title: Coherent cross-district professional development system for community school personnel
description: The West Kern Consortium built a professional development system for community school coordinators and social workers combining monthly virtual communities of practice, individual coaching from initiative leaders, and site visits to other districts or regions. The report states "these capacity-building opportunities coalesced to create a coherent professional development system, which is a critical systems-level support for high-quality community school implementation." title: Small rural districts should pool resources through cross-district consortiums to attain capacity no single district could achieve alone
description: The report's first lesson is "Working Stronger Together": by bringing together small, rural districts, the consortium "amassed and leveraged resources that individual districts likely would not have attained by working independently." These previously unavailable resources provided critical capacity and helped alleviate challenges in connecting students and families with resources—two common issues in rural schools. The principle applies the community schools strategy where economies of scale are unavailable.

article_title: Investing in a High-Quality Teacher Workforce: Lessons from Texas Teacher Preparation Programs
citation: Bland, J. A., Ralph, K., Wei, W., Wang, V., Wojcikiewicz, S. K., & Wechsler, M. E. (2025). Investing in a high-quality teacher workforce: Lessons from Texas teacher preparation programs. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/871.327
title: High-quality preparation pattern: practice-based coursework tightly coupled to a full-year, gradual-release clinical experience with trained mentor co-teachers
description: The three profiled programs share a design in which scaffolded, rigorous coursework is linked to "a full year of intensive, gradual-release clinical practice under the guidance of an experienced mentor teacher". Candidates experience the complete school year as co-teachers, take on responsibilities from day one, and follow delineated timelines for progression of responsibilities and co-teaching practices. Assessments shifted from evaluating what candidates know to what they can do, and course content is sequenced to add complexity progressively across preclinical and clinical years.

Structures delineating general timelines for candidates' progression of responsibilities throughout the school year
constraints: The report notes some structures are still being enhanced as implemented, and each case study emphasizes different program components to varying degrees
target_learners: Undergraduate and postbaccalaureate teacher candidates at minority-serving institutions
target_learning_goals: Day-one readiness to lead a classroom
Integration of coursework content with clinical teaching practice
examples: UH expanded student teaching from one semester to two and made the yearlong residency the standard for all undergraduate candidates (about 300 per year); UTRGV additionally offers a yearlong clinical experience called STEP UP

article_title: Investing in a High-Quality Teacher Workforce: Lessons from Texas Teacher Preparation Programs
citation: Bland, J. A., Ralph, K., Wei, W., Wang, V., Wojcikiewicz, S. K., & Wechsler, M. E. (2025). Investing in a high-quality teacher workforce: Lessons from Texas teacher preparation programs. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/871.327
title: Site coordinator role combining field supervision, coaching, seminar teaching, mentor training, and governance facilitation
description: The site coordinator, a role common to US PREP residency transformation sites, fulfills the responsibilities of traditional university field supervisors—"supervising, coaching, and conducting observations for residents during their clinical experience"—while also teaching practicum seminars and methods courses, training and collaborating with mentor teachers, supporting residents emotionally, and facilitating quarterly governance meetings with partner districts. Because site coordinators' work touches many dimensions of candidates' experiences, candidate support structures are well scaffolded and aligned.
requirements: Sufficient staffing to maintain a low ratio of teacher candidates to site coordinators, enabling frequent, meaningful feedback to each candidate
Personnel with both coaching and instructional expertise
constraints: The report recommends recruiting site coordinators from educators nearing retirement, senior teachers, and instructional leaders, implying supply considerations
target_learners: Teacher residents in yearlong clinical placements
target_learning_goals: Clinical skill development through frequent observation, coaching, and feedback
examples: At UH, site coordinators guide residents through scaffolded, graduated teaching responsibilities alongside mentor teachers

title: Common elements of high-quality teacher residencies
description: The report enumerates features that prior research identifies as common to effective teacher residencies: strong LEA–preparation program partnerships, a full year of residency "working alongside an accomplished mentor teacher who is the teacher of record," tightly integrated coursework and classroom practice, cohorts in teaching schools, postresidency induction support, recruitment for district needs, and financial support often tied to a teaching commitment. Coursework tightly integrated with classroom practice

citation: Wojcikiewicz, S. K., Ralph, K., Snyder, J., Bland, J. A., & Wechsler, M. E. (2025). Teacher residencies in Texas: Supporting successful implementation. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/630.675
title: Contextualized preparation model of teacher residencies
description: The Texas Education Agency framed the TCLAS residency model as "contextualized preparation": teachers are prepared within the district where they will work, learning from district context and culture, engaged in daily practice-based learning in district classrooms, coached daily by a high-quality mentor teacher, and building relationships within the school community during preparation. title: Kern County regional BLA workforce planning pilot
description: A regional BLA workforce planning pilot that "brought together county, district, and educator preparation program partners in Kern County for a series of planning workshops in 2025 to examine recruitment and retention data and identify workforce strategies." The pilot is presented alongside the EL-WIN initiative as a scalable, replicable proof point demonstrating how districts, counties, and preparation programs can jointly analyze and coordinate supply and demand to address critical workforce needs.

article_title: Community Schools in Lynwood Unified: Building Capacity for Districtwide Implementation
citation: Germain, E., Klevan, S., & Espinoza, D. (2026). Community schools in Lynwood Unified: Building capacity for districtwide implementation. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/947.934
title: Conduct a holistic districtwide analysis of existing services and unmet needs to target community schools funding and implementation
description: The principle holds that districts scaling community schools should first analyze what services already exist and what is still needed, using multiple data sources, so that new funds fill genuine gaps rather than duplicating provision. Lynwood leadership used "a combination of referral data tied to the district's health collaborative, climate surveys, and administrative data to pinpoint high areas of need" and gaps in resources, staffing, and partnerships. This analysis drove use of CCSPP funds, such as hiring student support analysts after referral analysis revealed a Tier 3 behavioral support gap.
requirements: Existing service and partnership infrastructure whose use can be traced through data such as referral records, climate surveys, and administrative data
constraints: The report presents this as a lesson from one rapidly scaling district implementing without a prior planning grant; effectiveness evidence is descriptive
target_learners: K-12 students in a high-need, majority low-income district
target_learning_goals: Student well-being, attendance, and access to integrated academic and non-academic supports
examples: Lynwood analyzed health collaborative referrals, climate surveys, and administrative data, then used CCSPP funds to hire four certified student support analysts to address a gap in Tier 3 behavioral supports for general education students without IEPs.
key_sources: Germain, E., Klevan, S., & Espinoza, D. (2026). Community schools in Lynwood Unified: Building capacity for districtwide implementation. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/947.934

article_title: Community Schools in Lynwood Unified: Building Capacity for Districtwide Implementation
citation: Germain, E., Klevan, S., & Espinoza, D. (2026). Community schools in Lynwood Unified: Building capacity for districtwide implementation. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/947.934
title: Clearly define the community school coordinator's skills, responsibilities, and position classification before hiring to support selection and onboarding
description: Because the community school coordinator is a role that previously did not exist in most schools, the report recommends defining its skills, disposition, and classification up front. The report states that "Clearly defining the skills, responsibilities, disposition, and position classification for the community school coordinator helped ensure the right people were hired and enabled a smooth onboarding process." Lynwood sought people with commitment to community, familiarity with existing resources, and relationship-building ability, and designated the position as classified management so coordinators could lead on campus without being diverted into certificated duties.
requirements: District vision for the coordinator role; a job description emphasizing relationship-building, assets and needs assessment, and governance committee development; collaboration with principals and unions
constraints: Classification choice (classified management) was made on the recommendation of the Los Angeles County Office of Education and may not transfer to districts with different labor contexts
target_learners: New community school coordinators and the students and families they serve
target_learning_goals: Effective coordination of integrated student supports and community school implementation
examples: Lynwood listed the coordinator position as classified management, onboarded coordinators by meeting with every campus entity to set expectations, and clarified collaboration points with community liaisons.

article_title: Community Schools in Lynwood Unified: Building Capacity for Districtwide Implementation
citation: Germain, E., Klevan, S., & Espinoza, D. (2026). Community schools in Lynwood Unified: Building capacity for districtwide implementation. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/947.934
title: Community schools as a whole child transformation strategy anchored by a cross-boundary coordinator role
description: The report frames community schools as an evidence-based school transformation strategy that unites students, families, educators, and community partners to improve learning and well-being through a whole child approach. Its central organizing concept is the coordinator: "a school-based staff member not traditionally found in schools, who is charged with organizing access to a range of public and private resources tailored to student and family needs and weaving them into the fabric and daily operations of the school." Coordinators act as cross-boundary leaders and connectors between schools, community partners, and families, and require targeted capacity building because the role is new and distinct from typical school positions.
requirements: Key practices such as expanded learning opportunities, family engagement, integrated systems of support, collaborative leadership, and a culture of belonging; systems-level supports including resources, shared governance, data systems, professional learning, and partnerships
constraints: The report notes quality depends on full implementation and that practitioners in different locations have different tools and resources available
target_learners: K-12 students and their families, particularly in marginalized or high-need communities
target_learning_goals: Improved student learning, well-being, attendance, connectedness, and reduced exclusionary discipline
examples: Lynwood applied the strategy districtwide, embedding coordinators within its Student Services Department alongside SEL specialists, clinical social workers, and community liaisons as a wraparound team.

article_title: Cultivating Math Mindsets: Teaching Practices That Enable Equitable Classroom Learning
citation: Price, H., & Fitz, J. (2026). Cultivating math mindsets: Teaching practices that enable equitable classroom learning. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/810.406
title: Composite daily math lesson structure with six engagement-oriented components
description: The observed middle school math lessons shared a common structure of six components: a warm-up, direct instruction, group activity, share-out, note-taking, and demonstration of understanding. Each teacher integrated at least five of these six components, whether the class period was 45 or 90 minutes. The structure deliberately builds in social interaction, with "Random assignment to groups; not ability-based grouping" at standing whiteboard stations, and low-stakes warm-ups and checks "with no grade."
requirements: Class time structured so students can move around and socially interact with a variety of classmates
constraints: Documented in 45- to 90-minute middle school periods across five California middle schools
target_learning_goals: engaged math learning
mathematical problem-solving
examples: Table 2 describes each component's goal, structure, and teacher and student roles, e.g., the share-out goal to "Celebrate multiple ways to represent and solve math problems."
key_sources: Price, H., & Fitz, J. (2026). Cultivating math mindsets: Teaching practices that enable equitable classroom learning. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/810.406

article_title: Cultivating Math Mindsets: Teaching Practices That Enable Equitable Classroom Learning
citation: Price, H., & Fitz, J. (2026). Cultivating math mindsets: Teaching practices that enable equitable classroom learning. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/810.406
title: Support math teachers with collaboration time, sustained professional learning, and coaching focused on contextual needs
description: The report identifies organizational practices that enable teachers to improve math classroom conditions: allocating school-day time for collaborative learning such as professional learning communities, shared planning, and peer observation, which can build teachers' efficacy and confidence; enabling access to well-designed professional learning, "particularly when these opportunities align with school goals and involve sustained engagement over an extended period of time"; and providing coaching or expert support focused on teachers' contextual needs. At the school level, teachers valued in-classroom support staff and structured collaboration norms set by leaders.
requirements: Staffing capacity and resources allocated to support organizational priorities
constraints: Findings reflect the supports identified by teachers in three California districts serving majority students of color and students from low-income families
target_learning_goals: improved math instruction
positive classroom learning conditions
examples: Teachers from schools with strong PLC collaboration and on-site math coaches described these as key supports; leaders' norms around collaboration time guided improvement-focused conversations between teachers.
key_sources: Price, H., & Fitz, J. (2026). Cultivating math mindsets: Teaching practices that enable equitable classroom learning. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/810.406

article_title: Cultivating Math Mindsets: Teaching Practices That Enable Equitable Classroom Learning
citation: Price, H., & Fitz, J. (2026). Cultivating math mindsets: Teaching practices that enable equitable classroom learning. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/810.406
title: Four positive classroom conditions framework for engaged math learning
description: The report organizes its findings around four classroom conditions under which, drawing on the science of learning and development and the authors' prior research synthesis, students learn math best: positive relationships with teachers and peers, a strong sense of classroom and mathematics belonging, support in adopting a growth mindset, and opportunities to engage with high-quality instruction. Figure 1 depicts these conditions, together with data access and use and school and district practices, as system factors supporting students' engagement in learning math. The framework holds that these conditions "can occur simultaneously with and reinforce high-quality instruction" and particularly matter for students from historically marginalized groups and during the middle school years.
requirements: System factors—data access and use, and school and district practices—that enable teachers to cultivate the conditions
constraints: Evidence base summarized from neuroscience, psychology, and developmental and learning sciences syntheses; classroom illustrations drawn from 10 case-study teachers
target_learning_goals: engaged math learning
positive math mindsets
reduced math anxiety
examples: The study documents how 10 teachers fostered each condition, e.g., routines such as welcoming students at the door, structuring daily group work, and creating a space of learning without fear of ridicule or shame.
key_sources: Price, H., & Fitz, J. (2026). Cultivating math mindsets: Teaching practices that enable equitable classroom learning. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/810.406

article_title: Strong Start, Strong Teachers: Supporting Teacher Preparation Programs for a Brighter Future

title: Talent Together registered teacher apprenticeship
description: Talent Together is a Michigan alternative certification program that "provides a free route to teacher certification and includes a registered apprenticeship to obtain paid work experience." It is a partnership between 56 intermediate school districts and 18 colleges and universities, prioritizes applications from uncertified current school employees in partner districts, and accepted 950 individuals in its first cohort while receiving 2,500 applications for 600 spots in its second cohort year. The report presents it as a promising path for growing and diversifying the teacher workforce.

citation: Charlotte Pierce. (2026). Strong Start, Strong Teachers: Supporting Teacher Preparation Programs for a Brighter Future. EdTrust-Midwest. https://midwest.edtrust.org
title: On the Rise Academy community-recruitment alternative certification program
description: On the Rise Academy, run by Detroit Public Schools Community District, "recruits new teacher candidates from the local community," with 75% of participants working in DPSCD as paraprofessionals, attendance agents, and academic interventionists. Candidates receive coaching cycles, observations, and intentional school placements under principals committed to their success. In 2021 about 90% of candidates were teachers of color, and DPSCD credits improvement in teacher vacancies partly to the Academy's pipeline of new teachers offsetting retirements and resignations.

title: MiCareer Rural Credentialing Hub for rural Michigan educators
description: The Michigan Consortium for Addressing Rural Education Expansion and Retention (MiCareer) Resource Hub is "an innovative partnership between educator preparation institutions and rural school districts that works to increase the number of qualified and credentialed educators in rural classrooms." citation: Charlotte Pierce. (2026). Strong Start, Strong Teachers: Supporting Teacher Preparation Programs for a Brighter Future. EdTrust-Midwest. https://midwest.edtrust.org
title: Provide strong coaching and continuous support to teacher candidates in alternative certification programs
description: The report states that "Strong coaching and support are essential ingredients for alternative programs to be successful," according to program administrators and teacher candidates. Support appears as intensive summer institutes, classroom observations, frequent professional development throughout the year, on-site coaching when the program is housed in the school building, and intentional candidate placement in supportive buildings. Because alternative-route candidates often work as teachers of record while training, the report says any certification training program should offer robust support and continuous feedback loops.

Support mechanisms such as summer institutes, observations, and professional development sessions

article_title: Trust and interaction design in AI-enabled systems: a systematic literature review
citation: Abramson SL, Sora-Cardenas J, Nandakumar P, Bruce JE, Gopinath N, Zangari LG and Feijóo-García PG (2026). Trust and interaction design in AI-enabled systems: a systematic literature review. Front. Psychol. 17:1932655. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1932655
title: Crampton Smith's four-dimensional framework for operationalizing interaction design factors in AI trust research
description: The review operationalizes interaction design factors—defined as "a design element that can be manipulated to shape how users interact with a system"—using Crampton Smith's four dimensions: Semantics (words, language, tone, linguistic framing), Visual representations (typography, iconography, diagrams, visual hierarchy), Physical embodiment (physical objects and spatial configurations), and Time (dynamic evolution of system behavior during interaction). The framework was chosen for its breadth in accommodating novel AI interaction paradigms, and the nine emergent design factors are interpreted as recurring manifestations within these dimensions rather than an alternative taxonomy.
requirements: Studies must examine how a design-related characteristic of the AI-enabled system or interaction influences trust for a factor to fall within this framework's scope as applied by the review.
constraints: The review notes Nielsen's taxonomy does not treat time as a manipulable design variable, whereas Crampton Smith's inclusion of time is particularly relevant for AI-enabled systems whose outputs may evolve adaptively.
target_learners: users of AI-enabled systems across domains such as healthcare, banking, and education
target_learning_goals: calibrated and appropriate trust in AI-enabled systems
examples: The review mapped its nine inductively coded factors onto the four dimensions, e.g., Semantics: Explainability, Confidence, Transparency; Physical embodiment: Anthropomorphism, Interface; Time: Errors, Perceived Control, Competence, Explainability.
key_sources: Abramson SL, Sora-Cardenas J, Nandakumar P, Bruce JE, Gopinath N, Zangari LG and Feijóo-García PG (2026). Trust and interaction design in AI-enabled systems: a systematic literature review. Front. Psychol. 17:1932655. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1932655

article_title: A Comprehensive Review of the Changing Landscape of Academic Dishonesty in Automated Proctoring in the Era of Artificial Intelligence
citation: Malhotra, M., & Chhabra, I. (2026). A comprehensive review of the changing landscape of academic dishonesty in automated proctoring in the era of artificial intelligence. Discover Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s44217-026-01275-6
title: Taxonomy of proctoring systems: offline proctoring and online proctoring subdivided into live, semi-automated, and fully automated
description: The review organizes proctoring systems into a classification derived from its literature study. It states that "various proctoring systems have been developed: offline proctoring, online proctoring", with online systems "categorized into live proctoring, semi-automated and automated proctoring systems". Offline proctoring requires a physical invigilator at an exam venue; live proctoring combines a virtual tool with a human proctor monitoring in real time; semi-automated proctoring records video and periodic images; fully automated proctoring uses AI tools without human involvement and generates a report at the end of the exam.
requirements: Fully automated proctoring requires infrastructure such as persistent internet connectivity, authentication, storage facilities, and security, which the review notes incur huge costs.
constraints: The review notes semi-automated proctoring has the drawback of lack of internet connectivity and the infrastructure required for processing images.
target_learners: high school students taking online exams
target_learning_goals: maintaining academic integrity during examinations
preventing cheating in online and offline assessments
examples: The review describes semi-automated image-based proctoring in which "the examinee's photos are taken at specified intervals: at the start of the exam, at the conclusion, and during the answering process, every 30 to 45 s."
key_sources: Malhotra, M., & Chhabra, I. (2026). A comprehensive review of the changing landscape of academic dishonesty in automated proctoring in the era of artificial intelligence. Discover Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s44217-026-01275-6

article_title: A Comprehensive Review of the Changing Landscape of Academic Dishonesty in Automated Proctoring in the Era of Artificial Intelligence
citation: Malhotra, M., & Chhabra, I. (2026). A comprehensive review of the changing landscape of academic dishonesty in automated proctoring in the era of artificial intelligence. Discover Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s44217-026-01275-6
title: Key functionalities of online proctoring systems: eye gaze tracking, head pose estimation, facial recognition, user verification, activity recognition, and authentication
description: The review identifies a set of core functionalities that online proctoring systems implement, stating that "Some key functionalities involved in online proctoring are eye gaze tracking, head pose estimation, facial recognition, user verification, activity recognition, and authentication." These functionalities are typically implemented with camera-based monitoring and browser lockdown components; the review devotes separate sections to the algorithms and datasets used for each functionality and their reported accuracies and limitations.

constraints: The review notes that in large exam settings the efficiency of online proctoring systems is hindered by the inability of teachers to invigilate properly.
target_learning_goals: ensuring academic integrity in online examinations
detecting cheating behavior during remote assessments
examples: The review's Fig. 3 presents a classification of key functionalities of online proctoring systems, and Tables 3 and 4 analyze systems for eye gaze estimation and head pose estimation respectively.

article_title: Acceptance of AI-Assisted English Language Learning Tools in Higher Education: Psychological Correlates Across Disciplinary and Proficiency Groups
citation: Wu J, Wang Y, He Y, Yin X, Chen F and Wan B (2026) Acceptance of AI-assisted English language learning tools in higher education: psychological correlates across disciplinary and proficiency groups. Front. Psychol. 17:1806457. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1806457
title: A learner-centered extension of TAM framing psychological resources, affective correlates, and contextual grouping variables alongside baseline acceptance constructs
description: The study retains the Technology Acceptance Model's baseline constructs — perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, behavioral intention, and satisfaction — and adds learner-centered correlates rather than replacing TAM. As the article states, "the present study retains PU, PEOU, BI, and satisfaction as baseline acceptance-related constructs, while examining learning motivation, self-eﬃcacy, anxiety, and risk perception as theoretically informed or exploratory correlates." Motivation (self-determination theory) addresses the value dimension, self-efficacy (social cognitive theory) the capability dimension, while anxiety and risk perception are treated as affective and evaluative correlates whose direction remains an empirical question. Disciplinary affiliation and English proficiency serve as contextual grouping variables for mean-level and subgroup-specific analyses.
requirements: Cross-sectional survey measurement of the four acceptance constructs and the psychological correlates; the framework organizes regression-based association analyses rather than causal or mediation models.
constraints: The article states the framework "does not imply causal ordering, mediation, temporal sequencing, or process-based eﬀects" given the cross-sectional design.
target_learners: Non-English-major undergraduates in higher education English courses
target_learning_goals: Acceptance and sustained use of AI-assisted English language learning tools
examples: The framework was applied to survey data from 210 Chinese undergraduates, with full-sample adjusted regressions, mean-level group comparisons by discipline and CET-4 proficiency, and exploratory subgroup-specific regressions.
key_sources: Wu J, Wang Y, He Y, Yin X, Chen F and Wan B (2026) Acceptance of AI-assisted English language learning tools in higher education: psychological correlates across disciplinary and proficiency groups. Front. Psychol. 17:1806457. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1806457

article_title: Access is Not Enough: Human Support Improves Engagement with AI Tutoring
citation: Robinson, Carly D., David Gormley, Ana Trindade Ribeiro, and Susanna Loeb. (2026). Access is Not Enough: Human Support Improves Engagement with AI Tutoring. EdWorkingPaper No. 26-1451, Annenberg Institute at Brown University. https://edworkingpapers.com/ai26-1451
title: Spectrum of relational intensity for models of personalized instruction
description: The article proposes a framework placing models of personalized instruction on a spectrum of relational intensity, from tech-led (low relational intensity), where humans oversee AI-student interactions from the backend, to human-led (high relational intensity), where a dedicated tutor uses AI as a supplement to direct instruction. The studied model sits near the midpoint: an in-person tutor supporting engagement, not delivering instruction. The article notes each modality spans a range, not a point, so the ordering is not fixed.
requirements: Comparing models across the spectrum requires accounting for differing personnel, training, and coordination costs the article says more human-intensive models require.
constraints: The article states the ordering is not fixed because each modality spans a range, not a point; for instance an AI-assisted human tutor can reach or even exceed the relational intensity of in-person tutoring.
target_learning_goals: literacy/reading engagement with AI-delivered personalized instruction
examples: The studied intervention assigned tutors to small groups of 2-5 students for sessions with a 10-minute check-in, 15 minutes of platform work, and a 2-5 minute reflection.
key_sources: Robinson, Carly D., David Gormley, Ana Trindade Ribeiro, and Susanna Loeb. (2026). Access is Not Enough: Human Support Improves Engagement with AI Tutoring. EdWorkingPaper No. 26-1451, Annenberg Institute at Brown University. https://edworkingpapers.com/ai26-1451

article_title: Access is Not Enough: Human Support Improves Engagement with AI Tutoring
citation: Robinson, Carly D., David Gormley, Ana Trindade Ribeiro, and Susanna Loeb. (2026). Access is Not Enough: Human Support Improves Engagement with AI Tutoring. EdWorkingPaper No. 26-1451, Annenberg Institute at Brown University. https://edworkingpapers.com/ai26-1451
title: Provide human support alongside AI tutoring tools; access alone does not ensure meaningful student engagement
description: The article's central design recommendation is that schools deploying AI-based learning tools should not rely on access alone: providing access to an AI tutor, whether after school or during school hours, did not ensure meaningful engagement. Pairing the platform with an in-person tutor focused on engagement, motivation, and troubleshooting increased both usage and content completion, suggesting that "implementation and student engagement may be equally important determinants of impact" as technology quality. Human support may be especially important for students least likely to persist with AI-based learning on their own.
requirements: Tutors need standardized training designed to help them support students while using the AI platform, and sites need capacity to assign tutors to small groups.
constraints: The article states human-intensive models require additional personnel, training, and coordination; and human support increased engagement but usage remained well below the levels recommended for measurable reading gains.
target_learners: elementary school students, including economically disadvantaged students (>80% of the sample)
target_learning_goals: reading/literacy engagement with AI-delivered personalized instruction

title: Agent-based educational science: formalizing educational theories as interacting agents and environments for in silico experimentation
description: Agent-based educational science (AES) is a research agenda in which educational theories are formalized as interacting agents and environments, enabling in silico experimentation on developmental processes. The authors frame it as "a coordinated invitation to the research community to reorient its priorities, workflows, data infrastructures, and validation practices around theory-constrained, dynamically updateable, and empirically examinable simulations of learner development." It targets developmental processes that are otherwise slow or infeasible to test empirically.

citation: Kamalov, F., Santandreu Calonge, D., Smail, L., Azizov, D., Thadani, D. R., Kwong, T., Atif, A. (2025). Evolution of AI in Education: Agentic Workflows. https://github.com/AzizovDilshod/Multi-agent-System-for-Essay-Assessment/tree/main
title: Four-paradigm taxonomy of agentic workflows in education: reflection, planning, tool use, and multi-agent collaboration
description: The article proposes a technological taxonomy that categorizes agentic workflows in education into four major design paradigms. As the article states, "Four major paradigms underpin many current agentic approaches" — 1) reflection, where the agent analyzes past actions to refine future behavior; 2) planning, where the agent creates and follows a sequence of steps or sub-goals; 3) tool use, where the agent leverages external resources such as calculators, code execution, web search, and APIs; and 4) multi-agent collaboration, where multiple specialized agents coordinate toward a common goal. The review applies this framework to map technical capabilities onto pedagogical affordances.
requirements: An LLM-based agent layer that orchestrates reasoning, tools, and coordination around a goal
constraints: The paradigms are distinct but often complementary strategies; implementations vary in degree of agenticness
target_learners: educators and instructional designers building agentic tools
target_learning_goals: designing and evaluating AI-agent-based educational systems

article_title: Adaptive Scaffolding for Cognitive Engagement in an Intelligent Tutoring System
citation: Tithi, S.D., Alam, N., Yasir, T., Shi, Y., Tian, X., Chi, M., Barnes, T. (2026). Adaptive Scaffolding for Cognitive Engagement in an Intelligent Tutoring System. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.07308
title: ICAP-based operationalization of cognitive engagement levels through worked example types in an ITS
description: This framework maps the ICAP engagement modes onto concrete problem representations in an intelligent logic tutor. Problem Solving is treated as "Interactive in the ICAP framework, since students receive explicit accuracy feedback on each step"; Guided worked examples, adapted from the Parsons format with subgoal structure, represent the "activeengagement level in ICAP"; and Buggy worked examples, containing expert-designed errors students must find and fix, represent the "constructiveengagement level in ICAP". The article uses this mapping as the theoretically grounded basis for adaptive scaffolding policies that select among engagement levels.
requirements: The tutor must provide problem-solving interleaved with the two worked-example types, and the ICAP level of each activity must be assigned; the article notes that "defining the ICAP level of a learning activity is non-trivial" because feedback-driven reflection could make either type more interactive.
constraints: The operationalization was implemented and evaluated in one logic tutor in an undergraduate discrete math course; the authors state the design "should be replicated in other problem-solving domains" to establish generalizability.
target_learners: undergraduate students in a discrete math / computer science course
target_learning_goals: propositional logic proof construction and rule application
examples: In the study tutor, Guided examples presented partial solutions with missing node connections students complete by applying rules, while Buggy examples presented solutions with expert-designed bugs students identify and correct.

article_title: Agentic Education with AI Coding Assistants
citation: Zain Naboulsi. (2026). Agentic Education: Using Claude Code to Teach Claude Code. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.17460
title: Persona progression model: a four-stage AI-instructor persona (Guide→Collaborator→Peer→Launcher) operationalizing the Gradual Release of Responsibility framework for AI-mediated instruction
description: The persona progression model ties the AI instructor's tone and scaffolding depth to the learner's position in the module sequence across four stages: Guide (patient teacher, explains every concept), Collaborator (working partner, asks before telling), Peer (senior colleague, terse and direct), and Launcher (states the goal and steps back). The article states that "The curriculum defines four personas, each specified as a prompt engineering directive in every module file", mapping 1:1 to GRR's four phases, with "I do it" reinterpreted so the learner is always hands-on. Persona boundaries are set at onboarding from three experience-level schedules (4/3/2/1, 3/3/3/1, 1/3/5/1) and can shift at module boundaries via the adaptive system. Implementation uses descriptive prompt directives alone, without fine-tuning, RLHF, or RAG.
requirements: Each module file must contain an explicit persona directive metadata line consumed by Claude Code when reading the module
constraints: The article notes a static tone either underwhelms beginners or patronizes experts, motivating stage-dependent personas; the adaptation is validated only for structural consistency, not instructional effectiveness
target_learners: professional software engineers learning an agentic AI coding tool, at beginner, intermediate, or advanced experience levels
target_learning_goals: compositional mastery of an agentic AI coding tool's features, from setup through multi-agent orchestration
examples: Module 1–3 use the Guide persona; the intermediate schedule assigns Guide to modules 1–3, Collaborator to 4–6, Peer to 7–9, and Launcher to module 10

article_title: Agentic Education with AI Coding Assistants
citation: Zain Naboulsi. (2026). Agentic Education: Using Claude Code to Teach Claude Code. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.17460
title: cc-self-train adaptive learning system: a three-layer hook-based engagement observation and scaffolding adjustment mechanism
description: The adaptive learning system observes learner engagement quality through keyword-heuristic classification of each learner message into six engagement categories with quality scores from 1 to 5, accumulated in a local learner profile. Layer 1 is a silent Stop hook that fires after every Claude response and computes streak booleans; Layer 2 injects a teaching note into Claude's context at session start based on the productive/unproductive ratio; Layer 3 adjusts the learner's Effective Level at module boundaries. The article describes "a two-timescale system" in which a slow clock adjusts the persona schedule at module boundaries using aggregate statistics while a fast clock triggers scaffolding changes mid-module using sequential patterns, governed by an asymmetric response principle that is quicker to increase scaffolding than to withdraw it.
requirements: Operates entirely through Claude Code's hook system with no external dependencies, no API calls for observation, and no web backend
constraints: Observation uses keyword heuristics rather than LLM-based classification, so individual classifications are noisy; Effective Level changes occur only at module boundaries; level changes are silent to the student
target_learners: developers learning an agentic AI coding tool through the cc-self-train curriculum
target_learning_goals: sustained productive engagement and appropriately paced scaffolding during tool-mastery learning
examples: A struggle streak (three or more consecutive answer_seeking or passive_acceptance classifications) produces the priority alert "Offer more scaffolding NOW"

title: Cross-domain unified curriculum: five project paths teach identical feature sequencing to enable transfer of tool mastery
description: This pattern fixes the instructional sequence across multiple parallel project domains so that tool knowledge transfers between them. The article states: "all five paths teach the same 10 Claude Code feature sets in the same order, designed to facilitate cross-domain transfer of tool mastery." Each path (Canvas portfolio site, Forge CLI toolkit, Nexus API gateway, Sentinel code analyzer, and BYOP) produces a different software artifact while adapting the same exercises to its domain; a feature coverage matrix documents that all covered features are taught in all 5 paths, enforced by an automated test class. The BYOP path serves as the ultimate transfer test, requiring learners to identify where each feature applies in their own codebase with no pre-specified exercises.
requirements: A feature coverage matrix enforced by the TestModuleConsistencyAcrossProjects test class, which fails the suite if a feature is added to one path but not the other four
constraints: The feature sequence is fixed; only project-specific application changes across domains
target_learners: developers choosing a project path by interest, including first-time users (Canvas) and learners applying the curriculum to an existing codebase (BYOP)
target_learning_goals: domain-independent transfer of agentic AI tool mastery
examples: Module 7's guard-rail exercises teach the same three hook mechanisms (deny, inject context, and modify input) in all five paths, contextualized per domain

citation: Zain Naboulsi. (2026). Agentic Education: Using Claude Code to Teach Claude Code. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.17460
title: cc-self-train auto-updating sync pipeline: an onboarding agent that detects upstream tool changes and updates teaching materials before instruction begins
description: The sync pipeline (/sync skill) addresses the content decay problem of curricula for rapidly evolving tools. The article states: "when a learner begins the curriculum, the onboarding agent checks whether its teaching materials cover the learner's installed version of Claude Code. If not, it updates the modules before instruction begins, so the learner always receives a current snapshot." The six-step pipeline detects the version gap, fetches and triages the upstream changelog, maps features to affected modules, researches new features, updates module and context files, and verifies structural integrity, reverting any file that fails. A safe-append rule never modifies or renumbers existing steps, inserting new content before the Checkpoint section.
requirements: A predefined feature-to-module mapping and a parametrized test suite that verifies structural integrity of updated files
constraints: During onboarding only the learner's chosen project variant is updated; standalone maintainer invocation updates all five variants in bulk
target_learners: developers learning agentic AI coding tools whose features change on a cadence measured in days
target_learning_goals: learning current tool features rather than outdated curriculum content
examples: Adding BYOP as a 5th path required generating 10 module files, which the pipeline then maintains alongside the original 40

article_title: A Formative Study of Brief Affective Text as a Complement to Wearable Sensing for Longitudinal Student Health Monitoring
citation: Tamunotonye Harry, Johanna Hidalgo, Matthew Price, Yuanyuan Feng, Kathryn Stanton, Connie Tompkins, Peter Sheridan Dodds, Mikaela Irene Fudolig, Laura Bloomfield, and Christopher Danforth. 2026. A Formative Study of Brief Affective Text as a Complement to Wearable Sensing for Longitudinal Student Health Monitoring. Proc. ACM Interact. Mob. Wearable Ubiquitous Technol. 10, 4, Article 219 (December 2026). https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14360
title: Use ultra-brief affective prompts to enrich the psychological interpretability of passive physiological data at minimal participant burden
description: The article's design guidance is that a single open-ended affective question, answered in the participant's own words, can complement passive wearable sensing by supplying psychological context the sensors cannot recover. Responses were extremely short — the median was three words — yet still associated with within-person variation in sleep and activity outcomes. The article concludes that "ultra-brief affective prompts enrich the psychological interpretability of passive physiological data at minimal burden", positioning this as a lightweight alternative to infrastructure-intensive sensor-language models.
requirements: A single open-ended concern prompt integrated into an existing study protocol (here, a bimonthly ecological momentary assessment delivered via a study mobile application), paired with concurrent wearable outcome data aggregated over the same two-week window.
constraints: The concern prompt is negatively valenced by construction, selectively surfacing worry and distress; the authors state findings should be read within that scope.
The bimonthly interval is a design constraint representing a middle point in the burden-versus-sensitivity tradeoff, not an optimum established by the study.
Associations are formative and exploratory; none survived correction for multiple comparisons.
target_learners: first-year university students in longitudinal health monitoring studies
target_learning_goals: psychological context for physiological monitoring
early detection of distress
timely clinical outreach
examples: Participants in the LEMURS study responded bimonthly to the prompt 'Of all the things that have happened in the last 2 weeks, what concerns you the most?', producing 3,073 concern-present responses with a median length of three words alongside continuous Oura ring wear.

article_title: Agentic Literacy Debt: A Structural Problem the AI Literacy Field Has Not Yet Named
citation: Nama, R. (2026). Agentic Literacy Debt: A Structural Problem the AI Literacy Field Has Not Yet Named. Author's accepted manuscript, AI and Ethics (Springer Nature). https://arxiv.org/
title: Agentic literacy debt: a compounding societal deficit from deploying agentic AI without literacy infrastructure
description: The paper defines agentic literacy debt as the accumulating deficit that grows "when agentic AI systems are deployed at scale without the literacy infrastructure users need to govern them." Borrowed from technical debt, it compounds through three reinforcing channels: normalization of opaque delegation (a ratchet effect of inherited, rarely revoked permission grants), multi-agent ecosystem complexity, and institutional path dependence. It extends Ladson-Billings' education debt and Petrozzino's ethical debt to systems that act autonomously on citizens' behalf.
requirements: Deployment of autonomous agents without frameworks enabling users to understand, supervise, and contest their actions is what adds to the debt.
constraints: Unlike ethical debt, incurred at design, it is incurred at the point of deployment and compounds with every user interaction without adequate literacy infrastructure.
target_learners: users, patients, consumers, and citizens on whose behalf agents act
target_learning_goals: governing autonomous AI agents: understanding, supervising, and contesting agent actions
examples: The author cites OpenClaw walletdrain attacks and the EchoLeak vulnerability as visible consequences of the gap.

It recommends transparency-by-design embedding literacy into agent interactions, AI tutoring simulating agentic scenarios, and contextual micro-learning at the point of risk.

Agents act on local observations, and a transition operator updates state, making trajectories generable, inspectable, and comparable rather than merely plausible dialogue.

title: Three validation targets for educational simulation: behavioral believability, educational mechanism fidelity, and institutional counterfactual usefulness
description: The paper argues that educational simulators are too often evaluated only on surface realism, and distinguishes three targets that are often conflated. As printed: "Behavioral believabilityasks whether generated dialogue resembles what teachers and students might say.Educational mechanism fidelityasks whether the internal process producing that dialogue corresponds to learning theory, such as knowledge restructuring, scaffolding, or misconception repair.Institutional counterfactual usefulnessasks whether the simulator can support 'what-if' reasoning about policies, spaces, or AI-mediated teaching arrangements that do not yet exist." AgentSchool is designed around the latter two targets, making internal learning states explicit and allowing scenarios to depart from present-day templates.
requirements: Calibration defined relative to the intended claim: discourse claims require turn-level calibration, growth claims require mastery-trajectory calibration, reform claims require institutional-pattern calibration
constraints: A classroom role-play system can satisfy behavioral believability while failing the other two targets; a single global realism score is insufficient because realism is multidimensional
target_learners: Educational researchers and policymakers evaluating educational AI
target_learning_goals: Valid inference about educational mechanisms
counterfactual policy reasoning
examples: AgentSchool records state transitions and supports scenario configurability so that mechanism fidelity and counterfactual usefulness can be assessed rather than dialogue realism alone

title: A4L Analytics Pipeline
description: The A4L Analytics Pipeline is a component of the Architecture for AI-Augmented Learning that performs statistical analyses on learner interaction data from educational AI assistants. It is "defined as a state machine that runs in a cloud environment" taking "a JSON-formatted analysis configuration payload as input". A data fetch module retrieves specified datasets into a staging area, and an analysis module performs pre-processing, transforms, and analysis, uploading results to durable object storage for the Visualization Pipeline's role-specific dashboards. Daily scheduled runs monitor the published data store for new data and run affected payloads.
requirements: Datasets must be loaded into the A4L published data store by the A4L Data Engine before the pipeline can fetch and analyze them.
An analysis configuration payload specifying dataset, variables, statistic, and result location must be supplied.
constraints: Extension of the pipeline's capabilities in this study was performed by research team members familiar with the system's architecture.
target_learners: graduate-level online computer science students at Georgia Tech
target_learning_goals: understanding AI assistant adoption, performance, need for cognition, and sense of belonging through learning analytics
examples: The pipeline ran Welch's t-tests, contingency tables, and power calculations across the JW, VERA, and SAMI research domains using one codebase.

title: Highly Configurable System design for cross-domain learning analytics
description: The pipeline applies Highly Configurable System (HCS) principles, "enabling a single underlying codebase to be applied to different scenarios through flexible configuration". Each statistical option's parameters — alternative hypothesis, dataset, independent and dependent variables, and result storage location — are programmed as variables whose values are read from keys in the JSON analysis configuration payload, so the same analysis-module code serves different domains. Santana et al 2025 found this yields a pipeline that is extensible and flexible while maintaining structural coherence, defined as the absence of invalid system configurations.
requirements: Analysis configuration payloads must supply valid values for each configurable key (statistic name, dataset, variables, result file name).
constraints: Structural coherence depends on configurations being valid; the balance between flexibility and structural coherence was established in prior work by Santana et al 2025.
target_learners: researchers and instructors analyzing educational AI assistant data
target_learning_goals: reproducible cross-domain analysis of learner interaction data
examples: Table 1 shows differing payload key values for JW, VERA, and SAMI Welch's t-tests feeding the same underlying analysis code.

citation: Steve Woollaston, Brendan Flanagan, Isanka Wijerathne, and Hiroaki Ogata. (2026). Agentic AI and Pedagogical Best Practice: The Tension Between Automation and Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.04543
title: Agentic AI systems defined by three behavioural traits: autonomy, proactivity, and reactivity
description: The article defines agentic systems as digital actors with three core behavioural traits: "autonomy to function without continuous human intervention, proactiveness to initiate goal-directed actions, and reactiveness to adapt to changing contexts". Unlike conventional dialogue systems, proactive AI agents can anticipate outcomes, take initiative, and strategically plan. A key functional advantage is the ability to use external tools (databases, APIs, microservices) while leveraging persistent memory across sessions and communicating across multi-agent networks. The article uses this framework to analyse how such systems interact with established pedagogical principles.
requirements: Persistent memory and access to external tools such as databases, APIs, and microservices to maintain continuity and act across the digital ecosystem
constraints: The framework is presented as a conceptual lens from the agentic AI literature, not empirically tested in educational settings in this article
target_learning_goals: personalised and real-time adaptive learning

title: Pedagogically Informed Agentic AI Implementation Matrix mapping six principles to agent actions and friction/fading strategies
description: Table 1 of the article operationalises six pedagogical principles into an actionable design framework, mapping each principle to a specific agent action, a friction or fading strategy, and a learning example. For example, for problem-based learning the agent generates an interactive simulation of a local real-world issue and "refuses to provide a direct 'solution pathway' when stuck, offering clues about where to look instead". The matrix is intended to bridge theory, system architecture, and practice, demonstrating how intentional instructional friction and dynamic scaffolding fading can be embedded across diverse learning contexts.

target_learning_goals: deep learning via productive struggle, self-regulation, and independent problem-solving

title: Design agentic AI for intentional instructional friction rather than friction-free interfaces
description: The article recommends that rather than aiming for seamless, friction-free interfaces, AI systems should be intentionally designed to withhold answers and support. By engineering strategic "instructional friction," agents can force the critical thinking and active inquiry necessary to cement knowledge, ensuring the learner remains the primary driver of the intellectual journey. Examples include an AI that asks the student to explain how their hobby relates to a new topic rather than explaining for them, and an AI that pauses the interface when it detects rapid clicking or superficial answers.
requirements: Agents must be able to detect when support is being over-used (e.g., rapid clicking or superficial answers) to time friction appropriately
constraints: The article presents this as a design recommendation grounded in pedagogical literature, not as a tested intervention
target_learners: students learning with proactive AI tutors
target_learning_goals: critical thinking, active inquiry, productive struggle

title: Implement dynamic fading: AI scaffolding must retreat as student competence increases
description: The article proposes that AI scaffolding be inherently transitional, explicitly designed to retreat as student competence increases. To prevent learned helplessness, agentic systems require robust, real-time analytics capable of distinguishing between temporary task completion and long-term mastery, allowing the AI to dynamically withdraw intermediate supports and systematically yield full cognitive autonomy back to the learner. In the matrix, feedback shifts from explicit corrections to subtle hints and eventually to zero cues as mastery increases.
requirements: Robust, real-time analytics that can distinguish temporary task completion from long-term mastery
constraints: The article notes it is hard to gauge when and how to withdraw support without hindering the learner, since generative AI provides implicit scaffolding through its adaptive, iterative nature
target_learners: students receiving AI tutoring or task support
target_learning_goals: student autonomy and independent problem-solving
examples: For essay writing the AI initially provides paragraph structures but removes the template entirely for the final paragraphs

title: Exercise AI usage restraint: prioritise Modification and Redefinition over Substitution and Augmentation
description: The article urges educators to critically assess which learning tasks genuinely benefit from AI support and which are better served through traditional methods that prioritise human interaction and internal cognitive processing. Applying the SAMR model it cites, educators should avoid using AI merely for Substitution or Augmentation, where the technology adds little pedagogical value, and instead prioritise instances where AI can facilitate true Modification or Redefinition of the learning experience. The article notes that sometimes the most effective tool for deep learning remains a conversation or a blank page.
requirements: Educators must critically assess each learning task's suitability for AI support before deployment
constraints: The article presents this as a recommendation applying the SAMR model, not as an empirically tested allocation rule

target_learning_goals: pedagogical integrity and deep human learning over task-completion efficiency

article_title: The Empirically Grounded Adaptive Virtual Patient for Psychotherapy Training: Disclosure That Responds to Therapist
citation: Angela Chen, Siwei Jin, Catherine Bao, Canwen Wang, Robert E. Kraut, Tongshuang Wu, and Haiyi Zhu. (2026). The Empirically Grounded Adaptive Virtual Patient for Psychotherapy Training: Disclosure That Responds to Therapist Micro-Skills. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10051
title: Adaptive Virtual Patient framework: separating behavioral state transitions from language generation
description: The AVP framework inserts an explicit behavioral-state module between the trainee's turn and the virtual patient's reply: LLM evaluators score empathy and exploration each turn, a dynamics module accumulates the scores into an ordinal disclosure level (G/M/H) using weights derived from a psychotherapy-data SEM, and an LLM generates the next utterance conditioned on that level. The article argues that "Keeping the behavioral logic separate from generation makes the VP’s adaptation inspectable, controllable, and fixed across experimental conditions in a way a prompt-only system cannot achieve." The level determines what the patient may reveal; the LLM determines how they say it.
requirements: Requires an external data-driven model of interaction dynamics (the SEM of Chen et al., 2026) to parameterize the state-update weights
Requires validated skill detectors scoring user behaviors each turn
constraints: The dynamics module is parameterized from psychotherapy data and encodes assumptions specific to therapeutic communication; broader-domain claims are not yet validated
The deployed 3:1 weight is an integer approximation, not an empirically optimized parameter
target_learners: clinicians and clinical trainees practicing psychotherapy micro-skills
target_learning_goals: empathic responding
exploratory probing
recognizing contingent patient disclosure
examples: In the evaluation, the AVP kept the guarded persona at G-level until accumulated empathy and exploration crossed the M threshold, while the static condition presented H-level topics from turn one

citation: Angela Chen, Siwei Jin, Catherine Bao, Canwen Wang, Robert E. Kraut, Tongshuang Wu, and Haiyi Zhu. (2026). The Empirically Grounded Adaptive Virtual Patient for Psychotherapy Training: Disclosure That Responds to Therapist Micro-Skills. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10051
title: Four measurable properties for evaluating adaptive virtual patients: responsiveness, gradual build-up, faithful realization, and skill sensitivity
description: The article proposes four measurable properties an adaptive virtual patient should satisfy, each with its own metric: P1 Responsiveness (state changes in the direction the data predicts), P2 Gradual Build-up (the state "climbs steadily across the session and only as the user earns it"), P3 Faithful Realization (generated text matches the intended state), and P4 Skill Sensitivity (different users get visibly different sessions). Each property comes with its own metric, so evaluators can locate exactly where a system fails rather than collapse the question into one number.
requirements: Each property requires its own metric: OLS regression for responsiveness, decile-slope fit for build-up, rater agreement for realization, and a median skill split for sensitivity
constraints: The P4 skill-sensitivity interaction test was underpowered at N= 20 per stratum in the article's own evaluation
target_learners: clinicians and clinical trainees practicing psychotherapy micro-skills
target_learning_goals: evaluating whether a simulated patient adapts to trainee behavior
examples: The article operationalized P2 by splitting each session into 10 deciles and fitting a linear slope and R2 across decile-averaged disclosure levels

title: Phoenix: a voice-based, non-embodied LLM conversational peer agent for group learning
description: Phoenix is a "voice-based, non-embodied conversational agent that joins real-time group discussions through spoken dialogue with multiple participants", positioned as an equal peer supporting knowledge co-construction rather than an authoritative tutor. title: Four-component lesson plan representation schema grounded in curriculum studies and differentiated instruction
description: AdaPT decomposes lesson plans into four components: curriculum standards, learning objectives, learning profile analysis, and learning tasks. The design draws on the Encyclopedia of Curriculum Studies' four common features of instructional design models and on Tomlinson's differentiated instruction framework, operationalizing readiness via Vygotsky's zone of proximal development. The authors state they "designed a structured representation that decomposes a lesson plan into four key components." Learning tasks are refined into atomic units with task, expected answer, detailed plan, implementation method, and design intent, enabling reuse and reflection on standards alignment.

constraints: Knowledge readiness remains initially unknown until enriched from teacher input or LMS data

description: AdaPT's backend is a multi-agent system in which each agent encapsulates distinct reasoning responsibilities. The LearningProfile Analysis Agent generates structured profiles from teacher natural-language descriptions, optionally retrieving knowledge readiness from the school's LMS via tool-calling. The authors state "The backend of AdaPT is designed as a multi-agent system (Figure 5), where each agent encapsulates distinct reasoning responsibilities aligned with the design requirements." title: Design AI lesson tools to support transformation of existing plans rather than generation from scratch
description: The article argues educational AI tools should align with teachers' actual practice of modifying existing high-quality plans rather than creating new ones. The formative study found the from-scratch generation prototype "was rejected because teachers' actual practice is often one of modification." AdaPT therefore reframes preparation as transformation: parsing existing plans, analyzing target student profiles, and adapting content with traceable changes. The authors derive design implications for future AI-based educational technologies that support adaptation practices and help mitigate educational inequality.
requirements: Systems must parse unstructured existing plans into editable structured formats and retain teacher agency over each change
constraints: The recommendation is grounded in Chinese K-12 contexts and cross-regional teaching support settings
target_learners: In-service K-12 teachers, especially those in cross-regional or differentiated teaching contexts
target_learning_goals: Efficient, contextually adapted lesson plans promoting educational equity
examples: AdaPT's one-click transformation generates adapted drafts with traces and reasons for each change, which teachers accept, modify, or regenerate

article_title: Do Gains from Generative AI-Enabled Adaptive Pretesting Persist? Evidence from a Retention Study
citation: Mahir Akgun and Sacip Toker. (2026). Do Gains from Generative AI–Enabled Adaptive Pretesting Persist? Evidence from a Retention Study. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22328
title: GenAI adaptive AI agent with response-contingent prompting and withheld solutions
description: The study's adaptive AI agent is a generative large language model configured via a structured system prompt defining its instructional role, response scope, and escalation logic. During pretesting it applied "response-contingent prompting": targeted probes for misconceptions, elaboration requests for superficial responses, and advancement for adequate engagement. "Direct solutions and posttest-relevant answers were explicitly excluded from the agent’s allowed outputs during pretesting." In the adaptive retrieval condition it additionally reviewed prior session performance signals to adjust conceptual depth.
requirements: A structured system prompt defining the agent's instructional role, response scope, and escalation logic, with direct solutions excluded from allowed outputs during pretesting
constraints: The study was conducted within a single instructional context; the article states replication across domains and task types is needed to assess generalizability
target_learners: undergraduate students in an upper-division applied statistics course
target_learning_goals: multiple linear regression concepts including predictor selection, multicollinearity detection, model comparison, and interpretation of regression coefficients
examples: In condition G1 the agent reviewed prior session performance signals, increasing conceptual depth for weaker content areas while maintaining challenge in stronger areas
key_sources: Mahir Akgun and Sacip Toker. (2026). Do Gains from Generative AI–Enabled Adaptive Pretesting Persist? Evidence from a Retention Study. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22328

article_title: Do Gains from Generative AI-Enabled Adaptive Pretesting Persist? Evidence from a Retention Study
citation: Mahir Akgun and Sacip Toker. (2026). Do Gains from Generative AI–Enabled Adaptive Pretesting Persist? Evidence from a Retention Study. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22328
title: Observed practice effort rubric scored from AI conversation logs
description: Observed practice effort is a behavioral engagement measure derived from students' submitted AI-agent conversation logs collected after each of three scheduled practice sessions. Two raters independently applied a consensus-developed rubric distinguishing substantive engagement (E), surface engagement (SE), compliance-driven submissions (CE), and non-engaged submissions (NE). Each student earned up to three engagement credits converted to a proportional 0.00–1.00 score, with qualitative adjustments within a band, yielding "an ordinal measure of behavioral engagement distinct from self-report or time-on-task."
requirements: Submitted AI-agent conversation logs after each scheduled practice session and two raters reaching agreement through structured discussion prior to scoring
constraints: The article states the measure "reflects behavioral indicators rather than internal motivational states"
target_learners: undergraduate students completing AI-supported practice sessions
target_learning_goals: behavioral engagement during AI-supported retrieval or study practice
examples: Scores took proportional values such as 0.00, 0.33, 0.66, 1.00, with within-band adjustments such as 0.77 or 0.88 where strict proportional scoring did not fully capture engagement patterns
key_sources: Mahir Akgun and Sacip Toker. (2026). Do Gains from Generative AI–Enabled Adaptive Pretesting Persist? Evidence from a Retention Study. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22328

article_title: Do Gains from Generative AI-Enabled Adaptive Pretesting Persist? Evidence from a Retention Study
citation: Mahir Akgun and Sacip Toker. (2026). Do Gains from Generative AI–Enabled Adaptive Pretesting Persist? Evidence from a Retention Study. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22328
title: Follow GenAI-enabled adaptive pretesting with structured spaced retrieval practice rather than learner-directed AI study to preserve gains
description: The article concludes that adaptive pretesting elevates initial understanding but that "sustained learning depends on how subsequent AI-supported practice is structured." When pretesting is followed by retrieval-based practice — especially adaptive retrieval — gains in retention and engagement persist; when followed only by learner-directed AI interaction, benefits may attenuate. AI access should be structured to elicit retrieval rather than enable passive review.
requirements: AI-supported practice sessions held constant in number and timing across learners, with interaction structure designed to elicit retrieval attempts
constraints: Evidence comes from a single instructional context (one applied statistics course and topic); the article calls for replication across domains and task types
target_learners: undergraduate students learning applied analytical content with GenAI support
target_learning_goals: long-term retention and near-transfer of concepts after AI-assisted pretesting
examples: Participants were randomly assigned to adaptive spaced retrieval, fixed spaced retrieval, or learner-directed AI study after a common adaptive pretesting and instruction phase, with the same posttest at semester's end
key_sources: Mahir Akgun and Sacip Toker. (2026). Do Gains from Generative AI–Enabled Adaptive Pretesting Persist? Evidence from a Retention Study. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22328

article_title: Agents That Teach: Towards Designing Incidental Learning Back into AI-Assisted Software Development
citation: Rohit Mehra, Samdyuti Suri, Prithviraj K Tagadinamani, Kapil Singi, Vikrant Kaulgud, Adam P. Burden. (2026). Agents That Teach: Towards Designing Incidental Learning Back into AI-Assisted Software Development. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.06101
title: Knowledge Debt: a developer-level analogue of Technical Debt incurred when agents change code the developer does not fully understand
description: Knowledge Debt is the article's central explanatory construct: "a developer-level analogue to Technical Debt, incurred when an agent makes changes to the codebase that the developer does not fully understand". Like Technical Debt, it "compounds silently and surfaces only when independent capability is required, at which point repayment through relearning becomes costly". The authors propose operationalizing it as a measurable construct as future work.
requirements: Applies in settings where developers delegate code changes to AI agents whose reasoning the developer does not fully verify.
constraints: The article presents Knowledge Debt as a posited construct; empirical operationalization is explicitly future work.
target_learners: Professional software developers using AI coding agents
target_learning_goals: Maintaining independent debugging, adaptation, and extension capability while working with AI-generated code
examples: The paper frames the accumulating gap between AI-generated code and developer understanding, building on prior work in cognitive offloading and skill atrophy.

article_title: Agents That Teach: Towards Designing Incidental Learning Back into AI-Assisted Software Development
citation: Rohit Mehra, Samdyuti Suri, Prithviraj K Tagadinamani, Kapil Singi, Vikrant Kaulgud, Adam P. Burden. (2026). Agents That Teach: Towards Designing Incidental Learning Back into AI-Assisted Software Development. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.06101
title: Six design principles for embedding incidental learning into developer-agent interactions
description: The article proposes six early design principles that "any approach embedding incidental learning into human-agent interactions should satisfy": Contextual (tied to the specific code or decision just engaged with), Grounded (based on the agent's reasoning, not artifacts alone), Ambient (out-of-band, flow-respecting), Selective (intervening only on genuine learning moments), Adaptive (calibrated to developer expertise), and Closed-Loop (verifying internalization via comprehension checks). They "do not specify a system" but "define what any such system must do".
requirements: Learning opportunities must be grounded in the agent's reasoning trace, which carries information such as alternatives considered and uncertainty that cannot be reconstructed from code artifacts alone.
constraints: The authors present the principles as early proposals and "invite the community to refine and extend them".
target_learners: Software developers at varying expertise levels using AI coding agents
target_learning_goals: Incidental acquisition of concepts such as API choices, design decisions, alternatives, and trade-offs during agent-assisted coding
examples: SHIELD is presented as an early instantiation that operationalizes these principles.

article_title: Agents That Teach: Towards Designing Incidental Learning Back into AI-Assisted Software Development
citation: Rohit Mehra, Samdyuti Suri, Prithviraj K Tagadinamani, Kapil Singi, Vikrant Kaulgud, Adam P. Burden. (2026). Agents That Teach: Towards Designing Incidental Learning Back into AI-Assisted Software Development. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.06101
title: SHIELD: a multi-agent system for embedding incidental learning in developer-agent interactions
description: SHIELD (Safeguarding Human Expertise and Incidental Learning in Software Development) is a multi-agent prototype operating within the developer's IDE alongside their AI coding agent. It instruments the agent to emit telemetry on every code change, then a Telemetry Observer Agent, Learning Orchestrator, Teachability Triage Agent, Probe Generator Agent, Knowledge Assessor Agent, and Microlearning Generator Agent identify genuine knowledge gaps and surface probes and microlearning asynchronously. It is implemented as a VSCode extension using CrewAI, Neo4j for the Concept Map, and GPT-5.1, currently instrumented for Claude Code.
requirements: Requires instrumenting the developer's AI coding agent to emit structured telemetry capturing changes, rationale, alternatives considered, and confidence.
constraints: The current prototype works only with Claude Code as the AI coding agent; no empirical user evaluation has been conducted yet.
target_learners: Professional software developers delegating coding tasks to AI agents
target_learning_goals: Repaying Knowledge Debt by addressing emerging knowledge gaps as they arise without interrupting development flow
examples: A walkthrough shows a developer delegating a webhook retry issue; the agent replaces fixed retry logic with exponential backoff and jitter, and SHIELD surfaces a probe, assesses partial understanding, and delivers microlearning followed by a comprehension check.
