article_title: Adversarial Stress Testing of Role-Playing Language Agents using Multi-Agent Evaluation
citation: Saqib Shouqi, Abdullah Nazly, Januki Wanniarachchi, Ravisha De Alwis. (2026). Adversarial Stress Testing of Role-Playing Language Agents using Multi-Agent Evaluation. ADScAI Conference, University of Moratuwa, Sri Lanka. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03166
title: Multi-agent adversarial evaluation framework coordinating Interrogator, Target, and Judging agents
description: The article proposes a modular multi-agent framework in which "a strategy-driven Interrogator Agent that applies six progressive adversarial strategies" probes a Target Agent representing the RPLA under evaluation, while "an automated Judging Agent that scores behavior across role fidelity, drift, ethical deviation, and consistency dimensions" evaluates the full transcript afterward. The Judging Agent does not participate in dialogue generation, ensuring evaluation does not alter the behavior measured. The framework treats the Target Agent as a black box and supports multiple LLM providers through a unified abstraction layer.
requirements: A persistent database storing experiment metadata, conversation transcripts, and evaluation results to enable replay, comparison, and auditing
A unified LLM provider abstraction layer so the same experimental setup runs across models without changing evaluation logic
constraints: The Target Agent is treated as a black box, reflecting deployment conditions where internal model parameters are not accessible
The framework focuses on prompt-based adversarial attacks and does not consider vulnerabilities arising from training, fine-tuning, or reinforcement learning processes
target_learners: Developers and researchers evaluating role-playing language agents for education, healthcare assistance, and customer support
target_learning_goals: Assessing robustness, reliability, and alignment of role-playing language agents under sustained adversarial conditions
examples: Experiments ran 10-turn interactions per experiment across three personas (Healthcare Assistant, Customer Support Agent, Financial Advisor) with three random seeds per condition
key_sources: Saqib Shouqi, Abdullah Nazly, Januki Wanniarachchi, Ravisha De Alwis. (2026). Adversarial Stress Testing of Role-Playing Language Agents using Multi-Agent Evaluation. ADScAI Conference, University of Moratuwa, Sri Lanka. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03166

title: Open-source adversarial stress-testing platform for RPLAs with FastAPI backend and React dashboard
description: The article releases "an open-source platform to support AI safety and reproducible RPLA benchmarking." The system follows a client-server design in which "A FastAPI-based backend manages experiment configuration, agent execution, scoring, and data persistence, while a React-based frontend provides an interactive interface for experiment creation, monitoring, and analysis." Metric computation code is available in the repository under agents/judging_agent/metrics.py, enabling reproducibility and community auditing of scoring algorithms.
requirements: Persistent storage of all prompts, responses, timestamps, and metadata for experiment replay and longitudinal analysis
constraints: The authors caution the framework could be misused to exploit deployed systems and emphasize responsible access and usage; automated evaluation should not be solely relied upon for critical decision-making
target_learners: AI safety researchers and developers of role-playing language agents
target_learning_goals: Systematic discovery of RPLA failure modes and reproducible benchmarking of agent robustness
examples: All experiments were executed using the proposed orchestration pipeline with 10-turn interactions per experiment across Groq, OpenAI, and Anthropic providers

description: The paper proposes an organizational framework in which a stable student-elected administrative board governs a dynamic portfolio of student-led projects, with faculty acting as mentors. Its central premise is that "students should occupy a leading role in both the conception and execution of projects, while faculty members act primarily as mentors and facilitators." Every project is expected to simultaneously promote student learning, generate knowledge, and produce extension outcomes, so the three university pillars are integrated continuously rather than treated as separate activities.

It synthesises features from experiential, transformative, reflective-practitioner, affective and self-regulated learning theories and incorporates the technological dimensions of GenAI. The article states it is proposed "to manage greater demand for reflection, ii) to address the limitations of the existing reflection models, iii) to consider technological aspects of GenAI."

article_title: Adaptive Scaffolding Needs Contingency: An AI Tutor That Escalates and Fades on What the Learner Does
citation: Hou, X., Weng, Y., Yeh, C. H., Lee, D. L., Zheng, L., Li, F., Wang, W., & Liu, Y. (2026). Adaptive Scaffolding Needs Contingency: An AI Tutor That Escalates and Fades on What the Learner Does. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22993
title: Preserved metacognitive demand: hold what the learner must decide constant and let carried load vary with demonstrated need
description: The principle states that "An AI learning system should hold the learner's metacognitive demand approximately constant, and let the cognitive load it carries vary with demonstrated need." It rests on the paper's separation of two quantities that giving-more-or-less designs run together: the load the system carries and the demand placed on the learner before help arrives. CoMeT implements it by escalating support at decision points on failure and fading on take-up, so the learner keeps deciding while the tutor's labour varies.
requirements: The tutor must be able to identify decision points and detect take-up from the learner's turns, via authored coverage patterns plus a take-up judgement
constraints: Demand is held approximately constant, not exactly; the principle was tested on adult learners on short Python tasks with authored decision points
target_learning_goals: planning and monitoring decisions in programming problem solving
self-regulated learning during AI-assisted coding
examples: Tutor C asks first, gives more help each time the learner does not use it, and pulls back as soon as the learner does, conceding one decision point at a time after three asks
key_sources: Hou, X., Weng, Y., Yeh, C. H., Lee, D. L., Zheng, L., Li, F., Wang, W., & Liu, Y. (2026). Adaptive Scaffolding Needs Contingency: An AI Tutor That Escalates and Fades on What the Learner Does. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22993

article_title: Adaptive Scaffolding Needs Contingency: An AI Tutor That Escalates and Fades on What the Learner Does
citation: Hou, X., Weng, Y., Yeh, C. H., Lee, D. L., Zheng, L., Li, F., Wang, W., & Liu, Y. (2026). Adaptive Scaffolding Needs Contingency: An AI Tutor That Escalates and Fades on What the Learner Does. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22993
title: The contingency dimension: separating the load a system carries from the demand it places on the learner
description: The paper defines a design axis on which tutor designs sit: "We call the line those positions lie on thecontingency dimension, and contingent tutoring is movement along it during a task." Structuring changes how much load the system carries; problematizing changes how much demand the learner faces. Existing LLM tutors fix one position at design time; contingent tutoring moves along the dimension during a task, escalating after failure and fading after success. The theory has three parts: direction (the contingent shift rule), unit (decision points), and warrant (what justifies fading).
requirements: A signal the tutor can read from the learner's writing to decide when support rises and falls
constraints: Positions of prior systems on the dimension are illustrative; the warrant part was tested only on a text-channel tutor with authored decision points
target_learners: adult novice programmers using AI tutors
target_learning_goals: regulatory work such as deciding, articulating and judging before help arrives
examples: Table 1 places prior LLM systems and the three study tutors on the dimension as five properties: withholds, structures, gates, escalates, fades

article_title: Adaptive Scaffolding Needs Contingency: An AI Tutor That Escalates and Fades on What the Learner Does
citation: Hou, X., Weng, Y., Yeh, C. H., Lee, D. L., Zheng, L., Li, F., Wang, W., & Liu, Y. (2026). Adaptive Scaffolding Needs Contingency: An AI Tutor That Escalates and Fades on What the Learner Does. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22993
title: CoMeT: a browser-based contingent AI programming tutor with a support ladder over authored decision points
description: CoMeT is "a browser-based environment in which a learner works through a short programming task beside a chat tutor", with a sketchpad and code editor. Tasks run three gated phases (Planning with the editor locked, Monitoring, Evaluating), and correctness is decided by authored test cases, never by the model. Tutor C escalates one rung at a time through three asks (Socratic question, specific hint, contrasting case), concedes a point after R = 3 rounds, and returns to the first rung on take-up; coverage is decided by authored patterns rather than holistic model judgement.
requirements: Decision points must be authored per task and phase, with coverage patterns and scaffold wording, so the difference between tutors is auditable
constraints: All three tutors ran on the same model backbone (Claude Haiku 4.5); take-up where patterns do not settle it falls to a one-word model judgement and a length threshold that errs on the learner's side
target_learners: adult learners with no prior programming threshold through over five years of Python experience
target_learning_goals: settling the decisions a program turns on before code is written
monitoring and evaluating one's own solution
examples: In the study, 131 adult learners met all three tutors across three Python tasks (bus-fare calculator, pizza order, staffing roster), one tutor per task in a Williams square design

article_title: AI-Assisted Social Story Intervention for Special Education: The Design of AdaptED Stories
citation: Buyankhishig Enkhjargal, Himanshi Lalwani, Hanan Salam. (2026). AI-Assisted Social Story Intervention for Special Education: The Design of AdaptED Stories. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24245
title: AdaptED Stories: practitioner-guided AI web application for authoring, personalizing, and delivering Social Stories
description: AdaptED Stories is a practitioner-facing web application for Social Story interventions with autistic children. Per the abstract, "The system uses student profiles to draft story text and visuals, supports review and refinement by practitioners, and includes reading-session support with comprehension activities and session records." Student profiles capture comprehension level, preferred story and sentence length, goals, interests, and a photograph converted into a reusable cartoon avatar. The library is pre-loaded with 200 validated Social Stories from the SS-GEN dataset across six thematic categories. Reading sessions use child-like text-to-speech narration, and analytics aggregate comprehension and behavioral scores with AI-generated recommendations.
requirements: Practitioner review and approval of AI-drafted text and visuals before use with children
Student profile information defined by the practitioner to ground personalization
constraints: Background inconsistencies may still occur in personalized visuals
Evaluated only for usability and acceptance, not yet for child outcomes
target_learners: Autistic children in special-education contexts, including non-speaking or minimally verbal children
target_learning_goals: Understanding and preparing for everyday social situations
Target behavior change and comprehension of social narratives
examples: Phase 3 participants completed five structured tasks: creating a student profile, generating a story, personalizing a library story, conducting a reading session, and reviewing analytics and recommendations.
key_sources: Buyankhishig Enkhjargal, Himanshi Lalwani, Hanan Salam. (2026). AI-Assisted Social Story Intervention for Special Education: The Design of AdaptED Stories. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24245

article_title: AI-Assisted Social Story Intervention for Special Education: The Design of AdaptED Stories
citation: Buyankhishig Enkhjargal, Himanshi Lalwani, Hanan Salam. (2026). AI-Assisted Social Story Intervention for Special Education: The Design of AdaptED Stories. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24245
title: Keep practitioners in control of AI-assisted authoring: treat AI outputs as reviewable drafts, not finished products
description: The article's first design goal holds that AI should reduce authoring effort while practitioners remain the main authors and decision-makers. As stated, "Our first goal was to keep practitioners as the main authors and decision-makers, with AI used to draft story text and visuals that are always subject to review and editing." In AdaptED Stories this is realized through staged workflows in which generated text and each scene visual are reviewed, edited, or regenerated and explicitly approved before saving. This preserves professional oversight and alignment with evidence-based practice.
requirements: Staged approval workflow separating text approval from visual approval
Practitioners with formal training in behavioral assessment and intervention design
constraints: Positioned for practitioner-facing rather than parent-facing authoring, since parent-centered authoring may create tensions between parental priorities and therapeutic goals
target_learning_goals: Therapeutically grounded, personalized Social Story interventions
examples: Across generation and personalization workflows, AI outputs are treated as reviewable drafts rather than finished products, with per-scene regeneration available.

article_title: Ticket to Nowhere: The Gap between Leaving High School and Entering College and High-Performance Jobs.
citation: Haycock, Kati, Ed.; Barth, Patte, Ed.; Mitchell, Ruth, Ed.; Wilkins, Amy, Ed. (1999). Ticket to Nowhere: The Gap between Leaving High School and Entering College and High-Performance Jobs. Thinking K-16; v3 n2 Fall 1999. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED457262
title: The K-16 Square: four interlocking commitments linking K-12 and higher education to bring all students to high standards
description: The K-16 Square is a framework drafted by state education CEOs from seven states (with the National Association of System Heads and the Education Trust) representing four interlocking and equally important commitments as the corners of a figure: ensure all high school graduates meet high standards; accept only teachers who can bring all students' performance to high standards; accept into college only students who meet high standards; and ensure all teacher candidates produced are prepared to bring student performance to high standards. The framework holds that "Change in one sector cannot be accomplished without change in the others," with standards for K-12 graduation congruent with college admission standards. The CEOs propose that about a third of states achieve the universal goal by 2010 and the rest by 2020.
requirements: Strong interaction among sectors: standards for graduation must be congruent with standards for college admission, and teacher preparation standards congruent with school employment standards
Publicly available, accurate data on the performance of schools, colleges, universities and their students
constraints: Each state must establish its own timetable because socioeconomic and political circumstances vary and may change suddenly
target_learners: all K-12 and college students, especially low-income and minority students
target_learning_goals: meeting high achievement standards from elementary through postsecondary education, preparation for work and citizenship
examples: The CEOs' statement cites El Paso, Texas, where a five-year collaboration between higher education, K-12, and community leaders raised academic performance for all students and reduced the minority achievement gap by about two-thirds

article_title: Priced out: How the Wrong Financial-Aid Policies Hurt Low-Income Students
citation: Mamie Lynch, Jennifer Engle, and José L. Cruz. (2011). Priced Out: How the Wrong Financial-Aid Policies Hurt Low-Income Students. The Education Trust. https://www.collegeresults.org
title: Evaluate financial-aid policies by whether they primarily benefit low-income students, remove access barriers, and provide awards large enough to influence choices and success
description: The report proposes that policymakers apply a set of screening questions to any financial-aid policy at the federal, state, or institutional level. The questions ask whether the policy "primarily benefit[s] low-income students," whether low-income students can "fully tap financial assistance" without technical barriers, and whether awards are "large enough to influence the choices—and success rates—of low-income students." The report grounds this in its finding that current aid choices increasingly steer funds toward affluent students.
requirements: Policymakers at federal, state, and institutional levels must apply the criteria when setting financial-aid policy
constraints: The report notes net-price data cannot show how institutions allocate aid across income brackets, only what low-income students pay after all grant aid
target_learning_goals: college access and affordability
postsecondary attainment
examples: The report's executive summary and conclusion both print the three-question test for decision makers setting financial-aid policy

title: VCU University College model: cohort-based first-year core curriculum with centralized support and proactive advising
description: Virginia Commonwealth University's University College, launched in 2006, is built around "a cohesive core curriculum with a limited set of course options and small class sizes," taught by dedicated cross-disciplinary faculty, with a full-year cohort class. It pairs this with proactive advising — required advisor meetings twice a semester, faculty attendance reporting, and outreach at the first sign of trouble — plus learning, writing, and supplemental instruction centers. After implementation, DFW rates in core courses decreased significantly and retention rose.

Dedicated faculty hired to work across disciplines
Professionally trained advisors tracking student data

examples: VCU narrowed its black-white gap from 7.4 points in 2004 to near parity by 2010, with black students graduating at 49.8 percent

college completion improvement

target_learners: students of color in higher education
target_learning_goals: Racial equity in higher education access, opportunity, and outcomes
examples: The report cites simulations showing income-based affirmative action yields less racial diversity than race-based policies, and performance-funding studies where low-income enrollment rose while Black enrollment stayed flat or fell

article_title: Teaching the Way Students Learn Best: Lessons from Bronxdale High School
citation: Ancess, J., Rogers, B., Duncan Grand, D., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2019). Teaching the way students learn best: Lessons from Bronxdale High School. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/social-and-emotional-learning-case-study-bronxdale
title: A framework of four principles for whole child education derived from the science of learning and development
description: The report organizes its case around four principles for educational practice drawn from syntheses of neuroscience, cognitive science, and the developmental sciences: (1) environmental conditions supporting positive, trusting relationships, safety, and belonging; (2) intentional development of social, emotional, and cognitive skills, mindsets, and habits, with "supports for behavior should be educative and restorative"; (3) curricular designs and instructional strategies featuring "well-scaffolded instruction and ongoing formative assessment"; and (4) multi-tiered systems of support based on a shared developmental framework. Figure 1 presents these as a Framework for Whole Child Education, and Appendix B maps Bronxdale practices onto the principles.
requirements: School structures and classroom practices must support positive, trusting relationships, physical and emotional safety including identity safety, and a sense of belonging and purpose.
constraints: The report presents the framework as derived from recently published research syntheses rather than testing it empirically in this case study.
target_learners: K–12 students, especially diverse learners and students experiencing adversity
target_learning_goals: Academic capacity, competence, motivation, metacognitive skills, social-emotional skills, and resilience
examples: The report uses the framework to structure its account of Bronxdale's culture, SEL teaching, instruction, and systems of support, with a mapping table in Appendix B.
key_sources: Ancess, J., Rogers, B., Duncan Grand, D., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2019). Teaching the way students learn best: Lessons from Bronxdale High School. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/social-and-emotional-learning-case-study-bronxdale

article_title: Teaching the Way Students Learn Best: Lessons from Bronxdale High School
citation: Ancess, J., Rogers, B., Duncan Grand, D., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2019). Teaching the way students learn best: Lessons from Bronxdale High School. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/social-and-emotional-learning-case-study-bronxdale
title: Whole-school design pattern combining community vision, inquiry instruction with social-emotional supports, restorative discipline, and a professional community of practice
description: The report identifies a constellation of four mutually reinforcing school-design factors that it argues produced Bronxdale's outcomes: "a compelling vision of students and school as a caring, safe, collaborative community," "the integration of inquiry instruction with social-emotional supports," "educative discipline that puts restorative practices into action," and a faculty committed to "teaching the way that students learn best" while "continuously learning together in a community of practice." The pattern treats culture, pedagogy, discipline, and adult learning as one integrated design rather than isolated programs.
requirements: Structures such as small class size and advisory to build close relationships; distributed leadership; intensive ongoing professional development; and multi-tiered academic, health, and social supports.
constraints: The report notes the school's evolution took about 7 years and that its first year, before these practices were in place, was "in disarray" with fights and an unsafe climate.
target_learners: Diverse high school learners, including students from low-income households and students with disabilities in inclusion settings
target_learning_goals: Self-reliant, independent learning; curiosity; creative problem-solving; agency; academic and emotional self-regulation
examples: Bronxdale implemented advisory, Peer Group Connections, restorative circles, peer mediation, youth court, small classes of about 22 students, and a senior capstone project presented to a jury of peers and faculty.

article_title: Taking the Long View: State Efforts to Solve Teacher Shortages by Strengthening the Profession
citation: Espinoza, D., Saunders, R., Kini, T., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2018). Taking the long view: State efforts to solve teacher shortages by strengthening the profession. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/long-view
title: Teacher residency model with eight key characteristics of strong programs
description: A teacher residency is an accelerated certification pathway in which candidates "work as paid apprentices to skilled expert teachers while completing highly integrated coursework" during a full-year clinical placement in a high-need classroom, with tuition and living support repaid through a multi-year service commitment. The report lists eight characteristics of strong residencies drawn from a research review, including strong district-university partnerships, tightly integrated coursework, expert mentor co-teaching, cohorts in partnership teaching schools, and ongoing mentoring for graduates. States including California, Texas, Pennsylvania, Michigan, and Louisiana fund or mandate residency models.
requirements: Strong district and university partnerships
A full year of residency teaching alongside an expert mentor teacher
Financial support for residents in exchange for a 3- to 5-year post-residency teaching commitment
Expert mentor teachers who co-teach with residents
constraints: Programs are typically targeted to postbaccalaureate candidates and hard-to-staff positions in sponsoring districts
target_learners: Career changers and paraprofessionals entering teaching
target_learning_goals: Effective teaching in high-need fields and school districts
Retention of new teachers in hard-to-staff positions
examples: California invested $75 million in a Teacher Residency Grant Program for special education, STEM, and bilingual shortage areas, funding more than 3,500 new teachers with up to $20,000 per teacher matched by districts
Louisiana adopted regulations requiring a yearlong residency as a pathway to licensure, with $7.3 million in transitional funding for stipends and mentor training
key_sources: Espinoza, D., Saunders, R., Kini, T., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2018). Taking the long view: State efforts to solve teacher shortages by strengthening the profession. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/long-view

article_title: Taking the Long View: State Efforts to Solve Teacher Shortages by Strengthening the Profession
citation: Espinoza, D., Saunders, R., Kini, T., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2018). Taking the long view: State efforts to solve teacher shortages by strengthening the profession. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/long-view
title: Address teacher shortages with a set of mutually reinforcing policies rather than any single policy in isolation
description: The report argues no single policy solves teacher shortages if enacted alone: research on hard-to-staff schools indicates it is important "both to raise salaries and to provide for more collegial, supportive, well-resourced environments," and induction works best alongside school-level collaboration and mentorship policies. It recommends that policymakers consider how to ensure a set of mutually reinforcing strategies spanning recruitment, preparation, induction, leadership, compensation, and retention. Washington State's comprehensive approach, profiled in the report, illustrates this combined strategy.
requirements: Coordination across multiple policy areas (scholarships, pathways, induction, leadership, compensation, recruitment)
constraints: Effectiveness hinges on the size, scope, and comprehensiveness of the policy, quality of implementation, and responsiveness to state, local, and labor market context
target_learners: State policymakers designing teacher workforce systems
Prospective and practicing teachers in shortage fields
target_learning_goals: Recruiting, developing, and retaining a strong, stable, diverse teacher workforce
examples: Washington State combined service scholarships, high school pathways and Grow Your Own programs, mentoring and induction, school leadership investment, competitive compensation, and recruitment policies in a single comprehensive approach
The report concludes states should continually evaluate implementation and outcomes to strengthen the effectiveness of their actions

article_title: Next Generation Accountability: A Vision for School Improvement under ESSA
citation: Adams, C. M., Ford, T. G., Forsyth, P. B., Ware, J. K., Olsen, J. J., Lepine, J. A., Sr., Barnes, L. B., Khojasteh, J., & Mwavita, M. (2017). Next generation accountability: A vision for improvement under ESSA. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/next-generation-accountability
title: Next generation accountability framework: shared accountability, adaptive improvement, and informational significance in a two-stage design
description: The report advances a framework for school accountability under ESSA governed by three principles: shared accountability, in which "performance responsibility is distributed across the system's components"; adaptive improvement, acknowledging that school capacities differ greatly; and informational significance, replacing a single composite with a broad palette of functionally significant indicators. It features a two-stage design: Stage One is formative, providing schools useful information for their own improvement decisions; Stage Two is aggressive, identifying and transforming schools in catastrophic failure. Schools are viewed as systems whose outcomes result from the quality of their resources and processes.
requirements: A support infrastructure capable of serving the developmental and resource needs of schools with differing needs
constraints: Stage Two applies to schools in catastrophic failure; Stage One is more formative than summative
target_learners: K-12 students in state accountability systems
target_learning_goals: deeper learning
college and career readiness
examples: The framework is operationalized in the Educational Quality and Improvement Profile (EQuIP) with resource, process, and outcome indicators

By reporting data on school resources, processes, and outcomes, "an EQuIP provides vital information for making judgments of school quality and helps focus school improvement efforts." school quality improvement

article_title: Building a System of College and Career Pathways in New Mexico
citation: Hoachlander, G. (2020). Building a system of college and career pathways in New Mexico. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/new-mexico-education
title: College and career pathways framework integrating CTE, core academics, work-based learning, and personalized supports
description: The report proposes a comprehensive high school redesign framework in which pathways "integrate CTE and core academic curriculum, combine classroom and work-based learning, and align secondary and postsecondary programs." Its state framework should include four essential components: college preparatory core academics "emphasizing real-world application, project-based learning, and performance assessment"; a sequence of four or more challenging CTE courses aligned to industry standards with dual enrollment and certifications; a continuum of work-based learning from career awareness in grade 9 to internships or school-based enterprise by grade 12; and personalized student supports including counseling, accelerated instruction, and social-emotional learning. The framework is grounded in the MDRC and SRI evidence the report reviews.
requirements: A task force to develop a state pathways framework and quality standards guiding pilots and eventual system design
constraints: The report notes H.B. 91 continued to situate CTE largely in isolation from the rest of students' high school experience
target_learners: All high school students in grades 9-12
target_learning_goals: College and career readiness
High school completion and postsecondary transition
Industry-related knowledge and skills integrated with core academics
examples: The report recommends New Mexico create demonstrations of pathways systems in 6 to 10 districts as part of the H.B. 91 CTE pilot.
key_sources: Hoachlander, G. (2020). Building a system of college and career pathways in New Mexico. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/new-mexico-education

article_title: Building a System of College and Career Pathways in New Mexico
citation: Hoachlander, G. (2020). Building a system of college and career pathways in New Mexico. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/new-mexico-education
title: Seven-dimension pathway quality standards spanning outcomes-driven practice, equity culture, industry themes, project-based learning, work-based learning, supports, and distributed leadership
description: The report proposes state quality standards for college and career pathways mirroring the seven dimensions on which certified Linked Learning pathways produced positive impacts. Standards include that "The progress of every student is the driving focus for evaluating pathway quality," a culture of high expectations with nondiscriminatory and inclusive practices, an industry-themed program of study offering dual credit, inquiry- and project-based learning that is "relevant, rigorous, outcome-focused, and collaborative in nature," a personalized continuum of work-based learning for every student, personalized academic and social-emotional supports, and shared responsibility among staff, leaders, and community partners.
requirements: A pathway quality assessment rubric tied to state quality standards, plus metrics and incentives for increasingly higher levels of quality implementation
constraints: The report warns tracking should ensure pathways do not regress into old systems that led to tracking and inequitable outcomes by race, ethnicity, gender, and special needs
target_learners: All high school students in pathway programs, including students with low prior achievement
target_learning_goals: College and career readiness
Mastery of college- and career-ready learning outcomes
Academic and professional skills demonstrated through work-based learning
examples: The report recommends metrics such as percentage of students participating in industry-centered, multidisciplinary project-based learning and percentage of students earning dual college credit aligned with their pathway.
key_sources: Hoachlander, G. (2020). Building a system of college and career pathways in New Mexico. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/new-mexico-education

article_title: California Teachers and COVID-19: How the Pandemic is Impacting the Teacher Workforce
citation: Carver-Thomas, D., Leung, M., & Burns, D. (2021). California teachers and COVID-19: How the pandemic is impacting the teacher workforce. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/california-covid-19-teacher-workforce
title: Teacher residency programs as district-preparation partnerships for high-need positions
description: Teacher residency programs are "partnerships between school districts and teacher preparation programs designed to recruit and prepare a diverse pool of candidates to teach in high-need positions." They are yearlong apprenticeships modeled on medical residencies, providing residents extensive clinical practice under an expert mentor teacher while completing tightly integrated coursework. Districts with residencies reported certainty about the number and quality of teachers they could expect to hire.

constraints: The report notes many residents struggle financially and such programs can be out of reach for smaller districts with lean administrative teams

target_learning_goals: Fully prepared, retained teachers for shortage fields

article_title: Students Experiencing Homelessness: The Conditions and Outcomes of Homelessness among California Students
citation: Burns, D., Espinoza, D., Ondrasek, N., & Yang, M. (2021). Students experiencing homelessness: The conditions and outcomes of homelessness among California students. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/students-experiencing-homelessness
title: Multi-tiered systems of support (MTSS) as a school-level structure for supporting students experiencing homelessness
description: MTSS is described as a school-level coordinative structure that integrates academic, behavioral, and social-emotional supports in tiers. The report states that "School-level structures like multi-tiered systems of support (MTSS) can support students experiencing homelessness by providing an intervention framework that integrates academic, behavioral, and social and emotional competencies." It recommends districts implement MTSS so services reach students who need them without cumbersome procedures, and notes MTSS can be tailored to individual students' specific needs, which matters given this group's complex needs.
requirements: Well implementation to provide services effectively, which the report notes can be made challenging by the highly mobile nature of homelessness
constraints: Implementation is challenged by the highly mobile nature of homelessness, as the article states
target_learning_goals: Integrated academic, behavioral, and social and emotional competencies
examples: The report recommends districts implement school-level coordinative structures such as MTSS to efficiently identify and meet student needs, alongside community school wraparound supports

article_title: Jim Crow Debt: How Black Borrowers Experience Student Loans
citation: Mustaffa, J. B., & Davis, J. C. W. (2021). Jim Crow Debt: How Black Borrowers Experience Student Loans. The Education Trust. https://edtrust.org/black-student-debt-study/
title: National Black Student Loan Debt Study (survey of 1,272 Black borrowers plus 100 in-depth interviews)
description: A sequential, equal status mixed-method study of Black borrowers' experiences with student loans, conducted by The Education Trust with Jalil B. Mustaffa. "In total, 1,272 Black borrowers completed our survey," recruited via social media ads, email alerts, and word of mouth, followed by in-depth interviews with 100 volunteers selected on demographic characteristics and analyzed with the constant comparative method. The sample is largely four-year and graduate-degree holders, women, borrowers aged 25 and older, earning $50,000 or more annually.
requirements: Participants must identify as Black borrowers; survey instrument elicits perspectives on mental health, information quality, pandemic impact, return on investment, and solutions
constraints: Non-random sampling scheme; sample skews toward degree holders, women, and borrowers earning $50,000 or more annually, so findings may not generalize to all Black borrowers
target_learners: Black student loan borrowers in higher education, including graduate-degree holders and parent borrowers
target_learning_goals: Understanding Black borrowers' lived experiences of student debt to inform student loan and college affordability policy
examples: Survey data were cleaned, recoded, and analyzed using frequencies and descriptive statistics; the study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the University of Pennsylvania

article_title: Educator Diversity State Profile: California
citation: The Education Trust. (2022). Educator Diversity State Profile: California. EDTRUST.ORG. https://edtrust.org/educator-diversity/
title: California Classified School Employee Teacher Credentialing Program (Grow Your Own)
description: A California Grow Your Own program that provides grants to adults who work in schools (classified staff) so they can complete their undergraduate education and prepare to become teachers. In July 2021 the state appropriated $125 million to expand the program for another five years. The California Center on Teaching Careers is described as an extension of the Credentialing Grant Program that supports classified staff pursuing teaching degrees. The brief rates California green on providing funding, guidance, and public support for GYO programs that attract candidates of color.
requirements: State-level funding and guidance for developing GYO programming
constraints: Described as serving adults already working in schools; the brief reports no outcome evaluation of the program
target_learners: classified school staff and paraprofessionals seeking teacher credentials
target_learning_goals: completing undergraduate education and teacher preparation
entering the teaching profession
examples: The brief cites Texas' Grow Your Own grant program as another state earning a green in this category

article_title: Educator Diversity State Profile: Illinois
citation: EdTrust. (2022). Educator Diversity State Profile: ILLINOIS. https://edtrust.org
title: Six-strategy state policy framework for increasing educator workforce diversity
description: The brief organizes state-level action into six strategies: making educator diversity data "visible and actionable to stakeholders"; setting clear state and district goals; investing in educator preparation programs; targeting resources to districts and schools for recruiting and hiring a diverse workforce; investing in retention through working conditions and growth opportunities; and using federal COVID relief funds for diversity strategies. Each strategy is operationalized as criteria rated on a three-level scale (meets all or most, some, one or no requirements), and Illinois is rated against each. The framework treats workforce diversity as a policy-design problem spanning data, goals, preparation, recruitment, and retention.
requirements: State education agencies must collect and share useful and timely educator workforce data so stakeholders can set goals and chart a path forward
constraints: The framework addresses state-level policy conditions; it rates what states do, not district or classroom practice
target_learners: K-12 public school students in Illinois, particularly students of color
target_learning_goals: Equitable student access to a racially diverse, high-quality educator workforce
examples: Illinois earned greens for scholarship programs, GYO funding, residency pathways, and numeric diversity goals, but reds or no-evidence ratings for investing in minority-serving institutions and for leader cultural-competence training
key_sources: EdTrust. (2022). Educator Diversity State Profile: ILLINOIS. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED622786

article_title: Educator Diversity State Profile: Illinois
citation: EdTrust. (2022). Educator Diversity State Profile: ILLINOIS. https://edtrust.org
title: Make educator diversity data publicly visible and actionable at the school level
description: The brief argues that increasing workforce diversity requires that "all stakeholders must have access to useful and timely educator workforce data to set goals and chart a path forward." State education agencies, as keepers of state data systems, should publish school-level racial demographics of the educator workforce in dashboards, report cards, or reports so stakeholders can make targeted decisions. Illinois posts only district-level data, and the brief recommends adding school-level data and easier interpretation, citing Massachusetts' dashboard as a model.
requirements: Data should be publicly available and easily accessible, at school level, in a dashboard, report card, or state report
constraints: Illinois currently meets only some requirements: it posts district-level rather than school-level data
target_learning_goals: Data-informed state and district decisions to diversify the educator workforce
examples: Illinois' Annual Program Reporting system publicly reports racial demographics of candidates entering and completing teacher preparation programs, earning green ratings
key_sources: EdTrust. (2022). Educator Diversity State Profile: ILLINOIS. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED622786

article_title: Educator Diversity State Profile: Illinois
citation: EdTrust. (2022). Educator Diversity State Profile: ILLINOIS. https://edtrust.org
title: Minority Teachers of Illinois scholarship program
description: A state scholarship program attracting students of color into teacher preparation. Recipients must have "achieved a secondary grade point average of 2.5 on a 4.0 scale" and be enrolled at least half-time in a course of study leading to teacher licensure while maintaining that GPA. In 2021 Illinois passed legislation to raise the scholarship ceiling to $7,500 and add a carve-out for bilingual candidates, pending appropriations. The brief rates Illinois green on this strategy and cites Florida's Minority Teacher Education Scholars Program as a comparable example.
requirements: Candidates must meet the 2.5 GPA threshold and half-time enrollment in a licensure program; the bilingual carve-out is pending appropriations
target_learners: Students of color pursuing teacher licensure in Illinois, including bilingual candidates
target_learning_goals: Recruiting candidates of color into the teaching profession
examples: 2021 legislation increased the scholarship ceiling to $7,500 and created a bilingual-candidate carve-out
key_sources: EdTrust. (2022). Educator Diversity State Profile: ILLINOIS. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED622786

article_title: Educator Diversity State Profile: Illinois
citation: EdTrust. (2022). Educator Diversity State Profile: ILLINOIS. https://edtrust.org
title: Grow Your Own Illinois program
description: A state-funded program that provides "scholarships and assistance for community members to become certified teachers and work in schools in the state." It also "facilitates partnership opportunities between districts, preparation programs, and Community Based Organizations," and is required to consider high school students enrolled in dual-credit courses as potential recruitment candidates. The brief rates Illinois green on both GYO funding and district-preparation-program partnerships, citing Texas and New York programs as peer examples.
requirements: Direct state funding and partnership structures between districts, preparation programs, and community-based organizations
target_learners: Community members and high school students in Illinois, traditionally attracting candidates of color
target_learning_goals: Community-based recruitment and preparation of certified teachers of color for local schools
examples: GYO Illinois is named in the brief's after-school pipeline recommendations as a recruitment relationship builder with OST providers

article_title: Equity First: Priorities for Higher Education Partnerships and Investments
citation: Byon, A. H., & Elliott, K. C. (2022). Equity First: Priorities for Higher Education Partnerships and Investments. The Education Trust. https://edtrust.org/resource/how-to-end-the-hunger-and-homelessness-crisis-among-college-students/
title: Three core areas of need for equity-focused higher education investment: institutional capacity building, wraparound supports with equity-focused funding, and asset-based student-centered approaches
description: A taxonomy of investment needs identified by convening participants. The report states that participants "identified three core areas of need that will require critical investments": "Institutional capacity building — including financial resources; physical infrastructure, such as facilities and internet connectivity; and human infrastructure, such as faculty and staff"; comprehensive wraparound student supports with flexible, equity-focused funding; and "Asset-based, human- and student-centered approaches that prioritize those who will be most affected by an investment or initiative." It organizes the report's funding recommendations for institutions serving marginalized students.
requirements: Investments must be aligned to the identified core areas to effectively serve Black, Latino, and Indigenous students and students from low-income backgrounds.
constraints: Derived from the perspectives of convening participants rather than from tested data.
target_learners: Black, Latino, and Indigenous students in higher education
target_learning_goals: equitable access to institutional resources and supports that enable completion and success

article_title: Understanding Teacher Compensation: A State-by-State Analysis
citation: Carver-Thomas, D., & Patrick, S. (2022). Understanding Teacher Compensation: A State-by-State Analysis. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/443.847
title: A three-indicator framework for describing state teacher compensation conditions
description: The report organizes teacher compensation analysis around three indicators: "(1) average annual starting salary for public school teachers, (2) average annual starting salary for public school teachers adjusted for cost-of-living differences across states, and (3) average weekly wage competitiveness". Together, the authors state, "these indicators signal the overall wage conditions underlying efforts to attract and retain well-prepared teachers across a state." Each indicator is presented as a national and state-level map and table.
requirements: Starting-salary data collected from district teacher salary schedules or district compensation plans
Cost-of-living adjustment requires Regional Price Parity data
Wage competitiveness requires comparison wages for other college-educated workers in each state
constraints: Teacher starting salaries and cost of living vary by district, so within states there are districts higher or lower than the state average on these indicators
target_learning_goals: Understanding state teacher compensation conditions that underlie teacher recruitment and retention
examples: The report applies the framework to all states and the District of Columbia, with a final table showing all three indicators and ranks for each state.
key_sources: Carver-Thomas, D., & Patrick, S. (2022). Understanding Teacher Compensation: A State-by-State Analysis. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/443.847

article_title: Understanding Teacher Compensation: A State-by-State Analysis
citation: Carver-Thomas, D., & Patrick, S. (2022). Understanding Teacher Compensation: A State-by-State Analysis. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/443.847
title: Teacher wage competitiveness index
description: An indicator defined as "the average public school teacher weekly wage as a percentage of the estimated weekly wage for other college-educated workers within each state". Weekly wages are used because they "adjust for any differences in the work year across occupations". The report transforms Economic Policy Institute weekly wage penalty data to a 0-100% scale and bands states from less competitive (below 75%) to more competitive (90% or above).
requirements: Population Survey data controlling for factors that typically influence wages
Weekly wage estimates for other college-educated workers in each state
constraints: State estimates are based on data from 2014 through 2019, and the national estimate is based on 2019 data
target_learning_goals: Assessing how competitively teacher pay compares with other college-educated occupations in a state
examples: The report reports state index values ranging from Wyoming at 98.0% down to Virginia at 67.3%, with a U.S. average of 80.8%.
key_sources: Carver-Thomas, D., & Patrick, S. (2022). Understanding Teacher Compensation: A State-by-State Analysis. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/443.847

article_title: Understanding Teacher Compensation: A State-by-State Analysis
citation: Carver-Thomas, D., & Patrick, S. (2022). Understanding Teacher Compensation: A State-by-State Analysis. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/443.847
title: Offer competitive teacher compensation to support recruitment and retention of a strong and diverse teacher workforce
description: The report's framing principle is that "Offering competitive teacher compensation is an important part of the solution to recruit and retain a strong and diverse teacher workforce." It treats compensation conditions as background factors underlying state efforts to attract and retain well-prepared teachers, and presents the three indicators as signals of those conditions.
requirements: State and district salary schedules that position teacher pay competitively against other college-educated work in the local labor market
constraints: The report presents compensation as one part of the solution, not the whole solution, and its indicators vary by district within states
target_learning_goals: Recruiting and retaining a strong and diverse teacher workforce
examples: The report documents state wage competitiveness values mostly below parity with other college-educated workers, framing this as the wage condition underlying recruitment and retention efforts.
key_sources: Carver-Thomas, D., & Patrick, S. (2022). Understanding Teacher Compensation: A State-by-State Analysis. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/443.847

article_title: Building a Well-Qualified Transitional Kindergarten Workforce in California: Needs and Opportunities
citation: Melnick, H., García, E., & Leung-Gagné, M. (2022). Building a well-qualified transitional kindergarten workforce in California: Needs and opportunities. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/826.674
title: Candidate pools and credentialing pathways for building the TK teaching workforce
description: The report identifies four pools of potential TK teacher candidates: current Multiple Subject credential holders who can teach while earning 24 ECE units; early childhood educators with a bachelor's degree, for whom "possible pathways this group might take to a credential include teacher residencies, postbaccalaureate credentialing programs, and internship programs"; early educators without a bachelor's degree, suited to apprenticeship and degree pathway programs; and new candidates for assistant positions, including recent high school graduates and career changers, buildable through dual enrollment pathways. Table 4 and Figure 6 map these pools to pathways.
requirements: Lead TK teachers must hold a Multiple Subject Teaching Credential plus, by August 2023, 24 units of ECE coursework, a Child Development Teacher Permit, or equivalent experience
Assistant TK teachers need a high school degree and a basic-skills/pedagogical-knowledge assessment
constraints: New candidates without credentials would not fill lead TK teacher positions in the short term
The state does not currently have data on the number of TK teachers employed by districts
target_learners: high school students in dual enrollment
target_learning_goals: early childhood teaching credentialing
ECE coursework completion
bachelor's degree attainment for early educators
examples: LEAs can organize and fund cohorts of teachers to take ECE-focused coursework at partner universities
Integrated teacher education programs allow candidates to earn a bachelor's degree and teaching credential in 4 years building on community college coursework
key_sources: Melnick, H., García, E., & Leung-Gagné, M. (2022). Building a well-qualified transitional kindergarten workforce in California: Needs and opportunities. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/826.674

article_title: Educator Diversity State Profile: Michigan
citation: The Education Trust. (2022). Educator Diversity State Profile: Michigan. https://edtrust.org/educator-diversity/
title: Six-strategy state policy framework for increasing the racial diversity of the educator workforce
description: The brief organizes state policy conditions into six strategies: making educator diversity data visible and actionable, setting clear state and district goals, investing in educator preparation programs, targeting resources to districts and schools for recruiting a diverse workforce, investing in retention of teachers of color, and using federal COVID-related relief funds. Each strategy is rated on a three-level scale from "Meets all or most of the requirements within the goal" down to "Meets one or no requirements within the goal", with printed rating methodologies for each criterion. The framework is applied to score Michigan's actions.
requirements: State education agencies must collect and share timely, publicly available educator workforce data so stakeholders can make targeted workforce decisions
constraints: Ratings reflect policy conditions as documented for Michigan in 2022; the brief states efforts to recruit teachers of color are compromised when districts struggle to retain them
target_learning_goals: increasing student access to diverse educators
recruiting, preparing, and retaining teachers of color
examples: Michigan earned green ratings for posting school-level workforce demographics, its stakeholder-input Top 10 Strategic Education Plan, Grow Your Own funding, and a three-year induction and mentoring program; it earned red for lacking scholarships and loan forgiveness targeting students of color
key_sources: The Education Trust. (2022). Educator Diversity State Profile: Michigan. https://edtrust.org/educator-diversity/

article_title: Educator Diversity State Profile: Michigan
citation: The Education Trust. (2022). Educator Diversity State Profile: Michigan. https://edtrust.org/educator-diversity/
title: Michigan Diverse Educator Advisory Group and director of diversity, equity, and inclusion
description: Michigan established the Diverse Educator Advisory Group in 2021 "to provide recommendations for changes to educator workforce policy", with results under review by department staff. The Michigan Department of Education also hired a director of diversity, equity, and inclusion responsible for developing and supporting internal and external efforts and strategies fostering greater fairness and inclusion in the state's public schools. The brief rates this criterion green, meaning the state meets all or most requirements for a leadership structure examining educator diversity.
requirements: A task force or advisory group with access to leadership to examine, create, and monitor strategies to increase the racial diversity of the educator workforce
target_learning_goals: increasing the racial diversity of the educator workforce
examples: The advisory group's recommendations were being reviewed by department staff at the time of the brief; Ohio's 2018 taskforce brief is offered as another green example
key_sources: The Education Trust. (2022). Educator Diversity State Profile: Michigan. https://edtrust.org/educator-diversity/

article_title: Educator Diversity State Profile: Ohio
citation: Educator Diversity State Profile: Ohio. (2020). EdTrust. http://education.ohio.gov/getattachment/Topics/Teaching/Diversifying-Education-Profession-Taskforce-Recommendations.pdf.aspx?lang=en-US
title: Five-goal state policy framework for increasing the racial diversity of the educator workforce
description: The brief organizes state policy conditions into five goals: making educator diversity data visible and actionable, setting clear state and district goals, supporting preparation programs to recruit and prepare teachers of color, targeting resources to recruit and hire a diverse workforce, and improving working conditions and growth opportunities for teachers of color. Each goal is scored on a three-level rating scale (meets, partially meets, does not meet criteria) with printed rating methodologies, and applied to Ohio with example policies from other states.
requirements: State education agencies must collect and share useful and timely educator workforce data so stakeholders can set goals and chart a path forward
constraints: The framework addresses state-level policy conditions, not classroom instructional practice
target_learning_goals: increasing student access to strong and diverse educators
examples: Ohio was rated against each goal; for example, its Diversifying the Education Profession Taskforce earned a green rated as a best practice, while scholarship investment earned a red

article_title: Educator Diversity State Profile: Pennsylvania
citation: The Education Trust. (2022). Educator Diversity State Profile: Pennsylvania. https://edtrust.org/educator-diversity/
title: Pennsylvania's Aspiring to Educate program: multiple pathways into teaching with financial supports and district-preparation partnerships
description: Aspiring to Educate is Pennsylvania's Grow Your Own-style investment providing "multiple pathways to high school students, adults, paraprofessionals, and college students to become teachers" with financial supports for preparation. It includes a $500K investment in partnerships between districts and teacher preparation programs, and a "Youth Pathway for Aspiring Educators" giving high school juniors a dual-enrollment path into a partnering institution of higher education with upwards of 30 credits available. The brief rates the state green on GYO support, teacher academies/dual enrollment, and district-preparation partnerships.
requirements: State funding, guidance, and public support for Grow Your Own programs that attract candidates of color
target_learners: High school students, adults, paraprofessionals, and college students
target_learning_goals: Pathways into the teaching profession, particularly for aspiring teachers of color
examples: In June 2022, an additional $1 million of state PAsmart funds went to supporting the next Aspiring to Educate pilot with a focus on diversifying the STEM teacher pipeline.
key_sources: The Education Trust. (2022). Educator Diversity State Profile: Pennsylvania. https://edtrust.org/educator-diversity/

article_title: Educator Diversity State Profile: Texas
citation: The Education Trust. (2022). Texas Educator Diversity State Profile. https://edtrust.org/educator-diversity/
title: Six-strategy state policy framework for increasing the racial diversity of the educator workforce
description: The brief organizes state policy conditions for a diverse educator workforce into six strategies: making educator diversity data visible and actionable, setting clear state and district goals, investing in educator preparation programs, targeting resources to districts and schools for recruiting and hiring, investing in retention of teachers of color, and using federal COVID-related relief funds. States are rated on each strategy using a three-level scale from "Meets all or most of the requirements within the goal" down to "Meets one or no requirements within the goal," with printed criteria and rating methodologies for each sub-component. The framework is applied to rate Texas green, yellow, or red on each criterion.
requirements: State education agencies must collect and share useful and timely educator workforce data so stakeholders "can make targeted, strategic workforce decisions at the school, district, and state level."
Ratings depend on publicly available, disaggregated data and documented state actions matching printed criteria.
constraints: The framework addresses state-level policy conditions; it rates states against printed criteria rather than measuring the effects of the strategies on workforce diversity.
target_learners: All K-12 public school students in the state
target_learning_goals: Equitable student access to a racially and culturally diverse, high-quality educator workforce
examples: Texas is rated green for posting school-level workforce racial demographics and program-completer data, red for lacking a numeric diversity goal and anti-bias training for hiring managers, and green as a best practice for Grow Your Own program funding.
key_sources: The Education Trust. (2022). Texas Educator Diversity State Profile. https://edtrust.org/educator-diversity/

article_title: Educator Diversity State Profile: Tennessee
citation: Educator Diversity State Profile: Tennessee. (2020). EdTrust. https://edtrust.org/
title: Five-goal state policy framework for increasing the racial diversity of the educator workforce
description: The brief organizes state policy conditions for a diverse educator workforce into five goals: making educator diversity data visible and actionable, setting clear state and district goals for student access to strong and diverse educators, supporting preparation programs to recruit and prepare teachers of color, targeting resources to recruit and hire a diverse workforce, and improving working conditions and growth opportunities for teachers of color. Each goal is operationalized into criteria rated "Meets Criteria," "Partially Meets Criteria," or "Does Not Meet Criteria," so the framework doubles as a rating rubric applied state by state.
requirements: State education agencies must collect and analyze educator workforce data to set goals and chart a path forward
constraints: The framework addresses state-level policy conditions rather than classroom instructional practice

article_title: Preparing Transitional Kindergarten to 3rd Grade Educators through Teacher Residencies
citation: Cathy Yun. (2022). Preparing Transitional Kindergarten to 3rd Grade Educators Through Teacher Residencies. Learning Policy Institute & EDPREPLAB. https://doi.org/10.54300/139.797
title: Common features of a high-quality teacher residency
description: The brief enumerates characteristics that research has identified in high-quality teacher residency programs: residencies "consist of strong partnerships between school districts, universities, and sometimes other organizations," tightly integrate coursework with classroom practice, require a full year of residency teaching alongside an accomplished mentor teacher, recruit diverse candidates for specific district needs, provide financial support in exchange for a teaching commitment, place cohorts in teaching schools modeling evidence-based practices, and offer ongoing mentoring for graduates. The brief presents these features as making early childhood-focused residencies part of a multipronged solution for preparing qualified, diverse teachers.
requirements: Strong district–university partnerships
Yearlong clinical experience with an accomplished mentor teacher
Financial supports for residents
target_learners: Teacher residency candidates preparing for TK–3 or elementary credentials
target_learning_goals: Preparation of credentialed teachers with early childhood expertise
examples: Fresno Unified's TK–3 residency and UCLA's IMPACT ECE program both exhibited these features, including paid apprenticeships, integrated coursework, and cohort placement in partner schools.
key_sources: Cathy Yun. (2022). Preparing Transitional Kindergarten to 3rd Grade Educators Through Teacher Residencies. Learning Policy Institute & EDPREPLAB. https://doi.org/10.54300/139.797

article_title: Preparing Transitional Kindergarten to 3rd Grade Educators through Teacher Residencies
citation: Cathy Yun. (2022). Preparing Transitional Kindergarten to 3rd Grade Educators Through Teacher Residencies. Learning Policy Institute & EDPREPLAB. https://doi.org/10.54300/139.797
title: Fresno TK–3 Teacher Residency Program
description: An 18-month residency (2017–2019) within Fresno Unified's workforce pipeline, run with California State University, Fresno, leading to a Multiple Subject credential and a master's degree in curriculum and instruction. The program focused on "early literacy, developmentally appropriate practices, and social and emotional learning" plus family engagement, with all credential coursework co-taught by district leaders paired with university faculty and quarterly curriculum meetings used to redesign syllabi around a developmental focus. Residents received an $11,000 stipend, clustered school-site placements, and courses held at a school site near their clinical placements.
requirements: District–university co-instruction of all credential coursework
Federal TQP grant funding for the resident stipend
constraints: The stipend was not enough to fully cover residents' cost of living; some residents substituted one day a week to supplement income
target_learners: Recent college graduates, career changers, and uncertified educators seeking TK–3 credentials
target_learning_goals: Developmentally appropriate pedagogy, early literacy, STEM integration, and social-emotional learning for TK–3
examples: Residents applied the project approach, investigated puzzles of practice, and taught literacy skills within content areas using informational text as starting points for science, social studies, or fine arts explorations.
key_sources: Cathy Yun. (2022). Preparing Transitional Kindergarten to 3rd Grade Educators Through Teacher Residencies. Learning Policy Institute & EDPREPLAB. https://doi.org/10.54300/139.797

article_title: Preparing Transitional Kindergarten to 3rd Grade Educators through Teacher Residencies
citation: Cathy Yun. (2022). Preparing Transitional Kindergarten to 3rd Grade Educators Through Teacher Residencies. Learning Policy Institute & EDPREPLAB. https://doi.org/10.54300/139.797
title: UCLA IMPACT ECE/Multiple Subject Program
description: A social justice–focused urban teacher residency run by LAUSD and UCLA Center X (2010–2014), through which candidates earned a Child Development Master Teacher Permit, Multiple Subject certification, and a Master of Education degree in 18 months. It began with a weeklong institute on child development and inclusion, required the eight early childhood core courses (the CAP 8) for the child development permit, and included extensive clinical placements in early childhood settings (6 hours a day, 4 days a week) and elementary classrooms (approximately 30 hours per week). Residents received a $10,000 fellowship; mentors received a $3,000 stipend and monthly "Methods With Mentors" professional development organized around UCLA's five dimensions of mentoring quality.
requirements: Completion of the CAP 8 early childhood core courses for the child development permit
Mentor selection and matching based on effective teaching and program values
constraints: The program required a large number of courses because residents pursued two certifications and a master's degree; the director noted integrating ECE and multiple subject courses would be a value add
target_learners: Candidates interested in early childhood education in traditionally underserved urban communities
target_learning_goals: Child development expertise, developmentally appropriate practice, social justice–oriented instruction, and inquiry-based reflective practice
examples: Residents' inquiries addressed puzzles of practice such as creating environments in which families feel welcome, differentiating instruction, and implementing classroom management strategies.
key_sources: Cathy Yun. (2022). Preparing Transitional Kindergarten to 3rd Grade Educators Through Teacher Residencies. Learning Policy Institute & EDPREPLAB. https://doi.org/10.54300/139.797

article_title: Faculty Diversity and Student Success Go Hand in Hand, so Why Are University Faculties so White?
citation: Jinann Bitar, Gabriel Montague, Lauren Ilano. (2022). Faculty Diversity and Student Success Go Hand in Hand, So Why Are University Faculties So White? The Education Trust. https://edtrust.org
title: Four-metric faculty equity grading framework (diversity relative to students, hiring equity, tenure equity, change over time)
description: The report develops a four-metric framework for auditing faculty racial equity at individual institutions. Metrics 1-3 produce 0-100 scores converted to letter grades: faculty diversity relative to student diversity, equity in tenure-track versus contingent hiring, and equity in tenure distribution. Metric 4 measures percentage point change in faculty representation between 2005 and 2020. The framework is designed so advocates can "use these metrics and findings to see what's happening at institutions and push for change."
requirements: Institutional IPEDS faculty survey completion, a tenure system, and institutionally reported enrollment and staff data
constraints: The diversity metric "does not take their appointment status — i.e., whether they are contingent or tenure track — into account"; IPEDS data limits analysis of other faculty of color groups
target_learning_goals: increasing Black and Latino faculty representation
improving college completion for students of color
examples: Bluefield State College scored 99 (A) on Black faculty diversity because 9.5% of faculty were Black versus 9.6% of students; Ball State scored 105 (A) on Latino hiring equity
key_sources: Jinann Bitar, Gabriel Montague, Lauren Ilano. (2022). Faculty Diversity and Student Success Go Hand in Hand, So Why Are University Faculties So White? The Education Trust. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED626440

article_title: Faculty Diversity and Student Success Go Hand in Hand, so Why Are University Faculties so White?
citation: Jinann Bitar, Gabriel Montague, Lauren Ilano. (2022). Faculty Diversity and Student Success Go Hand in Hand, So Why Are University Faculties So White? The Education Trust. https://edtrust.org
title: Faculty diversity pipeline programs (State Doctoral Scholars Program, STRIDE, California Pre-Doctoral Program)
description: The report profiles three initiatives it identifies as promising practices for diversifying the professoriate. The Southern Regional Education Board's State Doctoral Scholars Program provides "tailored faculty mentoring, networking, and financial support throughout their doctoral journey" and has helped more than 1,100 underrepresented students earn a Ph.D., with an 83% participant graduation rate. FIU's STRIDE offers mandatory best-practice workshops for hiring and promotion committees. The California Pre-Doctoral Program funds disadvantaged juniors, seniors, and graduate students for doctoral preparation, including GRE preparation and faculty mentoring.
requirements: Funding sources (e.g., NSF ADVANCE grants, state system funding) and institutional commitment to mentoring and financial support for underrepresented students
constraints: The report describes these as promising practices with output metrics, not as rigorously evaluated causal interventions
target_learners: undergraduate and graduate students facing economic or educational disadvantages
target_learning_goals: earning a Ph.D. and entering faculty careers
reducing bias in faculty hiring
building the professoriate pipeline for students of color
examples: State Doctoral Scholars Program participants finish their Ph.D.s 2-5 years ahead of the national average; 80% of graduates are currently faculty, administrators, or postdoctoral researchers in the U.S.
key_sources: Jinann Bitar, Gabriel Montague, Lauren Ilano. (2022). Faculty Diversity and Student Success Go Hand in Hand, So Why Are University Faculties So White? The Education Trust. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED626440

article_title: How States Can Use American Rescue Plan Funding and Federal Grants to Support Teacher Diversity
citation: The Education Trust. (2022). How States Can Use American Rescue Plan Funding and Federal Grants to Support Teacher Diversity. EdTrust.org. https://edtrust.org
title: State ESSER spending on teacher diversity falls into three categories: educator preparation, recruitment, and retention
description: The Education Trust collected state-level data on ESSER fund use and organized it into a three-part framework: "Supporting educator preparation programs that attract and support candidates of color," developing or implementing programs to recruit teachers of color, and developing or implementing programs to retain teachers of color. The brief uses this taxonomy to present state promising practices in each category.
requirements: States must have ESSER set-aside funds available through early 2025 to establish or supplement such programming
constraints: ESSER funds are set to expire in early 2025, limiting the time horizon of these investments
target_learning_goals: Diversifying the teacher workforce to improve equitable outcomes for all students
examples: Georgia used $5 million for fees, books, and certification preparation in an alternative certification program; Maryland, Texas, Missouri, Nevada, Georgia, and Tennessee funded Grow Your Own programs; Colorado, Illinois, Louisiana, Mississippi, Missouri, and Texas funded teacher residency programs
key_sources: The Education Trust. (2022). How States Can Use American Rescue Plan Funding and Federal Grants to Support Teacher Diversity. EdTrust.org. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED626513

article_title: How States Can Use American Rescue Plan Funding and Federal Grants to Support Teacher Diversity
citation: The Education Trust. (2022). How States Can Use American Rescue Plan Funding and Federal Grants to Support Teacher Diversity. EdTrust.org. https://edtrust.org
title: Augustus F. Hawkins Center for Excellence grant program for teacher preparation at HBCUs, minority-serving institutions, and tribal colleges
description: The Hawkins Center for Excellence program "provides competitive grants to teacher preparation programs at historically Black colleges and universities (HBCUs), minority-serving institutions, and tribal colleges and universities." Congress appropriated $8 million for Hawkins grants in 2022, the first funding since the program's creation in 2008. Required grant uses include inclusive pedagogical practices and sustained, high-quality preservice clinical experiences.
requirements: Competitive grant application; first FY23 funding round applications were invited in August 2022
constraints: The Education Trust requested at least $40 million for fiscal year 2023, implying current appropriations fall short of that ask
target_learners: Teacher candidates at HBCUs, minority-serving institutions, and tribal colleges
target_learning_goals: Preparing diverse educators through inclusive, clinically grounded teacher preparation
examples: In 2022 Congress appropriated $8 million, the first Hawkins funding since the program's creation in 2008
