article_title: Authentic Student Work in College Admissions: Lessons from the Ross School of Business
citation: Willis, L., & Martinez, M. R. (2022). Authentic student work in college admissions: Lessons from the Ross School of Business. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/756.774
title: Ross Admissions Portfolio (Business Case Discussion + Artifact)
description: A required student-created portfolio added to the Ross School of Business BBA first-year application in fall 2016. Per the report, "The Ross Admissions Portfolio consists of two components: a Business Case Discussion and an Artifact." The Business Case Discussion is a 500-word essay asking applicants to identify and solve a personally meaningful business-related issue; the Artifact is a 250-word description accompanying multimedia work showing learning applied in or beyond school. Every first-year BBA applicant completes it alongside University of Michigan application materials.
requirements: Aligned to central admission processes without altering University of Michigan deadlines or timelines
Technological capacity (SlideRoom) to accept and transfer multimedia submissions
Rubrics with clear criteria and detailed performance indicators
Trained, calibrated application readers
constraints: Required of all first-year BBA applicants, adding preparation time students estimated at 1 to 2 weeks
Open-ended prompts with no single right way to craft a successful portfolio
target_learners: High school seniors applying to the undergraduate BBA program
target_learning_goals: Demonstrating business mindsets such as problem definition and problem-solving
Demonstrating applied learning and college-success skills such as persistence and collaboration
examples: In the first implementation year the Ross School received nearly 5,000 Artifacts, including documents, images, videos, and audio files
key_sources: Willis, L., & Martinez, M. R. (2022). Authentic student work in college admissions: Lessons from the Ross School of Business. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/756.774

article_title: Authentic Student Work in College Admissions: Lessons from the Ross School of Business
citation: Willis, L., & Martinez, M. R. (2022). Authentic student work in college admissions: Lessons from the Ross School of Business. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/756.774
title: Six-step implementation process for an admissions portfolio review system
description: The report documents the process the Ross Undergraduate Admissions team used to build and run portfolio review: align the portfolio to central admission processes, establish technological capacity, develop rubrics, build reader capacity, conduct outreach, and iterate. Rubrics align with "skills and mindsets students need to flourish in the Ross program and community—including critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, and curiosity." The pattern balances a standard review's efficiency with qualitative portfolio depth inside existing university timelines.
requirements: Rubrics with clear criteria and detailed performance indicators for reliable qualitative review
A technology platform (SlideRoom) to accept and transfer media submissions
A hired team of 20 to 25 short-term contractual professional readers
constraints: Implemented within the University of Michigan's existing application deadlines, review timeline, and decision release, avoiding university-wide change
target_learning_goals: Reliable evaluation of applicants' critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, and curiosity
examples: In year one (2016), every submission was reviewed by the Ross Admissions Review Committee to determine whether submissions met the goals and identify needed guidance adjustments
key_sources: Willis, L., & Martinez, M. R. (2022). Authentic student work in college admissions: Lessons from the Ross School of Business. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/756.774

article_title: Inequitable Opportunity to Learn: Access to Advanced Mathematics and Science Courses
citation: Leung, M., Cardichon, J., Scott, C., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2020). Inequitable opportunity to learn: Access to advanced mathematics and science courses. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/crdc-course-access
title: Civil Rights Data Collection (CRDC) as a source for measuring school-level access to advanced courses
description: The Civil Rights Data Collection is a biennial dataset from the U.S. Department of Education's Office for Civil Rights, collected "every 2 years from all public schools and school districts in the United States since 1968." The 2017-18 dataset covers "17,604 school districts, 97,632 schools, and 50.9 million students." The report uses it, combined with the Common Core of Data, to compare advanced course offerings across school demographic quintiles at national and state levels.
requirements: School-level demographic data (percentage of students of color; free or reduced-price lunch eligibility) to sort schools into comparison quintiles
constraints: Most data are self-reported by local education agencies, so there may be discrepancies with other sources
Data are collected at the school level and cannot identify disparities at the student level within each school
target_learning_goals: Measuring equitable access to advanced mathematics and science curricula
examples: The report's analysis sample comprised 14,823 high schools offering all four grade levels 9 through 12, serving over 12.7 million students.
key_sources: Leung, M., Cardichon, J., Scott, C., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2020). Inequitable opportunity to learn: Access to advanced mathematics and science courses. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/crdc-course-access

article_title: 5 Questions to Ask District and School Leaders about Access to Advanced STEM Coursework in High School
citation: The Education Trust; Equal Opportunity Schools. (2023). 5 Questions to Ask District and School Leaders About Access to Advanced STEM Coursework in High School. https://edtrust.org
title: EOS Student Insight Card
description: The Student Insight Card is Equal Opportunity Schools' flagship tool for identifying students for advanced coursework. It "includes data about students’ interests and aspirations — such as expressed desire to enroll, student motivation, and recommendations from trusted school staff" so this data factors into academic opportunity and enrollment decisions. EOS states it "transforms the definition of readiness schools use to determine access to advanced courses."
requirements: Schools must factor the card's interest, motivation, and trusted-staff-recommendation data into enrollment decisions about academic opportunity
target_learners: Black and Latino high school students
target_learning_goals: Access to and success in advanced STEM coursework
examples: The brief recommends the card as a multiple-measures identification tool so students are not gated by a single test score or teacher recommendation
key_sources: The Education Trust; Equal Opportunity Schools. (2023). 5 Questions to Ask District and School Leaders About Access to Advanced STEM Coursework in High School. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED627984

article_title: 5 Questions to Ask District and School Leaders about Access to Advanced STEM Coursework in High School
citation: The Education Trust; Equal Opportunity Schools. (2023). 5 Questions to Ask District and School Leaders About Access to Advanced STEM Coursework in High School. https://edtrust.org
title: EOS Opportunity Chart
description: The EOS Opportunity Chart is a data tool that "allows schools and districts to see and report disaggregated course enrollments relative to the demographics of their school population to see where gaps exist." It supports the brief's first question about goals and monitoring data, enabling regular public reporting of seats, enrollment, and success in advanced courses across school levels.
requirements: Regular, public reports with detailed, disaggregated data around seats, enrollment, and success in advanced courses
target_learners: Black and Latino students across elementary, middle, and high school
target_learning_goals: Monitoring equitable access to advanced coursework
examples: The brief lists the Opportunity Chart under look-fors for leaders' goals and progress-monitoring data on advanced course access

article_title: Parent PLUS Loans Are a Double-Edged Sword for Black Borrowers
citation: Victoria Jackson, Brittani Williams, and Jalil B. Mustaffa. (2023). Parent PLUS Loans Are a Double-Edged Sword for Black Borrowers. The Education Trust. https://edtrust.org/resource/parent-plus-loans-are-a-double-edged-sword-for-black-borrowers
title: National Black Student Debt Study
description: The National Black Student Debt Study is the mixed-methods research project underlying this brief and the broader #BlackStudentDebt series, led by Jalil B. Mustaffa with the Equity Research Cooperative. The brief describes it as including "a survey of nearly 1,300 Black borrowers and in-depth interviews with 100 borrowers." This brief, the fourth in a series, combines the study's qualitative data and participant quotes (under pseudonyms at participants' request) with federal data to examine Black parents' Parent PLUS borrowing.
requirements: Participants' names are replaced with pseudonyms at their request, so quotes are anonymized in publication.
constraints: The study covers Black borrowers in the United States; this brief focuses specifically on parents holding Parent PLUS loans rather than all borrower experiences.
target_learners: Black undergraduate students and their parents financing college
target_learning_goals: Understanding how financing structures shape Black families' access to and persistence in higher education
examples: The brief quotes participants such as Marcus, Noelle, Marissa, Jade, and Walter describing room-and-board shortfalls, deferment cycles, and postponed retirement.
key_sources: Victoria Jackson, Brittani Williams, and Jalil B. Mustaffa. (2023). Parent PLUS Loans Are a Double-Edged Sword for Black Borrowers. The Education Trust. https://edtrust.org/resource/parent-plus-loans-are-a-double-edged-sword-for-black-borrowers

article_title: Creating Safer Schools: A Case Study
citation: Duchesneau, N., & Zapata, M. (2023). Creating Safer Schools: A Case Study. The Education Trust. https://edtrust.org
title: Five-type spectrum of school safety approaches, from school-to-prison pipeline schools to school-to-possibility pipeline schools
description: The report's authors categorize schools on a five-point spectrum of safety approaches. At one end, "School-to-prison pipeline schools" are "hardened schools with a high emphasis on physical security, no guardrails to prevent the harm that physical security can cause, and little to no attention on student well-being." Intermediate types add guardrails and scale up well-being practices while scaling down physical security. The ultimate goal, school-to-possibility pipeline schools, have fully adopted practices addressing root causes of violence and removed physical security. Leaders are advised to locate their schools on the spectrum and plan next steps toward the goal.
requirements: Leaders must first assess where their school or district currently stands on the spectrum in terms of current policies before planning next steps
constraints: The spectrum is a framework proposed by the report's authors based on this two-district case study and other research, not a validated measurement instrument
target_learners: students in urban districts serving majority Black, Latino, and/or low-income populations
target_learning_goals: creating safe, inclusive learning environments that support students' social, emotional, and academic development
examples: The report situates both case-study districts as retaining physical security while adopting well-being practices, placing them in intermediate spectrum categories rather than at the school-to-possibility end
key_sources: Duchesneau, N., & Zapata, M. (2023). Creating Safer Schools: A Case Study. The Education Trust. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED641760

article_title: Universal Prekindergarten Expansion in California: Progress and Opportunities
citation: Wang, V., Leung-Gagné, M., Melnick, H., & Wechsler, M. E. (2024). Universal prekindergarten expansion in California: Progress and opportunities. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/597.103
title: California universal prekindergarten mixed-delivery system and the 2022–23 UPK Planning and Implementation Grant Survey
description: California's UPK system is a mixed-delivery early learning arrangement comprising transitional kindergarten (TK), the California State Preschool Program (CSPP), Head Start, and locally funded early learning programs. The report states "California UPk includes several early learning programs, including transitional kindergarten (Tk), the California State Preschool Program (CSPP), Head Start, and locally funded early learning programs," with TK the only program that is free and universally available as part of the public school system and CSPP serving income-eligible 3- and 4-year-olds. Implementation is supported by the Universal Prekindergarten Planning and Implementation Grant (about $200 million in 2021 plus $300 million added in 2022), and monitored through the California Department of Education's August 2023 survey of all grant recipients, analyzed here for 1,384 LEAs (95% of public school districts and 65% of charter schools serving elementary grades).
requirements: All public LEAs are required to offer TK; offering CSPP and Head Start and partnering with community-based providers is encouraged but not required

TK curriculum must align with the California Preschool Learning Foundations, and state-funded TK classes must meet staffing requirements including the 2025–26 credential and early childhood coursework requirements
constraints: TK eligibility expands gradually, with all 4-year-olds eligible only by the 2025–26 school year
The report's findings describe the 2022–23 school year as captured in one survey administration
target_learners: Multilingual learners and students with disabilities in early learning programs
target_learning_goals: Universal access to prekindergarten education
School readiness across developmental domains
Developmentally appropriate early learning instruction
examples: In 2022–23, 25% of LEAs (343) operated a CSPP contract; 19% applied to expand their existing contract and 12% planned to apply in future years
The 2021 grant allocated $200 million to all LEAs serving kindergarteners, and the 2022 budget added another $300 million with funds released in 2023
The survey analyzed responses from 1,384 LEAs, representing 817 of 862 public school districts and 567 of 875 charter schools offering elementary grades
key_sources: Wang, V., Leung-Gagné, M., Melnick, H., & Wechsler, M. E. (2024). Universal prekindergarten expansion in California: Progress and opportunities. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/597.103

article_title: A Vision for Equitable Pathways: Enhancing Support and Innovation in College and Career Counseling
citation: Rebeca Shackleford and Kristen Hengtgen. (2024). A Vision for Equitable Pathways: Enhancing Support and Innovation in College and Career Counseling. EdTrust/All4Ed. https://edtrust.org
title: Ideal pathways system: intentional, supported trajectories with consistent guidance from middle school through adulthood
description: The brief defines pathways as "the full universe of intentional and supported trajectories that every learner understands and participates in as they move from adolescence through adulthood." The framework spans CTE, work-based learning including internships and apprenticeships, early postsecondary opportunities (advanced coursework, AP, IB, dual enrollment, early college), and postsecondary programs leading to industry-recognized credentials or degrees. Learners receive "consistent, knowledgeable guidance, beginning in middle school, from well-qualified counselors and navigators" and are supported over time to find, experience, and move among pathways aligned with their desired social, economic, and personal outcomes.
requirements: Well-qualified counselors and navigators with knowledge of the full range of options and capacity to connect students to opportunities
Guidance beginning in middle school and continuing through transitions
constraints: The current patchwork of programs and funding streams is described as inadequate to address the scale and urgency of the challenge
target_learners: Students ages 16-24, particularly low-income, first-generation students and students of color
target_learning_goals: College and career navigation and informed pathway choice
examples: The brief's convening of national partners in fall 2023 produced this collective definition to guide federal policy recommendations
key_sources: Rebeca Shackleford and Kristen Hengtgen. (2024). A Vision for Equitable Pathways: Enhancing Support and Innovation in College and Career Counseling. EdTrust/All4Ed. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED670956

article_title: A Vision for Equitable Pathways: Enhancing Support and Innovation in College and Career Counseling
citation: Rebeca Shackleford and Kristen Hengtgen. (2024). A Vision for Equitable Pathways: Enhancing Support and Innovation in College and Career Counseling. EdTrust/All4Ed. https://edtrust.org
title: Five elements of an ideal pathways system: clear choices, smart start, access for all, guided beginnings, final prep
description: The brief enumerates five essential elements an ideal pathways system ensures for students and families: "1. Clear choices: a clear understanding of all their options 2. A smart start: early outreach before entering high school 3. Access for all: information that is accessible and in multiple formats 4. Guided beginnings: regular touchpoints with a navigator 5. Final prep: dedicated and targeted support in high school." Each element is paired with promising state practices, such as Indiana's College Core planning tool, Connecticut's Student Success Plans, DCPS language access, Illinois' PaCE Framework, and Pinellas County college and career centers.
requirements: Dedicated pathways counselors in every school to connect students to these systems
Federal investment at scale, since implementation varies across states and underfunded districts struggle to offer additional resources
constraints: The brief notes other important elements exist (greater ROI, long-term economic mobility, employers seeing qualified employees) but focuses on the five navigation and counseling elements
target_learners: High school students and their families, particularly students of color and students from low-income backgrounds
target_learning_goals: Understanding and accessing college and career pathway options
examples: Connecticut requires individualized Student Success Plans starting in sixth grade; Illinois' PaCE Framework organizes career exploration, postsecondary preparation, and financial aid literacy
key_sources: Rebeca Shackleford and Kristen Hengtgen. (2024). A Vision for Equitable Pathways: Enhancing Support and Innovation in College and Career Counseling. EdTrust/All4Ed. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED670956

article_title: A Vision for Equitable Pathways: Enhancing Support and Innovation in College and Career Counseling
citation: Rebeca Shackleford and Kristen Hengtgen. (2024). A Vision for Equitable Pathways: Enhancing Support and Innovation in College and Career Counseling. EdTrust/All4Ed. https://edtrust.org
title: Pathways counselors: highly trained specialists providing personalized navigation support alongside grade-level counselors
description: The brief calls for "the creation and support of highly trained pathways counselors who can work in conjunction with grade-level school counselors and educators, but whose sole job is to provide students with a clear understanding of their options and outcomes; provide personalized, regular touchpoints to help students stay on track; and offer dedicated, targeted support on students' college and career journeys." The rationale is that it is nearly impossible for one school counselor to serve as general practitioner, provide grade-level supports, fulfill administrative tasks, offer mental health support, and be trained on all pathways. The brief also proposes national training and certification for this role.
requirements: Sufficient funds and clear expectations for districts to hire and support enough navigators
Professional learning, supports, and tools so school personnel can prepare all students for a high-quality pathways journey
constraints: The brief states solving the school counselor shortage is not possible anytime soon, motivating the specialist role
target_learners: High school students, especially traditionally underserved students
target_learning_goals: Clear understanding of college and career options and outcomes; staying on track toward postsecondary goals
examples: Pinellas County Schools staff every high school with a college and career center with a dedicated coordinator and trained volunteers, freeing counselors for more substantive conversations
key_sources: Rebeca Shackleford and Kristen Hengtgen. (2024). A Vision for Equitable Pathways: Enhancing Support and Innovation in College and Career Counseling. EdTrust/All4Ed. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED670956

article_title: A Vision for Equitable Pathways: Enhancing Support and Innovation in College and Career Counseling
citation: Rebeca Shackleford and Kristen Hengtgen. (2024). A Vision for Equitable Pathways: Enhancing Support and Innovation in College and Career Counseling. EdTrust/All4Ed. https://edtrust.org
title: Indiana College Core and My College Core planning tool for transferable college credits in high school
description: The Indiana College Core "lets students earn up to 30 college credits while in high school at low or no cost via Advanced Placement, International Baccalaureate, or dual enrollment/dual credit courses, and credits are easily transferable across all of Indiana's public postsecondary institutions." An accompanying interactive planning tool, My College Core, helps students plan and track coursework toward the Core and serves as a centralized resource with financial aid and transfer information. Students can share plans with school counselors, who help schedule classes aligned with their goals.
requirements: School counselor involvement to help students schedule classes and understand what they need to take
target_learners: Indiana high school students planning college coursework
target_learning_goals: Planning and completing transferable college-level coursework in high school
examples: The My College Core tool, in the brief's words, takes some of the guesswork out of individualized planning and gives families and counselors access to information about college-level coursework
key_sources: Rebeca Shackleford and Kristen Hengtgen. (2024). A Vision for Equitable Pathways: Enhancing Support and Innovation in College and Career Counseling. EdTrust/All4Ed. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED670956

article_title: Investing in Texas Teacher Preparation: Key Features of Successful Residency Programs
citation: Wojcikiewicz, S. K., & Wei, W. (2024). Investing in Texas teacher preparation: Key features of successful residency programs [Brief]. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/texas-teacher-preparation-brief
title: Six common features of high-quality teacher residencies: yearlong clinical experience, practice-based coursework, EPP–district partnerships, trained mentors, site coordinators, and stipends
description: Texas has used state guidance, grant provisions, and regulatory changes to incentivize residency programs to adopt a set of common features, "six of which stand out in contributing to quality preparation": a yearlong clinical experience, integrated practice-based coursework, partnerships between preparation programs and school districts, trained and experienced mentor teachers, clinical faculty site coordinators, and resident stipends. The features are based on the state's definition of a high-quality residency in which "the teacher candidate is paired with an experienced, highly effective mentor teacher for a full year of clinical training and co-teaching in a K–12 classroom."
requirements: State guidance, grant provisions, and administrative code changes that incentivize programs to adopt the features
constraints: The features are most difficult to establish and sustain in communities with higher needs, including smaller, under-resourced, and more rural districts
target_learning_goals: classroom teaching practice
professional readiness for teaching
examples: TCLAS-funded EPP–district partnerships launched with residency programs already meeting the state's vetted residency definition
key_sources: Wojcikiewicz, S. K., & Wei, W. (2024). Investing in Texas teacher preparation: Key features of successful residency programs [Brief]. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/texas-teacher-preparation-brief

article_title: Investing in Texas Teacher Preparation: Key Features of Successful Residency Programs
citation: Wojcikiewicz, S. K., & Wei, W. (2024). Investing in Texas teacher preparation: Key features of successful residency programs [Brief]. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/texas-teacher-preparation-brief
title: TCLAS High-Quality, Sustainable Residency Program grant
description: Launched in 2021 as part of the $1.4 billion Texas COVID Learning Acceleration Supports initiative underwritten by federal COVID-19 relief funds, the program "provided grant funding for paid placements supporting more than 2,100 residents at 85 school districts, offered in partnership with state-approved EPPs." Districts were required to partner with state-designated Vetted Teacher Residency programs. The grant also provided technical assistance for districts to adopt strategic staffing models intended to sustain paid residencies after grant funding ended in 2024.
requirements: Districts must partner with a state-designated Vetted Teacher Residency program to apply for funding
constraints: Grant funding ended in 2024, and some districts have struggled to maintain residency funding after grants ended
target_learning_goals: clinically intensive teacher preparation
examples: Grant-funded districts focused on strengthening partnerships, collaborative planning and governance, and adopting strategic staffing changes in K–12 schools
key_sources: Wojcikiewicz, S. K., & Wei, W. (2024). Investing in Texas teacher preparation: Key features of successful residency programs [Brief]. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/texas-teacher-preparation-brief

article_title: Investing in Texas Teacher Preparation: Key Features of Successful Residency Programs
citation: Wojcikiewicz, S. K., & Wei, W. (2024). Investing in Texas teacher preparation: Key features of successful residency programs [Brief]. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/texas-teacher-preparation-brief
title: Residency clinical faculty site coordinator role
description: The site coordinator is a clinical faculty role at residency partner educator preparation programs, described by US PREP as a "critical linchpin" to transformed residencies and much expanded compared to typical clinical field supervisor assignments. Beyond observing and coaching candidates, site coordinators provide mentor training and professional development, facilitate EPP–district partnership governance meetings, and compile and present resident clinical performance data to inform partnership improvement. As one US PREP staff member noted, "They're engaged with all stakeholders. They're the one responsible for gathering the data and supporting residents, mentors, and principals during the actual yearlong residency."
requirements: Site coordinators are EPP faculty embedded in school districts to work directly with mentor teachers, school leaders, and district administrators
target_learning_goals: clinical practice development
partnership governance and continuous improvement
examples: In TCLAS-supported partnerships, site coordinators participated in regular professional development sessions featuring data-driven discussions of resident progress
key_sources: Wojcikiewicz, S. K., & Wei, W. (2024). Investing in Texas teacher preparation: Key features of successful residency programs [Brief]. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/texas-teacher-preparation-brief

article_title: Investing in Texas Teacher Preparation: Key Features of Successful Residency Programs
citation: Wojcikiewicz, S. K., & Wei, W. (2024). Investing in Texas teacher preparation: Key features of successful residency programs [Brief]. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/texas-teacher-preparation-brief
title: Provide resident stipends covering living expenses so candidates can fully participate in yearlong clinical placements
description: Paid residency stipends intended to cover living expenses are an essential feature of Texas residencies. "Set by the TCLAS grant program at $20,000 per resident, stipends were aimed at eliminating the need for residents to take outside jobs during the yearlong clinical placement." Stipends made residencies a realistic option for a broader pool of candidates, and current residents consistently shared they could only participate because of the stipends. Implementing residencies without stipends may create barriers to full resident participation.
requirements: Stipend levels sufficient to eliminate the need for residents to take outside jobs during the clinical year
constraints: Implementation of residencies without stipends may create barriers to full resident participation in local contexts
target_learning_goals: full participation in yearlong immersive clinical placements
examples: TCLAS set stipends at $20,000 per resident to support living expenses during the yearlong placement
key_sources: Wojcikiewicz, S. K., & Wei, W. (2024). Investing in Texas teacher preparation: Key features of successful residency programs [Brief]. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/texas-teacher-preparation-brief

article_title: Investing in Texas Teacher Preparation: Key Features of Successful Residency Programs
citation: Wojcikiewicz, S. K., & Wei, W. (2024). Investing in Texas teacher preparation: Key features of successful residency programs [Brief]. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/texas-teacher-preparation-brief
title: Structure EPP–district partnerships around shared governance with joint data-informed decision-making
description: Texas interwove responsibility for teacher preparation across educator preparation programs (EPPs) and districts, with grants built on the assumption that the two work in tandem. As the TEA described, "In high-quality teacher residency models, the EPP and [district] have shared ownership over the preparation, support, and success of the teacher resident." Partnership requirements were instantiated through shared governance meetings that specified attendance by both parties, identified topics for collaborative planning, and called for joint data-informed decision-making, creating feedback loops for continuous improvement.
requirements: Shared governance meetings attended by both EPP and district personnel, with joint data-informed decision-making
target_learning_goals: coherent, contextually aligned teacher preparation
examples: Shared governance enabled EPPs to iterate on coursework, revisit assignments, and improve alignment to district contexts after practice-based redesigns
key_sources: Wojcikiewicz, S. K., & Wei, W. (2024). Investing in Texas teacher preparation: Key features of successful residency programs [Brief]. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/texas-teacher-preparation-brief

article_title: Humanizing Teacher Preparation: Claremont Graduate University's Teacher Residency
citation: Yun, C., & Fitz, J. (2025). Humanizing teacher preparation: Claremont Graduate University's teacher residency. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/338.812
title: Claremont Critical Social Justice Teaching Competencies and classroom ecology framework with nine domains
description: Claremont's Teacher Education Program uses its Critical Social Justice Teaching Competencies as the foundation for coursework and clinical programming, so that every assignment and class develops skills to interrupt deficit schooling. The framework centers relationships and interactions between and among students and teachers, emphasizing humanizing classroom experiences. The competencies explicitly address nine domains: "(1) philosophy of education, (2) pedagogy, (3) science of learning (data-driven instruction), (4) socio-emotional learning and experience, (5) funds of knowledge, (6) school climate and culture, (7) community and cultural wealth, (8) socio-political identity, and (9) worldview and global perspectives." Faculty operationalize the stance through concrete, observable teaching practices.
requirements: Competencies must be integrated into all courses, clinical observations, resident self-reflection, and evaluations rather than confined to one course
constraints: Applies to Claremont's own teacher preparation program; the report does not test the framework's effects experimentally
target_learners: teacher preparation candidates (residents) earning preliminary California credentials
target_learning_goals: critical social justice teaching practices
culturally and linguistically responsive pedagogy
humanizing classroom relationships
examples: The program aligned clinical observations, resident self-reflection, and evaluations with the competencies and centered the work of diverse scholars as course texts
key_sources: Yun, C., & Fitz, J. (2025). Humanizing teacher preparation: Claremont Graduate University's teacher residency. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/338.812

article_title: Humanizing Teacher Preparation: Claremont Graduate University's Teacher Residency
citation: Yun, C., & Fitz, J. (2025). Humanizing teacher preparation: Claremont Graduate University's teacher residency. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/338.812
title: Four-step reflection and analysis process for examining positionality, assumptions, and reimagining practice
description: TLP I teaches residents a four-step process for reflection and analysis that they apply throughout the program. The steps are: "1. Define the concept or artifact (what you are talking/thinking about). 2. Consider: What are the underlying values and assumptions... 3. Consider: Who or what is included or excluded in those assumptions and values? 4. How can you reimagine or reenvision it." Residents reported that reflecting on positionality and implicit biases also builds community, with one resident noting team-building discussion "makes us feel bound together in community."
requirements: Instructors guide residents in reflecting on their own school experiences and identifying their funds of knowledge
constraints: Described as implemented within Claremont's TLP I course; no independent effect evidence is reported
target_learning_goals: positionality reflection
examining implicit biases
critical analysis of schooling structures
examples: A graduate described reflecting on questions like "Who are we? Where do we come from? In what ways do we hold power?"
key_sources: Yun, C., & Fitz, J. (2025). Humanizing teacher preparation: Claremont Graduate University's teacher residency. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/338.812

article_title: Meeting Urban and Rural District Needs for Educators: California State University, Bakersfield's Teacher Residencies
citation: Fitz, J., & Yun, C. (2025). Meeting urban and rural district needs for educators: California State University, Bakersfield's teacher residencies. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/825.823
title: Teacher residency model with yearlong clinical apprenticeship, cohort coursework, stipend-for-commitment exchange, and LEA co-construction
description: The report describes a teacher residency preparation model in which candidates spend a full school year coteaching in a mentor teacher's classroom while taking residency-specific coursework in cohorts, receive a stipend in exchange for a multiyear teaching commitment in the partner district, and are prepared through university-LEA partnership. As printed, "All programs gave residents stipends to help cover their residency-year expenses, in exchange for a commitment to teach in the program's partner LEA(s) for 3 or 4 years following program completion." The model is organized around seven prioritized teaching practices aligned to California's Teacher Performance Expectations and the Danielson Framework for Teaching.
requirements: A partner LEA willing to co-construct programming, participate in admissions, and contribute funding
Mentor teachers with ongoing professional learning as clinical educators
A phase-in schedule pacing residents' progressive responsibility and focal Danielson Clusters
constraints: Residents commit to 3 or 4 years of teaching in partner LEAs after completion
Coordinators' heavily loaded combined role came at the expense of work-life balance and long-term retention in the role, per interviews
target_learners: Pre-service teacher credential candidates in urban and rural California districts
target_learning_goals: Preparation for preliminary teaching credentials with context-specific clinical competence
examples: Kern Urban paired residents with mentors and used a phase-in schedule breaking each semester into 2-week increments; TRRE placed residents in three rural districts via the Tulare County Office of Education
key_sources: Fitz, J., & Yun, C. (2025). Meeting urban and rural district needs for educators: California State University, Bakersfield's teacher residencies. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/825.823

article_title: Meeting Urban and Rural District Needs for Educators: California State University, Bakersfield's Teacher Residencies
citation: Fitz, J., & Yun, C. (2025). Meeting urban and rural district needs for educators: California State University, Bakersfield's teacher residencies. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/825.823
title: Phase-in schedule pacing resident responsibility and Danielson Clusters across the residency year
description: A reusable program-level design in which the clinical year is broken into 2-week increments that specify residents' coteaching roles, responsibilities, and strategies, plus focal Danielson Clusters that coursework reinforces in the same period. As printed, "These schedules broke each semester into 2-week increments and advised mentor teachers and residents about the roles, responsibilities, and coteaching strategies they should consider taking on during each period." Clusters are paced so residents cycle through all six once in fall and again in spring, reinforcing learning across semesters.
requirements: Mentor teachers able to shift the timeline based on their assessment of resident readiness
Course instructors who align coursework to the focal Cluster for each period
constraints: Mentor teachers may adjust the phase-in timeline according to resident readiness, so pacing is advisory rather than fixed
target_learners: Teacher residency candidates in yearlong clinical placements
target_learning_goals: Progressive development of teaching practice across the Danielson Framework Clusters
examples: Scheduled observations focused on the Cluster named for the period, with written feedback shared at weekly Coaching Time and with program coordinators
key_sources: Fitz, J., & Yun, C. (2025). Meeting urban and rural district needs for educators: California State University, Bakersfield's teacher residencies. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/825.823

citation: Fitz, J., & Yun, C. (2025). Meeting urban and rural district needs for educators: California State University, Bakersfield's teacher residencies. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/825.823
title: CSUB Teacher Residency Consortium, a monthly professional learning community of residency coordinators
description: The CSUB Teacher Residency Consortium is a professional learning community that brings together all of the university's residency coordinators monthly to align practices and share solutions across the seven residency programs. As printed, "In addition to supporting alignment across programs, it enabled residency coordinators to share successful practices, exchange ideas, and support each other through challenges." The coordinator leading it also attended California Teacher Residency Lab and National Center for Teacher Residencies meetings, cross-pollinating ideas between the institution and the national residency community.
requirements: A designated facilitator (Holly Gonzales led it in 2022–23) and monthly meeting time for all coordinators
target_learners: Residency coordinators and teacher education faculty
target_learning_goals: Cross-program alignment of residency practices and continuous improvement
examples: Consortium meetings supported alignment of coursework and clinical expectations around seven prioritized teaching practices across all CSUB residencies

article_title: Investing in Our Nation's Future: Advancing Educational Opportunity for Underserved Students
citation: García, E., Levin, H. (2025). Investing in Our Nation's Future: Advancing Educational Opportunity for Underserved Students. Los Angeles, CA: The Civil Rights Project/Proyecto Derechos Civiles, UCLA. https://escholarship.org/uc/item/29h9c9dn
title: Human capital theory as the framework linking education investment to productivity and societal returns
description: The report adopts human capital theory as its organizing framework, which "has established that education, or human capital more broadly, enhances a person's skills and increases productivity in the workplace, and that investments in education anticipate a wide range of benefits." The framework treats aggregate human capital as the nation's combined skills and attainment, weighted by demographic composition, and predicts both individual and collective economic gains, externalities, and nonmonetary benefits. The report cites empirical rates of return of about 10% for an additional year of education.
requirements: Requires treating education as an investment whose returns can be estimated and compared against costs
constraints: Returns estimates typically focus on increased earnings and the individual, though the report argues for broader accounting including externalities
target_learners: All students, with particular attention to those from historically disadvantaged racial/ethnic and income backgrounds
target_learning_goals: Educational attainment, skills, productivity, and long-term economic and social outcomes
examples: The report applies the framework to justify benefit-cost analysis of interventions from preschool through higher education.
key_sources: García, E., Levin, H. (2025). Investing in Our Nation's Future: Advancing Educational Opportunity for Underserved Students. Los Angeles, CA: The Civil Rights Project/Proyecto Derechos Civiles, UCLA. https://escholarship.org/uc/item/29h9c9dn

article_title: Investing in Our Nation's Future: Advancing Educational Opportunity for Underserved Students
citation: García, E., Levin, H. (2025). Investing in Our Nation's Future: Advancing Educational Opportunity for Underserved Students. Los Angeles, CA: The Civil Rights Project/Proyecto Derechos Civiles, UCLA. https://escholarship.org/uc/item/29h9c9dn
title: Design education investments with sufficient quality, intensity, duration, and dosage to yield strong benefit-cost ratios
description: The report's economic evaluations indicate that intervention design features drive returns: "the quality, intensity, and duration of the interventions are important, as higher benefit-to-cost ratios are usually associated with more resource-intense programs and those with stronger dosage effects and/or with longer exposure." This principle directs policymakers and program designers to resource interventions adequately rather than scaling back inputs, since under-resourced versions may fail to reproduce the returns documented in evaluations.
requirements: Programs must be funded and implemented at the quality, intensity, and duration levels associated with higher benefit-to-cost ratios in the evaluation literature
constraints: Higher benefit-to-cost ratios are associated with more resource-intense programs, implying greater upfront cost
target_learners: All students, with particular benefit for the most disadvantaged children
target_learning_goals: Maximizing net economic and educational returns on educational investment
examples: The report's synthesis of economic evaluations found stronger dosage effects and longer exposure linked to higher returns.
key_sources: García, E., Levin, H. (2025). Investing in Our Nation's Future: Advancing Educational Opportunity for Underserved Students. Los Angeles, CA: The Civil Rights Project/Proyecto Derechos Civiles, UCLA. https://escholarship.org/uc/item/29h9c9dn

article_title: Building Futures: Strengthening the Educator Workforce through Teacher Apprenticeships
citation: Nathan Kriha, Diarese George, Jonathan Feinstein, and Anna Skubel. (2025). Building Futures: Strengthening the Educator Workforce Through Teacher Apprenticeships. EdTrust. https://edtrust.org
title: Registered Teacher Apprenticeship Programs (RTAPs) and the National Guidelines for Apprenticeship Standards
description: RTAPs are a form of registered apprenticeship recognized by the U.S. Department of Labor in which apprentices hold paid positions with progressively increasing wages, complete at least 2,000 hours of structured on-the-job training under an experienced mentor, receive supplemental classroom instruction, and earn a portable, nationally recognized credential. The Pathways Alliance's National Guidelines add teacher-specific elements: competency-based completion, at least one academic year of on-the-job learning with a mentor-teacher at a ratio not exceeding two apprentices per mentor, at least 144 hours of related technical instruction, and no service as teacher of record. The report describes RTAPs as an "earn and learn" model intended to make teaching more accessible and affordable and to attract a more diverse candidate pool.
requirements: Programs must be registered with the U.S. Department of Labor or a state apprenticeship agency and operate as partnerships between districts and educator preparation programs
constraints: The report notes little research exists on the efficacy of these programs to produce high-quality, well-prepared, and diverse educators, and many programs have yet to graduate any apprentices
target_learners: adult learners and currently employed non-teacher school staff such as paraprofessionals and long-term substitutes seeking teacher licensure
target_learning_goals: full state teacher certification or licensure through competency-based, job-embedded educator preparation
examples: Programs studied in Tennessee and Texas placed apprentices in schools four to five days per week while completing coursework at night and on weekends, lasting one to three years depending on entry credentials

degree or credential completion

citation: Robbie Ha. (2026). Accreditation Needs Reform. ED’s Forthcoming Proposed Rule Misses the Mark. EdTrust. https://www.edtrust.org
title: The program integrity triad: ED, states, and accreditors as complementary quality guardrails for federal student aid
description: The brief describes American higher education quality assurance as a "program integrity triad" established under the Higher Education Act of 1965, designed to ensure Title IV funding flows only to institutions meeting standards for quality and integrity. As printed: "ED primarily evaluates institutions’ financial and administrative capacity; states focus on consumer protection; and accrediting agencies assess and promote academic quality." Accreditation is a powerful lever because losing it generally forfeits federal financial aid access, while accreditors remain independent nongovernmental organizations that Congress designed to operate free of direct federal control.
requirements: Accrediting agencies must maintain Department recognition to serve as gatekeepers for federal financial aid
constraints: Congress explicitly prohibited ED from exercising direction, supervision, or control over curriculum, programs, or accrediting agencies under the Department of Education Organization Act of 1979
target_learning_goals: institutional academic quality assurance
access to federal student aid
examples: The brief uses the triad to explain why losing accreditation would be a death knell for many institutions and why losing recognition eliminates an accreditor's primary value to its member institutions

description: The report organizes state universal FAFSA policy design around three main components: "who is responsible for fulfilling the requirement, whether an opt-out waiver is available, and whether funding is provided to local education agencies (LEAs)." States also differ in whether policies were created through regulation or statute and in statewide supports promoting college enrollment. The framework is used to compare Colorado, Illinois, Indiana, and Louisiana, whose policies vary across all three components — from Colorado's funded competitive grant program to Indiana's and Louisiana's unfunded requirements.

constraints: Louisiana and New Hampshire have repealed their policies, showing design choices affect policy durability

article_title: The Hidden Bias in College ROI Frameworks
citation: Michelle Chen and Sebastian Kane. (2026). The Hidden Bias in College ROI Frameworks. EdTrust. https://edtrust.org
title: Use continuous ROI measures rather than rigid pass-or-fail thresholds to assess institutional performance
description: The article argues that threshold-based accountability frameworks oversimplify institutional performance because institutions just below a cutoff are treated identically to those far below it, masking meaningful incremental differences. It recommends continuous measures: "Continuous measures, such as those used in the PEP framework, provide a more accurate assessment of institutional performance." This principle applies to designing accountability metrics for higher education.

constraints: The article notes threshold models make accountability easier to administer, a tradeoff policymakers weigh
target_learning_goals: accurate assessment of institutional value and student outcomes

title: Psychological resource account of AI-mediated learning grounded in Self-Determination Theory
description: The article frames AI-assisted autonomous learning as a learning context that reshapes students' experiences of autonomy, competence, and challenge rather than merely a tool for efficiency. Drawing on Self-Determination Theory, it argues that when AI "functions as a scaffold" students retain ownership, but when it replaces effortful engagement, "the learning process may appear autonomous but become externally guided in substance." Hardiness (commitment, control, challenge) is positioned as the psychological resource transmitting these effects to academic self-evaluation, with Cognitive Load Theory as a complementary explanation for reduced deep processing.

examples: The study modeled AI-assisted autonomous learning as a second-order latent variable predicting hardiness and reduced academic accomplishment in an SEM

description: The article recommends that AI tools be integrated "as supportive scaffolds rather than replacement systems": teachers should "intentionally retain moderately challenging tasks in AI-supported courses" and design activities requiring students to explain, reflect, revise, and decide independently. AI should provide prompting questions, step-by-step hints, alternative perspectives, or reflective feedback rather than complete solutions, so students keep a sense of control, persistence, and ownership while benefiting from AI support.
requirements: Instructional activities must still require students to explain, reflect, revise, and make decisions independently
constraints: The recommendation rests on cross-sectional correlational evidence, not on a test of the designed activities themselves
target_learners: vocational higher education students using generative AI tools
target_learning_goals: preserving sense of control, persistence, ownership, and academic accomplishment in AI-supported learning
examples: The authors suggest AI systems be designed or used to provide prompting questions, step-by-step hints, alternative perspectives, or reflective feedback rather than complete solutions

article_title: AI chatbot design principles to enhance the collective efficacy in collaborative learning
citation: Minji Kim, Cheolil Lim. (2025). AI chatbot design principles to enhance the collective efficacy in collaborative learning. Asia Pacific Education Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12564-025-10080-z
title: Four-element design framework for AI chatbots enhancing collective efficacy in collaborative learning
description: The article proposes a design framework for educational AI chatbots organized into four design elements: group cohesion support, affective cohesion support, support for collaborative learning activities, and inducing conversation (facilitation of dialogue). These elements are operationalized through ten design principles and 46 sub-guidelines. The framework is grounded in Social Cognitive Theory, Social and Emotional Learning, Social Presence Theory, and Transactional Distance Theory, and positions chatbots as "dynamic members of collaborative teams" that scaffold both social and cognitive processes.
requirements: The chatbot must automatically deliver team-specific feedback by analyzing accumulated conversation logs, without requiring learner prompts
constraints: The principles were developed as general guidelines across age groups; the authors state context-specific principles for project-based, maker, and discussion-based learning require further research
target_learners: learners working in collaborative learning teams across age groups
target_learning_goals: collective efficacy
collaboration
communication
problem-solving
examples: The final framework comprises four components operationalized through ten actionable design principles and 46 sub-guidelines, refined through three expert validation rounds and a usability test

citation: Minji Kim, Cheolil Lim. (2025). AI chatbot design principles to enhance the collective efficacy in collaborative learning. Asia Pacific Education Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12564-025-10080-z
title: Address data privacy and algorithmic bias when deploying educational AI chatbots
description: The article recommends that researchers and educators consider ethical factors when using AI chatbots in education. It identifies data privacy risks around storage and use of user logs and algorithmic bias such as cultural insensitivity or emotionally inappropriate responses as significant concerns, and prescribes informed consent, active bias monitoring, institutional policy standards for student data governance, and ethical guidelines for chatbot development and deployment to support responsible implementation and user trust.
requirements: Prior and informed consent from users; institutional policy standards governing collection, storage, and use of student data
target_learners: all learners interacting with educational AI chatbots
target_learning_goals: safe and responsible AI-supported learning environments
examples: The article recommends increasing awareness of implicit bias, actively monitoring chatbot behavior, and staying up to date with the evolving capabilities and limitations of generative AI in education

article_title: Artificial intelligence as a cognitive partner: a developmental framework for human-AI co-regulation in learning
citation: S P, Joseph J, Jose M, S M A, N R and Joseph J (2026) Artificial intelligence as a cognitive partner: a developmental framework for human–AI co-regulation in learning. Front. Dev. Psychol. 4:1835258. https://doi.org/10.3389/fdpys.2026.1835258
title: Human–AI co-regulation framework: cognitive regulation is distributed between the learner and an external intelligent system
description: The article proposes that interactions with AI be conceptualized as a co-regulation process in which planning, monitoring, and control of cognition are shared between a human learner and an adaptive intelligent system. It integrates sociocultural theory, executive function and metacognition research, and distributed cognition, extending classical developmental accounts to non-human regulating partners. The authors state they "hypothesize that the interaction with AI can be viewed as a co-regulation process, where cognitive regulation is distributed between the learner and the external intelligent system."
requirements: An adaptive AI system capable of real-time response generation, feedback, and decision support, not merely passive information presentation
constraints: The framework is conceptual and not yet empirically validated; the authors note there are "still only limited empirical findings, which are frequently inconsistent"
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning
metacognitive development
problem solving
examples: The authors frame everyday AI use — organizing work, checking answers, generating descriptions — as analogous to guided participation traditionally associated with teachers or peers
key_sources: S P, Joseph J, Jose M, S M A, N R and Joseph J (2026) Artificial intelligence as a cognitive partner: a developmental framework for human–AI co-regulation in learning. Front. Dev. Psychol. 4:1835258. https://doi.org/10.3389/fdpys.2026.1835258

article_title: Artificial intelligence as a cognitive partner: a developmental framework for human-AI co-regulation in learning
citation: S P, Joseph J, Jose M, S M A, N R and Joseph J (2026) Artificial intelligence as a cognitive partner: a developmental framework for human–AI co-regulation in learning. Front. Dev. Psychol. 4:1835258. https://doi.org/10.3389/fdpys.2026.1835258
title: Four roles of AI in cognitive regulation: scaffolding, metacognitive support, memory augmentation, and decision assistance
description: The proposed co-regulation model distinguishes four primary roles through which AI participates in cognition. As a scaffold, AI enables performance beyond independent capability; as metacognitive support, it prompts reflection and strategy evaluation; as external memory, it stores and generates content that offloads internal processing; as decision partner, it offers recommendations that shape action. The article states: "The model highlights four primary roles of AI in cognitive regulation: scaffolding, metacognitive support, memory augmentation, and decision assistance."
requirements: AI systems that actively engage in organizing cognitive activity rather than only storing or presenting information
constraints: The nature and intensity of AI involvement vary across developmental stages, becoming more prominent in later stages where metacognitive capacities are more developed
target_learning_goals: task performance
metacognitive monitoring
memory and reasoning support
decision making
examples: Figure 1 presents the conceptual model showing co-regulated cognition, temporary cognitive performance, and long-term developmental effects

title: AI integration should complement rather than replace human cognition, preserving human engagement in critical thinking and self-regulation domains
description: The article argues educators must distinguish domains where AI can productively support cognition (information processing, feedback, scaffolding, routine problem-solving) from domains requiring sustained human engagement (critical thinking, ethical reasoning, decision-making under uncertainty, self-regulation development). Its stated goal: "the goal of AI integration should not be to replace human cognition but to complement it, ensuring that external support enhances rather than substitutes the development of core cognitive competencies."
requirements: Deliberate domain-level decisions about where AI support is permitted and where human effortful processing is preserved
constraints: Over-reliance on AI in domains requiring effortful processing may limit opportunities for independent reasoning essential for long-term cognitive growth
target_learning_goals: critical thinking
ethical reasoning
self-regulation
independent reasoning
examples: The article identifies information processing, feedback provision, scaffolding, and routine problem-solving as domains where AI is particularly effective

citation: Abderrahim Agnaou; Hayat El Asri. (2025). Artificial Intelligence and Collaborative Learning: Impacts on Creativity, Critical Thinking, and Problem-Solving. JERAP Vol. 15 (2025) Iss. 1. https://doi.org/10.5590/JERAP.2025.15.2120
title: Mixed-methods design combining surveys, structured interviews, and analysis of student project outputs
description: The study used a mixed-methods approach combining quantitative questionnaires with qualitative follow-up interviews and analysis of student project outputs to investigate LLM use in team-based undergraduate work. Data came from 102 undergraduate students via questionnaires and 15 follow-up interviews, which the authors say "offered deeper insight into their experiences using LLMs in team-based projects." This design links perceived collaboration effects with actual project artifacts.
requirements: Both questionnaire data from 102 undergraduates and 15 follow-up interviews are needed for the combined quantitative-qualitative picture
constraints: Findings concern undergraduate students working in team-based projects using LLMs
target_learning_goals: collaborative learning, creativity, critical thinking, problem-solving, collective intelligence
examples: 102 undergraduate questionnaires plus 15 follow-up interviews and analysis of student project outputs in team-based LLM projects

title: Design LLMs that support rather than disrupt human collaboration, aligning AI tools with educational values
description: The article's forward-looking design recommendation is that as AI evolves, tools for collaborative learning should be built to reinforce group processes rather than undermine them. The authors "highlight the importance of designing LLMs that support rather than disrupt human collaboration," and pair this with "the need for alignment between AI tools and educational values." It directs AI developers and educators toward collaboration-preserving tool design.
requirements: AI tools used in collaborative learning must be aligned with educational values
constraints: Recommendation is framed as AI continues to evolve, based on a single study of undergraduate team projects

examples: The study's findings on LLM use in team-based projects are offered as the basis for emphasizing collaboration-supporting LLM design

article_title: 'Artificial Intelligence and Communities of Inquiry: Reimagining Educational Experiences'
citation: Stenbom, S., & Garrison, D. R. (2026). Artificial Intelligence and Communities of Inquiry: Reimagining Educational Experiences. The International Review of Research in Open and Distributed Learning, 27(2), 114–131. https://doi.org/10.19173/irrodl.v27i2.9314
title: The Community of Inquiry framework as a coherent theoretical framework for guiding educational adoption of AI
description: The article positions the Community of Inquiry (CoI) framework as the theoretical lens needed to navigate the tensions of generative AI in education, stating that "this article argues for the necessity of a coherent theoretical framework to guide the educational adoption of AI." It uses CoI and collaborative inquiry to show how AI can be integrated "in ways that preserve human agency and sustain deep and meaningful learning." The authors conclude the framework "has considerable potential to provide understanding and guidance in the adoption of AI tools."
requirements: AI adoption in education must be framed within a coherent conceptual perspective rather than adopted tool-by-tool
constraints: The framework guides adoption; the article argues its necessity rather than empirically testing it
target_learning_goals: deep and meaningful learning
critical thinking
collaborative inquiry
examples: The article outlines how collaborative inquiry can integrate AI while preserving human agency, drawing on CoI and shared metacognition

title: Shared metacognition—collective monitoring and management of thinking—as a responsible pathway for engaging critically with AI outputs
description: Shared metacognition is the CoI construct of "collective monitoring and management of thinking." The article argues it "offers a responsible pathway for educators and learners to engage critically with AI-generated outputs, ensuring that technology strengthens rather than supplants collaborative inquiry." It functions as the mechanism by which learning communities keep AI use subordinate to reflective, collaborative inquiry rather than replacing it.
requirements: Educators and learners must collectively monitor and manage their thinking when working with AI-generated outputs
constraints: The pathway is argued theoretically; the article reports no empirical test of it
target_learning_goals: critical engagement with AI-generated outputs
shared metacognitive regulation
examples: The article applies shared metacognition to the scenario of learners evaluating AI-generated outputs within a community of inquiry

title: A five-role taxonomy of AI within a community of inquiry: instructional design support, independent learner resource, instructor analytics, discussion participant, and dialogical partner
description: The article enumerates the potential roles AI can assume within a community of inquiry: "supporting instructional design, guiding learners as an independent resource, assisting instructors through analytics, participating in discussions, and sustaining dialogical partnerships with students." These roles, the authors state, "highlight the capacity of AI to enrich learning communities," while also carrying risks when reflective inquiry is bypassed. The taxonomy organizes how AI participation can be designed across the teaching, cognitive, and social dimensions of a community of inquiry.
requirements: AI roles must be designed so that reflective inquiry is not bypassed
constraints: Roles are outlined as potential; the article does not report empirical evaluation of any role

meaningful integration of AI in learning communities
examples: The article examines each role—from design support to dialogical partnership—as a distinct way AI may participate in a community of inquiry

title: Adopt AI in education only within a coherent conceptual perspective emphasizing skeptical engagement, collaborative reflection, and preservation of human purpose
description: The article's central design recommendation is that "AI can contribute to worthwhile educational experiences only when framed within a coherent conceptual perspective that emphasizes skeptical engagement, collaborative reflection, and the preservation of human purpose." Adoption should therefore be organized around a framework such as CoI rather than around tools, so that AI strengthens rather than supplants collaborative inquiry.

constraints: The article states this as a necessary condition for worthwhile educational experiences with AI; it does not claim tool-level adoption without a framework is impossible

preservation of human agency

article_title: The dark side of AI in education: AI dependency as a mediator linking academic self-efficacy and teacher support to learning burnout among university students
citation: Huang Q, Tu S, Lin J, Lu L and Lv C (2026). The dark side of AI in education: AI dependency as a mediator linking academic self-efficacy and teacher support to learning burnout among university students. Front. Psychol. 17:1889053. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1889053
title: Resource-depletion mediation framework: AI dependency as the mechanism linking personal and contextual resources to learning burnout
description: The article proposes an integrated framework in which academic self-efficacy (a personal psychological resource) and teacher support (a contextual resource) shape AI dependency, which in turn is associated with learning burnout. Grounded in Conservation of Resources, Cognitive Offloading, and Social Cognitive Theory, it treats AI dependency as "a comprehensive psychological phenomenon that encompasses emotional, cognitive, and behavioral dimensions". Dependency may temporarily conserve cognitive resources but gradually deplete internal learning resources such as critical thinking and autonomous learning competence, intensifying burnout.
requirements: Measurement of academic self-efficacy, teacher support, AI dependency, and learning burnout as distinct validated constructs
Theoretical framing in Conservation of Resources, Cognitive Offloading, and Social Cognitive Theory
constraints: The cross-sectional design limits the ability to establish causal relationships among the variables
The proposed model may capture only part of the mechanisms underlying AI dependency, indicating that its explanatory scope is not exhaustive
Reciprocal relationships may exist, such as higher burnout leading to greater AI dependency
target_learners: university students in AI-assisted learning environments
target_learning_goals: reducing learning burnout
promoting responsible and autonomous AI use
examples: The study tested the framework with a cross-sectional survey of 276 university students using PROCESS Model 4 mediation analysis with 5,000 bootstrap resamples.

article_title: The AI disruption in engineering education: an analysis of changing student norms through cultural historical activity
citation: Tiina Leino Lindell, Christian Stöhr. (2026). The AI disruption in engineering education: an analysis of changing student norms through cultural historical activity theory. Journal of Computing in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12528-025-09488-8
title: Cultural-Historical Activity Theory as a framework for analyzing how GenAI transforms educational activity systems
description: The study adopts Cultural-Historical Activity Theory (CHAT) as its analytical framework, understanding human action as mediated by tools within an activity system of six interconnected components: rules, tools, subjects, division of labor, community, and object. In CHAT, norms are "implicit rules that regulate activity", and contradictions are historically and culturally situated tensions that arise when new elements such as GenAI disrupt established practices. The article treats these contradictions not as obstacles but as "the driving force of change in activity", using them as analytical entry points to explain how students' GenAI use transforms norms and practices in engineering education.
requirements: Analysis requires identifying contradictions as tensions between components of the activity system, following the recommendations of Sannino and Engeström (2018) and Virtaluoto et al. (2016) as the article states
constraints: The authors call their introduction to CHAT "short and necessary incomplete"
The framework was applied to one technical university in Northern Europe, so the analysis is context-sensitive to that setting
target_learning_goals: Understanding how access to GenAI reshapes implicit rules, norms, and educational practices
examples: The article analyzes students using GenAI to 'enhance idea generation' as a shift from purely human-generated ideas to a hybrid approach, indicating changed division of labor and a new implicit rule about ideation tools

article_title: AI-Driven Educational Reform: Enhancing Talent Cultivation in Computer-Related Majors for the Digital Era
citation: Wang J and Li P (2026). AI-driven educational reform: enhancing talent cultivation in computer-related majors for the digital era. Front. Psychol. 17:1790916. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1790916
title: AI-driven talent cultivation reform framework with five interconnected components
description: The article proposes a comprehensive reform framework for computer-related majors grounded in the new engineering philosophy, integrating AI across curriculum, pedagogy, and practical training. As printed, "The framework is structured around five core components: curriculum restructuring, smart teaching integration, interdisciplinary and collaborative talent cultivation, practice-based learning enhancement, and multi-dimensional evaluation." The components form an interconnected system intended to deliver AI-empowered talent cultivation with academic depth and industrial relevance, and the framework was phased in across four undergraduate programs as a replicable model.
requirements: AI technologies must be systematically embedded across curriculum structures, instructional processes, and practice-oriented modules rather than confined to isolated courses
constraints: Implemented in computer-related majors at one Chinese institution under the new engineering education paradigm
target_learning_goals: technical proficiency in AI and computing
innovation capacity
practical problem-solving for real-world challenges
examples: The reform framework was phased in across four undergraduate programs, with new courses such as Artificial Intelligence and Big Data Analysis and partnerships such as the Huawei Cybersecurity Laboratory

description: To operationalize competency goals in the reformed curriculum, the authors developed a competency map that translates abstract professional requirements into measurable learning outcomes. constraints: The core competencies were drawn from the AI competency framework proposed by Huang (2021), recognized within China's educational reforms

title: Expanded AI competency framework adding technological adaptability and cross-cultural collaboration sub-competencies
description: Building on Huang's AI competency framework of knowledge, team, and learning competence with six sub-competencies, the authors extended it for the AI era. As printed, "we further expanded upon this framework by incorporating two additional sub-competencies: Technological Awareness and Adaptability Competence and Cross-cultural Collaboration Competence." The first emphasizes staying informed about emerging technologies and adapting to unforeseen technological change; the second equips students to communicate, collaborate, and problem-solve in diverse, multicultural teams as AI technologies are developed and deployed globally.
requirements: The expansion responds to fast-paced developments in AI requiring students to adapt quickly to new tools and technologies
constraints: Derived from Huang's framework as applied in China's AI education reforms

cross-cultural collaboration

description: The reform uses Performance Indicators as the assessment layer of the competency map. Each PI is defined as a specific observable action with clear scoring rubrics and paired assessment tools such as programming assignments, project reports, and peer reviews; standards are reviewed regularly using student, industry-expert, and faculty feedback, and are tested through interdisciplinary projects.

title: Three-phase AI smart teaching loop of pre-class diagnosis, in-class adaptation, and post-class analytics
description: The smart teaching integration organizes AI support across the instructional cycle. Before class, "AI-powered diagnostic systems analyze historical learning records, course performance data, and individual cognitive profiles to assess knowledge readiness" and generate personalized preparation materials. During class, AI-enabled assistants monitor engagement in real time and can push supplementary explanations, mini quizzes, or instructor alerts. After class, intelligent grading systems provide immediate formative feedback and dashboards feed a closed-loop mechanism connecting learning design, implementation, and continuous improvement.

constraints: The article notes existing research remains largely focused on tool- or course-level functional performance with limited attention to curriculum-level alignment

article_title: Responding to AI-generated emotional alerts: teachers' intervention and students' engagement in the mathematics classroom
citation: Osama Swidan. (2026). Responding to AI-generated emotional alerts: teachers' intervention and students' engagement in the mathematics classroom. ZDM-MathematicsEducation. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11858-026-01810-7
title: Goldin's engagement structures framework: affect as a representational system integral to mathematical engagement
description: The study draws on DeBellis and Goldin's and Goldin's framework in which affect operates as a representational system alongside cognition during mathematical work. Central to this perspective is the notion of engagement structures, defined in the article as "recurrent yet dynamically evolving conﬁgurations of affect, motiva- tion, behavior, social interaction, and mathematical reason- ing" that shape participation in problem-solving. Each structure is organized around a motivating desire (e.g., Get the Job Done, Help Me, I'm Really into This), and contexts can produce branching, replacement, or stabilization of structures. The article extends the framework to classrooms where AI-generated emotional alerts become elements of the situation that may interact with students' affective pathways.
requirements: Requires analyzing affect, motivation, behavior, social interaction, and mathematical reasoning together during in-the-moment mathematical activity rather than as separate predictors or outcomes.
constraints: The article states that constructs such as affective representations, affective pathways, motivating desires, and engagement structures are theoretically informed analytic interpretations rather than directly observable emotional states.
target_learners: high school mathematics students during problem-solving
target_learning_goals: sustained mathematical engagement during problem-solving
integration of affect with mathematical reasoning
examples: The author coded episodes for engagement processes of activation, stabilization, and branching, and for teacher responses including reframing, reinforcement, collective discussion, inquiry, and non-intervention.
