citation: Globerson, A., Keeling, A., Choudhury, A., et al. (2026). Towards Scalable Measurement of Durable Skills. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15864
title: The Executive LLM as a computerized adaptive test of complex behaviors
description: The Executive LLM is a single LLM that generates responses for all AI teammates, has access to the pedagogical rubrics, and is prompted to "create situations that will allow the subject to demonstrate their skill, so that their skill level can be quantitatively inferred". The article frames it as analogous to a computerized adaptive test: whereas traditional CAT varies only item difficulty in a narrow domain, the Executive LLM varies the flow of a group conversation — heightening or softening conflicts, creating project-management needs, or eliciting creative ideas — to maximize information about the test-taker while keeping the interaction naturalistic.
requirements: Access to the scoring rubrics as prompt input so steering targets the dimensions under assessment
constraints: Replacing human teammates with AI trades some authenticity for comparability and reliability
A completely unconstrained conversation likely will not efficiently provide the evidence of interest
target_learning_goals: Collaboration, creativity, and critical thinking proficiency measurement
examples: In the Debate task, the Executive LLM reasoned internally and responded as teammate Leo to steer toward conflict resolution evidence
key_sources: Globerson, A., Keeling, A., Choudhury, A., et al. (2026). Towards Scalable Measurement of Durable Skills. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15864

article_title: The Role of Implicit and Explicit Demographic Signals in Large Language Model-based Student Assessment
citation: Donya Rooein, Luca Benedetto, Dirk Hovy. (2026). The Role of Implicit and Explicit Demographic Signals in Large Language Model-based Student Assessment. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.16993
title: Require demographic invariance in high-stakes LLM scoring while allowing deliberate demographic adaptation only in instructional feedback
description: The article recommends that automated scoring must be invariant to demographic signals, since essay scores should depend solely on essay quality, whereas instructional contexts may legitimately adapt, for example readability, to student characteristics. Its evidence shows current models cannot be trusted to make this distinction themselves: "current LLMs cannot reliably separate task-relevant information from demographic cues". Deployers therefore need to explicitly control or strip demographic context in evaluative pipelines. The article frames this as essential for fairness, transparency, and avoiding amplification of educational inequities.
requirements: Evaluative tasks must hold demographic context out of scoring prompts, per the finding that implicit cues can inflate scores.
Educational uses should define which demographic adaptations are pedagogically intended versus biased before deployment.
constraints: The article states current LLMs cannot reliably separate task-relevant information from demographic cues, so invariance cannot be assumed from prompting alone.
target_learners: students assessed or given feedback by LLM-based systems, including second-language learners
target_learning_goals: fair and consistent automated assessment
pedagogically appropriate personalized feedback
examples: In the article's AES experiment, most models stayed relatively stable under explicit persona conditioning, but implicit cues produced significant score shifts for several models, motivating invariance requirements for scoring.
key_sources: Donya Rooein, Luca Benedetto, Dirk Hovy. (2026). The Role of Implicit and Explicit Demographic Signals in Large Language Model-based Student Assessment. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.16993

article_title: DataCanvas-EDU: An Agentic Framework for Instructor-Guided Synthetic Data Generation in Business Analytics Education
citation: Bang An, Maria Hamdani, Joseph Fox. (2026). DataCanvas-EDU: An Agentic Framework for Instructor-Guided Synthetic Data Generation in Business Analytics Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19617
title: DataCanvas-EDU: a four-phase agentic framework for instructor-guided synthetic data generation
description: DataCanvas-EDU is an agentic framework in which the instructor specifies a teaching brief (business setting, learner level, permitted tools, assignment scope) and intended patterns through conversation, while an AI agent writes generation code, checks the exported data, and prepares reference analyses, assignments, and rubrics. As the paper states, "Four phases—Plan, Create, Verify / Test Analysis, and Evaluate—organize the process and support instructor review and revision." A shared case specification connects each intended pattern to its generation rule, comparison groups, measurement, and sample-size requirements, guiding checks and revision.
requirements: Instructor approval of the complete design before the agent begins routine programming and numerical checks; changes to a substantive pattern or its intended difficulty require the instructor's review
constraints: The current workflow generates records from scratch and its numerical helper supports Python generation and a single CSV table; code execution is subject to the host environment's permissions
target_learning_goals: data investigation and visualization
formulating analytical questions and justifying findings
examples: The paper illustrates the framework's Plan phase with a healthcare conversation example proposing four patterns for a four-site clinic network, and demonstrates the full workflow with the WindowDash case
key_sources: Bang An, Maria Hamdani, Joseph Fox. (2026). DataCanvas-EDU: An Agentic Framework for Instructor-Guided Synthetic Data Generation in Business Analytics Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19617

description: The framework is implemented as a reusable AI Agent Skill: "a package of instructions, reference resources, and executable tools used within an existing agent environment." It is distributed as an installable folder, a versioned ZIP, and a plugin bundle, with an installation guide covering Claude, Claude Code, and compatible Codex/ChatGPT environments. The package and installation instructions are available on GitHub. The implementation described is version 0.1.3.

constraints: The numerical helper supports Python generation and a single CSV table; document, spreadsheet, and notebook exports rely on the host's tools
target_learners: instructors of business analytics and visualization courses
target_learning_goals: preparing synthetic teaching cases with verified reference analyses
examples: The paper's repository includes generation and verification programs, an instructor guide describing nine patterns, an assignment and rubric, and reference visualizations for WindowDash

article_title: DataCanvas-EDU: An Agentic Framework for Instructor-Guided Synthetic Data Generation in Business Analytics Education
citation: Bang An, Maria Hamdani, Joseph Fox. (2026). DataCanvas-EDU: An Agentic Framework for Instructor-Guided Synthetic Data Generation in Business Analytics Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19617
title: WindowDash: a synthetic food delivery teaching case with 15,000 orders and nine designed patterns
description: WindowDash is a fictional food delivery case for an undergraduate business analytics and visualization assignment, containing 15,000 orders with ten fields including timestamp, ZIP code, service type, cuisine, price, tip, customer rating, and delivery time. Students are asked to find at least five interesting, distinct patterns and submit at least five visualizations with explanations, hypotheses, and a management recommendation. The case includes generation and verification programs, an instructor guide describing nine patterns, an assignment and rubric, and reference visualizations.
requirements: Delivery time is missing for pickup orders because the field does not apply to that service type
constraints: The supplied rubric assigns 30 of the assignment's 50 points to identifying distinct patterns; the Price-Rating Sensitivity pattern rests on only three supporting observations
target_learning_goals: comparing groups and time windows
count-versus-share reasoning
interpreting conditional relationships and exceptions
examples: The Office Lunch Rush pattern requires students to identify the office location, restrict analysis to weekday lunch hours, and compare pickup shares rather than raw counts

article_title: DataCanvas-EDU: An Agentic Framework for Instructor-Guided Synthetic Data Generation in Business Analytics Education
citation: Bang An, Maria Hamdani, Joseph Fox. (2026). DataCanvas-EDU: An Agentic Framework for Instructor-Guided Synthetic Data Generation in Business Analytics Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19617
title: Designed-pattern authoring: linking each teaching pattern to its generation rule, check, and reference analysis
description: A designed pattern is "a trend, group difference, interaction, or exception intentionally built into a dataset for students to investigate." The workflow records each pattern in an executable case specification connecting it to its generation rule, comparison groups, measurement, and sample-size requirements, so that the generation rule, numerical check, reference chart, and rubric use the same definition of the intended finding. Verification examines the combined effect of interacting rules on the exported data, and the probability set in the generator is not itself evidence that the pattern appears in the data.
requirements: Each pattern requires one or more checks; the specification defines how overlapping rules interact, since an adjustment made for one pattern may affect another
constraints: The order of generation rules affects what students observe; in WindowDash the ZIP 10011 cuisine adjustment overrides earlier cuisine rules
target_learning_goals: investigating unfamiliar data with AI
distinguishing counts from shares
justifying conclusions from evidence
examples: The Office Lunch Rush specification records the business question, the office-versus-other comparison over the same weekday lunch interval, the pickup-probability generation rule, and acceptance criteria on the pickup-share difference with minimum sample sizes

article_title: DataCanvas-EDU: An Agentic Framework for Instructor-Guided Synthetic Data Generation in Business Analytics Education
citation: Bang An, Maria Hamdani, Joseph Fox. (2026). DataCanvas-EDU: An Agentic Framework for Instructor-Guided Synthetic Data Generation in Business Analytics Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19617
title: Give students newly designed datasets to investigate with AI rather than widely used public datasets with published worked analyses
description: Because widely used public datasets carry tutorials and worked analyses that models may have encountered during training, students may receive explanations drawn from existing analyses without practicing how to investigate unfamiliar data in collaboration with AI. The article argues teaching cases should feature "newly designed relationships that students must examine using the supplied data," with deliberately designed patterns and verified reference answers so instructors can assess discoveries and reasoning. In AI-assisted classes, assessment can consider the questions students ask, the comparisons they choose, and how they justify their conclusions.
requirements: Deliberately designed patterns plus verified reference answers so instructors can assess the discoveries and the reasoning behind them
constraints: A new case still contains familiar business concepts and analytical methods an AI model can use; students must establish which explanations fit their particular dataset
target_learners: undergraduate business analytics students working with AI assistants
target_learning_goals: investigating unfamiliar data
directing and evaluating AI assistance
checking supporting evidence
examples: WindowDash asks students to report at least five findings from a case with nine intended patterns, while the pattern inventory and reference solution remain with the instructor
key_sources: Bang An, Maria Hamdani, Joseph Fox. (2026). DataCanvas-EDU: An Agentic Framework for Instructor-Guided Synthetic Data Generation in Business Analytics Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19617

article_title: Edustories: A Collection of Real-world Case Studies from Classroom Practices
citation: Michal Štefánik, Jan Nehyba, Jirina Karasova, Martin Fico, Lucie Škarková, Markéta Košatková, David Kosatka. (2026). Edustories: A Collection of Real-world Case Studies from Classroom Practices. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20484
title: Edustories dataset of 1,492 teacher-written classroom case studies with expert annotations
description: Edustories is a public dataset of 1,492 teacher-authored case studies describing challenging classroom situations, each with "a narrative description of the situation, the teacher's chosen response or intervention, and the implied outcome". Stories were written by 241 trainee teachers during Czech teaching practice, enriched with categorical features peer-reviewed by two independent education experts, anonymized in two stages, and translated from Czech to English.
requirements: Stories follow a structured five-part format: situation narrative, anamnesis, problem, intervention, and perceived outcome
constraints: All stories originate from trainee teachers in the final years of university study, so the dataset may not capture strategies of older generations of teachers
The authors estimate 5–10% of English translations may contain typos or translationese
target_learners: elementary and high-school students in Czech classrooms
target_learning_goals: classroom management and teacher decision-making in collective instruction
examples: The most common outcome category is long-term success (44.63%); the most common intervention category is interview (30.35%)

article_title: Edustories: A Collection of Real-world Case Studies from Classroom Practices
citation: Michal Štefánik, Jan Nehyba, Jirina Karasova, Martin Fico, Lucie Škarková, Markéta Košatková, David Kosatka. (2026). Edustories: A Collection of Real-world Case Studies from Classroom Practices. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20484
title: Three-facet Behavior Management Framework decomposition used for expert evaluation
description: To assess interventions, five educational experts decomposed classroom behavior management into three facets drawn from Behavior Management Frameworks: "(1) Humanistic orientation, reflecting emphasis on empathy, dialogue, and student needs versus reinforced control; (2) Reactivity, capturing reactive (cf. preventive) strategies; and (3) Systematicity" distinguishing generalizable strategies from incident-specific actions. Experts rated each facet on a centered Likert scale (-2 to +2) and combined them into an overall Appropriateness score mapped to the dataset's outcome labels.
requirements: Ratings by trained education experts familiar with behavior management frameworks
A centered Likert scale with defined mapping to outcome categories
constraints: The mapping treats -1 and 0 ratings as partial or short-term success and +1/+2 as long-term success, preserving zero-centered semantics
target_learning_goals: evaluating the appropriateness of classroom behavior-management interventions
examples: Experts rated interventions on humanistic orientation, reactivity, and systematicity before constructing the overall Appropriateness judgment

title: GPT 5.2 selected as translation service after expert-based comparison
description: To make Edustories accessible to the broader research community, free-text features were translated from Czech to English. The authors compared four translation tools on a randomly chosen set of 50 samples, manually verifying fluency and semantic equivalence. They found "the GPT 5.2 outperforms other services in fluency, where our annotators did not identify any mistakes among the 50 samples", and GPT 5.2 performed on par with DeepL on semantic equivalence, so all translations were produced by GPT 5.2.
requirements: Original Czech features are retained in the collection for future translation improvement
constraints: The authors estimate 5–10% of stories may contain a typo or translationese text; human proofreading of all English versions was not feasible
target_learners: education and NLP researchers using the dataset
target_learning_goals: cross-lingual accessibility of classroom case-study data
examples: Annotators identified 2 of 50 samples with imperfect semantic equivalence, with minor mistakes occurring in Intervention texts

article_title: Reducing Barriers to Academic Support: Evaluating a Course-Specific RAG System for Addressing Help-Seeking Disparities in Higher Education
citation: Andy Gray, Jake Hobbs. (2026). Reducing Barriers to Academic Support: Evaluating a Course-Specific RAG System for Addressing Help-Seeking Disparities in Higher Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.21600
title: Beacon: a course-specific RAG academic support system grounding responses in approved teaching materials
description: Beacon is a web-based conversational support tool for computing students that combines a course-specific knowledge base with an open-source LLM. Rather than relying on the model's internal knowledge, "every response is generated using relevant teaching materials retrieved from the module knowledge base", so guidance stays aligned with module learning outcomes and assessment expectations. Its architecture comprises a curated knowledge base, a semantic retrieval component, an LLM, and a web-based user interface; retrieved passages carry source metadata so students can verify explanations against official module resources. It was built with open-source technologies (Flask, PostgreSQL with pgvector, Nomic Embed Text) allowing local or institutional deployment.
requirements: Only materials selected by the module teaching team are indexed, ensuring retrieved content remains course-specific and pedagogically appropriate; the knowledge base is updated when approved materials are added or revised.
constraints: The article states course-specific AI is not a substitute for effective teaching or student support services.
target_learners: undergraduate computing students in programming modules
target_learning_goals: programming concept understanding
assessment clarification
independent problem-solving and appropriate help-seeking
examples: The pilot used a minimalist Streamlit interface; Version 2 was reimplemented in Flask with a conventional chat interface displaying supporting source material alongside each response, and the model was upgraded from GPT-OSS-20B to GPT-OSS-120B.
key_sources: Andy Gray, Jake Hobbs. (2026). Reducing Barriers to Academic Support: Evaluating a Course-Specific RAG System for Addressing Help-Seeking Disparities in Higher Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.21600

citation: Andy Gray, Jake Hobbs. (2026). Reducing Barriers to Academic Support: Evaluating a Course-Specific RAG System for Addressing Help-Seeking Disparities in Higher Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.21600
title: Four educational design objectives for course-specific AI support: course-specificity, independent learning, transparency and trust, and complementing existing teaching
description: The article organises Beacon's educational design around four objectives: providing course-specific academic support aligned with module outcomes; supporting independent learning through explanations and guidance rather than complete solutions; promoting transparency and trust so students can verify where information originates; and complementing existing teaching practices by enhancing rather than replacing lecturer and tutor interaction. The authors state "RAGwasthereforeadoptednotsimplyasatechnicalsolution,butas aneducationaldesignchoicethatenablesAI‐generatedsupporttore maintransparent,contextuallyrelevant,andalignedwithinstitutional teachingpractices." These objectives informed each stage of development, from knowledge-base construction to interface design.
requirements: Approved teaching materials are treated as the authoritative foundation for all responses, with the LLM functioning as the conversational interface rather than the primary source of knowledge.
target_learners: higher education students in computing modules
target_learning_goals: module-aligned academic guidance
independent learning
trust and verification of AI-generated explanations
examples: Objective 3 states students should be able to verify explanations, for example by the system stating the material was from a specific session presentation and slide, or from a handout.

article_title: Reducing Barriers to Academic Support: Evaluating a Course-Specific RAG System for Addressing Help-Seeking Disparities in Higher Education
citation: Andy Gray, Jake Hobbs. (2026). Reducing Barriers to Academic Support: Evaluating a Course-Specific RAG System for Addressing Help-Seeking Disparities in Higher Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.21600
title: Course-specific RAG as an intermediary layer between independent study and formal academic support
description: The article proposes that course-specific RAG systems occupy an intermediary space between independent study and formal academic support: rather than replacing educators, they offer "private,immediate,andcourse‐specificguidance" as a low-friction first point of support before students engage lecturers or tutors. The account holds that help-seeking barriers extend beyond availability of services to confidence, anxiety, fear of judgement, and perceptions of whether questions are appropriate, so an accessible private channel can lower the threshold for initiating help-seeking while preserving the pedagogical role of educators. This framing informed both Beacon's design objectives and the study's evaluation questions on trust, learning support, and help-seeking.
requirements: Responses must be grounded in approved teaching materials and remain aligned with module learning outcomes, so guidance is educationally appropriate rather than unrestricted.
constraints: The article states course-specific AI is not a substitute for effective teaching or student support services, and the findings come from a single institution's computing modules.
target_learners: higher education students reluctant to seek help through conventional channels due to anxiety, low confidence, or fear of judgement
target_learning_goals: initiating help-seeking
accessing academically appropriate guidance
building confidence before engaging formal academic support
examples: Beacon was positioned as an accessible first point of support when students encountered difficulties outside scheduled teaching, complementing rather than replacing lecturers and tutorials.

article_title: E3Sense: Head-Confined Multimodal Sensing of Learner Engagement
citation: Sidharth Anupkrishnan, Itir Sayar, Jeongah Lee, Sri Harsha Musunuri, Guan-Ming Su, Madeline Endres, Ravi Karkar, Phuc Nguyen. (2026). E3Sense: Head-Confined Multimodal Sensing of Learner Engagement. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26569
title: E3Sense: a head-worn multimodal engagement-sensing platform co-locating dry-electrode EEG, eye-tracking glasses, and forehead EDA
description: E3Sense is a sensing platform that "co-locates three devices on the head": a four-channel dry-electrode EEG headband, Pupil Labs Neon eye-tracking glasses, and an EmotiBit EDA sensor with two dry forehead electrodes spaced by the eye-tracker frame. Software aligns the three independently clocked streams on device-native timestamps and computes a fixed 166-dimensional per-segment feature vector (28 EEG, 127 eye-tracking, 11 EDA features) from a 120 s analysis window, fed to classical model families for engagement prediction.
requirements: All sensing sites lie on the head, and the EEG and EDA electrodes are dry, enabling faster gel-free setup
Stream alignment on device-native timestamps and periodic clock anchors so features from one window trace to the same viewing stretch
constraints: The present configuration uses three devices, and its predictive performance does not establish comfort or ease of everyday use
Forehead EDA is characterized as relatively resistant to motion artifacts but less responsive than palmar recordings, motivating a feasibility evaluation rather than an equivalence claim
target_learners: adult university-campus participants watching educational videos
target_learning_goals: segment-level self-reported engagement during video learning, to inform engagement-aware adaptive interfaces
examples: In the lab study, 30 participants watched three of four educational videos in a 2×2 content/format design under continuous sensing, rating five segments per video, yielding 450 segment-level observations
key_sources: Sidharth Anupkrishnan, Itir Sayar, Jeongah Lee, Sri Harsha Musunuri, Guan-Ming Su, Madeline Endres, Ravi Karkar, Phuc Nguyen. (2026). E3Sense: Head-Confined Multimodal Sensing of Learner Engagement. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26569

article_title: E3Sense: Head-Confined Multimodal Sensing of Learner Engagement
citation: Sidharth Anupkrishnan, Itir Sayar, Jeongah Lee, Sri Harsha Musunuri, Guan-Ming Su, Madeline Endres, Ravi Karkar, Phuc Nguyen. (2026). E3Sense: Head-Confined Multimodal Sensing of Learner Engagement. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26569
title: Tripartite framework of engagement: behavioral, emotional, and cognitive dimensions
description: The article adopts the tripartite framework from educational psychology, which identifies "three interconnected aspects of engagement: behavioral participation and attention, emotional interest and enjoyment, and cognitive effort and depth of processing". The framework motivates E3Sense's measurement design and frames the qualitative analysis: learners' own interview definitions of engagement were found to align with these dimensions while showing that different learners emphasize different criteria when giving the same overall rating.
requirements: Used to motivate the system and discuss learners' accounts, while targeting a single overall self-reported engagement rating as the prediction outcome
constraints: The dimensions are related but dissociable, and none of the physiological channels provides a unique reading of one engagement dimension
target_learners: video-based learners whose engagement is being sensed
target_learning_goals: conceptualizing engagement as behavioral, emotional, and cognitive dimensions to guide measurement and personalized interpretation
examples: Exit-interview quotes illustrate each dimension: cognitive (learning something new), behavioral (not zoning out), and emotional (interest and curiosity)
key_sources: Sidharth Anupkrishnan, Itir Sayar, Jeongah Lee, Sri Harsha Musunuri, Guan-Ming Su, Madeline Endres, Ravi Karkar, Phuc Nguyen. (2026). E3Sense: Head-Confined Multimodal Sensing of Learner Engagement. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26569

citation: Sidharth Anupkrishnan, Itir Sayar, Jeongah Lee, Sri Harsha Musunuri, Guan-Ming Su, Madeline Endres, Ravi Karkar, Phuc Nguyen. (2026). E3Sense: Head-Confined Multimodal Sensing of Learner Engagement. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26569
title: Include learners in defining what an engagement estimate represents, using their own criteria as context for personalized prediction
description: The article's design implication is "to include learners in defining what an engagement estimate represents". Because a single self-report can reflect several engagement dimensions that learners weight differently, a future interface could briefly elicit whether a learner associates engagement with understanding, sustained attention, interest, or a combination, and use that information when mapping sensor-derived scores to ratings, letting learners review and update criteria as tasks or goals change.
requirements: Brief elicitation of the learner's engagement criteria, reviewable and updatable as tasks or goals change
Definition codes derived from the learner (the present codes came from interviews, not inferred as psychological traits from sensor data)
constraints: Prospective elicitation and its stability remain to be tested; current models predict reported engagement and do not establish the cause of a low rating or which intervention would help
target_learning_goals: personalized, accurate interpretation of sensor-derived engagement estimates
examples: In the study, 18 participants' interview-derived cognitive, behavioral, and emotional definition codes, entered with score interactions, raised exploratory balanced 1-off accuracy from 64.6% to 71.5%

article_title: EduBehaviors: Assertion-based Schemas for Auditable Coding of Educational Dialogues
citation: Julian Bernado, Ana Trindade Ribeiro, Xander Beberman, and Susanna Loeb. (2026). EduBehaviors: Assertion-Based Schemas for Auditable Coding of Educational Dialogues. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27043
title: EduBehaviors: decomposable assertion-based schemas separating behavior identification from construct labeling
description: EduBehaviors is an interpretable annotation framework in which researchers write explicit binary assertions about conversational behavior; LLMs annotate each assertion as true or false, and a rule or trained statistical model combines these values into a construct label. The article formalizes this as a decomposable schema S=(A,R), noting it is "an example of a concept bottleneck model". It is designed to make coding decisions inspectable and revisable.
requirements: Assertions must correspond to human-readable, directly observable aspects of utterances and be minimally ambiguous across unprepared human annotators
constraints: The article notes use still requires evidence that the assertions and resulting labels capture the intended constructs in the target context
target_learning_goals: valid measurement of educational constructs in conversational data
examples: On the TalkMoves Teacher TalkMoves task, corpus-derived and construct-derived assertions were annotated by a panel of five LLMs and mapped to labels with an L1-penalized logistic regression
key_sources: Julian Bernado, Ana Trindade Ribeiro, Xander Beberman, and Susanna Loeb. (2026). EduBehaviors: Assertion-Based Schemas for Auditable Coding of Educational Dialogues. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27043

citation: Julian Bernado, Ana Trindade Ribeiro, Xander Beberman, and Susanna Loeb. (2026). EduBehaviors: Assertion-Based Schemas for Auditable Coding of Educational Dialogues. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27043
title: EduBehaviors-Studio: LLM-assisted web app for developing and refining assertion-based schemas
description: EduBehaviors-Studio is a self-hosted, bring-your-own-key web application for generating construct-derived assertions, annotating them on a dataset, and iterating until they adequately reflect a construct of interest. Its five-step workflow centers the distinction between "definitional errors" and "predictive errors", letting reviewers see which assertions fired for an utterance and decide whether to rephrase assertions or revise the aggregation rule.
requirements: A researcher description of the construct of interest, its possible values, and which utterance speakers it manifests in
constraints: Use of the toolkit still requires evidence that the assertions and resulting labels capture the intended constructs in the target context
target_learning_goals: operationalizing educational constructs as inspectable assertion-based schemas
examples: A reviewer who agrees with all fired assertions but disagrees with the final label exposes a gap in the measure's definition; if only the rule changes, the counterfactual annotation is derived with no additional LLM calls
key_sources: Julian Bernado, Ana Trindade Ribeiro, Xander Beberman, and Susanna Loeb. (2026). EduBehaviors: Assertion-Based Schemas for Auditable Coding of Educational Dialogues. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27043

citation: Julian Bernado, Ana Trindade Ribeiro, Xander Beberman, and Susanna Loeb. (2026). EduBehaviors: Assertion-Based Schemas for Auditable Coding of Educational Dialogues. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27043
title: EduBehaviors-kit: open-source Python package with pretrained assertion encoder models
description: EduBehaviors-kit combines a pip-installable Python package (on GitHub and PyPI) with pretrained open-weights encoder models and training data on HuggingFace, so researchers can apply the EduBehaviors framework to their own datasets. It provides four objects (WordAnnotator, AssertionAnnotator, standard classifier, ClassificationPipeline) and pretrained SetFit classifiers for 49 corpus-derived assertions that "can be run on a laptop".
requirements: Applying the pretrained classifiers to a new corpus requires checking that they identify the intended behaviors in the new setting
constraints: All released encoder classifiers are trained on TalkMoves corpus-derived assertions and may not be valid for applications differing in significant dimensions
target_learners: education researchers with little to no experience with language model-based annotation
target_learning_goals: reproducible, low-cost behavioral annotation and construct classification
examples: An end-to-end pipeline annotating a dataset, splitting train/test sets, and training an interpretable classification model is as simple as calling ClassificationPipeline(data, words="all", assertions="all")
key_sources: Julian Bernado, Ana Trindade Ribeiro, Xander Beberman, and Susanna Loeb. (2026). EduBehaviors: Assertion-Based Schemas for Auditable Coding of Educational Dialogues. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27043

article_title: EduBehaviors: Assertion-based Schemas for Auditable Coding of Educational Dialogues
citation: Julian Bernado, Ana Trindade Ribeiro, Xander Beberman, and Susanna Loeb. (2026). EduBehaviors: Assertion-Based Schemas for Auditable Coding of Educational Dialogues. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27043
title: Share assertion definitions, annotated examples, trained classifiers, and combination rules so researchers can build on existing annotation work
description: The article recommends making behavioral annotation components reusable and inspectable: an assertion annotated once in a corpus can inform multiple construct labels, and assertion annotations can train smaller classifiers for later annotation. Sharing "assertion definitions, annotated examples, trained classifiers, and combination rules" reduces the need to develop every measure from the beginning, while each reused measure still requires validation for its intended use.
requirements: Assertion annotations must remain inspectable so researchers can assess how assertions contribute to each construct label
constraints: Applying trained classifiers to another corpus requires checking that they identify the intended behaviors in the new setting
target_learners: education researchers measuring teaching practices and student thinking in conversational data
target_learning_goals: reducing repeated development and annotation work across educational construct measures
examples: Identifying whether an educator asks a question can contribute to measures of focusing questions, funneling questions, responses to student mistakes, or relationship building, with other evidence distinguishing these uses

article_title: \"We'll Fix It Later\": Education, AI, and the Deferral of Student Privacy in EdTech
citation: Meghna Manoj Nair, Rachel Greenstadt. (2026). "We'll Fix It Later": Education, AI, and the Deferral of Student Privacy in EdTech. New York University. https://www.nyu.edu
title: The privacy deferral cycle in EdTech
description: A theory-building framework from the interview study, summarized in Figure 1, in which privacy deferral reproduces itself across the product lifecycle. As the article puts it, "Figure 1 summarizes the resulting theory": privacy struggles to enter the business case at strategy and funding stages, cloud delegation substitutes for internal engineering during build, pilots surface usability rather than privacy concerns, procurement can shift responsibility to schools with uneven capacity, AI introduces less visible downstream uses, and incidents finally create reactive attention. The cycle continues because underlying incentive, ownership, and feedback structures remain unchanged.
requirements: The framework was built from 12 interviews using Charmaz's grounded theory principles, with credibility grounded in convergence across roles and contexts rather than saturation
constraints: The article states the categories are an explanatory structure for findings, not evidence that every EdTech organization exhibits each pattern
The article does not claim analytical saturation or generalizability from the 12-person sample
target_learners: K-12 and higher-education students using institutionally mandated EdTech platforms
target_learning_goals: Protection of student data privacy and governance of AI-enabled learning tools
examples: Figure 1 depicts privacy deferral across the EdTech product lifecycle, where market pressure and delegation stabilize deferral and weak feedback loops sustain it
key_sources: Meghna Manoj Nair, Rachel Greenstadt. (2026). "We'll Fix It Later": Education, AI, and the Deferral of Student Privacy in EdTech. New York University. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28137

article_title: An Educator-Guided LLM Pedagogical Agent for Scaffolded Feedback in Conceptual Database Design
citation: Sara Riazi and Pedram Rooshenas. (2026). An Educator-Guided LLM Pedagogical Agent for Scaffolded Feedback in Conceptual Database Design. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00870v1
title: Educator-guided architecture separating artifact-grounded diagnosis, pedagogical workflow control, and student-facing LLM generation
description: The architecture places a hidden, artifact-grounded diagnosis inside an explicit, stateful pedagogical workflow so the language model is not solely responsible for instructional strategy. As the article puts it, "The educator defines the stages, student actions, and disclosure limits, while the LLM selects or generates content within those constraints." The controller assembles the context available to the LLM from the ERD diagnosis, educator resources, and episode history, and logs stage, context, responses, and disclosed information for later review. This preserves student authorship while making the timing, specificity, and extent of automated assistance explicit and configurable.
requirements: Educator-authored requirements, rubrics, concept-aligned questions and resources, and workflow definitions that express governance over disclosure and progression
constraints: Because the LLM may still produce content that exceeds stage limits, the system logs interactions for later review; staged disclosure cannot protect against wrong-relationship or wrong-concept selection, and the no-error route is unbuffered
target_learners: Undergraduate and mixed-level database systems students
target_learning_goals: Conceptual database design: translating requirements into entities, attributes, relationships, and semantic constraints in ER diagrams
examples: The deployed four-stage workflow in an ERD editor, where each request creates an episode linking the artifact, hidden diagnosis, active stage, and interaction
key_sources: Sara Riazi and Pedram Rooshenas. (2026). An Educator-Guided LLM Pedagogical Agent for Scaffolded Feedback in Conceptual Database Design. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00870

article_title: An Educator-Guided LLM Pedagogical Agent for Scaffolded Feedback in Conceptual Database Design
citation: Sara Riazi and Pedram Rooshenas. (2026). An Educator-Guided LLM Pedagogical Agent for Scaffolded Feedback in Conceptual Database Design. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00870v1
title: Four-stage learner-controlled workflow: concept check, guided application, guided feedback, and guided Q&A
description: The deployed workflow implements graduated prompting under learner control in an ERD editor. "The deployed workflow follows graduated prompting under learner control [3, 11, 33]. Each accessed stage consumes one feedback credit." Stage 1 uses an educator-authored question pool the LLM selects from without modifying; Stage 2 fills template slots from the selected ERD component and evaluates responses against a reference rubric; Stage 3 gives concise artifact-grounded feedback while withholding the localized correction; Stage 4 supports multi-turn requirement-grounded clarification without generating the complete ERD. After every interaction, students may revise the ERD or request more explicit assistance, so each stage can be a stopping point.
requirements: Educator-defined stage sequence, question pools, templates with reference rubrics, and feedback credits; the diagnostic pipeline from a prior requirement-grounded ERD feedback system
constraints: Progression is learner-controlled rather than automatic; the agent does not modify the ERD; each accessed stage consumes one credit
target_learners: Undergraduate database systems students revising ER diagrams
target_learning_goals: Applying modeling concepts such as identifying relationships, weak entities, cardinality, and participation constraints to specific requirements
examples: Stage 2 template "Do you think [Relationship] is identifying?" instantiated for the relationship under review, with the LLM evaluating the written response against the rubric
key_sources: Sara Riazi and Pedram Rooshenas. (2026). An Educator-Guided LLM Pedagogical Agent for Scaffolded Feedback in Conceptual Database Design. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00870

article_title: An Educator-Guided LLM Pedagogical Agent for Scaffolded Feedback in Conceptual Database Design
citation: Sara Riazi and Pedram Rooshenas. (2026). An Educator-Guided LLM Pedagogical Agent for Scaffolded Feedback in Conceptual Database Design. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00870v1
title: Episode memory linking feedback episodes to versioned ERD states
description: Each feedback request creates a session history containing stages shown, student answers, generated feedback, follow-up questions, credit use, and next actions, allowing later stages to condition on what has already occurred. "Episodes are linked to saved artifact states through the student, environment, selected relationship, feedback identifier, and ERD version." Returning to the editor ends the episode, and a later request reproceses the current ERD as a new episode rather than assuming the previous diagnosis remains valid. These records support analysis of progression, disclosure, repetition, and subsequent target-level changes, and are not treated as a persistent model of student knowledge.
requirements: Saved artifact states and logged interactions so episodes can be linked to ERD versions and analyzed
constraints: Records coordinate the current episode and are explicitly not a persistent student-knowledge model; a new request after revision creates a new diagnosis
target_learners: Students requesting feedback in an ERD editor
target_learning_goals: Revising conceptual database designs based on staged feedback
examples: The deployment's artifact-interaction-revision traces containing the initiating ERD, hidden context, stages accessed, student responses, and next saved ERD
key_sources: Sara Riazi and Pedram Rooshenas. (2026). An Educator-Guided LLM Pedagogical Agent for Scaffolded Feedback in Conceptual Database Design. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00870

article_title: Reimagining Success and Failure: Equitable Assessment Practices in an Age of Artificial Intelligence
citation: Dollinger, M., & Nieminen, J. (2026). Reimagining success and failure: equitable assessment practices in an age of AI. Journal of University Teaching and Learning Practice, 23(1). https://doi.org/10.53761/20z06b11
title: Two-dimension framing of equitable assessment reimagining: distribution of knowledge and agentic assessment
description: The paper organises its argument for equitable assessment in the age of generative AI around two key dimensions along which entrenched notions of student success can be challenged: "distribution of knowledge and agentic assessment". Distribution of knowledge concerns who gets recognised as knowing, moving beyond individual performance toward "diverse ways of knowing"; agentic assessment concerns valuing "collaboration and student agency over individual performance and predetermined standards". The framework is used to reposition GenAI from an integrity threat to a lever for redesigning assessment.
requirements: Applies to higher-education assessment contexts where generative AI is available to students
constraints: Proposed as a conceptual argument in a conceptual paper, not an empirically tested framework
target_learning_goals: equitable recognition of diverse ways of knowing; student agency in assessment
examples: The paper's abstract proposes exploring how GenAI may challenge entrenched and exclusionary notions of student success across these two dimensions.
key_sources: Dollinger, M., & Nieminen, J. (2026). Reimagining success and failure: equitable assessment practices in an age of AI. Journal of University Teaching and Learning Practice, 23(1). https://doi.org/10.53761/20z06b11

article_title: Reimagining Success and Failure: Equitable Assessment Practices in an Age of Artificial Intelligence
citation: Dollinger, M., & Nieminen, J. (2026). Reimagining success and failure: equitable assessment practices in an age of AI. Journal of University Teaching and Learning Practice, 23(1). https://doi.org/10.53761/20z06b11
title: Design assessment to value collaboration and student agency over individual performance and predetermined standards
description: This principle holds that in the age of generative AI, assessment should be designed as "a catalyst for more equitable assessment that values collaboration and student agency over individual performance and predetermined standards". Rather than treating GenAI use as an integrity violation to be policed, educators treat it as an occasion to redesign assessment so that success is not defined by individual performance against predetermined standards. The paper advances this as a design orientation for higher education.
requirements: Educators willing to reconsider entrenched definitions of student success and failure in assessment design
constraints: Advanced as a conceptual proposal; the supplied text reports no empirical evaluation of the redesign approach
target_learning_goals: equitable assessment; student agency; collaboration
examples: The paper proposes GenAI as an opportunity to move away from assessment practices that sort and rank students toward approaches that recognise diverse ways of knowing.
key_sources: Dollinger, M., & Nieminen, J. (2026). Reimagining success and failure: equitable assessment practices in an age of AI. Journal of University Teaching and Learning Practice, 23(1). https://doi.org/10.53761/20z06b11

article_title: 'AI Should Help Them Learn, Not Learn for Them': University Staff Perspectives on the Role of Generative AI in Education
citation: Enright, H., Horvath, D., Petrovic, K., & Šarkić, B. (2026). “AI Should Help them Learn, Not Learn for Them”: University Staff Perspectives on the Role of Generative AI in Education. Journal of University Teaching and Learning Practice. https://doi.org/10.53761/d5n2yh02
title: GenAI in education should support student learning rather than replace it — helping students learn, not learning for them.
description: The article's framing principle, drawn from its title, is that generative AI in education should serve student learning rather than substitute for it: "AI Should Help them Learn, Not Learn for Them." This principle captures staff views that GenAI risks eroding essential academic skills such as critical thinking and creativity, while its productive use lies in enhancing teaching practices and student-centred learning activities.
requirements: Institutional guidance that positions GenAI as a support for learning processes rather than a replacement for student effort.
constraints: Staff reported potential erosion of essential academic skills such as critical thinking and creativity when GenAI is used inappropriately.
target_learning_goals: Critical thinking
Creativity
Academic skill development
examples: Staff survey respondents at an Australian university articulated this framing in their perspectives on the role of GenAI in learning and teaching.

article_title: Mapping the Integration of AI into Business Education: Insights from a Decade of Research
citation: Espino, L., & Espino, C. (2026). Mapping the Integration of AI into Business Education: Insights from a Decade of Research. Journal of University Teaching and Learning Practice. https://doi.org/10.53761/5yhdnk13
title: Bibliometric mapping framework for the AI-in-business-education research landscape
description: The study organizes a decade of research on AI in business education through a bibliometric analysis framework. It states that "Bibliographic coupling and co-word analysis, facilitated through VOSviewer, were employed to uncover intellectual structures, thematic clusters, and conceptual linkages within the field." The framework combines document-level coupling (intellectual structure) with keyword co-occurrence (conceptual structure) to yield clusters, trends, and gaps that inform future research agendas and strategic reforms.
requirements: A corpus of peer-reviewed journal articles extracted from a database (here, 213 articles from Dimensions, 2015–2024)
VOSviewer tooling for bibliographic coupling and co-word analysis
constraints: Findings reflect the indexed literature in the Dimensions database for 2015–2024 and the field of business education specifically
target_learners: business education students in higher education
target_learning_goals: understanding how AI is integrated into business curricula and pedagogy
examples: The study applied the framework to 213 articles and reported four research clusters and three conceptual trends
key_sources: Espino, L., & Espino, C. (2026). Mapping the Integration of AI into Business Education: Insights from a Decade of Research. Journal of University Teaching and Learning Practice. https://doi.org/10.53761/5yhdnk13

article_title: Research on the optimization of the training system of university faculty development centers in the context of GenAI: a comparative analysis based on Chinese and Kazakhstani universities
citation: Bi T, Araily S, Lyu A and Xiu S (2026) Research on the optimization of the training system of university faculty development centers in the context of GenAI: a comparative analysis based on Chinese and Kazakhstani universities. Front. Psychol. 17:1890508. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1890508
title: GenAI pedagogical readiness: a seven-dimension faculty competence construct
description: The article defines GenAI pedagogical readiness as "university faculty members' capacity to use, evaluate, and regulate GenAI in course practice". The construct comprises seven dimensions — basic GenAI understanding, prompt design, AI-supported instructional design, AI-supported assessment, critical judgement, educational ethics, and disciplinary transfer — each measured by four items on a 1–5 agreement scale. It builds on TPACK, DigCompEdu, and AI literacy frameworks but focuses specifically on whether faculty can judge, revise, assess, and regulate generated materials in course practice. The framework connects baseline readiness, training design, and prompt-level evidence through situated professional learning, technology-integrated pedagogical judgement, and institutional mediation.
requirements: Measured through a seven-dimension scale with four items per dimension on a 1–5 agreement scale, translated into Chinese, English, Kazakh, and Russian with back-translation and reconciliation
constraints: Primarily self-report; the authors note concept interpretation and response styles across language backgrounds may still have affected part of the evidence
target_learners: University faculty with current higher education teaching responsibility
target_learning_goals: Using, evaluating, and regulating GenAI in course practice, including prompt design, assessment redesign, and responsible-use explanation
examples: The scale showed total-sample Cronbach's alpha ranging from 0.822 to 0.889 and McDonald's omega from 0.825 to 0.891, with partial scalar measurement invariance supported across the Chinese and Kazakhstani samples
key_sources: Bi T, Araily S, Lyu A and Xiu S (2026) Research on the optimization of the training system of university faculty development centers in the context of GenAI: a comparative analysis based on Chinese and Kazakhstani universities. Front. Psychol. 17:1890508. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1890508

citation: Bi T, Araily S, Lyu A and Xiu S (2026) Research on the optimization of the training system of university faculty development centers in the context of GenAI: a comparative analysis based on Chinese and Kazakhstani universities. Front. Psychol. 17:1890508. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1890508
title: Faculty development centers should build GenAI readiness by having faculty work on their own course artifacts under a structured prompt-task cycle
description: The article's practical lesson is that "faculty development centers can support prompt design, critical judgement, instructional design, and assessment capacity by asking faculty to work on their owncourseartifactsunderastructuredprompt-taskcycle". The cycle runs prompt formulation, generated-output review, course-material revision, and written reflection, organized around course-material preparation, learning-task design, assessment revision, and AI-use rule explanation. It outperformed conventional GenAI-focused faculty development (function introduction, teaching-case explanation, general application advice) on all seven readiness dimensions at post-test.
requirements: A structured prompt template requiring seven components: course objective, student level, task constraints, assessment criteria, faculty verification, student disclosure, and risk control
Four 90-minute onsite workshops with trained local facilitators and a shared training manual, task sheets, and performance checklist
constraints: Group assignment reflected voluntary sign-up and institutional scheduling, so training results are best interpreted as associations rather than strict causal estimates; delayed retention was examined only for prompt design
target_learners: University faculty in faculty development programs in higher education
target_learning_goals: Prompt design, critical judgement, instructional design, and assessment capacity for pedagogical uses of GenAI
examples: In the evaluated intervention, Session 1 rewrote a course objective into a prompt specifying objective, student level, prior knowledge, duration, language, and output format; Session 3 generated or revised a rubric with process evidence and student disclosure; Session 4 identified hallucination, bias, privacy, and overreliance risks and drafted course-level AI-use rules

article_title: Family-school autonomy support for children's responsible use of generative artificial intelligence
citation: Fan Y, Li X and Zhang R (2026). Family-school autonomy support for children's responsible use of generative artificial intelligence: a self-determination theory synthesis and developmental research agenda. Front. Psychol. 17:1969217. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1969217
title: A five-level family-school autonomy-support framework for children's responsible GenAI use, with evidence-tiered links
description: The review proposes a framework in which "Family-side and school-side inputs (Level 1) are hypothesized to act both directly and through a coordination layer (Level 2) on basic psychological need satisfaction (Level 3), which in turn supports moral and self-regulatory mediators (Level 4) and, through them, academic integrity and learning engagement (Level 5)." Links are graded into three evidence tiers: direct evidence in under-18s, indirect evidence from university samples, and theoretically specified but untested links. Table 1 operationalizes seven propositions (P1-P7) with family-side and school-side operationalizations and disconfirming results for each.
requirements: Comparable autonomy-support measures obtained from the same students in both settings to test the coordination layer
Behavioral rather than self-reported indices of responsible use
constraints: Because no reviewed study measured a family and a school input in the same participants, every link into and out of the coordination layer is Tier 3
The framework is a testable synthesis, not an established causal model
target_learners: children and adolescents using generative AI in learning
target_learning_goals: responsible, calibrated, and transparent GenAI use
learning engagement
academic integrity
examples: Table 1 states seven propositions P1-P7, each with family-side and school-side operationalizations, hypothesized processes, current evidence tier, and the result that would disconfirm it
key_sources: Fan Y, Li X and Zhang R (2026). Family-school autonomy support for children's responsible use of generative artificial intelligence: a self-determination theory synthesis and developmental research agenda. Front. Psychol. 17:1969217. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1969217

article_title: Family-school autonomy support for children's responsible use of generative artificial intelligence
citation: Fan Y, Li X and Zhang R (2026). Family-school autonomy support for children's responsible use of generative artificial intelligence: a self-determination theory synthesis and developmental research agenda. Front. Psychol. 17:1969217. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1969217
title: Three competing, falsifiable hypotheses for family-school coordination of autonomy support (additive, synergistic, compensatory)
description: Because family-side and school-side literatures rest on non-overlapping samples, the review states coordination as three competing hypotheses rather than an established effect. "H1 (additive): family and school autonomy support each predict responsible use, giving two main effects and no interaction. H2 (synergistic): the association between school autonomy support and responsible use is stronger where family autonomy support is high, giving a positive interaction." H3 (compensatory) holds that support in either setting is sufficient, giving a negative interaction. H2 is the version embedded in most current guidance and the one for which no evidence yet exists.
requirements: Discriminating the hypotheses requires comparable autonomy-support measures from the same students in both settings
A design powered for the interaction rather than for main effects
A factorial trial contrasting family-only, school-only, coordinated, and usual-practice guidance would be the strongest test
constraints: No equivalent test exists for GenAI; synergy should be treated as a hypothesis rather than an established effect
target_learning_goals: responsible GenAI use across home and school settings
examples: The review cites a meta-analysis of family-school partnership interventions improving children's social-emotional functioning in other domains, with efficacy moderated by which components are combined

citation: Fan Y, Li X and Zhang R (2026). Family-school autonomy support for children's responsible use of generative artificial intelligence: a self-determination theory synthesis and developmental research agenda. Front. Psychol. 17:1969217. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1969217
title: Pair clear GenAI policy boundaries with autonomy support rather than choosing between control and permissiveness
description: The review argues against a false choice between unrestricted autonomy and technological control, holding that "Clarity is most likely to support integrity when rules specify acceptable assistance, explain why boundaries matter, offer practice in disclosure and verification, and preserve meaningful choice within those boundaries." In SDT terms, autonomy support and structure are separable dimensions, and detection or punishment alone cannot cultivate judgment. The principle integrates transparent boundaries with AI literacy, reflective-use training, process-oriented assessment, and disclosure practice.
requirements: Rules that specify acceptable assistance and explain why boundaries matter
Practice in disclosure and verification
Meaningful choice preserved within the boundaries
constraints: Students in nursing education report insufficient guidance about acceptable GenAI use, so clarity alone may not reach learners without delivery
target_learners: children and adolescents using generative AI in learning
target_learning_goals: academic integrity
responsible and reflective GenAI use
examples: The review cites process-aware pedagogy, source verification, citation skills, and redesigned assessments as ways to make standards actionable, and a student-partnered Delphi study producing 14 consensus principles for responsible GenAI use in medical education

title: Use hybrid intelligent feedback systems in which teachers support students in interpreting and applying GenAI feedback
description: The article proposes combining GenAI feedback with teacher support so that teachers help students interpret and apply machine-generated comments. Although CoT-prompted GenAI produced the highest-rated feedback, "this higher feedback quality did not lead to significantly greater improvements in revisions", so the article argues that "students’ engagement with and uptake of feedback play a critical role" and highlights "hybrid intelligent feedback systems in which teachers support students in interpreting and applying GenAI feedback".

constraints: The article reports that feedback quality alone is insufficient to enhance writing outcomes
target_learners: higher education students writing argumentative essays
target_learning_goals: improving argumentative essay quality through feedback uptake and revision
examples: In the experiment, all three feedback conditions produced comparable revision gains, and feedback quality predicted revisions only in the teacher condition

Illuminating complex student realities of artificial intelligence through an entangled pedagogy framework. Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10734-026-01730-1
title: Entangled pedagogy as a lens for analysing student engagement with generative AI
description: Entangled pedagogy (Fawns, 2022) positions technology as integral to educational activity, "foregrounding its inseparability with context, purpose, values, and educational methods." The article applies it to three students' GenAI accounts, finding that the framework's "five initial categories—technology, methods, purposes, values, and context—were entangled with other considerations, including beliefs, identities, emotions, positionalities, and the perceived actions of others." It treats pedagogy as an emergent, distributed phenomenon co-produced through relations between teaching and learning.
requirements: Researchers make explicit decisions about what to include, exclude and foreground to bound the analysis, using selected excerpts as a viewfinder
constraints: All representations of entangled phenomena are necessarily partial; the article does not propose expanding the framework to every possible element
target_learning_goals: understanding how students negotiate GenAI in relation to studies, identities and practices
examples: The study analysed three participants from different focus groups as situated configurations of intersecting relations, using Barad's notion of agential cuts to bound the analysis

article_title: Fear and Awe: Making Sense of Generative AI Through Metaphor
citation: Carmen Vallis, Stephanie Wilson, Alison Casey. (2025). Fear and Awe: Making Sense of Generative AI Through Metaphor. Journal of Interactive Media Education. https://doi.org/10.5334/jime.972
title: Four-category taxonomy of GenAI metaphors in higher education: Functions, Roles, Qualities, Agency
description: The article proposes a four-category taxonomy of metaphors used to conceptualise generative AI in educational contexts, derived from thematic analysis of workshop artefacts. Functions metaphors "conceptualise GenAI in terms of its tasks and practical capabilities as tools or materials"; Roles position GenAI in human-like relationships; Qualities describe its "unknowable, unreliable, or magical nature"; and Agency attribute volition or autonomous action, often expressing concerns about control and power. Unlike prior AI metaphor studies, the authors argue their categories capture how metaphors emerge through collaborative social meaning-making linked to pedagogical concerns and lived experience.
requirements: Derived from collaborative workshop elicitation with multidisciplinary participant groups rather than individual elicitation
constraints: The authors acknowledge categories might reflect aspects of the workshop design in addition to participants' authentic conceptualisations
target_learning_goals: critical AI literacy
sensemaking about emerging technologies
examples: Sample metaphors include Swiss army knife (Functions), frenemy (Roles), black box (Qualities), and sinister robot (Agency).
key_sources: Carmen Vallis, Stephanie Wilson, Alison Casey. (2025). Fear and Awe: Making Sense of Generative AI Through Metaphor. Journal of Interactive Media Education. https://doi.org/10.5334/jime.972

citation: Carmen Vallis, Stephanie Wilson, Alison Casey. (2025). Fear and Awe: Making Sense of Generative AI Through Metaphor. Journal of Interactive Media Education. https://doi.org/10.5334/jime.972
title: Move beyond binary permit/prohibit GenAI policies toward frameworks acknowledging both opportunities and ethical risks
description: The article argues institutional responses to GenAI should not reduce to permitting or prohibiting the technology. Instead, institutions could develop frameworks that acknowledge both opportunities, as the "augmenting device" metaphors suggest, and the ethical risks reflected in "black box" concerns. Metaphor workshops are proposed as a means of gathering diverse stakeholder perspectives, and programs should address the gap between anthropomorphic perceptions and GenAI's actual capabilities.
requirements: Institutional willingness to gather diverse stakeholder perspectives, e.g. through metaphor workshops, before policy formation
constraints: Grounded in findings from a single university business school context with a small student sample
target_learning_goals: ethical and equitable AI implementation in education
examples: The article suggests professional development could address specific fears surfaced through metaphors, such as anxiety about AI replacing teaching roles.

article_title: The friction paradox: generative AI and the educational value of difficulty in education abroad
citation: Gupta, K. (2026). The friction paradox: generative AI and the educational value of difficulty in education abroad. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-10609387/v1
title: The friction paradox: generative AI can widen access to education abroad while weakening a principal learning mechanism
description: The friction paradox holds that the same generative AI system can remove an exclusionary language barrier in one context and eliminate a valuable communicative encounter in another. The article states that "generative AI can simultaneously make education abroad more inclusive and weaken one of its principal learning mechanisms". It extends desirable-difficulties and productive-failure arguments to relational difficulty within cross-cultural encounters, where difficulty is relational, interpretively open, and avoidance is socially invisible.
requirements: Institutional policy must distinguish barriers that exclude students from encounters that develop them, since removing both indiscriminately may leave education abroad more convenient but less educational
constraints: The framework is conceptual and untested; the article states the propositions in Section 6 may not survive examination
target_learners: students in cross-border education-abroad programmes, both short-term/semester and full-degree mobility
target_learning_goals: intercultural competence
independence
capacity to interpret unfamiliar perspectives
examples: The article contrasts translating an emergency medical instruction, which protects access, with translating every informal conversation, which may reduce language development and relationship formation
key_sources: Gupta, K. (2026). The friction paradox: generative AI and the educational value of difficulty in education abroad. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-10609387/v1

article_title: The friction paradox: generative AI and the educational value of difficulty in education abroad
citation: Gupta, K. (2026). The friction paradox: generative AI and the educational value of difficulty in education abroad. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-10609387/v1
title: The mediation gradient: five levels of interpretive agency transferred to AI, not volume of use
description: The mediation gradient organises AI use by "the degree of interpretive agency transferred to it" rather than by frequency or volume. Five levels are distinguished: access, preparation, co-interpretation, delegation and substitution. The level is diagnosed by five questions: who frames the question, who evaluates competing meanings, who chooses the response, whether a human encounter follows, and whether the student reflects afterwards. Timing interacts with the gradient: the same output may function as preparation, delegation or co-interpretation depending on when it is used.
requirements: Diagnosis requires asking who frames the question, who evaluates competing meanings, who chooses the response, whether a human encounter follows, and whether the student reflects afterwards
constraints: Access and preparation generally preserve agency; delegation and substitution may be justified for harmful friction but are most likely to erode learning when applied to productive friction
target_learning_goals: intercultural learning
interpretive agency
host-community engagement
examples: A lengthy AI-drafted message that the student interrogates and rewrites may transfer less agency than a brief cultural explanation accepted without examination
key_sources: Gupta, K. (2026). The friction paradox: generative AI and the educational value of difficulty in education abroad. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-10609387/v1

article_title: The friction paradox: generative AI and the educational value of difficulty in education abroad
citation: Gupta, K. (2026). The friction paradox: generative AI and the educational value of difficulty in education abroad. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-10609387/v1
title: Two-dimensional taxonomy of friction: harmful and productive friction by educational function, synthetic friction by technological origin
description: The taxonomy separates friction classified by educational function from friction generated by the technology itself. "Harmful friction and productive friction classify difficulty by educational function: whether it excludes the student from participation or creates conditions in which learning may occur." Synthetic friction classifies difficulty by technological origin — difficulty created or intensified by AI inaccuracy, cultural reduction, false confidence or inappropriate substitution — and its educational function remains open. The dimensions intersect rather than form three positions on one scale.
requirements: Synthetic friction should be made visible and contestable rather than simply eliminated, because its educational function depends on whether it is detected and examined
constraints: The taxonomy rejects friction romanticism, in which difficulty is presumed to build resilience and support is denied, and friction elimination, in which every uncertainty is treated as an inefficiency
target_learning_goals: distinguishing exclusionary barriers from developmentally productive difficulty
epistemic agency under AI mediation
examples: Table 1 lists examples: harmful friction includes inability to communicate a medical condition; productive friction includes attempting a host-language interaction; synthetic friction includes incorrect translation and stereotyped cultural explanation
key_sources: Gupta, K. (2026). The friction paradox: generative AI and the educational value of difficulty in education abroad. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-10609387/v1

article_title: The friction paradox: generative AI and the educational value of difficulty in education abroad
citation: Gupta, K. (2026). The friction paradox: generative AI and the educational value of difficulty in education abroad. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-10609387/v1
title: Immersion heuristic: crossing AI support with human engagement to target supported immersion
description: A two-by-two diagnostic aid for programme designers crossing AI support (low/high) with human engagement (low/high). The four cells are unmanaged struggle, traditional immersion, frictionless enclosure and supported immersion. "The target condition is supported immersion, not minimal technology." The heuristic also clarifies why volume of AI use is theoretically weak as a measure: two students may use AI equally often, one to prepare for and reflect on daily host-community interactions, the other to avoid them.
requirements: AI support and human engagement must be treated as varying independently when designing programmes
constraints: Offered as a diagnostic aid rather than as a further theoretical construct
target_learning_goals: host-community interaction
supported participation without frictionless enclosure
examples: Table 2 describes frictionless enclosure as AI translating, interpreting, reassuring and solving problems while host-community interaction remains limited
key_sources: Gupta, K. (2026). The friction paradox: generative AI and the educational value of difficulty in education abroad. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-10609387/v1

article_title: The friction paradox: generative AI and the educational value of difficulty in education abroad
citation: Gupta, K. (2026). The friction paradox: generative AI and the educational value of difficulty in education abroad. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-10609387/v1
title: Friction-conversion principle: reduce harmful friction, convert manageable difficulty, preserve interpretive role, expose synthetic friction
description: The article proposes that "responsible AI in education abroad should reduce harmful friction, convert manageable difficulty into supported participation, preserve the student's interpretive role in productive encounters, and make synthetic friction visible and contestable". Friction conversion differs from friction removal: the objective is to change the conditions under which difficulty is encountered rather than to eliminate the difficulty. The principle places educational purpose before technological efficiency.
requirements: Programmes must be able to classify friction by type before deciding whether to remove, convert or expose it
constraints: Productive friction should not be maximised indiscriminately but preserved in a form students can engage with safely and reflectively
target_learning_goals: intercultural learning
participation
interpretive agency
examples: Instead of writing the student's complaint to a landlord, AI helps identify the issue, explains possible tones, teaches relevant phrases and asks the student to select and personalise the message

article_title: When universities advocate GAI but practice falls short: student appraisals and creative process engagement in art education
citation: Chen Y (2026) When universities advocate GAI but practice falls short: student appraisals and creative process engagement in art education. Front. Psychol. 17:1955192. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1955192
title: Dual-path cognitive appraisal model of GAI advocacy–practice inconsistency
description: The article proposes a dual-path model grounded in the transactional theory of stress and coping, in which perceived GAI advocacy–practice inconsistency is appraised simultaneously as a hindrance and as a challenge, each carrying an opposing indirect association with creative process engagement. As the article states, "we propose a dual-path model in which GAI advocacy–practice inconsistency is associated with students' creative process engagement through hindrance and challenge appraisals." Pathways thinking is incorporated as a boundary condition that differentially shapes the two indirect relationships. The model extends organizational word–deed alignment research to GAI-supported art education.
requirements: Students must perceive a discrepancy between institutional GAI commitments and actual implementation for the appraisal process to operate
constraints: The scenario manipulation captured a broader experience of inconsistent implementation rather than an isolated word–deed inconsistency effect
target_learners: undergraduate and postgraduate art students in higher education
target_learning_goals: sustained engagement in creative processes such as problem identification, information searching and encoding, and idea generation in GAI-assisted art learning
examples: Study 2 tested the full model with PLS-SEM on 425 students' actual GAI-supported art-learning experiences, including direct, indirect, moderating, and conditional indirect relationships.

title: Universities should align GAI commitments with teaching, assessment, and support practices while helping students develop alternative coping routes
description: The article's practical implication is that institutional advocacy for generative AI must be matched by consistent implementation, and that students should simultaneously be supported in developing alternative routes for coping with implementation uncertainty. As the article puts it, "Universities should align GAI commitments with teaching, assessment, and support practices while helping students develop alternative routes for coping with implementation uncertainty." The principle rests on the finding that inconsistency evokes both hindrance and challenge appraisals with opposing engagement consequences.
requirements: Institutions must make public GAI commitments operational in course arrangements, instructor practices, resource support, and assessment standards
constraints: The findings are associational and specific to GAI-supported art education in Chinese higher education institutions
target_learners: art students in higher education using GAI tools
target_learning_goals: maintaining creative process engagement under uncertain institutional AI implementation
examples: The article recommends aligning commitments with teaching, assessment, and support practices and helping students develop alternative routes for coping with implementation uncertainty.
