article_title: Development and validation of the generative AI assessment literacy scale for higher education students
citation: Nie J, Zhang Z, Lu X, Zhang Y and Zhang M (2026) Development and validation of the generative AI assessment literacy scale for higher education students: psychometric evidence and associations with feedback engagement and academic integrity. Front. Educ. 11:1934632. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1934632
title: Generative AI assessment literacy as an assessment-specific integrative construct with five dimensions
description: The article defines generative AI assessment literacy as "students’ assessment-specific capacity to understand assessment criteria, judge the appropriateness of GenAI use, verify AI-generated content or feedback, disclose AI use ethically, and use AI-supported feedback for responsible revision in assessment-related learning tasks." It is positioned as an integrative construct, not a replacement for general AI literacy, assessment literacy, feedback literacy, or academic integrity literacy, becoming salient when GenAI is used within assessed work. The five GAA-LS dimensions represent a sequence of situated judgments moving from criteria and task boundaries to verification, disclosure, and feedback-based revision.
requirements: The construct applies when GenAI is used within assessed work, where students must make situated judgments about criteria, task boundaries, evidence quality, disclosure, and revision.
constraints: The article states it is not proposed as a replacement for general AI literacy, assessment literacy, feedback literacy, or academic integrity literacy.
target_learning_goals: responsible GenAI use in assessment-related tasks, including criteria interpretation, verification, disclosure, and feedback-based revision
examples: The GAA-LS operationalizes the construct as 18 items across five dimensions: assessment criteria awareness, AI-task appropriateness judgment, verification and evidence checking, ethical attribution and academic integrity, and feedback uptake and revision literacy.

title: Generative AI Assessment Literacy Scale (GAA-LS), an 18-item five-dimension instrument
description: The GAA-LS is a self-report questionnaire measuring higher education students' assessment-specific capacity to use GenAI responsibly. The final version includes 18 items across five dimensions: assessment criteria awareness (4 items), AI-task appropriateness judgment (4 items), verification and evidence checking (4 items), ethical attribution and academic integrity (3 items), and feedback uptake and revision literacy (3 items). article_title: Generative AI-supported instruction as a cognitive scaffold: effects on senior high school students' geometric reasoning and proof construction
citation: Davor I (2026) Generative AI-supported instruction as a cognitive scaffold: effects on senior high school students' geometric reasoning and proof construction. Front. Educ. 11:1869961. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1869961
title: Generative AI as a cognitive scaffold bridging Van Hiele level transitions and reducing extraneous cognitive load in geometry proof
description: The study grounds its intervention in Van Hiele's model of geometric thinking and Cognitive Load Theory. In this framework, "generative AI-assisted instruction is viewed as a scaffold that assists students in progressing from one level to another within the Van Hiele levels", supporting the transition from informal visual intuition to formal deduction. From the Cognitive Load perspective, AI-generated representations and prompts reduce extraneous load from diagram construction, freeing resources for selecting theorems, justifying choices, and ordering logical steps. The AI is positioned as a mediator of reasoning, not a provider of complete proofs.
requirements: The AI must provide vivid imagery, require justifications for what is observed, and assist in arranging deductive steps, without giving complete proofs or final answers.
constraints: The article states the cognitive mechanisms underlying the observed improvements were not directly measured, so the theoretical account remains an interpretation.
target_learners: senior high school students in geometry courses
target_learning_goals: geometric reasoning
proof construction
transition from visual intuition to deductive reasoning
examples: The intervention had the AI develop dynamic visual representations and provide guided prompts with which students justified relationships, identified relevant theorems, and arranged logical statements.

article_title: Generative AI in creative education: baseline-linked evidence on learning processes, artistic performance, and authorship
citation: Shen, N., Lee, L. S., and He, A. (2026). Generative AI in creative education: baseline-linked evidence on learning processes, artistic performance, and authorship. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1956939
title: Process–outcome decoupling in AI-supported creative education
description: The article develops process–outcome decoupling as an explanatory account for AI-supported creative learning: perceived support, fluency, and confidence can rise while assessed artistic competence, authorship, and judgment do not. The authors write that "This tension can be understood as a process–outcome decoupling pattern: AI may intensify the visible activity of creative learning without necessarily strengthening the artistic competence, ownership, or judgment through that learning is evaluated." The framework draws on illusions of learning and cognitive offloading research and motivates evaluating AI use by authorship, internalization, and transferable agency, not output quality alone.
requirements: Evidence must link reported learning-process experience with assessed performance rather than perceptions alone, as the study does by combining prior performance, final assessment, and questionnaire data.
constraints: The article frames the pattern as an association-based account from a single-institution, course-based design, not a causal demonstration.
target_learners: undergraduate art and design students in studio-based courses
target_learning_goals: creative agency and authorship
internalization of creative decisions
transferable artistic judgment
examples: The study operationalizes the framework by comparing AI-use associations with perceived support and skill transfer against baseline-adjusted final performance and performance-change models.

As the authors state, "AI mayfunctionasassistivesupportwhenstudentsuseitforideation, referencegathering,processmanagement,reﬁnement,ortechnique learning. title: Five-dimension creative-performance assessment rubric with blinded dual evaluation
description: Final artistic outcomes in the study were assessed with a standardized rubric across five 20-point dimensions — creativity, aesthetic quality, technique, authorship, and completion — summed to a 100-point total. The rubric defines authorship as "visible evidence of independent creative intention, decision-making, personal expression, and ownership in the ﬁnal artifact." Two doctoral-qualified instructors with more than 7 years of teaching experience evaluated all works blind to questionnaire responses and AI-use status, with a structured reconciliation protocol involving a third evaluator when score differences exceeded 5%.

article_title: GenAI dependence and graduate students’ research creativity: the roles of critical thinking and human–AI collaboration quality
citation: Yin S, Wu R, Liu X and Li R (2026) GenAI dependence and graduate students' research creativity: the roles of critical thinking and human–AI collaboration quality. Front. Psychol. 17:1896963. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1896963
title: Differentiated two-dimensional conceptualization of GenAI dependence: functional versus existential dependence
description: The article conceptualizes graduate students' GenAI dependence as two qualitatively distinct dimensions rather than a unitary construct. Functional dependence "refers to the instrumental and task-oriented use of GenAI to support speciﬁc academic or research-related activities," whereas existential dependence "refers to a deeper psychological and cognitive reliance on GenAI, in which individuals may feel less conﬁdent or less capable of completing research tasks independently without AI assistance." Functional dependence is described as an objective behavioral-level description and existential dependence as deep psychological involvement, drawing on the AI Dependence Questionnaire of Li et al. (2025) and Extended Mind Theory. The study uses this distinction to show differentiated associations with research creativity.
requirements: Measurement via the 18-item two-dimension AI Dependence Questionnaire rated on a 5-point Likert scale
constraints: The distinction is grounded in scale-development research by Li et al. (2025) as cited by the article; associations are cross-sectional and associative rather than causal
target_learning_goals: research creativity
critical engagement with AI-generated information
self-directed AI use in academic research
examples: The study modeled functional and existential dependence as separate independent variables in parallel PROCESS Model 6 mediation models and compared their total and indirect effects
key_sources: Yin S, Wu R, Liu X and Li R (2026) GenAI dependence and graduate students' research creativity: the roles of critical thinking and human–AI collaboration quality. Front. Psychol. 17:1896963. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1896963

article_title: Generative AI as a Didactic-Pedagogical Mediator: Rethinking Human Roles and Pedagogical Design in Higher Education
citation: Moganadas SR, Marín-González F, Nun SH and Gan CL (2026) Generative AI as a didactic-pedagogical mediator: rethinking human roles and pedagogical design in higher education. Front. Educ. 11:1856839. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1856839
title: Nested instructor-student-GenAI triadic conceptual model for higher education
description: The article proposes a triadic model that replaces the traditional instructor-student dyad with an interdependent relationship among instructors, students, GenAI outputs, and institutional conditions. It positions GenAI as "a bounded didactic-pedagogical mediator operating within a shared didactic mediation space." The model spans three interdependent levels: micro (course-and-lesson-level interactions), meso (institutional governance arrangements), and macro (stakeholder and infrastructural ecosystem). Knowledge construction emerges through students' active meaning-making among human participants, AI outputs, disciplinary criteria, and institutional expectations.
requirements: Human judgment, disciplinary validation, and institutional governance must frame GenAI outputs for them to become educationally meaningful
constraints: The model specifies proposed relationships rather than a fixed sequence of interaction or causal effects
It is a conceptual model derived from synthesis, not yet empirically validated
target_learners: higher education students, including novice learners new to HE, a subject, or GenAI use
target_learning_goals: learner agency
AI literacy
disciplinary knowledge construction
ethical judgment
examples: The article illustrates the model with a writing-task scenario in which GenAI generates an outline or formative feedback while the instructor specifies appropriate AI use, disclosure, and assessment criteria
key_sources: Moganadas SR, Marín-González F, Nun SH and Gan CL (2026) Generative AI as a didactic-pedagogical mediator: rethinking human roles and pedagogical design in higher education. Front. Educ. 11:1856839. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1856839

article_title: Generative AI as a Didactic-Pedagogical Mediator: Rethinking Human Roles and Pedagogical Design in Higher Education
citation: Moganadas SR, Marín-González F, Nun SH and Gan CL (2026) Generative AI as a didactic-pedagogical mediator: rethinking human roles and pedagogical design in higher education. Front. Educ. 11:1856839. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1856839
title: GenAI as a bounded didactic-pedagogical mediator, distinct from tool, tutor, assistant, scaffold, or co-educator
description: The article's central conceptual contribution is defining GenAI as a bounded didactic-pedagogical mediator: a non-human technological artifact that can support explanation, feedback, scaffolding, and knowledge representation while remaining dependent on human judgment, disciplinary validation, and institutional governance. The authors argue this role is conceptually distinct from adjacent interpretations "such as tool, tutor, assistant, scaffold, or co-educator." GenAI's pedagogical significance depends on how its outputs are framed, interpreted, questioned, verified, revised, and integrated by human actors within disciplinary and institutional contexts.
requirements: Outputs must be treated as provisional and evaluated through source verification, comparison with disciplinary evidence, and human pedagogical judgment
constraints: GenAI's fluency should not be presumed as sufficient grounds for assigning it epistemic authority or independent pedagogical responsibility
LLM outputs may contain fabricated claims, reproduce biases, or vary in quality across prompts and contexts
target_learning_goals: critical evaluation of AI-generated content
disciplinary reasoning
epistemic judgment
examples: The article contrasts this mediator role with AIEd frameworks that classify AI through functional roles such as tutoring, assessment, and analytics

article_title: From Unified to Differentiated Materials: Generative AI–Supported Adaptation of EAP Reading Materials
citation: Gao X (2026) From unified to differentiated materials: generative AI–supported adaptation of EAP reading materials. Front. Psychol. 17:1887565. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1887565
title: Proficiency-sensitive barrier-to-support mapping for EAP reading materials
description: The article organizes EAP reading adaptation around a mapping from proficiency-specific reading barriers to text-embedded supports, process indicators, and outcome foci. Low-proficiency learners face vocabulary and syntax load addressed by "glosses, short paraphrases, sentence unpacking, and clause segmentation"; intermediate learners face discourse navigation addressed by rhetorical labels, paragraph-function notes, and claim–evidence outlines; high-proficiency learners face evidence and stance evaluation addressed by critical prompts. Each pathway assigns a distinct process indicator (cognitive load, discourse awareness, critical engagement) so process variables are not treated as interchangeable.
requirements: Supports must be fixed, text-embedded, and task-bound, printed into the material as glosses, labels, notes, outlines, or prompts.
The dominant barrier for each proficiency group must be identified before selecting the support layer.
constraints: Teacher mediation during reading falls outside this operationalization of scaffolding.
The mapping was evaluated in one EAP instructional context with three source passages and 15 reviewed material versions.
target_learners: Adult undergraduate EAP readers at low, intermediate, and high proficiency
target_learning_goals: Academic reading comprehension
EAP task performance including summary, claim–evidence use, and critical response
examples: Low-proficiency versions added inline glosses such as "glucose = a typeofsugar" and process breakdowns listing stages of glycolysis; high-proficiency versions added stance and evidence prompts such as evaluating the power-plant analogy and considering counterexamples.
key_sources: Gao X (2026) From unified to differentiated materials: generative AI–supported adaptation of EAP reading materials. Front. Psychol. 17:1887565. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1887565

article_title: Generative AI technologies and educational outcomes: a comprehensive meta-analysis comparing traditional and AI-driven approaches
citation: Ying Dong. (2026). Generative AI technologies and educational outcomes: a comprehensive meta-analysis comparing traditional and AI-driven approaches. Humanities and Social Sciences Communications. https://doi.org/10.1057/s41599-026-06903-y
title: GenAI educational-effect framework: personalized learning, feedback, gamification, and contextual adaptation
description: The article proposes a framework in which GenAI improves educational outcomes through several mechanisms: it "may offer personalized learning experiences" and effective feedback, process and analyze large amounts of data to "provide timely and contextual feedback", integrate gaming factors to enhance real-time student interaction, and help teachers adjust teaching styles and modify content for diverse student needs. The framework organizes the meta-analysis's moderator structure (feedback, game assistance, country, educational level) and grounds each intervention type in a theory: constructivism for GenAI technologies, metacognition theory for GenAI feedback, and Self-Determination Theory for game-assisted GenAI.
requirements: GenAI interventions must be classified by type (GenAI technologies, GenAI feedback, game-assisted GenAI) for the framework's mechanisms to be tested separately
constraints: The article states over-reliance on GenAI as a replacement for human teachers negatively influences outcomes; GenAI should complement human instruction
target_learning_goals: academic achievement
higher-order thinking
writing skills
learning motivation
examples: The meta-analysis operationalized the framework's outcomes as academic achievements, higher-order thinking abilities, and writing skills, and its moderators as feedback type, game assistance, country, and educational level

citation: Ying Dong. (2026). Generative AI technologies and educational outcomes: a comprehensive meta-analysis comparing traditional and AI-driven approaches. Humanities and Social Sciences Communications. https://doi.org/10.1057/s41599-026-06903-y
title: 53-study PRISMA-screened evidence corpus on GenAI and educational outcomes
description: A corpus of 53 included studies assembled through a PRISMA-based screening process from an initial 1096 records across Web of Science, Scopus, Springer, ScienceDirect, and Wiley, with gray literature searched to minimize publication bias. The screening removed duplicates, ineligible records, and studies with unreliable designs or missing key data (mean, standard deviation, or sample size). Quality was rated on AERA reporting standards (6–18 points), yielding 28 high-quality (52.8%), 19 medium-quality (35.8%), and 6 low-quality (11.4%) studies, with inter-rater reliability Cohen's kappa = 0.82.
requirements: Included studies must report quantitative or qualitative data on the hypothesized outcomes and have a control group and reliable intervention
constraints: Studies lacking key data (mean, standard deviation, or sample size) were excluded; unpublished, retracted, or overlapped publications were excluded
target_learners: students across university and secondary levels
target_learning_goals: academic achievement
higher-order thinking
writing skills
examples: The corpus underpins the pooled estimates reported in Fig. 3 for academic achievements, higher-order thinking abilities, learning motivation, and writing skills

article_title: Human-centered GenAI feedback design in higher education: a multisite experiment on direct, reflective, and hybrid approaches to scientific argumentation
citation: Ates, H. (2026). Human-centered GenAI feedback design in higher education: a multisite experiment on direct, reflective, and hybrid approaches to scientific argumentation. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00614-9
title: Process model of GenAI-supported feedback: designs distribute evaluative work and act directly and indirectly through uptake and self-regulated learning
description: The article proposes a process model in which feedback design affects argument-quality gain, conceptual learning, and delayed AI-free transfer both directly and indirectly. As the model figure states, "feedback design affects four-dimension argument-quality gain, conceptual learning, and delayed AI-free transfer both directly and indirectly through feedback uptake and self-regulated learning during revision." The core theoretical claim is that alternative designs "distribute evaluative work differently across learners, peers, and AI-supported tools," so designs requiring comparison, selection, and justification of revision decisions better preserve evaluative judgment and epistemic agency.
requirements: Feedback designs must be understood as process configurations involving source, sequencing, and structured evaluative activity, not feedback-source exposure alone
constraints: Mediation models test statistical association between condition differences in outcomes and revision processes, not a strict within-cycle temporal causal sequence
target_learning_goals: scientific argumentation
evaluative judgment
self-regulated learning during revision
examples: The study tested the model with four conditions: peer only, direct GenAI, reflective GenAI, and hybrid combining self-evaluation, peer feedback, and GenAI critique

article_title: Human-centered GenAI feedback design in higher education: a multisite experiment on direct, reflective, and hybrid approaches to scientific argumentation
citation: Ates, H. (2026). Human-centered GenAI feedback design in higher education: a multisite experiment on direct, reflective, and hybrid approaches to scientific argumentation. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00614-9
title: Design GenAI feedback environments to preserve student agency, evaluative judgment, and ownership during revision
description: The article's central design principle is that the educational value of GenAI feedback depends less on AI access than on whether the feedback environment keeps learners responsible for judging quality. The abstract states that value "may depend less on AI access per se than on whether feedback environments preserve student agency, evaluative judgment, and ownership during revision." Designs that require students to articulate an initial judgment before receiving AI critique position AI feedback as a resource for comparison rather than a substitute for judgment.
requirements: Students must be positioned to interpret critique, compare it against criteria, and decide how revision should proceed
constraints: Reflective and hybrid designs require additional evaluative activity and time-on-task, so advantages reflect the whole designed process
target_learners: higher education students in science courses
target_learning_goals: feedback uptake
evaluative judgment
durable transfer of argumentation skill
examples: The hybrid condition required a 100–150 word revision memo explaining which suggestions students accepted, rejected, or modified

article_title: Effects of generative artificial intelligence on students' learning motivation: evidence from a meta-analysis
citation: Fang L, Li Z, Xiong B and Lu Z (2026). Effects of generative artificial intelligence on students' learning motivation: evidence from a meta-analysis. Front. Psychol. 17:1832451. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1832451
title: Self-determination theory as the explanatory framework for GenAI's motivational effects
description: The article uses self-determination theory (SDT), which "distinguishes intrinsic motivation (IM), rooted in interest and curiosity, from extrinsic motivation(EM),drivenbyexternalcontingenciessuchasrewards and grades," as its coding scheme and explanatory lens. In the discussion, the authors propose that GenAI may support autonomy (individualized pathways, pacing), competence (diagnosing status, adjusting task difficulty, scaffolding), and relatedness (prompt responses, targeted encouragement), thereby fostering motivation. These mechanisms are offered as interpretations, not tested results.
requirements: Motivation outcomes must be classifiable as intrinsic or extrinsic motivation per SDT, as the article's coding scheme requires
constraints: The proposed need-supportive mechanisms are the authors' interpretation and were not experimentally tested in the meta-analysis
target_learners: students in formal educational settings from primary school through university
target_learning_goals: learning motivation, including intrinsic and extrinsic motivation
examples: The article coded motivation outcomes as intrinsic or extrinsic motivation guided by SDT, and interpreted the pooled positive effect through need support for autonomy, competence, and relatedness

article_title: Critical AI Tutors: Empower or Enslave?
citation: Favero, L., Pérez-Ortiz, J. A., Käser, T., & Oliver, N. (2025). Do AI tutors empower or enslave learners? Toward a critical use of AI in education. Applications of Generative AI to support teaching and learning in Higher Education, co-located with AIED 2025, Palermo, Italy.
title: Four-area framework of AI-in-education risks: cognition, agency, emotion, and ethics
description: The paper organizes the risks of AI integration in education into four key areas of the learning process: cognition, emotion, ethics and agency. On the cognition side it identifies cognitive offloading, mental laziness, and limited creativity; on agency, dependency, outsource decision-making, passivity, and over-trusting; on emotion, AI guilt, damaged self-efficacy, stress and anxiety, and social isolation; on ethics, lack of privacy, surveillance, data exploitation, and academic integrity. The framework is summarized in Figure 1, which pairs each challenge with interventions such as AI literacy, scaffolding, stimulating thinking, and strong ethical frameworks and policy. It serves as the paper's organizing structure, with one section devoted to each area.
requirements: The framework is a position-paper synthesis drawing on cognitive science and pedagogy literature rather than a tested model
constraints: The paper states the risks are not inherent to the tools themselves but lie in how they are utilized
target_learners: students in education using AI chatbots, particularly higher education
target_learning_goals: critical thinking
learner autonomy
emotional well-being
academic integrity
examples: Figure 1 maps challenges such as cognitive offloading, dependency, AI guilt, and lack of privacy to interventions including AI literacy, scaffolding, and strong ethical frameworks and policy

article_title: Integrating Generative AI into Cybersecurity Education: A Study of OCR and Multimodal LLM-Assisted Instruction
citation: Patel, K., Lin, Y.-Z., Raul, G., Shih, B. P.-J., Redondo, M. W., Latibari, B. S., Pacheco, J., Salehi, S., & Satam, P. (2025). Integrating Generative AI into Cybersecurity Education: A Study of OCR and Multimodal LLM-assisted Instruction. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.02998
title: CLaaS platform with integrated OCR-to-LLM instructional assistant
description: CLaaS (Cybersecurity Labs-as-a-Service) is an AWS cloud-based platform delivering browser-accessible cybersecurity labs via EC2 virtual machines, supporting tasks such as DDoS attacks, buffer overflows, packet sniffing, and ransomware attacks. This paper extends it with an "Instruction Simplification" button that captures the current slide as an image, extracts text with Tesseract OCR, and sends the raw text with a crafted prompt to an LLM (gpt-4) via API to generate a simplified, zero-shot explanation delivered in the CLaaS interface. Students rate the output on a 1-10 feedback scale stored for later analysis and prompt personalization.
requirements: An existing instructional slide deck within the lab platform whose content can be captured as images
API access to a general-purpose LLM and the Tesseract OCR tool
constraints: Operates in a zero-shot setting with no domain-specific fine-tuning or preprocessing
OCR introduces noise, particularly from UI screenshots and slide templates
target_learners: undergraduate and graduate students in university cybersecurity courses
target_learning_goals: comprehension of technical cybersecurity lab instructions and procedures
examples: Deployed in a live university course where 42 student ratings averaged 7.83; the OCR pipeline runs in production on CLaaS

article_title: A principled way to think about AI in education: guidance for educators and policy makers based on goals, models
citation: Finkelstein, N. (2026). A principled way to think about AI in education: guidance for educators and policy makers on action based on goals, models of human learning, and use of technologies. Draft manuscript, University of Colorado, Boulder.
title: A principled framework bridging educational goals, models of human learning, and technology use in AI-era higher education
description: The article advances a framework positioned as a third path between discourse on AI's promise and peril and immediate implementation advice. It states: "a set of guiding principles can bridge the gap, connecting our implementation approaches to the large-scale goals we have for education." The framework connects broad goals (individual development, societal infrastructure, workforce) to actionable practices for educators, learners, and administrators, and is designed to be flexible across contexts.
requirements: Educators and policy makers must be explicit about the goals they are advancing before choosing technologies
constraints: The framework presupposes the value of institutions of higher education and focuses on colleges and universities, though the author notes many approaches will likely apply to pre- and post-college environments
target_learning_goals: meaningful learning, discernment, empathy, sense of self, preparation for dynamic futures
examples: The article applies the framework through scenarios including ubiquitous institution-supported AI access, basic skills catch-up, students training AI agents, and addressing TA shortages

citation: Finkelstein, N. (2026). A principled way to think about AI in education: guidance for educators and policy makers on action based on goals, models of human learning, and use of technologies. Draft manuscript, University of Colorado, Boulder.
title: Three broad classes of goals for educational systems: developing individuals, societal infrastructure, and workforce development
description: The article enumerates three broad classes of goals spanning why educational systems exist: "1) Developing individuals", "2) Societal infrastructure", and "3) Workforce development". It places them in the author's priority order, arguing that workforce goals are achieved by addressing the first two, and that being explicit about goals ought to guide technology use in creating educational environments.
requirements: Educators must prioritize among potentially multifaceted and contradictory goals before allocating technology responsibilities
constraints: The ordering is explicitly the author's own priority order, and the article acknowledges others may hold different goals for educational systems
target_learning_goals: individual development, citizenship and societal participation, career preparation
examples: The article cites AAC&U (2009) and Finley (2021) in arguing that workforce development and job training goals are achieved by developing learners and preparing them to engage in society

citation: Finkelstein, N. (2026). A principled way to think about AI in education: guidance for educators and policy makers on action based on goals, models of human learning, and use of technologies. Draft manuscript, University of Colorado, Boulder.
title: Discernment, empathy, and sense of self as three essential outcomes of AI-era education
description: The article identifies three objectives for educational practices in the modern era: "discernment: the abilities to ask and frame appropriate questions, validate and contextualize answers to these questions, and to act appropriately with the results"; empathy, which underpins communication and collaborative work; and sense of self, where students learn their roles, purposes, and belonging. It argues these practices support metacognition, ethics, and judgement, and underpin performance, engagement, and retention.
requirements: Educators must deliberately cultivate these outcomes, since instantaneous access to information and analyses makes discernment practices central
constraints: The article presents these as argued priorities rather than empirically tested outcomes
target_learning_goals: discernment, empathy, metacognition, ethics and judgement, agency and belonging
examples: The preamble frames these three objectives as particularly important because accessing information, calculations, and analyses has become nearly instantaneous with modern technologies

citation: Finkelstein, N. (2026). A principled way to think about AI in education: guidance for educators and policy makers on action based on goals, models of human learning, and use of technologies. Draft manuscript, University of Colorado, Boulder.

description: Principle 0 of the framework holds that "Know why you are acting -- whether at the highest level or specific class activity" — the goals one prioritizes ought to inform the actions one takes and how one leverages new technologies. The article treats this as the foundational move that makes the later role-allocation principles coherent, noting goals can be multifaceted and potentially contradictory.

citation: Finkelstein, N. (2026). A principled way to think about AI in education: guidance for educators and policy makers on action based on goals, models of human learning, and use of technologies. Draft manuscript, University of Colorado, Boulder.
title: Determine which educator and student activities remain human-led and which can be safely outsourced to AI technologies
description: The framework's central allocation principles state: "In our educational enterprise consider what domains of work are necessary or essential for educators to maintain as human led and directed, and what is feasible and safe to outsource to these new technologies", and in parallel determine which practices students must engage in as human-led and how technologies might advance learners' capacities. The article stresses these are not binary prescriptions: there are degrees of responsibility, and new responsibilities emerge as technologies develop.

article_title: Knowledge without Wisdom: Measuring Misalignment between LLMs and Intended Impact
citation: Michael Hardy, Yunsung Kim. (2026). Knowledge without Wisdom: Measuring Misalignment between LLMs and Intended Impact. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00883
title: A four-step methodological framework for measuring LLM alignment to intended impact in high-noise contexts
description: The article proposes a general framework for evaluating whether LLM judgments align with real-world outcomes when experimental control is infeasible. It comprises (1) correlating behaviors across the space of generalization with dCor2n dependence measures, (2) measuring best-proxy alignment on downstream tasks using Kendall's tau, described as "a simple, strong option that can be estimated with any datatype", (3) establishing real-world baselines such as teacher experience or prior VAM, and (4) decomposing misalignment error variance via Generalizability Theory. It was applied to classroom-transcript scoring against expert ratings and value-added measures.
requirements: requires external criteria representing both the downstream task and the intended impact of that task, however noisy
constraints: intended-impact data may be time-delayed after the downstream tasks or have grain-size mismatches, requiring real-world baselines for comparison
target_learning_goals: student academic growth as measured by value-added achievement gains
examples: Applied to 16 LLMs rating 479 primary mathematics lesson transcripts across seven tasks, with alignment measured against MQI/CLASS expert ratings and stacked value-added measures
key_sources: Michael Hardy, Yunsung Kim. (2026). Knowledge without Wisdom: Measuring Misalignment between LLMs and Intended Impact. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00883

citation: Michael Hardy, Yunsung Kim. (2026). Knowledge without Wisdom: Measuring Misalignment between LLMs and Intended Impact. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00883
title: NCTE Main Study dataset of classroom observations with expert ratings and value-added measures
description: The National Center for Teacher Effectiveness (NCTE) Main Study dataset provides the study's core data. The article states it "comprises ob- servations of roughly 350 4th and 5th-grade math- ematics teachers across four U.S. school districts." It is described as one of only two educational datasets containing measures of teaching practice, authentic classroom artifacts, and student learning outcomes at scale (VAMs). The study used anonymized transcripts of video-recorded lessons from its test set, rated by 63 MQI raters and 19 CLASS raters with rigorous certification and continual calibration.
requirements: requires linking of expert observation ratings with value-added measures of student learning, a combination the article says exists in only two extant datasets
constraints: the transcript data contain only fourth- and fifth-grade mathematics classrooms from the United States, limiting generalization to all classrooms
target_learners: 4th and 5th grade mathematics students in four U.S. school districts
target_learning_goals: student mathematics achievement growth measured by value-added scores
examples: The study prompted 16 LLMs on 479 lesson transcripts from 311 classrooms drawn from this dataset's test set, evaluating alignment against MQI and CLASS expert ratings and stacked VAMs

article_title: Expert Cognition Dashboard: From Learning Analytics to Cognition Intelligence in AI-Driven Education
citation: Yuan, A. (2026). Expert Cognition Dashboard: From Learning Analytics to Cognition Intelligence in AI-Driven Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17263
title: Cognition Intelligence: transforming learner behaviours into interpretable cognition structures for expert-level reasoning
description: The article introduces Cognition Intelligence as a new paradigm for AI-driven educational interpretation, defined as "the transformation of learner behaviours into interpretable cognition structures that support expert-level reasoning, adaptive intervention, and educational decision-making." It shifts the analytical object from observable behaviour to expert-informed cognition structures. The article states it "does not replace behavioural analytics; rather, it extends and reorganises behavioural analytics within a cognition-centred framework," with behavioural data as the first interpretive layer.
requirements: AI Tutors, reporting systems, and cognition-aware dashboards that collectively transform behavioural traces into higher-level cognition structures
constraints: Behavioural data remains necessary but becomes only the first layer in a larger interpretive process
target_learning_goals: expert-like interpretation of learner development, misconceptions, and adaptive pedagogical decision-making
examples: The article contrasts a conventional pipeline (behaviours to statistics to visualisation) with a cognition-centred pipeline in which AI Tutor analysis produces cognition structures before dashboard aggregation
key_sources: Yuan, A. (2026). Expert Cognition Dashboard: From Learning Analytics to Cognition Intelligence in AI-Driven Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17263

article_title: Expert Cognition Dashboard: From Learning Analytics to Cognition Intelligence in AI-Driven Education
citation: Yuan, A. (2026). Expert Cognition Dashboard: From Learning Analytics to Cognition Intelligence in AI-Driven Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17263
title: Expert Cognition Dashboard as cognitive middleware between learner behaviours and AI-driven expert reasoning
description: The ECD is defined as "a cognition-centred infrastructure that transforms learner behaviours into interpretable cognitive structures for AI-driven expert reasoning, adaptive intervention, and multi-level educational interpretation." Rather than a visualisation endpoint, the dashboard is an intermediate cognition layer that transforms fragmented behavioural signals into coherent cognition structures, enables multi-level aggregation, and provides interpretability for AI reasoning. The article argues dashboards become "perception infrastructures through which AI systems understand learners."
requirements: AI Tutor analysis to interpret learner behaviours before dashboard aggregation
constraints: The article states ECD is not intended to fully capture or automate expert judgment, and is not intended to replace human educators
target_learners: learners, educators, and AI agents in AI-native education systems
target_learning_goals: cognition-aware interpretation of learner development supporting adaptive intervention
examples: The ECD System (ECDS) prototype interface shows learner portraits, cognition summaries, class-level aggregation views, and AI Twin reasoning panels
key_sources: Yuan, A. (2026). Expert Cognition Dashboard: From Learning Analytics to Cognition Intelligence in AI-Driven Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17263

article_title: Expert Cognition Dashboard: From Learning Analytics to Cognition Intelligence in AI-Driven Education
citation: Yuan, A. (2026). Expert Cognition Dashboard: From Learning Analytics to Cognition Intelligence in AI-Driven Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17263
title: Three-level ECD architecture: individual, class, and AI Twin expert dashboards
description: The article proposes a multi-level cognition architecture of three interconnected layers: the Individual Cognition Dashboard (learning portrait, cognition radar, AI Tutor reports), the Class Cognition Dashboard (collective misunderstandings, group tension, cognition heatmaps), and the AI Twin Expert Dashboard (cross-group reasoning, intervention priorities, adaptive planning). Behaviours are "first interpreted through AI Tutor analysis and transformed into cognition structures before being aggregated across individual, class, and AI Twin levels."
requirements: AI Tutor interpretation layer producing cognition reports as foundational inputs for aggregation
constraints: The AI Twin does not observe raw learner behaviours directly but reasons through aggregated cognition structures
target_learners: individual learners, class groups, and cross-group educational ecosystems
target_learning_goals: multi-level cognition interpretation and adaptive educational intervention
examples: The cognition radar visualises conceptual understanding, interpretive consistency, identity confidence, value recognition, and cognitive tension
key_sources: Yuan, A. (2026). Expert Cognition Dashboard: From Learning Analytics to Cognition Intelligence in AI-Driven Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17263

article_title: Expert Cognition Dashboard: From Learning Analytics to Cognition Intelligence in AI-Driven Education
citation: Yuan, A. (2026). Expert Cognition Dashboard: From Learning Analytics to Cognition Intelligence in AI-Driven Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17263
title: AI Expert Feedback Ecology: a closed-loop cognition framework linking AI Twins, AI Tutors, dashboards, and learners
description: The article defines the AI Expert Feedback Ecology as "a closed-loop educational ecosystem in which AI Twins, AI tutors, dashboards, and learners continuously interact through cognition-aware feedback processes." AI Twins generate adaptive tasks; AI Tutors interpret behaviours into cognition reports; the ECD aggregates them; AI Twins reason through aggregated structures to generate interventions that start a new cycle. Cognition is treated as "an evolving interpretive structure continuously shaped through interaction, reflection, and intervention."
requirements: Continuous AI Tutor interpretation and dashboard aggregation to sustain the feedback loop
constraints: AI Twins perceive learners indirectly through cognition reports rather than raw behavioural logs
target_learning_goals: continuous adaptive feedback and expert-like pedagogical reasoning
examples: Figure 4 depicts learner interaction, AI Tutor interpretation, ECD aggregation, and AI Twin intervention as a continuous feedback loop

article_title: Expert Cognition Dashboard: From Learning Analytics to Cognition Intelligence in AI-Driven Education
citation: Yuan, A. (2026). Expert Cognition Dashboard: From Learning Analytics to Cognition Intelligence in AI-Driven Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17263
title: Five cognition structures as analytical objects: identity cognition, interpretation, cognitive tension, value recognition, and misunderstanding
description: The article enumerates five higher-order cognition structures that form "the core analytical objects of the ECD": identity cognition (how learners position themselves within a domain), interpretation (how learners construct meaning across situations), cognitive tension (conceptual conflicts and uncertainty marking cognitive transition), value recognition (negotiation of priorities and ethical judgments), and misunderstanding analysed as "structured cognitive divergence" rather than incorrect performance. These structures aim to represent learner development at a deeper interpretive level than behavioural outputs.
requirements: Dashboards must model these structures through AI Tutor interpretation rather than direct behavioural measurement
constraints: The article states these representations are not intended to fully capture learner cognition
target_learners: learners whose interpretive development is analysed in AI-native systems
target_learning_goals: interpreting conceptual understanding, identity formation, value negotiation, and cognitive transition
examples: Repeated hesitation around a concept may indicate unresolved cognitive tension; frequent revisions may suggest interpretive instability
key_sources: Yuan, A. (2026). Expert Cognition Dashboard: From Learning Analytics to Cognition Intelligence in AI-Driven Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17263

article_title: Gen-AI-tecture: using generative AI to support architectural students in design tasks
citation: Kapsalis, T. (2026). Gen-AI-tecture: using generative AI to support architectural students in design tasks. https://orcid.org/0000-0003-1598-6426
title: Gen-AI-tecture: a bespoke, locally run ComfyUI generative-AI image creation and editing workflow for architectural education
description: A bespoke generative-AI image workflow implemented as a localised ComfyUI environment in which students upload or select images, describe changes in natural language, and receive multiple visual alternatives. "The workﬂow is powered by the Flux 1 Kontext (dev) diffusion model (Black Forest Labs, 2025), which has been ﬁne-tuned with a curated set of interior-design images" using LoRA adaptation on the InteriorNet dataset. It offers three modes (text-driven, reference-image-driven, hybrid) and edits via in-painting that preserves surrounding context, acting as a visual co-pilot rather than replacing design thinking.
requirements: Runs locally within a ComfyUI node-based environment with the fine-tuned Flux 1 Kontext (dev) model
Used within scaffolded studio sessions with facilitator demonstration and structured design tasks
constraints: Fine-tuned for residential interior scenarios (bedroom and living/dining room scenes), so outputs support early design discussions "without claiming the status of resolved architectural drawings" and may not generalise to other design typologies or less supported studio environments
target_learning_goals: Architectural design ideation and visualisation
AI-handling skills for professional practice
examples: In the focus groups, students generated around 80 images per session, using Mode A to create bedroom designs from scratch and Modes B/C to edit provided living/dining-room images via in-painting
key_sources: Kapsalis, T. (2026). Gen-AI-tecture: using generative AI to support architectural students in design tasks. https://orcid.org/0000-0003-1598-6426

article_title: Gen-AI-tecture: using generative AI to support architectural students in design tasks
citation: Kapsalis, T. (2026). Gen-AI-tecture: using generative AI to support architectural students in design tasks. https://orcid.org/0000-0003-1598-6426
title: The GenAI workflow as a constructionist microworld and socio-constructivist cognitive mediator in studio education
description: The authors interpret their findings through constructionist and socio-constructivist lenses: "the bespoke, locally run GenAI workﬂow functions as a constructionist “microworld” for architectural ideation rather than as a mere image generator", echoing Papert's objects-to-think-with. They further read the AI as "a “more knowledgeable other” that suggested plausible yet negotiable alternatives", prompting students to articulate constraints and values, and as a connectivist interaction agent within students' personal learning environments. Learning is evidenced by cycles of making, inspecting and remaking, with the human-in-the-loop configuration preserving learner agency.
requirements: Outputs must be interrogated rather than accepted uncritically for the scaffold/ZPD effect to hold, per the article's reading
constraints: Interpretation drawn from a small, single-institution focus-group study with self-report data; the article notes instances where AI outputs risked narrowing exploration were identified and problematised in group discussion
target_learners: Undergraduate architecture students in studio-based education
target_learning_goals: Design reasoning and metacognitive talk about design moves
Critical management of human-AI learning networks
examples: Students described AI-edited images as provocations that opened up unforeseen options, especially when switching between masking modes

article_title: Mathematical Modelling of Ethical AI Use in Higher Education: A Coordination Game Framework for Future-Facing Learning
citation: Ndidi Bianca Ogbo, Zhao Song, Shatha Ghareeb, and The Anh Han. (2026). Mathematical Modelling of Ethical AI Use in Higher Education: A Coordination Game Framework for Future-Facing Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.27400
title: Coordination-based evolutionary game-theoretic framework of student AI use in assessment
description: The framework models student generative-AI use in assessment as a two-player symmetric coordination game in a well-mixed finite population, in which the institution is not a strategic player but shapes payoffs through assessment design. Strategies span responsible use with meaningful reflection, responsible use with superficial reflection, opportunistic use, and clear misuse, with parameters for learning value, effort costs, legitimacy costs, reflection reward and effort, and misconduct penalties. Behavioural change follows the Fermi imitation rule with small mutation probability, and long-run dynamics are approximated by a Markov chain over homogeneous states. The article writes that "we model interactions at the student–student level using a two-player symmetric game in a well-mixed population".
requirements: Reflective assessment incentives must be calibrated so that the reward for meaningful reflection is proportionate to its effort cost
constraints: The model treats each assessment task as a one-shot decision context in a well-mixed population; the article notes extending to multi-player and networked interactions and empirical validation as future work
target_learning_goals: responsible and learning-oriented use of generative AI in assessment
examples: Simulations with population size N = 100 and Fermi updating, varying reflection reward r, peer sensitivity β, and reflection effort cost κ across Figures 1–3
key_sources: Ndidi Bianca Ogbo, Zhao Song, Shatha Ghareeb, and The Anh Han. (2026). Mathematical Modelling of Ethical AI Use in Higher Education: A Coordination Game Framework for Future-Facing Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.27400

article_title: FOXGLOVE: Understanding Goal-Oriented and Anchored Writing Feedback from Experts and LLMs on Argumentative Essays
citation: Yijun Liu, Yifan Song, John Gallagher, Sarah Sterman, Tal August. (2026). FOXGLOVE: Understanding Goal-Oriented and Anchored Writing Feedback from Experts and LLMs on Argumentative Essays. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06271
title: FOXGLOVE: a parallel dataset of sentence-anchored, goal-labeled instructor and LLM writing feedback with urgency rankings and expert quality ratings
description: FOXGLOVE is a dataset of 2,340 feedback comments on 69 twelfth-grade argumentative essays from the PERSUADE 2.0 corpus: 696 comments from 14 trained writing instructors and 1,644 from four LLMs (GPT-5.2, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Llama 3.3 70B, Qwen3-Next 80B) produced under a shared protocol. It is, per the article, a dataset collected with "anchored, goal-labeled feedback comments" from trained human instructors and models. It adds expert quality ratings on 105 comments across seven dimensions (1,430 ratings), urgency rankings, and reusable annotation protocols for instructors, LLMs, and raters.
requirements: Feedback must follow the shared schema: sentence-anchored comments addressing one of five argumentative goals, an urgency ranking of the three most important comments, and one global comment per essay
constraints: The schema privileges feedback organized around predefined argumentative moves and may underrepresent feedback such as encouragement and praise
Feedback was collected for the study rather than drawn from authentic instructional settings, without an ongoing relationship with the writer
target_learners: writing instructors and LLM feedback system evaluators
target_learning_goals: argumentative writing revision through goal-oriented, anchored, prioritized feedback
examples: Each essay was independently annotated by two instructors via Google Docs, with comments anchored to sentences, goal labels recorded, and the top three comments ranked for urgency
key_sources: Yijun Liu, Yifan Song, John Gallagher, Sarah Sterman, Tal August. (2026). FOXGLOVE: Understanding Goal-Oriented and Anchored Writing Feedback from Experts and LLMs on Argumentative Essays. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06271

article_title: FOXGLOVE: Understanding Goal-Oriented and Anchored Writing Feedback from Experts and LLMs on Argumentative Essays
citation: Yijun Liu, Yifan Song, John Gallagher, Sarah Sterman, Tal August. (2026). FOXGLOVE: Understanding Goal-Oriented and Anchored Writing Feedback from Experts and LLMs on Argumentative Essays. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06271
title: Three-property schema for usable writing feedback: goal-orientation, anchoring, and prioritization
description: The article operationalizes three properties that writing research identifies as making feedback usable for revision: goal-orientation (engaging the rhetorical goal the writer is pursuing), anchoring (pointing to the specific text where revision should occur), and prioritization (ranking the most important revisions). The article states these address distinct revision needs: "what, where, and in what order", and that feedback usable for revision requires all three. In FOXGLOVE every feedback giver produces sentence-level comments labeled with one of five argumentative goals (Position, Claim, Evidence, Counterclaim, Rebuttal), anchors them to contiguous sentences, and ranks the three most urgent comments.
requirements: Feedback must be anchored to one or more contiguous full sentences, address exactly one goal per comment, and include an urgency ranking and a global comment
constraints: The schema encodes one particular view of what good feedback is and is intended as one lens on feedback quality, not a definitive standard
target_learning_goals: argumentative writing revision
formative feedback design
examples: Instructors and LLMs both produced feedback under this schema, enabling systematic comparison of where human and model feedback align and diverge

article_title: Report on CHIIR 2026 Workshop on Generative AI and Academic Search (GAI&AS)
citation: Yifan Liu, Jaime Arguello, Orland Hoeber, Chang Liu, Soo Young Rieh, Luanne Sinnamon, et al. (2026). Report on CHIIR 2026 Workshop on Generative AI and Academic Search (GAI&AS). ACM SIGIR Forum. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.08936
title: Three types of metacognitive laziness in academic search: plan-deficit, monitoring-deficit, and regulation-deficit
description: This framework, presented in a lightning talk by Song and Liu, identifies three types of metacognitive laziness during academic search behaviors: "plan-deficit, monitoring-deficit, and regulation-deficit". It characterizes ways learners offload metacognitive processes to GenAI systems, and it grounds two design challenges: evolving GenAI from fact-retrievers to problem-solving scaffolds at the strategy layer, and embedding metacognitive scaffolds to mitigate each type of laziness. The framework is used to foster adaptive collaboration and human-AI symbiosis in creative academic search.
requirements: GenAI systems should evolve from fact-retrievers to problem-solving scaffolds that help users break down ill-structured problems into manageable sub-problems at the strategy layer
target_learning_goals: metacognitive planning, monitoring, and regulation during academic search
examples: Song and Liu examined and identified the three laziness types from academic search behaviors, per the lightning talk

citation: Yifan Liu, Jaime Arguello, Orland Hoeber, Chang Liu, Soo Young Rieh, Luanne Sinnamon, et al. (2026). Report on CHIIR 2026 Workshop on Generative AI and Academic Search (GAI&AS). ACM SIGIR Forum. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.08936
title: GenAI systems should build trust by being transparent about process, purpose, and performance
description: A workshop roundtable principle of good GenAI design holds that "GenAI systems should build trust by being more transparent aboutprocess, purpose, and performance". Regarding process, systems should explain how an answer or output was generated, including which sources informed it; regarding purpose, systems should elicit the user's higher-level purpose to provide appropriate support; regarding performance, systems should convey their level of confidence about the accuracy and completeness of a response. The workshop also called for methodologies to measure the extent to which systems exhibit these principles.

target_learners: academic search system users, including researchers and students
target_learning_goals: trustworthy and responsible use of GenAI-mediated academic search

article_title: Structuring Transparency: Developing Domain-Specific Generative AI Declaration Frameworks in Higher Education
citation: Nicholas Micallef, Olga Petrovska. (2026). Structuring Transparency: Developing Domain-Specific Generative AI Declaration Frameworks in Higher Education. International Symposium on Artificial Intelligence and the Transformation of Higher Education Symposium (AITHE). https://www.swansea.ac.uk/staff/nicholas.micallef
title: Domain-specific GenAI declaration framework translating an activity taxonomy into task-specific disclosure instruments
description: The framework is a design artefact that translates the Bouvier et al. taxonomy of GenAI-mediated activities (Generate, Interpret, Evaluate, Get Feedback, Refine, Brainstorm, Design, Simulate, Reflect) into assessment-facing declaration categories for Computer Science coursework. It comprises two parallel task-specific structures (writing and coding) in which students indicate whether GenAI was used, its extent (Minor, Moderate, Extensive), and provide explanations with example prompts. The authors position it as operating "at the level of thestudent's declaration", complementing policy-level instruments such as the AI Assessment Scale, which operates at the educator's design-decision level.
requirements: Requires accurate self-reporting by students, accompanied by clear institutional guidance on which tools count as GenAI use
constraints: It does not itself detect misconduct
Transferability to disciplines beyond computing remains an open question
The goal is not a precise measurement instrument but a structured way to describe GenAI use
target_learners: Computer Science higher education students, including school-leavers, international students, career-changers, and degree apprentices
target_learning_goals: Academic integrity and transparent disclosure of GenAI use
Student reflection on their own learning process with GenAI
AI literacy and preparation for professional documentation of GenAI workflows
examples: A writing-focused form organised around six activity categories and a coding-focused form with five activity categories, both using the same Minor/Moderate/Extensive extent scale with explanations and example prompts

title: Writing-focused GenAI declaration structure with six activity categories
description: A declaration form for writing-focused activities (e.g., a short literature review on technology and society) organised around six activity categories: Planning & Structure, Textual Content Generation, Research & Analysis, Revision & Polish, Visual Content, and Evaluation & Feedback. For each category students (1) state whether GenAI was used (Yes/No), (2) specify the extent of use (Minor, Moderate, Extensive), and (3) provide a short explanation with example prompts. The categories operationalise aspects of the Bouvier et al. taxonomy in an essay-writing context, e.g., "Textual Content Generationaligns withGenerate".

constraints: Categories were derived from a computing-education activity taxonomy; the article notes the boundary of what counts as GenAI use is not always obvious to students

target_learning_goals: Transparent disclosure of GenAI use in writing tasks
Distinguishing acceptable assistance (e.g., limited revision support) from outsourcing of core content

title: Coding-focused GenAI declaration structure with five activity categories
description: A parallel declaration structure for coding assessments reflecting typical phases of software development and code-based learning, with five activity categories: Planning & Design, Code Generation, Code Improvement, Understanding & Learning, and Documentation & Reporting. As in the writing structure, students indicate whether GenAI was used and to what extent, with a short description and example prompts. The structure lets students and instructors "distinguish between GenAI as a learning aid (e.g., understanding error messages) and GenAI as an authoring tool (e.g., generating core solution code)".

target_learners: Computer Science students in programming-based assessments, from novices learning Python syntax to degree apprentices debugging legacy codebases
target_learning_goals: Transparent disclosure of GenAI use in coding tasks
Distinguishing GenAI as learning aid versus authoring tool
examples: Code Improvement covers debugging errors, refactoring, optimising performance, and requesting code review-style feedback; Understanding & Learning covers explaining error messages and learning syntax or design patterns

article_title: Structuring Transparency: Developing Domain-Specific Generative AI Declaration Frameworks in Higher Education
citation: Nicholas Micallef, Olga Petrovska. (2026). Structuring Transparency: Developing Domain-Specific Generative AI Declaration Frameworks in Higher Education. International Symposium on Artificial Intelligence and the Transformation of Higher Education Symposium (AITHE). https://www.swansea.ac.uk/staff/nicholas.micallef
title: Frame GenAI declarations as reflective instruments rather than compliance artefacts, using granularity, task specificity, intensity, prompt transparency, and reflection over punishment
description: The framework is guided by five principles that "collectively shift declarations from compliance artefacts to reflective instruments": granularity over a binary yes/no; task specificity; intensity as well as presence (Minor, Moderate, Extensive); prompt-level transparency via brief explanations and example prompts; and reflection over punishment, framing the declaration "as a description of process, not an admission of guilt". The last principle responds directly to empirical evidence that students avoid declaring GenAI use when they perceive the form as a penalty mechanism.
requirements: Declaration forms must offer multiple activity types per assessment, a shared extent scale, and space for explanations and example prompts
constraints: Relies on accurate self-reporting; novice programmers can experience an illusion of competence and misattribute GenAI contributions to their own work
target_learners: Higher education students, particularly in Computer Science
target_learning_goals: Honest self-assessment of GenAI use
Reflection on the learning process
Reducing perceived stigma of disclosure
examples: The framework asks students to indicate both whether and to what extent they used GenAI for each activity type, alongside short explanations and example prompts

article_title: Framing the 5% Problem: Teachers'' Perspectives on Persistence in Educational Technology
citation: Conrad Borchers. (2026). Framing the 5% Problem: Teachers’ Perspectives on Persistence in Educational Technology. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22294
title: Reframing the 5% problem as a situated instructional challenge requiring teacher-facing interpretive support
description: The article proposes that the 5% problem — only a small fraction of students engaging at levels sufficient for meaningful learning gains — should be understood not merely as a usage deficit but as a challenge of teacher interpretation. It argues that "the 5% problem extends beyond time-on-task and reflects challenges in interpreting meaningful student effort," and that teacher-facing systems should situate engagement patterns within broader instructional and contextual information rather than only detecting disengagement.
requirements: Teacher-facing systems would need to combine platform engagement data with instructional and contextual information to support teacher sensemaking about persistence.
constraints: Findings derive from an early needs-finding workshop with 12 volunteer teachers, one 90-minute session, one district, and one platform; transferability requires triangulation with observations, student interviews, or prototype trials.
target_learners: K-12 middle school mathematics students using adaptive learning platforms
target_learning_goals: Sustained student persistence and engagement in computer-assisted mathematics learning
examples: The workshop asked teachers for 'I wish I knew...' and 'I wish I could...' superpowers, such as knowing where students stall or reframing productive struggle.

article_title: Cross-Subject Predictive Validity for Learning Outcomes of Delayed Start Behavior
citation: Jordan Gutterman, Ashish Gurung, Lee Branstetter, Kenneth Koedinger, and Vincent Aleven. (2026). Cross-Subject Predictive Validity for Learning Outcomes of Delayed Start Behavior. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.25308
title: Session-level behavioral measures as content-independent, practitioner-aligned detectors of self-regulated learning
description: The article proposes that session-level measures like delayed start provide "a new opportunity for content-independent detectors, adding a behavioral component to the traditional usage and progress based on student engagement with content." Because the daily class period in K-12 is a bounded work space, its start and end times serve as behavioral anchors for defining self-regulation measures. The framework holds that detectors built from DLP log data already in use require no new diagnostics and frame results in minutes of delay, matching what educators observe. It bridges education research and classroom practice through interpretable measures.
requirements: Digital learning platform log data from which classwork sessions can be inferred via transaction density
K-12 class periods with bounded start and end times to anchor delay measurement
constraints: Results derived from one middle-school context with 45-minute class periods and one math platform; thresholds could differ in other contexts, e.g. 60-minute sessions
The raw minutes metric leaves the predictive power of classroom and contextual factors on the table
The work does not identify precisely which construct delayed start best represents
target_learners: Grade 7 middle school students using digital learning platforms
target_learning_goals: Self-regulated learning behaviors such as timely task initiation
Standardized math and ELA achievement
examples: The classwork-session inference algorithm classified practice instances with more than five concurrent students from the same class during school hours as classwork sessions, identifying 841 sessions across 26 classes

article_title: From Prompting to Epistemic Proactivity: Temporal Trajectories of Student-AI Interaction in Mathematics Learning
citation: Abdelghani, R., Kaiser, P., Murayama, K. (2026). Changes in Help-Seeking Strategies Predict unaided Performance during AI-based Mathematical Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.28472
title: Epistemic proactivity (EP): the extent to which learners retain responsibility for regulating and advancing their own knowledge-building while using AI
description: Epistemic proactivity characterizes "the extent to which learners retain this responsibility to carry out the important process for learning" during AI-supported learning. It concerns what role learners retain — whether they frame problems and originate learning trajectories or merely react to ones imposed by the AI — and goes beyond prompt sophistication or general engagement by focusing on how responsibility for knowledge-building is distributed between learner and AI. The study operationalizes EP through two behavioral dimensions: SRL functions (plan, monitor, request, evaluate) and the epistemic orientation of help-seeking (understanding-oriented versus closure-oriented requests), and treats EP as a developing property of the interaction rather than a fixed learner characteristic.
requirements: Behavioral codes capture only regulatory functions explicitly expressed in dialogue and should not be interpreted as a complete measure of internal self-regulation.
constraints: EP does not assume learners should perform every cognitive or regulatory operation independently; delegation becomes problematic when the learner increasingly relies on the model for determining what to pursue, generating reasoning, and judging understanding.
target_learning_goals: mathematical modelling with linear and quadratic functions
examples: The study coded 880 substantive student turns for SRL function and help-seeking orientation and related within-session change scores to unaided post-test performance.

article_title: Gaze-Informed Proactive AI Assistance for Children’s Picture Exploration
citation: Zekun Wu, Man Su, Huiyong Li, Tomohiro Nagashima, and Anna Maria Feit. (2026). Gaze-Informed Proactive AI Assistance for Children Exploring Picture Books. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.00445
title: Ollie: a gaze-informed LLM storytelling assistant for children's picture-book exploration
description: Ollie is an LLM-based (GPT-4o) proactive assistant that narrates picture-book scenes for children without requiring explicit requests. As the article describes it, "Ollie uses gaze-based attention detection to identify the child's current primary AOI, applies relevance-based AOI selection to choose a related but unassisted secondary AOI, and then prompts the LLM with the two AOIs and the full picture to produce spoken storytelling assistance." Narrations are delivered via text-to-speech, chain prior hooks, and end with an open-ended question to spark curiosity.
requirements: An eye tracker capturing the child's gaze during exploration, with predefined AOIs segmented into meaningful regions of the picture
A 5-second warm-start phase with no state inference to initialize the HMM parameters via batch EM
constraints: In the user study, assistance was limited to three initial instances per image with a minimum three-second interval between triggers, after pilot observations that overly frequent assistance interrupted self-directed exploration
The only parent preferring the baseline raised privacy and security concerns related to eye tracking
target_learners: preschool and early elementary-school children (ages 5-8 in the study)
target_learning_goals: sustaining attention and curiosity during open-ended picture exploration
narrative understanding and visual literacy support during picture-book reading
examples: In the within-subject study, children explored six Wimmelbook-style images, three per condition, with Ollie delivering spoken German narration via Azure text-to-speech

article_title: From Answer Generators to Reasoning Facilitators: Designing AI Tutors for Mathematical Reasoning in High-Stakes Environments
citation: Harry Feng, Yuan Tian, and Erica Zhao. 2026. From Answer Generators to Reasoning Facilitators: Designing AI Tutors for Mathematical Reasoning in High-Stakes Environments. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01692
title: Reasoning-Centered Product Loop: Orient, Visualize, Repair, Retrieve, Verify
description: A five-part design framework the authors propose for educational AI, moving beyond answer delivery. It holds that educational AI "should not hide answers under the guise of preventing cheating" but make answer access an entry point into reasoning; treat text and diagrams as one synchronized reasoning object; use contextual step-specific repair buttons; shift similar-problem recommendations into delayed spaced-retrieval workflows; and expose curriculum-fit signals before asking students to trust output. It emerged from the AITutor field deployment.
requirements: AI output must be decomposable into inspectable steps with curriculum-fit signals exposed before trust is requested
constraints: Evidence currently covers interaction behavior and perceived support, not measured learning gains; validated only in a 12-day deployment with 12 junior-high students in an exam-oriented Chinese context
target_learners: junior-high students preparing for high-stakes exams
target_learning_goals: mathematical reasoning inspection, local repair, and delayed retrieval
examples: AITutor implemented the loop via layered worked examples, step-linked visual grounding, contextual follow-up prompts, and an automated wrong-book review view

title: AITutor: an LLM-based iPad tutoring app translating pedagogical mechanisms into UI features
description: AITutor is a React Native/Expo iPad app with a Python/FastAPI backend that orchestrates LLM calls, curriculum-constrained prompting, retrieval over digitized course materials, and telemetry logging. Rather than "treating the AI as an open-ended chatbot, we constrained the interaction, translating pedagogical mechanisms into explicit UI features." Its features are layered worked examples (overview, orientation, explanation, final-answer checkpoint, exam-format layer), step-linked visual grounding, a contextual follow-up dock, and a delayed retrieval/wrong-book loop.

fast enough answer access for homework pressure
constraints: evaluated only as a prototype over a 12-day shared field window with a reliability outage on May 20–21

target_learning_goals: inspectable, repairable mathematical reasoning

title: GAIDE: A Guiding Framework for AI-Integrated Design for Educators
description: GAIDE is a framework supporting K-12 teachers in creating AI-powered learning technologies through vibe coding. It combines Design Thinking phases with adapted INTERACT design components, bookended by an initial Understand AI phase and a final Reflect on Ethical Application phase. Revisions from the empirical workshop included that "Learning Environment was removed, and Learning Objectives was newly introduced" in the Design phase, and the framework visualizes a non-linear, iterative cycle of collaborative design.

Mentor support during prototyping and testing phases

Developing AI literacy

title: Teacher-mentor-AI collaboration as a distributed expertise system in AI technology creation
description: The article conceptualizes workshop interactions among teachers, mentors, and AI as "a dynamically coordinated system of distributed expertise, grounded in distributed cognition theory". Evidence-based knowledge from mentors, practice-based knowledge from teachers, and generative knowledge from AI are integrated and reconfigured through interaction. AI is treated not merely as a tool but as a mediational artifact that shapes teachers' thinking, as teachers externalize tacit knowledge through prompt writing, prototype demonstration, and output review.

constraints: Conceptualized from one small workshop context; mentor interactions dominated the coded activity
target_learning_goals: Collaborative AI-powered learning technology design
Teacher professional learning

GAIDE instead "position[s] teachers as the primary designers, supported by AI-enabled vibe coding", which the authors say grants teachers greater agency and lets them shape technologies directly around their instructional goals. Structured guidance such as the GAIDE framework

Technology integration

title: Flowcode: an AI-powered creative coding environment integrating a code-structure flowchart with pedagogically constrained LLM explanations
description: Flowcode is a Node-based web application using GPT-4o that supports beginners iterating on found creative coding projects (Anime.js animations using HTML, CSS, and JS). Its interface has four components: code editors, a live preview, an LLM-generated flowchart summarizing project features across two abstraction levels, and an explanation panel producing "fill-in-the-blank code snippets" rather than full solutions. iterating on found creative coding projects by actively writing code

title: Introduce deliberate friction into AI-generated code assistance to prioritize learning over vibe coding
description: The article argues that code assistants for learning should deliberately slow learners down rather than maximize efficiency. Flowcode instruments friction by "revealing individual explanation steps one at a time and requiring users to directly edit blanks in generated code snippets rather than be given a full solution." The authors see this as distinct from friction arising from LLM misinterpretation, aiming to prioritize deeper learning and direct experimentation.
requirements: An LLM prompted to produce incomplete, fill-in-the-blank code rather than full solutions
An interface that reveals explanations step by step and avoids one-click code transfer
constraints: Friction slows prototyping speed, which the authors present as a trade-off favoring learning
Fill-in-the-blank behavior was not fully reliable even after prompt refinement
target_learners: novice programmers and new creative coders
target_learning_goals: understanding generated and found code
actively writing code rather than pasting AI solutions
examples: Flowcode removed the copy-to-clipboard button, stopped auto-inserting generated code into editors, and required clicking a 'Show Next Step' button to reveal each explanation step
