article_title: Judgment-Centred Software Engineering Education: A Post-Hype Review and Framework for AI-Augmented Learning
citation: Qusay H. Mahmoud. (2026). Judgment-Centred Software Engineering Education: A Post-Hype Review and Framework for AI-Augmented Learning. Preprint, September 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.29473
title: Comprehension debt: deferred learning and maintenance cost when AI-assisted production outpaces the ability to explain, test, modify, and justify software
description: Comprehension debt, building on Ahmad's socio-cognitive account of GenAI-assisted student projects, is defined in this review as "thedeferred learning, maintenance, and accountability cost incurred when AI-assisted artifact production outpaces the learner's or team's ability to explain, test, modify, and justify the artifact". Individual indicators include inability to explain control or data flow, poor defect localization, and inadequate test-oracle design; team indicators include uneven ownership and undocumented provenance. Conventional activities—delayed change requests, walkthroughs, independent tests, live debugging—can be repurposed as debt probes comparing what was produced with what can later be demonstrated. Frequency of AI use is a poor proxy: heavy use with active verification can carry low debt.
requirements: Assessment must compare what was produced with what can later be explained, tested, modified, and justified, using measures such as explanation quality, tracing accuracy, and independently designed tests
constraints: The construct remains a research agenda rather than a validated scalar metric
It is not identical to technical debt, academic misconduct, ordinary forgetting, or low code quality
target_learning_goals: retained code comprehension
independent verification and maintenance capability
accountability for AI-assisted artifacts
examples: Ahmad's underlying study drew on 621 reflective diaries from 207 students, identifying black-box acceptance, context mismatch, dependency-induced atrophy, verification bypass, and AI as a comprehension scaffold
key_sources: Qusay H. Mahmoud. (2026). Judgment-Centred Software Engineering Education: A Post-Hype Review and Framework for AI-Augmented Learning. Preprint, September 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.29473

article_title: Judgment-Centred Software Engineering Education: A Post-Hype Review and Framework for AI-Augmented Learning
citation: Qusay H. Mahmoud. (2026). Judgment-Centred Software Engineering Education: A Post-Hype Review and Framework for AI-Augmented Learning. Preprint, September 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.29473
title: AASEE framework: five non-linear AI integration levels crossed by four evidence-of-learning obligations (explain, verify, modify, account)
description: The AI-Augmented Software Engineering Education (AASEE) framework connects the scope of delegated engineering work and its lifecycle consequence to observable evidence of retained human competence. "Table 2 summarizes the five AASEE integration levels, their educational focus, typical forms of delegation, and the evidence or safeguards associated with each": tool awareness, guardrailed AI-assisted development, AI-collaborative engineering, AI governance, and agentic and AI systems engineering. Across all levels, four obligations—explain, verify, modify, and account—make retained competence visible; "Together, these obligations shift assessment from visible authorship to visible judgment". Levels are selected from the learning objective, not pursued as a maturity ladder.
requirements: Learning objectives are stated without reference to a tool before choosing an integration level
Evidence obligations (explanation, independent verification, modification under changed conditions, provenance and accountability) must accompany any delegation
constraints: Higher levels are not inherently better; a first-year tracing exercise may remain AI-restricted even where agent orchestration is taught elsewhere
Agentic curriculum proposals are not yet validated learning models
target_learning_goals: calibrated trust in AI output
disciplined delegation under lifecycle responsibility
supervision of agentic AI systems
retained independent competence
examples: A testing course at Level 3 has students obtain an initial test suite from an LLM, then classify the input space, justify oracles, add cases, and respond to a seeded defect or change request
A capstone combining Levels 4 and 5 defines task boundaries, permissions, sandboxes, acceptance tests, review ownership, and a recovery plan before an agent touches a repository
key_sources: Qusay H. Mahmoud. (2026). Judgment-Centred Software Engineering Education: A Post-Hype Review and Framework for AI-Augmented Learning. Preprint, September 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.29473

article_title: LearnAdapt Praxis: Controlled AI Assistance and Evidence Traces for Adult Workplace Learning
citation: Nizam Kadir. (2026). LearnAdapt Praxis: Controlled AI Assistance and Evidence Traces for Adult Workplace Learning. Technical research report. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02699
title: LearnAdapt Praxis five-stage learning workspace (Frame, Learn, Build, Validate, Transfer)
description: Praxis is a web application in the LearnAdapt ecosystem that structures an adult workplace-learning project across five stages: Frame, Learn, Build, Validate and Transfer. Learners "begin with their own starting response, engage with course material, develop a five-field specification, record validation observations and respond to a different scenario." The server stores a locked baseline, versioned specifications, hint records, validation observations and a separate transfer response, and enforces prerequisites such as a saved specification and validation observations before transfer begins.
requirements: A saved specification and validation observations are server prerequisites before transfer begins; a locked baseline is required before later substantive commands
constraints: The specification is a structured learning artefact, not an executable workplace application; the system does not execute external tests or certify deployment readiness
target_learning_goals: framing workplace problems, designing AI-supported services, validation reasoning, independent transfer
examples: The report's Table 1 relates each visible stage to its stored evidence and its interpretation limit, such as a saved reflection not establishing understanding
key_sources: Nizam Kadir. (2026). LearnAdapt Praxis: Controlled AI Assistance and Evidence Traces for Adult Workplace Learning. Technical research report. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02699

article_title: LearnAdapt Praxis: Controlled AI Assistance and Evidence Traces for Adult Workplace Learning
citation: Nizam Kadir. (2026). LearnAdapt Praxis: Controlled AI Assistance and Evidence Traces for Adult Workplace Learning. Technical research report. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02699
title: Retain inspectable provenance records of assisted and independent work, while treating them as application evidence rather than learning-gain evidence
description: The report argues that retaining versions, activity events, coaching records and authenticated actors makes future studies more interpretable by preserving the conditions under which an artefact was produced, but that these records support only limited inferences. It states that "an event label such as authenticated learning activity describes an application provenance category, not a psychological finding", and Table 5 distinguishes supported interpretations (e.g. text was saved in a particular sequence) from unsupported ones (e.g. that a change measures a learning gain).
requirements: Study design and collection context determine the evidential status of records; a course protocol must determine when facilitator feedback is delivered if unaided performance is an outcome of interest
constraints: The JSON schema is not a conformant W3C PROV serialisation, does not capture every interaction, and does not store a tamper-evident audit log or full model-request archive
target_learning_goals: independent reasoning and transfer in AI-supported design work
examples: The rehearsal's final exports retained the submitted transfer state, server-assigned reviewer identity, source-labelled timestamped events and notices separating activity records from learning-gain inference

article_title: From Learning Analytics to Educational Interventions: Enhancing Decision-Making and Learning Design
citation: Svetec, B., Divjak, B., & Kadoić, N. (2026). From learning analytics to educational interventions: enhancing decision-making and learning design. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00620-x
title: Seven-enabler framework for trustworthy LA-based educational interventions
description: A framework of seven institutional practices, capabilities or capacities that support, facilitate and enhance the implementation of educational interventions based on trustworthy learning analytics: institutional strategic orientation, pedagogical & other research foundations, available resources, pedagogical support, ethics & data governance, stakeholder engagement, and quality assurance. The article defines enablers as "institutional practices, capabilities or capacities that support, facilitate and enhance the implementation of educational interventions based on trustworthy LA" and positions trustworthiness as the prerequisite without which LA-based interventions are not meaningful. The framework was developed via survey, Delphi, and SNAP prioritization.
requirements: Trustworthy LA as a prerequisite: the article states trustworthiness is the prerequisite without which LA as a tool for informing educational interventions is not meaningful
constraints: The article states the enablers are not to be interpreted as dimensions of trustworthy LA but as conditions enabling LA-based educational interventions
The article states their relative importance may vary depending on institutional context and the maturity of LA systems
target_learners: Higher education institutions and educational leaders
target_learning_goals: Data-informed educational decision-making
Learning design and educational change based on trustworthy learning analytics
examples: The study identified the enablers through a survey of 34 e-course participants, a two-round Delphi with international experts, and SNAP prioritization with 12 experts

article_title: AI-based digital cheating at university, and the case for new ethical pedagogies
citation: Sandra Leaton Gray, Dominic Edsall, Dimitris Parapadakis. (2025). AI-Based Digital Cheating At University, and the Case for New Ethical Pedagogies. Journal of Academic Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10805-025-09642-y
title: Combined Theory of Planned Behaviour and Self-Efficacy account of AI-era cheating
description: The article combines Ajzen's Theory of Planned Behaviour with Bandura's Self-Efficacy Theory to explain student decisions to cheat with AI. TPB explains how "attitudes towards cheating, peer influence, and perceived ability to avoid detection" contribute to cheating decisions, while Self-Efficacy Theory explains how beliefs about competence shape perceived control. The combined account holds that a key aspect of cheating is "the interaction between technology's ease of misuse and the individual factors that influence students' choices". The article uses it to argue that banning technologies alone does not deal with the problem at source.
requirements: Understanding both motivational factors (attitudes, subjective norms, perceived behavioural control) and individual confidence in academic ability and AI-tool use
constraints: Self-Efficacy Theory does not factor in variables in the external environment or deal specifically with cheating, as the article states
The article sets aside external-to-the-student factors such as variable quality of tuition for reasons of space
target_learning_goals: academic integrity
ethical decision-making about AI tool use
examples: The article applies the combined account to argue that a student confident in using AI tools might see less risk of getting caught, increasing the likelihood of dishonesty
key_sources: Sandra Leaton Gray, Dominic Edsall, Dimitris Parapadakis. (2025). AI-Based Digital Cheating At University, and the Case for New Ethical Pedagogies. Journal of Academic Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10805-025-09642-y

article_title: AI-based digital cheating at university, and the case for new ethical pedagogies
citation: Sandra Leaton Gray, Dominic Edsall, Dimitris Parapadakis. (2025). AI-Based Digital Cheating At University, and the Case for New Ethical Pedagogies. Journal of Academic Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10805-025-09642-y
title: Design validity-driven, rehumanised assessments rather than relying on detection and surveillance
description: The article argues that safeguarding academic integrity requires moving beyond detection towards "validity-driven assessment designs that cultivate ethical agency". Its core validity argument is that "an assessment that can be answered by AI in a way that deceives an assessor is an assessment whose answer is intellectually trivial", so the technology exposes assessments that were already failing their fundamental purpose. Rehumanised approaches such as interactive viva-style examinations or peer-mediated assessments are proposed to foster engagement and reduce reliance on AI tools.
requirements: Assessments must genuinely reflect students' understanding and abilities rather than keyword identification, information compilation and paraphrasing
Investment in bespoke, single-use materials tailored to specific learning outcomes
constraints: Bespoke single-use materials take time, which conflicts with contemporary university workload models
Equitable access to resources (digital divides, accommodation quality, caring responsibilities) remains a fundamental barrier to academic integrity
target_learning_goals: deep learning
authentic demonstration of knowledge and ability
ethical formation
examples: Baird and Clare's case used weekly in-class invigilated tests, a red-flag system, random team reassignment, takedown notices, and single-use video case studies to rehumanise and personalise assessment

article_title: Analysing AI utilisation in education through learner question types: A constructivist approach
citation: Lee, H., Atif, A., & Kang, K. (2026). Analysing AI utilisation in education through learner question types: A constructivist approach. Australasian Journal of Educational Technology, 42(1), 79–96. https://doi.org/10.14742/ajet.10657
title: Constructivist three-role taxonomy of learner-generated questions: knowledge transmitter, facilitator and co-learner
description: The article organises learner-generated questions through a constructivist framework drawing on Piaget and Vygotsky's theories, in which student inquiries are categorised into three roles: "knowledge transmitter, facilitator and co-learner". This taxonomy serves as the class scheme that the NLP models are trained and evaluated against, linking question type to inquiry depth and to personalised learning and adaptive feedback in educational settings.
requirements: Learner-generated questions must be collected and expert labelled into the three roles before models can be trained on the taxonomy.
constraints: The article notes models struggle to distinguish the higher-order facilitator and co-learner categories, limiting automated use of those classes.
target_learners: higher education students in information technology courses
target_learning_goals: higher-order thinking through learner questioning
personalised learning and adaptive feedback
examples: Student inquiries from 11 students across 12 information technology courses were categorised into the three roles and used as classification targets.
key_sources: Lee, H., Atif, A., & Kang, K. (2026). Analysing AI utilisation in education through learner question types: A constructivist approach. Australasian Journal of Educational Technology, 42(1), 79–96. https://doi.org/10.14742/ajet.10657

citation: Lee, H., Atif, A., & Kang, K. (2026). Analysing AI utilisation in education through learner question types: A constructivist approach. Australasian Journal of Educational Technology, 42(1), 79–96. https://doi.org/10.14742/ajet.10657
title: Dataset of 434 expert-labelled authentic learner questions augmented to balance class distributions
description: A corpus of "434 authentic questions" collected from "11 students across 12 information technology courses", which were "expert labelled and augmented to balance class distributions". The dataset instantiates the constructivist three-role question taxonomy and serves as the training and evaluation data for the BERT, DeBERTa and RoBERTa classification models tested in the study.
requirements: Expert labelling of questions into the three role categories, plus augmentation to balance class distributions.
constraints: Data derive from 11 students across 12 information technology courses, a small single-discipline base the article itself flags via its call for cross-disciplinary validation.
target_learning_goals: classifying learner inquiry depth to support personalised feedback
examples: The corpus fed the evaluation in which DeBERTa reached the highest overall accuracy (86.36%).

article_title: Differential engagement with generative artificial intelligence in higher education: Gender, motivation, and achievement trajectories
citation: Yuan-Hsuan Lee and Jiun-Yu Wu. (2026). Differential engagement with generative artificial intelligence in higher education: Gender, motivation, and achievement trajectories. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00615-8
title: StatBot: a RAG-enhanced GPT-4 chatbot deployed as a voluntary virtual teaching assistant for graduate statistics courses
description: StatBot is a Retrieval-Augmented Generation chatbot built on GPT-4 that served as a virtual teaching assistant in three graduate statistics courses. As the article describes it, "StatBot was developed based on the GPT-4 large language model within a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) framework to support instructional interactions in the introductory statistics course." It retrieves from a curated corpus of lecture transcriptions, slides, textbooks, assignments, examinations, answer keys, and Q&A archives via vector-based semantic similarity, then applies a post-generation guardrail module that refines tone and pedagogical alignment, outputs "answer not found" when retrieval is insufficient, and appends source-based citations. It was integrated with the LINE messaging platform via Azure services and use was encouraged but not mandatory.
requirements: A curated internal knowledge base of course-specific instructional materials for retrieval
Deployment infrastructure (Azure Bot Service, OpenAI Service, Blob Storage, Key Vault, App Service) for real-time messaging integration
constraints: StatBot use was not permitted during quizzes and examinations
If retrieved source content is deemed insufficient, the system outputs "answer not found" rather than answering
target_learners: graduate students in introductory, advanced, and multivariate statistics courses
target_learning_goals: statistics content mastery
self-directed problem-solving during a semester-long data analytics project
examples: 97 graduate students across three courses generated 2,819 logged interactions over a 16-week semester under a policy encouraging transparent AI-use disclosure on the final project

article_title: The Impact of an LLM-Based Educational Agent on Learning Achievement, Cognitive Dynamics, and Student Perceptions in Computer Science Education
citation: Li, X., Liu, Z., Jiang, S., Chen, J., & Chen, W. (2026). The impact of an LLM-based educational agent on learning achievement, cognitive dynamics, and student perceptions in computer science education. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-026-00641-y
title: DBagent: an LLM-based educational agent combining RAG over a course knowledge base, external tool calling, memory, and ReAct reasoning
description: DBagent is a domain-specific educational agent built for an undergraduate database course on a university-wide educational AI infrastructure. It integrates a local course knowledge base via RAG, invokes external tools (search engine, image recognition, academic paper search, calculation, visualization), retains chat history in a memory module, and uses the ReAct reasoning pattern, which "enables LLMs to solve complex problems by alternating between logical reasoning and external execution". It uses Deepseek-r1-671b as base model and personalizes replies with the student's nickname.
requirements: A course-related knowledge base (courseware, teaching material, quizzes, handbook) converted to a unified data representation via an embedding model
Specialized training for students on interaction strategies such as Chain-of-thought prompting
constraints: Techniques for developing educational agents remain immature and their pedagogical efficacy is not yet well established, per the article's literature review
target_learners: sophomore computer-related majors in a database course
target_learning_goals: database knowledge and practical skills such as T-SQL programming and database design
examples: Used as a human-like tutor answering questions, clarifying concepts, and offering novel solutions during two practical sessions, replacing instructor-provided one-on-one help

article_title: GenAI assessment and language equity: Drawing the line between support and substitution
citation: Grace Li. (2026). GenAI Assessment and Language Equity: Drawing the Line between Support and Substitution. Journal of Academic Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10805-026-09760-1
title: Support–substitution framework: a purpose-based policy architecture for GenAI assessment in multilingual cohorts
description: The article's central framework separates legitimate language support (grammar, clarity, translation for comprehension, surface-level editing) from impermissible substitution (generation or material restructuring of reasoning, analysis, evidence, or sources). It is purpose-based rather than tool-based, ties permission to the assessment construct, and uses calibrated disclosure feasible for multilingual cohorts. As the article states, the framework is 'purpose-based rather than tool-based, uses calibrated disclosure that is feasible for multilingual cohorts, and links enforcement to reasons, proportionality, and evidence standards'. It is anchored in indirect discrimination logic, procedural fairness, and Kane's and Messick's validity accounts.
requirements: Permitted use must be expressly authorised in the assessment instructions for the specific task
The construct the task is intended to evidence must be re-specified to reflect the broader permission
Disclosure must be calibrated to make the permitted use visible without imposing disproportionate burden
constraints: The analysis is conceptual and governance-oriented, not empirical; it does not measure student behaviour or policy comprehension
Illustrative reference points are drawn from the Australian sector (TEQSA, Universities Australia)
target_learners: EAL and multilingual students in higher education

title: Box 1 quick tests for distinguishing support from substitution
description: Box 1 operationalises the support–substitution distinction with working definitions, quick tests, and illustrative edge cases. Permitted language support is defined as surface-level interventions improving readability 'without adding ideas, sources, or analytical structure'; substitution is defined as interventions creating or materially reshaping the substantive content. The quick tests ask whether an interaction would produce a new idea, a new source, or a re-ordering of analysis, functioning as a shared discretion-discipline device for markers.

title: Role-Adaptive AI Companion Framework: a Modular Adaptive Agent that dynamically switches between Student Peer, Teacher Assistant, and Parent Advisor roles
description: The framework conceptualizes an AI companion as a Modular Adaptive Agent (MAA), inspired by Multi-Agent Systems role-differentiation principles, that "dynamically transitions between three primary roles: the ‘Student Peer’ (facilitating low-stakes dialogue), the ‘Teacher Assistant’ (providing diagnostic analytics), and the ‘Parent Advisor’ (offering actionable home-based guid - ance)." Its core principle is context-aware role adaptability: the agent perceives the user and pedagogical task and modulates its functions, interactional style, and communication register through a modular configuration mechanism, triggered by cues such as user login or task selection. The framework is grounded in scaffolding theory, Learning Companion System principles, and socio-ecological views of family involvement, and its transition logic is justified by the article's empirical competence-gap findings.

Triggers such as user identity or task selection to activate the appropriate role
Access to student interaction data, curriculum data, and student profiles for adaptation

The framework itself was not implemented or evaluated; the empirical study tested only a fixed single-role instantiation

target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension and reflective book talk

title: Three role-integration design principles: integrated data governance, context-driven role switching, and synergistic human-AI collaboration
description: The article specifies three paramount design principles for orchestrating multiple AI roles into a cohesive whole. "Permissions and Data Sharing form the ethical backbone of the framework," implemented through Role-Based Access Control so the Teacher Assistant role provides detailed analytics while the Parent Advisor role generates aggregated, non-identifiable summaries. Context-driven adaptability operates on two levels: explicit role switching via pre-defined triggers and implicit stylistic adaptation that recalibrates scaffolding in real time. Synergistic human-AI collaboration requires communication protocols so insights from one role, such as the Student Peer mode, inform another, such as the Teacher Assistant interface.

title: GradeOpt: a multi-agent LLM coding framework with Grader, Reflector, and Refiner agents
description: GradeOpt is a multi-agent LLM framework for coding open-ended responses against human coding manuals. The article states that "GradeOpt automates the coding instruction process through collaboration among three LLM-powered agents: Grader, Reflector, and Refiner." article_title: LearnLM: Improving Gemini for Learning
citation: LearnLM Team, Google. (2024). LearnLM: Improving Gemini for Learning. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.16429
title: Pedagogical instruction following: conditioning model behavior on system-level pedagogy instructions
description: The report's central framework recasts injecting pedagogy into generative AI not as fixing one definition of good tutoring but as instruction following for pedagogical System Instructions. The authors "cast our work aspedagogical instruction following, meaning that we contextualize training and evaluation examples with system-level instructions that describe desired pedagogical behavior." This lets teachers or developers specify desired behavior, avoids conflicts of persona or style when mixing pedagogical data into Gemini's training mixture, and treats pedagogy as hard constraints (e.g. "do not reveal the answer") plus soft guidelines (e.g. "use a motivating tone").
requirements: Training and evaluation conversations must each begin with a specific System Instruction describing the pedagogical behavior present in that conversation; vague instructions are counterproductive because the model learns to ignore them.
constraints: The authors note pedagogy is "prohibitively difficult to define" across grade levels, subjects, languages, cultures and philosophies, so the framework deliberately avoids committing to any particular definition of pedagogy.
target_learners: learners across grade levels and subjects interacting with AI tutors
independent EdTech users and classroom students
target_learning_goals: tutoring and teaching interactions guided by teacher- or developer-specified pedagogical behavior
examples: LearnLM conversations were seeded with pedagogically focused System Instructions, and human preference raters labeled model samples on adherence to those instructions to train reward models for RLHF.

title: LearnLM: a Gemini 1.5 Pro-based model co-trained for pedagogical instruction following
description: LearnLM is an experimental model available on Google AI Studio, built on Gemini 1.5 Pro (gemini-1.5-pro-002) by co-training: the team mixed pedagogical SFT demonstration data and human preference data (reward model and RLHF) directly into Gemini's post-training stages. The authors state they "co-train with Gemini, meaning we mix our data directly with Gemini's SFT, RM, and RL stages", which lets the model learn new instruction following without forgetting core reasoning, multimodal, factuality, safety, or multi-turn properties, and keeps LearnLM in sync as the Gemini recipe evolves.
requirements: Pedagogical data must be conditioned on specific System Instructions so it can be mixed with general conversational data without conflicts of persona or style.
constraints: A subset of LearnLM improvements is part of the recently released Gemini 2.0 models; the evaluated version is a point-in-time artifact compared against model versions as of 2024-10-01.
target_learners: students and independent learners using AI tutoring products
target_learning_goals: interactive tutor-led exercises specified by teachers or developers through system instructions
examples: The model is offered as an experimental release on Google AI Studio with documentation of example use cases and suggested prompts.
key_sources: LearnLM Team, Google. (2024). LearnLM: Improving Gemini for Learning. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.16429

article_title: LLMs to Support K-12 Teachers in Culturally Relevant Pedagogy: An AI Literacy Example
citation: Jiayi Wang, Ruiwei Xiao, Xinying Hou, Hanqi Li, Ying Jui Tseng, John Stamper, and Ken Koedinger. (2025). LLMs to Support K–12 Teachers in Culturally Relevant Pedagogy: An AI Literacy Example. https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.08083
title: CulturAIEd: an LLM tool for culturally responsive adaptation of AI literacy lessons
description: CulturAIEd is an LLM-powered system built on streamlit with the gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18 model that helps teachers contextualize AI literacy activities through CRP principles. It combines "demographic characteristics of the students, rubric-based feedback, and just-in-time coaching" and offers two tiers of lesson modifications, basic and advanced, based on a CRT checklist, plus an interactive chatbot simulating instructional coaching.
requirements: Requires student demographic information as input for tailored culturally relevant content
constraints: Built as a demo with the gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18 model; the article lists needed improvements to workflow, UI, export functionality, and multilingual support
target_learning_goals: AI literacy instruction adapted to students' cultural contexts
examples: Pilot participants used CulturAIEd in Phase III to refine prior adaptations and modify a new activity on AI hallucinations

citation: Jiayi Wang, Ruiwei Xiao, Xinying Hou, Hanqi Li, Ying Jui Tseng, John Stamper, and Ken Koedinger. (2025). LLMs to Support K–12 Teachers in Culturally Relevant Pedagogy: An AI Literacy Example. https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.08083
title: Culturally Relevant Pedagogy as a three-component framework with Culturally Responsive Teaching as its operational extension
description: The article frames CRP, rooted in Ladson-Billings' foundational work, as "promoting academic success, developing cultural competence, and fostering sociopolitical consciousness." It presents Geneva Gay's Culturally Responsive Teaching (CRT) as a closely aligned concept emphasizing "more explicit strategies for operationalizing cultural responsiveness within daily teaching practices," particularly for modifying course materials. CulturAIEd operationalizes these ideas via a CRT checklist with levels from Contributions to Social Action.
requirements: Teachers need administrative support, professional training, and accessible tools to effectively integrate CRP/CRT methods
constraints: The article notes existing literature warns against the risk of routinizing CRP
target_learners: K-12 students in culturally diverse classrooms
target_learning_goals: Academic success, cultural competence, and sociopolitical consciousness
examples: Phase II of the pilot had teachers progress through CRT levels: Contributions, Additive, Transformation, and Social Action

article_title: Automatic Large Language Models Creation of Interactive Learning Lessons
citation: Jionghao Lin, Jiarui Rao, Sandy Yiyang Zhao, Yuting Wang, Ashish Gurung, Amanda Barany, Jaclyn Ocumpaugh, Ryan S. Baker, and Kenneth R. Koedinger. (2025). Automatic Large Language Models Creation of Interactive Learning Lessons. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.17356
title: RAG-based GPT-4o lesson generation system with task-decomposition prompting for tutor training lessons
description: A two-step system in which a lesson designer first retrieves research articles on effective tutoring practices, then uses them to prompt the GPT-4o model (gpt-4o-2024-05-13) to generate scenario-based lessons for training novice tutors of middle school mathematics online. The article states "The strength of RAG lies in its ability to produce contextually accurate content by incorporating the generated output into factual data." Lessons follow a five-section structure (Title Page, Scenario I, Instruction, Scenario II, Conclusion) and can be generated in one to five segments.
requirements: A lesson designer retrieves articles related to specific tutoring practices, providing the foundational knowledge on effective instructional strategies
The lesson follows the structured five-section tutor training format
constraints: Even with RAG integrating academic papers containing verified references, the model still produced references that did not exist
target_learners: novice human tutors teaching middle school mathematics online
target_learning_goals: effective tutoring practices
scenario-based tutoring skills
examples: Generated lessons for three topics: Encouraging Students' Independence, Encouraging Help-Seeking Behavior, and Turning on Cameras

article_title: AgenticMath: Enhancing LLM Reasoning via Agentic-based Math Data Generation
citation: Xianyang Liu, Yilin Liu, Shuai Wang, Hao Cheng, Andrew Estornell, Yuzhi Zhao, Jun Shu, Jiaheng Wei. (2025). AgenticMath: Enhancing LLM Reasoning via Agentic-based Math Data Generation. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.19361
title: AgenticMathQA: curated 30K/60K/90K math reasoning dataset
description: AgenticMathQA is the released training dataset produced by the AgenticMath pipeline, offered in curated 30K, 60K, and 90K versions. The article states: "We release AgenticMathQA, a curated dataset in 30K, 60K, and 90K versions." Unlike prior scale-focused approaches, it emphasizes "clarity, correctness, and diversity, providing higher-quality supervision for mathematical reasoning." The 30K version combines 15K seed problems with solutions and 15K AgenticMath-synthesized problem-solution pairs; larger sizes duplicate each problem with multiple solutions.
requirements: Built from GSM8K and MATH seed problems filtered at a quality threshold of score 3
Synthesized pairs must pass the Stage 4 ranking-based selection targeting 15K high-quality pairs
constraints: The article notes the study focuses primarily on text-based mathematical problems; extension to multimodal settings remains future work
Large-scale synthesis beyond the explored sample sizes was not conducted due to computational and resource constraints
target_learners: 3B-8B parameter large language models undergoing supervised fine-tuning
target_learning_goals: Mathematical reasoning on in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks
examples: The 30K setting consists of 15K seed problems and 15K AgenticMath-synthesized problems; scaling to 60K and 90K is achieved by duplicating each problem with multiple solutions
key_sources: Xianyang Liu, Yilin Liu, Shuai Wang, Hao Cheng, Andrew Estornell, Yuzhi Zhao, Jun Shu, Jiaheng Wei. (2025). AgenticMath: Enhancing LLM Reasoning via Agentic-based Math Data Generation. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.19361

article_title: AgenticMath: Enhancing LLM Reasoning via Agentic-based Math Data Generation
citation: Xianyang Liu, Yilin Liu, Shuai Wang, Hao Cheng, Andrew Estornell, Yuzhi Zhao, Jun Shu, Jiaheng Wei. (2025). AgenticMath: Enhancing LLM Reasoning via Agentic-based Math Data Generation. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.19361
title: AgenticMath four-stage multi-agent data generation framework
description: AgenticMath is an automated multi-agent framework enforcing quality control at every stage of mathematical data generation. It proceeds in four stages: seed problem filtering (LLM scoring on complexity, information value, and clarity with k-NN score curation), agentic problem generation (rephrase, review, and revise agents with an iterative loop), solution generation (one-shot chain-of-thought prompting), and synthetic-data evaluation with ranking-based selection. The article describes it as "an automated multi-agent framework that enforces quality control at every stage of mathematical data generation," following a "Less Is More" principle to yield a data-efficient, high-quality dataset.
requirements: LLM agents (GPT-4o-mini) for scoring, rephrasing, review, revision, and solution generation
Seed problems sourced from human-authored corpora (GSM8K and MATH)
Quality thresholds: seed filtering score of 3 and review-revise threshold of 4.5 with up to three iterations
constraints: The article notes current study focuses on text-based mathematical problems; multimodal extension remains future work
Scalability under substantially larger data budgets was not evaluated due to computational and resource constraints
target_learners: 3B-8B parameter large language models undergoing supervised fine-tuning
target_learning_goals: Generating high-quality mathematical question-answer pairs to improve LLM mathematical reasoning
examples: Each filtered seed problem is expanded into six rephrased variants; the review-revise loop runs at most three iterations with early stopping once the 4.5 threshold is met

article_title: Learning Context: A Unified Framework and Roadmap for Context-Aware AI in Education
citation: Naiming Liu, Brittany Bradford, Johaun Hatchett, Gabriel Diaz, Lorenzo Luzi, Zichao Wang, Debshila Basu Mallick, Richard Baraniuk. (2025). Learning Context: A Unified Framework and Roadmap for Context-Aware AI in Education. https://www.openstax.org
title: Learning Context Framework for AI Applications: five dimensions of learner context
description: The Learning Context (LC) Framework structures what AI education systems should know about a learner across five organizing questions: Who (learner factors such as prior knowledge, misconceptions, psychosocial traits), With whom (peers and instructors), What (content, task difficulty and domain), When (stable traits versus volatile states and intraindividual change), and Where (digital environment from micro- to meso-system, based on Bronfenbrenner's ecological levels). The article proposes it because "the ﬁeld lacks a computationally tractable theory for representing LC at scale," and pairs the dimensions with AI opportunities such as contextualized instructional design strategies and edtech affordances (feedback, prompts, practice quizzes).
requirements: Representation must be grounded in learning science, computationally amenable, machine-readable, and human-interpretable
constraints: Current AI systems capture only the context visible through direct user interaction, operationalizing a narrow subset of these dimensions
target_learners: K-12 and college learners using AI-based learning tools
target_learning_goals: Deep, robust learning via context-aware personalization rather than shallow mimicry
examples: The framework's dimensions were instantiated in four LLM vignettes and translated into the LC data structure of Theme 2
key_sources: Naiming Liu, Brittany Bradford, Johaun Hatchett, Gabriel Diaz, Lorenzo Luzi, Zichao Wang, Debshila Basu Mallick, Richard Baraniuk. (2025). Learning Context: A Unified Framework and Roadmap for Context-Aware AI in Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24362

article_title: Learning Context: A Unified Framework and Roadmap for Context-Aware AI in Education
citation: Naiming Liu, Brittany Bradford, Johaun Hatchett, Gabriel Diaz, Lorenzo Luzi, Zichao Wang, Debshila Basu Mallick, Richard Baraniuk. (2025). Learning Context: A Unified Framework and Roadmap for Context-Aware AI in Education. https://www.openstax.org
title: Multi-layered Learning Context graph data structure with modular design principles
description: The LC data structure translates the five framework dimensions into computational components: a learner vector, a dynamic social graph, graph-based content representations aligned to standards such as IEEE LOM and xAPI, a temporal index with recency weighting and spacing intervals, and environmental/platform metadata. "These ﬁve components form a multi-layered LC graph, where nodes correspond to entities (learner, content, peers, activities) and edges encode relationships and interactions." It can be structured as a JSON-LD schema or a knowledge graph compatible with graph databases such as Neo4j, enabling warm-start reasoning from accumulated context.
requirements: Modularity: each LC dimension forms an independently addressable module enabling selective access and updating
Extensibility: new dimensions can be added without schema overhaul
Interpretable embeddings: human-readable context snapshots for instructors and learners
Cross-system consistency: standardized metadata for interoperability across AI tools and platforms
constraints: Certain key components, such as belief-based models, are not yet fully developed
target_learners: Learners using AI-based teaching and learning systems across multiple tools
target_learning_goals: Personalized, context-aware instructional support across sessions and platforms
examples: Figure 6 illustrates four representation approaches with distinct trade-offs; Figure 7 shows an example belief-based model for a Grade-10 learner struggling with quadratic equations
key_sources: Naiming Liu, Brittany Bradford, Johaun Hatchett, Gabriel Diaz, Lorenzo Luzi, Zichao Wang, Debshila Basu Mallick, Richard Baraniuk. (2025). Learning Context: A Unified Framework and Roadmap for Context-Aware AI in Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24362

citation: Naiming Liu, Brittany Bradford, Johaun Hatchett, Gabriel Diaz, Lorenzo Luzi, Zichao Wang, Debshila Basu Mallick, Richard Baraniuk. (2025). Learning Context: A Unified Framework and Roadmap for Context-Aware AI in Education. https://www.openstax.org
title: Belief-based models (BBMs) capturing what learners actually believe
description: Belief-based models are a proposed LC component intended to capture learners' mental models, assumptions, preferences, and misconceptions—the beliefs that shape how they think, learn, and engage with content. The article positions them as under development: "we are working towards a BBM component that captures what learners actually believe." Their rationale is that beliefs shape learning trajectories in ways factual-knowledge modeling alone cannot capture, so beliefs must be represented as part of the broader Learning Context rather than only as mastered skills.
requirements: Beliefs must be represented as part of the broader LC, alongside factual knowledge models
constraints: The BBM component is not yet (fully) developed
target_learners: Learners whose misconceptions and beliefs shape their learning trajectories, e.g., Grade-10 algebra learners
target_learning_goals: Representing and responding to learner misconceptions and beliefs during instruction
examples: Figure 7 shows an example BBM for Sarah, a Grade-10 learner struggling with quadratic equations, including underlying belief, erroneous example, and triggering feature

article_title: Learning Context: A Unified Framework and Roadmap for Context-Aware AI in Education
citation: Naiming Liu, Brittany Bradford, Johaun Hatchett, Gabriel Diaz, Lorenzo Luzi, Zichao Wang, Debshila Basu Mallick, Richard Baraniuk. (2025). Learning Context: A Unified Framework and Roadmap for Context-Aware AI in Education. https://www.openstax.org
title: Model Context Protocol (MCP) as the interoperability layer for warm-starting AI education tools
description: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is the open-standards mechanism the article proposes for making Learning Context portable across AI tools, so that learner context accumulated in one system can be consumed by another. "By leveraging the Model Context Protocol (MCP), we will enable a wide range of AI tools to “warm-start” with durable context and achieve continual, long-term personalization." MCP addresses the problem that context is lost whenever a learner switches tools, and is one of the four research questions of the LC technology theme: how modern AI systems can interoperate securely through open standards.
requirements: Standardized metadata ensuring cross-system consistency and interoperability across AI tools and learning platforms
constraints: Realizing cross-tool context portability requires substantial R&D on scalable, privacy-aware data infrastructure
target_learners: Learners who use multiple AI tools and learning platforms across their learning journeys
target_learning_goals: Continual, long-term personalization via durable, portable learner context
examples: The article's implementation strategy embeds the LC in the OpenStax digital learning platform ecosystem with SafeInsights privacy-preserving enclaves

article_title: OpenLearnLM Benchmark: A Unified Framework for Evaluating Knowledge, Skill, and Attitude in Educational Large Language Models
citation: Unggi Lee, Sookbun Lee, Heungsoo Choi, Jinseo Lee, Haeun Park, Younghoon Jeon, Sungmin Cho, Minju Kang, Junbo Koh, Jiyeong Bae, Minwoo Nam, Juyeon Eun, Yeonji Jung, Yeil Jeong. (2026). OpenLearnLM Benchmark: A Unified Framework for Evaluating Knowledge, Skill, and Attitude in Educational Large Language Models. https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.13882
title: OpenLearnLM Benchmark dataset: 124K+ items spanning Knowledge, Skills, and Attitude axes
description: OpenLearnLM is an open benchmark dataset for evaluating educational LLMs across three axes. The article states: "Our benchmark comprises 124K+ items spanning multiple subjects, educational roles, and difficulty levels based on Bloom's taxonomy." The Knowledge domain contains 2,304 multiple-choice items (918 content, 1,386 pedagogical) sourced from C-Eval, GPQA, KICE, and the Pedagogy Benchmark; the Skills domain comprises 122,425 generated items (99.6% generation success rate, ~116,000 train / 6,100 test); the Attitude domain includes 14 scenario-based items. Quality assurance used an LLM-as-Judge rubric with a 99.9% pass rate (122,365 of 122,439 items).
requirements: Items must pass a five-criterion LLM-as-Judge quality rubric with a passing threshold of 20 points, including critical minimums for answer accuracy (3) and question clarity (2)
constraints: The Attitude domain contains only 14 scenario-based items (12 standard stances, 2 deception)
Skills items were generated by gpt-5-mini rather than authored by humans
target_learners: LLMs deployed as educational tutors, assessors, and instructional assistants
target_learning_goals: Evaluation of educational capability across knowledge, practical skill, and attitude
examples: Knowledge items were sourced from C-Eval and GPQA (918 items) and KICE and Pedagogy Benchmark (1,386 items) rather than solely synthetic generation
key_sources: Unggi Lee, Sookbun Lee, Heungsoo Choi, Jinseo Lee, Haeun Park, Younghoon Jeon, Sungmin Cho, Minju Kang, Junbo Koh, Jiyeong Bae, Minwoo Nam, Juyeon Eun, Yeonji Jung, Yeil Jeong. (2026). article_title: OpenLearnLM Benchmark: A Unified Framework for Evaluating Knowledge, Skill, and Attitude in Educational Large Language Models
citation: Unggi Lee, Sookbun Lee, Heungsoo Choi, Jinseo Lee, Haeun Park, Younghoon Jeon, Sungmin Cho, Minju Kang, Junbo Koh, Jiyeong Bae, Minwoo Nam, Juyeon Eun, Yeonji Jung, Yeil Jeong. (2026). OpenLearnLM Benchmark: A Unified Framework for Evaluating Knowledge, Skill, and Attitude in Educational Large Language Models. https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.13882
title: KSA three-axis evaluation framework with a four-level Skills hierarchy (Center→Role→Scenario→Sub-scenario)
description: The framework operationalizes educational LLM capability using the KSA (Knowledge-Skills-Attitude) model from educational assessment. The article states: "The Skills domain comprises 122,425 items across 6 Centers, 11 Roles, 46 Scenarios, and 81 Sub-scenarios." Knowledge covers curriculum-based content and pedagogical knowledge; Skills measures situated capability through tasks emulating real educational decisions, with difficulty tiers from Bloom's and Krathwohl's taxonomies; Attitude examines epistemic, instructional, and normative-ethical stances plus deception resistance via Alignment Faking. The hierarchy contextualizes tasks by institutional function (Center), professional responsibility (Role), task type (Scenario), and task variant (Sub-scenario).
requirements: Evaluation requires domain-matched methods: exact-match accuracy for Knowledge, LLM-as-Judge with scenario-specific 10-point rubrics for Skills, and LLM-as-Judge plus Alignment Faking comparison for Attitude
constraints: The framework is grounded in the KSA model from educational assessment and Bloom's/Krathwohl's taxonomies; the article notes future work is needed for multilingual contexts and real classroom interaction data
target_learners: LLMs acting as educational partners across teaching, learning, assessment, counseling, research, and administration contexts
target_learning_goals: Multidimensional educational competence beyond factual accuracy, including situated skill and pedagogical value alignment
examples: Each of the 81 sub-scenarios has a dedicated 10-point rubric defining quality levels from inadequate (1–2) to exemplary (9–10)

article_title: Can LLMs Model Incorrect Student Reasoning? A Case Study on Distractor Generation for Multiple-Choice Questions
citation: Yanick Zengaffinen, Andreas Opedal, Donya Rooein, Kv Aditya Srivatsa, Shashank Sonkar, Mrinmaya Sachan. (2026). Can LLMs Model Incorrect Student Reasoning? A Case Study on Distractor Generation for Multiple-Choice Questions. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.15547
title: A ten-strategy taxonomy of distractor-generation strategies grounded in learning-science literature and observed LLM reasoning
description: The article introduces a taxonomy of ten distractor-generation strategies, "grounded in learning-science literature and empirical observations of LLMs’ reasoning traces", spanning task understanding (INTER, CORR), candidate construction (LINK, ERR_DESC, ERR_SIM, INST), quality control and selection (PLAUS, DISCR, CURATE), and cross-cutting reconsideration (RECON). It was built by merging expert-practice strategies from the literature with strategies extracted via manual open coding of LLM traces, and is applied to annotate 885 reasoning traces span by span.
requirements: Requires reasoning traces (CoT or reasoning prompting) that can be annotated with strategy tags; direct prompting produces no intermediate traces to analyze.
constraints: The article notes reasoning traces are not guaranteed to faithfully reflect the underlying decision process, so strategies are descriptions of externalized reasoning rather than mechanistic claims.
target_learners: AI-in-education researchers and assessment designers modeling student misconceptions
target_learning_goals: Generating plausible, misconception-aligned distractors for multiple-choice assessment items
examples: The article annotates a DEEPSEEK-V3.2 trace for the problem "Simplify the following if possible: (6+9m)/3", labeling spans for correct-answer reference, error description, error simulation, outcome instantiation, plausibility assessment, final set curation, and discriminability check.
key_sources: Yanick Zengaffinen, Andreas Opedal, Donya Rooein, Kv Aditya Srivatsa, Shashank Sonkar, Mrinmaya Sachan. (2026). Can LLMs Model Incorrect Student Reasoning? A Case Study on Distractor Generation for Multiple-Choice Questions. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.15547

article_title: AI Assistance Reduces Persistence and Hurts Independent Performance
citation: Grace Liu, Brian Christian, Tsvetomira Dumbalska, Michiel A. Bakker, Rachit Dubey. (2026). AI Assistance Reduces Persistence and Hurts Independent Performance. Published as a conference paper at COLM 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.04721
title: Short-sighted AI collaboration: instant-answer assistance erodes persistence via shifted effort reference points and lost metacognitive calibration
description: The article frames current AI systems as "fundamentallyshort-termcollaborators" that provide instant, complete answers and rarely refuse, in contrast to good human collaborators who balance helping with fostering autonomy. It proposes two mechanisms for the observed persistence decline: hedonic-adaptation-like shifting of the reference point for how long a task should take, making unaided work feel counterfactually more effortful and self-reinforcing further offloading; and removal of the productive struggle through which people develop accurate self-knowledge, undermining the metacognitive calibration that sustains persistence. The theory situates the findings within the cognitive offloading and AI-induced deskilling literature.
requirements: AI systems currently optimized for short-term helpfulness and instant answers; the theory explains effects observed after brief (∼10 minute) AI-assisted problem-solving sessions.
constraints: The mechanisms are the authors' interpretation, not directly tested; experiments captured only brief AI exposure, and whether effects accumulate or attenuate with prolonged use remains an open question.
target_learners: Adult online research participants solving fraction and reading-comprehension tasks
Learners using AI assistants for reasoning-intensive tasks
target_learning_goals: Persistence through difficulty
Independent problem-solving and metacognitive calibration
examples: In the experiments, participants given a GPT-5 sidebar assistant for learning problems were then tested without it and showed lower solve rates and higher skip rates than never-assisted controls.
key_sources: Grace Liu, Brian Christian, Tsvetomira Dumbalska, Michiel A. Bakker, Rachit Dubey. (2026). AI Assistance Reduces Persistence and Hurts Independent Performance. Published as a conference paper at COLM 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.04721

article_title: What Don't You Understand? Using Large Language Models to Identify and Characterize Student Misconceptions About Challenging Topics
citation: Parker, M. J., & Zavala-Cerna, M. G. (2025). What Don't You Understand? Using Large Language Models to Identify and Characterize Student Misconceptions About Challenging Topics. https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09875
title: Framework for closing the learning analytics loop via LLM-characterized misconceptions
description: A cyclical framework in which data collection and analysis pinpoint challenging topics, LLMs characterize underlying misconceptions, and this analysis informs two intervention pathways: "cohort-level interventions for broad improvements and individualized learning paths for tailored support". Intervention effectiveness is then assessed with new data, refining the pedagogical process and revealing remaining or new misconceptions. The framework positions scalable misconception identification as the critical step toward closing the loop between learning analytics and instructional improvement.
requirements: Formative assessment data (topic-focused quizzes) collected across cohorts
LLM analysis grounded in quiz content, response patterns, and lecture transcripts
Follow-up data collection to evaluate intervention effectiveness
constraints: The study focuses primarily on cohort-level analysis; individual student analysis is proposed for future work
Intervention effectiveness measurement is proposed but not demonstrated in this study
target_learners: medical students in online biomedical science courses
target_learning_goals: identifying and remediating conceptual misconceptions in biomedical science
examples: The study applied the framework's first two stages (topic identification and misconception characterization) across five courses; intervention pathways remain proposed for future course iterations

citation: Parker, M. J., & Zavala-Cerna, M. G. (2025). What Don't You Understand? Using Large Language Models to Identify and Characterize Student Misconceptions About Challenging Topics. https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09875
title: Two-stage LLM misconception identification pipeline (GPT-4 misconception analysis plus Gemini topic synopses)
description: A pipeline combining quantitative quiz analysis with two LLM stages: GPT-4 (gpt-4o-2024-08-06, temperature 0.3) generates hypothesized misconceptions from structured question representations, most common incorrect answers, and Whisper-transcribed lecture transcripts; Gemini 2.0 Flash (temperature 0) creates topic synopses from titles and transcripts for instructors. The total LLM cost was minimal, "with the misconceptions work requiring only approximately one dollar and the topic synopsis work requiring one cent". The pipeline ran on an ordinary laptop via cloud APIs.

Lecture video transcripts (generated via Whisper large-v2)
Python coding skills for API-based batch processing
constraints: Drag-and-drop questions were excluded from misconception analysis due to difficulty of automatic characterization
Chat-based LLM interfaces lack reproducibility and reliable structured output compared to API access

citation: Parker, M. J., & Zavala-Cerna, M. G. (2025). What Don't You Understand? Using Large Language Models to Identify and Characterize Student Misconceptions About Challenging Topics. https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09875
title: Ground LLM misconception analysis in instructional content to mitigate hallucinations and produce instructor-actionable insights
description: Providing LLMs with relevant grounding context—lecture transcripts, question content, and response patterns—enables reliable misconception identification tied to how material was actually taught. The article reports that "The lack of hallucinations in this study suggests that providing relevant grounding/context is an effective strategy." Techniques like in-context learning and grounding mitigate hallucination risk by giving the model specific reference material and output format examples. This grounding also allows the model to relate misconceptions to instructional framing, producing feedback useful for instructors.

Structured output prompts with examples of desired format
constraints: Expert evaluation is still required; the article notes rigorous evaluation is needed even when no hallucinations are observed
target_learners: medical students in online biomedical science courses
target_learning_goals: accurate automated identification of student misconceptions
examples: GPT-4 prompts included the full lecture transcript, structured question representation, and most common incorrect answer for each problem

citation: Jana Gonnermann-Müller, Jennifer Haase, Nicolas Leins, Thomas Kosch, Sebastian Pokutta. (2026). LLM-Based Educational Simulation: Evaluating Temporal Student Persona Stability Across ADHD-Related Persona Specifications. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06307
title: Dual-assessment framework for evaluating LLM human simulations via joint self-report and observer-rated persona measurement
description: A methodology adapted from clinical psychology that jointly measures self-reported characteristics and observer-rated behavioral expressions of an LLM persona. Self-report scores measure how the persona agent characterizes itself when directly prompted with questionnaire items, while observer-report scores measure which persona-relevant behaviors are expressed in generated narratives or conversational segments. The framework's central contribution is exposing self–observer dissociation: "LLMs reliably report the assigned persona when directly asked, yet their spontaneous behavioral expression of that persona degrades in unscripted conversation." It also distinguishes between-conversation from within-conversation stability as complementary temporal dimensions.
requirements: Requires a validated instrument with parallel self-report and observer-report forms (here the CAARS ADHD Index) and independent raters blind to persona instructions
constraints: Neither measure provides direct access to the model's internal state; the framework measures consistency of expression, not representational validity or clinical authenticity
target_learners: LLM-simulated students with ADHD-related persona specifications
target_learning_goals: Temporal stability of simulated learner personas across and within interactions
examples: Experiment I administered the 26-item CAARS self-report short form to persona agents and had three independent LLM raters complete the 30-item observer short form on each narrative

title: Treat interaction structure as a primary design variable for stable LLM learner simulations, not an afterthought to model selection
description: When building simulation-based tools with sustained, path-dependent learner interactions, designers should engineer the conversational protocol itself: anchoring interactions with recurring task-relevant prompts standardizes opportunities for persona-relevant expression at each checkpoint. Across five models and two scenarios, "structured conversation design produced more temporally consistent observer-rated behavior" without model changes or fine-tuning. The article positions interaction structure as part of the measurement setup rather than a neutral delivery format.

constraints: A tightly scripted conversation can become less natural and can mechanically re-elicit the measured characteristics; higher measured stability does not by itself establish higher simulation fidelity

title: Curriculum cognition: structured understanding of how knowledge is organized and visually presented
description: The article names curriculum cognition as the construct that existing benchmarks fail to test and current instruction-tuning data fails to teach. It defines it as "the structured understanding of how knowledge is organized and visually presented, including prerequisite chains, concept taxonomies, experiment-concept links, and pedagogical sequencing." A competent teacher knows not only that a topic exists but what it requires as prerequisites, where it sits in the taxonomy, and where in the textbook it first appears. The K12-KGraph resources are designed to measure and teach this construct.

article_title: Simulating Students or Sycophantic Problem Solving? On Misconception Faithfulness of LLM Simulators
citation: Heejin Do, Shashank Sonkar, Mrinmaya Sachan. (2026). Simulating Students or Sycophantic Problem Solving? On Misconception Faithfulness of LLM Simulators. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.12748
title: Misconception faithfulness framework: misconception-contrastive feedback protocol and Selective Flip Score
description: The article proposes a diagnostic framework evaluating whether an LLM student simulator "preserves misconception-consistent belief state and selectively updates it only when feedback addresses the underlying misconception." Its core is a misconception-contrastive feedback protocol comparing targeted feedback (addressing the true misconception), misaligned feedback (targeting a different plausible misconception), and generic feedback (only signaling incorrectness), from which the Selective Flip Score SFS = FT − ½(FM + FG) quantifies selective sensitivity. The framework also includes a six-category student response taxonomy distinguishing content-sensitive updates (correct flip, constructive pushback) from content-insensitive ones (sycophantic flip, passive maintain).
requirements: A simulator must be evaluated with paired problem, misconception-driven wrong answer, and three contrastive feedback conditions for the same initial error
Feedback conditions must isolate semantic alignment as the primary source of variation
constraints: The framework focuses on mathematics domains with misconceptions drawn from existing taxonomies; extending to less structured domains remains future work
SFS measures observable behavioral updates rather than latent belief states directly
Teacher feedback and response classifications are generated by LLMs rather than human-authored
target_learners: LLM-based student simulators used to train and evaluate AI tutors and human educators
target_learning_goals: Diagnosing and responding to misconception-driven student reasoning during tutoring interaction
examples: The framework was applied to seven instruction-tuned LLMs (4B–120B) on the Malrule and EEDI datasets under base and reflective prompting, and used as the reward basis for SFT, DPO, and GRPO post-training.

title: Recurring failure modes of vision-LLM grading of handwritten math: blurry images, rotated text, hallucinated text, missing solution elements, and erroneous mathematical reasoning
description: The article's qualitative analysis of discrepant submissions identifies several recurring failure modes: transcription errors due to blurry submissions, transcription errors due to rotated text, hallucinated text, correctness assigned despite missing solution elements, and erroneous mathematical reasoning. The authors note LLMs "produced substantially more accurate transcripts for well-captured images, whereas blurred submissions were sometimes ambiguous even to course staff." Hallucinated text was most common with blurry or rotated images, suggesting higher-quality inputs may reduce this risk.
requirements: Well-captured, clear, well-organized submissions for reliable transcription
constraints: Correctness assigned despite missing solution elements may be an inherent LLM limitation
Penalization of rotated images may be impractical in high-stakes exams
target_learners: university STEM students submitting handwritten mathematical work
target_learning_goals: accurate automated rubric-based grading of handwritten multi-step solutions
examples: In Course 1, blurriness often resulted from students photographing solutions written on a tablet; the team added direct screenshot uploads supporting webcam capture, mobile photos, or direct file upload
key_sources: Jacob Levine, Miguel Aenlle, Craig Zilles, Matthew West, and Mariana Silva. (2026). Automated Grading of Handwritten Mathematics Using Vision-Capable LLMs. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.19043

article_title: Automated Grading of Handwritten Mathematics Using Vision-Capable LLMs
citation: Jacob Levine, Miguel Aenlle, Craig Zilles, Matthew West, and Mariana Silva. (2026). Automated Grading of Handwritten Mathematics Using Vision-Capable LLMs. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.19043
title: Deploy vision-LLM handwritten-math grading in low-stakes formative contexts first, with students informed feedback may contain mistakes
description: The article concludes that Gemini 3 Flash's accuracy appears sufficient for low-stakes, formative contexts such as practice problems, where immediate feedback outweighs occasional errors, provided students are informed the AI-generated feedback may contain mistakes. High-stakes deployment demands greater reliability in interpreting student work. This principle scopes deployment recommendations to the accuracy levels the study measured.
requirements: Students are informed the AI-generated feedback may contain mistakes
Accuracy sufficient for the stakes level, as measured against human ground truth
constraints: High-stakes deployment demands greater reliability in interpreting student work
target_learners: university STEM students in practice and formative assessment contexts
target_learning_goals: immediate feedback on handwritten mathematical problem solving
examples: The study evaluated the grader on extra-credit in-lecture activities and proctored midterm submissions, with students never exposed to AI-generated grading output

article_title: Exploring the Effectiveness of Using LLMs for Automated Assessment of Student Self Explanations in Programming Education
citation: Arun-Balajiee Lekshmi-Narayanan, Mohammad Hassany, Peter Brusilovsky. (2026). Exploring the Effectiveness of Using LLMs for Automated Assessment of Student Self–Explanations in Programming Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21614
title: SelfCode2.0 dataset of student and expert line-by-line code explanations
description: SelfCode2.0 is a recently released annotated corpus of code explanations used as the study's evaluation data. It "includes explanations produced by 60 students and 2 experts for individual lines of four code examples", with 3019 student–expert pairs in total, of which the study used 1854 single-statement pairs labeled correct or incorrect. The dataset's severe class imbalance (1794 correct vs 60 incorrect) motivated the paper's synthetic augmentation.
requirements: Annotator labels of student explanations as correct or incorrect
Single-statement pairs for sentence-level semantic similarity approaches
constraints: A stated limitation of the original dataset is variation among human experts in their assessments of student explanations
target_learning_goals: Code comprehension and self-explanation skills
examples: The study used a subset of 1854 of the 3019 pairs in which both student and expert explained the line with a single statement

article_title: LLM-assisted sentiment analysis for integrated computational and qualitative mixed methods education research: A case study of students' written reflection assignments
citation: Xiomara Gonzalez, Gabriella Coloyan Fleming, Andrew Katz, Maya Denton, Jessica Deters. (2026). LLM-assisted sentiment analysis for integrated computational and qualitative mixed methods education research: A case study of students' written reflection assignments. https://www.google.com/search?q=LLM-assisted+sentiment+analysis+for+integrated+computational+and+qualitative+mixed+methods+education+research
title: Quasi-mixed methods: an LLM-human workflow applying quantitative and qualitative analysis to the same qualitative dataset
description: The article proposes a "quasi-mixed" method in which "our “quasi-mixed” method applies quantitative and qualitative analysis to the same qualitative dataset", extending NLP-human mixed-methods workflows to an LLM-human workflow. It is operationalized as a six-stage pipeline: data familiarization, manual quote extraction, human and LLM-assisted sentiment labeling, human revision of LLM labels, parallel qualitative and quantitative analyses, and interpretation of qualitative findings considering quantitative results. The LLM is treated as an additional individual rater whose discrepancies inform deeper analysis.
requirements: Manually extracted quotes for downstream tasks, since the model's own quote extraction was unreliable
Human review of LLM sentiment labels to resolve discrepancies and ensure analytic coherence
Iterative prompt tuning and Python scripts to automate model inference and track outputs
constraints: Prompt designs are dataset- and context-specific, limiting generalizability across research settings
Upfront technical setup and administrative overhead may outweigh payoff for smaller datasets or single-use analyses
Only open source models were ethically usable because participants did not consent to data sharing with third-party commercial entities
target_learners: Undergraduate engineering students in study abroad programs
Education researchers analyzing qualitative reflection data
target_learning_goals: Cross-cultural communication skills
Critical self-assessment and meaning-making through written reflection
examples: The pipeline was applied to 535 quotations from 51 students across three reflection time points, partitioned by seven student identities and lived experiences, using MetaAI's Llama3 model (8 billion parameters) run locally via the Ollama framework with temperature set to 0

article_title: A Classroom Study of LLM-Generated Feedback Intervention in Introductory Programming
citation: Hasnain Heickal and Andrew Lan. (2026). A Classroom Study of LLM-Generated Feedback Intervention in Introductory Programming. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.08807
title: PROGFEED: a longitudinal dataset of randomized AI feedback conditions in introductory programming
description: PROGFEED is a released dataset from an IRB-approved classroom study in an introductory Python course, capturing "6,693 submissions from 215 consenting students across 17 labs and 43 problems". It links complete submission histories to feedback conditions, execution outcomes, and temporal ordering, and includes source code, test case outcomes, demographic and weekly survey responses, and course performance measures. The dataset is publicly available on GitHub and supports hierarchical analysis at student, problem, and lab levels.
requirements: Feedback conditions were randomized at the submission level within each lab, with students reassigned between labs; feedback was conditionally triggered only on failing submissions.
constraints: Because feedback delivery is conditionally triggered rather than fully randomized, all analyses on the dataset are associative, not causal.
target_learners: first-year introductory programming students, primarily computer science majors
target_learning_goals: debugging and reaching correct solutions on introductory Python programming problems
examples: The study randomized submissions across no-AI, failing test case, and natural language feedback conditions generated by gpt-4o-mini with fixed prompts across all labs.

article_title: Learning by Chatting? Investigating the Impact of Generative AI on Information Seeking and Learning
citation: Shravika Mittal, Su Lin Blodgett, Q. Vera Liao. (2026). Learning by Chatting? Investigating the Impact of Generative AI on Information Seeking and Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.11669
title: Ellis's model of information-seeking behaviors as an analytical lens for studying GenAI-mediated learning
description: Ellis's model (Ellis, Cox, and Hall 1993) characterizes information seeking as eight observable behaviors: "starting (initiating information seeking), chaining (following connections to pursue a line of inquiry), browsing (casually seeking information in potential areas of interest), differentiating (using known differences to filter information), monitoring (regularly following particular sources), extracting (selectively identifying relevant information), verifying (checking the correctness of information), and ending (wrapping up)." The article chose it because, unlike models emphasizing contextual or affective factors, it "focuses on observable behaviors," and used it as the deductive coding framework for thematic analysis of diary entries, with inductive sub-codes capturing condition-specific actions.
requirements: Diary or observational data describing how information seekers interact in an information environment, so the eight behavior stages can be coded
constraints: The article analyzed only responses to the first diary entry prompt and excluded day-1 entries as participants familiarized with the process
target_learners: Adult informal learners seeking everyday information (here, Prolific participants learning nutrition and meal planning)
target_learning_goals: Understanding and improving information-seeking behaviors that support informal learning
examples: The first author deductively coded diary entries from days 2 to 8 with Ellis's stages, generated inductive sub-codes (e.g., starting broad vs. narrow, extracting artifacts vs. information), and summarized the framework in Table 1
key_sources: Shravika Mittal, Su Lin Blodgett, Q. Vera Liao. (2026). Learning by Chatting? Investigating the Impact of Generative AI on Information Seeking and Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.11669

article_title: Are LLM-based Chatbots Good Enough to Support Computer Science Students in Multiple-Choice Exercises?
citation: Markos Stamatakis, Omkar Gavali, Joshua Berger, Christian Wartena, Anett Hoppe, and Ralph Ewerth. (2026). Are LLM-based Chatbots Good Enough to Support Computer Science Students in Multiple-Choice Exercises? https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15919
title: Integrate LLM-generated answers into assessment and study settings carefully, since their effect on performance depends on task domain and learners' prior knowledge
description: The article concludes that chatbot outputs in test settings can either support or hinder learning depending on the task and setup, calling for "careful educational integration" of such systems. It positions LLM output as possible scaffolding for lower-prior-knowledge learners while warning of cognitive offloading for higher-prior-knowledge learners, and recommends larger studies before reliable conclusions.
requirements: Larger user studies with more participants and questions to reliably assess the statistical significance of chatbot-output effects, as the article states.
constraints: The article states findings are limited by its dataset and the small group of participants; the quantitative effect of GPT-generated output was not statistically significant under LRT.
target_learning_goals: Answering domain-specific multiple-choice questions in computer science topics such as interactive visual data analysis and computer vision
examples: In the user study, participants were randomly assigned to three groups completing two test attempts with or without GPT-4o output in IVDA and CV lectures.
