title: AI adaptive learning environment perception scale (15 items, three dimensions)
description: A novel self-report instrument grounded in the Technology Acceptance Model and characteristics of adaptive studying systems, covering system adaptability (6 items), degree of personalization (5 items), and algorithmic transparency (4 items), refined after expert content-validity review and a pilot study. The article reports that "the overall scale demonstrated very strong internal consistency (Cronbach's α = 0.89), and second-order CFA gained support on the higher-order structure (χ2/df = 2.28, CFI = 0.95, RMSEA = 0.050)." Responses use a 5-point Likert format with the aggregate score used in primary analyses.
requirements: Content validity review by pedagogical psychology experts and pilot testing before use
constraints: It measures perceived adaptivity via self-report; only intelligent tutoring systems and course-specific recommendation tools in the sample provided true adaptivity
target_learners: undergraduate students using AI-based educational tools
target_learning_goals: measuring perceptions of AI-adaptive learning environments
examples: Used at T1 of the three-wave survey with 486 undergraduates in China

article_title: Students Prefer Personalized, AI-Generated Educational Videos over Non-Personalized, Human-Recorded Videos
citation: Tomlinson, B., Black, R.W., Patterson, D.J., van der Hoek, A., Ferguson, J. & Bietz, M.J. (2026). Students prefer personalized, AI-generated educational videos over non-personalized, human-recorded videos. Scientific Reports 16:21804. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-52798-9
title: Human-supervised AI video production pipeline for personalized instructional videos
description: A custom software pipeline produced 300 AI-generated personalized videos (100 topics × three interest variants: business, technology, society/biology) for a large online undergraduate course. LLMs (GPT-4o, Claude 3.7 Sonnet) drafted five-paragraph scripts from an instructor-defined "ethos" prompt; the instructor and project scientist reviewed and edited all scripts and checked examples for correctness. Videos composited a HeyGen AI avatar built from a recording of the instructor, Unsplash images, bullet points, titles, credits, and music into 3–5 minute videos uploaded to YouTube and embedded in Canvas pages.
requirements: Instructor oversight at multiple stages: script review, correctness checking of examples and images, and final video review
constraints: Producing and reviewing the scripts "was a time-consuming process, but still quicker than it would have been to write multiple versions of 100 scripts by hand"; numerous iterations were needed to adjust avatar expressiveness, intonation, lighting, and framing
target_learners: undergraduate students in a large online general education course
target_learning_goals: connections between information technology and global sustainability
examples: Students accessed the material through Canvas, shown approximately 10 topics per week across 10 weeks, choosing among three interest-tailored versions of each topic's video

article_title: Reimagining the Philosophy of Experimentation in Chemistry Education: Embracing AI as a Tool for Scientific Inquiry
citation: Reyes, R.L., & Regala, J.D. (2026). Reimagining the Philosophy of Experimentation in Chemistry Education: Embracing AI as a Tool for Scientific Inquiry. Sci & Educ, 35, 709–754. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11191-025-00667-8
title: Framework for integrating AI into chemistry education that maximizes benefits while preserving scientific reasoning and discovery
description: The article proposes that chemistry education needs "a framework for integrating AI into chemistry education that maximizes its benefits while preserving the essential elements of scientific reasoning and discovery." The framework is positioned as the article's central contribution, balancing AI's power with human-driven exploration in the experimental philosophy of chemistry education. The accessible text describes the framework's purpose and rationale but not its detailed components.
requirements: Integration must maximize AI's benefits while preserving the essential elements of scientific reasoning and discovery, as the article states
constraints: The accessible text does not print the framework's operational components; only its purpose is stated
target_learning_goals: scientific reasoning and discovery in chemistry experimentation
examples: The article positions this framework as its contribution to the future of chemistry education, per its abstract

citation: Reyes, R.L., & Regala, J.D. (2026). Reimagining the Philosophy of Experimentation in Chemistry Education: Embracing AI as a Tool for Scientific Inquiry. Sci & Educ, 35, 709–754. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11191-025-00667-8
title: Balance the power of AI with the irreplaceable aspects of human-driven scientific exploration in chemistry education
description: The article argues that integrating AI into chemistry education requires "balancing the power of AI with the irreplaceable aspects of human-driven scientific exploration," within a thoughtful reimagining of the philosophy of experimentation that challenges long-held epistemological, methodological, and ethical frameworks. The principle directs educators to adopt AI as a tool for scientific inquiry without displacing human agency in experimentation.
requirements: AI integration must be paired with preservation of human-driven scientific exploration, as the article states
constraints: The article frames this within chemistry education's philosophy of experimentation; scope beyond that domain is not claimed
target_learning_goals: scientific inquiry
experimental reasoning in chemistry
examples: The article's abstract presents this balancing as necessitated by AI's reshaping of experimental approaches in chemistry education

article_title: Artificial intelligence in initial teacher training for pre-service primary school teachers in mathematics: a systematic review
citation: Pinto F, Rodrigues RN, Brito-Costa S, Costa C, Gonçalves S, Pires NA and Martins F (2026) Artificial intelligence in initial teacher training for pre-service primary school teachers in mathematics: a systematic review. Front. Educ. 11:1934366. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1934366
title: Four-dimension framework for training pre-service primary teachers in AI integration
description: The review identifies four integrated dimensions for training pre-service primary school teachers in AI: "AI Awareness; AI Literacy and Prompting; Pedagogical Integration; and Critical Evaluation and Autonomous Professional Decision-Making". These range from knowledge and exploration of AI tools to pedagogically grounded use and critical evaluation of appropriateness. The dimensions are articulated with two cross-cutting needs: continuity of training and monitoring over time.
requirements: Training should progress from knowledge and exploration of AI tools to pedagogically grounded use and critical evaluation of their appropriateness
constraints: The framework synthesizes an evidence base of 11 studies published between 2024 and 2026, which the review describes as recent and limited
target_learners: Pre-service primary school teachers in initial teacher training
target_learning_goals: AI awareness and literacy
prompting competency
pedagogical integration of AI
critical evaluation and autonomous professional decision-making about AI-generated content
examples: The review grounds AI Awareness in the preparatory phases present in eight of the eleven studies, and Pedagogical Integration in practices ranging from problem solving and lesson planning to simulating professional situations

citation: Pinto F, Rodrigues RN, Brito-Costa S, Costa C, Gonçalves S, Pires NA and Martins F (2026) Artificial intelligence in initial teacher training for pre-service primary school teachers in mathematics: a systematic review. Front. Educ. 11:1934366. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1934366
title: Provide longer-term, continuous AI training that prepares teachers to evaluate and adapt AI-generated content rather than merely use AI tools
description: The review recommends that AI training extend beyond short-term tool use: it "should prepare Pre-Service Primary School Teachers to evaluate, adapt, and make informed decisions about AI-generated content based on their didactic and mathematical knowledge and critical thinking". Training should be embedded throughout initial teacher training rather than relying on isolated interventions, and supported by monitoring instruments implemented throughout the entire training process.

article_title: Agentic AI in educational environments and its association with social and motivational pathways to learning performance
citation: Dhanya Pramod and Kanchan Pranay Patil. (2026). Agentic AI in educational environments and its association with social and motivational pathways to learning performance. Discover Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s44217-026-02168-4
title: Integrated GDCT–SDT–SPT framework for agentic AI-supported online learning
description: The article proposes an integrated theoretical framework in which Holmberg's Guided Didactic Conversation Theory, Self-Determination Theory, and Social Presence Theory are "viewed not as additive, but as interlinked theoretical approaches". GDCT forms the pedagogical and interactional layer explaining dialogue, guidance, feedback, and responsiveness; SDT explains how psychological needs (autonomy, competence, relatedness) relate to learning motivation; SPT explains how interactivity, information sharing, and collaboration form social presence. The two pathways converge at learner engagement, which relates to perceived learner performance.
requirements: Learners must have prior experience with AI-based online learning platforms for the perceived constructs to be meaningful
constraints: The framework was tested with perception-based survey data among Indian business-school students, not with an experimental system or objective performance measures
target_learners: business and management students in higher education (MBA, PGDM, BBA)
target_learning_goals: learning motivation
social presence
learner engagement
perceived learning performance in AI-supported online learning
examples: The conceptual framework (Fig. 1) positions perceived agentic AI affordances, psychological perceptions, motivational and social-relational mechanisms, engagement, and perceived performance in one structural model tested with PLS-SEM
key_sources: Dhanya Pramod and Kanchan Pranay Patil. (2026). Agentic AI in educational environments and its association with social and motivational pathways to learning performance. Discover Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s44217-026-02168-4

article_title: Agentic AI in educational environments and its association with social and motivational pathways to learning performance
citation: Dhanya Pramod and Kanchan Pranay Patil. (2026). Agentic AI in educational environments and its association with social and motivational pathways to learning performance. Discover Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s44217-026-02168-4
title: Agentic AI-enabled online learning platforms as perceived autonomous learning facilitators
description: The study defines agentic AI as "an autonomous, adaptive learning facilitator that actively helps participants through personalised guidance, feedback, and decision-making support". Students in the sample used AI-powered platforms such as ChatGPT Agent, Claude with Agent, and Grammarly AI Agents for assignments, research, problem-solving, and case analysis; these were treated as examples of tools learners may perceive as exhibiting agentic characteristics rather than as technically equivalent agentic AI systems. Reported functions include developing study plans, step-by-step assignment help, recommending materials, proficiency-adjusted explanations, and proactive writing suggestions.
requirements: Respondents must have used agentic AI-powered platforms at least once in the previous three months to credibly report perceptions
constraints: The platforms were treated as examples of AI tools learners may perceive as agentic, not as technically equivalent agentic AI systems; the study assesses perceptions, not a specific system
target_learners: higher education students in business and management programs
target_learning_goals: academic coursework support
self-paced learning
personalized guidance and feedback
examples: Participants were given an example prompt asking an AI to act as a personal learning agent with a daily schedule, quizzes, feedback, and progress-adjusted lessons

article_title: Perceptions and Acceptance of Artificial Intelligence in Science Education Programmes: Voices of Pre-Service Science Teachers
citation: Amponsah, K. D., Adu-Boahen, J., Commey-Mintah, P., Kumassah, E. K., Ayittey, R. F., Nketsiah, J. (2026). Perceptions And Acceptance of Artificial Intelligence in Science Education Programmes: Voices of Pre-Service Science Teachers. Education Quarterly Reviews, 9(3), 51-65. https://doi.org/10.31014/aior.1993.09.03.724
title: Integrative UTAUT-TPB framework for AI adoption in science education
description: The study adapts the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (Venkatesh et al., 2003) and the Theory of Planned Behaviour (Ajzen, 1991) into an integrative framework in which "the influences of attitudes, norms, perceived behavioural control, and the performance and effort expected are channelled primarily through behavioural intention". UTAUT supplies performance expectancy and effort expectancy; TPB supplies attitude and perceived behavioural control; behavioural intention sits closest to behaviour. The authors argue UTAUT alone is "good at predicting a person's intention but weak at explaining the behaviour", motivating the integration.
requirements: Measurement of performance expectancy, effort expectancy, attitude, perceived behavioural control, behavioural intention, and actual use as distinct constructs
constraints: The article notes UTAUT alone is weak at explaining behaviour once intention is formed, motivating the TPB integration
target_learning_goals: technology acceptance and integration of AI in science teaching
examples: The study measured the six constructs with a structured questionnaire whose reliability and validity were confirmed (Cronbach's alpha and composite reliability above 0.70, AVE above 0.50 for all constructs).

article_title: Predictors of the ethical use of generative artificial intelligence in higher education
citation: Tabares-Cruz YB, Cevallos-Sánchez HA, Arteaga-Pita IG, Rodriguez-Alava LA, Carreño-Mendoza AL, Cedeño-Barreto MdlÁ, Castro-Castillo GJ, Cobacango-Villavicencio JG and Moreira-Choez JS (2026) Predictors of the ethical use of generative artificial intelligence in higher education. Front. Educ. 11:1942426. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1942426
title: Six-dimension structural model of ethical generative AI use
description: The article proposes and tests a structural framework in which ethical GenAI use is an integrative behavioral outcome predicted by six theoretically differentiated dimensions: ethical and technical AI literacy, academic integrity and transparency, critical thinking and content verification, self-regulation and academic responsibility, data protection/privacy/risk management, and institutional guidance and ethics education. The endogenous construct "captures whether these principles are translated into responsible academic practice across multiple domains." The model distinguishes responsible academic behavior from general AI adoption, frequency of use, or digital competence.
requirements: The six exogenous constructs must be modeled as distinct antecedents, with each observed indicator assigned exclusively to its theoretically corresponding latent construct
constraints: The cross-sectional design permits only predictive associations, not causal effects; the sample was non-probability purposive and does not warrant population-level representativeness
target_learners: higher education students across undergraduate, postgraduate, and continuing education levels
target_learning_goals: ethical and responsible use of generative AI in academic work, including integrity, transparency, verification, and data protection
examples: The model was estimated with CB-SEM in a sample of 980 students from different educational levels, fields of knowledge, and study modalities
key_sources: Tabares-Cruz YB, Cevallos-Sánchez HA, Arteaga-Pita IG, Rodriguez-Alava LA, Carreño-Mendoza AL, Cedeño-Barreto MdlÁ, Castro-Castillo GJ, Cobacango-Villavicencio JG and Moreira-Choez JS (2026) Predictors of the ethical use of generative artificial intelligence in higher education. article_title: Predictors of the ethical use of generative artificial intelligence in higher education
citation: Tabares-Cruz YB, Cevallos-Sánchez HA, Arteaga-Pita IG, Rodriguez-Alava LA, Carreño-Mendoza AL, Cedeño-Barreto MdlÁ, Castro-Castillo GJ, Cobacango-Villavicencio JG and Moreira-Choez JS (2026) Predictors of the ethical use of generative artificial intelligence in higher education. title: 44-item questionnaire measuring seven dimensions of ethical GenAI use
description: A newly developed self-administered instrument with 44 items across seven dimensions: six predictor constructs of six items each and an eight-item ethical-use dimension, answered on a five-point Likert scale. Reliability was satisfactory to high, with Cronbach's alpha ranging "from 0.861 for institutional guidance and ethics education to 0.924 for the ethical use of generative artificial intelligence," and composite reliability from 0.896 to 0.938. Seven reverse-worded items were retained after reverse-scoring.

constraints: The instrument was developed specifically for this study rather than adapted from a previously validated scale; validity evidence is from a single institutional sample
target_learners: university students at the State University of Milagro

examples: A sensitivity analysis showed excluding the reverse-worded indicator reduced Cronbach's alpha in every dimension, so no items were deleted

article_title: Preservice mathematics teachers’ noticing in AI-based simulations: transitions among attending, interpreting, and shaping
citation: Selen Galiç, Mathias Tejera, Sebastián Parodi, Markus Hohenwarter, Zsolt Lavicza. (2026). Preservice mathematics teachers' noticing in AI-based simulations: transitions among attending, interpreting, and shaping. ZDM – Mathematics Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11858-026-01805-4
title: Teacher Noticing of Rationality Framework (TNRF)
description: The TNRF builds on van Es and Sherin's expanded noticing framework of attending, interpreting, and shaping, and "extends van Es and Sherin's (2021) framework by specifying the object of noticing more precisely as students' mathematical thinking". It operationalises students' thinking through Habermas's theory of rationality as observable behaviours: justifying statements, selecting and using appropriate tools, and communicating with appropriate terminology and representations. Attending targets manifestations of rational behaviour rather than surface correctness; interpreting evaluates the quality of participation in mathematical practices; shaping structures conditions under which rational behaviour becomes visible.
requirements: Requires teachers' professional knowledge and an inquiry stance to interpret behaviours through the rationality lens rather than simple correctness judgments
constraints: The article applies the framework specifically to the equal-sign context, with coding adapted to the construct map of the equal sign (Matthews et al., 2012)
target_learning_goals: Noticing students' mathematical thinking in the context of the equal sign as equivalence
examples: The study used the TNRF to inform a deductive coding scheme with subcodes under each noticing dimension, applied to reflection papers and chat interactions

citation: Selen Galiç, Mathias Tejera, Sebastián Parodi, Markus Hohenwarter, Zsolt Lavicza. (2026). Preservice mathematics teachers' noticing in AI-based simulations: transitions among attending, interpreting, and shaping. ZDM – Mathematics Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11858-026-01805-4
title: AI-based simulation environment with virtual student and mentor chatbots built on GPT-4o
description: The environment comprises chatbots for three virtual secondary students (aged 11–12) each embodying a specific equal-sign misconception, paired with a targeted task and a video of the student's solution, plus a virtual mentor chatbot giving feedback on strengths, aspects to improve, and suggestions. "The AI-based simulations were built on OpenAI's GPT-4o (OpenAI, 2024)", with personas, aims, recipients, themes and chat structure defined through explicit prompt engineering following Park and Choo (2024). Prototypes were tested by researchers, then piloted with preservice teachers in Austria, inservice teachers in Spanish, and expert educators in Turkish before implementation.
requirements: Prompt engineering defining persona, aim, recipients, themes and chat structure with few-shot examples; iterative pilot testing to address overly elaborate student responses and descriptive rather than actionable mentor feedback
constraints: The article acknowledges the tasks used may have influenced noticing transitions, and that AI-generated responses may be overly verbose, mathematically inaccurate, or epistemically misleading, requiring scrutiny by users
target_learners: Preservice mathematics teachers in final-year programs in Austria, Türkiye, and Uruguay
target_learning_goals: Practising eliciting, interpreting, and responding to student thinking about the equal sign; rehearsing questioning strategies with feedback
examples: Each week preservice teachers watched a misconception video, interacted with one student chatbot, wrote guided reflections, and received mentor chatbot feedback

description: The implementation was organised as a repeating weekly structure in which "each week consisting of four phases". article_title: How Human-Centered Is AI-Aided Learning in Education?
citation: Katia Tödt, Corinne Büching, and Bastian Granas. (2026). Digital Education and Innovation: Objectives and Conceptual Classification of the Volume. In Digital Education and Innovation. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-26816-7_1
title: Knowledge triangle of research, education and innovation adapted to the educational context
description: The chapter adapts the innovation-economics 'knowledge triangle' to education as the volume's organising framework. It argues that education in this model 'encompasses the entire multi-level system of education', including administration and practice, not only university teaching. The triangle visualises interactions between research, education and innovation and frames transformation processes as interdisciplinary and innovation-oriented.
requirements: A broader understanding of education that incorporates the control, organisational, and action levels of the education system
constraints: The classic interpretation ties innovation to economic exploitation of research results, which the authors explicitly widen for the educational context
target_learning_goals: understanding and designing digital education innovation processes
examples: The chapter uses the adapted triangle to contextualise the volume's four thematic sections and to analyse why transfer of research knowledge into practice has been insufficient

title: Digital transformation in education as social innovation
description: The chapter proposes understanding digital transformation in education 'not only as technological modernisation or institutional reform, but also as a process of social innovation'. Drawing on the German national strategy, social innovations are 'new social practices and organisational models' that solve social problems, can arise independently of technology, and often develop bottom-up at the interfaces between state, market, civil society and science.
requirements: Cooperative and participatory approaches in which actors from learners to EdTech providers are jointly involved in innovation processes
constraints: The term social innovation has been used relatively rarely in education, where change is often framed as politically organised educational reform
target_learners: learners, teachers, educational institutions, administrators and policy actors
target_learning_goals: developing digital competences and future skills through changed forms of interaction in teaching and learning
examples: The chapter cites OER-based sharing and co-constructive development of materials and changed teaching-learning interactions through adaptive, data-based systems as developments interpretable as social innovation

Co-constructive, design-oriented research approaches are presented as a response.

article_title: Pedagogical Safety in Educational Reinforcement Learning
citation: Oluseyi Olukolaa, Nick Rahimia. (2026). Pedagogical Safety in Educational Reinforcement Learning: Formalizing and Detecting Reward Hacking in AI Tutoring Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.04237
title: Four-layer model of pedagogical safety for educational RL (structural, progress, behavioral, alignment) with the RHSI severity metric
description: The article formalizes pedagogical safety as four constraint classes: "Structural Safety (C1):Prerequisites are architecturally enforced via action masking", progress safety (C2, windowed mastery gain), behavioral safety (C3, minimum cognitive demand), and alignment safety (C4, engagement coupled to mastery). A policy is pedagogically safe if it simultaneously satisfies C1–C4, with an ε-relaxed weighted-norm version for practice. The Reward Hacking Severity Index quantifies the degree to which a policy simultaneously achieves high return and high violation, bounded in [0,1]. The authors argue via informal propositions that no proper subset of the four constraints implies the full set.
requirements: Constraint thresholds must be calibrated to the specific domain (e.g., εprog from a mastery-only baseline's per-window progress distribution; δmin=0.4 set at the ICAP passive/active boundary)
constraints: C1 is enforced architecturally and excluded from the aggregate violation vector (v1≡0 by convention)
The framework's safety guarantees hold with respect to estimated mastery, not necessarily true mastery
Constraint independence arguments are informal sufficiency arguments rather than formal proofs
target_learners: Learners in intelligent tutoring systems, simulated here as struggling, average, and advanced programming-education profiles
target_learning_goals: Genuine mastery of domain concepts (27 Python concepts) rather than proxy engagement maximization
examples: SmartTutor enforces C1 via action masking and C3 via an action selection module online; C2 and C4 are evaluated as offline safety metrics from session logs
key_sources: Oluseyi Olukolaa, Nick Rahimia. (2026). Pedagogical Safety in Educational Reinforcement Learning: Formalizing and Detecting Reward Hacking in AI Tutoring Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.04237

article_title: Pedagogical Safety in Educational Reinforcement Learning
citation: Oluseyi Olukolaa, Nick Rahimia. (2026). Pedagogical Safety in Educational Reinforcement Learning: Formalizing and Detecting Reward Hacking in AI Tutoring Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.04237
title: SmartTutor simulated Python tutoring testbed for evaluating pedagogical safety in educational RL
description: SmartTutor is a simulated Python tutoring environment comprising "a knowledge graph of 27 Python concepts (DAG, max depth 7", a student model with per-concept mastery tracking, a neural contextual bandit agent with UCB action selection over a 124-dimensional state representation, an action selection module enforcing C1 and C3 online, and a configurable reward system. Eight pedagogical actions span cognitive demand from d=0.0 (Encourage) to d=1.0 (Challenge), with Encourage producing zero mastery gain but the largest engagement boost (+0.8). Three learner profiles (Struggling, Average, Advanced) vary initial knowledge, gain multiplier, and confusion threshold.
requirements: A knowledge graph of prerequisite relationships, a student mastery model, and a configurable reward system with engagement, mastery, and pedagogical-appropriateness components
constraints: Simulated learners use a heuristic mastery update rather than full BKT inference and do not capture motivation, fatigue, or off-task behavior
The single domain (Python programming) limits generalizability to other subjects and curricula
target_learners: Simulated programming learners (struggling, average, advanced profiles)
target_learning_goals: Mastery of Python programming concepts
examples: Each main condition ran 30 sessions (3 profiles × 10 random seeds × 150 interactions per session), yielding 4,500 interactions per condition and 18,000 total across main conditions
key_sources: Oluseyi Olukolaa, Nick Rahimia. (2026). Pedagogical Safety in Educational Reinforcement Learning: Formalizing and Detecting Reward Hacking in AI Tutoring Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.04237

article_title: Pedagogical Safety in Educational Reinforcement Learning
citation: Oluseyi Olukolaa, Nick Rahimia. (2026). Pedagogical Safety in Educational Reinforcement Learning: Formalizing and Detecting Reward Hacking in AI Tutoring Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.04237
title: Reward design alone may be insufficient to ensure pedagogically aligned behavior in educational RL; pair reward shaping with architectural constraints
description: The article's central design recommendation is that weighted reward combinations do not by themselves prevent reward hacking when a zero-learning, high-engagement action exists; architectural constraints (prerequisite masking plus a minimum cognitive-demand floor) are needed. The abstract states that "reward design alone may be insufficient to ensure pedagogically aligned behavior in educational RL, at least in the simulated environment studied here", and the constrained architecture lowered RHSI from 0.317 to 0.102. The authors' future-work section suggests integrating constraints into the optimization itself as Lagrangian terms in a Constrained MDP, with C3 receiving the highest weight.
requirements: An action space in which cognitive demand per action can be quantified, and the ability to mask actions or filter action selection online
constraints: Demonstrated only in simulation with a single weight configuration for the multi-objective condition; human validation with real learners remains essential before deployment
target_learners: Learners using RL-based intelligent tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: Genuine mastery gains rather than proxy engagement maximization
examples: SmartTutor Full enforces C1 via action masking and C3 via a demand floor (δmin=0.4) during training, while C2 and C4 are monitored as offline metrics

article_title: Neural-Symbolic Knowledge Tracing: Injecting Educational Knowledge into Deep Learning for Responsible Learner Modelling
citation: Hooshyar, D.; Šír, G.; Yang, Y.; Kärkkäinen, T.; Hämäläinen, R.; Krivich, E.; Cukurova, M.; Gašević, D.; Azevedo, R. (2026). Neural-Symbolic Knowledge Tracing: Injecting Educational Knowledge into Deep Learning for Responsible Learner Modelling. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.08263
title: Responsible-DKT: a neural-symbolic deep knowledge tracing framework injecting symbolic educational knowledge into sequential neural architectures
description: Responsible-DKT is a neural-symbolic variant of DKT that unifies symbolic inputs, learnable embeddings, recurrent dynamics, output prediction, and pedagogical rules in a single differentiable logic program built with Lifted Relational Neural Networks. The article states it "is a neural-symbolic variant of DKT that injects symbolic educational knowledge into sequential neural architectures". Rules such as mastered and not_mastered modulate rather than override neural predictions, and the grounded computation graph supports local and global explanations. RNNs are used as a proof-of-concept, with the approach applicable to other architectures such as Transformers.
requirements: Symbolic educational knowledge (e.g., mastery and non-mastery rules) supplied by educators or domain experts for injection into the model
Interaction logs structured as ordered per-student sequences of skill, quiz, and correctness tuples
constraints: The injected rules in this study are simple pedagogical heuristics used as an illustrative example; the recurrent core is a proof-of-concept while richer architectures and rules remain future work
target_learning_goals: Tracking and predicting learners' evolving knowledge and next-step correctness in mathematics
examples: The model was trained and evaluated on Opiq interaction logs using a next-step prediction task, compared against BaseNS-DKT and Classic-DKT
key_sources: Hooshyar, D.; Šír, G.; Yang, Y.; Kärkkäinen, T.; Hämäläinen, R.; Krivich, E.; Cukurova, M.; Gašević, D.; Azevedo, R. (2026). Neural-Symbolic Knowledge Tracing: Injecting Educational Knowledge into Deep Learning for Responsible Learner Modelling. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.08263

citation: Hooshyar, D.; Šír, G.; Yang, Y.; Kärkkäinen, T.; Hämäläinen, R.; Krivich, E.; Cukurova, M.; Gašević, D.; Azevedo, R. (2026). Neural-Symbolic Knowledge Tracing: Injecting Educational Knowledge into Deep Learning for Responsible Learner Modelling. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.08263
title: PyNeuraLogic framework for lifted relational neural-symbolic learning
description: PyNeuraLogic implements the Lifted Relational Neural Networks paradigm, expressing data as logical predicates and model architectures as parameterized weighted logical rule templates that are grounded into differentiable computation graphs. The article states it "elevates neural-symbolic learning to the relational level, utilizing differentiable first-order logic programming". Because temporal sequences are a linear case of relational graphs, it can subsume RNN and graph architectures while enforcing explicit symbolic rules. The framework is released at the printed GitHub URL and is used here to implement Responsible-DKT.
requirements: Data expressed as logical ground facts and a declared rule template; grounding against available facts to unroll the computation graph before backpropagation
constraints: Propositional-level neural-symbolic models it supersedes struggle with structured or dynamically sized data; the framework's scope is relational, differentiable logic programming
target_learners: Researchers and developers of learner-modelling systems
target_learning_goals: Sequential learner knowledge modelling with injected symbolic educational knowledge
examples: Responsible-DKT was implemented as a single neural-symbolic template in PyNeuraLogic, grounded per student against interaction facts

citation: Hooshyar, D.; Šír, G.; Yang, Y.; Kärkkäinen, T.; Hämäläinen, R.; Krivich, E.; Cukurova, M.; Gašević, D.; Azevedo, R. (2026). Neural-Symbolic Knowledge Tracing: Injecting Educational Knowledge into Deep Learning for Responsible Learner Modelling. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.08263
title: Opiq 6th-grade mathematics interaction dataset from Estonia
description: The study uses time-ordered interaction logs of 6th-grade mathematics students collected in September 2021 from Opiq, a nationally adopted K-12 digital learning platform in Estonia. "The dataset contains 21,471 student–item interactions, each originally described by more than 20 raw attributes." Records were binarized using the first-quartile score threshold (37), students with fewer than two interactions were removed, and data were partitioned at the student level into train/validation/test sets at an approximate 7:1:2 ratio (14,057/2,969/4,428 interactions; 105/15/30 students) across 13 skills.
requirements: At least two recorded interactions per learner to support sequential modelling and next-step prediction
constraints: Scores binarized at the first quartile, so the correct label captures the top 75% of observed performance; sequence lengths truncated at the Tukey upper fence of 475 interactions
target_learning_goals: Next-step correctness prediction and knowledge tracing in mathematics
examples: Student-level partitioning prevented information leakage, ensuring evaluation on previously unseen learners

article_title: Neural-Symbolic Knowledge Tracing: Injecting Educational Knowledge into Deep Learning for Responsible Learner Modelling
citation: Hooshyar, D.; Šír, G.; Yang, Y.; Kärkkäinen, T.; Hämäläinen, R.; Krivich, E.; Cukurova, M.; Gašević, D.; Azevedo, R. (2026). Neural-Symbolic Knowledge Tracing: Injecting Educational Knowledge into Deep Learning for Responsible Learner Modelling. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.08263
title: Four-component pipeline for neural-symbolic knowledge tracing
description: The Responsible-DKT approach is organized as a reusable four-stage pipeline: raw logs are pre-processed into chronological per-student sequences, symbolic training samples are generated as sequence-to-sequence ground facts and queries, a neural-symbolic model integrates embeddings, recurrence, and symbolic rules, and evaluation combines predictive metrics with interpretability analyses. The article states that "the approach includes four main components: data pre-processing, sample generation, neural-symbolic modelling, and model evaluation and interpretation". Evaluation covers AUC, early-middle-late error comparison, prediction volatility and inconsistency, and skill-level mastery heatmaps.
requirements: Interaction logs with identifiers and performance information; a symbolic rule set R; student-level train/validation/test partitioning
constraints: Baselines without rule injection require post-hoc explanation methods, making direct interpretability comparison less meaningful per the article
target_learners: Learners in digital learning platforms producing sequential interaction logs
target_learning_goals: Next-step knowledge prediction with interpretable, pedagogically grounded updates
examples: Algorithm 1 summarizes the pipeline from pre-processing through local and global interpretability analyses

citation: Hooshyar, D.; Šír, G.; Yang, Y.; Kärkkäinen, T.; Hämäläinen, R.; Krivich, E.; Cukurova, M.; Gašević, D.; Azevedo, R. (2026). Neural-Symbolic Knowledge Tracing: Injecting Educational Knowledge into Deep Learning for Responsible Learner Modelling. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.08263
title: Inject conservative symbolic mastery and non-mastery rules to stabilize sequential knowledge-tracing predictions
description: The article recommends encoding pedagogically motivated constraints as learnable-weight symbolic rules that modulate neural predictions when simple evidence patterns occur in the interaction history. Specifically, "three incorrect responses on the same skill or quiz activate a not_mastered rule, providing a conservative signal that discourages premature overestimation of mastery", while two consecutive correct responses activate a mastered rule. These constraints help mitigate common DKT instabilities where mastery probabilities move contrary to recent responses, while preserving interpretability through the rule structure.
requirements: Interaction histories sufficient to detect the evidence patterns; rule weights learnable or fixed to enforce stronger pedagogical constraints when desired
constraints: Lower thresholds than prior mastery-learning work (e.g., seven learning opportunities) were adopted to suit the shorter and sparser sequences in this dataset; symbolic components modulate rather than override neural predictions
target_learners: K-12 learners in digital practice environments with sparse interaction sequences
target_learning_goals: Temporally consistent, pedagogically aligned mastery estimation
examples: In Responsible-DKT, triggered rules contribute additional evidence to the correctness predicate alongside the recurrent state and an averaged historical embedding pathway

article_title: Programming Intelligent Tutoring Systems
citation: Alina Deriyeva, Jesper Dannath, and Benjamin Paaßen. (2025). SCRIPT: Implementing an Intelligent Tutoring System for Programming in a German University Context. Artificial Intelligence in Education (Springer). https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-99261-2_16
title: SCRIPT: an adaptable Python programming ITS serving as both teaching and research platform
description: SCRIPT (Step-based Coding for Research and Intelligent Programming Tutoring) is a web-based ITS supporting advanced undergraduates learning Python for data science and machine learning. The article states it "functions both as a teaching and as a research tool by enabling to record fine-grained, keystroke-level data" and is "easily adaptable to novel learner models and pedagogical models as well as randomized experiments." It was offered as voluntary exam preparation for an Introduction to Data Mining course and has supported prior learner-model and feedback research. Source code is released on a GitLab repository, though the system is still in alpha stage.
requirements: Hosted in Docker containers on the university's own server infrastructure to meet regulatory requirements
Teachers must be able to upload new course material to adapt the system to different Python courses
constraints: The system is still in the alpha stage; the authors "can not yet recommend the system for deployment but only for research use"
At present the ITS is only used in a narrow, short-term setting (Python introduction and exam preparation)
target_learners: Advanced undergraduate (third year) and early postgraduate (first year) computer science students
target_learning_goals: Python programming for data science and machine learning
examples: Offered as voluntary exam preparation for the Introduction to Data Mining course with tasks across eight subdomains such as probability theory, clustering, and deep models

article_title: Programming Intelligent Tutoring Systems
citation: Alina Deriyeva, Jesper Dannath, and Benjamin Paaßen. (2025). SCRIPT: Implementing an Intelligent Tutoring System for Programming in a German University Context. Artificial Intelligence in Education (Springer). https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-99261-2_16
title: Four-model ITS architecture with inner and outer loop pedagogical model
description: SCRIPT adopts the standard four-models ITS approach: "a Pedagogical Model, a Learner Model, a Domain Model, and a User Interface." The pedagogical model follows VanLehn's inner/outer loop differentiation: "The outer loop is responsible for task selection and the inner loop is responsible for generating feedback to steps inside programming tasks." The domain model holds tasks, a competency model (Q-matrix), and difficulty information; the learner model derives competency states from UI actions via a knowledge tracing algorithm. Models are designed to be easily replaceable and can be randomly assigned for A/B-testing.
requirements: A knowledge tracing algorithm to derive learner competency from UI actions
Task-to-skill relations and task difficulty information from the domain model for outer-loop task selection
constraints: Only part of the features described in the outer and inner loop schemas are implemented; the system is in alpha stage

article_title: The Pedagogy of AI Mistakes: Fostering Higher-Order Thinking
citation: Hosseini, H. (2026). The Pedagogy of AI Mistakes: Fostering Higher-Order Thinking. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05472
title: AI-as-learning-companion: leveraging LLM fallibility through a critique-refinement cycle to develop higher-order thinking
description: The paper's central framework reframes generative AI errors and hallucinations as a pedagogical resource rather than a limitation. By treating AI as a "learning companion" whose imperfect outputs prompt analysis, evaluation, and reflection, instructors structure an "iterative critique-refinement cycle" in which "AI's imperfect outputs serve as catalysts for evaluation, positioning critique as the central mechanism driving higher-order cognition". The cycle of generation, evaluation, and revision is aligned with Bloom's taxonomy, shifting emphasis from knowledge and application toward analysis, evaluation, and creation, and fostering metacognitive engagement.
requirements: Instruction must extend beyond domain knowledge to include the ability to evaluate, contextualize, and revise AI-generated outputs
Structured opportunities for evaluation and revision with imperfect responses
constraints: Over-reliance on AI can impede the development of core cognitive skills, so use must be scaffolded
target_learning_goals: higher-order thinking (analysis, evaluation, creation)
metacognitive skills including self-monitoring and error detection
critical evaluation of AI-generated solutions
examples: Weekly AI Modules in a database design course structured prompting strategies, failure-mode analysis, and a recurring Santa's Workshop case study around the critique-refinement cycle

article_title: Prober.ai: Gated Inquiry-Based Feedback via LLM-Constrained Personas for Argumentative Writing
citation: Ran Bi, Shiyao Wei, Yuanyiyi Zhou. (2026). Prober.ai: Gated Inquiry-Based Feedback via LLM-Constrained Personas for Argumentative Writing Development. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05598
title: Pedagogical friction: reflection-gated feedback architecture in which cognitive effort precedes support
description: The article introduces pedagogical friction as a first-class architectural primitive: revision suggestions are gated behind an intelligent reflection gate that assesses the student's written defense for substance and, if thin, coaches rather than answers. The two-phase API design (/challenge → /unlock) ensures that "genuine cognitive effort—not merely a keystroke—precedes the delivery of revision support." The gate uses a deterministic assessment layer (length floor, reasoning markers, topical relevance) followed by a model-side status check, and after two coached attempts a genuine effort is released to a scaffolded hint.

A deterministic assessment layer checking length, reasoning markers, and question-specific relevance
constraints: The architecture supports only up to two coaching turns per question, not open-ended multi-turn dialogue
If an unlocked suggestion is misaligned, there is no mechanism for iteratively refining the defense–suggestion exchange
target_learners: K–12 students developing argumentative writing skills
students preparing for standardized assessments such as AP English Language and GRE Analytical Writing
target_learning_goals: argumentative writing quality
metacognitive reflection and self-explanation
examples: In the deployed system, a defense failing the deterministic layer receives a targeted coaching nudge such as adding a because-style reasoning link, and only a defense clearing both gate layers reaches the model-side unlock

title: Write–Challenge–Defend–Improve cyclical interaction loop
description: The system's user interaction follows a cyclical four-phase model: the student writes an essay, selects a critical persona and receives structured inquiry-based questions with no evaluative language, writes a reflective defense for each question, and only after the defense clears the reflection gate unlocks a concrete revision suggestion and writing tip built on the student's own reasoning. The student then incorporates these into the draft and may re-enter the loop with revised text. The article states the loop is designed so that "cognitive effort always precedes the delivery of suggestions, ensuring the student remains the primary agent of revision."

description: Prober.ai ships with a research-logging pipeline that "captures the full interaction without altering the student experience." An optional Study Setup mode records participant, session, condition, and prompt identifiers with a consent flag, and dedicated endpoints append newline-delimited JSON to six logs (sessions, events, drafts, challenges, unlocks, reflection-coaching). Fine-grained timestamped events let a researcher reconstruct each student's revision trajectory and the {question, defense, score, revision} tuples the reflection gate produces; each model call carries a hashed, privacy-preserving safety_identifier.

title: The AI should never write for the student: preserve cognitive effort in AI-assisted writing tools
description: The article's core design principle is that AI writing support must never reduce the cognitive load required for argumentation: the system functions exclusively as a structured questioner, asking rather than telling, and deliberately withholds solutions until the student has demonstrated reflective engagement. This is motivated by cited evidence that AI-generated text availability suppresses independent reasoning and that facilitative (question-based) feedback is more strongly associated with long-term learning gains than directive feedback. The article argues that "pedagogical friction is a feature, not a bug" in AI-assisted education design.
requirements: Feedback interaction must be question-based in its initial phase
Revision support must be gated behind assessed student reflection
constraints: Claims about cognitive engagement preservation and learning outcomes remain theoretical, grounded in prior literature rather than empirical validation specific to this system
target_learning_goals: durable argumentative writing skill development
metacognitive reflection
examples: Prober.ai refuses to generate or rewrite text, eliminating the cognitive shortcut that enables outsourcing, per the article's account of cited EEG and behavioral evidence

title: NSMQ Riddles: a benchmark of 1,840 scientific and mathematical riddles from Ghana's NSMQ competition
description: NSMQ Riddles is a benchmark dataset of scientific and mathematical riddles drawn from round 5 of Ghana's National Science and Maths Quiz, an annual live TV competition for senior secondary school students. The article states the dataset "consists of 1,840 riddle questions comprising 11 years of questions from round 5 of the NSMQ, ranging from 2009 to 2021". Each riddle contains a minimum of three clues that start vague and become more specific, with answers that are usually a number, word, or short phrase, allowing automatic evaluation via Exact Match and Fuzzy Match accuracy. It was curated from YouTube recordings and PDFs converted with OCR, manually reviewed, and preprocessed into CSVs with answer variants. A metadata sheet for 2019 and 2020 records which school answered each riddle and at which clue.

article_title: Explaining Too Much? Understanding How Large Language Model Reasoning Traces Influence Performance and Metacognition
citation: Fernandes, D., Buschek, D., Tankelevitch, L., Kosch, T., & Welsch, R. (2026). Explaining Too Much? Understanding How Large Language Model Reasoning Traces Influence Performance and Metacognition. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.25856
title: Reasoning traces as user-facing interface artifacts rather than transparent windows into model cognition
description: The article proposes that LLM reasoning traces are best understood as user-facing interface artifacts rather than windows into model cognition: what matters is not whether a trace faithfully reflects the model's computation but how its format shapes users' metacognitive processes. The authors state that "reasoning traces are best understood as user-facing interface artifacts rather than transparent windows into model cognition", positioning the faithfulness problem as a further design risk because users may calibrate reliance on unreliable representations of model thinking.
requirements: The framing applies to trace output treated from a user-facing perspective, regardless of its internal validity, as the article states.
constraints: A model's chain-of-thought output and the internal computations that produce its answer can diverge, so traces may not faithfully represent how the model arrived at its answer.
target_learners: adult problem-solvers using LLM assistants for reasoning tasks
target_learning_goals: calibrated self-evaluation and reliance on AI assistance during reasoning
examples: In the experiment, summary traces preserved performance while elevating trust and hedonic appeal, and full traces impaired performance and produced the largest overestimation gap.
key_sources: Fernandes, D., Buschek, D., Tankelevitch, L., Kosch, T., & Welsch, R. (2026). Explaining Too Much? Understanding How Large Language Model Reasoning Traces Influence Performance and Metacognition. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.25856

article_title: Explaining Too Much? Understanding How Large Language Model Reasoning Traces Influence Performance and Metacognition
citation: Fernandes, D., Buschek, D., Tankelevitch, L., Kosch, T., & Welsch, R. (2026). Explaining Too Much? Understanding How Large Language Model Reasoning Traces Influence Performance and Metacognition. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.25856
title: Scaffold metacognitive support by eliciting users' own reasoning before exposing the model's reasoning traces or answer
description: Because no trace format supported calibrated self-evaluation, the article argues that calibration is unlikely to emerge from the traces themselves and should instead be scaffolded by interactions that elicit users' own reasoning first. The authors write that "Metacognitive support must instead be scaffolded by interactions that elicit users' own reasoning before exposing the model's reasoning traces or answer." The Full-trace interface's Final Answer button, which required engagement with the trace before revealing the answer, illustrates deliberately sequencing exposure to encourage independent reasoning prior to model influence.
requirements: Interface designs must sequence exposure so that users commit to or articulate their own reasoning before the model's trace or answer is revealed.
constraints: The article presents this as a design direction argued from the finding that no trace format supported calibration; it was not itself manipulated as a condition in the experiment.
target_learners: adults solving reasoning problems with AI assistance
target_learning_goals: metacognitive accuracy and calibrated reliance on AI
examples: The Full-trace condition required participants to engage with the reasoning trace before a Final Answer button revealed the model's answer, encouraging independent reasoning prior to model influence.

description: PARE-M (Persistent Agentic Research Environment Measurement) v0.1 is a descriptive measurement framework the article introduces for evaluating persistent agentic research environments. description: The framework trains a variational autoencoder on standardized country-level indicators of autonomy, digital skills and teacher support, projecting them into a two-dimensional latent space interpreted as "a structural readiness space for digital and AI-related transformations in education". Geometric proximity reflects similarity in joint learning environment configurations, and a composite AI Readiness Index is formed as a linear aggregation of the two latent coordinates (α = 0.5). citation: Lala Yamazaki and Ramchandra Rimal. (2026). Leveraging Physiological Signals to Predict Exam Outcomes with Machine Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.14960
title: Encoder-only transformer with classification head adapted for numerical physiological data classification
description: The authors adapt the original transformer architecture for classification of tabular physiological data: the decoder is removed and a classification head (linear transformation followed by softmax over grade categories A–F) is added to the encoder output. Each physiological feature is treated as an individual token in the input sequence, with embedding and positional encoding preserving temporal structure, and multi-head self-attention capturing dependencies among physiological features. The article states, "Specifically, only the encoder component of the transformer was retained, as our task requires generating a single output—predicted performance category—rather than producing a sequential output," and reports this is the first attempt to implement transformer architecture to model academic outcomes using physiological signals.
requirements: Input physiological data embedded as dense vectors with positional encoding added to maintain sequence order; a classification head with softmax converts encoder output into grade-category probabilities
constraints: Tuned configuration used 8 heads, 3 layers, dropout probability 0, d_model 256, 128 hidden-layer neurons, batch size 128, and sequence length 128
target_learning_goals: predicting exam grade categories from multivariate physiological stress signals
examples: The adapted transformer achieved a mean test accuracy of 0.9039 ± 0.0081 over 30 replicates

title: Interpret physiological predictions within broader context; never use them as standalone decision-making tools
description: The article's ethics section recommends that predictions of academic performance derived from physiological data be treated as one input among many rather than as autonomous decision tools. It states that such predictions "should be interpreted within the context of other influential factors, such as personal circumstances, environmental conditions, and mental health considerations, to guarantee fairness and mitigate biases." High-stakes decisions such as educational interventions must incorporate these insights within a broader context to avoid imposing undue stress and unintended consequences on students.
requirements: Use of publicly accessible datasets and fully documented computational methodologies, including model parameters and hyperparameters, to promote reproducibility; averaging findings over multiple runs
constraints: Predictions are not intended to stand alone as decision-making tools; high-stakes decisions must incorporate broader context
target_learners: college students in high-stress exam settings
target_learning_goals: supporting student well-being and mental health awareness alongside academic performance monitoring
examples: The article suggests educators, mental health professionals, and stakeholders can leverage the study's framework to build stress-monitoring and performance-prediction tools that uphold ethical standards

title: Three-phase tutoring structure for math word problems: understanding, calculation, and summarization
description: The article identifies a three-phase structure organizing parent-child math word problem tutoring. The article states that "word problem solving was described as a process that embodies three recurrent phases, namely understanding, calculation, and summarization." Each phase establishes a temporary focus of attention and shared expectations about what counts as progress, regulating when reasoning advances and how instructional authority is distributed. Phase boundaries are actively enforced by parents rather than implicitly assumed, serving as an interactional script that guides instruction and regulates problem-solving behavior.
requirements: Parents must actively enforce phase boundaries and authorize transitions between phases for the structure to regulate tutoring interaction
constraints: Derived from interviews with 11 Chinese parents and 2 teachers in the context of upper-elementary math word problem tutoring
Aligns with classical problem solving models according to the article
target_learning_goals: Mathematical word problem solving including interpretation, calculation, and reflection
examples: Parents asked children to restate problems in their own words before calculation (understanding phase)
Teachers instructed students to return to the question instead of correcting numbers blindly (calculation to understanding transition)
Parents prompted children to articulate underlying principles after solving (summarization phase)
key_sources: LUO Lan, WANG Anqi, ZHOU Muzhi, ZHU Junhua, CAI Jie, YU Ao, and PAN Hui. (2024). ParaTutor: Coordinating Parent-Child Math Tutoring through Role-Separated LLM Scaffolding. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18030

article_title: ParaTutor: LLM Mediated Parent Child Tutoring through Role Separated Scaffolding Interface in Real Time
citation: LUO Lan, WANG Anqi, ZHOU Muzhi, ZHU Junhua, CAI Jie, YU Ao, and PAN Hui. (2024). ParaTutor: Coordinating Parent-Child Math Tutoring through Role-Separated LLM Scaffolding. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18030
title: Three-dimensional scaffolding design coordinating user roles, tutoring phases, and guidance strategies
description: ParaTutor organizes its support as a design that "coordinates user roles, tutoring phases, and guidance strategies during parent-child math tutoring." The role dimension differentiates support between parents (guidance for conducting tutoring) and children (visual grounding for interpreting problems). The phase dimension structures how support changes across understanding, calculation, and summarization. The strategy dimension translates tutoring goals into concrete parent-facing guidance including suggested actions, example language, and ways of using the child-facing visualization. Together these dimensions define ParaTutor as a scaffold for parent-led tutoring.
requirements: A shared internal state maintained by a Main Agent that stores the current problem, active phase, interaction history, selected mode, child progress, and visualization state
Phase transitions controlled by explicit rule-based conditions rather than LLM decisions
Two synchronized panels separating parent-facing and child-facing interfaces
constraints: Designed for parent-child dyads in home math word problem tutoring, not single-user learning
Visual grounding withholds procedural solution steps reserved for parent-facing scaffolding
target_learners: Parent-child dyads with children aged 10-12 in grades 4-6
target_learning_goals: Mathematical word problem solving with shared understanding and active reasoning
examples: In the understanding phase, agents prioritize segmentation and grounding prompts while withholding solution procedures
In the calculation phase, agents support error localization and guided questioning
In the summarization phase, agents support reflection, consolidation, and transfer prompts

article_title: ParaTutor: LLM Mediated Parent Child Tutoring through Role Separated Scaffolding Interface in Real Time
citation: LUO Lan, WANG Anqi, ZHOU Muzhi, ZHU Junhua, CAI Jie, YU Ao, and PAN Hui. (2024). ParaTutor: Coordinating Parent-Child Math Tutoring through Role-Separated LLM Scaffolding. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18030
title: ParaTutor: multi-agent LLM-based scaffolding system for home math word-problem tutoring
description: ParaTutor is "a multi-agent LLM-based scaffolding system for home math word-problem tutoring" that "distributes support across user roles by providing parents with strategy, language, repair, and phase scaffolds, while providing children with visual grounding for problem interpretation." The system consists of a Main Agent, phase-specific scaffolding agents, and a visual grounding module. The Main Agent maintains a shared internal state and invokes only scaffolding agents relevant to the current phase sequentially. A rule-based state-to-diagram generation pipeline renders interactive visualizations from the evolving shared state rather than revealing worked solutions.
requirements: An internet-connected computer for remote use
Parents attend an orientation session covering system use
Phase transitions require joint confirmation from parent and child
constraints: Evaluated with children aged 10-12 in grades 4-6 in Chinese home tutoring contexts
Visual grounding module is rule-based rather than LLM-generated
Positioned as a third party supporting parent-led tutoring rather than replacing parental involvement
target_learners: Parent-child dyads with children aged 10-12 in grades 4-6 in Chinese home tutoring contexts
target_learning_goals: Math word problem solving including perimeter-based counting, two-category constraint problems, and age-related reasoning
examples: The Main Agent prioritizes agents for task simplification and situational guidance in the understanding phase
The visual grounding module maps extracted entities, numerical attributes, and relational constraints to graphical primitives and layout rules
Children dragged age markers and adjusted time sliders to test whether interpretations were consistent with problem relations

article_title: ParaTutor: LLM Mediated Parent Child Tutoring through Role Separated Scaffolding Interface in Real Time
citation: LUO Lan, WANG Anqi, ZHOU Muzhi, ZHU Junhua, CAI Jie, YU Ao, and PAN Hui. (2024). ParaTutor: Coordinating Parent-Child Math Tutoring through Role-Separated LLM Scaffolding. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18030
title: Parent scaffolding strategies across three tutoring phases for math word problems
description: The formative study identified "recurring scaffolding moves that parents use" that "shape turn-taking, pacing, and the distribution of responsibility during problem solving." In the understanding phase, parents used task simplification and situational guidance. In the calculation phase, they used feedback and correction, demonstration and imitation, and independent-thinking strategies. In the summarization phase, they used review and consolidation and practical application. These strategies are organized by the three-phase tutoring structure and represent how parents without formal training distribute instructional responsibility during home math tutoring.
requirements: Parents must maintain distinct instructional roles where they guide the process while children remain responsible for reasoning and solution generation
constraints: Identified from interviews with 11 Chinese parents of children in grades 4-6
Some strategies such as systematic review were noted as too time-consuming by some parents
Demonstration and imitation raised concerns about differing from teachers' approaches
target_learners: Children in grades 4-6 (ages 10-12) receiving home math tutoring from parents
target_learning_goals: Mathematical word problem solving across understanding, calculation, and summarization phases
examples: A parent used a pen to circle parts of the problem on paper so the child could gradually understand it (task simplification)
A parent drew diagrams to clarify relationships when questions were too long (situational guidance)
A parent asked children to articulate their solution process before offering help (independent-thinking strategy)

article_title: Automated Recommendation of Programming Learning Content Using Pattern-based Knowledge Components
citation: Muntasir Hoq, Griffin Pitts, Zhangqi Duan, Arun Balajiee Lekshmi Narayanan, Mohammad Hassany, Andrew Lan, Peter Brusilovsky and Bita Akram. (2026). Automated Recommendation of Programming Learning Content Using Pattern-based Knowledge Components. CSEDM'26: 10th Educational Data Mining in Computer Science Education Workshop. https://educationaldatamining.org
title: Pattern-based knowledge component framework for representing programming learning activities
description: The framework defines knowledge components as "recurring, semantically meaningful structural patterns based on important subtrees from program Abstract Syntax Trees (ASTs)". Discovery proceeds in four steps: SANN-guided subtree extraction trained on topic labels, normalization that anonymizes identifiers and canonicalizes syntactic alternatives, context-aware encoding of normalized subtree sequences with a β-VAE, and K-means clustering of latent vectors into KCs. Activities are then mapped to IDF-weighted knowledge vectors and compared by cosine similarity, yielding finer-grained, implementation-level signals such as guarded loop traversals and accumulator updates.
requirements: Training the extraction pipeline requires coarse-grained topic labels for challenges and examples
Expert-defined bundle information is deliberately withheld from SANN training so patterns reflect topic-level regularities
constraints: The first pipeline step uses topic labels for training, limiting direct application to unlabeled corpora, as the authors state in Limitations
target_learning_goals: mastering foundational programming concepts and patterns
retrieving instructionally aligned worked examples and practice challenges
examples: Applied to the PCEX Python corpus, where each program is mapped to a binary KC-incidence vector, IDF-reweighted, L2-normalized, and ranked by cosine similarity

article_title: The Paternalistic Filter: Epistemic Injustice and Differential Refusal in LLM-Mediated History Education for Marginalized Romanian Students
citation: Alexis Popovici, Andrei Ionascu, Adrian Marius Dumitran. (2026). The Paternalistic Filter: Epistemic Injustice and Differential Refusal in LLM-Mediated History Education for Marginalized Romanian Students. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11292
title: Epistemic paternalism in LLM tutoring as hermeneutical injustice
description: The article's central explanatory framework holds that LLM tutors constitute "epistemic paternalism: withholding civic complexity from marginalized learners while replacing it with victimization-centered narratives." Drawing on Fricker's hermeneutical injustice—a gap in interpretive resources that disadvantages groups in understanding their social experience—the authors argue safety alignment acts as a paternalistic filter transforming conversational AI into "agents of narrative segregation." The framework unifies the audit's four empirical patterns (refusal, gatekeeping, lexical simplification, framing shifts) as one mechanism.
requirements: Requires deployment of LLMs as conversational tutors for politically contested historical content to marginalized learner populations
constraints: Established for a single contested event (the 1989 Romanian Revolution) and single-turn interactions; the authors state future work must verify whether the patterns are universal across other cultural contexts and multi-turn tutoring
target_learners: Marginalized secondary students, including Roma and low socio-economic tier learners
target_learning_goals: Understanding contested national history as political actors with access to interpretive tools and civic agency
examples: The audit operationalized the framework via five metrics: Differential Refusal, Coup Gap, Type-Token Ratio, Agency Theft Ratio, and Mean Justification Scores
key_sources: Alexis Popovici, Andrei Ionascu, Adrian Marius Dumitran. (2026). The Paternalistic Filter: Epistemic Injustice and Differential Refusal in LLM-Mediated History Education for Marginalized Romanian Students. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11292

title: Open audit dataset of 1,800 LLM history-tutor responses across five personas
description: The article releases a reproducible audit corpus: 1,800 independent API calls across four LLMs (GPT_OSS, LLaMA, Deepseek, Kimi K2) with five embedded student personas and three prompt types (general explanation, causes/consequences, justification score), run at temperature 0 with n=30 iterations per condition. The authors state "all exact prompts, persona definitions, and raw API data are available" publicly, enabling replication of differential refusal, coup-gap, TTR, agency-theft, and justification-score analyses.
requirements: Access to the four audited models' APIs; temperature control where configurable
constraints: Kimi K2's API temperature was unconfigurable, so some refusals may reflect stochastic behavior
target_learners: Researchers and auditors of educational AI systems
target_learning_goals: Auditing LLM tutoring systems for identity-conditioned bias in history education
examples: The preliminary UI pilot observed depoliticization of the Roma persona, which the controlled T=0 API study then quantified

citation: Steve Woollaston, Brendan Flanagan, Yuko Toyokawa and Hiroaki Ogata. (2026). Penny: Transition Network Analysis of Learner-Chatbot Interactions in Scaffolded EFL Writing. Preprint, accepted at the 1st Workshop on Transition Network Analysis (TNA) at LAK '26.
title: Penny: an LLM-powered EFL writing support chatbot with structured feedback guidelines
description: Penny is a generative AI chatbot powered by GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024–08–06) that scaffolds English writing practice three to four times per week with daily prompts. Learners must write at least 100 characters before requesting feedback, and feedback is given in English or Japanese. Its system prompt directs it to "Adapt to the student's level", review grammar and syntax, enhance vocabulary, encourage and support, limit responses to 50 words, and keep the student on topic.
requirements: Learners must write a minimum of 100 characters before the Check my writing button becomes active
The system prompt supplies the student's name, proficiency level, chat language and the day's writing prompt
constraints: Learners could not engage with future writing prompts past the present day
The writing textbox only accepted English characters
target_learners: Japanese junior high school EFL learners aged 14–16
target_learning_goals: English as a Foreign Language writing accuracy and engagement with written corrective feedback
examples: Used by three EFL classes (n = 119) at a high performing public school in Japan over four months

title: Transition Network Analysis as a framework for modelling temporal learner-chatbot interaction
description: Transition Network Analysis (TNA) models learning processes as networks of discrete behavioural states connected by directed, probabilistic transitions, computed here with a web-based TNA Shiny app. Unlike frequency counts, it "maps the temporal trajectory of learner actions", operationalising the error treatment sequence in interactionist SLA. In this study it revealed the Revision and Chat Loops and enabled network-level metrics (density, reciprocity) and proficiency-group comparisons.
requirements: Events must be coded into discrete states, with classification validated against human raters
Transitions below a chosen probability threshold (here 0.05) may be pruned for visualisation while metrics use the full dataset
constraints: The authors note their chi-squared analysis does not isolate specific edge-level differences and recommend permutation testing for specific transition pathways
target_learners: Researchers and designers analysing learner-chatbot interaction logs
target_learning_goals: Understanding temporal dynamics of feedback uptake and dialogue in AI-scaffolded writing
examples: Applied to 63,328 coded events from Japanese EFL learners using Penny, yielding a 10-node, 26-edge network

citation: Marina Lepp. (2026). Patterns of Learner–AI Interaction and Academic Performance in an Object-Oriented Programming Course. IEEE Frontiers in Education (FIE) 2026 Conference.
title: ICAP framework as a lens for interpreting learner–AI interaction patterns
description: The article uses the ICAP framework, which "distinguishes between passive, active, constructive, and interactive engagement", to interpret why different GenAI usage patterns relate differently to learning. Zero and Low usage patterns are read as predominantly active engagement without AI mediation, the "Smart" high usage pattern as closer to "constructive engagement that supports sense -making", and Very high usage as frequent interaction that remains largely active rather than constructive. The framework is applied as an interpretive lens rather than tested empirically.
requirements: Analyses must capture what learners do with AI (e.g., explanation seeking versus solution generation), not just usage frequency
constraints: The article notes ICAP has only recently begun to inform research on GenAI use in programming education
target_learners: undergraduate novice programmers in OOP courses
target_learning_goals: object-oriented programming concepts and problem-solving
examples: The discussion maps the five identified usage clusters onto ICAP engagement modes, treating explanation-focused use as constructive and very high-volume use as largely active
