article_title: When AI Does the Work, What Is Learning For? Post-Instrumental Learning and the Risk of Capacity Dissolution
citation: Kai Yao. (2026). When AI Does the Work, What Is Learning For? Post-Instrumental Learning and the Risk of Capacity Dissolution. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28041
title: Post-instrumental learning: formation of capacities needed for agency and accountability under extensive AI delegation
description: Post-instrumental learning is the article's central framework: the formation of capacities that remain necessary for agency, responsibility, and meaning when many products of learning can be delegated to AI. It is defined as "the formation of capacities that remain necessary for agency, responsibility, and meaning under extensive AI delegation". The term does not deny learning's instrumental value; it marks a shift in emphasis, from whether people must produce outputs unaided to whether they retain the capacities to set ends, ask for reasons, contest decisions, refuse harmful dependence, revise practices, and participate in the forms of life AI helps mediate.
requirements: Delegated work must remain connected to purposes, reasons, alternatives, and repair through people, intermediaries, and institutions
constraints: The account is a normative conceptual analysis, not an empirical measurement of learning loss or a design proposal for one educational technology
target_learners: citizens affected by AI-mediated institutional practices
target_learning_goals: preserving capacities for agency, responsibility, and accountability under AI delegation
key_sources: Kai Yao. (2026). When AI Does the Work, What Is Learning For? Post-Instrumental Learning and the Risk of Capacity Dissolution. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28041

article_title: When AI Does the Work, What Is Learning For? Post-Instrumental Learning and the Risk of Capacity Dissolution
citation: Kai Yao. (2026). When AI Does the Work, What Is Learning For? Post-Instrumental Learning and the Risk of Capacity Dissolution. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28041
title: Capacity dissolution: erosion of the practices that keep delegated work answerable, distinct from deskilling
description: Capacity dissolution is the article's name for the central risk of AI delegation: a breakdown in the relation among an output, the person or institution that claims or relies on it, and the practice that makes that claim answerable. The article defines it as "a breakdown in the relation among an output, the person or institution that claims or relies on it, and the practice that makes that claim answerable". It is distinguished from deskilling, automation complacency, and diminished contestability: its object is the institutional relation that keeps delegated work answerable, and it can arise while specialists retain skill, performance stays high, and a formal appeal route exists. Its warning sign is successful output production alongside erosion of the learning practices that sustain accountability.
requirements: Recurring occasions for use and institutions that make capacity use consequential, since capacity is sustained by practice rather than stored privately
constraints: Distinct from ordinary deskilling: a person may stop a routine calculation without losing meaningful agency; dissolution concerns the practices that make delegated work answerable
target_learning_goals: maintaining the judgment needed to set ends, use reasons, and make challenge consequential
key_sources: Kai Yao. (2026). When AI Does the Work, What Is Learning For? Post-Instrumental Learning and the Risk of Capacity Dissolution. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28041

article_title: When AI Does the Work, What Is Learning For? Post-Instrumental Learning and the Risk of Capacity Dissolution
citation: Kai Yao. (2026). When AI Does the Work, What Is Learning For? Post-Instrumental Learning and the Risk of Capacity Dissolution. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28041
title: Five-capacity framework: end-setting, reason-giving, contestability, refusal/revision, and participation as a minimum functional set
description: The article proposes five capacities as the core of post-instrumental learning: "end-setting, reason-giving, contestability,refusal/revision, and participation. They form a proposed minimum functional set, not a complete theory of education." End-setting keeps purposes open to judgment; reason-giving connects outputs to inspectable considerations; contestability supplies routes to challenge; refusal/revision makes exit and redesign possible; participation sustains the shared practices in which the others are learned. Table 1 translates each capacity into an institutional design question and a failure mode, for example that without contestability "Affected people encounter decisions as settled facts". The capacities are interdependent but not interchangeable and should be distributed across affected people, intermediaries, and communities.
requirements: Distribution across affected people, institutional intermediaries, and public or professional communities, so delegation remains accountable rather than private dependence on expertise
constraints: The claim is normative and functional rather than psychometric; the capacities may overlap and are not an empirically validated scale
target_learners: intermediaries such as teachers, clinicians, caseworkers, lawyers, engineers, and public officials
target_learning_goals: setting ends, giving reasons, contesting decisions, refusing and revising dependence, and participating in shared practices
key_sources: Kai Yao. (2026). When AI Does the Work, What Is Learning For? Post-Instrumental Learning and the Risk of Capacity Dissolution. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28041

article_title: When AI Does the Work, What Is Learning For? Post-Instrumental Learning and the Risk of Capacity Dissolution
citation: Kai Yao. (2026). When AI Does the Work, What Is Learning For? Post-Instrumental Learning and the Risk of Capacity Dissolution. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28041
title: Lightweight capacity impact statement: a five-judgment deliberative record for AI deployment review
description: A capacity impact statement is a governance artifact the article proposes to make deployment review concrete. It records five judgments: the changed practice and responsible roles; the capacity the prior practice formed or evidenced; who needs that capacity or relies on its certification; how the new workflow preserves an opportunity to exercise it and what evidence makes that opportunity credible; and an observable trigger for review or repair. The article describes it as "a deliberative record, not a validated scale or universal score", whose purpose is to make the institution's reasons inspectable and revisable. It can be incorporated into course approval, assessment moderation, procurement, or periodic review, with depth and review interval scaled to stakes and reversibility.
requirements: An observable trigger for review or repair, and credible evidence that the workflow preserves an opportunity to exercise the capacity
constraints: It is a deliberative record, not a validated scale or universal score; depth and review interval should scale with the stakes and reversibility of the workflow
target_learning_goals: maintaining institutional capacity to understand, challenge, and revise AI-mediated practices over time
examples: The article's example: an AI-supported research essay where repeated inability of students to defend source selection or revise arguments meets the review trigger, prompting task revision or restored guided practice

article_title: Students' Epistemological Beliefs and their Chatbot Preferences in AI-mediated Physics Learning
citation: Amogh Sirnoorkar and Omkar Mamidpalliwar. (2026). Students' Epistemological Beliefs and their Chatbot Preferences in AI-mediated Physics Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.29385
title: Custom-built online waves module with simulations integrated with a chatbot
description: A 10-page extra-credit online activity on wave concepts, built for a large-enrollment calculus-based physics course for future engineers using the Matter and Interactions textbook. Each content page presented "an interactive simulation and followed by four questions", with a chatbot integrated throughout. The first page collected anticipated chatbot preferences among three options, and the last page collected student ID, a 5-point activity rating, perceived learning, qualitative feedback, and retrospective reflections on content familiarity and chatbot preferences. Estimated completion time was around 30-45 minutes.
requirements: Administered as an extra-credit activity with students informed it was not part of course assessment, to encourage honest participation
constraints: The module covered waves because the topic was not covered in the host course
target_learners: introductory calculus-based physics students for future engineers
target_learning_goals: wave concepts not covered in the host course
examples: Deployed in Spring of 2026 in a course with total enrollment around 1800; 1191 students responded to the activity

article_title: Students' Epistemological Beliefs and their Chatbot Preferences in AI-mediated Physics Learning
citation: Amogh Sirnoorkar and Omkar Mamidpalliwar. (2026). Students' Epistemological Beliefs and their Chatbot Preferences in AI-mediated Physics Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.29385
title: EBAPS five-dimension framework of epistemological beliefs in physical sciences
description: The Epistemological Beliefs Assessment for Physical Sciences is a 30-item questionnaire of Likert-style and multiple-choice items, each scored from 0 (least sophisticated) to 4 (most sophisticated). "The questionnaire probes students' beliefs across the following five non-orthogonal dimensions": structure of scientific knowledge (10 items), nature of knowing and learning (8), real-life applicability (4), evolving knowledge (3), and source of ability to learn (5). The study uses weighted percentage scores per axis to compare belief sophistication across chatbot preference groups.
requirements: Scored via the prescribed rubric with weighted axis scores computed as item sums divided by maximum possible axis score
constraints: The survey authors argue against Cronbach's alpha for this instrument because "students were allowed to disagree with themselves within a subscale" and beliefs may be context-dependent; the study's alpha values were moderate to low (0.13–0.64)
target_learning_goals: epistemological beliefs about the structure, knowing, applicability, evolution, and learnability of scientific knowledge
examples: Administered via Qualtrics a week before the chatbot activity as an extra-credit task; 1408 students responded

article_title: NuclearDiffusion: Text-to-Image Foundation Models for Learning Nuclear Energy Concepts
citation: Mohammed I. Radaideh, Jeremy Moon, Andre Gala-Garza, Emma Son, Yug Shah, Majdi I. Radaideh. (2026). NuclearDiffusion: Text-to-Image Foundation Models for Learning Nuclear Energy Concepts. Preprint submitted to Peer Review. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04030
title: Curated dataset of 1,000 captioned nuclear energy images with automated extraction pipeline and released SDXL checkpoint
description: A curated dataset of 1,000 captioned nuclear energy images assembled from three sources: 348 images from books and encyclopedias, 119 from journal publications, and 533 from nuclear news websites. Images were extracted via a three-stage Python pipeline (CLIP-ViT-L/14 zero-shot classification, then GPT-4.1-nano and GPT-5-nano filtering) and preprocessed by upscaling to 1024x1024 with GPT-Image-2 while removing text and arrows. The article states the dataset "provides a foundation for future research in domain-specific generative AI". The best SDXL checkpoint and 300 testing prompts are released on GitHub.
requirements: Images require captions and preprocessing (upscaling, text and arrow removal) because the SD and Flux.1 models could not generate readable text even after fine-tuning
constraints: The article notes nuclear engineering has limited publicly accessible high-quality annotated images, so large-scale dataset expansion is challenging; captions from sources may be short and not sufficiently descriptive
target_learners: engineering students and learners of nuclear energy concepts
target_learning_goals: generating technically accurate visual representations of nuclear energy concepts such as reactors, fuel assemblies, fuel cycles, and radiation

Quality validation by preschool teachers acting as domain experts, with rejected samples discarded

article_title: Robust and Efficient Motion Reasoning for Privacy-Aware Classroom Incident Recognition
citation: Paritosh Parmar, Landy Lan, Hong Yang, Chen Yi, Chiat Pin Tay. (2026). Robust and Efficient Motion Reasoning for Privacy-Aware Classroom Incident Recognition. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05115
title: Hierarchical multi-order kinematic representation with multi-objective knowledge distillation framework
description: A motion-reasoning framework in which human actions are represented as a hierarchy of kinematic orders: "we represent motion using joint positions, velocities, and accelerations, which are later encoded by dedicated order-specific backbones." Order-specific representations are fused by weighted averaging into a multi-order teacher, which is distilled via a multi-objective loss (temperature-scaled KL distillation plus supervised classification) into a substantially smaller student operating only on zeroth-order joint positions. The design compresses along two axes: from multi-order inputs to a single zeroth-order stream, and from a larger teacher network to a smaller student.
requirements: Temporal preprocessing before computing derivatives, since higher-order kinematic features amplify errors present in lower-order pose estimates; missing joints are linearly interpolated and trajectories smoothed with a Savitzky–Golay filter
constraints: In the implementation the fusion weights are set manually
The deployed student operates only on a single zeroth-order joint-position stream at inference
target_learners: preschool students and teachers in monitored classrooms
target_learning_goals: privacy-preserving recognition of classroom safety incidents from pose sequences alone
examples: Instantiated with STGCN++ backbones: 64-base-channel order-specific teachers and a 32-channel student, with distillation temperature 4 and loss weights {λKD, λCls} = {0.3, 1.0}

citation: Kaushik Dutta. (2026). From Precision Medicine to Precision Education: A Vision for AI-Powered Student Digital Twins, Preventive Student Success, and Career-Aligned Academic Pathways. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06322
title: Precision Education: a healthcare-inspired framework of five analytics maturity stages culminating in autonomous, adaptive student success
description: Precision Education is a paradigm in which AI continuously analyzes academic, behavioral, financial, and career data to identify emerging risks, recommend personalized interventions, and align academic decisions with career success. The paper organizes the field's evolution across five stages, from descriptive reporting to what it calls "Stage 5: Autonomous and adaptive student success." It argues the field has invested heavily in Stage 3 predictive analytics while "The value proposition of Precision Education lives in Stages 4 and 5." The framing pairs data science with "warm humanity": technology identifies the signal, human judgment shapes the response.

constraints: Stages 4 and 5 require causal reasoning, not only correlation, per the article's own stage definitions

title: Student Digital Twin: a continuously updated learner model built for counterfactual simulation, not dashboard display
description: A Student Digital Twin is defined as "a continuously evolving model of an individual learner's academic performance, learning behavior, career interests, degree progression, financial circumstances, co-curricular engagement, and workforce preparedness." Its purpose is "to simulate": answering counterfactual questions such as what happens if a gateway course is repeated with tutoring, or if the student changes majors. The paper specifies three design properties: fidelity matched to purpose, calibration of predicted probabilities to observed rates, and validation of simulated causal claims against real outcomes. It cautions the twin "is not the person" and should be a decision aid, not an oracle.

article_title: Principal Trait Analysis: Towards Deriving 'Skills' in Human-AI Collaboration
citation: Hunter McNichols, Kai Du, Andrew Lan. (2026). PRINCIPAL TRAIT ANALYSIS: TOWARDS DERIVING "SKILLS" IN HUMAN-AI COLLABORATION. A preprint - August 13, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11460
title: Principal Trait Analysis (PTA): a four-stage, PCA-inspired pipeline for deriving behavioral traits from human-AI conversation corpora
description: PTA is a data-driven methodology that "produces a representative set of textual descriptions we callprincipal traitsfrom a corpus of human collaborator-AI collaborative conversation sessions." It runs four stages: LLM-prompted behavior-observation extraction (generic or theory-lens), embedding-based top-down and agglomerative clustering into candidate traits, LLM-as-a-judge scoring of each session on a 1-5 Likert scale, and greedy principal-trait selection trading off relevance (item-total correlation plus factor-analysis communality) against redundancy in score and text-embedding space. Trait selection mirrors PCA's variance-maximizing criterion adapted to text, where orthogonality is undefined.

LLM prompting and text-embedding infrastructure for extraction, clustering, scoring, and selection
constraints: The authors caution the derived traits "do not, by themselves, appear to be grounded enough to be interpreted as a definitive skill taxonomy in human-AI collaboration"

Professional software developers using AI coding agents
target_learning_goals: Effective collaboration with LLM-based tutors and coding agents

description: The review adapts a framework from Dello Russo et al. (2023) in which each policy implication is treated as "a short narrative that can be broken down into several parts": who it addresses, what actions it suggests, why they matter, when and where they apply, and how strongly they are framed (modal verbs such as must, should, could). The authors coded 31 implication narratives against these five dimensions, mapped onto their five research questions, using an a priori codebook refined through pilot coding with disagreement resolved in discussion with a third author.

constraints: Coding implicit policy implications can be subjective, as the authors state

article_title: The Policy Deficit in AI × Social-Emotional Learning Research
citation: Tran Van Cuong, Liu Yihan, Nguyen Van Tuong. (2026). The Policy Deficit in AI x Social-Emotional Learning Research.
title: The techno-solutionist trap: AI × SEL research foregrounds technical potential while leaving institutional conditions under-specified
description: The review characterizes the field as dominated by "techno-solutionism": the belief that AI applications will inherently solve SEL challenges without sufficient engagement with institutional or regulatory hurdles that prevent scaling. Policy, when mentioned, is treated as a "horizon" rather than practice-oriented tools, risking a "pilot-study paradox" where robust results fail to achieve real-world impact for lack of regulatory and resource-allocation frameworks. The authors propose reorienting from "implication-as-afterthought" to "implication-as-methodology", designing research with policy in mind from the start.
requirements: Researchers, reviewers, and editors must foreground policy considerations despite incentives prioritizing technical novelty
constraints: The authors note rapid technology lifecycles and rigid academic publication formats complicate integrating deep policy suggestions into short papers
target_learners: AI × SEL researchers, editors, reviewers, and policymakers
target_learning_goals: translating AI × SEL research findings into educational governance and implementation
examples: The review found some papers promise policy implications in impact statements yet ignore them in the main text

article_title: Privacy-Preserving Heterogeneous Multi-LLM Federated Inference for Cognitive Diagnosis
citation: Yagna Manasa Boyapati, Chong Yu, Tianyu Jiang, Justin Zhan. (2026). Privacy-Preserving Heterogeneous Multi-LLM Federated Inference for Cognitive Diagnosis. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02947
title: Privacy-preserving heterogeneous multi-LLM federated inference framework for cognitive diagnosis
description: A four-stage framework in which heterogeneous commercial LLMs (LLaMA-3.3-70B, GPT-4o-mini, Claude-3-Haiku) independently predict student knowledge states via engineered prompts, add calibrated Laplace noise locally to their prediction outputs, and aggregate with residual correction. The article describes it as "the first privacy-preserving heterogeneous multi-LLM federated inference framework for cognitive diagnosis", operating entirely at the prediction level with models frozen and accessible only via black-box APIs. It integrates Q-matrix theory to constrain prompts to relevant concepts and rests on an honest-but-curious trust paradigm.
requirements: Commercial LLM API access for each federated entity; a Q-matrix (expert-crafted or automatically generated) mapping questions to knowledge concepts; local calibration data per entity for residual correction terms.
constraints: The privacy guarantee follows an honest-but-curious trust paradigm: LDP shields published diagnostic outputs but does not prevent commercial API providers from logging submitted queries.
The framework is evaluated on structured educational domains; extension to open-ended assessment tasks may require adapted prompt engineering.
Residual correction may require periodic recalibration when providers release model updates.
target_learners: K-12 and secondary students in mathematics and academic assessment settings (ASSIST09, GSM8K, UCI Student Performance populations)
target_learning_goals: Diagnosing student mastery of specific knowledge concepts and skills to support intelligent tutoring and adaptive learning
examples: The framework was instantiated with LLaMA-3.3-70B via Groq API, GPT-4o-mini via OpenAI API, and Claude-3-Haiku via Anthropic API, each holding a disjoint local dataset subset for calibration, and evaluated on ASSIST09, GSM8K, and UCI Student Performance.

article_title: PRISMA-LLM: An Empirical Reporting Framework for AI-Assisted Systematic Reviews
citation: Zabaleta, M. & Lin, B. (2026). PRISMA-LLM: An Empirical Reporting Framework for AI-Assisted Systematic Reviews. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11559
title: PRISMA-LLM: a three-layer reporting framework for LLM-assisted systematic reviews
description: PRISMA-LLM is an evidence-informed reporting framework for LLM-assisted and AI-enabled systematic-review workflows, organized to complement PRISMA 2020. It has three layers: "a universal checklist specifies the information that should be reported across LLM-assisted review workflows"; five implementation-disclosure levels organize technical detail needed to reconstruct workflows; and consequence-sensitive evaluation expectations determine when validation should exceed the minimum associated with a disclosure level. Its empirical basis is the recurring evaluation and limitation dimensions observed in SciLitBench and the association between workflow type and reporting coverage.

constraints: The levels are disclosure tiers, not risk tiers

Its purpose is not to certify the quality or safety of an AI workflow
target_learners: review authors and auditors in evidence synthesis
target_learning_goals: transparent, auditable reporting of AI-assisted review workflows
distinguishing implementation disclosure from consequence-sensitive evaluation
examples: The framework was developed from SciLitBench reporting patterns, workflow choices encountered while building SciLitBench, and comparison with PRISMA 2020, PRISMA-S, and adjacent AI-reporting proposals

citation: Zabaleta, M. & Lin, B. (2026). PRISMA-LLM: An Empirical Reporting Framework for AI-Assisted Systematic Reviews. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11559
title: Five cumulative implementation-disclosure levels with a consequence-sensitive evaluation override
description: PRISMA-LLM organizes implementation disclosure into five cumulative levels: off-the-shelf software; prompt-only LLM; structured/engineered workflows; retrieval/adapted/single-agent workflows; and multi-agent/swarm systems, each adding the technical detail needed to reconstruct the workflow. citation: Mahbub Ul Alam. (2026). PAUSE: A Privacy-Preserving Self-Reflection Tool for AI-Associated Cognitive Offloading. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13155
title: Four-domain mapping of AI-associated cognitive offloading (D1-D4)
description: The article defines AI-associated cognitive offloading as the pattern where "what gets delegated is the thinking itself: reasoning through a problem, generating ideas, learning new material, or communicating with other people". It organises reflection around four domains grounded in the 2023-2026 literature: reasoning and critical thinking, creativity and originality, research and learning, and social and communicative capacity. Each domain is treated as a continuum on which self-reported behavioural patterns indicate offloading depth, not underlying ability. The author states these are "a working vocabulary grounded in the literature, not a tested factor structure".

constraints: The four-domain structure is a working organisation, not a confirmed factor structure

The emotional strand (anxiety, AI guilt, emotional dependence) falls outside the current scope

target_learning_goals: Maintaining reasoning, creativity, learning, and social-communicative capacities while using generative AI

citation: Mahbub Ul Alam. (2026). PAUSE: A Privacy-Preserving Self-Reflection Tool for AI-Associated Cognitive Offloading. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13155
title: PAUSE self-reflection web tool
description: PAUSE (Patterns of AI Use: Self-Examination) is a public, no-login web tool that "delivers a short, free, no-login self-check, scores it entirely in the browser, and returns descriptive, domain-aware reflections". It pairs reverse-scored behavioural Likert items with a claim-evaluation reasoning probe, a 90-second Alternative Uses creativity probe, and a retrospective before-and-after block reported separately as a trajectory indicator. Domain readings are scaled 0-100 and mapped to four fixed descriptive bands, with no overall composite. The author frames it as a reflective design probe, not a validated instrument.
requirements: At least three items answered per domain for a reading to display
JavaScript enabled, since rendering and scoring run client-side
Respondents aged 18 or over per the soft age check
constraints: Not a validated psychological instrument; presents no reliability or validity evidence
Cross-sectional, so it describes current patterns rather than accumulated change
Not designed for minors; readings must not drive consequential decisions
target_learners: Adults who regularly use LLM-based AI tools
target_learning_goals: Self-awareness of AI-associated cognitive offloading patterns and more deliberate AI engagement
examples: A worked example scores a fabricated creative professional at D1=71 (Moderate) and demonstrates a six-month comparison via return tokens

article_title: PAUSE: A Privacy-Preserving Self-Reflection Tool for AI-Associated Cognitive Offloading
citation: Mahbub Ul Alam. (2026). PAUSE: A Privacy-Preserving Self-Reflection Tool for AI-Associated Cognitive Offloading. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13155
title: Citation-grounded behavioural item design with reverse scoring
description: PAUSE's items follow a reusable design pattern: every LLM-era item is anchored to a 2023-2026 paper, items are behavioural rather than dispositional, and roughly one third per domain are reverse-scored, since "Roughly one third of the items per domain (two or three of seven) are reverse-scored to counter acquiescence". Each scored item carries an expandable rationale panel and a reference panel quoting the anchoring study with a resolvable DOI, so respondents can inspect the evidence behind a question. All items include a not-applicable option, and unanswered items are dropped rather than imputed.
requirements: Each item needs an anchoring study with an exact quotable passage and resolvable DOI
Probe non-responses must be scored as not applicable, never as uncritical acceptance
constraints: Anchors are supporting evidence for an item's framing, not validation of it
Several anchoring studies are recent preprints
Some items conflate early consultation with substitution, an imperfect proxy for whether reasoning stayed engaged
target_learning_goals: Accurate self-assessment of AI-use behaviours across four offloading domains
examples: Item B5 renders the behavioural task, a Why this question panel, and a Reference panel quoting Dergaa et al. (2024) with a DOI
key_sources: Mahbub Ul Alam. (2026). PAUSE: A Privacy-Preserving Self-Reflection Tool for AI-Associated Cognitive Offloading. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13155

title: Dynamic Learning Solutions pipeline: PDF-to-video educational explanation system
description: An automated pipeline that converts uploaded PDFs into video answers to user queries. A RAG model retrieves relevant content and generates a multi-scene script with narration and "visual prompts aligned with the textbook's explanatory style"; Stable Diffusion generates scene images, DynamiCrafter animates them, Google TTS produces synchronized narration, and MoviePy assembles the final video in a Streamlit interface. LLM backend (Groq llama-3.1-70b-versatile or Ollama llama3.2) with temperature 0 for consistent outputs
constraints: The RAG stage is optimized for NCERT textbook structure, so it performs better on content from those textbooks

examples: For each query, the system retrieved relevant textbook content, generated a multi-scene explanatory script, and produced synchronized visuals and narration

title: Figure-aware document extraction for NCERT diagram references in RAG indexing
description: A preprocessing component that detects standardized figure references such as "Fig 8.1" using regular expressions and extracts surrounding caption text into dedicated figure-related documents. These are "indexed alongside normal text chunks within the vector database, enabling the retriever to surface relevant diagram explanations when queries reference figures." It complements regex-based cleaning that removes structural noise like page headers and summary sections before chunking.

Regular-expression pattern matching over extracted PDF text before embedding

title: Multilingual synchronized narration module using Google Text-to-Speech
description: The voiceover component converts script dialogues into audio aligned with video segments. Speech-duration computation and text segmentation for scene-level timing

article_title: PersonaPath: Towards Knowledge-Centric Personalized Learning Path Planning
citation: Yu Liu, Zeming Liu, Tianle Zhang, Zihao Cheng, Yuhang Guo, Kehai Chen, Min Zhang, Yunhong Wang, Haifeng Wang. (2026). PersonaPath: Towards Knowledge-Centric Personalized Learning Path Planning. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18861
title: PersonaPath benchmark for Knowledge-Centric learning path planning
description: PersonaPath is a benchmark that "pairs 2,000 fine-grained learner personas with a hierarchical knowledge graph of 347 textbooks, 1,751 units, and 4,092 concepts across 77 subjects" connected by prerequisite dependencies. Given a learner profile, mastery state, and target unit, a model must generate a prerequisite-respecting path that adapts to prior knowledge and reaches the goal. Personas are stratified into Low-, Average-, and High-performing archetypes in an approximate 1:3:1 ratio, and paths are scored on Validity, Adaptivity, and Efficiency with a joint Final Pass criterion.
requirements: Explicit learner goals, a prerequisite knowledge structure, and learner-specific mastery states are the three inputs the pipeline is designed around
constraints: The benchmark is grounded in Chinese textbooks and curricula; learner states and mastery updates are synthetic
target_learners: learners from primary school to higher education in the Chinese curriculum
target_learning_goals: goal-directed, prerequisite-aware selection and ordering of knowledge toward a target unit
examples: Two educators independently rated 100 sampled personas on a 5-point Likert scale, with mean ratings from 4.11 to 4.68 and ICC(2,2) from 0.74 to 0.85
key_sources: Yu Liu, Zeming Liu, Tianle Zhang, Zihao Cheng, Yuhang Guo, Kehai Chen, Min Zhang, Yunhong Wang, Haifeng Wang. (2026). PersonaPath: Towards Knowledge-Centric Personalized Learning Path Planning. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18861

article_title: PersonaPath: Towards Knowledge-Centric Personalized Learning Path Planning
citation: Yu Liu, Zeming Liu, Tianle Zhang, Zihao Cheng, Yuhang Guo, Kehai Chen, Min Zhang, Yunhong Wang, Haifeng Wang. (2026). PersonaPath: Towards Knowledge-Centric Personalized Learning Path Planning. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18861
title: Knowledge-Centric (KC) paradigm for learning path planning
description: The KC paradigm contrasts with the dominant Exercise-Centric (EC) recommendation paradigm: instead of inferring the next exercise from item-level interaction logs, "a Knowledge-Centric (KC) paradigm, which decides what knowledge a learner should study and in what order." A KC planner reads each learner's progress and goal, selects knowledge from a structured knowledge space, and orders it into a path respecting prerequisite relations among concepts. Evaluation requires explicit learner personas, long-term goals, and curriculum-scale prerequisite structures together, since the goal sets the destination, the mastery state the starting point, and the prerequisite graph the routes between them.
requirements: Evaluation requires explicit learner personas, long-term goals, and curriculum-scale prerequisite structures jointly
constraints: Existing benchmarks primarily support exercise recommendation and rarely jointly provide these components, per the article
target_learners: learners with similar exercise records but different goals
target_learning_goals: selecting and ordering knowledge, not exercises, toward an explicit target
examples: Figure 1 contrasts two students with identical correctness records who need different paths because their targets differ

article_title: Penquiry: A Pen-based Interactive In-situ Q&A System Leveraging LLMs
citation: Jeongmin Rhee, Changhee Lee, Hyunwoo Kim, Kiroong Choe, Bohyoung Kim, Sungahn Ko, and Jinwook Seo. 2026. Penquiry: A Pen-based Interactive In-situ Q&A System Leveraging LLMs. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19870
title: Penquiry V2: in-situ pen-based Q&A system with Content Snapping and Question Autocompletion
description: Penquiry V2 is an in-situ question-and-answer system that lets learners query an LLM directly on digital study materials using a pen. It introduces Content Snapping, which "maps the sketch to nearby character-level PDF text elements and redraws it" to confirm referential targets, and Question Autocompletion, which generates "four autocomplete question candidates" from minimal ink keywords, categorized by question-content type, while retaining free-form questioning. It was evaluated in a within-subjects study against V1.
requirements: Requires pen-based digital devices with stylus input and PDF study materials with character-level text elements for snapping
Relies on GPT-4o across a multi-stage autocompletion, refinement and answering pipeline
constraints: Generated candidate questions may anchor learners to system-framed perspectives or narrow considered alternatives
Utility of autocompletion scales with domain expertise and can interfere when learners already have a specific question
target_learners: university undergraduate and graduate students studying textbook materials
target_learning_goals: concept clarification and inquiry during self-directed pen-based study
examples: In Study 2, 74.9% of submitted queries used autocompletion and the system achieved an average SUS score of 84.9, rated "Excellent"

article_title: OmniEdu: Open Foundation Models for Learning and Teaching
citation: Hao Liang, Qihan Lin, Meiyi Qiang, Linzhuang Sun, Hengyi Feng, Mingrui Chen, Sizhe Qiu, Wentao Zhang. (2026). OmniEdu: Open Foundation Models for Learning and Teaching. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23088
title: Four-capability taxonomy for organizing educational foundation-model supervision
description: OmniEdu organizes education-specific supervision around four complementary capability categories defined "according to the behaviors to be learned" rather than by source or subject. Subject competence covers solving K-12 problems and explaining answers across mathematics, science, reading, and writing; curriculum grounding captures grade-level alignment, knowledge points, prerequisite relations, and difficulty; diagnostic reasoning targets identifying errors and misconceptions and inferring missing prerequisites; pedagogical action and scaffolding covers selecting and executing interventions such as hints, questions, prerequisite review, or direct explanation. The taxonomy provides a common language for both data construction and evaluation.
requirements: Each example is assigned to a single primary capability according to its main supervision objective, with other properties retained as secondary metadata.
constraints: The taxonomy is designed for K-12 educational scenarios and is implemented through fine-grained task buckets within each capability.
target_learning_goals: Subject problem solving
Curriculum-structured knowledge
Error diagnosis and misconception repair
Pedagogically appropriate tutoring responses
examples: The final corpus allocates 45.5% of examples to subject competence, 20.3% to pedagogical action and scaffolding, 13.4% to curriculum grounding, and 7.8% to diagnostic reasoning, plus 12.9% general-purpose instruction.
key_sources: Hao Liang, Qihan Lin, Meiyi Qiang, Linzhuang Sun, Hengyi Feng, Mingrui Chen, Sizhe Qiu, Wentao Zhang. (2026). OmniEdu: Open Foundation Models for Learning and Teaching. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23088

article_title: OmniEdu: Open Foundation Models for Learning and Teaching
citation: Hao Liang, Qihan Lin, Meiyi Qiang, Linzhuang Sun, Hengyi Feng, Mingrui Chen, Sizhe Qiu, Wentao Zhang. (2026). OmniEdu: Open Foundation Models for Learning and Teaching. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23088
title: OmniEdu capability-oriented instruction-tuning corpus and six-stage data pipeline
description: A reproducible data-construction pipeline that curates an education-specific pool of approximately 1.34M examples drawn from more than 100 datasets and educational resources into 60,951 high-quality examples containing about 12.0M supervised response tokens. The six stages combine deterministic cleaning and evaluation decontamination, LLM-assisted semantic auditing and rewriting with 0-100 usability scoring, task-specific quality scoring, k-center greedy diversity selection over BGE-M3 embeddings under token budgets, and pedagogical instruction assignment. Together with 9,048 general-purpose examples, the final corpus contains 69,999 examples and 15.96M supervised response tokens, with provenance and audit metadata retained throughout.
requirements: Source and license information is retained for provenance tracking, and data with unclear usage conditions are excluded.
constraints: Examples overlapping the final evaluation set are removed to prevent evaluation contamination; rewritten examples are retained only if re-audited as keep.
target_learning_goals: Subject competence
Curriculum grounding
Diagnostic reasoning
Pedagogical action and scaffolding
examples: RACE is reduced from 60,180 to 5,000 examples via k-center greedy selection; auditing retains examples scoring 85-100, repairs those scoring 50-84, and discards those below 50.

article_title: A Workshop Series for Effective Use of AI in Uncertain Times: Building a Physics Faculty Learning Community
citation: Perl-Nussbaum, D., & Finkelstein, N. D. (2026). A Workshop Series for Effective Use of AI in Uncertain Times: Building a Physics Faculty Learning Community.
title: Framework for institutional change in the AI era: arrival technologies versus adoption technologies across six dimensions
description: The article applies the authors' framework for leading institutional change in the AI era, which distinguishes AI as an "arrival technology" that "disrupt[s] our practices and bypass[es] our evaluation and dissemination processes" from prior adoption technologies with strong evidence bases. Table 1 lays out six dimensions of AI-driven change (evidence base, rate of change, scope and intended use, faculty agency, change agent role, student role) with design implications: humble and local inquiries, approaches over tools, broadening learning goals, mapping disruption and needs, facilitating collective inquiry, and treating students as partners. The workshop series is presented as one instantiation of this framework.
requirements: Change initiatives proceed through local and humble exploration rather than dissemination of unevidenced practices
constraints: The framework addresses arrival technologies that lack a pedagogical evidence base and change rapidly, unlike evidence-based adoption technologies
target_learning_goals: Departmental capacity to respond collectively to AI-driven change in teaching and assessment
examples: The six-session workshop series operationalized the framework by surfacing local data, facilitating small-group inquiry, and building a shared repository
key_sources: Perl-Nussbaum, D., & Finkelstein, N. D. (2026). A Workshop Series for Effective Use of AI in Uncertain Times: Building a Physics Faculty Learning Community. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23887

citation: Perl-Nussbaum, D., & Finkelstein, N. D. (2026). A Workshop Series for Effective Use of AI in Uncertain Times: Building a Physics Faculty Learning Community.
title: Workshop session structure: local data, small-group testing, collective discussion
description: Each of the six sessions followed a common three-part structure: facilitators presented local data or department-sourced materials, faculty tested and reflected on the materials in small groups, and the whole group discussed them together. The article states: "We started by sharing local data, whether around AI policies and use or activities gathered from different courses, and then had faculty test and reflect on the materials in small groups, followed by collective discussion." This structure embodies the framework's principles of leading with student use and facilitating collective inquiry rather than disseminating best practices.
requirements: Local data and department-sourced materials must be available to anchor each session
constraints: Framed as collective, local inquiry rather than a general faculty training workshop
target_learners: University physics faculty in a departmental learning community
target_learning_goals: Developing shared departmental approaches to AI use in courses
examples: Session 3 opened with survey data on students' correctness-checking, then faculty tested AI chatbots on real anonymized homework in small groups before collective discussion

citation: Perl-Nussbaum, D., & Finkelstein, N. D. (2026). A Workshop Series for Effective Use of AI in Uncertain Times: Building a Physics Faculty Learning Community.
title: Shared departmental repository of AI-related teaching resources
description: The series' central product is a shared, evolving departmental repository pairing curated materials with framing for their use. The article reports: "Currently, it holds 5 entries, each pairing curated materials with brief framing for how to use them." Entries cover AI syllabus statements (including four sample policies spanning no use to full use), classroom discussion materials, student surveys with results across courses, homework tasks with AI integration, and assessment structures such as oral exams. Materials were shared with the department at the start of the following semester and continue to be updated.
requirements: Ongoing curation to keep the repository current as tools and practices evolve
constraints: The repository was also intended partly as a response to involving colleagues who did not participate in the series

article_title: From Content Generation to Learning Support: Pedagogy-Guided Generative Video Tutors for STEM Learning
citation: Xinchen Ma, Shuimu Wang, Gaole He, Yanbin Zhang, Chunyang Wang, Yunshi Lan, Weining Qian. (2026). From Content Generation to Learning Support: Pedagogy-Guided Generative Video Tutors for STEM Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24083
title: PIVOT: a three-stage pedagogy-guided instructional video tutoring framework
description: PIVOT is described as "a three-stage pedagogy-guided generative video tutoring framework for STEM education that supports active learning". Stage 1 generates structured instructional storyboards organizing objectives, prerequisite activation, explanations, visual plans, worked examples, and assessment probes. Stage 2 transforms the storyboard into shot-level Manim animations with a multimodal pedagogical verification harness covering layout, factual, and cognitive clarity, plus constrained layout prompting and automated code repair. Stage 3 generates storyboard-grounded quizzes and targeted remediation videos conditioned on learner responses, forming a closed feedback loop.
requirements: A learner-specified topic or learning goal as input
Storyboard generation must precede executable Manim code generation, narration synthesis, assessment construction, and multimodal verification
constraints: The system performs interaction-level adaptation conditioned on immediate learner responses rather than maintaining a fully personalized long-term learner model, with no long-term knowledge tracing or curriculum progression modeling
The multi-stage pipeline introduces substantially higher computational cost than direct multimedia synthesis approaches
target_learners: STEM learners at high-school and university level
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding of STEM knowledge points in mathematics, physics, chemistry, and computer science
Correction of misconceptions through targeted remediation
examples: For the topic Bubble Sort, the storyboard specifies learning objectives, prerequisite activation of arrays and loops, a worked example on array [5, 1, 4, 2, 8], and an assessment probe on which element is fixed after the first pass
key_sources: Xinchen Ma, Shuimu Wang, Gaole He, Yanbin Zhang, Chunyang Wang, Yunshi Lan, Weining Qian. (2026). From Content Generation to Learning Support: Pedagogy-Guided Generative Video Tutors for STEM Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24083

article_title: From Content Generation to Learning Support: Pedagogy-Guided Generative Video Tutors for STEM Learning
citation: Xinchen Ma, Shuimu Wang, Gaole He, Yanbin Zhang, Chunyang Wang, Yunshi Lan, Weining Qian. (2026). From Content Generation to Learning Support: Pedagogy-Guided Generative Video Tutors for STEM Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24083
title: Six-component pedagogically grounded instructional storyboard structure
description: The framework's instructional planning stage produces a storyboard whose components are "grounded in educational the-ory, each serving a clear pedagogical purpose": Learning Objectives, Prerequisite Activation, Concept Explanations, Visual Representation Plans, Worked Examples, and Diagnostic Assessment Probes. Each component is tied to an educational-theory rationale (e.g., Bloom's taxonomy for objectives, cognitive load for prerequisite activation, multimedia learning principles for visual plans, worked-example research for examples, formative assessment for probes). The storyboard serves as the semantic backbone for downstream code generation, narration, assessment, and verification.
requirements: Storyboard must progress from prerequisite knowledge to core concepts, then to examples and assessment
Each shot should focus on one local learning goal
Narration should explain why the concept works, not only describe what appears on screen
target_learners: STEM learners in high-school and university settings
target_learning_goals: Structured conceptual understanding of a specified STEM topic
Early detection of misconceptions via diagnostic probes
examples: The generated Bubble Sort storyboard defines the objective of understanding adjacent comparisons and swaps, activates prior knowledge of arrays and loops, and includes an assessment probe targeting the misconception that the smallest element is fixed first

article_title: From Sentiment Classification to Actionable and Responsible Feedback: A Scoping Review and Evidence Map of NLP in Student Evaluation of Teaching, 2015–2026
citation: Eicher, J., & da Silva, R. (2026). From Sentiment Classification to Actionable and Responsible Feedback: A Scoping Review and Evidence Map of NLP in Student Evaluation of Teaching, 2015–2026. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27939
title: Five-axis evidence map framework: a technical axis (RQ1) read against four value dimensions (analytical depth, methodological validation and reporting, actionability, responsible use)
description: The review's organizing framework separates technical sophistication (RQ1: tasks, methods, technological families, contexts) from four analytically separate value dimensions (RQ2–RQ5). The review states it "distinguishes technical sophistication (RQ1) from four related but analytically separate value dimensions (RQ2–RQ5)" covering depth, validation and reporting, actionability, and responsible use. Its core argument is that "Technical complexity should therefore not be used as a proxy for analytical depth, methodological robustness, educational usefulness, or responsible use." The framework is operationalized through seven extraction domains and versioned coding rules (D1–D5 depth, A0–A5 actionability, M1–M11 reporting indicators) applied to 421 studies.
requirements: Requires verbatim-evidence extraction with adjudication so that composite constructs (D1–D5, A0–A5) are derived by explicit, versioned coding rules rather than assigned directly by LLM judges
constraints: The review states all proportions and cross-tabulations are descriptive of the 421 mapped studies, not causal effects or population estimates, because the corpus was built without probability sampling
target_learners: higher education instructors and institutions using student evaluation of teaching
target_learning_goals: actionable and responsible use of NLP analysis of open-ended teaching-evaluation comments
examples: The review maps 421 studies along the five axes and identifies the A2+ to A3+ actionability cliff as the map's sharpest quantified gap

citation: Eicher, J., & da Silva, R. (2026). From Sentiment Classification to Actionable and Responsible Feedback: A Scoping Review and Evidence Map of NLP in Student Evaluation of Teaching, 2015–2026. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27939
title: Versioned reproducibility repository for the SET-NLP evidence map (code, study list, prompts, codebooks, adjudication bases)

constraints: The review notes reconstruction does not claim bit-for-bit re-execution on the same proprietary weights after deprecation

article_title: PhysicsMate: A Curriculum-Grounded Bengali Benchmark for Secondary Physics QA with Small-Model Adaptation
citation: Rashid Azraf Jahin, Saadman Sajid, Khan Raiyan Ibne Reza, Sumaiya Tabassum Nimi. (2026). PhysicsMate: A Curriculum-Grounded Bengali Benchmark for Secondary Physics QA with Small-Model Adaptation. IEEE CSDE 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00664v1
title: PhysicsMate benchmark of 1,834 curriculum-grounded Bengali physics QA pairs
description: PhysicsMate is a benchmark of 1,834 question-answer pairs derived from the official NCTB Grade 9-10 physics textbook (13 chapters, 359 pages), written in formal Bengali. Each pair is "linked to a specific knowledge node and originating semantic unit", giving curricular provenance back to textbook passages. The corpus is partitioned into training (n = 1,374; 74.9%), validation (n = 185; 10.1%) and held-out test (n = 275; 15.0%) sets, stratified by chapter, with programmatic checks that no question ID appears in more than one partition. The benchmark and knowledge graph are released with a Dataset Card.
requirements: Each benchmark item must be grounded in a specific NCTB textbook passage kept as metadata, so answers use the source curriculum's terminology, formulas and unit conventions.
constraints: The benchmark covers a single national curriculum, NCTB Grade 9-10 physics, and generalization to other syllabi or subjects has not been tested.
target_learners: Grade 9-10 secondary physics students in Bengali-medium education

title: Multi-relational knowledge graph of the NCTB physics syllabus with ten ontological node types
description: The knowledge graph formalizes the 13-chapter NCTB syllabus as a multi-relational structure with 1,760 nodes across 10 ontological types (concepts, questions, quantities, figures, examples, entities, definitions, formulas, laws, HSC topics) and 2,600 directed edges spanning 30 relation types. Relations include curricular hierarchy (part_of), applicability (applies_to), visual grounding (illustrates), example relations (example_of), dependency (depends_on) and provenance (derived_from). The graph serves as "a structured curricular index of the source material" used for category-level analysis, with every node traceable to source textbook pages.
requirements: Extraction uses a predefined domain ontology and a fixed structured prompt so equivalent curricular facts receive consistent representation, and each record retains source-page provenance.
constraints: The 10-node ontology maps directly to STEM domains; non-STEM or humanities curricula would require restructuring the declarative and procedural primitives into causal, temporal and narrative relation types.

target_learning_goals: Structured curricular knowledge representation enabling category-level evaluation of physics QA

title: CourseChat: an on-premises multi-course RAG tutor with course-isolated collections, twin serving nodes, and prebuilt quiz banks

citation: Yilmaz A (2026) The psychological mechanisms and behavioral determinants of academic integrity in the age of artificial intelligence. Front. Psychol. 17:1853790. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1853790
title: Stimulus–Organism–Response framework for AI-assisted academic dishonesty as a moderated mediation process
description: The article organizes AI-assisted academic dishonesty within the Stimulus–Organism–Response (SOR) framework, in which psychological vulnerabilities and socio-contextual conditions act as stimuli, cheating tendency is the organismic mechanism, and dishonesty is the behavioral response, with AI use as a moderating technological condition. The authors state the "SOR framework is well aligned with the proposed moderated mediation model, as it explains how psychological and contextual stimuli may be linked to AI-assisted academic dishonesty through cheating tendency." The model was tested with 1,045 undergraduates using PROCESS Model 14.
requirements: Measurement of psychological antecedents, cheating tendency, AI use, dishonesty, and social-contextual factors as distinct constructs
constraints: AI use is positioned as a behavioral amplifier in a non-causal statistical sense, not a direct cause of unethical behavior
target_learning_goals: academic integrity
ethical use of AI in academic work
examples: The study tested the model with seven measurement instruments, Pearson correlations, multiple regression, and Hayes' PROCESS Model 14 with 5,000-sample bootstrapping.

article_title: Governing generative AI in higher education: Emerging policy approaches and support ecosystems at innovative U.S. universities
citation: Qian, Y. (2026). Governing generative AI in higher education: emerging policy approaches and support ecosystems at innovative U.S. Universities. International Journal for Educational Integrity. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00233-x
title: Four-pillar framework for GenAI-era academic integrity: accountability, transparency, equity, and privacy
description: The article proposes that academic integrity when GenAI is permitted under stated conditions is organized by "a four-pillar framework for GenAI-era integrity: accountability, transparency, equity, and privacy." Accountability frames human agency in collaboration, with users expected to steer, critique, verify, and revise AI outputs rather than defer to them. Transparency operates through disclosure and attribution as a design principle reducing ambiguity before submission. Equity holds that integrity expectations are fair only when students have comparable opportunities to access and understand tools and norms. Privacy is treated as an integrity condition because inappropriate data sharing can undermine fairness and erode trust. Together the pillars define the conditions under which AI-assisted academic work can remain legitimate.
requirements: Integrity expectations must be paired with comparable student access to tools and norms for the equity pillar to hold
constraints: The framework is derived from document analysis of 50 innovation-oriented U.S. universities and is offered as analytically transferable insight, not statistical generalizability
target_learning_goals: responsible and ethical use of generative AI in academic work
academic integrity under AI-permitted conditions
examples: Arizona State's syllabus toolkit characterizes AI tools as partners in work while emphasizing that humans must iterate on AI outputs
Yale's guidance instructs community members not to enter confidential, legally restricted, or moderate/high-risk data into AI tools

title: Shift academic integrity effort from policing to design by pairing integrity policies with assessment innovation and AI literacy
description: The article recommends that institutions move away from detector-based enforcement toward a pedagogy-first integrity model. It advises investing in "process-rich assignments that include drafts, prompt logs, reflections, oral explanations, and revision histories" and mainstreaming AI literacy as a core academic capability rather than a remediation activity. This principle follows from the study's findings that institutions converge on detector skepticism and AI-literacy support while assignment-redesign resources remain scarce, indicating a gap between guidance and implementation supports.

It argues the study "challenges traditional cognitive taxonomies and calls for reimagining AI literacy as a multidimensional competence encompassing creativity, ethics, and critical reasoning essential for navigating AI-mediated learning environments." The framework arises from the study's finding that students' GenAI use engaged creativity, ethical reasoning, and epistemic vigilance together rather than separately.

title: Multi-layered safety architecture for teacher-supervised educational chatbots
description: Teachers in the study articulated a safety architecture for LLM-powered chatbots composed of four component types: "content scoping, presentation strategies, oversight mechanisms, and adaptation frameworks". This architecture gives teachers a reusable lesson/unit-level design that keeps chatbot behavior within professionally supervised bounds. It operationalizes the bounded authority model by layering protective mechanisms rather than relying on any single safeguard.
requirements: Human oversight mechanisms must be retained in the design
constraints: Articulated by secondary teachers for LLM-powered chatbots in educational settings
target_learning_goals: safe, scope-limited interaction with AI chatbots during learning
examples: Study participants prototyped chatbots with content scoping and oversight mechanisms during paper-prototype design sessions

title: Three protective layers: domain boundaries, content filtering, and teacher override
description: The article identifies three protective layers that operationalize bounded authority in educational chatbot design: "domain boundaries restricting scope, content filtering enabling safe personalization, and teacher override maintaining human authority". Domain boundaries limit what the chatbot addresses; content filtering makes personalization safe; teacher override preserves final human control. Together these layers form an implementable design pattern for supervised classroom AI.
requirements: A human teacher must be able to exercise override over the AI system
constraints: Designed for LLM-powered chatbots interacting with students under teacher supervision
target_learning_goals: safe personalized learning support from AI chatbots
examples: Teachers' paper prototypes included scoped domains, filtered content for personalization, and override controls

article_title: College students’ metacognitive awareness of generative-AI reliance: an experimental study of decision confidence and attribution bias
citation: Ren S (2026) College students’ metacognitive awareness of generative-AI reliance: an experimental study of decision confidence and attribution bias. Front. Psychol. 17:1926110. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1926110
title: Metacognitive dependence: a descriptive framework for perceived–behavioral reliance mismatch in AI-assisted decisions
description: The article introduces "metacognitive dependence" as an integrative conceptual label for a specific mismatch: students' observable reliance on generative-AI advice may diverge from their awareness of how strongly that advice shaped their judgment. The authors state the term is "not treated here as a validated unitary latent trait"; it organizes four theoretically related but distinct indicators — behavioral reliance, perceived reliance, decision confidence, and attributional responsibility. The framework also distinguishes overreliance (acceptance of incorrect AI advice) from trust calibration and metacognitive monitoring accuracy.
requirements: Behavioral reliance, awareness calibration, confidence, and attribution are analyzed separately rather than as one psychometric construct
constraints: The framework is descriptive; evidence that the measures change together is not psychometric proof of a single latent construct
target_learners: undergraduate students using generative AI for academic decisions
target_learning_goals: accurate metacognitive monitoring of AI influence on judgments and decisions
examples: In the experiment, open ChatGPT support produced a negative mean signed discrepancy (behavioral reliance exceeding perceived reliance), while reflection brought signed discrepancy near zero.
key_sources: Ren S (2026) College students’ metacognitive awareness of generative-AI reliance: an experimental study of decision confidence and attribution bias. Front. Psychol. 17:1926110. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1926110

article_title: College students’ metacognitive awareness of generative-AI reliance: an experimental study of decision confidence and attribution bias
citation: Ren S (2026) College students’ metacognitive awareness of generative-AI reliance: an experimental study of decision confidence and attribution bias. Front. Psychol. 17:1926110. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1926110
title: Insert a brief pre-decision metacognitive reflection prompt after AI consultation to promote discriminative reliance on AI advice
description: Before finalizing an AI-assisted answer, students respond to short prompts evaluating their own understanding, the AI's trustworthiness, and reasons for accepting or rejecting the recommendation. In the experiment the prompts asked, among other things, "Which part of the AI explanation is supported by evidence rather than ﬂuency?" This minimal intervention reduced acceptance of incorrect AI advice and improved perceived–behavioral correspondence without suppressing use of correct advice.
requirements: AI-assisted task setting where students submit an initial answer before consulting AI, allowing the prompt to sit between the AI interaction and the final answer
constraints: Findings concern bounded academic decision tasks rather than long-term learning; the model was queried dynamically so exact response replication is impossible
target_learning_goals: calibrated trust in AI advice; resistance to plausible but incorrect recommendations
examples: Participants in the reflection condition answered three metacognitive prompts after the ChatGPT interaction and before finalizing answers, and spent longer per AI-assisted trial (104.7 vs. 86.4 seconds).

article_title: Rethinking AI-assisted writing instruction: feedback literacy scripts, calibration training, and student writing development
citation: Dai (2026). Rethinking AI-assisted writing instruction: feedback literacy scripts, calibration training, and student writing development. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1829268
title: FRAC Feedback Literacy Script (Filter–Reason–Act–Check)
description: FRAC is a four-step feedback literacy script that guides students' processing of external AI feedback: "Filter, identifying the type of problem addressed by the feedback; Reason, judging whether the feedback was valid and relevant to the current task", then Act (implementing adopted feedback as a specific revision) and Check (reviewing whether the revision achieved the intended result). Training lasted approximately 15 to 25 minutes before T1 with brief reviews before T1 and T2; students recorded decision sheets at T1 and T2 as process data, with return rates exceeding 90% per round.
requirements: Students must process AI feedback systematically through the script and complete decision sheets recording how they handled each feedback item
constraints: In this study it was implemented with undergraduate English majors using Claude Sonnet 4 feedback during T1 and T2 only
target_learners: undergraduate English majors with basic academic writing skills
target_learning_goals: critical evaluation and effective uptake of AI-generated writing feedback
deep revision of argumentative essays
examples: FRAC group and combined group students completed decision sheets at T1 and T2 recording how they processed AI feedback; implementation was verified through submission rates, completeness checks, and classroom observations
key_sources: Dai (2026). Rethinking AI-assisted writing instruction: feedback literacy scripts, calibration training, and student writing development. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1829268

article_title: Rethinking AI-assisted writing instruction: feedback literacy scripts, calibration training, and student writing development
citation: Dai (2026). Rethinking AI-assisted writing instruction: feedback literacy scripts, calibration training, and student writing development. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1829268
title: APCA Assessment-Performance Calibration Activity
description: APCA is a self-assessment calibration training organized around "a process of “self-assessment-comparison-adjustment,” requiring students to repeatedly compare their own judgments with external evaluations across multiple task rounds". It has four stages: Anchor (reviewing sample texts at different quality levels), Predict (estimating one's score and confidence), Compare (identifying judgment bias against teacher ratings), and Adjust (modifying evaluation strategies based on recurring over- or underestimation). Each round lasted approximately 10 to 15 minutes with structured calibration logs, implemented continuously from T0 to T3, with log completion exceeding 90% per round.
requirements: Students complete structured calibration logs recording predicted score, confidence judgment, discrepancy from the teacher rating, and reflection on recurring bias, reviewed against a unified feedback protocol
constraints: The APCA group showed lower raw self-assessment error at baseline, so analyses used baseline-adjusted models; self-assessment and comparison stages were retained at T3 even though AI support was withdrawn
target_learners: undergraduate English majors with basic academic writing skills
target_learning_goals: accurate self-assessment of writing quality
reduction of overconfidence in self-judgment
examples: In each round students completed a calibration log and the researcher provided brief written comments for use in the next task
key_sources: Dai (2026). Rethinking AI-assisted writing instruction: feedback literacy scripts, calibration training, and student writing development. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1829268

article_title: Rethinking AI-assisted writing instruction: feedback literacy scripts, calibration training, and student writing development
citation: Dai (2026). Rethinking AI-assisted writing instruction: feedback literacy scripts, calibration training, and student writing development. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1829268
title: Embed AI writing tools within instructional support structures rather than treating them merely as instant feedback sources
description: The article concludes that when AI writing tools are used in teaching, "they should not be treated merely as sources of instant feedback. Instead, they should be embedded within specific instructional support structures", so students develop independent judgment and self-regulated learning while using feedback. The rationale is that AI feedback does not automatically improve writing; its value depends on whether learners can evaluate, select, and transform feedback into revision decisions, as shown by the differentiated effects of FRAC and APCA.
requirements: Structured metacognitive support (feedback-processing scripts and/or calibration activities) must accompany AI feedback access
constraints: Evidence comes from one study of English majors at a single university; the article calls for testing in more diverse contexts
target_learners: undergraduate L2/EFL writers using generative AI tools
target_learning_goals: independent revision judgment
self-regulated writing development with AI support
examples: The study embedded AI feedback within FRAC decision sheets and APCA calibration logs across four writing task points rather than providing AI feedback alone

article_title: ProductiveMath: A Generative-AI-Powered App to Support Productive Failure Teaching
citation: Antonio Laverghetta Jr., Simone Luchini, Averie Linell, Roni Reiter-Palmon and Roger Beaty. (2024). The creative psychometric item generator: a framework for item generation and validation using large language models. CREAI 2024: Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Creativity. https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.00202
title: CPIG: the creative psychometric item generator framework
description: CPIG is an iterative LLM-based framework for generating and validating creativity test items for the creative problem-solving (CPS) task. It uses LLMs as "item generators" to write items, "item response generators" to create human-like solutions under baseline, demographic, or psychometric prompting profiles, and an item scorer (a roberta-base originality model) to select k high-originality items as few-shot exemplars for the next generation round. The article hypothesizes that "items with high quality should enable more creative responses and will tend to elicit better originality scores on average than those that are of lower quality," making originality a proxy for item quality. It extends automated item generation, which has focused on multiple-choice cognitive and non-cognitive items, into the creativity domain.
requirements: Items must describe sufficiently complex yet ambiguous scenarios with no canonically correct solution, and the framework requires an automated originality scoring model validated against human ratings
constraints: The framework optimizes originality only, which the authors note is just one metric for judging creative outputs; item quality depends directly on the automated evaluation, and the authors caution against using CPIG items with human participants until more extensive review
target_learners: human test takers of creativity assessments
LLM test takers used as human simulacra
target_learning_goals: measuring creative problem-solving and originality of ideas
examples: In each trial, word lists generated by gpt-3.5-turbo constrain item generation, and four selected exemplar items are included in the prompt for the next of five iterations
key_sources: Antonio Laverghetta Jr., Simone Luchini, Averie Linell, Roni Reiter-Palmon and Roger Beaty. (2024). The creative psychometric item generator: a framework for item generation and validation using large language models. CREAI 2024: Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Creativity. https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.00202

article_title: ProductiveMath: A Generative-AI-Powered App to Support Productive Failure Teaching
citation: Antonio Laverghetta Jr., Simone Luchini, Averie Linell, Roni Reiter-Palmon and Roger Beaty. (2024). The creative psychometric item generator: a framework for item generation and validation using large language models. CREAI 2024: Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Creativity. https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.00202
title: Multi-stage prompting with rule-based quality filters for LLM item generation
description: CPIG's item generation follows a multi-stage prompting pattern: a first LLM produces word lists (three names, a place, and an action) that item-generator LLMs must incorporate, which the authors say helps "maximize diversity in scenario content by using different word lists to ensure no two item generation prompts are the same." Generated scenarios then pass rule-based validity filters: a Flesch reading-ease floor of 45 with a 140-token minimum, a string blacklist targeting priming (e.g., scenarios containing "on the one hand" or "is torn between"), and a required termination string. The pattern is meant to reduce, not replace, human expert review of items.
requirements: Human experts make the final decision on which items to include in a creativity assessment; the filters only eliminate items unlikely to be valid
constraints: The authors do not claim the priming string list is comprehensive, stating only that it eliminated most priming in generated scenarios
target_learners: human test takers of creativity assessments
target_learning_goals: generating valid, diverse creative problem-solving test items
examples: Scenarios are dropped if they lack the string "I am finished with this scenario." or score below 45 on Flesch reading ease; each word list gets at most 10 generation attempts

article_title: Teacher Involvement in Developing Sustainable Education Materials for AI Integration in Green Energy Education
citation: Riandi Riandi, Ismail Ismail, Ida Kaniawati, Wahyu Sopandi, Diana Ayu Rostikawati, Defrizal Hamka & Suhendar Suhendar. (2026). Teacher involvement in developing sustainable education materials for AI integration in green energy education. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-34422-4
title: Integrated conceptual model of AI integration in green energy education combining Constructivism, TAM, and TPACK
description: The article proposes a conceptual model integrating three theoretical frameworks to explain teachers' ability to integrate AI into green energy education. It states: "Figure 2 presents a revised conceptual model that integrates three main theoretical frameworks: Constructivism, Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), and Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK)." Constructivism frames ESD material development as reflective, collaborative practice; TAM contributes AI knowledge and attitudes as cognitive and affective readiness; TPACK is represented by a Perceived TPACK construct capturing self-assessed ability to integrate technology, pedagogy, and content. Five constructs are theorised to influence AI Integration Ability directly.
requirements: Measurement of the five constructs (AI knowledge, attitudes toward AI, use of AI in green education, ESD material development, ability to use AI) via validated questionnaire indicators
constraints: The model was tested as an exploratory baseline assessment in which participants received no specific AI training before the survey
target_learners: in-service teachers in professional development programs
target_learning_goals: integrating AI into sustainability-oriented (green energy) teaching practices
examples: The model was tested with PLS-SEM on survey data from 122 in-service teachers using five dichotomous-item constructs
key_sources: Riandi Riandi, Ismail Ismail, Ida Kaniawati, Wahyu Sopandi, Diana Ayu Rostikawati, Defrizal Hamka & Suhendar Suhendar. (2026). citation: Riandi Riandi, Ismail Ismail, Ida Kaniawati, Wahyu Sopandi, Diana Ayu Rostikawati, Defrizal Hamka & Suhendar Suhendar. (2026). Teacher involvement in developing sustainable education materials for AI integration in green energy education. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-34422-4
title: Five-construct dichotomous questionnaire measuring teacher AI readiness in green energy education
description: A structured questionnaire measuring five constructs aligned with TPACK domains: Knowledge of AI, Use of AI in Green Education, Development of ESD-Based Teaching Materials, Attitudes Toward AI, and Ability to Use AI. "Each construct was represented by five dichotomous items (Y es = 1, No = 0)." The binary format was chosen to accommodate varying technological familiarity and reduce respondent burden. The instrument was content-validated by three experts in science education and learning technology and distributed online via Google Forms between August and September 2024.
requirements: Content validation by subject-matter and learning-technology experts; PLS-SEM-compatible binary indicators handled via dummy-variable standardisation
constraints: The dichotomous 0/1 scale limited response variability and sensitivity, which the authors identify as likely weakening detection of knowledge and attitude effects
target_learners: in-service teachers without formal AI training
target_learning_goals: self-assessment of AI-related knowledge, attitudes, use, and integration ability in sustainability education
examples: Sample indicator: "I actively develop teaching modules with sustainability (ESD) principles."
