article_title: The impact of risk perception on perceived benefits of generative artificial intelligence users—an empirical study based on university students
citation: Du W, Ning S, Shi Y and Chen Y. (2026). The impact of risk perception on perceived benefits of generative artificial intelligence users—an empirical study based on university students. Front. Psychol. 17:1866428. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1866428
title: Integrated CAT–PMT–TAM/UTAUT2 risk–benefit framework for Gen AI use
description: The article integrates Cognitive Appraisal Theory, Protection Motivation Theory, and TAM/UTAUT2 into a unified framework explaining how risk perception dimensions relate to perceived benefits. Risk dimensions serve as primary appraisals of threat; students then conduct secondary appraisal of controllability and coping resources. Per PMT, high coping appraisal triggers adaptive, problem-focused coping associated with higher perceived benefits, while low coping appraisal triggers maladaptive coping. The framework predicts the risk–benefit relationship is "non-linear and dimension-speciﬁc".
requirements: Risk perception must be measured as multiple distinct dimensions rather than a unitary construct
The framework assumes students' coping self-efficacy and perceived controllability vary across risk types
constraints: The article states the relationship between risk perception and perceived benefit is non-linear and dimension-specific, so linear uniform-risk assumptions do not apply
target_learning_goals: understanding and managing AI-related risks
responsible and effective Gen AI use in academic and daily contexts
examples: The study operationalized five risk dimensions (information, security, technical, ethical, legal) and five benefit dimensions and tested the framework via hierarchical and threshold regression on 814 valid questionnaires
key_sources: Du W, Ning S, Shi Y and Chen Y. (2026). The impact of risk perception on perceived benefits of generative artificial intelligence users—an empirical study based on university students. Front. Psychol. 17:1866428. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1866428

article_title: AIED unplugged, teacher workload, and numeracy learning: a clustered quasi-experimental mixed-methods study
citation: Luiz Rodrigues, Guilherme Guerino, Thomaz Edson Silva, Luana Bianchini, Mariana Alves, Geiser Chalco Challco, Thales Vieira, Marcelo Marinho, Valmir Macario, Diego Dermeval, Ig Ibert Bittencourt, Seiji Isotani. (2026). AIED unplugged, teacher workload, and numeracy learning: a clustered quasi-experimental mixed-methods study. Smart Learning Environments. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40561-026-00465-x
title: AIED Unplugged (AIED-U): a paradigm for AI in education in resource-constrained settings, with the teacher as proxy
description: AIED-U is a paradigm for designing AIED for settings with limited technological infrastructure and digital skills, guided by five principles. The article states that "Conformity requires solutions to fit the infrastructure schools already have rather than demanding new hardware", Disconnect requires usability under intermittent or absent internet, Unskillfulness requires no advanced digital skills, Multi-user recognizes shared devices, and Proxy means "the teacher operates the system on behalf of students who continue to work with paper and pen". In this study the paradigm is instantiated by a numeracy app evaluated against usual practice.
requirements: Solutions must fit existing school infrastructure, remain usable without internet, and not demand advanced digital skills from users
constraints: The paradigm assumes no dedicated device per student, so students benefit through indirect interaction mediated by the teacher rather than direct student-system interaction
target_learners: elementary school students in low-resource Brazilian public schools
target_learning_goals: numeracy and arithmetic skills aligned with the BNCC curriculum
examples: In the evaluated system, the teacher photographs students' paper solution sheets with a smartphone; the app recognizes and evaluates the equations and generates error-specific feedback the teacher presents to students

(2026). AIED unplugged, teacher workload, and numeracy learning: a clustered quasi-experimental mixed-methods study. Smart Learning Environments. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40561-026-00465-x
title: [HIDDEN APP]: an AIED-U mobile system for numeracy education with exercise-list generation, automated assessment, learning analytics, and teacher autonomy preservation
description: [HIDDEN APP] is the AIED-U system for numeracy education evaluated in the study, a mobile app supporting four main functionalities. It generates personalized and diagnostic exercise lists using a student model with "a knowledge tracing component adapted for unplugged environments" combined with information gain theory; it offers personalized feedback by photographing paper sheets and applying object detection and handwritten math equation recognition with a knowledge-based system classifying errors; it provides individual and classroom learning analytics reports; and it preserves teachers' autonomy by allowing them to replace exercises or override the system's assessments.
requirements: A teacher smartphone with camera permission; teachers must photograph solutions and review reports; designed to work even when the teacher's smartphone lacks internet connectivity
constraints: Teachers reported the app sometimes failed to recognize students' calculations, particularly in multiplication tasks, and described reports as inaccurate; assessment reevaluation required many clicks and was one of the most challenging aspects
target_learners: third- and fourth-year Brazilian elementary students
target_learning_goals: BNCC numeracy skills EF02MA06 and EF03MA07 (arithmetic word problems)
examples: Teachers printed and administered app-generated lists, photographed solutions, and reviewed reports before planning the next lesson, over two lessons per week for two weeks

citation: Luiz Rodrigues, Guilherme Guerino, Thomaz Edson Silva, Luana Bianchini, Mariana Alves, Geiser Chalco Challco, Thales Vieira, Marcelo Marinho, Valmir Macario, Diego Dermeval, Ig Ibert Bittencourt, Seiji Isotani. (2026). AIED unplugged, teacher workload, and numeracy learning: a clustered quasi-experimental mixed-methods study. Smart Learning Environments. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40561-026-00465-x
title: Teacher-mediated AI offers a preliminary practical strategy for improving educational opportunities in resource-constrained settings
description: The article's findings support positioning the teacher, rather than the student, as the operator of AI systems where student devices are unavailable. The authors conclude that "these findings provide preliminary evidence that teacher-mediated AI may offer a practical strategy for improving educational opportunities in resource-constrained settings, calling for replications to establish whether this potential holds in longer interventions and other educational settings". The mechanism runs through the teacher: the system reduced reported effort, which was negatively associated with learning gains.
requirements: Teachers must be properly trained, and studies must experimentally control for training, since training itself enhanced students' learning outcomes in this study
constraints: Evidence is preliminary: the intervention lasted two weeks, the system showed technical and usability issues that added to teachers' work, and the indirect effect was exploratory
target_learners: students in under-resourced schools lacking per-student devices and reliable connectivity
target_learning_goals: mathematics/numeracy learning in elementary education
examples: In the study, experimental-condition teachers used the app on their own smartphones under intermittent classroom connectivity while students worked with paper and pen

article_title: Assessment twins: An approach for strengthening assessment validity in the age of generative AI
citation: Jasper Roe, Mike Perkins, Louie Giray. (2026). Assessment twins: An approach for strengthening assessment validity in the age of generative AI. Journal of Applied Learning and Teaching, 9(2). https://doi.org/10.37074/jalt.2026.9.2.3
title: Assessment twins: two deliberately linked assessment components addressing the same outcomes through different modes of evidence
description: The article names and substantively describes assessment twins as a redesign approach for the GenAI era. Twins are conceptualised as "two deliberately linked components that address the same learning outcomes through different modes of evidence, scheduled closely together to allow for cross-verification". The pairing lets instructors triangulate evidence across formats so that validity can be checked even when one format is vulnerable to generative AI misuse.
requirements: The two components must address the same learning outcomes and be scheduled closely together to allow cross-verification.
constraints: The authors acknowledge challenges including resource intensity, equity concerns, and the need for empirical validation.
target_learning_goals: course learning outcomes assessed through GenAI-vulnerable formats
examples: The article proposes pairing pedagogically valuable yet GenAI-vulnerable assessment formats so evidence can be triangulated across the twin tasks.
key_sources: Jasper Roe, Mike Perkins, Louie Giray. (2026). Assessment twins: An approach for strengthening assessment validity in the age of generative AI. Journal of Applied Learning and Teaching, 9(2). https://doi.org/10.37074/jalt.2026.9.2.3

article_title: Assessment twins: An approach for strengthening assessment validity in the age of generative AI
citation: Jasper Roe, Mike Perkins, Louie Giray. (2026). Assessment twins: An approach for strengthening assessment validity in the age of generative AI. Journal of Applied Learning and Teaching, 9(2). https://doi.org/10.37074/jalt.2026.9.2.3
title: Messick's unified validity framework used to map six facets of GenAI threat to assessment validity
description: The article applies Messick's unified validity framework as its organizing analytic axis, systematically mapping GenAI threats across six validity facets. As the abstract states, the authors "use Messick's unified validity framework to systematically map the ways in which GenAI threatens content, structural, consequential, generalisability, substantive, and external validity". This gives assessment designers a structured taxonomy for diagnosing which facets of validity a GenAI-vulnerable task loses.
requirements: Users must be able to analyse an assessment task against each of the six validity facets named in the framework.
target_learning_goals: validity-focused evaluation and redesign of assessment tasks
examples: The framework is used to organise the article's analysis of how GenAI undermines each validity facet before the twin approach is introduced.
key_sources: Jasper Roe, Mike Perkins, Louie Giray. (2026). Assessment twins: An approach for strengthening assessment validity in the age of generative AI. Journal of Applied Learning and Teaching, 9(2). https://doi.org/10.37074/jalt.2026.9.2.3

article_title: Assessment twins: An approach for strengthening assessment validity in the age of generative AI
citation: Jasper Roe, Mike Perkins, Louie Giray. (2026). Assessment twins: An approach for strengthening assessment validity in the age of generative AI. Journal of Applied Learning and Teaching, 9(2). https://doi.org/10.37074/jalt.2026.9.2.3
title: Respond to GenAI assessment threats with validity-focused redesign that prioritises pedagogy rather than surveillance or prohibition
description: The article's guiding design recommendation is that assessment responses to generative AI should be organised around assessment validity and pedagogy. The authors "contend that assessment twins represent a validity-focused response to GenAI that prioritises pedagogy while supporting meaningful student learning outcomes". Redesign should therefore preserve pedagogically valuable formats and strengthen evidence, rather than simply abandoning vulnerable task types.
requirements: Redesign must keep the targeted learning outcomes and meaningful student learning outcomes central when adapting vulnerable formats.
constraints: The authors acknowledge resource intensity and equity concerns as challenges for this approach.
target_learning_goals: maintaining assessment validity and meaningful learning outcomes in the age of generative AI
examples: The article frames assessment twins as its instantiation of this principle, pairing vulnerable formats so their pedagogical value is retained while evidence is cross-verified.

title: Assessment twin implementation challenges: resource intensity, equity concerns, and pending empirical validation
description: The article identifies a set of implementation challenges accompanying the assessment twin approach. As printed, the authors acknowledge "the challenges, including resource intensity, equity concerns, and the need for empirical validation". These challenges qualify the approach's readiness: designing and marking linked task pairs demands additional resources, may affect students unevenly, and the approach has not yet been empirically tested.
requirements: Adopters should plan for the additional resourcing that designing and marking two linked assessment components requires.
constraints: The approach currently lacks empirical validation, per the authors' own acknowledgement.

article_title: Integrating Generative Artificial Intelligence into University Curricula: Student Insights
citation: Rook, L., & Plumb, M. (2026). Integrating Generative Artificial Intelligence into University Curricula: Student Insights. Journal of University Teaching and Learning Practice, 23(2). https://doi.org/10.53761/jjzzd330
title: Three-area student-identified taxonomy of GenAI curriculum development priorities
description: This taxonomy organises student-identified priorities for GenAI curriculum development into three areas: understanding and optimising GenAI functionality, exploring GenAI applications across contexts, and navigating ethical and legal dimensions of GenAI. It emerged from thematic analysis of qualitative responses from 166 undergraduate business students in a capstone unit, who expressed "strong support for integrating GenAI knowledge and application into higher education curricula". The taxonomy functions as a framework for universities designing GenAI-integrated curricula and for structuring student consultation on digital capability and employability.
requirements: Curriculum design processes should gather student input, since the taxonomy derives from student-identified priorities rather than expert-defined categories
constraints: Derived from qualitative responses of business students in a single capstone unit; the article reports no quantitative validation of the three-area structure
target_learning_goals: generative AI literacy
career readiness with GenAI
ethical and legal use of GenAI
examples: The study asked 166 capstone business students about GenAI's role in academic learning and career readiness and thematically grouped their responses into the three priority areas

citation: Rook, L., & Plumb, M. (2026). Integrating Generative Artificial Intelligence into University Curricula: Student Insights. Journal of University Teaching and Learning Practice, 23(2). https://doi.org/10.53761/jjzzd330
title: Involve students in co-designing GenAI-integrated, future-ready curricula
description: The article argues that universities preparing students for a GenAI-integrated professional future should involve students in co-designing curricula, because students can directly identify which capabilities they need. The findings "highlight the value of student involvement in co-designing future-ready curricula" and contribute to conversations on digital capability and employability. In practice, this means treating student perceptions data, such as the qualitative responses analysed here, as design input for curriculum decisions about GenAI.
requirements: Mechanisms for collecting student perceptions (e.g., qualitative survey responses) must exist so student input can inform curriculum design
constraints: Evidence base is student perceptions from one capstone unit in business education; the article does not report tested outcomes of co-designed curricula
target_learning_goals: GenAI-related digital capability
employability and career readiness
examples: The authors drew on qualitative responses from 166 capstone business students and used the identified priority areas as the basis for recommending student involvement in curriculum co-design

article_title: Don't believe the hype. AI myths and the need for a critical approach in higher education
citation: Rudolph, J., Ismail, F., Tan, S., & Seah, P. (2025). Don't believe the hype. AI myths and the need for a critical approach in higher education. Journal of Applied Learning and Teaching, 8(1), 06-27. https://doi.org/10.37074/jalt.2025.8.1.1
title: Adopt a critical approach to AI in higher education rather than believing the hype
description: The editorial's organizing principle is that, amid hype and myth surrounding AI and GAI, "a critical re-evaluation of AI's role is imperative" in higher education. It positions educators to interrogate claims of AI autonomy, objectivity, and inevitable benefit rather than accept them. The principle underpins the authors' call for critical AI literacy and for ensuring AI enhances human insight and social justice rather than perpetuating technological illusions.
requirements: Educators must engage in critical re-evaluation of AI's role rather than accepting hype-driven narratives
target_learners: higher education faculty and institutional leaders
target_learning_goals: critical evaluation of AI technologies and their role in teaching and learning
examples: The editorial dismantles eight entrenched myths shaping current discourse on AI and GAI in higher education

article_title: Uncovering adoption personas for generative AI in higher education: a clustering-based segmentation approach
citation: Afef Saihi and Vian Ahmed. (2026). Uncovering adoption personas for generative AI in higher education: a clustering-based segmentation approach. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00583-z
title: Persona-based, person-centered framework for understanding GenAI chatbot adoption in higher education
description: The article introduces a persona-based framework that moves beyond aggregate, variable-centered adoption models such as TAM and UTAUT by identifying latent user segments. It argues that variable-centered models "rely on the assumption of user homogeneity, estimating average structural relationships across entire populations", which obscures meaningful variation. Using unsupervised clustering on validated adoption constructs, the framework yields personas grounded in "psychographic and behavioral clustering" rather than demographic segmentation, and is positioned as complementing, not replacing, the prior SEM model.
requirements: Requires validated, psychometrically sound multi-item constructs as clustering input, as established in prior SEM validation
constraints: The approach does not model causal relationships; it examines how perceptual constructs naturally combine into user configurations
target_learning_goals: understanding and supporting adoption of GenAI chatbots for academic support and learning-related activities
examples: The study applied hierarchical agglomerative clustering with Ward's linkage followed by k-means on 13 composite variables from 192 respondents to construct the personas.
key_sources: Afef Saihi and Vian Ahmed. (2026). Uncovering adoption personas for generative AI in higher education: a clustering-based segmentation approach. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00583-z

article_title: Uncovering adoption personas for generative AI in higher education: a clustering-based segmentation approach
citation: Afef Saihi and Vian Ahmed. (2026). Uncovering adoption personas for generative AI in higher education: a clustering-based segmentation approach. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00583-z
title: Validated 192-respondent GenAI chatbot adoption dataset with 13 clustering variables
description: A survey dataset originally collected via Qualtrics for prior SEM-based adoption research and repurposed here for person-centered clustering. It comprises 192 valid responses from students (n = 107) and educators (n = 85) across engineering, business, and health sciences, with approximately 70% reporting ChatGPT as their primary tool. Thirteen variables, including multi-item composites for trust, privacy concerns, and interaction quality plus single-item indicators such as intent to continue use, were standardized via z-score transformation before clustering.
requirements: Respondents required prior experience using GenAI chatbots in higher education contexts
constraints: Sampling used purposive and snowball strategies through professional and academic networks, which the article describes as targeting broad representation but not probability sampling
target_learning_goals: characterizing perceptions and experiences of GenAI chatbot use for academic support and learning
examples: The article reports the age of respondents ranged from 18 to over 65, with an approximately balanced gender distribution (54% female, 46% male).
key_sources: Afef Saihi and Vian Ahmed. (2026). Uncovering adoption personas for generative AI in higher education: a clustering-based segmentation approach. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00583-z

article_title: Uncovering adoption personas for generative AI in higher education: a clustering-based segmentation approach
citation: Afef Saihi and Vian Ahmed. (2026). Uncovering adoption personas for generative AI in higher education: a clustering-based segmentation approach. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00583-z
title: Two-stage clustering pattern: hierarchical clustering to determine k, then k-means for final segmentation
description: A reusable analytical pattern for constructing user personas from survey data. In the first stage, "hierarchical agglomerative clustering, using Ward's linkage method and Euclidean distance" is applied, with dendrograms and silhouette coefficients informing the choice of cluster count. In the second stage, that optimal k is used as input for k-means clustering, a centroid-based algorithm valued for scalability and interpretability. Cluster quality is then assessed with internal validation indices such as the Silhouette Score, Calinski-Harabasz Index, and Davies-Bouldin Index.
requirements: Requires standardized composite variables and internal validation indices to justify the chosen number of clusters
constraints: The article notes the highest silhouette score occurred at k = 2, so the selected solution balanced statistical fit against interpretability rather than maximizing a single index
target_learning_goals: identifying latent user segments to inform educational technology design and support
examples: The study executed the clustering in Python's scikit-learn library and validated the four-cluster solution with Silhouette, Calinski-Harabasz, and Davies-Bouldin indices.

grain_size: lesson/unit-level analytical pattern for persona construction

article_title: Knowing Its Name, Not Its Nature: Word Association Mapping of Student AI Cognition and Evidence-Based Micro-Credential Design in Turkish Higher Education
citation: İsmail Şan and Hanife Gülhan Orhan Karsak. (2026). Knowing its name, not its nature: word association mapping of student AI cognition and evidence-based micro-credential design in Turkish higher education. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00621-w
title: Word Association Test as a cognitive-structure diagnostic instrument for needs-assessment-driven curriculum design
description: The Word Association Test (WAT) is a psycholinguistic instrument grounded in spreading-activation and associationist models of semantic memory, used here to map the organisational structure of students' AI cognition. The article explains that the test "measures cognitive structure not as the presence or absence of individual concepts but as the pattern of associative connections among them". Early, frequent responses indicate highly integrated concepts; late or rare responses indicate peripheral or fragmented understanding. The study operationalises this through a seven-stage protocol — normalisation to 65 canonical codes, frequency and Z-score banding, Kendall's τ with FDR correction, PROXSCAL multidimensional scaling, and hierarchical threshold network analysis — and links the resulting map directly to micro-credential design decisions.
requirements: Administration with a time limit and no prompting to promote spontaneous activation, as the study implemented with a three-minute limit
constraints: The article notes semantic distance reveals the existence of a relationship rather than its specific nature

The sample excludes Turkey's most research-intensive and technologically advanced universities, so the authors advise against generalising to institutions of that profile without independent empirical verification
target_learning_goals: mapping learners' existing cognitive structures around AI to inform AI literacy curriculum sequencing
examples: The study administered an online written WAT with the stimulus word 'artificial intelligence' to 436 students at four Turkish public universities, yielding 1376 raw tokens analysed through the seven-stage protocol
key_sources: İsmail Şan and Hanife Gülhan Orhan Karsak. (2026). Knowing its name, not its nature: word association mapping of student AI cognition and evidence-based micro-credential design in Turkish higher education. title: Ethical AI and Workforce Readiness (EAWR) micro-credential framework
description: The Ethical AI and Workforce Readiness micro-credential framework is the study's proposed credential architecture, derived directly from the WAT diagnostic findings. The abstract states "the study proposes an Ethical AI and Workforce Readiness micro-credential framework that bridges the gap between functional use and conceptual mastery". Unlike approaches that treat AI ethics as a separate add-on to technical curricula, the framework embeds ethical considerations throughout the competency structure. Each analytical layer of the WAT protocol generates a specific design implication for the framework, targeting the diagnosed absences: algorithmic transparency, ethical governance, and technical mechanisms that remain conceptually absent from students' associative networks.
requirements: A clear specification of the target competency domain grounded in empirical needs assessment, since the article states each effectiveness factor necessitates a clear specification of the target competency domain that extends beyond what normative frameworks alone can provide
constraints: The framework is proposed as a design output of this needs assessment; the article reports no implementation or outcome evaluation of the credential itself
target_learners: undergraduate students in Turkish higher education with high AI tool use but low formal AI education
target_learning_goals: AI literacy spanning functional use, algorithmic understanding, and ethical governance for workforce readiness
examples: The study uses the frequency, τ, MDS and network findings as a curriculum roadmap, positioning ethical content as foundational rather than an afterthought

article_title: Scaffolding Systematic Reviews in Learning Design and Technology Through Mentoring and AI Integration
citation: Xiyu Wang, Fatemeh Dadashipour, Basori, Yukiko Maeda, & Jennifer C. Richardson. (2026). Scaffolding systematic reviews in learning design and technology through mentoring and AI integration. Educational technology research and development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10629-8
title: Systematic reviews as intentional learning experiences scaffolded by mentoring that combines methodological guidance with emotional scaffolding
description: The article frames systematic reviews "as intentional learning experiences that unfold across stages of the review and require mentoring and technological support." Mentoring is described as "an integrated support system that combined methodological guidance with emotional scaffolding" rather than solely procedural knowledge transmission. Mentoring was embedded across stages: guiding search refinement, joint discussion of borderline screening decisions, and collaborative coding, reducing the cognitive and emotional burden of evaluative judgments and supporting both technical competence and confidence.
requirements: Mentoring support embedded across multiple stages of the review process, or peer-based discussion groups when individual mentoring is not feasible
constraints: The account draws on one team's experience conducting an SR in the interdisciplinary LDT field; the authors position it as a practical guide for similarly complex fields
target_learners: graduate students and novice researchers conducting systematic reviews
target_learning_goals: systematic review methodology
critical appraisal skills
confidence in handling ambiguity and evaluative judgment
examples: Experienced researchers guided novices in refining search scopes and selecting databases; mentoring at screening involved joint discussion of inclusion and exclusion decisions for borderline cases
key_sources: Xiyu Wang, Fatemeh Dadashipour, Basori, Yukiko Maeda, & Jennifer C. Richardson. (2026). Scaffolding systematic reviews in learning design and technology through mentoring and AI integration. Educational technology research and development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10629-8

article_title: Scaffolding Systematic Reviews in Learning Design and Technology Through Mentoring and AI Integration
citation: Xiyu Wang, Fatemeh Dadashipour, Basori, Yukiko Maeda, & Jennifer C. Richardson. (2026). Scaffolding systematic reviews in learning design and technology through mentoring and AI integration. Educational technology research and development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10629-8
title: Treat automation in systematic reviews as a complement rather than a substitute, with careful documentation and human oversight
description: The article concludes that "the automation is best treated as a complement rather than a substitute" in systematic reviews. While automation reduced procedural burdens such as screening, "interpretive decisions still required substantial human oversight." The team tested LLM-based extraction tools (MetaMate) but chose not to integrate them because "currently available tools cannot ensure that the extracted content is verifiably grounded in the original text." Selective use can enhance efficiency while human verification safeguards interpretive rigor and credibility.
requirements: Careful documentation and human oversight to preserve interpretive rigor and credibility; researchers need both technical skills and methodological understanding to leverage emerging tools
constraints: Automation development and effectiveness are uneven across review stages; tasks requiring contextual interpretation, reconciliation of ambiguous reporting, or integrative synthesis remain difficult to automate
target_learners: SR teams in interdisciplinary fields such as LDT
target_learning_goals: balancing efficiency and credibility in technology-supported systematic reviews
examples: The team used Covidence's ML-based prioritization to reorder studies by previous screening decisions, but declined to substitute machine extraction for human coding

article_title: Designing a mobile chatbot-based learning journaling system for intrinsic motivation and engagement
citation: Sven Scheu, Simone N. Loeffler and Alexander Maedche. (2026). Designing a mobile chatbot-based learning journaling system for intrinsic motivation and engagement. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00589-7
title: Mobile chatbot-based learning journaling system with example-based course and LLM journaling assistant
description: A fully functional mobile chatbot-based learning journaling system that guides students through structured reflective journal entries. It instantiates two design principles: an example-based built-in course with a seven-day structure providing modeled responses, and an LLM-based journaling assistant that scaffolds entries by summarizing the user's preliminary response, asking a clarifying question, and generating up to three alternative first-person formulations using OpenAI's gpt−3.5-turbo-1106 model. The system also includes seven topic-based journal templates, a general template, optional daily summaries of the last five entries, and 9 P.M. reminders. It was evaluated in a 2×2 randomized field experiment over 22 days.
requirements: Students need a personal smartphone to install the application and native or near-native German-speaking proficiency
Journaling needs to be supported by instructions, as unguided learners do not engage sufficiently in germane processes
constraints: The chatbot was rule-based with a primarily linear conversation flow following templates
The assistant was used by only 55.91% of participants after the onboarding session
External support risks encouraging cognitive offloading if it formulates reflection on behalf of the student
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning
reflective journaling
intrinsic motivation for journaling
examples: In the field experiment, participants created 1904 journal entries, on average 10.64 entries per participant (SD = 6.46), and the course was completed by 75.58% of users with the course

article_title: Multidimensional perceived school support and AI learning anxiety among university students: the mediating roles of control-value appraisals
citation: Jiang H, Chen B and Chen Q (2026). Multidimensional perceived school support and AI learning anxiety among university students: the mediating roles of control-value appraisals. Front. Psychol. 17:1951992. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1951992
title: Control-value theory integrated with social support theory and TAM as an account of AI learning anxiety
description: The article proposes an integrated framework in which control-value theory is the principal account of AI learning anxiety: "achievement emotions reﬂect learners' judgments of how much control they have over activities and outcomes and how much value they place on them". AI learning self-efficacy operationalizes perceived control, and AI perceived usefulness (from TAM) operationalizes value. Social support theory supplies the three dimensions of perceived school support (emotional, informational, instrumental), specified as a distal contextual correlate of students' immediate appraisals. The model was tested with SEM in a sample of Chinese undergraduates.
requirements: Requires measurement of perceived school support, AI learning self-efficacy, AI perceived usefulness, and AI learning anxiety as distinct constructs
constraints: The article states the sequential ordering reflects the proposed structural model rather than an empirically established temporal process, and the design cannot establish causal mediation
target_learners: university undergraduates using AI tools in their learning
target_learning_goals: emotional adjustment to AI-supported learning, including reduced AI learning anxiety and informed judgments of AI's educational value
examples: The structural model specified PSS as a second-order construct with paths to ASE, APU, and ALA, and sequential mediation through self-efficacy then perceived usefulness.
key_sources: Jiang H, Chen B and Chen Q (2026). Multidimensional perceived school support and AI learning anxiety among university students: the mediating roles of control-value appraisals. Front. Psychol. 17:1951992. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1951992

article_title: Exploring interfaces and implications for integrating social-emotional competencies into AI literacy for education: a narrative review
citation: Adam Palmquist, Helga Dis Isfold Sigurdardottir, Hege Myhre. (2025). Exploring interfaces and implications for integrating social-emotional competencies into AI literacy for education: a narrative review. Journal of Computers in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40692-025-00354-1
title: Integrated framework embedding SEC within AI literacy for education
description: The review proposes a conceptual model that embeds social-emotional competencies within AI literacy, built by juxtaposing AI literacy frameworks (Long & Magerko; Ng et al.) with the SEC/CASEL framework. It states: 'By embedding SEC within AI literacy, this study contributes to understanding how AI technologies can foster emotional and relational skills while addressing ethical challenges in education.' The framework aims at a technologically adept and emotionally intelligent educational ecosystem, with AI literacy as the foundational concept and SEC/CASEL as complementary. It was derived through thematic analysis of a curated 19-source corpus.
requirements: A curated interdisciplinary knowledge base spanning AI literacy and SEC, as assembled by the SETCOM project
constraints: The review acknowledges potential selection bias and subjective interpretation of findings in narrative reviews
Synthesising concepts as of 2017 may not capture the most recent progressions in the rapidly evolving AI domain
target_learning_goals: AI literacy
social-emotional competencies
ethical and relational navigation of AI in education
examples: The SETCOM project used the framework to cross-pollinate SEC ideas into AI literacy as a transversal competency for educational stakeholders

article_title: Educational integrity in GenAI-augmented assessment: making judgment visible
citation: Sunaina Sharma. (2026). Educational integrity in GenAI-augmented assessment: making judgement visible. International Journal for Educational Integrity 22:6. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00216-y
title: Postplagiarism as an educational integrity framework reframing integrity around responsibility rather than control
description: The paper adopts Eaton's postplagiarism as a lens for rethinking educational integrity in GenAI-augmented contexts, recognizing hybrid human-GenAI writing as a contemporary condition of academic work. It states that postplagiarism "does not abandon integrity standards; it reframes them around responsibility rather than control", so integrity is defined not by whether GenAI was used but by how decisions were justified and disclosed. The paper extends this ethical orientation into structural assessment design.
requirements: Assessment design and institutional policy must support integrity as an enacted ethical practice rather than enforce it technologically
constraints: The framework addresses GenAI-augmented academic work in which responsibility for academic decisions remains with the human author
target_learning_goals: ethical academic practice and responsible GenAI use
examples: The paper operationalizes postplagiarism through four illustrative assessment practices that foreground transparency, justification, and accountability
key_sources: Sunaina Sharma. (2026). Educational integrity in GenAI-augmented assessment: making judgement visible. International Journal for Educational Integrity 22:6. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00216-y

article_title: Educational integrity in GenAI-augmented assessment: making judgment visible
citation: Sunaina Sharma. (2026). Educational integrity in GenAI-augmented assessment: making judgement visible. International Journal for Educational Integrity 22:6. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00216-y
title: Design assessment so that integrity is enacted through transparent, justified decision-making rather than inferred from technological absence
description: The paper's central design principle: assessment should be reconceptualized as the primary site where educational integrity is enacted, shifting attention "from whether GenAI was used to how academic choices were made and responsibility exercised". Assessment structures that foreground decision-making, transparency, and justification render integrity visible within hybrid human-GenAI work and scaffold accountability instead of relying on surveillance.
requirements: Assessment tasks must explicitly require justification, verification, and articulation of decision-making
Educators need shared criteria and professional calibration to interpret articulated judgement consistently
constraints: The paper notes these designs may become performative, with learners aligning discourse to expectations without internalizing commitments
target_learning_goals: accountable ethical reasoning and evaluative judgement in GenAI-augmented work
examples: The paper distinguishes integrity-oriented assessment from authentic assessment: authenticity asks whether a task mirrors real-world practice, whereas integrity-oriented design asks whether learners can justify decisions
key_sources: Sunaina Sharma. (2026). Educational integrity in GenAI-augmented assessment: making judgement visible. International Journal for Educational Integrity 22:6. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00216-y

article_title: Educational integrity in GenAI-augmented assessment: making judgment visible
citation: Sunaina Sharma. (2026). Educational integrity in GenAI-augmented assessment: making judgement visible. International Journal for Educational Integrity 22:6. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00216-y
title: Annotated decision trails as integrity artefacts documenting evaluative decisions about GenAI contributions
description: Annotated decision trails invite learners to document how GenAI contributed to their work and why particular outputs were retained, modified, or rejected in relation to disciplinary criteria. The paper describes them as "integrity artefacts, documenting how learners navigate responsibility within hybrid human-GenAI systems", rendering ethical decision-making observable without surveillance technologies. They also address equity by holding all learners accountable for articulating judgement regardless of language proficiency.
requirements: Scalability in larger enrolment contexts is supported by focused annotation of selected decision points and rubric criteria attending to quality of reasoning rather than volume of reflection
constraints: The paper offers these as illustrative rather than evidentiary mechanisms, not comprehensive pedagogical frameworks
target_learners: higher education students using GenAI tools
target_learning_goals: transparent disclosure of evaluative reasoning and accountability for academic decisions
examples: Appendix A models the practice reflexively, documenting the author's decisions to accept or reject ChatGPT5 revision suggestions during manuscript preparation

article_title: Educational integrity in GenAI-augmented assessment: making judgment visible
citation: Sunaina Sharma. (2026). Educational integrity in GenAI-augmented assessment: making judgement visible. International Journal for Educational Integrity 22:6. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00216-y
title: Verification and accountability practices requiring learners to demonstrate how GenAI-sourced claims were checked
description: Verification practices require learners to demonstrate how claims were checked, what sources were consulted, and how discrepancies or uncertainty were addressed. The paper positions verification as "an ethical responsibility inherent to academic work", operationalizing accountability: learners remain responsible for accuracy regardless of whether claims originated from GenAI. This makes integrity enacted through epistemic vigilance rather than presumed through trust in technological outputs.
requirements: Assessment must make verification an explicit component rather than treating GenAI inaccuracies as evidence of misconduct
constraints: Responds to the probabilistic nature of GenAI outputs, which may include fabricated citations or misleading summaries
target_learning_goals: critical information literacy and disciplinary accountability
examples: The paper connects such practices to emerging paired-component designs that verify learning outcomes in AI-vulnerable contexts

article_title: Educational integrity in GenAI-augmented assessment: making judgment visible
citation: Sunaina Sharma. (2026). Educational integrity in GenAI-augmented assessment: making judgement visible. International Journal for Educational Integrity 22:6. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00216-y
title: Oral defence and dialogic accountability as integrity artefacts evaluating understanding rather than artefacts
description: Oral defence practices provide a dialogic mechanism through which learners articulate and justify academic decision-making in GenAI-augmented work, with prompts about where and how GenAI supported the work and which outputs were rejected or revised and why. The paper argues that "responsiveness to probing questions, conceptual grasp of disciplinary ideas, and the ability to articulate boundaries of appropriateness provide more robust indicators of learning and responsibility than similarity metrics or probabilistic detection tools."
requirements: Clear criteria, shared calibration among instructors, and flexibility in modality are essential; evaluative criteria must prioritize conceptual understanding rather than rhetorical fluency alone
constraints: In larger classes, formats may need adaptation through brief structured conferences, small-group dialogic checks, or selective sampling
target_learners: higher education students, including those with diverse language backgrounds
target_learning_goals: ownership of meaning, limitations, and disciplinary implications of GenAI-augmented work
examples: Typical prompts ask where and how GenAI supported the work, or how the final product might be adapted for a specific learner, context, or disciplinary constraint

title: Draft differences and version history practices foregrounding developmental accountability across drafts
description: Draft comparison practices invite learners to compare selected versions of their work to explain what changed, what role GenAI played at different stages, and how revisions improved clarity, accuracy, or alignment with disciplinary criteria. Version history functions as an integrity artefact capturing learning trajectories.

title: On-premise OER-based AI knowledge-base assistant system for computer science education
description: A three-subsystem architecture comprising an LMS Layer, a Knowledge Base Layer with structured extraction and a FAISS vector index, and an AI Inference Layer with curriculum alignment and model optimization modules. Evaluation dataset drawn from English-medium OER platforms; multilingual extension is future work

citation: Qianrun Mao. (2024). Fostering Self-Directed Growth with Generative AI: Toward a New Learning Analytics Framework. https://www.google.com/search?q=Fostering+Self-Directed+Growth+with+Generative+AI+Toward+a+New+Learning+Analytics+Framework
title: Self-Directed Growth: a competency of independently driving iterative, sustainable SDL cycles fueled by Capacity to Aspire
description: Self-Directed Growth is defined as "a competency reflects by the increased progression to drive an ongoing, iterative, and sustainable SDL process independently, fueled by an enhanced Capacity to Aspire". It positions the learner as initiator, executor, assessor, and primary agent of their own SDL journey, extending SDL beyond achieving predefined outcomes in pre-assigned tasks toward independently constructing and assessing one's own SDL process guided by an internal compass. The article presents it as an advanced extension of the broader SDL framework and the central construct of the A2PL model.
requirements: Learners actively engage with GAI-supported feedback systems in a reflective and strategic manner
constraints: The article states its foundations remain largely conceptual and that variability in learners' intrinsic motivation, metacognitive maturity, and socio-cultural positioning is not fully accounted for in the model
target_learners: lifelong learners navigating transitions between educational and career phases
target_learning_goals: self-directed learning competency
capacity to aspire
sustained learner agency across contexts and tasks

title: A2PL framework: three foundational pillars (Capacity to Aspire, Complex Thinking, Self-Assessment) reconfigured around Self-Directed Growth
description: The Aspire to Potentials for Learners framework reconfigures the three foundational pillars of SDL summarized by Morris (2019): "The Capacity to Aspire represents the core essence of humanistic philosophy; Complex Thinking serves as the foundation of constructivist epistemology; and Self-Assessment embodies the principles of pragmatic philosophy". At the center is Self-Directed Growth, and together the pillars represent a learning process that is individual, purposeful, and developmental. The framework aligns summative self-assessment with the two layers of Capacity to Aspire within and across learning cycles.
requirements: Summative self-assessment must be combined with Capacity to Aspire to drive an ongoing, iterative, and sustainable SDL process
constraints: The article states detailed technical implementations, platform engineering, and algorithmic design fall outside its scope and are reserved for future research

title: A2PL three-level intervention design: Person, Task, and Person x Task levels
description: The A2PL intervention operates at three levels. At the Person level, learners reflect on aspirations and long-term vision of societal achievement and professional growth. At the Task level, "Learners and GAI co-create complex thinking tasks within real world scenarios that align with learners' aspirations". At the Person x Task level, learners construct a summative self-assessment framework by aligning identified ability, skill, and strategy gaps with task-aligned personal aims, fostering a more clearly defined strategic learning pathway. Starting from the second round, reflective practices adjust alignment and initiate a new SDL cycle.
requirements: GAI must refrain from disclosing that the assessment pertains directly to SDL, so learners' frameworks indicate internalized skills rather than prompted responses
constraints: The article states success is contingent on whether learners' summative self-assessment frameworks reflect analytical cognition of SDL into the depth of its procedures and components
target_learners: self-paced learners in non-synchronous online environments
target_learning_goals: self-monitoring, self-regulation, self-reflection, and self-evaluation
strategically aligned personal learning pathways

title: Aspire to Potential Scoring Rubric (APSR): a GAI-applied diagnostic rubric with undisclosed scores
description: Within the diagnostic analytics layer, the GAI evaluates students' summative self-assessment frameworks using the pre-designed Aspire to Potential Scoring Rubric (APSR), which "incorporates component weights, relational logistics, and vectorized progression, all mapped both within and across the phases of the SDL cycles". Component relevance, relational logistics, and vectorized progression refer to tailored assessment of each element's relative importance, their interconnections, and progression through key A2PL stages. Importantly, the GAI's scoring assessment is not disclosed to learners; interactive analytics build on the scores to deliver feedback.

title: Assess self-directed growth through learner-driven summative self-assessment frameworks rather than task-level engagement measures
description: The article argues that sustained, purposeful engagement across multiple contexts, not task-level behavior, indicates competency development, and that task-level engagement of learner agency cannot validly assess learner agency. It therefore adopts "a specific focus on learner-driven summative self-assessment", where the evolving trajectory of learners' self-assessment frameworks serves as a key indicator of emerging SDL skills and self-directed growth. This moves beyond post-task questionnaires and self-efficacy ratings toward post-task judgments of ability based on performance and procedures.
requirements: Assessment must capture developmental process across tasks and contexts, not single-task engagement
constraints: The article states summative self-assessment alone cannot drive a sustainable SDL process unless combined with Capacity to Aspire
target_learners: learners developing self-directed learning competencies across diverse tasks
target_learning_goals: accurate evaluation of sustained SDL competency development
examples: The article contrasts its approach with prior studies collecting self-efficacy assessments via backend data and summative self-assessments via researcher-administered post-task questionnaires

article_title: RoboBuddy in the Classroom: Exploring LLM-Powered Social Robots for Storytelling in Learning and Integration Activities
citation: Tozadore, D., Ertug, N., Chaker, Y., & Abderrahim, M. (2025). RoboBuddy in the Classroom: Exploring LLM-Powered Social Robots for Storytelling in Learning and Integration Activities. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.16706
title: RoboBuddy teacher interface for generating scenario-based robot activities from curriculum content
description: A browser-based system with three modules: a teacher-facing web interface for preparing storytelling activities, a web application connecting the interface to LLM modules, and a locally runnable fine-tuned LLM so data stays local. Teachers select predefined settings translated into specialized prompts, choose levels of AI assistance (five levels for Story Generation, three for Lecture Storification), specify the age group, and can edit, regenerate, or replace generated stories before approving questions for the robot. Activities run with a virtual avatar or an Alpha Mini robot, with DALL·E-3 image generation whose complexity is tailored to the age group. The article states the goal is to "grant teachers autonomy, using the AI as a supportive tool rather than the primary element in course creation".

constraints: The local model was chosen for setups with limited computing resources; the article notes concerns about data privacy motivated a local model

target_learning_goals: curriculum content approached through scenario-based activities
social integration and inclusion

title: PhinetunEd: a Phi-3 model fine-tuned for educational content creation
description: PhinetunEd is the authors' name for a Phi-3-Mini-128k-instruct model (3.8B parameters, 128K context window) fine-tuned with QLoRA on a consumer GPU using 2500 samples from Cosmopedia, a synthetic dataset of educational resources including story-generation instruction tasks. It was built because of "concerns about data privacy and the need for improved performance in pedagogical tasks" and runs on a laptop without an internet connection, keeping data locally processed and stored. In benchmarks it scored best of the compared models on story generation (7.46) while scoring below GPT-3.5-turbo on MMLU and Hellaswag.

constraints: The authors considered only small language models of around 3 billion parameters or fewer due to limited computing resources and the need for timely responses
target_learning_goals: story generation and Q&A creation from curriculum content
examples: Teachers shown outputs from both models said GPT stories could be more engaging while PhinetunEd provided more room for teacher intervention to dive deeper into concepts

citation: Elaheh Sanoubari, Neil Fernandes, Keith Rebello, Alicia Pan, Andrew Houston, and Kerstin Dautenhahn. (2026). Play-Testing REMind: Evaluating an Educational Robot-Mediated Role-Play Game. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.00300
title: REMind: a robot-mediated role-play game for rehearsing anti-bullying bystander intervention
description: REMind is a two-hour room-based installation in which a child plays a mentor to a robotic avatar while three Furhat robots enact a peer bullying scenario. The child uses a physical Bully-Detector prop, completes an empathy task, and in "Puppet Mode" records an improvised intervention and puppeteers AVATAR "through their own recorded voice and facial performance" to change the outcome of the live robotic drama. It was developed over 4 years of iterative co-design with children, teachers, and domain experts, orchestrated by a hidden Wizard and an in-room drama facilitator (the Joker).

constraints: Scalability is constrained by its semi-autonomous nature and the two-person Wizard-of-Oz facilitation protocol

self-efficacy for defending
examples: In the play-testing study, all participants rehearsed bystander intervention through Puppet Mode using one of the two strategies offered in the game

article_title: From Prototype to Classroom: An Intelligent Tutoring System for Quantum Education
citation: Iizalaarab Elhaimeur and Nikos Chrisochoides. (2026). From Prototype to Classroom: An Intelligent Tutoring System for Quantum Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.24807
title: Spoke-and-Wheel teaching architecture: three quantum-specialist agents in parallel coordinated by a Synthesizer
description: ITAS's teaching architecture decomposes tutoring by task: three specialist agents (Video, Guidance, Code) analyze each student question in parallel, each reasoning only within its designated scope, and a Synthesizer Agent integrates their outputs using a priority hierarchy with code errors first, then conceptual gaps, then video references. The design responds to the prototype's task-boundary hallucinations, which the authors attribute to cognitive overload of a single overloaded agent. Specialization is said to reduce hallucination via cognitive load reduction, task interference elimination, and synthesis filtering. The three-agent count "emerged empirically; two agents conflated code and concepts, while four added coordination overhead without reliability improvement."
requirements: Each agent must carry quantum-specific domain knowledge, e.g. a timestamp-indexed concept map for the Video Agent and a hand-curated Qiskit error catalog for the Code Agent
constraints: A controlled, blinded comparison against the prototype on the same input set remains future work
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of quantum information science
Qiskit implementation skills
video lecture comprehension
examples: A student question about a QiskitError applying Pauli-Z was handled by parallel Video, Code, and Guidance agent analyses synthesized into one response addressing video context, code diagnosis, and conceptual confirmation
key_sources: Iizalaarab Elhaimeur and Nikos Chrisochoides. (2026). From Prototype to Classroom: An Intelligent Tutoring System for Quantum Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.24807

citation: Iizalaarab Elhaimeur and Nikos Chrisochoides. (2026). From Prototype to Classroom: An Intelligent Tutoring System for Quantum Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.24807
title: ITAS conversational instructor analytics agent
description: A single-agent conversational analytics system that lets instructors interrogate deployment data through natural language while preserving student privacy. The agent "queries pre-aggregated BigQuery summaries, assembles results with lesson metadata, and produces a natural language response", narrating pre-queried data without writing SQL or performing calculations. It cross-references video seek data, code execution logs, and checkpoint submissions to surface aggregate pedagogical patterns, never returning individual transcripts or identifiable interaction logs. The narrow-scope design applies the same reliability principle as the teaching architecture.
requirements: Pre-aggregated BigQuery summaries and lesson metadata must exist for the agent to narrate
constraints: The agent never writes SQL or performs calculations, and never returns individual transcripts or identifiable interaction logs
target_learning_goals: instructor awareness of aggregate pedagogical patterns such as engagement gaps and failure types
examples: In the pilot, the agent surfaced the Module 2 dead zone finding without an explicit instructor query and distinguished a reading comprehension error from a genuine conceptual gap

citation: Iizalaarab Elhaimeur and Nikos Chrisochoides. (2026). From Prototype to Classroom: An Intelligent Tutoring System for Quantum Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.24807
title: Exercise coverage must match content coverage in self-paced quantum courses
description: Drawn from the dead zone finding, this principle holds that students treat exercises as the operational definition of required material in a self-paced course. The article states that "Any quantum concept without a corresponding implementation exercise risks being skipped regardless of its importance". In the pilot, students stopped watching the Module 2 lecture where exercise coverage ended, and the instructor closed the gap by adding multi-qubit checkpoints. Designers should map every lecture concept to at least one implementation exercise.
requirements: A checkpoint or exercise should exist for each lecture concept instructors expect students to engage with
constraints: Evidence comes from a single pilot deployment with five graduate students and no control group
target_learners: graduate students in self-paced quantum computing courses

title: Self-referential analytic assessment framework
description: An evaluation paradigm for analytic essay scoring that shifts from normative (inter-learner ranking) to within-learner interpretation of analytic profiles. "Self-referential analytic assessment focuses on intra-learner variability, identifying aspects where a student performs significantly better or worse than their average proficiency." Standardised analytic scores are averaged within a learner, and deviations of each aspect from that average define a dual binary classification task for positive and negative feedback, using a one-standard-deviation threshold. The article positions this as a stricter, more pedagogically relevant test of analytic assessment capability and the first such framework for L2 AES.

citation: Alexandre Cristovão Maiorano. (2026). Evaluating Prompt Injection Defenses for Educational LLM Tutors: Security-Usability-Latency Trade-offs. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06669
title: Four-layer defense-in-depth architecture for educational LLM guardrails
description: The article describes a "defense-in-depth mechanism comprising four distinct layers": deterministic lexical pattern filters (Layer 1), structural output validation (Layer 2), contextual sandboxing with explicit delimiters (Layer 3), and session-level behavioral heuristics (Layer 4). It is "designed as a progressive filter", starting with high-speed deterministic checks and escalating to structural, contextual, and session-level behavioral analysis, with each layer targeting a specific class of attack vectors while minimizing false positives on benign educational queries.

constraints: Layer 4 blocks zero attacks in the offline single-turn benchmark and is relevant only for online multi-turn enforcement; indirect injection is explicitly out of scope
target_learners: students in programming education tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: preventing answer extraction while permitting legitimate clarification, hint-seeking, and debugging help

title: Select educational AI guardrails as explicit trade-offs among bypass resistance, false-positive behavior, and latency
description: The article argues that "guardrail choices in educational AI should be made as explicit trade-offs among bypass resistance, false-positive behavior, and latency, rather than from isolated metrics." Because false positives carry direct pedagogical cost in tutoring systems, the optimal operating point depends on institutional risk and usability requirements: NeMo's balanced rail blocks all attacks but frustrates roughly 1 in 6 students, while the multi-layer pipeline preserves usability at higher residual bypass.
requirements: Institutional tolerance for false positives and latency must be specified before selecting a guardrail configuration
constraints: The article does not claim absolute security; a 46.34% input-gate bypass indicates significant residual risk, and latency figures are hardware-dependent

target_learning_goals: preserving pedagogical integrity and productive struggle while maintaining access to legitimate help

article_title: Reinforcement Learning Measurement Model
citation: Wenqian Xu, Feng Ji. (2026). Reinforcement Learning Measurement Model. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09305
title: Reinforcement Learning Measurement Model (RLMM)
description: The RLMM is a psychometric measurement framework for sequential process data that treats a person's inverse-temperature parameter βj as an ability to choose higher-valued actions under a Boltzmann policy. It replaces the MDP-MM's person-specific tabular value functions with "a shared parametric action-value function Qθ(s,a)", using centered and globally normalized advantages, a soft Bellman-consistency penalty encoding known task dynamics, and a block-coordinate MAP estimation procedure. It also yields step-level influence diagnostics that identify behaviorally critical decisions.
requirements: Known task dynamics (transition and reward structure) used in the soft Bellman-consistency penalty
Identification constraints: state-wise centering and global normalization of the advantage function to remove softmax translation and co-scaling freedom
constraints: Uses a single positive ability parameter, which the authors note cannot fully capture strategy selection, task persistence, and exploration patterns
In open-ended environments, estimates depend on how researchers define states, actions, and rewards
target_learning_goals: measuring latent decision-making ability from action-sequence process data
examples: Applied to peg-solitaire simulations with known true abilities and to AQUALAB gameplay logs from the Open Game Data export

title: KITE: an intent-aware RAG tutoring architecture combining multi-stage retrieval with pedagogical response strategies
description: KITE (Knowledge-Informed Tutoring Engine) is a RAG-based intelligent tutoring system for course-grounded dialogue on algorithmic reasoning and problem-solving. As the article states, "the system includes five components: document preprocessing, embedding generation, multi-stage retrieval, intent-aware response generation, and session management." Each query is classified by pedagogical intent, and the classified intent determines the response strategy: grounded explanations for direct and conceptual questions, Socratic assessment for validation, diagnostic hint progressions for debugging, and step-by-step state-tracing for algorithm tracing. Retrieval combines dense bi-encoder search, hybrid scoring (70% dense, 30% BM25), MMR with λ = 0.7, cross-encoder reranking, and source-based boosting, passing the top eight chunks to GPT-5.

constraints: The article notes strong retrieval alone does not ensure effective tutoring; responses may still be too direct or mismatched to the student's need

algorithm tracing
debugging
problem-solving

article_title: REC-CBM: Rubric-Aware Error-Correction Concept Bottleneck Models for Trustworthy Open-Ended Grading
citation: Chengshuai Zhao, Fan Zhang, Kumar Satvik Chaudhary, Yiwen Li, Lo Pang-Yun Ting, Ying-Chih Chen, Huan Liu. (2025). REC-CBM: Rubric-Aware Error-Correction Concept Bottleneck Models for Trustworthy Open-Ended Grading. https://github.com/scott-f-zhang/REC-CBM
title: REC-CBM framework: rubric-aware error-correction concept bottleneck model for trustworthy open-ended grading
description: REC-CBM is a concept bottleneck model for open-ended grading that integrates three components: a rubric-aware concept encoder that learns concept-specific representations over responses using a concept query bank, an ordinal pairwise calibration objective that preserves ranking structure among rubric dimensions, and a latent concept error-correction module that denoises concept predictions before final grade prediction while preserving interpretability. The framework uses two-stage training: Stage I learns rubric-aligned concept predictors, and Stage II fits latent-correction parameters on frozen concept outputs. The article states this design "preserves the interpretable bottleneck while cor-recting concept-level noise before grade prediction."
requirements: Requires human-annotated rubric-aligned concept labels for training, produced here through a human-in-the-loop annotation pipeline with three domain experts and LLM-assisted initial annotation
constraints: Applied to open-ended grading of short answers, essays, and reading-comprehension answers; the article notes future work will extend to multilingual and domain-specific assessment
target_learners: students whose written open-ended responses are graded
target_learning_goals: accurate and interpretable automated grading of open-ended responses
examples: Evaluated on Mohler short-answer grading, ASAP 2.0 essay scoring, and MOCHA reading-comprehension answer grading benchmarks

title: Route automated grading predictions through human-interpretable rubric-level concepts so educators can inspect, verify, and intervene
description: In high-stakes educational assessment, raw accuracy alone is insufficient; instructors need to understand why a score was produced and how to intervene on questionable judgments. Routing grading predictions through human-interpretable rubric-level concepts provides a mechanistic guarantee of transparency, decomposing the final grade into rubric-level concept predictions that educators can examine or modify. The article states this enables educators to "inspect, verify, and intervene on reasoning," supporting intervention and auditing and promoting pedagogical usefulness through concept-level outputs aligned with feedback categories.
requirements: Rubric-aligned concept annotations must cover the dominant rubric axes that determine the holistic grade, be non-redundant, and have ordinally interpretable anchored descriptors
constraints: Standard CBMs assume shared latent space and evenly spaced categories, requiring rubric-aware encoding and ordinal calibration to work well for fine-grained grading
target_learners: educators and instructors using automated grading systems
target_learning_goals: trustworthy and transparent automated grading of open-ended student responses
examples: REC-CBM implements this by decomposing grading into per-concept ordinal predictions with token-level attention evidence, corrected posteriors, and additive per-concept contributions to the grade logit

article_title: From Scoring to Explanations: Evaluating SHAP and LLM Rationales for Rubric-based Teaching Quality Assessment
citation: Ivo Bueno, Babette Bühler, Philipp Stark, Tim Fütterer, Ulrich Trautwein, Dorottya Demszky, Heather Hill, Enkelejda Kasneci. (2026). From Scoring to Explanations: Evaluating SHAP and LLM Rationales for Rubric-based Teaching Quality Assessment. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05180
title: A general framework for sentence-level interpretability of rubric-based scoring combining SHAP attributions with LLM rationales
description: The article proposes "a general framework for sentence-level interpretability of rubric-based scoring that combines model-agnostic Shapley value attributions with LLM-generated rationales". It casts rubric-based teaching quality assessment as text scoring with model-agnostic sentence-level explanations, where an explanation method maps an input and model to a ranked list of sentences claimed most influential. Faithfulness is evaluated via a deletion-based protocol that progressively removes top-k units and measures prediction change, extended to cross-model settings where explanations from one architecture perturb another. It was instantiated on the CLASS Quality of Feedback dimension using the NCTE corpus with fine-tuned PLMs and instruction-tuned LLMs.
requirements: Identical sentence segmentation, deletion rules, and deterministic LLM decoding across compared models, as the article states all experiments use
constraints: The deletion-based protocol perturbs natural discourse structure and may alter pragmatic meaning, limiting its ability to reflect true causal influence
The article does not evaluate whether identified sentences align with underlying rubric constructs (construct relevance)
target_learners: teachers receiving automated feedback on classroom transcripts
target_learning_goals: understanding which parts of classroom dialogue drive automated teaching quality assessments

title: Position automated rubric-based scoring systems as decision-support tools that augment rather than replace human raters in high-stakes settings
description: The article argues that in high-stakes educational contexts, automated scoring systems "should not replace human raters in high-stakes settings", because models trained on human annotations may inherit subjective judgments or structural biases and propagate them at scale. Instead, such systems "should be positioned as self-assessment or decision-support tools that augment, rather than replace, professional judgment". The article further stresses that scores and explanations are probabilistic and imperfect, and that interpretability methods are intended to support teacher reflection and informed decision-making rather than serve as authoritative assessments.

Model predictions and explanations risk being interpreted as objective ground truth

target_learning_goals: supporting teacher reflection and informed decision-making about automated teaching quality assessments

title: Verification spectrum: a graduate competency spanning informal code review and testing through static analysis and type-system-guided development to full formal verification
description: The verification spectrum is the whitepaper's articulation of verification as a durable graduate competency for the AI era, extending the CS2023 framework. In the faculty workshop's usage, "verification" in this context encompasses a spectrum of rigor: from informal code review and testing, through static analysis and type-system-guided development, to full formal verification using proof assistants. Humans act as a senior software engineer verifying AI-generated code, and the whitepaper argues this spectrum aligns with a three-level framework from the formal methods education literature that can be embedded in existing courses without additional curricular expansion.

article_title: Regulating the AI Tutor: Intentions, Help-Seeking, and Self-Regulated Learning in Adolescent GenAI Use
citation: Rania Abdelghani, Peter Kaiser, and Kou Murayama. (2026). Regulating the AI Tutor: Intentions, Help-Seeking, and Self-Regulated Learning in Adolescent GenAI Use. Accepted at the NextGen Learning Interfaces Workshop, AIED 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.08568
title: Turn-level coding framework combining SRL, help-seeking, and mathematical modeling codes with LLM-specific constructs of epistemic vigilance and agency over the AI
description: The article proposes a hybrid turn-level coding framework applied to each task-relevant student turn in AI-tutor conversations. Deductive codes follow Zimmerman's cyclical SRL model (PLAN, MONITOR, REQUEST, EVALUATE), with REQUEST turns further coded as instrumental or executive and by content type, plus a Blum-based modeling-process code. Two inductive LLM-specific constructs were derived via an exploratory pass with Gemini 2.5 Pro: "Epistemic vigilance is a three-valued code (not_applicable, caught, missed) capturing whether a student reacts to an inaccurate or mismatched AI turn", and a binary "Agency over the AI" marker capturing attempts to shape the AI's role, format, or scaffolding.
requirements: Task-relevant student turns from AI-tutor chat logs; a stratified human-validation pass by domain experts to establish per-construct reliability
constraints: Behavioral analyses currently rely on AI coding alone; human validation is ongoing
Derived from an exploratory pass on a randomly selected 30% of conversations
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning and help-seeking during AI-supported mathematics learning
examples: Applied to 1,616 chat turns (808 student turns) from 98 Grade-9 students using a web-based Mistral Large tutor on a mathematical-modeling task

title: Functionalist perspective of shame and guilt as social signals regulating behavior
description: The article adopts a functionalist perspective of social emotions, which "conceptualizes emotions as adaptive regulators of behavior in social contexts." Within this framing, guilt is oriented toward a specific behavior and motivates reparative action, whereas shame is oriented toward the self and elicits withdrawal, concealment, or identity threat. The framework guided the interview protocol and inductive coding, focusing on how students evaluated their behaviors and identities in relation to AI use, while remaining open to unanticipated patterns.
requirements: Applied via semi-structured interviews that avoid directly asking about specific emotions, letting emotional experiences emerge through students' own accounts
constraints: The article notes the functionalist lens may not fully capture the identity aspects uncovered in the findings

examples: The study used the lens to interpret hiding behaviors, selective disclosure, shaming, and cycles of use among 19 computing students
