article_title: StanBKT: Rethinking Parameter Estimation in Bayesian Knowledge Tracing
citation: Siddhartha Pradhan, Yanping Pei, Morgan Lee, Puyuan Zhang, Erin Ottmar, and Adam C. Sales. (2026). StanBKT: Rethinking Parameter Estimation in Bayesian Knowledge Tracing. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23048
title: StanBKT: an open-source Python package for Bayesian estimation of BKT models in Stan
description: StanBKT is an open-source Python package for estimating classical BKT models and several extensions using Bayesian inference in Stan. It provides a unified interface for model specification, parameter estimation, and posterior analysis, including filtered and smoothed latent-state estimation, posterior predictive prediction, visualization utilities, and diagnostics such as ESS, MCSE, and R-hat. Source code is public on GitHub, installable via pip, with online documentation and worked examples.

target_learners: students working in intelligent tutoring systems whose response sequences are modeled
target_learning_goals: estimating mastery, learning, forgetting, guessing, and slipping parameters from student interaction data
examples: The package fits models through a three-stage workflow of model specification, parameter estimation, and analysis, demonstrated in a worked example with simulated data for 100 students and 30 problems

article_title: StanBKT: Rethinking Parameter Estimation in Bayesian Knowledge Tracing
citation: Siddhartha Pradhan, Yanping Pei, Morgan Lee, Puyuan Zhang, Erin Ottmar, and Adam C. Sales. (2026). StanBKT: Rethinking Parameter Estimation in Bayesian Knowledge Tracing. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23048
title: Bayesian formulation of BKT: priors, posterior inference, and hierarchical partial pooling
description: The article frames BKT estimation as Bayesian inference: parameters are treated as random variables with prior distributions, and inference targets the posterior P(theta | Y), which "explicitly captures parameter uncertainty" and propagates it to downstream analyses such as mastery trajectories and group comparisons. The framework motivates Bayesian estimation on four grounds: principled uncertainty quantification, incorporation of prior knowledge for regularization, mitigation of BKT identifiability issues via informative priors, and natural extension to hierarchical models with partial pooling across students, skills, or items, which is "particularly beneficial in sparse-data settings common in educational experiments."
requirements: Approximate inference (MCMC or variational) is required because exact inference is intractable due to exponentially many latent state sequences
constraints: Approximate methods such as VI and Pathfinder produce biased approximations that often underestimate posterior uncertainty and simplify dependencies among parameters
target_learners: students in intelligent tutoring systems and educational experiments modeled via knowledge tracing
target_learning_goals: quantifying uncertainty in learning, forgetting, guessing, and slipping parameters for adaptive instruction and intervention comparison
examples: StanBKT implements this formulation with logit-scale priors, half-scaled-logit bounds on guess and slip, and hierarchical priors with learned between-group variance
key_sources: Siddhartha Pradhan, Yanping Pei, Morgan Lee, Puyuan Zhang, Erin Ottmar, and Adam C. Sales. (2026). StanBKT: Rethinking Parameter Estimation in Bayesian Knowledge Tracing. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23048

article_title: StanBKT: Rethinking Parameter Estimation in Bayesian Knowledge Tracing
citation: Siddhartha Pradhan, Yanping Pei, Morgan Lee, Puyuan Zhang, Erin Ottmar, and Adam C. Sales. (2026). StanBKT: Rethinking Parameter Estimation in Bayesian Knowledge Tracing. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23048
title: Three pooling formulations for BKT: standard, multi (group-specific), and hierarchical (partial pooling)
description: StanBKT organizes BKT formulations into three pooling types. Standard BKT shares a single parameter set across all students (full pooling, assuming homogeneous learning and response behavior). Multi BKT estimates a separate parameter set for each predefined group such as classrooms, treatment conditions, or individual students, enabling direct comparison across groups. Hierarchical BKT introduces partial pooling through hierarchical priors, decomposing each parameter into a global component and group-level deviations with a learned variance controlling shrinkage. The article states this formulation "stabilizes and regularizes estimates in sparse data contexts while preserving systematic differences across groups."
requirements: Grouped and hierarchical variants require a group identifier column in the interaction data
constraints: Standard BKT assumes homogeneous learning and response behavior across students and items
target_learners: students grouped by classroom, treatment condition, cohort, or individual
target_learning_goals: comparing learning dynamics across experimental conditions and stabilizing estimates in sparse-data settings
examples: The perceptual cue reanalysis used Multi BKT with condition-specific parameters across the nine spacing-by-color conditions, fit via MCMC

article_title: Socially fluent AI decouples conversational signals from source identity in online interaction
citation: Lixiang Yan, Yueqiao Jin, Xibin Han, Dragan Gasevic. (2026). Socially fluent AI decouples conversational signals from source identity in online interaction. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23426
title: Truth-default theory extended to presumed human identity in computer-mediated interaction
description: The article applies truth-default theory — the account that in ordinary interaction people default to presuming honesty and benign intent unless contextual triggers raise suspicion — to presumed human identity in synchronous text-based interaction. It argues that socially fluent AI "effectively decoupled social signaling from source identity, rendering established computer-mediated communication heuristics non-diagnostic". The theory explains why participants exhibited a slight bias toward human attribution and why suspicion cues such as perceived scriptedness or rapid response can be shared by both AI and human targets.

citation: Dimitri Eckert and Christian Kautz. (2026). How Students (Mis)understand Conditionals and Loops – A Taxonomy. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.26966v1
title: Extended Taxonomy Design Process (ETDP) as an iterative method for building taxonomies
description: The ETDP, described by Kundisch et al. and adopted as this article's method, is an iterative, user-centered taxonomy design methodology with six phases: problem specification, objective definition (including a meta-characteristic and ending conditions), development, demonstration and analysis, evaluation, and communication. The article emphasizes that "the ETDP is inherently iterative, allowing taxonomy designers to continuously update, extend, and refine existing taxonomies without restarting the entire design procedure". It supports both empirical-to-conceptual and conceptual-to-empirical building approaches.
requirements: Designers must determine the meta-characteristic, objective and subjective ending conditions, and evaluation goals upfront
constraints: Taxonomies should be judged by suitability for their intended purpose, not as right or wrong
target_learners: taxonomy designers and computing education researchers
target_learning_goals: structuring and classifying phenomena such as student difficulties
examples: This article applies the ETDP with a conceptual-to-empirical start, justified by the existing substantial body of research on student difficulties

article_title: How Students (Mis)understand Conditionals and Loops -- A Taxonomy
citation: Dimitri Eckert and Christian Kautz. (2026). How Students (Mis)understand Conditionals and Loops – A Taxonomy. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.26966v1
title: Distinctions among error, difficulty, and misconception, with misconceptions as potentially fragile knowledge
description: The article defines a terminology framework for classifying student problems: an error is a concrete incidence of a mistake, a difficulty is the underlying misunderstanding or erroneous cognitive behavior that causes errors, and a misconception is a difficulty grounded in an incorrect mental model. The authors define a misconception as "a specific kind of difficulty that is based in a concrete mental model about a specific programming concept that does not align with reality". They also argue misconceptions need not be stable, challenging prior definitions.
requirements: The terms must be used distinctly to avoid confusion, since they are sometimes used interchangeably in the literature
constraints: The authors challenge the definition that misconceptions are necessarily stable and systematically repeated, noting novice programming misconceptions can be fragile knowledge
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of programming constructs
examples: The framework treats misconceptions as non-binary, allowing students to hold semi-correct or multiple notions of a concept at the same time

title: Selection branch of the taxonomy: five categories of conditional-statement difficulties
description: The selection branch classifies difficulties with conditional statements into five categories: the selective nature of selection statements, boundaries of the selection body, the else-branch, timing of condition check, and nesting. Example categories include thinking all branches execute independent of their condition and confusion between "if(C) A; else B;" and "if (C) A; B;". Many categories carry literature references, while others are newly created from the authors' own research.
requirements: Applies to difficulties in reading code containing selection statements, within the paper's conceptual-knowledge scope
constraints: Syntactic and lexical errors are excluded as fundamentally different in nature

target_learning_goals: understanding conditional statements and their execution
examples: The nesting category includes confusion between sequencing versus nesting of if-statements and ignoring an if-condition inside a loop

title: Iteration branch of the taxonomy: seven categories of loop difficulties

article_title: 'It''s OK Because...": The Wild West of Student Rationalization of AI Use in Academic Writing'
citation: Kim, Jiyoon; Toyama, Kentaro; Kim, Sangmi; Carroll, John. (2026). "It's OK Because...": The Wild West of Student Rationalization of AI Use in Academic Writing. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.29090
title: Five-sites framework of AI-use expectations in a course
description: The article proposes that for any given course, concepts of appropriate AI use for academic writing are housed in five distinct sites: faculty intention, formal policy, student interpretation, student self-policy, and student practice. These sites, whether explicit or implicit, formal or informal, often differ from one another, and the divergences create openings for re-interpretation of ethically questionable AI use. The framework explains how instructor expectations are translated, interpreted, personalized, and enacted, with the boundary of acceptable use softening at each site.
requirements: Analysis of a course requires access to both syllabi or formal policy documents and student accounts of their interpretation and practice, as the article obtained through interviews, syllabi, chat logs, and submissions.
constraints: Faculty intention was not measured directly; the article states it was inferred from syllabi and participant interviews because faculty were not interviewed.
target_learning_goals: understanding and negotiating course AI policies in academic writing
examples: The article illustrates site mismatches with a student who copied AI text believing idea-generation permission covered it, students who misremembered or mixed up policies across courses, and students who violated their own stated norms in practice.
key_sources: Kim, Jiyoon; Toyama, Kentaro; Kim, Sangmi; Carroll, John. (2026). "It's OK Because...": The Wild West of Student Rationalization of AI Use in Academic Writing. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.29090

article_title: 'It''s OK Because...": The Wild West of Student Rationalization of AI Use in Academic Writing'
citation: Kim, Jiyoon; Toyama, Kentaro; Kim, Sangmi; Carroll, John. (2026). "It's OK Because...": The Wild West of Student Rationalization of AI Use in Academic Writing. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.29090
title: Taxonomy of 23 student rationalizations for AI use in six classes
description: The article presents a taxonomy of 23 distinct moral justifications, termed Rationalizations (R1–R23), that students use to justify AI use in writing assignments, grouped into six Rationalization Classes: victimless behavior, minimal AI contribution, ex ante contribution, post hoc contribution, responsibility denial, and perceived benefit. Definitions were developed inductively from participant accounts through thematic analysis of interviews, chat logs, and course documents, with representative participant quotes for each rationalization. The taxonomy classifies the justifications rather than the AI-use practices themselves, so the same practice can be justified through different rationalizations.
requirements: The taxonomy was built from semi-structured interview excerpts in which participants described or justified their AI use, consolidated from 46 subcodes through team consensus.
constraints: The article notes space limits prevented in-depth description of every rationalization, and the sample comprised students who self-reported at least sometimes using AI for writing.
target_learners: undergraduate students using generative AI for academic writing
target_learning_goals: moral sense-making about acceptable AI assistance in academic writing
examples: Class examples include R3 Busywork (AI acceptable for low-value assignments), R6 My Ideas (core ideas originated with the student), R12 My Style (output sounding like the student makes it theirs), R13 Normalization, and R19 Time Economy.

title: Interpretable decision layer for outcome-independent coordination of teacher and student feedback
description: A transparent mechanism that combines teacher and student feedback to rank course topics needing attention without grades or outcome labels. It integrates three signals — gap prevalence, survey disagreement, and teacher friction — into a topic priority score with a per-topic decision record explaining each ranking. The article states it "organizes teacher, student, and researcher roles around this shared decision process," positioning the layer as supporting human–AI co-agency rather than replacing instructor judgment.

article_title: Special-R1: Reinforcement Learning for Special Education — Aligning LLM Tutors to Diverse Learners through Disability-Adaptive Training
citation: Unggi Lee, Jihoi Na, Yeil Jeong, Haeun Park, Yeonju Jang. (2026). Reinforcement Learning for Special Education: Aligning LLM Tutors to Diverse Learners through Disability-Adaptive Training. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30670
title: Special-R1: disability-aware pedagogical RL coupling a two-dimensional adaptive prompt with a persona-aware Thinking Reward
description: Special-R1 is a framework extending pedagogical multi-turn RL to special education. It factors pedagogical support into two orthogonal dimensions: a support level (amount) mapped from the learner's baseline accuracy to Maximum, Moderate, or Minimum support following the I-Do / We-Do / You-Do progression, and a support style (manner) drawn from the learner's disability profile, so that "thewhatcomes from the support level, thehowcomes from the disability profile." Its second component is a persona-aware Thinking Reward whose judge is prompted with the learner's disability profile and scores whether the thinking trace reflects disability-appropriate reasoning, which the authors describe as "the first reward we are aware of that explicitly scoresdisability-appropriatereasoning."
requirements: Requires a pre-measured baseline accuracy of the student simulator on the given problem type to select the support level, and a structured disability rubric with learning characteristics, communication patterns, and recommended tutor strategies.
constraints: Every student in the framework is a disability-conditioned LLM simulator; improvements on judge-based metrics have not been validated with real learners with disabilities.
Experiments use 7-8B tutors; behavior at larger scales remains to be studied.
target_learners: Learners with disabilities across five profiles: intellectual disability, specific learning disability, autism spectrum disorder, ADHD, and emotional/behavioral disorder
target_learning_goals: Multi-domain tutoring covering mathematics, reading comprehension, social reasoning, and life skills
examples: The adaptive prompt maps baseline accuracy in [0.01, 0.20) to Maximum support (micro-steps, concrete examples), [0.20, 0.40) to Moderate support, and [0.40, 0.60) to Minimum support with open-ended questions.
key_sources: Unggi Lee, Jihoi Na, Yeil Jeong, Haeun Park, Yeonju Jang. (2026). Reinforcement Learning for Special Education: Aligning LLM Tutors to Diverse Learners through Disability-Adaptive Training. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30670

title: Released Special-R1 artifacts: multi-domain ZPD-filtered corpus, SPED-Tutor-Mix evaluation set, seven checkpoints, and disability-aware evaluation pipeline
description: The article releases the training and evaluation artifacts behind Special-R1. The training corpus contains approximately 54k problems across four domains (mathematics, reading comprehension, social reasoning, life skills), filtered to a ZPD window of 1-60% solve rate by the Llama-3.1-8B student simulator and annotated with baseline accuracy. The evaluation set is the persona-augmented SPED-Tutor-Mix test split in which "every item carries a disability profile so that persona-aware metrics can be computed." The disability rubric is released as disability_types.yaml alongside the code, together with all seven model checkpoints and the evaluation pipeline.
requirements: The corpus is ZPD-filtered to problems with 1-60% solve rate by the frozen student simulator before training.
constraints: The corpus contains a comparatively small number of LD-appropriate mathematics items, which the authors link to the sld_math weakness.
target_learners: LLM tutors being aligned for learners with disabilities
target_learning_goals: Multi-domain tutoring: mathematics, reading comprehension, social reasoning, and life skills

article_title: Special-R1: Reinforcement Learning for Special Education — Aligning LLM Tutors to Diverse Learners through Disability-Adaptive Training
citation: Unggi Lee, Jihoi Na, Yeil Jeong, Haeun Park, Yeonju Jang. (2026). Reinforcement Learning for Special Education: Aligning LLM Tutors to Diverse Learners through Disability-Adaptive Training. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30670
title: Calibrate both the amount and the style of tutor support to the learner: support level from baseline accuracy, style from disability-specific access needs
description: The article argues effective special-education tutoring demands two simultaneous adjustments: the amount of support, calibrated to the learner's zone of proximal development, and the style of support, calibrated to disability-specific access needs through Explicit Instruction, the Prompting Hierarchy, High-Leverage Practices, and Universal Design for Learning. Special-R1 operationalizes both axes inside the tutor's system prompt and the judge of its thinking trace, and its ablations show the prompt-style axis is the single largest driver of persona-aware Fit gains. The framework treats these as orthogonal dimensions rather than a single generic pedagogical prompt.
requirements: A pre-measured baseline accuracy per problem type to select the support level, and a structured disability profile specifying recommended tutor strategies, communication patterns, and learning characteristics.
constraints: The Thinking Reward component of the framework only becomes effective when combined with adaptive prompting; under static prompts the accept/reject judge saturates.
target_learners: Learners with disabilities in one-on-one LLM tutoring
target_learning_goals: Scaffolded problem-solving support tailored to disability-specific access needs
examples: The tutor prompt variants SPED-static and SPED-adaptive draw style verbatim from the disability profile's tutor_strategies, communication_patterns, and learning_characteristics fields, with SPED-adaptive selecting the support level dynamically from baseline accuracy.

article_title: Simulating Students' Java Programming Errors with Large Language Models
citation: Ali Keramati, Jie Cao, Iman Mohammadi, Mark Warschauer, Yang Shi. (2026). Simulating Students' Java Programming Errors with Large Language Models. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.14113
title: Diversity-alignment trade-off framework for LLM student-error simulation
description: The article proposes two dimensions, diversity and alignment, as central to the usefulness of LLMs as proxies for authentic student errors. Models strong in diversity (e.g., Gemini) often exhibit weaker alignment, and vice versa, with Claude Sonnet 4 described as "the most balanced option". The framework holds that model choice should be guided by analytic goals: diversity-oriented models explore the breadth of potential misconceptions, while alignment-oriented models approximate authentic error distributions. Struggling level acts as a moderator within this framework, raising diversity while lowering fidelity.
requirements: Evaluation must assess both diversity (e.g., pairwise AST edit distances) and alignment (nearest distance to authentic submissions) simultaneously
constraints: Even the most balanced model varied across tasks and prompts, so no single LLM is universally optimal
target_learning_goals: realistic simulation of novice logical errors for feedback design and misconception analysis
examples: Figure 5 plots the trade-off between alignment (fidelity) and diversity across the five evaluated models

article_title: What Robots Do Matters More Than What They Look Like: Task Context Shapes Trust in Educational HRI
citation: Anna-Maria Velentza, Konstantina Nikou, Anne-Gwenn Bosser, Nikolaos Fachantidis. (2026). What Robots Do Matters More Than What They Look Like: Task Context Shapes Trust in Educational HRI. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22What+Robots+Do+Matters+More+Than+What+They+Look+Like%22
title: Align robot behavior and interaction capabilities with task requirements rather than prioritizing anthropomorphic appearance when deploying educational robots
description: The article recommends that educational robot design and deployment focus on matching what robots do to interaction goals instead of relying on looks. It states that "designers of educational robots should prioritize aligning robot behavior and interaction capabilities with task requirements rather than focusing primarily on anthropomorphic appearance". Robots may be accepted as instructional guides regardless of embodiment, while emotionally sensitive tasks need extra design work such as transparency, privacy assurances, or enhanced socio-emotional behaviors.
requirements: Robots must be positioned within educational workflows according to task demands, with behavioral or relational mechanisms added before use in emotionally sensitive interactions
constraints: Findings come from video-based, script-controlled short-term evaluations with a homogeneous sample of Greek undergraduate future educators; the article notes video-mediation can mitigate appearance effects and calls for testing real-time, longitudinal, and broader-population interactions
target_learning_goals: trust in socially assistive robots across educational tasks (teaching, procedural instruction, personal-information discussion)
examples: In the experiment, all three robots delivered identical scripts across teaching, instruction, and personal-information tasks, and trust followed task type (T2 > T1 > T3) while robot type showed no meaningful effect

title: Ten-item Greek-language trust questionnaire assembled from established HRI trust scales with Lawshe content validation
description: A 10-item questionnaire rated on a five-point Likert scale after each video, developed by a multidisciplinary group of psychologists, engineers, and teachers by combining items from established trust and perception questionnaires (including trust perception, Jian et al., Kohn et al., and Godspeed items). Items cover willingness, competence, explicit trust, relative performance, reliability, and communication clarity. Content validity was assessed with Lawshe's CVR by five experts: "The resulting CVR met the critical threshold for five experts (CVR = .883, two-tailed p = .05)". Internal consistency across robot–task conditions ranged from α = .853 to .948.

title: Trust calibration account: users adjust reliance on robots according to perceived task risk, uncertainty, and expected competence rather than appearance
description: The article explains its findings through trust calibration theories from automation research. On this account, users calibrate trust to contextual demands: "users adjust their reliance on artificial agents according to perceived task risk, uncertainty, and expected system competence rather than agent appearance alone". Instructional tasks are structured, goal-oriented, and objectively verifiable, reducing uncertainty and promoting confidence, whereas personal conversations involving emotional disclosure introduce higher social and privacy sensitivity, leading users to apply stricter trust criteria.

examples: The article links the T2 > T1 > T3 trust ordering to lower perceived risk in verifiable instructional tasks and higher privacy sensitivity in personal-information discussions

article_title: Co-Creating Buildable and Open Social Robot Study Companions with University Students
citation: Farnaz Baksh, Matevž B. Zorec, Feiazie Baksh, and Karl Kruusamäe. (2026). Co-Creating Buildable and Open Social Robot Study Companions with University Students. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15239v1
title: Buildability and serviceability as social affordances of the human-robot relationship
description: The article proposes that hands-on assembly is an interaction-shaping variable rather than a hardware prerequisite: assembly establishes the user's stance toward the robot as a co-created artefact rather than a delivered product. It argues that treating buildability and serviceability as constituent elements of the human-robot relationship "reframes assembly as the opening move of social interaction", linking material co-creation to attachment, ownership, and sustained engagement. The framework draws on a lifecycle perspective that treats maintenance and repair as core components of the user experience, extending Design for Assembly and Design for Disassembly principles into the initial build phase.
requirements: The robot must be an open-source hardware platform whose build, repair, and maintenance are accessible to end users rather than pre-assembled or black-box.
constraints: Single-session study designs cannot capture long-term attachment or perceived agency, as the article states in its limitations.
target_learners: university students building open-source social robots
target_learning_goals: technical agency and self-efficacy through hands-on hardware building
psychological ownership of a co-created artefact
examples: Study 2 participants treated the partially-built robot as something worth protecting before any social interaction had taken place, and used affective vocabulary such as fun, engaging, and cool about the build.

title: Robot Study Companion (RSC) v4.1 open-source social robot chassis
description: The RSC is an affordable, compact, 3D-printed desktop social robot built around a Raspberry Pi with peripherals enabling multimodal interaction, including a touchscreen, servo-driven flippers, an LED ring, microphones, and speakers. article_title: PsyScore: A Psychometrically-Aware Framework for Trait-Adaptive Essay Scoring and ZPD-Scaffolded Feedback
citation: Wei Xia, Jin Wu, Haoran Shi, Xiangyu Wang, Chanjin Zheng. (2026). PsyScore: A Psychometrically-Aware Framework for Trait-Adaptive Essay Scoring and ZPD-Scaffolded Feedback. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20287
title: PsyScore: a psychometrically-aware framework unifying diagnostic scoring and ZPD-scaffolded feedback through a shared latent ability representation
description: PsyScore couples three modules: a Trait-Adaptive Neural GPCM Scorer that embeds the Graded Partial Credit Model in a BERT-based architecture to estimate latent ability θ; a ZPD-Conditional Feedback Generator that maps θ to instructional strategies via multi-agent fusion; and a Multi-Perspective Evaluation Strategy. The framework's premise is that "modeling student ability within a shared psychometric latent space can unify interpretable scoring and ZPD-aligned feedback", turning AES from summative scoring into formative diagnosis.
requirements: Requires fine-grained analytic trait labels (e.g., Voice, Organization) for trait-adaptive scorer training
Requires heterogeneous LLM agents plus a fusion model for feedback generation
constraints: Multi-agent consensus trades off inference latency, limiting real-time classroom deployment
Simulated revision cannot model motivational dynamics, epistemic trust, or cognitive fatigue
target_learners: K-12 and secondary essay writers across argumentative, source-based, and narrative genres
target_learning_goals: Writing proficiency across multiple traits (content, organization, conventions, voice, etc.)
examples: On ASAP++, the framework's scorer reached QWK 0.747 and its feedback module was evaluated via LLM-judge preference, simulated revision, and a three-expert blind study
key_sources: Wei Xia, Jin Wu, Haoran Shi, Xiangyu Wang, Chanjin Zheng. (2026). PsyScore: A Psychometrically-Aware Framework for Trait-Adaptive Essay Scoring and ZPD-Scaffolded Feedback. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20287

article_title: PsyScore: A Psychometrically-Aware Framework for Trait-Adaptive Essay Scoring and ZPD-Scaffolded Feedback
citation: Wei Xia, Jin Wu, Haoran Shi, Xiangyu Wang, Chanjin Zheng. (2026). PsyScore: A Psychometrically-Aware Framework for Trait-Adaptive Essay Scoring and ZPD-Scaffolded Feedback. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20287
title: ZPD-aligned strategy mapping: deterministic mapping of latent ability θ to explicit instruction, targeted scaffolding, or intellectual challenge
description: PsyScore defines a deterministic mapping from estimated ability to a pedagogical control token: explicit directive instruction for struggling learners (θ < −1.0), targeted scaffolding for developing learners (−1.0 ≤ θ ≤ 1.0), and intellectual challenge via Socratic questioning for advanced learners (θ > 1.0). The article states the "ZPD boundary values are designed to operationalize scaffolding theory within a computational framework", and traits with discrimination above 1.2 receive higher prompt attention.
requirements: A validated latent ability estimate (θ) from the IRT scorer is required to select the strategy
constraints: Strategy thresholds (−1.0, 1.0) are design values grounded in the authors' operationalization of scaffolding theory, not empirically derived optima
target_learners: Essay writers across proficiency levels, from struggling to advanced
target_learning_goals: Proficiency-appropriate writing feedback: error correction, guided improvement, or rhetorical refinement
examples: Table 10 maps θ < −1.0 to explicit directive instruction on grammar and mechanics, −1.0 ≤ θ ≤ 1.0 to targeted scaffolding balancing praise with 1-2 improvement areas, and θ > 1.0 to intellectual challenge via open-ended questions
key_sources: Wei Xia, Jin Wu, Haoran Shi, Xiangyu Wang, Chanjin Zheng. (2026). PsyScore: A Psychometrically-Aware Framework for Trait-Adaptive Essay Scoring and ZPD-Scaffolded Feedback. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20287

article_title: Estimating Learners' Skill Acquisition Without Temporal Information
citation: Ryosuke Nagai, Kyohei Atarashi, Koh Takeuchi, Jill-Jênn Vie, and Hisashi Kashima. (2026). Estimating Learners' Skill Acquisition Without Temporal Information. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20611
title: Pseudo-temporal ordering: inclusion relations among snapshot skill sets as a proxy for learning progression
description: The article proposes a framework in which, absent temporal logs, set-inclusion relations among learners' mastered-skill sets induce a pseudo-temporal axis: a learner whose mastered-skill set is a superset of another's can be viewed as a plausible later state. Learning is modeled as accumulation of expected one-skill increments, so that "a learner's mastered-skill set expands monotonically over time" under a non-forgetting assumption. This supports next-skill prediction from CDM-derived snapshot mastery patterns.
requirements: A predefined mapping between items and skills from cognitive diagnostic models to produce binary mastery patterns
The non-forgetting assumption that once a skill is mastered it remains mastered
constraints: Relies on a non-forgetting assumption; forgetting mechanisms are not incorporated
Evaluated on a restricted real-world subset of learners who attempted all skills
target_learners: Learners in large-scale periodic assessment settings with only snapshot data
target_learning_goals: Predicting the next skill to be acquired to support adaptive instruction
examples: Applied to PISA-style cross-sectional assessment settings where learner data are snapshots rather than temporal traces
key_sources: Ryosuke Nagai, Kyohei Atarashi, Koh Takeuchi, Jill-Jênn Vie, and Hisashi Kashima. (2026). Estimating Learners' Skill Acquisition Without Temporal Information. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20611

article_title: Estimating Learners' Skill Acquisition Without Temporal Information
citation: Ryosuke Nagai, Kyohei Atarashi, Koh Takeuchi, Jill-Jênn Vie, and Hisashi Kashima. (2026). Estimating Learners' Skill Acquisition Without Temporal Information. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20611
title: Neural expected-increment model with Upper Bounded Softmax for next-skill prediction
description: The article introduces a feed-forward neural model that maps a continuous mastery state to a distribution over the next skill using the Upper Bounded Softmax function, which assigns probability mass only to currently unmastered skills. Parameters are trained by minimizing squared reconstruction error of observed mastery patterns with L1 regularization that "promotes sparse and interpretable dependencies among skills." Repeatedly accumulating expected increments approximates intermediate acquisition states.
requirements: Continuous intermediate state representations relaxed from binary mastery patterns
Output constrained to the simplex intersected with unmastered skills
constraints: Direct path enumeration is infeasible as the number of possible acquisition paths grows exponentially, so complete paths are not modeled
target_learners: Learners assessed via cognitive diagnostic models in snapshot settings
target_learning_goals: Predicting the conditional distribution of the next acquired skill
examples: The model reconstructs each observed mastery pattern by applying the state update as many times as skills mastered
key_sources: Ryosuke Nagai, Kyohei Atarashi, Koh Takeuchi, Jill-Jênn Vie, and Hisashi Kashima. (2026). Estimating Learners' Skill Acquisition Without Temporal Information. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20611

article_title: Students' Perception Accuracy of Partners' AI Use and its Relation to Collaboration Performance
citation: Laura Graf, Ramona Beinstingel, Stephan Krusche, Oleksandra Poquet. (2026). Students' Perception Accuracy of Partners' AI Use and its Relation to Collaboration Performance. Preprint, Technical University of Munich. https://tum.de
title: Heuristic-inference account of partner AI-use beliefs under observability constraints
description: The article proposes that when a coordination-relevant behaviour such as AI use is not directly observable, collaborators form beliefs about partners through heuristic inference rather than partner-specific knowledge. Two heuristics are named: social projection, where "individuals assume partners to be similar to them and use their own behaviour as a reference point for judging others", and normative expectation, assumptions about what behaviour is typical or appropriate in a context. The study's partial-correlation results support the dominance of assumed similarity, reframing AI-use transparency as a coordination resource rather than only an integrity concern.
requirements: Requires a collaboration context where partners' AI use is private and observable work traces no longer distinguish own work from AI generation
constraints: Assumed-similarity effects may be pronounced when partners are already acquainted, as in this sample
The account is supported by observational, self-report data and should not be interpreted causally
target_learners: undergraduate students in introductory programming courses
target_learning_goals: accurate perception of collaborators' AI use during collaborative programming
effective team coordination in AI-supported collaborative work
examples: In the study, students' estimates of partners' task-level AI use correlated strongly with their own usage profiles (median r = .73), and partner-specific residual accuracy was low
key_sources: Laura Graf, Ramona Beinstingel, Stephan Krusche, Oleksandra Poquet. (2026). Students' Perception Accuracy of Partners' AI Use and its Relation to Collaboration Performance. Preprint, Technical University of Munich. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.23237

article_title: SupplyNet: Supporting Visual Exploratory Learning in Supply Chain via Contextual Multi-Agent Simulation
citation: Yanjia Li, Kelcy Kexin Han, Tianrui Hu, Yi-Fan Cao, Huamin Qu, Sicheng Song. (2026). SupplyNet: Supporting Visual Exploratory Learning in Supply Chain via Contextual Multi-Agent Simulation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.24694
title: SupplyNet: a gamified visual simulation system with graph-structured LLM multi-agent simulation, branching timeline, and analysis console
description: SupplyNet is a gamified visual simulation system for university SCM students, built on "a contextual graph-based LLM multi-agent framework that models interdependent supply chain dynamics and provides responsive feedback through tiered challenges." It integrates an interactive Graph Structure View, a Timeline Tree Map for branching what-if exploration, and a task-oriented Analysis Console with financial, operations, and logistics dashboards. Agents are powered by OpenAI's gpt-4o model, with agent-specific subgraph retrieval and heuristic Golden Rules as input.
requirements: Requires an LLM-backed multi-agent simulation core maintaining supply chain state as a directed graph, a database of temporal snapshots, and a front-end visual interface connected by a bidirectional data flow.
constraints: Designed and evaluated in the context of supply chain management, with the learning objective centered on inventory management.
target_learners: university students studying supply chain management
target_learning_goals: understanding dynamic supply chain interdependencies
inventory management decision making
counterfactual and causal reasoning about operational outcomes
examples: Users select a company role and challenge level in onboarding, manage the simulation in the Graph Structure View, branch parallel trajectories in the Timeline Tree Map, and inspect KPI dashboards in the Analysis Console.
key_sources: Yanjia Li, Kelcy Kexin Han, Tianrui Hu, Yi-Fan Cao, Huamin Qu, Sicheng Song. (2026). SupplyNet: Supporting Visual Exploratory Learning in Supply Chain via Contextual Multi-Agent Simulation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.24694

article_title: SupplyNet: Supporting Visual Exploratory Learning in Supply Chain via Contextual Multi-Agent Simulation
citation: Yanjia Li, Kelcy Kexin Han, Tianrui Hu, Yi-Fan Cao, Huamin Qu, Sicheng Song. (2026). SupplyNet: Supporting Visual Exploratory Learning in Supply Chain via Contextual Multi-Agent Simulation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.24694
title: Reusable simulation architecture for dynamic relational learning environments
description: The article abstracts SupplyNet's pipeline into "a reusable simulation architecture for dynamic relational learning environments." A graph represents domain entities, dependencies, and time-varying states; agents and learners observe relevant subgraphs, take domain-specific actions, and trigger state transitions; a database stores temporal snapshots supporting replay, branching, and comparison. The reusable layer separates from a domain-specific layer so other subjects can reuse the architecture by replacing the domain schema, transition rules, agent heuristics, event types, and learning metrics.
requirements: Subjects must be modelable as dynamic relational systems involving multiple connected entities, local decisions or disturbances, delayed propagation of effects, and trade-offs that learners need to diagnose over time.
constraints: The architecture was designed and evaluated only in the supply chain management context; cross-subject instantiations are discussed as future work.
target_learners: university students in domains modelable as dynamic relational systems
target_learning_goals: diagnosing delayed propagation of effects and trade-offs in interconnected systems
examples: In SupplyNet the architecture is instantiated with business entities, logistics links, inventory-related states, ordering decisions, disruption events, and operational KPIs.
key_sources: Yanjia Li, Kelcy Kexin Han, Tianrui Hu, Yi-Fan Cao, Huamin Qu, Sicheng Song. (2026). SupplyNet: Supporting Visual Exploratory Learning in Supply Chain via Contextual Multi-Agent Simulation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.24694

article_title: Touching and Feeling the Data: A Reusable Software Pipeline for Tactile Statistical Graphs in Accessible Education
citation: Lawrence Obiuwevwi, Krzysztof J. Rechowicz, Jessica M. Johnson, Erika Frydenlund, Vikas Ashok, Sachin Shetty, & Sampath Jayarathna. (2026). Touching and Feeling the Data: A Reusable Software Pipeline for Tactile Statistical Graphs in Accessible Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01214
title: Three-layer reusable pipeline for generating 3D-printed tactile statistical graphs
description: An open-source software pipeline of about 1,500 lines of JavaScript across 15 files that turns plate dimensions, chart type, and numeric data into print-ready binary STL files. Layer 1 derives tactile parameters from plate dimensions, Layer 2 provides shared chart scaffolding with five modular builders (scatter, bar, histogram, line, box plots), and an optional Layer 3 uses a multimodal LLM to extract chart specifications from uploaded images. The article states it is "the first open-source pipeline that automatically generates 3D-printed tactile statistical graphs from either typed data or chart images". Geometry runs locally via JSCAD with a Three.js browser preview; the Anthropic API key is needed only for image extraction.
requirements: Node.js (v18+) with Express for the server; an Anthropic API key only if the optional image-extraction layer is used
constraints: Plate dimensions are clamped to [80,250] mm; review of LLM-extracted specifications is mandatory before STL generation
target_learners: blind and low-vision students in statistics courses
target_learning_goals: exploring statistical distributions, trends, and relationships through haptic interaction with tactile graphs
examples: The pipeline produced a 150×150 mm tactile histogram plate with raised bars, axis rails, and dual-format labels, previewed in Three.js
key_sources: Lawrence Obiuwevwi, Krzysztof J. Rechowicz, Jessica M. Johnson, Erika Frydenlund, Vikas Ashok, Sachin Shetty, & Sampath Jayarathna. (2026). Touching and Feeling the Data: A Reusable Software Pipeline for Tactile Statistical Graphs in Accessible Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01214

article_title: Touching and Feeling the Data: A Reusable Software Pipeline for Tactile Statistical Graphs in Accessible Education
citation: Lawrence Obiuwevwi, Krzysztof J. Rechowicz, Jessica M. Johnson, Erika Frydenlund, Vikas Ashok, Sachin Shetty, & Sampath Jayarathna. (2026). Touching and Feeling the Data: A Reusable Software Pipeline for Tactile Statistical Graphs in Accessible Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01214
title: Derive tactile graph parameters from tactile perception research rather than ad hoc choices
description: The pipeline's parameter derivation layer computes feature heights and spacings automatically from plate dimensions using established tactile perception findings, so every generated chart is readable by touch without per-chart manual tuning. Data features are set at 1.5 mm, three times the "0.5 mm height discriminability floor" from Lederman and Klatzky, and scatter-point separation is 3.5 mm, exceeding the 2–3 mm two-point discrimination threshold. Axis rails are taller than data features so a sweeping finger distinguishes structural boundaries from encoded data.
requirements: Plate dimensions in millimeters as input; adherence to BANA guidelines and Library of Congress Braille dot geometry for labels
constraints: Parameters are derived for FDM-printed plates within the clamped [80,250] mm dimension range
target_learners: blind and low-vision students reading tactile graphs by fingertip
target_learning_goals: haptic discrimination of chart structure, data features, and labels
examples: The derivation layer sets baseplate thickness via a clamp formula, reserves an 18 mm margin for dual-format labels, and sets Braille dots at 0.6 mm per Library of Congress standard
key_sources: Lawrence Obiuwevwi, Krzysztof J. Rechowicz, Jessica M. Johnson, Erika Frydenlund, Vikas Ashok, Sachin Shetty, & Sampath Jayarathna. (2026). Touching and Feeling the Data: A Reusable Software Pipeline for Tactile Statistical Graphs in Accessible Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01214

citation: Lawrence Obiuwevwi, Krzysztof J. Rechowicz, Jessica M. Johnson, Erika Frydenlund, Vikas Ashok, Sachin Shetty, & Sampath Jayarathna. (2026). Touching and Feeling the Data: A Reusable Software Pipeline for Tactile Statistical Graphs in Accessible Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01214
title: Use multimodal AI as a data-entry accelerator with mandatory editable review, not as an autonomous producer of accessible artifacts
description: The article argues that in accessible-materials production, multimodal AI is most useful "as a data-entry accelerator, not as an autonomous producer of accessible artifacts", which makes mandatory editable review a safety requirement. In the pipeline, the optional vision layer converts chart images into structured JSON specifications that a teacher must review and correct in an editable form before STL generation. This positioning addresses observed failure modes such as unnecessary capital indicators and excessive numeric precision.
requirements: A teacher review step with an editable specification form between LLM extraction and print generation
constraints: Extraction accuracy was assessed only on an informal sample of textbook chart images; formal evaluation remains future work
target_learners: teachers preparing tactile materials for blind and low-vision students
target_learning_goals: producing accurate tactile statistical graphs from existing chart images
examples: The teacher workflow lets a user upload a chart image, receive a Claude vision extraction, and edit the extracted data in a review form before generating the STL

article_title: Uncovering Students' Mental Models of Generative Artificial Intelligence
citation: Amrita Ganguly, Sai Sharanya Garika, Aditya Johri. (2026). Uncovering Students' Mental Models of Generative Artificial Intelligence. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Uncovering+Students%27+Mental+Models+of+Generative+Artificial+Intelligence%22
title: Five-category taxonomy of undergraduate mental models of generative AI
description: The article proposes a taxonomy of students' mental models of GenAI derived from hierarchical clustering of concept maps. The five categories are technical-process based, educational tool based, transitional, consequence aware, and integrated; the authors state the clustering "revealed five distinct characteristics of student's mental model answering RQ1." Each category describes how students organize GenAI knowledge, from underlying technologies to collective responsibility. The taxonomy is positioned as preliminary and intended as a diagnostic lens for instruction and guideline design.
requirements: Concept map elicitation plus hierarchical clustering of map components to derive the categories
constraints: Preliminary WIP results; the authors state future qualitative analysis and validation via interviews or think-aloud studies is needed
target_learners: undergraduate students in information technology programs
target_learning_goals: AI literacy and responsible, ethical use of generative AI
examples: Cluster 5 grouped ethics, privacy, human oversight, and academic stakeholders, which the authors label an integrated and risk-aware mental model
key_sources: Amrita Ganguly, Sai Sharanya Garika, Aditya Johri. (2026). Uncovering Students' Mental Models of Generative Artificial Intelligence. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Uncovering+Students%27+Mental+Models+of+Generative+Artificial+Intelligence%22

article_title: Uncovering Students' Mental Models of Generative Artificial Intelligence
citation: Amrita Ganguly, Sai Sharanya Garika, Aditya Johri. (2026). Uncovering Students' Mental Models of Generative Artificial Intelligence. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Uncovering+Students%27+Mental+Models+of+Generative+Artificial+Intelligence%22
title: Use the five-cluster structure as a diagnostic framework for locating students' GenAI mental models and designing activities that stretch across cluster boundaries
description: The article recommends that faculty treat the five mental model clusters as a diagnostic framework: identify where individual students' mental models lie, then design learning activities that push thinking beyond that cluster. The authors write that faculty can use "the cluster structure as a diagnostic framework such as identifying where students' mental models lie and designing learning activities that stretch their thinking across cluster boundaries." The goal is an integrated mental model holding technical, educational, ethical, and governance dimensions as interdependent.
requirements: Faculty knowledge of the five-cluster taxonomy and a means of eliciting students' current mental models, such as concept mapping
constraints: Derived from a preliminary WIP study in one required technology ethics course at a single institution
target_learning_goals: integrated understanding of GenAI spanning technical, educational, ethical, and governance dimensions
examples: The authors suggest Cluster 1 students may benefit from human and societal context knowledge, while Cluster 2 students may need prompting to reflect on access, conditions, and risks
key_sources: Amrita Ganguly, Sai Sharanya Garika, Aditya Johri. (2026). Uncovering Students' Mental Models of Generative Artificial Intelligence. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Uncovering+Students%27+Mental+Models+of+Generative+Artificial+Intelligence%22

article_title: Uncovering Students' Mental Models of Generative Artificial Intelligence
citation: Amrita Ganguly, Sai Sharanya Garika, Aditya Johri. (2026). Uncovering Students' Mental Models of Generative Artificial Intelligence. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Uncovering+Students%27+Mental+Models+of+Generative+Artificial+Intelligence%22
title: Concept map elicitation with holistic scoring and hierarchical clustering for studying GenAI mental models
description: The article's methodology combines concept map collection, holistic scoring, and hierarchical clustering to externalize mental models. Maps from a technology ethics course assignment were scored by two researchers on comprehensiveness, organization, and correctness on a 1-to-3 scale with pluses and minuses, mapped to a nine-point scale and four levels; 64 of 86 enrolled students' maps were retained after exclusions. Components were coded with a 16-code inductive codebook and clustered, with merge height indicating dissimilarity. The authors offer this as an initial elicitation step to be validated with interviews or think-aloud studies.
requirements: Students with basic familiarity with concept maps; two independent raters with discussion to resolve scoring disagreements
constraints: Six maps excluded as Level 1 for being difficult to read or lacking meaningful connections; two unstructured maps retained for rich examples; 29 level-identification disagreements resolved by discussion
target_learning_goals: eliciting and diagnosing students' conceptual understanding of generative AI
examples: Maps were scored on a nine-point scale and categorized into four levels, with Level 1 maps lacking meaningful concepts or connections

article_title: Student Evaluation of Repeated AI Feedback Across a Semester of Writing
citation: Andres Karjus, Janika Leoste, Tiia Õun. (2026). Student Evaluation of Repeated AI Feedback Across a Semester of Writing. arXiv:2607.16115 [cs.CY]. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.16115
title: Design AI-feedback coursework so the intended learning work does not depend on the final text alone
description: The article argues that integrating AI feedback changes what a writing task becomes, and that AI feedback should not be evaluated only by whether students like it. Its educational value depends on the surrounding task: "whether students still have to write, and are motivated to interpret, question,andintegratefeedbackaspartoftheirownwritingprocess." The authors recommend requirements such as revision following feedback, comparison with reflection criteria, and follow-up rationales.
requirements: Assignments would need to directly incentivize reflection depth or require revision following feedback, comparison with explicit reflection criteria, follow-up questions, or a rationale for accepting or rejecting feedback
constraints: No single design feature completely prevents AI delegation of the parts meant to exercise student judgment; prohibition can be ignored and prescribed rationales, revisions, and self-reports can also be generated
target_learners: first-year humanities bachelor students in higher education
target_learning_goals: reflective writing
feedback literacy
critical and selective use of AI feedback
examples: The course tied writing and feedback use to earlier in-class contexts and the authors suggest version histories or brief peer- or teacher-facing explanations to shift the task toward showing situated decisions
key_sources: Andres Karjus, Janika Leoste, Tiia Õun. (2026). Student Evaluation of Repeated AI Feedback Across a Semester of Writing. arXiv:2607.16115 [cs.CY]. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.16115

article_title: Student Evaluation of Repeated AI Feedback Across a Semester of Writing
citation: Andres Karjus, Janika Leoste, Tiia Õun. (2026). Student Evaluation of Repeated AI Feedback Across a Semester of Writing. arXiv:2607.16115 [cs.CY]. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.16115
title: Estonian reflective-writing AI-feedback corpus of 2988 homework triplets from 283 students
description: An anonymized text corpus from a first-year humanities course on digital skills and AI, autumn semester 2025, collected as ordinary coursework with an opt-out (none received). As printed, "It consists of 2988 homework (HW) triplets from 283 students", each triplet being a 300–350-word reflective essay, paragraph-length AI feedback from a self-selected chatbot using a shared course prompt, and a 1–2 sentence student appraisal. GPT-5.4-assisted annotation coded appraisal theme, helpfulness stance, reflection depth, and feedback specificity, validated against human coding.
requirements: Feedback was obtained using a uniform course prompt, slightly revised after HW4 to request more concrete essay-grounded feedback
constraints: Corpus cannot be published as open data; exact model versions, settings, account tiers, and system prompts were unobserved, and provider labels come from shared chat URLs
target_learning_goals: reflective writing about lecture content
appraisal of AI-generated feedback
examples: ChatGPT was the most common tool (81% of parsed submissions), Gemini second (8%)

article_title: 'Why SuaCode?": Understanding African Students'' Motivations for Taking a Smartphone-Based Online Coding Course'
citation: Michael Addo, Nana Maryam Munagah, Victor Kumbol, Judith Uchidiuno, and George Boateng. (2026). “Why SuaCode?”: Understanding African Students’ Motivations for Taking a Smartphone-Based Online Coding Course. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22940
title: SuaCode: a 2-month smartphone-based online programming course for African high school, university, and recent-graduate learners
description: SuaCode Africa is described as "a 2-month online programming course targeted at high school, university, and recent graduates living in Africa and the diaspora." It is a smartphone-based coding curriculum covering basic programming concepts such as variables, conditionals, loops, functions, classes, objects, and arrays, taught in the Processing language (an open-source, Java-based language), with students writing and running programs in the APDE Android app. The course was the setting for the motivation survey analyzed in this poster.
requirements: Students need a smartphone running the APDE Android app to write and run their programs
constraints: The course covers basic programming concepts rather than advanced material, as printed in the course description
target_learners: High school students, university students, and recent graduates living in Africa and the diaspora
target_learning_goals: Basic programming concepts including variables, conditionals, loops, functions, classes, objects, and arrays
examples: Two cohorts of SuaCode courses supplied the over 3,000 open-ended survey responses analyzed in this study
key_sources: Michael Addo, Nana Maryam Munagah, Victor Kumbol, Judith Uchidiuno, and George Boateng. (2026). “Why SuaCode?”: Understanding African Students’ Motivations for Taking a Smartphone-Based Online Coding Course. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22940

article_title: 'Why SuaCode?": Understanding African Students'' Motivations for Taking a Smartphone-Based Online Coding Course'
citation: Michael Addo, Nana Maryam Munagah, Victor Kumbol, Judith Uchidiuno, and George Boateng. (2026). “Why SuaCode?”: Understanding African Students’ Motivations for Taking a Smartphone-Based Online Coding Course. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22940
title: Design programming MOOCs for African students around their interests and goals rather than relying on free, accessible content alone to drive enrollment
description: The article recommends that insights into students' motivations "can inform the design of MOOC content and assessments to align with students' interests." Because SuaCode students enrolled primarily for intrinsic reasons tied to interest and personal goals, while free and accessible content ranked low (4%) as a motivator, designers of programming MOOCs targeted at African students should foreground course theme and applicability to learners' goals rather than assuming no-cost access suffices to attract enrollees.
requirements: Understanding of the target students' motivations for enrolling, gathered for example via open-ended response surveys
constraints: The authors note this trend suggests accessible content alone may not suffice "without accounting for other factors"; the finding is from a preliminary analysis of one course's respondents
target_learners: High school, university, and recent-graduate learners in Africa and the diaspora
target_learning_goals: Computer programming skills
Sustained engagement and persistence in online coding courses
examples: SuaCode's enrollment was driven primarily by students' interest in the program's theme and its applicability to their goals, even though the course is freely accessible via smartphones
key_sources: Michael Addo, Nana Maryam Munagah, Victor Kumbol, Judith Uchidiuno, and George Boateng. (2026). “Why SuaCode?”: Understanding African Students’ Motivations for Taking a Smartphone-Based Online Coding Course. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22940

article_title: Make or Take: How Students Navigate Self-Created and Instructor-Provided Cheat Sheets
citation: Helen Weixu Chen, Victoria Sakhnini, and Lesley Istead. (2026). Make or Take: How Students Navigate Self-Created and Instructor-Provided Cheat Sheets. ACM Trans. Comput. Educ. https://doi.org/10.1145/3834566
title: Three recurring tensions shaping student cheat sheet decisions
description: The article organizes its qualitative findings around three tensions that recur in students' cheat sheet decisions: "1) trust in instructor judgment versus trust in their own knowledge needs, 2) coverage versus clarity, and 3) effort versus payoff." These tensions structure the themes of choice rationales (trust, cognitive efficiency, personalization), shifting attitudes over the term, and practical constraints such as legibility and information density. The framework also treats the tensions as evolving, with early convenience- or deference-based decisions giving way to more deliberate preparation strategies.
requirements: Applies in contexts where students genuinely choose between self-created and instructor-provided exam aids, as in the study's both-options design
constraints: Derived from a single term of one senior-level software requirements course with a specific instructor and policy
target_learning_goals: exam preparation strategies
self-regulated learning
student agency in assessment
examples: Table 1 maps themes to the three categories, e.g. P1's trust in instructor relevance, P23's anxiety reduction through control, and P15's realization of misalignment.

article_title: Is Solving Better Than Evaluating GenAI Solutions?
citation: Ethan Dickey, Marios Mertzanidis, Alexandros Psomas. (2026). Is Solving Better Than Evaluating GenAI Solutions? https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27586v1
title: Incorporate structured GenAI-evaluation activities into algorithms coursework without expecting automatic learning gains; scaffold evaluation beyond simple error diagnosis
description: The article's design recommendation is that GenAI-evaluation tasks can be incorporated into algorithms coursework safely, since "GenAI-evaluation activities can be incorporated into algorithms coursework without broad performance losses". However, meaningful gains require deliberate scaffolding: the authors recommend future assignments "push students beyond simple diagnosis" by asking students to identify the first invalid step, construct counterexamples, propose corrected algorithms or invariants, and explain why the corrected solution works. Pedagogical value depends more on scaffolding than on exposure to AI output itself.
requirements: Deliberate scaffolding that pushes students beyond simple error diagnosis, such as identifying the first invalid step, constructing counterexamples, and proposing corrected solutions
constraints: In this implementation, evaluation tasks produced no measurable summative or transfer gains over direct solving
target_learners: undergraduate students in junior-level algorithms courses
target_learning_goals: algorithm design, proof of correctness, runtime analysis, and transfer of abstract algorithmic reasoning
examples: The study asked evaluating students to grade a ChatGPT-4o solution, distinguishing minor bugs (e.g., calculation errors) from major bugs (wrong algorithm, invalid recurrence, missing invariant, flawed proof step), and found most students did not change study habits
key_sources: Ethan Dickey, Marios Mertzanidis, Alexandros Psomas. (2026). Is Solving Better Than Evaluating GenAI Solutions? https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27586

article_title: The Theoretical Foundation of Socratic Tests: Dynamic, Multimodal, Conversational Examinations
citation: Ilya Mikhelson. (2026). The Theoretical Foundation of Socratic Tests: Dynamic, Multimodal, Conversational Examinations. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.29624
title: The Socratic Test framework: decoupled Bloom's prompting and SOLO evaluation to map the Zone of Proximal Development
description: The Socratic Test is an adaptive, typed conversational assessment that standardizes the method of measurement without standardizing prompts. It decouples two taxonomies: "Bloom's Taxonomy dictates the cognitive difficulty of theprompt, the AI utilizes the SOLO Taxonomy... to measure the structural quality of theresponse." Rooted in Dynamic Assessment, it quantifies the ZPD by differentiating Independent from Assisted Performance via a scaffolding discount factor. SOLO's structural criteria are presented as observable and defensible, shifting grading from semantic interpretation to structural complexity.
requirements: An AI proctor capable of real-time Bloom-level prompting and provisional SOLO classification, with instructor calibration of the SOLO baseline before mass grading
constraints: Real-time SOLO assessment is strictly provisional and conservative; inaccuracies are absorbed by the oversampled evidence buffer and corrected in the post-exam pipeline
The author notes controlled comparisons against traditional oral and written exams are still required
target_learning_goals: mapping cognitive boundaries and mastery of disciplinary content at multiple Bloom levels
examples: The framework is instantiated in socratictest.com and demonstrated with a simulated Stair-Step Mode transcript on a Price Controls topic in Appendix A

article_title: The Theoretical Foundation of Socratic Tests: Dynamic, Multimodal, Conversational Examinations
citation: Ilya Mikhelson. (2026). The Theoretical Foundation of Socratic Tests: Dynamic, Multimodal, Conversational Examinations. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.29624
title: Non-compensatory capped-bucket grading across topic-by-tier matrix cells
description: The grading architecture rejects compensatory scoring in favor of "Non-Compensatory Grading": instructors configure capped buckets per topic and cognitive tier, and the total score aggregates min(cap, earned points) per cell. Points per interaction follow P(b,s,k) = γk·V(b,s), where V(b,s) is monotonically increasing with the Bloom level and γk discounts assisted performance. Once a bucket is full, further low-level answers yield zero additional points, preventing grinding of foundational questions from compensating for missing higher-order evidence.
requirements: Instructor-defined 2D grading matrix (or 1D topic-level caps in Organic Mode) with point capacities per tier and deterministic logging of Bloom level and hint count per interaction
constraints: Students cannot manually pivot between cognitive tiers within a topic, as foundational tiers must be completed to scaffold advanced topics
target_learners: higher education students in instructor-configured courses
target_learning_goals: demonstrating mastery at each required cognitive tier rather than accumulating low-level points
examples: Table 2 shows a conceptual matrix for an introductory Economics course with tier caps of 10-15 points and a 100-point total; Appendix A walks through a 40-point Price Controls topic at 120% oversampling

citation: Ilya Mikhelson. (2026). The Theoretical Foundation of Socratic Tests: Dynamic, Multimodal, Conversational Examinations. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.29624
title: socratictest.com: a summative conversational assessment platform with evidence buffers, shadow ledger, and human-AI grading pipeline
description: The author developed socratictest.com, "a custom software platform explicitly engineered to administer the Socratic Test modality," architected as a summative assessment engine with a decoupled design separating the real-time proctoring engine from the final deterministic gradebook. Core mechanics include an oversampled Evidence Buffer (e.g., 120%), a hidden Shadow Ledger logging baseline point values for skipped or exhausted prompts, user-directed pivoting with state resurrection, an Out-of-Scope audit protocol, and a 7-step grading pipeline with instructor calibration, validation, override, and an appeals queue.

constraints: Real-time SOLO evaluation is provisional and cannot gate progression directly, to avoid trapping students behind AI hallucinations; out-of-scope flags are initially treated as skips pending post-exam audit
target_learners: higher education students and instructors in pilot university courses
target_learning_goals: reliable summative assessment of conceptual mastery through adaptive conversation
examples: In the Appendix A case study, a verified hallucination (a Phillips Curve prompt) was converted from a 12-point shadow penalty into earned Synthesis points, and a Global Exclusion Rule protected other students who encountered the same flawed premise

article_title: Navigating the skill diversity frontier: How skill complexity explains worker resilience
citation: Carpanelli, M., Duszynski, J. & Stephany, F. (2026). Navigating the skill diversity frontier: How skill complexity explains worker resilience. Working paper, Oxford Internet Institute. https://oii.ox.ac.uk
title: Skill complexity framework: productive capital, adaptive capital, and the diversity frontier
description: The framework models human capital as a structured skill system rather than a list of attributes. It decomposes portfolios into productive capital, defined as "the market value associated with specialised expertise", and adaptive capital, "the flexibility generated by spanning multiple skill domains". It further postulates that specialisation constrains attainable diversity, yielding the diversity frontier: an inverse U-shaped upper envelope of diversity given specialisation. Workers on the frontier combine domain-specific expertise with cross-domain capabilities and are expected to be best positioned to learn, move, and adapt to technological change.
requirements: A directed skill network reconstructed from observed skill co-occurrence, with hierarchy inferred from asymmetric conditional probabilities and domains identified via community detection
constraints: The analysis remains associational rather than causal, despite the use of lagged explanatory variables and extensive controls
LinkedIn profiles over-represent digitally engaged and highly skilled occupations, and listed skills are self-reported
target_learners: Adult workers in knowledge-intensive labour markets facing technological change
target_learning_goals: Acquisition of new and AI-relevant skills
Occupational mobility and reskilling pathway identification
examples: The study operationalises the framework with specialisation as average inverse normalised local reaching centrality, diversity as Hill diversity across 12 Louvain skill domains, and a frontier score ranging from 0 to 1 within 100 specialisation groups

article_title: TACT: Taxonomy-Aligned Post-Training for Pedagogically Adaptive English Tutoring
citation: Dongjie Yang, Siyan Lin, Leixian Shen, Rui Sheng, Huamin Qu, and Zixin Chen. (2026). TACT: Taxonomy-Aligned Post-Training for Pedagogically Adaptive English Tutoring. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03952
title: TACT dual-taxonomy framework: a 13-strategy tutor-strategy taxonomy linked to a two-axis student-move taxonomy operationalizing conditional feedback decisions
description: TACT organizes ESL tutoring as a pedagogical decision space connecting learner-state annotation, tutor-strategy selection, and next-turn response generation. The student-move taxonomy records the learner's latest turn along two dimensions, move type and move status, where only Answer/Attempt moves can be Adequate or Problematic and other types are Non-evaluable. The tutor-strategy taxonomy "contains 13 strategies representing the intended pedagogical function of the next tutor turn", spanning prompting, backchanneling, affective feedback, verification, error flagging, hinting, guided revision, and direct correction. The mapping from student moves to strategies is conditional rather than deterministic, depending on proficiency, task difficulty, dialogue history, and prior support. Annotation reliability reached kappa of 0.708 for tutor strategy, 0.722 for move type, and 1.000 for move status.
requirements: Annotated authentic tutoring dialogue with codebooks and inter-annotator reliability checks to instantiate the two taxonomies
constraints: The article notes label abstraction is a limitation: real teachers blend instruction, affect, pacing, and rapport in ways a compact taxonomy does not always separate
target_learners: English-as-a-second-language learners across CEFR levels B1-C2
target_learning_goals: Conversational ESL proficiency through adaptive tutor feedback and scaffolding
examples: Expert annotators developed the coding scheme iteratively from 50 dialogue contexts, then independently double-coded 20 held-out contexts for inter-annotator reliability before corpus-scale annotation.

The GRPO reward combines a mean normalized task score with grounding, format, and strategy terms plus judge-level penalties for unacceptability, answer leakage or over-helping, and off-task errors, with a KL constraint against the frozen SFT reference policy. The article says the reward is "transparent and auditable rather than an opaque optimization of a single benchmark score", and model weights are released.

It is described as "a custom Socratic AI tutor built as a Django web application with a PostgreSQL backend and a retrieval-audmented generation pipeline over course materials", meaning LLM responses are conditioned on relevant course-material excerpts. Its system prompt instructed the model to use Socratic prompting and to scaffold conceptual setup before symbolic execution, and logging captured all turns at the message level.

article_title: A Bottom-Up Taxonomy of Student Discourse with a Socratic AI Physics Tutor
citation: Syed Furqan Abbas Hashmi and N. Sanjay Rebello. (2026). A bottom-up taxonomy of student discourse with a Socratic AI physics tutor. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07373
title: Emergent LLM coding plus embedding-based consolidation pipeline for large-scale student-discourse taxonomies
description: A two-step methodological framework, framed as the LLM analog of open coding in grounded theory, for converting large student-tutor transcript corpora into interpretable discourse categories. Step 1 asks an LLM coder to assign each turn an emergent free-text label using the previous four conversational turns as context, yielding 833 unique raw labels. Step 2 consolidates near-paraphrase labels via text embeddings, cosine distance, and agglomerative clustering with average linkage at a distance threshold of 0.40, followed by LLM-generated canonical category names, producing 357 consolidated categories. The approach follows computational grounded theory, letting categories be discovered rather than projected from a fixed codebook.
requirements: A context window of prior conversational turns (four turns was the smallest window recovering consistent labels for context-dependent moves); a distance-threshold sweep with human coherence inspection to select the clustering threshold; validation against expert coding.
constraints: Single-rater coherence judgments establish only face validity; rerunning consolidation with a different embedding model could shift category boundaries; specific category labels reflect the single mechanics problem context and will not transfer to tutors covering other content.
target_learners: introductory physics students interacting with AI tutors
target_learning_goals: characterizing student discourse and engagement with AI-tutor scaffolding
examples: The threshold 0.40 was selected as the largest setting at which ≥90% of inspected groups were judged coherent (47 of 50).

description: Spritz is a Discord-based AI conversational agent designed as a technology probe for interdisciplinary team communication, "enabling participants to reflect on the role, value, and boundaries of AI mediation rather than evaluating a mature system".
