title: Semantic and pragmatic disciplinary boundaries as the two recurring forms of boundary in interdisciplinary team communication
description: Drawing on boundary-crossing literature, the article frames interdisciplinary collaboration differences as two recurring boundary forms: "semantic boundaries, where the same term carries different meaning across fields, and pragmatic boundaries, where members’ goals and values conflict even when they understand one another". This taxonomy organizes what the Spritz probe was designed to detect and underpins the study's account of why text-based, facilitator-less student teams leave differences implicit until they surface as friction. It also connects to the perspective-making and perspective-taking framing the authors use to describe the probe's support functions.
requirements: Teams whose members hold different disciplinary meanings, goals, and values that must be negotiated through communication
constraints: The article focuses on text-based, unstructured channels such as Slack or Discord in temporary teams lacking a dedicated facilitator
target_learners: university students in interdisciplinary project-based learning teams
target_learning_goals: cross-disciplinary communication and coordination in collaborative problem-solving
examples: The probe's tension detector independently assigned semantic and pragmatic tension confidence scores, selecting the semantic path when both exceeded threshold to clarify interpretations before addressing competing interests
key_sources: Ching-Jung Cheng, Yu-Chan Chung, Bing-Chen Chiu, Yu-Hsuan Lin, and Jia-Wei Liao. 2026. Exploring AI-Supported Disciplinary Mediation in Student Project Teams' Text-Based Communication: A Probe-Grounded Co-Design Study. OzCHI '26. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07503

article_title: Structural Silence: When AI Infrastructure Fails Speakers of Underrepresented Languages
citation: Avijit Roy, Proma Roy. (2026). Structural Silence: When AI Infrastructure Fails Speakers of Underrepresented Languages — A Case Study in Bengali, the Digital Divide, and the Hidden Cost of English-Centric Design. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12278
title: Structural Silence: four interlocking infrastructure failures that systematically exclude a language from AI
description: Structural silence is the article's explanatory framework: "the systematic exclusion of a language from AI infrastructure not through explicit policy but through the accumulated weight of design decisions that were never made with that language in mind." It organizes four interlocking failures—web presence gap, training token deficit, tokenization penalty, and connectivity exclusion—that intensify one another over time. Bengali, with roughly 285 million speakers, classical recognition, and an active NLP research community, serves as the case demonstrating that uneven performance reflects infrastructure-level resource distribution rather than model quality alone.
requirements: Each failure compounds the others, so the framework requires analysis at corpus, tokenizer, benchmark, and deployment layers together
constraints: The article's contribution is explicitly explanatory and diagnostic rather than a new benchmark or empirical dataset
Evidence is drawn from published benchmarks, public indicators, and educational theory rather than newly collected learner data
target_learning_goals: Access to AI-assisted educational support (debugging help, concept explanation, feedback) in one's native language
examples: The paper consolidates Sangraha/Common Corpus token counts, BenLLM-Eval results, BBS ICT survey figures, and Cognitive Load Theory findings into one account of why Bengali AI support is uneven
key_sources: Avijit Roy, Proma Roy. (2026). Structural Silence: When AI Infrastructure Fails Speakers of Underrepresented Languages — A Case Study in Bengali, the Digital Divide, and the Hidden Cost of English-Centric Design. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12278

article_title: Structural Silence: When AI Infrastructure Fails Speakers of Underrepresented Languages
citation: Avijit Roy, Proma Roy. (2026). Structural Silence: When AI Infrastructure Fails Speakers of Underrepresented Languages — A Case Study in Bengali, the Digital Divide, and the Hidden Cost of English-Centric Design. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12278
title: Treat dataset construction for underrepresented languages as a primary research contribution, not supporting labor
description: The article argues dataset scarcity for underrepresented languages is a structural barrier shaped by funding and publication incentives, not a natural scarcity or individual researcher limitation. It states that "Recognizing dataset construction for underrepresented languages as a substantive research contribution, comparable to architectural innovation, is likely to be an important condition for changing that pattern." Researchers who treat such infrastructure as preliminary work reproduce the asymmetry that later appears in model performance.
requirements: Publication norms crediting benchmark creation, corpus development, and annotation methodology for high-resource languages must extend equal recognition to equivalent low-resource work
constraints: The principle is argued from an analysis of institutional incentives, not tested empirically
target_learning_goals: Availability of native-language AI-assisted educational tools
examples: The article describes researchers building Bengali AI tools who must curate training examples, validate translations, develop benchmarks, and establish annotation protocols from scratch

article_title: Structural Silence: When AI Infrastructure Fails Speakers of Underrepresented Languages
citation: Avijit Roy, Proma Roy. (2026). Structural Silence: When AI Infrastructure Fails Speakers of Underrepresented Languages — A Case Study in Bengali, the Digital Divide, and the Hidden Cost of English-Centric Design. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12278
title: Design offline-capable educational AI as an equity strategy for low-connectivity settings, and evaluate it under local bandwidth, device, and cost constraints
description: Offline-first deployment reframed as equity architecture rather than a degraded compromise: designing for local inference removes the connectivity assumption that excludes rural learners, extending the system's reach. The article argues educational AI for low-connectivity settings should be evaluated "not only for response quality under ideal conditions, but also for whether they remain usable under the bandwidth, device, and cost constraints that characterize the communities they are intended to serve." Quantization and parameter-efficient fine-tuning make local inference on consumer hardware feasible, with sustainability co-benefits.
requirements: Local inference feasibility depends on quantization techniques and parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods (e.g., quantized 7-billion-parameter models)
Evaluation frameworks must test usability under the target community's bandwidth, device, and cost constraints
constraints: The article frames this as a prioritization choice among users rather than claiming offline systems match cloud capability on response quality
target_learners: Rural learners in low-connectivity environments in Bangladesh and comparable contexts
target_learning_goals: Access to AI tutoring, debugging assistance, and native-language explanations without reliable connectivity
examples: The article notes local inference on a quantized 7-billion-parameter model consumes a fraction of the energy of routing each query through a remote cloud API, material at school computer-lab scale

article_title: From Substitution to Scaffolding: Breaking the Self-Reinforcing Harm Cycle of AI in Education (and Beyond)
citation: Lucile Favero, Juan Antonio Pérez-Ortiz, Tanja Käser, Nuria Oliver. (2026). From Substitution to Scaffolding: Breaking the Self-Reinforcing Harm Cycle of AI in Education (and Beyond). arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.17451
title: Self-reinforcing harm cycle linking cognition, agency, emotion, and ethics
description: An integrative conceptual framework organizing the risks of substitution-style AI in education into four interrelated dimensions — cognition, agency, emotional well-being, and ethics — connected by a reinforcing cycle. As the paper states, "These four dimensions are not independent; they interact through a reinforcing cycle." Cognitive offloading reduces effortful reasoning, diminished effort feeds illusory learning and overtrust, overtrust weakens agency, and reduced agency intensifies emotional harms such as anxiety, lower self-efficacy, and dependency, with ethical and structural factors amplifying individual-level effects. The framework is grounded in learning theory and in students' own reflections, with the clearest student-evidenced link being reliance on AI and diminished thinking.
requirements: Applies to AI systems that substitute for human cognitive effort rather than to every AI system or learner; the authors explicitly disclaim universal claims
constraints: The closing connection of the cycle is described as weakly evidenced in the students' exploratory data (dashed link in Figure 1); the essay cohort is illustrative, not representative
target_learners: school and higher-education learners using AI tools
target_learning_goals: critical thinking
learner agency
emotional resilience
academic integrity
examples: Figure 1 depicts the cycle: substitution erodes capacities while scaffolding builds critical thinking, agency, resilience, and trust
key_sources: Lucile Favero, Juan Antonio Pérez-Ortiz, Tanja Käser, Nuria Oliver. (2026). From Substitution to Scaffolding: Breaking the Self-Reinforcing Harm Cycle of AI in Education (and Beyond). arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.17451

article_title: From Substitution to Scaffolding: Breaking the Self-Reinforcing Harm Cycle of AI in Education (and Beyond)
citation: Lucile Favero, Juan Antonio Pérez-Ortiz, Tanja Käser, Nuria Oliver. (2026). From Substitution to Scaffolding: Breaking the Self-Reinforcing Harm Cycle of AI in Education (and Beyond). arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.17451
title: Scaffold, do not substitute: AI should support effort rather than replace it
description: The paper's unifying design principle: AI systems that mediate human thinking should preserve and manage cognitive friction — withholding immediate answers, prompting recall, asking questions, surfacing uncertainty — instead of delivering pre-digested solutions that bypass effort. As the authors put it, "The principle that emerges,scaffold, do not substitute, defines a challenge for the AI ecosystem as a whole." It extends beyond education to any system that mediates human cognition, which can either weaken human capabilities through substitution or strengthen them through scaffolding.
requirements: Systems must be able to decide when to withhold an answer, ask a question, surface uncertainty, or present alternative perspectives; builders must treat scaffolding as a first-class capability
constraints: The principle is derived from a small, homogeneous exploratory essay cohort and from argument rather than controlled testing; the authors make no claims of statistical generalizability
target_learning_goals: critical thinking
independent reasoning
learner agency
durable understanding
examples: Students requested an AI that does not provide solutions so they must find the correct answer themselves, and valued one that asks fundamental questions students must explain and answer

article_title: Analysis of Types of Inquiries in Student-AI Interaction: A case study of two CS2 tasks
citation: Matin Amoozadeh and Amin Alipour. (2026). Analysis of Types of Inquiries in Student-AI Interaction: A case study of two CS2 tasks. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.17919
title: The Graesser et al. question taxonomy adapted to student-AI programming interactions
description: The article adapts the Graesser et al. taxonomy, which "classifies student questions into 18 categories that reflect different cognitive functions of inquiry, including verification, explanation, causal reasoning, procedural guidance, and evaluation". Originally developed for tutoring dialogue, it is repurposed to distinguish prompts seeking conceptual clarification, procedural guidance, debugging explanations, and confirmation of correctness in programming contexts. The article applies it via a few-shot LLM classification approach to 830 CS2 student-AI prompts.
requirements: Prompts must be classifiable into the 18 categories, with prompts that do not clearly fit any category labeled as Other; classification requires category definitions plus example prompts for few-shot conditioning.
constraints: The article notes relatively little prior work has adapted these frameworks to student-generative-AI interactions in programming education, and categories were adapted to programming contexts by the authors.
target_learning_goals: Characterizing students' inquiry and help-seeking strategies during AI-supported programming problem solving
examples: The article applied the taxonomy to 830 prompts from two CS2 lab sessions using few-shot classification with GPT-5.2 and Claude, with disagreements resolved manually against the taxonomy definitions.
key_sources: Matin Amoozadeh and Amin Alipour. (2026). Analysis of Types of Inquiries in Student-AI Interaction: A case study of two CS2 tasks. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.17919

title: Web-based CS2 programming environment with integrated GPT-4 AI assistant and interaction logging
description: A web-based programming environment developed for this study in which "The system integrates the programming assign- ment description, a code editor, program execution output, and a conversational AI assistant within one single interface." The AI assistant was powered by GPT-4 accessed through the OpenAI API. The system automatically logged student prompts, AI responses, timestamps, user identifiers, and interaction metadata, enabling analysis of question-asking behavior during two 60-minute lab sessions.

constraints: The system was used during scheduled laboratory sessions of approximately 60 minutes in a single CS2 course at one university.

article_title: Do Not Copy/Paste: Soft Barriers for Copying in AI-Assisted Programming
citation: Iyiola E. Olatunji, Alberick Euraste Djire, Jacques Klein, and Tegawendé F. Bissyandé. 2026. Do Not Copy/Paste: Soft Barriers for Copying in AI-Assisted Programming. Proceedings of the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE '26). https://doi.org/10.1145/3832783.3834554
title: AI code handoff problem and handoff-aware AI-assisted programming as a design perspective
description: The paper identifies the AI code handoff problem: "the unmanaged transition from AI-generated text to executable or persistent software artifacts". It proposes handoff-aware AI-assisted programming, in which coding assistants explicitly shape how generated code is transferred, inspected, tested, or attributed, treating the handoff boundary as a software engineering design surface where transfer policies vary by context (education favors reconstruction; professional codebases require provenance, review, testing, or security checks).
requirements: A handoff-aware assistant applies a policy layer allowing direct transfer when appropriate or introducing explanations, metadata, review, tests, or soft barriers
constraints: Transfer policies should vary by context; educational and professional settings favor different defaults
target_learning_goals: code comprehension and reconstruction
responsible and reviewed use of AI-generated code
examples: The paper instantiates one point in this design space—soft-barrier handoff—using Unicode perturbations as a minimal technical probe

article_title: Do Not Copy/Paste: Soft Barriers for Copying in AI-Assisted Programming
citation: Iyiola E. Olatunji, Alberick Euraste Djire, Jacques Klein, and Tegawendé F. Bissyandé. 2026. Do Not Copy/Paste: Soft Barriers for Copying in AI-Assisted Programming. Proceedings of the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE '26). https://doi.org/10.1145/3832783.3834554
title: Unicode perturbation families implemented as system-prompt soft barriers
description: The paper implements soft barriers as a system prompt instructing the model to inject specific Unicode characters into user-defined identifiers during generation, leaving keywords, operators, literals, and built-in names unchanged. Four families are evaluated: "Invisible chars" (zero-width characters inside identifiers), "Homoglyphs" (ASCII letters replaced by visually identical Unicode equivalents), "BIDI reordering" (directionality overrides altering internal byte order), and "Deletions" (backspace/delete controls erasing adjacent rendered characters). The mechanism requires no model retraining or environment changes.
requirements: Only a system prompt; no model retraining, decoder change, or execution-environment modification
constraints: Any real deployment should be institutionally approved, disclosed at the policy level, and accessibility-tested; motivated users can bypass via clean-output requests, text normalizers, or retyping
target_learners: programming students using AI coding assistants
target_learning_goals: discouraging unexamined transfer of AI-generated code
promoting reading, editing, and reconstruction of generated code
examples: Full prompt templates for all families are released in the paper's repository; Figure 1 shows a homoglyph example where pasting triggers an execution error

title: Handoff design space for AI coding assistants: six handoff types from direct transfer to provenance marking
description: Table 1 enumerates the handoff design space the paper proposes for AI coding assistants: Direct (code transfers immediately with no intervention), Explanation-first (assistant provides reasoning before code, promoting inspection), Soft-barrier (code is readable but naive copy-paste execution fails), Review-gated (transfer requires a summary, test, or confirmation step), Test-gated (insertion is blocked until the learner runs or writes tests), and Provenance-marked (generated code carries metadata for attribution or auditing). These types could form a policy layer between an LLM and an IDE, LMS, or repository.
requirements: Different defaults for beginner exercises, production patches, security-sensitive code, and boilerplate generation
constraints: The paper studies only one point in this design space (soft-barrier handoff) technically
target_learning_goals: shaping how generated code is transferred, inspected, tested, or attributed
examples: Campus-managed assistants such as UniGPT-style services could support explanation-first, test-gated, or soft-barrier modes

article_title: Practical Implementation Report on Introducing Spec-Driven Development Using AI Agents in Software Development PBL
citation: Hidetake Tanaka, Hiroshi Igaki, Kazumasa Shimari, Kiyoshi Honda, and Naoki Fukuyasu. (2026). Practical Implementation Report on Introducing Spec-Driven Development Using AI Agents in Software Development PBL. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30572
title: Spec-Driven Development (SDD): a development methodology in which AI agents generate code from structured specification documents that developers must verify
description: SDD is a software development methodology proposed for use with AI agents, positioned as an alternative to Vibe Coding. "This approach involves deﬁning detailed speciﬁcations cl early at the early stages of development and having AI agents gener ate code based on those speciﬁcations." Its distinguishing feature is that agents proceed from structured specification documents rather than ambiguous natural-language instructions, with specifications describing architectural patterns, coding conventions, security requirements, and testing strategies that agents treat as constraints. Because developers must understand and verify the generated documents and code, the authors judge SDD more suitable than Vibe Coding for project-based courses where students take responsibility for AI outputs.
requirements: Developers must understand and verify AI-generated specifications and documents at each step to maintain code quality and consistency
constraints: SDD demands greater expertise compared to Vibe Coding, per the authors
target_learning_goals: application development skills
understanding and verifying AI-generated specifications and code
examples: In the SDPBL course, the existing SDD requirements-analysis and design phases were redefined as an investigation phase, and a review phase was added after implementation, yielding a four-phase workflow
key_sources: Hidetake Tanaka, Hiroshi Igaki, Kazumasa Shimari, Kiyoshi Honda, and Naoki Fukuyasu. (2026). Practical Implementation Report on Introducing Spec-Driven Development Using AI Agents in Software Development PBL. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30572

title: SDD template project with copilot-instructions.md custom instructions and docs/ artifact directories for AI-agent workflow in SDPBL
description: A template project directory for Visual Studio Code distributed to each team to operationalize SDD in the course. "copilot-instructions.md contains the workﬂow and project-speciﬁc rules as custom in structions." AI-generated artifacts are stored in the docs/ directory, with done/, investigate/, and review/ subdirectories holding the corresponding reports, alongside specs.md and tasks.md and a NewSpringBootProject directory registered as a GitHub repository. Based on their observations, the authors report these templates appeared to help students smoothly initiate development tasks using AI agents, and that a 30-minute lecture and one-hour demonstration accompanied distribution.

constraints: The study context is a specific Java/Spring Boot course with only four teams in 2025, limiting generalization per the authors
target_learners: third-year undergraduate information systems students working in teams of three to four
target_learning_goals: team-based web application development with Spring Boot
structuring instructions and specifications for AI agents

article_title: StudentSim: Training LLM-based Student Simulators
citation: Ke Yang, Chenglong Wang, Michel Galley, Chandan Singh, Jeevana Priya Inala, ChengXiang Zhai, Jianfeng Gao. (2026). StudentSim: Training LLM-based Student Simulators. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01591
title: The F/R decomposition: student simulators as jointly faithful and guidance-responsive proxies for tutor optimization
description: The article formalizes per-student student simulation as a measurable target with two properties. First, "behavioral fidelity: how well the simulator reproduces a student's own response to a problem, including that student's characteristic mistakes and strengths". Second, "guidance responsiveness", how readily the simulator updates its response in the direction tutor guidance steers. The framework is motivated by educational measurement's two targets — independent production and progress with support, the zone of proximal development that dynamic assessment operationalizes — and turns student simulation into an optimizable objective for AI tutor training.
requirements: A useful simulator must satisfy both properties together; the high-F, high-R corner is the target, since F and R measure separable capabilities.
constraints: The authors note F and R capture a student's state and its one-step update under guidance, not fuller learning dynamics such as acquisition, retention, and forgetting across many interactions.
target_learners: individual real learners in chess, second-language English writing, and mathematics
target_learning_goals: reproducing individual student responses and their revision under tutor guidance
examples: The framework scores every method on the same held-out per-student records, e.g. chess fidelity as move-prediction accuracy and responsiveness as corrected-move rate.
key_sources: Ke Yang, Chenglong Wang, Michel Galley, Chandan Singh, Jeevana Priya Inala, ChengXiang Zhai, Jianfeng Gao. (2026). StudentSim: Training LLM-based Student Simulators. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01591

article_title: StudentSim: Training LLM-based Student Simulators
citation: Ke Yang, Chenglong Wang, Michel Galley, Chandan Singh, Jeevana Priya Inala, ChengXiang Zhai, Jianfeng Gao. (2026). StudentSim: Training LLM-based Student Simulators. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01591
title: StudentSimEval: a standardized per-student simulator benchmark over 60 students in chess, L2 writing, and math with released code
description: StudentSimEval is a standardized evaluation protocol spanning 60 students across chess, second-language English writing, and mathematics. It "turns public learner corpora into a fixed per-student record schema with per-student train/held-out splits, and scores every method on two metrics, behavioral fidelity (F) and guidance responsiveness (R)". Because every method is fit on the same per-student records and scored on the same held-out records, simulators from any family are directly comparable; the authors release the construction pipeline, per-student splits, and evaluation code so others can score new methods and extend the benchmark.
requirements: Evaluation uses frozen per-student held-out sets scored identically for every method, with per-student evaluation records disjoint from training data.
constraints: The multi-turn corpora are real-teacher-annotated for L2 but LLM-tutor-generated under fixed style templates for chess and math, where the LLM determines only the wording of guidance.
target_learners: real human students: 30 chess players, 15 L2 English learners, 15 math students
target_learning_goals: measuring behavioral fidelity and guidance responsiveness of student simulators
examples: Chess records come from the Lichess May 2025 database, L2 essays from the EFCAMDAT corpus, and math from a foundational-assistance corpus of annotated open-ended problems.
key_sources: Ke Yang, Chenglong Wang, Michel Galley, Chandan Singh, Jeevana Priya Inala, ChengXiang Zhai, Jianfeng Gao. (2026). StudentSim: Training LLM-based Student Simulators. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01591

article_title: StudentSim: Training LLM-based Student Simulators
citation: Ke Yang, Chenglong Wang, Michel Galley, Chandan Singh, Jeevana Priya Inala, ChengXiang Zhai, Jianfeng Gao. (2026). StudentSim: Training LLM-based Student Simulators. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01591
title: Two-stage pooled-then-specialized training: pretrain a domain base simulator on pooled student data, then specialize one adapter per student
description: StudentSim overcomes sparse per-student data with a two-stage pipeline. Stage 1 trains one domain-specific base simulator on records pooled across all students, learning "common mistake patterns, the response format expected in the domain, and the pathway from natural-language tutor guidance to a changed response". Stage 2 initializes from that base and adapts it to one specific student using only that student's own recorded responses and tutor-guidance interactions, producing one LoRA adapter per student on a shared Qwen3-4B-Instruct backbone.
requirements: Stage 1 must supply what is shared across students and cannot be learned reliably from one student's sparse data alone; Stage 2 then supplies what is specific to each individual.
constraints: Per-student data is sparse: a learner in the L2 corpus writes three essays at the median, and more than two thirds write five or fewer; training one simulator end-to-end per student from such records would overfit.
target_learners: individual learners with sparse recorded interaction data in chess, L2 writing, or math
target_learning_goals: simulating an individual student's baseline responses and their revision after tutor guidance
examples: In chess, the article reports that performance drops when pooled records are replaced with repeated records from one student, supporting the pooled stage.
key_sources: Ke Yang, Chenglong Wang, Michel Galley, Chandan Singh, Jeevana Priya Inala, ChengXiang Zhai, Jianfeng Gao. (2026). StudentSim: Training LLM-based Student Simulators. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01591

article_title: Fairness-Aware Multimodal Transformer Modeling for Real-Time Student Attention Estimation
citation: Christoforos Fragkiadakis, Seyed Sahand Mohammadi Ziabari, and Ali Mohammed Mansoor Alsahag. (2026). Fairness-Aware Multimodal Transformer Modeling for Real-Time Student Attention Estimation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02232
title: DIPSER multimodal classroom dataset for in-person student engagement and attention recognition
description: DIPSER (Dataset for In-Person Student Engagement Recognition in the Wild) synchronizes camera recordings with smartwatch sensor data to capture student attention and emotional states during scheduled educational activities without experimental staging. It provides RGB facial images at 640× 480 pixels at approximately 10 frames per second, wearable sensors (heart rate, linear acceleration, gyroscope, rotation vector, ambient light) at up to 100 Hz, per-second attention labels on a scale from 1 to 5, emotion annotations across 9 categories, and automatically inferred demographic metadata. "The dataset contains recordings from 57 subjects, organized into three groups of 16–21 students, and comprises 9 distinct educational scenarios, ranging from passive learning settings (lectures) to highly interactive activities (robotics experimentation)."
requirements: Synchronized multimodal recordings with per-second attention labels and demographic metadata for subgroup-aware modeling
constraints: Approximately 95% of subjects were classified as white (Caucasian), leading to the exclusion of race as a fairness axis due to this imbalance
Demographic attributes are automatically inferred rather than self-reported
The authors note its real-world setting, demographic imbalance, and the subjectivity of human annotations introduce realistic sources of bias
target_learners: classroom students across secondary and higher education age groups (13–44)
target_learning_goals: continuous estimation of student attention during passive and interactive learning activities
examples: Used in this study with subject-level splits (39 train, 9 validation, 9 test subjects), 10-second rolling windows, and inverse-frequency weighting for imbalanced attention labels
key_sources: Christoforos Fragkiadakis, Seyed Sahand Mohammadi Ziabari, and Ali Mohammed Mansoor Alsahag. (2026). Fairness-Aware Multimodal Transformer Modeling for Real-Time Student Attention Estimation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02232

article_title: Fairness-Aware Multimodal Transformer Modeling for Real-Time Student Attention Estimation
citation: Christoforos Fragkiadakis, Seyed Sahand Mohammadi Ziabari, and Ali Mohammed Mansoor Alsahag. (2026). Fairness-Aware Multimodal Transformer Modeling for Real-Time Student Attention Estimation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02232
title: Subject-level demographic MAE-gap fairness regularization for multimodal attention models
description: An in-processing fairness framework that adds a demographic disparity penalty to the training objective of a multimodal attention model. Per-subject MAEs are averaged within each demographic group, and "The fairness penalty was defined as the gap between the highest and lowest group-level subject MAE", weighted by a trade-off parameter λ added to the weighted MSE task loss. Regularization is introduced after a two-epoch warm-up, with subject- and group-balanced batch sampling so every represented subject contributes equally to the penalty. λ is selected on validation data subject to a constraint that mean validation MAE increases by no more than 0.02 relative to the unregularized baseline.
requirements: Subject- and group-balanced batch sampling so all protected groups are represented in the penalty
A warm-up period optimizing only prediction MSE before adding the fairness term
Validation-based λ selection with an accuracy-degradation cap
constraints: In this study the validation-level fairness improvements did not consistently generalize to held-out subjects or repeated subject-level splits
Fairness constraints can modify the predictive optimum and create accuracy–fairness trade-offs
target_learners: classroom students in demographic subgroups defined by inferred gender and age
target_learning_goals: reducing demographic error disparities in continuous student attention estimation while preserving predictive performance
examples: Applied to the Residual Fusion Transformer with λ=0.7 for gender and λ=0.8 for age objectives, each evaluated across 10 training seeds
key_sources: Christoforos Fragkiadakis, Seyed Sahand Mohammadi Ziabari, and Ali Mohammed Mansoor Alsahag. (2026). Fairness-Aware Multimodal Transformer Modeling for Real-Time Student Attention Estimation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02232

article_title: Fairness-Aware Multimodal Transformer Modeling for Real-Time Student Attention Estimation
citation: Christoforos Fragkiadakis, Seyed Sahand Mohammadi Ziabari, and Ali Mohammed Mansoor Alsahag. (2026). Fairness-Aware Multimodal Transformer Modeling for Real-Time Student Attention Estimation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02232
title: Evaluate fairness-aware learning models with subgroup-aware metrics, repeated subject-level validation, and joint interpretation of disparity and accuracy
description: Because aggregate predictive metrics can conceal demographic disparities and single-split validation can overstate fairness gains, this principle holds that fairness claims require subgroup-level evaluation alongside overall and worst-group error, tested across repeated subject-level splits. The article concludes that "stable fairness improvements require stronger evidence than a single validation split or a reduction in one disparity metric." Disparity metrics should be interpreted jointly with predictive accuracy, since lower disparities do not necessarily correspond to better outcomes for all demographic groups.
requirements: Subgroup and worst-group error metrics computed per demographic axis
Repeated subject-level train-validation-test splits with paired comparisons
Sufficient numbers of independent subjects per subgroup
constraints: With very few subjects per subgroup, subgroup and worst-group metrics can be strongly influenced by individual participant behavior
Automatically inferred rather than self-reported demographic attributes add uncertainty
target_learners: students in demographic subgroups of educational AI deployments
target_learning_goals: reliable, fairness-aware evaluation of automated student attention and engagement estimation
examples: The study evaluated overall MAE, worst-group MAE, and best-to-worst subgroup MAE gaps for each fairness axis, and ran repeated subject-level split experiments with paired baseline and fairness-model comparisons

article_title: SWIM: Student Writing Simulation via Proficiency-Conditioned Generation
citation: Heejin Do, Jakub Kontak, Mrinmaya Sachan. (2026). SWIM: Student Writing Simulation via Proficiency-Conditioned Generation. arXiv preprint arXiv:2609.03215. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03215
title: SWIM: proficiency-conditioned essay generation task with AES-based profile-alignment evaluation and the Proficiency Alignment Reward
description: SWIM formalizes student writing simulation as proficiency-conditioned essay generation: given a writing prompt and a target trait-score profile, a generator produces an essay exhibiting the specified writing behavior, and "an AES-based evaluation framework for" measuring profile alignment scores the output with a frozen multi-trait AES verifier using QWK. The authors train generators via SFT on real (essay, profile) pairs and then refine them with GRPO using the Proficiency Alignment Reward, a dense per-sample reward based on trait-normalized accuracy against the target profile.
requirements: A trait-score-annotated essay corpus with prompt-specific rubrics and score ranges, and a frozen multi-trait AES verifier as external evaluator
constraints: Evaluation relies on AES as a proxy for fidelity and cannot fully replace human judgment of authenticity
Experiments cover a limited set of writing prompts and proficiency distributions on ASAP/ASAP++
Static proficiency profiles do not model evolving learner states such as knowledge, motivation, or writing strategies over time
target_learners: simulated K-12 and secondary student writers across grade levels in the ASAP/ASAP++ corpus
target_learning_goals: reproducing multidimensional writing proficiency (content, organization, lexical choice, sentence fluency, conventions) at specified levels
examples: GRPO-trained Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct generated qualitatively distinct essays for ASAP Prompt 5 at target Overall scores 1/4, 2/4, and 4/4, with length and structural sophistication scaling with the requested level
key_sources: Heejin Do, Jakub Kontak, Mrinmaya Sachan. (2026). SWIM: Student Writing Simulation via Proficiency-Conditioned Generation. arXiv preprint arXiv:2609.03215. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03215

article_title: Who Should Grade My Work? Student Perspectives on Transparent AI-Assisted Writing Assessment in Higher Education
citation: Rayed AlGhamdi. (2026). Who Should Grade My Work? Student Perspectives on Transparent AI-Assisted Writing Assessment in Higher Education. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-6277-2124
title: Feedback utility versus evaluative authority: a conceptual distinction between accepting AI as feedback mechanism and accepting AI as grader
description: The paper contributes a conceptual distinction "that has not been clearly named in the existing literature: between students' acceptance of AI as a feedback mechanism (feedback utility) and their acceptance of AI as an evaluator with grading authority (evaluative authority)." The two are analytically separate judgements rather than opposite ends of a single approval scale. The authors argue this distinction helps reconcile competing findings in the algorithm-trust literature, since students may appreciate AI for some functions and resist it for others within the same evaluation event.
requirements: Analysis must attend to how students separate functions of AI within the same evaluation event rather than asking whether students accept or reject AI evaluation as a whole
constraints: Derived from a small, purposive sample of 13 students in one Saudi computing course; the authors state the patterns should not be generalized without further research
target_learners: undergraduate computing students in higher education
target_learning_goals: reasoning about trust, fairness, and legitimacy of AI-mediated writing assessment
examples: Participants endorsed AI for initial feedback while questioning its use for final grading, and even enthusiastic participants framed endorsement as relating to learning support rather than grading authority
key_sources: Rayed AlGhamdi. (2026). Who Should Grade My Work? Student Perspectives on Transparent AI-Assisted Writing Assessment in Higher Education. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-6277-2124

article_title: Who Should Grade My Work? Student Perspectives on Transparent AI-Assisted Writing Assessment in Higher Education
citation: Rayed AlGhamdi. (2026). Who Should Grade My Work? Student Perspectives on Transparent AI-Assisted Writing Assessment in Higher Education. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-6277-2124
title: Three-principle framework for ethical GenAI integration in writing assessment: transparency, human mediation, reflective practice
description: The paper proposes "a three-principle framework (transparency, human mediation, reflective practice) for ethical GenAI integration in writing assessment." Transparency functions not merely as disclosure but as a pedagogical strategy that surfaces learners' assumptions, concerns, and values regarding GenAI. Human mediation reflects participants' positioning of the instructor as the appropriate authority over grading decisions and a safeguard against AI error. Reflective practice reflects the post-assessment reflective design in which students examined the evaluation itself.
requirements: GenAI evaluation must be aligned with a rubric-based prompt tied to task objectives; students must be explicitly informed that an AI generated the feedback and score
constraints: Proposed within the bounded context and sample of this study; the authors acknowledge other tools may offer enhanced data-protection guarantees and institutional policies on AI tool selection are evolving rapidly
target_learners: undergraduate students in higher education writing courses
target_learning_goals: critical engagement with AI-mediated feedback and assessment
examples: The study's design explicitly informed students that ChatGPT evaluated their handwritten work before a reflective task on agreement, learning, and opinions about AI as evaluator

article_title: Flawed but Memorable: Student Critical Reception of Interest-Personalized GenAI Analogies in Computing Education
citation: Seth Bernstein and Naaz Sibia. 2026. Flawed but Memorable: Student Critical Reception of Interest-Personalized GenAI Analogies in Computing Education. Koli Calling '26. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.06095
title: Two-sided analogy auditing: target-domain and source-domain knowledge jointly support evaluation of an analogical mapping
description: The article's conceptual account of how learners evaluate analogies. Target-concept knowledge identifies the relations an analogy must preserve, while source-domain knowledge determines whether those relations hold there; the article states "neither side is sufficient alone." A familiar source may make an analogy both more engaging and more inspectable, giving interest personalization a possible epistemic role in addition to its motivational role. The account reframes expertise as source-domain or target-domain expertise rather than a single construct.
requirements: Evaluating an analogy requires knowledge of both the computing concept and the analogy's source domain
constraints: Because explanation format and personalization varied together in the design, the study cannot isolate personalization as the cause of the observed scrutiny
target_learners: undergraduate computing students who have completed CS2
target_learning_goals: critically evaluating AI-generated analogical explanations of computing concepts such as linked lists and recursion
examples: Participants who knew an analogy's source domain well, such as P6 with One Piece, audited the source side of the mapping directly and located the point of structural divergence.
key_sources: Seth Bernstein and Naaz Sibia. 2026. Flawed but Memorable: Student Critical Reception of Interest-Personalized GenAI Analogies in Computing Education. Koli Calling '26. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.06095

article_title: Scalable AI-based clinical communication training and automated assessment
citation: Masum Hasan, Ron Epstein, Thomas Carroll, Ehsan Hoque. (2026). Scalable AI-based clinical communication training and automated assessment. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22517
title: SOPHIE 2.0: a browser-based self-service platform for AI-patient communication practice with automated feedback and assessment
description: SOPHIE 2.0 is a browser-based platform combining an audiovisual virtual avatar patient, real-time LLM-generated dialogue, and automated personalized feedback. Its library spans "24 clinical scenarios" across cardiology, primary care, oncology, critical care, pediatrics, neonatology, surgery, dental, and oral health, with virtual patients of diverse ages, genders, ethnicities, and appearances. Learners select a scenario, complete an encounter, receive immediate transcript-based feedback on the 3E skills, and repeat practice without a live facilitator, standardized patient, or human rater. Conversational backends are GPT-4o-mini and HAL, a Qwen2.5 14B model optimized with Direct Preference Optimization on approximately 7,500 medical conversation pairs.
requirements: An internet-connected device; the study required participants to have medical education or certification and English communication
constraints: The Tavus video avatar platform limits the maximum number of concurrent users depending on the payment plan
target_learning_goals: clinical communication skills: Empower, Be Explicit, and Empathize
examples: In the study, 59 participants completed two counterbalanced 3–10-minute AI-patient conversations with personalized feedback and an exit survey, fully automated without a live facilitator
key_sources: Masum Hasan, Ron Epstein, Thomas Carroll, Ehsan Hoque. (2026). Scalable AI-based clinical communication training and automated assessment. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22517

article_title: Scalable AI-based clinical communication training and automated assessment
citation: Masum Hasan, Ron Epstein, Thomas Carroll, Ehsan Hoque. (2026). Scalable AI-based clinical communication training and automated assessment. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22517
title: Deliver repeated communication practice, feedback, and assessment through a fully automated self-service platform to reduce the human-resource barriers of standardized-patient training
description: The article argues that scalability of communication training depends on removing two constraints: the availability of people to conduct simulations and the effort required to assess them. SOPHIE 2.0 lets learners "practice asynchronously with an embodied AI patient, receive personalized feedback, and repeat the experience without a live facilitator or rater", while an LLM assessor replaces expert rating effort. The study's findings on usability, agreement with human raters, and independent completion support the feasibility of this model.
requirements: An automated assessor whose agreement with human raters is adequate (here validated at r=0.759, ICC=0.746)
constraints: The present study demonstrates feasibility, not deployment at scale; performance gains could not be attributed specifically to training without a control condition
target_learners: healthcare professionals and students without prior communication training
target_learning_goals: clinical communication skills (3E framework)
serious illness and general clinical conversations
examples: SOPHIE 2.0 expanded a single-scenario, human-operated predecessor to 24 scenarios with automated assessment, and 59 participants completed successive encounters independently
key_sources: Masum Hasan, Ron Epstein, Thomas Carroll, Ehsan Hoque. (2026). Scalable AI-based clinical communication training and automated assessment. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22517

article_title: Scalable AI-based clinical communication training and automated assessment
citation: Masum Hasan, Ron Epstein, Thomas Carroll, Ehsan Hoque. (2026). Scalable AI-based clinical communication training and automated assessment. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22517
title: The 3E framework: Empower, Be Explicit, and Empathize as measurable dimensions of clinical communication
description: The 3E framework, drawn from the MVP (medical situation, values, and plan) model for serious illness conversations, defines three communication skills—Empower, Be Explicit, and Empathize—that the article treats as quantifiable dimensions of clinical communication. Scores are calculated with a Likert questionnaire, and both trained standardized-patient raters and the automated LLM judge apply the same rubric to transcripts. The framework serves as the platform's primary performance outcome and its domain-level outcomes, and structures the personalized feedback learners receive after each encounter.
requirements: A structured rubric and rating instructions, applied consistently by human or automated raters, to produce comparable Likert scores
constraints: Agreement was relatively weaker for the Be Explicit dimension for all LLM judges, for reasons the authors state remain unknown
target_learning_goals: empowering patients
explicit communication
empathic communication in clinical encounters
examples: Post-training self-ratings across the three domains ranged 3.75–4.08 out of 5, with Empathize rated highest
key_sources: Masum Hasan, Ron Epstein, Thomas Carroll, Ehsan Hoque. (2026). Scalable AI-based clinical communication training and automated assessment. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22517

article_title: What Fidelity Metrics Miss: A Structural Check on Synthetic Educational Data
citation: Inoue, H., & Yasutake, K. (2026). What Fidelity Metrics Miss: A Structural Check on Synthetic Educational Data. Proceedings of the 34th International Conference on Computers in Education. Asia-Pacific Society for Computers in Education. https://library.apsce.net
title: Weekly β0 structural check: connected components of a weekly proximity graph over learners tracked across a term
description: A structural summary of how a cohort divides in each week: learners are represented as points in a feature space, connected when Euclidean distance falls below a threshold ε, and β0 counts the connected components of the graph, read as "the number of distinct behavioural groups the cohort forms that week". Tracked across weeks it describes reorganisation rather than level. It requires no optimisation or random seed, is defined for disconnected graphs, and is computed identically on real and synthetic cohorts.
requirements: A choice of threshold ε, which must be controlled because the routine selection rule forces β0/N toward one quarter in every dataset
A complete learner-by-week feature grid with features standardised on a common scale across weeks
constraints: The platform's disclosure rules do not permit component-wise maxima
The authors do not argue β0 is a good measure of learning nor interpret its level educationally
Which structural descriptor serves non-stationarity description best is left open
target_learners: learners in annual cohorts of a lower-secondary study-habit logging system (117 to 120 learners per cohort)
target_learning_goals: describing week-to-week reorganisation of cohort behavioural structure in learning-process data
examples: Applied to four annual cohorts of lower-secondary study-habit logs with weekly study time in six time-of-day bands, and to four OULAD presentations with weekly click counts on six activity types
key_sources: Inoue, H., & Yasutake, K. (2026). What Fidelity Metrics Miss: A Structural Check on Synthetic Educational Data. Proceedings of the 34th International Conference on Computers in Education. Asia-Pacific Society for Computers in Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27265

article_title: Open Questions Towards Skill-Sustaining Reliance in Reflective AI Engagement
citation: Sander de Jong. (2026). Open Questions Towards Skill-Sustaining Reliance in Reflective AI Engagement. Workshop paper presented at CHIWORK'26 Workshop on Human Agency and Skill in AI-Supported Work. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27726
title: Skill-sustaining reliance: reflective AI engagement assessed for long-term sustainability of human agency and expertise
description: The paper introduces the concern of "skill-sustaining reliance": designing and evaluating reflective AI-engagement mechanisms not only for immediate decision quality but for whether professionals "still develop their own expertise or slowly lose the capacity for independent judgement". It organises the problem around four challenges: varying user effects, efficiency-driven workflows, habituation of scaffolding, and the short-term evidence gap. Its contribution is a set of open questions (Q1–Q4) for the research community about the conditions under which reflective AI engagement can be sustained in practice.
requirements: Evaluation must extend beyond single-session metrics such as task accuracy, reliance rate, and trust calibration to longitudinal outcomes of independent reasoning capacity.
constraints: The paper offers no empirical test of the framework; it explicitly frames its contributions as open questions, noting long-term evidence is currently insufficient.
target_learners: Professionals using AI decision support in high-stakes domains such as healthcare
target_learning_goals: Sustaining independent judgement and metacognitive capacity during long-term AI-assisted decision-making
examples: The paper's example of clinicians who routinely review AI-suggested diagnoses performing well in sessions while possibly not developing the diagnostic reasoning unassisted practice would have demanded.

article_title: StudentBench: AI and human tutoring yield equivalent GRE learning gains
citation: Curtis Northcutt, Inaara Hasmani, Kevin Feng, Trevor Khangi, Andreas Plesner, Jonas Mueller. (2026). StudentBench: AI and human tutoring yield equivalent GRE learning gains. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28470
title: StudentBench platform and open dataset for evaluating AI tutoring by real student learning gains
description: StudentBench is "a suite of AI teaching evaluations and a public platform that enables large-scale data collection with over 175,000 student–AI messages". It runs randomized pre/post learning-gain studies comparing AI tutors, human tutors, and control, and produces five leaderboards covering lesson planning, practice-problem creation, conversational pedagogy, cost, and engagement. Unlike prior LLM tutoring benchmarks judged by LLM evaluators or simulated students, it measures real students' unaided post-test gains after live tutoring. The de-identified data and reproduction code are open-sourced.
requirements: Human tutors, expert reviewers, students recruited via a career platform, and API access to LLM tutors
constraints: Latency is a first-class measured outcome; leaderboard scores should be compared only within panels
quality of teaching is characterized by expert evaluations and conversational behaviors, not by learning directly
target_learners: Adult students preparing for the GRE (primarily aged 18 to 23)
target_learning_goals: GRE Quantitative and Verbal reasoning gains
examples: 2,469 filtered sessions from 2,383 students in the learning-gain study; 51 expert tutors completing 2,028 pairwise rubric evaluations in the second study

article_title: StudentBench: AI and human tutoring yield equivalent GRE learning gains
citation: Curtis Northcutt, Inaara Hasmani, Kevin Feng, Trevor Khangi, Andreas Plesner, Jonas Mueller. (2026). StudentBench: AI and human tutoring yield equivalent GRE learning gains. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28470
title: Recursive human self-improvement (RHSI) framework for human–AI intelligence augmentation
description: RHSI is the authors' framework for a human-side singularity: "better teaching technologies help people learn, and greater human capabilities can in turn support better use and development of those technologies". The article states three conditions: the technology improves human capabilities; an improved human is better at using the technology; and better use leads to consistent further gains. The study tests only the first condition, using human tutoring as the benchmark for whether LLMs can augment human capabilities.
requirements: All three stated conditions must hold for recursive human self-improvement; this study addresses only the first
constraints: The article tests only the first condition for RHSI, via one-hour GRE tutoring sessions
target_learners: Adult learners using AI teaching technologies
target_learning_goals: Augmenting human learning capability through teaching technology
examples: The learning-gain study is framed as establishing the first condition for RHSI

article_title: SRJudge: Empowering Large Language Models with Selective Reasoning for Fine-Grained Knowledge Concept Tagging
citation: Zhiwei Yang, Jiahua Yang, Huiru Lin, Xing Chen, and Quanlong Guan. (2026). SRJudge: Empowering Large Language Models with Selective Reasoning for Fine-Grained Knowledge Concept Tagging. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36982
title: SRJudge: a three-stage Select-Reason-Judge framework for fine-grained knowledge concept tagging
description: SRJudge decomposes knowledge concept tagging into three stages. A fine-tuned BERT-based Selector first narrows the candidate space: "the Selector first picks K(≪ |Φ|)candidates ... reducing the decision space". A lightweight LLM Reasoner, trained with a pruned GRPO reinforcement-learning strategy and a task-specific reward combining format, accuracy and dynamic position rewards, recommends a concept with reasons over the shortlist. A frozen larger LLM Judger then evaluates the rationality of the reasoning and issues the final verdict from a global perspective. The framework addresses the problem that LLMs "struggle to select the correct concept from a large-scale candidate set due to the high dimensionality of the decision space".
requirements: A labeled dataset for supervised fine-tuning of the Selector, plus unlabeled instances for continued pre-training, as the article states the Selector is fine-tuned on a labeled dataset
constraints: The Reasoner operates only on the top-K shortlist produced by the Selector, so concepts outside the shortlist cannot be selected
target_learners: educational platforms and MOOCs tagging exercises for grade 7-12 mathematics, biology and physics
target_learning_goals: accurate assignment of fine-grained knowledge concept labels to exercises and solutions
examples: On S Math, S Bio and S Phy, the Selector shortlists K=5 candidates, the Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct Reasoner reasons over them under GRPO, and Qwen3-32B acts as Judger
key_sources: Zhiwei Yang, Jiahua Yang, Huiru Lin, Xing Chen, and Quanlong Guan. (2026). SRJudge: Empowering Large Language Models with Selective Reasoning for Fine-Grained Knowledge Concept Tagging. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36982

article_title: SRJudge: Empowering Large Language Models with Selective Reasoning for Fine-Grained Knowledge Concept Tagging
citation: Zhiwei Yang, Jiahua Yang, Huiru Lin, Xing Chen, and Quanlong Guan. (2026). SRJudge: Empowering Large Language Models with Selective Reasoning for Fine-Grained Knowledge Concept Tagging. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36982
title: S Bio and S Phy: two new knowledge concept tagging datasets for cross-discipline validation
description: The authors constructed two new benchmark datasets to address the lack of validation data outside mathematics: "we construct two new datasets, i.e., S Bio and S Phy, which will be made available to fill the gap in cross-validation of knowledge concept tagging methods across different disciplines". S Bio contains 9,941 exercises with 72 concept categories for grades 10-12, and S Phy contains 18,440 exercises with 135 categories for grades 10-12; both include questions, solutions, difficulty scores, and knowledge concepts, split 8:1:1 into training, validation and test sets with balanced concept distributions. Unsupervised corpora U Bio (15,669) and U Phy (32,138) support continued pre-training.
requirements: Labeled exercises with questions, solutions, difficulty scores and knowledge concept annotations, split stratified by concept category
constraints: Both datasets cover grades 10-12 biology and physics in a Chinese educational context
target_learners: senior secondary (grades 10-12) biology and physics students whose exercises are tagged
target_learning_goals: fine-grained knowledge concept tagging of exercises to support knowledge tracing, cognitive diagnosis and recommendation
examples: The datasets were used to evaluate SRJudge and all baselines alongside the existing S Math dataset

article_title: What Students Actually Ask: Demand Structure and Automation Potential in a Hybrid Support System
citation: Gupta, J., Ayinampudi, P., Aditya B.M.V., Hegade, P., Sharma, R., Sharma, S., Meenakshi, V., Iyengar, S.R.S. (2026). What Students Actually Ask: Demand Structure and Automation Potential in a Hybrid Support System. arXiv:2609.38967. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38967
title: Hybrid query-resolution platform routing queries across AI assistant, peer layer, curated FAQ corpus and administrator escalation
description: A deployed support platform for a large online internship programme that routes each raised query across four paths: an AI chatbot answering only from a curated FAQ corpus, a peer layer where any participant may answer, administrator handling, and a scripted facility. The article states that "The platform routes a raised query first to the AI chatbot, which answers only from a curated corpus of verified FAQ entries, a deliberate restriction that prevents unverified procedural guidance". Peer answers pass through administrator acceptance and senior-administrator final approval before release, and the corpus was revised daily so rule or schedule changes were reflected the same day.
requirements: A curated corpus of verified FAQ entries that is revised daily so procedural changes are reflected the same day
Administrator acceptance and senior-administrator approval of peer answers before release to the asker
constraints: The AI assistant answers only from the curated corpus and cannot report an individual participant's current status
The study covers a single programme across nine weeks of onboarding, with volume peaking in week 3 and tapering after, so it describes an onboarding period rather than a steady state
target_learners: Participants in a large-scale online internship programme during staggered-cohort onboarding
target_learning_goals: Resolving operational onboarding queries (eligibility, documentation, scheduling, status of pending submissions) with short turnaround without a dedicated mentor per student
examples: Over nine weeks (2 May to 6 July 2026) the system handled 4,093 queries from 1,434 participants; corpus reuse covered 21.3% of volume from 114 entries, participants self-resolved 12.2%, and 132 participants authored peer answers

article_title: Understanding Student Use of Large Language Models Across Computer Science Subfields
citation: Nizamani, S. B., Lee, Y., Donekal Chandrashekar, N., Ellis, M., & Ramakrishnan, N. (2026). Understanding Student Use of Large Language Models Across Computer Science Subfields. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01158
title: Demystify, use, and reflect: a structured LLM-intervention course design positioning LLMs as tools for supported learning
description: The course design centers on a structured intervention that works by "demystifying LLMs, how they work, their capabilities, and their probabilistic nature and limitations, alongside guided use through prompting strategies and iterative interaction". Rather than mandating or banning LLM use, the course leaves the decision to each student, requires students to understand, explain, and acknowledge AI-generated contributions, and adds a post-assignment reflection survey capturing prompt counts, role conceptualization, and verification strategies. This study extends the intervention by examining how its effects vary at the subfield level rather than only in aggregate.
requirements: Students need access to an LLM tool (institutionally licensed Microsoft Copilot Chat was available, though not restricted to a single tool)
Post-assignment reflection surveys must be administered immediately after task completion to capture interaction
constraints: The course did not explicitly encourage LLM use; the decision of whether and how to use them was left to each student
Findings are tied to the specific assignments and instructional practices of a single course context
target_learners: Undergraduate computer science students in a required post-CS1 problem-solving course
target_learning_goals: Informed and responsible LLM use
Effective prompting and iterative interaction
Assessing the reliability of LLM-generated responses
examples: One representative assignment per subfield: knapsack problem (Algorithms), Git commands practice (Software Engineering), HTTP request methods (Networking), HTML table design (Web Development), usability engineering report (HCI), SQL and Python (Databases), and Naive Bayes training and prediction (Machine Learning)
key_sources: Nizamani, S. B., Lee, Y., Donekal Chandrashekar, N., Ellis, M., & Ramakrishnan, N. (2026). Understanding Student Use of Large Language Models Across Computer Science Subfields. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01158

article_title: Understanding Student Use of Large Language Models Across Computer Science Subfields
citation: Nizamani, S. B., Lee, Y., Donekal Chandrashekar, N., Ellis, M., & Ramakrishnan, N. (2026). Understanding Student Use of Large Language Models Across Computer Science Subfields. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01158
title: Design assignments and reflection activities that promote effective and critical LLM interaction rather than restricting LLM use
description: The article concludes that assignment design shapes how students engage with LLMs, and recommends that "Rather than restricting LLM use, educators can design tasks and reflection activities that promote effective and critical interaction with AI tools". This works by pairing structured instruction on how LLMs work with post-assignment reflection, so that student decisions about LLM use become informed rather than ad hoc. The article's evidence shows that under one consistently applied instructional design, adoption, role conceptualization, and verification still varied by assignment, making task design a central lever.
requirements: Structured instruction on LLM capabilities, limitations, and prompting strategies
Post-assignment reflection surveys capturing LLM use
Ethical-use norms requiring students to understand, explain, and acknowledge AI-generated contributions
constraints: The study identifies associations between assignment characteristics and LLM usage patterns but does not establish causality
Results are tied to the specific assignments used and should not be generalized without caution to all tasks in the same subfields

Verification of LLM-generated outputs

article_title: Teacher intervention in K-12 AI-based instruction: a systematic review of processes, strategies, and effects
citation: Hansol Lee. (2026). Teacher intervention in K-12 AI-based instruction: a systematic review of processes, strategies, and effects. Smart Learning Environments. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40561-026-00461-1
title: Teacher intervention in AI-based instruction operates as a cyclical four-phase process of monitoring, judgment, intervention, and orchestration
description: The review conceptualizes teacher intervention as an integrated framework connecting AI-generated information with classroom practice. Analysis of the 29 included studies showed that "teacher intervention operates as a cyclical process comprising monitoring, judgment, intervention, and orchestration." AI outputs do not constitute pedagogical intervention by themselves; they gain instructional meaning only when teachers interpret, judge, and translate them into situated classroom support, and each link in the cycle is not automatic.
requirements: Teachers must interpret and judge AI-generated information before it becomes pedagogical action; the framework presupposes teacher presence in AI-based instruction
constraints: Derived from a synthesis of 29 K-12 studies published 2016-2025, relatively concentrated in middle and high school mathematics and science contexts
target_learning_goals: Transforming AI-generated information into pedagogical action and classroom adjustment
examples: The review presents the framework in Fig. 2, organizing the synthesis of processes, strategies, and effects across the 29 studies
key_sources: Hansol Lee. (2026). Teacher intervention in K-12 AI-based instruction: a systematic review of processes, strategies, and effects. Smart Learning Environments. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40561-026-00461-1

article_title: Teacher intervention in K-12 AI-based instruction: a systematic review of processes, strategies, and effects
citation: Hansol Lee. (2026). Teacher intervention in K-12 AI-based instruction: a systematic review of processes, strategies, and effects. Smart Learning Environments. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40561-026-00461-1
title: Three teacher intervention strategies in AI-based instruction: pedagogical translation of AI outputs, design of learning support, and reconstruction of interaction structures
description: The review identifies three strategies teachers use to intervene in AI-based instruction. "First, the pedagogical translation of AI outputs refers to the strategy by which teachers transform AI-generated information according to students' levels and classroom contexts, select what should be addressed, and turn it into actionable pedagogical practice." The second strategy organizes cognitive, affective-motivational, and procedural/self-regulatory support; the third coordinates peer interaction and student-AI interaction structures. The strategies are not mutually exclusive and can operate together within a single intervention scene.
requirements: Teachers need time and authority to interpret and select AI information, and the information itself must be interpretable, for translation to occur smoothly
constraints: Pedagogical translation can become a burden and increase teachers' cognitive load when information is excessive, hard to interpret, or there is insufficient time to review it
target_learning_goals: Supporting student learning through transformed AI information, designed support, and structured interactions
examples: In Yao et al. (2025), teachers selected, revised, supplemented, summarized, or deleted AI chatbot feedback according to students' writing levels and task purposes
key_sources: Hansol Lee. (2026). Teacher intervention in K-12 AI-based instruction: a systematic review of processes, strategies, and effects. Smart Learning Environments. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40561-026-00461-1

article_title: Teacher intervention in K-12 AI-based instruction: a systematic review of processes, strategies, and effects
citation: Hansol Lee. (2026). Teacher intervention in K-12 AI-based instruction: a systematic review of processes, strategies, and effects. Smart Learning Environments. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40561-026-00461-1
title: Teacher-facing AI tools should provide actionable information and preserve teachers' control over instructional decisions
description: Across design and co-design studies in the review, teachers perceived that AI tools supported orchestration when two conditions held: the tools "provided actionable information and preserved teachers' control." Relatedly, teachers preferred shared control in which they could accept, modify, reject, or override AI suggestions rather than fully automated decision-making. This principle guides the design of teacher-facing AI systems in K-12 classrooms.
requirements: AI tools must present interpretable, actionable information; systems must allow teachers to accept, modify, reject, or override AI suggestions
constraints: The degree of preferred control varied according to classroom context, trust in AI, and teachers' perceptions of the accuracy of AI recommendations
target_learning_goals: Classroom orchestration and teacher judgment in AI-based instruction
examples: In VanLehn et al. (2021), modifying the system so some questions went directly to students without passing through the teacher showed control could be redistributed between system and students

article_title: Teacher feedback vs. AI-assisted peer feedback in L2 writing: A quasi-experimental study in a Chinese university
citation: Tang J, Li P, Luo R (2026) Teacher feedback VS AI-assisted peer feedback in L2 writing: A quasi-experimental study in a Chinese University. PLoS One 21(6): e0345976. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0345976
title: Sociocultural account of feedback as scaffolding aligned to the Zone of Proximal Development
description: The article applies Vygotsky's Sociocultural Theory, specifically scaffolding and the Zone of Proximal Development, to L2 writing feedback: feedback is "an external scaffold whose value depends on its precise alignment with the learner's cognitive potential within the ZPD and its gradual withdrawal at appropriate moments". Within this account, teacher feedback acts as expert-provided dynamic scaffolding with authority and context sensitivity, while AI-assisted peer feedback acts as technology-mediated collaborative scaffolding offering real-time, standardized support. The study uses this framework to interpret its quasi-experimental comparison and to motivate a hybrid model.
requirements: Feedback must align with the learner's current ZPD and withdraw gradually to build independent task completion
constraints: The authors note the traditional SCT binary classifies technical tools only as static auxiliary intermediaries, leaving AI's scaffolding attributes inadequately theorized
target_learners: Second-language writing learners in higher education
target_learning_goals: L2 argumentative writing quality
lexical diversity
syntactic complexity
examples: The 8-week quasi-experiment interpreted teacher feedback's dynamic focus shift and AI-assisted peer feedback's stable learning-curve effect through this framework

title: Five-dimensional feedback checklist for structuring teacher and AI-assisted peer feedback
description: A standardized checklist adapted from Yang's (2022) Feedback Checklist and Orit Zeevy Solovey's (2022) Error Categories, covering "organizational structure, content and argumentation, grammar, vocabulary, and technical details". It guided both feedback modes in the study, providing "a structured operational framework for both scaffolding modes". Content validity was rated by three experts (CVI = 0.92), and pilot evaluation on 10 non-experimental essays yielded Cronbach's alpha coefficients from 0.78 to 0.86 across the five dimensions.

Unified training on the collaborative feedback procedure for students using it in AI-assisted peer review

target_learning_goals: Systematic coverage of organizational, content, grammar, vocabulary, and technical dimensions in writing feedback
examples: Both the control class teacher and the experimental class peer pairs applied the same checklist when generating feedback on argumentative drafts submitted via iWrite 2.0

article_title: Think First, ChatGPT Later: Guiding Human–AI Collaboration for Learning Gains in Independent Human Creativity
citation: Wong, S. S. H., & Qiu, S. X. (2026). Think First, ChatGPT Later: Guiding Human–AI Collaboration for Learning Gains in Independent Human Creativity. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10118-7
title: ISAR model: four types of AI effects on learning
description: The ISAR model proposed by Bauer et al. (2025) distinguishes four types of effects AI can exert on learning: inversion (AI leads to reduced cognitive processing and learning), substitution (AI provides instructional equivalence without changing cognitive processing), augmentation (AI enhances instruction with additional support without necessarily deepening processing), and redefinition (AI fosters deep constructive or interactive processes to enhance learning). The present study's findings align with the distinction between shallow appropriation (inversion-like) and deep collaborative engagement (redefinition-like) effects of AI.
requirements: Distinguishing between performance on assisted tasks and learning on subsequent unassisted tasks to classify AI effects
constraints: The model is cited from Bauer et al. (2025) as background; the present article tests its redefinition-type prediction only in creative problem-solving with university students
target_learning_goals: deep processing during AI-assisted learning
independent creative thinking
examples: The article frames free ChatGPT use that yields assisted-task gains but no unassisted gains as reliance rather than learning, and the guided approach as fostering deep constructive interaction
key_sources: Wong, S. S. H., & Qiu, S. X. (2026). Think First, ChatGPT Later: Guiding Human–AI Collaboration for Learning Gains in Independent Human Creativity. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10118-7

citation: Wong, S. S. H., & Qiu, S. X. (2026). Think First, ChatGPT Later: Guiding Human–AI Collaboration for Learning Gains in Independent Human Creativity. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10118-7
title: Seven sample prompts scaffolding collaborative ChatGPT interaction in creative problem-solving
description: A set of seven sample prompts presented to the regulated-AI group to scaffold collaborative interaction with ChatGPT during the creative product improvement task. The prompts covered processes such as seeking refinements and feedback, elaborating on promising ideas, comparing and evaluating ideas, connecting and combining ideas, identifying weaknesses, and refining selected ideas based on feedback. Participants were told the prompts were illustrative and could use their own prompts following the same principles.
requirements: Learners must have their own initial ideas to bring into the interaction
Access to ChatGPT during the collaboration phase
constraints: Designed for a creative product improvement task; participants could adapt wording freely
target_learning_goals: collaborative idea improvement with generative AI
metacognitive evaluation of ideas
examples: Sample prompt: asking ChatGPT what can be changed or added to make one's own initial bunny-improvement ideas better

article_title: Decoding symmetric and asymmetric pathways in generative AI learning adoption: a multi-method study
citation: Xin Tian, Musa Adekunle Ayanwale, Rethabile Rosemary Molefi, Preeti Manchanda, Nurgün Gençel and Barakat Olabisi Ogunjoun. (2026). Decoding symmetric and asymmetric pathways in generative AI learning adoption: a multi-method study. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00613-w
title: Integrated UTAUT3–ARCS hybrid-logic framework of Gen-AI adoption
description: The article integrates the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT3) with Keller's ARCS Motivation Model into a dual-layer account of Gen-AI adoption. UTAUT3 answers "Can I use this technology effectively?", whereas ARCS answers "Will I continue to engage with it for learning?". The framework posits a hybrid logic in which cognitive beliefs enable acceptance, motivational experiences sustain engagement, and habitual interaction normalizes use; ARCS is positioned as a motivational layer that reinforces or undermines cognitive evaluations and the pathway from intention to use.
requirements: Measurement of both acceptance beliefs (PE, EE, SI, FC, HM, HB, PI) and the four ARCS dimensions as distinct constructs, with satisfaction treated as an outcome-based evaluation distinct from hedonic motivation and habit
constraints: Tested in a low-resource higher education context (Lesotho) with cross-sectional data, so structural paths are interpreted as theory-consistent associations rather than definitive causal effects
target_learners: Higher education students in resource-constrained settings who have prior experience using ChatGPT or similar Gen-AI tools for academic work
target_learning_goals: Sustained adoption and use of generative AI tools for academic learning tasks
examples: The study operationalized the framework with ten constructs on a six-point Likert scale, validated via expert review (S-CVI/Ave = 0.94) and MGRM-IRT, and tested it with PLS-SEM, NCA, fsQCA, and machine learning on data from 842 Lesotho students
