article_title: A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research
citation: Panadero E. (2017). A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research. Front. Psychol. 8:422. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00422
title: Zimmerman's Cyclical Phases model of SRL: forethought, performance, self-reflection
description: Zimmerman's Cyclical Phases model organizes self-regulated learning into three recursive phases. Per the review, in the forethought phase "the students analyze the task, set goals, plan how to reach them" energized by motivational beliefs; in the performance phase they execute the task while monitoring progress and using self-control strategies; in the self-reflection phase they assess performance and make attributions whose self-reactions influence later task engagement. The review treats it as the individual-level process model comparable to the other five SRL models analyzed.
requirements: Describes SRL at the individual level, parallel to the other reviewed models
target_learning_goals: strategic self-regulated learning
examples: Cleary et al. trained 50 college students in basketball free throws across conditions training different numbers of SRL phases
key_sources: Panadero E. (2017). A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research. Front. Psychol. 8:422. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00422

article_title: A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research
citation: Panadero E. (2017). A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research. Front. Psychol. 8:422. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00422
title: Boekaerts' Dual Processing self-regulation model: mastery/growth versus well-being pathways
description: Boekaerts' Dual Processing self-regulation model describes how student appraisals determine which goal pathway activates during learning. The review states the model "described two parallel processing modes: (a) a mastery or learning mode and (b) a coping or well-being mode." When students perceive a task as threatening, negative cognitions and emotions trigger well-being protection; when the task fits their goals, positive cognitions trigger the mastery/growth pathway. The model assigns three purposes to self-regulation: expanding knowledge and skills, preventing threat to the self, and protecting commitments by re-routing attention from the well-being to the mastery pathway.
requirements: Student appraisals of the task determine which pathway is activated
constraints: Students who start in the mastery/growth pathway may switch to the well-being pathway if they detect cues they might not be successful
target_learners: students in secondary and vocational education
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning
emotion regulation during learning
examples: Boekaerts developed the On-line Motivation Questionnaire to measure task-specific feelings, thoughts and effort before and after tasks
key_sources: Panadero E. (2017). A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research. Front. Psychol. 8:422. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00422

article_title: A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research
citation: Panadero E. (2017). A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research. Front. Psychol. 8:422. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00422
title: Winne and Hadwin's metacognitive SRL model: four recursive phases and the COPES architecture
description: Winne and Hadwin's model takes a strongly metacognitive, information-processing view of SRL. The review states that "studying is powered by SRL across four linked phases that are open and recursive and are comprehended in a feedback loop": task definition, goal setting and planning, enacting study tactics and strategies, and metacognitively adapting studying. SRL deploys five task facets identified by "the COPES acronym" — Conditions, Operations, Products, Evaluations, Standards — with operations described as SMART (Searching, Monitoring, Assembling, Rehearsing, Translating). Students constantly monitor activities against standards, aligning the model with self-assessment research.
requirements: Scaffolding tools that record trace and log data are used to measure SRL under this model, since no classical questionnaires exist
constraints: The model figure contains no reference to emotions and only an allusion to motivation
target_learning_goals: metacognitive monitoring against standards
strategic study tactics
examples: Winne's team developed nStudy and gStudy, computer-supported learning environments that scaffold SRL while recording trace data
key_sources: Panadero E. (2017). A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research. Front. Psychol. 8:422. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00422

article_title: A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research
citation: Panadero E. (2017). A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research. Front. Psychol. 8:422. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00422
title: Pintrich's SRL model: four phases crossed with four areas for regulation
description: Pintrich's model, presented in the first SRL handbook, structures SRL as four phases — forethought/planning/activation, monitoring, control, and reaction and reflection — each crossed with four areas for regulation: cognition, motivation/affect, behavior and context. The review notes this combination "offers a comprehensive picture that includes a significant number of SRL processes." The behavior-regulation area, covering "individual's attempts to control their own overt behavior," is unique among the six reviewed models, and the context area covers students' attempts to monitor, control and regulate the learning context.
requirements: The model is operationalized in research primarily through the MSLQ questionnaire built on Pintrich's empirical work
constraints: The review states there is no empirical evidence directly addressing validation of Pintrich's model itself, only MSLQ validation data
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning integrating motivation and cognition
examples: Schunk reviewed Pintrich's six major contribution areas, including the SRL-motivation relationship and classroom contexts
key_sources: Panadero E. (2017). A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research. Front. Psychol. 8:422. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00422

article_title: A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research
citation: Panadero E. (2017). A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research. Front. Psychol. 8:422. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00422
title: Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire (MSLQ)
description: The MSLQ is Pintrich's widely used self-report instrument for measuring SRL and motivation. The review reports it "is composed of 15 scales, divided into a motivation section with 31 items, and a learning strategies (SRL) section with 50 items" subdivided into cognitive, metacognitive and resource management scales. Its strength is combining SRL and motivation measures, offering detailed information about students' learning strategy use. Versions exist for college and high school students, and two recent reviews found it the most used instrument in SRL and in self-efficacy measurement.
requirements: Used as a self-report instrument combining motivation and learning strategies scales
target_learning_goals: measuring motivation and learning strategy use
examples: The review cites reviews by Roth et al. and Honicke and Broadbent finding the MSLQ the most used instrument in SRL and self-efficacy measurement
key_sources: Panadero E. (2017). A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research. Front. Psychol. 8:422. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00422

article_title: A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research
citation: Panadero E. (2017). A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research. Front. Psychol. 8:422. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00422
title: Efklides' MASRL model: Person level and Task×Person level interaction of metacognition, motivation and affect
description: Efklides' Metacognitive and Affective Model of Self-Regulated Learning (MASRL) distinguishes two interacting levels. The Person level (macrolevel) is top-down and goal-driven, comprising cognition, motivation, self-concept, affect, volition, metacognitive knowledge and metacognitive skills. The Task×Person level (microlevel) is bottom-up and data-driven, where metacognitive activity takes control and attention moves to task-specific mechanisms. The review calls this distinction "probably the most salient feature of the MARSL model," and states the model clarifies how metacognition, motivation and affect interact via the macro and micro levels, with four basic functions at the microlevel: cognition, metacognition, affect, and regulation of affect and effort.
requirements: Empirical support rests on studies showing interactions among metacognition, motivation and affect at the two levels
constraints: Offers a different conceptualization of top-down/bottom-up processing than Boekaerts and Corno's account
target_learning_goals: metacognitive experiences during task execution
regulation of affect and effort
examples: Efklides created the Metacognitive Experiences Questionnaire exploring judgments and feelings about cognitive processing
key_sources: Panadero E. (2017). A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research. Front. Psychol. 8:422. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00422

article_title: A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research
citation: Panadero E. (2017). A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research. Front. Psychol. 8:422. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00422
title: SSRL model: three modes of regulation in collaborative learning (SRL, CoRL, SSRL)
description: The Hadwin, Järvelä and Miller model addresses regulation in collaborative and computer-supported learning. It proposes three modes: individual self-regulation adapting to interaction with group members; co-regulation, which "refers broadly to affordances and constraints stimulating the (student's) appropriation of strategic planning, enactment, reflection, and adaptation"; and socially shared regulation, where "deliberate, strategic and transactive planning, task enactment, reflection and adaptation" emerge through transactive exchanges among group members. SSRL unfolds in four loosely sequenced, recursively linked feedback loops adapted from Winne and Hadwin, extending regulation from the "I" or "you" level to collective activity.
requirements: Group members must commit to group work, establish shared common ground, and negotiate and share task perceptions, strategies and goals
constraints: The CoRL mode's use has not been consistent in the field and it has been the most disputed regulatory level; CoRL and SSRL can both occur as groups progress through different collaboration phases
target_learners: students in collaborative and computer-supported collaborative learning settings
target_learning_goals: shared regulation of group learning
collaborative planning and evaluation
examples: A review by Panadero and Järvelä found empirical evidence of SSRL occurrence in cognitive, metacognitive, motivational and emotional shared areas
key_sources: Panadero E. (2017). A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research. Front. Psychol. 8:422. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00422

citation: T. Sima Paribakht and Marjorie Wesche. (1996). Vocabulary enhancement activities and reading for meaning in second language vocabulary acquisition. Second Language Vocabulary Acquisition: A Rationale for Pedagogy, Cambridge University Press. https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9781139524643.013
title: Vocabulary Knowledge Scale (VKS)
description: The Vocabulary Knowledge Scale is a recently developed instrument for tracking the acquisition of targeted vocabulary words, created by Paribakht and Wesche. The authors describe it as "a recently developed instrument, the Vocabulary Knowledge Scale," with references to Paribakht & Wesche (1993) and Wesche & Paribakht (forthcoming).

citation: T. Sima Paribakht and Marjorie Wesche. (1996). Vocabulary enhancement activities and reading for meaning in second language vocabulary acquisition. Second Language Vocabulary Acquisition: A Rationale for Pedagogy, Cambridge University Press. https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9781139524643.013
title: Instructional intervention can support incidental L2 vocabulary acquisition through reading by making the process more directed and efficient
description: The chapter proposes that while incidental vocabulary acquisition through reading is slow and unpredictable, instructional intervention can support the process and make it more directed and efficient. It does so by using procedures that "increase the salience and cognitive processing of targeted words" encountered by L2 students in reading texts, combining reading for meaning with vocabulary enhancement activities rather than relying on reading alone or decontextualized exercises.

constraints: Incidental acquisition through reading alone is slow and unpredictable, which is the problem the intervention addresses

examples: The chapter's classroom experiments used instructional procedures designed to increase the salience and cognitive processing of targeted words in reading texts, tracking acquisition with the Vocabulary Knowledge Scale.

article_title: Assimilating complex information
citation: Pollock, Edwina Jane. (2000). Assimilating Complex Information. PhD thesis, School of Education, University of New South Wales. https://hdl.handle.net/1959.4/17813
title: The isolated-interacting elements two-phase instructional approach
description: The thesis develops a two-phase instructional approach for complex material. In the first phase the material's element interactivity is artificially reduced by presenting information as isolated elements that can be processed serially rather than simultaneously in working memory; in the second phase all the information for understanding is presented. The control instruction presented all information for understanding in both phases. The approach aims to promote schema construction in order to foster understanding while avoiding early working-memory overload.
requirements: Complex material whose element interactivity can be analysed and artificially reduced in a first instructional phase
A second phase in which all the information required for understanding is presented
constraints: A possible consequence of artificially reducing element interactivity may be an initial decrease in a student's capacity for understanding, per the thesis's own hypothesis statement
target_learners: Novice students learning complex information (e.g. apprentices at the Email training centre and BHP Ltd.)
target_learning_goals: Understanding of complex, high element-interactivity content and schema construction
examples: Experiments 1 and 2 used isolated and interacting elements instructional materials; Experiments 3 and 4 used oven baking and oven electrical circuit materials; Experiment 5 used fault finding tests

citation: Pollock, Edwina Jane. (2000). Assimilating Complex Information. PhD thesis, School of Education, University of New South Wales. https://hdl.handle.net/1959.4/17813
title: Schema construction as the mechanism underlying the isolated-interacting elements effect
description: The thesis proposes that schema construction is the mechanism underlying the success of the isolated-interacting elements instructional method. The first, isolated-elements phase is designed to allow learners to build component schemas without overwhelming working memory, and the second, interacting-elements phase then integrates them. The thesis states that evidence was provided in support of this proposal, linking the instructional sequence to the cognitive architecture in which schemas reduce working-memory load by storing organised knowledge in long term memory.
requirements: Instruction sequenced so that component schemas can be constructed before interacting elements are presented
constraints: The mechanism claim is supported within the five experiments of this thesis on complex technical material; the supplied text reports no test beyond these domains
target_learners: Novice and more experienced learners of complex technical information
target_learning_goals: Schema construction and understanding of complex, element-interactive material
examples: The thesis's experiments measured whether the isolated-then-interacting sequence produced better understanding, interpreted via schema construction

article_title: Assimilating complex information
citation: Pollock, Edwina Jane. (2000). Assimilating Complex Information. PhD thesis, School of Education, University of New South Wales. https://hdl.handle.net/1959.4/17813
title: Cognitive load theory as the generative framework of the thesis
description: The thesis is grounded in cognitive load theory, which is based on the assumption that features of human cognitive architecture have important implications for how we learn and understand. The theory distinguishes sources of cognitive load, including intrinsic load tied to element interactivity and extraneous load imposed by instructional design, and generates instructional techniques such as goal-free problems, worked examples, and split-attention, redundancy and modality effects. The five experiments reported in the thesis were generated by this theory.
requirements: Assumptions about human cognitive architecture, particularly limited working memory and long-term memory schema storage
constraints: The supplied text presents the theory as background framework; its detailed treatment of load sources lies in Chapter 2, not fully included in the supplied excerpt
target_learners: Learners of complex information across educational and training settings
target_learning_goals: Effective learning and understanding of complex material under working memory constraints
examples: The thesis's Chapter 2 lists instructional techniques generated by the theory, including goal free problems, worked examples, and the split attention, redundancy and modality effects

article_title: Assimilating complex information
citation: Pollock, Edwina Jane. (2000). Assimilating Complex Information. PhD thesis, School of Education, University of New South Wales. https://hdl.handle.net/1959.4/17813
title: Schemas reduce working memory load by incorporating interacting elements as single units
description: Within the thesis's account of cognitive architecture, human cognition circumvents the severely limited capacity of working memory by constructing schemas that organise elements of information categorically and store them in long term memory. Schemas shift the burden of storage to long term memory, and interacting elements that would otherwise overwhelm working memory can be incorporated in a schema that acts as a single element and imposes a minimal working memory load. This account underpins the thesis's rationale for reducing element interactivity during early instruction.
requirements: Prior knowledge organised into schemas stored in long term memory
constraints: The account is presented as the thesis's theoretical framing of memory and schema research, not as a new empirical result of the five experiments
target_learners: All learners processing complex, element-interactive information
target_learning_goals: Comprehension and learning of complex material within working memory limits
examples: The thesis illustrates the account with algebraic schemas: a/b = c can be transformed into a = cb and both equations processed easily in working memory by anyone competent at elementary algebra

citation: Hayo Reinders and Sorada Wattana. (2015). Affect and willingness to communicate in digital game-based learning. ReCALL, Volume 27, Issue 1. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0958344014000226

citation: Roessingh, H. (2006). BICS-CALP: An Introduction for Some, a Review for Others. TESL Canada Journal/Revue TESL du Canada, 23(2), Spring 2006. https://www.tesl.ca
title: Cummins' BICS-CALP framework as a four-quadrant developmental continuum overlaid on an iceberg metaphor
description: The article presents an adapted version of Cummins' (1982) framework in which context (embedded to reduced) forms the horizontal axis and cognitive demand (undemanding to demanding) the vertical axis, yielding four quadrants from BICS to CALP. The author overlays this on an iceberg image: "Like an iceberg, BICS may represent only about 10% of the overall proficiency of an academically competent learner." Quadrants 1-2 are BICS, quadrant 3 is transitional, and quadrant 4 involves metaphoric competence.
requirements: Understanding the role of first-language proficiency and age on arrival is described as key to understanding the relationship between above- and below-the-surface features
constraints: The author presents it as her own adaptation of Cummins' original framework and notes it is a work in progress

The author argues that "after BICS-level language has been acquired, the distances to the next benchmark or threshold become greater and more difficult to reach," and that quality and duration of ESL programming are crucial. She recommends continued support even for proficient older arrivals as they outgrow their L1.

article_title: A Theoretical Analysis of How Segmentation of Dynamic Visualizations Optimizes Students' Learning
citation: Spanjers, I. A. E., van Gog, T., & van Merriënboer, J. J. G. (2010). A Theoretical Analysis of How Segmentation of Dynamic Visualizations Optimizes Students' Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9135-6
title: Cognitive load / transience account: segmentation reduces extraneous load from information transience by dividing content into smaller units and providing processing pauses
description: This account, grounded in cognitive load theory and the time-based resource-sharing model of working memory, explains why transient dynamic visualizations can hinder learning: information is continuously replaced, so learners must maintain earlier information in working memory while processing new incoming information. Segmentation addresses this because "pauses between segments provide students with sufficient time to attend to necessary cognitive activities on the bit of information presented in the previous segment, without having to simultaneously attend to new incoming information." The review attributes the effectiveness of segmentation partly to this reduction of the co-occurrence of processing activities.
requirements: Applies to complex dynamic visualizations that are high in intrinsic load, where extraneous load must be decreased so learning is not hampered
constraints: Providing pauses increases total available learning time, but the review argues the effect is not simply due to learning time, citing Hasler et al. (2007) where learning time was equal across conditions
target_learners: Students learning from complex dynamic visualizations, especially novices
target_learning_goals: Understanding of processes and procedures depicted in animations and videos
examples: The review interprets the segmented-condition advantages in the Mayer and Chandler (2001), Moreno (2007), and Hasler et al. (2007) studies through this load-reduction mechanism

article_title: A Theoretical Analysis of How Segmentation of Dynamic Visualizations Optimizes Students' Learning
citation: Spanjers, I. A. E., van Gog, T., & van Merriënboer, J. J. G. (2010). A Theoretical Analysis of How Segmentation of Dynamic Visualizations Optimizes Students' Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9135-6
title: Event segmentation theory: people mentally segment dynamic visualizations during perception, and instructional segmentation can cue relevant event boundaries
description: Event segmentation theory (Zacks et al. 2007) "describes the processes underlying mental segmentation": people form event models in working memory, predict what happens next, and distinguish an event boundary when predictions and incoming sensory information differ too much. Physical and structural changes decrease predictability and mark boundaries; more extensive processing occurs at boundaries, so more information about them is stored in long-term memory. The review proposes that instructional segmentation works partly by cueing these boundaries — "rather than relying on students' ability to mentally segment the dynamic visualisations, this is done for them" — aiding perception of the underlying structure and chunking.
requirements: Event boundaries in the material should correspond to meaningful subevents or substeps of the depicted process or procedure
constraints: Students with higher levels of prior knowledge might not need these temporal cues or might even be hampered by them, because guidance must be reconciled with their available schemas
target_learners: Students learning from dynamic visualizations of processes and procedures, particularly novices
target_learning_goals: Perceiving the structure underlying a depicted process or procedure; remembering subevents and their temporal order
examples: The review links segmentation to Catrambone's work on labeled, visually isolated calculation substeps, which raised learning outcomes and prompted students to mention substeps in their procedure descriptions

Its core mechanism is that "Through game play, players are required to develop narrative accounts of scientific phenomena, a process that requires them to develop and argue scientific explanations." citation: Strobel, J., & van Barneveld, A. (2009). When is PBL More Effective? A Meta-synthesis of Meta-analyses Comparing PBL to Conventional Classrooms. Interdisciplinary Journal of Problem-Based Learning, 3(1). https://doi.org/10.7771/1541-5015.1046

description: The article's organizing approach is a qualitative meta-synthesis: rather than computing a new pooled estimate, it compares and contrasts the assumptions and findings of existing meta-analyses of PBL. The method treats divergent meta-analytic conclusions as data, explaining apparent contradictions (e.g., retention outcomes) by the type of outcome measured. As the article states, "This study used a qualitative meta-synthesis approach to compare and contrast the assumptions and findings of the meta-analytical research on the effectiveness of PBL."

citation: Su, Y.-L., & Reeve, J. (2011). A Meta-analysis of the Effectiveness of Intervention Programs Designed to Support Autonomy. Educational Psychology Review, 23, 159–188. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9142-7
title: Autonomy-supportive training programs as a class of interventions grounded in self-determination theory
description: The article treats autonomy-supportive training programs as an identifiable class of interventions designed to help people (teachers, parents, managers, health-care providers) support the autonomy of others, grounded in self-determination theory. Its purpose was "to determine whether training intervention programs designed to help people support the autonomy of others are effective and, second, to identify the set of conditions that allowed these interventions to be most effective." The framework organizes programs by trained elements, delivery format, and recipient characteristics.
requirements: Trainees must interact with others whose autonomy they can support (e.g., students, patients, employees)
constraints: Effectiveness conclusions rest on 19 studies, a small number the authors say warrants caution
target_learning_goals: supporting others' autonomy
adopting autonomy-supportive behaviors
examples: Included studies ranged from classroom teacher training (e.g., deCharms, Reeve) to medical-student and smoking-cessation interventions (e.g., Williams and colleagues)
key_sources: Su, Y.-L., & Reeve, J. (2011). A Meta-analysis of the Effectiveness of Intervention Programs Designed to Support Autonomy. Educational Psychology Review, 23, 159–188. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9142-7

article_title: Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design
citation: Sweller, J., van Merrienboer, J.J.G. & Paas, F.G.W.C. (1998). Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1022193728205
title: Cognitive load theory's model of human cognitive architecture: limited working memory with modality-based subcomponents and unlimited long-term memory holding schemas
description: The article's organizing framework is a model of human cognitive architecture underpinning cognitive load theory. It assumes "a limited capacity working memory that includes partially independent subcomponents to deal with auditory/verbal material and visual/2- or 3-dimensional information" alongside "an effectively unlimited long-term memory, holding schemas that vary in their degree of automation." These structures and functions are the basis from which the theory derives its instructional guidelines.
requirements: Instructional applications must respect the limited capacity of working memory when presenting information
constraints: The architecture is stated as the theory's assumption, not as a directly tested finding in the text available
target_learners: All learners processing new instructional material
target_learning_goals: Schema construction and automation in domain learning
key_sources: Sweller, J., van Merrienboer, J.J.G. & Paas, F.G.W.C. (1998). Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1022193728205

article_title: Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design
citation: Sweller, J., van Merrienboer, J.J.G. & Paas, F.G.W.C. (1998). Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1022193728205
title: Design instruction to reduce working memory load and encourage schema construction
description: The article's central design principle is that instruction should be built on "the assumption that working memory load should be reduced and schema construction encouraged." Because working memory is limited while schema construction drives learning, presentation of information should be arranged to lower unnecessary load and support schema building. The article reports that a variety of novel instructional procedures were designed on this basis.
requirements: Instructional designers must know which activities impose working memory load and which support schema construction
target_learners: All learners of instructional materials designed under cognitive load theory
target_learning_goals: Optimizing intellectual performance through schema construction
examples: The article states that cognitive architecture structures "have been used to design a variety of novel instructional procedures" based on the load-reduction and schema-construction assumption
key_sources: Sweller, J., van Merrienboer, J.J.G. & Paas, F.G.W.C. (1998). Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1022193728205

article_title: Benefits and Pitfalls of Multimedia and Interactive Features in Technology-Enhanced Storybooks
citation: Takacs, Z. K., Swart, E. K., & Bus, A. G. (2015). Benefits and Pitfalls of Multimedia and Interactive Features in Technology-Enhanced Storybooks: A Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research, 85(4), 698-739. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654314566989
title: Cognitive processing account: dual-channel multimedia integration helps, extraneous interactivity overloads young children's working memory
description: The article interprets its findings through the cognitive theory of multimedia learning and cognitive load theory. Dual coding theory holds that "verbal and nonverbal information are processed in two separate but interconnected channels," so congruent animation, music, and sound support comprehension rather than overload. Conversely, the coherence effect predicts deeper learning when extraneous materials are excluded; interactive features such as games and hotspots may act as seductive extraneous material, forcing task switching between story comprehension and play that places excessive load on young children's limited working memory.
requirements: Multimedia additions must be congruent with the narration to support rather than distract from comprehension
constraints: Even story-relevant interactive features may disturb comprehension because comprehending and playing are fundamentally different tasks requiring switching
target_learning_goals: story comprehension
vocabulary learning
code-related literacy skills
examples: The meta-analysis tested these predictions by contrasting multimedia-only, interactive-only, and multimedia-interactive stories across 43 studies
key_sources: Takacs, Z. K., Swart, E. K., & Bus, A. G. (2015). Benefits and Pitfalls of Multimedia and Interactive Features in Technology-Enhanced Storybooks: A Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research, 85(4), 698-739. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654314566989

article_title: SECOND LANGUAGE ANXIETY AND ACHIEVEMENT
citation: Yasser Teimouri, Julia Goetze, and Luke Plonsky. (2019). SECOND LANGUAGE ANXIETY AND ACHIEVEMENT: A META-ANALYSIS. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 41, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263118000311
title: Meta-analytic corpus of 97 reports, 105 independent samples, and 216 effect sizes on L2 anxiety and achievement
description: The study assembled a meta-analytic dataset on L2 anxiety and achievement. Following a comprehensive search, "a sample of 97 reports were identified, contributing a total of 105 independent samples (N = 19,933) from 23 countries," yielding 216 effect sizes (correlations). The corpus underpins the aggregate estimate and moderator analyses. The study earned an Open Data badge, with materials available at the IRIS database.
requirements: Comprehensive search to identify eligible reports of the anxiety–achievement relationship
target_learners: second language learners across 23 countries and multiple educational levels
target_learning_goals: second language achievement
examples: 97 reports contributing 105 independent samples (N = 19,933) from 23 countries
key_sources: Yasser Teimouri, Julia Goetze, and Luke Plonsky. (2019). SECOND LANGUAGE ANXIETY AND ACHIEVEMENT: A META-ANALYSIS. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 41, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263118000311

citation: Yasser Teimouri, Julia Goetze, and Luke Plonsky. (2019). SECOND LANGUAGE ANXIETY AND ACHIEVEMENT: A META-ANALYSIS. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 41, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263118000311
title: L2 anxiety as a negatively acting affective variable in L2 learning with (non)linguistic moderators
description: The article frames L2 anxiety as an affective variable with a demonstrably negative role in L2 learning, moderated by linguistic and nonlinguistic variables. It states the study "provides firm evidence for both the negative role of L2 anxiety in L2 learning and the moderating effects of a number of (non)linguistic variables." The framework builds on decades of empirical and theoretical attention to L2 anxiety and its relationship with achievement.
requirements: Measurement of both anxiety (various types) and language achievement to estimate the relationship
constraints: Effect sizes vary across achievement measure types, educational levels, target languages, and anxiety types, so the negative association is not uniform
target_learning_goals: second language achievement
examples: Meta-analysis of 216 correlations yielding a mean r = −.36

article_title: The effectiveness of peer tutoring in further and higher education: A typology and review of the literature
citation: Topping, K.J. (1996). The effectiveness of peer tutoring in further and higher education: A typology and review of the literature. Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00138870
title: A typology of peer tutoring in further and higher education
description: The article provides a clear definition and typology of peer tutoring as an organizing framework for the field. It argues that "The increasing use of peer tutoring in this context necessitates a clear definition and typology, which are outlined", and the review is organized around "the many different types and formats of peer tutoring within colleges and universities". The typology serves to structure the review of effectiveness research across these varied formats.
requirements: A clear definition and typology of peer tutoring is needed to make sense of the increasing use of peer tutoring in further and higher education.
target_learners: students in further and higher education (colleges and universities)
target_learning_goals: academic learning outcomes supported through peer tutoring arrangements
examples: The review uses the typology to organize the substantial existing research on the effectiveness of the many different types and formats of peer tutoring within colleges and universities.

article_title: Effectiveness of school-based programs to reduce bullying: a systematic and meta-analytic review
citation: Maria M. Ttofi, David P. Farrington. (2011). Effectiveness of school-based programs to reduce bullying: a systematic and meta-analytic review. J Exp Criminol. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11292-010-9109-1
title: Systematic review corpus of 622 reports yielding 53 program evaluations and 44 meta-analyzable effect sizes
description: The review assembled an evidence corpus by hand-searching all volumes of 35 journals from 1983 to the end of May 2009 and 18 electronic databases, including non-English reports and unpublished work. Of "622 reports concerned with bullying prevention", 89 reports describing 53 different program evaluations were included, and 44 provided calculable effect sizes for bullying or victimization. Evaluations spanned four design types: randomized experiments, before-and-after intervention-control comparisons, other intervention-control comparisons, and age-cohort designs.
requirements: Studies must compare an intervention group receiving an anti-bullying program with a control group that did not receive it
constraints: Nine evaluations (in 12 reports) were excluded from the meta-analysis due to missing values, lack of data, or implausible effect sizes
target_learners: school students in primary and secondary schools
target_learning_goals: reduction of bullying behavior
reduction of peer victimization
examples: Included programs range from the Olweus Bullying Prevention Program evaluations in Norway to the KiVa program, Steps to Respect, and the Sheffield project
key_sources: Maria M. Ttofi, David P. Farrington. (2011). Effectiveness of school-based programs to reduce bullying: a systematic and meta-analytic review. J Exp Criminol. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11292-010-9109-1

article_title: Dynamic Assessment of Young Children: Educational and Intervention Perspectives
citation: Tzuriel, D. (2000). Dynamic Assessment of Young Children: Educational and Intervention Perspectives. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1009032414088
title: Dynamic/interactive assessment grounded in Vygotsky's zone of proximal development and Feuerstein's mediated learning experience
description: Dynamic/interactive assessment (DA) is an assessment approach motivated by the inadequacy of conventional static tests, which fail "to provide accurate information about the individual's learning ability, specific deficient functions, change processes, and mediational strategies that are responsible for cognitive modifiability." The review states that "the theoretical foundations of the presented research derive from Vygotsky's sociocultural theory, specifically the zone of proximal development concept, and Feuerstein's mediated learning experience theory." DA is used with young children in educational and intervention contexts to assess learning potential rather than static performance.
requirements: An examiner mediates during assessment so that change processes and mediational strategies responsible for cognitive modifiability can be observed, rather than only static performance.
constraints: The review notes that crucial issues of cost-effectiveness, training, reliability and validity, and generalization remain to be addressed.
target_learning_goals: assessing learning potential and cognitive modifiability
learning how to learn skills
key_sources: Tzuriel, D. (2000). Dynamic Assessment of Young Children: Educational and Intervention Perspectives. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1009032414088

article_title: Dynamic Assessment of Young Children: Educational and Intervention Perspectives
citation: Tzuriel, D. (2000). Dynamic Assessment of Young Children: Educational and Intervention Perspectives. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1009032414088
title: Cognitive Modifiability Battery (CMB): a dynamic assessment and intervention instrument
description: The Cognitive Modifiability Battery (CMB) is a dynamic instrument named in the review's reference list as "The Cognitive Modifiability Battery (CMB): Assessment and Intervention-Instruction Manual" (Tzuriel, 1995a). It is cited both as a dynamic assessment instrument and, in conference papers listed by the review, as an intervention tool used in clinical and educational work with children with complex learning difficulties and in speech language therapy.
requirements: Use requires the instrument's instruction manual and training in dynamic assessment procedures.
target_learning_goals: assessment of cognitive modifiability
dynamic assessment-based intervention

article_title: Dynamic Assessment of Young Children: Educational and Intervention Perspectives
citation: Tzuriel, D. (2000). Dynamic Assessment of Young Children: Educational and Intervention Perspectives. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1009032414088
title: Use dynamic assessment with young children because treatment decisions should be made as early as possible
description: The review recommends dynamic assessment for young children because early identification matters: "a growing need for DA with young children has emerged recently because decisions about treatment should be made as early as possible." Static testing alone does not yield the information about learning ability and change processes needed for such early decisions, so DA is positioned as the assessment approach suited to early educational and intervention decision-making.
requirements: Examiners trained in dynamic assessment and mediational strategies are needed to administer DA with young children.
constraints: The review flags cost-effectiveness, training, reliability and validity, and generalization as crucial open issues for DA practice.
target_learning_goals: early identification of learning potential
informing early treatment decisions

article_title: Blueprints for complex learning: The 4C/ID-model
citation: van Merriënboer, J.J.G., Clark, R.E. & de Croock, M.B.M. (2002). Blueprints for complex learning: The 4C/ID-model. ETR&D. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02504993
title: The 4C/ID-model: a four-component instructional design system for training complex skills
description: The article describes the four-component instructional design system (4C/ID-model), developed originally by van Merriënboer and others in the early 1990s for the design of training programs for complex skills. The model structures training blueprints for complex learning around four interrelated components and specifies instructional methods for each component coupled to the basic learning processes involved in complex learning. The article presents the model's blueprint structure and illustrates it with a worked-out example.
requirements: Designers must produce training blueprints for complex learning that include all four interrelated components
constraints: The model was developed for the design of training programs for complex skills
target_learning_goals: complex skill acquisition and transfer
examples: A fully worked-out example of a training blueprint for searching for literature is provided in the article
key_sources: van Merriënboer, J.J.G., Clark, R.E. & de Croock, M.B.M. (2002). Blueprints for complex learning: The 4C/ID-model. ETR&D. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02504993

article_title: Blueprints for complex learning: The 4C/ID-model
citation: van Merriënboer, J.J.G., Clark, R.E. & de Croock, M.B.M. (2002). Blueprints for complex learning: The 4C/ID-model. ETR&D. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02504993
title: Couple instructional methods for each component to the basic learning processes involved in complex learning
description: In the 4C/ID approach, instructional methods are not chosen arbitrarily for each blueprint component; the article states that "Instructional methods for each component are coupled to the basic learning processes involved in complex learning". This principle directs designers to select methods for learning tasks, supportive information, just-in-time information, and part-task practice by reference to the learning processes those methods must support.
requirements: Designers must identify the basic learning processes involved in complex learning before selecting instructional methods for each component
target_learning_goals: complex skill acquisition
examples: The article's worked-out training blueprint for searching for literature applies this coupling of methods to learning processes
key_sources: van Merriënboer, J.J.G., Clark, R.E. & de Croock, M.B.M. (2002). Blueprints for complex learning: The 4C/ID-model. ETR&D. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02504993

title: Worked-out training blueprint for searching for literature
description: The article provides "a fully worked-out example of a training blueprint for 'searching for literature'" as a concrete instantiation of the 4C/ID-model. The blueprint demonstrates how the four components and their associated instructional methods are arranged in an actual training design for a complex skill, serving as a model designers can study when constructing their own blueprints.
requirements: Must be read alongside the four-component blueprint structure to serve as a design exemplar
constraints: The worked example targets the domain of searching for literature
target_learning_goals: literature searching as a complex skill

title: Training blueprint structure for complex learning with associated instructional methods
description: The article discusses "the structure of training blueprints for complex learning and associated instructional methods". A blueprint in this pattern is a design document that lays out the four interrelated components — learning tasks, supportive information, just-in-time information, and part-task practice — together with the instructional methods attached to each, providing the overall architecture for a training program for complex skills.
requirements: Blueprints must include the four interrelated components and associated instructional methods
constraints: Applies to complex learning rather than simple task training

article_title: The Four-Component Instructional Design Model : Multimedia Principles in Environments for Complex Learning
citation: Jeroen J. G. van Merriënboer and Liesbeth Kester. (2005). The Four-Component Instructional Design Model : Multimedia Principles in Environments for Complex Learning. The Cambridge Handbook of Multimedia Learning, pp. 71-94. https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511816819.006
title: The 4C-ID model claims four components are necessary to realize complex learning
description: The chapter presents the Four-Component Instructional Design (4C-ID) model as a framework for designing environments for complex learning. As the abstract states, "The Four-Component Instructional Design (4C-ID) model claims that four components are necessary to realize complex learning: (1) learning tasks, (2) supportive information, (3) procedural information, and (4) part-task practice." The chapter uses this framework to organize multimedia design guidance, relating multimedia principles to each of the four components.
requirements: Instruction for complex learning must include learning tasks, supportive information, procedural information, and part-task practice as distinct components
target_learning_goals: Complex learning integrating multiple knowledge and skill components
key_sources: Jeroen J. G. van Merriënboer and Liesbeth Kester. (2005). The Four-Component Instructional Design Model : Multimedia Principles in Environments for Complex Learning. The Cambridge Handbook of Multimedia Learning, pp. 71-94. https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511816819.006

article_title: The Four-Component Instructional Design Model : Multimedia Principles in Environments for Complex Learning
citation: Jeroen J. G. van Merriënboer and Liesbeth Kester. (2005). The Four-Component Instructional Design Model : Multimedia Principles in Environments for Complex Learning. The Cambridge Handbook of Multimedia Learning, pp. 71-94. https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511816819.006
title: Four learning processes are each facilitated by multimedia principles tied to one 4C-ID component
description: The chapter organizes 14 multimedia principles by mapping each of the four 4C-ID components to a distinct learning process and a matching multimedia environment. The abstract states the chapter "relates 14 multimedia principles to each of the four components," with inductive learning for learning tasks, elaboration and mindful abstraction for supportive information, knowledge compilation for procedural information, and psychological strengthening for part-task practice.
requirements: Multimedia principles must be selected to match the learning process each component is intended to facilitate
constraints: The framework is presented for design of multimedia learning environments; research implications and limitations are discussed in the chapter
target_learning_goals: Complex skill acquisition through coordinated multimedia environments

title: Electronic Performance Support Systems (EPSSs) as the environment for consulting procedural information
description: The chapter assigns Electronic Performance Support Systems (EPSSs) to the procedural-information component of 4C-ID. The abstract states: "They may consult procedural information in Electronic Performance Support Systems (EPSSs), where principles facilitate a process of knowledge compilation." In this arrangement, EPSSs serve as just-in-time repositories of procedural information that learners consult while working on tasks, with multimedia principles chosen to support knowledge compilation.
requirements: An EPSS in which procedural information can be consulted during task performance
target_learning_goals: Knowledge compilation of procedural information

title: Drill and practice Computer-Based Training (CBT) programs for part-task practice
description: The chapter assigns drill and practice Computer-Based Training (CBT) programs to the part-task-practice component of 4C-ID. The abstract states: "Finally, they may be involved in part-task practice with drill and practice Computer-Based Training (CBT) programs, where principles facilitate a process of psychological strengthening." CBT programs thus serve as the multimedia environment in which constituent skills are practiced to automaticity, with multimedia principles selected to support strengthening.

target_learning_goals: Automatization of recurring skill aspects through psychological strengthening

citation: Van Meter, P., Garner, J. (2005). The Promise and Practice of Learner-Generated Drawing: Literature Review and Synthesis. Educ Psychol Rev 17, 285–325. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-005-8136-3
title: A theoretical framework for learner-generated drawing built by extending Mayer's processes of selection, organization, and integration
description: The article proposes a theoretical framework for understanding the drawing strategy by extending R. E. Mayer's (1993) theoretical processes of selection, organization, and integration. The framework is intended to guide and organize future research efforts, and earlier proposed hypotheses are incorporated into its explanatory constructs. It serves as the review's organizing account of how learner-generated drawing supports learning.
requirements: The framework is grounded in current understandings of cognitive and strategic processing, as the review states it organizes hypotheses around such understandings.
target_learners: learners using drawing as a learning strategy across content areas
target_learning_goals: learning from text through construction of representative illustrations
examples: The review incorporates its earlier proposed hypotheses into the explanatory constructs of the theoretical perspective.

article_title: The Promise and Practice of Learner-Generated Drawing: Literature Review and Synthesis
citation: Van Meter, P., Garner, J. (2005). The Promise and Practice of Learner-Generated Drawing: Literature Review and Synthesis. Educ Psychol Rev 17, 285–325. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-005-8136-3
title: Learner-generated drawing as a learning strategy in which learners construct representative illustrations
description: Learner-generated drawing is a strategy in which learners construct representative illustrations in support of learning goals. The article reviews both applied and empirical literature on this strategy with the purpose of stimulating research on it. It treats the strategy as a comprehension strategy whose effectiveness depends on cognitive and strategic processing, as reflected in its key words: drawing, learning strategy, comprehension strategy, and cognitive processes.
requirements: Learners must construct representative illustrations in support of learning goals.
target_learners: learners from primary grades through adults, as represented in the reviewed literature
target_learning_goals: comprehension and learning from text
examples: The review covers applied readings and empirical studies of learners constructing illustrations to support learning goals.

article_title: Explicit Instruction and Input Processing
citation: Bill VanPatten and Teresa Cadierno. (1993). Explicit Instruction and Input Processing. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 15, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263100011979
title: Input processing: learner strategies in processing input as the basis for determining explicit instruction
description: Input processing is the framework the article uses to link second language acquisition to how learners process input data. It holds that "learner strategies in input processing" should serve as "the starting point for determining what explicit instruction should look like." Processing instruction operationalizes this by having learners practice processing input rather than producing output after grammar explanation.
requirements: Instruction must be designed around identified learner strategies in input processing.
target_learners: second language learners in classroom instruction
target_learning_goals: grammatical interpretation and production of the targeted linguistic form
examples: The experiment's processing instruction treatment involved "explanation and practice/experience processing input data."
key_sources: Bill VanPatten and Teresa Cadierno. (1993). Explicit Instruction and Input Processing. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 15, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263100011979

article_title: Explicit Instruction and Input Processing
citation: Bill VanPatten and Teresa Cadierno. (1993). Explicit Instruction and Input Processing. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 15, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263100011979
title: Design explicit grammar instruction around input processing rather than output practice
description: The article recommends structuring explicit grammar instruction so that, after explanation, learners practice processing input data instead of practicing output. This processing instruction approach "involves explanation and practice/experience processing input data, taking learner strategies in input processing as the starting point," in contrast to traditional instruction's explanation plus output practice.
requirements: A grammatical point to target and knowledge of the learner strategies in input processing for that point.
target_learning_goals: accurate comprehension and production of targeted grammatical forms
examples: The study's processing instruction condition paired grammatical explanation with input-processing practice activities.

citation: Bill VanPatten and Teresa Cadierno. (1993). Explicit Instruction and Input Processing. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 15, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263100011979
title: Sentence-level interpretation and production tasks as pretest-posttest measures of grammar instruction effects
description: This element is the assessment battery used in the experiment: pretest and posttest measures "involving both a sentence-level interpretation (comprehension) task and a sentence-level production task," with scores "submitted to an analysis of variance." It operationalizes comprehension and production outcomes for comparing explicit instruction treatments.
requirements: Target grammatical material expressible at the sentence level for both interpretation and production testing.
target_learners: second language learners in instructed settings
target_learning_goals: measuring sentence-level comprehension and production of a grammatical form

article_title: Sex Differences in Performance on the Mathematics Section of the Scholastic Aptitude Test: A Bidirectional Validity Study
citation: Howard Wainer, Linda Steinberg. (1992). Sex Differences in Performance on the Mathematics Section of the Scholastic Aptitude Test: A Bidirectional Validity Study. Harvard Educational Review. https://doi.org/10.17763/haer.62.3.1p1555011301r133
title: Bidirectional validity study: evaluating a test by matching examinees on the criterion the test predicts
description: The bidirectional validity approach examines a test's fairness by working backward from the criterion: examinees are matched on the outcome the test is supposed to predict (here, type of math course taken and grade received in first-year college math), and their test scores are compared. Wainer and Steinberg apply it to the SAT-M with "almost 47,000 men and women" and complement it with a prospective regression analysis of the same data. Differences in test scores among equally performing examinees indicate differences in the test's predictive validity across groups.
requirements: Requires a large dataset linking test scores to the criterion performance (course taken and grade received) so examinees can be matched on outcome.
constraints: The article states the data do not allow conclusions about the cause of the observed score differences.
target_learners: college students taking first-year mathematics courses
target_learning_goals: accurate and equitable prediction of college mathematics performance from admissions test scores
examples: Matching almost 47,000 men and women on type of math course taken and grade received, then comparing SAT-M scores; a prospective regression analysis of the same data.
key_sources: Howard Wainer, Linda Steinberg. (1992). Sex Differences in Performance on the Mathematics Section of the Scholastic Aptitude Test: A Bidirectional Validity Study. Harvard Educational Review. https://doi.org/10.17763/haer.62.3.1p1555011301r133

article_title: Design-based research and technology-enhanced learning environments
citation: Wang, F., & Hannafin, M. J. (2005). Design-based research and technology-enhanced learning environments. ETR&D, 53, 5–23. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02504682
title: The article defines design-based research and identifies its characteristics
description: The article undertakes to define design-based research and identify its characteristics as a methodology for technology-enhanced learning environments. According to the abstract, the authors "define and identify characteristics of design-based research", establishing what counts as DBR and how it differs from other educational research approaches. This definitional work organizes the paper's subsequent treatment of DBR's importance, implementation principles, and challenges for TELE development.
requirements: The methodology must be defined and its characteristics identified before it can be applied to TELE research and design, as the article's stated purpose requires.
target_learners: Educational researchers and instructional designers working with technology-enhanced learning environments
target_learning_goals: Understanding and applying design-based research methodology in TELE research and design
key_sources: Wang, F., & Hannafin, M. J. (2005). Design-based research and technology-enhanced learning environments. ETR&D, 53, 5–23. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02504682

citation: Wang, F., & Hannafin, M. J. (2005). Design-based research and technology-enhanced learning environments. ETR&D, 53, 5–23. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02504682
title: Implement design-based research with TELEs according to proposed principles
description: The article proposes principles for implementing design-based research in work on technology-enhanced learning environments. The abstract states that the authors "propose principles for implementing design-based research with TELEs", offering guidance for researchers who conduct DBR studies of TELEs. These principles are intended to make DBR implementation with TELEs systematic and disciplined.
requirements: Researchers implementing DBR with TELEs should follow the article's proposed principles for that implementation.

article_title: Mindfulness-based interventions in schoolsâ€”a systematic review and meta-analysis
citation: Charlotte Zenner, Solveig Herrnleben-Kurz and Harald Walach. (2014). Mindfulness-based interventions in schools—a systematic review and meta-analysis. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2014.00603
title: Common components of school-based mindfulness intervention programs
description: The review catalogued the components of the 24 school-based mindfulness programs. All programs used breath awareness, described as "the traditional essential exercise," and most combined multiple components including working with thoughts and emotions, psycho-education, awareness of senses and daily-life practices, and group discussion. Programs drew on mindfulness theory (100%), often linked to MBSR, MBCT, DBT, and ACT, and two thirds used manualized programs such as MindfulSchools or Learning to BREATHE.
requirements: Programs need well defined goals, explicit guidelines, training, and quality control described for evaluation, per Weare and Nind as cited by the review
constraints: Many manualized programs lacked sufficient guidance material for implementation, and only two had an enduring presence of more than five years
target_learners: pupils and students from grade 1 to 12
target_learning_goals: cultivating mindfulness, attentional and emotional self-regulation, and stress resilience
examples: Interventions varied from 4 to 24 weeks (median 8), typically 45 min once a week, totaling 160 to 3700 min of practice with a median of 420 min
key_sources: Charlotte Zenner, Solveig Herrnleben-Kurz and Harald Walach. (2014). Mindfulness-based interventions in schools—a systematic review and meta-analysis. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2014.00603

article_title: Mindfulness-based interventions in schoolsâ€”a systematic review and meta-analysis

title: Five-domain outcome taxonomy for evaluating school-based mindfulness interventions
description: The review organizes outcome measures into five domains: perceived stress and coping (S) and emotional problems (E) measured via self-report scales, factors of resilience (R) via self-report, cognitive performance (C) measured by performance tests, and third person ratings (T) from parent and teacher questionnaires. This taxonomy structures both the review's domain-specific effect size analysis and its overview of the measures used across studies, addressing the diversity of outcome measures in the field.
requirements: Outcome measures must be quantitative data referring to psychological aspects, per the review's inclusion criteria
constraints: Reliability of measures could not be used to adjust effect sizes because authors did not consistently report reliability and reported measures were not compatible
target_learners: pupils and students from grade 1 to 12
target_learning_goals: psychological outcomes of mindfulness training: stress, resilience, emotional problems, cognitive performance
examples: Cognitive performance was mostly quantified by attention tests; one study used a creativity test and another a mind wandering paradigm

article_title: SYNCHRONOUS COMPUTER-MEDIATED COMMUNICATION AND INTERACTION
citation: Nicole Ziegler. (2016). SYNCHRONOUS COMPUTER-MEDIATED COMMUNICATION AND INTERACTION: A Meta-Analysis. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, 38(3). https://doi.org/10.1017/S027226311500025X
title: Use interaction in either SCMC or FTF contexts to support L2 development, choosing mode by target outcome
description: This principle holds that conversational interaction supports second language development in both synchronous computer-mediated and face-to-face modes, so practitioners need not reserve interaction for physical classrooms. Because the meta-analysis found "no significant differences between SCMC and FTF" overall, mode selection can follow practical constraints. However, outcome type matters: SCMC showed advantages for "productive and written measures" while FTF favored "receptive and oral learning outcomes."
requirements: Interaction must occur in either synchronous computer-mediated or face-to-face communication contexts, as both were associated with significant L2 development
constraints: Mode-specific advantages are small; overall SCMC–FTF differences were not statistically significant
target_learners: second language learners in the studies meta-analyzed (1990–2012)
target_learning_goals: second language development across productive, written, receptive, and oral outcomes
examples: The meta-analysis synthesized 14 primary studies (journal articles and dissertations, 1990–2012) comparing interaction effectiveness across SCMC and FTF contexts
key_sources: Nicole Ziegler. (2016). SYNCHRONOUS COMPUTER-MEDIATED COMMUNICATION AND INTERACTION: A Meta-Analysis. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, 38(3). https://doi.org/10.1017/S027226311500025X

article_title: Are All Program Elements Created Equal? Relations Between Specific Social and Emotional Learning Components and Teacher–Student Classroom Interaction Quality
citation: Abry, T., Rimm-Kaufman, S.E. & Curby, T.W. (2017). Are All Program Elements Created Equal? Relations Between Specific Social and Emotional Learning Components and Teacher–Student Classroom Interaction Quality. Prevention Science, 18, 193–203. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11121-016-0743-3
title: Responsive Classroom core component indices: Morning Meeting, Rule Creation, Interactive Modeling, and Academic Choice
description: The Responsive Classroom approach is a school-based social and emotional learning program whose implementation was indexed through four core components. The article states that "Indices of teachers' implementation of Morning Meeting, Rule Creation, Interactive Modeling, and Academic Choice were derived from a combination of teacher-reported surveys and classroom observations." These component indices served as predictors of teacher–student classroom interaction quality among 143 treatment teachers in third, fourth, and fifth grade classrooms within a randomized controlled trial.
requirements: Implementation measured via a combination of teacher-reported surveys and classroom observations
target_learners: Elementary school students in third, fourth, and fifth grade
target_learning_goals: Social and emotional learning
Quality of teacher–student classroom interactions
examples: Ratings of teacher–student classroom interactions were aggregated across five observations conducted throughout the school year.

article_title: Are All Program Elements Created Equal? Relations Between Specific Social and Emotional Learning Components and Teacher–Student Classroom Interaction Quality
citation: Abry, T., Rimm-Kaufman, S.E. & Curby, T.W. (2017). Are All Program Elements Created Equal? Relations Between Specific Social and Emotional Learning Components and Teacher–Student Classroom Interaction Quality. Prevention Science, 18, 193–203. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11121-016-0743-3
title: Examine individual program components to identify active ingredients for intervention optimization and teacher professional development
description: Rather than treating a social and emotional learning program as an undifferentiated package, the article recommends analyzing variation in teachers' implementation of individual program components to find which carry the greatest leverage. As the authors state, "Results highlight the value of examining individual program components toward the identification of program active ingredients that can inform intervention optimization and teacher professional development." This component-level lens showed the four Responsive Classroom components were not equally related to interaction quality.
requirements: Implementation data on individual program components, derived from teacher-reported surveys and classroom observations
constraints: Findings come from variation in implementation among treatment teachers within one randomized controlled trial, not from manipulating components experimentally
target_learners: Elementary school students in grade 3–5 classrooms
target_learning_goals: Improving emotional, organizational, and instructional quality of teacher–student interactions
examples: The study indexed four Responsive Classroom components and found Morning Meeting, Rule Creation, Interactive Modeling, and Academic Choice differed in their relations to interaction quality.

article_title: The impact of educational chatbot on student learning experience
citation: Ait Baha, T., El Hajji, M., Es-Saady, Y., & Fadili, H. (2024). The impact of educational chatbot on student learning experience. Education and Information Technologies. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10639-023-12166-w
title: NLP- and deep-learning-based educational chatbot for teaching Logo to secondary school learners
description: The article presents an experimental educational chatbot built on recent Natural Language Processing and deep learning techniques, intended to instruct secondary school learners Logo, an educational programming language. It was "implemented and evaluated in Moroccan public schools" with support from teachers of the Regional Center for Education and Training Professions of Souss Massa. Its intended function is providing replies suited to each learner's specific needs within an e-learning setting.

constraints: Evaluated only with secondary school learners in Moroccan public schools learning Logo

article_title: ChatGPT: Revolutionizing student achievement in the electronic magnetism unit for eleventh-grade students in Emirates schools
citation: Alneyadi, S., & Wardat, Y. (2023). ChatGPT: Revolutionizing student achievement in the electronic magnetism unit for eleventh-grade students in Emirates schools. Contemporary Educational Technology, 15(4), ep448. https://doi.org/10.30935/cedtech/13417
title: Use language models like ChatGPT as supplementary resources rather than replacements for traditional teaching
description: The article recommends that language models support, not substitute for, conventional instruction. It states that because such models "may occasionally provide inaccurate or incomplete information," they "should be used as supplementary resources rather than replacements for traditional teaching and learning methods." The study's experimental group used ChatGPT alongside regular instruction whenever students needed help with course content.
requirements: Teachers must remain involved, since model outputs may be inaccurate or incomplete and require verification from credible sources.
constraints: The article notes ethical considerations related to data privacy and bias must be addressed when using language models in education.

target_learning_goals: Understanding electronic magnetism concepts and improving physics achievement
examples: The experimental group was instructed to utilize ChatGPT whenever they required assistance with the course content during the study period, while the control group received traditional teaching.

title: 25-item electronic magnetism cognitive achievement test
description: The study's achievement instrument is a test of 25 multiple-choice items categorized by Bloom's taxonomy levels (remember, understand, apply, analyze), scored one mark per correct answer for a maximum of 25. article_title: ONE SIZE FITS ALL?: Recasts, Prompts, and L2 Learning
citation: Ahlem Ammar and Nina Spada. (2006). ONE SIZE FITS ALL?: Recasts, Prompts, and L2 Learning. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 28, Issue 4. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263106060268
title: Four-week form-focused intervention on third-person possessive determiners his and her
description: An instructional intervention delivered to grade 6 intensive ESL classes over 4 weeks, targeting the English third-person possessive determiners his and her, described in the article as "a difficult aspect of English grammar for these Francophone learners of English." Two experimental conditions embedded corrective feedback (recasts for one group, prompts for the other) while a control group received no such feedback. Learner knowledge was measured with written and oral tasks at three time points.
requirements: Delivered within intact grade 6 intensive ESL classes in the Montreal area
constraints: Targeted a single grammatical structure (his and her) rather than grammar broadly
target_learners: Grade 6 Francophone learners of English in intensive ESL programs
target_learning_goals: Accurate use of third-person possessive determiners his and her
examples: Sixty-four students in three intact classes were assigned to recast, prompt, and control conditions; testing occurred before, immediately after, and 4 weeks after the intervention

article_title: ONE SIZE FITS ALL?: Recasts, Prompts, and L2 Learning
citation: Ahlem Ammar and Nina Spada. (2006). ONE SIZE FITS ALL?: Recasts, Prompts, and L2 Learning. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 28, Issue 4. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263106060268
title: Match corrective feedback technique to learner proficiency: prefer prompts for lower-proficiency learners
description: The article's proficiency-moderated findings support tailoring oral corrective feedback to learner proficiency rather than applying one technique to all learners. Because "low-proficiency learners benefited significantly more from prompts than recasts," while high-proficiency learners benefited equally from both, prompts are the safer default for lower-proficiency learners, and recasts remain a viable option for higher-proficiency learners.
requirements: Teachers must be able to assess or distinguish learner proficiency levels when choosing feedback techniques
constraints: Evidence concerns one grammatical structure (his and her) with young Francophone ESL learners in intensive grade 6 classes; the article's available text does not establish generalization to other structures or populations
target_learners: Grade 6 intensive ESL learners of varying proficiency
target_learning_goals: Improving grammatical accuracy through oral corrective feedback
examples: In the study, prompts and recasts were embedded in instruction on his and her across three intact grade 6 classes over 4 weeks

article_title: Investigating the higher education institutions’ guidelines and policies regarding the use of generative AI in teaching, learning, research, and administration
citation: Yunjo An, Ji Hyun Yu and Shadarra James. (2025). Investigating the higher education institutions' guidelines and policies regarding the use of generative AI in teaching, learning, research, and administration. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-025-00507-3
title: Faculty GenAI guidance pattern: syllabus statements, course policy communication, and redesigned authentic/process-oriented assessments
description: The article identifies a recurring pattern in faculty-targeted GenAI guidelines: providing template syllabus statements (e.g., Stanford's three categories from "AI tools permitted freely" to "AI tools not permitted"), advising faculty to set and communicate course policies (54%), and redesigning assignments and assessments (48%). Specifically, "authentic assessments (e.g., real-world tasks, projects), process-oriented assessments (e.g., low-stakes writing, drafts, presentations, oral exams, portfolios), and assignments requiring higher-order thinking were commonly recommended". This pattern operationalizes institutional guidance for teaching in the GenAI era.
requirements: Faculty must establish and communicate course-specific GenAI policies to students through syllabi and assignment prompts
constraints: The article notes guidance for faculty can become burdensome since continuous revisions are recommended in the policies (citing McDonald et al., 2024)
target_learning_goals: academic integrity
assessment design in the era of GenAI
AI literacy
examples: Stanford University provided template syllabus statements in three categories; the University of Chicago provided examples in four categories; 48% of universities advised redesigning assignments and assessments

title: Institutions should adopt flexible, stakeholder-specific GenAI policies addressing both opportunities and challenges
description: The article concludes that GenAI guidelines in higher education are rapidly evolving and that institutions need "flexible, stakeholder-specific policies that address both the opportunities and challenges presented by this technology". Its analysis shows guidelines vary widely by audience — 94% of universities had faculty guidelines but only 18% had researcher guidelines and 14% staff/administrator guidelines — supporting tailoring policies to each stakeholder group rather than issuing one generic policy.
requirements: Policies must be regularly updated as GenAI tools and guidelines constantly evolve; clear roles and responsibilities among faculty, students, and administrators are needed
constraints: The article notes many existing AI guidelines are generic and do not specifically address issues caused by GenAI in higher education

academic integrity
privacy and data protection
examples: The study analyzed guidelines for five audiences separately and found faculty guidelines covered seven themes while staff/administrator guidelines covered three, all seven staff-targeted guidelines addressing privacy and data protection
