article_title: Assisting self-explanation prompts are more effective than open prompts when learning with multiple representations
citation: Berthold, K., Eysink, T.H.S. & Renkl, A. (2009). Assisting self-explanation prompts are more effective than open prompts when learning with multiple representations. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9051-z
title: Provide assisting self-explanation prompts (assistance-giving-assistance-withholding) rather than open prompts when learners study multiple representations
description: The article recommends that, for enhancing high-quality self-explanations and both procedural knowledge and conceptual understanding, assisting self-explanation prompts should be provided. These prompts embed self-explanation support in an "assistance-giving-assistance-withholding procedure", gradually withdrawing help as learners explain the connections among multiple representations. The recommendation rests on the experiment showing assisting prompts particularly fostered conceptual knowledge.

article_title: Kindergarten teachers develop phoneme awareness in low-income, inner-city classrooms
citation: Blachman, B.A., Ball, E.W., Black, R.S. & Tangel, D.M. (1994). Kindergarten teachers develop phoneme awareness in low-income, inner-city classrooms. Read Writ 6, 1–18. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01027275
title: Classroom teachers and teaching assistants — not only researchers — can deliver effective phoneme awareness instruction in kindergarten
description: The study's central design choice was to have phonological awareness instruction delivered "by kindergarten teachers and their teaching assistants" in ordinary low-income, inner-city classrooms, rather than by outside researchers. The significant post-intervention advantages on phoneme segmentation, letter knowledge, reading, and invented spelling indicate classroom staff can implement this instruction effectively. This supports embedding phoneme awareness training in regular kindergarten practice.
requirements: Kindergarten teachers and teaching assistants deliver the instruction in their own classrooms over an extended period (11 weeks in this study)
constraints: Evidence comes from low-income, inner-city kindergarten classrooms in an urban district in upstate New York
target_learners: Kindergarten children in low-income, inner-city schools
target_learning_goals: Phoneme awareness, letter name and letter sound knowledge, beginning reading, and invented spelling
examples: The intervention was provided in low-income, inner-city kindergarten classrooms by kindergarten teachers and their teaching assistants over 11 weeks

article_title: Developing the theory of formative assessment
citation: Black, P., & Wiliam, D. (2009). Developing the theory of formative assessment. Educ Asse Eval Acc, 21, 5–31. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11092-008-9068-5
title: A framework that supplies a rationale for formative assessment within theories of pedagogy and unifies the diverse set of practices described as formative.
description: The article proposes a framework whose purpose is twofold: to give formative assessment a rationale located within broader theories of pedagogy, and to unify the heterogeneous practices that have been called formative. The authors state that "This paper aims to offer such a rationale, within a framework which can also unify the diverse set of practices which have been described as formative." The framework is then used analytically to connect formative assessment with other pedagogic initiatives and with literatures on self-regulated learning and classroom discourse, and to guide teacher implementation work.
requirements: Serves as an organizing rationale for practices already described as formative; it presupposes the existing body of formative assessment practice it seeks to unify.
constraints: The article presents it as a rationale and unifying framework, not as an empirically tested model; the full text beyond the abstract was not accessible here.
target_learning_goals: Improving learning through formative assessment practices embedded in pedagogy
examples: The article states the framework is used to relate formative assessment to cognitive acceleration, dynamic assessment, self-regulated learning models, and classroom discourse.
key_sources: Black, P., & Wiliam, D. (2009). Developing the theory of formative assessment. Educ Asse Eval Acc, 21, 5–31. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11092-008-9068-5

article_title: Developing the theory of formative assessment
citation: Black, P., & Wiliam, D. (2009). Developing the theory of formative assessment. Educ Asse Eval Acc, 21, 5–31. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11092-008-9068-5
title: Formative assessment is related to cognitive acceleration, dynamic assessment, models of self-regulated learning, and classroom discourse within the proposed framework.
description: A second organizing contribution of the article is a set of theoretical linkages: the framework connects formative assessment to neighbouring pedagogic initiatives and research literatures. The abstract states: "The analysis is used to relate formative assessment both to other pedagogic initiatives, notably cognitive acceleration and dynamic assessment, and to some of the existing literature on models of self-regulated learning and on classroom discourse." This positions formative assessment not as an isolated assessment technique but as continuous with pedagogies that regulate and accelerate learning, with dynamic assessment traditions, with self-regulation models, and with classroom dialogue research.
requirements: The linkages depend on the article's unifying framework for formative assessment within pedagogy.
constraints: The article presents these as relations established by theoretical analysis, not as empirically demonstrated equivalences.
target_learners: School students in classrooms served by formative, dialogic, and cognitive-acceleration pedagogies
target_learning_goals: Regulating and developing learning through assessment, dialogue, and cognitive acceleration
examples: The article's keywords list the linked constructs: formative assessment, assessment for learning, dynamic assessment, self-regulation, cognitive acceleration, and dialogue.
key_sources: Black, P., & Wiliam, D. (2009). Developing the theory of formative assessment. Educ Asse Eval Acc, 21, 5–31. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11092-008-9068-5

article_title: Developing the theory of formative assessment
citation: Black, P., & Wiliam, D. (2009). Developing the theory of formative assessment. Educ Asse Eval Acc, 21, 5–31. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11092-008-9068-5
title: Use a theoretical framework of formative assessment to open up new ways of helping teachers implement formative practices more effectively.
description: The article recommends that developing theory for formative assessment should serve practice directly: a sound framework should both guide research and support teacher implementation. The abstract states the framework "should indicate potentially fruitful lines for further enquiry, whilst at the same time opening up new ways of helping teachers to implement formative practices more effectively." The principle is that theoretical clarification of formative assessment is a route to more effective professional support for teachers, not merely an academic exercise.
requirements: A coherent framework delimiting formative assessment within pedagogy, so that implementation support can be grounded in it.
constraints: The article states this as an intended payoff of the framework; it does not report tested implementation outcomes in the accessible text.
target_learning_goals: More effective classroom implementation of formative assessment practices
examples: The article frames its framework as serving both further enquiry and teacher implementation support.

article_title: Developing the theory of formative assessment
citation: Black, P., & Wiliam, D. (2009). Developing the theory of formative assessment. Educ Asse Eval Acc, 21, 5–31. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11092-008-9068-5
title: Success criteria and learning intentions as components of formative practice.
description: In a note, the article identifies explicitly communicated goals for learning as an important component of formative classroom practice: "The importance of “success criteria” and “learning intentions” was emphasised by Clarke (2001)." Success criteria and learning intentions function as elements that make the intended learning visible to students, supporting the regulation of learning that the article's framework treats as central to formative assessment. The article cites this emphasis rather than developing it at length in the accessible text.
requirements: Teachers must articulate learning intentions and success criteria so that students know what valued learning looks like.
constraints: The article attributes the emphasis to Clarke (2001) and does not elaborate implementation detail in the accessible text.
target_learners: School students whose teachers share learning intentions and success criteria
target_learning_goals: Clarifying intended learning and criteria for success to support self-regulation
examples: The article's note cites Clarke (2001) as the source emphasising success criteria and learning intentions.
key_sources: Black, P., & Wiliam, D. (2009). Developing the theory of formative assessment. Educ Asse Eval Acc, 21, 5–31. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11092-008-9068-5

article_title: Developing the theory of formative assessment
citation: Black, P., & Wiliam, D. (2009). Developing the theory of formative assessment. Educ Asse Eval Acc, 21, 5–31. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11092-008-9068-5
title: A working definition of learning as an experience-driven increase in capacities to respond in valued ways.
description: To anchor its framework, the article offers an explicit definition of learning in a note: "we would define learning as an increase, brought about by experience, in the capacities of an organism to react in valued ways in response to stimuli." The definition is offered defensively — the authors supply it for those who think defining formative assessment merely shifts the definitional burden onto the word learning. It makes valued response capacities, experience, and change over time the constituents of learning, which in turn delimits what counts as formative evidence of learning.
requirements: Any account of formative assessment needs a working definition of learning; this one ties learning to experience and to valued ways of responding.
constraints: The authors present it as a stipulated definition for a specific objection, not as an established empirical result.
target_learners: All learners in instructional settings addressed by the framework
target_learning_goals: Increasing learners' capacities to respond in valued ways
examples: The note supplies the definition in response to the objection that defining formative assessment merely moves the burden of definition onto the word learning.
key_sources: Black, P., & Wiliam, D. (2009). Developing the theory of formative assessment. Educ Asse Eval Acc, 21, 5–31. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11092-008-9068-5

article_title: Developing the theory of formative assessment
citation: Black, P., & Wiliam, D. (2009). Developing the theory of formative assessment. Educ Asse Eval Acc, 21, 5–31. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11092-008-9068-5
title: Growth rather than mastery as the preferred term for a focus on learning achievement in formative assessment.
description: In discussing self-regulation literature, the article makes a deliberate terminological choice. The note records that "Boekearts and Corno use two terms, growth and mastery, with both, apparently interchangeable, to stand for a focus on learning achievement; we have preferred the first of these here because mastery denotes a sense of completion whereas growth does not." The choice reflects a theoretical stance: formative assessment concerns ongoing development of learning rather than terminal attainment, so growth is the more apt term within the article's framework.
requirements: Writers on formative assessment and self-regulation should choose achievement-focus terminology consciously, since connotations differ.
constraints: The choice is argued on the connotations of the two words, not on empirical evidence.
target_learners: Researchers and teachers working with formative assessment and self-regulation frameworks
target_learning_goals: Conceptualising learning achievement as ongoing growth rather than completed mastery
examples: The article adopts Boekaerts and Corno's growth term while explaining why mastery was set aside.

article_title: A meta systematic review of artificial intelligence in higher education: a call for increased ethics, collaboration, and rigour
citation: Bond, M., Khosravi, H., De Laat, M., Bergdahl, N., Negrea, V., Oxley, E., Pham, P., Chong, S. W. & Siemens, G. (2024). A meta systematic review of artificial intelligence in higher education: a call for increased ethics, collaboration, and rigour. title: Zawacki-Richter et al.'s (2019) four-area AIEd typology used as the review's organising classification
description: This typology classifies AI-in-education research into four broad areas: Profiling and prediction, Intelligent Tutoring Systems, Assessment and Evaluation, and Adaptive Systems and Personalisation. The tertiary review adopted it as the starting coding frame, stating it coded the corpus "using Zawacki-Richter et al. 's (2019) typology ... as a starting point", with reviews not specifying a focus coded as General AIEd. Each area is substantively described in the article, e.g. Profiling and Prediction covers dropout prediction and student models, while Adaptive Systems and Personalisation covers tailored content delivery and personalised learning pathways.
requirements: Reviews must be classifiable by their purported focus within title, abstract, keywords or search terms; reviews without a specified focus are coded General AIEd
constraints: The typology was developed for AIEd research generally and applied here to higher-education evidence syntheses; some reviews spanned multiple areas and were coded under both focus and key-findings categories
target_learning_goals: mapping applications of AI in formal higher education teaching, learning, and administration
examples: The review coded all 66 corpus reviews by primary focus under this typology, producing Table 5 counts (General AIEd 31, Profiling and Prediction 19, Adaptive Systems and Personalisation 18, Assessment and Evaluation 3, Intelligent Tutoring Systems 1)

article_title: Using generative ai as a simulation to support higher-order thinking
citation: Borge, M., Smith, B.K. & Aldemir, T. (2024). Using generative ai as a simulation to support higher-order thinking. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn 19, 479–532. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09437-0
title: GenAI as a social interaction and cultural simulation tool for practicing collective sensemaking skills
description: The article frames chat-based generative AI as a learning environment in which learners can engage in collaborative sense-making with an AI partner. Its initial findings "indicate the promise of GenAI as a valuable social interaction and cultural simulation tool for learners to practice collective sensemaking skills". The framework positions GenAI technology as capable of creating "stimulating new learning environments that support complex sense-making activities", with the AI serving as a partner rather than an answer source.
requirements: Requires a chat-based generative AI tool with which learners can interact collaboratively
constraints: Chat-based GenAI technologies have "a tendency to provide definitive answers unsupported by evidence"
target_learners: Students in larger courses or broader audiences
target_learning_goals: Collective sensemaking skills
Metacognition and sociometacognition
examples: The case study examined expert use of a chat-based generative AI tool (ChatGPT 3.5) in human–computer collaborative interactions

title: Sociometacognition: knowledge about, awareness of, and ability to regulate individual and collective cognition
description: The article defines metacognition and sociometacognition as "knowledge about, awareness of, and ability to regulate individual (meta) and collective (sociometa) cognition". This two-level construct distinguishes regulation of one's own cognition from regulation of a group's collective cognition, and the study asks whether human–GenAI collaborative interactions can support both levels. It grounds the paper's inquiry into how AI partners might participate in regulating collective thinking during sense-making.

article_title: Unpacking the Term “Self-Management”: Understanding Intervention Applications Within the School-Based Literature
citation: Briesch, A.M., Daniels, B. & Beneville, M. (2019). Unpacking the Term “Self-Management”: Understanding Intervention Applications Within the School-Based Literature. J Behav Educ 28, 54–77. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10864-018-9303-1
title: Taxonomy of eight primary self-management intervention configurations used in school-based single-case research
description: The review organizes the school-based self-management literature by the specific intervention configuration employed, distinguishing approaches such as prompted self-monitoring, self-monitoring plus reinforcement based on both accuracy and performance, and prompted self-monitoring plus graphing. The authors state that "eight primary approaches to self-management were utilized across more than one study" within the 56 studies reviewed. This taxonomy provides the organizing framework for evaluating component-level effectiveness.
requirements: Interventions must be describable by their specific component configuration (e.g., prompting, reinforcement, graphing) to be classified within the taxonomy.
constraints: Derived from single-case design studies in school-based literature only.
target_learners: K-12 students with behavioral needs, including students with disabilities
target_learning_goals: Improved classroom behavior such as on-task behavior and reduced disruptive or off-task behavior
examples: The review classified 56 single-case studies and found prompted self-monitoring in 23 of them, self-monitoring plus reinforcement in 6, and prompted self-monitoring plus graphing in 5.

article_title: Effects of mobile-app learning diaries vs online training on specific self-regulated learning components
citation: Broadbent, J., Panadero, E. & Fuller-Tyszkiewicz, M. (2020). Effects of mobile-app learning diaries vs online training on specific self-regulated learning components. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09781-6
title: Mobile-app based learning diaries for daily SRL self-monitoring
description: A novel mobile-app based diary used in the study as a daily self-monitoring tool administered before and after study sessions. The diary asks about affect (e.g. "How do you feel at moment?" with rated items such as Active and Determined), motivation (e.g. "Today, I am studying because I find the topic very interesting"), and learning strategies (e.g. "Today, I have made a time schedule"), using Likert-type response scales. It replaces paper-and-pencil diaries, which the authors note are limited in reach.
requirements: Administered as daily diary entries before and after study sessions via a mobile app
target_learners: University students from mixed disciplines and study modes
target_learning_goals: Self-regulated learning strategy use and motivation
examples: Appendix 2 prints example diary questions on affect, motivation, and learning strategies asked before and after study sessions

citation: Broadbent, J., Panadero, E. & Fuller-Tyszkiewicz, M. (2020). Effects of mobile-app learning diaries vs online training on specific self-regulated learning components. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09781-6
title: Three-session discipline-independent online SRL training program
description: An online SRL training program delivered in three sessions designed as mini-chapters containing "micro-learnings in the form of written and video content, activities, reflective tasks and quizzes". Session 1 covers SRL overview, components, the three phases of SRL, goal setting (SMART goals), barriers, and time management. Session 2 covers distractions and procrastination, learning strategies (critical thinking, organisation, elaboration, mnemonics, paraphrasing, note making, self-questioning), resource management, and metacognitive strategies. Session 3 covers dealing with failure, attribution theory, motivation, self-efficacy, and self-reflection.
requirements: Delivered online so it can reach large numbers of participants independent of discipline
target_learners: University students from mixed disciplines and study modes
target_learning_goals: SRL knowledge, metacognitive and cognitive strategies, resource management strategies
examples: Appendix 3 lists the session topics and content, including a time management planner and a time management style self-assessment quiz

title: Self-regulated learning as a multi-component construct with metacognitive, cognitive, and resource management strategies
description: The article treats self-regulated learning as a multi-component construct whose trainable components include SRL knowledge, metacognitive strategies, cognitive strategies, and resource management strategies. It reports that participants "improved on SRL knowledge, metacognitive strategies, cognitive strategies (elaboration, organisation and critical thinking), and resources management strategies (time-management and effort regulation)". The training program's structure mirrors this taxonomy, with dedicated content on learning strategies, resource management, and metacognitive strategies, and the three phases of SRL.
requirements: Measurement of distinct SRL components (e.g. via SRL knowledge test and strategy measures) to detect component-specific improvement
target_learning_goals: Self-regulated learning knowledge and strategy use
examples: The training program's three sessions map onto the taxonomy: learning strategies, resource management, and metacognitive strategies in session 2
key_sources: Broadbent, J., Panadero, E. & Fuller-Tyszkiewicz, M. (2020). Effects of mobile-app learning diaries vs online training on specific self-regulated learning components. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09781-6

article_title: The development of student feedback literacy: enabling uptake of feedback
citation: David Carless & David Boud. (2018). The development of student feedback literacy: enabling uptake of feedback. Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education, 43(8), 1315-1325. https://doi.org/10.1080/02602938.2018.1463354
title: Student feedback literacy framework: appreciating feedback, making judgments, managing affect, taking action
description: The article defines student feedback literacy as "the understandings, capacities and dispositions needed to make sense of information and use it to enhance work or learning strategies". It proposes four inter-related features — appreciating feedback, making judgments, managing affect, and taking action — represented in Figure 1 with bi-directional arrows linking the first three, whose combination is proposed to maximise potential for student action. Each feature is elaborated with three numbered characteristics of feedback literate students.
requirements: Students need opportunities to use feedback within the curriculum and appreciation of how feedback can operate effectively
constraints: The framework is proposed for undergraduates in higher education; the authors note postgraduate and workplace levels remain to be investigated
target_learning_goals: making sense of feedback information and using it to enhance work or learning strategies
examples: Figure 1 lists three numbered capacities under each of the four features, e.g. feedback literate students "maintain emotional equilibrium and avoid defensiveness when receiving critical feedback"
key_sources: David Carless & David Boud. (2018). The development of student feedback literacy: enabling uptake of feedback. Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education, 43(8), 1315-1325. https://doi.org/10.1080/02602938.2018.1463354

article_title: Using Spacing to Enhance Diverse Forms of Learning: Review of Recent Research and Implications for Instruction
citation: Carpenter, S.K., Cepeda, N.J., Rohrer, D., Kang, S.H.K., & Pashler, H. (2012). Using Spacing to Enhance Diverse Forms of Learning: Review of Recent Research and Implications for Instruction. Educational Psychology Review, 24, 369–378. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-012-9205-z
title: Incorporate spacing into everyday instruction by separating study sessions over time rather than massing them
description: The article closes by offering guidance on applying spacing research to teaching: it "conclude[s] with a list of recommendations on how spacing might be incorporated into everyday instruction". The principle is that instructors should schedule multiple study or review opportunities separated in time rather than in immediate succession, because spaced sessions improve final-test performance. The specific recommendations are listed in the article body, which is not available in the preview text.
requirements: Instruction must include multiple study opportunities that can be distributed across time rather than delivered in one massed session.
target_learning_goals: durable memory retention of studied material
examples: The authors state the article concludes with a list of recommendations on how spacing might be incorporated into everyday instruction.
key_sources: Carpenter, S.K., Cepeda, N.J., Rohrer, D., Kang, S.H.K., & Pashler, H. (2012). Using Spacing to Enhance Diverse Forms of Learning: Review of Recent Research and Implications for Instruction. Educational Psychology Review, 24, 369–378. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-012-9205-z

article_title: The role of feedback in adult second language acquisition: Error correction and morphological generalizations
citation: Susanne Carroll, Merrill Swain, and Yves Roberge. (1992). The role of feedback in adult second language acquisition: Error correction and morphological generalizations. Applied Psycholinguistics, Volume 13, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0142716400005555
title: Experimental French suffixation feedback-training task with feedback and guessing sessions
description: The study's instrument was an individual training task on two rules of French suffixation administered to 79 adult native speakers of English with intermediate (39) and advanced (40) proficiency in French. In the article's words, "Experimental subjects received correction if they gave erroneous responses to stimuli in a “feedback” session." Afterward all subjects guessed responses to novel stimuli and were retested twice on the feedback items, while comparison subjects "dealt with the same stimuli but were never corrected."
requirements: Subjects must be individually trained on the two suffixation rules before the feedback session
constraints: The task was administered in an experimental setting with adult intermediate and advanced French learners, not in ordinary classroom instruction
target_learners: adult intermediate and advanced learners of French
target_learning_goals: learning morphological generalizations of French suffixation, including absolute exceptions
examples: Experimental subjects were corrected for erroneous responses during the feedback session; comparison subjects handled the same stimuli without correction
key_sources: Susanne Carroll, Merrill Swain, and Yves Roberge. (1992). The role of feedback in adult second language acquisition: Error correction and morphological generalizations. Applied Psycholinguistics, Volume 13, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0142716400005555

article_title: The role of feedback in adult second language acquisition: Error correction and morphological generalizations
citation: Susanne Carroll, Merrill Swain, and Yves Roberge. (1992). The role of feedback in adult second language acquisition: Error correction and morphological generalizations. Applied Psycholinguistics, Volume 13, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0142716400005555
title: Expect explicit correction to improve performance on corrected items, not to guarantee generalized rule learning
description: This principle captures the study's central dissociation: correction improved responses on the corrected items themselves, yet "comparisons of guessing responses between experimental and comparison groups showed no evidence of learned generalizations." Designers of feedback activities should therefore treat explicit correction as supporting item-level accuracy, and should not assume that corrected practice alone produces learners' generalization of a morphological rule to new items.
requirements: Learners must encounter the corrected items in a feedback session and then be probed with novel stimuli to check whether generalization occurred
constraints: Demonstrated only for adult English speakers learning two rules of French suffixation in an experimental setting; generalization was not observed even with correction
target_learning_goals: morphological generalizations in a second language
examples: In the experiment, corrected learners outperformed comparison learners on feedback items while guessing responses to novel stimuli showed no learned generalizations in either group
key_sources: Susanne Carroll, Merrill Swain, and Yves Roberge. (1992). The role of feedback in adult second language acquisition: Error correction and morphological generalizations. Applied Psycholinguistics, Volume 13, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0142716400005555

article_title: Explicit and Implicit Negative Feedback
citation: Susanne Carroll and Merrill Swain. (1993). Explicit and Implicit Negative Feedback: An Empirical Study of the Learning of Linguistic Generalizations. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 15, Issue 3. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263100012158
title: Four-type negative feedback manipulation contrasted with a no-feedback comparison group
description: The study operationalizes negative feedback as four distinct types assigned between groups. Upon an error, "Group A subjects were given explicit metalinguistic information about the generalization we hoped they would learn"; "Group B subjects were told that their response was wrong"; "Group C subjects were corrected when they erred, giving them a model of the response desired along with implicit negative evidence that their response was incorrect"; and "Group D subjects, having made an error, were asked if they were sure about their response." A comparison group received no feedback. This taxonomy separates explicit metalinguistic, explicit rejection, model-plus-implicit-negative-evidence, and elicit-confirmation feedback types.
requirements: Learners must first be trained on the target structure so that errors can be elicited and feedback delivered upon error
constraints: Feedback was delivered in response to errors on a single trained structure, the English dative alternation, with adult Spanish-speaking ESL learners
target_learners: Adult Spanish-speaking learners of English as a second language
target_learning_goals: Learning abstract constraints on the English dative alternation
examples: Subjects were divided into groups according to the type of feedback they received when they made an error, with a no-feedback comparison group
key_sources: Susanne Carroll and Merrill Swain. (1993). Explicit and Implicit Negative Feedback: An Empirical Study of the Learning of Linguistic Generalizations. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 15, Issue 3. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263100012158

article_title: Explicit and Implicit Negative Feedback
citation: Susanne Carroll and Merrill Swain. (1993). Explicit and Implicit Negative Feedback: An Empirical Study of the Learning of Linguistic Generalizations. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 15, Issue 3. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263100012158
title: Dative alternation training task presented as a simple structural change
description: The learning target and task of the experiment: the English dative alternation, an abstract generalization that learners tend to overgeneralize. All subjects received training on the alternation before the feedback manipulation; the abstract states that "All subjects were trained on the alternation, which was presented in terms of a simple structural change." The task served to elicit errors on which the different feedback types were then delivered.
requirements: Training on the alternation precedes the feedback manipulation for all subjects
constraints: The structure was presented as a simple structural change rather than in full abstract complexity
target_learners: Adult Spanish-speaking learners of English as a second language
target_learning_goals: Acquisition of the English dative alternation and its abstract constraints
examples: All subjects were trained on the alternation before being divided into feedback groups
key_sources: Susanne Carroll and Merrill Swain. (1993). Explicit and Implicit Negative Feedback: An Empirical Study of the Learning of Linguistic Generalizations. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 15, Issue 3. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263100012158

article_title: AI literacy in K-12: a systematic literature review
citation: Casal-Otero, L., Catala, A., Fernández-Morante, C., Taboada, M., Cebreiro, B., & Barro, S. (2023). AI literacy in K-12: a systematic literature review. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-023-00418-7
title: Taxonomy of K-12 AI literacy approaches: learning experiences versus theoretical/implementation perspectives
description: The review organizes the K-12 AI literacy field into two broad thematic categories: learning experiences and theoretical perspectives on implementation. Learning experiences cover understanding AI concepts, how AI works, tools for AI, and living with AI; the implementation category covers curriculum design, AI as a subject, student perspective, teacher training, support resources, and gender diversity. The review states: "the papers were classified into two broad thematic categories according to the type of educational approach, namely, learning experience and theoretical perspective." Each main category was further subdivided to structure the field (Fig. 6).
requirements: Documents must concern AI literacy or AI education at the K-12 level, excluding computer-based learning and intelligent tutoring systems
constraints: Based on Scopus-indexed documents only; search conducted between 21 October 2021 and 9 March 2023
target_learning_goals: Understanding AI concepts and techniques
Critically evaluating AI technology
examples: Figure 6 shows the full taxonomy of identified categories and subcategories
key_sources: Casal-Otero, L., Catala, A., Fernández-Morante, C., Taboada, M., Cebreiro, B., & Barro, S. (2023). AI literacy in K-12: a systematic literature review. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-023-00418-7

article_title: AI literacy in K-12: a systematic literature review
citation: Casal-Otero, L., Catala, A., Fernández-Morante, C., Taboada, M., Cebreiro, B., & Barro, S. (2023). AI literacy in K-12: a systematic literature review. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-023-00418-7
title: K-12 AI literacy requires a competency framework to guide didactic proposals and define a sequenced, modular, personalized curriculum
description: The review concludes that a competency framework is needed to guide didactic proposals for AI literacy in K-12 and to define a curriculum reflecting sequence and academic continuity. It states: "These studies highlight the need for a competency framework to guide the design of didactic proposals for AI literacy in K-12 in educational institutions." Such a curriculum "should be modular and personalized" and adjusted to the conditions of the schools, and learning experiences should be based on clearly defined competencies within an AI literacy framework.
requirements: Clearly defined competencies in a particular AI literacy framework
Curriculum adjusted to the conditions of the schools
constraints: The review notes AI teaching at K-12 is not yet prevalent in formal settings and is considered challenging
target_learning_goals: AI literacy competencies across AI concepts, applications, and ethics and security
examples: Van Brummelen et al. (2021a) designed a five-day online workshop based on the AI competencies proposed by Long and Magerko (2020)
key_sources: Casal-Otero, L., Catala, A., Fernández-Morante, C., Taboada, M., Cebreiro, B., & Barro, S. (2023). AI literacy in K-12: a systematic literature review. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-023-00418-7

article_title: AI literacy in K-12: a systematic literature review
citation: Casal-Otero, L., Catala, A., Fernández-Morante, C., Taboada, M., Cebreiro, B., & Barro, S. (2023). AI literacy in K-12: a systematic literature review. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-023-00418-7
title: Teachers should be prioritized and involved in the co-design of AI literacy didactic proposals, supported by TPACK-based training
description: The review identifies teachers as key players for integrating AI literacy in K-12 and concludes didactic proposals must be co-designed and implemented by the teachers at the schools involved. It reports a shortage of teachers with AI training and proposes working with teachers in training or in schools as an effective solution. It highlights TPACK as the model for the knowledge teachers need: "teachers imparting AI to K-12 students require TPACK to build an environment and facilitate project-based classes that solve problems using AI technologies."
requirements: Teacher training following a framework of standard competencies
Identification of teachers' perceptions and knowledge about AI
constraints: Teachers can swing between total resistance and overconfidence; resistance could arise from inadequate, inappropriate, irrelevant, or outdated professional development
target_learning_goals: Teacher professional development in AI
Integration of AI into teaching-learning processes
examples: The review reports co-design of ML curricula between AI researchers and K-12 teachers as an important current issue
key_sources: Casal-Otero, L., Catala, A., Fernández-Morante, C., Taboada, M., Cebreiro, B., & Barro, S. (2023). AI literacy in K-12: a systematic literature review. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-023-00418-7

article_title: Students’ voices on generative AI: perceptions, benefits, and challenges in higher education
citation: Chan, C. K. Y., & Hu, W. (2023). Students’ voices on generative AI: perceptions, benefits, and challenges in higher education. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education, 20:43. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-023-00411-8
title: Five perceived benefit categories of GenAI in student learning: personalized support, writing and brainstorming, research and analysis, multimedia, and administrative support
description: Thematic analysis of open-ended survey responses (n = 387 coded by two coders with a consensus codebook) yielded five benefit categories students gave for willingness to use GenAI: "1. Personalized and immediate learning support", "2. Writing and brainstorming support", "3. Research and analysis support", "4. Visual and audio multi-media support", and "5. Administrative support" (Table 5). Students described GenAI as a virtual tutor giving immediate answers, a writing assistant for idea generation and polishing, a research aid for literature searching and hypothesis generation, and a handler of repetitive tasks.
requirements: Applies where students have access to GenAI tools and tasks suited to learning support, writing, research, multimedia creation, or administrative work
constraints: Perceptions from a convenience sample of Hong Kong university students; GenAI was not yet fully used in formal academic settings at the time of the study
target_learning_goals: learning support, writing skills, research and analysis skills, multimedia creation
examples: A student described ChatGPT as "a top student" offering help when no one else could; an English major proposed generating short texts to memorize vocabulary; science and engineering students used DALL-E and Stable Diffusion to create artwork.
key_sources: Chan, C. K. Y., & Hu, W. (2023). Students’ voices on generative AI: perceptions, benefits, and challenges in higher education. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education, 20:43. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-023-00411-8

article_title: Students’ voices on generative AI: perceptions, benefits, and challenges in higher education
citation: Chan, C. K. Y., & Hu, W. (2023). Students’ voices on generative AI: perceptions, benefits, and challenges in higher education. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education, 20:43. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-023-00411-8
title: Six perceived challenge categories of GenAI: accuracy and transparency, privacy and ethics, holistic competencies, career prospects, human values, and uncertain policies
description: Thematic analysis of open-ended responses yielded six challenge categories: "1. Accuracy and transparency", "2. Privacy and ethical issues", "3. Holistic competencies", "4. Career prospects", "5. Human values", and "6. Uncertain policies" (Table 5). Students worried they "cannot predict or accurately verify the accuracy or validity of AI generated information", about data privacy, plagiarism detection, over-reliance harming critical thinking and creativity, job replacement, value misalignment and inequality, and the absence of institutional guidance.
requirements: Relevant where institutions are integrating GenAI into coursework and need to anticipate student concerns
constraints: Perceptions from a convenience sample of Hong Kong university students; more than half of participants expressed concerns while some were optimistic
target_learning_goals: critical thinking, creativity, academic integrity awareness, career preparation
examples: A computer science student feared losing his job "due to the advent of ChatGPT"; a social science student worried AI "can obtain our private information easily"; one student noted "It is always dangerous to use things you cannot understand".
key_sources: Chan, C. K. Y., & Hu, W. (2023). Students’ voices on generative AI: perceptions, benefits, and challenges in higher education. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education, 20:43. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-023-00411-8

article_title: Students’ voices on generative AI: perceptions, benefits, and challenges in higher education
citation: Chan, C. K. Y., & Hu, W. (2023). Students’ voices on generative AI: perceptions, benefits, and challenges in higher education. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education, 20:43. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-023-00411-8
title: Biggs' 3P (Presage–Process–Product) model as the framework linking student perceptions of GenAI to learning approaches and outcomes
description: The article adopts John Biggs' 3P (Presage–Process–Product) model as its explanatory framework: "students’ perceptions of their learning environment, their abilities, and the teaching strategies used have a significant impact on their approach to learning", which in turn influences outcomes. Positive perceptions foster a deep approach seeking understanding and connections; negative perceptions foster a surface approach focused on memorizing minimum requirements. The authors use this to argue that understanding students' GenAI perceptions lets educators tailor integration so students adopt a deep approach.
requirements: Requires attention to how students perceive the learning environment, including technologies such as GenAI, when designing teaching and assessment
constraints: The model is applied interpretively; the study did not test the model's predictions about GenAI use empirically
target_learning_goals: deep approaches to learning, effective integration of GenAI into teaching and learning
examples: The authors argue that when students perceive GenAI as a valuable and supportive resource they are more likely to adopt a deep approach to learning, and that perception insights can inform institutional GenAI guidelines.
key_sources: Chan, C. K. Y., & Hu, W. (2023). Students’ voices on generative AI: perceptions, benefits, and challenges in higher education. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education, 20:43. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-023-00411-8

article_title: The Expertise Reversal Effect is a Variant of the More General Element Interactivity Effect
citation: Chen, O., Kalyuga, S. & Sweller, J. (2017). The Expertise Reversal Effect is a Variant of the More General Element Interactivity Effect. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-016-9359-1
title: Unified cognitive load account: the expertise reversal effect as a variant of the element interactivity effect
description: The article proposes, within cognitive load theory, a unifying account in which the expertise reversal effect is subsumed under the element interactivity effect. It argues that "the two effects may be intertwined with the expertise reversal effect constituting a particular example of the element interactivity effect." On this account, both effects reflect the same underlying mechanism — changes in the number of interacting elements that must be processed in working memory — triggered by different factors. The article supports the contention with empirical evidence from prior studies.
requirements: Both effects must be interpreted within the framework of cognitive load theory, where element interactivity determines working memory load
constraints: The article presents this as an argued contention supported by empirical evidence, not as a directly tested new hypothesis
target_learners: Learners across levels of expertise in cognitive load theory instructional contexts
target_learning_goals: Managing cognitive load when learning novel or complex material
key_sources: Chen, O., Kalyuga, S. & Sweller, J. (2017). The Expertise Reversal Effect is a Variant of the More General Element Interactivity Effect. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-016-9359-1

article_title: Effectiveness of AI-assisted game-based learning on science learning outcomes, intrinsic motivation, cognitive load, and learning behavior
citation: Alec Radford, Karthik Narasimhan, Tim Salimans, Ilya Sutskever. (2018). Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training. Preprint. Work in progress. https://cdn.openai.com/research-covers/language-unsupervised/language_understanding_paper.pdf
title: Generative pre-training followed by discriminative fine-tuning as a semi-supervised framework for language understanding
description: The article introduces a two-stage semi-supervised framework: a high-capacity language model is first trained on a large unlabeled corpus with a language modeling objective, then adapted to supervised target tasks. As the article states, "Our training procedure consists of two stages. The ﬁrst stage is learning a high-capacity language model on a large corpus of text." The goal is a universal representation that transfers with little adaptation across diverse tasks.
requirements: Access to a large corpus of unlabeled text and several datasets with manually annotated training examples for the target tasks
constraints: The target tasks are not required to be in the same domain as the unlabeled corpus, per the article's setup
target_learners: natural language processing researchers and practitioners
target_learning_goals: natural language understanding across inference, question answering, similarity, and classification tasks
examples: A 12-layer decoder-only transformer pre-trained on BooksCorpus and fine-tuned on twelve NLU benchmark datasets
key_sources: Alec Radford, Karthik Narasimhan, Tim Salimans, Ilya Sutskever. (2018). Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training. Preprint. Work in progress. https://cdn.openai.com/research-covers/language-unsupervised/language_understanding_paper.pdf

article_title: Effectiveness of AI-assisted game-based learning on science learning outcomes, intrinsic motivation, cognitive load, and learning behavior
citation: Alec Radford, Karthik Narasimhan, Tim Salimans, Ilya Sutskever. (2018). Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training. Preprint. Work in progress. https://cdn.openai.com/research-covers/language-unsupervised/language_understanding_paper.pdf
title: Task-aware input transformations for fine-tuning a pre-trained transformer on structured inputs
description: A set of task-specific input transformations that convert structured inputs (sentence pairs, document-question-answer triplets) into ordered token sequences the pre-trained model can process, using delimiter tokens and traversal-style processing. The article states: "we use a traversal-style approach [52], where we convert structured inputs into an ordered sequence that our pre-trained model can process." This enables effective transfer with minimal architectural change per task.
requirements: Randomly initialized start and end tokens added to every transformation, plus delimiter tokens between concatenated segments
constraints: The article notes the auxiliary LM objective during fine-tuning helps larger datasets but smaller datasets do not benefit
target_learners: natural language processing researchers and practitioners
target_learning_goals: transferring a single pre-trained model to entailment, similarity, question answering, and classification inputs
examples: For similarity tasks both sentence orderings are processed independently and the representations are added element-wise; for question answering, document, question, and each answer are concatenated with a delimiter and scored via softmax
key_sources: Alec Radford, Karthik Narasimhan, Tim Salimans, Ilya Sutskever. (2018). Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training. Preprint. Work in progress. https://cdn.openai.com/research-covers/language-unsupervised/language_understanding_paper.pdf

article_title: The Opportunity Atlas: Mapping the Childhood Roots of Social Mobility
citation: Raj Chetty, John N. Friedman, Nathaniel Hendren, Maggie R. Jones, and Sonya R. Porter. (2018). The Opportunity Atlas: Mapping the Childhood Roots of Social Mobility. NBER Working Paper No. 25147. http://www.nber.org/papers/w25147
title: The Opportunity Atlas: public tract-level dataset and interactive mapping tool of children's adult outcomes
description: The Opportunity Atlas is a publicly available dataset providing "the ﬁrst comprehensive estimates of children’s long-term outcomes across neigh­borhoods in the U.S." at the Census tract level, constructed from Census, tax, and ACS microdata covering 20.5 million children in the 1978-83 birth cohorts. It releases estimates of household income, incarceration, teenage birth, and other outcomes by parental income percentile, race, and gender, through "an interactive mapping tool and in downloadable ﬂat ﬁles" with a codebook, plus county and commuting-zone estimates.
requirements: Estimates are suppressed for cells based on 20 or fewer children, and noise is added for privacy, so users must account for sampling error and noise infusion when making tract comparisons.
constraints: Some estimates, particularly in more affluent areas, are based on extrapolation from higher-income children under the statistical model.
ACS-based outcomes such as college attendance are reported only at the county and CZ levels.
target_learners: families and housing-policy designers choosing where to live
target_learning_goals: identifying neighborhoods where children's opportunity is most lacking
targeting resources such as Head Start centers and Opportunity Zones
designing housing voucher programs to improve children's outcomes
examples: The article illustrates use with the Watts vs. Compton comparison and the Opportunity Zones re-targeting application.
key_sources: Raj Chetty, John N. Friedman, Nathaniel Hendren, Maggie R. Jones, and Sonya R. Porter. (2018). The Opportunity Atlas: Mapping the Childhood Roots of Social Mobility. NBER Working Paper No. 25147. http://www.nber.org/papers/w25147

article_title: Dual coding theory and education
citation: Clark, J.M., Paivio, A. Dual coding theory and education. Educ Psychol Rev 3, 149–210 (1991). https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01320076
title: Dual coding theory explains behavior and experience via associative processes on modality-specific verbal and nonverbal representations
description: Dual coding theory (DCT) is an explanatory framework in which human behavior and experience arise from dynamic associative processes operating over two classes of representation. As the article states, DCT "explains human behavior and experience in terms of dynamic associative processes that operate on a rich network of modality-specific verbal and nonverbal (or imagery) representations." The theory serves as the organizing framework the authors then apply to educational phenomena such as comprehension, memory, instruction, and motivation.
requirements: The theory presupposes a rich network of modality-specific verbal and nonverbal (imagery) representations on which associative processes operate
target_learning_goals: representation and comprehension of knowledge
learning and memory of school material
key_sources: Clark, J.M., Paivio, A. Dual coding theory and education. Educ Psychol Rev 3, 149–210 (1991). https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01320076

article_title: Dual coding theory and education
citation: Clark, J.M., Paivio, A. Dual coding theory and education. Educ Psychol Rev 3, 149–210 (1991). https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01320076
title: Use DCT's concrete models of student, teacher, and educational psychologist behavior to strengthen pedagogical practice
description: The article recommends grounding pedagogical practice in the concrete models that dual coding theory offers for the behavior and experience of educational participants. It argues that "the concrete models that DCT offers for the behavior and experience of students, teachers, and educational psychologists further our understanding of educational phenomena and strengthen related pedagogical practices." The principle treats DCT-based modeling as a route to improved educational design and understanding.
requirements: Practitioners and researchers must adopt DCT's concrete models of the behavior and experience of students, teachers, and educational psychologists
constraints: The article states that much additional research needs to be done
target_learning_goals: understanding of educational phenomena
strengthening pedagogical practices
examples: The article shows how basic DCT mechanisms model diverse educational phenomena including learning and memory of school material and effective instruction
key_sources: Clark, J.M., Paivio, A. Dual coding theory and education. Educ Psychol Rev 3, 149–210 (1991). https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01320076

article_title: Artificial intelligence in higher education: the state of the field
citation: Crompton, H., & Burke, D. (2023). Artificial intelligence in higher education: the state of the field. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-023-00392-8
title: Five usage codes for AI in higher education: Assessment/Evaluation, Predicting, AI Assistant, Intelligent Tutoring System, and Managing Student Learning
description: This systematic review used grounded coding of 138 articles to let uses of AI in higher education emerge from the data rather than fitting them to pre-existing frameworks. The review reports that "Five usage codes emerged from the data: (1) Assessment/Evaluation, (2) Predicting, (3) AI Assistant, (4) Intelligent Tutoring System (ITS), and (5) Managing Student Learning." Each code has axial codes as subcategories, e.g. automatic assessment, prediction of dropouts, chatbots, adaptive tutoring, and learning analytics.
requirements: Grounded coding of primary studies' descriptions of AI use, with in vivo codes and constant comparison until codes are theoretically saturated
constraints: Derived from peer-reviewed journal articles published 2016–2022 in English; conference proceedings and gray literature excluded
target_learning_goals: understanding how artificial intelligence is used across higher education contexts
examples: The review delineated each code with a figure of codes and axial codes, e.g. six axial codes under Assessment/Evaluation and ten axial codes under Predicting

article_title: Assessing the proficiency of large language models in automatic feedback generation: An evaluation study

title: Hattie and Timperley's feedback model: three dimensions (feeding up, feeding back, feeding forward) and four levels (task, process, self-regulation, self)
description: The article adopts this theoretical framework to analyse the effectiveness of textual feedback. It "categorized effective feedback into three dimensions (i.e., feeding up, feeding back and feeding forward) and four-level focuses (i.e., task, process, self-regulatory, and self )". Feeding up tells students where they are going; feeding back answers how they are going; feeding forward addresses where to go next. The authors chose it because it "has been adopted widely in previous research to analyse textual feedback", unlike Nicol and Macfarlane-Dick's principles judged too general.
requirements: Annotators trained in the framework's three dimensions and four levels to label feedback content
constraints: The article notes effectiveness of feedback goes beyond the content coverage of feedback, so this single framework does not capture relational or feedback-literacy dimensions
target_learning_goals: assessment feedback quality on writing tasks
examples: Two experts annotated 309 feedback pieces using the framework's dimensions and levels, with a third expert resolving inconsistencies

It examines "characteristics of students with ASD that react favorably to the intervention, what procedures are necessary for implementation, and how settings within schools affect outcomes". article_title: THE EXPERANTO EXPERIMENT
citation: Rick de Graaff. (1997). The Experanto Experiment: Effects of Explicit Instruction on Second Language Acquisition. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, 19(2). https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263197002064
title: Computer-controlled self-study course in the artificial language Experanto
description: The article's instructional element is a "computer-controlled self-study course in an artificial language" (Experanto), used to deliver L2 input and explicit instruction to university students under controlled conditions. Two groups of 27 students differing in exposure to explicit instruction worked through the course, and "computer-controlledposttests" measured acquisition of four L2 structures. The computer control of both instruction and testing is what allowed the presence or absence of explicit instruction to be manipulated experimentally.
requirements: Learners work through the course in self-study mode under computer control, with exposure to explicit instruction varied between groups.
constraints: The course teaches an artificial language rather than a natural second language, which limits generalization to natural L2 acquisition.
target_learning_goals: acquisition of L2 grammar structures
examples: Two groups of 27 university students, differing in the exposure to explicit instruction, followed the computer-controlled self-study course in the artificial language.

article_title: A Meta‐Analysis and Meta‐Regression of Incidental Second Language Word Learning from Spoken Input
citation: de Vos, J. F., Schriefers, H., Nivard, M. G., & Lemhöfer, K. (2018). A Meta-Analysis and Meta-Regression of Incidental Second Language Word Learning from Spoken Input. Language Learning. https://doi.org/10.1111/lang.12296
title: Involvement Load Hypothesis as a mechanism account of incidental word learning
description: The article presents the Involvement Load Hypothesis (Laufer & Hulstijn, 2001) as one mechanism explaining why incidental exposure can produce learning. It holds that "Involvement is seen as consisting of three dimensions: need, search, and evaluation", and that "activities that require a higher involvement from the learner are expected to lead to more learning". The article cites a prior meta-analysis finding support for it, and uses such mechanism accounts to motivate why meaning-focused activities differ in effectiveness.
requirements: Learning activities must differ in the motivational (need) and cognitive (search, evaluation) demands they place on learners for the hypothesis to predict differential learning.
constraints: The article reports the hypothesis as tested on output-versus-reading comparisons in prior work, not directly tested in its own meta-regression.
target_learning_goals: incidental L2 vocabulary learning from meaning-focused activities
examples: The article cites Huang, Willson, and Eslami (2012) finding that participants who completed an output task acquired more vocabulary than those who only read a text.

description: Preschool PATHS is "a universal, teacher-taught social-emotional curriculum that is designed to improve children's social competence and reduce problem behavior." In the trial, "Teachers in the 10 intervention classrooms implemented weekly lessons and extension activities across a 9-month period." It is an adaptation of the Promoting Alternative Thinking Strategies curriculum for preschool-age children in Head Start, delivered by classroom teachers as part of the universal program.

article_title: Long-Term Effects of Strategic Reading Instruction in the Intermediate Elementary Grades
citation: Droop, M.; van Elsäcker, W.; Voeten, M. J. M.; Verhoeven, L. (2016). Long-Term Effects of Strategic Reading Instruction in the Intermediate Elementary Grades. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness. https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2015.1065528
title: SRI program: sustained multiple-strategy instruction grounded in self-regulated learning and cognitive apprenticeship
description: The SRI program aims "to create independent self-regulated readers who are capable of applying appropriate reading strategies in various contexts." It draws on self-regulated learning theory and cognitive apprenticeship, teaching a limited set of nine strategies (predicting, relating to background knowledge, monitoring, deriving word meaning from context, visualizing, questioning, generating main idea, summarizing, evaluating) before, during, and after reading. Teacher modeling occurs in the meaningful context of reading aloud award-nominated children's literature three times weekly, followed by independent reading of self-chosen books with a strategy checklist on which students note problems and solutions, and weekly transfer lessons in content areas such as science. Regulation gradually shifts from teacher to students across the two years.
requirements: Teachers receive training (two three-hour meetings, a mid-year meeting, and an evaluation meeting) with video clips demonstrating strategy modeling, plus observation and coaching in November of each year
A collection of narrative and informative books at varied levels must be available for independent reading
constraints: Experimental schools were not allowed to use their own reading comprehension curriculum for the duration of the study
target_learners: Third and fourth grade elementary students of varying reading levels
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension
Knowledge and self-regulated use of reading strategies
examples: In Grade 3 strategies were introduced one by one over nine weeks; in Grade 4 three strategies were modeled at a time and students increasingly assisted in modeling

article_title: Long-Term Effects of Strategic Reading Instruction in the Intermediate Elementary Grades
citation: Droop, M.; van Elsäcker, W.; Voeten, M. J. M.; Verhoeven, L. (2016). Long-Term Effects of Strategic Reading Instruction in the Intermediate Elementary Grades. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness. https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2015.1065528
title: Read-aloud lesson structure integrating modeling, independent reading, and reflection
description: Each SRI lesson follows a fixed 40-minute structure: "(a) introduction of 5 minutes, (b) 15 minutes reading aloud including 5 minutes modeling of one or two strategies to the whole class, (c) 15 minutes individual independent reading with application of strategies and making notes, and (d) 5 minutes whole-class evaluation." The pattern embeds strategy modeling in authentic, motivating read-alouds of children's literature, then has students immediately apply the modeled strategies during independent reading of self-chosen books, recording problems and solutions on a strategy checklist, and closes with whole-class reflection on whether the strategy helped comprehension.
requirements: Well-written, interesting children's literature with manuals highlighting two or three moments to model a strategy
A strategy checklist and folder for each student
constraints: Teachers initially reported difficulty fitting the lessons in forty minutes, though they became accustomed to the structure during the year
target_learning_goals: Application of reading strategies during authentic reading
Self-regulated strategy use
examples: Books included works by Tosca Menten, Mirjam Oldenhave, and Lydia Rood; students chose books from classroom or school libraries at their own reading level

title: Teach a limited set of multiple reading strategies rather than an exhaustive amount of strategic activities
description: The article states "there is consensus that a limited set of multiple strategies is better than an exhaustive amount of strategic activities," citing Davis (2010), the National Reading Panel (2000), and the RAND Reading Study Group (2002). The SRI program operationalizes this by teaching nine strategies consistently over two years, deepening them across grades, rather than offering many activities exercised only once or twice — a weakness the authors note in many publisher materials.
requirements: Strategies should orient attention to the task (predicting, activating prior knowledge), support active processing (monitoring, visualizing, questioning, solving problems), and structure information after reading (summarizing, evaluating)
target_learners: Elementary students in the intermediate grades
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension
Strategic reading
examples: SRI selected nine strategies based on Block and Duffy (2008), the NRP (2000), and the RAND Reading Study Group (2002)

citation: Droop, M.; van Elsäcker, W.; Voeten, M. J. M.; Verhoeven, L. (2016). Long-Term Effects of Strategic Reading Instruction in the Intermediate Elementary Grades. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness. https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2015.1065528
title: Model strategies in a meaningful read-aloud context, then have students apply them during independent reading of self-chosen books
description: The article recommends that strategy instruction be embedded in meaningful contexts: "reading aloud children's books may offer a rich and meaningful context to model the strategies," and "Strategies modeled during read-aloud sessions may be applied during independent reading and transferred to content area reading." Teachers not only modeled the strategy but explicitly explained why they used it, following the cognitive apprenticeship principle of teacher-as-model. This contrasts with control curricula where students read identical short texts and answered written questions without a meaningful context.
requirements: Detailed scripts for teachers on when and how to model a strategy, what to say exactly, and which questions to ask during reading aloud
target_learners: Elementary students of varying reading levels
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension
Strategy application and transfer
examples: Manuals for each read-aloud book highlighted possible modeling moments with example sentences per strategy (Appendix A of the online supplement)

title: Sustain strategy instruction over multiple years, gradually shifting regulation from teacher to student
description: The article argues that "it takes time to become a strategic self-regulated reader" and that "strategy instruction should be sustained and should gradually shift from external regulation by the teacher to internal regulation by the students." Accordingly, SRI was implemented over two school years: in Grade 3 the teacher modeled all strategies, while in Grade 4 students were frequently asked to assist in modeling, and the visualizing strategy shifted from mental imagery to creating graphic representations of text.
requirements: A two-year implementation window in Grades 3 and 4 with repeated teacher training each year
target_learning_goals: Self-regulated reading strategy use
Independent strategic reading
examples: In Grade 4, when preparing a summary, the teacher and students together determined which information was more important

title: Consolidating AI risk management frameworks with utilitarian ethics for responsible generative AI use
description: This account proposes that organisations manage generative AI risks by combining the NIST Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework with utilitarian ethical reasoning. The NIST framework "can guide the organisations developing, adopting, and implementing AI solutions to systematically assess, understand, and manage risks", with risks mapped to the context of use. Utilitarianism then supplies "a flexible result-oriented lens for formulating and testing policies at each stage of the risk management cycle", prioritising impacts on each stakeholder. The article argues the two should be consolidated so decisions about ChatGPT design, adoption and evolution provide the most good or least harm for society.

Responsible AI toolkits and frameworks embedding ethical perspectives

title: Synergy account: explicit corrective feedback in communicative activity can foster implicit as well as explicit knowledge
description: The article frames corrective feedback via the implicit/explicit learning and knowledge distinction, drawing on connectionist models in which "conscious and unconscious processes are dynamically involved together in every cognitive task and in every learning episode." Metalinguistic time-outs from communicating are proposed as a context for melding conscious and unconscious processes, so explicit feedback caters to implicit as well as explicit learning. The study's delayed-posttest gains in oral imitation are presented as consistent with this account.
requirements: Feedback must be recognized by the learner as corrective and the error located, per Carroll's autonomous induction theory as cited in the article
constraints: The article notes no single exchange can guarantee that the targeted form will enter implicit memory; repeated exchanges directed at the same form might be expected to do so
target_learning_goals: acquisition of L2 grammar (regular past tense -ed), implicit and explicit L2 knowledge
examples: The study operationalized explicit feedback as metalinguistic explanation and implicit feedback as partial recasts during communicative tasks

article_title: Assessing student perceptions and use of instructor versus AI ‐generated feedback
citation: Er, Erkan; Akçapınar, Gökhan; Bayazıt, Alper; Noroozi, Omid; Banihashem, Seyyed Kazem. (2024). Assessing student perceptions and use of instructor versus AI-generated feedback. British Journal of Educational Technology. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjet.13558
title: AI should not be the sole source of feedback; human expertise remains crucial
description: The article's practitioner implication is that AI-generated feedback should not replace instructor feedback. Its experiment showed students receiving AI feedback had significantly lower score improvements, and the authors conclude that "AI should not be the sole source of feedback, as human expertise is crucial." They attribute this to instructors' contextual awareness and AI's risk of hallucination and generic feedback.
requirements: Instructors must remain available to provide or review feedback, particularly for nuanced, context-specific aspects of student work
constraints: Based on one Java programming course with 35 students; the authors note the finding may not generalise to other assignments, languages or larger samples
target_learning_goals: improving programming work based on feedback
examples: Students in the AI-feedback condition improved lab scores significantly less than the instructor-feedback condition after controlling for midterm scores
key_sources: Er, Erkan; Akçapınar, Gökhan; Bayazıt, Alper; Noroozi, Omid; Banihashem, Seyyed Kazem. (2024). Assessing student perceptions and use of instructor versus AI-generated feedback. British Journal of Educational Technology. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjet.13558

article_title: Assessing student perceptions and use of instructor versus AI ‐generated feedback
citation: Er, Erkan; Akçapınar, Gökhan; Bayazıt, Alper; Noroozi, Omid; Banihashem, Seyyed Kazem. (2024). Assessing student perceptions and use of instructor versus AI-generated feedback. British Journal of Educational Technology. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjet.13558
title: Four-dimension feedback perception framework: usefulness, fairness, developmental value and encouragement
description: The study organises student perceptions of feedback into four constructs: usefulness (how easy feedback is to understand and apply), fairness, developmental value (feedback's capacity to guide improvement) and encouragement (positive comments acknowledging effort). It operationalises these with subscales adapted from Strijbos et al. (2010) and Lizzio and Wilson (2008), noting that "these perceptions influence whether and how students engage with and utilise feedback."
requirements: Validated perception subscales; students must have received feedback to rate
constraints: Perceptions may not always relate to desired learning outcomes, as the article notes some studies show perceptions can deviate from actual learning gains
target_learning_goals: understanding student engagement with feedback
examples: The study measured all four dimensions with 5-point Likert subscales and compared them between instructor- and AI-feedback conditions

article_title: AI-generated feedback on writing: insights into efficacy and ENL student preference
citation: Escalante, J., Pack, A., & Barrett, A. (2023). AI-generated feedback on writing: insights into efficacy and ENL student preference. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education, 20:57. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-023-00425-2
title: Use a blended approach combining AI-generated and human feedback for ENL writing instruction
description: The article recommends a mixed approach to writing feedback that capitalizes on each modality's strengths: the clarity and specificity of AI-generated feedback and the engagement and speaking-practice benefits of human interaction. Since Study 1 found no outcome difference and Study 2 found a near-even preference split with "clear advantages to both forms of feedback apparent from the data", the authors conclude AI feedback "can likely be incorporated into ENL essay evaluation without affecting learning outcomes" alongside human tutoring.
requirements: Access to a GPT-4-based feedback pipeline with a carefully engineered prompt, and human tutors available to discuss AI-generated feedback with students
constraints: In this study students emailed AI feedback had no opportunity to ask follow-up questions to the AI, which the authors suggest limited AI preference
target_learners: University English-as-a-new-language (ENL) students at CEFR B1 or higher
target_learning_goals: Academic writing improvement in content, coherence, language use, and use of sources and evidence
examples: Students received weekly GPT-4 feedback on 300-word paragraphs and met weekly with human tutors; the authors suggest providing opportunities for students to discuss AI-generated feedback with a human tutor and ask follow-up questions
key_sources: Escalante, J., Pack, A., & Barrett, A. (2023). AI-generated feedback on writing: insights into efficacy and ENL student preference. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education, 20:57. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-023-00425-2

article_title: AI-generated feedback on writing: insights into efficacy and ENL student preference
citation: Escalante, J., Pack, A., & Barrett, A. (2023). AI-generated feedback on writing: insights into efficacy and ENL student preference. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education, 20:57. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-023-00425-2
title: Role-based GPT-4 prompt for six-area corrective writing feedback
description: A structured prompt, developed iteratively by two experienced language educators, that casts GPT-4 as "a professional language teacher who is an expert on providing feedback on the writing of English language learners". It instructs the model, using simple language, to comment on six areas: topic sentence, development of ideas, language lowering academic quality, transitional phrases, use of sources and evidence, and grammatical accuracy, with grammar feedback organized into a four-column error table (sentence, error type, description, suggestion). A teaching assistant ran the prompt per student and emailed feedback within two working days.
requirements: Prompt engineering following the framework of Ingley and Pack (2023); de-identified student drafts; GPT-4 access
constraints: GPT-4 is not optimized for AWE purposes, so features like text annotation common in existing AWE programs are cumbersome to reproduce
target_learners: ENL university students writing 300-word academic paragraphs
target_learning_goals: Formative corrective feedback on academic paragraph writing
examples: Appendix B prints the full sample prompt; Appendix C shows example feedback on a student paragraph about culture, including a grammar error table
