article_title: Intelligence, creativity, and cognitive control: The common and differential involvement of executive functions in intelligence and creativity
citation: Benedek Mathias, Jauk Emanuel, Sommer Markus, Arendasy Martin, Neubauer Aljoscha C. (2014). Intelligence, creativity, and cognitive control: The common and differential involvement of executive functions in intelligence and creativity. Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.intell.2014.05.007
title: Executive nature of creativity: controlled top-down processes (updating and inhibition) support creative thought
description: The article advances an executive account of creativity, arguing that creative idea generation "does not solely depend on spontaneous thought processes, but strongly relies on controlled top-down activity". Inhibition is thought to suppress dominant, obvious responses so that remote concepts can be retrieved, while working memory supports controlled search of memory and active maintenance of task goals and strategies during idea generation. The study's latent variable findings (updating and inhibition predicting creativity; shifting not) are presented as direct support for this account.
requirements: Measurement of both executive abilities and divergent thinking ability within the same individuals
constraints: Interpretation limited by latent EF factors each defined by task blocks of a single task, and by the possibility of task-specific method variance
target_learning_goals: creative idea generation (divergent thinking)
examples: The alternate uses task analysis in the discussion describes how working memory maintains goals such as generating creative uses while searching memory for remote applications

article_title: Intelligence, creativity, and cognitive control: The common and differential involvement of executive functions in intelligence and creativity
citation: Benedek Mathias, Jauk Emanuel, Sommer Markus, Arendasy Martin, Neubauer Aljoscha C. (2014). Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.intell.2014.05.007
title: Assess creativity via rated quality of top ideas rather than ideational fluency to avoid confounding with response count
description: The article scored divergent thinking tasks by the top-scoring method, in which creativity scores reflect the average creativity rating of the three highest-rated ideas per task. The authors state this method "was shown to avoid a confounding with the number of responses", allowing latent creativity to reflect the creative quality of ideas rather than sheer output volume. Four raters scored responses holistically on a four-point scale considering originality and appropriateness.
requirements: Multiple experienced raters with acceptable interrater reliability (ICC values reported between .57 and .79)
constraints: Requires holistic rating judgments; the article notes high creativity ratings should only be assigned to ideas that only few people could presumably come up with
target_learning_goals: assessment of creative potential (divergent thinking ability)
examples: Four DT tasks (two alternate uses, two instances) were administered with 2 min per task, and creativity scores reflected the average rating of the three top-rated ideas per task

article_title: <p>Developmental coordination disorder and dysgraphia: signs and symptoms, diagnosis, and rehabilitation</p>
citation: Biotteau M, Danna J, Baudou É, Puyjarinet F, Velay J-L, Albaret J-M, Chaix Y. (2019). Developmental coordination disorder and dysgraphia: signs and symptoms, diagnosis, and rehabilitation. Neuropsychiatric Disease and Treatment. https://doi.org/10.2147/NDT.S120514
title: Two-category framework of DCD interventions: bottom-up process-oriented versus top-down task-oriented approaches
description: The review organizes DCD intervention methods into two main categories. The bottom-up category contains process-oriented (deficit-oriented) approaches such as kinesthetic training and sensory integration, which assume "a deficit in a specific body function or part ... is responsible for the impaired motor skills" and aim to remediate that underlying deficit. The top-down category contains task-oriented (functional skill) approaches such as neuromotor task training and CO-OP, which teach children the ADLs they need, with children as actors encouraged to think about difficulties and find solutions while adults help explore and validate strategies.
requirements: Interventions supporting participation and activity are key to remediating motor impairments and associated problems in DCD
constraints: Process-oriented approaches were not included in European Academy of Childhood Disabilities recommendations or the 2012 American Academy of Pediatrics policy statement due to weak effects
target_learning_goals: Improving coordinated motor skills and activities of daily living
examples: Neuromotor task training and cognitive orientation to daily occupational performance (CO-OP) as named task-oriented approaches
key_sources: Biotteau M, Danna J, Baudou É, Puyjarinet F, Velay J-L, Albaret J-M, Chaix Y. (2019). Developmental coordination disorder and dysgraphia: signs and symptoms, diagnosis, and rehabilitation. Neuropsychiatric Disease and Treatment. https://doi.org/10.2147/NDT.S120514

article_title: <p>Developmental coordination disorder and dysgraphia: signs and symptoms, diagnosis, and rehabilitation</p>
citation: Biotteau M, Danna J, Baudou É, Puyjarinet F, Velay J-L, Albaret J-M, Chaix Y. (2019). Developmental coordination disorder and dysgraphia: signs and symptoms, diagnosis, and rehabilitation. Neuropsychiatric Disease and Treatment. https://doi.org/10.2147/NDT.S120514
title: Standardized assessment tools for DCD and dysgraphia diagnosis (MABC-2, TGMD-2, DCDQ, BHK, Minnesota Handwriting Assessment, ETCH)
description: The review catalogs the standardized instruments used to diagnose DCD and dysgraphia. The MABC-2, the most widely used DCD tool, consists of 8 items across three age ranges (3–6, 7–10, 11–16 years), lasts 40–50 mins, and covers manual dexterity, ball skills, and balance. The TGMD-2 is a norm-referenced measure of gross motor skills with 2 subtests probing 12 skills for children aged 3–10–11 years, lasting 15–20 mins. The DCDQ is a brief parental screening questionnaire for children aged 5–15 years. For dysgraphia, the BHK (standardized on 837 children aged 6–11) yields legibility and speed scores, alongside the Minnesota Handwriting Assessment and the ETCH.
requirements: Guidelines for administration must be followed to ensure reliability of standardized psychomotor batteries and scales
constraints: Unlike DCD, there is no gold standard for diagnosing dysgraphia, probably because writing systems differ substantially between countries and languages
target_learners: Children with suspected dysgraphia in Grades 1–6
target_learning_goals: Diagnosing motor coordination and handwriting difficulties and establishing baselines for intervention
examples: The BHK requires participants to copy a text for 5 mins on an unlined sheet, scored on 13 legibility criteria plus writing speed

article_title: Learning from others at work: communities of practice and informal learning
citation: David Boud and Heather Middleton. (2003). Learning from Others at Work: Communities of Practice and Informal Learning. Journal of Workplace Learning, 15, 5, 194-202.
title: Communities of practice are a useful but insufficient framework for informal workplace learning; loosely and tightly coupled variants and additional conceptualisations are needed
description: The article evaluates Lave and Wenger's and Wenger's communities of practice framework against qualitative data from four workgroups. It finds the framework "provides useful ways of accounting for the phenomenon we are considering", but is "not sufficient for our purposes of dealing with informal learning at work", because some learning networks are more loosely coupled groupings that do not build identity and meaning. The authors propose degrees of coupling, Bernstein's framing, and Engeström's expansive learning as complementary lenses.
requirements: The framework presupposes sustained relationships, shared ways of engaging, and mutual familiarity among members, as in the tightly coupled tiling teachers and HR group.
constraints: Communities of practice form naturally, are often strongly bounded, and may not be easily cultivated; an exclusive focus on them may limit accounts of workplace learning and the kinds of intervention possible.
target_learning_goals: Informal workplace learning, including mastering organisational processes, negotiating the political, and dealing with the atypical
examples: The tiling teachers and HR group were described as tightly coupled communities of practice; the educational planners, with more frequent reformation and changing membership, were looser and possibly more representative of contemporary organisations.
key_sources: David Boud and Heather Middleton. (2003). Learning from Others at Work: Communities of Practice and Informal Learning. Journal of Workplace Learning, 15, 5, 194-202. https://doi.org/10.1108/13665620310483895

article_title: Learning from others at work: communities of practice and informal learning
citation: David Boud and Heather Middleton. (2003). Learning from Others at Work: Communities of Practice and Informal Learning. Journal of Workplace Learning, 15, 5, 194-202.
title: Bernstein's construct of framing applied to communities of practice: strong framing means sharp boundaries on what is transmitted between members, weak framing blurred ones
description: The article imports Bernstein's (1990) construct of framing from studies of curriculum and schooling into the analysis of workplace learning networks. Framing of knowledge is strong "when there is a sharp boundary between what may be transmitted and what may not be transmitted in a learning relationship", and weak where the boundary is blurred. The authors identify strong framing with the tilers and weaker framing with the educational planners, and suggest loosely coupled communities of practice may be regarded as communities in which framing of knowledge is weak.
requirements: Applying framing requires identifying the boundary between what may and may not be transmitted within a learning relationship among network members.
constraints: The construct was developed from studies of curriculum and schooling; the article presents its application to workplace communities of practice as a proposal ('might also be applied').
target_learning_goals: Understanding the scope and consistency of knowledge transmission within workplace learning networks
examples: Strong framing was identified with the tiling teachers and weaker framing with the educational planners.
key_sources: David Boud and Heather Middleton. (2003). Learning from Others at Work: Communities of Practice and Informal Learning. Journal of Workplace Learning, 15, 5, 194-202. https://doi.org/10.1108/13665620310483895

article_title: Learning from others at work: communities of practice and informal learning
citation: David Boud and Heather Middleton. (2003). Learning from Others at Work: Communities of Practice and Informal Learning. Journal of Workplace Learning, 15, 5, 194-202.
title: Engeström's expansive learning: horizontal or sideways learning among peers without a conventional knowledge hierarchy, useful for conceptualising dealing with the atypical
description: The article draws on Engeström's (2001) activity-theoretical notion of expansive learning, articulated in the context of workplace learning. Engeström "draws attention to what he calls horizontal or sideways learning and development in which problem solving occurs essentially through interactions among peers without resort to a conventional knowledge hierarchy". The authors find this a potentially useful way of conceptualising their category of dealing with the atypical, where no set procedure exists and learning must address a problem or contradiction, often crossing workgroup boundaries.
requirements: The construct presupposes a focus on the social and organisational context rather than on individual learning, with contradictions or atypical events as sources of change.
constraints: The article presents expansive learning as a potentially useful conceptualisation for dealing with the atypical, not as a framework validated against the study data.
target_learning_goals: Dealing with atypical problems for which no set procedure or process exists
examples: The authors link dealing with the atypical to expansive learning because such problem solving can require crossing boundaries of workgroups and practices, which the well-bounded notion of communities of practice cannot adequately capture.

citation: Burin, D. I., Irrazabal, N., Injoque Ricle, I., Saux, G., & Barreyro, J. P. (2018). Self-reported internet skills, previous knowledge and working memory in text comprehension in E-learning. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education, 15:18. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-018-0099-9
title: Four-domain model of Internet skills (operational, formal, information, strategic)
description: The article adopts van Deursen and van Dijk's taxonomy of Internet skills, in which "Operational skills consist of the actions that allow a person to use digital tools", "Formal skills refer to navigation and orientation in structures specific to digital media", information skills concern searching, comparing, assessing and integrating information, and strategic skills involve using the Internet to achieve personal, professional, or social goals. The study adapts and validates the self-report scale for the first three domains in a Latin American college sample, excluding the strategic dimension because three items could not be culturally adapted.

constraints: The validated version covers only operational, formal/navigation, and informational/evaluation domains; strategic skills were not studied
target_learning_goals: digital reading and navigation skills for e-learning task completion
examples: Study 1 administered a 15-item adapted Likert-type scale and recovered the three factors via exploratory factor analysis

They recommend that teachers and instructional designers consider this before implementing the common practice of closed-question comprehension checks after lessons.

article_title: “When I Think of Black Girls, I Think of Opportunities”: Black Girls' Identity Development and the Protective Role of Parental Socialization in Educational Settings
citation: Burnett Marketa, McBride Margarett, Green McKenzie N., Cooper Shauna M. (2022). “When I Think of Black Girls, I Think of Opportunities”: Black Girls' Identity Development and the Protective Role of Parental Socialization in Educational Settings. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2022.933476
title: Phenomenological Variant of Ecological Systems Theory (PVEST)
description: PVEST is Spencer's model of how Black children process and make meaning of lived experiences. It begins with self-other appraisals—perceptions of how others view one, with attention to biases and stereotypes—and "PVEST posits that how someone makes meaning of these self-other appraisals also impacts their stress engagement which leads to their reactive coping strategies." Stable identities emerge through adaptive or maladaptive coping, leading to adverse or productive outcomes. The study used PVEST as its guiding framework for a theoretical thematic analysis of girls' meaning-making.
requirements: Codes and analysis aligned with PVEST and the research questions, emphasizing youths' own meaning-making as interpreters of their experiences
target_learners: adolescent Black girls in middle school and high school
target_learning_goals: identity development
coping with gendered racism in educational settings
examples: The study's codebook of seven overarching identity and socialization codes was developed to closely align with PVEST and the research questions

article_title: Comprehension skill, inference-making ability, and their relation to knowledge
citation: Kate Cain, Jane V. Oakhill, Marcia A. Barnes, and Peter E. Bryant. (2001). Comprehension skill, inference-making ability, and their relation to knowledge. Memory & Cognition, 29(6), 850-859. https://doi.org/10.3758/BF03196476
title: Mental models account of children's text comprehension difficulties: poor comprehenders construct incomplete, poorly integrated representations of text
description: The article interprets children's comprehension difficulties within the mental models framework, in which skilled comprehension requires building a coherent, integrated model of a text as a whole rather than only local links. The authors state that "poor comprehenders construct incomplete representations of text: They are often able to integrate information at a local level but are unable to produce a coherent integrated model of the text as a whole." In this study the framework motivated the distinction between coherence inferences, needed for cohesion, and elaborative inferences, which enrich the representation, and the finding that inference failures leave a poorly integrated text model.
requirements: Assessment of inference making must separate inferences essential for textual coherence from merely elaborative ones
Relevant background knowledge must be available to the learner for knowledge-based inferences to be possible
constraints: The account is applied to children with age-appropriate word-reading and vocabulary skills whose difficulties arise at the text level
The study tested 7- to 8-year-olds listening to a multiepisode story, so scope is limited to that age band and auditory presentation
target_learners: 7- to 8-year-old children with specific reading comprehension deficits despite adequate word-reading skills
target_learning_goals: Text comprehension
Inference making during narrative listening and reading
examples: Children heard a six-episode story about an imaginary planet after learning a 12-fact knowledge base, and answered coherence, elaborative, literal, and simile questions after each episode
key_sources: Kate Cain, Jane V. Oakhill, Marcia A. Barnes, and Peter E. Bryant. (2001). Comprehension skill, inference-making ability, and their relation to knowledge. Memory & Cognition, 29(6), 850-859. https://doi.org/10.3758/bf03196414

article_title: Behavioral and Brain Measures of Executive Attention and School Competence in Late Childhood
citation: Checa, P., & Rueda, M. R. (2011). Behavioral and Brain Measures of Executive Attention and School Competence in Late Childhood. Developmental Neuropsychology. https://doi.org/10.1080/87565641.2011.591857
title: Promote executive attention and effortful control to help children succeed at school
description: The article recommends that educators and intervention designers attend to children's executive attention and effortful control as foundations for school competence. It states: "Our data point out the importance of promoting executive attention and effortful control in order to help children to be successful at school." The authors argue this evidence "has the potential to guide the design of intervention programs aiming at enhancing school readiness."
requirements: Interventions should target the executive attention network and temperamental effortful control, which the study links to grades and schooling skills.
constraints: The authors note future research is needed to test whether attention training actually results in better academic performance and schooling competence.
target_learners: children in late childhood and early adolescence (around age 12)
target_learning_goals: academic achievement in mathematics and literacy
schooling skills such as rule following and student-role understanding
examples: The study measured executive attention with a combined Flanker-Go/No-Go task and linked interference suppression efficiency to math grades and schooling skills.
key_sources: Checa, P., & Rueda, M. R. (2011). Behavioral and Brain Measures of Executive Attention and School Competence in Late Childhood. Developmental Neuropsychology. https://doi.org/10.1080/87565641.2011.591857

article_title: Behavioral and Brain Measures of Executive Attention and School Competence in Late Childhood
citation: Checa, P., & Rueda, M. R. (2011). Behavioral and Brain Measures of Executive Attention and School Competence in Late Childhood. Developmental Neuropsychology. https://doi.org/10.1080/87565641.2011.591857
title: Executive attention network as the neural system underlying effortful control and self-regulation
description: Within Posner's neurocognitive model, executive attention is related to a neural network involving the anterior cingulate cortex and prefrontal regions. The article states that "the executive attention network in Posner's model constitutes the neural system underlying EC" (Rueda, Posner, & Rothbart, 2005a). Executive attention is required in situations involving "overcoming well-learned or dominant responses, facing novel and/or dangerous situations, detecting and correcting errors and planning actions." The study uses this framework to interpret correlations between temperament, brain, and school measures.
requirements: The framework assumes measures of executive attention through conflict tasks correlate with parent and/or self-reported measures of effortful control.
constraints: The article notes the influence of effortful control on school competence is not the same at different ages.
target_learners: children and adolescents in school settings
target_learning_goals: self-regulation of cognition and action
school competence and academic achievement
examples: The study used a combined Flanker and Go/No-Go task with EEG to index the efficiency of the executive attention network in twelve-year-olds.
key_sources: Checa, P., & Rueda, M. R. (2011). Behavioral and Brain Measures of Executive Attention and School Competence in Late Childhood. Developmental Neuropsychology. https://doi.org/10.1080/87565641.2011.591857

article_title: Self-Reported Sleep and Executive Function in Early Primary School Children
citation: Chen Y, Wang Y, Wang S, Zhang M and Wu N. (2021). Self-Reported Sleep and Executive Function in Early Primary School Children. Front. Psychol. 12:793000. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2021.793000
title: Chinese version of the Sleep Self-Report (SSR) with validated psychometrics
description: The Sleep Self-Report is a 23-item, 3-point self-report questionnaire assessing children's sleep habits and disturbance, with higher summed scores indicating more disturbed sleep. The authors developed a Chinese version by translation and back-translation and validated it in a separate sample: "Another 433 Chinese children (7–12  y ears old) were recruited to test the psychometric properties of the Chinese version, revealing that the Cronbach's α was 0.82 and retest-reliability (ICC) was 0.87." In the main study it served as the sleep disturbance measure for 204 children.
requirements: Requires children old enough for valid self-report; the article notes the youngest age adapted for SSR is 7 or 8 years old
constraints: Measures subjective multiple aspects of sleep (bedtime resistance, sleep anxiety, daytime sleepiness), not objective sleep duration
target_learning_goals: measurement of habitual sleep disturbance as a factor in children's cognitive development
examples: Administered collectively in groups of 20–40 children, with instructions read aloud and about 10 s per item
key_sources: Chen Y, Wang Y, Wang S, Zhang M and Wu N. (2021). Self-Reported Sleep and Executive Function in Early Primary School Children. Front. Psychol. 12:793000. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2021.793000

article_title: Self-Reported Sleep and Executive Function in Early Primary School Children
citation: Chen Y, Wang Y, Wang S, Zhang M and Wu N. (2021). Self-Reported Sleep and Executive Function in Early Primary School Children. Front. Psychol. 12:793000. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2021.793000
title: Extended 36-trial Red-Blue Test of inhibitory control with reported reliability
description: The Red-Blue Test is a Stroop/Day-Night-adapted computer task in which children name colors according to a reversed rule on an alien planet, scoring correct answers given within 2 s. The authors extended the original 16-trial preschool version to 36 trials for early primary school children, reasoning that children make more errors in later trials and that reliability increases with trial number. They report that "With the increase of trial number, the current test has gained sufficient reliability (split-half r = 0.82, Cronbach α = 0.71)."
requirements: One-to-one administration with two checking trials to ensure the child understands the rule
constraints: Scored by accuracy only, not reaction time; the authors note RT or speed may be more reliable in certain cognitive tests
target_learning_goals: assessment of inhibitory control as an executive function component
examples: Used as the inhibitory control measure in the 204-child study, with 36 trials total
key_sources: Chen Y, Wang Y, Wang S, Zhang M and Wu N. (2021). Self-Reported Sleep and Executive Function in Early Primary School Children. Front. Psychol. 12:793000. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2021.793000

article_title: Self-Reported Sleep and Executive Function in Early Primary School Children
citation: Chen Y, Wang Y, Wang S, Zhang M and Wu N. (2021). Self-Reported Sleep and Executive Function in Early Primary School Children. Front. Psychol. 12:793000. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2021.793000
title: Three-component model of executive function (inhibitory control, cognitive flexibility, working memory)
description: The article adopts the multidimensional conceptualization of executive function in which "It is often postulated in the literature that EF has three elementary components: inhibitory control, working memory, and cognitive flexibility." Each component is measured by a separate task (Red-Blue Test, Wisconsin Card Sorting Test, Backward Digit Span), and the components are moderately associated but separable. The study's design treats each component's link with sleep separately, which the authors say previous research neglecting the multidimensionality tended to miss.
requirements: Separate tasks for each component; the article notes few studies have systematically investigated sleep against all components
constraints: The structure of EF develops with age; the article notes shifting was found mixed with inhibition in young children, so correlation patterns may differ across age groups
target_learners: typically developing children in early primary school
target_learning_goals: understanding how sleep relates to distinct executive function components underlying school performance
examples: Applied in the current study with one classic task per component, administered counterbalanced in about 20 min per child
key_sources: Chen Y, Wang Y, Wang S, Zhang M and Wu N. (2021). Self-Reported Sleep and Executive Function in Early Primary School Children. Front. Psychol. 12:793000. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2021.793000

article_title: Working memory, inhibitory control, and reading disability
citation: Chiappe, P., Hasher, L., & Siegel, L. S. (2000). Working memory, inhibitory control, and reading disability. Memory & Cognition, 28(1), 8-17. https://www.psychonomic.org
title: Inhibitory control hypothesis: three functions (access, deletion, restraint) govern working memory contents
description: The article tests the Hasher and colleagues account in which inhibition controls the contents of working memory through three functions. As the article states, "These functions are access, deletion, and restraint": access prevents goal-irrelevant information from entering working memory, deletion suppresses information that has become irrelevant (whose failure yields proactive interference), and restraint prevents strong responses from seizing control so other responses can be considered. The study uses intrusion error types and a mixed span format to index these functions in relation to age and reading skill.
requirements: Assessment requires error analysis of span-task recall, classifying intrusions as current nonfinal, previous, or extraneous
constraints: The article reports the error analyses provided only mixed support for the hypothesis as applied to aging, with no age effects for previous or extraneous intrusions
target_learners: individuals aged 6-49, including those with reading disabilities
target_learning_goals: working memory capacity for storage during processing
word recognition and reading comprehension
examples: Experiment 1 used the blocked listening span format and Experiment 2 a mixed format to test whether reducing proactive interference would diminish age and reading-skill differences
key_sources: Chiappe, P., Hasher, L., & Siegel, L. S. (2000). Working memory, inhibitory control, and reading disability. Memory & Cognition, 28(1), 8-17. https://doi.org/10.3758/bf03211570

article_title: Working memory, inhibitory control, and reading disability
citation: Chiappe, P., Hasher, L., & Siegel, L. S. (2000). Working memory, inhibitory control, and reading disability. Memory & Cognition, 28(1), 8-17. https://www.psychonomic.org
title: Minimize proactive interference when measuring or supporting working memory across the lifespan
description: Because age-related declines in working memory span appear when trials are blocked and hence mutually interfering, task procedures that make trials distinctive reduce or eliminate those declines. The article shows that presenting the listening span task in a mixed format, in which each set contains two-, three-, and four-item trials, removed the adult decline seen with the blocked format. This supports designing assessment and instructional tasks so that earlier trials do not proactively interfere with later recall.
requirements: Trial formats must be arranged so that items from earlier trials are distinct from later targets, as in the mixed design
constraints: The mixed format did not eliminate differences between skilled and disabled readers, so reducing proactive interference does not remove reading-skill-related deficits
target_learners: learners across the lifespan, including middle-aged and older adults
target_learning_goals: accurate recall of target information during concurrent processing
examples: Experiment 2 administered three sets each containing a two-item trial followed by a three-item trial and ending with a four-item trial, rather than blocking trials by set size
key_sources: Chiappe, P., Hasher, L., & Siegel, L. S. (2000). Working memory, inhibitory control, and reading disability. Memory & Cognition, 28(1), 8-17. https://doi.org/10.3758/bf03211570

article_title: Language development and everyday functioning of children with hearing loss assessed at 3 years of age
citation: Ching Teresa Y. C., Crowe Kathryn, Martin Vivienne, Day Julia, Mahler Nicole, Youn Samantha, Street Laura, Cook Cassandra, Orsini Julia (2010). Language development and everyday functioning of children with hearing loss assessed at 3 years of age. International journal of speech-language pathology. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3094718/
title: Parents’ Evaluation of Aural/oral performance of Children (PEACH) questionnaire
description: The PEACH is an interview-administered parent questionnaire for assessing children’s functional performance in everyday life based on parents’ observations. The article describes it as "applicable for assessing children with hearing loss ranging from mild to profound degrees whose age ranges from 4 weeks to 18 years" and reports it was reliable for evaluating amplification effectiveness in real life. In this study, children’s performance was expressed as deviation from age-appropriate means, and PEACH scores correlated significantly with standardized language measures.
requirements: Administered as an interview with parents; uses normative data and critical differences (Ching & Hill, 2007) to relate performance to normal-hearing peers.
constraints: Performance expressed relative to normative data; applicable across mild to profound hearing loss.
target_learners: children with hearing loss aged 4 weeks to 18 years
target_learning_goals: evaluating aural/oral communicative functioning in everyday life
examples: Used with 61 parents of 3-year-old children in the LOCHI study; mean age-corrected score was −23.5.
key_sources: Ching Teresa Y. C., Crowe Kathryn, Martin Vivienne, Day Julia, Mahler Nicole, Youn Samantha, Street Laura, Cook Cassandra, Orsini Julia (2010). Language development and everyday functioning of children with hearing loss assessed at 3 years of age. International journal of speech-language pathology. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3094718/

article_title: Language development and everyday functioning of children with hearing loss assessed at 3 years of age
citation: Ching Teresa Y. C., Crowe Kathryn, Martin Vivienne, Day Julia, Mahler Nicole, Youn Samantha, Street Laura, Cook Cassandra, Orsini Julia (2010). Language development and everyday functioning of children with hearing loss assessed at 3 years of age. International journal of speech-language pathology. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3094718/
title: Use parents’ observations systematically to evaluate children’s communicative functioning in real life
description: The article recommends systematic use of parental observations to evaluate communicative functioning of children in real life, because structured tests may not reflect everyday ability. It reports that "the significant correlation with the PEACH provides evidence on convergent validity" of language skills measured in structured and unstructured settings. Parent report also extends assessment to children of non-English speaking background or whose primary mode of communication is not spoken English.
requirements: A validated parent questionnaire with normative data and critical differences, such as the PEACH.
constraints: Correlational evidence at 3 years of age; based on children with hearing loss using hearing aids.
target_learning_goals: assessing aural/oral communicative functioning in everyday life
examples: In the LOCHI study, parents completed the PEACH interview and scores correlated with PLS-4 and CDI measures.

article_title: Gaining control: changing relations between executive control and processing speed and their relevance for mathematics achievement over course of the preschool period
citation: Clark, C. A. C., Nelson, J. M., Garza, J., Sheffield, T. D., Wiebe, S. A., & Espy, K. A. (2014). Gaining control: changing relations between executive control and processing speed and their relevance for mathematics achievement over course of the preschool period. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2014.00107
title: Developmental cascade model: processing speed as a driving mechanism for higher-order cognition including EC
description: The developmental cascade model holds that growth in domain-general processing speed drives gains in higher-order cognition such as working memory and inhibitory control. The article states that "processing speed is conceptualized as a central mental capacity that drives changes in higher-order cognition", with age-related speed gains freeing cognitive resources for executive operations. This study tested the cascade account in early childhood by modeling EC and processing speed as overlapping latents across preschool age points, finding both support (speed contributes substantially to executive performance) and qualitative shifts in their interface over time.
requirements: Latent modeling that simultaneously loads executive tasks on EC and processing speed factors to parse their relative contributions
constraints: The article notes mediation analyses cannot reveal changes in the interplay of processing speed and EC over development, motivating its age-point approach
target_learning_goals: executive control development supporting mathematics achievement
examples: The study loaded each executive task simultaneously onto EC and processing speed factors at ages 3, 3.75, 4.5, and 5.25, covarying language proficiency
key_sources: Clark, C. A. C., Nelson, J. M., Garza, J., Sheffield, T. D., Wiebe, S. A., & Espy, K. A. (2014). Gaining control: changing relations between executive control and processing speed and their relevance for mathematics achievement over course of the preschool period. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2014.00107

article_title: First graders' literacy and self-regulation gains: The effect of individualizing student instruction
citation: Connor Carol McDonald, Ponitz Claire Cameron, Phillips Beth M., Travis Q. Monét, Glasney Stephanie, Morrison Frederick J. (2010). First graders' literacy and self-regulation gains: The effect of individualizing student instruction. Journal of School Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jsp.2010.06.003
title: Working model of self-regulation supporting academic growth through teacher practices
description: The article proposes a working model in which self-regulation, defined as "the deliberate modulation of one's responses to stimuli", enables students to focus cognitive resources on learning tasks, ignore distractions, and maximize learning time, thereby producing more efficient literacy learning. Key to the model is the assumption that teacher practices — planning, classroom management, use of routines, and opportunities to work independently and with peers — support the development of stronger self-regulation and hence stronger academic skills. The ISI intervention was designed to test this model (Fig. 1).
requirements: Teachers must be trained in planning, organizing, and classroom management strategies, and provide opportunities for students to practice managing their own behavior
constraints: The evidence for teacher practices contributing to self-regulation was largely correlational prior to this study; the self-regulation effect was evident only for students with initially weak self-regulation
target_learning_goals: Self-regulation (attention, working memory, inhibitory control)
Early literacy skills including reading comprehension and vocabulary
examples: The ISI intervention operationalized the model through professional development on organizing, minimizing non-instructional time, and planning, delivered via the A2i software
key_sources: Connor Carol McDonald, Ponitz Claire Cameron, Phillips Beth M., Travis Q. Monét, Glasney Stephanie, Morrison Frederick J. (2010). First graders' literacy and self-regulation gains: The effect of individualizing student instruction. Journal of School Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jsp.2010.06.003

article_title: First graders' literacy and self-regulation gains: The effect of individualizing student instruction
citation: Connor Carol McDonald, Ponitz Claire Cameron, Phillips Beth M., Travis Q. Monét, Glasney Stephanie, Morrison Frederick J. (2010). First graders' literacy and self-regulation gains: The effect of individualizing student instruction. Journal of School Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jsp.2010.06.003
title: Assessment-to-instruction (A2i) web-based planning software
description: The Assessment-to-instruction (A2i) software "translates assessment results into specific recommendations for amounts and types of instruction for each student in the classroom". It automatically records teachers' use, including total minutes of active use, which the study used as a metric of planning and a proxy for intervention fidelity. An integral part of the ISI intervention, A2i includes planning-specific components such as the Literacy Minutes Manager and the Group Activity Planner, and is available at http://isi.fcrr.org.
requirements: Teachers must be trained to use the software to plan individualized instruction, and assessment results must be available to generate recommendations
constraints: A2i use minutes are a proxy for fidelity, not a direct measure of instructional quality; treatment teachers' use ranged widely, from 15 to 370 minutes
target_learning_goals: Individualized literacy instruction matched to students' vocabulary and reading skills
examples: Treatment teachers used A2i on average about 160 minutes from September through May; the ISI Treatment variable coded control teachers as 0 and treatment teachers by their A2i minutes

article_title: Neurocognitive development of relational reasoning
citation: Crone Eveline A., Wendelken Carter, van Leijenhorst Linda, Honomichl Ryan D., Christoff Kalina, Bunge Silvia A. (2009). Neurocognitive development of relational reasoning. Developmental Science, 12(1), 55-66. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-7687.2008.00743.x
title: Relational integration account of rostrolateral prefrontal cortex function
description: The article endorses the account that RLPFC is specifically engaged when multiple relations must be jointly considered, whereas DLPFC is sensitive to task difficulty factors such as working memory and response selection rather than relational complexity per se. In adults, "RLPFC did not differentiate between REL-0 and REL-1 trials (REL-2 > REL-0, REL-1), whereas DLPFC exhibited an increase from REL-0 to REL-1 and from REL-1 to REL-2." The developmental findings extend this account: children recruit RLPFC for both 1st- and 2nd-order relational processing, and the adult specialization for integration is still undergoing change between ages 8 and 12.
requirements: Performance of problems that require joint consideration of multiple relations to detect RLPFC's selective engagement
constraints: The article notes alternative theoretical accounts of RLPFC involvement exist and are not adjudicated here
The account rests on cross-sectional age-group comparison rather than longitudinal within-person change
target_learning_goals: relational reasoning
relational integration
fluid intelligence
examples: Adults in the RPM-like task showed RLPFC activation selectively for REL-2 problems, replicating Christoff et al. (2001), while children engaged RLPFC for REL-1 as well as REL-2 problems
key_sources: Crone Eveline A., Wendelken Carter, van Leijenhorst Linda, Honomichl Ryan D., Christoff Kalina, Bunge Silvia A. (2009). Neurocognitive development of relational reasoning. Developmental Science, 12(1), 55-66. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-7687.2008.00743.x

article_title: Mothers, Intrinsic Math Motivation, Arithmetic Skills, and Math Anxiety in Elementary School
citation: Daches Cohen L and Rubinsten O (2017) Mothers, Intrinsic Math Motivation, Arithmetic Skills, and Math Anxiety in Elementary School. Front. Psychol. 8:1939. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.01939
title: Dual-measure framework of math anxiety: accessible self-representations versus inaccessible cognitive structures
description: The article organizes math anxiety assessment around two kinds of representation: accessible self-representations measured by explicit self-report questionnaires such as the AMAS, and inaccessible cognitive structures activated automatically, measured implicitly through attentional bias in the numerical dot-probe task. Its central organizing finding is that "diﬀerent factors predict accessible self-representations as compared to inaccessible cognitive structures of children's math anxiety" — cognitive factors predicted the explicit measure while environmental factors predicted the implicit one. The framework motivates using both kinds of tools when assessing math anxiety in children.
requirements: Assessment must include both an explicit self-report questionnaire and an implicit task such as the numerical dot-probe task, since the two measure distinct facets
constraints: The article notes the explicit and implicit measures were non-significantly correlated in this sample and that the relatively small sample size warrants caution
target_learning_goals: mathematics learning and math anxiety
arithmetic skills
intrinsic math motivation
examples: Sixth graders completed the AMAS self-report questionnaire and the numerical dot-probe task, whose congruency effect served as the implicit measure of attentional bias toward math-related stimuli
key_sources: Daches Cohen L and Rubinsten O (2017) Mothers, Intrinsic Math Motivation, Arithmetic Skills, and Math Anxiety in Elementary School. Front. Psychol. 8:1939. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.01939

article_title: Demystifying cognitive flexibility: Implications for clinical and developmental neuroscience
citation: Dajani, D. R., & Uddin, L. Q. (2015). Demystifying cognitive flexibility: Implications for clinical and developmental neuroscience. Trends in Neurosciences. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tins.2015.07.003
title: Cognitive flexibility as an emergent property of efficient executive function, measured by set shifting and task switching
description: The review defines cognitive flexibility as "the ability to appropriately adjust one's behavior according to a changing environment" and as "an emergent property of efficient executive function" typically measured with set shifting or task switching paradigms. It adopts Bunge and Zelazo's hierarchy in which set shifting is a lower-level form and task switching the most complex form. Both produce switch costs, reflecting inhibition of the previous response set and reconfiguration to the new task.
requirements: Tasks must produce a switch cost to be valid measures of cognitive flexibility
Consistent operationalization across studies is required
constraints: The construct is difficult to examine due to the multitude of ways it has been described in the literature
target_learning_goals: flexible adjustment of behavior to changing environments
set shifting and task switching
key_sources: Dajani, D. R., & Uddin, L. Q. (2015). Demystifying cognitive flexibility: Implications for clinical and developmental neuroscience. Trends in Neurosciences. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tins.2015.07.003

article_title: Demystifying cognitive flexibility: Implications for clinical and developmental neuroscience
citation: Dajani, D. R., & Uddin, L. Q. (2015). Demystifying cognitive flexibility: Implications for clinical and developmental neuroscience. Trends in Neurosciences. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tins.2015.07.003
title: Cognitive flexibility arises from interplay of nodes within the executive control network rather than a distinct substrate
description: The authors propose that "Cognitive flexibility likely emerges from the interplay of specific nodes in the frontal and parietal cortices" which are not flexibility-specific but are activated across executive functions. Within the domain-general executive control network, "the specific computations among nodes and their anatomical specificity within the broader frontoparietal networks determine which EF is behaviorally observed." Temporal dynamics of inter-node connectivity may distinguish executive functions; salience, dorsal and ventral attention networks, vlPFC and IFJ are proposed to act in sequence during a switch.
requirements: Working memory load must be controlled in task designs to avoid confounds
Causal modeling studies are needed for validation
constraints: The model is speculative at this time and remains to be validated with future causal modeling studies
target_learning_goals: understanding neural mechanisms of flexible cognition
key_sources: Dajani, D. R., & Uddin, L. Q. (2015). Demystifying cognitive flexibility: Implications for clinical and developmental neuroscience. Trends in Neurosciences. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tins.2015.07.003

article_title: Demystifying cognitive flexibility: Implications for clinical and developmental neuroscience
citation: Dajani, D. R., & Uddin, L. Q. (2015). Demystifying cognitive flexibility: Implications for clinical and developmental neuroscience. Trends in Neurosciences. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tins.2015.07.003
title: Dynamic functional connectivity as an analytic approach for relating brain dynamics to cognitive flexibility
description: Dynamic functional connectivity is described as "a new analytic approach" that "attempts to account for variations in brain network topology as a function of time". The review presents it as a tool for quantifying time-varying functional connectivity, commonly implemented with a sliding window approach in fMRI data. It proposes this approach will enable insights into the levels of neural flexibility required for optimal cognitive flexibility in typical and atypical development.
requirements: Quantifies changes in functional connectivity metrics over time
Sliding window approach uses a fixed-length time window shifted by a fixed number of data points
constraints: The functional significance of dynamic functional connectivity in the brain is still under investigation
target_learning_goals: characterizing neural flexibility underlying cognitive flexibility
key_sources: Dajani, D. R., & Uddin, L. Q. (2015). Demystifying cognitive flexibility: Implications for clinical and developmental neuroscience. Trends in Neurosciences. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tins.2015.07.003

article_title: Cognitive flexibility supports the development of cumulative cultural learning in children
citation: Davis, S., Rawlings, B., Clegg, J. M., Ikejimba, D., Watson-Jones, R. E., Whiten, A. & Legare, C. H. (2022). Cognitive flexibility supports the development of cumulative cultural learning in children. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-022-18231-7
title: Cumulative cultural evolution requires behavioral switching and maintenance of adopted improvements
description: The article frames cumulative cultural evolution (CCE) as "the process of accumulating knowledge and skills that increases the complexity and/or efficiency of technology and other forms of culture over time". It decomposes CCE into switching (relinquishing a current behavior for an improved version) and maintenance (resisting reversion to earlier versions and omitting redundant actions), arguing cognitive flexibility underpins these processes and their ontogeny in childhood.
requirements: Successful CCE requires both behavioral switching to improved versions and maintenance of what has been adopted
constraints: The framework is developed and tested with U.S. children aged 3–5 in a puzzlebox task
target_learning_goals: flexibly switching to more efficient solutions
maintaining adopted solutions and omitting redundant actions
examples: Children learned an inefficient Serialbox method by demonstration, witnessed a more efficient method, and were given multiple further interaction opportunities
key_sources: Davis, S., Rawlings, B., Clegg, J. M., Ikejimba, D., Watson-Jones, R. E., Whiten, A. & Legare, C. H. (2022). Cognitive flexibility supports the development of cumulative cultural learning in children. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-022-18231-7

article_title: Working Memory Model and Language Learning
citation: Demir, Bora. (2021). Working Memory Model and Language Learning. Shanlax International Journal of Education. https://doi.org/10.34293/education.v9iS2-Sep.4366
title: Baddeley's multi-component Working Memory model as a framework for language learning
description: The article takes Baddeley's (2012) Working Memory model as its theoretical framework for understanding language learning. WM is described as "a complex and limited cognitive system" that enables input "to be temporarily stored, monitored and manipulated". The model comprises a central executive and three slave systems — the phonological loop, the visuospatial sketchpad, and the episodic buffer — each handling different information types. The article uses this structure to map specific WM components onto specific language-learning processes.
requirements: The model is used as a theoretical framework for interpreting language-learning phenomena, requiring researchers to specify which WM component underlies a given language task
constraints: The article notes the model is "not perfectly specified" and "the components of the model and their interrelationships are underspecified" (Andrade, 2001, as cited)
The model's simplicity "fails in reflecting the nature of real cognition" and is "hard to apply to phenomena outside the domain of laboratory short-term memory tasks"
The central executive "remains the least understood component of the model"
target_learning_goals: language learning (vocabulary, reading, comprehension, production)

article_title: Metacognition and motivation as predictors for mathematics performance of Belgian elementary school children
citation: Desoete, A., Baten, E., Vercaemst, V., De Busschere, A., Baudonck, M., & Vanhaeke, J. (2019). Metacognition and motivation as predictors for mathematics performance of Belgian elementary school children. ZDM Mathematics Education, 51, 667–677. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11858-018-01020-w
title: Teachers should attend to both mathematical accuracy and fluency, and to metacognitive and motivational aspects, especially for poor performers
description: The article's practical recommendation, drawn from its longitudinal finding that accuracy and fluency have "overlapping yet different predictors", is that teachers pay attention to both aspects of mathematics. Because poor performers were found to be less intrinsically motivated, less metacognitively accurate, and to overestimate their performances more often than well-performing peers in all grades, the authors stress the importance of attending to these metacognitive and motivational aspects in mathematics education.
requirements: Instruction should address both accuracy and fluency as partly distinct outcome aspects of mathematics learning.
constraints: The recommendation rests on the study's Belgian elementary sample tested in January and June; the motivation–accuracy relation was reported for Grade 3.
target_learning_goals: Mathematical accuracy
Mathematical fluency
Metacognitive accuracy of performance evaluation
Intrinsic motivation for mathematics
examples: The study tested Belgian children from Grade 1 till 6 in January and June and derived the recommendation from the differing predictor sets for accuracy and fluency.

title: Opportunity–propensity (O–P) model of learning applied to mathematics achievement
description: The opportunity–propensity (O–P) model of learning is the organizing framework of the study, in which factors such as metacognitive postdiction skills, intrinsic motivation and prior proficiency in mathematics function as Propensity factors predicting mathematics performance. The article applies this model longitudinally to Belgian elementary children to test which propensity factors predict mathematical accuracy and fluency over a school semester, finding prior mathematical accuracy to be the especially important propensity factor.
requirements: Longitudinal measurement of prior performance and propensity factors to predict later mathematics outcomes.
constraints: Applied here to elementary mathematics (accuracy and fluency) in a Belgian sample; predictors for accuracy and fluency differ.

examples: The study investigated metacognitive postdiction skills, intrinsic motivation and prior proficiency in mathematics as Propensity factors within the O–P model.

article_title: ADHD Subtype Differences in Reinforcement Sensitivity and Visuospatial Working Memory
citation: Dovis, S., Van der Oord, S., Wiers, R.W., & Prins, P.J.M. (2015). ADHD subtype differences in reinforcement sensitivity and visuospatial working memory. Journal of Clinical Child and Adolescent Psychology, 44(5), 859-874. https://doi.org/10.1080/15374416.2014.895940
title: Dual-component model of visuospatial working memory: short-term memory and central executive
description: The article adopts a model in which visuospatial working memory "is composed of short-term memory (STM) and a central executive (CE)". It uses this decomposition to locate subtype-specific deficits: in ADHD-C both components seem impaired, whereas in ADHD-I only the CE appears impaired while STM is intact. The model also allows motivational impairments to be traced to their effects on the separate WM components. This componential framing organizes the study's experimental comparisons of STM, CE and WM performance across subtypes and reinforcement conditions.
requirements: Tasks must separately index STM and CE components of visuospatial working memory for the decomposition to be tested.
constraints: The article notes that in children with ADHD-C the components only "seem impaired", and no prior studies had investigated these WM components in children with ADHD-I.
target_learning_goals: visuospatial working memory performance
examples: The study examined effects of standard and high reinforcement on visuospatial WM-, STM-, and CE performance across the two ADHD subtypes and controls.
key_sources: Dovis, S., Van der Oord, S., Wiers, R.W., & Prins, P.J.M. (2015). ADHD subtype differences in reinforcement sensitivity and visuospatial working memory. Journal of Clinical Child and Adolescent Psychology, 44(5), 859-874. https://doi.org/10.1080/15374416.2014.895940

article_title: ADHD Subtype Differences in Reinforcement Sensitivity and Visuospatial Working Memory
citation: Dovis, S., Van der Oord, S., Wiers, R.W., & Prins, P.J.M. (2015). ADHD subtype differences in reinforcement sensitivity and visuospatial working memory. Journal of Clinical Child and Adolescent Psychology, 44(5), 859-874. https://doi.org/10.1080/15374416.2014.895940
title: Use high reinforcement to improve visuospatial STM and WM performance in children with ADHD
description: The article shows that raising reinforcement above a standard feedback-only level improves visuospatial STM and WM performance in children with ADHD. In the experiment, a high level of reinforcement was operationalized as "feedback + 10 euros" on top of standard feedback. The improvement occurred in both the ADHD-C and ADHD-I subtypes and was "equally pronounced in both subtypes", supporting reinforcement as a motivational lever for these children. The principle applies specifically to STM and WM tasks, not to CE-related performance.
requirements: Reinforcement must be substantially higher than standard feedback alone; the study used feedback plus a monetary reward of 10 euros.
constraints: High reinforcement did not improve CE-related performance, so the benefit is limited to STM and WM components.
The improvement was observed in children with ADHD but not in typically developing controls.
target_learning_goals: visuospatial working memory
visuospatial short-term memory
examples: The experiment compared a standard feedback-only condition with a high-reinforcement condition of feedback + 10 euros in children aged 9-12 with ADHD-I, ADHD-C, and controls.

article_title: The contribution of executive functions to narrative writing in fourth grade children
citation: Drijbooms, E., Groen, M. A., & Verhoeven, L. (2015). The contribution of executive functions to narrative writing in fourth grade children. Reading and Writing. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-015-9558-z
title: Microstructure/macrostructure framework mapping composition levels to word-, sentence-, and text-level language
description: The article organizes written composition assessment into microstructure (word-level productivity, sentence-level complexity) and macrostructure (text-level content and structure). As printed: "these micro- and macrostructural levels correspond very closely to the levels of language at which text is generated". This framework allowed the study to test whether different EF regulate different composition levels.
requirements: Measures of productivity, complexity, and story content derived from transcribed narratives
constraints: Only three measures (productivity, complexity, story content) were included; other components might tap different abilities
target_learning_goals: written narrative composition skills
examples: Text length indexed productivity, MLTUw indexed complexity, ERRNI story content scoring indexed macrostructure
key_sources: Drijbooms, E., Groen, M. A., & Verhoeven, L. (2015). The contribution of executive functions to narrative writing in fourth grade children. Reading and Writing. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-015-9558-z

article_title: The contribution of executive functions to narrative writing in fourth grade children
citation: Drijbooms, E., Groen, M. A., & Verhoeven, L. (2015). The contribution of executive functions to narrative writing in fourth grade children. Reading and Writing. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-015-9558-z
title: Assess a variety of low- and high-level executive functions with standard neuropsychological measures when studying developing writers
description: The authors argue that conceptualizing EF only as self-regulation strategies misses low-level EF contributions. They state "it is necessary to assess a variety of EF, including low-level EF with standard neuropsychological measures, in order to acquire more insight into the contribution of EF to writing outcome in developing writers". Their broad battery revealed direct and indirect EF contributions.
requirements: A broad test battery covering inhibition, updating, shifting, and planning
constraints: Findings are from one grade (fourth) and one genre (narrative)
target_learning_goals: written composition
examples: The study administered eight EF tasks including Tea-Ch subtests, WISC-IV Digit Span, D-KEFS tasks, and Tower of London

article_title: How executive functions predict development in syntactic complexity of narrative writing in the upper elementary grades
citation: Drijbooms, E., Groen, M. A., & Verhoeven, L. (2017). How executive functions predict development in syntactic complexity of narrative writing in the upper elementary grades. Reading and Writing, 30, 209–231. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-016-9670-8
title: Developmental model of writing: transcription skills, oral language skills, and executive functions as interacting component skills within working memory
description: The article frames writing development with a developmental model (Berninger & Winn, 2006) in which "three interrelated component skills underlie written text production, as they interact functionally during the writing process in an environment of working memory (WM): transcription skills, oral language skills, and executive functions (EF)." The model specifies constraints influencing the writing process and postulates that the relative influence of each component changes over time: transcription is critical early, and its automatization frees WM resources for language skills and EF, which constrain later composition. The present study tests the model's longitudinal predictions in the upper elementary grades.
requirements: The model assumes a working-memory environment in which component skills interact functionally during text production
constraints: The relative influence of components is hypothesized to shift with development, so predictor importance is age-dependent
target_learners: elementary school children, particularly upper elementary grades (fourth to sixth grade)
target_learning_goals: written composition, especially narrative writing and syntactic complexity of sentences
examples: The study assessed all three components in fourth grade with a broad neuropsychological battery and tested their longitudinal prediction of sixth-grade narrative writing
key_sources: Drijbooms, E., Groen, M. A., & Verhoeven, L. (2017). How executive functions predict development in syntactic complexity of narrative writing in the upper elementary grades. Reading and Writing, 30, 209–231. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-016-9670-8

article_title: How executive functions predict development in syntactic complexity of narrative writing in the upper elementary grades
citation: Drijbooms, E., Groen, M. A., & Verhoeven, L. (2017). How executive functions predict development in syntactic complexity of narrative writing in the upper elementary grades. Reading and Writing, 30, 209–231. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-016-9670-8
title: To improve children's sentence production in written composition in the upper elementary grades, instruction should attend to enhancing executive functions, particularly planning and inhibition
description: The article draws an instructional implication from its longitudinal findings: "in order to improve children's sentence production in written composition in the upper elementary grades, attention needs to be paid to enhancing children's EF, and particularly planning and inhibition skills." This aligns with the idea that children need more extensive training in self-regulation skills to manage written composition. The authors add that such training may be crucial because enhancing syntactic complexity positively impacts overall compositional quality.
requirements: Instruction targeting planning and inhibition should accompany writing instruction in the upper elementary grades
constraints: The recommendation rests on longitudinal correlational prediction, not on a manipulated intervention in this study
target_learners: typically developing children in upper elementary grades (fourth to sixth)
target_learning_goals: sentence production and syntactic complexity in written composition
examples: The study found fourth-grade planning and inhibition predicted improvement in narrative syntactic complexity by sixth grade

article_title: Life Stress Impairs Self-Control in Early Adolescence
citation: Duckworth, A. L., Kim, B., and Tsukayama, E. (2013). Life stress impairs self-control in early adolescence. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2012.00608
title: Hot/cool dual-process account: stress shifts processing toward the hot, impulsive system
description: The article interprets its findings through the hot/cool model (Metcalfe and Mischel, 1999), which "contrasts two opponent systems": a cool system that is "affectively-neutral, flexible, slow, and strategic" and a hot system that is "impulsive and reflexive, responding quickly to salient trigger features." Perceived stress is postulated to modulate the balance, so that as stress increases the cool system becomes dysfunctional and the hot system dominates. The authors present their longitudinal findings as direct, real-world evidence consistent with this account, which previously rested on animal and laboratory studies.
requirements: The account presupposes that perceived stress modulates the relative activity of the two systems
constraints: The article offers this as indirect interpretive support, not a direct test of the model
target_learning_goals: self-control over attentional, behavioral, and emotional impulses
examples: The three longitudinal studies are presented as direct evidence that children are more impulsive when negotiating stressful life circumstances

article_title: Exploring variation in measurement as a foundation for statistical thinking in the elementary school
citation: Lyn D English and Jane M Watson. (2015). Exploring variation in measurement as a foundation for statistical thinking in the elementary school. International Journal of STEM Education (2015) 2:3. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-015-0016-x
title: Build early statistical thinking on measurement activities that let students observe, represent and contrast variation in both hand-drawn and software formats
description: The article recommends an early instructional focus on variation and distribution through meaningful measurement activities. Students measure, observe the spread of values, create representations of their own choosing by hand and in software, and contrast two scenarios that embody different sources of variation. The authors conclude that findings "highlight the importance of an early focus on variation and distribution, with meaningful activities that motivate students to conduct and observe measurements, together with creating both hand-drawn and software representations to relate their experiences."
requirements: Activities must be aligned with the school curriculum so they form a core component rather than add-on learning experiences, as the authors state for their design
constraints: The article's evidence comes from year 4 classes in one middle socio-economic school within a 3-year design study; teachers needed preparatory meetings providing professional development on the core statistical ideas
target_learners: elementary school students, specifically year 4 (fourth grade)
target_learning_goals: appreciation of variation in data and measurement
representing and describing variability
using variability to make comparisons
informal inference and prediction
examples: Students measured one student's arm span repeatedly, then each class member once, created hand-drawn and TinkerPlots representations, and completed a delayed assessment 1 to 3 months later

article_title: Exploring variation in measurement as a foundation for statistical thinking in the elementary school
citation: Lyn D English and Jane M Watson. (2015). Exploring variation in measurement as a foundation for statistical thinking in the elementary school. International Journal of STEM Education (2015) 2:3. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-015-0016-x
title: Four-level developmental hierarchy of appreciation of variation (prerequisites, partial recognition, applications, critical aspects)
description: The article adopts, from Watson et al. (2003), a four-level hierarchy of increasing appreciation of variation used to frame its research questions and interpret student responses. Level 1 covers prerequisites such as interpreting context and simple graph reading; level 2, partial recognition, involves "putting ideas in context but focusing on single aspects and neglecting others"; level 3, applications, consolidates ideas in context with inconsistency on the most salient features; level 4, critical aspects, employs complex justification or critical reasoning. The study maps its three research questions to levels 2, 3 and 4 respectively.
requirements: Assessment of responses requires coding criteria that can distinguish descriptions, single-aspect focus, consolidation in context, and complex justification
constraints: The article states its assessment was more general than the Watson et al. survey and could only consider descriptively whether responses exhibited the type of thinking typical of the four levels
target_learners: elementary school students, with the hierarchy spanning grade levels 3 to 9 in its original development
target_learning_goals: understanding of variation in statistical investigations
statistical thinking and informal inference
examples: The study assumed all students had reached level 1, Prerequisites for Variation, and linked research question 1 to level 2, question 2 to level 3, and question 3 to level 4
