article_title: Self-regulation in the pre-adolescent brain
citation: Pas P., Hulshoff Pol H.E., Raemaekers M., Vink M. (2021). Self-regulation in the pre-adolescent brain. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dcn.2021.101012
title: Frontal control over subcortical regions as the developmental basis of proactive inhibitory control
description: The article works within a framework in which self-regulation develops through the integration of low-level executive functions such as reactive inhibition into higher-level proactive control, which "has been theorized to depend upon the establishment of frontal control over the rest of the brain, in particular subcortical regions". On this account, the shift from reactive to proactive inhibition strategies is linked to increased frontal activation and increased functional coupling between frontal and subcortical regions. The study tests this framework in pre-adolescent children by relating questionnaire-based self-regulation to frontal activation and cortico-subcortical coupling during a stop-signal anticipation task.
requirements: Measurement of both reactive and proactive inhibition with concurrent fMRI to index frontal activation and functional coupling
constraints: The article notes its cross-sectional data does not provide a definitive answer to how self-regulation increases relate to neural changes
target_learning_goals: Self-regulation and inhibitory control development
examples: The study related EATQ-R self-regulation scores to right mid frontal cortex activation and striatal-motor coupling in 640 children performing the Stop-Signal Anticipation Task
key_sources: Pas P., Hulshoff Pol H.E., Raemaekers M., Vink M. (2021). Self-regulation in the pre-adolescent brain. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dcn.2021.101012

article_title: Race Salience and Essentialist Thinking in Racial Stereotype Development
citation: Pauker, K., Ambady, N., & Apfelbaum, E. P. (2010). Race Salience and Essentialist Thinking in Racial Stereotype Development. Child Development, 81(6), 1799–1813. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8624.2010.01511.x
title: Developmental intergroup theory: psychological salience, categorization, and essentialism as core processes in stereotype formation
description: The article draws on Bigler and Liben's (2007) developmental intergroup theory, which proposes that "three core processes contribute to the formation of social stereotypes and prejudice: (a) establishing the psychological salience of different person attributes, (b) categorizing individuals by salient dimensions, and (c) developing sets of traits, behaviors, and emotions that are associated with particular salient social groups." The theory holds that once a dimension becomes salient, essentialism, in-group bias, and explicit and implicit attributions mold the development of stereotyping about that dimension, with perceptual discriminability, proportional group size, and explicit and implicit use shaping salience. The present study tested two components the theory suggests should affect racial stereotyping: race salience and essentialist thinking.
requirements: Race must become a psychologically salient dimension before categorization and stereotype development proceed along it
constraints: The article tested only the race salience and essentialist thinking components of the theory, not the full model
target_learning_goals: understanding the development of racial stereotypes and prejudice in childhood
examples: The study measured children's spontaneous sorting by race, racial justification, and racial constancy for self and others as operationalizations of the theory's salience and essentialism components
key_sources: Pauker, K., Ambady, N., & Apfelbaum, E. P. (2010). Race Salience and Essentialist Thinking in Racial Stereotype Development. Child Development, 81(6), 1799–1813. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8624.2010.01511.x

article_title: Gendered Pathways: How Mathematics Ability Beliefs Shape Secondary and Postsecondary Course and Degree Field Choices
citation: Perez-Felkner L, Nix S and Thomas K (2017) Gendered Pathways: How Mathematics Ability Beliefs Shape Secondary and Postsecondary Course and Degree Field Choices. Front. Psychol. 8:386. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00386
title: Enhance girls' beliefs about their mathematics ability under challenge, supported by social support from teachers, mentors, parents, and peers
description: The article recommends enhancing students' — especially girls' — beliefs about their mathematics ability when encountering challenging material, because these beliefs predict advanced science coursework and PEMC major selection at every stage. It states that "social support—from teachers, mentors, parents, peers—could be a valuable tool to scaﬀold students through challenges" and help girls counter lower beliefs about their mathematics ability. Recent interventions aiming to build resilience and malleable conceptions of intelligence are cited as promising approaches.
requirements: Feeling challenged is treated as a normal and necessary part of learning, so support should scaffold students through challenges rather than avoid difficulty
constraints: The recommendation rests on longitudinal observational associations, not on a test of the interventions themselves
target_learners: secondary school students, especially girls in mathematics-intensive course pathways
target_learning_goals: persistence in mathematics and science coursework and pursuit of PEMC degree fields
examples: The article cites science camps like SciGirls, recruiting girls into upper level science courses and extracurricular activities, informal science learning experiences, and increasing visibility of women scientists
key_sources: Perez-Felkner L, Nix S and Thomas K (2017) Gendered Pathways: How Mathematics Ability Beliefs Shape Secondary and Postsecondary Course and Degree Field Choices. Front. Psychol. 8:386. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00386

article_title: Spatial activity participation in childhood and adolescence: consistency and relations to spatial thinking in adolescence
citation: Emily Grossnickle Peterson, Adam B. Weinberger, David H. Uttal, Bob Kolvoord and Adam E. Green. (2020). Spatial activity participation in childhood and adolescence: consistency and relations to spatial thinking in adolescence. Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41235-020-00239-0
title: Bidirectional developmental model of spatial activities and spatial thinking across childhood and adolescence
description: The article proposes that relations between spatial activity participation and spatial thinking are bidirectional and can be examined at a single time point or across development (Fig. 1a, 1b). As the authors state, "participation in spatial activities may improve spatial thinking skills and strategies, and individuals with a greater capacity for spatial thinking may seek out opportunities to engage in spatial activities." The model distinguishes spatial skills from spatial habits of mind as distinct yet correlated facets of spatial thinking, and maps paths linking childhood activity participation, adolescent activity participation, and each facet. The present study tested the paths across development (Fig. 1b) rather than at a single point in time.
requirements: Measures of spatial activity participation at multiple developmental points (here, retrospective childhood CAQ and adolescent SAQ reports) and measures of both spatial skills and spatial habits of mind
constraints: The study was cross-sectional with retrospective self-report, so directionality of the relations could not be established; the authors call for longitudinal and intervention designs to test causal mechanisms
target_learners: Children and adolescents in STEM education contexts
target_learning_goals: Spatial thinking skills
Spatial habits of mind (spatial problem-solving strategies)
examples: The study regressed Paper Folding and SHOMI jointly on childhood and adolescent activity measures, testing paths B and C of the developmental model
key_sources: Emily Grossnickle Peterson, Adam B. Weinberger, David H. Uttal, Bob Kolvoord and Adam E. Green. (2020). Spatial activity participation in childhood and adolescence: consistency and relations to spatial thinking in adolescence. Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41235-020-00239-0

article_title: Spatial activity participation in childhood and adolescence: consistency and relations to spatial thinking in adolescence
citation: Emily Grossnickle Peterson, Adam B. Weinberger, David H. Uttal, Bob Kolvoord and Adam E. Green. (2020). Spatial activity participation in childhood and adolescence: consistency and relations to spatial thinking in adolescence. Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41235-020-00239-0
title: Attend to spatial activity participation during childhood, especially for girls, when planning spatial-thinking supports
description: The article recommends that educators and researchers consider when in development spatial activity participation matters, concluding that "Results highlight the importance of participating in spatial activities during childhood." Because childhood participation predicted later participation and later habits of mind, the authors argue that "spatial activity participation among young girls may be particularly important to consider in future research." Interventions should therefore target childhood participation rather than assuming adolescent participation can compensate for a childhood gap.
requirements: Opportunities for children to engage in spatial activities such as block play, puzzles, sports, and dance, with attention to activity participation across developmental stages
constraints: The study is cross-sectional and correlational; the authors note that future research will be necessary to directly assess whether interventions promoting childhood spatial activities increase later participation
target_learning_goals: Spatial thinking
Spatial habits of mind
STEM readiness
examples: The study found childhood activities predicted habits of mind even after controlling for adolescent activities, gender, and academic performance, and found no compensatory benefit of later participation

article_title: Fostering alphabet knowledge development: a comparison of two instructional approaches
citation: Piasta, S. B., Purpura, D. J., & Wagner, R. K. (2010). Fostering Alphabet Knowledge Development: A Comparison of Two Instructional Approaches. Reading and Writing, 23(6), 607-626. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-009-9174-x
title: Teach letter names and sounds together rather than letter sounds alone when fostering preschool alphabet knowledge
description: The article's central design recommendation is that for U.S. preschoolers, referring to each letter by its name and linking it to its corresponding sound (e.g., "the letter C that makes the sound/k/") fosters letter sound acquisition better than sound-only labeling. The authors state that "combined letter name and sound instruction may be most beneficial for U.S. preschoolers alphabet learning", while noting the mechanism is not entirely clear and more research is needed.
requirements: Instruction delivered in small groups (3-5 children) through scripted lessons of approximately 10-15 minutes, as in the study's 34-lesson curriculum
constraints: The advantage was specific to alphabet knowledge outcomes and did not generalize to other emergent literacy skills
The authors note the finding may not apply to children for whom letter sounds are a common, natural label, such as some children in the deaf community or UK-style instruction
Based on a small-scale study with observed power substantially lower than the intended 80%
target_learners: preschool-aged children (3- and 4-year-olds) with below-average letter knowledge
target_learning_goals: letter name knowledge
letter sound knowledge
examples: In the study, LNLS lessons referred to each letter by name and linked it to its sound, while LS lessons designated letters only by sound; both taught 26 uppercase letters plus 8 weekly review lessons over 9 weeks
key_sources: Piasta, S. B., Purpura, D. J., & Wagner, R. K. (2010). Fostering Alphabet Knowledge Development: A Comparison of Two Instructional Approaches. Reading and Writing, 23(6), 607-626. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-009-9174-x

article_title: Physical activity and creativity of children and youths
citation: Piya-amornphan N, Santiworakul A, Cetthakrikul S, Srirug P. (2020). Physical activity and creativity of children and youths. BMC Pediatrics. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12887-020-2017-2
title: Physical activity during childhood supports development of thinking processes including creativity
description: The article advances the account that childhood is a valuable period for developing creative skills because cognitive abilities attributed to prefrontal cortex function are required for creativity, and the prefrontal cortex does not completely mature until the early 20s. It concludes that "optimal physical activity is required during childhood for developing thinking process", positioning physical activity — especially active play — as supportive of cognitive development alongside previously reported links to intelligence and emotional quotients.
requirements: Physical activity during childhood, with active play as the directly reported indicator of physical activity in children and youths
constraints: The account rests on cross-sectional correlations; the article states many factors related to creativity remain and more information is needed to clarify other factors
target_learning_goals: creativity
cognitive function development
examples: The article cites cross-sectional studies in which increased physical activity was associated with higher intelligence quotient in 135 Saudi high school students and higher emotional quotient in 599 Taiwanese college students
key_sources: Piya-amornphan N, Santiworakul A, Cetthakrikul S, Srirug P. (2020). Physical activity and creativity of children and youths. BMC Pediatrics. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12887-020-2017-2

article_title: Costs of Selective Attention: When Children Notice What Adults Miss
citation: Plebanek, D. J., & Sloutsky, V. M. (2017). Costs of Selective Attention: When Children Notice what Adults Miss. Psychological Science, 28(6), 723-732. https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797617693005
title: Developmental shift from distributed to selective attention account
description: The article proposes that early attention is distributed across multiple stimulus dimensions because attention-control circuits are immature, so young children process task-irrelevant information well; with maturation, top-down selective attention develops, bringing efficiency for relevant information at the cost of attenuated processing of non-selected information. The article states that "Distributed attention early in development (stemming from the immaturity of attention-control circuits, Posner & Rothbart, 2007) results in greater processing of task-irrelevant information than more mature selective attention." Selection is described as supplementing, not replacing, diffuse attention within an attentional hierarchy.
requirements: Immature attention-control circuits in early development for the distributed-attention prediction; mature circuits for the selective-attention prediction
constraints: Young children are unlikely to exhibit top-down selectivity because supporting neural circuits are not fully developed; adults may distribute attention under high task demand such as high working memory load, and aging may also weaken top-down control
target_learning_goals: Processing of task-relevant and task-irrelevant information
development of selective attention
examples: Experiment 1 cued/uncued change detection and Experiment 2 visual search with recognition of relevant and irrelevant features, both showing the predicted reversal
key_sources: Plebanek, D. J., & Sloutsky, V. M. (2017). Costs of Selective Attention: When Children Notice what Adults Miss. Psychological Science, 28(6), 723-732. https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797617693005

article_title: Effects of Fact Retrieval Tutoring on Third‐Grade Students with Math Difficulties with and without Reading Difficulties
citation: Powell, S. R., Fuchs, L. S., Fuchs, D., Cirino, P. T., & Fletcher, J. M. (2009). Effects of Fact Retrieval Tutoring on Third-Grade Students with Math Difficulties with and without Reading Difficulties. Learning Disabilities Research & Practice, 24(1), 1-11. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-5826.2008.01272.x
title: MD subtype framework: MD-only versus MDRD differential difficulty
description: The article evaluates Geary's hypothesis that math difficulty subtypes represent distinct cognitive profiles. MDRD students' concurrent math and reading difficulty is attributed to weak phonological processing that hinders acquisition of vocabulary and math facts, whereas MD-only students' poor fact recall is attributed to weak number sense. The randomized trial's differential responsiveness finding is offered as support that MD-only versus MDRD "may represent a viable scheme for subtyping mathematics disability."
requirements: Subtype classification via math and reading screening cutoffs (WRAT Arithmetic and Reading percentiles)
constraints: The study was not designed to determine whether response differences are due to phonological processing or number sense skills
target_learning_goals: Automatic retrieval of basic number combinations
examples: Students were classified as MD-only (WRAT Arithmetic <26th percentile, WRAT Reading >39th percentile) or MDRD (Arithmetic <26th and Reading <25th percentile) and randomized within subtype.

article_title: Effects of Fact Retrieval Tutoring on Third‐Grade Students with Math Difficulties with and without Reading Difficulties
citation: Powell, S. R., Fuchs, L. S., Fuchs, D., Cirino, P. T., & Fletcher, J. M. (2009). Effects of Fact Retrieval Tutoring on Third-Grade Students with Math Difficulties with and without Reading Difficulties. Learning Disabilities Research & Practice, 24(1), 1-11. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-5826.2008.01272.x
title: Math Flash computer-assisted instruction for math fact practice
description: Math Flash is the computer-assisted instruction program used in both fact retrieval tutoring conditions. "In Math Flash, the student was presented with an addition or subtraction math fact with the answer; the math fact flashed on the screen for a second or two," after which the student typed the fact from memory while a number line shaded to represent addends or minuend and subtrahend. Correct answers earned sparkling numbers and applause; incorrect facts reappeared until typed correctly, and flashing speed adapted to performance, with treasure rewards for each five correct facts.
requirements: Tutor supervision during the 7.5-minute computer session
target_learning_goals: Automatic retrieval of addition and subtraction facts
examples: Used 7.5 minutes per session within FR-P and FR-C/P tutoring, three sessions per week over 15 weeks.

article_title: Language in the prediction of arithmetics in kindergarten and grade 1
citation: Praet, M., Titeca, D., Ceulemans, A., & Desoete, A. (2013). Language in the prediction of arithmetic in kindergarten and grade 1. Learning and Individual Differences (manuscript LAEIND-D-12-OO174R1). https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/LAEIND-D-12-OO174R1
title: Assess kindergarten language and number naming to inform targeted instruction and interventions for children at risk of arithmetic difficulties
description: The article argues that knowledge of kindergarten predictors should guide early support: "Such knowledge is necessary in order to inform targeted instruction and interventions that address the needs of children at risk". Because expressive language and number naming explained unique variance in early arithmetic, assessing these skills in kindergarten may identify children who need help before formal schooling compounds difficulties. The authors suggest future work test whether intervention on these skills raises grade 1 arithmetic.
requirements: Kindergarten assessment of expressive language and number naming before remediation decisions
constraints: The article notes it remains an open question whether intervention on language and/or number naming ability in kindergarten can increase grade 1 arithmetic skills
target_learners: children at risk of mathematical learning disabilities
target_learning_goals: early arithmetic skills
examples: The study tested 63 children in kindergarten on counting, estimation, logical thinking and language, then retested arithmetic in grade 1 to identify which kindergarten measures predicted later skill.
key_sources: Praet, M., Titeca, D., Ceulemans, A., & Desoete, A. (2013). Language in the prediction of arithmetic in kindergarten and grade 1. Learning and Individual Differences (manuscript LAEIND-D-12-OO174R1). https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/LAEIND-D-12-OO174R1

article_title: Physical Fitness Level Is Related to Attention and Concentration in Adolescents
citation: Reigal RE, Moral-Campillo L, Juárez-Ruiz de Mier R, Morillo-Baro JP, Morales-Sánchez V, Pastrana JL and Hernández-Mendo A (2020) Physical Fitness Level Is Related to Attention and Concentration in Adolescents. Front. Psychol. 11:110. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2020.00110
title: Physical activity for adolescents should be demanding enough to overcome a minimum adaptation threshold to benefit cognition
description: This principle holds that mere physical activity participation is not enough for cognitive benefit; activity must be sufficiently exigent to drive fitness adaptation, which the article links to better brain outcomes. It frames fitness level, not activity per se, as the relevant indicator. The article states "the practice of physical activity alone is not enough for the impact on the brain to be noticeable."
requirements: Physical activity of sufficient intensity/exigency to produce measurable fitness adaptation
constraints: The design does not allow causal relationships to be established; the threshold is an interpretation, not a tested optimum
target_learning_goals: selective attention and concentration as cognitive functions supporting academic and psychosocial adjustment
examples: The study classified participants into lower- and higher-fitness clusters via horizontal jump, 5×10 m speed and VO2max measures, and the higher-fitness cluster scored better on attention and concentration in both genders.
key_sources: Reigal RE, Moral-Campillo L, Juárez-Ruiz de Mier R, Morillo-Baro JP, Morales-Sánchez V, Pastrana JL and Hernández-Mendo A (2020) Physical Fitness Level Is Related to Attention and Concentration in Adolescents. Front. Psychol. 11:110. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2020.00110

article_title: Differences between presentation methods in working memory procedures: A matter of working memory consolidation.
citation: Ricker Timothy J., Cowan Nelson. (2014). Differences between Presentation Methods in Working Memory Procedures: A Matter of Working Memory Consolidation. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0034301
title: Working memory consolidation account of time-based forgetting
description: The article proposes that a post-encoding consolidation process, continuing after pattern masking, strengthens working memory traces and determines their vulnerability to time-based forgetting. Consolidation is distinguished from encoding: "consolidation is further processing that can occur even after a mask, and that helps makes the representation of the stimulus more resistant to forgetting". The experiments show that "the total amount of time available to consolidate the stimuli into working memory is what is important", reconciling studies that do and do not find duration-based forgetting. Candidate mechanisms discussed include attentional refreshing, neural desynchronization, and pattern identification or chunking.
requirements: Requires an encoded memory trace and central resources for consolidation to proceed after masking, as suggested by Jolicoeur and Dell'Acqua (1998)
constraints: The finding was obtained always with fairly substantial encoding times of at least 250 ms per item
The article does not try to distinguish short-term consolidation empirically from long-term consolidation, calling this a major and difficult future issue
The study did not manipulate interference, so consolidation's effect on interference-based forgetting is speculative
target_learners: adult college students performing working memory tasks
target_learning_goals: understanding maintenance of information in working memory over short retention intervals
examples: Across the four experiments, sequential conditions with post-mask free time showed 0.19-0.22 items forgotten between 1 and 12 s, while conditions without such free time showed 0.39-0.67 items forgotten.
key_sources: Ricker Timothy J., Cowan Nelson. (2014). Differences between Presentation Methods in Working Memory Procedures: A Matter of Working Memory Consolidation. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0034301

article_title: Creativity: The role of unconscious processes in idea generation and idea selection
citation: Ritter, S.M.; van Baaren, R.B.; Dijksterhuis, A.J. (2012). Creativity: The role of unconscious processes in idea generation and idea selection. Thinking Skills and Creativity, 7, 21-27. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tsc.2011.12.002
title: Unconscious thought theory: unconscious thought actively evaluates, weights, and integrates information
description: The article draws on dual process theories distinguishing a conscious, rule-based, controlled system from an unconscious, associative, automatic system, and on the theory of unconscious thought, under which "unconscious thought" is task-related thought occurring while conscious attention is directed elsewhere. It assumes unconscious thought is good at "evaluating, weighting, and integrating attribute information concerning various alternatives", which is why it predicts selection advantages after distraction. The paper extends this account to creativity, proposing the unconscious plays an active rather than merely passive role during incubation.
requirements: A distraction period during which conscious attention is directed elsewhere, so unconscious thought can operate on the task
constraints: The article notes prior research had yielded no sound empirical support for beneficial effects of unconscious processes on creative performance when only idea generation is measured
target_learning_goals: creative idea generation and selection of one's most creative idea
examples: In both experiments, participants in the unconscious thought condition clicked as quickly as possible on circles appearing at random screen locations for 2 min before listing ideas.

article_title: Creativity: The role of unconscious processes in idea generation and idea selection
citation: Ritter, S.M.; van Baaren, R.B.; Dijksterhuis, A.J. (2012). Creativity: The role of unconscious processes in idea generation and idea selection. Thinking Skills and Creativity, 7, 21-27. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tsc.2011.12.002
title: Insert a period of distraction before idea selection to improve selection of one's most creative idea
description: When learners have generated multiple ideas and must choose which to pursue, the article recommends a brief period of distraction during which unconscious thought can operate, rather than immediate selection or deliberate conscious deliberation. Participants "who had unconsciously thought about their ideas, however, were able to select their most creative and least creative idea from several self-generated ideas", whereas immediate and conscious-thought participants performed poorly at selection. The article presents this as "a means to enhance individuals' creative performance".
requirements: A set of self-generated ideas to choose among, and a roughly 2-minute unrelated distracting task to prevent task-relevant conscious thought
constraints: The benefit appeared for idea selection, not for the number or average creativity of generated ideas; the proposed evaluative-tagging mechanism is acknowledged as speculative
target_learning_goals: selecting one's most creative idea for further elaboration and implementation
examples: In both experiments, participants first listed ideas for 2 min, then unconscious-thought-condition participants performed a rapid circle-clicking distraction task for 2 min before selecting their most creative idea.

article_title: Consequences of Age-Related Cognitive Declines
citation: Salthouse, T. (2012). Consequences of Age-Related Cognitive Declines. Annual Review of Psychology, 63, 201-226. https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-psych-120710-100328
title: Typical versus maximal performance distinction as an explanation for absent real-world consequences of cognitive decline
description: This explanatory account holds that everyday outcomes reflect typical functioning whereas cognitive tests assess maximal functioning, so age-related deficits appear only when demands approach maximal levels. The review states: "what we do in daily life reflects our typical level of functioning, whereas cognitive tests attempt to assess our maximal level of functioning". Because people seldom need to function at their maximum, declines may go undetected in daily-life criteria. The review presents this as the first of four candidate explanations for the lab-life discrepancy.
requirements: Outcome criteria must reflect typical rather than maximal performance for the discrepancy to arise
constraints: The account does not deny real declines; it holds they are not detected because people seldom function at the level where deficits would appear
target_learning_goals: explaining why laboratory-measured cognitive declines do not necessarily impair everyday occupational and daily functioning
examples: The review contrasts the age distribution of top-scoring reasoning performers, which peaks before age 30, with the age distribution of Fortune 500 CEOs, which peaks near 60
key_sources: Salthouse, T. (2012). Consequences of Age-Related Cognitive Declines. Annual Review of Psychology, 63, 201-226. https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-psych-120710-100328

article_title: Sixth-grade students’ reasoning on the order relation of integers as influenced by prior experience: an inferentialist analysis
citation: Maike Schindler, Stephan Hußmann, Per Nilsson, Arthur Bakker. (2017). Sixth-grade students' reasoning on the order relation of integers as influenced by prior experience: an inferentialist analysis. Math Ed Res J 29:471–492. https://doi.org/10.1007/s13394-017-0202-x
title: Inferentialist epistemology for analyzing students' mathematical reasoning
description: The article develops an epistemological framework based on Brandom's inferentialism for studying students' reasoning on the order relation of integers. It treats reasoning as social, situated in the 'game of giving and asking for reasons' (GoGAR), implicitly normative, and holistic, with concepts interconnected in students' claims. It asks for the inferences students draw from out-of-school life, the mathematics classroom, contexts, and external representations such as the number line, prioritizing the reasoning itself over internal mental models.
requirements: Empirical settings must explicitly encourage students to make their reasons, inferences, and the origins of their inferences explicit
constraints: The framework does not aim to isolate individual knowledge or abstract mental models from students' utterances
target_learning_goals: reasoning on the order relation of integers
examples: Semi-structured, task-oriented clinical interviews in which the interviewer asked 'Why's that?' and 'Where do you know this from?' before and after a lesson series

citation: Maike Schindler, Stephan Hußmann, Per Nilsson, Arthur Bakker. (2017). Sixth-grade students' reasoning on the order relation of integers as influenced by prior experience: an inferentialist analysis. Math Ed Res J 29:471–492. https://doi.org/10.1007/s13394-017-0202-x
title: 'Out of the Debts' learning environment combining the debts-and-assets context with the number line
description: A learning environment developed by Hußmann and Schindler (2014a, b) in the KOSIMA project, which aims at teaching mathematics through real contexts. Students play a board game in groups of four in which each is an indebted person aiming to redeem debts; the board is a number line ('account bar') with positive and negative numbers, and players draw changing account balances with their pieces. Later problems invite reflection on positions on the account bar and the role of the minus sign, with temperatures and altitudes as further contexts.
requirements: Students should be involved in the GoGAR, drawing on out-of-school experiences and inferentially relating their reasoning to external representations
target_learners: sixth-grade students in German secondary school
target_learning_goals: understanding negative integers and the order relation
examples: In the study, students reflected on the context, e.g. on the possession of too many luxury goods ('I do not really need a car!')

article_title: The Contribution of Numerical Magnitude Comparison and Phonological Processing to Individual Differences in Fourth Graders’ Multiplication Fact Ability
citation: Schleepen TMJ, Van Mier HI, De Smedt B (2016) The Contribution of Numerical Magnitude Comparison and Phonological Processing to Individual Differences in Fourth Graders' Multiplication Fact Ability. PLoS ONE 11(6): e0158335. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0158335
title: Semantic-coding account: multiplication facts are stored as phonological/verbal codes in an interrelated semantic network, and symbolic magnitude comparison shares semantic mapping processes with fact retrieval
description: The article proposes that multiplication facts are stored in long-term memory as phonological (verbal) codes within a meaningfully organized, interrelated network of arithmetic facts. It argues that "magnitude" is a candidate dimension along which meaning is assigned to stored facts, so faster magnitude comparators can more easily access number-semantic fact representations. It further hypothesizes that symbolic magnitude comparison and multiplication fact retrieval "share the same semantic mapping processes", supported by cited neuroimaging work showing overlapping left temporo-parietal activation.
requirements: Multiplication facts must have been practiced enough that problem-answer pair associations are stored in long-term memory
constraints: The account is the authors' interpretation, supported by cited prior work rather than tested directly in this study
target_learners: elementary school children learning single-digit multiplication tables
target_learning_goals: multiplication fact retrieval fluency
examples: The study tested this account by correlating symbolic and nonsymbolic magnitude comparison speed with multiplication fact speed in 63 fourth graders

article_title: Enriching Mathematics Education with Visual Arts: Effects on Elementary School Students’ Ability in Geometry and Visual Arts
citation: Eveline M. Schoevers & Paul P. M. Leseman & Evelyn H. Kroesbergen. (2019). Enriching Mathematics Education with Visual Arts: Effects on Elementary School Students' Ability in Geometry and Visual Arts. International Journal of Science and Mathematics Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10763-019-10018-z
title: The MACE pedagogy: five key features for integrating geometry and visual arts
description: The MACE pedagogy is an explanatory framework for integrated geometry and visual arts instruction built on five features the article names: "visual arts perception, open activities, reflection, communication with peers, and a specific role of the teacher". Artworks are discussed whole-class with visual thinking strategies; open activities invite artwork production at the boundary of the two disciplines without predetermined solutions; lessons end with reflection making implicit knowledge explicit; peer communication supports creative thinking and geometrical language; and teachers act as facilitators asking open, activating questions. The framework underpins the MACE lesson series and PD program evaluated in the study.
requirements: A specific facilitator role of the teacher: asking open and activating questions and using academic geometrical vocabulary
Whole-class discussion of artworks, e.g. with an interactive whiteboard and visual thinking strategies
constraints: The article's evaluation found the PD component added no measurable student outcome effect beyond the lesson series and manual
target_learners: fourth, fifth, and sixth grade elementary students
target_learning_goals: geometrical ability (understanding and explaining geometric phenomena, geometrical vocabulary, creative geometrical problem solving)
visual arts perception
examples: In the lesson Playing with perspective, students discussed six artworks on perspective and viewpoints, then made photos creating visual illusions in groups of 3-4 students, followed by whole-class reflection

title: MACE program: nine integrated geometry-visual-arts lessons plus a five-session teacher professional development program
description: The MACE program is an instructional program consisting of "a lesson series for fourth, fifth, and sixth grade students in which geometry and visual arts education were integrated along with a PD program for teachers". The lesson series comprised nine lessons of 60-90 minutes each (five on the theme space, four on patterns), each with a whole-class introduction discussing artworks, an open activity in which students create an artwork in small groups, and a whole-class reflection. The PD program consisted of five 2.5-hour expert-guided sessions with interactive methods, with teachers teaching one or two MACE lessons after each session. It was evaluated in a quasi-experiment with 2909 students in 121 classes and 57 schools.
requirements: Teachers deliver the lesson series; the PD program is optional but was designed to assist implementation
constraints: Schools had to be within traveling distance of PD training locations, so random assignment of schools was not fully possible
target_learners: fourth, fifth, and sixth grade elementary students in the Netherlands

visual arts perception
creative skills in both disciplines

title: Use integrated visual arts and geometry lessons instead of regular geometry lessons to teach the geometry curriculum and visual arts perception
description: The article recommends that teachers replace regular textbook geometry lessons with the integrated MACE lesson series, because students reached the same level of geometrical understanding through open, creative lessons while additionally improving in perceiving geometrical aspects of visual artworks. citation: Seo S-M. (2018). The effect of fine motor skills on handwriting legibility in preschool age children. J. Phys. Ther. Sci. 30: 324–327. https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/4.0/
title: During handwriting instruction and treatment for preschool children, provide activities that develop fine motor precision and in-hand manipulation skills
description: The article recommends that occupational therapists embed fine-motor development activities into handwriting instruction and treatment for preschool-age children. Because fine motor precision and in-hand manipulation were the factors that affected legibility, "occupational therapists can provide activities that aid the development of fine motor precision and in-hand manipulation skills for children during the instruction and treatment of handwriting".
requirements: Children must first have sufficient handwriting readiness skills, since children without sufficient development of such readiness skills are at risk of bad handwriting habits
constraints: The supporting evidence is correlational and limited to normally developing children sampled from one region

examples: The study measured fine motor precision, manual dexterity, and Functional Dexterity Test performance in 52 preschool children and found these skills predicted handwriting legibility

article_title: Dynamics of Teacher–Student Relationships: Stability and Change Across Elementary School and the Influence on Children’s Academic Success
citation: Spilt, J. L., Hughes, J. N., Wu, J.-Y., & Kwok, O.-M. (2012). Dynamics of Teacher-Student Relationships: Stability and Change across Elementary School and the Influence on Children's Academic Success. Child Development, 83(4), 1180-1195. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8624.2012.01761.x
title: Bioecological and chronic-stress framing of teacher-student relationships as proximal processes whose cumulative exposure shapes development
description: The article applies the bioecological model (Bronfenbrenner & Morris, 2006), which posits four properties of development: "process, person, contexts, and time." Teacher-student interactions are proximal processes whose power depends on person, context, and time, and processes that recur over broader time intervals have greater impact than episodic ones. Combined with chronic stress models from peer-rejection research, this framing motivates modeling cumulative relationship trajectories rather than single-year snapshots, and interpreting chronic conflict's association with underachievement as an effect of prolonged relational adversity.
requirements: Longitudinal repeated measures of relationship quality across multiple years to capture cumulative exposure rather than single-time-point assessments
constraints: The article notes effects of a given process may differ across developmental periods, with long-term TSRQ effects possibly stronger in early school years than later years
target_learning_goals: academic achievement growth
school adjustment
examples: The study modeled grades 1-5 trajectories of conflict and warmth and tested their prediction of grade 6 achievement in 657 at-risk children

article_title: Violations of Core Knowledge Shape Early Learning
citation: Stahl Aimee E., Feigenson Lisa. (2019). Violations of Core Knowledge Shape Early Learning. Topics in Cognitive Science. https://doi.org/10.1111/tops.12389
title: Bayesian prior-strength account of surprise-driven learning from core versus acquired knowledge
description: The article proposes a Bayesian framework in which learners hold priors of varying strength—innate (core knowledge) or learned—and update them to posteriors upon observing events. The larger the prior-to-posterior discrepancy, the greater the surprise and "perhaps the greater the subsequent learning." On this quantitative view, priors set by core knowledge are stronger than those set by acquired associations, so their violation produces larger updates and greater learning enhancement. The authors offer this as one framework that might capture the potency of core versus acquired knowledge violations, while stressing it remains to be tested.
requirements: Empirical approaches capable of quantifying the degree of surprise learners experience and mapping it to subsequent learning, as the authors state will be needed
constraints: The article states this quantitative characterization of core versus acquired violations remains to be seen and will require extended efforts using multiple empirical approaches
target_learning_goals: acquisition of new object properties and word labels following expectancy violation
examples: The gumball machine experiments tested whether improbable events produce graded learning, as a continuous Bayesian account would predict, and found step-like performance instead

citation: Steacy LM, Fuchs D, Gilbert JK, Kearns DM, Elleman AM, Edwards AA. (2020). title: Lexical-feedback account: poor readers rely on the semantic processor when mapping orthography to phonology
description: The article interprets its findings within connectionist models of word reading (e.g., the triangle model), in which lexical feedback from semantics assists mapping between orthographic and phonological forms. It proposes that when sub-lexical mapping is difficult, "meaning is particularly important," and that "students with RD are relying heavily on the semantic processor in word learning efficiency." This explains why imageability and vocabulary grade mattered most for the poorest readers.
requirements: Applicable to word learning contexts where orthographic-phonological mapping is difficult, such as irregular or less decodable words
constraints: The authors state they do not have the correct data to make causal inferences about this relationship

target_learning_goals: Efficient acquisition of word-specific orthographic representations for high-frequency words
examples: The authors interpret the significant imageability and vocabulary-grade interactions as evidence that poor readers use semantic feedback to clean up mismatches between phonology and orthography

description: The Sight Word Challenge was a timed word recognition activity embedded in a yearlong multicomponent decoding intervention for at-risk first graders. Students read from lists of the 500 most frequent words (Educator's Word Frequency Guide) for one minute, with the tutor correcting errors by pronunciation only; "When a student read a word correctly on three consecutive days, the word was removed from the student's list." Tutors reviewed up to three unmastered words and awarded certificates at benchmarks of 10, 50, or 200 words mastered.

article_title: Development of abstract mathematical reasoning: the case of algebra
citation: Susac A, Bubic A, Vrbanc A and Planinic M (2014) Development of abstract mathematical reasoning: the case of algebra. Front. Hum. Neurosci. 8:679. https://doi.org/10.3389/fnhum.2014.00679
title: Teachers should repeatedly encourage formal reasoning rather than assuming equation-rearrangement skill transfers after one exposure
description: The article's concluding recommendation is that mastery of equation rearrangement cannot be presumed from a single exposure, because the concrete-to-abstract transition unfolds over years. As the authors state, "teachers should use every opportunity to encourage students to use formal reasoning – both pattern recognition and effective application of mathematical rules and known procedures." This applies across mathematics and science contexts such as physics problem solving.
requirements: Instruction must recur across grades and subjects, since all participants had been taught rearrangement at least one year prior yet still struggled with all-symbol equations.
constraints: The supporting evidence covers simple three-term equations with multiplication/division only; even 16–17-year-olds struggled with the slightly more complex C equations.
target_learners: Students aged 13–17 in lower-secondary and early-secondary mathematics and science courses
target_learning_goals: Abstract algebraic reasoning
equation rearrangement
transfer of equation-solving skill across contexts
examples: In the study, even students taught rearrangement a year earlier were only 82% accurate on all-symbol equations, and half of participants reported concrete strategies such as inserting numbers.

article_title: Sustained attention and prediction: distinct brain maturation trajectories during adolescence
citation: Thillay A, Roux S, Gissot V, Carteau-Martin I, Knight RT, Bonnet-Brilhault F and Bidet-Caulet A (2015) Sustained attention and prediction: distinct brain maturation trajectories during adolescence. Front. Hum. Neurosci. 9:519. https://doi.org/10.3389/fnhum.2015.00519
title: Distinct brain maturation trajectories account: sustained attention matures with frontal cortical development while prediction is mature by age 12
description: The article proposes that sustained attention and prediction, though both frontal-dependent optimization processes, follow distinct developmental trajectories through adolescence. Sustained attention continues to mature after age 12, evidenced by improved detection performance and "a frontal shift in P3 and CNV topographies with increasing age", whereas "predictive processing appeared to be mature at age 12". The account attributes the difference to a larger and longer recruitment of the frontal cortex when attention is sustained than during simple predictive processing, with prediction maintenance possibly achieved at lower hierarchical levels such as visual areas.
requirements: EEG recording with tasks that separately load on sustained attention and on manipulated target predictability, as in the visual target detection paradigm used
constraints: The study's gender distribution was biased towards males in the three subsamples
The authors note the study would have been stronger with larger samples, though effects showed large effect sizes
target_learning_goals: sustained attention
predictive processing
proactive cognitive control
examples: EEG recorded in 36 participants aged 12–24 in three age groups performing a visual target detection task with random versus predicted targets

article_title: Learning to Use an Alphabetic Writing System
citation: Treiman Rebecca, Kessler Brett. (2013). Learning to Use an Alphabetic Writing System. Language Learning and Development. https://doi.org/10.1080/15475441.2013.812016
title: Spelling instruction should go beyond rote memorization and explicitly teach sound-to-spelling patterns, including context-conditioned choices
description: The review argues that because implicit statistical learning of spelling patterns is slow and incomplete, explicit teaching has an important role. It recommends that instruction cover the sound-to-spelling direction, not only spellings-to-sounds, and teach how context helps choose among alternative spellings: "more direct instruction about the sound-to-spelling direction could be helpful" and it "could be helpful to draw children's attention to the fact that context can help in making these choices". Generic statements can convey generalizations that would otherwise require many instances.
requirements: Teachers need knowledge of phonology and spelling so they can interpret children's errors, e.g. recognizing that ‹CHRAP› for trap reflects careful listening plus a misclassification, not inattention.
constraints: The review notes current phonics approaches often rely on worksheets and drills that are boring for children, and that phoneme-level generic statements are harder for children to understand than everyday generics.
target_learners: children learning to spell in alphabetic writing systems, roughly ages 4 to 13
target_learning_goals: conventional spelling accuracy
understanding of sound-to-spelling correspondences and their context conditioning
examples: The review describes whole-language classrooms where children receive no explicit spelling instruction, and contrasts these with phonics instruction, recommending engaging word-pattern teaching methods (Joshi et al., 2008–2009).

article_title: Learning to Use an Alphabetic Writing System
citation: Treiman Rebecca, Kessler Brett. (2013). Learning to Use an Alphabetic Writing System. Language Learning and Development. https://doi.org/10.1080/15475441.2013.812016
title: Statistical learning account of spelling development
description: The review's organizing framework is statistical learning, defined as "the process whereby organisms pick up patterns by observing and internalizing the relative frequency with which objects and events occur and co-occur". On this account, children first learn salient graphic characteristics of print implicitly, then apply the same mechanisms to phoneme-spelling links, including context-conditioned and morphological patterns. Learning is shaped by the statistics of the writing children see, including their own names, and spelling learning in turn reshapes children's ideas about language.
requirements: Sufficient exposure to examples of writing in the child's environment, since the account holds that children learn letter and digram frequencies from the print around them.
constraints: The review states people are not ideal statistical learners: context conditioning is learned slowly, adults underuse context relative to its strength in the vocabulary, and the account's role in nonalphabetic systems needs further work.
target_learners: preschool and school-age children learning alphabetic writing systems
target_learning_goals: spelling development
implicit knowledge of orthographic patterns
examples: The review interprets prephonological spellers' language-specific letter and digram use, own-name letter use, and the gradual emergence of context sensitivity as manifestations of statistical learning.
key_sources: Treiman Rebecca, Kessler Brett. (2013). Learning to Use an Alphabetic Writing System. Language Learning and Development. https://doi.org/10.1080/15475441.2013.812016

article_title: Learning motivation mediates gene-by-socioeconomic status interaction on mathematics achievement in early childhood
citation: Tucker-Drob, Elliot M., & Harden, K. Paige. (2011). Learning Motivation Mediates Gene-by-Socioeconomic Status Interaction on Mathematics Achievement in Early Childhood. Learning and Individual Differences. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lindif.2011.11.015
title: Transactional gene-environment interaction account: high-opportunity environments let children select, evoke, and attend to learning experiences congruent with genetically influenced motivation
description: The article advances a transactional developmental account (citing Dickens and Flynn, Scarr, and Tucker-Drob & Harden) in which heritable variation in achievement is expressed through child-driven processes. As the authors write, "heritable variation in cognition and achievement comes to be expressed through a process by which children select, evoke, and attend to experiences that are congruent with their genetically influenced traits." In high-opportunity environments children can match learning experiences to their genotypes, so achievement becomes increasingly heritable; in low-opportunity environments this matching is constrained and heritable variation stays low. The study's mediation results are presented as evidence for this mechanism operating via learning motivation in early childhood.
requirements: Adequate environmental opportunity for enriching interactions with the proximal environment, so that motivated children can translate non-cognitive traits into cognitive skills
constraints: The authors note that in low-opportunity environments children are less able to match their learning experiences to their genotypes, suppressing heritable variation in achievement
target_learners: four-year-old children (early childhood, prior to formal schooling)
target_learning_goals: early mathematics achievement and school readiness
examples: The bivariate twin analyses showed only the genetic pathway from motivation to achievement varied with SES, which the authors interpret as support for this transactional process
key_sources: Tucker-Drob, Elliot M., & Harden, K. Paige. (2011). Learning Motivation Mediates Gene-by-Socioeconomic Status Interaction on Mathematics Achievement in Early Childhood. Learning and Individual Differences. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lindif.2011.11.015

article_title: Children's Effortful Control and Academic Achievement: Mediation Through Social Functioning
citation: Valiente Carlos, Eisenberg Nancy, Haugen Rg, Spinrad Tracy L., Hofer Claire, Liew Jeffrey, Kupfer Anne. (2011). Children's Effortful Control and Academic Achievement: Mediation Through Social Functioning. Early Education and Development, 22(3), 411-433. https://doi.org/10.1080/10409289.2010.505259
title: Effortful control as temperamentally based self-regulation grounded in the executive attention network
description: The article frames effortful control as "a group of temperamentally based skills viewed as the basis of self-regulation," defined by Rothbart and Bates as "the efficiency of executive attention—including the ability to inhibit a dominant response and/or to activate a subdominant response, to plan, and to detect errors." Drawing on Posner's attention networks, the study locates EC in the executive attention network, which monitors and resolves conflicts among other neural networks and is hypothesized to play a central role in regulatory efforts. EC is measured via adult reports of attentional and inhibitory control and behaviorally via persistence or delay tasks.
requirements: Measured through adult reports of attention shifting, attention focusing, and inhibitory control, or behavioral tasks such as persistence and delay of gratification
constraints: EC develops rapidly in the preschool years and continues improving in early school years; the study's sample was primarily Caucasian
target_learners: children in kindergarten through early elementary school
target_learning_goals: self-regulation supporting classroom attention, task completion, and academic achievement
examples: EC was measured with the Children's Behavior Questionnaire subscales and a puzzle task in which persistence without cheating over 4 minutes indexed EC
key_sources: Valiente Carlos, Eisenberg Nancy, Haugen Rg, Spinrad Tracy L., Hofer Claire, Liew Jeffrey, Kupfer Anne. (2011). Children's Effortful Control and Academic Achievement: Mediation Through Social Functioning. Early Education and Development, 22(3), 411-433. https://doi.org/10.1080/10409289.2010.505259

article_title: Children's Effortful Control and Academic Achievement: Mediation Through Social Functioning
citation: Valiente Carlos, Eisenberg Nancy, Haugen Rg, Spinrad Tracy L., Hofer Claire, Liew Jeffrey, Kupfer Anne. (2011). Children's Effortful Control and Academic Achievement: Mediation Through Social Functioning. Early Education and Development, 22(3), 411-433. https://doi.org/10.1080/10409289.2010.505259
title: Support children's effortful control development because it yields both social and academic advantages
description: The article recommends that educators and curriculum developers consider students' social and emotional functioning in models of school success, and that "a focused effort to improve EC is advantageous because growth in this area is likely to produce both social advantages (e.g., high levels of social competence and low levels of problem behaviors) and academic advantages." Many self-regulation activities are described as relatively inexpensive or free and classroom-administrable. Administrators are advised to give teachers clear messages supporting the modest time needed for such activities.
requirements: Administrators need to provide clear messages supporting the modest amount of time needed to promote students' EC for teachers to engage in such activities
constraints: The article cites mounting evidence that attentional abilities and inhibitory control can be improved via training, but this study itself is longitudinal-correlational, not an intervention trial
target_learners: children in preschool programs and elementary schools
target_learning_goals: self-regulation, social competence, and academic achievement
examples: The authors point to interventions such as the Head Start REDI program and the preschool PATHS curriculum as evidence that EC-related skills can be improved

article_title: Becoming original: effects of strategy instruction
citation: van de Kamp, M.-T., Admiraal, W., & Rijlaarsdam, G. (2016). Becoming original: effects of strategy instruction. Instructional Science, 44, 543–566. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9384-y
title: A model of twelve divergent thinking activities organised along two dimensions of remoteness and abstractness
description: The article presents a matrix of twelve divergent thinking activities organised along two dimensions: remoteness (the metaphorical distance from a stimulus, running from free association to bisociation) and abstractness (running from association through combination to abstraction). The authors state they "built a model of twelve divergent thinking activities, along two dimensions—remoteness and abstractness" to serve as a framework for teaching students how to generate more original ideas deliberately in visual arts education. Activities range from A1 (associate freely) to C4 (transform), with remoteness and abstractness treated as vectors along which learners can deliberately move to generate more original ideas.
requirements: Students must build up knowledge about the twelve specific generation activities and the two dimensions to use them as strategies for generating original ideas
constraints: The model was developed for and applied in the domain of visual arts education with secondary school students
target_learners: Grade-11 secondary school students aged 16–17 in pre-university visual arts education
target_learning_goals: Generate original ideas for visual art products through divergent thinking
examples: The article illustrates cell C1 (construct conceptually) with Mondrian's 'Pier and Ocean' composition, and cell C3 (restructure) with the NeoNurture incubator that used car parts for infant incubator design
key_sources: van de Kamp, M.-T., Admiraal, W., & Rijlaarsdam, G. (2016). Becoming original: effects of strategy instruction. Instructional Science, 44, 543–566. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9384-y

article_title: Becoming original: effects of strategy instruction
citation: van de Kamp, M.-T., Admiraal, W., & Rijlaarsdam, G. (2016). Becoming original: effects of strategy instruction. Instructional Science, 44, 543–566. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9384-y
title: A 50-minute metacognitive strategy instruction lesson on divergent thinking for visual arts
description: A single 50-minute lesson providing explicit instruction on metacognitive knowledge about creativity, twelve divergent thinking activities and strategies for originality in visual art products, and metacognitive skills for regulation (monitoring and control). The lesson "contained five lesson-phases" covering orientation on metacognitive knowledge, metacognitive strategy instruction, divergent thinking strategy instruction with exercises, and evaluation. It was delivered by the first author with a second teacher assisting, within a 14-week photography project on the theme of 'Time-grasping'.
requirements: Requires an instructor trained in the divergent thinking strategies and metacognitive instruction approach
Requires visual art examples to illustrate the twelve divergent thinking strategies
constraints: Tested as a single 50-minute lesson within a 14-week visual arts project with Grade-11 pre-university students in the Netherlands
target_learners: Grade-11 secondary school students aged 16–17 in pre-university visual arts education
target_learning_goals: Understand why, how and when to use specific divergent thinking activities and strategies to generate original ideas for visual art products
examples: Students exercised with an alternative uses test for a tablet computer, practised generating many different kinds of original ideas, and evaluated the originality of their own ideas in dyads and whole-class discussion
key_sources: van de Kamp, M.-T., Admiraal, W., & Rijlaarsdam, G. (2016). Becoming original: effects of strategy instruction. Instructional Science, 44, 543–566. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9384-y

article_title: Becoming original: effects of strategy instruction
citation: van de Kamp, M.-T., Admiraal, W., & Rijlaarsdam, G. (2016). Becoming original: effects of strategy instruction. Instructional Science, 44, 543–566. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9384-y
title: Nelson and Narens' two-level metacognition model applied to regulation of divergent thinking
description: The article applies Nelson and Narens' (1990) model of metamemory to divergent thinking in creative processes. The model posits two levels—an object-level running executive processes (task performance, learning processes) and a meta-level holding a dynamic representation of the object-level—connected by two types of information flow: monitoring (from object-level to meta-level) and control (from meta-level to object-level). The authors use this framework to explain how "regulation of executive processes is enhanced" through a cyclic flow between levels, grounding their instructional design for metacognitive strategy instruction in divergent thinking.
requirements: Learners must possess metacognitive knowledge about tasks, strategies and self to assess task demands and outcomes
Strategy knowledge about the specific executive process (here, divergent thinking) is needed for accurate control
constraints: Applied in the article specifically to divergent thinking processes in visual arts education
target_learners: Secondary school students in visual arts education
target_learning_goals: Monitor and control divergent thinking processes to generate more original ideas
examples: In the intervention lesson, monitoring was enhanced through clarifying knowledge and misunderstandings about creativity, while control was stimulated through interactive discussion providing examples of strategy selection and implementation
key_sources: van de Kamp, M.-T., Admiraal, W., & Rijlaarsdam, G. (2016). Becoming original: effects of strategy instruction. Instructional Science, 44, 543–566. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9384-y

article_title: Becoming original: effects of strategy instruction
citation: van de Kamp, M.-T., Admiraal, W., & Rijlaarsdam, G. (2016). Becoming original: effects of strategy instruction. Instructional Science, 44, 543–566. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9384-y
title: Teach divergent thinking through explicit instruction of metacognitive strategy knowledge rather than relying on brainstorming exercises alone
description: The article argues that regular brainstorming exercises in visual arts lessons may limit learning because students need many experiences before building a rich knowledge base for divergent thinking. Instead, it recommends that "students may develop enhanced divergent thinking skills through explicit instruction of metacognition, because then students may learn to understand why, how and when to use which specific divergent thinking activities and strategies." A previous intervention focusing mainly on association improved fluency and flexibility but not originality, motivating a redesign that added generation through combination and abstraction.
requirements: Instruction must cover declarative, procedural, conditional and contextual knowledge about divergent thinking strategies
Teacher modeling and visual examples are needed to make abstract strategy knowledge concrete
constraints: A prior version of the instruction that focused mainly on generation through association did not improve originality of ideas
target_learners: Secondary school students in visual arts education
target_learning_goals: Enhance divergent thinking skills including fluency, flexibility and originality of generated ideas
examples: The redesigned intervention lesson explicitly taught twelve divergent thinking strategies across association, combination and abstraction, illustrated with visual examples from art and design, and had students practise and evaluate their strategy use
key_sources: van de Kamp, M.-T., Admiraal, W., & Rijlaarsdam, G. (2016). Becoming original: effects of strategy instruction. Instructional Science, 44, 543–566. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9384-y

article_title: Becoming original: effects of strategy instruction
citation: van de Kamp, M.-T., Admiraal, W., & Rijlaarsdam, G. (2016). Becoming original: effects of strategy instruction. Instructional Science, 44, 543–566. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9384-y
title: A five-phase lesson structure for metacognitive strategy instruction on divergent thinking
description: The intervention lesson followed a structured sequence of five phases: (1) orientation on metacognitive knowledge activating prior conceptions of creativity, (2) metacognitive strategy instruction exemplifying divergent thinking with visual examples, (3) divergent thinking strategy instruction explaining and exercising the twelve strategies, (4) application through independent use of strategies, and (5) evaluation through reflection and prediction. The authors state that "the specific order of lesson phases was based on studies about the structuring of instructional-learning episodes," grounding the sequence in instructional design theory.
requirements: Each phase builds on the previous one; explicit instruction and teacher modeling are central to phases 2 and 3
Whole-class discussion and peer feedback are used to integrate and evaluate new knowledge
constraints: Designed and tested as a 50-minute lesson within a secondary visual arts curriculum
target_learners: Grade-11 secondary school students in visual arts education
target_learning_goals: Build metacognitive knowledge and skills for regulating divergent thinking strategies to generate original ideas
examples: In phase 3, twelve divergent thinking strategies were explained and exemplified through direct instruction and teacher modeling, then applied in an alternative uses test in phase 4

article_title: The Same yet Different: Oral and Silent Reading in Children and Adolescents with Dyslexia
citation: Madelon van den Boer, Loes Bazen, Elise de Bree. (2022). The Same yet Different: Oral and Silent Reading in Children and Adolescents with Dyslexia. Journal of Psycholinguistic Research. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10936-022-09856-w
title: Include silent reading in dyslexia diagnosis and treatment, especially for adolescents, alongside oral reading assessment
description: The article recommends that diagnosis and intervention for dyslexia consider both reading modes, because diagnosis is usually based on oral reading while accommodations target silent reading. It states "It seems important to include silent reading in diagnosing reading disabilities and dyslexia especially for adolescents", and that specific treatment of silent reading, in addition to oral reading, should be considered, with continued monitoring of both modes for individuals with dyslexia.
requirements: Valid measures of silent reading fluency for education and diagnostic examinations, which the authors note still need development
constraints: For primary school children oral and silent fluency are still interchangeable, so the need is greatest from adolescence onwards; the silent task used included simple task performance, which may have underestimated silent reading ability
target_learning_goals: reading fluency assessment and diagnosis
reading fluency intervention and accommodations
examples: Study 2 used an ecologically valid silent reading task in which adolescents read a text including instructions for six simple tasks, following the procedure of Gagliano et al. (2015).

article_title: Exploring the long-term relationship between academic-media multitasking and adolescents’ academic achievement
citation: W.A. van der Schuur, S.E. Baumgartner, S.R. Sumter, P.M. Valkenburg. (2020). Exploring the long-term relationship between academic-media multitasking and adolescents' academic achievement. New Media and Society. https://doi.org/10.1177/1461444819861956
title: Qualify concerns about the long-term impact of academic-media multitasking on adolescent achievement
description: Educators and policymakers should temper alarms that media use during academic activities durably damages adolescent achievement. The article concludes that "concerns regarding the long-term impact of academic-media multitasking on academic achievement need to be qualified", because a three-wave longitudinal study found no direct or indirect long-term achievement effect. Attention problems did increase, so caution remains warranted.
requirements: Base guidance on longitudinal evidence rather than cross-sectional associations, which the study shows can coexist with no long-term effect.
constraints: Findings apply to adolescents aged 11–15 studied over 3–4 month intervals; the study did not establish long-term equivalence, only absence of support for a long-term relationship.
target_learning_goals: academic achievement
academic attention
examples: The article's three-wave study with 1215 adolescents found cross-sectional links but no long-term achievement effect, grounding the recommendation to qualify concerns.

article_title: Learning multiplication: An integrated analysis of the multiplication ability of primary school children and the difficulty of single digit and multidigit multiplication problems
citation: S.H.G. van der Ven, M. Straatemeier, B.R.J. Jansen, S. Klinkenberg, H.L.J. van der Maas. (2015). Learning multiplication: An integrated analysis of the multiplication ability of primary school children and the difficulty of single digit and multidigit multiplication problems. Learning and Individual Differences. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lindif.2015.08.013
title: The computational efficiency model of multiplication problem difficulty
description: The computational efficiency model is an explanatory account of multiplication problem difficulty that the article evaluates against item data. It was contrasted with alternatives using data from two tasks: one in which children used predominantly computational strategies and one in which they were expected to rely mostly on retrieval. The article reports that "In both tasks we found most support for the computational efficiency model", making it the best-supported account of the models compared for both kinds of task data.
requirements: Item-level difficulty data from multiplication tasks, including tasks expected to elicit retrieval as well as tasks eliciting computational strategies, to test the model against alternatives.
target_learning_goals: mental multiplication ability and problem difficulty
examples: The article tested the model with data from two contrasted tasks and found most support for it in both.

article_title: (In)equitable Schooling and Mathematics of Marginalized Students: Through the Voices of Urban Latinas/os
citation: Maura Varley Gutiérrez, Craig Willey, & Lena L. Khisty. (2011). (In)equitable Schooling and Mathematics of Marginalized Students: Through the Voices of Urban Latinas/os. Journal of Urban Mathematics Education, 4(2), 26–43. http://education.gsu.edu/JUME
title: Counterstorytelling within critical race theory as a framework for understanding marginalized students' mathematics experiences
description: The article grounds its analysis in critical race theory and counterstorytelling, the practice of People of Color naming their own realities. A counterstory 'serves to illuminate these biases and the processes by which they operate and influence educational acts.' The authors combine counterstory with critical ethnography, weaving individual student stories into a collective voice of Latinas/os' lived experiences in mathematics education to counter deficit-based perspectives.
requirements: Experiential knowledge of non-dominant students must be treated as legitimate and critical data, per the article's key tenet of critical race theory
constraints: The counterstories represent a particular group of students across two urban sites and are presented as a collective reflection of shared systemic exclusion
target_learners: Urban Latina/o elementary and middle-grade students
target_learning_goals: Understanding students' perspectives on mathematics learning and schooling conditions
examples: The authors present four salient themes from students' spontaneous and structured comments across three years of after-school participation

title: After-school mathematics clubs as counter spaces using home language, community, and knowledge as learning resources
description: The after-school mathematics clubs were designed as alternative learning environments that 'explicitly defined and utilized students' home language, communities, and knowledge as learning resources.' They offered collaborative, project-based activities with cross-generational participants (students, preservice teachers, researchers), and became counter spaces that naturally provoked students to compare, analyze, question, and comment on their mathematics experiences in both settings.
requirements: Activities must value and integrate students' language, experiences, and communities; adults often spoke in Spanish and tasks were written in two languages
constraints: Students volunteered to participate; the clubs ran 8 to 12 weeks each school semester, meeting approximately two hours once or twice a week
target_learners: Third- to sixth-grade urban Latina/o students with a range of Spanish and English proficiencies
target_learning_goals: More advanced mathematics opportunities and practices than students typically received in their regular classes
examples: Approximately 34 students across a Midwestern dual-language site and a Southwestern site participated, many for all three years

article_title: Metacognition and self-regulation in young children: does it matter if metacognitive experiences are communicated?
citation: Ventura, Ana Clara. (2022). Metacognition and self-regulation in young children: does it matter if metacognitive experiences are communicated?. Early Years. https://doi.org/10.1080/09575146.2022.2065666
title: Promote and hear young children's voices and judgments about their metacognitive experiences to help them solve activities in educational contexts
description: The article argues that educational contexts should actively promote and attend to children's spoken judgments about their metacognitive experiences, particularly feelings of difficulty. Because communicating FOD "allowed children to mobilize resources and to achieve their goals", adults should invite and respond to these comments during challenging task engagement rather than treating them as off-task talk.
requirements: Tasks must be challenging enough to elicit feelings of difficulty that children can communicate
target_learning_goals: metacognitive knowledge
metacognitive regulation
emotional and motivational regulation
examples: Sixty first graders were individually interviewed while engaged in an ecological and challenging graphic task, and their spontaneous comments of FOD were coded

title: C.Ind.Le Coding Scheme-based coding of metacognitive knowledge, regulation, emotional and motivational regulation, and spontaneous FOD comments
description: The study's measurement approach applies the C.Ind.Le Coding Scheme to individual interviews of six-year-olds during an ecological and challenging graphic task. It codes "indicators of metacognitive knowledge (i.e., knowledge of persons, tasks and strategies), metacognitive regulation (i.e., planning, monitoring, control and evaluation) and emotional and motivational regulation (i.e., emotional and motivational monitoring and control)", plus children's spontaneous comments of feelings of difficulty.

examples: Applied with sixty first graders (57% boys; M age: 6.2 yr., SD = 3 months) individually interviewed during the graphic task
