title: Select-Organize-Integrate (SOI) model of meaningful learning
description: The article builds on the SOI information-processing model of meaningful learning by Mayer, in which "strategy guidance needs to target three essential cognitive processes involved in meaningful learning: selecting relevant information, organizing the selected information, and building a coherent mental representation that can be stored in long-term memory". The authors adapted SOI to a multiple document context by guiding students to highlight content in single documents, select and extract task-relevant content, and integrate information across documents. They also note Mayer treats SOI as applicable across problem-solving types, including writing an essay on an unsettled issue.
requirements: Guidance must address all three processes: selection, organization, and integration of information
constraints: The guidance was implemented before the task with a cue card available during the task, not as embedded tutoring
target_learning_goals: meaningful learning and comprehension from multiple documents
examples: LiquidText Guidance participants were guided to highlight information, select and extract task-relevant information, and conceptually and spatially organize information across documents

title: LiquidText multiple document reading application on iPad Pro
description: LiquidText is a reading application for tablets that "includes several additional functions adapted to working with multiple documents". Its screen areas support navigation (overview of documents), simultaneous viewing of up to three documents with highlighting, and a workspace in which learners can "group and link extracted information to construct an integrated understanding" and write the task product. In the experiment it was used on a 12.9-inch iPad Pro with a stylus with a set of five partly conflicting documents on sun exposure and health, under guidance, access-only, and non-guidance conditions.
requirements: Students may need explicit guidance to fully exploit the application's functions
constraints: In the Access condition technical removal of functions was not possible, so participants were instructed not to use certain functions while the application code was unchanged
target_learning_goals: comprehending and integrating multiple documents
examples: Participants working in the workspace moved extracted information there, grouped consistent content spatially, and wrote their answers in a textbox within the workspace

article_title: Constructivist learning (environments) and how to avoid another tower of Babel: reply to Renkl
citation: David Gijbels, Sofie M. M. Loyens. (2009). Constructivist learning (environments) and how to avoid another tower of Babel: reply to Renkl. Instructional Science, 37, 499–502. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-009-9100-2
title: Three perspectives on constructivism: theory of learning, philosophical position, and theory of instruction
description: The article argues that debates about constructivist learning environments turn on which of three perspectives one takes. Constructivism can be seen as a learning theory that is 'student-centered, since the emphasis is on students as active learners'; as a philosophical position focused on what knowledge is; or as a theory of instruction making claims at what Renkl calls the 'prescriptive level'. The authors recommend keeping theory and pedagogy apart while acknowledging that a learning theory carries implications for practice.
requirements: The perspectives must be distinguished explicitly, as Loyens and Gijbels (2008) did, to keep theory and pedagogy apart
constraints: The learning-theory perspective is descriptive, not prescriptive; the article notes that distinguishing perspectives is needed because debates misread one for another
target_learning_goals: understanding how constructivism is defined and applied in educational settings
examples: The article contrasts defining constructivism as a reaction to the traditional classroom (learning theory) with positions such as Colliver's that treat it as an insight into the nature of human knowledge
key_sources: David Gijbels, Sofie M. M. Loyens. (2009). Constructivist learning (environments) and how to avoid another tower of Babel: reply to Renkl. Instructional Science, 37, 499–502. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-009-9100-2

article_title: Constructivist learning (environments) and how to avoid another tower of Babel: reply to Renkl
citation: David Gijbels, Sofie M. M. Loyens. (2009). Constructivist learning (environments) and how to avoid another tower of Babel: reply to Renkl. Instructional Science, 37, 499–502. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-009-9100-2
title: Design instruction in any learning environment so students will engage in active sense-making and knowledge construction
description: The authors endorse Renkl's claim that one cannot deduce from constructivist assumptions that so-called constructivist environments are superior to traditional arrangements. Rather, 'instruction should be designed in such a way that there is a high probability students will engage in active sense-making and knowledge construction'. They extend this to recommending research on how to best induce sense-making irrespective of whether the environment is traditional or constructivist.
requirements: Instruction must be deliberately designed to make active sense-making and knowledge construction probable; the claim does not follow from constructivist assumptions alone
constraints: Traditional or constructivist labels alone do not guarantee better outcomes; the article explicitly denies that superiority can be deduced from the basic constructivist assumptions
target_learning_goals: meaningful learning
active sense-making
knowledge construction
examples: The special issue encouraged research looking at a wide range of effects in a wide range of learning environments, including traditional ones designed to induce meaningful learning activities

article_title: An experimental test of the Big-Fish-Little-Pond Effect using an immersive virtual reality classroom
citation: Lisa Hasenbein, Ulrich Trautwein, Jens-Uwe Hahn, Stephan Soller, Richard Göllner. (2024). An experimental test of the Big-Fish-Little-Pond Effect using an immersive virtual reality classroom. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09646-4
title: Fully preprogrammed immersive virtual reality (IVR) classroom simulating a computational thinking lesson
description: The article's IVR classroom is a 15-min simulated sixth-grade lesson on computational thinking (coding, sequences, loops), delivered via head-mounted displays to individual students in groups of up to 10. The lesson was "a fully preprogrammed simulation of a typical teaching situation based on audio recordings and motion captures stemming from a real classroom", with 24 virtual classmates whose hand-raising proportion (20/35/65/80%) was manipulated. The element works as an experimental apparatus preserving classroom authenticity while allowing strict control of social comparison information.
requirements: Requires head-mounted displays with noise-canceling headphones and technically reliable hardware; the study excluded 28 participants because of technical issues
constraints: Participants were asked to remain seated and quiet, and the lesson content assumes students have little to no prior computational thinking knowledge
target_learning_goals: basic principles of computational thinking, including coding, sequences, and loops
examples: Groups of up to 10 students at their own schools each experienced the identical IVR lesson in a virtual classroom resembling a blank-slate first-day class.
key_sources: Lisa Hasenbein, Ulrich Trautwein, Jens-Uwe Hahn, Stephan Soller, Richard Göllner. (2024). An experimental test of the Big-Fish-Little-Pond Effect using an immersive virtual reality classroom. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09646-4

article_title: An experimental test of the Big-Fish-Little-Pond Effect using an immersive virtual reality classroom
citation: Lisa Hasenbein, Ulrich Trautwein, Jens-Uwe Hahn, Stephan Soller, Richard Göllner. (2024). An experimental test of the Big-Fish-Little-Pond Effect using an immersive virtual reality classroom. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09646-4
title: Big-Fish-Little-Pond Effect (BFLPE)
description: The Big-Fish-Little-Pond Effect is the theoretical account that students' academic self-concept depends on the achievement level of their reference group: higher class-average achievement depresses self-concept at fixed individual achievement. As the article puts it, "two equally able students will evaluate themselves differently depending on the performance level of their classmates, whom they use as a reference for their self-evaluation." This study experimentally reproduces the effect in an IVR classroom and identifies students' perceived class performance level as the mediating mechanism.
requirements: A reference group of classmates whose performance-related behavior is visible to the student, so that social comparison information can be perceived
constraints: In this experiment the negative effect appeared only for situational self-concept and between the extreme conditions (20% vs. 80%), not for dispositional self-concept or moderate comparison standards
target_learning_goals: academic self-concept, self-evaluation of one's own abilities
examples: Virtual classmates who raised their hands in response to the teacher's questions served as the manipulated reference-group performance signal.
key_sources: Lisa Hasenbein, Ulrich Trautwein, Jens-Uwe Hahn, Stephan Soller, Richard Göllner. (2024). An experimental test of the Big-Fish-Little-Pond Effect using an immersive virtual reality classroom. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09646-4

article_title: Novice and expert self-regulated learning phase transitions in medical diagnosis: Implications for adaptive and intelligent systems
citation: Cloude, E. B., Chapman, R., Azevedo, R., Castiglioni, A., LaRochelle, J., Hernandez, C., & Torre, D. (2025). Novice and expert self-regulated learning phase transitions in medical diagnosis: Implications for adaptive and intelligent systems. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09729-4
title: Extending Zimmerman and Moylan's socio-cognitive model of SRL to include metacognitive feelings (uncertainty) as a phase in the clinical-reasoning cycle
description: The article applies Zimmerman and Moylan's socio-cognitive model of SRL, which organizes learning processes into "forethought, performance, and self-reflection" phases, to clinical reasoning in multimedia diagnosis. The authors extend the model by adding metacognitive feelings: they state they "extend the SCT model by including metacognitive feelings as a phase in this cycle", operationalized as a Feelings of Uncertainty code drawn from the Lajoie et al. line of work. The study's sequential pattern mining treats uncertainty as a full phase whose transitions (e.g., UNC→F) cycle back into forethought and performance, framing SRL as non-linear, bidirectional, and cyclical rather than unidirectional.
requirements: Think-aloud verbalizations coded with a scheme covering the three SCT phases plus an uncertainty code
constraints: Findings are from one medical domain (common cough cases) in one multimedia system; the article notes the excluded 20% of the sample has implications including reduced generalizability.
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning and diagnostic accuracy
self-regulated learning competency
examples: Participants were trained to think-aloud with a 3-min video of a physician thinking aloud during an anemia case in CResME before solving the five cough cases.

citation: Cloude, E. B., Chapman, R., Azevedo, R., Castiglioni, A., LaRochelle, J., Hernandez, C., & Torre, D. (2025). Novice and expert self-regulated learning phase transitions in medical diagnosis: Implications for adaptive and intelligent systems. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09729-4
title: CResME (Clinical-reasoning Mapping Exercise): a multimedia system eliciting clinical reasoning through illness-script matching across five cough cases
description: CResME is a multimedia system "built on assimilation (Ausubel, 2012) and illness script theories" that presents clinical information (history of present illness, laboratory tests/Data, physical exams) from five clinical cases with a chief complaint of a common cough. Critical findings are integrated across sources to activate illness scripts for specific diseases. Using the "drag & drop features", users must match physical exam and Data sources to the right history of present illness for each case, then write a diagnosis; identifying similarities, differences, and reconciling inconsistencies is designed to promote knowledge development and illness-script construction. The system has validity studies and was used with a diagnostic-performance rubric scoring illness script activation and diagnostic accuracy.
requirements: Users trained to think-aloud before using the system in the study workflow
A faculty-developed scoring rubric (e.g., a 0–3 scale) to quantify illness script activation and diagnostic accuracy
constraints: Assessed only five clinical cases related to the common cough in this study; electrodermal activity and eye-tracking data were collected but not analyzed.
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning
illness script development
diagnostic accuracy
examples: Each clinical case was structured vertically (1–5) on the right-hand side of the interface with the HPI provided; correct diagnosis required integrating prototypical features of the case.

article_title: Effects of immersion in inquiry-based learning on student teachers’ educational beliefs
citation: Voet, M. & De Wever, B. (2018). Effects of immersion in inquiry-based learning on student teachers' educational beliefs. Instructional Science, 46(3), 383-403. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-017-9439-8
title: Immersion in inquiry-based learning ('teach as you preach') as a professional development approach
description: Professional development on IBL commonly applies the teaching-as-you-preach principle: putting teachers through a substantive inquiry experience mirroring what they should do in class. The article states this roots in social learning theory, in which behaviors are "learned, either deliberately or inadvertently, through the influence of example". Rather than delivering information, immersion provides teachers with good practices they observe and potentially adopt.
requirements: Teachers work through a substantive amount of content in a way that mirrors the target pedagogical approach
constraints: Some scholars argue immersion may fail without meta-commentary making underlying ideas explicit
target_learning_goals: shifting teachers' educational beliefs toward inquiry-based learning
increasing self-efficacy for inquiry
examples: 302 student history teachers completed a four-hour WISE inquiry activity on the English Peasants' Revolt of 1381
key_sources: Voet, M. & De Wever, B. (2018). Effects of immersion in inquiry-based learning on student teachers' educational beliefs. Instructional Science, 46(3), 383-403. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-017-9439-8

citation: Voet, M. & De Wever, B. (2018). Effects of immersion in inquiry-based learning on student teachers' educational beliefs. Instructional Science, 46(3), 383-403. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-017-9439-8
title: Three design principles for IBL activities in professional development: authenticity, collaboration, and scaffolded inquiry
description: The IBL activity was designed around three principles. Authenticity meant a discovery-oriented approach using an ill-structured evaluative problem statement requiring students to form their own interpretations of evidence. Collaboration reflected the view that historical reasoning is a social activity in which interaction "stimulates students to elaborate their knowledge". Scaffolding sequenced key inquiry activities in a macro-script within a workflow.
requirements: an ill-structured problem leaving room for different plausible conclusions
sufficient guidance so learners forming their own interpretations from contradictory sources have a positive inquiry experience
constraints: sources were limited to five preselected ones to control the information used
target_learners: student teachers in teacher training programs
target_learning_goals: learning how historical knowledge is constructed
conducting historical inquiries
examples: the Peasants' Revolt task posed: "Do you think that 'Peasants' Revolt' is a fitting name for the uprisings that took place in England in 1381?" with five contradictory sources including Wikipedia, a TV documentary, a medieval chronicle and two monographs

title: WISE (Web-based Inquiry Science Environment) used to deliver a macro-scripted history inquiry in teacher education
description: WISE is an online platform for designing, developing, and implementing inquiry-based learning, described as well received by research and practitioner communities. In this study its navigation panel guided students through nine key inquiry activities, from studying historical context to writing a conclusion, with grayed-out buttons preventing access to an activity before completing previous ones. Students entered and stored notes alongside content for each step.

constraints: students could not visit an activity before completing the previous ones

article_title: Designing to support equity-as-transformation perspectives for multilingual science learners
citation: Ashlyn Pierson, D. Teo Keifert, Bethany Daniel, Sarah Lee, Tessaly Jen, Adam Bell, Heather Johnson, Rachel Askew, Andrea Henrie. (2024). Designing to support equity-as-transformation perspectives for multilingual science learners. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09674-8
title: Two conceptualizations of equity: equity-as-access and equity-as-transformation
description: The article organizes its analysis around two conceptualizations of equity drawn from Grapin et al. (2023): equity-as-access, in which "learners should have access to disciplinary knowledge, practices, and career paths" (Grapin et al), and equity-as-transformation, in which "learners should transform what it means to learn and participate in disciplines" (Grapin et al). The authors use this distinction to diagnose why their initial PD design failed to disrupt deficit ideologies and to guide redesign. They cite a NASEM report arguing both are necessary, in which "equity-as-access supports short-term achievement, whereas equity-as-transformation disrupts systemic oppression in the long-term" (NASEM report).
requirements: Teachers and facilitators need explicit opportunities to distinguish and discuss both conceptions for transformative perspectives to emerge
constraints: The article reports relatively little research exists on equity-as-transformation, and notes the section is in the authors' discussion
target_learners: K-4 science teachers in professional development
target_learning_goals: Teachers' conceptualizations of equity in science teaching for multilingual learners

citation: Ashlyn Pierson, D. Teo Keifert, Bethany Daniel, Sarah Lee, Tessaly Jen, Adam Bell, Heather Johnson, Rachel Askew, Andrea Henrie. (2024). Designing to support equity-as-transformation perspectives for multilingual science learners. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09674-8
title: PD design pattern pairing new activities with specific facilitation moves to support equity-oriented sensemaking
description: In the redesigned Summer 2 PD, each new activity was deliberately paired with a facilitation conversation targeting a specific ideological challenge: "Language Storybook was paired with a conversation about recognizing multilingual learners' assets; Jonathan and the Sun was paired with a conversation about surfacing deficit ideologies grounded in teachers' experiences" (Design section). This pairing links immersive experiences of being a nondominant-language learner to explicit discussion of ideologies, giving facilitators structured openings to surface and challenge deficit framings rather than pivoting back to safer content-focused ground.
requirements: Activities must be paired with conversations that connect the immersive experience to teachers' own planning, teaching, and ideological assumptions
constraints: The facilitation moves examined concern multilingual learners' assets and deficit ideologies in K-4 elementary science PD
target_learning_goals: Ideological sensemaking and rearticulation toward equity-as-transformation perspectives
examples: Summer 2 designers paired the French storybook debrief with asset recognition talk and the Jonathan and the Sun reading with surfacing deficit ideologies from teachers' experiences

Designing to support equity-as-transformation perspectives for multilingual science learners. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09674-8
title: Three sustained PD features—immersive learning, student work analysis, and video club—support reflection and collaboration
description: The article describes its PD as built on three features for supporting reflection and collaboration: "(1) immersive learning, (2) student work analysis, and (3) video club" (PD design section). Immersive lessons in which teachers participate as learners build shared grounding in science teaching; student work analysis helps teachers understand and evaluate student thinking; video clubs anchor sensemaking in the realities of teachers' own classrooms. These features ran through both summer workshops and academic-year sessions and provided the substrate for ideological sensemaking about equity.
requirements: Sustained opportunities across summer and academic-year sessions, including collaborative reflection grounded in perspectives of young children as capable science learners
constraints: The features were studied in a multi-year elementary science PD partnership with a metropolitan district
target_learning_goals: Collaborative reflection on representations, student sensemaking, and equity
examples: The Puddles demonstration lesson served as the immersive experience, academic-year workshops analyzed student work samples such as rainbow models, and video clubs examined classroom clips

citation: Ashlyn Pierson, D. Teo Keifert, Bethany Daniel, Sarah Lee, Tessaly Jen, Adam Bell, Heather Johnson, Rachel Askew, Andrea Henrie. (2024). Designing to support equity-as-transformation perspectives for multilingual science learners. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09674-8
title: Provide teachers explicit opportunities to connect new equity perspectives with day-to-day classroom teaching experiences
description: The article concludes that, for practice, PD must "underscore the importance of providing teachers with opportunities to explicitly connect new perspectives of equity with day-to-day experiences of classroom teaching" (Abstract, practice implications). The redesign succeeded when facilitators gave significant time for small-group discussion tying big ideas to practical, real-world stories, whereas abstract ideological debriefs alone reified deficit framings. The principle holds that transformative equity perspectives need structured occasions where teachers apply them to their own students' work, language, and classroom events.
requirements: Structured discussion time connecting concepts of equity to teachers' own teaching contexts, including student work and state assessment pressures
constraints: Applies to professional development design contexts; the article's evidence is a multi-year case study of one district partnership
target_learning_goals: Taking up equity-as-transformation perspectives in everyday science teaching
examples: In the second storybook iteration, facilitators tied discussion of big ideas to real-world stories through significant small-group discussion time

article_title: Factors that explain simulation-based inquiry performance in physics learning
citation: Gerdesmann, D., Schwichow, M., & Koerber, S. (2026). Factors that explain simulation-based inquiry performance in physics learning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09806-2
title: Extended SDDS framework: inquiry as structured search in hypothesis and experiment spaces
description: The Scientific Discovery as Dual Search framework describes inquiry as structured search in two interconnected spaces: a hypothesis space (divided by van Joolingen and de Jong into a variable space and a relation space) and an experiment space. The study maps cognitive factors onto these spaces: content knowledge constrains plausible hypotheses, CVS supports designing unconfounded experiments, and functional thinking supports reasoning about variable relations in the relation space. Seven measured inquiry facets were aligned to these spaces.
requirements: Guidance design requires knowing which cognitive skills support which inquiry facets within the SDDS spaces
constraints: The study applies the mapping in single-task, single-user digital simulation environments; the authors limit scope to such contexts
target_learners: young adults in physics inquiry learning
target_learning_goals: scientific inquiry skills including hypothesis generation, experiment design, and drawing conclusions
examples: The Cartesian diver task assessed seven facets spanning the variable, hypothesis, experiment, and relation spaces

description: The article grounds PDEODE in Posner et al.'s (1982) conceptual change conditions: dissatisfaction, intelligibility, plausibility and fruitfulness. Eliciting students' alternative conceptions before teaching is treated as "something deemed crucial for conceptual change"; the PDEODE sequence starts with elicitation of prior ideas before students re-examine them in groups and whole-class discussion and finally resolve contradictions between prior beliefs and observations.

The article states it "consist[ed] of five items ... developed based on the alternative conceptions derived from the literature", comprising one two-tier multiple-choice item, two true/false two-tiered items, and open-ended items. Items were piloted with 31 students and validated by a panel of three chemistry teachers and two teacher educators, then administered as pre-, post-, and delayed post-tests.

article_title: When failure fails to be productive: probing the effectiveness of productive failure for learning beyond STEM domains
citation: Valentina Nachtigall · Katja Serova · Nikol Rummel. (2020). When failure fails to be productive: probing the effectiveness of productive failure for learning beyond STEM domains. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09525-2
title: Productive Failure: design features and three hypothesized learning mechanisms
description: Productive Failure combines two successive phases: an initial phase in which students collaboratively invent solution ideas for a complex novel problem without instructional support, and a delayed instruction phase in which the instructor builds on erroneous student solutions. The article states the design features "are expected to trigger the following three learning-related mechanisms which are hypothesized to underlie the effectiveness of PF (Loibl et al. 2017): (1) activation of prior knowledge, (2) awareness of knowledge limitations, and (3) recognition of the deep features of the targeted learning concepts." It applies this framework to design and evaluate a non-STEM instantiation of PF.
requirements: The problem must meet a sweet spot of complexity, addressing prior knowledge related to the targeted concept while students cannot solve it canonically
The delayed instruction must build on students' erroneous solution ideas, comparing and contrasting them with components of the canonical solution
constraints: The targeted concept needs a canonical solution with clearly definable components that can be compared with erroneous ideas, per the article's own argument
target_learners: secondary school students (10th graders in the studies)
target_learning_goals: acquisition of conceptual knowledge of the targeted learning topic
examples: In the two studies, PF students invented solution ideas for a teacher-conference study-design problem before receiving instruction that contrasted four typical error features with the canonical 2 × 2 factorial design.
key_sources: Valentina Nachtigall · Katja Serova · Nikol Rummel. (2020). When failure fails to be productive: probing the effectiveness of productive failure for learning beyond STEM domains. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09525-2

article_title: When failure fails to be productive: probing the effectiveness of productive failure for learning beyond STEM domains
citation: Valentina Nachtigall · Katja Serova · Nikol Rummel. (2020). When failure fails to be productive: probing the effectiveness of productive failure for learning beyond STEM domains. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09525-2
title: Domain-structuredness hypothesis: PF effectiveness may be restricted to structured domains
description: The article argues that PF requires a canonical solution whose components can be compared and contrasted with features of erroneous student ideas during instruction. It reports that "Loibl et al. (2017) hypothesize that the effectiveness of PF may only emerge for learning in structured domains, which \"allow for clear identification of deep features and evaluation of solution attempts\" (p. 712)". It situates social science research-methods topics on a continuum as "rather structured topics", less structured than STEM topics like standard deviation but still evaluable, making them an apt test case for transferring PF beyond STEM.
requirements: The targeted concept should have a canonical or established solution whose crucial components can be presented and explained during instruction
The problem should remain complex and allow students to generate different solution ideas
constraints: Discipline traditions can vary the principles and criteria deemed appropriate, so non-STEM topics are typically less structured than STEM topics
target_learning_goals: learning research methods and scientific practices in the social sciences
examples: The article contrasts the standard deviation topic of Kapur's studies with social/educational science topics like social inequality (little structure) and experimental design analysis (rather structured).
key_sources: Valentina Nachtigall · Katja Serova · Nikol Rummel. (2020). When failure fails to be productive: probing the effectiveness of productive failure for learning beyond STEM domains. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09525-2

citation: Valentina Nachtigall · Katja Serova · Nikol Rummel. (2020). When failure fails to be productive: probing the effectiveness of productive failure for learning beyond STEM domains. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09525-2
title: Instruction that contrasts four typical erroneous solution features with components of the canonical solution
description: This instructional pattern structures the delayed instruction phase of a PF lesson: the instructor walks through ways in which typical student solutions fall short of each component of a canonical solution. For the experimental-design topic, the article's Table 3 pairs four error features (e.g. "No inclusion of a control condition") with corresponding canonical components (e.g. "Inclusion of a control condition"), presented in a step-by-step explanation based on pilot-test results, so that students can recognize their specific knowledge gaps and the deep features of the concept.
requirements: Typical erroneous solution features must be identified in advance (here via pilot tests) so the standardized lesson can target them
A canonical solution with clearly definable components must exist for the targeted concept
target_learning_goals: principles of experimental design, including control conditions, systematic variation of variables, pretest administration, and measurement of control variables
examples: Table 3 contrasts student solutions lacking control conditions, systematic variation, pretests, and control-variable measurement with the corresponding canonical design components.

description: The studies took place in an interdisciplinary out-of-school lab at a large German university, offering projects for secondary students. The article describes that "Out-of-school labs are non-formal learning settings that are assumed to be highly authentic environments for learning scientific ways of thinking and working due to their location\
examples: PF students role-played educational researchers designing a study to investigate teachers' and parents' suggestions about improving teaching, within the lab-based teacher-conference scenario.

citation: Valentina Nachtigall · Katja Serova · Nikol Rummel. (2020). When failure fails to be productive: probing the effectiveness of productive failure for learning beyond STEM domains. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09525-2
title: Definition of classical PF studies: three shared characteristics distinguishing them from PF-similar studies
description: The article defines classical PF studies (e.g. Kapur 2010-2012; Loibl and Rummel 2014a, b; Westermann and Rummel 2012) as those that focus on STEM learning and "share the following three characteristics": (a) the problem-solving condition fulfilled the crucial design features of collaboratively inventing solution ideas to a complex problem and having erroneous student solutions compared and contrasted with the canonical solution; (b) effectiveness was tested with secondary school or undergraduate students; and (c) effectiveness was examined by comparing PF to an instruction-prior-to-problem-solving control condition. This yardstick frames the article's own two studies as a faithful transfer to a non-STEM domain.
requirements: The control condition must be an instruction prior to problem-solving approach so that only timing of instruction varies between conditions
Participants should be secondary school or undergraduate students
constraints: Classical PF studies as defined here focus on students' learning in a STEM domain (i.e., mathematics)
target_learners: secondary school students or undergraduate students
target_learning_goals: acquisition of conceptual knowledge in the targeted domain
examples: The two studies of this article emulate these characteristics: PF condition with collaborative invention and error-based instruction, 10th graders, comparison against a DI condition.

article_title: Effects of short- and long-term prompting in learning journals on strategy use, self-efficacy, and learning outcomes
citation: Nadja M. Gentner, Lisa Respondek, Tina Seufert. (2024). Effects of short- and long-term prompting in learning journals on strategy use, self-efficacy, and learning outcomes. Instructional Science (2024) 52:919–950. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09671-x
title: Zimmerman's cyclical three-phase model of self-regulated learning (forethinking, performance, self-reflection)
description: The article adopts Zimmerman's (2005) model as its theoretical framework: self-regulation "refers to self-generated thoughts, feelings, and actions that are planned and cyclically adapted to the attainment of personal goals". It integrates cognitive, metacognitive, emotion-affective, and motivational components in three phases — forethought (task analysis, planning, strategy selection), performance (applying strategies, monitoring), and self-reflection (judging the process, selecting regulation strategies). Because the model treats self-regulated learning as a process unfolding over time, the authors chose it as the basis for their longitudinal design with continuous weekly measurement.
requirements: Continuous measurements over time are needed to capture the development of self-regulation components across phases.
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning strategy use and motivation in coursework
examples: The study measured cognitive and metacognitive strategy use and self-efficacy weekly at t1–t8 across two course units, following the model's process view.

article_title: Dynamics of university students’ epistemic emotions during game-based learning in an international relations course
citation: Ketonen, E. E., Kruskopf, M., Lonka, K., & Mattlin, M. (2026). Dynamics of university students' epistemic emotions during game-based learning in an international relations course. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09771-2
title: Integrated Diplomacy course design alternating lectures and game sessions
description: A university international relations course built around the board game Diplomacy, with alternating "1.5-hour lectures and 2-hour game sessions" in a weekly cycle of reading, lectures with small-group discussion, game sessions, and online discussion tasks. Students played in two-player teams including a peace-mediator team, a feature added by the teacher; game performance formed one-quarter of course evaluation. Three revised win-conditions correspond to offensive realism, liberal-institutionalism and constructivism.
requirements: Same teacher (a co-author) taught or supervised all course elements
Negotiation success is central, making it a combination of strategy game and conflict negotiation simulation
constraints: Course design allows only a very limited number of participants
Findings are specific to this particular game, as the authors state
target_learning_goals: Understanding international relations concepts such as the security dilemma, trust-building, and diplomatic negotiation
examples: Games were evaluated as one-quarter of the course grade; debriefing sessions at course end collected self-reported emotions including emotional exhaustion.

article_title: Dynamics of university students’ epistemic emotions during game-based learning in an international relations course
citation: Ketonen, E. E., Kruskopf, M., Lonka, K., & Mattlin, M. (2026). Dynamics of university students' epistemic emotions during game-based learning in an international relations course. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09771-2
title: Valence-activation classification of epistemic emotions
description: The article organises epistemic emotions — "curiosity, enjoyment, surprise, confusion, anxiety, frustration and boredom" — using a valence-activation classification (Pekrun et al., 2017). Enjoyment and curiosity are positive activating emotions; boredom is negative de-activating; surprise is neutral activating, experienced as pleasant or unpleasant; anxiety, confusion and frustration are negative activating emotions that can either drive incongruity-resolution strategies or provoke avoidance. Epistemic emotions arise from cognitive conflict between the known and unknown and are a subset of academic emotions.
requirements: Distinguishes epistemic emotions (tied to knowledge construction) from other academic emotions tied to achievement or social dynamics
constraints: Anxiety, frustration, boredom and enjoyment can also function as achievement or social emotions depending on their focus of attention
target_learners: University students in complex, knowledge-construction learning contexts
target_learning_goals: Supporting knowledge construction and cognitive processing through productive emotional experiences
examples: The study applies the framework to interpret which emotions game sessions activated and how their trajectories related to learning outcomes.
key_sources: Ketonen, E. E., Kruskopf, M., Lonka, K., & Mattlin, M. (2026). Dynamics of university students' epistemic emotions during game-based learning in an international relations course. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09771-2

citation: Ketonen, E. E., Kruskopf, M., Lonka, K., & Mattlin, M. (2026). Dynamics of university students' epistemic emotions during game-based learning in an international relations course. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09771-2
title: Use process-oriented intra-individual (time-series) analysis to capture emotion dynamics that group-level findings conceal
description: The study advocates measuring emotions repeatedly after every session and analysing them with dynamic structural equation modelling, a process-oriented, intra-individual approach "only recently applied in educational research". This distinguishes within-person processes, between-person differences and learning context. The unique individual emotional trajectories showed that group-level conclusions about emotion trends were not applicable to all individuals, since individuals with decreasing emotions learned better.
requirements: Intensive session-to-session self-report data (212 situational questionnaires across 22 students)
Bayesian estimation because of the small number of clusters
constraints: Performed at only the within level because of the small number of clusters at the between level; models assumed data missing at random
target_learners: University students in course-long intensive follow-up designs
target_learning_goals: Understanding and supporting emotional dynamics of learning over time
examples: Emotions were measured with single-item EES measures after each of 13 and 11 sessions across two course implementations, capturing situational fluctuation.

article_title: Significance of forms and foci of metacognitive regulation in collaborative science learning of less and more successful outcome groups in diverse contexts
citation: Iiskala, T., Volet, S., Jones, C., Koretsky, M., & Vauras, M. (2021). Significance of forms and foci of metacognitive regulation in collaborative science learning of less and more successful outcome groups in diverse contexts. Instructional Science, 49, 687–718. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09558-1
title: Forms and foci framework of metacognitive regulation in collaborative learning
description: A conceptual framework for describing metacognitive regulation (MR) in collaborative learning along two axes: forms (whose cognitive process is regulated and how the group is involved) and foci (the level of cognitive activity being regulated). Forms include VMSR ("observable evidence of a group member's MR of their own learning despite the joint effort"), IMR (a member attempting to regulate the group but being ignored), MOR ("asymmetric metacognitive interaction between partners"), and SSMR (several members' interdependent regulation of joint cognitive activity). Foci distinguish high-level (elaboration, constructing meaning) from low-level (simple acquisition, practical task aspects) cognitive activity. The article uses this framework to examine outcomes across three diverse contexts.
requirements: A shared group goal, since "the manifestation of social forms of MR, especially SSMR, presupposes the existence of a group's common goal."
constraints: Only verbalised MR is observable; most self-regulation is assumed internal and "not accessible to peers or researchers."
target_learning_goals: collaborative science learning
co-construction of shared conceptual understanding

article_title: Complete or faded double-content examples of video-based analyses: How do they impact student teachers’ professional vision of classroom management?
citation: Jasmin Lilian Bauersfeld, Bernadette Gold. (2025). Complete or faded double-content examples of video-based analyses: How do they impact student teachers' professional vision of classroom management? Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09738-3
title: Double-content examples as instructional support for video-based analysis in an ill-structured domain
description: Double-content examples integrate two levels: the learning domain level (the skill being taught, here analyzing classroom videos) and the exemplifying domain level (the content illustrating it, here classroom management). In this study, written analyses by an expert teacher with 38 years of experience served as examples, with highlighted text sequences marking professional vision indicators and instructional explanations added. The framework draws on cognitive load theory and the worked example effect, proposing that novices study expert solutions before producing their own analyses.
requirements: Learners study the double-content examples before conducting their own video-based analyses
constraints: The study found the examples hindered some professional vision outcomes in this ill-structured domain, so the framework's benefit in teacher education is not supported by this study
target_learning_goals: professional vision of classroom management: noticing, reasoning, generating alternatives of action, and expert features
examples: Three text-based double-content examples were developed from an expert teacher's written video-based analyses, with indicators highlighted in yellow, blue, and green, and validated with five experienced teachers in think-aloud interviews

article_title: Does inquiry-based learning work better in regular classrooms or computer-based settings?
citation: Hasan Ozgur Kapici. (2025). Does inquiry-based learning work better in regular classrooms or computer-based settings? Instructional Science (2025) 53:705–728. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09711-0
title: Self-determination theory framing of motivation quality in learning environments
description: The article adopts self-determination theory (SDT) as its motivation framework. SDT "differentiates the intensity and amount of motivation from the quality or type of motivation", refining the intrinsic/extrinsic split into "a distinction between autonomous (self-determined) and controlled motivation". Autonomous motivation arises when a learning environment satisfies needs for autonomy, self-efficacy (competence), and relatedness, and is associated with positive educational outcomes. The study assumed the virtual environment would support these needs, e.g. teachers refraining from disturbing interventions to provide psychological freedom.
requirements: A social context (learning environment) that satisfies learners' needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness to increase autonomous motivation
target_learning_goals: motivation for learning science
examples: The study assumed the inquiry-based virtual learning environment provided psychological freedom, self-efficacy, and a sense of belongingness; measured motivation nonetheless showed no group difference.

article_title: Does inquiry-based learning work better in regular classrooms or computer-based settings?
citation: Hasan Ozgur Kapici. (2025). Does inquiry-based learning work better in regular classrooms or computer-based settings? Instructional Science (2025) 53:705–728. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09711-0
title: Go-Lab/Graasp Inquiry Learning Spaces with online scaffolding tools
description: The experimental condition used virtual learning environments from the Go-Lab project, built on the Graasp platform. "The platform involves Inquiry Learning Spaces (ILSs) as learning resources that foster inquiry learning" by following "the inquiry cycle phases of orientation, hypothesis generation, experimentation, conclusion, and discussion". ILSs can include virtual/remote labs, scaffolding apps, and multimedia. In this study teachers developed nine ILSs for force and energy, each covered in about two hours over five weeks, using a hypothesis scratchpad and an experiment design tool as scaffolds.
requirements: Teachers/developers design personalized ILSs on the Graasp platform; hints on using online laboratories were provided so students mostly completed experiments
constraints: Students worked in pairs due to limited numbers of tablets and PCs
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of force and energy
inquiry skills
examples: Nine inquiry-based virtual learning spaces were developed by six science teachers; students used a hypothesis scratchpad with drag-and-drop domain terms and an experiment design tool.

title: Pair inquiry-based learning with technology-enabled scaffolding tools, since teacher guidance alone reaches students less individually
description: The article's discussion recommends that inquiry learning, especially for younger learners, be supported by online scaffolding tools such as hypothesis scratchpads and experiment design tools. It argues "teacher guidance may be less effective than online scaffolding tools, because teachers cannot follow each student in the classroom individually and cannot give appropriate feedback to them in the limited class time". Effective guidance in hypothesis formulation and experiment design is identified as a key factor in the experimental groups' success.
requirements: Scaffolding matched to inquiry phases (hypothesis generation, experiment design); teachers trained in IBL and virtual learning
constraints: The article also states a combination of inquiry-based methods and direct instruction is more effective than either alone, especially for younger learners
target_learners: primary and middle school science students
target_learning_goals: hypothesis formulation
experiment design
conceptual understanding
inquiry skills
examples: Experimental-group students used a hypothesis scratchpad with predefined domain terms and partial hypotheses, and an experiment design tool; control students developed hypotheses on their own with whole-class teacher guidance.

article_title: How preparation-for-learning with a worked versus an open inventing problem affect subsequent learning processes in pre-service teachers
citation: Inga Glogger-Frey, Anne-Katrin Treier, Alexander Renkl. (2022). How preparation-for-learning with a worked versus an open inventing problem affect subsequent learning processes in pre-service teachers. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09577-6
title: Use worked-example preparation rather than open inventing to prepare learners for subsequent instruction in complex, ill-structured domains
description: The article argues that when learning content has high element interactivity, preparing learners by having them study a worked-out solution of the invention problem deepens and focuses the subsequent learning phase. It concludes that "working through a worked example deepens future learning and thus is more beneficial for transfer than preparation with an open inventing problem" in comparable learning domains. The mechanism is more elaboration and more application of canonical criteria during future learning.
requirements: Learners with low prior knowledge facing complex learning contents, for whom direct guidance to canonical solutions and key concepts is argued to save time and cognitive resources
constraints: The authors state generalizations can be limited: effects may depend on learner expertise and element interactivity, and the opposite effect (inventing > worked example) was found when school students gained expertise through practice; only an immediate posttest was used
target_learners: novice learners with low prior knowledge in complex domains
target_learning_goals: assessing the quality of learning strategies
applying quality criteria to new instances
transfer of assessed skills
examples: In the experiment, the inventing group generated evaluation criteria from four contrasting learning-journal extracts while the worked-example group studied the same extracts with the criteria, ratings and notes already filled in by an experienced teacher, both for 15 minutes before learning in the CBLE

article_title: Fun beyond gamification: Universal elements to enhance children’s learning
citation: Kokarida, P., Markopoulos, P., & Tisza, G. (2026). Fun beyond gamification: Universal elements to enhance children's learning. Instructional Science (2026) 54:30. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09780-9
title: Six non-gamification elements of fun in formal learning for primary students
description: A thematic framework identifying six elements primary school students aged 9–12 perceive as making learning fun beyond gamification: "a sense of agency, challenge, diversity in learning, pleasure, a low-stress climate, and peer interaction." Derived via reflexive thematic analysis combining deductive coding against the FunQ model and inductive coding of focus group and observation data, then contextualized by an expert interview. It extends the FunQ model for formal primary settings.
requirements: Qualitative elicitation of student perspectives, since the elements are defined by students' own reported experiences of fun
constraints: Derived from one public primary school in Heraklion, Greece, in music and art sessions with students aged 9 to 12
target_learning_goals: motivation and engagement in formal learning activities
examples: Themes were corroborated by classroom observations of 48 students and reviewed by an expert in creative and fun learning

article_title: Instructional approaches to foster third graders’ adaptive use of strategies: an experimental study on the effects of two learning environments on multi-digit addition and subtraction
citation: Aiso Heinze, Julia Arend, Meike Gruessing, Frank Lipowsky. (2018). Instructional approaches to foster third graders' adaptive use of strategies: an experimental study on the effects of two learning environments on multi-digit addition and subtraction. Instr Sci 46:869–891. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9457-1
title: Two idealized instructional approaches to fostering adaptive strategy use: explicit demonstration versus implicit generation
description: The article contrasts two idealized learning environments for fostering adaptive use of strategies. The explicit approach reduces cognitive load by demonstrating and practicing strategies with explicit efficiency criteria, building a strategy repertoire and routine execution. The implicit approach capitalizes on the generation effect: children analyze number characteristics, categorize problems as "easy problems", "smart problems" or "other problems", generate their own strategies, and compare their efficiency, with the teacher acting as a mentor who avoids presenting official strategies or preferences. Both environments used the same problems and strategy comparison from the beginning.
requirements: Students must be able to generate the target strategies correctly; the article states a necessary condition for the generation effect is that students are able to generate the target information correctly
The teacher must avoid setting socio-mathematical norms that implicitly privilege particular strategies
constraints: The generation effect does not hold for strategies too complex for students to generate, such as indirect subtraction and simplifying for third graders
target_learners: primary school students (third grade, 9–10 years old)
target_learning_goals: adaptive use of computation strategies in multi-digit addition and subtraction
examples: In the explicit condition the five strategy types were successively demonstrated and practiced over the first three days; in the implicit condition children categorized problems and generated and compared their own strategies

article_title: Is drawing after learning effective for metacognitive monitoring only when supported by spatial scaffolds?
citation: Julia Kollmer, Katrin Schleinschok, Katharina Scheiter, Alexander Eitel. (2020). Is drawing after learning effective for metacognitive monitoring only when supported by spatial scaffolds? Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09521-6
title: Generative tasks foster metacognitive monitoring by prompting situation-model reasoning that yields more diagnostic JOL cues
description: The article's explanatory framework holds that inaccurate monitoring stems from learners basing JOLs on superficial cues such as the ease-of-processing heuristic. Generative tasks like drawing "require situation-model reasoning, because they require constructing a 'new' representation in a different code", transforming verbal relations into spatial ones and giving implicit feedback about knowledge gaps. JOLs grounded in situation-model comprehension are less inflated because less forgetting occurs at that level, improving calibration. The study tests this account by comparing drawing conditions against mental reactivation.
requirements: Learners must perform the generative task after reading and directly before providing JOLs, without access to the text (closed-book conditions).
constraints: The account was tested with high visuo-spatial content; the authors state it remains open whether drawing supports monitoring for contents lower in visuo-spatial reasoning demands.
target_learners: university students learning expository text independently
target_learning_goals: accurate metacognitive monitoring (calibration and resolution) of expository text comprehension
examples: Students drew the crucial concepts from each aurora-text paragraph and labeled the diagram before giving a JOL on an 11-point 0-100 scale.
key_sources: Julia Kollmer, Katrin Schleinschok, Katharina Scheiter, Alexander Eitel. (2020). Is drawing after learning effective for metacognitive monitoring only when supported by spatial scaffolds? Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09521-6

article_title: Self-regulation of secondary school students: self-assessments are inaccurate and insufficiently used for learning-task selection
citation: Nugteren, M. L., Jarodzka, H., Kester, L., & Van Merriënboer, J. J. G. (2018). Self-regulation of secondary school students: self-assessments are inaccurate and insufficiently used for learning-task selection. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9448-2
title: SRLTS model: a normative cyclical model for self-regulated learning-task selection based on self-assessments
description: The self-regulated learning-task selection (SRLTS) model describes "a systematic way in which students could select tasks to develop their knowledge and skills". Adapted from Zimmerman's SRL cycle and Van Merriënboer and Kirschner's dynamic task-selection model, it has students self-assess via performance estimates, mental effort ratings, and JOLs, compare these to internal standards, and use the gaps to choose a next task's difficulty, support, and content. It was added to existing models with two new elements: standards and a link between JOLs and content selection.
requirements: Self-assessments need to be accurate for task selections to be based on correct information
Students must be able to compare self-assessments to internal standards for performance and cognitive load
constraints: The article states the study does not yet establish that selecting tasks according to the SRLTS model leads to higher achievement
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning-task selection
self-assessment of performance
examples: Students selected genetics tasks varying in difficulty, support (completion vs. traditional problems), and content from a 75-task database while the authors compared selections to model prescriptions

article_title: Community and citizen science in schools: nested inquiries, productive tensions, and the role of communities
citation: Ballard, H. L. (2023). Community and citizen science in schools: nested inquiries, productive tensions, and the role of communities. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09643-7
title: Nested inquiries: students pursue their own investigations intertwined with partnering scientists' projects in school-based citizen science
description: Nested inquiries are cases where educators and scientists strike a balance between students' own questions and those of partnering professional scientists, offering a solution to the tension among the multiple goals of CCS in schools. The commentary states these cases "offer evidence of students' learning and deep engagement with scientific practices, the nature of science and uncertainty, and using their science for decision-making and action." It extends earlier work on youth working with nested data situated in larger datasets, projects, and communities.

nature of science and uncertainty
using science for decision-making and action
identity and agency development

A 4th and 5th grade class investigated birds on their school campus while submitting observations to eBird and developed schoolyard planting recommendations

article_title: Examining secondary school students’ views of model evaluation through an integrated framework of personal epistemology
citation: Lee, S. W.-Y., Wu, H., & Chang, H. (2021). Examining secondary school students' views of model evaluation through an integrated framework of personal epistemology. Instructional Science, 49, 223–248. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09534-9
title: Integrated framework of personal epistemology for model evaluation: Kuhn's three developmental stages crossed with Kitchener's three epistemic-cognition dimensions
description: The framework interlaces Kuhn's developmental levels (absolutist, multiplist, evaluatist) with Kitchener's dimensions of epistemic cognition (limits of knowing, certainty of knowing, criteria of knowing) to form a matrix for analyzing students' epistemic views of model evaluation. As the article states, "the three epistemic levels describing the absolutist, multiplist, and evaluatist... and the three epistemic dimensions describing limits of knowing, certainty of knowing, and criteria of knowing (Kitchener 1983) are interlaced to form a new framework for analyzing students' epistemic views of model evaluation." It was operationalized in coding themes and used to interpret students' justifications.
requirements: Written justifications and forced-choice assumption responses so that epistemic levels and dimensions can be coded and triangulated
constraints: The article notes relatively fewer students referred to the limits of knowing, and the framework was applied to two non-textbook science contexts with high uncertainty
target_learning_goals: epistemic understanding of scientific model evaluation
examples: Students' justifications were coded into themes mapped onto the framework's dimensions and levels, and each student's assumption choice was compared with the coded written response to confirm their epistemic level

article_title: Examining secondary school students’ views of model evaluation through an integrated framework of personal epistemology
citation: Lee, S. W.-Y., Wu, H., & Chang, H. (2021). Examining secondary school students' views of model evaluation through an integrated framework of personal epistemology. Instructional Science, 49, 223–248. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09534-9
title: Contextualized model-evaluation items presenting two competing models and three epistemic assumptions
description: The study developed model-evaluation items with three design characteristics: they are "contextualized by real scientific problems," they "present at least two competing models," and they "present three epistemic positions for the students to choose from." Two item sets were built on SARS virus infection models and dinosaur-extinction models, deliberately chosen as non-textbook science contexts with high uncertainty. After reading about the two models, students chose among three epistemic assumptions and wrote justifications explaining their choice.
requirements: Item review by co-authors and by two middle school teachers and one high school teacher to ensure construct, face, and content validity
constraints: The two contexts were intentionally non-textbook and possessed high levels of uncertainty, since scientists are still attempting to understand the mechanisms or causes
target_learning_goals: assessing students' epistemic views of scientific model evaluation
examples: Two models of SARS virus infection and two explanatory models of dinosaur extinction were presented, and students chose among assumptions such as "one model is better than another" and "depends on the evidence"

article_title: Walking the number line: towards an enactive understanding of integer arithmetic
citation: Jacqueline Anton, Dor Abrahamson. (2025). Walking the number line: towards an enactive understanding of integer arithmetic. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09707-w
title: Perspectival coordination framework: egocentric-to-allocentric coordination as the cognitive process of symbol grounding in embodied mathematics designs
description: The article proposes that embodied designs stage a coordination between an egocentric perspective, in which actions are experienced with respect to one's own body, and an allocentric perspective, in which objects are experienced with respect to other objects. Following Benally et al., it distinguishes "in perspectival substitution, one perspective replaces the other; in perspectival mutuality, individuals use an alternative perspective to validate their own; in perspectival synergy, a combination of two perspectives results in one that is greater than each perspective alone." The design operationalizes this as walking a body-scale number line (egocentric) then puppeteering a figurine on a desk-scale line (allocentric).
requirements: Students must experience the egocentric enaction first and then be guided to coordinate it with the allocentric normative display
constraints: Merely shifting unidirectionally from the BNL to a figurine on the SNL was often not enough, per the article's implications
target_learning_goals: understanding addition and subtraction with positive and negative integers
examples: Students walked the body-scale number line, then moved a puppy figurine on a desk-scale number line to mimic their movements
key_sources: Jacqueline Anton, Dor Abrahamson. (2025). Walking the number line: towards an enactive understanding of integer arithmetic. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09707-w

article_title: Walking the number line: towards an enactive understanding of integer arithmetic
citation: Jacqueline Anton, Dor Abrahamson. (2025). Walking the number line: towards an enactive understanding of integer arithmetic. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09707-w
title: Walking number line design: body-scale number line plus desk-scale number line with figurine, using a four-step orientation-and-movement procedure
description: The design consists of a body-scale number line (a 20' × 4' paper roll displaying a number line from −5 to +5, with step-spaced marks and addition/subtraction signs at the ends) and a small number line (an 8.5″ × 11″ sheet with a scaled-down line and a puppy figurine). Students follow four steps: "start by standing on the first number in the problem"; face the addition or subtraction direction; "walk forwards if the second number (the addend or subtrahend) is positive and backwards if the second number is negative"; and walk as many steps as the absolute value of that second number. The operation is enacted as a shift in orientation and the second number's polarity as direction of movement.
requirements: Signs marking addition and subtraction at the two ends of the body-scale line
A figurine on the desk-scale line for re-enacting the walking solution
constraints: The material boundaries at −5 and +5 led some students to reject solutions outside that range, per the limitations section
target_learners: Grade 7 students in general education inclusive math classes, pre-identified as struggling with integer operations
target_learning_goals: fluency with adding and subtracting positive and negative integers
examples: A student solving −1 + 3 stands on −1, faces addition, and walks forwards three steps to arrive at 2
key_sources: Jacqueline Anton, Dor Abrahamson. (2025). Walking the number line: towards an enactive understanding of integer arithmetic. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09707-w

article_title: Walking the number line: towards an enactive understanding of integer arithmetic
citation: Jacqueline Anton, Dor Abrahamson. (2025). Walking the number line: towards an enactive understanding of integer arithmetic. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09707-w
title: Scaffold perspective coordination explicitly: give students multiple body-scale sessions and bidirectional switching supports before expecting desk-scale transfer
description: From the pilot's breakdowns, the authors recommend that embodied designs not shift unidirectionally from enactive to normative media. They state that "students must be given scaffolded opportunities to coordinate between perspectives when learning curricular content in an experiential situation" and that "Merely shifting unidirectionally from the BNL to a figurine on the SNL was often not enough." For the next design iteration they specify multiple body-scale sessions before advancing, a longer number line, and switching back and forth between the two lines or teaching a peer how to walk the body-scale line.
requirements: Time for multiple sessions on the body-scale number line before advancing to the desk-scale line
constraints: The pilot's limited time within a typical school day restricted participants' opportunities to train adequately with the new resources
target_learners: middle-school students learning integer arithmetic, including students with disabilities
target_learning_goals: coordinating embodied and symbolic understandings of integer operations
examples: In the pilot, students who spontaneously returned to the body-scale line when stuck used it to validate desk-scale answers; the authors propose building in such switching deliberately

article_title: Students’ voices—the dynamic interactions between learning preferences, gender, learning disabilities, and achievements in science studies
citation: Oshra Aloni, Michal Zion, Ornit Spektor-Levy. (2024). Students' voices—the dynamic interactions between learning preferences, gender, learning disabilities, and achievements in science studies. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09666-8
title: Implement multi-faceted instructional strategies and an ongoing metacognitive dialogue with students about learning preferences to address student diversity in science classrooms
description: The article argues that because students favored all four learning modalities and expected variety, science instruction should be multi-faceted. The authors state that "the study results show the importance of implementing multi-faceted instructional strategies to address students' diversity and learning preferences", and that offering equal opportunities should be reflected in "an ongoing, metacognitive dialogue between the teachers and the students" about outcomes, achievements, and learning processes. Without such explicit discussion, they warn, providing learning choices may leave students confused and underachieving.
requirements: Explicit discussions with students about their learning preferences, so that offering learning choices does not end in confusion and unmet potential
constraints: The study addressed only a binary gender system and did not consider students who do not identify as male or female
Effect sizes for gender differences were low-moderate and the authors call for further examination
target_learners: Middle school (ninth-grade) science students in heterogeneous, inclusive classrooms, including students with and without learning disabilities
target_learning_goals: Scientific knowledge and skills in ninth-grade science (nutrition and the digestive system, scientific inquiry, graph reading)
examples: The study asked 305 ninth-grade students about their science learning preferences via a validated Learning Preferences Questionnaire based on Fleming's VARK model and the Multi-Faceted Holistic Approach, and found all four modalities preferred above the mid-point with visual and sensorimotor highest
key_sources: Oshra Aloni, Michal Zion, Ornit Spektor-Levy. (2024). Students' voices—the dynamic interactions between learning preferences, gender, learning disabilities, and achievements in science studies. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09666-8

article_title: Learning with concept maps: the effect of activity structure and the type of task
citation: Amante, C., Lucero, M., & Montanero, M. (2026). Learning with concept maps: the effect of activity structure and the type of task. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09764-1
title: Collective working memory account of why collaborative self-construction of concept maps supports learning
description: The article explains the advantage of collaborative map self-construction through a collective-working-memory account: dialogic conversation distributes the proposing and evaluating of representational alternatives across partners, so "the exchange and integration of information that characterizes dialogic conversation would generate a kind of collective working memory" that reduces the load on any single member's working memory. The authors link this to cognitive load theory, noting that individually constructing a map from a text requires producing and evaluating many alternatives, which overloads working memory. Peer help in the deep exploratory episodes of self-constructed CM pairs showed co-inference processes that offset this load.
requirements: Tasks complex enough that the intrinsic load justifies collaboration; the article states collaboration is only truly effective "when the task is sufficiently complex to justify the extra time and effort involved in collaborating with others".
constraints: Peer help showed no significant effect over individual work for relatively simple tasks such as completing a mutilated map, because the intrinsic load is much lighter.
target_learners: Undergraduate students with little or no experience using concept maps
target_learning_goals: Comprehension and delayed recall of academic text content
examples: Pairs who created complete maps showed deep exploratory episodes with co-inference, distributing the work of proposing and evaluating concept representations.
key_sources: Amante, C., Lucero, M., & Montanero, M. (2026). Learning with concept maps: the effect of activity structure and the type of task. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09764-1

article_title: Authentic evidence from the ‘SRL-AIDE’ simulative environment on explicitness and duration of in-class SRL teaching practices
citation: Orna Heaysman, Bracha Kramarski. (2026). Authentic evidence from the 'SRL-AIDE' simulative environment on explicitness and duration of in-class SRL teaching practices. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09787-2
title: SRL-AIDE: a professional development model combining direct and indirect SRL instruction through authentic, interactive, dynamic live-actor simulation experiences
description: SRL-AIDE (Authentic, Interactive, and Dynamic Experiences in SRL context) is a teacher professional development model combining explicit instruction in SRL theory and practice with simulations in which professional actors play student roles and one participant teaches. The article states it "involves live-actor simulations, where participants are highly engaged and immersed in the experience." After each simulation, participants analyze scenarios with metacognitive prompts, receive feedback from audience and actors, and take part in a guided video-based debriefing. The model addresses gaps in prior PD research that relied on pre-service teachers and self-report measures by measuring actual classroom implementation through observation.
requirements: Programs combining the model need theory–practice integration, simulations with professional actors, and materials such as video-recorded modelling, prompt cards, and reflection sessions as described in the program outline
constraints: The study examined the model with 70 elementary teachers of grades 3–5 (ages 8–10) in schools of medium–high/high socio-economic status in central Israel; the authors note future research should test impact on student outcomes and other practice types
target_learning_goals: teachers' knowledge and classroom implementation of self-regulated learning practices (MCS and KC)
examples: Over 10 three-hour sessions, the SRL-AIDE group received explicit SRL phase instruction, simulation workshops with professional actors (sessions 5 and 8), role-play, video observation, and collaborative lesson planning
key_sources: Orna Heaysman, Bracha Kramarski. (2026). Authentic evidence from the 'SRL-AIDE' simulative environment on explicitness and duration of in-class SRL teaching practices. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09787-2

article_title: Authentic evidence from the ‘SRL-AIDE’ simulative environment on explicitness and duration of in-class SRL teaching practices
citation: Orna Heaysman, Bracha Kramarski. (2026). Authentic evidence from the 'SRL-AIDE' simulative environment on explicitness and duration of in-class SRL teaching practices. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09787-2
title: Teacher PD for SRL should combine explicit theoretical instruction with authentic simulation-based practice, since promoting independence (KC) alone does not build metacognitive instruction capacity
description: The article recommends that effective SRL development for teachers requires "explicit theoretical instruction combined with authentic practice opportunities", because promoting independence through knowledge construction alone does not build teachers' capacity for explicit metacognitive instruction. PD programs should integrate direct and indirect SRL approaches with extended duration and simulation-based experiences allowing practice and reflection. The study's comparison of the SRL-AIDE group against a KC-focused comparison program provides the empirical basis for this recommendation.
requirements: PD programs need extended duration and simulation-based experiences allowing practice and reflection, per the article's implications section
constraints: The evidence comes from a quasi-experimental study of 70 elementary teachers in grades 3–5 in central Israel; the authors note student outcomes and other practice types remain untested
target_learning_goals: teachers' capacity to implement metacognitive strategic support and knowledge construction practices in class
examples: The SRL-AIDE group received explicit SRL theory instruction plus live-actor simulation workshops, while the comparison group received only KC-focused instruction; only the SRL-AIDE group's KC duration increased significantly
