citation: Brouhier, Q., Raemdonck, I., & März, V. (2026). Professional Learning of Late-career Teachers: A Systematic Literature Review. Educational Research Review, 50, 100757. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2025.100757
title: Design context-sensitive professional learning approaches that value late-career teachers' continued growth, contributions and well-being
description: The review concludes by "advocating for more nuanced, context-sensitive approaches to professional learning that value the continued growth, contributions and well-being of teachers in the later stages of their careers." This principle calls for professional development design that responds to late-career teachers' specific needs and circumstances rather than applying generic provision, and that recognises their ongoing capacity to grow and contribute.
requirements: Attention to the specific needs, context and well-being of late-career teachers when designing professional learning
constraints: The review highlights a notable gap in tailored interventions addressing late-career teachers' specific needs, so evidence on what such tailored approaches should contain is limited
target_learning_goals: Continued professional growth, contribution and well-being
examples: The review concludes with theoretical and practical implications advocating nuanced, context-sensitive approaches to professional learning for late-career teachers.
key_sources: Brouhier, Q., Raemdonck, I., & März, V. (2026). Professional Learning of Late-career Teachers: A Systematic Literature Review. Educational Research Review, 50, 100757. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2025.100757

article_title: Computer-assisted word reading intervention effects throughout the primary grades: A meta-analysis
citation: Verhoeven, L.T.W.; Voeten, M.J.M.; Segers, P.C.J. (2022). Computer-assisted word reading intervention effects throughout the primary grades: A meta-analysis. Educational Research Review, 37, article 100486. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2022.100486
title: Four-type taxonomy of computer-assisted word reading interventions
description: The article organizes computer-supported word reading interventions into four program types: foundational (comprehensive) reading instruction, supplementary alphabetics, reading fluency programs, and remedial reading programs for at-risk students in higher grades. It states "A distinction can be made between programs focusing on basic phonics instruction, supplementary alphabetic skills, reading fluency programs, and remedial reading interventions", and compares these four types on accuracy and speed of processing letters, phonological units, words, pseudowords, passages, and spelling. Comprehensive programs teach grapheme-phoneme correspondences explicitly in incremental sets; supplementary programs add phonological awareness and letter training; fluency programs build speeded word recognition; remedial programs give individualized or small-group tutoring.
requirements: Studies must report experimental comparisons between experimental and control conditions with a pre-test and post-test on the same outcome measure
constraints: Specific treatments focused solely on spelling or reading comprehension were left out for reasons of parsimony
target_learners: primary school children in grades 1 to 6
children at risk for reading difficulties
target_learning_goals: word reading accuracy
word reading speed and fluency
phonological awareness
letter knowledge
spelling
examples: The meta-analysis compared the four treatment types on accuracy and speed outcomes across 67 studies
key_sources: Verhoeven, L.T.W.; Voeten, M.J.M.; Segers, P.C.J. (2022). Computer-assisted word reading intervention effects throughout the primary grades: A meta-analysis. Educational Research Review, 37, article 100486. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2022.100486

article_title: A systematic review of the role of learning analytics in enhancing feedback practices in higher education
citation: Seyyed Kazem Banihashem, Omid Noroozi, Stan van Ginkel, Leah P. Macfadyen, Harm J.A. Biemans. (2022). A systematic review of the role of learning analytics in enhancing feedback practices in higher education. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2022.100489
title: Four-dimension LA reference model (what, how, why, who) guiding the review of LA for feedback
description: The review adopts Chatti et al.'s (2012) reference model in which "LA consists of four dimensions including (1) what (what types of data does the system capture and analyze), (2) how (how does the system perform analytics), (3) why (for what reasons does the system gather and analyze data), and (4) who (who is served by the analytics)". This framework structures the review's coding scheme and four research questions, and underpins the conceptual framework the authors propose to guide implementation of LA for feedback systems in higher education.
requirements: Included studies must report findings, implications or evidence addressing at least one of the four dimensions (data, methods, objectives, stakeholders) for LA feedback in higher education
constraints: The review restricts scope to peer-reviewed empirical studies in higher education settings published 2011–2022, excluding conceptual studies and K-12 contexts
target_learning_goals: improving feedback practices and feedback-supported learning in technology-mediated higher education environments
examples: The review coded all 46 papers in ATLAS.ti against the four categories (what, how, why, who), achieving 91 percent inter-rater agreement (κ = 0.84).
key_sources: Seyyed Kazem Banihashem, Omid Noroozi, Stan van Ginkel, Leah P. Macfadyen, Harm J.A. Biemans. (2022). A systematic review of the role of learning analytics in enhancing feedback practices in higher education. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2022.100489

article_title: Using student-centred learning environments to stimulate deep approaches to learning: Factors encouraging or discouraging their effectiveness
citation: Baeten, M., Kyndt, E., Struyven, K., & Dochy, F. (2010). Using student-centred learning environments to stimulate deep approaches to learning: Factors encouraging or discouraging their effectiveness. Educational Research Review, 5, 243–260. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2010.06.001
title: Approaches to learning framework: deep and surface approaches combining intention, motive and strategy
description: The review organises its synthesis around the approaches-to-learning construct, in which "An approach to learning embeds the intention of the student when starting a task and the learning processes and strategies used to carry out a task". Deep approaches combine an intention to understand with meaning-seeking strategies; surface approaches combine an intention to reproduce with rote memorisation and minimal effort. Approaches are measured by ASI- and SPQ-based questionnaires and are context-dependent rather than stable traits, which is why the review examines environmental and student factors shaping them.
requirements: Measurement by self-report questionnaires based on the ASI and SPQ traditions
constraints: Approaches depend on the context within which a task is experienced and the learner's interpretation thereof; recent SPQ research supports a two-factor deep/surface structure without a separate strategic scale
target_learning_goals: Fostering deep, meaningful learning and understanding rather than reproduction of content
examples: The review used this framework to select studies measuring approaches with ASI- and SPQ-based inventories and to classify encouraging and discouraging factors across context, perception and student characteristics
key_sources: Baeten, M., Kyndt, E., Struyven, K., & Dochy, F. (2010). Using student-centred learning environments to stimulate deep approaches to learning: Factors encouraging or discouraging their effectiveness. Educational Research Review, 5, 243–260. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2010.06.001

article_title: Let's talk evidence – The case for combining inquiry-based and direct instruction
citation: de Jong, T., Lazonder, A. W., Chinn, C. A., Fischer, F., Gobert, J., Hmelo-Silver, C. H., Koedinger, K. R., Krajcik, J. S., Kyza, E. A., Linn, M. C., Pedaste, M., Scheiter, K., & Zacharia, Z. C. (2023). Let's talk evidence – The case for combining inquiry-based and direct instruction. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2023.100536
title: Match instructional approach to learning goal: inquiry for deep, transferable understanding of ill-structured topics; direct instruction for foundational surface knowledge
description: The article's first design recommendation is to "employ inquiry-based methods if the instructional goal requires students to develop deep and transferrable conceptual understanding of topics that are open-ended or susceptible to misconceptions." Direct instruction is described as generally more appropriate and probably more efficient for acquiring well-structured and foundational (surface) knowledge. The recommendation draws on early instructional design theories and on Frey et al. (2017), who observed that inquiry-based methods were used effectively in lessons beyond the surface learning phase.
requirements: Teachers and curriculum designers should align instructional and assessment methods with the kind of learning outcomes they expect from students.
constraints: The article states direct instruction will not necessarily lead to deep conceptual understanding in less-well-structured domains.
target_learners: Science and STEM students in classroom settings
target_learning_goals: Deep and transferable conceptual understanding of science topics
Acquisition of well-structured foundational (surface) knowledge
examples: The article recommends inquiry for topics susceptible to misconceptions, such as how water's boiling point changes with altitude, and direct instruction for factual information such as the chemical formula of water.

article_title: Four key challenges to the design of blended learning: A systematic literature review
citation: Boelens, R., De Wever, B., & Voet, M. (2017). Four key challenges to the design of blended learning: A systematic literature review. Educational Research Review, 22, 1-18. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2017.06.001
title: Four-challenge framework for designing blended learning environments
description: The article presents a framework organizing blended learning design around four key challenges: incorporating flexibility, stimulating interaction, facilitating students' learning processes, and fostering an affective learning climate. The authors state: "This study presents a framework that is based on four key challenges to the design of blended learning: incorporating flexibility, stimulating interaction, facilitating students' learning processes, and fostering an affective learning climate." The framework was derived from a comparison of influential blended learning studies and used as the coding scheme for the systematic review. It can help designers create, communicate about, and evaluate blended learning designs.
requirements: Studies must define blended learning as a combination of face-to-face and online interventions and take an instructional, course-level design point of view
constraints: The framework excludes other dimensions such as which educational objectives are targeted in the online or face-to-face component
target_learning_goals: course-level design of blended learning environments
examples: The authors applied the framework as a coding scheme to 20 selected studies, with two coders reaching 74-95% percent agreement across 18 variables
key_sources: Boelens, R., De Wever, B., & Voet, M. (2017). Four key challenges to the design of blended learning: A systematic literature review. Educational Research Review, 22, 1-18. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2017.06.001

article_title: Four key challenges to the design of blended learning: A systematic literature review
citation: Boelens, R., De Wever, B., & Voet, M. (2017). Four key challenges to the design of blended learning: A systematic literature review. Educational Research Review, 22, 1-18. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2017.06.001
title: Vermunt and Verloop's categorization of regulative and affective instructional strategies
description: The review adopts Vermunt and Verloop's (1999) framework of instructional activities that assist students in regulating their learning. For learning processes, "this framework distinguishes between four categories of regulative strategies: orienting and planning, monitoring, adjusting, and evaluating." For the affective climate, it distinguishes five categories of affective strategies: motivating, concentrating and exerting effort, attributing and judging oneself, appraising, and dealing with emotions. The review used these categories as the basis of its coding scheme and derived specific instructional activities (e.g. peer assessment, tracking learners, reminders) inductively within them.
requirements: The framework focuses on aspects that can be dealt with during instruction, making it suitable for analyzing course-level design
target_learning_goals: self-regulation of learning
affective climate in blended courses
examples: The review's coding scheme mapped activities such as measuring prior knowledge to orienting and planning, and online tests and tracking systems to monitoring
key_sources: Boelens, R., De Wever, B., & Voet, M. (2017). Four key challenges to the design of blended learning: A systematic literature review. Educational Research Review, 22, 1-18. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2017.06.001

article_title: Four key challenges to the design of blended learning: A systematic literature review
citation: Boelens, R., De Wever, B., & Voet, M. (2017). Four key challenges to the design of blended learning: A systematic literature review. Educational Research Review, 22, 1-18. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2017.06.001
title: Systematic PRISMA-based review corpus of 20 blended learning design studies
description: The review's evidence base is a corpus of 20 studies on the design of blended learning environments, selected through a staged PRISMA-based procedure. "Starting from 640 sources, 20 studies on the design of blended learning environments were selected through a staged procedure based on the guidelines of the PRISMA statement, using predefined selection criteria." Most studies (n=18) were conducted in higher education contexts, and most (n=15) were intervention studies. Instructional activities were analyzed by two coders, with percent agreement between 74% and 95% across 18 variables.
requirements: Inclusion criteria required blended learning defined as a combination of face-to-face and online interventions, an instructional design point of view at course level, and a detailed description of the design
constraints: Studies focusing on one specific tool, short conference papers, book reviews, and non-English articles were excluded
target_learning_goals: blended course design and development
examples: The Web of Science search in February 2015 with blended/hybrid/flipped learning terms and design-related keywords yielded 496 hits, supplemented by literature suggested in prior reviews

article_title: Effects of innovative science and mathematics teaching on student attitudes and achievement: A meta-analytic study
citation: Savelsbergh, E. R., Prins, G. T., Rietbergen, C., Fechner, S., Vaessen, B. E., Draijer, J. M., & Bakker, A. (2016). Effects of innovative science and mathematics teaching on student attitudes and achievement: A meta-analytic study. Educational Research Review, 19, 158-172. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2016.07.003
title: Hierarchical framework of domain-specific attitude constructs for synthesizing attitude outcomes
description: The article proposes a hierarchical conceptual framework (Fig. 1) for classifying attitude measures at multiple grain sizes, balancing fine-grained and global analyses. The authors "consider attitude a multidimensional construct comprising: perceived relevance (personal and societal), interest (school, leisure, career), self-efficacy, and normality of scientists", with an overall attitude construct for aggregated measures. It was used to categorize attitude instruments across the 65 experiments and to justify separate meta-analyses for specific and global outcomes.
requirements: Attitude instruments must assess domain-specific attitudes and be validated or report reliability statistics and at least three sample items per scale
constraints: Scientific attitudes (critical stance, demand for verification) fall beyond the framework's scope as applied in this review
target_learners: primary and secondary students in science and mathematics education
target_learning_goals: domain-specific attitudes, interest, and motivation toward science and mathematics
examples: The framework sorted the 65 experiments' attitude measures into subscales such as general interest, career interest, self-efficacy, and normality of scientist, each meta-analyzed separately (Table 4).
key_sources: Savelsbergh, E. R., Prins, G. T., Rietbergen, C., Fechner, S., Vaessen, B. E., Draijer, J. M., & Bakker, A. (2016). Educational Research Review, 19, 158-172. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2016.07.003

article_title: School-based teaching for democracy: A systematic review of teaching methods in quantitative intervention studies
citation: Teegelbeckers, J.Y., Nieuwelink, H., & Oostdam, R.J. (2023). School-based teaching for democracy: A systematic review of teaching methods in quantitative intervention studies. Educational Research Review, 39, 100511. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2023.100511
title: Five-type taxonomy of teaching methods for democracy: instruction, small-group work, assignments, projects, and democratic decision-making
description: The review organizes democratic-schooling interventions into five types of teaching methods. As the article states, "We categorized these interventions into five types of teaching methods: instruction, small-group work, assignments, projects, and democratic decision-making." This taxonomy is the review's primary organizing axis for comparing which interventions were effective for which democratic competences, and it structures the analysis of educational characteristics across the 54 included interventions.
requirements: Quantitative intervention studies of school-based teaching for democracy that can be classified into one of the five method types
constraints: Derived from 51 quantitative effect studies written between 2010 and 2020; the review notes there is still much to be gained in the description of teaching methods
target_learners: School students in quantitative intervention studies of democratic education
target_learning_goals: Democratic competences (knowledge, attitude, skill, behavior)
examples: The review classified 54 interventions from 51 studies into the five method types and analyzed their effectiveness by democratic competence
key_sources: Teegelbeckers, J.Y., Nieuwelink, H., & Oostdam, R.J. (2023). School-based teaching for democracy: A systematic review of teaching methods in quantitative intervention studies. Educational Research Review, 39, 100511. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2023.100511

article_title: School-based teaching for democracy: A systematic review of teaching methods in quantitative intervention studies
citation: Teegelbeckers, J.Y., Nieuwelink, H., & Oostdam, R.J. (2023). School-based teaching for democracy: A systematic review of teaching methods in quantitative intervention studies. Educational Research Review, 39, 100511. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2023.100511
title: Four-component conceptualization of democratic competences: knowledge, attitude, skill, and behavior
description: The review conceptualizes democratic competences along four components. The article states it analyzed "for which democratic competences (i.e., knowledge, attitude, skill, behavior) they were effective." This four-part framework serves as the outcome axis of the review, paired against the five teaching-method types, allowing the authors to report which methods were effective for which competence components across the included interventions.
requirements: Studies must measure democratic competences in terms of knowledge, attitude, skill, and/or behavior
constraints: The review reports that there is still much to be gained in the conceptualization of democratic competences, indicating the framework's limits in the existing literature
target_learners: School students in democratic education interventions
target_learning_goals: Democratic knowledge, democratic attitudes, democratic skills, democratic behavior
examples: The review mapped each included intervention's outcomes onto the four competence components

article_title: School-based teaching for democracy: A systematic review of teaching methods in quantitative intervention studies
citation: Teegelbeckers, J.Y., Nieuwelink, H., & Oostdam, R.J. (2023). School-based teaching for democracy: A systematic review of teaching methods in quantitative intervention studies. Educational Research Review, 39, 100511. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2023.100511
title: Educational characteristics framework for analyzing democracy-teaching interventions: subject matter, classroom interaction, classroom management
description: Beyond teaching-method types, the review analyzes interventions through three educational characteristics. As the article prints, "We analyzed what the educational characteristics (i.e., subject matter, classroom interaction, classroom management) of these interventions were and for which democratic competences ... they were effective." This three-part lens describes how the 54 interventions were implemented in classrooms and links implementation features to effectiveness for democratic competences.
requirements: Interventions must be describable in terms of subject matter, classroom interaction, and classroom management
constraints: Applied to quantitative intervention studies of school-based teaching for democracy included in this review
target_learners: School students in democratic education interventions
target_learning_goals: Democratic competences (knowledge, attitude, skill, behavior)
examples: The review coded the 54 interventions on subject matter, classroom interaction, and classroom management characteristics

article_title: Scaffolding what, why and how? A critical thematic review study of descriptions, goals, and means of language scaffolding in Bilingual education contexts
citation: Ertugruloglu, E.O.; Mearns, T.L.; Admiraal, W.F. (2023). Scaffolding what, why and how? A critical thematic review study of descriptions, goals, and means of language scaffolding in Bilingual education contexts. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2023.100550
title: Hierarchy of language scaffolding goals: focusing on disciplinary literacy presupposes a focus on content and language
description: The review proposes an organizing account of language scaffolding goals in bilingual secondary education in which the goals form a hierarchy rather than a flat set. Within this hierarchy, "focusing on disciplinary literacy presupposes a focus on content and language", meaning that pursuing disciplinary literacy as a scaffolding goal builds on, and depends on, prior attention to content and language. The hierarchy emerged from the review's thematic synthesis of the four identified scaffolding goals.
requirements: Applies to language scaffolding by subject teachers in bilingual secondary education contexts
target_learners: secondary school students in bilingual education learning content through a partially known language
target_learning_goals: disciplinary literacy
content learning
language learning
examples: The review synthesizes studies of subject teachers teaching in bilingual secondary education contexts and orders their scaffolding goals into this hierarchy.
key_sources: Ertugruloglu, E.O.; Mearns, T.L.; Admiraal, W.F. (2023). Scaffolding what, why and how? A critical thematic review study of descriptions, goals, and means of language scaffolding in Bilingual education contexts. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2023.100550

article_title: Scaffolding what, why and how? A critical thematic review study of descriptions, goals, and means of language scaffolding in Bilingual education contexts
citation: Ertugruloglu, E.O.; Mearns, T.L.; Admiraal, W.F. (2023). Scaffolding what, why and how? A critical thematic review study of descriptions, goals, and means of language scaffolding in Bilingual education contexts. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2023.100550
title: Van de Pol et al.'s (2010) goals-and-means distinction and scaffolding characteristics as an analytic framework for language scaffolding
description: The review adopts Van de Pol et al.'s (2010) framework, which distinguishes scaffolding goals from scaffolding means and specifies characteristics of scaffolding, as its analytic lens. It uses this framework "to synthesize the various forms that scaffolding of language takes in the teaching practice of subject teachers teaching in bilingual secondary education contexts". The framework structures the review's findings into characteristics, means and goals of language scaffolding.
requirements: Distinguishing between scaffolding goals and scaffolding means when analyzing descriptions of scaffolding practice
target_learners: secondary school students in bilingual education
target_learning_goals: content and language learning supported by teacher scaffolding
examples: The review applied the framework to studies of subject teachers in bilingual secondary education to classify scaffolding descriptions.

article_title: Dialogic literary gatherings: A systematic review of evidence to overcome social and educational inequalities
citation: Ruiz-Eugenio, L., Soler-Gallart, M., Racionero-Plaza, S., & Padrós, M. (2023). Dialogic literary gatherings: A systematic review of evidence to overcome social and educational inequalities. Educational Research Review, 39, 100534. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2023.100534
title: Dialogic learning framework with seven principles underpinning DLGs
description: The review frames DLGs within dialogic learning (Flecha, 2000), an intersubjective, dialogic account of learning drawing on Bakhtin, Bruner, Freire, Mead, and Vygotsky. Flecha defined "the seven principles of DL", beginning with egalitarian dialogue in which "Participants' contributions are considered according to the validity of their arguments instead of their positions of power", followed by cultural intelligence, transformation, the instrumental dimension, creation of meaning, solidarity, and equality of differences. The review uses this framework both to define eligible studies and to organize its seven impact categories.
requirements: DLGs must be based on Flecha's principles of dialogic learning, which was the review's inclusion criterion
constraints: The review only covers evidence from gatherings based on Flecha's principles of dialogic learning, excluding other types of literary gatherings and dialogic learning environments
target_learners: children, adolescents, and adults across primary, secondary, high, special, and adult schools, family and community education, foster care, and prisons
target_learning_goals: critical thinking through dialogic interaction
collective construction of meaning from universal literature
instrumental learning of knowledge and skills
examples: DLG sessions in which participants choose passages from works such as The Odyssey or Crime and Punishment and argue agreements based on validity claims
key_sources: Ruiz-Eugenio, L., Soler-Gallart, M., Racionero-Plaza, S., & Padrós, M. (2023). Dialogic literary gatherings: A systematic review of evidence to overcome social and educational inequalities. Educational Research Review, 39, 100534. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2023.100534

article_title: Dialogic literary gatherings: A systematic review of evidence to overcome social and educational inequalities
citation: Ruiz-Eugenio, L., Soler-Gallart, M., Racionero-Plaza, S., & Padrós, M. (2023). Dialogic literary gatherings: A systematic review of evidence to overcome social and educational inequalities. Educational Research Review, 39, 100534. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2023.100534
title: Dialogic Literary Gathering as an educational action and learning environment
description: A DLG is "an educational action and learning environment based on the collective construction of meaning and knowledge through reading and dialogue the best universal literary works". Participants choose a classic work, agree on pages to read, and in weekly one-to-two-hour sessions share selected fragments, explaining why they chose them and giving reasons for agreeing or disagreeing, while the teacher chairs so everyone can speak. Originating in 1979–80 at La Verneda-Sant Martí School for Adults in Barcelona, DLGs are now applied in more than 10,000 schools and other educative and social settings in Europe and Latin America.
requirements: selection of high-quality universal literary works or adaptations
a teacher or moderator who chairs the discussion so that everyone has a chance to speak
participants read agreed pages before the session and choose passages to share
target_learners: preschool, primary, secondary, special education, and adult learners, families, and prison inmates
target_learning_goals: reading and dialogue about universal literature
communicative and argumentative skills
examples: weekly DLGs reading Oliver Twist in a foster care centre, and online DLGs during COVID-19 confinement

article_title: Why do we know so little about the factors associated with gifted underachievement? A systematic literature review
citation: White, Sonia, Graham, Linda, & Blaas, Sabrina (2018). Why do we know so little about the factors associated with gifted underachievement? A systematic literature review. Educational Research Review, 24, pp. 55-66. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2018.03.001
title: Use individually referenced benchmarks, not researcher-determined cut-offs, when identifying gifted underachievement
description: This principle holds that identification of gifted underachievement should compare a student's achievement to their own expected achievement based on cognitive ability, rather than to an arbitrary group cut-off set by researchers. The review argues researcher-determined benchmarks are "conceptually inconsistent with the discrepancy model" and can misclassify capable students. It recommends designs aligned with the discrepancy model that underpins the definition of gifted underachievement.
requirements: Studies must report both a cognitive ability measure and an achievement measure so an individual discrepancy can be computed
constraints: The review notes only three of nine reviewed studies used individually referenced benchmarks; the approach assumes gifted students' characteristics can vary across domains
target_learners: intellectually gifted elementary and secondary school students
target_learning_goals: accurate identification of gifted underachievement for research and support
examples: Dixon et al. (2006), Obergriesser and Stoeger (2015) and Stoeger et al. (2008) identified underachievers whose achievement was more than one standard deviation below their own expected achievement based on cognitive ability score
key_sources: White, Sonia, Graham, Linda, & Blaas, Sabrina (2018). Why do we know so little about the factors associated with gifted underachievement? A systematic literature review. Educational Research Review, 24, pp. 55-66. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2018.03.001

article_title: Personalization through adaptivity or adaptability? A meta-analysis on simulation-based learning in higher education
citation: Chernikova, O., Sommerhoff, D., Stadler, M., Holzberger, D., Nickl, M., Seidel, T., Kasneci, E., Küchemann, S., Kuhn, J., Fischer, F., & Heitzmann, N. (2025). Personalization through adaptivity or adaptability? A meta-analysis on simulation-based learning in higher education. Educational Research Review 46 (2025) 100662. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2024.100662
title: Adaptivity–adaptability framework for personalization of simulation-based learning
description: The article organizes personalization by decision-making authority: adaptivity is "a modification made by a computer", where the system identifies learner characteristics and tailors support, whereas adaptability "pertains to systems that human actors, including the learners themselves, can adjust", e.g. via a hint button. The framework links this distinction to the Plass and Pawar (2020) adaptivity framework and Kucirkova et al.'s (2021) personalization forms, and applies it to two personalization targets: scaffolding (amount, timing, type of prompts) and task progression (order of tasks), each of which can be adaptive, adaptable, mixed, or non-personalized. Theoretical mechanisms draw on self-regulated learning and self-determination theory (positive expectations) and cognitive load theory (negative expectations).
requirements: Realizing adaptivity requires an accurate learner model, which entails data collection and interpretation within the simulation
constraints: Learner models with even 80–90% accuracy may lead to sub-optimal personalization; adaptability may increase extraneous cognitive load especially for learners with low prior knowledge
target_learners: higher education students learning complex skills
target_learning_goals: complex skills such as diagnosing, decision-making, problem solving, and planning

The categories emerged from the data analysis rather than being imposed a priori, and they describe distinct ways of structuring dramatic activity in teacher education to provoke critical reflection on equity and diversity.

article_title: Using think-aloud protocol in self-regulated reading research
citation: Hu, Jingjing; Gao, Xuesong (Andy). (2017). Using think-aloud protocol in self-regulated reading research. Educational Research Review, v.22, pp. 181-193. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2017.09.004
title: Think-aloud protocol validity framework: reactivity and veridicality as the two central methodological concerns
description: The review organizes methodological concerns about think-aloud protocols around two constructs. Reactivity "concerns whether reporting cognitive/metacognitive processes alters the processes being reported (e.g., reading process) and/or its outcomes (e.g., comprehension or remembering of reading texts)", while veridicality "concerns whether the cognitive/metacognitive processes can be accurately and completely reported". The framework explains why design choices like training and prompting involve trade-offs: solutions to one concern may create risks for the other, a dilemma the authors highlight for self-regulated reading research.
requirements: Researchers must consider reactive effects when participants produce metacognitive verbal reports during reading tasks
Design choices must balance reactivity reduction against veridicality risks
constraints: Reactive effects are moderated by type of report, language of verbal report or learning task, and age of participants
Individual readers may no longer be conscious of habitual metacognitive processes, making them impossible to verbalize
target_learners: Researchers of self-regulated reading across educational levels
target_learning_goals: Accurate measurement of cognitive and metacognitive reading processes
examples: The review analyzed six experimental studies (Set 1) examining reactivity and veridicality and 23 studies using think-aloud as data collection
key_sources: Hu, Jingjing; Gao, Xuesong (Andy). (2017). Using think-aloud protocol in self-regulated reading research. Educational Research Review, v.22, pp. 181-193. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2017.09.004

article_title: Using think-aloud protocol in self-regulated reading research
citation: Hu, Jingjing; Gao, Xuesong (Andy). (2017). Using think-aloud protocol in self-regulated reading research. Educational Research Review, v.22, pp. 181-193. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2017.09.004
title: Treat think-aloud data as indicators of only part of the self-regulated reading process and triangulate with other data sources
description: Because think-aloud protocols face reactivity and veridicality risks, the review recommends that researchers "view think-aloud data as indicators of only a part of self-regulated reading process rather than a full picture of it". One or more other data sources — pre- and post-interviews, questionnaires, observations, on-line computer logs, and eye-movement registration — should be combined with think-aloud reports for a fuller picture. The review also recommends reporting details such as languages used for reading and verbalizing and participant ages.
requirements: Combine think-aloud with at least one other data collection tool
Provide detailed descriptions of participant demographics and task design in studies using think-aloud
constraints: The optimal integration of data sources is not yet identified and requires further research
target_learners: Researchers studying self-regulated reading and learning processes
target_learning_goals: Valid and complete measurement of self-regulated reading processes
examples: The review's Appendix III lists suggested solutions including combining data sources and viewing think-aloud as partial indicators

article_title: Keep the hands in mind: A meta-analysis of correlations between fine motor skills and reading, writing, mathematics, and cognitive development in children and adolescents
citation: Sebastian P. Suggate, Viktoria L. Karle, Tanja Kipfelsberger, Heidrun Stoeger. (2025). Keep the hands in mind: A meta-analysis of correlations between fine motor skills and reading, writing, mathematics, and cognitive development in children and adolescents. Educational Research Review 49 (2025) 100748. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2025.100748
title: Four contrasting theoretical accounts of FMS–academic-cognitive links: amodal, maturation, functionalism, and shared processes
description: The article organises the fragmented theoretical literature into four contrasting accounts. Amodal theories see FMS as "simply the executors of centrally informed intentions" predicting no offline links; maturation attributes correlations to age variance; functionalism claims FMS "provide unique opportunities to engage in skillful actions that benefit academic learning"; and shared processes holds that FMS and cognitive skills draw on common neural and behavioural processes, including the nimble-hands nimble-minds hypothesis. The meta-analysis was designed to test these accounts against each other.
requirements: Correlational data covering FMS, academic skills, and cognitive skills simultaneously, enabling MASEM tests of direct versus mediated paths
constraints: The authors state their analyses "are certainly not sufficient for a final conclusion, especially since many of the theoretical approaches overlap"
target_learning_goals: reading
writing
mathematics
cognitive development
examples: The meta-analysis tested amodal predictions via moderator control, maturation via age moderation, and functionalism versus shared processes via MASEM mediation comparison

description: A systematically assembled corpus of correlational studies linking fine motor skills to academic-cognitive skills in children aged 3–16, identified from 21,225 search hits across five databases and coded with interrater reliability of IRR = .98. It comprises 118 articles, 143 samples, and 1110 effect sizes, mostly cross-sectional (71.5%) and peer-reviewed (88.2%), with samples averaging 7.16 years (SD = 2.59). All meta-analytic data, analysis code, and coding materials are shared on OSF.

article_title: Embodied learning and teaching approaches in language education: A mixed studies review
citation: Sofia Jusslin, Kaisa Korpinen, Niina Lilja, Rose Martin, Johanna Lehtinen-Schnabel, Eeva Anttila. (2022). Embodied learning and teaching approaches in language education: A mixed studies review. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2022.100480
title: Two-strand taxonomy of embodied learning in language education: orchestrated embodied teaching versus embodied learning in naturally occurring interactions
description: The review organizes the empirical literature into two strands: "embodied learning through orchestrating embodied language learning and teaching", and "embodied learning in naturally occurring language learning interactions". The first strand covers designed interventions and activities where teachers deliberately orchestrate bodily engagement; the second covers analyses of embodiment arising in ordinary classroom and interactional language use. L1, L2, and FL studies were identified within both strands, making this the review's central organizing axis for RQ1.
requirements: Studies must theoretically use an embodied framework for learning and teaching, not merely mention embodiment
constraints: Taxonomy derived from studies published 1990–2020 in English, Swedish, Finnish, Norwegian, and Danish; signed languages excluded
target_learners: learners across preschool, primary, secondary, higher, adult, and non-formal language education
target_learning_goals: first, second, and foreign language learning and teaching
examples: The review's thematic analysis grouped all 41 studies under these two strands, with different characteristics of embodied learning distinguished within each

citation: Sofia Jusslin, Kaisa Korpinen, Niina Lilja, Rose Martin, Johanna Lehtinen-Schnabel, Eeva Anttila. (2022). Embodied learning and teaching approaches in language education: A mixed studies review. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2022.100480
title: Embodied learning as holistic engagement: bodily engagement beyond motor action, grounded in 4E cognition
description: The review defines embodied learning as "a conception of learning where learners are holistically engaged and intertwined in their social and material surroundings", rooted in the embodied turn and phenomenology. Drawing on Barsalou's grounded/4E cognition account, it argues embodied activity goes beyond visible movement to include inner bodily sensations and physiological changes, and proposes that "embodied learning extends beyond learning through movement and that a more suitable term for learning through motor action could be bodily learning". This framework underpins the review's analysis and its openness to multiple theoretical perspectives.
requirements: Understanding cognition as embodied connecting brain, body, and environment, rather than a modular brain-bound view
constraints: The review contests the claim that all learning is embodied simply because the brain is part of the body, requiring more detailed argumentation
target_learners: language learners from early childhood to adulthood
target_learning_goals: language learning and teaching understood as an embodied process
examples: The review distinguishes embodied learning from kinesthetic learning, which it describes as pedagogical practices emphasizing sensory (kinesthetic) experiences generated through bodily activity

article_title: Self-regulated learning strategies in continuing education: A systematic review and meta-analysis
citation: Yvonne M. Hemmler, Dirk Ifenthaler. (2024). Self-regulated learning strategies in continuing education: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2024.100629
title: Four-category framework of factors associated with SRL strategies in continuing education
description: The article organizes the factors associated with learners' use of SRL strategies in continuing education into four inductively derived categories. Factors were "inductively extracted from the primary studies and assigned to one of the following four main categories: learning process-related, learner-related, CE-related, or work-related factors." Learning process-related factors cover behavior, motivational states, and performance during a CE activity; learner-related factors cover general dispositions and beliefs; CE-related factors cover instructional characteristics and learner perceptions; work-related factors cover job characteristics and the work environment. The framework structures both the narrative synthesis and the meta-analyses.
requirements: Empirical primary studies that report an empirical measure of SRL strategies in relation to other variables in a CE context
constraints: Learners with disabilities were excluded from the evidence base
Only studies published in English in peer-reviewed journals were included
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning strategy use in continuing education

article_title: The connection between the social network perspective and teacher professional development: A systematic literature review
citation: Coppe, T., Thomas, L., Strijbos, J.-W., & Vanderlinde, R. (2026). The connection between the social network perspective and teacher professional development: A systematic literature review. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2026.100818
title: Integrated conceptual model of four rationales connecting the social network perspective and teacher professional development
description: The review proposes an integrated conceptual model organizing how empirical studies connect the social network perspective and TPD. From 51 studies, thematic analysis yielded "four distinct rationales for connecting the social network perspective and TPD": the network as a source of TPD, as a catalyst for enactment and sustainability of reforms with TPD, as purposefully (re)shaped by professional development initiatives, and as a (latent) school capacity for teacher and school development. The model gives researchers "conceptual clarity to situate their own work within the different theoretical rationales" and helps practitioners and policy-makers understand the different roles teacher networks can play.
requirements: Empirical studies using a social network perspective in relation to TPD, restricted to on-site primary and secondary school teacher networks
constraints: Excludes online/digital social networks, higher education, and conceptual or review studies; covers publications 2000–2024
target_learning_goals: teacher professional development understood as growth in work-related knowledge, skills and attitudes through formal or informal dynamics
examples: The model was built from a two-stage analysis: a 12-item data extraction table followed by iterative deductive and inductive thematic coding of the 51 included studies

article_title: Change in team learning behaviours in work teams – A systematic review
citation: Andreas Widmann, Regina H. Mulder. (2025). Change in team learning behaviours in work teams – A systematic review. Educational Research Review 49. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2025.100736
title: Four-type taxonomy of behavioural change in team learning behaviours: dynamics, pattern, development, and minor change
description: The review defines four types of change in team learning behaviours, distinguished by the shape of the sequence of increases and decreases. Dynamics is "a sequence of increases and/or decreases in frequency, duration, intensity, or quality of team learning behaviours in a chaotic way without any regularity". Patterns are repetitive sequences, development is a sequence of major increases possibly with minor decreases, and minor change is a sequence of minor increases and/or decreases. The taxonomy was built from the theoretical framework and used to categorise the findings of the 15 included studies.
requirements: Longitudinal data with repeated measurement of team learning behaviours to distinguish the types of change
constraints: Precise definitions and clear distinctions were largely lacking in prior research, so the definitions are the review's own alignment
target_learners: members of natural work teams in organisations
target_learning_goals: understanding and fostering change in team learning behaviours over time
examples: The review classified the results of eight quantitative and seven qualitative studies into the four change categories

citation: Andreas Widmann, Regina H. Mulder. (2025). Change in team learning behaviours in work teams – A systematic review. Educational Research Review 49. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2025.100736
title: Seven primary team learning behaviours framework used to categorise change
description: The review adopts the framework of seven primary team learning behaviours: knowledge sharing, constructive conflict, co-construction, boundary crossing, team activity, team reflexivity, and storage and retrieval. These are forms of social interaction between team members while accomplishing work tasks, such as "giving feedback, sharing, storing and retrieving knowledge, jointly reflecting on work strategies, and communicating with individuals outside the team". The seven behaviours served as the categories in the narrative synthesis of the included studies.

constraints: The review focuses on single team learning behaviours separately rather than combinations or sequences
target_learners: members of natural work teams in organisations
target_learning_goals: understanding which team learning behaviours change over time and relate to outcomes
examples: The synthesis categorised study variables such as sharing, reflection, boundary spanning, and asking for feedback under these seven behaviours

article_title: A systematic review of the role of dialogic leadership: Characterization and impacts
citation: Shiza Khaqan, Gisela Redondo-Sama. (2024). A systematic review of the role of dialogic leadership: Characterization and impacts. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2024.100618
title: Dialogic leadership: a leadership framework in which community members develop leadership practices through egalitarian dialogue
description: Dialogic leadership is an educational leadership approach grounded in the dialogic framework, in which teachers, students, family members, volunteers and other stakeholders engage in dialogue to achieve common goals and, through that interaction, develop leadership practices. The review characterizes it as egalitarian and social-justice oriented, contrasting it with hierarchical models such as instructional leadership: "in dialogic leadership, the leadership role can be taken on by any community member (Padr´os & Flecha, 2014)". It was conceptualized from the INCLUD-ED project, from which Successful Educational Actions such as interactive groups were identified.
requirements: Dialogue among all participants of the educational community, with equal importance given to each individual's contribution regardless of role or education level
constraints: The review reports the approach is still in early stages of research expansion, with all included studies qualitative
target_learning_goals: inclusive quality education
reducing inequalities in education
community participation in school transformation
examples: Interactive groups in which children interact through dialogue on subject-related activities under volunteer guidance, one of the Successful Educational Actions identified in INCLUD-ED

article_title: Recalibrating impact in STEM education: Empirical benchmarks for interpreting intervention effects
citation: Mehmet Bicakci, Heidrun Stoeger, Diana Wengler, Albert Ziegler. (2026). Recalibrating impact in STEM education: Empirical benchmarks for interpreting intervention effects. Educational Research Review 52. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2026.100803
title: Interpret STEM education intervention effects against empirically derived, context-sensitive benchmark distributions rather than Cohen's universal thresholds
description: The article argues that labeling an effect small, medium, or large with inherited conventions is insufficient because STEM effect distributions vary by field, intervention type, outcome domain, and valence. It states researchers "should instead interpret effects relative to benchmark distributions that reflect the relevant field, intervention type, and outcome orientation." The study supplies the benchmark tables that make this possible.
requirements: Researchers need access to benchmark distributions for the relevant STEM field, intervention category, outcome domain, and valence orientation.
constraints: Benchmarks reflect prior review decisions and reporting practices; subgroup coverage is uneven, with engineering, technology, collaborative learning, and nonacademic outcomes sparse.
Adjusted benchmarks are more conservative estimates, not definitive population values.
target_learning_goals: Accurate interpretation of the practical significance of STEM intervention effect sizes
examples: The study derived quartile benchmarks from 95 meta-analyses and 5,956 effect sizes, showing raw overall quartiles of 0.21, 0.48, and 0.86 that fell after bias adjustment.

article_title: Exploration of domains of educational purpose in K-12 data literacy education research
citation: Fagerlund, J., Palsa, L., & Mertala, P. (2025). Exploration of domains of educational purpose in K-12 data literacy education research. Educational Research Review, 46, Article 100663. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2024.100663
title: Biesta's three domains of educational purpose (qualification, socialization, subjectification) as an organizing framework for data literacy education
description: The review applies Gert Biesta's (2009) account of "good education" to K-12 data literacy education, treating education as impacting three interconnected domains: qualification (equipping individuals with knowledge, skills, and dispositions), socialization (becoming part of social orders), and subjectification (becoming the subject of one's own life). The framework is used deductively to code 611 purpose expressions and inductively to map themes and their intersections. The review states the domains are "unique but also interconnected, and the effectiveness of education lies in how they intersect".
requirements: Purpose expressions in source literature must be sufficiently clear to code against the three domains; the review accepted only sufficiently clear arguments regarding educational purposes
constraints: The framework does not provide clear themes usable with minimal interpretation when operationalized in a new domain, which the authors say justified consensus-building coding
Conflicts between domains are possible; subjectification is described as the opposite of socialization in encouraging non-conformity
target_learning_goals: Data literacy education purposes spanning skills, social integration, and self-determination in data-rich contexts
examples: The review coded 611 expressions from 77 studies against the three domains and their intersecting areas, producing themes such as data competencies under qualification

citation: Fagerlund, J., Palsa, L., & Mertala, P. (2025). Exploration of domains of educational purpose in K-12 data literacy education research. Educational Research Review, 46, Article 100663. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2024.100663
title: Four macro strands of educational purpose in K-12 data literacy education: coping, training and studying, personal value, and critical engagement
description: To connect the themes produced by its analysis, the review discerns four thematic macro strands of DLE purpose: coping in data-intensive contexts, data-related training and studying, finding personal value in data, and critical engagement with data (fication). Each strand bundles themes positioned within and across Biesta's three domains; for example, data competencies can be ends in themselves or prerequisites for professional qualifications. The review notes that "Some themes may have additional relevance to others in intricate ways" and that not all relationships are theorized systematically.
requirements: Themes must first be produced by analysis of expressed educational purposes before being (re)positioned into macro strands
constraints: The authors state relationships among themes are not theorized systematically due to their potentially immense amount and nature
target_learning_goals: Understanding the range of educational purposes data literacy education can serve
examples: Fig. 3 depicts the macro strands as discerned from the themes and their relationships, e.g., reaching personal goals may involve acquiring professional qualifications

article_title: Exploration of domains of educational purpose in K-12 data literacy education research
citation: Fagerlund, J., Palsa, L., & Mertala, P. (2025). Exploration of domains of educational purpose in K-12 data literacy education research. Educational Research Review, 46, Article 100663. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2024.100663
title: Two broad approaches to data literacy: disciplinary data-science-anchored versus socio-technical and critical perspectives
description: The review distinguishes two broad approaches to data literacy: one anchored in the disciplinary paradigm of data science, statistics, and informatics, treating literacy instrumentally as a subject-object relationship in which the human learns to master data; and a more socio-technically oriented perspective that accounts for data's pervasive presence and its personal and societal implications. The latter includes "critical data literacy", which the review characterizes as "not a judgmental or negativistic attitude, but a reflective and a questioning approach". The review argues data literacy should build upon other literacies rather than replace them.
requirements: Conceptualizations of data literacy vary in relation to social, technological, and cultural contexts
constraints: The review notes theorization of data literacy is still ongoing
target_learning_goals: Both skill-centric and reflective, self-determination-oriented competencies in data-intensive contexts
examples: The review cites definitions such as an ability to collect, manage, evaluate, and apply data in a critical manner (Ridsdale et al., 2015) for the disciplinary approach
key_sources: Fagerlund, J., Palsa, L., & Mertala, P. (2025). Exploration of domains of educational purpose in K-12 data literacy education research. Educational Research Review, 46, Article 100663. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2024.100663

article_title: Exploration of domains of educational purpose in K-12 data literacy education research
citation: Fagerlund, J., Palsa, L., & Mertala, P. (2025). Exploration of domains of educational purpose in K-12 data literacy education research. Educational Research Review, 46, Article 100663. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2024.100663
title: Corpus of 77 peer-reviewed K-12 data literacy education studies yielding 611 purpose expressions
description: The review's final corpus comprises 77 peer-reviewed journal articles and conference papers on K-12 data literacy education, identified through multi-database keyword searching, cleaning, two-stage screening, and a snowball search of prior reviews. From these studies the authors collected "argumentation and justification of its educational goals, intents, and/or purposes were gathered (total: 611 expressions in the 77 studies)", drawn from the early and final sections of IMRaD-structured articles. The corpus is the empirical basis for all thematic findings.
requirements: Included studies had to use the term data literacy within a K-12 or general-education context and be written in English
constraints: Book chapters, dissertations, editorials, and non-K-12 contexts (e.g., medicine, higher education) were excluded
target_learning_goals: Mapping expressed educational purposes of data literacy education
examples: Search stages included identification, cleaning in Zotero, cursory screening, content screening, and an additional snowball search revisiting prior reviews

citation: Aleknavičiūtė, V., Lehtinen, E., & Södervik, I. (2023). Thirty years of conceptual change research in biology – A review and meta-analysis of intervention studies. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2023.100556
title: Conceptual change theory landscape: Posner's conditions model most used in biology interventions, alongside Vosniadou's framework theory and Chi's ontological shift
description: The review organises intervention studies by the conceptual change theory each builds on, coding papers into 14 framework groups (Posner, Chi, Vosniadou, diSessa, Carey, Driver, Nussbaum and Novick, Clement, Klein, Duit, Pintrich, Sinatra, multidimensional CC theory, and no CC theory). Posner's theory, which holds that learners must be "dissatisfied with existing conceptions and view scientific concepts as meaningful, plausible and fruitful", was the most frequently cited basis for biology interventions. Vosniadou's and Chi's theories were used equally frequently, with Chi's ontological shift theory particularly common in evolution interventions and usually combined with other theories. Nineteen studies referenced no conceptual change theory at all.
requirements: Interventions applying these theories should make learners aware of the conflict between prior thinking and new concepts, as the theory theories prescribe
constraints: Chi's ontological shift theory was more often combined with other CC theories than used as the sole basis for interventions
19 intervention studies did not refer to any specific theory of conceptual change
target_learners: kindergarten through university students, including natural science majors and student teachers
target_learning_goals: restructuring of biological misconceptions toward scientifically accepted understanding
examples: The review coded all 96 articles by theoretical framework and found Posner's theory applied across topics from climate change to genetics and respiration, with populations from lower secondary to college students.
key_sources: Aleknavičiūtė, V., Lehtinen, E., & Södervik, I. (2023). Thirty years of conceptual change research in biology – A review and meta-analysis of intervention studies. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2023.100556

article_title: Thirty years of conceptual change research in biology – A review and meta-analysis of intervention studies
citation: Aleknavičiūtė, V., Lehtinen, E., & Södervik, I. (2023). Thirty years of conceptual change research in biology – A review and meta-analysis of intervention studies. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2023.100556
title: Distinction between knowledge enrichment and knowledge restructuring as two outcome types in conceptual change research
description: The review adopts the field's core distinction between two types of conceptual change. Knowledge enrichment is learning in which "new knowledge is simply added to existing knowledge structures, enriching the knowledge base", whereas knowledge restructuring (also called revision) is "a more demanding process that requires fundamental changes and restructuring of one's existing knowledge structures", in which existing concepts may take on new meanings and misconceptions are revised. The distinction grounds the review's coding of outcome-measure quality and its finding that many studies capture only enrichment. Either multiple-choice or open-ended formats can capture either type; what matters is deliberate item design.
requirements: Assessing restructuring with multiple-choice items requires deliberately planned items systematically comparing correct scientific concepts with widely held misconceptions, complemented by open-ended questions
constraints: The data collection method alone does not determine which type of conceptual change is captured
target_learners: learners at all educational levels studied, from kindergarten to university
target_learning_goals: distinguishing genuine restructuring of scientific concepts from simple addition of facts
examples: The review coded each study's outcome measures as enrichment or restructuring, resolving coder disagreements through discussion until inter-rater reliability reached 100%.

article_title: Studies of expansive learning: Foundations, findings and future challenges
citation: Engeström, Y., Sannino, A. (2010). Studies of expansive learning: Foundations, findings and future challenges. Educational Research Review, 5. https://www.sciencedirect.com/journal/educational-research-review
title: Teoria ekspansywnego uczenia się jako trzecia metafora wykraczająca poza przyswajanie i uczestnictwo
description: Teoria ekspansywnego uczenia się (Engeström, 1987), zakorzeniona w kulturowo-historycznej teorii działalności Wygotskiego, Leontjewa, Iljenkowa i Dawidowa, wraz z ideami Batesona i Bachtina, utrzymuje, że uczenie się nie jest ani przyswajaniem, ani uczestnictwem, lecz rozszerzaniem: „teoria ekspansywnego uczenia się musi bazować na własnej metaforze, a mianowicie na poszerzeniu”. Uczący się wspólnie tworzą i wdrażają nowe obiekty i koncepcje dla ich kolektywnej działalności. Przegląd redefiniuje strefę najbliższego rozwoju Wygotskiego jako zbiorową odległość między codziennymi działaniami a historycznie nową formą działalności.
requirements: Analiza musi być wielowymiarowa, obejmująca to, czy uczenie się utrwala czy przekształca kulturę, ruch pionowy czy poziomy oraz przyswajanie/uczestnictwo czy formowanie pojęć teoretycznych
constraints: Artykuł argumentuje, że dychotomia przyswajanie–uczestnictwo Sfard prowadzi do nadmiernych uproszczeń i że teoria nie mieści się w żadnej z tych metafor
target_learners: społeczności i sieci praktyków w miejscach pracy i organizacjach
target_learning_goals: kolektywne przekształcanie obiektów i form wspólnej działalności
examples: Przykłady otwierające: pracownicy opieki społecznej w Helsinkach wspierający starszych klientów w domu oraz biblioteka uniwersytecka w Helsinkach redefiniująca swoje usługi dla naukowców
key_sources: Engeström, Y., Sannino, A. (2010). Studies of expansive learning: Foundations, findings and future challenges. Educational Research Review, 5. https://www.sciencedirect.com/journal/educational-research-review

article_title: Studies of expansive learning: Foundations, findings and future challenges
citation: Engeström, Y., Sannino, A. (2010). Studies of expansive learning: Foundations, findings and future challenges. Educational Research Review, 5. https://www.sciencedirect.com/journal/educational-research-review
title: Cykl ekspansywnego uczenia się jako sekwencja działań uczenia się od kwestionowania do konsolidacji
description: Cykl ekspansywny modeluje kolektywne uczenie się jako sekwencję działań poznawczych: kwestionowanie, analiza (historyczno-genetyczna i faktyczno-empiryczna), modelowanie nowego związku, badanie modelu, wdrażanie go, a następnie refleksja i konsolidacja w nową stabilną formę praktyki. Artykuł podkreśla, że „cykl ekspansywnego uczenia się nie jest uniwersalną formułą poszczególnych faz i etapów”, lecz heurystycznym narzędziem opartym na przejściu od abstrakcji do konkretu, testowanym i wzbogacanym przy każdym użyciu.
requirements: Punkt początkowy cyklu to moment, w którym kwestionowany jest stabilny wzorzec działalności; punkt końcowy to moment, w którym nowy wzorzec jest konsolidowany
constraints: Artykuł stwierdza, że żaden rzeczywisty kolektywny proces prawdopodobnie nie podąża wyraźnie za wzorcowym modelem
target_learners: kolektywy, takie jak zespoły nauczycieli, grupy pracowników i sieci organizacyjne
target_learning_goals: generowanie i konsolidacja nowej, historycznie nowej formy działalności
examples: Model rozszerza sześć działań uczenia się Dawydowa, dodając krytyczne kwestionowanie oraz wdrażanie i konsolidację rzeczywistych, kulturowo nowych praktyk

article_title: Beyond inquiry or direct instruction: Pressing issues for designing impactful science learning opportunities
citation: Ton de Jong, Ard W. Lazonder, Clark A. Chinn, Frank Fischer, Janice Gobert, Cindy E. Hmelo-Silver, Ken R. Koedinger, Joseph S. Krajcik, Eleni A. Kyza, Marcia C. Linn, Margus Pedaste, Katharina Scheiter, Zacharias C. Zacharia. (2024). Beyond inquiry or direct instruction: Pressing issues for designing impactful science learning opportunities. Educational Research Review, 44. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2024.100623
title: Inquiry-based learning is grounded in both cognitive (knowledge-integration, generative learning) and sociocultural theories
description: The article argues inquiry-based instruction is not theory-free: cognitive theories explain its success through "the active integration of knowledge," generative learning activities, and schema (re)construction, while sociocultural theory treats learning as "changes in patterns of participation in social activity" supported by scaffolds, tools, and collaborative engagement with meaningful tasks. Together these accounts explain why guided inquiry fosters deep conceptual knowledge and motivation, and they guide the design of instructional interventions.
requirements: Cognitive effort must stay within learners' cognitive capacities, supported by scaffolds and guidance.
target_learning_goals: Deep conceptual knowledge in science domains
Scientific inquiry practices
examples: The article cites Eysink et al. (2009) as a cognitive explanation and traces the sociocultural line to Rousseau, Dewey, and Vygotsky.
key_sources: Ton de Jong, Ard W. Lazonder, Clark A. Chinn, Frank Fischer, Janice Gobert, Cindy E. Hmelo-Silver, Ken R. Koedinger, Joseph S. Krajcik, Eleni A. Kyza, Marcia C. Linn, Margus Pedaste, Katharina Scheiter, Zacharias C. Zacharia. (2024). Beyond inquiry or direct instruction: Pressing issues for designing impactful science learning opportunities. Educational Research Review, 44. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2024.100623

article_title: Beyond inquiry or direct instruction: Pressing issues for designing impactful science learning opportunities
citation: Ton de Jong, Ard W. Lazonder, Clark A. Chinn, Frank Fischer, Janice Gobert, Cindy E. Hmelo-Silver, Ken R. Koedinger, Joseph S. Krajcik, Eleni A. Kyza, Marcia C. Linn, Margus Pedaste, Katharina Scheiter, Zacharias C. Zacharia. (2024). Beyond inquiry or direct instruction: Pressing issues for designing impactful science learning opportunities. Educational Research Review, 44. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2024.100623
title: Select and orchestrate instructional strategies based on contextual factors rather than declaring one method superior
description: The article's central position is that "adequate instruction always involves different strategies, which should be thoughtfully selected based on contextual factors." Most real learning environments mix telling students things with opportunities to explore and invent; the key difference between methods is whether full explanation precedes investigation or students generate part of the content themselves. Designers and teachers should therefore orchestrate both approaches depending on topic, goal, student, teacher, and design.
requirements: Teachers need thorough training in the theoretical background of inquiry-based learning and its classroom implementation.
constraints: The distinction between direct instruction and guided inquiry is not always straightforward because student activity plays a role in both.
target_learners: Science students from elementary through secondary education
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding of science domains
examples: The article notes Open Science curricula and project-based programs contain "a rich mixture of telling students certain things and having them figure out other things."
