article_title: Exploring the dimensions of electronic work integrated learning (eWIL)
citation: Schuster, Lisa & Glavas, Charmaine (2017). Exploring the dimensions of electronic work integrated learning (eWIL). Educational Research Review, 21, pp. 55-66. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2017.04.001
title: Two-dimensional typology of eWIL: function of technology (support vs. deliver) by degree of technological involvement (low vs. high)
description: The review develops a typology classifying eWIL experiences along two dimensions: the function of the technology (supporting administrative WIL processes vs. delivering the WIL experience pedagogically) and the degree of technological involvement (low vs. high). Iterative open and pattern coding of 22 studies produced "four broad codes: "Technology-Supported", "Technology-Facilitated", "Technology-Blended" and "Technology-Based"", validated by independent recoding with no inconsistencies between researchers. The typology extends Kaider et al. (2009) by recognizing that technology can deliver, not just support, WIL.
requirements: Studies must be classifiable by both the function the technology serves in the WIL experience and the extent of technological involvement
constraints: The authors acknowledge that theoretically there are likely to be numerous attributes which may influence the implementation of the typology, and the study aimed to identify preliminary attributes rather than be exhaustive
target_learners: higher education students participating in work integrated learning
target_learning_goals: integrating theory with workplace practice
graduate employability
examples: Technology-Supported: a web-based portal for industry partners; Technology-Facilitated: digital platforms such as OpenSim used to prepare students; Technology-Blended: face-to-face placements combined with online role-plays; Technology-Based: WIL through virtual reality
key_sources: Schuster, Lisa & Glavas, Charmaine (2017). Exploring the dimensions of electronic work integrated learning (eWIL). Educational Research Review, 21, pp. 55-66. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2017.04.001

article_title: Exploring learning and fit in the transition from higher education to the labour market: A systematic review
citation: Grosemans, I., Coertjens, L., & Kyndt, E. (2017). Exploring learning and fit in the transition from higher education to the labour market: A systematic review. Educational Research Review, 21, 67-84. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2017.03.001
title: Four types of fit distinguish the higher-education-to-labour-market transition: vertical, horizontal, competence, and person-environment fit
description: The review organises the fit construct in the transition from higher education to the labour market as a four-part taxonomy. As the review states, "four types of fit are distinguished: vertical, horizontal, competence, and person-environment fit." This taxonomy structures how congruence between graduates' education and their work context is analysed in the reviewed literature, and it connects to findings that background characteristics influence fit and that fit relates to outcomes such as career progress.
requirements: The taxonomy presupposes a transition context in which a graduate's educational background can be compared with characteristics of the work context.
constraints: The supplied text presents the taxonomy as the review's organising distinction without printing definitions of each fit type.
target_learners: higher education students and recent graduates entering the labour market
target_learning_goals: understanding person-context congruence during the school-to-work transition
key_sources: Grosemans, I., Coertjens, L., & Kyndt, E. (2017). Exploring learning and fit in the transition from higher education to the labour market: A systematic review. Educational Research Review, 21, 67-84. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2017.03.001

article_title: Theoretical foundations and approaches in research on educational escape rooms: A systematic review
citation: Vorderobermeier, A., Abel, J., & Sailer, M. (2024). Theoretical foundations and approaches in research on educational escape rooms: A systematic review. Educational Research Review, 44, 100625. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2024.100625
title: Educational escape rooms as an instructional concept grounded in game methods adapted to learning goals
description: An educational escape room transfers the methods of a commercial escape room - "live action team-based games where players discover clues, solve puzzles, and accomplish tasks" (quoting Nicholson's definition) - to a learning context with a defined learning goal tailored to a target group. Puzzles and challenges align with curriculum content, often through a background story, creating authentic learning contexts that encourage meaningful activity and provide space for failure. Variants include pop-up rooms, puzzle boxes, puzzle hunts, serial stories, hybrid games, and virtual EERs. The review describes EERs as implemented in primary/secondary education, higher education, and professional development.
requirements: A defined learning goal tailored to a specific target group must be prioritized over the game mechanics alone
Time limits typically adjusted to fit within school hours or teaching units
constraints: The review restricts its analysis to formal educational settings and articles developed by lecturers rather than students
target_learning_goals: content knowledge
content-related and general skills
affective goals
examples: Bassford et al.'s 'CrashEd' embeds STEM subjects into a realistic criminal case
Around 79% of EERs are utilized in classrooms or laboratories, per Fotaris and Mastoras (2019)
key_sources: Vorderobermeier, A., Abel, J., & Sailer, M. (2024). Theoretical foundations and approaches in research on educational escape rooms: A systematic review. Educational Research Review, 44, 100625. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2024.100625

article_title: Theoretical foundations and approaches in research on educational escape rooms: A systematic review
citation: Vorderobermeier, A., Abel, J., & Sailer, M. (2024). Theoretical foundations and approaches in research on educational escape rooms: A systematic review. Educational Research Review, 44, 100625. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2024.100625
title: Six patterns of theoretical integration in EER research, from general statements to empirical validation
description: The review develops a six-category typology of how deeply EER articles integrate theory, classifying each of the 24 included articles along four dimensions: didactic considerations, implementation of a specific EER, theoretical foundation connected with didactic considerations, and empirical verification of the theoretical foundation. The patterns range from "general statements on theoretical grounding in EERs without connection to didactic considerations" through loose connections, combined theoretical-didactic treatments without a specific EER or without empirical validation, up to "theoretical grounding with empirical validation". Each pattern is labeled with the dominant category of its articles.
requirements: Articles must be classifiable on the four dimensions of didactic considerations, specific EER implementation, theory-didactics connection, and empirical verification
constraints: The typology was developed from only 24 articles that passed a strict theoretical-foundation screening criterion
target_learning_goals: understanding the theoretical integration of instructional design in EERs
examples: Abdul Rahim et al. (2022) exemplifies general statements without didactic connection, where SDT classification appeared only in the discussion without relating findings to it
Piñero (2020) exemplifies combining theoretical grounding and didactic considerations without empirical validation
key_sources: Vorderobermeier, A., Abel, J., & Sailer, M. (2024). Theoretical foundations and approaches in research on educational escape rooms: A systematic review. Educational Research Review, 44, 100625. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2024.100625

article_title: Theoretical foundations and approaches in research on educational escape rooms: A systematic review
citation: Vorderobermeier, A., Abel, J., & Sailer, M. (2024). Theoretical foundations and approaches in research on educational escape rooms: A systematic review. Educational Research Review, 44, 100625. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2024.100625
title: Debriefing as the structured consolidation phase of experiential learning in EERs
description: Within experiential learning in EERs, a sequenced debriefing phase operationalizes reflective observation and abstract conceptualization, and was "extensively discussed in seven articles" of the review. The emphasis lies in self-assessment and critical reflection on performance, re-expressing learning objectives, discussing emotions and approaches during the game, and providing feedback on cooperation and to game developers. Implementations may start with an outro video, prepared questions on learning objectives and team-based skills, and open-ended questions to initiate dialogue; Fotaris and Mastoras (2022) suggested the reflection phase take up approximately one-third of lesson time.
requirements: Learning objectives must be clearly expressed once again during debriefing
Reflection should be planned as a substantial share of lesson time (about one-third suggested)
constraints: Debriefing descriptions come from development/evaluation articles; the review reports no effect sizes for debriefing
target_learning_goals: consolidation of learning content
self-assessment and critical reflection
teamwork and communication skills
examples: Egan et al. (2021) mapped Kolb's four abilities of effective learners onto their EER, with sequenced debrief covering reflective observation, abstract conceptualization, and active experimentation
key_sources: Vorderobermeier, A., Abel, J., & Sailer, M. (2024). Theoretical foundations and approaches in research on educational escape rooms: A systematic review. Educational Research Review, 44, 100625. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2024.100625

article_title: Theoretical foundations and approaches in research on educational escape rooms: A systematic review
citation: Vorderobermeier, A., Abel, J., & Sailer, M. (2024). Theoretical foundations and approaches in research on educational escape rooms: A systematic review. Educational Research Review, 44, 100625. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2024.100625
title: Interweave theory, didactic instruction, and practice in future EER research and development
description: The review's central recommendation is that future EER research move beyond superficial name-dropping toward genuine interweaving of theoretical foundations with didactic decisions and practical implementation, because "the theoretical foundation in current research on EERs is weak". Studies like Veldkamp et al. (2022) and Hamilton et al. (2021), which empirically investigated whether and how a named theory (e.g., collaborative learning) is promoted in an EER, "can be particularly valuable for instructional decisions" and reveal mechanisms behind successful learning environments.
requirements: Research designs must connect a named theory to specific didactic decisions and measure the outcome empirically
constraints: The recommendation rests on only a few included studies reaching the empirical-validation pattern
target_learning_goals: understanding mechanisms behind successful learning environments with EERs
examples: Veldkamp et al. (2022) studied collaborative learning in an EER through pre/post-test, experience questionnaire, interviews, and classroom observation
Hamilton et al. (2021) formulated research hypotheses comparing linear and open path escape room settings

article_title: The impacts of open inquiry on students’ learning in science: A systematic literature review
citation: Muhamad Dah, N., Mat Noor, M. S. A., Kamarudin, M. Z., & Syed Abdul Azziz, S. S. (2024). The impacts of open inquiry on students' learning in science: A systematic literature review. Educational Research Review, 43. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2024.100601
title: Four-level model of inquiry teaching (confirmation, structured, guided, open)
description: The review organises inquiry-based science teaching around a four-level model established by Rezba et al. (2007), drawing on Schwab (1958) and Herron (1971). The levels differ by how much is given to students: "questions, procedures, and solutions are offered (confirmation inquiry); questions and processes are given to students (structured inquiry); questions are merely provided to students (guided inquiry); and students develop questions, procedures, and solutions (open inquiry)". Open inquiry is the fourth and highest level, in which students generate their own questions and design investigations, most closely following the work of actual scientists.
requirements: Requires students to develop their own questions, procedures, and solutions, with teacher support and classroom management
constraints: The review notes open inquiry is not a popular pedagogical practice due to challenges in relation to time and resources, and has rarely been implemented
target_learning_goals: Scientific inquiry skills
Conceptual understanding of science
examples: The review located 24 empirical studies of open inquiry across elementary, middle and high school levels, with high school students (ages 15–19) in 14 cases
key_sources: Muhamad Dah, N., Mat Noor, M. S. A., Kamarudin, M. Z., & Syed Abdul Azziz, S. S. (2024). The impacts of open inquiry on students' learning in science: A systematic literature review. Educational Research Review, 43. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2024.100601

article_title: Effectiveness of relationships and sex education: A systematic review of terminology, content, pedagogy, and outcomes
citation: van Leent, Lisa, Walsh, Kerryann, Moran, Claire, Hand, Kirstine, & French, Sally (2023). Effectiveness of relationships and sex education: A systematic review of terminology, content, pedagogy, and outcomes. Educational Research Review, 39, Article number: 100527. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2023.100527
title: A taxonomy of terminology for school-based relationships and sexuality education
description: The review presents a taxonomy of the terms used to describe school-based relationships and sexuality education, identifying terms including "sexuality education, sex education, holistic sexuality education, sexual and reproductive health, relationships and sex education, sexual health/education, comprehensive sex/sexual education/health education". It charts how often each term was defined and which sources (UNESCO, SIECUS, WHO, IPPF, author-defined) supplied definitions, concluding the terms used in the field are vast and inconsistently defined.
requirements: Studies must report the term used and a definition for the taxonomy to classify them
constraints: Applies to universal school-based RSE for children aged 4-18 published in English 2000-2020; excludes targeted cohorts and abstinence-only approaches
target_learning_goals: relationships and sexuality education
examples: The most frequently-defined term was sexuality education, defined in 9 of 33 clearly defined papers, drawing variously on UNESCO, SIECUS, and author-defined sources

citation: van Leent, Lisa, Walsh, Kerryann, Moran, Claire, Hand, Kirstine, & French, Sally (2023). Effectiveness of relationships and sex education: A systematic review of terminology, content, pedagogy, and outcomes. Educational Research Review, 39, Article number: 100527. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2023.100527
title: A taxonomy of teaching approaches used to deliver school-based RSE
description: The review classifies the pedagogical approaches reported in RSE studies into categories including multiple strategies, health promotion, delivery personnel, a suite of active learning pedagogies, cross-curriculum approaches, UNESCO guidance, philosophy/ethics, and sex/gender-based approaches. It reports a "striking lack of standardised use of pedagogical terms" and that detail explaining the approaches used was starkly missing, hindering replication and further testing.
requirements: Studies must describe their program approach for classification; the review argues reporting guidelines for RSE studies are needed
constraints: Only 38 of 134 studies provided approach information; 66 provided none
target_learning_goals: relationships and sexuality education
examples: Four studies espoused active learning pedagogies incorporating role-play, discussion, demonstrations, simulations and games; 11 studies used multiple strategies

article_title: Two decades of research on children's creativity development during primary education in relation to task characteristics
citation: O.T.A. Potters, T.J.P. van Schijndel, S. Jak, J. Voogt. (2023). Two decades of research on children's creativity development during primary education in relation to task characteristics. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2023.100532
title: A taxonomy of creativity tasks differentiating open- versus close-ended and integrating versus fragmenting tasks
description: The review introduces a taxonomy for mapping creativity tasks used in primary education research. It is "based on a broad conceptualization of creativity, and differentiates between open- and close-ended, and integrating and fragmenting creativity tasks", producing quadrants such as the open-ended fragmenting quadrant. The review also analyzes tasks by the domains of the stimulus and response. The taxonomy is offered as useful for clarifying discussions in creativity research and for designing creativity activities in educational practice.
requirements: Tasks must be classifiable on the two dimensions of open- versus close-ended and integrating versus fragmenting, and can additionally be characterized by stimulus and response domain.
target_learning_goals: creativity development
examples: The review used the taxonomy to classify the tasks in 52 studies, finding open-ended integrating and open-ended fragmenting tasks were frequently used.
key_sources: O.T.A. Potters, T.J.P. van Schijndel, S. Jak, J. Voogt. (2023). Two decades of research on children's creativity development during primary education in relation to task characteristics. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2023.100532

article_title: Two decades of research on children's creativity development during primary education in relation to task characteristics
citation: O.T.A. Potters, T.J.P. van Schijndel, S. Jak, J. Voogt. (2023). Two decades of research on children's creativity development during primary education in relation to task characteristics. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2023.100532
title: Corpus of 52 studies on creativity development in primary education analyzed descriptively and meta-analytically
description: The review's evidence base is a systematically assembled set of studies on children's creativity development in primary education in relation to task characteristics, published in the last 20 years. As the abstract states, "A total of 52 studies published in the last 20 years were systematically analyzed with a combination of descriptive analyses and meta-analyses." The corpus supported both descriptive characterization of task use and meta-analytic synthesis of developmental patterns.
requirements: Studies must concern children's creativity development during primary education and relate to task characteristics.
target_learning_goals: creativity development
examples: The corpus was analyzed with descriptive analyses of task characteristics and meta-analyses of developmental patterns.

article_title: Adolescent flourishing in a digitally connected world: A qualitative systematic review and meta-synthesis
citation: Gordon, C. S., Brake, N., Hammond, S. P., Picton, I., Notley, T., Rowston, K., Gutierrez, A., Basarkod, G., Costello, K., Gupta, M., West, M., & Dicke, T. (2025). Adolescent flourishing in a digitally connected world: A qualitative systematic review and meta-synthesis. Preprint. https://osf.io/j48k5/?view_only=8b6423082746439abb4106526e953aaf
title: Self-Determination Theory framework organising adolescent digital flourishing into autonomy, competence, and relatedness themes
description: The review uses Self-Determination Theory as the organising framework for synthesising adolescents' positive online experiences. "Guided by the tenets of Self-Determination Theory, the analysis generated ten subthemes organised under the core categories of autonomy, competence, and relatedness." SDT holds that individuals flourish when basic psychological needs for autonomy (agency and self-endorsed action), competence (mastery and effectiveness), and relatedness (connection and belonging) are met. The synthesis presents these dimensions as interconnected, displayed in a layered concept map showing fluid, overlapping relationships between subthemes.
requirements: Qualitative studies capturing adolescents' own narrative accounts, with at least two meaningful participant quotes
constraints: The review focuses on adolescents aged 12–19 and on positive experiences, explicitly not denying negative experiences but balancing a deficit-focused conversation
target_learning_goals: wellbeing and flourishing in digitally connected learning and social contexts

article_title: An integrative review of the cognitive costs and benefits of note-taking
citation: Jansen, R. S., Lakens, D., & IJsselsteijn, W. (2017). An integrative review of the cognitive costs and benefits of note-taking. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2017.10.001
title: Cognitive load framework of note-taking: five recursive processes whose load explains divergent encoding effects
description: The review proposes that note-taking is a multi-stage process in which a note-taker must "(1) comprehend the lecture material, (2) identify key points, (3) link the material to prior knowledge and prior notes, (4) paraphrase or summarize, and (5) transform to written form", performed recursively during a lecture. Because note-taking induces load beyond comprehension alone, it can overload some individuals in some situations and become detrimental. The framework links lecture structure, modality, speed, note-taking style and structure, and cognitive ability to load on specific phases, integrating the divergent empirical findings reviewed.
requirements: Applicable to individual (non-collaborative) note-taking in educational settings without note review, as scoped by the review's inclusion criteria
constraints: The review states further research is warranted to test the effects of note-taking on cognitive load, and that which effect of typing (resource savings versus shallower processing) is stronger should be explored in more detail
target_learners: students in primary, secondary, and higher education attending lectures
target_learning_goals: memory for lecture content
examples: The review uses the framework to explain why organised note-taking hurt memory with an audio lecture (Bui et al., 2013) but helped with a text (Bretzing & Kulhavy, 1979): with text, phases 2 and 3 can be performed sequentially rather than simultaneously with comprehension
key_sources: Jansen, R. S., Lakens, D., & IJsselsteijn, W. (2017). An integrative review of the cognitive costs and benefits of note-taking. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2017.10.001

article_title: Researchers under the spell of the arts: Two decades of using arts-based methods in community-based inquiry with vulnerable populations
citation: Sara Coemans, Karin Hannes. (2017). Researchers Under the Spell of the Arts: Two Decades of Using Arts-Based Methods in Community-Based Inquiry with Vulnerable Populations. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2017.08.003
title: Definition and classification framework for arts-based methods in community-based inquiry
description: The review proposes a shared definition to address the "confusing plethora of terms" in the field: "The use of artistically inspired methods by researchers and participants in a collaborative research environment where members of the community are actively involved either in creating art in the search for meaning or in providing a critical, situated response to artistically inspired formats of research dissemination from others." It also distinguishes research about art, art as research, and art in research, including only the latter in the review. ABR methods operate as data collection techniques, where art forms are data in their own right, or as dissemination vehicles replacing traditional textual reports.
requirements: Researchers or participants actively create art or respond critically to artistic dissemination within a collaborative community research environment
constraints: The review's definition covers art in research projects only, excluding art therapy and medically inspired projects
target_learners: community members and vulnerable populations participating in community-based inquiry
target_learning_goals: expressing experiences that are difficult to verbalize
developing specific skills through art-making
fostering reflection and dialogue
examples: The review included only studies meeting its art in research definition, where art is used in one or more phases of a research process with active researcher involvement

article_title: A systematic review of the key components of online peer feedback practices in higher education
citation: Xingshi Gao, Omid Noroozi, Judith Gulikers, Harm J.A. Biemans, Seyyed Kazem Banihashem. (2024). A systematic review of the key components of online peer feedback practices in higher education. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2023.100588
title: The MISCA model as a five-component framework for evaluating feedback practices
description: The review adopts the MISCA (Message, Implementation, Student Characteristics, Context, Agents) model proposed by Panadero and Lipnevich (2022), which integrates five common components for classifying feedback practices: Content, Function, Student Characteristics, Presentation, and Source. The article states that "The model shows the complexity of feedback process and provides a theoretical framework for understanding and evaluating the key components that influence feedback practices." Student Characteristics is placed at the center of the model as "the unique component that influences the other four." The review uses these five components as the deductive coding scheme for analyzing online peer feedback studies.
requirements: The framework requires analyzing feedback practices across all five components (content, function, student characteristics, presentation, source) rather than in isolation
constraints: The review applies the model to written peer feedback comments in online or blended higher-education settings
target_learning_goals: improving task performance through peer feedback
feedback quality and uptake
examples: The review coded 73 articles deductively under the five MISCA components, producing Tables 3–7 of categories and sub-categories

article_title: A systematic review of the key components of online peer feedback practices in higher education
citation: Xingshi Gao, Omid Noroozi, Judith Gulikers, Harm J.A. Biemans, Seyyed Kazem Banihashem. (2024). A systematic review of the key components of online peer feedback practices in higher education. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2023.100588
title: Corpus of 73 peer-reviewed studies on online peer feedback in higher education (2000–2022)
description: The review's evidence base is a corpus of 73 peer-reviewed journal articles published between 2000 and 2022, identified through searches of Scopus, ERIC, and Web of Science following PRISMA guidelines. The review reports that "The number of participants involved in the reviewed publications varied from 3 to 2421" and that more than half of the studies (n = 39) were conducted in Asian areas, particularly Taiwan (n = 21; 28%). Content analysis (n = 34; 47%) and questionnaires (n = 31; 42%) were the most regularly used data collection instruments.
requirements: Included articles focused on feedback between students, were performed in online or blended environments, included empirical experiments, and were conducted in higher education
constraints: Only peer-reviewed journal articles in English were included; studies not investigating written feedback comments were excluded
target_learning_goals: peer feedback practices in online settings
examples: Inter-rater reliability was checked with Kappa results (κ = 0.86, p < .001) at the title/abstract stage and (κ = 0.68, p < .001) at full-text screening

article_title: When personal becomes relational: A meta-analysis and narrative review on personality traits and children's affective relationships with adults
citation: Du, Q., Roorda, D. L., Koomen, H. M. Y., Jak, S., & Zee, M. (2025). When personal becomes relational: A meta-analysis and narrative review on personality traits and children's affective relationships with adults. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2025.100688
title: Attend to the personality traits of children and adults when seeking to understand children's affective relationships with adults
description: The article proposes that focusing on personality — of children, parents, and teachers, and of their similarity — is a useful lens for understanding the affective quality of adult–child relationships across contexts. It concludes that "focusing on personality may be a promising way to better understand children's affective relationships with adults in various contexts (e.g., family, school)." The recommendation rests on the meta-analytic and narrative findings that traits of both dyad members relate to relationship quality.
requirements: Practitioners or researchers need information on the personality traits of both the child and the adult in the dyad, since traits of both were associated with relationship quality.
constraints: The authors note the associations were "small to medium in magnitude", so personality is one factor among others rather than a decisive determinant.
target_learners: children in family and school contexts
target_learning_goals: understanding and supporting the affective quality of parent–child and teacher–child relationships
examples: The meta-analysis of k = 39 studies linked children's and parents' traits to parent–child relationship quality, and narrative reviews extended the pattern to teacher–child relationships and personality similarity.

article_title: Fostering creativity in formal schooling: A systematic review of explicit and implicit interventions for young learners
citation: Gu, X., Ritter, S. M., Frossard, F., van den Boom, L., Delfmann, L. R. & Barajas, M. (2026). Fostering creativity in formal schooling: A systematic review of explicit and implicit interventions for young learners. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2026.100784
title: Explicit vs. implicit interventions as a two-branch taxonomy of school-based creativity support
description: The review organizes school-based creativity support into two branches. Explicit interventions are 'intentionally designed programs or instructional units aimed at developing creativity as a specific learning objective', typically structured, time-bound, and measurable. Implicit interventions are 'not framed as direct creativity training but are embedded in everyday classroom practices and broader school environments', operating through pedagogical strategies and contextual conditions. The taxonomy builds on Jeffrey and Craft's distinction between teaching for creativity and creative teaching, and structures the review's three research questions.
requirements: Interventions must be classifiable by whether creativity is the explicit instructional objective or an indirect outcome of pedagogy and context
constraints: Distinction drawn for formal K-12 school settings; the review notes implicit interventions are more diffuse and context-dependent than explicit ones
target_learners: K-12 students in formal education (primary ages 6–12, secondary ages 13–18)
target_learning_goals: Creative thinking (divergent and convergent), creative self-efficacy, creative problem solving
examples: The review categorized 101 studies under RQ1 (explicit interventions) versus RQ2/RQ3 (implicit pedagogical and contextual approaches), e.g., brainstorming programs under ideation and inquiry-based STEM activities under student-centered inquiry learning
key_sources: Gu, X., Ritter, S. M., Frossard, F., van den Boom, L., Delfmann, L. R. & Barajas, M. (2026). Fostering creativity in formal schooling: A systematic review of explicit and implicit interventions for young learners. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2026.100784

article_title: Fostering creativity in formal schooling: A systematic review of explicit and implicit interventions for young learners
citation: Gu, X., Ritter, S. M., Frossard, F., van den Boom, L., Delfmann, L. R. & Barajas, M. (2026). Fostering creativity in formal schooling: A systematic review of explicit and implicit interventions for young learners. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2026.100784
title: Multidimensional developmental frameworks of creativity (4-C model and 4Ps model) grounding the review
description: The review grounds its synthesis in two frameworks. Kaufman and Beghetto's 4-C model 'categorizes creativity into four levels: mini-c (personal insights), little-c (everyday problem-solving), pro-C (professional-level creativity), and big-C (eminent, historically recognized creativity)', treating creativity as a developmental continuum. Rhodes' 4Ps model—Person, Process, Press (environment), and Product—provides a taxonomy underscoring that creativity is shaped by individual traits, cognitive and affective processes, environmental influences, and creative outcomes. Together these frameworks motivate the review's contextualized, multidimensional approach to intervention design.
requirements: Interventions must address cognitive, motivational, and environmental factors together rather than treating creativity as a fixed trait
constraints: Frameworks are theoretical background the review adopts; the review applies them to K-12 formal schooling contexts
target_learning_goals: Understanding creativity as multidimensional and developmental to guide intervention design
examples: The review uses the mini-c to big-C continuum to argue educators must support developmental pathways from early creative dispositions toward more complex forms
key_sources: Gu, X., Ritter, S. M., Frossard, F., van den Boom, L., Delfmann, L. R. & Barajas, M. (2026). description: The intervention model characterizing most included studies combined a systematic and direct instruction approach with one-to-one delivery. The abstract states that "In the majority of the studies, phonics instruction was carried out using a systematic and direct instruction approach and a one-to-one format." This describes the dominant instructional pattern the meta-analysis found effective for teaching decoding to students with intellectual disability.

article_title: The Social Side of School: Why Teachers Need Social Psychology
citation: Gehlbach, Hunter. (2010). The social side of school: Why teachers need social psychology. Educational Psychology Review 22, no. 3: 349-362. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9138-3
title: Social perspective taking as a two-dimensional aptitude with ability and motivational components
description: The review presents social perspective taking (SPT) as the construct of "discerning the thoughts and feelings of others with particular attention to how others perceive the situation." Following Gehlbach (2004), it characterizes SPT as "a complex aptitude, consisting of an ability dimension as well as a motivational dimension," so that real-world impact requires both accurate reading of others and motivation to engage frequently. The review proposes that teachers' SPT, once biases are mitigated, can improve monitoring of student progress and pedagogy.
requirements: For SPT to impact outcomes in the real world, people need both the ability to read thoughts and feelings accurately and the motivation to engage in SPT frequently
constraints: The review notes that little of the bias research has focused specifically on teachers, presuming they are as susceptible as anyone else
target_learning_goals: accurately perceiving students' thoughts, feelings, and motivations to improve pedagogy and monitoring of student progress
examples: A science teacher used SPT to anticipate where chemistry students struggled due to their non-analytic, sequential way of thinking, tailoring lessons and reading facial expressions to gauge comprehension
key_sources: Gehlbach, Hunter. (2010). The social side of school: Why teachers need social psychology. Educational Psychology Review 22, no. 3: 349-362. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9138-3

article_title: The Social Side of School: Why Teachers Need Social Psychology
citation: Gehlbach, Hunter. (2010). The social side of school: Why teachers need social psychology. Educational Psychology Review 22, no. 3: 349-362. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9138-3
title: Cognitive dissonance as a self-persuasion mechanism with free-choice and foreseeable-consequence conditions
description: The review describes cognitive dissonance (Festinger) as the finding that "the arguments we perceive to be most persuasive tend to come from our own mouths," so that preaching a position increases the likelihood of practicing it. It specifies two caveats from Cooper and Fazio (1984): dissonance requires perceived free choice and foreseeable negative consequences. Classroom applications include peer tutoring in which students advocate homework's importance, and having students voice, explain, and publicly post their goals.
requirements: People must feel they freely chose the behavior, and the behavior must have foreseeable negative consequences, for dissonance to arise
constraints: The review hedges that the preach-then-practice rule holds true only subject to a couple of caveats
target_learning_goals: bolstering student motivation and effort on homework and academic goals
examples: Eighth graders mentoring fourth graders were encouraged to stress homework's importance, with free choice established via an onerous worksheet alternative and consequences instilled through class discussion of setting a good example

article_title: The Influence of Diagnostic Labels on the Evaluation of Students: a Multilevel Meta-Analysis
citation: Franz, D. J., Richter, T., Lenhard, W., Marx, P., Stein, R., & Ratz, C. (2023). The Influence of Diagnostic Labels on the Evaluation of Students: a Multilevel Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09716-6
title: Stigma account of diagnostic labels: labels activate stereotypes, prejudice, and discrimination
description: The article frames diagnostic labels within a stigma process in which a diagnosis functions as a label that carries stereotypical surplus meaning. It cites the account that "mental disorder diagnoses can be the cause of stereotypes (i.e., beliefs or cognitive schemas about people suffering from mental illness), prejudice (i.e., evaluative reactions towards mentally ill persons), and discrimination (i.e., overt negative behavior towards the mentally ill)". In the school context, the article links this to expectancy effects, interpreting the Golem effect as the negative flipside of the Pygmalion effect, with diagnostic labels as one student characteristic that can shape teacher expectations and evaluations.
requirements: The label must be stated explicitly to the evaluator while other information about the child is held constant, as in the experimental vignette and video designs the meta-analysis includes.
constraints: The article notes that findings regarding negative effects of teacher expectations are somewhat mixed, and that the empirical evidence on information amount as a moderator was inconclusive in prior studies.
target_learners: children and teenagers under 21 who receive psychological or educational diagnoses
target_learning_goals: fair and accurate evaluation of diagnosed students' academic skills, behavior, and personality by teachers and other professionals
examples: The meta-analysis tested this account by synthesizing experiments in which teachers or other adults evaluated vignettes, videos, or labels of children with and without a diagnostic label.
key_sources: Franz, D. J., Richter, T., Lenhard, W., Marx, P., Stein, R., & Ratz, C. (2023). The Influence of Diagnostic Labels on the Evaluation of Students: a Multilevel Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09716-6

article_title: The Influence of Diagnostic Labels on the Evaluation of Students: a Multilevel Meta-Analysis
citation: Franz, D. J., Richter, T., Lenhard, W., Marx, P., Stein, R., & Ratz, C. (2023). The Influence of Diagnostic Labels on the Evaluation of Students: a Multilevel Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09716-6
title: Open Science Framework repository with data, R code, and forest plots for the label-effect meta-analysis
description: The article releases its research materials openly: "Data and R-Code underlying all results and comprehensive forest plots are available at the repository of the Open Science Framework". The repository contains the extracted effect-size dataset (284 effects nested in 60 experiments), the R analysis code, and comprehensive forest plots, enabling reuse and verification of the meta-analytic results. It supports the multilevel meta-analytic approach implemented with the metafor package in R.
requirements: Access requires the view-only link printed in the article; analyses were run with the metafor package in R and an adapted version of the R-code approach recommended by Assink and Wibbelink (2016).
constraints: The repository link is a view-only URL, so reuse permissions beyond viewing are not stated in the article.
target_learners: researchers and meta-analysts studying label effects and teacher evaluation biases
target_learning_goals: transparent replication and reanalysis of the multilevel meta-analysis of diagnostic label effects
examples: The article points readers to https://osf.io/g72nt/ (view-only link) for the data, R code, and forest plots underlying all reported results.

article_title: An Individual Participant Data Meta-analysis of the Joint Effects of Social, Dimensional, and Temporal Comparisons on Students’ Academic Self-Concepts
citation: Fabian Wolff · Jens Möller. (2022). An Individual Participant Data Meta-analysis of the Joint Effects of Social, Dimensional, and Temporal Comparisons on Students' Academic Self-Concepts. Educational Psychology Review (2022) 34:2569–2608. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09686-1
title: The 2I/E model: joint effects of social, dimensional, and temporal comparisons on academic self-concepts
description: The 2I/E model extends Marsh's classic internal/external frame of reference model by adding temporal comparisons as a second internal comparison. It "describes the effects of students' math and verbal achievements on their math and verbal self-concepts in a more differentiated fashion than the classic I/E model by considering achievement information from different points in time, and separating students' achievement levels from their achievement changes." It predicts positive within-subject effects of achievement levels and changes, negative between-subject level effects, and orders effect strength: social > dimensional > temporal. The meta-analysis tested it on pooled data from 10 datasets (N = 45,248).
requirements: Achievement and self-concept measures in two subjects (math and first language) at the beginning and end of a temporal comparison period, so achievement levels and achievement changes can be computed
constraints: The models are simplified representations that do not claim to capture all determinants of self-concept formation, and the regression approach does not allow causal conclusions
Dimensional comparisons are specified only between math and verbal achievements, and social comparisons refer to all other students examined in the study rather than local reference groups
target_learners: school students in math and first-language domains, grades 6–11
target_learning_goals: formation of subject-specific academic self-concepts
examples: The IPD meta-analysis regressed math self-concept on math achievement level, the math–verbal achievement-level difference, and math achievement change, and analogously for verbal self-concept, across 10 pooled datasets

article_title: A Meta-analytic Review of the Effectiveness of Spacing and Retrieval Practice for Mathematics Learning
citation: Murray, E., Horner, A. J., & Göbel, S. M. (2023). A Meta-analytic Review of the Effectiveness of Spacing and Retrieval Practice for Mathematics Learning. https://osf.io/
title: Study-phase retrieval hypothesis as an explanation for the smaller spacing effect in course-embedded settings
description: The article invokes the study-phase retrieval hypothesis, under which a key mechanism of the spacing effect is the retrieval of the initial study phase. It proposes that in course settings, where students work in classrooms or on homework, learners may have prior material or notes accessible during practice, so they "may not have to retrieve the original memory, instead relying on external guides", reducing the spacing benefit. The authors use this to explain why the course-embedded effect was numerically smaller, while noting it is difficult to know the extent to which participants actually used such materials.
requirements: For the mechanism to operate as described, learners must actually be prompted to recall the required information rather than access external guides during practice.
constraints: The article states it is difficult to understand to what extent participants made use of accessible materials, so whether retrieval occurred could not be coded accurately.
target_learners: Students learning mathematics in classroom courses or via homework, from primary school to university
target_learning_goals: Retention of mathematics material (procedures, facts, concepts) on delayed post-tests
examples: The article quotes Nazari & Ebersbach (2019) and Emeny et al. (2021) describing practice conditions in which students had access to summary sheets or their own prior written work during practice sessions.
key_sources: Murray, E., Horner, A. J., & Göbel, S. M. (2023). A Meta-analytic Review of the Effectiveness of Spacing and Retrieval Practice for Mathematics Learning. https://osf.io/

article_title: Placebo or Assistant? Generative AI Between Externalization and Anthropomorphization
citation: Skulmowski, A. (2024). Placebo or Assistant? Generative AI Between Externalization and Anthropomorphization. Educational Psychology Review, 36, 58. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09894-x
title: Computers as Social Actors (CASA) framework
description: The CASA framework holds that "humans expect computers to function in alignment with certain social rules, leading them to perceive technology as a human-like partner". The essay extends this account to AI systems, smartphones, and smartwatches, and uses it to organize findings on anthropomorphization triggers, such as humanized chatbot elements increasing social presence and thereby trust, empathy, and satisfaction. It serves as the essay's explanatory backdrop for why users might be expected to credit AI contributions, and highlights a research gap regarding relationships with AI collaborators in education.
requirements: The framework applies to human-technology interaction in which social-rule expectations can be triggered by design factors.
constraints: The essay notes most studies in this section predate the 2023 widespread adoption of generative AI, and that little is known about these relationships with AI collaborators in educational contexts.
target_learning_goals: accurate monitoring and attribution of one's own versus AI contributions to learning tasks
examples: The essay applies CASA to interpret why users might treat chatbots as partners, and to frame the conflict between liking AI output quality and taking credit for it.

article_title: Placebo or Assistant? Generative AI Between Externalization and Anthropomorphization
citation: Skulmowski, A. (2024). Placebo or Assistant? Generative AI Between Externalization and Anthropomorphization. Educational Psychology Review, 36, 58. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09894-x
title: Three-layer model of learning activities (semantic, proximal, motor)
description: The essay presents Skulmowski's (2024) model of activity-based learning, built on Pacherie's (2008) conceptualization of action planning, in which "an educational task commonly consists of a semantic part at a high level of abstraction" (e.g., the intention to write an essay), realized through proximal activities (formulating paragraphs and sentences), which are usually realized through motor activities such as typing. The semantic layer carries considerable cognitive load and requires planning, decisions, and acquired skills. The model is proposed as a guide for deciding which task layers can be externalized to AI without significant risk, with lower layers lending themselves to externalization and the semantic layer at greatest risk.
requirements: Learning tasks and objectives must be analyzed with high precision to derive guidelines on skill levels at which task parts can be offloaded.
constraints: The essay states the model is plausible as a starting point but that more empirical research is needed on effectiveness and transferability across subjects, domains, and task types.
target_learners: learners across education levels using AI tools for writing and other complex tasks
target_learning_goals: distributing learning tasks between learner effort and AI externalization without diminishing skill acquisition
examples: For essay writing: semantic activities include knowledge of style, composition, and content; proximal activities are formulating paragraphs and sentences; motor activities are typing or handwriting letters.
key_sources: Skulmowski, A. (2024). Placebo or Assistant? Generative AI Between Externalization and Anthropomorphization. Educational Psychology Review, 36, 58. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09894-x

article_title: Intensive Longitudinal Methods in School Research: A Systematic Literature Review
citation: Carina Schreiber & Michael Becker. (2026). Intensive Longitudinal Methods in School Research: A Systematic Literature Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10203-x
title: Comprehensive checklist of reporting criteria for intensive longitudinal studies
description: The review offers "a comprehensive checklist of reporting criteria for intensive longitudinal methods", integrating the APA Journal Article Reporting Standards, the Trull and Ebner-Priemer (2020) guidelines, and the review's own findings. The checklist covers sample justification, sampling scheme and scheduling, item text and psychometrics, hardware and software, compliance procedures, valid and missing data, the final dataset, analysis preparation, and analysis details. It is operationalised in Table 2, where each criterion was coded met or not met per article.
requirements: Researchers should justify sample and sample size (e.g., using multilevel power analyses) and give rationales for sampling scheme, assessment frequency, and questionnaire density
constraints: Adherence rates for the majority of guidelines were questionably low even among articles published in the past five years
target_learners: school researchers designing intensive longitudinal studies
target_learning_goals: transparent, replicable reporting of intensive longitudinal study methods
examples: The review coded each of the 257 included articles against the checklist criteria, e.g., reporting full text of response options was met by 92.2% of articles, while justifying sample size was met by only 4.7%
key_sources: Carina Schreiber & Michael Becker. (2026). Intensive Longitudinal Methods in School Research: A Systematic Literature Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10203-x

article_title: Intensive Longitudinal Methods in School Research: A Systematic Literature Review
citation: Carina Schreiber & Michael Becker. (2026). Intensive Longitudinal Methods in School Research: A Systematic Literature Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10203-x
title: Methodological parameter framework for designing intensive longitudinal studies
description: The review organises the design of intensive longitudinal studies around core methodological parameters: study duration, assessment frequency, sampling scheme (fixed, random, semi-random, event-based), item phrasing and questionnaire density, and data-collection device. It argues these choices "contain, rather implicitly, theoretical assumptions about the psychological processes under investigation and delimit the kinds of inferences that can be drawn from the data", requiring alignment between parameters, research questions, and constructs. For example, low-frequency assessments implicitly assume no meaningful within-day fluctuations.
requirements: Methodological decisions should be explicitly justified in light of the specific research questions, theoretical assumptions, and study populations under investigation
Assessment frequency should be balanced with study duration to keep participant burden acceptable while generating sufficient data points
constraints: Established validated trait-level measures are usually too long and retrospective, so researchers often must adapt or develop state-level instruments, which may alter the construct measured
Time-varying confounders and lagged effects remain an issue for within-person causal inference
target_learners: students and teachers as study participants
target_learning_goals: capturing within-person fluctuations in students' and teachers' experiences, emotions, cognitions, and behaviours in everyday school life
examples: The review illustrates the framework with a hypothetical study of students' motivation, showing how different parameter specifications yield fundamentally different insights
key_sources: Carina Schreiber & Michael Becker. (2026). Intensive Longitudinal Methods in School Research: A Systematic Literature Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10203-x

article_title: The Associations Between Parenting Self-Efficacy and Parents’ Contributions to the Home-School Partnership Among Parents of Primary School Students: a Multilevel Meta-analysis
citation: Tianyi Ma, Cassandra L. Tellegen, Julie Hodges, Matthew R. Sanders. (2024). The Associations Between Parenting Self-Efficacy and Parents' Contributions to the Home-School Partnership Among Parents of Primary School Students: a Multilevel Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09937-3
title: Hoover-Dempsey model of the parental involvement process
description: The article describes the Hoover-Dempsey model as explaining "the antecedents of parental involvement, consequences on child adjustments, and mediation pathways". It highlights three key family-level antecedents: parental motivational beliefs (active role construction and "a strong sense of self-efficacy that they can make positive impacts on children's learning"), perceptions of whether school, teacher, or child want involvement, and contextual family factors. The meta-analysis findings support the model's placement of parenting self-efficacy as a key antecedent of parents' contributions to the home-school partnership.
requirements: Requires the self-efficacy component of motivational beliefs to be measured alongside involvement outcomes
constraints: The article notes only the self-efficacy component of motivational beliefs was considered in its inclusion criteria
target_learning_goals: parents' contributions to home-school partnership (involvement, communication, expectations)
examples: The meta-analysis tested the model's prediction that parenting self-efficacy is a key antecedent of parents' partnership contributions

The Associations Between Parenting Self-Efficacy and Parents' Contributions to the Home-School Partnership Among Parents of Primary School Students: a Multilevel Meta-analysis. article_title: The Associations Between Parenting Self-Efficacy and Parents’ Contributions to the Home-School Partnership Among Parents of Primary School Students: a Multilevel Meta-analysis
citation: Tianyi Ma, Cassandra L. Tellegen, Julie Hodges, Matthew R. Sanders. (2024). The Associations Between Parenting Self-Efficacy and Parents' Contributions to the Home-School Partnership Among Parents of Primary School Students: a Multilevel Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09937-3
title: Parental self-regulation framework with parenting self-efficacy as a core element
description: The article describes parental self-regulation as extending Bandura's work on self-efficacy and personal agency, viewed as "a more comprehensive explanatory framework for parenting self-efficacy". The framework views parenting self-efficacy as a core element strongly associated with parents' capacity to self-monitor, regulate attributions, emotions, and behaviors, and problem-solve to achieve parenting goals; other core elements are self-sufficiency, self-management, personal agency, and problem-solving. Parenting self-efficacy has been found to be a strong indicator of overall self-regulatory capacity (r ≈ 0.70, factor loading = 0.94).
requirements: Measures of parental self-regulation, which have only been recently developed
constraints: Very limited research has investigated associations between parental self-regulation and parents' contributions to the home-school partnership; all studies in the meta-analysis measured only the parenting self-efficacy component
target_learning_goals: parents' self-regulatory capacity supporting engagement in children's education
key_sources: Tianyi Ma, Cassandra L. Tellegen, Julie Hodges, Matthew R. Sanders. (2024). The Associations Between Parenting Self-Efficacy and Parents' Contributions to the Home-School Partnership Among Parents of Primary School Students: a Multilevel Meta-analysis. citation: Tianyi Ma, Cassandra L. Tellegen, Julie Hodges, Matthew R. Sanders. (2024). The Associations Between Parenting Self-Efficacy and Parents' Contributions to the Home-School Partnership Among Parents of Primary School Students: a Multilevel Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09937-3
title: Corpus of 50 studies with 185 effect sizes on parenting self-efficacy and home-school partnership
description: The meta-analytic dataset comprises 50 independent samples (43 studies, 7 with multiple cohorts) published between 1992 and 2024, with 72% published in the last 15 years; 30 were journal articles and 20 doctoral dissertations. It includes "A total of 20,043 children" with sample sizes from 35 to 8152. Most studies were conducted in the USA (31/50), used cross-sectional methodology (44/50), and recruited general samples (41/50); all included studies measured only the parenting self-efficacy component of parental self-regulation.
requirements: Studies needed to report Pearson's r correlations or sufficient information to estimate effect sizes
constraints: Studies presenting only multivariate results (multiple regression, SEM, multilevel modeling) were excluded due to inability to obtain independent effect sizes
target_learning_goals: synthesis of associations between parenting self-efficacy and home-school partnership contributions
examples: Searches of six databases completed in late October 2023; screening conducted in Covidence with 98.4% inter-rater agreement
