article_title: Correlates of K-12 Students’ Intertextual Integration
citation: Daniel R. Espinas, Brennan W. Chandler. (2024). Correlates of K-12 Students' Intertextual Integration. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09889-8
title: Documents Model Framework: integration via an integrated situations model and an inter-text model
description: The Documents Model Framework (DMF; Britt et al., 1999; Perfetti et al., 1999) is the review's anchor theoretical account of how meaning is constructed from multiple documents. It proposes that "integration is accomplished by constructing two representations: an integrated situations model and an inter-text model" — the situations model holds semantic content about the common topic, while the inter-text model holds meta-document information such as source author, publication, date, and purpose. The review describes three possible representational outcomes: a mush model, a separate representations model, and a documents model, and notes the DMF "provided the foundation for much of the theorizing and empirical work that has followed."
requirements: Tasks and contexts in which well-formed intertextual representations matter, such as history-class research reports, for readers to construct a documents model
constraints: The likelihood a reader constructs a particular representational form depends in part on the context and task at hand; effortful connection formation may not occur when readers view connections as unnecessary or are unable to form them
target_learners: K-12 students reading multiple text documents
target_learning_goals: Constructing coherent integrated representations of situations presented across multiple documents, including linking content to sources
examples: The review uses the DMF to organize its taxonomy of individual difference predictors and illustrates the three representational outcomes (mush model, separate representations model, documents model) in Fig. 1
key_sources: Daniel R. Espinas, Brennan W. Chandler. (2024). Correlates of K-12 Students' Intertextual Integration. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09889-8

article_title: Five Educational-Psychology Lenses for Training and Evaluating AI Models
citation: Peng Wang, Fred Paas. (2026). Five Educational-Psychology Lenses for Training and Evaluating AI Models. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10195-8
title: Five educational-psychology lenses for interpreting AI training: curriculum design, scaffolding, social learning, assessment validity, and ethical alignment
description: The article organizes AI training analysis around five educational-psychology domains, mapping each construct onto a concrete AI analogue and validity risk. It states that its reflection "focuses on five interrelated domains where the analogy between AI training and human education is especially illuminating": curriculum design, instructional scaffolding, social learning via feedback, assessment and construct validity, and ethical alignment. Table 1 pairs each lens with practical design checks, such as planning fading tests for scaffolds and auditing teacher signals for feedback.
requirements: The framework is used as a design heuristic for interpreting training interventions, not as a claim of shared mechanisms between human and machine learning
constraints: The article states the mapping "is not a claim that human learning and model optimization share underlying mechanisms"
target_learners: AI researchers and developers acting as trainers of models
educational psychologists evaluating AI capability claims
target_learning_goals: Evaluating whether AI training gains reflect robust competence rather than support dependence or proxy optimization
examples: Table 1 maps constructs such as hints and worked examples to prompting supports, and formative versus summative assessment to benchmarks and reward functions
key_sources: Peng Wang, Fred Paas. (2026). Five Educational-Psychology Lenses for Training and Evaluating AI Models. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10195-8

article_title: Five Educational-Psychology Lenses for Training and Evaluating AI Models
citation: Peng Wang, Fred Paas. (2026). Five Educational-Psychology Lenses for Training and Evaluating AI Models. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10195-8
title: Messick's unified validity framework applied to AI evaluation, with six sources of construct-validity evidence
description: The article anchors its validity discussion in Messick's unified theory of validity, which holds that validity is a property of inferences and decisions based on scores, not of instruments. It enumerates six interlocking evidence sources (content, substantive, structural, generalizability, external, and consequential) and gives each an AI analogue, such as item-level factor analysis for structural evidence and out-of-distribution testing for generalizability evidence.
requirements: Validity questions must be asked about the inferences drawn from benchmark scores for an intended use and context, not merely about whether a score is produced
constraints: The consequential strand becomes central when a benchmark is itself a training target, because optimizing against it changes what it measures
target_learners: educational psychologists assessing AI capability claims
target_learning_goals: Judging whether benchmark scores warrant inferences about capability, safety, or alignment
examples: The article reads specification gaming, shortcut learning, dataset contamination, and reward hacking as concrete forms of validity failure in LLM evaluation
key_sources: Peng Wang, Fred Paas. (2026). Five Educational-Psychology Lenses for Training and Evaluating AI Models. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10195-8

article_title: Five Educational-Psychology Lenses for Training and Evaluating AI Models
citation: Peng Wang, Fred Paas. (2026). Five Educational-Psychology Lenses for Training and Evaluating AI Models. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10195-8
title: Test prompting supports with fading and perturbation checks before attributing a performance gain to stable model competence
description: The article recommends treating prompting supports such as chain-of-thought and few-shot exemplars as scaffolds whose gains must be validated against scaffold removal. It states: "A useful validity check is the educational analogue of scaffold fading: evaluate performance when intermediate steps are no longer requested, and when prompts are modified to prevent simple template completion." If accuracy collapses under fading, the gain reflects dependence on external structure rather than stable competence.
requirements: Paired evaluation in which a gain attributed to chain-of-thought, retrieval, or tool use is reported alongside a matched run with the support removed
constraints: The article notes it is an open question whether AI models internalize the benefits of scaffolding or merely exploit the temporary crutch
target_learners: educational psychologists reviewing AI capability claims
target_learning_goals: Distinguishing support-independent competence from scaffold dependence in model performance
examples: The article proposes evaluating chain-of-thought gains with prompts modified to prevent simple template completion, and interpreting persistence under perturbation as evidence of more general solution procedures
key_sources: Peng Wang, Fred Paas. (2026). Five Educational-Psychology Lenses for Training and Evaluating AI Models. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10195-8

article_title: Five Educational-Psychology Lenses for Training and Evaluating AI Models
citation: Peng Wang, Fred Paas. (2026). Five Educational-Psychology Lenses for Training and Evaluating AI Models. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10195-8
title: Training data functions as a hidden curriculum that socializes AI models into the values and biases implicit in their corpus
description: The article extends the educational concept of the hidden curriculum to AI: "In the context of AI, the training data serves as a hidden curriculum for the model (Bender et al., 2021)." Models trained on open internet text learn patterns reflecting societal biases, stereotypes, and power structures, effectively socializing them into the worldview implicit in the corpus. This motivates auditing and curating datasets and treating feedback loops as value-laden pedagogical signals.
requirements: Developers must audit teacher signals, including labelers and training data, because models derive behavior from human-generated examples and judgments
constraints: The socialization is functional rather than conscious, and the analogy risks oversimplifying because AI does not develop genuine understanding or independent moral reasoning
target_learning_goals: Recognizing and mitigating implicit bias and norms transmitted to models through training data and feedback
examples: The article notes that an LLM trained on open internet text learns societal biases, spurring work on auditing and curating datasets to educate the AI more fairly
key_sources: Peng Wang, Fred Paas. (2026). Five Educational-Psychology Lenses for Training and Evaluating AI Models. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10195-8

article_title: Sex Differences in Mathematics: A Meta-analytic Review Across Content, Grades, and Geographic Regions
citation: Sara Caviola, David Giofrè, Enrico Toffalini, Lorenzo Esposito, Irene Tonizzi, David C. Geary. (2026). Sex Differences in Mathematics: A Meta-analytic Review Across Content, Grades, and Geographic Regions. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10125-8
title: Spatial-ability account of content- and grade-specific sex differences in mathematics
description: The article organizes its findings around an explanatory framework in which sex differences in mathematics are content- and grade-specific because mathematical domains differ in their reliance on visuospatial abilities. It notes that boys' advantage in spatial abilities increases from childhood into adolescence, and that mathematical domains influenced by spatial abilities, such as geometry, show correspondingly growing male advantages. The framework also incorporates socio-cultural factors, including mathematics anxiety and stereotype-related mechanisms, and school practices such as tracking and course placement that may mitigate or amplify gaps.
requirements: Distinguishing mathematics content by its visuospatial component and relating domain-specific gaps to developmental trajectories of spatial abilities
constraints: The article states the findings do not mean boys have advantages in all aspects of geometry, such as writing geometric proofs, but only content involving active manipulation of visuospatial information
target_learning_goals: mathematics performance across content domains and grade levels
examples: The article links the growing geometry advantage to boys' increasing spatial-ability advantage from childhood into adolescence
key_sources: Sara Caviola, David Giofrè, Enrico Toffalini, Lorenzo Esposito, Irene Tonizzi, David C. Geary. (2026). Sex Differences in Mathematics: A Meta-analytic Review Across Content, Grades, and Geographic Regions. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10125-8

article_title: Interactivity in Video-based Models
citation: Wouters, P., Tabbers, H. K., & Paas, F. (2007). Interactivity in Video-based Models. Educational Psychology Review, 19, 327–342. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-007-9045-4
title: Social cognitive model of sequential skill acquisition
description: This model describes how learners move from observing a model to independent, self-regulated performance. As the review states, "The model contends that skills can be optimally acquired in four sequential stages": observation, emulation or imitation, self-control, and self-regulation. The review uses it as the organizing framework, arguing that the transition from observing to self-regulated practice is accompanied by different cognitive processes and different forms of interactivity, and that both delayed and premature starts with actual performance can hamper learning.
requirements: Learners must transition from observation to performance in a timely way; both delayed and premature transitions can hamper learning
constraints: Initially learners depend heavily on the performance and standards of the model and must gradually rely more on their own self-regulation processes
target_learners: novices learning complex motor or cognitive skills
target_learning_goals: acquisition of complex skills through observation leading to self-regulated performance
examples: The review maps each interactivity guideline to one or more of the four stages, e.g., pacing in the observation stage and reflection prompts in the self-control and self-regulation stages
key_sources: Wouters, P., Tabbers, H. K., & Paas, F. (2007). Interactivity in Video-based Models. Educational Psychology Review, 19, 327–342. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-007-9045-4

article_title: Interactivity in Video-based Models
citation: Wouters, P., Tabbers, H. K., & Paas, F. (2007). Interactivity in Video-based Models. Educational Psychology Review, 19, 327–342. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-007-9045-4
title: Two-level model of interactivity: functional and cognitive interactivity
description: Adopting Kennedy's (2004) model, the review distinguishes two levels of interactivity centered on instructional events. "The first level, functional interactivity, comprises the behavioral responses learners engage in when they face an instructional event," while the second level, cognitive interactivity, proposes that these behavioral responses mediate between instructional events and (meta)cognitive processes. The review argues guidelines for interactivity should address both components, and that clicking a button without the purpose of eliciting desired cognitive processes is not interaction relevant for learning.
requirements: Guidelines must describe both the behavioral actions addressed and the cognitive processes they mediate
constraints: The effect of an instructional event and its behavioral response may depend on factors outside interactivity itself, most importantly prior knowledge
target_learning_goals: engaging learners in cognitive and metacognitive processes during interaction with learning materials
examples: A prediction prompt is functional interactivity (answering a question) whose behavioral response may trigger selection, organization and integration of information with prior knowledge
key_sources: Wouters, P., Tabbers, H. K., & Paas, F. (2007). Interactivity in Video-based Models. Educational Psychology Review, 19, 327–342. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-007-9045-4

article_title: Interactivity in Video-based Models
citation: Wouters, P., Tabbers, H. K., & Paas, F. (2007). Interactivity in Video-based Models. Educational Psychology Review, 19, 327–342. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-007-9045-4
title: Guidelines for interactivity in video-based modeling mapped to cognitive processes and skill-acquisition stages
description: The review identifies a set of guidelines for implementing interactivity in video-based models, classified by required prior knowledge, behavioral component, cognitive processes supported, and stage of the social cognitive model. As the abstract states, "Pacing, cues, control over appearance, prediction, working in dyads, personalized task selection, and reflection prompts are identified as guidelines that might support learners to interactively construct schemas." Each guideline specifies who implements control (learner or system), which processes (elaboration, induction, compilation, strengthening) it mediates, and the stage where it applies.
requirements: Implementation must match the learner's level of prior knowledge, since a guideline effective for low-experience learners may be ineffective for high-experience learners
constraints: The guidelines are presented in isolation and it is not clear how they are related or whether an ideal sequence exists; hardly any research has investigated interactivity in cognitive modeling directly
target_learners: novices through experienced learners of complex motor and cognitive skills
target_learning_goals: schema construction and schema automation during observation and practice of modeled skills
examples: Table 1 classifies each guideline; e.g., dissolving cues for low prior knowledge in the observation stage, personalized task selection for high prior knowledge in the self-control and self-regulation stages, and personalized task selection with part-task practice for compilation and strengthening
key_sources: Wouters, P., Tabbers, H. K., & Paas, F. (2007). Interactivity in Video-based Models. Educational Psychology Review, 19, 327–342. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-007-9045-4

article_title: Historical Reasoning: Towards a Framework for Analyzing Students’ Reasoning about the Past
citation: Jannet van Drie & Carla van Boxtel. (2008). Historical Reasoning: Towards a Framework for Analyzing Students' Reasoning about the Past. Educ Psychol Rev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-007-9056-1
title: Six-component framework of historical reasoning
description: The article defines historical reasoning as "an activity in which a person organizes information about the past in order to describe, compare, and/or explain historical phenomena". The framework comprises six analytically separable but interrelated components: asking historical questions, using sources, contextualization, argumentation, using substantive concepts, and using meta-concepts. It was developed and refined through coding student essays, chat discussions, small-group and whole-class discussions, and is intended to describe progression and task effects in secondary history education.
requirements: Quality of reasoning can only be judged relative to the nature of the task, the topic or theme, the historical materials, and the background knowledge expected of the student
constraints: The components are analytical tools and do not occur clearly separated in reality; the framework defines no fixed categories of high and low level historical reasoning
target_learning_goals: historical reasoning: describing, comparing, and explaining historical phenomena
examples: The authors used the framework's coding schemes to identify differences in the amount and quality of historical reasoning between tasks and between experts and novices in various studies
key_sources: Jannet van Drie & Carla van Boxtel. (2008). Historical Reasoning: Towards a Framework for Analyzing Students' Reasoning about the Past. Educ Psychol Rev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-007-9056-1

article_title: Four Decades After the Big-Fish–Little-Pond Effect: Critical Boundary Tests and Integrative Models of Mean-Context, Ordinal-Standing, and Distributional-Scaling in 46 Countries
citation: Herbert W. Marsh. (2026). Four Decades After the Big-Fish–Little-Pond Effect: Critical Boundary Tests and Integrative Models of Mean-Context, Ordinal-Standing, and Distributional-Scaling in 46 Countries. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10200-0
title: The Statistical–Mechanism Gap Fallacy: statistical contextual indicators are not psychologically transparent mechanisms
description: The article names and defines the Statistical–Mechanism Gap Fallacy as "the tendency to collapse the gap between statistical indicators and the psychological, social, or cognitive mechanisms they are presumed to represent". Contextual means, ordinal ranks, and dispersion statistics are treated as "partially overlapping statistical representations of socially experienced comparison environments rather than as isolated psychological mechanisms". The framing motivates modeling mean, rank, and dispersion jointly rather than assuming any single statistic uniquely represents the comparison process.
requirements: Analyses must model contextual means, ordinal standing, and dispersion jointly so their distinct and overlapping contributions can be evaluated without assuming any single statistic uniquely represents the comparison process.
constraints: The issue is not whether students consciously compute classroom means, percentile ranks, or formal distributional statistics; the indicators are representations of evaluative environments, not the mechanisms themselves.
target_learners: Grade 8 mathematics students in cross-national assessments
target_learning_goals: Academic self-concept formation through social comparison in classrooms
examples: The study models contextual means, ordinal standing, and classroom dispersion jointly in TIMSS 2019 data rather than treating any one indicator as the mechanism.
key_sources: Herbert W. Marsh. (2026). Four Decades After the Big-Fish–Little-Pond Effect: Critical Boundary Tests and Integrative Models of Mean-Context, Ordinal-Standing, and Distributional-Scaling in 46 Countries. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10200-0

article_title: Motivating Self-Regulation: Utility Value, Interest Development, and the Potential for Intervention
citation: Carol Sansone, K. Ann Renninger, Judith M. Harackiewicz. (2026). Motivating Self-Regulation: Utility Value, Interest Development, and the Potential for Intervention. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10142-7
title: Situated expectancy-value theory: expectancies and subjective task value as proximal predictors of achievement choices
description: SEVT is the conceptual framework that initially grounded utility-value interventions. The article states that "SEVT identifies individuals' expectancies of success and subjective task value as the most proximal predictors of students' achievement-related choices." Task value has components including intrinsic value, attainment value, and utility value, with perceived cost also discussed, and value components are combined and weighed relative to perceived cost to predict engagement and persistence.
requirements: The theory presupposes intervening processes between external factors (e.g., culture, parents' beliefs) and students' expectancies and values, including students' perceptions of those factors
constraints: The article notes the model's depiction may suggest external factors matter only as precursors, but Eccles and Wigfield view expectancies and values as enmeshed in and influenced by different levels of environments and cultures
target_learning_goals: achievement-related choices and persistence in coursework
examples: UVIs target the utility value component of SEVT because it has been systematically evaluated through experimental research and randomized control trials in high school and college classes
key_sources: Carol Sansone, K. Ann Renninger, Judith M. Harackiewicz. (2026). Motivating Self-Regulation: Utility Value, Interest Development, and the Potential for Intervention. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10142-7

article_title: Motivating Self-Regulation: Utility Value, Interest Development, and the Potential for Intervention
citation: Carol Sansone, K. Ann Renninger, Judith M. Harackiewicz. (2026). Motivating Self-Regulation: Utility Value, Interest Development, and the Potential for Intervention. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10142-7
title: Four-phase model of interest development: from triggered situational interest to well-developed individual interest
description: The four-phase model describes how interest develops over time from a temporary response to features of the task and context into an integrated aspect of identity. The article states the model "includes four phases: triggered situational interest, maintained situational interest, emerging individual interest, and well-developed individual interest." Each phase has affective and cognitive components; earlier phases are relatively more affective, later phases more cognitive, requiring ongoing development of knowledge and value.
requirements: Support through interactions with educators and peers and the design of the environment can trigger and develop interest at any age
constraints: How interest connects to learning and how it should be supported depends on the phase of the students' interest
target_learners: students at any age developing interest in course topics
target_learning_goals: sustained engagement and reengagement with topics and domains
examples: In earlier phases learners respond to triggers encouraging meaningful connections to related content; in later phases learners generate questions that go beyond what they are assigned
key_sources: Carol Sansone, K. Ann Renninger, Judith M. Harackiewicz. (2026). Motivating Self-Regulation: Utility Value, Interest Development, and the Potential for Intervention. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10142-7

article_title: Motivating Self-Regulation: Utility Value, Interest Development, and the Potential for Intervention
citation: Carol Sansone, K. Ann Renninger, Judith M. Harackiewicz. (2026). Motivating Self-Regulation: Utility Value, Interest Development, and the Potential for Intervention. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10142-7
title: Self-Regulation of Motivation (SRM) model: reciprocal relationship between goal-based value motivation and interest experience
description: The SRM model addresses the reciprocal relationship between value and interest when students self-regulate. The article states it "integrates motivation to reach goals (predicted by value and expectancy of reaching the goals) and motivation based on the subjective experience of interest while working towards those goals." When interest ebbs, individuals consider whether there is a sufficient reason to continue; if so, they may either continue as is or engage in strategies to enhance the experience of interest, potentially changing how they perform the activity.
requirements: Goal-based motivation (expectancy and value) may be necessary to initiate engagement; in-the-moment interest experience becomes important for persistence and reengagement decisions
constraints: There may be limits to how successful a particular interest-enhancing strategy may be; strategic actions differ based on task characteristics, individual preferences, and constraints of the environment
target_learners: high school and college students managing motivational challenges
target_learning_goals: persistence and reengagement with course content and domains
examples: Students may look up something triggered by reading, work with other students if allowed, or think about how content connects to their own life
key_sources: Carol Sansone, K. Ann Renninger, Judith M. Harackiewicz. (2026). Motivating Self-Regulation: Utility Value, Interest Development, and the Potential for Intervention. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10142-7

article_title: Motivating Self-Regulation: Utility Value, Interest Development, and the Potential for Intervention
citation: Carol Sansone, K. Ann Renninger, Judith M. Harackiewicz. (2026). Motivating Self-Regulation: Utility Value, Interest Development, and the Potential for Intervention. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10142-7
title: Framework: effects of generating utility value on motivation differ by phase of interest development depending on compatibility of useful and interesting content
description: The article's integrative framework hypothesizes that generating utility value affects motivation differently at earlier and later phases of interest. Figure 1 "displays the hypothesized effect of generating utility value for course content on students' motivation to engage with that content" and illustrates that "useful content may align with interest at earlier phases of interest but may diverge at later phases of interest." At earlier phases, perceived utility and interest can work in sync; at later phases, divergence between useful and interesting content can create conflict about where to invest effort, while compatibility is mutually reinforcing.
requirements: Understanding the effects requires considering the degree to which the learning content perceived as useful is compatible with the content that is the focus of developing interest
constraints: The framework is hypothesized; the article states exploration of these questions requires data capturing students' perceptions, feelings, and behaviors over time, and the nature of differences in how students with more developed interest regulate motivation are not yet known
target_learners: high school and college students in courses with required content
target_learning_goals: motivation to engage with course content and sustained engagement over time
examples: A student may generate utility for fungi as food or brewing beer without wanting to learn more, while the 'wood wide web' possibility triggers interest with little immediate practical use
key_sources: Carol Sansone, K. Ann Renninger, Judith M. Harackiewicz. (2026). Motivating Self-Regulation: Utility Value, Interest Development, and the Potential for Intervention. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10142-7

article_title: Spacing and Interleaving Effects Require Distinct Theoretical Bases: a Systematic Review Testing the Cognitive Load and Discriminative-Contrast Hypotheses
citation: Ouhao Chen & Fred Paas & John Sweller. (2021). Spacing and Interleaving Effects Require Distinct Theoretical Bases: a Systematic Review Testing the Cognitive Load and Discriminative-Contrast Hypotheses. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09613-w
title: Spacing effect as a cognitive load effect: working memory resource depletion during learning with recovery during rest-from-deliberate-learning
description: The review proposes that the spacing effect is a cognitive load effect: continuous mental effort depletes limited working memory resources, depressing subsequent performance, and rest-from-deliberate-learning periods allow those resources to be restored, enhancing later learning. The authors state that "CLT assumes that inserted spacing with rest-from-deliberate-learning during spaced practice allows the restoration of depleted working memory resources, thus enhancing subsequent learning." Unlike most cognitive load effects, this one does not require high element interactivity materials.
requirements: A rest-from-deliberate-learning period between learning episodes during which intentional learning does not occur
constraints: The article notes it is not known whether depletion is greater with high than low element interactivity information
Only Chen et al. (2018) directly assessed working memory resources; the authors are not aware of other studies that did
target_learners: students across all stages of education
target_learning_goals: retention and learning outcomes across verbal, motor, and academic domains
examples: Chen et al. (2018) administered a working memory capacity test immediately before the content test to massed and spaced groups, finding recovery after rest associated with superior learning
key_sources: Ouhao Chen & Fred Paas & John Sweller. (2021). Spacing and Interleaving Effects Require Distinct Theoretical Bases: a Systematic Review Testing the Cognitive Load and Discriminative-Contrast Hypotheses. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09613-w

article_title: Spacing and Interleaving Effects Require Distinct Theoretical Bases: a Systematic Review Testing the Cognitive Load and Discriminative-Contrast Hypotheses
citation: Ouhao Chen & Fred Paas & John Sweller. (2021). Spacing and Interleaving Effects Require Distinct Theoretical Bases: a Systematic Review Testing the Cognitive Load and Discriminative-Contrast Hypotheses. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09613-w
title: Discriminative-contrast hypothesis: interleaving assists learners to discriminate between similar topics
description: The review explains the interleaving effect via the discriminative-contrast hypothesis, initially proposed by Kornell and Bjork (2008) for category learning. It posits that alternating episodes of different but similar skills or topics helps learners distinguish between them, unlike blocked practice. The authors write that "Interleaving does not involve mental rest-from-deliberate-learning but rather assists learners to discriminate between similar concepts or topics of a domain." It builds on the contextual interference hypothesis, which makes identical predictions.
requirements: Learning materials from the same domain that are similar and not readily discriminable, so learners must contrast and discriminate between them
constraints: For very obviously different, immediately discriminable materials the interleaving effect is unlikely to be obtained
The effect is not moderated by varying working memory capacity according to Sana et al. (2018) as cited in the review
target_learners: students across all stages of education, primarily novices
target_learning_goals: category learning, discrimination between similar concepts, problem-type identification
examples: Kang and Pashler (2012) interleaved paintings by the same artist with easily discriminated cartoons to test discriminative practice
key_sources: Ouhao Chen & Fred Paas & John Sweller. (2021). Spacing and Interleaving Effects Require Distinct Theoretical Bases: a Systematic Review Testing the Cognitive Load and Discriminative-Contrast Hypotheses. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09613-w

article_title: Spacing and Interleaving Effects Require Distinct Theoretical Bases: a Systematic Review Testing the Cognitive Load and Discriminative-Contrast Hypotheses
citation: Ouhao Chen & Fred Paas & John Sweller. (2021). Spacing and Interleaving Effects Require Distinct Theoretical Bases: a Systematic Review Testing the Cognitive Load and Discriminative-Contrast Hypotheses. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09613-w
title: Use spaced instruction when learners need mental rest and interleaved instruction when learners must discriminate between similar areas
description: From the review's practical conclusion, the two effects call for different instructional conditions: spacing supports learning when gaps provide genuine rest from deliberate learning, while interleaving supports learning when learners must learn to tell apart apparently similar but different topics. The authors state: "Spacing should be used when learners need to mentally rest from learning while interleaving should be used when learners need to discriminate between apparently similar but in fact different instructional areas."
requirements: For spacing: gaps filled with rest-from-deliberate-learning; for interleaving: multiple similar, difficult-to-discriminate learning areas
constraints: Interleaving with obviously different materials or knowledgeable learners is unlikely to produce an effect, per the five null studies
target_learners: students across all stages of education
target_learning_goals: retention of learned material and discrimination between similar concepts or problem types
examples: The review's coding classified 48 studies as spacing (with rest) and 67 as interleaving (without rest), including lag designs as interleaving
key_sources: Ouhao Chen & Fred Paas & John Sweller. (2021). Spacing and Interleaving Effects Require Distinct Theoretical Bases: a Systematic Review Testing the Cognitive Load and Discriminative-Contrast Hypotheses. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09613-w

article_title: Epistemic Beliefs in Science—A Systematic Integration of Evidence From Multiple Studies
citation: Julia Schiefer, Peter A. Edelsbrunner, Andrea Bernholt, Nele Kampa, Andreas Nehring. (2022). Epistemic Beliefs in Science—A Systematic Integration of Evidence From Multiple Studies. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09661-w
title: Four-dimensional model of epistemic beliefs in science (Conley et al., 2004)
description: The model conceptualizes epistemic beliefs in science along four dimensions: certainty (stability of scientific knowledge), development (science as an evolving discipline), source (whether knowledge resides in external authorities or can be generated through one's own thinking), and justification (the role of experiments and evidence in evaluating claims). According to the article, 'central epistemic beliefs in the domain of science include beliefs about the certainty, development, source, and justification of knowledge.' Each dimension ranges from naïve to sophisticated stances, with the sophisticated end valuing change, critical evaluation, and evidence-based reasoning.
requirements: Assessment instruments must cover all four dimensions to enable profile identification
constraints: The model was originally developed for students in Grade 5, and Likert-scale assessment may work best when instruments are adapted to specific age groups, particularly for younger participants
target_learners: Elementary to upper secondary school students (Grades 3–12) in science education
target_learning_goals: Development of sophisticated epistemic beliefs about the source, certainty, development, and justification of scientific knowledge
examples: The six integrated studies administered the 26-item Conley et al. (2004) instrument (German version by Urhahne & Hopf, 2004) with subscales for source (5 items), certainty (6 items), development (6 items), and justification (9 items)
key_sources: Julia Schiefer, Peter A. Edelsbrunner, Andrea Bernholt, Nele Kampa, Andreas Nehring. (2022). Epistemic Beliefs in Science—A Systematic Integration of Evidence From Multiple Studies. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09661-w

article_title: Time Management and Achievement Motivation: A Review of What We Know and Directions for Where to Go
citation: Christopher A. Wolters, Anna C. Brady, Hyun Ji Lee. (2025). Time Management and Achievement Motivation: A Review of What We Know and Directions for Where to Go. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10032-4
title: Time management within SRL comprises forethought, performance-phase monitoring, and control strategic processes
description: The review frames time management as a self-regulatory process within SRL, defined as students' strategic efforts to plan, monitor, and regulate when and for how long they engage in academic work. Core processes include goal setting, prioritizing, planning, and time estimation in the forethought phase; monitoring of time passage in the performance phase; and control processes that adjust time allocation. The article states that "Effective goal setting, prioritization, and planning all rely on students' anticipations... of how long it will take to finish academic work." Procrastination is treated as antithetical to time management and indicative of a failure in SRL.
requirements: Students must form expectations about the duration of academic work, though the article notes estimation "can be challenging and fraught with errors"
constraints: No well-established canon of fundamental time management tactics exists, and no widespread standard conceptual definition has been established
target_learners: students in academic contexts from secondary school through post-secondary education
target_learning_goals: effective self-regulated management of academic study time
key_sources: Christopher A. Wolters, Anna C. Brady, Hyun Ji Lee. (2025). Time Management and Achievement Motivation: A Review of What We Know and Directions for Where to Go. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10032-4

article_title: Time Management and Achievement Motivation: A Review of What We Know and Directions for Where to Go
citation: Christopher A. Wolters, Anna C. Brady, Hyun Ji Lee. (2025). Time Management and Achievement Motivation: A Review of What We Know and Directions for Where to Go. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10032-4
title: Research and practice on time management should treat motivation and time management as reciprocally related within SRL
description: The review argues that within SRL, motivation and time management are "expected to be reciprocally and dynamically related processes": motivation energizes strategic time management, while managing time may in turn shape confidence and values. It recommends that future research move beyond cross-sectional bivariate correlations toward longitudinal and experimental designs that can test these reciprocal causal pathways. Practitioners should therefore attend to both motivational beliefs and time management skills rather than treating either in isolation.
requirements: Testing reciprocal pathways requires longitudinal and/or experimental designs rather than cross-sectional correlations
constraints: The review notes only a small proportion of motivation-strategy research has focused on time management, and evidence for each causal path is limited
target_learners: students across academic levels, from secondary school through post-secondary education
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning, effective time management, and adaptive academic motivation
examples: The review highlights cross-lagged findings such as self-efficacy predicting later time management but not vice versa, and time management predicting later intrinsic motivation
key_sources: Christopher A. Wolters, Anna C. Brady, Hyun Ji Lee. (2025). Time Management and Achievement Motivation: A Review of What We Know and Directions for Where to Go. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10032-4

article_title: Unifying the Ability-as-Compensator and Ability-as-Enhancer Hypotheses
citation: Tim Kühl, Benedict C. O. F. Fehringer, Stefan Münzer. (2022). Unifying the Ability-as-Compensator and Ability-as-Enhancer Hypotheses. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09650-5
title: Unifying conceptualization: ability-as-enhancer and ability-as-compensator interactions occupy different ranges of one ability continuum
description: The article proposes a unifying conceptualization in which the ability-as-enhancer and ability-as-compensator aptitude-treatment interactions are 'not necessarily mutually exclusive, but pro[pose]... two different interaction forms' along a broad ability continuum. The ability-as-enhancer interaction results from comparing low-to-medium ability learners, where the optimized visualization's regression line is steeper; the ability-as-compensator interaction results from comparing medium-to-high ability learners, where the optimized design's regression line is flatter. The conceptualization implies the largest difference between visual designs occurs for medium-ability learners.
requirements: Comparisons must be made between different points of a broad ability continuum relative to task demand, with one visualization variant identifiable as optimized and one as suboptimal for the task
constraints: The article notes which format counts as optimized 'depends on the processes that dynamic and static visualizations require and support, respectively'
target_learners: learners with varying spatial ability in multimedia learning settings
target_learning_goals: learning from visualizations in educational materials
examples: Fig. 1 illustrates five possible regression-line forms (a–e) that all represent the same unifying principle across low, medium, and high ability levels
key_sources: Tim Kühl, Benedict C. O. F. Fehringer, Stefan Münzer. (2022). Unifying the Ability-as-Compensator and Ability-as-Enhancer Hypotheses. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09650-5

article_title: Unifying the Ability-as-Compensator and Ability-as-Enhancer Hypotheses
citation: Tim Kühl, Benedict C. O. F. Fehringer, Stefan Münzer. (2022). Unifying the Ability-as-Compensator and Ability-as-Enhancer Hypotheses. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09650-5
title: Analytical approach: regression model with two design dummies and quadratic interaction terms to test the unifying conceptualization
description: The article introduces a multiple regression model in which the aptitude variable enters as a continuous predictor and visual design is coded with two dummy variables, dumOpt and dumSub, each carrying a quadratic interaction term with ability. The relevant coefficients are 'b 41 and b 42 indicating the specific progression of the regression lines presented in Fig. 1', and the five possible coefficient combinations 'can be summarized by the simple hypothesis "b42 > b41" indicating a higher benefit from the optimized visual design than from the suboptimal visual design in the medium ability range'. This approach detects nonlinear interactions that linear moderation tests would miss.
requirements: A continuous ability predictor and treatment coding with two complementary dummy variables so that both design conditions can have nonlinear regression lines
constraints: The article states the low/medium/high labels are illustrative only: 'our verbal descriptions and the illustrations in Figure 1 refer to low, medium, and high ability ranges for illustrative purposes only'
target_learners: researchers analyzing aptitude-treatment interactions in multimedia learning
target_learning_goals: analysis and interpretation of ability-by-design interactions in learning research
examples: In Study 1 the model was tested with a multi-level model with visual design on Level 1 and subjects on Level 2
key_sources: Tim Kühl, Benedict C. O. F. Fehringer, Stefan Münzer. (2022). Unifying the Ability-as-Compensator and Ability-as-Enhancer Hypotheses. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09650-5

article_title: There is an Evidence Crisis in Science Educational Policy
citation: Lin Zhang, Paul A. Kirschner, William W. Cobern, John Sweller. (2022). There is an Evidence Crisis in Science Educational Policy. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09646-1
title: Three-category taxonomy of educational research evidence: program-based studies, randomized controlled studies, and correlational studies
description: The article organizes science education evidence into three research categories with different methodological strengths and different implications for policy. Program-based studies evaluate whole programs with pre-post or business-as-usual designs; controlled studies "alter only one target factor at a time to examine the effectiveness of an instructional procedure over alternatives" using random assignment; correlational studies use large datasets such as TIMSS and PISA to examine associations over large populations. The article argues the three categories yield divergent findings about inquiry-based teaching and that policy should draw on all three.
requirements: Policy recommendations should draw on all three categories rather than a single methodology
constraints: Correlational studies are limited in their capacity to claim causal relationships
Program-based studies cannot attribute program gains to any single instructional component
target_learning_goals: science conceptual and procedural understanding
examples: The article contrasts the KGS and LeTUS program evaluations (program-based) with controlled comparisons of investigation versus explicit instruction and with TIMSS/PISA correlational analyses
key_sources: Lin Zhang, Paul A. Kirschner, William W. Cobern, John Sweller. (2022). There is an Evidence Crisis in Science Educational Policy. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09646-1

article_title: There is an Evidence Crisis in Science Educational Policy
citation: Lin Zhang, Paul A. Kirschner, William W. Cobern, John Sweller. (2022). There is an Evidence Crisis in Science Educational Policy. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09646-1
title: Cognitive load theory account of why explicit instruction outperforms inquiry for novice learners acquiring complex novel information
description: The article invokes cognitive load theory (Sweller et al., 2011, 2019) as a cognitively based theory underpinning explicit, structured instruction. Its assumptions are that humans evolved to obtain novel information from others because this is more efficient than generating it by problem solving; novel information must be processed by a limited capacity, limited duration working memory before transfer to long-term memory; and stored information governs action without known working-memory limits. On this basis the article argues "there never is a justification for engaging in inquiry-based learning or any other pedagogically identical approaches when students need to acquire complex, novel information."
requirements: Applies when students need to acquire complex, novel information
constraints: The article's argument targets acquisition of complex novel information by novices; it does not claim inquiry is never useful for other learning goals
target_learners: novice learners in a complex area
target_learning_goals: acquisition of complex novel information
science conceptual and procedural understanding
examples: The article cites the worked example effect, in which studying worked examples yields superior performance over solving equivalent problems for novices
key_sources: Lin Zhang, Paul A. Kirschner, William W. Cobern, John Sweller. (2022). There is an Evidence Crisis in Science Educational Policy. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09646-1

article_title: There is an Evidence Crisis in Science Educational Policy
citation: Lin Zhang, Paul A. Kirschner, William W. Cobern, John Sweller. (2022). There is an Evidence Crisis in Science Educational Policy. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09646-1
title: Educational standards should represent a balanced view of all available research categories rather than relying on one methodology
description: The article recommends that educational standards and policy documents draw on program-based, randomized controlled, and correlational studies together rather than privileging one category. It argues that "none of them alone should be used to definitively recommend any particular instructional procedure" and that program-based studies should never be the sole evidence base for recommending inquiry-based learning. The concern is not the inclusion of program-based studies but the complete exclusion of controlled studies from standards.
requirements: Policy writers must consider findings from controlled and correlational studies alongside program-based studies
constraints: The article focuses its argument on students' learning of science concepts and procedures, not all possible science learning outcomes
target_learning_goals: science conceptual and procedural understanding
evidence-informed instructional policy
examples: The article documents that NGSS and the 1996 NSES both promoted investigation-based teaching while controlled and correlational findings unfavorable to inquiry were excluded from consideration
key_sources: Lin Zhang, Paul A. Kirschner, William W. Cobern, John Sweller. (2022). There is an Evidence Crisis in Science Educational Policy. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09646-1

article_title: Meta-Bias: A Practical Theory of Motivated Thinking
citation: Gehlbach, H., & Vriesema, C. C. (2018). Meta‐bias: A practical theory of motivated thinking. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-018-9454-6
title: Meta-bias theory: two competing motives derail the default goal of accurate person perception
description: The article proposes an organizing theory in which perceivers default to accurately reading themselves and others, but two meta-biases regularly trump this accuracy motive: a desire for cognitive efficiency and a need to protect or enhance one's sense of self. The authors state that "two competing motives—meta‐biases—often derail this default goal: a desire for cognitive efficiency and a need to protect or enhance one's sense of self." The theory distills large families of person-perception biases into these two motives to make them usable by educators and researchers.
requirements: Perceivers must have a default goal of accurately understanding others and themselves that the two motives can override
constraints: The authors make no claims as to when and where one meta-bias might override the other, and Figure 1 is not necessarily drawn to scale
Generalizability across cultures is flagged as an important area for future research
target_learning_goals: accurate social perspective taking
recognizing and mitigating bias in person perception
examples: The article maps a sample of biases (anchoring and adjusting, stereotyping, fundamental attribution error, availability heuristic, self-serving biases, spotlight effect, naïve realism, confirmation bias, in-group/out-group bias) onto the two motives in Figure 1
key_sources: Gehlbach, H., & Vriesema, C. C. (2018). Meta‐bias: A practical theory of motivated thinking. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-018-9454-6

article_title: Revisiting Picture Functions in Multimedia Testing: A Systematic Narrative Review and Taxonomy Extension
citation: Schewior, L., & Lindner, M. A. (2024). Revisiting Picture Functions in Multimedia Testing: A Systematic Narrative Review and Taxonomy Extension. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09883-0
title: Four-function taxonomy of pictures in multimedia testing (decorative, representational, organizational, informational)
description: The review organizes pictures in test items by their functional relationship to the accompanying text, adapting Levin's MML classification. Decorative pictures "can be loosely associated with the item context but do not display task or solution relevant information"; representational pictures represent part or all of task-relevant text content; organizational pictures support the solution procedure by providing visuospatial structure; and informational pictures "depict information that is essential for the solution of the problem." The review uses this taxonomy to classify 62 studies and proposes simplification and extension in its discussion.
requirements: Pictures must be displayed simultaneously with the text-based problem statement or question in a testing context
constraints: The taxonomy was developed for multimedia testing contexts, not multimedia learning generally
Pictures in the same functional category can vary considerably in abstraction level
target_learning_goals: Accurate measurement of constructs in assessment
Problem-solving performance in testing situations
examples: The review classified 62 studies by picture function with high inter-rater reliability (Cohen's Kappa = 0.957)
key_sources: Schewior, L., & Lindner, M. A. (2024). Revisiting Picture Functions in Multimedia Testing: A Systematic Narrative Review and Taxonomy Extension. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09883-0

article_title: Teachers’ Attitudes Toward Bullying and Intervention Responses: A Systematic and Meta-analytic Review
citation: Dawes, M., Malamut, S. T., Guess, H., & Lohrbach, E. (2024). Teachers' Attitudes Toward Bullying and Intervention Responses: A Systematic and Meta-analytic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09951-5
title: Theory of Planned Behavior applied to teachers' bullying intervention responses
description: The review is guided by the Theory of Planned Behavior (Ajzen), in which "behavior is guided by intentions which are influenced by (1) attitudes toward the behavior, (2) subjective norms, and (3) self-efficacy beliefs." Applied to bullying, teachers' intervention intentions are assumed to be guided by their attitudes toward bullying, subjective norms for intervening, and self-efficacy for intervening. The framework's utility is that each component is assumed malleable and thus targetable through intervention efforts. The review tests the attitude–response link this framework predicts.
requirements: Studies must measure teachers' attitudes toward bullying and an outcome measure assessing teachers' intervention response to bullying, and report the association between them.
constraints: The review addresses the attitude component's association with responses; subjective norms and self-efficacy components are covered by other reviews it cites.
target_learning_goals: responding appropriately to bullying and victimization incidents
key_sources: Dawes, M., Malamut, S. T., Guess, H., & Lohrbach, E. (2024). Teachers' Attitudes Toward Bullying and Intervention Responses: A Systematic and Meta-analytic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09951-5

article_title: Meta-analysis of Interventions for Monitoring Accuracy in Problem Solving
citation: Noortje Janssen · Ard W. Lazonder. (2024). Meta-analysis of Interventions for Monitoring Accuracy in Problem Solving. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09936-4
title: For problem-solving tasks, use whole-task, metacognitive knowledge, or external standard interventions and avoid timing interventions
description: This principle guides educators choosing interventions to improve students' monitoring accuracy in problem-solving tasks. The meta-analysis recommends interventions "addressing the whole task, metacognitive knowledge, and external standards" because these significantly improved monitoring accuracy, while advising educators to "refrain from implementing" timing interventions until further research ascertains their effectiveness.
requirements: The intervention must target monitoring accuracy in problem-solving tasks; effectiveness evidence comes from (quasi-)experimental comparisons against untreated or non-monitoring control conditions.
constraints: Timing interventions adversely affected monitoring accuracy in the included studies, though only two studies tested this type.
Caution is needed when generalizing results to educational practice because each study has unique contextual features.
target_learners: Elementary, secondary, and adult students in formal education
target_learning_goals: Accurate monitoring (calibration) of problem-solving performance
examples: The meta-analysis pooled 35 studies in which interventions such as practice problems (whole task), metacognitive questions during the task, and receiving the correct answer after judgment (external standard) were compared with control conditions.
key_sources: Noortje Janssen · Ard W. Lazonder. (2024). Meta-analysis of Interventions for Monitoring Accuracy in Problem Solving. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09936-4

article_title: Meta-analysis of Interventions for Monitoring Accuracy in Problem Solving
citation: Noortje Janssen · Ard W. Lazonder. (2024). Meta-analysis of Interventions for Monitoring Accuracy in Problem Solving. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09936-4
title: Nelson and Narens' metamemory model as a normative framework for designing monitoring accuracy interventions
description: The article uses Nelson and Narens' (1990) metamemory model, which distinguishes an object level of cognitive processes and a meta level of metacognitive judgment, with monitoring informing the meta level and judgments driving control decisions. The meta-analysis concludes that "Monitoring accuracy can thus be improved by providing support on each component of Nelson and Narens' (1990) metamememory model," suggesting the descriptive model can serve as a normative framework for developing successful instructional interventions.
requirements: Interventions must target components of the monitoring-control loop (learning-task cues, judgment process, or standards) for the model to guide design.
constraints: The model is descriptive; the authors' proposal to use it normatively for intervention research is their own interpretation from this meta-analysis.
target_learners: Students in formal education and adults solving problems
target_learning_goals: Accurate metacognitive monitoring of problem-solving performance
examples: The meta-analysis mapped its six intervention types onto the model: whole-task and knowledge interventions target the object level, while timing, external standard, and training interventions target the meta level's judgment processes.
key_sources: Noortje Janssen · Ard W. Lazonder. (2024). Meta-analysis of Interventions for Monitoring Accuracy in Problem Solving. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09936-4

article_title: What If We Look at the Body? An Embodied Perspective of Collaborative Learning
citation: Juliene Madureira Ferreira. (2021). What If We Look at the Body? An Embodied Perspective of Collaborative Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09607-8
title: Embodied cognition theory as a framework for investigating collaborative learning
description: The review proposes embodied cognition (EC) as a theoretical lens for collaborative learning, holding that 'the only way that the brain talks to the environment is through the body, sensory tissues, and organs.' EC spans moderate approaches based on bodily formats and embodied simulation, radical enactive approaches where perception directly picks up others' mental states, and extended cognition where the cognitive loop encompasses brain, body, and environment. The article argues this lens can reveal how collaboration skills emerge through bodily engagements and intersubjectivity, dimensions regulatory-systems frameworks cannot reach.
requirements: Researchers must acknowledge the brain as embodied, treating sensorimotor experiences as a fundamental unit of analysis in investigating cognitive processes including knowledge construction.
constraints: The article states EC theories do not refute the validity of traditional cognitivist approaches but provide an alternative explanation for how human knowledge is constructed.
target_learners: students in group-based learning from early childhood to higher education
target_learning_goals: collaboration as a transversal competence
knowledge construction in groups
examples: The review applies EC to propose analyzing bodily engagements, nonverbal behaviors, physiological synchrony, and intersubjectivity during face-to-face collaborative tasks.
key_sources: Juliene Madureira Ferreira. (2021). What If We Look at the Body? An Embodied Perspective of Collaborative Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09607-8

article_title: What If We Look at the Body? An Embodied Perspective of Collaborative Learning
citation: Juliene Madureira Ferreira. (2021). What If We Look at the Body? An Embodied Perspective of Collaborative Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09607-8
title: Taxonomy of regulatory frameworks in collaborative learning: from self-regulation to socially shared regulation
description: The review organizes CL research around regulatory systems of learning at individual and group levels. Zimmerman's sociocognitive model conceptualized self-regulated learning (SRL) around essential elements such as time control, goal setting, self-reflection, and self-efficacy. The sociocultural model frames coregulation as 'a transitional process; an ability that starts with the regulations imposed by the teacher and then evolves to the SRL.' The constructionist model addresses socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL), the joint metacognitive regulation among group members, and the situative model adds context and nonverbal behaviors. The article stresses these are 'distinct ways of theorizing and investigating learning process,' not a gradual evolution.
requirements: Each model requires its own analytical unit: individual metacognition for SRL, teacher–learner mediation for coregulation, group dialogue for SSRL, and situated context for the situative model.
constraints: The article notes nonverbal behaviors are still analyzed as a separate aspect of the storyline of events even under the situative approach.
target_learners: students across educational stages working in groups
target_learning_goals: regulation of learning in collaborative tasks
metacognitive and socio-emotional aspects of collaboration
examples: The review traces how SRL research decentralized the teacher's role, how coregulation studies linked socioemotional interactions to self-regulation, and how SSRL research revealed joint metacognition patterns in group dialog.
key_sources: Juliene Madureira Ferreira. (2021). What If We Look at the Body? An Embodied Perspective of Collaborative Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09607-8

article_title: Making the Black Box of Collaborative Learning Transparent: Combining Process-Oriented and Cognitive Load Approaches
citation: Janssen, J., Kirschner, F., Erkens, G., Kirschner, P. A., & Paas, F. (2010). Making the Black Box of Collaborative Learning Transparent: Combining Process-Oriented and Cognitive Load Approaches. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9131-x
title: Groups as information processing systems: a cognitive load account of collaborative learning balancing distribution advantage against transaction costs
description: The article advances a CLT-based account in which collaborating learners are viewed as information processing systems whose task information and associated load "can be divided across multiple collaborating WMs." This distribution advantage means collaborating individuals invest less cognitive effort than individuals learning alone, but interindividual communication and coordination impose transaction costs that can be germane (fostering shared understanding, argumentation, coordination) or extraneous (fostering errors, conflicts, unnecessary duplication). Whether collaboration beats individual learning depends on whether the distribution advantage compensates for extraneous transaction costs.
requirements: Communication and coordination between group members for the load to be divided across a larger reservoir of cognitive capacity
constraints: The article states CLT was developed for individual learning situations and that CLT-based collaborative studies did not monitor or analyze the specific transaction-cost processes
target_learning_goals: complex cognitive task learning
schema construction and automation
examples: The article interprets F. Kirschner et al.'s experiments on task complexity as demonstrating the trade-off between distribution advantage and transaction costs
key_sources: Janssen, J., Kirschner, F., Erkens, G., Kirschner, P. A., & Paas, F. (2010). Making the Black Box of Collaborative Learning Transparent: Combining Process-Oriented and Cognitive Load Approaches. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9131-x

article_title: Association of Teacher Well-Being With Student Motivation and Achievement: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
citation: Dicke, T., Ferber, K., Devine, E., Collie, R., Granziera, H., Parker, P., Guo, J., Marsh, H., et al. (2026). Association of Teacher Well-Being With Student Motivation and Achievement: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10216-6
title: Four-domain taxonomy of teacher well-being and ill-being indicators
description: The review organizes heterogeneous teacher functioning constructs into four theory-informed domains: self-efficacy, teacher motivation, job satisfaction and commitment, and psychological functioning. The authors "grouped individual constructs into four broader categories that reflect common distinctions in the literature". Psychological functioning is defined by a positive criterion — teachers' experienced affective and health-related states and adaptive capacities — and is split into well-being indicators (positive affect, enjoyment, vitality, coping, resilience) and ill-being indicators (stress, burnout, adverse emotional experiences, mental health difficulties), reflecting the view that positive functioning and distress are related but distinct dimensions rather than opposite ends of one continuum.
requirements: Constructs must be mappable to a domain via theoretical alignment and operationalization similarity, as coded in Table 1
constraints: The domains are theory-informed organizing categories rather than mutually exclusive theoretical constructs
The categorization was not preregistered and was derived after screening, so domain comparisons are post hoc
target_learning_goals: teacher functioning as a lever for student motivation and achievement
examples: Table 1 maps search terms such as burnout, self-efficacy, job satisfaction, and coping onto the four domains and the JD-R, Transactional Stress, PERMA, SDT, and Social Cognitive frameworks
key_sources: Dicke, T., Ferber, K., Devine, E., Collie, R., Granziera, H., Parker, P., Guo, J., Marsh, H., et al. (2026). Association of Teacher Well-Being With Student Motivation and Achievement: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10216-6

article_title: Association of Teacher Well-Being With Student Motivation and Achievement: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
citation: Dicke, T., Ferber, K., Devine, E., Collie, R., Granziera, H., Parker, P., Guo, J., Marsh, H., et al. (2026). Association of Teacher Well-Being With Student Motivation and Achievement: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10216-6
title: Classroom-behavior transmission account: teacher well-being relates to student outcomes through teachers' classroom behavior
description: The review's organizing explanatory account holds that teacher well-being is associated with student motivation and achievement indirectly, through teachers' classroom behavior and interactions rather than a direct pathway. The authors write that the frameworks "converge in suggesting that teacher well-being is transmitted to students through teachers' classroom behavior rather than affecting student outcomes directly": within JD-R, personal resources spill over into instructional quality and classroom management; within SDT, need-satisfied teachers adopt autonomy-supportive practices; the prosocial classroom model similarly links well-being to classroom management and teacher–student relationships.
requirements: Plausible explanatory pathways only; the account presupposes that teacher well-being shapes instructional, motivational, and relational practices
constraints: The present review does not directly test mediation
The evidence base is largely correlational, so causal mechanisms and direction of effects remain unclarified
target_learning_goals: student motivation and academic achievement
examples: The review draws on the JD-R model, Transactional Stress Model, SDT, and the PERMA model as complementary organizing lenses for coding and interpretation
key_sources: Dicke, T., Ferber, K., Devine, E., Collie, R., Granziera, H., Parker, P., Guo, J., Marsh, H., et al. (2026). Association of Teacher Well-Being With Student Motivation and Achievement: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10216-6

article_title: Teachers’ Beliefs About Inclusive Education and Insights on What Contributes to Those Beliefs: a Meta-analytical Study
citation: Dignath, C., Rimm-Kaufman, S., van Ewijk, R., & Kunter, M. (2022). Teachers' Beliefs About Inclusive Education and Insights on What Contributes to Those Beliefs: a Meta-analytical Study. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09695-0
title: Three-component model of teachers' belief systems about inclusive education: cognitive appraisals, emotional appraisals, and self-efficacy
description: The article organizes teachers' belief systems about inclusive education into three inter-related components: "teachers' cognitive appraisals (e.g., thoughts), emotional appraisals (e.g., feelings), and self-efficacy (e.g., agency to teach inclusive classrooms)". Drawing on Gregoire's (2003) cognitive-affective model of conceptual change, it treats these components as entangled subcomponents of a dynamic belief system that guides perceptions, interprets incoming information, and acts as a working model of the world. The framework underpins the meta-analysis's three separate syntheses and its claim that beliefs are malleable through training.
requirements: Belief components are measured separately (cognitive appraisals, emotional appraisals, self-efficacy), as the meta-analysis required three separate meta-analyses of standardized mean scores
constraints: The article notes the belief subcomponents are often entangled, and that research on teachers' beliefs about inclusive education differs from research on the effectiveness of inclusive education, which is beyond its scope
target_learning_goals: implementation of inclusive education practices
examples: The meta-analysis quantified each component separately across 102 studies and examined how career point, teacher type, and interventions contribute to each.
key_sources: Dignath, C., Rimm-Kaufman, S., van Ewijk, R., & Kunter, M. (2022). Teachers' Beliefs About Inclusive Education and Insights on What Contributes to Those Beliefs: a Meta-analytical Study. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09695-0

article_title: Integrating Fractions into Physical Education classes can improve Mathematical Performance in 11–13-Year-Olds - The Basketball Mathematics project
citation: Jensen, O. E., Damsgaard, L., Rohde, R. A., Nielsen, G., Fosnaes, O., Hauge, J., Wienecke, J. (2026). Integrating Fractions into Physical Education classes can improve Mathematical Performance in 11–13-Year-Olds - The Basketball Mathematics project. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10175-y
title: Integrate subject-specific academic content into existing PE lessons to strengthen learning without adding instructional hours
description: The article advocates targeted integration of academic content into physical education as an add-in to the regular timetable. It reports that "the structure of the school timetable can be rethought without necessarily adding more hours" and that "with a small change physical education-classes can contribute meaningfully to learning and academic performance." The BM program replaced one weekly PE lesson, keeping total instructional hours constant while adding mathematics practice.
requirements: Integration must be thoughtfully designed and targeted rather than merging all subjects; mathematical content was tailored to each class's proficiency level with input from the mathematics teacher.
constraints: Teachers were instructed not to conduct similar mixed exercises between pre- and post-testing; the authors note alignment between gym and classroom content could have been stronger.
target_learning_goals: fraction understanding
general mathematical performance
examples: One weekly 60-minute BM session replaced regular PE for 8 weeks; each session had an introduction, warm-up, two-three integrated exercises, and a concluding summary, with mathematical themes integrated into basketball drills.
key_sources: Jensen, O. E., Damsgaard, L., Rohde, R. A., Nielsen, G., Fosnaes, O., Hauge, J., Wienecke, J. (2026). Integrating Fractions into Physical Education classes can improve Mathematical Performance in 11–13-Year-Olds - The Basketball Mathematics project. article_title: Integrating Fractions into Physical Education classes can improve Mathematical Performance in 11–13-Year-Olds - The Basketball Mathematics project
citation: Jensen, O. E., Damsgaard, L., Rohde, R. A., Nielsen, G., Fosnaes, O., Hauge, J., Wienecke, J. (2026). Integrating Fractions into Physical Education classes can improve Mathematical Performance in 11–13-Year-Olds - The Basketball Mathematics project. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10175-y
title: Basketball Mathematics (BM) intervention program
description: A play-based 8-week program in which one weekly 60-minute PE lesson combines basketball drills with fraction tasks. "The mathematical theme was seamlessly integrated into the exercises, requiring children to collect and calculate mathematical information during various basketball drills." Sessions mix motor-enriched exercises with high-intensity cardiovascular activities, follow a structured format with a concluding summary, and were delivered by trained instructors with researcher observation. Full materials are published on a project video site and in Supplementary Material 5.
requirements: Delivered within existing PE lessons by trained instructors with mathematical content tailored to class proficiency and aligned with the national curriculum focus on fractions.
constraints: The intervention was originally intended as a shorter, higher-frequency four-week program; the authors suggest higher frequency could allow better scaffolding.
target_learning_goals: fractions
mathematical performance
basketball skills
examples: Weekly themes paired a basketball skill with a fraction topic; children calculated fractions from data they collected themselves during drills.
