article_title: From RAMSing to Rigor: Improving Moderator Analysis in STEM Education Meta-Research
citation: Bicakci, M., Heller, F., Stoeger, H., & Ziegler, A. (2026). From RAMSing to Rigor: Improving Moderator Analysis in STEM Education Meta-Research. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10172-1
title: RAMSing: reporting after moderators are significant
description: RAMSing is the article's name for a selective reporting practice in meta-research: "the practice of conducting multiple moderator tests but reporting only those effect sizes that meet conventional significance thresholds (e.g., p < .05) or exceed conventional effect-size benchmarks (e.g., d = 0.20, d = 0.50), while omitting the remaining results from the published record." It is distinguished from p-hacking, HARKing, and study-level publication bias because it operates within the meta-analysis itself. By suppressing null effect sizes it can inflate apparent explanatory power of moderator analyses, compress effect size distributions, and distort heterogeneity estimates, while obscuring true boundary conditions for theory and practice.
requirements: Detection requires explicit auditing of planned versus reported analyses where available, bias-robust statistical adjustment, and routine reporting of adequately powered moderator tests
constraints: The article notes only about half of moderator analyses are ever published, so observable red flags likely reveal only a subset of the problem
target_learners: researchers in fields relying on meta-analytic moderator evidence
target_learning_goals: Understanding selective reporting bias in moderator analysis
Interpreting moderator evidence with appropriate caution
examples: Full-text screening of more than 100 STEM meta-analyses found indicators including moderators announced in introductions but absent from results, inconsistent summary tables, and vague statements such as "no other moderators were significant" without accompanying statistics
key_sources: Bicakci, M., Heller, F., Stoeger, H., & Ziegler, A. (2026). From RAMSing to Rigor: Improving Moderator Analysis in STEM Education Meta-Research. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10172-1

article_title: From RAMSing to Rigor: Improving Moderator Analysis in STEM Education Meta-Research
citation: Bicakci, M., Heller, F., Stoeger, H., & Ziegler, A. (2026). From RAMSing to Rigor: Improving Moderator Analysis in STEM Education Meta-Research. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10172-1
title: Anti-RAMSing toolkit: annotated R scripts and worked example dataset on OSF
description: The authors developed "a comprehensive toolkit, implemented as fully annotated R scripts and accompanied by a worked example dataset, which is publicly available on the Open Science Framework." Its workflow is explicitly sequential and integrates four components: structural mapping, robust Bayesian meta-analysis and meta-regression (RoBMA-PSMA and RoBMA-Regression), effect-size benchmarking, and prospective power analysis. Once a domain-specific dataset is constructed with the shared coding framework, the toolkit can reproduce the core analytic procedures and extend them to other fields; the structural mapping stage itself depends on systematic qualitative coding and cannot be automated in R.
requirements: A domain-specific dataset constructed using the shared coding framework
Systematic qualitative coding for the structural mapping stage
constraints: The structural mapping stage cannot itself be automated in R because it depends on systematic qualitative coding
target_learners: Researchers in psychology, management, and health sciences conducting moderator analyses
target_learning_goals: Detecting and bias-adjusting selective moderator reporting
Planning adequately powered moderator tests
examples: In the worked example, RoBMA-PSMA used 36 candidate models with default priors, estimation in JAGS with four MCMC chains, and RoBMA-Regression averaged across 72 candidate models
key_sources: Bicakci, M., Heller, F., Stoeger, H., & Ziegler, A. (2026). From RAMSing to Rigor: Improving Moderator Analysis in STEM Education Meta-Research. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10172-1

article_title: From RAMSing to Rigor: Improving Moderator Analysis in STEM Education Meta-Research
citation: Bicakci, M., Heller, F., Stoeger, H., & Ziegler, A. (2026). From RAMSing to Rigor: Improving Moderator Analysis in STEM Education Meta-Research. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10172-1
title: First field-specific structural variable map of STEM education interventions
description: As the toolkit's first stage, the authors "catalogued every co-occurrence of intervention, moderator, and outcome variables in the corpus, generating, to our knowledge, the first field-specific structural variable map of STEM education interventions." Coding across four layers (STEM domain, outcome, intervention, moderator theme) used iterative constant-comparative procedures until theoretical saturation, visualized as an alluvial (Sankey) diagram. The map shows moderator attention is heavily asymmetric: intervention specifications accounted for 41.61% of all moderators and sample/context variables for 23.36%, while study design/quality (10.70%), disciplinary focus (13.55%), and publication metadata (10.81%) received less attention; mathematics dominated the corpus at 49.91% of effect sizes.
requirements: Qualitative coding of interventions, moderators, and outcomes across the literature before quantitative modeling
constraints: The map reflects the 2000–2023 corpus of STEM intervention meta-analyses screened from four databases
target_learning_goals: Auditable moderator selection grounded in the evidence base
Preregisterable, theory-driven moderator sets
examples: The ten most common intervention–moderator–outcome triads accounted for 1,056 of 1,786 effect sizes (59.12%), led by instructional models with intervention-specification moderators and academic outcomes
key_sources: Bicakci, M., Heller, F., Stoeger, H., & Ziegler, A. (2026). From RAMSing to Rigor: Improving Moderator Analysis in STEM Education Meta-Research. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10172-1

article_title: A Systematic Review of Mathematical, Motivational, and Socioemotional Propensities Related to Algebraic Thinking
citation: Silla, E. M., Guba, T.-P., Rodrigues, A., Anisiobi, O. C., Scanniello, A., & Barbieri, C. A. (2026). A Systematic Review of Mathematical, Motivational, and Socioemotional Propensities Related to Algebraic Thinking. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10111-6
title: Opportunity-Propensity model of achievement as the review's organizing framework
description: The review frames student-level factors related to algebra achievement using the Opportunity-Propensity (O-P) model, which 'suggests that multiple factors influence academic achievement, including opportunities for achievement, propensities or student-level characteristics, and antecedents to these opportunities and propensities.' The authors selected it because it 'provides a clear distinction between student-level characteristics (i.e., propensities) and other factors that influence achievement.' They restrict scope to malleable student-level propensities (mathematical and motivational/socioemotional), excluding cognitive, antecedent, and contextual factors.
requirements: The model requires considering propensity factors in conjunction with broader environmental (opportunity and antecedent) factors when interpreting findings about any single factor.
constraints: The review explicitly does not examine cognitive factors such as working memory and executive functioning, nor contextual opportunity factors, focusing solely on mathematical and motivational and/or socioemotional propensities.
target_learners: U.S. students in grades 6-12 taking algebra
target_learning_goals: Algebraic thinking and algebra achievement
examples: The authors used the O-P model to categorize the 61 reviewed studies' factors as propensities, distinguishing them from opportunities such as instructional practices and societal policies.
key_sources: Silla, E. M., Guba, T.-P., Rodrigues, A., Anisiobi, O. C., Scanniello, A., & Barbieri, C. A. (2026). A Systematic Review of Mathematical, Motivational, and Socioemotional Propensities Related to Algebraic Thinking. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10111-6

article_title: A Systematic Review of Mathematical, Motivational, and Socioemotional Propensities Related to Algebraic Thinking
citation: Silla, E. M., Guba, T.-P., Rodrigues, A., Anisiobi, O. C., Scanniello, A., & Barbieri, C. A. (2026). A Systematic Review of Mathematical, Motivational, and Socioemotional Propensities Related to Algebraic Thinking. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10111-6
title: Taxonomy of algebraic thinking operationalizations: global measures versus specific facets
description: The review organizes algebra outcome measures into a taxonomy distinguishing global constructs from specific facets. It states that 'some studies focus on conceptual understanding of algebraic concepts, such as the equal sign, negative sign, variables, and exponents; this is often referred to as algebraic feature knowledge.' Other operationalizations include equation encoding, 'their ability to perceptually process and represent equation structures, components, and terms,' and equation-solving accuracy on linear equations. The review argues propensities 'may be differentially related to algebra understanding depending on the algebra outcome measure used.'
requirements: Studies must use a standalone performance measure of algebra specifically, not a general math measure or course grade.
constraints: The taxonomy was applied to U.S. studies of students in grades 6-12; college algebra was excluded as distinct from secondary education.
target_learners: U.S. middle and high school students (grades 6-12)
target_learning_goals: Algebraic thinking, including algebraic feature knowledge, equation encoding, and equation-solving
examples: Twelve of the 61 reviewed studies measured specific facets of algebra knowledge, with equation-solving and algebraic feature knowledge the most prevalent assessments.
key_sources: Silla, E. M., Guba, T.-P., Rodrigues, A., Anisiobi, O. C., Scanniello, A., & Barbieri, C. A. (2026). A Systematic Review of Mathematical, Motivational, and Socioemotional Propensities Related to Algebraic Thinking. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10111-6

article_title: Social Presence: Conceptualization and Measurement
citation: Karel Kreijns, Kate Xu, Joshua Weidlich. (2022). Social Presence: Conceptualization and Measurement. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09623-8
title: Reformulated definition of social presence as perceived 'realness' of other persons in technology-mediated communication
description: The review reformulates Short et al.'s (1976) definition of social presence, which it finds ambiguous and non-operationalizable because 'salience' admits multiple interpretations. The reformulated definition treats social presence as 'the psychological phenomenon in which, to a certain extent, the others are perceived as physical "real" persons in technology-mediated communication enabled by CMC tools and electronic platforms'. It is a sense of others being present in the here and now even when they are not — 'the illusion of being together with other persons as if the communication is not mediated at all'. This makes 'realness' the underlying latent construct that can be assessed.
requirements: The construct must be operationalized by assessing perceived 'realness' of the other persons, not attitudes toward the communication medium
constraints: The article states the reformulated definition departs from Short et al.'s technological determinism, so realness is not determined solely by medium attributes
target_learners: online distance education learners in group learning settings
target_learning_goals: interpersonal communication and group dynamics in online group learning
examples: The authors ground the reformulation in Short et al.'s own statements that social presence depends on the degree to which the other person is perceived as a 'real' person, including their expectation of three-dimensional electronic reconstitution of distant individuals
key_sources: Karel Kreijns, Kate Xu, Joshua Weidlich. (2022). Social Presence: Conceptualization and Measurement. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09623-8

article_title: Social Presence: Conceptualization and Measurement
citation: Karel Kreijns, Kate Xu, Joshua Weidlich. (2022). Social Presence: Conceptualization and Measurement. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09623-8
title: Triangle model interrelating social presence, sociability, and social space with social interaction at the center
description: The review identifies two constructs closely linked to social presence: sociability, defined as 'the capacity of CMC tools and electronic platforms to allow for the expression of social presence and the experience of it as well as for the emergence of a social space', a medium attribute; and social space, 'the network of interpersonal relationships embedded in group structures of norms and values, rules and roles, and beliefs and ideals', a group attribute manifested by sense of community, group climate, mutual trust, social identity, and group cohesion. The three constructs are shown as a triangle whose sides represent their interrelations, with social interaction at the center, since together they influence how social interaction in groups is established and maintained.
requirements: The three constructs must be treated as interrelated rather than in isolation, because together they influence how social interaction in groups is established and maintained
constraints: The article states most social presence researchers, unaware of sociability and social space, collapse the three constructs into one 'social presence' construct
target_learners: learners in online group learning and learning networks
target_learning_goals: establishing and maintaining social interaction in online groups
examples: Figure 1 visually depicts the triangle with social presence, sociability, and social space as vertices and social interaction positioned in the center
key_sources: Karel Kreijns, Kate Xu, Joshua Weidlich. (2022). Social Presence: Conceptualization and Measurement. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09623-8

article_title: Social Presence: Conceptualization and Measurement
citation: Karel Kreijns, Kate Xu, Joshua Weidlich. (2022). Social Presence: Conceptualization and Measurement. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09623-8
title: Social Presence Measure (Kreijns et al., 2020): a Rasch-validated 27-item two-dimensional measure of perceived 'realness'
description: The review presents the Social Presence Measure of Kreijns et al. (2020) as an instrument that 'operationalizes "realness" of the other persons in the communication in accordance with the reformulated social presence definition'. Rasch analyses were performed to establish construct validity; aiming at a unidimensional measure, the multidimensionality test instead revealed two dimensions, 'awareness of others' (15 items) and 'proximity with others' (12 items), with the former indicating lower and the latter higher perceptions of social presence. It uses five-point Likert scales and requires a conversion table to convert total scores to Rasch person measures.
requirements: A conversion table is needed to convert total scores to Rasch person measures
constraints: The Rasch test for multidimensionality revealed two dimensions rather than the intended unidimensional structure
target_learning_goals: assessing perceived 'realness' of communication partners in online learning
examples: Validation was by Rasch analysis with Cronbach α of 0.92 and 0.94 for the two dimensions (n = 82)
key_sources: Karel Kreijns, Kate Xu, Joshua Weidlich. (2022). Social Presence: Conceptualization and Measurement. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09623-8

article_title: Social Presence: Conceptualization and Measurement
citation: Karel Kreijns, Kate Xu, Joshua Weidlich. (2022). Social Presence: Conceptualization and Measurement. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09623-8
title: Whiteside and Garrett Dickers' Social Presence Model with five components for structuring online and blended courses
description: The review describes the social presence model (SPM) of Whiteside and Garrett Dickers, which sees social presence as 'a critical literacy for cultivating emotions and relationships' that serves an influential role in advancing and sustaining successful, meaningful learning experiences. The model is used to organize the structure of an online or blended course and encompasses five components: affective association, community cohesion, instructor involvement, interaction intensity, and knowledge and experience. The review positions it as a conceptualization that fits neither end of Lowenthal's continuum of social presence definitions.
requirements: The model is used to organize the structure of an online or blended course
constraints: The review notes this model cannot be placed on Lowenthal's social presence continuum because it treats social presence neither as a perception nor as an interpersonal connection
target_learners: students in online or blended courses
target_learning_goals: cultivating emotions and relationships to support meaningful learning experiences
examples: The five components include instructor involvement, defined as encouraging students to participate in higher order thinking and critical inquiry and developing relationships and social connections among students
key_sources: Karel Kreijns, Kate Xu, Joshua Weidlich. (2022). Social Presence: Conceptualization and Measurement. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09623-8

article_title: Practice Recommendations or Not? The LoGeT Model as Empirical Approach to Generate Localized, Generalized, and Transferable Evidence
citation: Lachner, A., Sibley, L., & Wagner, S. (2024). Practice Recommendations or Not? The LoGeT Model as Empirical Approach to Generate Localized, Generalized, and Transferable Evidence. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09876-z
title: The LoGeT model: a three-stage, reciprocal framework integrating co-design, ManyClasses, and transfer strategies
description: The LoGeT model is a methodological framework for generating educational evidence that is localized, generalizable, and transferable. The authors state: "we propose the localize, generalize, and transfer (LoGeT) model to localize, generalize, and transfer scientific evidence for educational practice." It comprises a localization stage (co-design of interventions with teachers via context inquiry, participatory design, product design, and prototype-as-hypothesis phases), a generalization stage (implementing the interventions across diverse subjects, cohorts, and contexts and aggregating results with meta-analytic techniques such as mixed effect models), and a transfer stage (publishing materials as OER and communicating findings through practice-oriented outlets). The model is explicitly reciprocal rather than sequential, so transfer insights feed back into localization and generalization.
requirements: Interdisciplinary design teams including several subject-matter teachers and researchers simultaneously, so abstract design principles are localized in authentic subject-specific teaching experiences
A joint design framework and iterative formative feedback workshops to warrant comparability and implementation fidelity across localized realizations
constraints: Contextual findings from the generalization stage cannot be interpreted as causal, but rather inform future experimental studies
Findings may be confounded by teacher motivation and implementation fidelity because participation depends on motivated teachers
The procedure requires considerable research efforts, infrastructure, funding for teachers, and professionals for science communication
target_learners: School students across subjects and school types
target_learning_goals: Effectiveness of instructional interventions across instructional contexts
Evidence-based design and transfer of educational interventions
examples: Three long-term projects applied the model: a TPACK teacher-education project with five design teams, a 4-year adaptive-teaching project at comprehensive schools, and a minimal-invasive non-interactive teaching project in a master's program.
key_sources: Lachner, A., Sibley, L., & Wagner, S. (2024). Practice Recommendations or Not? The LoGeT Model as Empirical Approach to Generate Localized, Generalized, and Transferable Evidence. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09876-z

article_title: Practice Recommendations or Not? The LoGeT Model as Empirical Approach to Generate Localized, Generalized, and Transferable Evidence
citation: Lachner, A., Sibley, L., & Wagner, S. (2024). Practice Recommendations or Not? The LoGeT Model as Empirical Approach to Generate Localized, Generalized, and Transferable Evidence. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09876-z
title: Design transfer products co-constructively and early, using formative testing to foster acceptance and adoption
description: Within the LoGeT model's transfer stage, evidence and interventions are processed and published so other stakeholders can adopt them, with transfer activities planned from the outset and outputs tailored to the targeted audience (compact summaries, intervention descriptions, OER materials; print, multimedia, social media formats). The article recommends that "co-constructive, formative design and testing could contribute to the acceptance and adoption of the different transfer products," and suggests presentation in application-related specialist outlets and practice-related conferences. In the example projects, materials were published as OER in repositories and scaled through professional networks and practice journals.
requirements: Transfer activities considered early in the localization and generalization stages
Professionals to effectively communicate the obtained evidence
constraints: Cascade-transfer strategies via clearing houses may create a natural bottleneck for in-time, state-of-the-art evidence
OER materials vary greatly in quality and may not integrate empirical research testing their effectiveness
target_learners: Schools not participating in the original design studies
target_learning_goals: Adoption of evidence-based instructional practices in educational practice
examples: The TPACK and adaptive-teaching projects published materials as OER in repositories; non-interactive teaching findings were incorporated into federal professional development programs and short explanation videos for German teachers.
key_sources: Lachner, A., Sibley, L., & Wagner, S. (2024). Practice Recommendations or Not? The LoGeT Model as Empirical Approach to Generate Localized, Generalized, and Transferable Evidence. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09876-z

article_title: The Development of Cognitive Load Theory: Replication Crises and Incorporation of Other Theories Can Lead to Theory Expansion
citation: John Sweller. (2023). The Development of Cognitive Load Theory: Replication Crises and Incorporation of Other Theories Can Lead to Theory Expansion. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09817-2
title: Current cognitive load theory: biologically secondary knowledge, limited working memory, vast long-term memory, and element interactivity determining intrinsic and extraneous load
description: The article outlines the current version of cognitive load theory, which is 'concerned with the acquisition of biologically secondary knowledge and is based on the cognitive architecture associated with the acquisition of such knowledge'. Novel information is processed by a working memory with severe capacity and duration limits and stored in long-term memory with no known limits. Element interactivity determines working memory load: high interactivity yields intrinsic cognitive load, while presentation-driven complexity yields extraneous load that instruction should minimise.
requirements: Instruction must be designed to minimise or eliminate extraneous cognitive load
The theory applies to biologically secondary knowledge that requires explicit teaching
constraints: Germane cognitive load is no longer considered an independent source of load
Element interactivity cannot be accurately measured because it relies on knowledge of the exact contents of long-term memory, but it can be estimated
target_learners: students acquiring biologically secondary knowledge in educational institutions
target_learning_goals: acquisition of biologically secondary knowledge such as reading, writing, and mathematics
key_sources: John Sweller. (2023). The Development of Cognitive Load Theory: Replication Crises and Incorporation of Other Theories Can Lead to Theory Expansion. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09817-2

article_title: The Development of Cognitive Load Theory: Replication Crises and Incorporation of Other Theories Can Lead to Theory Expansion
citation: John Sweller. (2023). The Development of Cognitive Load Theory: Replication Crises and Incorporation of Other Theories Can Lead to Theory Expansion. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09817-2
title: Incorporation of Geary's biologically primary versus secondary knowledge distinction into cognitive load theory
description: The article incorporates Geary's categorisation of knowledge into biologically primary knowledge, which humans have evolved to acquire easily and unconsciously through immersion, and biologically secondary knowledge, which culture deems important and which requires conscious effort and explicit teaching. The author states that 'The incorporation of Geary's distinction between biologically primary and secondary knowledge has considerably strengthened the cognitive architecture that underlies cognitive load theory.' This distinction explains why minimal-guidance discovery approaches, which assume school learning proceeds like primary acquisition, conflict with randomised controlled trial results favouring explicit instruction for school-based material.
requirements: Educational institutions and explicit instruction are needed for biologically secondary knowledge because it is not acquired automatically
constraints: The theory's instructional procedures apply to biologically secondary knowledge, not to biologically primary knowledge acquired through species-typical childhood behaviours
target_learners: students in formal educational institutions acquiring biologically secondary knowledge
target_learning_goals: explicit instruction of biologically secondary knowledge such as reading, writing, and mathematics
examples: The article notes that randomised controlled trials on the worked example effect showed novice learners studying worked examples frequently proved superior to solving the equivalent problems, the reverse of what discovery learning advocates expected
key_sources: John Sweller. (2023). The Development of Cognitive Load Theory: Replication Crises and Incorporation of Other Theories Can Lead to Theory Expansion. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09817-2

article_title: The Development of Cognitive Load Theory: Replication Crises and Incorporation of Other Theories Can Lead to Theory Expansion
citation: John Sweller. (2023). The Development of Cognitive Load Theory: Replication Crises and Incorporation of Other Theories Can Lead to Theory Expansion. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09817-2
title: Analogy between human cognition and evolution by natural selection as natural information-processing systems underpinning cognitive load theory
description: The article proposes that the information processing characteristics of human cognitive architecture and evolution by natural selection are analogous, with both constituting natural information-processing systems. Problem solving corresponds to random generation and test analogous to random mutation, learning from others corresponds to reproduction, working memory corresponds to the epigenetic system, and long-term memory corresponds to the unlimited genetic code. The author argues this analogy strengthens the theory's base and underpins the emphasis on building stores of information in long-term memory as the major aim of instruction.
requirements: The analogy's validity is conditional: the article states that if the analogy is valid, the factors relevant to instructional design can be refined
constraints: The article presents this as an analogy whose validity is asserted rather than experimentally tested in this essay
target_learning_goals: building stores of relevant information in long-term memory for later use
examples: The article maps each cognitive component onto an evolutionary counterpart, e.g. retrieval from long-term memory to govern action is analogous to the epigenetic system using environmental cues to turn genes on or off
key_sources: John Sweller. (2023). The Development of Cognitive Load Theory: Replication Crises and Incorporation of Other Theories Can Lead to Theory Expansion. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09817-2

article_title: Interventions as Probes of Cognitive Architecture: Commentary on Zhang et al. (2026)
citation: David Moreau, Kristina Wiebels. (2026). Interventions as Probes of Cognitive Architecture: Commentary on Zhang et al. (2026). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10150-7
title: Perturbation-based framework: structured interventions as diagnostic probes of cognitive architecture
description: The article advances a framework in which interventions that alter physiological or motivational states in predictable ways serve as diagnostic tools for probing the organization of cognitive systems, analogous to lesion studies and pharmacological or stimulation manipulations. Its core inferential logic is that "What unites these approaches is not the severity of the manipulation, but its structured nature." When constructs change in parallel, shared mechanisms are implicated; when they decouple, claims of functional unity are weakened. Null effects and selective effects are both treated as theoretically informative outputs of this framework.
requirements: Perturbations must alter broad physiological or motivational states in predictable ways so researchers can observe which cognitive functions covary and which remain stable
constraints: Frequentist null effects do not constitute affirmative evidence for invariance; the framework's inferences require methodologically sound conditions where change would otherwise be plausible
target_learning_goals: understanding how executive processes are recruited and expressed during instruction
examples: The commentary interprets Zhang et al. (2026)'s dissociation between a mathematics-specific negative priming task and the Flanker task through this framework, with the logic summarized schematically in Fig. 1.
key_sources: David Moreau, Kristina Wiebels. (2026). Interventions as Probes of Cognitive Architecture: Commentary on Zhang et al. (2026). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10150-7

article_title: Interventions as Probes of Cognitive Architecture: Commentary on Zhang et al. (2026)
citation: David Moreau, Kristina Wiebels. (2026). Interventions as Probes of Cognitive Architecture: Commentary on Zhang et al. (2026). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10150-7
title: Measurement local optima: canonical executive function tasks may reflect measurement inertia rather than genuine invariance
description: The article argues that operationalizations of psychological constructs settle into "local optima": "definitions that are reliable, interpretable, and widely accepted, yet not necessarily epistemically optimal for addressing all theoretical questions." Canonical tasks like the Flanker and Stroop are optimized for reliability, comparability, and stable individual differences, which can reduce sensitivity to transient, state-based perturbations. Apparent stability under perturbation may therefore reflect properties of the measurement instrument rather than genuine invariance of the underlying process.
requirements: Detecting measurement inertia requires deploying canonical tasks alongside alternative, context-aligned operationalizations within the same study
constraints: The article notes the observed sensitivity of the domain-aligned measure could reflect idiosyncratic task-specific measurement properties rather than construct-level differences
target_learning_goals: refining construct definitions and measurement of executive function in learning contexts
examples: The mathematics-specific negative priming task in Zhang et al. (2026) is presented as an alternative operationalization that prioritizes alignment with instructional content over generality.
key_sources: David Moreau, Kristina Wiebels. (2026). Interventions as Probes of Cognitive Architecture: Commentary on Zhang et al. (2026). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10150-7

article_title: Interventions as Probes of Cognitive Architecture: Commentary on Zhang et al. (2026)
citation: David Moreau, Kristina Wiebels. (2026). Interventions as Probes of Cognitive Architecture: Commentary on Zhang et al. (2026). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10150-7
title: Design interventions to maximize theoretical insight, not only efficacy
description: The article proposes that when interventions are leveraged as probes of cognitive architecture, their design should prioritize interpretability alongside feasibility. It enumerates principles: "First, temporal specificity is critical." — aligning assessment timing with the perturbation's time course; treating content alignment between intervention context and measurement as a design variable; combining broad perturbations with specific measurement; and anticipating null effects in the inferential framework. Dissociations across aligned and non-aligned measures provide direct evidence about contextual recruitment of cognitive processes.
requirements: Cognitive assessment must be aligned with the expected time course of the perturbation, and measures must be sufficiently challenging to engage the processes of interest
constraints: When task demands are too low, even well-aligned measures may fail to reveal modulation
target_learners: school-aged learners in authentic classroom settings
target_learning_goals: mapping which cognitive processes are modifiable, under what conditions, and at what timescales
examples: Brief exercise embedded into classroom routines without altering instructional content, paired with measures differing in instructional alignment, as in Zhang et al. (2026).
key_sources: David Moreau, Kristina Wiebels. (2026). Interventions as Probes of Cognitive Architecture: Commentary on Zhang et al. (2026). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10150-7

article_title: Interventions as Probes of Cognitive Architecture: Commentary on Zhang et al. (2026)
citation: David Moreau, Kristina Wiebels. (2026). Interventions as Probes of Cognitive Architecture: Commentary on Zhang et al. (2026). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10150-7
title: Dynamic, context-sensitive view of cognition: classrooms as contexts where cognitive processes are selectively recruited
description: The article argues for viewing cognition as dynamic and context-sensitive, in which "classrooms are contexts in which cognitive processes are selectively recruited, constrained, and expressed." Ecological complexity is treated as a source of theoretical leverage rather than a confound to be controlled away. On this view, executive processes are conditionally recruited as a function of task context and representational demands, which is more consistent with the selective exercise effects than accounts treating executive function as a unitary, globally malleable capacity.
requirements: Interventions embedded within authentic educational settings, paired with theoretically aligned measurement, to reveal how cognitive systems function in practice
constraints: The article states the present findings do not adjudicate decisively between competing frameworks; they only help place constraints on theories predicting broad, content-independent modulation
target_learners: students learning within structured classroom activities
target_learning_goals: understanding how cognitive control is expressed in authentic instructional contexts
examples: Zhang et al. (2026) observed a differential pattern of effects that would likely remain invisible under more abstract or decontextualized testing conditions.
key_sources: David Moreau, Kristina Wiebels. (2026). Interventions as Probes of Cognitive Architecture: Commentary on Zhang et al. (2026). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10150-7

article_title: Linking Language Attitudes to Proficiency Across Learning Contexts: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Correlational Evidence
citation: Maria Adelina Ianos, Andrei Rusu, Ramona Paloş, Cristina Petreñas, Clara Sansó. (2026). Linking Language Attitudes to Proficiency Across Learning Contexts: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Correlational Evidence. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10193-w
title: Four-object taxonomy of language attitudes (language, speakers, learning, learning situation)
description: The article organizes language attitudes as an umbrella term covering four distinct attitude objects: "attitudes toward the language itself, (2) attitudes toward its speakers, (3) attitudes toward learning the language, and (4) attitudes toward the language learning situation." Evaluations of a language concern its perceived value or aesthetic qualities, while evaluations of speakers involve social judgements tied to group identity; the language–culture discrepancy hypothesis supports their non-interchangeability. The meta-analysis is the first to test all four objects against proficiency systematically.
requirements: Attitude-object measures must specify which object is targeted, since the objects have often been conflated although they are not interchangeable
constraints: The learning-situation category contained only three effects from two clusters, precluding reliable subgroup inference in the meta-analysis
target_learners: language learners in foreign-language and local-language contexts
target_learning_goals: understanding how affective factors relate to language proficiency
designing language education policies that foster favorable language attitudes
examples: The meta-analysis decomposed 132 effect sizes by the four attitude objects, with attitudes toward the language (k = 93) the most studied category
key_sources: Maria Adelina Ianos, Andrei Rusu, Ramona Paloş, Cristina Petreñas, Clara Sansó. (2026). Linking Language Attitudes to Proficiency Across Learning Contexts: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Correlational Evidence. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10193-w

article_title: Re-Experiencing vs. Self-Explaining: Comparing Generative Learning Activities in VR
citation: Valdemar Stenberdt, Ban Mouid Shiwalia, Guido Makransky. (2025). Re-Experiencing vs. Self-Explaining: Comparing Generative Learning Activities in VR. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10096-2
title: Re-experiencing: a generative learning activity in which learners watch a 3D VR replay of their own past performance to engage visualizing and enacting modes
description: Re-experiencing is a newly conceptualized generative learning activity in which a learner is recorded performing a task and then rewatchs the recording in immersive VR, shifting "from being the one carrying out a task to being a reflective observer". Building on the generative sense-making framework, it is designed to engage the visualizing mode (the replay provides visual material as an instructional scaffold) and the enacting mode (learners can move freely, watch from any angle, and mimic the replay), while reducing the extraneous load of recalling past actions. The replay pauses at mistakes and displays temporally aligned feedback on a wrist info screen.
requirements: An immersive VR implementation that records the learner's performance and replays it in 3D with free movement and a first-person embodied perspective
Corrective feedback that can be temporally aligned with mistakes in the replay
constraints: The article notes re-experiencing is not restricted to immersive VR lessons, but the study's implementation builds on technological features of the VR medium
Expected benefits rest on the affordances of agency, presence, and embodiment as theorized, not directly manipulated
target_learners: high school students learning laboratory procedures
target_learning_goals: procedural and motor skills such as pipetting
reflection on and improvement of one's own performance
examples: In the study, students assigned re-experiencing watched a replay of their first pipetting task in VR, with the corrective feedback visible on a clipboard and mistake-specific feedback shown on a wrist info screen as the replay paused at each mistake.
key_sources: Valdemar Stenberdt, Ban Mouid Shiwalia, Guido Makransky. (2025). Re-Experiencing vs. Self-Explaining: Comparing Generative Learning Activities in VR. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10096-2

article_title: Learning Foreign Language Vocabulary with Gestures and Pictures Enhances Vocabulary Memory for Several Months Post-Learning in Eight-Year-Old School Children
citation: Andrä, C., Mathias, B., Schwager, A., Macedonia, M., & von Kriegstein, K. (2020). Learning Foreign Language Vocabulary with Gestures and Pictures Enhances Vocabulary Memory for Several Months Post-Learning in Eight-Year-Old School Children. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09527-z
title: Enrich auditorily presented L2 vocabulary with self-performed gestures or pictures to boost children's vocabulary memory over months
description: The article supports enriching foreign-language vocabulary instruction with semantically congruent gestures performed by the children themselves, or with pictures, rather than audio-only learning. In three classroom experiments, both enrichment types "enhanced children 's test performance compared with non-enriched learning," with benefits persisting up to 6 months. Training involved 5 consecutive days of short blocks in ordinary primary school classrooms.
requirements: Auditory presentation of L2 words paired with their L1 translations
Gestures must be semantically congruent (iconic) with word meanings and performed by the children
Repeated training over multiple consecutive days with counterbalanced conditions
constraints: Benefits were demonstrated in 8-year-old German third-graders learning English nouns in a movement-oriented school
Gesture enrichment did not outperform picture enrichment in children, unlike in adults
Overall test accuracy was low relative to the number of stimuli in Experiment 1
target_learners: Primary school children (grade three, around 8 years old)
target_learning_goals: Foreign language (L2) vocabulary acquisition and long-term retention
examples: Children heard English words, their German translations, and repetitions while viewing gesture videos or pictures, then performed gestures or recited words with their teacher over 5 days
Tests were free recall, German-English, and English-German translation administered orally at 3 days, 2 months, and 6 months post-learning
key_sources: Andrä, C., Mathias, B., Schwager, A., Macedonia, M., & von Kriegstein, K. (2020). Learning Foreign Language Vocabulary with Gestures and Pictures Enhances Vocabulary Memory for Several Months Post-Learning in Eight-Year-Old School Children. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09527-z

article_title: How to Optimize Self-Assessment Accuracy in Cognitive Skill Acquisition When Learning from Worked Examples
citation: Waldeyer, J., Endres, T., Roelle, J., Baars, M., & Renkl, A. (2024). How to Optimize Self-Assessment Accuracy in Cognitive Skill Acquisition When Learning from Worked Examples. Educational Psychology Review, 36, 103. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09944-4
title: Cue-utilization framework of self-assessment
description: The article adopts the cue-utilization framework (attributed to Koriat) as its theoretical model of how learners form self-assessments and why these are often inaccurate. According to the article, "learners infer their self-assessments from cues, which they can monitor during learning", such as solution fluency, retrievability, or interest. Accuracy is thought to depend on how diagnostic the utilized cues are in the given context, so inaccurate self-assessments are assumed to result from monitoring cues of low diagnosticity. The study applies this framework by manipulating which cue learners are prompted to monitor during the initial problem-solving phase of worked-example learning.
requirements: Learners must be able to monitor the relevant cue during learning, as the framework assumes cues are monitored while learning proceeds.
constraints: The article notes the diagnosticity of a cue is context-dependent, so a cue that is diagnostic in one setting may be misleading in another, such as shallowly solved problems.
target_learners: university students in self-regulated example-based learning
target_learning_goals: accurate self-assessment of one's level of understanding during cognitive skill acquisition
examples: The experiments prompted learners to infer self-assessments either from how well they solved the four problems or from how well they could explain how the problems are solved.
key_sources: Waldeyer, J., Endres, T., Roelle, J., Baars, M., & Renkl, A. (2024). How to Optimize Self-Assessment Accuracy in Cognitive Skill Acquisition When Learning from Worked Examples. Educational Psychology Review, 36, 103. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09944-4

article_title: How to Optimize Self-Assessment Accuracy in Cognitive Skill Acquisition When Learning from Worked Examples
citation: Waldeyer, J., Endres, T., Roelle, J., Baars, M., & Renkl, A. (2024). How to Optimize Self-Assessment Accuracy in Cognitive Skill Acquisition When Learning from Worked Examples. Educational Psychology Review, 36, 103. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09944-4
title: Four-stage model of cognitive skill acquisition through the worked-example approach
description: The article describes the worked-example approach as a procedure that "usually involves four stages" of cognitive skill acquisition. In Stage 1 learners receive instructional explanations communicating basic knowledge of principles and concepts; in Stage 2 they study worked examples with self-explanation prompts; in Stage 3 they turn to initial problem-solving, which deepens understanding and can serve self-assessment; in Stage 4 they practice extensively to enhance problem-solving speed and accuracy. The first three stages correspond to the early and intermediate phases of skill acquisition, focused on understanding the rationale of solutions, while Stage 4 corresponds to the late phase focused on efficiency. The present study targets the transition out of Stage 3, where accurate self-assessment decides whether learners restudy examples or proceed.
requirements: Learners navigating the sequence in a self-regulated manner must accurately self-assess their level of understanding after initial problem-solving to decide whether to proceed to Stage 4.
constraints: The article states it is generally unclear how many problems learners need to solve at what times to effectively consolidate the acquired schemata in Stage 4.
target_learners: learners acquiring cognitive skills through example-based learning, such as university students learning mathematical urn model problems
target_learning_goals: understanding the rationale of solution procedures
enhancing speed and accuracy of problem-solving
examples: The experiments implemented Stages 1–3 with instructional explanations, four worked examples with self-explanation prompts, and four problems to solve before self-assessment.
key_sources: Waldeyer, J., Endres, T., Roelle, J., Baars, M., & Renkl, A. (2024). How to Optimize Self-Assessment Accuracy in Cognitive Skill Acquisition When Learning from Worked Examples. Educational Psychology Review, 36, 103. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09944-4

article_title: How to Optimize Self-Assessment Accuracy in Cognitive Skill Acquisition When Learning from Worked Examples
citation: Waldeyer, J., Endres, T., Roelle, J., Baars, M., & Renkl, A. (2024). How to Optimize Self-Assessment Accuracy in Cognitive Skill Acquisition When Learning from Worked Examples. Educational Psychology Review, 36, 103. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09944-4
title: Inform learners about the to-be-monitored self-assessment cue before, not after, the problem-solving phase
description: When learners must self-assess their understanding at the end of an initial problem-solving phase, tell them at the start of that phase which cue they should monitor for their self-assessment. In Experiment 1, learners "informed about the to-be-monitored cue already before the problem-solving phase showed better self-assessment accuracy" than learners informed only afterwards, apparently because attending to the cue during problem-solving is less error-prone than reconstructing it afterwards. The authors found no evidence that this advance information overloaded learners or compromised problem-solving.
requirements: Learners must be told the specific cue (e.g., problem-solving performance or ability to explain) they will later use for their self-assessment.
constraints: The benefit was shown when mental effort was relatively low (M = 5.37 on a 9-point scale); the article notes high cognitive load could in principle compromise performance or lead learners to disengage from monitoring.
target_learners: university students in self-regulated example-based learning
target_learning_goals: accurate self-assessment of understanding after initial problem-solving
examples: In Experiment 1, learners in the before conditions received instructions such as "please pay attention to how well you can solve the problems" at the start of the problem-solving phase, with the note "You will need this information afterwards."
key_sources: Waldeyer, J., Endres, T., Roelle, J., Baars, M., & Renkl, A. (2024). How to Optimize Self-Assessment Accuracy in Cognitive Skill Acquisition When Learning from Worked Examples. Educational Psychology Review, 36, 103. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09944-4

article_title: Cracking Chicken-Egg Conundrums: Juxtaposing Contemporaneous and Lagged Reciprocal Effects Models of Academic Self-Concept and Achievement’s Directional Ordering
citation: Marsh, H. W., Guo, J., Pekrun, R., Lüdtke, O., & Núñez-Regueiro, F. (2024). Cracking Chicken-Egg Conundrums: Juxtaposing Contemporaneous and Lagged Reciprocal Effects Models of Academic Self-Concept and Achievement's Directional Ordering. Educational Psychology Review, 36. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09887-w
title: Taxonomy of causality theories: sequential, simultaneous, and reciprocal
description: The article organizes philosophical, theological, and scientific perspectives on causation into three families relevant to interpreting cross-lagged panel models. "Sequential theories of causation posit that causes and effects are temporally distinct, with causes preceding effects" — the traditional Western view from Aristotle onward and the default in psychological research. Simultaneous theories (from Nagarjuna and Dogen to Descartes, Kant, and Cramer's transactional interpretation) allow cause and effect to co-occur. "Reciprocal causation occurs when two or more variables mutually influence each other, forming a causal loop", combining bidirectionality with temporal ordering. The article uses this taxonomy to motivate testing lag0 alongside lag1 and lag2 paths.
requirements: Testing reciprocal directional ordering requires both constructs measured across at least two, preferably three or more, waves of data
constraints: The article adheres to a Granger predictive-causality perspective, under which truly instantaneous lag0 effects might not fit as prospective effects
target_learning_goals: understanding directional ordering of academic self-concept and achievement
examples: The article illustrates time-interval dependence with Gollob and Reichardt's aspirin example: no effect in 2 minutes, maximum effect after several hours, little effect after 24 hours
key_sources: Marsh, H. W., Guo, J., Pekrun, R., Lüdtke, O., & Núñez-Regueiro, F. (2024). Cracking Chicken-Egg Conundrums: Juxtaposing Contemporaneous and Lagged Reciprocal Effects Models of Academic Self-Concept and Achievement's Directional Ordering. Educational Psychology Review, 36. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09887-w

article_title: Cracking Chicken-Egg Conundrums: Juxtaposing Contemporaneous and Lagged Reciprocal Effects Models of Academic Self-Concept and Achievement’s Directional Ordering
citation: Marsh, H. W., Guo, J., Pekrun, R., Lüdtke, O., & Núñez-Regueiro, F. (2024). Cracking Chicken-Egg Conundrums: Juxtaposing Contemporaneous and Lagged Reciprocal Effects Models of Academic Self-Concept and Achievement's Directional Ordering. Educational Psychology Review, 36. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09887-w
title: Reciprocal effects model (REM) of academic self-concept and achievement
description: The REM is the article's substantive explanatory framework, integrating the earlier skill-development model (prior achievement leads to subsequent self-concept) and self-enhancement model (prior self-concept leads to subsequent achievement) into one bidirectional account. Marsh "argued for a reciprocal model of effects whereby better ASCs lead to better achievement, and better achievement leads to better ASCs." Support for the skill-development path is described as well-established, so the critical issue is the self-enhancement path. The framework underpins the article's a priori hypotheses and its claim that interventions should concurrently enhance self-concept and achievement.
requirements: Longitudinal panel data with multiple waves of both constructs, and statistical models whose assumptions are made explicit
constraints: Causal interpretations from longitudinal correlational models remain susceptible to third-variable confounding, as the article notes citing Wu et al.'s caution
target_learning_goals: academic self-concept and mathematics achievement development
examples: The article cites meta-analyses (Huang 2011; Valentine et al. 2004; Wu et al. 2021) as extensive support for REM predictions, nearly all based on traditional lag1-only CLPMs
key_sources: Marsh, H. W., Guo, J., Pekrun, R., Lüdtke, O., & Núñez-Regueiro, F. (2024). article_title: Cracking Chicken-Egg Conundrums: Juxtaposing Contemporaneous and Lagged Reciprocal Effects Models of Academic Self-Concept and Achievement’s Directional Ordering
citation: Marsh, H. W., Guo, J., Pekrun, R., Lüdtke, O., & Núñez-Regueiro, F. (2024). Cracking Chicken-Egg Conundrums: Juxtaposing Contemporaneous and Lagged Reciprocal Effects Models of Academic Self-Concept and Achievement's Directional Ordering. Educational Psychology Review, 36. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09887-w
title: Taxonomy of reciprocal effect panel models: CLPM, RI-CLPM, PCPM, and CCLPM with lag0, lag1, and lag2 effects
description: The article's methodological contribution is a taxonomy of structural equation models for directional ordering, extending Muthén and Asparouhov's contemporaneous-effects models with latent measurement factors, lag2 paths, random intercepts, and covariate strategies. "We focus on four basic models (Fig. 2): CLPMs (lag1 effects; no RI; no lag0 effects), RI-CLPMs (with lag1 and RI effects, but no lag0 effects), pure contemporaneous panel models with only contemporaneous effects (PCPM; RI and lag0 effects, but no lag1 cross-paths), and reciprocal models (RI-CCLPM; RI, lag0 and lag1 effects)." Lag0 paths are reciprocal paths within each wave; lag2 paths link non-adjacent waves. The models were fit to five annual waves of PALMA data.
requirements: Three or more waves of data for models combining lag0 and lag1 reciprocal paths, since two waves do not identify them; parsimonious constrained versions to circumvent convergence issues
constraints: Models with both lag0 and lag1 effects may have convergence problems; residual covariances were excluded from fully reciprocal models following Muthén and Asparouhov's recommendation
Models without lag2 effects make the critical, typically untested assumption that lag2 paths are zero, which can bias estimates
target_learning_goals: directional ordering of academic self-concept and achievement
examples: Covariate effects were modeled either via paths to global trait (RI) factors or directly to measurement factors, with invariance of covariate effects over time testable in the latter

article_title: Cracking Chicken-Egg Conundrums: Juxtaposing Contemporaneous and Lagged Reciprocal Effects Models of Academic Self-Concept and Achievement’s Directional Ordering
citation: Marsh, H. W., Guo, J., Pekrun, R., Lüdtke, O., & Núñez-Regueiro, F. (2024). Cracking Chicken-Egg Conundrums: Juxtaposing Contemporaneous and Lagged Reciprocal Effects Models of Academic Self-Concept and Achievement's Directional Ordering. Educational Psychology Review, 36. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09887-w
title: Juxtapose results from competing panel models rather than selecting a single best model by goodness-of-fit
description: The article recommends that longitudinal model evaluation rest on substantive interpretation alongside fit indices, following Muthén and Asparouhov's advice. Because alternative models may be formally equivalent or hard to distinguish by fit, "conclusions should be based on the juxtaposition of different results rather than selecting a single "best" model based on goodness-of-fit" when competing models each support a priori theory-based hypotheses. Researchers should report results from competing models and consider more parsimonious constrained versions when convergence problems arise.
requirements: A priori theory-based hypotheses to differentiate models whose fit is similar, and reporting of results from multiple competing models
constraints: Convergence problems are common in fully reciprocal lag0-plus-lag1 models, so parsimonious versions constraining non-significant parameters may be needed
target_learning_goals: valid causal-ordering inference from longitudinal panel data
examples: The article fit CLPM, RI-CLPM, PCPM, RI-CCLPM and lag2 variants to the PALMA data and interpreted them jointly rather than choosing one winner

article_title: Cracking Chicken-Egg Conundrums: Juxtaposing Contemporaneous and Lagged Reciprocal Effects Models of Academic Self-Concept and Achievement’s Directional Ordering
citation: Marsh, H. W., Guo, J., Pekrun, R., Lüdtke, O., & Núñez-Regueiro, F. (2024). Cracking Chicken-Egg Conundrums: Juxtaposing Contemporaneous and Lagged Reciprocal Effects Models of Academic Self-Concept and Achievement's Directional Ordering. Educational Psychology Review, 36. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09887-w
title: Treat tests of contemporaneous (lag0) effects as a sensitivity analysis of whether panel-design time intervals are appropriate
description: Because effect sizes vary with the interval between measurement waves and there is no optimal interval, the article proposes testing lag0 paths within each wave as a practical check on design. "Tests of contemporaneous (lag0) effect in CLPMs are heuristic and offer a practical sensitivity analysis of whether the research design is based on appropriate time intervals." Significant lag0 effects may not be truly instantaneous but may signal that effects occur between waves, motivating shorter intervals; researchers should consider alternative intervals since failure to find lagged effects at one interval does not preclude effects at others.
requirements: Multi-wave panel data allowing both within-wave (lag0) and between-wave (lag1, lag2) reciprocal paths, and theoretical reasoning about the causal processes' temporality
constraints: Significant lag0 effects might reflect proximal events between waves rather than truly instantaneous causation; testing ever-shorter intervals with new data collections may not be feasible
target_learning_goals: appropriate longitudinal design and causal interpretation of self-concept-achievement relations
examples: The article's hypothetical model with waves falling between actual data waves illustrates how apparent lag0 effects may be proximal lag1 effects at unmeasured shorter intervals

article_title: The Murky Distinction Between Curiosity and Interest: State of the Art and Future Prospects
citation: Pekrun, R. (2019). The Murky Distinction Between Curiosity and Interest: State of the Art and Future Prospects. Educational Psychology Review, 31, 905–914. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09512-1
title: Common-core definition of curiosity as recognition of an information gap combined with a sense that closing it is possible and intrinsically valuable
description: The article proposes deriving definitions from the common core of typical usages. On this approach, curiosity is defined as a psychological state including recognition of an information gap, anticipation that it may be possible to close it, and an intrinsically motivated desire to do so. The article argues that information gaps alone are insufficient, since gaps may alternatively cause surprise, confusion, or frustration, so a sense of control must be added.
requirements: The definition treats perception of an information gap as a necessary constituent, plus a sense of control that the gap can be closed and intrinsic value of closure
constraints: At this stage of research, the article states there is insufficient evidence to consider additional components, such as negative deprivation affect, as necessary constituents of curiosity
target_learning_goals: fostering curiosity and knowledge acquisition
key_sources: Pekrun, R. (2019). The Murky Distinction Between Curiosity and Interest: State of the Art and Future Prospects. Educational Psychology Review, 31, 905–914. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09512-1

article_title: The Murky Distinction Between Curiosity and Interest: State of the Art and Future Prospects
citation: Pekrun, R. (2019). The Murky Distinction Between Curiosity and Interest: State of the Art and Future Prospects. Educational Psychology Review, 31, 905–914. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09512-1
title: Common-core definition of interest as intrinsically motivated engagement with a specific activity, object, or content
description: The article defines interest as intrinsically motivated engagement with any specific object, content, or activity. The common core of definitions is engagement with an activity, object, or content because such engagement is intrinsically valuable. Additional components such as positive emotion are treated as possible but not necessary ingredients, since situational interest can be associated with either positive or negative feelings.
requirements: Definitions of interest should be derived from the common core of typical usages, with engagement and intrinsic value as the core elements
constraints: Positive emotion is not a necessary component; the article notes cases in which interest involves negative emotions, such as students' disgust when fascinated by dissecting frogs
target_learners: students across age groups and cultural contexts
target_learning_goals: fostering interest and engagement in learning
key_sources: Pekrun, R. (2019). The Murky Distinction Between Curiosity and Interest: State of the Art and Future Prospects. Educational Psychology Review, 31, 905–914. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09512-1

article_title: The Murky Distinction Between Curiosity and Interest: State of the Art and Future Prospects
citation: Pekrun, R. (2019). The Murky Distinction Between Curiosity and Interest: State of the Art and Future Prospects. Educational Psychology Review, 31, 905–914. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09512-1
title: Use the state-trait distinction to treat momentary and enduring curiosity and interest in conceptually parallel ways
description: The article recommends applying the state-trait distinction to both curiosity and interest instead of the situational/individual terminology used for interest. State and trait terms denote temporal specificity, align with the general psychological literature, and make it possible to discuss curiosity and interest in conceptually parallel ways. Trait denotes habitual patterns and does not imply genetic predisposition or immutability.
requirements: Trait is used as a descriptive category denoting habitual patterns of thought, affect, and action, not implying genetic predisposition
constraints: The article notes an asymmetry: trait curiosity is broad-situational while trait interest is re-engagement with specific contents; it remains open whether this asymmetry should be reduced
target_learning_goals: measurement and conceptual clarity about curiosity and interest
examples: The article proposes domain-specific trait curiosity and domain-general trait interest as constructs aligned with the common-core definitions

article_title: The Murky Distinction Between Curiosity and Interest: State of the Art and Future Prospects
citation: Pekrun, R. (2019). The Murky Distinction Between Curiosity and Interest: State of the Art and Future Prospects. Educational Psychology Review, 31, 905–914. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09512-1
title: Five options for defining contested psychological concepts, from dropping terms to listing variants
description: The article enumerates five strategies for reducing gaps between research traditions' definitions: dropping terms, definition by common core, definition by components and causes, definition by prototype, and definition by listing variants. It recommends the common core approach for curiosity and interest, since dropping terms is not viable for communication, and component definitions must assemble elements in nonarbitrary ways based on structural and functional covariation.
requirements: Component-based definitions should be assembled in nonarbitrary ways so their usefulness can be empirically scrutinized
constraints: Definitions cannot be discovered by empirical investigation; they must be constructed and are subject to theoretical preferences
target_learning_goals: conceptual clarity and consistent measurement in motivation research
examples: The article illustrates the common core principle with the definition of personality as characteristics that vary between persons and are relatively stable over time

article_title: A Systematic Review of Teachers’ Knowledge of Self-Regulated Learning and its Assessment
citation: Yves Karlen · Charlotte Dignath. (2026). A Systematic Review of Teachers' Knowledge of Self-Regulated Learning and its Assessment. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10171-2
title: TK-SRL framework: three interrelated dimensions of teachers' knowledge of self-regulated learning
description: The Teacher Knowledge of SRL (TK-SRL) framework adapts Shulman's teacher knowledge theory to SRL, distinguishing three interrelated dimensions: "content knowledge of SRL (CK-SRL), pedagogical content knowledge for promoting SRL (PCK-SRL), and assessment knowledge for diagnosing SRL (AK-SRL)". CK-SRL covers phases, components, and conditional strategy knowledge; PCK-SRL covers direct promotion and indirect activation of SRL; AK-SRL covers diagnosing largely non-observable regulatory processes. General pedagogical knowledge is deliberately excluded as non-SRL-specific. The framework served as an a priori lens for coding the 33 included studies.
requirements: Teachers need knowledge of regulatory phases (forethought, performance, reflection) and of cognitive, metacognitive, motivational, emotional, and resource-oriented components
AK-SRL requires interpreting indirect indicators of learning rather than solely observable products
constraints: The framework does not directly address teachers' beliefs, motivational orientations, or learning environments; it focuses on the knowledge component only
target_learning_goals: understanding and promoting students' self-regulated learning
diagnosing students' SRL processes
examples: The review illustrates the three dimensions with a writing-task scenario in which CK-SRL identifies regulatory difficulties, AK-SRL gathers diagnostic evidence via learning diaries and observations, and PCK-SRL translates the diagnosis into modeled planning strategies and scaffolded reflection
key_sources: Yves Karlen · Charlotte Dignath. (2026). A Systematic Review of Teachers' Knowledge of Self-Regulated Learning and its Assessment. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10171-2

citation: Yves Karlen · Charlotte Dignath. (2026). A Systematic Review of Teachers' Knowledge of Self-Regulated Learning and its Assessment. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10171-2
title: PRISMA-guided corpus of 33 studies on teachers' knowledge of SRL (1990–2024)
description: The review's evidence base is a corpus of 33 empirical studies identified through PRISMA-guided searching of nine databases plus citation tracking, from 7,120 initially identified records. Screening was conducted by two independent raters on the Rayyan platform, and coding reached "Cohen's κ = 0.84". Studies span 1990 to 2024, with 28 published after 2014, and cover Europe, North America, Australia, and China, with Germany (n = 9), Switzerland (n = 6), and the United States (n = 5) most frequent.
requirements: Included studies had to report at least one explicit measure of teachers' SRL knowledge with adequate instrument description
Studies had to be set in compulsory education academic subject contexts with pre-service or in-service teachers
constraints: Only peer-reviewed journal articles or doctoral dissertations in English or German were included; the search covers publications up to October 2024
target_learners: pre-service and in-service teachers in compulsory education
target_learning_goals: conceptualization and assessment of teachers' knowledge of self-regulated learning
examples: The PRISMA flow diagram (Fig. 2) traces the pathway from 8,207 screened records to 176 full-text assessments and the final 33 included studies

article_title: A Systematic Review of Evidence-Based Wellbeing Initiatives for Schoolteachers and Early Childhood Educators
citation: Emily Berger, Andrea Reupert, Timothy C. H. Campbell, Zoe Morris, Marie Hammer, Zane Diamond, Rochelle Hine, Pamela Patrick, Chantel Fathers. (2022). A Systematic Review of Evidence-Based Wellbeing Initiatives for Schoolteachers and Early Childhood Educators. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09690-5
title: Bronfenbrenner's ecological framework as applied to educator wellbeing
description: The review applies Bronfenbrenner's original ecological framework to organise understanding of educator wellbeing, in which "educator wellbeing is determined by six, interrelated factors": the individual educator, microsystem, mesosystem, exosystem, macrosystem and chronosystem. The individual layer covers predisposing factors such as life experiences and temperament; the microsystem covers teacher, student and parent relationships and classroom interactions; the exosystem covers indirect structures such as district procedures; the macrosystem covers political, economic, legal and cultural influences; and the chronosystem covers change across time. The review uses this lens to identify strengths and gaps in the evidence on wellbeing initiatives.
requirements: Application of the framework requires analysis across all six ecological layers, which the review notes has not been extensively analysed
constraints: The review states the influence of the ecological layers on educator wellbeing is not well understood
target_learning_goals: understanding and supporting educator wellbeing as a determinant of teaching quality and student outcomes
examples: The review grouped the 19 identified initiatives by therapeutic approach and assessed how well they respond to individual, organisational and structural factors

citation: Emily Berger, Andrea Reupert, Timothy C. H. Campbell, Zoe Morris, Marie Hammer, Zane Diamond, Rochelle Hine, Pamela Patrick, Chantel Fathers. (2022). title: Nineteen educator wellbeing initiatives organised into six therapeutic categories plus school leadership and policy change
description: The review's central artifact is a structured inventory of 19 distinct educator wellbeing initiatives drawn from 23 studies, organised by therapeutic approach: "The six therapeutic categories of "mindfulness", "social-emotional", "mental health literacy", "cognitive behavioural", "positive psychology", and "integrative" were used to organise the results", with a final non-therapeutic category of school leadership and policy change. For each initiative the review records target group, underpinning theory, key content, delivery format and facilitator, and appraises evidence quality via NHMRC levels, WWC standards or the CASP checklist.
requirements: Peer-reviewed primary-data evaluation studies published in English between 2010 and 2020 in early learning, primary, secondary or specialist settings
constraints: Evidence quality is modest, especially for early childhood educators; no initiative has Level I evidence
target_learning_goals: educator wellbeing, stress reduction, mental health literacy and resilience
examples: Seven initiatives were mindfulness-based, five social-emotional, two mental health literacy, one positive psychology, one school leadership and policy change, one cognitive behavioural, and two integrative

article_title: Emotions Are Not Random: Machine Learning Reveals Predictable Patterns in a 21-Day Second Language Learning Trajectory
citation: Peng Wang, Lesya Ganushchak, Camille Welie, Roel van Steensel. (2026). Emotions Are Not Random: Machine Learning Reveals Predictable Patterns in a 21-Day Second Language Learning Trajectory. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10141-8
title: Dynamic, context-sensitive account of L2 emotions: emotions as emergent episodes shaped by appraisals, contextual configurations and temporal adjacency
description: The article reconceptualizes second language emotions as "emergent and context-dependent, shaped by real-time interactions with learning activities and self-perceptions", drawing on complex dynamic systems theory and Pekrun's control–value appraisal account. It argues emotions unfold as episodes rather than stable dispositions, carry over across adjacent episodes (affective inertia), and are conditioned by configurations of contextual features such as activity type, modality combinations, pacing and spacing. The study operationalizes this account through an analytic pipeline combining unsupervised profile discovery with supervised short-horizon forecasting.
requirements: Multivariate time-series data combining momentary emotions and contextual features with preserved temporal adjacency, which the authors obtain via Ecological Momentary Assessment
constraints: The authors state profile labels are "descriptive and provisional, secondary to their utility for prediction"
target_learning_goals: momentary emotional states (anxiety, enjoyment, boredom) and self-perceived proficiency during language learning
examples: The 21-day EMA study tracked 92 learners across 6,918 episodes, identifying five emotional profiles and quantifying within-person variability and short-run dependence.
key_sources: Peng Wang, Lesya Ganushchak, Camille Welie, Roel van Steensel. (2026). Emotions Are Not Random: Machine Learning Reveals Predictable Patterns in a 21-Day Second Language Learning Trajectory. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10141-8

title: 21-day EMA dataset of 6,918 language-learning episodes with momentary emotions, perceived proficiency and contextual features
description: An intensive longitudinal dataset in which 92 adult foreign language learners completed momentary surveys via the Avicenna app (four per day at 2-hour intervals plus one end-of-day survey) over 21 days, yielding "6,918 momentary surveys (EMA prompts)". Each survey captured single-item ratings of anxiety, enjoyment, boredom and perceived proficiency (0–10 scales) plus contextual features: modality, activity type (self-directed vs. classroom), episode duration, time since the last activity and time until the next. Overall response rate was 71.4% with median per-person compliance of 83.3%.
requirements: Smartphone-based EMA prompting with one-hour response windows to minimize recall bias, and single-item indicators justified by dense sampling
constraints: Compliance ranged from 1.9% to 100% across participants; most learning was self-directed (85.0%) and speaking and writing episodes were relatively rare
target_learners: adult foreign language learners (Chinese university students, mean age 20.1)
target_learning_goals: tracking momentary emotions and self-perceived proficiency during self-directed and classroom language learning
examples: 41.5% of episodes mixed at least two modalities; mean episode length was 40.9 minutes.
