article_title: Disentangling the Association Between the Big Five Personality Traits and Student Achievement: Meta-Analytic Evidence on the Role of Domain Specificity and Achievement Measures
citation: Meyer, J., Jansen, T., Hübner, N., & Lüdtke, O. (2023). Disentangling the Association Between the Big Five Personality Traits and Student Achievement: Meta-Analytic Evidence on the Role of Domain Specificity and Achievement Measures. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09736-2
title: PASH: the personality–achievement saturation hypothesis framework
description: PASH (personality–achievement saturation hypothesis; Hübner et al., 2022) is a framework describing when personality manifests more strongly in achievement measures. It holds that personality shows "higher personality saturation" under certain circumstances reflected in different achievement measures, and "distinguishes between five different features of achievement measures" — standardization, relevance, curricular validity, instructional sensitivity, and cognitive ability saturation. Grades are characterized as low in standardization with high curricular validity and instructional sensitivity, whereas standardized tests are highly standardized, lower in relevance and instructional sensitivity, and high in cognitive ability saturation. This meta-analysis tests PASH-derived predictions about differential trait–measure associations.
requirements: Achievement measures must be distinguishable on the five features (standardization, relevance, curricular validity, instructional sensitivity, cognitive ability saturation) for differential saturation predictions to be made
constraints: The framework is attributed by this article to Hübner et al. (2022); this meta-analysis tests but does not originate it
target_learning_goals: academic achievement across subject domains and achievement measures
examples: The meta-analysis tested PASH-consistent predictions, e.g., that conscientiousness relates more closely to low-standardization measures such as course grades

title: Choose achievement measures based on the research question; there is no best or more objective measure
description: Because personality–achievement associations differ substantially by subject domain and achievement measure, researchers should not treat any single measure as universally preferable. The article concludes "there is no “best” or “more objective” achievement measure but, instead, that achievement measures should be chosen based on the research question of interest." Computing means across domains and measures may not be the most appropriate estimate of how personality and achievement relate. This principle guides study design in educational research on student characteristics and achievement.
requirements: Researchers must specify the subject domain and achievement measure of interest when designing studies of personality–achievement associations
constraints: The article addresses research on personality–achievement associations in elementary and secondary education; it does not claim generalizability to all achievement research
target_learning_goals: accurate measurement of academic achievement in research on student characteristics
examples: The meta-analysis of 78 studies showed moderating effects of measure or domain for all five traits, with differences in the direction of the effects

citation: Keller, L., Lüdtke, O., Preckel, F., & Brunner, M. (2023). Educational Inequalities at the Intersection of Multiple Social Categories: An Introduction and Systematic Review of the Multilevel Analysis of Individual Heterogeneity and Discriminatory Accuracy (MAIHDA) Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09733-5
title: The MAIHDA approach models individuals nested within intersectional strata to quantify intersectional effects and discriminatory accuracy
description: MAIHDA (Multilevel Analysis of Individual Heterogeneity and Discriminatory Accuracy) is a statistical framework in which individuals are nested within intersectional strata defined by combinations of social categories. It partitions variance within and between strata, yielding global measures (VPC, adjusted VPC, PCV) and specific measures (strata means and strata-level residuals) of intersectionality. The article introduces it to educational psychology, noting that 'the intersectional MAIHDA approach is considered the "new gold standard" for studying social inequalities in epidemiology (Merlo, 2018)'.
requirements: Very large and diverse samples are required to apply the intersectional MAIHDA approach for reliably estimating effects, so that strata have sufficient sample sizes
constraints: Meaningful cut points must be chosen when transforming continuous variables into categories or collapsing categories to reduce the number of strata
target_learning_goals: Understanding and quantifying educational inequalities in achievement outcomes across intersecting social categories
examples: The article demonstrates the approach with PISA 2018 German data, assigning each student to one of 40 strata combining gender, immigrant background, parental education, and parental occupational status

title: Annotated R syntax and OSF repository for replicating MAIHDA analyses
description: The article provides a hands-on tutorial consisting of a step-by-step table of analytical steps with corresponding R code (using brms via the brm function) and a thoroughly annotated R syntax released with supplemental materials. The authors state: "The supplemental materials and R code for reproducing the results and figures from the present study can be accessed via https:// osf. io/ qdcna/." constraints: If missing data are imputed using multiple imputation techniques, each preprocessing step needs to be repeated for each multiply-imputed data set

target_learning_goals: Replicating and applying intersectional MAIHDA analyses to educational inequality data

article_title: Are Some People Generally More Creative Than Others? A Systematic Review of Fifty Years’ Research
citation: Sébastien Miravete, André Tricot. (2024). Are Some People Generally More Creative Than Others? A Systematic Review of Fifty Years' Research. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09926-6
title: Three variants of the domain-general creativity hypothesis: mechanist, minimalist, and maximalist
description: The review organizes claims that creativity is domain-general into three non-equivalent variants. The mechanist variant holds that "the cognitive or neural mechanisms involved in creative tasks are domain-general". The minimalist variant requires general factors with a non-negligible positive impact (e.g., Cohen's d ≥ 0.2) that are all teachable; the maximalist variant requires at least one unteachable general factor, such as a genetic one. The variants carry different educational consequences: minimalism supports teaching general creativity, maximalism supports selecting potentially creative individuals.
requirements: A theory of creativity must specify which general factors it posits and whether they are teachable, since the three variants imply different educational recommendations
constraints: Minimalism and maximalism are not compatible with each other, though the mechanistic hypothesis is compatible with both
target_learning_goals: creative performance across domains
examples: The review classifies its 36 selected studies by these variants in Table 1's last column
key_sources: Sébastien Miravete, André Tricot. (2024). Are Some People Generally More Creative Than Others? A Systematic Review of Fifty Years' Research. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09926-6

article_title: Are Some People Generally More Creative Than Others? A Systematic Review of Fifty Years’ Research
citation: Sébastien Miravete, André Tricot. (2024). Are Some People Generally More Creative Than Others? A Systematic Review of Fifty Years' Research. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09926-6
title: Four-c model of creativity: mini-c, little-c, pro-c, and big-c levels
description: The review adopts Kaufman and Beghetto's (2009) Four-c model as its framework for levels of creativity. "mini-c (…) encompass the creativity inherent in the learning process"; little-c is everyday amateur creativity; pro-c requires roughly ten years of daily professional effort; big-c creators revolutionize a field and must appear as geniuses to "the gatekeepers who comprise the field". The review uses these levels to scope its research question and notes that no researcher claims big-c or pro-c creativity is possible without lengthy training.
requirements: Distinguishing creativity levels requires judging novelty and appropriateness relative to a reference community (novice, amateur, professional, field gatekeepers)
constraints: The review's corpus only explores little-c creativity because participants are always students
target_learners: learners at all levels, from novices (mini-c) to professionals (pro-c)
target_learning_goals: understanding what level of creative performance a learner can attain
examples: The review defines the domain-general question separately for mini-c, little-c, pro-c and big-c
key_sources: Sébastien Miravete, André Tricot. (2024). Are Some People Generally More Creative Than Others? A Systematic Review of Fifty Years' Research. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09926-6

article_title: Are Some People Generally More Creative Than Others? A Systematic Review of Fifty Years’ Research
citation: Sébastien Miravete, André Tricot. (2024). Are Some People Generally More Creative Than Others? A Systematic Review of Fifty Years' Research. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09926-6
title: Do not yet integrate general creative skills training into curricula or select for a presumed creative profile
description: Because the evidence for domain-general creativity fails the review's validity conditions — uncontrolled prior knowledge and artificial tasks — the authors advise against, for now, the two educational recommendations they derive from minimalist and maximalist theories: integrating general creativity training into curricula, and selecting students or employees by a general creative profile. They state "it seems premature to recommend the integration of general creative skills into school or training programs, as well as the selection of students or employees with a presumed 'creative profile'".
requirements: Any future adoption of general creativity training or profile-based selection would require studies controlling prior knowledge and using realistic creative tasks
constraints: This is a recommendation against current adoption, not evidence that general creativity training is ineffective; the review's corpus covers only little-c creativity among students
target_learning_goals: creative performance across domains
examples: The review contrasts minimalist educational recommendation 1 (integrate general creativity training) and maximalist recommendation 2 (select by creative profile) and defers both

article_title: Separating Myth from Reality in Education: Introduction to the Special Issue
citation: Andrew C. Butler & Shana K. Carpenter. (2015). Separating Myth from Reality in Education: Introduction to the Special Issue. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-015-9344-0
title: A four-step evaluative framework for judging educational practices and beliefs
description: The editorial describes a shared evaluation process modeled by every article in the special issue. Each article first documents that a practice or belief exists, then sets objective criteria for what would count as good experimental evidence, then weighs the evidence for and against, and finally draws conclusions and recommendations. The editors argue this process "provides a roadmap for evaluating other practices and beliefs in education as well as other fields."
requirements: Delineation of objective criteria for judging efficacy or accuracy before weighing evidence, since "Many of the disagreements about practices and beliefs stem from a lack of common understanding about criteria for evaluating claims."
target_learning_goals: identifying effective practices and accurate beliefs about learning
correcting misconceptions about ineffective practices
examples: Each special-issue article "begin[s] by defining and documenting the existence of the practice or belief," then evaluates evidence against criteria it sets up.

article_title: The Forward Effect of Judgements of Learning on Memory and Transfer in Inductive Learning
citation: Ritter, C., Hausman, H., Gaschler, R., Tiffin-Richards, S. P., & Kubik, V. (2025). The Forward Effect of Judgements of Learning on Memory and Transfer in Inductive Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10094-4
title: Covert-retrieval account of forward effects of judgments of learning
description: The article advances and tests the account that JOLs benefit new learning "by inducing covert retrieval—that is, causing learners to search their memory for the target information to judge the likelihood they will be able to recall on a later test." Cue-only JOLs, given when only partial information is present, should trigger more retrieval than cue–target JOLs, which can rest on familiarity. The two-stage model holds that a JOL involves an initial familiarity assessment followed by retrieval only when familiarity is moderate, producing the inverted U-shaped JOL–RT relationship observed for cue-only JOLs.
requirements: JOL prompts must be item-level and cue-only (target information absent) to engage retrieval-based monitoring
constraints: The truncated search hypothesis warns that retrieval efforts that stop prematurely will fail to support future learning
Aggregate JOLs rely on broader heuristics and may be less sensitive to retrieval-based mechanisms
target_learners: university students learning visual natural categories
target_learning_goals: inductive learning of natural categories (memory and transfer of category memberships)
examples: Experiment 1 compared overt retrieval, cue-only JOLs, cue–target JOLs, and restudy as interim tasks between study phases
Experiment 2 added a feedback manipulation to cue-only JOLs to test retrieval-based versus metacognitive-effort explanations

citation: Keles, S., ten Braak, D., Hagen, Å. M., & Melby-Lervåg, M. (2025). Validity of Early-Grade Screening Tools in the Three Tier (RTI/MTSS) Model: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Literacy, Language, and Mathematics. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10077-5
title: The Three Tier (RTI/MTSS) model as a data-informed tiered support framework in which screening is one component of broader placement decisions
description: The Three Tier model (also called MTSS with three tiers or a three-tier RTI model) is a prevention-oriented framework providing universal Tier 1 instruction, targeted Tier 2 supplemental interventions, and intensive, individualized Tier 3 support. The review emphasizes that "universal screening is not intended to serve as a definitive placement mechanism into Tiers 1, 2, or 3"; instead, screening is an initial risk-identification step within a dynamic process combining teacher judgment, contextual information, and response to intervention. The review synthesizes the validity of the screening tools that feed this process.
requirements: Screening measures should be highly predictive of future outcomes to ensure accurate identification of students at risk
Appropriate assignment of students to tiers, with ongoing adjustments informed by progress monitoring, is described as the most important prerequisite for effective implementation
constraints: The review focuses on models explicitly structured with three tiers, in ECEC through grade 2, in language, literacy, or mathematics domains
target_learners: Children in early childhood education and care (preschool/kindergarten) through grade 2 of primary school
target_learning_goals: Early identification of students at risk of learning difficulties in literacy, language, and mathematics
Accurate assignment to tiered levels of academic support
examples: The review included 127 studies in which screening tools were used as part of tier assignment, with all screeners used in Tier 1

Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10077-5
title: Treat screening as one input in a dynamic, data-informed tier placement process rather than a single gatekeeping assessment
description: The article argues that within the Three Tier model, screening functions as an initial step to flag potential risk, while tier placement is refined over time through teacher judgment, contextual information, and students' responses to intervention. Contemporary models, the authors note, emphasize "the integration of multiple data sources—including universal screening, progress monitoring, and teacher judgment—to guide instructional decisions and tier placement in a dynamic, iterative manner". This framing treats screening as part of a responsive, evidence-based process rather than a static gatekeeping tool.
requirements: Progress monitoring and additional diagnostic assessments to guide movement into more intensive tiers
Teacher judgment and contextual information alongside screening scores
constraints: Screening occurs about three times per year and progress monitoring even monthly, so assessments must be brief and fit for purpose; resource limitations may prevent schools from serving all students who might benefit
target_learners: Children in ECEC through grade 2 in tiered support systems
target_learning_goals: Accurate identification of students at risk and responsive allocation of tiered interventions
examples: The review included studies where screening data informed—but did not necessarily solely determine—tier placement within broader tiered support systems

article_title: Integrating Insights from Volitional Personality Change Interventions to Improve Self-Regulated Learning
citation: Mathias Allemand, Brent W. Roberts, Ulrich Trautwein. (2026). Integrating Insights from Volitional Personality Change Interventions to Improve Self-Regulated Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10127-6
title: VPC theory of change: enduring trait change arises from interplay of top-down volitional strategies and bottom-up behavioral repetition
description: The review describes VPC interventions as resting on the assumption that "traits can be modified through two complementary pathways: top-down and bottom-up." Top-down processes involve goal setting, self-reflection, and motivational alignment; bottom-up processes rely on repeated enactment of trait-relevant behaviors and repertoire expansion that accumulate into trait change. Supporting frameworks include TESSERA, Behavioral Activation, Intentional Change theories, and the General (Common) Change Factors model, whose four mechanisms are discrepancy awareness, activating strengths and resources, targeting thoughts and feelings to achieve insight, and targeting behaviors to be practiced.
requirements: Sustained motivation to change is a prerequisite that remains critical throughout the change process
Behavioral practice with feedback from coaches or peers to stabilize change through habit formation and reinforcement
constraints: Participants in research on personality change goals are typically aged 18 or older
The number of studies on VPC remains too limited to examine differences in the effects of various intervention methods
target_learning_goals: enduring self-regulatory development
persistence and transfer of intervention effects
examples: The review describes the General (Common) Change Factors model's four mechanisms, including actuating discrepancy awareness by contrasting actual with desired personality profiles

article_title: Learning by Doing or Doing Without Learning? The Potentials and Challenges of Activity-Based Learning
citation: Alexander Skulmowski. (2024). Learning by Doing or Doing Without Learning? The Potentials and Challenges of Activity-Based Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09869-y
title: Integrated cognitive framework for analyzing activity-based learning: cognitive load theory, biologically primary/secondary knowledge, and layers of action planning
description: The review analyzes learning activities by combining cognitive load theory, Geary's (2008) distinction between biologically primary and secondary knowledge, and Pacherie's (2008) model of distal, proximal, and motor intentions. Activities are decomposed into layers: complex distal plans requiring task-related, biologically secondary knowledge generate load, while ingrained motor components do not. The review states it analyzes "different forms of activity-based learning... using the framework of cognitive load theory... and Geary's (2008) distinction between evolved and acquired knowledge." Figure 2 summarizes the combination.
requirements: Analysts must be able to decompose an activity into distal, proximal, and motor intention layers and classify required knowledge as biologically primary or secondary
constraints: The review states it is not its focus to discuss whether biologically primary knowledge causes little load exclusively due to evolutionary factors
target_learners: learners across educational settings using activity-based instruction
target_learning_goals: optimizing the design of learning activities to avoid extraneous cognitive load
examples: The review applies the framework to learning by drawing, distinguishing low-load relational drawings from load-heavy representational drawings requiring perspective and shading skills

article_title: Learning by Doing or Doing Without Learning? The Potentials and Challenges of Activity-Based Learning
citation: Alexander Skulmowski. (2024). Learning by Doing or Doing Without Learning? The Potentials and Challenges of Activity-Based Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09869-y
title: Taxonomies of embodied learning classifying interventions by bodily engagement, task integration, and relevance
description: The review organizes movement-based learning research through successive classification systems. Johnson-Glenberg et al. (2014) proposed three factors: motoric engagement, gestural congruency, and immersion. Skulmowski and Rey (2018) simplified this to "the two dimensions bodily engagement and task integration," finding bodily engagement has a nonlinear influence on learning. Mavilidi et al. (2022) proposed a 2x2 system with the dimensions integration (temporal connection between movements and tasks) and relevance (correspondence between movements and content). These taxonomies predict when motor activity helps or hinders learning.
requirements: Classification of an intervention requires judging its level of bodily engagement and how well its actions match the learning content
constraints: Skulmowski and Rey (2018) describe excessive bodily activity as linked to extraneous cognitive load, so more engagement is not always better
target_learners: learners in embodied and movement-based learning interventions
target_learning_goals: selecting and designing motor activities that support rather than distract from learning
examples: The review uses the taxonomies to explain why whole-body movement studies do not always outperform less bodily activity

article_title: Learning by Doing or Doing Without Learning? The Potentials and Challenges of Activity-Based Learning
citation: Alexander Skulmowski. (2024). Learning by Doing or Doing Without Learning? The Potentials and Challenges of Activity-Based Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09869-y
title: Design activity-based learning to avoid redundant demands and provide guidance, favoring biologically primary activity components
description: The review recommends that if activity-based interventions are used, designers should strip out redundant aspects, supply guidance, and shift focus toward low-demand components. It states that "as many redundant aspects as possible need to be avoided while providing additional guidance to learners," and that learning activities "may be more effective if the extraneous task demands are removed and the focus is shifted towards the less demanding components, such as gesturing." Guidance for drawing and restricting drawing to easier, familiar topics are offered as ways to avoid overload.
requirements: Activities must be analyzed for their cognitive demands so that guidance can target the biologically secondary components
constraints: The review warns that more passive methods can be preferable when extraneous load cannot be avoided, and that digital transfer can increase demands
target_learners: learners in activity-based and generative learning settings, including novices
target_learning_goals: protecting working memory capacity for the actual learning content during hands-on activities
examples: The review notes Fiorella and Zhang (2018) found simplifying the drawing task can have a positive effect, and Wang et al. (2023) reduced social load by having learners teach toward a webcam

citation: Emhardt, S. N., Kok, E., van Gog, T., Brandt-Gruwel, S., van Marlen, T., & Jarodzka, H. (2023). Visualizing a Task Performer's Gaze to Foster Observers' Performance and Learning—a Systematic Literature Review on Eye Movement Modeling Examples. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09731-7
title: Three mechanisms underlying EMME effectiveness: attention guidance, revealing perceptual strategies, and inducing a social learning situation
description: The review adopts Krebs et al.'s account that EMME effectiveness rests on three mechanisms. Gaze visualizations act as "visual cue to guide the observer's attention", helping observers select relevant information at the right time in transient instructional videos; they reveal "a performer's perceptual strategies that would otherwise not be accessible to observers", since people have limited insight into their own viewing behavior; and they induce a stronger social learning situation, evoking more social presence than abstract cues such as animated arrows. The review coded which of these rationales each included study used.
requirements: Gaze visualization must be displayed on top of to-be-learned task material with the goal of fostering observer performance or learning
constraints: The review treats these as rationales stated by study authors, not as mechanisms tested within this review
target_learners: observers of instructional videos across primary, secondary, tertiary, and professional education
target_learning_goals: attention allocation to relevant task information
acquisition of expert perceptual and cognitive strategies
learning from multimedia task demonstrations

article_title: Spaced Retrieval Practice Imposes Desirable Difficulty in Calculus Learning
citation: Keith B. Lyle, Campbell R. Bego, Patricia A. S. Ralston, Jason C. Immekus. (2022). Spaced Retrieval Practice Imposes Desirable Difficulty in Calculus Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09677-2
title: Protracted knowledge acquisition account of spacing as desirable difficulty in calculus
description: The authors propose that answering multiple quiz questions gives students opportunities to construct new knowledge, and that spacing "imposed difficulty by protracting the knowledge acquisition process": equivalent knowledge was ultimately acquired in both conditions, as revealed by third-question performance, but the process unfolded over weeks when spaced versus minutes when massed. Drawing on the learning-versus-performance distinction, they suggest spreading acquisition over weeks, while newer objectives were also being learned, offered opportunities to integrate older and newer knowledge into a more cohesive mental model of calculus. This account is distinct from the idea that spacing makes retrieval more effortful.
requirements: The account presupposes practice via multiple quiz questions on the same objective and, in the massed condition, the ability to move back and forth between questions before submitting the quiz
constraints: The authors argue that in this context no amount of retrieval effort would allow students to retrieve knowledge they have not yet acquired, distinguishing the account from retrieval-effort explanations
The account is the authors' interpretation of the practice-phase pattern, not a directly tested mechanism
target_learning_goals: retention of calculus learning objectives such as limits, derivatives, and implicit differentiation
examples: In the spaced condition performance was lowest on the first question, intermediate on the second, and highest on the third, converging with the massed condition once prior practice was equated
key_sources: Keith B. Lyle, Campbell R. Bego, Patricia A. S. Ralston, Jason C. Immekus. (2022). Spaced Retrieval Practice Imposes Desirable Difficulty in Calculus Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09677-2

article_title: Spaced Retrieval Practice Imposes Desirable Difficulty in Calculus Learning
citation: Keith B. Lyle, Campbell R. Bego, Patricia A. S. Ralston, Jason C. Immekus. (2022). Spaced Retrieval Practice Imposes Desirable Difficulty in Calculus Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09677-2
title: Distribute calculus practice across multiple quizzes and accept lower short-term practice performance for better long-term retention
description: Because spacing improved end-of-semester test scores while reducing practice-quiz performance, the article recommends that instructors distribute quiz questions on a learning objective across several quizzes rather than presenting all variants on one quiz. The authors "encourage instructors and students alike to embrace the short-term pain of spacing in order to reap its long-term gain", noting spacing is a low- or no-cost intervention requiring no increase in the amount of work assigned. Practice performance alone is a misleading basis for choosing massing, since manipulations facilitating performance during training can reduce the quality of learning.
requirements: Quizzes administered on a schedule that permits distributing questions on an objective across at least three quizzes spaced weeks apart
Use of algorithmic question variants so repeated questions differ only in superficial features
constraints: Practice-quiz scores will be lower in the short term, which matters when quizzes are credit-bearing; the decrement falls mainly on the first two questions on an objective
target_learners: undergraduate engineering students in calculus courses
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of objective-specific calculus knowledge
examples: In the study, three algorithmic variants of each objective's question appeared either all on the first quiz after introduction (massed) or one per quiz across three consecutive quizzes (spaced), with the criterial test counting toward course grades

article_title: Spaced Retrieval Practice Imposes Desirable Difficulty in Calculus Learning
citation: Keith B. Lyle, Campbell R. Bego, Patricia A. S. Ralston, Jason C. Immekus. (2022). Spaced Retrieval Practice Imposes Desirable Difficulty in Calculus Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09677-2
title: Spaced versus massed MyMathLab quizzing procedure with end-of-semester criterial test
description: A classroom research procedure embedded in a hybrid calculus course for engineering undergraduates using the MyMathLab online platform. For each of 24 target learning objectives, MyMathLab generated "three random algorithmic variants of the question for each student", which were presented either on a single quiz (massed) or distributed across three consecutive biweekly quizzes (spaced), with assignment of objective sets to condition counterbalanced across students. Retention was measured by a 24-question criterial test on the last day of class, proctored via ProctorU, with quizzes and the test averaged to count for 7% of the course grade.

Biweekly quizzes accessible within a timed window, completed in one sitting
Counterbalanced assignment of objective sets to massed versus spaced conditions
constraints: Quizzes were not proctored; the authors relied on time limits, randomized question order, and algorithmic variants to deter answer sharing
Attrition left slightly unbalanced counterbalancing groups (92 vs. 88 of N = 180)

target_learning_goals: retention of fundamental calculus objectives from the first seven weeks of the course
examples: Quizzes were administered at the end of weeks 3, 5, 7, 9, and 11, with approximately 3 minutes allowed per question

article_title: Emotional Wellbeing in the Context of Primary-Secondary School Transitions: A Concept Analysis Paper
citation: Bagnall, C. L., Jindal-Snape, D., Banwell, E., Panayiotou, M., Mason, C., & Qualter, P. (2025). Emotional Wellbeing in the Context of Primary-Secondary School Transitions: A Concept Analysis Paper. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09990-6
title: Conceptual model of emotional wellbeing in the context of primary-secondary school transitions with three defining attributes
description: The paper's central contribution is a concept analysis (Walker and Avant, 2005 method) defining emotional wellbeing in the context of primary-secondary school transitions as a distinct construct. Its defining attributes are that it includes "children's affective experience of navigating primary-secondary school transitions, in the here-and-now", children's evaluations of their emotional functioning globally and in specific social, academic, environmental, and personal transition domains, and children's perceptions of their internal and external resources to manage transition demands and maintain a stable affective state. The model is grounded in hedonia and eudaimonia perspectives and mapped onto Jindal-Snape's Multiple and Multi-dimensional Transitions Theory domains.
requirements: Conceptualisation must be developed in partnership with children to be contextually and experientially relevant, age and stage appropriate
constraints: The construct is specific to the primary-secondary school transitions context; the authors state general emotional wellbeing or transitions appraisals alone do not fully represent children's experiences during this time
target_learners: Children aged 10-14 navigating primary-secondary school transitions (Year 6/7 in England, P7/S1 in Scotland)
target_learning_goals: Emotional wellbeing during school transitions
Adaptation to multiple and multi-dimensional transition changes
examples: A fictional model case, James, a Year 7 pupil, illustrates all defining attributes: feeling excited and confident before the move, evaluating school size within a specific domain, and drawing on supportive family as an external resource

article_title: How Learners Use Their Hands for Learning: an Eye-Tracking Study
citation: Babette Park · Andreas Korbach · Paul Ginns · Roland Brünken. (2023). How Learners Use Their Hands for Learning: an Eye-Tracking Study. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09833-2
title: Attention-directing explanation of the tracing effect (near-hand prioritization)
description: The article presents an explanation derived from basic cognitive science research on near-hand effects: hand position and activity fundamentally affect cognitive processes, so touch-based actions direct and focus visual attention on relevant material. The article states that "Near-hand position should evoke faster target detection and effective direction of attention, as well as potent shielding of attention from interferences." Under this view, learning benefits should specifically appear in recall-type performance such as remembering new terminologies or identifying recently learned contents, and not necessarily in comprehension. The present experiment was designed to test this explanation against the multimodal memory model via hypotheses H1a–H1c.
requirements: Learning material with separable text and illustration elements whose corresponding parts learners can point at or trace over with the index finger
constraints: Some studies on near-hand effects show the fragility of this effect (Andringa et al., 2018; Dosso & Kingstone, 2018), and reduced semantic processing of near-hand information has been reported (Davoli et al., 2010)
Yeo and Tzeng (2019) suggest tracing may only affect learning with highly visuospatial-based material
target_learners: School students learning from multimedia lessons
target_learning_goals: Retention and identification of newly learned terms from text-and-illustration lessons
examples: The present study operationalized this explanation as H1a–H1c, predicting higher performance, cognitive activity, and visual attention in both touch-based groups versus the no-touch group with no pointing–tracing difference

article_title: How Learners Use Their Hands for Learning: an Eye-Tracking Study
citation: Babette Park · Andreas Korbach · Paul Ginns · Roland Brünken. (2023). How Learners Use Their Hands for Learning: an Eye-Tracking Study. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09833-2
title: Multimodal memory model explanation of the tracing effect
description: The article introduces the multimodal memory model (Engelkamp & Zimmer, 1994) as a novel system-oriented explanation for tracing effects. It posits a non-verbal output system for action besides output-lexica, such that "The execution of action should make motor information on the cognitive level available, which becomes part of memory traces that can affect the later recall in a positive way." The model grew out of subject-performed task effect research, and its limits suggest tracing effects should appear in comprehension of complex systems with visuospatial information rather than pure recall of single terms. This yielded hypotheses H2a–H2b, predicting only the tracing group would outperform the other two groups.
requirements: Learning tasks involving kinesthetic experience during the learning phase, e.g., finger tracing against a surface, so motor information enters memory traces
constraints: The subject-performed task effect was not found for recall of associated word pairs or serial recall, implying episodic-relational information limits, though some self-performed task effects do support relational processing (Kormi-Nouri & Nilsson, 2001)
target_learners: School students learning from multimedia lessons
target_learning_goals: Comprehension of complex systems involving visuospatial information
examples: H2a predicted the tracing group would outperform pointing and no-touch groups only on comprehension; the experiment instead found pointing superior, contradicting this hypothesis

article_title: A Complete SMOCkery: Daily Online Testing Did Not Boost College Performance
citation: Robinson, D. H. (2021). A Complete SMOCkery: Daily Online Testing Did Not Boost College Performance. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09588-0
title: Vet widely cited educational claims for internal-validity threats before acting on them, and expose unsupported extravagant claims
description: The article demonstrates a practice of re-examining influential findings by checking threats to internal validity — history, selection bias, and differential attrition — before accepting causal claims from non-randomized comparisons. The author writes that "our field needs watchdogs who expose such unsupported extravagant claims— especially those appearing in pay-to-publish journals." The reanalysis of the SMOC data shows how alternative explanations can fully account for apparent effects.

constraints: Applies to comparisons that do not randomly assign students to conditions; the author notes the original study was an ex post facto comparison of 2008 and 2011 cohorts
target_learning_goals: accurate evaluation of educational intervention evidence
examples: The author computed major-weighted average GPAs for the 2008 and 2011 introductory psychology cohorts and found the 0.11 weighted difference matched the originally reported advantages

article_title: A Cognitive Load Theory Approach to Understanding Expert Scaffolding of Visual Problem-Solving Tasks: A Scoping Review
citation: Christine C. A. van Nooijen · Bjorn B. de Koning · Wichor M. Bramer · Anna Isahakyan · Maryam Asoodar · Ellen Kok · Jeroen J. G. van Merrienboer · Fred Paas. (2024). A Cognitive Load Theory Approach to Understanding Expert Scaffolding of Visual Problem-Solving Tasks: A Scoping Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09848-3
title: A cognitive load theory framework classifies expert scaffolding behaviours into cueing and chunking relative to the working memory bottleneck
description: The review proposes that scaffolding behaviours be organised by their cognitive function relative to the working memory bottleneck. Cueing behaviours direct attention before information enters working memory, reducing load; chunking behaviours encourage novices to construct, enrich and retrieve schemas after the bottleneck. As the authors state, "We propose that scaffolding behaviours may be categorised into two conceptual groups based on their function relative to the cognitive load bottleneck. These groups are cueing and chunking." The framework is intended to unify diverse scaffolding research and connect behaviours to underlying cognitive processes.
requirements: Experts interacting one-on-one with novices on visual problem-solving tasks
constraints: The review notes no prior framework connected scaffolding to underlying cognitive mechanisms; the framework is proposed, not empirically validated as a whole
target_learners: Novices in visual domains (medicine, physics, design, craftsmanship) learning through expert-novice dyads
target_learning_goals: Domain-specific visual problem-solving and visual expertise
examples: Excerpts from 18 articles were categorised on cueing/chunking and verbal/nonverbal deductive categories, with tree diagrams providing conceptual definitions and practical examples

title: A two-axis expression-and-activity taxonomy: scaffolding behaviours vary in verbal/nonverbal expression and active/passive engagement
description: Beyond cognitive strategy, the review codes scaffolding behaviours by method of expression (verbal/auditory vs. nonverbal/visual, which can co-occur, e.g. an expert narrating actions) and by an inductively derived activity category. The active/passive category, derived from Tambaum's concept of indirect scaffolding, captures purposeful absence: "the turns in which the tutor is available for the learner but only observes the learner acting independently and does not interfere even when the learner faces a problem". Passive excerpts were not further coded into expression or strategy categories because they describe the absence of behaviour.
requirements: Coding of excerpts requires isolating each expert-novice interaction event reported close to the original dataset
constraints: Passive excerpts cannot be sub-categorised as verbal/nonverbal or cueing/chunking because the category describes absence of behaviour
target_learners: Novices in visual domains taught in one-on-one apprenticeship-style settings
target_learning_goals: Visual expertise and visual problem-solving skill
examples: Of 164 included excerpts, 13 were coded passive; combined verbal-nonverbal expression occurred in 28 excerpts

article_title: A Meta-Analysis of Perfectionism and Academic Achievement
citation: Madigan, D. J. (2019). A meta-analysis of perfectionism and academic achievement. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09484-2
title: Two higher-order dimensions of perfectionism: perfectionistic strivings and perfectionistic concerns
description: The article conceptualizes perfectionism as a multidimensional personality trait supported by factor analytic studies into two higher-order dimensions. Perfectionistic strivings "capture personal standards and a self-oriented striving for perfection" while perfectionistic concerns "capture concern over mistakes, feelings of discrepancy between one's expectations and performance, and negative reactions to imperfection." The two dimensions show different and sometimes opposite relationships with outcomes, which is why the meta-analysis analyses them separately.
requirements: Measurement via multidimensional perfectionism scales whose subscales map onto the two higher-order dimensions
constraints: The dimensions overlap substantially (r+ = .32 in this meta-analysis), so their unique relationships require semi-partial correlations
target_learners: school, high school, and college students
target_learning_goals: understanding how perfectionism relates to academic achievement
examples: The meta-analysis coded subscales such as personal standards and self-oriented perfectionism as strivings indicators, and concerns over mistakes, socially prescribed perfectionism, and discrepancy as concerns indicators

article_title: Special Issue on Cognitive Load Theory: Editorial
citation: Paul Ginns & Jimmie Leppink. (2019). Special Issue on Cognitive Load Theory: Editorial. Educational Psychology Review, 31, 255–259. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09474-4
title: Cognitive load theory: working-memory limits and schema-based instructional design
description: Cognitive load theory draws on models of cognitive architecture, including a working memory whose limits are reduced when domain-specific schemas are activated from long-term memory, to generate and test instructional design hypotheses. The editorial states that "When working memory is overloaded by the competing demands of these processes, CLT argues, student learning is impaired." Researchers have typically used experimental methods to test designs targeting obstructions such as split attention or circumventing them with worked examples.
requirements: Instructional designs must be tested against models of human cognitive architecture, particularly working memory capacity and duration limits
target_learning_goals: schema construction and automation
problem solving
comprehension
examples: The Special Issue presents theoretical reviews, meta-analyses, and intervention studies all focused on advancement of CLT

title: Integrated working memory model with a common finite attentional resource across modalities
description: Sepp et al. (2019) propose a new integrated working memory model to help understand how the human motor system may influence learning and cognition. Its central tenet is "a common and finite attentional resource that can be distributed across multiple modalities." The model may help researchers understand effects of gestures and other movements on cognitive load, and the authors call for increased use of eye tracking and motion tracking technology in future experiments.

target_learning_goals: understanding effects of gestures and movement on cognitive load

title: EVCT-CLT model linking motivational beliefs directly to cognitive load

Integrating the two research traditions combines EVCT's perspective on motivation and self-regulation with CLT's tradition of carefully designed randomized controlled experiments, and the authors suggest designs for new experiments and measurement approaches.

citation: Tino Endres, Lisa Bender, Stoo Sepp, Shirong Zhang, Louise David, Melanie Trypke, et al. (2025). Developing the Mental Effort and Load–Translingual Scale (MEL‑TS) as a Foundation for Translingual Research in Self‑Regulated Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09978-8
title: Mental effort versus mental load as the appropriate distinction of cognitive demand in self-regulated learning
description: The article proposes that in self-regulated learning, cognitive demand is best captured by two constructs: mental load, passively experienced, and mental effort, actively invested. It argues the classical CLT distinction (ICL/ECL/GCL) fits instructor-regulated settings but has less predictive value when learners self-regulate, since learners monitor an aggregation of demands rather than their source. The paper notes the mental load construct "is also referred to as data-driven demand (Koriat, 1997) and task-centered dimension of load", while the active component is also called goal-driven demand or goal-driven appraisals of cognitive load.
requirements: Assessment items must be interpretable across a broad range of learning situations, including learner-regulated contexts where learners cannot choose the design of materials
constraints: The distinction is argued to suit SRL contexts; classical CLT load types remain the focus in structured, instructor-regulated instructional design settings
target_learners: self-regulating learners across school and higher education
target_learning_goals: monitoring and regulating cognitive demand during self-regulated learning
examples: The authors use the terminology of mental load and mental effort (Klepsch & Seufert, 2021) because these terms were most idiomatic to participants in their qualitative interviews

title: MEL-TS: a translingual set of mental effort and mental load self-rating items in six languages
description: The MEL-TS is a set of self-rating items assessing mental effort and mental load during self-regulated learning, developed in English, Dutch, Spanish, German, Mandarin Chinese, and French. The initial pool comprised ten items — "five for mental effort and five for mental load" — inspired by established measures (Paas, 1992; Klepsch & Seufert, 2021; Krell, 2017; Leppink et al., 2013), with reversed items to mitigate response bias. The final quantitative version used four items per construct plus a 'heart and soul' intensity item and a difficulty item, with all items available on the Open Science Framework.
requirements: Items must be rated with attention to cultural context, as translations are not expected to be literal matches across languages
constraints: The 'lifeblood' (heart and soul) item proved suitable only in Mandarin Chinese and Spanish contexts; item intensity differences across languages may produce floor or ceiling effects
target_learners: first-language speakers of English, Dutch, Spanish, German, Mandarin Chinese, and French in learning contexts
target_learning_goals: assessing invested mental effort and perceived mental load during self-regulated learning

description: The article's closing recommendation is a best practice for measuring cognitive demand across languages: "As best practice, we recommend four items within a reference point evaluation." This means administering the validated four-item mental effort and four-item mental load subscales with a reference point so ratings are anchored to a comparable learning situation across languages and cultures. The recommendation follows from the scale's demonstrated criterion, convergent, and incremental validity in English, Chinese, and German samples.

article_title: The Role of Teachers’ Emotions and Their Assessment in Professional Development Research: A Systematic Review
citation: Mareike Ehlert, Carola Grunschel, Friederike Koehler. (2025). The Role of Teachers' Emotions and Their Assessment in Professional Development Research: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10048-w
title: Adjusted framework integrating teacher emotions into Desimone's four-component PD process model
description: The review proposes an adjusted version of Desimone's (2009) PD framework in which emotions both influence and are influenced by each of the four PD components (core features, knowledge/attitude change, instructional change, student outcomes). The article states that "emotions can both influence and be influenced by each component of the PD process" and that emotions experienced in one component spill over into others, making emotions in PD context-sensitive and time-sensitive. It is offered as a conceptual map for future research and PD design.

constraints: The framework is presented as theoretical integration; the article notes existing ideas are largely theoretical or based on single case studies

target_learning_goals: teachers' emotional engagement with and adoption of new instructional practices during PD

title: Attentional anchor: a strategically useful imaginary or real Gestalt that orients perception to facilitate goal movement
description: The attentional anchor is a hypothetical construct from enactivist theory denoting a strategically useful imaginary Gestalt, such as a diagonal line between the hands, that learners generate to solve motor-control problems. The article defines it as something that "orients, focalizes, and shapes perception toward an environment to facilitate the situated enactment of some goal movement form". It serves as the central ontological innovation linking Abrahamson's mathematics-education program with Mechsner's movement science, and the authors propose that any purposeful movement may be tacitly guided by such anchors.

title: Mathematics Imagery Trainer: a technologically enabled activity architecture for embodied mathematics learning
description: The Mathematics Imagery Trainer is a technologically enabled activity architecture in which students manipulate a geometrical figure, such as a rectangle, with both hands along orthogonal axes while color feedback signals a target ratio. The student is "tasked first to make the rectangle green and, once that is accomplished, to keep moving the two vertices while keeping the rectangle green". After a performance criterion is met, a human or virtual tutor introduces grids and numerals, and activities then move to paper-and-pen tasks formalizing the attentional anchor.
requirements: Real-time color feedback tied to the target quantitative relation; supplementary inscriptions (grid, numerals) introduced only after a pre-specified minimal performance criterion
constraints: Reported studies are cross-sectional rather than longitudinal; the program has focused primarily on extremity (hand) actions without explicit regard to whole-body sub-movements
target_learning_goals: proportionality and ratio; trigonometry graphs; parabolas; quantitative reasoning grounded in movement
examples: The Orthogonal Proportion task with a 1:2 height-to-width green rectangle; grid and numeral overlays; paper-and-pen generation of further green triangles using hand-gauge and unit-counting techniques

title: Embodied-design instructional sequence: motor challenge, emergent attentional anchor, quantitative re-articulation, then formal mathematical discourse
description: This lesson-level pattern from the embodied-design genre sequences learning from a bimanual motor-control problem, through the spontaneous emergence of an attentional anchor, to its quantitative and formal mathematical articulation. Overlaid grids and numerals let students "describe their strategy quantitatively" and "predict properties of yet-unenacted geometrical shapes satisfying the interaction regimen", after which paper tasks materialize the anchor and a teacher names the new equivalence class, e.g. proportionality.

constraints: Documented in cross-sectional qualitative studies; the article notes studies have been cross-sectional rather than longitudinal
target_learning_goals: proportionality and equivalent ratio classes; coordinating perceptual strategies with formal mathematical notation
examples: The Orthogonal Proportion lesson moving from red/green rectangle feedback, to grid and numeral overlays, to paper-and-parallel-line drawing of green triangles negotiated with a revoicing teacher

article_title: Effects of School-led Greenspace Interventions on Mental, Physical and Social Wellbeing in Children and Adolescents: A Systematic Review
citation: Vi Ly · Dianne A. Vella-Brodrick. (2024). Effects of School-led Greenspace Interventions on Mental, Physical and Social Wellbeing in Children and Adolescents: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09963-1
title: Attention Restoration Theory and Stress Reduction Theory explain nature's restorative effects on wellbeing
description: The review presents two complementary theories for the human–nature connection. Attention Restoration Theory "posits that exposure to nature provides a restorative effect by recovering directed (effortful) attention after prolonged mental activity", with restorative settings requiring being away, extent, and compatibility. Stress Reduction Theory "proposes that natural environments have a restorative effect that reduces physiological stress and negative emotions" after stressful situations. Together with the Biophilia Hypothesis, they frame why school nature exposure may enhance wellbeing for learning.

constraints: The review notes these theories are frameworks proposed to explain nature–health links, applied here to school settings

stress reduction and attention restoration
examples: The review uses ART and SRT to motivate examining school-led nature interventions on affect, stress, PA and social outcomes

article_title: Augmentation or Erosion? Regulating Cognitive Offloading in Generative AI-Supported STEM Learning
citation: Daiki Nakamura. (2026). Augmentation or Erosion? Regulating Cognitive Offloading in Generative AI-Supported STEM Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10224-6
title: The augmentation–erosion framework: offloading augments learning when the offloaded process is peripheral to the learning goal and erodes it when the process is constitutive
description: The framework treats the educational effect of GenAI as a property of the partition of cognitive labor between learner and machine rather than of the tool. It holds that offloading is augmentative when the handed-off process is peripheral, freeing working-memory resources for germane processing, and erosive when the process is constitutive of the learning target, bypassing the processing learning was supposed to involve. Erosion covers both acquisition erosion (failing to build a competence) and maintenance erosion (decay of an acquired competence through non-exercise). Outcomes are defined relative to a comparison condition, by default unaided work with time on task held constant.
requirements: A specified learning goal against which operations are classified as peripheral or constitutive
A comparison condition (default: unaided work, time on task held constant) against which augmentation and erosion are defined
constraints: A conceptual article advancing propositions as hypotheses to be tested, not data-reported conclusions
Focal outcome is durable, unaided learning assessed at a delay, not AI-assisted performance
target_learners: STEM learners in secondary and undergraduate education
target_learning_goals: Durable, unaided disciplinary competence in STEM practices such as modeling, justification, and proof
examples: Student A offloads data entry, plotting, and parameter fitting but selects and justifies the model herself, an augmentative partition; Student B pastes data and transcribes the AI's answer, an episode at high risk of acquisition erosion
key_sources: Daiki Nakamura. (2026). Augmentation or Erosion? Regulating Cognitive Offloading in Generative AI-Supported STEM Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10224-6

article_title: Augmentation or Erosion? Regulating Cognitive Offloading in Generative AI-Supported STEM Learning
citation: Daiki Nakamura. (2026). Augmentation or Erosion? Regulating Cognitive Offloading in Generative AI-Supported STEM Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10224-6
title: Two goal-relative criteria — specification and assessment demand — locate operations on a graded peripheral–constitutive continuum
description: The framework supplies criteria applicable before instruction for classifying cognitive operations relative to a learning goal. The specification criterion asks whether the operation or its reasoning is named in the learning goal or its underlying standard; the assessment-demand criterion asks whether the criterion assessment, an unaided task at a delay, would require the learner to perform the operation or its equivalent. These yield a graded quantity, constitutive weight, with erosion risk rising monotonically in that weight. The learner's developmental status is kept separate, modulating how much practice a given learner still needs without changing the classification.
requirements: Explicit specification of the learning goal, which the article treats as an instructional design act
Measurement of learners' prior competence on constitutive operations before instruction to set the level of protection each operation warrants
constraints: Classification is goal-relative: the same content can be peripheral in one context and constitutive in another
target_learning_goals: Constructing and justifying models, solutions, and proofs within specified learning goals
examples: In a bacterial-growth modeling task, selecting and justifying a model family and interpreting fitted parameters are constitutive by both criteria, while entering data and writing up are peripheral
key_sources: Daiki Nakamura. (2026). Augmentation or Erosion? Regulating Cognitive Offloading in Generative AI-Supported STEM Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10224-6

article_title: Augmentation or Erosion? Regulating Cognitive Offloading in Generative AI-Supported STEM Learning
citation: Daiki Nakamura. (2026). Augmentation or Erosion? Regulating Cognitive Offloading in Generative AI-Supported STEM Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10224-6
title: Offloading regulation: a learning-oriented dimension of AI literacy comprising partition discernment, calibrated monitoring, disciplinary verification, and re-internalization
description: The article proposes offloading regulation as the competence to govern the cognitive partition between learner and GenAI, positioned as a learning-oriented dimension of AI literacy with domain-general and discipline-specific components. It comprises partition discernment (judging what may be offloaded without erosion), calibrated monitoring of whether understanding is developing, disciplinary verification of AI outputs, and re-internalization of offloaded content through re-deriving, self-explaining, or unaided attempts. It is enacted through metacognitive control and conditioned by learners' goals and motivation.
requirements: Metacognitive monitoring whose signal tracks actual understanding rather than fluency-based ease
Disciplinary competence sufficient to evaluate AI outputs, which novices may lack
constraints: Conditioned by learners' goals and motivation; the review notes learners who know which strategies work often do not use them
target_learners: STEM learners in K–12 and higher education
target_learning_goals: Governing the learner–AI division of cognitive labor so that offloading supports rather than supplants durable learning
examples: Student C treats an AI-generated model as a worked example, checks the fit against residuals, explains why a linear model fails, and later re-derives the doubling time unaided
key_sources: Daiki Nakamura. (2026). Augmentation or Erosion? Regulating Cognitive Offloading in Generative AI-Supported STEM Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10224-6

article_title: Augmentation or Erosion? Regulating Cognitive Offloading in Generative AI-Supported STEM Learning
citation: Daiki Nakamura. (2026). Augmentation or Erosion? Regulating Cognitive Offloading in Generative AI-Supported STEM Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10224-6
title: Peripheral–constitutive mapping across STEM disciplines: routine operations tend to augment, generating the disciplinary product itself unprocessed tends to erode
description: Table 1 maps the peripheral–constitutive distinction across mathematics, physics, chemistry, computer science, and engineering at the level of typical focal learning targets. For each discipline it lists the constitutive process (e.g., constructing and justifying a solution method in mathematics; designing an algorithm in computer science), peripheral offloads that tend to augment (routine arithmetic, unit conversion, boilerplate syntax), and constitutive offloads that tend to erode when unprocessed (generating the solution method, mechanism, or design rationale itself). The distinction is graded and goal-relative, not content-intrinsic.
requirements: Application of the specification and assessment-demand criteria within each discipline cell
A specified focal learning target for the activity
constraints: Whether an offload is peripheral or constitutive is defined relative to the focal learning target, not by the content as such; a mastered process may be peripheral for acquisition but sustained non-exercise can still erode maintenance
target_learners: STEM learners across mathematics, physics, chemistry, computer science, and engineering
target_learning_goals: Disciplinary practices such as modeling, mechanism proposal, algorithm design, and design reasoning under constraint
examples: In mathematics, offloading routine arithmetic tends to augment while generating the solution method or proof itself unprocessed tends to erode
key_sources: Daiki Nakamura. (2026). Augmentation or Erosion? Regulating Cognitive Offloading in Generative AI-Supported STEM Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10224-6

article_title: Augmentation or Erosion? Regulating Cognitive Offloading in Generative AI-Supported STEM Learning
citation: Daiki Nakamura. (2026). Augmentation or Erosion? Regulating Cognitive Offloading in Generative AI-Supported STEM Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10224-6
title: Design tasks and tools so that constitutive work stays with the learner: withhold answers, demand justification, and reward unaided capability
description: The article identifies task and assessment design as the system-side lever on the cognitive partition: whether tasks demand justification and exhibition of process, whether assessment rewards a finished product or evidence of unaided capability, and whether the tool surrenders answers or offers only hints all determine what it is rational to offload. Design can compensate for weak regulation, as hint-based tutors protected students who would not have regulated their own offloading with a permissive tool. Design and regulation function as partial substitutes and complements toward keeping offloading peripheral to the target.
requirements: Tasks and assessments that demand justification and evidence of unaided capability
Tool configurations that sequence assistance after an unaided attempt or require verification
constraints: Protection engineered into the environment prevented erosion without, by itself, producing augmentation
target_learners: STEM learners, including novices doubly exposed because they least equipped to vet AI output
target_learning_goals: Preserving goal-constitutive processing such as model selection, justification, and proof construction
examples: Bastani et al.'s GPT Tutor provided teacher-crafted hints rather than solutions and eliminated the learning penalty of the answer-giving interface; Kestin et al.'s tutor guided, questioned, and paced rather than surrendering solutions

article_title: A Review of Reminiscing in Early Childhood Settings and Links to Sustained Shared Thinking
citation: Dave Neale & Deborah Pino-Pasternak. (2016). A Review of Reminiscing in Early Childhood Settings and Links to Sustained Shared Thinking. Educ Psychol Rev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-016-9376-0
title: Elaborative style: an utterance-level coding framework for adult–child reminiscing
description: Elaborative style is a dimension of adults' language assessed in reminiscing research, classified on a continuum from high to low. High elaborative style uses open-ended questions, details and embellished descriptions producing co-constructed dialog with a strong narrative thread; coding proceeds "on an utterance-by-utterance basis followed by a quantitative assessment of the amount ofelaborationsand repetitionsa parent uses". Elaborations add new information; repetitions repeat the gist of a prior turn; evaluations confirm or negate and extend the child's utterance. The review proposes this framework as a transferable model for analyzing other adult–child conversations.
requirements: Conversations are coded utterance-by-utterance with quantitative counts of elaborations and repetitions
Adult–child conversation about past events, or by extension other adult–child dialog
constraints: The review focuses solely on research in the Western context due to cultural differences in reminiscing and elaborative style
target_learning_goals: Language and vocabulary development
Narrative and autobiographical memory skills
Social and emotional development
examples: The review presents Reese et al. (1993) transcripts contrasting a low elaborative mother who repeats the same question with a high elaborative mother who adds new details or asks new questions
key_sources: Dave Neale & Deborah Pino-Pasternak. (2016). A Review of Reminiscing in Early Childhood Settings and Links to Sustained Shared Thinking. Educ Psychol Rev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-016-9376-0

article_title: A Review of Reminiscing in Early Childhood Settings and Links to Sustained Shared Thinking
citation: Dave Neale & Deborah Pino-Pasternak. (2016). A Review of Reminiscing in Early Childhood Settings and Links to Sustained Shared Thinking. Educ Psychol Rev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-016-9376-0
title: Sustained shared thinking: an episode-level construct for adult–child dialog in early childhood
description: Sustained shared thinking is a construct developed in the EPPE and REPEY studies, defined by Sylva et al. (2004) as an episode in which two or more individuals "work together" in an intellectual way to solve a problem, clarify a concept, evaluate activities, or extend a narrative, with both parties contributing and thinking developing and extending. The review characterizes it as exemplifying the field's focus on explicit learning situations and macro-level episode identification, contrasting it with the utterance-by-utterance elaborative style approach. It reports the construct as developmentally significant in large-scale research.
requirements: Identification of valid episodes of joint intellectual activity between adult and child
constraints: The review argues its identification involves a proscriptive focus on explicit learning tasks and lacks close utterance-by-utterance structural analysis, limiting usefulness in some ways
target_learners: Preschool children in formal early childhood settings
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding and problem solving
Emergent literacy
Extension of narrative
examples: The review compares sustained shared thinking criteria with elaborative style analysis to draw out synergies and differences in classification and analysis

article_title: A Meta-Analysis of the Relations Between Achievement Goals and Internalizing Problems
citation: Diaconu-Gherasim, L. R., Elliot, A. J., Zancu, A. S., Brumariu, L. E., Măirean, C., Opariuc-Dan, C., & Crumpei-Tanasă, I. (2024). A Meta-Analysis of the Relations Between Achievement Goals and Internalizing Problems. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09943-5
title: Goal-orientation model of depression vulnerability
description: The article identifies Dykman's (1998) goal-orientation model of depression vulnerability as "the most influential model of achievement goals and internalizing problems." It postulates that "achievement goals lead to specific cognitive sets and appraisal patterns that have important implications for people's mental health": mastery-focused individuals perceive negative outcomes as growth opportunities and show lower depressive symptoms, while performance-focused individuals tie self-worth to social comparison and are more vulnerable to depression. The article extends the model to anxiety and to the approach-avoidance distinction.
requirements: The model presupposes that competence is a basic human need whose satisfaction sustains mental health and well-being, as the article states.
constraints: The article notes the relation between achievement goals and internalizing problems is posited to be reciprocal, so the model is not strictly unidirectional.
target_learners: children, adolescents, and young adults in educational settings
target_learning_goals: understanding how achievement goal adoption relates to anxiety and depression vulnerability
examples: The meta-analysis tested the model's prediction that mastery-approach goals relate negatively and performance-approach/avoidance goals positively to internalizing problems.

article_title: Learning Styles, Preferences, or Strategies? An Explanation for the Resurgence of Styles Across Many Meta-analyses
citation: John Hattie, Timothy O'Leary. (2025). Learning Styles, Preferences, or Strategies? An Explanation for the Resurgence of Styles Across Many Meta-analyses. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10002-w
title: Two-stories framework: matching-hypothesis (d) studies versus correlational (r) studies of learning styles
description: The article's central organizing framework distinguishes two types of learning styles meta-analyses that "effectively measure different things": d-studies testing whether "students do better when taught to their preferred learning style" and r-studies correlating learning style inventory scores with achievement. The framework explains the apparent resurgence of learning styles: the higher correlational average (r = 0.24) is mistaken for support of matching, which itself shows d = 0.04. The review uses this distinction to argue that correlational evidence cannot establish causation nor support the matching hypothesis.
requirements: Meta-analyses must be classified by whether they randomly assign learners within style groups to different teaching methods, per Pashler et al.'s design criteria
constraints: Correlational studies fail Pashler et al.'s criteria because they do not divide learners into groups or randomly assign methods, so they cannot support matching claims
target_learners: all school and higher education students
target_learning_goals: academic achievement
examples: The review classifies the 17 MetaX meta-analyses in Table 1 into four matching studies (pooled d = 0.04) and thirteen correlational studies (pooled r = 0.24)

article_title: Eye-Tracking in Educational Practice: Investigating Visual Perception Underlying Teaching and Learning in the Classroom
citation: Jarodzka, H., Skuballa, I., & Gruber, H. (2020). Eye-Tracking in Educational Practice: Investigating Visual Perception Underlying Teaching and Learning in the Classroom. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09565-7
title: Actor-perspective by setting taxonomy for classroom eye-tracking research
description: The article organizes eye-tracking research in education along two axes: the actor perspective studied (teacher vs. learner vs. teacher-learner interaction) and a continuum from laboratory to real-life settings. Figure 1 clusters existing research and the Special Issue articles into these boxes, showing that classic eye-tracking research sits in the learner-laboratory corner while interaction studies in real classrooms are the newest and scarcest. The authors state that existing research beyond the classic learner-laboratory box "is extremely scarce."
requirements: Eye-tracking methodology, optionally enriched with verbal protocols, to capture what actors saw and how they interpreted it
constraints: Apart from classic learner-on-material laboratory research, existing research in the other boxes is extremely scarce
target_learning_goals: understanding the role of visual perception in teaching and learning
examples: Figure 1 places the six Special Issue empirical articles into the learner, teacher, and interaction boxes along the lab-to-real-life continuum

citation: Jarodzka, H., Skuballa, I., & Gruber, H. (2020). Eye-Tracking in Educational Practice: Investigating Visual Perception Underlying Teaching and Learning in the Classroom. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09565-7
title: Wolff, Jarodzka, and Boshuizen's model of teachers' classroom management scripts linking knowledge, perception, and situational awareness
description: The article presents the first detailed theoretical framework for research on teachers' professional vision: a model of teachers' classroom management scripts incorporating organized knowledge and perception with their effects on situational awareness and representations of classroom events, developed by contrasting novice and expert teachers. The review states this model "can not only help to synergize existing research into a broader picture but also clearly point towards new research avenues." It is expected to enable a shift from exploration to hypothesis-driven research.
requirements: Future empirical research to test and improve the model, moving beyond mere explorations
constraints: The field previously lacked specific theoretical models of cognitive and perceptual processes underlying teachers' classroom behavior and had to borrow from adjacent fields, which did not allow for specific predictions
target_learning_goals: understanding how teachers' knowledge and visual perception support classroom management and situational awareness
examples: The model contrasts novice and expert teachers' organized knowledge, perception, situational awareness, and representations of classroom events
