article_title: Not New, but Nearly Forgotten: the Testing Effect Decreases or even Disappears as the Complexity of Learning Materials Increases
citation: van Gog, T., & Sweller, J. (2015). Not New, but Nearly Forgotten: the Testing Effect Decreases or even Disappears as the Complexity of Learning Materials Increases. Educational Psychology Review, 27, 247–264. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-015-9310-x
title: Element interactivity as a measure of learning task complexity that depends on learner expertise
description: The review defines complex learning tasks as tasks "high in element interactivity", containing related information elements that must be processed simultaneously in working memory, as when learning how components of a hydraulic brake system interact. The measure incorporates human cognitive architecture: what is complex for a novice may constitute a single element for an expert, because knowledge held in long-term memory allows automatic processing without excessive working memory load.
requirements: Complexity judgements must simultaneously consider the knowledge base of individuals, since information complex for a novice is simple for someone with relevant expertise
constraints: Element interactivity "cannot be specified just by reference to the material" because it changes with the learner's level of expertise
target_learners: school and university students learning curriculum content
target_learning_goals: identifying which learning materials and tasks are complex for a given learner

article_title: Not New, but Nearly Forgotten: the Testing Effect Decreases or even Disappears as the Complexity of Learning Materials Increases
citation: van Gog, T., & Sweller, J. (2015). Not New, but Nearly Forgotten: the Testing Effect Decreases or even Disappears as the Complexity of Learning Materials Increases. Educational Psychology Review, 27, 247–264. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-015-9310-x
title: Association-building explanations for why the testing effect decreases with material complexity
description: The review advances an explanatory account built on two existing explanations for low element interactivity materials: free recall improves retention through organization of information during recall, and paired-associate testing strengthens memory traces via mediators. Both hinge on "elaborative processes that establish relations between information elements", which are less necessary when such relations are inherent to complex material, and restudy may instead afford relational processing of elements while maintaining student motivation.
requirements: The account assumes testing benefits arise mainly from establishing associations between elements during retrieval
constraints: The review notes "very few studies have systematically evaluated theoretical explanations for the memorial benefits of testing"
target_learners: school and university students learning curriculum content
target_learning_goals: explaining when and why retrieval practice benefits retention
key_sources: van Gog, T., & Sweller, J. (2015). Not New, but Nearly Forgotten: the Testing Effect Decreases or even Disappears as the Complexity of Learning Materials Increases. Educational Psychology Review, 27, 247–264. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-015-9310-x

article_title: Not New, but Nearly Forgotten: the Testing Effect Decreases or even Disappears as the Complexity of Learning Materials Increases
citation: van Gog, T., & Sweller, J. (2015). Not New, but Nearly Forgotten: the Testing Effect Decreases or even Disappears as the Complexity of Learning Materials Increases. Educational Psychology Review, 27, 247–264. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-015-9310-x
title: Consider the complexity of learning materials when deciding between practice testing and further study
description: Because the testing effect shrinks or vanishes for high element interactivity materials, teachers and instructional designers should weigh material complexity when choosing between practice tests and restudy. The review argues that research on complexity as a boundary condition "would help teachers and instructional designers to know for which learning tasks they can and cannot expect benefits of having their students take practice tests instead of engage in further study".
requirements: Judgement of the element interactivity of learning tasks and test items before assigning practice testing
constraints: In several special-issue studies, other known boundary conditions such as test format, retrieval success on the initial test, feedback, or test spacing "cannot be ruled out entirely as an alternative explanation"
target_learning_goals: choosing between practice testing and restudy for complex learning tasks
examples: Worked example studies in the special issue found no testing effect for problem-solving tasks, while scrambled sentences and word lists showed benefits on delayed tests

article_title: The Multicomponent Working Memory Model, Attention, and Long-term Memory in Multimedia Learning: A Comment on Schweppe and Rummer (2014)
citation: Soemer, A. (2015). The Multicomponent Working Memory Model, Attention, and Long-term Memory in Multimedia Learning: A Comment on Schweppe and Rummer (2014). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-015-9303-9
title: Baddeley's multicomponent model is a functional, not structural, working memory model compatible with activated long-term memory representations forming part of working memory
description: The multicomponent model of working memory (Baddeley and Hitch 1974; Baddeley 2000) separates working memory from long-term memory functionally, not structurally, in order to account for functionality beyond mere activation of long-term memory traces, such as learning new information. The commentary quotes Baddeley and Logie (1999) that working memory and LTM "comprise two functionally separable cognitive systems", and notes the model's subcomponents have direct connections to long-term memory that do not involve the episodic buffer. This reading contradicts the characterization in multimedia learning theories that the model posits structural separation.
requirements: Interpreting the model requires distinguishing functional from structural separation, as the commentary argues structural separation "is nowhere asserted in Baddeley (2000)"
constraints: The commentary notes multimedia learning theories deviate from the multicomponent model by assuming visual and auditory, rather than visuospatial and verbal, components
target_learning_goals: theoretical foundations for explaining learning from multimedia materials
examples: The commentary cites work on the phonological loop's heavy involvement in verbal learning (Baddeley et al. 1998) as establishing long-term memory contributions to subcomponent processing within the framework.
key_sources: Soemer, A. (2015). The Multicomponent Working Memory Model, Attention, and Long-term Memory in Multimedia Learning: A Comment on Schweppe and Rummer (2014). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-015-9303-9

article_title: The Multicomponent Working Memory Model, Attention, and Long-term Memory in Multimedia Learning: A Comment on Schweppe and Rummer (2014)
citation: Soemer, A. (2015). The Multicomponent Working Memory Model, Attention, and Long-term Memory in Multimedia Learning: A Comment on Schweppe and Rummer (2014). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-015-9303-9
title: Cowan's embedded-processes model details a single central executive attentional mechanism that can reactivate any long-term memory trace irrespective of content
description: Cowan's (1999) embedded-processes model is presented as filling a gap the multicomponent model left until recently: an underspecified central executive. The commentary states it details "a single central executive (i.e., attentional) mechanism that is able to (re)activate any long-term memory trace irrespective of its content". Cowan argued for this general mechanism based on experiments showing working memory capacity estimates do not differ much between single and dual span tasks with verbal and visual materials under certain conditions. The commentary treats this model as complementary to, not a replacement for, the multicomponent model.
requirements: The model's single-capacity assumption is supported, per the commentary, by dual-task evidence such as Saults and Cowan (2007)
constraints: The commentary notes functional specialization is "not paid attention to in the embedded-processes model"
target_learning_goals: theoretical foundations for explaining attention and capacity limits in learning from multimedia

article_title: One Instructional Sequence Fits all? A Conceptual Analysis of the Applicability of Concreteness Fading in Mathematics, Physics, Chemistry, and Biology Education
citation: Tommi Kokkonen & Lennart Schalk. (2021). One Instructional Sequence Fits all? A Conceptual Analysis of the Applicability of Concreteness Fading in Mathematics, Physics, Chemistry, and Biology Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09581-7
title: Structure-mapping theory's four domain-general processes as a framework for analyzing learning from multiple external representations
description: The article proposes theories of analogical and relational reasoning, especially structure-mapping theory, as a framework for examining how combinations of external representations trigger learning processes. It states that "Structure-mapping theory postulates four basic, domain-general processes: abstraction, re-representation, inference projection, and difference detection." Abstraction extracts a schema capturing commonalities across representations; re-representation changes an internal representation when a novel example does not fit; inference projection generates inferences from a well-understood to a less well-understood concept; difference detection distinguishes superficially similar but conceptually distinct representations. The authors use these processes to predict how MER combinations influence knowledge development.
requirements: A unified framework is needed to systematically examine cognitive aspects of learning from MERs
constraints: The authors note other processes may be involved; the four-process collection is offered as a parsimonious model
target_learners: students in mathematics and natural science education
target_learning_goals: understanding how combinations of external representations trigger learning processes

title: DeFT framework's three normative functions of multiple external representations
description: The article describes Ainsworth's Design-Functions-Tasks (DeFT) framework as the guiding framework for research on multiple external representations, covering design parameters, normative functions, and cognitive tasks. It states that "The DeFT framework lays out three major functions for MERs": complementary roles, constraining interpretation, and allowing construction of deeper understanding. Complementary roles mean different representations convey different pieces of information; constraining interpretation works by familiarity or inherent properties; deeper understanding arises, for example, when analogies support abstract, transferable mental representations. The framework also captures how cognitive tasks influence construction of and changes to internal representations.
requirements: The framework prescribes what external representations are supposed to do (normative functions)
constraints: The article notes the framework's description of learning is rather unspecific and requires precise description of triggered learning processes

title: Lin et al.'s taxonomy extending concreteness fading levels across mathematics, physics, chemistry, and biology
description: Lin et al.'s taxonomy, presented in the article's Table 1, extends the concreteness fading sequence from mathematics to the natural sciences. The article states it is "conceptually based on the chemistry triplet," mapping the concrete level to the macro scale of phenomena observable through the senses, the faded/intermediate level to nano- or micro-scale schematic representations of atoms and molecules, and the symbolic level to chemical symbols, equations, or biochemical notation. The article uses this taxonomy to show that progressing across levels in the natural sciences varies along more than one dimension and cannot be directly aligned with mathematics progressions.
requirements: Three external representations per sequence, corresponding to the Fyfe and Nathan definition of concreteness fading
constraints: The article notes the intermediate nano/micro-scale level is less obviously aligned with intermediate examples used in mathematics, and that the taxonomy is not the only possible way to conceptualize concreteness fading across disciplines
target_learners: students in mathematics, physics, chemistry, and biology education
target_learning_goals: understanding concepts and principles across representational levels
examples: Table 1 maps concrete examples to the macro scale in physics, chemistry, and biology, faded examples to invisible forces, nano scale, and micro scale, and symbolic notation to symbolic or biochemical representations

title: Biology's complex systems hierarchy of components, interactions, and emergent behaviors as a framework for representational levels
description: For biology, the article presents a framework conceptualizing three levels of complex systems. It states the framework "conceptualizes three levels of complex systems: components, interactions, and emergent behaviors (Buckley and Quellmalz 2013)." The component level corresponds to the concrete level, capturing phenomena as experienced; the interaction level consists of descriptions or dynamic models of interactions between components with significant idealization; the emergent behavior level may consist of mathematical descriptions such as population dynamics devoid of contextual details. The article argues the biochemical level constitutes its own conceptual sphere rather than a more idealized representation of macro-level phenomena, and that biology spans nested hierarchies of multiple entities.
requirements: Learners must make sense of complex interdependencies and causalities within and across levels
constraints: The article notes emergent phenomena are counterintuitive with non-linear interaction patterns, and cross-level relations are not present in mathematical descriptions of population-level dynamics
target_learning_goals: understanding hierarchical and complex biological systems and emergent phenomena
examples: Buckley and Quellmalz use an animation with life-like depictions of organisms such as grass, lizards, and crickets to illustrate ecosystem components

citation: Gary D. Phye. (2012). Commentary on the Special Issue. Educ Psychol Rev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-012-9211-1
title: Gibson's correspondence principle: research findings should correspond across levels of analysis
description: The commentary invokes Gibson (1994)'s correspondence principle to address poor communication between basic and applied psychologists. Different specialties study the same human behavior "from quite different levels of observation and analysis" but "there should be a correspondence among levels in terms of research findings." The author explicitly rejects a reductionist reading, framing the principle as correspondence between levels rather than a prescriptive cause-effect chain, and applies it to educational research on classroom learning.
requirements: Researchers studying the same behavior at different levels must seek correspondence among their findings rather than treating levels as incommensurable
constraints: The author states this is not a reductionist view proposing a prescriptive cause-effect relationship from brain cell to classroom performance
target_learning_goals: Academic learning and classroom performance
examples: The commentary contrasts a global constructivist analysis of fourth-grade academic growth with the more precise functional study of memory and cognition conducted by applied cognitive psychologists

title: A three-tier level of analysis implicitly exists in the study of learning, memory, and cognition
description: The author proposes that "a three-tier level of analysis implicitly exists in the study of learning, memory, and cognition (educational research, educational psychology, applied cognition)". The tiers range from global educational research on academic growth, through educational psychology, to applied cognitive psychology providing "principles of learning, memory and cognition" with classroom application. He notes someone could propose a four- or five-tier model and views the journal's special issue as a step toward enhancing communication among these research communities.

constraints: The author states there is a scarcity of testable models that would serve as the basis for model-based reasoning, which is critical for communication across disciplines

title: Involve teachers and building administrators in partnerships when implementing learning principles in schools
description: Commenting on the Agarwal, Bain, and Chamberlain article, the author argues that successful classroom implementation of basic learning principles depends on collaboration: "The involvement of both teachers and building administration is a critical factor in the successful implementation of the principles discussed herein." His stated concern is that only a small number of students were impacted over a 5-year period, raising dissemination and scaling questions.

title: Hybrid interleaving format: 12 training sessions of 10 problems ordered by cognitive processing type and material nature
description: The cognitive training programs reviewed by Klauer and Phye (2008) followed "a program format consisting of 12 training sessions over a 3- to 4-week period with a total of 120 problem solving episodes," each session containing 10 problems. The sessions "follows a hybrid interleaving format ordered in difficulty of cognitive processing (generalization then discrimination, then the combination) as well as the nature of the material (attributes then relations)." The author states this format promotes durability of problem solving commonly maintained over a 6-month interval.

article_title: Using Primary Knowledge: an Efficient Way To Motivate Students and Promote the Learning of Formal Reasoning
citation: Florence Lespiau, André Tricot. (2019). Using Primary Knowledge: an Efficient Way To Motivate Students and Promote the Learning of Formal Reasoning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09482-4
title: Geary's evolutionary approach to knowledge: primary versus secondary knowledge
description: The article organizes its predictions around Geary's evolutionary approach, in which "humans are able to easily acquire primary knowledge and, with more efforts, secondary knowledge". Primary knowledge is evolutionarily salient content such as rules about food and animals, while secondary knowledge is culturally invented content such as formal mathematics and grammar. The authors use this distinction to predict that framing formal logical problems in primary contexts should raise efficiency, motivation and engagement, and propose the approach as "a framework for developing a way to present new content that is cost-efficient in keeping learners motivated".
requirements: Learning tasks must distinguish content that is evolutionarily salient (primary) from culturally invented formal content (secondary)
target_learning_goals: formal logical reasoning (syllogisms)
examples: Syllogism training materials framed as rules about invented food and animals (primary) versus fictitious mathematics and grammar rules (secondary)

description: The article recommends using primary knowledge contents to facilitate learning of formal logical rules: "Framing formal logical problems in evolutionary salient contexts should increase learners' efficiency, motivation and engagement in learning compared with framing logical problems in secondary knowledge". In practice, formal problems are given concrete, evolutionarily familiar cover stories (food, animals) rather than abstract or school-like content. The authors present this as a cost-efficient way of keeping learners motivated whatever their age or personal characteristics.

article_title: To Grade or Not To Grade? Demystifying a Centuries-Old Debate
citation: Nicolas Hübner, Juliane Rutsch, Ann-Kathrin Schnelle, Mia Herkommer, Evelin Ruth-Herbein, Benjamin Fauth. (2026). To Grade or Not To Grade? Demystifying a Centuries-Old Debate. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10156-1
title: Three overarching theoretical foundations structure the grades debate: motivation research, assessment and feedback research, and measurement research
description: The article's literature review of 136 studies organized the theoretical foundations of the school-grades debate into recurring fields. As the authors report, "the results of the literature review revealed three overarching recurring theoretical foundations, which stemmed from the fields of: (1) motivation research, (2) assessment and feedback research, and (3) measurement research." Within motivation research the prevalent theories were self-determination theory and its subtheories (cognitive evaluation theory, organismic integration theory); within assessment and feedback research, summative versus formative assessment and formative feedback theory; within measurement research, validity and standardization of grades and standards-based grading. Occasional topics were scored as a fourth 'other research' category.
requirements: The taxonomy emerged from a systematic literature search across four databases with AI-aided screening in ASReview, yielding 136 studies rated with a two-category scheme (interrater κ = 0.85 and κ = 0.94)
constraints: Topics that came up only occasionally were scored as a separate 'other research' category rather than integrated into the three main foundations
target_learning_goals: understanding how grading practices relate to student motivation, learning, and measurement quality
examples: The LPF school trial's features were explicitly linked back to these three theoretical foundations in Table 1

title: LPF school trial: grade abolishment with standards-based competency grids, learning-development meetings, and formative feedback
description: The Learning-enhanced Performance Feedback (LPF) school trial was a quasi-experimental intervention in 35 Baden-Württemberg elementary schools beginning in the 2022/2023 school year, compared with 40 control schools. Trial schools abolished written grades and report cards and instead gave "standards-based competency grids" on a 4-point scale from "You still need to work on this" to "You are an expert", at least two oral learning-development meetings per school year, and formative assessment and feedback practices integrated throughout instruction. The grids share many similarities with standards-based grading systems as defined by Welsh et al. (2013) and Guskey and Bailey (2001).
requirements: Trial schools were required to eliminate written grades from Grade 2 onward; implementation was evaluated on behalf of the Ministry of Education and Cultural Affairs
constraints: The trial was implemented with minimal requirements: teachers received no comprehensive professional development and no detailed guidance on formative assessment or feedback practices; standardization of features decreased from the first to the third feature

subject-specific self-concepts and interests
well-being and classroom climate
examples: Competency grids covered predefined areas in German, mathematics, and social studies (e.g., "You read texts fluently", "You can measure sizes") plus behavior, work attitude, and learning process

citation: Bjorklund, D.F. (2022). Children's Evolved Learning Abilities and Their Implications for Education. Educational Psychology Review, 34, 2243-2273. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09688-z
title: Four evolved learning mechanisms make humans highly educable
description: The article organizes human educability around four evolved mechanisms: "skeletal perceptual and cognitive mechanisms that get fleshed out over the course of development, mainly through play"; plasticity greatest early but persisting into adulthood; remarkable social-learning capabilities; and dispositions toward exploration and play. It uses this framework to explain how children are prepared to learn and why modern schooling sometimes conflicts with it.

constraints: Framed as an evolutionary account of children's learning rather than a tested instructional intervention

title: Evolutionary mismatches explain conflicts between evolved learning mechanisms and modern schooling
description: The article defines evolutionary mismatches as "conflicts between psychological mechanisms evolved in ancient environments and their utility in modern ones," examined "specifically with respect to modern educational systems." This account explains why some school practices fit poorly with children's evolved learning abilities and motivates the article's recommendations for aligning education with those abilities.

citation: Demetriou, A., Spanoudis, G., & Mouyi, A. (2011). Educating the Developing Mind: Towards an Overarching Paradigm. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-011-9178-3
title: Four-system architecture of the mind: specialized structural systems, representational capacity, inference, and consciousness
description: The article proposes that the mind is organized into interacting systems: specialized structural systems interfacing with environmental domains, a representational capacity system serving as the work space of the mind, an inference system connecting information toward the goal of the moment, and a consciousness system that monitors, controls, and regulates processing, including metarepresentation. The systems interact dynamically so that changes in each are related to changes in others.

constraints: The essay focuses on cognitive processes, integrating motivational and emotional considerations only briefly
target_learning_goals: understanding, problem solving, and learning across domains

citation: Demetriou, A., Spanoudis, G., & Mouyi, A. (2011). Educating the Developing Mind: Towards an Overarching Paradigm. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-011-9178-3
title: Developmental milestones of representation: dual representation, logical necessity, and conditional representations
description: The review organizes representational development into milestones. Around ages 3-4 children differentiate representations from the objects they represent, which DeLoache called dual representation and which opens the way for intentional symbol use. Around ages 7-8 children grasp that representations constrain each other, the beginning of logical necessity. In early adolescence, conditional representations let thinkers view systems of representations from the point of view of each other, making thought suppositional and foresighted.
requirements: Gradual emergence of language bringing representations as such into focus for reflection
constraints: Milestone ages are modal characterizations of development, not strict boundaries
target_learning_goals: symbol use, systematic classification, hypothetical and proportional reasoning

title: Metarepresentation as the generative mechanism of consciousness and cognitive change
description: The review defines metarepresentation as the generative aspect of consciousness: an ideoplastic process that looks for, encodes, and typifies similarities between mental experiences and representations. Through it, new mental operations, higher-order rules, and representations standing for them are created. Metarepresentation also builds self-evaluated maps of mental functions that guide problem solving, and links mind and personality through a personal constant moderating self-evaluations.

constraints: There are large individual differences in the accuracy of self-generated maps of mental functions

description: The article proposes a model for education specifying educational priorities for different phases of development according to the cognitive developmental milestones associated with each phase. It further specifies how education can help students construct mental models for conceptual change, use central representational capacity efficiently, advance analogical and deductive reasoning, learn how to learn, and become critical and creative thinkers, summarized in a table of principles spanning working memory, conceptual change, reasoning, learning to learn, and critical thinking.

target_learning_goals: conceptual change, efficient use of working memory, analogical and deductive reasoning, learning to learn, critical and creative thinking

article_title: An Interactive Layers Model of Self-Regulated Learning and Cognitive Load
citation: Joachim Wirth, Ferdinand Stebner, Melanie Trypke, Corinna Schuster, & Detlev Leutner. (2020). An Interactive Layers Model of Self-Regulated Learning and Cognitive Load. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09568-4
title: Interactive layers model of self-regulated learning and cognitive load
description: The article proposes a model that represents self-regulated learning across three layers — a content layer, a learning strategy layer, and a metacognitive layer — each spanning sensory memory, working memory, and long-term memory. It distinguishes conscious self-regulation in working memory, which induces cognitive load, from unconscious self-regulation initiated by resonant states in sensory memory, which does not. Layers interact through monitoring and control processes, both consciously in working memory and automatically in sensory memory.
requirements: The model assumes the three structural memory components proposed by Atkinson and Shiffrin (1968): sensory memory, working memory, and long-term memory
constraints: The model is proposed as a theoretical framework substantiated by a narrative review; the authors state it must be tested empirically in future research
target_learners: learners across educational levels engaged in self-regulated learning
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning
metacognitive monitoring and control
cognitive load management
examples: The authors use the model to re-interpret inconsistent findings on self-regulation correlations, questionnaire validity, the underconfidence-with-practice effect, and the expertise reversal effect
key_sources: Joachim Wirth, Ferdinand Stebner, Melanie Trypke, Corinna Schuster, & Detlev Leutner. (2020). An Interactive Layers Model of Self-Regulated Learning and Cognitive Load. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09568-4

article_title: An Interactive Layers Model of Self-Regulated Learning and Cognitive Load
citation: Joachim Wirth, Ferdinand Stebner, Melanie Trypke, Corinna Schuster, & Detlev Leutner. (2020). An Interactive Layers Model of Self-Regulated Learning and Cognitive Load. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09568-4
title: Resonant states as a mechanism of unconscious self-regulation in sensory memory
description: Adapting Grossberg's Adaptive Resonance Theory, the authors propose that when sensory information matches expectations retrieved from long-term memory, bottom-up and top-down processes amplify each other, creating a resonant state in sensory memory. Resonant states can stay unconscious, allowing information to interact with long-term memory and contribute to learning without being transferred to working memory, without achieving consciousness, and without inducing cognitive load. Strong mismatched information instead transfers to working memory and induces cognitive load.
requirements: Resonance requires a match between bottom-up sensory information and top-down long-term memory information, such as schemes or expectations
constraints: Resonance is proposed as necessary but not sufficient for consciousness; resonant states that stay in sensory memory remain unconscious
target_learning_goals: implicit and incidental learning
automatic strategy use
unconscious metacognitive regulation
examples: The authors illustrate the mechanism with driving a car: steering remains unconscious as long as the road is straight, but a construction area with unexpected traffic signs transfers information to working memory and induces cognitive load
key_sources: Joachim Wirth, Ferdinand Stebner, Melanie Trypke, Corinna Schuster, & Detlev Leutner. (2020). An Interactive Layers Model of Self-Regulated Learning and Cognitive Load. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09568-4

article_title: An Interactive Layers Model of Self-Regulated Learning and Cognitive Load
citation: Joachim Wirth, Ferdinand Stebner, Melanie Trypke, Corinna Schuster, & Detlev Leutner. (2020). An Interactive Layers Model of Self-Regulated Learning and Cognitive Load. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09568-4
title: Design strategy instruction to move learners from declarative to proceduralized strategy knowledge through repeated practice
description: The article describes how learning strategy interventions typically begin by verbally explaining and demonstrating a strategy, then give learners repeated opportunities to apply it to similar tasks, moving through declarative, knowledge compilation, and procedural phases. As knowledge is proceduralized, conscious interpretation of conceptual and conditional strategy information decreases and the cognitive load of strategy use decreases. This principle follows the article's account of the learning strategy layer.
requirements: Interventions must include phases of skill acquisition as described by Anderson (1982): verbal explanation and demonstration followed by repeated application to different but similar learning tasks
constraints: In the declarative phase, strategy knowledge is conscious and induces cognitive load; the load reduction applies only once knowledge is proceduralized
target_learners: learners acquiring learning strategies across educational levels
target_learning_goals: learning strategy knowledge and use
reducing cognitive load during strategy application
examples: The article describes typical interventions, citing Leopold and Leutner (2015), that start with verbally explaining the strategy and its steps, demonstrating its use, and then giving repeated application opportunities

article_title: A Conceptual Framework to Integrate Research Programs on Self-Regulation in Education
citation: Wortha, F., Gerjets, P., Azevedo, R., Bernacki, M., Brucker, B., Bühler, B., Ehlis, A.-C., Kasneci, E., Miyake, A., Murayama, K., Nagengast, B., Roberts, B., Tibus, M., & Trautwein, U. (2026). A Conceptual Framework to Integrate Research Programs on Self-Regulation in Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10196-7
title: Integrative framework conceptualizing self-regulation in education as a dynamic, interdependent person-situation system of four research traditions
description: The article proposes a conceptual framework that unifies four SR research traditions—Stable Dispositions, Limited Resources, Driving Forces, and Learning Activities—into one architecture. It states: "our framework positions SR as a dynamic, interdependent system, emphasizing how interactions and compensatory mechanisms explain individual differences and influence learning outcomes." The framework maps how stable traits shape situation-specific regulatory processes that jointly produce learning outcomes, and how situated processes over time give rise to enduring traits.
requirements: Integration of constructs that differ in granularity and temporal scope, from real-time metacognitive judgments to semester-level strategy use
constraints: The framework is limited to four internal individual-level mechanisms; social context, co-regulation, environment, gender, and socioeconomic status are treated as antecedent or contextual variables, not SR mechanisms
target_learners: Learners across educational contexts and trajectories
target_learning_goals: Self-regulation of cognition, motivation, emotion, and behavior in pursuit of learning goals
examples: Fig. 2 depicts the integrative framework with arrows indicating hypothesized relationships, darker arrows for temporal and causal influences and lighter arrows for reciprocal effects
key_sources: Wortha, F., Gerjets, P., Azevedo, R., Bernacki, M., Brucker, B., Bühler, B., Ehlis, A.-C., Kasneci, E., Miyake, A., Murayama, K., Nagengast, B., Roberts, B., Tibus, M., & Trautwein, U. (2026). A Conceptual Framework to Integrate Research Programs on Self-Regulation in Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10196-7

article_title: A Conceptual Framework to Integrate Research Programs on Self-Regulation in Education
citation: Wortha, F., Gerjets, P., Azevedo, R., Bernacki, M., Brucker, B., Bühler, B., Ehlis, A.-C., Kasneci, E., Miyake, A., Murayama, K., Nagengast, B., Roberts, B., Tibus, M., & Trautwein, U. (2026). A Conceptual Framework to Integrate Research Programs on Self-Regulation in Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10196-7
title: Taxonomy of four SR research traditions distinguished by core explanatory construct families and Lakatosian hard cores
description: Using a Lakatosian framework of research programs, the article categorizes SR research into four traditions, each with a hard core of foundational assertions protected by a belt of auxiliary hypotheses and methods. The article states: "we categorize existing research programs into four broad traditions, each of which is characterized by its core explanatory construct family: (1) Stable Dispositions, (2) Limited Resources, (3) Driving Forces, and (4) Learning Activities." The traditions differ in stability assumptions, methodologies, and temporal levels of analysis.
requirements: Each tradition is treated as a family of research programs structured around a common hard core of foundational assertions
constraints: The traditions were selected because they present distinct assumptions, mechanisms, and constructs of individual-level SR; contextual factors are excluded from the taxonomy
target_learners: Learners in educational settings from school to higher education
target_learning_goals: Understanding how dispositions, cognitive resources, motivation, and learning strategies each explain self-regulation
examples: The Learning Activities tradition's hard core centers on metacognitive monitoring and control of learning activities (Winne & Hadwin), while the Limited Resources tradition foregrounds working-memory capacity and executive functions

article_title: A Conceptual Framework to Integrate Research Programs on Self-Regulation in Education
citation: Wortha, F., Gerjets, P., Azevedo, R., Bernacki, M., Brucker, B., Bühler, B., Ehlis, A.-C., Kasneci, E., Miyake, A., Murayama, K., Nagengast, B., Roberts, B., Tibus, M., & Trautwein, U. (2026). A Conceptual Framework to Integrate Research Programs on Self-Regulation in Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10196-7
title: Hierarchical model of nested self-regulatory cycles at macro, meso, and micro levels
description: Drawing on action regulation theory, the framework proposes that self-regulatory processes occur across nested cycles at three levels of granularity and timescale. The article states: "These cycles can be conceptually segmented into three distinct levels: the macro-level (e.g., managing long-term goals such as preparing for an examination across multiple study sessions or an entire semester), the meso-level (e.g., executing within-session cycles of planning, performance, and appraisal), and the micro-level (e.g., adjusting strategies in response to real-time feedback or moment-to-moment monitoring)."
requirements: Success or failure at one level can systematically influence processes at another, requiring multi-level investigation
constraints: The segmentation is conceptual, proposed by the authors drawing from action regulation theory rather than empirically tested in this article
target_learners: Students managing study across sessions, within sessions, and moment to moment
target_learning_goals: Coordinating long-term goal pursuit, within-session regulation, and real-time strategy adjustment
examples: A poor micro-level self-test result may trigger motivational regulation inflected by trait conscientiousness, leading to deeper strategies in future meso-level sessions

article_title: The Impasse on Gender Differences in Intelligence: a Meta-Analysis on WISC Batteries
citation: D. Giofrè · K. Allen · E. Toffalini · S. Caviola. (2022). The Impasse on Gender Differences in Intelligence: a Meta-Analysis on WISC Batteries. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09705-1
title: CHC theory and the cross-battery approach as the framework for locating WISC gender differences across ability levels
description: The article adopts the Cattell-Horn-Carroll (CHC) theory and the cross-battery approach as its organizing framework, in which "the CHC model divides cognitive abilities into different levels": the g-factor at the top, broad abilities (gF, gV, gC, gSM, gS, gQ) in the middle, and narrow abilities at the base. WISC subtests are assigned to broad factors by their CHC loadings, allowing female/male differences to be estimated at factor and subtest levels rather than only on FSIQ. The framework also motivates comparing results across WISC battery versions.
requirements: WISC subtests must be classifiable into CHC broad factors by their loadings, as the article codes them (e.g. Block design to gV, Coding to gS).
constraints: The article did not calculate a gQ factor because only one subtest (arithmetic) measured it, making the factor unnecessary in its words.
target_learners: school-aged children assessed with the WISC
target_learning_goals: accurate assessment of cognitive ability differences between genders in children
examples: The meta-analysis used subtests such as vocabulary and information as indicators of gC, and matrix reasoning and picture concepts as indicators of gF, fitting separate models per factor.
key_sources: D. Giofrè · K. Allen · E. Toffalini · S. Caviola. (2022). The Impasse on Gender Differences in Intelligence: a Meta-Analysis on WISC Batteries. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09705-1

article_title: Research Avenues Supporting Embodied Cognition in Learning and Instruction
citation: Juan C. Castro-Alonso, Paul Ayres, Shirong Zhang, Björn B. de Koning, Fred Paas. (2024). Research Avenues Supporting Embodied Cognition in Learning and Instruction. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09847-4
title: Six research avenues framework for embodied cognition effects on learning and instruction
description: The review organizes embodied learning research into six interconnected avenues: physical activity, generative learning, and offloaded cognition explain benefits of making human movements; specialized processor and signaling explain benefits of observing movements; and social cognition applies to both. As the review states, "The first three research avenues (physical activity, generative learning, and offloaded cognition) apply when students make human movements." Each avenue is paired with influencing features (e.g., movement relevance, working memory load, redundancy, meaningfulness) that modulate the size of embodied learning effects.
requirements: Movements must be made or observed in instructional settings, primarily hand gestures and object manipulation
constraints: The avenues are complementary and not mutually exclusive; the review's primary focus is on hand movements rather than whole-body movements
target_learners: students across domains including math, science, statistics, and astronomy
target_learning_goals: learning enhanced by making or observing gestures and object manipulations
examples: Table 1 lists each avenue with its explanation, example, influencing feature, and a review article, e.g., offloaded cognition illustrated by using manipulative objects for complex calculations
key_sources: Juan C. Castro-Alonso, Paul Ayres, Shirong Zhang, Björn B. de Koning, Fred Paas. (2024). Research Avenues Supporting Embodied Cognition in Learning and Instruction. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09847-4

article_title: When Fine is Large and Gross is Small: A Meta-Analysis of Links Between Fine and Gross Motor Skills with Academic-Cognitive Skills
citation: Karle, V. L., Suggate, S. P., Winter, R., & Stoeger, H. (2026). When Fine is Large and Gross is Small: A Meta-Analysis of Links Between Fine and Gross Motor Skills with Academic-Cognitive Skills. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10161-4
title: Functionalism and shared action-cognition accounts of motor–academic-cognitive links
description: The article organizes theoretical explanations for motor–academic-cognitive associations into two perspectives. Functionalism holds that "children with better motor skills can more easily access and engage in learning opportunities", including writing facilitating reading and lower cognitive load in combined motor-cognitive tasks. The shared action-cognition account holds that academic-cognitive skills "share and can recruit motor networks during task performance" (e.g., handwriting networks during reading, finger perception networks during mathematics). The authors state the two perspectives "are not necessarily mutually exclusive" and use both to interpret the FiMS advantage.
requirements: Both perspectives are used to interpret correlational evidence; the article notes experimental evidence for a functional mechanism exists mainly for older children (motor skills facilitating writing, which improves reading).
constraints: The meta-analysis is correlational, so these accounts are interpretations rather than tested mechanisms; the article notes the lack of an age moderating effect makes one functionalist exploration-based explanation unlikely for middle childhood and adolescence.
target_learners: children and adolescents aged 3–16 in typical (non-clinical) samples
target_learning_goals: academic skills (reading, writing, mathematics, language, general attainment)
cognitive skills (intelligence, executive functions)
examples: The discussion reads the stronger FiMS associations as support for functionalism's emphasis on engaging with learning materials and dealing with fine motor demands of school tasks, while also invoking shared neural activation between motor and cognitive areas.

article_title: From Passive to Metacognitive: The Role of Mode of Engagement in Enabling Lasting Learning Using Digital Media
citation: Yoana Omarchevska, Brendan A. Schuetze, Juliane Richter, Sascha Schanze, Nina Ulrich, Katharina Scheiter. (2026). From Passive to Metacognitive: The Role of Mode of Engagement in Enabling Lasting Learning Using Digital Media. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10120-z
title: Extension of the ICAP framework adding metacognitive engagement as an additional mode
description: The article proposes extending the ICAP framework (passive, active, constructive, interactive modes of cognitive engagement) with metacognitive engagement, operationalized as the frequency of making judgments of learning. The authors "propose metacognitive engagement as an additional mode of engagement", arguing it is particularly relevant for self-regulated, individual learning with open-ended digital environments. Their findings that profiles differing mainly in metacognitive engagement showed the largest knowledge differences support this extension correlationally.
requirements: A learning environment that logs or affords observable metacognitive activities such as judgments of learning
constraints: The empirical support is correlational, from a single classroom study with one digital textbook
target_learners: secondary school students (eighth grade) learning science individually with digital media
target_learning_goals: durable domain-specific chemistry knowledge (particle model of matter)
examples: In the eChemBook, students could optionally rate on a traffic light scale how well they could explain each unit and check which concepts they could explain

description: The eChemBook is a digital chemistry textbook developed with German Research Foundation funding as "a collaboration between scientists, a textbook publisher, and an interactive whiteboard manufacturer". It contains six learning units on the particle model of matter, each with a motivational teaser, basic text, video experiment, two learning activities, and a summary page. Students navigate non-linearly, and all activities are logged, yielding passive, active, constructive, and metacognitive engagement indicators.

constraints: Studied here with eighth-grade German students in regular chemistry lessons; only high-interactivity condition data were analyzed

examples: Each unit included drawing and matching exercises, cloze tests alongside simulations, and optional traffic-light judgments of learning on the summary page

article_title: Integrating Motivation and Instruction: Towards a Unified Approach in Educational Psychology
citation: Andrew J. Martin. (2023). Integrating Motivation and Instruction: Towards a Unified Approach in Educational Psychology. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09774-w
title: Two-step integration process: intra-domain then inter-domain unification of motivation and instruction
description: The review articulates a two-step process for unifying fragmented domains in educational psychology. Step 1 involves intra-domain integration, drawing together key concepts within motivation (Step 1a) and within instruction (Step 1b); Step 2 involves inter-domain integration, drawing the unified motivation and instruction frameworks together. The author states that "the joint operation of intra- and inter-domain integration of motivation and instruction holds potential for more coherent theorizing, measurement, and practical application." The process is presented as an illustrative meta-view rather than a definitive framework.
requirements: A unified motivation framework and a unified instruction framework must first be developed before inter-domain integration can proceed
constraints: The review presents the process as tentative and illustrative, emanating from the author's own program of theorizing
target_learning_goals: coherent integration of motivation and instructional theory to support student learning
examples: The Motivation and Engagement Wheel illustrates Step 1a; Load Reduction Instruction illustrates Step 1b; their nexus illustrates Step 2
key_sources: Andrew J. Martin. (2023). Integrating Motivation and Instruction: Towards a Unified Approach in Educational Psychology. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09774-w

article_title: Integrating Motivation and Instruction: Towards a Unified Approach in Educational Psychology
citation: Andrew J. Martin. (2023). Integrating Motivation and Instruction: Towards a Unified Approach in Educational Psychology. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09774-w
title: Motivation and Engagement Wheel: four higher-order dimensions subsuming eleven lower-order factors
description: The Motivation and Engagement Wheel is an integrative framework organizing multidimensional motivation and engagement. It comprises four higher-order dimensions—positive motivation, positive engagement, negative motivation, and negative engagement—each subsuming convergent lower-order factors such as self-efficacy, valuing, mastery orientation, planning, task management, persistence, anxiety, failure avoidance, uncertain control, self-handicapping, and disengagement. The article states "There are four higher order dimensions and eleven lower order factors in the Motivation and Engagement Wheel." It was developed to reflect multidimensionality, positive/negative demarcation, and lower-order factors under broader dimensions.
requirements: Measurement via the parallel Motivation and Engagement Scale to assess students on each part of the Wheel
constraints: The Wheel is not intended to be exhaustive, definitive, or prescriptive; factors such as intrinsic motivation, autonomy, and participation are excluded; it represents predominantly intra-personal constructs, with interpersonal factors such as relatedness beyond its composition
target_learning_goals: academic motivation and engagement
examples: Figure 2 graphically represents the synthesis of four positive and negative higher-order dimensions and the eleven specific factors subsumed under them
key_sources: Andrew J. Martin. (2023). Integrating Motivation and Instruction: Towards a Unified Approach in Educational Psychology. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09774-w

article_title: Integrating Motivation and Instruction: Towards a Unified Approach in Educational Psychology
citation: Andrew J. Martin. (2023). Integrating Motivation and Instruction: Towards a Unified Approach in Educational Psychology. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09774-w
title: Motivation and Engagement Scale (MES): 44-item self-report instrument with three educational-level versions
description: The Motivation and Engagement Scale is the measurement instrument accompanying the Wheel, comprising "44 items (4 items for each of the 11 factors)" for student self-report. It comes in elementary school, high school, and university/college versions. The review reports, citing Liem and Martin (2012), that responses to the MES factors are normally distributed, internally consistent, and perform well in lower-order and higher-order confirmatory factor analysis, and that MES factors are significantly associated with academic outcomes such as achievement.
requirements: Used to assess students on each part of the Wheel
constraints: A detailed account of MES psychometrics and construct validity is beyond the scope of this review
target_learning_goals: assessment of multidimensional motivation and engagement
examples: Other multidimensional instruments noted in a footnote include PALS, MSLQ, SEI, AMS, and ISM

article_title: Integrating Motivation and Instruction: Towards a Unified Approach in Educational Psychology
citation: Andrew J. Martin. (2023). Integrating Motivation and Instruction: Towards a Unified Approach in Educational Psychology. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09774-w
title: Load Reduction Instruction: five sequenced principles from difficulty reduction to guided independent learning
description: Load Reduction Instruction (LRI) is an integrative instructional framework drawing on Cognitive Load Theory that harmonizes explicit instruction with guided independent learning. Its first four principles build long-term memory and fluency: "Reduce the difficulty of instruction in the initial stages of learning", provide support and scaffolding, allow sufficient opportunity for practice, and provide feedback-feedforward. The fifth principle, guided independent learning, is introduced once fluency and automaticity develop, and "represents a fundamental unification of explicit and constructivist instructional approaches." Teaching strategies operationalizing each principle are mapped in Tables 1 through 5.
requirements: Sequencing is pivotal: explicit principles #1-4 precede guided independence (#5), calibrated to the learner's prior knowledge and novice-to-expert status
constraints: LRI targets reduction of extraneous cognitive load as the main yield and intrinsic load as a subsidiary yield; failure to reduce load for novices risks a failure to learn
target_learners: school students moving from novice to more expert status
target_learning_goals: managing cognitive load to optimize learning and enable guided independent learning
examples: Table 1 strategies for difficulty reduction include pre-training, modelling, segmenting, and preliminary and spaced reviews; Table 2 includes worked examples, templates, prompting, and personalizing
key_sources: Andrew J. Martin. (2023). Integrating Motivation and Instruction: Towards a Unified Approach in Educational Psychology. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09774-w

article_title: Integrating Motivation and Instruction: Towards a Unified Approach in Educational Psychology
citation: Andrew J. Martin. (2023). Integrating Motivation and Instruction: Towards a Unified Approach in Educational Psychology. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09774-w
title: Treat explicit and constructivist instruction as synergistic rather than mutually exclusive
description: The review argues that framing explicit and constructivist instruction as mutually exclusive sets in place "a false dichotomy"; there are synergies and neither approach has exclusive claims to particular instructional strategies. High-quality learning relies on students experiencing both explicit and independent approaches, and privileging one risks denying students learning opportunities the other affords. LRI operationalizes this synthesis so students benefit from the strengths each approach offers.
requirements: Educators must recognize points in learner development where each approach is appropriate, with effectiveness of one intertwined with the other
constraints: The divergence between the approaches lies mainly in the amount and type of instruction provided
target_learning_goals: comprehensive instructional support across novice-to-expert learning phases
examples: The review quotes Liem and Martin (2013): constructivist approaches are better assisted by direct and structured teacher input that builds knowledge needed for subsequent meaningful discovery and enquiry-based learning
key_sources: Andrew J. Martin. (2023). Integrating Motivation and Instruction: Towards a Unified Approach in Educational Psychology. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09774-w

article_title: The AIR and Apt-AIR Frameworks of Epistemic Performance and Growth: Reflections on Educational Theory Development
citation: Sarit Barzilai & Clark A. Chinn. (2024). The AIR and Apt-AIR Frameworks of Epistemic Performance and Growth: Reflections on Educational Theory Development. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09927-5
title: The AIR framework characterizes epistemic thinking as three interdependent components: epistemic aims, epistemic ideals, and reliable epistemic processes
description: The AIR framework provides a structure for analyzing epistemic thinking in terms of three interdependent components. Epistemic aims are goals involving developing a representation of the world, such as models, theories, explanations, and beliefs. Epistemic ideals are the standards or criteria people use to evaluate whether epistemic aims have been achieved. Reliable epistemic processes are the individual and collective strategies or methods people use to try to achieve their epistemic aims in light of the associated ideals. The article states that "epistemic aims, ideals, and reliable processes are inextricably interconnected in the AIR framework" and that people "deploy aims, ideals, and reliable processes in concert when engaged in epistemic thinking."
requirements: Researchers or educators analyzing epistemic thinking must attend to how aims, ideals, and processes interact rather than treating them in isolation
constraints: The interdependence of the AIR components does not mean that researchers must always study all three together; researchers may focus on one component when seeking a rich and detailed portrait of it
target_learners: elementary through university students and teachers engaged in inquiry, argumentation, and fact-checking tasks
target_learning_goals: growth in epistemic thinking including evaluating online claims, constructing knowledge from multiple documents, and model-based inquiry in science
examples: Table 1 presents examples of aims, ideals, and processes expressed by ninth graders constructing knowledge from multiple historical documents and seventh graders constructing and evaluating scientific models
key_sources: Sarit Barzilai & Clark A. Chinn. (2024). The AIR and Apt-AIR Frameworks of Epistemic Performance and Growth: Reflections on Educational Theory Development. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09927-5

article_title: The AIR and Apt-AIR Frameworks of Epistemic Performance and Growth: Reflections on Educational Theory Development
citation: Sarit Barzilai & Clark A. Chinn. (2024). The AIR and Apt-AIR Frameworks of Epistemic Performance and Growth: Reflections on Educational Theory Development. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09927-5
title: The Apt-AIR framework unpacks fully apt epistemic performance into five interwoven aspects of competent engagement with aims, ideals, and reliable processes
description: The Apt-AIR framework was developed to address the normative question of what the goals of epistemic education should be. It proposes that fully apt epistemic performance is facilitated by five interwoven aspects of competent engagement with aims, ideals, and reliable processes: cognitive engagement, adapting epistemic performance across tasks and contexts, metacognitively regulating and understanding epistemic performance, caring about and enjoying epistemic performance, and participating in epistemic performance with others. The article states that "the aspects are interrelated and are not independent or mutually exclusive dimensions" and that the heuristic value is "to identify important aspects of epistemic performance that require instructional support."
requirements: Instructional designers must consider how each aspect of epistemic performance connects to specific aims, ideals, and reliable processes rather than treating the aspects as free-standing skills
constraints: The order in which the five aspects are presented does not reflect their importance or temporal sequence; many activities involve multiple intersecting aspects simultaneously
target_learners: learners across diverse educational contexts from elementary school to teacher education
target_learning_goals: fully apt epistemic performance including adaptive, metacognitively regulated, motivated, and socially engaged epistemic thinking
examples: The framework was applied in a case study illustrating how teachers might promote epistemic performance by attending to all five aspects through their activities and discourse
key_sources: Sarit Barzilai & Clark A. Chinn. (2024). The AIR and Apt-AIR Frameworks of Epistemic Performance and Growth: Reflections on Educational Theory Development. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09927-5

article_title: The AIR and Apt-AIR Frameworks of Epistemic Performance and Growth: Reflections on Educational Theory Development
citation: Sarit Barzilai & Clark A. Chinn. (2024). The AIR and Apt-AIR Frameworks of Epistemic Performance and Growth: Reflections on Educational Theory Development. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09927-5
title: Sosa's reliabilist virtue epistemology grounds the Apt-AIR goal of fully apt epistemic performance through success, competence, and aptness conditions
description: The Apt-AIR framework is grounded in the reliabilist virtue epistemology of philosopher Ernest Sosa. Sosa proposed that an epistemic performance can be evaluated by examining three conditions: its success in attaining its aim, whether it is an exercise of competence using appropriate strategies, and whether it is apt, meaning successful because it is competent. Real achievement requires not just success but apt success, because competent performance reduces the risk of failure. Performance guided by meta-level awareness of one's competence is described as fully apt performance. The article states that "the aim of epistemic education should be to promote learners' fully apt epistemic performance."
requirements: Educators adopting this goal must consider not only whether learners succeed but whether success derives from reliable processes rather than guessing or luck
constraints: What counts as good epistemic performance can be task- and situation-dependent and requires metacognitive judgment about when particular strategies are applicable
target_learners: learners engaged in online inquiry, model-based science, and belief formation across diverse tasks
target_learning_goals: forming accurate beliefs through reliable processes guided by metacognitive awareness of when and how skills can be used successfully
examples: Table 2 illustrates how successful, competent, apt, and fully apt performance apply to forming beliefs, judging online claim accuracy, and model-based inquiry in science
key_sources: Sarit Barzilai & Clark A. Chinn. (2024). The AIR and Apt-AIR Frameworks of Epistemic Performance and Growth: Reflections on Educational Theory Development. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09927-5

article_title: The AIR and Apt-AIR Frameworks of Epistemic Performance and Growth: Reflections on Educational Theory Development
citation: Sarit Barzilai & Clark A. Chinn. (2024). The AIR and Apt-AIR Frameworks of Epistemic Performance and Growth: Reflections on Educational Theory Development. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09927-5
title: Design epistemic learning environments by creating opportunities for learners and teachers to collaboratively notice, articulate, elaborate, and evaluate epistemic ideals and processes
description: This design principle from the Apt-AIR framework addresses growth in metacognitive understanding of epistemic performance. The article states that "a key design principle for supporting growth in metacognitive understanding of epistemic performance is creating opportunities for learners and teachers to collaboratively notice, articulate, elaborate, and evaluate epistemic ideals and processes." The authors implemented this by encouraging middle school students to develop and refine their own class lists of criteria for evaluating models, arguments, or sources, and by prompting students to evaluate source trustworthiness and discuss their justifications.
requirements: Learners need appropriate materials and prompts that scaffold the articulation and evaluation of epistemic ideals and processes
constraints: More research is needed to examine how designs for supporting learners' epistemic growth can be adapted to different educational levels and contexts
target_learners: middle school students through undergraduates and teacher education students
target_learning_goals: metacognitive understanding of epistemic aims, ideals, and processes including why they are valuable and how to apply them
examples: Encouraging middle school students to develop and refine class lists of criteria for evaluating models, arguments, or sources; prompting students to evaluate source trustworthiness and discuss justifications
key_sources: Sarit Barzilai & Clark A. Chinn. (2024). The AIR and Apt-AIR Frameworks of Epistemic Performance and Growth: Reflections on Educational Theory Development. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09927-5

article_title: The AIR and Apt-AIR Frameworks of Epistemic Performance and Growth: Reflections on Educational Theory Development
citation: Sarit Barzilai & Clark A. Chinn. (2024). The AIR and Apt-AIR Frameworks of Epistemic Performance and Growth: Reflections on Educational Theory Development. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09927-5
title: Support students' autonomy and agency as they collaboratively work on meaningful and interesting challenges to foster caring about epistemic performance
description: This design principle addresses the fourth aspect of the Apt-AIR framework—caring about and enjoying epistemic performance. The article states that "to foster caring about epistemic performance, our key design principle has been to support students' autonomy and agency as they collaboratively work on meaningful and interesting challenges." The authors observed that "students appeared unlikely to care about aims, ideals, and processes unless they had some agency in choosing and/or applying them."
requirements: Learning environments must provide students with genuine choices about which epistemic aims, ideals, and processes to adopt or apply
constraints: The principle was derived from the authors' design observations rather than from controlled experimental comparisons
target_learners: K-12 and higher education students engaged in epistemic inquiry tasks
target_learning_goals: motivation and positive dispositions toward epistemic performance including caring about valuable epistemic aims and ideals
examples: The authors applied this principle in design studies where students collaboratively worked on model-based inquiry and source evaluation challenges
key_sources: Sarit Barzilai & Clark A. Chinn. (2024). The AIR and Apt-AIR Frameworks of Epistemic Performance and Growth: Reflections on Educational Theory Development. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09927-5

article_title: The AIR and Apt-AIR Frameworks of Epistemic Performance and Growth: Reflections on Educational Theory Development
citation: Sarit Barzilai & Clark A. Chinn. (2024). The AIR and Apt-AIR Frameworks of Epistemic Performance and Growth: Reflections on Educational Theory Development. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09927-5
title: The Multifaceted Framework of Epistemic Thinking defines cognitive and metacognitive aspects of epistemic thinking aligned with central models of metacognition
description: The Multifaceted Framework of Epistemic Thinking, developed by Barzilai and Zohar, defined the cognitive and metacognitive aspects of epistemic thinking in ways aligned with central models of metacognition. Following Flavell, the cognitive aspects were defined as those used to make cognitive progress, including thinking about the epistemic status and properties of specific information, knowledge claims, and sources. The metacognitive aspects were defined as knowledge, skills, and experiences related to the nature of knowledge and knowing, such as knowledge about criteria and strategies for evaluating claims or sources. The article states this framework "has informed research on self-regulated learning and was, along with the AIR framework, central to the development of the Apt-AIR framework."
requirements: Researchers using this framework must situate epistemic thinking within existing theoretical models of the meta/cognitive system rather than treating it as disconnected
constraints: The framework was developed to increase coherence between epistemic thinking research and metacognition research, which had mostly developed in distinct niches
target_learners: researchers and educators studying or supporting epistemic thinking across educational levels
target_learning_goals: understanding the cognitive and metacognitive dimensions of epistemic thinking including evaluating claims and sources
examples: The framework informed research on self-regulated learning and was central to developing the Apt-AIR framework's cognitive and metacognitive engagement aspects
key_sources: Sarit Barzilai & Clark A. Chinn. (2024). The AIR and Apt-AIR Frameworks of Epistemic Performance and Growth: Reflections on Educational Theory Development. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09927-5

article_title: Compositional Analysis of Writing Instructional Practices Performed with Digital Tools: A Meta-Analysis
citation: López, P., Fidalgo, R., Álvarez-Moreno, C., Díaz-Tejedor, R., van den Bergh, H., & Rijlaarsdam, G. (2026). Compositional Analysis of Writing Instructional Practices Performed with Digital Tools: A Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10153-4
title: Component-based instructional design framework for analyzing ICT-supported writing interventions
description: The article adopts a component-based instructional design perspective, coding each intervention on four design aspects: Merrill's instructional principles (problem centered, activation, demonstration, application, integration), the instructional activities that operationalize them, the types of feedback, and the types of scaffolding. Each element is additionally coded by delivery agent (teacher, ICT, or both). The article argues that "analyzing ICT-supported writing interventions at a fine-grained, componential level provides clearer insight into how instructional design shapes learning outcomes" than aggregating interventions as a single category.
requirements: Studies must report sufficient description of the instructional intervention to code principles, activities, feedback, scaffolding, and delivery agent
constraints: Applied to ICT-supported writing interventions targeting higher-level cognitive writing processes (planning, drafting, revising, genre-based text structuring) in typically developing students
target_learners: typically developing students in primary, secondary, and higher education writing instruction
target_learning_goals: improvement of writing quality through higher-level writing processes such as planning, text structuring, and revision
examples: The framework was applied to 42 empirical studies contributing 53 effect sizes, coded with interrater reliability (Cohen's kappa ranging from 0.805 to 1.00)
key_sources: López, P., Fidalgo, R., Álvarez-Moreno, C., Díaz-Tejedor, R., van den Bergh, H., & Rijlaarsdam, G. (2026). Compositional Analysis of Writing Instructional Practices Performed with Digital Tools: A Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10153-4

article_title: Task Characteristics Associated with Mathematical Word Problem-Solving Performance Among Elementary School-Aged Children: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
citation: T. Vessonen, M. Dahlberg, H. Hellstrand, A. Widlund, J. Korhonen, P. Aunio, A. Laine. (2024). Task Characteristics Associated with Mathematical Word Problem-Solving Performance Among Elementary School-Aged Children: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09954-2
title: Cognitive load account of word problem-solving task difficulty
description: The article frames task characteristics as moderators of the cognitive demands of word problem-solving: solving requires integrating multiple linguistic and numerical elements simultaneously, drawing on limited working memory, executive functions, and reading comprehension. "According to such theory, performing learning tasks imposes cognitive demands (or load) on a student's limited cognitive capacity (e.g., working memory)". The amount of demand is determined by element interactivity, so characteristics such as irrelevant information, lexical inconsistency, and multiple operations increase the elements to process and may especially challenge elementary schoolers whose cognitive capacity is still developing.
requirements: Applies to tasks requiring simultaneous integration of linguistic and numerical elements within limited working memory
constraints: The article presents this as a theoretical framing for interpreting associations, not as a tested mechanism in the meta-analysis itself
target_learners: Elementary school-aged children in Grades 1 to 6
target_learning_goals: Mathematical word problem-solving
key_sources: T. Vessonen, M. Dahlberg, H. Hellstrand, A. Widlund, J. Korhonen, P. Aunio, A. Laine. (2024). Task Characteristics Associated with Mathematical Word Problem-Solving Performance Among Elementary School-Aged Children: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09954-2

article_title: Task Characteristics Associated with Mathematical Word Problem-Solving Performance Among Elementary School-Aged Children: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
citation: T. Vessonen, M. Dahlberg, H. Hellstrand, A. Widlund, J. Korhonen, P. Aunio, A. Laine. (2024). Task Characteristics Associated with Mathematical Word Problem-Solving Performance Among Elementary School-Aged Children: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09954-2
title: Taxonomy of linguistic and numerical task characteristics of mathematical word problems
description: The review organizes word problem task characteristics into two categories with named dimensions. Linguistic characteristics cover structure of the word problem (order-consistency, position of the unknown), schematic structure, semantic relationships, situational narrative familiarity, non-standard problems (unsolvable, multiple solutions, irrelevant linguistic information, realistic considerations), lexical consistency, code of numerical values, and length. Numerical characteristics cover number properties, required operation (additive vs. multiplicative, number of operations), solution strategy, relevance of information, and carrying. For schematic structure, "word problems fall into three additive (Total, Difference, Change) and five multiplicative categories (Equal groups, Comparison, Combination, Ratios and proportions, Product of measures)". Each dimension carries a presumable direction of association with performance.
requirements: Each dimension required at least five studies for robust variance estimation, since results "cannot be held reliable if there are under four degrees of freedom"
constraints: Multiplicative schematic structures could not be compared because too few independent studies investigated them; order-consistency, number properties, and other dimensions were dropped for the same reason
target_learners: Elementary school-aged children in Grades 1 to 6
target_learning_goals: Mathematical word problem-solving
key_sources: T. Vessonen, M. Dahlberg, H. Hellstrand, A. Widlund, J. Korhonen, P. Aunio, A. Laine. (2024). Task Characteristics Associated with Mathematical Word Problem-Solving Performance Among Elementary School-Aged Children: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
