article_title: Task Characteristics Associated with Mathematical Word Problem-Solving Performance Among Elementary School-Aged Children: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
citation: T. Vessonen, M. Dahlberg, H. Hellstrand, A. Widlund, J. Korhonen, P. Aunio, A. Laine. (2024). Task Characteristics Associated with Mathematical Word Problem-Solving Performance Among Elementary School-Aged Children: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09954-2
title: Design word problem instruction and assessment to be appropriate and progressive based on task demandingness
description: The article recommends that understanding which task characteristics challenge elementary schoolers should shape the design of instruction and assessment. Assessment tools "may be designed to encompass a comprehensive range of different mathematical word problems to understand students' varying performance", and "through understanding how demanding different tasks are, progressive instruction may be designed by simultaneously ensuring that students understand foundational concepts and appropriate strategies for solving more challenging tasks". Instruction should advance in a sequence aligned with students' cognitive capacity.
requirements: Knowledge of the relative demandingness of task characteristics, as provided by the meta-analytic findings
constraints: The article states the findings may guide design and steer future research into interactions among task and individual characteristics; it does not itself test an instructional intervention
target_learners: Elementary school-aged children in Grades 1 to 6
target_learning_goals: Mathematical word problem-solving
examples: The meta-analysis identified realistic considerations, multiple operations, lexical inconsistency, and first-position unknowns as the characteristics elementary schoolers especially struggle with, informing sequencing decisions

article_title: How Representation Matters: Conceptualizing Systemic Racism to Develop Diversity Research Agendas for Undergraduate STEM Education
citation: Sedlacek, Q., Villa, A. M., III, Friend, M., Pérez, G., Dozier, S., Haeger, H., Lomelí, K., & Mejia, J. A. (2025). How Representation Matters: Conceptualizing Systemic Racism to Develop Diversity Research Agendas for Undergraduate STEM Education. Educational Psychology Review, 37:49. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10021-7
title: Ecological systems model of systemic racism in STEM higher education across micro- to macro-levels
description: The review adapts Bronfenbrenner's ecological systems theory to theorize systemic racism in STEM higher education, nesting individual students within classrooms, departments, institutions, labor markets, and societal/historical contexts. The authors state that "Bronfenbrenner's (1979) ecological systems theory was developed to examine the interdependent relationships between individuals and their environments," and use it to explicate manifestations of systemic racism at each level (Table 1), from White supremacist STEM history and racist stereotypes at the macrosystem to belonging uncertainty and stereotype threat at the individual level.
requirements: Analysis must consider multiple ecological levels concurrently, since mechanisms at lower levels are shaped by phenomena at higher levels
constraints: The authors apply it as a narrow theorization of systemic racism within STEM higher education, specifically in relation to instructor diversity
target_learners: undergraduate STEM students in US higher education
target_learning_goals: understanding how systemic racism shapes STEM learning environments and student outcomes
examples: Table 1 maps manifestations such as Eurocentric curriculum at the mesosystem and micro- or macroaggressions in classrooms at the microsystem level
key_sources: Sedlacek, Q., Villa, A. M., III, Friend, M., Pérez, G., Dozier, S., Haeger, H., Lomelí, K., & Mejia, J. A. (2025). How Representation Matters: Conceptualizing Systemic Racism to Develop Diversity Research Agendas for Undergraduate STEM Education. Educational Psychology Review, 37:49. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10021-7

article_title: How Representation Matters: Conceptualizing Systemic Racism to Develop Diversity Research Agendas for Undergraduate STEM Education
citation: Sedlacek, Q., Villa, A. M., III, Friend, M., Pérez, G., Dozier, S., Haeger, H., Lomelí, K., & Mejia, J. A. (2025). How Representation Matters: Conceptualizing Systemic Racism to Develop Diversity Research Agendas for Undergraduate STEM Education. Educational Psychology Review, 37:49. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10021-7
title: Multi-path model of hypothesized mediators of instructor diversity benefits in STEM
description: The review proposes a path model in which exposure to racially marginalized STEM instructors relates to positive outcomes for racially marginalized students through multiple hypothesized mediators: instructors' use of inclusive pedagogy (Arrow B), changes in peer interaction patterns at the classroom level (Arrow C), and students' belonging (Arrow D) and group-as-target stereotype threat (Arrow E). The authors state, "We present such a model in Fig. 2, and will expand on this model throughout the paper," elaborating it with additional mediators such as instructors' experiences of marginalization and racial ideology.
requirements: Future empirical tests of the hypothesized mediation paths, which the review generates as predictions
constraints: The model is hypothesized, not tested; the review notes few studies provide direct causal evidence identifying the specific mechanisms
target_learning_goals: explaining how and under what circumstances instructor racial/ethnic diversity benefits racially marginalized students
examples: Arrow A depicts exposure to racially marginalized instructors increasing grades and/or persistence, potentially mediated by inclusive pedagogy (Arrow B) or classroom interaction patterns (Arrow C)

article_title: How Representation Matters: Conceptualizing Systemic Racism to Develop Diversity Research Agendas for Undergraduate STEM Education
citation: Sedlacek, Q., Villa, A. M., III, Friend, M., Pérez, G., Dozier, S., Haeger, H., Lomelí, K., & Mejia, J. A. (2025). How Representation Matters: Conceptualizing Systemic Racism to Develop Diversity Research Agendas for Undergraduate STEM Education. Educational Psychology Review, 37:49. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10021-7
title: Intersectionality as a framework for analyzing interlocking oppressions in STEM education research
description: The review presents intersectionality theory as a framework holding that multiple systems of oppression must be analyzed together rather than in isolation. It states that "Intersectionality theory suggests that since multiple systems of oppression shape our world simultaneously with each other, these systems of oppression cannot necessarily be understood in isolation from each other," forming a matrix of domination. In diversity research, it pushes researchers to center multiply marginalized persons, such as Black women and LGBTQ+ people of color, to avoid unidimensional analyses focused only on racism.
requirements: Researchers must theorize racialized and gendered oppression together rather than isolating effects of racism from sexism or cisheterosexism
constraints: The review notes intersectionality is not an Oppression Olympics ranking identities by oppression, nor a tool to explore infinite combinations of difference
target_learning_goals: avoiding overlooking the needs and experiences of multiply marginalized populations in STEM diversity research
examples: The review cites Rodriguez and Blaney (2021)'s qualitative study in which Latina students reported belonging experiences distinct from their male Latino peers

article_title: The Effects of Contextual Interference Learning on the Acquisition and Relatively Permanent Gains in Skilled Performance: A Critical Systematic Review with Multilevel Meta-Analysis
citation: Achraf Ammar, Khaled Trabelsi, Mohamed Ali Boujelbane, Atef Salem, Omar Boukhris, Jordan M. Glenn, Piotr Zmijewski, Haitham A. Jahrami, Hamdi Chtourou, Wolfgang I. Schöllhorn. (2024). The Effects of Contextual Interference Learning on the Acquisition and Relatively Permanent Gains in Skilled Performance: A Critical Systematic Review with Multilevel Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09892-z
title: Do not assume high contextual interference (random) practice guarantees a longer-term performance advantage in PE and sports
description: The meta-analysis finds "very limited evidence supporting the recommendation to employ high CI practices to gain a longer-term performance advantage, calling into question the generalization of the CI model to PE and sports practices." Practitioners should therefore not schedule random/serial practice on the expectation of guaranteed retention benefits over blocked practice; gains differences were negligible acutely and non-significant long-term. The authors instead call for "High-quality follow-up research evaluating alternative motor-learning models."
requirements: Decisions about practice schedules should rest on outcome gains (Δ pre-post, Δ post-retention, Δ pre-retention) rather than on post-test group comparisons alone, as the article argues prior conclusions lacked gain analyses.
constraints: Evidence base is gross motor skills in healthy populations in PE and sports contexts; studies on cognitive performance, fine motor skills, and populations with physical or mental disability were excluded.
target_learners: sports participants across age groups from children to older adults
target_learning_goals: acquisition and retention of gross motor and sports skills
examples: The meta-analysis pooled 183 outcomes from 36 studies and found only 20% agreed with the paradoxical CI prediction.
key_sources: Achraf Ammar, Khaled Trabelsi, Mohamed Ali Boujelbane, Atef Salem, Omar Boukhris, Jordan M. Glenn, Piotr Zmijewski, Haitham A. Jahrami, Hamdi Chtourou, Wolfgang I. Schöllhorn. (2024). The Effects of Contextual Interference Learning on the Acquisition and Relatively Permanent Gains in Skilled Performance: A Critical Systematic Review with Multilevel Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09892-z

article_title: The Effects of Contextual Interference Learning on the Acquisition and Relatively Permanent Gains in Skilled Performance: A Critical Systematic Review with Multilevel Meta-Analysis
citation: Achraf Ammar, Khaled Trabelsi, Mohamed Ali Boujelbane, Atef Salem, Omar Boukhris, Jordan M. Glenn, Piotr Zmijewski, Haitham A. Jahrami, Hamdi Chtourou, Wolfgang I. Schöllhorn. (2024). The Effects of Contextual Interference Learning on the Acquisition and Relatively Permanent Gains in Skilled Performance: A Critical Systematic Review with Multilevel Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09892-z
title: The contextual interference (CI) paradox model of practice scheduling
description: The CI model holds that "When practice trials are interrupted by the execution of other tasks, detrimental effects can be observed immediately after the acquisition phase but are followed by greater benefits in the subsequent retention phase compared to uninterrupted sequence." Two mechanisms are proposed: the "elaborative hypothesis" (deeper, more elaborate information processing during random practice) and the "forgetting/reconstruction hypothesis" (increased forcing retrieval practice and reconstruction of tasks' plans-of-action); working-memory overload during random practice is suggested to hinder acquisition. This meta-analysis tests and largely fails to support the model's generalization to gross motor skills.
requirements: A design contrasting low CI (blocked) practice with high CI (random/serial) practice, with acquisition and retention test phases, to exhibit the paradoxical pattern.
constraints: The article reports the effect "could only be systematically demonstrated for sequences of fine motor movements with a high visual-spatial component," and finds very limited evidence for generalization to PE and sports practices.
target_learners: learners of gross motor and sports skills in physical education settings
target_learning_goals: skill acquisition and relatively permanent retention of motor skills
examples: Blocked practice completes all trials of a task before moving to a different task in predictable patterns; random practice interleaves tasks in unpredictable order.

article_title: Embodied Learning Activities Focusing on Letter-Sound Knowledge Increase Spelling Performance in 1st Grade Children with Low and High Reading Ability
citation: Damsgaard, L., Nielsen, A.-M. V., Topor, M. K., Hansen, R. A., Jensen, S. K., Markers, R. L., Gejl, A. K., Malling, A. S. B., & Wienecke, J. (2023). Embodied Learning Activities Focusing on Letter-Sound Knowledge Increase Spelling Performance in 1st Grade Children with Low and High Reading Ability. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09791-9
title: Embodied cognition and the enactment effect as the explanatory framework for movement-based literacy learning
description: The article frames its intervention in embodied cognition, which "describes how our body and environment are related to cognitive processes," integrating the mind into body sensorimotor systems. Its proposed mechanism is the enactment effect: "the engagement of the motor system reinforces encoding in addition to just observing, listening, pronunciations, and mental visual representations." Embodied learning here means using movement in close connection with the learning content, applied through movement-phonemes coupled to letter-sounds.
requirements: Movement must be meaningfully integrated with the learning content rather than added as generic activity
constraints: The authors state embodied exercises must not require too much cognitive effort to avoid the risk of cognitive overload, especially for low-performing children
target_learners: Grade 1 children aged 6-7 learning early literacy
target_learning_goals: Letter-sound knowledge and spelling performance
examples: Children made specific whole-body movements to letter-sounds (movement phonemes), executed left to right, with crisp sounds coupled to quick movements and high-pitch phonemes placed above lower-pitch ones.
key_sources: Damsgaard, L., Nielsen, A.-M. V., Topor, M. K., Hansen, R. A., Jensen, S. K., Markers, R. L., Gejl, A. K., Malling, A. S. B., & Wienecke, J. (2023). Embodied Learning Activities Focusing on Letter-Sound Knowledge Increase Spelling Performance in 1st Grade Children with Low and High Reading Ability. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09791-9

article_title: Embodied Learning Activities Focusing on Letter-Sound Knowledge Increase Spelling Performance in 1st Grade Children with Low and High Reading Ability
citation: Damsgaard, L., Nielsen, A.-M. V., Topor, M. K., Hansen, R. A., Jensen, S. K., Markers, R. L., Gejl, A. K., Malling, A. S. B., & Wienecke, J. (2023). Embodied Learning Activities Focusing on Letter-Sound Knowledge Increase Spelling Performance in 1st Grade Children with Low and High Reading Ability. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09791-9
title: Movement-phoneme activity program: paired whole-body letter-sound exercises over 4 weeks
description: A 4-week intervention of three 25-minute weekly sessions in which children "were taught to make specific whole-body movements to letter-sounds (movement phonemes)" across 25 letters, working in pairs under a trained instructor with a 1:2 teacher-student fraction. Activities included letter-sound relay, alphabet chaos, become-a-letter, miming, letter salad, sound duel, rime-twister, and hidden-word games, built on the Danish teaching material Fandango Mini.
requirements: A trained instructor delivering activities to pairs of children with positive and corrective feedback
constraints: The 1:2 teacher-student fraction may not be easily applicable for teachers in a whole-class school setting, as the authors note
target_learners: Grade 1 children, both low and high reading performers
target_learning_goals: Letter-form knowledge, standard and conditional letter-sound correspondences, spelling short words
examples: In the letter-sound relay, children ran to grab a letter, returned, and made the letter-sound and movement-phoneme while teammates guessed the letter.

article_title: Understanding Cognitive Load in Digital and Online Learning: a New Perspective on Extraneous Cognitive Load
citation: Alexander Skulmowski & Kate Man Xu. (2022). Understanding Cognitive Load in Digital and Online Learning: a New Perspective on Extraneous Cognitive Load. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09624-7
title: The 1998 triarchic cognitive load theory model partitions working memory demands into intrinsic, extraneous, and germane load
description: The review describes the 1998 CLT model (Sweller et al.) as partitioning working memory demands into three load types: intrinsic cognitive load, extraneous cognitive load, and germane load. Intrinsic load stems from element interactivity and varies with prior knowledge; extraneous load arises from design choices; germane load covers resources devoted to schema construction. The model assumes an additive relationship, so "intrinsic load and extraneous load must be low enough in order to leave sufficient cognitive resources for processes associated with germane load to occur".
requirements: Learning materials must be designed so extraneous load is minimized to leave capacity for intrinsic load and germane processing
constraints: Intrinsic load cannot be lowered by instructional design, only varied by learner prior knowledge
target_learning_goals: managing working memory demands during acquisition of biologically secondary knowledge
key_sources: Alexander Skulmowski & Kate Man Xu. (2022). Understanding Cognitive Load in Digital and Online Learning: a New Perspective on Extraneous Cognitive Load. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09624-7

article_title: Understanding Cognitive Load in Digital and Online Learning: a New Perspective on Extraneous Cognitive Load
citation: Alexander Skulmowski & Kate Man Xu. (2022). Understanding Cognitive Load in Digital and Online Learning: a New Perspective on Extraneous Cognitive Load. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09624-7
title: The revised 2019 CLT model removes germane load from total load, recasting it as germane processing
description: The review reports that Sweller et al. (2019) revised CLT in response to debates over germane load's definition and relevance, including factor-analytic arguments for a two-factor model. "The major change from the 1998 model is that Sweller et al. (2019) have removed germane load from the additive equation of total load, but rather a dimension now called 'germane processing.'" Consequently, increased germane load "is no longer believed to lead to cognitive overload and can thus no longer be assumed to be detrimental to learning performance".
requirements: Distinguishing germane processing from components of total mental load when measuring or designing for load
constraints: The review notes germane load's definition and theoretical basis remained controversial, motivating calls for a dyadic intrinsic/extraneous model
target_learning_goals: understanding relations between load components and learning performance
key_sources: Alexander Skulmowski & Kate Man Xu. (2022). Understanding Cognitive Load in Digital and Online Learning: a New Perspective on Extraneous Cognitive Load. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09624-7

article_title: Understanding Cognitive Load in Digital and Online Learning: a New Perspective on Extraneous Cognitive Load
citation: Alexander Skulmowski & Kate Man Xu. (2022). Understanding Cognitive Load in Digital and Online Learning: a New Perspective on Extraneous Cognitive Load. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09624-7
title: Cost-benefit model links specific design factors to extraneous load types with associated germane processing benefits
description: The review's organizing framework treats design factors as cognitive costs (extraneous load) paired with benefits (germane processing). "The cost-benefit model links different design factors to extraneous load types that feature associated forms of germane processing." Digital learning often involves "a trade-off between risks of exposing learners to extraneous load and the benefit of letting them profit from novel and engaging experiences", so a small extraneous investment can be worthwhile when its germane benefit exceeds the cost.
requirements: Designers must identify which germane process a given extraneous load component supports and compare cost against benefit for the specific task
constraints: The review states a cost-benefit approach alone does not suffice to explain divergent effects on different outcome measures such as retention versus transfer
target_learners: learners using digital and online learning environments
target_learning_goals: balancing engagement and cognitive load in digital learning design
key_sources: Alexander Skulmowski & Kate Man Xu. (2022). Understanding Cognitive Load in Digital and Online Learning: a New Perspective on Extraneous Cognitive Load. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09624-7

article_title: Correlates of teachers’ classroom management self-efficacy: A systematic review and meta-analysis
citation: Duan, S., Bissaker, K., & Xu, Z. (2024). Correlates of teachers' classroom management self-efficacy: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09881-2
title: Three-strand conceptual framework of CMSE correlates: teacher-level, classroom-level, and school-level factors
description: The article proposes a conceptual framework, adapted from Fackler et al.'s three categories of TSE-related factors, that organizes correlates of classroom management self-efficacy into three strands: "(1) personal characteristics of teacher (teacher-level factors); (2) characteristics of classroom composition (classroom-level factors); (3) teachers' working conditions (school-level factors)". The framework, presented in Fig. 1, guided both the synthesis of the literature and the discussion of areas needing further exploration.
requirements: Correlates must be empirically tested in studies measuring teacher self-efficacy for classroom management with quantifiable relationships
constraints: The framework captures correlates that are both theoretically and empirically tested, per the article
target_learners: in-service teachers in mainstream school settings
target_learning_goals: classroom management self-efficacy
examples: The meta-analysis used the framework to cluster 22 identified correlates into the three categories and to structure the discussion of results
key_sources: Duan, S., Bissaker, K., & Xu, Z. (2024). Correlates of teachers' classroom management self-efficacy: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09881-2

article_title: Exploring the Nature-Creativity Connection Across Different Settings: A Scoping Review
citation: Vella-Brodrick, D. A., Lewis, K. J., & Gilowska, K. (2024). Exploring the Nature-Creativity Connection Across Different Settings: A Scoping Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09964-0
title: Attention Restoration Theory and the alternating attention orientation model as explanations for how nature enhances creativity
description: The review presents Attention Restoration Theory (ART; Kaplan) as the most commonly used explanation for how nature's restorative effects indirectly enhance creativity by reducing cognitive fatigue and renewing attention. Under ART, "goal-directed attention is a finite resource" that fatigues, and nature restores it via "soft fascination" — effortless attention held by low-stimulation yet fascinating surroundings, contrasting with absorption-driven hard fascination. The review also describes Williams et al.'s alternating attention orientation model, in which attention alternates between fascinating natural surroundings and inward mind-wandering, both placing low demand on attentional control and potentially strengthening the illumination and evaluation phases of the four-stage creative process.
requirements: Exposure to low-stimulation natural surroundings during or after cognitively demanding preparation, consistent with the incubation phase of the creative process
constraints: The review notes mindfulness and soft fascination are distinct constructs whose exact relationship, and thus their relationship to creativity, remains unclear
target_learners: adults across education, workplace, and arts contexts
target_learning_goals: divergent and convergent creative thinking
creative problem-solving
examples: The review describes placing nature exposure after the cognitively demanding preparation phase so attention renews while ideas incubate unconsciously
key_sources: Vella-Brodrick, D. A., Lewis, K. J., & Gilowska, K. (2024). Exploring the Nature-Creativity Connection Across Different Settings: A Scoping Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09964-0

article_title: Growing Out of the Experience: How Subjective Experiences of Effort and Learning Influence the Use of Interleaved Practice
citation: Onan, E., Wiradhany, W., Biwer, F., Janssen, E. M., & de Bruin, A. B. H. (2022). Growing Out of the Experience: How Subjective Experiences of Effort and Learning Influence the Use of Interleaved Practice. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09692-3
title: Visual Feedback Prompt (VFP): individualized line graphs of perceived effort and perceived learning across study units with reflection questions
description: The VFP is a metacognitive prompt that fed back participants' own ratings as "individualized visual summaries, in which we presented two separate line graphs, one for perceived effort and one for perceived learning". Study units were grouped on the x-axis as beginning, middle, and end periods, and four open questions prompted participants to compare strategies, describe changes across time, and reason about why their experiences changed in relation to strategy efficacy. In this study the VFP did not increase interleaved-practice choices over control, but qualitative reports indicated it changed some decisions and increased decision confidence.
requirements: Participants must first have rated perceived effort and perceived learning after each study unit so individualized graphs can be generated
Participants must be able to understand the line-graph summaries; the article checked correspondence between prompt responses and actual ratings
constraints: In this study it did not significantly change strategy choices relative to a control reading condition
The article notes it could act as a double-edged sword by reinforcing inaccurate monitoring of effort and learning
target_learning_goals: accurate monitoring of effort and learning
making effective learning strategy decisions in category learning
examples: Participants in the VFP condition inspected line graphs of their effort and learning ratings and answered four open prompt questions before making their final strategy choice

article_title: Inconclusive Evidence for a Prospective Effect of Academic Self-Concept on Achievement: A Simulated Reanalysis and Comment on Marsh et al. (2024)
citation: Kimmo Sorjonen, Bo Melin, Gustav Nilsonne. (2025). Inconclusive Evidence for a Prospective Effect of Academic Self-Concept on Achievement: A Simulated Reanalysis and Comment on Marsh et al. (2024). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10008-4
title: Extended Skill Development Model (ESDM)
description: The ESDM is the authors' alternative to the reciprocal effects model of academic self-concept and achievement. It "posits a unidirectional effect of trait-like academic achievement on trait-like self-concept", and holds that time-specific scores on both constructs arise from those trait-like levels "in addition to common time-specific state factors, e.g., illness or mood", with autoregressive effects among the state factors and no direct prospective effects between occasion-specific scores. In this article it is fitted to simulated PALMA-like and TRAIN-like data, where its good fit suggests observed cross-lagged effects may be spurious.
requirements: Longitudinal multi-wave measures of both constructs; the model is estimated via SEM on covariances/correlations and sample size
constraints: The unidirectional trait effect is an assumption that cannot be distinguished statistically, at least not in observational data, from a confounder affecting both trait-like factors
target_learning_goals: academic self-concept in math
math achievement
examples: Fitted to simulated PALMA-like data (χ2 = 597, CFI = 0.977) and TRAIN-like data (χ2 = 821, CFI = 0.934) with good fit in both
key_sources: Kimmo Sorjonen, Bo Melin, Gustav Nilsonne. (2025). Inconclusive Evidence for a Prospective Effect of Academic Self-Concept on Achievement: A Simulated Reanalysis and Comment on Marsh et al. (2024). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10008-4

article_title: Inconclusive Evidence for a Prospective Effect of Academic Self-Concept on Achievement: A Simulated Reanalysis and Comment on Marsh et al. (2024)
citation: Kimmo Sorjonen, Bo Melin, Gustav Nilsonne. (2025). Inconclusive Evidence for a Prospective Effect of Academic Self-Concept on Achievement: A Simulated Reanalysis and Comment on Marsh et al. (2024). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10008-4
title: Test alternative longitudinal models and juxtapose their results and interpretations before drawing causal conclusions
description: The article endorses Marsh et al.'s (2024) recommendation that researchers "test alternative models and juxtapose their results and interpretations". When findings from alternative models converge, causal conclusions are corroborated; when they diverge, "caution is advised and causal conclusions appear premature". The authors demonstrate this by fitting RI-CLPM, LCSM, ESDM and STARTS models to the same simulated data and finding contradictory positive, negative, and null effects.
requirements: Multiple competing longitudinal models fitted to the same data; willingness to withhold causal claims when findings diverge
constraints: The article's demonstration rests on simulated data resembling the original studies, and on observational data from which causality is difficult, maybe impossible, to infer
target_learning_goals: academic self-concept
academic achievement
examples: The authors fitted four (and two additional modified) models to simulated PALMA-like data and validated the divergence on simulated TRAIN-like data, concluding that claims of reciprocal causal effects appear premature
key_sources: Kimmo Sorjonen, Bo Melin, Gustav Nilsonne. (2025). Inconclusive Evidence for a Prospective Effect of Academic Self-Concept on Achievement: A Simulated Reanalysis and Comment on Marsh et al. (2024). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10008-4

article_title: Critiquing and Reimagining Belonging in Public Spaces in Higher Education
citation: Bart-Plange, D.-J., Henderson, K., Hoffman, K., & Trawalter, S. (2025). Critiquing and Reimagining Belonging in Public Spaces in Higher Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10061-z
title: Universities as defensible spaces: a territorial, surveilled, and symbolic space framework
description: The article adapts Newman's Defensible Space Theory—originally a model for residential environments that 'inhibits crime by creating the physical expression of a social fabric that defends itself'—to university campuses. It proposes that campuses are (1) territorial, (2) surveilled, and (3) symbolic spaces, and that these features sharpen ingroup-outgroup boundaries and reify racial and class disparities, leaving marginalized students feeling like trespassers. Table 1 summarizes each feature's definition, examples, and implications for belonging.
requirements: The framework applies to campuses whose territorial boundaries, surveillance, and symbols fall along historical lines of race and class; the authors state they use their own institution as an example because they know it well, not because it is unique.
constraints: The authors note the theory and its application have received sharp criticism, having led to gated enclaves and privatized public space, and that the present evidence does not yet test the framework's central tenets.
target_learners: racially minoritized students in higher education
target_learning_goals: sense of belonging at the university
empowered use of campus public space
examples: The article maps surveillance cameras on one campus via an ArcGIS survey and catalogs symbols such as antebellum architecture, statues of Thomas Jefferson, and Greek organization houses.
key_sources: Bart-Plange, D.-J., Henderson, K., Hoffman, K., & Trawalter, S. (2025). Critiquing and Reimagining Belonging in Public Spaces in Higher Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10061-z

article_title: The Past, Present, and Future of the Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning
citation: Richard E. Mayer. (2024). The Past, Present, and Future of the Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09842-1
title: Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning (CTML): dual channels, limited capacity, active processing
description: CTML is an evidence-based account of how people learn academic material from words and graphics. Its three guiding assumptions are that "dual channels (i.e., humans have separate information processing channels for verbal and visual information)", that "processing capacity is severely limited", and that meaningful learning involves active selecting, organizing, and integrating of material in working memory with prior knowledge from long-term memory. The theory is depicted in a stable flowchart with sensory, working, and long-term memory stores and yields multimedia design principles.
requirements: Applies to academic material consisting of words and graphics presented as multimedia instructional messages
constraints: The theory focuses on how to help people learn academic content rather than on the capabilities of the latest educational technologies
target_learners: students learning academic material from multimedia lessons
target_learning_goals: meaningful learning that transfers to new situations
examples: The theory is represented in Fig. 8 with an auditory row across the top and a visual row across the bottom, boxes for sensory, working, and long-term memory, and arrows for selecting, organizing, and integrating.
key_sources: Richard E. Mayer. (2024). The Past, Present, and Future of the Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09842-1

article_title: The Past, Present, and Future of the Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning
citation: Richard E. Mayer. (2024). The Past, Present, and Future of the Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09842-1
title: SOI model: selecting, organizing, and integrating as the core cognitive processes of CTML
description: The SOI model holds that meaningful learning depends on three cognitive processes: selecting relevant material for further processing, organizing it into a coherent cognitive representation, and integrating it with relevant prior knowledge. The article states that "The SOI model was a major conceptual breakthrough for me, and has remained at the core of CTML ever since". In the current model CTML has five cognitive processes: selecting words, selecting images, organizing words, organizing images, and integrating.
requirements: Learners must engage in appropriate cognitive processing during learning for meaningful learning to occur
target_learners: students learning from multimedia instructional messages
target_learning_goals: meaningful learning of academic material
examples: Instructional design is intended to guide these processes, such as prompting learners to write a summary or self-test during pauses in a lesson.
key_sources: Richard E. Mayer. (2024). The Past, Present, and Future of the Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09842-1

article_title: The Past, Present, and Future of the Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning
citation: Richard E. Mayer. (2024). The Past, Present, and Future of the Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09842-1
title: Three demands on limited cognitive capacity: extraneous, essential, and generative processing
description: A central tenet of CTML is that working memory capacity is limited and faces three demands during learning. The article states: "there are three demands on that limited cognitive capacity during learning: extraneous processing, essential processing, and generative processing." Extraneous processing does not support the instructional goal and depends on poor instructional design; essential processing represents the material in working memory and depends on the inherent complexity of the material; generative processing makes sense of the incoming information and depends on the learner's motivation.
requirements: Working memory capacity is limited, so capacity used for one kind of processing takes away from capacity available for the others
target_learning_goals: efficient allocation of cognitive capacity during multimedia learning
examples: Extraneous processing depends on the degree of poor instructional design, such as presenting extraneous verbal or pictorial information in a lesson.
key_sources: Richard E. Mayer. (2024). The Past, Present, and Future of the Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09842-1

article_title: The Past, Present, and Future of the Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning
citation: Richard E. Mayer. (2024). The Past, Present, and Future of the Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09842-1
title: Three instructional goals for multimedia design: minimize extraneous, manage essential, foster generative processing
description: CTML translates the three demands on cognitive capacity into a lesson-level design pattern. The article states: "The three demands on cognitive capacity give rise to three instructional goals: minimize extraneous processing, manage essential processing, and foster generative processing." Minimizing is accomplished by eliminating unneeded words and graphical elements, managing by breaking a continuous lesson into learner-paced chunks, and fostering by prompting generative learning activities such as writing a summary or self-testing.
requirements: Designers must diagnose which demand on capacity is the binding constraint for a given lesson before choosing techniques
constraints: Each design principle is subject to boundary conditions including for whom the principle applies, for which kind of lesson the principle applies, and under what circumstances the principle applies
target_learners: students in multimedia instruction across print, screen, and virtual reality
target_learning_goals: meaningful learning of academic content
examples: Managing essential processing can be accomplished by breaking a continuous lesson into manageable chunks that can be paced by the learner.
key_sources: Richard E. Mayer. (2024). The Past, Present, and Future of the Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09842-1

article_title: The Past, Present, and Future of the Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning
citation: Richard E. Mayer. (2024). The Past, Present, and Future of the Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09842-1
title: Adjunct theories extending CTML: social agency theory and cognitive-affective models of learning with media
description: As CTML expands beyond purely cognitive processing, the article reports supplementing it with adjunct theories. The article states: "we supplemented CTML with 'social agency theory' ... which incorporates social processes during learning, and with the 'cognitive-affective theory of learning with media' ... and the 'cognitive-affective model of e-learning' ... which incorporates affective processes during learning." Social agency theory posits that learners try harder to understand a lesson when they feel the instructor is working with them; the affective models posit learners try harder when they experience positive emotion while learning.
requirements: More work is needed to incorporate new components into CTML, especially given ongoing advances in theories of self-regulated learning and motivation
constraints: The article notes we are now grappling with how to represent these additions to CTML
target_learners: students learning from online and multimedia lessons
target_learning_goals: meaningful learning supported by social and affective processing
examples: Research showing students learn better from a statistics lesson when given prompts intended to boost their self-efficacy and decrease anxiety during learning.
key_sources: Richard E. Mayer. (2024). The Past, Present, and Future of the Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09842-1

article_title: Blending Teacher Autonomy Support and Provision of Structure in the Classroom for Optimal Motivation: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
citation: Alexandra Patzak, Xiaorong Zhang. (2025). Blending Teacher Autonomy Support and Provision of Structure in the Classroom for Optimal Motivation: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09994-2
title: Autonomy support as a multi-component instructional construct (ten defining components)
description: The review synthesizes how 94 studies conceptualize teacher autonomy support as teachers' efforts to support students' need for autonomy through instructional strategies. A detailed analysis "yielded ten distinct components of autonomy support", the most common being "providing students with choices" and "providing explanatory rationales", plus acknowledging negative feelings, taking students' perspective, promoting students' voice, inviting pursuit of interests, invitational language, need-satisfying activity design, patience, and respect. Definitions of individual components vary across studies, hampering generalizability.
requirements: Studies must define autonomy support via identifiable instructional strategy components for the taxonomy to apply
constraints: Component definitions are inconsistent across studies; e.g., choices are variably described as aligned with interests or merely 'offering choice' without elaboration
target_learning_goals: Autonomous motivation
sense of autonomy
engagement
examples: Offer choice was referenced by 62 studies; provide explanatory rationales by 35; acknowledge negative feelings by 23 (Table 2)
key_sources: Alexandra Patzak, Xiaorong Zhang. (2025). Blending Teacher Autonomy Support and Provision of Structure in the Classroom for Optimal Motivation: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09994-2

article_title: Blending Teacher Autonomy Support and Provision of Structure in the Classroom for Optimal Motivation: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
citation: Alexandra Patzak, Xiaorong Zhang. (2025). Blending Teacher Autonomy Support and Provision of Structure in the Classroom for Optimal Motivation: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09994-2
title: Provision of structure as a three-theme instructional construct (guidance, expectations, encouragement)
description: The review synthesizes how studies conceptualize provision of structure as strategies teachers use to foster students' understanding of course materials and sense of competency. Three key themes emerged: "Offer guidance, provide and clarify expectations, and encourage students." The most common components were "offering guidance, clarifying expectations, giving informational feedback, and offering encouragement", with additional components including consistent behavior, adjusting instruction to ability level, learning strategies, and explaining consequences of rule-breaking. Definitions of components such as informational feedback vary across studies.
requirements: Instructional strategies must be identifiable as guidance, expectation clarification, or encouragement to map onto the taxonomy
constraints: Components are inconsistently defined across studies; encouragement overlaps with positive feedback, and ambiguity may cause unclear teacher application
target_learning_goals: sense of competence
academic engagement
understanding of course materials
examples: Offer guidance was referenced by 95 studies; provide and clarify expectations by 61; encourage by 32 (Table 3)
key_sources: Alexandra Patzak, Xiaorong Zhang. (2025). Blending Teacher Autonomy Support and Provision of Structure in the Classroom for Optimal Motivation: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09994-2

article_title: Blending Teacher Autonomy Support and Provision of Structure in the Classroom for Optimal Motivation: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
citation: Alexandra Patzak, Xiaorong Zhang. (2025). Blending Teacher Autonomy Support and Provision of Structure in the Classroom for Optimal Motivation: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09994-2
title: Teacher as Social Context Questionnaire (TASC) and Situations in School Questionnaire (SIS) as measures of autonomy support and structure
description: The review identifies the two most frequently used measures of autonomy support and structure. The TASC (Belmont et al., 1988) comprises 41 items and three sub-scales (autonomy support 12 items, structure 15 items, involvement 14 items), usable as student or teacher report, with Cronbach's alpha 0.66–0.90 (student) and 0.73–0.90 (teacher). The SIS (Aelterman et al., 2019) is "a vignette-based questionnaire" with fifteen vignettes rated on a 7-point scale, with alpha 0.80–0.92 (student) and 0.73–0.85 (teacher). Both measure autonomy support and structure alongside their opposites, control and chaos.
requirements: Measures must include items operationalizing both autonomy support and structure for paired assessment
constraints: Studies in the sample varied widely in the number of items used, from 1 to 12 for autonomy support and 1 to 15 for structure
target_learning_goals: assessment of teacher autonomy support and provision of structure
examples: Student-report TASC sample items include 'My teacher listens to my ideas' (autonomy support) and 'My teacher makes sure I understand before they move on' (structure)
key_sources: Alexandra Patzak, Xiaorong Zhang. (2025). Blending Teacher Autonomy Support and Provision of Structure in the Classroom for Optimal Motivation: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09994-2

article_title: Blending Teacher Autonomy Support and Provision of Structure in the Classroom for Optimal Motivation: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
citation: Alexandra Patzak, Xiaorong Zhang. (2025). Blending Teacher Autonomy Support and Provision of Structure in the Classroom for Optimal Motivation: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09994-2
title: Blend teacher autonomy support with provision of structure rather than treating them as opposites
description: The article's central recommendation is that teachers should blend autonomy support and provision of structure, because the two constructs reinforce each other and both elevate student outcomes. The authors state: "Our findings suggest blending autonomy support and structure for optimal growth of students and teachers." The recommendation rests on the pooled positive correlation between the constructs and their independent associations with student motivation, engagement, and need satisfaction, and on evidence that students benefit most when structure is provided in an autonomy-supportive rather than controlling manner.
requirements: Teachers must distinguish structure from control, since control undermines motivation while structure supports competence
constraints: The relationship between the two constructs was moderated by data collection method and school level; teacher-report studies sometimes showed negative correlations
target_learning_goals: student motivation
engagement
need satisfaction
teacher motivation and effectiveness
examples: The review found 86 of 94 studies described the two constructs as independent but positively related aspects of teachers' instructional approaches
