article_title: Interrelations Among Achievement Goals and Achievement Emotions: A Meta-Analytic Examination
citation: Tanja Bross, Ulrike Elisabeth Nett, & Martin Daumiller. (2024). Interrelations Among Achievement Goals and Achievement Emotions: A Meta-Analytic Examination. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09931-9
title: Control-value theory of achievement emotions with activity/outcome object focus
description: Control-value theory defines achievement emotions as "emotions tied directly to achievement activities or achievement outcomes" and explains them via control- and value-appraisals. Emotions are classified by valence and by object focus into activity emotions (e.g., enjoyment, boredom, anger during an activity) and outcome emotions (e.g., hope, pride, shame, hopelessness regarding outcomes), each with prospective, concurrent, or retrospective temporal relations. The article uses this taxonomy to differentiate goal-emotion associations at a specific level rather than only at the affective valence level, and predicts mastery-approach goals correlate positively with enjoyment and negatively with boredom and anger, while performance-approach goals link to positive outcome emotions such as hope and pride.
requirements: Achievement emotions must be measured with their object focus (activity vs. outcome) and temporal relation distinguished, not only by valence
constraints: The article notes the relationships among work-avoidance goals and emotions as well as among relational goals and emotions are not addressed in either theoretical model it reviews
target_learning_goals: understanding how achievement goals relate to achievement emotions in educational settings
examples: The article's Table 2 maps emotions such as anticipatory joy, hope, hopelessness, anxiety, enjoyment, boredom, anger and frustration onto object focus, value and control appraisals
key_sources: Tanja Bross, Ulrike Elisabeth Nett, & Martin Daumiller. (2024). Interrelations Among Achievement Goals and Achievement Emotions: A Meta-Analytic Examination. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09931-9

article_title: Interrelations Among Achievement Goals and Achievement Emotions: A Meta-Analytic Examination
citation: Tanja Bross, Ulrike Elisabeth Nett, & Martin Daumiller. (2024). Interrelations Among Achievement Goals and Achievement Emotions: A Meta-Analytic Examination. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09931-9
title: Bidirectional goal-emotion model linking achievement goals to positive and negative emotions via perceived progress
description: The article describes a bidirectional conceptual model in which "achievement goals shape individuals' emotions, as the rate of progress made towards achieving a goal leads to the experience of certain emotions," while affective experiences (mood) in turn impact achievement goals. Built on Carver and Scheier's (1998) predictions and the 2 x 2 goal taxonomy, it generates concrete predictions: mastery-approach goals should increase positive and decrease negative emotions, performance-approach goals carry risk of anxiety and dissatisfaction, and avoidance goals relate negatively to positive emotions. The article uses this model, alongside control-value theory, as a complementary theoretical anchor for interpreting goal-emotion interrelations.
requirements: Both mastery and performance goal dimensions must be distinguished, since the model's predictions derive from these dimensions
constraints: The article notes the argument primarily focuses on the direction from goals to emotions and does not fully address the reciprocal influence of emotions on goals
target_learning_goals: understanding how achievement goals shape emotional experiences and vice versa
examples: The article derives from this model that people with mastery-approach goals should not experience negative emotions when progress is insufficient, as this signals insufficient effort without taking the self negatively into account
key_sources: Tanja Bross, Ulrike Elisabeth Nett, & Martin Daumiller. (2024). Interrelations Among Achievement Goals and Achievement Emotions: A Meta-Analytic Examination. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09931-9

article_title: Ten Years of Dimensional Comparison Theory: On the Development of a Theory from Educational Psychology
citation: Jens Möller. (2024). Ten Years of Dimensional Comparison Theory: On the Development of a Theory from Educational Psychology. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09918-6
title: The Generalized I/E (GI/E) model: dimensional comparisons between any life domains, with multiple criteria and possible assimilation effects
description: The generalized I/E model (Möller et al., 2016) is the main extension of the classic I/E model within DCT. It removes three restrictions of the original model: it covers comparisons between more subjects than math and first language, criteria beyond self-concept, and effect directions beyond negative contrast. The review states that "the GI/E model postulates that dimensional comparisons occur between achievements in more subjects than just math and the first language, also between perceptions of teacher characteristics (such as agency or communion, self-concepts, interests) and even indeed beyond academic domains." It further holds that "dimensional comparisons need not lead to negative contrast effects but rather may lead to near-zero or even positive assimilation effects."
requirements: Dimensional comparisons are defined as comparisons between a person's ability in one domain against those in one or more other domains
constraints: The direction and strength of effects depend on the perceived similarity of the compared domains, with near comparisons yielding weaker contrast or assimilation effects
target_learning_goals: academic self-concept formation
subject-specific task values and motivation
examples: Studies extending comparisons to physics, second language, history, physical education, earth science, social studies, and music, and to perceived teacher characteristics as predictors
key_sources: Jens Möller. (2024). Ten Years of Dimensional Comparison Theory: On the Development of a Theory from Educational Psychology. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09918-6

article_title: Ten Years of Dimensional Comparison Theory: On the Development of a Theory from Educational Psychology
citation: Jens Möller. (2024). Ten Years of Dimensional Comparison Theory: On the Development of a Theory from Educational Psychology. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09918-6
title: Integration of dimensional comparisons into situated expectancy-value theory (SEVT): relativistic expectancy and value formation across domains
description: Eccles and Wigfield (2020) developed SEVT to explain individual differences in expectancies, values, and their consequences for achievement and choices; Wigfield et al. (2020) presented the connection of DCT with SEVT in detail. The review explains that this extension affords a more relativistic reading, where "the question being asked is less "Can I do X?" and more "How well can I do X compared to Y?," less "Do I want to do X?" and more "Do I want to do X more than Y?"." All facets playing a role in SEVT can also be predictors, moderators, and criteria in dimensional comparisons, underpinning that dimensional comparisons impact the formation of both expectancy and subjective task values.
requirements: Subjective task values are heterogeneous in domain-specificity, so they should be influenced to different extents by dimensional comparisons
constraints: The review notes costs, which differ strongly between domains, should be more strongly determined by dimensional contrast effects than utility values, which vary less strongly between subjects
target_learning_goals: expectancy formation
subjective task value formation
academic choice
examples: Wigfield et al. (2020) presented in detail the connection of DCT with SEVT in a separate theoretical paper
key_sources: Jens Möller. (2024). Ten Years of Dimensional Comparison Theory: On the Development of a Theory from Educational Psychology. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09918-6

article_title: A Computational Model of School Achievement
citation: Brendan A. Schuetze. (2024). A Computational Model of School Achievement. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09853-6
title: CoMSA: A computational model of school achievement unifying cognitive, metacognitive, and motivational theory
description: The CoMSA is a formal mathematical model of the relationship between learning over time and exam achievement. It simulates individual student trajectories using logistic learning curves with three parameters (slope, intercept, inflection point), modulated by metacognitive bias and precision, and bounded by motivational circuit breakers (norm of study and maximum willingness to study). The model acts as an interface between construct-focused educational psychology and achievement outcomes by modeling the downstream behavioral effects of cognition, motivation, and metacognition.
requirements: Explicit encoding of assumptions in computer code enabling modification, theory testing, and novel predictions
Assumption that the S-shaped logistic curve is generally acceptable for modeling learning
constraints: The three steps (curve establishment, metacognitive modulation, stopping rule) are laid out in strict sequence for tractability; in real-world settings contingencies exist between steps
All inputs are assumed to be set once at the beginning of the study session and do not change over the course of the learning period
The analyses do not directly test the ability of the CoMSA to model individual-level data
target_learning_goals: Exam achievement
Self-regulated learning
examples: The model was used to simulate classroom-level data from two meta-analytic sources: Godwin et al. (2021) on time-on-task and Simonsmeier et al. (2022) on prior knowledge
key_sources: Brendan A. Schuetze. (2024). A Computational Model of School Achievement. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09853-6

article_title: A Computational Model of School Achievement
citation: Brendan A. Schuetze. (2024). A Computational Model of School Achievement. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09853-6
title: CoMSA simulation database of 184,032 simulation runs representing over 1.8 billion simulated students
description: A publicly available database hosted on OSF (https://osf.io/z8n3a/) containing the full simulation output from the CoMSA project. It includes N = 184,032 simulation runs representing over 1.8 billion individual simulated students, including runs rejected due to the second and third filtering criteria. The database can be queried, filtered, plotted, and analyzed to understand effects of different individual and contextual factors.
requirements: Access to the OSF project at https://osf.io/z8n3a/
constraints: Includes runs rejected due to the second and third filtering criteria, not just the final 100,000 used in analyses
target_learning_goals: Understanding effects of individual and contextual factors on achievement
examples: The database was used for proof-of-concept analyses comparing simulated correlations to two meta-analytic sources
key_sources: Brendan A. Schuetze. (2024). A Computational Model of School Achievement. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09853-6

article_title: A Computational Model of School Achievement
citation: Brendan A. Schuetze. (2024). A Computational Model of School Achievement. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09853-6
title: Learning curve parameterization: slope, intercept, and inflection point map to distinct educational constructs
description: The CoMSA conceptualizes educational differences through three logistic curve parameters. Slope (Logis a) represents learning rate per unit of time invested. Intercept (Logis c) represents floor performance when time spent studying is zero, associated with prior knowledge and guessing floors. Inflection point (Logis d) determines the amount of prerequisite learning needed before performance gains appear on the tested material. Interventions are modeled as modifications to these parameters.
requirements: Assumption that learning follows a logistic (S-shaped) curve within the 0-100 percent grading scale
Three-parameter logistic (3PL) model from psychometrics
constraints: Slope and all parameters are not directly mappable to any one contextual or psychological variable
The relationship between floor and prior knowledge also depends on the inflection point
target_learning_goals: Predicting exam achievement from student and contextual characteristics
examples: A medical student studying for a licensing exam would have a much shallower learning curve than a fifth-grade student studying for a ten-word vocabulary quiz
key_sources: Brendan A. Schuetze. (2024). A Computational Model of School Achievement. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09853-6

article_title: How Do We Deal with Uncertain Information? Effects of Verbal and Visual Expressions of Uncertainty on Learning
citation: Glaser, M., Lengyel, D., Toulouse, C., & Schwan, S. (2022). How Do We Deal with Uncertain Information? Effects of Verbal and Visual Expressions of Uncertainty on Learning. Educational Psychology Review (2022) 34:1097–1131. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09659-4
title: Integrated model of processing evidence and its uncertainty values in multimedia learning
description: The article proposes an integrated theoretical approach combining the knowledge generation model for visual analytics (Sacha et al.), the cognitive theory of multimedia learning, and the multimedia principle to explain how learners process content marked with uncertainty. The model "describes how knowledge is built based on the awareness of uncertainty markers and trust building cues" and identifies "an exploration loop, a verification loop, and a knowledge generation loop" of cognitive processing. It predicts that certain content is processed with higher priority and that the multimedia effect extends to metainformation such as uncertainty values.
requirements: Learners must become aware of uncertainty information and hold it in working memory for it to influence processing
constraints: Presented as a first step in validating the integrated model, applied to archeological reconstructions with deficient/epistemic uncertainty
target_learners: Students and laypersons learning scientific content with uncertain information
target_learning_goals: Learning scientific content while understanding the epistemic uncertainty of that content
examples: The study operationalized the model with temple reconstructions whose elements carried lexical hedges and visual uncertainty markers in a 4×3 design
key_sources: Glaser, M., Lengyel, D., Toulouse, C., & Schwan, S. (2022). How Do We Deal with Uncertain Information? Effects of Verbal and Visual Expressions of Uncertainty on Learning. Educational Psychology Review (2022) 34:1097–1131. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09659-4

article_title: How Do We Deal with Uncertain Information? Effects of Verbal and Visual Expressions of Uncertainty on Learning
citation: Glaser, M., Lengyel, D., Toulouse, C., & Schwan, S. (2022). How Do We Deal with Uncertain Information? Effects of Verbal and Visual Expressions of Uncertainty on Learning. Educational Psychology Review (2022) 34:1097–1131. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09659-4
title: Use stop light colors rather than value-suppressing geometric contrast to visualize uncertainty in multimedia learning materials
description: The article recommends stop light colors as the uncertainty visualization style for learning materials because they support dual coding of uncertainty information. The authors state that stop light colors "should be easier to comprehend, discriminate, and transfer, thus being better for dual coding and therefore for the learning of uncertainty information compared to geometric contrast." The experiment's results on memory of uncertainty values and uncertain-element appearance are consistent with this recommendation, and the article closes by giving recommendations for designing learning material including uncertainty visualizations.
requirements: Learners must be introduced to the meaning of the color code, as done via an explanatory text and manipulation check in the study
constraints: Geometric contrast was superior for memory of the appearance of certain elements, so the recommendation is limited to learning uncertainty information
target_learners: Adult learners and students without background in the subject domain
target_learning_goals: Remembering uncertainty values and the appearance of uncertain content elements
examples: In the experiment, uncertain elements were colored red, medium yellow, and certain green in the stop light condition, versus coarse-to-fine geometric detail in the geometric contrast condition
key_sources: Glaser, M., Lengyel, D., Toulouse, C., & Schwan, S. (2022). How Do We Deal with Uncertain Information? Effects of Verbal and Visual Expressions of Uncertainty on Learning. Educational Psychology Review (2022) 34:1097–1131. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09659-4

article_title: How Do We Deal with Uncertain Information? Effects of Verbal and Visual Expressions of Uncertainty on Learning
citation: Glaser, M., Lengyel, D., Toulouse, C., & Schwan, S. (2022). How Do We Deal with Uncertain Information? Effects of Verbal and Visual Expressions of Uncertainty on Learning. Educational Psychology Review (2022) 34:1097–1131. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09659-4
title: Pergamon multimedia learning environment with temple reconstructions and uncertainty expressions
description: A computer-based, linear learning environment about the ancient city Pergamon used as the study material. Participants worked through "a computer-based, linear learning environment about the ancient city Pergamon and two of its most important buildings—the temple of Athena and the temple of Demeter", including pictures of reconstructions with audio explanations in which lexical hedges expressed uncertainty values of twelve architectural elements per temple, each with a scientific justification. Four picture conditions varied the uncertainty visualization: none, stop light colors, geometric contrast, or both combined.
requirements: Audio explanations with the reconstructions had to be played in full length and could not be paused; navigation backwards was not possible
constraints: Uncertainty values and their verbal scientific justifications were fictional, created for experimental reasons
target_learners: Adult participants from a broad variety of disciplines without archeology, history, or architecture background
target_learning_goals: Memory for architectural elements, uncertainty values, and their scientific justifications
examples: Lexical hedges ranged from "maybe" (uncertain) through "highly probable" (medium) to "definitely" (certain)
key_sources: Glaser, M., Lengyel, D., Toulouse, C., & Schwan, S. (2022). How Do We Deal with Uncertain Information? Effects of Verbal and Visual Expressions of Uncertainty on Learning. Educational Psychology Review (2022) 34:1097–1131. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09659-4

article_title: Student Teachers’ and Experienced Teachers’ Professional Vision of Students’ Understanding of the Rational Number Concept
citation: Maikki Pouta, Erno Lehtinen & Tuire Palonen. (2020). Student Teachers' and Experienced Teachers' Professional Vision of Students' Understanding of the Rational Number Concept. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09536-y
title: Professional vision as selective attention, knowledge-based reasoning, and decision-making bridging teacher knowledge and practice
description: The article applies a framework in which professional vision in education consists of selective attention and knowledge-based reasoning including "description, explanation and prediction", later expanded to a third interrelated component, decision-making of action. It treats professional vision as "not only an integrated model of a teacher's knowledge but also a system bridging knowledge and practice", developmentally shaped by teachers' knowledge and beliefs and learnable through guided video observation rather than a natural talent.
requirements: Development is strongly guided by teachers' knowledge and beliefs
Execution of decisions demands additional, complex skills beyond noticing
target_learning_goals: noticing and interpreting students' mathematical thinking
instructing students' understanding of fractions
examples: The study coded CRR episodes into descriptive, evaluative and interpretive levels and instruction into supportive versus non-supportive categories to operationalise the framework.
key_sources: Maikki Pouta, Erno Lehtinen & Tuire Palonen. (2020). Student Teachers' and Experienced Teachers' Professional Vision of Students' Understanding of the Rational Number Concept. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09536-y

article_title: Cognitive Load Theory and Time Considerations: Using the Time-Based Resource Sharing Model
citation: Sébastien Puma, Nadine Matton, Pierre-Vincent Paubel, André Tricot. (2018). Cognitive Load Theory and Time Considerations: Using the Time-Based Resource Sharing Model. Educational Psychology Review, 30 (3). https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-018-9438-6
title: The Time-Based Resource Sharing model as a working-memory model for Cognitive Load Theory that accounts for time
description: The article introduces the Time-Based Resource Sharing model into Cognitive Load Theory as a working-memory model in which time matters. Unlike slot-based models where working memory is "composed of a discrete number of slots (i.e., chunks) that can be kept active", the TBRS model "enables time to be taken into account when describing working memory solicitation". The authors use it to generate testable hypotheses about how presentation pace during learning affects performance.
requirements: Learning scenarios must be describable in terms of the pace and timing of information presentation for the model to characterize working memory solicitation.
target_learners: learners studying instructional materials with time-paced information presentation
target_learning_goals: understanding how presentation pace affects working memory load during learning
examples: The authors used the model to derive hypotheses tested in two experiments on information presentation pace effects during learning.
key_sources: Sébastien Puma, Nadine Matton, Pierre-Vincent Paubel, André Tricot. (2018). Cognitive Load Theory and Time Considerations: Using the Time-Based Resource Sharing Model. Educational Psychology Review, 30 (3). https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-018-9438-6

article_title: Cognitive Load Theory and Time Considerations: Using the Time-Based Resource Sharing Model
citation: Sébastien Puma, Nadine Matton, Pierre-Vincent Paubel, André Tricot. (2018). Cognitive Load Theory and Time Considerations: Using the Time-Based Resource Sharing Model. Educational Psychology Review, 30 (3). https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-018-9438-6
title: When investigating presentation-pace effects during learning, take learners' prior knowledge into account
description: This principle follows from the article's experimental findings: the TBRS model assisted investigation of information presentation pace effects during learning only "as long as prior knowledge is taken into account". Researchers and designers studying time-paced instruction should therefore measure or control learners' prior knowledge, since it conditions whether pace effects can be characterized with the model.
requirements: Learners' prior knowledge must be measured or accounted for when studying or designing for presentation-pace effects.
target_learning_goals: optimizing information presentation pace for learning
examples: In the article's two experiments, hypotheses from the TBRS model were tested and the model's usefulness for investigating pace effects was shown conditional on prior knowledge.
key_sources: Sébastien Puma, Nadine Matton, Pierre-Vincent Paubel, André Tricot. (2018). Cognitive Load Theory and Time Considerations: Using the Time-Based Resource Sharing Model. Educational Psychology Review, 30 (3). https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-018-9438-6

article_title: Introducing the FoRe-Squares Model: Focus Support and Reward as Key Predictors of Effective Technology-Augmented Instruction
citation: Eitel, A., Krebs, M.-C., Schöne, C. (2025). Introducing the FoRe-Squares Model: Focus Support and Reward as Key Predictors of Effective Technology-Augmented Instruction. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10045-z
title: The FoRe-Squares model: instruction is effective when it provides both focus support and reward
description: The FoRe-Squares (Focus-Support-Reward-Squares) model is a teaching model, not a learning model, synthesizing cognitive and motivational theory for technology-augmented instruction. It postulates two continuous independent variables — focus support and reward — that drive the mediating variable of active goal-directed processing and thus learning outcomes. As the article states, "the combination of focus support (cognitive factor) and reward (motivational factor) predicts and fosters good learning outcomes." The model takes an augmentation perspective in which technology supports, but cannot replace, human teachers and learners, and aims to serve as "a parsimonious schema to explain many instructional design effects." It draws on situated expectancy-value theory for its reward factor, using the value component to explain what learners may find rewarding.
requirements: Both focus support and reward must be present at least at a medium degree for active goal-directed processing and good learning outcomes
constraints: The model is not a learning model but a teaching model; it specifies causal relations between independent, mediating, and dependent variables rather than replacing existing theories
target_learning_goals: recall and transfer of key terms, principles, and procedures
key_sources: Eitel, A., Krebs, M.-C., Schöne, C. (2025). Introducing the FoRe-Squares Model: Focus Support and Reward as Key Predictors of Effective Technology-Augmented Instruction. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10045-z

article_title: Introducing the FoRe-Squares Model: Focus Support and Reward as Key Predictors of Effective Technology-Augmented Instruction
citation: Eitel, A., Krebs, M.-C., Schöne, C. (2025). Introducing the FoRe-Squares Model: Focus Support and Reward as Key Predictors of Effective Technology-Augmented Instruction. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10045-z
title: Active goal-directed processing as the SOISG mediator of learning outcomes
description: The model's mediating variable, active goal-directed processing, consists of five cognitive processes abbreviated SOISG: selecting, organizing, and integrating (SOI, per cognitive theory of multimedia learning), strengthening (S, via rehearsal and retrieval), and generating (G, inferences mapping to similar and novel situations). The article notes "the more an instruction stimulates SOISG processing (selecting-organizing-integrating-strengthening-generating) in an active and goal-directed manner, the more likely the instruction is to foster learning outcomes." Strengthening is described as especially important for fluent recall, while generating is especially important for transfer. The construct is not directly observable but is indicated by behavioral data such as eye movements, think-aloud protocols, and key presses, enriched with physiological and questionnaire data.
requirements: Measurement via behavioral data best enriched with physiological data such as pupil dilation or EEG, plus questionnaire data on mental effort and mind wandering
constraints: Active goal-directed processing is not directly observable from the outside
target_learning_goals: recall and transfer of instructionally relevant content
key_sources: Eitel, A., Krebs, M.-C., Schöne, C. (2025). Introducing the FoRe-Squares Model: Focus Support and Reward as Key Predictors of Effective Technology-Augmented Instruction. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10045-z

article_title: Teacher Wellbeing: The Importance of Teacher–Student Relationships
citation: Jantine L. Spilt, Helma M. Y. Koomen, & Jochem T. Thijs. (2011). Teacher Wellbeing: The Importance of Teacher–Student Relationships. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-011-9170-y
title: Hypothetical model: mental representations of teacher–student relationships affect teacher wellbeing through everyday emotional responses
description: The review proposes a hypothetical model, depicted in Fig. 1, in which teachers' mental representations of teacher–student relationships affect wellbeing "through their everyday emotional responses." Grounded in Lazarus's Transactional Model of Stress and Coping, it holds that appraisal of stressors triggers discrete emotions whose prolonged experience changes wellbeing. Teachers are postulated to have a basic need for relatedness and to internalize relationship experiences into representational models at global, domain-specific, and relationship-specific levels, which may "mediate or moderate the well-studied effects of perceived student behavior on teacher wellbeing."
requirements: Teachers must have a need or desire for personal relationships with students for relationships to be harmful or beneficial to their wellbeing
constraints: The review states there is virtually no research that has directly tested the propositions of the conceptual model represented in Fig. 1
The model assumes causal effects, but wellbeing in turn most likely influences the ability to form personal relationships with children
target_learners: teachers in preschool, primary, and secondary education
target_learning_goals: teacher wellbeing
stress and burnout prevention
professional development and retention
key_sources: Jantine L. Spilt, Helma M. Y. Koomen, & Jochem T. Thijs. (2011). Teacher Wellbeing: The Importance of Teacher–Student Relationships. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-011-9170-y

article_title: Teacher Wellbeing: The Importance of Teacher–Student Relationships
citation: Jantine L. Spilt, Helma M. Y. Koomen, & Jochem T. Thijs. (2011). Teacher Wellbeing: The Importance of Teacher–Student Relationships. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-011-9170-y
title: Hierarchical structure of teachers' mental relationship representations at global, domain-specific, and relationship-specific levels
description: Drawing on attachment theory, the review proposes that teachers internalize relationship experiences into mental representations at "different levels of generalization": a global interpersonal orientation, domain-specific models of relationships with students containing beliefs about teaching roles and self-efficacy, and relationship-specific models for individual children containing "a teacher's image of the child, a sense of her- or himself in interaction with the child as well as internalized feelings." The relationship-specific models are nested within the domain-specific model, which is nested in the global model, explaining how individual relationships can affect teachers' professional and personal self-esteem.
requirements: Physical proximity between teachers and students is believed to trigger the development of domain-specific and relationship-specific models
constraints: The review states it is aware of no studies that have tested whether teachers construct relationship models at different levels of generalization
target_learners: teachers in preschool through upper elementary education
target_learning_goals: understanding teacher emotional responses to individual students
teacher self-esteem and wellbeing
key_sources: Jantine L. Spilt, Helma M. Y. Koomen, & Jochem T. Thijs. (2011). Teacher Wellbeing: The Importance of Teacher–Student Relationships. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-011-9170-y

article_title: Teacher Wellbeing: The Importance of Teacher–Student Relationships
citation: Jantine L. Spilt, Helma M. Y. Koomen, & Jochem T. Thijs. (2011). Teacher Wellbeing: The Importance of Teacher–Student Relationships. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-011-9170-y
title: Student–Teacher Relationship Scale (STRS) measuring conflict, closeness, and dependency
description: The review describes the Student–Teacher Relationship Scale as a widely used and well-validated teacher-report questionnaire measuring perceptions of conflict, closeness, and sometimes dependency in relationships with specific children from preschool to upper elementary school. Conflict items include "Dealing with this child drains my energy"; closeness items include "My interactions with this child make me feel effective and confident." The review notes teachers' reports of relationship quality are unique predictors of children's school functioning above direct reports of student behavior, supporting their validity, though some researchers have questioned the validity of the dependency subscale.
requirements: Relies on teacher self-report perceptions of the dyadic relationship rather than observed behavior
constraints: Some researchers have questioned the validity of the dependency subscale, arguing it may be a marker of child adjustment problems rather than a relational dimension
target_learners: teachers of children from preschool to upper elementary school
target_learning_goals: measuring teacher-perceived relationship quality with individual students
key_sources: Jantine L. Spilt, Helma M. Y. Koomen, & Jochem T. Thijs. (2011). Teacher Wellbeing: The Importance of Teacher–Student Relationships. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-011-9170-y

article_title: Worth the Effort: the Start and Stick to Desirable Difficulties (S2D2) Framework
citation: Anique B. H. de Bruin, Felicitas Biwer, Luotong Hui, Erdem Onan, Louise David, Wisnu Wiradhany. (2023). Worth the Effort: the Start and Stick to Desirable Difficulties (S2D2) Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09766-w
title: S2D2 framework: supporting self-regulation of effort when engaging in desirable difficulties
description: The S2D2 framework describes how learners can be supported to self-regulate effort when engaging in desirable difficulties, building on the Effort Monitoring and Regulation model. It centers on the interrelations between perceived effort, perceived learning, and use of desirable difficulties, and organizes support into accepting, reducing, or silencing perceived effort. As the authors state, "Here, we present a framework that describes how to support self-regulation of effort when engaging in desirable difficulties: the \"Start and Stick to Desirable Difficulties (S2D2)\" framework." The framework targets self-study contexts with (older) adolescents and adult learners.
requirements: Support depends on addressing perceived effort, perceived learning, and actual learning effects simultaneously
constraints: The framework focuses on learners' self-regulated use of desirable difficulties in the self-study context, not on how teachers directly incorporate desirable difficulties in teaching
target_learners: older adolescents and adult learners in self-study contexts
target_learning_goals: self-regulated use of effective, desirably difficult learning strategies such as retrieval practice and interleaving
examples: The framework organizes interventions at strategy, task, and learner levels into accept, reduce, or silence approaches (Table 1)
key_sources: Anique B. H. de Bruin, Felicitas Biwer, Luotong Hui, Erdem Onan, Louise David, Wisnu Wiradhany. (2023). Worth the Effort: the Start and Stick to Desirable Difficulties (S2D2) Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09766-w

article_title: Worth the Effort: the Start and Stick to Desirable Difficulties (S2D2) Framework
citation: Anique B. H. de Bruin, Felicitas Biwer, Luotong Hui, Erdem Onan, Louise David, Wisnu Wiradhany. (2023). Worth the Effort: the Start and Stick to Desirable Difficulties (S2D2) Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09766-w
title: Effort Monitoring and Regulation (EMR) model: effort as a basis for monitoring and control of learning
description: The EMR model, on which S2D2 builds, describes how cycles of monitoring and regulation of learning characterize learning task engagement, extending the Nelson and Narens metalevel/object-level architecture. Monitoring results are brought to the metalevel, and control is exerted to translate decisions back to the object level. The article states: "The EMR model outlines how effort is used as a basis for monitoring and control of learning, and how effort needs to be managed in self-regulated learning environments." S2D2 focuses on the model's first two research questions, how students monitor and regulate effort.
requirements: Monitoring and regulation cycles in which learners evaluate what happens during the learning task
constraints: S2D2 addresses only the first two EMR research questions (monitoring and regulating effort)
target_learning_goals: accurate monitoring and effective regulation of invested mental effort during learning
examples: Fig. 1 presents the EMR framework integrating cognitive load theory and self-regulated learning theory

title: Provide adequate teacher training on effective learning strategies before student training
description: Because strategy-level training programs depend on teachers or mentors, the article argues that student training on desirable difficulties must be preceded by teacher training. Teachers, like students, hold misbeliefs about effective learning, so programs delivered by untrained teachers risk transmitting those misbeliefs. The article states: "Providing adequate teacher training therefore should precede student training." This principle applies whenever educators deliver instruction about desirably difficult learning strategies.
requirements: Teachers and mentors must endorse the importance of and understand how to teach the use of desirable difficulties
constraints: The article notes teachers suffer from misbeliefs and lack adequate knowledge about effective learning strategy use, citing Morehead et al. (2016) and Surma et al. (2018)
target_learners: teachers and mentors delivering learning strategy training
target_learning_goals: accurate teacher knowledge of effective learning strategies to support student strategy training
examples: The article cites the Study Smart framework (Biwer & de Bruin, 2023) and the KBCP framework (McDaniel & Einstein, 2020) as starting points for such training programs

title: Conduct Indigenous educational research to test the cross-cultural applicability of motivation theories
description: This principle, drawn from McInerney's agenda as described in the tribute, holds that motivation research should include Indigenous educational research so that mainstream theories are examined "to understand the extent to which mainstream motivation theories apply to culturally diverse groups". It directs researchers to subject established motivation theories to cross-cultural testing rather than assuming universality.
requirements: Motivation theories must be tested against data from culturally diverse groups, including Indigenous students, rather than only mainstream samples.
constraints: The tribute presents this as McInerney's belief and research agenda, not as a validated recommendation with evidence in the accessible text.
target_learning_goals: Academic motivation
Achievement motivation
examples: The tribute notes McInerney dedicated a significant part of his career to researching problems associated with studying culture in motivation research.

title: The multilevel latent covariate model as the method of choice for unbiased estimation of class-level climate-outcome relations from student ratings
description: The article recaps Lüdtke et al.'s (2008) multilevel latent covariate model, in which students' ratings of classroom climate are latently aggregated to a latent class mean that is regressed on an outcome at the class level. The model is presented as "the method of choice because it allows researchers to obtain unbiased estimates of the relations between classroom climate and outcome variables even when the ICC(2) values are not very high." It applies to reflective group-level constructs such as student-rated classroom management or teacher support.
requirements: Student ratings of a classroom climate characteristic are aggregated latently on the class level, and the outcome is regressed on the latent class mean at the class level
constraints: The model is most appropriate for reflective class-level constructs, not formative group-level constructs such as the percentage of girls in a class
The procedures in the article target the between slope; they might not provide optimal solutions for other parameters such as the within slope
target_learners: Students in classrooms participating in classroom climate research
target_learning_goals: Estimating relations between classroom climate constructs (e.g., teaching quality, classroom management) and student outcomes such as achievement and motivation
examples: The article illustrates the model with research on classroom management, where students rate whether their teacher does not have to wait a long time for students to quiet down, and with Arens and Morin's (2016) study of teacher support and reading achievement in the German PIRLS 2006 sample

title: Shiny App for finding optimal designs in classroom climate studies
description: An interactive web application the authors created "to help researchers plan classroom climate studies and learn about optimal designs and the impact of the quantities that need to be considered when planning such studies." It has two tabs corresponding to the two scenarios: maximizing power under a fixed budget and minimizing the budget for a given power level. With default values (budget 20,000€, costs 68.20€ and 7.05€, ICC(1)s and slopes .2), it returns 130 classes, 12 students per class, and 98% power in Scenario 1, and 61 classes, 12 students, and a budget of 9,311€ in Scenario 2.
requirements: Users must understand the underlying multilevel latent covariate model and the quantities involved (the two ICC(1)s, the standardized slopes, costs per class and per student)
constraints: The app is based on approximate formulas and the multilevel latent covariate model, so it is intended for reflective class-level construct predictors; the authors recommend avoiding it for formative constructs unless only a small number of students is sampled per class
target_learners: Educational researchers planning classroom climate studies
target_learning_goals: Study planning and power analysis for multilevel latent variable classroom climate studies
examples: The app can be accessed at https://psychtools.shinyapps.io/optimalDesignsClassroomClimate and updates output immediately as input values change

title: Treat optimal designs as locally optimal and apply a rule of thumb when the optimal number of students per class exceeds typical class size
description: The article cautions that "the optimal design is only 'locally optimal,' meaning that it is optimal only for the specific values that the researcher specified for the quantities and can be suboptimal for other values," suggesting maximin designs as a workaround. It also notes that power computations assume unbiased estimation, which holds in large samples but not small ones, and offers a practical rule: "set this number to 25 and then increase the number of classes to compensate for the loss of power" when the optimal students per class exceeds typical class size.
requirements: Planners must specify plausible values for the ICC(1)s and slopes, ideally drawn from previous studies, and consider boundary conditions such as typical class size
constraints: Optimal designs can deviate from what is really optimal when assumed values are wrong or when sample sizes are small (results tend to be biased when sample sizes are small, e.g., below N > 1,000)
target_learners: Educational researchers planning classroom climate studies
target_learning_goals: Designing sufficiently powered, cost-efficient classroom climate studies
examples: The article suggests maximin designs, which maximize the minimum variability across a range of reasonable values for the quantities, as one workaround for the local optimality problem

citation: Lisette Hornstra, Kim Stroet, Christine Rubie-Davies, Annaline Flint. (2023). Teacher Expectations and Self-Determination Theory: Considering Convergence and Divergence of Theories. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09788-4
title: Integrated HET–SDT model with need satisfaction mediating between teaching practices and student outcomes
description: The article proposes an integrative model (Fig. 1) combining high expectation theory and self-determination theory. It maps HET's three principles and SDT's need-supportive teaching dimensions as convergent teaching practices, with teacher beliefs and contextual conditions shaping whether teachers enact them. The model's central mechanism is that "need satisfaction" mediates between teaching practices and student outcomes: practices may be effective "because they help to satisfy students' needs and help stu dents to feel autonomous, competent, and related to others." The mediational pathways are offered as hypotheses for future empirical work.
requirements: Empirical work is needed to test the hypothesized mediational pathways from teaching practices through need satisfaction to student outcomes
constraints: Some relations in the model (dashed arrows) are stated to be beyond the scope of the present paper
target_learners: school students in primary and secondary classrooms
target_learning_goals: motivation
learning
well-being
examples: The model positions mixed ability grouping (HET) as expected to satisfy students' need for competence (SDT), a pathway the authors propose for empirical investigation

title: High expectation theory's three key principles: mixed/flexible grouping, class climate, and goal setting
description: High expectation theory describes three interconnected principles teachers use to communicate high expectations to all students: "mixed ability or flexible grouping (coupled with high-level learning opportunities), class climate, and goal setting." Mixed grouping reduces the salience of ability and provides high-level learning opportunities for all, including high-level questions asked of every student. Class climate involves warm teacher-student relationships, peer support, and collaboration rather than reward for out-performing others. Goal setting gives all students clear learning goals, success criteria, and frequent targeted feedback tied to progress toward those goals.
requirements: Teachers hold beliefs that all students can achieve at high levels given a supportive classroom environment, so expectations are high for all students relative to achievement
constraints: HET does not encompass classroom clarity in the sense of clear rules and expectations as proposed in SDT's notion of structure
target_learners: all students in a classroom, regardless of achievement level
target_learning_goals: academic achievement
student self-beliefs
motivation and engagement
examples: High expectation teachers offer skill-based workshops that students opt into, with workshop membership changing daily so ability is not made salient

citation: Lisette Hornstra, Kim Stroet, Christine Rubie-Davies, Annaline Flint. (2023). Teacher Expectations and Self-Determination Theory: Considering Convergence and Divergence of Theories. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09788-4
title: Need-supportive teaching in SDT: three dimensions (autonomy support, structure, involvement) and their thwarting counterparts
description: Within SDT's Basic Psychological Needs Theory, educational literature identifies "three dimensions of need-supportive teaching" that support students' needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness. Autonomy support includes offering choices, fostering relevance, and cognitive autonomy support via open questions. Structure provides contingent information, guidance, optimal challenge, clear guidelines, and non-comparative feedback. Involvement shows unconditional positive regard and commitment to students' learning. Need support and need thwarting are "two independent dimensions": controlling teaching, chaos, and disaffection actively threaten needs and can cause need frustration and outcomes such as amotivation or dropout.
requirements: Need support should be tailored to the individual student and contingent on students' needs, abilities, and actions, rather than applied as a one-size-fits-all approach
constraints: SDT research has focused mostly on between-teacher differences in need support, with little attention to ability grouping or within-teacher variation
target_learning_goals: intrinsic motivation
engagement
well-being
need satisfaction
examples: In a multiple case study the review cites, socio-constructivist schools provided autonomy support via scaffolding in one-on-one interactions, while a traditional school used open, cognitively engaging questions in whole-class instruction

title: Common acceptability thresholds for psychometric evidence in education research (review Table 1)
description: The review assembles a framework of psychometric indicators and their common acceptability thresholds in educational research, covering content validity, structural validity, internal consistency, reliability, and criterion validity. For example, it lists "RMSEA < .06; CFI > .95; TLI > .95" for confirmatory factor analysis, internal consistency and test–retest/inter-rater correlations at ≥ .70, diagnostic accuracy at "Sensitivity ≥ .90; Specificity ≥ .70", and criterion correlations at ≥ .60. Tools were rated Acceptable, Mixed, or Low against these thresholds.
requirements: Longitudinal data, preferably at least six months between measurements, to produce predictive validity evidence
Gold Standard measurement tools as reference for criterion validity evaluations
constraints: Gold Standard measurement tools are infrequently available in many countries and cultures in mathematical learning and development research, per the review

examples: The review rated each tool's psychometric evidence as Acceptable, Mixed, or Low against these thresholds across five indicators

Task groups span nine spatial factors, with four higher-difficulty factors aimed at adolescents including mental rotation and spatial visualisation. citation: Núñez-Regueiro, F., Marsh, H. title: Contemporaneous-Lagged Reciprocal Effects Model (CL-REM): a timescales continuum refinement of the Reciprocal Effects Model
description: The CL-REM is the article's proposed refinement of the Reciprocal Effects Model, drawing on the timescales continuum framework to formalize how self-concept and skills influence each other at different speeds. It distinguishes three levels: a "Contemporaneous skill development effect (microlevel timescale)", a "Lagged self-enhancement effect (mesolevel timescale)", and covariance of stable traits at the macrolevel estimated through random intercepts. The model predicts that skills modify self-concept quickly (within a semester) while self-concept shapes skills gradually (across semesters), and that detectability depends on aligning measurement intervals with these timescales.
requirements: Mesolevel designs with yearly or multi-month measurement intervals are needed to detect both contemporaneous skill-development effects and lagged self-enhancement effects.
At least three measurement occasions are required to capture the stable trait component via random intercepts with sufficient precision.
constraints: The study only tests the temporal structure posited by the CL-REM; putative mediators are not investigated.
With very short intervals fast effects may appear lagged, and with long intervals slow processes may appear contemporaneous while fast processes become undetectable.
target_learning_goals: academic self-concept in mathematics and French (language arts)
academic skills in mathematics and French
examples: The ProFAN design with 8-month intervals was used to test fast skill-development effects as lag0 effects and slower self-enhancement effects as lag1 effects.

title: Align intervention strategies and model specifications with the timescales of the underlying psychological processes
description: The article argues that because perceived competence and skills influence each other at different speeds, both intervention design and longitudinal modeling must match the timescales of the processes targeted. The abstract states the findings "underscore the importance of aligning intervention strategies and model specifications with the timescales of the underlying psychological processes". Fast skill-to-self-concept effects call for immediate feedback after performance; slow self-concept-to-skill effects call for sustained motivational support across semesters.
requirements: Knowledge of the relevant timescale (fast within-semester vs slow across-semester dynamics) for the targeted process.
Measurement or intervention schedules whose intervals align with the timescale of the process being targeted or modeled.
constraints: Detectability of the effects depends on measurement intervals: very short or very long intervals can distort or obliterate fast or slow processes.
target_learning_goals: academic self-concept
academic skill development
examples: The CL-REM framework links fast skill effects to proximal feedback mechanisms such as teacher praise shortly after a test, and slow self-concept effects to gradual motivational internalization over semesters.

article_title: Cubic Relations of Autonomous and Controlled Motivation to Achievement: A Cross-National Validation of Self-Determination Theory Using Response Surface Analysis
citation: Núñez-Regueiro, F. (2024). Cubic Relations of Autonomous and Controlled Motivation to Achievement: A Cross-National Validation of Self-Determination Theory Using Response Surface Analysis. Educational Psychology Review, 36 (3). https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09905-x
title: Bidimensional (circumplex) approach to SDT's motivational regulations, projecting the six regulation types onto combined autonomous and controlled motivation dimensions
description: The article advances a bidimensional projection of SDT's taxonomy in which the six motivational regulations are expressed as combined levels of autonomous motivation (AM) and controlled motivation (CM). It argues that "autonomous and controlled motivations may co-exist or exist independently from one another", so students may feel both, only one, or neither (non-regulation/amotivation). This circumplex approach integrates internal, external, introjected, identified, integrated regulation and non-regulation in one two-dimensional spectrum used to model achievement via cubic response surfaces.
requirements: Measures of autonomous and controlled motivation must be commensurate (standardized) so parametric constraints defining polynomial families are structurally valid.
constraints: The unidimensional simplex approach is reported not to fit data for specific disciplines and to contradict findings that AM and CM indicators correlate positively or non-significantly.
target_learning_goals: Mathematics achievement
Motivational regulation in school learning
examples: The study operationalizes AM via the Students Like Learning Mathematics scale and CM via the Students Value Mathematics scale in TIMSS 2019, then relates the two dimensions to achievement with cubic polynomial regression.

article_title: Peer Victimization: an Integrative Review and Cross-National Test of a Tripartite Model
citation: Herbert W. Marsh, Jiesi Guo, Philip D. Parker, Reinhard Pekrun, Geetanjali Basarkod, Theresa Dicke, et al. (2023). Peer Victimization: an Integrative Review and Cross-National Test of a Tripartite Model. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09765-x
title: Tripartite model of victimization: relational, verbal, and physical components as distinct constructs
description: The tripartite model holds that peer victimization comprises three distinguishable components — relational, verbal, and physical — that relate differently to antecedents and outcomes such as gender, well-being, and anti-bullying attitudes. The article argues support for unidimensional models stems from poor measurement and inappropriate theoretical models, noting that "Marsh et al. (2011, 2022; also see Bear et al., 2014) argue for a tripartite model that distinguishes between physical, relational, and verbal components." The model is positioned against bivariate (overt vs. relational) accounts that combine verbal with physical victimization, and against global scores such as the PISA three-item composite. Cyberbullying is treated within this framework as a manifestation of relational bullying rather than a fourth component, since it "largely parallels and strongly correlates with relational bullying".
requirements: Appropriate measurement tools that yield well-differentiated, not overly highly correlated, components with discriminant validity
Statistical tools such as ESEM that allow cross-loadings rather than traditional CFA
constraints: Support for the model in victimization research has been limited because most studies use global or two-component measures
target_learners: adolescents in primary, middle, and high school
target_learning_goals: understanding and reducing peer victimization and bullying
protecting student well-being and mental health
shaping anti-bullying attitudes
examples: PISA2018 six victimization items mapped onto relational, verbal, and physical components and tested against five competing structural models
key_sources: Herbert W. Marsh, Jiesi Guo, Philip D. Parker, Reinhard Pekrun, Geetanjali Basarkod, Theresa Dicke, et al. (2023). Peer Victimization: an Integrative Review and Cross-National Test of a Tripartite Model. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09765-x

article_title: Peer Victimization: an Integrative Review and Cross-National Test of a Tripartite Model
citation: Herbert W. Marsh, Jiesi Guo, Philip D. Parker, Reinhard Pekrun, Geetanjali Basarkod, Theresa Dicke, et al. (2023). Peer Victimization: an Integrative Review and Cross-National Test of a Tripartite Model. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09765-x
title: Interventions and anti-bullying policies should address relational and verbal victimization, not only physical victimization
description: Because relational and verbal victimization are more strongly and negatively related to well-being and mental health than physical victimization, interventions and policies focused mainly on physical victimization miss the most harmful forms. The article observes that "physical victimization is the focus of many interventions and anti-bullying policies" even though "relational victimization is more detrimental to well-being and mental health than is physical victimization." Designing multifaceted interventions that address the different components follows from the tripartite model's discriminant validity.
requirements: Measurement and monitoring that distinguish the three victimization components rather than relying on global scores
constraints: The article notes previous intervention research has produced weak effects overall, so component-targeting alone does not guarantee effectiveness
target_learning_goals: reducing peer victimization
supporting student well-being and mental health
examples: The article recommends simultaneous evaluation of multiple parallel components of victimization and bullying and capitalizing on anti-bullying attitudes in future research and intervention design

article_title: The Role of Mental Effort in Fostering Self-Regulated Learning with Problem-Solving Tasks
citation: Tamara van Gog & Vincent Hoogerheide & Milou van Harsel. (2020). The Role of Mental Effort in Fostering Self-Regulated Learning with Problem-Solving Tasks. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09544-y
title: Cue-utilization framework: monitoring judgments rest on cues whose diagnosticity determines accuracy, with invested mental effort as a candidate cue
description: The cue-utilization framework (Koriat 1997), as applied in this review, holds that learners base monitoring judgments on sources of information (cues) arising from the study material and their studying experience, and that judgment accuracy depends on how predictive those cues are of actual test performance. The review uses it to explain why generative activities improve monitoring: they give learners access to cues about their understanding. It further develops an effort-as-cue account, noting that "Several studies have found students'effort ratings to correlate negatively with their monitoring judgments", while cautioning that effort is informative only when it reflects mental-model quality rather than extraneous processing or instructional support.
requirements: Effort ratings must be interpretable relative to the quality of the associated performance, and activity design must tie effort cues to mental-model quality rather than extraneous factors
constraints: Evidence that students use effort as a cue is correlational; effort ratings can be influenced by feedback valence and reporting timing, and students likely cannot distinguish the origin of invested effort
target_learners: higher education students learning problem-solving tasks
target_learning_goals: accurate self-monitoring of problem-solving performance
adaptive task selection in self-regulated learning
examples: The review interprets Baars et al. (2013): completion-condition students reported more effort and negatively correlated effort with judgments of learning, possibly using high effort as a cue for poor understanding
key_sources: Tamara van Gog & Vincent Hoogerheide & Milou van Harsel. (2020). The Role of Mental Effort in Fostering Self-Regulated Learning with Problem-Solving Tasks. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09544-y

article_title: The Role of Mental Effort in Fostering Self-Regulated Learning with Problem-Solving Tasks
citation: Tamara van Gog & Vincent Hoogerheide & Milou van Harsel. (2020). The Role of Mental Effort in Fostering Self-Regulated Learning with Problem-Solving Tasks. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09544-y
title: Teach students a simple task selection rule that combines self-assessed performance and invested mental effort when choosing the next problem-solving task
description: This principle holds that self-regulated learning with problem-solving tasks improves when students are explicitly taught, via video modeling examples, to select their next task by combining their self-assessed performance and self-reported invested mental effort on the prior task. The review concludes that "teaching students a relatively simple task selection rule based on a combination of their self-assessed performance and invested mental effort improves their self-regulated learning outcomes", a replicated finding rare among monitoring interventions. The rule must stay simple enough for students to understand, remember, and apply during self-study.
requirements: Video modeling examples demonstrating the full performance-assessment-selection cycle, and a task database ordered from simple to complex with support faded within complexity levels
constraints: Training did not transfer to a different problem domain (math posttest performance was not improved); any algorithm must be much simpler than adaptive-system algorithms, and effort ratings affected by extraneous variables will limit effectiveness
target_learners: secondary education students learning biology problem solving
target_learning_goals: accurate self-assessment
adaptive task selection
improved posttest performance on problem-solving tasks
examples: Kostons et al. (2012) and Raaijmakers et al. (2018b) trained students with video models using a selection table advising, e.g., high performance with low effort: select a task with much less support or more complexity
key_sources: Tamara van Gog & Vincent Hoogerheide & Milou van Harsel. (2020). The Role of Mental Effort in Fostering Self-Regulated Learning with Problem-Solving Tasks. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09544-y

article_title: Learning Mechanisms Explaining Learning With Digital Tools in Educational Settings: a Cognitive Process Framework
citation: Frank Reinhold, Timo Leuders, Katharina Loibl, Matthias Nückles, Maik Beege, Jan M. Boelmann (2024). Learning Mechanisms Explaining Learning With Digital Tools in Educational Settings: a Cognitive Process Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09845-6
title: CoDiL framework: a cognitive process framework on the learning mechanisms of digital tools in educational settings
description: CoDiL is a high-level conceptual integration of the KLI framework, the SOI model, and the ULO framework explaining how learning with digital tools succeeds. It distinguishes external instructional events and student-tool interactions from internal cognitive processes and knowledge components. Instructional features offer learning opportunities that, if utilized, trigger learning activities which—mediated by selecting, organizing, and integrating and in interaction with prior knowledge—lead to knowledge gains. The authors state it "can be used to theoretically ground, firstly, the design of digital tools for learning, and secondly, the empirical analysis of students' learning activities in digitally enriched educational settings via the analysis of specific student-tool interactions."
requirements: The framework's degrees of freedom must be specified for the concrete educational scenario of interest, since it is a high-level conceptual integration requiring more detailed empirical integration into specific studies
constraints: The authors state the current framework represents a high-level conceptual integration of KLI, SOI, and ULO, providing a basic starting point but requiring further empirical integration
target_learners: students in digitally enriched educational settings across subject domains
target_learning_goals: subject-matter knowledge acquisition with digital tools
examples: The authors frame Koedinger et al. (2010) formative assessment study and Lalley et al. (2010) virtual frog dissection study through the framework
key_sources: Frank Reinhold, Timo Leuders, Katharina Loibl, Matthias Nückles, Maik Beege, Jan M. Boelmann (2024). Learning Mechanisms Explaining Learning With Digital Tools in Educational Settings: a Cognitive Process Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09845-6

article_title: Learning Mechanisms Explaining Learning With Digital Tools in Educational Settings: a Cognitive Process Framework
citation: Frank Reinhold, Timo Leuders, Katharina Loibl, Matthias Nückles, Maik Beege, Jan M. Boelmann (2024). Learning Mechanisms Explaining Learning With Digital Tools in Educational Settings: a Cognitive Process Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09845-6
title: Taxonomy of learning activities relevant for digitally enriched educational settings
description: The CoDiL framework enumerates learning activities that digital instructional features may initiate and stimulate, each with an external behavioral side (observable student-tool interactions) and an internal cognitive side. The article lists abstraction, conducting experiments, creating examples, exploration, formulating hypothesis, refinement, revision, and self-explanation, each defined with cited literature. These activities function as a link between external behavior and internal cognitive processes and are understood as theoretical predictors of learning outcomes. The authors state that "students' engagement in these learning activities as necessity for successful learning—in line with the ULO framework and generative learning theory."
requirements: Content-specific analysis of knowledge components as a fundamental basis for understanding which learning activities are at play
constraints: The article notes such content-specific learning activities are often not specified in detail in educational research, especially research on learning with digital tools
target_learners: students learning with digital tools in educational settings
target_learning_goals: engagement in generative learning activities leading to knowledge component acquisition
examples: The framework's discussion section centers the model on learning activities shown relevant to digital learning, e.g., abstraction, conducting experiments, creating examples, exploration, formulating hypothesis, refinement, revision, self-explanation
key_sources: Frank Reinhold, Timo Leuders, Katharina Loibl, Matthias Nückles, Maik Beege, Jan M. Boelmann (2024). Learning Mechanisms Explaining Learning With Digital Tools in Educational Settings: a Cognitive Process Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09845-6

article_title: Learning Mechanisms Explaining Learning With Digital Tools in Educational Settings: a Cognitive Process Framework
citation: Frank Reinhold, Timo Leuders, Katharina Loibl, Matthias Nückles, Maik Beege, Jan M. Boelmann (2024). Learning Mechanisms Explaining Learning With Digital Tools in Educational Settings: a Cognitive Process Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09845-6
title: Digitally enriched instructional features as affordance-and-constraint learning opportunities
description: The framework conceptualizes instructional features as digitally enriched instructional events that have the potential to stimulate learning activities, are subject of affordances and constraints, and should be designed to lower extraneous load and increase generative processing. The article argues, in line with the media debate, that it is not the digital tool itself but the implemented features that initiate learning. It enumerates essential features: adaptive feedback, opportunities to try and fail (PS-I), prompting, prompting to summarize and explain, and contrasting cases, each mapped to the learning activities it may stimulate.
requirements: Features should be designed to foster learning activities, i.e., to lower extraneous load and increase generative processing compared to non-digitally enriched settings
constraints: Some of these instructional features can be included in classical non-digital classroom instruction as well; digital implementation is described as potentially particularly promising, not uniquely effective
target_learners: students in digitally enriched educational settings
target_learning_goals: stimulation of content-specific generative learning activities
examples: Adaptive feedback may stimulate refinement and revision activities by revealing the limits of students' prior knowledge; contrasting cases may stimulate revision by comparing examples
key_sources: Frank Reinhold, Timo Leuders, Katharina Loibl, Matthias Nückles, Maik Beege, Jan M. Boelmann (2024). Learning Mechanisms Explaining Learning With Digital Tools in Educational Settings: a Cognitive Process Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09845-6

article_title: Learning Mechanisms Explaining Learning With Digital Tools in Educational Settings: a Cognitive Process Framework
citation: Frank Reinhold, Timo Leuders, Katharina Loibl, Matthias Nückles, Maik Beege, Jan M. Boelmann (2024). Learning Mechanisms Explaining Learning With Digital Tools in Educational Settings: a Cognitive Process Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09845-6
title: Design digital tools by starting from content-specific knowledge components and learning activities, not by picking a tool first
description: The article recommends that research on digitally enriched learning start with analyses of the to-be-learned content, the necessary knowledge elements, and the required learning activities, rather than selecting a digital tool first. Knowledge about content-specific learner models should be used to design instructional features well-suited to stimulate the relevant generative cognitive processes. The authors state they "consider it necessary for researchers to engage in the development (or selection) of digital prototype tools that are explicitly designed to align with the learning mechanisms assumed."
requirements: Detailed specification of the content-specific knowledge components students need to acquire, and of the learning activities leading to their acquisition
constraints: The article notes this design endeavor may be demanding as it can vary between domains, content, and learning goals
target_learners: students in digitally enriched educational settings across domains
target_learning_goals: acquisition of specified content-specific knowledge components
examples: For a fraction-arithmetic online math tutor, adaptive feedback and adaptive increase in task difficulty were suggested; for physics, a simulation enabling the control of variables strategy

article_title: Learning Mechanisms Explaining Learning With Digital Tools in Educational Settings: a Cognitive Process Framework
citation: Frank Reinhold, Timo Leuders, Katharina Loibl, Matthias Nückles, Maik Beege, Jan M. Boelmann (2024). Learning Mechanisms Explaining Learning With Digital Tools in Educational Settings: a Cognitive Process Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09845-6
title: Measure utilization of instructional features via process data rather than only comparing learning outcomes
description: The article argues that research focusing only on the direct path—the effect of digital tools on outcomes versus another scenario—allows only limited interpretation. Instead, students' interaction with implemented instructional features (the external behavioral side of learning activities) should be treated as a theoretical and empirical mediator of achievement. The framework treats "process data" as an umbrella term encompassing tool-logged interactions and other process indicators obtained from accompanying assessments during learning.
requirements: A solid theoretical foundation and appropriate indicators inside the process data files to allow differentiated statements about the effects of implemented instructional features
constraints: The article notes the link between behavior and cognition must be established validly; unobtrusive capture of student-tool interactions is named as ongoing future work
target_learners: students in digitally enriched educational settings
target_learning_goals: valid inference about cognitive learning activities from behavioral data
examples: Koedinger et al. (2010) assessed engagement in learning activities by labeling students low or high usage based on items completed in the tool

article_title: Does Retrieval Demand Moderate the Effectiveness of Covert Retrieval Practice? Comparing Covert and Overt Retrieval Practice for Learning Key Terms and Definitions
citation: Michelle L. Rivers, Paige E. Northern, Sarah K. Tauber. (2025). Does Retrieval Demand Moderate the Effectiveness of Covert Retrieval Practice? Comparing Covert and Overt Retrieval Practice for Learning Key Terms and Definitions. Educational Psychology Review (2025) 37:61. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10040-4
title: Retrieval dynamics hypothesis
description: The retrieval dynamics hypothesis explains when overt and covert retrieval practice differ in effectiveness. It posits that retrieving a single unit of information is relatively automatic and easy, whereas retrieving multiple interconnected units (e.g., definitions) is more demanding and, when done covertly, may terminate prematurely or be non-exhaustive. The article states that "retrieving multiple interconnected units of information (e.g., definitions, especially for novice learners) imposes higher retrieval demands, making overt retrieval more effective because it promotes exhaustive recall and self-monitoring during the process." The two experiments tested and found partial support for its predictions.
requirements: Material whose retrieval demand can be characterized along a low-to-high continuum (the article operationalizes demand as the type of to-be-retrieved material)
constraints: The article found only partial support: the overt advantage did not significantly differ by number of idea units, and the authors call the idea-unit operationalization of retrieval demand overly simplistic.
target_learners: undergraduate students learning declarative concepts (key terms and definitions)
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of key terms and definitions of declarative concepts
key_sources: Michelle L. Rivers, Paige E. Northern, Sarah K. Tauber. (2025). Does Retrieval Demand Moderate the Effectiveness of Covert Retrieval Practice?
