article_title: Does Retrieval Demand Moderate the Effectiveness of Covert Retrieval Practice? Comparing Covert and Overt Retrieval Practice for Learning Key Terms and Definitions
citation: Michelle L. Rivers, Paige E. Northern, Sarah K. Tauber. (2025). Does Retrieval Demand Moderate the Effectiveness of Covert Retrieval Practice? Comparing Covert and Overt Retrieval Practice for Learning Key Terms and Definitions. Educational Psychology Review (2025) 37:61. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10040-4
title: Students should prioritize overt retrieval when mastering complex information such as definitions
description: This principle follows from the article's recommendation that learners who want to maximize performance use overt retrieval (typing or writing responses) rather than covert retrieval for demanding material. The article states: "Until then, we recommend students prioritize overt retrieval when mastering complex information." Overt retrieval consistently produced the best criterion-test performance across both experiments, though it costs more practice time than covert retrieval.
requirements: Learners must be able to produce written or oral responses during practice (e.g., typing into a text field) and receive feedback
constraints: Overt retrieval takes longer per item than covert retrieval; if the objective is efficiency rather than maximum performance, covert retrieval may be preferable.
target_learners: students studying declarative concepts and definitions
target_learning_goals: maximizing delayed recall of complex material such as definitions
examples: In both experiments, undergraduates practiced key-term definitions by typing responses (overt), silently retrieving (covert), or restudying, with a criterion test two days later.

article_title: When Does Learning by Non-interactive Teaching Work? A Large-Scale Analysis of Learner Characteristics in a Classroom Setting
citation: Lachner, A., Russ, H., Hübner, N., Sibley, L., & Scheiter, K. (2025). When Does Learning by Non-interactive Teaching Work? A Large-Scale Analysis of Learner Characteristics in a Classroom Setting. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10060-0
title: Aptitude-treatment interaction framework applied to non-interactive teaching via a competence-oriented approach
description: The article organizes its moderation analysis around the aptitude-treatment interaction (ATI) paradigm, which "states that the effectiveness of an intervention can be conceptualized as a result of the complex interplay between the distinct features of the intervention and students' ability and willingness to utilize them". It extends this with a competence-oriented approach following Weinert, treating (meta-)cognitive and motivational dispositions as competence and demographic background and personality traits as precursors, testing nine learner characteristics simultaneously in a multilevel IPD framework.
requirements: Well-powered samples, since ATI effects are subtle and prior small-sample studies produced inconsistent findings
constraints: Prior ATI evidence in non-interactive teaching was inconsistent, with non-significant or even reversed findings across studies
target_learners: secondary physics students in grades 7 and 8
target_learning_goals: scientific understanding of optics (converging lens image formation)
metacognitive monitoring accuracy
examples: The study tested prior knowledge, academic self-concept, interest in physics, interest in technology, conscientiousness, gender, mother tongue, and socio-economic status simultaneously as moderators.
key_sources: Lachner, A., Russ, H., Hübner, N., Sibley, L., & Scheiter, K. (2025). When Does Learning by Non-interactive Teaching Work? A Large-Scale Analysis of Learner Characteristics in a Classroom Setting. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10060-0

article_title: When Does Learning by Non-interactive Teaching Work? A Large-Scale Analysis of Learner Characteristics in a Classroom Setting
citation: Lachner, A., Russ, H., Hübner, N., Sibley, L., & Scheiter, K. (2025). When Does Learning by Non-interactive Teaching Work? A Large-Scale Analysis of Learner Characteristics in a Classroom Setting. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10060-0
title: GRAIL combined dataset of three classroom experiments on non-interactive teaching in optics
description: The GRAIL (generative tasks and retrieval practice in inquiry learning) combined dataset comprises three analogous classroom experiments with German secondary physics students in seventh and eighth grade from k = 11 schools, embedded in a curricular teaching unit on the converging lens. After the unit, students were randomly assigned to restudy or to record a voice message explaining the content to a fictitious peer, Mia, via a mock-up messenger on a tablet, with time-on-task held constant at 15 minutes. The final analyzed sample was N = 1074 after exclusions.
requirements: Random assignment after a common teaching unit with time-on-task kept constant across conditions
constraints: The analyzed sample was fixed due to the secondary data analysis approach; Monte Carlo simulation indicated power of .81 to detect interaction effects of d = 0.14
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of image formation with converging lenses
examples: In Study 1 (N = 590) students were assigned to restudy, teaching-only, teaching with a pre-provided visualization, or teaching with drawing; Study 2 (N = 317) crossed learning activity with timing; Study 3 (N = 344) crossed generation with retrieval.

article_title: A Framework for Motivating Teacher-Student Relationships
citation: Robinson, C. D. (2022). A Framework for Motivating Teacher-Student Relationships. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09706-0
title: The Motivating Teacher-Student Relationships framework: three motivational beliefs drive teachers' relationship-building behaviors
description: The Motivating TSRs framework is an explanatory model integrating multiple motivation theories to explain why some teachers invest more in building relationships with students. It hypothesizes that teachers' beliefs about roles, values, and self-efficacy determine whether they "direct (and sustain) energy and effort toward building relationships with their students," which in turn shapes TSR quality. The beliefs are interdependent, reciprocal with experiences, and underpinned by sociocultural contexts. The article states it "does not elevate one theory of motivation over another" but integrates aspects of each.
requirements: Teachers must attend to all three beliefs with high salience and a favorable overall valence for relationship-building behaviors to occur at a given moment
constraints: The framework addresses teachers' motivations only; students' motivational beliefs about TSRs are explicitly outside the article's scope
The association between beliefs and TSR quality is hypothesized, not experimentally tested in this article
target_learning_goals: Building positive teacher-student relationships that support student achievement and engagement
examples: Figure 1 presents the hypothesized pathway from motivational beliefs through relationship-building behaviors to TSR quality, with sociocultural contexts as the foundation
key_sources: Robinson, C. D. (2022). A Framework for Motivating Teacher-Student Relationships. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09706-0

article_title: A Framework for Motivating Teacher-Student Relationships
citation: Robinson, C. D. (2022). A Framework for Motivating Teacher-Student Relationships. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09706-0
title: Design TSR interventions to target teachers' motivational beliefs, not just behaviors
description: The article recommends that interventions to improve teacher-student relationships be grounded in the Motivating TSRs framework by addressing teachers' role beliefs, values, and relational self-efficacy rather than only delivering relationship-building techniques. It hypothesizes that past interventions had "mixed success in improving TSRs" partly because they "do not adequately address teachers' underlying beliefs about TSRs." Interventions aligned with teachers' ideal roles and values should be more successful at changing behavior.
requirements: Intervention designers must diagnose which of the three beliefs (role, value, self-efficacy) is limiting a teacher's motivation
Belief-targeting components should draw on the four sources of self-efficacy, such as mastery and vicarious experiences
constraints: The evidence base for TSR interventions is small and correlational research cannot confirm that improving TSRs causes improved outcomes
target_learners: Teacher educators and professional development designers
target_learning_goals: Improving the quality of teacher-student relationships
Sustaining teachers' motivation to invest in relationship-building
examples: The article proposes that interventions leveraging mastery experiences, vicarious models, verbal persuasion, and positive affective states could raise teachers' relational self-efficacy and thereby their relationship-building efforts

article_title: The Effectiveness of Concept Maps on Students’ Achievement in Science: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Dimitris Anastasiou · Clare Nangsin Wirngo · Pantelis Bagos. (2024). The Effectiveness of Concept Maps on Students' Achievement in Science: A Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09877-y
title: Three-theory account of concept-mapping effectiveness: Ausubel's subsumption theory, Paivio's dual coding theory, and cognitive load theory
description: The article organizes explanations of concept-mapping effects around three theories. Ausubel's subsumption theory holds that learning is facilitated when knowledge is "meaningfully acquired and hierarchically organized", matching concept maps' hierarchical structure. Dual coding theory proposes that information encoded in both verbal and visual modalities "can be more efficiently integrated and retained". Cognitive load theory holds that concept maps reduce extraneous cognitive load by visually simplifying verbal information and providing a higher degree of organization that helps students structure material into schemas.
requirements: Concept maps must connect concepts with linking words or short prepositional phrases and typically use a hierarchical structure with general concepts at the top or center
constraints: The article presents these as potential mechanisms of action explaining the observed effects, not as directly tested within the meta-analysis
target_learners: Elementary, intermediate, and secondary education students (Grades 3–12) learning science
target_learning_goals: Science achievement, including vocabulary development, understanding, and reading comprehension of scientific texts
examples: The article explains the larger physics effect by noting concept maps can help students bridge the gap between abstract theories and physical phenomena

article_title: Facilitating Flexible Problem Solving: A Cognitive Load Perspective
citation: Slava Kalyuga, Alexander Renkl, Fred Paas. (2010). Facilitating Flexible Problem Solving: A Cognitive Load Perspective. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9132-9
title: Generalized knowledge structures of medium generality as a sensible compromise between generality and power for flexible expertise
description: The paper argues that knowledge structures neither narrowly task-specific nor fully general occupy a medium level of generality and are essential for flexible expertise. Such structures, like the FPS schema, act as deep explanatory principles that transfer across task classes. The authors state that knowledge structures of medium generality are important for flexible expertise as a "sensible compromise between generality and power" and allow adapting not-yet-fully-developed expertise to new demands.
requirements: Domain-specific knowledge base within which the generalized structures are developed; generalized structures are applicable within relevant domains only
constraints: Classical CLT formulations considering only routine low-level domain-specific knowledge are described as unnecessarily limited
target_learners: advanced learners in specific subject domains
target_learning_goals: flexible problem solving and transfer to novel situations within a domain
examples: The Function-Process-Structure schema in technical domains is given as an example of a medium-generality generalized knowledge structure
key_sources: Slava Kalyuga, Alexander Renkl, Fred Paas. (2010). Facilitating Flexible Problem Solving: A Cognitive Load Perspective. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9132-9

article_title: Facilitating Flexible Problem Solving: A Cognitive Load Perspective
citation: Slava Kalyuga, Alexander Renkl, Fred Paas. (2010). Facilitating Flexible Problem Solving: A Cognitive Load Perspective. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9132-9
title: Function-Process-Structure (FPS) schema as a generalized framework for technical domains
description: The FPS schema is a triarchic generalized schema for technical knowledge: a technical object is characterized by its functions (what it is for), the natural processes utilized in its operation (how it operates), and its internal structure (what it consists of). Understanding means establishing mental connections between these components, each describable at multiple levels of generality. The paper states the framework "provides a generalized schema that can be used as a deep explanatory principle that may allow effective reasoning about complex systems" and captures expert-novice differences, with novices focusing on perceptually available structural components while experts organize knowledge around processes and functions.
requirements: Learners must establish mental connections between the function, process, and structure components; basic concepts and routine procedures need to be well automated to release cognitive resources
constraints: Developed for technical domains; related but distinct approaches such as the structure-behaviour-function framework exist
target_learners: novices learning about technical devices and systems
target_learning_goals: deep understanding of complex technical systems and flexible reasoning about them
examples: The paper illustrates levels of generality with an air-conditioning system whose function can be described from lowering room temperature down to refrigerant phase transformation
key_sources: Slava Kalyuga, Alexander Renkl, Fred Paas. (2010). Facilitating Flexible Problem Solving: A Cognitive Load Perspective. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9132-9

article_title: The Associations Between Discrete Emotions and Political Learning: A Cross-Disciplinary Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
citation: Elisabeth Graf, Johanna L. Donath, Elouise Botes, Martin Voracek, Thomas Goetz. (2024). The Associations Between Discrete Emotions and Political Learning: A Cross-Disciplinary Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09893-y
title: Control-value theory four-category framework (activation × valence) applied to political learning
description: The article applies the control-value theory of achievement emotions (Pekrun, 2006) to political learning by sorting discrete emotions into four categories: "(1) positive-activating, (2) positive-deactivating, (3) negative-activating, and (4) negative-deactivating emotions". The theory proposes that positive-activating emotions foster learning while negative-deactivating emotions hinder it, with variable expectations for the other two categories. Using this framework let the authors "combine multiple discrete emotions to these categories with uniform expectations regarding their associations with learning" and derive Hypotheses 1 and 2 for the meta-analysis.
requirements: Emotions must be classifiable along the activation and valence dimensions, and discrete emotion measures must be available or categorizable into one of the four emotion groups
constraints: The article notes consequences for learning are not clear for positive-deactivating and negative-activating emotions, as they "often depend on the specific emotion or learning aspect considered"; the framework was developed for achievement settings and applied to politics as a novel context
target_learners: adults and university students in political learning contexts
target_learning_goals: political knowledge and knowledge gain
attention to politics
political information seeking
political discussions
examples: The meta-analysis tested Hypothesis 1 on positive-activating emotions and Hypothesis 2 on negative-deactivating emotions, and explored negative-activating emotions (anxiety, anger) separately by design type

The Associations Between Discrete Emotions and Political Learning: A Cross-Disciplinary Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09893-y

article_title: Intervention Programs Targeting the Mental Health, Professional Burnout, and/or Wellbeing of School Teachers: Systematic Review and Meta-Analyses
citation: Joanne R. Beames, Samantha Spanos, Anna Roberts, Lauren McGillivray, Sophie Li, Jill M. Newby, Bridianne O'Dea, Aliza Werner-Seidler. (2023). Intervention Programs Targeting the Mental Health, Professional Burnout, and/or Wellbeing of School Teachers: Systematic Review and Meta-Analyses. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09720-w
title: Design future teacher mental health program research with methodologically rigorous designs, co-design with teachers, and attention to implementation factors
description: The review's stated research priorities are "using methodologically rigorous designs, developing programs for teachers with teachers (i.e. co-design), and considering implementation factors to ensure feasibility, acceptability, and uptake." The authors also call for increased consistency in measurement using standardised, teacher-validated measures, more comprehensive follow-up evaluation, and measurement of program fidelity and adherence, which they argue must be a priority in future research.
requirements: Studies should use standardised measures with sound psychometric properties that are validated with teachers and the school context.
constraints: The review found an inadequate number of comparisons to perform sub-group analyses, meta-regression, or publication bias analyses.
target_learning_goals: Mental health
Professional burnout reduction
Wellbeing
examples: The review measured risk of bias with ROB-II for RCTs and ROBINS-I for nRCTs and found quality generally poor, particularly in non-randomised trials.

article_title: Short-Term Exposure to Nature and Benefits for Students’ Cognitive Performance: a Review
citation: Lucia Mason, Angelica Ronconi, Sara Scrimin, Francesca Pazzaglia. (2022). Short-Term Exposure to Nature and Benefits for Students' Cognitive Performance: a Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09631-8
title: Attention Restoration Theory: nature restores directed attention through soft fascination
description: Attention restoration theory (ART; Kaplan, 1995) explains the salutary effects of nature on cognitive functioning. It distinguishes involuntary attention, which is automatic and requires no mental resources, from voluntary or directed attention, which is effortful, goal-directed, and susceptible to fatigue. Restorative environments generate "soft fascination" as they gently attract involuntary attention without overwhelming the attentional system, allowing directed attention to rest and recover. The review uses ART as the main framework for interpreting cognitive benefits of green exposure.
requirements: Exposure to a natural environment rich in stimuli that softly capture involuntary attention, minimizing the need for voluntary attention
constraints: Urban environments have only poor restorative power because their bottom-up stimuli require directed attention to be overcome
target_learners: students at all educational levels, from elementary school to university
target_learning_goals: restoration of directed attention supporting executive functioning and self-regulation
key_sources: Lucia Mason, Angelica Ronconi, Sara Scrimin, Francesca Pazzaglia. (2022). Short-Term Exposure to Nature and Benefits for Students' Cognitive Performance: a Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09631-8

article_title: Short-Term Exposure to Nature and Benefits for Students’ Cognitive Performance: a Review
citation: Lucia Mason, Angelica Ronconi, Sara Scrimin, Francesca Pazzaglia. (2022). Short-Term Exposure to Nature and Benefits for Students' Cognitive Performance: a Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09631-8
title: Stress Reduction Theory: nature sustains physiological stress recovery
description: Stress reduction theory (SRT; Ulrich, 1981; Ulrich et al., 1991) explains the salutary effects of nature on emotional functioning. According to SRT, exposure to nature sustains stress recovery as physiological parameters indicate, for example, reduction in blood pressure and stress hormone. Natural environments have restorative power because of the role they played during human evolution, activating the parasympathetic nervous system and reducing physiological arousal. The review pairs SRT with ART, noting the two theories are not incompatible: mental fatigue drives restoration for ART, physiological stress for SRT.
requirements: Contact with a natural environment after a stress-inducing or arousal-raising situation
constraints: SRT addresses emotional and physiological restoration, whereas ART addresses cognitive restoration of directed attention
target_learning_goals: stress recovery and wellbeing supporting cognitive functioning
key_sources: Lucia Mason, Angelica Ronconi, Sara Scrimin, Francesca Pazzaglia. (2022). Short-Term Exposure to Nature and Benefits for Students' Cognitive Performance: a Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09631-8

article_title: Why Do Learners (Under)Utilize Interleaving in Learning Confusable Categories? The Role of Metastrategic Knowledge and Utility Value of Distinguishing
citation: Roman Abel, Anique de Bruin, Erdem Onan, Julian Roelle. (2024). Why Do Learners (Under)Utilize Interleaving in Learning Confusable Categories? The Role of Metastrategic Knowledge and Utility Value of Distinguishing. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09902-0
title: Conditional-knowledge framework of learners' (under)utilization of interleaving in confusable category learning
description: The article models learners' spontaneous interleaving as depending on conditional (if–then) links among motivational and metacognitive processes. Learners first need "awareness-that-differences-matter": "learners need to be aware that detecting differences is essential for being able to distinguish confusable categories". Second, they need "awareness-that-interleaving-highlights-differences": awareness "that interleaving is supportive in detecting subtle differences between confusable categories". A motivational gap — low utility value of distinguishing — can break the first link, so that even aware learners do not invest effort in finding differences.
requirements: Learners must hold both conditional knowledge components — that differences matter for distinguishing and that interleaving highlights differences — for the if–then links to translate into spontaneous interleaving use.
constraints: The framework is stated for adult learners with advanced learning skills such as university students, for whom a mediation deficiency (not knowing how to execute interleaving) appears unlikely.
target_learning_goals: distinguishing easily confusable categories by detecting their predictive differences
examples: Experiment 1 factorially varied utility value of distinguishing (poisonous/edible vs. soil labels) and the differences-matter instruction; Experiment 2 additionally varied the instruction that interleaving highlights differences.
key_sources: Roman Abel, Anique de Bruin, Erdem Onan, Julian Roelle. (2024). Why Do Learners (Under)Utilize Interleaving in Learning Confusable Categories? The Role of Metastrategic Knowledge and Utility Value of Distinguishing. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09902-0

article_title: Community and Participatory Evidence and Research Synthesis: Enhancing Alignment and Usability of Research Synthesis Methods
citation: Jason C. Chow · Ruben G. Martinez. (2026). Community and Participatory Evidence and Research Synthesis: Enhancing Alignment and Usability of Research Synthesis Methods. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10152-5
title: CAPERS: a prospective mixed-methods framework integrating community participatory methods into research synthesis
description: CAPERS (Community and Participatory Evidence and Research Synthesis) is a mixed-methods framework that engages community partners prospectively in research synthesis rather than post hoc. The article describes it as "a novel mixed-methods synthesis framework" that shifts community engagement "from a post hoc interpretive activity/responsibility to a prospectively planned component of the research synthesis design." It applies across synthesis types including meta-analyses, scoping reviews, and qualitative meta-syntheses.
requirements: Requires identifying community members "aligned with the goals of the synthesis" who have relevant practical perspectives on feasibility, adoptability, and sustainability
constraints: The article presents it as a proposal to "stimulate dialogue and provide a guidance" rather than a validated method with empirical evidence of effectiveness
target_learners: Practitioners and policymakers using synthesis evidence
target_learning_goals: Improve relevance, usability, and implementation readiness of research syntheses for practice
examples: Integrating meta-analytic findings with practitioner and student perspectives to identify contextually-grounded mechanisms of change in school-based interventions
key_sources: Jason C. Chow · Ruben G. Martinez. (2026). Community and Participatory Evidence and Research Synthesis: Enhancing Alignment and Usability of Research Synthesis Methods. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10152-5

article_title: Community and Participatory Evidence and Research Synthesis: Enhancing Alignment and Usability of Research Synthesis Methods
citation: Jason C. Chow · Ruben G. Martinez. (2026). Community and Participatory Evidence and Research Synthesis: Enhancing Alignment and Usability of Research Synthesis Methods. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10152-5
title: Five mixed-methods integration functions organize CAPERS: convergence, complementarity, development, expansion, and sampling
description: CAPERS organizes the integration of participatory and synthesis methods through "five mixed-methods functions (Palinkas et al. 2011a, b) that are tailored to the research synthesis workstream": Convergence (same question, both methods), Complementarity (related questions, elaboration), Expansion (one method extends the other), Development (one method informs the design or coding of the other), and Sampling (one method guides selection for the other). Each function is defined with rationale, an extant-literature example, and an educational psychology application.
requirements: Researchers must decide which function(s) fit their synthesis purpose; the article notes "it is possible to integrate PAR and RS methods in more than one way in each study"
constraints: Adapted from Palinkas et al. (2011a, b); the taxonomy is borrowed rather than newly validated in this article
target_learning_goals: Structure intentional integration of qualitative participatory data with research synthesis
examples: Complementarity: a scoping review of Tier 2 mathematics tutoring implementation strategies followed by school-team implementation blueprinting
key_sources: Jason C. Chow · Ruben G. Martinez. (2026). Community and Participatory Evidence and Research Synthesis: Enhancing Alignment and Usability of Research Synthesis Methods. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10152-5

article_title: Community and Participatory Evidence and Research Synthesis: Enhancing Alignment and Usability of Research Synthesis Methods
citation: Jason C. Chow · Ruben G. Martinez. (2026). Community and Participatory Evidence and Research Synthesis: Enhancing Alignment and Usability of Research Synthesis Methods. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10152-5
title: Eight-stage synthesis process with participatory integration actions at each stage
description: The article maps community integration onto eight synthesis stages: planning and protocol development, literature search, study identification, coding and data extraction, data analysis, results interpretation, reporting, and dissemination. Each stage carries actionable steps and integration examples, e.g., at coding, "Coding expands beyond effect sizes to include implementation features, participation outcomes, equity relevant variables." The pattern transforms a review "from a retrospective aggregation of effects into a mechanism- and context-informed synthesis."
requirements: A synthesis protocol with planned participatory integration developed at stage 1, including registered goals and equity checkpoints
constraints: Depth of integration varies "depending on the research, practice, and policy goals of the synthesis"
target_learners: Researchers conducting systematic reviews or meta-analyses in education
target_learning_goals: Produce community-aligned, implementation-ready synthesis findings
examples: Table 3 maps a teacher professional development review onto the stages, with shareholders co-defining priorities and co-interpreting findings through structured sensemaking
key_sources: Jason C. Chow · Ruben G. Martinez. (2026). Community and Participatory Evidence and Research Synthesis: Enhancing Alignment and Usability of Research Synthesis Methods. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10152-5

article_title: Community and Participatory Evidence and Research Synthesis: Enhancing Alignment and Usability of Research Synthesis Methods
citation: Jason C. Chow · Ruben G. Martinez. (2026). Community and Participatory Evidence and Research Synthesis: Enhancing Alignment and Usability of Research Synthesis Methods. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10152-5
title: Select and engage community members through structured, documented partner-selection processes
description: CAPERS recommends "a structured approach to partner selection and engagement that includes (a) mapping relevant community groups, (b) establishing clear engagement structures and expectations, (c) iteratively evaluating the composition of the group, and (d) documenting recruitment and decision-making processes." Teams should designate whether members are research participants or co-production partners, with implications for IRB oversight, and include individuals representing multiple roles: deliverers, receivers, indirectly impacted people, policy/legal experts, and methodological experts.
requirements: Early communication of engagement length, intensity, roles, and compensation; a decision-tracking system recording who was invited, participated, or declined
constraints: Composition should be revisited iteratively so important perspectives are not underrepresented as the project progresses
target_learning_goals: Ensure equitable representation and transparent, credible community engagement in synthesis
examples: Recruitment pathways include existing partnerships, professional organizations, open online recruitment, and community engagement studios for focused consultation
key_sources: Jason C. Chow · Ruben G. Martinez. (2026). Community and Participatory Evidence and Research Synthesis: Enhancing Alignment and Usability of Research Synthesis Methods. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10152-5

citation: Jason C. Chow · Ruben G. Martinez. (2026). Community and Participatory Evidence and Research Synthesis: Enhancing Alignment and Usability of Research Synthesis Methods. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10152-5
title: AI synthesis tools such as Abstrackr for machine-assisted evidence synthesis
description: The article notes that "Artificial intelligence (AI) methods for evidence synthesis are on the rise" and cites Abstrackr (Wallace et al., 2012) as synthesis software that has "leveraged natural language" processing for synthesis tasks. It appears in a section on leveraging AI within CAPERS, positioning AI tools as complements to community-integrated synthesis processes. The supplied text is truncated mid-description of this section.
requirements: AI tools support but do not replace the participatory integration decisions CAPERS specifies
constraints: The article's discussion of AI is introductory; the supplied text truncates before full treatment
target_learning_goals: Increase efficiency of screening and synthesis workflows
examples: Abstrackr cited as an example of synthesis software using natural language methods

article_title: The Yet Underestimated Importance of Communicating Findings from Educational Trials to Teachers, Schools, School Authorities, or Policy Makers (Comment on Brady et al. (2023))
citation: Zitzmann, S., Machts, N., Hübner, N., Schauber, S., Möller, J., & Lindner, C. (2023). The Yet Underestimated Importance of Communicating Findings from Educational Trials to Teachers, Schools, School Authorities, or Policy Makers (Comment on Brady et al. (2023)). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09776-8
title: Communicate findings from educational trials to stakeholders in a way they can easily understand, because recommendations derive from the findings
description: The article argues that researchers should report findings to teachers, schools, school authorities, and policy makers in a meaningful, understandable form. It states that "recommendations are derived from the findings, and a correct understanding of them is essential for stakeholders to evaluate the usefulness of recommendations and strengthen stakeholders' beliefs in their added value." Practical recommendations should be preceded by a stakeholder-appropriate summary of findings.
requirements: A summary of findings that is meaningful to stakeholders and communicated so these persons will easily understand them
target_learners: teachers, schools, school authorities, and policy makers as research stakeholders
target_learning_goals: stakeholder understanding and evaluation of research-based recommendations
examples: The authors precede their own recommendation by summarizing findings in plain terms and propose responder rates as an understandable summary format

citation: Zitzmann, S., Machts, N., Hübner, N., Schauber, S., Möller, J., & Lindner, C. (2023). The Yet Underestimated Importance of Communicating Findings from Educational Trials to Teachers, Schools, School Authorities, or Policy Makers (Comment on Brady et al. (2023)). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09776-8
title: Report responder rates in addition to effect sizes so stakeholders can understand the consequences of implementing a treatment
description: Adapting a practice from clinical research, the article recommends that alongside an effect size measure, findings from a responder analysis be communicated: the relative frequencies of students whose outcomes improved substantially. Because responder rates "emerge from individual students’ percentages change and are thus an intuitive way of summarizing findings, stakeholders can better infer their practical significance." This applies to learning research and other outcomes such as stress reduction.
requirements: Percentage change computed for each student as (post − pre) / pre · 100%, classification into categories of change based on reasonable cutoffs, and counting students per category to yield responder rates
constraints: The efficacy of communicating responder rates needs to be tested empirically before conclusive recommendations can be formulated
target_learners: teachers, schools, school authorities, policy makers
target_learning_goals: stakeholder understanding of practical significance of treatment effects on student outcomes
examples: The article presents a hypothetical trial's responder rates as an easy-to-interpret bar chart (Fig. 1) with cutoffs of 0% and 50%

title: Choose responder-analysis cutoffs from theory or empirical research rather than arbitrarily
description: The article acknowledges the criticism that cutoffs for classifying students' percentage change into categories may seem arbitrary, and answers it: "the cutoffs may come from theory; for example, from expert considerations of what should at least be learned during a course/period of time. Or, they may come from empirical research." When theory is vague and findings rare, illustrative cutoffs may provide a starting point but not a definite definition.

examples: The authors used cutoffs of 0% and 50% in their Fig. 1 example, explicitly labeled as illustrative and not very valid

article_title: Measuring the Quality of Adult–Child Interactions in the Context of ECEC: a Systematic Review on the Relationship with Developmental and Educational Outcomes
citation: Steven J. Howard, Kate L. Lewis, Emma Walter, Irina Verenikina, & Lisa K. Kervin. (2024). Measuring the Quality of Adult–Child Interactions in the Context of ECEC: a Systematic Review on the Relationship with Developmental and Educational Outcomes. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09832-3
title: Classification framework distinguishing global quality, global process quality, quality pedagogical interactions, and quality interactions related to curriculum content
description: The review's organising taxonomy for grouping interaction quality characteristics. Beyond the consensus distinction of structural and process quality, it delineates process quality into ECEC global quality, ECEC process quality, quality pedagogical interactions, and quality interactions related to curriculum content. Quality pedagogical interactions are "further subdivided into four categories: (i) building positive relationships; (ii) routines and structure; (iii) educator–child conversations and questioning; (iv) supporting play". Curriculum-content interactions are subdivided into seven categories including global instructional support, literacy, language, mathematics, science and environment learning, diversity, and educator use of materials/resources. The frame permitted evaluating differential associations of global versus finer-grained indices with child outcomes.
requirements: Studies must report interaction quality measures classifiable into the framework's categories, with interactional-quality domains tabled at subscale level where reported
constraints: The article states there is less agreement on delineations within process quality, that overlap exists between dimensions (e.g. conversations and questioning are essential to each), and that other groupings are possible with potential implications for findings
target_learners: Children aged 3–5 years in formal ECEC settings
target_learning_goals: Cognitive-academic outcomes (cognitive and academic) and social-emotional outcomes (prosociality and socio-emotional competence)
examples: Studies using overall ECERS-R ratings were grouped as ECEC global quality; total CLASS-Pre-K as ECEC process quality; the CLASS-PreK Emotional Support subscale and ORCE as quality pedagogical interactions; and ECERS-E Literacy, Mathematics, Science and Environment, or Diversity subscales as curriculum-content interactions

citation: Steven J. Howard, Kate L. Lewis, Emma Walter, Irina Verenikina, & Lisa K. Kervin. (2024). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09832-3
title: Process–structural quality distinction in ECEC, with structural quality setting conditions for process quality
description: A conceptual distinction the review describes as guiding ECEC quality research: quality is commonly separated into "distinct yet related process and structural dimensions, rather than conceiving of quality as a unidimensional global construct". Process quality relates to children's interactions with adults and other children and to learning experiences shaped by curricula, resources and materials, whereas structural quality refers to organisational aspects such as adult qualifications, child-to-adult ratios, group size, funding and management. The review states the general view that "structural quality sets the conditions for process quality", i.e. structural quality is necessary but not sufficient for robust child-level impacts.
requirements: Both dimensions must be measured if the distinction is to be applied in evaluating ECEC provision
constraints: The review notes some studies instead conceive of global quality indices as meaningful, so the distinction is a dominant but not universal convention
target_learners: Children aged 3–5 years in formal ECEC settings
target_learning_goals: Developmental and educational outcomes of early childhood provision
examples: The review's own classification of quality measures (e.g. ECERS-R global ratings vs CLASS interaction domains) operationalises this distinction

Measuring the Quality of Adult–Child Interactions in the Context of ECEC: a Systematic Review on the Relationship with Developmental and Educational Outcomes. article_title: Help! I Need Somebody: A Systematic Review of Academic Help-Seeking Among Pre-Service Teachers
citation: Navarro-Ibáñez, M., Balladares, J., Sprovera, I., Manaut, C., & Infante, M. (2026). Help! I Need Somebody: A Systematic Review of Academic Help-Seeking Among Pre-Service Teachers. Educational Psychology Review, 38, 115. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10208-6
title: AHS as a socially embedded regulatory process within self-regulated learning
description: The review proposes an integrated conceptualization of academic help-seeking as a contextually and motivationally influenced regulatory process rather than a stable individual disposition. It argues that "help-seeking has a strong social component, as it heavily depends on the context and environment to encourage or discourage students from seeking help", and offers "a more integrated conceptualization of AHS as a socially embedded regulatory process within self-regulated learning". In teacher education, this framing highlights the relational nature of AHS and its potential implications for professional identity development.
requirements: Conceptualizing AHS within social-cognitive self-regulated learning frameworks rather than as a trait-like disposition
constraints: The review presents this as an integrative conceptualization suggested by the evidence, not as a directly tested model
target_learners: preservice teachers in teacher education programs
target_learning_goals: adaptive academic help-seeking
self-regulated learning
professional identity development
examples: The review synthesizes 32 empirical studies of AHS in preservice teachers to support this conceptualization

citation: Navarro-Ibáñez, M., Balladares, J., Sprovera, I., Manaut, C., & Infante, M. (2026). Help! I Need Somebody: A Systematic Review of Academic Help-Seeking Among Pre-Service Teachers. Educational Psychology Review, 38, 115. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10208-6
title: Karabenick and Dembo's eight-stage help-seeking model with instrumental versus executive help-seeking
description: The review describes the eight-stage model as "a widely recognized help-seeking model in the literature", which "highlights various cognitive, social, affective-emotional, and contextual competencies required at each stage", from identifying a problem through processing received help. It also presents Nelson-Le Gall's distinction "identifying two types: instrumental (or adaptive) help-seeking and executive (or non-adaptive) help-seeking", where instrumental help-seeking promotes learning and independence while executive help-seeking obtains immediate answers without deepening understanding.
requirements: Learners must deploy cognitive, social, affective-emotional, and contextual competencies across the eight stages, from problem identification to processing received help
constraints: The review notes there is no consensus on the exact structure of help-seeking
target_learning_goals: adaptive (instrumental) help-seeking
metacognitive monitoring of learning needs
examples: The review uses the model to frame how preservice teachers decide whether, whom, and how to ask for help during coursework and practicum

article_title: Emotion Regulation and Academic Burnout Among Youth: a Quantitative Meta-analysis
citation: Ioana Alexandra Iuga · Oana Alexandra David. (2024). Emotion Regulation and Academic Burnout Among Youth: a Quantitative Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09930-w
title: Gross's process model of emotion regulation as the explanatory framework linking ER strategies to academic burnout
description: The article adopts Gross's process model of emotion regulation, which "lays out the sequential actions people take to regulate their emotions during the emotion-generative process": situation selection, situation modification, attentional deployment, cognitive change, and response modulation. It uses this model to explain how students' ER strategies, as adaptive or maladaptive reactions to academic stressors, shape their susceptibility to school burnout. The article also distinguishes ER abilities from ER strategies as interconnected approaches.
requirements: The model presumes an emotion-generative circumstance in which strategies are deployed; the article notes strategies are employed when there is a discrepancy between current and desired emotional state
constraints: The article states the included studies are predominantly cross-sectional, so the model's causal directionality from ER to burnout cannot be established from this evidence
target_learners: children, adolescents, and youth aged 18 to 25 in elementary, middle, secondary, and tertiary education
target_learning_goals: managing academic stress and emotions to protect academic well-being and reduce burnout
examples: The article frames the ER–burnout link through the model: whether a student employs efficient ER strategies or encounters ER difficulties could influence their susceptibility to school burnout
key_sources: Ioana Alexandra Iuga · Oana Alexandra David. (2024). Emotion Regulation and Academic Burnout Among Youth: a Quantitative Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09930-w

article_title: Cultural Insights into the Motivation Paradox of East Asian Learners
citation: Bong, M., Jeong, D., Park, S., Suh, J., Kim, S. G., Park, J. C., & Kim, J. (2026). Cultural Insights into the Motivation Paradox of East Asian Learners. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10140-9
title: Funnel model of East Asian achievement motivation: cultural forces flow from collectivism and Confucianism through nested ecological systems into unique motivational currencies
description: The article proposes a conceptual framework, depicted as a funnel, in which the cultural doctrines of collectivism and Confucianism form the macrosystem and filter through exosystem, mesosystem, and microsystem layers toward family and school. The authors state the framework 'takes the form of a funnel to illustrate how cultural influences flow from broader to more immediate systems, with the influence becoming more concentrated as one enters more immediate surroundings.' From this cultural core of interdependent self-construal and constant self-discipline emerge distinctive motivational patterns the authors call 'motivational currencies.'
requirements: Focuses solely on factors related to East Asian learners' academic motivation, not their development or learning processes
constraints: The model addresses East Asian learners under East Asian culture, defined as China, Japan, Korea, and Taiwan; the authors present only three motivational currencies for illustrative purposes
target_learners: East Asian students in achievement contexts
target_learning_goals: Understanding culturally shaped achievement motivation
examples: The framework organizes seven cultural characteristics, including relational self-understanding, familism, collective attribution, low self-enhancement, self-criticism, meritocratic exam-oriented pedagogy, and role responsibilities
key_sources: Bong, M., Jeong, D., Park, S., Suh, J., Kim, S. G., Park, J. C., & Kim, J. (2026). Cultural Insights into the Motivation Paradox of East Asian Learners. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10140-9

article_title: Learning to Read in Chinese: A Meta-analytic Structural Equation Modeling Analysis of Cognitive-Linguistic Skills in Chinese Word Reading
citation: Learning to read in Chinese: A Meta-analytic Structural Equation Modeling analysis of cognitive-linguistic skills in Chinese word reading. (2025). https://osf.io/s7tjp/?view_only=4865c0558529407aa0a9e35777761117
title: Lexical Quality Hypothesis as a framework for cognitive-linguistic underpinnings of word reading
description: The article adopts the Lexical Quality Hypothesis (Perfetti, 2007) as its organizing theoretical framework, contending that "successful word reading depends on readers' high-quality orthographic representations, well-specified phonological representations, and rich and elaborated semantic representations" of a word. When these components are firmly connected, word reading becomes faster and more effortless, freeing resources for comprehension. The MASEM model operationalizes these representations as five cognitive-linguistic skills predicting word reading.
requirements: Models of word reading must include the covariance among skills and control for nonverbal reasoning to estimate each skill's unique effect, as the article argues univariate approaches obscured unique contributions
constraints: The framework is applied here to typically developing native Chinese-speaking children under age 18 in mainland China, Taiwan, and Hong Kong
target_learners: Native Chinese-speaking children (kindergarten through elementary school)
target_learning_goals: Word reading (character and multi-character word recognition) in Chinese
examples: The study fitted a path model in which RAN, OA, PA, MA, and vocabulary predicted word reading, testing the interplay the LQH implies

title: Pooled correlational dataset of 288 independent samples (N = 47,121) with OSF repository
description: A pooled dataset of correlation matrices for RAN, OA, PA, MA, vocabulary, word reading, and nonverbal reasoning, drawn from 244 primary studies comprising "288 independent samples (N = 47,121)" of native Chinese-speaking children. Coding achieved 100% agreement on moderator coding and a Cohen's Kappa of .91 for correlation coefficients. The correlation matrices, sample sizes, and study features are available in Online Resource 2 on OSF.
requirements: Studies included native Chinese-speaking children under 18 with at least one focal correlation, published in peer-reviewed English-language journals
constraints: Excluded adults, heritage/non-native speakers, bilingual settings such as Singapore, children with dyslexia or other learning disabilities, and meta-analyses/reviews/case studies
target_learners: Native Chinese-speaking children in mainland China, Taiwan, and Hong Kong
target_learning_goals: Word reading in Chinese

article_title: Learning to Read in Chinese: A Meta-analytic Structural Equation Modeling Analysis of Cognitive-Linguistic Skills in Chinese Word Reading
citation: Learning to read in Chinese: A Meta-analytic Structural Equation Modeling analysis of cognitive-linguistic skills in Chinese word reading. (2025). https://osf.io/s7tjp/?view_only=4865c0558529407aa0a9e35777761117
title: Choose early literacy instruction methods in awareness of their trade-off between phonological and morphological reliance in Chinese word reading
description: The article's moderator results show that how children are taught to read reshapes which skills carry word reading: phonetic coding systems (Pinyin, Zhuyin Fuhao) strengthen reliance on PA while reducing reliance on MA, whereas look-and-say instruction leaves greater weight on MA. The article reports that phonological instruction via Pinyin and Bopomofo "has been found to promote children's sub-syllabic awareness, such as rime/onset awareness and phonemic awareness." Educators should therefore expect instructional method, not just script, to shape the skill profile children draw on.
requirements: Requires knowing which instructional method (phonetic coding system vs. look-and-say) a child population receives when interpreting or planning assessment of cognitive-linguistic skills
constraints: Instructional method was coded from study site (mainland China/Taiwan vs. Hong Kong), so script and instructional differences were confounded in the coding; the article cautions that interpretations of site differences need caution
target_learners: Children learning to read Chinese in kindergarten and elementary school
target_learning_goals: Word reading in Chinese; phonological and morphological awareness
examples: The MASEM compared Hong Kong look-and-say children with mainland China and Taiwan children taught via Pinyin or Zhuyin Fuhao, finding Δβ = .071 for PA and Δβ = -.093 for MA

article_title: Relationships Between Experiences of Autonomy and Well(Ill)-Being for K-12 Youth: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Amanda Vite, Erika A. Patall, Man Chen. (2024). Relationships Between Experiences of Autonomy and Well(Ill)-Being for K-12 Youth: A Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review (2024) 36:127. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09967-x
title: Dual process model of basic psychological need satisfaction and frustration
description: The dual process model treats need satisfaction and need frustration as distinct psychological processes rather than opposite ends of one continuum. As the article states, "The dual process model defines need satisfaction and need frustration as distinct processes, with experiences of need satisfaction primarily leading to more optimal outcomes and experiences of need frustration primarily leading to non-optimal outcomes." The meta-analysis used it to predict that matched-valence correlations (ANS with well-being, ANF with ill-being) would be stronger than mismatched ones, a pattern the results supported.
requirements: Studies must measure need satisfaction and need frustration separately to test the model's distinct-process prediction
constraints: The article notes low need satisfaction differs from need frustration: frustration can provoke negative outcomes whereas low satisfaction may only elicit decreased positive outcomes
target_learning_goals: Understanding autonomy need satisfaction and frustration as mechanisms of youth psychological well- and ill-being
examples: The meta-analysis tested and found stronger pooled correlations for matched-valence pairs (ANS-well-being r = .37; ANF-ill-being r = .34) than mismatched pairs
key_sources: Amanda Vite, Erika A. Patall, Man Chen. (2024). Relationships Between Experiences of Autonomy and Well(Ill)-Being for K-12 Youth: A Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review (2024) 36:127. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09967-x

article_title: Relationships Between Experiences of Autonomy and Well(Ill)-Being for K-12 Youth: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Amanda Vite, Erika A. Patall, Man Chen. (2024). Relationships Between Experiences of Autonomy and Well(Ill)-Being for K-12 Youth: A Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review (2024) 36:127. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09967-x
title: Four competing cultural hypotheses for the role of culture in psychological need effects
description: The article organizes debate about cultural universality of autonomy need effects as a continuum of four positions. As it states, "we review four competing hypotheses regarding the role of culture in psychological needs and outcomes including a strict universalist perspective (Ryan & Deci, 2000b), a compensatory perspective (Lee et al., 2023; Gewirtz & Baer, 1958), a cultural matching perspective (Schüler et al., 2013), and a strict cultural relativist perspective (Markus & Kitayama, 1991)." The strict universalist view expects no cultural variation; the compensatory view predicts stronger satisfaction effects where autonomy is inconsistently satisfied; cultural matching predicts stronger effects where autonomy is culturally embedded; the strict relativist view treats needs as entirely context-specific.
requirements: Testing these hypotheses requires studies spanning multiple cultural contexts with comparable autonomy and well(ill)-being measures
constraints: The article notes it could not examine variation in the definition of autonomy due to insufficient data, and SDT researchers distinguish autonomy-as-endorsement from independence and independent choice
target_learners: K-12 youth across cultural contexts worldwide
target_learning_goals: Understanding how cultural context moderates the relationship between autonomy experiences and well(ill)-being
examples: The meta-analysis framed its cultural moderator analyses against these four hypotheses, with the region findings described as in line with the compensatory hypothesis

article_title: Cognitive Load and Challenges in Self-regulation: An Introduction and Reflection on the Topical Collection
citation: de Bruin, A. B. H., Janssen, E. M., Waldeyer, J., & Stebner, F. (2025). Cognitive Load and Challenges in Self-regulation: An Introduction and Reflection on the Topical Collection. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10042-2
title: The Effort Monitoring and Regulation (EMR) model integrates self-regulated learning and cognitive load theory
description: The EMR model "integrates self-regulated learning and cognitive load theory to examine how students monitor, regulate, and optimize effort during learning." Introduced in 2020 by an EARLI and Jacobs Foundation-sponsored Emerging Field Group, it poses three research questions: how students monitor effort, how they regulate effort, and how cognitive load on SRL tasks can be optimized during and after the primary task. The topical collection papers are mapped onto the model and used to refine it.
requirements: Research addressing how learners monitor effort, regulate effort, and optimize cognitive load on self-regulated learning tasks
constraints: The editorial notes critical questions remain, including how learners transition from data-driven to goal-driven interpretations of effort
target_learning_goals: accurate monitoring and regulation of mental effort during learning
examples: The eleven topical collection papers are positioned within the EMR model's three research questions in Fig. 1

article_title: Cognitive Load and Challenges in Self-regulation: An Introduction and Reflection on the Topical Collection
citation: de Bruin, A. B. H., Janssen, E. M., Waldeyer, J., & Stebner, F. (2025). Cognitive Load and Challenges in Self-regulation: An Introduction and Reflection on the Topical Collection. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10042-2
title: Grund et al. (2024) categorize mental effort by psychological sources: effort-by-complexity, effort-by-need frustration, and effort-by-allocation
description: A review by Grund et al. (2024) introduces "a novel categorization of how to conceptualize effort based on its underlying psychological sources of experiencing and allocating mental effort: effort-by-complexity, effort-by-need frustration, and effort-by-allocation." The authors argue that motivational and emotional factors shape both willingness to invest effort and whether effort is experienced as manageable or taxing, and call for including affective components when measuring cognitive mental effort.
requirements: Measurement of cognitive mental effort should consider its affective components
target_learners: learners working on effortful learning tasks
target_learning_goals: conceptualization and measurement of mental effort in learning
examples: The editorial recommends disentangling effort due to task complexity from effort due to need frustration, optimizing the first while minimizing the latter

article_title: Gamification on Mathematics Engagement and Motivation in Secondary School and Higher Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
citation: Ratinho, E., Figueiredo, M., Estêvão, D., Faísca, L., & Martins, C. (2026). Gamification on Mathematics Engagement and Motivation in Secondary School and Higher Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10108-1
title: Self-Determination Theory as the dominant motivational framework for gamification, complemented by ARCS, SCT, AGT, and Flow Theory
description: The review organizes gamification's motivational effects through established frameworks, with Self-Determination Theory the most frequently used (n = 13), followed by SCT (n = 8) and the ARCS model (n = 6). Under SDT, "the satisfaction of autonomy, competence, and relatedness is essential to fostering intrinsic motivation", and game elements can be aligned with these needs: points and levels support competence, avatars and team leaderboards support relatedness, and task choice supports autonomy. The review argues controlling or comparative elements may undermine autonomy and competence, while feedback, scaffolding, and self-paced progression tend to support basic psychological needs.
requirements: Gamified designs must be aligned with students' psychological needs (autonomy, competence, relatedness) rather than adding elements superficially
constraints: The review notes a recurring reliance on non-validated or ad hoc measures of motivation, often with limited theoretical grounding, which restricts comparability across studies
target_learners: Secondary and higher education students in mathematics courses
target_learning_goals: Sustaining motivation and engagement in mathematics learning
examples: Points and levels framed as progress feedback for competence; team leaderboards for relatedness; task or difficulty choice for autonomy
key_sources: Ratinho, E., Figueiredo, M., Estêvão, D., Faísca, L., & Martins, C. (2026). Gamification on Mathematics Engagement and Motivation in Secondary School and Higher Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10108-1

article_title: Gamification on Mathematics Engagement and Motivation in Secondary School and Higher Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
citation: Ratinho, E., Figueiredo, M., Estêvão, D., Faísca, L., & Martins, C. (2026). Gamification on Mathematics Engagement and Motivation in Secondary School and Higher Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10108-1
title: Align gamification design with students' psychological needs, limiting excessive competition and prioritizing personal progress and cooperative tasks
description: The review concludes that gamification enhances motivation and engagement in mathematics "when designs are aligned with students’ needs, balancing competition with mastery and cooperation". Elements added superficially are unlikely to be effective; instead, mastery-oriented structures, gradual progression through increasing difficulty, individual progress indicators, and cooperative mechanics that foster relatedness are recommended. Educators should "limit excessive competition and prioritize personal progress and cooperative tasks that foster social interaction".
requirements: Designs must balance competition with mastery and cooperation, supporting autonomy, competence, and relatedness
constraints: Competitive features can be motivating, but if overemphasized, they risk discouraging less competitive students; external rewards require careful use
target_learners: Secondary and higher education mathematics students
target_learning_goals: Sustaining motivation and engagement in mathematics
examples: The review reports that interventions combining gamification with interactive or narrative structures tended to increase participation and attention, and that cooperative mechanics fostered relatedness while balancing competition

citation: Ratinho, E., Figueiredo, M., Estêvão, D., Faísca, L., & Martins, C. (2026). Gamification on Mathematics Engagement and Motivation in Secondary School and Higher Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10108-1
title: Table 4 mapping of gamification elements to learner motivational characteristics
description: The review provides a synthesis table (Table 4) mapping eight game elements — avatar, badges, progress/levels, ranking/leaderboards, collaborative rankings/team tasks, score/points, timer/time pressure, and rewards — to the learner profiles for which each is "Possibly effective" and "Possibly less effective", with example studies. For instance, badges suit learners low in intrinsic motivation but may be perceived as controlling by learners initially high in intrinsic motivation; leaderboards suit learners high in extrinsic motivation but may reduce autonomy and competence for learners high in intrinsic motivation.
requirements: Matching elements to learners' motivational profiles requires knowledge of learner characteristics; the review points to player typologies such as the HEXAD model as validated tools to identify motivational preferences
constraints: The table's entries are qualified as "possibly" effective or less effective, drawn from the included studies rather than tested as moderator hypotheses
target_learners: Secondary and higher education mathematics students with varying motivational profiles
target_learning_goals: Tailoring gamification elements to learner motivation and engagement needs
examples: Leaderboards listed as possibly effective for learners high in extrinsic motivation and possibly less effective for learners high in intrinsic motivation, citing Lee et al. (2023) and Reyssier et al. (2022)

article_title: Stirring a Secret Sauce: A Literature Review on the Conditions and Effects of Authentic Learning
citation: Valentina Nachtigall, David Williamson Shaffer, Nikol Rummel. (2022). Stirring a Secret Sauce: A Literature Review on the Conditions and Effects of Authentic Learning. Educational Psychology Review (2022) 34:1479–1516. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09676-3
title: Synthesized framework of eight design elements of authentic learning settings
description: The review synthesizes four prior operationalizations (Herrington & Oliver 2000; Rule 2006; Betz et al. 2016; Hod & Sagy 2019) into eight main design elements: collaboration, complex problems/tasks, inquiry/investigation, experts/practitioners, real-life/professional setting, real-life materials/cultural tools, authentic assessment, and technology. It states that "authentic learning is assumed to emerge from the interaction of multiple design elements", with rarer elements such as reflection, coaching and scaffolding overlapping with the more common ones.
requirements: Authentic learning settings combine multiple design elements; the review analyzes how the eight elements interact rather than treating any single element as sufficient
constraints: Authentic assessment is treated as a design element rather than an intention of authenticity, and teacher authenticity is excluded because it can hardly be achieved by implementing design elements
target_learners: Undergraduate and vocational learners as represented in the reviewed studies
target_learning_goals: Cognitive outcomes such as knowledge acquisition and problem-solving
Motivational outcomes such as interest and intrinsic motivation
examples: The review's codebook illustrates each element with reviewed studies, e.g., learners visiting an agritourism farm to learn about aquaponics as a real-life/professional setting
key_sources: Valentina Nachtigall, David Williamson Shaffer, Nikol Rummel. (2022). Stirring a Secret Sauce: A Literature Review on the Conditions and Effects of Authentic Learning. Educational Psychology Review (2022) 34:1479–1516. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09676-3

article_title: Stirring a Secret Sauce: A Literature Review on the Conditions and Effects of Authentic Learning
citation: Valentina Nachtigall, David Williamson Shaffer, Nikol Rummel. (2022). Stirring a Secret Sauce: A Literature Review on the Conditions and Effects of Authentic Learning. Educational Psychology Review (2022) 34:1479–1516. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09676-3
title: Taxonomy of four intentions of authenticity underlying authentic learning design
description: The review synthesizes five prior classifications of authenticity (Shaffer & Resnick 1999; Polman 2012; Strobel et al. 2013; Doyle 2000; Fougt et al. 2019) into four intentions: creating personally meaningful learning activities, emulating the work of professionals, connecting learners with a community of practitioners, and reflecting experiences from real/daily life. The review states it "extracted the fol- lowing four intentions of authenticity" and treats intentions as "the overarch- ing determination or definition of authenticity in learning settings" that determine how design elements are selected and implemented.
requirements: Design elements are selected and implemented in ways determined by the intended authenticity; certain elements are presumed more strongly linked to certain intentions
constraints: Authentic assessment and teacher authenticity are deliberately not treated as equivalent intentions of authenticity in this taxonomy
target_learners: Higher education and vocational learners as represented in the reviewed studies
target_learning_goals: Contextualizing learning so learners recognize the value, utility, meaning, and functionality of the knowledge to be acquired
examples: The codebook example for community of practice: teacher candidates connected to professional learning communities and supervised by experienced teachers
