article_title: Digital Prompting in Education: A Design Framework and Bibliometric Analysis
citation: Jasmin Breitwieser, André Bittermann, Maria Theobald, Tim Lauer, Mirijam Schaaf, Garvin Brod. (2026). Digital Prompting in Education: A Design Framework and Bibliometric Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10164-1
title: Guiding framework of digital prompts as dynamic scaffolds with a four-dimension design typology
description: The article proposes a guiding framework that conceptualizes digital prompts as feed-forward scaffolds that directly trigger beneficial learning activities students might not initiate on their own, situating prompts within scaffolding theory with contingency, fading, and transfer of responsibility as core principles. Prompt design is characterized through a typology of four dimensions: content, function, presentation, and source, adapted from Panadero and Lipnevich's feedback typology. The framework treats prompting as a dynamic, iterative scaffolding process in which student responses inform subsequent prompting, such as gradually fading support as competence increases.
requirements: Relevant student characteristics (e.g., prior knowledge, SRL skills) and momentary needs should inform the design of a prompt to provide contingent support
constraints: Unlike feedback, prompts do not necessarily communicate discrepancies between students' current state and a target goal; evaluative subdimensions such as verification and valence may be less relevant for prompting
target_learners: K-12 and university students using digital learning environments
target_learning_goals: Activation of cognitive, metacognitive, and self-regulated learning strategies through digital prompts
key_sources: Jasmin Breitwieser, André Bittermann, Maria Theobald, Tim Lauer, Mirijam Schaaf, Garvin Brod. (2026). Digital Prompting in Education: A Design Framework and Bibliometric Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10164-1

article_title: On Being Accepted: Interrogating How University Cultural Scripts Shape Personal and Political Facets of Belonging
citation: Rebecca Covarrubias. (2024). On Being Accepted: Interrogating How University Cultural Scripts Shape Personal and Political Facets of Belonging. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09970-2
title: Place-belongingness and politics of belonging framework for student belonging in higher education
description: The framework characterizes belonging both as an intimate personal feeling of 'being at home' and as tied to social forces that include and exclude. It specifies six factors of place-belongingness—auto-biographical, relational, cultural, economic, legal, and elective—and holds that these must be read against structures of power that delineate who gets to belong. The article applies it to universities, arguing that systems of whiteness and intersecting oppression shape students' diverse constellations of belonging needs.
requirements: Analysis must attend to both the personal feeling of belonging and the power structures that afford or constrain it
constraints: The framework theorizes broadly around migration, nationalism, and citizenship, and its higher-education application is attributed to Covarrubias (2023)
target_learners: low-income, first-generation-to-college students of color in higher education
target_learning_goals: fostering students' sense of belonging and acceptance in university settings
examples: The article uses the framework to organize its review of harmful and transformative institutional acceptance practices and to analyze how scripts of multiculturalism and exceptionalism erase relational, legal, and economic belonging needs
key_sources: Rebecca Covarrubias. (2024). On Being Accepted: Interrogating How University Cultural Scripts Shape Personal and Political Facets of Belonging. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09970-2

article_title: On Being Accepted: Interrogating How University Cultural Scripts Shape Personal and Political Facets of Belonging
citation: Rebecca Covarrubias. (2024). On Being Accepted: Interrogating How University Cultural Scripts Shape Personal and Political Facets of Belonging. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09970-2
title: Taxonomy of cultural scripts of acceptance: sameness, difference, and pluralism
description: The article organizes institutional acceptance practices into three cultural scripts (Table 1). Scripts of acceptance through sameness require assimilation into dominant culture; scripts of acceptance through difference acknowledge cultural differences substantively via identity-conscious approaches such as culturally relevant cues and pedagogy; and scripts of acceptance through pluralism acknowledge the plurality of students' identities and interrogate the politics of belonging. Harmful scripts communicate a trade-off in which students must hide or contort parts of the self to be accepted, while pluralist scripts 'communicate how marginalized students need not trade important parts of themselves to be accepted.'
requirements: Scripts must be analyzed for whether they attend to the politics of belonging, not merely whether they signal acceptance
constraints: Culturally sustaining pedagogy reflects acceptance through pluralism but is organized under acceptance through difference in the main text to analyze similarities with culturally relevant pedagogy
target_learning_goals: designing institutional practices that foster belonging without demanding assimilation
examples: Table 1 lists illustrative examples: multiculturalism and exceptionalism under sameness; culturally relevant cues and culturally relevant pedagogy under difference; culturally sustaining pedagogy and loving playfulness under pluralism
key_sources: Rebecca Covarrubias. (2024). On Being Accepted: Interrogating How University Cultural Scripts Shape Personal and Political Facets of Belonging. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09970-2

article_title: On Being Accepted: Interrogating How University Cultural Scripts Shape Personal and Political Facets of Belonging
citation: Rebecca Covarrubias. (2024). On Being Accepted: Interrogating How University Cultural Scripts Shape Personal and Political Facets of Belonging. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09970-2
title: Counterspaces with three processes for sustaining marginalized students' belonging
description: Counterspaces are relational spaces where students with shared marginalization share, affirm, and analyze counter-stories, satisfying relational and cultural place-belongingness needs. The article describes them as psychological and relational sites of resistance that reshape dominant power structures 'through three distinct processes: narrative identity work, direct relational transactions, and acts of resistance (Case & Hunter, 2012).' Many institutional spaces, including research labs and ethnic studies courses, can function as counterspaces, though they sit outside the main fabric of the institution.
requirements: Participants must be able to feel accepted within safe parameters while a critical approach heightens awareness of the politics of belonging
constraints: Counterspaces are considered 'counter' because they do not exist within the main fabric of the institution
target_learners: marginalized undergraduate students, e.g., undergraduate women of color in STEM at a predominantly white institution
target_learning_goals: fostering belonging, navigational competence in dominant culture, and resistance to structural marginalization
examples: A year-long community initiative at a PWI served as a counterspace and fostered belonging for undergraduate women of color in STEM (Wilkins-Yel et al., 2022); a counterspace for first-generation students of color mobilized navigational and resistance capital
key_sources: Rebecca Covarrubias. (2024). On Being Accepted: Interrogating How University Cultural Scripts Shape Personal and Political Facets of Belonging. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09970-2

article_title: On Being Accepted: Interrogating How University Cultural Scripts Shape Personal and Political Facets of Belonging
citation: Rebecca Covarrubias. (2024). On Being Accepted: Interrogating How University Cultural Scripts Shape Personal and Political Facets of Belonging. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09970-2
title: Nepantla and world-traveling: multiple selves at the margins of social worlds
description: Drawing on Anzaldúa and Lugones, the article theorizes that individuals hold multiple selves that move across social worlds, and that marginalized people must 'travel' between worlds as a matter of necessity and survival. Nepantla is 'an in-between liminal state of being that is the result of world traveling,' a painful but potentially transformative space where clashing worldviews collide. Moving through nepantla can liberate individuals from constraining norms and enable re-narration of limiting cultural scripts, linking psychological processes with structural realities.
requirements: Transformation requires moving through the discomfort of nepantla rather than retreating from it, which Anzaldúa argues thwarts its transformative potential
constraints: The account is theoretical and draws on scholars theorizing life at the margins of multiple social worlds; it is not an empirically tested model in this article
target_learners: marginalized undergraduate students navigating multiple cultural worlds
target_learning_goals: sustaining authentic plural selves while succeeding in dominant institutional settings
examples: Valle and Covarrubias (2024) documented five low-income, first-generation Mexican American women resisting racist, sexist, and classist scripts and creating new narratives; Bernal (2001) explored Chicana undergraduates leveraging plurality to navigate college challenges
key_sources: Rebecca Covarrubias. (2024). On Being Accepted: Interrogating How University Cultural Scripts Shape Personal and Political Facets of Belonging. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09970-2

article_title: On Being Accepted: Interrogating How University Cultural Scripts Shape Personal and Political Facets of Belonging
citation: Rebecca Covarrubias. (2024). On Being Accepted: Interrogating How University Cultural Scripts Shape Personal and Political Facets of Belonging. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09970-2
title: UCLA Migrant Student Leadership Institute as a third space
description: The MSLI is presented as an illustrative example of a third space—an approach or zone of development that transforms 'conflict and difference into rich zones of collaboration and learning.' It reorganized educational practices so that college-bound students of color from migrant farmworker backgrounds could see themselves as learners and social change agents, drawing on rigorous texts, mini-lectures, discussions, writing and reading conferences, field trips, theater, and college preparation workshops, and connecting students' community histories to present-day realities.
requirements: Organizers must work outside pre-existing conventions of what a learning space and its tools are
constraints: The third space emerges from the collision of official and unofficial scripts; redirecting students back to the official curriculum thwarts its transformative potential
target_learners: college-bound students of color from migrant farmworker backgrounds
target_learning_goals: critical inquiry, seeing oneself as a learner and social change agent, and revising constructions of self, community, and schooling
examples: Students used traditional tools such as dictionaries and conventional writing rules in new ways to reflect on, contest, and revise their constructions of themselves and their schooling experiences
key_sources: Rebecca Covarrubias. (2024). On Being Accepted: Interrogating How University Cultural Scripts Shape Personal and Political Facets of Belonging. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09970-2

article_title: Opting Out as an Untapped Resource in Instructional Design: Review and Implications
citation: Yael Sidi · Rakefet Ackerman. (2024). Opting Out as an Untapped Resource in Instructional Design: Review and Implications. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09879-w
title: Region of Proximal Learning framework for strategic opting out
description: The Region of Proximal Learning framework explains learners' self-regulated choices about which task components to engage. Learners "continue to work on each task item as long as they metacognitively sense progress while thinking", and disengage from tasks exceeding their self-perceived trajectory. The review extends this framework to opting out, proposing that effective strategic opting out rests on "a fine-tuned balance between the perceived challenge level of each task item and the motivation to overcome it", so motivated students can be taught when and what to quit.
requirements: Learners must metacognitively sense progress while thinking to sustain engagement on task items
constraints: Tasks perceived as overly simplistic fail to stimulate cognitive advancement, while excessively challenging tasks may exceed current cognitive capacity
target_learners: students in learning and assessment contexts, from primary school to higher education
target_learning_goals: strategic effort regulation and self-regulated learning task choice
examples: The review interprets output-bound accuracy findings through this framework: by adjusting confidence thresholds to motivation and opting out of uncertain responses, learners engage tasks at the right challenge level
key_sources: Yael Sidi · Rakefet Ackerman. (2024). Opting Out as an Untapped Resource in Instructional Design: Review and Implications. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09879-w

article_title: The Validity of Heart Rate Variability (HRV) in Educational Research and a Synthesis of Recommendations
citation: Hyun Jin Kim, Yuyi Park, Jihyun Lee. (2024). The Validity of Heart Rate Variability (HRV) in Educational Research and a Synthesis of Recommendations. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09878-x
title: HRV as a psychophysiological index of autonomic nervous system balance underlying self-regulation
description: The review presents HRV as "a quantitative expression of balance in the functioning of the autonomic nervous system (ANS)", reflecting sympathetic (alertness) versus parasympathetic (relaxation) modulation. Via brain–heart connections — inhibitory GABAergic pathways from prefrontal cortex to amygdala and amygdala regulation of the ANS through hormones and neurotransmitters — HRV indexes physiological, emotional, and cognitive regulation, so high HRV implies balanced ANS allowing flexible, resilient responses, while lower HRV can signal imbalance. Educational studies use it to objectively track learner stress and attention states in real time.
requirements: HRV measurement must account for physiological factors such as cardiac function, respiration rate, age, health status, and medications that influence the signal
constraints: HRV is influenced by a wide range of physiological, emotional, and cognitive factors, so the review warns the information it provides can be easily misconstrued and interpretation difficulties can limit real-world implications
target_learners: learners in educational contexts aged 5 to 65, including primary, secondary, undergraduate, and professional learners
target_learning_goals: measuring learner stress
measuring learner attention
understanding learners' emotional and cognitive self-regulation during learning
examples: The review's 48 included studies applied HRV during exams, learning activities, and experiments to capture changes in learner states over time
key_sources: Hyun Jin Kim, Yuyi Park, Jihyun Lee. (2024). The Validity of Heart Rate Variability (HRV) in Educational Research and a Synthesis of Recommendations. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09878-x

article_title: The Dynamic Nature of Emotions in Language Learning Context: Theory, Method, and Analysis
citation: Peng Wang, Lesya Ganushchak, Camille Welie, Roel van Steensel. (2024). The Dynamic Nature of Emotions in Language Learning Context: Theory, Method, and Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09946-2
title: Refined CDST interpretation of emotions in SLA emphasizing temporal relationships among emotional factors over time
description: The article proposes a refinement of complex dynamic systems theory for second language acquisition in which emotions such as anxiety, enjoyment and boredom are conceptualized as trajectories that fluctuate across timescales, from seconds for word production to years for overall development. The authors state: "we emphasize the importance of examining the dynamic interplay among emotional factors over time, particularly the temporal relationship among factors." Unlike the current CDST framework, which focuses on longitudinal aggregate properties, this interpretation operationalizes both macro levels (development across conversations and classes) and micro levels (fluctuations within a single speech or sentence production), and treats temporal succession as a basis for inferring causality.
requirements: High-frequency time series data on emotions and language behaviours across timescales, since the framework requires observing how changes in one factor are followed by changes in another over time
constraints: The article notes that with the contemporary CDST understanding and traditional methodology, only a static relationship may be researched and demonstrated
target_learning_goals: Understanding and supporting emotional dynamics during second language learning and use
examples: The article presents a hypothetical graph (Fig. 2) in which an initial surge in enjoyment is followed by a fall in anxiety and later by an increase in boredom, illustrating potential temporal relationships among emotions concurrent with language behaviours
key_sources: Peng Wang, Lesya Ganushchak, Camille Welie, Roel van Steensel. (2024). The Dynamic Nature of Emotions in Language Learning Context: Theory, Method, and Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09946-2

article_title: The Dynamic Nature of Emotions in Language Learning Context: Theory, Method, and Analysis
citation: Peng Wang, Lesya Ganushchak, Camille Welie, Roel van Steensel. (2024). The Dynamic Nature of Emotions in Language Learning Context: Theory, Method, and Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09946-2
title: Idiodynamic method for capturing micro-level emotion dynamics in language use
description: The idiodynamic method tracks moment-to-moment changes in subjective emotional intensity during communication events. Operationally, "the idiodynamic method relies on post hoc recalling of language behaviours stimulated by according video": participants review recordings of short communication episodes and continuously rate target factors by pressing buttons indicating increases or decreases, with ratings returning to a neutral value when no button is pressed. The review reports it has revealed that anxiety and enjoyment levels can vary significantly within a single task or interaction, but that correlation-based analyses still yield largely static results.
requirements: Specialized software facilitating granular analysis of communication events, and video recordings of the communication episodes for post hoc review
constraints: The button-clicking and value-returning mechanism may introduce task switching and multitasking that could promote anxiety and affect cognitive load and working memory, interfering with the natural cognitive processes of language use
The only available idiodynamic software has limited compatibility with high-resolution tools like EEG, restricting concurrent capture of subjective and physiological data
target_learners: Second language learners in communication tasks
target_learning_goals: Capturing real-time fluctuations of emotions such as anxiety and enjoyment during language use
examples: The review cites studies applying the method to SLA factors, finding that anxiety and enjoyment levels can vary significantly within a single task or interaction
key_sources: Peng Wang, Lesya Ganushchak, Camille Welie, Roel van Steensel. (2024). The Dynamic Nature of Emotions in Language Learning Context: Theory, Method, and Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09946-2

article_title: The Dynamic Nature of Emotions in Language Learning Context: Theory, Method, and Analysis
citation: Peng Wang, Lesya Ganushchak, Camille Welie, Roel van Steensel. (2024). The Dynamic Nature of Emotions in Language Learning Context: Theory, Method, and Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09946-2
title: Experience sampling method (ESM) for capturing macro-level emotion dynamics in language learning
description: ESM, also known as ecological momentary assessment, originated in psychiatry and collects real-time data on participants' behaviours, experiences and psychological states in natural environments. Participants are prompted "multiple times per day over a specified period ranging from days to weeks", via fixed, random, or event-contingent prompts on smartphones or wearable devices. The review proposes ESM to fill the gap of methodologies examining emotion dynamics from a macro, developmental perspective in language studies, illustrating a hypothetical two-week exam-period design with prompts after language activities plus contextual questions.
requirements: Mobile technologies such as smartphones or wearable devices to deliver prompts, and specialized statistical techniques handling multilevel intensive longitudinal data
constraints: Participant burden from intensive sampling may lead to fatigue or noncompliance over time
Repeated assessments may introduce reactivity, though studies have shown reactivity tends to be minimal and short-lived in ESM designs
target_learners: Second language learners in daily learning contexts
target_learning_goals: Tracking variability, stability and trajectories of emotions and their antecedents and consequences during language development
examples: The article sketches a hypothetical study prompting students after conversations, classes, essays, or reading to report emotions toward their most recent language use experience, alongside questions about topic complexity, conversational effort, and learning environment
key_sources: Peng Wang, Lesya Ganushchak, Camille Welie, Roel van Steensel. (2024). The Dynamic Nature of Emotions in Language Learning Context: Theory, Method, and Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09946-2

article_title: The Dynamic Nature of Emotions in Language Learning Context: Theory, Method, and Analysis
citation: Peng Wang, Lesya Ganushchak, Camille Welie, Roel van Steensel. (2024). The Dynamic Nature of Emotions in Language Learning Context: Theory, Method, and Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09946-2
title: Vector autoregression (VAR) as an analytical method for temporal relationships between emotions and language behaviours
description: The review introduces vector autoregression as a statistical technique for analysing how a vector of observations at a given time-point is influenced by vectors of observations at previous time-points. In the simplest VAR(1) model, observations at time t are regressed on observations at time t-1; higher-order models capture dependencies at further distances. Its power lies in accounting for both within-variable and between-variable dynamics, revealing how a variable's future values are predicted by its own past values and by past values of other variables, addressing temporal relationships that the review says have never been validly explored in SLA emotion studies.
requirements: Intensive longitudinal time series data on the emotions and language behaviours of interest, collected at a sampling rate matching the timescale of the hypothesized temporal relationships
target_learners: Second language learners studied at individual or group level
target_learning_goals: Identifying temporal (auto-)correlations among emotions and language behaviours to inform timely interventions
examples: The review illustrates that if a hypothetical VAR model showed anxiety at a previous time-point positively predicting later anxiety while negatively predicting enjoyment, educators could design interventions that proactively address anxiety before it undermines enjoyment
key_sources: Peng Wang, Lesya Ganushchak, Camille Welie, Roel van Steensel. (2024). The Dynamic Nature of Emotions in Language Learning Context: Theory, Method, and Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09946-2

article_title: Revisiting the Role of Social and Dimensional Comparisons in the Internal/External Frame of Reference Model: A Systematic Comparison of the Classic and the Difference I/E Model
citation: Fabian Wolff, Jennifer Schumacher, Jens Möller. (2026). Revisiting the Role of Social and Dimensional Comparisons in the Internal/External Frame of Reference Model: A Systematic Comparison of the Classic and the Difference I/E Model. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10212-w
title: Classic Internal/External Frame of Reference (I/E) Model
description: The classic I/E model (Marsh, 1986) describes the formation of students' math and verbal self-concepts through two comparison processes. It assumes "students compare their achievements in a given domain with the achievements of their classmates in the same domain," producing positive within-domain effects, and that dimensional (internal) comparisons between domains produce negative between-domain effects. The model has shaped educational-psychological research on academic self-concept for over 40 years and served as the starting point for dimensional comparison theory.
requirements: Achievement data from at least two domains (e.g., math and verbal) and domain-specific self-concept measures from the same students
constraints: Negative between-domain effects have been found particularly among secondary school students, with less consistent findings for primary school students in lower grades
Between-domain effects were positive or close to zero in some countries, suggesting cultural context moderates the contrast process
target_learning_goals: academic self-concept formation in domain-specific subjects
key_sources: Fabian Wolff, Jennifer Schumacher, Jens Möller. (2026). Revisiting the Role of Social and Dimensional Comparisons in the Internal/External Frame of Reference Model: A Systematic Comparison of the Classic and the Difference I/E Model. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10212-w

article_title: Revisiting the Role of Social and Dimensional Comparisons in the Internal/External Frame of Reference Model: A Systematic Comparison of the Classic and the Difference I/E Model
citation: Fabian Wolff, Jennifer Schumacher, Jens Möller. (2026). Revisiting the Role of Social and Dimensional Comparisons in the Internal/External Frame of Reference Model: A Systematic Comparison of the Classic and the Difference I/E Model. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10212-w
title: Difference I/E Model as a Reparameterization of the Classic I/E Model
description: The difference I/E model, proposed by Wolff (2021), is a reparameterization of the classic I/E model in which "self-concept in one domain is regressed on achievement in the same domain and on the difference between achievement in the same domain and achievement in the other domain." This operationalization aims to separate within-domain achievement effects (including social comparisons) from between-domain achievement effects (including dimensional comparisons), assigning each type of comparison to only one path. Both specifications yield identical model fit and explain the same variance in self-concepts.
requirements: Achievement data from two domains and computation of the difference between standardized achievement scores
constraints: Both model specifications yield identical model fit; differences in effect sizes reflect parameterization and variance allocation, not different psychological processes
The redistribution of variance in the difference I/E model is not unique; other transformations are conceivable
target_learning_goals: academic self-concept formation in domain-specific subjects
key_sources: Fabian Wolff, Jennifer Schumacher, Jens Möller. (2026). Revisiting the Role of Social and Dimensional Comparisons in the Internal/External Frame of Reference Model: A Systematic Comparison of the Classic and the Difference I/E Model. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10212-w

article_title: Revisiting the Role of Social and Dimensional Comparisons in the Internal/External Frame of Reference Model: A Systematic Comparison of the Classic and the Difference I/E Model
citation: Fabian Wolff, Jennifer Schumacher, Jens Möller. (2026). Revisiting the Role of Social and Dimensional Comparisons in the Internal/External Frame of Reference Model: A Systematic Comparison of the Classic and the Difference I/E Model. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10212-w
title: Avoid labeling within-domain effects in the classic I/E model as pure social comparison effects
description: The article recommends that researchers avoid interpreting within-domain effects in the classic I/E model as exclusively reflecting social comparisons. The authors state that "labeling the within-domain effects in the classic I/E model as 'social comparison effects', as occasionally done in the literature... should be avoided" because these effects likely also reflect dimensional comparisons, criterion-based comparisons against individual or objective standards, and temporal comparisons. They recommend the more cautious terms "within-domain effects" and "between-domain effects."
requirements: Researchers interpreting I/E model coefficients should consider that multiple comparison processes (social, dimensional, criterion-based, temporal) may contribute to within-domain effects
constraints: This recommendation applies specifically to the interpretation of effects in the classic I/E model parameterization
target_learning_goals: accurate interpretation of academic self-concept formation processes
examples: The authors use the terms 'within-domain effects' and 'between-domain effects' throughout their six studies rather than 'social comparison effects'
key_sources: Fabian Wolff, Jennifer Schumacher, Jens Möller. (2026). Revisiting the Role of Social and Dimensional Comparisons in the Internal/External Frame of Reference Model: A Systematic Comparison of the Classic and the Difference I/E Model. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10212-w

article_title: A Systematic Review on Students’ Perceptions of Self-Assessment: Usefulness and Factors Influencing Implementation
citation: Zi Yan · Ernesto Panadero · Xiang Wang · Ying Zhan. (2023). A Systematic Review on Students' Perceptions of Self-Assessment: Usefulness and Factors Influencing Implementation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09799-1
title: Two-aspect framework of students' perceptions of self-assessment: perceived usefulness and perceived factors influencing implementation
description: The review organises students' perceptions of self-assessment around two key aspects: perceived usefulness of self-assessment, and the factors students perceive as influencing its implementation. Within each aspect it distinguishes individual factors (e.g., age, self-efficacy, psychological safety) from instructional or design factors (e.g., external feedback, instruments, purpose, practice, environmental support). The framework is used to synthesise 44 empirical studies and to guide the design of self-assessment activities. As the review states, it "aimed to synthesise the findings on two key aspects of the students' perceptions of self-assessment: usefulness and factors influencing implementation."
requirements: Empirical studies that present students' perceptions of self-assessment, whether or not perceptions are the central topic
constraints: The review focused on explicit and/or structured self-assessment, excluding implicit self-assessment such as spontaneous self-questioning
target_learning_goals: self-assessment engagement
self-regulated learning
examples: The review coded 44 studies against this framework, reporting usefulness findings for RQ2-RQ3 and implementation factors for RQ4.
key_sources: Zi Yan · Ernesto Panadero · Xiang Wang · Ying Zhan. (2023). A Systematic Review on Students' Perceptions of Self-Assessment: Usefulness and Factors Influencing Implementation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09799-1

article_title: Does Individual Performance Feedback Increase the Use of Retrieval Practice?
citation: Luotong Hui, Anique B. H. de Bruin, Jeroen Donkers, & Jeroen J. G. van Merriënboer. (2021). Does Individual Performance Feedback Increase the Use of Retrieval Practice? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09604-x
title: Show learners their own performance feedback comparing strategies so they experience a strategy's benefits before expecting them to adopt it
description: This principle holds that learners adopt an effective learning strategy more readily when shown their own actual learning outcomes under that strategy versus an alternative, rather than only receiving general instruction about the strategy's benefits. The article found that "individual feedback led to enhanced use in the long term by those who had actually experienced its benefits". General instruction alone did not sustain long-term use.
requirements: Learners must actually experience the strategy's benefit (obtain a higher score under it) for the feedback to change their strategy choices
Feedback must compare the learner's own outcomes across strategies rather than only presenting class averages or general claims
constraints: Only about half of students benefited from retrieval practice in these experiments, so many learners will not experience the benefit
Individual feedback showed no impact when students who benefited from restudy or had equal scores were included
The general-feedback group came to consider retrieval practice less useful after trying it, so instruction without personal outcome information may backfire in the long term
target_learners: university students studying new factual material
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of factual material
adoption of effective learning strategies such as retrieval practice
examples: In Experiment 2, students on day 8 received either individual feedback showing their own 7-day delayed test scores after each strategy, or general feedback presenting the average rate at which retrieval practice was found superior to restudy from prior studies
key_sources: Luotong Hui, Anique B. H. de Bruin, Jeroen Donkers, & Jeroen J. G. van Merriënboer. (2021). Does Individual Performance Feedback Increase the Use of Retrieval Practice? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09604-x

article_title: Without Integration, Everything Is Nothing: A Meta-Analysis of the Effectiveness of Instructional Support for Drawing-to-Learn
citation: Detlev Leutner · Johanna Biele. (2025). Without Integration, Everything Is Nothing: A Meta-Analysis of the Effectiveness of Instructional Support for Drawing-to-Learn. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10067-7
title: Three-component framework of drawing support based on generative learning and cognitive load theory
description: The article differentiates drawing support into three components: support expected to reduce extraneous cognitive load (e.g., a partially drawn background, selecting main ideas before drawing), support expected to increase germane cognitive load (e.g., explaining before or while drawing), and support expected to facilitate the integration sub-process of generative learning (e.g., comparing self-generated drawings with provided illustrations). The components are features a measure may or may not have, and are "not mutually exclusive": all integration-facilitating measures also increase germane load, but not vice versa. The framework rests on Mayer's SOI model and Cognitive Load Theory.
requirements: Studies must contrast a drawing-only condition with a drawing-support condition on a comprehension or transfer test for the components to be evaluated as moderators
constraints: The components describe potential impact on cognitive processing, not mutually exclusive categories; a single measure can address multiple sub-processes
Learners' characteristics (age, schooling level, prior knowledge) and other support kinds (extra time, drag-and-drop, tablet drawing) were not considered in greater detail
target_learners: students learning science content from text, from school to undergraduate level
target_learning_goals: comprehension and transfer of complex science content through generative drawing
examples: The meta-analysis coded each study's support measure binary on the three components and tested them as moderators of comprehension effects
key_sources: Detlev Leutner · Johanna Biele. (2025). Without Integration, Everything Is Nothing: A Meta-Analysis of the Effectiveness of Instructional Support for Drawing-to-Learn. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10067-7

article_title: Without Integration, Everything Is Nothing: A Meta-Analysis of the Effectiveness of Instructional Support for Drawing-to-Learn
citation: Detlev Leutner · Johanna Biele. (2025). Without Integration, Everything Is Nothing: A Meta-Analysis of the Effectiveness of Instructional Support for Drawing-to-Learn. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10067-7
title: Design drawing support to facilitate integration of verbal and pictorial models, not merely to reduce load or increase generative activity
description: When students draw to learn, support should specifically guide them to integrate their verbal and pictorial models with prior knowledge into a coherent mental model. The article concludes that "it seems essential to help students make sense by integrating the verbal and pictorial models into a coherent mental model that can consistently be stored in long-term memory." Support that only keeps learners active or eases drawing demands did not reliably help.
requirements: Support must prompt learners to build referential connections between their verbal and pictorial models, e.g., explaining while drawing or comparing their drawing with a provided illustration
constraints: Evidence covers comprehension of science content learned from text with hand drawing; transfer moderator analysis was not conducted (k = 7 effect sizes, below the k = 10 rule of thumb)
target_learners: school, high-school, and undergraduate students in STEM learning contexts
target_learning_goals: deeper comprehension of complex science content through drawing-to-learn activities
examples: In the meta-analysis, support such as explaining while drawing, viewing a teacher drawing while checking one's own drawing, and revising drawings by inspecting a provided illustration was coded as facilitating integration and showed g = 0.35
key_sources: Detlev Leutner · Johanna Biele. (2025). Without Integration, Everything Is Nothing: A Meta-Analysis of the Effectiveness of Instructional Support for Drawing-to-Learn. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10067-7

article_title: Should we Tell Teachers That They Are (In)Correct? How Personalized Refutation Text Promotes or Hampers Conceptual Change
citation: Anna-Sophia Dersch · Ian Thacker · Alexander Eitel (2026). Should we Tell Teachers That They Are (In)Correct? How Personalized Refutation Text Promotes or Hampers Conceptual Change. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10116-9
title: Knowledge Revision Components (KReC) framework of conceptual change
description: The article adopts the Knowledge Revision Components Framework by Kendeou and O'Brien (2014), which it says "is supported by strong evidence in the subject of reducing misconceptions". According to the framework, "conceptual change occurs through (1) co-activation of the misconception and the correct information that is aimed to refute the misconception", followed by (2) integration of the correct information into the relevant cognitive schema, and (3) competing-activation, in which the correct information is activated iteratively more strongly than the misconception, which is inhibited in relevant situations. Refutation texts are presented as a way to achieve co-activation.
requirements: Conceptual change requires deliberate processing, which requires active mental effort and motivation to engage with the presented information
target_learning_goals: revising math-gender misconceptions
conceptual change about scientifically unsupported beliefs
examples: The study's refutation texts name a common math-gender misconception, state that it is incorrect, and provide the correct alternative explanation to achieve co-activation
key_sources: Anna-Sophia Dersch · Ian Thacker · Alexander Eitel (2026). Should we Tell Teachers That They Are (In)Correct? How Personalized Refutation Text Promotes or Hampers Conceptual Change. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10116-9

article_title: Should we Tell Teachers That They Are (In)Correct? How Personalized Refutation Text Promotes or Hampers Conceptual Change
citation: Anna-Sophia Dersch · Ian Thacker · Alexander Eitel (2026). Should we Tell Teachers That They Are (In)Correct? How Personalized Refutation Text Promotes or Hampers Conceptual Change. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10116-9
title: Backfire effects: knowledge, attitude, and worldview backfire in refutation
description: The article defines backfire effects as "the ironic reinforcement of a misconception after an attempted refutation". It distinguishes knowledge backfire (misconceptions reinforced), attitude backfire (related stereotypes reinforced when misconceptions are strongly related to attitudes), and worldview backfire, which "occurs due to a refutational message contradicting learners’ core values, threatening their self-concept and/or identity", potentially triggering anger as negative affect of external blame. Math and gender are argued to be identity-relevant domains, making worldview and attitude backfire plausible when refuting math-gender misconceptions.
requirements: Backfire is expected when the refutational message threatens learners' identity or self-concept, with anger (external blame) as a proposed mediator
constraints: The article notes prior topics differed: worldview backfire was found for genetically modified foods but not for multimedia learning, depending on identity relevance
target_learning_goals: avoiding reinforcement of misconceptions during refutation
examples: The study tested whether personalized refutation texts on math-gender misconceptions trigger stronger worldview backfire via increased self-implication and threat appraisal
key_sources: Anna-Sophia Dersch · Ian Thacker · Alexander Eitel (2026). Should we Tell Teachers That They Are (In)Correct? How Personalized Refutation Text Promotes or Hampers Conceptual Change. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10116-9

article_title: Should we Tell Teachers That They Are (In)Correct? How Personalized Refutation Text Promotes or Hampers Conceptual Change
citation: Anna-Sophia Dersch · Ian Thacker · Alexander Eitel (2026). Should we Tell Teachers That They Are (In)Correct? How Personalized Refutation Text Promotes or Hampers Conceptual Change. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10116-9
title: Math-gender Misconceptions Questionnaire short version (MGMQ-s)
description: The MGMQ-s is the pre- and post-test measure of teachers' math-gender misconceptions. It "consists of two misconceptions scales (empathizing-systemizing ... and girls' compensation" with four items each, plus eight correct filler items to balance the questionnaire. For each item participants indicate agreement dichotomously and certainty on a five-point Likert scale; misconception scores are computed by multiplying agreement (−1/+1) by certainty (0–4), yielding item values from −4 to +4, with higher scores expressing stronger misconceptions. Items are presented in a newly randomized order per participant.
requirements: A criterion determines a misconception as prevalent if a participant agreed to at least one item per scale with high certainty (certain or absolutely certain)
target_learning_goals: measuring empathizing-systemizing and girls' compensation misconceptions
examples: Used as pre-test and post-test in the 2×2 experiment; conceptual change scores were calculated by subtracting pre-test from post-test results
key_sources: Anna-Sophia Dersch · Ian Thacker · Alexander Eitel (2026). Should we Tell Teachers That They Are (In)Correct? How Personalized Refutation Text Promotes or Hampers Conceptual Change. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10116-9

article_title: Should we Tell Teachers That They Are (In)Correct? How Personalized Refutation Text Promotes or Hampers Conceptual Change
citation: Anna-Sophia Dersch · Ian Thacker · Alexander Eitel (2026). Should we Tell Teachers That They Are (In)Correct? How Personalized Refutation Text Promotes or Hampers Conceptual Change. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10116-9
title: Video task measuring awareness of math-gender stereotype-reinforcing behaviors
description: A behavioral measure in which participants watch four scripted classroom videos, each showing "a female model teacher’s math-gender stereotype-reinforcing behavior in a math lesson, for example the teacher praising girls exaggeratedly for very easy tasks while praising boys moderately for more difficult tasks", plus distractor behaviors. Participants answer an open-ended question about which teaching strategies and behaviors they notice and would adopt; detection (0/1) and critical evaluation (−3 to +3) are summed into an awareness score. Two condition-blinded raters quantified answers with good interrater reliability (κ Cohen = 0.73).
requirements: Participants were not told in advance that stereotype-reinforcing behaviors would appear, to increase ecological validity; each video could be watched only once but paused freely
constraints: The article states the measure "must be considered exploratory and its transfer validity is hence limited" due to null-correlations with the misconception measures
target_learning_goals: detecting and critically evaluating stereotype-reinforcing teacher behaviors
examples: Administered as post-test 2 after the learning phase and misconception post-test in the online experiment
key_sources: Anna-Sophia Dersch · Ian Thacker · Alexander Eitel (2026). Should we Tell Teachers That They Are (In)Correct? How Personalized Refutation Text Promotes or Hampers Conceptual Change. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10116-9

article_title: Should we Tell Teachers That They Are (In)Correct? How Personalized Refutation Text Promotes or Hampers Conceptual Change
citation: Anna-Sophia Dersch · Ian Thacker · Alexander Eitel (2026). Should we Tell Teachers That They Are (In)Correct? How Personalized Refutation Text Promotes or Hampers Conceptual Change. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10116-9
title: Adapt personalized (refutation) interventions to individuals' prior knowledge and misconceptions
description: The article recommends tailoring refutation-based interventions to what learners actually believe, rather than addressing all readers as if they held the misconception. Personalized feedback was "contingent upon participants' answers", telling them whether their answers were in line with scientific evidence, reflected uncertainty, or were not in line with it, thereby creating an impasse experience that increases self-implication. The authors conclude: "we recommend that personalized (refutation) interventions be adapted to individuals' prior knowledge and misconceptions", because personalization benefits misconception holders but can harm those without misconceptions.
requirements: Personalized feedback must be adapted to learners' prior performance in a misconception assessment, so that feedback is contingent on participants' answers
constraints: If misconceptions are not prevalent, personalized refutation text may lead to familiarity backfire: by repeatedly naming a misconception, it gains familiarity and becomes more credible than the intended refutation information
target_learning_goals: reducing math-gender misconceptions
promoting conceptual change
examples: Participants received performance feedback on each misconception scale just before the matching text, with three possible feedback versions depending on their pre-test answers

article_title: Tracing and Pointing Support Multimedia Learning: A Cross-Cultural Replication
citation: Yining Wang, Kexin Han, Paul Ginns. (2025). Tracing and Pointing Support Multimedia Learning: A Cross-Cultural Replication. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10005-7
title: Biologically primary tracing and pointing actions support acquisition of biologically secondary knowledge (cognitive load theory evolutionary account)
description: Within cognitive load theory's evolutionary framing, knowledge is split into biologically primary knowledge, acquired effortlessly without explicit instruction, and biologically secondary knowledge, which requires extensive working memory investment. The article contends touch-based pointing and tracing with the index finger are biologically primary actions that "can potentially enhance the learning process because they support learning-related processing without overly taxing working memory", reducing extraneous load by directing attention between text and diagrams. The present study tests this account cross-culturally by instructing Chinese-speaking adults to trace and point while learning heart anatomy.
requirements: Pre-lesson instructions directing learners to make touch-based pointing and tracing actions linking text and diagram elements
constraints: Effects on intrinsic load and intrinsic motivation were not supported in this study; the attention-direction (extraneous load) account is the one the authors treat as supported
target_learners: adult university students learning biologically secondary knowledge such as anatomy
target_learning_goals: comprehension of multimedia lesson material combining expository text and diagrams
examples: Participants were instructed to point at words and corresponding diagram locations, leave a finger on the diagram, and trace along arrows indicating blood flow during a 25-minute paper-based lesson
key_sources: Yining Wang, Kexin Han, Paul Ginns. (2025). Tracing and Pointing Support Multimedia Learning: A Cross-Cultural Replication. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10005-7

article_title: Tracing and Pointing Support Multimedia Learning: A Cross-Cultural Replication
citation: Yining Wang, Kexin Han, Paul Ginns. (2025). Tracing and Pointing Support Multimedia Learning: A Cross-Cultural Replication. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10005-7
title: Give learners omnibus pre-lesson instructions offering multiple hand-action options rather than one restricted action
description: When multimedia lessons require learners to connect text and diagram elements, the article recommends "omnibus" pre-lesson instructions that offer several touch-based options — pointing, leaving a finger on the diagram, using both hands, tracing arrows — rather than a single restricted action. The authors argue such combined instructions "appear to support learning more than more restricted (one-handed) actions on lesson materials", based on a comparison with recent studies that restricted learners to pointing or tracing alone. The present study's instruction sheet modelled this omnibus approach.
requirements: Lesson materials combining expository text with diagrams so that hand actions can link related elements
constraints: The recommendation contrasts this study's combined instructions with computer-based studies using restricted actions; it is the authors' comparative interpretation, not a manipulation tested within this experiment
target_learners: adult learners studying multimedia expository lessons
target_learning_goals: integrating textual and diagrammatic information in multimedia lessons
examples: The instruction sheet offered four options: point at text and corresponding diagram location, leave a finger on the diagram while reading, use more than one finger/hand, and trace along arrows indicating blood flow
key_sources: Yining Wang, Kexin Han, Paul Ginns. (2025). Tracing and Pointing Support Multimedia Learning: A Cross-Cultural Replication. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10005-7

article_title: Should researchers make causal inferences and recommendations for practice on the basis of nonexperimental studies?
citation: Grosz, M. P. (2023). Should researchers make causal inferences and recommendations for practice on the basis of nonexperimental studies? Educational Psychology Review, 35, 57. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09777-7
title: Researchers should discuss practical implications in their articles regardless of design, while transparently communicating limitations and assumptions
description: The article recommends that educational researchers "talk about practical implications in their articles regardless of the design and analysis they used", because practitioners cannot usually postpone decisions and because researchers know their studies' strengths and limitations best. Alongside this, researchers should "clearly and transparently communicate the limitations and assumptions of their findings and how they affect the practical implications", enabling educators and policy makers to make evidence-aligned decisions.
requirements: Researchers must be transparent about relevant limitations and assumptions, discuss them critically, and take them into account when contemplating causal effects and implications for practice
constraints: Experimental studies will usually be more causally informative than nonexperimental studies, so the strength of causal claims should match the design
target_learning_goals: transfer of research findings into educational practice and decision making
examples: The author argues that if nonexperimental researchers stay silent, practitioners may base decisions on anecdotal evidence and personal experiences, which are less trustworthy than nonexperimental evidence
key_sources: Grosz, M. P. (2023). Should researchers make causal inferences and recommendations for practice on the basis of nonexperimental studies? Educational Psychology Review, 35, 57. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09777-7

article_title: Study Demands–Resources Theory: Understanding Student Well-Being in Higher Education
citation: Arnold B. Bakker, Karina Mostert. (2024). Study Demands–Resources Theory: Understanding Student Well-Being in Higher Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09940-8
title: Study Demands–Resources (SD–R) theory explains student burnout and engagement through demands, resources, behaviors, and feedback loops
description: SD–R theory is an explanatory framework for student well-being in higher education, built on the Job Demands–Resources model. It holds that "higher education students’ experiences can be categorized as being demanding or resourceful", that study demands and resources instigate a health impairment process and a motivational process, and that study environments trigger either reactive maladaptive behaviors or proactive adaptive behaviors. The theory includes feedback loops and is graphically depicted in the article's Fig. 1.
requirements: Study environment features must be classifiable as either a study demand or a study resource
constraints: Developed for the higher education context, although the article notes it may also be relevant for other educational contexts such as primary school and high school
target_learning_goals: student well-being (burnout and engagement)
academic engagement and performance
examples: The article aligns empirical evidence from existing SD–R models (e.g., Lesener et al., 2020; Salmela-Aro et al., 2022) with recent JD–R theory developments
key_sources: Arnold B. Bakker, Karina Mostert. (2024). Study Demands–Resources Theory: Understanding Student Well-Being in Higher Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09940-8

article_title: Making the Executive ‘Function’ for the Foundations of Mathematics: the Need for Explicit Theories of Change for Early Interventions
citation: Scerif, G., Blakey, E., Gattas, S., Hawes, Z., Howard, S., Merkley, R., O'Connor, R., & Simms, V. (2023). Making the Executive 'Function' for the Foundations of Mathematics: the Need for Explicit Theories of Change for Early Interventions. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09824-3
title: Four-mechanism taxonomy of EF–mathematics relationships: performance foe, learning foe, learning ally, explicit learning ally
description: The review proposes four non-mutually-exclusive mechanisms by which EF relates to early mathematics. EF may be "a performance foe" (a constraint on demonstrating skills), "a learning foe" (learning mathematics is EF-demanding), "a learning ally" (EF challenge deepens processing of mathematical concepts), or "an explicit learning ally" (adult-guided EF challenge in play-based activities builds metacognitive appreciation of challenge). The taxonomy implies different intervention designs: reducing EF demands suits struggling older learners, whereas well-calibrated increasing EF challenge should facilitate transfer for beginning learners.
requirements: Explicit operationalisation of the mechanism by which EF and mathematics interact during learning, since differing relationships lead to different intervention designs
constraints: The review argues the performance-foe account may fit older struggling learners but that preschool evidence does not point in that direction; remediation for later difficulties is distinguished from laying foundations for all learners
target_learners: Preschool and early primary children beginning mathematics learning
target_learning_goals: Foundational numeracy and executive function co-development
examples: The review's dots-estimation game: keeping mathematical content within the child's range while adaptively increasing EF demands (shorter estimation time, mixed-colour dots) is hypothesised to make EF a learning ally
key_sources: Scerif, G., Blakey, E., Gattas, S., Hawes, Z., Howard, S., Merkley, R., O'Connor, R., & Simms, V. (2023). Making the Executive 'Function' for the Foundations of Mathematics: the Need for Explicit Theories of Change for Early Interventions. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09824-3

article_title: Making the Executive ‘Function’ for the Foundations of Mathematics: the Need for Explicit Theories of Change for Early Interventions
citation: Scerif, G., Blakey, E., Gattas, S., Hawes, Z., Howard, S., Merkley, R., O'Connor, R., & Simms, V. (2023). Making the Executive 'Function' for the Foundations of Mathematics: the Need for Explicit Theories of Change for Early Interventions. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09824-3
title: Developmental cognitive neuroscience account: interactive specialisation explains why isolated EF training transfers poorly in children
description: The review argues that adult models of EF transfer — training frontoparietal control networks to better gate expert systems — apply poorly to developing brains. Because "control networks (involved in EFs) and expert systems (involved in mathematical expertise) are not yet as efficient and specialised as in their adult counterparts", training them in isolation is inefficient; instead they should co-ordinate so they specialise via interactive specialisation processes. The account also notes that session number does not moderate computerised training gains, suggesting such training improves task-specific strategies rather than underlying systems, and that optimal arousal levels support frontoparietal engagement.
requirements: Interventions should co-ordinate developing control and expert systems rather than training control networks in isolation
constraints: The account is framed for developing (child) brains; the review notes EFs remain relevant to adult mathematics, especially for novel and challenging content
target_learning_goals: Understanding mechanisms of transfer from EF training to mathematics
examples: The review cites child–adult differences in frontoparietal recruitment during mathematics, and adults showing child-like recruitment for novel tasks such as negative numbers

article_title: Self-Regulated Learning Interventions for Pre-service Teachers: a Systematic Review
citation: Alazne Fernández Ortube, Ernesto Panadero, Charlotte Dignath. (2024). Self-Regulated Learning Interventions for Pre-service Teachers: a Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09919-5
title: Teachers' dual role in SRL: self-regulated professional and promoter of students' SRL
description: The review frames teachers as occupying a dual role in SRL: they must "apply the SRL principles to their own learning" as self-regulated professionals, and they must be "promoters of their students' SRL". The professional role requires metacognitive knowledge and SRL content knowledge; the promoter role requires pedagogical content knowledge, awareness of students' strategy use, and SRL assessment. The review also cites a proposed third role, self-regulation for teaching actions, and codes interventions against four dual-role subcategories (SRL knowledge, SRL practice, teaching SRL, SRL diagnosis).
requirements: Pre-service teachers need SRL content knowledge and metacognitive knowledge to reflect on their own learning before mastering the pedagogical practice of teaching SRL
constraints: The review notes few studies exist on how teachers assess students' SRL, and that many teachers hold SRL conceptions inconsistent with SRL theory
target_learners: pre-service teachers in initial teacher education
target_learning_goals: regulating one's own learning
teaching and promoting students' SRL
assessing students' SRL strategy use
examples: The review coded 66 interventions against the four dual-role subcategories and found only three covered all of them
key_sources: Alazne Fernández Ortube, Ernesto Panadero, Charlotte Dignath. (2024). Self-Regulated Learning Interventions for Pre-service Teachers: a Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09919-5

article_title: Self-Regulated Learning Interventions for Pre-service Teachers: a Systematic Review
citation: Alazne Fernández Ortube, Ernesto Panadero, Charlotte Dignath. (2024). Self-Regulated Learning Interventions for Pre-service Teachers: a Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09919-5
title: SRL interventions for pre-service teachers rely mainly on indirect instruction within constructivist environments, with a guiding trainer
description: The review classifies pedagogical characteristics into direct promotion of SRL (direct instruction of strategies, work on beliefs, specific methodologies) and indirect activation of SRL (constructivist environments where learners drive their own regulated learning). Among the coded interventions, 34 promoted constructivist environments, pre-service teachers were given opportunities to "actively explore, reflect, and seek for learning" in 62 interventions, and the trainer acted as a guide in 50. Direct instruction most often took the form of metacognitive training.
requirements: A learning environment offering meaningful activities and cooperation with peers and instructors so learners can practise self-regulation and take responsibility for their learning
constraints: Only five interventions targeted pre-service teachers' beliefs towards SRL and learning
target_learners: pre-service teachers in initial teacher education
target_learning_goals: acquiring SRL strategies
developing SRL teaching practices
examples: Interventions used cooperative learning environments and problem-based learning as indirect instruction; direct instruction used metacognitive training, concept maps and rubrics

article_title: Looking at Mental Effort Appraisals through a Metacognitive Lens: Are they Biased?
citation: Scheiter, K., Ackerman, R., & Hoogerheide, V. (2020). Looking at Mental Effort Appraisals through a Metacognitive Lens: Are they Biased? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09555-9
title: Effort appraisals are a type of metacognitive judgment that may be prone to biases through heuristic cue utilization
description: The review proposes that mental effort appraisals function as metacognitive judgments—subjective assessments based on how a person thinks about their cognition rather than on the cognition itself. Like judgments of learning and confidence, they may rely on heuristic cues with varying diagnosticity and be prone to biases, yet still guide regulatory decisions. The review states that "effort appraisals are, in fact, a type of metacognitive judgment" and suggests "the possibility that also effort appraisals may hence be prone to biases, but nevertheless guide people's actions."
requirements: Effort appraisals must be treated as subjective measures requiring validation against objective effort indicators
target_learners: students performing learning or problem-solving tasks
adults and children across cognitive domains
target_learning_goals: accurate self-assessment of cognitive effort investment during learning
key_sources: Scheiter, K., Ackerman, R., & Hoogerheide, V. (2020). Looking at Mental Effort Appraisals through a Metacognitive Lens: Are they Biased? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09555-9

article_title: Looking at Mental Effort Appraisals through a Metacognitive Lens: Are they Biased?
citation: Scheiter, K., Ackerman, R., & Hoogerheide, V. (2020). Looking at Mental Effort Appraisals through a Metacognitive Lens: Are they Biased? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09555-9
title: CLT distinguishes three load indicators—mental load, mental effort, and task performance—that map onto data-driven and goal-driven effort in metacognitive research
description: The review describes a taxonomy of three cognitive load indicators that differ in their causing factors. "Mental Load refers to the demands a task imposes on a person's cognitive resources," seen as independent of person characteristics and corresponding to data-driven effort. "Mental Effort addresses the human-centered dimension of cognitive load," affected by task, person, and their interaction, corresponding to goal-driven effort. Task performance results from the accumulation of all effort types, with effort moderating the relationship between mental load and performance.
requirements: Assumes learners are sufficiently motivated to invest all available resources in task accomplishment
constraints: CLT is commonly conceptualized as a cognitive theory that does not address student motivation
target_learning_goals: understanding how cognitive load components relate to task performance
key_sources: Scheiter, K., Ackerman, R., & Hoogerheide, V. (2020). Looking at Mental Effort Appraisals through a Metacognitive Lens: Are they Biased? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09555-9

article_title: Looking at Mental Effort Appraisals through a Metacognitive Lens: Are they Biased?
citation: Scheiter, K., Ackerman, R., & Hoogerheide, V. (2020). Looking at Mental Effort Appraisals through a Metacognitive Lens: Are they Biased? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09555-9
title: Paas 9-point mental effort rating scale
description: A single-item subjective measure asking people to "rate on 9-point Likert scale the mental effort that was invested to accomplish a task." It is the most prominent effort assessment in CLT research, used in the majority of studies. Benefits include being "easy to administer, cost- and time-efficient, sensitive to variations in task complexity," and causing "only minimal interference with task accomplishment."
requirements: Respondents must be able to introspect on cognitive processes and provide a reliable estimate of effort expenditure
constraints: Single-item appraisal makes reliability difficult to establish
Wording and framing of the question may affect how people interpret effort
It is an open issue whether a person can discriminate between nine different levels of effort
target_learners: students performing learning or problem-solving tasks
target_learning_goals: measuring mental effort investment during task performance

article_title: Integration in the Achievement Motivation Literature and the Hierarchical Model of Achievement Motivation
citation: Andrew J. Elliot · Nicolas Sommet. (2023). Integration in the Achievement Motivation Literature and the Hierarchical Model of Achievement Motivation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09785-7
title: Hierarchical model of achievement motivation: energization and direction as separate, hierarchically linked components
description: The hierarchical model of achievement motivation is an integrative framework in which energization and direction are separate, equally important components of motivation. Energization is the 'why' of behavior and exerts a distal, indirect influence, while direction channels it into concrete goal pursuit that proximally predicts behavior. The model is hierarchical in focus (abstract-to-concrete constructs) and function (energizing vs. guiding roles), and the authors present it as 'a theoretical foundation from which integrative work may be organized and carried out.'
requirements: Constructs must be precisely defined and conceptualized so their nature and boundaries are clearly understood before integration
constraints: The model requires competence to be present in either the energization or the direction component for achievement motivation to be implicated
target_learners: learners across school, sport, and work domains
target_learning_goals: competence-relevant behavior and achievement outcomes
examples: The model links achievement motives (energization) to achievement goals (direction), which in turn proximally predict intrinsic motivation and academic performance
key_sources: Andrew J. Elliot · Nicolas Sommet. (2023). Integration in the Achievement Motivation Literature and the Hierarchical Model of Achievement Motivation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09785-7

article_title: Integration in the Achievement Motivation Literature and the Hierarchical Model of Achievement Motivation
citation: Andrew J. Elliot · Nicolas Sommet. (2023). Integration in the Achievement Motivation Literature and the Hierarchical Model of Achievement Motivation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09785-7
title: 2 × 2 standards model of achievement goals: definition and valence components
description: Within the hierarchical model, achievement goals are conceptualized in the 2 × 2 standards model in terms of two components of competence: definition (task-/self-based mastery vs. other-based performance standard) and valence (approach of success vs. avoidance of failure). Crossing these yields four goals: mastery-approach, mastery-avoidance, performance-approach, and performance-avoidance. An achievement goal is defined as 'a cognitive representation of a future competence-based possibility that a person is committed to approach or avoid.'
requirements: Goals are viewed as the conceptual centerpiece or hub of the hierarchical model, emerging from and serving underlying energization
constraints: Achievement goals alone are not sufficient to account for competence-motivated behavior; the energization source must also be identified
target_learning_goals: competence strivings and achievement goal adoption
examples: Example goals as printed: 'I am trying to do better than I have done before' (mastery-approach) and 'I am trying to avoid doing poorly compared to others' (performance-avoidance)
key_sources: Andrew J. Elliot · Nicolas Sommet. (2023). Integration in the Achievement Motivation Literature and the Hierarchical Model of Achievement Motivation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09785-7

article_title: Integration in the Achievement Motivation Literature and the Hierarchical Model of Achievement Motivation
citation: Andrew J. Elliot · Nicolas Sommet. (2023). Integration in the Achievement Motivation Literature and the Hierarchical Model of Achievement Motivation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09785-7
title: Achievement goal complex: fused reason-goal construct operative in self-regulation
description: The goal complex concept captures the idea that energization and direction become enmeshed during self-regulation: when energization prompts a goal, they 'fuse together to create a third reason-goal combined construct that is represented in memory and operative in self-regulation.' Structurally it takes the form 'Try to X in order to Y' or 'Try to X because Y.' The concept is highly flexible, broadly applicable to competence-based and non-competence-based reasons, and ecologically valid in capturing idiographic daily self-regulation.
requirements: Both the energization source and the goal must be identified, since the same goal can be fused with different energization sources and the same energization with different goals
constraints: The billiard ball metaphor, in which energization is left behind after prompting the goal, does not adequately capture how energization and direction work together in actual daily self-regulation
target_learning_goals: competence-relevant self-regulation and goal pursuit
examples: Example complexes as printed: 'Try to do well compared to others in order to experience the satisfaction of competitive success' versus 'in order to avoid losing my scholarship and go further into debt'

article_title: Integration in the Achievement Motivation Literature and the Hierarchical Model of Achievement Motivation
citation: Andrew J. Elliot · Nicolas Sommet. (2023). Integration in the Achievement Motivation Literature and the Hierarchical Model of Achievement Motivation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09785-7
title: Prioritize integrative research over siloed, competitive study of motivational constructs
description: The article argues that because the primary explanatory constructs in achievement motivation have been identified and sufficiently understood, research should now integrate them rather than study them in isolation or cast them as competitors. The authors contend that 'the major advances of the next decade (and, likely, beyond) within the achievement motivation literature will be integrative in nature,' and that failing to move from isolation to integration risks stagnation and incompleteness.
requirements: Clear, precise construct definition and conceptualization must come first, since without such clarity jingle and jangle fallacies abound
constraints: Initial independent study of constituent constructs is described as necessary and beneficial before integration
target_learners: researchers and theorists studying learner motivation
target_learning_goals: a comprehensive account of achievement motivation in educational settings
examples: The hierarchical model's two-step process—first separating and defining energization and direction, then joining them—is offered as a template for how existing frameworks emphasizing one component can be brought together in a single model
