article_title: Cognitive Load Theory: Advances in Research on Worked Examples, Animations, and Cognitive Load Measurement
citation: Tamara van Gog & Fred Paas & John Sweller. (2010). Cognitive Load Theory: Advances in Research on Worked Examples, Animations, and Cognitive Load Measurement. Educ Psychol Rev (2010) 22:375–378. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9145-4
title: Cognitive load theory: instruction should optimize intrinsic load, reduce extraneous load, and foster germane load
description: Cognitive load theory concerns learning complex cognitive tasks in which learners may be overwhelmed by "the number of interactive information elements that need to be processed simultaneously". Its central tenet is that instruction should be designed at an optimal level of complexity (intrinsic load), reduce load from processes not contributing to learning (extraneous load), and optimize load from processes fostering learning (germane load). This editorial uses the framework to organize advances in example-based learning, animation design, and load measurement.
requirements: Instruction must be designed so complexity is at an optimal level for the learner's working memory capacity
constraints: Applies to complex cognitive tasks where interactive elements must be processed simultaneously before meaningful learning can commence
target_learners: novice learners of complex cognitive tasks
target_learning_goals: learning and transfer of complex cognitive task skills
examples: The special issue applies the theory to worked examples in tutoring systems, animation segmentation, and EEG load measurement
key_sources: Tamara van Gog & Fred Paas & John Sweller. (2010). Cognitive Load Theory: Advances in Research on Worked Examples, Animations, and Cognitive Load Measurement. Educ Psychol Rev (2010) 22:375–378. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9145-4

article_title: Cognitive Load Theory: Advances in Research on Worked Examples, Animations, and Cognitive Load Measurement
citation: Tamara van Gog & Fred Paas & John Sweller. (2010). Cognitive Load Theory: Advances in Research on Worked Examples, Animations, and Cognitive Load Measurement. Educ Psychol Rev (2010) 22:375–378. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9145-4
title: Electroencephalography (EEG) as a continuous, objective, online measure of cognitive load
description: Antonenko et al. (2010) describe the possibilities offered by "electroencephalography (EEG) to provide a continuous and objective measure of cognitive load". Unlike offline mental-effort ratings, online process measures indicate cognitive load at specific points in time, allowing hypotheses to be tested in more detail. The element identifies which EEG components can assess load and reviews EEG studies of learning from hypertext and multimedia materials.
requirements: Rapid technological advances making online, continuous measurement methods accessible to educational researchers
constraints: Offline measures such as mental effort ratings yield only indirect evidence because they do not capture load at the relevant specific points in time
target_learners: participants learning from hypertext and multimedia materials
target_learning_goals: measuring cognitive load during learning from multimedia and hypertext
examples: Antonenko and Niederhauser (2010) used EEG's fine temporal resolution to detect load differences when participants accessed hyperlinks with or without content-preview leads

article_title: Motivational Apprenticeship: An Apprenticeship Framework for Developing Students’ Motivational Competencies
citation: Shan Li, Juan Zheng. (2026). Motivational Apprenticeship: An Apprenticeship Framework for Developing Students' Motivational Competencies. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10114-3
title: Motivational apprenticeship: a six-component framework for developing learners' motivational self-regulation
description: The article proposes motivational apprenticeship, a conceptual framework extending cognitive apprenticeship to motivation, so learners "develop autonomous motivational regulation skills". It operationalizes six components: modeling, coaching, scaffolding, articulation, reflection, and exploration, treating motivation as "a teachable skill set rather than solely an internal state". The framework aims to make motivational processes visible and teachable through guided expert support that fades over time.
requirements: Experts who can demonstrate and articulate their own motivational strategies and processes
Authentic learning contexts in which motivational skills are practiced
constraints: The manuscript focuses on students from elementary through postsecondary education; adaptations for teachers, coaches, or other adult learners are stated to be beyond its scope
target_learners: Students at varying developmental stages, from elementary through postsecondary education
target_learning_goals: Autonomous motivational regulation skills
Metacognitive awareness of motivation
Lifelong motivational self-regulation
examples: Table 1 lists sample techniques per component, such as live demonstrations and recorded video examples for modeling, and reflective journals for reflection
key_sources: Shan Li, Juan Zheng. (2026). Motivational Apprenticeship: An Apprenticeship Framework for Developing Students' Motivational Competencies. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10114-3

article_title: Motivational Apprenticeship: An Apprenticeship Framework for Developing Students’ Motivational Competencies
citation: Shan Li, Juan Zheng. (2026). Motivational Apprenticeship: An Apprenticeship Framework for Developing Students' Motivational Competencies. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10114-3
title: Four core principles underpinning motivational apprenticeship: visible, situated, guided, and metacognitive motivation
description: The framework rests on four principles. Visible motivation makes implicit motivational processes explicit, with experts "transparently sharing their struggles with motivation". Situated motivation treats motivation as context-dependent and develops it in authentic contexts. Guided experience provides structured support that gradually increases independence. Metacognitive awareness builds learners' capacity to monitor and regulate their own motivational states, extending Wolters' facets of motivational regulation.
requirements: Experts able to verbalize motivational strategies and struggles
Scaffolded practice opportunities within authentic tasks
constraints: The principles are conceptual; the article presents no empirical test of the principle set itself
target_learning_goals: Metacognitive awareness of motivation
Application of motivational strategies in authentic contexts
examples: A teacher coaching students on an actual multi-week research project as they encounter real motivational challenges

citation: Televantou, I., Marsh, H. W., Xu, K. M., Guo, J., & Dicke, T. (2023). Peer Spillover and Big-Fish-Little-Pond Effects with SIMS80: Revisiting a Historical Database Through the Lens of a Modern Methodological Perspective. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09816-3
title: Doubly latent models for compositional effects
description: Doubly latent models are multilevel latent variable models that estimate compositional effects while correcting for two sources of error: measurement error in individual-level measures, controlled "by using multiple indicators," and sampling error in aggregates, "adjusted for by using latent rather than a manifest aggregation to form the group-level aggregates." The article applies multi-group doubly latent models in Mplus 8 to SIMS80 data to test peer spillover and BFLPE effects, showing they change substantive conclusions relative to manifest models.
requirements: Multiple indicators of the individual-level construct to control measurement error
Latent aggregation of group-level measures to adjust sampling error
Longitudinal or otherwise controlled data supporting prior-achievement controls
constraints: The article notes concern about overcorrecting for sampling error with intact classes, though juxtaposed latent-manifest estimates showed no substantial differences
target_learning_goals: estimating class-level compositional effects on achievement and academic self-concept
examples: Multi-group doubly latent models applied to SIMS80 pre- and post-test mathematics achievement and four-item mathematics self-concept measures

citation: Televantou, I., Marsh, H. W., Xu, K. M., Guo, J., & Dicke, T. (2023). Peer Spillover and Big-Fish-Little-Pond Effects with SIMS80: Revisiting a Historical Database Through the Lens of a Modern Methodological Perspective. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09816-3
title: Phantom peer spillover effects: measurement error and selection bias as sources of misleadingly positive compositional effects
description: The article adopts the concept of phantom effects, coined by Harker and Tymms, defined as "misleadingly positive effects of aggregated variables in compositional models — peer spillover effects that are simply an artifact of the inadequacy in the statistical procedures used." Two facets of student-level under-specification produce them: measurement error bias, which can make non-existent compositional effects appear positive and significant, and omitted variable (selection) bias, whose direction depends on correlations among omitted and aggregated variables. The SIMS80 re-analysis empirically illustrates both facets.
requirements: Statistical models accommodating measurement error (e.g., multiple indicators)
Controls for student-level background variables to address selection bias
constraints: The direction of omitted variable bias is not straightforward to predict; the article notes unmeasured confounding positively related to class-average achievement may never be fully resolved in observational studies
target_learning_goals: interpreting compositional (peer) effects in educational research
examples: SIMS80 re-analysis in which positive spillover effects from a linear-in-means model disappeared under doubly latent models with student background controls

title: SIMS80 cross-national longitudinal database
description: The Second International Mathematics Study (SIMS80), administered by the IEA in the 1980s, is a cross-national database of 13-year-old students from the USA, Canada (Ontario), and New Zealand (13,656 students, 340 schools). Uniquely among IEA and PISA collections, "SIMS80 is based on a pre- and post-measurement design, allowing for controls for the effects of prior achievement on subsequent achievement." The study used forty common mathematics test items across four rotated forms, four-item mathematics self-concept measures, and rich student- and class-level background variables.
requirements: Pre- and post-measurement design enabling prior-achievement controls
constraints: Data are dated (1980s), which the authors state limits their use for informing current educational policy
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement and mathematics self-concept outcomes
examples: Re-analysis replicating Zimmer and Toma (2000) with a subset of SIMS80 data; data publicly available in SPSS format without restrictions

article_title: The Role of School in Adolescents’ Identity Development. A Literature Review
citation: Verhoeven, M., Poorthuis, A. M. G., & Volman, M. (2019). The Role of School in Adolescents' Identity Development. A Literature Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-018-9457-3
title: Sociocultural perspective: identity as multidimensional self-understandings developed through participation in sociocultural contexts
description: The review describes the sociocultural perspective, under which identity is understood as "a multidimensional phenomenon rather than a single entity": people develop a range of self-understandings (e.g., science identity, literacy identity) that are integrated into learner, student, social, and personal identities. Identity develops through participation in contexts such as home, school, and work, where interaction makes identity positions available and tools, norms, and values guide action. Half of the reviewed articles (n = 55) employed this perspective.
requirements: Studies adopting this perspective examine how identity positions and their evaluation, and how tools, norms, and values communicated through educational activities, inform adolescents' identities
constraints: The review reports this perspective as used by the included studies, not as a tested result
target_learning_goals: development of personal, social, and school- and learning-related identity dimensions
examples: Sociocultural scholars in the review studied identities as narratives in interviews, used classroom observations of engagement, or combined both with ethnographic methods
key_sources: Verhoeven, M., Poorthuis, A. M. G., & Volman, M. (2019). The Role of School in Adolescents' Identity Development. A Literature Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-018-9457-3

article_title: The Role of School in Adolescents’ Identity Development. A Literature Review
citation: Verhoeven, M., Poorthuis, A. M. G., & Volman, M. (2019). The Role of School in Adolescents' Identity Development. A Literature Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-018-9457-3
title: Psychosocial perspective: identity development as exploration and commitment processes
description: The review describes the psychosocial perspective, focused on internal psychological processes, in which "two key stages in the identity development of adolescents are distinguished: exploration and commitment." Exploration involves inquiring into new interests and trying out activities to learn what values and goals one deems important; commitment involves making durable life decisions about education, profession, and worldview. Eight reviewed articles adopted this perspective, favoring large-scale quantitative survey studies of identity stage.
requirements: Educational activities that provide opportunities to try out and reflect upon various activities are stressed as fostering exploration and commitment
constraints: Scholars adopting this perspective are generally concerned with the process of identity development rather than the content of specific identity dimensions
target_learning_goals: identity exploration and commitment processes
examples: Survey studies in the review examined the effect of educational characteristics such as education level on the identity stage adolescents find themselves in

article_title: Does Embodiment in Virtual Reality Boost Learning Transfer? Testing an Immersion-Interactivity Framework
citation: Klingenberg, S., Bosse, R., Mayer, R. E., & Makransky, G. (2024). Does Embodiment in Virtual Reality Boost Learning Transfer? Testing an Immersion-Interactivity Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09956-0
title: Immersion-interactivity framework of embodiment
description: The article proposes a 2x2 framework of embodiment for virtual learning environments built on the taxonomies of Johnson-Glenberg et al. (2014) and Skulmowski and Rey (2018). The immersion dimension ranges from low-immersion desktop or tablet simulations to high-immersion HMD-based VR, and the interactivity dimension ranges from incidental gestures (e.g., a laser pointer) to congruent gestures relevant to the learning task. The authors state: "In the context of VR, we propose a 2 × 2 framework of embodiment based on immersion and interactivity, building on these taxonomies." Unlike Johnson-Glenberg's ranked taxonomy, it does not specify whether immersion or interactivity matters more, and it predicts the greatest embodiment when both are high.
requirements: A virtual learning environment whose immersion and interactivity levels can be independently varied so the four combinations can be instantiated
constraints: The framework does not specify whether immersion or interactivity has a greater impact, unlike the Johnson-Glenberg et al. (2014) ranking
target_learners: high school students learning procedural science skills
target_learning_goals: procedural knowledge and transfer of technical procedures
examples: The study instantiated the four cells as VR congruent, VR incidental, PC congruent, and PC incidental versions of a pipetting lesson
key_sources: Klingenberg, S., Bosse, R., Mayer, R. E., & Makransky, G. (2024). Does Embodiment in Virtual Reality Boost Learning Transfer? Testing an Immersion-Interactivity Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09956-0

article_title: Does Embodiment in Virtual Reality Boost Learning Transfer? Testing an Immersion-Interactivity Framework
citation: Klingenberg, S., Bosse, R., Mayer, R. E., & Makransky, G. (2024). Does Embodiment in Virtual Reality Boost Learning Transfer? Testing an Immersion-Interactivity Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09956-0
title: Cognitive Affective Model of Immersive Learning (CAMIL) pathways for embodiment and cognitive load
description: CAMIL is described as "an evidence-based theoretical framework that explains how highly immersive learning environments, such as VR, can influence learning outcomes." It proposes six cognitive-affective pathways through which presence and agency influence knowledge acquisition and transfer. The article draws on two: a pathway in which "higher levels of presence and agency lead to more embodied learning experiences, which should result in better procedural learning outcomes," and a pathway in which immersion and interactivity raise extraneous cognitive load, which can impair learning and transfer. The study tests the embodiment pathway against the cognitive-load pathway.
requirements: Measures of presence, agency, embodiment, cognitive load, and learning outcomes to test the proposed pathways
constraints: The article notes existing evidence does not clarify how the goals of increased embodiment and reduced extraneous cognitive load are congruent
target_learners: learners in immersive virtual learning environments, here high school students
target_learning_goals: procedural learning outcomes and transfer in immersive VR
examples: The study's hypotheses H1-H5 were derived from CAMIL's embodiment and cognitive-load pathways

citation: Klingenberg, S., Bosse, R., Mayer, R. E., & Makransky, G. (2024). Does Embodiment in Virtual Reality Boost Learning Transfer? Testing an Immersion-Interactivity Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09956-0
title: Virtual pipetting simulation with tutorial and test phases in four condition variants
description: The learning material was an adapted version of a simulation used by Petersen et al. (2022a), set in a virtual laboratory with a workstation, micropipette, pipette tips, test tubes, and beakers. It "taught students how to use a micropipette" and "how to correctly perform a serial dilution—a scientific procedure in which the concentration of a given substance is reduced through a series of steps." The simulation "consisted of two parts: a tutorial and a test": a virtual agent guided students through pipetting steps, then students performed a serial dilution alone and received feedback on mistakes. Four versions varied immersion (VR vs. PC) and interactivity (congruent gestures vs. laser-pointer pointing).
requirements: A HMD with controllers or a Windows laptop with mouse and keyboard to deliver the four condition variants
constraints: The narration was in English, so English proficiency was measured in the pre-questionnaire
target_learning_goals: procedural skill in micropipette use and serial dilution, plus declarative knowledge of pipetting
examples: In the VR congruent condition, students physically walked to the station and pressed the controller button to the first or second stop with haptic feedback; in the incidental conditions they aimed a laser pointer and clicked

article_title: Does Embodiment in Virtual Reality Boost Learning Transfer? Testing an Immersion-Interactivity Framework
citation: Klingenberg, S., Bosse, R., Mayer, R. E., & Makransky, G. (2024). Does Embodiment in Virtual Reality Boost Learning Transfer? Testing an Immersion-Interactivity Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09956-0
title: Real-life transfer test with behavior-anchored rating scale rated from head-mounted camera video
description: The main outcome measure was a real-life transfer test in which each student individually performed a serial dilution with concrete laboratory assets identical to the virtual ones. It "measured a total of 22 items, which were grouped into three overall domains: laboratory safety, dexterity, and accuracy of serial dilution," developed with a psychometrics expert and a subject matter expert. Each participant wore a head-mounted action camera, and "the real-life transfer test video of each participant was rated by two independent raters, using a behaviour-anchored rating scale." Interrater reliability (linear weighted Kappa) was 0.877 for safety, 0.575 for dexterity, and 0.361 for accuracy.
requirements: Two independent raters trained on the behavior-anchored rating scale, and head-mounted cameras recording first-person video of each performance
constraints: Interrater reliability for accuracy of serial dilution was rated poor (Kappa = 0.361) and for dexterity fair (0.575) by the article's own standards
target_learners: high school students who completed the virtual pipetting lesson
target_learning_goals: transfer of a learned technical procedure from a virtual environment to real-world performance
examples: Dexterity items such as 'put on a pipette tip correctly' were scored 0-4, and disagreements between raters were resolved by using the mean score

title: Immersion principle: pair highly immersive media with instructional methods that amplify benefits and mitigate drawbacks
description: The article invokes the immersion principle in multimedia learning, which "proposes that people learn more effectively with highly immersive media when accompanied by effective instructional methods that amplify the benefits and mitigate the drawbacks of these technologies." It is used to argue that instructional design in immersive virtual lessons should reduce unnecessary extraneous load and keep learners focused on the content, since highly immersive and interactive experiences can either aid learning or act as seductive details depending on design.

constraints: The article notes gesticulations can in some studies increase cognitive load and impair learning, so embodied interaction is not uniformly beneficial
target_learners: students learning in immersive VR environments
target_learning_goals: acquisition of factual, conceptual, and procedural knowledge and transfer
examples: The study's pre-registered predictions acknowledged that immersion and interactivity could serve as aids to learning or as seductive details that distract from learning in VR

article_title: Screening Smarter, Not Harder: A Comparative Analysis of Machine Learning Screening Algorithms and Heuristic Stopping Criteria for Systematic Reviews in Educational Research
citation: Campos, D. G., Fütterer, T., Gfrörer, T., Lavelle-Hill, R., Murayama, K., König, L., Hecht, M., Zitzmann, S., & Scherer, R. (2024). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09862-5
title: ASReview open-source machine-learning abstract screening software
description: ASReview is an open-source machine-learning tool for abstract screening in systematic reviews, used in this study's retrospective simulation. The article states that "the ASReview software, an open-source platform, provides multiple learning algorithms for both feature extraction and classification." Researchers install it, load a study database (titles and abstracts), classify a small initial subset, then choose a feature extraction method, classifier, balancing strategy (default dynamic resampling), and query strategy (default certainty-based sampling). The algorithm iteratively suggests the study predicted most relevant for the reviewer's include/exclude decision.
requirements: A study database including at least the titles and abstracts of the searched studies, in formats such as .csv, .txt, or .xlsx, plus initial classification of a small subset of relevant and irrelevant studies for training.
constraints: The article states that ASReview currently lacks clear guidelines for when to stop, and it continues to suggest studies until all records have been reviewed.
target_learners: Researchers conducting systematic reviews and meta-analyses in education and educational psychology
target_learning_goals: Efficient and reliable identification of relevant studies during the abstract screening phase of systematic reviews
examples: The study ran 270 retrospective simulation runs (ten learning algorithms across 27 abstract collections) in ASReview's simulation mode, using dynamic resampling and certainty-based sampling.

article_title: Homo Curious: Curious or Interested?
citation: Shin, D. D., & Kim, S. (2019). Homo Curious: Curious or Interested? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09497-x
title: Curiosity as an appetite-like drive to fill an information gap
description: The review develops an appetite analogy for curiosity: hunger is to appetite as uncertainty is to curiosity, so that "curiosity is a desire for information in order to reduce the psychological discomfort of uncertainty." Under drive theory, curiosity is a homeostatic state reduced by filling the information gap, which reinforces information-seeking. The review uses this account to explain why curiosity is aversive yet rewarding, and why information seeking follows a cost–benefit analysis.
requirements: A recognizable information gap between current and desired knowledge that the learner is aware of
constraints: The curiosity–uncertainty relationship is inverted U-shaped: too much information or too large a gap kills curiosity
target_learning_goals: Information-seeking and knowledge acquisition driven by curiosity
key_sources: Shin, D. D., & Kim, S. (2019). Homo Curious: Curious or Interested? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09497-x

article_title: Homo Curious: Curious or Interested?
citation: Shin, D. D., & Kim, S. (2019). Homo Curious: Curious or Interested? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09497-x
title: Forward and backward curiosity: a two-type taxonomy of state curiosity
description: The review proposes a conceptual distinction of state curiosity by its two primary determinants: "We refer to the curiosity elicited by unpredictability and incongruity as forward and backward curiosity, respectively." Forward curiosity (curiosity for what) requires minimal knowledge, involves no prediction or surprise, shows an inverted-U relationship with its cause, and serves knowledge acquisition. Backward curiosity (curiosity for why) requires moderate-to-high knowledge, involves prediction, surprise and confusion, scales linearly with incongruity, and serves knowledge revision through causal search.
requirements: Backward curiosity requires sufficient prior knowledge to make predictions and recognize incongruity
constraints: Not all unpredictability produces forward curiosity unless a discernable information gap is created
target_learning_goals: Distinguishing curiosity experiences to design curiosity-inducing instruction
key_sources: Shin, D. D., & Kim, S. (2019). Homo Curious: Curious or Interested? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09497-x

article_title: Homo Curious: Curious or Interested?
citation: Shin, D. D., & Kim, S. (2019). Homo Curious: Curious or Interested? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09497-x
title: Design learning environments around an optimal knowledge gap, valued information, and curiosity-reinforcing feedback
description: The review translates its curiosity account into design guidance: "The first step to instigate curiosity is creating an optimal knowledge gap and helping students to be aware of it," for example by introducing cognitive incongruity after basic knowledge, posing provocative questions, or withholding critical information. Teachers should also raise the perceived value and lower the perceived cost of information seeking, and use prompt informative feedback so students learn to enjoy being curious.
requirements: Learners must be aware of the information gap for curiosity to spark
constraints: Outcome-oriented assessment and normative evaluation can undermine curiosity by promoting anxiety about competence
target_learning_goals: Curiosity initiation, maintenance, and deep cognitive exploration
examples: The review recommends introducing an exception that deviates from previously learned knowledge, ill-defined problems or problem-based learning, and personalizing material to increase relevance
key_sources: Shin, D. D., & Kim, S. (2019). Homo Curious: Curious or Interested? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09497-x

article_title: Homo Curious: Curious or Interested?
citation: Shin, D. D., & Kim, S. (2019). Homo Curious: Curious or Interested? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09497-x
title: Appendix table of self-report measures of situational interest and curiosity
description: The article's appendix compiles sample items from self-report scales used to measure situational interest and curiosity, organized by citation year. It illustrates measurement problems: the review states that "measures of curiosity and situational interest suffer from both jingle ... and jangle ... fallacies," with some interest items actually measuring curiosity and vice versa, and items relying on transparent self-report susceptible to social desirability.
requirements: Triangulating assessment approaches and developing valid measures to capture the two constructs distinctly
constraints: The validity of alternative measures (related constructs, observation, resource spending, fMRI) remains in question per the review
target_learners: Researchers measuring curiosity and interest in learners
target_learning_goals: Accurate measurement of curiosity versus situational interest
key_sources: Shin, D. D., & Kim, S. (2019). Homo Curious: Curious or Interested? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09497-x

article_title: Future Directions for Theory and Research with Instructional Manipulatives:Commentary on the Special Issue Papers
citation: Scott C. Marley & Kira J. Carbonneau. (2014). Future Directions for Theory and Research with Instructional Manipulatives: Commentary on the Special Issue Papers. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-014-9259-1
title: Concreteness fading: systematic shift from enactive to iconic to symbolic representations to support generalization of deep structure
description: Concreteness fading is an instructional approach in which representations systematically become more abstract over instruction: learners begin with enactive (physical) representations, move through iconic intermediaries, and end with symbolic ones. The commentary describes it as seeking "an appropriate level of instructional guidance" and notes that, unlike providing multiple external representations, "concreteness fading requires that the representations systematically become more abstract". It is grounded in long-standing interest dating to Bruner (1964) and is exemplified in the special issue by Fyfe et al.'s math and science strategy.
requirements: Representations must shift systematically from enactive to symbolic, with iconic representations as an intermediary
constraints: After a period of instruction with external representations learners often fail to generalize learning, which the approach is designed to address; model breaking points may impede transfer when deep structure implied by manipulatives fails to generalize
target_learners: Elementary and secondary mathematics and science learners
target_learning_goals: Generalization of the deep structure of mathematical and scientific concepts to related circumstances
examples: Fyfe et al. (2014/this issue) develop and empirically test a mathematics and science instructional strategy based on concreteness fading; related reading and listening comprehension research used imagined manipulation as an iconic intermediary
key_sources: Scott C. Marley & Kira J. Carbonneau. (2014). Future Directions for Theory and Research with Instructional Manipulatives: Commentary on the Special Issue Papers. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-014-9259-1

article_title: Future Directions for Theory and Research with Instructional Manipulatives:Commentary on the Special Issue Papers
citation: Scott C. Marley & Kira J. Carbonneau. (2014). Future Directions for Theory and Research with Instructional Manipulatives: Commentary on the Special Issue Papers. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-014-9259-1
title: Groundedness continuum of external representations: grounded versus idealized manipulatives
description: Belenky and Schalk's framework, as discussed in the commentary, views manipulatives as a particular form of external representation arranged along a groundedness continuum. As the commentary puts it, "On one end of the continuum are grounded representations that share the visual appearances of objects they represent (e.g., pizzas to represent fractions) while on the other end are idealized representations with superficial characteristics stripped away". The framework organizes predictions about learning, transfer, and interest, with idealized representations expected to facilitate transfer more than grounded ones.
requirements: Classification of a manipulative's position on the groundedness continuum to generate predictions about learning and transfer
constraints: Related research is inconsistent: some studies suggest grounded manipulatives may inhibit learning relative to idealized representations (Kaminski et al. 2009; McNeil and Jarvin 2007)
target_learners: Classroom learners, particularly children in mathematics instruction
target_learning_goals: Learning, transfer, and interest outcomes from manipulative-based instruction
examples: Pizzas representing fractions as grounded representations; plastic circles representing fractions as idealized representations
key_sources: Scott C. Marley & Kira J. Carbonneau. (2014). Future Directions for Theory and Research with Instructional Manipulatives: Commentary on the Special Issue Papers. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-014-9259-1

article_title: Future Directions for Theory and Research with Instructional Manipulatives:Commentary on the Special Issue Papers
citation: Scott C. Marley & Kira J. Carbonneau. (2014). Future Directions for Theory and Research with Instructional Manipulatives: Commentary on the Special Issue Papers. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-014-9259-1
title: Embedded and embodied cognition account: perceptually rich, interactive manipulatives may improve transfer through internalization of multimodality routines
description: Pouw, van Gog, and Paas's account, discussed in the commentary, draws on embedded and embodied cognitive viewpoints to propose that learning with manipulatives is "a complex interplay between structuring and restructuring the environment (i.e., embedded cognition) and a cognitive system consisting of manipulations of perceptual symbols (i.e., embodied cognition)". On this view, perceptual and interactive richness may invite predictable interactions that support targeted meanings, and internalization of multimodality routines for offline processing requires extensive time interacting with manipulatives.
requirements: Extensive amounts of time interacting with manipulatives, more than commonly examined in empirical studies, to allow construction of robust fully grounded representations
constraints: Convincing evidence supporting this and related predictions is currently scarce, as the commentary notes
target_learning_goals: Transfer of learning and construction of internal representations supporting offline processing
examples: The commentary contrasts this account with concreteness fading: if strategies focus on internalization, educators must provide substantial opportunities for physical interaction rather than shifting to abstract symbols
key_sources: Scott C. Marley & Kira J. Carbonneau. (2014). Future Directions for Theory and Research with Instructional Manipulatives: Commentary on the Special Issue Papers. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-014-9259-1

article_title: Future Directions for Theory and Research with Instructional Manipulatives:Commentary on the Special Issue Papers
citation: Scott C. Marley & Kira J. Carbonneau. (2014). Future Directions for Theory and Research with Instructional Manipulatives: Commentary on the Special Issue Papers. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-014-9259-1
title: ICAP framework as a lens for examining instructional support and manipulatives efficacy
description: The commentary proposes Chi's Interactive-Constructive-Active-Passive (ICAP) framework as a potential framework for examining instructional support and manipulatives efficacy. As printed, "The ICAP model differentiates learning tasks by categorizing learning activities as interactive, constructive, active, or passive and links these behaviors to different cognitive processes". Systematically examining learning tasks within this framework may identify specific recommendations for producing high performance on learning outcomes.
requirements: Learning tasks must be categorizable as interactive, constructive, active, or passive
target_learners: Classroom learners across manipulative-based instruction contexts
target_learning_goals: Performance on multiple learning outcome types
examples: The commentary suggests future research focus on quantitative and qualitative factors of instructional activities, including modality of outcome tasks, examined within the ICAP framework
key_sources: Scott C. Marley & Kira J. Carbonneau. (2014). Future Directions for Theory and Research with Instructional Manipulatives: Commentary on the Special Issue Papers. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-014-9259-1

article_title: Future Directions for Theory and Research with Instructional Manipulatives:Commentary on the Special Issue Papers
citation: Scott C. Marley & Kira J. Carbonneau. (2014). Future Directions for Theory and Research with Instructional Manipulatives: Commentary on the Special Issue Papers. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-014-9259-1
title: Allow extended instructional time with manipulatives and examine delay between learning and assessment
description: Drawing on embodied theories and discovery-learning arguments, the commentary recommends that future studies allow more instructional time spent interacting with manipulatives, because successful construction of internal representations likely requires extensive sensorimotor experience. It also recommends examining time between learning and assessment, since "it is likely that the effectiveness of approaches are overestimated when instruction and assessment occur in one session". This principle follows Pouw, van Gog, and Paas's argument that internalization of multimodality routines requires extensive interaction time.
requirements: Instructional designs must provide learners substantial opportunities to physically interact with manipulatives over extended periods
constraints: A review cited in the commentary found less than 5% of educational psychology studies accounted for time spent learning and time between learning and outcome measurement, with most research performed in periods of less than 1 day
target_learning_goals: Construction of robust internal representations and durable learning outcomes
examples: The commentary cites Hsieh et al. (2005) finding that the majority of educational psychology research is performed in abbreviated periods, usually less than 1 day
key_sources: Scott C. Marley & Kira J. Carbonneau. (2014). Future Directions for Theory and Research with Instructional Manipulatives: Commentary on the Special Issue Papers. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-014-9259-1

article_title: Mental Effort, Workload, Time on Task, and Certainty: Beyond Linear Models
citation: Jimmie Leppink & Patricia Pérez-Fuster. (2019). Mental Effort, Workload, Time on Task, and Certainty: Beyond Linear Models. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-018-09460-2
title: Effort–certainty–performance conceptual framework (De Bruin et al., 2017)
description: The article describes a conceptual framework, attributed to De Bruin et al. (2017) and supported by Blissett et al. (2018), in which "mental effort directly influences diagnostic accuracy (performance) and also indirectly influences it through certainty (monitoring judgment)". It treats the mental effort–certainty relation as linear, an assumption the reanalysis challenges by finding a cubic relation. The reanalysis's logistic models tested the framework's suggested causal paths and found evidence favouring simplification to certainty alone predicting performance.
requirements: The framework as specified assumes a linear mental effort–certainty relation, which the article's reanalysis did not support
constraints: The reanalysis found evidence against the framework in its original form, favouring a model in which certainty alone predicts performance
target_learning_goals: accurate self-monitoring (certainty) of task performance
diagnostic accuracy
examples: The reanalysis compared five logistic models (L0–L4) representing the framework, its simplification, extension, or revision
key_sources: Jimmie Leppink & Patricia Pérez-Fuster. (2019). Mental Effort, Workload, Time on Task, and Certainty: Beyond Linear Models. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-018-09460-2

article_title: Mental Effort, Workload, Time on Task, and Certainty: Beyond Linear Models
citation: Jimmie Leppink & Patricia Pérez-Fuster. (2019). Mental Effort, Workload, Time on Task, and Certainty: Beyond Linear Models. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-018-09460-2
title: Test the linearity assumption before reporting linear models for mental-effort relations
description: The article recommends that researchers check whether relations involving self-rated mental effort are linear before fitting and interpreting linear models, because "predictions based on linear models may be substantially biased for most of the range of mental effort". It demonstrates a pragmatic approach: fit competing models of increasing polynomial complexity (none, linear, quadratic, cubic, more complex) in two-level mixed-effects models and compare them on R2M, AIC and BIC. The response-time finding is presented as "a clear example of why testing the linearity assumption and reporting the core outcomes of that check is important".
requirements: Data with multiple measurements per participant on the variables of interest, or sufficiently large samples (the article mentions e.g. 200 students in a course) for single-measurement designs
constraints: With small samples, more flexible random-effects structures and multiple imputation are not to be trusted; the article used compound-symmetry random-intercept models and omitted a small percentage of missing covariate observations
target_learners: researchers and practitioners measuring cognitive load in learning or task-performance settings
target_learning_goals: valid interpretation of self-rated mental effort as a predictor of workload, time on task, or metacognitive variables
examples: The authors reanalysed data from four published studies, comparing Models 0–4 per study on R2M, AIC and BIC in Jamovi
key_sources: Jimmie Leppink & Patricia Pérez-Fuster. (2019). Mental Effort, Workload, Time on Task, and Certainty: Beyond Linear Models. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-018-09460-2

article_title: Mental Effort, Workload, Time on Task, and Certainty: Beyond Linear Models
citation: Jimmie Leppink & Patricia Pérez-Fuster. (2019). Mental Effort, Workload, Time on Task, and Certainty: Beyond Linear Models. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-018-09460-2
title: Model-comparison approach for linear vs non-linear mental-effort relations (Models 0–4)
description: A reusable analytic procedure the article introduces: five competing two-level mixed-effects models (random participant intercepts) ordered by complexity — no relation, linear, quadratic, cubic, and more complex than cubic (mental effort as factor) — compared on marginal R2, AIC and BIC. Model 4 sets "the maximum possible R2M for a set of fixed effects", letting researchers quantify what is lost by simplifying. The authors state "the approach we have provided is applicable to any study that involves sufficiently large samples and/or includes multiple measurements from the same participants".
requirements: Same random-effects structure and identical data across compared models; repeated measurements per participant or large samples
constraints: Compound-symmetry (random-intercept) models were used because more flexible random-effects structures are unreliable in small samples; multiple imputation was avoided in small samples
target_learners: researchers analysing repeated-measurement cognitive load data
target_learning_goals: accurate modelling of relations between mental effort and other learning-relevant variables
examples: Analyses were run in Jamovi version 0.9.5.11, chosen because it is open source and provides marginal and conditional R2 statistics
key_sources: Jimmie Leppink & Patricia Pérez-Fuster. (2019). Mental Effort, Workload, Time on Task, and Certainty: Beyond Linear Models. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-018-09460-2

article_title: Effects of a Reading Strategy Training Aimed at Improving Mental Simulation in Primary School Children
citation: Björn B. de Koning, Lisanne T. Bos, Stephanie I. Wassenburg & Menno van der Schoot. (2017). Effects of a Reading Strategy Training Aimed at Improving Mental Simulation in Primary School Children. Educational Psychology Review, 29, 869–889. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-016-9380-4
title: Embodied situation model account of reading comprehension via mental simulation
description: The article frames reading comprehension as constructing a situation model whose representations are partially based on reactivations of the brain areas governing analogous perception and action. It states that "understanding text involves a mental simulation of described events by reactivating and integrating traces of earlier experiences from multiple perceptual and motor modalities in the brain". Readers who simulate perceptual and motoric elements build an embodied situation model assumed to yield deeper understanding; the training tested whether this process can be taught.
requirements: Readers must retrieve and integrate their stored sensorimotor experiences with the events and objects mentioned in the text
constraints: The article notes mental simulation is a multifaceted concept of which the administered tasks capture only a specific aspect
target_learners: primary school children in Grades 3 and 4
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension via construction of an embodied situation model
examples: The training taught children to use all their senses to represent described events, to simulate implicitly described object shapes, and to simulate implied movement directions
key_sources: Björn B. de Koning, Lisanne T. Bos, Stephanie I. Wassenburg & Menno van der Schoot. (2017). Effects of a Reading Strategy Training Aimed at Improving Mental Simulation in Primary School Children. Educational Psychology Review, 29, 869–889. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-016-9380-4

article_title: Effects of a Reading Strategy Training Aimed at Improving Mental Simulation in Primary School Children
citation: Björn B. de Koning, Lisanne T. Bos, Stephanie I. Wassenburg & Menno van der Schoot. (2017). Effects of a Reading Strategy Training Aimed at Improving Mental Simulation in Primary School Children. Educational Psychology Review, 29, 869–889. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-016-9380-4
title: Mental simulation training program: eight 30-min lessons alternating group instruction and individual computer-based practice
description: A 4-week reading strategy training in which "Mental simulation was taught in a 4-week training program containing eight 30-min lessons (two lessons per week)", alternating group instruction lessons with individual computer-based lessons. The lessons used "a balanced approach of direct instruction, modeling, guided practice, and individual practice", covered multisensory, visual, and motor simulation, and replaced the school's regular reading comprehension lessons during the training period.
requirements: Trained research assistants following standardized instructions delivered the lessons, with each computer-based lesson preceded by an instruction lesson
constraints: The eight lessons replaced the school's regular reading comprehension lessons for the 4-week training period
target_learners: third and fourth graders in regular primary schools
target_learning_goals: connecting sensorimotor experiences to text to build an embodied situation model and improve reading comprehension
examples: Instruction lessons had children describe what they saw, heard, smelled, tasted and felt for a described situation; computer-based lessons used cloze and movement-direction matching exercises
key_sources: Björn B. de Koning, Lisanne T. Bos, Stephanie I. Wassenburg & Menno van der Schoot. (2017). Effects of a Reading Strategy Training Aimed at Improving Mental Simulation in Primary School Children. Educational Psychology Review, 29, 869–889. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-016-9380-4

article_title: Mapping and Drawing to Improve Students’ and Teachers’ Monitoring and Regulation of Students’ Learning from Text: Current Findings and Future Directions
citation: Janneke van de Pol, et al. (2020). Mapping and Drawing to Improve Students’ and Teachers’ Monitoring and Regulation of Students’ Learning from Text: Current Findings and Future Directions. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09560-y
title: Cue utilization framework for monitoring accuracy in learning from text
description: The review adopts the cue utilization framework (Koriat, 1997) as its organizing account of monitoring accuracy in learning from text. It holds that monitoring judgments depend on the cues people use, defined as "bits of information that might potentially be drawn upon or referred to [ … ] to inform a judgment." Cues diagnostic of students' text comprehension should be used and non-diagnostic cues ignored; students and teachers tend to use low-diagnosticity cues such as text length or effort, which harms accuracy. Generative activities like mapping and drawing make diagnostic cues available, and the framework underpins the review's analysis of cue diagnosticity and cue utilization.
requirements: Cues coded from generative-activity products must be reliably measurable so their relation to judgments (cue utilization) and to test performance (cue diagnosticity) can be determined
constraints: The framework is applied in this review to complex text comprehension tasks with mapping and drawing activities
target_learners: students learning from texts in primary, secondary, and university education
target_learning_goals: accurate monitoring and regulation of text comprehension
key_sources: Janneke van de Pol, et al. (2020). Mapping and Drawing to Improve Students’ and Teachers’ Monitoring and Regulation of Students’ Learning from Text: Current Findings and Future Directions. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09560-y

article_title: A Testing Load: Investigating Test Mode Effects on Test Score, Cognitive Load and Scratch Paper Use with Secondary School Students
citation: James Pengelley · Peter R. Whipp · Nina Rovis-Hermann. (2023). A Testing Load: Investigating Test Mode Effects on Test Score, Cognitive Load and Scratch Paper Use with Secondary School Students. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09781-x
title: Tripartite cognitive load model applied to assessment: intrinsic, extraneous, and additive total load
description: The article draws on the tripartite model of cognitive load, in which "intrinsic load (IL) is associated with the complexity of the material being learned" and extraneous load arises from instructional design or environment rather than content. IL and EL are additive: when their combined demands exceed working memory capacity, students experience poorer test performance and comprehension. The study applies this framework to assessment, treating test mode as a manipulation of extraneous load and question difficulty as a manipulation of intrinsic load.
requirements: Assessment of mode effects requires within-subjects comparison, since the subjective experience of intrinsic load varies with individual learner characteristics such as prior knowledge and working memory capacity
constraints: Germane load has been removed from the tripartite model as a discrete type of load and incorporated into intrinsic load
The model is applied here to school-aged students completing physics revision quizzes in authentic classroom contexts
target_learning_goals: physics problem-solving assessed via Ohm's Law calculation questions
examples: The study manipulated extraneous load via computer versus paper test mode and intrinsic load via four low and four high element-interactivity Ohm's Law questions validated by expert teachers
key_sources: James Pengelley · Peter R. Whipp · Nina Rovis-Hermann. (2023). A Testing Load: Investigating Test Mode Effects on Test Score, Cognitive Load and Scratch Paper Use with Secondary School Students. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09781-x

article_title: Examining the Academic Effects of Cross-age Tutoring: A Meta-analysis
citation: Chang, A., Mauer, E., Wanzek, J., Kim, S., Scammacca, N., & Swanson, E. (2025). Examining the academic effects of cross-age tutoring: A meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review, 37, 19. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09997-z
title: Vygotsky's social constructivist theory and the Zone of Proximal Development as the theoretical foundation for cross-age tutoring
description: The article grounds cross-age tutoring in Vygotsky's social constructivist theory, which posits that child development relies on "adult-supervised or peer-mediated experiences with social interaction, critical thinking, and problem solving." The Zone of Proximal Development represents "the range of tasks that a learner cannot yet perform independently, but could perform with the assistance of a more knowledgeable individual." In tutoring, the tutor serves as the more knowledgeable other, providing "support and scaffolding to help tutees accomplish tasks they cannot do alone." The article also draws on Chi's ICAP framework, noting that tutors engage in constructive learning by verbalizing explanations and may reach the interactive mode, "which represents the highest level of cognitive engagement."
requirements: A more knowledgeable tutor who can provide scaffolding within the tutee's zone of proximal development
constraints: The framework is theoretical; the article notes that empirical support comes from observed positive effects consistent with, not directly testing, the mechanism
target_learners: Older student tutors in grades 5 through 12
target_learning_goals: Reading and mathematics academic outcomes
examples: The article interprets tutee gains as learning from a more knowledgeable other and tutor gains as practice of self-explanation, making implicit learning explicit
key_sources: Chang, A., Mauer, E., Wanzek, J., Kim, S., Scammacca, N., & Swanson, E. (2025). Examining the academic effects of cross-age tutoring: A meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review, 37, 19. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09997-z

article_title: How Similar Are Students’ Aggregated State Emotions to Their Self-Reported Trait Emotions? Results from a Measurement Burst Design Across Three School Years
citation: Keller, M. M., Yanagida, T., Lüdtke, O., & Goetz, T. (2025). How Similar Are Students' Aggregated State Emotions to Their Self-Reported Trait Emotions? Results from a Measurement Burst Design Across Three School Years. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09995-1
title: Aggregation of momentary emotional states as a measurement route to trait emotions (Epstein's resolution of the person-situation debate)
description: This framework holds that emotional traits are stable dispositions that can be inferred by repeatedly measuring momentary emotional states and aggregating them per person, resolving the person-situation debate methodologically. The article explains that Epstein "recommends collecting momentary responses from a wide array of situations and time points to identify correlations with stable traits", so that common variance in repeated states captures a person-specific, trait-like component. The study applies this by aggregating experience-sampling state emotions over ten school days per year and comparing the aggregates to one-time trait self-reports on convergence, mean levels, stability, and predictive validity.
requirements: Repeated state assessments across multiple situations and time points (the study used ten consecutive school days of experience sampling per wave)
constraints: Traits here are conceived narrowly as classroom/domain-specific dispositions rather than lifelong dispositions; trait consistency across situations and stability over time cannot be assumed to be absolute
target_learners: secondary school students in the high-achieving track of the Swiss educational system, grades 9-11
target_learning_goals: measuring students' domain-specific academic emotions (enjoyment, anger, pride, anxiety, shame, boredom) in German, English, French, and mathematics
examples: Students activated iPod Touch devices at the start of German, English, French, and mathematics lessons and reported momentary emotions when randomly signaled 10-35 min after activation, once per year across three school years
key_sources: Keller, M. M., Yanagida, T., Lüdtke, O., & Goetz, T. (2025). How Similar Are Students' Aggregated State Emotions to Their Self-Reported Trait Emotions? Results from a Measurement Burst Design Across Three School Years. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09995-1

article_title: Does Touching Real Objects Affect Learning?
citation: Magdalena Novak & Stephan Schwan. (2021). Does Touching Real Objects Affect Learning? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09551-z
title: Cognitive-Affective Theory of Learning with Media (CATLM) as a framework for haptic learning
description: CATLM extends multimedia learning theory by adopting two-channel processing, limited working memory, and active construction, and supplementing them with assumptions about episodic memory, motivation and affect, metacognition, and learner differences. The article uses CATLM to organize empirical findings on haptics along situational interest, attention and information selection, working memory processing, long-term memory storage, and affect. It "also considers tactile, olfactory, and gustatory sensory input as additional information sources that may affect the learning process."
requirements: Learning with haptic input occurs in concert with other learning materials such as verbal explanations, texts, or illustrations
constraints: The article notes systematic research on affective effects of haptic exploration in educational contexts is virtually absent
target_learners: adult learners in informal and museum settings
target_learning_goals: multimodal integration of sensory input with verbal content
knowledge acquisition about real objects and artifacts
key_sources: Magdalena Novak & Stephan Schwan. (2021). Does Touching Real Objects Affect Learning? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09551-z

article_title: Student Characteristics in the Eyes of Teachers: Differences Between Novice and Expert Teachers in Judgment Accuracy, Observed Behavioral Cues, and Gaze
citation: Seidel, T., Schnitzler, K., Kosel, C., Stürmer, K., & Holzberger, D. (2021). Student Characteristics in the Eyes of Teachers: Differences Between Novice and Expert Teachers in Judgment Accuracy, Observed Behavioral Cues, and Gaze. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09532-2
title: Teacher gaze as an additional operationalization of the noticing component of the cognitive model of teacher professional vision
description: The article works within a cognitive model of teachers' professional vision comprising perceptual noticing and knowledge-based reasoning (Lachner et al. 2016). It argues that gaze, measured with eye-movement methodology, "provides a suitable operationalization for noticing processes in the forefront of further processing and interpreting observed events." The study extends this model to diagnosing individual student characteristics, distinguishing bottom-up (stimulus-driven) and top-down (goal-driven) gaze drivers, and tentatively concludes that "adding teacher gaze to the model can enrich our understanding of the processes involved in knowledge-based reasoning."
requirements: Eye-tracking methodology with defined areas of interest on the observed students is needed to operationalize noticing through gaze.
constraints: The article notes the findings are limited in generalizability and replicability as a first study, and that marking students with visible letters might have forced bottom-up processing due to the letters' saliency.
target_learning_goals: teacher diagnostic competence in judging student characteristic profiles
teacher professional vision (noticing and reasoning about student engagement)
examples: In the study, teachers' eye movements were recorded while observing five marked students in whole-class instruction and seatwork scenes of an 11-min geometry video.
key_sources: Seidel, T., Schnitzler, K., Kosel, C., Stürmer, K., & Holzberger, D. (2021). Student Characteristics in the Eyes of Teachers: Differences Between Novice and Expert Teachers in Judgment Accuracy, Observed Behavioral Cues, and Gaze. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09532-2

article_title: Student Characteristics in the Eyes of Teachers: Differences Between Novice and Expert Teachers in Judgment Accuracy, Observed Behavioral Cues, and Gaze
citation: Seidel, T., Schnitzler, K., Kosel, C., Stürmer, K., & Holzberger, D. (2021). Student Characteristics in the Eyes of Teachers: Differences Between Novice and Expert Teachers in Judgment Accuracy, Observed Behavioral Cues, and Gaze. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09532-2
title: Video-based student-profile diagnosis task with eye tracking (11-min geometry lesson, five marked students)
description: The study's core element is an 11-min video of an eighth-grade introductory geometry lesson from a German high school, containing a whole-class question-answer scene (bottom-up drivers assumed) and an individual seatwork scene (top-down drivers assumed). Five students marked with letters B, E, K, P, T each represented one empirically identified profile (strong, struggling, overestimating, underestimating, uninterested) from a latent profile analysis. Participants watched the video under eye tracking, then assigned each student to one profile and wrote down the indicators they had used, with a second-choice option for possible confusions.
requirements: Participants must first be introduced to the student characteristics and the five profiles, and watch a short trailer to become familiar with the lesson and classroom.
constraints: Only the strong, struggling, overestimating, and underestimating profiles were identified by latent profile analysis in percentages of 26%, 21%, 12%, and 9%, with a fifth intermediate low-interest group (31%) treated as comparable to the uninterested profile.
target_learning_goals: diagnostic judgment of individual student characteristic profiles from observed engagement
examples: The underestimating student raised the hand twice and took notes; the struggling student never raised her hand and often rested her head on her hands.
