article_title: Comments on Integration, Theory Conflicts, and Practical Implementations: Some Contrarian Ideas for Consideration
citation: Richard M. Ryan. (2024). Comments on Integration, Theory Conflicts, and Practical Implementations: Some Contrarian Ideas for Consideration. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09858-1
title: True theoretical integration as coherent synthesis grounded in an explicit meta-theory, distinct from aggregation
description: The article distinguishes true theoretical integration from mere combination of variables or measures. In the author's organismic tradition, integration means "bringing them into a truly coherent, organized whole" rather than adding elements. A genuine synthesis creates new insights and frameworks that capture the strengths and address the limitations of the integrated theories, and is grounded in a consistent set of assumptions and meta-theory. The article uses this criterion to evaluate cross-theoretical fusion efforts in the special issue, warning that fused theories may become lists of variables with unclear inclusion criteria and problematic psychometrics.
requirements: An explicit meta-theory and philosophic grounding
A solid set of links between abstract constructs and empirical data
A consistent set of priorities and aims
constraints: A model cannot integrate a theory, but a theory can integrate a model
Theories differ in integrative span; some have no business trying to integrate others
target_learning_goals: Understanding how motivation theories can be legitimately combined or integrated
examples: The author evaluates AGT's combination of mastery versus performance goals with SDT's autonomy construct into a goal complex, asking whether AGT can absorb autonomy's organismic implications
key_sources: Richard M. Ryan. (2024). Comments on Integration, Theory Conflicts, and Practical Implementations: Some Contrarian Ideas for Consideration. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09858-1

article_title: Comments on Integration, Theory Conflicts, and Practical Implementations: Some Contrarian Ideas for Consideration
citation: Richard M. Ryan. (2024). Comments on Integration, Theory Conflicts, and Practical Implementations: Some Contrarian Ideas for Consideration. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09858-1
title: Coordinate distinct theories within interventions when their techniques are compatible and non-contradictory
description: The article argues that practical integration in interventions differs from theoretical integration: distinct theories can be combined in interventions "as long as techniques and processes within different theories can be coordinated and are not contradictory to one another". Different theories address different aspects of the classroom, and applying multiple frameworks is common in professions like engineering and psychotherapy. The author cites pairings such as teacher expectation theory with SDT, and SDT with socio-emotional learning strategies, as readily combined in practice.
requirements: Techniques and processes from the combined theories must be coordinable and non-contradictory
constraints: Some theories cannot be easily integrated and some may be contradictory, e.g. differing definitions of basic psychological need
Social cognitive theory could not incorporate SDT's views of competence growth without radical change in its philosophical foundations
target_learning_goals: Supporting student motivation, engagement, and classroom climate
examples: The article cites Hornstra et al. (2023) combining teacher expectation theory with SDT around positive classroom climate, and Ng (2023) pairing SDT with SEL strategies
key_sources: Richard M. Ryan. (2024). Comments on Integration, Theory Conflicts, and Practical Implementations: Some Contrarian Ideas for Consideration. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09858-1

article_title: Overcoming Fragmentation in Motivation Science: Why, When, and How Should We Integrate Theories?
citation: Reinhard Pekrun. (2024). Overcoming Fragmentation in Motivation Science: Why, When, and How Should We Integrate Theories? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09846-5
title: Two types of theoretical integration: metatheoretical organizing versus merging constructs and propositions
description: The article distinguishes two meanings of integration. Metatheoretical integration organizes constructs and propositions from different theories in a common conceptual space while keeping them as they are, whereas theoretical integration reduces their number by merging them. The author states that "Metatheoretical integration can be useful as a first step towards such integration, but cannot replace it," and uses the term integration throughout to denote merging that simplifies the conceptual space used to describe, explain, or predict phenomena.
requirements: Theories to be integrated must target the same or related phenomena and show convergence of constructs and propositions
constraints: Metatheoretical integration alone cannot replace merging of constructs and propositions
target_learning_goals: academic motivation
examples: The frameworks in the collection (e.g., Skinner's guideposts and buckets) exemplify metatheoretical organization; reciprocal-effects models exemplify true merging
key_sources: Reinhard Pekrun. (2024). Overcoming Fragmentation in Motivation Science: Why, When, and How Should We Integrate Theories? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09846-5

article_title: Overcoming Fragmentation in Motivation Science: Why, When, and How Should We Integrate Theories?
citation: Reinhard Pekrun. (2024). Overcoming Fragmentation in Motivation Science: Why, When, and How Should We Integrate Theories? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09846-5
title: Six options for integrating propositions across theories (Table 2 heuristic model)
description: The article presents a heuristic model of six ways to integrate causal or predictive propositions: identical effects, reciprocal effects, chains of effects, joint causes, joint outcomes, and new effects. Options such as joint causes and joint outcomes reduce the number of propositions by merging constructs, while the new-effects option increases propositions but "allows new insights and creates a broader theory that contains the original theories as subtheories." Options 4 and 5 require functional homogeneity of the merged constructs.
requirements: Constructs subsumed under a merged umbrella construct must show functional homogeneity — the same effects on the outcome — or explanatory power is lost
constraints: Options 4 and 5 lose explanatory power if the functional homogeneity principle is violated; option 6 increases rather than decreases the number of propositions
target_learning_goals: academic motivation
examples: Reciprocal-effects models integrated self-enhancement and skill-development models of self-concept and achievement; joint-cause merging of emotions into positive and negative affect works for hedonic well-being but not task performance
key_sources: Reinhard Pekrun. (2024). Overcoming Fragmentation in Motivation Science: Why, When, and How Should We Integrate Theories? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09846-5

article_title: Overcoming Fragmentation in Motivation Science: Why, When, and How Should We Integrate Theories?
citation: Reinhard Pekrun. (2024). Overcoming Fragmentation in Motivation Science: Why, When, and How Should We Integrate Theories? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09846-5
title: Four levels of functional specificity of theoretical propositions, from non-causal association to functionally specified causal effects
description: The article proposes that propositions differ in specificity, which determines their falsifiability. Table 1 depicts four levels: non-causal association, weak causal effect, moderate causal effect with specified direction, and strong causal effect with a defined functional form. The author notes that "almost all propositions of the motivation theories addressed are located on Levels 1–3" and argues that moving to Level 4 would make contradictions between theories and between theory and evidence easier to detect.
requirements: Precise theoretical propositions and precise measurement are needed, otherwise contradictions may not be detectable
constraints: Even specified Level 1 associations remain weak from a causal inference perspective
target_learning_goals: academic motivation
examples: The article classifies Martin's wheel factors being correlated as Level 1, feedback impacting engagement as Level 2, and teacher support positively affecting outcomes as Level 3
key_sources: Reinhard Pekrun. (2024). Overcoming Fragmentation in Motivation Science: Why, When, and How Should We Integrate Theories? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09846-5

article_title: Overcoming Fragmentation in Motivation Science: Why, When, and How Should We Integrate Theories?
citation: Reinhard Pekrun. (2024). Overcoming Fragmentation in Motivation Science: Why, When, and How Should We Integrate Theories? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09846-5
title: Core motivation: mental processes that directly influence goal direction, intensity, and persistence of behavior
description: The article argues that broad energy-and-direction definitions of motivation are overinclusive, implying that neurohormonal processes, nutrition, and emotions would all count as motivation. It instead proposes "core motivation, defined as mental processes that directly influence goal direction, intensity, and persistence of behavior," comprising proximal mental determinants such as goals, expectancies, values, and intentions combined with feelings of desire. The author recommends defining the conceptual space theoretically before integrating theories located in it.
requirements: The conceptual space of motivation should be defined theoretically rather than by lists of theories that happen to exist
constraints: The author presents core motivation as one possibility among several, not the only defensible definition
target_learning_goals: academic motivation
examples: The theories synthesized in the collection focus on mental representations such as goals, ability beliefs, expectancies, attributions, values, and needs
key_sources: Reinhard Pekrun. (2024). Overcoming Fragmentation in Motivation Science: Why, When, and How Should We Integrate Theories? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09846-5

article_title: Finger Use and Arithmetic Skills in Children and Adolescents: a Scoping Review
citation: Maëlle Neveu, Marie Geurten, Nancy Durieux, Laurence Rousselle. (2023). Finger Use and Arithmetic Skills in Children and Adolescents: a Scoping Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09722-8
title: Roesch and Moeller's three-stage developmental model of fingers' contribution to numerical development
description: The review presents a developmental model proposed by Roesch and Moeller (2015) that assigns fingers a changing role across three stages of numerical development. At the first stage, when children learn the number-word sequence, "fingers support the segmentation of this sequence by the association of each raised finger with a specific number word," and procedural counting with fingers supports early conceptual knowledge such as cardinality. At the second stage, number gestures communicate the cardinal of a set and support learning cardinal values of new number words. At the third stage, when children start to calculate, they "mobilizing fingers as an external support" while drawing on counting and cardinal skills. The review uses this model to frame why the role of fingers may differ across numerical tasks and developmental stages.
requirements: Children progress through stages of learning the number-word sequence, the cardinal principle, and initial calculation, with fingers serving a different function at each stage.
constraints: The model was proposed to clarify fingers' contribution across numerical development generally; the review notes the benefit of finger use is mainly debated specifically for arithmetic development.
target_learners: Children from preschool through primary school learning number words, cardinality, and early arithmetic
target_learning_goals: Number-word sequence learning
Cardinality understanding
Early arithmetic calculation skills
examples: The review cites finger counting supporting segmentation of the number-word sequence, tagging items during procedural counting, communicating set cardinality, and serving as external support during early calculation.
key_sources: Maëlle Neveu, Marie Geurten, Nancy Durieux, Laurence Rousselle. (2023). Finger Use and Arithmetic Skills in Children and Adolescents: a Scoping Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09722-8

article_title: Hybridizing Motivational Strains: How Integrative Models Are Crucial for Advancing Motivation Science
citation: Ronnel B. King, Luke K. Fryer. (2024). Hybridizing Motivational Strains: How Integrative Models Are Crucial for Advancing Motivation Science. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09850-9
title: Theoretical fragmentation of motivation science as a field-level problem hindering cumulative progress
description: The essay argues that motivation research in educational psychology is divided into camps, each with its own theory, that ignore findings from other camps. It documents repeated calls for integration from leading scholars and argues that without integration the field risks 'unchecked and likely unsustainable growth in the number of theories', undermining reliable findings and the field's reputation with practitioners and policymakers.
requirements: Researchers must recognize that no single theory can fully capture the complexity of motivation and learning
constraints: The essay attributes fragmentation partly to researchers themselves and to misaligned incentives rather than to the theories' content
target_learning_goals: understanding student motivation and learning through cumulative theoretical knowledge
examples: The essay quotes Murphy & Alexander (2000), Eccles & Wigfield (2002), Dweck (2017), Koenka (2020), Anderman (2020), Hattie et al. (2020), Wentzel (2021), and Greene (2022) all calling for integration
key_sources: Ronnel B. King, Luke K. Fryer. (2024). Hybridizing Motivational Strains: How Integrative Models Are Crucial for Advancing Motivation Science. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09850-9

article_title: Hybridizing Motivational Strains: How Integrative Models Are Crucial for Advancing Motivation Science
citation: Ronnel B. King, Luke K. Fryer. (2024). Hybridizing Motivational Strains: How Integrative Models Are Crucial for Advancing Motivation Science. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09850-9
title: Three routes to theoretical integration: competition among theories, unified frameworks, and bridge-building integration of existing theories
description: Drawing on Gigerenzer (2010), the essay presents three routes researchers can take toward integration. Route 1 is competition among theories in the Popperian tradition, using Kuhn's criteria of accuracy, consistency, scope, simplicity, and fruitfulness. Route 2 is the formation of unified frameworks, exemplified by Dweck's program and SDT's five mini-theories. Route 3, which the authors advocate and call hybridization, is 'growth through bridge-building' — building networks between existing theories and detecting coherence among them.
requirements: Researchers must revisit their own theoretical assumptions and be willing to cross theoretical borders
constraints: The authors state Route 3 is 'perhaps the most reasonable and practical in the field of educational psychology' and nearly all special issue authors took this approach
target_learning_goals: conducting cross-theoretical research that produces cumulative knowledge
examples: Martin (2023) bridged motivation and instructional theories; Elliot bridged SDT and achievement goal theory; Hornstra et al. integrated SDT with high expectations theory; Fryer and Leenknecht integrated self-efficacy and perceived control work with higher education theorizing
key_sources: Ronnel B. King, Luke K. Fryer. (2024). Hybridizing Motivational Strains: How Integrative Models Are Crucial for Advancing Motivation Science. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09850-9

article_title: Hybridizing Motivational Strains: How Integrative Models Are Crucial for Advancing Motivation Science
citation: Ronnel B. King, Luke K. Fryer. (2024). Hybridizing Motivational Strains: How Integrative Models Are Crucial for Advancing Motivation Science. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09850-9
title: Skinner's system approach: four guideposts (motivational resilience, academic identity, complex social ecologies, developmental embeddedness) for principled motivational integration
description: In the special issue's final paper, Skinner advances a 'system approach' in which all theories describe parts of a larger motivational system. Integration begins by identifying 'big ideas' common to the field. She proposes four guideposts: motivational resilience covering 'the energy, direction, and durability of action'; academic identity covering self-system processes; complex social ecologies incorporating classroom and meso-/macro-environmental factors; and developmental embeddedness. She locates constructs from different theories within this system and gives teachers concrete recommendations.
requirements: Integration should proceed by identifying common 'big ideas' rather than merging constructs wholesale
constraints: The essay presents this as one paper's proposal within the special issue, not a field consensus
target_learning_goals: locating motivational theories within a common system to improve teaching and learning
examples: Skinner provides specific examples of how different motivational theories and constructs can be located within the larger motivational system
key_sources: Ronnel B. King, Luke K. Fryer. (2024). Hybridizing Motivational Strains: How Integrative Models Are Crucial for Advancing Motivation Science. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09850-9

article_title: Hybridizing Motivational Strains: How Integrative Models Are Crucial for Advancing Motivation Science
citation: Ronnel B. King, Luke K. Fryer. (2024). Hybridizing Motivational Strains: How Integrative Models Are Crucial for Advancing Motivation Science. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09850-9
title: Integrate theories with care for meta-theoretical assumptions and boundary conditions, not for integration's sake
description: The essay cautions that integration must not be done haphazardly: 'Careful attention to meta-theoretical assumptions and boundary conditions must be made.' Quoting Ryan (2024), it warns that good theories 'can often collapse under the weight of swallowing too much'. It also notes, citing Pekrun (2024), that integration is only one strategy among others including differentiating, revising, generating, and discarding theories, and that the ultimate goal is promoting learning and academic development for all students.
requirements: Researchers must reconcile the meta-theoretical, ontological, and epistemological bases of the theories they integrate
constraints: Integration may be unhelpful in some situations; it should be pursued independently or alongside other theory-improvement strategies depending on the phenomenon
target_learning_goals: producing integrative theoretical models that genuinely improve understanding of student motivation
examples: Commenter Alexander urged authors to evaluate integration efforts by their prospective value to learning and academic development for all students
key_sources: Ronnel B. King, Luke K. Fryer. (2024). Hybridizing Motivational Strains: How Integrative Models Are Crucial for Advancing Motivation Science. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09850-9

article_title: Effectiveness of Computer-Based Scaffolding in the Context of Problem-Based Learning for Stem Education: Bayesian Meta-analysis
citation: Nam Ju Kim, Brian R. Belland, & Andrew E. Walker. (2018). Effectiveness of Computer-Based Scaffolding in the Context of Problem-Based Learning for STEM Education: Bayesian Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-017-9419-1
title: Differentiate scaffolding design according to which level of higher-order thinking is addressed in problem-based learning
description: The article's meta-analytic results show scaffolding effects differ sharply by the level of higher-order thinking targeted: analysis-level scaffolding reached g = 0.537 while synthesis (g = 0.156) and evaluation (g = 0.147) effects were small. The authors draw the design implication that "scaffolding design for improving students ' higher-order thinking should be differentiated according to which level (i.e., analysis, synthesis, and evaluation) of higher-order thinking is addressed in PBL." Computer-based scaffolding can effectively support analysis with current technology, while synthesis and evaluation may need integration with one-to-one teacher scaffolding.
requirements: Scaffolding design must specify which level of higher-order thinking (analysis, synthesis, or evaluation) it intends to address in PBL.
constraints: Current technology and designs often struggle to support students' more advanced and complicated learning processes in PBL such as synthesis, application, and reflection, per the authors' discussion.
target_learners: Students engaged in problem-based learning in STEM education
target_learning_goals: Higher-order thinking skills at the analysis, synthesis, and evaluation levels of Bloom's taxonomy
examples: The Bayesian meta-analysis compared scaffolding outcomes coded as analysis, synthesis, or evaluation subcategories across 21 PBL-STEM studies, finding analysis-level effects much higher than synthesis or evaluation effects.
key_sources: Nam Ju Kim, Brian R. Belland, & Andrew E. Walker. (2018). Effectiveness of Computer-Based Scaffolding in the Context of Problem-Based Learning for STEM Education: Bayesian Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-017-9419-1

article_title: What Makes Learners Overestimate Their Text Comprehension? The Impact of Learner Characteristics on Judgment Bias
citation: Stefanie Golke, Tim Steininger, & Jörg Wittwer. (2022). What Makes Learners Overestimate Their Text Comprehension? The Impact of Learner Characteristics on Judgment Bias. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09687-0
title: Cue-utilization framework extended to learner characteristics as sources of judgment bias in metacomprehension
description: The article organizes its predictions with the cue-utilization framework (Koriat, 1997), in which metacomprehension accuracy depends on the cues learners use to infer comprehension because "cues differ in their validity in indicating actual understanding." Representation-based cues emerge from monitoring text processing and are rather valid; heuristic cues such as self-perceptions of ability are available whether or not a text has been read and are usually less valid. The study extends this account by treating learner characteristics as sources of these cues and argues such characteristics "should be incorporated explicitly in theories of judgment accuracy."
requirements: Learners make comprehension judgments before and/or after answering comprehension questions, providing judgment-bias measures
constraints: The article notes which characteristics impact judgment bias also depends on task requirements, such as factual versus inference questions
target_learning_goals: accurate monitoring and judgment of one's own text comprehension
examples: The study assessed 255 university students' predictions and postdictions for factual and inference questions on three expository texts and regressed judgment bias on cognitive, metacognitive, motivational, and personality characteristics simultaneously
key_sources: Stefanie Golke, Tim Steininger, & Jörg Wittwer. (2022). What Makes Learners Overestimate Their Text Comprehension? The Impact of Learner Characteristics on Judgment Bias. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09687-0

article_title: Facilitating Understanding of Movements in Dynamic Visualizations: an Embodied Perspective
citation: Björn B. de Koning & Huib K. Tabbers. (2011). Facilitating Understanding of Movements in Dynamic Visualizations: an Embodied Perspective. Educ Psychol Rev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-011-9173-8
title: Embodied cognition: cognition grounded in perception and action via multimodal simulations
description: The article adopts embodied theories of cognition, in which psychological processes are shaped by the body and its interaction with the world, as the theoretical framework for improving learning from animations. Central to the account are simulations, defined as "the reenactment of perceptual and motor states that were acquired during experiences with the physical world"; even abstract concepts are understood by mapping concrete, bodily grounded concepts onto them. The article uses this framework to argue that sensorimotor experiences during learning become part of the mental simulation and enrich learners' multimodal representations of depicted movements.
requirements: Learning content must be linkable to learners' perceptual and motor experiences for embodiment to support representation building
constraints: The article notes the mirror neuron variant of this account remains speculative because the exact mechanisms translating neural activation into learning benefits have yet to be identified
target_learners: learners studying mechanical or technical processes via dynamic visualizations
target_learning_goals: building accurate mental representations of the movements of dynamic systems
examples: The article interprets action–sentence compatibility effects and motor cortex activation during language comprehension as evidence that comprehension entails mental simulation of described actions
key_sources: Björn B. de Koning & Huib K. Tabbers. (2011). Facilitating Understanding of Movements in Dynamic Visualizations: an Embodied Perspective. Educ Psychol Rev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-011-9173-8

article_title: Facilitating Understanding of Movements in Dynamic Visualizations: an Embodied Perspective
citation: Björn B. de Koning & Huib K. Tabbers. (2011). Facilitating Understanding of Movements in Dynamic Visualizations: an Embodied Perspective. Educ Psychol Rev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-011-9173-8
title: Mirror neuron account: dynamic visualizations work best for human-movement tasks because observation activates the action system
description: The review reports Van Gog et al.'s explanation for when animations help: watching a human perform a task is observational learning relying on the mirror neuron system, so an animation showing human movement automatically activates the cortical circuits involved in executing that action, priming similar actions and easing processing of transient information. Animations of non-human movements do not activate the learner's action system, which the account uses to explain their weaker effectiveness. The article treats this as a plausible but speculative explanation and extends the underlying logic to non-human movements via the learner's own motor system.
requirements: Explains effectiveness differences only relative to whether depicted movements are human or non-human
constraints: The article states the argument "remains rather speculative because the exact mechanisms of how the activation of mirror neurons translates into learning benefits have yet to be identified"
target_learners: learners studying dynamic systems or processes via animation or video
target_learning_goals: understanding movements depicted in dynamic visualizations
examples: The review cites animation advantages for first-aid procedures, origami folding, and knot-tying and puzzle construction as tasks involving human movements
key_sources: Björn B. de Koning & Huib K. Tabbers. (2011). Facilitating Understanding of Movements in Dynamic Visualizations: an Embodied Perspective. Educ Psychol Rev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-011-9173-8

article_title: Grasping Virtual Objects Benefits Lower Aptitude Learners’ Acquisition of Foreign Language Vocabulary
citation: Manuela Macedonia, Brian Mathias, Astrid E. Lehner, Susanne M. Reiterer, Claudia Repetto. (2023). Grasping Virtual Objects Benefits Lower Aptitude Learners' Acquisition of Foreign Language Vocabulary. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09835-0
title: Procedural–declarative memory account of differential sensorimotor enrichment benefits in L2 vocabulary learning
description: The article interprets its findings via embodied/grounded cognition and the interplay of declarative memory (hippocampal, engaged by reading and listening) and procedural memory (premotor and motor cortices, basal ganglia, cerebellum, engaged by movement-related input). It proposes that high-aptitude learners "may inherently rely on their declarative memory for L2 learning", while low-aptitude learners' word learning "may be supported to a greater extent by the recruitment of procedural memory systems", so sensorimotor enrichment disproportionately helps the latter. Grasping is also framed as cognitive offloading that saves working-memory resources.
requirements: Sensorimotor enrichment must be congruent with the to-be-learned stimuli for actions to enhance task performance, per the article's cited work
constraints: The article states the recruitment of procedural memory in LLA learners "does not occur intentionally" and appears to be an innate strategy
target_learners: Adult foreign-language learners with low or high language aptitude
target_learning_goals: Foreign language vocabulary acquisition and retention
examples: In the VR-cave study, grasping movements during word learning were proposed to have engaged LLA learners' procedural memory, enhancing their vocabulary acquisition relative to HLA learners who benefited from higher declarative memory capacities.
key_sources: Manuela Macedonia, Brian Mathias, Astrid E. Lehner, Susanne M. Reiterer, Claudia Repetto. (2023). Grasping Virtual Objects Benefits Lower Aptitude Learners' Acquisition of Foreign Language Vocabulary. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09835-0

article_title: Transforming Self-regulated Learning – Multimodal Insights and Future Directions
citation: Tina Seufert. (2026). Transforming Self-regulated Learning – Multimodal Insights and Future Directions. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10119-6
title: SMA Grid: a two-dimensional classificatory framework for multimodal SRL research
description: The Self-regulated learning, Multimodal data and Analysis Grid (SMA Grid) is a classificatory and organizing framework for multimodal SRL research, with one dimension differentiating cognitive, metacognitive, affective, and motivational (CAMM) components and a second dimension characterizing multimodal measurements. The paper states it "serves as a valuable tool for structuring the rapidly growing field of multimodal SRL research," promoting transparency, comparability, and conceptual orientation. It functions from heuristic classification to guiding analytic design, but does not claim to be a fully developed theoretical model of SRL.
requirements: Theoretical grounding is the responsibility of the individual study, since the grid remains open to various theoretical interpretations.
constraints: The grid does not provide a fully developed theoretical model of SRL; it supports existing frameworks by visualizing how modalities and process components connect.
target_learners: Researchers and designers of learning environments studying self-regulated learning
target_learning_goals: Understanding and classifying how self-regulated learning is measured and analyzed with multimodal data
examples: The reviews by de Mooij et al. and Bühler et al. systematically used the SMA Grid to classify studies; Kubsch et al. exemplify one of the few genuinely integrative applications within the Topical Collection.
key_sources: Tina Seufert. (2026). Transforming Self-regulated Learning – Multimodal Insights and Future Directions. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10119-6

article_title: Transforming Self-regulated Learning – Multimodal Insights and Future Directions
citation: Tina Seufert. (2026). Transforming Self-regulated Learning – Multimodal Insights and Future Directions. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10119-6
title: CAMM framework and its proposed CAMMS extension adding social and somatic dimensions
description: CAMM is a conceptual taxonomy differentiating the cognitive, metacognitive, affective, and motivational components of SRL, aligned with current SRL models describing their interrelatedness. The paper argues the Moreno et al. study "introduces an additional dimension: social processes and dynamics in socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL)," suggesting expansion into a CAMMS model. An expanded CAMMS model may better reflect the embodied and distributed nature of regulation in complex learning environments, particularly collaborative or high-stakes settings.
requirements: Integrated approaches that examine the dynamic interplay of the four components over time, which the paper says would strengthen theoretical development.
constraints: The paper reports motivational and affective components are frequently neglected in reviewed studies, and Törmänen et al. focus on motivation without connecting it to other CAMM domains.
target_learners: Learners in collaborative and high-stakes learning environments studied with multimodal data
target_learning_goals: Understanding self-regulated learning as interrelated cognitive, metacognitive, affective, motivational, social, and somatic processes
examples: Moreno et al. modeled collective regulatory dynamics in medical simulation, which the paper treats as evidence for extending CAMM toward CAMMS.

article_title: Transforming Self-regulated Learning – Multimodal Insights and Future Directions
citation: Tina Seufert. (2026). Transforming Self-regulated Learning – Multimodal Insights and Future Directions. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10119-6
title: Resource-based model of SRL: regulation as a function of the balance between learner resources, task demands, and instructional context
description: Drawing on cognitive load theory and Seufert's (2018) model integrating cognitive load with self-regulated learning, the paper proposes that SRL should be understood as a function of the dynamic balance between learners' resources, task demands, and instructional context. It states that "regulation is most likely to occur when learners operate within a zone of optimal challenge—where the task is demanding enough to require regulation, but not so complex as to exceed their cognitive capacity." This adds an explanatory dimension to CAMM: regulation is shaped by the interplay between task demands and available learner resources.
requirements: Cognitive and motivational resources must be available and not entirely consumed by external demands or task-related load for planning, monitoring, or regulation to take place.
constraints: Under high cognitive load or in complex tasks, even well-developed regulatory skills may fail to unfold.
target_learners: Learners in multimodal and classroom learning environments, particularly those facing high task complexity
target_learning_goals: Enabling self-regulated learning by matching task demands to learners' cognitive and motivational resources
examples: The paper cites Kubsch et al.'s finding that prior knowledge becomes relevant later in the regulation process as support for treating learner characteristics as temporally sensitive rather than stable moderators.
key_sources: Tina Seufert. (2026). Transforming Self-regulated Learning – Multimodal Insights and Future Directions. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10119-6

article_title: When Can AI Models Explain Learning? Validity Criteria for AI as Cognitive Models in Education
citation: Peng Wang, Olga Viberg, Effie Lai-Chong Law, Samuel Greiff. (2026). When Can AI Models Explain Learning? Validity Criteria for AI as Cognitive Models in Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10202-y
title: Eight validity criteria determine when an AI system should count as a cognitive model of learning
description: The review's central contribution is an evaluative framework of eight criteria that an AI system must satisfy before its cognitive-model status is granted rather than assumed: theoretical grounding, construct validity, mechanistic transparency, alignment with human learning trajectories, error-signature matching, causal-intervention tests, ecological validity, and instructional usefulness. The framework shifts the question from whether AI can model cognition to when it should be allowed to count as one, treating the criteria as "a structured set of validity criteria that together determine when an AI system should be allowed to count as a cognitive model of learning".
requirements: Internal components must be transparent enough to support meaningful mappings to theory, and these mappings must be empirically validated rather than asserted by intuition
constraints: The cognitive status of any virtual-learner proxy must be earned through the validity criteria rather than assumed from the label
target_learners: Educational researchers using computational models of learners
target_learning_goals: Mechanistic explanation of learning processes such as memory, strategy use, motivation, and self-regulation
examples: The review uses a running example of math anxiety and problem solving, operationalized as an anxiety signal that narrows attention or pre-empts working memory, tested via representation analysis and targeted ablation against human error trajectories
key_sources: Peng Wang, Olga Viberg, Effie Lai-Chong Law, Samuel Greiff. (2026). When Can AI Models Explain Learning? Validity Criteria for AI as Cognitive Models in Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10202-y

article_title: When Can AI Models Explain Learning? Validity Criteria for AI as Cognitive Models in Education
citation: Peng Wang, Olga Viberg, Effie Lai-Chong Law, Samuel Greiff. (2026). When Can AI Models Explain Learning? Validity Criteria for AI as Cognitive Models in Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10202-y
title: Four AI model families as complementary lenses on educational cognition, organized by learning flexibility and mechanistic transparency
description: The review organizes AI approaches to modeling educational cognition into four families treated as different lenses rather than a formal taxonomy: neural networks, reinforcement learning agents, cognitive architectures, and large language models. It situates them along two dimensions, learning flexibility and scale, and mechanistic transparency and construct alignment, arguing that "neural networks emphasize learning from experience through gradual parameter change; reinforcement learning formalizes adaptation through feedback and incentives; cognitive architectures enforce psychologically motivated structure and capacity limits; and large language models bring broad, pretrained competence for language-mediated tasks". The families are complementary and increasingly integrable through hybrid approaches.
requirements: Model choice should be theory-driven, depending on whether the target phenomenon is practice-driven skill acquisition, sequential decision making under feedback, structured procedure under capacity limits, or language-mediated reasoning
constraints: The four families are neither mutually exclusive nor strictly parallel, and figure placements are illustrative rather than exact, intended for qualitative comparison only
target_learners: Educational psychology researchers and learning scientists selecting computational modeling approaches
target_learning_goals: Explaining learning trajectories, error patterns, strategy selection, cognitive load, self-regulation, and transfer
examples: Figure 2 places LLMs in the high-flexibility, low-transparency region and cognitive architectures in the opposite region, with neural networks and RL agents between the poles
key_sources: Peng Wang, Olga Viberg, Effie Lai-Chong Law, Samuel Greiff. (2026). When Can AI Models Explain Learning? Validity Criteria for AI as Cognitive Models in Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10202-y

article_title: When Can AI Models Explain Learning? Validity Criteria for AI as Cognitive Models in Education
citation: Peng Wang, Olga Viberg, Effie Lai-Chong Law, Samuel Greiff. (2026). When Can AI Models Explain Learning? Validity Criteria for AI as Cognitive Models in Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10202-y
title: Comparative guide table of AI model families mapping phenomena, interpretability risks, and validity checks
description: The review provides a summary table (Table 1) comparing the four major AI model families as cognitive models for educational psychology. For each family it lists best-suited phenomena, internal variables, explanatory strengths, key limitations and risks, and priority validity checks mapped to the review's criteria. The table is described as "a compact guide to what each modeling family naturally represents (e.g., practice-driven learning, feedback-driven decisions, capacity limits, language-mediated reasoning), the main interpretability/construct-validity risks, and the evaluation checks that strengthen mechanistic claims".
requirements: The final column maps recommended checks to the review's validity criteria: construct validity, trajectory alignment, error-signature matching, and causal-intervention tests
constraints: The table summarizes family-level trade-offs and recommended checks rather than quantitative rankings of model families
target_learners: Educational researchers choosing among AI modeling approaches
target_learning_goals: Selecting and validating AI models for explaining memory, strategy use, cognitive load, and language-mediated learning
examples: For neural networks the table lists representation probing, learning-curve fitting, structured error patterns, and ablations or counterfactuals as priority validity checks

article_title: Motivation-Achievement Cycles in Learning: a Literature Review and Research Agenda
citation: Vu, T., Magis-Weinberg, L., Jansen, B. R. J., van Atteveldt, N., Jansen, T. W. P. J., Lee, N. C., van der Maas, H. L. J., Raijmakers, M. E. J., Sachisthal, M. S. M., & Meeter, M. (2021). Motivation-Achievement Cycles in Learning: a Literature Review and Research Agenda. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09616-7
title: The motivation-achievement cycle: a synthesis model of reciprocal motivation-achievement interactions
description: The review proposes a summary model (Fig. 1) capturing commonalities across prominent academic motivation theories, in which motivation arises from an appraisal combining value and expectancy, which drives achievement behaviors (quantity and quality of learning) and academic emotions, and achievement feeds back through perceived performance and flow. As the authors state, "Figure 1 represents an attempt to synthesize, fo r the purposes of this paper, some of the commonalities of well-established theories". The model also marks external influences (culture, social influence, rewards, feedback form, instruction quality) that affect the cycle without being part of it.
requirements: Multiple motivation constructs and their behavioral mediators must be measured to study the cycle's reciprocal links empirically
constraints: The authors state the goal is not to comprehensively review and synthesize existing theories but to illustrate commonalities suggesting a framework
target_learners: school and college students in academic domains
target_learning_goals: academic motivation and academic achievement (knowledge, skill)
examples: The model distinguishes two routes from motivation to achievement (quantity and quality of academic behaviors) and two routes from achievement to motivation (perceived performance and flow)
key_sources: Vu, T., Magis-Weinberg, L., Jansen, B. R. J., van Atteveldt, N., Jansen, T. W. P. J., Lee, N. C., van der Maas, H. L. J., Raijmakers, M. E. J., Sachisthal, M. S. M., & Meeter, M. (2021). Motivation-Achievement Cycles in Learning: a Literature Review and Research Agenda. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09616-7
title: The mutualistic network approach to motivation-achievement relations
description: The review advocates a network approach in which motivation and achievement constructs are nodes and bidirectional partial correlations are edges, so constructs emerge empirically as clusters rather than being assumed a priori. "The network approach is different; it does not assume an a priori structure of motivation factors." Central nodes are proposed as efficient intervention targets: in Sachisthal et al.'s science-interest study, "enjoyment emerged as the central node in the network of Dutch students, whereas engagement behaviors emerged as central in the network of Colombian students", so different intervention approaches were advised for the two countries.
requirements: Multiple motivation constructs must be measured in one single study to model clusters of motivation, behavior, and achievement
constraints: Central variables may differ between contexts and populations, so network findings may not generalize across groups
target_learners: students in science-learning contexts (e.g., Dutch and Colombian students in the cited example)
target_learning_goals: science interest, engagement, and achievement
examples: Sachisthal et al. (2019) modeled value of science, science engagement, and achievement as a network in which interpretable clusters emerged; Zwicker et al. (2020) identified guilt as a central node and successfully manipulated it

citation: Vu, T., Magis-Weinberg, L., Jansen, B. R. J., van Atteveldt, N., Jansen, T. W. P. J., Lee, N. C., van der Maas, H. L. J., Raijmakers, M. E. J., Sachisthal, M. S. M., & Meeter, M. (2021). Motivation-Achievement Cycles in Learning: a Literature Review and Research Agenda. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09616-7
title: Treat external factors (rewards, norms, requirements, feedback form, instruction quality) as entry points for interventions on the motivation-achievement cycle
description: The review argues that external influences — extrinsic rewards, autonomy support, cultural norms, verbal persuasion, outside requirements such as deadlines, quality of teaching, and the form of feedback — can start, sustain, or redirect a motivation-achievement cycle that might otherwise not start or falter. Such factors matter because "they offer entry points for interventions that enhance motivation, achievement, or both". For example, feedback framed as mastery rather than ranking changes perceived achievement, so true high achievement can still fail to support motivation.
requirements: Educational design elements (feedback form, requirements, instruction quality) must be adjustable to influence perceived performance, effort, or value
constraints: Extrinsic rewards may detract from intrinsic motivation as described in self-determination theory, though they may also jolt a cycle that would otherwise not start
target_learners: school students, including those whose motivation-achievement cycles have not started
target_learning_goals: motivation, achievement, or both
examples: The review cites feedback form (De Kraker-Pauw et al., 2017) and attributional processes as design elements shaping perceived achievement independently of true achievement

article_title: Peer Mindset Culture as a Developmental Context for Belonging
citation: Eunjin Seo, Margarett Clapper, Cameron A. Hecht, Robert Crosnoe, David S. Yeager. (2025). Peer Mindset Culture as a Developmental Context for Belonging. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10082-8
title: Peer mindset culture framework: two pathways linking fixed-mindset peer norms to belonging
description: The article proposes that peer mindset culture—"peers' shared beliefs about whether ability is fixed or can grow"—functions as a developmental context shaping adolescent belonging. Drawing on the Many Questions of Belonging and Integrative Framework of Belonging perspectives, it maps two broad pathways: identity threat and reduced opportunities for connection. Within these, five empirically testable mechanisms are proposed: stereotype threat, mindset-culture mismatch, social contagion, peer selection, and low social support, each with stated applicability to particular student populations.
requirements: The five mechanisms are proposed as illustrative and testable, not exhaustive or mutually exclusive
constraints: The mechanisms are currently theoretical and require rigorous testing to establish their validity and impact
The pathways are not necessarily equally potent, nor are they exhaustive
target_learners: adolescents and early adulthood students in academic settings
target_learning_goals: sense of belonging in learning environments
examples: Figure 1 presents the proposed mediation model of peer mindset culture and belonging; Table 1 defines the five mechanisms and their applicability

citation: Herbert W. Marsh, Reinhard Pekrun, Jiesi Guo, John Hattie, Eyal Karin. (2023). Too Much of a Good Thing Might Be Bad: the Double-Edged Sword of Parental Aspirations and the Adverse Effects of Aspiration-Expectation Gaps. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09768-8
title: Sum-and-difference within-person transformation for testing aspiration-expectation gaps
description: A statistical method the article applies to disentangle highly correlated parent aspiration and expectation variables. The two variables are orthogonally transformed into a sum (expectations + aspirations) and a difference (aspirations - expectations), preserving degrees of freedom, fit, and other parameters while giving the difference a within-person interpretation. The article states the transformation "provided a within-person perspective (i.e., the difference between aspirations and expectations of a given parent)", avoiding confounding of within- and between-person effects and enabling direct tests of the gap hypothesis with appropriate standard errors.
requirements: Two highly correlated predictors whose difference is substantively meaningful
An orthogonal transformation that leaves variance explained, degrees of freedom, and other parameter estimates unchanged
constraints: Applied in the article to parent aspirations and expectations only; teacher and student aspiration data were not available
target_learners: high school students (Year 10) and their parents
target_learning_goals: educational expectations and aspirations as predictors of academic outcomes
examples: The article tested the parent aspiration-expectation gap with two equivalent SEMs (Fig. 1A untransformed, Fig. 1B transformed) and estimated direct, mediated, and total effects of the difference

title: ELS:2002 longitudinal database
description: The US Educational Longitudinal Survey 2002 is the public secondary dataset the article analyzes: "16,197 high school Year-10 students from 751 schools followed up through age 26". It used a two-stage complex sample design with sampling weights yielding a nationally representative probability sample of public, Catholic, and other private schools, with follow-ups 2, 4, and 10 years after baseline, transcript collection for more than 90% of baseline students, and a 78.2% age-26 response rate.
requirements: Sampling weights and complex-design standard-error adjustment for the two-stage school-and-student sampling
constraints: Expectation and aspiration items use a 7-category response scale; parent aspirations were collected only for parents, not teachers or students

article_title: Does Professional Development Effectively Support the Implementation of Inclusive Education? A Meta-Analysis
citation: Johanna L. Donath, Timo Lüke, Elisabeth Graf, Ulrich S. Tran, Thomas Götz. (2023). Does Professional Development Effectively Support the Implementation of Inclusive Education? A Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09752-2
title: Design inclusive-education professional development with active learning, practical relevance, and participation prerequisites to facilitate transfer to schools
description: The meta-analysis examined the Desimone design criteria (content focus, coherence, active learning, collective participation, duration) plus certification for professional development addressing inclusive education. It found that "long-term training with high practical relevance and active learning opportunities facilitates transfer to schools", though support for the classic criteria was limited overall. Active learning significantly moderated skill gains, and participation prerequisites and specific content focus improved some subcategory outcomes.
requirements: Programs should provide practice opportunities within sessions, case studies, and alternating input and praxis phases rather than blocked input-only sessions.
Participation prerequisites (e.g., having a relevant student in the classroom) and coherent additional learning activities support transfer.
constraints: Descriptions of program design in primary studies were scarce, so design effects may be underestimated.
Moderator analyses were limited to intensive intervention programs; data from short-term one-shot programs were lacking.
Duration showed no influence when analyses were limited to programs up to 200 h.
target_learning_goals: knowledge about inclusive education
inclusive teaching skills
positive beliefs toward inclusive education
improved student behavior
examples: Programs with alternating input and praxis phases showed larger changes in use of teaching methods (g = 0.78) than blocked-design programs (g = 0.03).

Programs requiring teachers to fulfill participation prerequisites reported larger changes in perception of teaching methods (g = 0.60) and student achievement (g = 0.71) than programs open to all teachers.

article_title: Editor’s Note
citation: Daniel H. Robinson. (2013). Editor's Note. Educ Psychol Rev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-013-9226-2
title: Discourage authors from including prescriptive statements in empirical research journal articles
description: This principle holds that empirical research articles should not include prescriptive statements recommending practice, because such recommendations face generalization problems even when grounded in strong causal evidence. It emerged from a 2-day meeting whose participants "ended with the decision to write a position paper discouraging authors from including prescriptives in empirical research journal articles."
requirements: A position paper articulating the rationale, as decided by the meeting participants
constraints: The article itself notes the position is controversial and warrants a range of informed responses
target_learners: Authors of empirical research journal articles in educational psychology
target_learning_goals: Responsible communication of research findings for educational practice
examples: The Meadows Center meeting participants decided to write a position paper discouraging prescriptives, and the journal solicited short responses from scholars for a subsequent issue

article_title: Examining the Effects of Family-Implemented Literacy Interventions for School-Aged Children: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Dahl-Leonard, K., Hall, C., Cho, E., Capin, P., Roberts, G. J., Kehoe, K. F., Haring, C., Peacott, D., & Demchak, A. (2025). Examining the Effects of Family-Implemented Literacy Interventions for School-Aged Children: A Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09985-3
title: Bioecological systems framework: home-based family literacy interactions as proximal processes in the microsystem
description: The article frames family-implemented literacy interventions using Bronfenbrenner's bioecological systems framework, in which context comprises five interrelated systems (microsystem, mesosystem, exosystem, macrosystem, chronosystem). Home experiences influence children's learning at the same level as school experiences because both sit in the microsystem, the system most proximal to the child. In the discussion, the authors describe interactions between a child and a family member in home-based literacy interventions as "proximal processes, occurring at the level of the microsystem", which Bronfenbrenner called "the primary engines of development". The framework motivates the meta-analysis's premise that families can improve both code-related and meaning-related skills supporting reading comprehension.
requirements: Interventions must be implemented by a family member or caregiver in the home, as proximal processes arise from reciprocal interactions within the microsystem.
target_learners: School-aged children in grades K-12, including students with or at risk for reading difficulties
target_learning_goals: Code-focused literacy skills (phonological awareness, decoding/word reading, spelling, text reading)
Meaning-focused literacy skills (vocabulary, listening comprehension, reading comprehension)
examples: The meta-analysis included 25 interventions across 22 studies in which parents or primary caregivers delivered literacy activities such as paired reading, dialogic reading, repeated reading, and interactive homework at home.

article_title: Facilitating Diagnostic Competences in Higher Education—a Meta-Analysis in Medical and Teacher Education
citation: Olga Chernikova, Nicole Heitzmann, Maximilian Christian Fink, Venance Timothy, Tina Seidel, Frank Fischer, DFG Research group COSIMA. (2020). Facilitating Diagnostic Competences in Higher Education—a Meta-Analysis in Medical and Teacher Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09492-2
title: Diagnostic competences as coordinated application of professional knowledge in epistemic-diagnostic activities
description: The article's conceptual framework defines diagnostic competences as "dispositions enabling goal-oriented gathering and integration of information in order to make medical or educational decisions." Diagnostic processes are conceptualized as a set of epistemic activities, "including (a) identifying a problem, (b) questioning, (c) generating hypotheses, (d) constructing artifacts, (e) generalizing evidence, (f) evaluating evidence" and drawing conclusions and communicating results. The framework links learners' prior professional knowledge (conceptual and practical) and the quality of diagnostic processes and outcomes, and it organizes the meta-analysis's coding of moderators.
requirements: Outcome measures must address diagnostic quality or one or more of the epistemic-diagnostic activities for a study to be coded within the framework
constraints: The article states the current research is not specific enough to infer the type of knowledge representations—declarative or procedural—suggested by ACT-R
target_learners: higher education students in medical and teacher education
target_learning_goals: diagnostic competences: gathering and integrating case-specific information to make medical or educational decisions
examples: The coding scheme for professional knowledge base, instructional support, and diagnostic context in the meta-analysis was based on this conceptual framework (Heitzmann et al. 2018b).

citation: Olga Chernikova, Nicole Heitzmann, Maximilian Christian Fink, Venance Timothy, Tina Seidel, Frank Fischer, DFG Research group COSIMA. (2020). Facilitating Diagnostic Competences in Higher Education—a Meta-Analysis in Medical and Teacher Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09492-2
title: Scaffolding types arranged on a continuum of self-regulation of problem-solving
description: The article proposes ordering scaffolding techniques by the degrees of freedom they leave the learner: "we suggest locating the scaffolding types on different positions on a scale of self-regulation of problem-solving, with examples located from a rather low level followed by role assignments and prompts with increasing levels of self-regulation potential." Reflection phases and unscaffolded problem-solving sit at the high end. The continuum builds on scaffolding as a temporary shift of control from learner to teacher or advanced peer, and it underpins the meta-analysis's moderator analysis of which scaffolding type fits which knowledge level.
requirements: Classifying a scaffolding intervention requires coding which techniques it realizes (examples, prompts, roles, reflection phases) and the guidance level provided
constraints: The article states that a convincing framework to integrate the different types of scaffolding does not yet exist and offers this classification heuristically
target_learners: higher education learners in medical and teacher education with varying prior professional knowledge
target_learning_goals: diagnostic competences through scaffolded problem-solving
examples: The meta-analysis coded examples, prompts, roles, and reflection phases as distinct instructional support categories and located them on the self-regulation scale.

citation: Olga Chernikova, Nicole Heitzmann, Maximilian Christian Fink, Venance Timothy, Tina Seidel, Frank Fischer, DFG Research group COSIMA. (2020). Facilitating Diagnostic Competences in Higher Education—a Meta-Analysis in Medical and Teacher Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09492-2
title: Two-dimensional classification of diagnostic situations: information base and collaboration requirement
description: Adopting Heitzmann et al. (2018b), the article distinguishes diagnostic situations along two dimensions. The first is that "The first dimension is information base (e.g., where the information for diagnosis comes from), spanning the spectrum from document-based to interaction-based": document-based diagnosis uses recorded information with little time pressure, while interaction-based diagnosis processes information in real time with more time pressure and fewer opportunities for reflection. The second dimension runs from individual diagnoses to diagnoses requiring collaboration and communication with other professionals, which the article notes can be problematic even for experts.
requirements: Describing a diagnostic situation requires coding both its information base and whether collaboration with other professionals is needed
constraints: The article notes empirical studies provide evidence that collaboration and social aspects of working on the case can be problematic even for experts
target_learners: medical and teacher education students learning to diagnose
target_learning_goals: diagnostic competences across varied diagnostic situations
examples: The meta-analysis coded each primary study's diagnostic situation as document-based or interaction-based and as individual or collaborative (Table 1).
