citation: Noroozi, O., Kirschner, P. A., Biemans, H. J. A., & Mulder, M. (2018). Promoting Argumentation Competence: Extending from First- to Second-Order Scaffolding Through Adaptive Fading. Educational Psychol Rev, 30, 153–176. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-017-9400-z
title: Script Theory of Guidance (SToG): interplay of internal and external collaboration scripts with hierarchical components
description: SToG explains how external and internal scripts interplay during collaborative learning. Internal scripts are prior procedural knowledge structured from repeated experiences; external scripts are supports embedded in the environment that "activate existing internal scripts or help create new internal scripts". Knowledge of a CABLe practice "consists of a set of somewhat hierarchical components including plays, scenes, scriptlets, and roles", which this article applies to argumentation rather than collaboration as such.
requirements: External scripts are effective only when they trigger an accompanying specific constellation of internal script components, or do not conflict with or duplicate them
constraints: The article applies SToG to argumentation in CABLe settings rather than collaboration generally
Internal argumentative scripts vary among individuals and are not fixed across situations
target_learners: learners engaged in collaborative argumentation-based learning, from primary school to university
target_learning_goals: argumentation competence
collaborative knowledge co-construction
examples: The article uses SToG components to specify when feedback authoring tools should send reminder versus direct instructions during CABLe
key_sources: Noroozi, O., Kirschner, P. A., Biemans, H. J. A., & Mulder, M. (2018). Promoting Argumentation Competence: Extending from First- to Second-Order Scaffolding Through Adaptive Fading. Educational Psychol Rev, 30, 153–176. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-017-9400-z

article_title: Promoting Argumentation Competence: Extending from First- to Second-Order Scaffolding Through Adaptive Fading
citation: Noroozi, O., Kirschner, P. A., Biemans, H. J. A., & Mulder, M. (2018). Promoting Argumentation Competence: Extending from First- to Second-Order Scaffolding Through Adaptive Fading. Educational Psychol Rev, 30, 153–176. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-017-9400-z
title: Distinction between first-order scaffolding (task performance) and second-order scaffolding (self-directed learning)
description: Drawing on Van Merriënboer and Kirschner's Ten Steps to Complex Learning, the article distinguishes two scaffold types: "first-order (i.e., regular) scaffolding refers to providing support and guidance for the acquisition and performance of domain-specific complex skills, second-order scaffolding provides support and guid- ance for self-directed learning". Applied to argumentation, first-order scaffolding supports desirable argumentation within a task, while second-order scaffolding aims at argumentation competence transferable to similar tasks once support is removed.
requirements: Second-order scaffolding requires taking learners' internal scripts into account
Argumentation competence includes knowledge, skill, and attitude/willingness to apply it
constraints: Transfer is framed as within the same discipline, not across disciplines or areas, because disciplines differ in argumentation rules, goals, and epistemology
target_learners: students dealing with complex, ill-defined, controversial issues, e.g., in the natural sciences
target_learning_goals: transferable argumentation competence
self-directed learning
examples: The article argues second-order scaffolding should be prioritized in class situations where students frequently deal with complex authentic problems
key_sources: Noroozi, O., Kirschner, P. A., Biemans, H. J. A., & Mulder, M. (2018). Promoting Argumentation Competence: Extending from First- to Second-Order Scaffolding Through Adaptive Fading. Educational Psychol Rev, 30, 153–176. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-017-9400-z

article_title: Promoting Argumentation Competence: Extending from First- to Second-Order Scaffolding Through Adaptive Fading
citation: Noroozi, O., Kirschner, P. A., Biemans, H. J. A., & Mulder, M. (2018). Promoting Argumentation Competence: Extending from First- to Second-Order Scaffolding Through Adaptive Fading. Educational Psychol Rev, 30, 153–176. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-017-9400-z
title: Design second-order argument scaffolding through a three-step guideline: diagnose internal scripts, adapt support, fade adaptively
description: The article's central design principle is that argument scaffold design should extend beyond first-order scaffolding to second-order scaffolding via a guideline with three steps: "diagnosis of the internal argumentative script, adaptive external support, and adaptive fading of this external support". Diagnosis identifies learners' internal argumentative scripts; adaptive support targets missing or non-enacted script components; adaptive fading withdraws support as learners internalize the strategy, complemented by peer, automatic, and self-assessment.
requirements: Adequate and proper diagnosis of the discourse and situation is essential for realization of adaptive fading
Fading should occur only when the learner can carry out the required action, with support gradually reduced
constraints: Fading something that is not understood is not adequate for fostering acquisition of targeted argumentation activities
Evidence for fading in CABLe is mixed, so the guideline is a design proposal rather than an empirically validated recipe
target_learners: learners in natural-science education facing controversial societal issues
target_learning_goals: acquisition and transfer of argumentation competence across similar tasks
examples: The article proposes using automated analysis techniques and AI/computer-linguistic tools to detect internal scripts during discourse and deliver dynamic support and adaptive fading
key_sources: Noroozi, O., Kirschner, P. A., Biemans, H. J. A., & Mulder, M. (2018). Promoting Argumentation Competence: Extending from First- to Second-Order Scaffolding Through Adaptive Fading. Educational Psychol Rev, 30, 153–176. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-017-9400-z

article_title: Promoting Argumentation Competence: Extending from First- to Second-Order Scaffolding Through Adaptive Fading
citation: Noroozi, O., Kirschner, P. A., Biemans, H. J. A., & Mulder, M. (2018). Promoting Argumentation Competence: Extending from First- to Second-Order Scaffolding Through Adaptive Fading. Educational Psychol Rev, 30, 153–176. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-017-9400-z
title: Automated analysis techniques and tools for diagnosing argumentation during discourse
description: The article identifies automated analysis techniques for detecting learners' internal argumentative scripts during CABLe. "Scheuer et al. ( 2012) classified available automated analysis techniques to this effect into four categories, namely syntactical anal ysis, problem-specifi c analysis, reasoning analysis, and collaborative filtering analysis." Named educational technologies using AI and language content analysis to analyze student argumentation moves and structures include ARGUNAUT, TagHelper, Rashi, Belvédère, and LARGO; NLP has also been used to code micro-argumentation prior to a learning phase.
requirements: Advancement in artificial intelligence systems and analysis techniques to process discourse in real time
constraints: The article presents these as means toward diagnosis and adaptive support; it reports no evaluation of them itself
target_learners: learners in computer-supported collaborative argumentation environments
target_learning_goals: diagnosis of internal argumentative scripts for adaptive support and fading
examples: Feedback authoring tools alerting students to rule violations, e.g., when a claim is not backed up
key_sources: Noroozi, O., Kirschner, P. A., Biemans, H. J. A., & Mulder, M. (2018). Promoting Argumentation Competence: Extending from First- to Second-Order Scaffolding Through Adaptive Fading. Educational Psychol Rev, 30, 153–176. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-017-9400-z

article_title: Social Network Analysis in E-Learning Environments: A Preliminary Systematic Review
citation: Cela, K.L., Sicilia, M.Á. & Sánchez, S. (2015). Social Network Analysis in E-Learning Environments: A Preliminary Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-014-9276-0
title: Social network analysis as an approach to understanding and improving e-learning systems
description: The review frames social network analysis (SNA) as a methodological approach for describing and analysing network behaviours in e-learning. It notes SNA "has proven extremely powerful at describing and analysing network behaviours in business, economics and medicine, but its application to e-learning has been relatively limited." The review positions SNA as a way to understand and improve e-learning systems, operationalised through measures such as centrality and density applied to learner interaction networks, most often in forum-based one-mode networks.
requirements: Interaction data from an e-learning environment (e.g. forum posts) that can be represented as a network of relations between members.
constraints: Application to e-learning has been relatively limited compared with business, economics and medicine, per the review.
target_learning_goals: Understanding and improving interaction patterns and course design in e-learning systems
examples: The review's included studies applied SNA methods to analyse interaction patterns in discussion forums in e-learning courses.
key_sources: Cela, K.L., Sicilia, M.Á. & Sánchez, S. (2015). Social Network Analysis in E-Learning Environments: A Preliminary Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-014-9276-0

article_title: Understanding Learning Strategy Use Through the Lens of Habit
citation: Ann-Kathrin Krause, Jasmin Breitwieser, Garvin Brod. (2025). Understanding Learning Strategy Use Through the Lens of Habit. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10087-3
title: Habit-based lens on learning strategy use: strategies can be driven by automatic cue-response associations alongside deliberate regulation
description: The article proposes framing learning strategy use through modern habit theory, in which a habit is "a learned association between a contextual cue and a behavioral response" that develops through repeated cue-behavior pairing. Drawing on dual-process models, it argues strategy use can stem from both controlled, reasoned decisions and automatic, cue-driven habitual impulses. The lens complements self-regulated learning models, which acknowledge automaticity but treat automatic routines as readily adjustable, whereas habits are cue-bound and hard to disrupt.
requirements: Repeated performance of the behavior in a stable context with a salient cue for a habit to form
constraints: The authors note habitual behavior exists on a continuum and is not necessarily non-intentional or unconscious
target_learners: students in secondary and higher education
target_learning_goals: self-regulated use of effective cognitive learning strategies for long-term retention
examples: The article illustrates the lens with highlighting while reading: opening a text becomes the cue that triggers the impulse to grab a pencil and highlight, even though highlighting may not enhance long-term retention
key_sources: Ann-Kathrin Krause, Jasmin Breitwieser, Garvin Brod. (2025). Understanding Learning Strategy Use Through the Lens of Habit. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10087-3

article_title: Understanding Learning Strategy Use Through the Lens of Habit
citation: Ann-Kathrin Krause, Jasmin Breitwieser, Garvin Brod. (2025). Understanding Learning Strategy Use Through the Lens of Habit. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10087-3
title: Breaking entrenched strategy habits requires targeted disruption of cue-response links, not reflection or feedback alone
description: Contrasting habit theory with self-regulated learning models, the article argues that because habits are tightly bound to environmental cues, they are difficult to detect and disrupt. It states that "Reflection or feedback alone may be insufficient; targeted strategies are usually needed to weaken or replace entrenched cue-response links, a process that is both effortful and time-consuming." This supports interventions that restructure contexts rather than only informing students.
requirements: Sustained, deliberate effort over an extended time horizon to break cue-response links
constraints: The article notes this process is effortful and time-consuming, and that whether students' strategy reversion under stress is habitual or deliberate remains uncertain
target_learners: students whose ineffective strategy use is entrenched
target_learning_goals: replacing ineffective strategy habits with effective strategy routines
examples: The article cites qualitative reports from David et al. (2024) and Biwer et al. (2020) in which students found shifting toward more effective strategies difficult and fell back on entrenched habits, particularly under setbacks or time pressure
key_sources: Ann-Kathrin Krause, Jasmin Breitwieser, Garvin Brod. (2025). Understanding Learning Strategy Use Through the Lens of Habit. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10087-3

article_title: Systematic Review of Educational Approaches to Misinformation
citation: Rau, M. A., & Premo, A. E. (2025). Systematic Review of Educational Approaches to Misinformation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10012-8
title: Four lines of research on educational interventions against misinformation
description: The review's data-driven approach organizes the 107-article corpus into four distinct research lines, each with its own theoretical perspective, study designs, and intervention types: research on moderators of the misinformation effect (memory literature), lie detection trainings (deception literature), information-literacy trainings (curriculum and instruction), and fraud trainings at the intersection of human behavior and information technology, plus an "other" category for singular articles. The authors state that "The data-driven approach identified four distinct categories that examine educational interventions about misinformation from different angles." Comparing each line to an idealized model of educational interventions reveals research gaps such as missing delayed posttests and unmeasured prior knowledge.
requirements: Articles must describe a concrete implemented intervention with an empirical evaluation of misinformation susceptibility via pretest-to-posttest or control comparisons
constraints: Coding was limited to interventions targeting cognitive processes in individual learners; emotional, behavioral, and stable-factor interventions were excluded
target_learners: adults and children across lab and field studies, depending on the research line
target_learning_goals: recognizing and resisting misinformation
detecting deception
evaluating information credibility
examples: Forty of the 107 articles concerned moderators of the misinformation effect; 30 concerned lie detection trainings; 23 concerned information-literacy trainings
key_sources: Rau, M. A., & Premo, A. E. (2025). Systematic Review of Educational Approaches to Misinformation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10012-8

article_title: Systematic Review of Educational Approaches to Misinformation
citation: Rau, M. A., & Premo, A. E. (2025). Systematic Review of Educational Approaches to Misinformation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10012-8
title: Taxonomy of diagnostic misinformation features
description: The review's theory-driven axis classifies misinformation characteristics that can signal falsity into four feature types: content features (quality elements such as typos, linguistic cues, rhetorical features), source features (lack of sources, obscure or fabricated sources, reliable sources), structural features (delivery format such as URLs or clickbait), and network features (how information is obtained or distributed, e.g., spreading patterns). The authors note that "Several features can signal that a piece of information is false (Molina et al., 2021)" and use this taxonomy to code which features each intervention line targets. Only two articles in the corpus targeted network features.
requirements: A definition of misinformation must be complemented by feature knowledge for detection to be possible
constraints: Feature diagnosticity varies; nonverbal behaviors are reported as mostly unreliable cues
target_learners: learners being trained to detect misinformation
target_learning_goals: identifying misinformation via content, source, structural, and network cues
examples: Lie detection trainings targeted content features in 22 articles and structural features in 23; all 23 information-literacy articles targeted specific features
key_sources: Rau, M. A., & Premo, A. E. (2025). Systematic Review of Educational Approaches to Misinformation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10012-8

article_title: Systematic Review of Educational Approaches to Misinformation
citation: Rau, M. A., & Premo, A. E. (2025). Systematic Review of Educational Approaches to Misinformation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10012-8
title: Design misinformation education to enhance discrepancy detection
description: Based on its synthesis, the review recommends that interventions to reduce misinformation susceptibility be designed to enhance learners' noticing of discrepancies between original information and subsequent misinformation. The authors state that "our review suggests that specific pre-warnings and explicit types of attention-focusing interventions might be better suited to enhance discrepancy detection and reduce susceptibility to misinformation." Retrieval practice alone did not seem suited to this goal, though detail-focused and criterion testing were exceptions. The review also recommends testing combinations of intervention types.
requirements: Interventions must direct learners' attention to discrepancies, e.g., via explicit discrepancy-indication instructions, veracity judgments, or specific warnings
constraints: General pre-warnings and mindfulness approaches mostly failed; retrieval practice often increased susceptibility except under verbatim or criterion testing
target_learners: adults and children learning to resist misinformation
target_learning_goals: detecting discrepancies between original and post-event information
reducing misinformation endorsement
examples: The review found explicit instructions to press a button when noticing discrepancies and veracity-judgment instructions were effective across studies
key_sources: Rau, M. A., & Premo, A. E. (2025). Systematic Review of Educational Approaches to Misinformation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10012-8

article_title: Does Spelling Still Matter—and If So, How Should It Be Taught? Perspectives from Contemporary and Historical Research
citation: Steven C. Pan, Timothy C. Rickard, Robert A. Bjork. (2021). Does Spelling Still Matter— and If So, How Should It Be Taught? Perspectives from Contemporary and Historical Research. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09611-y
title: Contemporary multi-component definition of spelling skills
description: The review describes a contemporary, expanded definition of spelling skills that goes beyond correct spelling to include component knowledge domains: "phonological knowledge (i.e., phonemics and phonics), morphological knowledge (e.g., prefixes and suffixes), orthographic knowledge (e.g., phoneme-grapheme relationships), etymological knowledge (i.e., word origins), and visual knowledge", many of which may develop in stages. It also includes functional skills such as dictionary use, spellcheck use, and spelling or learning unfamiliar words. This framework underpins the review's argument that modern explicit instruction should target these components rather than word-by-word memorization.
requirements: Instruction targeting the components requires learners to develop phonological, morphological, orthographic, etymological, and visual knowledge, which may develop in stages
constraints: The review focuses its evidence base on normally developing learners, excluding much of the literature on students with learning disabilities
target_learning_goals: spelling proficiency
literacy skills including reading and writing
key_sources: Steven C. Pan, Timothy C. Rickard, Robert A. Bjork. (2021). Does Spelling Still Matter— and If So, How Should It Be Taught? Perspectives from Contemporary and Historical Research. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09611-y

article_title: Does Spelling Still Matter—and If So, How Should It Be Taught? Perspectives from Contemporary and Historical Research
citation: Steven C. Pan, Timothy C. Rickard, Robert A. Bjork. (2021). Does Spelling Still Matter— and If So, How Should It Be Taught? Perspectives from Contemporary and Historical Research. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09611-y
title: Horn-Ashbaugh Speller weekly curriculum: distributed practice and retrieval practice with pretesting, self-testing, and spaced review
description: The Speller's curriculum assigned a new word list each Monday with a pretest, self-testing study routines on Tuesday and Thursday (look, visualize, cover, write from memory, check, repeated three times), diagnostic tests on Wednesday and Friday that also assessed the list from one month prior, and a spelling notebook tracking errors and progress. The review characterizes these as implementations of "distributed practice" and "practice testing" (retrieval practice), two techniques "now regarded as evidence-based and highly robust". The pattern also included reviewing difficult words at the start of each school year.
requirements: Requires daily instructional time devoted to spelling, weekly word lists, and teacher-administered pretests and diagnostic tests with corrective feedback
constraints: The review judges the Speller overall obsolete: its visualization-heavy drill routines rested on an incomplete view of spelling's cognitive mechanisms, and it lacked grade-level benchmarks and systematic error diagnosis
target_learning_goals: correct spelling of assigned word lists
development of a spelling conscience and motivation to spell correctly
examples: The Speller contained grade-appropriate lists totaling 4578 words and prescribed a daily routine of testing, writing, and word study exercises, remaining a bestseller for at least 25 years
key_sources: Steven C. Pan, Timothy C. Rickard, Robert A. Bjork. (2021). Does Spelling Still Matter— and If So, How Should It Be Taught? Perspectives from Contemporary and Historical Research. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09611-y

article_title: The Effect of Testing on the Retention of Coherent and Incoherent Text Material
citation: de Jonge, M., Tabbers, H. K., & Rikers, R. M. J. P. (2015). The Effect of Testing on the Retention of Coherent and Incoherent Text Material. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-015-9300-z
title: Elaborative retrieval account of the coherence-moderated testing effect
description: The authors offer the elaborative retrieval hypothesis as a possible explanation of their pattern of results. The hypothesis "suggests that testing will result in more elaborate memory traces compared to passive restudy of information." Applied to their data, the coherent text's organizational structure may itself serve as a retrieval cue, so testing added little elaborative processing beyond what the context already invited, whereas the absence of supporting context for isolated statements in Experiment 2 may have forced more elaborative processing during testing. The authors present this as one way to explain the results, to be investigated in future research.
requirements: Testing must involve retrieval that can produce elaborative processing beyond the cue support already provided by the material's structure.
constraints: The authors present this as a possible explanation only, noting that investigating it "could be a fruitful avenue to pursue in future research."
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of text material
examples: In Experiment 1, the coherent text's context may have functioned as a retrieval cue, so the fill-in-the-blank test added no elaborative processing; in Experiment 2, isolated statements without supporting context may have elicited more elaborative processing on the test.
key_sources: de Jonge, M., Tabbers, H. K., & Rikers, R. M. J. P. (2015). The Effect of Testing on the Retention of Coherent and Incoherent Text Material. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-015-9300-z

article_title: The Effect of Testing on the Retention of Coherent and Incoherent Text Material
citation: de Jonge, M., Tabbers, H. K., & Rikers, R. M. J. P. (2015). The Effect of Testing on the Retention of Coherent and Incoherent Text Material. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-015-9300-z
title: Use completion tests for retention of unconnected materials rather than highly structured texts
description: The article's central design implication is that the benefit of fill-in-the-blank testing depends on material connectedness. As the abstract states, "Testing with a completion test seems most beneficial for unconnected materials and less so for highly structured materials." When material is already coherent and structured, the text's organization may serve as a retrieval cue, leaving the completion test little additional processing to add; when material is a list of facts, testing slows forgetting relative to restudy.
requirements: Material whose connectedness is low (e.g., lists of facts) for the testing benefit to emerge.
constraints: Conclusions are limited to the short-answer (fill-in-the-blank) test format; the authors state they "would not want to imply that testing as a general learning activity might not be a useful tool for learning texts."
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of learned material
examples: Experiment 2 presented the black hole text as a scrambled list of facts and found testing slowed forgetting; Experiment 1 with the coherent text found no benefit.
key_sources: de Jonge, M., Tabbers, H. K., & Rikers, R. M. J. P. (2015). The Effect of Testing on the Retention of Coherent and Incoherent Text Material. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-015-9300-z

article_title: Validity of Eye-Tracking Measures in Immersive Virtual Reality: Using Cognitive Theories of Learning
citation: Lee, J. Y., Moon, J., Paas, F., Cho, M., Darejeh, A., Holmer, S., & Ayres, P. (2026). Validity of Eye-Tracking Measures in Immersive Virtual Reality: Using Cognitive Theories of Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10186-9
title: Theory-driven classification of six IVR learning processes and nine eye-trackable constructs
description: The article develops a classification mapping eye-tracking metrics onto learning processes in IVR, grounded in CTML, CATLM, CASTLE, CAMIL, and Cognitive Load Theory. It proposes "a classification of six key learning processes (i.e., cognitive, motivational, affective, social, metacognitive, media-specific) and nine associated constructs (i.e., attention, visual strategy, cognitive load, motivation, emotion, social attention, self-regulation, immersion, usability) measurable through eye tracking in IVR." The media-specific category was added to capture IVR-specific processes such as embodiment, and review literature supplied the construct subcategories used as the coding scheme.
requirements: Eye-tracking indicators must be matched to constructs via established classifications of fixation-, saccade-, pupil-, blink-, AOI-based, and combined measures
constraints: Classification was developed for IVR delivered through head-mounted displays; AR, MR, and desktop virtual environments were excluded
target_learners: IVR learners across professional, medical, and educational training contexts
target_learning_goals: Assessing cognitive, motivational, affective, social, metacognitive, and media-specific learning processes in IVR
examples: The classification was applied as the coding scheme for a systematic review of 38 empirical IVR eye-tracking studies
key_sources: Lee, J. Y., Moon, J., Paas, F., Cho, M., Darejeh, A., Holmer, S., & Ayres, P. (2026). Validity of Eye-Tracking Measures in Immersive Virtual Reality: Using Cognitive Theories of Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10186-9

article_title: Validity of Eye-Tracking Measures in Immersive Virtual Reality: Using Cognitive Theories of Learning
citation: Lee, J. Y., Moon, J., Paas, F., Cho, M., Darejeh, A., Holmer, S., & Ayres, P. (2026). Validity of Eye-Tracking Measures in Immersive Virtual Reality: Using Cognitive Theories of Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10186-9
title: Four-component validity scoring scheme for eye-tracking measures (0–4 points)
description: A structured scoring system adapted from Cook et al. and Naismith and Cavalcanti for evaluating validity evidence of eye-tracking measures, comprising four components: content, relations with other variables, data quality, and consequences. "The total validity score was calculated by summing the scores across all four components, yielding possible scores ranging from 0 to 4." Internal structure and response process were reinterpreted as data quality for eye tracking. The scheme enabled comparison of validity strength across learning constructs in the review.
requirements: Validity evidence from accumulated studies must be available for each component to assign points
constraints: Originally designed for broader measurement tools such as questionnaires and observation, requiring adaptation for eye-tracking methodologies
target_learners: Researchers evaluating eye-tracking measures in IVR learning environments
target_learning_goals: Evaluating and improving measurement validity of learning-process indicators
examples: Applied to score eye-tracking measures across 38 studies, with component scores reported per construct
key_sources: Lee, J. Y., Moon, J., Paas, F., Cho, M., Darejeh, A., Holmer, S., & Ayres, P. (2026). Validity of Eye-Tracking Measures in Immersive Virtual Reality: Using Cognitive Theories of Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10186-9

article_title: How Do Children Socially Learn from Narrative Fiction: Getting the Lesson, Simulating Social Worlds, or Dialogic Inquiry?
citation: Luciano Gasser · Yvonne Dammert · P. Karen Murphy. (2022). How Do Children Socially Learn from Narrative Fiction: Getting the Lesson, Simulating Social Worlds, or Dialogic Inquiry? Educational Psychology Review (2022) 34:1445–1475. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09667-4
title: Three reading stances (efferent, expressive, critical-analytic) as a taxonomy of sociomoral learning through narrative fiction
description: Drawing on Rosenblatt's transactional reading theory, the review organizes conceptions of sociomoral learning through narrative fiction into three stances. From the efferent stance, attention focuses on abstract moral propositions; from the expressive stance, readers develop mindreading and empathy by becoming immersed in the story; from a critical-analytic stance, readers critically reflect on initial responses through argument-based dialogues with peers. The review uses this taxonomy to systematize both psychological assumptions and educational programs, noting that stances are not exclusive and often overlap.
requirements: Studies and programs must be classified by their dominant stance, since readers and studies often include elements of several stances
constraints: The three stances are not exclusive; readers can take a single specific stance, but more often various stances overlap
target_learners: children and adolescents in literary education
target_learning_goals: sociomoral competence including theory of mind, empathy, and social reasoning
examples: Table 1 summarizes the three conceptions across learning mechanism, developmental outcomes, type of narrative fiction, instructional principles, and educational relationships
key_sources: Luciano Gasser · Yvonne Dammert · P. Karen Murphy. (2022). How Do Children Socially Learn from Narrative Fiction: Getting the Lesson, Simulating Social Worlds, or Dialogic Inquiry? Educational Psychology Review (2022) 34:1445–1475. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09667-4

article_title: How Do Children Socially Learn from Narrative Fiction: Getting the Lesson, Simulating Social Worlds, or Dialogic Inquiry?
citation: Luciano Gasser · Yvonne Dammert · P. Karen Murphy. (2022). How Do Children Socially Learn from Narrative Fiction: Getting the Lesson, Simulating Social Worlds, or Dialogic Inquiry? Educational Psychology Review (2022) 34:1445–1475. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09667-4
title: Sociomoral competence defined through theory of mind, empathy, and social reasoning
description: The review defines sociomoral competence as the ability to take the perspective of and feel emotional concern for another person as well as engage in complex social reasoning that aims to balance conflicting interests. It builds on three developmental concepts: ToM (understanding mental states), empathy (an affective response stemming from apprehension of another's emotional state), and social reasoning, which the authors consider more complex than ToM and empathy because it requires coordinating moral, social-conventional, and personal concerns in context-specific ways.
requirements: Assessment of sociomoral outcomes should distinguish ToM, empathy, and social reasoning, as they differ in developmental complexity
constraints: Social reasoning requiring coordination of multiple concerns represents a more complex sociomoral competence than ToM and empathy, which contribute to basic social functioning
target_learning_goals: perspective-taking, empathic concern, and contextualized moral judgment
examples: The review describes Social Domain Theory findings that preschoolers judge straightforward moral transgressions as wrong independently of authority, rules, and context
key_sources: Luciano Gasser · Yvonne Dammert · P. Karen Murphy. (2022). How Do Children Socially Learn from Narrative Fiction: Getting the Lesson, Simulating Social Worlds, or Dialogic Inquiry? Educational Psychology Review (2022) 34:1445–1475. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09667-4

article_title: How Do Children Socially Learn from Narrative Fiction: Getting the Lesson, Simulating Social Worlds, or Dialogic Inquiry?
citation: Luciano Gasser · Yvonne Dammert · P. Karen Murphy. (2022). How Do Children Socially Learn from Narrative Fiction: Getting the Lesson, Simulating Social Worlds, or Dialogic Inquiry? Educational Psychology Review (2022) 34:1445–1475. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09667-4
title: Support argumentative peer dialogues that require children to justify perspectives and consider divergent views about narrative fiction
description: From the critical-analytic stance, children learn socially from narrative fiction by engaging in argumentative dialogues that require them to reason for their own perspectives and consider divergent perspectives. Through such dialogues with peers or adults, children learn to justify their interpretation, respectfully listen to others' ideas, critically examine others' arguments, and develop openness toward alternative views. The review positions this stance as going beyond both moral-message extraction and perspective simulation by emphasizing reasoned and justified judgments about complex sociomoral issues.
requirements: Classroom dialogues about narrative fiction need to fulfill specific characteristics if educators aim to promote more than basic sociomoral competences
constraints: Initial expressive responses are a necessary but insufficient condition for intellectual and sociomoral growth and must be expanded by critical reflection
target_learners: children and adolescents in classroom literary discussions
target_learning_goals: social reasoning, critical evaluation of perspectives, and balanced text interpretation
examples: The review describes argumentative dialogues in which children legitimize their own perspectives while considering peers' alternative perspectives on complex sociomoral issues raised in narrative fiction
key_sources: Luciano Gasser · Yvonne Dammert · P. Karen Murphy. (2022). How Do Children Socially Learn from Narrative Fiction: Getting the Lesson, Simulating Social Worlds, or Dialogic Inquiry? Educational Psychology Review (2022) 34:1445–1475. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09667-4

article_title: Student Burnout and Educational Dropout: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Dropout Behavior and Intentions
citation: Daniel J. Madigan, Hanna L. Glandorf. (2026). Student Burnout and Educational Dropout: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Dropout Behavior and Intentions. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10191-y
title: Study Demands-Resources theory as an account of how student burnout develops and leads to dropout
description: The review adopts Study Demands-Resources Theory (Bakker & Mostert, 2024) as its organizing explanatory framework. It posits that "student burnout is primarily the consequence of an imbalance between study demands and resources": high demands (workload, time pressures, cognitive complexity) deplete energy and produce exhaustion, cynicism, and reduced efficacy, while resources (social support, feedback, autonomy) buffer demands. Burnout also drives self-undermining behaviors such as procrastination, creating a loss spiral, and acts as a mediator between study demands and negative academic outcomes including dropout.
requirements: Requires measurement of both study demands and study resources to model burnout development as the theory specifies
constraints: The article notes few theoretical models of student burnout exist and further work is necessary to integrate and test theory, including examining possible mechanisms underpinning these relationships
target_learners: students in post-compulsory education (secondary, undergraduate, postgraduate)
target_learning_goals: understanding and reducing educational dropout risk via burnout
examples: The review draws on stress theory and self-efficacy/expectancy-value theory to explain how exhaustion and cynicism reinforce avoidant coping and withdrawal, while reduced efficacy undermines motivation
key_sources: Daniel J. Madigan, Hanna L. Glandorf. (2026). Student Burnout and Educational Dropout: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Dropout Behavior and Intentions. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10191-y

article_title: Developing Personalized Education: A Dynamic Framework
citation: Leonard Tetzlaff, Florian Schmiedek & Garvin Brod. (2021). Developing Personalized Education: A Dynamic Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09570-w
title: A dynamic framework of personalized education on three timescales
description: The article proposes a framework that 'conceptualizes learners as dynamic entities that change during and in interaction with the instructional process.' It classifies learner dynamics on three timescales—macroscale (months to years, developmental processes), mesoscale (days to weeks, intervention-induced changes), and microscale (minutes to hours, short-term fluctuations)—and maps each to an instructional lever: goal setting, design of instructional units/task selection, and giving or withholding assistance. It serves as a frame of reference for localizing personalization research questions.
requirements: Repeated measurements throughout the learning process to supplement and adjust the initial assessment of learning prerequisites
constraints: Decisions on the macro level are often predetermined by context and thus difficult to truly personalize
target_learners: learners across laboratory, classroom, and digital learning environments
target_learning_goals: adapting instruction to individual learners' changing characteristics
examples: The framework updates a general personalization loop (Fig. 1) with timescale-specific decision processes (Fig. 3)
key_sources: Leonard Tetzlaff, Florian Schmiedek & Garvin Brod. (2021). Developing Personalized Education: A Dynamic Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09570-w

article_title: Developing Personalized Education: A Dynamic Framework
citation: Leonard Tetzlaff, Florian Schmiedek & Garvin Brod. (2021). Developing Personalized Education: A Dynamic Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09570-w
title: Measure relevant learner characteristics repeatedly during learning and adapt instruction systematically
description: The review's central design recommendation is that personalization is most successful when 'relevant learner characteristics are measured repeatedly during the learning process' and the resulting data drive systematic instructional adaptation. Static, single-point modeling risks aptitude-treatment mismatch and can deprive learners of opportunities to acquire lacking aptitudes. Repeated measures at different timescales let the teaching agent identify whether performance is typical, whether an intervention worked, or whether a learner needs help on a specific day.
requirements: A student model that accounts for potential changes in relevant learner characteristics during the instructional process
Sufficiently dense temporal resolution of measurements to capture nonlinear dynamics
constraints: The dynamic conceptualization brings an additional load for teaching agents, who must regularly assess relevant parameters and use them for instructional decisions
target_learners: individual learners in classrooms, digital environments, and laboratories
target_learning_goals: improving learning gains through data-based adaptation of instruction
examples: ITS and formative assessment both use dynamic assessment procedures to create and update student models
key_sources: Leonard Tetzlaff, Florian Schmiedek & Garvin Brod. (2021). Developing Personalized Education: A Dynamic Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09570-w

article_title: Spaced Retrieval Practice: Can Restudying Trump Retrieval?
citation: Higham, P. A., Fastrich, G. M., Potts, R., Murayama, K., Pickering, J. S., & Hadwin, J. A. (2023). Spaced Retrieval Practice: Can Restudying Trump Retrieval? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09809-2
title: Reactivity of memory judgments as an explanatory framework for the restudy-versus-retrieval reversal
description: The article explains its unexpected restudy advantage through theories of reactivity of memory judgments, analogous to Judgment of Learning (JOL) reactivity. The authors hypothesized that the post-feedback rating "may have interfered with retrieval (negative reactivity) and/or boosted restudy performance (positive reactivity)". They note JOL reactivity is sometimes positive, sometimes negative, and sometimes absent, and that positive reactivity is seldom observed with unrelated word pairs, making the translation-pair setting novel. Experiment 2 tested this by manipulating the rating requirement.
requirements: A post-feedback memory rating prompt (e.g., "Was your answer correct?" or "Would you have remembered the correct translation?") must be administered during practice for reactivity to occur.
constraints: The article notes positive JOL reactivity is seldom observed with unrelated word pairs, and the detailed reactivity mechanisms for translation pairs had not previously been investigated.
target_learners: Adult online learners studying foreign-language vocabulary
target_learning_goals: Long-term retention of paired-associate material (e.g., Swahili–English translations)
examples: Experiment 2 manipulated whether the memory rating was required after feedback; with ratings, restudy exceeded retrieval, replicating Experiment 1, and without ratings the pattern was descriptively reversed.
key_sources: Higham, P. A., Fastrich, G. M., Potts, R., Murayama, K., Pickering, J. S., & Hadwin, J. A. (2023). Spaced Retrieval Practice: Can Restudying Trump Retrieval? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09809-2

article_title: What Are Teacher–Student Relationships in Adolescent Motivation Research? A Systematic Review of Conceptualizations, Measurement, and Analysis
citation: Emma C. Burns · Penny Van Bergen. (2025). What Are Teacher–Student Relationships in Adolescent Motivation Research? A Systematic Review of Conceptualizations, Measurement, and Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09998-y
title: Attachment theory conceptualizes teacher–student relationships as multidimensional bonds comprising closeness, conflict, and dependency
description: Attachment theory, one of three relational theories consistently employed in adolescent motivation research, argues that positive and secure emotional bonds are critical to adaptive functioning. Within it, "teacher–student relationships are multidimensional and can be considered via three dimensions: closeness, conflict, and dependency", with positive relationships high in closeness and low in conflict and dependency. More recent work attends to relationships outside a positive–negative binary, including complicated and reserved relationships.
requirements: Measurement should treat closeness and conflict as separate but co-occurring dimensions of the same relationship
constraints: The relevance of dependency in adolescence has been debated, with suggestions that teachers as a safe haven may not be developmentally appropriate
target_learning_goals: Academic motivation supported by positive teacher–student relationships
examples: The review notes adolescent motivation research often references attachment theory to support hypotheses but has not typically operationalized and integrated it with motivation theory
key_sources: Emma C. Burns · Penny Van Bergen. (2025). What Are Teacher–Student Relationships in Adolescent Motivation Research? A Systematic Review of Conceptualizations, Measurement, and Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09998-y

article_title: What Are Teacher–Student Relationships in Adolescent Motivation Research? A Systematic Review of Conceptualizations, Measurement, and Analysis
citation: Emma C. Burns · Penny Van Bergen. (2025). What Are Teacher–Student Relationships in Adolescent Motivation Research? A Systematic Review of Conceptualizations, Measurement, and Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09998-y
title: The Model for Interpersonal Teacher Behavior (MITB) describes teacher–student relationships via a circumplex of influence and proximity, typically measured with the QTI
description: The MITB uses a communicative systems approach in which all teacher behavior functions as nonverbal communication and students' perceptions of that behavior reflect the underlying relationship. "The MITB is presented as a circumplex model", with behavior located on two orthogonal axes: influence (perceptions of teacher behavior as controlling) and proximity (perceptions of teacher behavior as socially and academically approachable). Research typically assesses relationships via these axes, sometimes via eight octants; the most common measure is the Questionnaire on Teacher Interaction (QTI).
requirements: Consistent specification of interpersonal behaviors as relating to an individual student or multiple students, so dyadic relationships can be disentangled from broader classroom climates
constraints: QTI items framing teacher behavior as an independent observation, not in relation to students, cannot be considered equivalent to behavioral interactions with students
target_learning_goals: Understanding how teacher interpersonal behavior shapes students' perceptions of the relationship and their motivation
examples: Some MITB research aggregates relationships to the classroom level or examines them as multilevel systems
key_sources: Emma C. Burns · Penny Van Bergen. (2025). What Are Teacher–Student Relationships in Adolescent Motivation Research? A Systematic Review of Conceptualizations, Measurement, and Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09998-y

article_title: What Are Teacher–Student Relationships in Adolescent Motivation Research? A Systematic Review of Conceptualizations, Measurement, and Analysis
citation: Emma C. Burns · Penny Van Bergen. (2025). What Are Teacher–Student Relationships in Adolescent Motivation Research? A Systematic Review of Conceptualizations, Measurement, and Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09998-y
title: Self-determination theory frames relationships via relatedness support, alongside autonomy support and structure as distinct needs-supportive practices
description: SDT is a meta-theory spanning development and motivation, arguing that optimal motivation requires three psychological needs: autonomy, competence, and relatedness. "In classrooms, needs can be met through teachers' provision of autonomy support (i.e., asking student opinions, offering choice, providing explanatory rationales), structure (i.e., instructional guidance, clear expectations), and relatedness support (i.e., care, warmth, also referred to as involvement)". Relatedness support is the only explicitly relational component; autonomy support and structure reflect more unidirectional dynamics and are not intended as relationship measures.
requirements: Approaches using autonomy support or collective needs support as relationship indicators should disentangle interpersonal aspects (e.g., trust, respect) from pedagogical aspects (e.g., offering choice)
constraints: Relatedness support is relatively under-researched compared to autonomy support and structure, and there is very little research regarding relatedness thwarting
target_learning_goals: Supporting students' autonomy, competence, and relatedness needs to foster academic motivation
examples: Some researchers have used autonomy support as an indicator of relationship quality, arguing autonomy supportive behaviors capture ongoing patterns of interpersonal dynamics
key_sources: Emma C. Burns · Penny Van Bergen. (2025). What Are Teacher–Student Relationships in Adolescent Motivation Research? A Systematic Review of Conceptualizations, Measurement, and Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09998-y

article_title: What Are Teacher–Student Relationships in Adolescent Motivation Research? A Systematic Review of Conceptualizations, Measurement, and Analysis
citation: Emma C. Burns · Penny Van Bergen. (2025). What Are Teacher–Student Relationships in Adolescent Motivation Research? A Systematic Review of Conceptualizations, Measurement, and Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09998-y
title: Match the level of analysis to the referents used in relationship measurement items, using multilevel analyses for plural or averaged referents
description: Because relationship items differ in their referents — dyadic ("I like my teacher"), plural ("this teacher likes us"), or averaged ("I like my teachers") — the referent should determine the level at which analysis takes place. The review states that "Where referents are plural or averaged, analyses should be multilevel to account for shared group-level variance and ensure appropriate interpretation". This matters because implications for practice and intervention differ depending on whether individual relationships, multiple relationships, or classroom culture is being addressed.
requirements: Researchers must identify the referent of each measurement item before selecting an analytic level
constraints: The review notes it is unclear how frequently multilevel analyses are in fact used for plural or averaged configuration types
target_learning_goals: Accurate inference about relationships and motivation at the dyadic, plural, or classroom level
examples: The review cites Marsh et al. (2012) and Stapleton and Johnson (2019) on referent-driven levels of analysis
key_sources: Emma C. Burns · Penny Van Bergen. (2025). What Are Teacher–Student Relationships in Adolescent Motivation Research? A Systematic Review of Conceptualizations, Measurement, and Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09998-y

article_title: Dimensionality, Reliability, and Validity of Academic Resilience Scales: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
citation: Könül Karimova, Hsing-Fen Tu. (2026). Dimensionality, Reliability, and Validity of Academic Resilience Scales: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10207-7
title: Academic resilience as a contextually embedded adaptive capacity, distinguished from lower-intensity academic buoyancy
description: The review frames academic resilience as students' capacity to sustain or recover adaptive academic motivation, engagement, learning behavior, and performance under substantial academic adversity, emphasizing "exposure to academic adversity and adaptive functioning in response to that adversity." Academic buoyancy is distinguished as a lower-intensity form covering everyday setbacks such as poor grades and negative feedback. Drawing on resilience theory, ecological systems, and motivational perspectives, the framework treats resilience as an adaptive process situated within learning environments rather than a purely individual disposition, and evaluates competing unidimensional, multidimensional, hierarchical, and bifactor measurement operationalizations without assuming one in advance.
requirements: Instruments must explicitly anchor items, instructions, or validation purposes to academic adversity, schoolwork, learning, grades, examinations, or school contexts
constraints: The review notes a general factor may emerge from homogeneous self-report items or restrictive analytic models rather than a genuinely broad construct; dimensionality evidence was interpreted alongside item content and scoring purpose
target_learners: students in primary, secondary, and higher education
target_learning_goals: adaptive academic functioning under academic stressors, setbacks, failure, or threat
examples: Table 1 summarizes frequently used measures including the ARS-30, ABS, ARRS, SRS, SRQ, MRS, and domain-specific scales for pharmacy, English learning, programming, and nursing education
key_sources: Könül Karimova, Hsing-Fen Tu. (2026). Dimensionality, Reliability, and Validity of Academic Resilience Scales: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10207-7

article_title: Dimensionality, Reliability, and Validity of Academic Resilience Scales: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
citation: Könül Karimova, Hsing-Fen Tu. (2026). Dimensionality, Reliability, and Validity of Academic Resilience Scales: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10207-7
title: Corpus of 46 studies of academic resilience and buoyancy instrument validation (48 study–instrument combinations, 51 records)
description: The review's analytic dataset comprised quantitative studies published between 2000 and February 2026, identified through five databases following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. The final dataset included "46 unique studies, 48 unique study–instrument combinations, and 51 study–sample–instrument records," all restricted to academic- or education-specific instruments; no domain-general resilience measure was retained. Studies were double coded with discrepancies resolved through deliberation, and covered dimensionality, internal consistency, and construct validity evidence across educational levels and geographic regions.
requirements: Studies had to report extractable psychometric evidence such as model-fit indices, reliability coefficients, or validity correlations with sufficient statistical information
constraints: Formal meta-analytic tests of measurement invariance were not conducted because item-level covariance matrices or comparable parameter estimates were unavailable for most studies
target_learners: students in formal education (primary, secondary, higher education)
target_learning_goals: psychometric evaluation of academic resilience measurement
examples: The search yielded 2,325 records across five databases, of which 46 studies were included after screening
key_sources: Könül Karimova, Hsing-Fen Tu. (2026). Dimensionality, Reliability, and Validity of Academic Resilience Scales: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10207-7

article_title: Dynamic or Static Goal Regulation: Implications of Weak and Strong Bonds Between Autonomous/Controlled Reasons and Aims for Achievement Goal Striving
citation: Janke, S. (2024). Dynamic or Static Goal Regulation: Implications of Weak and Strong Bonds Between Autonomous/Controlled Reasons and Aims for Achievement Goal Striving. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09968-w
title: Dynamic versus static goal regulation: two accounts of how aims and autonomous/controlled reasons align
description: The article contrasts two accounts of achievement goal regulation. Dynamic goal regulation treats any aim as energizable by multiple autonomous or controlled reasons, forming goal complexes as flexible composites. Static goal regulation treats aims as agents of chronically available overarching aspirations, with intrinsic aspirations fueling mastery striving and extrinsic aspirations fueling performance striving. The synthesis concludes that "mastery aims show primarily strong bounds with autonomous reasons, whereas performance aims are more ambiguously aligned with underlying reasons", calling for integration of both perspectives rather than treating them as merely coexisting research strains.
requirements: Distinguishing aims (aspired end-states) from reasons (autonomous vs. controlled energizing forces) as separately measurable constructs
constraints: Anchored measurement of reasons after aims may artificially inflate aim-reason associations
Evidence on performance-aim bonds is ambiguous and heterogeneous across methodologies
target_learning_goals: achievement goal adoption (mastery vs. performance)
quality of motivation for goal striving
examples: The scoping review pooled goal-complex studies and life-aspiration studies to locate where bonds are strong (mastery-autonomous) versus ambiguous (performance)
key_sources: Janke, S. (2024). Dynamic or Static Goal Regulation: Implications of Weak and Strong Bonds Between Autonomous/Controlled Reasons and Aims for Achievement Goal Striving. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09968-w

article_title: Dynamic or Static Goal Regulation: Implications of Weak and Strong Bonds Between Autonomous/Controlled Reasons and Aims for Achievement Goal Striving
citation: Janke, S. (2024). Dynamic or Static Goal Regulation: Implications of Weak and Strong Bonds Between Autonomous/Controlled Reasons and Aims for Achievement Goal Striving. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09968-w
title: Foster mastery goals through autonomous rather than controlled motivators such as rewards
description: Because mastery aims appear strongly bound to autonomous reasons, educational practice seeking to foster mastery goals should rely on motivators aligned with autonomous regulation rather than external pressure. The article warns that if educators assume aims are equidistant to reasons, "such a practice could undermine autonomous reasons for goal striving in the sense of an overjustification effect and as a result effectively reduce mastery goal striving". Practice should therefore center on the primarily energizing reasons for the desired aim.
requirements: Knowledge of which reasons primarily energize the target aim in the given population
constraints: If an aim were genuinely equidistant to reasons, a broader range of motivators would be suitable; the evidence base for performance aims remains ambiguous
Large external pressure may in some conditions enforce bonds between controlled reasons and an aim
target_learning_goals: mastery goal adoption
autonomous motivation for learning
examples: The article's illustrative case of teachers using rewards for learning, which could backfire for mastery goals given their stronger bond to autonomous reasons
key_sources: Janke, S. (2024). Dynamic or Static Goal Regulation: Implications of Weak and Strong Bonds Between Autonomous/Controlled Reasons and Aims for Achievement Goal Striving. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09968-w

article_title: Classroom Management Scripts: a Theoretical Model Contrasting Expert and Novice Teachers’ Knowledge and Awareness of Classroom Events
citation: Charlotte E. Wolff, Halszka Jarodzka, Henny P.A. Boshuizen. (2020). Classroom Management Scripts: a Theoretical Model Contrasting Expert and Novice Teachers' Knowledge and Awareness of Classroom Events. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09542-0
title: Classroom management scripts: knowledge structures comprising enabling conditions, event representations, and consequences
description: The article defines classroom management scripts as "specific knowledge structures comprising a common sequence of events necessary to achieve management goals in the classroom", including actors, locations, and objects. The basic construct comprises enabling conditions (background factors influencing event probability), the classroom event representation, and consequences (signals and potential sources of problems). Scripts are framed around classroom events, are activated as wholes for familiar event types, and are built up and restructured through classroom experience.
requirements: Scripts develop through exposure to numerous events and varied experiences in the classroom
constraints: Scripts are domain-specific knowledge structures, though similarities in tasks across domains yield similar knowledge structures
target_learning_goals: classroom management knowledge
professional vision
event awareness
examples: The article illustrates enabling conditions with a boring lesson, missing learning materials, and unchecked distracting behavior leading to spreading disengagement
key_sources: Charlotte E. Wolff, Halszka Jarodzka, Henny P.A. Boshuizen. (2020). Classroom Management Scripts: a Theoretical Model Contrasting Expert and Novice Teachers' Knowledge and Awareness of Classroom Events. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09542-0

article_title: Classroom Management Scripts: a Theoretical Model Contrasting Expert and Novice Teachers’ Knowledge and Awareness of Classroom Events
citation: Charlotte E. Wolff, Halszka Jarodzka, Henny P.A. Boshuizen. (2020). Classroom Management Scripts: a Theoretical Model Contrasting Expert and Novice Teachers' Knowledge and Awareness of Classroom Events. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09542-0
title: Two-part model linking classroom management scripts to situational awareness, mode of cognition, and event representation
description: The second part of the model depicts how activated classroom management scripts influence teachers' visual perception, situational awareness, mode of cognition, and event representation. It draws on Endsley's theory of situational awareness, whose "three levels" are perception, comprehension, and projection, and on Eraut's theory of workplace learning for mode of cognition. The model presumes novices become overloaded in perceiving, understanding, and responding, while experts' scripts guide perceptual attention efficiently, equating integrated situational awareness with withitness.
requirements: Situational awareness is tightly coupled with mode of cognition; perception and event representation interact in a recurring loop of input and interpretation
constraints: The model itself is not entirely linear, as indicated by the arrows in the model
target_learning_goals: withitness
situational awareness of classroom events
classroom management decision-making
examples: The model is presented in Fig. 3 contrasting novices' continual image-driven scanning and prolonged analysis with experts' automatic scanning and pattern recognition
key_sources: Charlotte E. Wolff, Halszka Jarodzka, Henny P.A. Boshuizen. (2020). Classroom Management Scripts: a Theoretical Model Contrasting Expert and Novice Teachers' Knowledge and Awareness of Classroom Events. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09542-0

article_title: Classroom Management Scripts: a Theoretical Model Contrasting Expert and Novice Teachers’ Knowledge and Awareness of Classroom Events
citation: Charlotte E. Wolff, Halszka Jarodzka, Henny P.A. Boshuizen. (2020). Classroom Management Scripts: a Theoretical Model Contrasting Expert and Novice Teachers' Knowledge and Awareness of Classroom Events. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09542-0
title: Frame classroom management as a learning concern rather than a behavioral concern in teacher education
description: The article argues that because experts center student learning in interpreting events while novices emphasize behavior, teacher education should reframe classroom management around learning. It recommends "making new teachers aware that enabling conditions can be rather subtle, and reframing classroom management as a learning concern rather than a behavioral concern" as an area programs could explore more thoroughly, and reinforcing teachers' agency to counter the tendency to blame students.
requirements: Teacher education programs must address enabling conditions and teacher agency explicitly with beginner teachers
target_learning_goals: classroom management expertise
interpretation of classroom events
examples: The article suggests reinforcing the agency and influence of teachers on classroom situations may aid novices in overcoming the tendency to finger students as the cause of problems

article_title: The Long-Term Effects of the COVID-19 Pandemic on Children’s Writing: a Follow-up Replication Study
citation: Skar, G. B., Graham, S., & Huebener, A. (2023). The Long-Term Effects of the COVID-19 Pandemic on Children's Writing: a Follow-up Replication Study. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09729-1
title: Writer(s)-within-Community (WWC) model of writing development
description: The Writer(s)-within-Community model (Graham, 2018a, 2018b) is the theoretical framework that guided both the prior first-grade study and this longitudinal replication. The article states that "The WWC proposed that writing development is simultaneously and interactively shaped and bound by where it is learned and the cognitive capabilities and resources of those learning to write." This framing motivated restricting the study to a single country (Norway), since writing instruction is shaped by unique cultural, social, institutional, political, and historical factors. The model also motivated the choice of measures: attitude toward writing fuels effort, while limited cognitive resources make slow transcription skills such as handwriting interfere with conceptualization and ideation for beginning writers.
requirements: Assessment of writing should capture motivation (attitude), transcription resources (handwriting fluency), and the end product (text quality), as the model treats these as interacting components
constraints: The model led the authors to focus on a single country, since the teaching of writing in any single country is influenced by its own unique cultural, social, institutional, political, and historical factors
target_learning_goals: writing quality
handwriting fluency
attitude toward writing
examples: The model guided the assessment of attitude toward writing, handwriting fluency, and overall writing quality in Norwegian first- and second-graders
key_sources: Skar, G. B., Graham, S., & Huebener, A. (2023). The Long-Term Effects of the COVID-19 Pandemic on Children's Writing: a Follow-up Replication Study. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09729-1

article_title: Prospective Educational Applications of Mental Simulation: A Meta-review
citation: Meer, J.P. van & Theunissen, N.C.M. (2009). Prospective educational applications of mental simulation: A meta-review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-009-9097-8
title: Five explanation models for why mental simulation works
description: The review presents five theoretical accounts of MS effectiveness: motivational, symbolic learning, attentional-arousal, bio-informational and psychoneuromuscular theory. The bio-informational theory "holds that every overt and covert behavior creates a specific and unique pattern of interconnected nodes in the brain", strengthened by rehearsal; symbolic learning ties MS effects to a task's cognitive component; psychoneuromuscular theory points to minute muscle innervations with EMG evidence. The authors note no clear-cut answer exists and models may jointly explain the phenomenon.
requirements: Future studies exploring how the models together explain MS effectiveness, as the authors recommend
constraints: The review states there is no clear-cut answer to why MS is effective; some researchers do not find the neuromuscular theory very likely
target_learners: healthy adults practicing motor or cognitive skills
target_learning_goals: understanding mechanisms of mental practice for skill performance enhancement
examples: EMG action potentials during MS are cited as physiological evidence; symbolic learning theory is used to explain why MS appears more useful for cognitive than physical tasks.
key_sources: Meer, J.P. van & Theunissen, N.C.M. (2009). Prospective educational applications of mental simulation: A meta-review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-009-9097-8

article_title: Learning a Language Through Reading: A Meta-analysis of Studies on the Effects of Extensive Reading on Second and Foreign Language Learning
citation: Sangers, N. L., van der Sande, L., Welie, C., Dobber, M., & van Steensel, R. (2025). Learning a Language Through Reading: A Meta-analysis of Studies on the Effects of Extensive Reading on Second and Foreign Language Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10068-6
title: Three-mechanism theoretical rationale for extensive reading: implicit learning, comprehensible input, and motivation via choice
description: The article grounds extensive reading in three interrelated mechanisms. First, "extensive reading is expected to promote reading fluency by supporting implicit learning", via frequent exposure that strengthens lexical entries. Second, Krashen's Input Hypothesis holds that acquisition occurs through comprehensible input containing structure "a bit beyond our current level of competence (i + 1)". Third, choice-based motivation (Self-Determination Theory, the Affective Filter) is assumed to lower affective barriers so input is used for acquisition.
requirements: Frequent exposure to large amounts of textual input for implicit learning of co-occurrence patterns
Texts attuned to learners' proficiency so input remains comprehensible
Learner self-selection of reading material to support autonomous motivation
constraints: The Input Hypothesis has been criticized for being untestable, since i + 1 has not been operationalized
target_learners: Second and foreign language learners across primary, secondary, and tertiary education
target_learning_goals: Second and foreign language skills: reading comprehension, vocabulary, decoding/fluency, motivation, writing, oral proficiency, general language proficiency

Learning a Language Through Reading: A Meta-analysis of Studies on the Effects of Extensive Reading on Second and Foreign Language Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10068-6

article_title: Individual and Structural Factors Associated with Interactive Skills of Child-Care Professionals in Early Childhood Education and Care: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
citation: Støve, L. L., Dalgaard, N. T., Mohr, J. W., Hansen, J. E., Wendelboe, K. I., Hestbaek, E., Vieira, C. C., Væver, M. S., & Smith-Nielsen, J. (2026). Individual and Structural Factors Associated with Interactive Skills of Child-Care Professionals in Early Childhood Education and Care: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10162-3
title: Structure-Process-Outcome and Person-Process-Context-Time models as the review's organizing framework for caregiver interactive skills
description: The review organizes factors associated with caregiver interactive skills within two frameworks. The Structure-Process-Outcome model "proposes that structural characteristics of care settings (e.g., group sizes, child-caregiver ratios) create the conditions in which caregivers operate," with process quality (caregiver-child interactions) as the proximal mechanism linking structure to child outcomes. The Person-Process-Context-Time model extends this by "emphasizing the dynamic interplay between individual and contextual characteristics over time in shaping interaction quality." The review uses this integrative lens to situate structural and individual correlates in one conceptual framework.
requirements: Studies must assess interactive skills at the individual caregiver level for the framework's individual-level correlates to be disentangled
constraints: The framework is applied to formal ECEC settings for children up to 6.0 years
target_learners: Child-care professionals working with children aged 0–6 years in formal ECEC settings
target_learning_goals: Improving quality of caregiver-child interactions (responsiveness, sensitivity, developmental stimulation)
examples: The review interprets stronger negative ratio and group-size effects in higher-quality studies through a PPCT lens, suggesting contextual systems jointly shape proximal interactions

article_title: Emotional Artificial Intelligence in Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
citation: Heng Zhang, Yuhan Liu, Meilin Jiang, Juanjuan Chen, Minhong Wang, Fred Paas. (2025). Emotional Artificial Intelligence in Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10086-4
title: Control-value theory as an explanatory framework for AI-based cognitive and emotional support effects
description: The review interprets effects of AI-based learning support through Pekrun's control-value theory of achievement emotions, which "posits that achievement emotions stem from learners’ appraisals of control over tasks and the value they assign to those tasks." In AI-supported learning, cognitive support such as personalized feedback can raise perceived control, while emotional support can stabilize achievement emotions; the authors therefore expected the largest knowledge and skill effects when supports are integrated. This framework organizes the meta-analysis's directional expectations and its interpretation of why integrated supports outperformed emotional-only support on cognitive outcomes.
requirements: AI-based cognitive support that raises perceived task control and emotional support that regulates achievement emotions must be distinguishable and combinable in the intervention design
constraints: The authors describe their expectations as "theory-informed expectations rather than confirmatory hypotheses"; heterogeneity suggests mechanisms depend on task complexity, adaptivity, and how tightly emotional signals are coupled to instructional actions
target_learners: students across pre-school, elementary, secondary, and tertiary education
target_learning_goals: knowledge acquisition
skill acquisition
affective experience regulation
examples: The review expected integrated support to outperform emotional-only support on cognitive outcomes by increasing perceived control while regulating emotions
key_sources: Heng Zhang, Yuhan Liu, Meilin Jiang, Juanjuan Chen, Minhong Wang, Fred Paas. (2025). Emotional Artificial Intelligence in Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10086-4

article_title: Emotional Artificial Intelligence in Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
citation: Heng Zhang, Yuhan Liu, Meilin Jiang, Juanjuan Chen, Minhong Wang, Fred Paas. (2025). Emotional Artificial Intelligence in Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10086-4
title: Taxonomy of eight AI-based cognitive support types and five AI-based emotional support types in education
description: From 172 included articles, the review identified "eight types of AI-based cognitive support and five types of AI-based emotional support." Cognitive support types include providing individualized feedback (65 articles), real-time task guidance (45), simulating human conversations for communication skills (32), personalized learning resources (31), answering questions (26), prompting questions (13), metacognitive advice (10), and translating images/text (5). Emotional support types include tailored affective responses (34), emotional interaction without monitoring (22), reminders to relax or regulate emotions (4), instructing teachers to demonstrate empathetic behaviors (1), and grouping students with similar knowledge levels (1). This taxonomy maps the intervention space of emotional AI in education and underpins the three-category meta-analytic comparison.
requirements: Interventions must be classifiable as AI-based cognitive support, AI-based emotional support, or an integration of both, based on the nature of the support provided
constraints: The taxonomy reflects the 172 articles included in this review (2000–2025); support types were identified from the included literature rather than proposed a priori
target_learners: students across pre-school, elementary, secondary, and tertiary education
target_learning_goals: cognitive learning support
emotional regulation during learning
examples: Table 4 lists all support types with article counts, e.g., CS1 providing feedback based on individual circumstances (65 articles) and ES1 offering affective responses tailored to individual circumstances (34 articles)
