article_title: The Development, Testing, and Refinement of Eccles, Wigfield, and Colleagues’ Situated Expectancy-Value Model of Achievement Performance and Choice
citation: Jacquelynne S. Eccles · Allan Wigfield. (2024). The Development, Testing, and Refinement of Eccles, Wigfield, and Colleagues' Situated Expectancy-Value Model of Achievement Performance and Choice. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09888-9
title: Situated expectancy-value theory (SEVT) of achievement performance and choice
description: SEVT holds that achievement-related performance and choice are most directly influenced by individuals' "expectations for success at and the subjective task value (STV) of the action chosen compared to" available alternatives. Subjective task value comprises four components: intrinsic value, utility value, attainment value, and perceived cost. Expectancies and values are themselves shaped by task-specific beliefs, goals, self-schemata, and affective memories, which develop through socializers' beliefs and behaviors, prior achievement experiences, and the cultural milieu. The 2020 renaming to situated expectancy-value theory emphasizes that beliefs, values, and decisions are situated and specific rather than global, and that cultural influences are infused throughout the model rather than only exogenous.
requirements: Validated measures of the central constructs; the authors note attaining consensus on measurement is a key future need
constraints: The article states trying to test all proposed links in one study would not be possible; support is built gradually, part by part
The figure depiction does not fully capture the situative and culturally infused character the authors intend; a new depiction is in preparation
target_learning_goals: achievement-related choices such as course enrollment and career choice
academic performance motivation
examples: The 1976 precursor model had four boxes including cultural norms and expectations, current situational factors, socialization in home and schools, and personal attitudes and values
The model was developed to explain why girls were less likely to participate in STEM courses and careers
key_sources: Jacquelynne S. Eccles · Allan Wigfield. (2024). The Development, Testing, and Refinement of Eccles, Wigfield, and Colleagues' Situated Expectancy-Value Model of Achievement Performance and Choice. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09888-9

article_title: A Systematic Review of Peer Assessment Design Elements
citation: Alqassab, M., Strijbos, J.-W., Panadero, E., Fernández Ruiz, J., Warrens, M., & To, J. (2023). A Systematic Review of Peer Assessment Design Elements. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09723-7
title: Five prototypical peer assessment design patterns from latent class analysis
description: The review's LCA of 891 cases yielded a five-class solution describing latent patterns of peer assessment designs. Class 1 is "Online asynchronous formative anonymous random-matched bi-direc tional intragroup (individually assessed) peer assessment via written comments [with revision]"; Class 2 is the summative scoring counterpart without revision; Class 3 is face-to-face synchronous formative non-anonymous self-selection matched with oral and written comments and revision; Class 4 is online asynchronous formative intergroup scoring plus written comments with revision; Class 5 is online asynchronous summative non-anonymous domain-matched intra- and intergroup scoring without revision. Classes 1, 2, and 3 were large (32.8%, 25.7%, 21.6%); Classes 4 and 5 small (13.1%, 6.8%).
requirements: Design elements must be reported in sufficient detail for coding; the review notes vagueness of design descriptions in most published articles limited reliable coding
constraints: Patterns derive from studies published 2011–October 2018 in peer-reviewed journals, excluding grey literature and workplace settings
target_learning_goals: domain-specific knowledge or skills
social skills
examples: Class 1 (32.8% of sample): formative, written comments, revision, intragroup, anonymous, online asynchronous, random matching
Class 3 (21.6%): face-to-face synchronous, formative, non-anonymous, self-select matching, oral and written comments, with revision

article_title: A Systematic Review of Peer Assessment Design Elements
citation: Alqassab, M., Strijbos, J.-W., Panadero, E., Fernández Ruiz, J., Warrens, M., & To, J. (2023). A Systematic Review of Peer Assessment Design Elements. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09723-7
title: Refined definition of peer assessment as a learning phenomenon in social constellations, organized by a four-category coding scheme
description: The review defines peer assessment as "a learning phenomenon where individuals or social constellations (e.g., pair, group, team, community)—within a physical and/or virtual environment—exchange, react to, interact and/or act upon information about individual performance and/or individual contributions" with the purpose of accomplishing shared and individual learning goals. It extends Topping's (1998) definition to cover social constellations and virtual environments, and frames instructional scaffolds provided by agents (teacher, peer, self, technology) as fadable supports. The definition underpins a coding scheme of 27 design elements grouped into four categories: context (what designers cannot manipulate), instructional design (what designers can manipulate), outcomes, and moderators/mediators.
requirements: Peer assessment must be clearly distinguished from other peer-assisted learning activities such as peer tutoring, peer modelling, peer monitoring, and peer coaching
constraints: The coding scheme was built on Gielen et al.'s (2011) refinement of Topping's (1998) typology, with variables refined from contemporary reviews
target_learning_goals: domain-specific knowledge or skills
social skills
examples: The coding scheme includes 22 instructional design elements such as purpose, object, privacy, contact, matching, training, and revision

article_title: Yes Children Need to Learn Their GPCs but There Really Is Little or No Evidence that Systematic or Explicit Phonics Is Effective: a response to Fletcher, Savage, and Sharon (2020)
citation: Jeffrey S. Bowers. (2021). Yes Children Need to Learn Their GPCs but There Really Is Little or No Evidence that Systematic or Explicit Phonics Is Effective: a response to Fletcher, Savage, and Sharon (2020). Educational Psychology Review (2021) 33:1965–1979. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09602-z
title: Structured Word Inquiry (SWI): teaching GPCs within morphology from the start, rejecting the 'phonology first' assumption
description: Structured Word Inquiry is an approach to reading instruction that explicitly teaches grapheme-phoneme correspondences together with morphology, etymology, spelling, and vocabulary from the start, rather than teaching letter-sound correspondences first in isolation. As the article states, "Structured Word Inquiry (SWI) teaches GPCs in the context of morphology in an attempt to teach GPCs more effectively." It uses tools such as word sums and morphological matrices to highlight consistent spelling-meaning connections in morphological families — for example, showing that the spelling of <do> is preserved in <does>, <doing>, and <done>, making sense of spellings phonics treats as exceptions. SWI can be used at any stage of reading instruction, unlike phonics, which is ideally finished after grade 2 or 3.
requirements: Instruction must teach phonological and semantic regularities of English spellings together from the start, because they interact in ways that make sense of GPCs
constraints: The article states the SWI approach needs more empirical support, and more work is needed on implementing SWI at larger scale given many concepts are unfamiliar to teachers
target_learners: children in the early stages of learning to read (grade 1–2 in the cited preliminary studies)
target_learning_goals: reading
spelling
vocabulary
knowledge of grapheme-phoneme correspondences and morphological structure of English spellings
examples: A SWI lesson on <does> begins with the meanings of <does> and <do> in spoken sentences, then uses word sums and morphological matrices to show the spelling of <do> is preserved in <does>, <doing>, and <done>
key_sources: Jeffrey S. Bowers. (2021). Yes Children Need to Learn Their GPCs but There Really Is Little or No Evidence that Systematic or Explicit Phonics Is Effective: a response to Fletcher, Savage, and Sharon (2020). Educational Psychology Review (2021) 33:1965–1979. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09602-z

article_title: The Effect of Playback Speed and Distractions on the Comprehension of Audio and Audio-Visual Materials
citation: Ashley Chen, Suchita E. Kumar, Rhea Varkhedi, Dillon H. Murphy. (2024). The Effect of Playback Speed and Distractions on the Comprehension of Audio and Audio-Visual Materials. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09917-7
title: Dual-channel cognitive load account of speeded multimedia comprehension
description: The article explains preserved comprehension at accelerated speeds via cognitive load theory and the multimedia principle: because visual and verbal information are processed in separate working memory channels, adding visual content to narration divides processing demands and frees capacity. The authors state that "multimedia presentations can help mitigate the negative costs of accelerated speeds, especially when information is processed by separate working memory components (i.e., narration in the auditory channel, text or pictures in the visual channel), which reduces cognitive load." This account frames why audio-only content is more vulnerable to overload at high speeds and why visual supports buffer accelerated narration.
requirements: Learning materials must pair narration with visual content (text or pictures) presented in the visual channel so processing is split across channels
constraints: The account is offered as the authors' interpretation of why speed effects were absent up to 2.5x; performance is expected to decline beyond the 2x threshold per prior work the article cites
target_learners: undergraduate students learning from pre-recorded audio and audio-visual lectures
target_learning_goals: comprehension of narrated instructional content at accelerated playback speeds
examples: Experiment 2 compared audio-only versus audio-visual clips (slides plus instructor images) at 1x and 2x speed; Experiment 3 compared textual versus pictorial slides accompanying narration
key_sources: Ashley Chen, Suchita E. Kumar, Rhea Varkhedi, Dillon H. Murphy. (2024). The Effect of Playback Speed and Distractions on the Comprehension of Audio and Audio-Visual Materials. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09917-7

article_title: The Effect of Playback Speed and Distractions on the Comprehension of Audio and Audio-Visual Materials
citation: Ashley Chen, Suchita E. Kumar, Rhea Varkhedi, Dillon H. Murphy. (2024). The Effect of Playback Speed and Distractions on the Comprehension of Audio and Audio-Visual Materials. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09917-7
title: Advise learners not to exceed 2x playback speed, and pair accelerated narration with visual content to protect comprehension
description: The article recommends two practices for speeded lecture consumption: keep acceleration at or below 2x, and prefer audio-visual over audio-only formats when learning at faster speeds. The authors write "we still do not advise exceeding 2x speed since performance tends to quickly decline beyond that point," and conclude that viewing information in dual modalities "may thus be preferable when learning at faster speeds." The recommendation rests on their own experiments showing a near-significant 1x-to-2.5x decline and a significant multimedia advantage.
requirements: Pre-recorded audio or audio-visual lectures with user-controlled playback speed
Visual components (slides, text, or images) available to accompany narration
constraints: The speed caution is based on a 6% difference between 1x and 2.5x groups that only approached significance (ptukey = 0.051); distraction findings apply to passive, non-interactive notifications
target_learners: undergraduate and other students watching pre-recorded lectures, including MOOC learners
target_learning_goals: preserving comprehension while accelerating lecture playback
examples: Experiment 1 assigned listeners across 1x, 1.5x, 2x, and 2.5x speeds; Experiment 2's 2x audio-only group scored about 12% lower than the 1x audio-visual group
key_sources: Ashley Chen, Suchita E. Kumar, Rhea Varkhedi, Dillon H. Murphy. (2024). The Effect of Playback Speed and Distractions on the Comprehension of Audio and Audio-Visual Materials. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09917-7

article_title: Interest, Self-efficacy, and Belonging in Classroom Learning
citation: Renninger, K. A., Barton, L. K., Bautista, G., Garcia-Barrios, M., Ogunyinka, I., & Riley, K. R. (2026). Interest, Self-efficacy, and Belonging in Classroom Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10102-7
title: Four-phase model of interest development
description: The article follows Hidi and Renninger's model in which interest is "a cognitive and affective motivational variable that may develop." Development "is initiated by an initial triggering," which, if sustained, "continues to deepen in knowledge and value, and may continue to develop into a well-developed individual interest." Across populations and subject matters the developmental course is the same, yet individual pathways are idiosyncratic; the process may take a short time or extend over several years. The article uses this model to organize its review of interest's indicators, pedagogical supports, and relations to the other variables.
requirements: Sustained support after triggering, through interactions with people and/or environment design, for interest to deepen in knowledge and value
constraints: Students may not be fully aware of their interest, which may impact their ability to self-report it
target_learners: K-16 students in disciplinary classrooms, including science
target_learning_goals: Sustained engagement and re-engagement with disciplinary content
Development of individual interest in a discipline
examples: The pilot workshop designed NGSS-aligned modules on everyday phenomena so students with no formal science training could make connections and trigger interest
key_sources: Renninger, K. A., Barton, L. K., Bautista, G., Garcia-Barrios, M., Ogunyinka, I., & Riley, K. R. (2026). Interest, Self-efficacy, and Belonging in Classroom Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10102-7

article_title: Interest, Self-efficacy, and Belonging in Classroom Learning
citation: Renninger, K. A., Barton, L. K., Bautista, G., Garcia-Barrios, M., Ogunyinka, I., & Riley, K. R. (2026). Interest, Self-efficacy, and Belonging in Classroom Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10102-7
title: Bandura's four sources of self-efficacy beliefs
description: The article presents Bandura's (1997) model of the sources of individuals' self-efficacy beliefs: "mastery experiences," "vicarious experience (the observations of others' actions)," "social persuasion (encouragement from community members)," and "emotional and physiological states." The review reports that study of these sources does not consistently indicate which are most important in aggregate populations, prompting analysis by gender, race, ethnicity, and classroom environment variables. It uses the model to identify practices teachers could promote, such as proximal goal setting and peer modeling.
requirements: Opportunities for students to recognize their own competence when working on activities, e.g., through mastery experiences and social persuasion
constraints: Which sources are most important is not consistent across populations studied in aggregate
target_learners: Middle school, secondary, and college students in academic domains
target_learning_goals: Students' beliefs about their capacity to succeed on academic tasks
Academic achievement, persistence, and self-directed learning
examples: Usher and Pajares (2006) found social persuasion was a predictive source of academic self-efficacy for girls and African American students more of the time
key_sources: Renninger, K. A., Barton, L. K., Bautista, G., Garcia-Barrios, M., Ogunyinka, I., & Riley, K. R. (2026). Interest, Self-efficacy, and Belonging in Classroom Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10102-7

article_title: Interest, Self-efficacy, and Belonging in Classroom Learning
citation: Renninger, K. A., Barton, L. K., Bautista, G., Garcia-Barrios, M., Ogunyinka, I., & Riley, K. R. (2026). Interest, Self-efficacy, and Belonging in Classroom Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10102-7
title: Educators should sustain content connections, affirm students can be successful, and provide contextual support
description: Across the three literatures, the review concludes that "the role of the educator was shown to be particularly important, as the educator is positioned to encourage students and/or design the learning environment to" (a) sustain connections to disciplinary content that triggered interest, (b) help students know they can be successful, and (c) provide contextual support for working with content. These three supports jointly provide "a basis for developing interest, and associated self-efficacy and belonging." The principle integrates the review's practice implications rather than privileging one variable.
requirements: Educators positioned to design the learning environment and encourage students across all three motivational variables
constraints: The review notes the relations among the variables and their implications for working with students remain largely unexplored
target_learners: Classroom students across K-16, including minoritized students in science
target_learning_goals: Sustained engagement with disciplinary content
Self-efficacy for learning
Classroom belonging
examples: The pilot workshop paired students as lab partners, used real-world phenomena such as how energy travels through systems, and was facilitated by a professor sharing students' racial identity who engaged them in individual conversation

article_title: Generative Learning: Which Strategies for What Age?
citation: Garvin Brod. (2021). Generative Learning: Which Strategies for What Age? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09571-9
title: Developmental prerequisites framework: knowledge, cognitive capacities, and metacognitive abilities explain age-related differences in generative learning strategy effectiveness
description: The review proposes that age-related differences in the effectiveness of generative learning strategies stem from three developmental processes: "Increases in knowledge", "Increases in cognitive capacities", and "Increases in metacognitive abilities". World knowledge provides a richer semantic network and frees cognitive capacity; working memory and inhibition — "collectively termed executive functions" — underlie reasoning and mental-model revision; and monitoring and control skills follow a late-maturing trajectory. Differences between strategies' developmental trajectories are attributed to their differing specific prerequisites, such as reasoning for explaining and metacognitive monitoring for questioning.
requirements: Strategies capitalizing on prior-knowledge activation require learners to have sufficient world knowledge, executive functions, and metacognitive monitoring for the strategy's specific mechanisms
constraints: The review restricts this account to individually performed generative strategies targeting declarative knowledge enrichment, excluding collaborative generation, procedural knowledge, and children below school age
target_learners: school-age students from elementary school through university
target_learning_goals: acquisition of declarative knowledge through generative learning strategies
examples: The review links lower elementary students' failure to profit from the forward testing effect to difficulties combating interference related to executive-function development
key_sources: Garvin Brod. (2021). Generative Learning: Which Strategies for What Age? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09571-9

article_title: Generative Learning: Which Strategies for What Age?
citation: Garvin Brod. (2021). Generative Learning: Which Strategies for What Age? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09571-9
title: Match the amount of instructional support in generative learning activities to learners' age, giving younger learners more structure
description: The review concludes that generative learning strategies must be implemented with age-appropriate support: "younger learners generally need more support than older learners", and "a suboptimal implementation of the technique for a particular age group can render it ineffective". Support can take the form of pre-structured materials, such as high-coherence concept maps or fill-in maps, or prompts to compare generated products with provided ones. Without such scaffolding, younger children may produce poor-quality generative products and gain nothing.
requirements: Instructional support must be calibrated to the age group's prior knowledge, working memory, and self-regulation capacities
constraints: For drawing, even high support did not suffice for fourth-graders, who may need additional practice in the technique; guided question stems may not truly involve generation
target_learning_goals: effective use of generative learning strategies for declarative knowledge acquisition
examples: Late-elementary children who only filled in parts of an existing concept map did significantly better than children generating the entire map themselves
Sixth-graders' drawing benefit was enhanced when prompted to compare their drawing with a provided illustration

article_title: The Cognitive Architecture of Digital Externalization
citation: Alexander Skulmowski. (2023). The Cognitive Architecture of Digital Externalization. Educational Psychology Review, 35:101. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09818-1
title: Cognitive architecture of digital externalization: cognitive load determines when learners offload information
description: The article presents a model of digital externalization grounded in cognitive load theory, in which the decision to externalize information is driven by five factors: lower actual or perceived working memory capacity, higher extraneous cognitive load, higher intrinsic cognitive load, and the perceived value of information. As the article states, "the model presented in Fig. 1 presents extraneous cognitive load as a triple barrier for information in the selection, offloading, and long-term memorization stages." Extraneous load can block information from entering working memory, from being stored in long-term memory, and from being externalized via complex artifact controls. Strategy selection is metacognitive, drawing on learners' beliefs about their capabilities and the task.
requirements: Grounded in the current iteration of cognitive load theory distinguishing intrinsic and extraneous cognitive load
Learners make metacognitive strategy-selection decisions based on beliefs about capabilities and task demands
constraints: The article notes memory and intention offloading "might need to be considered as distinct phenomena following their own sets of rules"
The model is a synthesis of prior studies rather than a directly tested prediction
target_learners: learners using digital technologies for learning
target_learning_goals: understanding when learners internalize versus externalize information
key_sources: Alexander Skulmowski. (2023). The Cognitive Architecture of Digital Externalization. Educational Psychology Review, 35:101. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09818-1

article_title: The Cognitive Architecture of Digital Externalization
citation: Alexander Skulmowski. (2023). The Cognitive Architecture of Digital Externalization. Educational Psychology Review, 35:101. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09818-1
title: Design digital learning to rely on biologically primary knowledge instead of technology-related secondary knowledge
description: The principle holds that digital learning tasks should be analyzed for elements requiring biologically secondary knowledge (e.g., learning game rules or unfamiliar interfaces) and replaced with counterparts drawing on biologically primary knowledge such as intuitive gestures. The review reports that "Several studies have utilized biologically primary knowledge in the form of intuitive actions, such as pointing gestures on tablets, with positive effects on learning." Requiring substantial technology-related secondary knowledge before content learning can encumber digital learning.
requirements: An analysis of which task elements rely on biologically secondary versus primary knowledge
Technology-related secondary demands must be minimized before intrinsic content is encountered
constraints: The review notes certain forms of digital learning encumber learning specifically when learners must master substantial technology-related secondary knowledge first
target_learning_goals: reducing extraneous cognitive load in digital learning tasks
examples: Studies using pointing gestures on tablets showed positive learning effects while keeping cognitive load at a minimum
key_sources: Alexander Skulmowski. (2023). The Cognitive Architecture of Digital Externalization. Educational Psychology Review, 35:101. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09818-1

article_title: Let Learners Monitor the Learning Content and Their Learning Behavior! A Meta-analysis on the Effectiveness of Tools to Foster Monitoring
citation: Dignath, C., van Ewijk, R., Perels, F., & Fabriz, S. (2023). Let Learners Monitor the Learning Content and Their Learning Behavior! A Meta-analysis on the Effectiveness of Tools to Foster Monitoring. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09718-4
title: Reactivity and reminder effects as the mode of action of monitoring tools
description: The article explains monitoring tools' operation through two mechanisms. The reactivity effect holds that directing attention to one's learning already changes behavior: "This shift of attention focus alone is already assumed to elicit behavior change, also called the reactivity effect (Zimmerman, 2002)." The reminder effect holds that tool questions act as cues that prompt strategy use in the moment of learning. Tools thus engage learners in monitoring and control processes within the SRL cycle, drawing on Winne and Hadwin's COPES model in which monitoring compares products against standards.
requirements: Tools must include questions or prompts that focus the learner's attention on their understanding or learning behavior during the learning process.
constraints: The reactivity account is presented as an assumption from prior theory rather than a mechanism tested within this meta-analysis.
target_learners: students from primary school through higher education and adult learners
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning skills, metacognitive monitoring of comprehension and learning behavior
examples: Learning journals with self-recording prompts such as registering one's actions during task performance; prompts for monitoring understanding such as asking which main points have not yet been understood.

article_title: Synthesizing Cognitive Load and Self-regulation Theory: a Theoretical Framework and Research Agenda
citation: de Bruin, A. B. H., Roelle, J., Carpenter, S. K., & Baars, M. (2020). Synthesizing Cognitive Load and Self-regulation Theory: a Theoretical Framework and Research Agenda. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09576-4
title: The Effort Monitoring and Regulation (EMR) framework integrates cognitive load theory with self-regulated learning theory
description: The EMR framework builds on the Nelson and Narens model, positing a meta level at which metacognitive monitoring and regulation occur based on input from the object level where learners engage with a learning task. Cognitive load is positioned in the middle, with direct links to both levels and both processes. The authors state it "outlines how monitoring and regulation of effort are neglected but essential aspects of self-regulated learning" and emphasize optimizing cognitive load during self-regulated learning by reducing unnecessary primary-task load or distributing load between the primary task and metacognitive aspects.
requirements: Requires investigation of how learners incorporate mental effort into monitoring processes and how learners regulate mental effort, per the article's three research questions
constraints: Beyond effort cues, various other cues (e.g., fluency, familiarity) affect monitoring, regulation, and learning
Interactions with individual differences, task characteristics, and learning context need to be taken into account
Integrated CLT-SRL research is in its embryonal stage, with little empirical data to date
target_learners: students learning from texts, hypermedia, problem-solving tasks, and other learning environments
target_learning_goals: accurate self-monitoring of learning and effort
effective regulation of mental effort during learning
examples: The framework structures the special issue's contributions around three research questions: how students monitor effort, how they regulate effort, and how cognitive load on self-regulated learning tasks can be optimized during and after the primary task

article_title: Synthesizing Cognitive Load and Self-regulation Theory: a Theoretical Framework and Research Agenda
citation: de Bruin, A. B. H., Roelle, J., Carpenter, S. K., & Baars, M. (2020). Synthesizing Cognitive Load and Self-regulation Theory: a Theoretical Framework and Research Agenda. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09576-4
title: The interactive layers model describes self-regulated learning as occurring in three layers, consciously or unconsciously
description: The special-issue paper by Wirth, Stebner, Trypke, Schuster, and Leutner introduces what the editorial calls "a novel, interactive layers model of self-regulated learning and cognitive load". It describes how self-regulated learning can be unconscious, not loading onto working memory but relying on resonant states in sensory memory, or conscious and related to schema construction in working memory. Both conscious and unconscious self-regulation is described to take place in three layers: a content layer, a learning strategy layer, and a metacognitive layer. The model is then applied to explain existing inconsistent empirical findings in the literature.
requirements: The model is applied to explain existing inconsistent empirical findings, requiring empirical phenomena to interpret
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning and management of cognitive load
examples: The editorial illustrates unconscious self-regulation with an experienced highway driver responding effectively to traffic without remembering it seconds later

title: Seufert's discussion paper models self-regulation as an inverted U-shaped function of task difficulty
description: In the first discussion paper of the special issue, Seufert describes "how self-regulation can be seen as an inverted U-shaped function of task difficulty, with an optimal balance between resources and load, and thus optimal self-regulation, at medium task difficulty". She emphasizes understanding how learners' effort is used as a cue and how it can bias students' judgments of their learning. She concludes that more elaborate analyses of effort appraisals, including research into the different origins of load, are needed, and that research should broaden the scope to include appraisals of learning resources, including motivational and affective states.
requirements: More elaborate analyses of effort appraisals, including research into the different origins of load, are needed
constraints: The scope should broaden to include appraisals of learning resources, including motivational and affective states
target_learning_goals: accurate effort appraisals and self-regulation of learning
examples: The model posits optimal self-regulation at medium task difficulty, where resources and load are balanced

article_title: The Powerful Teacher: A Power Hypothesis for the Benefits of Learning-by-Teaching
citation: Sarah Shi Hui Wong, Stephen Lim. (2026). The Powerful Teacher: A Power Hypothesis for the Benefits of Learning-by-Teaching. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10097-1
title: Power hypothesis of learning-by-teaching
description: The article advances a novel mechanism account: "when taking on the role of a teacher and teaching others, students might experience a heightened sense of power that may be beneficial for their own learning." Power is defined as a psychological state of perceived capacity to influence others, distinct from social presence, autonomy, self-efficacy, and productive agency. Drawing on French and Raven's power bases, the account holds that the teacher role carries expectations of authoritative knowledge, and that power triggers approach orientation, energized cognition, and self-regulation that improve task performance.
requirements: The learner must take on the role of a teacher, which carries socially structured expectations of authoritative knowledge and responsibility for the audience's learning.
constraints: The account is presented as a hypothesis tested in non-interactive, written teaching with a fictitious peer audience; the article distinguishes power from social presence, which can manifest without interaction.
target_learning_goals: deep learning of studied material
create-level research question generation
examples: Participants in the teaching condition wrote a verbatim teaching script as how they would orally deliver a lecture to their peers, and rated their sense of power during the intervention.
key_sources: Sarah Shi Hui Wong, Stephen Lim. (2026). The Powerful Teacher: A Power Hypothesis for the Benefits of Learning-by-Teaching. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10097-1

citation: Sarah Shi Hui Wong, Stephen Lim. (2026). The Powerful Teacher: A Power Hypothesis for the Benefits of Learning-by-Teaching. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10097-1
title: Three extant theoretical accounts of learning-by-teaching benefits
description: The article organizes prior mechanism accounts into a three-part framework: "Three main non-mutually exclusive accounts have been proposed to explain the benefits of learning-by-teaching: (a) the retrieval hypothesis, (b) the generative hypothesis, and (c) the social presence hypothesis." The retrieval hypothesis attributes benefits to retrieval practice; the generative hypothesis to selecting, organizing, integrating, and metacognitive monitoring during teaching; the social presence hypothesis to feelings that an audience is real and present. The review argues each account has contested evidence.
requirements: Each account is evaluated against empirical tests; the article treats them as non-mutually exclusive and requires process measures (retrieval, elaborations, monitoring statements, self-other referential terms) to test them.
constraints: The article reports mixed or contested evidence for each account: the social presence hypothesis is summarized as showing that increasing social presence does not necessarily enhance learning outcomes.
target_learners: learners in peer tutoring and teachable-agent settings
target_learning_goals: retention and comprehension of studied material
higher-order outcomes such as question generation and argumentative reasoning
examples: The article reviews Koh et al.'s teaching-with-retrieval versus teaching-no-retrieval comparison and Sibley et al.'s open- versus closed-book teaching as tests of the retrieval hypothesis.

title: Question generation training handout based on Bloom's taxonomy
description: A training handout that "introduced and explained the features of all six question levels corresponding to Bloom's taxonomy" with sample action prompts for each level from remember to create. Before the intervention, all participants practiced generating at least two create questions from a 199-word practice text on enzymes in 5 minutes and received concise verbal feedback on whether their questions reflected the create level. The handout was reprinted from Wong, Lim, and Lim (2023).

constraints: The handout defines create questions as those creating new knowledge by compiling information in a different way, combining elements in a new pattern, or proposing alternative solutions; generic questions answerable without deep understanding are scored as non-create.

examples: Sample create questions included asking what new methods could preserve the chemical composition of lunar rocks for better analysis; sample non-create questions included generic questions such as alternative hypotheses for how the moon was formed.

These workshops are the setting in which the three recurring concerns about workload, scope of usefulness, and test anxiety surfaced, and in which the authors attempted to address them by discussing nuances of the retrieval practice literature. article_title: Null and Void? Errors in Meta-analysis on Perceptual Disfluency and Recommendations to Improve Meta-analytical Reproducibility
citation: Sophia C. Weissgerber, Matthias Brunmair & Ralf Rummer. (2021). Null and Void? Errors in Meta-analysis on Perceptual Disfluency and Recommendations to Improve Meta-analytical Reproducibility. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09579-1
title: Methods Reproducibility framework for meta-analysis: four levels from Computational Reproducibility to Outcome Reproducibility
description: The article introduces a framework targeted at facilitating the reproducibility of meta-analysis, organized in four levels building on the TOP-guidelines, the Reproducibility Enhancement Principles, and Lakens et al.'s recommendations. It addresses "numerical accuracy (Computational Reproducibility: Level 1) and numerical validity (Computational Verification: Level 2)", then Analysis Reproducibility (Level 3) and Outcome Reproducibility (Level 4), which target researchers' degrees of freedom in analytical choices and database creation. The framework specifies what original authors must provide and what independent researchers or reviewers check at each level, and is demonstrated on the TRANSFER outcome of the Xie et al. meta-analysis.
requirements: Original authors provide original data including raw data used to estimate effect sizes, understandable analysis code, and description of used analysis tools; higher levels additionally require a codebook, workflow log of subjective decisions, and computational formulas
constraints: Level 1 and Level 2 are positioned prior to publication; the framework's logic moves from reliability to include validity aspects, per the article's own footnote
target_learning_goals: improving the credibility and reproducibility of meta-analytical evidence about learning interventions
examples: The appendices and supplemental materials demonstrate the approach on TRANSFER performance of Xie et al. (2018), with OSF-hosted check files for Levels 1–4
key_sources: Sophia C. Weissgerber, Matthias Brunmair & Ralf Rummer. (2021). Null and Void? Errors in Meta-analysis on Perceptual Disfluency and Recommendations to Improve Meta-analytical Reproducibility. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09579-1

article_title: Null and Void? Errors in Meta-analysis on Perceptual Disfluency and Recommendations to Improve Meta-analytical Reproducibility
citation: Sophia C. Weissgerber, Matthias Brunmair & Ralf Rummer. (2021). Null and Void? Errors in Meta-analysis on Perceptual Disfluency and Recommendations to Improve Meta-analytical Reproducibility. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09579-1
title: Meta-analyses should mandatorily publish their dataset and complete analysis code prior to publication
description: The article argues that open-science practices should be mandatory rather than voluntary for meta-analyses: "it should thus be mandatory (and not voluntary) to publish the data set as a separate file alongside the manuscript", and it should be mandatory prior to publication to provide the complete analysis code via a repository such as OSF. This enables independent researchers to exactly recreate reported results and supports future re-analysis as statistical tools evolve. The principle rests on the TOP-guidelines and the Reproducibility Enhancement Principles.
requirements: Data files must include all relevant texts from primary studies underlying coding decisions, statistical raw values, and a link to data files directly analyzable with statistical software
constraints: The article notes existing guidelines such as PRISMA are not always formulated specifically enough for reproducibility
target_learning_goals: ensuring meta-analytical results about learning effects can be independently verified and re-analyzed
examples: The commentary could not apply Level 1 checks as outlined because Xie et al. provided no data or code files, illustrating the consequence of non-compliance

citation: Janssen, E. M., van Gog, T., van de Groep, L., de Lange, A. J., Knopper, R. L., Onan, E., Wiradhany, W., & de Bruin, A. B. H. (2023). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09797-3
title: Effort Monitoring and Regulation (EMR) framework
description: The EMR framework, attributed by the article to De Bruin et al. (2020), "proposes that students use mental effort as a cue for monitoring their learning and for making study decisions." It explains why students avoid effective but effortful strategies: they may misinterpret experienced effort during studying, treating the experience that studying costs much effort as an indication that they are not learning well. The present experiments tested this account by relating effort ratings to judgments of learning, perceived strategy effectiveness, and willingness to use blocked and interleaved study.
requirements: Students must report their experienced mental effort during studying for the framework's cue-based monitoring account to apply
constraints: The article applies the framework to conditions, like interleaved studying, where high effort investment may actually result in higher learning outcomes
target_learners: higher-education students self-regulating their study strategy choices
target_learning_goals: category learning (recognizing painters' styles from paintings) and study-strategy selection for similar learning tasks
examples: Both experiments measured self-reported mental effort, judgments of learning, perceived effectiveness, and willingness to use each strategy at multiple measurement moments

article_title: Agency in Educational Technology: Interdisciplinary Perspectives and Implications for Learning Design
citation: Garvin Brod, Natalia Kucirkova, Joshua Shepherd, Dietsje Jolles, Inge Molenaar. (2023). Agency in Educational Technology: Interdisciplinary Perspectives and Implications for Learning Design. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09749-x
title: Agency personalization loop: adaptive assignment of agency levels based on a student model and learning progress
description: The agency personalization loop is a three-step conceptualization for how personalized EdTech can adaptively assign levels of agency to learners. As the article describes it, "The simplified version of such a personalization loop consists of three steps: (1) Identification and assessment of relevant learner characteristics (e.g., prior domain knowledge, executive function, and metacognitive skills), which form a student model", followed by algorithmic assignment of agency level and learning-progress assessment that updates the student model. The loop lets agency "vary both between different learners and within a particular learner over time," balancing free choice against assigned optimal content.
requirements: A student model of learner characteristics such as prior domain knowledge, executive function, and metacognitive skills
Task performance data used to update the student model and re-assign agency level
constraints: The article states that, to its knowledge, such adaptive assignment of agency has not been implemented in current EdTech beyond task-selection examples
The loop is deliberately generic and assumed applicable to various ways control can be shared between students and EdTech
target_learners: children and young learners using personalized EdTech
target_learning_goals: balancing learning effectiveness with learner engagement and self-regulated learning development
examples: Corbalan et al.'s personalized task-selection model, in which the scope of preselected tasks is inversely related to learners' prerequisites
Long and Aleven's shared control over problem selection in intelligent tutoring systems

citation: Garvin Brod, Natalia Kucirkova, Joshua Shepherd, Dietsje Jolles, Inge Molenaar. (2023). Agency in Educational Technology: Interdisciplinary Perspectives and Implications for Learning Design. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09749-x
title: Interdisciplinary taxonomy of agency: types, levels, and developmental prerequisites across philosophy, education, and psychology
description: The review organizes agency along two philosophical axes: types of agency defined by the normative structures they are sensitive to, and levels or degrees of agency varying in sophistication of capacities. Types include epistemic agency, which "is the kind of agency that is sensitive to epistemic norms (e.g., norms regarding when a belief or action is justified)", plus skilled, aesthetic, moral, practical, and group agency. The educational perspective highlights child-adult-technology interactions, and the psychological perspective treats agency beliefs and perceived control as mechanisms whose effective exercise depends on prior knowledge, executive functions, and metacognition that develop across childhood.
requirements: Distinguishing which dimension of agency a design decision targets, since agency is multi-dimensional and EdTech choices impact multiple facets at once
constraints: The article notes philosophy has little advanced understanding of children's agency, and the conceptualization excludes anthropology, sociology, and neuroscience
target_learning_goals: fostering learners' agency in technology-supported learning
examples: EdTech prompts that let learners explore the epistemic space, gaining familiarity with evidence assessment, propaganda detection, and decisions to change one's mind

title: Wh-question design levers for agency in EdTech: what, who, when, and where choices can be made
description: The review proposes a set of guiding questions and design levers for researching and designing agency in EdTech, organized as what can be chosen (content, progress, appearance, self-representation), who has choice (learner, shared with EdTech or teachers, or EdTech), when choices can be made, and where. The article states "The ordering along wh-questions (i.e., what, when, where, who) is intended to illustrate that there is no hierarchy among the options, nor is it the case that learner agency either is or is not present." Designers should aim for an optimal balance across options at different points in the learning journey.
requirements: Designers must make choices and provide justifications for which agency dimensions to emphasize and which to ignore
constraints: The article notes the level of agency provided by EdTech has not been considered in previous evaluation rubrics, which it calls a significant gap

target_learning_goals: supporting children's active participation and agency in learning activities
examples: Young students without the cognitive capacity to make effective learning-path decisions could be given choices regarding problem selection, while older or more advanced learners may benefit from more autonomy over task content and progression

citation: de Koning, B., Zhang, S., & Sepp, S. (2025). Integrating Human Movement in Learning: Advancements in Language Instruction, Multimedia, and Theory. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10027-1
title: Embodied cognition with biologically primary movement supporting biologically secondary knowledge acquisition
description: The article frames the collection with embodied cognition, the view that "cognition is situated in a real-world environment where bodies and brains are inextricably linked," so movements are not only outputs of thinking but can impact cognitive processing. Within Cognitive Load Theory, biologically primary knowledge (e.g., gesturing) is evolved, requires little cognitive effort and no explicit instruction, while biologically secondary knowledge (e.g., arithmetic) requires instruction and deliberate investment. Primary movements can support secondary knowledge acquisition, such as using hands to represent an object in space when learning the meaning of a word.
requirements: Instruction and deliberate cognitive investment are needed for biologically secondary knowledge to benefit from primary-movement support.
constraints: The framework distinguishes biologically primary from biologically secondary knowledge; the article presents it as theorizing within CLT rather than a tested result of this collection.

target_learning_goals: vocabulary learning
arithmetic and other instructed secondary knowledge
examples: The article cites Montessori embedding the tracing of letters on sandpaper to support children's writing more than 100 years ago.

title: Six interrelated research avenues explaining why embodied cognition can enhance learning and instruction
description: The review describes Castro-Alonso et al.'s (2024) framework of "six interrelated research avenues that explain why embodied cognition can enhance learning and instruction." Three avenues concern mechanisms underlying making movements: physical activity, generative learning, and offloaded cognition. Two avenues pertain to observing movements: the specialized processor and signaling. A final avenue, social cognition, applies to both making and observing movements. For each avenue the authors discuss supporting evidence, key influencing factors, and instructional implications.
requirements: For each avenue, supporting evidence, key influencing factors, and instructional implications are discussed.
constraints: The review notes the authors emphasize the need for future research to consider instructional, cognitive, and cultural aspects to deepen understanding of embodiment in learning.

title: Balance Board Math: a pedagogical intervention integrating stimming as a learning tool
description: Balance Board Math is a pedagogical intervention presented by Tancredi and Abrahamson (2024) in their critical-pedagogy conceptual paper. The article describes it as an illustration of a pedagogical shift that recognizes stimming — self-stimulatory behavior such as rocking and fidgeting — as "a legitimate epistemic resource." The paper argues, drawing on post-cognitivist embodied cognition theory and neuro-cognitive empirical studies, that stimming is an intrinsic part of adaptive cognitive functioning and should be embraced as a form of thinking, particularly for neurodivergent individuals.
requirements: A pedagogical shift that recognizes stimming as a legitimate epistemic resource.
constraints: The article presents this as a conceptual argument and illustration rather than an empirically tested intervention in this collection.
target_learning_goals: mathematics learning through embodied movement
examples: The authors present Balance Board Math to illustrate integrating stimming as a learning tool.
key_sources: de Koning, B., Zhang, S., & Sepp, S. (2025). Integrating Human Movement in Learning: Advancements in Language Instruction, Multimedia, and Theory. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10027-1

article_title: Associations Between Teacher-Student Relationship Quality and Middle and Secondary School Teachers’ Wellbeing: A Systematic Review
citation: Rhoda Lai, Jennifer Southam, Luella Mageean, Sue Roffey, Kelly-Ann Allen. (2026). Associations Between Teacher-Student Relationship Quality and Middle and Secondary School Teachers' Wellbeing: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10107-2
title: PERMA model as a framework for teacher wellbeing in the review
description: The PERMA model posits that wellbeing is built on five main elements: positive emotion, engagement, relationships, meaning, and accomplishment (Seligman, 2011). The review used it to structure its synthesis because it captures both hedonic and eudaimonic elements and, per Hone et al. (2014), "demonstrated the highest level of correlation to each of the other theories" among positive psychology wellbeing theories. The review widened wellbeing definition to include each PERMA facet beyond stress and burnout.
requirements: Studies must report at least one PERMA element or its opposite (e.g., negative emotions) as a wellbeing outcome.
constraints: The review does not explore links between clinically relevant symptoms or diagnoses of ill mental health and teacher-student relationships; elements of other theories such as self-esteem and social contribution are not treated as wellbeing components.
target_learning_goals: teacher wellbeing
teacher-student relationship quality
examples: The review classified each included study's wellbeing measures by PERMA element (e.g., MBI for emotions, work enthusiasm scales for engagement, efficacy scales for accomplishment).

Associations Between Teacher-Student Relationship Quality and Middle and Secondary School Teachers' Wellbeing: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10107-2

article_title: Associations Between Teacher-Student Relationship Quality and Middle and Secondary School Teachers’ Wellbeing: A Systematic Review
citation: Rhoda Lai, Jennifer Southam, Luella Mageean, Sue Roffey, Kelly-Ann Allen. (2026). Associations Between Teacher-Student Relationship Quality and Middle and Secondary School Teachers' Wellbeing: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10107-2
title: Internal working models of teacher-student relationships (Spilt et al., 2011) as a framework for teacher wellbeing
description: The review adopts Spilt and colleagues' (2011) model, in which teachers form internal working models of their relationships with students that shape interpretations of student behaviour and emotional responses. The article states "the internal working models that teachers form of these relationships are important for them as they relate to their sense of meaning and perceptions of their professional identities". Teachers hold general models of students as well as individual models per student, and bring biases and efficacy beliefs to these representations. Relationship quality is treated as a subjectively perceived phenomenon.
requirements: Relationship quality must be measured as subjective personal perceptions of teachers or students, not third-party observations of behaviours.
constraints: Attachment theory does not explain why teachers would require fleeting attachment bonds with students or why such relationships matter for teacher wellbeing relative to colleague relationships; limited contact time leads students to use teachers as 'ad hoc' attachments.
target_learning_goals: understanding how relationship perceptions shape teacher emotional responses and wellbeing
examples: A negative internalised relationship model leads a teacher to interpret challenging behaviour as threatening, whereas a positive model supports interpreting it as situational.
