Associations Between Teacher-Student Relationship Quality and Middle and Secondary School Teachers' Wellbeing: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10107-2

article_title: Classroom Carrying Capacity: A Resource and Limiting Factors Framework
citation: Kristen L. Granger, Jason C. Chow. (2025). Classroom Carrying Capacity: A Resource and Limiting Factors Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09999-x
title: Classroom Carrying Capacity framework: an index of the maximum quality of support a classroom can provide students
description: Classroom Carrying Capacity adapts the biological concept of carrying capacity to classrooms, conceptualizing it as "an index of the maximum quality of support that is available to a student in the ecology of a classroom." Unlike traditional environmental models with binary thriving outcomes, CCC is a continuous metric reflecting the balance of resource factors (e.g., positive teacher-child relationships, effective instruction) outweighing limiting factors (e.g., problem behaviors, teacher burnout). The framework extends the bioecological model by shifting focus to the classroom as a collective entity and by providing a structured method to categorize and quantify resource and limiting factors.
requirements: A structured method to categorize and quantify resource and limiting factors within and across spheres of influence, which the authors state the bioecological model lacks
constraints: The authors state CCC "is not a fixed threshold but a dynamic and context-sensitive state that adapts to the needs of individual students and the collective classroom"
The framework does not specify which factors research is required to measure; it is a first step in advancing an integrative model
target_learning_goals: Student functioning and development across social-emotional, academic, and engagement domains
examples: The authors illustrate CCC with a fishbowl ecosystem analogy and with classroom examples such as high rates of externalizing problem behaviors lowering capacity, offset by a teacher with high classroom management efficacy implementing positive behavioral supports
key_sources: Kristen L. Granger, Jason C. Chow. (2025). Classroom Carrying Capacity: A Resource and Limiting Factors Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09999-x

article_title: Classroom Carrying Capacity: A Resource and Limiting Factors Framework
citation: Kristen L. Granger, Jason C. Chow. (2025). Classroom Carrying Capacity: A Resource and Limiting Factors Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09999-x
title: Four-domain taxonomy of classroom resource and limiting factors: external, collective classroom, teacher, and individual student
description: The CCC framework organizes resource and limiting factors across four interdependent domains "external, collective classroom, teacher, and individual student," built from previous conceptual models. External factors include teacher-caregiver partnerships, school climate, and neighborhood conditions; collective classroom factors include aggregate student group characteristics and supplies; teacher factors include self-efficacy, burnout, and health; student factors include relationship perceptions, social-emotional skills, sleep quality, and food insecurity. The domains are conceptualized as interdependent with interactive and potentially additive influence on Classroom Carrying Capacity.
requirements: The delineation is intended to assist stakeholders and researchers in conceptualizing and organizing research questions, teacher training, approaches to measurement, and theories of change
constraints: The authors note "these domains do not include an exhaustive list of factors"; the goal is to guide future identification and study of resource and limiting factors
target_learning_goals: Understanding how multi-level classroom factors cumulatively influence student functioning and development
examples: Table 1 presents a conceptualization of environmental, psychosocial, density-dependent, and density-independent factors across the four domains
key_sources: Kristen L. Granger, Jason C. Chow. (2025). Classroom Carrying Capacity: A Resource and Limiting Factors Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09999-x

article_title: Classroom Carrying Capacity: A Resource and Limiting Factors Framework
citation: Kristen L. Granger, Jason C. Chow. (2025). Classroom Carrying Capacity: A Resource and Limiting Factors Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09999-x
title: Categorization schema for classroom factors: density dependent vs. independent and psychosocial vs. environmental
description: The framework operationalizes classroom factors along two dimensions: density dependency and type. The framework "operationalizes these factors by introducing dimensions of density dependency (dependent vs. independent) and type (psychosocial vs. environmental), enabling a systematic evaluation of their cumulative and interactive effects on classroom outcomes." Density-dependent factors (e.g., instructional time, student-teacher ratios) change in effect as collective student needs increase, while density-independent factors (e.g., classroom space, teacher training) affect support quality regardless of density. Environmental factors are tangible (space, materials, time), psychosocial factors include efficacy, relationships, and behaviors.
requirements: Researchers should define measurements of CCC, in part, by their density (dependent vs. independent) and whether they are physical or psychosocial across the four domains
constraints: The authors state these categorizations attribute importance to varying and multiple, potentially cumulative factors, and that malleability and influence of factors may differ in strength
target_learning_goals: Systematic evaluation of cumulative and interactive effects of classroom factors on student outcomes
examples: A fixed amount of instructional time for a reading lesson is density dependent: when collective student needs are high, available time becomes insufficient, leaving some students without their required intensity of instruction
key_sources: Kristen L. Granger, Jason C. Chow. (2025). Classroom Carrying Capacity: A Resource and Limiting Factors Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09999-x

article_title: Commentary on Highly Successful Female Educational Psychologists: Equity and Intersectionality in Success Definitions
citation: Kucirkova, N. (2023). Commentary on Highly Successful Female Educational Psychologists: Equity and Intersectionality in Success Definitions. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09727-3
title: Intersectionality framework for interpreting academic success narratives
description: The commentary applies intersectionality, "an interdisciplinary critical framework that refers to the connections and dependencies between various identity types", coined by Kimberlé Crenshaw in 1989 and rooted in Black feminism and Critical Race Theory. It is used as both method and epistemology to interrogate how power and intersecting identities are embedded in social relations, highlighting "accumulated advantages for dominant social groups". The author uses it to show that factors like research specialisation and placements at top universities exemplify cumulative benefits that intersect with inequalities.
requirements: Analysis must attend to power dynamics and the mutual influence of social positionings rather than treating identity categories separately
constraints: The commentary notes prior studies showed the relationship between gender and ethnicity, rather than each as separate categories, affected female academics' experiences
target_learners: academic women and minority scholars in higher education
target_learning_goals: understanding systemic barriers to academic career progression and equitable definitions of scholarly success
examples: The commentary reinterprets Prinz et al.'s (2021) and Kiewra et al.'s (2021) success trajectories of interviewees as exemplifying cumulative benefits that intersect with inequalities
key_sources: Kucirkova, N. (2023). Commentary on Highly Successful Female Educational Psychologists: Equity and Intersectionality in Success Definitions. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09727-3

article_title: Reporting of Methodological Rigor in Empirical Mixed Methods Research in Educational Psychology
citation: Matthew T. McCrudden · Macy Bowman · Gala Sofia Campos Oaxaca. (2025). Reporting of Methodological Rigor in Empirical Mixed Methods Research in Educational Psychology. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10090-8
title: Creswell and Plano Clark's three core mixed methods designs (convergent, explanatory sequential, exploratory sequential)
description: A taxonomy of three basic mixed methods research designs in which researchers combine quantitative and qualitative approaches in a single study. The review adopts this typology "because it is widely used in educational psychology and many other disciplines" and uses it both to explain design logic (rationales of comparison, explanation, and exploration) and to classify the designs of the 57 reviewed articles. Each design specifies the timing and sequence of the two strands and the typical rationale for mixing.
requirements: Researchers choose a design and report the quantitative and qualitative strands and their interface (e.g., timing, integration)
constraints: Other design types and typologies/labels exist beyond the three core designs
target_learning_goals: designing and reporting mixed methods empirical studies
examples: The review classified 30 reviewed articles as explanatory sequential, 23 as convergent, and 4 as exploratory sequential using this typology
key_sources: Matthew T. McCrudden · Macy Bowman · Gala Sofia Campos Oaxaca. (2025). Reporting of Methodological Rigor in Empirical Mixed Methods Research in Educational Psychology. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10090-8

article_title: Reporting of Methodological Rigor in Empirical Mixed Methods Research in Educational Psychology
citation: Matthew T. McCrudden · Macy Bowman · Gala Sofia Campos Oaxaca. (2025). Reporting of Methodological Rigor in Empirical Mixed Methods Research in Educational Psychology. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10090-8
title: Three integration strategies in mixed methods research: connecting, building, and merging (with meta-inferences)
description: A framework describing how researchers link quantitative and qualitative strands. Integration is "the linking of qualitative and quantitative approaches and dimensions together to create a new whole or a more holistic understanding than achieved by either alone". Connecting uses results from one strand to inform participant selection for the other; building uses one strand's data collection and analysis to inform the other's; merging brings findings together for comparison and to generate meta-inferences — insights not possible from either strand alone. The review used these strategies as criteria for evaluating reporting of integration.
requirements: Integration must be planned at the start of a study (how and why strands will be integrated) and communicated transparently to readers
constraints: Reporting integration within journal word-count limits is a stated barrier; meta-inference types relate to the design rationale
target_learning_goals: achieving and reporting integration of quantitative and qualitative strands
examples: McCrudden et al. (2016) used connecting (purposeful sampling from experiment results), building (quantitative findings informed the interview protocol), and merging (qualitative findings explained quantitative findings)
key_sources: Matthew T. McCrudden · Macy Bowman · Gala Sofia Campos Oaxaca. (2025). Reporting of Methodological Rigor in Empirical Mixed Methods Research in Educational Psychology. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10090-8

article_title: Reporting of Methodological Rigor in Empirical Mixed Methods Research in Educational Psychology
citation: Matthew T. McCrudden · Macy Bowman · Gala Sofia Campos Oaxaca. (2025). Reporting of Methodological Rigor in Empirical Mixed Methods Research in Educational Psychology. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10090-8
title: Six-element coding scheme for evaluating reporting of methodological rigor in mixed methods articles (adapted from Harrison et al., 2020)
description: A scoring rubric the authors adapted from Harrison et al. (2020) to evaluate reporting quality across six elements: aims and purposes, mixed methods study design, data collection, data analysis, integration, and elements of writing, each scored high/medium/low (Table 1). Two reviewers independently coded all 57 articles; pre-reconciliation agreement was 94.7% (324/342 ratings) with Cohen's kappa of 0.925 overall, and the first author adjudicated 18 adjacent score differences.
requirements: Two independent trained raters coding all articles, with reconciliation of differences by adjudication
constraints: Eligibility was limited to articles with primary quantitative AND primary qualitative data collection and analysis; data-transformation studies were excluded
target_learning_goals: evaluating and improving reporting of methodological rigor in mixed methods research
examples: The rubric's design element distinguished clearly labeled designs from identifiable-but-unlabeled and difficult-to-identify designs
key_sources: Matthew T. McCrudden · Macy Bowman · Gala Sofia Campos Oaxaca. (2025). Reporting of Methodological Rigor in Empirical Mixed Methods Research in Educational Psychology. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10090-8

article_title: How Personality Matters for Education Research
citation: Hayley K. Jach, Lisa Bardach, Kou Murayama. (2023). How Personality Matters for Education Research. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09807-4
title: Big Five trait framework: traits as continuous, hierarchical, context-dependent dimensions
description: The review frames personality traits as "characteristic patterns of thoughts, feelings, and behaviours manifest in isomorphic situations", organised hierarchically with facets below broad Big Five dimensions. Traits are continuous dimensions, not types: trait scores correspond to the average of density distributions of momentary states, and expression is context-dependent. The framework serves as a shared nomenclature that reduces redundancy and locates narrower traits such as grit within conscientiousness.
requirements: High-quality measurement with established scales (e.g. BFI-2) to reflect target constructs accurately
constraints: Most factor-structure research was performed in WEIRD nations; a cited systematic review found little support for stricter forms of measurement invariance across cultures
target_learners: students across primary, secondary, and tertiary education
target_learning_goals: predicting and supporting academic performance, motivation, engagement, and wellbeing
examples: The review uses the Big Five to organise discussion of predictors, interventions, personalised learning, and outcome measurement throughout
key_sources: Hayley K. Jach, Lisa Bardach, Kou Murayama. (2023). How Personality Matters for Education Research. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09807-4

article_title: How Personality Matters for Education Research
citation: Hayley K. Jach, Lisa Bardach, Kou Murayama. (2023). How Personality Matters for Education Research. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09807-4
title: BESSI hierarchical framework organising socio-emotional skills into five domains aligned with Big Five traits
description: The review describes the BESSI framework (Soto et al., 2021, 2022), a hierarchical framework of socio-emotional skills built on a structure similar to the Big Five. It organises skills into five domains — "social engagement, cooperation, self-management, emotional resilience, and innovation skills" — each strongly positively correlated with a Big Five trait. The review proposes a conceptual distinction whereby traits describe average tendencies while skills describe the capacity to engage in certain emotions, behaviours, and cognitions.
requirements: Assessing both a BESSI skill domain and its correlated Big Five trait when researchers want to track whether developing capacity increases tendency
constraints: Positive correlation between a skill domain and a trait does not mean they describe the same thing, per the review
target_learners: school students in intervention and assessment studies
target_learning_goals: socio-emotional skill development including self-regulated learning, cooperation, and emotional resilience
examples: The review suggests assessing Big Five conscientiousness alongside BESSI self-management skills when studying whether capacity to work hard increases tendency to work hard
key_sources: Hayley K. Jach, Lisa Bardach, Kou Murayama. (2023). How Personality Matters for Education Research. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09807-4

article_title: How Personality Matters for Education Research
citation: Hayley K. Jach, Lisa Bardach, Kou Murayama. (2023). How Personality Matters for Education Research. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09807-4
title: Table 1 overview of current Big Five personality scales with the BFI-2 recommended for education research
description: Table 1 of the review lists the most popular current personality trait scales with item counts, facets per trait, and open-access status, spanning medium-length scales (BFI-2, BFI-2-Short, Big Five Aspect Scales, NEO-FFI, HEXACO, BFI), large scales (IPIP-NEO, NEO-PI-R), and super-short scales (Ten Item Personality Inventory, BFI-2-Extra-Short, Mini-IPIP). The review recommends the BFI-2 for its breadth without compromising efficiency.
requirements: Researchers should match scale length and facet coverage to survey space and the specificity of the target outcome, using narrow measures when the bandwidth/fidelity trade-off favours them
constraints: Super-short scales are "recommended only when brevity is essential"; the NEO-FFI and NEO-PI-R are not open access
target_learners: students in education research studies at any level
target_learning_goals: measuring personality traits as predictors, personalisation dimensions, or outcome measures in educational studies
examples: The review recommends including a global Big Five measure alongside narrow scales when survey space allows, to enable cross-study comparison and meta-analysis
key_sources: Hayley K. Jach, Lisa Bardach, Kou Murayama. (2023). How Personality Matters for Education Research. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09807-4

article_title: Enhancing School Students’ Self-Regulated Learning through Generative AI Support: A Randomized Controlled Trial
citation: Tim Fütterer, Lisa Bardach, Jochen Kuhn, Stefan Daniel Keller, Peter Gerjets. (2026). Enhancing School Students’ Self-Regulated Learning through Generative AI Support: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10133-8
title: Integrative framework of self-regulation in education (Wortha et al.) with four interacting components
description: The study draws on an integrative model situating SRL within a broader account of self-regulation in education. "This model distinguishes four key components that interact to shape learning outcomes: personal dispositions (e.g., personality traits such as conscientiousness), driving forces (e.g., current motivation), limited resources (e.g., cognitive capacity, executive functions), and learning activities (e.g., cognitive learning strategies)". The components are assumed to interact in complex, partially compensatory ways, and the framework is grounded in a person–situation interaction view. The study targeted driving forces and learning activities because these can be directly affected by short-term interventions.
requirements: Interventions should target components amenable to change, such as driving forces and learning activities, rather than stable dispositions
constraints: Personal dispositions and limited cognitive resources are described as less likely to be changed by short-term instructional support
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning, including motivation and cognitive learning strategies
examples: The RCT operationalized the framework by contrasting a utility value (driving forces) intervention with a cognitive learning strategy (learning activities) intervention
key_sources: Tim Fütterer, Lisa Bardach, Jochen Kuhn, Stefan Daniel Keller, Peter Gerjets. (2026). Enhancing School Students’ Self-Regulated Learning through Generative AI Support: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10133-8

article_title: Examining Black and Latine Students’ Sense of Belonging within the Mathematics Classroom: A Narrative Review
citation: Harris-Thomas, B., Nicolai, K. D., Chen, X.-Y., & Areizaga Barbieri, C. (2026). Examining Black and Latine Students' Sense of Belonging within the Mathematics Classroom: A Narrative Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10181-0
title: Three considerations for researching and supporting Black and Latine students' mathematics belonging
description: The review's organizing framework proposes that belonging researchers consider three areas "that would allow them to study belonging in productive and not harmful ways": "(1) Contextual Factors that Shape a Sense of Belonging to Mathematics, (2) Positionality and Framing of Investigations of Belonging, and (3) Recognizing the Whole Student." Each consideration is broken down into practical ways researchers might consider context, framing, and the whole student, along with future research considerations. The framework rests on the review's premise that belonging is dynamic, situated, and shaped by race, ethnicity, and culture.
requirements: Researchers must examine the educational contexts in which Black and Latine students engage with mathematics alongside the prevailing frameworks and assumptions of their studies
constraints: The review presents the list of contextual factors as non-exhaustive and based on the 20 reviewed studies
target_learners: Black and Latine adolescent mathematics students in U.S. schools
target_learning_goals: Supporting students' sense of belonging in mathematics learning environments
examples: The review organizes its Findings and Interpretation section around the three considerations, drawing on studies such as Gray et al. (2024) and Maloney and Matthews (2020)
key_sources: Harris-Thomas, B., Nicolai, K. D., Chen, X.-Y., & Areizaga Barbieri, C. (2026). Examining Black and Latine Students' Sense of Belonging within the Mathematics Classroom: A Narrative Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10181-0

article_title: Examining Black and Latine Students’ Sense of Belonging within the Mathematics Classroom: A Narrative Review
citation: Harris-Thomas, B., Nicolai, K. D., Chen, X.-Y., & Areizaga Barbieri, C. (2026). Examining Black and Latine Students' Sense of Belonging within the Mathematics Classroom: A Narrative Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10181-0
title: DeCuir-Gunby and Schutz's five purposes for considering race in educational psychology research
description: The review adopts DeCuir-Gunby and Schutz's (2014) classification as a common language for analyzing each article's approach to race. The five purposes are "descriptive or demographic (i.e., to describe the sample or another level of demographics; explanatory (i.e., to use race or ethnicity to explain variance); comparative (i.e., to compare racial and/or ethnic groups to each other); race-focused (i.e., to center race in the analysis and build upon race-based or cultural theories); and race-reimaged (i.e., to build upon race-based or cultural theories or lenses as a means to add nuance to traditional constructs) purposes." The authors turned these categories into a decision tree (Fig. 1) to classify each study's treatment of participants' race/ethnic identity and to center studies going beyond treating race as a "diverse sample."
requirements: Researchers code each study's approach to race/ethnicity using the decision tree rather than treating racial identity as merely a demographic descriptor
constraints: The classification descriptions are taken from DeCuir-Gunby and Schutz's 2014 paper, not developed anew by this review
target_learners: Black and Latine adolescent mathematics students in U.S. schools
target_learning_goals: Guiding belonging research that centers students' race and ethnicity without causing harm
examples: The review used the categories to classify its 20 included studies, e.g., labeling Barbieri and Miller-Cotto (2021) as comparative and Matthews et al. (2021) as race-focused
key_sources: Harris-Thomas, B., Nicolai, K. D., Chen, X.-Y., & Areizaga Barbieri, C. (2026). Examining Black and Latine Students' Sense of Belonging within the Mathematics Classroom: A Narrative Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10181-0

article_title: Examining Black and Latine Students’ Sense of Belonging within the Mathematics Classroom: A Narrative Review
citation: Harris-Thomas, B., Nicolai, K. D., Chen, X.-Y., & Areizaga Barbieri, C. (2026). Examining Black and Latine Students' Sense of Belonging within the Mathematics Classroom: A Narrative Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10181-0
title: Reviewed corpus of 20 studies on Black and Latine adolescents' mathematics belonging
description: The review's evidence base comprises 20 manuscripts: 14 identified through systematic search methods (five databases, ancestry search, grey literature request, Covidence screening) plus 13 added during the narrative review phase via backward snowballing. Studies span quantitative surveys (e.g., 2,938 Algebra I students in Morales-Chicas & Graham, 2021), qualitative interviews, focus groups, observations, and video data. Each study was coded for data sources, sample characteristics, belonging or related constructs, and approach to race/ethnicity using DeCuir-Gunby and Schutz's classification.
requirements: Included studies reported results or findings specifically for Black and/or Latine students, focused on adolescents in U.S. school mathematics settings, and named belonging or a closely related construct
constraints: The review transitioned from systematic to narrative review methods, expanding inclusion criteria and weighting studies unequally based on the authors' expertise
target_learners: Black and Latine adolescent mathematics students in U.S. middle and high schools
target_learning_goals: Understanding and supporting sense of belonging and related constructs (math identity, connectedness, engagement) in mathematics classrooms
examples: Table 2 snapshots each study, e.g., Maloney and Matthews (2020) with 12 teachers and 321 Black and Latine students, and Gray et al. (2024) with 255 sixth-grade students

article_title: How Learners’ Visuospatial Ability and Different Ways of Changing the Perspective Influence Learning About Movements in Desktop and Immersive Virtual Reality Environments
citation: Birgit Brucker, Georg Pardi, Fabienne Uehlin, Laura Moosmann, Martin Lachmair, Marc Halfmann, Peter Gerjets. (2024). How Learners' Visuospatial Ability and Different Ways of Changing the Perspective Influence Learning About Movements in Desktop and Immersive Virtual Reality Environments. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09895-w
title: GES framework: grounding, embodiment, and situatedness as a cognitive framework for VR interaction design
description: The GES framework, introduced by Fischer and Brugger (2011) and cited by the article, is a model of cognition emphasizing the role of the body, and has been used to inform interaction guidelines for VR user interface design. It comprises three components: "Grounding refers to universal principles applicable to all individuals, such as physical laws"; embodiment captures individual-specific bodily traits such as handedness and sensory-motor proficiency; and situatedness encompasses context-specific experiences arising from interaction within a particular environment. The article uses it to reason about how VR interactions should follow real-world principles.
requirements: The framework treats grounding principles as a foundational element of cognitive architecture that is resistant to change, so designs should align with physical laws
constraints: The article presents it as a framework for informing interaction guidelines, not as a tested intervention in this study
target_learners: adults learning about movements in VR environments
target_learning_goals: understanding dynamic 3D content from multiple perspectives
examples: The article uses the GES framework, via Lachmair et al. (2022), to argue that whole-body immersive VR interactions might overwhelm users

citation: Birgit Brucker, Georg Pardi, Fabienne Uehlin, Laura Moosmann, Martin Lachmair, Marc Halfmann, Peter Gerjets. (2024). How Learners' Visuospatial Ability and Different Ways of Changing the Perspective Influence Learning About Movements in Desktop and Immersive Virtual Reality Environments. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09895-w
title: Cognitive Affective Model of Immersive Learning (CAMIL): presence and agency as key benefits of immersive VR
description: The article describes CAMIL, introduced by Makransky and Petersen (2021), as a model that "highlights presence and agency as the key benefits of immersive VR", because these aspects are facilitated by immersion, interactive control, and representational fidelity. CAMIL identifies six factors influencing learning that can be enhanced by presence and agency: interest, motivation, self-efficacy, embodiment, cognitive load, and self-regulation. The article uses CAMIL to frame why embodiment and agency in immersive VR may affect learning outcomes.
requirements: Presence and agency are assumed to be facilitated by immersion, interactive control, and representational fidelity
constraints: The article cites CAMIL as background theory; it does not test CAMIL itself in the reported studies
target_learning_goals: learning about dynamic movements with 3D-models
examples: The article invokes CAMIL alongside Dalgarno and Lee (2010) when motivating the comparison of interaction formats across Desktop-VR and immersive VR

article_title: How Learners’ Visuospatial Ability and Different Ways of Changing the Perspective Influence Learning About Movements in Desktop and Immersive Virtual Reality Environments
citation: Birgit Brucker, Georg Pardi, Fabienne Uehlin, Laura Moosmann, Martin Lachmair, Marc Halfmann, Peter Gerjets. (2024). How Learners' Visuospatial Ability and Different Ways of Changing the Perspective Influence Learning About Movements in Desktop and Immersive Virtual Reality Environments. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09895-w
title: Ability-as-enhancer versus ability-as-compensator assumptions for visuospatial ability as an instructional moderator
description: The article presents two alternative assumptions about how learners' visuospatial ability moderates the effectiveness of instructional formats. Under the ability-as-compensator assumption, well-designed formats such as dynamic visualizations act as compensatory tools enabling lower-visuospatial-ability learners to reach similar outcomes to higher-ability learners. In contrast, "the ability-as-enhancer assumption suggests that learners with higher visuospatial ability might even be able to utilize specific instructional formats, even if these formats are less optimally designed", for example by more accurately imagining how to rotate a model to an optimal viewing position. The study's research question R1 asks which assumption fits the observed moderation.
requirements: Both assumptions presuppose that visuospatial ability is measured as a continuous learner factor (here via the paper folding test)
constraints: The article treats these as alternative assumptions to be explored, not as settled findings
target_learning_goals: learning about movements with dynamic visualizations and 3D-models
examples: Study 1 explored whether visuospatial ability acts as compensator or enhancer by testing interaction format × visuospatial ability interactions on learning outcomes

article_title: Navigating Spatial Ability for Mathematics Education: a Review and Roadmap
citation: Kelsey E. Schenck, Mitchell J. Nathan. (2024). Navigating Spatial Ability for Mathematics Education: a Review and Roadmap. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09935-5
title: Three-family taxonomy of spatial ability structures: specific-factor, broad-factor, and unitary
description: The review organizes the sprawling spatial ability literature into three general types of taxonomies. Specific-factor structures use factor-analytic methods to identify subcomponents such as spatial orientation, mental rotation, and non-rotational spatial visualization; broad-factor structures use theoretically motivated categories such as large- versus small-scale or the intrinsic-extrinsic by static-dynamic 2x2; unitary structures treat spatial ability as a single factor. The review states these were chosen "to highlight the main sub-factor dissociations in the literature" and to make definitions navigable for non-specialist mathematics education researchers.
requirements: Researchers selecting a taxonomy must match it to the data collected and the theoretical framework of the inquiry, since the review states a taxonomy shapes interpretation and generalization of findings.
constraints: The review states the three-type account is not comprehensive, and that no validated instruments exist for the broad-factor or unitary taxonomies.
target_learners: mathematics education researchers and practitioners selecting spatial measures
target_learning_goals: measuring and theorizing spatial ability as it relates to mathematics learning
examples: The review details exemplar dissociations within the specific-factor family, such as spatial orientation versus rotational spatial visualization, and mental rotation versus non-rotational spatial visualization.
key_sources: Kelsey E. Schenck, Mitchell J. Nathan. (2024). Navigating Spatial Ability for Mathematics Education: a Review and Roadmap. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09935-5

article_title: Navigating Spatial Ability for Mathematics Education: a Review and Roadmap
citation: Kelsey E. Schenck, Mitchell J. Nathan. (2024). Navigating Spatial Ability for Mathematics Education: a Review and Roadmap. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09935-5
title: Compiled table of spatial ability instruments mapped to sub-components and populations
description: The review compiled Table 1, an alphabetical list of spatial ability instruments matched with their associated spatial sub-components and intended populations, organized by the specific sub-components that overlap with mathematics curricula per Ramful et al. (2017). It lists instruments such as the Mental Rotations Test, Paper Folding Test, Embedded Figures Test, Perspective Taking/Object Perspective Test, and water level tasks, with population ranges from preschool children to adults. The review notes most instruments are psychometric tests "created by psychologists for use in controlled laboratory-based studies rather than in classroom contexts."
requirements: Researchers should match task selection to stated research goals, theoretical frameworks, the spatial skills of interest, and the populations under investigation, per the review.
constraints: The review states the instrument slate is dominated by tasks tested only on adults, few measures test more than one subcomponent, and no published validated instruments for large-scale spatial orientation met its inclusion criteria.
target_learners: learners from preschool children to adults, per the populations listed in Table 1
target_learning_goals: assessing spatial sub-components relevant to mathematics education research
examples: Table 1 maps each instrument to alternative factor labels such as small-scale, intrinsic-dynamic, or extrinsic-static, and flags instruments likely combining multiple factors into one task.
key_sources: Kelsey E. Schenck, Mitchell J. Nathan. (2024). Navigating Spatial Ability for Mathematics Education: a Review and Roadmap. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09935-5

article_title: Navigating Spatial Ability for Mathematics Education: a Review and Roadmap
citation: Kelsey E. Schenck, Mitchell J. Nathan. (2024). Navigating Spatial Ability for Mathematics Education: a Review and Roadmap. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09935-5
title: Make three explicit design decisions — taxonomy, analytical framework, and task selection — when studying spatial ability in mathematics education
description: The review proposes a guiding framework identifying three major design decisions for scholars using spatial skills in mathematics education research: selecting a spatial ability taxonomy, selecting corresponding analytical frameworks, and selecting spatial tasks for assessing spatial performance. The review states this framework "is intended to provide educational researchers and practitioners with a common language and decision-making process for conducting research and instruction that engages learners' spatial abilities," aiming to improve understanding of associative and causal links between spatial and mathematical abilities.
requirements: Researchers must align taxonomy, analytical framework, and task choices with one another and with their research goals, since the review shows divergent choices yield conflicting interpretations.
constraints: The review explicitly declines to offer overly optimistic proposals for resolving long-standing complexities, instead helping researchers operate within them from an informed perspective.
target_learners: mathematics and STEM education researchers and practitioners
target_learning_goals: designing spatial skills interventions and selecting appropriate spatial measures for mathematics education studies
examples: The review compiled Table 1 of instruments organized by Ramful et al.'s (2017) three-factor framework and grouped tasks into spatial orientation, non-rotational spatial visualization, and mental rotation categories chosen for their empirical links to mathematical thinking.

article_title: Patterns in Student Learning: Relationships Between Learning Strategies, Conceptions of Learning, and Learning Orientations
citation: Vermunt, J. D. & Vermetten, Y. J. (2004). Patterns in Student Learning: Relationships Between Learning Strategies, Conceptions of Learning, and Learning Orientations. Educational Psychology Review. https://dspacelibrary.uu.nl/handle/1874/11958
title: Integrative theory of student learning uniting cognitive, regulative, metacognitive, and motivational components and the interplay of self- and external regulation
description: The article presents an integrative learning theory in which student learning comprises cognitive processing activities, affective activities, and regulation activities that steer the other two, plus conceptions of learning and learning orientations. It focusses on "the interplay between self-regulation and external regulation of learning processes as a theoretical framework," and the ILS instrument was built from it. The theory also distinguishes teaching/learning functions and predicts congruence or friction (constructive and destructive) between teaching and learning strategies.
requirements: Measurement of processing, regulation, conceptions, and orientations together, as operationalized in the ILS
constraints: Developed and validated mainly with students in the beginning years of higher education; structures deviate in other populations and contexts
target_learning_goals: self-regulation of learning
quality of learning strategies and conceptions
examples: Vermunt (1996, 1998) discerned three processing strategies (deep, stepwise, concrete) and three regulation strategies (self-regulated, externally regulated, lack of regulation) in empirical studies
key_sources: Vermunt, J. D. & Vermetten, Y. J. (2004). Patterns in Student Learning: Relationships Between Learning Strategies, Conceptions of Learning, and Learning Orientations. Educational Psychology Review. https://dspacelibrary.uu.nl/handle/1874/11958

article_title: Patterns in Student Learning: Relationships Between Learning Strategies, Conceptions of Learning, and Learning Orientations
citation: Vermunt, J. D. & Vermetten, Y. J. (2004). Patterns in Student Learning: Relationships Between Learning Strategies, Conceptions of Learning, and Learning Orientations. Educational Psychology Review. https://dspacelibrary.uu.nl/handle/1874/11958
title: Inventory of Learning Styles (ILS): 120-item diagnostic questionnaire covering processing, regulation, conceptions, and orientations
description: The ILS is a diagnostic instrument developed from phenomenographic interview analyses and factor, reliability, item, and test-retest analyses. "The final version of the ILS consists of 120 statements that cover four learning components: cognitive processing strategies, metacognitive regulation strategies, conceptions of learning, and learning orientations." It assesses five scales in each component, rated on 5-point scales, and has been used in at least ten countries since 1992.
requirements: Administration to students able to report on their own study behavior; adapted language and school context for younger or non-Dutch populations
constraints: Regulation-strategy scales showed lower internal consistencies (alphas from .48) in some regular-university samples
target_learning_goals: diagnosis of learning strategies, conceptions, and orientations
examples: Used in studies across the Netherlands, Belgium, Finland, England, Cyprus, USA, Brazil, Argentina, Indonesia, and Sri Lanka

citation: Vermunt, J. D. & Vermetten, Y. J. (2004). Patterns in Student Learning: Relationships Between Learning Strategies, Conceptions of Learning, and Learning Orientations. Educational Psychology Review. https://dspacelibrary.uu.nl/handle/1874/11958
title: Design teaching for a gradual transfer of regulation from teacher to students, addressing all learning components
description: Process-oriented instruction integrates the teaching of domain knowledge with learning and thinking strategies, aiming to discourage undirected and reproduction-directed patterns and promote meaning- and application-directed ones. Its emphasis is on "a gradual transfer of control over student learning processes from the teacher and/or other instructional agents to students." The review argues successful change requires addressing all learning components, not just strategies.
requirements: Interventions must address all learning components (strategies, conceptions, orientations), not just learning strategies
Diagnosis of students' own way of learning and preconceptions, as in Vermunt (1995)
constraints: Change will probably not be possible from one day to another; initial slowing of study pace was observed in one innovation study
target_learning_goals: learning to learn
self-regulation of learning
meaning- and application-directed learning patterns
examples: Schatteman et al. (1997) implemented interactive working groups in which the instructor interacted on a metacognitive level with students; Vermunt (1995) linked ILS diagnosis to individually tailored instructional measures

article_title: Do Females Outperform Males on Second/Foreign Language (L2) Achievement? A Meta-Analytical Review across Three Decades
citation: Chen, X., Zhou, Z., & Padilla, A. M. (2026). Do Females Outperform Males on Second/Foreign Language (L2) Achievement? A Meta-Analytical Review across Three Decades. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10092-6
title: Avoid gender stereotyping in L2 educational practice; cultivate inclusive environments addressing individual needs
description: Because the pooled female advantage is small and highly context-dependent, the article recommends that educators not attribute achievement differences broadly to gender. It states educators "should focus on cultivating inclusive learning environments that address individual needs, encourage participation across all skill domains, and mitigate potential gender biases in instruction and assessment." This guards against stereotype-driven disparities in academic and professional choices.
requirements: Educators and policy makers must treat the small average gap as insufficient grounds for gender-based expectations or tracking in language instruction.
constraints: The recommendation rests on a small effect size (g = 0.17) with very high heterogeneity; the article warns a belief in a female advantage may contribute to disparities in college admissions or special education placements.
target_learners: L2 learners across elementary, secondary, and university settings
target_learning_goals: Second/foreign language achievement across speaking, listening, reading, and writing
examples: The meta-analysis pooled 137 effect sizes and found the advantage diminishes to non-significance at university level, supporting individualized rather than gendered expectations.
key_sources: Chen, X., Zhou, Z., & Padilla, A. M. (2026). Do Females Outperform Males on Second/Foreign Language (L2) Achievement? A Meta-Analytical Review across Three Decades. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10092-6

article_title: Do Females Outperform Males on Second/Foreign Language (L2) Achievement? A Meta-Analytical Review across Three Decades
citation: Chen, X., Zhou, Z., & Padilla, A. M. (2026). Do Females Outperform Males on Second/Foreign Language (L2) Achievement? A Meta-Analytical Review across Three Decades. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10092-6
title: Stereotype threat and social cognitive theory as explanatory accounts of the male disadvantage in L2 learning
description: The article explains the female advantage in L2 achievement through two named theoretical frameworks. Stereotype threat theory (Steele & Aronson, 1995) holds that when negative stereotypes about a group become obvious in a performance context, members of the stereotyped group are threatened, which lowers task performance. Social cognitive theory (Bandura, 1991, 2011) emphasizes the interaction between personal, environmental, and behavioral factors: when males believe L2 learning is feminized, their self-efficacy weakens, they restrict effort, and achievement falls. The article applies both accounts to the L2 domain, where language learning is often stereotyped as a "female-domain" subject.
requirements: The account presupposes that learners and teachers hold gendered beliefs about language learning as a feminized subject, and that these beliefs are salient in the performance context.
constraints: The article presents these as plausible explanatory mechanisms for the observed gender gap, not as tested predictions within the meta-analysis itself; it also notes that research reporting a female biological verbal advantage was based on very small differences or none.
target_learners: Male and female L2 learners, particularly adolescents in secondary school
target_learning_goals: L2 learning achievement, motivation, self-efficacy, and persistence
examples: The article cites the Chinese context, where L2 learning is believed to be a feminized area of study and males interested in L2 learning may experience criticism or disapproval, as one setting where stereotype threat may operate.
key_sources: Chen, X., Zhou, Z., & Padilla, A. M. (2026). Do Females Outperform Males on Second/Foreign Language (L2) Achievement? A Meta-Analytical Review across Three Decades. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10092-6

article_title: The Relationship Between Cognitive Offloading and the Transient Information Effect
citation: Chen, O., Allen, R., Waterman, A., & Sweller, J. (2026). The Relationship Between Cognitive Offloading and the Transient Information Effect. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10132-9
title: Cognitive Load Theory provides the fundamental basis for the transient information effect
description: The article states that Cognitive Load Theory is an instructional theory designed to improve learning by managing cognitive load, and that the transient information effect is grounded in this framework. It holds that working memory is limited in capacity and duration, and that when information disappears before it can be adequately processed, learning suffers. The article presents this as the theoretical foundation for understanding why transient information impairs learning.
requirements: Learning materials must be designed with awareness of working memory capacity limits
constraints: The effect applies to biologically secondary knowledge rather than biologically primary knowledge
target_learning_goals: acquisition of biologically secondary knowledge such as reading and writing
key_sources: Chen, O., Allen, R., Waterman, A., & Sweller, J. (2026). The Relationship Between Cognitive Offloading and the Transient Information Effect. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10132-9

article_title: The Relationship Between Cognitive Offloading and the Transient Information Effect
citation: Chen, O., Allen, R., Waterman, A., & Sweller, J. (2026). The Relationship Between Cognitive Offloading and the Transient Information Effect. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10132-9
title: Cognitive offloading is a learner-driven process of externalising internal information onto the environment
description: The article defines cognitive offloading as the use of physical action to alter the information processing requirements of a task so as to reduce cognitive demand. It distinguishes two forms: environmental adjustments or external normalisation, and direct externalisation of to-be-remembered information to the environment such as note-taking or setting reminders. The learner is active and drives the offloading behaviour.
requirements: Learners must have access to external tools or representations to offload information onto
constraints: Offloading can become problematic if overused or if it distracts from learning
target_learners: children and adults across a range of educational and everyday contexts
target_learning_goals: reducing memory and processing demands during task performance
key_sources: Chen, O., Allen, R., Waterman, A., & Sweller, J. (2026). The Relationship Between Cognitive Offloading and the Transient Information Effect. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10132-9

article_title: The Role of Direct Strategy Instruction and Indirect Activation of Self-Regulated Learning—Evidence from Classroom Observation Studies
citation: Charlotte Dignath & Marcel V. J. Veenman. (2021). The Role of Direct Strategy Instruction and Indirect Activation of Self-Regulated Learning—Evidence from Classroom Observation Studies. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09534-0
title: Framework of direct and indirect teacher approaches to activate self-regulated learning
description: The article presents a framework in which "teachers can promote strategies directly, and they can indirectly activate SRL by providing a learning environment that incites students to self-regulate their learning." Direct promotion splits into explicit and implicit strategy instruction, while indirect promotion operates through powerful learning environments grounded in constructivist theory. The framework organizes the review's analysis of classroom observation studies, which coded teachers' practice as direct strategy instruction, indirect activation of SRL, or a combination of both.
requirements: Teachers need knowledge of metacognition and strategies so they can instruct strategies explicitly and design learning environments conducive to SRL
constraints: The review notes that as a conceptual paper it does not present a complete state-of-the-art and there is a lack of quantitative synthesis of teachers' promotion of SRL
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning
metacognitive strategy knowledge and use
examples: The 17 reviewed observation studies were classified according to the framework as focusing on direct strategy instruction, indirect activation of SRL, or a combination of both
key_sources: Charlotte Dignath & Marcel V. J. Veenman. (2021). The Role of Direct Strategy Instruction and Indirect Activation of Self-Regulated Learning—Evidence from Classroom Observation Studies. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09534-0

article_title: The Role of Direct Strategy Instruction and Indirect Activation of Self-Regulated Learning—Evidence from Classroom Observation Studies
citation: Charlotte Dignath & Marcel V. J. Veenman. (2021). The Role of Direct Strategy Instruction and Indirect Activation of Self-Regulated Learning—Evidence from Classroom Observation Studies. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09534-0
title: Three levels of strategy instruction: blind, informed, and self-control training (WWW&H rule)
description: Drawing on Brown et al., the article differentiates three levels of strategy instruction. In blind training, students are induced to use a strategy without information about its significance; informed training adds information about the strategy's benefits; and "the self-control training, the highest level of instruction, combines the informed training with an explicit instruction of how to manage, monitor, check, and evaluate strategy application." Self-control training best facilitates transfer. Explicit instruction follows the WWW&H rule—What to do, When, Why, and How—so students develop metacognitive knowledge about strategies.
requirements: Students first need explicit training in self-regulation strategies before they can benefit from implicit instruction and modeling
constraints: Blind training might fail to maintain strategy production in the future and its generalization to similar useful contexts
target_learning_goals: metacognitive strategy use
transfer of strategy application
examples: The article's Table 1 lists examples of explicit strategy instruction: explicit demonstration, explicit explanation, explicit call, and explicitly asking about strategy use
key_sources: Charlotte Dignath & Marcel V. J. Veenman. (2021). The Role of Direct Strategy Instruction and Indirect Activation of Self-Regulated Learning—Evidence from Classroom Observation Studies. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09534-0

article_title: The Role of Direct Strategy Instruction and Indirect Activation of Self-Regulated Learning—Evidence from Classroom Observation Studies
citation: Charlotte Dignath & Marcel V. J. Veenman. (2021). The Role of Direct Strategy Instruction and Indirect Activation of Self-Regulated Learning—Evidence from Classroom Observation Studies. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09534-0
title: Instructional elements of learning environments that foster SRL indirectly: complex activities, choices, and evaluation criteria
description: The article identifies instructional elements of learning environments relevant for students' engagement in SRL, including "offering complex and meaningful activities" and "providing choices about the content, the place, or the cooperation partner while working on an assignment", choices about the level of challenge, and providing evaluation criteria. These elements, drawn from Perry's research, have proven to distinguish between classrooms that support students in enacting SRL and those that do not. Related preconditions include self-direction, cooperative learning, constructivist learning principles, and fostering transfer.
requirements: A balance between self-directed and teacher-directed learning, with internal control by the student and external control by the teacher balanced
constraints: Complex learning environments with much information but minimal structure or guidance will be detrimental for learning since they increase cognitive load; constructivist environments are more effective when they provide explicit guidance
target_learning_goals: engagement in self-regulated learning
independent learning
examples: Butler et al. supported teachers in using inquiry-oriented or problem-based learning approaches to engage students in authentic learning tasks, and found achievement gains associated with teachers who stimulated independence during learning

article_title: The Role of Direct Strategy Instruction and Indirect Activation of Self-Regulated Learning—Evidence from Classroom Observation Studies
citation: Charlotte Dignath & Marcel V. J. Veenman. (2021). The Role of Direct Strategy Instruction and Indirect Activation of Self-Regulated Learning—Evidence from Classroom Observation Studies. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09534-0
title: Developmental levels of self-regulation: adaptive scaffolding from observation to self-regulation
description: The article describes models in which teachers' support changes over time in accordance with students' developmental level. Collins et al.'s cognitive apprenticeship distinguishes modeling, scaffolding, fading, and coaching; Zimmerman describes four levels—observation, emulation, self-control, and self-regulation. At the highest level, "the students monitor their behavior, and are able to adjust their learning systematically to changing requirements and conditions", and the teacher offers an environment allowing performance without supervision. Both approaches share that teacher control is reduced as students move to the next self-regulatory level.
requirements: Learners first need to learn regulation strategies before they can regulate their learning effectively; teachers gradually fade scaffolding as students practice under supervision
constraints: Modeling of strategy use can take place implicitly, but may become explicit once the teacher addresses metacognitive aspects of strategy use
target_learning_goals: development of self-regulated learning
gradual assumption of responsibility for learning
examples: At the emulation level, students attempt to follow behavior modeled by their teacher or peer, and the teacher supports, encourages, and provides feedback

article_title: A More Comprehensive, More Reliable Multilevel Approach for Assessing and Modeling Teacher Judgment Accuracy Using Latent Variables
citation: Julian F. Lohmann, Nils Machts, Jens Möller, Steffen Zitzmann. (2025). A More Comprehensive, More Reliable Multilevel Approach for Assessing and Modeling Teacher Judgment Accuracy Using Latent Variables. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10029-z
title: A multilevel latent variable model (ML-LVM) of judgment accuracy that represents rank, level, and differentiation components as raters' latent abilities
description: The article introduces the ML-LVM, in which each rater's judgments are modeled with a rater-specific bivariate normal distribution whose mean, variance, and covariance parameters correspond to the level, differentiation, and rank components of judgment accuracy. The three components follow a multivariate normal distribution across raters, so the model yields both population-level means and variances quantifying between-rater differences. The authors note that in a traditional two-step approach, person-specific scores 'are calculated in the first stage for each teacher separately and then treated as observed variables in subsequent analyses,' which the ML-LVM avoids by accounting for sampling error from a limited number of judgments. Estimation uses Bayesian MCMC in Stan.
requirements: A benchmark vector of judgments and corresponding criterion scores (e.g., test scores or simulated student ability) for each rater
Bayesian MCMC estimation in Stan, since random variances and covariances cause estimation problems in frequentist estimation
constraints: Variance components for the benchmark can be fixed to zero only when all raters judge identical stimuli; both variance components can be fixed to zero when all raters are provided with the same judgment stimuli
target_learners: teachers and pre-service teachers whose judgment accuracy is being assessed
target_learning_goals: assessment competence (diagnostic competence): accurate teacher judgments of student characteristics such as cognitive ability or performance
examples: In the illustrative scenario, 20 teachers each evaluate 30 students; teacher A's class mean of 70 versus a population mean of 60 is captured by the random intercept uj, and an average rank correlation of 0.55 versus teacher A's 0.45 illustrates the rank component
key_sources: Julian F. Lohmann, Nils Machts, Jens Möller, Steffen Zitzmann. (2025). A More Comprehensive, More Reliable Multilevel Approach for Assessing and Modeling Teacher Judgment Accuracy Using Latent Variables. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10029-z

citation: Julian F. Lohmann, Nils Machts, Jens Möller, Steffen Zitzmann. (2025). A More Comprehensive, More Reliable Multilevel Approach for Assessing and Modeling Teacher Judgment Accuracy Using Latent Variables. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10029-z
title: Simulated classroom environment for assessing pre-service chemistry teachers' judgment accuracy
description: The article's first empirical application used a simulated classroom environment in which pre-service chemistry teachers interacted with 12 virtual eighth-graders by selecting and posing questions, with three false answers and one correct answer per question covering four chemistry competence domains. Participants were 'required to assess the correctness of the given responses themselves' and after a 30-minute virtual lesson rated each student's ability on a 0–100 scale. Student ability levels were randomly sampled per student and teacher, so the true benchmarks varied across participants. The sample consisted of N = 53 pre-service chemistry teachers.
requirements: Benchmark ability levels defined by the simulation's student-specific probabilities of correct answers
Participants rating students on a 0–100 scale after the virtual lesson
constraints: The article text available here ends before the application's results are reported, so no outcome findings from this study are recorded
target_learners: pre-service chemistry teachers (teacher students) preparing to teach at upper track secondary schools
target_learning_goals: judgment accuracy (rank, level, differentiation) regarding student ability in chemistry
examples: Moderators tested in this application were education status (Bachelor = 0, Master = 1) and the number of questions asked during the virtual class

article_title: A More Comprehensive, More Reliable Multilevel Approach for Assessing and Modeling Teacher Judgment Accuracy Using Latent Variables
citation: Julian F. Lohmann, Nils Machts, Jens Möller, Steffen Zitzmann. (2025). A More Comprehensive, More Reliable Multilevel Approach for Assessing and Modeling Teacher Judgment Accuracy Using Latent Variables. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10029-z
title: Easy-to-use R code and step-by-step tutorial for applying the ML-LVM judgment accuracy model
description: The article states that 'Easy-to-use R code is provided to simplify the application of the new judgment accuracy model,' and Appendix 1 presents 'a step-by-step tutorial on how to apply the ML-LVM in R.' The model is estimated in the Bayesian environment of Stan using MCMC, with normal priors for intercepts and component means, half-Cauchy priors for population-level variances, and a Lewandowski–Kurowicka–Joe prior for random-effect covariances. The analysis code and dataset for the first empirical application are available on an OSF repository.
requirements: Bayesian estimation environment (Stan) with MCMC sampling
constraints: Runtime was up to 270 min per dataset in the largest sample size condition of the simulations (three chains run in parallel)
target_learners: researchers studying teacher judgment accuracy who wish to apply the ML-LVM
target_learning_goals: assessment and modeling of teacher judgment accuracy components
examples: The tutorial in Appendix 1 walks through applying the ML-LVM to the pre-service chemistry teacher dataset, including comparing results with PS-method calculations

article_title: Advancing Contextual Interference: Addressing Methodological Debates, Reflecting on Meta-Analytic Practices and Generalizability, and Guiding Future Directions in Motor Learning
citation: Ammar, A., Trabelsi, K., Salem, A., Jahrami, H., & Schöllhorn, W. I. (2025). Advancing Contextual Interference: Addressing Methodological Debates, Reflecting on Meta-Analytic Practices and Generalizability, and Guiding Future Directions in Motor Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10043-1
title: The two-effect contextual interference hypothesis: high-CI practice yields inferior acquisition but superior retention and transfer
description: The contextual interference (CI) hypothesis holds that practice schedule structure produces two distinct effects: a first effect during acquisition and a second effect on relatively permanent learning. As the article states, the hypothesis "posits that high CI (e.g., random practice) leads to inferior acquisition (1st effect), but superior learning capabilities (2nd effect), operationalized in form of retention and/or transfer tests, compared to low CI (i.e., blocked practice)". The article uses this framework to organize its meta-analytic evaluations and to criticize reviews that analyze only the second effect while neglecting acquisition. It also notes serial practice lies conceptually between blocked and random formats, and that mechanisms such as elaboration and reconstruction are debated.
requirements: Studies must compare higher vs lower contextual interference practice conditions and measure acquisition plus retention and/or transfer outcomes
constraints: The article limits its synthesis to gross motor skills in applied sport and physical education settings
target_learners: learners of gross motor / sport skills in physical education and sports training
target_learning_goals: motor skill acquisition
motor skill retention
transfer of motor learning
examples: The authors' meta-analyses evaluated outcome measures at post-test, retention and transfer, and computed changes across phases to capture both acquisition and relatively permanent gains

Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10043-1
title: Evidence syntheses of practice-schedule effects should ensure or stratify by baseline group equivalence before pooling post-test comparisons
description: This principle holds that reviews comparing practice conditions must verify that groups were equivalent at pre-test, or otherwise analyze pre-post deltas rather than raw post-tests, because unequal starting performance can be mistaken for an intervention effect. The article recommends that "reviews adhere to more rigorous inclusion criteria or conduct stratified/sensitivity analyses specifically designed to account for baseline imbalances in order to provide more valid, less biased and interpretable effect estimate". The authors implemented this by excluding studies without verified baseline comparability and by analyzing changes across phases.
requirements: Pre-test data must be reported or retrievable so baseline comparability can be verified or statistically modeled
constraints: The article states post-test comparisons without baseline control are vulnerable to bias and leave conclusions uncertain
target_learners: learners of gross motor / sport skills
target_learning_goals: valid estimation of practice-schedule effects on motor learning
examples: Ammar et al. excluded 25 studies lacking verified baseline comparability and analyzed pre-post deltas or retention gains relative to acquisition

article_title: Happy Together? On the Relationship Between Research on Retrieval Practice and Generative Learning Using the Case of Follow-Up Learning Tasks
citation: Julian Roelle, Tino Endres, Roman Abel, Niklas Obergassel, Matthias Nückles, Alexander Renkl. (2023). Happy Together? On the Relationship Between Research on Retrieval Practice and Generative Learning Using the Case of Follow-Up Learning Tasks. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09810-9
title: Retrieval practice as consolidation of mental representations in memory
description: The review characterizes retrieval practice (test-enhanced learning) as learning tasks requiring learners to retrieve studied information from memory, whose main theoretical function is consolidation. It states that retrieval practice is assumed to consolidate the respective retrieved knowledge in memory and hence enable learners to maintain their knowledge or performance originating from that knowledge over long periods of time. The review uses this function as one of two complementary functions organizing follow-up learning task design.
requirements: Tasks must require learners to retrieve the studied information from memory, e.g., via closed-book format
constraints: Benefits are largest when the format of the posttest questions matches the answer formats of the follow-up learning task, per the review
target_learners: learners studying factual and conceptual content after initial instruction
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of studied content

On the Relationship Between Research on Retrieval Practice and Generative Learning Using the Case of Follow-Up Learning Tasks. citation: Julian Roelle, Tino Endres, Roman Abel, Niklas Obergassel, Matthias Nückles, Alexander Renkl. (2023). Happy Together? On the Relationship Between Research on Retrieval Practice and Generative Learning Using the Case of Follow-Up Learning Tasks. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09810-9
title: Generative learning activities as construction of coherent mental representations
description: The review characterizes generative learning tasks as tasks requiring sense-making through organization, elaboration, and inference generation. It states that according to various generative learning theories, such activities foster the coherence of learners' mental representations of the to-be-learned content and the integration of these mental representations with prior knowledge. This constructing function is presented as complementary to the consolidating function of retrieval practice when designing follow-up learning tasks.
requirements: Task instructions must require generative activities such as organization, elaboration, or inference generation
constraints: The review distinguishes this concept from the classical generation effect, noting the activities restructure information rather than generate parts of it
target_learners: learners studying expository texts or multimedia material
target_learning_goals: conceptual knowledge and transfer

On the Relationship Between Research on Retrieval Practice and Generative Learning Using the Case of Follow-Up Learning Tasks. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09810-9
title: Reflect on each task's implementation quality when comparing retrieval practice, generative learning, or their combination
description: The review proposes that future research comparing retrieval practice, generative learning activities, or their combination must attend to how well each activity is implemented. It argues that in both research fields the other activity type has often been implemented in low quality, which limits what can be learned about their interaction, stating that in such comparisons "it is crucial to reflect on each task's implementation quality." This tenet is one of three the review offers for consolidating the relationship between the two research strands.
requirements: Comparisons should implement each task feature at adequate quality, e.g., retrieval practice with sufficient retrievability, repetition, and spacing
constraints: The review notes prior horse-race comparisons often pitted tasks of unequal implementation quality, making them uninformative
target_learners: researchers and designers of follow-up learning tasks
target_learning_goals: valid comparison of learning-task features and their combination
examples: The review cites Karpicke and Blunt (2011) as pitting a poorly implemented concept-mapping task against a well-implemented free-recall task

article_title: Making Sense of Generative Learning
citation: Fiorella, L. (2023). Making Sense of Generative Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09769-7
title: Generative sense-making framework: explaining, visualizing, and enacting modes with grounded sense-making
description: The article proposes a framework in which sense-making involves three qualitatively distinct modes: explaining (coherent verbal representations), visualizing (coherent visual representations), and enacting (coherent motor representations). Its core assumption is that 'the visualizing and enacting modes function to facilitate the explaining mode', so learners mentally organize and simulate material to support generalizing it through explanation. The framework maintains SOI/ICAP assumptions (limited working memory, role of prior knowledge, GLA advantage over non-generative activities) while specifying how instructor-provided and learner-generated representations interact to support internal sense-making.
requirements: Learners must have sufficient background knowledge and GLA guidance for GLAs to be effective, as the framework assumes
constraints: The framework targets conceptual learning materials, such as scientific phenomena and mathematics principles
target_learners: Learners of conceptual science and mathematics material
target_learning_goals: Constructing coherent mental representations that support comprehension and transfer
examples: Fig. 1 depicts how instruction, learner characteristics, and GLAs interact with internal sense-making processes to support comprehension and transfer

article_title: What Can Eye Movements Tell us about Visual Perception Processes in Classroom Contexts? Commentary on a Special Issue
citation: Kaakinen, J. K. (2021). What Can Eye Movements Tell us about Visual Perception Processes in Classroom Contexts? Commentary on a Special Issue. Educational Psychology Review, 33, 169-179. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09573-7
title: Classroom management scripts: a theoretical model contrasting expert and novice teachers' knowledge and awareness of classroom events
description: The commentary describes the theoretical paper by Wolff et al. (this issue), which introduces "classroom management scripts" to conceptualize differences between expert and novice teachers. The model explains how knowledge structures and cognitive processes differ, producing different situational awareness and action decisions. Experts are assumed to engage in automatic scanning of the visual environment for relevant cues with top-down control of eye movements guided by knowledge; whether experts show a greater perceptual span or focus on fewer relevant areas depends on the classroom event representation the teacher has formed.
requirements: The model assumes experts' top-down, knowledge-guided control of eye movements and automatic scanning for relevant cues.
constraints: Whether experts show greater perceptual span or narrower focus depends on the classroom event representation formed in the situation.
target_learning_goals: professional vision and classroom management awareness
examples: The commentary uses the model to reconcile why experts show wider scanning in some contexts and narrower focus in others.
key_sources: Kaakinen, J. K. (2021). What Can Eye Movements Tell us about Visual Perception Processes in Classroom Contexts? Commentary on a Special Issue. Educational Psychology Review, 33, 169-179. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09573-7

article_title: What Can Eye Movements Tell us about Visual Perception Processes in Classroom Contexts? Commentary on a Special Issue
citation: Kaakinen, J. K. (2021). What Can Eye Movements Tell us about Visual Perception Processes in Classroom Contexts? Commentary on a Special Issue. Educational Psychology Review, 33, 169-179. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09573-7
title: Eye movement data analysis should use measures and statistical methods that capture the time-course of processing and the data's correlational structure
description: The author argues that eye tracking's main advantage is detailed time-course information, which total fixation time or gaze duration fails to exploit because it "sums up all fixations or gazes made to a particular area of interest." She recommends first-pass and reinspection measures, fixation probability over time, and scanpath analysis, and notes that traditional ANOVA or t test approaches are often not optimal because eye movement data have correlational structure, missing observations, and unbalanced data.
requirements: AOI definitions should be guided by theory and support hypothesis testing; statistical methods must handle correlational structure, missing observations, and unbalanced data.
constraints: Mixed-effects methods require sufficient statistical power, which depends on the number of participants and observations per participant; recruiting classroom participants is difficult.
target_learning_goals: valid analysis of visual perception and attention processes in learning contexts
examples: The author notes linear mixed models are the gold standard in reading research, with Poisson models for fixation counts and mixed logit models for fixation probability.
