article_title: The Case for Multifaceted, Integrative Motivation Interventions Embedded in Classrooms
citation: Linnenbrink-Garcia, L., Wigfield, A., Cabrera, L., Mouzaoir, S., McKinney, D., Liu, P. P., Marchand, G., Schmidt, J. A., Harris, C. J., & Guthrie, J. (2026). The Case for Multifaceted, Integrative Motivation Interventions Embedded in Classrooms. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10177-w
title: A two-axis classification of motivation interventions: targeted versus multifaceted focus, and add-on versus embedded implementation on a continuum
description: This paper proposes classifying motivation interventions along two independent axes: their focus (targeted, addressing one form of motivation or problem, versus multifaceted, addressing multiple forms) and their implementation mode — whether they are "embedded within the curriculum versus implemented as an "add-on" module or activity". The authors argue the add-on–embedded distinction operates on a continuum, from fully stand-alone lessons to in-depth reframing of curricula and instructional approach, and that the two axes are often but not always confounded. The classification is illustrated with examples in Fig. 1 and used to organize the paper's argument for multifaceted, embedded interventions.
requirements: The two axes must be treated as separable dimensions of an intervention rather than collapsed into one targeted-versus-multifaceted contrast
constraints: The authors present this as a conceptual proposal for thinking about interventions, not a tested taxonomy
target_learning_goals: students' motivation and engagement
examples: The paper locates targeted mindset and utility value interventions as typically add-on, and CORI and M-PLANS as multifaceted and embedded

citation: Linnenbrink-Garcia, L., Wigfield, A., Cabrera, L., Mouzaoir, S., McKinney, D., Liu, P. P., Marchand, G., Schmidt, J. A., Harris, C. J., & Guthrie, J. (2026). The Case for Multifaceted, Integrative Motivation Interventions Embedded in Classrooms. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10177-w
title: Complex dynamic systems (CDS) framing of student motivation: self-organizing, non-linear change, developmental cascades, and attractor states
description: The paper presents a primer on CDS as applied to motivation: psychological processes are organized systems embedded in layered environments; they are "self-organizing, adaptive, and emergent", change is non-linear, and small events can produce large change through developmental cascades. A central concept is that "there are certain patterns of psychological processing or behavior that students gravitate towards; these are called attractor states", which stabilize behavior but are hard to change; Heino et al.'s landscape metaphor represents them as valleys that interventions can deepen or flatten. The authors contend motivation is compatible with CDS because theories already posit socialization within nested systems, motivation shifts over time, and motivational forms are interconnected in emergent, reinforcing belief systems.
requirements: Interventions using this framing should consider how changes to classroom context (curricula, teacher practice) shift the attractor state landscape
constraints: The authors state it is beyond the article's scope to develop a complete integrated model of motivation based on this premise; empirical motivation research has largely used linear models
target_learning_goals: understanding and sustaining students' motivation, engagement, and learning
examples: The M-PLANS science motivation intervention used CDS as an underlying framework; Geerling et al. applied CDS to confusion and interest during a utility value intervention
key_sources: Linnenbrink-Garcia, L., Wigfield, A., Cabrera, L., Mouzaoir, S., McKinney, D., Liu, P. P., Marchand, G., Schmidt, J. A., Harris, C. J., & Guthrie, J. (2026). citation: Linnenbrink-Garcia, L., Wigfield, A., Cabrera, L., Mouzaoir, S., McKinney, D., Liu, P. P., Marchand, G., Schmidt, J. A., Harris, C. J., & Guthrie, J. (2026). The Case for Multifaceted, Integrative Motivation Interventions Embedded in Classrooms. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10177-w
title: Theoretical integration rationale: no single motivation theory captures all relevant constructs, so interventions should integrate carefully across theories
description: The paper argues that "no theory captures all relevant motivation constructs that impact student learning outcomes. Perhaps no one theory ever can", echoing Graham and Kelly that theories have foci and a range of convenience. Because constructs overlap across theories yet each theory holds unique constructs, integrative approaches should let interventions reach more students. The authors caution, following Pekrun and Ryan, that integration must be done carefully and conceptually: integrate theories studying the same phenomena or making converging predictions, and specify how integration yields new insights rather than merely adding constructs.
requirements: Integration should follow Pekrun's rules: same phenomena or converging predictions, plus a specified account of new insights gained
constraints: The authors state the motivation field's knowledge about integrating across motivation, metacognition, self-regulation, and personality is not complete enough to recommend interventions spanning those constructs
target_learning_goals: designing motivation interventions that support multiple forms of student motivation
examples: CORI integrated goal, interest, self-determination, expectancy-value, and social cognitive theories; M-PLANS built on five motivational design principles integrated across theories

citation: Linnenbrink-Garcia, L., Wigfield, A., Cabrera, L., Mouzaoir, S., McKinney, D., Liu, P. P., Marchand, G., Schmidt, J. A., Harris, C. J., & Guthrie, J. (2026). The Case for Multifaceted, Integrative Motivation Interventions Embedded in Classrooms. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10177-w
title: Design motivation interventions that are multifaceted, theoretically integrated, and embedded in classrooms, creating sustained supports — a "fertile soil" for motivation
description: The paper's central recommendation is a paradigm shift: develop interventions that integrate across motivation theories, address multiple forms of motivation, and are embedded in classroom curricula and instruction with teachers as partners, so that "students will have sustained supports for their motivation that creates a "fertile soil" for motivation to develop further". Multifaceted interventions can meet the motivational challenges of more students in a single classroom than single-construct targeted interventions, and changing the educational context can shift the attractor state landscape toward more adaptive motivation.
requirements: Work with classroom instructors and embed supports in curriculum and instructional practice rather than delivering stand-alone add-on modules
Integrate multiple motivation theories deliberately, following the paper's integration guidelines
constraints: Multicomponent interventions may cost more researcher time and resources, take more teacher implementation time, and make it harder to isolate which components drive effectiveness (per Rosenzweig et al., 2022, as cited in the paper)
target_learning_goals: students' motivation, engagement, and learning across reading and science domains
examples: CORI embedded motivational practices in a 12-week science-reading program; M-PLANS used CDS as its underlying framework for teacher professional learning

article_title: Effects and Characteristics of Mathematics Interventions for Students with Co-Occurring Difficulties in Mathematics and Reading: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis
citation: Ellinor Waaland, Vibeke Rønneberg, Dieuwer ten Braak. (2026). Effects and Characteristics of Mathematics Interventions for Students with Co-Occurring Difficulties in Mathematics and Reading: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10184-x
title: Multiple cognitive deficit model as the framework for understanding co-occurring mathematics and reading difficulties
description: The review adopts the multiple cognitive deficit model as "the most plausible framework for understanding learning difficulties as well as their co-occurrence." The model posits that learning difficulties are multifactorial and arise from interacting risk factors that partly overlap across disorder pairs. Within this framework, the review identifies executive function, language, and rapid naming as shared risk factors for co-occurring mathematics and reading difficulties, with students showing greater challenges in these processes than students with isolated difficulties. Phonological processing is linked more specifically to reading, and numerical/magnitude processing to mathematics.
requirements: Explains co-occurrence as arising from partly overlapping multifactorial risk factors rather than a single cause or a fully distinct disorder
constraints: The review notes the evidence for domain-general skills accounting for shared variance "remains somewhat inconclusive"
target_learners: Early elementary students (grades 1-3) with co-occurring mathematics and reading difficulties
target_learning_goals: Mathematics achievement
Understanding responsiveness to mathematics interventions
examples: The review cites Viesel-Nordmeyer et al. (2023) finding an additive pattern for mathematics and reading skills but an under-additive pattern in executive function among students with co-occurring difficulties, suggesting executive function is a shared risk factor.

article_title: Learning to Argue Through Dialogue: a Review of Instructional Approaches
citation: Chrysi Rapanta & Mark K. Felton. (2022). Learning to Argue Through Dialogue: a Review of Instructional Approaches. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09637-2
title: MeDOL framework for reviewing learning-to-argue (LTA) instructional approaches
description: The MeDOL framework is the review's organizing scheme, adapting Morrison et al.'s instructional effectiveness model to the diversity of LTA research. It codes each study on four components: Methods (how dialogue is framed and fostered), Dialogue goals (epistemic goals participants pursue), Outcomes (LTA gains), and Learners (age/grade, learning structure, disciplinary field). The authors state: "Our MeDOL framework adapts Morrison et al.'s( 2019) effectiveness components as follows: Methods refer to the authors ' approach of framing educationally effective dialogue, and to the fostering methods used to increase LTA outcomes". Eleven coding categories emerged from applying it to 143 studies.
requirements: Studies must describe framing of dialogue, dialogue goals, LTA outcomes, and learner characteristics to be codable within the framework
constraints: The authors state applying Morrison et al.'s generic instructional effectiveness model directly to the LTA literature was not possible due to the great variety of approaches, so the framework is a transformed adaptation
target_learners: K-16 students across primary, middle, secondary, and university levels
target_learning_goals: Learning to argue through argumentative dialogue
examples: All 143 reviewed studies were coded on the framework's eleven categories, with inter-rater reliabilities of κ = .776, κ = .727, and κ = .702 for three high-inference variables
key_sources: Chrysi Rapanta & Mark K. Felton. (2022). Learning to Argue Through Dialogue: a Review of Instructional Approaches. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09637-2

article_title: Learning to Argue Through Dialogue: a Review of Instructional Approaches
citation: Chrysi Rapanta & Mark K. Felton. (2022). Learning to Argue Through Dialogue: a Review of Instructional Approaches. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09637-2
title: Three dialogue goals for LTA: sensemaking, articulation, and deliberation
description: The review proposes a typology of epistemic dialogue goals enacted by students in LTA settings, extending Berland and Reiser's (2009) proposal. Sensemaking dialogues aim at making sense of what others say or a phenomenon; articulation focuses on articulating relationships between sources of evidence or coordinating theories with evidence; persuasion dialogues focus on arriving at consensus (deliberation) or proving one's position best. The authors write: "Examples of such dialogue goals are the ones proposed by Berland and Reiser ( 2009), namely: sensemaking, articulation, and persuasion". They prefer the term deliberation to persuasion to avoid the misconception that persuasion must be confrontational.
requirements: Sensemaking is treated as a starting point for any constructive dialogue; deliberation presupposes sensemaking and articulation as elements of the deliberative process
constraints: The authors note it is still not clear what a dialogue-goal typology in educational contexts should take into consideration as a 'goal'
target_learners: K-16 students in classroom dialogue settings
target_learning_goals: Sensemaking, articulation of evidence relations, and deliberative persuasion through dialogue
examples: Studies coded with deliberation as primary task include science students using critical dialogue to evaluate solutions to a socio-scientific problem and students in a historical debate through role-playing
key_sources: Chrysi Rapanta & Mark K. Felton. (2022). Learning to Argue Through Dialogue: a Review of Instructional Approaches. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09637-2

citation: Chrysi Rapanta & Mark K. Felton. (2022). Learning to Argue Through Dialogue: a Review of Instructional Approaches. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09637-2
title: Five-level taxonomy of argument quality for coding reasoning gains
description: The review codes argumentative reasoning gains on five levels combining structural and functional elements: main (claims/reasons), elaborated (evidence, questions, TAP structure), complex (internal relationships and quality of evidence/justification), dialogic (transactivity, critique, rebuttal), and dialectic (revision or integration of alternative theories, quality of counterarguments, critical questions). The authors state: "we had previously identified five types or levels of arguments, comprising both structural and functional elements, namely: main, elaborated, complex, dialogic, and dialectic". Table 1 details the codes per level, e.g., level 4 codes T, CAR, CAR/E for dialogic argument.
requirements: Coding requires identifying presence or combination of elements such as claims, reasons, evidence, TAP structure, transactive moves, counterarguments, and revisions
constraints: The authors note that asserting specific argument elements are effective may require additional pragmatic criteria such as conceptual complexity, coherence, and relevance
target_learning_goals: Argumentative reasoning gains as products of dialogue
examples: Pattern 2 studies were mostly coded at the elaborated level (TAP-structure arguments) while Pattern 4 studies were mostly coded at the dialectic level
key_sources: Chrysi Rapanta & Mark K. Felton. (2022). Learning to Argue Through Dialogue: a Review of Instructional Approaches. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09637-2

article_title: Learning to Argue Through Dialogue: a Review of Instructional Approaches
citation: Chrysi Rapanta & Mark K. Felton. (2022). Learning to Argue Through Dialogue: a Review of Instructional Approaches. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09637-2
title: Match dialogue structure to the intended LTA goal: low structure for sensemaking, high structure for articulation, dialectic framing for deliberation
description: The review's four study patterns show that instructional framing of argumentative dialogue aligns with the epistemic goal pursued: low-structure framing suits sensemaking, high-structure framing suits articulation and deliberation, and dialectic framing with disagreement as a starting point suits deliberation aimed at integrated arguments. The authors identify "low-structured sensemaking, high-structured articulation, high-structured deliberation, and dialectic deliberation" as the four relationships driving their findings. Designers should choose framing deliberately according to which argumentative gains they target.
requirements: The intended dialogue goal (sensemaking, articulation, or deliberation) must be identified before choosing the framing structure
constraints: The patterns derive from cross-tabulated frequencies in a review of 143 studies, not from a controlled comparison of framings; the authors note outcomes are not defined similarly across studies and methods do not always involve controlled comparison
target_learners: K-16 students in whole-class, small-group, or one-to-one dialogue settings
target_learning_goals: Learning to argue through argumentative dialogue
examples: Pattern 4 studies established disagreement as a necessary starting point and leveraged it to drive gains in counter-argumentation, rebuttals, and argument-counterargument integration
key_sources: Chrysi Rapanta & Mark K. Felton. (2022). Learning to Argue Through Dialogue: a Review of Instructional Approaches. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09637-2

article_title: An Evolutionary Approach to Motivation and Learning: Differentiating Biologically Primary and Secondary Knowledge
citation: Kate M. Xu, Sarah Coertjens, Florence Lespiau, Kim Ouwehand, Hanke Korpershoek, Fred Paas, David C. Geary. (2024). An Evolutionary Approach to Motivation and Learning: Differentiating Biologically Primary and Secondary Knowledge. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09880-3
title: Evolutionary framework distinguishing biologically primary from biologically secondary knowledge and motivation
description: The article builds on Geary's framework distinguishing "biologically secondary knowledge and skills learned in schools from those acquired nearly automatically during development (e.g., language, face recognition)". Primary knowledge emerges through built-in cognitive and motivational scaffolds organized as folk psychology, folk biology, and folk physics; secondary domains such as physics and mathematics lack these biases, "require more explicit, organized instruction", and their evolutionary novelty explains declining motivation during schooling. The study tests this framework empirically with a vocabulary task.
requirements: Distinguishing content by evolutionary relevance of the knowledge being learned
constraints: The built-in cognitive and motivational biases do not extend to most academic domains
target_learners: school and university students learning academic content
target_learning_goals: academic knowledge and skills in evolutionarily novel domains such as mathematics, physics, and reading
examples: The study embedded primary (e.g., mother, love) and secondary (e.g., computer, gravity) concepts in Dutch-fictional word pairs and contrasted recall, motivation, and cognitive load between the two knowledge types.
key_sources: Kate M. Xu, Sarah Coertjens, Florence Lespiau, Kim Ouwehand, Hanke Korpershoek, Fred Paas, David C. Geary. (2024). An Evolutionary Approach to Motivation and Learning: Differentiating Biologically Primary and Secondary Knowledge. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09880-3

article_title: Development and Validation of a Theory-Based Questionnaire to Measure Different Types of Cognitive Load
citation: Krieglstein, F., Beege, M., Rey, G. D., Sanchez-Stockhammer, C., & Schneider, S. (2023). Development and Validation of a Theory-Based Questionnaire to Measure Different Types of Cognitive Load. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09738-0
title: Three types of cognitive load within Cognitive Load Theory: intrinsic, extraneous, and germane
description: The article organizes cognitive load into three types within Cognitive Load Theory. Intrinsic load "refers to the load imposed by the learning task's complexity", reflected in element interactivity and reduced by prior knowledge. Extraneous load "results from processes that are not relevant to learning" and is determined by the presentation format of the material. Germane load is the learning-relevant, productive load: learners "must actively invest cognitive resources" to construct and automate schemata, so GCL should be as high as possible. ICL and ECL are assumed to be additive, and design aims to reduce ECL to free resources for dealing with ICL.
requirements: Measurement instruments must be able to differentiate between the three load types to assess the effectiveness of specific instructional designs and principles.
constraints: The article states the role of GCL within CLT is still controversial concerning its measurement and theoretical embedding.
target_learners: learners acquiring secondary knowledge in educational and training contexts
target_learning_goals: efficient use of limited working memory for construction and automation of schemata in long-term memory
examples: The questionnaire items were formulated to reflect these definitions: ICL items address perceived task complexity and prior knowledge, ECL items address the design of the learning material, and GCL items address mental effort and schema construction.
key_sources: Krieglstein, F., Beege, M., Rey, G. D., Sanchez-Stockhammer, C., & Schneider, S. (2023). Development and Validation of a Theory-Based Questionnaire to Measure Different Types of Cognitive Load. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09738-0

article_title: Development and Validation of a Theory-Based Questionnaire to Measure Different Types of Cognitive Load
citation: Krieglstein, F., Beege, M., Rey, G. D., Sanchez-Stockhammer, C., & Schneider, S. (2023). Development and Validation of a Theory-Based Questionnaire to Measure Different Types of Cognitive Load. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09738-0
title: A 15-item theory-based questionnaire measuring intrinsic, extraneous, and germane cognitive load separately
description: The instrument measures the three cognitive load types separately with multiple items on a 9-point Likert-type scale, developed from a 17-item catalog and reduced to 15 items (five per type). Items intended to measure ICL and ECL "were formulated passively", while "the items designed to measure GCL were formulated from a first-person perspective (“I”)" to make the active investment of cognitive resources easier to assess. The strict use of "learning content" (ICL) versus "design or structure of the learning material" (ECL) wording was chosen because learners have problems differentiating ICL from ECL, and one ICL item explicitly addresses prior knowledge.
requirements: Appropriate instruction is needed so respondents assess the learning intervention rather than a subsequent learning test.
constraints: The article states the construct germane cognitive load remains controversial concerning its measurement and theoretical embedding in cognitive load theory.
target_learning_goals: differentiated measurement of perceived intrinsic, extraneous, and germane cognitive load during learning
examples: Studies 3–5 were designed so that "each cognitive load type was manipulated separately (Study 3: ICL; Study 4: ECL; Study 5: GCL) to further validate the questionnaire" in between-subjects online experiments.
key_sources: Krieglstein, F., Beege, M., Rey, G. D., Sanchez-Stockhammer, C., & Schneider, S. (2023). Development and Validation of a Theory-Based Questionnaire to Measure Different Types of Cognitive Load. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09738-0

article_title: The Reliability, But Not the Cronbach’s Alpha, of Knowledge Tests Matters: Response to Zitzmann and Orona (2025)
citation: Peter A. Edelsbrunner, Bianca A. Simonsmeier, Michael Schneider. (2025). The Reliability, But Not the Cronbach's Alpha, of Knowledge Tests Matters: Response to Zitzmann and Orona (2025). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10023-5
title: Semantic similarity heuristic: alpha indicates reliability to the degree that test items are semantically similar
description: The article proposes a heuristic for judging when Cronbach's alpha can be read as a reliability index: researchers should examine how semantically similar a test's items are. When items vary only in wording but not content, as in the Satisfaction with Life Scale, wording variation cancels measurement error across items and alpha is meaningful. The article states: "a good heuristic is to examine semantic similarity among items: the higher the similarity, the more accurately alpha indicates reliability." For knowledge tests, whose items tap different facets, the heuristic signals that alpha should not be read as reliability.
requirements: Applicable when judging whether a test's items assess the same homogeneous construct or different facets of a heterogeneous construct
constraints: The article presents this as a heuristic, not a formal test
target_learners: Researchers and test developers in educational measurement
target_learning_goals: Evaluating the reliability of knowledge tests
examples: The Satisfaction with Life Scale illustrates high semantic similarity; Hofer et al.'s bMCU mechanics test illustrates low semantic similarity because its items tap inertia, force and acceleration, balance of forces, and reciprocal action
key_sources: Peter A. Edelsbrunner, Bianca A. Simonsmeier, Michael Schneider. (2025). The Reliability, But Not the Cronbach's Alpha, of Knowledge Tests Matters: Response to Zitzmann and Orona (2025). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10023-5

article_title: The Reliability, But Not the Cronbach’s Alpha, of Knowledge Tests Matters: Response to Zitzmann and Orona (2025)
citation: Peter A. Edelsbrunner, Bianca A. Simonsmeier, Michael Schneider. (2025). The Reliability, But Not the Cronbach's Alpha, of Knowledge Tests Matters: Response to Zitzmann and Orona (2025). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10023-5
title: Abandon fixed alpha cutoff values for knowledge tests; report alpha and its confidence interval for studying item interrelatedness instead
description: The article recommends that fixed cutoff values for knowledge tests' alphas be abandoned because they do not ensure reliability and instead increase publication bias. Researchers should still report alpha and its confidence interval, but as indices of item interrelatedness rather than reliability. As the authors conclude: "Fixed cutoff values for the alphas of knowledge tests must be abandoned because they do not ensure reliability but instead increase publication bias." Methodological rigor instead requires flexible, theory-guided application of methods.
requirements: Researchers should still report alpha and its confidence interval for knowledge tests to derive and study item interrelatedness
constraints: The recommendation applies to heterogeneous constructs like knowledge; alpha remains appropriate as a reliability index for homogeneous constructs
target_learning_goals: Sound measurement of domain-specific knowledge
Methodological rigor in test construction
examples: The authors contrast the homogeneous Satisfaction with Life Scale, where alpha is meaningful, with the heterogeneous bMCU mechanics knowledge test, where it is not
key_sources: Peter A. Edelsbrunner, Bianca A. Simonsmeier, Michael Schneider. (2025). The Reliability, But Not the Cronbach's Alpha, of Knowledge Tests Matters: Response to Zitzmann and Orona (2025). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10023-5

article_title: A Systematic Review of Self-Regulated Learning through Integration of Multimodal Data and Artificial Intelligence
citation: Susanne de Mooij, Joni Lämsä, Lyn Lim, Olli Aksela, Shruti Athavale, Inti Bistolfi, Flora Jin, Tongguang Li, Roger Azevedo, Maria Bannert, Dragan Gašević, Sanna Järvelä, Inge Molenaar. (2025). A Systematic Review of Self-Regulated Learning through Integration of Multimodal Data and Artificial Intelligence. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10028-0
title: The SMA grid: a two-dimensional framework mapping CAMM processes against data streams and four analytic approaches
description: The Self-Regulated Learning Processes, Multimodal Data, and Analysis (SMA) grid, introduced by Molenaar et al. (2023) and applied in this review, maps SRL research along two axes: CAMM processes (cognition, metacognition, affective states, motivation) and data streams (behavioural, physiological, contextual). It distinguishes four analytic approaches: "The unimodal approach is a classical approach, focusing on a single CAMM process with one data stream", horizontal (multiple processes, one stream), vertical (one process, multiple streams), and integrated (multiple streams, multiple processes). The review mapped 141 studies onto the grid to visualise typical combinations.
requirements: Studies must report process data capturing the sequence and timing of events during a learning task and apply process-oriented analysis to be mappable onto the grid
constraints: The review notes prior data taxonomies (Di Mitri et al. 2018; Sailer et al. 2024) are insufficiently granular for SRL-model-specific characteristics
target_learners: formal education students across primary, secondary, and higher education
target_learning_goals: measuring and diagnosing self-regulated learning processes (cognitive, metacognitive, affective, motivational)
examples: The review's Fig. 2 maps 141 studies onto the grid, with the most prevalent combination being log data used to investigate cognitive and metacognitive processes through a horizontal approach (N = 26 studies, 18.8%)
key_sources: Susanne de Mooij, Joni Lämsä, Lyn Lim, Olli Aksela, Shruti Athavale, Inti Bistolfi, Flora Jin, Tongguang Li, Roger Azevedo, Maria Bannert, Dragan Gašević, Sanna Järvelä, Inge Molenaar. (2025). A Systematic Review of Self-Regulated Learning through Integration of Multimodal Data and Artificial Intelligence. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10028-0

article_title: A Systematic Review of Self-Regulated Learning through Integration of Multimodal Data and Artificial Intelligence
citation: Susanne de Mooij, Joni Lämsä, Lyn Lim, Olli Aksela, Shruti Athavale, Inti Bistolfi, Flora Jin, Tongguang Li, Roger Azevedo, Maria Bannert, Dragan Gašević, Sanna Järvelä, Inge Molenaar. (2025). A Systematic Review of Self-Regulated Learning through Integration of Multimodal Data and Artificial Intelligence. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10028-0
title: Open-source database of SRL constructs and multimodal indicators
description: To address variation in operational definitions of CAMM processes when applying multimodal data and analytics, the review's authors provide an open-source database hosted on Zenodo (https://zenodo.org/records/15481052). The article states "This database can be utilized to gain more detailed information about the SRL constructs within each CAMM process and the related indicators derived from multimodal data and analytics." It supports researchers in comparing how constructs and indicators were operationalised across the 142 included studies.
requirements: Researchers seeking construct-level detail on CAMM operationalisations across the included studies
target_learners: SRL researchers and learning analytics practitioners
target_learning_goals: valid and reliable measurement of CAMM processes underlying self-regulated learning
examples: The database accompanies the review's mapping of studies onto the SMA grid and its coding of CAMM processes, data streams, and analytical methods
key_sources: Susanne de Mooij, Joni Lämsä, Lyn Lim, Olli Aksela, Shruti Athavale, Inti Bistolfi, Flora Jin, Tongguang Li, Roger Azevedo, Maria Bannert, Dragan Gašević, Sanna Järvelä, Inge Molenaar. (2025). A Systematic Review of Self-Regulated Learning through Integration of Multimodal Data and Artificial Intelligence. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10028-0

article_title: Investigating Success in the Transition to University: A Systematic Review of Personal Risk and Protective Factors Influencing Psychosocial Success
citation: Ball, I., Banerjee, M., Holliman, A., & Tyndall, I. (2025). Investigating Success in the Transition to University: A Systematic Review of Personal Risk and Protective Factors Influencing Psychosocial Success. https://osf.io/vxu5q?view_only=ee23e20f57c54891b842c92b7a4858de
title: PHABS-PSS framework: Personal disposition, Health and wellbeing, Acclimation, Background, and Social factors influencing Psychosocial Success
description: The PHABS-PSS framework is the review's organising taxonomy, grouping the 96 identified risk and protective factors into five higher-order domains: "Personal disposition, Health and wellbeing, Acclimation, Background, and Social factors influencing PsychoSocial Success". It was built to reduce the complexity of a disparate literature, make findings conveyable to diverse audiences, and provide "a more practical basis for formulating interventions with real world impact". Personal disposition covers personality, adaptive self-regulation and coping; health and wellbeing covers positive and negative wellbeing dimensions and addictive behaviours; acclimation covers adjustment variables and academic attitudes; background covers demographic and education-context variables; social covers support, skills and motivations.
requirements: Further work should explore the framework and confirm its predictive power over students' psychosocial success in the transition to university
constraints: The thematic groupings lose some nuance of lower-order factors, an argument the authors acknowledge while defending the lumping approach
target_learners: traditional first-year university students transitioning from pre-tertiary education
target_learning_goals: psychosocial success in the transition to university, including wellbeing, adjustment, and social functioning
examples: The review's Figure 2 visually represents the identified risk and protective factor domains in relation to psychosocial outcomes, and Figure 3 presents the PHABS-PSS framework
key_sources: Ball, I., Banerjee, M., Holliman, A., & Tyndall, I. (2025). Investigating Success in the Transition to University: A Systematic Review of Personal Risk and Protective Factors Influencing Psychosocial Success. https://osf.io/vxu5q?view_only=ee23e20f57c54891b842c92b7a4858de

article_title: Involving the Body to Improve Letter Knowledge and Script: an Experimental Study in French Kindergarten
citation: Fernando Núñez-Regueiro, Natacha Boissicat, Fanny Gimbert, Céline Pobel-Burtin, Marie-Caroline Croset, Marie-Line Bosse, and Cécile Nurra. (2024). Involving the Body to Improve Letter Knowledge and Script: An Experimental Study in French Kindergarten. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09923-9
title: Hierarchical memory-trace framework for sensorimotor training design
description: The article proposes that bodily experiences be organized by the proximity of their memory traces to the learning content: specific (pencil-and-paper), intermediate (arm), and general (body) levels. It assumes "memory traces generated by bodily experiences more distal to the content of the activity" need to be "nested within memory traces of more proximal levels" to create synergies in learning. Training conditions are nested: arm training combines specific and intermediate traces, arm-body training all three levels. The framework draws on embodied cognition, the modality-like "multimodality effect", the variability effect, and the human movement effect from cognitive load theory.
requirements: Higher-level bodily movement training must be combined with lower-level training (e.g., handwriting exercises in all conditions) so that distal memory traces are nested within proximal ones
constraints: A pilot study without handwriting exercises in the arm and arm-body conditions showed null or negative effects of bodily engagement, which the authors attributed to the lack of specific sensorimotor experiences
target_learners: Kindergarten students (around 5 years old) acquiring pre-reading skills
target_learning_goals: Letter knowledge (letter recognition, letter-name knowledge)
Letter script skills (dictation, stroke direction, legibility)
examples: The experiment nested conditions: pencil-and-paper training allocated 100% of time to writing activity traces; arm training allocated 45% to handwriting and 55% to arm tracing; arm-body training allocated 45% handwriting, 11% arm, 44% body training
key_sources: Fernando Núñez-Regueiro, Natacha Boissicat, Fanny Gimbert, Céline Pobel-Burtin, Marie-Caroline Croset, Marie-Line Bosse, and Cécile Nurra. (2024). Involving the Body to Improve Letter Knowledge and Script: An Experimental Study in French Kindergarten. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09923-9

article_title: Involving the Body to Improve Letter Knowledge and Script: an Experimental Study in French Kindergarten
citation: Fernando Núñez-Regueiro, Natacha Boissicat, Fanny Gimbert, Céline Pobel-Burtin, Marie-Caroline Croset, Marie-Line Bosse, and Cécile Nurra. (2024). Involving the Body to Improve Letter Knowledge and Script: An Experimental Study in French Kindergarten. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09923-9
title: When adding bodily movement to handwriting instruction, keep handwriting exercises in all conditions and introduce arm movements before whole-body movements
description: The article recommends a hierarchical instructional design in which ordinary handwriting exercises remain the core of all conditions, and bodily movements are added in increasing degrees of integration (arm tracing, then walking letter outlines). This design was chosen to minimize "the possibility that the beneficial effects of higher-level embodied learning were offset by a lack of memory traces from lower-level embodied learning". It also ensures ecological validity for ordinary kindergarten time and personnel requirements.
requirements: All conditions must include ordinary pencil-and-paper handwriting exercises (the common training session)
Bodily-movement exercises should be adapted to kindergarten time and personnel constraints
constraints: Arm-body training showed negative effects on letters written under dictation and on the composite measure, and its benefits depended on students' initial skill level
target_learners: Kindergarten students learning letter knowledge and script
target_learning_goals: Letter recognition and name knowledge
Handwriting and letter script quality
examples: Twelve training sessions over 6 weeks, one specific and one common session per week, each pair training a single letter; arm training traced letters in the air and over the desk, arm-body training added walking over ground letter outlines with and without blindfolds
key_sources: Fernando Núñez-Regueiro, Natacha Boissicat, Fanny Gimbert, Céline Pobel-Burtin, Marie-Caroline Croset, Marie-Line Bosse, and Cécile Nurra. (2024). Involving the Body to Improve Letter Knowledge and Script: An Experimental Study in French Kindergarten. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09923-9

article_title: Self-regulated Learning in the Digitally Enhanced Science Classroom: Toward an Early Warning System
citation: Kubsch, M., Strauß, S., Grimm, A., Gombert, S., Drachsler, H., Neumann, K., & Rummel, N. (2025). Self-regulated Learning in the Digitally Enhanced Science Classroom: Toward an Early Warning System. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10011-9
title: CAMM framework of self-regulated learning processes in technology-enhanced classrooms
description: The article organizes self-regulated learning around four components—"cognition, affect, metacognition, and motivation"—referred to as CAMM processes, drawing on Winne and Perry's COPES model and cyclical SRL accounts. Learners set goals, monitor progress, and regulate their cognitions, affects, metacognition, and motivation; the cycle is recursive rather than strictly linear. The study operationalizes the cognitive, affective, and metacognitive dimensions (motivation data was unavailable) as data streams for predicting learning productivity in inquiry classrooms.
requirements: Data streams capturing cognitive, affective, and metacognitive processes must be collectable unobtrusively, validly, economically, and within legal and ethical bounds in real classrooms
constraints: The dataset did not include data on students' motivation during learning, so the motivational component was not modeled
target_learners: middle school students in grades 7 and 8
target_learning_goals: physics energy concept understanding
self-regulated learning during inquiry
examples: The study scored 36 workbook tasks into 107 cognitive scores per student and assessed epistemic emotions and metacognitive judgments after each of five unit parts
key_sources: Kubsch, M., Strauß, S., Grimm, A., Gombert, S., Drachsler, H., Neumann, K., & Rummel, N. (2025). Self-regulated Learning in the Digitally Enhanced Science Classroom: Toward an Early Warning System. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10011-9

article_title: Self-regulated Learning in the Digitally Enhanced Science Classroom: Toward an Early Warning System
citation: Kubsch, M., Strauß, S., Grimm, A., Gombert, S., Drachsler, H., Neumann, K., & Rummel, N. (2025). Self-regulated Learning in the Digitally Enhanced Science Classroom: Toward an Early Warning System. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10011-9
title: Technology-enhanced digital workbook (Moodle-based) for inquiry-based physics instruction
description: A Moodle course implementing a technology-enhanced workbook that "replaced paper-based worksheets and notebooks" in an inquiry-based energy unit. It featured task formats from multiple-choice to open-ended answers, recorded student artifacts across 36 tasks, and gave each student a personal laptop or tablet. The recorded artifacts supplied the cognitive data stream (107 scores per student via evidence-centered design scoring), while self-report instruments after each of five unit parts supplied affective and metacognitive data.
requirements: Each student needs access to a laptop or tablet; teachers participate in professional learning on project-based pedagogy and the workbook
constraints: Data collection is limited by classroom affordances such as missed lessons and teacher instructions to skip tasks, which produced missing task responses
target_learners: middle school students in grades 7 and 8 in Gymnasium and Gemeinschaftsschule school types
target_learning_goals: energy concept understanding
scientific practices such as planning investigations and constructing explanations
examples: Students investigated the driving question about mounting solar cells on a house through three sub-driving questions across five unit parts
key_sources: Kubsch, M., Strauß, S., Grimm, A., Gombert, S., Drachsler, H., Neumann, K., & Rummel, N. (2025). Self-regulated Learning in the Digitally Enhanced Science Classroom: Toward an Early Warning System. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10011-9

article_title: The Effective Design of Tasks Involving Learning by Drawing: Current Trends and Methodological Progress in Research on Drawing to Learn
citation: Dechamps, T., & Skulmowski, A. (2025). The Effective Design of Tasks Involving Learning by Drawing: Current Trends and Methodological Progress in Research on Drawing to Learn. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10026-2
title: Two-level classification of visualizations in drawing tasks: abstractness level and representational vs. relational drawing type
description: The review proposes describing visualizations in learning-by-drawing studies on two levels: the level of visual abstractness (concrete vs. abstract) and the drawing type, distinguishing "visualizations representing tangible real-world objects, labeled as representational images" from "non-tangible concepts or abstract relationships, labeled as relational images," following Hegarty (2011) and Skulmowski (2024). Complex drawings such as multiple representations or animations form an additional category. The authors apply these labels to both provided reference images and learner-generated drawings to make studies comparable.
requirements: Studies should classify both provided and learner-generated visualizations using a shared terminology so results can be compared.
constraints: The classification is proposed for learning-oriented drawing tasks and relies on the conceptual systems of Hegarty (2011), Quillin and Thomas (2015), and Skulmowski (2024).
target_learners: learners using drawing as a learning strategy across educational domains
target_learning_goals: designing and comparing drawing-to-learn tasks and their visualizations
examples: The review classifies Schwamborn et al.'s (2010) drawing prompt as predominantly abstract, and Bobek and Tversky's (2016) tire-pump drawings as combining representational and relational elements with predominantly concrete elements.
key_sources: Dechamps, T., & Skulmowski, A. (2025). The Effective Design of Tasks Involving Learning by Drawing: Current Trends and Methodological Progress in Research on Drawing to Learn. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10026-2

article_title: The Effective Design of Tasks Involving Learning by Drawing: Current Trends and Methodological Progress in Research on Drawing to Learn
citation: Dechamps, T., & Skulmowski, A. (2025). The Effective Design of Tasks Involving Learning by Drawing: Current Trends and Methodological Progress in Research on Drawing to Learn. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10026-2
title: Align assessment modality and knowledge types with the learning strategies under study when evaluating drawing to learn
description: The review argues that because drawing evokes nonverbal, pictorial processing, assessments should cover the modalities and knowledge types targeted in the learning phase. It recommends that "a variety of outcomes including retention, transfer, and inferential knowledge (see Cromley et al., 2020) should optimally be covered by an assessment when studying the learning strategy of drawing." Studies that aligned verbal and pictorial tests with all compared strategies allowed more differentiated and comparable conclusions.
requirements: Assessment batteries must include tests matching the modality of every learning strategy compared, including pictorial (drawing) tests alongside verbal tests.
constraints: The review notes some results suggest drawing can be effective beyond pictorial learning situations, so alignment alone does not guarantee detecting benefits.
target_learners: researchers and educators assessing drawing-based learning tasks
target_learning_goals: accurate measurement of drawing effects on retention, transfer, and inferential knowledge
examples: Schwamborn et al. (2010) and Schmeck et al. (2014) used transfer, retention, and drawing tests covering verbal and pictorial modalities, yielding differentiated results, whereas Bobek and Tversky (2016) used only verbal tests.
key_sources: Dechamps, T., & Skulmowski, A. (2025). The Effective Design of Tasks Involving Learning by Drawing: Current Trends and Methodological Progress in Research on Drawing to Learn. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10026-2

article_title: Effectiveness of Reading Interventions on Literacy Skills for Chinese Children with and Without Dyslexia: a Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
citation: Yijun Ruan, Urs Maurer, Catherine McBride. (2024). Effectiveness of Reading Interventions on Literacy Skills for Chinese Children with and Without Dyslexia: a Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09915-9
title: Six-moderator framework for reading intervention efficacy in Chinese children
description: The article organizes its meta-analysis around six potentially important moderators of reading intervention efficacy for Chinese children: "intervention outcome, intervention method, intervention timing, participant type, intervention form, and intervention implementer". Interventions were classified into five types based on core linguistic components for reading acquisition (phonological, morphological, orthographic, fluency, and working memory), grounded in the Interactive Dynamic Literacy Model. Meta-regression analyses tested each moderator's influence on effect sizes.
requirements: Studies must use a pretest–posttest control-group randomized controlled design and report at least one word-level literacy indicator
constraints: Limited to school-aged native Chinese speakers from preschool to sixth grade; only RCTs were included
target_learners: typically developing Chinese children in preschool through grade 6
target_learning_goals: word reading
word spelling
examples: The meta-analysis coded 49 effect sizes from 28 studies on these six moderators with interrater Cohen's kappas ranging from 0.68 to 1
key_sources: Yijun Ruan, Urs Maurer, Catherine McBride. (2024). Effectiveness of Reading Interventions on Literacy Skills for Chinese Children with and Without Dyslexia: a Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09915-9

article_title: Effectiveness of Reading Interventions on Literacy Skills for Chinese Children with and Without Dyslexia: a Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
citation: Yijun Ruan, Urs Maurer, Catherine McBride. (2024). Effectiveness of Reading Interventions on Literacy Skills for Chinese Children with and Without Dyslexia: a Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09915-9
title: Corpus of 28 randomized controlled trials of Chinese reading interventions
description: The evidence base of the meta-analysis: 28 independent RCT studies yielding 49 standardized mean-change effect sizes (37 for word reading and 12 for word spelling), identified through database searches of ERIC, PsycINFO, PubMed, ProQuest, and CNKI following PRISMA guidelines. Studies used pretest–posttest control-group designs with children with dyslexia or typically developing children, native Chinese speakers from preschool to sixth grade. Study characteristics coded included participant type, intervention method, outcome, implementer, duration, technology use, and form.
requirements: Included studies must provide sufficient statistics (sample sizes, means, and standard deviations) for computing effect size
constraints: Only randomized controlled trials were included; participants limited to school-aged native Chinese speakers with no other developmental, mental, or physical disorders
target_learning_goals: character/word reading
word spelling
examples: The initial database search resulted in 18814 records; 98 full-text articles were evaluated and 28 studies were finally included
key_sources: Yijun Ruan, Urs Maurer, Catherine McBride. (2024). Effectiveness of Reading Interventions on Literacy Skills for Chinese Children with and Without Dyslexia: a Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09915-9

article_title: Testing the Relative Universalism of Psychological Theories: A Person-Centered Analysis of Control-Value Theory
citation: Dirk Tempelaar · Alexandra Niculescu. (2026). Testing the Relative Universalism of Psychological Theories: A Person-Centered Analysis of Control-Value Theory. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10155-2
title: Person-centered analysis (latent profile analysis) as a framework for testing the relative universalism of psychological theories
description: The article proposes testing a theory's relative universalism—functional forms invariant while parameter magnitudes vary—by combining latent profile analysis with within-profile structural equation modeling. Person-centered methods, following Howard and Hoffman (2018), "balance both" parsimony and specificity by "grouping individuals into relatively homogeneous subpopulations while maintaining analytical tractability," addressing the homogeneity condition of ergodicity for static cross-sectional models. Four pre-specified criteria operationalize the test: functional-form invariance, sign stability, bounded magnitude flexibility, and contextual robustness after covariates. The framework is offered as replicable for other educational-psychology theories.
requirements: Large samples, since mixture modeling methods are described as data-intensive and require large samples
Integration of person-centered subgroup identification with variable-centered model testing, since identifying profiles alone does not test theory-driven relations
constraints: Person-centered methods do not address the stationarity condition of ergodicity, which the authors deem non-critical for static theories like CVT
Cross-sectional data mean all reported associations are predictive rather than causal
Within-profile variance restriction can mechanically attenuate standardized coefficients and R2
target_learning_goals: achievement emotions in learning processes
motivation and engagement
examples: Applied to 14,534 first-year business and economics students, the framework identified five emotion profiles and showed CVT relations hold across demographic groupings but partially diverge across profiles
key_sources: Dirk Tempelaar · Alexandra Niculescu. (2026). Testing the Relative Universalism of Psychological Theories: A Person-Centered Analysis of Control-Value Theory. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10155-2

article_title: Editor’s Note: Remembering Roxana Moreno
citation: Robinson, D. (2010). Editor's Note: Remembering Roxana Moreno. Educational Psychology Review, 22, 363–374. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9147-2
title: Moreno's cognitive–affective theory of learning with media incorporates motivational and metacognitive factors within cognitive theories of multimedia learning
description: This editorial describes the cognitive–affective theory of learning with media as Roxana Moreno's extension of emerging cognitive theories of multimedia learning. According to Mayer's tribute, along the way she was able to "incorporate motivational and metacognitive factors within the emerging cognitive theories of multimedia learning, creating her cognitive – affective theory of learning with media." The theory integrates affective and motivational processes with the cognitive account of learning from words and pictures, and Park and Brünken note a final paper she valued because it "integrates the cognitive and affective perspectives on learning with multimedia instruction."
requirements: The theory is presented as an extension of cognitive theories of multimedia learning, building on that prior theoretical base as the article describes
target_learning_goals: learning from words and pictures in multimedia environments
examples: The editorial reports that Moreno applied the theory across media ranging from narrated animation to virtual reality to educational games to training video
key_sources: Robinson, D. (2010). Editor's Note: Remembering Roxana Moreno. Educational Psychology Review, 22, 363–374. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9147-2

article_title: Editor’s Note: Remembering Roxana Moreno
citation: Robinson, D. (2010). Editor's Note: Remembering Roxana Moreno. Educational Psychology Review, 22, 363–374. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9147-2
title: The lightning-formation multimedia lesson used in Mayer and Moreno's 1998 split-attention study
description: This is the multimedia lesson on lightning formation that Moreno developed for her first major study on multimedia learning with Mayer, published in the Journal of Educational Psychology in 1998. The editorial opens the lesson with the sentence "Cool moist air moves over a warmer surface and becomes heated" and reproduces early words and graphics from it as Fig. 1. Mayer reports that "the lightning passage has been used in more than a dozen published experiments conducted at UCSB and around the world," making it a widely reused stimulus in multimedia learning research.
requirements: The lesson was designed for experiments on how people learn from words and pictures, pairing narration text with graphics as shown in the article's Fig. 1
target_learners: novice learners in multimedia learning experiments
target_learning_goals: understanding lightning formation from narrated multimedia instruction
examples: Mayer and Moreno's 1998 Journal of Educational Psychology study of a split-attention effect in multimedia learning used this lesson
key_sources: Robinson, D. (2010). Editor's Note: Remembering Roxana Moreno. Educational Psychology Review, 22, 363–374. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9147-2

article_title: Editor’s Note: Remembering Roxana Moreno
citation: Robinson, D. (2010). Editor's Note: Remembering Roxana Moreno. Educational Psychology Review, 22, 363–374. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9147-2
title: Mayer and Moreno's 1998 split-attention effect study as the first of nine joint Journal of Educational Psychology articles
description: This element is the 1998 Journal of Educational Psychology study by Mayer and Moreno, which the reference list titles "A split-attention effect in multimedia learning: Evidence for dual processing systems in working memory." Mayer's tribute describes it as based on work Moreno started in her first years of graduate study at UCSB, and reports it "was the first of what was to become a string of nine research articles we published together in the Journal of Educational Psychology." The editorial characterizes it as a significant contribution to cognitive theories of how people learn from words and pictures.
requirements: The study used the lightning-formation multimedia lesson developed by Moreno during her graduate work at UCSB
target_learning_goals: learning from words and pictures under split-attention conditions
examples: The editorial reports the lightning passage from this study was subsequently used in more than a dozen published experiments at UCSB and around the world
key_sources: Robinson, D. (2010). Editor's Note: Remembering Roxana Moreno. Educational Psychology Review, 22, 363–374. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9147-2

article_title: Editor’s Note: Remembering Roxana Moreno
citation: Robinson, D. (2010). Editor's Note: Remembering Roxana Moreno. Educational Psychology Review, 22, 363–374. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9147-2
title: Moreno's summary article on nine ways to reduce cognitive load
description: This element is Moreno's summary article on nine ways to reduce cognitive load, cited by Reisslein as the work through which he first encountered her research. The editorial's reference list does not print this article's full citation, but Reisslein's tribute identifies it as a summary of methods for reducing cognitive load in multimedia learning, the research area the editorial describes as one of Moreno's primary research areas. It connects to the edited volume on cognitive load theory she later co-edited with Plass and Brünken.
requirements: The article summarizes methods for reducing cognitive load, presupposing the cognitive load framework of multimedia learning research
target_learning_goals: reducing cognitive load during learning from multimedia instruction
examples: Reisslein reports first reading this summary article before beginning his collaboration with Moreno on engineering education research

article_title: Editor’s Note: Remembering Roxana Moreno
citation: Robinson, D. (2010). Editor's Note: Remembering Roxana Moreno. Educational Psychology Review, 22, 363–374. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9147-2
title: NSF-funded longitudinal study of elementary and middle school math learning among ethnic minority students
description: Shell's tribute describes a research thread few in the field knew about: an NSF-funded in-depth longitudinal study of elementary and middle school student math learning and the factors influencing that learning, with a focus on understanding achievement of ethnic minority students, especially Native Americans. He reports that those involved "were actively engaged in manuscript writing right up to her passing," and hopes that as results are published the work will advance theory and practice in learning and motivation in the classroom.
requirements: The study was funded by the National Science Foundation and designed as an in-depth longitudinal study of math learning factors
constraints: At the time of the editorial the study's manuscripts were still being written and its results had not yet been published
target_learners: elementary and middle school students, especially ethnic minority students including Native Americans
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement and the factors influencing math learning
examples: The editorial reports collaborators were writing manuscripts from the study up to Moreno's passing, with results forthcoming
key_sources: Robinson, D. (2010). Editor's Note: Remembering Roxana Moreno. Educational Psychology Review, 22, 363–374. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9147-2

article_title: Editor’s Note: Remembering Roxana Moreno
citation: Robinson, D. (2010). Editor's Note: Remembering Roxana Moreno. Educational Psychology Review, 22, 363–374. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9147-2
title: The edited volume Cognitive Load Theory (Plass, Moreno, & Brünken, 2010) and its involved coherence review process
description: This element is the edited volume Cognitive Load Theory, published in 2010 by Cambridge University Press and edited by Plass, Moreno, and Brünken. Plass's tribute describes the very involved review process implemented for the 12 chapters of the book, aimed at assuring the coherence and quality of the individual contributions. He acknowledges that the editing process and resulting revisions delayed publication, but reports that the rigor of the process was justified by the resulting strength of the chapters by all contributing authors.
requirements: The volume comprised 12 chapters that were subjected to an involved review process to assure coherence and quality across contributions
constraints: The editing process and resulting revisions delayed the book's publication, and some authors were not used to this level of editing
target_learners: educational psychology researchers and scholars engaging with cognitive load theory
target_learning_goals: understanding cognitive load theory and its applications to instruction
examples: Plass, Moreno, and Brünken edited the volume together, with Moreno contributing the coherence-oriented review process for its chapters

article_title: Developing Digital Self-Regulation in Adolescence: A Developmental Self-Determination Model of Digital Self-Regulation
citation: Wang, M.-T. (2026). Developing Digital Self-Regulation in Adolescence: A Developmental Self-Determination Model of Digital Self-Regulation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10183-y
title: Developmental Self-Determination Model of Digital Self-Regulation (DSMDS)
description: DSMDS is an SDT-grounded conceptual framework that treats adolescent digital self-regulation as a developmental process rather than a problem of exposure control. The article states the model "conceptualizes digital self-regulation as a developmental process through which adolescents learn to navigate digital environments as their executive functions, motivational capacities, and social ecologies mature." It integrates two core components—digital literacy competence as the knowledge and meaning-making foundation, and regulatory strategies as the enactment layer—shaped by autonomy-supportive or controlling conditions across family, school, peer, and policy contexts. Internalization of regulation is hypothesized but treated as contingent rather than inevitable.
requirements: Requires consideration of adolescents' developing executive function and basic psychological needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness
constraints: The article states the coordination framework "remains a conceptual proposition intended to organize future research rather than a settled empirical sequence in the digital-specific literature"
target_learning_goals: intentional, self-directed digital engagement
sustained attention and goal-directed technology use
digital literacy development
examples: The article presents Fig. 1 as a visual conceptualization of the model and applies it to devices, platforms, and activities including social media, gaming, messaging, and AI-based platforms
key_sources: Wang, M.-T. (2026). Developing Digital Self-Regulation in Adolescence: A Developmental Self-Determination Model of Digital Self-Regulation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10183-y

article_title: Developing Digital Self-Regulation in Adolescence: A Developmental Self-Determination Model of Digital Self-Regulation
citation: Wang, M.-T. (2026). Developing Digital Self-Regulation in Adolescence: A Developmental Self-Determination Model of Digital Self-Regulation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10183-y
title: Parental mediation typology: developmental implications depend on how mediation is enacted
description: The article interprets parental strategies to monitor, guide, and limit digital engagement as forms of external regulatory scaffolding whose effects depend on enactment. It states that "the developmental implications of parental mediation depend on how it is enacted, including whether it supports adolescents' autonomy and competence, whether it is experienced as legitimate and predictable, and whether it is calibrated to adolescents' developmental readiness." Table 2 maps active mediation, restrictive mediation, non-intrusive inspection, and authoritarian surveillance onto adolescent strategy types, distinguishing collaborative, competence-supporting scaffolds from controlling constraints.
requirements: Mediation must be experienced as legitimate, predictable, and calibrated to developmental readiness to support internalization
constraints: The article states parental mediation is not uniformly beneficial or harmful in itself; authoritarian surveillance is described as likely to thwart autonomy and bypass adolescent executive function development
target_learning_goals: internalization of digital self-regulation
autonomy-supportive socialization
examples: Active mediation such as discussing disclosure and explaining risks; restrictive mediation such as platform bans; non-intrusive inspection such as knowing accounts; authoritarian surveillance such as password requirements
key_sources: Wang, M.-T. (2026). Developing Digital Self-Regulation in Adolescence: A Developmental Self-Determination Model of Digital Self-Regulation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10183-y

article_title: Developing Digital Self-Regulation in Adolescence: A Developmental Self-Determination Model of Digital Self-Regulation
citation: Wang, M.-T. (2026). Developing Digital Self-Regulation in Adolescence: A Developmental Self-Determination Model of Digital Self-Regulation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10183-y
title: Time parental scaffolding shifts to match adolescents' demonstrated competence
description: The article argues parental mediation should be developmentally contingent: authority and autonomy are adjusted in tandem with demonstrated competence. It states that "optimal timing involves gradually increasing adolescents' decision-making authority in tandem with their demonstrated competence, ensuring that autonomy is experienced as supported rather than abandoned." Introducing autonomy-supportive strategies too late after strict control may undermine trust, while withdrawing scaffolds too early may increase risk exposure and regulatory failure.
requirements: Parental strategies must be responsive to adolescents' developmental signals such as growing self-awareness, expressed values, or responsible behavior
constraints: The article warns that introducing autonomy-supportive strategies too late after prolonged strict control may be experienced as abrupt or inconsistent, and withdrawing scaffolds too early may increase risk exposure and regulatory failure
target_learning_goals: internalization of digital self-regulation
autonomy-supportive parent-adolescent regulation
examples: The article describes parents shifting from restrictive mediation and closer monitoring early in adolescence toward non-intrusive inspection, active mediation, and collaborative rule-setting as adolescents demonstrate competence
key_sources: Wang, M.-T. (2026). Developing Digital Self-Regulation in Adolescence: A Developmental Self-Determination Model of Digital Self-Regulation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10183-y

article_title: Advances in Cognitive Psychology Relevant to Education: Introduction to the Special Issue
citation: Pooja K. Agarwal. (2012). Advances in Cognitive Psychology Relevant to Education: Introduction to the Special Issue. Educational Psychol Rev (2012) 24:353–354. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-012-9212-0
title: Apply a century of cognitive psychology research on human learning and memory to real-world education to ground practice in evidence rather than doctrine
description: The article argues that cognitive and educational scientists should, in the author's words, take "what we have learned over the course of at least 100 years about human learning and memory and apply it to the 'real world' of education." By giving research away, scientists could add scientific rigor to education debates, strengthen teacher training standards, and improve data-based decision making, moving practice away from history and doctrine toward evidence-based methods.
requirements: Researchers must widely disseminate evidence-based practices rather than keeping findings within the field
constraints: The article notes that year after year new initiatives are implemented yet often fail to obtain significant improvements, so translation alone is not a quick fix
target_learners: K-12 students in national education systems
target_learning_goals: Improved educational outcomes through evidence-based instructional practices
examples: The special issue itself is presented as an initial step: each article reviews recent advances in learning and memory research and addresses potential implementation of cognitive strategies in authentic classroom settings
key_sources: Pooja K. Agarwal. (2012). Advances in Cognitive Psychology Relevant to Education: Introduction to the Special Issue. Educational Psychol Rev (2012) 24:353–354. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-012-9212-0

article_title: Teachers’ Feedback on Oral Reading: A Critical Review of its Effects and the use of Theory in Research
citation: Grønli, K. M., Walgermo, B. R., McTigue, E. M., & Uppstad, P. H. (2024). Teachers' Feedback on Oral Reading: A Critical Review of its Effects and the use of Theory in Research. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09957-z
title: Eleven-component taxonomy of teacher feedback during oral reading, organized into four main feedback types
description: The review codes the feedback practices in 24 K–5 oral-reading studies into a taxonomy of feedback content. It reports: "We identified 11 components of feedback content in the various feedback practices reviewed. These components fall into four main types of feedback: performance feedback, supporting elements, explicit corrective feedback, and implicit feedback encouraging independent thinking about their reading". The components range from reading-rate and error information through goals and rewards to word-reading, comprehension, and prosody instruction and questions as feedback.
requirements: Feedback practices in primary studies must be codable into the 11 content components, with combined practices treated as single practices with measured effects
constraints: Visual elements appeared in several studies but their effects were not uniquely measured and were not further analyzed
target_learners: K–5 students (age 5–11) in school-based reading instruction
target_learning_goals: Reading fluency
Reading comprehension
Reading motivation
examples: The review's bubble chart (Table 1) maps the frequency of studies across the 11 feedback types and their examined effects on fluency, comprehension, and motivation
key_sources: Grønli, K. M., Walgermo, B. R., McTigue, E. M., & Uppstad, P. H. (2024). Teachers' Feedback on Oral Reading: A Critical Review of its Effects and the use of Theory in Research. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09957-z

article_title: Moving Beyond Fulfillment: Wisdom Years Stories of Passion, Perseverance, and Productivity
citation: Kiewra, K.A., Walsh, J. & Labenz, C. (2023). Moving Beyond Fulfillment: Wisdom Years Stories of Passion, Perseverance, and Productivity. Educ Psychol Rev 35, 20. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09747-z
title: Retire to something rather than simply retiring
description: The article's first conclusion advises readers: "Do not retire, but if you do, retire to something." The principle holds that continued productivity in the wisdom years comes from avoiding an aimless retirement and instead redirecting one's energies toward a purposeful pursuit, as illustrated by the interviewed participants who shun retirement and remain productive.
requirements: A purposeful pursuit or goal to retire toward, rather than retirement as an end in itself.
constraints: Grounded in the experiences of seven exceptionally productive interviewees; the article does not test this advice experimentally.
target_learning_goals: maintaining purpose and productivity after career transitions
examples: The article's conclusion lists "Do not retire, but if you do, retire to something" as its first advice-laden conclusion.
key_sources: Kiewra, K.A., Walsh, J. & Labenz, C. (2023). Moving Beyond Fulfillment: Wisdom Years Stories of Passion, Perseverance, and Productivity. Educ Psychol Rev 35, 20. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09747-z

article_title: Moving Beyond Fulfillment: Wisdom Years Stories of Passion, Perseverance, and Productivity
citation: Kiewra, K.A., Walsh, J. & Labenz, C. (2023). Moving Beyond Fulfillment: Wisdom Years Stories of Passion, Perseverance, and Productivity. Educ Psychol Rev 35, 20. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09747-z
title: Be a life-long learner to remain productive in the wisdom years
description: Among the article's seven conclusions is the advice to "be a life-long learner." The principle holds that sustained learning across the lifespan supports the passion, perseverance, and productivity the interviewed participants displayed in their wisdom years, and it connects the article to its stated keywords of lifelong learning and talent development.
requirements: Continued engagement in learning activities throughout adulthood.
constraints: The advice is drawn from qualitative interviews with seven highly productive individuals and is not experimentally validated.
target_learners: older adults in their wisdom years
target_learning_goals: lifelong learning
sustained personal development and productivity
examples: The article lists "be a life-long learner" as conclusion (f) among its seven advice-laden conclusions.
