article_title: Inhibitory Control and Mathematical Ability in Elementary School Children: A Preregistered Meta-Analysis
citation: Zhu, X., Tang, Y., Lu, J., Song, M., Yang, C., & Zhao, X. (2025). Inhibitory Control and Mathematical Ability in Elementary School Children: A Preregistered Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review, 37(1), 1. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09976-w
title: Constrained and unconstrained model of mathematical skills
description: The constrained and unconstrained model categorizes mathematical skills by whether they can be mastered and automated. The article states that "constrained skills involve a relatively small and finite pool of knowledge (e.g., counting, single-digit arithmetic), which can be fully automated through learning or experience", whereas "unconstrained skills involve an infinite pool of knowledge (e.g., word problem-solving), which may be slow or even impossible to automate". It integrates intrinsic cognitive load theory and dual-processing theory, predicting that the inhibitory control–mathematical ability relationship is weaker for constrained skills and stable for unconstrained skills. The meta-analysis uses it to motivate the mathematical-domain moderator and to interpret the weaker elementary-school correlation.
requirements: Requires distinguishing mathematical skills that can be automated from those that cannot
constraints: The meta-analysis found no significant moderation by mathematical ability domain, which runs against the model's prediction of domain-dependent correlations
target_learning_goals: mathematical ability
inhibitory control development
examples: The meta-analysis coded six domains of mathematical ability, including numerical ability, arithmetical ability, logical reasoning ability, geometric ability, standardized mathematics tests scores, and school examinations scores, to test the model's predictions
key_sources: Zhu, X., Tang, Y., Lu, J., Song, M., Yang, C., & Zhao, X. (2025). Inhibitory Control and Mathematical Ability in Elementary School Children: A Preregistered Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review, 37(1), 1. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09976-w

article_title: Factors Associated with Teacher Wellbeing: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Sijing Zhou, Gavin R. Slemp & Dianne A. Vella-Brodrick. (2024). Factors Associated with Teacher Wellbeing: A Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09886-x
title: Job Demands-Resources theory as a framework for classifying antecedents, consequences, and correlates of teacher wellbeing
description: The article uses JD-R theory to position factors in the nomological network of teacher wellbeing. The theory "proposes that job-related phenomena can be modelled using two broad categories: job demands and job resources," with demands activating a health impairment process and resources a motivational process, plus personal resources as aspects of the self. The authors build a conceptual model (Fig. 1) grouping antecedents into individual differences and personal characteristics, interpersonal characteristics, and workplace characteristics, with correlates and consequences classified separately.
requirements: Requires distinguishing wellbeing (hedonic, eudaimonic, general, occupational) from its exogenous antecedents and endogenous consequences, excluding models that conflate them
constraints: The article notes moderator results may highlight boundary conditions of JD-R theory, and moderator analyses were exploratory
target_learning_goals: supporting teacher wellbeing
reducing turnover intentions
informing school leadership and policy practice
examples: The meta-analysis coded 173 studies' correlates into JD-R-based antecedent, consequence, and correlate categories and meta-analyzed each association corrected for sampling and measurement error
key_sources: Sijing Zhou, Gavin R. Slemp & Dianne A. Vella-Brodrick. (2024). Factors Associated with Teacher Wellbeing: A Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09886-x

article_title: Dosage Response in Intensive Mathematics Interventions for Early Elementary Students With or At-Risk for Mathematics Learning Disability
citation: Anna H. Miller, Daniel R. Espinas, Daniel McNeish, & Marcia A. Barnes. (2025). Dosage Response in Intensive Mathematics Interventions for Early Elementary Students With or At-Risk for Mathematics Learning Disability. Educational Psychology Review, 37, 91. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10070-y
title: Dose–response framework with dosage defined as cumulative intensity (session duration × frequency × treatment length)
description: The article applies the dose–response framework, borrowed from medicine and pharmacology, to academic intervention: the dose–response curve represents the relation between an intervention's intensity and its effects. Dosage is operationalized following Warren et al. (2007) as "the product of an intervention's session duration (e.g., 30 min), frequency (e.g., three times per week), and length of treatment (e.g., 15 weeks)", quantified as total instructional hours per student. The framework distinguishes a linear dose–response relation, where "the effect of the treatment increases in direct proportion to the amount of treatment delivered", from a nonlinear one that peaks and then plateaus or diminishes. The authors use it to test whether K-3 mathematics interventions show diminishing returns as reading interventions do.
requirements: Studies must adequately report intervention frequency, duration, and length so dosage can be calculated as total hours per student
constraints: Analyses excluded computerized or partially computerized interventions and adaptive/SMART designs, so the framework's application here is limited to human-delivered, fixed-dosage interventions compared to non-active controls
target_learners: Kindergarten through third grade students with or at risk for mathematics learning disability
target_learning_goals: Foundational mathematics skills including number knowledge, operations, and word-problem solving
examples: The authors meta-analyzed 164 effect sizes from 24 studies with dosages ranging from 3.12 to 42.0 hours (Mdn = 20 h) using this framework
key_sources: Anna H. Miller, Daniel R. Espinas, Daniel McNeish, & Marcia A. Barnes. (2025). Dosage Response in Intensive Mathematics Interventions for Early Elementary Students With or At-Risk for Mathematics Learning Disability. Educational Psychology Review, 37, 91. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10070-y

article_title: The Relation Between Teacher-Student Eye Contact and Teachers’ Interpersonal Behavior During Group Work: a Multiple-Person Gaze-Tracking Case Study in Secondary Mathematics Education
citation: Haataja, E., Salonen, V., Laine, A., Toivanen, M., & Hannula, M. S. (2021). The Relation Between Teacher-Student Eye Contact and Teachers' Interpersonal Behavior During Group Work: a Multiple-Person Gaze-Tracking Case Study in Secondary Mathematics Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09538-w
title: Interpersonal theory's agency-communion cycle extended to micro-level reciprocal teacher-student gaze interaction
description: The article applies interpersonal theory, in which "human interaction is conceptualized as a continuous cycle of initiatives and responses between people", conceptualized "with two dimensions: agency and communion". It extends this framework from whole-class interaction to reciprocal communication between the teacher and individual students, arguing that interpersonal adaptation in the classroom is visible at the level of gaze behavior and that both teachers and students can use gaze to take initiative. The authors conclude that such individualization of micro-level interactions should be included in further developments of interpersonal theory.
requirements: Momentary, continuous coding of teacher interpersonal behavior (e.g., the computer-joystick method) synchronized with gaze data is needed to link micro-level gaze to communion and agency.
constraints: The article states its results are not necessarily generalizable to other contexts, and the effect sizes of the statistical results were relatively low throughout the research.
target_learners: Secondary school students (15-16-year-old ninth-grade mathematics students)
target_learning_goals: Teacher-student interaction and classroom communication during collaborative mathematical problem solving
examples: The study coded three teachers' interpersonal behavior continuously with the computer-joystick method and synchronized it with ELAN-coded gaze dwells during 16-18-minute collaborative problem-solving phases.
key_sources: Haataja, E., Salonen, V., Laine, A., Toivanen, M., & Hannula, M. S. (2021). The Relation Between Teacher-Student Eye Contact and Teachers' Interpersonal Behavior During Group Work: a Multiple-Person Gaze-Tracking Case Study in Secondary Mathematics Education. article_title: The Relation Between Teacher-Student Eye Contact and Teachers’ Interpersonal Behavior During Group Work: a Multiple-Person Gaze-Tracking Case Study in Secondary Mathematics Education
citation: Haataja, E., Salonen, V., Laine, A., Toivanen, M., & Hannula, M. S. (2021). The Relation Between Teacher-Student Eye Contact and Teachers' Interpersonal Behavior During Group Work: a Multiple-Person Gaze-Tracking Case Study in Secondary Mathematics Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09538-w
title: Multiple-person mobile gaze-tracking combined with continuous interpersonal coding for studying classroom eye contact
description: The article introduces a methodological approach described as "A novel approach in educational science, multiple-person mobile gaze-tracking", which "allows us to gather data on these momentary processes of nonverbal interaction". Teachers and target students wore mobile gaze-tracking glasses (accuracy 1.5 degrees of visual angle) while stationary cameras recorded the classroom; gaze dwells were coded in ELAN by target and duration, and teachers' interpersonal behavior was continuously coded with Sadler's computer-joystick method. The two codings were synchronized in half-second intervals to relate gaze types and durations to momentary communion and agency.
requirements: Gaze and joystick codings must be synchronized (here by dividing gazes into half-second intervals), and coding validity must be confirmed, e.g., by double coding with inter-rater reliability checks.
constraints: Despite high device accuracy, the authors cannot be sure that all face-directed gazes were targeted at the eyes of the other person; they interpreted mutual gazing at faces as essentially eye contact.
target_learners: Secondary school students in authentic classroom lessons
target_learning_goals: Studying momentary teacher-student nonverbal interaction and eye contact in natural classroom settings
examples: In the study, three teachers and 47 students participated; target students wore the glasses in groups of three to four during collaborative problem-solving phases of 16-18 minutes.

The Relation Between Teacher-Student Eye Contact and Teachers' Interpersonal Behavior During Group Work: a Multiple-Person Gaze-Tracking Case Study in Secondary Mathematics Education. article_title: Learning Stories Through Gesture: Gesture’s Effects on Child and Adult Narrative Comprehension
citation: Dargue, N; Sweller, N. (2020). Learning Stories Through Gesture: Gesture's Effects on Child and Adult Narrative Comprehension. Educational Psychology Review, 32 (1). https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09505-0
title: Semantic relatedness account: typical gestures benefit narrative comprehension because they are more semantically related to accompanying speech
description: The article proposes an explanatory account in which gesture type matters for narrative comprehension because of the semantic relationship between gesture and speech. As the authors put it, "It may be that typical gestures benefit narrative comprehension more than atypical gestures due to the typical gestures being more semantically related to accompanying speech." The account is supported by the second study's finding that typical gestures were rated as more semantically related to speech than atypical gestures. It explains why gesture observation benefits learning by providing an external support to speech.
requirements: Gestures used must be semantically related to the accompanying speech for the benefit to arise
constraints: The article frames this as a proposed explanation ("It may be that..."), supported by a rating study rather than a direct test of the mechanism
target_learners: Children and adults learning from narrated stories
target_learning_goals: Narrative comprehension
examples: The second study had participants rate how semantically related typical and atypical gestures were to the accompanying speech.
key_sources: Dargue, N; Sweller, N. (2020). Learning Stories Through Gesture: Gesture's Effects on Child and Adult Narrative Comprehension. Educational Psychology Review, 32 (1). https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09505-0

article_title: Learning Stories Through Gesture: Gesture’s Effects on Child and Adult Narrative Comprehension
citation: Dargue, N; Sweller, N. (2020). Learning Stories Through Gesture: Gesture's Effects on Child and Adult Narrative Comprehension. Educational Psychology Review, 32 (1). https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09505-0
title: Educators should use typical, frequently produced iconic gestures that are adequately semantically related to speech to enhance student understanding
description: This principle translates the article's findings into educator practice: when narrating stories or explaining content, speakers should produce typical, frequently produced iconic gestures that are adequately semantically related to their speech. The article argues that "educators' use of typical, frequently produced iconic gestures that are adequately semantically related to speech may enhance student understanding." The recommendation follows from the finding that typical, not atypical, gestures benefited narrative comprehension across child and adult learners.
requirements: Gestures must be typical and frequently produced
Gestures must be adequately semantically related to the accompanying speech
constraints: The article hedges the benefit with "may enhance student understanding"
target_learners: Children and adults in educational settings
target_learning_goals: Narrative comprehension and understanding of spoken content
examples: Across two studies, observing typical gestures during narrated stories significantly benefited narrative comprehension compared with atypical or no gestures.

article_title: Watch Your Step Children! Learning Two-Digit Numbers Through Mirror-Based Observation of Self-Initiated Body Movements
citation: Margina Ruiter & Sofie Loyens & Fred Paas. (2015). Watch Your Step Children! Learning Two-Digit Numbers Through Mirror-Based Observation of Self-Initiated Body Movements. Educ Psychol Rev (2015) 27:457–474. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-015-9324-4
title: Integrate task-related full-body movements into conventional math number building exercises because they improve performance at low cost
description: The principle is to embed meaningful, task-related full-body movements into standard math exercises: children build two-digit numbers by making steps of different sizes along a floor ruler, with "tens were represented by large steps, fives by mediate, and ones by very small steps", while verbalizing the count. The article argues this improves performance over the predominant sit-and-write method and fits the trend toward more physical activity in primary schools.
requirements: A floor ruler with marks indicating ones, fives, and tens, and exercises in which step size is proportionate to the number units being built
constraints: The article cautions that one must be careful drawing educational-practice conclusions from a single study; the specific active ingredient of the movements could not be determined from the design
target_learners: first-grade elementary school children learning two-digit numbers
target_learning_goals: numerical concept understanding: positioning of numbers on a number line, number magnitude, and number structure
examples: In the experiment, children in movement conditions construed numbers like 36 by saying 10, 20, 30, 35, 36 while making three big steps, one medium, and one small step on a 3.2 m ruler across the gym floor
key_sources: Margina Ruiter & Sofie Loyens & Fred Paas. (2015). Watch Your Step Children! Learning Two-Digit Numbers Through Mirror-Based Observation of Self-Initiated Body Movements. Educ Psychol Rev (2015) 27:457–474. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-015-9324-4

article_title: Watch Your Step Children! Learning Two-Digit Numbers Through Mirror-Based Observation of Self-Initiated Body Movements
citation: Margina Ruiter & Sofie Loyens & Fred Paas. (2015). Watch Your Step Children! Learning Two-Digit Numbers Through Mirror-Based Observation of Self-Initiated Body Movements. Educ Psychol Rev (2015) 27:457–474. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-015-9324-4
title: Embodied cognition account of using biologically primary body movements to support biologically secondary learning
description: The article frames its intervention with embodied cognition theories, which propose that "cognitive processes are grounded in perception and bodily action", in contrast to cognitivist approaches treating mind and body as separate. Building on Paas and Sweller's evolutionary account and cognitive load theory, it distinguishes biologically primary knowledge (e.g., learning to move, acquired effortlessly without instruction) from biologically secondary knowledge (e.g., math and reading, requiring explicit instruction and conscious effort), and argues "it may be advantageous to use primary information, such as body movements, to assist in the acquisition of secondary information".
requirements: Task-related movements that are meaningfully connected to the content of the secondary knowledge being learned
constraints: The account is the article's framing; the study's design could not determine which specific element of the movements produced the learning benefit
target_learning_goals: acquisition of biologically secondary knowledge such as mathematics, supported by primary bodily actions
examples: The study operationalized the account by having first-graders build two-digit numbers with full-body steps whose sizes corresponded to tens, fives, and ones on a floor ruler
key_sources: Margina Ruiter & Sofie Loyens & Fred Paas. (2015). Watch Your Step Children! Learning Two-Digit Numbers Through Mirror-Based Observation of Self-Initiated Body Movements. Educ Psychol Rev (2015) 27:457–474. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-015-9324-4

article_title: Striking the Balance: How Variability Shapes Retrieval Practice and Worked Examples for Transfer Learning
citation: Meng Cao & Paulo F. Carvalho. (2026). Striking the Balance: How Variability Shapes Retrieval Practice and Worked Examples for Transfer Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10169-w
title: Exemplar-based account of how variability shapes retrieval practice for transfer
description: The article proposes that retrieval practice is fundamentally memory-based, and that item variability determines the scope and organization of what is remembered. Drawing on exemplar-based models of category learning, it argues that "Repeated retrieval can be viewed as strengthening memory for specific exemplars, supporting accurate recall but offering limited transfer," whereas varied retrieval strengthens memory for multiple related exemplars whose overlapping representations support generalization. This account extends existing memory-strengthening theories of retrieval practice, which the article says were developed from repeated-item studies and do not explain how variability shapes transfer.
requirements: Learners must engage in retrieval attempts across multiple related exemplars for overlapping representations to form
constraints: The account is offered as the authors' interpretation of their two experiments with artificial rule-learning tasks, not as a directly tested model
target_learners: adult learners in rule- and skill-learning contexts
target_learning_goals: generalization of learned rules to novel problems
examples: In Experiment 2, varied retrieval practice produced final-test performance comparable to varied worked examples, which the authors explain via overlapping exemplar representations
key_sources: Meng Cao & Paulo F. Carvalho. (2026). Striking the Balance: How Variability Shapes Retrieval Practice and Worked Examples for Transfer Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10169-w

article_title: Striking the Balance: How Variability Shapes Retrieval Practice and Worked Examples for Transfer Learning
citation: Meng Cao & Paulo F. Carvalho. (2026). Striking the Balance: How Variability Shapes Retrieval Practice and Worked Examples for Transfer Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10169-w
title: Align learning strategy choice with the instructional goal: induction versus memory consolidation
description: The article recommends that instructional decisions be guided by whether students are discovering a rule or strengthening one they already understand. For rule induction, teachers can "present varied worked examples and ask students to identify the underlying pattern to promote inductive learning through practice," or use varied problem solving with feedback. Once students can articulate and apply the rule, the goal shifts to consolidation, where retrieval practice such as short quizzes and cumulative review becomes especially effective.
requirements: The instructional goal (rule induction vs. consolidation) must be identifiable at a given moment
Retrieval practice in the study was paired with corrective feedback, which the authors say likely supported rule induction
constraints: Under consolidation conditions, the article warns that introducing additional variability may impose unnecessary cognitive demands without benefit
Findings come from artificial language and mathematics rule-learning tasks with adults; ecological validity to authentic classrooms is untested
target_learners: school and adult learners acquiring rules or skills, e.g., in mathematics
target_learning_goals: rule induction and schema formation
retention and stable application of learned rules
examples: The article's mathematics example: students examine expressions such as 2(x + 3) = 2x + 6, 4(x + 5) = 4x + 20, and 3(x + 1) = 3x + 3 to induce the distributive property, then later retrieve and apply the rule via structurally similar problems
key_sources: Meng Cao & Paulo F. Carvalho. (2026). Striking the Balance: How Variability Shapes Retrieval Practice and Worked Examples for Transfer Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10169-w

article_title: Culture and school belonging: Towards a global research agenda
citation: Ronnel B. King, Faming Wang. (2026). Culture and school belonging: Towards a global research agenda. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10213-9
title: Three forms of cultural variation in school belonging: level-oriented, structure-oriented, and meaning-oriented differences
description: The commentary organizes how culture can shape school belonging into three forms, drawing on van de Vijver and Leung's distinction between level-oriented and structure-oriented differences and adding meaning-oriented differences. Culture "could impact the mean levels of school belonging in a given population (i.e., level-oriented differences)", could "modify the relationship between school belonging and other constructs in the nomological network", and could shape the very meaning of belonging across contexts. The commentary uses this framework to structure its PISA 2018 reanalyses and its argument for emic approaches.
requirements: Cross-cultural studies must specify which form of cultural variation they are testing (means, associations, or meanings)
constraints: Level comparisons of means can be open to numerous interpretations, per the authors
target_learners: K-12 and higher education students across cultural contexts
target_learning_goals: Understanding how cultural context shapes students' sense of school belonging and its links to motivation and achievement
examples: The commentary's PISA 2018 reanalyses illustrate level-oriented differences (Table 3 rankings) and structure-oriented differences (Figure 2 ecological correlations)
key_sources: Ronnel B. King, Faming Wang. (2026). Culture and school belonging: Towards a global research agenda. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10213-9

article_title: Culture and school belonging: Towards a global research agenda
citation: Ronnel B. King, Faming Wang. (2026). Culture and school belonging: Towards a global research agenda. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10213-9
title: Multilevel cultural framework for school belonging: individual, classroom, school/institutional, national, and global culture
description: Transposing Erez and Gati's (2004) hierarchical model of culture into educational psychology, the commentary proposes that cultural influence on belonging operates at nested levels: "individual, classroom, school/institutional, national, and global culture". Each level offers a distinct unit of analysis, from students' values and self-construals, through peer mindset cultures and school climates, to national value orientations and global narratives such as meritocracy and neoliberalism. The model also emphasizes top-down and bottom-up dynamic processes across levels.
requirements: Researchers must specify which level of culture they are theorizing, how they are measuring it, and how processes across levels interact over time
constraints: The framework was originally developed for organizational contexts and is transposed by the authors into educational psychology
target_learners: Students at individual, classroom, school, national, and global levels of analysis
target_learning_goals: Multilevel theorizing of how culture shapes school belonging
examples: The commentary maps topical-collection constructs onto levels: Browman's goal fit (individual), Seo et al.'s peer mindset culture (classroom), Byrd et al.'s racial climate (school), Hofstede-style value comparisons (national), and global brilliance/meritocracy narratives
key_sources: Ronnel B. King, Faming Wang. (2026). Culture and school belonging: Towards a global research agenda. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10213-9

article_title: Culture and school belonging: Towards a global research agenda
citation: Ronnel B. King, Faming Wang. (2026). Culture and school belonging: Towards a global research agenda. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10213-9
title: Etic–emic distinction applied to school belonging: Western-derived definitions may not capture culture-specific meanings
description: The commentary argues that much belonging research adopts "an etic approach, which involves testing concepts developed in Western psychology across different cultural groups", applying Goodenow and Grady's Western-derived definition globally through translated instruments that assume conceptual equivalence. Emic approaches, by contrast, ask students how they understand belonging, exclusion, and acceptance in their own contexts. The commentary cites Li's (2003) prototype analysis—Americans view learning primarily as cognitive while Chinese students associate it with social and moral development—as a model of what etic instruments miss.
requirements: In-depth qualitative studies across diverse cultural contexts to uncover both etic commonalities and emic variations
constraints: The commentary presents this as an argument for future research; no new emic belonging data are collected here
target_learners: Students in non-WEIRD and marginalized cultural contexts
target_learning_goals: Culturally valid conceptualization and measurement of school belonging
examples: Saravi et al. (2020) developed an emic understanding of belonging among disadvantaged Mexican students, showing stigmatization and institutional practices shape belonging in ways WEIRD-dominated research seldom captures
key_sources: Ronnel B. King, Faming Wang. (2026). Culture and school belonging: Towards a global research agenda. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10213-9

article_title: Disentangling the Long-Term Compositional Effects of School-Average Achievement and SES: a Substantive-Methodological Synergy
citation: Marsh, H. W., Pekrun, R., Dicke, T., Guo, J., Parker, P. D., & Basarkod, G. (2023). Disentangling the Long-Term Compositional Effects of School-Average Achievement and SES: a Substantive-Methodological Synergy. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09726-4
title: The BFLPE model: social comparison processes explain adverse effects of school-average achievement on academic self-concept
description: The BFLPE model hypothesizes that students compare their own achievements with those of classmates and use this social comparison as a basis for forming academic self-concept. The article states "Individual achievement positively predicts ASC (the better I perform, the higher my ASC). In contrast, school-average achievement negatively predicts ASC (the brighter my classmates, the lower my ASC)." The model integrates relative deprivation theory, psychophysical judgment, social judgment, and social comparison theory, and holds that BFLPE size depends substantially on the extent of ability stratification in schools.
requirements: Students must be able to perceive the relative achievement levels of their classmates for social comparison to operate
constraints: If all schools had the same school-average achievement, the BFLPE would disappear
target_learning_goals: academic self-concept
examples: The article applies the model as the theoretical basis for predicting negative compositional effects of school-average achievement in the ELS:2002 analysis (Hypothesis 1).
key_sources: Marsh, H. W., Pekrun, R., Dicke, T., Guo, J., Parker, P. D., & Basarkod, G. (2023). Disentangling the Long-Term Compositional Effects of School-Average Achievement and SES: a Substantive-Methodological Synergy. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09726-4

article_title: Stimming as Thinking: a Critical Reevaluation of Self-Stimulatory Behavior as an Epistemic Resource for Inclusive Education
citation: Sofia Tancredi, Dor Abrahamson. (2024). Stimming as Thinking: a Critical Reevaluation of Self-Stimulatory Behavior as an Epistemic Resource for Inclusive Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09904-y
title: A multi-E (post-cognitivist) model of stimming as integral to cognitive-affective dynamics
description: The article proposes a model of stimming grounded in 4E (and beyond) embodied cognition, treating stimming as an intrinsic part of the cognitive system rather than peripheral noise. It advances five precepts: stimming as embodied (impacting thought and cognitive load), enactive (a substrate for complex actions and concepts), embedded and emotional (reflecting and regulating cognitive-affective system dynamics), ecological (responding to environmental properties), and extended (functioning as socially communicative). The authors state that "post-cognitivist theory offers an alternative conceptualization of stimming as part of the cognitive system's dynamic interactions, through the body, with the physical and social environment." The model reinterprets constructs from psychiatry, psychology, HCI, occupational therapy, and communication studies under the unifying term stimming.
requirements: Recognizes neurodivergent testimony of sensory experiences and practices, and models self-regulative, communicative, and cognitive functions of stimming
constraints: The authors acknowledge contention among post-cognitivist theorists, who endorse the Es to different extents and disagree on topics such as mental representations
target_learners: the full spectrum of the general population
target_learning_goals: curricular content learning through sensorimotor engagement
self-regulation supporting attention and affect during learning
examples: The article reinterprets fidgeting, stereotypies, sensation seeking, embodied self-regulation, adapters, and stimming semiosis as overlapping constructs along axes of focal population, scope (overt vs. covert), and consciousness
key_sources: Sofia Tancredi, Dor Abrahamson. (2024). Stimming as Thinking: a Critical Reevaluation of Self-Stimulatory Behavior as an Epistemic Resource for Inclusive Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09904-y

article_title: Stimming as Thinking: a Critical Reevaluation of Self-Stimulatory Behavior as an Epistemic Resource for Inclusive Education
citation: Sofia Tancredi, Dor Abrahamson. (2024). Stimming as Thinking: a Critical Reevaluation of Self-Stimulatory Behavior as an Epistemic Resource for Inclusive Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09904-y
title: SpEED: special education embodied design framework for inclusive embodied instruction
description: SpEED is a design-based research framework for inclusive design grounded in embodied cognition, introduced in prior work by the first author and applied here to analyze how instructional designs privilege sensory modalities. The article explains that "SpEED differentiates the sensory and motor systems engaged, such as vision (modality), materials, such as printed textbooks (media), and system of meaning making, such as diagrams and language (semiotic mode) of instructional designs and highlights their interrelation." SpEED names modalism as the privileging of a dominant modality (e.g., vision in geometry teaching) that makes content less accessible to learners with different sensory access, and calls for instruction rooted in the modalities through which a learner explores the world. Its principles hold that learning happens through sensorimotor engagement, begins from learners' existing embodied resources, and must flexibly adapt to sensorimotor diversity.
requirements: Instruction must flexibly adapt to learners' sensorimotor diversities and build from learners' existing embodied resources
constraints: The framework diagnoses exclusionary design (e.g., oculocentric geometry instruction) rather than inherent learner pathology
target_learning_goals: disciplinary concepts such as geometry accessible through non-dominant modalities
equitable access to embodied sense-making
examples: The article uses SpEED parameters to analyze the Balance Board Math design, which leverages the vestibular modality commonly engaged in stimming but uncommonly engaged in learning contexts
key_sources: Sofia Tancredi, Dor Abrahamson. (2024). Stimming as Thinking: a Critical Reevaluation of Self-Stimulatory Behavior as an Epistemic Resource for Inclusive Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09904-y

article_title: Stimming as Thinking: a Critical Reevaluation of Self-Stimulatory Behavior as an Epistemic Resource for Inclusive Education
citation: Sofia Tancredi, Dor Abrahamson. (2024). Stimming as Thinking: a Critical Reevaluation of Self-Stimulatory Behavior as an Epistemic Resource for Inclusive Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09904-y
title: Balance Board Math (BBM): sensor-equipped balance board environment eliciting rocking as mathematical thinking
description: Balance Board Math is a design-based research project and pedagogical tool in which children rock on large wooden sensor-equipped balance boards to explore mathematical concepts such as the frequency and amplitude of sinusoidal functions. Inclinometer sensors capture rocking movements and generate real-time graphs projected on a screen, with color changes and tones signaling period length and extrema. The article states the design conjecture directly: "The BBM project investigates the design conjecture that movement for learning and movement for self-regulation can be integrated to strengthen instructional efficacy." BBM is presented as a proof-of-concept of inclusively harnessing stims as content-oriented epistemic actions, following SpEED principles.
requirements: Novel media (a sensor-equipped balance board and interface) that facilitate and capture rocking movements and project real-time graphs
constraints: The article presents BBM as a proof-of-concept illustrative context within an ongoing design-based research project, not as a validated intervention
target_learners: including neurodivergent learners whose stimming includes rocking
target_learning_goals: understanding mathematical functions, specifically frequency and amplitude of sinusoidal graphs
examples: In the frequency exploration activity, the screen background changes color depending on rocking period length, and learners work through rounds of graphing and reflection to control the period of their rocking to generate a consistent color

article_title: Twelve- and Fourteen-Year-Old School Children Differentially Benefit from Sensorimotor- and Multisensory-Enriched Vocabulary Training
citation: Brian Mathias, Christian Andrä, Anika Schwager, Manuela Macedonia, Katharina von Kriegstein. (2022). Twelve- and Fourteen-Year-Old School Children Differentially Benefit from Sensorimotor- and Multisensory-Enriched Vocabulary Training. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09648-z
title: Multisensory learning theory: enrichment benefits are driven by modality-specific sensory and motor representations
description: The article describes multisensory learning theory as the notion that "brain regions that support the processing of enrichment also drive enrichment-based learning benefits". At a neural level, the same sensory and motor regions that process visuo-motor enrichment information during learning are causally relevant for subsequent auditory L2 recognition. This implies benefits arise from specific motor and sensory representations formed under the learning conditions, rather than from general mechanisms such as enhanced attention or arousal. The theory sits alongside embodied, dual coding, mental imagery, and predictive coding accounts, which share the premise that novel information can be mentally represented in terms of its perceptual and motor features.
requirements: Learning must present congruent information in the enrichment modality alongside the primary auditory stimulus
constraints: Benefits may be partially limited by the high dependence of semantics on linguistic context
target_learners: foreign language learners across age groups
target_learning_goals: L2 vocabulary learning and retention
key_sources: Brian Mathias, Christian Andrä, Anika Schwager, Manuela Macedonia, Katharina von Kriegstein. (2022). Twelve- and Fourteen-Year-Old School Children Differentially Benefit from Sensorimotor- and Multisensory-Enriched Vocabulary Training. article_title: Twelve- and Fourteen-Year-Old School Children Differentially Benefit from Sensorimotor- and Multisensory-Enriched Vocabulary Training
citation: Brian Mathias, Christian Andrä, Anika Schwager, Manuela Macedonia, Katharina von Kriegstein. (2022). Twelve- and Fourteen-Year-Old School Children Differentially Benefit from Sensorimotor- and Multisensory-Enriched Vocabulary Training. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09648-z
title: Integrate gestures rather than pictures into L2 vocabulary pedagogy starting at 14 years of age
description: Because gesture-enriched learning was more beneficial than picture-enriched learning for 14-year-olds but not for 12-year-olds, the authors conclude these "findings provide evidence for opting to integrate gestures rather than pictures into L2 pedagogy starting at 14 years of age". Both enrichment forms still beat auditory-only learning at every age tested, so pictures remain valuable for younger learners. The recommendation follows from a classroom intervention in which children performed gestures with their teacher while reciting translations.
requirements: Training integrated within regular course meetings with teacher-led recitation and gesture performance
Words not yet encountered in lessons and excluded from the curriculum during the study period
constraints: For 12-year-olds, gesture and picture enrichment were equivalently effective, so the gesture preference applies from age 14 onward rather than universally
Gestures and other sensorimotor-based interventions may be more challenging for educators to integrate into pedagogy than multisensory-based interventions
target_learners: secondary school foreign language learners aged 12 and 14
target_learning_goals: foreign language vocabulary learning and long-term retention
examples: Children learned Spanish words over three in-class training days, performing gestures with their teacher in the gesture condition and viewing line drawings in the picture condition, with tests at 3 days, 2 months, and 6 months

article_title: The Interplay of Cognitive Load, Learners’ Resources and Self-regulation
citation: Seufert, T., Hamm, V., Vogt, A., & Riemer, V. (2024). The Interplay of Cognitive Load, Learners' Resources and Self-Regulation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09890-1
title: Seufert's model of self-regulation as a function of resources and perceived cognitive load
description: The model describes how task difficulty drives two counteracting forces that determine the intensity of self-regulatory activities: cognitive load, which increases with difficulty, and learner resources, which decrease with difficulty. It predicts an inverted U-shaped curve, since "Optimal self-regulation occurs with tasks of moderate difficulty, where resources and load are balanced". The present study operationalized the model's parameters across four exams and tested its mediation assumptions empirically.
requirements: Empirical support for its assumptions about task difficulty, load, and resources as parameters of self-regulatory activity
constraints: The article notes resource-based strategies are not specifically focused in the model and were excluded from analysis
target_learners: secondary school students preparing for exams
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning strategy use during exam preparation
examples: The study surveyed 67 grade-11 students after each of four exams (English, Mathematics, German, profile subject) on difficulty, load, resources, and strategy use
key_sources: Seufert, T., Hamm, V., Vogt, A., & Riemer, V. (2024). The Interplay of Cognitive Load, Learners' Resources and Self-Regulation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09890-1

article_title: The Interplay of Cognitive Load, Learners’ Resources and Self-regulation
citation: Seufert, T., Hamm, V., Vogt, A., & Riemer, V. (2024). The Interplay of Cognitive Load, Learners' Resources and Self-Regulation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09890-1
title: Balance task difficulty with learner resources and cognitive load to promote self-regulation
description: If the model is valid, it offers teachers and learners a framework for supporting self-regulation by "balancing task affordances with learner resources and cognitive load, to promote self-regulation". Tasks of moderate difficulty keep load manageable while still catalyzing self-regulatory activity, whereas very easy tasks do not activate regulation and very difficult tasks exhaust resources. Designers should therefore match task demands to learners' available resources.
requirements: Assessment of learners' resources (e.g., prior knowledge, interest, self-efficacy) and perceived task difficulty so the two can be matched
constraints: The study's exam difficulty ranged only from rather easy to moderately difficult, so the decline of self-regulation at high difficulty could not be fully explored; the authors call for a broader range of task difficulty in future investigations
target_learning_goals: promoting use of cognitive and metacognitive learning strategies
examples: The four exams were selected via expert assessment to span a range of perceived difficulty, and students rated each exam's difficulty before and after taking it
key_sources: Seufert, T., Hamm, V., Vogt, A., & Riemer, V. (2024). The Interplay of Cognitive Load, Learners' Resources and Self-Regulation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09890-1

article_title: On acquiring expertise in medicine
citation: Schmidt, H.G., Boshuizen, H.P.A. (1993). On acquiring expertise in medicine. Educational Psychology Review 5. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01323044
title: Expertise development in medicine proceeds through consecutive phases with functionally different knowledge structures
description: The article introduces a theory describing "expertise development as the progression through a series of consecutive phases, each of which is characterized by functionally different knowledge structures underlying performance." The phases move from accumulation of causal disease knowledge, to narrative illness scripts, to use of episodic patient memories in diagnosis. The article states it presents "the empirical evidence available" for this theory.
requirements: Experience with real cases is needed for the transition from causal knowledge to illness scripts
target_learning_goals: development of diagnostic expertise in medicine
key_sources: Schmidt, H.G., Boshuizen, H.P.A. (1993). On acquiring expertise in medicine. Educational Psychology Review 5. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01323044

article_title: Modeling Interactions Between Multivariate Learner Characteristics and Interventions: a Person-Centered Approach
citation: Tetzlaff, L., Edelsbrunner, P., Schmitterer, A., Hartmann, U., & Brod, G. (2023). Modeling Interactions Between Multivariate Learner Characteristics and Interventions: a Person-Centered Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09830-5
title: Two-step person-centered approach: latent profile analysis of learner characteristics followed by BCH-based modeling of profile-by-intervention interactions
description: The article proposes moving "the focus of analysis from the interactions of single variables to entire persons and their characteristic constellation of learning prerequisites". In step one, learners are grouped by latent profile analysis, chosen because it is "a model-based clustering approach" allowing measurement-error-corrected estimates. In step two, profiles are related to instructional parameters via the manual BCH approach, which "enables relating latent profiles to any parameters that can be modeled in the framework of structural equation modeling". Grouping many learners into few categories helps achieve high statistical power while capturing multivariate, potentially non-linear information.
requirements: Learner characteristics that presumably interact with instructional effects must be measurable on multiple indicator variables and grouped via latent profile analysis or similar model-based clustering
Instructional parameters must be assessed so profiles can be related to treatment effects in a structural equation modeling framework
constraints: The study is exploratory and not pre-registered; inference relies on 90% confidence intervals rather than significance testing
Very small profiles (poor readers, about 16 students in the subsample) cannot support reliable differential-effectiveness estimates
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension
differential effectiveness of instruction across learner profiles
examples: Applied to German third-grade reading instruction: profiles of decoding, syntactic comprehension, vocabulary, and pretest reading comprehension were related to teachers' instructional foci over one school year
key_sources: Tetzlaff, L., Edelsbrunner, P., Schmitterer, A., Hartmann, U., & Brod, G. (2023). Modeling Interactions Between Multivariate Learner Characteristics and Interventions: a Person-Centered Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09830-5

article_title: Modeling Interactions Between Multivariate Learner Characteristics and Interventions: a Person-Centered Approach
citation: Tetzlaff, L., Edelsbrunner, P., Schmitterer, A., Hartmann, U., & Brod, G. (2023). Modeling Interactions Between Multivariate Learner Characteristics and Interventions: a Person-Centered Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09830-5
title: Simple view of reading: reading comprehension as the product of decoding and language comprehension, implying four reader quadrants
description: The article describes the simple view of reading (SVR; Hoover & Gough, 1990) as a prominent theory in which "reading comprehension can be modeled as the product of language comprehension (LC) and decoding (D) abilities". Decoding is the ability to recognize printed words accurately and quickly; language comprehension is the ability to extract and construct literal and inferred meaning from spoken discourse. "The multiplicative nature of the model implies a difficulty in compensating for deficits in one of the two abilities with improved performance in the other", yielding four quadrants: good readers, poor readers, poor decoders, and poor comprehenders.
requirements: Measures of both decoding and language comprehension (here syntactic comprehension and vocabulary as two indicators) are needed to classify readers into the four quadrants
constraints: The article acknowledges the SVR does not fully describe all possible aspects of reading performance, citing Castles et al. (2018)
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension
examples: The study used the SVR to label the four latent profiles and to predict that poor comprehenders benefit from comprehension-targeted instruction
key_sources: Tetzlaff, L., Edelsbrunner, P., Schmitterer, A., Hartmann, U., & Brod, G. (2023). Modeling Interactions Between Multivariate Learner Characteristics and Interventions: a Person-Centered Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09830-5

article_title: Modeling Interactions Between Multivariate Learner Characteristics and Interventions: a Person-Centered Approach
citation: Tetzlaff, L., Edelsbrunner, P., Schmitterer, A., Hartmann, U., & Brod, G. (2023). Modeling Interactions Between Multivariate Learner Characteristics and Interventions: a Person-Centered Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09830-5
title: Match instructional focus to learners' multivariate reading profiles rather than to single characteristics
description: The article argues that individualized instruction requires knowing for whom which instruction works, per Hunt's definition of differential effectiveness: "Given this kind of person, which of these approaches is more effective for a given objective?" Because learner characteristics interact (aptitude complexes), teachers and researchers should consider constellations of characteristics rather than one variable at a time. The study's findings illustrate this: vocabulary focus benefited good readers but not poor decoders or poor comprehenders, while advanced reading focus benefited poor comprehenders.
requirements: Learner profiles must be diagnosed on multiple relevant characteristics, and instructional foci must be measurable and variable across classrooms
constraints: Findings are exploratory, from German third-grade reading instruction, with teacher self-reported foci; the article notes self-reports showed a tendency to report the presence rather than absence of foci
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension
examples: Teachers' aggregated self-reported emphasis on vocabulary, advanced reading abilities, and reading motivation was related to profile-specific reading-comprehension gains over one school year
