article_title: The Cognitive-Affective-Social Theory of Learning in digital Environments (CASTLE)
citation: Sascha Schneider, Maik Beege, Steve Nebel, Lenka Schnaubert, Günter Daniel Rey. (2021). The Cognitive-Affective-Social Theory of Learning in digital Environments (CASTLE). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09626-5
title: CASTLE: social processes triggered by social cues mediate cognitive processing in individual digital learning
description: CASTLE extends the CTML and CATLM by adding a basic assumption: "Social processes triggered by social cues mediate the cognitive processing of information when learning with digital materials." Social cues activate social schemata in long-term memory, leading to enhanced (para-)social, motivational, emotional, and metacognitive processes that influence selection, organization, integration, and retrieval. The theory applies to individual learners interacting with digital material and excludes truly collaborative scenarios. It is illustrated in Fig. 1 of the article as an extension of the CATLM according to Moreno (2006).
requirements: Social cues must be present in the digital learning material to raise the probability of activating the social potential of human–technology interaction
constraints: The theory "only refer[s] to an instructional interaction that is designed as learning or retrieving task for one learner, therefore excluding truly collaborative learning scenarios involving direct interaction of more than one learner"
target_learners: individual learners with digital learning materials
target_learning_goals: knowledge construction and learning outcomes with digital multimedia materials
key_sources: Sascha Schneider, Maik Beege, Steve Nebel, Lenka Schnaubert, Günter Daniel Rey. (2021). The Cognitive-Affective-Social Theory of Learning in digital Environments (CASTLE). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09626-5

article_title: An Evolutionary Upgrade of Cognitive Load Theory: Using the Human Motor System and Collaboration to Support the Learning of Complex Cognitive Tasks
citation: Fred Paas & John Sweller. (2011). An Evolutionary Upgrade of Cognitive Load Theory: Using the Human Motor System and Collaboration to Support the Learning of Complex Cognitive Tasks. Educ Psychol Rev (2012) 24:27–45. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-011-9179-2
title: Evolutionary upgrade of cognitive load theory: biologically primary vs. biologically secondary knowledge
description: The article amends cognitive load theory using Geary's evolutionary account. Working memory limitations are critical only for biologically secondary information — culturally important knowledge we have not evolved to acquire, such as reading and mathematics — while biologically primary information, which the brain has evolved to process, is acquired "without a discernible working memory load". The paper uses this distinction to reinterpret cognitive load effects and to ask whether primary systems can facilitate secondary learning.
requirements: The distinction applies to instructional design for biologically secondary subject matter taught in educational and training contexts
constraints: It may not always be obvious in the absence of an evolutionary history into which category a particular skill should be placed; many skills may combine primary and secondary knowledge, forming more a continuum than a dichotomy
target_learners: school and university students acquiring biologically secondary subject matter
target_learning_goals: acquisition of culturally important, explicitly taught knowledge such as reading and mathematics
examples: Speaking and face recognition are given as primary knowledge acquired unconsciously and effortlessly; reading and mathematics as secondary knowledge requiring explicit instruction and extrinsic motivation
key_sources: Fred Paas & John Sweller. (2011). An Evolutionary Upgrade of Cognitive Load Theory: Using the Human Motor System and Collaboration to Support the Learning of Complex Cognitive Tasks. Educ Psychol Rev (2012) 24:27–45. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-011-9179-2

article_title: An Evolutionary Upgrade of Cognitive Load Theory: Using the Human Motor System and Collaboration to Support the Learning of Complex Cognitive Tasks
citation: Fred Paas & John Sweller. (2011). An Evolutionary Upgrade of Cognitive Load Theory: Using the Human Motor System and Collaboration to Support the Learning of Complex Cognitive Tasks. Educ Psychol Rev (2012) 24:27–45. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-011-9179-2
title: Use biologically primary skills (communication, gesture, movement, object manipulation) to scaffold acquisition of biologically secondary knowledge
description: The article's central design recommendation: because biologically primary skills make minimal demands on working memory, they can be galvanized to assist acquisition of the high-load secondary content of instruction. As the authors put it, "Organizing general skills to assist in the acquisition of subject matter knowledge may be more productive than attempting to teach skills that we have evolved to acquire automatically." The recommendation is grounded in the collective working memory, human movement, and embodied cognition findings reviewed.
requirements: The communication and coordination costs of the primary activity must be largely biologically primary rather than task-specific secondary processes
constraints: Task-specific communication and coordination costs can be substantial; they may need to be decreased by training or by carefully structured or scripted learning environments
target_learners: learners acquiring biologically secondary school subject matter, including children not yet capable of high-level verbal interaction
target_learning_goals: complex cognitive tasks in domains such as mathematics, science concepts, and reading comprehension
examples: Shoval's (2011) mindful movement study: children using body movements in cooperative geometry learning obtained better results than the conventionally taught control group
key_sources: Fred Paas & John Sweller. (2011). An Evolutionary Upgrade of Cognitive Load Theory: Using the Human Motor System and Collaboration to Support the Learning of Complex Cognitive Tasks. Educ Psychol Rev (2012) 24:27–45. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-011-9179-2

article_title: The Relationship between Visuospatial Working Memory and Mathematical Performance in School-Aged Children: a Systematic Review
citation: Katie Allen & Steve Higgins & John Adams. (2019). The Relationship between Visuospatial Working Memory and Mathematical Performance in School-Aged Children: a Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09470-8
title: Researchers should use standardised mathematics measures when investigating the VSWM–mathematics relationship
description: This principle directs researchers studying the VSWM–mathematics relationship to prefer standardised mathematics assessments over study-specific measures, because the review found the choice of measure significantly influences the estimated effect size. The review states that "researchers ought to be cautious of devising their own measures of mathematics attainment where a suitable standardised measure is available." It applies to study design in research on cognitive predictors of mathematics attainment.
requirements: A suitable standardised mathematics measure must be available for the age group and mathematics domain being studied
constraints: The finding concerns effect-size estimation in correlational studies of VSWM and mathematics, not instructional outcomes
target_learners: school-aged children aged 0–16 in mainstream schools
target_learning_goals: mathematics performance (numerical operations and mathematical reasoning)
examples: The review's subsection analysis compared mean effect sizes of 0.44 for standardised versus 0.25 for unstandardised mathematics measures across 35 studies
key_sources: Katie Allen & Steve Higgins & John Adams. (2019). The Relationship between Visuospatial Working Memory and Mathematical Performance in School-Aged Children: a Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09470-8

article_title: The Relationship between Visuospatial Working Memory and Mathematical Performance in School-Aged Children: a Systematic Review
citation: Katie Allen & Steve Higgins & John Adams. (2019). The Relationship between Visuospatial Working Memory and Mathematical Performance in School-Aged Children: a Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09470-8
title: Distinction between simultaneous and sequential visuospatial working memory
description: The review adopts a working-memory framework in which the visuospatial sketchpad is subdivided into simultaneous and sequential VSWM components, citing evidence of a double dissociation. Simultaneous VSWM tasks present all information at once and require recall of stimulus positions, as in the visual patterns task, while sequential tasks present stimuli in a sequence, as in the Corsi block task. The review treats this distinction as an organizing axis for assessing the predictive power of VSWM for mathematics.
requirements: Tasks must separately tap each component, since the review states there is evidence for the dissociation of these tasks supporting their independent investigation
constraints: The review notes no included studies investigated the influence of sequential VSWM on Mathematical Reasoning, highlighting a gap in the research
target_learners: school-aged children aged 0–16 in mainstream schools
target_learning_goals: mathematics performance (numerical operations and mathematical reasoning)
examples: Included studies used simultaneous tasks such as the visual patterns task and dot matrix, and sequential tasks such as the Corsi block task
key_sources: Katie Allen & Steve Higgins & John Adams. (2019). The Relationship between Visuospatial Working Memory and Mathematical Performance in School-Aged Children: a Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09470-8

article_title: Motivation and Personality: Current Integrative Perspectives and the Way Ahead
citation: Lisa Bardach, Luise von Keyserlingk, Jacque S. Eccles. (2026). Motivation and Personality: Current Integrative Perspectives and the Way Ahead. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10147-2
title: Five-group organizing framework for motivation–personality integration in educational psychology
description: The article proposes an organizing framework that maps five groups of theories offering pathways toward integrating motivation and personality: theories from personality psychology that include motivational elements, motivational theories that implicitly or explicitly incorporate personality, cognitive-domain theories, construct-specific integrative theories, and process-oriented theories of learning. The authors state their aim to combine "motivation" primarily in terms of motivational constructs commonly examined in educational psychology (e.g., subject- or domain-specific expectancies, values, interests, and goals) with a Big Five personality focus, noting the work is "intentionally asymmetrical". Integration is said to operate at multiple levels, including dynamic state-level interplay, long-term trait development, compensatory mechanisms, and principles of sustainable and self-regulated learning.
requirements: Integration combines education-relevant motivational constructs with broad Big Five personality aspects, requiring researchers to work across disciplinary borders
constraints: The article states it is not intended as a comprehensive review; it is meant to encourage deeper reflection on integration
target_learning_goals: understanding learning behaviors, engagement, performance, and educational choices
key_sources: Lisa Bardach, Luise von Keyserlingk, Jacque S. Eccles. (2026). Motivation and Personality: Current Integrative Perspectives and the Way Ahead. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10147-2

article_title: Motivation and Personality: Current Integrative Perspectives and the Way Ahead
citation: Lisa Bardach, Luise von Keyserlingk, Jacque S. Eccles. (2026). Motivation and Personality: Current Integrative Perspectives and the Way Ahead. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10147-2
title: Characteristic adaptations as the bridge between personality traits and educational motivation
description: Drawing on McAdams and colleagues, the article treats characteristic adaptations (e.g., motives, goals, plans, strivings, strategies, values, self-images) as intermediate constructs between personality traits and specific behaviors within a situation, and describes them as capturing "how traits interact with changing situational demands". Because these adaptations "closely map onto the social ecology of everyday life", they include everyday learning situations. The article argues educational psychology's clearly defined motivational constructs can specify the broad category of characteristic adaptations, which personality researchers have criticized as vague, and illustrates how a conscientious student may adopt mastery goals when facing demanding learning materials.
requirements: Personality traits are understood as relatively enduring and automatic patterns of thoughts, feelings, and behaviors, not as completely fixed and unaffected by experience
constraints: The article notes the characteristic adaptation perspective is somewhat limited in that personality usually remains restricted to the trait level
target_learning_goals: goal adoption, learning engagement, and learning behaviors in demanding situations
examples: A highly conscientious student facing difficult learning materials activates goals conducive to engaging with them, such as mastery goals of really understanding the materials
key_sources: Lisa Bardach, Luise von Keyserlingk, Jacque S. Eccles. (2026). Motivation and Personality: Current Integrative Perspectives and the Way Ahead. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10147-2

article_title: Motivation and Personality: Current Integrative Perspectives and the Way Ahead
citation: Lisa Bardach, Luise von Keyserlingk, Jacque S. Eccles. (2026). Motivation and Personality: Current Integrative Perspectives and the Way Ahead. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10147-2
title: TESSERA framework: repeated short-term personality states drive long-term trait development
description: The TESSERA framework (Wrzus & Roberts, 2017) elaborates how "repeated short-term, situational processes lead to long-term personality development" through recursive sequences of Triggering situations, Expectancy, States/State expressions, and Reactions. Momentary motivation in the form of expectancies influences which personality state emerges after a trigger, and reactions (internal reinforcement through positive emotions or external feedback) help sustain sequences. The article makes the framework educationally relevant by situating it in learning situations, e.g., a selective advanced mathematics program repeatedly prompting high state conscientiousness that feeds into trait development, and stresses effects are not one-way but likely reciprocal between motivation states and personality states.
requirements: Repeated experiences of personality states that differ from one's typical trait level, accompanied by reinforcing reactions, are needed for trait change over time
constraints: The article notes external expectations should lead to smaller personality changes than internal expectations, per the TESSERA framework's own reasoning
target_learners: students in selective programs, school groups, and everyday learning settings
target_learning_goals: sustained engagement and personality development through learning situations
examples: A student in a school theatre group behaves more outgoing than usual due to context-specific expectations, and repeated higher-than-usual state extraversion may feed into trait development
key_sources: Lisa Bardach, Luise von Keyserlingk, Jacque S. Eccles. (2026). Motivation and Personality: Current Integrative Perspectives and the Way Ahead. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10147-2

article_title: Motivation and Personality: Current Integrative Perspectives and the Way Ahead
citation: Lisa Bardach, Luise von Keyserlingk, Jacque S. Eccles. (2026). Motivation and Personality: Current Integrative Perspectives and the Way Ahead. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10147-2
title: Anchoring Big Five personality traits and states within Situated Expectancy–Value Theory
description: The article proposes concrete placements for personality within Situated Expectancy–Value Theory: Big Five traits are added to the component relabeled "Goals, general self-schemata, and personality traits", and personality states are added to the box containing affective reactions and memories. The authors argue "Personality traits likely influence both expectancies and task value beliefs", illustrating that trait curiosity may raise task value, while state neuroticism in a learning situation is likely to interfere with assigning high value to the task. Because SEVT is situationally specific and culturally bound, the authors deem it a compelling framework for embedding motivation–personality integrations and for deriving testable hypotheses.
requirements: SEVT components represent general categories whose example listings are not exhaustive, which is what allows the proposed additions
constraints: The authors note their proposal for where traits and states belong in the model differs from that of Eccles et al. (in press), and researchers should examine which approach better aligns with their theoretical assumptions
target_learning_goals: formation of expectancies and task value beliefs, learning behaviors, performance, and educational choices
examples: A student low in trait curiosity whose curiosity is sparked in the moment (state curiosity) may come to see the value of the task at hand
key_sources: Lisa Bardach, Luise von Keyserlingk, Jacque S. Eccles. (2026). Motivation and Personality: Current Integrative Perspectives and the Way Ahead. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10147-2

article_title: Motivation and Personality: Current Integrative Perspectives and the Way Ahead
citation: Lisa Bardach, Luise von Keyserlingk, Jacque S. Eccles. (2026). Motivation and Personality: Current Integrative Perspectives and the Way Ahead. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10147-2
title: Mutualism theory applied to motivation–personality co-development
description: Mutualism theory (van der Maas et al., 2006), originally an alternative account of the positive manifold in cognitive abilities, proposes that positive correlations may be "a by-product of increasingly beneficial interactions that develop over time between initially undeveloped and uncorrelated cognitive processes". The article transfers this principle to motivation and personality, foregrounding mutually reinforcing developmental interactions between motivational and personality processes rather than isolated examples. The theory also accounts for differentiation and specialization: some mutualistic interactions strengthen during development while others weaken or shift toward competitive relationships, for instance conscientiousness supporting interest early in skill acquisition but becoming a barrier with ill-structured problems.
requirements: Developmental interactions between motivation and personality processes must be modeled as mutually reinforcing rather than as isolated effects
constraints: Mutualistic couplings can be interrupted: highly conscientious individuals may lose the link with task-specific interests when tasks require creativity, and highly agreeable individuals may inhibit engagement in competitive evaluation contexts
target_learners: students across educational levels and developmental transitions
target_learning_goals: co-development of motivation, personality, and learning-related outcomes
examples: The article cites the meta-analysis by Mammadov (2022) finding the link between agreeableness and academic achievement was stronger in earlier educational levels (elementary/middle school) than in later ones, aligning with mutualism-inspired reasoning
key_sources: Lisa Bardach, Luise von Keyserlingk, Jacque S. Eccles. (2026). Motivation and Personality: Current Integrative Perspectives and the Way Ahead. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10147-2

article_title: Motivation and Personality: Current Integrative Perspectives and the Way Ahead
citation: Lisa Bardach, Luise von Keyserlingk, Jacque S. Eccles. (2026). Motivation and Personality: Current Integrative Perspectives and the Way Ahead. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10147-2
title: Intellectual investment trait theory: reciprocal enrichment and success pathways
description: Intellectual Investment Trait Theory is a family of theories linking investment traits (e.g., intellectual curiosity, interests, typical intellectual engagement, need for cognition) with cognitive abilities. Building on Cattell's idea that crystallized intelligence develops through investment of fluid intelligence, Ackerman (1996) proposed that certain personality traits and motivations contribute to crystallized intelligence beyond fluid intelligence. The article highlights "the environmental enrichment hypothesis" (investment traits lead individuals to seek learning opportunities that foster cognitive development) and "the environmental success hypothesis" (higher cognitive abilities enable more effective engagement in enriching experiences that shape investment traits), assuming a reciprocal relationship, and extends the reasoning to Big Five traits and educational motivation such as expectancies and task values.
requirements: The theory assumes a reciprocal relationship between investment traits and cognitive abilities rather than mutually exclusive directional hypotheses
constraints: Recent extensions reformulate the two key hypotheses as situation exploration and situation exploitation hypotheses to reflect reciprocal state-level interplay
target_learners: students and learners across domains and professions
target_learning_goals: knowledge acquisition, information-seeking behaviors, and cognitive development
examples: A highly conscientious person seeks a well-structured environment, does well there, which contributes to expectancies of success and domain value, reinforcing conscientiousness
key_sources: Lisa Bardach, Luise von Keyserlingk, Jacque S. Eccles. (2026). Motivation and Personality: Current Integrative Perspectives and the Way Ahead. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10147-2

article_title: Motivation and Personality: Current Integrative Perspectives and the Way Ahead
citation: Lisa Bardach, Luise von Keyserlingk, Jacque S. Eccles. (2026). Motivation and Personality: Current Integrative Perspectives and the Way Ahead. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10147-2
title: Reward-learning framework of knowledge acquisition and motivation transformations
description: The reward-learning framework of knowledge acquisition (Murayama, 2022) explains how individuals initiate and sustain learning: individuals engage in learning "because gaining knowledge is intrinsically rewarding and often linked to positive emotional experiences". Awareness of a knowledge gap triggers curiosity and expectation of the rewarding value of new information, and acquired knowledge reinforces future learning via an internal loop, while an external loop sustains long-term interest through generating new questions, increasing valuation, and enhancing capability. The article extends the framework with extrinsic rewards (Bardach & Murayama, 2025) as an entry point for unmotivated learners, whereby extrinsic-reward motivation can transform into intrinsic-reward motivation—referred to as motivation transformations—and links the framework to TESSERA-based personality development.
requirements: Extrinsic rewards act as an entry point that sets in motion the positive feedback loop of internally rewarding learning processes
constraints: The article argues extrinsic factors do not contradict intrinsic ones and can go hand in hand, countering views that extrinsic rewards undermine intrinsic motivation
target_learning_goals: initiation and sustained engagement in learning, curiosity, interest, and long-term trait development
examples: Students who initially learn to satisfy parents' or teachers' expectations experience rewarding engagement and knowledge acquisition, kick-starting the intrinsically rewarding learning process
key_sources: Lisa Bardach, Luise von Keyserlingk, Jacque S. Eccles. (2026). Motivation and Personality: Current Integrative Perspectives and the Way Ahead. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10147-2

article_title: Is a Preference for Realism Really Naive After All? A Cognitive Model of Learning with Realistic Visualizations
citation: Skulmowski, A., Nebel, S., Remmele, M., & Rey, G. D. (2022). Is a Preference for Realism Really Naive After All? A Cognitive Model of Learning with Realistic Visualizations. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09638-1
title: GSR model: realism as three independently manipulable dimensions of geometry, shading, and rendering
description: The geometry, shading, and rendering (GSR) model is a technical taxonomy of realism grounded in the actual production process of computer-generated imagery in 3D software. It replaces unidimensional realism continua with three dimensions that 'can individually range from simplified to highly realistic', so that each dimension's contribution to realism can be assessed separately. The authors present it as a common terminology for educators, designers, and researchers, exemplified with renderings of the patella created in Blender (Fig. 2).
requirements: Researchers and practitioners must have enough information about learning materials to recreate a particular level of realism, including software packages, plug-ins, and design choices such as whether the same 3D model underlies realistic and schematic versions
constraints: Realism studies usually compare only a few possible combinations of the three dimensions, so results concern specific GSR combinations rather than realism in general
target_learners: designers and researchers of instructional visualizations
target_learning_goals: describing and categorizing the realism of instructional visualizations
examples: Figure 2 exemplifies the model with renderings of the patella varying geometry detail, shading (solid white, color texture, specular), and rendering style (toon with contour line vs. realistic lighting)
key_sources: Skulmowski, A., Nebel, S., Remmele, M., & Rey, G. D. (2022). Is a Preference for Realism Really Naive After All? A Cognitive Model of Learning with Realistic Visualizations. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09638-1

article_title: Is a Preference for Realism Really Naive After All? A Cognitive Model of Learning with Realistic Visualizations
citation: Skulmowski, A., Nebel, S., Remmele, M., & Rey, G. D. (2022). Is a Preference for Realism Really Naive After All? A Cognitive Model of Learning with Realistic Visualizations. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09638-1
title: Cognitive model of learning with realistic visualizations: perception, schema construction, and testing stages
description: The article's cognitive model traces learning outcomes with realistic visualizations through three stages: perception, schema construction, and testing. In the perceptual stage learners segment contents and form a 3D representation; realism dimensions contribute to a perceptual load that can be lightened with cues. At schema construction, elements and their visual relationships form a primarily visual form of element interactivity integrated into long-term memory, moderated by learner characteristics such as spatial ability. At testing, the realism level of the learned visualization interacts with test type in determining performance.
requirements: The model assumes stages may be completed in a different order or in a continuous loop, for example in virtual reality environments where several objects are perceived and learned in succession
constraints: The model is presented as a framework for formulating predictions and guiding research, not as directly tested in this article
target_learners: learners using realistic visualizations, e.g., in anatomy learning and virtual reality environments
target_learning_goals: retention and transfer of visually presented learning content
examples: The model explains how realistic details created using shading and texture maps induce perceptual load that can be lowered using cues, and how learning goals can transform realistic details from extraneous load towards intrinsic load
key_sources: Skulmowski, A., Nebel, S., Remmele, M., & Rey, G. D. (2022). Is a Preference for Realism Really Naive After All? A Cognitive Model of Learning with Realistic Visualizations. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09638-1

article_title: Is a Preference for Realism Really Naive After All? A Cognitive Model of Learning with Realistic Visualizations
citation: Skulmowski, A., Nebel, S., Remmele, M., & Rey, G. D. (2022). Is a Preference for Realism Really Naive After All? A Cognitive Model of Learning with Realistic Visualizations. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09638-1
title: Specify the geometry, shading, and rendering design choices of learning materials to create reproducible realism comparisons
description: The article recommends that research papers provide standardized information about learning materials so that a particular level of realism can be recreated with the same or other learning contents. A well-defined degree of realism is achieved when 'researchers and practitioners have enough information concerning the learning materials available to recreate that particular level of realism'. Authors should report software packages, plug-ins, unusual settings, and design choices such as whether the same 3D model underlies realistic and schematic versions and whether texture maps were used.
requirements: Reports should include the name of the software package(s) used, whether special plug-ins or unusual settings were utilized, and design choices made during production of the learning materials
constraints: The article notes most papers already include excerpts of the learning materials but that categorization of existing research is often impossible due to missing information
target_learning_goals: comparable, replicable research on realism in learning materials
examples: The article proposes assessing visualizations concerning their geometry, shading, and rendering, and categorizing previous studies along these dimensions in Table 2

article_title: Interventions and Approaches Targeting Early Self-Regulation or Executive Functioning in Preschools: A Systematic Review
citation: Rosalyn A. Muir · Steven J. Howard · Lisa Kervin. (2023). Interventions and Approaches Targeting Early Self-Regulation or Executive Functioning in Preschools: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09740-6
title: Four-category taxonomy of 12 preschool SR/EF intervention approaches
description: The review organises preschool SR/EF interventions into a taxonomy building on Takacs and Kassai (2019), in which "four higher-order categories comprised of 12 distinct intervention approaches were identified": Play (mediated structured play, semi-structured creative play), Social-Emotional (mindfulness, SEL programs), Curricula and Pedagogy (curricula, multicomponent training, music, mathematics, language training, integrated arts), and Non-routine Activities (task training including digitalised, physical activity). The taxonomy allows results to be synthesised separately for each approach and then reconciled across approaches to identify which content and features yield comparatively more robust child-level effects.
requirements: Studies must target SR and/or EF in typically developing children aged 3–6 in preschool settings with a control group and validated pre/post measures
constraints: Two studies could have been assigned to more than one category; multi-arm interventions were assigned by the stated emphasis and intent of the authors' paper
target_learning_goals: self-regulation
executive function (inhibitory control, working memory, cognitive flexibility)
examples: The review charted 85 studies into the 12 approaches and synthesised results separately for each approach before reconciling them in the Discussion

article_title: Collaboration Scripts – A Conceptual Analysis
citation: Kollar, I., Fischer, F. & Hesse, F.W. (2006). Collaboration Scripts – A Conceptual Analysis. Educational Psychology Review, 18, 159–185. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-006-9007-2
title: Collaboration scripts as scaffolds structuring interactive processes between learning partners
description: The article defines collaboration scripts as instructional scaffolds for collaborative learning. As the abstract states, collaboration scripts are scaffolds that aim to improve collaboration through structuring the interactive processes between two or more learning partners. The concept is grounded in the script notion from Schank and Abelson and applied to both face-to-face and computer-mediated collaborative learning settings.
requirements: At least two learning partners whose interactive processes are to be structured
target_learners: Collaborative learners in face-to-face or computer-mediated settings
target_learning_goals: Improved collaboration and individual knowledge acquisition

citation: Kollar, I., Fischer, F. & Hesse, F.W. (2006). Collaboration Scripts – A Conceptual Analysis. Educational Psychology Review, 18, 159–185. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-006-9007-2
title: Five-component taxonomy of collaboration scripts
description: The article proposes that collaboration scripts can be analyzed into five components, which serve as a basis for comparing different script approaches. As printed, collaboration scripts consist of at least five components: (a) learning objectives, (b) type of activities, (c) sequencing, (d) role distribution, and (e) type of representation. These components function as an analytical taxonomy for describing and comparing prototypical script approaches.
requirements: A script design must specify each of the five components to be fully described
constraints: The list is stated as a minimum: at least five components

target_learning_goals: Systematic design and comparison of collaboration scripts

article_title: Collaboration Scripts – A Conceptual Analysis
citation: Kollar, I., Fischer, F. & Hesse, F.W. (2006). Collaboration Scripts – A Conceptual Analysis. Educational Psychology Review, 18, 159–185. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-006-9007-2
title: Conceptual framework of script-based learning incorporating external and internal collaboration scripts
description: The article closes with a conceptual framework on script-based learning that incorporates both external and internal collaboration scripts. External scripts are instructional scaffolds provided by the environment, while internal collaboration scripts are the learners' own knowledge structures about collaboration. The framework holds that research on collaboration scripts needs to consider the learners' internal collaboration scripts as a further determinant of collaboration behavior, alongside the external scaffolds designers provide.
requirements: Design and research must consider both the provided external script and the learners' internal scripts
target_learners: Collaborative learners in schools and computer-mediated settings
target_learning_goals: Understanding and designing collaboration support that fits learners' internal scripts

citation: Kollar, I., Fischer, F. & Hesse, F.W. (2006). Collaboration Scripts – A Conceptual Analysis. Educational Psychology Review, 18, 159–185. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-006-9007-2
title: Design collaboration scripts that support both participation and coordination and induce individual knowledge acquisition and metacognition
description: The article recommends consolidating the two research lines so that scripts both support participation and coordination, as well as induce learning activities closely related to individual knowledge acquisition and metacognition. This design principle follows directly from the analysis showing that face-to-face scripts emphasize acquisition activities while computer-mediated scripts emphasize coordination, so integrated scripts should address both functions.
requirements: Script designers must address both the communicative-coordinative dimension and the individual knowledge acquisition dimension
target_learners: Collaborative learners in face-to-face and computer-mediated settings
target_learning_goals: Collaboration quality, individual knowledge acquisition, and metacognition

title: Scripted cooperation and structured dyadic learning approaches as prototypical face-to-face collaboration scripts
description: The article's reference base treats scripted cooperation (O'Donnell & Dansereau) and structured dyadic learning environments as prototypical face-to-face collaboration script approaches. article_title: Visuospatial Processing Decline Due to Cannabis Consumption in Nondependent High School Students
citation: Goycolea, Rodrigo; Castro Alonso, Juan; Dörr Álamos, Anneliese. (2020). Visuospatial Processing Decline Due to Cannabis Consumption in Nondependent High School Students. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09564-8
title: Three-type taxonomy of correlational studies of cannabis-related visuospatial decline
description: The review organizes its correlational evidence into three types: comparisons of declines between visuospatial processing and other cognitive tasks, studies comparing declines between high school students and adult participants, and stringent correlational studies such as large samples, longitudinal data, and twin studies. This taxonomy structures how the review weighs evidence of visuospatial processing decline associated with cannabis use in nondependent high school students, alongside experimental evidence and evidence from abstinent conditions.
requirements: Correlational evidence must be classified by design features such as sample size, longitudinal data, or twin design to count as stringent
constraints: The taxonomy applies to correlational studies of cannabis-related cognitive decline in nondependent or nonclinical high school students

learning performance

article_title: Why Some Gestures Work Better than Others: Toward a Model of Gesture-Supported Vocabulary Learning
citation: Manuela Macedonia, Lihui Hu, Brian Mathias. (2026). Why Some Gestures Work Better than Others: Toward a Model of Gesture-Supported Vocabulary Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10222-8
title: Gesture Memory Support Model (GMSM): seven dimensions for characterizing instructional gestures
description: The GMSM is a preliminary theoretical and operational framework for characterizing instructional gestures in L2 vocabulary learning. As the article states, it is "a preliminary theoretical and operational framework, accompanied by provisional rating guidance, for characterizing instructional gestures according to seven dimensions hypothesized to be relevant to their potential mnemonic contribution to L2 vocabulary learning". The dimensions capture properties of the gesture stimulus and its relationships with the target word, learners, and context, and are retained as a multidimensional profile rather than combined into one effectiveness score. The dimensions are not assumed to be statistically independent or additive.
requirements: Rating guidance for characterizing gestures dimension by dimension; dimensions rated in relation to the intended lexical meaning rather than gesture category membership
constraints: Not an empirically validated diagnostic or predictive instrument; reliability and empirical distinctiveness of dimensions remain to be established; grounded primarily in L2 research; facial expression considered only for emotional salience fit, with prosody, gaze, and posture outside the core dimensions
target_learning_goals: L2 vocabulary encoding and retention
examples: The article contrasts the GMSM's multidimensional profile approach with traditional taxonomies such as McNeill's Quartet and Kendon's Continuum, which classify spontaneous co-speech gestures rather than designed instructional gestures
key_sources: Manuela Macedonia, Lihui Hu, Brian Mathias. (2026). Why Some Gestures Work Better than Others: Toward a Model of Gesture-Supported Vocabulary Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10222-8

article_title: Promoting Temporal Investigations of Development in Context: a Systematic Review of Longitudinal Research Linking Childhood Circumstances and Learning-related Outcomes
citation: Molly Grant, Kane Meissel, Daniel Exeter. (2023). Promoting Temporal Investigations of Development in Context: a Systematic Review of Longitudinal Research Linking Childhood Circumstances and Learning-related Outcomes. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09734-4
title: Temporality framework: duration, developmental timing, and mobility as longitudinal dimensions through which childhood context affects learning and development
description: The review organizes evidence on how childhood social and economic circumstances affect educational and cognitive outcomes through three temporal dimensions grounded in ecological systems theory (the chronosystem) and life course theory. As the review defines it, "temporality" refers to "the timing-related dynamics of the duration of exposure, developmental time points of exposure, and changes in exposure to contextual factors across time." The framework structures the review's four themes and identifies when children are particularly vulnerable to contextual effects.
requirements: Longitudinal data with circumstances assessed at least twice within childhood (pregnancy to age 12) to distinguish duration, timing, and mobility effects
constraints: The review restricts circumstances to family and neighborhood levels, excluding school and early childhood education factors
target_learning_goals: educational outcomes (academic performance, qualifications, school engagement)
cognitive outcomes (language, attention, memory, executive function, general cognitive composites)
examples: The four themes (duration effects, developmental timing effects, mobility effects, no temporal effects) were constructed via reflexive thematic analysis of 75 studies

Promoting Temporal Investigations of Development in Context: a Systematic Review of Longitudinal Research Linking Childhood Circumstances and Learning-related Outcomes. article_title: Mapping the Heterogeneity of Emotional Design Features in Multimedia Research: A Systematic Review
citation: Juliette C. Désiron, Julien Venni, Mireille Bétrancourt. (2026). Mapping the Heterogeneity of Emotional Design Features in Multimedia Research: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10138-3
title: Integrated Cognitive-Affective Model of Learning with Media (ICALM)
description: ICALM (Plass & Kaplan, 2016) refines the cognitive-affective theory of multimedia learning by attributing the induction of positive affective states to multimedia characteristics. The review describes how "Multimedia stimuli engage both cognitive and affective resources, with these processes being closely linked and interacting reciprocally—emotions influence content processing and vice versa". Integration into a coherent mental model in long-term memory includes affect in the form of emotion schemas. The review uses ICALM, with CTML and CATML, as its theoretical grounding for how visual features guide attention, load, affect and motivation.
requirements: Theoretical grounding assumes design elements can induce affective states that interact reciprocally with cognitive processing during selection, organization, and integration.
target_learners: multimedia learners in the reviewed studies (school and higher education)
target_learning_goals: retention, transfer and comprehension of instructional multimedia content
key_sources: Juliette C. Désiron, Julien Venni, Mireille Bétrancourt. (2026). Mapping the Heterogeneity of Emotional Design Features in Multimedia Research: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10138-3

article_title: Mapping the Heterogeneity of Emotional Design Features in Multimedia Research: A Systematic Review
citation: Juliette C. Désiron, Julien Venni, Mireille Bétrancourt. (2026). Mapping the Heterogeneity of Emotional Design Features in Multimedia Research: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10138-3
title: Endogenous versus exogenous anthropomorphism: the semantic function of anthropomorphic design
description: The review distinguishes anthropomorphic cues that are visually embedded in the represented entity itself (endogenous) from those conveyed through contextual or metaphorical human associations (exogenous). Endogenous features can fulfil a semantic function by conveying content-relevant information, e.g. "representing viruses with an angry appearance to signify their danger or virulence". Following Mayer (2011), the review states "such endogenous visual characteristics should be favoured over an exogenous use, where the anthropomorphic characteristics do not relate to the content's information". The distinction was operationalised in the review's coding of 15 materials (Table 6, Fig. 4).
requirements: Anthropomorphic elements should bear endogenous meaning relevant to the instructional content to serve a semantic function.
constraints: Anthropomorphic depictions may risk introducing misconceptions about underlying scientific concepts, creating a trade-off between affective engagement and conceptual accuracy.
target_learners: learners of science topics in multimedia instruction
target_learning_goals: content comprehension through semantically meaningful visual representations
examples: Bülbül and Kuzu (2021) represented a protostar as a baby on a fluffy cloud, conveying its early stage of formation surrounded by interstellar dust.

article_title: Effectiveness of Unproctored vs. Teacher-Proctored Exams in Reducing Students’ Cheating: A Double-Blind Randomized Controlled Field Experimental Study
citation: Li Zhao, Junjie Peng, Shiqi Ke, Kang Lee. (2024). Effectiveness of Unproctored vs. Teacher-Proctored Exams in Reducing Students’ Cheating: A Double-Blind Randomized Controlled Field Experimental Study. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09965-z
title: Fake Question Paradigm for objective measurement of exam cheating
description: The Fake Question Paradigm is an objective behavioral measure of cheating in real exams. "This paradigm involved adding researcher-prepared fill-in-the-blank target questions to the exam questions prepared by the professors"; the target questions appear course-related but test fictional concepts with fake answers unavailable online or in books. The answer key is posted to the class portal after the exam starts, so "any correct answer would indicate cheating and the number of correct answers would measure the extent of cheating." Fill-in-the-blank format minimizes guessing, and different target questions per section prevent answer sharing.
requirements: Target questions must test fictional concepts whose answers do not exist on the internet or in books, verified by pilot testing and internet searches
The answer key must be posted online during the exam while students are told not to check it, so correct target answers can only arise from cheating
constraints: Requires a context where posting answer keys to a class portal during exams is routine practice
Students must put away electronic devices before the exam starts so portal access constitutes cheating
target_learning_goals: objective assessment of academic dishonesty in actual course exams
examples: In Study 1, five fill-in-the-blank target questions about fictional concepts (e.g., a fake tenth force in Western psychology) were added to a 17-question professor-prepared midterm, after a pilot study (N = 64) verified students could not answer them correctly
key_sources: Li Zhao, Junjie Peng, Shiqi Ke, Kang Lee. (2024). Effectiveness of Unproctored vs. Teacher-Proctored Exams in Reducing Students’ Cheating: A Double-Blind Randomized Controlled Field Experimental Study. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09965-z

article_title: Effectiveness of Unproctored vs. Teacher-Proctored Exams in Reducing Students’ Cheating: A Double-Blind Randomized Controlled Field Experimental Study
citation: Li Zhao, Junjie Peng, Shiqi Ke, Kang Lee. (2024). Effectiveness of Unproctored vs. Teacher-Proctored Exams in Reducing Students’ Cheating: A Double-Blind Randomized Controlled Field Experimental Study. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09965-z
title: Incorporate unproctored exams together with pre-exam integrity reminders into university assessment practices to reduce cheating
description: The article concludes that "incorporating unproctored exams and pre-exam academic integrity reminders into a university's assessment practices may be a useful strategy for reducing academic dishonesty and upholding assessment validity." Across four double-blind randomized field experiments and a mini-meta-analysis, the unproctored (trust exam) format outperformed teacher-proctored exams on both cheating rate and cheating extent, and reminders added an independent rate reduction. The principle rests on a university population experienced with unproctored exams.
requirements: Students should be familiar with the unproctored exam process and academic integrity expectations; at the study university, 10% of exams were unproctored and students had decades of institutional experience with the Trust Exam system
constraints: The exam-format effect on cheating rate was not significant in Study 3 when reminders were present, though the pooled analysis favored the unproctored format
Findings come from second-year undergraduates at one Chinese university without an honor code system
target_learning_goals: reducing academic dishonesty and upholding assessment validity
examples: Students from the same class were randomly assigned within double-blind field experiments to unproctored or proctored conditions, with professors and students unaware of assigned conditions before the exam

article_title: How Are Curiosity and Interest Different? Naïve Bayes Classification of People’s Beliefs
citation: Donnellan, E., Aslan, S., Fastrich, G. M., & Murayama, K. (2021). How Are Curiosity and Interest Different? Naïve Bayes Classification of People's Beliefs. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09622-9
title: Reward-learning framework: curiosity and interest as folk psychological concepts constructed from knowledge-acquisition experiences
description: The reward-learning framework of knowledge acquisition holds that curiosity and interest are labels people assign to their own experiences of information seeking. Under this account, "curiosity and interest are commonsense (also termed naïve or folk) psychological concepts, intuitively and subjectively constructed by people to describe feelings resulting from underlying psychological processes to which they lack true introspective access". Because no agreed expert definitions exist, the framework proposes that the non-expert consensus view can serve as the reference definition for future empirical work, complementing top-down theoretical approaches.
requirements: Requires treating definitional consensus as a starting point for, not evidence of, distinct underlying psychological processes
constraints: The article states we cannot currently make hard distinctions at the level of specific psychological or neural processes
target_learners: adult online participants defining curiosity and interest
target_learning_goals: conceptual clarity on the distinction between curiosity and interest in knowledge acquisition
examples: Study 1 elicited free-text definitions (minimum 80 words each) from online participants and trained a Naïve Bayes classifier on them
key_sources: Donnellan, E., Aslan, S., Fastrich, G. M., & Murayama, K. (2021). How Are Curiosity and Interest Different? Naïve Bayes Classification of People's Beliefs. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09622-9

article_title: How Are Curiosity and Interest Different? Naïve Bayes Classification of People’s Beliefs
citation: Donnellan, E., Aslan, S., Fastrich, G. M., & Murayama, K. (2021). How Are Curiosity and Interest Different? Naïve Bayes Classification of People's Beliefs. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09622-9
title: Five proposed state-level distinctions between curiosity and interest: triggers, information-seeking character, knowledge states, affect, and incentive salience
description: The article's theoretical review organises proposed distinctions between state curiosity and situational interest into five facets. As printed: "In this section, we outline five distinctions between state-level interest and curiosity proposed by researchers who maintain that the concepts are meaningfully separable." These are (1) triggers — curiosity requires collative variables inducing information gaps while interest has broader, possibly subjective triggers; (2) character of information seeking — curiosity ceases on closing a specific gap whereas interest lacks stopping rules and can last longer; (3) knowledge states — curiosity follows an inverted U-shaped function of perceived knowledge, interest does not; (4) affect — curiosity is initially aversive then pleasant, interest pleasant from triggering; (5) incentive salience — D-type curiosity involves higher initial "wanting" distinct from "liking".
requirements: Distinguishing state-level forms is required because trait-level distinctions depend on whether traits are tendencies to experience corresponding states
constraints: The article notes lines demarcating one dimension may not demarcate others, and situational interest and state curiosity may be indistinguishable under some accounts
target_learners: educational researchers designing curiosity- or interest-based interventions
target_learning_goals: understanding how curiosity and interest differ as motivations for information seeking and learning
examples: The review cites Litman's I/D-type framework, Loewenstein's information-gap theory, and the four-phase model of interest development as the frameworks from which the distinctions derive
key_sources: Donnellan, E., Aslan, S., Fastrich, G. M., & Murayama, K. (2021). How Are Curiosity and Interest Different? Naïve Bayes Classification of People's Beliefs. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09622-9

citation: Núñez-Regueiro, F., Marsh, H. W., Pekrun, R., Lüdtke, O., & Guo, J. (2026). On Model Interpretability and Time-Reversal Testing in Analyses of Reciprocal Effects: Clarifying Modeling Issues in Sorjonen et al.'s (2025a, 2025b) Commentaries. Educational Psychology Review, 38(80). https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10179-8
title: Make modeling assumptions fully explicit when comparing alternative longitudinal models, so differences reflect substantive mechanisms rather than specification issues
description: This principle holds that debates over alternative longitudinal models should distinguish defensible modeling choices from specification errors that depart from SEM logic. The authors argue that "what appeared to be contradictory results from alternative models ... are better understood as consequences of specification issues that, once resolved, yield results consistent with the REM". Explicit assumptions ensure interpretability of reciprocal-effect estimates.
requirements: Model comparisons must state temporal ordering, identification, and parameter-interpretability assumptions explicitly
constraints: Improper solutions (non-positive definite matrices) invalidate interpretation of parameters under standard SEM principles
target_learners: researchers analyzing longitudinal data on academic self-concept and achievement
target_learning_goals: valid causal interpretation of reciprocal effects between academic self-concept and achievement
examples: The commentary restates the LCSM, STARTS, and ESDM misspecifications in Table 1 and shows corrected versions yield proper solutions corroborating Marsh et al. (2024)

article_title: On Model Interpretability and Time-Reversal Testing in Analyses of Reciprocal Effects: Clarifying Modeling Issues in Sorjonen et al.’s (2025a, 2025b) Commentaries
citation: Núñez-Regueiro, F., Marsh, H. W., Pekrun, R., Lüdtke, O., & Guo, J. (2026). Educational Psychology Review, 38(80). https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10179-8
title: Time-reversal testing for assessing directional consistency of prospective effects
description: Time-reversal testing, introduced for neuroimaging analysis by Haufe et al. (2013), assesses the Granger-causal strength of prospective effects in noisy contexts. Its rationale is that "since causes must precede effects, reversing the temporal order of a model should result in attenuating or reversing the sign of a prospective effect presumed to be causal", while contemporaneous effects should remain unchanged. The authors adapt it to contrast time-aligned and time-reversed REM variants.
requirements: The time-reversed model must mirror the original model's structure (same lagged and contemporaneous paths, autoregressive structures reversed for both constructs) for commensurability
constraints: Results are compatible with, but do not establish, a causal interpretation; reversing time for only one construct breaks commensurability
target_learners: researchers evaluating directional ordering in longitudinal panel data
target_learning_goals: testing whether observed ASC-ACH lagged patterns are consistent with hypothesized temporal ordering
examples: The authors estimated time-reversed REM variants on Sorjonen et al.'s simulated data and the PALMA data (Fig. 1, B.2 and C.2), with reproducible code in their OSF repository

article_title: Process Account of Curiosity and Interest: A Reward-Learning Perspective
citation: Kou Murayama, Lily FitzGibbon & Michiko Sakaki. (2019). Process Account of Curiosity and Interest: A Reward-Learning Perspective. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09499-9
title: Reward-learning framework of autonomous knowledge acquisition
description: The article presents a framework in which knowledge acquisition itself serves as a reward: recognizing a knowledge gap motivates information-seeking, acquisition generates a rewarding experience, and that experience "strengthens the further information-seeking behavior by increasing the expected reward value of new information." An expanded knowledge base also generates new questions, forming a positive feedback loop that enables sustainable learning. The framework is built on reinforcement-learning models but incorporates knowledge-specific features such as new knowledge creating room for further gaps.
requirements: The framework centers on reward learning as the key to understanding sustainable knowledge acquisition, so a rewarding experience upon knowledge acquisition is required for the loop to form
constraints: The authors acknowledge that the framework is still preliminary
target_learning_goals: sustained autonomous knowledge acquisition
information-seeking behavior
examples: The article illustrates the loop with a student learning to solve quadratic equations, whose understanding may prompt wondering whether cubic equations can be solved similarly
key_sources: Kou Murayama, Lily FitzGibbon & Michiko Sakaki. (2019). Process Account of Curiosity and Interest: A Reward-Learning Perspective. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09499-9

article_title: Availability to Learn: An Essential, Achievable Condition for Self-Regulated Learning
citation: Adar Ben-Eliyahu · Matthew L. Bernacki. (2026). Availability to Learn: An Essential, Achievable Condition for Self-Regulated Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10144-5
title: Availability to learn is a prerequisite condition, established by a summative ratio of contributors to challenges, that must be met before SRL can activate
description: The article's central framework holds that availability to learn is a prerequisite stage preceding even preparatory phases of SRL process models. Learners weigh and sum psychological and environmental conditions, and "We propose a ratio function when contributors to availability can outweigh detractors and SRL can activate." When detractors outweigh contributors, learners can self-activate SRL by recruiting assets to flip the ratio. The construct extends Kahn's psychological availability to learning contexts and adds an intraindividual summation process.
requirements: Learners must surpass a personal minimal threshold of contributors relative to detractors before SRL processes can initiate and be sustained
constraints: The framework is proposed theoretically; the article presents no empirical test of the ratio or threshold
target_learners: Adolescent and adult learners in academic settings
target_learning_goals: Initiating and sustaining self-regulated engagement in academic tasks under suboptimal conditions
examples: Sarah's scenario: a learner who cleared her desk, met bodily needs, and set intent to study was rendered unavailable by a loud noise, illustrating how environmental detractors can overwhelm antecedent preparation

article_title: Availability to Learn: An Essential, Achievable Condition for Self-Regulated Learning
citation: Adar Ben-Eliyahu · Matthew L. Bernacki. (2026). Availability to Learn: An Essential, Achievable Condition for Self-Regulated Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10144-5
title: Person × Task × Circumstances perspective extends MASRL and information processing SRL models to the learner's broader ecological system
description: The article extends Efklides' MASRL model and Winne and Hadwin's personal and task affordances and constraints "to a Person × Task × Circumstances perspective." It applies Bronfenbrenner's ecological systems theory, mapping the intraindividual system, microsystem, exosystem, and macrosystem around a focal learning task, building on the authors' earlier integrated SRL (iSRL) model. This captures idiosyncratic affordances and constraints learners appraise when engaging a task within their larger learning ecosystem.
requirements: Modeling requires mapping internal and external conditions at layers of the ecological system relative to the focal task
constraints: The article notes contemporary SRL models' constrained focus enabled online behavioral measures; the broadened view is a theoretical proposal, not an empirically validated model
target_learners: Learners across ecological contexts, including those facing poverty, crisis, or disrupted environments
target_learning_goals: Representing task context comprehensively in models of self-regulated learning
examples: Figure 2 depicts the ecological system of the learner, with distal systems exerting depleting or replenishing effects on students' limited resources to self-regulate in a learning task
key_sources: Adar Ben-Eliyahu · Matthew L. Bernacki. (2026). Availability to Learn: An Essential, Achievable Condition for Self-Regulated Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10144-5

article_title: Availability to Learn: An Essential, Achievable Condition for Self-Regulated Learning
citation: Adar Ben-Eliyahu · Matthew L. Bernacki. (2026). Availability to Learn: An Essential, Achievable Condition for Self-Regulated Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10144-5
title: When availability does not arise naturally, learners should recruit antecedent strategies and behavioral scripts to self-activate SRL and flip the contributor-detractor ratio
description: The article recommends that learners who find themselves unavailable to learn can "recognize the assets at their disposal, recruit these into their perception of their capacity as a learner who can succeed in a task and overcome challenges sufficient to activate their capacity for SRL." Antecedent strategies include clearing the environment, meeting bodily needs, establishing intent, and enacting familiar behavioral scripts such as reviewing notes to initiate productive learning behavior.
requirements: Learners need metacognitive knowledge of themselves, their learning process, and their learning environment to recruit sufficient resources
constraints: The article states this applies to experienced adolescent and adult learners with sufficient metacognitive knowledge; disruptions can still overwhelm antecedent preparation, as in Sarah's scenario
target_learning_goals: Establishing availability to learn under suboptimal internal and external conditions
examples: Sarah investigated the noise source, made a pact to return within a few minutes, and initiated a familiar note-review strategy, thereby regulating emotion, attention, and behavior to establish availability

article_title: Detecting Instruction Effects—Deciding Between Covariance Analytical and Change-Score Approach
citation: Köhler, C., Hartig, J., & Naumann, A. (2021). Detecting Instruction Effects—Deciding Between Covariance Analytical and Change-Score Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09590-6
title: Hypothetical data-generating model with trait and state components for diagnosing bias in instruction-effect estimation
description: The article proposes representing, via graphs, a hypothetical data-generating model containing all observed and unobserved variables affecting the outcome at T1 and T2 and the instruction variable. As the article states, "we use graphs to represent the state component, the trait component, their effects on the variables of interest (outcome at T1, outcome at T2, and instruction), and the instruction effect, denoted by δ". Researchers formulate assumptions about which components influence which variables, then deduce for which scenario the true effect δ is mirrored by the ANCOVA or CHANGE coefficient. Bias is defined as the difference between the true effect in the data generation and the estimated effects.
requirements: Researchers must formulate assumptions, based on apparent plausibility or empirical findings, about the presence of third variables and the relative sizes of trait- and state-specific influences.
constraints: The article notes assumptions regarding the model might not hold and alternative data-generating scenarios cannot be ruled out; interaction effects between instruction and the outcome at T2 were not considered and would make the model much less feasible.
target_learning_goals: unbiased estimation of instruction effects in two-occasion nonrandomized studies
examples: Applied to the DESI study, the Kunter et al. (2013) PCK example, the Holzberger et al. (2013) self-efficacy example, and the Lazarides and Buchholz (2019) teaching-quality example.
key_sources: Köhler, C., Hartig, J., & Naumann, A. (2021). Detecting Instruction Effects—Deciding Between Covariance Analytical and Change-Score Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09590-6

article_title: Cognitive Load Theory and Its Relationships with Motivation: a Self-Determination Theory Perspective
citation: Evans, P., Vansteenkiste, M., Parker, P., Kingsford-Smith, A., & Zhou, S. (2024). Cognitive Load Theory and Its Relationships with Motivation: a Self-Determination Theory Perspective. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09841-2
title: Self-determination theory as an integrative framework linking cognitive load theory and motivation
description: The article proposes self-determination theory as a unifying motivational framework for cognitive load theory research, which has historically studied motivation with unitary constructs or no unifying framework. SDT contributes two key mechanisms: fulfillment of the basic psychological needs of "competence, relatedness, and autonomy," and a motivation continuum "from amotivation, an absence of motivation, through controlled motivation... to autonomous motivation." The study operationalizes these via the relative autonomy index and teacher motivating styles, showing that strategies supporting autonomous motivation also minimize extraneous load.
requirements: Adoption of multidimensional motivation measures (e.g., the SDT motivation continuum) rather than unitary motivation constructs
constraints: The article makes no claims about whether one motivation theory should be preferred over another; basic psychological need experiences were not measured in the present study
target_learning_goals: self-regulated motivation and engagement in school subjects
examples: The study computed a relative autonomy index from the Self-Regulation Questionnaire-Academic and modeled engagement as behavioral, emotional, cognitive, and agentic factors.
key_sources: Evans, P., Vansteenkiste, M., Parker, P., Kingsford-Smith, A., & Zhou, S. (2024). Cognitive Load Theory and Its Relationships with Motivation: a Self-Determination Theory Perspective. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09841-2

article_title: Cognitive Load Theory and Its Relationships with Motivation: a Self-Determination Theory Perspective
citation: Evans, P., Vansteenkiste, M., Parker, P., Kingsford-Smith, A., & Zhou, S. (2024). Cognitive Load Theory and Its Relationships with Motivation: a Self-Determination Theory Perspective. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09841-2
title: Circumplex model of teachers' motivating styles organized by need support and directiveness
description: Teachers' motivating styles are depicted on a circumplex with two orthogonal dimensions: "the support, relative to the thwarting, of basic needs and the extent to which the teacher takes the lead and is directive or instead transfers the lead to students." The four quadrants represent four overarching teaching styles (autonomy support, structure, control, chaos), each divided into two subareas (attuning, participative; clarifying, guiding; domineering, demanding; awaiting, abandoning), for eight subareas total. Empirically, subareas correlate in sinusoidal patterns with outcomes, with peaks at need-supportive areas and decreasingly positive or negative correlations toward need-thwarting areas.
requirements: Measurement via the SIS vignette instrument (15 vignettes, 60 items) assessing the eight subareas
constraints: Validated previously in Belgian samples and here with Australian students; the demanding subarea's correlates were ambiguous in this data
target_learning_goals: motivation, engagement, and achievement in classroom learning
examples: Multidimensional scaling of SIS items confirmed the circular arrangement around the need-support and directiveness dimensions, comparable to previous research.
key_sources: Evans, P., Vansteenkiste, M., Parker, P., Kingsford-Smith, A., & Zhou, S. (2024). Cognitive Load Theory and Its Relationships with Motivation: a Self-Determination Theory Perspective. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09841-2

article_title: Cognitive Load Theory and Its Relationships with Motivation: a Self-Determination Theory Perspective
citation: Evans, P., Vansteenkiste, M., Parker, P., Kingsford-Smith, A., & Zhou, S. (2024). Cognitive Load Theory and Its Relationships with Motivation: a Self-Determination Theory Perspective. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09841-2
title: Teachers can combine load-reducing instructional strategies with an autonomy-supportive, structured motivating style, since the same strategies reduce cognitive load and support autonomous motivation
description: The article concludes that strategies for motivating students and strategies for reducing cognitive load are not antagonistic: "the same strategies that support students' autonomous motivation can also be those that minimize extraneous cognitive load." Teachers should use load reduction instruction (reducing difficulty, scaffolding, practice, feedback, guided independent work) while adopting motivating styles high in autonomy support and structure, because control and chaos pose risks of increased load and reduced motivation and engagement.
requirements: Teachers able to enact load reduction instruction principles and autonomy-supportive, structured motivating styles in whole-class settings
constraints: Evidence is cross-sectional and correlational; the article notes minimal risk for motivation and engagement from load-reducing strategies but causal conclusions await longitudinal designs
target_learning_goals: reducing extraneous cognitive load while fostering autonomous motivation, engagement, and achievement
examples: In the survey of 88 classes, student-perceived load reduction instruction correlated negatively with extraneous load (r = -.679) and positively with engagement (r = .646).
key_sources: Evans, P., Vansteenkiste, M., Parker, P., Kingsford-Smith, A., & Zhou, S. (2024). Cognitive Load Theory and Its Relationships with Motivation: a Self-Determination Theory Perspective. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09841-2

article_title: Cognitive Load Theory and Its Relationships with Motivation: a Self-Determination Theory Perspective
citation: Evans, P., Vansteenkiste, M., Parker, P., Kingsford-Smith, A., & Zhou, S. (2024). Cognitive Load Theory and Its Relationships with Motivation: a Self-Determination Theory Perspective. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09841-2
title: Load Reduction Instruction (LRI) framework of five instructional principles
description: Load reduction instruction integrates cognitive load theory findings into "a framework of instructional principles hypothesized to reduce cognitive load: reduce difficulty, provide support and scaffolding, create opportunities for practice, give useful feedback, and design guided, independent projects when learners have sufficient prior knowledge to experience success." It is measured by the 25-item LRIS as a higher-order factor with five principle subscales, validated with high school students and positively associated with motivation and achievement across school subjects.
requirements: Student survey measurement via the LRIS; the principles vary in effectiveness depending on the prior knowledge of the learner (Kalyuga, 2007)
constraints: Guided independent projects are recommended only when learners have sufficient prior knowledge to experience success
target_learning_goals: reducing extraneous and intrinsic cognitive load in classroom instruction
examples: Sample LRIS items include "when we learn new things in class, the teacher makes it easy at first" and "once we know what we're doing in this class, the teacher gives us schoolwork to figure it out by ourselves."
key_sources: Evans, P., Vansteenkiste, M., Parker, P., Kingsford-Smith, A., & Zhou, S. (2024). Cognitive Load Theory and Its Relationships with Motivation: a Self-Determination Theory Perspective. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09841-2

article_title: Effects of Nature (Greenspace) on Cognitive Functioning in School Children and Adolescents: a Systematic Review
citation: Dianne A. Vella-Brodrick · Krystyna Gilowska. (2022). Effects of Nature (Greenspace) on Cognitive Functioning in School Children and Adolescents: a Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review (2022) 34:1217–1254. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09658-5
title: Attention Restoration Theory, Stress Reduction Theory and the Biophilia hypothesis as complementary accounts of nature's cognitive benefits
description: The review organizes underlying mechanisms around three theoretical perspectives, each "a distinctive but complementary explanation for why nature could benefit cognitive functioning". Attention Restoration Theory holds that natural environments elicit "soft fascination" that releases goal-directed attention and permits cognitive restoration; Stress Reduction Theory proposes that physiological stress reduction induced by nature enhances cognition; the Biophilia hypothesis posits an innate drive to affiliate with nature for survival and psychological restoration. The review maps included studies to these frameworks using corresponding measures such as the Perceived Restorativeness Scale, vagal tone and affect scales.
requirements: Studies testing these theories employ corresponding measurement approaches, e.g. perceived restorativeness scales, physiological stress instruments, and eye-tracking for soft fascination
constraints: The review notes Stevenson et al. found no significant difference on executive attention, which is central to ART, and that van den Berg et al. provided no additional support for ART
target_learning_goals: attention and cognitive restoration
stress reduction supporting learning
examples: Amicone et al.'s studies reported higher Perceived Restorativeness Scale scores for natural than built environments; Stevenson et al. used mobile eye-tracking and found more eye fixations per minute in nature, which the authors linked to soft fascination
