article_title: The Theory of Immersive Collaborative Learning (TICOL)
citation: Guido Makransky · Gustav Bøg Petersen. (2023). The Theory of Immersive Collaborative Learning (TICOL). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09822-5
title: TICOL: a theory of immersive collaborative learning organized around four psychological factors
description: TICOL is a theoretical framework describing how collaboration through head-mounted-display immersive media differs from collaboration through traditional systems such as laptops. It proposes that technological features, social affordances, and pedagogical techniques foster four psychological factors—social presence, physical presence, body ownership, and agency—which the authors hypothesize influence the quality of cognitive and socio-emotional social interaction, the social space, and ultimately learning outcomes through ten hypothesized paths. The article states: "In TICOL, we propose that technological features, social affordances, and pedagogical techniques can foster four psychological factors that we define as fundamentally different in XRCL compared to collaboration that occurs through traditional systems (e.g., laptops)". TICOL builds on CSCL frameworks (Kreijns et al.), collaborative cognitive load theory, the immersion principle in multimedia learning, and CAMIL.
requirements: XRCL environments accessed through head-mounted displays, where two or more people interact via avatars with the objective of learning
constraints: The authors state XRCL research is in its infancy and present TICOL as hypotheses to be empirically challenged and built on, not tested predictions
target_learners: distributed learners collaborating across locations, e.g., higher education students
target_learning_goals: collaborative knowledge construction and co-construction of knowledge and skills
examples: The framework is illustrated with examples such as co-constructing an enlarged virtual cell during a virtual tour through the human bloodstream, and the Engage VR meet-and-greet high-five affordance
key_sources: Guido Makransky · Gustav Bøg Petersen. (2023). The Theory of Immersive Collaborative Learning (TICOL). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09822-5

article_title: The Landscape of Research on Prior Knowledge and Learning: a Bibliometric Analysis
citation: Bittermann, A., McNamara, D., Simonsmeier, B. A., & Schneider, M. (2023). The Landscape of Research on Prior Knowledge and Learning: a Bibliometric Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09775-9
title: Multidimensional Knowledge in Text Comprehension (MDK-C) framework
description: The MDK-C framework describes how four dimensions of prior knowledge — amount, accuracy, specificity, and coherence — determine learners' understanding of texts. It assumes prior content knowledge is represented as a multidimensional mental model or semantic network in which spreading activation makes semantically related and interconnected knowledge more likely, and faster, to be activated. The article presents it as a recent development aimed at enabling more nuanced predictions about knowledge use during comprehension.
requirements: Clearer definitions and boundaries around the dimensions of prior knowledge, which the article states is the framework's underlying motivation
constraints: The framework concerns text and discourse comprehension specifically, not learning in general
target_learners: readers of texts and discourse, including students in comprehension research
target_learning_goals: text and discourse comprehension supported by prior knowledge
examples: The article cites the framework (McCarthy & McNamara, 2021) as an example of recent work distinguishing amount, accuracy, specificity, and coherence of prior knowledge

article_title: Looking Beyond the Hype: Understanding the Effects of AI on Learning
citation: Bauer, E., Greiff, S., Graesser, A. C., Scheiter, K., & Sailer, M. (2025). Looking Beyond the Hype: Understanding the Effects of AI on Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10020-8
title: ISAR model of four types of AI effects on learning: inversion, substitution, augmentation, and redefinition
description: The ISAR model classifies four types of AI effects on learning compared to non-AI conditions. It builds on the SAMR model and an ICAP-inspired SAMR model, retaining substitution, augmentation, and redefinition as mechanisms the authors say were 'empirically supported by a second-order meta-analysis on technology-enhanced learning', and adds inversion effects, 'referring to reduced cognitive learning when learners over-rely on AI'. The model is used to classify AI implementations and define research directions for AI-enhanced learning.
requirements: Requires explicit comparison conditions to assess when and where AI provides instructional benefits over non-AI-enhanced instruction
constraints: The article states the model's assumption is that the greater the instructional enhancement relative to a comparison condition, the greater the transformative potential, but implementations must avoid inversion effects
target_learning_goals: cognitive learning processes and outcomes, including knowledge and skills
key_sources: Bauer, E., Greiff, S., Graesser, A. C., Scheiter, K., & Sailer, M. (2025). Looking Beyond the Hype: Understanding the Effects of AI on Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10020-8

article_title: Looking Beyond the Hype: Understanding the Effects of AI on Learning
citation: Bauer, E., Greiff, S., Graesser, A. C., Scheiter, K., & Sailer, M. (2025). Looking Beyond the Hype: Understanding the Effects of AI on Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10020-8
title: Mitigate AI over-reliance by keeping learners actively engaged in reflective processes before or during AI output generation
description: This principle holds that risks of learners uncritically accepting AI outputs can be reduced by structuring reflective human input around AI use. The article states that "the risks of over-reliance on potentially suboptimal outputs can be mitigated if professionals are actively engaged in reflective processes before or during the generation of AI outputs", citing cognitive forcing functions that elicit initial judgments before AI outputs appear. It recommends designing AI-enhanced learning opportunities that prioritize cognitive engagement.
requirements: Learners or professionals must be prompted to make initial judgments or engage in reflection before or while AI outputs are generated
constraints: The article notes effective prevention strategies in educational contexts are yet to be explored; the supporting evidence comes from workplace learning contexts
target_learning_goals: critical thinking
self-regulated learning
maintaining domain-specific and transversal skills
examples: The article describes cognitive forcing functions that initiate human inputs, such as initial judgments, before AI outputs are generated, and notes explanations accompanying AI outputs can help users critically assess information

article_title: The More the Better? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Benefits of More than Two External Representations in STEM Education
citation: Rexigel, E., Kuhn, J., Becker, S., & Malone, S. (2024). The More the Better? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Benefits of More than Two External Representations in STEM Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09958-y
title: The DeFT framework: design parameters, functions, and tasks of multirepresentational learning
description: The Design, Functions, and Tasks (DeFT) framework (Ainsworth, 2006) is an overarching framework for describing external representation compositions of any kind and making assumptions about their usage. Its design parameters are "the number of representations, the distribution of information among the representations, the form of the representations, the sequence of their presentation, and the provision of support to translate between representations." Its functions component holds that MERs can complement each other, constrain each other's interpretation, and help learners construct deeper understanding; its tasks component relates to the cognitive activities learners engage in when using representations. The review uses DeFT to organize its moderator analysis.
requirements: Learners need to understand how information is encoded within each provided representation and how to relate the individual representations to each other.
target_learners: Students in STEM education at primary, secondary, and postsecondary levels
target_learning_goals: Conceptual knowledge and problem-solving with multiple external representations
examples: The review coded the presence of support, mode of presentation, and informational redundancy of MERs as moderators following the DeFT framework.
key_sources: Rexigel, E., Kuhn, J., Becker, S., & Malone, S. (2024). The More the Better? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Benefits of More than Two External Representations in STEM Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09958-y

article_title: The More the Better? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Benefits of More than Two External Representations in STEM Education
citation: Rexigel, E., Kuhn, J., Becker, S., & Malone, S. (2024). The More the Better? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Benefits of More than Two External Representations in STEM Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09958-y
title: Three categories of representational competencies for learning with multiple external representations
description: Drawing on Rau (2017), the article distinguishes three categories of representational competencies needed to profit from MERs. Conceptual representational competencies are the abilities and knowledge learners apply when associating an external representation with a specific concept and drawing conclusions from it, including discerning superficial versus conceptually significant similarities between representations. Perceptual representational competencies include visual fluency (effortlessly reading a representation) and connectional fluency (quickly matching and connecting multiple representations). Meta-representational competencies are essential for selecting an appropriate representation according to the task and one's own abilities. These skills can be developed through targeted interactions with representations.
requirements: To benefit from MERs, learners need representational competence; when it is lacking, students face a representational dilemma of learning unfamiliar content from as-yet-unfamiliar representations.
constraints: Representational competencies are rarely studied as outcomes of learning with multimedia educational resources.
target_learners: Students of any age learning with multiple external representations
target_learning_goals: Developing representational competencies for learning and problem-solving with MERs
examples: The article cites eye-tracking studies showing different combinations of representations triggered distinct processing of mathematical problems.
key_sources: Rexigel, E., Kuhn, J., Becker, S., & Malone, S. (2024). The More the Better? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Benefits of More than Two External Representations in STEM Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09958-y

article_title: The More the Better? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Benefits of More than Two External Representations in STEM Education
citation: Rexigel, E., Kuhn, J., Becker, S., & Malone, S. (2024). The More the Better? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Benefits of More than Two External Representations in STEM Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09958-y
title: Systematic review corpus of 46 STEM studies on more than two external representations
description: The article's evidence base is a systematic review corpus of 46 eligible studies identified through searches of Scopus, ERIC, and PsycINFO plus conference proceedings (AERA, EARLI, ICLS, ESERA, NARST), "comprising 170 individual measurements." Studies were screened by two independent raters against eight predefined inclusion criteria using Rayyan. Of the 46 studies, 23 were selected for the meta-analysis based on having a control group with two or fewer representations, sufficient data to calculate effect sizes, and a focus on students' learning. Publication years spanned 1984 to 2022, and contexts included mathematics, electrical engineering, chemistry, biology, physics, and computer science.
requirements: Included studies required a comparative design, students of any age, STEM scope, cognitive outcomes, at least one condition with more than two external representations, and data allowing effect-size calculation.
constraints: Only a few of the included studies investigate students' problem-solving with MERs, and studies solely investigating learning with different types of more than two representations are sparse.
target_learners: Students of any age in STEM education
target_learning_goals: Learning and problem-solving with multiple external representations
examples: The Results section reports a subset of 20 studies for the meta-analysis, while the Method section states 23 studies were selected; the article prints both figures.

article_title: The More the Better? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Benefits of More than Two External Representations in STEM Education
citation: Rexigel, E., Kuhn, J., Becker, S., & Malone, S. (2024). The More the Better? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Benefits of More than Two External Representations in STEM Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09958-y
title: Do not assume a universal ideal number of external representations; tailor representational sets to learners and context
description: The article explicitly cautions against seeking one optimal number of representations: "it is not reasonable to assume that there is a universal, ideal number of representations for learning and problem-solving in STEM." Because personal and environmental factors vary significantly across individuals and contexts, the meaningful number of representations may vary across contexts and disciplines. Design decisions about how many representations to use should therefore be conditioned on moderators the review identifies, above all the provision of appropriate instructional support, rather than on a fixed rule.
requirements: Design decisions should account for moderating factors such as educational level, instructional support, informational redundancy, mode of presentation, and representational homogeneity.
constraints: The possible influences of including more than two external representations in STEM learning remain unknown in several respects, and future research on representation novelty is needed.
target_learners: Students of any age in STEM education
target_learning_goals: Effective design of multirepresentational learning materials
examples: The review examined educational level, support, mode of presentation, redundancy, and homogeneity as moderators rather than prescribing a fixed number of representations.

article_title: The Relation Between Perceived Mental Effort, Monitoring Judgments, and Learning Outcomes: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Louise David, Felicitas Biwer, Martine Baars, Lisette Wijnia, Fred Paas, Anique de Bruin. (2024). The Relation Between Perceived Mental Effort, Monitoring Judgments, and Learning Outcomes: A Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09903-z
title: Cue-utilization framework for metacognitive monitoring in self-regulated learning
description: The framework holds that learners who cannot access their learning outcomes directly infer them from indirect cues arising from study experiences or materials, such as processing fluency or perceived mental effort. The article states that "three elements are involved in self-regulated learning: cues, monitoring judgments, and actual learning or performance". Cue diagnosticity is the extent to which cues predict outcomes, and monitoring accuracy is the extent to which judgments predict outcomes. The article operationalizes this triangle in its MASEM with perceived mental effort as cue, monitoring judgments as mediator, and learning outcomes as performance approximation.
requirements: Cues, monitoring judgments, and learning outcomes must be measured in the same study or experiment on the same task for the triangular relationships to be estimated
constraints: Often learners utilize cues that are not diagnostic of actual learning outcomes, which the article states leads to inaccurate monitoring
target_learners: learners across education levels, from primary grades to postgraduate education
target_learning_goals: accurate metacognitive monitoring of learning during self-regulated learning
examples: The article specified perceived mental effort as the cue, monitoring judgments as the mediator, and learning outcomes as the outcome in its full mediation MASEM
key_sources: Louise David, Felicitas Biwer, Martine Baars, Lisette Wijnia, Fred Paas, Anique de Bruin. (2024). The Relation Between Perceived Mental Effort, Monitoring Judgments, and Learning Outcomes: A Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09903-z

article_title: The Relation Between Perceived Mental Effort, Monitoring Judgments, and Learning Outcomes: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Louise David, Felicitas Biwer, Martine Baars, Lisette Wijnia, Fred Paas, Anique de Bruin. (2024). The Relation Between Perceived Mental Effort, Monitoring Judgments, and Learning Outcomes: A Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09903-z
title: Open meta-analytic dataset of effort–monitoring–outcome correlations on OSF
description: The authors released the coded meta-analytic dataset underlying the MASEM on the Open Science Framework. It contains extracted Pearson correlations and sample sizes from 35 papers, comprising 83 independent samples and 236 effect sizes (83 effort–monitoring, 77 monitoring–outcome, 76 effort–outcome correlations), with a total sample size of N = 3973. The article states "Our data set can be found on OSF via https:// osf. io/ hc5fk/", and the final coding scheme is likewise available at OSF, supporting reproducibility of the moderator coding.
requirements: Users need the OSF repository access to retrieve the dataset and the final coding scheme
constraints: Only studies measuring perceived mental effort via self-report were included; physiological and behavioral effort indicators were excluded
target_learners: researchers studying metacognitive monitoring and cognitive load
target_learning_goals: secondary analysis and replication of effort–monitoring–outcome relationships
examples: The dataset coded moderators including education level, effort measurement wording, monitoring timing, task type, and task difficulty
key_sources: Louise David, Felicitas Biwer, Martine Baars, Lisette Wijnia, Fred Paas, Anique de Bruin. (2024). The Relation Between Perceived Mental Effort, Monitoring Judgments, and Learning Outcomes: A Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09903-z

article_title: Effects of 8 Weeks with Embodied Learning on 5–6-Year-Old Danish Children’s Pre-reading Skills and Word Reading Skills: the PLAYMORE Project, DK
citation: Linn Damsgaard, Anne-Mette Veber Nielsen, Anne Kær Gejl, Anne Sofie Bøgh Malling, Søren Kildahl Jensen, Jacob Wienecke. (2022). Effects of 8 Weeks with Embodied Learning on 5–6-Year-Old Danish Children's Pre-reading Skills and Word Reading Skills: the PLAYMORE Project, DK. Educational Psychology Review (2022) 34:1709–1737. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09671-8
title: Use high bodily engagement with high task integration as a supplement to handwriting when teaching letter-sound associations
description: The authors recommend that letter-sound instruction combine movements closely integrated with the learning content, since their intervention groups with "high bodily engagement and high task integration" outperformed a handwriting-only control on letter-sound knowledge. The recommendation is explicitly positioned as a supplement to, not a replacement for, handwriting.
requirements: Movements must be meaningfully and congruently coupled to the letter-sounds being learned, performed while pronouncing the sound
constraints: Benefit was shown for letter-sound knowledge, not word reading; the control group still involved handwriting and hearing, described as a lesser degree of embodiment
target_learning_goals: Letter-sound knowledge, including standard and conditional pronunciations
examples: Children in WM stood in a circle making whole-body phoneme movements left to right while pronouncing sounds; HM children made arm-and-hand movements seated; CON children did seated pencil-and-paper activities
key_sources: Linn Damsgaard, Anne-Mette Veber Nielsen, Anne Kær Gejl, Anne Sofie Bøgh Malling, Søren Kildahl Jensen, Jacob Wienecke. (2022). Effects of 8 Weeks with Embodied Learning on 5–6-Year-Old Danish Children's Pre-reading Skills and Word Reading Skills: the PLAYMORE Project, DK. Educational Psychology Review (2022) 34:1709–1737. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09671-8

article_title: Effects of 8 Weeks with Embodied Learning on 5–6-Year-Old Danish Children’s Pre-reading Skills and Word Reading Skills: the PLAYMORE Project, DK
citation: Linn Damsgaard, Anne-Mette Veber Nielsen, Anne Kær Gejl, Anne Sofie Bøgh Malling, Søren Kildahl Jensen, Jacob Wienecke. (2022). Effects of 8 Weeks with Embodied Learning on 5–6-Year-Old Danish Children's Pre-reading Skills and Word Reading Skills: the PLAYMORE Project, DK. Educational Psychology Review (2022) 34:1709–1737. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09671-8
title: Embodied cognition: sensorimotor recruitment supports memory for academic content
description: The article frames its intervention with embodied cognition, the account that "cognitive processes are mental representations derived from our senses" integrated into the sensorimotor system, so that recruiting the motor system during learning can enhance understanding and recall. It draws on the enactment effect — information is memorized better when the learner performs the described action — to explain why movement-coupled letter-sound teaching beat verbal-only teaching.
requirements: Congruence between the bodily movement and the learning task is treated as the key condition for enhanced performance
constraints: High bodily engagement carries a noted risk of cognitive overload, and some researchers suggest a medium degree of interactivity; the article also notes embodied learning need not involve the learner's own body
target_learning_goals: Letter-sound knowledge and early word decoding
examples: The PLAYMORE intervention coupled phoneme movements to letter-sounds, executed left to right in reading direction, with long sounds as slow fluent movements and staccato sounds as fast powerful movements
key_sources: Linn Damsgaard, Anne-Mette Veber Nielsen, Anne Kær Gejl, Anne Sofie Bøgh Malling, Søren Kildahl Jensen, Jacob Wienecke. (2022). Effects of 8 Weeks with Embodied Learning on 5–6-Year-Old Danish Children's Pre-reading Skills and Word Reading Skills: the PLAYMORE Project, DK. Educational Psychology Review (2022) 34:1709–1737. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09671-8

article_title: Relations between Teachers’ and Students’ Social-emotional Competence: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-analysis
citation: Nguyen, T.-A., Hidajat, T., Zhou, T., Ma, T., Hoang, A., Poed, S., & Edwards, E. J. (2026). Relations between Teachers' and Students' Social-emotional Competence: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10218-4
title: CASEL five-domain framework of social-emotional competence as the review's organizing taxonomy
description: The review adopts the CASEL framework as its multidimensional conceptual model for classifying teachers' and students' SEC. The article states that "The CASEL framework conceptualises SEC as five distinct yet interrelated domains (self-awareness, self-management, social awareness, relationship skills, and responsible decision-making; CASEL, 2020)." Constructs were coded as domain-specific or broad/mixed SEC based on definitions and measurement content rather than authors' labels, with interrater reliability of κ = 0.87 for teacher codes and κ = 0.85 for student codes. The framework enabled domain-specific meta-analytic models of teacher-student SEC associations.
requirements: Studies must report SEC constructs mappable to CASEL domains, coded by construct definitions and measurement content rather than scale labels
constraints: SEC domains are conceptually related rather than fully discrete, and some overlap between categories is theoretically expected
Constructs spanning three or more domains were coded as broad SEC rather than a discrete domain
target_learners: K-12 students from preschool/kindergarten to upper secondary
target_learning_goals: Social-emotional competence across self-awareness, self-management, social awareness, relationship skills, and responsible decision-making
examples: Coding mapped constructs such as teachers' caring to responsible decision-making or relationship skills depending on dominant conceptual function
key_sources: Nguyen, T.-A., Hidajat, T., Zhou, T., Ma, T., Hoang, A., Poed, S., & Edwards, E. J. (2026). Relations between Teachers' and Students' Social-emotional Competence: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10218-4

article_title: Relations between Teachers’ and Students’ Social-emotional Competence: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-analysis
citation: Nguyen, T.-A., Hidajat, T., Zhou, T., Ma, T., Hoang, A., Poed, S., & Edwards, E. J. (2026). Relations between Teachers' and Students' Social-emotional Competence: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10218-4
title: Socialisation, co-regulation, and prosocial classroom mechanisms linking teacher SEC to student SEC
description: The review organises explanatory accounts of the teacher-student SEC link into three named frameworks. It states "Teachers are often viewed as socialisers of students' emotions (Denham et al., 2012), a process by which children learn culturally acceptable knowledge, values, and skills about social and emotional situations from a significant adult (Eisenberg et al., 1998)." The Co-regulation Framework holds that teachers guide students' social and emotional behaviours towards shared goals shaped by teachers' emotional schemas, while Jennings and Greenberg's prosocial classroom framework proposes reciprocal interaction through teachers' well-being, relationships, classroom management, SEL programs, and climate. The review notes less theoretical work has examined the reverse pathway from student SEC to teacher SEC.
requirements: Mechanisms operate through teachers modelling competencies, providing effective SEL, and responding supportively rather than dismissively to students' emotions
constraints: Empirical findings on the prosocial classroom mechanisms are mixed, with discrepancies partly attributable to common method bias of self-reports versus more objective tools
Less theoretical work has examined how student SEC may influence teacher SEC
target_learning_goals: Development of students' social-emotional competence through teacher modelling, co-regulation, and classroom climate
examples: A teacher with strong self- and social awareness who views emotions as teachable opportunities may respond to a heated group dispute by calmly labelling feelings and scaffolding problem-solving
key_sources: Nguyen, T.-A., Hidajat, T., Zhou, T., Ma, T., Hoang, A., Poed, S., & Edwards, E. J. (2026). Relations between Teachers' and Students' Social-emotional Competence: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10218-4

article_title: Multi-Level Meta-Analysis of Physical Activity Interventions During Childhood: Effects of Physical Activity on Cognition and Academic Achievement
citation: Vasilopoulos, F., Jeffrey, H., Wu, Y., & Dumontheil, I. (2023). Multi-Level Meta-Analysis of Physical Activity Interventions During Childhood: Effects of Physical Activity on Cognition and Academic Achievement. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09760-2
title: Differential mechanisms of impact of different types of physical activity on different aspects of cognition
description: This account holds that different categories of physical activity affect different cognitive and academic outcomes through distinct mechanisms, rather than PA acting as a uniform cognitive enhancer. The meta-analysis found that "aerobic PA with moderate to vigorous intensity benefitted executive function outcomes", while PA integrated with academic instruction benefited mathematics and enriched PA programmes benefited language. The article situates this within cognitive explanations for change, including the skills acquisition theory, which "postulates that the motor and cognitive complexity of PA influence cognitive processes", and embodied cognition. It frames dose–response characteristics (intensity, duration, frequency, type) as the levers that select which outcome is affected.
requirements: Interventions must be characterised by type, intensity, duration and frequency so that dose–response moderators can be distinguished
constraints: Moderator analyses were exploratory and heterogeneity was high; on-task behaviour had an insufficient sample size for moderator analysis
target_learning_goals: Executive functions (working memory, inhibitory control, cognitive flexibility, attention, planning)
Fluid intelligence, creativity, on-task behaviour, mathematics and language achievement
examples: The meta-analysis contrasted PA with academic instruction, aerobic, sports, cognitively enriched, dance, PE and holistic movement interventions as distinct activity types
key_sources: Vasilopoulos, F., Jeffrey, H., Wu, Y., & Dumontheil, I. (2023). Multi-Level Meta-Analysis of Physical Activity Interventions During Childhood: Effects of Physical Activity on Cognition and Academic Achievement. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09760-2

article_title: Multi-Level Meta-Analysis of Physical Activity Interventions During Childhood: Effects of Physical Activity on Cognition and Academic Achievement
citation: Vasilopoulos, F., Jeffrey, H., Wu, Y., & Dumontheil, I. (2023). Multi-Level Meta-Analysis of Physical Activity Interventions During Childhood: Effects of Physical Activity on Cognition and Academic Achievement. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09760-2
title: Match the type of physical activity integration to the targeted outcome: embed PA in academic instruction for mathematics and use enriched PA for language
description: This principle recommends selecting the form of school-based physical activity according to the outcome a designer wants to improve, because the meta-analysis found outcome-specific moderator patterns. PA combined with academic instruction — for example children answering a sum by moving as many times as the answer — showed significant mathematics benefits (g = 0.32), while enriched PA programmes benefited language outcomes. The article's own conclusion is that "These results therefore suggest differential mechanisms of impact of different types of PA on different aspects of cognition", so a single PA format cannot be assumed to serve all academic goals.
requirements: Interventions need at least three sessions over more than one week, as single bouts were excluded from the evidence base
constraints: The mathematics benefit was observed for 6–10-week interventions of moderate or moderate-to-vigorous intensity; moderator analyses were exploratory with high heterogeneity
target_learners: Typically developing primary-school children aged 5–12 years
target_learning_goals: Mathematics achievement
Language achievement
examples: Close integration examples in the article include giving the answer to a sum by star jumps or jumping on letters to spell a word; the moderator analysis found PA with academic instruction constituted 67% of AA effect sizes
key_sources: Vasilopoulos, F., Jeffrey, H., Wu, Y., & Dumontheil, I. (2023). Multi-Level Meta-Analysis of Physical Activity Interventions During Childhood: Effects of Physical Activity on Cognition and Academic Achievement. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09760-2

article_title: The Value of Pretend Play for Social Competence in Early Childhood: A Meta-analysis
citation: Smits-van der Nat, M., van der Wilt, F., Meeter, M., & van der Veen, C. (2024). The Value of Pretend Play for Social Competence in Early Childhood: A Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09884-z
title: Vygotsky's cultural-historical activity theory account of pretend play as a context for social competence development
description: Cultural-historical activity theory (CHAT) holds that children develop higher mental functions, such as social competence, through collaborative participation in socio-cultural practices. In early childhood settings these practices (a restaurant, supermarket, bookshop, or museum) are often imitated within pretend play, where children imitate adults engaging in socially desirable behavior and practice negotiating play themes, social roles, and rules. The meta-analysis frames its hypothesis in these terms and interprets the age moderation as possible confirmation of the CHAT tenet that the 3–6 year period is crucial.
requirements: Engagement in pretend play in which children re-enact the surrounding socio-cultural world, typically within early childhood education and care contexts
constraints: The article states empirical support for the causal conjecture is limited and that no claims of causality can be drawn from the correlational evidence
target_learners: Children aged 3–8 years in early childhood education and care
target_learning_goals: Social competence, including negotiating play themes, social roles, and rules and solving peer conflicts
examples: The meta-analysis of 34 studies tested the CHAT-derived hypothesis that pretend play is positively related to children's social competence
key_sources: Smits-van der Nat, M., van der Wilt, F., Meeter, M., & van der Veen, C. (2024). The Value of Pretend Play for Social Competence in Early Childhood: A Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09884-z

article_title: The Value of Pretend Play for Social Competence in Early Childhood: A Meta-analysis
citation: Smits-van der Nat, M., van der Wilt, F., Meeter, M., & van der Veen, C. (2024). The Value of Pretend Play for Social Competence in Early Childhood: A Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09884-z
title: Prism model of social competence with three layers and five underlying skills
description: The meta-analysis defines social competence using the prism model developed by Rose-Krasnor (1997) and elaborated by Junge et al. (2020), which consists of three layers: a theoretical layer defining social competence as successful participation in interactions, an indexical layer of behavioral manifestations such as sociometric status and prosocial behavior, and a skills layer of underlying skills. The five identified skills are social encoding, social problem solving, emotion regulation, communicative competence, and empathy. The meta-analysis used this model to categorize the social competence measures of the included studies into underlying skills and indices.
requirements: Measurement of social competence must be mapped onto one of the model's layers, as the meta-analysis did when coding included studies
constraints: The article notes social competence is a complex and multifaceted construct, and that the extensive variety in operationalization across studies made comparing studies difficult
target_learners: Children aged 3–8 years in early childhood education and care
target_learning_goals: Social competence, spanning underlying skills (social encoding, social problem solving, emotion regulation, communicative competence, empathy) and indices (social behavior, sociometric status)
examples: The meta-analysis coded the 34 included studies' social competence outcomes as either underlying skills (21 studies) or indices (23 studies) of the prism model
key_sources: Smits-van der Nat, M., van der Wilt, F., Meeter, M., & van der Veen, C. (2024). The Value of Pretend Play for Social Competence in Early Childhood: A Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09884-z

article_title: Is Boredom the Opposite of Interest? A Longitudinal Reciprocal Effect Study
citation: Katharina Luisa Boehme, Thomas Goetz, Markus Feuchter, Franzis Preckel. (2025). Is Boredom the Opposite of Interest? A Longitudinal Reciprocal Effect Study. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09991-5
title: Boredom and lack of interest as distinct constructs with different emotional and motivational consequences
description: The article's conceptual framework holds that although boredom and interest overlap phenomenologically, boredom is not the absence of interest. Lack of interest is affectively neutral, whereas boredom is an unpleasant, aversive state with low arousal that provokes avoidance motivation and the wish to escape the situation; lack of interest implies only an absence of approach motivation. The framework also holds that academic boredom and interest are domain-specific and that boredom arises from interactions of task, person (value and perceived control), and environment characteristics, whereas interest is object-specific. The study's CFA and cross-lagged results are presented as empirical support for this separability.
requirements: Measurement models must establish at least metric longitudinal measurement invariance before interpreting stability and cross-lagged path coefficients, and scalar invariance for comparing latent means
constraints: The empirical evidence comes from upper-track German Gymnasium students in mathematics and German only; the article notes limited evidence of between-domain predictive patterns except in grade 5
target_learners: secondary school students in upper-track German Gymnasium, grades 5–8
target_learning_goals: students' academic emotions and motivational development in mathematics and German
examples: The study operationalised boredom with two AEQ-M items and interest with a three-item PALMA scale, rated on 5-point Likert scales, across four waves
key_sources: Katharina Luisa Boehme, Thomas Goetz, Markus Feuchter, Franzis Preckel. (2025). Is Boredom the Opposite of Interest? A Longitudinal Reciprocal Effect Study. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09991-5

article_title: Is Empathy the Key to Effective Teaching? A Systematic Review of Its Association with Teacher-Student Interactions and Student Outcomes
citation: Karen Aldrup · Bastian Carstensen · Uta Klusmann. (2022). Is Empathy the Key to Effective Teaching? A Systematic Review of Its Association with Teacher-Student Interactions and Student Outcomes. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09649-y
title: Heuristic working model linking teacher empathy to interaction quality and student outcomes (based on the prosocial classroom model)
description: The review proposes a heuristic working model (Fig. 1), largely based on the prosocial classroom model (Jennings & Greenberg, 2009), in which teacher empathy — defined as including both "affective and cognitive components" — supports high-quality teacher-student interactions, especially emotional support, and thereby indirectly fosters student development. Cognitive empathy enables reading students' nonverbal signals and understanding their perspectives; affective empathy motivates sensitive responses. Expected associations are strongest for emotional support and weakest for student achievement.
requirements: Empathy must be measured in accordance with the review's dual-component (affective plus cognitive) definition; fantasy and personal distress subscales were excluded as not measuring empathy
constraints: The model is heuristic; the review found empirical support only for the empathy–bullying-intervention path, not consistently for emotional support, classroom management, instructional support, or student outcomes
target_learners: teachers from preschool to tertiary education
target_learning_goals: quality of teacher-student interactions (emotional support, classroom management, instructional support) and student cognitive and psychosocial development
key_sources: Karen Aldrup · Bastian Carstensen · Uta Klusmann. (2022). Is Empathy the Key to Effective Teaching? A Systematic Review of Its Association with Teacher-Student Interactions and Student Outcomes. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09649-y

article_title: Active Student Participation in Whole-School Interventions in Secondary School. A Systematic Literature Review
citation: Sara Berti, Valentina Grazia, Luisa Molinari. (2023). Active Student Participation in Whole-School Interventions in Secondary School. A Systematic Literature Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09773-x
title: Five-level scale of Active Student Participation (ASP) in whole-school intervention activities
description: The review proposes an organizing structure that grades program activities on a 5-point scale of active student participation, partly following the school participation scale of the HBSC questionnaire (De Róiste et al., 2012). As the review states, "It ranged from Very high levels of ASP, attributed to activities in which students were given a fully decision-making role, to Very low levels of ASP, given to activities in which students were just the recipients of activities delivered by adults." Very high ASP covers decision-making processes and school action teams with students; high ASP covers student artifacts, student-led activities for peers and for adults; moderate ASP covers platforms, interactive assemblies and data collection; low ASP covers trainings, group and individual activities within adult-designed formats. Levels are not mutually exclusive, and coding was based on the qualitative analysis of students' role, not the number of students involved.
requirements: Activities must be coded by qualitative analysis of the role attributed to students, not by the number of students involved
Levels are not mutually exclusive, so each program may include different levels of ASP
constraints: In the reviewed sample, no program involved students solely as passive recipients (Very low ASP), since such studies were excluded by the inclusion criteria
target_learning_goals: student participation in school activities and decision-making
improving the school learning environment
examples: The review coded all 13 programs on this scale (Table 5): e.g., SEHER included activities at every level from decision-making committees to teacher-led workshops, while STAC's activities were limited to peer-leader trainings
key_sources: Sara Berti, Valentina Grazia, Luisa Molinari. (2023). Active Student Participation in Whole-School Interventions in Secondary School. A Systematic Literature Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09773-x

article_title: Self-Regulation Competence as a Superpower: An Integrated Framework for K-12
citation: Ulrich Trautwein, Janina Eberhart, Charlotte Dignath, Cavan V. Bonner, Brent W. Roberts. (2026). Self-Regulation Competence as a Superpower: An Integrated Framework for K-12. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10190-z
title: Integrated multicomponent model of self-regulation competence unifying SRL, executive functions, and conscientiousness
description: The article proposes an integrated multicomponent model that treats self-regulation competence as a broad, integrative capacity encompassing cognitive, motivational, affective, and behavioral components, uniting the SRL, EF, and conscientiousness research traditions. It rests on three propositions: the construct predicts broad outcomes, the three traditions share a core of "goal-directedness, monitoring, and control", and the construct is malleable through instruction. The model frames self-regulation competence as a developmental "superpower" that schools can deliberately cultivate.
requirements: Integration requires sufficient conceptual and empirical overlap among SRL, EFs, and conscientiousness to warrant grouping them under one construct
Evidence must show the construct predicts a broad range of educational and developmental outcomes
constraints: The authors acknowledge parts of the multicomponent-promotion argument are somewhat more speculative and essentially a task for the future
EF components, particularly working memory beyond early childhood, are seen as difficult to train
target_learning_goals: Self-regulation competence: monitoring and controlling cognition, emotion, and behavior adaptively to achieve personal goals
examples: The article reviews three research traditions—SRL in educational psychology, EFs in developmental psychology, and conscientiousness in personality psychology—and reports its own 313-student canonical correlation study of their overlap.
key_sources: Ulrich Trautwein, Janina Eberhart, Charlotte Dignath, Cavan V. Bonner, Brent W. Roberts. (2026). Self-Regulation Competence as a Superpower: An Integrated Framework for K-12. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10190-z

article_title: Measuring Children’s Engagement in Early Childhood Education and Care Settings: A Scoping Literature Review
citation: Ritoša, A., Åström, F., Björck, E., Borglund, L., Karlsson, E., McHugh, E., & Nylander, E. (2023). Measuring Children's Engagement in Early Childhood Education and Care Settings: A Scoping Literature Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09815-4
title: State–trait temporality as an organizing axis of child engagement conceptualization and measurement in ECEC
description: The review organizes variation in engagement measurement around assumptions about temporality: engagement can be treated as a momentary, transient state of immersion in an activity, assessed by observations and experience sampling, or as a relatively stable tendency to behave in certain ways, assessed by questionnaires about typical behavior. It concludes that "the variations in the observational schedules, such as duration and number of observations in measuring child engagement, reflect a variety in the conceptualizations of child engagement on a state-trait continuum." This axis explains why observation schedules differ so widely across studies.
requirements: Researchers must make their temporal assumptions about engagement explicit when choosing observation duration, frequency, or questionnaire format.
constraints: The review notes conceptualizations do not always match the measurement approach, e.g., few definitions of academic engagement described it as a stable trait despite survey measurement.
target_learners: young children (approximately ages 1–6) attending ECEC settings
target_learning_goals: measuring and understanding children's engagement in learning activities
examples: The review reports 10- or 15-second time sampling in 10-minute observations as the most common time frame, with short observations repeated and averaged to obtain individual engagement scores.
key_sources: Ritoša, A., Åström, F., Björck, E., Borglund, L., Karlsson, E., McHugh, E., & Nylander, E. (2023). Measuring Children's Engagement in Early Childhood Education and Care Settings: A Scoping Literature Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09815-4

article_title: Measuring Children’s Engagement in Early Childhood Education and Care Settings: A Scoping Literature Review
citation: Ritoša, A., Åström, F., Björck, E., Borglund, L., Karlsson, E., McHugh, E., & Nylander, E. (2023). Measuring Children's Engagement in Early Childhood Education and Care Settings: A Scoping Literature Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09815-4
title: Inventory of 77 established measures of young children's engagement in ECEC (Table 4)
description: The review compiles a categorized inventory of 77 unique established measures of child engagement in ECEC, grouped by measured concept (engagement, involvement, academic, social, task, joint, negative, reading, play, music, and computer engagement), with method (observation or survey), informant, and notes on subscales, dimensions, and school-age origin. It reports that "Of the identified engagement measurements, 202 relied on established measures of child engagement," and that five established tools were general observational protocols or software adapted to include child engagement. The inventory is presented in Table 4 with references in supplementary material.
requirements: Users should consult the supplementary reference list, as an existing citation indicated but did not guarantee that a measure was validated in earlier publications.
constraints: The review notes about one-third of established survey measures were primarily intended for school-aged children but were used in ECEC settings in the identified studies.
target_learners: young children attending ECEC, preschool, kindergarten, or pre-K settings
target_learning_goals: quantitative assessment of child engagement and involvement in ECEC
examples: Examples include the Leuven Involvement Scale for Young Children (LIS-YC, used in 15 studies) and the Individualized Classroom Assessment Scoring System (InCLASS, used in 22 studies).
key_sources: Ritoša, A., Åström, F., Björck, E., Borglund, L., Karlsson, E., McHugh, E., & Nylander, E. (2023). Measuring Children's Engagement in Early Childhood Education and Care Settings: A Scoping Literature Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09815-4

article_title: Linking Disparate Strands: A Critical Review of the Relationship Between Creativity and Education
citation: Bruce S. Rawlings & Sarah J. Cutting. (2024). Linking Disparate Strands: A Critical Review of the Relationship Between Creativity and Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09973-z
title: Divergent and convergent thinking as the two core components of creativity used to organize the education–creativity debate
description: The review organizes its synthesis around a two-component account of creativity as "the ability to generate novel and useful ideas", comprising "divergent thinking—the capacity to produce multiple novel ideas, solutions or possibilities" and "convergent thinking—homing in on single, correct solutions from a range of options". Divergent thinking involves fluent, original, flexible and elaborate production; convergent thinking requires logical thinking, accuracy, precision and deduction to evaluate and select optimal solutions. Both are required for creativity, yet divergent thinking has received far more scientific focus and is often used as a proxy for overall creative ability.
requirements: Both divergent and convergent thinking are required for creativity; the former produces novel ideas and the latter evaluates them to optimise value
constraints: The review restricts its scope to divergent and convergent thinking because they are the most widely used creativity measures in education, setting aside debates over the validity and reliability of other creativity measures
target_learning_goals: creative thinking
divergent idea generation
evaluative and convergent problem solving
examples: The PISA 2022 Assessment and Analytical Framework breaks creative thinking into generating diverse ideas, generating creative ideas, and evaluating and improving ideas—facets the review says are captured by both divergent and convergent thinking
key_sources: Bruce S. Rawlings & Sarah J. Cutting. (2024). Linking Disparate Strands: A Critical Review of the Relationship Between Creativity and Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09973-z

article_title: Comparing Mental Effort, Difficulty, and Confidence Appraisals in Problem-Solving: A Metacognitive Perspective
citation: Emely Hoch, Yael Sidi, Rakefet Ackerman, Vincent Hoogerheide, Katharina Scheiter. (2023). Comparing Mental Effort, Difficulty, and Confidence Appraisals in Problem-Solving: A Metacognitive Perspective. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09779-5
title: Goal-driven versus data-driven effort as two framings of mental effort appraisals
description: The article applies Koriat et al.'s distinction to CLT self-report items: effort phrased as personal investment captures "goal-driven effort", which "relies on top-down processing, reflecting voluntary decisions made by learners", whereas effort phrased as task demand captures "data-driven effort", based on bottom-up task characteristics the learner cannot control, similar to difficulty. The study operationalized these as two distinct appraisal conditions and tested their differential relationships with response time and accuracy.
requirements: Appraisal items must be phrased to distinguish voluntary investment of effort from effort the task demands, as in the article's two effort conditions
constraints: The article notes the intrinsic/extrinsic load-type distinction and germane load as a category are under debate in the CLT literature, and focuses on the classic framing of mental effort
target_learners: Adult problem-solvers in online reasoning experiments (Prolific participants)
target_learning_goals: Metacognitive monitoring of effort, difficulty, and confidence during problem solving
examples: Experiment 1 used the goal-driven phrasing "How much effort did you invest in solving the problem?" and the data-driven phrasing "How much effort did the problem require?" on 0–100 sliders
key_sources: Emely Hoch, Yael Sidi, Rakefet Ackerman, Vincent Hoogerheide, Katharina Scheiter. (2023). Comparing Mental Effort, Difficulty, and Confidence Appraisals in Problem-Solving: A Metacognitive Perspective. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09779-5

article_title: Comparing Mental Effort, Difficulty, and Confidence Appraisals in Problem-Solving: A Metacognitive Perspective
citation: Emely Hoch, Yael Sidi, Rakefet Ackerman, Vincent Hoogerheide, Katharina Scheiter. (2023). Comparing Mental Effort, Difficulty, and Confidence Appraisals in Problem-Solving: A Metacognitive Perspective. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09779-5
title: Treat mental effort and difficulty self-reports as heuristic metacognitive appraisals rather than reliable reflections of cognitive load
description: The article argues that load-related self-reports should be interpreted through the metacognitive cue-utilization lens: like confidence judgments, they are inferential and "prone to misleading cues like other metacognitive judgments", so researchers and designers should not treat them as direct readouts of cognitive load. The principle follows from the finding that effort and difficulty appraisals track response time more strongly than confidence does, and predict success less strongly than difficulty and confidence appraisals.
requirements: Interpretation of effort/difficulty ratings should account for heuristic cues such as response time and item complexity rather than assuming direct correspondence with cognitive load
constraints: The article notes the distinction between cognitive load types, and germane load as a category, is under debate; its findings concern classic global mental effort and difficulty scales
target_learners: Adult problem-solvers in online reasoning experiments (Prolific participants)
target_learning_goals: Accurate interpretation of self-reported cognitive load in learning research and instructional design evaluation
examples: Across three experiments, the authors conclude these findings "challenge the accepted notion that mental effort appraisals can serve as reliable reflections of cognitive load"
key_sources: Emely Hoch, Yael Sidi, Rakefet Ackerman, Vincent Hoogerheide, Katharina Scheiter. (2023). Comparing Mental Effort, Difficulty, and Confidence Appraisals in Problem-Solving: A Metacognitive Perspective. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09779-5

article_title: Benefits of Taking a Virtual Field Trip in Immersive Virtual Reality: Evidence for the Immersion Principle in Multimedia Learning
citation: Guido Makransky · Richard E. Mayer. (2022). Benefits of Taking a Virtual Field Trip in Immersive Virtual Reality: Evidence for the Immersion Principle in Multimedia Learning. Educational Psychology Review (2022) 34:1771–1798. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09675-4
title: The immersion principle in multimedia learning
description: The immersion principle "proposes that immersive virtual environments promote better learning when they incorporate multimedia design principles" and holds that "immersive media per se do not necessarily improve learning". It predicts people learn better with immersive media (e.g., a 3D HMD video) than less immersive media when lessons follow instructional design principles and the affordances of the media. The article tests it with a media-comparison experiment in a real middle-school intervention, and the results support it.
requirements: Lessons must be designed according to instructional design principles and the affordances of the media, promoting selecting, organizing, and integrating information.
constraints: Higher immersion is not automatically beneficial; cognitive load, seductive details, distraction, and poor pedagogy are stated boundary conditions under which immersion can be counterproductive.
target_learning_goals: declarative science knowledge about climate change (greenhouse effect, albedo effect)
examples: The study implemented evidence-based design principles (multimedia, signaling, split attention, redundancy, modality, personalization) in both versions of the Greenland virtual field trip and compared HMD to 2D video within a six-lesson IBSL intervention.
key_sources: Guido Makransky · Richard E. Mayer. (2022). Benefits of Taking a Virtual Field Trip in Immersive Virtual Reality: Evidence for the Immersion Principle in Multimedia Learning. Educational Psychology Review (2022) 34:1771–1798. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09675-4

article_title: Benefits of Taking a Virtual Field Trip in Immersive Virtual Reality: Evidence for the Immersion Principle in Multimedia Learning
citation: Guido Makransky · Richard E. Mayer. (2022). Benefits of Taking a Virtual Field Trip in Immersive Virtual Reality: Evidence for the Immersion Principle in Multimedia Learning. Educational Psychology Review (2022) 34:1771–1798. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09675-4
title: Cognitive Affective Model of Immersive Learning (CAMIL)
description: CAMIL describes how the level of immersion influences learning through affective factors. "According to the CAMIL ..., the main affordances of learning in immersive environments are a higher sense of presence (the psychological sense of 'being there') and agency (being in control of one's actions)". The model links immersion to presence, presence to enjoyment and interest, and these affective factors to immediate and delayed retention. The study's SEM provided "evidence for two pathways within the cognitive affective model of immersive learning—the enjoyment pathway and the interest pathway".
requirements: Structural equation modeling of the hypothesized links between immersion, presence, enjoyment, interest, and retention measures.
constraints: Cognitive load is identified as a potential limitation of learning with IVR; boundary conditions include cognitive load, reflection opportunities, and self-regulated learning support.
target_learning_goals: retention of instructional content
affective outcomes (presence, enjoyment, interest)
examples: Figure 1's hypothesized model with nine links (immersion→presence; presence→enjoyment and interest; enjoyment and interest→immediate and delayed retention) was tested via SEM in the Greenland virtual field trip experiment.
