article_title: Learning scientific concepts through material and social activities: Conversational analysis meets conceptual change
citation: Roy D. Pea. (1994). Learning Scientific Concepts Through Material and Social Activities: Conversational Analysis Meets Conceptual Change. Educational Psychologist, 28(3), pp.265-277. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00190572
title: A sociocultural framework informed by conversation analysis explains conceptual change through meaning negotiation and appropriation
description: The article describes a sociocultural framework for learning scientific concepts that is informed by studies of conversation analysis. Within this framework, "meaning negotiation and appropriation are identified as mechanisms for achieving such conceptual change" — that is, learners' conceptual change in scientific thinking is explained by social and material processes of negotiating meanings in activity and appropriating them. The framework is offered as a bridge between macrosocial theories of cultural learning and microanalytic details of situated human learning activities.
requirements: The framework is applied to learning situated in a material and social world, connecting macrosocial cultural-learning theory with microanalysis of situated activity.
constraints: The framework is presented for conceptual change in scientific thinking as the central case domain.
target_learning_goals: conceptual change in scientific thinking
key_sources: Roy D. Pea. (1994). Learning Scientific Concepts Through Material and Social Activities: Conversational Analysis Meets Conceptual Change. Educational Psychologist, 28(3), pp.265-277. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00190572

article_title: Learning scientific concepts through material and social activities: Conversational analysis meets conceptual change
citation: Roy D. Pea. (1994). Learning Scientific Concepts Through Material and Social Activities: Conversational Analysis Meets Conceptual Change. Educational Psychologist, 28(3), pp.265-277. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00190572
title: Design and study of learning environments should follow from a sociocultural perspective on conceptual change
description: The article outlines key implications of its sociocultural, conversation-analytic perspective for the design and study of learning environments. Because "meaning negotiation and appropriation are identified as mechanisms for achieving such conceptual change," environments for learning scientific concepts should be designed and studied so that learners can negotiate meanings in material and social activity and appropriate them. The abstract states that "Key implications of this perspective for the design and study of learning environments are outlined."
requirements: Learning environments should be designed and studied in terms of the sociocultural mechanisms of meaning negotiation and appropriation.
constraints: The perspective is developed for conceptual change in scientific thinking as the central case.
target_learning_goals: conceptual change in scientific thinking
key_sources: Roy D. Pea. (1994). Learning Scientific Concepts Through Material and Social Activities: Conversational Analysis Meets Conceptual Change. Educational Psychologist, 28(3), pp.265-277. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00190572

article_title: How Mathematicians Obtain Conviction: Implications for Mathematics Instruction and Research on Epistemic Cognition
citation: Keith Weber, Matthew Inglis & Juan Pablo Mejia-Ramos. (2013). How mathematicians obtain conviction: Implications for mathematics instruction and research on epistemic cognition. https://dspace.lboro.ac.uk/
title: Epistemic aims framework for mathematical conviction
description: The article adopts the construct of epistemic aims—"goals related to finding things out, understanding them, and forming beliefs"—and argues that the sources of evidence mathematicians use depend on which aim they pursue. It distinguishes four aims: convincing oneself an assertion is true, producing a peer-sanctioned deductive proof, verifying a proof's correctness, and increasing understanding of the mathematics behind the assertion. The framework underpins the paper's argument that empirical or authoritarian evidence can rationally persuade for some aims while deductive evidence is needed for understanding-generating learning opportunities.
requirements: Research on justification must distinguish the epistemic aim a person pursues, since different aims license different types of evidence
constraints: A full account of the understanding aim is beyond the scope of the paper, which treats understanding as explanation, new methods, new relationships, and new representations via cited sources
target_learning_goals: justifying mathematical assertions
gaining conviction in mathematical claims
understanding why theorems are true
examples: The paper uses the four aims to reinterpret studies of students' empirical justifications, arguing the studies did not establish which aim students pursued
key_sources: Keith Weber, Matthew Inglis & Juan Pablo Mejia-Ramos. (2013). How mathematicians obtain conviction: Implications for mathematics instruction and research on epistemic cognition. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2013.865527

article_title: Promoting Social Inclusion in Educational Settings: Challenges and Opportunities
citation: Juvonen, J., Lessard, L.M., Rastogi, R., Schacter, H.L., & Smith, D.S. (2019). Promoting social inclusion in educational settings: Challenges and opportunities. Educational Psychologist, 54, 250-270. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2019.1655645
title: Proactive inclusion model: four school-level strategies for promoting social inclusion
description: The article's organizing framework for promoting social inclusion, presented as Figure 1. Rather than reacting to exclusion after it occurs, the model proposes that "students fare best when schools take a proactive approach to maximizing cross-group contact and purposefully facilitating positive peer interactions and relationships across diverse students." It specifies four strategies: "(1) maximizing diversity and ensuring equitable access, (2) increasing teachers' awareness and use of inclusive strategies, (3) promoting shared goals outside of the classroom context, and (4) facilitating cross-group friendships." The model treats inclusive practices as built-in preventions embedded in school organization and instruction.
requirements: School administrators and teachers must be aware of group and interpersonal dynamics that divide and marginalize students
Equitable access and fair distribution of students across classes must be monitored
constraints: The article notes lack of inclusion is likely to arise unless schools disrupt typical social dynamics such as homophily and avoid segregating practices
target_learning_goals: Peer acceptance and cross-group friendships
Engagement and academic performance protected from exclusion
examples: The article cites jigsaw and other group-based cooperative activities, extracurricular activities requiring collaboration, gay-straight alliances, buddy programs, and peer mentoring as practical instantiations of the strategies
key_sources: Juvonen, J., Lessard, L.M., Rastogi, R., Schacter, H.L., & Smith, D.S. (2019). Promoting social inclusion in educational settings: Challenges and opportunities. Educational Psychologist, 54, 250-270. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2019.1655645

article_title: Promoting Social Inclusion in Educational Settings: Challenges and Opportunities
citation: Juvonen, J., Lessard, L.M., Rastogi, R., Schacter, H.L., & Smith, D.S. (2019). Promoting social inclusion in educational settings: Challenges and opportunities. Educational Psychologist, 54, 250-270. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2019.1655645
title: Conceptual accounts of peer exclusion: homophily, social norms, and intergroup dynamics
description: The article's explanatory framework for why classmates bully, reject, and avoid befriending some peers, approached from the perspective of those showing prejudice rather than presuming something is wrong with excluded students. It integrates three accounts. First, ingroup favoritism and homophily: "Students of all ages gravitate toward similar peers and away from dissimilar classmates, thereby contributing to lack of integration." Second, social norms: deviation from classroom behavioral norms predicts rejection, and high-status peers police norms, making attributes salient. Third, intergroup dynamics: lack of proximity, unequal status, competition, and absence of authority sanctioning maintain prejudice and exclusionary behaviors.
requirements: Educators must comprehend these dynamics to prevent and decrease social exclusion
constraints: The article states homophily does not promote inclusion for groups small in number and students with stigmatized identities and attributes
target_learners: K-12 students, particularly those with stigmatized identities or attributes
target_learning_goals: Understanding and preventing peer victimization, rejection, and friendlessness
examples: The review cites experiments and classroom observations showing aggressive boys in non-aggressive groups and socially withdrawn boys in aggressive groups are most likely to be rejected
key_sources: Juvonen, J., Lessard, L.M., Rastogi, R., Schacter, H.L., & Smith, D.S. (2019). Promoting social inclusion in educational settings: Challenges and opportunities. Educational Psychologist, 54, 250-270. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2019.1655645

article_title: Reassessing Aptitude: Introduction to a Special Issue in Honor of Richard E. Snow
citation: Patrick C. Kyllonen & Susanne P. Lajoie (2003). Reassessing Aptitude: Introduction to a Special Issue in Honor of Richard E. Snow. Educational Psychologist, 38(2), 79–83. https://doi.org/10.1207/S15326985EP3802_2
title: Snow's transactional conception of aptitude: aptitude as person–situation transactions rather than a static trait
description: The article presents Snow's conceptualization of aptitude, developed in Corno et al. (2002), as emphasizing transactions between personal characteristics and the affordances of particular situations. As summarized from Lohman, persons bring propensities and situations make some actions more likely, and "which propensities function as aptitudes (or inaptitudes) depend ultimately on the transactions that occur on a moment by moment basis". This reframes aptitude as dynamic rather than a fixed test score.
requirements: Requires treating aptitude as any personal characteristic that affects learning, including cognitive, affective, and conative characteristics
constraints: The article notes Snow's own research on will, determination, cognitive flexibility, fluidity, and playfulness remained speculative and was not tested empirically
target_learning_goals: understanding how learner characteristics relate to learning outcomes
examples: The Stanford Aptitude Seminar completed the posthumous project as the book Remaking the Concept of Aptitude: Extending the Legacy of Richard E. Snow (Corno et al., 2002)
key_sources: Patrick C. Kyllonen & Susanne P. Lajoie (2003). Reassessing Aptitude: Introduction to a Special Issue in Honor of Richard E. Snow. Educational Psychologist, 38(2), 79–83. https://doi.org/10.1207/S15326985EP3802_2

article_title: Reassessing Aptitude: Introduction to a Special Issue in Honor of Richard E. Snow
citation: Patrick C. Kyllonen & Susanne P. Lajoie (2003). Reassessing Aptitude: Introduction to a Special Issue in Honor of Richard E. Snow. Educational Psychologist, 38(2), 79–83. https://doi.org/10.1207/S15326985EP3802_2
title: Aptitude complexes versus trait complexes: interaction-based and commonality-based configurations of learner variables
description: The article contrasts two frameworks for studying configurations of learner variables. Snow's aptitude complexes treat a complex as an interaction between factors whose interaction term may account for variance in treatment outcomes independently of the components. Ackerman's trait complexes instead treat a complex as a collection of intercorrelating variables, an "amalgamation" of variables that go together, derived from factor analyses of ability, interest, and personality data.
requirements: Single-predictor, single-outcome studies are presumed unfruitful for understanding aptitude–instruction relations; variables must be studied as sets
constraints: The article states the two schemes are complementary rather than competing: Snow's complexes may be most useful for predicting treatment outcomes, Ackerman's for studying coherences among personal characteristics
target_learners: learners characterized by multiple ability, interest, and personality variables
target_learning_goals: predicting instructional treatment outcomes from learner characteristic configurations
examples: Ackerman proposes four trait complexes emerging from factor analyses: social, clerical–convention, science–mathematics, and intellectual–cultural, against Snow's five candidate aptitude complexes
key_sources: Patrick C. Kyllonen & Susanne P. Lajoie (2003). Reassessing Aptitude: Introduction to a Special Issue in Honor of Richard E. Snow. Educational Psychologist, 38(2), 79–83. https://doi.org/10.1207/S15326985EP3802_2

article_title: Reassessing Aptitude: Introduction to a Special Issue in Honor of Richard E. Snow
citation: Patrick C. Kyllonen & Susanne P. Lajoie (2003). Reassessing Aptitude: Introduction to a Special Issue in Honor of Richard E. Snow. Educational Psychologist, 38(2), 79–83. https://doi.org/10.1207/S15326985EP3802_2
title: SMART: a microadaptive and macroadaptive student-modeling system that selects learning objects to fit learner needs
description: SMART (Student Modeling Approach for Responsive Tutoring) is a student modeling system reviewed by Shute and Towle (2003) that "selects learning objects according to its estimate of how much a student knows and how fast a student is learning". It combines microadaptive estimates (learning speed within the current session) and macroadaptive estimates (general learning speed from separate tasks) to choose appropriate learning objects—small instructional components such as videos, tutorials, demonstrations, and simulations—at a given moment.
requirements: Requires assessment of the learner both in a domain-dependent and domain-independent way; learning speed may be estimated via regression or Bayesian inference methods
constraints: The article reports only Shute and Towle's expressed optimism that the approach shows promise; no effectiveness evaluation of SMART is printed here
target_learning_goals: delivering tailored, adaptive instruction matched to current knowledge and learning speed
examples: Shute and Towle argue e-learning increases effectiveness insofar as it becomes adaptive, delivering the right instruction at the right time, place, path, and pace
key_sources: Patrick C. Kyllonen & Susanne P. Lajoie (2003). Reassessing Aptitude: Introduction to a Special Issue in Honor of Richard E. Snow. Educational Psychologist, 38(2), 79–83. https://doi.org/10.1207/S15326985EP3802_2

article_title: Reassessing Aptitude: Introduction to a Special Issue in Honor of Richard E. Snow
citation: Patrick C. Kyllonen & Susanne P. Lajoie (2003). Reassessing Aptitude: Introduction to a Special Issue in Honor of Richard E. Snow. Educational Psychologist, 38(2), 79–83. https://doi.org/10.1207/S15326985EP3802_2
title: Adapt instruction to individual learner aptitudes (aptitude–treatment interactions)
description: The article presents as a central Snow theme the belief that "instruction ought to be adapted to accommodate the aptitudes of individual learners", in the formulation known as aptitude–treatment interactions or ATIs, developed with Cronbach. Shute and Towle extend this into e-learning, arguing that with computers ATIs will be found and replicated, and that e-learning increases effectiveness insofar as it becomes adaptive.
requirements: Requires measuring relevant learner aptitude characteristics and offering instructional treatments that differ in fit for different aptitude profiles
constraints: The article notes Cronbach and Snow's ATI results were somewhat inconsistent, as Cronbach and Snow themselves admitted, and that early classroom studies investigated the phenomenon under noisy conditions
target_learners: individual learners with differing aptitudes in instructional settings
target_learning_goals: matching instructional treatments to learner aptitudes to improve outcomes
examples: Shute and Towle's electricity learning environment found an interaction between exploratory time and rule-induction versus rule-application treatments
key_sources: Patrick C. Kyllonen & Susanne P. Lajoie (2003). Reassessing Aptitude: Introduction to a Special Issue in Honor of Richard E. Snow. Educational Psychologist, 38(2), 79–83. https://doi.org/10.1207/S15326985EP3802_2

article_title: Connecting Sociocultural Theory and Educational Practice: Galperin's Approach
citation: Arievitch, I.M., & Haenen, J.P.P. (2005). Connecting Sociocultural Theory and Educational Practice: Galperin's Approach. Educational Psychologist, 40(3), 155-165. https://doi.org/10.1207/s15326985ep4003_2
title: Galperin's spiral model of stepwise formation of mental actions
description: The article presents Galperin's teaching strategy as a spiral model in which learning proceeds through alternating levels of acting while the quality of the action improves. The authors state that "the stepwise process of the formation of actions can be most adequately represented by a spiral model," with five levels per cycle, each cycle ending in more advanced orienting activity. The model operationalizes internalization: material actions are progressively transformed into mental actions that orient further learning.
requirements: Teaching must be specially organized so learners pass through material, verbal, and mental levels, with orienting charts and guided formation rather than mere observation
constraints: The complete sequence of steps is a theoretical model assuming the action is perfectly new to the learner; in real learning situations steps may be abbreviated, combined, or skipped depending on prior knowledge
target_learners: adult learners acquiring substantially new content
target_learning_goals: formation of mental actions
generalization and abbreviation of learned actions
self-regulation and orienting ability
examples: Teaching experiments in handwriting, attention, geometry, elementary mathematics, history, grammar, and foreign languages from the 1950s through the 1980s
key_sources: Arievitch, I.M., & Haenen, J.P.P. (2005). Connecting Sociocultural Theory and Educational Practice: Galperin's Approach. Educational Psychologist, 40(3), 155-165. https://doi.org/10.1207/s15326985ep4003_2

article_title: Connecting Sociocultural Theory and Educational Practice: Galperin's Approach
citation: Arievitch, I.M., & Haenen, J.P.P. (2005). Connecting Sociocultural Theory and Educational Practice: Galperin's Approach. Educational Psychologist, 40(3), 155-165. https://doi.org/10.1207/s15326985ep4003_2
title: Three levels of action abstraction: material, verbal, and mental
description: Galperin classified each concrete form of an action into three basic levels of abstraction: material, verbal, and mental, each associated with a dominant way of thinking (operative, figurative, communicative, dialogical, conceptual). The article reports that "Galperin classified each concrete form of an action into three basic levels of abstraction which he called the material, the verbal, and the mental levels." Passing through all levels supports generalization (isolating essential from non-essential properties) and abbreviation (reducing operations), which together yield a fully-fledged mental action.
requirements: Each level should have its place in the teaching-learning process; several different representations of the material must be used to draw attention to essential and non-essential properties
target_learning_goals: conceptual thinking
generalization of actions
action mastery and automatization
examples: At the material level actions use hands-on manipulation or models, diagrams, and displays; at the verbal level learners think aloud; at the mental level action is performed internally
key_sources: Arievitch, I.M., & Haenen, J.P.P. (2005). Connecting Sociocultural Theory and Educational Practice: Galperin's Approach. Educational Psychologist, 40(3), 155-165. https://doi.org/10.1207/s15326985ep4003_2

article_title: Semantic congruence in arithmetic: A new conceptual model for word problem solving
citation: Hippolyte Gros, Jean-Pierre Thibaut, Emmanuel Sander. (2020). Semantic Congruence in Arithmetic: A New Conceptual Model for Word Problem Solving. Educational Psychologist. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2019.1691004
title: The SECO model: semantic congruence between world semantics and mathematical semantics governs arithmetic word problem encoding, recoding, and solving
description: The SECO model is a theoretical account of arithmetic word problem solving in which solvers abstract an interpreted structure from a problem statement under the joint constraints of world semantics (daily-life knowledge about the entities) and mathematical semantics (applicable mathematical knowledge). The article introduces it as "a theoretical model depicting how world and mathematical semantics interact in the encoding, recoding and solving of arithmetic word problems". When the interpreted structure cannot be specified into a tractable algorithm, a costly recoding process drawing on mathematical semantics builds a representation closer to the problem's deep structure; experts may encode the deep structure directly.
requirements: Solvers possess world semantics about the problem entities and mathematical semantics applicable to the problem's relations
constraints: The article states SECO does not intend to resort solely to world semantics to account for every variation in solving, since other sources of differences exist, such as algorithm computation abilities or reading comprehension
target_learners: kindergarten to adult learners solving arithmetic word problems
target_learning_goals: selecting and flexibly switching solving algorithms for arithmetic word problems
overcoming semantically incongruent initial problem representations
examples: The article reinterprets six case studies, including Bassok et al.'s transfer asymmetry and Coquin-Viennot and Moreau's bouquet factorization effect, through the SECO architecture with figures S1-S7 in supplemental materials
key_sources: Hippolyte Gros, Jean-Pierre Thibaut, Emmanuel Sander. (2020). Semantic Congruence in Arithmetic: A New Conceptual Model for Word Problem Solving. Educational Psychologist. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2019.1691004

article_title: The framework of prior knowledge in online credibility evaluation
citation: Carita Kiili, Ivar Bråten, and Julie Coiro. (2026). The framework of prior knowledge in online credibility evaluation. Educational Psychologist. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2026.2717081
title: The Framework of Prior Knowledge in Online Credibility Evaluation
description: The article proposes a framework in which online credibility evaluation by a motivated, strategic reader draws on five interconnected prior knowledge types. As printed, "the framework consists of four main interacting components: prior knowledge, evaluation strategies, metastrategic knowledge and regulation, and justified integrated understanding." Activated knowledge supports inferences about content, source, and context credibility, and resulting understanding can be integrated into existing knowledge structures to support future evaluations.
requirements: Readers must be motivated and strategic; the framework intentionally focuses on evaluation processes of a motivated and strategic reader rather than heuristic processing
constraints: The framework enjoys preliminary empirical support and is proposed to promote further empirical work investigating its crucial assumptions
The five knowledge types are distinguished for analytical purposes and may be highly intertwined in practice
target_learners: online readers evaluating the credibility of web information
adolescent and adult students in educational settings
target_learning_goals: critical online reading and credibility evaluation of online information
key_sources: Carita Kiili, Ivar Bråten, and Julie Coiro. (2026). The framework of prior knowledge in online credibility evaluation. Educational Psychologist. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2026.2717081

article_title: Preregistration and registered reports
citation: Preregistration and Registered Reports. (2021). https://osf.io/ya594
title: Registered reports: a two-phase publication format with in-principle acceptance before results are known
description: Registered reports are a journal publication format, developed by the journal Cortex for neuroscience, that integrates preregistration with peer review in two phases. Authors submit a Phase I manuscript with introduction, background, and method including pre-specified analytic plans; if reviewers and editors find merit, "the article is then granted “in-principle” acceptance", meaning publication is agreed regardless of the direction or magnitude of findings, provided the study is conducted as agreed with documented modifications. The article edited an AERA Open special topic publishing some of the first registered reports in educational psychology.
requirements: Peer review must occur at least before data analysis, and ideally before data collection begins, so reviewers evaluate design without knowing results
constraints: Field studies requiring negotiation with local stakeholders may be incompatible with rigid preregistration timelines; articles can still be rejected after in-principle acceptance for implementation flaws
target_learning_goals: increasing transparency and replicability of educational research
reducing publication bias against null findings
examples: The AERA Open special topic (2018-2020) published registered reports on student-teacher relationships, researcher trustworthiness perceptions, text framings for college matriculation, and gifted education identification policies; three of seven articles had graduate student lead authors
key_sources: Preregistration and Registered Reports. (2021). https://osf.io/ya594

article_title: Preregistration and registered reports
citation: Preregistration and Registered Reports. (2021). https://osf.io/ya594
title: Start preregistrations short and concise, then develop more detail over a research trajectory and for the study's most important parts
description: The article recommends three principles for preregistration in educational psychology: begin with short, concise documents because lower burden increases willingness to write and read them; develop more robust preregistrations as researchers gain familiarity with settings, designs, and analysis plans; and preregister more detail on correspondingly important parts of the study, such as subgroup analyses central to the theory. This follows Duflo et al.'s argument that in field settings, documenting all contingencies rapidly becomes prohibitive.
requirements: Preregistration content should match the maturity of the research line and the importance of specific analyses, with more detail where subgroup effects are predicted and theoretically central
constraints: Thorough pre-analysis plans down to analytic code may be inappropriate for less mature research lines or field settings where flexibility is needed to negotiate access
target_learning_goals: distinguishing confirmatory predictions from exploratory post hoc analyses
preserving the interpretability of null-hypothesis tests
examples: The author's own preregistrations ranged from a short narrative for a planning-prompt study to a complete package including exact analytic code for a MOOC intervention study
key_sources: Preregistration and Registered Reports. (2021). https://osf.io/ya594

article_title: Moving Beyond Reflection: Reflexivity and Epistemic Cognition in Teaching and Teacher Education
citation: Feucht, F. C., Lunn Brownlee, J., & Schraw, G. (2017). Moving beyond reflection: Reflexivity and epistemic cognition in teaching and teacher education. Educational Psychologist, 52(4), 234-241. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2017.1350180
title: The 3R-EC Framework: Reflection, Reflexivity and Resolved action for Epistemic Cognition
description: The 3R-EC Framework is a three-step process for changing teachers' epistemic cognition, adapted from Lunn and Schraw's original 3R Model and refined at a 2015 EARLI Advanced Study Colloquium. First, teachers 'identify a teaching issue of concern (Reflection)'; second, they engage in 'internal dialogue that included the weighing up of diverse structural, cultural and personal factors, including one's personal epistemologies (Reflexivity)'; third, 'decision making would be enacted in classroom contexts (Resolved action)'. The framework was retitled from 3R to 3R-EC to reflect the shift from personal epistemology to the broader construct of epistemic cognition, and served as the conceptual platform for the special issue's articles.
requirements: Teachers must identify a specific teaching issue of concern as the reflection step before internal dialogue and action can proceed
constraints: The framework is described as 'an evolving conceptual framework' whose theory-of-change for when, how and why epistemic cognition changes still requires empirical identification
target_learning_goals: changing epistemic cognition and personal epistemologies about knowledge and knowing
transformative change in classroom teaching practices
examples: The article by Lunn et al. in the special issue uses the framework to guide the process of developing a lesson plan in social studies
key_sources: Feucht, F. C., Lunn Brownlee, J., & Schraw, G. (2017). Moving beyond reflection: Reflexivity and epistemic cognition in teaching and teacher education. Educational Psychologist, 52(4), 234-241. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2017.1350180

article_title: Moving Beyond Reflection: Reflexivity and Epistemic Cognition in Teaching and Teacher Education
citation: Feucht, F. C., Lunn Brownlee, J., & Schraw, G. (2017). Moving beyond reflection: Reflexivity and epistemic cognition in teaching and teacher education. Educational Psychologist, 52(4), 234-241. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2017.1350180
title: Three waves of personal epistemology research: development, beliefs, and justification/epistemic cognition
description: Drawing on Hofer (2016), the article organizes five decades of personal epistemology research into three waves: epistemological development, epistemological beliefs, and more recent work on justification and epistemic cognition. Developmental frameworks (Perry; Kuhn & Weinstock) describe progression from absolutist through subjectivist to evaluativist positions. Schommer-Aikins proposed independent multidimensional beliefs, while Hofer's epistemological theories and Elby and Hammer's epistemological resources offer fine-grained, context-specific accounts. The article notes that 'no specific framework (or even framework type) has achieved prevalence to enable systematic and focused research'.
requirements: Understanding of the framework distinctions requires familiarity with the cited primary works, which this article only summarizes
constraints: The article presents these as descriptive overviews of others' frameworks rather than tested models
target_learning_goals: understanding the nature of knowledge and processes of knowing
framing research on teachers' personal epistemologies
examples: The article applies the developmental levels to teachers: absolutist teachers view knowledge as transmissible, subjectivist teachers as personal opinion, evaluativist teachers as requiring adjudication among perspectives
key_sources: Feucht, F. C., Lunn Brownlee, J., & Schraw, G. (2017). Moving beyond reflection: Reflexivity and epistemic cognition in teaching and teacher education. Educational Psychologist, 52(4), 234-241. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2017.1350180

article_title: Moving Beyond Reflection: Reflexivity and Epistemic Cognition in Teaching and Teacher Education
citation: Feucht, F. C., Lunn Brownlee, J., & Schraw, G. (2017). Moving beyond reflection: Reflexivity and epistemic cognition in teaching and teacher education. Educational Psychologist, 52(4), 234-241. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2017.1350180
title: The epistemic climate construct and the Educational Model for Personal Epistemology
description: The epistemic climate construct (Bendixen & Rule; Feucht; Muis & Duffy) provides the broader classroom context for the 3R-EC Framework. The Educational Model for Personal Epistemology (Feucht, 2010a) describes how the nature of knowledge and knowing emerge from epistemic entities in classrooms: 'the epistemic cognition of learners and teachers, the epistemic underpinning of instruction ... and of educational materials ... and the reciprocal relations among these entities'. The model was developed to account for changes in epistemic climate across context, culture and time, and its entities can become the targeted focus of self-reflection leading to epistemic reflexivity.
requirements: Application requires attention to the reciprocal relations among learner cognition, teacher cognition, instruction and materials rather than any single entity
constraints: The model was developed for classroom settings and extended to cross-context, cross-culture and cross-time comparison
target_learning_goals: awareness of epistemic aspects of learning and instruction
aligning instructional approaches and materials with epistemic cognition
examples: The article proposes that these epistemic entities and their relations 'can be incorporated into the process of self-reflection that lead to epistemic reflexivity in the classroom setting'
key_sources: Feucht, F. C., Lunn Brownlee, J., & Schraw, G. (2017). Moving beyond reflection: Reflexivity and epistemic cognition in teaching and teacher education. Educational Psychologist, 52(4), 234-241. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2017.1350180

article_title: Moving Beyond Reflection: Reflexivity and Epistemic Cognition in Teaching and Teacher Education
citation: Feucht, F. C., Lunn Brownlee, J., & Schraw, G. (2017). Moving beyond reflection: Reflexivity and epistemic cognition in teaching and teacher education. Educational Psychologist, 52(4), 234-241. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2017.1350180
title: Chinn and colleagues' AIR model of epistemic cognition: Aims, Ideals and Reliable processes
description: The article describes the AIR model as a comprehensive, philosophically-driven framework for epistemic cognition developed by Chinn and colleagues, which re-conceptualizes aspects of existing frameworks. An earlier version focused on five components: epistemic aims and epistemic value; structure of knowledge and other epistemic achievements; sources and justification of knowledge; epistemic virtues and vices; and reliable and unreliable processes for achieving epistemic aims. 'Its current version, the AIR model, focuses specifically on epistemic Aims, Ideals and Reliable processes to better understand and explain the nature of knowledge and processes of knowing.'
requirements: Application requires attention to all three components—aims, ideals and reliable processes—rather than beliefs alone
constraints: The article presents the model as described by Chinn et al. (2011, 2014) and does not evaluate it empirically
target_learning_goals: understanding and explaining the nature of knowledge and processes of knowing
examples: Bråten, Muis and Reznitskaya's special-issue article uses the framework's aims and reliable processes constructs to analyze dialogic teaching for deep understanding

article_title: A critical analysis of the current motivation theories in educational psychology: Why the same theories continue to dominate
citation: Murayama, K., & von Keyserlingk, L. (2025). A critical analysis of the current motivation theories in educational psychology: Why the same theories continue to dominate.
title: The common formula of motivation theories: core constructs with antecedents and outcomes
description: The article describes a shared structural scheme across major motivation theories (Figure 1): each theory posits one or more core motivation constructs (e.g., need satisfaction, self-efficacy, achievement goals, expectancy and task values), plus antecedents (e.g., school environment, social support) and outcomes (e.g., achievement, engagement). "Usually, some adaptive form of motivation ... is posited to positively predict some adaptive outcome(s)", while maladaptive forms predict maladaptive outcomes. The authors argue most empirical motivation research, including person-centered profile approaches, largely adheres to this formula, which maps readily onto regression models.
requirements: A core motivation construct or set of constructs
Posited antecedents and outcomes of those constructs
constraints: The article notes theories are "far more complex and nuanced" than this general scheme, which captures only part of them
target_learning_goals: understanding motivated behavior such as engagement, achievement, and educational choice
examples: The article illustrates the formula with adaptive constructs (need satisfaction, mastery goals, self-efficacy, subjective task values) predicting positive outcomes and maladaptive constructs (amotivation, performance-avoidance goals) predicting negative ones
key_sources: Murayama, K., & von Keyserlingk, L. (2025). A critical analysis of the current motivation theories in educational psychology: Why the same theories continue to dominate. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2025.2473894

article_title: A critical analysis of the current motivation theories in educational psychology: Why the same theories continue to dominate
citation: Murayama, K., & von Keyserlingk, L. (2025). A critical analysis of the current motivation theories in educational psychology: Why the same theories continue to dominate.
title: Distinction between descriptive and explanatory aspects of theory, and between theory, phenomenon, and data
description: Drawing on Greene (2022) and Borsboom et al. (2021), the article distinguishes the descriptive aspect of a theory (a broad, concise picture of a phenomenon) from its explanatory aspect (an account of the causal mechanisms, the "how"). It further distinguishes data (direct observations such as survey responses or classroom behavior) from phenomena (robust empirical generalizations across data, such as the positive manifold or named effects), with "A theory provides a causal explanation for the phenomena". The authors argue existing motivation theories largely describe phenomena in the Figure 1 scheme but lack detailed causal explanation, making them hard to falsify.
requirements: A theory should make predictions about new phenomena that can be tested with empirical data
constraints: The distinction between data and phenomenon is relative, not absolute, per the article
target_learning_goals: understanding how theories are formulated and evaluated in motivation science
examples: The article uses the positive manifold as an example: general intelligence theory and mutualism-style accounts (van der Maas et al., 2006) are alternative theories explaining the same phenomenon
key_sources: Murayama, K., & von Keyserlingk, L. (2025). A critical analysis of the current motivation theories in educational psychology: Why the same theories continue to dominate. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2025.2473894

article_title: A critical analysis of the current motivation theories in educational psychology: Why the same theories continue to dominate
citation: Murayama, K., & von Keyserlingk, L. (2025). A critical analysis of the current motivation theories in educational psychology: Why the same theories continue to dominate.
title: Reward-learning framework of knowledge acquisition: long-term intellectual engagement as a positive feedback process
description: Murayama and colleagues' reward-learning framework extends reward learning models and "explains long-term voluntary engagement as a causal positive feedback process that surrounds the rewarding value of information, knowledge structure, and information-seeking behavior". Learning is motivated by meta-cognitive awareness of uncertainty; acquired knowledge produces a rewarding feeling, elicits new questions, increases the value of topic knowledge, and increases the ability to understand new information, sustaining engagement without external rewards. The framework explains engagement without using constructs like interest, curiosity, or intrinsic motivation, treating them as emergent properties.
requirements: The framework still relies on some theoretical constructs (value or perceived competence) and does not explain how value is represented and calculated in the mind
constraints: The authors avoided calling it a theory because it remains underspecified; it is a first step toward a more elaborative theory
target_learners: learners engaging in voluntary intellectual activities
target_learning_goals: sustaining long-term voluntary engagement and information-seeking in a domain
examples: The article illustrates the framework with a person persisting in learning statistics: acquired knowledge reveals knowledge gaps, raising the expected rewarding value of further information
key_sources: Murayama, K., & von Keyserlingk, L. (2025). A critical analysis of the current motivation theories in educational psychology: Why the same theories continue to dominate. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2025.2473894

article_title: A consideration of racial/ethnic diversity conceptualization and measurement: Clarifying ambiguities and advancing scholarship
citation: Chan, M.-k., & Benner, A. D. (2023). A Consideration of Racial/Ethnic Diversity Conceptualization and Measurement: Clarifying Ambiguities and Advancing Scholarship. Educational Psychologist (accepted manuscript). https://orcid.org/0000-0001-6451-2417
title: A multidimensional conceptual model of diversity: attributes, three evaluative frameworks (normic, dual-concept, representative), and static versus dynamic social spaces
description: The article proposes a conceptual model, built on Steel et al.'s (2018) framework plus dynamic diversity (Graham, 2018; Garces & Jayakumar, 2014), in which diversity conceptualization varies along three axes. "Figure 1 is a conceptual model detailing the multidimensional nature of diversity conceptualization." Attributes are the categorization used (e.g., race/ethnicity); evaluative frameworks define what counts as diverse — normic (divergence from a "norm"), dual-concept (variety plus even concentration), and representative (similarity to a reference population); social spaces distinguish static context-level from person-specific dynamic diversity. The model is used to map and critique existing measures.
requirements: Researchers must specify the attribute, its categorization, the norm or reference population, and the social space when defining diversity for a study
constraints: The authors state these frameworks are not the only available approaches, though they encompass the major conceptualizations actively studied in the literature
target_learning_goals: characterizing school racial/ethnic composition to study its impact on student adjustment, academic performance, intergroup interactions, and school climate
examples: A San Francisco school (38% White, 40% Asian, 16% Hispanic, 3% Black, 3% other) is judged diverse or not depending on which of the three evaluative frameworks is applied
key_sources: Chan, M.-k., & Benner, A. D. (2023). A Consideration of Racial/Ethnic Diversity Conceptualization and Measurement: Clarifying Ambiguities and Advancing Scholarship. Educational Psychologist (accepted manuscript). https://orcid.org/0000-0001-6451-2417

article_title: A consideration of racial/ethnic diversity conceptualization and measurement: Clarifying ambiguities and advancing scholarship
citation: Chan, M.-k., & Benner, A. D. (2023). A Consideration of Racial/Ethnic Diversity Conceptualization and Measurement: Clarifying Ambiguities and Advancing Scholarship. Educational Psychologist (accepted manuscript). https://orcid.org/0000-0001-6451-2417
title: Frequentist-based Representative Diversity (FRD) index: a new measure capturing dual-concept and representative diversity simultaneously
description: The FRD index is a proposed measure that modifies the dissimilarity (segregation) index to "assess the degree of similarity between a target and a reference population", computed as one minus the summed absolute differences between target and reference group proportions. The researcher specifies a target distribution and a reference population "set by the researcher to represent maximum diversity in a given context." The authors state it "can capture two different aspects of diversity, is easy to interpret, and potentially broadens the scope of diversity research." It addresses the absence of tools for representative diversity and limitations of existing dual-concept indices.
requirements: The researcher must specify a target distribution and a reference population representing maximum diversity in the given context
constraints: Proposed in an accepted manuscript; the supplied text does not report empirical validation studies of the index
target_learning_goals: quantifying school racial/ethnic diversity in a way that preserves minority-representation information and compares contexts to reference populations
examples: The article illustrates the formula with a school that is 50% White, 30% Latina/o/x, and 20% Black, comparing its AP Calculus class composition to the school composition
key_sources: Chan, M.-k., & Benner, A. D. (2023). A Consideration of Racial/Ethnic Diversity Conceptualization and Measurement: Clarifying Ambiguities and Advancing Scholarship. Educational Psychologist (accepted manuscript). https://orcid.org/0000-0001-6451-2417

article_title: A consideration of racial/ethnic diversity conceptualization and measurement: Clarifying ambiguities and advancing scholarship
citation: Chan, M.-k., & Benner, A. D. (2023). A Consideration of Racial/Ethnic Diversity Conceptualization and Measurement: Clarifying Ambiguities and Advancing Scholarship. Educational Psychologist (accepted manuscript). https://orcid.org/0000-0001-6451-2417
title: Match the diversity measure to the diversity conceptualization: researchers should explicitly define which aspect of diversity they intend to assess before selecting a measure
description: The article's central methodological recommendation is that measure selection follow conceptualization. "The selection of a given diversity measure should be driven by the diversity conceptualization researchers intend to assess." Because different measures operationalize different frameworks (normic, dual-concept, representative), a study that defines diversity one way but measures it another produces inappropriate or misleading conclusions. The review found many studies did not explicitly delineate their diversity definition, obscuring what aspect of diversity was studied and hindering cross-study comparison.
requirements: Studies should explicitly state their definition of school racial/ethnic diversity and specify diversity terminology, since using "diversity" without specification makes results hard to interpret and compare
constraints: The review documents that current practice frequently violates this principle, with the same term used for different concepts and different terms for the same construct
target_learning_goals: valid operationalization of school racial/ethnic diversity in research on student outcomes
examples: The review shows bullying-victimization studies using minority proportion versus dual-concept indices support fundamentally different claims about how diversity relates to victimization

article_title: Supporting Learners' Agentic Engagement With Feedback: A Systematic Review and a Taxonomy of Recipience Processes
citation: Winstone, N. E., Nash, R. A., Parker, M., & Rowntree, J. (2014). Supporting Learners' Agentic Engagement with Feedback: A Systematic Review and a Taxonomy of Recipience Processes. Educational Psychologist (in press). https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2017.1359635
title: SAGE taxonomy of four recipience processes targeted by feedback interventions
description: The SAGE taxonomy is a data-driven framework of four distinct recipience processes that feedback interventions target: Self-appraisal (making judgments about oneself, one's traits, or one's behavior), Assessment literacy (understanding the grading process and applying it to make academic judgments), Goal-setting and self-regulation (articulating desired outcomes and monitoring progress), and Engagement and motivation (being enthusiastic about and open to receiving performance information). It was generated by coding the stated or implied rationales of 105 intervention papers. The authors report the processes are empirically distinct: "the correlations for all pairs of SAGE processes were either negative, or only very weakly positive (r's ranged from -.43 to .12)".
requirements: Interventions must be coded against researchers' stated or implied rationales to identify which SAGE processes they target
constraints: Derived from researchers' rationales in the reviewed literature rather than from direct measurement of learner processes
target_learning_goals: Active, agentic engagement with feedback processes
self-appraisal
assessment literacy
goal-setting and self-regulation
engagement and motivation
examples: Two authors jointly classified each of the 105 intervention papers into one or more SAGE categories, with a third author independently classifying 20% of the subset and 81% identical coding
key_sources: Winstone, N. E., Nash, R. A., Parker, M., & Rowntree, J. (2014). Supporting Learners' Agentic Engagement with Feedback: A Systematic Review and a Taxonomy of Recipience Processes. Educational Psychologist (in press). https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2016.1207538

article_title: Supporting Learners' Agentic Engagement With Feedback: A Systematic Review and a Taxonomy of Recipience Processes
citation: Winstone, N. E., Nash, R. A., Parker, M., & Rowntree, J. (2014). Supporting Learners' Agentic Engagement with Feedback: A Systematic Review and a Taxonomy of Recipience Processes. Educational Psychologist (in press). https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2017.1359635
title: Design feedback interventions to target learners' recipience processes, not only feedback delivery
description: Because feedback benefits learners only when they actively receive, engage with, and implement it, educators should design interventions that build learners' recipience processes rather than treating learners as passive recipients. The review proposes the SAGE taxonomy (self-appraisal, assessment literacy, goal-setting and self-regulation, engagement and motivation) as "a theoretical basis for conceptualizing learners' responsibility within feedback dialogues, and for guiding the strategic design and evaluation of interventions." Intervention components such as peer-assessment, self-assessment, and engaging with grading criteria each map onto one or more of these processes.
requirements: Educators must diagnose which recipience process an intervention targets, since the four SAGE processes are empirically distinct and no two co-occurred systematically in researchers' rationales
constraints: Evidence on intervention effectiveness is largely descriptive and anecdotal; the review found no existing theoretical frameworks for categorizing recipience processes before SAGE
target_learning_goals: Proactive recipience of feedback
self-regulation of learning
assessment literacy
examples: The review catalogued 14 intervention component categories, including peer-assessment, self-assessment, and engaging with grading criteria, and mapped which SAGE processes each targets in Table 2

article_title: The Work of Writing: Raiding the Inarticulate
citation: Galbraith, D., & Baaijen, V. M. (2018). The Work of Writing: Raiding the Inarticulate. Educational psychologist, 53(4), 238-257. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2018.1505515
title: Dual-process model of content generation during writing
description: The article proposes a dual-process model in which two processes generate content during writing. The first is "an active, knowledge-constituting process in which content is synthesized by constraints within semantic memory representing the implicit structure of the writer's understanding". The second is "a reflective, knowledge-transforming process in which content retrieved from episodic memory is manipulated in working memory to satisfy rhetorical goals". The article outlines how these processes are combined and relates them to current models of writing.
requirements: Both processes must operate for effective writing, since "both processes are required for effective writing".
target_learning_goals: generation of content during writing
development of writing ability

article_title: A critical review of the refutation text literature: Methodological confounds, theoretical problems, and possible solutions
citation: Allison Zengilowski, Brendan Schuetze, Brady Nash, Diane Schallert. (2020). Coding Notes for “A Critical Review of the Refutation Text Literature: Methodological Confounds, Theoretical Problems, and Possible Solutions”. Version 2. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=%22A+Critical+Review+of+the+Refutation+Text+Literature%22
title: Taxonomy of general-knowledge misconception topics (sets A–D) used across refutation-text studies
description: The notes organise the general-knowledge misconceptions used as refutation-text topics in the reviewed studies into four labelled sets. Set A collects ten common folk beliefs such as "Chameleons change color to match their surroundings" and "People only use ten percent of their brains"; set B collects psychology-related myths such as learning-styles matching; set C collects everyday factual misconceptions; and set D combines a personality-development misconception with topics drawn from sets A and B, with each set tied to the studies that featured it.
requirements: Each topic entry is tied to the specific reviewed studies (e.g., Kendeou et al. 2014, 2019; van Loon et al. 2015; Beker et al. 2019) in which the misconception appeared as stimulus material.
constraints: The taxonomy covers only topics the authors label "General Knowledge"; scientific and socio-political topics were coded in separate, non-exclusive categories.
target_learners: Participants in refutation-text studies reviewed by the authors, spanning general-knowledge and psychology-related misconception content
target_learning_goals: Conceptual change and correction of persistent misconceptions through refutation texts
examples: Set A's ten topics include "Seasons are caused by the Earth being closer to the Sun in the summer than in the winter" and "Lightning never strikes the same place twice"; set B includes "Students learn best when teaching styles are matched to their learning styles".

article_title: A developmental perspective on feedback: How corrective feedback influences children’s literacy, mathematics, and problem solving
citation: Fyfe Emily R., Borriello Giulia, Merrick Megan. (2023). A developmental perspective on feedback: How corrective feedback influences children's literacy, mathematics, and problem solving. Educational Psychologist. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2022.2108426
title: Five-Stage Model of feedback processing
description: The review adopts the Bangert-Drowns et al. (1991) Five-Stage Model, a cycle of learner mental states: initial state, retrieval, response with confidence, evaluation of the feedback message, and adjustment of knowledge, goals, and interests that feed back into the initial state. The authors use it as a springboard for developmental questions, noting it "highlights the multistep nature of the feedback process, the mindfulness of the learner, and the mutual influence between the learner and the environment."
requirements: Learners must notice feedback, be able to interpret its form, and view it as credible for Stage 4 evaluation to occur
constraints: The authors do not test the model directly; they use it as a springboard for identifying open questions about feedback in childhood
target_learners: preschool and elementary school children ages 3-11
target_learning_goals: learning from task-level corrective feedback in literacy, mathematics, and problem solving
examples: The review proposes feedback alerts may constitute a new pre-task stage, and that Stage 4 should be broken into notice, decode, evaluate, and act-upon steps
