article_title: Changing Teachers' Epistemic Cognition: A New Conceptual Framework for Epistemic Reflexivity
citation: Jo Lunn Brownlee, Leila E. Ferguson & Mary Ryan (2017). Changing Teachers' Epistemic Cognition: A New Conceptual Framework for Epistemic Reflexivity. Educational Psychologist, 52(4), 242–252. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2017.1333430
title: The 3R-EC Framework theorizes change in teachers' epistemic cognition through reflection, reflexivity, and resolved action
description: The 3R-EC Framework (Reflection, Reflexivity and Resolved Action for Epistemic Cognition) is a three-step model for changing teachers' epistemic cognition in specific teaching contexts. Step 1 involves reflecting on classroom practices and identifying associated epistemic aims; Step 2 involves reflexive deliberation calibrating practices with reliable processes for achieving those aims; Step 3 is resolved action. The article states that "The 3R-EC Framework for epistemic reflexivity focuses on making the epistemic aims and reliable processes explicit" and draws on Chinn and colleagues' AIR model to embed the epistemic in everyday teaching interactions.
requirements: Teachers identify epistemic aims embedded in teaching practices, not just the practices themselves
Examination of epistemic cognition in specific teaching and learning contexts rather than as broad epistemic beliefs
constraints: The authors do not suggest the framework would form the basis of every classroom interaction or lesson; it is described as useful for contested forms of knowledge and complex concepts
Its strength can be tested only through further empirical work such as longitudinal classroom interventions
target_learners: Student teachers in teacher education programs
target_learning_goals: Adaptive epistemic cognition for teaching
Calibrating epistemic aims with teaching practices
examples: The framework is exemplified through teaching for active citizenship, where scenarios and provocations support children to reason about injustice, exclusion, and inclusion
key_sources: Jo Lunn Brownlee, Leila E. Ferguson & Mary Ryan (2017). Changing Teachers' Epistemic Cognition: A New Conceptual Framework for Epistemic Reflexivity. Educational Psychologist, 52(4), 242–252. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2017.1333430

article_title: Changing Teachers' Epistemic Cognition: A New Conceptual Framework for Epistemic Reflexivity
citation: Jo Lunn Brownlee, Leila E. Ferguson & Mary Ryan (2017). Changing Teachers' Epistemic Cognition: A New Conceptual Framework for Epistemic Reflexivity. Educational Psychologist, 52(4), 242–252. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2017.1333430
title: The AIR framework models epistemic cognition as epistemic Aims, Ideals, and Reliable processes
description: The article describes the AIR framework, developed by Chinn and colleagues from an extensive review of educational and philosophical literature, as a model with three components. Epistemic aims and values cover goals such as developing true beliefs, understanding, or wisdom; epistemic ideals are "criteria or standards that must be met" for judging that aims have been achieved; and reliable processes are strategies, procedures, and activities for achieving epistemic aims, such as argumentation or logical reasoning. The 3R-EC Framework draws specifically on this AIR model to relate epistemic cognition to reflexivity in teaching contexts.
requirements: Epistemic aims, ideals, and reliable processes must be identified within specific teaching and learning contexts
constraints: The article notes that understanding reliable processes includes explicating the conditions in which processes may be considered reliable, a focus it says is not present in other epistemic cognition frameworks
target_learning_goals: Understanding the components of epistemic cognition
Developing justified true beliefs, understanding, and explanations
examples: In the active citizenship example, reliable processes for promoting understanding and explanation include accountable talk, argumentation, scaffolds, epistemic categories, and classroom norms
key_sources: Jo Lunn Brownlee, Leila E. Ferguson & Mary Ryan (2017). Changing Teachers' Epistemic Cognition: A New Conceptual Framework for Epistemic Reflexivity. Educational Psychologist, 52(4), 242–252. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2017.1333430

article_title: Changing Teachers' Epistemic Cognition: A New Conceptual Framework for Epistemic Reflexivity
citation: Jo Lunn Brownlee, Leila E. Ferguson & Mary Ryan (2017). Changing Teachers' Epistemic Cognition: A New Conceptual Framework for Epistemic Reflexivity. Educational Psychologist, 52(4), 242–252. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2017.1333430
title: Epistemic reflexivity extends reflection by adding internal dialogue evaluating multiple perspectives and leading to action
description: Drawing on Archer and on Ryan and Bourke, the article distinguishes reflection from reflexivity. Reflection is treated as a necessary component of reflexivity, but reflexivity adds an internal dialogue that evaluates multiple perspectives — the individual's and those situated in the broader social context — and maintains or changes courses of action. Reflexivity is characterized by discernment (reflecting on a key issue or aim), deliberation (weighing personal and contextual concerns), and dedication (resolved action). The article argues this distinction matters because metacognitive thinking strategies alone fail to account for changes in learning behavior.
requirements: Internal dialogue that evaluates multiple perspectives including school policies, curriculum expectations, and social justice agendas
Deliberative action following reflective thought
constraints: Reflexivity is described as always situated and potentially transformative, so its impact depends on the immediate and broader political and social context
target_learning_goals: Changing epistemic cognition for teaching practice
Moving from reflection to resolved action in classrooms
examples: Ryan and Bourke's account of reflexivity as bending-back thought upon self, taking the form of subject-object-subject, is used to frame teachers' deliberation about teaching to the test versus student well-being
key_sources: Jo Lunn Brownlee, Leila E. Ferguson & Mary Ryan (2017). Changing Teachers' Epistemic Cognition: A New Conceptual Framework for Epistemic Reflexivity. Educational Psychologist, 52(4), 242–252. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2017.1333430

article_title: Embodied guidance fading: When embodiment supports STEM learning by optimizing cognitive load
citation: Fred Paas, Nadine Marcus, Kevin Sigayret, Peng Wang, Kim Ouwehand, Liye Zou. (2026). Embodied guidance fading: When embodiment supports STEM learning by optimizing cognitive load. Educational Psychologist. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2026.2717080
title: Embodied guidance fading: least embodied task-relevant support matched to knowledge and element interactivity, then faded as schemas develop
description: The article reformulates the Perform First Hypothesis as embodied guidance fading, an account grounded in cognitive load theory. It prescribes to "use the least embodied, task-relevant support needed for the learner's current knowledge and the task's element interactivity, then fade that support as schemas develop". The aim is better learning, transfer, and flexible use of formal representations, not movement or lower load for its own sake.
requirements: Embodied support must be task-relevant and matched to the learner's current knowledge and the task's element interactivity
constraints: The account is formulated for embodied instruction in STEM
target_learners: STEM learners, especially novices early in expertise development
target_learning_goals: Concept understanding, transfer, and flexible use of formal representations
examples: Tracing a graph helps novices coordinate slope, variables, and change
key_sources: Fred Paas, Nadine Marcus, Kevin Sigayret, Peng Wang, Kim Ouwehand, Liye Zou. (2026). Embodied guidance fading: When embodiment supports STEM learning by optimizing cognitive load. Educational Psychologist. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2026.2717080

article_title: Embodied guidance fading: When embodiment supports STEM learning by optimizing cognitive load
citation: Fred Paas, Nadine Marcus, Kevin Sigayret, Peng Wang, Kim Ouwehand, Liye Zou. (2026). Embodied guidance fading: When embodiment supports STEM learning by optimizing cognitive load. Educational Psychologist. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2026.2717080
title: Optimize cognitive load in embodied instruction: aim for better learning and transfer, not movement or lower load for its own sake
description: This principle holds that the central instructional aim of embodied instruction is not movement or reduced load per se, but improved outcomes. The article states: "The central instructional aim is not movement or lower load for its own sake, but better learning, transfer, and flexible use of formal representations." Embodied activity should therefore be judged by whether it optimizes cognitive load toward learning, transfer, and flexible use of formal representations.
requirements: Embodied activities must be evaluated against learning, transfer, and flexible use of formal representations rather than amount of movement
target_learning_goals: Learning, transfer, and flexible use of formal representations
examples: Tracing a graph is justified when it helps novices coordinate slope, variables, and change
key_sources: Fred Paas, Nadine Marcus, Kevin Sigayret, Peng Wang, Kim Ouwehand, Liye Zou. (2026). Embodied guidance fading: When embodiment supports STEM learning by optimizing cognitive load. Educational Psychologist. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2026.2717080

article_title: Teachers' Epistemic Cognition in Classroom Assessment
citation: Fives, Helenrose, Barnes, Nicole, Buehl, Michelle, Mascadri, Julia, & Ziegler, Nathan. (2017). Teachers’ epistemic cognition in classroom assessment. Educational Psychologist, 52(4), pp. 270-283. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2017.1323218
title: Model of epistemic cognition in teaching embedded in pedagogical decision making
description: The article presents a nested model situating teachers' epistemic cognition within pedagogical decision making situated in the task of teaching, informed by domain knowledge and the teacher's self-system. It comprises epistemic aims, reliable processes, and consideration and evaluation of epistemic matters, producing epistemically informed praxis. The authors state: "Figure 1 provides a model of epistemic cognition in teaching informed by the work of Buehl and Fives (2016), Chinn et al. (2011, 2014), and Greene et al. (2008)." The process is iterative rather than linear in practice.
requirements: Epistemic cognition is only invoked when pedagogical decision making is knowledge focused, relating to the construction, use, or justification of knowledge
constraints: The authors note the process "visually depicted and described here as linear, in practice is more recursive, iterative, and multi-directional"
target_learning_goals: teachers' epistemic cognition in planning, constructing, and using classroom assessment events
examples: A hypothetical educational psychology instructor, Dr. Jones, works through the model while assessing students' understanding of learning theories
key_sources: Fives, Helenrose, Barnes, Nicole, Buehl, Michelle, Mascadri, Julia, & Ziegler, Nathan. (2017). Teachers’ epistemic cognition in classroom assessment. Educational Psychologist, 52(4), pp. 270-283. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2017.1323218

article_title: Teachers' Epistemic Cognition in Classroom Assessment
citation: Fives, Helenrose, Barnes, Nicole, Buehl, Michelle, Mascadri, Julia, & Ziegler, Nathan. (2017). Teachers’ epistemic cognition in classroom assessment. Educational Psychologist, 52(4), pp. 270-283. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2017.1323218
title: Assessment Triangle Model: cognition, observation, and interpretation as interdependent elements of classroom assessment
description: The article adopts Pellegrino, Chudowsky, and Glaser's (2001) Assessment Triangle Model to structure how teachers engage in classroom assessment. The authors write: "According to this model, assessment involves the three core elements of cognition, observation, and interpretation, which Pellegrino and colleagues represented as three vertices of a triangle to highlight their interdependency." Cognition concerns models of student learning, observation concerns designing sensitive assessment events, and interpretation concerns making meaning from evidence to inform teaching.
requirements: Teachers must attend to all three interdependent components to create assessment events that measure learning, allow valid interpretation, and inform teaching decisions
constraints: Teachers often struggle to transform assessment information into instructional actions even with access to student responses
target_learning_goals: designing and interpreting classroom assessment events
examples: Dr. Jones applies the three components when assessing students' understanding of Piaget, Vygotsky, and Information Processing Theory
key_sources: Fives, Helenrose, Barnes, Nicole, Buehl, Michelle, Mascadri, Julia, & Ziegler, Nathan. (2017). Teachers’ epistemic cognition in classroom assessment. Educational Psychologist, 52(4), pp. 270-283. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2017.1323218

article_title: Teachers' Epistemic Cognition in Classroom Assessment
citation: Fives, Helenrose, Barnes, Nicole, Buehl, Michelle, Mascadri, Julia, & Ziegler, Nathan. (2017). Teachers’ epistemic cognition in classroom assessment. Educational Psychologist, 52(4), pp. 270-283. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2017.1323218
title: Align reliable processes with the epistemic aims they are meant to achieve
description: The principle holds that strategies teachers select — rubrics, scoring guides, taxonomies, assessment formats — must align with the epistemic aims they are intended to serve. The article states: "Chinn et al. (2014) indicated that there must be alignment between the epistemic aim and the reliable process employed." For example, a single-point rubric better serves an aim of understanding student work, while a detailed analytic rubric better serves an aim of justifying grades to parents.
requirements: Teachers must identify their epistemic aim before selecting a reliable process, and evaluate whether required tools align with aims they hold
constraints: School curricula and policies often dictate the evaluation system teachers must implement, which may have been developed for an aim the teacher does not hold
target_learning_goals: selecting assessment tools and strategies that serve identified epistemic aims
examples: A teacher choosing between a single-point rubric and an analytic rubric depending on whether the aim is understanding students or justifying grades
key_sources: Fives, Helenrose, Barnes, Nicole, Buehl, Michelle, Mascadri, Julia, & Ziegler, Nathan. (2017). Teachers’ epistemic cognition in classroom assessment. Educational Psychologist, 52(4), pp. 270-283. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2017.1323218

article_title: Teachers' Epistemic Cognition in Classroom Assessment
citation: Fives, Helenrose, Barnes, Nicole, Buehl, Michelle, Mascadri, Julia, & Ziegler, Nathan. (2017). Teachers’ epistemic cognition in classroom assessment. Educational Psychologist, 52(4), pp. 270-283. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2017.1323218
title: 3R-EC model: a protocol for fostering reflexivity as an epistemic virtue targeting epistemic cognition
description: The 3R-EC model (Reflection-discernment, Reflexive-deliberation, Resolved Action-dedication, for Epistemic Cognition) is offered as a protocol for engaging teachers in reflexive practice aimed at epistemic cognition. The authors write that it "represents one protocol for fostering a disposition toward reflexive practice that targets epistemic cognition and can potentially be used to engage teachers in a habit of thinking about their assessment (and other teaching) practices with epistemic aims in mind." Reflexivity here extends reflection to a transformative level where understandings shift and actions are reconsidered.
requirements: A reflexive disposition, treated as an epistemic virtue, is positioned as necessary for teachers' epistemic cognition
constraints: The likelihood of routinely engaging in epistemic cognition may rest on the extent to which the individual has the epistemic virtue of a reflexive disposition
target_learning_goals: developing reflexive dispositions that support epistemic cognition in assessment practice
examples: The model is attributed to Brownlee Lunn, Ferguson, and Ryan and elaborated with the Dr. Jones assessment example
key_sources: Fives, Helenrose, Barnes, Nicole, Buehl, Michelle, Mascadri, Julia, & Ziegler, Nathan. (2017). Teachers’ epistemic cognition in classroom assessment. Educational Psychologist, 52(4), pp. 270-283. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2017.1323218

article_title: Teachers' Epistemic Cognition in Classroom Assessment
citation: Fives, Helenrose, Barnes, Nicole, Buehl, Michelle, Mascadri, Julia, & Ziegler, Nathan. (2017). Teachers’ epistemic cognition in classroom assessment. Educational Psychologist, 52(4), pp. 270-283. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2017.1323218
title: Table of Specifications (TOS) as a tool supporting epistemic cognition in test development
description: A Table of Specifications is presented as a reliable process teachers can use when constructing traditional summative tests. The article defines it: "A TOS is a conceptual and tangible table that helps teachers to align learning objectives with class time and expected cognitive levels of understanding." Teachers use it to determine the number and nature of test items so that multiple cognitive levels, low and high, are appropriately represented, thereby supporting alignment between objectives and the assessment event.
requirements: Learning objectives, ideally guided by a cognitive taxonomy, must exist for the TOS to align items against
target_learning_goals: developing summative tests that reflect multiple cognitive levels of understanding
examples: Dr. Jones could use a TOS when building a summative test for her learning theories unit
key_sources: Fives, Helenrose, Barnes, Nicole, Buehl, Michelle, Mascadri, Julia, & Ziegler, Nathan. (2017). Teachers’ epistemic cognition in classroom assessment. Educational Psychologist, 52(4), pp. 270-283. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2017.1323218

article_title: Beyond Amplification: Using the computer to Reorganize Mental Functioning
citation: Roy D. Pea. (1985). Beyond Amplification: Using the Computer to Reorganize Mental Functioning. Educational Psychologist, 20(4), pp.167-182. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00190536
title: Computer as reorganizer of mental functioning: an alternative to the amplifier view of computing in cognition
description: Pea contrasts two conceptualizations of the computer's role in cognition. The classical view treats computers as "amplifiers of cognition," while his alternative treats the computer as a "reorganizer of mental functioning," meaning that cognitive technologies change what people do and thus who they become, rather than merely speeding up existing processes. He argues this reframing opens new visions of the potential cognitive benefits of computers in education.
requirements: Educational software and cognitive technologies must be analyzed in terms of how they restructure activity, not only how much faster or more of it learners produce.
constraints: The article presents this as a conceptualization supported by software analyses, not as a tested experimental result.
target_learners: learners using computers in educational settings
target_learning_goals: general cognitive skills and reorganized mental functioning
examples: The article reports software analyses used to illuminate the advantages of the reorganizer view over the amplifier view.
key_sources: Roy D. Pea. (1985). Beyond Amplification: Using the Computer to Reorganize Mental Functioning. Educational Psychologist, 20(4), pp.167-182. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00190536

article_title: Beyond Amplification: Using the computer to Reorganize Mental Functioning
citation: Roy D. Pea. (1985). Beyond Amplification: Using the Computer to Reorganize Mental Functioning. Educational Psychologist, 20(4), pp.167-182. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00190536
title: Because cognitive technologies redefine what learners do, defining educational values must be a foreground issue in educational computing
description: The principle holds that choosing and designing cognitive technologies for education is a values-laden act, since these tools "shap[e] who we are by changing, not just amplifying, what we do." Therefore educators must explicitly define educational values when adopting computing tools, rather than treating technology adoption as value-neutral amplification of existing practice.
requirements: Educators must explicitly articulate educational values before selecting or designing cognitive technologies for learning.
constraints: Grounded in the article's conceptual argument rather than in empirical testing.
target_learners: all learners affected by educational computing
target_learning_goals: alignment of educational goals with the reorganizing effects of cognitive technologies
examples: The article's software analyses are offered as illustrations of how the reorganizer view changes the perceived cognitive benefits of computing.
key_sources: Roy D. Pea. (1985). Beyond Amplification: Using the Computer to Reorganize Mental Functioning. Educational Psychologist, 20(4), pp.167-182. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00190536

article_title: Improving norms in research culture to incentivize transparency and rigor
citation: Mellor, D. (2021). Improving norms in research culture to incentivize transparency and rigor. Educational Psychologist, 56(2). https://orcid.org/0000-0002-3125-5888
title: Five-stage diffusion-of-innovations roadmap for changing research culture
description: The article adapts Rogers' diffusion of innovations into a strategy for normalizing open science practices in educational psychology. Adoption proceeds through adopter groups, each needing a different condition: "Innovators only need a new practice to be possible in order to pick it up", early adopters need practices designed to be easy, the early majority needs a community of practice, the late majority needs specific rewards, and laggards come on board only when practices are required. Stakeholders supply the matching opportunity at each stage.
requirements: Each adopter group must be offered the opportunity or incentive matching its stage: possibility, ease, community of practice, rewards, or requirements
constraints: The article states the recommendations are "by no means exhaustive" and that making practices required is appropriate only once they are widely possible, easy, normal, and rewarded
target_learners: academic policy makers at journals, funders, and universities
target_learning_goals: adopting open science practices such as data sharing and preregistration
shifting community norms toward transparency and rigor
examples: The article maps each stage to concrete mechanisms: digital repositories make practices possible, the OSF makes them easy, Open Science Badges and unconferences make them normative, Registered Reports and hiring criteria make them rewarding, and the TOP Guidelines and funder policies make them required
key_sources: Mellor, D. (2021). Improving norms in research culture to incentivize transparency and rigor. Educational Psychologist, 56(2). https://orcid.org/0000-0002-3125-5888

article_title: Improving norms in research culture to incentivize transparency and rigor
citation: Mellor, D. (2021). Improving norms in research culture to incentivize transparency and rigor. Educational Psychologist, 56(2). https://orcid.org/0000-0002-3125-5888
title: TOP Guidelines for transparency and openness in publishing and funding
description: The Transparency and Openness Promotion (TOP) Guidelines, developed in 2014 among social scientists, editors, and funders, are a policy framework for journals and funders. The article states they "cover eight specific standards where open science can be practiced in publishing and funding", including data citation; data, materials, and code transparency; design and analysis transparency; preregistration; and replication research. Each standard has three levels of increasing rigor, and TOP provides specific policy recommendations and a plan for increasing rigor over time.
requirements: Journals and funders select which of the eight standards and levels to adopt; Level 2 mandates transparency with exceptions only for legal or ethical constraints, and Level 3 requires verification or computational reproducibility
constraints: Level 0 represents the ineffective status quo and is not compliant with TOP; the article notes data sharing in education research raises ethical and legal feasibility limits that policies must accommodate
target_learning_goals: adopting journal and funder policies that incentivize transparency, preregistration, and reproducibility
examples: The article describes a signatory campaign with over 5,000 journals, societies, publishers, and funders, and the TOP Factor rubric that awards 0 to 3 points per standard
key_sources: Mellor, D. (2021). Improving norms in research culture to incentivize transparency and rigor. Educational Psychologist, 56(2). https://orcid.org/0000-0002-3125-5888

article_title: Improving norms in research culture to incentivize transparency and rigor
citation: Mellor, D. (2021). Improving norms in research culture to incentivize transparency and rigor. Educational Psychologist, 56(2). https://orcid.org/0000-0002-3125-5888
title: Open Science Framework and research data repositories as infrastructure for sharing
description: The article describes digital infrastructure that makes open practices possible and easy. End-of-life repositories archive materials "not commonly preserved or rarely published, such as protocols, stimuli, questionnaires, raw data, analytical code". The Open Science Framework (OSF) is an open-source workspace connecting project pages to registries, repositories, and preprint servers, providing persistent, citable, timestamped links so authors need not reorganize materials at project's end. The Re3data registry catalogues repositories, including many supporting restricted access for sensitive data.
requirements: Persistent, unique identifiers (PUIDs) for datasets and instruments; for sensitive data, restricted-access workflows with an ethical check prior to access; when data cannot be shared, code, instruments, and surveys can still be shared
constraints: The article notes that in education research, quick and easy data sharing is particularly challenging, and that complete transparency is sometimes not ethical or legally feasible
target_learners: research lab members managing ongoing projects
target_learning_goals: documenting and preserving research materials
enabling verification and reuse of data and code
examples: The article cites the Re3data catalogue of over 2,000 repositories, over 1,100 offering restricted access, and the Qualitative Data Repository at Syracuse University for ethical sharing of qualitative data
key_sources: Mellor, D. (2021). Improving norms in research culture to incentivize transparency and rigor. Educational Psychologist, 56(2). https://orcid.org/0000-0002-3125-5888

article_title: Possibility mindset: A theory of motivation under constraint, with neurodivergence as a revealing interpretive case
citation: Srinivasan, H. (2026). Possibility Mindset: A Theory of Motivation Under Constraint, with Neurodivergence as a Revealing Interpretive Case. Preprint (v1) posted to PsyArXiv on January 18, 2026. https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv
title: Possibility mindset: a context-specific appraisal of 'room to move' grounded in three belief dimensions
description: Possibility mindset is defined as a learner's integrated appraisal of perceived room to move within a specific learning context, grounded in three belief dimensions: self-change beliefs (can I develop in ways that matter here?), environment-change beliefs (will this setting adapt reliably in practice?), and pathway-flexibility beliefs (are there multiple legitimate routes to valued goals?). The article positions it within the attributional tradition, specifying how attributions about systems, rather than solely about the self, shape motivational decisions under enduring constraint. It is offered as complementary to growth mindset, not a replacement for it.
requirements: Measurement of beliefs about environments and pathways alongside self-beliefs, so that misalignment profiles are not misread as motivational failure
constraints: Applies to contexts where effort alone cannot reliably secure access; the article states it is not a need-based or autonomy-based theory but an appraisal of feasibility
target_learners: Disabled and neurodivergent learners, including autistic learners
Learners in educational contexts where effort alone cannot reliably remove barriers
target_learning_goals: Persistence and engagement under constraint
Help-seeking and strategy switching
examples: The article defines the construct via three questions: 'Can I change? Will the setting change? Are there legitimate routes?'
key_sources: Srinivasan, H. (2026). Possibility Mindset: A Theory of Motivation Under Constraint, with Neurodivergence as a Revealing Interpretive Case. Preprint (v1) posted to PsyArXiv on January 18, 2026. https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv

article_title: Possibility mindset: A theory of motivation under constraint, with neurodivergence as a revealing interpretive case
citation: Srinivasan, H. (2026). Possibility Mindset: A Theory of Motivation Under Constraint, with Neurodivergence as a Revealing Interpretive Case. Preprint (v1) posted to PsyArXiv on January 18, 2026. https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv
title: Pair psychological mindset messages with visible structural flexibility ('aligned' interventions)
description: The article proposes aligned interventions that combine psychological messages with visible structural flexibility, so that growth-oriented messages are not delivered into settings that contradict them. It argues that instructional design choices matter because they provide credible evidence that the environment will adapt and that alternative pathways are treated as real in practice. The principle follows the wise-interventions insight that meaning shifts stick when the surrounding setting stops contradicting the new story.
requirements: Instructors and institutions must make flexibility concrete and credible, since persistence depends less on slogans about effort than on visible, reliable adaptation
constraints: Growth-mindset language delivered without corresponding changes in learning conditions can land as added pressure to push through when the real bottleneck is access, design, or institutional follow-through
target_learners: Students in settings with enduring structural constraints
target_learning_goals: Sustained engagement and persistence under constraint
examples: Structuring a lab into complementary roles when equipment demands exceed a student's fine-motor capacity, such as one student handling apparatus setup while another leads data logging and analysis
key_sources: Srinivasan, H. (2026). Possibility Mindset: A Theory of Motivation Under Constraint, with Neurodivergence as a Revealing Interpretive Case. Preprint (v1) posted to PsyArXiv on January 18, 2026. https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv

article_title: Academic Emotions in Students' Self-Regulated Learning and Achievement: A Program of Qualitative and Quantitative Research
citation: Reinhard Pekrun, Thomas Goetz, Wolfram Titz, & Raymond P. Perry. (2002). Academic Emotions in Students' Self-Regulated Learning and Achievement: A Program of Qualitative and Quantitative Research. https://doi.org/10.1207/s15326985ep3702_4
title: Academic Emotions Questionnaire (AEQ): a multidimensional self-report instrument measuring nine academic emotions across class-, learning-, and test-related situations
description: The AEQ is a multidimensional self-report instrument developed from the authors' qualitative data, measuring "students' enjoyment, hope, pride, relief, anger, anxiety, shame, hopelessness, and boredom." It uses multiple items per emotion to represent affective, cognitive, physiological, and motivational components, with separate scales for class-related, learning-related, and test-related emotions, and trait, course-related, and state versions. Short eight-item versions and an English-language version (average reliability α = .86) are also reported.
requirements: Domain-specific items constructed from exploratory student reports and test anxiety measurement standards
Separate scales for the three academic situations (class, learning, test)
constraints: Relief is measured for test emotions only; boredom for learning-related and class-related emotions only
target_learning_goals: measuring academic emotions as predictors of self-regulated learning and achievement
examples: Trait scale reliabilities reported in Table 3 range up to α = .94 (test anxiety, hopelessness)
key_sources: Reinhard Pekrun, Thomas Goetz, Wolfram Titz, & Raymond P. Perry. (2002). Academic Emotions in Students' Self-Regulated Learning and Achievement: A Program of Qualitative and Quantitative Research. https://doi.org/10.1207/s15326985ep3702_4

article_title: Academic Emotions in Students' Self-Regulated Learning and Achievement: A Program of Qualitative and Quantitative Research
citation: Reinhard Pekrun, Thomas Goetz, Wolfram Titz, & Raymond P. Perry. (2002). Academic Emotions in Students' Self-Regulated Learning and Achievement: A Program of Qualitative and Quantitative Research. https://doi.org/10.1207/s15326985ep3702_4
title: Cognitive-motivational model of academic emotion effects: valence × activation categories influence motivation, learning strategies, cognitive resources, and self-regulation
description: Pekrun's cognitive-motivational model assumes emotion effects on learning and achievement are mediated by motivation to learn, learning strategies, cognitive resources, and self-regulation. It distinguishes four emotion categories by valence and activation: "positiveactivatingemotions (such as enjoyment of learning, hope for success, or pride); positive deactivating emotions (e.g., relief...); negative activatingemotions (such as anger, anxiety, and shame); and negative deactivating emotions(e.g., boredom, hopelessness)." Positive activating emotions are hypothesized to enhance motivation and flexible learning; negative deactivating emotions to be detrimental; the other two categories to have ambivalent effects.
requirements: Mediating mechanisms of motivation, strategies, cognitive resources, and self-regulation link emotions to achievement
constraints: The valence-activation simplification has stated exceptions: anxiety may lead to behavioral freezing, and some boredom variants may be arousing
target_learning_goals: understanding how emotions shape self-regulated learning and achievement
examples: The model explains why test anxiety-achievement correlations rarely explain more than 10% of achievement variance
key_sources: Reinhard Pekrun, Thomas Goetz, Wolfram Titz, & Raymond P. Perry. (2002). Academic Emotions in Students' Self-Regulated Learning and Achievement: A Program of Qualitative and Quantitative Research. https://doi.org/10.1207/s15326985ep3702_4

article_title: Academic Emotions in Students' Self-Regulated Learning and Achievement: A Program of Qualitative and Quantitative Research
citation: Reinhard Pekrun, Thomas Goetz, Wolfram Titz, & Raymond P. Perry. (2002). Academic Emotions in Students' Self-Regulated Learning and Achievement: A Program of Qualitative and Quantitative Research. https://doi.org/10.1207/s15326985ep3702_4
title: Control-value theory of academic emotion antecedents: control-related and value-related appraisals are main sources of students' academic emotions
description: The control-value theory integrates expectancy-value and attributional theories, holding that "control-related and value-related appraisals are main sources of students' academic emotions." Control cognitions take forms of retrospective attributions, state control cognitions, or future expectancies (self-efficacy, situation-outcome, action-outcome), interacting with intrinsic and extrinsic values such that, for most emotions, both control and values are necessary antecedents. Environmental factors (instruction quality, autonomy support, expectancies, feedback, social support) are assumed to affect emotions indirectly via these appraisals.
requirements: Both control and value appraisals are necessary antecedents for most academic emotions
constraints: The authors state they have not yet tested the mediational assumptions implied by control-value theory in more direct ways
target_learning_goals: understanding origins of academic emotions to inform prevention and instructional design
examples: In a statistics-course study, enjoyment was high when both control and value were high, whereas anxiety showed a pattern of low control combined with high value

article_title: Critical culturalized comprehension: Exploring culture as learners thinking about texts
citation: Alexandra List, Gala S. Campos Oaxaca, Hongcui Du, Hye Yeon Lee, Bailing Lyu. (2023). Critical culturalized comprehension: exploring culture as learners thinking about texts. Educational Psychologist. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2023.2266028
title: Culturalized comprehension: culture as a way of thinking about texts, not an individual difference
description: The article proposes culturalized comprehension as a framework in which culture is conceptualized as a way of thinking rather than an individual difference factor. It defines it as "individuals' reasoning about the commonalities and differences in their and others' worldviews and the linking of these to underlying values". When this reasoning is engaged in reference to texts, the article names it culturalized comprehension, positioning it as an extension of comprehension theories centered on cognitive representation of texts.
requirements: Learners must engage in reasoning that links commonalities and differences across their own and others' worldviews to underlying values.
constraints: The framework applies when such worldview reasoning is engaged in reference to texts, as the article states.
target_learners: readers in educational psychology research contexts
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension
critical reasoning about texts
key_sources: Alexandra List, Gala S. Campos Oaxaca, Hongcui Du, Hye Yeon Lee, Bailing Lyu. (2023). Critical culturalized comprehension: exploring culture as learners thinking about texts. Educational Psychologist. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2023.2266028

article_title: Critical culturalized comprehension: Exploring culture as learners thinking about texts
citation: Alexandra List, Gala S. Campos Oaxaca, Hongcui Du, Hye Yeon Lee, Bailing Lyu. (2023). Critical culturalized comprehension: exploring culture as learners thinking about texts. Educational Psychologist. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2023.2266028
title: Support learners to question and analyze the mental representations they form from texts
description: The article recommends that because readers' text representations reflect their understandings of the real world, "individuals should be supported to question and analyze the mental representations that they form". The authors use the term culture to capture precisely such questioning and analysis, making this support central to their account of comprehension rather than an add-on.
requirements: Instruction must create opportunities for learners to question and analyze the mental representations they form while reading.
target_learning_goals: comprehension of texts
critical analysis of one's own text representations
examples: The article's abstract states the recommendation directly: individuals should be supported to question and analyze the mental representations that they form.
key_sources: Alexandra List, Gala S. Campos Oaxaca, Hongcui Du, Hye Yeon Lee, Bailing Lyu. (2023). Critical culturalized comprehension: exploring culture as learners thinking about texts. Educational Psychologist. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2023.2266028

article_title: The “simple” view of learning from illustrated texts and videos
citation: Haavisto, M., Lepola, J., & Jaakkola, T. (2025). The “simple” view of learning from illustrated texts and videos. Learning and Instruction, 100, 102200. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102200
title: Incorporate videos into primary science instruction to support learners with weaker reading skills
description: The article concludes that videos are beneficial across reading skill levels and especially for weaker readers: among fifth and sixth graders, "children with weaker decoding skills remembered more of what they learned from videos, while the benefit was less for those with average decoding and almost nonexistent for those with high decoding." Videos were not harmful for any reader group and produced more equitable retention. Teachers can identify likely beneficiaries with common decoding tests.
requirements: Access to video materials with spoken audio and learner controls on classroom devices
Decoding tests are common and easy to implement, allowing teachers to identify students most likely to benefit from video-based learning
constraints: Findings are from primary school science learning; extension to other domains and younger students needs further research
The modality effect was weaker when material was available during testing than in retention-based studying
target_learners: Fifth and sixth grade primary school students across reading skill levels
target_learning_goals: Science topic learning: retrieval, transfer, and long-term retention of expository content
examples: In the within-subjects experiment, children studied climate change and balance in nature from videos and illustrated texts on iPads in authentic lessons, with delayed tests one week later

article_title: Little and often: Causal inference machine learning demonstrates the benefits of homework for improving achievement in mathematics and science
citation: Nathan McJames, Andrew Parnell, and Ann O'Shea. (2023). Little and Often: Causal Inference Machine Learning Demonstrates the Benefits of Homework for Improving Achievement in Mathematics and Science. https://timssandpirls.bc.edu/timss2019/international-results
title: Multivariate Bayesian Causal Forests for estimating homework treatment effects on multiple outcomes
description: This study adopts a multivariate extension of Bayesian Causal Forests (BCF), a non-parametric causal inference machine learning model built on Bayesian Additive Regression Trees. The article states it "adopts a multivariate extension of BCF developed by McJames et al. (2023), which allows BCF to be applied to multiple outcome variables such as mathematics and science achievement simultaneously". The model estimates baseline achievement (mu) and treatment effects (tau) for four treatment groups covering higher frequencies and longer durations, with a classroom random intercept, capturing interactions and non-linear relationships without assuming linearity.
requirements: Observational data with a rich set of confounding covariates that can be controlled for, since the model assumes all confounding can be accounted for
Sufficiently large samples; the authors chose the Irish sample of 4118 students because it is large enough for the model to detect relationships and interactions
constraints: The model assumes all possible sources of confounding are accounted for; unmeasured confounders not collected in TIMSS could bias results
Imputed missing values (6% of data) carry uncertainty not reflected in the reported credible intervals
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement
science achievement
examples: The model was fit with 50 trees in the mu part and 20 trees in each tau part, 5000 MCMC iterations with the first 3000 discarded as burn-in, applied to five plausible values per student

article_title: Emotions in flipped and lecture-based math courses
citation: Hartikainen, S., Nokelainen, P., Puhakka, I., & Kangaslampi, R. (2026). Emotions in flipped and lecture-based math courses. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2026.102474
title: Control-value theory of achievement emotions as the study's organizing framework
description: The study is organized around the control-value theory (CVT) of achievement emotions, which "views individual appraisals of control and value as antecedents of emotions". CVT categorizes achievement emotions by valence (positive/negative) and arousal (activating/deactivating) plus object focus, and holds that positive activating emotions are most beneficial to learning while negative deactivating emotions may hinder it. The article uses CVT to select the measured emotions (hope, joy, relief, anxiety, hopelessness before events; joy, pride, contentment, relief, shame, anger, sadness, disappointment, gratitude after), to code arousal, and to interpret learning-mode and implementation differences as differences in perceived control, value, autonomy, and support.
requirements: Appraisal of control and value as antecedents: emotions arise from students' perceived control over actions and outcomes and the perceived value of the activity
constraints: The article notes negative activating emotions such as anxiety may sometimes mobilize effort, so their effects are context-dependent
target_learning_goals: achievement emotions in mathematics learning events
examples: The study coded each self-reported emotion into CVT valence × arousal quadrants, finding positive–activating emotions most common before events (48.2%) and positive–deactivating most common after (49.3%)

article_title: Fostering teenagers' assessment of information reliability: Effects of a classroom intervention focused on critical source dimensions
citation: Ana Pérez, Anna Potocki, Marc Stadtler, Mônica Macedo-Rouet, Johanna Paul, Ladislao Salmerón, Jean-François Rouet. (2018). Fostering Teenagers' Assessment of Information Reliability: Effects of a Classroom Intervention focused on Critical Source Dimensions. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2018.04.006
title: Content-Source Integration (CSI) model of processing conflicting documents
description: The Content-Source Integration model, attributed to Stadtler and Bromme (2014), explains how readers handle conflicting texts. It "posits that content-source integration involves three processing stages": detection of a conflict, regulation of the conflict (e.g., attributing the contradiction to different sources), and resolution of the conflict (e.g., evaluating information reliability). The article uses it, together with the D-ISC effect, to justify building the training workshops on the presentation and discussion of documents providing conflicting views, and predicts that readers with low prior knowledge rely on second-hand evaluation of source trustworthiness.
requirements: Readers must notice contradictions across texts dealing with the same topic for content-source integration to be triggered
constraints: When prior knowledge is low, readers may rather evaluate the trustworthiness of the sources (second-hand evaluation) rather than judge truth value from subject matter
target_learning_goals: evaluating information reliability when comprehending multiple conflicting documents
examples: The three workshops were largely based on the presentation and discussion of short documents providing conflicting views on a given topic

title: Knowledge application task: rating search-result links contrasted on three source dimensions
description: An assessment instrument in which students imagine searching for a topic and "rate on a Likert scale from 0 (certainly not) to 4 (certainly), whether they would consult or not several links". Author position, author motivation and media quality were manipulated to create four link types: good (reliable on all three dimensions), fair (two dimensions), poor (one), and bad (none), plus a filler link. The dependent variable was the mean normalized rating score from 0 to 1, with three counterbalanced topic versions.
requirements: Topic versions counterbalanced across phases and schools to prevent biases due to topic knowledge or interest
constraints: The distinction between more reliable (good, fair) and less reliable (poor, bad) links is described by the authors as merely indicative

examples: Topics included "The period of world history called Cold War", "Opinion polls in democratic societies", and "The health risks of electromagnetic waves emitted by mobile phones"

article_title: Congruence and friction between learning and teaching
citation: Jan D. Vermunt, Nico Verloop. (1999). Congruence and friction between learning and teaching. Learning and Instruction 9, 257–280. http://hdl.handle.net/1874/18753
title: Three-component taxonomy of learning activities: cognitive processing, affective, and metacognitive regulation
description: The article organizes student learning activities into three components drawn from Pintrich's comparison of taxonomies: cognitive processing, affective, and metacognitive (regulative) activities. Cognitive processing activities are "those thinking activities that students use to process subject matter and that lead directly to learning outcomes in terms of changes in students' knowledge base". Six processing categories (relating/structuring, analyzing, concretizing/applying, memorizing/rehearsing, critical processing, selecting), five affective categories, and five regulative categories (orienting/planning through evaluating/reflecting) are described, with the caveat that categories are neither exhaustive nor mutually exclusive.
requirements: Applies to upper secondary and higher education learning contexts as scoped by the article
constraints: The authors state the taxonomy is "not the ultimate solution but a helpful balance between simplified dichotomous categories and complex and elaborate categorical systems" and that categories are neither exhaustive nor mutually exclusive
target_learners: upper secondary and higher education students
target_learning_goals: self-regulated knowledge construction across cognitive, affective and regulative learning activities
examples: Table 1 summarizes the categorization of learning activities across the three components
key_sources: Jan D. Vermunt, Nico Verloop. (1999). Congruence and friction between learning and teaching. Learning and Instruction 9, 257–280. http://hdl.handle.net/1874/18753

article_title: Congruence and friction between learning and teaching
citation: Jan D. Vermunt, Nico Verloop. (1999). Congruence and friction between learning and teaching. Learning and Instruction 9, 257–280. http://hdl.handle.net/1874/18753
title: Four learning styles: undirected, reproduction-directed, meaning-directed and application-directed
description: The article defines learning style as a coherent whole of learning activities, learning orientation and conception of learning characteristic of a student in a certain period. Citing Vermunt's (1996, 1998) research, it reports "four qualitatively different learning styles as conceptualized above: undirected, reproduction-directed, meaning-directed and application-directed learning". Each style combines a processing strategy, a regulation strategy, a learning conception and an orientation; for example, the meaning-directed style combines deep processing, self-regulation, a knowledge-construction conception and personal interest.
requirements: Learning style is used broadly, including conceptions and orientations, not only consistent activity patterns
constraints: The article scopes this conceptualization to higher education students and notes family resemblances to Biggs's and Entwistle's orientations
target_learning_goals: diagnosing students' learning strategies and styles to tailor teaching
examples: The reproduction-directed style links stepwise processing and external regulation with a conception of learning as intake of teacher-provided knowledge
key_sources: Jan D. Vermunt, Nico Verloop. (1999). Congruence and friction between learning and teaching. Learning and Instruction 9, 257–280. http://hdl.handle.net/1874/18753

article_title: Congruence and friction between learning and teaching
citation: Jan D. Vermunt, Nico Verloop. (1999). Congruence and friction between learning and teaching. Learning and Instruction 9, 257–280. http://hdl.handle.net/1874/18753
title: Three teacher-regulation strategies: strong, shared and loose control of learning functions
description: The article places teaching methods on a dimension "ranging from very strongly teacher-regulated to very loosely teacher-regulated" and singles out three positions. Under strong control the teacher substitutes learning functions for students (e.g. presenting overviews, giving analogies); under shared control the teacher activates students to perform the functions themselves (e.g. asking for main points, letting students invent test questions); under loose control students perform all functions and the teacher mainly presents subject matter and tests outcomes. Teacher control includes regulation exerted by tasks, materials and other instructional agents, and every form of teaching can be characterized by a three-by-fifteen matrix of strategies by learning functions.
requirements: A task division between teachers and students in fulfilling learning functions always exists in practice
constraints: Complete teacher control or total absence of teacher control rarely occur; the three positions are a simplification of a continuum with many intermediate positions, including mixed control
target_learners: upper secondary and higher education students
target_learning_goals: regulation of students' learning and thinking activities during instruction
examples: Tables 2 and 3 give examples of teacher substitution and teacher activation of learning functions for each of the fifteen functions
key_sources: Jan D. Vermunt, Nico Verloop. (1999). Congruence and friction between learning and teaching. Learning and Instruction 9, 257–280. http://hdl.handle.net/1874/18753

article_title: Congruence and friction between learning and teaching
citation: Jan D. Vermunt, Nico Verloop. (1999). Congruence and friction between learning and teaching. Learning and Instruction 9, 257–280. http://hdl.handle.net/1874/18753
title: Process-oriented teaching promotes congruence and constructive friction while avoiding destructive friction
description: Process-oriented teaching focuses on the processes of knowledge construction and utilization, teaching domain-specific knowledge and learning-and-thinking strategies in coherence. The article states that "Process-oriented teaching tries to promote congruence and constructive friction, and to avoid destructive friction", with "a gradual transfer of learning functions from teachers to students". It aims to stimulate meaning- and application-directed learning styles and discourage undirected and reproduction-directed ways of learning.
requirements: Teachers must diagnose students' learning and thinking strategies to tailor teaching to functions students do not yet master
constraints: The article notes not all parts of the theory can yet be documented equally well with empirical research results
target_learners: upper secondary and higher education students
target_learning_goals: domain knowledge and self-regulated knowledge-construction skills developed in coherence
examples: The article derives four teacher roles from this view: diagnostician, challenger, model learner and activator

article_title: Coaching for the PISA test
citation: Brunner, M.; Artelt, C.; Krauss, Stefan; Baumert, J. (2007). Coaching for the PISA test. Learning and Instruction 17 (2), S. 111-122. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2007.01.002
title: Interpret low-stakes large-scale assessment scores with caution because coaching plus pretesting can raise performance
description: Because this study found that "only the combined effects of pretesting and coaching have substantial positive effects on student performance" on the low-stakes PISA assessments, score gains in large-scale assessments may partly reflect coaching and pretesting rather than pure achievement. The article draws implications for the interpretation of large-scale assessment programs from this finding.
requirements: Applies to low-stakes tests, which the article defines as tests with no personal relevance for the students taking them
constraints: The substantial positive effect required the combination of pretesting and coaching, not either alone
target_learners: Students taking large-scale assessments such as PISA
target_learning_goals: Valid interpretation of reading and mathematics achievement scores from large-scale assessment programs
examples: A pre-/posttest quasi-experimental study in German Hauptschule and Gymnasium schools examined coaching and pretest effects on PISA reading and mathematics performance separately by content domain
key_sources: Brunner, M.; Artelt, C.; Krauss, Stefan; Baumert, J. (2007). Coaching for the PISA test. Learning and Instruction 17 (2), S. 111-122. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2007.01.002

title: PISA coaching quasi-experiment (Hauptschule and Gymnasium, reading and mathematics)
description: A pre-/posttest quasi-experimental study in which "Coaching and pretest effects were studied for each content domain separately" on the PISA reading and mathematics assessments. Samples were drawn from German Hauptschule and Gymnasium schools to examine differential effects of academic tracks. The key result was that only combined pretesting and coaching showed substantial positive effects on performance.

article_title: Exploring the links between students' engagement in cooperative learning, their goal preferences and appraisals of instructional conditions in the classroom
citation: Hijzen, D., Boekaerts, M., & Vedder, P. H. (2007). Exploring the links between students' engagement in cooperative learning, their goal preferences and appraisals of instructional conditions in the classroom. Learning And Instruction, 17(6), 673-687. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2007.09.020
title: Three types of engagement during cooperative learning: task-relevant, task-irrelevant, and socially oriented task engagement
description: Following Chapman (2003), the article distinguishes "three types of engagement that may occur during CL". Task-relevant engagement characterizes students who are active, focus on the task and persist; task-irrelevant engagement characterizes disaffected students who "do not try hard, give up easily" and chat or disturb others; socially oriented task engagement involves students "primarily involved in social activities such as providing help and emotional support". The study operationalizes these as subscales of an observation rating list and uses them to define effective versus ineffective CL teams.
requirements: Engagement must be observed during actual CL sessions and rated with items covering the three engagement types
constraints: The article treats engagement as students' actual involvement, distinct from motivation, which concerns underlying cognitions
target_learning_goals: engagement in cooperative learning tasks
examples: The 18-item rating list contained three subscales with sample items such as "this student chats" (α = 0.89), "this student concentrates on the task" (α = 0.95), and "this student offers team members help" (α = 0.90).

title: 18-item engagement rating list for observing CL engagement
description: An observational instrument developed "to rate engagement levels of the individual students in CL", based on Skinner and Belmont (1993) and the Quality of CL questionnaire. It contains three subscales measuring task-irrelevant engagement (sample item "this student chats", α = 0.89), task-relevant engagement ("this student concentrates on the task", α = 0.95), and socially oriented engagement ("this student offers team members help", α = 0.90), rated on four response categories from "almost never" to "very often". Two trained raters achieved Cohen's Kappa of 0.66 (p = 0.006).
requirements: A scoring guide with item examples and trained raters to optimize interrater reliability
constraints: Ratings were made on 10-minute video recordings of CL sessions
target_learning_goals: measuring task-relevant, task-irrelevant and socially oriented engagement
examples: Raters rated the engagement levels of the 57 students on one video-tape, the same recording used in the stimulated-recall session.

article_title: Maternal homework assistance and children's task-persistent behavior in elementary school
citation: Viljaranta, J., Silinskas, G., Lerkkanen, M.-K., Hirvonen, R., Pakarinen, E., Poikkeus, A.-M., & Nurmi, J.-E. (2017). Maternal Homework Assistance and Children’s Task-Persistent Behavior in Elementary School. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Maternal+Homework+Assistance+and+Children%E2%80%99s+Task-Persistent+Behavior+in+Elementary+School
title: Self-determination theory-based typology of maternal homework assistance: help, monitoring, and autonomy granting
description: The article applies self-determination theory to distinguish three types of maternal homework assistance by their level of direct involvement. Autonomy granting means trusting the child to work independently; help is active, direct involvement — "in terms of the parent actively and directly helping the child with homework tasks by, for example, sitting next to the child and working on the task together"; monitoring is lower-involvement checking that homework is complete and correct. Help and monitoring are seen as more controlling practices that may diminish children's feelings of autonomy and competence, whereas autonomy granting satisfies needs for autonomy and competence and supports motivated, persistent behavior.
requirements: Distinguishing the three types requires measuring the amount of each practice separately, as different types are differently related to children's outcomes
constraints: The article measures the amount (frequency) of assistance via mothers' self-reports, not its quality, and treats help and monitoring as general rather than subject-specific constructs
target_learning_goals: task-persistent behavior in learning situations
academic performance in math and reading
examples: Mothers rated the frequency of help, monitoring, and autonomy granting on identical 10-item questionnaires in Grades 2, 3, and 4, with three factors extracted at all time points

article_title: Effects of heterogeneity simulations on beliefs
citation: Baier-Mosch, Franziska; Dignath, Charlotte; Kunter, Mareike (2026). Effects of heterogeneity simulations on beliefs. Learning and Instruction 101, Art. 102258. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102258
title: Empathy-and-internalization account of self-experience simulations
description: The article grounds heterogeneity simulations in experience-based learning theory drawn from disability-simulation research: simulations in which people self-experience situations of others are argued to be effective "because they lead to empathy", which comprises affective and cognitive components. Empathy is said to trigger internalization, whereby external social regulations become "internalized, personally endorsed values and beliefs". The article applies this account to explain why self-experience, but not reading a factual text, should change heterogeneity-responsive teaching beliefs.
requirements: The learner must directly experience the simulated situation (self-experience), not merely receive factual information about it
constraints: The article notes empathy was not directly measured as an explanatory mechanism in its own research
target_learning_goals: beliefs about the importance of heterogeneity-responsive teaching
examples: The heterogeneity simulation operationalized the account by having participants read simulated peer feedback revealing different perceived difficulty of the same text

article_title: Effects of heterogeneity simulations on beliefs
citation: Baier-Mosch, Franziska; Dignath, Charlotte; Kunter, Mareike (2026). Effects of heterogeneity simulations on beliefs. Learning and Instruction 101, Art. 102258. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102258
title: Text-based heterogeneity simulation with simulated peer feedback
description: A short, stand-alone online intervention in which pre-service teachers read a 302-word text on learning theories, rate its difficulty, and then read "the written feedback from six fictitious other students (143 words long)" whose difficulty ratings were heterogeneous (two very easy, two very difficult, two appropriate), followed by a written reflection on their own and peers' heterogeneity in prior knowledge. Manipulation credibility was supported because participants' own difficulty ratings (Study 1: M =32.42, SD =21.28, min =1, max =85) spanned almost the entire 1-100 range. It takes about 30 minutes including measures and can be integrated into university teacher education economically.
requirements: A base learning task on which participants give difficulty ratings, plus heterogeneous simulated peer feedback and a reflection prompt
constraints: The article states word length of materials across conditions was not fully standardized and suggests a homogeneous-feedback condition is needed to isolate the pure effect of heterogeneity information
target_learners: pre-service teachers in university teacher education
target_learning_goals: beliefs about the importance of responding to students' heterogeneity in prior knowledge
examples: In both studies participants were randomly assigned to the simulation, a heterogeneity text, or a control condition, fully online

article_title: Classroom emotions in civic education: A multilevel approach to antecedents and effects
citation: Graf, E., Stempfer, L., Muis, K. R., & Goetz, T. (2023). Classroom emotions in civic education: A multilevel approach to antecedents and effects. Draft version 1.0, University of Vienna / McGill University (not peer-reviewed preprint).
title: Control-value theory applied to civic education: classroom context as distal antecedent and valence/arousal-categorized emotions as mediators of civic learning
description: The study applies Pekrun's control-value theory, in which "the classroom context is an important factor in determining the experience of classroom emotions," and emotions are categorized by valence (positive/negative) and arousal (activating/deactivating). Distal environmental antecedents such as classroom climate shape emotions, which in turn relate to learning processes and outcomes and can mediate between context and outcomes. The article reports that results "strongly support the theoretical assumptions of the control-value theory" in the civic education domain.
requirements: Emotions are measured as discrete class-related emotions (enjoyment, shame, anxiety, boredom) distinguished by valence and activation
constraints: Tested in civic education with vocational-school students in Austria; observational and cross-sectional, so causal claims are not supported
target_learning_goals: political knowledge
intended political participation
examples: The study tested CVT hypotheses with doubly-latent multilevel SEM on survey and knowledge-test data from 1,117 students

article_title: Mapping students' interest in a new domain: Connecting prior knowledge, interest, and self-efficacy with interesting tasks and a lasting desire to reengage
citation: Fryer, L. K., Shum, A., Lee, A., & Lau, P. (2021). Mapping students' interest in a new domain: Connecting prior knowledge, interest and self-efficacy with interesting tasks and a lasting desire to reengage. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2021.101493
title: Task-Course-Domain refocusing of the Four Phase Model of interest development for university courses
description: The article refocuses the Four Phase Model of interest development (Hidi & Renninger) onto three measurable interest objects within a university course: Task interest (consistent with situational interest, with a specific task as its object), Course interest (a combination of interest in the learning environment and the content under study), and Domain interest (consistent with individual interest, not confined to a course). As the article states, "on the way to the development of an individual's Domain interest, for example, teaching, the student will encounter the specific localised levels of Task interest and the more general level of course interest within that broader domain." This structure makes it realistic to model interconnections between readiness, task experiences, and longer-term interest across a single course.
requirements: Readiness components (prior Domain interest, prior knowledge, self-efficacy) must be assessed to model forward connections to and through Task interest
constraints: Applied here to a mandatory introductory course for research postgraduate students new to the teaching domain
target_learners: research postgraduate students in an introductory university teaching course
target_learning_goals: development of Domain interest in teaching
examples: The study measured interest in seven strategically chosen tasks immediately after each task, Course interest in module seven, and Domain interest in the final module
key_sources: Fryer, L. K., Shum, A., Lee, A., & Lau, P. (2021). Mapping students' interest in a new domain: Connecting prior knowledge, interest and self-efficacy with interesting tasks and a lasting desire to reengage. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2021.101493

article_title: Dimensional comparisons in students' perceptions of the learning environment
citation: Arens, A.K., & Möller, J. (2016). Dimensional comparisons in students' perceptions of the learning environment. Learning and Instruction, 42, 22–30. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2015.11.001
title: The generalized internal/external frames of reference (GI/E) model extends the classic I/E model and dimensional comparison theory to outcome variables beyond academic self-concepts.
description: The GI/E model generalizes the internal/external frames of reference model, which explains near-zero correlations between math and language self-concepts via simultaneous social and dimensional comparisons. Building on dimensional comparison theory, the GI/E model assumes "dimensional comparisons to become evident by negative or near-zero cross-domain relations between any kinds of independent and outcome variables." This study applies the model to students' perceptions of the learning environment — perceived instructional quality and student-teacher relations — as outcome variables, finding the predicted pattern of positive within-domain and negative or near-zero cross-domain relations with achievement.
requirements: Requires at least two domains with comparable achievement and outcome measures to test cross-domain versus within-domain relations
constraints: The classic I/E model was restricted to math and language achievement as independent variables and self-concepts as outcomes; the GI/E model opens this logic to other variables but the present evidence is limited to achievement as the independent variable
target_learning_goals: understanding how social and dimensional comparison processes shape students' perceptions of their learning environment
examples: The study tested the GI/E model with N = 4926 students, using math and language grades as achievement indicators and four-item scales for perceived teacher relations and instructional quality in each domain.
key_sources: Arens, A.K., & Möller, J. (2016). Dimensional comparisons in students' perceptions of the learning environment. Learning and Instruction, 42, 22–30. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2015.11.001

article_title: Early childcare enrollment and the pursuit of higher education: A Canadian longitudinal study
citation: Garon-Carrier, G., Ansari, A., Letarte, M.-J., & Fitzpatrick, C. (2022). Early childcare enrollment and the pursuit of higher education: A Canadian longitudinal study. Learning and Instruction, 80. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101615
title: Compensatory effect and lost-resource effect accounts of childcare outcomes
description: The article uses two explanatory accounts for heterogeneous childcare effects. The compensatory hypothesis "suggests that childcare may be particularly beneficial for children from low-income families", which the authors see supported by the finding that childcare attendance increased enrollment probability for children from low-income and non-working families. The lost-resource effect (Desai et al., 1989) describes how "children with cognitively and linguistically stimulating home environment may be comparatively deprived of learning opportunities when receiving formal out of home childcare", which the authors invoke for higher-income children in formal care.
requirements: Distinguishing family contexts (e.g., household income, parental employment) to identify which children benefit from which arrangement
constraints: The authors present these as interpretations of observational matched data, not tested mechanisms; unmeasured factors could also account for the associations
target_learners: Children from low-income or non-working families
target_learning_goals: Long-term educational attainment (enrollment in higher education)
examples: The study found formal childcare attendance mitigated disparities in pursuit of higher education for vulnerable children while being associated with reduced chances for children from higher-income, fully-employed families
