article_title: Do easy-to-read adaptations really facilitate sentence processing for adults with a lower level of education? An experimental eye-tracking study
citation: Miriam Rivero-Contreras, Paul E. Engelhardt, David Saldaña. (2023). Do easy-to-read adaptations really facilitate sentence processing for adults with a lower level of education? An experimental eye-tracking study. Learning and Instruction 84 (2023) 101731. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101731
title: Apply Easy-to-Read adaptations—visual support and lexical simplification—to facilitate adult sentence processing
description: The article supports the Easy-to-Read guideline recommendations of accompanying text with contextualizing images and replacing low-frequency words with high-frequency ones. The authors state that "general contextualizing pictures which include all elements of a sentence can be moderately supportive of its comprehension," and both adaptations facilitated processing and comprehension in adults with lower and higher education levels.
requirements: Images should be visual representations of the sentence content, including the target word, created for the text
Lexical simplification substitutes low-frequency words with higher-frequency words more common in oral language
constraints: The effect sizes for pictures were small to moderate, and the authors note more research is needed on which type of visual support is most useful
Perceived text difficulty did not differ by adaptation, so reader ratings alone do not capture the benefit
target_learners: adults with a lower level of education
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension
sentence processing
examples: In the experiment, sentences were accompanied by a contextualizing image below the text, and sentence pairs differed only in the frequency of one target word, with comprehension assessed by true/false statements
key_sources: Miriam Rivero-Contreras, Paul E. Engelhardt, David Saldaña. (2023). Do easy-to-read adaptations really facilitate sentence processing for adults with a lower level of education? An experimental eye-tracking study. Learning and Instruction 84 (2023) 101731. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101731

article_title: Effects of supplemental instruction on grades, mental well-being, and belonging: A field experiment
citation: Dekker, I., Luberti, M., & Stam, J. (2022). Effects of supplemental instruction on grades, mental well-being, and belonging: A field experiment. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-6858-4001
title: Supplemental Instruction (SI): structured peer-led weekly sessions attached to historically difficult courses
description: Supplemental Instruction is peer learning in which "experienced peers (the SI-leaders) are trained to design and execute 50-100 minute voluntary sessions for a classroom of students on a weekly basis". SI leaders do not introduce new concepts but stimulate discussion and application of class content via collaborative learning techniques and practice assessments. In this study, 7 weekly 100-minute sessions were offered to randomly assigned first-year students across 10 courses, with leaders trained via a Dutch adaptation of the Texas State University program.
requirements: SI leaders must have recently successfully completed the supported course and be extensively trained and observed by a certified SI-supervisor
SI leaders prepare sessions with opening, middle, and closing activities using collaborative learning techniques
constraints: In this study the requirement that SI leaders attend at least 60% of the supported course's lectures was not met; leaders watched lecture recordings instead
target_learners: first-year higher-education students in historically difficult courses
target_learning_goals: consolidation of course subject matter and improved course grades
examples: 42 groups combined into 39 SI groups across 10 courses of study; leaders uploaded lesson plans a week ahead for supervisor and lecturer feedback
key_sources: Dekker, I., Luberti, M., & Stam, J. (2022). Effects of supplemental instruction on grades, mental well-being, and belonging: A field experiment. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-6858-4001

article_title: Capturing teacher priorities: Using real-world eye-tracking to investigate expert teacher priorities across two cultures
citation: McIntyre, N. A., Jarodzka, H., & Klassen, R. M. (2019). Capturing teacher priorities: Using real-world eye-tracking to investigate expert teacher priorities across two cultures. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2017.12.003
title: Gaze proportions as implicit micro-level indicators of explicit macro-level teacher priorities, analysed separately for attentional and communicative gaze
description: The article proposes that gaze proportions—how much a person looks at one region relative to alternatives—serve as implicit, intensive measures of teachers' enduring decision-making priorities, extending a decision-making analytic approach to educational psychology. It distinguishes attentional gaze (information-seeking, e.g., questioning) from communicative gaze (information-giving, e.g., lecturing), classifying gaze events by the speech co-occurring with them. Higher gaze proportions toward a region are interpreted as greater priority for that region.
requirements: Real-world mobile eye-tracking recordings of teaching, with simultaneous speech used to classify each gaze event as attentional or communicative
Relativized gaze proportion measures computed per participant due to uneven occurrences of gaze events across individuals
constraints: The measure accesses teachers' cognitive habits only; the article states it "does not offer an avenue for understanding teaching styles or personality as such"
Gaze proportions revealed more about teacher priorities during communicative than attentional gaze in this study
The priority measure was not triangulated with an explicit self-report measure of teacher priority
target_learning_goals: teacher expertise development
classroom prioritisation of students
examples: 40 teachers in the UK and Hong Kong wore Tobii eye-tracking glasses during ten-minute teacher-centred episodes; gaze was coded to students, student material, teacher material, and non-instructional regions
key_sources: McIntyre, N. A., Jarodzka, H., & Klassen, R. M. (2019). Capturing teacher priorities: Using real-world eye-tracking to investigate expert teacher priorities across two cultures. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2017.12.003

article_title: Capturing teacher priorities: Using real-world eye-tracking to investigate expert teacher priorities across two cultures
citation: McIntyre, N. A., Jarodzka, H., & Klassen, R. M. (2019). Capturing teacher priorities: Using real-world eye-tracking to investigate expert teacher priorities across two cultures. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2017.12.003
title: Teachers should prioritise students, as a foundational, culture-transcending element of teacher training curricula
description: Because experts in both cultures directed higher gaze proportions toward students during both attentional and communicative instruction, the article contends that "student-centredness is one aspect of teacher cognition that deserves to be foundational universally, in both Western European and East Asian teacher training curricula." The recommendation rests on the observed expert–novice gaze difference and the absence of cultural differences in student gaze.
requirements: Teacher education programmes willing to treat student-centredness as a foundational component across cultural settings
constraints: The recommendation derives from gaze-proportion evidence in one study of secondary teachers in two cultural settings; the article notes no cultural differences emerged in student prioritisation
target_learning_goals: student-centred teaching
classroom prioritisation of students
examples: Expert teachers in both the UK and Hong Kong samples used higher proportions of student gaze than novices during questioning and lecturing episodes
key_sources: McIntyre, N. A., Jarodzka, H., & Klassen, R. M. (2019). Capturing teacher priorities: Using real-world eye-tracking to investigate expert teacher priorities across two cultures. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2017.12.003

article_title: Is the clique a pond? The big-fish-little-pond effect and the relative meaning of clique and classroom
citation: Tanja Auer, Marion Reindl, Burkhard Gniewosz. (2025). Is the clique a pond? The big-fish-little-pond effect and the relative meaning of clique and classroom. Learning and Instruction 95 (2025) 101997. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2024.101997
title: Local dominance extension of the BFLPE: self-selected cliques as the most proximal reference group for adolescent ASC
description: This framework extends the big-fish-little-pond effect by adding the informal, self-selected clique as a reference group alongside the formal classroom. Building on social comparison theory and the local dominance effect, it holds that reference groups must fulfill "similarity, accessibility, and proximity", and that cliques fulfill these better than classrooms because members are voluntarily selected, interact more routinely inside and outside class, and share tighter social bonds. The article concludes the reference-group hierarchy extends "from the broader school environment to the classroom (both formal environments) and then to peer groups (moving from formal to informal contexts)".
requirements: Reference groups must fulfill the criteria of similarity, accessibility, and proximity to serve as comparison standards
constraints: Findings are limited to mathematics ASC among sixth- and eighth-grade German secondary students in one school year; peer nominations were restricted to same-classroom peers, and only clique members were analyzed
target_learning_goals: development of academic self-concept in mathematics
examples: In the study, clique-average achievement negatively predicted ASC change while classroom-average achievement did not, supporting the clique as the more proximal reference group
key_sources: Tanja Auer, Marion Reindl, Burkhard Gniewosz. (2025). Is the clique a pond? The big-fish-little-pond effect and the relative meaning of clique and classroom. Learning and Instruction 95 (2025) 101997. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2024.101997

article_title: Creative problem solving in primary school students
citation: Van Hooijdonk, M., Mainhard, T., Kroesbergen, E. H., & Van Tartwijk, J. (2023). Creative problem solving in primary school students. Learning and Instruction, 88, 101823. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2023.101823
title: The CPS model describes creative problem solving as four main elements, with the first three applied flexibly and iteratively
description: The Creative Problem Solving (CPS) model of Isaksen, Treffinger and colleagues describes creative problem solving as a set of behaviors organized into four main elements: "understanding the challenge, generating ideas, preparing for action and planning your approach". The first three elements are flexible and dynamic in ordering, so students may switch back and forth between them iteratively, while the fourth element covers planning and monitoring the process. The article applies this education-oriented model to study how primary school students solve everyday problems creatively.
requirements: Students work on an open, everyday problem situation that allows interpretation and idea generation
constraints: The model was adapted specifically for the educational context by Treffinger, Isaksen and colleagues
target_learning_goals: creative problem solving of everyday problems in science, social, and entrepreneurial domains
examples: In Study 1, 13 fourth graders thought aloud while completing a structured science problem task, and their verbalized behaviors were coded against the four CPS elements
key_sources: Van Hooijdonk, M., Mainhard, T., Kroesbergen, E. H., & Van Tartwijk, J. (2023). Creative problem solving in primary school students. Learning and Instruction, 88, 101823. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2023.101823

article_title: Creative problem solving in primary school students
citation: Van Hooijdonk, M., Mainhard, T., Kroesbergen, E. H., & Van Tartwijk, J. (2023). Creative problem solving in primary school students. Learning and Instruction, 88, 101823. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2023.101823
title: Four creative problem solving product indicators: fluency, originality, completeness, and practicality
description: The article treats the products of creative problem solving as ideas rated on four indicators. Fluency is the number of ideas a student generates, while "Solutions that a student ends up with after a creative problem solving process are usually regarded as creative when they are original, complete and practical". This extends classic divergent thinking scoring (fluency, flexibility, originality, elaboration) by emphasizing usefulness: ideas should be assessed not only for quantity and originality but also for how complete and practical they are. In Study 2 these indicators were operationalized as latent factors rated via a modified Consensual Assessment Technique.
requirements: Ideas generated in response to a problem situation, with top-scoring selection to fix the number of rated ideas per student
constraints: The flexibility factor is less frequently applied in later creativity assessment because of its strong correlations with fluency
target_learning_goals: evaluating the creativity of students' problem-solving ideas
examples: In Study 2, two trained raters rated students' self-selected top-three ideas on 5-point scales for originality, completeness, and practicality, and counted fluency as the number of different ideas listed
key_sources: Van Hooijdonk, M., Mainhard, T., Kroesbergen, E. H., & Van Tartwijk, J. (2023). Creative problem solving in primary school students. Learning and Instruction, 88, 101823. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2023.101823

article_title: Creative problem solving in primary school students
citation: Van Hooijdonk, M., Mainhard, T., Kroesbergen, E. H., & Van Tartwijk, J. (2023). Creative problem solving in primary school students. Learning and Instruction, 88, 101823. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2023.101823
title: Structured creative problem solving task with vignette-based problem situations and four pre-structured steps
description: The article constructed structured tasks in which students read a short vignette describing an everyday problem (science, social, or entrepreneurial domain) and are "guided through four pre-structured steps of the task": exploring relevant knowledge in a mind map, framing the problem as a question, generating as many different and original ideas as possible in ten minutes, and selecting their three most creative ideas. Six design criteria governed the vignettes, e.g. "The problem situations are open and non-directive, enabling the participant to form his/her own interpretation of the described situation". Three problems were selected by nine-year-old students ranking six candidate situations on complexity, importance, realism, efficacy, and experience.
requirements: Problem descriptions written in short sentences with word choices suitable for children between 9 and 12 years old; problems presented on paper and read aloud
constraints: The three selected problems ranked lowest on complexity but highest on realism, efficacy, and experience per student rankings
target_learning_goals: eliciting creative problem solving processes and products across science, social, and entrepreneurial domains
examples: The science problem described Lisa and Tom whose ice cream melted on the way home; the social problem involved Simon being distracted by his friend Julian; the entrepreneurial problem described Aron who wants a new bicycle but owns only a two-euro coin
key_sources: Van Hooijdonk, M., Mainhard, T., Kroesbergen, E. H., & Van Tartwijk, J. (2023). Creative problem solving in primary school students. Learning and Instruction, 88, 101823. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2023.101823

article_title: Complexity affects performance, cognitive load, and awareness
citation: Ines Zeitlhofer, Joerg Zumbach, Judith Schweppe. (2024). Complexity affects performance, cognitive load, and awareness. Learning and Instruction 94 (2024) 102001. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2024.102001
title: Expose learners to consistently high task complexity to stimulate germane processing without harming intrinsic interest
description: This principle holds that, contrary to the standard cognitive load recommendation of gradually increasing complexity, presenting learners with consistently high complexity problem-solving tasks can stimulate germane cognitive processing and metacognitive engagement. The authors conclude that "exposing learners to consistently high complexity tasks can have beneficial effects on learning without negatively influencing intrinsic interest." It applies to problem-solving tasks where complexity can be manipulated, such as the Tower of Hanoi task used in the study.
requirements: Learners must tackle problem-solving tasks whose complexity can be manipulated, such as varying the number of disks in the Tower of Hanoi task
constraints: The immediate-performance advantage did not carry over to a delayed post-test two days later
Only germane cognitive load was assessed, not overall cognitive load
The study used a standardized problem-solving activity rather than authentic learning materials
target_learners: university students with no prior familiarity with the learning task
target_learning_goals: problem-solving schema construction
metacognitive awareness of solution strategies
examples: Participants repeatedly solved a six-disk Tower of Hanoi task (consistently high complexity) or progressed from four to six disks (gradually increasing), with performance assessed by time and number of moves
key_sources: Ines Zeitlhofer, Joerg Zumbach, Judith Schweppe. (2024). Complexity affects performance, cognitive load, and awareness. Learning and Instruction 94 (2024) 102001. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2024.102001

article_title: Effects of SI-PASS on a high-risk course – A randomized controlled trial
citation: Puttaert, N., Dachet, D., Baye, A., Quertemont, E., Leduc, L., Nyssen, A.-S., & Verpoorten, D. (2025). Effects of SI-PASS on a high-risk course – A randomized controlled trial. Learning and Instruction, 95, 102042. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2024.102042
title: Encourage students to attend more SI-PASS sessions rather than altering the scheme itself
description: Because performance benefits emerged only above an attendance cut point, the authors recommend that support efforts target participation levels. As they state, "any endeavors aimed at improving the support to students should not involve altering the SI-PASS scheme itself but directed towards encouraging students to elevate their level of participation in the weekly sessions." The principle rests on the threshold finding that at least five meetings were needed for significant improvement.
requirements: SI-PASS sessions must be attached to a high-risk course with weekly meetings students can attend repeatedly
constraints: The exact threshold likely varies across contexts; the optimal attendance level remains an open question, and the five-meeting cut point was found in one RCT on a statistics course
target_learners: first-year university students in high-risk courses
target_learning_goals: academic performance in a high-risk discipline course
examples: In the RCT, students attending at least 5 of 12 weekly meetings scored significantly higher (mean difference of 2.08 on a 20-point scale) than those attending fewer

article_title: Are both classroom autonomy support and structure equally important for students' engagement? A multilevel analysis
citation: Hospel, V., & Galand, B. (2016). Are both classroom autonomy support and structure equally important for students’ engagement? A multilevel analysis. Learning and Instruction, 41(1), 1-10. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2015.09.001
title: Self-determination theory as the framework linking teacher autonomy support and structure to student engagement
description: The study is carried out "within the framework of self-determination theory", which the authors use to organize two distinct classroom-level teacher provisions — autonomy support and structure — and to investigate their "specific, additive and combined effects" on students' behavioral, cognitive and emotional engagement. The framework treats the learning environment as a classroom-level context whose provisions relate differentially to engagement components, with structure linked to all three and autonomy support to emotional engagement.
requirements: Both teacher provisions are measured as students' perceptions at the classroom level, requiring aggregation across students within classes
constraints: Evidence concerns ninth-grade students in language classes; the abstract does not generalize beyond this setting
target_learning_goals: behavioral, cognitive and emotional engagement in classroom learning
examples: 744 ninth-grade students from 51 classes completed a questionnaire about their engagement during language classes and their perceptions of the teacher's provision of autonomy support and structure
key_sources: Hospel, V., & Galand, B. (2016). Are both classroom autonomy support and structure equally important for students’ engagement? A multilevel analysis. Learning and Instruction, 41(1), 1-10. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2015.09.001

article_title: Experiencing fear appeals as a challenge or a threat influences attainment value and academic self-efficacy
citation: The appraisal of fear appeals as a challenge or a threat influences a subsequent decline or increase in attainment value and academic self-efficacy. (2014). https://eric.ed.gov/?q=appraisal+of+fear+appeals+challenge+threat+attainment+value+academic+self-efficacy
title: Challenge and threat appraisal framework for classroom fear appeals grounded in EVT and control-value theory
description: The article frames teacher fear appeals prior to high-stakes examinations as appraised on two dimensions: primary appraisal of personal relevance and secondary appraisal of response options. It states that "A challenge appraisal occurs when the fear appeal is judged as being relevant and the student believes that they can respond effectively to the demands posed in the message", accompanied by positive emotions such as hope, whereas a threat appraisal occurs when demands are believed to outweigh one's ability to respond, accompanied by anxiety. Attainment value (from expectancy-value theory) establishes relevance and academic self-efficacy establishes response options, and a CVT feedback loop from emotions back to control and value beliefs explains how appraisals subsequently change those beliefs.
requirements: Fear appeals must be personally relevant to students for appraisal processes to operate
Constructs should be operationalised at the same level of domain specificity (here subject-specific, per the matching-specificity principle)
constraints: The study examined student-level appraisals only and did not measure actual teacher behaviour such as frequency or strength of fear appeals
Only attainment value was examined; other subjective task values, in particular cost, were not included
target_learners: Secondary school students in the final two years of education preparing for high-stakes examinations
target_learning_goals: Maintaining attainment value and academic self-efficacy in the run-up to high-stakes examinations
examples: Students with high attainment value and high academic self-efficacy (+1 SD) at T1 were projected to report a challenge score of 4.17 and a threat score of 2.56, with above-average T3 academic self-efficacy (3.86) and attainment value (4.24).

article_title: Scaffolding of learning activities: Aptitude-treatment-interaction effects in math?
citation: Sarah I. Hofer, Frank Reinhold. (2025). Scaffolding of learning activities: Aptitude-treatment-interaction effects in math?. Learning and Instruction 99 (2025) 102177. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102177
title: Expanded scaffolding framework: scaffolds as modifications of learning activities classified by cognitive, motivational, and metacognitive intentions
description: The article proposes an expanded conception of scaffolding that goes beyond providing additional information to include modifications in the implementation of a learning activity itself, such as dynamic instead of static visualizations or performance-adapted task difficulty. It classifies scaffolds by 'scaffolding intentions' — cognitive, motivational, and metacognitive — noting that "these classifications are not supposed to be deterministic" since one scaffold can serve several functions. The framework connects scaffolds to the specific mechanisms underlying established learning activities, guiding which scaffold fits which activity.
requirements: Scaffolds must tap underlying cognitive, motivational, or metacognitive processes required for the learning activity to work as intended
The learning activity and its affordances must first be identified before choosing scaffolds
constraints: Metacognitive scaffolding is defined but was not investigated in the present study
target_learners: 6th-grade secondary school students in mathematics classrooms
target_learning_goals: Conceptual and procedural knowledge of fractions on the number line
examples: Dynamic visualizations as a cognitive information-processing scaffold for learning with analogies; adaptive task difficulty as a motivational scaffold and individualized explanations based on typical mistakes as a cognitive information scaffold during repeated practice
key_sources: Sarah I. Hofer, Frank Reinhold. (2025). Scaffolding of learning activities: Aptitude-treatment-interaction effects in math?. Learning and Instruction 99 (2025) 102177. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102177

article_title: The effects of achievement goal instructions in game-based learning on students’ achievement goals, performance, and achievement emotions
citation: Hu, Y., Wouters, P., van der Schaaf, M., & Kester, L. (2024). The effects of achievement goal instructions in game-based learning on students' achievement goals, performance, and achievement emotions. Learning and Instruction, 93, 101943. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2024.101943
title: Multiple goal perspective mechanisms and match/mismatch hypotheses for achievement goal instructions
description: The article organizes its predictions through the multiple goal perspective (Barron & Harackiewicz, 2001), which proposes four mechanisms by which combined mastery-approach and performance-approach goals may produce optimal outcomes: the "specialized mechanism", "additive mechanism", "selective mechanism", and "interactive mechanism". It pairs these with the match hypothesis (instructions work best when they match prior achievement goals) and mismatch hypothesis (mismatched instructions may be vibrated, migrated, or exacerbated) from Murayama & Elliot. The study tested the specialized, additive, and interactive mechanisms and the moderation hypotheses in chemistry game-based learning.
requirements: Achievement goal instructions that assign learners' goals beforehand, and measurement of prior achievement goals before the intervention
constraints: The study tested only state-based approach goals, excluding avoidance goals because they may not be as prevalent among secondary school students as theory expected
target_learners: secondary school students in chemistry game-based learning
target_learning_goals: chemistry content learning (separation techniques) in game-based learning
examples: The 2×2 experiment assigned 450 students to mastery-approach, performance-approach, multiple goal, or no goal instructions conditions before playing CosmiClean
key_sources: Hu, Y., Wouters, P., van der Schaaf, M., & Kester, L. (2024). The effects of achievement goal instructions in game-based learning on students' achievement goals, performance, and achievement emotions. Learning and Instruction, 93, 101943. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2024.101943

article_title: General introduction to the special issue on resilience in learning
citation: van Viersen, S., Psyridou, M., & Torppa, M. (2026). General introduction to the special issue on resilience in learning. Learning and Instruction, 101, Article 102254. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102254
title: Promotive, protective, and compensatory effects framework for academic resilience research
description: The special issue's theoretical backbone distinguishes promotive effects (factors benefiting all learners), protective effects (factors offsetting risk), and compensatory mechanisms. Slomowitz et al. introduce "the seesaw metaphor" and provide "definitions and methodological guidelines for analysis and interpretation of promotive and protective effects, as well as compensatory mechanisms in academic resilience research". Appels et al. add guidelines for interpreting main and interaction effects in variable- and person-centered designs.
requirements: Designs and statistical techniques that allow discerning between promotive, protective, and skill-enhancing effects, as the editors state is essential
constraints: The editors note no studies in the issue manipulated protective factors through experiments or interventions, and hypotheses about specific compensatory mechanisms were largely absent
target_learners: At-risk learners, including learners with specific learning disabilities
target_learning_goals: Development of foundational academic skills: reading, writing, and mathematics
examples: Slomowitz et al. used examples from the context of learning disabilities, mainly dyslexia, to illustrate the framework
key_sources: van Viersen, S., Psyridou, M., & Torppa, M. (2026). General introduction to the special issue on resilience in learning. Learning and Instruction, 101, Article 102254. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102254

article_title: How feedback affects emotions, performance and self-concept in mathematics
citation: Van der Beek, J.P.J.; Van der Ven, S.H.G.; Van de Weijer-Bergsma, E.; Kroesbergen, E.H. (2025). How feedback affects emotions, performance and self-concept in mathematics. Learning and Instruction 99, 102169. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102169
title: Control-Value Theory as framework for feedback effects on achievement emotions, performance and self-concept
description: The study is framed by Pekrun's Control-Value Theory, in which "performance feedback is regarded as an important antecedent of achievement emotions, which subsequently affect performance and self-concept". Emotions are classified as positive or negative, activating or deactivating, and activity- or outcome-focused; feedback effects are shaped by control appraisals, value appraisals and achievement goals. The article's findings on hope as the key mediator are interpreted within this framework.
requirements: Feedback must be appraised by students through control and value appraisals for emotional effects to arise, per the theory's structure as described
constraints: The article notes control-value appraisals, achievement goals and emotions can be domain- and even situation-specific, so effects need not generalize across subjects
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement emotions
math performance
math self-concept
examples: The experiment operationalized feedback as an antecedent and measured anxiety, anger, enjoyment and hope as mediators of performance and self-concept effects
key_sources: Van der Beek, J.P.J.; Van der Ven, S.H.G.; Van de Weijer-Bergsma, E.; Kroesbergen, E.H. (2025). How feedback affects emotions, performance and self-concept in mathematics. Learning and Instruction 99, 102169. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102169

article_title: How feedback affects emotions, performance and self-concept in mathematics
citation: Van der Beek, J.P.J.; Van der Ven, S.H.G.; Van de Weijer-Bergsma, E.; Kroesbergen, E.H. (2025). How feedback affects emotions, performance and self-concept in mathematics. Learning and Instruction 99, 102169. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102169
title: Avoid normative feedback in educational practice; prefer self-referential, task- and process-level feedback
description: The authors conclude that "normative feedback should be avoided in educational practices" because even a single instance of positive or negative normative feedback affected students' emotions, performance and self-concept in largely undesirable ways. They recommend self-referential feedback comparing performance to students' own past performance, and feedback aimed at the task- and process-level that provides specific information on how to improve skills, which fosters positive achievement emotions like hope and enjoyment and makes students experience control.
requirements: Feedback should provide specific information on how to improve skills and be delivered within a responsive teacher-student relation, per the article's recommendations
constraints: The article notes negative feedback can still offer hope for improvement only when it meets the requirements of constructive criticism; long-term effects of repeated normative feedback remain unstudied
target_learning_goals: protecting achievement emotions
maintaining math self-concept
sustaining math performance
examples: In the experiment, students receiving negative normative feedback showed more anxiety and less enjoyment and hope than controls, and positive feedback diminished pre-existing low math self-concepts
key_sources: Van der Beek, J.P.J.; Van der Ven, S.H.G.; Van de Weijer-Bergsma, E.; Kroesbergen, E.H. (2025). How feedback affects emotions, performance and self-concept in mathematics. Learning and Instruction 99, 102169. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102169

article_title: Two hands and a tale: When gestures benefit adult narrative comprehension
citation: Dargue, N; Sweller, N. (2020). Two hands and a tale: When gestures benefit adult narrative comprehension. Learning and Instruction, 68. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2020.101331
title: Adult narrative comprehension gesture observation-and-production experiment
description: An experimental study with adult learners that manipulated gesture observation (typical versus atypical gestures) and gesture production to test their roles in narrative comprehension. The article describes it as a study that "examined the role of gesture observation and production in adult narrative comprehension, through investigating whether gesture production moderates the effect of gesture observation." It provides evidence that iconic gestures can benefit adult narrative comprehension and highlights conditions of benefit.
requirements: Adult learners comprehending narrative (verbal message) material
Gesture stimuli distinguishable as typical versus atypical
target_learning_goals: narrative comprehension
comprehension of verbal messages
examples: The study compared observing typical gestures with observing atypical gestures and assessed gesture production as a potential moderator
key_sources: Dargue, N; Sweller, N. (2020). Two hands and a tale: When gestures benefit adult narrative comprehension. Learning and Instruction, 68. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2020.101331

article_title: Solving graphics tasks: Gender differences in middle-school students
citation: Lowrie, Tom and Diezmann, Carmel. (2010). Solving graphics tasks: Gender differences in middle-school students. Learning and Instruction. http://eprints.qut.edu.au/
title: Mackinlay's six graphical languages framework for classifying graphics tasks
description: The study adopts Mackinlay's (1999) model, derived from Bertin (1967/1983), in which graphics are categorised into six "graphical languages" that "represent mathematical relationships among perceptual elements and use particular encoding techniques": Axis, Apposed-position, Map, Retinal-list, Connection, and Miscellaneous. Each language is defined by its encoding technique — Axis encodes by mark position on one axis, Apposed-position by marks on both x and y axes, Map by fixed positions and map-specific techniques, Connection by linking node and link objects, Retinal-list without position encoding, and Miscellaneous by conventions of particular graphics. The framework provides the perceptual basis for analysing students' decoding performance on the GLIM test.
requirements: Items must be classifiable by expert panels into the six graphical-language categories (the GLIM categorisation achieved Cronbach's alpha 0.9)
constraints: Miscellaneous languages can have various graphical structures, whereas the other languages each have a unique graphical structure
target_learners: primary school students in the last three years of primary education (ages 9-12)
target_learning_goals: decoding and interpreting mathematical information represented in graphs, maps, diagrams and number lines
examples: The GLIM test comprised six items from each of the six language categories, with items drawn from state, national and international year-level mathematics and science tests
key_sources: Lowrie, Tom and Diezmann, Carmel. (2010). Solving graphics tasks: Gender differences in middle-school students. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2009.11.005

article_title: Solving graphics tasks: Gender differences in middle-school students
citation: Lowrie, Tom and Diezmann, Carmel. (2010). Solving graphics tasks: Gender differences in middle-school students. Learning and Instruction. http://eprints.qut.edu.au/
title: The GLIM test: a 36-item instrument for assessing decoding of six graphical languages
description: The Graphical Languages in Mathematics (GLIM) test is a "36-item test" developed to determine students' decoding performance for each of the six graphical languages (Mackinlay, 1999). Items were selected from a bank of 58 items trialled with primary-aged children, drawn from state, national and international year-level mathematics and science tests, with high-literacy-demand items removed. In its final form it comprised six items from each language category, organised into Easy, Moderate and Difficult subtests of 12 items each, scored 0 or 1 per item with a maximum of 12 per difficulty category.
requirements: Items must vary in complexity, require substantial levels of graphical interpretation, and conform to reliability and validity measures
constraints: The instrument was developed for students in the final three years of primary school (Grades 4-6, ages 9-12)
target_learning_goals: decoding graphical languages in mathematics, including number lines, graphs, maps and diagrams
examples: Administered to 317 students approximately 12 months apart in Grades 4, 5 and 6 in approximately 50 minutes within intact classes of 24-31 participants
key_sources: Lowrie, Tom and Diezmann, Carmel. (2010). Solving graphics tasks: Gender differences in middle-school students. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2009.11.005

article_title: Designs for learning about climate change as a complex system
citation: Jacobson, Michael, Markauskaite, Lina, Portolese, Alisha, Kapur, Manu, Lai, Polly, & Roberts, Gareth (2017). Designs for learning about climate change as a complex system. Learning and Instruction, 52, pp. 1-14. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2017.03.007
title: Productive Failure two-phase learning design
description: PF is a learning design approach with two phases: an initial Generation and Exploration phase in which students solve complex problems, activating prior knowledge and generating multiple Representations and Solution Methods (RSMs), followed by a Consolidation and Knowledge Assembly phase in which a teacher helps students compare and contrast their suboptimal RSMs with canonical ones. The article contrasts it with Direct Instruction, where instructional structure is provided initially. Proposed mechanisms include activation and differentiation of prior knowledge and schema abstraction.
requirements: Problems designed to be challenging but not frustrating to students
A teacher-led Consolidation and Knowledge Assembly phase comparing student-generated RSMs with canonical RSMs
constraints: The study was a small-scale quasi-experiment in a single all-girls selective school, so internal validity and generalization are limited
target_learners: ninth-grade (Year Nine) secondary science students, approximately 14 years old
target_learning_goals: explanatory knowledge of climate systems and complex systems ideas such as feedback, emergence, dynamic equilibrium, tipping points, and non-linearity
near and far transfer of complex systems knowledge
examples: In the study, PF pairs worked 15-20 minutes on Challenge Problem 1 with a complexity model and Challenge Problem 2 with a climate model, then received about 15 minutes of teacher instruction, then applied ideas on Challenge Problem 3
key_sources: Jacobson, Michael, Markauskaite, Lina, Portolese, Alisha, Kapur, Manu, Lai, Polly, & Roberts, Gareth (2017). Designs for learning about climate change as a complex system. Learning and Instruction, 52, pp. 1-14. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2017.03.007

article_title: Designs for learning about climate change as a complex system
citation: Jacobson, Michael, Markauskaite, Lina, Portolese, Alisha, Kapur, Manu, Lai, Polly, & Roberts, Gareth (2017). Designs for learning about climate change as a complex system. Learning and Instruction, 52, pp. 1-14. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2017.03.007
title: NetLogo agent-based computer models for climate and complex systems learning
description: The study used eight agent-based computer models developed with the NetLogo modeling and visualization system; four focusing on complex systems ideas were taken from the NetLogo model library. Models included the Ants Foraging Model and a Climate Model with Feedback developed by a collaborating teacher. Student pairs used the models on two computers—one running the models, one for entering responses—to work on challenge problems aligned to daily complexity and climate topics such as feedback, emergence, dynamic equilibrium, and tipping points.
requirements: Teachers received professional development covering the teaching approaches, use of the computer models, and the climate and complex systems content
constraints: The same models and challenge problems were used in both treatment conditions, with only the instructional sequence varying
target_learning_goals: understanding complex systems ideas such as positive and negative feedback, emergence, dynamic equilibrium, tipping points, and non-linearity as they relate to climate systems
examples: Day 2 introduced positive and negative feedback processes relevant to global temperature, greenhouse effect, and cloud cover; Day 5 introduced tipping points and non-linearity relevant to atmospheric water feedback and albedo
key_sources: Jacobson, Michael, Markauskaite, Lina, Portolese, Alisha, Kapur, Manu, Lai, Polly, & Roberts, Gareth (2017). Designs for learning about climate change as a complex system. Learning and Instruction, 52, pp. 1-14. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2017.03.007

article_title: A scoping review on word-reading resilience in literacy: Evaluating empirical evidence for protective factors
citation: Appels, S., van Viersen, S., van Erp, S., Hornstra, L., & de Bree, E. (2024). A scoping review on word-reading resilience in literacy: Evaluating empirical evidence for protective factors. Learning and Instruction, 93, 101969. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2024.101969
title: A framework and operationalization of study designs and statistical approaches for studying academic resilience in literacy
description: The review provides a framework for studying academic resilience that distinguishes promotive, protective, and skill-enhancing factors in atypical literacy development. It aims to "provide a framework and operationalize study designs and statistical approaches for studying academic resilience", giving researchers concrete design and analysis tools for resilience research in word-level reading.
requirements: Studies must include samples of children with a detectable (risk of) word-level reading difficulty and at least one relevant literacy outcome measure
target_learners: 6- to 16-year-old children with (a risk of) word-level reading difficulties
target_learning_goals: Word-level literacy outcomes in the face of reading difficulty
examples: The review applied the framework to 22 empirical studies of compensation in literacy development, evaluating whether their designs could distinguish factor types
key_sources: Appels, S., van Viersen, S., van Erp, S., Hornstra, L., & de Bree, E. (2024). A scoping review on word-reading resilience in literacy: Evaluating empirical evidence for protective factors. Learning and Instruction, 93, 101969. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2024.101969

article_title: A digital game-based training improves spelling in German primary school children – A randomized controlled field trial
citation: Holz, H., Ninaus, M., Schwerter, J., Parrisius, C., Beuttler, B., Brandelik, K., & Meurers, D. (2023). A Digital Game-Based Training Improves Spelling in German Primary School Children – A Randomized Controlled Field Trial. Learning and Instruction, 87, 101771. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2023.101771
title: Prosodiya: adaptive digital game-based spelling training for unassisted home use
description: Prosodiya is "an adaptive digital game-based spelling training for mobile touch devices" that systematically teaches orthographic knowledge in combination with syllable stress awareness. It consists of five curriculum units moving from stress-pattern identification and syllable segmentation, through vowel length distinction and open/closed syllables, to orthographic markers, spelling, and consolidation/automation. Game design elements (fantasy-themed setting, points, stars, unlocked levels, tutorials, scaffolding and KCR feedback) support motivation and unassisted use at home.
requirements: Requires mobile touch devices and basic reading skills, since it targets spelling skills covered from second grade onward
constraints: For the field trial, the subchapter on the silent h and capitalization rules was excluded to reduce load; children were asked to train five days per week twenty minutes each following an eight-week plan of 66 levels
target_learners: German second- to fourth-grade primary school children with poor spelling skills, with and without developmental dyslexia
target_learning_goals: Syllable stress awareness
syllable segmentation
vowel length distinction
orthographic marking of long and short vowels
spelling of words
examples: In the field trial, families received Android tablets and children trained at home following a training plan, with new weekly content unlocked on Monday mornings to avoid binge-playing
key_sources: Holz, H., Ninaus, M., Schwerter, J., Parrisius, C., Beuttler, B., Brandelik, K., & Meurers, D. (2023). A Digital Game-Based Training Improves Spelling in German Primary School Children – A Randomized Controlled Field Trial. article_title: A digital game-based training improves spelling in German primary school children – A randomized controlled field trial
citation: Holz, H., Ninaus, M., Schwerter, J., Parrisius, C., Beuttler, B., Brandelik, K., & Meurers, D. (2023). A Digital Game-Based Training Improves Spelling in German Primary School Children – A Randomized Controlled Field Trial. Learning and Instruction, 87, 101771. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2023.101771
title: Five-unit curriculum progressing from syllable stress awareness to automation of spelling
description: The training's pedagogical structure is a five-unit progression: "The training consists of five curriculum units" covering syllable stress awareness, syllable structure, orthographic markers, spelling, and consolidation & automation. Each part starts with easy exercises and difficulty continuously increases and adapts individually across units, chapters, subchapters, and levels, so children first attend to stress patterns, then learn vowel-length marking rules, then consolidate and automate their knowledge.
requirements: Difficulty must adapt individually and content must be unlocked progressively to keep children on track
constraints: The acquisition phase covered the first two-thirds of the 66-level schedule, with the last third devoted to training and automation
target_learners: German primary school children in grades 2–4 with poor spelling skills
target_learning_goals: Orthographic knowledge of vowel length marking combined with syllable stress awareness
examples: Unit 1 teaches identifying stress patterns and segmenting words into syllables; unit 3 teaches rules of orthographic marking of long and short vowels; unit 5 practices all games in medium or hard difficulties to automate reading and spelling processes

article_title: Self-regulated learning processes vary as a function of epistemic beliefs and contexts: Mixed method evidence from eye tracking and concurrent and retrospective reports
citation: Gregory Trevors, Reza Feyzi-Behnagh, Roger Azevedo, François Bouchet. Self-Regulated Learning Processes Vary as a Function of Epistemic Beliefs and Contexts: Mixed Method Evidence from Eye Tracking and Concurrent and Retrospective Reports. Learning and Instruction, 2016, 42, pp.31-46. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2015.11.003
title: Epistemic cognition as a determinant of phase- and component-specific self-regulated learning under varying learning conditions
description: The article frames epistemic cognition as related to "specific phases and components of self-regulated learning and its adaptation to learning conditions of varying quality." In this account, learners' beliefs about knowledge interact with the quality of learning conditions: when science content relays conceptual discrepancies, learners' epistemic cognition shapes how they behaviorally process, notice, and resolve the discrepancies across SRL phases. The framework is instantiated empirically through eye tracking, study times, metacognitive ratings, think-aloud protocols, and retrospective interviews.
requirements: Learners must encounter science content that relays conceptual discrepancies for the epistemic-cognition-driven adaptation to be observable
constraints: Evidence reported is from university students in science content contexts
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning of science content involving conceptual discrepancies
epistemic cognition and evaluation of conflicting knowledge
examples: Study 1 collected eye tracking patterns, study times, and metacognitive ratings while students processed discrepant science content; Study 2 added concurrent and retrospective verbal reports.
key_sources: Gregory Trevors, Reza Feyzi-Behnagh, Roger Azevedo, François Bouchet. Self-Regulated Learning Processes Vary as a Function of Epistemic Beliefs and Contexts: Mixed Method Evidence from Eye Tracking and Concurrent and Retrospective Reports. Learning and Instruction, 2016, 42, pp.31-46. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2015.11.003

citation: Gregory Trevors, Reza Feyzi-Behnagh, Roger Azevedo, François Bouchet. title: Science content with conceptual discrepancies as a learning task for studying epistemic cognition in SRL
description: The studies used science content deliberately designed to relay conceptual discrepancies, presented to university students within a multi-study mixed method design. The authors state they "presented university students with science content that relayed conceptual discrepancies and collected quantitative and qualitative data to study how students responded to discrepancies." This material serves as the stimulus context in which eye tracking, study times, metacognitive ratings, think-aloud protocols, and retrospective interviews were collected.
requirements: Content must relay conceptual discrepancies so that learners' responses to discrepancies can be observed
target_learning_goals: responding to conceptual discrepancies in science content
examples: Both Study 1 (n = 42) and Study 2 (n = 20) presented this discrepant science content to university students.

article_title: Variation in situation-specific engagement among lower secondary school students
citation: Pöysä, S., Vasalampi, K., Muotka, J., Lerkkanen, M.-K., Poikkeus, A.-M., & Nurmi, J.-E. (2018). Variation in situation-specific engagement among lower secondary school students. Learning and Instruction, 53, 64-73. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2017.07.007
title: InSitu mobile-based instrument for lesson-to-lesson ratings of situation-specific engagement
description: The InSitu (InSituations) instrument is a mobile application pre-programmed into smart phones with which students rate their situation-specific engagement at the end of lessons; "InSitu consists of 17 items (Table 1) rated on a 5-point scale (1 = not at all; 5 = very much)." Confirmatory factor analysis established a five-factor structure (behavioral/cognitive engagement, emotional engagement, disaffection, competence experiences, help-seeking) with acceptable fit (CFI = .932; RMSEA = .058; SRMR = .051). The present study used the first three latent factors.
requirements: Ratings are collected at the end of each lesson with phones handed out simultaneously and collected a few minutes later, requiring device logistics per lesson
constraints: The instrument has not yet been widely used in previous research
It did not distinguish between cognitive and behavioral engagement
target_learning_goals: situational behavioral/cognitive engagement, emotional engagement, and disaffection in lessons
examples: In the study, 57 students produced 1,328 time-stamped ratings with a total response rate of 81.8% during a one-week intensive follow-up
key_sources: Pöysä, S., Vasalampi, K., Muotka, J., Lerkkanen, M.-K., Poikkeus, A.-M., & Nurmi, J.-E. (2018). Variation in situation-specific engagement among lower secondary school students. Learning and Instruction, 53, 64-73. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2017.07.007

article_title: Training for fostering knowledge co-construction from collaborative inference-drawing
citation: Deiglmayr, A., & Spada, H. (2011). Training for fostering knowledge co-construction from collaborative inference-drawing. Learning and Instruction, 21(3), 441-451. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2010.06.004
title: A priori taxonomy of three inference types defined by how interdependent information is distributed between collaborators
description: The article distinguishes three types of solution-relevant inferences, defined a priori by the experimental distribution of two interdependent pieces of information in a dyad: "Collaborative inferences" result from unshared, distributed information and "can only be drawn collaboratively"; individual inferences result from unshared information located with the same person; shared inferences result from information known to both partners. The taxonomy allows systematic comparison of inference difficulty, since the distribution is manipulated experimentally.
requirements: Information distribution between group members must be experimentally controlled so that each inference type can be identified a priori
constraints: Defined and tested in dyads working on hidden-profile-style tasks in which complementary pieces of information yield solution-relevant inferences
target_learning_goals: drawing solution-relevant inferences from distributed information during collaborative problem solving
examples: Murder-mystery testing case in which 12 solution-relevant inferences (four of each type) were distributed across counterbalanced text versions
key_sources: Deiglmayr, A., & Spada, H. (2011). Training for fostering knowledge co-construction from collaborative inference-drawing. Learning and Instruction, 21(3), 441-451. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2010.06.004

article_title: Training for fostering knowledge co-construction from collaborative inference-drawing
citation: Deiglmayr, A., & Spada, H. (2011). Training for fostering knowledge co-construction from collaborative inference-drawing. Learning and Instruction, 21(3), 441-451. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2010.06.004
title: Semi-computerized inference tutoring tool providing adaptive feedback and prompts during collaborative training
description: A semi-computerized tutoring tool developed for the training phase, controlled by a human observer who monitored the discussion and sent four types of messages based on an observation matrix: new information feedback announcing when "a piece of case information was mentioned for the first time", complete inference feedback on drawn inferences, missing information reminders, and missing information hints. It provided "just-in-time feedback on their performance, pointed out relevant cues... and prompted strategy application".
requirements: A human observer able to identify solution-relevant information mentions and inferences in real time and fill in the observation matrix
constraints: Guidance was provided during the training phase only, and not available during the unscaffolded testing phase
target_learners: university students in dyads collaborating via audio connection and shared word processor
target_learning_goals: applying information connection, pooling, and take-up strategies during collaboration
examples: Tutored training dyads received tutor messages displayed in both participants' rooms while collaborating on the medical-diagnosis case; 7 of 9 tutored dyads solved the training case correctly
key_sources: Deiglmayr, A., & Spada, H. (2011). Training for fostering knowledge co-construction from collaborative inference-drawing. Learning and Instruction, 21(3), 441-451. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2010.06.004

article_title: Teacher self-efficacy and self-reported cognitive activation and classroom management: A multilevel perspective on the role of school characteristics
citation: Holzberger, D., & Prestele, E. (2021). Teacher Self-Efficacy and Self-Reported Instructional Quality: A Multilevel Perspective on the Role of School Characteristics. Learning and Instruction, 76, 101513. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2021.101513
title: Multilevel motivation-to-performance framework: teacher self-efficacy modeled at both individual and school level with context effects and cross-level interactions
description: The article transfers a work-team motivation framework (Chen & Kanfer) to teaching, modeling teacher self-efficacy simultaneously as an individual variable and as a composite school variable (collective efficacy), and distinguishing Level 2 associations, unique context effects, and cross-level interactions. It defines a context effect in terms of "equally motivated teachers reporting more or less instructional quality in a more or less efficacious school". The framework organizes the study's three research questions and its multilevel modeling strategy.
requirements: Multiple teachers per school and school-level aggregates of individual efficacy ratings to separate within- from between-school associations
constraints: Applied to self-reported instructional quality in a cross-sectional secondary dataset, so causal direction cannot be established
target_learning_goals: instructional quality (cognitive activation and classroom management) as an outcome of teacher motivation
examples: Austrian TALIS 2018 data from 4,255 teachers at 246 schools analyzed with grand-mean and school-mean centering to separate Level 1 and Level 2 associations
key_sources: Holzberger, D., & Prestele, E. (2021). Teacher Self-Efficacy and Self-Reported Instructional Quality: A Multilevel Perspective on the Role of School Characteristics. Learning and Instruction, 76, 101513. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2021.101513

article_title: Teacher self-efficacy and self-reported cognitive activation and classroom management: A multilevel perspective on the role of school characteristics
citation: Holzberger, D., & Prestele, E. (2021). Teacher Self-Efficacy and Self-Reported Instructional Quality: A Multilevel Perspective on the Role of School Characteristics. Learning and Instruction, 76, 101513. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2021.101513
title: When investigating teacher self-efficacy and instructional quality, model the school context rather than treating self-efficacy as purely individual
description: The article argues that research on teacher motivation and instruction should not neglect the school context: teachers' self-efficacy should be modeled both as an individual variable and as a school-level composite, and school characteristics (collective efficacy, collaboration, participation, leadership) should be tested as context predictors and moderators. The authors state the findings "indicate the differential importance of addressing the school context when investigating teacher self-efficacy and instructional quality".
requirements: Multilevel data with multiple teachers per school; separation of teacher-level and school-level variance via centering
constraints: School-level differences in self-efficacy and instructional quality were small (1–5% between-school variance), and effects were rather small and not consistent across all indicators
target_learning_goals: understanding how teacher motivation relates to instructional quality across organizational levels
examples: The study modeled teacher self-efficacy as a school aggregate and tested context effects and cross-level interactions in multilevel regression on TALIS 2018 data
key_sources: Holzberger, D., & Prestele, E. (2021). Teacher Self-Efficacy and Self-Reported Instructional Quality: A Multilevel Perspective on the Role of School Characteristics. Learning and Instruction, 76, 101513. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2021.101513

article_title: Balancing situativity and formality: the importance of relating a formal language to interactive graphics in logic instruction
citation: Jelke van Der Pal, Tessa Eysink. (1999). Balancing situativity and formality: the importance of relating a formal language to interactive graphics in logic instruction. Learning and Instruction, 9 (4), pp.327-341. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197363
title: Developmental situativity theory: situated learning from a Vygotskian perspective
description: The article presents a situated cognition framework, the developmental situativity theory, in which "situated learning is viewed from a Vygotskian perspective". It assumes learning is "basically a non-symbolic inductive process that is greatly enhanced by formal systems which act as tools", so formal systems function as culturally provided instruments for an otherwise inductive learning process. The theory is used to derive an instructional balance between situated activity and formal tools, and was tested through logic instruction with Tarski's World.
requirements: Instruction must provide an environment containing elements for situated activity together with appropriate formal tools for the theory to be enacted.
target_learners: Students learning formal logic and conditional reasoning
target_learning_goals: Conditional reasoning in formal logic
examples: The authors present the theory and test it empirically by comparing instruction based on only-situated tasks, only-formal tasks, and a combination.
key_sources: Jelke van Der Pal, Tessa Eysink. (1999). Balancing situativity and formality: the importance of relating a formal language to interactive graphics in logic instruction. Learning and Instruction, 9 (4), pp.327-341. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197363

article_title: Balancing situativity and formality: the importance of relating a formal language to interactive graphics in logic instruction
citation: Jelke van Der Pal, Tessa Eysink. (1999). Balancing situativity and formality: the importance of relating a formal language to interactive graphics in logic instruction. Learning and Instruction, 9 (4), pp.327-341. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197363
title: Balance situated activity with formal tools in instruction
description: The principle states that "Instruction should provide students with an environment containing elements to allow for situated activity as well as with appropriate formal tools". It follows from developmental situativity theory: since situated, inductive learning is greatly enhanced when formal systems act as tools, neither purely situated nor purely formal instruction suffices. The article operationalizes the principle by relating a formal language to interactive graphics in logic instruction.
requirements: An environment with elements allowing situated activity, plus appropriate formal tools, must both be provided.
target_learning_goals: Conditional reasoning and mastery of a formal language
examples: Tarski's World relates a formal logic language to interactive graphics so students can engage in situated activity while using formal tools.
key_sources: Jelke van Der Pal, Tessa Eysink. (1999). Balancing situativity and formality: the importance of relating a formal language to interactive graphics in logic instruction. Learning and Instruction, 9 (4), pp.327-341. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197363

article_title: Balancing situativity and formality: the importance of relating a formal language to interactive graphics in logic instruction
citation: Jelke van Der Pal, Tessa Eysink. (1999). Balancing situativity and formality: the importance of relating a formal language to interactive graphics in logic instruction. Learning and Instruction, 9 (4), pp.327-341. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197363
title: Tarski's World: an instructional Interactive Graphical Representation System for formal logic
description: Tarski's World is described as "an instructional Interactive Graphical Representation System in formal logic". It exemplifies instruction that balances situativity and formality by relating a formal language to interactive graphics, thereby embodying the developmental situativity principle in which formal systems act as tools for situated, inductive learning. The system was empirically evaluated against only-situated and only-formal instruction for supporting conditional reasoning.
requirements: A formal language must be related to interactive graphics so the environment offers both situated activity and formal tools.
target_learning_goals: Conditional reasoning
examples: Used in logic instruction as the combined situated-plus-formal condition against which only-situated and only-formal instruction were compared.
