article_title: Interaction between orthographic and graphomotor constraints in learning to write
citation: Danna, J., Longcamp, M., Nalborczyk, L., Velay, J.-L., Commengé, C., & Jover, M. (2021). Interaction between orthographic and graphomotor constraints in learning to write. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-3596-880X
title: Parallel processing of spelling and graphomotor modules in handwriting production (van Galen's model)
description: The article frames handwriting production within van Galen's (1991) psychomotor model, in which spelling (high-level) and graphomotor (low-level) modules operate in parallel, with higher modules running ahead of real-time output. The study's findings are taken to support this account: the authors write that their finding "supports the idea of a parallel activation of spelling (high-level) and graphomotor (low-level) modules". The related parallel and cascading model (Olive, 2014) makes the dynamics of this parallel processing flexible according to the cognitive resources allocated to spelling versus motor control.
requirements: Handwriting must be produced under measurable orthographic and graphomotor constraints for the interaction of the two processing levels to be observed
constraints: The article notes further studies are necessary to better understand the emergence of the cascading phenomenon between spelling and motor processes in learning to write
target_learners: primary school students learning cursive handwriting (Grades 1, 3 and 5)
target_learning_goals: learning to spell words and to form cursive letters fluently
examples: Grade 1 students produced more stops when writing a difficult first letter in a low-frequency word, which the authors read as spelling processes interfering with motor processing
key_sources: Danna, J., Longcamp, M., Nalborczyk, L., Velay, J.-L., Commengé, C., & Jover, M. (2021). Interaction between orthographic and graphomotor constraints in learning to write. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-3596-880X

article_title: Interaction between orthographic and graphomotor constraints in learning to write
citation: Danna, J., Longcamp, M., Nalborczyk, L., Velay, J.-L., Commengé, C., & Jover, M. (2021). Interaction between orthographic and graphomotor constraints in learning to write. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-3596-880X
title: Evaluate spelling and graphomotor skill together: low word frequency with difficult letters can mimic graphomotor difficulty
description: Because orthographic and graphomotor constraints interact in beginning writers, assessing them separately can mislead teachers. The article states that this interaction "calls into question the relevance of evaluating spelling and graphomotor processes separately". If the word to be written is infrequent and contains difficult letters, handwriting performance may drop and the teacher could wrongly interpret this as a graphomotor difficulty. The principle therefore asks evaluators to consider word orthographic properties when judging handwriting quality, and letter difficulty when judging spelling.
requirements: Evaluation tasks must be designed so that the orthographic properties of the words (frequency, graphemic complexity) and the motor difficulty of their letters are known or controlled
constraints: The article notes the main limit is the reduced number of items used, due to the very controlled material, and further studies are necessary to confirm the combined effect
target_learners: primary school students, especially beginning writers in Grade 1
target_learning_goals: accurate assessment of handwriting quality and spelling proficiency
examples: The article warns that handwriting performance on infrequent words containing difficult letters could be wrongly interpreted as a graphomotor difficulty, which might explain some handwriting difficulties observed in children with reading disorders
key_sources: Danna, J., Longcamp, M., Nalborczyk, L., Velay, J.-L., Commengé, C., & Jover, M. (2021). Interaction between orthographic and graphomotor constraints in learning to write. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-3596-880X

article_title: Teacher personality domains and facets: Their unique associations with student-ratings of teaching quality and teacher enthusiasm
citation: Burić, Irena, Butković, Ana and Kim, Lisa (2023) Teacher personality domains and facets: Their unique associations with student-ratings of teaching quality and teacher enthusiasm. Learning and Instruction. 101827. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2023.101827
title: Bifactor-(S-1) approach to modeling the hierarchy of teacher personality
description: The bifactor-(S-1) approach (Eid et al., 2017) models hierarchical constructs by using items of a theoretically chosen reference facet as indicators of the general reference factor, while non-reference facets load on both the general factor and their specific factors, which may correlate. The article applies it to teacher Big Five personality because facets "cannot be viewed as randomly chosen facets from a set of all possible facets that are inherently substitutable", making it more suitable than the classic bifactor approach for examining the incremental predictive power of facets over domains.
requirements: A priori selection of a theoretically meaningful reference facet to define the general factor clearly
constraints: The general reference factor does not represent the overarching domain but is defined by the items of the reference facet
Specific factors are residualized with respect to the reference facet
target_learning_goals: understanding how teacher personality domains and facets relate to teaching quality and teacher enthusiasm
examples: The study chose factor-pure facets as references: sociability for extraversion, compassion for agreeableness, organization for conscientiousness, anxiety for negative emotionality, and intellectual curiosity for open-mindedness
key_sources: Burić, Irena, Butković, Ana and Kim, Lisa (2023) Teacher personality domains and facets: Their unique associations with student-ratings of teaching quality and teacher enthusiasm. Learning and Instruction. 101827. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2023.101827

article_title: School grades and students’ emotions: Longitudinal models of within-person reciprocal effects
citation: Reinhard Pekrun, Herbert W. Marsh, Felix Suessenbach, Anne C. Frenzel, Thomas Goetz. (2022). School grades and students' emotions: Longitudinal models of within-person reciprocal effects. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101626
title: Control-value theory reciprocal effects model of achievement feedback and emotions
description: Control-value theory (CVT) proposes that feedback about achievement drives achievement emotions via appraisals of control and value, and that these emotions in turn affect performance and subsequent feedback, producing reciprocal effects over time. As the article states, "CVT proposes that feedback about achievement is a prime driver of achievement emotions, due to its impact on appraisals of control and value related to achievement." Positive emotions are triggered by high control and high value, negative emotions by low control and high value. The present study used CVT to derive preregistered hypotheses about within-person reciprocal links between grades and emotions.
requirements: Feedback interpreted as success or failure must be appraised by students in terms of control and value for emotions to be aroused as theorized
constraints: The article notes positive emotions can occasionally undermine performance and negative emotions can sometimes support performance, so overall effects are described as typically positive or negative
target_learning_goals: achievement emotions such as enjoyment, pride, anger, anxiety, shame, boredom, and hopelessness in mathematics
examples: The study operationalized feedback as end-of-the-year mathematics grades across five annual assessments in the PALMA study
key_sources: Reinhard Pekrun, Herbert W. Marsh, Felix Suessenbach, Anne C. Frenzel, Thomas Goetz. (2022). School grades and students' emotions: Longitudinal models of within-person reciprocal effects. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101626

article_title: Adaptive teaching with technology enhances lasting learning
citation: Sibley, L., Fabian, A., Plicht, C., Pagano, L., Ehrhardt, N., Wellert, L., Bohl, T., & Lachner, A. (2025). Adaptive teaching with technology enhances lasting learning. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102141
title: Adaptive teaching framework: formative assessment, macro-level and micro-level adaptations
description: The article's organizing framework defines adaptive teaching as an instructional model for handling student heterogeneity. As the authors state, "Adaptive teaching systematically combines formative assessment, differentiation (i.e., macro adaptation), and individual support (i.e., micro adaptation) to enhance students' meaningful and lasting learning." Formative assessment is the backbone: continuous informal diagnoses that inform both pre-planned group-level adaptations and moment-to-moment individual support. The constructs are iterative rather than sequential, and educational technology can supply instant assessment data and automated feedback for each level.
requirements: Formative assessments must continuously provide data on students' learning progress to inform macro- and micro adaptations
constraints: The constructs do not follow a strict sequential order but occur simultaneously or in any sequence as needed
target_learners: secondary school students in heterogeneous classrooms (grades 7-12)
target_learning_goals: subject-matter knowledge across STEM, humanities, and language subjects
examples: In the Euclidean plane mathematics unit, online quizzes informed proficiency grouping (macro-adaptation), computer-based feedback supported individuals (micro-adaptation), and results adjusted practice-task numbers
key_sources: Sibley, L., Fabian, A., Plicht, C., Pagano, L., Ehrhardt, N., Wellert, L., Bohl, T., & Lachner, A. (2025). Adaptive teaching with technology enhances lasting learning. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102141

article_title: Adaptive teaching with technology enhances lasting learning
citation: Sibley, L., Fabian, A., Plicht, C., Pagano, L., Ehrhardt, N., Wellert, L., Bohl, T., & Lachner, A. (2025). Adaptive teaching with technology enhances lasting learning. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102141
title: LoGeT framework: Localize-Generalize-Transfer for scaling educational interventions
description: The Localize-Generalize-Transfer (LoGeT) framework by Lachner et al. structures implementation research so evidence is grounded in real classrooms yet generalizable. "The LoGeT model integrates three essential stages: localization, generalization, and transfer." Localization uses co-design with teachers as key stakeholders; generalization applies the ManyClasses approach, running the same experimental setup across multiple settings, subjects, and student groups; transfer creates practical resources such as instructional guides so educators can implement the strategies beyond the original study. This study instantiated LoGeT by combining co-design with a ManyClasses design across 12 units.
requirements: Research team participation in co-design support meetings to ensure implementation fidelity
constraints: ManyClasses units are intentionally diverse and not directly comparable in difficulty across subjects
target_learners: secondary school students across varied subjects and grade levels
target_learning_goals: generalizable, transferable evidence about instructional interventions
examples: The study combined a co-design professional development program with a ManyClasses quasi-experiment across 12 teaching units in six schools
key_sources: Sibley, L., Fabian, A., Plicht, C., Pagano, L., Ehrhardt, N., Wellert, L., Bohl, T., & Lachner, A. (2025). Adaptive teaching with technology enhances lasting learning. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102141

article_title: Adaptive teaching with technology enhances lasting learning
citation: Sibley, L., Fabian, A., Plicht, C., Pagano, L., Ehrhardt, N., Wellert, L., Bohl, T., & Lachner, A. (2025). Adaptive teaching with technology enhances lasting learning. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102141
title: Implement adaptive teaching with high fidelity: apply adaptive elements constantly, since benefits emerge only in highly adaptive units
description: The article's central practical recommendation is that adaptive teaching pays off only when implemented with many adaptive elements. As the authors put it, "teachers need to carefully apply adaptive elements constantly, since our results demonstrated that adaptive teaching units were only more effective than regular teaching when the degree of adaptivity was high." Degree of adaptivity was measured as the number of formative assessments, macro- and micro-level adaptations, and consolidation phases implemented per unit. Units above the sample mean of adaptive elements outperformed control classes; units below it did not.
requirements: Frequent formative assessments and tailored instructional supports across the four levels: formative assessments, macro- and micro-level adaptations, and consolidation phases
Professional development and research-team support so digital tools support rather than dictate adaptivity
constraints: The 18-element cut-off was derived from the conditions' mean degree of adaptivity, not tested as an optimum
Benefits in STEM and humanities were not significant, so high adaptivity alone may not suffice in every domain
target_learning_goals: lasting subject-matter knowledge and self-efficacy in using technology
examples: Teachers in the study co-designed units over two to three months in tandems with workshops and feedback sessions, integrating online quizzes, group-work platforms, and automated feedback systems
key_sources: Sibley, L., Fabian, A., Plicht, C., Pagano, L., Ehrhardt, N., Wellert, L., Bohl, T., & Lachner, A. (2025). Adaptive teaching with technology enhances lasting learning. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102141

article_title: Observational, student, and teacher perspectives on interpersonal teacher behavior: Shared and unique associations with teacher and student emotions
citation: Donker, M. H., van Vemde, L., Hessen, D. J., van Gog, T., & Mainhard, T. (2021). Observational, student, and teacher perspectives on interpersonal teacher behavior: Shared and unique associations with teacher and student emotions. Learning and Instruction, vol. 73, 101414. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2020.101414
title: Interpersonal theory and the Interpersonal Circle for Teachers (IPC-T): Agency and Communion as two sufficient dimensions of interpersonal teacher behavior
description: Interpersonal theory is the framework the article uses to operationalize teachers' interpersonal behavior in class. It "postulates that to describe behavior of people in interaction with others two dimensions are at the same time needed and sufficient", denoted by the meta-labels Agency (taking the lead, social influence, control) and Communion (friendliness, affection, warmth). Wubbels, Créton, and Hooymayers adapted this theory to the classroom setting as the Interpersonal Circle for Teachers (IPC-T), in which all prototypical teacher behaviors around the circle are specific combinations of agency and communion, such as being hesitant (low agency) or imposing (high agency, moderately low communion).
requirements: Both dimensions are needed at the same time to describe interpersonal behavior; all teacher behaviors are characterized as a specific combination of agency and communion
target_learning_goals: understanding interpersonal teacher behavior as antecedent of teacher and student emotions
examples: The article illustrates combinations: a teacher can be hesitant to act (uncertain; moderately low communion and low agency) or employ strict classroom management (imposing; moderately low communion and high agency)
key_sources: Donker, M. H., van Vemde, L., Hessen, D. J., van Gog, T., & Mainhard, T. (2021). Observational, student, and teacher perspectives on interpersonal teacher behavior: Shared and unique associations with teacher and student emotions. Learning and Instruction, vol. 73, 101414. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2020.101414

article_title: Observational, student, and teacher perspectives on interpersonal teacher behavior: Shared and unique associations with teacher and student emotions
citation: Donker, M. H., van Vemde, L., Hessen, D. J., van Gog, T., & Mainhard, T. (2021). Observational, student, and teacher perspectives on interpersonal teacher behavior: Shared and unique associations with teacher and student emotions. Learning and Instruction, vol. 73, 101414. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2020.101414
title: Novel regression-based correction method for splitting shared and unique explained variance of multiple predictors
description: The article introduces a novel statistical approach based on multiple regression that "allows to calculate the explained variance of different combinations of predictors, and the shared and unique variance of each (set of) predictors", even in the case of suppressor effects or large overlap between variables. It works by correcting the explained variance in several steps, combining information from various multiple regression analyses with one, two, or three predictors; an explanation and the R code are provided in Appendix B. The empirical part of the paper serves as an illustration of the method with data on teacher interpersonal behavior and emotions.
requirements: Multiple regression analyses with single and combined predictors (7 options in the study); listwise deletion to compare Sum of Squares across analyses
constraints: Simple addition and subtraction of effects only leads to correct calculation of shared and unique parts when there are no suppressor effects
target_learning_goals: separating shared and unique variance of raters or perspectives predicting outcomes
examples: Applied to 76 teachers' data to split variance of observer, student, and teacher perspectives predicting teacher and student positive and negative emotions
key_sources: Donker, M. H., van Vemde, L., Hessen, D. J., van Gog, T., & Mainhard, T. (2021). article_title: A Bayesian approach to students’ perceptions of teachers’ autonomy support
citation: Flunger, B., Verdonschot, A., Zitzmann, S., Hornstra, L., & van Gog, T. (2024). A Bayesian approach to students' perceptions of teachers' autonomy support. Learning and Instruction, 91, 101873. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2023.101873
title: Multilevel conceptualization of autonomy support: climate, contextual, and perceived-difference constructs
description: The article conceptualizes teachers' autonomy support as a multilevel construct with distinct operationalizations: class-directed support measured with class-referent items forms an L2 climate construct reflecting the "overall classroom-specific autonomy-supportive climate"; individual support is an L1 construct whose class aggregate forms a contextual construct indicating how similarly teachers support students; and perceived differences (including relative lack of support) capture within-classroom inequality. The overall autonomy-supportive atmosphere is a shared perception combining class-aggregated individual and class-directed support. This framework motivated the study's doubly latent multilevel modeling of student perceptions.
requirements: Measures must make the referent explicit ("me/I" vs "us/class" items) so individual and class-directed support can be distinguished
constraints: Uniform ratings of a class-level construct by students are unlikely because within-cluster differences in subjective perceptions are expected
target_learners: primary school students in mathematics classrooms
target_learning_goals: students' intrinsic motivation, extrinsic regulation, effort, and persistence
examples: The study measured four autonomy-supportive strategies (choice provision, rationale provision, interest stimulation, frustration acknowledgment) with parallel individual and class-directed items, plus newly developed perceived-difference items
key_sources: Flunger, B., Verdonschot, A., Zitzmann, S., Hornstra, L., & van Gog, T. (2024). A Bayesian approach to students' perceptions of teachers' autonomy support. Learning and Instruction, 91, 101873. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2023.101873

article_title: A Bayesian approach to students’ perceptions of teachers’ autonomy support
citation: Flunger, B., Verdonschot, A., Zitzmann, S., Hornstra, L., & van Gog, T. (2024). A Bayesian approach to students' perceptions of teachers' autonomy support. Learning and Instruction, 91, 101873. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2023.101873
title: Support autonomy at both the individual and class level; class-directed support alone omits essential information
description: Because students perceive individual and class-directed autonomy support as distinct at the student level, and both positively predict intrinsic motivation, effort, and persistence, teachers should provide autonomy support both to the whole class and to individual students. The article concludes that "Both individual and class-level support should be high to yield optimal results" and warns that "Focusing solely on class-directed autonomy support may omit essential information" about how students experience support relative to classmates.
requirements: Teachers need strategies addressing both the class as a whole and individual students, across strategies such as choice provision, rationales, interest stimulation, and frustration acknowledgment
constraints: Students who perceive receiving less support than classmates show higher extrinsic regulation, so differentiation must be managed carefully to avoid perceived unfairness
target_learning_goals: fostering intrinsic motivation and behavioral engagement (effort, persistence)
examples: In the studied mathematics classes, teachers could direct strategies such as explaining math's relevance to the whole class while also acknowledging individual students' frustrations
key_sources: Flunger, B., Verdonschot, A., Zitzmann, S., Hornstra, L., & van Gog, T. (2024). A Bayesian approach to students' perceptions of teachers' autonomy support. Learning and Instruction, 91, 101873. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2023.101873

article_title: A Bayesian approach to students’ perceptions of teachers’ autonomy support
citation: Flunger, B., Verdonschot, A., Zitzmann, S., Hornstra, L., & van Gog, T. (2024). A Bayesian approach to students' perceptions of teachers' autonomy support. Learning and Instruction, 91, 101873. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2023.101873
title: Bayesian doubly latent multilevel CFA/SEM for autonomy-support perceptions with small Level-2 samples
description: The study employed Bayesian Multilevel-CFA and Multilevel-SEM with doubly latent modeling, in which latent factors are modeled at both student and classroom levels to control for measurement error and latent aggregation to control for sampling error. Because the sample included only 22 classrooms (below 50), conventional maximum-likelihood estimation risked biased estimates; the authors note that "Bayesian analyses allow for complex multilevel analyses with relatively small sample sizes at Level 2." Analysis codes, outputs, and the codebook are available on OSF.
requirements: Specification of approximately uninformative or weakly informative priors; unit variance identification for scaling; posterior predictive p-values and DIC for model fit and comparison
constraints: With Level-2 sample size below 25, frequentist multilevel models risk downwardly biased variance components and inflated Type-I error rates, motivating the Bayesian approach
target_learners: primary school students (data source for the multilevel models)
target_learning_goals: valid measurement of student-perceived teaching quality and its associations with motivation and engagement
examples: The item ICC(1)s ranged from 0.017 to 0.128, and models were estimated in Mplus 8.6 with the Bayesian estimator

article_title: Linking parental scaffolding with self-regulated learning in Chinese kindergarten children
citation: Heyi Zhang, David Whitebread. (2014). Linking parental scaffolding with self-regulated learning in Chinese kindergarten children. Faculty of Education, University of Cambridge. https://www.repository.cam.ac.uk
title: Three-dimensional parental scaffolding framework: cognitive support, emotional support, and contingency
description: The article organises parental scaffolding during joint problem-solving into three aspects: "cognitive support, emotional support, and contingency". Cognitive support covers parents' provision of metacognitive information such as task management strategies and rationales; emotional support covers encouragement and rejection; contingency is the degree to which parents adjust instructional demand in response to children's ongoing evidence of task understanding, operationalised via the shift rule of raising demand after success and lowering it after failure. The framework structures the study's coding and regression analyses.
requirements: Coding requires dividing each 10-minute task into 2-minute segments and rating each scaffolding aspect on a 5-point scale
constraints: The framework was applied to play-based puzzle and origami problem-solving tasks with Chinese kindergarten dyads in Beijing
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning strategic behaviours in problem-solving tasks
examples: Parents were coded utterance-by-utterance for instructional demand (D1-D3) against children's five levels of task understanding (U0-U4) to classify contingent and non-contingent behaviours
key_sources: Heyi Zhang, David Whitebread. (2014). Linking parental scaffolding with self-regulated learning in Chinese kindergarten children. Faculty of Education, University of Cambridge. https://www.repository.cam.ac.uk

article_title: Linking parental scaffolding with self-regulated learning in Chinese kindergarten children
citation: Heyi Zhang, David Whitebread. (2014). Linking parental scaffolding with self-regulated learning in Chinese kindergarten children. Faculty of Education, University of Cambridge. https://www.repository.cam.ac.uk
title: Support children's problem solving contingently: adjust instructional demand to the child's ongoing evidence of task understanding
description: The article's findings indicate that the effectiveness of parental scaffolding lies in its contingency rather than its quantity: parents should provide "less specific instructions and higher cognitive demand after a child's success and more specific instructions and lower cognitive demand after a child's failure". In the study, contingency was the only independent scaffolding predictor of children's SRL strategic behaviours and task performance, and it mediated the effect of parental education. This principle applies the shift rule to any adult supporting a child's problem solving.
requirements: The adult must monitor the child's ongoing evidence of task understanding and adjust demand level accordingly
constraints: Evidence comes from parent-child problem-solving tasks with Chinese kindergarten children; the longer-term influence the authors propose needs testing in longitudinal studies
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning strategic behaviours
independent problem-solving performance
examples: In the study, parents' contingent instructional demand (D1-D3 matched to children's understanding levels U0-U4) was coded utterance-by-utterance in puzzle and origami tasks
key_sources: Heyi Zhang, David Whitebread. (2014). Linking parental scaffolding with self-regulated learning in Chinese kindergarten children. Faculty of Education, University of Cambridge. https://www.repository.cam.ac.uk

article_title: Subtraction by addition in children with mathematical learning disabilities
citation: Peters, G., De Smedt, B., Torbeyns, J., Verschaffel, L., & Ghesquière, P. (2014). Subtraction by addition in children with mathematical learning disabilities. Learning and Instruction, 30, 1-8. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learn.instruc.2013.11.001
title: Supplement routine direct-subtraction instruction for children with MLD with explicit teaching of subtraction by addition
description: The article argues that mathematics instruction for children with MLD need not be restricted to routine mastery of direct subtraction. Because MLD children spontaneously switch between direct subtraction and subtraction by addition on large-distance problems, the authors propose that "the current focus on the direct subtraction strategy is supplemented by the teaching of subtraction by addition as an alternative strategy", together with attention to the inverse relation between addition and subtraction and practice in flexibly applying both strategies.
requirements: Explicit attention to the conceptual underpinnings of subtraction by addition, i.e., the inverse relation between addition and subtraction, as the article states
Plenty of opportunities to practice and flexibly apply both strategies, as the article states
constraints: The article notes this recommendation rests on reaction-time evidence from problems with extremely large subtrahends or extremely small differences, and calls for intervention studies testing different instructional settings
target_learners: children with mathematical learning disabilities in special education
target_learning_goals: flexible use of mental calculation strategies in multi-digit subtraction
examples: In the study, none of the eight participating special education schools except one explicitly taught subtraction by addition for symbolically presented two-digit subtractions, yet children used it flexibly on large-distance problems
key_sources: Peters, G., De Smedt, B., Torbeyns, J., Verschaffel, L., & Ghesquière, P. (2014). Subtraction by addition in children with mathematical learning disabilities. Learning and Instruction, 30, 1-8. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2013.11.001

article_title: Subtraction by addition in children with mathematical learning disabilities
citation: Peters, G., De Smedt, B., Torbeyns, J., Verschaffel, L., & Ghesquière, P. (2014). Subtraction by addition in children with mathematical learning disabilities. Learning and Instruction, 30, 1-8. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learn.instruc.2013.11.001
title: Strategy choice model: switching between direct subtraction and subtraction by addition predicted by the minimum of subtrahend and difference
description: The Switch-Model is a reaction-time regression model representing a strategy use pattern in which solvers switch between direct subtraction and subtraction by addition based on the relative magnitude of the subtrahend. Reaction times are predicted by min[D, S]: for problems with the subtrahend smaller than the difference, times increase with subtrahend size (direct subtraction expected); for problems with the subtrahend larger than the difference, times increase with difference size (subtraction by addition expected). It contrasts with the DS-Model (times predicted by subtrahend size) and the SBA-Model (times predicted by difference size).
requirements: Symbolically presented two-digit subtraction problems allowing classification by subtrahend size, difference size, and their minimum, with reaction time measurement
constraints: The article notes the non-verbal methods did not allow strategy identification at the item level
target_learning_goals: understanding flexible strategy choice in mental multi-digit subtraction

article_title: A domain-specific perspective on adaptivity
citation: Anselm Strohmaier, Fien Depaepe, Michael Nickl, Andreas Obersteiner. (2026). A domain-specific perspective on adaptivity. Learning and Instruction 104. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2026.102364
title: Plass and Pawar's three-dimension framework of adaptive support
description: The editorial adopts Plass and Pawar's (2020) conceptualization, in which adaptive support is organized around three questions: which learner variables to adapt for, how these variables can be reliably measured, and what adaptations can be made during learning. The authors state that Plass and Pawar (2020) "conceptualize adaptive support through three dimensions" and use this structure to analyze where domain-specificity matters in each dimension, since these dimensions are also apparent in most other adaptivity frameworks.

constraints: Without this interpretive bridge, more data do not necessarily yield better adaptation.

article_title: The impact of executive functions on English academic performance among Chinese primary school students: A network analysis
citation: Ma, C., Song, M., & Zhao, X. (2023). The impact of executive functions on English academic performance among Chinese primary school students: A network analysis. https://www.nwnu.edu.cn
title: Network analysis framework for relating executive function components to English academic performance
description: The article applies psychological network analysis as an alternative to latent variable modelling, modelling executive function subcomponents and English subskills as nodes with edges whose thickness indicates association strength. It combines Gaussian Graphical Models with LASSO regularisation, Expected Influence and Bridge Expected Influence centrality indices, NetworkComparisonTest invariance tests, and bootstrap accuracy/stability checks. The authors argue this approach captures "variable interactions" that latent variable models neglect and offers "multiplevalidationtests(e.g.,networkaccuracy,stabilitytests,anddifferencetests)to ensurethereliabilityoftheresults".

constraints: Cross-sectional design: causality between executive function and academic performance remains unestablished; significant partial correlations only indicate potential causal effects

target_learning_goals: English listening, reading, and writing achievement
examples: An eight-node, 28-edge regularised network was estimated for the overall sample, with gender-stratified networks compared via global and local invariance tests

By random assignment, "kits were either “guided” (included embedded stories, parent tips, and extension ideas; n = 50) or “basic” (identical construction activities without guidance features; n = 25)." article_title: Intraindividual relations between achievement goals and discrete achievement emotions: An experience sampling approach
citation: Goetz, T., Sticca, F., Pekrun, R., Murayama, K., & Elliot, A. J. (2016). Intraindividual relations between achievement goals and discrete achievement emotions: An experience sampling approach. Learning and Instruction, 41, 115-125. https://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2015.10.007
title: Pekrun et al.'s control-value-based model linking trichotomous achievement goals to discrete achievement emotions
description: The article tests and supports a theoretical model grounding goal-emotion links in "control-value theory which posits that the perceived controllability and the subjective value of achievement activities and outcomes function as proximal antecedents of achievement emotions." Within this model, mastery goals focus attention on the controllability and positive value of activities (fostering enjoyment, reducing boredom and anger), performance-approach goals on success outcomes (fostering pride), and performance-avoidance goals on possible failure and uncontrollability (fostering anxiety and shame). The study's experience sampling design provides the first direct intraindividual test of these propositions in classrooms.
requirements: Assessment of both state (or trait) achievement goals and discrete achievement emotions so goal-emotion propositions can be tested at the intended level of analysis
constraints: The model posits goals influencing emotions, but the article notes reciprocal causation (emotions influencing goal adoption) cannot be ruled out and the ESM design did not allow causal analysis
target_learning_goals: Fostering adaptive achievement emotions (enjoyment, pride) and reducing maladaptive emotions (boredom, anger, anxiety, shame) through goal foci
examples: The study assessed mastery, performance-approach, and performance-avoidance goals against six emotions (enjoyment, pride, anxiety, shame, anger, boredom) in mathematics, German, English, and French classrooms
key_sources: Goetz, T., Sticca, F., Pekrun, R., Murayama, K., & Elliot, A. J. (2016). Intraindividual relations between achievement goals and discrete achievement emotions: An experience sampling approach. Learning and Instruction, 41, 115-125. https://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2015.10.007

article_title: Intraindividual relations between achievement goals and discrete achievement emotions: An experience sampling approach
citation: Goetz, T., Sticca, F., Pekrun, R., Murayama, K., & Elliot, A. J. (2016). Intraindividual relations between achievement goals and discrete achievement emotions: An experience sampling approach. Learning and Instruction, 41, 115-125. https://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2015.10.007
title: Experience sampling protocol with single-item state measures on handheld devices for classroom goal and emotion assessment
description: The study's measurement instrument is an experience sampling procedure in which students carried iPod Touch 4G devices running iDialog Pad software for ten school days, activating them at the start of 45-minute classes and completing a digital questionnaire at one random audible signal. State goals and emotions were assessed with single-item measures because multi-item scales could compromise state validity by prompting reflection and recall biases. Of 1779 initiated questionnaires, 1409 (79%) were completed, averaging 11.74 per student. ICC(2) reliability of aggregated state scores ranged from .734 to .921.
requirements: Single-item state measures to keep lesson interruption minimal and avoid recall bias; random signal timing within class; trait assessment administered after the state assessment to avoid influencing state reports
constraints: The restricted lesson time did not allow including more than three goals and six emotions; non-completion reasons included taking a test (51%) and other priority tasks (25%)
target_learners: 10th grade students in regular subject-matter classrooms
target_learning_goals: Assessing momentary achievement goals and discrete achievement emotions during authentic classroom activities
examples: State items included "My goal at this moment is to learn as much as possible" (mastery) and "At this moment I am experiencing [EMOTION]" on 5-point Likert scales

citation: Nuria Vita-Barrull, Verónica Estrada-Plana, Jaume March-Llanes, Pablo Sotoca-Orgaz, Núria Guzmán, Rosa Ayesa, Jorge Moya-Higueras. (2024). Do you play in class? Board games to promote cognitive and educational development in primary school: A cluster randomized controlled trial. Learning and Instruction, 93. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2024.101946
title: Conectar Jugando classroom board-game programme
description: Conectar Jugando (Connecting Through Play) is a school intervention programme in which students play commercial analogue board games during school hours to train basic executive functions and support academic skills. "The Conectar Jugando Group received 12 gaming sessions over six weeks", each lasting one hour and held twice a week, with students in groups of three to five playing two games face-to-face. Teachers received a manual specifying session organisation and which games to use; commercial games were selected by an expert committee for the executive functions and curriculum competencies they could train.

Games must fit the educational competencies of the Spanish curriculum and suit recommended ages and durations

reading and maths skills
examples: In the trial, students played games such as Monster Match and La Morada Maldita, chosen for cognitive domains like working memory updating, inhibition and shifting

Board games to promote cognitive and educational development in primary school: A cluster randomized controlled trial. Learning and Instruction, 93. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2024.101946
title: Emergent and embedded learning in game-based learning
description: This framework distinguishes two ways learning arises in playful formats. "Emergent learning is understood as the acquisition of new skills and knowledge every time we face challenges that need to be overcome", whereas "embedded learning refers to learning linked to a particular context" — the inclusion of specific concepts and content in game elements, such as writing information on cards, to achieve didactic objectives. The article presents modern board games as a playful methodology that combines both: learning emerges from participation and interaction around the game while curricular content is embedded in game elements, so children playing for fun are inadvertently engaging cognitive abilities and curricular knowledge.
requirements: Games must pose challenges whose difficulty aligns with participants' capacity to sustain engagement
constraints: In these commercial games the learning content is emergent rather than explicit
target_learning_goals: executive functions
curricular academic skills
examples: In Monster Match, winning requires recognising dice numbers and counting monsters' eyes, legs, hands and doughnuts; in La Morada Maldita, higher-point cards include counting, simple arithmetic and polygon identification

title: Include board-game play in primary classrooms as an alternative or complement to regular direct instruction for cognitive and academic development
description: The article concludes that classroom time spent playing modern board games can serve cognitive and educational development at least as well as regular teaching. Based on the trial results, it states that "the inclusion of board games in the classroom could favour the development of executive functions in primary school children just as much as, or even better than, regular classes", and that commercial games designed to entertain nevertheless led to reading and maths benefits. The recommendation is grounded in the trial's measured group-time effects rather than in motivation ratings, which were not collected.
requirements: Games selected for the executive functions and curricular competencies they can train, with sessions organised by a programme manual
constraints: The direction of transfer from executive-function training to academic skills was not tested; inhibition and flexibility gains did not favour the play group in grades two to six
target_learners: primary school students from first to sixth grade
target_learning_goals: executive functions
reading and maths skills

citation: Szczygieł M.; Szűcs D.; Toffalini E. (2024). Math anxiety and math achievement in primary school children: Longitudinal relationship and predictors. LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION. https://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2024.101906
title: Reciprocal Theory of the math anxiety–math achievement relationship
description: The Reciprocal Theory holds that math anxiety and math achievement influence each other over time, rather than one direction alone. The article tested it against the Deficit Theory (achievement predicts anxiety) and the Debilitating Anxiety Theory (anxiety predicts achievement), reporting that "MATH at T1 predicted MA at T2 and MA at T1 predicted MATH at T2 (supporting the Reciprocal Theory)" in 337 Polish primary school children.
requirements: Longitudinal data with math anxiety and math achievement measured at multiple time points to test cross-lag prediction in both directions
constraints: Evidence comes from primary school children in Poland across first and second grade; the article does not print effect sizes in the available text
target_learners: Primary school children (first and second grade)
target_learning_goals: Mathematics achievement and math anxiety development
examples: The study analyzed longitudinal data at three time points: T0 (beginning of first grade), T1 (end of first grade), and T2 (end of second grade).

article_title: What can moment-by-moment learning curves tell about students’ self-regulated learning?
citation: Inge Molenaar, Anne Horvers, Ryan S. Baker. (2021). What can moment-by-moment learning curves tell about students' self-regulated learning? Learning and Instruction, 72, 101206. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2019.05.003
title: Moment-by-moment learning curves as personalized visualizations of students' accuracy regulation in hybrid human-system self-regulated learning with ALTs.
description: Moment-by-moment learning curves visualize "the probability that a student learned a specific skill at a particular problem during learning", derived automatically from ALT log data via Bayesian Knowledge Tracing and the P(J) estimate. Distinct from classic learning curves, they show "a distillation of student progress" rather than accuracy or effort directly. The article frames them as personalized visualizations that could help learners make valid inferences about how their effort and accuracy relate to progress, addressing utilization deficiency in a hybrid form of human-system regulation where the ALT executes part of the control and monitoring loop.
requirements: Log data from an adaptive learning technology capturing per-problem correctness and knowledge estimates, sufficient practice opportunities per subskill (graphs with 15 or more problems were included).
constraints: The studied ALT's only adaptive mechanism was problem selection; it offered no scaffolding, prompting or error classification.
The curves did not show effort directly, and no associations between curve form and effort were found in this study.
target_learners: Primary education students (grade five, ages 10-12) practicing arithmetic with adaptive learning technologies
target_learning_goals: Self-regulated learning of arithmetic subskills, including regulation of effort and accuracy during practice
examples: In the study, 265 curves coded into four forms were differentially associated with accuracy, prior knowledge, gain and transfer, supporting the curves' value as indicators of accuracy regulation.

description: The article positions cognitive load theory as a lens for analyzing CSCL environments where students share external representations of argumentation. CLT is said to "contribute to our understanding of CSCL by pinpointing situations in which high levels of cognitive load are generated" and to "help identify mismatches between representational schemes and execution of (sub)tasks." It thus functions as a diagnostic framework for locating load problems in collaborative settings rather than as a tested model.

citation: De Wever, B., Van Keer, H., Schellens, T., & Valcke, M. (2007). Learning and Instruction, 17, 436-447. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2007.04.001
title: Multilevel modelling as the appropriate statistical framework for analysing content analysis data from CSCL environments
description: The article presents multilevel modelling as a statistical approach for hierarchically clustered data in collaborative learning research, in which messages are nested within students (and measurement occasions) within groups. It argues that traditional unilevel techniques violate the independence assumption, that "conventional modelling can result in underestimation of standard errors", and that multilevel modelling handles "the hierarchical nesting, the interdependency, and the unit of analysis problem in a natural way". The article demonstrates the framework through three-level and four-level random intercept models with roles, themes, and ASIMeC dimensions as predictors.

Decomposition of variance via a random intercept null model before adding explanatory variables
constraints: The article states a demonstration of the full power of multilevel modelling was beyond the scope of the article

target_learning_goals: Methodologically sound analysis of collaborative learning processes in asynchronous discussion groups
examples: Three-level model testing role effects and four-level model with measurement occasions nested within subjects, estimated with RIGLS in MLwiN 2.01

title: ASIMeC — analysis scheme identifying message characteristics along five dimensions
description: ASIMeC is a content analysis scheme developed by the authors to identify message characteristics along five dimensions: moderating, summarising, adding new discussion points, adding theory, and adding external information. Unlike the Gunawardena et al. (1997) interaction analysis model, it "is specifically related to the different roles", and was developed "to provide more information about the actual role adoption in the discussion groups". Each unit of analysis (the complete message) receives a code along each dimension, with ordered categories such as mentioning versus actively discussing theory or sources. Krippendorff's alpha reliabilities ranged from 0.59 to 0.75 across dimensions.

Interrater reliability checked on a sample of transcripts using Krippendorff's alpha
constraints: Applied to transcripts of asynchronous discussion groups in an educational sciences course; approximately 2859 of 3345 messages were analysed along its five dimensions
target_learners: Freshmen students in asynchronous discussion groups
target_learning_goals: Identifying role adoption and message characteristics in collaborative discussion transcripts

article_title: Relations between the worked example and generation effects on immediate and delayed tests
citation: Relations Between the Worked Example and Generation Effects on Immediate and Delayed Tests. (2016). Submitted 29/01/2016.
title: Match the level of instructional guidance to the element interactivity of the material and the expertise of the learners
description: The article's central design recommendation is that guidance must be calibrated to material complexity and learner knowledge. It states that "the required level of instructional guidance cannot be determined without considering the level of complexity of learning materials which is dependent on the level of element interactivity". For novices facing complex, high element interactivity content, explicit worked examples are recommended; for simple content, or complex content handled by more expert learners, self-generation is recommended, especially for longer-term retention. The recommendation rests on the delayed- and immediate-test findings of the trigonometry experiment reported in this article.
requirements: Learner expertise and the element interactivity of the materials must be assessable so guidance can be matched to them.
constraints: The delayed worked-example effect for novices on high element interactivity material only approached significance on a 2-tailed test (p = .06), and the Year 11 delayed test had low internal reliability, so replications are required.
target_learners: Secondary school mathematics students (Year 10 novices and Year 11 more knowledgeable learners)
target_learning_goals: Learning to simplify trigonometry expressions and memorising trigonometry formulae
examples: Year 10 novices studying worked examples for high element interactivity simplification problems while generating low element interactivity formulae from name cues
key_sources: Relations Between the Worked Example and Generation Effects on Immediate and Delayed Tests. (2016). Submitted 29/01/2016. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2016.06.007

article_title: Relations between the worked example and generation effects on immediate and delayed tests
citation: Relations Between the Worked Example and Generation Effects on Immediate and Delayed Tests. (2016). Submitted 29/01/2016.
title: Element interactivity as the cognitive load theory measure reconciling the worked example and generation effects
description: Within cognitive load theory, element interactivity is the measure of material complexity: "Interactive elements are defined as elements that must be processed simultaneously in working memory in order to complete a task". It determines intrinsic and extraneous cognitive load and varies with learner expertise, since experts retrieve interacting elements from long-term memory as single units. The article uses it to resolve the contradiction between the worked example effect (guidance helps) and the generation effect (generation helps): the worked example effect "relies on high element interactivity material while the generation effect relies on low element interactivity material", with expertise reducing effective element interactivity. Human cognitive architecture is described via five principles, including the information store, borrowing and reorganizing, randomness as genesis, narrow limits of change, and environmental organizing and linking principles.
requirements: Applying the measure requires counting interacting elements for the specific learners, since expertise changes the effective count.
constraints: The article scopes its claims to acquisition of domain-specific schemas in long-term memory, citing Kalyuga and Singh (2015) that cognitive load theory may not apply to goals such as motivating learners or acquiring generalized schemas for transfer.
target_learners: Novice and more expert learners of curriculum-based problem-solving and memorization tasks
target_learning_goals: Acquisition of domain-specific schemas in long-term memory
examples: Estimating about 71 interacting elements in a trigonometry simplification task for Year 10 novices versus a count of one for formula memorization
key_sources: Relations Between the Worked Example and Generation Effects on Immediate and Delayed Tests. (2016). Submitted 29/01/2016. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2016.06.007

citation: Niolaki, G., Vousden, J., Terzopoulos, A., Shepherd, D.-L., Debney, L., & Masterson, J. (2022). title: Interpretive Spelling Test (IST)
description: The Interpretive Spelling Test is a spelling-to-dictation assessment distinguishing three letter string types: irregular words, regular words and pseudowords. The article states "The IST comprises three sections: 36 irregular words, 36 regular words and 34 pseudowords", matched on psycholinguistic variables such as zipf frequency, letters, phonemes and syllables. It was designed because standardised spelling tests do not distinguish letter string types, allowing separate analysis of lexical and sublexical spelling processes across year groups.
requirements: Administered as spelling to dictation with target word, embedded sentence, and repetition; pseudoword items repeated three times
constraints: Regularity defined parsimoniously by the most frequent context-insensitive phoneme-grapheme correspondence, which the authors note is somewhat subjective
target_learners: Primary school children aged 4–12 (Yr R to Yr 6)
target_learning_goals: Single-word spelling of regular words, irregular words and pseudowords
examples: Children in all year groups spelled all 106 IST items, scored one point per correct regular or irregular word and against a bank of phonologically acceptable pseudoword responses

citation: Niolaki, G., Vousden, J., Terzopoulos, A., Shepherd, D.-L., Debney, L., & Masterson, J. (2022). Spelling predictors; investigating the role of phonological ability and rapid naming in a large cross-sectional British study. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101635
title: Dual-route (DR) model of spelling
description: The article adopts the dual-route model of spelling (Barry, 1994), which "proposes that children use both lexical-semantic and sublexical processes to spell." Irregular words rely predominantly on lexical-semantic processes, pseudowords on sublexical processes, and regular words on both. The study used this framework to generate hypotheses about how PA, RAN, reading and letter-sound knowledge should relate to each letter string type, and reports that the observed dissociation between irregular and pseudoword spelling supports the model.
requirements: Assessment tools that distinguish regular words, irregular words and pseudowords so the two routes can be examined separately
constraints: The authors note they do not suggest there are clearly distinct processes for each word type; reliance differs by age and word type and the processes are not used exclusively
target_learners: Primary school children learning to spell English
target_learning_goals: Understanding and predicting single-word spelling development
examples: The study predicted irregular word spelling taps lexical-semantic processes and pseudoword spelling taps sublexical processes, then tested these predictions with the IST

article_title: Latent motivational-emotional profiles and their effects on strategy use and performance in online multimodal reading tasks: A mixed-methods investigation
citation: Zhu, S., Yao, Y., Cheong, C. M., & Zhu, X. (2026). Latent motivational-emotional profiles and their effects on strategy use and performance in online multimodal reading tasks: A mixed-methods investigation. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2026.102386
title: Cognitive-Affective Engagement Model extended with a person-centered approach to online multimodal reading
description: The study is grounded in the Cognitive-Affective Engagement Model (CAEM) of List and Alexander, which integrates "warm" motivational-emotional variables with "cold" analyses of observable behavior and strategy use in multiple-source comprehension. The article operationalizes the model's default stance as a motivational-emotional profile of OMR self-efficacy and emotional states, and extends it "by integrating a person-centered approach, which captures individual heterogeneity by identifying distinct combinations of variables within learners." Profiles are then linked to strategy use and performance outcomes.
requirements: Self-efficacy measures must be task-specific to OMR, covering traditional reading, multiple-source use, and ICT self-efficacy, rather than adapted paper-based scales
constraints: The article notes prior OMR studies using variable-centered approaches pay less attention to how motivational-emotional factors co-occur within individuals
target_learners: fourth-grade primary students reading online multimodal texts
target_learning_goals: online multimodal reading comprehension and strategy use
examples: The study measured OMR self-efficacy across three sub-dimensions and three emotions (enjoyment, anxiety, boredom), then used latent profile analysis to instantiate the model's default stance construct.

article_title: Learning by explaining orally or in written form? Text complexity matters
citation: Jacob, L., Lachner, A., & Scheiter, K. (2019). Learning by Explaining Orally or In Written Form? Text Difficulty Matters. https://aspredicted.org/sv3zv.pdf
title: Indirect social presence account of the explaining modality effect
description: The article advances an account in which the learning benefit of oral over written explaining arises because oral explaining raises awareness of social presence, which in turn triggers more generative processing. The authors state their "findings rather support the indirect social presence hypothesis, as we only obtained a significant serial mediation effect of the explaining modality on students' learning via social presence and comprehensiveness of explanations but not a direct effect solely via social presence." Social presence is operationalized as the number of personal references in explanations, and generative processing as comprehensiveness (number of concepts).
requirements: Explanations must be coded for personal references and concepts to trace the indirect pathway
constraints: Supported only for high-difficult text material and inference-based questions in this laboratory study
Based on explanation products rather than online process measures
target_learners: university students from non-biology study programs
target_learning_goals: deep comprehension of expository texts
higher-order inference-based knowledge
examples: In the experiment, oral explanations contained more personal references (d = 0.50) and more concepts (d = 0.83) than written explanations, and the serial mediation via references → concepts was significant

article_title: University students in COVID-19 lockdown: The role of adaptability and fluid reasoning in supporting their academic motivation and engagement
citation: Martin Andrew J., Ginns Paul, Collie Rebecca J. (2023). University students in COVID-19 lockdown: The role of adaptability and fluid reasoning in supporting their academic motivation and engagement. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101712
title: Job Demands-Resources theory and its academic adaptation, the Academic Demands-Resources (AD-R) model
description: JD-R theory holds that contextual demands (aspects of work "that require physical and/or psychological exertion") and resources (aspects supporting goal attainment) predict motivation and performance, alongside modifiable personal resources; it also posits buffering and boosting moderation effects. The AD-R model adapts these processes to students' academic experience. The study operationalizes lockdown as demand, adaptability and fluid reasoning as personal resources, self-efficacy as motivation, and engagement/disengagement as outcomes.
requirements: Demands, resources, motivation, and outcomes must be measured so main effects and moderation (interaction) terms can be modeled
constraints: The article notes demands and resources can be appraised differently by individuals, so effects may vary in sign or size across students
target_learning_goals: academic motivation and self-efficacy
engagement and disengagement during disruption
examples: The study modeled lockdown status, perceived adaptability, and fluid reasoning as predictors of self-efficacy, which in turn predicted participation, aspirations, enjoyment, and disengagement
key_sources: Martin Andrew J., Ginns Paul, Collie Rebecca J. (2023). University students in COVID-19 lockdown: The role of adaptability and fluid reasoning in supporting their academic motivation and engagement. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101712

article_title: University students in COVID-19 lockdown: The role of adaptability and fluid reasoning in supporting their academic motivation and engagement
citation: Martin Andrew J., Ginns Paul, Collie Rebecca J. (2023). University students in COVID-19 lockdown: The role of adaptability and fluid reasoning in supporting their academic motivation and engagement. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101712
title: Measurement battery: Adaptability Scale – Short, ICAR Letter and Number Series, and MES-UC motivation/engagement items
description: The study's instruments operationalize the JD-R constructs for university students: lockdown status as a dichotomous item, adaptability via the 3-item Adaptability Scale – Short, fluid reasoning via the 9-item ICAR Letter and Number Series sub-test (30 s per item, formed into three item parcels), and self-efficacy, participation, aspirations, enjoyment, and disengagement via MES-UC items rated 1 (Strongly Disagree) to 7 (Strongly Agree). Reliabilities (coefficient omega) ranged from .64 (fluid reasoning) to .87 (participation).
requirements: Administered via online questionnaire with screening and quality checks (straight-lining and speeder exclusion, IP cross-referencing)
constraints: The authors note the fluid reasoning measure was brief and restricted to 30 s per item, truncating variance so the effect of fluid reasoning may have been under-estimated
target_learning_goals: measuring adaptability, fluid reasoning, self-efficacy, engagement, and disengagement
examples: Fluid reasoning items ask participants to identify the next element in short digit or letter sequences, e.g. "C, F, I, L, O, …"

article_title: Methodological issues in developing a multi-dimensional coding procedure for small-group chat communication
citation: Jan Willem Strijbos, Gerry Stahl. (2007). Methodological issues in developing a multi-dimensional coding procedure for small group chat communication. Learning and Instruction. https://hal.science/hal-00703042
title: Multi-dimensional coding procedure for small group chat communication
description: A multi-dimensional coding procedure for analyzing small group chat communication in CSCL research, developed by the authors to address three methodological issues: "the unit of analysis and unit fragmentation", "the reconstruction of the response structure" and "determining reliability without overestimation". The procedure treats analysis units and the connections between them — threading — as central, since threading "proved essential to handle unit fragmentation, to reconstruct the response structure and for reliability of coding". It extends chat analysis beyond the dyadic settings that have dominated CSCL research.
requirements: Analysis units must be defined for chat communication, with threading (connections between analysis units) incorporated to handle fragmentation and reconstruct the response structure.
Reliability must be determined in a way that avoids overestimation.
constraints: The procedure was developed for small group chat communication; the article notes CSCL chat research has primarily studied dyadic settings, so extension to small groups is its distinguishing scope.
target_learners: small groups of learners collaborating through chat in CSCL settings
target_learning_goals: analysis and understanding of collaborative learning processes in chat communication
examples: The article reports the procedure's development for small group chat communication in Learning and Instruction, illustrating unit fragmentation, response-structure reconstruction, and a reliability overestimation risk.
key_sources: Jan Willem Strijbos, Gerry Stahl. (2007). Methodological issues in developing a multi-dimensional coding procedure for small group chat communication. Learning and Instruction. https://hal.science/hal-00703042

article_title: Methodological issues in developing a multi-dimensional coding procedure for small-group chat communication
citation: Jan Willem Strijbos, Gerry Stahl. (2007). Methodological issues in developing a multi-dimensional coding procedure for small group chat communication. Learning and Instruction. https://hal.science/hal-00703042
title: When coding small group chat communication, incorporate threading between analysis units to handle fragmentation and support reliability
description: A design principle for chat communication analysis methodology: coding procedures for small group chat should build in threading, i.e. "connections between analysis units", because the article found threading "proved essential to handle unit fragmentation, to reconstruct the response structure and for reliability of coding". Without threading, unit fragmentation and an unreconstructable response structure undermine both the analysis and the trustworthiness of reliability figures.
requirements: Coding must operate on defined analysis units; threading connections between those units must be reconstructed as part of the procedure.
constraints: Established for small group chat communication in CSCL; the article also warns of "a risk for reliability overestimation", so reliability determination must be designed to avoid overestimation.
target_learners: researchers and analysts coding small group chat collaboration in CSCL
target_learning_goals: valid, reliable analysis of collaborative learning processes in chat communication
examples: The article's multi-dimensional coding procedure for small group chat communication was developed around threading to handle unit fragmentation, reconstruct the response structure, and support reliability of coding.
key_sources: Jan Willem Strijbos, Gerry Stahl. (2007). Methodological issues in developing a multi-dimensional coding procedure for small group chat communication. Learning and Instruction. https://hal.science/hal-00703042

article_title: Change and transmission of students' and teachers’ lesson-specific emotions
citation: Sorkkila, M., Malmberg, L.-E., Pöysä, S., Kiuru, N., Lerkkanen, M.-K., & Pakarinen, E. (2026). Change and transmission of students' and teachers' lesson-specific emotions. Learning and Instruction, 102, Article 102298. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102298
title: Cross-directional lesson-specific emotion transmission between teachers and students as an extension of contagion and shared-emotional-experience accounts
description: The article proposes that emotional spirals between teachers and students are cross-directional rather than symmetric: teachers' negative emotions lower students' positive emotions, and students' positive emotions lower teachers' negative emotions. It contributes to "the previous theories of emotion contagion and shared emotional experience" a "novel perspective of cross-directional transmission of positive and negative emotions between teachers and students." Because positive and negative emotions were not shared as prior theories would expect, the article concludes "emotional transmission can be more complex and multifaceted phenomenon, which depends on the roles and relationships between individuals."
requirements: Examining teachers' and students' emotions together in the same lessons, since the article notes it may be more fruitful to investigate them together than separately
constraints: The article notes contagion or desire for similar emotional experiences did not take place between students and teachers as prior theories would expect, possibly because these theories apply particularly to peer networks
The terms predict or transmit do not refer to causality
target_learning_goals: Understanding and supporting classroom emotional dynamics and wellbeing
examples: The article illustrates the spiral with a teacher excited about a topic raising student excitement, students asking more questions, and teacher excitement increasing further
key_sources: Sorkkila, M., Malmberg, L.-E., Pöysä, S., Kiuru, N., Lerkkanen, M.-K., & Pakarinen, E. (2026). Change and transmission of students' and teachers' lesson-specific emotions. Learning and Instruction, 102, Article 102298. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102298

title: InSitu and InSituT mobile-based lesson-specific emotion instruments
description: The InSituations (InSitu) student instrument and its teacher version (InSituT) are mobile-based questionnaires administered towards the end of each lesson to capture lesson-specific emotions in real time. The student version contributed three emotional-engagement items (positive emotions) and two disaffection items (negative emotions) on a 5-point Likert scale; the teacher version contributed three items each. The article states the instruments "allowed us to collect multi-informant 'real--time' data and observe both change and spill-over of emotions" and reports good reliability and validity among Finnish adolescents and teachers.
requirements: Research assistants provide mobile phones and administer the questionnaire towards the end of each lesson; short questionnaires are needed to keep response rates high in real-time data collection
constraints: In this study the reliability of teachers' negative emotions was relatively low (α = .58; ω = 0.64), and the reader is advised to be careful in interpreting results for this scale
target_learning_goals: Measuring momentary emotional engagement and disaffection during lessons
examples: In this study 672 student lesson-reports nested in 61 lessons and 61 teacher lesson-reports nested in 20 teachers were collected on one school day

article_title: Physiological synchrony amongst medical residents during crisis management simulation training and a video-based assessment of leaders’ performance
citation: Lucia Patino Melo, Sebastian Wallot, Keerat Grewal, Matthew Moreno, Osamu Nomura, Jason M. Harley. (2026). Physiological synchrony amongst medical residents during crisis management simulation training and a video-based assessment of leaders' performance. Learning and Instruction 102 (2026) 102302. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102302
title: Control-Value Theory of Achievement Emotions as a framework for interpreting physiological arousal in simulation
description: The study draws on the Control-Value Theory of Achievement Emotions (CVT) to operationalize and interpret EDA as an emotional expression component. CVT treats emotional arousal as a key dimension of emotion alongside valence and object focus, and holds that "the learner's perceived control over the learning situation and the value the learner places on the learning situation" are antecedents of emotions. The authors use CVT to hypothesize that residents' high value appraisals and uncertain control appraisals arouse emotions like anxiety, and that shared goals (saving the patient) produce parallel appraisal changes that become visible as physiological synchrony. They caution that valence and object focus were not measured, so claims about discrete emotions require caution.
requirements: Interpretation of EDA as emotional arousal requires acknowledging which emotional dimensions (valence, object focus) are not measured
constraints: Appraisals were inferred from context rather than measured; the article states claims about valence and discrete emotions require caution
target_learners: medical residents in crisis resource management simulation training
target_learning_goals: understanding and managing emotional arousal during team-based crisis management practice
examples: The authors hypothesize residents' appraisals of control decline when the simulated patient deteriorates, producing shared arousal visible in EDA synchrony

title: Socially shared regulated learning (SSRL) as a lens for team emotional dynamics in simulation
description: The study uses self- and socially-shared regulated learning (SSRL) theory to situate team-level emotional processes in CRM simulation. SSRL concerns collaboratively regulating learning among multiple individuals, requiring teams to "negotiate personal interests, set common goals, and manage the team as members progress in accomplishing these goals". The authors draw on SSRL's proposition that "shared emotional responses can be indicators of adaptive learning" to motivate their hypothesis that physiological synchrony relates to team performance. They note shared monitoring was not measured but helps interpret and situate the findings.
requirements: Team members need baseline understanding of individual regulatory abilities and skills to contribute to team goals; SSRL presupposes prerequisite SRL abilities
constraints: Shared monitoring and other SSRL processes were not measured in this study; the theory is used for interpretation only
target_learners: medical residents working in teams during simulation training
target_learning_goals: collaborative regulation of learning and emotion in high-stakes team performance
examples: The authors use SSRL's shared-emotion proposition to justify expecting PS to positively correlate with leader performance

Learning and Instruction 102 (2026) 102302. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102302
title: MdRQA %REC with surrogate-data comparison for detecting group physiological synchrony
description: Multidimensional Recurrence Quantification Analysis (MdRQA) is the analytic method the article uses to quantify physiological synchrony in multivariate EDA time series. It extends cross-recurrence analysis and "can handle multivariate time series data... and is not limited to bi-variate analyses". The study focused on the %REC output, the proportion of recurrent points in phase space, and validated detected synchrony by comparing real teams' %REC against surrogate datasets created by randomizing each participant's z-scored EDA values within a group. Radius was tuned so %REC ranged from 5 to 20% for comparability across datasets.
requirements: Time-delayed embedding parameters (emb: 1, del = 21, rad = 0.2, Euclidean norm) and radius tuning to keep %REC between 5 and 20% for comparability
constraints: Surrogate datasets with non-group members were not feasible due to differing recording lengths and sample size limitations; no in situ movement-artifact controls were used, with artifacts addressed post hoc via visual inspection and filtering
target_learners: medical trainees in team-based simulation education
target_learning_goals: detecting shared emotional arousal in collaborative learning teams
examples: Applied to EDA from 29 residents in 9 teams wearing Empatica E4 wristbands before and during CRM scenarios

title: Adapted Ottawa Global Rating Scale scoring team leaders' leadership and communication
description: The Ottawa Global Rating Scale (GRS) is the expert-rating instrument used to score team leaders' CRM performance on video. The original scale divides CRM skills into five categories including "problem solving, situational awareness, leadership, resource utilization, and communication", each on a 7-point anchored ordinal scale from novice (1) to experienced physician (7). The research team adapted it by removing categories not aligned with the leadership-and-communication learning objectives, supported by Kane's validity framework, and two Emergency Medicine physicians scored each video, reaching perfect agreement after negotiation (Cohen's Kappa 0.77 before negotiation).

constraints: The scale was adapted by removing overall performance, problem solving, situational awareness, and resource utilization categories, and was not used for summative clinical evaluation of learners

target_learning_goals: assessing leadership and communication performance in crisis resource management training
examples: Two physicians scored leaders' videos individually, then negotiated differences until perfect agreement, averaging Leadership and Communication items into one global CRM score
