article_title: Knowledge development and restructuring in the domain of medicine: The role of theory and practice
citation: Boshuizen, H. P. A., Schmidt, H. G., Custers, E. J. F. M., & van de Wiel, M. W. (1995). Knowledge Development and Restructuring in the Domain of Medicine: The Role of Theory and Practice. Learning and Instruction. https://www.sciencedirect.com/journal/learning-and-instruction
title: Theory of medical expertise development through knowledge encapsulation and illness script formation
description: A theory of medical knowledge development in which students first build rich causal pathophysiological networks, then restructure knowledge in two ways: knowledge encapsulation, in which "encapsulating concepts that more or less summarize the detailed ones" function as shorthand in clinical reasoning, and illness script formation, in which scripts of enabling conditions, fault and consequences develop through exposure to real patients. Earlier structures are assumed not to decay but to "sediment into multiple layers" accessible when newer structures fail.
requirements: Requires repeated application of knowledge in diagnostic tasks for encapsulation
Illness scripts require both conceptual learning and practical experience with patients
constraints: Novices in medicine do not have experientially grounded illness scripts, though their lay knowledge may have a similar structure
target_learning_goals: diagnostic reasoning
clinical knowledge organisation
development of medical expertise
examples: In Experiment 1, experts' explanations used higher-level concepts such as "urine retention" while a fourth-year student's protocol activated detailed anatomical and pathophysiological concepts across over ten organs

article_title: Perceived social-emotional competence: A multidimensional examination and links with social-emotional motivation and behaviors
citation: Collie, R.J. (2022). Perceived social-emotional competence: A multidimensional examination and links with social-emotional motivation and behaviors. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101656
title: SEC School Model
description: The Social and Emotional Competence (SEC) School Model (Collie, 2020) frames social-emotional competence as a process involving mechanisms and manifestations. It posits two intrapsychic mechanisms—social-emotional perceptions and motivation—that drive socially and emotionally competent behaviors. As the article states, "the SEC School Model posits that social-emotional perceptions promote social-emotional motivation and that both factors boost adaptive behaviors." The present study tested this central process using perceived-SEC as the perception mechanism.
requirements: Grounding in motivation theories (self-determination theory, social-cognitive theory) linking perceptions to motivation and adaptive behaviors
constraints: Examined here cross-sectionally among 13-16-year-old Australian adolescents; causal ordering could not be assessed
target_learning_goals: social-emotional competence, social-emotional motivation, prosocial behavior, reduced conduct problems
examples: The study operationalized the model's central process with perceived-SEC, autonomous/controlled motivation, and parent-reported prosocial behavior and conduct problems
key_sources: Collie, R.J. (2022). Perceived social-emotional competence: A multidimensional examination and links with social-emotional motivation and behaviors. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101656

article_title: Perceived social-emotional competence: A multidimensional examination and links with social-emotional motivation and behaviors
citation: Collie, R.J. (2022). Perceived social-emotional competence: A multidimensional examination and links with social-emotional motivation and behaviors. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101656
title: Perceived Social-Emotional Competence Scale (five dimensions)
description: A student self-report scale (Collie, 2021b) assessing five dimensions of perceived-SEC on a 1-7 agreement scale. As printed: "Five dimensions of perceived-SEC were assessed: perceived competence for assertiveness (4 items; e.g., “I feel capable to make sure my ideas are heard in group work at school”), tolerance (3 items; e.g., “I feel capable to be respectful of different cultures”)" plus social regulation, emotion regulation, and emotional awareness. In this study it was analyzed via bifactor ESEM with adequate omegas (global ω = .95).
requirements: Student self-report administration; omega estimates of ≥ .50 considered adequate for specific-factors in bifactor ESEM
constraints: The five dimensions are not all-encompassing; different dimensions may be required in different cultures and contexts
target_learning_goals: assessing perceived competence for social-emotional skills
examples: Used with 414 Australian secondary students in 2021 via an online questionnaire

article_title: The differential development of epistemic beliefs in psychology and computer science students: A four-wave longitudinal study
citation: Rosman, T., Mayer, A.-K., Kerwer, M., & Krampen, G. (2019). The differential development of epistemic beliefs in psychology and computer science students: A four-wave longitudinal study. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2017.01.006
title: Epistemic sophistication as flexible adaptation of epistemic judgments to specific contexts, not a generalized developmental sequence
description: This account reconceives epistemic 'sophistication' as, in the authors' words, "a flexible adaptation of epistemic judgments to the characteristics of specific contexts, and not as a generalized developmental sequence." It emerged from the finding that belief trajectories diverged by discipline: absolute beliefs increased in computer science while multiplistic beliefs in psychology rose and then steeply decreased. The framework implies that domain context shapes which belief changes count as developmentally advanced.
requirements: Learning contexts must have discernible discipline-specific characteristics of knowledge to which epistemic judgments can adapt.
constraints: Derived from a single four-wave study of undergraduates in two disciplines (computer science and psychology).
target_learning_goals: development of discipline-appropriate epistemic beliefs about the nature of knowledge
examples: The authors suggest the account after observing divergent belief trajectories across the two disciplines in their longitudinal data.

article_title: The differential development of epistemic beliefs in psychology and computer science students: A four-wave longitudinal study
citation: Rosman, T., Mayer, A.-K., Kerwer, M., & Krampen, G. (2019). The differential development of epistemic beliefs in psychology and computer science students: A four-wave longitudinal study. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2017.01.006
title: Three-semester four-wave longitudinal design with multi-group growth modelling for parallel epistemic-belief processes
description: The study's methodological element is a "three-semester long four-wave study with 226 undergraduates" in which "Data were analysed by multi- group growth modelling for parallel processes." This design permits modelling of belief trajectories across disciplines in parallel, enabling the differential-development analysis that grounded the article's conclusions about epistemic sophistication.
requirements: Repeated measurement across four waves spanning three semesters to model belief trajectories.
constraints: Applied to undergraduates in computer science and psychology; findings reported for these two disciplines.
target_learning_goals: measuring change in epistemic beliefs about the nature of knowledge over time
examples: Hypotheses about discipline-specific belief trajectories were tested in this design.

article_title: A sequence of learning processes in an intelligent tutoring system from topic-related appraisals to learning gains
citation: Chevalère, J., Yun, H. S., Henke, A., Pinkwart, N., Hafner, V., & Lazarides, R. (2023). A sequence of learning processes in an intelligent tutoring system from topic-related appraisals to learning gains. Learning and Instruction, 87, 101799. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2023.101799
title: Control-value theory sequence applied to ITS learning: partial correlational support but difficult causal establishment
description: The article tests Pekrun's control-value theory (CVT), which posits a sequence from topic-related cognitive appraisals of control and value, through activity-related emotions (enjoyment, boredom), to engagement, task performance, and learning gains, including reciprocal feedback loops. In the ITS context the authors found "partial support for the application of CVT to the ITS context on a correlational basis", while "causation was more difficult to establish due to the influence of multiple confounders challenging the expected unidirectional and reciprocal relations". The theory served as the framework for hypotheses and a three-step path-analytic testing procedure.
requirements: Measurement of appraisals, emotions, engagement, performance, and knowledge at temporally ordered phases (pretest, test, posttest) as in the study's three-day protocol
constraints: The article states the difficulty of establishing sequential causation in the current ITS context due to confounders
Multilevel analyses were not performed due to the small number of schools (N = 5) and classrooms (N = 11)
target_learning_goals: Science learning (climate change knowledge) in an open-ended ITS environment
examples: Path analyses of 140 students' data across pretest, four one-hour Betty's Brain sessions, and posttest

article_title: Creativity in dialogues: How do children interact with parents vs. strangers for generating creative ideas?
citation: Bai, H.; Chan, L.; Luo, A.; Kroesbergen, E.H.; Christie, S. (2026). Creativity in dialogues: How do children interact with parents vs. strangers for generating creative ideas? Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102286
title: Perspective-affordance theory (PAT) of creativity as the framework linking perspective taking to creative idea generation
description: The article adopts Glăveanu's (2020) perspective-affordance theory as its explanatory framework for how creativity emerges in social interaction. It defines perspective as a relational construct linking a person and the world, and affordance as the action possibilities of materials relative to people's perspectives. The article states that "perspective diversities increase the creative potential of individuals and groups, and creativity essentially emerges from perspective taking—a relational, dialogical process that consists of an exchange of perspectives". The study operationalizes this framework in its two-part coding scheme distinguishing cognitive and social-emotional perspective taking.
requirements: Perspective taking requires an exchange of positions between social partners, which the article states can be challenging when differences are substantial and surface positions are incompatible.
constraints: The article notes social-emotional unease while changing positions, rooted in the difficulty of being truly open to others' perspectives and in perceived judgement, can make partners defensive of their own ideas.
target_learners: children aged 4-6 years in dyadic creative activities with adults
target_learning_goals: generation of creative (original and appropriate) ideas through social interaction
examples: The study built its coding scheme on the PAT theory and applied it to child-adult dyads generating unusual uses for everyday objects in the AUT.
key_sources: Bai, H.; Chan, L.; Luo, A.; Kroesbergen, E.H.; Christie, S. (2026). Creativity in dialogues: How do children interact with parents vs. strangers for generating creative ideas? Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102286

article_title: Creativity in dialogues: How do children interact with parents vs. strangers for generating creative ideas?
citation: Bai, H.; Chan, L.; Luo, A.; Kroesbergen, E.H.; Christie, S. (2026). Creativity in dialogues: How do children interact with parents vs. strangers for generating creative ideas? Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102286
title: Novel coding scheme for cognitive and social-emotional perspective taking in dyadic AUT dialogues
description: A novel observational coding scheme designed by the authors, based on the PAT theory and inspirations from Chiu (2008), applied utterance-by-utterance to videotaped and transcribed AUT sessions. It contains two broad categories, cognitive perspective taking (Listen/understand and Extend/revise) and social-emotional perspective taking (Direct deny/doubt, Polite deny/doubt, Recognize/agree, Appreciate/praise), plus Inviting behavior and Utterance number as controls. Reliability testing showed that "Kappa was 0.63 (95 % CI [0.59,0.66]) for the whole coding scheme (with mutual-exclusive categories)".
requirements: Videotaped, verbatim-transcribed dialogue sessions segmented into utterances, and coders blinded to the study hypotheses applying one mutually exclusive code per utterance.
constraints: Per-category agreement was lower for the disagreement codes: Kappa was 0.40 (95 % CI [0.13, 0.75]) for Direct deny/doubt and 0.50 (95 % CI [0.29, 0.70]) for Polite deny/doubt, described as moderate to substantial inter-coder agreement overall.
target_learners: children aged 4-6 years interacting with adults in creative tasks
target_learning_goals: quantifying social processes (exchange of ideas, open accepting atmosphere) during collaborative creative idea generation
examples: The scheme was applied to 102 dyads' transcripts; five transcripts (incl. 1807 utterances) were double coded to establish inter-coder agreement.

article_title: The moderating role of the teacher-child relationship in the association between peer rejection and language competence in early childhood education
citation: Femke van der Wilt, Jantine Spilt, Sharisse van Driel, Hilde Colpin. (2025). The moderating role of the teacher-child relationship in the association between peer rejection and language competence in early childhood education. Learning and Instruction 100 (2025) 102217. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102217
title: Support teachers in building close and non-conflictual relationships with pupils to protect rejected children's language development
description: Because peer rejection was related to poorer later language competence only when teacher-child closeness was below median or conflict above median, the authors argue schools should "support teachers in building close and non-conflictual relationships with their pupils". They note existing interventions have improved poor teacher-child relationships and that fostering positive relationships may create a classroom environment benefiting both peer interactions and language development.
requirements: Teacher professional development that emphasizes relationship-building, both between teachers and pupils and among peers
constraints: The moderating findings come from one longitudinal study of Dutch children aged four to six with predominantly highly educated, Dutch-speaking families
target_learners: children aged four to six in early childhood education
children at risk of peer rejection
target_learning_goals: language competence (pragmatic skills)
social integration
examples: The study measured teacher-child closeness and conflict with the Student-Teacher Relationship Scale and found the peer rejection-language link absent above-median closeness and below-median conflict

citation: Femke van der Wilt, Jantine Spilt, Sharisse van Driel, Hilde Colpin. (2025). title: Extended attachment perspective on teacher-child relationships: dyadic affective quality with closeness, conflict, and dependency dimensions
description: The article adopts the extended attachment perspective, which "emphasizes the dyadic, affective quality of teacher-child relationships, distinguishing three dimensions: closeness, conflict, and dependency". Closeness refers to warmth, support and positive affect, with the teacher as a secure base and safe haven; conflict describes struggles, tension and negative affect. The study focuses on closeness and conflict as moderators of the peer rejection-language competence link, framed by attachment theory and the academic risk hypothesis.
requirements: Measurement of the dyadic affective quality of the teacher-child relationship, e.g. via the Student-Teacher Relationship Scale
constraints: The study examined only the affective quality, without considering the cognitive dimension such as instructional support
target_learning_goals: language competence
social-emotional adjustment
examples: The study used the shortened Closeness and Conflict subscales of the Dutch Student-Teacher Relationship Scale (Cronbach's alpha .82 and .81)

article_title: Short- and long-term effects of COVID-related kindergarten and school closures on first- to eighth-grade students’ school readiness skills and mathematics, reading and science learning
citation: Gyöngyvér Molnár & Zoltán Hermann. (2023). Short- and long-term effects of COVID-related kindergarten and school closures on first- to eighth-grade students' school readiness skills and mathematics, reading and science learning. Learning and Instruction, 83, 101706. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101706
title: eDia computer-based diagnostic assessment system
description: The eDia system is the online platform through which all assessments in this study were delivered. The article describes it as "an integrated online assessment platform that supports all assessment processes from technology-based test administration and IRT-based data analyses to an easy-to-use and well-interpretable feedback module." Students received immediate feedback on total and dimension-level achievement, and tests were drawn from domain-specific item banks scaled with the Rasch model (mean 500, SD 100).
requirements: Students in Grades 1–3 completed mouse and keyboard training and warm-up tasks, and could listen to pre-recorded voiceover instructions, to use the platform at the required level
constraints: Participating schools self-select into the eDia system, so the school sample is self-selected and can change from year to year
target_learning_goals: Diagnosing mathematics, reading, science and school-readiness skills across reasoning, application and disciplinary knowledge dimensions
examples: All tests lasted one 45-minute school lesson supervised by teachers; in Grades 2–8 the system randomly selected one grade-appropriate test per student from 220 tests per domain

article_title: Seeking academic help: The case of lower secondary students with autism spectrum disorder and their teachers
citation: Sabine Zorn, Minna Puustinen. (2022). Seeking academic help: The case of lower secondary students with autism spectrum disorder and their teachers. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101624
title: Ecologically valid video analysis of the help-seeking and help-giving process in inclusive classrooms
description: The study frames help seeking as a social process to be analyzed in real classroom interaction rather than only through interviews. It complements prior interview data by "analyzing video data on the same students’ (i.e., 11 students with ASD) actual help-seeking behavior as well as their teachers’ (n = 17) subsequent help-giving behavior." The article states that "The importance of analyzing the helpseeking process in an ecologically valid context is emphasized."
requirements: Video recordings of everyday classroom situations in both general and resource class contexts
constraints: Conducted within a single mainstream lower secondary school with 11 students with ASD
target_learners: lower secondary students with autism spectrum disorder
target_learning_goals: academic help seeking and help-giving social interaction
examples: Video data on 11 students with ASD and 17 teachers in general and resource class within a mainstream lower secondary school

article_title: Linguistic precursors of sixth-grade geometric and fraction skills in children with and without Developmental Language Disorder
citation: Kleemans, T., Vissers, C. T. W. M., & Segers, E. (2025). Linguistic precursors of sixth-grade geometric and fraction skills in children with and without Developmental Language Disorder. Learning and Instruction, 95, 102019. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2024.102019
title: Identify individual cognitive strengths and integrate them into standardized test batteries and treatment approaches for children with DLD
description: The article argues that because children with DLD are highly heterogeneous, compensatory strengths may only appear at the individual level, so "identifying individual strengths should be integrated into standardized test batteries and treatment approaches." The case-series analysis showed a verbal-reasoning strength brought DLD children's geometry and fraction scores into the normal range, so assessment should profile strengths rather than only deficits.
requirements: Individual-level (case-series) analysis in addition to group comparisons, because group-level analyses did not identify specific strengths for children with DLD
constraints: The DLD sample attended Dutch special education, so generalization to children with DLD in mainstream education was not supported by the study
target_learners: Upper-primary-grade children with Developmental Language Disorder
target_learning_goals: Geometric skills
Fraction skills
examples: The study defined strengths as scores 1 SD above the TD-group mean and used a follow-up MANCOVA to show DLD children with a verbal-reasoning strength scored within the average range on geometry and fractions

article_title: It is autonomous, not controlled motivation that counts: Linear and curvilinear relations of autonomous and controlled motivation to school grades
citation: Mouratidis, A., Michou, A., Sayil, M., & Altan, S. (2021). It is autonomous, not controlled motivation that counts: Linear and curvilinear relations of autonomous and controlled motivation to school grades. Learning and Instruction, 73, 101433. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2020.101433
title: Self-Determination Theory quality-of-motivation account of academic achievement
description: Self-Determination Theory distinguishes autonomous motivation — acting out of interest, enjoyment, or personal importance (intrinsic and identified regulation) — from controlled motivation — acting under internal or external pressure (introjected and external regulation). The article applies SDT's key proposition that "high quality of motivation (i.e., high autonomous motivation and low controlled motivation) which matters for positive outcomes" to school grades, testing it with polynomial regression. Autonomous motivation is said to foster an internal locus of causality and fuller recruitment of inner resources, while controlled motivation produces a less adaptive mode of functioning.
requirements: Measures distinguishing autonomous (intrinsic + identified) from controlled (introjected + external) regulation, validated via higher-order CFA in each sample
constraints: Formulated and tested here for Turkish adolescent students in middle and high school using the Self-Regulated Questionnaire tradition; recent findings (Phillips & Johnson, 2018; Brunet et al., 2015) have cast partial doubt on the incongruence tenet in other domains
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement as reflected in school grades in mathematics and Turkish language
examples: Both samples' motivation was measured with translated Likert scales; grades came from school records rather than self-report to reduce common method bias
key_sources: Mouratidis, A., Michou, A., Sayil, M., & Altan, S. (2021). It is autonomous, not controlled motivation that counts: Linear and curvilinear relations of autonomous and controlled motivation to school grades. Learning and Instruction, 73, 101433. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2020.101433

article_title: How to foster STEM learning during Covid-19 remote schooling: Combining virtual and video experiments
citation: Flegr, S., Kuhn, J., & Scheiter, K. (2023). How to foster STEM learning during Covid-19 remote schooling: Combining virtual and video experiments. Learning and Instruction, 86, 101778. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2023.101778
title: Use virtual experiments, optionally combined with video experiments, for guided inquiry learning when hands-on experimentation is not possible
description: The article concludes that "virtual and video experiments can be recommended to teachers if hands-on experimentation is not possible". In its study, guided inquiry learning with these formats during Covid-19 remote schooling significantly fostered seventh-graders' conceptual understanding of converging lenses, with guidance embedded in worksheets and instructional videos. Because combinations and sequences conferred no advantage over the virtual experiment alone, the virtual experiment is the essential component, with the video experiment an optional enrichment.
requirements: Guidance must be embedded in the learning material, such as experimentation worksheets and instructional videos, since a teacher cannot provide just-in-time support during remote schooling
Students need access to the digital experiments and materials, which were provided via links and regular mail in the study
constraints: The study was conducted during Covid-19 remote schooling with seventh-graders learning individually at home on the topic of converging lenses, so scope is limited to that setting and topic
No hands-on control group in a traditional classroom could be included, so learning cannot be compared to traditional classroom experimentation
The video experiment lacks interactivity, as students are "in the role of an attentive observer without having any opportunity to actively manipulate variables"
target_learners: Seventh-grade secondary school students (Gymnasium, highest German track) learning individually at home during remote schooling
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding in physics, specifically geometrical optics and image formation by converging lenses
examples: 154 seventh-graders were randomly assigned within classes to video-virtual, virtual-video, or virtual-only conditions and worked through a guided inquiry unit on converging lenses entirely from home
key_sources: Flegr, S., Kuhn, J., & Scheiter, K. (2023). How to foster STEM learning during Covid-19 remote schooling: Combining virtual and video experiments. Learning and Instruction, 86, 101778. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2023.101778

article_title: Development of numerical relational and counting skills as components of early numeracy
citation: Verkerk, J. C., van de Rijt, B., & van Viersen, S. (2026). Development of numerical relational and counting skills as components of early numeracy. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102313
title: Two-component framework of early numeracy: numerical relational skills and counting skills
description: The article adopts and substantiates a two-dimensional framework of early numeracy in which "another two-dimensional approach to EN concerns a distinction between numerical relational skills (NRS) and counting skills (CS". NRS comprises comparing, classifying, one-to-one correspondence, and seriation, involving logical inferences about quantitative relationships including transitivity. CS comprises using number words in sequence, structured counting, resultative counting, and general number knowledge including early symbolic addition. The framework is supported by factor analyses in this study and prior work, and offers "a more precise framework to understand EN and its role in later mathematical development".
requirements: Measurement instruments must capture both components separately, e.g., the ENT-3 subtests for NRS (comparison, classification, correspondence, seriation) and CS (counting words, synchronized and shortened counting, resultative counting, general number knowledge).
constraints: The article notes the components are interrelated yet distinct; NRS reliability was lower in Grade 1 (Cronbach's α .43–.60), and the estimation and measurement subtests were excluded from analysis.
target_learners: Dutch children in Kindergarten year 1 through Grade 1 (ages 4 to 7), including at-risk low-performing learners
target_learning_goals: Early numeracy: numerical relational skills (comparing, classifying, one-to-one correspondence, seriation) and counting skills (number-word sequences, structured and resultative counting, early number operations)
examples: The Dutch Early Numeracy Test-3 operationalizes the framework with ten subtests, four per component, scored dichotomously and Rasch-scaled.
key_sources: Verkerk, J. C., van de Rijt, B., & van Viersen, S. (2026). Development of numerical relational and counting skills as components of early numeracy. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102313

article_title: The relation between text comprehension and computation in mathematical word-problem solving
citation: Strohmaier, A. R., Schons, C., Knabbe, A., Vogel, M., Saado, K., & Obersteiner, A. (2025). The relation between text comprehension and computation in mathematical word-problem solving. Learning and Instruction, 101, 102235. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102235
title: Four-type taxonomy of word-problem process models by process order and mental representation
description: The article organizes existing cognitive models of word-problem solving along two axes: whether text comprehension and computation occur in a "linear" or "flexible" order, and whether they use "separable or integrated mental representations". This yields four model types (linear-separable, flexible-separable, linear-integrated, flexible-integrated), each predicting distinct patterns of canonical, phase-crossover, and attention-crossover effects on eye-tracking data. The taxonomy is used to judge which model best fits the observed solution process.
requirements: Requires process data (e.g., eye-tracking) that distinguishes solution phases and areas of interest to discriminate between model types
constraints: The direct translation strategy is excluded from the taxonomy because it is "generally unreliable" and expected mostly in low-achieving solvers
target_learning_goals: understanding the cognitive process of mathematical word-problem solving
key_sources: Strohmaier, A. R., Schons, C., Knabbe, A., Vogel, M., Saado, K., & Obersteiner, A. (2025). The relation between text comprehension and computation in mathematical word-problem solving. Learning and Instruction, 101, 102235. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102235

article_title: The relation between text comprehension and computation in mathematical word-problem solving
citation: Strohmaier, A. R., Schons, C., Knabbe, A., Vogel, M., Saado, K., & Obersteiner, A. (2025). The relation between text comprehension and computation in mathematical word-problem solving. Learning and Instruction, 101, 102235. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102235
title: Three categories of attentional effects (canonical, phase-crossover, attention-crossover) for discriminating process models
description: The article proposes a categorization of effects on cognitive processing during word-problem solving: "Canonical effects" are predicted by all process models; "Phase-crossover effects" occur when a difficulty or ability affects the phase opposite to its canonical one (predicted by flexible models); "Attention-crossover effects" occur when a factor affects attention on the problem part opposite to its canonical one (predicted by integrated models). This framework converts model differences into empirically testable predictions about fixation durations on numbers and situational text in two solution phases.
requirements: Independent variation of linguistic and mathematical problem difficulty, standardized ability measures, and phase-distinguishing process data
constraints: Flexible and integrated models predict opposite attention-crossover effects for question position, "which might also cancel each other out"
target_learning_goals: diagnosing the sequence and integration of comprehension and computation processes
key_sources: Strohmaier, A. R., Schons, C., Knabbe, A., Vogel, M., Saado, K., & Obersteiner, A. (2025). The relation between text comprehension and computation in mathematical word-problem solving. Learning and Instruction, 101, 102235. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102235

article_title: The relation between text comprehension and computation in mathematical word-problem solving
citation: Strohmaier, A. R., Schons, C., Knabbe, A., Vogel, M., Saado, K., & Obersteiner, A. (2025). The relation between text comprehension and computation in mathematical word-problem solving. Learning and Instruction, 101, 102235. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102235
title: Teach word-problem text-comprehension strategies that prepare the mathematical model rather than strip away the story context
description: Because the study found that linguistic and mathematical processes share a joint mental representation, the authors argue that "teaching text-comprehension strategies for word-problem solving should be particularly valuable if those strategies are working towards preparing the mathematical model". Strategies aimed merely at identifying keywords or removing the context risk building an incomplete mental representation that takes longer to transform into an adequate mathematical model.
requirements: Instruction should connect comprehension of the problem text to the construction of the mathematical model, since both draw on one shared mental representation
constraints: The authors warn that supporting text comprehension superficially "might initially lead to quicker linguistic processing, but might result in an incomplete mental representation"
target_learning_goals: mathematical word-problem solving
examples: The study found question-first placement accelerated initial processing but lengthened the second solution phase, which the authors read as evidence that superficial comprehension support can backfire
key_sources: Strohmaier, A. R., Schons, C., Knabbe, A., Vogel, M., Saado, K., & Obersteiner, A. (2025). The relation between text comprehension and computation in mathematical word-problem solving. Learning and Instruction, 101, 102235. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102235

article_title: The happy-fish-little-pond effect on enjoyment: Generalizability across multiple domains and countries
citation: Basarkod, G., Marsh, H. W., Guo, J., Parker, P. D., Dicke, T., & Pekrun, R. (2023). The Happy-Fish-Little-Pond Effect on Enjoyment: Generalizability Across Multiple Domains and Countries. https://osf.io/kb29h/
title: Control-value theory and the relative universality principle as the framework for achievement-emotion formation
description: Control-value theory (CVT; Pekrun, 2006, 2018) holds that emotions are a consequence of cognitive appraisals of control over, and subjective value placed on, achievement activities and outcomes. The article applies CVT to enjoyment: success in a valued, controllable subject raises control appraisals and thus enjoyment, while high class-average achievement lowers relative control via social comparison. CVT assumes "general functional mechanisms of human emotions are universal", with contents and intensities varying across individuals and groups — the relative universality principle this study tests.
requirements: Emotions arise from control and value appraisals, so testing CVT-based predictions requires measures of achievement contexts and appraisals
constraints: CVT assumes functional relations are universal but levels of emotions may differ across domains and cultural contexts
target_learning_goals: Academic enjoyment in mathematics, science, and reading
examples: The study tested CVT-derived hypotheses that student-level achievement positively and class-average achievement negatively predict enjoyment across three domains and 37 countries.
key_sources: Basarkod, G., Marsh, H. W., Guo, J., Parker, P. D., Dicke, T., & Pekrun, R. (2023). The Happy-Fish-Little-Pond Effect on Enjoyment: Generalizability Across Multiple Domains and Countries. https://osf.io/kb29h/

article_title: Strategies for regulating achievement emotions: Conceptualization and relations with university students’ emotions, well-being, and health
citation: Stockinger, K., Dresel, M., Marsh, H. W., & Pekrun, R. (2025). Strategies for regulating achievement emotions: Conceptualization and relations with university students' emotions, well-being, and health. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102089
title: Six-group model of achievement emotion regulation strategies derived from control-value theory
description: The article proposes a theoretical model in which university students regulate achievement emotions using six strategy groups. As the authors state, the model "is derived from the control-value theory of achievement emotions (Pekrun, 2006) and Harley et al.'s (2019) model of emotion regulation in achievement settings" and "considers six groups of strategies: situation selection, social support, reappraisal, expression,suppression,andcompetencedevelopment." Strategies target different elements of reciprocal feedback loops between emotions, appraisals, situations, and competence.
requirements: Measures must be context- and emotion-specific, since the model holds that emotion regulation is context-specific and emotion-specific
constraints: The model was developed and tested with university students in Germany and England
target_learning_goals: regulating achievement emotions such as enjoyment, anxiety, and boredom during studying, attending class, and taking tests
key_sources: Stockinger, K., Dresel, M., Marsh, H. W., & Pekrun, R. (2025). Strategies for regulating achievement emotions: Conceptualization and relations with university students' emotions, well-being, and health. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102089

article_title: Strategies for regulating achievement emotions: Conceptualization and relations with university students’ emotions, well-being, and health
citation: Stockinger, K., Dresel, M., Marsh, H. W., & Pekrun, R. (2025). Strategies for regulating achievement emotions: Conceptualization and relations with university students' emotions, well-being, and health. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102089
title: Regulation of Achievement Emotions Questionnaire (RAEQ)
description: The RAEQ is a newly developed context- and emotion-specific self-report instrument assessing students' use of the six regulation strategies for enjoyment, anxiety, and boredom. The article reports that "the RAEQcomprises 18 subscales (3 emotions; 6 strategies per emotion)" with "a totalof 80items across all 18 scales" and "Mean alpha was .77". Items are answered on a five-point Likert-type scale and assess prohedonic regulation in studying, class attendance, and test situations.
requirements: Administration with university students experiencing achievement-related enjoyment, anxiety, and boredom
constraints: Items were partly derived from existing instruments and newly developed items; reliability was considered acceptable because analyses were conducted on a latent level
target_learning_goals: self-regulation of achievement emotions
key_sources: Stockinger, K., Dresel, M., Marsh, H. W., & Pekrun, R. (2025). Strategies for regulating achievement emotions: Conceptualization and relations with university students' emotions, well-being, and health. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102089

article_title: Strategies for regulating achievement emotions: Conceptualization and relations with university students’ emotions, well-being, and health
citation: Stockinger, K., Dresel, M., Marsh, H. W., & Pekrun, R. (2025). Strategies for regulating achievement emotions: Conceptualization and relations with university students' emotions, well-being, and health. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102089
title: Support students in reappraising control and value appraisals to increase enjoyment and decrease anxiety and boredom
description: Grounded in control-value theory, the article argues that reappraisal of achievement-related appraisals is a key lever for regulating achievement emotions: "Boostingperceivedcontrolshouldhelpincreaseenjoymentand decrease anxiety or boredom resulting from overchallenge". Across the three studies, reappraisal and competence development showed the most pronounced links with target emotions and were implied to be especially adaptive strategies for educators to foster.
requirements: Instruction should target students' perceived control and value appraisals, the proximal antecedents of achievement emotions in control-value theory
constraints: Evidence is largely correlational; the article states cross-sectional relations may reflect different causal feedback loops, so causal direction is unresolved
target_learning_goals: regulating enjoyment, anxiety, and boredom in academic settings
examples: The RAEQ includes reappraisal items targeting perceived value of learning materials and perceived competence and control over learning, such as reminding oneself there are more important things in life when nervous during studying

article_title: A movement and story-telling intervention improves language and fundamental movement skills and is feasible for delivery by teachers in the first year of school
citation: Cunningham, Anna J.; Baikousi, Violeta; Eyre, Emma; Duncan, Michael; Crotti, Matteo; Martins, Ricardo; Wood, Clare. (2025). A movement and story-telling intervention improves language and fundamental movement skills and is feasible for delivery by teachers in the first year of school. LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION. https://hdl.handle.net/10446/299265
title: Upskill early years educators and educate school management on the importance of teaching movement and language skills to young children
description: The article draws an implementation implication from its trial of MAST, a 12-week whole-class combined movement and story-telling approach delivered by teachers. Because the programme proved feasible but fidelity varied, the authors state that "Implications include the need to upskill early years educators and to educate school management on the importance of teaching movement and language skills to young children". This positions educator training and management buy-in as prerequisites for successfully delivering integrated movement and language programmes in school.
requirements: Teachers need upskilling to deliver combined movement and story-telling programmes as delivered in MAST
constraints: Fidelity varied: one of five schools did not consistently deliver all key components of MAST
target_learners: four-to-five-year-old children in the first year of primary school
target_learning_goals: language development
fundamental movement skills
examples: MAST, a 12-week whole-class combined movement and story-telling approach, was delivered by teachers across five primary schools in a cluster-randomised controlled trial with 214 children

article_title: Resilience research in learning disabilities: Guiding principles from developmental psychopathology
citation: Slomowitz R. F., Narayan A. J., & McGrath L. M. (2025). Resilience research in learning disabilities: Guiding principles from developmental psychopathology. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102090
title: Developmental psychopathology resilience framework: resilience as a dynamic process of better-than-expected outcomes in the context of risk
description: The paper adapts the DP resilience framework to LD research, defining resilience as "the process of obtaining better-than-expected outcomes or developmentally appropriate functioning due to successful adaptation in the context of risk or adversity". Two core tenets are that risk is a prerequisite for resilience (without adversity the mechanisms are called competence) and that resilience is a dynamic process, not a trait or single-point outcome. The framework distinguishes promotive from protective factors as quantifiable resilience mechanisms.
requirements: Risk or adversity must be present as a prerequisite condition for resilience mechanisms to be identified
constraints: The paper focuses on individual-level factors because these are most commonly studied in academic resilience research, with less focus on systemic factors
target_learners: children at risk for learning disabilities
target_learning_goals: academic outcomes in reading and math despite risk for learning disabilities
key_sources: Slomowitz R. F., Narayan A. J., & McGrath L. M. (2025). Resilience research in learning disabilities: Guiding principles from developmental psychopathology. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102090

article_title: Resilience research in learning disabilities: Guiding principles from developmental psychopathology
citation: Slomowitz R. F., Narayan A. J., & McGrath L. M. (2025). Resilience research in learning disabilities: Guiding principles from developmental psychopathology. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102090
title: Study academic resilience with tests of both main and interaction effects embedded in a full 2×2 risk-by-resilience-factor design
description: The paper's central methodological recommendation is that analyses of resilience in LD research must include "a statistical test of main and interaction effects" and "the full 2 × 2 conceptual matrix of presence/absence of a suspected resilience factor and high/low risk groups" (HR+, HR−, LR+, LR−) to determine gap-maintaining versus gap-closing effects. Without the low-risk group divided by factor presence, interactions cannot be tested and promotive versus protective status cannot be determined.
requirements: Sufficient numbers of individuals in the lower-risk/non-LD group both with and without the resilience factor of interest when applying the matrix to pre-existing datasets
Careful investigation and plotting of interaction forms, since a significant interaction is not necessarily protective
constraints: The matrix can be applied categorically or dimensionally, with risk status and resilience factor entered as continuous main effects and interaction terms
target_learners: children at risk for learning disabilities
target_learning_goals: identifying promotive and protective factors for academic outcomes
examples: Slomowitz et al. (2021) used dimensional measurement of risk and resilience factors with a categorical follow-up of the interaction to show vocabulary was promotive but not protective
key_sources: Slomowitz R. F., Narayan A. J., & McGrath L. M. (2025). Resilience research in learning disabilities: Guiding principles from developmental psychopathology. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102090

article_title: Feedback complexities interact with prior knowledge
citation: Fynn Töllner, Poldi Kuhl, Michael Besser. (2026). Feedback complexities interact with prior knowledge. Learning and Instruction 105 (2026) 102413. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2026.102413
title: Provide elaborated feedback, especially conceptual feedback, to learners with low prior knowledge
description: The article recommends that teachers give elaborated feedback and, for struggling learners, base it on conceptual knowledge, because conceptual feedback nearly nullified the effect of prior knowledge on achievement in their RCT. As the authors put it, "especially those learners who perform poorly in class should receive teacher feedback based on conceptual knowledge." This addresses heterogeneity by reducing achievement differences between low- and high-prior-knowledge students.
requirements: Feedback must be elaborated with conceptual knowledge explaining why the procedure works, e.g. visualized fraction representations
constraints: Transferability to other subjects and contexts is unknown per the article's limitations; the study was underpowered
target_learners: seventh-grade secondary mathematics students, especially those with low prior knowledge
target_learning_goals: fraction addition; conceptual and procedural knowledge of adding fractions
examples: In the study, students in the conceptual feedback group received illustrated explanations of why fraction addition works after incorrect answers, and low-prior-knowledge students in this group reached posttest scores similar to their more knowledgeable peers.
key_sources: Fynn Töllner, Poldi Kuhl, Michael Besser. (2026). Feedback complexities interact with prior knowledge. Learning and Instruction 105 (2026) 102413. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2026.102413

article_title: It's all a matter of expectancy: How expectancies about task execution perspective influence learning through video modeling examples
citation: de Jonge, T. H. S., de Koning, B. B., & van Wermeskerken, M. (2026). It's all a matter of expectancy: How expectancies about task execution perspective influence learning through video modeling examples. Learning and Instruction, 105, 102422. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2026.102422
title: Expectation Alignment Hypothesis (EAH)
description: The Expectation Alignment Hypothesis is the article's proposed dynamic account of the perspective effect: "the benefit of a particular recording angle depends on how well it aligns with the viewer's expectations about the task angle". When recording angle and expected task angle mismatch, viewers must perform mental transformations (mental rotation or perspective taking) during observation, which "induce a significant degree of cognitive load" and reduce working memory available for encoding, impairing performance. The experiment supported the EAH: alignment effects on performance and load were larger than the recording-angle main effect.
requirements: The learner holds (or is induced to hold) an expectation about the angle from which the task will be performed, which can align or misalign with the recording angle
constraints: The article notes the ERH and EAH may both operate simultaneously and hold to varying degrees, with potentially additive effects
target_learners: undergraduate psychology students learning procedural tasks from video modeling examples
target_learning_goals: procedural knowledge and task performance in circuit-board assembly from video modeling examples
examples: The experiment oriented a physical circuit next to the monitor and told participants they would perform the task from that orientation, manipulating expected angle independently of recording angle
key_sources: de Jonge, T. H. S., de Koning, B. B., & van Wermeskerken, M. (2026). It's all a matter of expectancy: How expectancies about task execution perspective influence learning through video modeling examples. Learning and Instruction, 105, 102422. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2026.102422

article_title: The process of tool innovation in young children: An attempt to bridge the Gestalt and the perception-action theories
citation: Guo, J.; Bai, H.; Long, X.; Su, X.; Pang, W. (2025). The process of tool innovation in young children: An attempt to bridge the Gestalt and the perception-action theories. Learning and Instruction, 99, article 102182. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102182
title: Task difficulty level as a mechanism bridging the Gestalt and perception-action theories of tool innovation
description: The article proposes that the Gestalt and perception-action theories differ in their assumptions about initial problem representations — a fixed, complete representation requiring sudden reconstruction versus a partial representation refined through exploratory interaction. The authors conjecture that "the Gestalt theory better explains the process of problems with lower task difficulty level" while "the perception-action theory better explains the process of problems with higher task difficulty level", because harder situations may overwhelm full representation. Task difficulty thus serves as the moderating mechanism reconciling the two accounts, tested via fixation and flexibility effects across tasks of varied difficulty.
requirements: Tasks spanning a range of difficulty levels relative to the sample, with difficulty indexed by success rate
Process measures coding fixation (repeating the same unsuccessful actions) and flexibility (shifting to novel actions)
constraints: Difficulty level is relative to the sample used; it was determined post-hoc rather than pre-determined
The flexibility-by-difficulty moderation held for ideal manipulation but not task success
target_learning_goals: tool innovation
creative problem solving
examples: The study tested the conjecture by coding 139 children's exploration processes across nine tasks of varied difficulty and examining difficulty-moderated fixation and flexibility effects in multilevel logistic regressions.
key_sources: Guo, J.; Bai, H.; Long, X.; Su, X.; Pang, W. (2025). The process of tool innovation in young children: An attempt to bridge the Gestalt and the perception-action theories. Learning and Instruction, 99, article 102182. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102182

article_title: The process of tool innovation in young children: An attempt to bridge the Gestalt and the perception-action theories
citation: Guo, J.; Bai, H.; Long, X.; Su, X.; Pang, W. (2025). The process of tool innovation in young children: An attempt to bridge the Gestalt and the perception-action theories. Learning and Instruction, 99, article 102182. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102182
title: Nine tool innovation tasks spanning three paradigms and three tool types
description: A validated task battery for studying tool innovation in 3- to 6-year-olds: "nine tasks spanning three tool innovation test paradigms (Hook task, Push task, and Cling task) and three types of tools (add, subtract, and reshape)". Each task has one intended manipulation and a warm-up with exercise materials manipulable in the same way. The new Cling Task requires retrieving a reward from an upstanding tube through clinging. Performance is coded as task success and ideal manipulation, and the exploration process is coded for fixation and flexibility behaviors.
requirements: A warm-up session familiarizing children with the manipulative actions
Prompts such as "please try another way" when children repeatedly use an ineffective strategy
Two trained coders per child for reliability
constraints: The Cling-subtract task showed a low factor loading (0.17) on task success and is subject to further improvement
Task order was only partially counterbalanced
target_learning_goals: tool innovation
creativity
problem solving
examples: Children were tested individually in kindertartens in two 20–30 minute sessions; inter-coder ICCs ranged from 0.69 (fixation) to 1.00 (task success).
key_sources: Guo, J.; Bai, H.; Long, X.; Su, X.; Pang, W. (2025). The process of tool innovation in young children: An attempt to bridge the Gestalt and the perception-action theories. Learning and Instruction, 99, article 102182. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102182

article_title: COVID-19: A cross-national analysis with PISA data
citation: Giang Pham, Franziska Maria Locher, Dimitra Kolovou, Eliane Arnold. (2026). COVID-19: A cross-national analysis with PISA data. Learning and Instruction 105 (2026) 102366. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2026.102366
title: Dynamic Model of Educational Effectiveness as framework for pandemic-era teaching and learning conditions
description: The study draws on the Dynamic Model of Educational Effectiveness (DMEE; Creemers & Kyriakides, 2008), which "provides a general framework for exploring interactions among factors operating at four levels (student, teacher/classroom, school, and system/context)". The authors chose it because it emphasises the system level, which shaped pandemic schooling through measures such as closure duration, and because it has been used in cross-national PISA research. Pandemic-specific distance-learning elements were supplemented from related distance-education models.
requirements: Applicable when system-level policy factors (e.g. school-closure duration) are measured alongside classroom- and student-level conditions
constraints: The article notes new distance-learning elements gained importance during the pandemic that are not explicitly defined in the DMEE
target_learning_goals: Sustaining student performance in mathematics, reading, and science during irregular schooling
examples: The authors operationalised system-level conditions via school-closure and stringency indices and teacher/classroom and student conditions via the PISA 2022 Global Crises Module
key_sources: Giang Pham, Franziska Maria Locher, Dimitra Kolovou, Eliane Arnold. (2026). COVID-19: A cross-national analysis with PISA data. Learning and Instruction 105 (2026) 102366. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2026.102366

article_title: COVID-19: A cross-national analysis with PISA data
citation: Giang Pham, Franziska Maria Locher, Dimitra Kolovou, Eliane Arnold. (2026). COVID-19: A cross-national analysis with PISA data. Learning and Instruction 105 (2026) 102366. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2026.102366
title: PISA 2022 Global Crises Module (GCM) student questionnaire
description: The PISA 2022 Global Crises Module was administered to students to measure teaching and learning conditions during school closures. "The student GCM comprised 62 items grouped into 11 questions" (Bertling et al., 2020). The study used items ST348–ST354 covering school actions to sustain learning, digital devices, learning resources, self-directed learning problems, family support, and feelings about learning at home, with country-level intraclass correlations ranging from .02 to .17.
requirements: Country-level aggregation of student responses; rescaled ESCS indices for trend analyses across PISA cycles
constraints: Country-level ICCs were low (M = .06), and the article notes small differences between countries may attain statistical significance due to small standard errors
target_learning_goals: Measuring teaching and learning conditions for sustaining learning during COVID-19 school closures
examples: Items ST348–ST354 with response options from Never to Every day or almost every day, and Strongly disagree to Strongly agree
key_sources: Giang Pham, Franziska Maria Locher, Dimitra Kolovou, Eliane Arnold. (2026). COVID-19: A cross-national analysis with PISA data. Learning and Instruction 105 (2026) 102366. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2026.102366

article_title: Better together: Simultaneous presentation of speech and gesture in math instruction supports generalization and retention
citation: Congdon Eliza L., Novack Miriam A., Brooks Neon, Hemani-Lopez Naureen, O'Keefe Lucy, Goldin-Meadow Susan. (2017). Better together: Simultaneous presentation of speech and gesture in math instruction supports generalization and retention. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2017.03.005
title: Simultaneity account of gesture's effect on learning: temporal synchrony between speech and gesture enables integration of complementary messages
description: The article advances an account in which instructor gesture promotes durable, generalizable learning because it conveys a complementary message simultaneously with speech, allowing learners to integrate two strategies across modalities. The authors write that "speech and gesture appeared to encourage learners to simultaneously attend to and integrate ideas conveyed in the two modalities and thus create long-lasting and flexible new concepts." This account is framed within dual-channel theories of multimedia learning and the Contiguity Principle, and is contrasted with an embodied-cognition account in which gesture's bodily origin alone would suffice. The experiment supports the simultaneity account because sequential cross-modal presentation conferred no advantage over speech alone.
requirements: The two channels must carry different but complementary strategies (a conceptual principle in speech and a procedural algorithm in gesture), as in the EQ and AS strategies used here
The gesture must be interpretable within the context provided by concurrent speech
constraints: The account concerns instructor-produced gesture watched by learners; the authors note it may not extend to self-produced gesture
The design did not test gesture-first sequencing or algorithm-in-speech/principle-in-gesture combinations
target_learning_goals: conceptual and procedural understanding of mathematical equivalence
generalization to novel problem formats
retention over delays
examples: Third graders solved missing-addend problems (e.g., 4+3+7=__+7) after instruction pairing the Equalizer principle in speech with the Add-Subtract algorithm in gesture, simultaneously or sequentially
key_sources: Congdon Eliza L., Novack Miriam A., Brooks Neon, Hemani-Lopez Naureen, O'Keefe Lucy, Goldin-Meadow Susan. (2017). Better together: Simultaneous presentation of speech and gesture in math instruction supports generalization and retention. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2017.03.005

article_title: Better together: Simultaneous presentation of speech and gesture in math instruction supports generalization and retention
citation: Congdon Eliza L., Novack Miriam A., Brooks Neon, Hemani-Lopez Naureen, O'Keefe Lucy, Goldin-Meadow Susan. (2017). Better together: Simultaneous presentation of speech and gesture in math instruction supports generalization and retention. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2017.03.005
title: Present complementary problem-solving strategies simultaneously in speech and gesture rather than sequentially
description: When teaching a concept paired with a complementary procedure, deliver the conceptual strategy in speech while simultaneously performing the procedural strategy in gesture, rather than presenting the two messages one after the other. The article concludes that "for an instructor's gesture to facilitate deep learning, generalization, and retention over time, it must be presented simultaneously with speech." In the supporting experiment, only simultaneous presentation produced delayed retention and generalization advantages; sequential cross-modal presentation was no better than speech alone.
requirements: The gesture must convey a strategy complementary to, not redundant with, the spoken strategy
Both strategies must be presented within a single presentation of the problem, without a break
constraints: Sequential speech-then-gesture presentation may cause children to discount the gestured information as meaningless movement
The article did not test gesture-first sequencing, which prior work it cites suggests might sometimes help learners with high prior knowledge
target_learners: learners naive to the taught material
target_learning_goals: retention of taught procedures over days and weeks
generalization to novel problem formats
integration of conceptual and procedural strategies
examples: In the experiment, children in the simultaneous condition heard the Equalizer explanation while watching Add-Subtract hand movements on the same equation, and showed the highest delayed performance (e.g., .64 mean proportion correct on generalization problems at four weeks)
key_sources: Congdon Eliza L., Novack Miriam A., Brooks Neon, Hemani-Lopez Naureen, O'Keefe Lucy, Goldin-Meadow Susan. (2017). Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2017.03.005

article_title: Teachers’ immigration attitudes and students’ performance
citation: Anatolia Batruch, Nicolas Sommet, Eva G.T. Green. (2026). Teachers' immigration attitudes and students' performance. Learning and Instruction 102 (2026) 102303. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102303
title: Aggregated teachers' explicit immigration attitudes as an exogenous institutional indicator of school diversity climate (normative climate / structural bias account)
description: The article proposes measuring school diversity climates through teachers' immigration attitudes aggregated at the school level, rather than through students' perceptions. It argues this captures "exclusionary versus inclusionary 'normative climates'" and systemic or structural bias, because aggregation reflects "the prevalence of teachers' biases within schools but also the broader institutional norms that foster or legitimize them." The account holds that biases are embedded in institutional climates that shape outcomes for marginalized students, and that collective teacher attitudes act as social environmental cues of socioecological inclusion.
requirements: Requires teachers' explicit immigration attitudes to be measured and aggregated within schools; the article reports ICC(1) = 0.30 and ICC(2) = 0.91 supporting aggregation
constraints: Self-reports may still reflect social desirability; the study is cross-sectional and limited to public schools in OECD countries
target_learning_goals: academic achievement in science, mathematics, and reading
academic integration of immigrant students
examples: The authors aggregated four teacher questionnaire items on immigrant rights and opportunities (α = .84) into a school-level score ranging from exclusionary to inclusionary climate
key_sources: Anatolia Batruch, Nicolas Sommet, Eva G.T. Green. (2026). Teachers' immigration attitudes and students' performance. Learning and Instruction 102 (2026) 102303. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102303

article_title: Teachers’ immigration attitudes and students’ performance
citation: Anatolia Batruch, Nicolas Sommet, Eva G.T. Green. (2026). Teachers' immigration attitudes and students' performance. Learning and Instruction 102 (2026) 102303. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102303
title: Foster inclusionary school diversity climates to promote the academic integration of first-generation immigrant students
description: The article's central design recommendation is that schools should cultivate inclusionary diversity climates—reflected in teachers' pro-immigration attitudes—because such climates are associated with higher first-generation immigrant students' performance and narrower achievement gaps. It states that "fostering inclusionary school climates may meaningfully improve first-generation students' achievement" given the observed effect sizes, and that interventions can target students, teachers, or structural features like leadership and policy, with results pointing especially to teacher-focused efforts.
requirements: Requires addressing teachers' explicit attitudes toward immigrant rights and opportunities, e.g., through professional development that reduces prejudice and builds multicultural competencies
constraints: The cross-sectional design limits causal inference; generalizability is constrained to public schools in OECD countries
target_learning_goals: academic achievement
reducing achievement disparities between immigrant and non-immigrant students
examples: In the PISA 2018 data, first-generation students in more inclusionary schools scored up to 29.18 points higher in reading than in more exclusionary schools
key_sources: Anatolia Batruch, Nicolas Sommet, Eva G.T. Green. (2026). Teachers' immigration attitudes and students' performance. Learning and Instruction 102 (2026) 102303. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102303

article_title: Civic Education Outcomes After Emergency Lockdowns: International Evidence from the COVID-19 Pandemic
citation: Kennedy, A. I., Mejía-Rodríguez, A. M., Strietholt, R. (2026). Civic Education Outcomes After Emergency Lockdowns: International Evidence from the COVID-19 Pandemic. Preprint submitted to Learning and Instruction. https://github.com/OxCGRT/covid-policy-dataset
title: Bronfenbrenner's ecological systems theory as a framework for civic education outcomes
description: The article uses Bronfenbrenner's ecological systems theory to frame how civic education outcomes are shaped beyond formal schooling. It states the theory "provides a valuable framework for understanding civic education, emphasizing how an individual's development is shaped by interactions across multiple environments". The model nests microsystem, mesosystem, exosystem, macrosystem, and chronosystem around the individual student, with the chronosystem capturing historical events such as the COVID-19 pandemic. The authors use it to justify hypothesizing that lockdown measures influenced civic knowledge, trust, and expected participation through home, parental, societal, and event-related layers.
requirements: Civic learning is understood as occurring across multiple nested environments, not only within educational institutions
constraints: The article applies the framework to grade 8 students' civic outcomes in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic
target_learning_goals: Civic knowledge
Trust in civic institutions
Expected civic participation
examples: The authors hypothesize that students confined to the microsystem of their home may have developed decreased trust in institutions and increased propensity for protest, shaped by parents, significant adults, and media
key_sources: Kennedy, A. I., Mejía-Rodríguez, A. M., Strietholt, R. (2026). Civic Education Outcomes After Emergency Lockdowns: International Evidence from the COVID-19 Pandemic. Preprint submitted to Learning and Instruction. https://github.com/OxCGRT/covid-policy-dataset

article_title: Civic Education Outcomes After Emergency Lockdowns: International Evidence from the COVID-19 Pandemic
citation: Kennedy, A. I., Mejía-Rodríguez, A. M., Strietholt, R. (2026). Civic Education Outcomes After Emergency Lockdowns: International Evidence from the COVID-19 Pandemic. Preprint submitted to Learning and Instruction. https://github.com/OxCGRT/covid-policy-dataset
title: OxCGRT stringency index and weighted school-closure duration measures
description: The study draws two explanatory measures from the Oxford COVID-19 Government Response Tracker (OxCGRT), a publicly available dataset collecting daily information on pandemic policy measures. The stringency index is described as "a continuous scale ranging from 0 (none of these measures are in place) to 100 (all policy measures are in place affecting the largest portion of the population possible)", averaged from January 2020 to February 2022. School-closure duration is a weighted sum of required closure days (weights 0 to 1 by geographic and sectoral scope), excluding weekends and academic holidays. These measures are combined with ICCS civic outcome scales in country-fixed-effects regressions.
requirements: Daily policy coding from OxCGRT combined with ICCS data for countries participating in both the 2016 and 2022 cycles
constraints: The two measures are positively correlated (r = 0.7) and are not used together in the same model due to multicollinearity
For the benchmarking participant (Germany's North Rhine-Westphalia), lockdown policies are measured at the national level rather than regional
target_learning_goals: Civic knowledge
Trust in civic institutions
Expected civic participation
examples: Sensitivity analyses compared alternative measures including the standard deviation of the stringency index, days above 50, a 'Fully closed' measure, and UIS-based closure durations (r = 0.89 with OxCGRT measures)

article_title: On the challenges of investigating lasting learning: A commentary
citation: Katharina Scheiter, Alexander Renkl. (2026). On the challenges of investigating lasting learning: A commentary. Learning and Instruction 105 (2026) 102417. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2026.102417
title: Differentiated conception of lasting learning as heterogeneous phenomenon types
description: The commentary proposes that a theory of lasting learning must begin with an elaborated description of the phenomenon's variants, because "lasting learning is not a homogeneous, uniform phenomenon". It sketches two contrasting cases: topics treated once in school, such as a classical literature piece belonging to general cultural knowledge, and core concepts or principles of a discipline that recur across years, such as energy in physics. The two cases differ in learning goals, instructional demands (e.g., coherence over long periods, spiral curriculum, connectable initial teaching), and appropriate assessment, so a theory may either cover multiple variants or restrict its scope to a clearly described selected type.
requirements: An elaborated description of the types of phenomena under focus, consistent with all major variants to be explained
Alignment of learning goals, instructional methods, and assessment, following the constructive alignment triangle
constraints: The commentary does not propose a specific type of assessment; it pleads for a deliberate decision aligned to goals and methods
A first-step theory may be restricted to selected types of lasting learning
target_learners: school students across subjects and grade levels
target_learning_goals: retention and flexible use of knowledge over long periods
mastery of core concepts and principles of a discipline
examples: The commentary contrasts remembering basic aspects of a literature piece such as Faust I or Romeo and Juliet with re-occurring core concepts like energy in physics or natural selection in biology

article_title: On the challenges of investigating lasting learning: A commentary
citation: Katharina Scheiter, Alexander Renkl. (2026). On the challenges of investigating lasting learning: A commentary. Learning and Instruction 105 (2026) 102417. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2026.102417
title: Treat prior knowledge as a resource for learning rather than a nuisance variable when evaluating instructional effects
description: The commentary argues that research aiming to inform educational practice should adopt a multidimensional stance on ecological validity, including "treating prior knowledge as a resource for learning rather than a variable to be controlled for when evaluating instructional effects". In real-world scenarios prior knowledge facilitates acquisition of novel content, and instructional techniques activate it, whereas most lab studies minimize or statistically control it. Only two special-issue studies explicitly tested whether instructional approaches had similar effects at different prior-knowledge levels, and both found interactions.
requirements: Studies must measure prior knowledge and analyze its role, e.g., by testing interactions between instructional approach and prior knowledge
constraints: Fully integrating prior knowledge into school-curriculum studies reduces possibilities for far-reaching experimental control
target_learners: school and university students with varying prior knowledge
target_learning_goals: acquisition of novel declarative and procedural knowledge built on existing knowledge
examples: Klimovich and Richter used simple-slope analyses showing interleaving helped high and average prior-knowledge students but not low ones; Ruitenburg et al. tested approach-by-prior-knowledge interactions

citation: Becker, Michael; Neumann, Marko. (2016). Context-related changes in academic self concept development. On the long-term persistence of big-fish-little-pond effects. Learning and instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2016.06.003
title: Big-Fish-Little-Pond Effect (BFLPE) framework of contextual influences on academic self-concept
description: The BFLPE framework holds that academic self-concept develops not only from individual factors but also from contextual characteristics of the learning environment, especially the abilities of classmates. As the article states, "Besides individual factors, contextual characteristics play an important role in driving changes in self-perception", and "The abilities of classmates are especially important". The framework predicts that equally able students form lower ASCs in higher-achieving classrooms, and the article extends it by testing whether the effect persists across consecutive school contexts.
requirements: Contextual information about classmates' achievement in each school context the student passes through
constraints: The article's evidence covers students transitioning from elementary to secondary school; the prior-context effect faded within one year
target_learning_goals: academic self-concept development
examples: The study drew on a sample of fourth graders who transitioned from elementary school to secondary school, using contextual information from both settings.

title: When interpreting students' academic self-concept, account for the achievement level of the classroom context
description: Because classroom ability composition shapes academic self-concept, educators and researchers interpreting a student's ASC should consider the achievement level of the surrounding classroom. The article shows that "contextual characteristics play an important role in driving changes in self-perception" and that equally able students report different ASCs depending on classroom achievement. It also cautions that contextual effects can change across school transitions, so the current context matters most.
requirements: Knowledge of the achievement composition of the student's current classroom
constraints: The elementary-school context's influence was no longer discernible after one year in secondary school, so prior-context information has limited lasting value
target_learning_goals: accurate interpretation of academic self-concept
supporting healthy academic self-concept
examples: The longitudinal study followed fourth graders through the elementary-to-secondary transition, tracking how BFLPEs from each context affected their ASCs over time.

citation: Mielicki, M. K., Kacinik, N. A., & Wiley, J. (2017). Bilingualism and symbolic abstraction: Implications for algebra learning. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2017.03.002
title: Metalinguistic awareness account of the bilingual advantage in symbolic abstraction
description: The article proposes that prolonged bilingual experience may improve the ability to separate symbols from their referents, a form of metalinguistic awareness that supports symbolic abstraction in algebra. Building on Vygotsky's suggestion that expressing a thought in different languages lets one "separate labels from their referents", the authors argue bilinguals may be "better able to attend tothemeaningofthesymbolsthanmonolinguals". The account is offered as an interpretation of the hard-item advantage, alongside the alternative that bilinguals adapt faster to novel tasks.

constraints: The article presents this as an interpretation consistent with its results, not a directly tested mechanism
