This positions reduced achievement as a key mechanism linking disorderly classrooms to lower competence self-perceptions, higher test anxiety, and lower engagement.

article_title: Differentiated instruction in primary mathematics: Effects of teacher professional development on student achievement
citation: Prast, E. J., Van de Weijer-Bergsma, E., Kroesbergen, E. H., & Van Luit, J. E. H. (2018). Differentiated instruction in primary mathematics: Effects of teacher professional development on student achievement. Learning and Instruction, 54, 22-34. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2018.01.009
title: The cycle of differentiation: a five-step expert-consensus model for differentiating primary mathematics instruction
description: The cycle of differentiation is the GROW project's expert-consensus model of what teachers should do to implement differentiation in daily mathematics practice. It comprises five steps: identification of educational needs (including diagnostic interviews and analysis of daily work), setting differentiated goals that are challenging but realistic, differentiated instruction (broad whole-class instruction, tailored subgroup instruction, individual adaptations), differentiated practice (quantitatively and qualitatively, including compacting and enriching material for high achievers), and evaluation of progress and process, which feeds back into needs identification. Students work in flexible within-class achievement groups part of the time and can switch groups as needs change.
requirements: Teachers need extensive subject matter knowledge as well as advanced diagnostic, didactical, pedagogical, and classroom management skills
Ongoing refined diagnostic measures beyond achievement tests to determine qualitative educational needs
Flexible within-class grouping so students can switch groups based on changes in educational needs
constraints: The article states the cycle represents best practice recommended by experts based on experiential knowledge, and quantitative empirical evidence proving differentiation has positive effects was scarce at the time of design
target_learners: Primary school students in grades 1-6 of diverse achievement levels
target_learning_goals: Mathematics achievement and growth
Meeting diverse educational needs in primary mathematics
examples: The PD programme taught teachers the cycle of differentiation and strategies for each step over ten three-hour team meetings spread across the schoolyear

title: GROW teacher professional development programme for differentiated mathematics instruction
description: The GROW PD programme is a multi-component, year-long professional development intervention designed following characteristics of effective teacher PD from the literature. It consisted of three main components: PD for all teachers (ten three-hour team meetings across the schoolyear, six led by educational consultants and four by school-based project coaches, using interactive lectures, practical exercises, and adapted Lesson Study), additional training for internal project coaches (five regional meetings, coaching and lesson-observation duties, follow-up and train-the-trainer packages), and active involvement of the principal (intake meetings, intervision meetings, a school-level implementation plan). Materials were organised as a toolbox so schools could adapt the focus to their needs.

Active principal involvement and administrative support
Teachers attend team meetings (certificate required presence at least eight out of ten)
Teachers read selected literature and apply differentiation strategies in their lessons
constraints: The programme balanced specification with adaptation to school needs; the cycle of differentiation was the common core while schools determined their own focus in consultation with the consultant

Student mathematics achievement growth
examples: In Year 1, 81.0% of Cohort 1 teachers obtained their certificate; in Year 2, 90% of Cohort 2 teachers did

title: Use flexible within-class ability grouping coupled with instructional adaptation to protect low-achieving students from negative grouping effects
description: The article argues that negative effects of ability grouping for low-achieving students, ascribed to stigmatization and lower educational quality in low-ability groups, can be prevented. Negative stigma may be overcome by ensuring subgroups are within-class and flexible and by promoting a growth mindset, communicating additional instruction as an opportunity to learn rather than a sign of fixed low ability. When grouping is used to adapt education to the specific needs of students in the groups, it may enhance rather than reduce educational quality for low achievers because instruction is better attuned to their needs.
requirements: Subgroups must be within-class and flexible
Participation in additional instruction should be communicated as an opportunity to learn, not as a sign of fixed low ability
Instruction and practice must actually be adapted to the educational needs of the different ability groups
constraints: Reviews found slight negative effects of within-class ability grouping in primary school across three studies in which variations in instructional treatment were not explicitly described
target_learners: Primary school students of low, average and high achievement levels
target_learning_goals: Mathematics achievement growth for all achievement groups, including low-achieving students
examples: The GROW study used flexible within-class achievement groups (typically low-, average-, and high-achieving) that students could switch between based on changes in educational needs

citation: David W. Putwain, Andrea Mallaburn, Hanna Gaspard. (2026). Student perceptions of teacher messages about the value of science in the classroom. Learning and Instruction 104 (2026) 102365. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2026.102365
title: Situated Expectancy Value Theory (SEVT)
description: Situated Expectancy Value Theory is described as "an influential theory of educational achievement and choice that combines dynamic relations between contextually sensitive developmental and socio-cultural influences with socio-cognitive task appraisals." Task appraisals comprise expectancy of success, subjective task values (intrinsic, attainment, utility), and cost. The study uses SEVT to model perceived teacher value messages as proximal socio-cultural classroom cues shaping motivational beliefs, which in turn predict achievement and aspirations, with relations hypothesized as recursive rather than unidirectional.
requirements: Relations between motivational beliefs, achievement, and choices are modeled as recursive, requiring longitudinal data with autoregressive controls
constraints: The study focused on utility value and effort cost as the appraisals most responsive to teacher value messages, since intrinsic and attainment value are more task-intrinsic

target_learning_goals: science achievement
science career and study aspirations
motivational beliefs about science

Training should therefore target both the processing subphase (noticing discrepancies) and the use subphase (time on the essay, higher order comments, incremental correction, final proofreading).

title: Coding scheme of young learners’ metacognitive SRL activities with domain-general and task-specific sublevel categories
description: A think-aloud coding scheme for metacognitive SRL activities in lower secondary students, developed from theory and data using Bannert’s (2007) and van der Stel and Veenman’s (2014) schemes as a basis. citation: Goetz, T., Bieleke, M., Gogol, K., van Tartwijk, J., Mainhard, T., Lipnevich, A. A., & Pekrun, R. (2021). title: Control-value theory applied to student-teacher relationships and emotions
description: Control-value theory (CVT; Pekrun, 2006) is a comprehensive account of the antecedents and effects of achievement emotions that the article uses to motivate reciprocal hypotheses. The article operationalizes relationship quality as interpersonal closeness, a social facet of the learning environment whose effects on emotions are mediated by control and value appraisals.

constraints: The article states CVT does not yield specific assumptions about differences in associations across discrete emotions, making hypotheses about emotion-specific strengths difficult to formulate

examples: In the experiment, dyads and individuals worked on computer lab-based simulations under adaptive or static feedback conditions

article_title: A short teacher-led intervention using direct instruction enhances 5th graders' purposeful reading skills
citation: Potocki, A., Ayroles, J., & Rouet, J.-F. (2023). A short teacher-led intervention using direct instruction enhances 5th graders' purposeful reading skills. Learning and Instruction, 86, 101781. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2023.101781
title: MD-TRACE model of purposeful reading
description: MD-TRACE (Rouet & Britt, 2011) describes purposeful reading as a cyclical sequence of steps: the reader builds a task model from the instruction, searches for relevant information, selectively processes and integrates it into a task product, and checks the product against the question's requirements, recycling if needed. The article highlights "the role of goal formation and monitoring, and the cyclical nature of the activity, with several recycling loops corresponding to metacognitive processes". The training program's five modules were mapped onto the model's four steps plus an integrative module.
requirements: Readers must understand task instructions to build an appropriate task model, which the article identifies as key to reading outcomes
target_learning_goals: purposeful reading: constructing task models, locating, extracting and integrating information, and evaluating answers
examples: The Purposeful Reading Training Program devoted its first four modules to Steps 1-4 of MD-TRACE and a final module to coordinating all steps
key_sources: Potocki, A., Ayroles, J., & Rouet, J.-F. (2023). A short teacher-led intervention using direct instruction enhances 5th graders' purposeful reading skills. Learning and Instruction, 86, 101781. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2023.101781

article_title: A short teacher-led intervention using direct instruction enhances 5th graders' purposeful reading skills
citation: Potocki, A., Ayroles, J., & Rouet, J.-F. (2023). A short teacher-led intervention using direct instruction enhances 5th graders' purposeful reading skills. Learning and Instruction, 86, 101781. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2023.101781
title: Five-module direct instruction program for purposeful reading strategies
description: The Purposeful Reading Training Program comprised five modules, each with two 45-minute workshops pairing a student workbook and a teacher guide. Each workshop followed explicit instruction phases: "presentation of the learning objective", "modelling", "guided practice" in pairs with corrective feedback, "individual practice", and a final "objectification phase" in which students make explicit the essential skills and knowledge to be retained. The first four modules targeted the MD-TRACE steps and the last coordinated them.
requirements: Teachers received a one-day training session and materials ahead of time, with ongoing researcher-teacher communication during implementation
constraints: Some teachers reported the workshops were sometimes too dense and difficult to carry out in 45 minutes only
target_learning_goals: declarative and procedural knowledge of purposeful reading strategies: question analysis, using textual cues, extracting and integrating information, constructing and checking answers
examples: Module tasks included underlining question keywords, choosing titles where answers were likely found, and assessing proposed answers for relevance and sufficiency

article_title: Levels of comprehension of scientific prose: the role of text variables
citation: Vidal-Abarca, E., & Sanjosé, V. (1998). Levels of comprehension of scientific prose: The role of text variables. Learning and Instruction, 8(3), 215-233. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0959475297000200
title: Textbase and situation model: two levels of comprehension that textual changes affect differently
description: The article adopts van Dijk and Kintsch's (1983) distinction between comprehension levels: the textbase, the semantic and rhetorical relationships encoded from the text, and the situation model, a deeper level where "theinformationprovidedbythetext iselaboratedfrompriorknowledgeandisintegratedintoit". The article uses this framework to predict that coherence changes mainly affect the textbase (main ideas, recall) while deep problem solving requires a situation model built by integrating text information with background knowledge, which the authors argue occurs only when readers first form good textbases.
requirements: Deep comprehension requires text information to be integrated with previously assimilated knowledge, so good textbase formation is described as a necessary prior stage
constraints: The article notes studies showing good situation models with poor textbases, but argues those used short, familiar paragraphs and recognition tasks unlike normal scientific text reading
target_learners: tenth-grade high school students reading unfamiliar scientific texts
target_learning_goals: deep comprehension of scientific prose enabling problem solving in novel contexts
examples: Four text versions manipulated coherence and linking changes separately and in tandem to test level-specific predictions
key_sources: Vidal-Abarca, E., & Sanjosé, V. (1998). Levels of comprehension of scientific prose: The role of text variables. Learning and Instruction, 8(3), 215-233. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0959475297000200

article_title: Growth trajectories of self-concept and interest in mathematics and language – Individual differences and cross-domain relations
citation: Anna Widlund, Markku Niemivirta, Heta Tuominen, Johan Korhonen. (2023). Growth Trajectories of Self-Concept and Interest in Mathematics and Language – Individual Differences and Cross-Domain Relations. Preprint version 1. https://orcid.org/0000-0001-5563-5044
title: Internal/external frame of reference and dimensional comparison theory as an account of domain-specific motivational development
description: The article applies the I/E model and dimensional comparison theory to explain why students' competence perceptions and interests become increasingly differentiated across math and L1 during adolescence. Students make external (social) comparisons of their performance against other students, and internal (dimensional) comparisons of performance in one domain against another, which "sometimes leading to negative predictions between performance and competence perceptions across domains". The study's negative cross-domain correlations, especially among girls, are read as support for this framework.
requirements: Students must experience and evaluate performance in at least two comparable academic domains for dimensional comparisons to operate.
constraints: The article states it is challenging to conclude whether dimensional comparison processes cause the gender differences or are a result of already-differentiated motivational beliefs.
target_learners: adolescent students in lower secondary education (Grades 7–9)
target_learning_goals: domain-specific academic self-concept and interest in mathematics and language
examples: The study tested the theory by estimating cross-domain correlations between intercept and slope factors of math and L1 self-concept and interest, separately for boys and girls.
key_sources: Anna Widlund, Markku Niemivirta, Heta Tuominen, Johan Korhonen. (2023). Growth Trajectories of Self-Concept and Interest in Mathematics and Language – Individual Differences and Cross-Domain Relations. Preprint version 1. https://orcid.org/0000-0001-5563-5044

article_title: The longitudinal relationship between internalizing and externalizing behavioral problems with academic achievement in elementary school
citation: Kulakow, S., Mahlau, K., & Kocaj, A. (2023). The longitudinal relationship between internalizing and externalizing behavioral problems with academic achievement in elementary school. https://osf.io/cyqak/?view_only=37eade9dd7c142e88fe9bef9451c125e
title: Four theoretical models of the interplay between behavioral problems and academic achievement
description: The article organizes prior theory, based on Hinshaw (1992) as described by Chen et al. (2022), into four models of how behavior and achievement interrelate: "The adjustment erosion model", the academic incompetence model, the reciprocal model, and the shared risk model. Each specifies a different direction of influence, including third-variable common antecedents. The study tests these against cross-lagged data and finds no clear preference for any single model across domains.
requirements: Longitudinal data with repeated measures of both behavior and achievement to distinguish directional paths
constraints: The study's data gave no clear preference for any of the four models; support varied by achievement domain
target_learning_goals: academic achievement in reading, writing, and mathematics; behavioral development
examples: The study mapped domain-specific results onto the models: shared risk for reading, academic incompetence for writing, adjustment erosion and reciprocal for mathematics.
key_sources: Kulakow, S., Mahlau, K., & Kocaj, A. (2023). The longitudinal relationship between internalizing and externalizing behavioral problems with academic achievement in elementary school. https://osf.io/cyqak/?view_only=37eade9dd7c142e88fe9bef9451c125e

article_title: The longitudinal relationship between internalizing and externalizing behavioral problems with academic achievement in elementary school
citation: Kulakow, S., Mahlau, K., & Kocaj, A. (2023). The longitudinal relationship between internalizing and externalizing behavioral problems with academic achievement in elementary school. https://osf.io/cyqak/?view_only=37eade9dd7c142e88fe9bef9451c125e
title: Use classroom-level, evidence-based procedures such as the good behavior game and Daily Behavior Report Cards to prevent behavioral problems in elementary classrooms
description: The authors argue that, unlike individual case-based psychologically oriented support systems, only a few classroom-level support procedures have proven effective in school contexts. They name "the good behavior game", an interdependent group contingency procedure using playful elements to reduce classroom and behavioral disruptions, and "Daily Behavior Report Cards", in which the teacher works with the child to develop behaviors or goals for specific situations. Both are recommended as preventive measures within multi-tiered school-based support systems.
requirements: Whole-class implementation capacity (good behavior game) or teacher–child goal setting (Daily Behavior Report Cards)
constraints: The article cites effectiveness from prior reviews and meta-analyses (Flower et al., 2014; Pyle & Fabiano, 2017); this study did not test these procedures itself
target_learners: elementary school students, especially children with early behavioral problems
target_learning_goals: reducing classroom disruptions and externalizing problem behaviors; supporting adequate learning progress
examples: The authors state the good behavior game can be conducted with the entire class, and Daily Behavior Report Cards target reducing externalizing problem behaviors.

article_title: A red button does it all: A red button nudges students to close their knowledge gaps in an intelligent tutoring system
citation: Spitzer, M. W. H., Moeller, K., Richter, E., Frede, L., & Bardach, L. (2025). A red button does it all: A red button nudges students to close their knowledge gaps in an intelligent tutoring system. Learning and Instruction 99 (2025) 102181. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102181
title: Adaptive knowledge gap mechanism: repeated-error detection triggers tailored additional learning materials closed at 60% accuracy
description: The bettermarks ITS automatically detects knowledge gaps when students commit the same error repeatedly, reflecting specific misconceptions such as adding fractions with uncommon denominators. It then adaptively assigns tailored additional learning materials in a separate Knowledge gaps tab, which students work through on their own schedule. A gap counts as closed when students "achieve a minimum accuracy of 60 %" on the additional materials, at which point the red badge is removed or its count reduced. The mechanism operates alongside teacher-assigned work, so the materials are system- rather than teacher-assigned.
requirements: Students must engage with the additional learning materials in the separate tab on their own initiative, which the article notes relies on self-regulation skills and motivation.
constraints: The mechanism was studied within bettermarks, an ITS for mathematics used in grades 4 to 12; gap closure is operationalized as 60% accuracy on the assigned materials.
target_learners: Students in grades 4 to 12 learning mathematics
target_learning_goals: Closing misconception-specific knowledge gaps in mathematics
examples: When a student repeatedly errs as in 1/2 + 1/3 = 2/5, the system recognizes the misconception and assigns additional explanations and problem sets on expanding fractions.
key_sources: Spitzer, M. W. H., Moeller, K., Richter, E., Frede, L., & Bardach, L. (2025). article_title: A red button does it all: A red button nudges students to close their knowledge gaps in an intelligent tutoring system
citation: Spitzer, M. W. H., Moeller, K., Richter, E., Frede, L., & Bardach, L. (2025). A red button does it all: A red button nudges students to close their knowledge gaps in an intelligent tutoring system. Learning and Instruction 99 (2025) 102181. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102181
title: Incorporate notification badges as low-effort nudges to prompt students to engage with adaptively provided learning materials
description: Because adaptively provided additional learning materials sit in a separate tab that students may never open, ITSs can add notification badges (e.g., a small red button showing the number of open gaps) as automatic, low-effort nudges. The article argues badges "direct attention without requiring active thought" and so likely reduce extraneous cognitive load, consistent with Cognitive Load Theory, and draws on color-in-context theory for red's attention-drawing urgency. The study's natural experiment supports the badge's effectiveness at raising gap closing.
requirements: The badge must signal system-identified knowledge gaps and update (be removed or reduced) as gaps are closed.
constraints: Offering materials directly may disrupt lesson plans when all students are expected to work on the same teacher-assigned tasks; the badge approach relies on students still choosing to engage with the materials.
target_learners: Students in grades 4 to 12 learning mathematics using an ITS
target_learning_goals: Engaging with adaptively assigned additional learning materials to close knowledge gaps
examples: In bettermarks, a red notification badge on the knowledge gaps tab displayed a white digit reflecting the number of additional learning materials a student should complete.

article_title: Effects of instructional design, instructional preferences, and cognitive load on problem solving and knowledge acquisition in a computer-based office simulation
citation: Sabrina Ludwig, Andreas Rausch, Michelle Taub. (2026). Effects of instructional design, instructional preferences, and cognitive load on problem solving and knowledge acquisition in a computer-based office simulation. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102255
title: LUCA browser-based office simulation for business learning and assessment
description: LUCA is a browser-based office simulation developed as a learning and assessment environment in business contexts. It "provides learners with typical office tools such as an email client, a file system, a PDF viewer, a spreadsheet application, a calculator, a notepad, and a reduced enterprise resource planning (ERP) system". An integrated authoring environment allows developing and modifying authentic work scenarios, and questionnaires and traditional test items are implemented within it. In this study, all questionnaires, the instructional video, and the 40-min supplier selection problem-solving scenario ran inside LUCA, with log data (mouse clicks and keystrokes) collected during the scenario.
requirements: An integrated authoring environment to develop and modify authentic work scenarios for learning or assessment purposes
constraints: In the reported study, participants worked under individual observation and could not influence the order of the phases
target_learners: undergraduate business and economic education students
target_learning_goals: supplier selection and multi-attribute utility analysis in business education
domain-specific problem solving with typical office tools
examples: Participants received an email task, read two supplier offers, calculated purchase prices, evaluated suppliers in a decision table, and communicated a well-founded decision via email reply

article_title: Exploring paths of change: Analyzing teachers’ emotion regulation repertoire over time using multi-level latent profile analysis
citation: Hilger, K. J. E., Scheibe, S., Frenzel, A. C., Grund, S., & Keller, M. M. (2025). Exploring paths of change: Analyzing teachers’ emotion regulation repertoire over time using multi-level latent profile analysis. Learning and Instruction, 101, Article 102234. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102234
title: Person-level emotion regulation repertoire profiles as an organizing framework for teachers' combined strategy use
description: The article organizes teachers' emotion regulation not as isolated strategies but as person-level profiles combining multiple strategies. Daily-diary assessments covered 12 ER strategies, including "acceptance, positive reappraisal, social support, situation modification, situation selection, expressive suppression, experience suppression, distraction, acting-out, self-blame, rumination, substance use". Multilevel latent profile analysis identified profiles "at the person level", yielding five profiles whose members differ in the specific combination of strategies, which the article then links to job experience and occupational well-being.
requirements: Daily-diary measurement of multiple ER strategies at the daily level across at least two measurement bursts
Multilevel latent profile analysis applied to identify ER profiles at the person level
constraints: Profiles were identified in German primary and secondary school teachers across two bursts spaced six months apart
target_learning_goals: Regulation of negative emotions in teaching
Occupational well-being of teachers
examples: The study assessed 12 ER strategies daily in two bursts and derived five profiles, three common and two unique to the bursts

description: This instrument is the study's measurement design: daily-diary assessments of 12 emotion regulation strategies administered at two time points in a measurement-burst design. The strategies assessed are "acceptance, positive reappraisal, social support, situation modification, situation selection, expressive suppression, experience suppression, distraction, acting-out, self-blame, rumination, substance use". It was administered to German primary and secondary school teachers, with NBurst1 = 268 and NBurst2 = 164, and its data fed the multilevel latent profile analyses.

constraints: Sampled German primary and secondary school teachers

article_title: Boosting debiasing: Impact of repeated training on reasoning
citation: Nina Franiatte, Esther Boissin, Alexandra Delmas, Wim De Neys. (2024). Boosting Debiasing: Impact of Repeated Training on Reasoning. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2023.101845
title: Repeat debiasing training sessions to further boost sound intuiting beyond a single-shot intervention
description: A repeated debias training approach schedules multiple short explanation-based training sessions on classic reasoning tasks rather than a single session. The article's Studies 1 and 2 show the first session lets most trained reasoners answer correctly already at the intuitive stage, and repetition adds further gains: the second session lifted final accuracy by a further 11.2 points, and the authors present the results "as a proof-of-principle for a repeated debias training approach."
requirements: Training uses brief plain-English explanations that state both the correct response and the typical biased response, with no performance feedback and no formal algebraic equations
constraints: The second-session gain was much smaller than the first (approximately 11.6 vs 43.1 points) with only marginal Block x Group interactions
Session 2 Block x Group interactions reached only marginal significance (p = .05 final, p = .06 initial)
Task order within the battery may matter: the training effect trended weaker for the last task, possibly due to fatigue
target_learners: adult reasoners recruited via Prolific Academic
initially biased reasoners on classic heuristics-and-biases tasks
target_learning_goals: avoiding biased intuitive responses on conflict reasoning problems
applying probabilistic and logical principles such as the conjunction rule and base-rate use
examples: Participants received a first one-hour training session with pre-intervention, intervention, and post-intervention blocks on three tasks, a second session two days later with modified problem contents, and a third session two months later in Study 2

article_title: Teacher self-efficacy, instructional quality, and student motivational beliefs: An analysis using multilevel structural equation modeling
citation: Burić, Irena and Kim, Lisa (2020) Teacher self-efficacy, instructional quality, and student motivational beliefs: An analysis using multilevel structural equation modeling. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2019.101302
title: Doubly latent multilevel structural equation modeling for climate-effect research
description: The article employs doubly latent multilevel SEM (Marsh et al., 2009) to test relationships between teacher and classroom constructs at the correct level of analysis. Its stated advantages are "the ability to control for measurement error at both L1 and L2 levels by using multiple indicators of a construct, as well as the ability to control for sampling error through the aggregating individual student responses to represent teacher level characteristic". It treats instructional quality as a classroom climate effect with the class, not the individual student, as referent.
requirements: Students nested within teachers, with each student rating the same teacher-referent classroom characteristic so aggregation at the teacher level is valid.
constraints: The article notes many classroom constructs must be tested at the teacher level; residual student-level ratings may reflect method effects rather than substantive climate.
target_learners: high school students in grammar-school programs
target_learning_goals: student self-efficacy and intrinsic motivation in subject-specific learning
examples: The study aggregated reports from on average 22 students per teacher to form latent teacher-level constructs while controlling measurement and sampling error.

article_title: Students' and mathematics teachers' perceptions of teacher enthusiasm and instruction
citation: Kunter, M.; Tsai, Y.-M.; Klusmann, U.; Brunner, M.; Krauss, Stefan; Baumert, J. (2008). Students' and mathematics teachers' perceptions of teacher enthusiasm and instruction. Learning and Instruction 18 (5), S. 468-482. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2008.06.008
title: Two-facet model of teacher enthusiasm: subject-matter enthusiasm versus enthusiasm for teaching
description: The article proposes that teacher enthusiasm is not a single construct but has two distinguishable facets. As the authors state, "We distinguished teachers' enthusiasm for the subject matter of mathematics from their enthusiasm for teaching mathematics." This two-facet framework organises the study's measurement and its finding that the two facets relate differently to instructional behaviour: enthusiasm for teaching tracks student-perceived instructional quality, whereas subject-matter enthusiasm tracks only teachers' self-reports. It serves as an explanatory account of why enthusiasm relates to instruction only in some of its forms.
requirements: Both facets must be measured separately, e.g. via questionnaires addressing enthusiasm for the subject and enthusiasm for teaching
constraints: The framework was developed and tested in the domain of mathematics with 9th-grade classes
target_learning_goals: quality of mathematics instruction as perceived by teachers and students
examples: The study operationalised the two facets with teacher questionnaires and linked them to teacher self-reports and student ratings of instructional behaviour via structural equation modelling

article_title: The interplay of positivity and self-verification strivings: Feedback preference under increased desire for self-enhancement
citation: Szumowska, Ewa; Szwed, Paulina; Wójcik, Natalia; Kruglanski, Arie W. (2023). The interplay of positivity and self-verification strivings : feedback preference under increased desire for self-enhancement. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101715
title: Two-motive account of feedback preference: self-enhancement versus self-verification
description: The article frames feedback preference as motivated by two main drivers in the educational context: "the desire for positive evaluation (self-enhancement motive) and the desire for subjectively accurate information (self-verification motive)". The self-enhancement motive "produces positivity bias", while self-verification "is seen in the preference for feedback consistent with one's established self-perception". The two laboratory studies test how these motives interact when self-enhancement motivation is increased.
requirements: Measuring or manipulating self-enhancement motivation and assessing established self-perception to distinguish the two motives' effects on feedback preference.
constraints: Studied in the educational context with feedback about social abilities; the positivity effect under increased self-enhancement was mainly observed for participants with positive self-perception.
target_learners: learners receiving evaluative feedback on their abilities
target_learning_goals: feedback processing and self-perception in educational evaluation
examples: Participants were presented with two evaluations of their social abilities, one positive and one negative, and their preferences were tested under increased self-enhancement motivation.
key_sources: Szumowska, Ewa; Szwed, Paulina; Wójcik, Natalia; Kruglanski, Arie W. (2023). The interplay of positivity and self-verification strivings : feedback preference under increased desire for self-enhancement. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101715

article_title: The interplay of positivity and self-verification strivings: Feedback preference under increased desire for self-enhancement
citation: Szumowska, Ewa; Szwed, Paulina; Wójcik, Natalia; Kruglanski, Arie W. (2023). The interplay of positivity and self-verification strivings : feedback preference under increased desire for self-enhancement. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101715
title: Account for learners' self-enhancement and self-verification motives when designing feedback
description: Because "feedback preference is motivated", feedback design in educational settings should recognize that learners' acceptance of feedback depends on competing motives: the desire for positive evaluation and the desire for subjectively accurate information. The article shows that when self-enhancement motivation is increased, learners may prefer positive feedback "regardless of its perceived accuracy", so accuracy-focused feedback may be discounted under such motivation.
requirements: Awareness of learners' current self-enhancement motivation and their established self-perception in the relevant domain.
constraints: Evidence concerns feedback on social abilities under laboratory conditions; the positivity preference was mainly observed for participants with positive self-perception.
target_learning_goals: effective feedback processing and uptake
examples: In the laboratory studies, participants chose between one positive and one negative evaluation of their social abilities under varying self-enhancement motivation.
key_sources: Szumowska, Ewa; Szwed, Paulina; Wójcik, Natalia; Kruglanski, Arie W. (2023). The interplay of positivity and self-verification strivings : feedback preference under increased desire for self-enhancement. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101715

article_title: Improving (meta)comprehension: Feedback and self-assessment
citation: Hepner, S. L., Oudman, S., Carlson, T. E., van de Pol, J., & van Gog, T. (2024). Improving (meta)comprehension: Feedback and self-assessment. Learning and Instruction, 92, 101922. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2024.101922
title: Situation-Model Approach to Metacomprehension (cue-utilization account)
description: The article frames monitoring accuracy via the Situation-Model Approach to Metacomprehension, built on Koriat's cue-utilization framework: learners lack direct insight into comprehension and rely on cues, some diagnostic (e.g., summarizing gist) and some not (e.g., ease of reading, interest, font size). Generative activities like delayed diagramming give access to diagnostic cues about the situation model, because the diagram is completed from the mental model in long-term memory rather than degraded surface features. The study tests whether model-answer feedback adds further diagnostic cues.
requirements: Learners must engage in a generative activity (e.g., diagramming) that exposes the quality of their situation model, ideally at a delay so judgments rest on the mental model rather than surface features
constraints: Effects of diagramming on monitoring accuracy are described as only moderate (g = 0.72 in prior meta-analytic work cited by the article), leaving room for further improvement
target_learners: secondary school students reading expository texts
target_learning_goals: accurate comprehension monitoring and self-regulated learning from text
examples: Participants read four texts and completed delayed causal diagrams of the texts' underlying causal structure before making judgments of learning
key_sources: Hepner, S. L., Oudman, S., Carlson, T. E., van de Pol, J., & van Gog, T. (2024). Improving (meta)comprehension: Feedback and self-assessment. Learning and Instruction, 92, 101922. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2024.101922

article_title: Understanding the structure of the set of rational numbers: a conceptual change approach
citation: Xenia Vamvakoussi, Stella Vosniadou. (2004). Understanding the structure of the set of rational numbers: a conceptual change approach. Learning and Instruction. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00190233
title: The conceptual change approach to learning can apply to mathematics learning
description: The article argues that conceptual change, a framework usually applied to science learning, extends to mathematics. It states that "the conceptual change approach to learning can apply in the case of mathematics", provided the account takes into consideration "the particular nature of mathematical knowledge and the neurobiological bases of mathematical cognition". The framework is then used to interpret ninth graders' understanding of rational numbers.
requirements: The application must take into consideration the particular nature of mathematical knowledge and the neurobiological bases of mathematical cognition, as the article states.

article_title: Increasing the use of conceptually-derived strategies in arithmetic: using inversion problems to promote the use of associativity shortcuts
citation: Joanne Eaves, Nina Attridge, Camilla Gilmore. (2018). Increasing the use of conceptually-derived strategies in arithmetic: using inversion problems to promote the use of associativity shortcuts. Learning and Instruction. https://figshare.com/s/230ee9491e0b67d9d3f3
title: Three proposed mechanisms linking inversion problem exposure to associativity shortcut use
description: The article proposes three non-mutually-exclusive mechanisms through which solving inversion problems may encourage associativity shortcut use: conceptual knowledge association, spatial attention, and strategy validation. The authors state they "suggest three possible (not mutually exclusive) mechanisms through which this could operate, a) conceptual knowledge, b) spatial attention, and c) validation of a strategy." Conceptual association activates linked principles in memory; spatial attention directs focus to the right-hand side where the shortcut is located; validation communicates that a right-to-left strategy is legitimate. The mechanisms are likely to interact.
requirements: For the conceptual mechanism, individuals must have at least some understanding of both principles stored in memory
For the validation mechanism, top-down manipulation of arithmetic knowledge is required rather than a simple general stimulus
constraints: The mechanisms are proposed as explanations, not independently tested in the available text; the authors note they are likely to interact and are discussed separately only for clarity
target_learning_goals: use of associativity shortcuts in arithmetic
conceptual knowledge of arithmetic principles
examples: Study 3 was designed to discriminate between mechanisms by comparing 'a + b – b' inversion, 'a + b – a' inversion, and two-term control conditions

citation: Joanne Eaves, Nina Attridge, Camilla Gilmore. (2018). Increasing the use of conceptually-derived strategies in arithmetic: using inversion problems to promote the use of associativity shortcuts. Learning and Instruction. https://figshare.com/s/230ee9491e0b67d9d3f3
title: SCADS* strategy discovery model attributing shortcut discovery to attentional mechanisms
description: SCADS* (Strategy Change and Discovery Simulation Model) is a computational model "designed to predict when arithmetic strategies are discovered," developed partly from performance patterns on inversion problems. It proposes that on each trial familiar strategies race against alternative strategies; over trials alternatives gain strength and are eventually applied. Attention is "proposed to be the first process required for shortcut discovery": an individual must direct attention to the right-hand side to discover the shortcut. The article applies SCADS* to associativity, suggesting the same attentional mechanisms may be required, and invokes its 'dynamic feature selection' process to explain how salient features become associated with strategy efficiency.
requirements: Attention must be directed to the right-hand side of the problem for shortcut discovery to occur
Alternative strategies must gain strength over repeated trials before application
constraints: The model was developed from inversion problems; its application to associativity is an extension proposed by Robinson & LeFevre (2012), not a direct derivation
target_learners: learners solving multi-term arithmetic problems (children and adults)
target_learning_goals: discovery and use of arithmetic shortcut strategies
examples: The article cites Dubé & Robinson (2010), who primed participants to look left or right at three-term problems and found faster reaction times in the right-prime condition on large inversion problems

article_title: Education, not age, linked to narrative comprehension
citation: Markus Huff, Natalia Gagarina, Ekaterina Varkentin, Irina R. Brich. (2025). Education, Not Age, Linked to Narrative Comprehension. https://aspredicted.org/WT9_TK6
title: Structure building framework as an account of codality-general narrative comprehension
description: The article adopts the structure building framework (Gernsbacher) to explain narrative comprehension across codalities. It "postulates three processes for building mental models of a narrative: laying a foundation containing the information within a scene, continually mapping new information onto the preexisting model, and, if new information is largely inconsistent with the current model, shifting to a new foundation." The mapping process draws on bridging inference generation, and the framework underpins the article's hypothesis of a general comprehension skill applying to both written and pictorial narratives.
requirements: Comprehension requires generating bridging inferences to connect explicitly depicted narrative scenes and maintain a coherent mental model held in working memory.
constraints: The article notes the framework's processes may require less effort for pictorial narratives, and that the observed pictorial advantage might instead stem from material difficulty rather than different cognitive processes.
target_learners: adults across the adult age span (18–87 years)
learners across low, middle, and high education levels
target_learning_goals: narrative comprehension via bridging inference generation

title: Use pictorial narratives to enhance comprehension and accessibility across education and age groups
description: The article recommends pictorial narratives as a way to convey information beyond text and lower comprehension barriers. Because "pictorial stories enhance comprehension across all education levels, they could still be a viable method to engage these groups more effectively," including less educated groups and people with literacy challenges. The recommendation rests on the observed pictorial advantage holding uniformly across demographics.
requirements: Pictorial materials must be designed for clarity; the MAIN narratives used were "tailored for clarity and universal appeal."
constraints: Targeting less educated groups with pictorial narratives alone "may not be particularly effective" because comprehension still depends on education; the pictorial advantage may partly reflect material difficulty differences.
target_learning_goals: comprehension of narrated information and societal participation
examples: In the main experiment, participants viewed MAIN-based story clips with the bridging event replaced by an empty frame and judged true or false inference statements about the missing part.

description: The study's data collection and analysis instrument: students wrote anonymous autobiographical narratives recalling positive and negative PE experiences across compulsory primary and secondary education, connecting them to primary emotions. citation: Stephen R. Earl, Ian M. Taylor, Carla Meijen and Louis Passfield (2016). Learning and Instruction, 49, 32-40. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2016.12.001
title: Avoid psychologically controlling strategies in the classroom to prevent both active and passive disengagement
description: The article recommends that teachers refrain from psychologically controlling tactics such as guilt induction, criticism and suppressing pupil opinion, because these thwart autonomy and competence and were associated with both disengagement pathways. It states that "teacher directed interventions may be required to help teachers understand the consequences of employing psychological control and methods to avoid such strategies". Teachers are advised to demonstrate relevance and invite pupil opinion instead.
requirements: Teachers must be able to recognise controlling language and tactics in their own practice, which the authors say may require targeted interventions.
constraints: The supporting evidence is cross-sectional, so causal benefits of removing control are not established by this study.
target_learning_goals: Classroom engagement and reducing active and passive disengagement
examples: The study measured pupil perceptions of teacher psychological control with items such as "My teacher does not allow me to work at my own pace" and linked those perceptions to need frustration and disengagement.

citation: Stephen R. Earl, Ian M. Taylor, Carla Meijen and Louis Passfield (2016). Learning and Instruction, 49, 32-40. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2016.12.001
title: Dual-process model of need frustration underpinning active versus passive classroom disengagement
description: Drawing on basic psychological needs theory, the article proposes two separate maladaptive processes: perceived teacher psychological control frustrates autonomy, which directly manifests as energetic, disruptive active disengagement; and frustrates competence, which reduces subjective vitality and thereby produces passive withdrawal such as daydreaming. The authors state the study will "identify different mechanisms underpinning two separate types of pupil disengagement". The structural model in Figure 1 depicts these as independent pathways from teacher control to the two disengagement forms.
requirements: Measurement of pupil-perceived teacher psychological control, autonomy and competence frustration, subjective vitality, and teacher-rated active and passive disengagement in a specific class context.
constraints: The model was tested cross-sectionally with teacher-rated behavioural disengagement only; the authors note emotional and cognitive engagement components were not assessed.
target_learners: Young adolescent pupils aged 11-14 in secondary school classrooms
target_learning_goals: Understanding and reducing distinct forms of classroom disengagement
examples: In the fitted SEM, teacher control loaded positively on both frustration factors (.86 and .74 as printed in Figure 1), which then routed to active and passive disengagement through the two distinct mechanisms.

citation: Grazia, V., Molinari, L., Mameli, C. (2024). Contrasting school dropout: The protective role of perceived teacher justice. LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION, 89, 1-9. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2023.101826
title: Treat students fairly to protect against early school leaving
description: The article argues that a feature of the proximal learning environment — students' perception of being treated fairly by teachers — can act as a protective factor against dropout. It reports that "perceptions of teacher justice had a negative association with the increase" in dropout intentions across the school year. Teachers' fair treatment is therefore positioned as a lever for dropout prevention.

constraints: The finding is an observational association from one three-wave study of 9th graders in Italy, not a tested intervention

examples: 547 9th-grade students answered questionnaires on teacher justice and dropout intentions at the beginning, middle and end of the school year

The framework links everyday classroom treatment to students' intention to persist in school.

citation: Xenidou-Dervou, I., Molenaar, D., Ansari, D., van der Schoot, M., & van Lieshout, E.C.D.M. (2017). Because the two skills showed different developmental trajectories and different predictive strengths for mathematics, studies of early numerical cognition should not rely on a single measure type. The article's own results motivate including both measure types in longitudinal designs.

article_title: Self-derivation through memory integration: A model for accumulation of semantic knowledge
citation: Bauer, P. J., Esposito, A. G., & Daly, J. J. (2020). Self-derivation through memory integration: A model for accumulation of semantic knowledge. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2019.101271
title: Self-derivation through memory integration as a model for accumulation of semantic knowledge
description: Self-derivation through memory integration is the authors' proposed model of how semantic knowledge accumulates: information explicitly taught in separate learning episodes is integrated into a single memory representation, and inferential processes over that representation generate new factual knowledge that was never directly taught. The article argues it is a particularly viable candidate model because it uses true, factual knowledge, its products are rapidly incorporated into the knowledge base, and they are retained over time. The classroom experiments reported here test its retention, generalizability to science curricula, and episodic consequences.
requirements: Both members of a pair of related facts must be explicitly learned in separate episodes; if only one member is taught, children do not self-derive new knowledge.
A prompt or demand to integrate (e.g., a question such as How does a pod talk?) is needed for children to engage the integration process at test.
constraints: In children, the processes supporting self-derivation seemingly occur on demand at the time of test rather than at encoding; performance falls substantially when delay is imposed before the self-derivation test.
Classroom performance is nominally lower than laboratory performance, and cue-distinctiveness is lacking in classroom contexts.
target_learners: Elementary school children, particularly second-grade students ages 7-9 years
target_learning_goals: Accumulation of factual semantic knowledge, including science curriculum content
examples: Second-graders heard pairs of illustrated story passages in class (e.g., tigers are the largest cats; the largest cats swim to cool off) and answered questions requiring integration, such as What do tigers do to cool off?

citation: Cerni, Tania; Lonciari, Isabella; Job, Remo. (2025). Learning by writing: The influence of handwriting and typing on novel word learning in typically developing readers and readers with dyslexia. LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102119
title: Nonword learning paradigm comparing typing and handwriting with spelling and nonword-image association tests
description: The study used a paradigm in which participants learned nonwords varying in transcription regularity, each paired with an image, through either typing or handwriting. Learning was tested with spelling and nonword-image association tasks. The article states that "Recorded metrics included accuracy, writing duration during learning and spelling tasks, and reaction time in the nonword-image mapping task." Eighteen Italian middle school students with developmental dyslexia and eighteen age-matched typically developing readers participated.
requirements: Nonwords must vary in transcription regularity and be paired with images
Both a spelling task and a nonword-image mapping task are needed to assess orthographic and semantic learning
constraints: Evaluated with Italian middle school students, so findings are scoped to that language and age group
target_learning_goals: orthographic learning
semantic word-referent association
examples: Participants learned a set of nonwords, varying in transcription regularity, paired with images, either through typing or handwriting
key_sources: Cerni, Tania; Lonciari, Isabella; Job, Remo. (2025). Learning by writing: The influence of handwriting and typing on novel word learning in typically developing readers and readers with dyslexia. LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102119

article_title: Primary school students’ awareness of their monitoring and regulation judgment accuracy
citation: Oudman, S., van de Pol, J., Janssen, E., & van Gog, T. (2024). Primary school students' awareness of their monitoring and regulation judgment accuracy. Learning and Instruction, 92, 101907. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2024.101907
title: Second-order judgments (SOJs) as a measure of accuracy awareness in self-regulated learning
description: This framework distinguishes first-order monitoring and regulation judgments (evaluating performance and deciding on subsequent learning actions) from second-order judgments — students' ratings of their confidence in the accuracy of those first-order judgments. Students show accuracy awareness when they "feel relatively more confident about the accuracy of a more accurate judgment than of a less accurate judgment." The article applies this framework to primary school mathematics, measuring SOJ-m and SOJ-r on a 6-point Likert scale with smiley faces, and analyzing within-student relationships across two measurement days. It argues awareness matters because confidence affects whether students act upon their judgments.
requirements: Multiple measurement points per student to analyze within-student relationships between judgment accuracy and confidence
Students must understand the second-order judgment questions, which the authors verified through pilot interviews
constraints: The article notes awareness findings depend on analysis level: between-student analyses (as in Nederhand et al., 2021) can yield different conclusions than within-student analyses
target_learning_goals: Accurate monitoring and regulation of mathematics problem solving
Effective self-regulated learning
examples: Students completed parallel multiplication and division tasks on two days, making monitoring/regulation judgments, SOJs, and self-scoring on both occasions
key_sources: Oudman, S., van de Pol, J., Janssen, E., & van Gog, T. (2024). Primary school students' awareness of their monitoring and regulation judgment accuracy. Learning and Instruction, 92, 101907. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2024.101907

article_title: Primary school students’ awareness of their monitoring and regulation judgment accuracy
citation: Oudman, S., van de Pol, J., Janssen, E., & van Gog, T. (2024). Primary school students' awareness of their monitoring and regulation judgment accuracy. Learning and Instruction, 92, 101907. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2024.101907
title: Analyze accuracy awareness at the within-student level using multiple measurement points
description: The article argues that true awareness of judgment accuracy requires analyzing whether an individual student's increase in judgment accuracy is accompanied by an increase in confidence, which demands multiple measurements per student. Between-student analyses answer a different question — whether students with higher accuracy are generally more confident — and "could have concluded that students showed awareness of their monitoring and regulation accuracy on the division task" even though within-student analyses showed no awareness. Researchers studying accuracy awareness should regress SOJs on judgment accuracy at the day (within-student) level with group-mean centering.
requirements: At least two measurement points per student (e.g., parallel task versions on different days)
Multilevel regression with judgment accuracy centered at the group mean for within-student effects
constraints: Between-student and within-student analyses answer different questions and may lead to different conclusions about the same data
target_learning_goals: Accurate measurement of monitoring and regulation accuracy awareness
examples: The authors regressed SOJ-m/SOJ-r on monitoring/regulation accuracy at the day level in three-level multilevel models (day, student, class) using Mplus with MLR estimation
key_sources: Oudman, S., van de Pol, J., Janssen, E., & van Gog, T. (2024). Primary school students' awareness of their monitoring and regulation judgment accuracy. Learning and Instruction, 92, 101907. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2024.101907

article_title: Bridging the gap: Fraction understanding is central to mathematics achievement in students from three different continents
citation: Torbeyns, J., Schneider, M., Xin, Z., & Siegler, R. S. (2015). Bridging the Gap: Fraction Understanding is Central to Mathematics Achievement in Students from Three Different Continents. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2014.03.002
title: Integrated theory of numerical development
description: Siegler, Thompson, and Schneider's (2011) integrated theory of numerical development unites whole number and fraction learning in a single framework, in contrast to conceptual change theories that posit a gap between them. It holds that numerical development is a "steadily expanding understanding of the connection between numbers and their magnitudes", involving both expansion of the range of whole numbers whose magnitudes are understood and a conceptual change toward understanding rational numbers via their single defining feature, their magnitudes. The theory views interference from whole number knowledge as only one of several sources of difficulty in learning fractions, and recognizes the positive role of whole number magnitude knowledge in learning fractions. This study tested its major assumption cross-culturally.
requirements: Fraction magnitude understanding must be assessable, e.g., via number line estimation and magnitude comparison tasks, for the theory's central relation to be tested.
constraints: The theory's applicability to irrational numbers had not been tested empirically, according to the article.
target_learners: Elementary and middle school students (6th and 8th graders)
target_learning_goals: Understanding of fraction magnitudes
General mathematics achievement
examples: The study tested the theory's assumption that fraction magnitude understanding is crucial to overall mathematics learning in Belgium (Flanders), China, and the U.S., countries differing in teachers' knowledge, instructional practices, and student performance.
key_sources: Torbeyns, J., Schneider, M., Xin, Z., & Siegler, R. S. (2015). Bridging the Gap: Fraction Understanding is Central to Mathematics Achievement in Students from Three Different Continents. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2014.03.002

article_title: The linguistic nature of Children's scientific reasoning
citation: Van de Sande, E., Kleemans, T., Verhoeven, L., & Segers, E. (2019). The linguistic nature of children's scientific reasoning. Learning and Instruction, 62, 20-26. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2019.02.002
title: Dual-route (spatial and verbal) framework of individual differences in children's scientific reasoning
description: The article frames scientific reasoning as drawing on parallel visuospatial and linguistic processing, aligned with Baddeley's working-memory model: "there is both a spatial and verbal route to retrieve and restore information from long-term memory", with an episodic route enabling their interaction. Visuospatial inferencing serves pattern discovery in evidence and graphs, while academic vocabulary and linguistic inferencing serve conceptualising, mental-model construction and syllogistic deduction. The study tested this framework by relating both ability types to the full cycle of scientific reasoning skills in sixth graders.
requirements: Assessment of both visuospatial (e.g., Raven's matrices) and linguistic (reading comprehension, academic vocabulary) abilities alongside scientific reasoning measures
constraints: Framework tested only in a cross-sectional design with paper-and-pencil measures at the end of primary school
target_learners: children in the upper years of primary education (sixth grade, mean age 11.8)
target_learning_goals: scientific reasoning skills: generating investigable questions, evaluating evidence, designing controlled experiments, generating conclusions
examples: The path model related Raven's matrices, a reading comprehension test, and an academic vocabulary test to the three SRI factors
key_sources: Van de Sande, E., Kleemans, T., Verhoeven, L., & Segers, E. (2019). The linguistic nature of children's scientific reasoning. Learning and Instruction, 62, 20-26. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2019.02.002

article_title: The linguistic nature of Children's scientific reasoning
citation: Van de Sande, E., Kleemans, T., Verhoeven, L., & Segers, E. (2019). The linguistic nature of children's scientific reasoning. Learning and Instruction, 62, 20-26. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2019.02.002
title: Scientific Reasoning Inventory (SRI)
description: The SRI is "a paper-and-pencil test that consists of 20 multiple-choice questions with sub-questions (40 items in total)", rooted in five STEM contextual stories with a common question structure covering generating investigable questions, evaluating evidence, designing experiments (CVS), and generating conclusions (syllogistic reasoning). Its structure is based on the Argumentative Sensemaking Measure for middle-school students. The authors present it as an easy-to-administer group assessment that can help teachers tailor enquiry-based education to individual needs.
requirements: 45 minutes administration time; practice items precede CVS items to introduce the line of reasoning
constraints: Measured with paper-and-pencil tasks although the skills also have an active, hands-on nature; conclusion generation was operationalised narrowly as syllogistic reasoning only
target_learning_goals: scientific reasoning across the enquiry cycle
examples: Administered classroom-wide with a randomly counterbalanced order relative to the academic vocabulary test
key_sources: Van de Sande, E., Kleemans, T., Verhoeven, L., & Segers, E. (2019). The linguistic nature of children's scientific reasoning. Learning and Instruction, 62, 20-26. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2019.02.002

article_title: The linguistic nature of Children's scientific reasoning
citation: Van de Sande, E., Kleemans, T., Verhoeven, L., & Segers, E. (2019). The linguistic nature of children's scientific reasoning. Learning and Instruction, 62, 20-26. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2019.02.002
title: Exercise linguistic abilities — linguistic inferencing and academic vocabulary — in science education, not only visuospatial skills
description: Because linguistic inferencing predicted all three scientific reasoning components and academic vocabulary supported early-stage hypothesis validation, the authors argue that science education, which currently stresses visuospatial inferencing, underestimates the role of linguistic abilities. They conclude that "linguistic abilities – both linguistic inferencing and academic vocabulary – can and should be exercised as well". This extends the theoretical framework of individual differences in scientific reasoning to include verbal processing routes.
requirements: Attention to academic vocabulary (domain-general enquiry words and STEM words) and inferencing practice, e.g., in reading comprehension contexts
constraints: Based on cross-sectional correlational evidence; the authors call for longitudinal and intervention research
target_learners: primary school children in enquiry-based science education
target_learning_goals: scientific reasoning: hypothesis validation, experimentation, generating conclusions
examples: The study measured academic vocabulary with a 54-item test covering physics, engineering, biology, mathematics, Earth and space, and general science

article_title: Longitudinal predictors of reading comprehension in French at first grade: Unpacking the oral comprehension component of the simple view
citation: Jessica Massonnié, Maryse Bianco, Laurent Lima, Pascal Bressoux. (2018). Longitudinal predictors of reading comprehension in French at first grade: Unpacking the oral comprehension component of the simple view. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2018.01.005
title: Unpacked simple view of reading: oral comprehension comprises lower level language skills and discourse skills as dissociable dimensions
description: The study refines the simple view of reading by unpacking its oral comprehension component. Rather than one broad oral language factor, the article reports that "lower level language skills (vocabulary, syntax) and discourse skills (oral text comprehension) emerged as two dimensions of 'oral comprehension'". LLL skills cover vocabulary breadth and syntactic skills assessed at word and sentence level, while discourse skills cover comprehension of whole oral texts requiring inference-making and integration. The framework was operationalised in longitudinal structural equation models predicting end-of-first-grade reading comprehension in French.
requirements: Assessment must separately measure vocabulary, syntax, and oral text comprehension rather than aggregating them, since sentence-level and text-level interpretation "might not involve similar cognitive mechanisms".
constraints: The two factors were highly correlated (.81 at T1, .73 at T2), and the structure was established in French first-graders, a moderately transparent orthography.
target_learners: First-grade pupils (around 6 years old) learning to read in French
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension development
Oral language comprehension
examples: Confirmatory factor analyses at T1 and T2 with 556 pupils compared three-factor models against two-factor alternatives, favouring the three-factor structure at both time points.
key_sources: Jessica Massonnié, Maryse Bianco, Laurent Lima, Pascal Bressoux. (2018). Longitudinal predictors of reading comprehension in French at first grade: Unpacking the oral comprehension component of the simple view. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2018.01.005

article_title: Longitudinal predictors of reading comprehension in French at first grade: Unpacking the oral comprehension component of the simple view
citation: Jessica Massonnié, Maryse Bianco, Laurent Lima, Pascal Bressoux. (2018). Longitudinal predictors of reading comprehension in French at first grade: Unpacking the oral comprehension component of the simple view. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2018.01.005
title: Assess vocabulary, syntax and oral text comprehension separately when predicting early reading comprehension
description: The article recommends a fine-grained conceptualisation of oral comprehension in early reading instruction and assessment. Because a three-factor structure distinguishing "lower level language skills (vocabulary, syntax) and discourse skills (oral text comprehension)" fit better than a single oral language factor, aggregating these measures risks masking which component drives reading comprehension. In this study LLL skills, but not discourse skills, predicted end-of-first-grade reading comprehension, so aggregated measures would have obscured this differential contribution.
requirements: Measures of vocabulary breadth, syntactic skills and oral text comprehension must each be administered separately rather than combined into one oral comprehension score.
constraints: Evidence comes from French first-graders in a moderately transparent orthography; the two oral factors were highly correlated (.81 at T1, .73 at T2).
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension
Oral language assessment
examples: The study assessed vocabulary breadth, syntactic skills and oral text comprehension as separate measures at T1 and T2 and entered them as distinct latent factors in SEMs.
key_sources: Jessica Massonnié, Maryse Bianco, Laurent Lima, Pascal Bressoux. (2018). Longitudinal predictors of reading comprehension in French at first grade: Unpacking the oral comprehension component of the simple view. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2018.01.005

article_title: The role of rhythm in learning to read in children with and without reading difficulties: an intervention study
citation: Gutiérrez-Palma, N., Calet, N., Robles-Bello, M.A., & Valencia-Naranjo, N. (2026). The role of rhythm in learning to read in children with and without reading difficulties: an intervention study. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102273
title: Temporal sampling theory of dyslexia (Goswami)
description: Temporal sampling theory, as described in this article, holds that phonological problems in dyslexia originate in a subtle deficit in detecting rise times, the acoustic correlate of rhythm. The article states that "this deficit would, in turn, be caused by a difficulty in sampling the speech signal at low frequencies, Delta (1–4 Hz) and Theta (4–10 Hz)", which correspond to stress and syllables. The study tests the theory's prediction that rhythm training facilitates attention to lower frequencies and improves phonological awareness, reporting partial support.
requirements: Rhythm perception is assumed to operate through sampling the speech signal at Delta (1–4 Hz) and Theta (4–10 Hz) frequencies corresponding to stress and syllables
constraints: The article reports only partial support: the combined training group was not the best on reading measures, contrary to the theory-based hypothesis H1
target_learners: children in the first year of primary education learning to read
target_learning_goals: phonological awareness
word reading
pseudoword reading
key_sources: Gutiérrez-Palma, N., Calet, N., Robles-Bello, M.A., & Valencia-Naranjo, N. (2026). The role of rhythm in learning to read in children with and without reading difficulties: an intervention study. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102273

article_title: Joy is reciprocally transmitted between teachers and students: Evidence on facial mimicry in the classroom
citation: Frenzel, A. C., Dindar, M., Pekrun, R., Reck, C., & Marx, A. K. G. (2024). Joy is reciprocally transmitted between teachers and students: Evidence on facial mimicry in the classroom. Learning and Instruction, 91, 101896. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2024.101896
title: Facial mimicry as a micro-level bottom-up mechanism driving macro-level teacher–student emotional contagion
description: The article proposes that macro-level covariation between teachers' and students' self-reported habitual joy experiences is fueled, in a bottom-up fashion, by micro-level covariation: repeated instances of joint joy experiences during instruction. Facial mimicry is positioned as a key mechanism, defined as one person facially expressing their emotional state which is "mirrored, or imitated, by their interaction partner within seconds". The framework draws on the "social glue" function of emotional mimicry, which fosters affiliation between interaction partners, and proposes that persistent micro-level mimicry processes lead habitual emotional experiences in the joint context to converge over time.
requirements: Both interaction partners must engage in a joint activity during which they can mimic each other's facial expressions for substantial proportions of their interaction.
constraints: The article notes the degree of emotional mimicry depends on individual, contextual, and relational factors such as prior affiliation, group membership, and attitudes, and occurs less in competitive or hostile settings.
target_learning_goals: positive emotional experiences during instruction
teacher-student relational and emotional convergence
examples: The study operationalized the mechanism using cross-recurrence quantification analysis on frame-by-frame facial joy expression time series from 69 instructor–student dyads, identifying a critical lag window of -54 to +85 lags.
key_sources: Frenzel, A. C., Dindar, M., Pekrun, R., Reck, C., & Marx, A. K. G. (2024). Joy is reciprocally transmitted between teachers and students: Evidence on facial mimicry in the classroom. Learning and Instruction, 91, 101896. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2024.101896

article_title: Training children’s spatial language skills improves their numerical magnitude understanding
citation: Nadja Lindner, Korbinian Moeller, Frauke Hildebrandt, Marcus Hasselhorn, Jan Lonnemann. (2025). Training children's spatial language skills improves their numerical magnitude understanding. Learning and Instruction 99 (2025) 102191. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102191
title: Mental number line account of the spatial language–numerical magnitude link
description: The article frames its intervention within the notion that "numerical magnitudes are represented spatially along a mental number line" (citing Dehaene, 1992; Siegler, 2016). Mastery of spatial language terms is expected to facilitate early numerical skills by helping children grasp spatial relations between numerical magnitudes on this line. The training effect on number words comparison is interpreted as consistent with spatial language facilitating associations of numerical magnitudes with physical space.
requirements: Mastery of spatial terms such as in front of, behind, to the left, and to the right within the egocentric frame of reference
constraints: The design cannot decide whether the effect reflects spatial mapping of serial order in working memory or of magnitude representations in long-term memory; both may apply
target_learning_goals: Numerical magnitude understanding
Spatial language production and comprehension
examples: Six small-group training sessions of about 20 min using a treasure hunt cover story in which children named and placed a wooden cube relative to a wooden half-sphere
key_sources: Nadja Lindner, Korbinian Moeller, Frauke Hildebrandt, Marcus Hasselhorn, Jan Lonnemann. (2025). Training children's spatial language skills improves their numerical magnitude understanding. Learning and Instruction 99 (2025) 102191. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102191

article_title: Training children’s spatial language skills improves their numerical magnitude understanding
citation: Nadja Lindner, Korbinian Moeller, Frauke Hildebrandt, Marcus Hasselhorn, Jan Lonnemann. (2025). Training children's spatial language skills improves their numerical magnitude understanding. Learning and Instruction 99 (2025) 102191. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102191
title: Working-memory serial-order and symbolic-representation alternative explanations
description: The article presents two alternative mechanisms attributed to Georges et al. (2023) and Gilligan-Lee et al. (2021). One holds that mastery of spatial terms may facilitate "the spatialization of ordered sequences in working memory and/or spatial attentional scanning processes". The other holds that spatial terms and symbolic numbers both require associating verbal labels with concepts, so spatial language training may have facilitated symbolic number representations. The authors state their design cannot decide between these accounts.
requirements: Further studies, e.g. training spatial language from another category not expected to facilitate numerical processing, to evaluate the symbolic-representation account
constraints: The study design does not allow deciding whether the effect is based on working-memory serial-order mapping, long-term-memory magnitude mapping, or both
target_learning_goals: Numerical magnitude comparison
Understanding of symbolic number representations
examples: The authors note some children produced above/below instead of behind/in front of, suggesting vertical as well as sagittal and horizontal dimensions may be associated with numerical magnitudes
