article_title: Feedback processing and emotion regulation in nursing students during internship
citation: Feedback processing and emotion regulation in nursing students during internship. (2022). https://eric.ed.gov/?q=feedback+processing+and+emotion+regulation+in+nursing+students+during+internship
title: Integrated model of internship feedback processing in nursing students
description: A four-phase, circular model of how nursing students process internship feedback, integrating emotional processing with prior findings on self-esteem and learning behavior. Phase one activates determinants (personal dispositions, task perception, context); phase two interprets feedback content and form through cognitive and emotional processes; phase three concerns deciding about feedback; phase four concerns consequences for motivational beliefs and behaviors oriented toward self-protection or learning regulation. The article states "this model operates in a circular dynamic," with consequences feeding back into dispositions and perceptions of the next task. Emotions and their regulation are central and appear in bold in the model.
requirements: Feedback situations recur over time so that consequences of one episode can influence dispositions and perceptions in the next
constraints: Developed in the context of nursing internships in French-speaking Belgium
Emotion regulation strategies were often unconscious and could not always be identified as such from T1 interview data
target_learners: nursing students on internship (higher education, vocational bachelor's)
target_learning_goals: constructive processing and use of clinical feedback
emotion management during feedback
self-regulated learning
examples: The model was built by integrating this study's findings on emotions and regulation with the authors' previous publications on self-esteem and feedback interpretation

article_title: Exploring the short-term and long-term effects of the COVID-19 school closures on reading fluency in Southern Germany: A longitudinal causal effects analysis
citation: Kraus, E. B., Wild, J., Schilcher, A., & Hilbert, S. (2024). Exploring the Short-Term and Long-Term Effects of the COVID-19 School Closures on Reading Fluency in Southern Germany: A Longitudinal Causal Effects Analysis. https://osf.io/bu2ad/
title: Control time-dependent trends in causal learning-loss analyses by choosing a homogeneously developing, narrowly defined ability measured with a standardized instrument
description: This design principle holds that causal estimates of instructional disruptions require tight confinement of the counterfactual trend. The authors achieved this by restricting the outcome to reading fluency, "a readily measurable and well-defined construct", and by noting that "the choice of an ability with a homogeneous development, a narrow definition of the construct reading fluency, and the measurement with a standardized instrument allowed us to control time-dependent trends in our causal analysis." Multiple measurement points additionally separated short-term from long-term effects.
requirements: A standardized, normed test instrument usable across the full study period
Large sample sizes and high data quality for pre-trend and matched control comparison
Pre-trend estimation and propensity score weighting to validate the parallel assumption
constraints: Findings apply to a skill assumed mostly internalized and automated before the disruption; skills still developing, such as third-grade reading comprehension, may show more severe impact
Sample restricted to one region (Bavaria) and one grade, limiting generalization
target_learners: elementary school students (grades two to four)
target_learning_goals: reading fluency
examples: The study restricted the sample to Southern German third graders, used the SLS across five measurement points, and validated linear pre-trends before estimating DiD effects.

citation: Kraus, E. B., Wild, J., Schilcher, A., & Hilbert, S. (2024). Exploring the Short-Term and Long-Term Effects of the COVID-19 School Closures on Reading Fluency in Southern Germany: A Longitudinal Causal Effects Analysis. https://osf.io/bu2ad/
title: Salzburger Lesescreening (SLS) reading fluency test
description: The Salzburger Lesescreening (SLS) is a standardized reading fluency test in which students "indicate the substantive correctness of as many sentences as possible out of a maximum of 100 sentences, during a three-minute period". The article used SLS 1-4 and SLS 2-9 versions, equated via equipercentile equating after scalar non-invariance, and describes it as "a validated four-version test with appropriate psychometric properties, such as a convergent validity with reading comprehension of r = .43" and internal consistency up to α = .98 in this study.
requirements: Trained teachers or university staff to administer assessments
Version equating across test versions due to metric but not scalar measurement invariance
constraints: Psychometric modeling indicated metric but not scalar measurement invariance for test versions, requiring equating

examples: Rasch models per test version fit the data with non-significant Andersen likelihood ratio tests (all ps > .920).

article_title: The timing of executive function development is associated with growth in math achievement from preschool through second grade
citation: Sammy F. Ahmed, Janelle J. Montroy, Lori E. Skibbe, Ryan P. Bowles, & Frederick J. Morrison. (2022). The Timing of Executive Function Development is Associated with Growth in Math Achievement from Preschool through Second Grade. Manuscript in-press at Learning and Instruction. https://orcid.org/0000-0003-3814-2955
title: Three-class classification of EF developmental timing: early, intermediate, and later developers
description: The article uses a previously established growth mixture modeling (GMM) classification in which young children follow distinct EF growth trajectories relative to peers. Children were classified as developing EF early, intermediate, or later: "24% of children were classified as developing EF “early”", while "Almost half (i.e., 48%) of children were “intermediate developers”" and 28% were later developers. Early developers start preschool with higher EF and grow rapidly across preschool; intermediate developers start lower and grow more slowly; later developers start comparable to the intermediate group but show minimal preschool growth, with major EF gains occurring later. The present study used these classifications as multigroup predictors of math growth.
requirements: EF scores grouped into six-month developmental windows between preschool and second grade and parameterized with an exponential growth model before GMM classification
constraints: Acceleration and deceleration rates were constrained to equality across trajectory classes, so trajectories differed in timing rather than variation; class membership was implicitly treated as directly observed and should be interpreted with caution
target_learners: children in preschool through second grade
target_learning_goals: executive function development
math achievement growth
examples: In the present study's sample, 24% were early, 48% intermediate, and 28% later EF developers; a 3-step robustness check produced the same patterns of results

article_title: Effects of dialogic learning on value-loaded critical thinking
citation: Frijters, S., ten Dam, G., & Rijlaarsdam, G. (2008). Effects of dialogic learning on value-loaded critical thinking. Learning and Instruction, 18(1), 66-82. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2006.11.001
title: Paired Dialogic and Non-Dialogic lesson series for value-loaded critical thinking in Biology
description: The article describes two lesson series developed for teaching value-loaded critical thinking: "a Dialogic lesson series and a Non-Dialogic one". They were implemented in the school subject of Biology in pre-vocational secondary education with a sample of 297 students, allowing a controlled comparison of dialogic versus non-dialogic approaches to the same competences.
requirements: Lesson series must be embedded in a domain-specific school subject (here Biology) so critical thinking is taught alongside subject-matter knowledge.
constraints: Developed and evaluated for pre-vocational secondary education.
target_learning_goals: Value-loaded critical thinking
Biology subject-matter knowledge
examples: The study developed two lesson series and compared their effects on critical-thinking competences and Biology knowledge with 297 students.

article_title: Effects of dialogic learning on value-loaded critical thinking
citation: Frijters, S., ten Dam, G., & Rijlaarsdam, G. (2008). Effects of dialogic learning on value-loaded critical thinking. Learning and Instruction, 18(1), 66-82. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2006.11.001
title: Teach democratic-participation competences such as value-loaded critical thinking within domain-specific school subjects
description: The article argues that education should "endeavour to include the competences that students need to participate in a democratic society in a responsible and adequate way", and addresses the question of how this can be realized in a curriculum organized in school subjects. Its answer is to embed value-loaded critical thinking in the domain-specific subject of Biology, where it was taught without sacrificing subject-matter knowledge.
requirements: A curriculum aimed at domain-specific knowledge and skills organized in school subjects, in which critical-thinking competences are integrated rather than taught separately.
constraints: Demonstrated in pre-vocational secondary education within Biology.
target_learning_goals: Value-loaded critical thinking for responsible participation in a democratic society
examples: The study implemented value-loaded critical thinking in the school subject of Biology in pre-vocational secondary education.
key_sources: Frijters, S., ten Dam, G., & Rijlaarsdam, G. (2008). Effects of dialogic learning on value-loaded critical thinking. Learning and Instruction, 18(1), 66-82. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2006.11.001

article_title: Putting excellence first: How rubric performance level order and feedback type influence students’ reading patterns and task performance
citation: Panadero, E., Delgado, P., Zamorano, D., Pinedo, L., Fernández-Ortube, A., & Barrenetxea-Mínguez, L. (2025). Putting excellence first: How rubric performance level order and feedback type influence students' reading patterns and task performance. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102168
title: Multimodal process-tracing approach to rubric use: triangulating eye-tracking and think-aloud protocols
description: The article adopts a methodological framework combining eye-tracking with think-aloud protocols to capture students' real-time engagement with rubrics during academic tasks. Eye-tracking supplies fixation times, number of visits, and gaze transitions between rubric and task stimuli, while think-aloud protocols capture verbalized reasoning and strategies. The authors state that "The integration of these two data sources follows a logic of triangulation common in mixed-methods research", allowing them to identify convergences (prioritization of PL4) and divergences (visual behavior predicting performance while verbal references did not). No prior study had combined both methods to examine how students read and use rubrics.
requirements: Concurrent collection of eye-tracking and think-aloud data during task performance; tasks of moderate cognitive demand so participants can verbalize without being overwhelmed
constraints: Triangulation operates at the level of interpretive patterns rather than fine-grained synchronized episode-level coding; think-aloud independence assumptions were not always met when participants contributed multiple protocols
target_learning_goals: understanding how students read and use rubrics formatively during complex academic tasks
examples: The study combined eye-tracking (fixation times, visits, gaze transitions) with coded think-aloud protocols across five task phases, using the two streams in parallel to identify converging and diverging patterns.
key_sources: Panadero, E., Delgado, P., Zamorano, D., Pinedo, L., Fernández-Ortube, A., & Barrenetxea-Mínguez, L. (2025). Putting excellence first: How rubric performance level order and feedback type influence students' reading patterns and task performance. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102168

article_title: Longitudinal associations between academic motivation and school-related stressors in adolescents transitioning to secondary school
citation: Wang, J., Kaufman, T., Mastrotheodoros, S., & Branje, S. (2025). Longitudinal associations between academic motivation and school-related stressors in adolescents transitioning to secondary school. Learning and Instruction, 98, 102144. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102144
title: Self-Determination Theory account of controlled and autonomous academic motivation shaped by relationships with parents, peers, and teachers
description: The article organizes its hypotheses with Self-Determination Theory, under which individuals regulate behavior along controlled and autonomous orientations: "Controlled motivation is often associated with external pressures and rewards, while autonomous motivation is characterized by self-determination and intrinsic drive." Relationships Motivation Theory, a mini theory of SDT, supplies the mechanism: people have an innate need for connection and belonging, so stressors from parents, peers, and teachers can create an unsupportive environment that shifts motivation toward controlled or away from autonomous forms.
requirements: Assessment of both controlled and autonomous motivation as distinct constructs (e.g., external, introjected, identified, and intrinsic regulation subscales)
Measurement of adolescents' subjective perceptions of relationship quality with parents, peers, and teachers
constraints: The study assesses adolescents' subjective perceptions via self-report, which the authors note may reflect perceptual biases or shared method variance rather than actual differences in parental or teachers' behaviors
target_learners: adolescents transitioning from primary to secondary school
target_learning_goals: academic motivation (controlled and autonomous regulation of academic behavior)
examples: The study tested SDT-derived hypotheses by correlating growth factors of three school-related social stressors with growth factors of controlled and autonomous motivation across four waves spanning the secondary school transition
key_sources: Wang, J., Kaufman, T., Mastrotheodoros, S., & Branje, S. (2025). Longitudinal associations between academic motivation and school-related stressors in adolescents transitioning to secondary school. Learning and Instruction, 98, 102144. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102144

article_title: Achievement emotions and arithmetic fluency – Development and parallel processes during the early school years
citation: Rawlings, A. M., Niemivirta, M., Korhonen, J., Lindskog, M., Tuominen, H., & Mononen, R. (2023). Achievement emotions and arithmetic fluency – Development and parallel processes during the early school years. Preprint Version 3, Accepted for publication, 27 March 2023.
title: Control-value theory of achievement emotions as the framework for mathematics emotions
description: The article adopts Pekrun's control-value theory, in which "emotions directly related to achievement activities or outcomes that are judged on competence-related standards are defined as achievement emotions". Emotions arise from appraisals of perceived control over task demands and the subjective value of the activity or outcome. The theory organises emotions along a three-dimensional taxonomy of object focus, valence, and arousal level, which the study uses to select enjoyment, anxiety, and boredom as the emotions representing its main dimensions.
requirements: Measurement of domain-specific emotions tied to mathematics activities and outcomes, as the theory treats achievement emotions as domain-specific
constraints: The study measures only three emotions representing the taxonomy's main dimensions, within the mathematics domain of early primary school
target_learning_goals: mathematics-related achievement emotions (enjoyment, anxiety, boredom) and arithmetic fluency development
examples: The study used the framework to hypothesise that enjoyment is instigated by high control and value appraisals, anxiety by high value but low control, and boredom when both are low
key_sources: Rawlings, A. M., Niemivirta, M., Korhonen, J., Lindskog, M., Tuominen, H., & Mononen, R. (2023). Achievement emotions and arithmetic fluency – Development and parallel processes during the early school years. Preprint Version 3, Accepted for publication, 27 March 2023. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2023.101776

article_title: Training flexibility in dealing with additive situations
citation: Laura Gabler, Stefan Ufer. (2024). Training flexibility in dealing with additive situations. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2024.101902
title: Flexibility in dealing with additive situations: restructuring situation models via the Inversion and Dynamization strategies
description: The article defines "flexibility in dealing with additive situations as the skill to restructure situation models of additive one-step word problems by inferring additional features of the situation structure (a/s wording, semantic structure, unknown set)". It is operationalized through two strategies: the Inversion Strategy, which reverses subject and object and inverts additive/subtractive wording to turn inconsistent problems into consistent ones, and the Dynamization Strategy, which restructures static compare problems as dynamic equalize problems. The framework builds on Kintsch's text comprehension model and Riley et al.'s problem-type taxonomy, and holds that inferring additional situation-structure features can ease identifying an adequate mathematical model even with restricted conceptual knowledge.
requirements: Learners need conceptual knowledge about how features of a situation structure relate to mathematical concepts, and the relevant schemata must be individually available and activated
constraints: The framework addresses additive one-step word problems without irrelevant information; equalize problems have little evidence on difficulty since they were not included in the majority of studies
target_learning_goals: solving additive one-step word problems
flexibly restructuring situation models of additive situations
examples: The flexibility test contrasted statement pairs equivalent via the Dynamization Strategy (contrasting semantic structures) or the Inversion Strategy (contrasting a/s wordings), embedded in a story about twins reporting on a birthday party
key_sources: Laura Gabler, Stefan Ufer. (2024). Training flexibility in dealing with additive situations. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2024.101902

article_title: Training flexibility in dealing with additive situations
citation: Laura Gabler, Stefan Ufer. (2024). Training flexibility in dealing with additive situations. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2024.101902
title: Ten-session small-group training on restructuring additive situations without word problem solving
description: A training program comprising "ten 40–50 min small-group sessions over five weeks", delivered by pre-service teachers following a script and piloted with four students from another school. It contained learning activities on difference sets, the Dynamization Strategy, and the Inversion Strategy, moving from verifying and matching statements about given situations to generating different descriptions of given situations. Crucially, "No word problems were solved during the training", meaning students did not encounter word problems in their typical form and were not asked to write equations or calculate; learners instead contrasted and analyzed features of given statements collaboratively, explaining differences and commonalities between statements such as symmetrical relational statements.
requirements: Pre-service tutors followed a script outlining content, procedure, and duration of activities as well as wording options for student support; specific care was taken to support learners with low language skills regarding the linguistic challenges of the re-wording approach
constraints: The training deliberately excluded word problem solving, equation writing, and calculation, so it targets restructuring of situation models only; it was evaluated as a feasibility study with a neutral control group
target_learners: grade 2 students in German primary schools, grouped in small groups of six per classroom with heterogeneous language skills
target_learning_goals: restructuring situation models of additive one-step word problems
generating and comparing different perspectives on given situations
examples: One activity type involved verifying if a statement corresponds to a given situation; another involved matching a statement with several given situations; in the second half learners generated different descriptions of given situations
key_sources: Laura Gabler, Stefan Ufer. (2024). Training flexibility in dealing with additive situations. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2024.101902

article_title: Role of home math environment in the intergenerational transmission of math skills
citation: Torppa, M., Psyridou, M., Khanolainen, D., Koponen, T., & Salminen, J. (2025). Role of home math environment in the intergenerational transmission of math skills. Learning and Instruction, 97, Article 102080. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102080
title: Home Numeracy Model: formal vs. informal home math activities as distinct categories
description: The Home Numeracy Model (Skwarchuk et al., 2014), adopted in this study, divides math-related parent–child interactions into two categories. Formal activities are instructional, with the "purposeful aim of parents teaching math content to their children," such as counting objects or printing numbers. Informal activities are playful or real-world tasks in which math content is incidentally present, such as playing board games or measuring ingredients while cooking. The study adopted this categorization because it was empirically well fitted to the data structure and enables comparison with previous research.
requirements: Parental self-report questionnaires on frequency of shared math-related activities, rated on a Likert scale from 1 (not at all or rarely) to 5 (several times a day)
constraints: The authors acknowledge that assessment of HME is very intricate and this categorization is a simplified representation of the complex nature of HME
target_learning_goals: Early arithmetic fluency development
examples: In this study, factor analyses identified one formal and one informal HME factor at age 2, and three factors (formal, games, everyday activities) at age 5 and Grade 1
key_sources: Torppa, M., Psyridou, M., Khanolainen, D., Koponen, T., & Salminen, J. (2025). Role of home math environment in the intergenerational transmission of math skills. Learning and Instruction, 97, Article 102080. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102080

article_title: Role of home math environment in the intergenerational transmission of math skills
citation: Torppa, M., Psyridou, M., Khanolainen, D., Koponen, T., & Salminen, J. (2025). Role of home math environment in the intergenerational transmission of math skills. Learning and Instruction, 97, Article 102080. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102080
title: Formal math teaching activities at home can alleviate familial risk for children of parents with lower math skills
description: The study concludes that teaching activities at home have the potential to alleviate familial risk for children whose parents have lower math skills. For children at risk of developing math difficulties because of parental math difficulties, it was beneficial to support development via formal activities, "such as showing how objects are calculated or teaching how to count." The protective effect was strongest when formal activities occurred before school entry (ages 2 and 5).
requirements: Formal home math activities provided particularly before school entry, targeting children at higher familial risk
constraints: The protective effect of formal HME was smaller at school age; among lower-risk children, more formal HME was associated with worse performance
target_learners: Children at familial risk of math difficulties due to parental math difficulties, ages 2–9
target_learning_goals: Arithmetic fluency in early grades
examples: Higher-risk children with higher levels of formal HME before school entry had better arithmetic skills than higher-risk children with less formal HME
key_sources: Torppa, M., Psyridou, M., Khanolainen, D., Koponen, T., & Salminen, J. (2025). Role of home math environment in the intergenerational transmission of math skills. Learning and Instruction, 97, Article 102080. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102080

article_title: Cognitive load theory: implications of cognitive load theory on the design of learning
citation: Kirschner, P.A. (2002). Cognitive load theory: implications of cognitive load theory on the design of learning. https://dspace.library.uu.nl/handle/1874/16884
title: Cognitive load theory's cognitive architecture: limited working memory with partly independent visual and audio units interacting with unlimited long-term memory
description: The editorial presents the cognitive architecture on which cognitive load theory is based. As printed, it "is based on a cognitive architecture that consists of a limited working memory, with partly independent processing units for visual and audio information, which interacts with an unlimited long-term memory." This architecture grounds the special issue's instructional implications, framing why instruction must manage load across modality-specific channels and why long-term memory schemata offset working-memory limits.
requirements: Instructional designs derived from the theory must respect the limited capacity of working memory and its partly independent visual and audio processing units
target_learners: learners generally, across the domains covered in the special issue
target_learning_goals: optimising intellectual performance through load-managed instruction
examples: The editorial uses this architecture to introduce six articles on instructional techniques for managing cognitive load
key_sources: Kirschner, P.A. (2002). Cognitive load theory: implications of cognitive load theory on the design of learning. https://dspace.library.uu.nl/handle/1874/16884

article_title: Cognitive load theory: implications of cognitive load theory on the design of learning
citation: Kirschner, P.A. (2002). Cognitive load theory: implications of cognitive load theory on the design of learning. https://dspace.library.uu.nl/handle/1874/16884
title: Present information in ways that encourage learner activities that optimise intellectual performance
description: The editorial frames cognitive load theory as a source of presentation guidelines for instruction. It states that "Cognitive load theory (CLT) can provide guidelines to assist in the presentation of information in a manner that encourages learner activities that optimise intellectual performance." The principle directs designers to arrange information presentation so that learner activity is channeled productively rather than wasted on extraneous load, and the special issue articles instantiate this for worked examples, multimedia, and CSCL.
requirements: Designers need an analysis of which learner activities the presentation induces and how these relate to working-memory load
target_learners: learners generally, across the domains covered in the special issue
target_learning_goals: optimising intellectual performance through information presentation
examples: The special issue applies the principle to worked examples, example elaboration training, high element interactivity material, older learners, multimedia learning, and CSCL external representations
key_sources: Kirschner, P.A. (2002). Cognitive load theory: implications of cognitive load theory on the design of learning. https://dspace.library.uu.nl/handle/1874/16884

article_title: Cognitive load theory: implications of cognitive load theory on the design of learning
citation: Kirschner, P.A. (2002). Cognitive load theory: implications of cognitive load theory on the design of learning. https://dspace.library.uu.nl/handle/1874/16884
title: A cognitive theory of multimedia learning (Mayer & Moreno)
description: The editorial announces that the special issue includes "a cognitive theory of multimedia learning (Mayer & Moreno)". Within the issue's framing, this theory addresses how multimedia instruction relates to the cognitive architecture of limited working memory with partly independent visual and audio processing units, making modality-relevant presentation a central design concern. The editorial itself does not describe the theory's mechanisms beyond naming it as part of the issue's coverage.
requirements: A multimedia learning theory under this framing must connect presentation formats to the load limits of working memory
constraints: The editorial names the theory but does not describe its content
target_learners: learners generally, across the domains covered in the special issue
target_learning_goals: learning from multimedia presentations under working-memory constraints
examples: The special issue includes the Mayer and Moreno article on a cognitive theory of multimedia learning
key_sources: Kirschner, P.A. (2002). Cognitive load theory: implications of cognitive load theory on the design of learning. https://dspace.library.uu.nl/handle/1874/16884

article_title: Evaluating and diversifying philosophy education
citation: Timmenga, F., & van der Zande, I. (2026). Evaluating and diversifying philosophy education. Learning and Instruction, 104, 102369. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2026.102369
title: Facilitate encounters with philosophical difference carefully to prevent disorientation
description: The article reports that philosophy teachers cautioned that exposing students to diverse perspectives requires deliberate facilitation. Teachers "cautioned that encounters with difference can be disorienting if not carefully facilitated, emphasizing the need for balance." The principle holds that educators designing intercultural or diversifying learning experiences should balance exposure to difference with careful facilitation so that encounters remain productive rather than disorienting.
requirements: Careful facilitation of encounters with difference, as emphasized by the teachers interviewed
constraints: Encounters with difference can be disorienting if not carefully facilitated
target_learning_goals: critical reflection
responsible engagement with difference
examples: Teachers in the study described balancing intellectual development, transformative education, and engagement with philosophical diversity in their pedagogical approaches.
key_sources: Timmenga, F., & van der Zande, I. (2026). Evaluating and diversifying philosophy education. Learning and Instruction, 104, 102369. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2026.102369

article_title: Examining myside bias on a controversial historical event after engagement in dialogic argumentation: Insights from a think aloud study
citation: Iordanou, K., Fotiou, C., Manoli, A., & Zembylas, M. (2025). Examining myside bias on a controversial historical event after engagement in dialogic argumentation: Insights from a think aloud study. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102209
title: Think-aloud methodology as a tool for identifying myside bias and the conditions that facilitate or impede its change
description: The article proposes the think-aloud methodology, in which participants read sentence-by-sentence flashcards and verbalize thoughts and feelings, as a way to assess myside bias during reading rather than only in argument generation or evaluation tasks. It argues the method captures not just final judgments but the reasoning behind them, and that "it uncovers when and under which conditions myside bias occurs, changes, or fails to change." The study applied it pre- and post-intervention with authentic biased historical texts.
requirements: Participants must be able to meet the demands of thinking aloud while reading; in this study teachers selected students on that criterion.
constraints: Assessed myside bias for one ethnic community's students on one controversial historical event; the method was previously validated for this purpose in an adult sample.
target_learning_goals: reasoning and myside bias during reading of conflicting historical accounts
examples: Pre- and post-intervention think-aloud sessions of 20-25 minutes with flashcards of sentences from Greek-Cypriot and Turkish-Cypriot historian texts, coded with an adapted reading-comprehension scheme (inter-rater κ = 0.849).
key_sources: Iordanou, K., Fotiou, C., Manoli, A., & Zembylas, M. (2025). Examining myside bias on a controversial historical event after engagement in dialogic argumentation: Insights from a think aloud study. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102209

article_title: Examining myside bias on a controversial historical event after engagement in dialogic argumentation: Insights from a think aloud study
citation: Iordanou, K., Fotiou, C., Manoli, A., & Zembylas, M. (2025). Examining myside bias on a controversial historical event after engagement in dialogic argumentation: Insights from a think aloud study. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102209
title: Expose learners to the other side's narrative, authentically expressed by its representatives, to foster understanding of and empathy toward the other side
description: The principle holds that engaging with an alternative position, even through a text written by individuals who hold it, is a facilitative condition for understanding the other side and reflecting on one's own position. The article reports that "Being exposed to the narrative of the “other-side,” as authentically expressed by its representatives, appears to be a facilitative condition for understanding the “other-side” and showing empathy toward the “other-side.”" It extends prior work on hearing opposing arguments to engagement via authentic texts.
requirements: The alternative account should authentically represent the other side's position, written by members of that group.
constraints: Exposure evoked understanding and self-reflection but did not eliminate myside bias; evaluative comments remained in favor of students' own position.
target_learners: elementary school students in ethnically divided contexts
target_learning_goals: understanding of the other side's perspective, empathy, self-reflection on one's own position
examples: Students read a Turkish-Cypriot historian's account of the 1974 war; against-own-side comments doubled and own-side support halved at post-test when reading it.
key_sources: Iordanou, K., Fotiou, C., Manoli, A., & Zembylas, M. (2025). Examining myside bias on a controversial historical event after engagement in dialogic argumentation: Insights from a think aloud study. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102209

article_title: Need-supportive teaching and student engagement in the classroom: Comparing the additive, synergistic, and global contributions
citation: Olivier, E., Galand, B., Morin, A., & Hospel, V. (2021). Need-supportive teaching and student engagement in the classroom: Comparing the additive, synergistic, and global contributions. Learning and Instruction, 71, 101389. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2020.101389
title: Global need-supportive teaching configuration: engagement depends on the global level across autonomy support, structure, and involvement
description: This framework holds that classroom engagement is best supported not by each need-supportive practice separately (additive) nor by their combination at high levels (synergistic), but by the overall level a teacher provides across autonomy support, structure, and involvement, "captured by a global factor". The study tested this against two rival configurations using multilevel analyses and found the global account optimal, with imbalance factors playing a secondary role.
requirements: Teachers must provide measurable levels of autonomy support, structure, and involvement that can be modeled as a global factor across practices
constraints: Evidence comes from 8th grade math classrooms in Belgium; the global factor was supported over additive and synergistic alternatives in this setting
target_learners: 8th grade students in secondary mathematics classrooms
target_learning_goals: behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement in the classroom
examples: Multilevel analyses among 1,193 8th grade Belgian students nested in 57 math classrooms contrasted the three configurations of teacher need-supporting practices.
key_sources: Olivier, E., Galand, B., Morin, A., & Hospel, V. (2021). Need-supportive teaching and student engagement in the classroom: Comparing the additive, synergistic, and global contributions. Learning and Instruction, 71, 101389. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2020.101389

article_title: Contrasting orthographically similar words facilitates adult second language vocabulary learning
citation: Baxter, P.A.; Bekkering, H.; Dijkstra, A.F.J.; Droop, W.; Hurk, M.M. van den; Léoné, F.T.M. (2022). Contrasting orthographically similar words facilitates adult second language vocabulary learning. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101582
title: Representational specification account of similarity and contrasting in L2 vocabulary learning
description: The article proposes that new L2 word representations are initially underspecified and that similarity between items sharpens them: "representations sharpen over time, allowing learners to make increased distinctions between words as vocabulary grows." Contrasting tasks draw attention to distinctive lexical information, enabling more specific form and form-meaning representations. The account yields three hypotheses: contrasting as a general desirable difficulty, direction-dependent effects, and benefits only for underspecified (new L2) dimensions.
requirements: Learners must encounter similar items whose representations are not yet fully specified, so that attention to distinctive information drives sharpening
constraints: Form and meaning similarity mainly cause errors while representations are still underspecified; once stabilized, similarity should no longer confuse learners
target_learning_goals: L2 vocabulary acquisition and form-meaning linking
examples: Experiment 1 contrasted orthographically or semantically similar L2 words via sorted versus shuffled multiple-choice triplets with identical word lists across conditions
key_sources: Baxter, P.A.; Bekkering, H.; Dijkstra, A.F.J.; Droop, W.; Hurk, M.M. van den; Léoné, F.T.M. (2022). Contrasting orthographically similar words facilitates adult second language vocabulary learning. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101582

article_title: Contrasting orthographically similar words facilitates adult second language vocabulary learning
citation: Baxter, P.A.; Bekkering, H.; Dijkstra, A.F.J.; Droop, W.; Hurk, M.M. van den; Léoné, F.T.M. (2022). Contrasting orthographically similar words facilitates adult second language vocabulary learning. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101582
title: Multiple-choice contrasting task with sorted/shuffled word-list shuffling system
description: A multiple-choice vocabulary learning task in which learners select the correct translation among three options and receive feedback. A shuffling system creates a sorted condition, where triplets contain similar answer options inducing contrasting, and a shuffled condition with dissimilar options. Crucially, "we used a shuffling system that enabled the words to be learned to be identical across conditions, eliminating list effects as an explanation during group comparison." The task includes repeated retrieval (a testing effect) and can test learning in both productive and receptive directions.
requirements: Triplets must be constructed so sorted and shuffled conditions contain exactly the same words, avoiding word or list confounds
constraints: Participants were instructed to avoid their own learning strategies, and a response time limit limited conscious association strategies
target_learning_goals: L2 vocabulary form-meaning acquisition in productive and receptive directions
examples: Experiment 1 used 75 words in orthographically similar, semantically similar, and fully dissimilar conditions, six blocks of 75 trials with feedback highlighting correct translations in green
key_sources: Baxter, P.A.; Bekkering, H.; Dijkstra, A.F.J.; Droop, W.; Hurk, M.M. van den; Léoné, F.T.M. (2022). Contrasting orthographically similar words facilitates adult second language vocabulary learning. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101582

article_title: Contrasting orthographically similar words facilitates adult second language vocabulary learning
citation: Baxter, P.A.; Bekkering, H.; Dijkstra, A.F.J.; Droop, W.; Hurk, M.M. van den; Léoné, F.T.M. (2022). Contrasting orthographically similar words facilitates adult second language vocabulary learning. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101582
title: Use contrasting of orthographically similar new L2 words to sharpen form representations
description: When teaching new L2 vocabulary, present orthographically similar words together so learners must contrast them, because contrasting "underspecified representations serves as a learning mechanism that guides attention to relevant lexical information." In Experiment 1 this improved recall of orthographically similar words and made errors more target-like. The benefit is dimension-specific: it applied to orthographically similar L2 words, not semantically similar ones, and appeared in recall rather than recognition.
requirements: The contrasted words should be new, underspecified L2 forms whose distinctive features learners must attend to
constraints: The benefit appeared in recall posttests but not recognition, and contrasting lowered accuracy during the learning phase itself
target_learning_goals: productive L2 vocabulary recall and representational specificity
examples: Participants in the sorted condition saw triplets of orthographically similar pseudowords (e.g., maximum Levenshtein distance 2) as answer options and had to carefully compare them to select the correct translation
key_sources: Baxter, P.A.; Bekkering, H.; Dijkstra, A.F.J.; Droop, W.; Hurk, M.M. van den; Léoné, F.T.M. (2022). Contrasting orthographically similar words facilitates adult second language vocabulary learning. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101582

article_title: Reading comprehension resiliency in adolescents with and without dyslexia relates to vocabulary, listening comprehension and socioeconomic status
citation: Lefèvre, E., Law, J. M., Prado, J., Anders, R., & Cavalli, E. (2024). Reading Comprehension Resiliency in Adolescents with and without Dyslexia relates to Vocabulary, Listening Comprehension and Socioeconomic Status. https://osf.io/fzyeh/?view_only=84fc51248a0d48ba9a505835e525efdc
title: Double mediation model of reading comprehension resiliency linking SES, vocabulary, listening comprehension and RCR
description: The article proposes and tests a double mediation model in which "the relationship between SES and listening comprehension is mediated by vocabulary", and "the direct effect of vocabulary on RCR is mediated by listening comprehension". RCR is operationalized as a continuous index computed by subtracting standardized reading fluency from standardized reading comprehension, so positive values reflect high comprehension despite low fluency. The fitted model retained direct paths and showed excellent fit on standard SEM diagnostics.
requirements: Assessment of vocabulary, listening comprehension, reading fluency and reading comprehension on comparable standardized scales
A sample large enough for the number of estimated path parameters (the article cites a 10-observations-per-parameter minimum)
constraints: The design is correlational and cross-sectional, so the model supports no causal claims; alternative models could also fit the findings
The sample over-represents individuals with dyslexia relative to the general population, limiting generalisability
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension development
Vocabulary and listening comprehension as semantic supports for reading
examples: A path analysis on 95 French adolescents fit the double mediation model with excellent SEM diagnostics (X² = 0.02, p = .89; CFI = 1.00), and bootstrapped standard errors (n = 3000) replicated the initial results

title: Control-value theory of achievement emotions extended to e-learning
description: The control-value theory (CVT) is an integrative framework describing interrelations between achievement emotions, their antecedents, and outcomes. It defines achievement emotions as "those emotions which are felt in relation to learning activities and outcomes", organized by valence and activation into four categories (e.g., positive activating emotions such as enjoyment; negative deactivating emotions such as boredom). It differentiates proximal individual antecedents such as control appraisals and self-efficacy, which act directly, from distal environmental antecedents such as cognitive and motivational quality of tasks, which act through mediation, and proposes the relative universality of these links across individuals, genders, areas of study, and cultures. This study tested and largely confirmed the CVT's mediation structure for e-learning during the COVID-19 pandemic.

constraints: Cross-country comparability was limited: only configural invariance held across the 13 countries

citation: Jacobson, Michael, Goldwater, Micah, Markauskaite, Lina, Lai, Polly, Kapur, Manu, Roberts, Gareth, & Hilton, Courtney. (2020). Schema abstraction with productive failure and analogical comparison: Learning designs for far across domain transfer. Learning and Instruction, 65, Article number: 101222. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2019.101222
title: Hybrid productive failure with analogical comparison: schema abstraction through comparing contrasting models
description: The article proposes a hybrid learning design that combines productive failure's two phases (Exploration and Generation, then Consolidation and Knowledge Assembly) with analogical comparison scaffolds. In the exploration phase students compare two highly contrasting computer models that share deep structure, which the authors argue activates structural prior knowledge so that teacher-led consolidation elicits "the cognitive process of schema abstraction" and assembly of new knowledge. The design was operationalized as the Two Models condition, where students "were instructed (i.e., scaffolded) to write out similarities and differences of the models" across climate and non-climate domains.
requirements: Two computer models implementing the same underlying complexity principles but from contrasting surface domains
Explicit scaffolding prompting students to write out similarities and differences between the models
A teacher-led consolidation phase presenting correct solutions and targeted concepts
constraints: The study included no non-PF and no non-computer-model control conditions, so the design's advantage over those alternatives is not tested here
The schema abstraction account is the authors' proposed explanation for the far transfer finding, not a directly measured process
target_learning_goals: weather and climate concepts
complex systems principles such as feedback, emergence, and tipping points
far across domain transfer of structural concepts
examples: Two Models Group students compared the Day 3 Climate with Feedback model with the Ants Foraging model, which shared "the deep structure conceptual similarity of feedback in dynamic systems" while differing in surface features

title: Scaffold comparison of two contrasting-domain models during productive failure exploration to foster far across domain transfer
description: When learners explore problems with productive failure, pairing the target-domain model with an analog model from a different domain and explicitly scaffolding learners to write out the models' similarities and differences can foster far across domain transfer without harming domain knowledge. The article grounds this in evidence that "without explicit instruction to write out similarities, learners often will not deeply compare pairs of analog cases", and in its finding that the scaffolded two-model comparison group outperformed the single-model group on far transfer while matching it on knowledge and near transfer.
requirements: Analog models that implement the same underlying principles as the target-domain model
Explicit comparison scaffolds (writing similarities and differences), since unscaffolded comparison is often shallow
Equal instructional time and identical consolidation scripts across conditions
constraints: The far transfer advantage emerged on a posttest-only item; knowledge and near transfer showed no condition differences
The comparison scaffold was tested with ninth-grade students in an all-girls high-achieving school using NetLogo models
target_learning_goals: far across domain transfer of complex systems principles
climate change understanding
examples: The Two Models Group used four non-climate NetLogo analog models (Wolf-Sheep Predation, Ants Foraging, Birds Flocking, Forest Fire) alongside the climate models and wrote out model similarities and differences each day

article_title: Teacher self-efficacy and burnout: Determining the directions of prediction through an autoregressive cross-lagged panel model.
citation: Kim, Lisa E. and Burić, Irena. (2020). Teacher self-efficacy and burnout: Determining the directions of prediction through an autoregressive cross-lagged panel model. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000424
title: Conservation of Resources theory account of the TSE–burnout relationship
description: The article uses Hobfoll's (1989) Conservation of Resources theory to explain why burnout may precede low self-efficacy rather than only the reverse. Under this account, "prolonged exposure to stressors (e.g., lack of collegiality) results in resource depletion, which can be manifested as burnout symptoms," and depleted resources hinder confidence and self-efficacy. The theory also permits the reverse cycle: exhausted, disengaged individuals are less able to restore personal resources, perpetuating a cycle in which low-resource teachers concurrently experience exhaustion, disengagement, and low self-efficacy. The article presents this theory as the framework consistent with its finding that burnout predicts future TSE.
requirements: The account presupposes that individuals strive to obtain, conserve, and build resources for their positive well-being, and that prolonged stressor exposure occurs without resource replacement
constraints: The theory is offered as an interpretation of the observed cross-lagged paths, not as a mechanism directly tested in the study
target_learners: teachers across elementary, middle, and secondary educational levels
target_learning_goals: understanding the directional relationship between teacher well-being (burnout) and teacher self-efficacy beliefs
examples: The article invokes the theory in its Discussion to explain why experiencing burnout more strongly colors future TSE levels than TSE colors future burnout levels

title: Teacher scholarship should be selected for its bearing on the situations the high school teacher will meet, centered on adolescents' interests and development.
description: The editorial proposes a standard of teacher scholarship judged by relevance to teaching situations rather than amount or technical elevation. It states the needed scholarship "should be a scholarship that has some bearing upon the situations that the high school teacher will meet," with its center in the interests and activities of adolescent boys and girls. It argues this standard calls for a complete reorganization of the college courses currently recommended for prospective high school teachers.

constraints: The editorial presents this as an argued standard, not a tested result; it offers no empirical evidence for the claim.

examples: The editorial asks what advantage courses in analytical geometry, calculus, the Punic wars, or early English would give a teacher of high school algebra, history, or English, and notes teachers' ignorance of subjects like economics, sociology, and ethics that help interpret culture to adolescents.

article_title: Silver linings and storm clouds: Divergent profiles of student momentary engagement emerge in response to the same task.
citation: Symonds, J. E., Schreiber, J. B., & Torsney, B. M. (2021). Silver linings and storm clouds: Divergent profiles of momentary engagement emerge in response to the same task. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000605
title: Momentary task engagement as a dynamic system of emotion, cognition, agency and behavior at micro-level grain size
description: The article frames momentary task engagement as a multidimensional construct with affective-motivational, cognitive and behavioral components, occurring at the "micro-level grain size of momentary time, at the micro-level grain size of a specific task, and at the micro-level grain size of individual student experiences". It proposes that momentary engagement "is proposed to operate as a rapid, non-linear dynamic system where motivation, emotion, and mental and physical action continually shape and are shaped by the emergent property of engagement as they co-act in context". The framework motivates person-oriented latent profile analysis, since components can co-act divergently within one student during one task. Its opposite, momentary disaffection, includes inattention, negative academic emotions, and disengagement as a behavioral indicator.
requirements: Data collected at the micro-level grain size of a single task and momentary time, measuring at least two engagement dimensions
constraints: The system responds sensitively to task context and setting, so patterns and predictors are task specific rather than general across tasks
target_learning_goals: Momentary engagement and disaffection during academic classwork
examples: The study operationalized the framework with self-reported emotional and cognitive engagement and observed on-task behavior during one ten-minute literacy task

title: Class composition effects framework
description: The article organizes its inquiry around composition effects, which "occur when individual student characteristics (e.g., individual academic achievement) are combined into a class-level composite score (e.g., mean academic achievement) and that score is related to individual-level outcomes (e.g., academic achievement) beyond student-level characteristic." The framework spans mean-level composition (achievement, interest) and within-class heterogeneity dimensions, tested at the classroom level with individual-level outcomes, and extended to motivational composition and learning-environment mediators. It guides the study's hypotheses about who benefits from which composition.
requirements: Class-level composites must be estimated beyond student-level characteristics (e.g., subtracting individual prior achievement) to isolate composition effects and avoid phantom effects.
constraints: The study focuses on classmates, since in German secondary schooling the class is the most proximal school-related developmental context.

subject-specific academic interest

title: Social contagion account of motivational composition effects
description: The article draws on social contagion theory to explain motivational composition effects: "Social contagion describes the transmission of psychological characteristics (e.g., attitudes, behaviors, motivation) among individuals in a network (Levy & Nail, 1993)." In class settings, contagion may emerge through interactions that convey and reinforce motivation, such as discussing a topic and asking thought-provoking questions in classes with higher average interest. The account is linked to self-determination theory via feelings of relatedness and to vicarious experiences (Bandura), and predicts that adolescents may adjust their own interest to conform to the class norm.
requirements: Peer interactions that convey and reinforce motivation, which are presumed more frequent in language lessons involving collaborative work with a range of classmates.
constraints: The article notes an alternative mechanism: students with similar interest levels may group together and reinforce each other's initial levels, so heterogeneity in interest may not raise individual interest.
target_learning_goals: subject-specific academic interest development
examples: The article cites King and Mendoza's findings that classmates' goal orientations predicted individual students' goal orientations months later as empirical support for motivational composition effects.

title: MoMa (Motivation in Mathematics) 90-minute classroom-based relevance intervention
description: MoMa is a 90-minute classroom-based relevance intervention for ninth-grade academic-track math students in Germany. "The 90-min intervention consists of a psychoeducational presentation for the whole class and relevance-inducing reflection tasks, on which students work individually." The presentation covers research on effort and self-concept in math achievement (targeting growth mindsets and inoculating against backfire effects for low-expectancy students) and examples of mathematics' utility across life domains; students then evaluate six interview quotations from young adults about the usefulness of mathematics for personal relevance. Materials were optimized from the efficacy trial (e.g., traffic-light cards as ice-breaker, take-home message slides, updated daily-life examples).
requirements: A trained deliverer (master's student or teacher) who received the intervention materials including a lesson plan, PowerPoint slides, and a script with detailed notes for the presentation
constraints: Developed for ninth-grade academic track students in Germany; the waitlist control had no access to materials to limit diffusion
target_learning_goals: perceived utility value of mathematics
growth mindsets about math ability
mathematics achievement
examples: In the effectiveness trial, 28 classes received MoMa from master's students and 25 from their regular math teachers after brief training; observers noted only very few severe deviations from the standardized procedure across 15 pre-defined phases

title: Expectancy-value theory as the grounding framework for relevance interventions
description: The article grounds relevance interventions in Eccles et al.'s expectancy-value theory, in which students' academic behavior and choices are predicted by expectancies for success and the value they attach to tasks. "Eccles and colleagues (1983) distinguish four major components that contribute to subjective task value": intrinsic value, attainment value, and utility value contribute positively, while cost contributes negatively. Recent work decomposes these into subfacets (e.g., utility value by life domain and time horizon; cost into effort, emotional, and opportunity cost). Utility value is targeted by interventions because it is assumed more malleable than attainment and intrinsic value.
requirements: Interventions targeting value should account for the interplay of expectancies and values, since the highest outcomes are predicted when both are high
constraints: The article uses the term expectancies to cover self-concept and self-efficacy, which differ in malleability and frame-of-reference sensitivity
target_learning_goals: academic motivation in mathematics
subjective task value
examples: The MoMa intervention logic model (Figure 1) details intervention components triggering expectancies, mindsets, and utility value, which should ultimately enhance achievement

title: Combine direct communication of utility value with relevance-inducing reflection tasks and an expectancy component to reach more students
description: The article argues that neither intervention approach alone serves all students: directly communicating utility value benefits students with high interest or expectancies but can backfire for students with low expectancies, whereas relevance-inducing reflection tasks particularly benefit students with low expectancies. It therefore recommends that "One potential approach might be to combine the communication of utility value with relevance-inducing reflection tasks" and to add an expectancy component such as a growth-mindset element, so that as many students as possible benefit. MoMa operationalizes this by pairing a utility-communication presentation with individual reflection tasks and an effort/mindset segment.
requirements: An expectancy component (e.g., emphasizing effort over talent) to prevent utility communication from backfiring for students with low expectancies
constraints: Directly communicated utility value alone can undermine interest and performance for students with low expectancies, per prior lab studies the article cites
target_learners: secondary school students in mathematics classrooms
target_learning_goals: perceived relevance and utility value of school content
expectancies for success
examples: MoMa's psychoeducational presentation first inoculates students against negative effects of relevance highlighting for low-expectancy students, then presents utility examples, followed by individual quotation-evaluation reflection tasks

article_title: Validation processes and reading purpose: Is validation against knowledge and prior text influenced by reading goal?
citation: Moort, M. L. van, Koornneef, A. W., Wilderjans, T. F., & Broek, P. W. van den. (2022). Validation processes and reading purpose: Is validation against knowledge and prior text influenced by reading goal? Journal of Educational Psychology, 114(7), 1533-1552. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000769
title: Two-component architecture of validation: coherence-detection and postdetection epistemic elaboration
description: The article describes theoretical models of validation that assume distinct components: a coherence-detection component involved in detecting (in)consistencies, and a postdetection processing component involving optional epistemic elaboration to resolve inconsistencies. The coherence-detection component is described as "a routine part of comprehension" that is "memory-based, pose little demands on cognitive resources, and are not dependent on readers' goals." Postdetection elaboration processes are "slow, resource-demanding and under strategic control of the reader." Two named models instantiate this architecture: the RI-Val model (resonance, integration, validation) and the two-step model of validation (epistemic monitoring followed by epistemic elaboration).
requirements: Incoming information must be validated against a reader's evolving situation model comprising both textual and world knowledge information
constraints: The coherence-detection component is assumed to be passive and not under strategic control of the reader
Epistemic elaboration only occurs when readers are motivated and have enough cognitive resources available
target_learning_goals: Monitoring text coherence and accuracy during reading
Building accurate mental representations of text content
examples: The study tested predictions from this architecture by examining whether reading goals modulate coherence-detection (they did not) versus postdetection representation-building (they did, for congruent targets)

article_title: Age norms of psycho-motor capacity.
citation: Wallin, J. E. W. (1915). Age Norms of Psycho-Motor Capacity. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://search.worldcat.org/search?q=Age+Norms+of+Psycho-Motor+Capacity
title: Age norms of psycho-motor capacity and the psycho-motor versus motor test distinction
description: The article defines a normal age norm of psycho-motor capacity as the average quantitative or qualitative score made by normal children of a given chronological age when incited to best effort on a task requiring both muscular movement and "the ability to make the basic intellectual analyses and comparisons." It distinguishes motor tests, which depend primarily on neuro-muscular qualities, from psycho-motor tests, which also demand sensory discrimination, association, memory for relationships, and adaptation to novel situations. Psycho-motor tests are held more valuable for grading mental development because they measure intelligence as well as motor ability.
requirements: Norms must be based on selected groups of normal children, since norms from unselected groups would likely be too low because there are more subnormal than supernormal children.
constraints: The author acknowledges it is impossible to draw an absolutely fixed and sharp line between motor and psycho-motor tests.
target_learners: children of chronological ages two to seventeen
children of varying ability levels including bright, average, dull, feeble-minded, and epileptic
target_learning_goals: assessment of mental capacity and psycho-motor development
examples: The modified Seguin form board (Stoelting's Catalogue Number 78,002), requiring discrimination of ten detached insets, association of forms with recesses, memorization of locations, and quick accurate insertion.

title: Construct graded developmental scales with norm step size matched to age, using semi-yearly norms for young children
description: The article recommends constructing graded scales of intellectual or motor development by establishing norms separately for numerous individual traits, with the lower end based on children who can just barely do the test and the upper end extended to ages where additional improvement ceases. Step size should vary with age: "It is advisable to utilize semi-yearly norms up to about the age of 8. From about 8 to 12 yearly norms and from 12 to 17 bi-yearly" norms, because yearly steps are too large at lower ages.
requirements: Scales must be based on performance of children so young they can just barely do the test at the lower end, and extended to individuals so old that increased age shows no additional improvement.
constraints: No data are available after age 17, so the recommendation covers ages up to 17 only.
target_learning_goals: accurate classification of developmental level on individual mental and motor traits
examples: The author established both whole-yearly (Graph I) and half-yearly (Graph II) norms for the form board, with half-yearly norms constructed so no child varies more than three months from his age classification.

article_title: Methods and results of a class experiment in learning.
citation: Dearborn, W. F., and Brewer, J. M. (1918). Methods and Results of a Class Experiment in Learning. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Vol. IX, No. 2. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu/9/2/
title: Classification of individual learning curves by initial rapidity of progress: convex, concave, and rectilinear types, with plateaus common in code learning
description: From individually plotted practice curves, the article classifies learning curves "on the basis of the rapidity of the initial progress into three groups": rapid initial rise with slower later progress (convex to base line), slow initial progress with later acceleration (concave), and rectilinear even progress. The prevailing type in the code practice "approximates the rectilinear with a tendency to a small initial acceleration," and plateaus were very common and of longer duration than in digit-letter substitution practice. The article uses this taxonomy to illustrate characteristics of the learning curve in class experiments.
requirements: A practice series of sufficient trials plotted individually by each student on cross-section paper, as the class did for the twenty-two code trials.
constraints: The classification is described as rough, and the article notes initial gains were less marked in code learning than in digit-letter substitution because the associations to be formed were more difficult.
target_learning_goals: understanding of learning curves, individual differences, and effects of practice
examples: Plates I to IV reproduce characteristic curves selected from the students' own graphs, including curves with frequent fluctuations or ups and downs.

article_title: Methods and results of a class experiment in learning.
citation: Dearborn, W. F., and Brewer, J. M. (1918). Methods and Results of a Class Experiment in Learning. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Vol. IX, No. 2. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu/9/2/
title: Class experiment pattern: a practiced class and unpracticed control classes taking identical pre- and post-tests to study practice, transfer, and interference
description: The article demonstrates a class experiment in which one class practices a skill (translating English into a code) for twenty-two trials while control classes take the same five tests without intervening practice, twelve working days apart. Students plot their own learning curves, compute percentage gains, compare morning and evening performances, and write discussions of transfer and interference. The design lets a class illustrate individual differences, learning-curve characteristics, correlation, and facilitation or interference, with the article noting that "An unpracticed or control group is needed in order to test this question."
requirements: Test intervals should be the same in all groups; the article notes circumstances made this impossible in the present experiment, with intervals of sixteen, nine, and nineteen calendar days.
constraints: Materials must be tasks in which the student is not already practiced and in which improvement is possible within a relatively short practice; the article calls the tasks used artificial and recommends more useful ones.
target_learning_goals: understanding of practice effects, transfer, interference, and experimental method
examples: The practiced class in educational psychology was practiced twenty-two times in the use of a code between the two administrations of the five tests, while classes in teaching and school administration took the tests without intervening practice.

article_title: Massed vs. Distributed Effort in Learning.
citation: Pechstein, L. A. (1921). Massed vs. Distributed Effort in Learning. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0070137
title: Elimination and mechanization as the two principles explaining when massed or distributed effort is efficient
description: The article explains its findings through two learning principles. The principle of elimination "connotes the detection of critical points in the problem, the careful study of all the details, the formation of proper associations, the rejection of others"; it operates with maximum effectiveness on short, easy problems under massed effort but ceases to operate efficiently when massed effort strains the organism on a long, hard problem. The principle of mechanization renders the activity habitual; whole-method learning delays and repeatedly nullifies it by re-injecting the conscious eliminative principle, while the part method lets each operate in turn, provided effort is massed.
requirements: The part method must be combined with massed effort for full utilization of both principles
constraints: The explanation is offered for motor learning of the maze type; the author states the results hold for selected animals and the human adult in that domain
target_learning_goals: motor maze learning
formation of serial unit habits
examples: The author explains that massed practice on short units builds habits of long application, which is exactly what the complex act of connection requires
