citation: Hall-Quest, Alfred L. (1918). Present Tendencies in Educational Psychology. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ
title: Educational psychology as a distinct experimental science whose standard course takes the learning process as its backbone
description: The article argues that educational psychology deserves status as a distinct discipline because education is a significant field of application of psychological truth, comparing it to agriculture: "Experimental pedagogy is just as important and just as possible as experimental farming." It holds that the learning process should form the backbone of standard courses, studied experimentally rather than a priori, preferably in the school system, with constant application in laboratories or schools and differentiation of courses by the type of educator being prepared.
requirements: Experiments carried out throughout the entire field of education, ideally under school conditions normal for scientific investigation
Laboratory training of instructors in pedagogical apparatus such as Binet tests before laboratory work is attempted
constraints: The author admits much laboratory work is at present inexact and subject to constant revision, and that mental phenomena elude absolutely exact measurement
Articulating experimentation with the public school system presents difficulties the article acknowledges, though it sees no other wholly adequate means of arriving at pedagogical truth
target_learners: College and university students preparing to be teachers, supervising school officers, normal school instructors, and educational investigators
target_learning_goals: Understanding the laws of the learning process and their experimental investigation
Applying psychological principles to school subjects and teaching methods
examples: Colvin at Brown University paired a one-semester undergraduate course with a practical Introduction to Secondary Teaching course involving observation and slight practice
Kohl of Mount Holyoke presented actual concrete school situations drawn from more than 200 visited high school classes for students to psychologize
key_sources: Hall-Quest, Alfred L. (1918). Present Tendencies in Educational Psychology. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ

article_title: Do children’s executive functions account for associations between early autonomy-supportive parenting and achievement through high school?
citation: Bindman, S. W., Pomerantz, E. M., & Roisman, G. I. (2015). Do Children's Executive Functions Account for Associations Between Early Autonomy-Supportive Parenting and Achievement Through High School? Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000017
title: Self-Determination Theory-based account: autonomy-supportive parenting fosters executive functions via autonomous motivation and practice on challenging activities
description: The article draws on Self-Determination Theory to explain why autonomy-supportive (vs. controlling) parenting may build children's executive functions. It argues that "when parents support children's autonomy rather than attempt to control children, they foster children's fulfillment of the basic need for autonomy," producing autonomous rather than controlled motivation. Autonomously motivated children are proposed to sustain engagement in challenging activities that require executive functions, practicing and strengthening these skills; autonomy support may also foster language skills used in self-talk for inhibition and switching. The study tests this account's prediction that early autonomy support predicts later executive functions and achievement.
requirements: Parenting must be ongoing over time; the article states brief interludes of autonomy support are unlikely to suffice for developing executive functions
constraints: The account is tested with correlational longitudinal data, so causal conclusions are not possible per the article
target_learners: children from infancy through high school
target_learning_goals: executive functions (inhibition, delay of gratification, sustained attention)
academic achievement in math and reading
examples: The study combined observations of autonomy support at 6, 15, 24, and 36 months into a single index, reflecting the argument that support must be ongoing
key_sources: Bindman, S. W., Pomerantz, E. M., & Roisman, G. I. (2015). Do Children's Executive Functions Account for Associations Between Early Autonomy-Supportive Parenting and Achievement Through High School? Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000017

article_title: Do children’s executive functions account for associations between early autonomy-supportive parenting and achievement through high school?
citation: Bindman, S. W., Pomerantz, E. M., & Roisman, G. I. (2015). Do Children's Executive Functions Account for Associations Between Early Autonomy-Supportive Parenting and Achievement Through High School? Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000017
title: Caregivers and educators should support children's autonomy rather than control, because early autonomy support uniquely predicts later executive functions and achievement
description: The article's findings support giving children choice, initiative, and opportunities to solve problems on their own rather than relying on pressure and directives. Autonomy support "over the first 3 years of life predicted enhanced executive functions... and academic achievement in elementary and high school" even after covarying warmth, cognitive stimulation, temperament, and early cognitive skills. Because the design is correlational, the principle is framed as consistent with, not causally proven by, the evidence.
requirements: Support should be sustained over time rather than brief interludes, per the article's argument about ongoing experiences
constraints: The evidence is ultimately correlational; the sample was primarily middle- to upper-middle class, and the article calls for research with lower socioeconomic status families
target_learners: young children (6 months to kindergarten entry)
target_learning_goals: executive function development
long-term academic achievement
examples: Mothers' autonomy support was observed in semi-structured play tasks at 6, 15, 24, and 36 months, coded for flexibility, following children's pace and interests, and allowing children to take the lead
key_sources: Bindman, S. W., Pomerantz, E. M., & Roisman, G. I. (2015). Do Children's Executive Functions Account for Associations Between Early Autonomy-Supportive Parenting and Achievement Through High School? Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000017

article_title: Some observations on the learning of sensible material.
citation: Dell, John A. (1911). Some Observations on the Learning of Sensible Material. Journal of Educational Psychology, 2, 401-406.
title: Rational learning builds associations by similarity with prior knowledge rather than by contiguity, explaining the absence of serial-position effects for sensible material
description: The article proposes a mechanism account contrasting nonsense-syllable learning with the learning of sensible material. With meaningless syllables, connections depend "almost entirely on their contiguity in space or time", which yields the serial-position curve Bolton showed. In rational learning, associations "depend almost entirely on associations by similarity with various facts", many outside the memorized series; the learner builds up concurrent mental series and places each new fact in its correct position in one of them. This account explains why position in the presented series had negligible influence on recall in all three experiments.
requirements: The material must be a series of facts having a rational relation to one another, so learners can connect new facts to pre-existing knowledge by similarity
constraints: The account is offered as the authors' interpretation of the three experiments, not as a separately tested prediction
target_learning_goals: retention of meaningful lesson and lecture content
examples: In the bud lesson, recall tracked subject-matter section rather than the order in which the two forms received the groups of facts
key_sources: Dell, John A. (1911). Some Observations on the Learning of Sensible Material. Journal of Educational Psychology, 2, 401-406. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0074801

article_title: Some observations on the learning of sensible material.
citation: Dell, John A. (1911). Some Observations on the Learning of Sensible Material. Journal of Educational Psychology, 2, 401-406.
title: Do not alter the natural sequence of lesson facts to exploit primacy or recency, because other causes of remembering dominate position
description: The article draws a practical recommendation from its three experiments: although "the beginning and the end of a lesson are the best places for facts which have to be remembered" other things being equal, for rational material other things are generally not equal. Since recall depends on associations by similarity with prior knowledge rather than on serial position, "it is not worth while to alter the natural sequence of the facts in order to bring any particular fact to the beginning or end". Teachers should preserve the logical order of meaningful content instead of reordering it for position effects.
requirements: Applies to sensible material whose facts bear a rational relation to one another; meaningless series behave differently
constraints: The recommendation rests on classroom experiments with schoolboys and on the author's interpretation, not on a direct test of reordering outcomes
target_learning_goals: retention of meaningful lesson and lecture content
examples: The bud lesson was actually taught to two forms with its three groups of facts in different orders, and the reordering made no difference to which section was best remembered
key_sources: Dell, John A. (1911). Some Observations on the Learning of Sensible Material. Journal of Educational Psychology, 2, 401-406. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0074801

article_title: Timing matters! Explaining between study phases enhances students’ learning.
citation: Lachner, A., Backfisch, I., Hoogerheide, V., van Gog, T., & Renkl, A. (2020). Timing matters! Explaining between study phases enhances students' learning. Journal of Educational Psychology, 112(4), 841–853. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000396
title: Prepone explaining to between study phases when designing learning environments
description: The principle holds that the instructional timing of explaining matters: placing an explanation activity between study phases, rather than only at the end of the study phase, fosters learning because it raises learners' awareness of knowledge gaps early, which they can remedy during further studying. The authors state that "preponing explaining between study phases enhances learning more than explaining at the end of the entire study phase" and that "the timing of explaining is crucial, and should be considered during designing learning environments".
requirements: Learners must get the opportunity to repair detected knowledge gaps during subsequent study phases after the in-between explaining activity.
constraints: The benefit was demonstrated with university students learning from an expository text on combustion engines; transfer performance was very low and not improved in either experiment.
target_learners: university students in self-study with expository texts
target_learning_goals: conceptual knowledge of expository text content
examples: In Experiment 1, students in the in-between explaining condition recorded a video explanation for a fictitious fellow student after studying the first of two text units, before studying the second.
key_sources: Lachner, A., Backfisch, I., Hoogerheide, V., van Gog, T., & Renkl, A. (2020). Timing matters! Explaining between study phases enhances students' learning. Journal of Educational Psychology, 112(4), 841–853. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000396

article_title: Social perspective taking: A professional development induction to improve teacher–student relationships and student learning.
citation: Gehlbach, H., Mascio, B., & McIntyre, J. (2021). Social perspective taking: A professional development induction to improve teacher-student relationships and student learning. Journal of Educational Psychology (in press). https://osf.io/suhvj/
title: Social perspective taking as a complex aptitude encompassing motivation and ability dimensions
description: The article defines social perspective taking as "the process in which a perceiver attempts to discern the thoughts, feelings, and motivations of one or more targets." It treats it as a complex aptitude with a motivation component (effort and confidence, with confidence less studied) and an ability component (information-gathering approaches, information sources, and inference strategies). The framework grounds the intervention design and three hypothesized pathways: motivation, perceived similarity, and effective strategies.
requirements: Perceivers must first be motivated to take a target's perspective and then bring cognitive resources to accomplish the task
constraints: Confidence's role is less clear; the article notes equivocal past findings regarding social perspective taking confidence
target_learners: K-9 teachers in a charter school network
target_learning_goals: Understanding students' thoughts, feelings, and motivations to improve teacher-student relationships
examples: The intervention scaffolds teachers to develop their own approaches by encouraging different strategies, colleague feedback, and continued classroom practice
key_sources: Gehlbach, H., Mascio, B., & McIntyre, J. (2021). Social perspective taking: A professional development induction to improve teacher-student relationships and student learning. Journal of Educational Psychology (in press). https://osf.io/suhvj/

article_title: Social perspective taking: A professional development induction to improve teacher–student relationships and student learning.
citation: Gehlbach, H., Mascio, B., & McIntyre, J. (2021). Social perspective taking: A professional development induction to improve teacher-student relationships and student learning. Journal of Educational Psychology (in press). https://osf.io/suhvj/
title: Six-step social perspective taking induction for teachers with a focal student
description: A 90-minute professional development induction in which "teachers progressed through the social perspective taking induction steps with a partner, concentrating on the focal student whose behavior they found perplexing." Teachers identify a puzzling behavior, share stories from their own perspective, retell the stories from the student's perspective (role-taking), present background information, develop multiple hypotheses with their partner, and identify concrete action steps to test the hypotheses. Teachers then record hypotheses and proposed action steps, with a December follow-up email reminding them of their steps.
requirements: Each teacher identifies a focal student who behaves in ways that make little sense, will remain their student, and whom they want to work with better
A partner for the paired induction steps
constraints: Control teachers received the same training only after the study concluded
target_learning_goals: Improving teachers' understanding of perplexing students and teacher-student relationships
examples: Treatment teachers completed the induction at a central location in November, then recorded hypotheses and proposed action steps for their focal student
key_sources: Gehlbach, H., Mascio, B., & McIntyre, J. (2021). Social perspective taking: A professional development induction to improve teacher-student relationships and student learning. Journal of Educational Psychology (in press). https://osf.io/suhvj/

article_title: Social perspective taking: A professional development induction to improve teacher–student relationships and student learning.
citation: Gehlbach, H., Mascio, B., & McIntyre, J. (2021). Social perspective taking: A professional development induction to improve teacher-student relationships and student learning. Journal of Educational Psychology (in press). https://osf.io/suhvj/
title: In field settings, design relationship interventions holistically so teachers can flexibly use strategies from their existing repertoire
description: The article argues that in noisy, complex field settings, interventions targeting narrowly defined constructs risk having their effects drowned out, and that precisely specified interventions may be dropped once a study ends. Instead, it recommends that "an intervention that engages teachers in using strategies from their existing repertoire that they can flexibly incorporate into their daily practices, would seem to have a greater chance of adoption over the long term." The study's own induction followed this logic by scaffolding multiple pathways rather than prescribing one strategy.
requirements: Interventions must offer teachers sufficient latitude to execute the approach in ways that work for them
Constructs should be conceptualized broadly enough that discrete-component improvements can propagate to broader outcomes
constraints: The article presents this as a design rationale for field experiments, not as a directly tested manipulation
target_learning_goals: Improving teacher-student relationships and downstream student outcomes
examples: The induction encouraged use of different strategies, provided colleague feedback, and asked teachers to propose their own action steps rather than prescribing a single perspective taking routine
key_sources: Gehlbach, H., Mascio, B., & McIntyre, J. (2021). Social perspective taking: A professional development induction to improve teacher-student relationships and student learning. Journal of Educational Psychology (in press). https://osf.io/suhvj/

article_title: Cooperative learning in middle school: A means to improve peer relations and reduce victimization, bullying, and related outcomes.
citation: Van Ryzin, M. J., & Roseth, C. J. (2018). Cooperative Learning in Middle School: A Means to Improve Peer Relations and Reduce Victimization, Bullying, and Related Outcomes. Journal of Educational Psychology, 110(8), 1192-1201. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000265
title: Peer-relations prevention theory: positive interdependence breaks down bully homophily and reduces social isolation
description: The article proposes that bullying prevention can work through peer relations alone: cooperative learning structures goals so that "individuals can attain their goals if (and only if) others in their group also reach their goals," producing mutual assistance and support. These positive interactions increase interpersonal attraction, reduce isolation, and are theorized to break down homophily among bullies while giving marginalized students a mechanism to form new friendships. The trial tested this account as a stand-alone alternative to curriculum-based anti-bullying programs.
requirements: Group-based learning activities must be carefully structured with positive interdependence; simply putting students in groups does not guarantee positive social interaction
constraints: Imposing contact across cliques without a cooperative structure can exacerbate perceived differences, per the social psychology of intergroup contact the article cites
target_learning_goals: positive peer relations
reduced bullying and victimization
reduced perceived stress and emotional problems
examples: Teachers in the 7 intervention schools received 3 half-day training sessions on the Johnsons' approach and applied positive interdependence within existing curricula
key_sources: Van Ryzin, M. J., & Roseth, C. J. (2018). Cooperative Learning in Middle School: A Means to Improve Peer Relations and Reduce Victimization, Bullying, and Related Outcomes. Journal of Educational Psychology, 110(8), 1192-1201. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000265

article_title: Cooperative learning in middle school: A means to improve peer relations and reduce victimization, bullying, and related outcomes.
citation: Van Ryzin, M. J., & Roseth, C. J. (2018). Cooperative Learning in Middle School: A Means to Improve Peer Relations and Reduce Victimization, Bullying, and Related Outcomes. Journal of Educational Psychology, 110(8), 1192-1201. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000265
title: Use cooperative learning as a sustainable, stand-alone component of bullying prevention that does not sacrifice instructional time
description: The article recommends embedding cooperative learning in everyday classroom instruction as a prevention approach, rather than adding a separate anti-bullying curriculum. It argues this "does not require the sacrifice of instructional time, and can be used in any subject," and that techniques "can be shared among staff members, modified to fit new academic curricula and learning objectives, and taught to new teachers by existing staff," sustaining implementation despite teacher turnover.
requirements: Teacher training in the cooperative learning approach (the trial used 3 half-day in-person sessions plus videoconference check-ins)
constraints: Evidence comes from a relatively homogeneous rural sample that was about three-quarters White, limiting external validity; all measures were self-report, some with low reliability
target_learning_goals: reduced bullying and victimization
positive peer relations
academic achievement alongside social outcomes
examples: The trial trained intervention-school staff with 3 half-day sessions using Cooperation in the Classroom, 9th Edition, and teachers applied cooperative learning within existing curricula

article_title: The Effect of Rate of Silent Reading on Ability to Recall.
citation: Gilliland, A. R. (1922). The effect of rate of silent reading on ability to recall. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/record/1922-02093-001
title: Teachers should insist upon accurate, rapid silent reading to save preparation time and increase efficiency
description: The article recommends that reading instruction push pupils toward faster silent reading, because recall did not drop when reading rate increased while time saved was substantial. As the author puts it, "the teacher of reading by insistence upon accurate, rapid, silent reading would be able to reduce not only the time required by pupils in the schools in the preparation of their lessons but also and more important still greatly increase their efficiency in life."
requirements: Reading material of the ordinary kind used in the study; the author concedes there are limits in speed beyond which one should not go.
constraints: The recommendation is grounded in short, relatively easy paragraphs with immediate recall; the author flags longer, vaguer selections and delayed recall as untested.
target_learning_goals: efficient silent reading with retained comprehension
examples: In the supporting experiment each subject read two paragraphs at each of three rates and immediately wrote down everything remembered, with comprehension roughly constant across rates.

article_title: Supplemental Material for A Growth-Theory-of-Interest Intervention Increases Interest in Math and Science Coursework Among Liberal Arts Undergraduates
citation: Paul A. O'Keefe, E. J. Horberg, Carol S. Dweck and Gregory M. Walton. (2024). A Growth Theory of Interest Intervention Increases Interest in Math and Science Coursework Among Liberal Arts Undergraduates. https://tinyurl.com/2yjm7rf9
title: Preregistered pilot and main studies with pre-matriculation and semester follow-up registrations
description: The article's open-practices disclosure documents preregistrations for both a pilot study and a main study, each with a pre-matriculation registration and follow-up registrations (pilot follow-up, Semester 1 follow-up, and Semester 2 follow-up for the main study). The authors state they "pre-registered hypotheses but not specific analyses", and that all pre-registered hypotheses were reported. Time-stamped registrations are hosted in public repositories via the listed links.

constraints: The analysis plan itself was not registered prior to examining the data; only hypotheses were pre-registered

math/science course grades

article_title: The problem of sex education.
citation: Cook, W. A. (1913). The problem of sex education. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 4(5), 253-260. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22The+problem+of+sex+education%22+Cook+1913
title: Answer children's honest spontaneous questions about sex truthfully but with guard, at any age, even though formal instruction has a grade limit
description: The author pairs a proposed lower limit for formal sex instruction with an exception for spontaneous questions: 'there probably should be no inferior limit set to the truthful, but guarded, answering of honest spontaneous questions from the children.' The principle separates formal curriculum, which should begin at a chosen grade, from responsive answering, which should not be refused on age grounds. It functions as an administration guideline for schools deciding when to begin instruction.
requirements: Teachers must answer truthfully while guarding the content appropriately for the child's age
constraints: The author sets this only for honest spontaneous questions from children, not for initiating formal instruction below the chosen limit
target_learners: children of any age who ask spontaneous questions about sex
target_learning_goals: accurate understanding of sex and reproduction
examples: The author proposes establishing the formal grade limit by starting instruction at the top of the school and working carefully down, while keeping truthful guarded answers available to younger children throughout
key_sources: Cook, W. A. (1913). The problem of sex education. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 4(5), 253-260. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22The+problem+of+sex+education%22+Cook+1913

article_title: Transfer between reading comprehension and word-problem solving among children with learning difficulty in both domains.
citation: Fuchs, L. S., Seethaler, P. M., Sterba, S. K., Fuchs, D., Cutting, L. E., Mancilla-Martinez, J., Martin, B. L. N., & Espinas, D. (2024). Transfer between Reading Comprehension and Word-Problem Solving among Children with Learning Difficulty in Both Domains. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000911
title: Kintsch and Greeno's model of word-problem solving as text processing
description: The study's theoretical framework is Kintsch and Greeno's (1985) model of WPS, rooted in discourse-processing theory. It holds that WP representations, like other text, have three components: a coherent text structure, a situation model supplemented with world knowledge about quantity relations, and knowledge of problem models that formalizes relations and guides solution strategies within schema. The article states "The model assumes that word-problem (WP) representations, as with other forms of text, have three components." Building these representations makes strong demands on memory, attentive behavior, reasoning, and language comprehension.
requirements: Problem solvers must coordinate world knowledge about quantity relations with problem-model knowledge to build representations
constraints: Incorrect solutions may arise from text-processing failures or from computational error, so the model does not attribute all WPS errors to text processing
target_learners: elementary students solving arithmetic word problems
target_learning_goals: constructing mental representations of word problems
identifying problem schemas
applying solution strategies
examples: The article walks through a combine-schema puppy/kitten problem showing how propositions are stored in working memory and the schema is filled (Part 1 + Part 2 = Total)
key_sources: Fuchs, L. S., Seethaler, P. M., Sterba, S. K., Fuchs, D., Cutting, L. E., Mancilla-Martinez, J., Martin, B. L. N., & Espinas, D. (2024). Transfer between Reading Comprehension and Word-Problem Solving among Children with Learning Difficulty in Both Domains. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000911

article_title: Transfer between reading comprehension and word-problem solving among children with learning difficulty in both domains.
citation: Fuchs, L. S., Seethaler, P. M., Sterba, S. K., Fuchs, D., Cutting, L. E., Mancilla-Martinez, J., Martin, B. L. N., & Espinas, D. (2024). Transfer between Reading Comprehension and Word-Problem Solving among Children with Learning Difficulty in Both Domains. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000911
title: Parallel single-domain text-structure intervention design with diagrams, text-type vocabulary, summarization, and transfer instruction
description: Both interventions taught a domain-specific strategy for constructing text-level representations via close reading, analytical reasoning, and text-structure vocabulary with a domain-specific diagram or equation mapping the text type's structure. Design elements drawn from meta-analyses included two text types, a writing component with graphic organizers, rule-based summarization, text-structure naming, signal words, and a short explicit transfer-instruction unit. The article states the interventions "were designed to maximize parallelisms between the processing of text with and without numbers, while preserving the domain-specificity of each text-processing strategy."
requirements: 45 lessons over 15 weeks, three 30-minute 1:1 lessons per week
tutors trained to fidelity criteria with weekly coaching
constraints: Only two text types were included because intervention lasted only 15 weeks; designed for second graders with comorbid difficulty and broadly average intellectual ability
target_learners: second-grade children with comorbid reading comprehension and word-problem solving difficulty
target_learning_goals: cause-effect and compare-contrast text-structure knowledge in passages and word problems
text comprehension
word-problem solving
examples: WP.INT used WP-type number sentences (ST + C = E; B − s = D) with diagrams gradually faded; RC.INT used parallel diagrams and summarization-guideline retells

article_title: The elimination of Freshmen from the University of Texas.
citation: E. D. Jennings. (1911). The Elimination of Freshmen from the University of Texas. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=elimination+of+freshmen+from+the+university+of+texas
title: Close the high-school-to-university grading gap by raising university freshman ratings and lowering high-school senior ratings by about 10 per cent (one letter)
description: The article recommends adjusting marking standards on both sides of the school-to-university transition so that students' scholarship ratings do not drop sharply when they enter the university. It argues the current break "tends to discourage him and to drive him out of school," and that closing "the unnatural and harmful breach between them" would reduce the large percentage of elimination. The recommendation rests on the finding that university ratings ran about 16 per cent below high-school ratings for the same students.
requirements: Institutional coordination between university and high school marking systems, since the adjustment must be made on both sides of the transition
constraints: The article frames the 10 per cent, or one-letter, adjustment as an estimate tied to the observed 16 per cent gap and the two-thirds rating ratio, not as a tested optimum
target_learning_goals: persistence through the first years of university study
fair and continuous assessment across the secondary-to-higher-education transition
examples: The article reports that the same students averaged 85 per cent in the last year of high school and 70 per cent at the university, and that reducing grades to arbitrary percentages again showed a difference of about 16 per cent between the two systems' standards.
key_sources: E. D. Jennings. (1911). The Elimination of Freshmen from the University of Texas. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=elimination+of+freshmen+from+the+university+of+texas

article_title: Phonological processing in children with specific reading disorder versus typical learners: Factor structure and measurement invariance in a transparent orthography.
citation: Brandenburg, Janin; Klesczewski, Julia; Schuchardt, Kirsten; Fischbach, Anne; Büttner, Gerhard; Hasselhorn, Marcus (2017). Phonological processing in children with specific reading disorder versus typical learners. Factor structure and measurement invariance in a transparent orthography. The Journal of educational psychology 109 (2017) 5, S. 709-726. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000162
title: Wagner and Torgesen's tripartite model of phonological processing (PA, RAN, PL)
description: The article adopts Wagner and Torgesen's (1987) account in which "phonological processing consists of 3 distinct constructs: phonological awareness (PA), rapid automatized naming (RAN), and the phonological loop (PL) of working memory." The study treats these as separable latent constructs measurable by a test battery and tests the model's structure via confirmatory factor analysis in German third graders, including children with reading disorder.
requirements: A comprehensive test battery assessing PA, RAN, and PL separately, as used in the study
constraints: Originally developed for English orthography; the article tests its applicability to the transparent orthography of German
target_learners: German-speaking third-grade primary school children, including children with specific reading disorder
target_learning_goals: Phonological processing skills underlying reading: phonological awareness, rapid automatized naming, and phonological loop functioning
examples: 209 German-speaking 3rd graders completed a comprehensive test battery assessing PA, RAN, and PL, and confirmatory factor analyses compared the latent structure across groups.

Phonological processing in children with specific reading disorder versus typical learners. Factor structure and measurement invariance in a transparent orthography. The Journal of educational psychology 109 (2017) 5, S. 709-726. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000162

article_title: Category change in the absence of cognitive conflict.
citation: Ramsburg, J. T., & Ohlsson, S. (2015). Category Change in the Absence of Cognitive Conflict. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Category+Change+in+the+Absence+of+Cognitive+Conflict%22
title: Resubsumption Theory of non-monotonic conceptual change without cognitive conflict
description: Resubsumption Theory explains how non-monotonic cognitive change can occur without cognitive conflict. Its core idea is that "An object, event, or phenomenon subsumed under some concept, schema, or (informal) theory X can be understood differently by being assimilated to, or subsumed under, an alternative concept, schema, or (informal) theory Y." Because knowledge structures created in one domain can apply to other domains, two structures may be activated in parallel and compete for control of action; competition is resolved by accumulated evidence of higher cognitive utility, not by logical falsification or dissatisfaction with the prior conception.
requirements: Multiple knowledge structures that can each apply to the same domain must be available for parallel activation and response competition
constraints: The theory only claims knowledge representations are abstract, not bound to their domain of origin, and is agnostic about other aspects of knowledge; its processes are not logic-like and conflicts are competitions among knowledge structures rather than logical contradictions
target_learners: Learners with entrenched prior conceptions undergoing conceptual change, e.g., science students
target_learning_goals: Non-monotonic conceptual change: replacing an initial conception with a contradictory alternative conception
examples: The article's re-categorization experiments operationalize the theory: participants master an initial category (black nuclei determine oxygen resistance), the definition silently changes to bent ribosomes, and learners shift without falsifying feedback
key_sources: Ramsburg, J. T., & Ohlsson, S. (2015). Category Change in the Absence of Cognitive Conflict. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Category+Change+in+the+Absence+of+Cognitive+Conflict%22

article_title: Category change in the absence of cognitive conflict.
citation: Ramsburg, J. T., & Ohlsson, S. (2015). Category Change in the Absence of Cognitive Conflict. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Category+Change+in+the+Absence+of+Cognitive+Conflict%22
title: Test cognitive-conflict necessity in simple, successful learning scenarios with manipulation checks and independent tracking of unlearning and re-learning
description: The article argues that weak effects of cognitive conflict interventions in complex classroom scenarios are uninterpretable because learning has multiple determinants. It recommends that "One response to this problem is to study simple situations in which there are fewer factors that determine the outcome, and those factors can be identified, measured, or controlled." It further recommends studying scenarios where learning is already successful, implementing an accurate manipulation check that learners experienced conflict, and using assessments that track reliance on the prior and new conceptions independently of each other.
requirements: Learning scenarios simple enough that determinants of outcome can be identified, measured, or controlled
A manipulation check verifying learners actually experienced the intended conflict
Assessment forms that track unlearning of the prior conception and learning of the new conception independently
constraints: In complex, realistic subject matters where outcomes have many determinants, a negative outcome of a conflict intervention is not interpretable; the recommendation is limited to simple scenarios with successful baseline learning
target_learners: Researchers designing studies of conceptual change; instructors of science topics
target_learning_goals: Evaluating whether cognitive conflict is a necessary prerequisite for non-monotonic conceptual change
examples: The authors applied this approach themselves: the re-categorization paradigm offers experimental control over prior knowledge, simple subject matter, controlled feedback content, and posttests probing reliance on initial versus target categories
key_sources: Ramsburg, J. T., & Ohlsson, S. (2015). Category Change in the Absence of Cognitive Conflict. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Category+Change+in+the+Absence+of+Cognitive+Conflict%22

article_title: An investigation on the value of drill work in the fundamental operations of arithmetic. Part II.
citation: Brown, J. C. (1915). An Investigation on the Value of Drill Work in the Fundamental Operations of Arithmetic. Part II. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu/
title: Direct drill work toward the poorest pupils, where its effect is greatest and it reduces class variability
description: This principle holds that drill practice in arithmetic fundamentals yields its largest benefit for the lowest-performing pupils, and that drill decreases the variability of a class. The article reports that the effect of drill "seems to be greatest on the poorest portion of the class" and that drill classes improved from two to three times as much as non-drill classes. It supports using drill as a remedial and equalizing practice rather than only as extension for proficient pupils.
requirements: A drill period of repeated recitations on the fundamental operations (20 recitations in this study) with pre- and post-testing to identify the poorest pupils
constraints: The effect-size ordering is the author's hedged interpretation ("seems to be greatest"); the poorest drill pupils still averaged a negative gross gain of -3.1 points, so drill did not fully overcome their deficit
target_learners: elementary school pupils in arithmetic, especially the lowest-performing third of a class
target_learning_goals: accuracy and speed in the fundamental operations of arithmetic (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division)
examples: The study compared the poorest 19 and best 19 pupils of drill and non-drill sections on first and second tests, finding poorest drill pupils moved from 50.7 percent below the drill-section average to 23.7 percent below it
key_sources: Brown, J. C. (1915). An Investigation on the Value of Drill Work in the Fundamental Operations of Arithmetic. Part II. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu/

article_title: Instruction, teacher–student relations, and math achievement trajectories in elementary school.
citation: Crosnoe, R., Morrison, F., Burchinal, M., Pianta, R., Keating, D., Friedman, S. L., Clarke-Stewart, K. A., & the NICHD Early Child Care Research Network. (2010). Instruction, Teacher–Student Relations, and Math Achievement Trajectories in Elementary School. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0017762
title: Pair higher order instruction with socioemotional support rather than defaulting low-skill children to basic skills curricula
description: The article argues that equity in elementary math requires breaking the link between entry skills and pedagogy: "the answer is not simply more challenging classes but, instead, classes that are advanced and supportive." Challenging coursework without instrumental and emotional support risks failure for children entering with limited skills, so higher order instruction must be coupled with basic-skills supplements and positive teacher relations.
requirements: Teachers able to provide encouragement, emotional support, and comfort while implementing demanding higher order activities
constraints: Exposing unprepared children to challenging instruction without support could be counterproductive and add to cumulative disadvantage
target_learners: Elementary school children with low entry-level math skills in mixed-skill classrooms
target_learning_goals: Math achievement growth and narrowing of entry-skill achievement gaps
examples: The study tested this by crossing inference instruction and teacher–student conflict with early skill group in repeated measures HLM of SECCYD math scores
key_sources: Crosnoe, R., Morrison, F., Burchinal, M., Pianta, R., Keating, D., Friedman, S. L., Clarke-Stewart, K. A., & the NICHD Early Child Care Research Network. (2010). Instruction, Teacher–Student Relations, and Math Achievement Trajectories in Elementary School. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0017762

article_title: Relation between teachers' early expectations and students' later perceived competence in physical education classes: Autonomy-supportive climate as a moderator.
citation: David Trouilloud, Philippe Sarrazin, Pascal Bressoux, Julien Bois. (2006). Relation between teachers’ early expectations and students’ later perceived competence in physical education classes: Autonomy-supportive climate as a moderator. Journal of Educational Psychology, 98, 75-86. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-0663.98.1.75
title: Self-determination theory account of autonomy-supportive climate as a moderator of social influence on students
description: The article applies self-determination theory (Deci & Ryan, 2002) to the teacher-expectations paradigm. It defines an autonomy-supportive climate as "a motivational style including behaviors such as offering choices, encouraging independent problem solving, involving students in the decision process, and minimizing the use of pressure". Because such climates enhance self-determination, students in them are theorized to be less susceptible to conforming to social factors such as teachers' expectations, whereas controlling climates reduce self-determination and increase susceptibility. The study used this framework to derive its moderation hypothesis.
requirements: Teachers must create a motivational climate perceived by students as autonomy supportive, measured here via students' shared perceptions of the classroom climate
constraints: The moderation account was tested only in naturalistic French junior-high physical education classes over one school year; the authors state their explanatory mechanisms (student motivational orientation, teacher beliefs about ability) are hypothetical and require further study
target_learners: students in grades 7-11 in physical education classes
target_learning_goals: students' perceived competence and motivational development
examples: The study measured students' perceptions of the autonomy-supportive climate with a French version of the Learning Climate Questionnaire (α = .75) aggregated to the classroom level (Rwg = .65 to .80), then tested the climate as a cross-level moderator of teacher expectation effects.
key_sources: David Trouilloud, Philippe Sarrazin, Pascal Bressoux, Julien Bois. (2006). Relation between teachers’ early expectations and students’ later perceived competence in physical education classes: Autonomy-supportive climate as a moderator. Journal of Educational Psychology, 98, 75-86. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-0663.98.1.75

article_title: Shall we teach spelling by rule?
citation: Cook, W. A. (1917). Shall we teach spelling by rule? The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=%22Shall+we+teach+spelling+by+rule%22
title: If spelling rules are taught at all, they must be introduced in the elementary school during the habit-forming period and given in widely-separated doses
description: This principle states the author's concluding recommendation about when and how spelling rules may profitably be taught. He argues that rules "do not teach themselves", that they "cannot be taught once and then dismissed from attention like an event in history", and that "they must be introduced, if at all, in the elementary school during the habit-forming period, while the pupil still spells reflectively rather than automatically". It is drawn from his test results rather than from a tested manipulation.
requirements: Teachers must insist upon the rules being learned and give them in widely-separated doses for thoroughness of digestion.
constraints: The author states the presumption is against a favorable outcome even under these conditions, except with a superior teacher.
target_learners: elementary school pupils in the habit-forming period
target_learning_goals: correct spelling of common words in written discourse
examples: University freshmen and academy students taught the rules the previous winter or six weeks before the test largely failed to recall or profit from them.
key_sources: Cook, W. A. (1917). Shall we teach spelling by rule? The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=%22Shall+we+teach+spelling+by+rule%22

article_title: A person-centered approach to action-control beliefs of students with special educational needs and their relation to student performance and time on task.
citation: Nyman, L., Koivuhovi, S., Greiff, S., Hotulainen, R., Little, T. D., & Vainikainen, M.-P. (2025). A person-centered approach to action-control beliefs of students with special educational needs and their relation to student performance and time on task. Journal of Educational Psychology. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0001000
title: Action-control theory of motivational beliefs (agency beliefs, means-ends beliefs, control expectancy)
description: Action-control theory (Skinner et al., 1988) conceptualizes control-related beliefs that mediate motivated action in the school domain. It integrates perceived-control theories including locus of control, causal attributions, learned helplessness, and self-efficacy. The article states these beliefs "form a belief system with a sequential distinction among agent, means and ends," comprising agency beliefs (perceived ability to utilize means such as effort and ability), means-ends beliefs (beliefs about which means produce desired outcomes, including internal means like effort and ability and external ones like luck), and control expectancy (perceived control over actions toward desired outcomes). The study uses these constructs as profile indicators.
requirements: Measurement of agency beliefs for ability and effort, control expectancy, and means-ends beliefs for ability and luck as distinct but related belief constructs
constraints: The article notes means-ends belief for ability can be adaptive or maladaptive depending on its conjunction with other beliefs such as perceived own ability or control expectancy
target_learners: secondary school students, including students with special educational needs
target_learning_goals: academic achievement and effort exertion in learning tasks
examples: The study measured agency beliefs for ability (e.g., "I have suf ﬁcient ability to succeed at school") and effort, control expectancy, and means-ends beliefs for ability and luck with three-item 7-point Likert scales
key_sources: Nyman, L., Koivuhovi, S., Greiff, S., Hotulainen, R., Little, T. D., & Vainikainen, M.-P. (2025). A person-centered approach to action-control beliefs of students with special educational needs and their relation to student performance and time on task. Journal of Educational Psychology. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0001000

article_title: A person-centered approach to action-control beliefs of students with special educational needs and their relation to student performance and time on task.
citation: Nyman, L., Koivuhovi, S., Greiff, S., Hotulainen, R., Little, T. D., & Vainikainen, M.-P. (2025). A person-centered approach to action-control beliefs of students with special educational needs and their relation to student performance and time on task. Journal of Educational Psychology. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0001000
title: Use person-centered approaches to identify distinct motivational patterns that variable-centered analyses miss
description: The article argues that a person-centered approach to motivational factors reveals heterogeneity between and within individuals, enabling identification of key patterns of values across variables. It states this makes it possible "to more accurately detect hindering nonlinear and interactive effects compared to the variable-centered approach." Applied to students with SEN, this approach uncovered four distinct belief profiles and showed that SEN status relates probabilistically, not deterministically, to maladaptive motivation. The authors highlight its importance for identifying different reasons and consequences for performance.
requirements: Motivational belief measures suitable for latent profile analysis and a sufficiently large sample for profile enumeration
constraints: Fit indices for class enumeration are sample-size dependent, especially information criteria in large samples, requiring supplementary elbow-plot and theoretical judgment
target_learners: students with diverse motivational profiles, including students with special educational needs
target_learning_goals: understanding and supporting motivation and effort related to academic performance
examples: Latent profile analysis of 6,942 Finnish ninth graders identified agentic, moderate, avoidant, and mixed profiles, with SEN students distributed across all four
key_sources: Nyman, L., Koivuhovi, S., Greiff, S., Hotulainen, R., Little, T. D., & Vainikainen, M.-P. (2025). A person-centered approach to action-control beliefs of students with special educational needs and their relation to student performance and time on task. Journal of Educational Psychology. article_title: A person-centered approach to action-control beliefs of students with special educational needs and their relation to student performance and time on task.
citation: Nyman, L., Koivuhovi, S., Greiff, S., Hotulainen, R., Little, T. D., & Vainikainen, M.-P. (2025). A person-centered approach to action-control beliefs of students with special educational needs and their relation to student performance and time on task. Journal of Educational Psychology. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0001000
title: Use log-data time on task as an objective indicator of effort in computer-based assessment
description: The article recommends using log data on time on task (TOT) to overcome the subjectivity limits of self-reported motivation and effort. It argues that with log data, researchers can "more objectively and comprehensively analyze how motivation and effort are connected to performance." TOT is extracted from logfiles as the time from task opening to submission, and is considered valid for tasks requiring higher-order thinking and complex problem solving where rapid automatized processes do not help. This enables identifying task-behavior-related factors explaining performance differences, including among academically struggling students.
requirements: Tasks that require controlled rather than automatic cognitive processes (novel problem-solving tasks), so that time use reflects effortful cognitive investment rather than task familiarity
constraints: The article notes criticism that simply spending more time does not necessarily lead to better outcomes for all students; TOT's meaning depends on task demands and student ability levels
target_learners: secondary school students in low-stakes computer-based assessment, including students with special educational needs
target_learning_goals: measuring effort exertion and task engagement during assessment
examples: TOT was extracted from logfiles for each task in the Finnish national learning-to-learn assessment, with outlier exclusions for delayed submissions and zero-second technical artifacts
key_sources: Nyman, L., Koivuhovi, S., Greiff, S., Hotulainen, R., Little, T. D., & Vainikainen, M.-P. (2025). article_title: Expanding the Direct and Indirect Effects Model of Writing (DIEW): Reading–writing relations, and dynamic relations as a function of measurement/dimensions of written composition.
citation: Grace Kim Young-Suk & Graham Steve. (2022). Expanding the Direct and Indirect Effects Model of Writing (DIEW): Reading-Writing Relations, and Dynamic Relations As a Function of Measurement/Dimensions of Written Composition. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000564
title: Expanded DIEW dynamic relations hypothesis: component skills relate to written composition as a function of measurement and dimensions of written composition
description: The expanded Direct and Indirect Effects Model of Writing adds a dynamic relations hypothesis stating that "the relations of component skills to the written composition vary as a function of measurement and dimensions of written composition." Measurement refers to how writing is assessed (format, genre, evaluation), while dimensions refer to aspects evaluated in the composition, such as writing quality, writing productivity, and correctness in writing. The article argues that because the outcome is multidimensional, a theoretical model must recognize both predictors and outcome dimensions, and it tests this hypothesis with Grade 2 data, finding differential relations for higher order cognitions and reading comprehension.
requirements: A theoretical model of writing must specify both the component skills (predictors) and the dimension of written composition (outcome) being predicted, since demands of component skills differ by focal dimension.
constraints: The article elaborates only the evaluation facet (dimensions of written composition); assessment format and genre facets are noted as beyond the scope of the paper.
The hypothesis was tested with English-speaking second graders in a semirural southeastern US context; the authors call for testing across developmental phases, writing systems, and L1/L2 learners.
target_learners: Elementary school students, specifically Grade 2 beginning writers
target_learning_goals: Written composition skills including writing quality, writing productivity, and correctness in writing
examples: Structural equation models with 350 Grade 2 children showed higher order cognitive skills related to writing quality but not productivity, and reading comprehension related only to writing quality.
key_sources: Grace Kim Young-Suk & Graham Steve. (2022). Expanding the Direct and Indirect Effects Model of Writing (DIEW): Reading-Writing Relations, and Dynamic Relations As a Function of Measurement/Dimensions of Written Composition. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000564

article_title: Expanding the Direct and Indirect Effects Model of Writing (DIEW): Reading–writing relations, and dynamic relations as a function of measurement/dimensions of written composition.
citation: Grace Kim Young-Suk & Graham Steve. (2022). Expanding the Direct and Indirect Effects Model of Writing (DIEW): Reading-Writing Relations, and Dynamic Relations As a Function of Measurement/Dimensions of Written Composition. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000564
title: DIEW component skills model of writing: hierarchical, interactive, and dynamic structural relations among component skills
description: The Direct and Indirect Effects Model of Writing is a component skills model hypothesizing that background knowledge, socio-emotions, transcription skills, knowledge of phonology/orthography/semantics, discourse oral language, higher order cognitive and regulation skills, vocabulary and grammatical knowledge, and executive function contribute to writing. The article states that "DIEW hypothesizes and specifies hierarchical relations among the component skills," with lower order skills related to written composition via higher order skills, and posits interactive, bidirectional relations among skills. It maps component skills onto writing processes: idea generation draws on topic knowledge and reading, translation on oral language, transcription on spelling and handwriting, and evaluation on language, reading, higher order cognitions, and discourse knowledge.
requirements: Assessment and instruction can be operationalized only when the model's component skills are explicitly specified, which the authors describe as the model's singular advantage.
constraints: The model is not a model of a particular genre or task; the extent of component skill contributions varies with development and assessment factors.
Component skills are involved in the writing process only as needed, not all during the entire writing process.
target_learners: K-12 students learning to write, particularly elementary-grade developing writers
target_learning_goals: Written composition, writing processes (planning, translation, transcription, revision), and component skills such as oral language, transcription, and higher order cognition
examples: The article maps DIEW component skills onto writing processes (Figure 2) and tests the model's hypotheses with Grade 2 structural equation models.
key_sources: Grace Kim Young-Suk & Graham Steve. (2022). Expanding the Direct and Indirect Effects Model of Writing (DIEW): Reading-Writing Relations, and Dynamic Relations As a Function of Measurement/Dimensions of Written Composition. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000564

article_title: Expanding the Direct and Indirect Effects Model of Writing (DIEW): Reading–writing relations, and dynamic relations as a function of measurement/dimensions of written composition.
citation: Grace Kim Young-Suk & Graham Steve. (2022). Expanding the Direct and Indirect Effects Model of Writing (DIEW): Reading-Writing Relations, and Dynamic Relations As a Function of Measurement/Dimensions of Written Composition. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000564
title: Multidimensional written composition scoring protocol: writing quality, writing productivity, and correctness in writing from two expository prompts
description: The study assessed written composition with two expository prompts (the WIAT-III Essay Composition task and an experimental Beaver source-based prompt, 15 minutes each) and scored compositions on three dimensions. "Writing quality was operationalized as the extent and clarity of idea development and organization" on a 1-to-7 modified 6+1 Trait rubric (kappa .87–.95); writing productivity was the number of words written (agreement .95); and correctness in writing used the CBM correct minus incorrect word sequences (CIWS) score (similarity coefficients .94–.95). Spelling was corrected for quality and productivity scoring but handwritten versions were used for correctness scoring.
requirements: Typed-up versions with corrected spelling are needed for quality and productivity evaluation because spelling errors and handwriting legibility influence evaluators' judgments.
constraints: Compositions that were mostly verbatim copies of the source text were scored zero (six students' compositions on the Beaver prompt).
target_learning_goals: Assessment of written composition across quality, productivity, and correctness dimensions
examples: Children wrote about their favorite game (WIAT-III) and about beavers after reading an illustrated 297-word passage, with 15 minutes per prompt.
key_sources: Grace Kim Young-Suk & Graham Steve. (2022). Expanding the Direct and Indirect Effects Model of Writing (DIEW): Reading-Writing Relations, and Dynamic Relations As a Function of Measurement/Dimensions of Written Composition. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000564

article_title: School belonging predicts whether an emerging adult will be not in education, employment, or training (NEET) after school.
citation: Philip Parker, Kelly-Ann Allen, Rhiannon Parker, Jiesi Guo, Herbert W Marsh, Geetanjali Basarkod, and Theresa Dicke. (2021). School Belonging Predicts whether an Emerging Adult will be Not in Education, Employment, or Training (NEET) after School. https://www.pwc.com.au/government/government-matters/youth-unemployment.html
title: Identity capital and the politics of belonging as an explanatory framework linking school belonging to NEET
description: The article frames school belonging and NEET via two sociological theories. Identity capital is "the tangible (connections, ways of speaking, memberships of a group, and ways of dressing) and intangible (self-belief, self-regulatory skills...) resources that provide access to opportunities". The politics of belonging examines how "social positions and identities are diﬀerentially valued and contested" and how community boundaries determine who belongs. Low school belonging may signal low identity capital, which then disadvantages youth in labor-market and tertiary 'identity markets', making belonging a psychological precursor to wider institutional exclusion.
requirements: The framework assumes youth identities must compete in institutional 'identity markets' of school, labor market, and tertiary education
constraints: The article presents this as a theoretical interpretation of the belonging-NEET link, not a tested mechanism; other mechanisms such as social exclusion experience and mental-health costs are flagged for future research
target_learners: secondary school students approaching the post-compulsory transition
target_learning_goals: social inclusion and belonging at school
successful transition to further education, employment, or training
examples: The study tested whether belonging's effect operated through high-school graduation and found it did not, leaving identity-based mechanisms as candidate explanations
key_sources: Philip Parker, Kelly-Ann Allen, Rhiannon Parker, Jiesi Guo, Herbert W Marsh, Geetanjali Basarkod, and Theresa Dicke. (2021). School Belonging Predicts whether an Emerging Adult will be Not in Education, Employment, or Training (NEET) after School. https://www.pwc.com.au/government/government-matters/youth-unemployment.html

article_title: School belonging predicts whether an emerging adult will be not in education, employment, or training (NEET) after school.
citation: Philip Parker, Kelly-Ann Allen, Rhiannon Parker, Jiesi Guo, Herbert W Marsh, Geetanjali Basarkod, and Theresa Dicke. (2021). School Belonging Predicts whether an Emerging Adult will be Not in Education, Employment, or Training (NEET) after School. https://www.pwc.com.au/government/government-matters/youth-unemployment.html
title: Monitor school belonging as an early indicator of NEET risk and intervene while youth are still in school
description: Because low school belonging at age 15 predicts NEET status at ages 16-20 even after graduation and covariates are controlled, the article recommends that "school personnel and, at a national level, policymakers, should monitor school belonging as one of a range of indicators of NEET risk". Measures of belonging let teachers, schools, and policymakers identify at-risk students and implement interventions that may break a pattern of social exclusion before youth leave the institution.
requirements: Ongoing measurement of students' sense of school belonging (e.g., PISA-style belonging scales) during schooling
constraints: The evidence is comparative rather than causal; the article states results are most safely interpreted comparatively, not as the causal effect of belonging on NEET
target_learners: adolescents around age 15 in secondary school
youth at risk of social exclusion after school
target_learning_goals: reducing post-school social exclusion (NEET)
fostering school belonging
examples: The two-cohort LSAY analysis showed belonging predicted NEET among non-graduates, where five percentage points separated strong-belonging from weak-belonging youth

article_title: Variability in memory span.
citation: Mitchell, David. (1918). Variability in Memory Span. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Variability+in+Memory+Span%22+Mitchell+1918
title: Do not grade a child's ability from a single examination, since performance varies from day to day
description: The article argues that educational and intelligence grading has assumed individual performance is constant, and that its memory span results show "The performance ability of children is not a static or fixed quantity." Because a child may score very differently on the same task on different days, a single examination can misrank him. The author recommends that "the doubt should always be in favor of the child until a wider range of experiment with him has been possible."
requirements: Multiple testing occasions are needed before a single low score is treated as evidence of a child's inability.
constraints: The author notes the results are not conclusive evidence that mental testing rests on a false assumption, and that variability under intelligence-scale procedures still needs to be determined.
target_learning_goals: accurate assessment of individual ability and intelligence
examples: The study tested 192 fifth graders on two days five weeks apart and 97 seventh graders on ten successive school days, finding individual scores varying by as much as six within a range of ten.
key_sources: Mitchell, David. (1918). Variability in Memory Span. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Variability+in+Memory+Span%22+Mitchell+1918

article_title: Attitude as a determinant in spelling efficiency in immediate and delayed recall.
citation: Arps, G. P. (1917). Attitude as a determinant in spelling efficiency in immediate and delayed recall. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Arps+attitude+spelling+efficiency
title: Accidental spatial-temporal contiguity acts as a temporary recall crutch that aids immediate reproduction but interferes with permanent retention
description: The article's explanatory account of why the two procedures reverse between immediate and delayed recall. Under orderly assignment, words acquire "a unique, temporary, and accidental contiguity" that functions during immediate reproduction but fades almost wholly by delayed recall, and whose total final effect is negative because it interferes with clear phonetic connections of a word's literal elements. The article illustrates this with a pupil who, when March followed missed in the learned order, said "I was thinking of 'smell.'"
requirements: Recall situations in real life lack the spatial and temporal references present in orderly school assignments, so the crutch cannot transfer
constraints: Derived from observation of a single learner in initial spelling work, within the limits of that study
target_learners: primary-grade children in initial spelling work
target_learning_goals: permanent retention and accurate reproduction of spelling words
examples: When March in the reproductive order followed missed, the pupil was confused, stating "I was thinking of 'smell.'"
key_sources: Arps, G. P. (1917). Attitude as a determinant in spelling efficiency in immediate and delayed recall. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Arps+attitude+spelling+efficiency

article_title: Supported self-explaining during fraction intervention.
citation: Fuchs, L. S., Malone, A., Schumacher, R. F., Namkung, J., Hamlett, C. L., Jordan, N. C., Siegler, R. S., Gersten, R., & Changas, P. (2016). Supported Self-Explaining during Fraction Intervention. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000073
title: Supported self-explaining: learners operate on high-quality explanations already created for them
description: The article distinguishes three forms of self-explaining: spontaneous, elicited, and supported. In supported self-explaining, "learners operate on high-quality explanations already created for them"; tutors model explanations and provide practice analyzing and applying them, encouraging elaboration and discussion. The authors chose this form because at-risk learners with cognitive limitations may invent subpar explanations, and because the key ingredient appears to be processing high-quality explanations rather than inventing them.
requirements: Tutors model high-quality explanations and scaffold practice in analyzing and applying them
constraints: Designed for learners with histories of poor mathematics achievement who may be vulnerable to inventing subpar explanations
target_learning_goals: explaining why fraction magnitudes differ
fraction magnitude comparison

title: Fraction Face-Off! multi-component fraction intervention
description: Fraction Face-Off! is the multi-component fraction intervention in which both the explaining and word-problem components were embedded. "Sessions occurred 3 times per week for 12 weeks with pairs of children," each 35 minutes, with 28 shared minutes focused on the measurement interpretation: comparing, ordering, placing fractions on number lines, and equivalencies. Instruction was explicit with worked examples, efficient strategies, cumulative review, and a motivation system of checkmarks, fraction dollars, and a weekly Fraction Store.

citation: Fuchs, L. S., Malone, A., Schumacher, R. F., Namkung, J., Hamlett, C. L., Jordan, N. C., Siegler, R. S., Gersten, R., & Changas, P. (2016). Supported Self-Explaining during Fraction Intervention. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000073
title: Use supported self-explaining to compensate for weak working memory in at-risk learners
description: Because inventing explanations is cognitively demanding for learners with weak cognitive resources, this principle recommends modeling high-quality explanations and having students analyze and apply them rather than invent their own. The article's moderator results support it: the effect favoring the explaining condition "transitioned to nonsignificance at 1.09 SDs above the at-risk sample mean on working memory," so supported self-explaining was most beneficial for students with weaker working memory.
requirements: Intervention must model high-quality explanations and provide scaffolded practice in analyzing and applying them, embedded in a program teaching the same fraction content
constraints: The compensatory benefit was demonstrated for magnitude comparison accuracy, not word-problem outcomes; effects favoring EXP were not significant for students with more adequate working memory
target_learners: at-risk fourth-grade mathematics learners with weak working memory

accurate fraction magnitude comparison
examples: EXP tutors modeled a 4-step sequence in which students wrote explanations such as "same number of parts, but fourths are bigger than eighths"

article_title: Pitfalls in Rating Schemes.
citation: Knight, F. B., & Franzen, R. H. (1921). Pitfalls in rating schemes. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org
title: Interpret ratings as behavior rather than as truthful accounts of the rated person
description: The article argues that a rating's value lies in what it reveals about the rater's judgments and point of view, not in its accuracy as a report of fact. As the authors put it, "ratings are of value only when these are interpreted as behavior and not as truthful accounts." A self-report that a person thinks something is important data regardless of whether the person really thinks it. The article demonstrates this by reading self-versus-peer rating discrepancies as evidence of self-defense mechanisms rather than as measurement error alone.
requirements: Ratings must be interpreted with awareness of tendencies such as self-overrating and the spread of a general impression across traits
constraints: The article states the fluctuations of the self-overrating tendency are unknown, and whether it extends to rating liked or disliked others is unknown
target_learners: users of rating schemes in educational and psychological assessment
target_learning_goals: accurate interpretation of self-ratings and peer ratings of traits and interests
examples: The 110-junior study read the +0.13 introspective-objective correlation as difference in the rater's point of view rather than difference in facts

article_title: A change of scenery: Does the setting of an instructional video affect learning?
citation: Merkt, M., Lux, S., Hoogerheide, V., van Gog, T., & Schwan, S. (2020). A Change of Scenery: Does the Setting of an Instructional Video Affect Learning? Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000414
title: Competing hypotheses: an authentic video setting as distraction versus as a cue for instructor expertise
description: The article frames two competing theoretical accounts of what an authentic setting does during video learning: the setting may draw the learner's attention away from the content, or it may signal the instructor's expertise and thereby support learning. Experiment 1 was designed to pit these accounts against each other, exploring "whether an authentic setting would serve as a distraction or as a cue for the instructor's expertise." The mixed experimental outcomes across the two experiments left the competition between the hypotheses unresolved.
requirements: The hypotheses rest on theoretical assumptions about how learners interpret the setting of an instructional video.
constraints: The retention benefit observed in Experiment 1 did not replicate in Experiment 2, leaving the hypotheses unresolved.
target_learners: learners watching instructional videos in laboratory experiments
target_learning_goals: retention of video content
application of video content

title: Setting-manipulated instructional videos on floral diagrams and floral formulas (greenhouse vs. white wall)
description: Two versions of an instructional video about floral diagrams and floral formulas were produced, differing only in setting: one was "shot in a greenhouse (authentic setting)" and one "in front of a white wall (neutral setting)". Experiment 1 used these videos to test whether the setting affects retention and application of the content, and the same learning materials were used again in Experiment 2.
requirements: Content is held constant across versions so that the setting is the differing factor between the authentic and neutral videos.
constraints: The retention benefit observed with these materials in Experiment 1 did not replicate in Experiment 2 despite the same learning materials and a comparable sample.
target_learners: adult participants watching instructional videos in laboratory experiments
target_learning_goals: retention of video content
application of video content

description: In Experiment 2, the video's setting was reinstated during assessment: after watching the video, participants worked on the retention and application test "while a screenshot of the authentic or the neutral setting was presented as a background". This manipulation tested whether the setting could act as a contextual cue that further improves test performance, but the article reports no evidence for context effects.

article_title: Teacher behavior and peer liking and disliking: The teacher as a social referent for peer status.
citation: Hendrickx, M. M. H. G., Mainhard, M. T., Oudman, V. S., Boor-Klip, H. J., & Brekelmans, J. M. G. (2017). Teacher Behavior and Peer Liking and Disliking: The Teacher as a Social Referent for Peer Status. Journal of Educational Psychology, 109(4), 546-558. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000157
title: Social referencing theory applied to the teacher as a social referent for peer status
description: The article applies social referencing theory to classroom peer relations: according to this account, peers take cues from the teacher's positive and negative behavior toward a student, and these cues affect the student's peer liking and disliking status. The study extends the account with a mediation mechanism in which peers' perceptions of the teacher's liking and disliking for the student transmit the teacher's behavioral cues to peer status. As the article states, "According to social referencing theory, cues peers take from positive and negative teacher behavior toward a student affect the student's peer liking and disliking status."
requirements: Peers must observe teacher behavior directed toward individual students and form perceptions of the teacher's liking or disliking for that student.
constraints: In this study the referent function was supported only through negative teacher behavior and peer disliking, not positive behavior or liking.
target_learning_goals: Healthy peer relationships and peer status in the classroom
examples: The study tested the hypothesized mediation model longitudinally across three time points within one school year in 56 classes.
