citation: Hendrickx, M. M. H. G., Mainhard, M. T., Oudman, V. S., Boor-Klip, H. J., & Brekelmans, J. M. G. (2017). Teacher Behavior and Peer Liking and Disliking: The Teacher as a Social Referent for Peer Status. Journal of Educational Psychology, 109(4), 546-558. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000157
title: Teachers should refrain from openly negative behavior toward students, particularly those at risk of peer rejection
description: Because negative teacher behavior toward a student was transmitted to peers' disliking of that student via peers' perceptions of the teacher's disliking, the article draws a practical implication for classroom practice: teachers should avoid openly negative behavior directed at individual students. As the abstract puts it, "it may be important for teachers to refrain from openly negative behavior toward students, particularly those at risk of peer rejection." This targets the disliking pathway, the one the study supported.
requirements: Teachers must be aware that their behavior toward individual students is observed by the peer group and interpreted as a signal of the teacher's liking or disliking.
constraints: The recommendation is hedged by the authors ("may be important") and rests on evidence concerning negative behavior and peer disliking only.
target_learners: Elementary school students, particularly those at risk of peer rejection
target_learning_goals: Preventing peer rejection and supporting positive peer relationships
examples: The study found negative teacher behavior predicted peers' disliking of a student six months later via perceived teacher disliking.

At the first time point, video data were recorded and teacher behavior toward specific students was coded. As the abstract reports, "At the first time point video data was also recorded, and teacher behavior toward specific students was coded." The design controlled for peer perceptions of student behavior.

article_title: Mental adaptation during the school day as measured by arithmetical reasoning - Part I.
citation: Winch, W. H. (1911). Mental adaptation during the school day as measured by arithmetical reasoning.—Part I. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Mental+adaptation+during+the+school+day%22+Winch+1911
title: Place severe mental work of a rational kind later in the school session, except in very poor schools whose boys work before school
description: The article derives a timetabling principle from its adaptation experiments: hard reasoning work such as problematic arithmetic should not occupy the earliest school period. It states that "Severe mental work of a rational kind, except in the very poor schools where the boys rise early and \"go to work\" before school, should be placed later in the school session than it is at present", arguing that if well grounded "a considerable change in school time-tables seems desirable".
requirements: The class must be one whose children's mental adaptation is not already at its height early in the morning, as the article claims for boys who work before school.
constraints: The article excepts very poor schools where boys rise early and go to work before school, for which early placement may suit better.
target_learners: elementary school children in England, of various social classes, ages, and grades of mental ability as measured by school standards
target_learning_goals: problematic arithmetic and other severe rational mental work
examples: In the experiments, one equal group worked the same problematic arithmetic tests early in the morning session and the other worked them later, under the same teacher.

article_title: Mental adaptation during the school day as measured by arithmetical reasoning - Part I.
citation: Winch, W. H. (1911). Mental adaptation during the school day as measured by arithmetical reasoning.—Part I. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Mental+adaptation+during+the+school+day%22+Winch+1911
title: Mental adaptation as the cognate of mental fatigue, identifying the best times for school functions
description: The article frames mental adaptation as a school-day phenomenon parallel to mental fatigue: where fatigue knowledge shows the "worst times" for functions, adaptation knowledge shows the "best times". It complains that educationists have attended to fatigue but paid little attention to "the cognate phenomena of mental adaptation", and treats adaptation as the reason the same arithmetical tests yield better improvement at some morning hours than others, peaking at different times for different children.
requirements: Detecting adaptation effects requires dividing a class into equal groups on preliminary tests and comparing improvement when the same work is done at different times of day.
constraints: The article's evidence concerns problematic arithmetic in elementary school classes during the morning session; the general summary notes conclusions contradict current English pedagogical practice.
target_learning_goals: scheduling rational mental work such as problematic arithmetic at the time of day favoring improvement
examples: The experiments compared groups working identical test sets at 9.40 A.M. versus 11.25 A.M. (boys) and 9.40 A.M. versus 11.15 A.M. (girls).

title: Problematic arithmetic tests scored for rational steps toward solution
description: The measuring instrument in both experiment series: cyclostyled sets of multi-step problematic arithmetic questions, with marking that ignores the numerical answer. The marker asked "Was the problem done the right way!" and scored by "allowing one mark for every rational'' step'' which wa& on the way to a correct solution, even though no solution was actually ar- rived at", with figures chosen so mechanical computation difficulties were avoided and a fixed maximum mark per set (12 in the first series, 23 in the second).
requirements: Tests of the right pitch of difficulty and practice tests before scoring counts, since first-test results were discarded and preliminary sets established steadiness.
constraints: In the first series the order of problems was kept constant across sets, while in the second series both wording and problem order varied from set to set.
target_learners: elementary school children in Standards III to VII
target_learning_goals: problematic arithmetical reasoning, marked for rational method rather than numerical correctness
examples: Sample problems include one-step, two-step, three-step and four-step questions such as combining pole lengths or computing a profit per pound of bacon.

article_title: Conceptual knowledge of decimal arithmetic.
citation: Lortie-Forgues, Hugues and Siegler, Robert S (2017) Conceptual knowledge of decimal arithmetic. Journal of Educational Psychology. pp. 374-391. ISSN: 0022-0620. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000148
title: Three theoretical interpretations of incorrect direction of effect judgments: strong conviction, operation knowledge, and cognitive conflict
description: The article distinguishes three interpretations of incorrect direction of effect judgments, to be separated by confidence ratings: "The strong conviction hypothesis, which posits that students are highly confident that multiplication produces answers greater than either operand"; the operation knowledge hypothesis, in which students are less confident about multiplication and division than addition and subtraction regardless of operand size; and the cognitive conflict hypothesis, in which confidence is lower specifically for multiplication and division of numbers between zero and one. Confidence data supported the operation knowledge account for most students, with a grade-related emergence of cognitive conflict in 8th graders.
requirements: Confidence ratings collected immediately after each direction of effect judgment on a 5-point scale
constraints: The confidence pattern differed between the subgroup whose judgments always followed whole number arithmetic and the remaining students
target_learning_goals: understanding the direction of effect of rational number arithmetic operations
examples: Study 1 collected 5-point confidence ratings after each of 16 direction of effect judgments and compared them across operation and operand size

article_title: Problems in reading.
citation: J. C. Bell. (1919). Problems in Reading. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Volume X, Number 8. https://psycnet.apa.org/journal/edu
title: Pool the ratings of competent judges to build a scale of expression-comprehension in oral reading that steadies individual teachers' judgments
description: The editorial proposes that, although objective measurement of expression in oral reading is difficult, it may not be insurmountable to work out, "by pooling the ratings of competent judges," a scale of expression-comprehension in oral reading usable to steady individual teachers' judgments, as composition and handwriting scales do. It argues such a scale would be significant for rating pupils because school reading is and will likely remain chiefly oral reading.
requirements: Requires competent judges whose pooled ratings can be standardized into a scale, analogous to composition and handwriting scales.
constraints: Objective measurement of expression and voice modulation is difficult, which is why Gray's oral reading scale ignores these finer points.
target_learning_goals: accurate assessment of reading comprehension in oral reading
examples: The editorial asks whether pooling competent judges' ratings could produce a scale usable to steady individual teacher judgments, as existing composition and handwriting scales do.

article_title: Mental measurements in education.
citation: J. C. B. (1919). Measurements in education [Editorial]. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 10(1). https://archive.org/search?query=Journal+of+Educational+Psychology+1919
title: Advocates of scientific studies in education should wage a vigorous campaign to arouse public opinion to demand such studies in the schools.
description: The principle holds that the obstacle to school measurement work is not trained personnel but public conviction of its practical value. The editorial states it is "now incumbent upon all those who believe in the value of scientific studies in education to engage in a vigorous and aggressive campaign to arouse public opinion" so such studies are demanded as enlightened policy.

title: Remediation for scholastic laggards should target habits of application and resistance to distraction rather than instruction in content
description: The article proposes that the supplementary teacher or college advisor faces a problem bigger than teaching the laggard the lesson: developing habits of application and resistance to distracting temptations, framed as the general problem of interest and control. article_title: Some results of practice in addition under school conditions.
citation: H. H. Hahn and E. L. Thorndike. (1914). Some Results of Practice in Addition Under School Conditions. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Volume V, Number 2. https://www.google.com/search?q=Hahn+Thorndike+1914+Some+Results+of+Practice+in+Addition+Under+School+Conditions
title: Hahn-Thorndike school addition practice experiment with self-competition and no-practice control groups
description: A school-based experiment in which pupils in grades 4 through 7 added columns, each of ten one-place numbers, as rapidly as was consistent with accuracy. Each pupil competed against his own record: "Each child was led to compete with his own past record—was told repeatedly 'to beat himself.'" Seven sheets of forty-eight columns of equal difficulty were used; practice groups took an initial 15-minute test, 90 minutes of practice in periods from 5 to 22.5 minutes, and a final test, while control groups took only the two tests.
requirements: Pupils must have formed the fundamental associations required for addition, as the 4B group had not and was excluded from main comparisons
constraints: Out-of-school practice was not prevented and could not be detected or subtracted from the obtained results
target_learning_goals: speed and accuracy in adding columns of one-place numbers
examples: Practice periods of 5, 7.5, 10, 15, 20 and 22.5 minutes were assigned to different groups across an October-November schedule

article_title: Mental fatigue in day school children as measured by immediate memory: Part I.
citation: W. H. Winch. (1910). Mental Fatigue in Day School Children as Measured by Immediate Memory. Part I. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://books.google.com
title: Visual immediate-memory test of twelve consonants used as a fatigue measure in day school children
description: A mechanical memory test used by Winch to measure fatigue: "Twelve consonants, arranged in the following way" were "exposed to view for 25 seconds", after which boys wrote down as much as they could remember with 1 minute 35 seconds for writing and rest. Ten tests formed a 20-minute exercise, scored three marks per correctly remembered and rightly placed consonant, two for one place out, one for two places out. Study was visual, audible articulation not permitted.
requirements: New material each test so "the process can be mechanized, but the acquisition required is always a new matter"
A preliminary series of tests to establish steady performance before fatigue comparisons
constraints: Contemporary opinion held that immediate memory tests "will not give satisfactory indices of fatigue" in children, due to irregularity in the first exercises of a series
target_learners: School children around 13 years of age (Standard VI class)
target_learning_goals: Immediate memory for visual percepts of non-connotative material
examples: Used with 45 boys in a municipal boys' school in a poor London neighborhood, morning tests following Scripture lessons and afternoon tests after spelling, drill, recreation and algebra

article_title: The benefits of successive relearning on multiple learning outcomes.
citation: Philip A. Higham, Bettina Zengel, Laura Bartlett, and Julie A. Hadwin (2020). The Benefits of Successive Relearning on Multiple Learning Outcomes. https://osf.io/nx4va/?view_only=049ee04aab4f420e9fa0091b3b69b9d0

metacognitive accuracy about future test performance

citation: Lowell, Frances. (1917). A Preliminary Report of Some Group Tests of General Intelligence. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu
title: Design criteria for group intelligence tests in the primary grades
description: Lowell sets out a framework of requirements a test must meet to be administered to a group of young children rather than individually. She states that "Simplicity is an important criterion in the selection of the group test; simplicity of material; of directions; of response; and of scoring." Tests must permit only one correct response with one interpretation, be scored "all or none" so the examiner's judgment never enters, and directions must be clear, brief and repetitively illustrated since young children are limited in vocabulary and attention.
requirements: Material must be easily carried and quickly distributed to a large group, which the author achieved by arranging all pages and blanks in numbered booklets
constraints: Directions cannot be too varied, because too many instructions may destroy the value of the test, since ability to follow directions is itself a test of intelligence
target_learners: Children in first, second and third grades of elementary school
target_learning_goals: Screening for general intelligence level to identify children needing individual Binet testing
examples: The battery of twenty-five tests arranged as five-, six-, seven-, eight- and nine-year tests, adapted from Binet-Simon, Kuhlmann's 1917 Revision, Terman's Revision, the New York Bureau standards, and original tests
key_sources: Lowell, Frances. (1917). A Preliminary Report of Some Group Tests of General Intelligence. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu

article_title: A preliminary report of some group tests of general intelligence.
citation: Lowell, Frances. (1917). A Preliminary Report of Some Group Tests of General Intelligence. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu
title: Use group tests as an impersonal first-stage screener to sort out subnormal children for individual Binet testing
description: The article recommends group tests as an impersonal method for locating children of doubtful mentality, because teachers' estimates are unreliable: teachers judge a sweet, docile child bright and overlook age. As the author states, "The use of the group tests in the survey has been to sort out the subnormal children, or those whose mentality is questionable, for further individual testing." Classification by number of tests passed approximates the intelligence quotient for borderline children.
requirements: If more complete standardization of the tests confirms the present results, grade- and age-normed numbers of tests passed must be available for comparison
constraints: The author states that only if further standardization confirms present results will such classification be readily possible; borderline classifications still need individual testing before mental status can be correctly gauged
target_learners: Primary-grade school children in a county-wide school survey
target_learning_goals: Identifying subnormal or borderline mentality for diagnostic follow-up
examples: The author's worked example: an eight-year-old first grader passing only 6.3 tests would be placed around I.Q. .70-.79, the borderline group, needing individual testing
key_sources: Lowell, Frances. (1917). A Preliminary Report of Some Group Tests of General Intelligence. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu

article_title: A preliminary report of some group tests of general intelligence.
citation: Lowell, Frances. (1917). A Preliminary Report of Some Group Tests of General Intelligence. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu
title: Lowell's 25-test primary-grade group intelligence battery in booklet form
description: A series of 25 group tests, divided into five groups designated as five, six, seven, eight and nine year tests, administered to whole classrooms via 7.25 x 11.5 inch booklets (first grade: five-, six-, seven-year tests; second: six through eight; third: seven through nine). The author writes that "Altogether, twenty-five tests have been selected which seem to fulfill the requirements mentioned above." Tests were adapted from Binet-Simon, Kuhlmann's 1917 Revision, Terman's Revision, New York Bureau standards, and original tests by Lowell.
requirements: Booklets keep each child's responses together and allocate definite numbered spaces per test to avoid confusion from loose sheets
constraints: Scoring is all-or-none by design, since the purpose is not to rank relative performance but to identify children who fail a task entirely
target_learners: First, second and third grade pupils
target_learning_goals: Sorting children of doubtful mentality for individual Binet testing
examples: The tests were given to 566 school children distributed by age: 74 six-year-olds, 132 seven-year-olds, 155 eight-year-olds, 115 nine-year-olds, and 90 ten-year-olds
key_sources: Lowell, Frances. (1917). A Preliminary Report of Some Group Tests of General Intelligence. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu

article_title: The National Research Council.
citation: Bell, J. C. (1919). Editorial: The National Research Council. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Volume X, No. 9. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journal_of_Educational_Psychology
title: National Research Council group tests of general intelligence
description: A set of "two series of group tests of general intelligence of a high degree of reliability" developed by an NRC committee with a General Education Board grant, trialed on five thousand children and on several thousand more. The editorial describes them as giving as satisfactory a measure of intelligence as any scale then available and as enabling mass administration in schools.
requirements: Group administration with subsequent scoring and tabulating of results by school staff
constraints: The editorial reports the tests were not yet released: the committee "will shortly be able to offer to the country" the two series
target_learning_goals: Measurement of general intelligence and pupils' abilities and attainments
examples: The committee selected some twenty candidate tests, gave them a careful trial on five thousand children, and re-tried the selected series on several thousand more children to perfect the procedure

article_title: Social contagion and high school dropout: The role of friends, romantic partners, and siblings.
citation: Dupéré, V., Dion, E., Cantin, S., Archambault, I., & Lacourse, E. (2021). Social contagion and high school dropout: The role of friends, romantic partners, and siblings. Journal of Educational Psychology, 113, 572-584. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000484
title: Social contagion of dropout through recent exposure within networks of same-age intimates
description: Social contagion refers to "the transmission of behaviors through contact with others who exhibit these behaviors". Applied to dropout, the article argues contagion is unlikely to occur through imitation of high-status models, since dropping out is uncorrelated or negatively correlated with peer-group status; it may instead operate through transmission of educational norms in communities where dropout is prevalent. Contagion is theorized to depend on recency of exposure, with dropout contagious only for a short period, and to be especially likely when adolescents with pre-existing vulnerabilities are in contact.
requirements: Contact between adolescents and same-age intimates who have recently exhibited the behavior
constraints: Only experimental or detailed longitudinal evidence with proper statistical controls can fully disentangle social influences from homophily and similarity-based selection
The mechanisms underlying contagion were not assessed in the present study
target_learners: Adolescents in disadvantaged communities with high dropout rates
target_learning_goals: Understanding and preventing the social propagation of high school dropout
examples: The study's finding that only dropout occurrences within the past year predicted participants' dropout, and that risk was highest with multiple types of intimates who had dropped out, supports the recency-based contagion account.
key_sources: Dupéré, V., Dion, E., Cantin, S., Archambault, I., & Lacourse, E. (2021). Social contagion and high school dropout: The role of friends, romantic partners, and siblings. Journal of Educational Psychology, 113, 572-584. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000484

article_title: To confirm or to conform? Performance goals as a regulator of conflict with more-competent others.
citation: Sommet, N., Darnon, C., & Butera, F. (2015). To Confirm or to Conform? Performance Goals as a Regulator of Conflict With More-Competent Others. Journal of Educational Psychology, 107(2), 580–598. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0037240
title: Performance goals as social tools regulating interpersonal behavior with more-competent others
description: The article conceives performance goals not merely as intrapersonal motivators but as "a social tool for regulating interpersonal behaviors with more-competent others." Drawing on the interpersonal circumplex model's agentic dimension, it proposes that performance-approach goals trigger an appetitive self–other regulation system producing dominant behavior, while performance-avoidance goals trigger an aversive system producing submissive behavior. This account explains why responses to socio-cognitive conflict with more-competent others vary between self-confirmation and compliance.
requirements: A competence-relevant social setting in which the learner confronts a disagreeing other whose relative competence is salient (higher, equal, or unspecified).
constraints: The account targets relational (not epistemic) conflict regulation in confrontations with more-competent others; the approach/avoidance distinction within mastery goals is explicitly not brought into play.
target_learning_goals: Regulation of interpersonal behavior during socio-cognitive conflict and disagreement in collaborative learning
examples: In Study 2, performance-approach versus performance-avoidance goal instructions were given before participants rated a confirmation versus compliance model after disagreeing with a partner presented as same-grade or higher-grade.
key_sources: Sommet, N., Darnon, C., & Butera, F. (2015). To Confirm or to Conform? Performance Goals as a Regulator of Conflict With More-Competent Others. Journal of Educational Psychology, 107(2), 580–598. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0037240

article_title: Pedagogical suggestions from memory tests.
citation: Patterson, T. L. (1909). Pedagogical Suggestions from Memory Tests. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://books.google.com
title: Teach educational subjects from the grapho-motor standpoint, alongside the other special senses, to approach maximal teaching efficiency
description: The article recommends that because the grapho-motor power exceeds the visual-motor power in acquiring knowledge through memory, "all educational subjects from the graded schools to the university, as far as possible and as far as time will permit, should be taught from the grapho-motor standpoint, as well as by the other special senses." It urges teachers to train the grapho-motor sense through drawing rather than relying only on receptive stimuli to the other senses.
requirements: The subject must lend itself to writing or drawing activity within available time, since the article qualifies the recommendation with as far as possible and as far as time will permit
constraints: The article states this cannot be applied to all subjects alike, singling out the biological sciences as a most satisfactory application and other subjects in varying degrees
target_learning_goals: memory for educational content
retention of subject-matter knowledge
examples: The author administered about 50 figure-reproduction tests at Anson Academy in 1909 using Meyerhardt's method before drawing the pedagogical recommendation.
key_sources: Patterson, T. L. (1909). Pedagogical Suggestions from Memory Tests. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://books.google.com

article_title: Some experimental evidence in regard to formal discipline.
citation: Linus W. Kline, Ph.D. (1909). Some Experimental Evidence in Regard to Formal Discipline. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Some+experimental+evidence+in+regard+to+formal+discipline%22+Kline
title: Attention-gateway account of transfer: mental life levies a tax on special processes through attention
description: The article offers an explanatory account of why practice transfers positively or negatively: attention directed to mere form in one task can prejudice performance on a task requiring meaning, and general mental functioning is affected through attention. The author writes, "It is as if our mental life, as a whole, levies a tax for general purposes upon special processes and that the manner and application of the levy are made through the gateway of attention." This interprets both studies' transfer asymmetries as changes in attitudes of attention rather than generic discipline of faculties.
requirements: Both the practiced and transfer tasks must be performed under conditions where attention can be directed to form versus meaning, as in the letter-versus-parts-of-speech tasks.
constraints: The account is the authors' interpretation of two small experiments, not a separately tested mechanism; the article cites Angell and Judd's symposium as its theoretical support.
target_learners: adult students in educational psychology courses
target_learning_goals: understanding how practice on one task affects performance on related tasks
examples: Subjects reported that e's and t's claimed attention even in irrelevant words, and the author noted the illusion persisted for six months.
key_sources: Linus W. Kline, Ph.D. (1909). Some Experimental Evidence in Regard to Formal Discipline. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Some+experimental+evidence+in+regard+to+formal+discipline%22+Kline

article_title: Social and emotional behavioral profiles in kindergarten: A population-based latent profile analysis of links to socio-educational characteristics and later achievement.
citation: Collie, Rebecca; Martin, Andrew; Nassar, N; Roberts, CL. (2018). Social and Emotional Behavioral Profiles in Kindergarten: A Population-Based Latent Profile Analysis of Links to Socio-Educational Characteristics and Later Achievement. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000262
title: Use population-based SEB profiling in kindergarten to target early academic intervention
description: The article demonstrates identifying social-emotional behavior profiles among whole kindergarten populations via latent profile analysis on five SEBs (cooperative, socially responsible, helpful, anxious, aggressive-disruptive). Because profiles were linked to later achievement, the authors state the "findings have implications for healthy student development and academic intervention", supporting early identification of groups such as SE-Vulnerable students.
requirements: SEB ratings on multiple behaviors (cooperative, socially responsible, helpful, anxious, aggressive-disruptive) for a student population
standardized achievement data to establish profile-outcome links
constraints: Findings are from New South Wales, Australia kindergarten populations (2012 and 2009 cohorts); profiles were associated with, not experimentally manipulated for, later achievement
target_learning_goals: social and emotional behavior development
academic achievement in elementary grades
examples: Study 1 profiled the 2012 NSW kindergarten population (N = 100,776); Study 2 replicated with the 2009 cohort (n = 52,661) and linked profiles to Grades 3 and 5 test scores

article_title: School instruction in matters of sex.
citation: Foster, W. S. (1911). School Instruction in Matters of Sex. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22School+Instruction+in+Matters+of+Sex%22+Foster
title: Answer children's sex questions as they arise, treating sexual enlightenment as a natural, integral part of general enlightenment rather than an isolated special topic.
description: This principle holds that adults should satisfy children's curiosity about sexual matters immediately and naturally, rather than marking sex off as a special, embarrassing topic. The essay states "It should be a rule to answer questions and to satisfy curiosity as soon as it arises," so that sex enlightenment becomes "a natural and integral part of general enlightenment." It rests on the psycho-analytic claim that false explanations fill any silence left by adults.
requirements: Adults must be prepared to give true, frank and simple explanations whenever curiosity arises, since withheld answers are replaced by false ones heard or invented.
constraints: Later attempts at instruction must overcome acquired ideas and feelings of shame and embarrassment if the groundwork was not laid early.
target_learners: young children at home and in kindergarten
target_learning_goals: proper attitudes toward sex
accurate early understanding of reproduction and the body
examples: The essay recommends that the child be made to feel free to ask the mother any questions and be assured of a correct answer, treated with absolute frankness and honesty.
key_sources: Foster, W. S. (1911). School Instruction in Matters of Sex. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22School+Instruction+in+Matters+of+Sex%22+Foster

article_title: School instruction in matters of sex.
citation: Foster, W. S. (1911). School Instruction in Matters of Sex. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22School+Instruction+in+Matters+of+Sex%22+Foster
title: Sex instruction should be continuous, progressive, and suited to the learner's development, beginning at home with the mother before school age.
description: The essay organizes instruction into three periods—home and kindergarten, pre-pubertal, and adolescent—insisting that "Sexual enlightenment, like any other enlightenment, should be continuous, progressive and suited to the development and needs of the learner." Because "the mother is the natural teacher in early years," she should begin instruction before the child meets sources of misinformation, with the school supplementing her teaching. Marking off one specific time for complete instruction is explicitly not recommended.
requirements: A groundwork satisfying all insistent curiosity should be secured before the child goes to school or becomes open to misinformation.
constraints: If early information has not been given, the teacher is no longer so free to speak nor so influential, so words are left unsaid or come with little force.
target_learning_goals: developmentally appropriate sexual knowledge
preparation for puberty changes
rational attitudes toward marriage, prostitution and venereal disease
examples: The essay assigns habit formation and simple facts to the mother in the first stage, puberty preparation to the pre-pubertal stage, and facts of marriage, prostitution and venereal disease before school leaving.
key_sources: Foster, W. S. (1911). School Instruction in Matters of Sex. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22School+Instruction+in+Matters+of+Sex%22+Foster

Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000964.supp
title: Sympathetic arousal inferred from EDA as a physio-psychological measure distinct from challenge and threat appraisal
description: The article treats electrodermal activity as an accessible, non-invasive window on the sympathetic nervous system's fight-or-flight response, categorized as a physio-psychological measure because it is measured physiologically though it originates in the brain. It stresses that arousal intensity is not the same construct as challenge and threat appraisal. The study used EDA-derived sympathetic arousal alongside self-report indicators in classroom science tasks.
requirements: Signal and noise separation methods are needed to extract a usable sympathetic arousal signal from raw EDA recordings
constraints: The article states sympathetic arousal "is not synonymous with challenge and threat" and does not convey whether the response will be fight or flight
target_learning_goals: understanding students' challenge and threat states during academic tasks and assessments
examples: The present research utilized a measure of sympathetic arousal inferred from EDA analysis to uncover a dimension of students' orientation toward science tasks

title: CytonRK: a custom head-mounted portable EEG recorder for classroom use
description: The CytonRK is a bespoke head-mounted EEG device built by the lead author because no commercial device met classroom requirements. It uses an OPENBCI Cyton board with an ADS1299 8-channel converter, records at 250Hz to local micro-SD memory with a battery-backed real-time clock, and uses dry Silver Chloride comb electrodes on a 25mm elasticized harness designed for minimal invasiveness in hair.
requirements: Local memory recording was chosen because Bluetooth pairing of up to 26 devices in one classroom was impractical and school WiFi networks were infeasible
constraints: The article notes temporal electrode placement was moved from just in front to just behind the ears after participant feedback about pressure irritation
target_learners: high school students in naturalistic classroom settings
target_learning_goals: recording EEG-based indicators of attention and working memory during real classroom assessments
examples: Neurometric validation in UNSW's Future Minds Lab showed 12Hz flicker responses at O1/O2 and eyes-closed alpha peaks at parietal electrodes

title: Automated Matlab signal pipeline synchronizing EDA, EEG, and survey data
description: The signal pipeline is an autonomous Matlab program into which raw signals from the Empatica E4, the CytonRK headsets, and Qualtrics survey data are fed, producing a synchronized and processed dataset without subjective human intervention. Each recording has an independent layered database so raw data or any processing step can be revisited, and a graphical interface allows visual inspection of each stage, including automated peak-alpha frequency identification.
requirements: Individual per-participant data files were needed because some steps, such as Fourier transforms into time slices, took nearly 10 hours to process
constraints: Ledalab's conservative curve-matching approach may produce false negatives, so the research measured event amplitude rather than frequency
target_learning_goals: processing multimodal physiological and survey data for observational classroom research
examples: Raw EDA data were batch-processed outsourced to Ledalab for deconvolution and flowed back into the pipeline

title: EEG-alpha task-related synchronization as an inferred measure of internal attention
description: The article frames alpha rhythms (8-13 Hz) as sensory gating rather than cortical idling: alpha synchronization suppresses responsiveness of networks to irrelevant sensory input, allowing priority processing of internal processes such as top-down predictions. Internal attention is inferred from alpha task-related synchronization computed against a person-specific baseline, using a person-specific peak alpha frequency identified via Klimesch's lowest-desynchronization criterion.
requirements: A non-task baseline recording is required to compute task-related synchronization relative to each person's own baseline
constraints: The study's equipment had insufficient electrodes for spatial localization, so spatial information was excluded
target_learning_goals: inferring students' internal attentional focus during science tasks and tests
examples: High alpha task-related synchronization indicates a focus on internal processes, while low synchronization indicates focus on external stimuli

title: EEG-theta task-related synchronization as an exploratory inferred measure of working memory activity
description: The article links theta oscillations to encoding of new information via hippocampo-cortical feedback loops, with higher theta power indicating more efficient memory circuits and greater access to working memory. EEG-theta is computed as the proportionalized difference between task and baseline theta power over a person-specific band defined 6 to 4 Hz below the individual's peak alpha frequency, used exploratively alongside other indicators.
requirements: Theta power must be referenced to an individual's own baseline and proportionalized to account for factors such as scalp thickness and electrode connection
constraints: The article cautions that theta synchronization is linked to working memory but is not its sole determinant, necessitating cautious interpretation
target_learning_goals: inferring working memory activity during classroom science assessment
examples: Castro-Meneses et al. (2019) identified a correlation between theta power and cognitive load, suggesting theta as a real-time measure of working memory activity

title: Teacher-designed standardized science achievement test aligned to NSW Stage 4 and 5 syllabuses
description: The science achievement test was built from NSW Stage 4 and 5 syllabus units, administered in two halves around an online science survey. Questions were developed by a lead science teacher with 26 years of experience, reviewed by a panel of five science educators for difficulty and syllabus alignment, with an additional review for linguistic accessibility for students from non-English speaking backgrounds. Items were coded dichotomously and scores standardized by year level.
requirements: An iterative review panel ensured content, format, structure, and accessibility met the panel's satisfaction, including a spread of difficulty levels typical of science assessments
constraints: The test measured selected content outcomes aligned with the NSW Stage 4 and Stage 5 science curriculum only
target_learners: high school science students, including students from non-English speaking backgrounds
target_learning_goals: measuring science achievement as the study's primary outcome
examples: A sample unit with introductory information supported by visual aids was presented to students using Qualtrics

title: Select neuro-psychological measures against four explicit criteria before classroom EEG studies
description: The article proposes screening candidate neuro-psychological measures against four criteria: potential to add unique information about challenge and threat states, compatibility with portable EEG devices, a strong empirical and theoretical basis for inference from EEG data, and the ability to remain meaningful when aggregated over time in observational studies. Applying these criteria iteratively led to selecting alpha-based internal attention and theta-based working memory activity.
requirements: Candidate measures must have a plausible connection between the measured quantity and the cognitive states of interest, and must remain meaningful when averaged over extended periods
constraints: The criteria exclude measures needing precise brain signal localization, millisecond timing or relative phase, event-related potentials, and measures exceeding device frequency specifications
target_learners: high school science students in observational classroom studies
target_learning_goals: measuring cognitive processing and engagement during academic tasks
examples: The criteria excluded event-related potentials because the observational design involved no stimulus manipulation, and identified dominant brain rhythms such as alpha as having the greatest potential

article_title: Improving second-grade reading comprehension through a sustained content literacy intervention: A mixed-methods study examining the mediating role of domain-specific vocabulary.
citation: Mosher, D. M., Burkhauser, M. A., & Kim, J. S. (2024). Improving second-grade reading comprehension through a sustained content literacy intervention: A mixed-methods study examining the mediating role of domain-specific vocabulary. Journal of Educational Psychology, 116(4), 550–568. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000868
title: Theory of change: networks of domain-specific vocabulary as the visible components of schemas mediate comprehension transfer
description: The article's theoretical framework holds that schemas are "an abstract knowledge structure" whose visible components are semantically related networks of vocabulary words. Teaching domain-specific words in conceptually related networks helps students build topic and domain schemas, instantiate them during reading via construction-integration processes, and transfer them to related topics. The intervention theory of change links thematic lessons, concept mapping, interactive read alouds, argumentative writing, collaborative research, and word inquiry to vocabulary growth, which in turn supports word-to-text integration on transfer passages.
requirements: Sustained, aligned content literacy instruction across grades so topic schemas accumulate over time
Vocabulary taught in semantic networks rather than in isolation
constraints: Building science and social studies topic knowledge takes time in the early grades; most studies examine only one year
target_learning_goals: domain-specific reading comprehension in science
depth of domain-specific vocabulary knowledge
examples: The Grade 2 MORE unit on how paleontologists study dinosaurs used concept maps, read alouds, notetaking, word inquiry, and collaborative research across five 9-lesson cycles

article_title: The benefits of combining value for the self and others in utility-value interventions.
citation: Priniski, S. J., Rosenzweig, E. Q., Canning, E. A., Hecht, C. A., Tibbetts, Y., Hyde, J. S., & Harackiewicz, J. M. (2019). The Benefits of Combining Value for the Self and Others in Utility-Value Interventions. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000343
title: Combine self-focused and other-focused utility-value assignments through variety or choice rather than repeating one assignment type
description: The article recommends that when implementing utility-value writing interventions, instructors expose students to both self-focused essays and other-focused letters, either by assigning a fixed variety of both types or by letting students choose between them each time. The authors state that students "benefitted most from the UV intervention when the assignment structure exposed them to both types of UV assignments, rather than instructing them to complete the same type of assignment three times."
requirements: Assignments must be authentic coursework integrated into the curriculum, graded for scientific accuracy, and returned before unit exams, as in the study procedure.
constraints: Evidence comes from one introductory biology course for prospective majors at a single institution; the article states more work is needed to determine whether other assignment structures generalize, and the overall intervention contrast versus control was not significant.
target_learners: Undergraduate students in introductory college science courses
target_learning_goals: Course performance in introductory science
Motivation, interest, and perceived utility value of course material
examples: Students were randomly assigned to six conditions: control summaries, self-first variety, other-first variety, self-focused only, other-focused only, or choice between essay and letter on each of three assignments.
key_sources: Priniski, S. J., Rosenzweig, E. Q., Canning, E. A., Hecht, C. A., Tibbetts, Y., Hyde, J. S., & Harackiewicz, J. M. (2019). The Benefits of Combining Value for the Self and Others in Utility-Value Interventions. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000343

article_title: Does motivation predict changes in academic achievement beyond intelligence and personality? A multitheoretical perspective.
citation: Lavrijsen, J., Vansteenkiste, M., Boncquet, M., & Verschueren, K. (2022). Does motivation predict changes in academic achievement beyond intelligence and personality? A multitheoretical perspective. JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL PSYCHOLOGY, 114(4), 772–790. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000666
title: Improving student motivation is a worthwhile undertaking because motivational dynamics are more malleable than intelligence and personality
description: The article recommends investing in student motivation on the grounds that motivational dynamics are more malleable than intelligence and personality differences, while motivation still carries unique, positive associations with achievement. It states that "the unique, positive associations between motivation and achievement suggest that improving student motivation is a worthwhile undertaking." The Educational Impact Statement adds that parents, teachers and schools could do well to promote motivation in students.
requirements: Motivation's unique association with achievement beyond intelligence and personality, as established in the study
constraints: The recommendation rests on predictive associations in one sample of Flemish seventh graders, not on a tested intervention
target_learning_goals: academic achievement
examples: The study controlled for intelligence and personality and found motivational constructs still explained about a quarter of the explained variance in school results
key_sources: Lavrijsen, J., Vansteenkiste, M., Boncquet, M., & Verschueren, K. (2022). Does motivation predict changes in academic achievement beyond intelligence and personality? A multitheoretical perspective. JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL PSYCHOLOGY, 114(4), 772–790. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000666

article_title: Latent profiles as predictors of response to instruction for students with reading difficulties.
citation: Kulesz, P. A., Roberts, G. J., Francis, D. J., Cirino, P., Walczak, M., & Vaughn, S. (2024). Latent profiles as predictors of response to instruction for students with reading difficulties. Journal of Educational Psychology, 116(3). https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000832
title: Active View of Reading (AVR): reading comprehension depends on active self-regulation skills alongside word recognition and linguistic comprehension, with vocabulary as a bridging process
description: The Active View of Reading (Duke & Cartwright, 2021) extends the Simple View of Reading by adding self-regulation to the reading domains. As the article states, "The AVR model posits that for students to successfully comprehend text, in addition to having adequate skills in the reading domains, successful readers need to employ active self-regulation skills, which includes motivation, strategy use, and EF." Within AVR, vocabulary bridges word recognition and linguistic comprehension rather than belonging solely to linguistic comprehension. The article uses AVR to justify including executive functioning and attention measures and to interpret why the attention-stronger profile benefited more from intervention.
requirements: Adequate skills in the reading domains (word recognition and linguistic comprehension) plus active self-regulation skills including motivation, strategy use, and executive functioning
constraints: The article applies AVR to elementary students with reading difficulties in Grades 4–5; the framework is cited from Duke and Cartwright (2021) rather than tested directly in this study
target_learners: Elementary school students, including students with reading difficulties
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension
key_sources: Kulesz, P. A., Roberts, G. J., Francis, D. J., Cirino, P., Walczak, M., & Vaughn, S. (2024). Latent profiles as predictors of response to instruction for students with reading difficulties. Journal of Educational Psychology, 116(3). https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000832

article_title: Latent profiles as predictors of response to instruction for students with reading difficulties.
citation: Kulesz, P. A., Roberts, G. J., Francis, D. J., Cirino, P., Walczak, M., & Vaughn, S. (2024). Latent profiles as predictors of response to instruction for students with reading difficulties. Journal of Educational Psychology, 116(3). https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000832
title: Match reading intervention design to students' cognitive-language profiles: students with lower basic language but stronger attention may succeed with a non-customized multi-component intervention, while students with better language but weaker attention may need attention supports and more linguistic-comprehension focus
description: The article argues that latent cognitive-language profiles can guide customization of reading interventions. It reports that "Profile 1 students could benefit from a more customized intervention targeting attention and linguistic comprehension, while Profile 2 students may benefit from a non-customized (but evidence-based) multi-component reading intervention." Tailoring to a group profile rather than one-on-one customization may also yield cost savings, since customized one-on-one instruction is costly and time consuming.
requirements: Latent profile classification of students on basic language, cognitive, and attention measures to identify profile membership before assigning intervention components
constraints: The authors state it is conceivable but remains to be further examined that customized intervention based on cognitive-language profiles improves outcomes; profiles are sample specific and generalizability is unknown
target_learners: Upper elementary students with reading difficulties
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension
examples: In the study, Profile 2 students (lower basic language, higher attention) in the intervention condition outperformed controls on the Gates post-test, while Profile 1 students did not, prompting the recommendation that Profile 1 students need attention supports plus linguistic-comprehension instruction.
key_sources: Kulesz, P. A., Roberts, G. J., Francis, D. J., Cirino, P., Walczak, M., & Vaughn, S. (2024). Latent profiles as predictors of response to instruction for students with reading difficulties. Journal of Educational Psychology, 116(3). https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000832

article_title: The point of view of genetic psychology.
citation: E. A. Kirkpatrick. (1910). The Point of View of Genetic Psychology. The Journal of Educational Psychology.
title: Genetic psychology is a point of view and method that traces mental activities back to their origins and development, not a separate body of knowledge
description: The article defines genetic psychology as psychology that inquires how present mental states originated and traces them back to their beginnings. It argues the term indicates 'a point of view and a method of studying the phenomena in question' rather than a separate body of knowledge, analogous to evolutionary botany or zoology. In its special sense it denotes the evolutionary study of mind in the race.
requirements: The search for origins must be 'made prominent and carried back farther and farther toward ultimate beginnings' for a psychology to count as genetic
constraints: In its special sense the term designates only the evolutionary study of the beginnings of mind in lower organisms and the development of consciousness in the race
target_learners: learners across species and developmental stages
target_learning_goals: understanding how mental activities and learning processes develop from their beginnings
examples: The author classifies introspective, experimental, physiological, comparative and social psychology as genetic only insofar as each investigates processes of development rather than present states
key_sources: E. A. Kirkpatrick. (1910). The Point of View of Genetic Psychology. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0074078

article_title: The point of view of genetic psychology.
citation: E. A. Kirkpatrick. (1910). The Point of View of Genetic Psychology. The Journal of Educational Psychology.
title: Teach by favoring natural development rather than molding the child's mind into mature form
description: On the genetic view, the child's mind and every idea in it go through a process of development, and attempts to quickly mold the mind or a single idea into mature form are 'sure to fail'. The teacher's role is like the gardener's: make external conditions favorable, supply proper material for development, and give the necessary stimuli to activity, which for humans are chiefly social.
requirements: The teacher must make external conditions favorable, supply proper material for development, and give necessary stimuli to activity
constraints: Methods of teaching evolved by old-time psychologists 'distort and retard rather than hasten' development, per the article
target_learners: children at different stages of development
target_learning_goals: healthy development of the child's mind and ideas toward mature form
examples: The article contrasts the gardener's provision of thermal stimuli for plants with the social stimuli a teacher provides for human development
key_sources: E. A. Kirkpatrick. (1910). The Point of View of Genetic Psychology. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0074078

article_title: Test boredom: Exploring a neglected emotion.
citation: Goetz, T., Bieleke, M., Yanagida, T., Krannich, M., Roos, A.-L., Frenzel, A. C., Lipnevich, A. A., & Pekrun, R. (2023). Test boredom: Exploring a neglected emotion. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://osf.io/ftr4g/?view_only=beac4ca87987492294aeac4a1bb96c86
title: Control-value theory account of test boredom and its antecedents
description: The article applies Pekrun's control-value theory (CVT) of achievement emotions to testing situations, defining test boredom as a subtype of academic boredom: "Test boredom is the experience of boredom in situations that are labeled and/or experienced as tests." CVT posits that perceived control and perceived value are the key psychosocial antecedents: the control-boredom relation is curvilinear (boredom rises at very low and very high control), and "CVT posits a negative relation between perceived value and test boredom." The theory's relative universality assumption holds that structural relations with antecedents and outcomes are similar across academic settings, while test-specific features (task difficulty spread, low stakes) shape boredom magnitude.
requirements: Assessment of students' control and value appraisals (e.g., over-/underchallenge, intrinsic and extrinsic value) alongside boredom measures
constraints: The article notes the predicted curvilinear control relation has only partial support; perceived control was commonly found to relate linearly and negatively to boredom in prior studies
target_learners: school students in achievement testing situations
target_learning_goals: understanding and managing achievement emotions during tests
examples: Study 1 induced non-optimal control by splitting a low-stakes math test into easy and difficult blocks and assessing state boredom during each
key_sources: Goetz, T., Bieleke, M., Yanagida, T., Krannich, M., Roos, A.-L., Frenzel, A. C., Lipnevich, A. A., & Pekrun, R. (2023). Test boredom: Exploring a neglected emotion. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://osf.io/ftr4g/?view_only=beac4ca87987492294aeac4a1bb96c86

article_title: Test boredom: Exploring a neglected emotion.
citation: Goetz, T., Bieleke, M., Yanagida, T., Krannich, M., Roos, A.-L., Frenzel, A. C., Lipnevich, A. A., & Pekrun, R. (2023). Test boredom: Exploring a neglected emotion. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://osf.io/ftr4g/?view_only=beac4ca87987492294aeac4a1bb96c86
title: Test Boredom Scale (TBS-Trait and TBS-State)
description: The Test Boredom Scale is a multi-item self-report instrument constructed by modifying class- and learning-related boredom items from the Academic Emotions Questionnaire (AEQ). It comprises four sub-scales of three items each, representing the affective (e.g., "I'm bored during math exams"), cognitive, motivational, and physiological/expressive components of boredom, with parallel trait and state wordings on a 5-point response scale. Reliability "was α = .86 for the overall score comprising all four components" for the trait version, and coefficient α ranged from .83 to .94 across the five state assessments in Study 1.
requirements: Administration embedded in or alongside a test situation; the state version was administered five times before, during, and after the test
constraints: Developed and evaluated for mathematics tests with secondary-school students in the reported studies
target_learning_goals: measuring habitual and real-time boredom during tests
examples: Study 1 used the TBS-Trait one to three weeks before the test and the TBS-State within the test booklets
key_sources: Goetz, T., Bieleke, M., Yanagida, T., Krannich, M., Roos, A.-L., Frenzel, A. C., Lipnevich, A. A., & Pekrun, R. (2023). Test boredom: Exploring a neglected emotion. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://osf.io/ftr4g/?view_only=beac4ca87987492294aeac4a1bb96c86

article_title: Tentative order of difficulty of the Terman vocabulary with very young children.
citation: Cobb, Margaret V. (1921). Tentative Order of Difficulty of the Terman Vocabulary with Very Young Children. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journal_of_Educational_Psychology
title: Revised two-column word order for the Terman vocabulary test with young children
description: A reordered two-column word list for the Terman (Stanford Revision) vocabulary test, arranged from tabulated credit totals for kindergarten and Grade I children. The author states the new order "makes the two lists more nearly equal in difficulty, so that the use of one alone is somewhat more accurate," and that mimeographed sheets may easily be made up in this order or in a similar order derived from the data.
requirements: Mimeographed sheets made up in the revised order, or in a similar order anyone wishes to derive from the data
constraints: The author states it is her belief that using one list alone is "almost never advisable"
Scoring conventions were noted since "a different rule might have altered the result"
target_learning_goals: accurate assessment of children's vocabulary during individual intelligence examining
examples: The article prints a proposed 19-word order for each of the two vocabulary columns with tabulated credit totals for each word

article_title: Measuring teaching effectiveness in secondary schools: Multitrait–multimethod analyses of student–teacher agreement across 15 teaching effectiveness factors and student growth.
citation: Marsh, H. W., Knoester, C. E., Pfeiffer, M., Hattie, J., Dicke, T., Guo, J., Reeve, J., Pekrun, R., Lüdtke, O., Vasconcellos, D., & Huang, D. (2026). Measuring teaching effectiveness in secondary schools: Multitrait–multimethod analyses of student–teacher agreement across 15 teaching effectiveness factors and student growth. Journal of Educational Psychology. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0001035
title: SEEQ-S and TEEQ-S: parallel 15-factor student and teacher instruments for secondary-school teaching effectiveness
description: The article introduces two parallel multidimensional instruments: the Student Evaluation of Educational Quality–Secondary, gathering student feedback, and the parallel Teacher Evaluation of Educational Quality–Secondary, a self-evaluation tool for teachers. Both "assess the same 15 factors of teaching effectiveness", with TEEQ-S items rephrasing SEEQ-S items for teacher self-evaluation. They are designed for formative use within an ongoing school feedback program.
requirements: Administered to intact classes with the teacher completing a parallel self-rating for the same class, linked by class identifiers
constraints: Designed for formative feedback and professional learning rather than summative evaluation
The study sample is a convenience sample and is not nationally representative
target_learning_goals: Multidimensional evaluation of teaching effectiveness for teacher reflection and professional growth
examples: Students completed the SEEQ-S on school devices via Qualtrics and later a TXcel platform; each student evaluated a single identified class while the corresponding teacher completed a parallel self-rating
key_sources: Marsh, H. W., Knoester, C. E., Pfeiffer, M., Hattie, J., Dicke, T., Guo, J., Reeve, J., Pekrun, R., Lüdtke, O., Vasconcellos, D., & Huang, D. (2026). Measuring teaching effectiveness in secondary schools: Multitrait–multimethod analyses of student–teacher agreement across 15 teaching effectiveness factors and student growth. Journal of Educational Psychology. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0001035

article_title: Measuring teaching effectiveness in secondary schools: Multitrait–multimethod analyses of student–teacher agreement across 15 teaching effectiveness factors and student growth.
citation: Marsh, H. W., Knoester, C. E., Pfeiffer, M., Hattie, J., Dicke, T., Guo, J., Reeve, J., Pekrun, R., Lüdtke, O., Vasconcellos, D., & Huang, D. (2026). Measuring teaching effectiveness in secondary schools: Multitrait–multimethod analyses of student–teacher agreement across 15 teaching effectiveness factors and student growth. Journal of Educational Psychology. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0001035
title: A 15-dimension taxonomy of secondary teaching effectiveness organized by self-determination theory need-supportive facets
description: The article articulates 15 theoretically and empirically grounded dimensions of teaching effectiveness for secondary schools, nine adapted from the university SEEQ tradition and six added as secondary-appropriate scales: classroom management, cognitive activation, organization/explaining, choice, relevance, and technology. Self-determination theory organizes the profile: "Autonomy-supportive practices (e.g., choice, relevance, elements of group interaction/climate) foster students' sense of volition", while competence-supportive and relatedness-supportive practices scaffold challenge and belonging. Table 2 provides concise conceptual definitions for all 15 scales.
requirements: Items must be lesson-proximal practices directly experienced by students during lessons
Facets retained require strong theoretical grounding and consistent empirical links to student learning or well-being
constraints: Additional possible facets (e.g., management of time) were not retained because they lacked strong theoretical grounding and/or consistent empirical links
Using fewer facets would underrepresent theoretically and empirically established components of instructional quality
target_learning_goals: Comprehensive multidimensional definition and feedback on teaching effectiveness
examples: Table 2 defines each dimension with what high student ratings indicate, e.g., cognitive activation: the teacher encourages students to think deeply and figure out and complete classroom activities for themselves
key_sources: Marsh, H. W., Knoester, C. E., Pfeiffer, M., Hattie, J., Dicke, T., Guo, J., Reeve, J., Pekrun, R., Lüdtke, O., Vasconcellos, D., & Huang, D. (2026). article_title: Measuring teaching effectiveness in secondary schools: Multitrait–multimethod analyses of student–teacher agreement across 15 teaching effectiveness factors and student growth.
citation: Marsh, H. W., Knoester, C. E., Pfeiffer, M., Hattie, J., Dicke, T., Guo, J., Reeve, J., Pekrun, R., Lüdtke, O., Vasconcellos, D., & Huang, D. (2026). Measuring teaching effectiveness in secondary schools: Multitrait–multimethod analyses of student–teacher agreement across 15 teaching effectiveness factors and student growth. Journal of Educational Psychology. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0001035
title: Use student and teacher teaching-effectiveness ratings formatively for reflection and professional learning, not summative evaluation
description: The article positions the SEEQ-S and TEEQ-S as formative diagnostic tools: they are "Designed for formative feedback and professional learning rather than summative evaluation", transforming multidimensional evidence into actionable feedback for reflective practice and targeted professional growth. Multidimensional evaluations suit this purpose because they offer fine-grained information about specific teaching behaviors that can guide instructional improvement over time.
requirements: Feedback must be tailored to individual strengths and growth areas using the 15-factor profile
Integration into routine school improvement cycles with ongoing, longitudinal feedback
constraints: The article states the present study did not directly test feedback interventions; the instruments were designed with this formative purpose in mind
target_learning_goals: Teacher self-reflection, instructional improvement, and targeted professional growth
examples: The TXcel initiative integrates SEEQ-S and TEEQ-S into feedback reports to inform goal setting and instructional planning

article_title: Measuring teaching effectiveness in secondary schools: Multitrait–multimethod analyses of student–teacher agreement across 15 teaching effectiveness factors and student growth.
citation: Marsh, H. W., Knoester, C. E., Pfeiffer, M., Hattie, J., Dicke, T., Guo, J., Reeve, J., Pekrun, R., Lüdtke, O., Vasconcellos, D., & Huang, D. (2026). Measuring teaching effectiveness in secondary schools: Multitrait–multimethod analyses of student–teacher agreement across 15 teaching effectiveness factors and student growth. Journal of Educational Psychology. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0001035
title: Analyze student evaluations of secondary teaching at the class-mean level, aligned with parallel teacher reports for the same class
description: The article argues that because inferences concern the shared classroom experience and the teacher's practice, student ratings should be aggregated to class means rather than analyzed at the student level: "we evaluate student ratings at the class-mean level and align them with parallel teacher reports for the same class." Student-level analyses confound within- and between-class variance and underreport reliability at the teacher/class level, a critique the article traces to prior secondary-school SET research.
requirements: Ratings collected in intact classrooms with each student evaluating a single identified class
Class records linked to the corresponding teacher's parallel self-rating via class identifiers
constraints: Classes with fewer than five students were excluded to reduce unreliability in small aggregates
target_learning_goals: Valid measurement of classroom-level teaching effectiveness for formative feedback
examples: In the validation analyses, student ratings were aggregated to 1,013 class-mean responses aligned with 549 teacher self-evaluations

article_title: An experimental critique of the Binet-Simon scale.
citation: Carl C. Brigham. (1914). An Experimental Critique of the Binet-Simon Scale. The Journal of Educational Psychology.
title: Classify Binet-Simon results by the difference between mental and chronological age, computed in tenths of a year
description: The article proposes a standardized method of classifying Binet-Simon results: calculate chronological age in tenths or fifths of a year, place the mental age in tenths or fifths giving credit for every test passed above the basal age, and classify by the difference between the two. The writer "would therefore suggest the following as the standardized method of classifying the results obtained from the Binet-Simon tests." This method avoids the double smoothing error that afflicts classifying first by chronological and then by mental age.
requirements: Calculate the chronological age in tenths or fifths of a year and the mental age in tenths or fifths, giving credit for every test passed above the basal age, then classify by years or half-years according to the amount of analysis the data will stand
constraints: Classification by age difference remains liable to one source of error — smoothing the figures to years or half-years
target_learners: school children in the first six grades assessed with the Binet-Simon scale
target_learning_goals: accurate measurement and grading of intelligence and individual differences
examples: In this study the chronological ages were calculated in tenths of a year, and the age difference computed in tenths, applied to the 294 cases in the regular grades of the Princeton Model School.
key_sources: Carl C. Brigham. (1914). An Experimental Critique of the Binet-Simon Scale. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0071183

article_title: Intelligence and its measurement: A symposium--VII.
citation: Pressey, S. L. (1920). Intelligence and Its Measurement. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Intelligence+and+Its+Measurement+Pressey
title: Evaluate intelligence tests by their efficiency at the concrete practical problem they were built for, not by intrinsic psychometric appeal
description: Pressey proposes a problem-driven standard for test construction and evaluation: a test is satisfactory only insofar as it deals efficiently with the practical problem that motivated it, such as surveying a school system to find children who should be placed in special classes. As he puts it, "there is no value in measuring intelligence simply for the sake of measuring it; the tests are given in an effort to deal with some practical problem."
requirements: The practical problem the test is meant to solve must be specified before the test is built and evaluated
constraints: Pressey frames this for prognosis and class-placement problems in schools, not as a general theory of what intelligence is
target_learners: school children being screened for special or regular classes
target_learning_goals: appropriate educational placement and prognosis of school capacity
examples: For placing children in special classes, he recommends building an examination not involving matters taught specifically in school, but as much like school work as possible in other respects
key_sources: Pressey, S. L. (1920). Intelligence and Its Measurement. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Intelligence+and+Its+Measurement+Pressey

article_title: Intelligence and its measurement: A symposium--VII.
citation: Pressey, S. L. (1920). Intelligence and Its Measurement. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Intelligence+and+Its+Measurement+Pressey
title: General intelligence as a working hypothesis for prognosis, to be kept only while it works better than alternatives
description: Pressey's account treats the concept of general intelligence not as a discovered entity but as a pragmatic tool that arose from an educational situation. He states that "the concept of general intelligence is for the writer, primarily, simply a working hypothesis which has been very helpful in the first attack upon problems of prognosis," and that it "should continue as a working hypothesis until other hypotheses are found to work better." The hypothesis earns its keep by suggesting general lines of approach and giving investigators courage to attack the otherwise impossibly complex prognosis problem, but it must not prevent analysis of that problem.
requirements: The hypothetical nature of the concept, and the educational situation which first gave rise to such tests, must be kept in mind
constraints: Pressey warns against being dominated by the concept or hypnotized by statistics, and against the notion that intelligence testing is a short-cut that will put everything in the schools to rights
target_learners: school children whose educational prognosis is being assessed
target_learning_goals: prognosis of capacity for school work
key_sources: Pressey, S. L. (1920). Intelligence and Its Measurement. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Intelligence+and+Its+Measurement+Pressey

article_title: A criticism of the Yerkes-Bridges Point Scale, with alternative suggestions.
citation: ARTHUK S. OTIS (Stanford University). (1917). A Criticism of the Yerkes-Bridges Point Scale, with Alternative Suggestions. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Vol. VIII, No. 3. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Otis+criticism+Yerkes-Bridges+point+scale
title: Otis's absolute grade of intelligence scale with coefficient of brightness
description: The article proposes expressing intelligence on an arbitrary absolute scale whose median adult grade is 100 and whose unit is one-tenth of the quartile of the distribution of absolute degrees, so that adult grades fall in a normal distribution. Brightness is then expressed as a coefficient of brightness: the quotient of a person's absolute grade by the absolute grade normal for his age. Because degrees of brightness are assumed constant for a given child, this "absolute intelligence quotient" lets one predict the probable ultimate absolute grade, and hence maximum attainments, from a child's rank at any age. The article states the scale is "a means to an end," discarded once percentages of persons exceeded are read off.
requirements: Assumes the distribution of absolute grades of intelligence is normal for each age and that degrees of brightness are constant for a given individual
constraints: The exact relation between a child's brightness at one age and another awaits repeated testing of the same children in successive years; the mental-age method cannot express degrees above normal adult ability
target_learners: children of all ages being assessed for intelligence
target_learning_goals: measurement of general intelligence and prediction of ultimate intellectual attainment
examples: The article tabulates theoretical percentages of adults attaining grades 60 to 140 with the quartile taken as 8 points and median at 100, and illustrates a 12-year-old with 880 points on the 75% curve having a coefficient of brightness of 1.10
key_sources: ARTHUK S. OTIS (Stanford University). (1917). A Criticism of the Yerkes-Bridges Point Scale, with Alternative Suggestions. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Vol. VIII, No. 3. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Otis+criticism+Yerkes-Bridges+point+scale

article_title: A criticism of the Yerkes-Bridges Point Scale, with alternative suggestions.
citation: ARTHUK S. OTIS (Stanford University). (1917). A Criticism of the Yerkes-Bridges Point Scale, with Alternative Suggestions. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Vol. VIII, No. 3. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Otis+criticism+Yerkes-Bridges+point+scale
title: The Binet Point Scale: a paper reorganization of the Stanford Revision giving one point per month of mental age
description: The article constructs a Binet Point Scale by reorganizing the Stanford Revision of the Binet Scale on paper into six lists, each list composed of tests representing different degrees of the same ability, with point values read from a correspondence table in which one point equals one month of mental age. Administration and scoring are identical to the ordinary Binet; only the mode of expression changes, from mental age to a summed point-score. The article argues that "the present Binet Scale is already a point scale, for all the purposes for which Yerkes' and Bridges' alteration of the Binet Scale could be used," and that this conversion preserves more nearly equal point values than the Yerkes-Bridges rearrangement.
requirements: The tests are given and scored exactly as in the regular Binet Scale; the correspondence table assumes passing six tests (12 points) indicates mental age III and twelve tests (24 points) mental age IV

citation: ARTHUK S. OTIS (Stanford University). (1917). A Criticism of the Yerkes-Bridges Point Scale, with Alternative Suggestions. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Vol. VIII, No. 3. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Otis+criticism+Yerkes-Bridges+point+scale
title: Weight test scores according to each test's significance as a measure of intelligence before combining them

target_learning_goals: accurate composite measurement of general intelligence
examples: The article's Table V illustrates a weighted average of 84 versus an unweighted 80 for a seven-test series with weights from 1 to 5, and Table VI converts sentence-test performance into weighted points
