citation: Greene, H. A. (1928). Tests for the Measurement of Certain Phases of Linguistic Organization in Sentences. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org
title: Greene's tentative analysis of language ability into oral and written expression with mechanical, grammatical and rhetorical factors
description: The article presents a tentative analysis dividing language ability into oral expression (voice, articulation, grammatical errors, vocabulary, audience attitudes, logical organization) and written expression. Written expression is further divided into "Mechanical factors" such as spelling, punctuation and form, "Grammatical factors", and "Rhetorical factors" including choice of words, interestingness of material, and logical organization at sentence, paragraph and larger-unit levels. The author calls the analysis "crude and incomplete" and uses it to locate the unmeasured element his tests target.

constraints: The author states the analysis is crude and incomplete and that a number of elements were purposely omitted

title: Organization Test: sentence-rearrangement exercises measuring organization ability within the sentence
description: The Organization Test confronts the subject with a limited number of ideas presented in jumbled order which, when properly arranged, make a complete logical statement. Sentences from lower grade readers and primers were divided into thought units, jumbled by randomized number permutations, and answered by writing the numbers in the proper order rather than rewriting the sentence. Two parallel forms of ten exercises each were standardized, with a total possible score of 100 points per form.
requirements: Sentences must be simple straightforward statements of fact whose meaning remains clear when removed from context, so that vocabulary difficulties are eliminated
constraints: The tests represent but a single phase of Organization ability, namely organization within the sentence and not paragraph organization

target_learning_goals: logical organization of material within sentences

article_title: In-class attention, spatial ability, and mathematics anxiety predict across-grade gains in adolescents’ mathematics achievement.
citation: Geary, D. C., Hoard, M. K., Nugent, L., & Scofield, J. E. (2021). In-Class Attention, Spatial Ability, and Mathematics Anxiety Predict Across-Grade Gains in Adolescents' Mathematics Achievement. Journal of Educational Psychology, 113(4), 754-769. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000487

description: The article argues that because many factors have been proposed as contributing to mathematics growth, interventions risk being unfocused; its broad assessment identified the most plausible contributors for middle school students. The results "have implications for how to best target interventions for students at risk for long-term difficulties with mathematics," pointing to in-class attention, spatial ability, and prior competence as the factors to prioritize. This is a targeting principle grounded in the study's Bayesian and multilevel findings, not a tested intervention.

article_title: Some recent literature upon fatigue.
citation: G. M. W. (1910). Abstracts and Reviews: Some Recent Literature upon Fatigue; Studies in Arithmetic. The Journal of Educational Psychology.
title: MacDougall's synaptic-resistance account: fatigue reflects the balance between available energy and resistance at the synapses, with special energy reserves explaining struggle against fatigue
description: The review presents MacDougall's theory of fatigue, which rejects Verworn's simpler waste-product account and instead follows Sherrington in viewing neuro-muscular activity via the reflex-arc concept and the 'resistance' or 'blocking' of nerve paths at the synapses. On this view, "Fatigue is, therefore, a matter of the relative balance between available energy and the resistance against which this energy must work." Individual differences in this balance yield the neurasthenic constitution (feeble resistances) or the hysteric type (chronically deficient energy), and special energy reserves explain how interest or powerful incentives permit work without felt fatigue.
requirements: The account presupposes the reflex-arc concept and the notion of synaptic blocking or resistance of nerve paths, as utilized by Sherrington and others.
constraints: The reviewer warns that these views of the ultimate nature of fatigue are, and seem likely to remain, a matter of conjecture and speculative opinion, not demonstrated facts.
target_learners: school children whose fatigue and recuperation the school program must manage
target_learning_goals: regulation of mental work and management of fatigue in study and schooling
examples: MacDougall cites Darwin and Spencer as individuals who can work effectively for a short time but tire quickly and demand rest before resuming.

article_title: Verbal and abstract elements in intelligence examinations.
citation: Herring, J. P. (1923). Verbal and Abstract Elements in Intelligence Examinations. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org
title: Two continuous scales, C (concrete–abstract) and N (non-verbal–verbal), for describing and rating test content and behavior
description: The article proposes that human behavior and test content be described on two continuous seven-point scales rather than dualistic categories: scale C runs from concrete (pertaining to things or objects) to abstract (pertaining to relations between objects, involving analytic and synthetic thinking), and scale N from non-verbal to verbal (involving use of words and symbols). The article states it is "false to classify human behavior dualistically" and that responses are distributed "continuous throughout both scale C and scale N." Five judges rated 63 test units on both scales, producing subjective scales against which any homogeneous portion of test material may be rated for abstractness and symbolism.
requirements: Judged classification of test units by multiple judges, with each judge given a voice in determining the meaning of the concepts as well as classifying material
constraints: The definitions of abstract, concrete, and verbal are not regarded as final or even as necessarily valid, but as starting points for classification
target_learners: School children in grades IV–VII assessed with group intelligence examinations
target_learning_goals: Measurement and prediction of general intelligence
examples: Digit symbol tests were rated distinctly concrete and very non-symbolic; the Army Beta Maze Test as concrete as anything found; arithmetical problems rated very abstract.

article_title: Verbal and abstract elements in intelligence examinations.

title: Prefer abstract and verbal test content when selecting material for intelligence examinations
description: For prediction and control, the article recommends building intelligence examinations chiefly from abstract and verbal content, because such tests "afford better means for the prediction of human intelligence" than concrete and non-verbal tests, and because they also "have higher coefficients of reliability." The middle portions of both scales are distinguishably better material than the extreme concrete and non-verbal ends but inferior to the abstract extremes.

constraints: The data do not permit the conclusion that concrete and non-verbal tests may not properly supplement the others in a battery of tests; there are circumstances in which they are the feasible form of procedure

target_learning_goals: Prediction of general intelligence and selection of examination content
examples: The study correlated segments of the Dearborn, Army Beta, Pressey Primer, Indiana Cross-cut and Thorndike Visual Vocabulary examinations, classified by judges, against a seven-part weighted composite criterion.

description: Baldwin advocates the individualizing method: following the same children consecutively over years with both physical and mental measurements, rather than cross-sectional snapshots. He argues that "The day for the study of physical growth processes by single measurements is over" and that prediction of later status requires identifying a child's growth-curve type, chronological and physiological age. The method underpins all the paper's prediction analyses and his call for intensive consecutive studies of the same individuals across a series of years.

constraints: The author notes no complete longitudinal mental-development data comparable to the physical data yet existed, and that exact prediction error for various examination intervals could not be determined from his data

article_title: The education and control of the emotions.
citation: Henry, T. S. (1916). The Education and Control of the Emotions. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu/
title: Reward desired emotional expression with pleasure and attach unpleasant consequences to harmful emotions
description: A general rule for teachers developing good emotions: provide every opportunity for desirable emotions to originate, then ensure their proper expression is 'rewarded with pleasure, so that a definite connection may be set up between the emotional state and the pleasurable consequences'. Conversely, situations calling forth harmful emotions should be avoided and unpleasant consequences connected with their expression. The article presents this as the application of consequence experience to emotional life.
requirements: Opportunities for the desired emotion to originate must be provided so that pleasurable consequences can be connected with its proper expression
constraints: The article frames the rule as an application of Spencer's 'doctrine of natural punishments', relying on experience with natural individual and social consequences rather than teacher-imposed rewards alone
target_learning_goals: development of desirable emotions
inhibition of harmful emotional expressions
examples: The article prescribes avoiding every situation which tends to call forth a harmful emotion and connecting unpleasant consequences with its expression, citing Thorndike's Principles of Teaching.

article_title: The education and control of the emotions.
citation: Henry, T. S. (1916). The Education and Control of the Emotions. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu/
title: Cultivate a desired emotion or disposition by voluntarily performing its outward bodily manifestations
description: A method of emotional control, described as an outgrowth of the James-Lange theory though acted on earlier: assume the bodily attitude characteristic of an emotion to further its development. James states that 'when we wish to cultivate a certain disposition, we should go through with the movements which make up the outward manifestation of that disposition'. Thorndike and Münsterberg endorse the same principle, the latter treating feelings as essentially motor reactions controllable through voluntary movement.
requirements: The learner must voluntarily assume the movements and attitudes that make up the outward manifestation of the desired emotion or disposition
constraints: The article states it is impossible to say to just what extent one can control his emotions and feelings by assuming appropriate bodily attitudes, while affirming there must be something in the principle
target_learning_goals: cultivation of desired emotional dispositions such as courage, cheerfulness, and affection
examples: Thorndike's illustrations: a frightened person walking steadily toward the enemy, shouting defiance and brandishing his weapon so fear may be replaced by courage; and a kindergarten teacher treating a disfigured baby with lap, smiles and caresses until disgust gives way to tolerance and even affection.

article_title: The education and control of the emotions.
citation: Henry, T. S. (1916). The Education and Control of the Emotions. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu/
title: Control emotion by reclassifying the stimulus through judgment, changing the attitude taken toward it
description: Following Pillsbury, the article holds that real control of emotion is effected at the source by classifying, and thus controlling, the situation which calls the emotion forth. 'Sensations and stimuli which are capable of being classified in different ways arouse different emotions upon the basis of that classification' — the same remark may be an insult from a stranger or a jest from a friend. Thorndike frames this as learning to judge the situation objectively by the facts, not subjectively by the feelings.
requirements: The stimulus must fall outside the class of fundamental instincts most closely linked with their stimuli, since the attitude is only to a considerable extent under one's control
constraints: The article notes this control is available only to some degree, and that the attitude is chiefly controllable for stimuli outside fundamental instinct-linked classes
target_learning_goals: inhibition of undesirable emotional reactions such as anger through objective judgment of the situation
examples: The article describes a teacher relieving an over-emotional state in a child by counseling and reasoning, where explanation of the situation may change the object of the feeling and draw it into harmless or useful channels; and directing the attention elsewhere until the occasion for the emotion is past.
key_sources: Henry, T. S. (1916). The Education and Control of the Emotions. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu/

article_title: The education and control of the emotions.
citation: Henry, T. S. (1916). The Education and Control of the Emotions. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu/
title: Redirect emotions toward proper objects and sublimate primitive feelings by attaching them to other objects and processes
description: For emotions good or bad only according to their objects, such as ambition, pride and anger, control involves proper direction; the article argues it matters to be able to hate aright. Closely allied is sublimation, defined by Colvin and Bagley as 'the method which attempts to lift a strong feeling bodily out of the instinct to which it naturally belongs and to fasten it firmly to another object and to an entirely different process'. Effective control thus lies in forming attitudes, ideals and sentiments attached to the original emotion as a core.
requirements: Appropriate ideas must be attached to the original emotion as a core to form attitudes, ideals and sentiments
constraints: The Freudians use the term sublimation exclusively for the sexual instincts, though the article extends it by a similar interpretation to other emotions
target_learning_goals: directing emotions such as ambition, pride and anger toward proper objects
sublimating primitive instincts into socially valuable sentiments
examples: Colvin and Bagley's illustrations: the Salvation Army enlisting a military organization with suggestions of physical combat in the service of peaceable ideals, and the Boy Scout movement attaching feelings connected with primitive instincts to objects insuring only symbolic responses.

article_title: Multimedia effects during retrieval practice: Images that reveal the answer reduce vocabulary learning.
citation: van den Broek, G., Van Gog, T., Jansen, E., Pleijsant, M., & Kester, L. (2021). Multimedia Effects During Retrieval Practice: Images That Reveal the Answer Reduce Vocabulary Learning. Journal of Educational Psychology, 113(8), 1587-1608. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000499
title: Avoid informative images during vocabulary retrieval practice because they can harm learning
description: The article concludes that during vocabulary retrieval practice, "informative images are thus potentially harmful and students have limited insight into these effects." The principle is to omit images that help learners retrieve the answer during practice, or present them only after the retrieval attempt, because such images reduce later recall while inflating feelings of competence.
requirements: Retrieval practice of vocabulary items where the image could reveal or hint at the answer
constraints: Findings come from secondary education classroom experiments on foreign vocabulary with posttests 1 to 4 days after practice
target_learners: secondary education students learning foreign vocabulary
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of foreign vocabulary
examples: In the experiments, images that helped students retrieve the answer weakened posttest recall relative to no images or images after the retrieval attempt.

article_title: Reading comprehension on handheld devices versus on paper: A narrative review and meta-analysis of the medium effect and its moderators.
citation: Salmerón, L., Altamura, L., Delgado, P., Karagiorgi, A., & Vargas, C. (2023). Reading comprehension on handheld devices vs. on paper: A narrative review and meta-analysis of the medium effect and its moderators. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://dx.doi.org/10.1037/edu0000830
title: Reading for Understanding framework organizing screen inferiority moderators into reader, text, activity, and socio-cultural context
description: The article uses the Reading for Understanding framework (Snow et al., 2002) as its organizing taxonomy for potential moderators of the screen inferiority effect on handheld devices. The framework conceives comprehension as extracting and constructing knowledge, where "Comprehension occurs as the interaction of three main elements: reader (individual abilities, knowledge and attitudes), text (any form of print or digital text), and activity (purpose, processes, and consequences of reading), that take place within a particular socio-cultural context." The review maps moderator evidence onto these four elements and codes study variables accordingly for meta-regression.
requirements: Applied to reading-medium research, requires coding of study characteristics into reader, text, activity, and socio-cultural context variables for moderator analysis
constraints: The authors note most previous research has focused on the text and activity levels, and to a lesser extent the reader and socio-cultural context
target_learners: autonomous readers across educational stages, from primary school to undergraduates
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension of print and digital texts
examples: The review's coding scheme classified educational stage, text genre and length, navigation mode, device type, time limit, question type, session modality, and publication year as moderators within the four framework elements.

article_title: Reading comprehension on handheld devices versus on paper: A narrative review and meta-analysis of the medium effect and its moderators.
citation: Salmerón, L., Altamura, L., Delgado, P., Karagiorgi, A., & Vargas, C. (2023). Reading comprehension on handheld devices vs. on paper: A narrative review and meta-analysis of the medium effect and its moderators. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://dx.doi.org/10.1037/edu0000830
title: Shallowing hypothesis as an explanatory account of the screen inferiority effect
description: The review presents the shallowing hypothesis (Annisette & Lafreniere, 2017) as one of the most influential theoretical accounts of the screen inferiority effect. It "assumes that typical interactions with digital devices involve quick episodes with short pieces of texts, which favors a mindset aiming to browse as much information as possible, without in-depth elaboration." When reading on a digital device, readers may activate this shallow mindset and allocate cognitive resources less efficiently, which should be most visible in challenging contexts demanding self-regulation. The review uses it to generate moderator predictions, several of which existing evidence does not support.
requirements: As an account, it presupposes that digital reading habits transfer a browsing-oriented mindset to comprehension tasks
constraints: The review notes existing evidence does not support the prediction of higher screen inferiority for older students, and similar comprehension on tablets versus e-readers does not support it for handheld devices
target_learners: readers across ages who use digital devices, from primary students to undergraduates
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension of print and digital texts
examples: The review derived moderator predictions from the hypothesis, including larger effects for expository texts, longer texts, scrolling, tablets, time limits, and group settings.

title: Foster print reading in schools while developing effective ways to incorporate handheld devices for reading
description: Based on their synthesis showing a small but significant comprehension advantage for print over handheld devices, the authors recommend that schools continue promoting print reading while also working out how handheld devices can be incorporated effectively for reading purposes. They state: "We discuss the need to continue fostering print reading in schools while developing effective ways to incorporate handheld devices for reading purposes." The educational impact statement adds that in-print reading can be considered an efficient way to promote students' text comprehension.

constraints: The recommendation rests on a small pooled effect with high heterogeneity across studies
target_learners: school students who read on tablets and e-readers
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension
examples: The meta-analyses pooled 38 between-participants and 21 within-participants effect sizes comparing handheld-device and print reading comprehension.

article_title: Cooperative learning reduces the gender gap in perceived social competences: A large-scale nationwide longitudinal experiment.
citation: Rudmann, O., Batruch, A., Visintin, E. P., Sommet, N., Bressoux, P., Darnon, C., ... Butera, F. (2023). Cooperative Learning Reduces the Gender Gap in Perceived Social Competences. A Large-Scale Nationwide Longitudinal Experiment. Journal of Educational Psychology (accepted for publication). https://osf.io/qarxk/?view_only=e772332576a5421cbf61b3092e567ac9
title: Jigsaw classroom as cooperative learning with positive goal and resource interdependence
description: The Jigsaw classroom is a cooperative learning method in which "each group member possesses a unique portion of the learning materials" and all members pursue the same goal, creating positive goal and resource interdependence. In the ProFAN experiment it was implemented in five stages: Jigsaw groups of 3-5 students each study a sub-section, meet in expert groups, return to present their sub-section, and produce a collective assignment requiring articulation of all sub-sections. The article positions this structure as what allows all students to practice social competences.
requirements: Each student must feel responsible for attaining their learning goal as well as helping groupmates attain the same goal
A unique portion of the learning materials must be distributed to each group member so resources must be combined
constraints: Some criticism has recently emerged about the effectiveness of this method as far as performance and achievement are concerned
target_learning_goals: social competences such as communication, collaboration, and collective problem solving
examples: In the ProFAN experiment students went four times through three pedagogical sequences (12 sequences over two years) under the Jigsaw method in 108 French vocational high schools

article_title: Pedagogical psychology of report.
citation: Lipmann, O. (1911). Pedagogical Psychology of Report. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://archive.org
title: Distribution-of-attention account of children's report errors, with Stern's developmental stages of report content
description: The article explains children's poorer reports not by weaker concentration but by a qualitatively different distribution of attention: children notice details adults miss and overlook details adults call essential, so questioning about adult-essential details yields errors. If the child formulated the questions, the adult would report the child's essential details equally poorly. The account draws on Stern's stages, in which "the child at first notices mainly objects; later he turns his attention to their properties and to actions, and only during the last stage does he notice the relations between objects."
requirements: Applies when the report concerns details of an experience rather than material deliberately memorized for reproduction
constraints: The author states the argument is not strictly proved but made very probable, and that no one has yet determined how the child's distribution of attention differs from the adult's
target_learning_goals: accurate reporting of observed experiences
examples: The author argues that if attention distribution were identical across observers, the order of objects ranked by report accuracy would be the same for all classes of observers, which is not the case.
key_sources: Lipmann, O. (1911). Pedagogical Psychology of Report. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0070700

article_title: Pedagogical psychology of report.
citation: Lipmann, O. (1911). Pedagogical Psychology of Report. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://archive.org
title: Childhood imagination as reality: imagined content initially bears the character of a memory-image
description: The article proposes a fundamental characteristic of the childish imagination as a further cause of faulty reports: "everything that is imagined is imagined as real." Whether an image comes as a memory-image, from fancy, or from suggestion, it at first plays the role of a real experience for the child, so imagined fillings of memory gaps are reported as actual memories. The author limits this crude formulation to the very small child, since accumulating experience teaches that fancy differs from reality, but even school children's recognition remains relatively little developed.
requirements: Explains wrong reports that arise when children fill gaps in memory with material from fancy, custom, or suggestion
constraints: The author states the crude formulation holds only for the very small child, and that the role of fancy does not admit of experimental treatment
target_learning_goals: accurate reporting of past experiences
examples: The author cites observation-based material on fancy as a source of wrong reports, noting it cannot be treated experimentally.
key_sources: Lipmann, O. (1911). Pedagogical Psychology of Report. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0070700

article_title: The influence of improvement in one simple mental process upon other related processes.
citation: Poffenberger, A. T., Jr. (1915). The influence of improvement in one simple mental process upon other related processes. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 6(8), 459-474.
title: Specific stimulus-response bonds and identical elements as the mechanism of transfer of training
description: The article explains transfer through Thorndikean bonds between situation and response: improvement spreads only when the two tasks share identical elements or when one process incorporates bonds previously formed. "This test seems to indicate that learning is facilitated by incorporating into the process to be learned previously formed bonds between situation and response, or, in other words, it indicates the transfer of identical elements." Interference arises when a new response to the same stimulus requires breaking an old bond. The experiment was designed to isolate these specific bonds by eliminating general factors such as adaptation to the experimental conditions.
requirements: Tasks must be analyzable into stimulus and response components so that identical or conflicting bonds can be identified
constraints: The authors note it will probably never be possible to analyze any process into stimulus and response terms within the nervous system, where any real transfer must finally be located
target_learners: adult subjects familiar with psychological tests
target_learning_goals: efficiency of simple mental processes such as naming, cancellation, and arithmetic operations
examples: The seven test comparisons varied the relation between training and test processes from close similarity to complete antagonism
key_sources: Poffenberger, A. T., Jr. (1915). The influence of improvement in one simple mental process upon other related processes. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 6(8), 459-474. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0075269

article_title: The influence of improvement in one simple mental process upon other related processes.
citation: Poffenberger, A. T., Jr. (1915). The influence of improvement in one simple mental process upon other related processes. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 6(8), 459-474.
title: Transfer experiments should train to a level practice curve and use control subjects before testing transfer
description: The article argues that earlier transfer studies were unconvincing because training was too short and controls were missing. It states that "the training series was continued long enough to bring the curves of improvement practically to a level, before the transfer effect was tested," and notes that Ebert and Meumann "used no control subjects." General factors such as adaptation to the experiment were eliminated by using subjects familiar with the tests and discarding the first two trials of the first and last test series.
requirements: A control group tested over the same interval
Training continued until improvement curves level off
Familiar subjects and discarded preliminary trials to remove general sources of improvement
constraints: With few subjects, results are expressed in absolute amounts with probable errors rather than percentages
target_learning_goals: valid measurement of transfer of training between mental processes
examples: The training group practiced four tests 100 times over nine days before the combined groups were retested on the seven original tests

article_title: The correlation of general intelligence tests and school standing.
citation: E. B. Skaggs. (1918). The Correlation of General Intelligence Tests and School Standing. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journal/edu
title: Never brand a child as feeble-minded on the bare intelligence rating alone; consider heredity, training, environment, disease history, and sense-organ conditions
description: A diagnostic-caution principle: an intelligence rating should never by itself determine a label of feeble-mindedness. The article states that "No one would think of branding a child as feeble-minded until many other factors besides the bare intelligence rating had been taken into consideration, as heredity, training, environment, disease history, sense-organ conditions, etc." It follows from the author's argument that tests tap only part of the child.
requirements: Multiple factors beyond the bare intelligence rating must be taken into consideration before any diagnostic label is applied.
constraints: The article frames this for diagnostic and prognostic use of mental tests, which it says have many weak points.
target_learning_goals: accurate diagnosis and prognosis of student ability
examples: The author reports illustrations of each stated limitation from limited use of prominent mental tests over the last four years.

title: Pressey's new silent-reading test: children cross out the wrong word in paragraphs
description: A new form of silent reading test devised at Indiana University by Mrs. S. L. Pressey. It "consists of paragraphs in each of which there is a word which spoils the meaning of the paragraph or makes a false statement," and children are told to cross out the wrong word in each paragraph. The test is being validated against pooled teacher ratings of reading ability.
requirements: Validation against an independent statement of reading ability based on pooled ratings from four teachers for each child in a large junior high school.

examples: The article gives the sample item about men in shoe factories striking for shorter hours, lower wages, and recognition of their union.

article_title: Explanatory models in the processing of science text: The role of prior knowledge activation through small-group discussion.
citation: Schmidt, H. G., De Volder, M. L., De Grave, W. S., Moust, J. H. C., & Patel, V. L. (1989). Explanatory Models in the Processing of Science Text: The Role of Prior Knowledge Activation Through Small-Group Discussion. Journal of Educational Psychology, 81(4), 610-619. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-0663.81.4.610
title: Activation hypothesis: problem analysis packages activated prior knowledge into explanatory models that speed access and integration of new text information
description: The article's explanatory framework holds that discussing a problem mobilizes relevant prior knowledge, which is "packaged" in a problem-specific explanatory model. Because the task demands explanation, the activated knowledge tends to be explanatory in nature and is therefore more easily accessed when the text is processed, enabling integration of new concepts into existing cognitive structures. The theory explains both greater overall recall and the specific advantage for explanatory information, since causally linked propositions are more coherent and easier to retrieve.
requirements: Learners must possess some prior knowledge, however imprecise, that can be activated by the problem description
constraints: If subjects' knowledge is insufficient to make any sense of a problem, facilitative effects of problem analysis are not expected, per the article's own analysis
target_learners: secondary school and college science students, novices and experts alike
target_learning_goals: comprehension and integration of causal, explanatory concepts from expository science text
examples: In Experiment 2, subjects analyzing the blood cell problem before reading a text on osmosis and diffusion recalled significantly more explanatory propositions than controls

article_title: Differential effects of the classroom on African American and non-African American’s mathematics achievement.
citation: Schenke, K., Nguyen, T., Watts, T. W., Sarama, J. H., & Clements, D. H. (2017). Differential effects of the classroom on African American and non-African American’s mathematics achievement. Journal of Educational Psychology, 109(6), 794–811. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000165
title: Three observed dimensions of the early-childhood classroom learning environment
description: The article organizes the observed classroom-learning environment into three dimensions measured with the COEMET observation protocol: (1) teachers' expectations and the developmental appropriateness of their instruction, (2) teachers' confidence and enthusiasm in their teaching, and (3) teachers' support for mathematical discourse. The authors state, "we described the classroom environment as: (1) teachers’ expectations and the developmental appropriateness of their instruction... (2) teachers’ confidence and enthusiasm in their teaching, and (3) teachers’ support for mathematical discourse." Factor composites were weighted by standardized factor loadings, and the three factors were moderately to strongly intercorrelated (r = .48 to .66).
requirements: Trained observers blind to experimental condition conducting COEMET observations twice during the school year, with ratings averaged across time points and mathematics activities
constraints: Developmental appropriateness is operationalized specifically as the expectations teachers have of what preschool students are capable of learning, including engagement in higher-level thinking rather than only play-based activities
target_learning_goals: early mathematics achievement (number and geometry skills)
examples: The dimensions were used as mediators in multigroup multilevel mediation models linking the TRIAD treatment to student posttest mathematics achievement

article_title: Differential effects of the classroom on African American and non-African American’s mathematics achievement.
citation: Schenke, K., Nguyen, T., Watts, T. W., Sarama, J. H., & Clements, D. H. (2017). Differential effects of the classroom on African American and non-African American’s mathematics achievement. Journal of Educational Psychology, 109(6), 794–811. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000165
title: COEMET — Classroom Observation of Early Mathematics Environment and Teaching
description: The COEMET is a live classroom observation instrument used to measure the quality of early mathematics environments. Its first section documents the number of computers and the start and end times of all activities via interval coding; its second section contains 28 indicators rated on a 5-point Likert scale during each mathematics activity, covering constructs such as supporting children's conceptual understanding, teaching strategies, and expectations. In this study, inter-rater reliability was 88% of Likert items coded identically, and coefficient alpha ranged from .95 to .97 in previous research.
requirements: Observers who spend about half a day in each classroom and are blind to experimental condition; pair visits for reliability checking
constraints: Ratings for each mathematics activity are averaged to obtain mean scores; the instrument was used with preschool classrooms in this study
target_learning_goals: early mathematics instruction quality
examples: Observations were conducted twice during the school year (October–December and March–May) and averaged to obtain a school-year rating of the classroom environment

article_title: 'Bright' and 'slow' pupils in elementary and high school.
citation: Cummins, R. A. (1917). 'Bright' and 'Slow' Pupils in Elementary and High School. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org
title: The Scholastic Quotient (S. Q.), a weighted-mark formula for ranking pupils' scholarship
description: A formula devised by the author to rank pupils from high school record cards, weighting the counts of A, B, C and D marks as 3A+2B+C−D over A+B+C+D to yield a 'Scholastic Quotient'. The article states the quotient "has a range of from minus 1 to plus 3" and that the limits hold whether a pupil has one mark or a thousand and one. It was used to classify the upper quartile as 'Bright' and the lower quartile as 'Slow'.
requirements: Counts of each kind of mark received (A, B, C, D) from pupils' high school record cards
constraints: The formula "assumes an equal weight for all the subjects for which marks are given", which can place a pupil high on the S. Q. while teachers rate the pupil much lower, as in a case where 11 of 15 A's were in physical training
target_learners: elementary and high school pupils at a private college-preparatory school
target_learning_goals: ranking pupils' scholastic standing and predicting success or failure in school subjects
examples: The author ranked 52 early-entering graduates by S. Q. from .75 to 2.49 and split them into quartiles of 13 pupils each

citation: Cummins, R. A. (1917). 'Bright' and 'Slow' Pupils in Elementary and High School. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org
title: Equalize high/low mark ratios across subjects by combining adjusted subject-matter difficulty with within-class ranking and curve-based mark distribution
description: The author proposes that schools make the relative frequency of high and low marks practically the same across subjects by combining two methods: introducing more difficult subject-matter where ratios are high and less difficult material where they are low, and ranking class members from best to poorest using all available information, then distributing marks along a curve approximating the normal surface of frequency. He states this should be done "in all cases where there are as many as 50 pupils in a subject".

article_title: Improving performance and retention in introductory biology with a utility-value intervention.
citation: Canning, E. A., Harackiewicz, J. M., Priniski, S. J., Hecht, C. A., Tibbetts, Y., & Hyde, J. S. (2018). Improving Performance and Retention in Introductory Biology with a Utility-Value Intervention. Journal of educational psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000244
title: Time utility-value writing assignments to students' performance history: early for struggling students, late for high performers, with full dosage for the broadest benefit
description: The article's design recommendations follow from its timing and dosage findings: assignments asking students to explain why course material is useful to them personally should be scheduled deliberately across a course. The authors conclude that "full dosage (three UV assignments) is optimal to obtain the highest level of articulated UV, the beneficial early (first UV) effect on performance for low performers, and the beneficial late (3rd UV) effect on continuation for high performers." Because one or three doses worked but two did not, implementers should either commit to a dose for every unit or a single well-timed essay, not an arbitrary middle number.
requirements: Assignments must be graded for scientific content with feedback, and instructors kept blind to condition as in the study implementation.
UV prompts must ask students to explain how specific course content applies personally or to someone close to them, not merely summarize.
constraints: Two doses were not effective for performance or continuation in this study.

The timing moderation is exploratory: the early-benefit-for-low-performers effect on continuation did not reach significance (p = .063), and late UV may decrease enrollment for students more than 1 SD below the mean prior GPA.
Effects were tested in one introductory biology course at a large Midwestern university.
target_learners: Undergraduate students in introductory STEM gateway courses
target_learning_goals: Course performance
Persistence in the STEM major
Continuation in a course sequence
examples: Students were blocked on gender and randomly assigned to a fully crossed 2×2×2 design in which each of three five-week unit essays was either a UV essay or a control summary, assigned three weeks before each unit exam.

title: Books preparing teachers for school subjects should be grounded in scientific analyses of learning in those subjects rather than in empirical, a-priori pedagogy

article_title: A developmental extension to the multidimensional structure of interests.
citation: Akkerman, D. M., Vulperhorst, J. P., & Akkerman, S. F. (2020). A developmental extension to the multidimensional structure of interests. Journal of Educational Psychology, 112(1), 183-203. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000361
title: Six-dimensional framework underlying the development of interests
description: The article organizes interest development around six dimensions identified in prior literature: "time, value, agency, frequency, intensity, and mastery". These dimensions serve as the measurement structure for characterizing students' multiple interests and how their profiles of scores change across contexts and over time. The framework is used empirically to test developmental models of interest rather than proposed as a new taxonomy.
requirements: Empirical measurement of interests on all six dimensions, here via experience sampling, to support developmental models of interest
constraints: The dimensions are identified in prior literature, not derived anew in this article
target_learning_goals: Understanding the structure and development of individual interests as a basis for learning
examples: The six dimensions structured latent profile analyses of 7,226 interest reports from 204 students at two time points

title: Smartphone experience-sampling application for measuring multiple interests over time
description: The study used "experience-sampling methodology through a smartphone application" to measure students' multiple interests and their development across contexts and over time. Students reported interests at two time points three months apart, yielding 7,226 interest reports from 204 Dutch high school students. The tool enables capturing interest dimensions in situ rather than via retrospective questionnaires.
requirements: Repeated in-the-moment reports from students across contexts and over time
constraints: Applied here with high school students at two measurement occasions three months apart
target_learning_goals: Measuring the structure, persistence, stability, and development of interests

article_title: Early intervention for children at risk for reading disabilities: The impact of grade at intervention and individual differences on intervention outcomes.
citation: Lovett, Frijters, Wolf, Steinbach, Sevcik, & Morris. (2017). Early intervention for children at risk for reading disabilities: The impact of grade at intervention and individual differences on intervention outcomes. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000181
title: The Triple-Focus Program: an integrated multiple-component remediation combining PHAST decoding and comprehension strategy training with RAVE-O lexical enrichment
description: The Triple-Focus Program integrates the PHAST Reading Program (decoding and comprehension parts) with the RAVE-O Program into one intervention for children with reading disabilities. The article states it "provides tailored and intensive remediation that combines explicit phonological instruction with word identification strategy training, reading comprehension strategy training, and instructional activities that foster enriched lexical representations". PHAST teaches five metacognitive word-identification strategies plus comprehension strategies (predicting, summarizing, clarifying, questioning), while RAVE-O develops accuracy and fluency in phonological, orthographic, semantic, syntactic, and morphological skills and their interconnections. It was delivered as a pull-out program on a 1:4 ratio for an hour a day, totaling 100–125 hours.
requirements: Small instructional groups of four children matched on single-word reading level, taught by trained research teachers with scripted lessons and monitored treatment integrity
constraints: Designed for children in Grades 1–3 meeting low-achievement criteria for reading disabilities; full 125 hours were implemented as planned for only 68% of the sample (n = 117)
target_learners: Children at risk for or meeting criteria for reading disabilities in Grades 1–3
target_learning_goals: Word reading and decoding
Reading fluency
Reading comprehension
Metacognitive word-identification and comprehension strategies
examples: Delivered an hour a day, five days a week, in the child's home school across three sites (Atlanta, Boston, Toronto)
key_sources: Lovett, Frijters, Wolf, Steinbach, Sevcik, & Morris. (2017). Early intervention for children at risk for reading disabilities: The impact of grade at intervention and individual differences on intervention outcomes. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000181

citation: Lovett, Frijters, Wolf, Steinbach, Sevcik, & Morris. (2017). Early intervention for children at risk for reading disabilities: The impact of grade at intervention and individual differences on intervention outcomes. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000181
title: Provide early intensive evidence-based reading intervention starting in 1st grade, supported by school-level infrastructure for screening, monitoring, and booster intervention
description: The article's findings support starting intensive, evidence-based small-group reading intervention in 1st grade rather than waiting, because earlier intervention yielded larger and more durable gains. The authors also state that such efforts "require coordinated infrastructure and investment at the school level, including universal early screening for academic risk, access to effective early intervention within the school, teacher preparation and confidence in such procedures, regular progress monitoring for all children, and access to booster interventions when needed".
requirements: Universal early screening for academic risk
Access to effective early intervention within the school
Teacher preparation and confidence in intervention procedures
Regular progress monitoring for all children
Access to booster interventions when needed
constraints: Evidence comes from a quasi-experimental design with a small control group; schools frequently waited until 3rd grade to identify children needing help during the study years
target_learners: Children at risk for or with reading disabilities in the primary grades
target_learning_goals: Foundational word reading
Decoding
Reading comprehension and fluency
examples: Children taught in small groups an hour a day for 125 hours in 1st, 2nd, or 3rd grade; 1st- and 2nd-grade participants made greater basic-skill gains than 3rd-grade participants

article_title: Psychology in the schoolroom.
citation: J. D. Heilman. (1916). Psychology in the Schoolroom. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0073918
title: Select curriculum subjects for their content value and teach them for both content and formal values, avoiding radical views on mental discipline
description: The article argues that psychology shows both the older belief in formal mental training and the newer reaction against it were extreme. It recommends that "the safest procedure in practice is to select the subjects of the curriculum for their content value and to teach them for both their content and their formal values." The author adds that no one should hold radical views on mental discipline and predicts formal value will prove greater in the elementary school.
requirements: Curriculum decisions should draw on the psychological literature on formal training, which the article says presents problems by no means easy of solution
constraints: The article states the subject is not yet well understood and that valuable psychological contributions will continue to be made
target_learning_goals: curriculum content knowledge and transferable formal value of school subjects
examples: The article describes the shift from faculty psychology through the writings of James and Thorndike to an unwarranted disbelief in formal value
key_sources: J. D. Heilman. (1916). Psychology in the Schoolroom. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0073918

article_title: Psychology in the schoolroom.
citation: J. D. Heilman. (1916). Psychology in the Schoolroom. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0073918
title: Organizing educational psychology around the divisions of education rather than psychological headings
description: The article proposes that educational psychology be treated under educational headings instead of psychological ones such as instinct, memory, and fatigue. It argues that "Instead of a chapter on mental fatigue, there should be a chapter on the daily program and fatigue," and that attention should be discussed under the psychology of each school subject. It further proposes that a single volume give way to volumes addressing the history of education, principles of education, school administration, school management, school supervision, and the principles of teaching, because general and child psychology differ in purpose from education and supply only a starting point for schoolroom problems.
requirements: A third individual, the educational psychologist, must study schoolroom problems with the aid of psychological knowledge, since general and child psychology alone fall short
constraints: The article states that in some phases of school administration the psychologist's teachings must be ignored on account of other factors, such as social conditions affecting school-leaving age
target_learners: teachers, principals, and superintendents in the schoolroom
target_learning_goals: applying psychological knowledge to practical educational problems across the divisions of education
examples: The article illustrates the reorganization with chapters on the daily program and fatigue and on conditions of attention for reading, writing, and other school subjects
key_sources: J. D. Heilman. (1916). Psychology in the Schoolroom. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0073918

article_title: Empirical Studies in School Reading.
citation: L. Z. (1921). New Publications: Review of Empirical Studies in School Reading. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Empirical+Studies+in+School+Reading
title: Design literature study around sympathetic approach and imaginative picturing of the selection's experiences rather than technique and factual detail
description: The reviewed study's experimental comparison supports designing literature instruction so that the method "emphasized the sympathetic approach and gave opportunity for picturing and imaging the experiences in the selection", rather than stressing technique, analysis and factual detail. The review recommends the conclusions to those interested in improving textbooks and to those who value the aesthetic experiences literature study may open. It rests on the controlled experimental comparison and the expert rankings reported above.
requirements: Study questions should draw on the pupil's related experiences and assist realization in imagination of the experiences of the poet, as the rankings emphasized.
constraints: The review notes those advocating formal language training considered it essential; the sympathetic approach was contrasted with, not shown to replace all value of, technique-focused work.
target_learners: Pupils in grades IV to VIII studying literature
target_learning_goals: Literary appreciation and imaginative realization of literary selections
examples: The reviewed study set up and used two methods experimentally under controlled conditions, one sympathetic and imaging-oriented, one technique- and fact-stressing.

article_title: Mediators that matter: Psychological distress, developmental assets, and educational outcomes among Black youth.
citation: Rose, T., Joe, S., & Hancock, G. R. (2024). Mediators that Matter: Psychological Distress, Developmental Assets, and Educational Outcomes among Black Youth. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000876
title: Positive youth development theory and the developmental asset framework as an asset-based lens on Black adolescent educational outcomes
description: The study is guided by positive youth development theory (PYDT), under which "adolescents are seen as “co-producers” of their development, as they are influenced by and influence their contexts". Building on PYDT, the Search Institute's developmental asset framework treats assets as "opportunities, experiences, and supports" that serve protective or promotive functions. The authors apply this asset-based lens to challenge deficit-based narratives about Black students, focusing on internal assets — positive identity (self-esteem, mastery) and commitment to learning (school bonding, aspirations, expectations) — as mediators between psychological distress and educational outcomes.
requirements: Assets are described as malleable, making them suitable targets for individual- or group-level, particularly school-level, interventions
constraints: The study examined only a limited set of internal assets, some with varied reliability, using cross-sectional secondary data
target_learners: Black adolescents ages 13–17 (African American and Caribbean Black)
target_learning_goals: Educational outcomes including grades, grade repetition, suspensions, and expulsions
examples: The study modeled five assets (self-esteem, mastery, school bonding, educational aspirations, educational expectations) as mediators in path analyses of NSAL-A data
key_sources: Rose, T., Joe, S., & Hancock, G. R. (2024). Mediators that Matter: Psychological Distress, Developmental Assets, and Educational Outcomes among Black Youth. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000876

article_title: The Binet Scale for measuring intelligence and retardation.
citation: Huey, E. B. (1911). The Binet Scale for Measuring Intelligence and Retardation. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Binet_Scale_for_Measuring_Intelligence_and_Retardation
title: The complete Binet-Simon 1908 test series with record form and supplementary administration notes
description: The article presents the complete series of Binet-Simon tests, from the 1905 one- and two-year items through the thirteen-year tests, "stating each test as simply and briefly as possible, for the most part in the form of record used for reference in the files of this institution." The record form yields a mental age level and a retardation figure, and supplementary notes give directions, sample sentences, pictures, and scoring criteria for tests that are not self-explanatory. Responses are marked plus, minus, exclamation point, or letters for inattention, timidity, resistance, and ignorance.
requirements: The examiner must first make a careful reading of Binet's article in L'Annee Psychologique for 1908, since brief notes cannot replace it
constraints: Huey's translations are often very free, with a few changes adapted to American conditions
target_learners: children being examined for mental retardation in schools and institutions
target_learning_goals: determining the fact and amount of mental retardation
examples: The record form credits the child with the age level at which he passes all tests or all but one, adding one year for each five tests passed at higher levels
key_sources: Huey, E. B. (1911). The Binet Scale for Measuring Intelligence and Retardation. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Binet_Scale_for_Measuring_Intelligence_and_Retardation

article_title: The Binet Scale for measuring intelligence and retardation.
citation: Huey, E. B. (1911). The Binet Scale for Measuring Intelligence and Retardation. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Binet_Scale_for_Measuring_Intelligence_and_Retardation
title: Use the Binet tests only under the direction and supervision of an experienced psychologist familiar with Binet's directions
description: Huey urges that the tests be administered only by competent persons working under psychological supervision, because the scale measures the ability to use knowledge in a standardized situation rather than knowledge alone. Testing should begin a little below the child's apparent level, continue until there is no possibility of going further, and the child "should be encouraged and praised whenever possible, and failures should never be dwelt upon." Responses should be copied verbatim with notes on conduct.
requirements: The examiner must have familiarized himself with Binet's directions in the 1908 article
constraints: Usually it is far better to be alone with the child, and the test must not be discussed or interfered with
target_learners: children referred for possible mental retardation
target_learning_goals: valid measurement of mental level and retardation
examples: Huey's institutional record form marks failures through inattention, timidity, resistance, or ignorance with separate symbols

title: The Binet classification of tested children into idiots, imbeciles, feeble-minded, backward, and unstable
description: The article reports the Binet classification of tested children by mental level: "retarded children who cannot pass beyond the tests for two years are classed as idiots. Above this but below the eight-year level they are imbeciles. Children passing tests for eight years or higher are classed as feeble-minded, using the term in a restricted sense for the higher grade defectives." The terms backward (or retarded) and unstable name the two main transition classes between the feeble-minded and the normal.
requirements: A completed Binet scale administration yielding the child's mental level
constraints: The term feeble-minded is used in a restricted sense for the higher grade defectives
target_learners: children examined with the Binet scale
target_learning_goals: classifying degree of mental retardation
examples: Huey's institution records half years, so a child's age may be 10 1/2 and his mental level 8 1/2

article_title: Fish swimming into the ocean: How tracking relates to students’ self-beliefs and school disengagement at the end of schooling.
citation: Dumont, Hanna; Protsch, Paula; Jansen, Malte; Becker, Michael. (2017). Fish swimming into the ocean. How tracking relates to students' self-beliefs and school disengagement at the end of schooling. The Journal of educational psychology 109 (2017) 6, S. 855-870. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000175
title: Two-feature framework of tracking: tracks as social contexts versus tracks as pathways to future opportunities
description: The article proposes disentangling two distinguishing features of secondary school tracking. As the abstract states, "we disentangled 2 distinguishing features of tracking: tracks as social contexts(operationalized via track level and the mean achievement of students' schoolmates) and tracks as pathways to different future opportunities (operationalized via educational certificates)." This framework allows separate estimation of contextual and credentialing effects on self-beliefs and disengagement. In the Berlin study the pathway feature (certificates) dominated, while the social-context features showed limited or null relations.
requirements: Data allowing simultaneous operationalization of track level, schoolmates' mean achievement, and educational certificates
constraints: Tested at the end of schooling in Berlin's tracked secondary system; track level showed no predictive power for the outcomes considered
target_learners: secondary school students at the end of schooling
target_learning_goals: academic self-concept
beliefs about labor market chances
school engagement
examples: The study operationalized social contexts via track level and schoolmates' mean achievement, and pathways via educational certificates, using data from low-track, intermediate-track, and comprehensive schools in Berlin

The multi-source design links self-report measures of self-beliefs and disengagement with achievement and administrative records on track level and certificates, enabling the disentangling of tracking features at the end of schooling.

article_title: The role of authoritative and authoritarian parenting in the early academic achievement of Latino students.
citation: Kim Yeonwoo, Calzada Esther J., Barajas-Gonzalez R. Gabriela, Huang Keng-Yen, Brotman Laurie M., Castro Ashley, Pichardo Catherine. (2018). The Role of Authoritative and Authoritarian Parenting in the Early Academic Achievement of Latino Students. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000192
title: Cultural framework of Latino parenting and student academic achievement
description: The article tests a cultural framework (Calzada, Fernandez, & Cortes, 2010; Figure 1) in which "mothers' acculturative status is expected to influence socialization messages of respeto or independence and the authoritarian or authoritative parenting practices that reinforce them; both, in turn, are expected to influence child developmental outcomes." Cultural socialization is the process through which parents transmit cultural values, beliefs, traditions, and behavioral norms. The framework was tested with multi-group SEM, separately for Mexican and Dominican American families, with school readiness (academic and social-emotional) as the mediator between parenting and first-grade achievement.
requirements: Measures of maternal acculturative status (acculturation and enculturation), cultural socialization messages, and authoritative/authoritarian parenting practices
constraints: The framework was tested with cross-sectional data for the acculturation-to-parenting-readiness paths, so temporal ordering and causality cannot be inferred
Findings cannot be generalized to Latino families beyond Mexican and Dominican origin
target_learners: Latino children entering pre-kindergarten or kindergarten in urban public schools
target_learning_goals: Early academic achievement
Social-emotional school readiness
examples: The framework was tested with longitudinal data from 750 Mexican and Dominican American mother-child pairs in 24 New York City public elementary schools

article_title: A tentative standardization of certain 'opposites tests'.
citation: Irving King and Hugo Gold. (1911). A Tentative Standardization of Certain "Opposites Tests". University of Iowa. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=A+Tentative+Standardization+of+Certain+Opposites+Tests
title: Frequency tables of responses to the opposites stimulus words with graded credit values
description: The article's appendix tabulates all reactions to the opposites stimulus words from 100 adult subjects, printing for each stimulus word the response words, their frequencies, and their credit values (full, two-thirds, one-half, one-third, or none). The authors state that "Since there were exactly one hundred subjects these frequencies are also percentages" and that the numbers following stimulus words "measure the relative difficulty of the various stimulus words". The tables serve as the basis for constructing lists of uniform or graded difficulty.
requirements: Oral responses recorded accurately (the authors used shorthand records) so response frequencies are not confounded with writing speed
constraints: Two words occurred twice in the easy lists, so there should have been 160 words rather than the 158 counted
target_learners: adult subjects in education and psychology departments
target_learning_goals: controlled association and selective thinking measured through opposites naming
examples: The easy-list table shows above answered below by 80 of 100 subjects; the hard-list table shows precise answered exact by only 2 subjects
key_sources: Irving King and Hugo Gold. (1911). A Tentative Standardization of Certain "Opposites Tests". University of Iowa. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=A+Tentative+Standardization+of+Certain+Opposites+Tests

article_title: A tentative standardization of certain 'opposites tests'.
citation: Irving King and Hugo Gold. (1911). A Tentative Standardization of Certain "Opposites Tests". University of Iowa. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=A+Tentative+Standardization+of+Certain+Opposites+Tests
title: Time-penalty grading rules separating easy and hard opposites into ranked credit classes
description: The authors propose a standardized grading scheme in which errors and omissions are converted into added seconds: for easy opposites "The penalty for an omitted word was four seconds", with exact opposites given full credit and a second class given one-half credit; for hard opposites an omitted or entirely wrong word drew an eighteen-second penalty, with intermediate response classes ranked at two-thirds and one-third value. Separate rule sets were adopted because easy opposites test rapidity of association while hard opposites test selective thinking. The scheme aims to make results from different investigators comparable.
requirements: A tabulated, valued set of common responses to each stimulus word so graders can classify responses consistently
constraints: Grading was more or less arbitrary but consistent; no claim is made for scientific precision and the rules are recognized as improvable
target_learners: adult test subjects in education and psychology departments
target_learning_goals: controlled association (easy opposites) and logical keenness in selecting contrary ideas (hard opposites)
examples: In hard-list grading, tardy = on time was ranked at two-thirds value as a phrase of common usage expressing an exact opposite idea, while synonyms and repeated stimulus words received no credit and the full eighteen-second penalty

article_title: The measurement of ability in Latin. Part II. Sentence tests.
citation: Henmon, V. A. C. (1917). The Measurement of Ability in Latin. Part II. Sentence Tests. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Henmon+Measurement+of+Ability+in+Latin+Sentence+Tests
title: P.E.-based scaling of sentence difficulty assuming normal distribution and equal year variability
description: The article scales each sentence's difficulty by the same method used for vocabulary words: given the per cent of pupils translating it correctly, its position is located on the base line of the normal frequency surface in P.E. deviations. Two assumptions are made: "that ability to translate Latin is distributed normally, and that the real variability for each year is approximately the same." A reference zero point of -3.8 P.E. obviates plus and minus values, and general scale values combine year values using the intervals between year medians.
requirements: Per cent correct for each sentence in each year must be known from large administrations
The two stated assumptions of normality and approximately equal year variability must hold
constraints: The design of uniformly stepping, year-equal lists "has not as yet been fully realized"; a much larger number of sentences must be constructed and tried out
target_learners: first- to fourth-year secondary school Latin pupils
target_learning_goals: ability to translate Latin sentences
knowledge of Latin grammar
examples: Intervals between year medians were averaged from six direct and derived P.E. values: Test A M I-II 1.151 P.E., M I-III 2.490 P.E., M I-IV 3.011 P.E.
key_sources: Henmon, V. A. C. (1917). The Measurement of Ability in Latin. Part II. Sentence Tests. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Henmon+Measurement+of+Ability+in+Latin+Sentence+Tests

citation: Henmon, V. A. C. (1917). The Measurement of Ability in Latin. Part II. Sentence Tests. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Henmon+Measurement+of+Ability+in+Latin+Sentence+Tests
title: Latin Sentence Tests A, B, I, II and III with printed scale values
description: A set of Latin translation tests: Test A of thirty sentences and Test B of fourteen easier sentences, both built exclusively from the 239-word Standard Vocabulary so that pupils meet no unknown words. From these, the author derives "Two arrangements of ten sentences each of equal difficulty and grading up by fairly uniform steps" (Tests I and II, perfect scores 28.0 and 28.4), plus a ten-sentence equal-difficulty Test III judged too difficult to be satisfactory. Each sentence carries a printed general scale value.
requirements: Sentences must contain no words outside the 239-word Standard Vocabulary list
Alternative lists are desirable, as a few hours coaching on the tests would vitiate their value
constraints: The number of sentences studied is not yet large enough to furnish a genuinely satisfactory scale; experimentation with several hundred sentences is required
target_learners: first- to fourth-year secondary school Latin pupils
target_learning_goals: accuracy of Latin sentence translation
examples: Test A was given in June 1916 and 1917 in seventeen schools; Test B in June 1917 in sixteen schools; sentences were scored right or wrong with no partial credit.

article_title: Experimental researches on learning to spell. Part I.
citation: Winch, W. H. (1913). Experimental researches on learning to spell. I. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org/stable/1412810
title: Direct teacher attention during spelling practice, guiding learners letter by letter with combined sensory channels, benefits young children learning to spell
description: The article supports directing young learners' attention during spelling practice rather than leaving them to work independently. In the experiment, the teacher "spelt each word carefully, with slight pauses between the syllables" and boys spelt each word twice aloud while looking at each letter. This directed combined method outperformed undirected silent visual learning. The principle applies specifically to young children whose attention is not yet self-regulating for orthographic learning.
requirements: A teacher or experimenter must direct attention letter by letter during the spelling practice
constraints: Demonstrated only with young Standard II boys (average age 8 years 9 months) of relatively low ability in a poor London school; the author cautions results may not generalize to older or more able children
target_learners: young elementary school children (Standard II, average age 8 years 9 months)
target_learning_goals: correct spelling of common words
examples: The Head Master spelt each word on a black-board with slight pauses between syllables and clear pronunciation, and boys simultaneously spelt each word twice aloud looking at each letter
key_sources: Winch, W. H. (1913). Experimental researches on learning to spell. I. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org/stable/1412810

article_title: Experimental researches on learning to spell. Part I.
citation: Winch, W. H. (1913). Experimental researches on learning to spell. I. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org/stable/1412810
title: Equal-difficulty word list methodology for classroom spelling experiments
description: The article describes a methodology for constructing and validating two lists of spelling words of equal difficulty for a given class. Words are selected from reading material slightly above the class level, tested by preliminary dictation, and confirmed as matched when averages are practically identical and the correlation between individual performance on the two lists is very high. This enables controlled comparison of teaching methods with actual school words rather than nonsense syllables.
requirements: Preliminary test must confirm equal difficulty: averages practically identical and positive correlation very high
Practice periods must be arranged so neither list has advantage in time of day or curriculum placement
Multiple practice sessions are needed; single practice exercises are unsafe
constraints: Lists suitable for one class may not be suitable for another even of the same standard or grade
Words must be ones no boy can spell entirely and most can partially accomplish
target_learning_goals: correct spelling of curriculum vocabulary words

title: Five modes of rapid reading and skimming
description: The article proposes that skimming is not one process but embraces at least five varieties: (a) fast reading in which every word is read, (b) trailing, perceiving without apperceiving, (c) covering, like trailing but possibly vertical as well as horizontal, (d) omitting logically, and (e) omitting arbitrarily. article_title: Factors associated with children’s understanding of mathematical equivalence: An investigation across six countries.
citation: Şimşek, E., Xenidou-Dervou, I., Hunter, J., Gillon Dowens, M., Pang, J., Lee, Y., McNeil, N., Kirkland, P., & Jones, I. (2021). Factors Associated with Children's Understanding of Mathematical Equivalence: An Investigation across Six Countries. https://figshare.com/s/78625a6b0061200db6b7
title: Change-resistance account of children's poor equivalence performance
description: The change-resistance account of McNeil and Alibali (2005), described in this article's literature review, proposes that "excessive practice with only a traditional arithmetic presentation" reinforces three operational patterns (answer blank after equals sign, use all given numbers, equals sign means 'do something') and hinders performance on complex equations. It hypothesises that richer classroom instruction can support students to develop understanding beyond an operational conception. The present study tested a textbook-format implication of this account and found no relation with equivalence understanding.
requirements: Requires variation in the format of arithmetic practice presented to students for its textbook-format prediction to be testable
constraints: The article's own large-scale data found no relation between non-traditional textbook practice and equivalence understanding, qualifying the account's textbook prediction

relational meaning of the equals sign

description: A four-item teacher instrument asked teachers to identify possible correct and incorrect student answers and the strategies students might use when solving equivalence problems and defining the equals sign. citation: Zimmerman, J. (1914). The Binet-Simon Scale and the Yerkes Point Scale: A Comparative Study Based on the Examination of 100 Cases. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journal/edu
title: Use divergence between two intelligence scales to trigger supplementary testing before diagnosis
description: The article recommends administering more than one intelligence scale and treating marked divergence between their mental-age results as diagnostic information in itself. Where the scales agree, the examiner may feel considerable certainty; where they diverge, divergence "prevents over hasty conclusions" and "makes clear the need of supplementary tests before a definite diagnosis is made". This turns disagreement between instruments into a safeguard against premature classification.
requirements: Both scales must be administered under favorable, distraction-free conditions with rapport established with the child before testing begins.
constraints: Agreement between scales supports confidence in the mental-age estimate, but the article notes Binet results themselves are not very reliable after age ten.

target_learning_goals: accurate determination of children's mental age for placement and diagnosis decisions
examples: The examiner gave both the Binet-Simon and Point Scale tests at one sitting to 100 children and used the status-difference column to identify cases needing further testing.
