article_title: Science as Subject-Matter and as Method.
citation: J. Dewey. (1910). Science as Subject-Mattcr and as Method. Science, 31: 787. https://www.science.org/journal/science
title: Teach science for its method-value — cultivating the scientific attitude through pupil inquiry — rather than primarily for informational subject-matter
description: The principle, drawn from Dewey's address as reported in the review, is that science instruction should constantly aim at the pupil's "scientific attitude and habit of mind" rather than placing informational subject-matter value uppermost. It works by leading pupils to take a hand in the making of knowledge, so that guess and opinion become belief authorized by inquiry. The review presents this as Dewey's remedy for the partial failure of school science.
requirements: Instruction must lead the pupil to participate in the making of knowledge rather than only receive information, per Dewey's stated condition that this is the only way to accomplish the aim.
constraints: The review notes some maintained this disciplinary attitude coincided with a relative falling off in science-registrations during the past ten years.
target_learning_goals: scientific attitude and habit of mind
inquiry-based belief formation
examples: The review reports Dewey's Boston address as the statement of this position, and notes secondary course organization and the spirit of instruction already seem to represent an attempt to realize this disciplinary value.

article_title: Sex differences in developmental pathways to mathematical competence.
citation: Geary David C., Hoard Mary K., Nugent Lara, Ünal Zehra E. (2023). Sex Differences in Developmental Pathways to Mathematical Competence. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000763
title: Differential contributions hypothesis of sex differences in mathematical development
description: The hypothesis holds that sex differences in math-relevant traits shape distinct developmental pathways to mathematics: boys' advantage in spatial abilities contributes relatively more to their mathematical development, while girls' advantage in in-class attention contributes relatively more to theirs. The article states that "the sex differences in spatial abilities and in-class attention differentially contribute to the mathematical development of boys and girls and counteract one another," explaining why overall mean sex differences in mathematics are small or non-existent despite trait differences. The longitudinal SEM study confirmed the hypothesis with significant sex-to-trait and trait-to-mathematics paths.
requirements: Longitudinal assessment of both spatial abilities and in-class attention alongside mathematics outcomes
Statistical control of general cognitive ability to isolate the specific pathway contributions
constraints: The article notes the data are correlational and do not allow definitive causal inferences
The spatial boost is likely unimportant in some mathematics areas and more important in others than the modest effect for general mathematics abilities found here
Lower achieving students were less likely to enroll in the longitudinal component, which could influence generalizability
target_learners: adolescents in middle school and early high school (grades 6 to 9)
target_learning_goals: mathematical competence from arithmetic fluency to algebra
examples: Model 4 fitted paths from sex to Spatial and In-Class Attention and resulted in a significant improvement in model fit, with all paths significant (ps < .028)

article_title: Expanding the developmental models of writing: A direct and indirect effects model of developmental writing (DIEW).
citation: Kim Young-Suk Grace, Schatschneider Christopher. (2017). Expanding the developmental models of writing: A direct and indirect effects model of developmental writing (DIEW). Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000129
title: The direct and indirect effects model of developmental writing (DIEW)
description: The DIEW model extends the simple view and not-so-simple view of writing by explicitly specifying direct and indirect relations among component skills and their relations to writing. It hypothesizes that working memory is a foundational cognitive ability supporting vocabulary, grammatical knowledge, higher-order cognitive skills (inference, theory of mind), and transcription skills; these feed discourse-level oral language and transcription skills, which in turn directly support writing. The article states the model 'extends them by explicitly hypothesizing direct and indirect relations among components skills and their relations to writing based on theory and empirical evidence.'
requirements: Discourse-level oral language and transcription skills (spelling, handwriting fluency) as upper-level skills directly related to writing
constraints: Tested with beginning writers (Grade 1) for writing quality operationalized as idea development; the authors note relations might vary for older children and different writing outcomes
target_learning_goals: Writing quality (idea development and organization)
examples: Structural equation modeling with 193 Grade 1 children compared four DIEW variations (complete mediation, two partial mediation models, and a working-memory direct-path model)

title: Three levels of mental representation in discourse comprehension and production
description: The article describes theoretical models of discourse comprehension and production positing three levels of mental representations: the situation model, textbase, and surface code. The situation model, the highest level, requires linking propositions across the text and to background knowledge to integrate and infer meanings. The article maps language and cognitive skills onto these levels, with higher-order cognitive skills (inference, theory of mind) supporting global coherence (situation model) and foundational skills supporting textbase construction. As printed: 'The situation model is the interlocutor's representation of the events, actions, and characters (what the text is about; van Dijk & Kintsch, 1983), and is the highest level of mental representation.'
requirements: Linking propositions across the text and to general background knowledge to establish a coherent whole
target_learning_goals: Discourse-level oral language comprehension and production
examples: The direct and mediated model of discourse-level language maps inference and theory of mind onto the situation model and vocabulary, grammatical knowledge, and working memory onto the textbase

The article states that 'more multi-faceted systematic attention beyond vocabulary would be beneficial to improve discourse-level oral language.'

title: Composite of all measures as criterion for evaluating classification measures
description: The article constructs a composite mental age as the standard against which each survey measure is evaluated. As printed, "this composite is the average mental age found by adding the mental ages obtained from the Stanford Revision, the two group tests, and the teachers' estimates, the Terman mental age being doubled". Each measure's worth for classification and promotion is judged by its correlation with this composite. The authors acknowledge the composite cannot be evaluated against an independent criterion in this survey.

constraints: The measures compared are contained within the composite itself, so correlations with it are far higher than they would otherwise be; no independent criterion was available

title: Statistical procedures for converting varied measures into mental ages
description: The article details procedures for reducing heterogeneous survey data to the common basis of mental age. For the Stanford Revision, mental ages at a common date were obtained "by using the intelligence quotients already determined as multipliers". For the group tests, tables of norms by months were constructed, since "it was necessary to build up a table of norms by months". Teachers' rankings were transmuted into mental ages by three methods: assuming a normal distribution, treating the distribution as rectangular, and treating ranks as gross scores.

article_title: College students’ reasons for leaving biomedical fields: Disenchantment with biomedicine or attraction to other fields?
citation: Rosenzweig, E. Q., Harackiewicz, J. M., Hecht, C. A., Priniski, S. J., Canning, E. A., Tibbetts, Y., Asher, M. W., & Hyde, J. S. (2021). College Students’ Reasons for Leaving Biomedical Fields: Disenchantment with Biomedicine or Attraction to Other Fields? Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000456
title: Expectancy-value theory as a framework for biomedical attrition
description: The article grounds its predictive models in Eccles and colleagues' expectancy-value theory of motivation, which "posits that there are two primary psychological variables that influence academic choices": expectations for success and the value of the field in terms of how "useful, interesting, and important it is". The theory assumes course experiences affect choices indirectly by shaping expectancies and task values, so students leave STEM because of low confidence and/or low value. The study operationalized the competence side through course grades and the value side through interest measures.
requirements: Requires measures of competence-related beliefs (here proxied by grades) and task value (here interest in biology) at relevant time points in students' trajectories
constraints: The study used grades rather than competence-related beliefs because grades are more frequently used in prior attrition research, limiting direct tests of the belief construct

article_title: Predicting age of becoming a cardinal principle knower.
citation: Geary David C., vanMarle Kristy, Chu Felicia W., Hoard Mary K., Nugent Lara. (2019). Predicting Age of Becoming a Cardinal Principle Knower. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000277
title: Carey's bootstrapping model of cardinality learning via analogical reasoning and enumeration
description: The article invokes Carey's (2004) bootstrapping model as a theoretical account of how children learn cardinal value. On this view, children learn the cardinality of the first few number words through "analogical reasoning and inductive inference to form a conceptual link between count words and the number of objects" in focus of visual attention. Enumeration of collections of three or four items is critical to initial insights about cardinal value, with diminishing returns beyond that. The study's findings on early and delayed CPK status are interpreted through this framework.
requirements: Children must learn the count list before understanding the quantities represented by number words
constraints: The ability to enumerate up to three or four is critical, with diminishing returns for enumeration of larger collections
target_learning_goals: understanding the cardinal value of number words
examples: The article interprets delayed CPKs' enumeration deficit (averaging up to about four) as consistent with Carey's proposal that enumerating three or four items is critical to initial cardinal value insights

description: The article argues that interventions focused only on preschoolers' quantitative deficits "will not be sufficient, if they do not also include features that address these children's difficulties with attentional and inhibitory control." Following Fuchs et al. (2016), well-designed interventions can compensate for domain-general weaknesses by integrating domain-specific instruction with compensatory supports. Explicit, teacher-directed instruction may help compensate for domain-general deficits, and instruction pace may need to be slower for children with below-average FSIQ.

article_title: Measurement of some abilities in scientific thinking.
citation: Herring, J. P. (1918). Measurements of some abilities in scientific thinking. The Journal of Educational Psychology, IX(10), 535-558.
title: Herring's analysis of scientific method into eleven measurable abilities
description: The article defines scientific method as "a complex of processes used in the attempts to explain," analyzable but neither finally nor universally, since scientists alter its use across ages and fields. From this complex the author selects eleven abilities of scientific work: value, feasibility, definition, clarity, statistics, relevancy, recording, comparison, classification, arrangement, and sufficiency. Each is defined and measured by three exercises in the test.
requirements: Each ability must be important with reference to scientific work and feasible for inclusion in a group test
constraints: The eleven abilities together are stated to be very far from constituting the whole of scientific method
target_learning_goals: elements of scientific method and scientific thinking
examples: Each catch-word appears at the top of three exercises; for example, relevancy exercises ask pupils to select facts showing that air is colder high up than low down.

title: The 33-exercise scientific method test in geography content

The author states the test "is a test of method, not of content," aiming to measure ability to use scientific method in geography rather than recall of geographical content.

constraints: All content falls within the subject of geography; four scores only are possible per ability (none to three right)

title: Base school conclusions on primary data from immediate experience rather than on secondary data alone
description: The article distinguishes primary data, "selected by the individual from immediate experience," from secondary data, selected from representations of others' experience, arguing primary data are more educative and that secondary data are subject to prejudice, carelessness, and greed. It urges schools to train children to rely much upon the testimony of their own senses and to seek primary data rather than habitually accept conclusions of others.

citation: The Dynamic Interplay Between Goal Setting, Performance, and Emotions in Self-Regulated Learning: A Computational Modeling Approach — Supplementary Materials. (2022). https://gpemodel.shinyapps.io/gpe-model/
title: A dynamic computational model of goal setting, performance, and emotions in self-regulated learning
description: The article presents a three-equation dynamic model in which goals, performance, and emotions at each time point are each computed as a baseline intercept, an autoregressive carry-over component, a goal-performance discrepancy (GPD) component, an emotions component (for goals and performance), and random error. The model relies on tasks where participants specify goals, complete a task, and report emotion valence across repeated goal-striving episodes. It is estimated hierarchically in Stan with 95% HDIs used for significance.

No constraints on the values that goal levels, performances, and emotions could take were set

article_title: Number knowledge and the approximate number system are two critical foundations for early arithmetic development.
citation: Malone, SA; Burgoyne, K; Hulme, C. (2020). Number Knowledge and the Approximate Number System Are Two Critical Foundations for Early Arithmetic Development. Journal of Educational Psychology, 112 (6), pp. 1167-1182. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000426
title: Triple Code Model of numerical cognition
description: The article cites the Triple Code Model (Dehaene & Cohen, 1995) as the theoretical framework its findings support. The model holds that arithmetic development depends on distinct representational codes, and the authors state their results are "consistent with the Triple Code Model (Dehaene & Cohen, 1995) suggesting that both nonsymbolic representations of numerosity and visual symbolic representations of number are critical for the development of arithmetic". The study's two unique predictors map onto these two codes: numerosity discrimination to nonsymbolic numerosity and number knowledge to visual symbolic representations.
requirements: The framework is invoked to interpret longitudinal predictor findings; the article does not test the model's mechanisms directly.
constraints: The article's support is correlational/longitudinal consistency, not a direct test of the model's processing assumptions.

target_learning_goals: early arithmetic development
numerical cognition
examples: Latent variable path modeling in 569 children showed number knowledge (symbolic) and numerosity discrimination (nonsymbolic) as the only unique predictors of arithmetic growth.

article_title: How you read affects what you gain: Individual differences in the functional organization of the reading system predict intervention gains in children with reading disabilities.
citation: Siegelman, N., Rueckl, J. G., van den Bunt, M., Frijters, J. C., Zevin, J. D., Lovett, M. W., Seidenberg, M. S., Pugh, K. R., & Morris, R. D. (2022). How you read affects what you gain: Individual differences in the functional organization of the reading system predict intervention gains in children with reading disabilities. Journal of Educational Psychology, 114(4). https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000672
title: Triangle Model of Reading as a framework for predicting intervention response via functional organization of the reading system
description: The article grounds its predictors in the Triangle Model of Reading, "a computational theory positing that reading acquisition entails the formation of associations between the representations of the orthographic (O), phonological, (P) and semantic (S) properties of written words". Because O-P regularities are more consistent than O-S associations, they are acquired earlier, and individual differences in reliance on O-P versus imageability index the functional organization of the reading system. The authors use individual slope scores from a word reading task as proxies of this organization and interpret greater imageability reliance as a marker of a suboptimal, overfitting organization in which semantics contributes more to naming.
requirements: A word reading task with items varying independently in O-P regularity, imageability, and frequency, from which individual logistic-regression slope scores can be extracted
constraints: Reliance on imageability should not be conflated with reliance on all O-S regularities; it is a non-systematic, arbitrary cue
Slope-score reliability may be limited for children at the edges of the accuracy distribution
target_learners: Children with reading disabilities in grades 3-4
target_learning_goals: Word reading and decoding skill
Reading comprehension
examples: Children read 160 monosyllabic words aloud pre- and post-intervention; per-child logistic regressions on trial-level accuracy yielded O-P and imageability slope scores

Future studies should account for differential variability in gains across outcomes while recognizing that component skills ultimately impact one another.

article_title: Students’ motivational trajectories and academic success in math-intensive study programs: Why short-term motivational assessments matter.
citation: Daria Katharina Benden and Fani Lauermann. (2021). Students' Motivational Trajectories and Academic Success in Math-Intensive Study Programs: Why Short-Term Motivational Assessments Matter. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000708
title: Situated expectancy-value theory (SEVT) as a framework for understanding situationally sensitive motivational fluctuations
description: The article draws on Eccles and Wigfield's (2020) situated expectancy-value theory, which posits that students' expectancy and subjective task values are not only developmental but also "situationally sensitive (i.e., influenced by situational characteristics)." The framework distinguishes expectancy from self-concept of ability and differentiates intrinsic value, utility value, attainment value, and cost components (effort, opportunity, psychological). The authors apply SEVT to argue that short-term, situation-specific motivational fluctuations in gateway math courses can serve as early warning signs of academic struggles and dropout.
requirements: Situation-specific assessments that reference lesson-, class-, or content-specific expectancies and values rather than global motivations
constraints: Educational research on situation-specific motivational fluctuations is still relatively scarce; it is not yet clear whether, when, and for whom these fluctuations serve as early warning signs
target_learners: First-semester university students in math-intensive study programs
target_learning_goals: Persistence in math-intensive STEM study programs
Academic achievement in gateway math courses
examples: The study measured expectancy, intrinsic value, utility value, psychological cost, and effort cost at multiple time points during the semester using situation-specific items referencing the specific math course.

article_title: Students’ motivational trajectories and academic success in math-intensive study programs: Why short-term motivational assessments matter.
citation: Daria Katharina Benden and Fani Lauermann. (2021). Students' Motivational Trajectories and Academic Success in Math-Intensive Study Programs: Why Short-Term Motivational Assessments Matter. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000708
title: Use short-term motivational assessments as early warning signs of academic struggles and course dropout in math-intensive fields
description: The article recommends that educators and researchers consider short-term motivational changes as early indicators of later academic difficulties. The authors state that "short-term declines in students' expectancy and value beliefs—especially at the beginning of college—are a precursor to later declines in academic performance, and can thus function as early warning signs of academic struggles and intentions to leave college." Their own data support this: motivational changes in the first weeks predicted end-of-term satisfaction, exam performance, and dropout.
requirements: Intensive short-term assessments (weekly or at critical time points) rather than only beginning- and end-of-semester measurements
constraints: Most existing research has used only two or three measurement points, limiting understanding of trajectory shape and sensitive time points
target_learners: First-semester university students in math-intensive study programs
target_learning_goals: Early identification of students at risk of academic struggle and course dropout
examples: Study 1b assessed students weekly in the first four weeks of the semester and found the motivational shock between Weeks 2 and 3 predicted end-of-term outcomes.

article_title: The contributions of domain-general and numerical factors to third-grade arithmetic skills and mathematical learning disability.
citation: Cowan, R., & Powell, D. (2014). The Contributions of Domain-General and Numerical Factors to Third-Grade Arithmetic Skills and Mathematical Learning Disability. Journal of Educational Psychology, 106(1), 214-229. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0034097
title: Multiple deficits framework for mathematical learning disability
description: The article evaluates and supports a multiple deficits view of number difficulties, in which arithmetical difficulties arise from combinations of deficits in domain-general factors (working memory, reasoning, processing speed, oral language) and numerical factors (single digit processing, multidigit skills). The authors state that "Most children with number difficulties exhibit deficits in both domain-general and numerical factors." This contrasts with accounts attributing difficulties solely to single-digit processing deficits. The framework was tested by examining deficit incidence in MLD, LA, and TA groups.
requirements: Assessment of both domain-general and numerical factors to identify deficit combinations
constraints: Findings are from a single cohort of children assessed in one grade over one year; the article notes findings might vary with year of schooling
target_learners: Third-grade children with mathematical learning difficulties
target_learning_goals: Arithmetic skills including calculation fluency, written computation, and word problems
examples: Children categorized as having deficits if their score on one or more constituent factors was more than 1SD below the mean, examined across MLD, LA, and TA groups

description: A numerical estimation measure in which children estimated the position of 22 numbers on a scale from 0-1,000, using a different 25 cm number line for each estimate. Estimates were converted into numerical values and mean percent absolute errors were calculated as in Booth and Siegler (2006). This measure served as the estimation factor in the study's regression models and was one of the two multidigit skills assessed.

article_title: Needed research in method.
citation: Clayton C. Kohl. (1911). Needed Research in Method. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Needed+Research+in+Method%22+Kohl
title: Kohl's four-class taxonomy of books on method
description: The article organizes the method literature into a four-part classification: works on general method that emphasize the psychology of the learning process, works that summarize principles and apply them across a curriculum, works on special method by subject, and experimental studies emerging from the psychological laboratory. As the article states, "Books on method may be roughly divided into four classes." The taxonomy frames the paper's critical survey and its argument for a new research program in method.
requirements: A body of method literature to classify by emphasis: general psychology, applied principles, subject-specific method, or laboratory experiment
constraints: The article presents the division as rough, not exhaustive
target_learning_goals: understanding the organization of the literature on teaching method

article_title: Needed research in method.
citation: Clayton C. Kohl. (1911). Needed Research in Method. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Needed+Research+in+Method%22+Kohl
title: The true province of method is the scientific study of the child's mind acquiring a given piece of subject-matter
description: The article proposes that method should be redefined as a branch of educational psychology that psychologizes definite subject-matter from the child's viewpoint. In the author's words, "The true province of method would seem to lie right here: it is the scientific study of the child's (not the adult's) mind as it acquires a given experience involved in a given piece of subject-matter." Under this view all method becomes essentially special, general method being elaborated, modified and corrected rather than ignored. The article argues this is the only way to remove adult faculty psychology from method.
requirements: Educational psychology standing as an independent science rather than trailing behind general psychology
Research that considers general psychology, the particular psychology of the subject taught, and the child being instructed
constraints: The article presents this as the author's argued position, not a tested result
target_learning_goals: defining the scope of method as a field of study

title: Book's Psychology of Skill as a model of experimental research in method

The article describes it as "an experimental study of habit-formation as exemplified in typewriting," studying specific habits and general aspects of mental life such as merging of smaller habits, fatigue, mental inertia, warming up, and kinds of practice that counted most for efficiency. The author argues such work shows the crucial points in a learning process and yields vital, definite suggestions for teachers.

constraints: The article cites it as an example from the psychological laboratory, not as research done in classrooms

article_title: The social class test gap: A worldwide investigation of the role of academic anxiety and income inequality in standardized test score disparities.
citation: Nele Claes, Annique Smeding, Arnaud Carré, Nicolas Sommet. (2024). The social class test gap: A worldwide investigation of the role of academic anxiety and income inequality in standardized test score disparities. Journal of Educational Psychology, 116(6), 871-888. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000881
title: Multidimensional conceptualization of family social class: economic capital and cultural capital as related yet distinct resources
description: The article defines family social class by unequal access to resources and distinguishes two critical forms. It states that "economic capital refers to access to economic resources and is typically measured using household income and material possessions", while "cultural capital refers to access to cultural resources and is typically measured using parental education and cultural possessions". The two are "related yet conceptually distinct", associated with different psychological processes and school experiences. The article argues that prior studies often combined them, making it difficult to disentangle their contributions, and uses fine-grained indicators separating the two across its PISA studies.
requirements: Operationalizing social class requires separate indicators for economic capital (household income, material possessions) and cultural capital (parental education, cultural possessions) to disentangle their effects.
constraints: Many extant studies operationalized social class as a combination of economic and cultural capital, which the article says makes it difficult to disentangle their relative contributions.
target_learning_goals: Standardized test performance in mathematics, reading, and science
examples: Studies 2a-2b measured parental education and cultural possessions as culturally based indicators and a twelve-item wealth measure as the economically based indicator, in separate model series.

article_title: Research versus Propaganda in Visual Education.
citation: Frank N. Freeman. (1922). Research Versus Propaganda in Visual Education. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Vol. XI, No. 5. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu/13/5/
title: Three-stage model of how educational movements are adopted: propaganda, reaction, and equilibrium
description: Freeman proposes that an educational movement typically passes through three stages: undiscriminating propaganda that awakens enthusiasm, a second stage of reaction and decline in which claims are found overstated, and a third stage of equilibrium in which the movement's true value is estimated. He argues the wasteful cycle could be shortened if the critique of later stages were applied at the beginning and classroom trial supplemented by systematic experimentation.
requirements: Scientific technique of investigation, including laboratory experimentation and statistical methods, must be available to test new movements before adoption
constraints: The analysis is framed for new materials or methods adopted through large-scale schoolroom practice rather than tested in advance
target_learning_goals: judicious adoption of new instructional materials and methods
examples: Freeman applies the model to visual education, which he sees as showing signs of the first, propaganda stage
key_sources: Frank N. Freeman. (1922). Research Versus Propaganda in Visual Education. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Vol. XI, No. 5. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu/13/5/

article_title: Research versus Propaganda in Visual Education.
citation: Frank N. Freeman. (1922). Research Versus Propaganda in Visual Education. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Vol. XI, No. 5. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu/13/5/
title: Treat each presentation problem as a special case decided on its merits rather than applying a wholesale sensory doctrine
description: Freeman's thesis is that choices among modes of presentation cannot be settled by any general principle about the supremacy of a sense. While certain senses have advantages in particular cases and some experiences can only be initiated by particular sensations, "It is necessary rather that each case be examined for itself, in order that it may be determined what the most advantageous type of sensory stimulus may be."
requirements: Each presentation problem must be examined individually, and analysis should be supplemented and verified by careful scientific procedure
constraints: Freeman regards his own psychological analysis as somewhat tentative, pointing out only the most probable lines of development
target_learning_goals: selecting the most advantageous mode of presentation for given content
examples: Freeman grants special cases such as music depending on hearing and appreciation of painting on sight, but denies wholesale arguments can be based on them
key_sources: Frank N. Freeman. (1922). Research Versus Propaganda in Visual Education. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Vol. XI, No. 5. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu/13/5/

article_title: Research versus Propaganda in Visual Education.
citation: Frank N. Freeman. (1922). Research Versus Propaganda in Visual Education. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Vol. XI, No. 5. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu/13/5/
title: Visual materials' distinctive advantages: sensory appeal, spatial and mechanical relationships, temporal transformation, and diffusion of expert presentation
description: Freeman identifies the probable advantages of visual materials to set against their limitations. Pictures possess immediate sensory appeal and share with textbooks the advantage of diffusing expert examples of presentation. Visual devices are particularly suitable for representing spatial relations, mechanical construction and operation, and graphs for presenting comparisons and trends, while motion pictures can slow rapid motion or speed up very slow movements to render them perceptible.
requirements: Concrete materials should be employed only for meanings that can be conveyed through sensory channels, since language remains essential for abstract meanings
constraints: Freeman notes H. G. Wells emphasized the diffusion advantage in an exaggerated fashion
target_learning_goals: concrete, spatial, mechanical, and temporal understandings conveyable through sensory channels
examples: Freeman's examples: a clearer notion of a geographic region from a map, mechanical contrivances better shown than described, and graphs as an unrivalled method for certain relationships

article_title: Problems in the experimental pedagogy of chemistry.
citation: Ellwood B. Spear. (1915). Problems in the Experimental Pedagogy of Chemistry. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org/journal/jeducpsych
title: Connect laboratory experiments illustrating related phenomena so pupils more readily correlate ideas.
description: The article recommends choosing laboratory experiments that are correlated with one another rather than isolated illustrations of single points. It argues that "the pupil's chances of realizing the relation between synthesis and metathesis would be greatly enhanced by having the experiments illustrating the two phenomena closely connected," yet notes this device is seldom used in laboratory manuals. The copper-sulphur sequence (combination then treatment with nitric acid) is given as a worked example.
requirements: Experiments must be selected so that successive ones illustrate related chemical phenomena, such as synthesis and metathesis, using shared materials.
constraints: The article presents this as a reasoned expectation, stating it holds "until we have evidence to the contrary," and notes the device is seldom made use of in existing laboratory manuals.
target_learning_goals: correlation of ideas
connecting chemical facts and theory
examples: Heating copper and sulphur to show combination, then treating the copper sulphide with nitric acid to show metathesis, followed by seven linked experiments extending from copper nitrate through deliquescence, diffusion, and hydrates.

article_title: The measurement of efficiency in spelling and the overlapping of grades in combined measurements of reading, writing and spelling.
citation: Starch, D. (1910). The Measurement of Efficiency in Spelling, and the Overlapping of Grades in Combined Measurements of Reading, Writing and Spelling. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=The+Measurement+of+Efficiency+in+Spelling
title: Starch's 600-word dictionary-sampled spelling test in six comparable 100-word lists
description: A spelling test constructed by taking the first defined word on every even-numbered page of Webster's New International Dictionary (1910 edition), yielding 1186 words, then discarding technical, scientific and obsolete words to leave 600 words arranged by length and divided into six 100-word lists by systematic rotation. The author states the method "would give a random sampling of the entire non-technical English vocabulary" and that the lists can be duplicated by anyone else. Scoring is by counting words correct, each list of 100 making the score also a percentage.
requirements: Administered as a dictated test with words pronounced clearly but not phonetically, each grade tested twice on two successive days with two different lists
Grade-specific list lengths: first 40 words in grade 1, 65 in grade 2, 80 in grade 3, and the full list in higher grades
constraints: The author notes the standard scores are probably not quite as reliable as those for reading and writing because they are based on a smaller number of tests
target_learners: Elementary school pupils in grades 1 through 8
target_learning_goals: Measuring spelling ability and attainment
examples: The full six lists of 100 words each are printed in the article, from 'add' and 'but' up to 'ineffectually' and 'irresponsibility'

article_title: Communications and discussions: The doctrine of formal discipline: two neglected instances of transfer of training.
citation: J. E. Wallace Wallin. (1905). The Doctrine of Formal Discipline: Two Neglected Instances of Transfer of Training. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://archive.org
title: Central (cortical) account of cross-education: practice effects establish cortical tendencies and mental attitudes that generalize
description: The article proposes that transfer of practice between organs is explicable on the assumption that "the effects of practice are central: the training of the one eye established certain cortical tendencies and mental attitudes," so the unused retina responds in harmony with the central predisposition. It allows that peripheral elements, such as sympathetic fixation of the two eyes functioning as a unity, could be involved conjointly. The account is offered as an explanation of the cross-education observed in the reversible-perspective experiments.
requirements: Practice must establish a general disposition or tendency strong enough that an organ not directly exercised shares in it
constraints: The author states the explanation is an assumption and that a tendency of training to spread or generalize holds "whatever the explanation"
target_learners: adult experimental subjects practicing perceptual control tasks
target_learning_goals: perceptual control of reversible perspective figures
transfer of trained perceptual dispositions to unpracticed organs
examples: The author's reversible-perspective series, in which monocular practice transferred to the covered eye, which "acquired by cross-induction a favorable fixation set."
key_sources: J. E. Wallace Wallin. (1905). The Doctrine of Formal Discipline: Two Neglected Instances of Transfer of Training. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://archive.org

article_title: Communications and discussions: The doctrine of formal discipline: two neglected instances of transfer of training.
citation: J. E. Wallace Wallin. (1905). The Doctrine of Formal Discipline: Two Neglected Instances of Transfer of Training. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://archive.org
title: Specific training can insure general training under certain limitations, supporting formal discipline
description: The article argues that recent experimental results offer cumulative evidence that the doctrine of formal discipline "is still good pedagogical doctrine under certain limitations," because "Specific training does, under certain conditions and in varying measure, insure general training." It presents transfer of training between analogous functions and corresponding organs as the basis for this position, offering its reversible-perspective instances as further evidence in favor of the doctrine.
requirements: Transfer occurs between analogous or similar functions and organs, under certain conditions and in varying measure
constraints: The author notes some cited experimental results are discrepant with this conclusion, and offers the instances with no attempt to further justify, limit and explain the doctrine
target_learners: learners in educational settings generally, as framed by the doctrine of formal discipline
target_learning_goals: general mental training arising from specific practice
transfer of trained ability to new situations
examples: The article cites practice transferring across hands, senses, school subjects such as neatness from geography to arithmetic, and verbal memorizing, plus its own reversible-perspective experiments.
key_sources: J. E. Wallace Wallin. (1905). The Doctrine of Formal Discipline: Two Neglected Instances of Transfer of Training. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://archive.org

article_title: The Rôle of the Teacher in the Most Expeditious and Economic Learning.
citation: Book, William Frederick. (1908). The Role of the Teacher in the Most Expeditious and Economic Learning. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=The+Role+of+the+Teacher+in+the+Most+Expeditious+and+Economic+Learning
title: Hierarchy-of-habits account: skills form as hierarchies of manipulation and control habits in which elemental and higher-order habits develop together
description: Book describes skill acquisition as the formation of two groups of habits: "habits of manipulation, a complicated hierarchy of psycho-physical habits having to do with the writing as such, and (b) habits of control," the latter characterized as learning to learn. Elemental associations are adapted from old familiar activities, selected and eliminated into letter associations, then short-circuited into word habits and higher complexes. Crucially, the levels develop together: "the lower-order habits are perfected in and through the formation of the higher even as the further development of the higher is dependent upon the perfection of the lower." The teacher's role is to see this natural method followed rather than an artificial, logical one.
requirements: Elemental habits must be thoroughly learned and perfected before higher-order habits can safely be built on them
Practice with the highest-order habits possible so all units are learned in their proper setting
constraints: The account is drawn from studies of acquisition such as typewriting and telegraphy; the most economic periods of work and rest in different fields still required further investigation
target_learners: Learners acquiring complex skills such as typewriting or telegraphy
target_learning_goals: Formation and progressive organization of skill habits
Learning to learn, i.e., habits of control
examples: The typewriting learners' first circuitous writing methods were simplified and reorganized into direct letter associations, then into word habits and higher complexes
key_sources: Book, William Frederick. (1908). The Role of the Teacher in the Most Expeditious and Economic Learning. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=The+Role+of+the+Teacher+in+the+Most+Expeditious+and+Economic+Learning

article_title: Fluctuations in elementary school children’s working memory performance in the school context.
citation: Dirk, Judith; Schmiedek, Florian. (2016). Fluctuations in elementary school children's working memory performance in the school context. The journal of educational psychology 108 (2016) 5, S. 722-739. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000076
title: Educational practice should account for substantial WM fluctuations at all timescales and adopt interventions that increase children's attentional focus and self-regulation
description: The article recommends that practice respond to the demonstrated instability of children's working memory. It states that "Educational practice may be informed by the substantial WM fluctuations at all timescales and adopt interventions that increase children's attentional focus and self-regulation." The recommendation rests on the ambulatory assessment findings that daily WM performance fluctuates substantially within person across days, occasions, and moments.
requirements: Practitioners need awareness that a child's WM performance varies substantially from day to day, occasion to occasion, and moment to moment
constraints: The article presents this as a possibility informed by the findings, not as an intervention tested in the study
target_learners: elementary school students in Grades 3 and 4 (8 to 11 years old)
target_learning_goals: maintaining attentional focus
self-regulation
working memory-dependent learning performance
examples: Grade 3 and 4 students completed WM tasks on smartphones 3 times a day in school and at home for 4 weeks, revealing substantial within-person fluctuations
key_sources: Dirk, Judith; Schmiedek, Florian. (2016). Fluctuations in elementary school children's working memory performance in the school context. The journal of educational psychology 108 (2016) 5, S. 722-739. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000076

article_title: Fluctuations in elementary school children’s working memory performance in the school context.
citation: Dirk, Judith; Schmiedek, Florian. (2016). Fluctuations in elementary school children's working memory performance in the school context. The journal of educational psychology 108 (2016) 5, S. 722-739. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000076
title: Performance fluctuations across and within days as a consideration for theories of cognitive development and learning
description: The article proposes that accounts of cognitive development and learning should incorporate short-timescale performance variability. It argues that "Theories about cognitive development and learning should consider performance fluctuations across and within days to understand the processes underlying long-term changes." The proposal is grounded in the finding that day-to-day, occasion-to-occasion, and moment-to-moment variability each contribute roughly equally to observed daily WM fluctuations, with large individual differences.
requirements: Theories must model within-person variability at multiple timescales, not only long-term average performance
constraints: The article presents this as a foundation for future research on antecedents and consequences of fluctuating cognitive resources, not as a tested theory
target_learners: elementary school children (8 to 11 years old)
target_learning_goals: understanding processes underlying long-term cognitive development and learning
examples: The ambulatory assessment study decomposed daily WM variability into day-to-day, occasion-to-occasion, and moment-to-moment components

article_title: Hierarchical nature of arithmetic skills: Similarities and differences between arithmetic operations.
citation: Rautiainen, J., Aro, T., Aro, M., Tolvanen, A., & Koponen, T. (2026). Hierarchical Nature of Arithmetic Skills: Similarities and Differences Between Arithmetic Operations. Journal of Educational Psychology, Early online. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0001066
title: Hierarchical development framework of arithmetic operations with operation-specific cognitive architectures
description: The article frames arithmetic skill development as hierarchical: prior operations contribute greatly to subsequent ones (subtraction is the inverse of addition, multiplication is repeated addition), while each operation retains a partially distinct cognitive architecture of numerical and non-numerical precursors. The article states that "Arithmetic development is suggested to be hierarchical in the sense that prior skills contribute greatly to subsequent skills." The study operationalizes this by modeling how fall-of-second-grade numerical abilities, serial retrieval fluency, and working memory predict third-grade multiplication fluency, with addition, subtraction, or reading fluency as hierarchically positioned lower skills whose covariance is partialled out via specific factors.
requirements: Requires longitudinal measurement of both hierarchically lower skills (addition, subtraction fluency in spring of second grade) and the target skill (multiplication fluency in spring of third grade)
constraints: The article notes the interrelatedness of operations may partly stem from educational practices rather than shared cognitive architecture
Findings are situated in the Finnish instructional context; instructional and curricular approaches were not examined in the study
target_learning_goals: arithmetic fluency development across addition, subtraction, and multiplication
examples: The study modeled 207 children across five assessment points from first to third grade using structural equation modeling with hierarchically lower skills captured in specific factors (F1)
key_sources: Rautiainen, J., Aro, T., Aro, M., Tolvanen, A., & Koponen, T. (2026). Hierarchical Nature of Arithmetic Skills: Similarities and Differences Between Arithmetic Operations. Journal of Educational Psychology, Early online. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0001066

article_title: Intelligence and its measurement: A symposium--I.
citation: E. L. Thorndike and L. M. Terman. (1921). Intelligence and Its Measurement. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://archive.org/search?query=Journal+of+Educational+Psychology+1921
title: Thorndike's definition of intellect as the power of good responses with respect to truth or fact, specialized by data and operation
description: Thorndike defines intellect pragmatically as "the power of good responses from the point of view of truth or fact", and separates varieties by whether the situation is taken grossly or abstractly and whether it is experienced directly or thought of. The abstract, idea-directed variety is called "the more intellectual variety of intellect". Each variety is further specialized by the data operated on and the form of the operation, so goodness of response varies with the particular task. The framework underlies his argument that no single test score captures a general power determining every intellectual task.
requirements: Definitions and distinctions are treated as pragmatic rather than absolute, accepting that behavior shows intermediate forms between directly sensed and planned, concrete and abstract responses
constraints: Thorndike warns against trying to separate responses to directly sensed situations from those concerned with planning, or concrete from abstract responses, as behavior shows all sorts of intermediate forms
target_learners: children and adults whose intellectual status is being measured
target_learning_goals: general intellectual performance across varied tasks and data
examples: Thorndike illustrates specialization by noting the child best at mental multiplication of two-place numbers will not be best at thinking out verbal puzzles
key_sources: E. L. Thorndike and L. M. Terman. (1921). Intelligence and Its Measurement. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://archive.org/search?query=Journal+of+Educational+Psychology+1921

article_title: The worked example effect, the generation effect, and element interactivity.
citation: Chen, Ouhao. (2016). The Worked Example Effect, the Generation Effect, and Element Interactivity. PhD thesis, School of Education, UNSW. https://hdl.handle.net/1959.4/55865
title: Human cognitive architecture as the base of cognitive load theory
description: The thesis presents human cognitive architecture — the organization of components such as working memory and long-term memory — as the theoretical base on which cognitive load theory rests. It argues that "instructional design issues and human cognitive architecture are inseparably intertwined", and reviews sensory registers, working memory with its limited capacity and short duration for novel information, long-term memory with effectively unlimited storage, and schema theory. It also outlines five principles of this architecture, including borrowing and reorganizing, randomness as genesis, narrow limits of change, information store, and environmental organizing and linking.
requirements: The framework applies to biologically secondary knowledge that requires explicit instruction, since biologically primary knowledge is acquired without special courses
target_learners: school and university students learning formal curricula such as mathematics
target_learning_goals: acquisition of biologically secondary knowledge and schemas in domains like geometry and trigonometry
examples: The thesis's five experiments in geometry and trigonometry are designed on the basis of this architecture
key_sources: Chen, Ouhao. (2016). The Worked Example Effect, the Generation Effect, and Element Interactivity. PhD thesis, School of Education, UNSW. https://hdl.handle.net/1959.4/55865

article_title: The worked example effect, the generation effect, and element interactivity.
citation: Chen, Ouhao. (2016). The Worked Example Effect, the Generation Effect, and Element Interactivity. PhD thesis, School of Education, UNSW. https://hdl.handle.net/1959.4/55865
title: Biologically primary versus biologically secondary knowledge distinction
description: Drawing on Geary's theory, the thesis distinguishes two knowledge categories relevant to instructional design: "Biologically primary knowledge is learnable but not teachable, whereas biologically secondary knowledge is learnable as well as teachable." Primary knowledge, such as speaking one's mother language or general problem-solving strategies like means-ends analysis, is acquired naturally and effortlessly without explicit instruction. Secondary knowledge, such as writing, is culture-specific, effortful and conscious, and requires formal instruction — so the design of its teaching matters. An informal test is whether acquisition requires instructional supports.
requirements: Instructional design effort is directed at biologically secondary knowledge, which needs formal or informal explicit instruction
target_learning_goals: distinguishing knowledge that needs explicit teaching from knowledge acquired automatically
examples: The thesis cites learning to speak versus learning to write: speaking is acquired automatically in a speaking society, writing is not
key_sources: Chen, Ouhao. (2016). The Worked Example Effect, the Generation Effect, and Element Interactivity. PhD thesis, School of Education, UNSW. https://hdl.handle.net/1959.4/55865

article_title: The worked example effect, the generation effect, and element interactivity.
citation: Chen, Ouhao. (2016). The Worked Example Effect, the Generation Effect, and Element Interactivity. PhD thesis, School of Education, UNSW. https://hdl.handle.net/1959.4/55865
title: Schema theory: schemas as cognitive constructs organising long-term memory
description: The thesis reviews schema theory as the answer to how information is stored in long-term memory. "A schema can be regarded as a cognitive construct which lets us categorize multiple elements of information into a single element based on the way in which the multiple elements are used." Schemas allow similar situations to be treated similarly, are built through assimilation and accommodation, and reduce working memory load by letting many elements be processed as one entity. The thesis traces the theory from Piaget and Bartlett and gives the example of an equation schema for problems like x+5=8.
requirements: Schemas must already exist or be formed through active, constructive acquisition processes for their load-reduction function to operate
target_learners: students learning structured domains such as algebra and geometry
target_learning_goals: schema acquisition that organises knowledge and reduces working memory load
examples: The thesis uses the algebra problem x+5=8: a learner with a schema for it treats all similar problems as one entity and applies the same procedure
key_sources: Chen, Ouhao. (2016). The Worked Example Effect, the Generation Effect, and Element Interactivity. PhD thesis, School of Education, UNSW. https://hdl.handle.net/1959.4/55865

article_title: Measurement of the drawing ability of two thousand one hundred and seventy-seven children in Indiana City School systems by a supplemented Thorndike scale.
citation: Childs, H. G. (1915). Measurement of the drawing ability of two thousand one hundred and seventy-seven children in Indiana city school systems by a supplemented Thorndike scale. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 6(7), 391-408.
title: The supplemented Thorndike drawing scale of snow scenes with human figures in action
description: A rating scale for children's drawings constructed by supplementing the Thorndike drawing scale with additional samples. The author explains that "it occurred to us to construct a scale every unit of which should represent a snow scene with human figures in action, placing houses, landscapes, etc., as accessory features." Sample values were fixed by having seventeen judges rank drawings and by anchoring supplementary samples to Thorndike scale points, yielding a scale of approximately unit differences running from 0 to 17.6. It was used to rate over 2,000 pupils' ten-minute drawings in two Indiana school systems.
requirements: Ratings are made by comparing a pupil's drawing against the scale samples, with each paper rated by two judges and the ratings averaged
A variety of samples of approximately equal value aids greatly in rating drawings
constraints: Teachers and supervisors protested that it was unfair to judge drawing achievement by a scale based on a type of drawing given little emphasis in their courses of study
The scale lacks samples in the units 1 to 1.99, 2 to 2.99, 3 to 3.99, 4 to 4.99, and 12 to 12.99
It does not admit of easy and accurate comparison of all types of drawings
target_learners: Elementary and high school pupils in grades IB through high school
target_learning_goals: Drawing achievement, specifically snow scenes with human figures in action
examples: Used in February and May 1914 to test 1,405 elementary and 285 high school pupils in system A and 487 pupils in one school of system B, with ten minutes of drawing time
key_sources: Childs, H. G. (1915). Measurement of the drawing ability of two thousand one hundred and seventy-seven children in Indiana city school systems by a supplemented Thorndike scale. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 6(7), 391-408. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0075575

article_title: A new textbook on fundamental principles of learning and study.
citation: A. I. G. (1920). New Publications. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org/journal/jeducpsych
title: Edwards' textbook The Fundamental Principles of Learning and Study
description: A textbook by Professor A. S. Edwards of the University of Georgia, directed primarily to college students of education and adapted to school principals, supervisors, and parts to high school students. It treats learning broadly as habit formation and "abounds in definite practical directions," including admonitions such as "Review frequently" and "Have an intention to remember." The reviewer calls it "a useful collection of suggestions with regard to methods of study," with merits over popular How to Study books, though weakly grounded in experimental work.
requirements: Intended for college students of education, school principals, and supervisors; parts suitable for high school students
constraints: Not a compendium of experimental studies on learning nor a novel systematic treatise on principles; much experimental work of merit not drawn upon
target_learning_goals: methods of study
memorizing
efficient thinking and working
emotional control
examples: Two chapters consist almost wholly of practical admonitions, and suggestions cover diet, humidity, temperature, change of work, sleep, naps, and light

article_title: A new textbook on fundamental principles of learning and study.
citation: A. I. G. (1920). New Publications. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org/journal/jeducpsych
title: Lloyd and Gray bulletin Reading in a Texas City: Diagnosis and Remedy
description: A University of Texas Bulletin (No. 1853) prepared especially for elementary teachers of Texas, reporting a city school system's program for diagnosing and remediating pupils' reading ability. From available reading tests described in its first chapter, two were chosen and used as described in chapter two; chapters four and five describe the diagnosis and remedial program in detail. The reviewer judges that its "numerous charts and diagrams should make it quite possible for any teacher to make regular use of the procedures devised," and that its literature listing supplements the meagre diagnosis-and-remedy literature.
requirements: Teachers using the procedures rely on the bulletin's charts and diagrams and the illustrative records in its final Summary and Suggestions chapter
constraints: The available literature of diagnosis and remedy as listed in chapter III and the Bibliography is described as meagre
target_learning_goals: reading diagnosis
reading remediation
examples: Two reading tests were chosen from those available and used as described in chapter two; the final chapter gives illustrative records and practical suggestions

article_title: A new textbook on fundamental principles of learning and study.
citation: A. I. G. (1920). New Publications. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org/journal/jeducpsych
title: Edwards' thesis that all learning is habit formation of permanent, generalized value
description: The organizing thesis of Edwards' textbook, as reported by the reviewer: accepting the word habit to express the acquisition of memories, skills, interests, and all more or less permanent tendencies of mind and body, the author holds that "while all learning is habit formation, it should be of permanent value, and generalized improvement, as well as specific improvement, should be sought." The book applies this thesis across types of mental work, discussing acquisition of ideals and habits of efficient thinking, working, memorizing, studying, and emotional control. The reviewer notes the repetition in applying the principles to several types of mental work may advantage students even though the principles are not most economically handled.
requirements: Learning should be directed toward permanent value and generalized improvement, not only specific improvement
constraints: The reviewer judges the general principles are not most economically handled, with repetition across applications
target_learning_goals: habit formation
generalized improvement in study and thinking
memorizing
emotional control
examples: The thesis is applied in turn to ideals, efficient thinking, working, memorizing, studying, and emotional control

article_title: An Improved Form for Rating by the Order of Merit Method.
citation: Stenquist, J. L. (1918). An Improved Form for Rating by the Order of Merit Method. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=An+Improved+Form+for+Rating+by+the+Order+of+Merit+Method
title: The 'Card list': a perforated carbon-duplicate ranking form producing separable miniature name cards
description: The Card list is a printed form on heavy paper, 9 x 15 1/4 inches, "perforated to fold lengthwise in the center." Its left half is ruled for entering the list of names to be ranked with rank-number columns at the left margin; its right half is "a continuous row of small separable slips" matching the opposite ruling. With carbon paper inserted while folding, names typed or pencilled on the left simultaneously appear on individual slips, which are torn off and sorted. The author designed it to overcome the inconvenience of copying names onto cards and their bulk in the mails.
requirements: A folded sheet with carbon paper inserted so duplicate names are made on the separable slips while the original list is entered

examples: Used by Mr. John Slawson in an intensive study of the order of merit method as applied to the rating of teachers, and by Mr. H. A. Toops in practical tests of shopworkmen in factories and laboratories in New England.

article_title: An Improved Form for Rating by the Order of Merit Method.
citation: Stenquist, J. L. (1918). An Improved Form for Rating by the Order of Merit Method. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=An+Improved+Form+for+Rating+by+the+Order+of+Merit+Method
title: Reduce the labor of a rating task to increase judges' willingness to perform it

The principle generalizes the author's design rationale for the form: restructure rating as manipulation of reusable slips rather than writing, re-copying and erasing.

title: Bell Chemistry Test and appended Payne correction sheet
description: The Bell Chemistry Test is a 25-question chemistry achievement test covering electrolysis, oxidation and reduction definitions, valence, water purification, and commercial chemistry. article_title: The contribution of psychology to education.
citation: Thorndike, E. L. (1910). The contribution of psychology to education. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0074512
title: Decide competing teaching methods with controlled comparative trials and measurement, rather than from unaided classroom experience.
description: The article argues that psychology, by its methods of measuring knowledge and skill, can test and verify or refute the claims of any teaching method. Its worked example is whether to teach the spelling of a pair of homonyms together or apart in time, a question teachers had failed to decide from classroom experience. The prescribed recipe is a controlled comparison with measurement of errors afterwards.
requirements: Enough teachers using both methods with enough different classes
keeping everything else except the method constant
measuring the errors in spelling the words thereafter in the two cases
target_learning_goals: spelling accuracy
examples: The homonym-spelling comparison: the article states teachers could not decide the question from classroom experience, but measuring errors in the two cases would decide it for any given pair.

article_title: The contribution of psychology to education.
citation: Thorndike, E. L. (1910). The contribution of psychology to education. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0074512
title: Teaching methods may be deduced outright from the laws of human nature, as when habit interference explains pupils' difficulty dividing by a fraction.
description: The article's first way psychology contributes to teaching method is deduction from psychological laws. Its example: pupils' difficulty in dividing by a fraction is attributed largely to the entrenched habit from thousands of previous divisions that the result is smaller than the number divided. A method should then be devised or selected that reduces this interference from old habits without weakening them in their proper functioning.
requirements: knowledge of the laws of human nature and of the prior habits that interfere with the new learning
target_learners: elementary and secondary pupils learning arithmetic
target_learning_goals: division by fractions
examples: The fraction-division analysis: the interference is traced to the habit of division-decrease, and method design aims to reduce it to a minimum.
key_sources: Thorndike, E. L. (1910). The contribution of psychology to education. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0070113

article_title: The contribution of psychology to education.
citation: Thorndike, E. L. (1910). The contribution of psychology to education. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0074512
title: Bidirectional relation: psychology guides education, and school life is a vast laboratory that contributes back to psychology.
description: The article frames the psychology-education relation as two-way. Psychology's laws from simple, specially arranged experiments help interpret and control mental action under schoolroom conditions, while school-room life is a vast laboratory whose thousands of experiments interest pure psychology. Children's arithmetic mistakes, for example, afford material for studies of the action of the laws of association, analysis and selective thinking. The author predicts this journal will report psychological questions answered from educational experience.
requirements: experts in education studying responses to school situations for the sake of practical control, so that results advance knowledge of the mind

title: Three-way taxonomy of readers of illegible writing: combined form-and-meaning readers, meaning-dominant readers, and form-dominant readers
description: The article classifies subjects' procedures in reading illegible writing into three classes. Some place 'dependence being placed exclusively on neither meaning or form, but on a combination of both as occurs in ordinary reading'; a second class depends largely on meaning, making substitutions on a meaning basis without noticing the difference; a third depends greatly on form while paying little attention to meaning, producing context-free substitutions. The authors stress these divisions shade into each other, and the same three classes recur with mutilated specimens where meaning plays a smaller part.

constraints: The divisions are not hard and fast but shade into each other; the article says it is often difficult to tell whether a person is using a meaning or form basis

examples: In Test C 1 a subject read 'latest list of all' as 'taxes this year' (meaning-based); in Test A 1 a subject read 'Review Monograph Series' as 'Reverend Negotiable Fines' (form-based)

description: The Educational Survey Test is a short composite achievement test assembled from eight standard educational tests and requiring about 30 minutes; the authors state it was devised because existing educational tests had practically no age norms and required too long to administer. article_title: Examining general and specific factors in the dimensionality of oral language and reading in 4th–10th grades.
citation: Foorman Barbara R., Koon Sharon, Petscher Yaacov, Mitchell Alison, Truckenmiller Adrea. (2015). Examining General and Specific Factors in the Dimensionality of Oral Language and Reading in 4th–10th Grades. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000026
title: Bifactor model of lexical knowledge: a general oral language factor of syntax and vocabulary, not specific factors, drives reading comprehension
description: The article proposes that oral language in adolescence is best characterized by a bifactor structure in which syntax and vocabulary measures load on both specific factors and a general oral language factor. The authors state that "it is the general oral language factor consisting of second-order factors of vocabulary and syntax that explained a large amount of the variability in reading comprehension (with correlations ranging from .72 to .96) and not the specific factors themselves." They present this as supporting the Simple View of Reading from a latent-variable perspective and as consistent with Perfetti's (1999) Reading Systems Framework, in which integrated syntactic and semantic lexical knowledge links word identification with comprehension.
requirements: Latent variable modeling with multiple measures of syntax and vocabulary to separate general from specific factor variance
Measures of decoding fluency and reading comprehension to test structural relations
constraints: Cross-sectional rather than longitudinal data
Results depend on the measures used; no productive orthographic measure such as spelling dictation was included
No separate listening-comprehension passage test; PPVT-4 served as a proxy
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension
Oral language (syntax and vocabulary) development
examples: Bifactor models were fit separately at each of seven grades, with the general oral language factor indicated by all syntax and vocabulary measures and orthogonal specific factors

title: Interpret vocabulary or syntax effects on adolescent reading comprehension cautiously, because a general oral language factor absorbs their unique variance
description: The article recommends that studies presenting vocabulary or syntax as the sole oral language predictor of reading comprehension in adolescence be interpreted with caution, because latent modeling shows their unique contributions largely vanish once a general oral language factor is estimated. The authors write that findings "suggest cautious interpretation of studies that present vocabulary (e.g., Clarke et al., 2010; Cromley & Azevedo, 2007; Eason et al., 2013; Ouellette & Beers, 2010) or syntax (e.g., Nation et al., 2004; Catts et al., 2006) as sole oral language predictors of reading comprehension in fourth through 10th grades."

Understanding predictors of comprehension
examples: The bifactor structural models showed unique syntax prediction only in fourth grade and unique vocabulary prediction only in seventh grade

title: Tekster: a comprehensive strategy-focused writing instruction program for Grades 4–6
description: Tekster is a program of 16 grade-level specific lessons in a student workbook with a teacher's manual, developed for fourth- through sixth-grade Dutch general education classrooms. "Tekster incorporates several different research-based practices to address both the focus and the mode of instruction." Its three design principles are writing strategies, text structures, and self-regulation skills, operationalized through observational learning (teacher and peer modeling, reader reaction), explicit instruction, and guided practice with scaffolding. Lessons use mnemonic acronyms (VOS, DODO, EKSTER) and authentic writing tasks across genres with specified communicative goals and audiences.
requirements: Teachers receive a 4-hour training session, a teacher's manual with 16 lesson plans, and a DVD with peer modeling video clips and examples of teacher modeling
constraints: In implementation, teachers taught an average of 10 of the intended 16 lessons, and 8% of students completed fewer than four lessons
target_learners: fourth-, fifth-, and sixth-grade students in general education classrooms in the Netherlands
target_learning_goals: writing quality across descriptive, narrative, and persuasive genres
use of a general writing strategy
self-regulation skills such as setting communicative goals and monitoring progress
examples: Grade 4 students learned the VOS (fox) strategy: Verzinnen, Ordenen, Schrijven; Grade 6 students learned EKSTER (magpie), which adds evaluating and revising steps
Writing tasks included personal advertisements, newspaper articles, emails nominating a TV program, recipes, and party invitations

citation: Bouwer, R., Koster, M., & van den Bergh, H. (2018). Effects of a Strategy-Focused Instructional Program on the Writing Quality of Upper Elementary Students in the Netherlands. Journal of Educational Psychology, 110(1), 58–71. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000206
title: Tekster lesson format: mnemonic strategy steps taught through modeling, explicit instruction, and gradual release across a consistent lesson sequence
description: Tekster lessons follow a generally consistent format lasting 45–60 minutes, in which a mnemonic acronym (an animal name whose letters spell the strategy steps) anchors instruction. Each lesson explicitly states its goal, introduces text-type characteristics through modeling or explicit instruction, names the strategy acronym, and moves through generating content in keywords to writing, with "gradual release of responsibility from 1a to 1c, 3a to 3c" as printed in the lesson format table. Later phases have students read, evaluate, and revise texts based on feedback.
requirements: A student workbook and teacher's manual with detailed lesson plans
A DVD with peer modeling video clips and examples of teacher modeling
constraints: Phases 8a–10b (reading, evaluating, revising texts) apply only to Grades 5 and 6, with revision only in Grade 6

evaluating and revising texts on the basis of criteria

title: Goal congruity theory: role attitudes depend on congruity between a role's communal/agentic goal affordances and personally valued goals
description: Goal congruity theory, rooted in expectancy-value theory, holds that attitudes toward a social role such as being a scientist are shaped by the goal affordances the role offers and how well those affordances match personally endorsed goals. The article states that "Goal congruity theory posits that individuals' attitudes towards a social role (e.g., being a scientist) are influenced by the communal/agentic goal affordances associated with that role and the congruity between those affordances and personally valued goals." Communal goals concern collaboration and helping others; agentic goals concern advancement and recognition. The study extends the theory to Indigenous STEM populations longitudinally, with belonging as a mediating mechanism.
requirements: Measurement of both perceived goal affordances in the role and personal goal endorsement, operationalized here via POMP-converted difference scores for incongruity
constraints: The article notes most prior goal congruity research used White middle-class samples, limiting generalizability, and that evidence for incongruity effects has been inconsistent across communal and agentic goals
target_learners: Indigenous undergraduate, graduate, and professional STEM students
target_learning_goals: STEM career persistence intentions
sense of belonging in STEM disciplines
examples: The study measured four communal goals (including serving community and nation-building) and three agentic goals (recognition, success, independence) across three survey waves over 12 months

description: The article recommends incorporating speed drills into reading teaching, on the grounds that its seven-month experiment showed a relative improvement of 18.7% in speed without injuriously affecting quality. The drills used easy, interesting narrative matter, occupied five to ten minutes of the reading period, and paired silent reading under speed exhortation with oral reproduction checked by questioning to guard against skimming.

Oral reproduction with questioning must accompany the drills as a guarantee against skimming
Total reading time must not exceed that given to comparison instruction

Comparisons between groups under different teachers and buildings were not ideal for experiment
