article_title: The cost of multiple representations: Learning number symbols with abstract and concrete representations.
citation: Amy Bennett, Matthew Inglis and Camilla Gilmore. (2018). The Cost of Multiple Representations: Learning Number Symbols with Abstract and Concrete Representations.
title: Seductive details account of the multiple-representation cost
description: The authors propose that the so-called 'seductive details' effect explains why single representations outperformed multiple ones. Concrete pictures activate irrelevant prior knowledge — for example, "showing a child an array of five frogs may bring to mind knowledge about frogs that is irrelevant to the fiveness of the representation" — which the child must inhibit to succeed. Inhibition is easier when the same knowledge is activated on every trial than when new knowledge is activated from trial to trial, accounting for the single-concrete advantage in Experiment 3.
requirements: Learners must inhibit irrelevant prior knowledge activated by concrete items for the account to apply
constraints: The article presents this as an interpretive account of the findings, not a directly tested mechanism
target_learners: young children learning number words and symbols
target_learning_goals: attaching magnitude meanings to number symbols
examples: In Experiment 3, children learning with one repeated picture (e.g. fish only) outperformed children learning with twenty different pictures

article_title: The cost of multiple representations: Learning number symbols with abstract and concrete representations.
citation: Amy Bennett, Matthew Inglis and Camilla Gilmore. (2018). The Cost of Multiple Representations: Learning Number Symbols with Abstract and Concrete Representations.
title: Design number books and early number materials with simple, consistent representations of quantity
description: Because learning from multiple concrete representations was less effective than learning from a single consistent representation, the authors recommend that materials introducing number words and symbols use simple representations. The implications statement concludes that "number books designed to introduce children to the magnitude meanings of number words and symbols should consider using simple representations", whether a single concrete item set or abstract dot arrays. This challenges the dominant number-book convention of varying counted items page by page.
requirements: Materials should pair each number word or symbol with a consistent set of representations so learners can map magnitude without extraneous variation
constraints: Evidence comes from artificial symbol learning with children aged roughly 6-10 in short training sessions; the authors note their setting differs from how children typically first encounter Arabic numerals
target_learners: preschool and early primary school children learning number words and symbols
target_learning_goals: attaching magnitude meanings to number words and symbols
examples: Across three experiments, children trained with dot arrays or one repeated picture set outperformed children trained with twenty different familiar pictures varying from trial to trial

title: Electrically instrumented mirror-drawing apparatus that automatically registers errors
description: A laboratory apparatus for the mirror-drawing test consisting of two concentric metal stars with the intervening star-shaped space filled with hardened plastic, connected to an electric counter and a metal-tipped stylus. The article reports that "Any and every time the stylus moves from the inscribed star the counter registers", so that at the conclusion of the test the number of errors is read from a dial just as elapsed time is. The inscribed star "measures ten centimetres from point to point, and is one and a half millimetres in width", with brass strips five millimetres wide, a pivoted mirror, and a screen separating hand from eyes.
requirements: Two concentric metal stars electrically connected to a counter, power source and metal-pointed stylus, plus a mirror and screen
constraints: The article notes that in later types some more suitable material than cement may be found for the base
target_learners: students taking mirror-drawing tests in a psychological laboratory
target_learning_goals: measuring motor learning performance via error counts in mirror drawing
examples: Used in the psychological laboratory of Ohio Wesleyan University with a cement base embedding two brass stars

title: Eliminate unavoidable computational labor in experimental procedures wherever possible
description: Because measurement work in experimental psychology is inherently laborious, the article argues that instrumentation should remove avoidable computation. It states that "just because so much labor of computation is unavoidable in experimental psychology it is worth while to eliminate it wherever possible", and offers the electrically counting mirror-drawing apparatus as its worked example, claiming the form "will reduce the amount of work and the time required for performing the test very considerably".
requirements: An automated recording mechanism that yields the measure directly, as a readable dial does
target_learning_goals: efficient and accurate measurement of learning performance
examples: The electric counter apparatus replaces counting errors on printed star figures with reading a dial

article_title: Group Tests of Intelligence. An Annotated List.
citation: Bell, J. C. (1920). Group Tests of Intelligence: An Annotated List. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 103-108. https://psycnet.apa.org
title: Group intelligence tests arose because individual Binet-scale examination was impractical for school-wide testing and was intensified by wartime Army testing
description: The article organizes the emerging field of group intelligence testing as a historical development: the Binet Scale and its revisions "demand the individual examination of the child", which made routine school testing impractical, and demand for group tests was "greatly intensified by our sudden entry into the World War". The wholesale testing of recruits stimulated publication of many tests, creating "great need for comparison, analysis and evaluation".
requirements: Group tests must be administrable to whole classes or groups rather than one child at a time, since individual examination of thousands of children prohibits incorporation of mental testing into regular school routine
constraints: The compiled list is acknowledged by the author as likely far from complete
target_learners: school children in grades 1 through college
target_learning_goals: measurement of general intelligence and mental ability at scale

title: Pintner's Mental Survey: six group tests standardized on over 3000 school children with percentile norms
description: Rudolf Pintner's The Mental Survey (1918, 116 pages) is a group testing instrument of "Six mental tests, taken chiefly from Whipple", standardized as group tests on over 3000 school children of chronological ages 6-16, with "elaborate tables of percentile norms". It appears in the annotated list as one of the early individually-published group scales.

constraints: Standardized on children of chronological ages 6-16 as printed

The Army Alpha examination is noted as based largely on the Otis tests.

article_title: The Psychopathology of Every-day Life.
citation: Mayer, H. (1911). The Psychopathology of Everyday Life. American Journal of Psychology, 22, 477-527. https://www.jstor.org/stable/1412853
title: Psychoanalytic account of everyday errors: an unconsciously operative repressed wish conditions slips and failures
description: The article presents a psychoanalytic explanatory framework in which everyday imperfections of mental functioning — "slips of the tongue, slips of the pen, symptomatic acts, certain failures to perceive or to remember, as well as false perceptions and false recollections" — are conditioned by an unconsciously operative repressed wish, whether directly or indirectly. The framework denies that such acts are purposeless, holding instead that determinism prevails in mental operations, and links these minor errors to the mechanism of more serious pathological disturbances.
requirements: Interpretation of an error requires uncovering the unconscious motive or repressed wish assumed to condition it
constraints: The account is presented as a psychoanalytic interpretation rather than an experimentally tested result
target_learners: adults reflecting on their own mental functioning
target_learning_goals: understanding the determinants of everyday errors of perception, memory, and action
examples: The review enumerates the deficiencies covered: slips of the tongue, slips of the pen, symptomatic acts, failures to perceive or remember, and false perceptions and recollections.
key_sources: Mayer, H. (1911). The Psychopathology of Everyday Life. American Journal of Psychology, 22, 477-527. https://www.jstor.org/stable/1412853

citation: Mayer, H. (1911). The Psychopathology of Everyday Life. American Journal of Psychology, 22, 477-527. https://www.jstor.org/stable/1412853
title: An introductory textbook should be judged chiefly by whether it induces pupils to think, with class exercises that stimulate introspection
description: In a companion book notice, the reviewer states that "Probably the chief function of an introductory textbook is to induce the pupils to think," and praises the reviewed text for accomplishing this through a terse, vigorous style and short, easily grasped sentences. The chapter-end class exercises are singled out as "admirably chosen to stimulate introspection," making introspective exercises a design feature of an introductory psychology text.
requirements: Exercises placed at the end of each chapter, chosen to prompt pupils' introspection
constraints: Stated for introductory psychology textbooks
target_learners: pupils in an introductory psychology course
target_learning_goals: stimulating thinking and introspection about mental facts
examples: The reviewed textbook's class exercises follow each chapter and are described as admirably chosen to stimulate introspection.

article_title: Instructional compensation for age-related cognitive declines: Effects of goal specificity in maze learning.
citation: Paas, F., Camp, G., & Rikers, R.M.J.P. (2001). Instructional compensation for age-related cognitive declines: Effects of goal specificity in maze learning. Journal of Educational Psychology, 93(1), 181-186. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-0663.93.1.181
title: Use nonspecific rather than specific goals when instructing older learners on complex tasks
description: The article shows that presenting a task's finish point "in more general terms" rather than as a specific location reduced the performance disadvantage of old adults in maze learning. Because a specific goal disproportionately compromised elderly performance while its absence disproportionately enhanced it, designers of instruction for older learners should favor nonspecific goal formulations. The recommendation rests on the authors' conclusion that cognitive load theory-based instruction can compensate for age-related cognitive declines.
requirements: Instruction must involve a task, such as maze navigation, whose goal can be formulated either specifically or in general terms.
constraints: Evidence comes from a single computerized maze-learning study with 40 young and 40 old adults; the article does not claim generalization beyond such tasks.
target_learning_goals: complex task performance such as maze navigation
examples: In the experiment, the maze finish point was presented either as a specific location or in more general terms, and the age difference was much smaller in the nonspecific goal conditions.
key_sources: Paas, F., Camp, G., & Rikers, R.M.J.P. (2001). Instructional compensation for age-related cognitive declines: Effects of goal specificity in maze learning. Journal of Educational Psychology, 93(1), 181-186. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-0663.93.1.181

article_title: Emotional transmission in the classroom: Exploring the relationship between teacher and student enjoyment.
citation: Frenzel, A. C., Goetz, T., Lüdtke, O., Pekrun, R., & Sutton, R. E. (2009). Emotional Transmission in the Classroom: Exploring the Relationship Between Teacher and Student Enjoyment. Journal of Educational Psychology, 101(3), 705–716. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0014695
title: Social–cognitive value-induction account of emotional transmission from teachers to students
description: The article frames teacher-to-student enjoyment transmission using social–cognitive learning theories and social construction approaches. Students can learn that a task is valuable by observing their teacher's enjoyment, a process the article calls "value induction" (citing Pekrun, 2000), also described as "appreciation-oriented modeling" (Brophy, 2004). Wild et al.'s constructive social perception model holds that even implicit hints about a target's motivational orientation elicit perceivers' expectations of enjoyment, which then shape students' own enjoyment. The article operationalizes the behavioral side of this account as teacher enthusiasm and tests it via mediation analysis.
requirements: Teachers' enjoyment must be made visible through socially perceivable behavior (enthusiasm) for transmission to occur
constraints: The account was tested in mathematics classrooms with students aged 13–15 in Bavaria; the authors argue basic mechanisms should generalize but call for tests in other domains and age groups
target_learning_goals: students' pleasant achievement emotions, specifically enjoyment of learning
examples: Wild et al.'s experiments: participants taught by seemingly extrinsically motivated teachers reported lower interest and less task enjoyment than those taught by seemingly intrinsically motivated teachers, despite identical lessons
key_sources: Frenzel, A. C., Goetz, T., Lüdtke, O., Pekrun, R., & Sutton, R. E. (2009). Emotional Transmission in the Classroom: Exploring the Relationship Between Teacher and Student Enjoyment. Journal of Educational Psychology, 101(3), 705–716. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0014695

title: Teacher enjoyment scale developed for this study (5 class-referenced items)
description: Because no scales measuring teacher enjoyment existed, the authors developed a five-item scale referring to teaching a specific group of students, with items such as "I really enjoy teaching mathematics in this class" and "Teaching in this class gives me many reasons to be pleased," answered on a 5-point Likert scale. Internal consistency was high (Cronbach's α = .90). It was administered to the 71 Grade 8 mathematics teachers, whose mean rating was 3.69 (SD = 0.68).
requirements: Items refer to the specific class of students being taught, consistent with the study's context-specific, traitlike approach to emotions
target_learning_goals: assessment of teachers' enjoyment of teaching a particular class
examples: Observed range of the teacher enjoyment scale was 1.80 to 5.0, per Table 1

article_title: A study of superior children.
citation: Sandiford, P., & R. P. (1922). New Publications: reviews of Baldwin's mental growth study, Root's A Socio-Psychological Study of 53 Supernormal Children, and Ballard's Group Tests of Intelligence. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journal/edu
title: Root's central common factor theory of superior intelligence, in which the common factor may be environmental as well as innate
description: The review describes Root's explanatory framework for his results: a central common factor theory in which the common factor underlying superior performance "could just as well be environmental as innate." Root states the factor "may be a varying admixture of innate ability, formal training, incidental education and social conditions." The reviewer reports that Root stresses environmental factors throughout the thesis more than most psychologists would, and the reviewer questions some of these opinions.
requirements: The theory is offered as Root's explanation of his own test and case-history results with superior children, per the review.
constraints: The reviewer reports the conclusions and opinions of the author are open to much debate.
target_learning_goals: explaining the basis of superior intelligence and test performance
examples: Root's monograph presents sociological and psychological study of a small group of superior-IQ children with extensive case histories.

article_title: Teacher coaching in upper secondary school: Examining the effects on teacher–student interaction and student engagement.
citation: Ertesvåg, S. K., Vaaland, G. S., Tvedt, M. S., Virtanen, T. E., Idsoe, T., Panayiotou, M., Lerang, M. S., Sølvik, R. M., & Lerkkanen, M.-K. (2026). Teacher coaching in upper secondary school: Examining the effects on teacher–student interaction and student engagement. Journal of Educational Psychology, 118(1), 118-137. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000986
title: Teaching Through Interactions (TTI) framework: three domains of teacher–student interaction
description: The TTI framework conceptualizes teacher–student interaction as comprising three domains of teacher support: emotional support, classroom organization, and instructional support. Emotional support promotes motivation and security, classroom organization organizes students' behavior, time, and attention, and instructional support comprises teachers' facilitation of learning opportunities. The article states that "TSI can be conceptualized as comprising three domains of teacher support for student development and learning: emotional support, classroom organization, and instructional support," and uses this framework to structure both the INTERACT intervention topics and the outcome measures.
requirements: The domains are grounded in their presumptive salience for social-emotional development, self-regulation and attention, and cognitive development and achievement
target_learning_goals: social and academic learning supported by high-quality teacher–student interaction
examples: The INTERACT coaching cycles addressed emotional support (first), instructional support (second, fourth, and sixth), classroom organization (third), student engagement (fifth), and a repeated topic of own choice (seventh)
key_sources: Ertesvåg, S. K., Vaaland, G. S., Tvedt, M. S., Virtanen, T. E., Idsoe, T., Panayiotou, M., Lerang, M. S., Sølvik, R. M., & Lerkkanen, M.-K. (2026). Teacher coaching in upper secondary school: Examining the effects on teacher–student interaction and student engagement. Journal of Educational Psychology, 118(1), 118-137. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000986
title: INTERACT video-based, web-mediated teacher coaching intervention
description: INTERACT is a structured, personalized, and interactive coaching process built on "coaching dialogues based on authentic video-recorded classroom practice from the teacher's classroom." Delivery involves three components: seven coaching cycles of six steps each using the IRIS Connect recording system, implementation support (webinars, workshops, video library, podcasts, articles), and data- and knowledge-driven decision making guided by TTI and the CLASS-S. Ten trained coaches each worked with assigned teachers across the 2022–2023 school year.
requirements: Teachers record lessons approximately every third week using the IRIS Connect system
Coaches complete 5-day coach training plus 2-day CLASS-S observer training with certification
constraints: Evaluated in Norwegian upper secondary schools; no prior studies of teacher coaching on TSI and engagement had been conducted outside the United States at this level
target_learning_goals: improve teacher–student interaction quality and student engagement
examples: Teachers in the intervention group were assigned to a coach (10 coaches in total) and participated in seven coaching cycles throughout the 2022–2023 school year

article_title: A cross-lagged study of students’ motivation, academic achievement, and relationships with teachers from kindergarten to 6th grade.
citation: M. Zee, K. Moritz Rudasill, R.J. Bosman. (2021). A Cross-Lagged Study of Students' Motivation, Academic Achievement, and Relationships With Teachers From Kindergarten to 6th Grade. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000574
title: Transactional model of motivation, teacher-student relationships, and achievement from kindergarten to 6th grade
description: The article proposes and tests a transactional framework in which students' motivation (motivational attitudes and beliefs), relationships with teachers (closeness, conflict, and dependency), and academic achievement (reading comprehension and math performance) are mutually informing over time. The framework holds that these three domains "inform one another from kindergarten through 6th grade", rather than one domain unidirectionally driving the others. It was operationalized through cross-lagged panel models fitted to three waves of data.
requirements: Longitudinal data with repeated measures of relationship quality, motivation, and achievement across at least three waves
constraints: Tested in the Dutch elementary school context from kindergarten through 6th grade
target_learners: Elementary school students from kindergarten through 6th grade
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension and math performance
Motivational attitudes and beliefs including self-efficacy and task motivation
examples: Fitted to three waves of the Dutch COOL cohort study with teacher and student reports

constraints: Dutch national cohort; student-reported measures available only at Waves 2 and 3

article_title: Academic acceleration in gifted youth and fruitless concerns regarding psychological well-being: A 35-year longitudinal study.
citation: Bernstein Brian O., Lubinski David, Benbow Camilla P. (2021). Academic Acceleration in Gifted Youth and Fruitless Concerns Regarding Psychological Well-Being: A 35-Year Longitudinal Study. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000500
title: Allow intellectually precocious students who desire advanced subject matter the freedom to pursue it
description: The article recommends that when precocious students want more advanced learning, educators and families should not block acceleration on social/emotional grounds. It argues that "students should be allowed the freedom to choose to pursue their passions" because 35-year evidence shows no well-being decrement and prior work shows academic and creative benefits. The principle treats acceleration as one form of matching curriculum to a student's learning rate.
requirements: Above-level assessments to identify precocity so that acceleration decisions rest on evidence of rapid learning rates
constraints: The evidence base covers high-potential populations identified via talent searches and elite graduate programs, not all students
target_learning_goals: matching curriculum pace and depth to advanced learning needs
examples: Study 1 tracked three cohorts of talent-search participants for over 35 years and found acceleration did not covary with age-50 well-being; Study 2 replicated this in elite STEM graduate students.
key_sources: Bernstein Brian O., Lubinski David, Benbow Camilla P. (2021). Academic Acceleration in Gifted Youth and Fruitless Concerns Regarding Psychological Well-Being: A 35-Year Longitudinal Study. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000500

article_title: Academic acceleration in gifted youth and fruitless concerns regarding psychological well-being: A 35-year longitudinal study.
citation: Bernstein Brian O., Lubinski David, Benbow Camilla P. (2021). Academic Acceleration in Gifted Youth and Fruitless Concerns Regarding Psychological Well-Being: A 35-Year Longitudinal Study. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000500
title: Appropriate developmental placement as the general continuum underlying acceleration
description: The article frames acceleration not as an isolated intervention but as one location on a broader best-practice continuum. It states, "The more general dimension is the continuum for what all students require, that is, appropriate developmental placement (Lubinski & Benbow, 2000)." Presenting curriculum at the depth and pace at which a student assimilates new knowledge is beneficial; for talented students, above-level assessments indicate when an above-level curriculum is needed. Several acceleration modalities are described as likely functionally equivalent.
requirements: Above-level assessments (for precocity) are useful in determining when an above-level curriculum (for acceleration) is needed
constraints: The modalities of acceleration studied are described as but a few examples of a broader class of educational interventions for intellectually precocious youth
target_learners: all students, as the continuum is described as what all students require
target_learning_goals: matching educational curriculum to the depth and pace at which students assimilate new knowledge
examples: The article operationalized acceleration via an acceleration composite (AP courses, college courses, grades skipped) and age of high school graduation, both treated as locations on the placement continuum.
key_sources: Bernstein Brian O., Lubinski David, Benbow Camilla P. (2021). Academic Acceleration in Gifted Youth and Fruitless Concerns Regarding Psychological Well-Being: A 35-Year Longitudinal Study. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000500

article_title: Comparative tests of home work and school work.
citation: Heck, W. H. (1914). Comparative tests of home work and school work. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org/stable/1412814
title: Do not assign home work that requires equipment, literature, or assistance many homes cannot furnish
description: The article draws an equity boundary for home work assignments: tasks "requiring equipment, literature, assistance, etc., which many homes of the students concerned cannot furnish, are manifestly unjust and should not be given in public schools." Sensible assignments instead call for independent work on topics previously discussed in school, for which the majority of homes are about as favorable as the majority of schools.
requirements: Home work topics should have been previously discussed in school so no outside resources are needed
constraints: Assignments depending on equipment, literature, or assistance unavailable in many homes are unjust in public schools
target_learners: public school students in grammar and high school grades
target_learning_goals: independent practice of school-taught content
examples: The composition topics ('The Harrisonburg High School', 'The Town of Harrisonburg') were chosen so any high school student had enough facts in mind, with no need to consult outsiders or literature.
key_sources: Heck, W. H. (1914). Comparative tests of home work and school work. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org/stable/1412814

article_title: Comparative tests of home work and school work.
citation: Heck, W. H. (1914). Comparative tests of home work and school work. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org/stable/1412814
title: Home work and school work are about equal and both depend on good teaching
description: The article's final conclusion from experiments in arithmetic and English composition, chosen to represent two contrasted types of school requirements, is that "home work and school work are or can be made about equal to each other, are about equally dependent on good teaching, and will therefore develop as the teaching develops." Objections to home work on grounds of supposed inferiority are not justified; the two should not be pitted against each other but improved together through clear instruction, assignment, interest, and checking of results.
requirements: Good teaching in school and home co-operation, including clear instruction and assignment, creation of interest, and strict checking-up of results
constraints: As a matter of daily routine children may not know how or may not will to do either well without good teaching
target_learning_goals: arithmetic computation and reasoning
English composition
examples: The Harrisonburg experiments assigned matched test forms to balanced groups so each group did one computation and one reasoning test, or one composition, in each environment.

article_title: An experiment in learning an abstract subject.
citation: Thorndike, E. L., & Upton, C. B. (1922). An Experiment in Learning an Abstract Subject. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 13(6). https://doi.org/10.1037/h0072644
title: Four-factor account of what makes 'hard' subjects hard beyond abstractness, organization, rigor and precision
description: The article proposes that part of the greater difficulty of subjects like mathematics, Latin, or physics is due not only to abstractness, organization, rigor and precision, but to four additional factors: "the sheer unfamiliarity of the date, the greater amount to be learned per unit of time, the more subtle symbolism, and the larger number of missing links—facts that have to be read between the lines." In the experiment all four appeared: strange concepts, thirteen formulas in six hours, symbolism that is at first a burden, and many required inferences. The account reframes subject difficulty as partly incidental rather than intrinsic.
requirements: The account is offered as highly probable from the facts of this one experiment with adult learners of electricity and magnetism, not as a tested result.
constraints: The authors state the common view (abstractness, organization, rigor, precision) is true; the four factors are additions deserving consideration alongside it, not replacements.
target_learners: adult learners of novel abstract material
target_learning_goals: understanding elementary laws of electricity and magnetism
learning abstract, symbolically represented subject matter
examples: The authors illustrate with a half-page textbook passage on magnetic flux requiring multiple inferences, and with hypothetical ways unfamiliar data, symbols, and omitted statements would make history harder.
key_sources: Thorndike, E. L., & Upton, C. B. (1922). An Experiment in Learning an Abstract Subject. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 13(6). https://doi.org/10.1037/h0065229

article_title: An experiment in learning an abstract subject.
citation: Thorndike, E. L., & Upton, C. B. (1922). An Experiment in Learning an Abstract Subject. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 13(6). https://doi.org/10.1037/h0072644
title: Apply each item of fact or principle as soon as learned, give many short problems first, and enable learners to ascertain correctness very soon and very often
description: The experiment corroborates pedagogical doctrines about sequencing and feedback in learning organized abstract subjects. There was general agreement among the adult learners "that each item of fact or principle should be applied as soon as learned, that miscellaneous problems requiring the selection of appropriate principles should be given later, and that many short problems with a minimum of computation" should come first. Learners also agreed the problems explained the text as truly as the text explained the problems, and that correctness should be ascertainable very soon after finishing any part of the work.
requirements: A supply of short problems requiring minimal computation, sample problems solved in the text as illustrations of formulas, and a means for learners to check their work along its course.
constraints: The agreement is the subjects' reported opinion after the experiment, not a manipulated comparison; the article reports no test of these arrangements.
target_learners: adult learners of novel abstract material
high school pupils in abstract subjects
target_learning_goals: understanding and applying principles of electricity and magnetism
mastering organized abstract subject matter
examples: Subjects studied Franklin and Esty's text for six hours, then worked problems 4 to 18 with the textbook answers erased, keeping notes of difficulties.
key_sources: Thorndike, E. L., & Upton, C. B. (1922). An Experiment in Learning an Abstract Subject. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 13(6). https://doi.org/10.1037/h0065229

article_title: Inspector Winch's experiments on transfer.
citation: Locke, L. L. (1913). Inspector Winch's experiments on transfer. https://www.google.com/books/search?q=%22Inspector+Winch%27s+Experiments+on+Transfer%22
title: Formal discipline: the doctrine defending mathematics courses through transfer since Plato
description: The article names formal discipline as the long-standing doctrine that training in mathematics quickens and disciplines the mind generally. It observes that the doctrine 'has been invoked from Plato's time to the present as a defense of the courses in mathematics,' and treats Inspector Winch's experiment as preliminary research on whether accuracy in reasoning transfers from arithmetical to other situations.
requirements: The doctrine rests on the assumption that arithmetical training produces gains, in quickness at least, in other kinds of knowledge.
constraints: The article notes that the almost universal lay belief in transfer persists regardless of theoretical argument, so the doctrine's popularity does not depend on evidence.
target_learning_goals: transfer of accuracy in reasoning from arithmetical to other situations
key_sources: Locke, L. L. (1913). Inspector Winch's experiments on transfer. https://www.google.com/books/search?q=%22Inspector+Winch%27s+Experiments+on+Transfer%22

article_title: Preliminary study of the relative efficiency of inductive and deductive teaching of logical reasoning.
citation: Felix Sachs. (1913). Preliminary Study of the Relative Efficiency of Inductive and Deductive Teaching of Logical Reasoning. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org/journal/jeducpsyc
title: Teach forms of fallacious reasoning inductively through drill on concrete everyday examples rather than by deductive presentation of rules
description: The article recommends replacing deductive logic teaching, accompanied as it too often is by sheer memorizing of logical figures and rules, with painstaking drill in analyzing concrete examples of argumentation taken from various phases of everyday life. Instruction proceeded by having observers understand each fallacy from a typical example, then labelling it, then drilling with valid and fallacious examples until each could state validity, reasons, and fallacy name.
requirements: Requires a collection of suitable concrete, non-technical examples of each fallacy type, which the author reports was no easy task to assemble
constraints: The author concedes the experiment does not prove the conviction incontestably and calls it a preliminary study; the comparison confounded inductive with deductive and individual with classroom instruction
target_learning_goals: detecting fallacious reasoning
explaining and naming logical fallacies
examples: About 20 hours of tutoring in which examples such as a strike argument were varied premise by premise until observers themselves identified which inferences were wrong, after which the fallacy names Denying the Antecedent and Affirming the Consequent were given
key_sources: Felix Sachs. (1913). Preliminary Study of the Relative Efficiency of Inductive and Deductive Teaching of Logical Reasoning. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org/journal/jeducpsyc

article_title: Preliminary study of the relative efficiency of inductive and deductive teaching of logical reasoning.
citation: Felix Sachs. (1913). Preliminary Study of the Relative Efficiency of Inductive and Deductive Teaching of Logical Reasoning. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org/journal/jeducpsyc
title: Formal discipline as development of transferable patterns or forms of thought
description: The article frames its experiment within the doctrine of formal discipline as discussed by Meiklejohn, according to which training along a specific line develops patterns or forms of thought that may thereafter function in other and different activities. The study sought to see whether practice in detecting fallacies would build up inductively in observers' minds patterns of these fallacies that could be subsumed and ticketed when the fallacies recurred in other settings and material.
requirements: Access to observers skilled in introspection to study the formation and transfer of patterns, which the author recommends for future repetitions
constraints: The hoped-for introspective account of the genesis and nature of these forms was not realized, whether from error in method, incapacity of observers, or actual impossibility of the task
target_learning_goals: transfer of reasoning patterns to new material
examples: One tutored observer reported in several instances making a deliberate comparison of the test-example with the typical example used in his training

article_title: Problems in the experimental pedagogy of geometry.
citation: William H. Metzler. (1912). Problems in the Experimental Pedagogy of Geometry. The Journal of Educational Psychology.
title: Three lines of experimental investigation for the pedagogy of geometry
description: The article organizes experimental work on geometry teaching around three questions: whether the desired results are obtained under a given method, what the best method of obtaining them is, and whether obtaining them transfers to other subjects. It states that "If the three lines of investigation indicated were carefully carried out and the questions involved settled, there would be no doubt as to the correct aims and proper methods in teaching the subject." The framework links aim-verification, method comparison, and transfer testing into one research program.
requirements: Experiments must be performed "with the utmost care and under the most certain conditions," since overlooked factors can spoil an experiment's value
constraints: Testing for transfer is described as not easy and in some phases almost, if not entirely, impossible
target_learning_goals: logical thinking
concentration
transfer of general powers
examples: The article derives suggested tests for knowledge of fundamentals, reasoning, and concentration from the first line of investigation
key_sources: William H. Metzler. (1912). Problems in the Experimental Pedagogy of Geometry. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0070947

article_title: Problems in the experimental pedagogy of geometry.
citation: William H. Metzler. (1912). Problems in the Experimental Pedagogy of Geometry. The Journal of Educational Psychology.
title: Three recognized general methods of teaching geometry: textbook, suggestive, and syllabus methods
description: The article identifies "the textbook method, the suggestive method, and the syllabus method" as the three fairly well recognized general methods of teaching geometry, alongside many special devices. It proposes that their relative merits be determined by well-selected experiments testing the results, and that because different schools use different methods, the same test could be given across schools to compare outcomes.
requirements: Method comparison requires well-selected experiments testing the results, or same tests administered across schools using different methods
target_learning_goals: acquisition of the ten desired outcomes of geometry study
examples: The article suggests giving the same test to different schools that use different methods as one route to comparison
key_sources: William H. Metzler. (1912). Problems in the Experimental Pedagogy of Geometry. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0070947

article_title: Problems in the experimental pedagogy of geometry.
citation: William H. Metzler. (1912). Problems in the Experimental Pedagogy of Geometry. The Journal of Educational Psychology.
title: Teach general powers explicitly and across all subjects, never leaving them to accidental acquirement
description: The article recommends that powers such as concentration, accuracy, and honesty be made objects of instruction in themselves and be insisted upon in connection with every school subject, so that pupils apply them to everything they undertake. It argues that what is impressed from only one or two subjects "is not likely to be considered of much importance in others, and will not become a habit in all."
requirements: Teachers must explicitly point out the general value of the ability rather than limit it to the subject at hand
constraints: The article concedes there may be some truth to the objection that teaching accuracy in connection with everything dilutes subject-specific teaching
target_learning_goals: transferable habits such as concentration, accuracy, and honesty
examples: The article's analogy: a boy would hardly be expected to be honest if honesty were mentioned only in relation to his teacher
key_sources: William H. Metzler. (1912). Problems in the Experimental Pedagogy of Geometry. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0070947

article_title: The learning of delinquent adolescent girls as shown by a substitution test.
citation: Baldwin, B. T. (1913). The learning of delinquent adolescent girls as shown by a substitution test. The Journal of Educational Psychology, IV(6), 317-332.
title: Wig-wag code substitution test with typewriter-layout keyboard
description: A code-transliteration learning task in which girls translate a portion of Benjamin Franklin's Autobiography into a modified wig-wag code. The letters of the alphabet are "distributed in the form of the universal typewriter keyboard, with the code equivalents attached, at the top of each of five pages", and the code consists of combinations of the numbers 1 and 2, signifying short horizontal marks to the left or right of vertical red lines. The task was administered for sixteen five-minute practice periods and yielded counts of substitutions and errors per girl.
requirements: Subjects receive careful initial instructions and a worked illustration of writing the first two words before starting.
constraints: No information was given in regard to errors after the first two trials, except to apparently feeble-minded girls.
target_learners: delinquent adolescent girls aged thirteen to twenty-one in a reformatory school
target_learning_goals: learning capacity as measured by speed and accuracy of code substitution
examples: Administered to five classes of girls for sixteen consecutive practice periods of five minutes each, between 2:45 and 4:30 in the afternoon.

article_title: Achievement in large-scale national numeracy assessment: An ecological study of motivation and student, home, and school predictors.
citation: Martin, Andrew; Lazendic, G. (2018). Achievement in large-scale national numeracy assessment: An ecological study of motivation and student, home, and school predictors. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000231
title: Ecological and transactional framework of student, student/home, and school factors predicting motivation and numeracy achievement
description: The article organizes predictors of numeracy achievement through "ecological and transactional conceptualizing involving student, student/home, and school factors." Student factors comprised mathematics ability, gender, and year group; student/home factors comprised tutoring, competition participation, computer support, and practice tests; school factors included school-average ability, practice tests, competition participation, and socioeducational status. These factors were modeled as predictors of mathematics motivation, which along with the ecology factors predicted numeracy achievement.
requirements: Data from students nested within schools, enabling multilevel (Level 1 and Level 2) modeling of the three factor groups
constraints: Applied to large-scale national numeracy assessment contexts, as modeled in this study
target_learners: Australian elementary (Years 3 and 5) and secondary (Years 7 and 9) school students
target_learning_goals: Mathematics motivation
Numeracy achievement in large-scale assessment
examples: The framework was tested with multilevel structural equation modeling on data from 12,736 students in 231 schools participating in a national numeracy assessment exercise.
key_sources: Martin, Andrew; Lazendic, G. (2018). Achievement in large-scale national numeracy assessment: An ecological study of motivation and student, home, and school predictors. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000231

citation: Martin, Andrew; Lazendic, G. (2018). Achievement in large-scale national numeracy assessment: An ecological study of motivation and student, home, and school predictors. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000231
title: National numeracy assessment dataset: 12,736 Australian students from 231 schools
description: The study's empirical base is a large-scale national numeracy assessment dataset. The article states that "Data were drawn from N = 12,736 Australian elementary (Years 3 and 5) and secondary (Years 7 and 9) school students from 231 schools participating in a national numeracy assessment exercise." The dataset spans four year groups and supports multilevel modeling of student- and school-level effects.
requirements: Participation data from students nested within schools in a national assessment exercise
constraints: Limited to Australian elementary and secondary students in Years 3, 5, 7, and 9
target_learners: Elementary and secondary school students (Years 3, 5, 7, and 9)
target_learning_goals: Numeracy achievement
Mathematics motivation
examples: The dataset was analyzed with multilevel structural equation modeling to predict motivation and numeracy achievement.

article_title: Multimedia effects in initial instruction and feedback on problem solving.
citation: Gök, S., Zhang, T., Goldstone, R. L., & Fyfe, E. R. (2025). Multimedia Effects in Initial Instruction and Feedback on Problem Solving. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000943
title: Provide multimedia materials in feedback to improve problem-solving performance, and in initial instruction when the aim is spontaneous diagram generation
description: The article recommends placing multimedia materials (text plus diagrams) selectively depending on the instructional goal. It states: "It may be important for practitioners to provide multimedia materials in feedback to improve problem-solving performance, whereas they may include them in initial instruction if the aim is for students to spontaneously generate diagrams in their own solutions." The recommendation follows directly from the experiment's dissociated effects: feedback modality drove posttest accuracy, instruction modality drove perceptions and drawings.
requirements: Feedback or instruction materials must combine text with content-based diagrams (icon arrays and tables in this study) aligned with multimedia learning design principles of contiguity and coherence.
constraints: Effects were demonstrated only for conditional probability problems with undergraduate students; the study's design and analysis were not pre-registered.
target_learning_goals: problem-solving accuracy on conditional probability problems
spontaneous diagram generation during problem solving
examples: In the experiment, 129 undergraduates were randomly assigned across four conditions crossing text-only vs multimedia initial instruction with text-only vs multimedia feedback on conditional probability problems.

article_title: Developmental change in the influence of domain-general abilities and domain-specific knowledge on mathematics achievement: An eight-year longitudinal study.
citation: Geary David C., Nicholas Alan, Li Yaoran, Sun Jianguo. (2017). Developmental Change in the Influence of Domain-General Abilities and Domain-Specific Knowledge on Mathematics Achievement: An Eight-Year Longitudinal Study. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000159
title: Prioritize domain-specific mathematical skills, not domain-general abilities, as intervention targets for long-term mathematics gains
description: Because the importance of prior mathematical knowledge for further gains increases across grades while domain-general effects remain stable, the article recommends interventions focused on domain-specific skills. It states that "interventions focused on improving domain-specific skills, such as fractions knowledge, will likely yield longer-term gains in mathematics achievement than will interventions focused on domain-general abilities, such as working memory." Prerequisite skills identified include number knowledge and basic arithmetic in early grades and fractions knowledge in later grades.
requirements: Interventions must address the prerequisite domain-specific skills identified for the relevant grade band: number knowledge and basic arithmetic early, fractions knowledge later.
constraints: The data are correlational and do not support strong causal inferences; the article notes follow-up studies are needed to test whether improving domain-specific skills reduces individual differences in later achievement.
target_learning_goals: Mathematics achievement, number knowledge, arithmetic skills, fractions knowledge
examples: The longitudinal study indexed domain-specific knowledge with number sets, number line, addition retrieval, decomposition, and fractions comparison measures and showed their increasing importance across grades.
key_sources: Geary David C., Nicholas Alan, Li Yaoran, Sun Jianguo. (2017). Developmental Change in the Influence of Domain-General Abilities and Domain-Specific Knowledge on Mathematics Achievement: An Eight-Year Longitudinal Study. article_title: Developmental change in the influence of domain-general abilities and domain-specific knowledge on mathematics achievement: An eight-year longitudinal study.
citation: Geary David C., Nicholas Alan, Li Yaoran, Sun Jianguo. (2017). Developmental Change in the Influence of Domain-General Abilities and Domain-Specific Knowledge on Mathematics Achievement: An Eight-Year Longitudinal Study. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000159
title: Mixed functional data analysis for estimating grade-by-grade longitudinal predictor effects
description: The article applies longitudinal mixed functional data analysis (FDA) to estimate regression effects as functions of grade, using linear splines for fixed and random effect functions. It argues FDA "is not constrained by the parametric assumptions of cross-lagged and related models" and enables simultaneous estimation of overall domain-general and domain-specific effects, grade-by-grade contributions of individual variables, and linear and non-linear across-grade change in these effects on subsequent mathematics achievement.
requirements: Longitudinal data with repeated assessments across multiple grades for the outcome and predictors, standardized at each grade to a common metric.
constraints: The article notes the correlational data do not support strong causal inferences, and the relatively small sample may have reduced statistical power for some analyses.
target_learners: Children followed longitudinally from kindergarten through 8th grade
target_learning_goals: Mathematics achievement development
examples: The %fmixed SAS macro following Liu and Guo (2011) was used to fit models estimating domain-general and domain-specific effects from 2nd to 8th grade.

article_title: Adult tests of the Stanford revision applied to college students.
citation: Caldwell, Helen Hubbert. (1919). Adult Tests of the Stanford Revision Applied to College Students. The Journal of Educational Psychology, X(10). https://www.jstor.org
title: Use standardized adult intelligence tests to advise college students, but always interpret IQs in light of character study
description: The article recommends the Stanford Adult Tests for advisory work because their correlation with scholastic standing is as high as any other test set and they are standardized, providing "a common basis for the comparison of results." It simultaneously insists that IQs "must always be interpreted in the light of character study," since factors like verbal fluency, popularity, and outside activities distort both grades and estimates of intelligence.
requirements: Standardized administration and scoring by trained examiners, as in the study where student examiners were trained and supervised before data collection began
constraints: Adult IQs have less meaning than children's; the highest attainable adult IQ is 121.8, making identification of adult genius impossible
The alternate Average Adult tests are misplaced or need changing, and the Superior Adult group carries too many auditory memory tests
target_learning_goals: diagnosis of unsatisfactory scholarship and academic advising
examples: The author suggests the tests could help advisory officers diagnose unsatisfactory scholarship among Freshmen and Upper-classmen, and could screen candidates where a long waiting list is the rule
key_sources: Caldwell, Helen Hubbert. (1919). Adult Tests of the Stanford Revision Applied to College Students. The Journal of Educational Psychology, X(10). https://doi.org/10.1037/h0074484

article_title: Supplemental Material for Test Boredom While Working on Difficult Versus Easy Tasks: The Same Emotion but Different Effects on Performance
citation: Test Boredom While Working on Difficult Versus Easy Tasks: Online Supplementary Materials. (2022). https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Test+Boredom+While+Working+on+Difficult+Versus+Easy+Tasks%22
title: Assessment-timing rationale separating over-/underchallenge and boredom measures within experimental blocks
description: Supplemental Material S6 documents the authors' rationale for when and where state assessments were placed during Study 2's experimental blocks. They separated the assessment of over-/underchallenge and boredom "to keep the individual assessments as brief as possible," assessed both constructs "as late as possible within the manipulation blocks" so the manipulation had time to take effect, and assessed over-/underchallenge first because these perceptions were assumed to be antecedents of boredom. The authors acknowledge this ordering does not permit causal conclusions.
requirements: Over-/underchallenge perceptions must be assessed before boredom, as the authors assumed these perceptions to be antecedents of boredom.
constraints: The authors acknowledge that this assessment order does not allow for causal conclusions.
target_learners: Adult participants completing working-memory tasks in a laboratory experiment
target_learning_goals: Understanding how task difficulty (overchallenge vs. underchallenge) relates to state boredom and performance during cognitive tasks
examples: In Study 2, over-/underchallenge and boredom were assessed at separate, late points within each manipulation block of difficult or easy digit-span tasks.

article_title: Recent studies in handwriting.
citation: Thompson, M. E. (1911). Recent Studies in Handwriting. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 2, 41-45.
title: Thorndike's objective scale for measuring handwriting quality
description: Thorndike devised a standard scale for objectively measuring the quality of handwriting, resting on the consensus of many competent judges rather than on individual biased impressions. Samples from pupils in grades V to VIII were sorted into twenty quality groups by thirty or forty judges, and scale points were constructed equidistant from each other, with a copy-book model at the top and artificially produced very bad writing at the bottom.
requirements: Several competent judges independently compare a sample with the scale and indicate the quality it most resembles
constraints: The author admits the scale is not yet perfect; few of the steps contain a sufficient number of different styles of writing
Individuals will vary somewhat in their ratings, so the scale will not work automatically
target_learners: pupils in grades V to VIII
target_learning_goals: handwriting quality measurement
examples: A scale of six points was also constructed for the quality of adult women's handwriting

article_title: Recent studies in handwriting.
citation: Thompson, M. E. (1911). Recent Studies in Handwriting. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 2, 41-45.
title: Freeman's recommendations: emphasize letter form from the start, postpone strenuous movement drill, and combine sentence and letter methods
description: On the basis of his own and other experiments, Freeman discusses five questions in the teaching of writing. He argues that form, which is fundamental, should be emphasized from the start while strenuous drill in movement may be postponed until the third or fourth grade, that slant writing has a physiological basis for greater ease and rapidity, and that a combination of sentence and letter method is advantageous.
requirements: Further experimentation is recognized as needed throughout the discussion
constraints: Drill in arm movement shows little progress in the first three or four grades, with marked development in grades IV to VI
target_learning_goals: handwriting form and movement
examples: Freeman suggests taking one component at a time, practicing finger movement at the desk and arm movement at the blackboard, and uniting the two later; a combination of free arm movement, muscular movement, and finger movement is advocated

article_title: Recent studies in handwriting.
citation: Thompson, M. E. (1911). Recent Studies in Handwriting. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 2, 41-45.
title: Thompson's resume organizes psychological research on writing for teachers, from alphabet history to neural bases to pedagogy
description: Thompson's book brings together widely scattered experimental data on handwriting, published in technical journals inaccessible to the average teacher, and presents them in orderly fashion with emphasis on their pedagogical applications. It traces the historical development of the alphabet, summarizes views on the neural activities underlying writing including the agraphia question, and reviews experimental studies of movement, practice, and intelligence before re-examining the results from the teacher's practical standpoint.
requirements: Intended for teachers and laymen rather than the psychological expert
constraints: For the specialist in psychology she has nothing new to offer; she made no original researches nor novel theories
The historical sketch ends with the printing form of the Latin alphabet and does not trace cursive development
target_learning_goals: evidence-based understanding of handwriting pedagogy
examples: The final chapter on the pedagogy of writing incorporates a portion of Thorndike's scale and includes a bibliography of 44 numbers and an index

article_title: Optimizing multiple-choice questions for retrieval practice: Delayed display of answer alternatives enhances vocabulary learning.
citation: van den Broek, G., Gerritsen, S. L., Oomen, I. T. J., Velthoven, E., van Boxtel, F. H. J., Kester, L., & van Gog, T. (2023). Optimizing multiple-choice questions for retrieval practice: Delayed display of answer alternatives enhances vocabulary learning. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000810
title: Stepwise MCQ: a multiple-choice item that presents the question word for 4 s before the answer options appear
description: A stepwise MCQ is a modified multiple-choice item for vocabulary retrieval practice in which the question is presented before the answer options, creating an opportunity for cued recall. As the article describes the manipulation, "in stepwise MCQs, it was shown for 4 s before the translations appeared", whereas in standard MCQs a word was presented with three possible translations simultaneously. The element was tested against standard MCQs in one classroom and three online experiments.
requirements: The question must be displayed before the answer options (a 4 s delay in the reported experiments) so learners can attempt cued recall.
constraints: The retention benefit did not appear in one of the four experiments and was most robust for noncompetitive answer options.
target_learners: school students in the classroom experiment
target_learning_goals: vocabulary learning (word-translation retention)
examples: In the reported experiments, a vocabulary word was shown for 4 s before its three possible translations appeared, and learners practiced with either standard or stepwise MCQs.
key_sources: van den Broek, G., Gerritsen, S. L., Oomen, I. T. J., Velthoven, E., van Boxtel, F. H. J., Kester, L., & van Gog, T. (2023). article_title: Optimizing multiple-choice questions for retrieval practice: Delayed display of answer alternatives enhances vocabulary learning.
citation: van den Broek, G., Gerritsen, S. L., Oomen, I. T. J., Velthoven, E., van Boxtel, F. H. J., Kester, L., & van Gog, T. (2023). Optimizing multiple-choice questions for retrieval practice: Delayed display of answer alternatives enhances vocabulary learning. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000810
title: Use a stepwise display in MCQ-based retrieval practice: present the question before the answer options to create a cued-recall opportunity.
description: Because retrieval during MCQ practice may not always occur, for example with easy-to-guess answers, the article recommends presenting the question before the options: "a stepwise display, which presents the question before the answer options. This creates an opportunity for cued recall." The authors conclude that "a stepwise display is a promising and easy-to-implement manipulation to optimize MCQs for retrieval practice."
requirements: MCQ practice in which learners might otherwise guess without retrieving; the delay must give learners a chance to attempt retrieval from memory.
constraints: The benefit was most robust for noncompetitive answer options and for learners who reported actually retrieving during the delay; it did not appear in one of the four experiments.
target_learners: vocabulary learners in classrooms and online settings
target_learning_goals: delayed retention of vocabulary
examples: The experiments implemented the stepwise display by showing the word for 4 s before the translations appeared, in a classroom study and three online studies.
key_sources: van den Broek, G., Gerritsen, S. L., Oomen, I. T. J., Velthoven, E., van Boxtel, F. H. J., Kester, L., & van Gog, T. (2023). article_title: Distribution of grades.
citation: J. L. Zerbe. (1917). Distribution of Grades. The Journal of Educational Psychology, VIII(10), 575-588.
title: Normal-curve-based uniform grading standard (George Washington University committee plan)
description: A grading framework grounded in the psychological finding that mental ability, "when sufficiently large numbers are considered," is distributed in the bell-shaped probability curve. The George Washington University committee translated this into fixed grade percentages: "The grade of A or excellent should be assigned to about 4 per cent, of the students, B or good to about 24 per cent., C or medium to about 44 per cent., D or sub-medium to about 24 per cent, and E or failure to about 4 per cent." The article presents this plan, adopted since the University of Missouri's 1908 system, as the leading institutional attempt to replace personal-opinion grading with a uniform standard, while insisting it does not curtail teachers' freedom.
requirements: Faculty-wide adoption so that all teachers use approximately the same standard with all students, preserving uniformity across courses and instructors.
constraints: The committee itself allowed that failure percentages may properly be higher in lower classes and in professional schools, so the fixed percentages are adjustable rather than absolute.
target_learning_goals: fair and uniform evaluation of student achievement for credits, honors, and recommendations
examples: The George Washington University committee report of March 1914, quoted in the article, and the University of Missouri's 1908 adoption of a defined grading method.
key_sources: J. L. Zerbe. (1917). Distribution of Grades. The Journal of Educational Psychology, VIII(10), 575-588. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0074694

article_title: Distribution of grades.
citation: J. L. Zerbe. (1917). Distribution of Grades. The Journal of Educational Psychology, VIII(10), 575-588.
title: Base grading standards on empirically derived distribution curves rather than instructors' personal opinion
description: The article argues that because instructor grading rests on personal opinion and varies wildly, institutions need "definite scales, absolute units of value for school work." It proposes that "a curve which expresses the correlation of mental tests of the students within the institution with the distribution of grades as assigned by many instructors through many years ought to give a distribution which would maintain the traditional standards of that institution and at the same time give the individual student full justice." Until a per-subject measuring scale exists, an empirically derived curve is the recommended scientific method of grading.
requirements: Either well-devised psychological tests of the students, or a multi-year distribution of grades within the institution, as the basis for the curve.
constraints: The author notes a test-based curve limits the institution's standard to the general mental ability of its students, and a curve based on former grades, while upholding tradition, "is not just in the long run to many of the students."
target_learning_goals: just, uniform recognition of school work in grades, honors, and elimination decisions

article_title: Chance or Purpose in the Origin and Evolution of Adaptation.
citation: Paul Knuth and W. C. B., abstractors. (1910). Journal of Educational Psychology abstracts page: theory of sleep; T. H. Morgan, Chance or Purpose in the Origin and Evolution of Adaptation. Science, 33: 789.
title: Theory of sleep as an actively induced passive state explained by cell energy and stimulus exhaustion
description: The abstracted theory explains sleep in terms of cell energy and stimulus exhaustion: living tissue discharges energy in response to a stimulus, and responsiveness has a limit, so that repeated stimulation of constant intensity eventually fails to incite a response. The abstract states that "the monotony of stimula- tion raises the threshold," and that an organism is asleep to an environment it fails to respond to while remaining awake to stimuli not yet exhausted. Sleep is characterized as an "actively induced passive state in relation to the external environment," developed out of the hypnoidal state, with implications for dream-life and subconscious activities.
requirements: The account presupposes that responsiveness of living tissue to a stimulus has a finite limit, so that constant-intensity stimulation progressively loses effectiveness.
constraints: The theory is stated at the level of cells and organisms generally, not derived from learning tasks or instructional settings.
target_learners: human organisms generally, as discussed in the source
target_learning_goals: understanding responsiveness and threshold changes under repeated stimulation
examples: The abstract describes subjects passing into and out of sleep through a brief, unstable hypnoidal state oscillating between waking and sleep or hypnosis.

article_title: Chance or Purpose in the Origin and Evolution of Adaptation.
citation: Paul Knuth and W. C. B., abstractors. (1910). Journal of Educational Psychology abstracts page: theory of sleep; T. H. Morgan, Chance or Purpose in the Origin and Evolution of Adaptation. Science, 33: 789.
title: Morgan's account of adaptation: an initial accidental adaptation loads the dice for further variation in the same direction
description: The abstract reports T. H. Morgan's argument against explaining adaptation purely by chance fit between variations and environments. Morgan posits "some closer bond that 'insures the continuance in a given direction of variations once begun'": once germinal material shows itself susceptible of change in an environment, it tends to vary further in the same direction in that environment. The abstract quotes Morgan's summary that "Each step that the organism has taken guarantees further responses in the same direction," so that the mechanism of survival insures success where it is most called for.
requirements: The account presupposes germinal material that, once susceptible of change in an environment, tends to vary further in the same direction in that environment.
constraints: The theory concerns the origin and evolution of biological adaptation, not human learning or instruction.
target_learners: readers of evolutionary theory in educational psychology, as addressed by the abstract
target_learning_goals: understanding directedness of variation in the evolution of adaptation
examples: The abstract presents Morgan's dissatisfaction with the chance-explanation of adaptation and his proposed germinal-tendency alternative as printed in Science, 33: 789.

article_title: Communications and discussions: The organization of the Department of Education at the University of Vermont.
citation: Communications and Discussions. (1910). The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov
title: University of Vermont Department of Education organized so education strengthens teaching of other subjects
description: The Department of Education at the University of Vermont was organized around the premise that education study should serve teachers of other subjects rather than stand as an isolated elective. As Messenger writes, "The chief function of the department of education is to strengthen them as teachers of those subjects." Students completing two years of required work receive the Bachelor of Science in Education, and students enrolled in other departments may take education courses and have the words "in education" appended to their baccalaureate degree.

constraints: Admission to education courses by students enrolled elsewhere requires permission of the dean of the department in which he is enrolled and of the dean of the department of education

College graduates who are not teachers but will hold positions on school boards and boards of trustees

Strengthening subject-matter teachers with educational theory

Education courses are open as free electives to juniors and seniors in any department

article_title: Disparity between Intelligence and Scholarship.
citation: Stone, Charles Leonard. (1924). Disparity Between Intelligence and Scholarship. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org
title: A four-part test battery measuring tension, perseverance, environmental assimilation, and aggression
description: The article describes a battery administered to 87 summoned students to probe factors behind intelligence–scholarship discrepancy. It included "a modification of the Downey will-profile test" in which a phrase was written at normal, rapid, and slow rates to yield tension and perseverance quotients; an abbreviated Rosanoff, Martin, and Rosanoff High Standard Frequency Test scored by agreement with responses of 100 eminent men of science; and three story-based deletion tests for fear, sex, and aggression, with the aggression time divided by total time of the three tests.
requirements: Requires subjects able to write at normal, rapid, and slow rates for the Downey-derived quotients
Requires the normative response distribution of a group of 100 eminent men of science for scoring the frequency test

article_title: Adolescent well-being and school engagement as a function of teacher and peer relatedness: The more (relatedness) is not always the merrier.
citation: Núñez-Regueiro, F., & Wang, M.-T. (2024). Adolescent Well-Being and School Engagement as a Function of Teacher and Peer Relatedness: The More (Relatedness) Is Not Always the Merrier. Journal of Educational Psychology, 117(3), 466-484. https://hal.science/hal-04920252v1
title: Complex social ecology of school relatedness operationalized through cubic response surface analysis with five congruence hypotheses
description: The article extends the complex social ecology model, which conceptualizes the "collective influences" that social partners may have on youth development, by operationalizing collective effects of peer and teacher relatedness with cubic polynomial regression. Its cubic RSA uses a model "composed of 9 regression parameters" whose constraints instantiate five congruence hypotheses (cumulative coaction, interdependent needs, peer-specific, teacher-specific, and complete compensatory processes), tested in Study 1 and cross-validated in Study 2 with alternative measures. The approach mixes variable-centered predictive effects with person-centered typological patterns along the lines of congruence and incongruence.
requirements: Commensurable, standardized predictors and outcomes so response surfaces along the LOC and LOIC can be interpreted
Sufficient sample and measures of both relatedness sources and the outcome to fit and compare constrained polynomial families
constraints: In Study 1, data clustering could not be modeled because student class membership was unknown
RSA had never been applied in this context, so unexpected congruence processes could fit better than the five hypotheses
target_learning_goals: student well-being
school engagement
examples: Study 1 fit a congruence-effect family to well-being (R2 = .171) and an asymmetric congruence family to engagement (R2 = .284), selected via absolute fit, AIC/BIC weights, and 1000 bootstrapped samples.

title: Design interventions and theories around peer and teacher relatedness as interdependent, rather than independent, factors of adolescent development
description: The article's implications state that "peer and teacher relatedness appear to be interdependent factors of positive development", which "changes the way psychological needs for relatedness are conceived in educational theories". Interventions should therefore foster healthy socialization processes with both peers and teachers together, since benefits of one source depend on the other. The principle rests on the two-study cubic RSA evidence that single-source relatedness was often not adaptive.
requirements: Interventions must assess and address both peer and teacher relatedness rather than a single source
constraints: Peer relatedness did not contribute to well-being in the absence of teacher relatedness, and teacher relatedness alone did not contribute to well-being
target_learning_goals: student well-being
school engagement
examples: The Educational Impact and Implications Statement reports that the findings open new avenues for interventions aiming to foster healthy socialization processes at school.

article_title: Achievement goals, reasons for goal pursuit, and achievement goal complexes as predictors of beneficial outcomes: Is the influence of goals reducible to reasons?
citation: Sommet, N., Darnon, C., & Butera, F. (2015). To Confirm or to Conform? Performance Goals as a Regulator of Conflict With More-Competent Others. Journal of Educational Psychology, 107(2), 580–598. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0037240
title: Performance goals as social tools regulating conflict with more-competent others: competitive vs. protective relational regulation
description: The article proposes that performance goals function as regulators of interpersonal behavior during socio-cognitive conflict with a more-competent disagreeing other. Drawing on the interpersonal circumplex's agency dimension, it predicts that "performance-approach goals (focus on approaching normative competence) should be associated with more-dominant behavior (i.e., competitive conflict regulation), whereas performance-avoidance goals (focus on avoiding normative incompetence) should be associated with more-submissive behavior (i.e., protective conflict regulation)". Competitive regulation means confirming one's own viewpoint and invalidating the other's; protective regulation means complying with the other's viewpoint and subordinating one's own. The framework treats the superior competence of a partner as a self-evaluation threat that activates these opposing self–other regulation systems.
requirements: A competence-relevant disagreement situation in which the partner's relative competence is perceived as equal, superior, or unspecified
Learners' endorsement (or induced adoption) of performance-approach or performance-avoidance goals
constraints: The framework concerns relational conflict regulation with more-competent others, not epistemic regulation in which the other is treated as an informational support
The approach/avoidance distinction applies to performance goals; mastery goals are not brought into the account
target_learners: learners in dyadic or group interactions with more-competent peers
target_learning_goals: regulation of disagreement during collaborative learning
socio-cognitive conflict resolution
examples: In Studies 1 and 3 participants reacted to a fictitious disagreeing partner on the Internet; in Study 2 goals were induced via instructions; in Study 4 participants took part in face-to-face videotaped interaction

title: Design dynamic learning systems for competence-asymmetric interactions with learners' performance goals in mind
description: Because interventions promoting interaction with more-knowledgeable peers expose learners to self-evaluation threat, designers should anticipate that performance-approach goals push learners toward dominant, self-confirming responses and performance-avoidance goals toward submissive compliance. The article argues that "understanding the motivational determinants of its regulation may be of utmost importance to design facilitating interventions" for confrontations with more-competent others, a situation it calls common in educational settings such as unequal-status classroom interactions.

constraints: The evidence concerns disagreement (socio-cognitive conflict) with a more-competent or equally competent partner, not all collaborative learning
target_learners: students in peer tutoring and collaborative learning
target_learning_goals: constructive engagement with a more-competent disagreeing partner
coordinated rather than dominant or compliant conflict regulation
examples: The four studies manipulated or measured partner competence via academic status, bogus test scores, or dyadic score asymmetry while assessing competitive and protective regulation
