article_title: Long-term positive effects of repeating a year in school: Six-year longitudinal study of self-beliefs, anxiety, social relations, school grades, and test scores.
citation: Marsh, H. W., Pekrun, R., Parker, P. D., Murayama, K., Guo, J., Dicke, T. and Lichtenfeld, S. (2017). Long-term positive effects of repeating a year in school: six-year longitudinal study of self-beliefs, anxiety, social relations, school grades, and test scores. Journal of Educational Psychology, 109 (3). pp. 425-438. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000144
title: Developmental equilibrium perspective on retention effects
description: The article introduces an apparently new developmental equilibrium perspective in retention research, evaluating whether retention effects are consistent across the potentially volatile early-to-middle adolescent period. It defines equilibrium as when "a system achieves a state of balance between the potentially counter-balancing effects of opposing forces". Applied here, the hypothesis is that retention effects are the same for students retained in Years 5-8; support indicates the self-system has achieved developmental balance in relation to retention effects over this period.
requirements: Longitudinal data with multiple retention groups spanning the age range of interest, so lagged effects can be constrained equal across groups and tested for invariance
constraints: The article notes this is an apparently new strategy in retention research and that future research should test the generalizability of the retention effects to students of other ages
target_learners: German secondary school students in Years 5-8 (early-to-middle adolescents)
target_learning_goals: Academic self-beliefs, anxiety, social relations, and math achievement following grade retention
examples: The study tested a developmental invariance model constraining lagged retention effects equal across four retention groups (Years 5-8), imposing 60 invariance constraints

citation: Sunne, Dagny. (1917). The Relation of Class Standing to College Tests. The Journal of Educational Psychology, VIII(4), 193-211.
title: Use group testing of college students as a feasible, time-saving measurement approach, with repeated trials and both quantitative and qualitative scoring for memory tests
description: The article concludes that group administration of standardized tests is practical and efficient for college students. It states "Group testing of college students is feasible and an economy of time especially in measuring speed and accuracy of association and memory", and recommends at least two trials of association and memory tests and both quantitative and qualitative scoring of memory results.
requirements: Standardized time limits and adapted group instructions, as the article notes individual and group method differences affect results
constraints: Some tests proved too easy for the majority and may become mainly tests of writing speed if the time limit is shortened; the Ink Blot test was least suited to group work

article_title: Associations between teacher and student mathematics, science, and literacy anxiety in fourth grade.
citation: McLean, L., Janssen, J., Espinoza, P., Lindstrom Johnson, S., & Jimenez, M. (2023). Associations Between Teacher and Student Mathematics, Science, and Literacy Anxiety in Fourth Grade. Journal of Educational Psychology. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000790
title: Direct emotional transmission between teachers and students, framed by Sociocultural, Appraisal, and Control-Value Theories
description: The article organizes its inquiry around emotional transmission, defined via Frenzel et al. as a process "whereby an emotion expressed by one participant in an interaction is induced in their interaction partner(s), either directly or indirectly." Sociocultural Theory positions the teacher as the "more knowledgeable other" whose affective cues students observe; Appraisal Theory holds that individuals use others' emotional, behavioral, and affective cues to interpret and respond to their environment; Control-Value Theory describes how students' achievement emotions are shaped by appraisals of teacher-initiated social antecedents such as instruction, feedback, and classroom values. The article uses this framework to hypothesize that teachers' content-area anxiety transmits to students, potentially creating a "snowball effect" of anxiety, and to argue the teacher is the highest-leverage point for intervention even if relations are bi-directional.
requirements: Requires that students notice and appraise teachers' affective cues, as the framework posits students interpret and respond to emotional, behavioral, and affective cues from others in their environment.
constraints: The article notes teachers' and students' emotions likely influence each other bi-directionally and/or reciprocally, and the study's correlational design speaks only to associations, not directionality of effects.
target_learning_goals: Students' content-area anxiety in mathematics, science, and English language arts
examples: The article illustrates the mechanism with a teacher who experiences mathematics anxiety displaying rushed/nervous speech patterns, posturing that turns them away from students, and concerned/nervous facial expressions, which students may appraise as mathematics being threatening or intimidating.

article_title: The problem of sense training.
citation: G. M. W. (1915). The Problem of Sense Training. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Vol. VI, No. 9. https://worldcat.org/search?q=Journal+of+Educational+Psychology+Volume+VI+1915
title: The doctrine of sense training as commonly interpreted
description: The editorial names and critiques the doctrine of sense training: the assumption, taken for granted in modern kindergarten practice, methods of educating the feeble-minded, and the Montessori fad, that devices for training the senses of young children are both necessary and valuable. The author argues that apparent sensory improvements reflect central factors like attention rather than training of the sense organs themselves, and calls for a careful critique of the doctrine.
requirements: The doctrine, to be meaningful as commonly interpreted, would require that presenting sense impressions improves sensory capacity in ways not attributable to central factors
constraints: The author's argument applies to sense training as commonly interpreted, while conceding that systematic instruction with concrete objects may in some instances produce noticeable, measurable improvement in young children's capacity to identify objects

examples: The editorial cites kindergarten practice, education of the feeble-minded, and the Montessori movement as practices that take the doctrine for granted

article_title: Supporting parents to support children: A U.K. randomized controlled trial testing a text message intervention to cultivate the home learning environment.
citation: O'Reilly, F., Loeb, S., Farrell, A., & Scerif, G. (2026). Supporting Parents to Support Children: A U.K. Randomized Controlled Trial Testing a Text Message Intervention to Cultivate the Home Learning Environment. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000973
title: Tips by Text: a 12-month FACT/TIP/GROWTH text message program for parents of reception children
description: Tips by Text is a 12-month text messaging intervention for parents of Reception students aged 4–5 years, adapted from a U.S. program and delivered through schools' existing texting platforms. Each week parents received three messages: a FACT message with information about the targeted skill, a TIP message with a practical activity using common household objects, and a GROWTH message reinforcing long-term benefits. The article reports that "The split of content was 50% language and early literacy, 25% socioemotional skill development, and 25% numeracy." Fidelity was high, with 81% of treatment parents receiving at least 150 of 165 messages.
requirements: Parents' telephone numbers shared by schools and entered into a texting platform; messages delivered on a fixed weekly schedule
constraints: Messages were sent in English, which the article notes may have reduced effectiveness for non-English-speaking parents; parents received no responses from the research team
target_learners: Parents of 4- to 5-year-old reception students in England
target_learning_goals: Children's language, literacy, numeracy, and socioemotional skills via enriched home learning interactions
examples: In the trial, messages were sent at 3.45 p.m. on Mondays and Wednesdays and 10.30 a.m. on Saturdays, timings chosen after two rounds of piloting with parents and teachers

article_title: Achievement emotions and academic achievement: Reciprocal relations and the moderating influence of academic buoyancy.
citation: Putwain, D. W., Wood, P., & Pekrun, R. (2021). Achievement emotions and academic achievement: Reciprocal relations and the moderating influence of academic buoyancy. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000671
title: Control-value theory of achievement emotions
description: Control-value theory (CVT) is a framework incorporating the antecedents and outcomes of achievement emotions. Appraisals of value (importance of activities/outcomes) and control (expectancies and attributions) are proximal antecedents of emotions; emotions influence cognitive and motivational processes underpinning performance, and performance outcomes reciprocally influence emotions in "a cycle of reciprocal causation". The present study tested CVT's reciprocal predictions for enjoyment, boredom, and anxiety in primary mathematics.
requirements: Requires measurement of both emotion appraisals (control and value) and achievement outcomes over time to test reciprocal relations
constraints: The article notes effects of emotions on learning may be complex, depending on interactions of mediating mechanisms with task demands
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement
academic emotional development
examples: The study tested CVT-predicted reciprocal relations between three classroom emotions and mathematics test performance over four waves in Year 5 students

article_title: Achievement emotions and academic achievement: Reciprocal relations and the moderating influence of academic buoyancy.
citation: Putwain, D. W., Wood, P., & Pekrun, R. (2021). Achievement emotions and academic achievement: Reciprocal relations and the moderating influence of academic buoyancy. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000671
title: Academic buoyancy as adaptive response to minor academic adversity
description: Academic buoyancy is "the ability to respond adaptively to the everyday challenges, setbacks, and pressures experienced by students during their studies", such as poor performance, dips in confidence, negative feedback, and test demands. It is distinguished from academic resilience, which concerns major adversities. The construct is theorized to buffer the detrimental impact of negative emotions on achievement; this study tested that buffering role with a mathematics-specific buoyancy measure in primary students.
requirements: Domain-specific measurement is recommended; the article notes relations with achievement are stronger when analyzed in a domain-specific fashion
constraints: Buoyancy's benefit for performance diminished at higher anxiety levels; it did not protect performance against anxiety at high levels
target_learning_goals: coping with everyday academic setbacks
mathematics achievement
examples: Buoyancy was measured at T3 with a four-item mathematics-specific adaptation of the Academic Buoyancy Scale

citation: Whipple, G. M. (1910). The effect of practise upon the range of visual attention and of visual apprehension. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://books.google.com/books?q=Whipple+effect+of+practise+range+of+visual+attention+apprehension
title: Eight-factor account of the conditions determining efficiency in quick visual apprehension
description: From a qualitative analysis of the apprehension data, the article proposes that efficiency in visual apprehension is conditioned upon eight factors: native capacity, degree of attention, type of material, ease of assimilation, obstruction or distraction, ideational type, voluntary restriction, and grouping. The article states that "apprehension is greatly facilitated by any scheme that permits of grouping the constituent elements in the field," calling grouping perhaps the most important single factor in practise-improvement after habituation.
requirements: Performance must be scored per material type (dots, pictures, drawings, nonsense syllables, poetry, objects) for the factors to be distinguished
constraints: The article states native capacity was believed unaffected by practise
The account derives from a qualitative analysis of three adult observers, not a quantitative test of the factors
target_learners: adult observers in laboratory perception tasks
target_learning_goals: quick visual perception and attentive observation
examples: Observers arbitrarily rearranged irregular dot groups into two to four groups of three to six dots, and split drawings into components recombined by analysis and synthesis
key_sources: Whipple, G. M. (1910). The effect of practise upon the range of visual attention and of visual apprehension. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://books.google.com/books?q=Whipple+effect+of+practise+range+of+visual+attention+apprehension

article_title: The effect of practice upon the range of visual attention and of visual apprehension.
citation: Whipple, G. M. (1910). The effect of practise upon the range of visual attention and of visual apprehension. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://books.google.com/books?q=Whipple+effect+of+practise+range+of+visual+attention+apprehension
title: Do not expect brief daily perception exercises to train a general capacity to attend
description: The article argues against classroom exercises, like Miss Aiken's, that claim to train concentration of attention through brief daily drills. Its experiments show practise effects on quick visual perception are negligible once habituation and grouping devices are removed, and individual differences are material-specific. It concludes these considerations "make it still more improbable that a series of classroom exercises, like Miss Aiken's, will train and develop general capacity to attend."
requirements: Any claim of attention training must be tested against material other than that used in the training exercises
constraints: The article concedes the negative outcome is not entirely conclusive: practise may not have been sufficiently long, and observers were adults rather than children
target_learners: school pupils and adult learners targeted by mind-training exercises
target_learning_goals: concentration of attention and quick visual perception
examples: Whipple replicated Aiken-style exercises under laboratory conditions with college students and adults and measured the extent and nature of the improvement
key_sources: Whipple, G. M. (1910). The effect of practise upon the range of visual attention and of visual apprehension. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://books.google.com/books?q=Whipple+effect+of+practise+range+of+visual+attention+apprehension

article_title: Educational psychology and college administrators.
citation: J. C. H. (1915). Editorials: Educational Psychology and College Administrators; The Lecturer's Illusion. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 6(2), 121-122.
title: The lecturer's illusion: a teacher's warm feeling of successful presentation is mistaken for evidence of learning
description: The editorial names and describes 'the lecturer's illusion': the lecturer feels satisfaction over the ease, clearness, correctness and economy of the presentation, and this subjective well-being is reinforced by students' hearty approval and absence of friction. The fallacy is that these signs of smooth delivery are taken as evidence that learning occurred, when lecturing supplies 'predigested intellectual food' rather than eliciting the pupil's own reaction. The article uses this account to explain why the information lecture persists from graduate school to kindergarten despite long-standing condemnation by educational economy.
requirements: The illusion operates where the teacher judges success by subjective ease and student approval rather than by evidence of pupil reaction or learning.
constraints: The article offers this as a psychological interpretation, not a tested result.
target_learners: pupils and students at all levels, from kindergarten to graduate school
target_learning_goals: genuine learning through the pupil's own reaction rather than passive reception of predigested information
examples: The editorial describes the elementary teacher who 'explains' the lesson because pupils lack the habit of reacting to the lesson itself, and the secondary mathematics teacher who 'prepares' the lesson because the text lacks the right point of view.
key_sources: J. C. H. (1915). Editorials: Educational Psychology and College Administrators; The Lecturer's Illusion. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 6(2), 121-122. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0063797

article_title: Educational psychology and college administrators.
citation: J. C. H. (1915). Editorials: Educational Psychology and College Administrators; The Lecturer's Illusion. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 6(2), 121-122.
title: Skillfully elicit pupils' reactions rather than lecture, because lecturing delivers predigested intellectual food
description: The editorial recommends replacing the information lecture with the skillful eliciting of pupils' reactions. It argues that lectures at every level are 'all of the same brand of predigested intellectual food', that lecturing persists because it is easy and satisfies the pupil's craving for authority and ready-made knowledge, and that the lecturer's sense of success is an illusion. The design implication is that instruction should require learners to react to the lesson itself rather than receive explanations.
requirements: Teachers must accept the harder work of eliciting pupil reactions, which the article contrasts with the ease of lecturing.
constraints: The article presents this as an argument from educational economy and psychological reasoning, not from experimental evidence.
target_learners: elementary, secondary, college and graduate students
target_learning_goals: active responding to lessons instead of passive reception of information
examples: The editorial contrasts lecturing with 'the skillful eliciting of a pupil's reaction' across school levels, from dictated zoology manuals to elementary lesson explanations.
key_sources: J. C. H. (1915). Editorials: Educational Psychology and College Administrators; The Lecturer's Illusion. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 6(2), 121-122. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0063797

article_title: Vocational interest profiles in secondary school: Accounting for multiplicity and exploring associations with future-oriented choices.
citation: Slot, E. M., Bronkhorst, L. H., Akkerman, S. F., & Wubbels, T. (2021). Vocational Interest Profiles in Secondary School: Accounting for Multiplicity and Exploring Associations With Future-Oriented Choices. Journal of Educational Psychology, 113(5), 1059–1071. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000475
title: Multiplicity of vocational interests: profiles as combinations of RIASEC domains rather than single dominant interests
description: This framework treats vocational interests as combinations across the six RIASEC domains (realistic, investigative, artistic, social, enterprising, conventional) rather than assuming one dominant interest per student. The article argues that "vocational interest assessment tools generally do not account for the possibility that students are interested in multiple vocational domains", which can challenge future-oriented decision-making. Latent profile analysis operationalizes this by identifying seven distinct profiles, spanning nondifferentiated (low, neutral, or broad) and differentiated (domain-dominant) structures.
requirements: Assessment of all six RIASEC interest domains so that combinations and profile structures can be identified
constraints: Studied among Dutch secondary school Grade 9 students facing early educational career decisions
target_learning_goals: vocational interest assessment
educational and career decision-making
key_sources: Slot, E. M., Bronkhorst, L. H., Akkerman, S. F., & Wubbels, T. (2021). Vocational Interest Profiles in Secondary School: Accounting for Multiplicity and Exploring Associations With Future-Oriented Choices. Journal of Educational Psychology, 113(5), 1059–1071. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000475

article_title: Vocational interest profiles in secondary school: Accounting for multiplicity and exploring associations with future-oriented choices.
citation: Slot, E. M., Bronkhorst, L. H., Akkerman, S. F., & Wubbels, T. (2021). Vocational Interest Profiles in Secondary School: Accounting for Multiplicity and Exploring Associations With Future-Oriented Choices. Journal of Educational Psychology, 113(5), 1059–1071. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000475
title: Vocational interest assessment in secondary school should account for students holding interests in multiple vocational domains
description: Because many secondary students show similar levels of interest across different vocational activities, interest assessment should capture multiplicity rather than force a single dominant domain. The article notes that "vocational interest assessment tools generally do not account for the possibility that students are interested in multiple vocational domains, potentially challenging students' future-oriented decisionmaking processes". Profile-based assessment (e.g., latent profile analysis over RIASEC scales) is the article's approach to this.
requirements: Interest measures covering multiple vocational domains so combinations can be detected
constraints: The article does not claim nondifferentiated profiles indicate uncertainty; it finds the opposite pattern is not necessary
target_learning_goals: accurate vocational interest assessment
informed educational career decisions
examples: A latent profile analysis on six RIASEC interests in 358 Grade 9 students identified seven profiles, of which 40.8% were nondifferentiated

article_title: A scale in ancient history.
citation: Sackett, L. W. (1922). A Scale in Ancient History. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu
title: Eight-test ancient-history recall scale with weighted score cards
description: A packet of eight ten-item tests covering who figures are noted for, naming men by role, historical significance of events, battle combatants and victors, approximate dates, civilizations' contributions, ethnic classification, and map locations. The article states "Four minutes were allowed to each of the eight tests thus bringing the whole series with the preliminary information and the supplementary comments well within the 45-minute period." Weighted score cards assign point values to the ideas present in answers, and Test VII items were eliminated from calculations because chance alone would give 33 1/3%.
requirements: Questions must meet with general approval from teachers of ancient history so every pupil feels a sense of familiarity with each item
Grading should be done under common standards, with directors coaching assistants on the score-card weightings
constraints: Test VIII had no score card devised and its returns were not yet employed in scaling
Test VII items were eliminated from the calculations because chance alone would give 33 1/3%
target_learning_goals: recall of definite facts in ancient history
prompt recognition of historical figures, events, dates, and contributions
examples: Test No. I asks what ten men including Hannibal, Khufu or Cheops, and Demosthenes are noted for
Test No. V asks approximate dates for events such as the Fall of Rome and the Battle of Marathon
key_sources: Sackett, L. W. (1922). A Scale in Ancient History. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu

article_title: A scale in ancient history.
citation: Sackett, L. W. (1922). A Scale in Ancient History. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu
title: Use scale points as a quantitative, not rigidly qualitative, measure of retention in a school subject
description: The article's scale-use method converts class averages per question into fractions of a perfect grade, multiplies each into the question's scale value, and sums the products into total scale points located on a linear scale via subtotals. The article states "Thus, the scale becomes a quantitative rather than a rigidly qualitative measure of ability in these particular aspects of ancient history," comparable with other scales measuring retention after training, and notes it can be made more qualitative by scaling each test separately.
requirements: Pupils take the original tests in whole or in part, work is graded on the basis of 10 per cent per question using the score card, and class averages are found for each question before multiplying into scale values
constraints: The scale measures ability only in these particular aspects of ancient history, and the qualitative and quantitative lapsing of information over time remains to be determined
target_learners: individual pupils and classes in ancient-history courses
target_learning_goals: measuring amount of retention in ancient history after instruction
examples: A class scale grade of 3.6 on question 10 of Test II yields .36 x 151 = 64 scale points; a total of 3200 points places the class between scale values 217 and 219
key_sources: Sackett, L. W. (1922). A Scale in Ancient History. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu

article_title: Elementary tests in psychology.
citation: Seashore, C. E. (1922). Elementary tests in psychology. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://archive.org
title: Elemental tests: the distinction between psycho-physic sensibility and the apperceptive use of a sense
description: Seashore proposes that a test is "elemental" when it is so simple and direct that no improvement can be made in the record by training, and that the record of such a test should not vary with age or phenomenal use of the sense. The framework distinguishes inborn sensory capacity (physiological threshold) from acquired skill in using a sense (cognitive threshold). The Iowa laboratory sought verification through two lines of experiment: measurement of the effect of extraordinary use of a sense (the blind) and prolonged training on a presumably elemental test.
requirements: Tests must be reduced to simple, direct impressions reportable by the most natural response, with no skill in action involved, to approximate a physiological rather than a cognitive threshold.
constraints: No test can be made absolute, since even the most elemental test involves some general power of observation acquired by training; a child must be old enough to apply himself to the task.
target_learning_goals: measuring inborn sensory capacity distinct from trained skill
examples: The six measurements on blind and seeing pupils, and the thirteen-observer training study on intensity of sound, were designed as verifications of this principle.
key_sources: Seashore, C. E. (1922). Elementary tests in psychology. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://archive.org

article_title: Elementary tests in psychology.
citation: Seashore, C. E. (1922). Elementary tests in psychology. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://archive.org
title: Before attributing a developmental trait to a subject, ascertain the test of capacity has been made elemental
description: Seashore draws a practical implication for educational psychology and mental testing: the findings "constitute a challenge to a large part of current systems of mental tests". Before attributing a developmental trait to a subject, the tester must ascertain that the measured variable is not an artifact of failing to make the test of capacity elemental, since a non-elemental test can reflect training, age-related apperceptive skill, or cognitive difficulty rather than native capacity.
requirements: Tests intended to measure capacity must be reduced to simple, direct impressions requiring no skill in action, so that training cannot improve the record.
constraints: The article states no test can be made absolute, because even the most elemental test involves some acquired power of observation.
target_learners: all subjects of mental and sensory testing, including school children
target_learning_goals: accurate measurement of capacity versus developmental or trained traits
examples: The Iowa laboratory's two experiment lines — comparing blind and seeing pupils, and prolonged training on intensity-of-sound discrimination — were undertaken to verify the principle before applying it to test design.
key_sources: Seashore, C. E. (1922). Elementary tests in psychology. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://archive.org

article_title: Measuring arithmetic: A psychometric approach to understanding formatting effects and domain specificity.
citation: Rhodes Katherine T., Branum-Martin Lee, Washington Julie A., Fuchs Lynn S. (2017). Measuring arithmetic: A psychometric approach to understanding formatting effects and domain specificity. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000189
title: Four competing theories of arithmetic cognition as measurement hypotheses (Abstract Code, Encoding Complex, Triple Code, Exact versus Approximate)
description: The article frames four leading theories of arithmetic cognition as competing, testable measurement hypotheses. Abstract Code Theory holds that a single abstract code represents all numeric information regardless of format, so "formatting exerts no effect on numeric processing." Encoding Complex Theory posits format-specific codes in an associative network relying on domain-general capacities. Triple Code Theory posits visual Arabic, verbal word frame, and analog magnitude representations determined by stimulus format, with Exact versus Approximate Calculations as its extension for calculation tasks. The study operationalizes each theory as a confirmatory factor model.
requirements: Measurement requires multitrait multimethod data: arithmetic measured across formats alongside language and executive attention measures, analyzed with confirmatory factor analysis.
constraints: The factor analytic framework cannot distinguish the abstract-code and encoding-complex single-factor models, which the authors note as a limitation.
target_learning_goals: arithmetic cognition and measurement of mathematical ability
examples: The study tested 11 models, presenting full results for the four theory-guided full measurement models plus a post-hoc hybrid model.
key_sources: Rhodes Katherine T., Branum-Martin Lee, Washington Julie A., Fuchs Lynn S. (2017). Measuring arithmetic: A psychometric approach to understanding formatting effects and domain specificity. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000189

article_title: Measuring arithmetic: A psychometric approach to understanding formatting effects and domain specificity.
citation: Rhodes Katherine T., Branum-Martin Lee, Washington Julie A., Fuchs Lynn S. (2017). Measuring arithmetic: A psychometric approach to understanding formatting effects and domain specificity. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000189
title: Arithmetic assessment and intervention should account for problem format and the role of executive attention and language, not treat all arithmetic scores as measures of one ability
description: Because formatting affects what arithmetic measures tap, the article argues that scores from differently formatted arithmetic items should not be interpreted interchangeably as indicators of one math ability. It concludes that "in addition to arithmetic-focused interventions, interventions targeting executive attention, language, and/or the interplay between them (i.e., internal speech during problem-solving) may be a promising avenues of mathematical problem-solving intervention." This principle follows from the finding that executive attention directly predicted all arithmetic outcomes while language contributed only to language-formatted items.
requirements: Assessment batteries must measure arithmetic in multiple formats alongside language and executive attention measures so that construct contributions can be separated.
constraints: The intervention implication is stated prospectively by the authors as promising, not tested in this study, which used only baseline data.
target_learning_goals: arithmetic problem-solving and valid measurement of mathematical ability
examples: The study assessed 1,314 third graders with 11 arithmetic measures spanning language-formatted word problems, Arabic numeral computation, and estimation tasks, plus language and executive attention batteries.
key_sources: Rhodes Katherine T., Branum-Martin Lee, Washington Julie A., Fuchs Lynn S. (2017). Measuring arithmetic: A psychometric approach to understanding formatting effects and domain specificity. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000189

article_title: The supernormal child.
citation: William Stern. (1910). The Supernormal Child. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://archive.org/search?query=Journal+of+Educational+Psychology
title: Supernormality as quantitatively superior capacities, divided into specifically and universally supernormal groups
description: Stern's taxonomy distinguishes supernormality from genius: it is "not something qualitatively sui generis, but the possession in quantitatively superior forms of capacities that are generally exhibited by individuals at large." The supernormal divide into two groups: the specifically supernormal, in whom one mental phase (musical, artistic, mathematical, technical, linguistic) is strongly developed while others may be merely normal, and the universally supernormal, whose general superiority appears across diverse mental activity. The pedagogy of the supernormal must cover all forms and apply different programs to different phases.
requirements: Criteria for drawing the line between normal and supernormal must be determined by future psychological research and pedagogical practice
constraints: A satisfactory psychological definition is impossible just now because scientific psychology is only beginning to study the problem; true geniuses are too rare for a special pedagogy
target_learning_goals: realization of exceptional talent and endowment
key_sources: William Stern. (1910). The Supernormal Child. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://archive.org/search?query=Journal+of+Educational+Psychology

article_title: The supernormal child.
citation: William Stern. (1910). The Supernormal Child. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://archive.org/search?query=Journal+of+Educational+Psychology
title: Support supernormal children through systematic pedagogical measures rather than fortuitous stipends and patronage
description: Stern argues that existing support for able poor children — free tuition, scholarships, patrons — is "how fortuitous, how unsystematic, it all is!" and compares it to disorganized almsgiving that social charity has already outgrown. He calls for simultaneous, systematic pedagogical measures for the supernormal, holding that measures applied to hundreds of gifted children may bear more abundant fruit than a ten-times-greater expenditure on thousands of subnormal children.
requirements: Systematic identification of talent, such as testing programs like Kerschensteiner's Munich drawing experiments, rather than reliance on chance discovery
constraints: The number of supernormal individuals is relatively small, and critics regard special provision for the able as a luxury while defectives' schools remain insufficient
target_learners: supernormal children, especially poor public-school children with conspicuous ability
target_learning_goals: full realization of exceptional capacities for the individual and for society
examples: Kerschensteiner assigned children whose exceptional drawing talent had gone unnoticed to art schools and arts and crafts schools, where they could develop their special gifts
key_sources: William Stern. (1910). The Supernormal Child. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://archive.org/search?query=Journal+of+Educational+Psychology

article_title: Artificial intelligence enhances children’s science learning from television shows.
citation: Ying Xu, Kunlei He, Julian Levine, Daniel Ritchie, Zexuan Pan, Andres Bustamante, and Mark Warschauer. (2023). Artificial Intelligence Enhances Children's Science Learning from Television Shows. https://osf.io/j7upd
title: AI-powered interactive Elinor Wonders Why videos with contingent dialogue
description: Interactive science videos built with PBS KIDS on two Elinor Wonders Why episodes (aerodynamics and reptile molting), in which "the main character, powered by artificial intelligence (AI), engaged in conversation with children by asking them questions and providing responsive feedback". They use "automatic speech recognition and intent detection, powered by Google's cloud services"; when the AI did not comprehend an answer, Elinor rephrased the question in simpler language, e.g. converting an open-ended question to multiple choice. Questions and feedback were based on the Next Generation Science Standards and vetted by PBS KIDS' science learning advisory board.
requirements: Automatic speech recognition and intent detection (Google cloud services) to classify children's utterances by semantic intent
Questions and feedback aligned to the Next Generation Science Standards and vetted by a science learning advisory board
constraints: Speech data may need to be shared with third-party services, raising privacy concerns; COPPA does not explicitly cover AI technologies
Speech recognition performance may vary with children's linguistic profiles per related phonemic-recognition research
target_learners: Children aged 3–7, predominantly bilingual English–Spanish, preschool and early elementary
target_learning_goals: Science concepts (aerodynamics, reptile molting)
Observation, prediction, pattern finding, and problem solving
examples: In the RCT, 79 children watched the interactive videos and outperformed the pseudo-interactive (n = 80) and non-interactive (n = 81) conditions on post-viewing science assessments

article_title: Mastery and performance goals predict epistemic and relational conflict regulation.
citation: Darnon, C., Muller, D., Schrager, S. M., Pannuzzo, N., & Butera, F. (2006). Mastery and Performance Goals Predict Epistemic and Relational Conflict Regulation. Journal of Educational Psychology, 98(4), 766–776. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-0663.98.4.766
title: Sociocognitive conflict regulation framework: epistemic versus relational modes
description: The article builds on the sociocognitive conflict framework, in which disagreement between collaborators carries both a cognitive component (doubt about the task content) and a social component (doubt about relative competence). It specifies two modes of regulation: "epistemic regulation, which is focused on task understanding and examination of the validity of each proposition", and relational regulation, which defends one's own competence by affirming one's point of view. The article contributes by linking these modes, previously inferred from influence outcomes, to mastery and performance goals and by showing they can be measured directly or via competence attributions.
requirements: A sociocognitive conflict situation in which a partner's disagreement is credible and plausible, as induced by the prerecorded incorrect but plausible partner answers in Study 2
constraints: Regulation here is not conflict resolution: regulating a conflict in either mode does not necessarily imply the conflict is terminated
Only the approach form of performance goals was examined
target_learning_goals: regulating disagreement over academic material to support understanding
examples: Study 2 induced real sociocognitive conflict by sending participants prerecorded incorrect but plausible partner answers in a computer-mediated cooperative task
Study 1 assessed regulation via direct self-report items such as trying to examine the conditions under which each point of view could help understanding
key_sources: Darnon, C., Muller, D., Schrager, S. M., Pannuzzo, N., & Butera, F. (2006). Mastery and Performance Goals Predict Epistemic and Relational Conflict Regulation. Journal of Educational Psychology, 98(4), 766–776. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-0663.98.4.766

article_title: Mastery and performance goals predict epistemic and relational conflict regulation.
citation: Darnon, C., Muller, D., Schrager, S. M., Pannuzzo, N., & Butera, F. (2006). Mastery and Performance Goals Predict Epistemic and Relational Conflict Regulation. Journal of Educational Psychology, 98(4), 766–776. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-0663.98.4.766
title: Orient students toward mastery goals to favor epistemic regulation of sociocognitive conflict
description: The article concludes that enhancing mastery goals is one way to orient students toward epistemic conflict regulation when they discuss conflicting viewpoints. Because "sociocognitive conflict leads to more positive outcomes when it is regulated in an epistemic way than when it is regulated in a relational way", and mastery goals predict epistemic regulation while performance goals predict relational regulation, the authors present mastery-goal enhancement as a lever for productive peer disagreement.
requirements: A learning situation involving genuine disagreement with a partner over academic material
constraints: Both studies were correlational, so a causal link between goals and regulation is not established
The research sample was mainly composed of women
target_learners: students working in pairs or groups on academic material
target_learning_goals: productive resolution of sociocognitive conflict during collaborative learning
examples: The authors state that these two studies show that one way to orient students to epistemic conflict regulation is to enhance mastery goals

article_title: The use of a composition scale.
citation: Truman L. Kelley; Ernest C. Witham. (1918). Communications and Discussions. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journal_of_Educational_Psychology
title: Determine that a test is highly reliable before using grade-overlapping figures to judge the adequacy of classification
description: Kelley's recommendation for interpreting overlapping between grade distributions: overlapping is evidence about classification only after the measuring instrument has been vetted. As the article puts it, "great overlapping is as much an indictment of the test as it is the adequacy of the classification, unless it has been determined that the test itself is highly reliable." The correction he derived is presented as easy to apply, requiring only a normal-distribution frequency table and the reliability coefficient.
requirements: A table of the frequencies in a normal distribution and the coefficient of reliability are the only new data required to apply the correction
target_learning_goals: accurate classification of pupil ability
examples: Kelley derived a correction to previously reported overlapping measures and applied it to the overlapping reported by F. J. Kelly, revising correct classification from 17 to 33 per cent
key_sources: Truman L. Kelley; Ernest C. Witham. (1918). Communications and Discussions. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journal_of_Educational_Psychology

article_title: The use of a composition scale.
citation: Truman L. Kelley; Ernest C. Witham. (1918). Communications and Discussions. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journal_of_Educational_Psychology
title: Nassau Supplement: a composition rating scale scored in steps 0–9, used alongside percentage ratings
description: The Nassau Supplement is a scale for rating the quality of written compositions, scored in steps from 0 to 9. In Witham's account, students first rated a composition "on the percentage basis" and, the following day, "rated the same composition by the Nassau Supplement", yielding frequency distributions across the ten scale steps that were compared with the ten percentage groups.
requirements: Raters must study the scale before applying it, as Witham's students did after a further study of the scale
target_learners: normal-school students learning tests and measurements
seventh-grade pupils whose compositions are rated
target_learning_goals: reliable evaluation of written composition quality
examples: A mixed class on Tests and Measurements of 16 students in a summer normal school rated a typewritten composition first on the percentage basis and then by the Nassau Supplement
key_sources: Truman L. Kelley; Ernest C. Witham. (1918). Communications and Discussions. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journal_of_Educational_Psychology

article_title: Promoting positive attitudes toward peers with disabilities: The role of information and imagined contact.
citation: Ginevra, M. C.; Vezzali, Loris; Camussi, E.; Capozza, D.; Nota, L.. (2021). Promoting positive attitudes toward peers with disabilities: The role of information and imagined contact. JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL PSYCHOLOGY. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000661
title: Combine positive information about disabilities with imagined contact exercises to strengthen improvement of children's attitudes toward peers with disabilities
description: The article's implication statement recommends providing positive information about disabilities together with imagination exercises. It reports that "The combination of the 2 interventions (information about disability and imagination) allows to get stronger effects." This principle supports pairing informational content about peers with sensory disability, intellectual disability, or behavioral difficulties with guided imagined interactions.
requirements: Provide positive information about the disabilities and strategies to encourage participation in educational and extracurricular activities.
constraints: Tested with typically developing elementary school children; effects on other populations are not established in this study.
target_learning_goals: positive attitudes toward peers with disabilities
intentions to engage in contact with peers with disabilities
examples: The study randomly assigned 142 typically developing children to a cognitive intervention, a behavioral intervention, a combined intervention, or a no-intervention control condition.

article_title: A tentative standardization of a completion test.
citation: Walter R. Miles and Julian E. Butterworth. (1912). A Tentative Standardization of a Completion Test. The Journal of Educational Psychology, pp. 329-336. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22A+Tentative+Standardization+of+a+Completion+Test%22
title: A standardization method for completion tests combining per-unit timing with subjects' introspective difficulty marking of elisions
description: The article develops a method for assigning differential credit to the blanks of a completion test. Subjects complete sentence units under timing, then "immediately underline the words which gave difficulty," marking especially hard words twice. The relative difficulty of each elision is "estimated by the frequency with which it was marked by all subjects as of one of the three degrees of difficulty," combined with unit times to produce per-elision values. The authors offer it as an approach "which may be applied to any test of this character."
requirements: Subjects must complete units one at a time and retrospectively mark three degrees of word difficulty after each sentence, with marking time measured and deducted from total test time.
constraints: The authors note it was originally intended to correlate difficulty with correctness but no way was found to determine time for absolutely correct work, so the two elements were kept separate.
target_learners: students or faculty at the State University of Iowa
target_learning_goals: accurate scoring of completion (cloze) test performance
examples: Twenty-five university subjects completed the test with telegraph-key signalling to a time-recording apparatus in an adjoining sound-proof room; values were then validated with 100 first-year normal school girls as a mass test.

article_title: A tentative standardization of a completion test.
citation: Walter R. Miles and Julian E. Butterworth. (1912). A Tentative Standardization of a Completion Test. The Journal of Educational Psychology, pp. 329-336. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22A+Tentative+Standardization+of+a+Completion+Test%22
title: Score completion-test blanks with difficulty-based weights rather than assuming every blank is of equal value
description: The article argues against the practice in which "each blank space is of equal value with every other blank." Because comparisons based on equal-difficulty grading are "open to serious question" when omissions differ in difficulty, the authors recommend using a table of individual elision values, holding that the more accurate results justify "the little additional labor that will be required to use or apply them."
requirements: A standardization study must first establish the per-unit time values and per-elision difficulty weights before unequal scoring can be applied.
constraints: If the test is expected to yield only a very rough measure, rating papers by the fractional part performed would, in the authors' words, do well enough.

article_title: The interplay of mastery and performance goals in social comparison: A multiple-goal perspective.
citation: Darnon, C., Dompnier, B., Gilliéron, O., & Butera, F. (2010). The Interplay of Mastery and Performance Goals in Social Comparison: A Multiple-Goal Perspective. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0018161
title: Multiple-goal perspective: achievement goals are pursued simultaneously and interact rather than operate in isolation
description: The multiple-goal perspective holds that learners pursue several achievement goals at once — mastery goals (the desire to acquire knowledge), performance-approach goals (the desire to outperform others), and performance-avoidance goals (not to be outperformed by others) — and that these goals interact in shaping outcomes. The article uses this perspective to motivate testing the interaction between mastery and performance-approach goals in predicting social comparison. Its results are discussed "in terms of the importance of multiple-goal pursuit in academic settings."
requirements: Educational settings must be considered as containing multiple co-occurring goals, since settings are rarely free from performance-approach goals even when mastery goals are promoted
target_learning_goals: understanding how achievement goal pursuit shapes learners' social comparison behavior
examples: Study 1 measured self-set mastery, performance-approach, and performance-avoidance goals together; Study 2 manipulated goal conditions to test their joint effect on social comparison interest.
key_sources: Darnon, C., Dompnier, B., Gilliéron, O., & Butera, F. (2010). The Interplay of Mastery and Performance Goals in Social Comparison: A Multiple-Goal Perspective. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0018161

article_title: The interplay of mastery and performance goals in social comparison: A multiple-goal perspective.
citation: Darnon, C., Dompnier, B., Gilliéron, O., & Butera, F. (2010). The Interplay of Mastery and Performance Goals in Social Comparison: A Multiple-Goal Perspective. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0018161
title: Design mastery-goal learning settings assuming performance-approach goals remain present and shape how mastery goals operate
description: Because "educational settings are rarely free from performance-approach goals, even when mastery goals are promoted", designers should anticipate that mastery goals will coexist with performance-approach goals and that the latter moderate the former's effects. The article shows that mastery goals lead to social comparison only when performance-approach goals are endorsed or induced, so designers should account for this interplay rather than treating goal conditions in isolation.
requirements: Awareness of learners' performance-approach goal endorsement when promoting mastery goals
constraints: Mastery goals predicted social comparison interest only in the performance-approach goal condition in Study 2
target_learning_goals: managing goal conditions when designing mastery-oriented learning environments
examples: Study 2 manipulated goal conditions and found mastery goals predicted interest in social comparison only in the performance-approach goal condition.

The construct links achievement goal theory to learners' informational behavior in academic settings.

article_title: Tests for Mental Alertness.
citation: L. W. Sackett. (1917). Tests for Mental Alertness. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://books.google.com/books?q=%22Tests+for+Mental+Alertness%22
title: Sackett's mental alertness tests (story recall plus story exercises) with Alertness Quotient scoring
description: A two-part paper-and-pencil battery: Test 1 is a short story the pupil reads and reproduces from memory in his own words, and Test 2 is a set of fifteen questions and exercises based on the story. Scoring divides accomplishment by time: "In each case the 'score' forms the numerator and the 'time' the denominator of a fraction while the resulting quotient is the index of ability in the test," designated the Alertness Quotient. Test 2's parts have printed differential weights (1, 4, 2, 5, 5, 8, 8, 6, 9, 5, 3, 4, 3, 5, 12), though these were not used in the reported study.
requirements: Administered by teachers furnished with full instructions, cautions, grading directions, A.Q. calculation blanks, and original papers inspected before scores were accepted
Future use should employ the weighted values in scoring Test 2
constraints: Reading difficulties preclude extensive use below the fourth grade
Test 2 parts are not of equal difficulty, and the seventh grade showed technical difficulties with the second test
target_learners: Elementary school pupils in grades four to seven, with suggested extension to high school and university
target_learning_goals: Measuring speed and accuracy of simple school-like reading, recall, and direction-following tasks (mental alertness)
examples: One large city tested 4961 pupils in grades four to seven after the writer briefed principals and demonstrated the administration; smaller cities were run by cooperating principals and superintendents
key_sources: L. W. Sackett. (1917). Tests for Mental Alertness. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://books.google.com/books?q=%22Tests+for+Mental+Alertness%22

article_title: Tests for Mental Alertness.
citation: L. W. Sackett. (1917). Tests for Mental Alertness. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://books.google.com/books?q=%22Tests+for+Mental+Alertness%22
title: Use quick mass-administered alertness tests to inform borderline promotion versus non-promotion decisions
description: The article recommends administering its short story-based tests to a whole class at once, because they are comparable with school work and can be given "as a mass test by an untrained and inexpert examiner." Because the Alertness Quotient combines accuracy and time, the resulting index is argued to reflect the qualities that govern promotion and retardation, and the author concludes that use for borderline cases between promotion and non-promotion is justified.
requirements: Tests carefully administered with the printed instructions and inspected scoring, so results reflect actual conditions of promotion and retardation
constraints: The diagnostic result is more reliable for subnormal than for supernormal pupils
Reading difficulties preclude extensive use below the fourth grade
target_learners: Elementary pupils in grades four to seven, especially borderline cases
target_learning_goals: Identifying retardation related to mental sluggishness and informing promotion decisions
examples: In each test the score formed the numerator and time the denominator, and teachers marked finishing times on pupils' papers as they passed through the room
key_sources: L. W. Sackett. (1917). Tests for Mental Alertness. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://books.google.com/books?q=%22Tests+for+Mental+Alertness%22

article_title: Measurements of the physical growth of two children.
citation: King, Irving. (1930). Measurements of the Physical Growth of Two Children. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journal/edu
title: Developmental period scheme dividing the growth charts into six motor and mental phases
description: The article organizes its growth charts by dividing the measurement span into numbered developmental periods: a pre-grasping period to the fourth month, development of grasping from the fourth to sixth month, movements preliminary to creeping, creeping and walking, a preliminary talking period from the seventeenth to twenty-fourth month, and rapid development of speech in the third year, with questioning, drawing and collecting interests in the fourth to sixth years. The article states "The following explanation of the periods into which the charts are divided should be here noted." The periods are marked on the charts with dotted vertical lines and slightly different age boundaries for the two children.
requirements: Longitudinal individual records taken at regular intervals from birth, with chart divisions anchored to observed motor and mental developments
constraints: Period boundaries differ between the two children (e.g., movements preliminary to creeping at 6th to 10th month for the first child, 6th to 8th month for the second)
target_learners: infants and young children from birth to six years
target_learning_goals: relating motor and speech development periods to physical growth patterns
examples: Charts I and II mark the periods with dotted vertical lines; the years are indicated by heavy lines

article_title: The persistence of preschool effects from early childhood through adolescence.
citation: Ansari, A. (2018). The persistence of preschool effects from early childhood through adolescence. Journal of Educational Psychology, 110(7). https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000255
title: Three developmental models of long-term preschool effects: persistence, convergence, and sleeper effects
description: The article organizes its inquiry around three conceptual models proposed to explain whether and why preschool programs may have long-term academic and psychosocial benefits: "models of persistence, convergence, and sleeper effects." Persistence holds that early skills lay foundations for later success; convergence holds that initial advantages dissipate as non-attendees catch up or attendees fade; sleeper effects hold that benefits emerge later without initial gains. The study tests these models against matched ECLS-K data.
requirements: The models are evaluated using longitudinal data following children from kindergarten through the end of middle school, with propensity-score-matched preschool and informal care samples
constraints: The article notes there was limited empirical evidence about when and why convergence occurs prior to this study, and that proximal indicators of preschool quality were not available in the ECLS-K: 1998 Cohort
target_learners: middle-class children attending preschool at age 4 in the United States
target_learning_goals: long-term academic achievement and psychosocial development following early childhood education
examples: The study operationalizes persistence as significant preschool paths through eighth grade, convergence as shrinking effect sizes between waves, and sleeper effects via three stated conditions on paths B1 and B2-B6
key_sources: Ansari, A. (2018). The persistence of preschool effects from early childhood through adolescence. Journal of Educational Psychology, 110(7). https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000255

citation: Herring, J. P. (1919). Derivation of a scale to measure abilities in scientific thinking. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journal/edu
title: Scientific Method Test scale of 33 problems administered to about 500 pupils in each of grades III–VIII
description: The Scientific Method Test is a series of 33 scientific-thinking problems whose scale values are derived in this article. The data came from administering the test to about 500 pupils in each of grades III to VIII, with printed numbers tested of 362, 482, 518, 449, 500 and 498 across grades III to VIII. The final scale (Table X) orders the problems by difficulty, with problem 1 at 1.952 P.E. and problem 32 at 6.415 P.E. above zero, column C carrying values to the nearest tenth of a P.E. multiplied by 10.
requirements: A normal distribution of the abilities studied
Approximately equal variability of large randomly selected groups of pupils
constraints: Per cents near 0% and 100% are distrusted and weighted low in the derivation
Only in the case of an infinite number of randomly selected measures would the curve correspond perfectly to its formula
target_learners: pupils in school grades III to VIII
target_learning_goals: abilities in scientific thinking
examples: Table II shows 50 of the 362 third-grade pupils scored 0 and the third-grade median score was 4.362 problems right
231 pupils of the third grade and 381 of the fourth solved problem 1

article_title: College marking systems.
citation: Kohl, C. C., & Hughes, P. (1911). Communications and discussions. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Journal+of+Educational+Psychology
title: Design instruction and student progress so that no student needs to fail
description: This principle holds that because a failure mark signals a student should not proceed without repeating work, instructors should not expect any fixed share of students to fail. Hughes argues that "under proper conditions no one would be invited to commence a term's work with the expectation that he must fail and repeat it," and that with attention to planning, admission, and progress-tracking it is often possible to insure that none shall fail.
requirements: Due attention to planning the work, admitting men to classes, and keeping track of their progress
constraints: The article concedes more men may be passed in some classes and fewer in others than believed should pass
target_learning_goals: successful completion of coursework without failure and repetition
examples: Hughes cites the Michigan Department of Literature, Science and the Arts, where failures remained below 3 per cent after adopting a standard ranking scale

article_title: College marking systems.
citation: Kohl, C. C., & Hughes, P. (1911). Communications and discussions. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Journal+of+Educational+Psychology
title: The distinction between ranking marks and passing marks
description: Hughes proposes that college marks divide into two fundamentally different kinds. Ranking marks (A through D) place students along a distribution and are meaningful only when the percentage admitted to each rank accords with a recognized standard; the failure mark instead indicates that "the student would better not proceed along a certain line of work without repeating the subject." The article calls this distinction fundamental and uses it to argue against prescribing a fixed percentage of failures.
requirements: A recognized standard for the percentage of students admitted to each ranking mark
constraints: The framework addresses college marking systems and does not prescribe how many students should fail
target_learning_goals: accurate interpretation and assignment of academic marks
examples: The suggested scale: A 10 per cent, B 15 to 20 per cent, C 40 to 50 per cent, D 15 to 20 per cent, with failure treated separately from the ranking scale

article_title: Top-performing math students in 82 countries: An integrative data analysis of gender differences in achievement, achievement profiles, and achievement motivation.
citation: Keller, L., Preckel, F., Eccles, J. S., & Brunner, M. (2021). Top-Performing Math Students in 82 Countries: An Integrative Data Analysis of Gender Differences in Achievement, Achievement Profiles, and Achievement Motivation. Journal of Educational Psychology. http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/edu0000685
title: Integrative data analysis of six PISA cycles with harmonized protocol and OSF-released materials
description: The article built a harmonized individual participant dataset from "six PISA cycles" (PISA 2000–2015, 82 countries, 113,864 top-performing math students defined as the top 5% in mathematics per country and cycle). The same analysis protocol was applied to each country-cycle, and results were integrated with meta-analytical random coefficient models. Protocols, R code, and additional materials are released: "Protocols can be accessed via the Open Science Framework (OSF; Soderberg, 2018) at https://osf.io/ych6q/", and the PISA databases "can be downloaded from https://www.oecd.org/pisa/pisaproducts/".

constraints: Students from Liechtenstein were excluded due to fewer than 30 top-5% students per cycle
In PISA 2000, mathematics scores were available for only 56% of students
Gender equality moderator data were incomplete and estimated via multilevel multiple imputation

examples: Country-specific cut-off values for the top 5% in mathematics per PISA cycle are reported in supplemental Table S4

article_title: A New Handbook on Sex Education.
citation: L. Z. (1921). New Publications. https://eric.ed.gov
title: Chapter structure of discussion topics, introductory statement, and question-answer pairs with source references
description: The review praises the organization of Galloway's sex-education handbook: each chapter opens with listed discussion topics, followed by an introductory statement and then brief specific question-and-answer items linked to source materials. The reviewer calls this organization noteworthy, making it a reusable lesson-level instructional pattern. It works by preparing learners with an orienting statement and then engaging them with specific questions anchored to readings.
requirements: Discussion topics must be listed at the start of each chapter, and questions must be paired with references to source materials.

character development

article_title: Research Problems Raised in Recent Issues of Educational Periodicals.
citation: Zirbes, L. (1922). Research problems raised in recent issues of educational periodicals. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 13(1), 1-6.
title: Zirbes's seven-category classification of educational research problems raised in periodicals
description: The article organizes the unsolved problems it assembles into seven headings: mental tests, curriculum studies, administration and supervision, educational test problems, learning studies, rating-scale problems, and the need for statistical devices and methods. Each category lists the problems with periodical and page references so researchers can find the original statements. The author reports that classification "was not seriously hampered by overlapping," and that counting references per heading yields relative frequencies of the grouped problems.

constraints: The search was confined to the three most recent (autumn 1921) issues of the listed periodicals, except as noted, so the taxonomy reflects a restricted body of literature
target_learners: educational researchers and graduate students in education
target_learning_goals: identifying urgent, unsolved problems for educational research
examples: Category II lists curriculum problems such as scientific determination of curricula in history and reconstruction of college curricula in terms of individual differences

article_title: Research Problems Raised in Recent Issues of Educational Periodicals.
citation: Zirbes, L. (1922). Research problems raised in recent issues of educational periodicals. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 13(1), 1-6.
title: Zirbes's periodical-search method for rescuing statements of unsolved research problems
description: The article describes a search procedure that reads recent issues of nine educational periodicals and extracts statements of unsolved research problems, which are usually mentioned incidentally in connection with practical situations. Problems are recorded with periodical number and page references "so that those who are in a position to conduct research may readily find the original statement of any problem in its setting," and original phrasing is retained wherever possible. The article is presented as one of a series intended to define research trends and hasten solutions by re-statement and accessibility.

constraints: The search was limited to autumn 1921 issues because several publications lack summer numbers, and the author argues several carefully limited searches serve better than one more inclusive investigation

article_title: The meetings at Mobile, Alabama, February 22-25, 1911.

title: Kansas Silent Reading Tests (Kelly), a three-test objective silent reading series with weighted exercises
description: A silent reading test series devised by F. J. Kelly and distributed by the Bureau of Educational Measurements and Standards. It comprises "Three tests" for grade spans 3-5, 6-8 and 9-12, each consisting of sixteen exercises scored in five minutes. Each exercise has a value proportional to the average time required to do it correctly, and the tests are objective in that "there is little opportunity for differences of opinion in marking the test papers". citation: Kim Young-Suk Grace, Wolters Alissa, Mercado Janet, & Quinn Jamie. (2022). Crosslinguistic Transfer of Higher Order Cognitive Skills and Their Roles in Writing for English-Spanish Dual Language Learners. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000516
title: Linguistic interdependence hypothesis extended to higher order cognitive skills as underlying cross-language competence
description: The article works with the linguistic interdependence hypothesis (Cummins, 1979), which holds that L2 competence is partially "a function of the type of competence already developed in L1". It notes the hypothesis left the underlying cognitive competences "a black box" and extends the candidate set to higher order cognitive skills. Its bifactor finding — a general factor common across languages plus language-specific factors — is read as evidence that higher order cognitive skills are part of the cross-language "underlying cognitive/academic language proficiency" and likely transfer between languages.
requirements: The article states future work with an experimental design is needed to confirm cross-linguistic transfer of higher order cognitive skills
constraints: Findings are limited to Spanish-English dual language learners in primary grades in the US; the transfer interpretation is correlational, not causal

description: The article describes the direct and indirect effects model of writing (DIEW), in which writing processes draw on oral language skills, executive function, background knowledge, social-emotional factors, and transcription skills. DIEW "posits that higher order cognitive skills and regulation such as reasoning, inferencing, perspective taking, and monitoring are important to compositional quality, particularly for establishing coherence". Inferencing supports understanding relations among ideas, perspective taking helps writers anticipate readers' interpretations, and monitoring supports detecting and repairing breakdowns in coherence. The study's findings are framed as corroborating DIEW for dual language learners.

title: Formal training in visualizing and visual reproduction has limited general value; specific practice is demanded for best results and becomes quickly effective.
description: The article concludes that "the value of formal training of our kind had been greatly overestimated", because little ability is gained by continuing practice beyond a relatively short time and gains are specific to identical ability-conditioning factors. It recommends specific practice targeted at the exact material and conditions rather than general formal visualizing exercises.

title: Orthographic facilitation account of Set for Variability: a phonological clean-up process augmented by phonology-to-orthography knowledge
description: The article proposes that the SfV task taps a phonologically-based "clean-up" process, analogous to phonological cleanup units in connectionist reading models, that allows children to disambiguate the mismatch between a decoded form and the actual lexical pronunciation. It further hypothesizes orthographic facilitation: children may use phonology-to-orthography associations to translate a mispronounced spoken word into an orthographic form and access the correct phonological form, a process rooted in the orthographic skeleton hypothesis. The account predicts facilitation only for children with sufficient decoding skill and for items with greater phonology-orthography consistency.

Word reading development

title: Point-hour ratio: a weighted quantitative index of college academic standing
description: The point-hour ratio is the academic-standing measure Bridges constructed from registrar grade records. article_title: Practice and transference in normal and feeble-minded children.
citation: Woodrow, H. (1915). Practice and transference in normal and feeble-minded children. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=%22Practice+and+Transference+in+Normal+and+Feeble-Minded+Children%22
title: Incapacity for mental development reflects inability to grow rather than inability to learn
description: The author proposes that the capacity to gain from practice (learning) is separable from the capacity for mental development (growth). The practice data showing equal improvement in feeble-minded and normal children of the same mental age suggest that "it is not inability to learn which characterizes incapacity for mental development, but inability to grow, and that the two are quite distinguishable." The author argues that prejudice against admitting equal practice effects stems from wrongly identifying mental development capacity with ability to learn.
requirements: Requires comparing feeble-minded children with normal children of the same mental age and initial ability, not the same chronological age
constraints: The author notes the conclusion is based on one type of work and small groups, and that the matter of the spread of training remains to be considered in a subsequent paper
target_learners: normal children of the same mental age
target_learning_goals: practice effects on perceptual-motor sorting tasks
capacity for improvement with repetition
examples: The four-group experiment compared practice curves and found equal improvement, leading the author to distinguish learning from growth as separate capacities

Each trial involves sorting 250 wads within 4 minutes, using one hand, picking up one wad at a time. The box order is changed every second day to prevent the task from becoming too automatic. Scoring is the total number correctly sorted.

title: Compare learners of different ability groups at the same mental age, not the same chronological age, to isolate differences in learning capacity
description: The author argues that comparing feeble-minded children with normal children of the same chronological age reveals only differences attributable to developmental level, not to feeble-mindedness itself. Characteristics such as inability to learn, lack of attention, and incapacity for sustained effort "characterize a six-year-old child compared with a ten-year-old child." Only by matching on mental age and initial ability can genuine differences in learning capacity be detected, which is how the four groups in this study were constructed.

title: Town's four-section adult test series organized around three fundamental mental processes and their volitional expression
description: For examining adult subjects, the author uses a series of selected tests designed to give an approximately complete mental analysis. It is 'arranged in four sections in accordance with the recognition of three fundamental mental processes—sensation, reproductive memory, and apperception—and their final expression in volitional movements.' Each section is extensively subdivided, each subdivision carrying one or more tests. The design allows tests calling on the same mental processes but requiring less mental content to be substituted when necessary.
requirements: Subdivision must permit substitution of tests calling on the same mental processes but requiring less mental content when necessary.
constraints: Described for the examination of adult subjects in clinical appraisal.

target_learning_goals: approximately complete mental analysis of individual adults

article_title: The murky distinction between self-concept and self-efficacy: Beware of lurking jingle-jangle fallacies.
citation: Marsh, H. W., Pekrun, R., Parker, P. D., Murayama, K., Guo, J., Dicke, T. and Arens, A. K. (2019). The murky distinction between self-concept and self-efficacy: beware of lurking jingle-jangle fallacies. Journal of Educational Psychology, 111 (2). pp. 331-353. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000281
title: Jingle-jangle fallacies as a construct-validation framework for positive self-belief measures
description: The article re-introduces Kelley's classic jingle-jangle fallacies as a construct-validation framework: a jingle fallacy occurs when 'two scales with similar names might measure different constructs', and a jangle fallacy when 'apparently dissimilar labels might measure similar constructs'. The framework prescribes testing convergent and discriminant validity with CFA, SEM, and multitrait-multimethod logic, using frame-of-reference effects and longitudinal prediction of outcomes as validation criteria. The authors apply it to five math self-belief measures.
requirements: Construct validity studies comparing multiple candidate measures in a single factor analysis are needed, because a scale loading on one factor alone does not test discriminant validity against other constructs
constraints: Scale labels alone are not sufficient evidence of how a scale relates to other constructs
target_learning_goals: academic self-beliefs and motivation in mathematics
examples: The authors classify five math self-belief measures a priori as self-concept-like or self-efficacy-like and test that classification empirically
