title: Internal/external frame-of-reference (I/E) model of academic self-concept formation
description: The I/E model explains why verbal and math self-concepts are nearly uncorrelated even though verbal and math achievements are substantially correlated: self-concepts form relative to an external social comparison with other students and an internal dimensional comparison across one's own domains. Its 'key theoretical prediction is that the cross-paths leading from achievement in one domain to ASCs in a different (non-matching) domain (e.g., verbal achievement to math self-concept) are negative'. The article cites meta-analytic support (r = .10 for math-verbal self-concepts; cross-path β = −.27) and tests whether the model extends to other self-belief constructs.
requirements: Measures of achievement in at least two school subjects plus domain-specific self-belief measures, analyzed with path models
constraints: The model as originally developed concerns self-concept measures; the article predicts it does not apply to pure self-efficacy items
target_learning_goals: formation of academic self-concept across school subjects
examples: Meta-analytic path analysis cited in the article: math achievement to math self-concept β = .61; verbal achievement to math self-concept β = −.27

title: Big-fish-little-pond effect (BFLPE): social comparison effects of school-average achievement on self-concept
description: The BFLPE posits that students form academic self-concepts by comparing their abilities with classmates'. As the article states, 'students in schools that have a high school-average achievement will have lower ASCs than will equally able students in schools where the school-average ability is not high'. The article reviews extensive cross-national support and negative effects on aspirations, grades, and later attendance, and tests whether the effect extends to self-efficacy-like measures.
requirements: School-average achievement as a contextual predictor and individual-level self-belief measures analyzed in multilevel or contextual-effect models
constraints: The article predicts the BFLPE is attenuated or eliminated for pure self-efficacy responses
target_learning_goals: academic self-concept and educational aspiration outcomes
examples: PISA-based reviews cited in the article found negative school-average-achievement effects on academic self-concept in 122 of 123 country samples

citation: Marsh, H. W., Pekrun, R., Parker, P. D., Murayama, K., Guo, J., Dicke, T. and Arens, A. K. (2019). The murky distinction between self-concept and self-efficacy: beware of lurking jingle-jangle fallacies. Journal of Educational Psychology, 111 (2). pp. 331-353. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000281
title: Three-part theoretical distinction between self-concept and self-efficacy (prospective, descriptive-evaluative, frame-of-reference)
description: The article proposes three characteristics distinguishing self-efficacy from self-concept. First, self-efficacy is prospective and task-specific ('what I can do') whereas self-concept rests on past accomplishments. Second, 'appropriately constructed self-efficacy responses are designed to be purely descriptive, whereas self-concept responses are both descriptive and evaluative', with self-concept incorporating worthiness and social comparison. Third, negative frame-of-reference effects (BFLPE and I/E) should be largely eliminated in pure self-efficacy items that contain their own referent. The authors argue against globality and content specificity as useful distinguishing features.
requirements: Distinguishing features hold only for appropriately constructed pure self-efficacy items with an explicit criterion of successful performance
constraints: The distinction depends more on item wording than on construct labels; some generalized self-efficacy measures are indistinguishable from self-concept
target_learning_goals: measurement and interpretation of math self-beliefs
examples: The article cites experimental work showing that more purely worded can-do self-efficacy items reduced predictive validity compared with items conflating capability and motivation

title: A priori classification of five math self-belief constructs into self-concept-like and self-efficacy-like categories
description: This classification pattern sorts self-belief measures by item construction rather than by label: whether items provide 'a specific description of a referent against which to judge competence'. The article states it 'classify a priori the five math self-belief constructs ... into two categories: three self-concept-like constructs (math self-concept, outcome expectancy, and generalized math self-efficacy) and two self-efficacy-like constructs', namely test-related and functional math self-efficacy. The classification is then validated against factor structure, frame-of-reference effects, and outcome prediction.
requirements: Item wording must be inspected for an explicit referent criterion before assigning a measure to either category
constraints: The classification is a priori and validated empirically; the article treats test-related and functional self-efficacy as not fully clear-cut in practice

examples: Test-related self-efficacy items asked 'How confident are you that you can solve this math problem?' about items administered prior to the test; functional items asked about everyday tasks such as working out a discounted price

title: PALMA longitudinal dataset of math achievement and self-beliefs in Bavarian secondary schools
description: PALMA (Project for the Analysis of Learning and Achievement in Mathematics) is the article's secondary dataset, 'a representative sample of 3,350 students from math classes in 43 German schools' with six measurement waves (Years 5-10) plus Year 4 primary-school grades. Students (N = 3,530; 50% girls; mean age = 11.7 in Year 5) were tracked into Gymnasium, Realschule, or Hauptschule, and surveys were anonymized with a 91.8% parental acceptance rate. The study uses five math self-belief measures, standardized math tests, and school grades.

constraints: Data following Year 9 are no longer representative regarding ability and achievement tracks because compulsory education ends after Year 9 in Germany

title: Build pure self-efficacy items so the frame of reference and context are contained in the item itself
description: The article's design recommendation for self-belief instrumentation is that self-efficacy items should supply their own explicit criterion: 'if the appropriate frame of reference and context are fully contained in the self-efficacy item itself, then social and dimensional comparison effects should be substantially attenuated'. Operationally this means showing students example tasks (test-like or everyday functional problems) and asking for confidence in accomplishing them, with a stated standard of successful performance, rather than asking generalized evaluations of performing well.

citation: Gilbert, J. P. (1909). An experiment on methods of teaching zoology (preliminary report). The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journal/edu
title: Parallel-groups comparison of matched class sections as a method for investigating questions of teaching method
description: The article pilots a classroom-experiment design in which two sections of the same course, matched on sex, age, environment and intended occupation, are taught by different approaches with the same teacher, laboratory, texts and examinations. The author writes that "[t]he method of conducting the experiment, by the use of parallel groups ... is comparatively new, and should prove of service in questions of method of teaching", and the summary judges it "promises to yield valuable results" if refined through repeated tests.

Careful study and refinement of technique through repeated tests, including control of the experimenter's personal equation

target_learning_goals: relative merits of pure-science versus applied-science approaches to secondary-school science instruction
examples: Two beginners' zoology sections of 17 and 15 students in the Academy of the University of Illinois, first semester 1909-10, one taught with cultural/disciplinary emphases and one with economic emphases on the same topics, compared on examination grades, semester grades, an experimentation test, and interest.

article_title: Supplemental Material for Important Text Characteristics for Early-Grades Text Complexity
citation: J. Fitzgerald et al. (2014). Important Text Characteristics for Early-Grades Text Complexity. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0037289
title: Multiple-perspective measurement of early-grades text complexity at the intersection of texts, readers, and tasks
description: The article defines text complexity not as an intrinsic text property but relationally: "Because text complexity was defined at the intersection of printed texts with students reading them for particular purposes and doing particular tasks, a multiple-perspective measure of text complexity was created using student responses during a reading task and teachers’ ordering of texts according to complexity." Two Rasch logit scales (student maze responses, teacher comparative judgments) are linked by linear equating and transformed to a 0–100 developmental scale. This framework grounds the study's outcome measure for identifying important text characteristics.
requirements: Both student response data from a reading task and teacher complexity orderings of the same texts are needed before equating onto a single scale
constraints: The resulting 0–100 scale was developed for first- and second-grade readers and early-grades texts, with scores ranging from 0 to 100
target_learning_goals: Reading development and matching text difficulty to early readers
examples: 1,258 students completed maze tasks on 89 texts while 90 teachers compared digitized text pairs side by side; the two logit scales were equated and linearly transformed to a 0–100 scale
key_sources: J. Fitzgerald et al. (2014). Important Text Characteristics for Early-Grades Text Complexity. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0037289

article_title: Supplemental Material for Important Text Characteristics for Early-Grades Text Complexity
citation: J. Fitzgerald et al. (2014). Important Text Characteristics for Early-Grades Text Complexity. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0037289
title: Taxonomy of early-grades text characteristics organized by linguistic level from sounds to text density
description: Table S1 organizes quantifiable text characteristics by linguistic level: sounds in words (number of phonemes, phonemic Levenshtein distance, internal phonemic predictability), word structure (decoding demand, orthographic Levenshtein distance, syllables, sight words), word meaning (age of acquisition, abstractness, word rareness), within-sentence/syntax (sentence length, grammar link type, distance to verb, link distance), discourse (linear edit distance, word overlap, cohesion triggers, type-token ratio, phrase diversity, edit distance, Cartesian word overlap), text density (information load), and non-compressibility (compression ratio). Each characteristic has a definition, a source, a possible score range with a complexity interpretation, and multiple variable operationalizations. The taxonomy structures which characteristics were tested as predictors of text complexity.
requirements: Each characteristic must be operationalized computationally from the text (e.g., via the MRC Psycholinguistic Database, CMU Pronouncing Dictionary, or researcher computer coding)
constraints: Score ranges are specific to this study's texts, e.g., linear edit distance ran "0 (if all sentences are identical or there is only one sentence; lots of redundancy, less complex) to approximately 110 in our study"
target_learning_goals: Identifying which text features make early-reading texts more or less complex
examples: Abstractness scored 0–700 from the Paivio index; information load exemplified by comparing a highly redundant text scoring .28 with a denser text scoring .58

article_title: Supplemental Material for Important Text Characteristics for Early-Grades Text Complexity
citation: J. Fitzgerald et al. (2014). Important Text Characteristics for Early-Grades Text Complexity. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0037289
title: Rationale for random forest regression over linear regression when identifying important text characteristics
description: Supplemental Material 4 gives six reasons random forest regression suits text-complexity analysis: it is nonparametric with no distributional assumptions, accommodates very large numbers of variables and higher-order interactions, assumes no fixed functional form, yields Importance values ("the amount of increased error in the model when that variable is prevented from influencing the outcome measure") rather than significance tests, averages hundreds to thousands of decision trees to reduce overfit, and validates on hold-out data. The authors argue these properties matter because text-characteristic distributions in early-grades texts are unknown and characteristics may interact.
requirements: A validation phase with previously unseen data is used to test model predictive power
constraints: Importance values do not carry probability values; variables with higher Importance values often are involved in interactions with other variables, so importance is not a clean main-effect estimate
target_learning_goals: Determining most-important text characteristics while acknowledging potential interactions
examples: The authors contrast linear regression's required homoscedasticity with random forest's freedom from distributional assumptions about data or population

citation: J. Fitzgerald et al. (2014). Important Text Characteristics for Early-Grades Text Complexity. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0037289
title: Corpus of 350 early-grades texts used for complexity measurement and prediction
description: The study's material base is a set of 350 early-grades texts, stratified by six categories and publisher-designated difficulty level for sampling. The 350 texts were digitized (including images) for teacher comparison, all 350 were assigned teacher-judgment logit scores and 0–100 complexity measures, and a random stratified sample of 90 texts (89 analyzed) was read by students. Text characteristics were computer- operationalized for these texts as predictors on the text-complexity outcome measure.
requirements: Texts must be digitizable, including images, for side-by-side computer-screen comparison by teachers
constraints: Student maze testing sampled only a subset of 90 texts from the 350, so student-based logits exist for fewer texts than teacher-based logits
target_learning_goals: Measuring and predicting early-reader text-complexity level
examples: A random sample of 90 texts was selected stratified by the six categories and by publisher-designated difficulty level; one passage was later rejected due to a printing error

article_title: The limits set to educational achievement by limited intelligence.
citation: Cobb, Margaret V. (1922). The Limits Set to Educational Achievement by Limited Intelligence. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Vol. XIII, No. 8. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=The+Limits+Set+to+Educational+Achievement+by+Limited+Intelligence
title: Conversion table relating median Army Alpha scores to median Stanford-Binet mental ages
description: The article builds a working table (Table III) pairing median Army Alpha scores from 175 down to 10 with median mental ages from 20-6 down to 9-6, so that its high school figures can be "expressed, so far as possible, both as Alpha scores, and in terms of the Stanford-Binet Scale." The table was made up after a study of the Army, Kohs-Proctor, Kansas State Normal School, and Doll norms, and the authors state it is far from being considered final. Examples of the pairings include Alpha 175 with MA 20-6, Alpha 130 with MA 17-6, and Alpha 65 with MA 14-6.
requirements: Relies on the Army, Kohs-Proctor, Kansas State Normal School and Doll norms from which the median pairings were compiled
constraints: The authors state the table, though used throughout the study, is far from being considered final
target_learners: high school pupils assessed with Army Alpha or Stanford-Binet measures
target_learning_goals: estimating the mental-age equivalent of Army Alpha scores for educational guidance and placement decisions
examples: The study uses the table to translate freshman and senior Alpha medians into mental ages, e.g. the freshman median of the total group corresponds to MA 15-3

article_title: Morphology in reading comprehension among school-aged readers of English: A synthesis and meta-analytic structural equation modeling study.
citation: Zhang, D., Ke, S. (E.), & Mo, Y. (2023). Morphology in Reading Comprehension Among School-Aged Readers of English: A Synthesis and Meta-Analytic Structural Equation Modeling Study. Journal of Educational Psychology, 115(5), 683–699. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000797
title: Direct and Indirect Routes Framework of Morphological Awareness to Reading Comprehension
description: The article proposes a theory-driven path model (Figure 1) in which MA influences reading comprehension through one direct route and two indirect routes. Path 1 is "MA → Word Reading → Reading Comprehension", grounded in the lexical quality hypothesis and the binder-of-representations account. Path 2 is "MA → Vocabulary Knowledge → Reading Comprehension", grounded in morphological problem-solving and meaning inference. Paths 3a/3b represent a contingent direct route where MA supports in-situ lexical problem-solving and syntactic parsing during reading.
requirements: Studies must measure MA, word reading, vocabulary knowledge, and reading comprehension to test the full path model
constraints: The model was tested only in English, a deep orthography where morphology offers "islands of regularity"
The syntactic aspect (Path 3b) is noted as "the least studied yet can play a role that should not be ignored"
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension
Word reading
Vocabulary knowledge
examples: The MASEM study fitted this model to a pooled correlation matrix from 107 effect sizes (N = 21,818) and found very good model fits (CFI = 0.994, RMSEA = 0.039)
key_sources: Zhang, D., Ke, S. (E.), & Mo, Y. (2023). Morphology in Reading Comprehension Among School-Aged Readers of English: A Synthesis and Meta-Analytic Structural Equation Modeling Study. Journal of Educational Psychology, 115(5), 683–699. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000797

article_title: Morphology in reading comprehension among school-aged readers of English: A synthesis and meta-analytic structural equation modeling study.
citation: Zhang, D., Ke, S. (E.), & Mo, Y. (2023). Morphology in Reading Comprehension Among School-Aged Readers of English: A Synthesis and Meta-Analytic Structural Equation Modeling Study. Journal of Educational Psychology, 115(5), 683–699. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000797
title: Morphological instruction should include a strong meaning focus, especially for bilingual and older school-aged readers
description: The authors recommend that morphological instruction emphasize meaning-oriented aspects of morphology (morphological problem-solving, meaning inference) rather than only code/form-based decoding. This is because the vocabulary-mediated route (Path 2) was the larger indirect effect in the whole sample and grew stronger with age, and because bilingual readers rely more on vocabulary than on word reading. As stated in the implications: "morphological instruction may need to be differentiated and responsive to children's language status and stage of schooling."
requirements: Instruction should target the specific routes (chunking for decoding, morphological problem-solving for meaning) that are developmentally most relevant to the learner group
constraints: The recommendation is based on correlational MASEM findings, not experimental intervention data
Existing morphological interventions have sometimes shown very small or non-significant effects on reading comprehension, possibly reflecting a lack of direct-effect focus
target_learners: Older school-aged readers (upper elementary and middle/high school)
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension
Vocabulary knowledge
examples: The study found that the indirect effect via vocabulary knowledge (β = .190) exceeded that via word reading (β = .140), and that bilinguals showed a more salient reliance on vocabulary than on word reading for comprehension

article_title: Dimensional comparison effects on (gendered) educational choices.
citation: Jansen, M., Becker, M., & Neumann, M. (2020). Dimensional Comparison Effects on (Gendered) Educational Choices. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 113(2), 330-350. https://nbn-resolving.org/urn:nbn:de:0111-pedocs-220459
title: Dimensional comparison theory and the internal/external frame of reference model
description: Dimensional comparison theory (DCT) holds that "these beliefs are themselves affected by students comparing their ability across different domains", so students with similar achievement in one domain can hold different self-concepts depending on achievement in other domains. The classic operationalization is the internal/external frame of reference (I/E) model: "After controlling for the positive effect of achievement on self-concept in the same domain... dimensional comparison effects can be observed as a negative effect of achievement on self-concept across domains". This study tests DCT within an expectancy-value framework, modeling cross-domain paths from achievement, self-concept, and value to course choices and STEM intentions.
requirements: Path modeling with achievement and outcome measures in at least two domains (here mathematics and German), with within-domain effects controlled when estimating cross-domain effects
constraints: Effects here estimated from observational longitudinal data on academic-track Berlin students choosing between advanced mathematics and German courses; no causal manipulation of comparisons
target_learners: Upper-secondary academic-track students approaching course and university-major choices
target_learning_goals: Educational choice behavior, domain-specific academic self-concept, domain-specific value, STEM study intentions
examples: The article estimated a full SEM with within- and cross-domain paths from gender to achievement (grades and test-scores) to self-concept and value to advanced course choice to STEM study intentions, and found the model with cross-domain paths fit better (AIC/BIC) than a model without them
key_sources: Jansen, M., Becker, M., & Neumann, M. (2020). Dimensional Comparison Effects on (Gendered) Educational Choices. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 113(2), 330-350. https://nbn-resolving.org/urn:nbn:de:0111-pedocs-220459

article_title: Parental math input is not uniformly beneficial for young children: The moderating role of inhibitory control.
citation: Silver, A. M., Elliott, L., & Libertus, M. E. (2022). Parental math input is not uniformly beneficial for young children: The moderating role of inhibitory control. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000679
title: Opportunity-Propensity framework extended: opportunity and propensity factors interact to shape children's achievement
description: The Opportunity-Propensity framework explains children's development by the learning opportunities provided in the environment and children's propensity to learn, including antecedent factors like socioeconomic status. This article notes the framework "has typically employed mediational path modeling" treating opportunity and propensity as independent predictors, and extends it by showing the two interact: children's inhibitory control (propensity) determines whether parental number talk (opportunity) relates to math achievement. The authors state that "opportunities and propensities interact to shape children's performance rather than independently predicting math achievement."
requirements: Requires measuring both an environmental opportunity factor and a child-level propensity factor in the same sample, and testing their interaction rather than only main effects.
constraints: Evidence in this article is concurrent and correlational, drawn from a predominantly White, highly educated sample, so the authors caution the findings "may not extend to other populations in other contexts" and causal conclusions cannot be drawn.
target_learning_goals: Early math achievement
examples: Regressing TEMA-3 math scores on parent number talk, child inhibitory control, and their interaction while controlling for overall talk, parent math achievement, vocabulary, age, and gender.
key_sources: Silver, A. M., Elliott, L., & Libertus, M. E. (2022). Parental math input is not uniformly beneficial for young children: The moderating role of inhibitory control. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000679

article_title: Individual differences in addition strategy choice: A psychometric evaluation.
citation: Rhodes, K. T., Lukowski, S., Branum-Martin, L., Opfer, J., Geary, D. C., & Petrill, S. A. (2018). Individual Differences in Addition Strategy Choice: A Psychometric Evaluation. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11360214/
title: Explanatory Item Response Theory (EIRT) as a psychometric framework for jointly estimating item and person effects on problem solving
description: EIRT is described as "a special name given to models of multilevel, categorical responses, in which latent estimates are generated for both item and person parameters and explanatory variables can be modeled as predictors of responses across levels of analysis". It combines experimental design with observational measurement to yield explanatory measurement. The article maps SCM postulates onto crossclassified, mixed-effects, and bivariate EIRT specifications, using random intercepts and slopes for items and persons in adolescent addition data.
requirements: Responses must be crossclassified in items and persons; models are estimated with Bayesian methods (Mplus 7 in this study)
constraints: Mplus 7 does not allow estimation of categorical outcome residual variance at the within level of crossclassified models
Twin dyadic clustering could not be modeled, so twin pairs were split into random singletons
target_learning_goals: arithmetic problem-solving strategy use
solution time and accuracy
examples: Applied to 376 adolescents solving 30 addition problems with interview-coded strategies and bivariate solution time and accuracy outcomes
key_sources: Rhodes, K. T., Lukowski, S., Branum-Martin, L., Opfer, J., Geary, D. C., & Petrill, S. A. (2018). Individual Differences in Addition Strategy Choice: A Psychometric Evaluation. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11360214/

article_title: Individual differences in addition strategy choice: A psychometric evaluation.
citation: Rhodes, K. T., Lukowski, S., Branum-Martin, L., Opfer, J., Geary, D. C., & Petrill, S. A. (2018). Individual Differences in Addition Strategy Choice: A Psychometric Evaluation. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11360214/
title: Strategy Choice Model: adaptive strategy choice balancing goals, problem demands, and cognitive constraints
description: The SCM holds that "people's adaptive strategy choices require balancing conflicting problem-solving goals (e.g., speed and accuracy) and managing problem-specific demands (e.g., varying levels of problem difficulty) and cognitive constraints (e.g., the ability to retrieve a solution from memory)". Counting builds problem-answer associative strength, eventually yielding retrieval and decomposition strategies. The article evaluates the SCM's central tenet — that solving is a joint function of item difficulty and individual knowledge — and confirms it empirically.
requirements: Evaluation should model strategy variety across problems, mixed item/person effects, and trade-offs such as speed versus accuracy simultaneously
constraints: Most prior SCM evaluations relied on averaging methods that collapse across items or persons and can obscure individual differences
target_learning_goals: addition strategy choice
development of retrieval-based problem solving
examples: Addition is described as perhaps the best understood domain of strategy development, with counting, min-counting, decomposition, and retrieval as characteristic strategies

title: Standardized trade tests in four formats (oral, picture, performance, written) for measuring trade proficiency
description: Chapman's volume, as reviewed, presents trade tests developed under government-financed war research to classify skilled personnel, showing "the gradual development of technique in the construction and administration of trade tests" across oral, picture, performance, and written formats. article_title: Recent literature on the Binet tests.
citation: J. C. B. (1912). Recent Literature on the Binet Tests. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://openlibrary.org/search?q=recent+literature+on+the+binet+tests
title: The Binet-Simon age-scale principle: arranging graded tests in a scale whose steps correspond to normal intelligence at each age from three to thirteen
description: The article describes the organizing idea of the Binet-Simon scale as an age-graded series of tests. After early trials, Binet and Simon, following 1908 testing on Parisian school children, "hit upon their great idea... that of arranging the tests in a scale, each step of which should correspond to the normal intelligence of a given age between three and 13 years." The 1908 scale held 56 tests with three to eight per age; the 1911 revision reduced tests to five per age and rearranged placements to better represent normal children's performance.
requirements: Tests must be empirically graded age for age against performance of normal children, as Goddard's distribution about the at-age group was taken to show
constraints: The reviewer reports the statistical basis for individual test placement was not altogether convincing, and the scale was found too easy at the bottom and too hard at the top
target_learners: school children ages three to thirteen
target_learning_goals: measurement of intelligence level for detecting mentally retarded pupils
examples: The 1911 series is presented in a translated table with each test's 1908 position and its age rank according to six applications to normal children

article_title: A meta-analysis of the relation between RAN and mathematics.
citation: Koponen, T., Georgiou, G., Salmi, P., Leskinen, M., & Aro, M. (2017). A Meta-Analysis of the Relation Between RAN and Mathematics. Journal of Educational Psychology, 109(7), 977-992. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000182
title: Shared phonological access-and-retrieval account of the RAN–mathematics relationship
description: The article proposes that the RAN–mathematics relationship arises from shared underlying processing: "rapid access from visual stimuli to phonological representation stored in long-term memory." Fluent calculation depends on retrieving arithmetic facts stored as phonological forms, the same capacity RAN indexes; the article also notes neuroimaging evidence linking both skills to the left angular gyrus. The moderator pattern (arithmetic > achievement, single-digit > multi-digit, fluency > accuracy) is read as support for this account, and the equally strong non-alphanumeric correlations suggest the relationship also involves conceptual processing factors.
requirements: Applies to mathematics tasks whose solution depends on retrieving arithmetic facts or phonologically stored answers, not to tasks dominated by procedural or conceptual knowledge.
constraints: The article states the relationship is only partially explained by phonological access; conceptual and semantic processing factors also contribute, and much moderator variance remains unexplained.
target_learners: children at risk for arithmetic dysfluency
target_learning_goals: arithmetic calculation fluency
early identification of mathematics difficulties

title: Teacher-preparation programs should place a training school at their center rather than at the margin
description: The article argues that any institution preparing teachers should make a training school the central feature of its plan, rather than treating the training department as secondary work fitted into vacant periods of the theory department. It states that "Every school that plans to prepare teachers, whether normal 6chool, college or university, should have a training school as the central fea- ture of such a plan." It criticizes training departments that are too small or function as show rooms for observation.
requirements: A training department large enough to serve its function adequately, with conditions resembling outside experience rather than show rooms.
target_learners: Prospective teachers in normal schools, colleges, and universities
target_learning_goals: Practical teaching competence developed through observation and practice in a training school
examples: The article describes training departments fitted into vacant periods of theory departments and children put through mental gymnastics for the benefit of teachers in training, which it calls observation.

citation: Pintner, R. (1921). New Publications in Educational Psychology and Related Fields of Education. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22New+Publications+in+Educational+Psychology+and+Related+Fields+of+Education%22
title: Badenes' monograph: a trait list and teacher rating chart for selecting gifted children
description: A short monograph reviewed here proposes identifying gifted children through teacher judgement: it "lists nine pages of items or traits, mental, emotional, physical and so forth" and "supplies a chart on which the teacher is supposed to evaluate or describe these traits." The reviewer found the approach disappointing because it disregards mental tests and ignores recent rating-scale progress.

article_title: Pedagogy at the Berlin Psychological Congress.
citation: Peters, W. (1912). Pedagogy at the Berlin Psychological Congress. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 3, 452-457. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Pedagogy+at+the+Berlin+Psychological+Congress
title: Kupp's two-function theory of memory: perseveration and association with threefold psychic effects
description: A systematic survey of the characteristics of memory presented by Kupp at the Berlin congress. It posits two elementary functions of memory: "perseveration, or the tendency for an impression to persist in consciousness," and "association, or the connection between two or more impressions." Their psychic effects are threefold: revival of the experience, a mere increase in receptivity for this or a similar impression, and arousal of the consciousness of familiarity on repetition of this or a like impression. The report presents this as a classificatory framework for memory research of educational interest.
requirements: Memory phenomena are to be analyzed into the two elementary functions of perseveration and association as Kupp defines them.
target_learners: school learners studied in experimental pedagogy
target_learning_goals: retention and reproduction of learned material
examples: Presented as a systematic survey address at the congress, organizing memory phenomena into two elementary functions and three kinds of psychic effects.

article_title: Pedagogy at the Berlin Psychological Congress.
citation: Peters, W. (1912). Pedagogy at the Berlin Psychological Congress. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 3, 452-457. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Pedagogy+at+the+Berlin+Psychological+Congress
title: Spearman's theory of general intelligence, defended against the similarity theory and the type theory
description: In his address on general mental capacity, Spearman distinguished three theories of the relations of single mental abilities: "The similarity theory, which assumes that high correlation exists only between those activities which are very similar; the type theory, which affirms that correlation of mental abilities is a function of certain types, and Spearman's own theory of 'general intelligence.'" He critically examined the literature of the past 32 years and endeavored to demonstrate in it the presence of a general intelligence factor, also including physiological data favorable to his contention. The report presents this as a defense of general intelligence as distinct from special abilities.
requirements: Demonstration rests on critical re-examination of the existing correlation literature plus physiological data.
target_learning_goals: understanding and measurement of general mental capacity versus special aptitudes
examples: Spearman's congress address critically examined 32 years of literature to argue for a general intelligence factor, alongside Stern's report defending general intelligence as distinct from special abilities.

citation: Peters, W. (1912). Pedagogy at the Berlin Psychological Congress. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 3, 452-457. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Pedagogy+at+the+Berlin+Psychological+Congress
title: The principle of emphasis on sense perception (Anschauung) in instruction is in need of revision
description: In closing, the report endorses Külppe's observation that "the fundamental principle of modern instruction, the principle of emphasis on sense perception (Anschauung), is in need of revision." This follows from the shift of experimental psychology's center of interest from sensation and perception to complex psychic processes such as imageless thought and determining tendencies. The report frames this as one of the new demands for pedagogical investigation raised at the congress, alongside extending educational psychology to fields previously accessible only to rough, casual observation.
requirements: Revision should be grounded in exact psychological methods rather than casual observation.
target_learning_goals: balancing sense-perception-based instruction with training in abstract thinking
examples: The report's closing section cites Külppe's observations as the basis for revising the Anschauung principle and calls for applying exact methods to new pedagogical questions.

article_title: Alleged elements of waste in learning a motor problem by the "part" method.
citation: Pechstein, L. A. (1917). Alleged Elements of Waste in Learning a Motor Problem by the "Part" Method. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://books.google.com
title: Place association account of waste in part learning
description: The article's explanatory framework holds that mastering each maze unit establishes temporal and spatial positional relationships, locating each turn, cul de sac, and section relative to the time span, distance, the food-box, the starting place, and the experimenter. All waste in part learning "occurs in the act of connection and is here traceable almost entirely to the influence of place association," because connecting units demands breaking up these positional establishments.
requirements: Units must first be mastered as units, with positional establishments formed as necessary by-products of that mastery
constraints: The account is offered for the field of motor learning represented by the maze; the author waives a demonstrable comparison with rote learning
target_learning_goals: serial motor skill acquisition
examples: Behavior in the initial act of connection showed constant returning to the starting place, delay at closed exits, hesitation, confusion, and discouragement as runners vainly relied on short time and distance relationships

citation: Pechstein, L. A. (1917). Alleged Elements of Waste in Learning a Motor Problem by the "Part" Method. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://books.google.com
title: Withhold verdicts of whole-method superiority until modified part methods have been tested
description: Because modified part methods that progressively and distributively eliminate positional factors beat the whole method in maze learning, the article argues that its demonstrated advantages "lead the writer to question a thor- ough-going statement of the superiority of the whole method" in verbatim learning. Verdicts should wait "until the results of certain modified forms of part learning have been obtained and found inferior."
requirements: Modified part methods must provide a steady and progressive elimination of positional factors while the separate units are being mastered and connected
constraints: The article's remarks are meant to apply to that field of motor learning represented by the maze
target_learning_goals: efficient serial learning
motor skill acquisition
examples: The progressive part method: learn the first two units as units and proceed at once to the act of connection, then master Section III and join it to the established unity, then Section IV

article_title: The Teaching of Natural Science.
citation: J. C. B. (1915). Editorial. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Volume VI, Number 10. Warwick & York. https://archive.org
title: Reorganize science teaching from bottom to top to develop students' keenest interest in broader knowledge of scientific discoveries.
description: The editorial's central design recommendation: science teaching at every level should be reorganized so that instruction develops, in the author's words, "the keenest possible interest in the student for a broader knowledge of scientific discoveries in the world about him." It is offered as a corrective to the formal disciplinary and specialization-dominated approaches criticized throughout the editorial. No implementation details or supporting data are provided.
requirements: Science instruction must shift away from insistence on consecration to scientific method and from technical and mathematical treatment that obscures the cultural and general aspects of science.
constraints: The recommendation is stated as an editorial opinion for general education, not a tested intervention; the article offers no evidence of its effectiveness.
target_learning_goals: developing interest in scientific discoveries
cultivating a scientific temper of thought
examples: The editorial contrasts its recommendation with current practice: elementary observational study of nature decried as unscientific, high school physics overemphasizing experimentation and mathematics, and college courses eliminating the general student body.
key_sources: J. C. B. (1915). Editorial. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Volume VI, Number 10. Warwick & York. https://archive.org

article_title: An outline for institutional education and treatment of young offenders.
citation: William Healy and Augusta F. Bronner. (1916). An Outline for Institutional Education and Treatment of Young Offenders. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org
title: Diagnosis of each individual's needs is essential for successful institutional treatment of young offenders
description: The authors make diagnosis of individual needs the cornerstone of institutional treatment, insisting it be "absolutely essential for carrying out successful treatment" and correlated with educational and other therapy throughout institutional life. Diagnosis covers physical, psychological, and moral-background domains, and continues beyond admission to explain treatment failures and conduct outbreaks.
requirements: A trained diagnostician must know earlier causative factors of the delinquency, such as defective heredity and conditions of environment, in detail
constraints: The authors state that deliberately ignoring the delinquent's prior record is justifiable only when no thorough diagnosis of causation is available
target_learners: young offenders in training or industrial schools
target_learning_goals: moral recovery and social adjustment
examples: The outline specifies physical diagnosis of diseases and sensory defects, psychological diagnosis of disabilities, talents, mental content, and habits, and diagnosis of the moral background to find what normal experiences were left out or perverted
key_sources: William Healy and Augusta F. Bronner. (1916). An Outline for Institutional Education and Treatment of Young Offenders. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0071384

article_title: An outline for institutional education and treatment of young offenders.
citation: William Healy and Augusta F. Bronner. (1916). An Outline for Institutional Education and Treatment of Young Offenders. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org
title: Reward-based discipline outperforms punishment in institutions for young offenders
description: The authors recommend highly individualized discipline built on rewards rather than penalties, holding that "stimulus to doing better is more apt to result from the promise of rewards than the administering of penalties." Delinquents should have goals to work toward as the reward of good behavior, and with constructive treatment discipline problems largely tend to disappear.
requirements: Punishments must be highly individualized according to the personalities involved
constraints: The authors state that coercion and punishment by inflicting pain are the lowest levels of control
target_learning_goals: improved behavior and character building
examples: The outline advises goals toward which the delinquent works as the reward of good behavior, and warns against deceit, pedantry, and demonstrations of irrationality as methods
key_sources: William Healy and Augusta F. Bronner. (1916). An Outline for Institutional Education and Treatment of Young Offenders. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0071384

article_title: An outline for institutional education and treatment of young offenders.
citation: William Healy and Augusta F. Bronner. (1916). An Outline for Institutional Education and Treatment of Young Offenders. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org
title: Institutional life should be wholly educational and highly individualized to fit delinquents for outside environment
description: The authors state that "the entire institutional life should be adjusted with the idea that it is treatment, that it is educational," aimed at fitting the delinquent for an outside environment. This requires high individualization: both education and work must be adapted to individual needs, and the method should be elastic in all ways, particularly in institutions for girls.
requirements: Staff must avoid deceit, pedantry, and any demonstration of irrationality, modeling rationality and honesty by example
constraints: Modification cannot always be thought of in terms of building up; some offenders have self-will too strong or physical vigor too redundant, and harmful modifications can come from throwing delinquents together
target_learners: young offenders in training or industrial schools
target_learning_goals: coping with all phases of an ordinary social environment
examples: The outline allows for outbreaks and explosions of pent-up emotions and energies in institutions for girls, and for physical fluctuations
key_sources: William Healy and Augusta F. Bronner. (1916). An Outline for Institutional Education and Treatment of Young Offenders. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0071384

article_title: An outline for institutional education and treatment of young offenders.
citation: William Healy and Augusta F. Bronner. (1916). An Outline for Institutional Education and Treatment of Young Offenders. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org
title: School training for delinquents organized around social values of each curriculum subject
description: The outline's school plan rests on the general underlying principle of "emphasis of the social values in each subject of the curriculum," with specific purposes of creating good habits of thought and conduct, permanent wholesome interests, and knowledge for better social functioning. The central idea is social life and its manifold relations, centering about the home for girls and the industries for boys.
requirements: Application must be according to the needs of the pupils and the opportunities of the locality
constraints: The authors note no regular series of readers will suffice for older pupils who have had wide experience but little educational training, requiring specially prepared leaflets
target_learners: young offenders of varied ages and limited educational training
target_learning_goals: habits of thought and conduct, wholesome interests, and better social functioning
examples: Subjects include reading via prepared leaflets and good literature, language through free discussion of living problems, arithmetic based on household accounts and banking, applied art and music for appreciation, self-government, physical training, and vocational training possibly as the core of school work
key_sources: William Healy and Augusta F. Bronner. (1916). An Outline for Institutional Education and Treatment of Young Offenders. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0071384

article_title: Modeling writing development: Contribution of transcription and self-regulation to Portuguese students' text generation quality.
citation: Limpo, T., & Alves, R. A. (2013). Modeling writing development: Contribution of transcription and self-regulation to Portuguese students' text generation quality. Journal of Educational Psychology, 105, 401-413. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0031391
title: Not-so-simple view of writing with a capacity account of transcription–self-regulation development
description: The article organizes writing development around the not-so-simple view of writing (Berninger & Winn, 2006), in which "text generation is supported by the collaboration between transcription (handwriting and spelling) and high-level cognitive skills for self-regulation, such as planning and revising." Within working-memory constraints, transcription and self-regulation compete for attentional resources; as transcription automatizes across schooling, spare resources support planning and revising, shifting writers from knowledge telling toward knowledge transforming. The study's SEM results are offered as support for this account.
requirements: Assessment separating transcription skill from text-quality scoring, since poor spelling and penmanship bias holistic quality judgments
constraints: The account is tested only at Grades 4-6 and 7-9 with the specific indicators used; working memory and writing knowledge were not included in the model
target_learning_goals: Written composition quality in narrative and opinion genres
examples: Multiple-group SEM across Grades 4-6 and 7-9 with 376 students tested the model's developmental shift from direct to indirect transcription effects
key_sources: Limpo, T., & Alves, R. A. (2013). Modeling writing development: Contribution of transcription and self-regulation to Portuguese students' text generation quality. Journal of Educational Psychology, 105, 401-413. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0031391

article_title: Modeling writing development: Contribution of transcription and self-regulation to Portuguese students' text generation quality.
citation: Limpo, T., & Alves, R. A. (2013). Modeling writing development: Contribution of transcription and self-regulation to Portuguese students' text generation quality. Journal of Educational Psychology, 105, 401-413. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0031391
title: Teach transcription to automaticity and promote planning, revising, and self-efficacy in the middle grades
description: The article recommends that "transcription should be taught and practiced until a proficient level of automaticity is achieved," because transcription continues to constrain older students' writing indirectly through planning maturity and self-efficacy. It further argues that Grades 4-6 "may be a sensitive period to promote planning and revising as well as to nurture self-efficacy beliefs," with particular attention to revising skills, and calls for intervention programs tapping both low- and high-level skills.
requirements: Intervention programs addressing both low-level transcription skills and high-level self-regulatory skills, as the authors state is "clearly warranted"
constraints: Conclusions are limited to the indicators used and to writing assessment, as writing instruction was not studied in this project; these skills tend to be neglected by teachers beyond the initial years of learning to write
target_learners: Students in Grades 4-9, with particular attention to Grades 4-6 as a sensitive period
target_learning_goals: Written composition quality, including handwriting and spelling automaticity, planning, revising, and realistic self-efficacy beliefs
examples: The authors cite educational research showing positive effects of interventions targeting handwriting and spelling, and recommend designing programs tapping low- and high-level skills
key_sources: Limpo, T., & Alves, R. A. (2013). Modeling writing development: Contribution of transcription and self-regulation to Portuguese students' text generation quality. Journal of Educational Psychology, 105, 401-413. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0031391

article_title: The abilities of pupils in Detroit prevocational classes.
citation: Renshaw, S. (1915). The abilities of pupils in Detroit prevocational classes. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org/journal/jeduapsy
title: Train each prevocational pupil to do some one thing with creditable skill rather than attempting academic subjects with all
description: The article recommends that instead of trying to do the impossible with academic subjects, schools should give each prevocational pupil focused training toward one marketable skill. It argues that "each of these pupils could be taught or trained to do some one thing with creditable skill, provided there were no indigenous limitations to prevent," citing follow-up evidence that most unemployed men seeking non-skilled labor were rated backward or feeble-minded. The author cautions that manual and industrial teaching in these classes may be open to the same criticism as the academic instruction.
requirements: There must be no indigenous limitations in the individual pupil to prevent acquiring the skill, as the article states.
constraints: The article states the common notion that all defectives can be trained to acquire a high degree of skill in the manual and industrial arts is not borne out in fact.
target_learners: adolescent pupils in prevocational classes for atypical children
target_learning_goals: vocational skill sufficient for self-sustaining employment
examples: The article cites Pintner and Toops finding 82 per cent of 94 unemployed men seeking non-skilled labor rated backward, border-cases or definitely feeble-minded.
key_sources: Renshaw, S. (1915). The abilities of pupils in Detroit prevocational classes. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org/journal/jeduapsy

article_title: Teachers’ self-efficacy in relation to individual students with a variety of social–emotional behaviors: A multilevel investigation.
citation: M. Zee, P.F. de Jong, H.M.Y. Koomen. (2016). Teachers' self-efficacy in relation to individual students with a variety of social-emotional behaviors: A multilevel investigation. Journal of Educational Psychology, 108(7), 1013-1027. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000106
title: Dyadic perspective on teacher self-efficacy
description: The article argues that teacher self-efficacy should be viewed from a dyadic perspective, meaning it is conceptualized in relation to individual students rather than only as a general classroom-level belief. The multilevel design operationalizes this by modeling students' externalizing, internalizing, and prosocial behaviors as predictors of teachers' domain-specific self-efficacy toward each student, with teachers' perceived classroom misbehavior and teaching experience as moderators. The authors state these findings "illustrate the importance of viewing TSE from a dyadic perspective."
requirements: Measuring teacher self-efficacy separately for individual students and for distinct teaching domains, as the study did with its multilevel design
constraints: Studied among third- to sixth-grade students and their teachers in regular classrooms
target_learning_goals: Teachers' self-efficacy for instructional strategies, behavior management, student engagement, and emotional support
examples: The study modeled 526 students nested under 69 teachers, predicting domain-specific self-efficacy from each student's behavior ratings.
key_sources: M. Zee, P.F. de Jong, H.M.Y. Koomen. (2016). Teachers' self-efficacy in relation to individual students with a variety of social-emotional behaviors: A multilevel investigation. Journal of Educational Psychology, 108(7), 1013-1027. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000106

article_title: Teacher personality and teacher effectiveness in secondary school: Personality predicts teacher support and student self-efficacy but not academic achievement.
citation: Kim, Lisa, Dar-Nimrod, Ilan and MacCann, Carolyn (2018) Teacher Personality and Teacher Effectiveness in Secondary School: Personality Predicts Teacher Support and Student Self-Efficacy but not Academic Achievement. Journal of Educational Psychology. pp. 309-323. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000217
title: Emotional contagion and social modeling account for teacher neuroticism lowering student performance self-efficacy
description: The article proposes a mechanism account in which teachers high in neuroticism transmit negative emotions to students. Teachers act as social models: when a teacher "behaves anxiously and verbalizes their doubts and worries about their teaching and students' skills, students may model the teacher's low self-efficacy and nervous behaviors". Teachers' emotional expressions may also foster emotional contagion, in which students unconsciously synchronize their emotions with their teachers', raising student anxiety and self-doubt and diminishing the approach-oriented construct of performance self-efficacy. The study uses this account to motivate its hypothesis that teacher neuroticism negatively predicts PSE.
requirements: Requires observable teacher emotional expression in the classroom that students can perceive and model
constraints: The article presents this as a theoretical argument; it did not directly test the contagion or modeling mechanism
target_learners: Secondary school students in mathematics and English classes
target_learning_goals: Student performance self-efficacy and academic self-confidence
examples: The study's hypothesis H4c, that teacher neuroticism would negatively predict PSE, was derived from this account and received partial support in the multilevel regressions.
key_sources: Kim, Lisa, Dar-Nimrod, Ilan and MacCann, Carolyn (2018) Teacher Personality and Teacher Effectiveness in Secondary School: Personality Predicts Teacher Support and Student Self-Efficacy but not Academic Achievement. Journal of Educational Psychology. pp. 309-323. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000217

article_title: Which class matters? Juxtaposing multiple class environments as frames-of-reference for academic self-concept formation.
citation: Fleischmann, M., Hübner, N., Marsh, H. W., Guo, J., Trautwein, U., & Nagengast, B. (2021). Which Class Matters? Juxtaposing Multiple Class Environments as Frames-of-Reference for Academic Self-Concept Formation.
title: Local dominance effect: proximal comparison environments dominate academic self-concept formation
description: The frame-of-reference account holds that academic self-concept is formed through social comparison with the achievement of surrounding educational environments, producing the big-fish-little-pond effect (BFLPE). The local dominance effect specifies that the most locally proximal comparison group matters most: prior three-level work "found the class to be the pivotal frame-of-reference for academic self-concept formation," and local comparison information "matters the most for ability self-evaluations." This study extends the account to course-by-course tracked systems with multiple class environments.
requirements: Data must allow reliable achievement aggregates at every level of student nesting, which large-scale datasets like PISA and TIMSS typically do not provide
constraints: The article notes average achievement of educational environments is highly correlated, making the relative strength of frames-of-reference difficult to identify
target_learners: eighth-grade students in course-by-course tracked secondary school systems
target_learning_goals: academic self-concept in mathematics
examples: The study regressed math self-concept on average math achievement of students' school, math class, and regular class simultaneously in cross-classified multilevel models.
key_sources: Fleischmann, M., Hübner, N., Marsh, H. W., Guo, J., Trautwein, U., & Nagengast, B. (2021). Which Class Matters? Juxtaposing Multiple Class Environments as Frames-of-Reference for Academic Self-Concept Formation. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000491

article_title: Which class matters? Juxtaposing multiple class environments as frames-of-reference for academic self-concept formation.
citation: Fleischmann, M., Hübner, N., Marsh, H. W., Guo, J., Trautwein, U., & Nagengast, B. (2021). Which Class Matters? Juxtaposing Multiple Class Environments as Frames-of-Reference for Academic Self-Concept Formation.
title: Austrian national educational standard assessment 2012 (mathematics, eighth grade)
description: A comprehensive census survey that measured "the entire population of Austrian eighth-grade students in the domain of mathematics in 2012," provided by BIFIE. Because it covers the full population, reliable achievement aggregates can be computed at all nesting levels—school, regular class, and ability-grouped math class—overcoming the sampling limitation of typical large-scale assessments. General secondary school students were ability-grouped in the core subjects (mathematics, German, English) while regular class composition stayed the same in other subjects.
requirements: Full-population coverage so achievement aggregates are reliable on all levels of student nesting
constraints: Limited to the mathematics domain and the Austrian 2012 eighth-grade cohort
target_learners: Austrian eighth-grade students, including general secondary school students in ability-grouped core subjects
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement and math academic self-concept
examples: General secondary school students were grouped according to ability in mathematics, German, and English, while regular class composition was unchanged in all other subjects.
key_sources: Fleischmann, M., Hübner, N., Marsh, H. W., Guo, J., Trautwein, U., & Nagengast, B. (2021). Which Class Matters? Juxtaposing Multiple Class Environments as Frames-of-Reference for Academic Self-Concept Formation. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000491

article_title: Which class matters? Juxtaposing multiple class environments as frames-of-reference for academic self-concept formation.
citation: Fleischmann, M., Hübner, N., Marsh, H. W., Guo, J., Trautwein, U., & Nagengast, B. (2021). Which Class Matters? Juxtaposing Multiple Class Environments as Frames-of-Reference for Academic Self-Concept Formation.
title: When placing students in high-achieving classes, weigh domain-specific classes most heavily for self-concept costs
description: In course-by-course tracked systems, grouping decisions should anticipate that the BFLPE is strongest in the domain-specific class: students' self-concept "may be hurt when placing them in high achieving domain-specific classes" and "to a lesser extent also be hurt when placing them in high achieving domain-unrelated classrooms." Placement policy should therefore prioritize the achievement composition of domain-specific classes when managing self-concept risks.
requirements: A course-by-course tracked system in which students belong to both domain-specific and domain-unrelated class environments
constraints: Findings are limited to mathematics self-concept among Austrian eighth-graders in 2012
target_learners: eighth-grade students in course-by-course tracked systems
target_learning_goals: protecting academic self-concept under ability grouping
examples: The study refined BFLPE implications for course-by-course tracked systems using population-wide Austrian data with cross-classified multilevel models.
key_sources: Fleischmann, M., Hübner, N., Marsh, H. W., Guo, J., Trautwein, U., & Nagengast, B. (2021). Which Class Matters? Juxtaposing Multiple Class Environments as Frames-of-Reference for Academic Self-Concept Formation. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000491

article_title: Correlation of excellence in different school subjects based on a study of school grades.
citation: L. E. Frailey and C. M. Crane. (1912). Correlation of Excellence in Different School Subjects Based on a Study of School Grades. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journal_of_Educational_Psychology
title: Matched 32-pupil grade-record cohort from Urbana High School (1908-1912)
description: A dataset of school grades for 32 pupils, 18 girls and 14 boys, who entered Urbana High School in the fall of 1908 and graduated in the spring of 1912, studied the same subjects under the same instructors, and were selected after examining "the records of the pupils for the past six years." The authors tabulated ranks and grades in algebra, civics, American history, geometry, Latin and four years of English, dividing pupils into four equal groups of eight as the unit of comparison.
requirements: Pupils must have undergone the same treatment and lived under the same conditions, including identical instructors, subjects, and years of schooling, to give what the authors call a constant basis for trustworthy results.
constraints: The group is a single small cohort from one school; the authors repeatedly qualify conclusions with 'so far as this group is concerned' and 'with regard to the group studied.'
target_learning_goals: academic achievement across school subjects
examples: The authors ranked pupils by algebra grades, divided them into four groups of eight, and checked whether a pupil in group I in algebra appeared in group I in civics and the other subjects.
key_sources: L. E. Frailey and C. M. Crane. (1912). Correlation of Excellence in Different School Subjects Based on a Study of School Grades. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journal_of_Educational_Psychology

article_title: Correlation of excellence in different school subjects based on a study of school grades.
citation: L. E. Frailey and C. M. Crane. (1912). Correlation of Excellence in Different School Subjects Based on a Study of School Grades. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journal_of_Educational_Psychology
title: Control instructional conditions by studying a cohort with identical instructors, subjects and years before comparing grade-based ability correlations
description: The article's method is to first establish constancy of conditions, then compare standings. The authors write that "in order to make our investigations as constant as possible it was necessary that we should select from the many students a certain group which had passed through the same conditions in respect to time of studying the subjects investigated, years of schooling, instructors, etc." This makes grade-based group comparisons interpretable as reflecting pupil ability rather than differing instruction.
requirements: Access to multi-year pupil records allowing selection of pupils whose study experiences were identical in instructors, subjects, and years of schooling.
constraints: The authors note the unequal numbers of boys (14) and girls (18), saying the difference is so slight as to have little or no effect on general conclusions.
target_learning_goals: measuring consistency of academic achievement
examples: The study secured 32 pupils who all entered in fall 1908, graduated spring 1912, and studied algebra, civics, American history, geometry, Latin and English together under the same instructors.
key_sources: L. E. Frailey and C. M. Crane. (1912). Correlation of Excellence in Different School Subjects Based on a Study of School Grades. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journal_of_Educational_Psychology

article_title: How can the blow of math difficulty on elementary school children’s motivational, cognitive, and affective experiences be dampened? The critical role of autonomy-supportive instructions.
citation: Baten, E., Vansteenkiste, M., De Muynck, G., De Poortere, E., Desoete, A. (2020). How Can the Blow of Math Difficulty on Elementary School Children's Motivational, Cognitive and Affective Experiences be Dampened? The Critical Role of Autonomy-Supportive Instructions. Journal of Educational Psychology. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000444
title: Introduce difficult math tasks with autonomy-supportive instructions to buffer their impairing effects
description: When learners must work on tasks that are too difficult for them, the article recommends introducing them in an autonomy-supportive rather than controlling way — using inviting language, offering choice, and providing a meaningful rationale. In the experiment, such instructions "were dampened when the exercises were introduced in an autonomy -supportive manner" in their harmful need-related effects, fully cancelling the autonomy-frustrating effect of difficulty and minimizing its competence-impairing impact. The authors state this is especially valuable for poor performers and children with Mathematical Learning Disabilities.
requirements: The instructional style must include inviting language, choice in how and in what order to solve exercises, and a meaningful rationale, as operationalized in the comic-book vignette.
constraints: The buffering was partial for competence-based experiences: autonomy-supportive instructions minimized but did not cancel out the competence-impairing impact of difficulty.
The style manipulation was vignette-based and one-time; its main effects were limited compared to the difficulty manipulation, and replication with real teachers is needed.
target_learners: Elementary school children learning mathematics, especially poor performers and children with Mathematical Learning Disabilities
target_learning_goals: Maintaining interest, engagement and challenge seeking when working on difficult math exercises
examples: Children read a comic book in which a teacher introduced math exercises either autonomously-supportively (choice, rationale, inviting language) or controllingly (pressure, no rationale, exercises framed as a test) before solving easy-medium or difficult exercises.
key_sources: Baten, E., Vansteenkiste, M., De Muynck, G., De Poortere, E., Desoete, A. (2020). How Can the Blow of Math Difficulty on Elementary School Children's Motivational, Cognitive and Affective Experiences be Dampened? The Critical Role of Autonomy-Supportive Instructions. Journal of Educational Psychology. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000444

article_title: Supplemental Material for School-Level Academic and Cultural Demands and Resources: Their Role in Immigrant Students’ Motivation and Achievement
citation: Andrew J. Martin, Gregory Arief D. Liem, Rebecca J. Collie, Lars-Erik Malmberg, Tim Mainhard. (2025). School-Level Academic and Cultural Demands and Resources: Their Role in Immigrant Students' Motivation and Achievement. Journal of Educational Psychology.
title: PISA 2018 school-level measures of academic and cultural demands and resources
description: The study operationalises school-level factors using PISA (2018) codebook indices. Academic demands comprise resource shortage (item code "SC017"), reflecting instruction hindered by staffing or resourcing issues, and hindered learning ("SC061"); the academic resource is student assistance ("SC052"). Cultural demands are immigrant socioeconomic disadvantage ("SC048Q03NA"), and cultural resources comprise cultural learning ("SC165"), shared cultural values ("SC166") and immigrant (remedial) language support ("SC150").
requirements: Researchers must consult the full set of PISA items via the printed codebook item codes to use these measures
constraints: Measures are school-level indices drawn from the PISA 2018 codebook/dataset, not researcher-collected scales
target_learning_goals: school-level influences on immigrant students' motivation (self-efficacy, valuing) and achievement
examples: Resource shortage was represented by three item parcels built from SC017Q01–SC017Q08 items

School-Level Academic and Cultural Demands and Resources: Their Role in Immigrant Students' Motivation and Achievement. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000972.supp
