article_title: Language-independent and language-specific aspects of early literacy: An evaluation of the common underlying proficiency model.
citation: Goodrich J. Marc, Lonigan Christopher J. (2017). Language-Independent and Language-Specific Aspects of Early Literacy: An Evaluation of the Common Underlying Proficiency Model. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000179
title: Common Underlying Proficiency Model (Cummins)
description: The common underlying proficiency model holds that proficiencies in a first and second language are not separate abilities: "As proficiency in one language develops, so does language-independent knowledge (i.e., the common underlying proficiency) that supports the development of skills in both languages." Exposure to either language contributes to this shared proficiency, which may permit cross-language transfer. This study evaluated the model empirically for the first time using bifactor confirmatory factor analysis with language-minority preschoolers.
requirements: Sustained exposure to both languages so that language-independent knowledge can develop in either
constraints: The article notes evidence of a common underlying proficiency is not necessarily evidence of cross-language transfer; further research is needed on conditions under which transfer occurs
target_learning_goals: Early literacy: phonological awareness, print knowledge, oral language
examples: The study estimated bifactor models in which Spanish and English items loaded on language-specific factors and all items also loaded on a general factor for each skill
key_sources: Goodrich J. Marc, Lonigan Christopher J. (2017). Language-Independent and Language-Specific Aspects of Early Literacy: An Evaluation of the Common Underlying Proficiency Model. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000179

article_title: Language-independent and language-specific aspects of early literacy: An evaluation of the common underlying proficiency model.
citation: Goodrich J. Marc, Lonigan Christopher J. (2017). Language-Independent and Language-Specific Aspects of Early Literacy: An Evaluation of the Common Underlying Proficiency Model. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000179
title: Evidence-based instruction in either language should build code-related skills in both languages for language-minority preschoolers, but language instruction benefits only the language of instruction
description: Because code-related skills showed a common underlying proficiency, the authors argue "the presence of language-independent early literacy skills suggests that instruction in L1 will improve code-related skills in both L1 and L2." For oral language, however, "beneficial effects of language exposure and instruction will only be seen in the language of instruction." Educators can therefore choose either language for code-related foundations but must target each language separately for vocabulary and language skills.
requirements: Instruction should be evidence-based; the common underlying proficiency applies to code-related skills, not oral language
constraints: The authors caution results should be interpreted with caution, noting some studies of older children find L1 vocabulary uniquely predicts L2 reading comprehension, contrasting with this pattern
target_learning_goals: Phonological awareness, print knowledge, and oral language development
examples: The study found code-related skills of language-minority children approximately equivalent to monolingual peers despite lower language skills, a pattern the authors say this explains
key_sources: Goodrich J. Marc, Lonigan Christopher J. (2017). Language-Independent and Language-Specific Aspects of Early Literacy: An Evaluation of the Common Underlying Proficiency Model. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000179

article_title: Expanding autonomy psychological need states from two (satisfaction, frustration) to three (dissatisfaction): A classroom-based intervention study.
citation: Sung Hyeon Cheon, Johnmarshall Reeve, Youngsun Lee, Nikos Ntoumanis, Nicolas Gillet, Bo Ram Kim, Yong-Gwan Song. (2019). Expanding Autonomy Psychological Need States from Two (Satisfaction, Frustration) to Three (Dissatisfaction): A Classroom-Based Intervention Study. Journal of Educational Psychology, 111(4), 685-702. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000306
title: Three-state model of the psychological need for autonomy: satisfaction, frustration, and dissatisfaction
description: The article expands the SDT dual-process model by adding autonomy dissatisfaction as a third need state. It argues that "need satisfaction represented the 'bright side' of student motivation" while need frustration represented the "dark side," and that dissatisfaction arises when the learning environment is indifferent to students' needs. Teacher indifference—neglecting students' needs, goals, or concerns—produces an "energy-depleting experience" of dissatisfaction marked by boredom, amotivation, and apathy, distinct from the energy-disorganizing frustration produced by teacher control.
requirements: A learning environment that offers need indifference—activities unrelated or disconnected from students' psychological needs—for dissatisfaction to occur
constraints: The study focused only on the psychological need for autonomy, not competence or relatedness
target_learners: secondary school students in physical education
target_learning_goals: classroom engagement and prevention of disengagement
examples: Figure 1 illustrates how a teacher's motivating style (need supportive, need indifferent, or need thwartive) yields one of three student need states during instruction
key_sources: Sung Hyeon Cheon, Johnmarshall Reeve, Youngsun Lee, Nikos Ntoumanis, Nicolas Gillet, Bo Ram Kim, Yong-Gwan Song. (2019). Expanding Autonomy Psychological Need States from Two (Satisfaction, Frustration) to Three (Dissatisfaction): A Classroom-Based Intervention Study. Journal of Educational Psychology, 111(4), 685-702. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000306

article_title: In-FUSE-ing STEAM learning with spatial reasoning: Distributed spatial sensemaking in school-based making activities.
citation: Ramey, K. E., Stevens, R., & Uttal, D. H. (2019). In-FUSE-ing STEAM Learning with Spatial Reasoning: Distributed Spatial Sensemaking in School-based Making Activities. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000422
title: Distributed spatial sensemaking: spatial reasoning as distributed practices drawing on social and material resources
description: The article frames spatial reasoning not only as internal cognitive skills but as "a set of distributed practices, which draw on context- and activity-specific social and material resources (i.e. distributed spatial sensemaking)". Drawing on distributed theories of thinking and learning, the study examines interactions between people, tools, and representations through which spatial reasoning is enacted, and traces spatial representations across representational media. It translates the Uttal et al./Newcombe and Shipley two-by-two spatial-skills taxonomy into qualitative codes applicable to observable talk or action.
requirements: Requires studying reasoning within the sociomaterial context in which it is authentically learned and applied, using qualitative categorical coding and interaction analysis of multimodal idea units.
constraints: The framework addresses types of spatial reasoning beyond the intrinsic-dynamic skills typically measured by psychometric tests; it supplements rather than replaces laboratory, quasi-experimental, and correlational approaches.
target_learners: fifth- and sixth-grade students in school-based making activities
target_learning_goals: spatial reasoning and STEAM problem-solving
examples: The authors applied the framework via a modified version of Ramey and Uttal's (2017) coding scheme to approximately 88 hours of video from five FUSE classrooms.
key_sources: Ramey, K. E., Stevens, R., & Uttal, D. H. (2019). In-FUSE-ing STEAM Learning with Spatial Reasoning: Distributed Spatial Sensemaking in School-based Making Activities. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000422

article_title: The effects of explicit teaching of strategies, second-order concepts, and epistemological underpinnings on students’ ability to reason causally in history.
citation: Stoel, G.L., van Drie, J.P., & van Boxtel, C.A.M. (2017). The effects of explicit teaching of strategies, second-order concepts, and epistemological underpinnings on students' ability to reason causally in history. Journal of Educational Psychology, 109(3), 321-337. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000143
title: Model of domain learning as the framework for multidimensional explicit teaching in history
description: The article underpins its intervention with the model of domain learning, treating explicit teaching as multidimensional: it "focus[s] on strategies and second-order concepts to generate and verbalize causal explanations and epistemological underpinnings connected to causal reasoning in history". The model motivates measuring knowledge, epistemological beliefs, and interest as interrelated outcomes of domain learning.
requirements: Explicit teaching must address multiple dimensions simultaneously: strategies, second-order concepts, and epistemological underpinnings
constraints: The study applies the framework to causal reasoning in history with 11th-grade students
target_learning_goals: Constructing causal explanations in history
Second-order historical reasoning
Epistemological understanding of history
examples: The randomized experiment (N = 95) operationalized the framework as a treatment condition targeting strategies, second-order concepts, and epistemological underpinnings.
key_sources: Stoel, G.L., van Drie, J.P., & van Boxtel, C.A.M. (2017). The effects of explicit teaching of strategies, second-order concepts, and epistemological underpinnings on students' ability to reason causally in history. Journal of Educational Psychology, 109(3), 321-337. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000143

article_title: A New Statistical Book for Research Workers.
citation: H. O. R. (1922). New Publications. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org/journal/jeduropsych
title: Jones' A First Course in Statistics (1921), a two-part statistics textbook for education and psychology research workers
description: The reviewed artifact is Jones' textbook 'A First Course in Statistics' (G. Bell & Sons, London, 1921, pp. IX + 286). Part I, using economic and biological illustrations, covers "variables and frequency distribution; classification and tabulation of materials; averages, dispersion, graphs and correlation." Part II gives students "access to a treatment of probability, sampling, curve fitting and type distribution curves."
requirements: Intended for research students in psychology and education who need mathematical foundations beyond existing American measurement books
constraints: The reviewer notes partial correlation is not discussed, so students must still consult Yule's detailed original publication
target_learners: Research students in psychology and education
target_learning_goals: Statistical treatment of data: frequency distributions, averages, dispersion, correlation, probability, sampling, curve fitting
examples: The reviewer cites Part I's use of economic and biological illustrations and Part II's treatment of probability, sampling, curve fitting and type distribution curves
key_sources: H. O. R. (1922). New Publications. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org/journal/jeduropsych

article_title: A New Statistical Book for Research Workers.
citation: H. O. R. (1922). New Publications. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org/journal/jeduropsych
title: Davis' Technique of Teaching (1922), a general methods book organized by general principles plus per-subject chapters
description: The reviewed artifact is Davis' Technique of Teaching (Macmillan, New York, 1922, pp. VIII + 346). The reviewer describes it as "but another of a long stream of such books written largely out of the experience and observation of the author." It "contains a chapter of general principles of teaching, followed by a series of chapters, one devoted to the teaching of each of the principal school subjects."
requirements: Intended for prospective teachers being prepared in technique of teaching across school subjects
constraints: The reviewer judges it only partially in touch with the newest scientific and philosophic developments
target_learning_goals: General principles of teaching and subject-specific teaching technique for spelling, reading and literature, composition and grammar, arithmetic, history and geography
examples: The reviewer identifies the set of exercises at the close of each chapter as the best thing in the book

article_title: Spelling development in young children: A case of representational redescription?
citation: Critten, S., Pine, K., & Steffler, D. (2006). Spelling Development in Young Children: A Case of Representational-Redescription? Manuscript submitted for publication (Date of Submission: Thursday 3rd August 2006).
title: Karmiloff-Smith's Representational-Redescription model applied to spelling development
description: The RR model describes how knowledge is represented and changes with development through four levels: Implicit (behavioral mastery without understanding or verbal access), E1 (abstraction of an internal theory that dominates external data, producing overgeneralization errors and U-shaped performance), E2 (integration of theory with environmental data with improved performance), and E3 (fully explicit, verbalizable, flexible knowledge). Applied to spelling, E1 children over-apply phonological (E1A) or morphological -ed (E1B) theories, and E3 children can "recognize exceptions to those rules" such as -ed being only for regular verbs.
requirements: Children's verbal justifications about spelling choices must be elicited and coded, since levels beyond Implicit are indexed by explanation quality, not accuracy alone
constraints: Development through RR levels is domain specific to spelling (and possibly reading), not indicative of similar development in domains such as numeracy
No children in this study were predominantly at the Implicit level, so U-shaped performance at the representational level could not be commented upon
target_learners: young children aged 5-7 learning to spell
target_learning_goals: phonological and morphological spelling knowledge, including the -ed past-tense convention and its exceptions
examples: Children at E1B justified choices with the -ed rule, e.g. explaining that slepted was correct "it has an -ed", while an E3 child explained called was correct because "it has the word call with an -ed on the end to make it past (tense)"
key_sources: Critten, S., Pine, K., & Steffler, D. (2006). Spelling Development in Young Children: A Case of Representational-Redescription? Manuscript submitted for publication (Date of Submission: Thursday 3rd August 2006). https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-0663.99.1.207

article_title: Supplemental Material for Spontaneous Use of Retrieval and Rereading: Relation to Achievement Goals and Exam Performance
citation: Aleza Wallace, Andrew J. Elliot, & Ronald Rogge. Spontaneous Use of Retrieval and Rereading: Relation to Achievement Goals and Exam Performance. https://osf.io/53z6x
title: Open Science Framework repository (osf.io/53z6x) with the study's data and materials
description: A public, open-access OSF repository associated with the study on spontaneous use of retrieval and rereading. The disclosure form lists it for both the Open Data Badge and the Open Materials Badge, stating it provides "the URL , doi , or other permanent path for accessing the time-stamped and immutable data in a public, open-access repository". The authors confirm "sufficient information for an independent researcher to reproduce all of the reported results" and the methodology. No year of posting is printed in the supplied text.
requirements: A qualifying public, open-access repository that keeps the shared information accessible via the web in perpetuity, with the information in a format that is time-stamped, immutable, and permanent, as the form requires for badge eligibility
constraints: The form notes there are circumstances in which sharing participants' data could violate confidentiality, and publicly posted data must not contain information that would allow individuals to be identified without consent
target_learners: college students in the underlying exam-performance study
target_learning_goals: self-regulated study behavior, specifically spontaneous use of retrieval and rereading
examples: The authors checked the Open Data and Open Materials badges and supplied osf.io/53z6x as the permanent path for both the data and the materials
key_sources: Aleza Wallace, Andrew J. Elliot, & Ronald Rogge. Spontaneous Use of Retrieval and Rereading: Relation to Achievement Goals and Exam Performance. https://osf.io/53z6x

article_title: A study of initial spurt in the case of addition.
citation: Chapman, J. C. (1914). A Study of Initial Spurt in the Case of Addition. The Journal of Educational Psychology.
title: Initial spurt doctrine: maximum efficiency at the very commencement of mental work
description: The article names and states the doctrine of initial spurt as a candidate general characteristic of mental work: "At the very commencement of work, other things being equal, the individual tends to exhibit his maximum efficiency." The proposed explanation is that the individual "commences work with a too exacting standard" and is soon compelled to relax it. The article treats the doctrine as attractive but previously unsupported, and sets out to test it with short time periods and many subjects.
requirements: Testing the doctrine requires measuring continuous work divided into periods short enough to capture the spurt, with a sufficient number of subjects
constraints: The article notes the subject is usually so mixed up with accidental variations that selection can make them look like a general law
target_learning_goals: efficiency of sustained mental work over time
examples: The author tested the doctrine with 46 college students adding columns of numbers, scoring five successive two-minute periods within each ten-minute test
key_sources: Chapman, J. C. (1914). A Study of Initial Spurt in the Case of Addition. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0070019

article_title: A study of initial spurt in the case of addition.
citation: Chapman, J. C. (1914). A Study of Initial Spurt in the Case of Addition. The Journal of Educational Psychology.
title: Two-minute-mark continuous addition procedure for measuring initial spurt
description: An experimental procedure in which subjects add columns of ten one-place numbers continuously for ten minutes while the experimenter calls "mark" every two minutes, prompting subjects to tick the column they are on. "Forty-six male college students worked at addition of columns of ten one place numbers for ten ten-minute periods", over five days with two periods per day separated by a two-hour interval, using seven Thorndike addition sheets in rotation to prevent memorizing. Scores are columns added correctly, corrected for beginning and end effects.
requirements: Practice session the day before to make the routine automatic
Rotation of seven sheets to eliminate the possibility of memorizing
A correction of three-quarters of a column for beginning and end effects
constraints: The tick records only the column reached, not the point within the column, because subjects add in different directions
Subjects were not told the fifth two-minute period was the close of each test, so the data cannot investigate end spurt
target_learning_goals: measuring efficiency of sustained arithmetic work over short time periods
examples: Testing was conducted with four subjects a week over twelve weeks, with previous day's results announced to keep interest and competition at a maximum
key_sources: Chapman, J. C. (1914). A Study of Initial Spurt in the Case of Addition. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0070019

article_title:
Preservice teachers’ epistemic and achievement emotions when
                        confronted with common misconceptions about education.
citation: Berweger, B., Kracke, B., & Dietrich, J. (2023). Preservice Teachers' Epistemic and Achievement Emotions When Confronted With Common Misconceptions About Education. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000792
title: Epistemic versus achievement emotions distinguished by object focus, with epistemic emotions arising from information-oriented appraisals of cognitive incongruity
description: The article organizes learning-related emotions by their object focus, drawing on Pekrun's control-value theory and Muis et al.'s account of epistemic emotions. Epistemic emotions (surprise, curiosity, confusion, and enjoyment, frustration, anxiety when knowledge-focused) "result from information-oriented appraisals about the (mis-)alignment between new information and existing knowledge structures," and motivate critical reflection and exploration. Achievement emotions (anger, pride) are tied to success or failure outcomes. The study operationalizes this distinction by measuring state-level emotions after feedback on misconception statements.
requirements: Requires in-the-moment (state-level) measurement across multiple occasions per person, since the framework concerns intra-individual appraisal-emotion links rather than trait differences.
constraints: The same emotion (e.g., anxiety) belongs to different categories depending on the object focus of attention, so category membership is context-dependent, as the article states.
target_learners: preservice teachers in teacher education programs
target_learning_goals: revising faulty educational knowledge and misconceptions
engaging in evidence-based knowledge exploration
examples: Participants judged 15 misconception statements about class size, grade retention, and direct instruction, received refutational or confirming feedback, rated eight emotions, and could request explanations to resolve discrepancies.
key_sources: Berweger, B., Kracke, B., & Dietrich, J. (2023). Preservice Teachers' Epistemic and Achievement Emotions When Confronted With Common Misconceptions About Education. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000792

article_title: What is reading ability?
citation: Wyman, J. B., & Wendle, M. (1921). What is Reading Ability? The Journal of Educational Psychology, 518-531. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=%22What+is+Reading+Ability%22
title: A reliability coefficient alone cannot establish what function a test measures; other objective information about a test is necessary
description: The article argues that a reliability coefficient only measures agreement between forms of a test and "do their reliability coefficients or their norms guarantee that they are good tests of reading ability?" It therefore validates tests against external criteria — teachers' estimates and expert-weighted test combinations — before saying what they measure. The studies demonstrate this method on reading and English tests.
requirements: An external criterion of the ability in question must be obtained, such as teacher estimates or a weighted combination of expert-judged tests, against which each test is correlated
constraints: Teachers' estimates are themselves fallible; the article reports their reliability as only 0.84 in the grade VIII study and an estimated 0.45 for high school teachers' grades
target_learning_goals: silent reading ability
English ability
examples: Two criteria were built: the averaged independent rankings of two teachers, and a combination of all tests weighted by averaged judgments of two professors and three graduate students
key_sources: Wyman, J. B., & Wendle, M. (1921). What is Reading Ability? The Journal of Educational Psychology, 518-531. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=%22What+is+Reading+Ability%22

article_title: The Toronto Meeting of the Sections on Psychology and Education of the American Association for the Advancement of Science.
citation: Frank N. Freeman. (1924). The Toronto Meeting of the Sections on Psychology and Education of the American Association for the Advancement of Science. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/search?q=Freeman%20Toronto%20Meeting%20Journal%20of%20Educational%20Psychology
title: Intelligence tests imported from another country should be restandardized for local use
description: Sandiford's paper on test standardization, as reported at the Toronto meeting, argued that tests developed in one national context cannot be assumed valid in another. The report states he "emphasized particularly the necessity of restandardizing tests for use in Canada which are imported from the United States." This principle applies to any educational setting adopting tests normed on a different population.
requirements: Norms must be re-established on the local population before imported tests are used for decisions.
constraints: Stated in the context of Canadian use of United States tests; the report prints no supporting data.
target_learners: school children entering school in Canada
target_learning_goals: accurate measurement of ability for educational decisions
examples: Sandiford's paper on the standardization of tests presented at the Toronto meeting's session on mental tests.

article_title: Identifying reciprocities in school motivation research: A review of issues and solutions associated with cross-lagged effects models.
citation: Fernando Núñez-Regueiro, Jacques Juhel, Pascal Bressoux, Cécile Nurra. (2021). Identifying Reciprocities in School Motivation Research: A Review of Issues and Solutions Associated With Cross-Lagged Effects Models. Journal of Educational Psychology, 114 (5), pp.945-965. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000700
title: Violating the convergence assumption of cross-lagged models confounds between- and within-person processes of change
description: The review's central explanatory account is that the reliability of cross-lagged models "rests on the assumption that students do not differ in their trajectories of growth over time". When this convergence assumption is violated — for example, when high- or low-achievers follow different growth trajectories — the estimated cross-lagged effects become unreliable because they mix between-person differences with within-person processes of change. The article frames this as the core methodological issue underlying questionable findings in school motivation research.
requirements: Longitudinal panel data with repeated measures of the constructs across occasions
constraints: Standard cross-lagged models are unreliable when students differ in their trajectories of growth over time
target_learning_goals: school motivation
academic self-concept
school achievement
key_sources: Fernando Núñez-Regueiro, Jacques Juhel, Pascal Bressoux, Cécile Nurra. (2021). Identifying Reciprocities in School Motivation Research: A Review of Issues and Solutions Associated With Cross-Lagged Effects Models. Journal of Educational Psychology, 114 (5), pp.945-965. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000700

article_title: Identifying reciprocities in school motivation research: A review of issues and solutions associated with cross-lagged effects models.
citation: Fernando Núñez-Regueiro, Jacques Juhel, Pascal Bressoux, Cécile Nurra. (2021). Identifying Reciprocities in School Motivation Research: A Review of Issues and Solutions Associated With Cross-Lagged Effects Models. Journal of Educational Psychology, 114 (5), pp.945-965. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000700
title: Reciprocal-effects theory of motivation: development as a function of reciprocal effects between beliefs about the self and school achievement
description: The article uses as its case study "the pervading theory that motivation develops as a function of reciprocal effects between beliefs about the self (e.g., academic self-concept) and school achievement". This theory posits bidirectional, cross-occasion influences: self-beliefs such as academic self-concept affect subsequent achievement, and achievement in turn affects subsequent self-beliefs. Much of the supporting evidence for such school motivation theories comes from cross-lagged modeling of longitudinal data, which is precisely the method the review critiques.
requirements: Longitudinal panel data suitable for estimating cross-lagged effects between self-beliefs and achievement
constraints: Evidence for the theory relies on modeling methods whose reliability depends on the convergence assumption the review questions
target_learning_goals: school motivation
academic self-concept
school achievement

Identifying Reciprocities in School Motivation Research: A Review of Issues and Solutions Associated With Cross-Lagged Effects Models. Journal of Educational Psychology, 114 (5), pp.945-965. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000700

article_title: An approach to the synthetic study of interest in education: Part I.
citation: Waples, D. (1920). An Approach to the Synthetic Study of Interest in Education: Part I. The Journal of Educational Psychology, XI(6).
title: Three types of interest: intrinsic, practical, and cognitive
description: Waples proposes a theoretical classification of expressed interest into three attitudes distinguished by types of experience: "the types are three: an intrinsic, which seeks indulgence of feeling toward the situation; practical, which seeks usefulness, or directs action towards the situation; and cognitive, which seeks meaning." Each type is conceived to be differentiated by socialized expression, with some elements becoming prominent only after infancy. He argues discovery of the appropriate type and knowledge of its limitations is the theoretical prerequisite of effective motivation, and notes substantial agreement among authorities on this logical classification.
requirements: Diagnosis of the individual's appropriate type of interest and knowledge of its limitations before applying motivational principles
constraints: The pure type probably exists only in abstraction, so the classification's application depends largely on the specific case
target_learners: school pupils at successive stages of development
target_learning_goals: effective motivation through accurate diagnosis of pupil interest
examples: Waples traces the classification to Herbart's three-fold division under knowledge and participation and lists Kilpatrick, Dewey, McDougall, and others as employing substantially the same terms
key_sources: Waples, D. (1920). An Approach to the Synthetic Study of Interest in Education: Part I. The Journal of Educational Psychology, XI(6). https://doi.org/10.1037/h0076045

article_title: An approach to the synthetic study of interest in education: Part I.
citation: Waples, D. (1920). An Approach to the Synthetic Study of Interest in Education: Part I. The Journal of Educational Psychology, XI(6).
title: Three-class taxonomy of sources on interest: introspective, descriptive-psychological, and statistical
description: The article organizes previous investigations of interest into three general classes: works where analysis is largely introspective (with or without direct pedagogical reference), descriptive psychology ranging from laboratory analysis to childhood and adolescence biographies, and statistical child-study investigations recording group preferences and reactions. Each class is further distributed between strictly pedagogical and strictly psychological approaches and between direct and incidental study of interest. Waples judges the incidental classes generally the more reliable despite greater difficulty of adaptation.
requirements: Selection of representative works from each class so the student can cover the field with the greatest economy of time
constraints: Very few of the statistical studies had made any real contribution to the theory of interest, rendering those few easy to distinguish
target_learners: education researchers and students of educational psychology
target_learning_goals: understanding the nature, development, and educational bearing of interest
examples: Illustrative works named include Herbart's Outlines and Science of Education, Mitchell's The Structure and Growth of the Mind, and Croswell's, Chapman and Feeler's, and Thorndike's studies
key_sources: Waples, D. (1920). An Approach to the Synthetic Study of Interest in Education: Part I. The Journal of Educational Psychology, XI(6). https://doi.org/10.1037/h0076045

article_title: An approach to the synthetic study of interest in education: Part I.
citation: Waples, D. (1920). An Approach to the Synthetic Study of Interest in Education: Part I. The Journal of Educational Psychology, XI(6).
title: Begin motivation by diagnosing the learner's currently most intense varieties of interest, then instruct so that expression is evoked in useful content through voluntary effort of attention
description: Waples states a design principle for motivation grounded in his analysis of interest: "The first step in motivation consists in determining the varieties of interest in which expression is temporarily most intense and thereafter in such instruction as will evoke expression in useful content as the result of voluntary effort of attention." The principle presupposes individual study of the learner, since principles derived from groups require such individual study for their application. It connects interest diagnosis to the standardization of the learning process he outlines in the study's final chapter.
requirements: Individual diagnosis of the varieties of interest in which expression is temporarily most intense
Instruction designed so expression occurs in useful content via voluntary effort of attention
constraints: Principles derived from groups presuppose individual study for their application; the principles are valueless except as applied to the specific situation
target_learners: school pupils, particularly at secondary level
target_learning_goals: effective motivation of voluntary effort of attention toward useful content
examples: Waples cites Chapman and Feeler's incentive experiment as showing that diagnosis of individual interest responsive to direct appeal and standardization of the stimulus is a study of the first importance
key_sources: Waples, D. (1920). An Approach to the Synthetic Study of Interest in Education: Part I. The Journal of Educational Psychology, XI(6). https://doi.org/10.1037/h0076045

article_title: Understanding instructions.
citation: Marcus, N. (1998). Understanding Instructions. PhD thesis, University of New South Wales. https://hdl.handle.net/1959.4/70247
title: Element interactivity account of understanding instructions within cognitive load theory
description: The thesis proposes that understanding of instructions is governed by cognitive load theory: material is hard to understand when many interacting elements must be held in working memory simultaneously, and schemas in long-term memory are what allow elements to be combined. As the abstract states, "Instructional material may be difficult to understand if it consists of many elements that must be held in working memory simultaneously." The thesis uses this account to organise its literature review and to motivate five experiments on presentation mode.
requirements: Materials whose interacting elements exceed working-memory capacity require schemas before they can be understood
target_learners: school students learning science and mathematics problem-solving procedures
target_learning_goals: understanding written or diagrammatic instructions for problem-solving tasks
examples: The abstract frames Experiments 1 to 5, which manipulated whether instructions were presented as diagrams cueing pre-existing schemas or as text.
key_sources: Marcus, N. (1998). Understanding Instructions. PhD thesis, University of New South Wales. https://hdl.handle.net/1959.4/70247

article_title: Understanding instructions.
citation: Marcus, N. (1998). Understanding Instructions. PhD thesis, University of New South Wales. https://hdl.handle.net/1959.4/70247
title: Five-experiment instructional materials: resistor problems and angle construction tasks
description: The empirical core of the thesis is a series of five experiments using electrical resistor problems and angle construction tasks, comparing instruction presented as diagrams that cue pre-existing schemas against text, and in Experiment 5 also against diagrams unlikely to cue pre-existing schemas. The abstract states: "In Experiments 1 to 4, three different electrical resistor problems were given to students to complete, with instructions presented using diagrams (which cue pre-existing schemas) or text." Subjective rating scales were used in Experiments 4 and 5 (Appendix D).
requirements: Instructions must be presentable in both diagrammatic and textual modes for comparison
target_learners: primary and high school students from the participating Sydney schools
target_learning_goals: understanding instructions for electrical resistor and angle construction problems
examples: Experiment 5 presented four different angle construction tasks under three presentation conditions: schema-cueing diagrams, non-cueing diagrams, or text.
key_sources: Marcus, N. (1998). Understanding Instructions. PhD thesis, University of New South Wales. https://hdl.handle.net/1959.4/70247

article_title: Understanding instructions.
citation: Marcus, N. (1998). Understanding Instructions. PhD thesis, University of New South Wales. https://hdl.handle.net/1959.4/70247
title: Schema theory as a framework for expert-novice differences in problem solving
description: The thesis adopts schema theory to characterise expert-novice differences: schemas are organised knowledge structures in long-term memory that let solvers chunk information, recognise problem categories, and apply appropriate solution moves. In the problem-solving context, "a schema is defined as a cognitive structure which allows problem solvers to recognise a problem as belonging to a particular category of problems that usually require particular moves to reach a solution." The framework organises the thesis's review of memory, categorisation, and strategy research.
requirements: A large domain-specific knowledge base acquired through extensive experience within the domain
constraints: Expertise is domain-specific; expert problem solvers in one domain are not necessarily good problem solvers in other domains
target_learning_goals: schema acquisition and problem categorisation by solution mode
examples: The thesis reviews chess, electronics, algebra, programming, and physics studies showing experts' superior memory for meaningful configurations that disappears with random materials.
key_sources: Marcus, N. (1998). Understanding Instructions. PhD thesis, University of New South Wales. https://hdl.handle.net/1959.4/70247

article_title: Engaging Latinx or Hispanic-Identifying families in science education: A longitudinal intervention study.
citation: Jiang Su, Woodcock Anna, Haddad Kamel, Hernandez Paul R. (2026). Engaging Latinx or Hispanic-Identifying Families in Science Education: A Longitudinal Intervention Study. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0001047
title: Latent Trait-State Theory (Revised) applied as a latent single-trait multiple-states model for intervention outcomes
description: LST-R is a longitudinal latent measurement framework distinguishing stable traits from situationally fluctuating states: "latent traits typically change little over time and situations (although trait change is possible), while latent states reflect the influence of persons in situations or person × situation interactions". The article applies its latent single-trait multiple-states model to parent-child outcomes with up to four repeated measures, estimating the ICC for each outcome and testing treatment effects on state variability at T2 and T3 after removing trait variance. It was adopted because prior pre-post designs conflated trait-like and state-like variability.
requirements: At least three repeated measures, per the article's stated assumption that sufficient numbers of repeated measures are assessed
Longitudinal measurement invariance, which the article verified via configural, metric, and scalar invariance testing before estimating treatment effects
constraints: The article acknowledges this latent trait-state modeling approach deviated from the pre-registered ANCOVA analysis plan
Treatment effects estimated under the model apply to state-like person-in-situation variability, not to stable trait-like differences
target_learners: First-year Latinx or Hispanic-identifying STEM undergraduates
target_learning_goals: Parental support for STEM persistence
Parent-child STEM conversations and values
examples: The study estimated the model separately for Parent Support, STEM Conversations, STEM Value, and Family Obligations using FIML with auxiliary variables
key_sources: Jiang Su, Woodcock Anna, Haddad Kamel, Hernandez Paul R. (2026). Engaging Latinx or Hispanic-Identifying Families in Science Education: A Longitudinal Intervention Study. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0001047

article_title: Engaging Latinx or Hispanic-Identifying families in science education: A longitudinal intervention study.
citation: Jiang Su, Woodcock Anna, Haddad Kamel, Hernandez Paul R. (2026). Engaging Latinx or Hispanic-Identifying Families in Science Education: A Longitudinal Intervention Study. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0001047
title: Familias por el Éxito en STEM: Spanish-language virtual parent workshops delivered with PIQE
description: A culturally responsive parent intervention developed with the Parent Institute for Quality Education (PIQE), a community-based organization with over 30 years of experience with the local Spanish-speaking community. "The parent intervention workshops consisted of five virtual (Zoom) seminars, each meeting for 90 minutes once a week over five consecutive weeks", held after work hours (6:00-7:30 pm). Sessions covered the value of STEM education, STEM and Latinx identity, university resources, and STEM career pathways, and included Latinx STEM alumni role models and a graduation ceremony. Grounded in Yosso's Community Cultural Wealth, the design emphasized familial, aspirational, linguistic, and social capital.
requirements: Training and materials conducted in Spanish to value parents' linguistic capital
Delivery via community partner organization staff bilingual in Spanish and English
Sessions scheduled after typical work hours to accommodate working parents
constraints: Originally planned in person but moved online due to COVID-19
Parents who partially participated were included in the treatment group
target_learners: Spanish-speaking parents of first-year Latinx or Hispanic-identifying STEM undergraduates, predominantly of Mexican descent
target_learning_goals: Parents' utility value of STEM careers
Supportive parent behaviors including STEM conversations and balancing family and school obligations
examples: Session four, "Prestigious and Well-Paid Careers in STEM," involved interactions with STEM alumni role models highlighting the utility value and cultural relevance of STEM degrees
key_sources: Jiang Su, Woodcock Anna, Haddad Kamel, Hernandez Paul R. (2026). Engaging Latinx or Hispanic-Identifying Families in Science Education: A Longitudinal Intervention Study. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0001047

article_title: The function of selection of assessment leads evaluators to artificially create the social class achievement gap.
citation: Autin, Frédérique; Batruch, Anatolia; Butera, Fabrizio. (2019). The function of selection of assessment leads evaluators to artificially create the social class achievement gap. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000307
title: Use assessment for learning (formative comments) rather than selection (normative grading) to avoid evaluator bias against low-SES students
description: The article shows that the function assessment serves shapes evaluator behavior: when assessment is used to compare, rank and track students (normative grading), evaluators judge low-SES students' work more harshly; when used for learning (formative comments), this bias is reduced. The article reports the SES difference in mistakes was "reduced in the assessment for learning condition". This supports designing assessment to serve learning rather than selection where the goal is equitable evaluation.
requirements: Assessment tasks must be evaluated under a clearly learning-oriented framing (formative comments) rather than a selection framing (compare, rank and track students).
constraints: The bias-reduction effect did not reach significance in Experiment 4, though the internal meta-analysis confirmed the overall effect.
target_learners: lower and higher socio-economic status (SES) students in educational settings
target_learning_goals: equitable assessment of student performance
examples: Participants graded a test attributed to a high- or low-SES student using normative grading or formative comments; the low-SES penalty appeared under normative grading and was reduced under formative comments.
key_sources: Autin, Frédérique; Batruch, Anatolia; Butera, Fabrizio. (2019). The function of selection of assessment leads evaluators to artificially create the social class achievement gap. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000307

article_title: Teacher motivational strategies and student self-determination in physical education.
citation: Taylor, I. M., & Ntoumanis, N. (2007). Teacher motivational strategies and student self-determination in physical education. Journal of Educational Psychology, 99, 747-760. https://dspace.lboro.ac.uk/
title: Self-determination theory motivational sequence in physical education
description: The article applies self-determination theory (SDT; Ryan & Deci) to PE, in which a "continuum of different types of motivation exists depending upon the level of self-determination" ranging from intrinsic motivation through identified, introjected, and external regulations to amotivation. Self-determination is determined by satisfaction of three innate psychological needs—autonomy, competence, and relatedness—and teachers' motivational strategies (autonomy support, structure, involvement) map onto these needs in a social-contextual sequence tested in this study.
requirements: The strategy-to-outcome sequence operates through students' perceptions of the social context (functional significance), not through teachers' own reports
constraints: Integrated regulation has rarely been investigated in PE contexts because adolescents have not reported it, possibly due to an underdeveloped sense of the self
target_learners: Secondary school students (ages 11-16) in physical education classes
target_learning_goals: Self-determined motivation for physical activity and participation in PE
examples: The study tested the SDT sequence with 787 British PE students and 51 teachers using multilevel mediation models
key_sources: Taylor, I. M., & Ntoumanis, N. (2007). Teacher motivational strategies and student self-determination in physical education. Journal of Educational Psychology, 99, 747-760. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-0663.99.4.747

article_title: An absolute point scale for the group measurement of intelligence.- Part II.
citation: Arthur S. Otis. (1917). An Absolute Point Scale for the Group Measurement of Intelligence.—Part II. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://archive.org
title: Correlational-spread account: the sums of a test's intercorrelations with all other tests measure the relative degree to which it shares a common factor
description: In Appendix III, Otis develops a mathematical argument that if each test measures a general factor plus specifics, the relative degrees to which two tests correlate with the general factor are expressed by their relative correlations with the other tests. He demonstrates with a four-test example that "the sums of the correlations of each of the tests with all of the others afford meaures of the relative correlational spread of the tests," and shows average intercorrelations can be derived from each test's correlation with the composite without computing all pairwise coefficients.
requirements: Assumes each test measures only a general factor common to all tests plus factors specific to that test alone, so that the general factor is the only source of correlation.
constraints: The derivation assumes equal weights and standard deviations where stated, and the author notes the ratios hold only subject to the chance errors of the coefficients.
target_learners: pupils administered group intelligence tests in grades 3 through 8
target_learning_goals: measurement of general intelligence via group-administered point scales
examples: Otis illustrates the argument with a hypothetical four-test group whose elements overlap in known proportions, showing correlation sums of 1.80 : 1.80 : 1.60 : 1.20 match the elemental-overlap proportions 9 : 9 : 8 : 6.
key_sources: Arthur S. Otis. (1917). An Absolute Point Scale for the Group Measurement of Intelligence.—Part II. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0074753

article_title: An absolute point scale for the group measurement of intelligence.- Part II.
citation: Arthur S. Otis. (1917). An Absolute Point Scale for the Group Measurement of Intelligence.—Part II. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://archive.org
title: Otis Absolute Point Scale (Scale I and Scale II) for group measurement of intelligence
description: The Absolute Point Scale is a group intelligence test composed of ten tests per scale (including Spelling, Arithmetic, Synonyms, Proverbs, Relation, Narrative Completion, Following Directions, Geometric, Disarranged Sentences, and Digits), administered in two parallel forms whose correlation provides the scale's reliability. Scores are expressed on an absolute point scale with grade norms, and inter-test correlations are reported both raw and "corrected for attenuation due to errors of measurement."
requirements: Two parallel forms (Scale I and Scale II) are needed to obtain the double measures from which the reliability coefficient and probable error are computed.
constraints: The author notes the Spelling Test is too easy and the Synonym Test somewhat too easy for the group tested, and that refinement of item difficulty is not of great value until more obvious defects of the scale are eliminated.
target_learning_goals: group measurement of general intelligence and mental age
examples: Applied to 121 pupils across the fourth, sixth, and eighth grades, yielding grade norms of 385, 514, and 605 points and a median score of 500 for the whole group.
key_sources: Arthur S. Otis. (1917). An Absolute Point Scale for the Group Measurement of Intelligence.—Part II. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0074753

article_title: Criteria to Employ in Choice of Tests.
citation: Franzen, R., & Knight, F. B. (1921). Criteria to Employ in Choice of Tests. The Journal of Educational Psychology.
title: Nine-criterion framework for judging the value of educational tests
description: The article enumerates nine virtues a test may possess to varying degrees, from validity ('Measure what it purports to measure') through reliability, objectivity, scaling, norms, interest to the child, range of abilities registered, diagnostic discrimination between failures, and correlation with intelligence at maximum ability. The framework is offered as 'a convenient assembly of important test virtues' to guide administrators who must choose among many existing tests rather than find one.
requirements: Tests must be evaluated against all nine virtues before selection, with published data such as correlation with a criterion, reliability coefficients, and scale determinations available for inspection
constraints: The authors disclaim originality: 'No credit is here given or taken for originality in the formulation of criteria'
Some virtues are superfluous or undesirable for particular uses, e.g. high intelligence correlation is not desirable for mechanical ability tests
target_learners: school students in grades 3 through senior high school
target_learning_goals: measurement of school abilities and capacities such as reading and arithmetic for comparison, experimentation, classification, diagnosis and goal definition
examples: The authors apply the framework to reading tests and intelligence tests, noting that an 'arithmetic' test stressing time may actually measure speed in writing figures
key_sources: Franzen, R., & Knight, F. B. (1921). Criteria to Employ in Choice of Tests. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0075312

article_title: Criteria to Employ in Choice of Tests.
citation: Franzen, R., & Knight, F. B. (1921). Criteria to Employ in Choice of Tests. The Journal of Educational Psychology.
title: Decide primary psychological and statistical values of a test first; consider price, time and convenience only in ratio to benefits derived
description: The article holds that administrative exigencies (price, administration time, scoring convenience) are secondary criteria, admissible only after establishing how much service each candidate test performs. An administrator should 'decide primary values first; then let him consider price, time and convenience in ratio to the benefits derived', because often the only affordable test is the one that does not perform the needed service.
requirements: The administrator must first know how much service can be expected from each of a group of tests before weighing cost, time and scoring convenience
constraints: Cost, time and convenience remain legitimate factors once all considered tests perform the needed service
target_learners: school students measured by district testing programs
target_learning_goals: accurate measurement of abilities such as reading for school decision-making
examples: The authors argue that if a test does not really measure reading, it would pay an administrator to use the test that did the service even though it cost more, took longer, and was scored with great time and energy
key_sources: Franzen, R., & Knight, F. B. (1921). Criteria to Employ in Choice of Tests. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0075312

article_title: The left-handed child.
citation: CHARLES HUGHES JOHNSTON; GUY MONTROSE WHIPPLE. (1907). THE LEFT-HANDED CHILD. THE JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL PSYCHOLOGY. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=THE+LEFT-HANDED+CHILD
title: Whipple's open solicitation of reader reports on attempts to correct left-handedness
description: A journal communication in which Whipple, having found the literature thin, uses the discussion pages to gather data: "I shall be glad to receive information from readers who have noted attempts to correct left-handedness, whether the outcome was successful or unsuccessful." Cases with concomitant speech disturbance are of particular interest. It functions as an early crowdsourced case-collection instrument rather than a study.
requirements: Requires readers who have observed attempts to correct left-handedness to submit reports of the outcomes
target_learning_goals: understanding consequences of correcting left-handedness
identifying concomitant speech disturbance
examples: Whipple solicits instances of concomitant speech disturbance in particular, inviting both successful and unsuccessful outcomes

article_title: Communications and discussions. The conference on mental hygiene at Boston.
citation: Wm. H. Burnham. (1913). The Conference on Mental Hygiene at Boston. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/
title: Train children by example: the report names example as the best method of training
description: Among the conference's printed practical suggestions, the report states that "The best method of training is example; and what is good for your child is usually good for you." As a design principle, adults should model the habits and dispositions they wish children to develop, because example rather than precept is named as the primary training method. The report offers this assertion without supporting data or argument.
requirements: Adults in the child's environment must themselves practice the habits and dispositions being modeled
constraints: Stated as a conference suggestion with no evidence or argument reported; it stands as expert assertion from 1913
target_learning_goals: health habits and dispositions
cheerful, generous disposition
examples: The conference program pairs the example principle with suggestions such as cultivating a cheerful, generous and charitable disposition and keeping one's own health habits.
key_sources: Wm. H. Burnham. (1913). The Conference on Mental Hygiene at Boston. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/

article_title: Communications and discussions. The conference on mental hygiene at Boston.
citation: Wm. H. Burnham. (1913). The Conference on Mental Hygiene at Boston. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/
title: Mental hygiene extending beyond the pathological to normal mental processes and school practice
description: The report highlights as noteworthy that "considerable attention was given at this conference to normal mental processes," in contrast to recent mental-hygiene writing that concerned the pathological. This framing extends mental hygiene into education: Dr. Burnham spoke on "Mental Hygiene in the School," Professor Yerkes on "Hygiene and Mental Development," and Dr. Cabot on "Four Laws for Mental Hygiene." The account treats mental health as something cultivated through schooling and child training, with prevention rather than treatment as the guiding aim.
requirements: Educational settings must attend to normal mental processes and child development, not only pathology
constraints: The report frames this as a notable shift of emphasis at one 1913 conference; it presents no data on outcomes in schools
target_learning_goals: mental health and prevention
mental development
examples: Talks at the conference on mental hygiene in the school and on hygiene and mental development exemplify the extension to normal processes.
key_sources: Wm. H. Burnham. (1913). The Conference on Mental Hygiene at Boston. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/

article_title: Communications and discussions. The conference on mental hygiene at Boston.
citation: Wm. H. Burnham. (1913). The Conference on Mental Hygiene at Boston. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/
title: The Boston Mental Hygiene Conference and its accompanying exhibit
description: A Mental Hygiene Conference was "held in Boston, March 31 to April 4, inclusive, conducted by the National Committee for Mental Hygiene and the newly formed Massachusetts Society for Mental Hygiene." In connection with it was an exhibit similar to those given at earlier hygiene congresses. The program included addresses by Dr. Paton, President-Emeritus Eliot, Dr. Putnam, President G. Stanley Hall, and other medical and institutional speakers, plus an elaborate printed program of facts and practical suggestions.
requirements: Organization by a national committee and a newly formed state society, with speakers and an accompanying exhibit
constraints: A one-time 1913 event; the article gives no evaluation of the conference's effects
target_learners: the general public addressed by the conference program
target_learning_goals: mental hygiene awareness
prevention of mental illness
examples: The closing session included Dr. Putnam on "Our Obligation to Understand the Working of Our Own Minds" and President G. Stanley Hall on "Mind and Food."

article_title: Do Spanish-English bilingual children outperform monolingual English-speaking children on executive function tasks in early childhood? A propensity score analysis.
citation: Goodrich, J. M., Koziol, N. A., Yoon, H., & Leiva, S. (2019). Do Spanish-English Bilingual Children Outperform Monolingual English-Speaking Children on Executive Function Tasks in Early Childhood? A Propensity Score Analysis. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.apa.org/pubs/journals/edu
title: Doebel's ecological framework: executive function develops in the context of goal-directed behavior
description: The article adopts Doebel's (2020) re-conceptualization of executive function, which criticizes componential models (e.g., the tripartite and unity/diversity models) for isolating EF components from the contexts in which they develop. Instead, "a more appropriate theoretical framework would involve conceptualizing and measuring EF as skills that develop in the context of a need to achieve specific goals." Under this view, children's experiences, knowledge, values, and cultural norms shape goals, and environment interactions in service of goals drive EF development. The study uses this framework to predict bilingual advantages on ecologically valid, report-based measures rather than abstract laboratory tasks.
requirements: Measures of EF should capture the real-world contexts in which children use EF in pursuit of goals, such as teacher or parent report questionnaires
constraints: The article notes it was unable to account for cultural heterogeneity among different populations of Spanish speakers within its sample
target_learning_goals: executive function development, including inhibitory control, attentional focus, working memory, and cognitive flexibility
examples: The study tested the framework by comparing report-based (CBQ) and performance-based (DCCS, Numbers Reversed) EF measures in a matched bilingual-monolingual comparison
key_sources: Goodrich, J. M., Koziol, N. A., Yoon, H., & Leiva, S. (2019). Do Spanish-English Bilingual Children Outperform Monolingual English-Speaking Children on Executive Function Tasks in Early Childhood? A Propensity Score Analysis. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.apa.org/pubs/journals/edu

article_title: Do Spanish-English bilingual children outperform monolingual English-speaking children on executive function tasks in early childhood? A propensity score analysis.
citation: Goodrich, J. M., Koziol, N. A., Yoon, H., & Leiva, S. (2019). Do Spanish-English Bilingual Children Outperform Monolingual English-Speaking Children on Executive Function Tasks in Early Childhood? A Propensity Score Analysis. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.apa.org/pubs/journals/edu
title: Bialystok's executive attention reformulation of the bilingual advantage
description: The article describes Bialystok's reformulated bilingual advantage hypothesis, in which the advantage is no longer attributed to inhibition practice. Bialystok (2017) is described as "highlighting that what is common across different components of EF is the use of 'executive attention.'" Increased novelty in bilingual children's environments, such as shifts between multiple languages, draws attention and requires selective allocation to the target language, with the largest expected advantage in selective attention that trickles down to other EF domains. The study empirically tested this executive attention conceptualization in early childhood.
requirements: Bilingual experience involving attention to and selection among multiple languages in the child's environment
constraints: The article notes the hypothesis predicts advantages most strongly for selective attention, with trickle-down effects to other EF components rather than uniform advantages
target_learners: bilingual and monolingual children in early childhood
target_learning_goals: executive function, particularly selective attention and inhibitory control
examples: The study evaluated the executive attention account using teacher-rated attentional focus and inhibitory control alongside performance-based EF tasks in a nationally representative matched sample
key_sources: Goodrich, J. M., Koziol, N. A., Yoon, H., & Leiva, S. (2019). Do Spanish-English Bilingual Children Outperform Monolingual English-Speaking Children on Executive Function Tasks in Early Childhood? A Propensity Score Analysis. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.apa.org/pubs/journals/edu

article_title: Do Spanish-English bilingual children outperform monolingual English-speaking children on executive function tasks in early childhood? A propensity score analysis.
citation: Goodrich, J. M., Koziol, N. A., Yoon, H., & Leiva, S. (2019). Do Spanish-English Bilingual Children Outperform Monolingual English-Speaking Children on Executive Function Tasks in Early Childhood? A Propensity Score Analysis. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.apa.org/pubs/journals/edu
title: Propensity score matching design with 48 covariates and a simulation-based sensitivity analysis for the bilingual advantage question
description: The study's methodological artifact is a comprehensive propensity score matching analysis of ECLS-K:2011 data, in which "a total of 48 child- and school-level covariates were included in the propensity score model," spanning demographics, health-related factors, parent-child engagement, and school-level factors. One-to-one nearest neighbor matching without replacement within a .2 SD caliper produced 252 matched pairs, and a simulation-based sensitivity analysis generated a synthetic unmeasured confounder modeled on SES across 100 replications to test robustness of effects.
requirements: Large secondary datasets with detailed child-, family-, and school-level information; the strong ignorability assumption that all confounders are measured
constraints: Causal inference about early bilingualism is described as unattainable because early bilingualism is not a manipulable variable; the analysis estimates an average controlled difference instead
The article notes it could not account for cultural heterogeneity among Spanish-speaking populations
target_learners: U.S. kindergarten children (bilingual Spanish-English and monolingual English)
target_learning_goals: executive function outcomes in early childhood
examples: Matching yielded 252 bilingual-monolingual pairs; the sensitivity analysis simulated an unobserved confounder based on SES, the covariate with the largest pre-match SMDs

Do Spanish-English Bilingual Children Outperform Monolingual English-Speaking Children on Executive Function Tasks in Early Childhood? A Propensity Score Analysis. article_title: Experimental researches on learning to spell. Part II.
citation: Winch, W. H. (1913). Experimental Researches on Learning to Spell, Part II. The Journal of Educational Psychology.
title: Teachers should improve instruction through controlled experiments with exact measurement, supported by educational psychologists rather than directives from superior persons
description: The article argues that teachers who try instructional issues for themselves are driven, by the logic of events, toward "controlled procedure with exact measurement," and that educational psychologists should be appointed to help teachers find out which methods work, not to tell them what to adopt. The subsidiary experiments in the article illustrate, in the author's words, "genetically the pathway to experimental pedagogy."
requirements: Teachers need guidance from educational psychologists to frame valid experiments; the article says teachers "cannot usually invent valid experiments, but they can carry them out."
constraints: The article notes the superior persons appointed to direct teachers "do not really know any more than the teachers do," so the principle excludes top-down prescription.
target_learners: elementary school children in poor urban neighbourhoods
target_learning_goals: spelling and orthography
examples: The Head Master's twelve-week home-copy method, the flash-card methods, and the head-to-head teaching contest each failed or proved inconclusive until the controlled First and Second Experiments were run.
key_sources: Winch, W. H. (1913). Experimental Researches on Learning to Spell, Part II. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0076021

article_title: Solution of Problems in Geometry.
citation: Wood, B. D., & Bell, J. C. (1914). Solution of problems in geometry. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Wood+Bell+Solution+of+Problems+in+Geometry
title: Prerequisite life habits of attention, precise language, and conscious motor control should precede instruction aimed at developing skilled geometry problem solvers
description: The study's authors argue that success in geometry problem solving rests on "neural organization" — readiness to grasp significant features and reject irrelevant ones — built from life habits of noting and recalling details, precise language use, and conscious motor control. They warn that "unless these life habits are already well formed, the prospect of developing a good geometer is not a very favorable one." Design of geometry instruction should therefore attend to these habits as prerequisites.
requirements: Learners must already have well-formed habits of accurately noting and recalling details, care and precision in language use, and conscious control of motor activities for such readiness to be present.
constraints: The authors state that the extent to which these life habits are developed by the study of formal geometry remains an open question for experimental investigation.
target_learners: secondary and teacher-training students studying plane geometry
target_learning_goals: geometry problem solving
locus reasoning
geometrical construction
examples: The six good students showed faultless verbal description and inhibited motor activity, while poor students like PD produced unstable, incorrect figures and uncontrollable pencil use.
