article_title: Do processing patterns of strengths and weaknesses predict differential treatment response?
citation: Miciak Jeremy, Williams Jacob L., Taylor W. Pat, Cirino Paul T., Fletcher Jack M., Vaughn Sharon. (2016). Do Processing Patterns of Strengths and Weaknesses Predict Differential Treatment Response? Journal of Educational Psychology, 108(6), 898-909. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000096
title: Processing strengths and weaknesses (PSW) approaches to LD identification, operationalized by the XBA and C/DM methods
description: PSW methods operationalize a cognitive discrepancy approach to LD identification based on identifying an intraindividual pattern of processing strengths and weaknesses. The XBA approach "utilizes a series of normative comparisons to identify deficient and normal academic and cognitive abilities," requiring an achievement deficit, a normal cognitive profile, and a theoretically related cognitive deficit. The C/DM instead "calculates difference scores across a number of cognitive and achievement tests and compares these difference scores against computed critical values," requiring concordance between achievement and cognitive deficits and discordance with a cognitive strength. Both are aligned with CHC theory in this study.
requirements: Requires a comprehensive psychoeducational assessment battery covering the seven CHC broad cognitive abilities plus reading, administered individually by a trained examiner
constraints: The article notes the two methods are often presented as equivalent but demonstrate key differences in how they identify PSW patterns and in theoretical orientation
target_learners: K-12 students with academic difficulties being evaluated for learning disabilities
target_learning_goals: Accurate LD identification and planning of individualized academic intervention
examples: Applied at pretest to 206 fourth graders with GMRT reading comprehension standard scores below 85 to classify students as LD or not LD prior to a 16-week intensive reading intervention
key_sources: Miciak Jeremy, Williams Jacob L., Taylor W. Pat, Cirino Paul T., Fletcher Jack M., Vaughn Sharon. (2016). Do Processing Patterns of Strengths and Weaknesses Predict Differential Treatment Response? Journal of Educational Psychology, 108(6), 898-909. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000096

article_title: From individual word recognition to word list and text reading fluency.
citation: Altani, A., Protopapas, A., Katopodi, K., & Georgiou, G. K. (2019). From Individual Word Recognition to Word List and Text Reading Fluency. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000359
title: Multi-item sequence processing account of reading fluency development
description: The article advances and tests the account that fluent reading of multiple words is co-determined, after basic word recognition is mastered, by an additional ability to process multi-item sequences, indexed by serial naming tasks. Readers process one stimulus while articulating the previous one and previewing upcoming items, buffering information about "items that have already been viewed but not yet pronounced." This endogenously controlled sequential processing is proposed as the mechanism underlying the transition from word-by-word reading to efficient processing of word sequences, potentially underpinning prosody via syntactic and semantic planning.
requirements: Basic accuracy and speed in individual word recognition must first be achieved (around Grade 3 for high-frequency short words) before the sequence-processing component contributes unique fluency variance
constraints: The aspect of multiword processing addressed is word-level multi-item processing, not supralexical processing involving syntactic, semantic, and discourse structures of text
target_learners: Elementary school children in Grades 1, 3, and 5 learning to read in alphabetic orthographies
target_learning_goals: Reading fluency development, including word-list reading fluency and text reading fluency
examples: A two-predictor regression model with discrete word reading and serial digit naming was tested across grades and languages; serial digit naming uniquely predicted fluency in Grades 3 and 5 in both Greek and English
key_sources: Altani, A., Protopapas, A., Katopodi, K., & Georgiou, G. K. (2019). From Individual Word Recognition to Word List and Text Reading Fluency. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000359

article_title: Recent publications in history [Four articles and two books].
citation: J. C. B. (1917). Recent Publications in History. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org
title: Dynes's primary-grade program for developing the historic sense through the immediate social environment
description: Dynes's book Socializing the Child proposes beginning history in Grade I rather than relegating it to upper grades, using "play, construction work, pictures and stories" to familiarize children with their immediate social environment, including community workers and public enterprises. Grade II covers primitive life, fire, occupations and existing tribes such as Eskimos and American Indians; Grade III studies home life and customs of Holland, Germany, Japan and France, plus stories of Bible characters, Greek and Roman heroes and Columbus. The reviewer judges the work well planned and valuable for building a foundation for later systematic historical study.
requirements: Reference book lists for the teacher's use, which the author supplies
target_learning_goals: Developing the historic sense and familiarity with the social environment as a foundation for later systematic historical study
examples: Grade I familiarizes children with the policeman, fireman, mail carrier and public enterprises such as water works, parks and schools; Grade II takes up primitive man and tribes like the Eskimos and American Indians
key_sources: J. C. B. (1917). Recent Publications in History. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org

article_title: Recent publications in history [Four articles and two books].
citation: J. C. B. (1917). Recent Publications in History. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org
title: History examinations should test interpretation and use of historical materials rather than memoriter reproduction of isolated facts
description: In his chapter on the history examination, Johnson, as reported by the reviewer, "deplores the emphasis placed upon the memoriter reproduction of isolated historical facts, and urges a type of examination which will show the pupils' ability to interpret and utilize historical materials, situations or generalizations." The principle holds that assessment in history should reveal whether pupils can work with historical content, not merely recall it. The reviewer presents this as Johnson's central recommendation for examination practice.
requirements: Examination tasks built around historical materials, situations or generalizations that pupils must interpret and utilize
target_learners: Elementary and secondary school history students
target_learning_goals: Ability to interpret and utilize historical materials, situations or generalizations
examples: Johnson contrasts the recommended interpretive examination with the prevailing emphasis on reproducing isolated historical facts
key_sources: J. C. B. (1917). Recent Publications in History. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org

article_title: Recent publications in history [Four articles and two books].
citation: J. C. B. (1917). Recent Publications in History. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org
title: Johnson's conception of history teaching: making the social world intelligible as the permanent aim
description: Johnson's book, which the reviewer calls the most recent, most incisive and most illuminating study of history teaching yet to appear, contrasts the simple narrative and moralist-didactic types of historical account with the modern scientific conception that strives for objective interpretation of social conditions. Of all proposed aims, the reviewer reports Johnson holds "the only really permanent aim is to under- stand the world in which we live,—to make the social world intelligible," so history is studied for its own sake rather than for disciplinary or moral advantage. Johnson's task for the teacher is making the past real, employing all imaginable aids and allowing pupils' self-activity.
requirements: History work confined to interpreting the past; Johnson recommends leaving imaginative re-creation of historic characters to literature and treating today's governmental organizations as contemporary rather than historical phenomena
constraints: Johnson expresses doubt that correlation schemes with geography, literature and government may be detrimental to history itself and disorganizing for other subjects
target_learning_goals: Understanding the present social world through acquaintance with the life of the past
examples: The book's first five chapters survey the history of the teaching of history, and chapters four and five survey history's curricular place from the sixteenth century onward, with reference to France, Germany and the United States
key_sources: J. C. B. (1917). Recent Publications in History. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org

article_title: The child's speech. I. The impulse to speech.
citation: Robert MacDougall. (1912). The Child's Speech. I. The Impulse to Speech. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=none-in-text
title: MacDougall's account of the impulse to speech as arising from inherited developmental factors plus external social-practical demands
description: The article presents a theory in which the incentives to speech are internal and external: they 'spring from the new forces which are growing up within his own nature' as well as 'in the world about the child'. Speech appears as a spontaneous product of maturation, driven by expressive and social instincts, imitation, and play, and sustained by the practical need to make wants known and secure social mediation.
requirements: the child must have reached a phase of organic development in which brain and organs of speech are sufficiently matured for articulation and understanding
constraints: the account is a theoretical argument rather than an empirical test; it is the first in a series of papers, with imitation's later role deferred to subsequent installments
target_learning_goals: early language acquisition and articulate expression
examples: the article describes the infant's widening activity — looking, listening, reaching, handling — as the developmental context in which the craving for expression arises
key_sources: Robert MacDougall. (1912). The Child's Speech. I. The Impulse to Speech. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=none-in-text

article_title: The child's speech. I. The impulse to speech.
citation: Robert MacDougall. (1912). The Child's Speech. I. The Impulse to Speech. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=none-in-text
title: Do not anticipate the child's wants or interpret rudimentary expressions once speech is expected; let speaking bring reward and its absence bring consequences
description: The article recommends that, to hasten speech acquisition, the child 'should be made to feel as fully as possible the rewards of success in speaking', through profit (getting what is asked for) and praise. It adds that 'it is unwise to anticipate the child's wants and interpret his most rudimentary expressions', because this removes the motive for acquiring speech.
requirements: the child must be of an age to acquire the verbal symbol or already have attempted to use it before gratification is withheld
constraints: the article frames this as a method for children at the stage of acquiring verbal symbols, not for younger infants
target_learners: young children at the stage of acquiring first verbal symbols
target_learning_goals: acquisition and motivated use of spoken language
examples: the article's example: refusing to attend or gratify a desire indicated by gesture or inarticulate cry when the child can use verbal symbols
key_sources: Robert MacDougall. (1912). The Child's Speech. I. The Impulse to Speech. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=none-in-text

article_title: The child's speech. I. The impulse to speech.
citation: Robert MacDougall. (1912). The Child's Speech. I. The Impulse to Speech. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=none-in-text
title: Show the child he is understood and appreciated when he speaks, since sympathetic response is essential to acquiring speech
description: The article urges that 'the teacher should be no less careful to let the child see that he is understood and appreciated when he speaks', because the child 'seeks recognition in word and look' and 'may be seriously discouraged if it be found lacking'. Feeling understood is described as clarifying, educative, and a ratification of the child's thought.
requirements: an attentive, responsive hearer must be present when the child speaks
constraints: the article warns that amused attention to quaint or vulgar phrases can fix persistent idiosyncrasies of child speech through delighted repetition
target_learning_goals: confident, motivated use of spoken language
examples: the article notes adults' own speech and thought are readily disturbed by an inattentive or unresponsive hearer, as grounds for the child's need for sympathetic response

article_title: Promoting persistence in the biological and medical sciences: An expectancy-value approach to intervention.
citation: Hecht, C. A., Harackiewicz, J. M., Priniski, S. J., Canning, E. A., Tibbetts, Y., & Hyde, J. S. (2019). Promoting Persistence in the Biological and Medical Sciences: An Expectancy-Value Approach to Intervention. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000356
title: Expectancy-value theory: positive expectancy x value interaction in academic choices, extended to a two-process account of UVI effects
description: The article applies Eccles' expectancy-value theory, in which "students are most likely to pursue an education in a particular domain if they both value the domain and believe they can succeed in it." It extends this with a two-process account: UVIs initiate task engagement, which improves performance for struggling students, and personal relevance reflection, which amplifies confident students' persistence decisions. The UVI x confidence interaction on persistence is read as consistent with the theorized synergistic expectancy x value effect.
requirements: Effects on persistence are expected only when the intervention increases subjective task value in a domain students are considering pursuing, such as an introductory course for intended majors.
constraints: The authors note the personal-relevance process may be a double-edged sword: students with doubts may decide to pursue a field where they perceive both value and a high likelihood of success instead.
target_learners: undergraduate students in introductory biomedical science courses
target_learning_goals: persistence in biomedical STEM majors
course performance in gateway science courses
examples: The UVI x confidence interaction on two-year persistence was interpreted as consistent with the positive expectancy-value interaction, since only in the value-emphasizing UVI condition did confidence predict persistence.
key_sources: Hecht, C. A., Harackiewicz, J. M., Priniski, S. J., Canning, E. A., Tibbetts, Y., & Hyde, J. S. (2019). Promoting Persistence in the Biological and Medical Sciences: An Expectancy-Value Approach to Intervention. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000356

article_title: Promoting persistence in the biological and medical sciences: An expectancy-value approach to intervention.
citation: Hecht, C. A., Harackiewicz, J. M., Priniski, S. J., Canning, E. A., Tibbetts, Y., & Hyde, J. S. (2019). Promoting Persistence in the Biological and Medical Sciences: An Expectancy-Value Approach to Intervention. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000356
title: Utility-value writing assignments in an introductory biology course for biomedical majors
description: The intervention consisted of three graded writing assignments in the first course of a two-course introductory biology sequence. In both conditions students selected a lecture concept, formulated a question, and wrote a 1-2 page essay; UVI students additionally "discuss[ed] the relevance of the concept or issue to your own life" (essay variation) or wrote a letter connecting material to another person (letter variation). Assignments were cumulatively worth 1.8% of the course grade and were graded by biology graduate students for scientific accuracy.
requirements: Assignments were presented as graded course assignments within a gateway course taken by prospective biomedical majors, and instructional staff were blind to condition.
constraints: The article notes findings are limited to the context of the biomedical fields and to students who were all at least considering a biomedical major.
target_learners: undergraduate students in introductory biology, including first-generation and underrepresented minority students
target_learning_goals: engagement with course material
reflection on personal relevance of course topics
course performance and STEM persistence
examples: In a double-blind randomized controlled trial across four semesters, 2,378 students enrolled; the analyzed sample comprised 1,039 consenting students, with 579 assigned to the UVI condition and 460 to control.
key_sources: Hecht, C. A., Harackiewicz, J. M., Priniski, S. J., Canning, E. A., Tibbetts, Y., & Hyde, J. S. (2019). Promoting Persistence in the Biological and Medical Sciences: An Expectancy-Value Approach to Intervention. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000356

article_title: Early prediction of math difficulties with the use of a neural networks model.
citation: Psyridou, M., Koponen, T., Tolvanen, A., Aunola, K., Lerkkanen, M.-K., Poikkeus, A.-M., & Torppa, M. (2024). Early prediction of math difficulties with the use of a neural networks model. Journal of Educational Psychology, 116(2), 212-232. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000835
title: Neural networks (multilayer perceptron) models as a prediction-oriented approach to early identification of learning difficulties
description: The article frames deep neural networks as machine-learning models that, unlike classical linear, inference-focused statistics, can identify linear and non-linear associations, interaction effects, or combinations of these, and can handle many correlated predictors. A multilayer perceptron learns connection weights from labelled training data and is then applied to a held-out testing sample to forecast a dichotomized outcome. The authors position this as a complement to inference models: "Prediction allows, for example, the identification of whether an individual will experience MD without requiring an understanding of the underlying mechanisms". They also name the approach's key limitation: neural networks are often referred to as black boxes.
requirements: A supervised, labelled outcome for training, with training and testing samples split from the data
Sufficient sample size; the article notes missing cases must be imputed because the MLP cannot be performed with missing data
constraints: Limited interpretability: neural networks models are often referred to as black boxes due to lack of transparency in decision-making
The study was not preregistered; the cut-off defining MD is somewhat arbitrary
target_learners: kindergarten-age children (age 6) in longitudinal school samples
target_learning_goals: early identification of children at risk of math difficulties (arithmetic fluency)
examples: The MLP was trained 20 times on 70% of the First Steps data and evaluated on 30%, using the SPSS Version 26 neural networks module with binary cross-entropy loss and scaled conjugate gradient descent
key_sources: Psyridou, M., Koponen, T., Tolvanen, A., Aunola, K., Lerkkanen, M.-K., Poikkeus, A.-M., & Torppa, M. (2024). Early prediction of math difficulties with the use of a neural networks model. Journal of Educational Psychology, 116(2), 212-232. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000835

article_title: The causal ordering of academic achievement and self-concept of ability during elementary school: A longitudinal study.
citation: Helmke, A., & van Aken, M. A. G. (1995). The causal ordering of academic achievement and self-concept of ability during elementary school: A longitudinal study. Journal of Educational Psychology, 87(4), 624-637. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-0663.87.4.624
title: Model marks and test performance as separate achievement constructs in longitudinal studies of self-concept and achievement
description: The article recommends that future investigations on causal ordering include both marks and test performance as distinct latent variables rather than a single achievement indicator, because single-indicator models yield artificially reciprocal patterns. The authors state this complex model was "recommended for future investigations on this issue," and that single-indicator use "may lead to artificially high regression coefficients." This applies to longitudinal panel research on motivation–achievement relations.
requirements: Longitudinal data with both teacher-given marks and standardized achievement tests collected at each measurement wave, as in the SCHOLASTIC project
constraints: Requires school systems where both marks and tests are available; the article notes that in German schools only one official mark per year and domain exists, and that using a single indicator for marks requires assumptions about reliability
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement
self-concept of academic ability
examples: Models 2a/2b (single indicator) versus Model 3c (separate latents with cross-lagged paths between marks and tests) were fit to 3 waves of data from 697 students
key_sources: Helmke, A., & van Aken, M. A. G. (1995). The causal ordering of academic achievement and self-concept of ability during elementary school: A longitudinal study. Journal of Educational Psychology, 87(4), 624-637. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-0663.87.4.624

article_title: The causal ordering of academic achievement and self-concept of ability during elementary school: A longitudinal study.
citation: Helmke, A., & van Aken, M. A. G. (1995). The causal ordering of academic achievement and self-concept of ability during elementary school: A longitudinal study. Journal of Educational Psychology, 87(4), 624-637. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-0663.87.4.624
title: Two distinct sources of children's self-evaluation of ability: competence and evaluation by significant others
description: Drawing on developmental psychology (Harter), the article interprets its findings as supporting a conception of "two distinct sources of self-evaluation in children": competence (speed and quality of performance, indicated by test performance) and evaluation by significant others (teachers, indicated by marks). The article reports that both sources "appear to operate (at least, to some degree) independently from each other," since both marks and actual test competence influenced self-concept development, even though students were not informed of individual test results.
requirements: Achievement feedback channels that can be separated into objective performance experience and socially communicated evaluation
constraints: Interpretation offered in the discussion; the article notes one cannot rule out informal within-classroom social comparison processes after tests
target_learning_goals: self-concept of ability in mathematics
examples: Test performance influenced later self-concept although students were not told individual results, suggesting direct competence experience feeds self-evaluation

article_title: A report on the teaching and practice of hygiene in the public normal schools of the United States.
citation: Arthur Heche. (1909). A Report on the Teaching and Practice of Hygiene in the Public Normal Schools of the United States. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org/journal/jeducreducpsyc
title: Correlate hygiene throughout the whole curriculum so prospective teachers habitually consider school problems from the point of view of hygiene
description: The article recommends that hygiene pervade the whole curriculum rather than appear only in physiology. It describes one school that "offers several courses in hygiene, and in addition deals in various other courses with the hygienic aspects of school problems," including sanitation with school administration and hygiene in practice-school observation. The author states that "Such correlation of hygiene with other courses unifies the student's knowledge and instils the habit of considering all school problems" hygienically.
requirements: Every instructor must be awake to the problems involved, according to the article, for such a program to be carried out successfully
target_learning_goals: personal, school, and community hygiene; habitual hygienic evaluation of school problems such as discipline, daily programs, and pupil classification
examples: One surveyed school deals with hygienic aspects of school problems in courses on school administration, practice-school observation, educational psychology, and child psychology.

article_title: Sex differences in mathematics anxiety and attitudes: Concurrent and longitudinal relations to mathematical competence.
citation: Geary, D. C., Hoard, M. K., Nugent, L., Chu, F., Scofield, J. E., & Hibbard, D. F. (2019). Sex Differences in Mathematics Anxiety and Attitudes: Concurrent and Longitudinal Relations to Mathematical Competence. Journal of Educational Psychology, 111(8), 1447-1461. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000355
title: Two-facet structure of adolescent mathematics anxiety: evaluations versus learning
description: The article's mathematics anxiety measure factored into two facets: a learning facet explaining 43% of item covariance (e.g., "Having to use the tables in the back of a math book") and an evaluation facet explaining 13% (e.g., "Taking an examination in a math course"), moderately correlated (r = .47). This structure parallels Baloglu and Koçak's test/coursework factors, and the sex difference emerged only for the evaluation facet, showing global assessments can obscure specific differences.
requirements: A measure whose items distinguish evaluative situations (tests, examinations) from general learning situations; the authors note their measure lacked numerical-activity items so that facet could not be assessed.
constraints: Adolescent sample using adapted Hopko et al. items; no numerical-activity items included, so whether that facet exists in adolescents was untestable.
target_learning_goals: mathematics anxiety
mathematics attitudes
mathematics achievement
examples: Factor analysis of 10 adapted items in the sixth-grade sample yielded the two composites (α = .76 learning, α = .81 evaluation).

citation: Geary, D. C., Hoard, M. K., Nugent, L., Chu, F., Scofield, J. E., & Hibbard, D. F. (2019). title: Mathematics efficacy and utility beliefs form a single mathematics-attitudes construct in this sample
description: Unlike studies separating utility (value) beliefs from self-efficacy, the article's principal components, parallel, and MAP analyses indicated utility and efficacy items defined a single factor for mathematics, so an overall mathematics attitudes score (7 items, α = .84) was used. The authors suggest the collapse may reflect uniformly high utility ratings across students, reducing variation and discriminating power.
requirements: Attitude items assessing both self-evaluated efficacy and long-term utility beliefs, e.g., "How much do you like doing math?" on a 1-to-7 scale, with factor-structure checks before compositing.
constraints: The single-factor result may be sample- or era-specific; the article notes it might reflect a secular increase in students' beliefs about the importance of mathematics.

academic self-efficacy
utility value of mathematics
examples: The Michigan Study of Adolescent and Adult Transitions attitudes measure was analyzed with PCA, parallel, and MAP procedures before compositing.

article_title: Zur Erkennung jugendlichen Schwachsinns.
citation: Paul Wilhelm Knuth. (1909). Zur Erkennung jugendlichen Schwachsinns [review of Gustav Major's monograph]. Zeitschrift für Experimentelle Pädagogik, 9, 425. none in text
title: Major's three-class taxonomy of feeble-mindedness: debility, imbecility, and idiocy
description: The review reports that Major classifies the feeble-minded by severity: "The feeble-minded are grouped into three classes,debility.imbecihtv and idiocy, corresponding to light, medium and severe cases." The organizing axis is defect type as well as severity: "The leading characteristic of the first class is their ethical defect, that of the last two intellectual defect." This taxonomy structures Major's discussion of teachability, moral treatment, and diagnosis throughout the monograph.
requirements: Diagnosis must first distinguish the severity class, since the leading defect differs by class: ethical defect in the light cases and intellectual defect in the medium and severe cases
target_learners: children identified as feeble-minded (debility, imbecility, idiocy)
target_learning_goals: identification and classification of degree of mental weakness to guide educational placement and treatment
examples: Major's diagnostic outline assigns children to debility, imbecility, or idiocy corresponding to light, medium, and severe cases

article_title: Zur Erkennung jugendlichen Schwachsinns.
citation: Paul Wilhelm Knuth. (1909). Zur Erkennung jugendlichen Schwachsinns [review of Gustav Major's monograph]. Zeitschrift für Experimentelle Pädagogik, 9, 425. none in text
title: Major's diagnostic procedure for detecting mental debility in youth
description: The element is Major's full diagnostic outline for detecting mental debility, described as "fairly simple and can be applied by the capable parent and teacher." It consists of "the chief tests being (1) mathematical problems; (2) questions involving discrimination; (3) tests of school learning, and (4) various tests by the psychoanalytic method" such as association reactions, mental imagery tests, and story analysis, plus "an elaborate outline for medical examination."
requirements: Application by a capable parent or teacher, per the review's statement that the method is simple enough for lay use
target_learning_goals: detection and diagnosis of mental debility to inform educational decisions
examples: Test components include mathematical problems, discrimination questions, tests of school learning, association reactions, tests of mental imagery, and analysis of stories

article_title: Effects of peers’ emotions on students’ emotions, achievement goals, mental effort, and performance.
citation: Hu, Y., Elliot, A. J., Wouters, P., van der Schaaf, M., Kester, L., & Pekrun, R. (2024). Effects of peers' emotions on students' emotions, achievement goals, mental effort, and performance. Journal of Educational Psychology, 116(7), 1283–1299. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000895
title: Three coexisting mechanisms of emotion transmission
description: The article frames emotion transmission — people "catching" the emotions of others — via three proposed mechanisms that "can coexist and affect the outcomes". Primitive emotional contagion holds that observers mimic facial, vocal, and postural expressions and afferent feedback triggers the same state; emotion categorization holds that categorizing an expression as an emotional state activates a similar state; social appraisal holds that appraising the situation from the expresser's expression triggers the emotion. The study uses this framework to motivate expecting transmission from peers to students in observational learning.
requirements: An expresser displaying emotional expressions (here a peer model's facial, postural, and vocal expressions in videos) that observers are exposed to
constraints: Transmission can be moderated by activity characteristics, individual differences such as the tendency to catch emotions, and social factors such as liking the expresser
target_learners: University students in observational learning of a science game
target_learning_goals: Achievement emotions during learning
Achievement goals
Mental effort and performance
examples: The article illustrates with witnessing a smile: one may mimic it, categorize it as enjoyment, or appraise that another is happy, all possibly triggering one's own enjoyment
key_sources: Hu, Y., Elliot, A. J., Wouters, P., van der Schaaf, M., Kester, L., & Pekrun, R. (2024). Effects of peers' emotions on students' emotions, achievement goals, mental effort, and performance. Journal of Educational Psychology, 116(7), 1283–1299. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000895

article_title: Effects of peers’ emotions on students’ emotions, achievement goals, mental effort, and performance.
citation: Hu, Y., Elliot, A. J., Wouters, P., van der Schaaf, M., Kester, L., & Pekrun, R. (2024). Effects of peers' emotions on students' emotions, achievement goals, mental effort, and performance. Journal of Educational Psychology, 116(7), 1283–1299. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000895
title: CosmiClean game and peer-model emotion videos
description: CosmiClean is a game "designed ... to teach secondary school and university students the principles of separation processes for recycling materials", in which players build separation chains of conveyors, separators, and receptors across cargo levels with corrective feedback. For the intervention, three recorded videos (about 23 minutes each, 13 game levels) showed a male peer model playing the same script with enjoyment, frustration, or a neutral expression, filmed from a first-person perspective and hosted on Edpuzzle.
requirements: Participants watch the video carefully and cannot skip it; a manipulation check after the posttest verifies perceived emotion
constraints: The study used a virtual peer participants did not know, and an online rather than classroom format, to keep exposure to a single emotion clearly controlled
target_learning_goals: Chemistry separation processes: using nine separators, twelve materials, and eight properties
examples: Videos asked multiple-answer questions about which separators to use, gave corrective feedback, then the peer model explained and ran the recycling

article_title: How the Dearborn Intelligence Examination Standards were Obtained.
citation: Walter F. Dearborn and Edward A. Lincoln. (1922). How the Dearborn Intelligence Examination Standards Were Obtained. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org
title: Dearborn separate-community age-standards method
description: A test-standardization method in which scores from each community are treated separately rather than lumped, distributed by months so both median score and median age can be found, then plotted so standards can be chosen at each half year. The aim is that "the median child of each age should have an intelligence quotient within the normal group (0.90 to 1.10) no matter which community he was in." The article presents this as an alternative to the customary large-N norming that produced classes placed too high or too low and inconsistent rankings across tests.
requirements: Examinations administered in every grade from the second through the senior high school class
Scores distributed by months within each community so median ages as well as median scores can be computed
constraints: Series I lacked enough upper-grade children, so standards from the twelfth year on had to be estimated from the continuation of the plotted lines
The towns were near Boston with agriculture and manufacturing and a sprinkling of children of foreign parents, so generalization to other town types is not directly established
target_learners: school pupils from grade two through senior high school
target_learning_goals: age- and grade-based intelligence-test norms
fair classification of pupils relative to standards

Series II was administered in three towns in every grade from the second through the senior class of high school, while Series I was standardized the same way but "it was not practicable to get results from so many upper grade children," so its upper standards were estimated. article_title: Accuracy in school children. Does improvement in numerical accuracy "transfer"?
citation: Winch, W. H. (1910). Accuracy in school children. Does improvement in numerical accuracy "transfer"? The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org
title: Seek numerical accuracy in school arithmetic for its practical value in life, not on the expectation that it will transfer to arithmetical reasoning
description: This pedagogical principle holds that drill aimed at numerical computation should be justified by computation's own usefulness rather than by expected gains in reasoning. Winch concludes that teachers may in some cases improve one function by improving another, but for arithmetic "numerical accuracy should be sought for because it is valuable in actual life, and not because we can feel confident that an improvement in it will transfer to accuracy of arithmetical reasoning". The principle is pending more conclusive experiments.
requirements: The article states indirect improvement of a function should only be attempted if the indirect method is quantitatively better than the direct one, or the direct method is not available.
constraints: The author hedges the conclusion pending more conclusive experiments, and the experimental results across the four schools were too irregular to warrant a conclusion of definite transfer.
target_learners: Elementary school children in Standards II-VII studying arithmetic
target_learning_goals: Accuracy in numerical computation
Accuracy in arithmetical reasoning
examples: In the four experiments, one matched half of each class practised rule sums while the other did history, drawing, geography or English composition, and both were retested on problems marked for reasoning only.

description: Because grades operate partly through the affective reactions they elicit, the article argues grading practices should attend to students' emotional responses. It finds that "teachers should be aware of the potential negative consequences of the grades they give and try to reduce these," while not recommending abandoning grades, which "can provide vital information to teachers, students, and parents." Low-performing students perceiving high class performance norms, and boys, are named as particularly vulnerable.

title: Control-value theory of achievement emotions
description: Control-value theory explains achievement emotions through students' appraisals: 'achievement emotions are based on students' appraisals of control and value of the learning activities and achievement outcomes.' It distinguishes activity emotions (enjoyment, boredom, anger) from outcome emotions (pride, anxiety, shame, hopelessness), tying activity emotions mainly to intrinsic value and outcome emotions to achievement value. The study invokes it to predict how parental expectations and over-aspiration shift perceived control and the value of failure.

constraints: The article notes boredom can also occur when perceived control is too high, making its relation to control non-linear

examples: The study used the theory to predict that high expectations raise perceived control, increasing positive and reducing negative emotions, while over-aspiration shifts outcome appraisals toward failure.

citation: Sakaki, M., Murayama, K., Frenzel, A. C., Goetz, T., Marsh, H. W., Lichtenfeld, S., Wünsch, M., & Pekrun, R. (2025). Parents' academic expectations and aspirations predict students' achievement emotions. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000959
title: Parents should balance their expectations and aspirations to support students' emotional well-being
description: The article recommends that parents align their aspirations with their realistic expectations rather than aspiring far beyond them: 'These results highlight the need for parents to balance their expectations and aspirations to support their children's emotional well-being and academic success.' Higher expectations contemporaneously accompany more positive emotions, but over-aspiration contemporaneously predicts greater anxiety and lower pride, and high expectations predict more anxiety, anger, and shame a year later.

article_title: Short- and long-term effects of over-reporting of grades on academic self-concept and achievement.
citation: Sticca, F., Götz, T., Nett, U. E., Hubbard, K., & Haag, L. (2017). Short- and Long-Term Effects of Over-Reporting of Grades on Academic Self-Concept and Achievement. Journal of Educational Psychology, 109(6), 842-854. https://dx.doi.org/10.1037/edu0000174
title: Self-enhancement as a short-term self-concept booster that risks a vicious cycle of declining self-concept and achievement
description: The article proposes that over-reporting grades raises self-concept in the short term but, because the boost rests on unrealistic self-evaluation, it sets up expectations students cannot meet, threatening the self-concept and re-triggering self-enhancement. As the authors put it, "a vicious cycle could arise from these dynamics." Protective causal attributions (success to ability, failure to luck) and underestimated learning effort are proposed as reinforcing and moderating factors, though these roles remain hypothetical and untested in this study.
requirements: Short-term self-concept benefits depend on unrealistic self-evaluation that later fails to match attained achievement
constraints: The potential moderating role of learning effort and the mediating role of attributions remain hypothetical and would need to be examined in future studies
No causal interpretations are possible from the latent growth models
target_learning_goals: Maintaining accurate academic self-concept
Sustaining academic achievement over multiple school years
examples: The three-wave TPPLGM showed self-enhancement raised self-concept in Grade 9 (β = .28) while predicting more negative self-concept slopes and, via self-concept, more negative achievement slopes

He writes that "numerical accuracy should be sought for because it is valuable in actual life, and not because we can feel con- fident that an improvement in it will transfer to accuracy of arithmetical reasoning." article_title: Daily affective-motivational experiences during exam preparation: Feedback loops, stability, and change over time.
citation: Berweger, B., Breitwieser, J., Kracke, B., Brod, G., & Dietrich, J. (2024). Daily Affective-Motivational Experiences During Exam Preparation: Feedback Loops, Stability, and Change Over Time. PsychArchives preprint. https://hdl.handle.net/20.500.12034/10953
title: Three-measure framework for temporal dynamics of affective-motivational experiences: carryover, instability, and variability
description: The article organizes the question of whether affective-motivational experiences remain stable or fluctuate using three complementary dynamic measures. It investigates "the extent to which affective-motivational experiences remained stable or fluctuated from one situation to the next, using carryover (autoregressive effects), instability (rMSSD), and variability (within-person SD) as dyamic measures". Carryover captures how strongly a state persists to the next occasion, rMSSD captures moment-to-moment instability, and within-person SD captures overall variability. The framework is applied to medical students' motivation and emotions during exam preparation and analyzed with DSEM in Mplus.
requirements: Intensive longitudinal (daily diary) data with repeated measures of the affective-motivational states of interest, analyzed with time series modeling (DSEM in Mplus)
constraints: Applied in this article to a 40-day exam preparation period with medical students; the article does not claim generalization beyond this setting
target_learning_goals: understanding and regulating motivational and emotional dynamics during self-regulated exam preparation
examples: The study used the three measures to show that anxiety and boredom were more stable than positive emotions and anger across the 40-day period

article_title: Aphasic performance in the Terman Vocabulary Test.
citation: Wells, F. L. (1922). Aphasic performance in the Terman vocabulary test. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0072510
title: Word knowledge splits into ability to use/complete a word versus ability to define it by relation to other words
description: The article proposes that vocabulary testing taps two separable abilities: the ability to complete and use a word, and the ability to relate it to the words that describe it. As the author puts it, "Defining a word is not a test of 'knowing' the word itself, but of knowing its relation to certain other words that describe it." In the aphasic case, combination remained relatively intact while definitional association was disturbed; the author also notes people use function words they cannot define, and that some words are more fairly tested one way than the other.

target_learning_goals: vocabulary knowledge
word meaning
examples: The patient answered definition items with fragmentary or insufficient responses (e.g. impolite, quake, plumbing) that the author calls fair examples of word-amnesia, while completing the same words in context

citation: Pressey, L. W. (1919). A Group Scale of Intelligence for Use in the First Three Grades. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org
title: Five special requirements for group testing young children
description: A framework of five problems in building group tests for first-grade children that do not arise for older children: literacy, fatigue, directions, integration, and motivation. The first requirement is that all elements of school training must be avoided, since no reading or writing can be involved for young children.

article_title: Mentality tests: A symposium.
citation: Hollingworth, H. L. (1917). Mentality Tests: A Symposium. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Mentality+Tests%3A+A+Symposium%22+Hollingworth
title: Standardize individual tasks on graded bases and build graded series of single-process tests before combining them into composite scales
description: This principle orders test-development work from the bottom up: particular tasks and tests are first standardized on graded bases, and graded series of tests of a single, definite, objectively describable process are built. Hollingworth states his interest is "in seeing particular tasks and tests standardized on some graded basis, such as age, school grades or standing, occupational success." Only once many such single tasks exist, in duplicate or triplicate sets, may testers "combine them as we like into sectioned or universal scales," correlate them with other characteristics, and classify the scales by the mental functions they involve.
requirements: A considerable number of single tasks must first be standardized on a graded basis such as age, school grades or standing, or occupational success, and be available in duplicate or triplicate sets.
target_learners: individuals of different ages, school grades, and occupations assessed with mental tests
target_learning_goals: objective description and grading of specific mental processes such as language ability, musical ability, and reading
examples: Hollingworth cites Roemer's study of association reactions, Sylvester's study of the form board, tests of musical ability, Trabue's scales for language ability, Pintner's work with the Knox cube, and Thorndike's reading scales as work of this character.

article_title: Individual differences in grammar grade children. A comparative study of forty-four seventh and eighth grade pupils.
citation: Chambers, W. G. (1909). Individual Differences in Grammar Grade Children: A Comparative Study of Forty-Four Seventh and Eight Grade Pupils. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov
title: Grade rigid grading and promotion on natural rather than artificial distinctions, since a rigid system works injustice to individuals
description: The article argues that because pupils of a given grade are not equally endowed in any one subject and no pupil holds the same rank across studies, "a rigid system of grading and promotion must work injustice to individuals." Since grading is nonetheless necessary, it "should be made to depend on natural, rather than artificial, distinctions." This challenges the assumption that all members of a class should proceed at the same pace in all subjects.
requirements: Knowledge of individual pupils' abilities across mental and physical traits, obtained through testing
constraints: The article accepts that grading remains necessary under present conditions and does not propose abolishing it
target_learning_goals: fair and accurate placement and promotion of pupils according to their actual abilities
examples: Rank analysis of 44 pupils showed the least variation of ability in any pupil was five different ranks in ten different traits; the poorest eighth-grade addition and spelling records were surpassed by a randomly selected third-grade child.

article_title: A stitch in time: Strategic self-control in high school and college students.
citation: Duckworth Angela L., White Rachel E., Matteucci Alyssa J., Shearer Annie, Gross James J. (2016). A Stitch in Time: Strategic Self-Control in High School and College Students. Journal of educational psychology, 108(3), 329-341. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000062
title: The process model of self-control organizes strategies into five categories corresponding to stages of impulse generation
description: The process model of self-control organizes self-control strategies by their underlying mechanism and the stage at which they are employed during impulse generation. Impulses develop through a recursive "situation-attention-appraisal-response sequence," yielding "five categories of self-control strategies can be identified, corresponding to distinct stages of impulse generation": situation selection, situation modification, attentional deployment, cognitive change, and response modulation. Its central prediction is that "intervening earlier in the cycle of impulse generation, when impulses are still developing, is more effective than intervening later." The article uses it as a coding taxonomy and as the framework for the interventions.
requirements: Strategies are classifiable by mechanism and by the stage of impulse generation at which they operate
constraints: Direct empirical evidence on situation selection in adolescent students is lacking, per the article
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning
self-control in everyday academic and interpersonal dilemmas

citation: King, I., and Johnson, H. (1914). The Writing Abilities of the Elementary and Grammar School Pupils of a City School System Measured by the Ayres Scale. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0072531
title: The Ayres scale as a workable instrument for measuring and comparing handwriting legibility across ages, grades and schools
description: The Ayres scale grades handwriting on eight supposed equal steps designated 20 to 90, with three specimen styles (vertical, medium slant and full slant) under each grade; grade 20 is very poor writing and 90 is excellence "seldom attained in the public schools." The article uses it to grade 966 specimens copied "in their ordinary hand," to compare grade with grade, age with age, and school with school, and to test the scale's practicability. It concludes the scale is workable but that subjective judging cannot be fully eliminated.

article_title: Mentality and school progress.
citation: Toops, H. A., and Pintker, R. (1918). Mentality and School Progress. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Mentality+and+School+Progress+Toops+Pintner
title: Use extreme school-grade limits (four or more grades retarded; more than one grade advanced) as diagnostic indicators of mental status
description: The article proposes that when a middle 'normal' band is retained and extreme school-grade limits are applied, school position becomes a near-perfect indicator of mental diagnosis: "no individual who is four or more grades retarded in school is above normal in mentality", and none more than one grade advanced is below normal. This was demonstrated on group mental-test and grade data from three schools of differing social status (ages 6 to 16), yielding a perfect association under these limits. The principle allows screening questions about children to be answered without mental testing of large numbers.
requirements: Age-at-grade expectations must be defined per age (e.g., grades 3B/3A as normal for eight-year-olds), and children without the possibility of being retarded or advanced at least one year (ages 6, 14, 15 and above as applicable) must be excluded from the computation.
constraints: The coefficient of +.97 obtained without a middle mentality class was described by the authors as not such as to warrant using school grade as a prediction of mentality until the middle classes are eliminated; the perfect association holds only for the extreme classes defined by the stated limits.
target_learners: Elementary and junior-high school children, ages 6 to 16
target_learning_goals: Diagnosis of mental subnormality or advancement from school progress
examples: In the three-school survey, four grades or more of retardation perfectly indicated a mentality not higher than normal, and two grades or more of advancement at least a normal mentality.

article_title: The dynamics of motivation.
citation: Bell, J. C. (1919). The dynamics of motivation. The Journal of Educational Psychology, X(5-6). https://eric.ed.gov/?q=journal+of+educational+psychology+volume+X
title: The mechanism-drive framework: every mechanism requires a drive, and any mechanism may act as a drive for another
description: The editorial proposes an explanatory account of motivation built on Woodworth's Dynamic Psychology, in which behavior rests on the sensory-motor arc and its modifications. It states the fundamental distinction between "mechanism" and "drive": a mechanism is the neural structure that acts, while a drive is the impetus that sets it going. The article asserts that "any mechanism may act as a 'drive' to bring about a reaction of any other 'mechanism,'" so that complex behavior such as reflective action involves elaborately combined drives and mechanisms rather than a single stimulus-response link.
requirements: An adequate psychology of motivation to develop the account further, which the article says is yet to be written
constraints: The framework is presented as a theoretical account, not a tested result; the article says much current discussion of motivation is superficial or mystical
target_learning_goals: sustained motivation and effort in school learning
examples: The article applies the framework to explain how simple reflex arcs obtain drive from sensory stimulation while complex reflective behavior involves drives that reinforce or inhibit each other through memory and habit formation

citation: Bell, J. C. (1919). The dynamics of motivation. The Journal of Educational Psychology, X(5-6). https://eric.ed.gov/?q=journal+of+educational+psychology+volume+X
title: Study pupils' drives in order to build up motives for school learning rather than merely cater to their whims
description: This principle directs educators to diagnose the motivational makeup of individual learners and to cultivate durable motivational dispositions rather than simply indulging momentary preferences. The article urges that "Educators need to study the 'drives' of individual pupils, not so much to cater to their whims, as to build up those emotional complexes, those likes, desires, aspirations, that will constitute a motive power for the effort required in school learning." In the editorial's framing, this is how the mechanism-drive framework should be applied in educational procedure.
requirements: Teachers must attend to the individual pupil's drives and emotional attitudes rather than assume a learning attitude can be elicited at command
constraints: Part of attitude depends on native endowment and is little subject to modification, per the article
target_learners: school pupils in compulsory universal education
target_learning_goals: sustained effort and a zest for learning across school subjects
examples: The editorial points to fostering a zest for learning by combining and developing pupils' drives as the practical payoff of the analysis

article_title: The dimensions of reading comprehension in Dutch children: Is differentiation by text and question type necessary?
citation: M.M.L. Muijselaar, N.M. Swart, E.G. Steenbeek-Planting, M. Droop, L. Verhoeven, P.F. de Jong. (2017). The dimensions of reading comprehension in Dutch children: Is differentiation by text and question type necessary? Journal of Educational Psychology, 109(1), 70-83. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000120
title: Unidimensional account of reading comprehension
description: The article advances the account that reading comprehension, as measured across varying texts and question types, is best described by a single general factor rather than multiple specific dimensions. Its analyses found specific measures "hardly reflected systematic variation" once a general factor was modeled, so items "largely reflect a common factor". This account challenges the frequent implicit assumption that reading comprehension is multidimensional.
requirements: Requires item pools sampling different text and question types so that specific dimensions, if present, could emerge in factor models
constraints: Evidence comes from Dutch fourth-grade children and the item pool and text/question types studied
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension
examples: Multitrait, multimethod and confirmatory factor models applied to the administered item pool

title: Reading comprehension item pool varying by text and question type
description: A large pool of reading comprehension items constructed so that items differ "according to text and question type", allowing the dimensionality of comprehension to be tested with multitrait, multimethod modeling. The pool was administered to 996 fourth-grade children, and factor scores from the resulting measures were correlated with word reading speed, vocabulary, and working memory.
requirements: Items must systematically cross text type with question type to support multitrait, multimethod modeling
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension assessment
examples: Administered to 996 fourth-grade children in the dimensionality study

article_title: The dimensions of reading comprehension in Dutch children: Is differentiation by text and question type necessary?
citation: M.M.L. Muijselaar, N.M. Swart, E.G. Steenbeek-Planting, M. Droop, L. Verhoeven, P.F. de Jong. (2017). The dimensions of reading comprehension in Dutch children: Is differentiation by text and question type necessary? Journal of Educational Psychology, 109(1), 70-83. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000120
title: Do not assume separate comprehension abilities by text or question type when assessing fourth-grade reading comprehension
description: Because specific measures of comprehension differing by text and question type showed little systematic variation beyond a general factor, assessments of fourth-grade reading comprehension need not be differentiated by text or question type to capture distinct underlying abilities. The article's question — "Is differentiation by text and question type necessary?" — is answered negatively in its data: items largely reflect a common factor.
requirements: Applies to summarizing overall reading comprehension ability rather than diagnosing item-format-specific skills
constraints: Based on Dutch fourth-grade children and the text and question types studied
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension assessment and interpretation
examples: Multitrait, multimethod modeling of a text-by-question-type item pool administered to 996 children

article_title:
Students’ emotion regulation and school-related well-being:
                        Longitudinal models juxtaposing between- and within-person
                        perspectives.
citation: Beaumont, J., Putwain, D. W., Gallard, D., Malone, E., Marsh, H. W., & Pekrun, R. (2022, in press). Students' emotion regulation and school-related wellbeing: Longitudinal models juxtaposing between- and within-person perspectives. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://osf.io/W5CPE
title: Reciprocal reappraisal-wellbeing loop account grounded in Gross's process model, control-value theory, broaden-and-build theory, and the ERAS model
description: The article frames reappraisal-wellbeing reciprocity using Gross's process model of emotion regulation, which organizes strategies into "'antecedent-focused' strategies" implemented before the emotional response and "'response-focused' strategies" implemented after it, and Pekrun's control-value theory. It draws on Harley et al.'s (2019) emotion regulation in achievement situations (ERAS) model, in which control and value appraisals drive the cognitive-change stage, and on broaden-and-build theory, whereby wellbeing broadens cognition enabling positive reinterpretation. These accounts predict a reciprocal loop: reappraisal raises positive emotions and wellbeing, which in turn facilitate further positive reappraisal.
requirements: Requires that students can reframe control and value appraisals of academic situations (e.g., viewing an exam as an opportunity to demonstrate knowledge) before the emotional response develops
constraints: The article notes students have fewer regulation strategies available at school than outside it, limiting alternatives such as situation modification or distraction
target_learners: secondary and upper secondary students aged 11-19
target_learning_goals: school-related wellbeing
emotion regulation in academic situations
examples: The article illustrates ERAS with a student reminding themselves they have prior knowledge for a class discussion (a control appraisal increasing enjoyment) or that a boring lesson matters for an exam (a value appraisal reducing boredom)
key_sources: Beaumont, J., Putwain, D. W., Gallard, D., Malone, E., Marsh, H. W., & Pekrun, R. (2022, in press). Students' emotion regulation and school-related wellbeing: Longitudinal models juxtaposing between- and within-person perspectives. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://osf.io/W5CPE

article_title: The relation between text reading and reading comprehension varies as a function of developmental phase, orthographic depth, and measurement characteristics: Evidence from a meta-analysis.
citation: Leachman, M., Wolters, A., & Kim, Y.-S. G. (2025). The Relation Between Text Reading and Reading Comprehension Varies as a Function of Developmental Phase, Orthographic Depth, and Measurement Characteristics: Evidence From a Meta-Analysis. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000932
title: Dynamic relations hypothesis of the Direct and Indirect Effects Model of Reading (DIER)
description: DIER proposes that relations among reading component skills are not fixed but vary systematically. The article states the "dynamic relations hypothesis, which posits that the relations between component skills and reading are not uniform, but dynamic", varying as a function of reading development, text characteristics such as orthographic depth, and measurement characteristics such as task types. Within DIER, text reading fluency acts as a mediator or bridge connecting word reading and listening comprehension to reading comprehension, and it increasingly mediates these relations with development, completely mediating word reading's relation at some developmental point but never completely mediating listening comprehension's relation. The meta-analysis tested and found support for these hypotheses.
requirements: Reading comprehension and component skills must be assessed with specified tasks, since the theory holds that measurement characteristics shape observed relations
constraints: The theory concerns correlational relations among skills; the present meta-analysis did not examine directionality of the relation
target_learners: learners from kindergarten through adulthood learning to read in alphabetic and morphosyllabic languages
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension
text reading fluency
word reading
examples: The meta-analysis of 401 studies tested the hypothesis that the text reading–comprehension relation varies by developmental phase, orthographic depth, and task type, and the patterns matched the predictions
key_sources: Leachman, M., Wolters, A., & Kim, Y.-S. G. (2025). The Relation Between Text Reading and Reading Comprehension Varies as a Function of Developmental Phase, Orthographic Depth, and Measurement Characteristics: Evidence From a Meta-Analysis. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000932

article_title: Bringing Assessment-to-Instruction (A2i) technology to scale: Exploring the process from development to implementation.
citation: Connor, Carol McDonald; May, Henry; Sparapani, Nicole; Hwang, Jin Kyoung; Adams, Ashley; Wood, Taffeta S.; Siegal, Sarah; Wolfe, Cassidy; Day, Stephanie. (2022). Bringing Assessment-to-Instruction (A2i) Technology to Scale: Exploring the Process from Development to Implementation. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000758
title: The Lattice Model of literacy development
description: The Lattice Model is the theoretical account underlying A2i that places instruction as a central force in students' literacy learning. Aligned with aptitude-by-treatment interactions, it holds that "the effect of instruction depends on each student’s linguistic, text-specific, cognitive, and social-emotional skills", so instructional effects differ by students' baseline skills across developmental domains. It further posits reciprocal, bi-directional effects: instruction improves literacy and linguistic, cognitive, and social-emotional skills, which in turn support literacy. This child-characteristics-by-instruction premise motivates individualizing instruction via A2i's algorithms.
requirements: Assessment information about individual students' language and literacy skills is needed so instruction can be matched to student characteristics
target_learners: kindergarten through third grade students, including English learners
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension
word decoding
vocabulary and language comprehension
examples: A2i's dynamic forecasting intervention algorithms compute recommended minutes of four instruction types based on individual students' language and literacy skills
key_sources: Connor, Carol McDonald; May, Henry; Sparapani, Nicole; Hwang, Jin Kyoung; Adams, Ashley; Wood, Taffeta S.; Siegal, Sarah; Wolfe, Cassidy; Day, Stephanie. (2022). Bringing Assessment-to-Instruction (A2i) Technology to Scale: Exploring the Process from Development to Implementation. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000758

article_title: A Novel Approach to Reading.
citation: L. Z. (1922). A Novel Approach to Reading. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=journal+of+educational+psychology
title: A silent reading method for beginners built on printed commands executed as action responses
description: Watkins' Silent Reading Method teaches beginners to read by having each pupil carry out printed commands physically in front of the class. The commands mix parts of speech and varied actions, e.g. pupils must 'Draw an oblong, a circle and a square' or ask a visitor a question and report the answer. The materials were made 'available so that anyone may attempt to do what she has found possible by actual trial.'
requirements: available printed materials so that anyone may attempt the method
class activities involving other people, objects and actions in the room
constraints: the reviewer notes it is not supposed to displace instruction in literary appreciation and extensive reading
target_learners: beginning readers in the first school year
target_learning_goals: silent reading comprehension of printed commands
examples: pupils in a class of forty carried out printed commands such as telling a visitor a fact and showing a time on a large dial
key_sources: L. Z. (1922). A Novel Approach to Reading. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=journal+of+educational+psychology

article_title: Longitudinal relations among self-concept, intrinsic value, and attainment value across secondary school years in three academic domains.
citation: Arens, A. Katrin; Schmidt, Isabelle; Preckel, Franzis. (2019). Longitudinal relations among self-concept, intrinsic value, and attainment value across secondary school years in three academic domains. The Journal of educational psychology 111 (2019) 4, S. 663-684. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000313
title: Temporal reciprocal relations among motivation constructs in expectancy-value theory
description: The article applies expectancy-value theory's account of temporal relations among motivation constructs, examining how academic self-conpect, intrinsic value, and attainment value predict each other over time in cross-lagged panel models. It reports that "former academic self-concept was positively related to later intrinsic value and attainment value" in math and English, while in German "former intrinsic value and attainment value were positively related to later academic self-concept," with domain-specific patterns and stable relation sizes across Grades 5 to 9.
requirements: Requires longitudinal data with multiple annual measurement waves and cross-lagged panel modeling
Requires domain-specific measures of self-concept and separate value facets
constraints: Findings are domain-specific; directional patterns differ between math, English, and German
Based on German secondary school students in Grades 5 to 9
target_learners: German secondary school students in Grades 5 to 9
target_learning_goals: Academic self-concept and motivational value beliefs in math, German, and English

Longitudinal relations among self-concept, intrinsic value, and attainment value across secondary school years in three academic domains. The Journal of educational psychology 111 (2019) 4, S. 663-684. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000313

article_title: Multiple pathways to success: An examination of integrative motivational profiles among upper elementary and college students.
citation: Linnenbrink-Garcia, L., Wormington, S. V., Snyder, K. E., Riggsbee, J., Perez, T., Ben-Eliyahu, A., & Hill, N. E. (2018). Multiple Pathways to Success: An Examination of Integrative Motivational Profiles Among Upper Elementary and College Students. Journal of Educational Psychology, 110(7), 1026-1048. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000245
title: Integrative motivational profile framework combining Expectancy-Value Theory and Achievement Goal Theory
description: This framework integrates constructs from Expectancy-Value Theory and Achievement Goal Theory to describe how students' motivational beliefs cohere into profiles. As the authors state, "we aimed to identify integrative motivational profiles consisting of competence beliefs (representing expectancies from Expectancy-Value Theory), task value, and three types of achievement goal orientations (mastery, performance-approach, performance-avoidance)". Competence beliefs address whether students believe they can succeed, while task value and goals address why they engage. The framework underpins the person-oriented analyses in both studies.
requirements: Measures of perceived competence, task value, mastery goals, performance-approach goals, and performance-avoidance goals on comparable scales, combined via latent profile analysis.
constraints: Profiles identified are by design unique to each sample, raising generalizability concerns the authors note from prior person-oriented research.
target_learning_goals: academic engagement
achievement in schooling and science
examples: In Study 1, fifth graders' domain-general schooling motivation was profiled into four groups; in Study 2, college students' science motivation was profiled in a gateway chemistry context.
