article_title: Supplemental Material for Learning With Animation and Illusions of Understanding
citation: Animation and Illusions of Understanding: Experiment Protocol Users Guide. http://get.adobe.com/flashplayer/
title: Experiment Protocol.swf: a Flash-based multimedia program that administered the animation experiment and recorded participant responses
description: The guide describes an interactive multimedia computer program, provided as the Adobe Flash file "Experiment Protocol.swf", that administered the experiment and "recorded all participant responses". The program "provides aural narration, which was a significant component of the protocol". Examiners can start the protocol at any point using drop-down list boxes for treatment condition and protocol location, controls that participants were not shown. Condition codes are entered on a code entry screen: "magenta" for the no animation condition, "purple" for directive animation only, "crimson" for representational animation only, or "violet" for both animations.
requirements: Requires an appropriate version of Adobe Flash Player, which at the time of publication was available freely at http://get.adobe.com/flashplayer/.
constraints: The "no connection" message signifies the program cannot connect to the server needed to capture user input; the guide states that not connecting to the server will not impact how the program behaves from the participant's point of view.
The drop-down list boxes for treatment condition and protocol location were not provided to participants; they exist so examiners can view different sections without starting from the beginning.
target_learners: participants in the animation-and-understanding experiment administered by this program
target_learning_goals: learning from a narrated multimedia protocol under four animation treatment conditions (none, directive only, representational only, both)
examples: Running the program and clicking Start without adjusting the list boxes reproduces the protocol exactly as participants saw it.
Entering the code "violet" on the code entry screen presents the condition with both directive and representational animations.
key_sources: Animation and Illusions of Understanding: Experiment Protocol Users Guide. http://get.adobe.com/flashplayer/

article_title: Pupils' estimates of teachers.
citation: Grace E. Bird. (1917). Pupils' Estimates of Teachers. Journal of Educational Psychology.
title: Teachers should endeavor to fulfil the requirements of both supervisor and pupil, since pupils appreciate the ordinary virtues fundamental to character.
description: The article argues that because employers and supervisors "are forced to rely upon appearances" and can rarely observe instructors' work, while pupils possess intimate daily acquaintance with teachers, the effective teacher should satisfy both audiences' criteria. It concludes "it behooves the instructor of youth to endeavor to fulfil all the requirements of both supervisor and pupil." Pupils' lists emphasize social-character virtues, and the author argues the parallelism between the two lists is closer than it seems because loose general terms hide similar ideas.
requirements: The teacher must be evaluated by both supervisor criteria (instructional skill, discipline, initiative, experience) and pupil criteria (kindness, fairness, sociability, humor and related virtues).
constraints: The article notes pupils appreciate most "the ordinary virtues fundamental to character," and that standardized methods of rating teachers' fitness are often absent.
target_learning_goals: teacher effectiveness and teacher selection
examples: The study collected unsigned written answers from 139 high school girls, 253 high school boys, and 150 normal school students naming the best qualities of their best teachers, then compared these with employers' qualification lists and documented causes of teacher failure.
key_sources: Grace E. Bird. (1917). Pupils' Estimates of Teachers. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0072302

article_title: Response to instruction in preschool: Results of two randomized studies with children at significant risk of reading difficulties.
citation: Lonigan, C. J., & Phillips, B. M. (2016). Response to Instruction in Preschool: Results of Two Randomized Studies with Children At Significant Risk of Reading Difficulties. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000054
title: Intensified Tier II design: narrowed content targets, smaller groups, separated strands, and progress-monitoring-based pacing
description: This design pattern describes how the authors revised their Tier II preschool intervention between studies. They narrowed content within each strand "to allow more time on topic across fewer distinct content targets", reduced the maximum small-group size from 6 to 4 children, separated phonological awareness and print knowledge into distinct strands, and added regular progress-monitoring assessments that determined whether groups advanced or repeated lessons. Lesson plans also explicitly included upward and downward scaffolding instructions so within-group instruction could be differentiated.
requirements: Detailed written lesson plans describing daily activities, duration, and scripts; interventionists trained (approximately 20 hours in Study 2) with audio-recorded sessions reviewed for fidelity and weekly feedback
constraints: Evaluated with 11-week small-group supplemental instruction for preschoolers already failing to progress under an evidence-based Tier I curriculum in Title I preschools
target_learners: preschool children at significant risk of reading difficulties identified via RTI screening
target_learning_goals: phonological awareness, print knowledge (letter names and sounds), and oral language/vocabulary
examples: In Study 2, letter instruction covered only letters in each child's name plus 11 target letters with cumulative weekly review, and PA focused only on compound words, two-syllable words, and onset-rime
key_sources: Lonigan, C. J., & Phillips, B. M. (2016). Response to Instruction in Preschool: Results of Two Randomized Studies with Children At Significant Risk of Reading Difficulties. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000054

article_title: Response to instruction in preschool: Results of two randomized studies with children at significant risk of reading difficulties.
citation: Lonigan, C. J., & Phillips, B. M. (2016). Response to Instruction in Preschool: Results of Two Randomized Studies with Children At Significant Risk of Reading Difficulties. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000054
title: Preschoolers identified for Tier II within an RTI framework need more intensive and more narrowly focused instruction than children at general risk
description: The article's central design recommendation is that the population identified for Tier II instruction matters. Children who fail to progress under a high-quality, evidence-based Tier I curriculum represent a more difficult-to-remediate group, so the authors conclude that "Children identified as eligible for Tier II in an RTI framework likely require more intensive and more narrowly focused instruction than do children at general risk of later academic difficulties." The two studies support this: broad-scope Tier II activities with prior efficacy evidence produced minimal impacts in Study 1, while the intensified, narrowed Study 2 version produced significant impacts.
requirements: Tier I must first be a high-quality, evidence-based core curriculum so that Tier II identification reflects genuine non-response rather than weak core instruction
constraints: Evidence comes from Title I preschool settings with children averaging standard scores of roughly 78 to 86 at qualification; the authors state the context of identification may alter the nature of Tier II instruction required
target_learners: preschool children who fail to make adequate progress under evidence-based core classroom instruction
target_learning_goals: early literacy skills: phonological awareness, print knowledge, and oral language
examples: After Study 1's minimal impacts, the authors revised the protocols to be more intensive, more focused, and more explicit, and Study 2 showed significant and moderate-to-large impacts
key_sources: Lonigan, C. J., & Phillips, B. M. (2016). Response to Instruction in Preschool: Results of Two Randomized Studies with Children At Significant Risk of Reading Difficulties. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000054

article_title: Response to instruction in preschool: Results of two randomized studies with children at significant risk of reading difficulties.
citation: Lonigan, C. J., & Phillips, B. M. (2016). Response to Instruction in Preschool: Results of Two Randomized Studies with Children At Significant Risk of Reading Difficulties. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000054
title: Response to Instruction (RTI) three-tier framework for organizing instructional intensity
description: The article describes RTI as two interrelated approaches: a method for identifying learning disabilities via universal screening, risk identification, increasing instructional intensity, and progress monitoring; and a framework of tiers of instructional intensity. In the standard three-tiered model, "Tier II represents an increased intensity of instruction, often administered as small-group instruction, with membership in the small-groups differentiated by students' skill levels", while Tier III provides even smaller-group or one-on-one instruction often delivered by specialists. Tier I is the core, evidence-based classroom instruction expected to meet 75 to 90 percent of children.
requirements: Universal screening and frequent progress monitoring with curriculum-based measures; a core Tier I curriculum that is high-quality and evidence-based
constraints: The article notes it is not clear the high-quality Tier I presumption is met in many preschool classrooms, where most commonly used curricula lack WWC evidence of efficacy
target_learners: preschool and elementary children at risk of academic difficulties
target_learning_goals: early identification and remediation of academic skill deficits, particularly early literacy
examples: The studies operationalized Tier II as 11 weeks of need-aligned small-group instruction in phonological awareness, print knowledge, and oral language strands, randomized against Tier I only
key_sources: Lonigan, C. J., & Phillips, B. M. (2016). Response to Instruction in Preschool: Results of Two Randomized Studies with Children At Significant Risk of Reading Difficulties. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000054

article_title: Mental development and the measurement of the level of intelligence.
citation: De Sanctis, S. (1911). Mental development and the measurement of the level of intelligence. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 2, 498-507.
title: Two-tier theory of ideation: lower associative processes and higher ideation, with intelligence as elaboration of the lower
description: De Sanctis divides mental processes into immediate ones governed by the laws of association (sense perception, imagination, memory) and mediate or higher processes (judgment, concept formation, reasoning). He holds that "Intelligence, properly so called, or intellectual capacity, is a manifestation of higher ideation," while insisting there is "no discontinuity between them, but rather a progressive evolution." The framework grounds his argument that intelligence tests must engage higher ideation rather than elementary psychic states.
requirements: Measurement of intelligence must be interpreted as measurement of the level of higher ideation, not of elementary sensations, attention or memory alone
constraints: The author warns against positing new metaphysical entities, which he calls superfluous and even dangerous for experimental psychology
target_learning_goals: understanding the structure of intellectual capacity as a basis for its measurement
examples: He classifies empirical or associative thought as lower ideation and judgment, concepts and reasoning as higher ideation, noting higher ideation is noticeable even in children of eight to ten years
key_sources: De Sanctis, S. (1911). Mental development and the measurement of the level of intelligence. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 2, 498-507. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0069835

article_title: Mental development and the measurement of the level of intelligence.
citation: De Sanctis, S. (1911). Mental development and the measurement of the level of intelligence. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 2, 498-507.
title: De Sanctis six-test series for measuring and grading mental deficiency
description: A six-test series proposed by De Sanctis in 1906 (tests of 1905) and printed here in operational detail: handing a named colored ball, recognizing the ball just given, selecting cubes from mixed shapes, matching a cube to a form chart, counting and comparing graduated cubes, and weight and optical-illusion questions. Scoring rules grade deficiency: failing the second test indicates high-grade deficiency, and completing the sixth test without mistake indicates no mental deficiency. The author states the tests were designed to measure the degree of mental defect, not primarily the level of intelligence.
requirements: A table, a screen, five glass balls of different colors, twelve graduated wooden cubes, three cones, two parallelopipeds, a form chart of triangles, rectangles and squares, and a stop-watch measuring fifths of a second
constraints: The tests divide institutionalized defectives into three grades (idiots and imbeciles versus morons) and are intended for medico-pedagogical placement rather than fine-grained intelligence measurement
target_learning_goals: classification of degree of mental deficiency for educational placement
examples: The author reports the tests are in general use in certain American, Russian, and Italian institutions and quickly distinguish idiots and imbeciles from morons
key_sources: De Sanctis, S. (1911). Mental development and the measurement of the level of intelligence. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 2, 498-507. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0069835

article_title: Mental development and the measurement of the level of intelligence.
citation: De Sanctis, S. (1911). Mental development and the measurement of the level of intelligence. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 2, 498-507.
title: Graded-question scale: questions of progressive difficulty grouped into levels to classify subjects by degree
description: A general psychological method in which a list of questions of increasing difficulty is used to grade the level of intelligence: with forty questions of progressive difficulty, some subjects master the first ten, others reach the first thirty-five, and a small minority answer all forty. Grouping the questions (four groups of ten, or ten groups of ten from one hundred questions) yields classification into as many degrees. De Sanctis reports using this method with great success on mental defectives ten years old and over, and identifies it as the principle underlying the Binet-Simon scale.
requirements: A pool of questions ordered by increasing difficulty, grouped into equal-sized sets so that the group reached indexes the subject's level
constraints: The Binet-Simon version adds the assumption that each stage corresponds to the intellectual development characteristic of a given age, an assumption the author says must be verified before judging the scale's applicability
target_learners: mental defectives ten years old and over
target_learning_goals: grading and classifying the level of intelligence
examples: De Sanctis describes dividing one hundred questions of increasing difficulty into ten groups of ten to classify subjects into ten different grades
key_sources: De Sanctis, S. (1911). Mental development and the measurement of the level of intelligence. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 2, 498-507. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0069835

article_title: Report of the twenty-fourth annual meeting of the American Psychological Association, Chicago, December 28-30, 1915.
citation: Kelley, T. L. (1915). Report of the Twenty-fourth Annual Meeting of the American Psychological Association, Chicago, December 28-30, 1915. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org/journal/jeducpsych
title: Judd's thesis that general psychology fails to ground school practice, and that teachers need 'educational psychology' or 'experimental education' instead
description: Judd's framework holds that general psychology, as then taught, does not supply a scientific background for school practice because it is too broad and its internal disputes distract prospective teachers. He argues that "Students do not and can not make the applications" of general psychology to educational situations, so application must be built into the course itself. He proposes "educational psychology," or perhaps better "experimental education," for the rank and file of teachers, while agreeing with Haggerty on the value of general psychology for leaders in educational science.
requirements: A first course must make beginning education students aware of the problems of education and give them specific facts contributing to solving those problems.
constraints: The thesis is presented as an address position at the 1915 meeting, not as a tested result; it applies to courses for prospective teachers rather than to psychology training for research leaders.
target_learning_goals: applying psychological principles to educational situations
understanding problems of education
examples: Haggerty presented the University of Indiana's course of study, including elementary, experimental, educational and other psychology courses, recommended as preparation for advanced research work in education.
key_sources: Kelley, T. L. (1915). Report of the Twenty-fourth Annual Meeting of the American Psychological Association, Chicago, December 28-30, 1915. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org/journal/jeducpsych

article_title: Report of the twenty-fourth annual meeting of the American Psychological Association, Chicago, December 28-30, 1915.
citation: Kelley, T. L. (1915). Report of the Twenty-fourth Annual Meeting of the American Psychological Association, Chicago, December 28-30, 1915. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org/journal/jeducpsych
title: Pintner's standardized non-language performance test scale (15 tests, eight standardized so far)
description: Rudolf Pintner reported progress in standardizing performance tests that are independent of language, intended for examining individuals with poor language endowment or limited English. The report states a scale of such tests "will be very serviceable in examining non-English-speaking individuals." The tests standardized at the time of the report were the Feature Profile, Manikin, Five Figure Board, Two Figure Board, Casuist Form Board, Seguin Form Board, Adaptation Board, and Healy's Five Block Frame Test.
requirements: Standardization work on the performance tests, of which some 15 were reported in progress.
constraints: Only the eight named tests were standardized at the time of the report; the scale was still in progress.
target_learning_goals: language-independent assessment of mental ability
examples: The named standardized tests include the Feature Profile, Manikin, Seguin Form Board, and Healy's Five Block Frame Test.
key_sources: Kelley, T. L. (1915). Report of the Twenty-fourth Annual Meeting of the American Psychological Association, Chicago, December 28-30, 1915. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org/journal/jeducpsych

article_title: Graded mental tests. Part I. Attention, perception, comprehension and memory.
citation: Squire, C. R. (1912). Graded Mental Tests. Part I. Attention, Perception, Comprehension and Memory. The Journal of Educational Psychology, III(7). https://www.jstor.org/journal/jeducpsych
title: Seven critical points of mental efficiency as the organizing axis for graded mental age-norms
description: The article proposes that mental efficiency in school children be estimated by "sinking shafts" at seven critical points: attention, perception, comprehension, memory, association, invention/construction, and judgment. The author argues these are "some of the most significant factors in the determination of mental efficiency" and that age-norms at these points would furnish more accurate evidence of a child's development than examination of school-subject knowledge. The tests reported in this paper operationalize the first four points, with the remainder to follow in later installments.
requirements: Tests must be applicable to all stages of development and comparable from age to age
Each test must present a problem the child can grasp and arouse effort
Tests must be completable without undue fatigue, with a minimum of apparatus, within two or three school periods of at most thirty minutes
constraints: The series is offered as a tentative answer; norms are established only for unretarded pupils whose chronological, physiological, pedagogical and psychological ages correspond
This installment covers only attention, perception, comprehension and memory; association, invention and judgment are deferred to later parts
target_learners: elementary school children aged six to thirteen
target_learning_goals: diagnosis of mental development stage
establishment of age-norms of mental capacity
examples: Eight groups of ten children from the School of Education, University of Chicago, were tested individually with a series requiring no apparatus except a stopwatch

article_title: Graded mental tests. Part I. Attention, perception, comprehension and memory.
citation: Squire, C. R. (1912). Graded Mental Tests. Part I. Attention, Perception, Comprehension and Memory. The Journal of Educational Psychology, III(7). https://www.jstor.org/journal/jeducpsych
title: Individual administration of mental tests is essential to reliability when working with children
description: The article recommends giving mental tests to children individually rather than in groups, because individual testing "gives every individual an equal opportunity". The experimenter and child come into close rapport, questions can be adapted to the individual child's comprehension, and the exercise can feel like a pleasant game rather than a test, which is requisite to a good working mood in a child. All of this, the author argues, is impossible in group testing.
requirements: Standard conditions maintained throughout the series, with tests adapted to each age and individual
constraints: Individual testing consumes more time than group testing
target_learners: elementary school children aged six to thirteen
target_learning_goals: accurate measurement of mental capacity for diagnosis and grading
examples: All tests in the series were given individually; with the six-year-old group responses were oral and recorded by the examiner, while older children wrote their own responses where time was not the determinant

article_title: Communications and discussions: Notes on the recall of nonsense syllables.
citation: Whipple, G. M. (1917). Notes on the recall of nonsense syllables. Cornell University. https://psycnet.apa.org
title: Use documented incidental-retention incidents as classroom illustrations of the nature of retention and recall in educational psychology teaching
description: The author proposes that observations like the nonsense-syllable case have value for teaching educational psychology, because they give students a verifiable, classmate-sourced instance of long-term retention. He notes stock anecdotes such as the Coleridge servant-girl story are striking but lack the certainty of an instance "drawn from the experience of classmates". Such illustrations can also address the familiar student query of whether anything is absolutely forgotten.
requirements: The original learning experience must be a matter of record so that recall can be verified against it
target_learning_goals: understanding the nature of retention and recall
evaluating the reliability of memory for long-forgotten incidents

article_title: A latent profile analysis of math achievement, numerosity, and math anxiety in twins.
citation: Hart, Sara A.; Logan, Jessica A.R.; Thompson, Lee; Kovas, Yulia; McLoughlin, Gráinne; & Petrill, Stephen A. (2015). A latent profile analysis of math achievement, numerosity, and math anxiety in twins. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000045
title: Attentional control theory as an account of the math anxiety–achievement link
description: The article invokes attentional control theory (Eysenck & Calvo, 1992; Eysenck et al., 2007) to explain how math anxiety harms math performance: anxiety directs attention away from the goal toward threat-related stimuli, and 'These ruminations occupy the working memory system, and because math achievement is highly dependent on working memory, math achievement suffers.' The theory predicts anxiety should impair complex skills like math achievement but not basic skills like numerosity, which the LPA results were interpreted as supporting.
requirements: Math achievement tasks that depend on working memory for the anxiety-driven rumination mechanism to reduce performance
constraints: The article presents this as an interpretive account; the study design does not establish the causal mechanism
target_learners: school-age children and adolescents learning mathematics
target_learning_goals: math achievement
examples: Class 5 children had typical numerosity but low achievement with the highest math anxiety, which the authors read as consistent with the theory

article_title: A study of association in defectives.
citation: Otis, M. (1915). A Study of Association in Defectives. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Vol. VI, No. 5. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22A+Study+of+Association+in+Defectives%22+Otis
title: Five-type classification of word-association responses as an index of mental level or abnormality
description: Otis proposes a taxonomy of association-test responses into five types: repetition of the stimulus, non-logical responses, sound reactions, more-than-one-word reactions, and normal single-word reactions matching the Kent-Rosanoff frequency tables. A child is assigned to a type only when "50 per cent, of a child's reactions must be clearly of a given type to consider the child as belonging to that type," with mixed types otherwise classified by their two most frequent components. The types are interpreted as marking stages of language development from imitation through sentence-thought to single-word analysis, and are examined for diagnostic and age-test value.
requirements: Administration of a standard word list (the Kent-Rosanoff 100-word list) with individually recorded, timed responses so reaction types can be classified per child.
constraints: A child is assigned to a type only when at least 50 per cent of reactions clearly belong to it; otherwise the child is classified as a mixed type.
target_learning_goals: diagnosis of mental status and language-development level through associational tendencies
examples: Illustrative papers are given for each type, e.g. a boy of 11 testing 6-1 for Type I and a Mongolian male of 33 testing 3-4 for Type II.
key_sources: Otis, M. (1915). A Study of Association in Defectives. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Vol. VI, No. 5. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22A+Study+of+Association+in+Defectives%22+Otis

article_title: A study of association in defectives.
citation: Otis, M. (1915). A Study of Association in Defectives. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Vol. VI, No. 5. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22A+Study+of+Association+in+Defectives%22+Otis
title: Kent-Rosanoff 100-word association list with standardized frequency tables
description: The Kent-Rosanoff list of 100 stimulus words is a standardized word-association instrument with published frequency tables providing "a standard of comparison in the frequency tables published at the close of their work." Otis used it so that "a comparison with normal reactions could be made," administering the words individually in list order with stop-watch timing. Normal-type (Type V) responses were scored against the Kent-Rosanoff frequency tables, and new frequency tables compiled from the defectives and normal school children were placed on file at the Vineland laboratory.
requirements: Individual administration in a private room with a reliable stop-watch, recording responses verbatim and timing in tenths of seconds.
constraints: Some list words are beyond the comprehension of very young children, though the author judges enough words are adapted to a child's understanding to make the test fair.
target_learning_goals: assessment of associational tendencies and mental status
examples: Frequency tables compiled from the defectives' and normal children's responses were placed on file at the Vineland laboratory for consultation.

article_title: Psychology Coming into Its Own in the Making of Children's Books.
citation: A. I. G.; H. O. R. (1922). New Publications. The Journal of Educational Psychology, pp. 186-187. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journal_of_Educational_Psychology
title: Here and Now Story Book (Mitchell, 1921)
description: Here and Now Story Book, published by E. P. Dutton & Co., New York, 1921, p. 360, is a collection of stories for young children built from what Mitchell and her colleagues learned by living with children at the City and Country School of New York City. The reviewer calls it "quite revolutionary" and lists sample stories including The Dinner Hour, The Grocery Man, The Journey, How the Engine Learned the Knowing Song, The Fog Boat Story, Hammer and Saw and Plane, The Skyscraper, and Things that Loved the Lake.
requirements: The reviewer states that readers should study the book's introduction, which explains "the why and wherefore of all the change" in children's reading material.
constraints: The stories are intended for primary-grade children and young children in homes, per the reviewer's recommendation.
target_learning_goals: reading material matched to children's spontaneous interests
examples: The reviewer recommends the introduction to teachers and lists story titles such as The Dinner Hour and How the Engine Learned the Knowing Song.

article_title: Psychology Coming into Its Own in the Making of Children's Books.
citation: A. I. G.; H. O. R. (1922). New Publications. The Journal of Educational Psychology, pp. 186-187. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journal_of_Educational_Psychology
title: The Child and His School (Hartman, 1922) with a classified bibliography of 850 children's books
description: The Child and His School by Gertrude Hartman (E. P. Dutton & Co., New York, 1922, pp. XI + 248) is a Bureau of Educational Experiments product that gives teachers "a good bibliography of books and materials (850 of them)" for children in the lower and intermediate grades, classified into community study, national life, and the study of other nations. It also summarizes, quotes from and interprets the scientific basis of education for teachers.
requirements: Intended as a tool for teachers making curricula who need evidence on social needs, children's learning, interests, heredity, intelligence and growth.
constraints: The reviewer notes that "many of the books listed are very poor readings for children," but that they are all that is currently available.
target_learners: children in the lower and intermediate grades
target_learning_goals: curriculum planning grounded in biology, psychology and sociology of the child
examples: The bibliography's community-study category covers food, shelter, clothing, transportation, communication, conservation of wealth, education, recreation, religion, government and primitive life.

article_title: Psychology Coming into Its Own in the Making of Children's Books.
citation: A. I. G.; H. O. R. (1922). New Publications. The Journal of Educational Psychology, pp. 186-187. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journal_of_Educational_Psychology
title: Teachers need an up-to-date, described bibliography of the biological, psychological and sociological evidence about the child as an essential curriculum-making tool
description: The reviewer argues that in making a curriculum, teachers constantly need evidence on mooted points about children, and that "one of the essential tools of the progressive and experimentalist in school practice is an up-to-date, complete and described bibliography" of what biology, psychology and sociology say about the child and the educative process. Hartman's The Child and His School is offered as a book that does this well, adding liberal quotations from leaders and definite suggestions about usable books and materials.
requirements: The bibliography must be up to date, complete, and described, and ideally supplies liberal quotations from leaders of prestige plus suggestions of materials usable with children.
target_learners: teachers making curricula for school children
target_learning_goals: evidence-informed curriculum decisions about children's needs, learning and interests
examples: The reviewer recommends Hartman's book as supplying a classified 850-item bibliography plus an interpreted summary of the scientific basis of education.

article_title: No evidence that playing a linear number board game improves numerical skills beyond teaching as usual: A randomized controlled trial in 4- to 5-year-old primary school children.
citation: James-Brabham, E., Jay, T., & Sella, F. (2024). No evidence that playing a linear number board game improves numerical skills beyond teaching as usual: a randomized controlled trial in four- to five-year-old primary school children. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000857
title: Co-developed linear number board game with forward-only and bidirectional conditions
description: A classroom number game in which pairs of children place number food cards in order on a tablecloth-shaped mat to feed a monster, building a linear number line. Children in the forward condition placed cards ascending (e.g., 1-10 or 6-15); bidirectional children placed cards forward then backward (e.g., 10-1 or 15-6). The interval moved from 1-10 in the first three sessions to 6-15 in the remaining five after pilot testing. The game was designed to "required limited input from adults to play, and children found highly playable, fun, and engaging."
requirements: Played in small pairs in a quiet corner of the classroom with an experimenter prompting children to find the successive or preceding number and checking card order with scaffolded support
constraints: The article notes it used a one-size-fits-all difficulty level, with all children playing the same number intervals
target_learners: four- to five-year-old children in primary schools in socioeconomically disadvantaged areas
target_learning_goals: early numerical skills: counting, number naming, number order, number line estimation, number comparison
examples: Eight gameplay sessions across five weeks (twice weekly for four weeks with a one-week break), approximately ten minutes per session, with number-game pairs playing twice per session to match card placements with the alphabet control

article_title: Within-year stability and changes in adolescents’ cross-domain motivational profiles: Predictions on academic achievement and educational choices.
citation: Polso, K.-M., Tuominen, H., Ihantola, P., & Niemivirta, M. (2025). Within-year stability and changes in adolescents' cross-domain motivational profiles: Predictions on academic achievement and educational choices. Journal of Educational Psychology, 117(6), 960-979. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000955
title: Situated expectancy-value theory: socialization and interpretation of prior experiences shape goals, self-concepts, expectancies, and subjective task values that drive achievement and choices
description: Situated expectancy-value theory (SEVT), the renamed framework of Eccles' expectancy-value theory, explains educational outcomes such as achievement and program choice through domain-specific motivational beliefs. The article states that "These beliefs are tightly intertwined with identity formation and impact success expectancies as well as the subjective task value in a given activity or, for example, school subject." Task value comprises intrinsic, attainment, and utility facets plus perceived cost, and the study uses these constructs to profile ninth-graders' math and language arts motivation. The framework underpins the study's four research questions on profiles, stability, predictors, and outcomes.
requirements: Motivational beliefs are measured as domain-specific (subject-specific) expectancies, values, and costs rather than global traits
constraints: The framework emphasizes the context-specific and dynamic nature of motivational processes, so findings are situated in the specific educational transition context studied
target_learners: adolescents in the final year of lower secondary education
target_learning_goals: educational pathway choices and academic achievement
examples: The study operationalized SEVT constructs as self-concept, intrinsic value, attainment value, utility value, and opportunity cost for math and language arts, measured twice across the ninth-grade year.

article_title: The range of information in Biology: III. Botany.
citation: Grier, N. M. (1918). The Range of Information in Biology. III. Botany. Journal of Educational Psychology, 9, 509-516. https://psycnet.apa.org
title: 100-word range of information test in botany
description: A vocabulary-based diagnostic instrument consisting of 100 botanical terms drawn from grade-school spellers and readers and from Boy Scout and Camp Fire Girls publications, chosen as frequently occurring words. Words were selected to indicate the range of information about plant life pupils might know from nature study and school gardens, and familiarity with biological principles. Pupils were told the terms pertained directly or indirectly to plants.
requirements: Words must be drawn from materials the pupils actually used in grade school work and out-of-school publications
constraints: The method of giving the test is only referenced to previous papers in the series; only the word list is given here
target_learners: first-year high school pupils entering or completing botany
target_learning_goals: range of botanical vocabulary and concepts carried from nature study into secondary biology
examples: The word list printed in the article includes terms such as absorption, anther, carbohydrate, cell, germinate, pollen, and stigma

article_title: The range of information in Biology: III. Botany.
citation: Grier, N. M. (1918). The Range of Information in Biology. III. Botany. Journal of Educational Psychology, 9, 509-516. https://psycnet.apa.org
title: High school botany instruction and textbooks should take account of botanical knowledge gained from grade-school nature study
description: The article argues that effective teaching of high school botany should inquire to what extent the ground has been broken by nature study, since the nature study course constantly tends to include more botanical knowledge. It notes that no current textbook takes serious consideration of this prior knowledge, and that more elementary botany could safely be included in nature study.

constraints: The author notes parts of plant natural history, such as complicated life cycles, seem too difficult for pupils of an early age

target_learning_goals: effective teaching and persistence of botany in the secondary curriculum
examples: The author's range of information test was used to measure how much ground nature study had broken for high school botany

article_title: A randomized controlled trial of a smartphone-based well-being training in public school system employees during the COVID-19 pandemic.
citation: Hirshberg Matthew J., Frye Corrina, Dahl Cortland J., Riordan Kevin M., Vack Nathan J., Sachs Jane, Goldman Robin, Davidson Richard J., Goldberg Simon B. (2022). A Randomized Controlled Trial of a Smartphone-Based Well-Being Training in Public School System Employees During the COVID-19 Pandemic. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000739
title: Awareness, Connection, Insight, and Purpose (ACIP) training-based model of well-being
description: The ACIP model, proposed by Dahl and colleagues, holds that well-being rests on four trainable pillars: "awareness, connection, insight, and purpose (ACIP)". Awareness comprises attention and meta-awareness skills; connection emphasizes prosocial dispositions such as gratitude and kindness; insight targets clarity about the nature of one's identity and experience; and purpose aims to clarify values and apply them in daily life. The model claims these pillar skills "demonstrate plasticity" and that this plasticity "can be harnessed through intentional practice," specifically meditation training. The Healthy Minds Program app and this trial's hypotheses were constructed around this framework.
requirements: Skills in each pillar are strengthened through repeated, intentional meditation practice over time
constraints: The authors did not preregister predicted improvements in purpose for the four-week intervention, assuming changes in purpose occur over a longer timescale
target_learners: School system employees, including teachers and other adult staff
target_learning_goals: Reduced psychological distress and strengthened well-being skills (attention, prosocial dispositions, defusion, purpose)
examples: The four-week Healthy Minds Program Foundations course delivered one week of content per ACIP pillar to school system employees
key_sources: Hirshberg Matthew J., Frye Corrina, Dahl Cortland J., Riordan Kevin M., Vack Nathan J., Sachs Jane, Goldman Robin, Davidson Richard J., Goldberg Simon B. (2022). A Randomized Controlled Trial of a Smartphone-Based Well-Being Training in Public School System Employees During the COVID-19 Pandemic. article_title: A randomized controlled trial of a smartphone-based well-being training in public school system employees during the COVID-19 pandemic.
citation: Hirshberg Matthew J., Frye Corrina, Dahl Cortland J., Riordan Kevin M., Vack Nathan J., Sachs Jane, Goldman Robin, Davidson Richard J., Goldberg Simon B. (2022). A Randomized Controlled Trial of a Smartphone-Based Well-Being Training in Public School System Employees During the COVID-19 Pandemic. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000739
title: Healthy Minds Program (HMP) four-week smartphone meditation course
description: The Healthy Minds Program is a free smartphone-based meditation app constructed around the ACIP model. The four-week Foundations course studied here "includes two introductory audio lessons and two introductory guided meditations... followed by one week of content for each pillar of well-being," with two brief podcast lessons (5 to 7 minutes each) and three guided meditations per week. "In total, the intervention contains 10 lessons and 14 guided meditations." Participants choose between two guides, active or sitting practices, and practice lengths of 5 to 30 minutes, requiring only minutes a day.
requirements: A smartphone capable of downloading the HMP app
constraints: Participants with prior HMP use, meditation retreat experience, or a regular meditation practice were excluded from the trial
target_learners: Public school system employees (teachers, instructional, building, and administrative staff)
target_learning_goals: Reduction of psychological distress and training of awareness, connection, insight, and purpose skills
examples: Delivered remotely to 344 Wisconsin school system employees during summer 2020 or the first month of the school year, with automated REDCap reminder emails supporting download and use

article_title: An educational survey test.
citation: Rudolf Pintner and Florence Fitzgerald. (1918). An Educational Survey Test. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journal/edu
title: The Pintner-Fitzgerald Educational Survey Test
description: A 30-minute group test booklet covering eight subject areas: vocabulary (Thorndike), arithmetic (Woody-Stone), two reading tests (Kelly and Thorndike), completion/language (Trabue), punctuation-grammar (Starch), geography (Hahn-Lackey) and history (Van Wagenen). Items were drawn from the Standard Educational Tests and Measurements "at approximately equal intervals" of difficulty. Timed subtests total twenty-five and one-half minutes, with about thirty minutes for the full administration, and scoring uses stencils and keys with subject weights summing to a highest possible score of 141.
requirements: Printed instructions simple enough that children are merely told to do what the test tells them to do
constraints: Not intended for teachers seeking detailed, accurate knowledge of a pupil's ability in one subject or for diagnosing particular difficulties and weaknesses
Five to eight minutes per subject cannot give an accurate measure of individual attainment in each subject
target_learners: Elementary school pupils in grades 2 to 8
target_learning_goals: Rough measurement of general educational attainment across the main elementary-school subjects
examples: The booklet reverses alternate pages so the pupil cannot read the next test, keeping attention on the current subtest

article_title: An educational survey test.
citation: Rudolf Pintner and Florence Fitzgerald. (1918). An Educational Survey Test. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journal/edu
title: Use short group survey tests to obtain fair measures of general attainment for groups and school systems
description: The article argues that just as group mental tests survey general mental ability, group educational survey tests are needed to sum a child's educational attainment in a single value. It states there is "great practical need of a short scale covering the chief subjects that will give a fair measure of the general attainment of the individual and a good measure of the group," enabling accurate comparison of grades, schools and school systems within one sitting of about thirty to forty minutes.
requirements: A careful selection of a few items from the main standard school subjects, coverable in one sitting
Time limits short enough that even the brightest pupils cannot complete everything
constraints: Suitable for group-level survey purposes, not for individual diagnosis within a subject
target_learning_goals: General educational attainment measurement for administration and supervision
examples: The authors' test puts general attainment in a single value comparable with mental-test measures, supporting efficiency in administration and supervision

article_title: Effects of discipline techniques on children's personality trait inferences.
citation: Rice, W. K., Jr. (1973). Effects of Discipline Techniques on Children's Personality-Trait Inferences. Ph.D. dissertation, The University of Oklahoma. University Microfilms No. 74-12,322. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Effects+of+Discipline+Techniques+on+Children%27s+Personality-Trait+Inferences
title: Kelley's attribution theory and its discounting principle as the explanatory framework for peer trait inferences from discipline episodes
description: The article adopts Kelley's informational-processing model of attribution theory, in which observers use the covariation principle with multiple observations and the discounting principle with a single observation: "The role of a given cause in producing a given effect is discounted if other Plausible causes are also present". Under minimal information, trait attribution is greatest when external causes are minimal, and negative information is weighted more heavily than positive. The study uses this framework to predict that approval-focused desists, whose negative content targets the child, yield more negative and more confident trait inferences.
requirements: Applies when the observer has only a single observation or minimal information about the behavior and its possible causes
constraints: When observers have information from multiple observations, the covariation principle applies and different results might be obtained
target_learning_goals: forming trait inferences about peers and teachers from observed social interactions
examples: The dissertation tested the framework's prediction with a tape-recording experiment in which observers heard either approval-focused or task-focused desists and rated the child and teacher on trait and confidence scales
key_sources: Rice, W. K., Jr. (1973). Effects of Discipline Techniques on Children's Personality-Trait Inferences. Ph.D. dissertation, The University of Oklahoma. article_title: Effects of discipline techniques on children's personality trait inferences.
citation: Rice, W. K., Jr. (1973). Effects of Discipline Techniques on Children's Personality-Trait Inferences. Ph.D. dissertation, The University of Oklahoma. University Microfilms No. 74-12,322. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Effects+of+Discipline+Techniques+on+Children%27s+Personality-Trait+Inferences
title: Keep approval-focused desists of a negative quality to a minimum in classroom discipline
description: Because observers attribute less desirable traits to both the disciplined child and the teacher after approval-focused desists, and because self-concept is influenced by how others view a person, the authors recommend limiting this discipline technique. As they state, "it is suggested that the use of approval- focused desists of a negative quality b e  kept minimal." The recommendation rests on the laboratory finding that desist type changes how the child and teacher are viewed.
requirements: Teachers must have alternative desist forms available, such as task-focused desists that direct negative content at the activity rather than the child
constraints: The finding comes from a laboratory tape-listening setting with minimal information; the authors note that significant laboratory results frequently do not translate into significant classroom effects, and that under normal classroom conditions the covariation principle applies and different results might be obtained
target_learning_goals: maintaining a classroom climate that protects the school-self concept and peer standing of disciplined students
examples: The experiment presented eighth graders with tape-recorded approval-focused or task-focused desists and measured their trait and confidence ratings of the target child and the teacher

article_title: Explanatory models in the processing of science text: The role of prior knowledge activation through small-group discussion.
citation: Schmidt, H. G., De Volder, M. L., De Grave, W. S., Moust, J. H. C., & Patel, V. L. (1989). Explanatory Models in the Processing of Science Text: The Role of Prior Knowledge Activation Through Small-Group Discussion. Journal of Educational Psychology, 81(4), 610-619. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-0663.81.4.610
title: Prior-knowledge activation through problem analysis: explanatory models as vehicles for text comprehension
description: The article proposes that discussing a problem mobilizes relevant prior knowledge, which is packaged in a problem-specific explanatory model—a set of concepts connected by causal links interpreting phenomena in terms of their underlying structure. This model, constructed before reading, facilitates comprehension of a relevant text because activated explanatory knowledge is more easily accessed and causally linked propositions are more coherent. The account explains why problem analysis aids recall of explanatory but not descriptive information.
requirements: Learners must analyze a problem describing natural phenomena and generate explanations in terms of underlying processes, principles, or mechanisms before encountering the relevant text
constraints: The effect was demonstrated for recall of explanatory propositions; retention of descriptive facts was not specifically supported by the procedure
target_learners: secondary-school and college science students, both novices and experts
target_learning_goals: acquisition of causal, explanatory concepts from expository science text
examples: Small groups discussed why a red blood cell swells and bursts in pure water but shrinks in salt solution, then read a text on osmosis and diffusion

article_title: The Binet-Simon measuring scale for intelligence: An annotated bibliography. Part II.
citation: Kohs, S. C. (1914). The Binet-Simon Measuring Scale for Intelligence: An Annotated Bibliography. Part II. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Binet-Simon+Measuring+Scale+for+Intelligence%22+Kohs+annotated+bibliography
title: Binet-Simon measuring scale for intelligence as a widely applied diagnostic instrument
description: The bibliography documents the Binet-Simon scale as a measuring instrument for intellectual level applied across institutions, courts, schools and hospitals in America and Europe between 1908 and 1914. Entries describe translations and adaptations, including Goddard's condensed translation of Binet's 1908 scale, a standard method for administration, and extensions to the deaf and to the insane. One annotation reports that the scale was found 'wonderfully accurate' in Vineland use, while another notes it 'is not yet sufficiently satisfactory' in England.
requirements: Standardized administration procedure, as in the annotated entry describing 'An attempt to standardize the experimental procedure.'
constraints: An annotated entry states the scale 'is not yet sufficiently satisfactory,' and another entry reports doubt about the mental quotient beyond age twelve.
target_learning_goals: measurement and diagnosis of intellectual level
classification of mental defectives
examples: Goddard's revised scale in use at Vineland after testing two thousand normal children
Huey's directions for applying the scale to the deaf

article_title: The Binet-Simon measuring scale for intelligence: An annotated bibliography. Part II.
citation: Kohs, S. C. (1914). The Binet-Simon Measuring Scale for Intelligence: An Annotated Bibliography. Part II. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Binet-Simon+Measuring+Scale+for+Intelligence%22+Kohs+annotated+bibliography
title: Mental-age-based classification of mental defectives
description: The bibliography records the proposal, attributed to Goddard, of 'a classification of mental defectives according to mental age' — ranking individuals by the age level their Binet performance attains rather than by chronological age alone. This organizing idea underlies the diagnostic and institutional applications the bibliography documents, including grading of institutional populations. Kuhlmann's entry criticizes the underlying quantity, arguing the difference between mental and chronological age 'does not represent the true degree of deficiency' and choosing rate of mental progress as more representative.
requirements: A normed scale yielding a mental-age estimate, such as the Binet-Simon scale with its age-graded tests.
constraints: Kuhlmann's annotated entry argues that the mental-age/chronological-age difference does not represent the true degree of deficiency; Kulpe's entry doubts the comparative value of mental age.
target_learning_goals: classification of mental defectives
diagnosis of retardation
examples: Goddard's prognostical classification of mental defectives in institutional settings
Kuhlmann's grading of thirteen hundred feeble-minded children with the tests

article_title: An absolute point scale for the group measurements of intelligence. Part I.
citation: Otis, A. S. (1918). An absolute point scale for the group measurements of intelligence. Part I. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 9(5), 239-261. https://books.google.com/books/about/the_journal_of_educational_psychology.html
title: Group tests should require very simple responses with one correct answer so that administration and scoring are rapid and comparable across investigators
description: Otis argues that the rationale for group testing is time economy, achieved by arranging items so that each has a single objectively scorable answer. As printed: "The chief object of testing in groups, of course, is economy of time. One of the most essential means of accomplishing this purpose is that the responses required be very simple." Answers are indicated by making a letter or figure or drawing a line, so papers "may be scored with dispatch by the use of scoring forms" and every investigator scores the same way, assuring comparability.
requirements: Responses must be very simple so administration and scoring are fast
Each item must have only one correct answer
Answers should be placeable in a single column for scoring-form scoring
constraints: The design is aimed at administration to groups of at least 50 pupils in grades 4 to 8 of the elementary school
target_learners: pupils in grades 4, 5, 6, 7, and 8 of the elementary school
target_learning_goals: measurement of general mental ability in groups
examples: Tests in the scale were arranged so answers were marked with a letter, figure, or drawn line, and partially correct answers were avoided entirely
key_sources: Otis, A. S. (1918). An absolute point scale for the group measurements of intelligence. Part I. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 9(5), 239-261. https://books.google.com/books/about/the_journal_of_educational_psychology.html

article_title: An absolute point scale for the group measurements of intelligence. Part I.
citation: Otis, A. S. (1918). An absolute point scale for the group measurements of intelligence. Part I. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 9(5), 239-261. https://books.google.com/books/about/the_journal_of_educational_psychology.html
title: The Absolute Point Scale: ten objective tests compiled in duplicate forms for group measurement of general mental ability
description: The scale is a battery of ten tests—Spelling, Arithmetic, Synonyms and Antonyms, Memory for Digits, Proverbs, Disarranged Sentences, Relation, Geometric, Following Directions, and Narrative Completion—compiled in duplicate. As printed: "The scale was compiled in duplicate. There were, in other words, two complete tests of each kind." The two forms of each kind were made as alike as possible without using the same material, and the ideas were drawn chiefly from the Stanford Revision of the Binet Scale, with the remaining tests designed especially for this study.
requirements: Each test exists in two near-identical forms to support reliability estimation
Scoring rules are fixed per test, e.g. one count per correct answer with deductions for incorrect answers on some tests
constraints: The Spelling Test, though a strong measure, was later dropped from the scale
The Disarranged Sentence Test is a speed test requiring fixed time limits
target_learners: pupils in grades 4 to 8 of the elementary school
target_learning_goals: measurement of general mental ability
examples: The Arithmetic Test used 16 problems with easy computation so emphasis fell on reasoning; the Proverb Test asked pupils to match ten proverbs to explaining statements among twelve

article_title: An absolute point scale for the group measurements of intelligence. Part I.
citation: Otis, A. S. (1918). An absolute point scale for the group measurements of intelligence. Part I. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 9(5), 239-261. https://books.google.com/books/about/the_journal_of_educational_psychology.html
title: The Absolute Point Scale framework and the Coefficient of Brightness: ability units defined so equal point increments equal ability increments and zero points mean absence of ability
description: The framework holds that scores from different tests can be averaged fairly only after transmutation into common absolute units, or points, such that equal increments of ability receive equal increments of points. Otis defines the Coefficient of Brightness as "the quotient that would be obtained by dividing the measure of the absolute amount of mental ability of any individual by the measure of the absolute amount of mental ability which was normal for the age of that individual." The scale's zero is set so that zero points represent "just absence of ability," and the framework was applied in this study by dividing each pupil's total point score by the age norm taken from the curve of Fig. 2.
requirements: Measures must be in terms where equal increments of ability are measured by equal increments of the scale and twice as many units represent twice as much ability
Age norms must be available for the pupil's age, taken from the smoothed curve for fractional ages
constraints: Reliable norms were obtained only for ages 10 to 14; the straight line to age zero was an assumed extrapolation, and norms above age 15 are only roughly approximate because older pupils were selected
target_learners: pupils in grades 4 to 8 of the elementary school
target_learning_goals: measuring general mental ability on an absolute scale and comparing individuals to age norms
examples: Each pupil's coefficient of brightness was found by dividing his total point score by the score normal for his age, with norms for fractional ages read from the Fig. 2 curve

article_title: A Significant Conference Report on Sex Education.
citation: New Publications, The Journal of Educational Psychology. (1920). https://journals.apa.org/edp/
title: Embed sex education within the whole purpose of education and of life, treating it as character education rather than a segregated special subject
description: The principle holds that sex education should not be isolated as a special subject. The 1920 conference report reviewed here argues it is "not in its nature a special form of education" but character education that addresses pervasive human incentives, and that segregation arouses apprehension. It recommends psychological gradation of training respecting individual differences.
requirements: Issue definition first: because many question whether anything can or ought to be attempted in sex education, objectives must be carefully defined before training is planned.
constraints: The reviewed report deals rather exclusively with boys and young men; restatement for girls and young women was only contemplated.
target_learners: boys and young men (as addressed by the reviewed report)
target_learning_goals: character education addressing sexual attitudes and conduct as part of general education
examples: The American Social Hygiene Association's 1920 preliminary synthesis and integration of the returns of the sex education conference, prepared under the active direction of Dr. Thomas W. Galloway for the International Committee of Young Men's Christian Association.
key_sources: New Publications, The Journal of Educational Psychology. (1920). https://journals.apa.org/edp/

article_title: A Significant Conference Report on Sex Education.
citation: New Publications, The Journal of Educational Psychology. (1920). https://journals.apa.org/edp/
title: Avoid rigidly dividing a lesson period into fixed minutes per activity, since fixed time allocation may formalize the lesson
description: This principle cautions against lesson plans that bind each activity to a fixed number of minutes. The reviewer of a 7th-grade lesson scheme, which allocated a 50-minute period across review, assignment, silent study, oral expression, and summary, suggests that to assign periods of different kinds of work within the class hour "may quite completely formalize the lesson." Flexible use of lesson time is implied as preferable.
requirements: A lesson plan whose activities would otherwise be pinned to fixed per-activity minute allocations within one period.
constraints: The caution rests on questions the reviewer raises from his own experiment in fifth grade social studies; no results of that experiment are reported.
target_learning_goals: maintaining flexible, non-formulaic lesson structure in secondary classroom teaching
examples: The reviewed proposal's allocation of a 50-minute period: 9 minutes review, 10 minutes assignment, 6 minutes silent study, 20 minutes oral expression, and 5 minutes summary, against which the reviewer states the caution.
key_sources: New Publications, The Journal of Educational Psychology. (1920). https://journals.apa.org/edp/

article_title: “So no one feels left out”: Latinx youths’ and parents’ reimagined school realities in the context of cultural stressors.
citation: Lorenzo-Blanco, Elma I., Henriquez, Kimberly L., Romero, Michelle Y. Martin, Stein, Gabriela Livas, & Isaza, Alejandra Garcia. (2025). “So no one feels left out:” Latinx youths’ and parents’ re-imagined school realities in the context of cultural stressors. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000956
title: Community cultural wealth, freedom dreaming, and desire-based frameworks positioning youths’ and parents’ reimagined realities as precursors for social change
description: The article draws on community cultural wealth (Yosso, 2005), freedom dreaming (Kelley, 2002), desire-based research (Tuck, 2009), and the integrative model of minority child development. These frameworks challenge deficit views and position hopes and dreams as “a precursor for social change.” The study focuses on aspirational capital, which “involves youths’ and families’ ability to maintain hopes and dreams in the face of structural inequality.” Participants’ magic-wand re-imaginations elicit this aspirational capital to identify school-level intervention targets.
requirements: Research must center youths’ and parents’ voices, positioning them as experts in naming their reality and desired changes.
constraints: The frameworks were applied to Latinx youth and parents in six high schools with high Latinx and economically disadvantaged enrollment in one Central Texas district.
target_learners: Latinx high school students and their parents
target_learning_goals: School belonging and engagement
Socio-emotional well-being
Healthy youth adjustment despite cultural stressors
examples: Youth and parents responded to the magic-wand prompt describing ideal school realities, which the authors read as expressions of aspirational capital in the context of cultural stressors.
key_sources: Lorenzo-Blanco, Elma I., Henriquez, Kimberly L., Romero, Michelle Y. Martin, Stein, Gabriela Livas, & Isaza, Alejandra Garcia. (2025). “So no one feels left out:” Latinx youths’ and parents’ re-imagined school realities in the context of cultural stressors. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000956

article_title: An inquiry into the statistical basis of a conclusion concerning sex differences.
citation: Frasier, George W. (1915). An Inquiry Into the Statistical Basis of a Conclusion Concerning Sex Differences. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov
title: Do not base conclusions about group differences on modal values of small, arbitrarily grouped distributions
description: The article argues that a modal value is sensitive to the arbitrary size and position of class intervals, quoting Rugg that the modal value "depends, within a certain range over the scale, upon the size and position of class-intervals." Group comparisons should instead use measures such as the arithmetic mean and refined median with their probable errors, and should rest on adequate numbers of cases.
requirements: Distributions must be checked under alternative class-interval sizes and positions before interpreting modes
Comparisons of central tendency should be reported with measures of dispersion such as the P.E.
constraints: The demonstration concerns a single 53-child Point Scale dataset; the article states no attempt was made to justify the interval of eight used in one illustration
target_learners: ten-year-old school children assessed on mental ability scales
target_learning_goals: fair evaluation of individual test results across sex groups
examples: The article regrouped the Yerkes monograph data with shifted five-point intervals and with eight-point intervals, showing the ten-point modal separation shrink to five points and then disappear, and compared mean (63.9 vs 60.8) and median (65.8 vs 59.7) differences with their probable errors.
key_sources: Frasier, George W. (1915). An Inquiry Into the Statistical Basis of a Conclusion Concerning Sex Differences. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov

article_title: A Comparison of Results Obtained by the Terman Binet Tests and the Healy Picture Completion Test.
citation: E. B. Skaggs. (1920). A Comparison of Results Obtained by the Terman Binet Tests and the Healy Picture Completion Test. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org
title: Two-aspect general intelligence: an abstract (Binet-tapped) and a concrete, mechanical (Picture-Completion-tapped) form
description: The article proposes that general intelligence splits into two forms, drawing on Thorndike's suggestion of abstract, concrete-mechanical, and social intelligence. The author writes that "there is ground for the twofold general grouping," holding that the "Picture Completion test is the concrete and more mechanical form of test" while the Terman Binet taps the abstract form far more. The theory rests on the near-zero correlations between the two tests in the 65-case comparison. The author declines to endorse a separate social general intelligence and speculates that the abstract form is evolutionarily later and superior.
requirements: Both an abstract-type test such as the Terman Binet and a concrete performance-type test such as the Healy Picture Completion must be administered to the same individuals to reveal the divergence.
constraints: The author states the theory is grounded in one 65-case sample of children, most below normal mental age and all under 14, and partly on theorizing about racial evolution that the article itself labels speculative.
target_learners: children under 14, most between 8 and 14, including ungraded-class and clinic-referred cases
target_learning_goals: assessment of general intelligence and its abstract versus concrete components
examples: The article's 65-case comparison, in which some children classified feebleminded by Binet tested years advanced on the Picture Completion test, is offered as the basis for the two-aspect account.
key_sources: E. B. Skaggs. (1920). A Comparison of Results Obtained by the Terman Binet Tests and the Healy Picture Completion Test. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0076088

article_title: A Comparison of Results Obtained by the Terman Binet Tests and the Healy Picture Completion Test.
citation: E. B. Skaggs. (1920). A Comparison of Results Obtained by the Terman Binet Tests and the Healy Picture Completion Test. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org
title: Healy Picture Completion Test (administered by Pintner and Anderson procedures)
description: The Healy Picture Completion Test is a performance test in which the child completes pictures, scored by score and completion time, and classified into age levels such as Below 5, Age 8, and Adult. The article administered it following "the procedure and standards laid down by Pintner and Anderson," noting the test is relatively useless for adults, so no adult cases appear. Across 65 children it produced scores, times, and age-level classifications compared against Terman Binet IQs and ratings.
requirements: Pintner and Anderson's published procedure and standards must be followed for administration and scoring.
constraints: The article states the test is relatively useless for adults; it was applied here only to children under 14.
target_learners: children under chronological age 14, mostly aged 8 to 14
target_learning_goals: mental testing and classification of children's general mental ability
examples: In the article, 26 children in an ungraded class at the Ann Arbor Perry School and other clinic cases were given the Healy test personally, with Binet ratings partly loaned by Professor Jackson.

article_title: Results in Silent Versus Oral Reading.
citation: Mead, C. D. (1916). Results in Silent Versus Oral Reading. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov
title: Alice in Wonderland silent-versus-oral reproduction tests
description: A reading-comprehension test format in which pupils read an 'Alice in Wonderland' passage under both silent and oral reading conditions and reproduce the points covered. The purpose "was to find by which method pupils were able to reproduce the more points included in the" material read. Scoring counted lines read and points reproduced, and compared the percentage of possible points covered by each method across timed tests.
requirements: Material is read under both silent and oral methods so the two conditions can be compared for the same pupils.
target_learners: Pupils from the third to the tenth grade
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension measured by reproduction of points in a passage
examples: Six two-minute tests per method with 112 sixth-grade pupils in 1914; six one-minute tests per method with 340 pupils from grades 3–10 in 1915 and 1916.

article_title: Warning students of the consequences of examination failure: An effective strategy for promoting student engagement?
citation: Putwain, D. W., Nicholson, L. J., & Kutuk, G. (2021). Warning Students of the Consequences of Examination Failure: An Effective Strategy for Promoting Student Engagement? https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1329876
title: Appraisal-based framework for student evaluation of teacher fear appeals as challenge or threat
description: The article proposes that teacher fear appeals about high-stakes examinations do not directly link to motivation, engagement and achievement but depend on how students evaluate them, drawing on Expectancy Value Theory, Control-Value Theory and the Cognitive Theory of Stress and Coping. Challenge arises when "coping resources are judged to outweigh task demands" and threat when they cannot. The framework treats fear appeals as prompts for evaluative processes shaped by competence beliefs and utility value.
requirements: Students must perceive the examination as personally meaningful (high utility value) for a challenge or threat evaluation to arise
constraints: The article notes it remains unclear whether challenge and threat are opposite states or can co-occur
target_learners: Secondary school students aged 14-16 preparing for high-stakes examinations
target_learning_goals: Behavioral engagement in mathematics
GCSE mathematics achievement
examples: The study operationalised challenge evaluation as interpreting fear appeals as inspiring hard work, effort and hope, and threat evaluation as interpreting them as worrying and indicating likely failure
key_sources: Putwain, D. W., Nicholson, L. J., & Kutuk, G. (2021). Warning Students of the Consequences of Examination Failure: An Effective Strategy for Promoting Student Engagement? https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1329876

article_title: Between- and within-domain relations of students' academic emotions.
citation: Goetz, T., Frenzel, A. C., Pekrun, R., Hall, N. C., & Lüdtke, O. (2006). Between- and Within-Domain Relations of Students' Academic Emotions. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu
title: Control–value theory of achievement emotions as an explanatory framework for domain-specific academic emotions
description: Pekrun's control–value theory holds that academic emotions are joint products of two appraisal types: appraisals of control over achievement activities and outcomes, and appraisals of their value. The article states that "any emotion related to academic achievement can be understood as a joint product of control and value appraisals, including students' enjoyment, pride, anxiety, anger, and boredom." Because control- and value-related constructs (self-efficacy, attributions, self-concepts, task values, achievement goals) are organized domain-specifically, the theory implies academic emotions should show weak between-domain relations — a corollary the study's results corroborate.
requirements: Appraisal of control and of value are both needed for the arousal of academic emotions, per the theory's account.
constraints: The theory's domain-specificity corollary applies to the extent that control- and value-related constructs are themselves organized in domain-specific ways, as the article states.
target_learners: secondary school students (Grades 8 and 11 in the study)
target_learning_goals: academic emotions related to classroom learning and achievement in specific subject domains
examples: The study tested the theory's corollary that academic emotions should show weak between-domain relations, finding disattenuated cross-domain emotion correlations that were generally weak.
key_sources: Goetz, T., Frenzel, A. C., Pekrun, R., Hall, N. C., & Lüdtke, O. (2006). Between- and Within-Domain Relations of Students' Academic Emotions. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu

article_title: A constructive ability test.
citation: Kelley, Truman Lee. (1916). A constructive ability test. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Vol. VII, No. 1. https://www.google.com/search?q=Kelley+1916+A+Constructive+Ability+Test+Journal+of+Educational+Psychology
title: The Constructive Ability Test: block-building task with four design criteria and a structured record blank
description: A test in which the child is given blocks and instructed in his native tongue "to build the best thing he can and whatever he chooses", so that the end is not set by the examiner. It was designed to meet four criteria: to be free from dependence upon language, free from preceding formal training, to test initiative as well as manipulative ability, and to be capable of objective grading and standardization. Administration uses a time limit of twice as many minutes as the child is years old, and a record blank scoring purpose, dominance of purpose, symmetry, interest in building versus playing, and merit of each successive structure.
requirements: A set of limited building material as shown in Plate I, a trained grader, and the 40-sample stereoscopic photograph scale for merit grading
constraints: Structures incomplete because of lack of material are not graded as high as structures incomplete because of lack of time
Time may be a trifle short for adults around twenty years of age
The norms so far drawn up rest on boys, so if high-school boys differ from boys in general they would be those of a select group
target_learners: exceptional children (twice the mental age allowed)
target_learning_goals: constructive and executive ability
initiative in setting one's own task
manipulative ability
examples: Children are asked at sixty seconds what they are going to build, and graded excellent=5 to no purpose=0 for dominance of purpose
A large wheel is included in the material as a distraction that suggests playing, to observe interest in building versus aimless play
