article_title: The Constancy of Intelligence Quotients. (A Case Study.).
citation: Lincoln, Edward A. (1922). The Constancy of Intelligence Quotients (A Case Study). The Journal of Educational Psychology, 14, 484-495. https://archive.org/details/journalofeducat14
title: Lincoln's taxonomy of causes of IQ discrepancies between successive examinations
description: The article groups the causes of large differences between successive intelligence quotients under a few general heads. These are fluctuations in ability, interest or attention; unstable or psychopathic personality indicated by failure of previously passed tests; temporary retardation of mental growth paralleling physical retardation; and deficiencies in training or environment, including unfamiliarity with English, poor health keeping a child from school, and lack of experience in superior young children. The taxonomy is built from the case analyses in the paper: "The causes of the Intelligence Quotient differences which have been pointed out in the previous case studies may be grouped under a few general heads."
requirements: Interpreting a discrepancy requires supplementary case information such as teacher reports, physical measurements and examination records
constraints: The taxonomy is derived from a small set of individual cases examined with the Stanford-Binet scale, not from a systematic experiment
target_learners: children examined at a psycho-educational clinic
target_learning_goals: accurate classification of children's intelligence for educational placement
examples: Case 49's low first IQ was traced to linguistic difficulty; case 16's rise was linked to a period of rapid physical growth
key_sources: Lincoln, Edward A. (1922). The Constancy of Intelligence Quotients (A Case Study). The Journal of Educational Psychology, 14, 484-495. https://archive.org/details/journalofeducat14

article_title: The Constancy of Intelligence Quotients. (A Case Study.).
citation: Lincoln, Edward A. (1922). The Constancy of Intelligence Quotients (A Case Study). The Journal of Educational Psychology, 14, 484-495. https://archive.org/details/journalofeducat14
title: Classify a child's intelligence on the basis of several averaged IQ examinations plus a scientific case study, not a single test
description: The article argues that a single intelligence examination should not ground a definite classification because measurement conditions can never be identical between testings and performance fluctuates. It recommends that "no definite classification should be made on the basis of one examination alone, but that a number of Intelligence Quotients should be obtained and averaged for each individual," and closes that discrepancies increase the IQ's usefulness "providing always that a scientific case study of the individual is made." This functions as a testing-practice design principle: repeated measurement plus contextual case study yields more trustworthy classification.
requirements: Multiple examinations of the same individual at different times
Supplementary data such as teacher reports, physical measurements and examination records for the case study
constraints: Identical testing conditions are impossible because prior examination itself changes the subject and time lapses between testings
target_learners: children being examined for intelligence classification
children not getting along in school work
target_learning_goals: accurate and fair educational classification and placement
examples: The study interprets discrepancies across four years of summer-school testing and sixteen clinic retestings to show why single-exam classification is risky
key_sources: Lincoln, Edward A. (1922). The Constancy of Intelligence Quotients (A Case Study). The Journal of Educational Psychology, 14, 484-495. https://archive.org/details/journalofeducat14

article_title: Profiles of teachers’ striving and wellbeing: Evolution and relations with context factors, retention, and professional engagement.
citation: De Clercq, Mikaël, Helen Watt, & Paul Richardson. (2021). Profiles of Teachers’ Striving and Wellbeing: Evolution and relations with context factors, retention and professional engagement. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000702
title: Five-profile typology of teachers' striving and wellbeing
description: The study applies and empirically grounds an existing typology of teacher striving and wellbeing, identifying "Five profiles ... (Sparing, Good health, Ambitious, Burnout and Wornout)" among a longitudinal sample of Australian teachers. The profiles combine dimensions of striving (ambition, effort) and wellbeing (health, burnout), and are used as the states between which teachers transition over career stages.
requirements: Longitudinal measurement of teachers' striving and wellbeing indicators to assign profiles and track transitions
constraints: Profiles were identified among Australian secondary and primary teachers from early to mid-career

target_learning_goals: understanding and supporting teacher wellbeing, striving and professional development

article_title: Complex problem solving in educational contexts—Something beyond g: Concept, assessment, measurement invariance, and construct validity.
citation: Greiff, S., Wüstenberg, S., Molnár, G., Fischer, A., Funke, J., & Csapó, B. (2013, February 18). Complex Problem Solving in Educational Contexts—Something Beyond g: Concept, Assessment, Measurement Invariance, and Construct Validity. Journal of Educational Psychology. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0031856
title: Two-process cognitive framework of complex problem solving: knowledge acquisition and knowledge application
description: This framework, drawn from the European CPS research tradition (Dörner, Funke), holds that "two main demands specify a problem solver's performance within the realm of CPS: knowledge acquisition and knowledge application" (Funke, 2001). Knowledge acquisition concerns building a problem representation of an unknown, dynamic system through exploration; knowledge application concerns using that representation to reach goal states. The article operationalizes the two processes as separate MicroDYN phases and tests them as distinct but correlated latent dimensions. It connects to problem-representation and problem-solution research in the Newell and Simon tradition.
requirements: Assessment must present an unknown dynamic system whose regularities can only be revealed through active exploration, since pencil-and-paper formats cannot capture interactive system behavior
constraints: The framework targets domain-general processes when solvers first face an unknown system; domain-specific knowledge becomes increasingly involved with repeated exposure and is deliberately minimized in the tasks
target_learners: high school students in Grades 5 to 11 (ages 11 to 17)
target_learning_goals: cross-curricular complex problem solving, including exploring unknown systems and applying acquired knowledge to reach goals
examples: MicroDYN implements the framework in two phases: an evaluation-free exploration phase in which solvers draw the connections between variables onscreen, and a phase in which they reach given target values on output variables
key_sources: Greiff, S., Wüstenberg, S., Molnár, G., Fischer, A., Funke, J., & Csapó, B. (2013, February 18). Complex Problem Solving in Educational Contexts—Something Beyond g: Concept, Assessment, Measurement Invariance, and Construct Validity. Journal of Educational Psychology. article_title: Tests of Trade Proficiency and Their Adaptation to Educational Use.

title: Self-administrative performance tests in trades as incentive and economy device
description: A testing arrangement recommended in Toops' book in which learners administer performance tests themselves and see immediately how their performance compares with a norm or scale point. The review states "the person tested can see how his performance compares with the norm or with any point on a scale without the loss of interest due to delayed scoring," citing use in two engineering schools. article_title: Dynamics of change in math self-efficacy, sources of self-efficacy, and math skills.
citation: Peura, P., Koponen, T., Aro, T., Viholainen, H., & Aro, M. (2026). Dynamics of change in math self-efficacy, sources of self-efficacy, and math skills. Journal of Educational Psychology, 118(2), 209-223. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0001006
title: Dynamic person-oriented account of math self-efficacy change within social cognitive theory's triadic reciprocity
description: The article applies a person-oriented, growth-mixture approach to social cognitive theory's claim that personal beliefs (self-efficacy), environmental inputs (the four sources of self-efficacy), and behavior (math skills) interact dynamically. Rather than mean-level trends, it models unobserved subgroups with differing levels, rates, and directions of change, testing what it calls the theoretical tenets of triadic reciprocity between personal, environmental, and behavioral processes. The four identified trajectories provide evidence that self-efficacy is dynamic and co-develops with skills and learning experiences.
requirements: Longitudinal data with repeated measures of self-efficacy, its sources, and skills at multiple time points
Person-oriented modeling (growth mixture modeling) to reveal subgroups masked by mean-level analyses
constraints: The design assessed sources, self-efficacy, and skills at the same time points, so causal inferences cannot be made
Only three time points, limiting the change shapes that could be modeled
target_learning_goals: Math self-efficacy and beliefs about capability in mathematics
examples: Growth mixture modeling over 11 months in grades 2–4 identified high stable, low stable, increasing, and decreasing self-efficacy trajectories related to co-occurring changes in skills and sources

article_title: Autonomy and task performance: Explaining the impact of grades on intrinsic motivation.
citation: Pulfrey, C., Darnon, C., & Butera, F. (2013). Autonomy and task performance: Explaining the impact of grades on intrinsic motivation. Journal of Educational Psychology, 105(1), 39–57. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0029376
title: Integrative model differentiating the mediational roles of task performance and task autonomy in the grading–intrinsic motivation link
description: The article proposes an integrative model that treats posttask intrinsic motivation as two distinct but related constructs — self-report task interest and continuing motivation for the task — and tests two mediators simultaneously. It holds that both perceived task autonomy and reward-contingent task performance mediate the link between grading context and task interest, whereas task autonomy, and not task performance, mediates the link between grading context and continuing motivation. The model was tested in a school context using two contrasts against a standard-grade reference condition. As the authors state, the model tests "the mediational role of task performance and of perceived task autonomy on the relationship between grading and both self-report task interest and continuing motivation for the task."
requirements: Two experimental contrasts against a standard-grade reference condition: a reward contrast (high grade vs. standard grade) and an autonomy contrast (no grade vs. standard grade)
Simultaneous measurement of task performance and perceived task autonomy as mediators, with task autonomy measured before the main task to preserve chronological order
constraints: Tested in the ecologically valid context of Swiss secondary school classrooms with anagram tasks
Grounded in the SDT versus GIT debate over performance-contingent rewards
target_learners: Secondary school pupils in academic tracks (Grades 7–9)
target_learning_goals: Intrinsic motivation for academic tasks, measured as task interest and continuing motivation for the task
examples: Experiment 1 with 89 lowest-track pupils and Experiment 2 with 122 seventh graders across three tracks used anagram exercises under no-grade, high-grade, and standard-grade conditions

article_title: Two Important Points with Regard to Age-Grade Tables.
citation: Pressey, S. L. (1920). Two Important Points with Regard to Age-Grade Tables. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Two+Important+Points+with+Regard+to+Age-Grade+Tables
title: Report grade norms together with the median age of the grade instead of attempting general age norms
description: For achievement testing, the article recommends abandoning general age norms and instead publishing grade norms accompanied by each grade's median age. This "will permit of allowance for differences in the age-grade make-up of different schools", largely allows for selection differences, removes the advantage highly retarding schools gain on tests, and eases adjustment for testing at different times of year.
requirements: A census of the age-grade distribution must be available so the median age per grade can be computed and reported alongside the norms.
constraints: The author frames this for tests of achievement (and, he believes, intelligence), noting age norms are even more difficult than grade norms because of uneven coverage of ages within schools.
target_learners: K-12 school pupils whose age-grade distribution is being summarized for testing and comparison purposes
target_learning_goals: Fair and interpretable standardization of achievement and intelligence test norms across schools and school systems
examples: The author urges treating age-grade data "according to some such standard statistical procedure" — medians and 10th/90th percentiles — and demonstrates the method on age-grade tables from Cities C and F.

article_title: A brief scale of intelligence for use in school surveys.
citation: Pressey, S. L. (1920). A Brief Group Scale of Intelligence for Use in School Surveys. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journal/edu
title: The Pressey 'Cross-out' brief group intelligence scale for grades 4-8
description: A four-test group scale of general intelligence printed as a four-page 9-inch by 12-inch folder, with "four tests each of twenty-five items (a total of 100 'points')": verbal ingenuity, logical judgment, arithmetical ingenuity, and moral judgment, all using a cross-out response. It was intended (a) for survey comparisons between sections, schools, or systems and (b) as an aid in individual diagnosis.
requirements: Administered by teachers or field workers without special training in mental tests, with directions read verbatim from a one-page script and blanks scored by crossing out one word or number per line
constraints: "Sufficient accuracy for the final diagnosis of any individual case can, of course, not be expected from such a brief scale"; it is for preliminary selection of individuals deserving further study
target_learning_goals: measurement of level and distribution of general ability in groups and preliminary individual diagnosis
examples: Given to all children from the third grade through high school in three Indiana city surveys, with the final form based on item analysis by P.E. deviations against a sixth-grade base

citation: Pressey, S. L. (1920). A Brief Group Scale of Intelligence for Use in School Surveys. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journal/edu
title: Design brief group tests for convenience, brevity, and teacher-interpretable scores
description: The article argues that group intelligence tests for schools should be built around "convenience, brevity, cost and ready interpretation of results in terms of school practice". The Cross-out scale realizes this: one 9" by 12" sheet, twenty-five minutes of testing, scoring at "90 an hour" by student help or one minute per blank by a teacher, and cheap blanks, so a survey is possible "at a minimum of expense and labor".
requirements: Directions occupy one side of a typewritten sheet, are read verbatim, and scoring requires only counting correctly crossed-out words, one per line
constraints: Insufficient attention to such practical considerations is criticized in other group scales; individual-diagnosis accuracy is limited by brevity
target_learners: school children in grades 4-8 surveyed at class, school, or system level
target_learning_goals: efficient measurement of general ability for survey comparisons and preliminary diagnosis
examples: All cases in one city survey were examined by the writer in one school day, and total scoring-blank cost with student help was $5.00

article_title: A standardization of certain opposites tests.
citation: Harry A. Greene. (1918). A Standardization of Certain Opposites Tests. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0070589
title: Graded 80-word opposites-test list with difficulty point values from .5 to 2.0 totaling 100 points
description: A scored stimulus-word list for opposites tests in which each of eighty words carries a difficulty-derived point value. Values were derived from freshmen responses and "range from .5 point for the words beautiful and straight, up to 2.0 points for the word suave". The article states that "by using the complete list of eighty words and considering each word at its point value a test with a total possible score of 100 points is obtained", allowing direct combination of two opposites tests into one score. Table I groups words of equal point value in ascending order of difficulty.
requirements: A tabulation of correct and half-correct responses to each stimulus word from a large group administration, keyed to the King and Gold response table
constraints: Word values were calibrated on University of Iowa freshmen in the fall of 1916 and 1917, so difficulty values reflect that population

target_learning_goals: measurement of verbal association and word knowledge via opposites tests
examples: Responses from 990 individuals to the first half of the list and 710 to the second half were tabulated and scaled
The published list gives each stimulus word with its point value, full value responses in italics, and half value responses in ordinary type

article_title: A standardization of certain opposites tests.
citation: Harry A. Greene. (1918). A Standardization of Certain Opposites Tests. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0070589
title: Probability-curve percentile weighting of item difficulty for scoring opposites tests
description: A scoring account in which each stimulus word's difficulty is estimated from the percentage of subjects failing it, then converted to a percentile value by reading from a table based on the area of the probability curve, assuming the tested ability fits that curve. The article states that "the percentage scores were changed directly into percentile values by reading directly from table based upon the area of the probability curve" with 0 set at -3σ, 50 at the mean, and 100 at +3σ. This replaces earlier scoring that treated every error identically. As an illustration, the word suave, "missed by 96% of the subjects", is valued at 79 on the percentile scale.
requirements: Group-administration response data large enough to estimate the percentage failing each stimulus word
A conversion table based on the area of the normal probability curve
constraints: The scaling assumes the particular abilities involved in the test fit the probability curve
Scores are calculated for group use; the time-to-correct-response method is presented as better suited to individual testing
target_learners: school children assessed with opposites tests
target_learning_goals: accurate, difficulty-weighted scoring of opposites tests in educational measurement
examples: Word values were derived from responses of University of Iowa freshmen in 1916 and 1917
Percentile values were totaled and divided by the total to yield relative point values from .5 to 2.0

article_title: The reading comprehension and vocabulary knowledge of children with poor reading comprehension despite adequate decoding: Evidence from a regression-based matching approach.
citation: Spencer, M., Wagner, R. K., & Petscher, Y. (2019). Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000274
title: Simple View of Reading classification system and its additive versus multiplicative variants
description: The Simple View of Reading holds that reading comprehension is the product of decoding and linguistic comprehension, and it underwrites a four-group classification: adequate reader, dyslexia, SCD, and mixed deficit/garden-variety poor reader. The article tests whether the SCD cell's predicted oral-language weakness is sufficient to explain its comprehension difficulty, contrasting additive (main-effects) and multiplicative (interactive) variants. It concludes the results "do not support an additive version the Simple View of Reading" and that vocabulary and decoding are "necessary but not sufficient components of reading comprehension."

constraints: The article states an interactive version still lacks "a theoretical explanation with empirical support of any interactive effect that is observed"
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension
examples: The study classified second graders as SCD or typical readers using SAT-10 reading comprehension and DIBELS-6 NWF decoding percentile cutoffs and tested the additive versus multiplicative models via the magnitude of vocabulary versus comprehension weaknesses.

description: A statistical technique described by Stanovich and Siegel (1994) that tests whether a skill is developmentally delayed or deficient by predicting the skill from achievement level and then adding a group contrast. The article states it "does not introduce the possibility of regression artifacts, allows the entire sample to be retained for analysis, and allows for a wide range of achievement levels to be included within a single continuous framework." Here it predicted PPVT vocabulary from SAT-10 comprehension, then entered an SCD/typical-reader grouping variable.

article_title: Preliminary study of the effect of dental treatment upon the physical and mental efficiency of school children.
citation: Emma Kohnky, M.A. (1913). Preliminary Study of the Effect of Dental Treatment upon the Physical and Mental Efficiency of School Children. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org/journal/jeducpsych
title: Kohnky 1913 two-class dental-treatment comparison design with a Whipple test battery and coin-toss assignment
description: This element is the study design of Kohnky's 1913 preliminary study: two fifth-grade classes in one down-town school, matched on grading, neighborhood, and foreign-birth composition, with the experimental class chosen "decided by the toss of a coin." The treated class received full dental care including "treatment, tooth-brush drills, dinners," while a nurse and social visitor monitored compliance. Outcome measures were Whipple's tapping, cancellation, memory-span, and substitution tests plus weight and height, administered in October and May by two experimenters. The untreated class "received only such attention as they sought, which was found to be practically none."
requirements: Tests must be given by the same experimenters at both testing occasions, as the article arranged
A non-treated comparison class must be available in the same school with like home and social conditions
constraints: The author concedes the ongoing dental work itself introduced "the disturbing factor introduced by the actual carrying on of the dental work in the experimental class"
Only children present at both testings were counted
Results use medians rather than averages to neutralize extremes
target_learning_goals: physical and mental efficiency of school children
examples: Room 21 received dental treatment while Room 18 served as the comparison class; Room 21 was chosen experimentally by the toss of a coin

citation: Keller, L., Preckel, F., & Brunner, M. (2020). Nonlinear Relations Between Achievement and Academic Self-Concepts in Elementary and Secondary School: An Integrative Data Analysis Across 13 Countries. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000533
title: Self-protection as a mechanism underlying nonlinear achievement–self-concept relations
description: The article proposes self-protection as the mechanism that weakens the achievement–self-concept relation for low achievers: negative self-evaluations threaten the self, so "low-achieving students are likely to engage in self-protective strategies that lead to more positive self-evaluations". Strategies include changing the comparison group, poorer recall of self-threatening feedback, and downplaying negative events. The authors argue this mechanism plausibly drives the observed nonlinearity.

article_title: Nonlinear relations between achievement and academic self-concepts in elementary and secondary school: An integrative data analysis across 13 countries.

title: Do not assume a general linear trend when assessing and interpreting students' academic self-concepts
description: Because relations between achievement and self-concepts are nonlinear for a substantial share of students, practitioners "should be aware that there is no general linear trend between students' achievement and their corresponding academic self-concepts" and should account for this "when assessing and interpreting students' academic self-concepts in counseling contexts". Researchers are similarly advised to specify nonlinear models, including for elementary students, to avoid missing nonlinear relations.

target_learning_goals: valid assessment and interpretation of academic self-concepts in counseling
examples: The integrative data analysis applied quadratic and interrupted regression analyses to TIMSS, PIRLS, and PISA data as nonlinear alternatives to linear regression models

article_title: A new scale of mental and physical measurements for adolescents and some of its uses.
citation: Woolley, Helen Thompson. (1915). A new scale of mental and physical measurements for adolescents, and some of its uses. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 6(9), 521-550.
title: A composite adolescent measurement scale built from averaged ten-percentile ranks on mental and physical tests
description: The scale ranks each child from one to ten on every mental and physical test according to the percentile in which the result falls, averages these ranks separately for physical measures (excluding height and weight) and mental measures, and places the average on general ten-percentile tables normed separately by sex and age. It was based on 750 fourteen-year-old children dropping out of school to work and 680 of the same children at fifteen, and places each individual 'in comparison with a large group of supposedly normal people of his own age and sex'. The article calls it 'a first attempt to formulate this kind of a standard, and is very rough in form'.
requirements: Requires giving the child the same series of tests on which the percentile tables are based and ranking each result by the printed percentile tables for the child's age and sex
constraints: Norms apply to fourteen and fifteen year old native born white working children; school-child scales were not yet published
The authors call the method 'a very rough one' and suggest increasing the number, variety and difficulty of tests and finer divisions
target_learners: fourteen and fifteen year old working children (native born white)
target_learning_goals: assessment of native mental and physical endowment for educational and vocational guidance
examples: Percentile tables for vital capacity, grip, steadiness, tapping, fatigue index, card sorting, cancellation, memory, substitution, sentence completion, opposites, and puzzle boxes are appended for ages fourteen and fifteen
key_sources: Woolley, Helen Thompson. (1915). A new scale of mental and physical measurements for adolescents, and some of its uses. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 6(9), 521-550. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0075644

article_title: A new scale of mental and physical measurements for adolescents and some of its uses.
citation: Woolley, Helen Thompson. (1915). A new scale of mental and physical measurements for adolescents, and some of its uses. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 6(9), 521-550.
title: Sort children early by mental and manual endowment into differentiated curriculum tracks, kept flexible
description: The article recommends that children be sorted into large ability groups early — low in both abilities toward industrial training, good manual but poor mental toward skilled trades, medium toward business and secondary positions, high mental with low manual toward professions, and high in both toward professions like medicine and engineering — with corresponding public school curriculum modifications. It stresses that the system must remain flexible: children 'whose diagnosis was uncertain, or those who developed unexpectedly could be shifted from one course to another', supplemented by scholarships for gifted children of limited means.
requirements: A feasible early sorting based on native endowment, using tests such as the composite percentile scale
Flexibility to shift children between courses and scholarships for gifted children of limited means
constraints: The sorting makes no pretense of singling out artistic ability; the authors had no experimental data on artistic genius and general intelligence
Success depends on many factors beyond endowment, including ambition, manner, and home conditions
target_learners: adolescents of fourteen to eighteen in public schools
target_learning_goals: alignment of educational and vocational training with individual endowment
examples: The article proposes grammar-school identification of children unable to profit from high school, and high-school separation of medium from exceptionally good endowment with experimental-science versus humanities emphasis

article_title: Writing fluency: Its relations with language, cognitive, and transcription skills, and writing quality using longitudinal data from kindergarten to grade 2.
citation: Kim Young-Suk Grace. (2024). Writing Fluency: Its Relations With Language, Cognitive, and Transcription Skills, and Writing Quality Using Longitudinal Data From Kindergarten to Grade 2. Journal of Educational Psychology, 116(4). https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000841
title: Developmental dynamic relations hypothesis: what writing fluency taps changes across writing development
description: The article invokes the DIEW dynamic relations hypothesis (Kim & Graham, 2022), which holds that component skills' contributions to writing vary as a function of development. In the beginning phase, transcription skills are not automated and "transcription skills act as a primary determinant of writing process and outcomes", so writing fluency largely taps the transcription process; as transcription automates, other processes and associated skills become increasingly tapped. The study's null relations of oral language skills to fluency support this account for beginning writers.
requirements: Applies within a theoretical framework distinguishing writing phases and component skills (transcription, translation, revision) that draw on language, cognitive, and transcription resources
constraints: The article presents this as one of two speculative possibilities, noting sentence skills such as sentence construction might alternatively be the direct correlate of fluency, and calls for future work
target_learners: Beginning writers in primary grades (kindergarten to Grade 2)
target_learning_goals: Written composition quality
examples: The longitudinal SEM found complete mediation of transcription skills by writing fluency and no independent relation of oral language skills to fluency, consistent with the developmental hypothesis for beginning writers

article_title: Teachers “finding peace in a frantic world”: An experimental study of self-taught and instructor-led mindfulness program formats on acceptability, effectiveness, and mechanisms.
citation: Montero-Marin et al. (2021). Teachers “Finding Peace in a Frantic World”: An Experimental Study of Self-Taught and Instructor-Led Mindfulness Program Formats on Acceptability, Effectiveness, and Mechanisms. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000542
title: Mindfulness and self-compassion skills as psychological mechanisms linking mindfulness training implementation to teacher occupational well-being
description: The article draws on a comprehensive theoretical framework in which adequate implementation of mindfulness training enables teachers to develop the skills of mindfulness and self-compassion, which, applied in daily life through practice, lead to improved occupational health and well-being. Mindfulness skills help teachers "recognize their distress without judgment, be open to it, and learn to self-soothe," while self-compassion skills increase the ability to regulate intense negative emotions in response to stressors. This framework motivated the study's mediation analyses and the hypothesis that the two delivery formats might produce different patterns of skill acquisition and mediation.
requirements: An adequate implementation of mindfulness training so that skills are developed and applied in daily life through practice
constraints: The framework's causal links between skills and outcomes were tested via mediation analysis without a no-intervention arm in this study
target_learning_goals: managing occupational stress and improving well-being through mindfulness and self-compassion skills
examples: The trial tested whether mindfulness and self-compassion gains mediated improvements in well-being, stress, anxiety, depression, and burnout in each delivery format
key_sources: Montero-Marin et al. (2021). Teachers “Finding Peace in a Frantic World”: An Experimental Study of Self-Taught and Instructor-Led Mindfulness Program Formats on Acceptability, Effectiveness, and Mechanisms. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000542

title: M-FP mindfulness curriculum sequencing four understandings-and-skills themes across eight sessions with daily home practice
description: The Mindfulness: A Practical Guide to Finding Peace in a Frantic World (M-FP) curriculum is an introductory, skills-based training built on mindfulness-based cognitive therapy core elements and designed for improving well-being in the general population. It develops four sequenced themes: recognizing autopilot and bringing mindfulness to everyday present-moment experience; recognizing thoughts, emotions, sensations, and impulses while stabilizing attention; recognizing unhelpful patterns of thinking, feeling, and acting; and learning skills for keeping balanced and responding skillfully when difficulties arise. "The curriculum has eight sessions that work sequentially through these four main themes," with home practices including a daily 20-minute mindfulness practice.
requirements: Participants engage in a range of home practices that support learning, including a daily 20-minute mindfulness practice
constraints: Designed as an introductory program for the general population, applied here to secondary school teachers
target_learning_goals: dispositional mindfulness
self-compassion
responding skillfully to difficulties
examples: Both trial arms delivered this same M-FP manualized curriculum, one instructor-led in eight 90-minute weekly group sessions and one self-taught from the book with an accompanying app

article_title: The Devious Path of Slow Work.
citation: Bird, Grace E. (1921). The Devious Path of Slow Work. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ123456
title: Encourage learners to attain standard speed of motions as early as possible.
description: Bird, drawing on Gilbreth's motion study, argues that because "fast motions are different in character from slow motions," the learner "should be encouraged to attain standard speed of motions as early as possible." If motions cannot be made at standard speed by the beginner, rapidity should approach that of the expert, since habits initiated slowly may later cause retroactive inhibition when speed is sought.
requirements: Work should be provided in which the finest quality is not essential, so the beginner can approximate standard speed.
constraints: Undue haste can arouse anxiety, fear, or annoyance which interfere with rational processes; standard speed is not always high speed.
target_learning_goals: accurate and rapid execution of learned procedures
examples: Bird suggests that in arithmetic, approximations of the answer rather than exact results give the child opportunity to attain initial speed, paralleling the industrial beginner given work where fine quality is not essential.
key_sources: Bird, Grace E. (1921). The Devious Path of Slow Work. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ123456

article_title: The Devious Path of Slow Work.
citation: Bird, Grace E. (1921). The Devious Path of Slow Work. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ123456
title: Pupils should think in terms of results more than in terms of the process.
description: Bird concludes that pupils "should think in terms of results more than in terms of the process," because this economical method encourages speed and is more conducive to concentration, being in less danger of distraction elements which tend to alter the character of the work. The recommendation follows from her observation that rapid calculation crowds out irrelevant intermediate performances.
requirements: Practice must be properly focalized and motivated so that learners exercise optimum effort.
target_learning_goals: rapid and accurate computation
concentration on task goals
examples: In her experiment, students during rapid adding stated as their central thought a desire to get the answer, while slow adding produced varied distractions.
key_sources: Bird, Grace E. (1921). The Devious Path of Slow Work. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ123456

article_title: The Devious Path of Slow Work.
citation: Bird, Grace E. (1921). The Devious Path of Slow Work. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ123456
title: Fast motions are essentially different from slow motions in both industrial and intellectual work.
description: Bird's central thesis, stated in her conclusion, is that "Fast motions are essentially different from slow motions not only in industrial but in intellectual work." Drawing on Gilbreth's observation that a bricklayer used different motions when working slowly than when working rapidly due to different muscle tension, and on her own addition experiments showing more errors and distractions under slow work, she argues slow work follows a devious path cluttered with irrelevant bonds.
requirements: The distinction rests on the assumption that rapid, properly focalized practice establishes habits that eliminate superfluous intermediate performances.
constraints: Bird notes further investigation might show decreased efficiency even more marked than the reduction of accuracy observed.
target_learning_goals: efficient skill automatization
speed with accuracy
examples: Bird describes how in slow addition a person may revert to wasteful childhood habits such as counting on fingers, lip movement, and vocalization.

article_title: Reading for university or for myself? Effects of context and beliefs about science on college students’ document selection.
citation: Cornelia Schoor, Jean-François Rouet, and M. Anne Britt (2024). Reading for University or for Myself? Effects of Context and Beliefs about Science on College Students' Document Selection. Journal of Educational Psychology, 116 (3), pp.317-345. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000849
title: RESOLV theory of reading as problem solving with context and task models
description: RESOLV (REading as problem SOLVing) posits that most reading serves a specific purpose, so readers decide what to read and how. According to the article, "these decisions are based on a context model and a task model": readers build a context model by feature extraction of external elements (task, requester, audience, supports and obstacles) and internal aspects (knowledge, values, beliefs, skills), and an activated task schema yields a task model that "will drive reading decisions such as what to read, how to read, and when to stop". The study uses RESOLV to predict that the same task question produces different selection decisions depending on the external context scenario.
requirements: Readers must have acquired task schemata from many exposures to certain types of tasks within a situation or context
target_learners: college and university students reading about science
target_learning_goals: adaptive selection of appropriate reading strategies and sources for a given task and context
examples: In both experiments, a university seminar scenario versus a personal podcast scenario was used to activate different task schemata for the identical task question.

title: SERP-based document-selection task with scientific-expertise and personal-experiences sources
description: The core experimental material was a simulated Google search result list for each of four target topics (health, sports, or education domains), from which participants ticked checkboxes for documents to read further. Per the article, "Four of the relevant documents had a source with scientific expertise (e.g., a professor of a relevant field), while another four had a source with personal experiences (e.g., the head of a support group)", plus two irrelevant titles to conceal the study's intent; SERP order, title-source pairings, and topic order were counterbalanced. The task question (write an overview vs. write an opinion) was manipulated independently from the external context.
requirements: Topics must be addressable by both scientific studies and personal experiences
Participants must encode the external context scenario before selecting
constraints: Sources and titles were fictitious, created only for the experiment
target_learners: university students from a German university, mainly teacher education and social science enrollees

examples: For each topic participants received the topic question and selected as many documents as they wanted from the ten-title SERP for later essay writing.

title: Battery measuring explicit and implicit beliefs about science and knowledge about how science works
description: The study's self-variable instruments comprised a perceived-utility-of-science questionnaire, a German short version of the Nadelson trust-in-science questionnaire, and two implicit association tests contrasting science with opinion (utility and trustworthiness evaluation dimensions, D scores per Greenwald et al.), plus a scenario-based knowledge test. As the article states, "As measures of implicit beliefs about science, two implicit association tests (IAT; e.g., Greenwald et al., 2003; Rudolph et al., 2008) were applied (Schoor & Schütz, 2021)". The knowledge test covers nine scenarios including research design, probability, double-blind procedure, meta-analysis, significance, falsification, peer review, operationalization, and generalizability.
requirements: Explicit scales need confirmatory factor analysis support and acceptable internal consistency
IAT administration requires routing participants to a separate assessment environment
constraints: Internal consistency of the knowledge sum score was low (.37), attributed to heterogeneous knowledge aspects
target_learning_goals: assessing beliefs about science and knowledge about how science works as predictors of source selection
examples: Each knowledge scenario asked the participant to choose the correct option from four alternatives, yielding a maximum score of 9.

title: Foster both knowledge about how science works and positive beliefs about science in education to support expert-source selection
description: Based on both experiments' finding that more positive beliefs about science and greater knowledge about how science works predict fewer selections of personal-experiences sources, the article's educational impact statement concludes that "these findings indicate the importance of fostering both knowledge and beliefs about science in education". The principle holds that instruction should target not only scientific content knowledge but also learners' trust in and perceived utility of science, since these dispositions shape which sources students consider appropriate for further reading in both academic and personal reading situations.
requirements: Instruction must address both explicit knowledge about how science works and beliefs (trust in and utility of science)
constraints: The evidence base is document selection about science by university students in the studied contexts
target_learning_goals: selecting trustworthy, scientifically expert sources for further reading
examples: The experiments measured utility of science, trust in science, implicit associations, and scenario-based methodology knowledge as the belief and knowledge variables tied to selection behavior.

article_title: Comparison of the work done in the successive minutes of a ten minute practice period in the fundamentals of arithmetic.
citation: Phillips, F. M. (1916). Comparison of the work done in the successive minutes of a ten minute practice period in the fundamentals of arithmetic. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0072031
title: A one-minute arithmetic test is a fair measure of pupil ability, but scores should be interpreted knowing first-minute output runs slightly higher
description: The article concludes that pupil ability in the fundamentals of arithmetic can be fairly determined by one minute of work, since first- and later-minute performance correlate highly. However, it cautions that "The product of the first minute is a little better than that of the later minutes, a point which should be borne in mind in giving a one minute test." Test designers should treat one-minute scores as valid but slightly elevated estimates.
requirements: Test administered as a timed one-minute period in the fundamentals, with pupils instructed to work as rapidly as possible
constraints: The first-minute advantage diminishes with repeated daily practice, so the elevation applies to initial rather than well-practiced testing
target_learners: Pupils in grades four through eight
target_learning_goals: Measuring computational ability in the four fundamentals of arithmetic
examples: The study administered two figure combinations in the four fundamentals, with 240 combinations per practice sheet, marking minute boundaries verbally during the ten-minute period

article_title: Do jigsaw classrooms improve learning outcomes? Five experiments and an internal meta-analysis.
citation: Arnaud Stanczak, Céline Darnon, Anaïs Robert, Marie Demolliens, Camille Sanrey, Pascal Bressoux, Pascal Huguet, Céline Buchs, Fabrizio Butera, and PROFAN Consortium. (2022). Do Jigsaw classrooms improve learning outcomes? Five experiments and an internal meta-analysis. Journal of Educational Psychology, 114 (6), pp.1461-1476. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000730
title: The classical three-step jigsaw procedure: jigsaw groups on subtopics, expert groups, then teaching back to the jigsaw group
description: This pattern structures positive interdependence by distributing complementary resources among group members across three steps. As the article describes it, "In the jigsaw classroom, students work in groups on pedagogical content divided into several subtopics. The classical procedure usually follows three major steps": students first work individually on their assigned subtopic, then meet in expert groups with peers who studied the same subtopic to check understanding, then return to their jigsaw groups and take turns teaching their topic to the other members. In the experiments, this procedure was compared against individualistic or teaching-as-usual conditions on identical content.
requirements: Pedagogical content divided into subtopics with complementary resources distributed so each member is responsible for explaining one part
Expert-group meetings so students can check understanding before teaching back
constraints: The article reports that the three-step procedure "generates different dynamics between members", with the expert step linked to individualistic dynamics and the jigsaw step involving both positive and negative dynamics
target_learning_goals: academic learning outcomes across mathematics, life and earth sciences, physics and chemistry
examples: Experiment 3A adapted a physics-chemistry topic into jigsaw subtopics where expert groups tested specific predictions (e.g., mass conservation with sugar, sand, salt, or vinegar in water) and reported results back to their jigsaw groups

citation: Arnaud Stanczak, Céline Darnon, Anaïs Robert, Marie Demolliens, Camille Sanrey, Pascal Bressoux, Pascal Huguet, Céline Buchs, Fabrizio Butera, and PROFAN Consortium. (2022). Do Jigsaw classrooms improve learning outcomes? Five experiments and an internal meta-analysis. Journal of Educational Psychology, 114 (6), pp.1461-1476. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000730
title: Positive interdependence theory of cooperative learning
description: The article organizes its rationale around positive interdependence theory (Johnson & Johnson, 2009), which "suggests that individuals engage in the task and help each other because they identify with the group and want others to succeed". The theory holds that beneficial effects of cooperation emerge when group members feel responsible for their own learning and that of others; positive interdependence generates opportunities for promotive interactions such as help giving and seeking. A second essential element is individual accountability, because "resource interdependence allows group members to become both positively interdependent and individually accountable", which also counters social loafing.
requirements: Achievement of a group member positively linked to others (common goals, collective rewards, or complementary tasks, resources and roles)
Individual contributions visible and accountable
Group- and individual-level feedback so learners can reflect on group processing
constraints: The article notes the theory's promised benefits depend on these structural elements being present; its five experiments suggest jigsaw, which embodies the elements, did not yield learning gains
target_learners: school students in cooperative classroom settings
target_learning_goals: academic achievement through promotive peer interactions
examples: The jigsaw classroom is presented as an implementation of the theory: positive interdependence is ensured by both the means (complementary resources) and the goal (ensuring everyone has understood the content).

article_title: When academic achievement (also) reflects personality: Using the personality-achievement saturation hypothesis (PASH) to explain differential associations between achievement measures and personality traits.
citation: Nicolas Hübner, Marion Spengler, Benjamin Nagengast, Lex Borghans, Trudie Schils, and Ulrich Trautwein. (2022). When Academic Achievement (Also) Reflects Personality: Using the Personality-Achievement Saturation Hypothesis (PASH) to Explain Differential Associations Between Achievement Measures and Personality Traits. American Psychological Association. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000571
title: Personality-Achievement Saturation Hypothesis (PASH): five features of achievement measures explain differential personality-achievement associations
description: The PASH is an overarching framework proposing that the traditional dichotomy between grades and standardized tests is too simplistic, and that personality-achievement associations instead vary with five features of achievement measures: "level of standardization, relevance for the student, curricular validity, instructional sensitivity, and cognitive ability saturation." It predicts that conscientiousness saturates measures low on standardization and high on curriculum validity and instructional sensitivity, while openness saturates measures high on standardization and cognitive ability saturation but low on relevance, curriculum validity, and instructional sensitivity. The article developed and systematically tested the PASH across three large-scale studies, calling it "currently not part of any other model or theory."
requirements: Achievement measures must be positioned along all five features in each social context; the article states the positioning "should be carefully reconsidered in each social context."
constraints: The article's test focused on conscientiousness and openness only; associations with the other Big Five traits were explored, not hypothesized.
The five features "overlap to some degree" while remaining distinct.
Prior supporting evidence was from studies not tailored to test the PASH.
target_learners: Upper secondary school students (end of Grade 13)
target_learning_goals: Understanding which student characteristics different achievement measures reflect (grades vs. standardized tests)
examples: Table 1 positions measures such as course grades, Zentralabitur final examination grades, GPA, TIMSS-based mathematics tests, and TOEFL along the five features.

article_title: Students' motivational profiles and achievement outcomes in physical education: A self-determination perspective.
citation: Julie Boiché, Philippe Sarrazin, Frederick Grouzet, Luc Pelletier, Julien Chanal. (2008). Students’ Motivational Profiles and Achievement Outcomes in Physical Education. Journal of Educational Psychology, 100 (3), pp.688-701. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-0663.100.3.688
title: Self-Determination Theory's taxonomy of intrinsic and extrinsic motivation types as combinable motivational profiles
description: Self-Determination Theory distinguishes different types of motivation — intrinsic and extrinsic — that prior educational research typically collapsed into a single global indicator of self-determined motivation. This article treats these types as combinable, using cluster analysis to identify "distinct profiles as identified by cluster analysis" and then relating those profiles to "objective criteria of achievement." The framework shifts the unit of analysis from global motivation to the configuration of motivation types a student holds.
requirements: Requires measurement of the separate SDT motivation types rather than only a global self-determination index, so that combinations can be detected via cluster analysis.
constraints: Studied in the domain of physical education (gymnastics teaching cycles) with high school students.
target_learners: high school students in physical education
target_learning_goals: motor skill performance and achievement in physical education
examples: Cluster analyses in the two studies yielded self-determined, non self-determined, and moderate profiles among gymnastics students.

article_title: Students' motivational profiles and achievement outcomes in physical education: A self-determination perspective.
citation: Julie Boiché, Philippe Sarrazin, Frederick Grouzet, Luc Pelletier, Julien Chanal. (2008). Students’ Motivational Profiles and Achievement Outcomes in Physical Education. Journal of Educational Psychology, 100 (3), pp.688-701. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-0663.100.3.688
title: Assess students' motivation as distinct profiles rather than a single global self-determination index
description: Because different types of motivation can combine into distinct profiles with different achievement consequences, educators and researchers should assess students' motivational profiles instead of relying only on a global indicator of self-determined motivation. The article states its purpose was to examine "whether the different types of motivation proposed by SDT can combine into distinct profiles" and discusses "the implications for the assessment of students' motivational profile." Identifying a student's profile allows targeting interventions at the dominant motivation types.
requirements: Measurement instruments capturing the separate intrinsic and extrinsic motivation types, plus a clustering procedure, to assign students to profiles.
constraints: Evidence comes from physical education settings with high school students over 10-week gymnastics cycles.
target_learning_goals: achievement, effort, and performance in physical education
examples: Two studies assessed motivation at the start of gymnastics cycles and linked cluster-derived profiles to end-of-cycle performance, effort, and grades.

article_title: The Significance of Alpha in Colleges.
citation: Stone, Charles Leonard. (1920). The significance of alpha in colleges. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22The+significance+of+alpha+in+colleges%22+Stone
title: Compare intelligence percentiles with scholarship percentiles to identify students whose achievement diverges from measured ability
description: The article recommends pairing intelligence-test percentiles with scholarship percentiles for individual students to flag extreme disparity between ability and achievement. It names the candidates this surfaces: "idlers, men too heavily loaded with extra-curricular activities, and men with unusual capacity to develop their potential." Disparity cases should then be eliminated or explained, with motivation and accessory case-study data considered. The author presents this as a step toward scientific educational administration rather than a tested finding.
requirements: Intelligence test percentiles and scholarship percentiles for the same individual students, plus accessory data such as case studies and instinct tests.
constraints: The article bases the recommendation on tentative trust in intelligence tests; it is offered as a direction for educational administration, not a tested procedure.
target_learning_goals: Identifying students whose scholarship diverges from measured ability, including underperformers and students with undeveloped potential
examples: The Dartmouth study compared Alpha test performance with scholarship quarters and reported 18.2 per cent of A men below the class Alpha average and 32.8 per cent of E men above it.

article_title: A class experiment with the Hillegas scale.
citation: Kate Gordon. (1916). A Class Experiment with the Hillegas Scale. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org/journal/jeducpsych
title: Gordon's reconciliation account: the scale steadies judgment of a single composition but does not alter relative judgments of a series
description: Gordon proposes that the scale's effect is to reduce inconsistency in marking any one composition, while leaving each judge's and the group's ordering of the compositions relatively intact. She writes that "whereas the scale does steady the judgment of a group with respect to its marking of a single composition, it does not alter the judgment... with respect to the relative merits of a series of compositions." This accounts for the coexistence of reduced ranges and standard deviations with unchanged correlations.
requirements: Requires untrained judges grading the same set of compositions twice, once without and once with the objective scale
constraints: Inferred from one class experiment with forty-one inexperienced judges and twenty-five freshman compositions; the author frames it as her interpretation of seemingly conflicting results
target_learners: Junior and Senior students in educational psychology
target_learning_goals: Reliable measurement of English composition quality using an objective scale
examples: The class experiment had students grade twenty-five Marble Statue reproductions by college freshmen, first by impression and then with the Hillegas Scale

article_title: Educational measurement and the classroom teacher.
citation: J. C. B. (1919). Educational Measurements and the Classroom Teacher. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 10(2), 111–112. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journal_of_Educational_Psychology
title: Supervising staff must actively encourage classroom teachers to use educational measurements for the practice to take hold
description: This principle holds that classroom teachers will adopt educational measurement as routine practice only if superintendents and principals actively encourage and support them in doing so. The editorial states that "The recognition of the value of measurements for the teacher can only come about through the encouragement of the supervising staff." It pairs with the authors' vision of united staff effort to study "the needs and capacities of individual children" and base school work on those findings.
requirements: Whole-hearted cooperation of superintendent, principal, and teacher in studying the needs and capacities of individual children and basing school work on their findings, as the editorial states: "When superintendent, principal and teacher unite whole-heartedly to study the needs and capacities of individual children and to base the school work upon their findings."
target_learners: K-12 school pupils assessed by their classroom teachers
target_learning_goals: Determining the needs and capacities of individual pupils and adjusting teaching effort accordingly
examples: The editorial cites directors of research bureaus as "making noteworthy contributions" toward equipping teachers to use measurements as everyday tools.

article_title: Tests for originality.
citation: Chassell, L. M. (1916). Tests for Originality. The Journal of Educational Psychology, VII (June, 1916).
title: Battery of twelve tests for originality with self-recording time device
description: A battery of twelve individual and group-administered tests for originality, five devised in the Northwestern University psychological laboratory and seven adapted or modified from prior tests, covering word-building, picture writing, analogues, puzzles, completion, economic prophecy, code translation, invention, and novel hypothetical situations. Instructions were given orally and by placard, and a constructed time-keeping device let subjects record their own time. The article states, "the following twelve were selected and modified for subsequent use." Scores ranged from timed solutions to graded originality of suggestions, and each student's final group rank was the median of his twelve ranks.
requirements: Oral plus placard presentation of instructions, and a time-keeping device allowing subjects to record their own time
constraints: Raw scores were omitted from the article, and several tests required scoring adjustments (fines for errors, quality adjustments to recorded time)
target_learning_goals: Ranking individuals in terms of originality
examples: Applied to 100 students from all classes at Northwestern University and to one inventor of international reputation

article_title: Department for discussion of research problems. A problem for careful research: How does the ability to make rapid mental adjustments affect test scores and pupil achievements?
citation: Zirbes, L. (1919). A Problem for Careful Research: How Does the Ability to Make Rapid Mental Adjustments Affect Test Scores and Pupil Achievements? The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22How+Does+the+Ability+to+Make+Rapid+Mental+Adjustments+Affect+Test+Scores+and+Pupil+Achievements%22+Zirbes
title: Mental set and rapid mental adjustment as a skill factor in achievement
description: The article proposes that many achievement errors arise not from lack of mathematical or reading ability but from 'a failure on the part of the child to set his mind for the particular reading task in hand, or to the persistence of one mental set through different types of reading'. Rapid mental adjustment — the ability to shift set quickly and to see the necessity of change — is framed as a general skill factor contributing to test scores across subjects, trainable in principle. The framework generates six stated research problems on its influence on standard tests, Binet scores, training and transfer.
requirements: Training and testing situations must make the need for change in mental set inhere in the material, since pupils may not see the need themselves
constraints: The ability is not distinctly characterized as mathematical ability, and the article states it is unknown to what extent training of this ability must be special rather than transferring
target_learners: elementary grade pupils (grades IV-VI in the illustrations)
target_learning_goals: accurate and flexible performance across mixed tasks
appropriate reading rate and comprehension
recall of learned material under varied conditions
examples: The Courtis arithmetic error analysis and the four-part timed reading test are the article's own illustrations of set effects and adjustment

article_title: Differential codevelopment of vocabulary knowledge and reading comprehension for students with and without learning disabilities.
citation: Quinn, Jamie M.; Wagner, Richard K.; Petscher, Yaacov; Roberts, Greg; Menzel, Andrew J.; Schatschneider, Christopher. (2020). Differential Co-Development of Vocabulary Knowledge and Reading Comprehension for Students with and without Learning Disabilities. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000382
title: Developmental lag versus developmental deficit accounts of reading growth differences for students with learning disabilities
description: Two competing developmental theories the article tests against its longitudinal data. The "developmental lag model posits that children with an LD start out lower in reading than their peers without an LD, but grow much faster in their reading to catch up over time," whereas "the developmental deficit model posits that children with an LD... are poor readers because of a deficit in a skill that does not properly develop." The study's multiple-group LCS results are used to adjudicate between them: the persistent reading comprehension gap favoring a deficit interpretation, while vocabulary trajectories remained similar across groups.
requirements: Longitudinal multi-year measurement of the target skills to distinguish starting-level differences from growth-rate differences
constraints: The authors caution their model may have covered too narrow a developmental period for a catch-up effect to manifest, leaving the lag account not fully ruled out
Results come from a Title 1 Florida sample under Reading First-era instruction, with no information on curriculum or instructional practices
target_learners: Students in kindergarten through fourth grade
Typically developing students in Title 1 schools
target_learning_goals: Vocabulary knowledge (receptive vocabulary breadth)
Reading comprehension growth
examples: The study compared fitted LCS growth trajectories for 627 students with a school-identified LD against 14,146 typically developing peers from kindergarten through fourth grade

article_title: Differential codevelopment of vocabulary knowledge and reading comprehension for students with and without learning disabilities.
citation: Quinn, Jamie M.; Wagner, Richard K.; Petscher, Yaacov; Roberts, Greg; Menzel, Andrew J.; Schatschneider, Christopher. (2020). Differential Co-Development of Vocabulary Knowledge and Reading Comprehension for Students with and without Learning Disabilities. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000382
title: Bivariate latent change score modeling as a method for testing dynamic co-development of two constructs
description: The article's methodological framework combines cross-lagged panel and parallel-process growth modeling. "Bivariate latent change score (LCS) models make use of longitudinal data to define the nature of dynamic relations between two variables over time," with change decomposed into a constant change component (α ∗ η), a proportional autoregressive component (β), and a cross-lagged component (γ) that "estimates whether one construct is a leading indicator of change in the second construct." The authors argue this approach detects bidirectional influences that growth-curve models miss, because "LCS models have a parallel process growth curve model embedded in them, which allows for testing of bidirectional influences between two constructs above and beyond the influence of correlated intercepts and slopes and proportional change parameters."
requirements: Longitudinal data with equally spaced measurement occasions
Measurement invariance constraints across time and groups
Handling of missing data (the article used full-information maximum likelihood) and clustering correction (Huber-White sandwich estimator)
constraints: The models assume equally spaced measurement occasions
Individual LCS parameters should not be interpreted in isolation but within full change score equations
Standardization choices (z-scoring centered at first grade) shape interpretability of parameter estimates
target_learners: Students in kindergarten through fourth grade in longitudinal reading research
target_learning_goals: Modeling developmental relations between vocabulary knowledge and reading comprehension
examples: Four competing bivariate LCS models per group (bidirectional, two unidirectional, and no-coupling) were compared using Satorra-Bentler chi-square difference and Wald tests

article_title: Using choice and utility value to promote interest: Stimulating situational interest in a lesson and fostering the development of interest in statistics.
citation: Asher, M. W., & Harackiewicz, J. M. (2025). Using Choice and Utility Value to Promote Interest: Stimulating Situational Interest in a Lesson and Fostering the Development of Interest in Statistics. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000921
title: Hidi and Renninger four-phase model of interest development
description: The article organizes its seven experiments around the four-phase model of interest development, in which "interest is both a cognitive and affective state and a motivational variable" and is content specific. The model differentiates situational interest (phases 1 and 2: triggered and maintained) from individual interest (phases 3 and 4: emerging and well-developed), and holds that "individuals don't skip phases of interest development: interest must be triggered before it can be maintained." The authors use it to predict that choice targets triggered situational interest while utility value targets later phases.
requirements: Instructional practices must be matched to the phase of interest development being targeted
constraints: The model concerns interest in a particular topic or content area, not interest in general
target_learning_goals: developing situational and individual interest in academic content
examples: Seven experiments mapped manipulations onto phases: choice was expected to trigger situational interest; utility value to promote maintained situational and emerging individual interest, measured via voluntary resource requests.

article_title: Certain abilities fundamental to the study of geometry.
citation: Minnick, J. H. (1925). Certain abilities fundamental to the study of geometry. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Certain+Abilities+Fundamental+to+the+Study+of+Geometry
title: Four abilities fundamental to the formal demonstration of a geometry theorem
description: The article names and describes an explanatory framework of four abilities that it argues success in formal geometric demonstration depends upon: "The ability to draw a figure for the theorem", "The ability to state correctly and accurately the hypothesis and conclusion of the theorem", the ability to recall additional facts about a figure when some are given, and the ability to select from available facts those necessary for a proof and arrange them toward the conclusion. The framework organizes the four diagnostic tests and the diagnosis of class weaknesses.
requirements: Each ability must be measured separately by a test arranged to measure only that one ability, as the article designed Tests A-D to do
constraints: The investigation was limited to classes which had recently completed the first two books of geometry
target_learners: High school geometry students who have completed the first two books of geometry
target_learning_goals: Formal demonstration of geometry theorems
examples: Four tests, known as A, B, C, and D, were developed, each testing one of the abilities in question

article_title: Certain abilities fundamental to the study of geometry.
citation: Minnick, J. H. (1925). Certain abilities fundamental to the study of geometry. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Certain+Abilities+Fundamental+to+the+Study+of+Geometry
title: Tests A, B, C, and D: four diagnostic tests for the fundamental geometry abilities
description: An element consisting of four paper-and-pencil diagnostic tests, each arranged to measure only one of the four abilities. Test A asked pupils to draw the figure for stated exercises; in Test B the figure was drawn and the pupil stated hypothesis and conclusion; in Test C a drawn figure with given facts was supplemented by as many more facts as the pupil could add; in Test D the figure, started hypothesis and conclusion, and a list of facts were given, and the pupil was asked to give the proof. Each test was given to not less than one thousand pupils in sixty-three schools.
requirements: Simple and definite directions so teachers can administer the tests uniformly; the author tried them out with high school classes and made changes before use
constraints: Two schools whose returns indicated a variation from the directions were rejected; scoring required the author to mark all papers personally to insure uniformity
target_learners: High school geometry pupils in classes that recently completed the first two books of geometry
target_learning_goals: Diagnosis of weaknesses in the abilities fundamental to geometric proof
examples: Each test yielded two scores: a positive score for correct necessary statements and a negative score for incorrect and unnecessary statements, which the author held should not be combined

article_title: The truth sandwich format does not enhance the correction of misinformation.
citation: Swire-Thompson, Briony, Butler, Lucy, & Rapp, David N. (2025). The truth sandwich format does not enhance the correction of misinformation. Journal of Educational Psychology, 117(6), 851–862. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000961
title: Prioritize clear, coherent correction content over the ordering format of corrective information
description: This principle holds that what matters in a misinformation correction is the quality and completeness of the corrective content, not the order of its components. In two experiments, fact-first and misinformation-first corrections were equally effective, leading the authors to conclude that "Making corrections clear and coherent is likely far more important than ensuring they buttress or bookend misinformation in any particular way." Communicators should therefore invest effort in correction clarity rather than in elaborate formats.
requirements: Corrections must contain the necessary components — the misinformation identified as false plus factual corrective information — which the article states are "highly useful for fostering belief change, irrespective of their format".
constraints: Evidence comes from short format, health-based misinformation; the authors note future research should replicate the findings with other misinformation content, correction types, or contexts.
target_learners: US adults encountering health misinformation (Prolific samples over age 18)
target_learning_goals: Reduce belief in false claims
Reduce reliance on misinformation when reasoning
examples: Participants received corrections in which the same three sections were simply reordered into truth sandwich or bottom-loaded refutation formats, counterbalanced in a Latin Square design across participants.

article_title: Rules Versus Drill in Teaching Spelling.
citation: Turner, E. A.; Markus, H. P. (1912). Rules versus drill in teaching spelling; Some results in manual training. Journal of Educational Psychology.
title: Pair spelling-rule instruction with type words and minimal drill when transfer to new words is the goal
description: This principle holds that spelling instruction which teaches rules and associates them with type words, requiring only a minimum of drill, is the arrangement to use when the instructional goal includes transfer to new, similar words. In the reported experiment, the rules group's instruction consisted of "three 25-minute exercises, in two of which rules were taught and associated with type words and a minimum of drill required." The rules group showed a distinct advantage on the new-word transfer test, supporting the principle for that outcome.
requirements: Instruction must include explicit teaching of rules associated with type words, not rules alone; the article's condition paired rules with type words across two of three 25-minute exercises.
constraints: The article's evidence comes from one small parallel-group experiment (16 pupils per group) with eighth-grade pupils, separate teachers per group, and no time on the words outside the 25-minute exercises; the drill group retained repeated words relatively better after five days.
target_learning_goals: spelling of new words similar to taught words
examples: Group II received three 25-minute exercises in which rules were taught and associated with type words with a minimum of drill, and outperformed the drill-only group on the new-word 'D' test.
