article_title: How the predictors of math achievement change over time: A longitudinal machine learning approach.
citation: Lavelle-Hill, R., Frenzel, A. C., Goetz, T., Lichtenfeld, S., Marsh, H. W., Pekrun, R., Sakaki, M., Smith, G., & Murayama, K. (2024). How the Predictors of Math Achievement Change Over Time: A Longitudinal Machine Learning Approach. Journal of Educational Psychology, 116(8), 1383–1403. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000863
title: All-inclusive machine learning approach to modeling achievement predictors
description: The article coins an "all-inclusive approach": modeling the entire set of potential predictors, including their nonlinear and complex interactions, at once, rather than testing a small subset of predictors. Machine learning makes this feasible because regularization and out-of-sample evaluation protect against overfitting and multicollinearity that destabilize traditional regression with many predictors. The approach is applied to the PALMA longitudinal data with Elastic Net and Random Forest models, using a pipeline of training/test splitting, five-fold cross-validation, and SHAP-based variable importance for interpretation.
requirements: A large longitudinal data set containing an extensive set of predictor variables assessed consistently over time
Machine learning pipeline with cross-validation and out-of-sample testing to guard against overfitting
constraints: Variable importance measures are model- and method-dependent and should be interpreted with caution, ideally in combination with relevant theories
These measures are unlikely to reflect only the causal effects of the predictors on the outcome
The pipeline does not explicitly account for the hierarchical structure of students nested within classes
target_learning_goals: predicting and understanding longitudinal change in mathematics achievement
examples: The article states: "the current paper takes a different approach: Analyzing all of the variables included in a large longitudinal data set to predict math achievement over time, which we coin an 'all-inclusive approach'"

citation: Lavelle-Hill, R., Frenzel, A. C., Goetz, T., Lichtenfeld, S., Marsh, H. W., Pekrun, R., Sakaki, M., Smith, G., & Murayama, K. (2024). description: The PALMA study (project for the analysis of learning and achievement in mathematics) is a longitudinal panel following German secondary school students with annual assessments from Year 5 to Year 10, representative of Bavaria's three school types. Across five assessments it covered 3,425 students, one parent each, and 419 mathematics teachers, with student, parent, and teacher surveys plus an IQ test and a Rasch-scaled standardized math achievement test. In this article it supplied 105 predictors (88 before dummy coding) for the machine learning analyses.

constraints: Compulsory vocational-track schooling ends after Year 9, so the analysis uses only Years 5–9
target_learners: German secondary school students in vocational-, intermediate-, and academic-track schools
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement development across secondary school
examples: The article reports: "Across all five assessments, a total of 3,425 students (50.0% female) and one of their parents, as well as the mathematics teachers of the participating classes (N = 419 teachers; 65.7% male) participated in the study."

citation: Lavelle-Hill, R., Frenzel, A. C., Goetz, T., Lichtenfeld, S., Marsh, H. W., Pekrun, R., Sakaki, M., Smith, G., & Murayama, K. (2024). How the Predictors of Math Achievement Change Over Time: A Longitudinal Machine Learning Approach. Journal of Educational Psychology, 116(8), 1383–1403. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000863
title: SHAP-based variable importance for interpreting achievement prediction models
description: Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) values are a post hoc, model-agnostic interpretation method used in this article to quantify which variables and variable groups predict math achievement and how their importance changes over time. The authors argue SHAP has three key benefits: it indicates each predictor's direction of contribution, it is computed per individual student enabling heterogeneity analysis, and it is additive so it aggregates to sample-level importance. Group importance was computed by summing absolute SHAP values across variables within theoretically defined predictor groups.
requirements: A fitted prediction model whose per-instance contributions can be decomposed via Shapley values
Grouping of predictors into conceptually similar sets to yield stable, interpretable group importance scores
constraints: Variable importance depends on the model and calculation method and should be interpreted with caution
Importance values are unlikely to reflect only causal effects given reciprocal influences among predictors
target_learning_goals: identifying which predictors contribute to math achievement predictions
examples: The article states: "we argue that SHAP values have three key benefits: (a) They indicate the direction in which each predictor contributes to the prediction (i.e., whether there is a positive or negative predictive relationship)"

title: Five-group classification of exceptional children via teacher questionnaire census

article_title: Cues to generality: Integrating linguistic and visual information when generalizing biological information.
citation: David Menendez. (2023). Cues to generality: Integrating linguistic and visual information when generalizing biological information. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000812
title: Cues to generality hypothesis
description: The cues to generality hypothesis is the article's proposed account of "how students use information in lessons to determine how far to generalize." It holds that learners treat features of both the linguistic and visual modalities — such as generic noun phrases and perceptual richness — as cues signaling whether a taught fact applies narrowly or broadly, and integrate these cues when deciding how far to extend the information to untaught exemplars. The eight studies substantiate it by showing that text-type cues operate similarly across ages, while the weight given to visual cues changes with development and with whether visual attention is split between text and image.
requirements: Lessons must present information in both linguistic and visual modalities for the cue-integration account to apply
constraints: The account was developed from studies of animal-fact generalization with undergraduate and elementary-school participants; the author notes the advantage of bland visualizations is context dependent, varying with task and learner
target_learning_goals: generalizing biological facts from multimedia lessons to untaught category members
examples: In Study 8, children generalized most when the text was generic and the visualization was rich, the most common text-image combination found in the elementary science books analyzed in Study 1

article_title: Problems in the scientific study of the teaching of arithmetic.
citation: Stone, C. W. (1913). Problems in the Scientific Study of the Teaching of Arithmetic. The Journal of Educational Psychology, IV(1). https://psycnet.apa.org/journal/edu
title: Stone's two-phase framework for determining the subject-matter of arithmetic: a practical-sociological phase and a cultural-psychological phase
description: The article organizes the question of what arithmetic ought to be taught into two phases. As printed: "There are, then, two phases of the question, viz.: the practical one, What Arithmetic is needed in order best to make a living? and the cultural one, What Arithmetic is needed in order to make the best living?" The practical phase is answered from economic and social life, including games and recreation, and asks what minimum of arithmetic all people need and what additional arithmetic each trade or profession requires. The cultural phase concerns mental-discipline values, the stages of child development, and the transferability of discipline within and beyond arithmetic.
requirements: Answers to the practical phase must rest on full knowledge of the values of arithmetic in the economic and other social needs of life
Answers to the cultural phase must rest on full knowledge of the values of arithmetic in the mental aspects of life
constraints: The article states that certain phases of the disciplinary-values problem seem at present impossible of exact solution because psychological and statistical research have not yet developed sufficiently
target_learners: all boys and girls of normal ability in public elementary schools
pupils entering respective trades and professions
target_learning_goals: determining which arithmetic topics merit inclusion in the course of study
examples: The article enumerates seven practical-phase questions, such as what minimum of arithmetic is needed by all people in the economic activities of life, and seven cultural-phase questions, including at what ages developmental stages are reached and to what extent disciplinary values are transferable

article_title: Why grades engender performance-avoidance goals: The mediating role of autonomous motivation.
citation: Pulfrey, C., Buchs, C., & Butera, F. (2011). Why grades engender performance-avoidance goals: The mediating role of autonomous motivation. Journal of Educational Psychology, 103(3), 683–700. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0023911
title: Self-determination theory's perceived-locus-of-causality framework as the mechanism linking grading to avoidance goals
description: The article uses the perceived-locus-of-causality framework at the heart of self-determination theory to explain why grading breeds avoidance. The framework "organizes reasons for acting into a range going from controlled to autonomous", with controlled motivation comprising external and introjected regulation and autonomous motivation comprising identified and intrinsic regulation. The authors argue that graded evaluation places students in dependence and powerlessness vis-à-vis the teacher who controls the valued resource, reducing autonomy, and that this erosion of autonomous motivation renders performance-avoidance, rather than performance-approach, goals salient.
requirements: The account presupposes that the student perceives the grade as dispensed by an external controlling authority on whom the grade's value depends.
constraints: The account is developed for normative, grade-based evaluation in classroom settings; the experiments were carried out in Swiss professional schools.
target_learners: secondary and postsecondary students in graded courses (Swiss professional school students, ages ~15–30)
target_learning_goals: motivational quality of engagement (autonomous versus controlled motivation) and pretask achievement goal adoption
examples: Experiment 3 measured autonomous motivation with the Reported Autonomy Index after a graded or nongraded exercise and tested it as a mediator of subsequent performance-avoidance goal adoption.

article_title: Why grades engender performance-avoidance goals: The mediating role of autonomous motivation.
citation: Pulfrey, C., Buchs, C., & Butera, F. (2011). Why grades engender performance-avoidance goals: The mediating role of autonomous motivation. Journal of Educational Psychology, 103(3), 683–700. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0023911
title: Use comment-only formative feedback rather than grades when the aim is to avoid fostering performance-avoidance goals
description: Because expecting a grade raised performance-avoidance goals even when accompanied by formative comments, while comment-only assessment did not, the article's findings support assessing student work with individualized comments alone where avoidance-oriented motivation is a concern. In the experiment, "Assessment based uniquely on comments produced lower levels of performance avoidance than the other two conditions", i.e., than grade-only and grade-with-comment feedback. Comments specified mastered areas and how to improve, following the formative-assessment tradition the authors cite.
requirements: Comments must be individualized, specifying areas of the work mastered and giving indications how to improve, as in the comment-only condition.
constraints: The effect was demonstrated for in-class EFL exercises in Swiss professional schools; comment-based feedback could still be perceived as potentially threatening, per the literature the authors cite.
target_learners: secondary and postsecondary students in graded courses
target_learning_goals: reducing performance-avoidance goal adoption prior to assessment tasks
examples: In Experiment 2, comment-only students received an individualized comment such as 'You have shown you have understood the main theme of the discussion. Now try to distinguish more precisely the viewpoint of each speaker' with no grade, and showed lower performance-avoidance goal adoption (M = 4.95) than graded students (M = 5.73).

article_title: Cognitive predictors of calculations and number line estimation with whole numbers and fractions among at-risk students.
citation: Namkung, J. M., & Fuchs, L. S. (2016). Cognitive Predictors of Calculations and Number Line Estimation with Whole Numbers and Fractions among At-Risk Students. Journal of Educational Psychology, 108(2), 214-228. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000055
title: Geary's (2004) model of mathematics learning distinguishing concepts, procedures, and supporting cognitive systems
description: The study's conceptual framework is Geary's (2004) model of mathematics learning, which the authors extend with additional cognitive variables. The model "distinguishes between mathematics concepts and mathematics procedures," treats conceptual and procedural knowledge as mutually supportive, and holds that "general cognitive processes, such as working memory and attention, support learning of both math concepts and procedures." It further identifies symbolic and nonverbal systems: language for number names and counting, and nonverbal reasoning for representing and comparing numerical magnitudes. The authors state this model "guided the processes that were assessed in the present study."
requirements: Assessment of both conceptual (number line estimation) and procedural (calculations) outcomes to capture the model's distinction
constraints: The study extends the model by adding attentive behavior, processing speed, and concept formation, which were not part of the original formulation
target_learners: at-risk fourth-grade students performing below the 35th percentile in calculations
target_learning_goals: whole-number and fraction calculation skill
whole-number and fraction number line estimation (numerical magnitude representation)
examples: The study operationalized the model's constructs as seven cognitive predictors (numerical working memory, working memory-sentences, language, attentive behavior, processing speed, nonverbal reasoning, concept formation) plus incoming calculation skill, tested against whole-number and fraction outcomes in one structural model.

article_title: Test anxiety, emotion regulation, and achievement: Lagged and contemporaneous reciprocal relations.
citation: Putwain, D. W., Nicholson, L. J., & Pekrun, R. (2025). Test anxiety, emotion regulation, and achievement: Lagged and contemporaneous reciprocal relations. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://repository.essex.ac.uk/40904/
title: Reciprocal effects model of anxiety and achievement (within control-value theory)
description: The reciprocal effects model (REM), proposed by Pekrun and later part of control-value theory, integrates the interference and deficit accounts of the anxiety-achievement correlation. In this model, anxiety lowers achievement through cognitive-motivational processes including impaired working memory functions and avoidance motivation, while poor achievement provides negative competence feedback that lowers control appraisals, a proximal antecedent of anxiety. Over successive iterations, "test anxiety and achievement would relate in reciprocal vicious cycles". The present study's five-wave findings provide direct support for the model for test anxiety specifically.
requirements: Longitudinal data with repeated measures of both anxiety and achievement allowing autoregressive controls
constraints: The model proposes that anxiety often, although not always, lowers achievement
target_learners: upper-secondary students preparing for high-stakes exit exams
target_learning_goals: reducing anxiety-related underachievement in exam performance
examples: The study tested the REM with five waves of data and found the predicted negative reciprocal relations between test anxiety and achievement

article_title: Intelligence and its measurement: A symposium--IV.
citation: Colvin, S. S., & Pintner, R. (1921). Intelligence and Its Measurement. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.apa.org/pubs/journals/edu
title: Colvin's definition of intelligence as the capacity to learn
description: Colvin proposes that intelligence is best understood as learning capacity: an individual possesses intelligence insofar as he has learned, or can learn, to adjust to his environment. He argues this view avoids overemphasizing the problem aspect of intelligence and rightly attributes intelligence to animals whose learning is confined to trial and error. As he writes, intelligence "is equivalent to the capacity to learn." The article presents this as a definitional position, not a tested result.
requirements: The definition is offered as a conceptual viewpoint for considering intelligence, to guide how intelligence examinations are interpreted.
constraints: Colvin notes the broader definition of intelligence as mental adaptability to environment is too broad because it includes instinctive adaptations as well as those acquired through experience.
target_learners: school and college students assessed with intelligence tests
target_learning_goals: understanding and measuring general intelligence as learning ability
examples: Colvin points to existing intelligence examinations, which measure intelligence largely in terms of what the examinee has learned, as practical acceptance of this definition.
key_sources: Colvin, S. S., & Pintner, R. (1921). Intelligence and Its Measurement. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.apa.org/pubs/journals/edu

article_title: Intelligence and its measurement: A symposium--IV.
citation: Colvin, S. S., & Pintner, R. (1921). Intelligence and Its Measurement. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.apa.org/pubs/journals/edu
title: Intelligence testing should include untimed tests emphasizing deliberation, analysis, synthesis, and extended attention span
description: Colvin recommends developing test elements that emphasize deliberation and sustained rational ability, in which speed is relatively unimportant and analysis, synthesis, and an extensive attention span are the chief factors. He argues current tests overemphasize speed and that tests of higher intellectual processes are needed in greater degree than simple tests of facts, memory, and perception. As he puts it, "we need at present test elements that emphasize, more than any now existing do, deliberation and substained rational ability."
requirements: Tests must give the individual who thinks carefully, accurately, but sometimes ponderously, an opportunity to show his ability.
constraints: Colvin notes pioneer work on such tests had been done by Thorndike, particularly in his tests for college freshmen, indicating such tests were not yet standard.
target_learners: students from primary grades through college taking intelligence tests
target_learning_goals: accurate measurement of higher intellectual processes and learning capacity
examples: Colvin cites Thorndike's tests for college freshmen as pioneer work emphasizing deliberation rather than speed.

citation: Colvin, S. S., & Pintner, R. (1921). Intelligence and Its Measurement. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.apa.org/pubs/journals/edu
title: Teachers and administrators should be better informed about the value and limitations of intelligence test results
description: Colvin argues that for mental tests to have practical value, teachers and administrators must be more carefully informed about what testing results can and cannot tell them for instruction and supervision. He observes that tests are frequently given whose results are never utilized, and that results are often wrongly interpreted and applied. As he states, "teachers and administrators should be more carefully informed as to the value and limitations of the results of intelligence testing in solving problems of instruction and supervision."
requirements: Test results must actually be utilized, and interpreted correctly, in solving problems of instruction and supervision.
constraints: Colvin notes that at present norms are lacking or have been imperfectly and inadequately devised, limiting sound interpretation.

target_learning_goals: appropriate interpretation and application of intelligence testing in instruction and supervision

title: Pintner's definition of intelligence as adaptation to relatively new situations, grounded in nervous-system modifiability
description: Pintner conceives of intelligence as the individual's ability to adapt adequately to relatively new situations in life, including the capacity for getting along well in all sorts of situations. This implies ease and rapidity in making adjustments, and hence ease in breaking old habits and forming new ones. He traces this capacity fundamentally to the general modifiability of the nervous system, writing that "An organism whose nervous system is very modifi-" (the excerpt breaks off here). The article presents this as a definitional position rather than a tested result.

citation: Poull, L. E. (1921). Constancy of I. Q. in mental defectives, according to the Stanford-revision of Binet tests. The Journal of Educational Psychology.
title: Use composite ratings combining non-language and performance scales with the Stanford-Binet for truer evaluation of problem cases
description: The article recommends that classification decisions about persons with suspected mental defect should not rest on a single Stanford-Binet administration. Instead, "Composite ratings, including non-language and performance scales, together with the Stanford-Binet, have been found to give truer evaluations of problem cases", because they weight manual abilities that language inhibitions can hide. This is offered as an assessment practice for problem cases in institutional settings.

constraints: The advantage is stated for problem cases above the obvious imbecile type, where language inhibitions may hide intelligence

article_title: The moderating role of popular peers’ achievement goals in 5th- and 6th-graders’ achievement-related friendships: A social network analysis.
citation: Laninga-Wijnen, L., Ryan, A., Harakeh, Z., Shin, H., & Vollebergh, W. A. M. (2018). Journal of Educational Psychology, vol. 110, no. 2, pp. 289-307. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000210
title: Reputational salience of popular peers' achievement goals as a classroom norm mechanism
description: The article proposes that popular peers make achievement goals salient in the classroom, setting norms that shape friendship selection, maintenance, and influence around achievement. Popularity norms are measured as "the within-classroom correlation between popularity and behaviors or attitudes" (also called norm salience). Because adolescents are "highly attuned to the behaviors and attitudes of popular peers, as these behaviors and attitudes are reputationally salient," the goals popular students endorse become positively valued classroom standards. This extends prior work on how teachers make goals salient to the peer-driven pathway.

target_learning_goals: Academic achievement in math and science
examples: The study operationalized popularity norms as within-classroom correlations between peer-nominated popularity and mastery or performance goals, splitting 46 classrooms into low, moderate, and high norm types by quartiles.

citation: W. H. Winch. (1911). Mental Fatigue in Day School Children as Measured by Immediate Memory. Part II. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journal_of_Educational_Psychology

Ten sets constituted one 15-minute test. Scoring gave "Three marks for each consonant correctly remembered and rightly placed", two for one place out, and one for two places out, with spaces left for forgotten consonants.

constraints: The author judged these tests relatively, as well as absolutely, easier than those given in the previous experiment with older and abler boys

citation: E. A. Doll. (1912). Inexpert Binet Examiners and Their Limitations. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org
title: Fault for misdiagnosis with the Binet tests lies with inexpert examiners, not with the tests themselves

The analogy is drawn to inexperienced nurses who incorrectly interpret thermometric readings, where blame falls on the nurse and not the thermometer. The principle holds that determining normality or abnormality requires expertise beyond Binet testing itself.

citation: Haggerty, M. E. (1917). Tests of Applicants for Admission to University of Minnesota Medical School. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://books.google.com
title: Mental test scores measure a complex mental state including non-intellectual functions, so correlations of .60-.80 may be the maximum expected
description: The article argues that test performance is not a purely intellectual product: association is "shot through with the very interests and emotions" discriminated from it in discussion, and a reading-scale product also indirectly tests "his interest, his endurance, persistence and other emotional and instinctive attitudes." On this account a correlation of .70 between test and marks means the test measures intellectual and non-intellectual factors all partially, and a test of purely intellectual functions could cap correlations near .60-.80, while a test capturing the complex state could conceivably approach a perfect relationship.

target_learning_goals: prognosis of success in a medical curriculum
examples: The author reasons that a time score recorded at the end of the association test is a measure of the complex mental state involving desire to succeed, speed, error avoidance, and affective states prompted by surprise, absurdity and complexity.

article_title: Tests of applicants for admission to University of Minnesota Medical School.
citation: Haggerty, M. E. (1917). Tests of Applicants for Admission to University of Minnesota Medical School. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://books.google.com
title: Two-test admission battery: omnibus association test plus Thorndike reading scale
description: The battery used for 1916 medical school applicants comprised an omnibus test "fashioned after the one reported by Scott," arranged in triplicate to prevent communication between groups tested on different days, and sets of the Thorndike Improved Scale for Reading Ability, Scale Alpha 2. Both tests were given at one sitting, scored for rate and quality, with each omnibus error penalized by adding ten seconds to raw time to give a weighted time. The article states the two tests occupied two examiners for not to exceed one and one-half hours and that a hundred applicants may be examined at a sitting.
requirements: Accurate time keeping on both tests and scoring by persons familiar with the work.
constraints: No applicants were examined who did not meet the academic requirements for entrance to the Medical School.
target_learners: applicants to a university medical school
target_learning_goals: evaluation of mental capacity and general mental fitness for medical study
examples: 93 candidates were tested individually or in groups ranging up to 25, and 69 were accepted and entered in September 1917.

article_title: Educational psychology at the Chicago meetings of scientific societies.
citation: Gates, A. I. (1921). Educational Psychology at the Chicago Meetings of Scientific Societies. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 12(2). https://psycnet.apa.org/journal/edu
title: New group tests presented at the 1920 Chicago meetings: Kingsbury pictorial primary scale, Pintner combined mental-educational survey test, and Pressey seventh-grade attainment scale
description: The report describes three newly devised instruments. Kingsbury's group intelligence scale for the primary grades is "pictorial in character and involving no reading, writing, or complicated drawing" and yielded an average correlation of +0.69 with Stanford-Binet mental age of 1300 primary pupils. Pintner's combined mental-educational test, standardized on 4300 cases, affords a measure of class mental status and evaluates attainments in terms of ability to profit by instruction. Pressey presented a scale measuring seventh-grade attainments in history, reading vocabulary, English composition, and arithmetical reasoning, the composition part scored by children's judgments of compositions of known value.
requirements: Intended for group administration in schools: the Kingsbury scale requires no reading or writing from primary pupils, and the Pintner test is designed for quick survey use with results sufficiently accurate for school surveys.
constraints: The Kingsbury scale was standardized only tentatively, as the report states.

Measurement of educational attainments in history, reading vocabulary, English composition, and arithmetical reasoning
examples: The Kingsbury scale was tentatively standardized on 1300 primary pupils with an average correlation of +0.69 with Stanford-Binet mental age; the Pintner test was standardized on 4300 cases.

citation: M.S.M. Sachisthal, B.R.J. Jansen, T.T.D. Peetsma, J. Dalege, H.L.J. van der Maas, M.E.J. Raijmakers. (2019). Introducing a Science Interest Network Model to Reveal Country Differences. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000327
title: Science Interest Network Model: interest as a dynamic relational construct
description: The SINM models science interest as a dynamic relational construct rather than a latent score. In it, "affective, behavioral, and cognitive components and related motivational components mutually reinforce one another within the development of interest", and these mutual interactions are hypothesized to underlie interest development. The article operationalizes the model with network analysis over interest-related indicators and applies it to PISA 2015 data from two countries.

article_title: A Further Criterion for the Selection of Mental Test Elements.
citation: Chapman, J. Crosby and Dale, A. Barbara. (1921). A Further Criterion for the Selection of Mental Test Elements. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://archive.org/search?query=A+Further+Criterion+for+the+Selection+of+Mental+Test+Elements
title: The matched-groups criterion: ranking test elements by their weight on hereditary brightness versus environmental training
description: The article proposes "A new criterion ... which will rank tests with reference to the weight placed on hereditary brightness rather than on environmental training." It works by selecting two groups of children matched in total intelligence-test score but differing widely in chronological age, then comparing their average scores on each test element. Elements on which the Young Bright group exceeds the Old Dull group are judged to favor native intelligence; the reverse order ranks elements by dependence on training. This loads age and training factors in opposite directions, unlike the usual criteria of age-increase and coherence.
requirements: A large sample of complete intelligence-test administrations from which two total-score-matched groups of differing chronological age can be selected
constraints: Where ratios differ only slightly from unity, nothing can be inferred; the criterion yields order of merit, not absolute quantitative estimates
target_learners: school-age children in elementary grades being assessed with group intelligence tests
target_learning_goals: distinguishing native intellectual endowment from environmentally trained performance in test-element selection
examples: Applied to the National Intelligence Test Series A with 50 matched pairs from Mount Vernon, N. Y. elementary schools, using the five subtests arithmetical reasoning, sentence completion, logical sequence, opposites, and symbol-digit substitution
key_sources: Chapman, J. Crosby and Dale, A. Barbara. (1921). A Further Criterion for the Selection of Mental Test Elements. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://archive.org/search?query=A+Further+Criterion+for+the+Selection+of+Mental+Test+Elements

article_title: A Further Criterion for the Selection of Mental Test Elements.
citation: Chapman, J. Crosby and Dale, A. Barbara. (1921). A Further Criterion for the Selection of Mental Test Elements. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://archive.org/search?query=A+Further+Criterion+for+the+Selection+of+Mental+Test+Elements
title: Test elements intended to measure higher mental processes must be freed from non-essential experience factors
description: Because intelligence is measured through higher complex processes that must reveal themselves in young bright children, the article argues "The test elements which measure the presence or absence of these powers must be freed from non-essential experience factors." Otherwise a young precocious child may fail, not from lack of conceptual thought, but from inadequate vocabulary or reading facility acquired through practice. Tests constructed to demand facility and information closely correlated with grade position effectively substitute school selection for the mental test as criterion.
requirements: Test elements must not require facility or information that younger children have not yet had the opportunity to acquire
constraints: Some confounding of age and training is acknowledged as unavoidable; the authors state the young bright may be prejudiced by absence of reading practice even in tests like opposites
target_learners: young bright children assessed before they have acquired school-taught facility
target_learning_goals: valid measurement of higher conceptual processes independent of environmental training
examples: The authors note the opposites test performance of a young precocious child may be prejudiced by inadequate vocabulary or lack of reading practice rather than lack of speed of conceptual thought
key_sources: Chapman, J. Crosby and Dale, A. Barbara. (1921). A Further Criterion for the Selection of Mental Test Elements. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://archive.org/search?query=A+Further+Criterion+for+the+Selection+of+Mental+Test+Elements

article_title: A Further Criterion for the Selection of Mental Test Elements.
citation: Chapman, J. Crosby and Dale, A. Barbara. (1921). A Further Criterion for the Selection of Mental Test Elements. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://archive.org/search?query=A+Further+Criterion+for+the+Selection+of+Mental+Test+Elements
title: Interpret matched-group ratios only where they differ greatly from unity; small differences permit no inference
description: The article warns that in its matched-groups procedure, inferences are safe only for large deviations. Where ratios "differ greatly from unity it is safe to draw deductions", but where the differences are small, nothing can be inferred, because a young group's extra score on one test must be compensated by slightly lower scores on other tests when totals are matched. The method therefore supports only an order of merit among tests, not absolute quantitative estimates.
requirements: Total scores of the two matched groups must be held equal, which forces compensating deviations across tests
constraints: No absolute quantitative estimates are possible; the article also notes an exception where the Young Bright have recently practiced a function the Old Dull have forgotten
target_learners: school-age children in group intelligence testing
target_learning_goals: ranking mental test elements as measures of native intelligence versus training
examples: The authors illustrate with a hypothetical battery of four tests in which one test favors native intelligence and the other three favor neither group

article_title: A longitudinal randomized trial of a sustained content literacy intervention from first to second grade: Transfer effects on students’ reading comprehension.
citation: Kim, J. S., Burkhauser, M. A., Relyea, J. E., Gilbert, J. B., Scherer, E., Fitzgerald, J., Mosher, D., & McIntyre, J. (2023). A Longitudinal Randomized Trial of a Sustained Content Literacy Intervention From First to Second Grade: Transfer Effects on Students' Reading Comprehension. Journal of Educational Psychology, 115(1), 73-98. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000751
title: Model of Reading Engagement (MORE): schema instantiation account of sustained content literacy transfer
description: The MORE framework holds that thematic lessons give students an intellectual framework connecting new learning to a general schema, such as how scientists study past events. The article defines sustained content literacy intervention as an approach in which "thematic lessons are designed to provide sustained and recurrent exposure to schema-building activities so that knowledge is more accessible to children as they build coherent text representations." Schema instantiation is the proposed mechanism of transfer: "schema instantiation can facilitate transfer across topics within a domain and enhance comprehension of novel material that fits the same situation." Domain-specific vocabulary networks supply retrieval cues that activate the general schema.
requirements: Sustained instruction across grades so that general schemas have time to develop
Topic-specific schemas sharing structural components that map onto the general schema
Domain-specific academic vocabulary networks embedded across topics to cue schema activation
constraints: The article notes transfer is difficult to achieve and measure in reading comprehension, and few early-grade interventions have targeted generalized schema development
target_learners: Early elementary grade students (Grades 1-2) in urban elementary schools
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension of complex informational texts
Domain and topic knowledge in science and social studies
Academic vocabulary knowledge
examples: Grade 1 unit on animal survival laid the foundation for the Grade 2 unit on how paleontologists study prehistoric events, both instantiating the general schema of how scientists study past events.

Journal of Educational Psychology, 115(1), 73-98. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000751
title: Near-, mid-, and far-transfer passage framework for measuring transfer in reading comprehension
description: The authors developed a sensitivity framework for assessing transfer on an end-of-Grade-2 science reading comprehension measure, building on the content and context dimensions of transfer. Passages differed in exposure to taught vocabulary: "the content of the near-, mid-, and far-transfer passages provided extensive, limited, and no exposure, respectively, to the domain-specific vocabulary networks that children learned in the lessons." The context dimension captured similarity to the taught thematic lessons, with near-transfer contexts similar to instruction and mid and far contexts less similar.
requirements: Passages must vary systematically in exposure to directly taught vocabulary networks
Comprehension items must be aligned to the content and context dimensions of transfer
constraints: The framework was developed for a Grade 2 science content reading comprehension outcome in this study
target_learners: Second-grade students reading science informational texts
target_learning_goals: Transfer of domain and topic knowledge to novel reading comprehension tasks
examples: Near- and mid-transfer passages were designed to activate the schema children learned, whereas the far-transfer passage provided no cues for schema activation.

description: The MORE intervention organizes content literacy instruction as recurring thematic lesson sequences built on a pyramid structure in which a general schema unifies topics in a domain. Teachers "interleaved practices involving direct teaching of domain-specific academic vocabulary networks, interactive read-alouds to provide recurrent exposures to schema-related vocabulary, and wide reading of thematically related informational texts with autonomy and competence supports." The Grade 2 science unit contained 45 lessons with nine lesson activity types repeated five times across a 10-week unit, ending each sequence with a reflection activity.

Reading comprehension of informational texts

description: The article recommends that content and instruction be aligned and sustained across grades so children accumulate related topic knowledge over time. Its implications statement argues that "sustained content literacy intervention efforts that gradually build thematic connections across grades and across school and home contexts may help young children connect new learning to a general schema and transfer their knowledge to related topics." The intervention operationalized this by sequencing a Grade 1 animal-survival unit before a Grade 2 paleontology unit and extending school lessons with summer wide reading of thematically related texts.

title: Control-value theory of achievement emotions as a framework linking negative emotion to academic functioning
description: The article draws on Pekrun's control-value theory of achievement emotions, in which achievement emotions are "emotions directly tied to achievement activities or achievement outcomes" and are proposed to affect cognitive resources, motivation, learning strategies, self-regulated learning, and subsequent achievement. The study uses this framework, alongside temperament perspectives, to motivate testing whether observed classroom negative expressivity predicts academic outcomes. It frames negative expression as limiting attention and interest relevant to academic tasks.

article_title: The power of the eye to sustain clear seeing under different conditions of lighting.
citation: C. E. Ferree and Gertrude Rand. (1917). The Power of the Eye to Sustain Clear Seeing Under Different Conditions of Lighting. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://archive.org
title: Three-minute acuity-sustain test of the eye's power to sustain clear seeing under lighting conditions
description: A laboratory test combining two principles: visual acuity may be measured by the smallest angle the eye can discriminate, and loss of efficiency shows more plainly in prolonged than momentary performance. As printed, "The power of the eye to sustain a certain standard of acuity for three minutes is measured before and after a period of reading from uniform type and paper under the lighting conditions to be tested." A kymograph and chronograph record time at standard versus below it, and the ratio measures the ability to sustain clear seeing. Observers were trained to precision and results were accepted only when condition effects exceeded the mean variation.
requirements: Observers trained to satisfactory precision in the three-minute record and the three-hour test before taking part
Results accepted only when the variation from changing conditions largely exceeded the mean variation for the condition
target_learners: adult observers under 30 years of age with no uncorrected defects of consequence
target_learning_goals: measuring sustained visual efficiency under different lighting conditions
examples: Used to compare direct, semi-indirect, and indirect installations at four positions in a test room and across lamp wattages and reflector densities

article_title: The power of the eye to sustain clear seeing under different conditions of lighting.
citation: C. E. Ferree and Gertrude Rand. (1917). The Power of the Eye to Sustain Clear Seeing Under Different Conditions of Lighting. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://archive.org
title: Install lighting so that the field of vision is uniformly illuminated, well diffused, and free of extremes of surface brightness, because distribution factors govern the eye's comfort and efficiency
description: The article's central design recommendation for lighting spaces used for sustained visual work: the ideal condition is to have the field of vision "uniformly illuminated with light well diffused and no extremes of surface brightness," since such gradation of retinal illumination supports accurate and comfortable fixation and accommodation. The authors derive this from six years of tests showing distribution factors are fundamental to the eye's welfare, and they rank lighting systems by how well they realize it.
requirements: Light sources concealed or diffused so no extremes of surface brightness enter the field of view
Bright sources kept out of the zone of most harmful influence on the eye, easiest in rooms with higher ceilings
constraints: In rooms of low or medium height, protecting the eye is the most difficult feature of the problem; the difficulty decreases with increase in the height of the ceiling
target_learners: students and workers doing sustained reading or visual work in artificially and daylit rooms
target_learning_goals: sustaining clear seeing and visual comfort during prolonged reading and study
examples: The authors report the best control of the distribution factors in daylight rooms and, among artificial systems, in indirect and high-density semi-indirect installations

article_title: The measurement of ability in Latin. Part I. Vocabulary.
citation: V. A. C. Henmon. (1917). The Measurement of Ability in Latin. Part I. Vocabulary. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22The+Measurement+of+Ability+in+Latin%22+Henmon
title: P. E. scale values for vocabulary difficulty via Buckingham's normal-distribution method
description: The article adapts Buckingham's spelling-scaling method to assign each Latin word a difficulty weight. Percent-correct values are converted to probable-error equivalents on the base line of a normal frequency surface, referenced to a zero point 3.8 P. E. below the median, so that equal raw percentage differences near the tails count as larger difficulty differences than near the median. The article states that assuming ability "follows the normal distribution," a 2 percent difference between words remote from the median "is not the same as the difference between par 64 percent correct and occido 62 percent correct." Year scale values and a general scale value averaging positions across four years are produced for the 239-word list.
requirements: Percent-correct data for each word from a sufficiently large sample of pupils at each year level
An assumed zero point in ability, taken as a word missed by 5 out of 1000 pupils (3.8 P. E. below the median)
constraints: Scale values rest on the assumption that ability in translating the words follows the normal distribution
Words not missed by third- and fourth-year pupils have indeterminate P. E. equivalents and were arbitrarily assigned the value -3.8 P. E.
target_learners: first- through fourth-year high school Latin pupils
target_learning_goals: scope and accuracy of Latin vocabulary knowledge
examples: On this scale the easiest first-year word, pulcher, received a value of .3 while the most difficult, conficio, received 5.2; a correct translation of ab earned 1.6 points toward a first-year perfect score of 735.2

title: Standard Vocabulary Test of 239 words derived from thirteen beginner books and Lodge's Caesar-Cicero-Vergil tabulation
description: A standardized Latin vocabulary test constructed by tabulating all words in thirteen recent or widely used beginners' books (vocabularies of 750 to 1750 words), yielding 3350 different words of which 319 were common to all books. Words not used by all three of Caesar, Cicero, and Vergil, per Lodge's frequency tabulation, were dropped, reducing the list to 239 words. The article says the list "would seem to be in the real sense a standard vocabulary for high school Latin," encountered by all pupils regardless of textbook. Blanks with the words in alphabetical order were printed and used in schools over two years.

target_learning_goals: recognition of standard high-school Latin vocabulary

article_title:
The good cheat: Benevolence and the justification of collective
						cheating.
citation: Caroline Pulfrey, Kevin Durussel, and Fabrizio Butera. (2018). The Good Cheat: Benevolence and the Justification of Collective Cheating. Journal of Educational Psychology, Vol. 110, No. 6. http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/edu0000247
title: Benevolence-loyalty account of collective cheating: group-loyalty values justify pro-in-group cheating when competition is salient
description: The article integrates Schwartz's values theory, moral foundations theory, and in-group favoritism research into an account of collective cheating, defined as "students cheating together with in-group peers". It posits that benevolence values, which encapsulate the prioritization of loyalty toward one's in-group, can justify unethical pro-in-group behavior: when competition is salient, loyalty-motivated students accept collective cheating while rejecting individual cheating. Three forms of collective cheating are distinguished: in-group resource sharing, individual altruism toward the group, and in-group versus out-group copying.
requirements: A salient form of competition (societal, grades-based, or internalized power values) for the benevolence-cheating link to appear
An in-group of peers with whom the student is in frequent contact
constraints: The effect was demonstrated for collective cheating attitudes and behavior, not for individual cheating, which benevolence values did not predict positively
The account is framed for academic contexts in which group work is encouraged but evaluation is largely individual
target_learners: management and social sciences students in the reported studies
target_learning_goals: understanding the motivational underpinnings of academic dishonesty
distinguishing collective from individual forms of academic dishonesty
examples: Study 1 exposed students to a portrayal of a competitive versus cooperative society before measuring cheating attitudes
Study 2 used vignettes set in an end-of-year exam context portraying individual and three collective cheating forms
key_sources: Caroline Pulfrey, Kevin Durussel, and Fabrizio Butera. (2018). The Good Cheat: Benevolence and the Justification of Collective Cheating. Journal of Educational Psychology, Vol. 110, No. 6. http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/edu0000247

article_title: The interplay of personal and situational factors in situated expectancy-value theory: Cross-classified analyses of students’ situation-specific motivations in the Math domain.
citation: Benden, D. K., & Lauermann, F. (2026). The Interplay of Personal and Situational Factors in Situated Expectancy-Value Theory: Cross-Classified Analyses of Students' Situation-Specific Motivations in the Math Domain. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0001032
title: Situated expectancy-value theory (SEVT) as a framework for person- and situation-specific motivational beliefs
description: SEVT holds that students' "expectancies for success and the subjective value they assign to a task—are proximal predictors of their achievement-related choices," including engagement, persistence, and disengagement from math tasks. Within a situation, beliefs are shaped by person factors (stable attributes and cumulative experience histories), situational factors (task demands, domains, social contexts), and their interactions. The study applies SEVT by measuring situation-specific ability self-concept, intrinsic and utility value, and cost four times during one math test, and by modeling Person × Situation interactions theorized by SEVT but not previously tested for situation-specific beliefs.
requirements: Measurement of motivational beliefs referring to specific time points and contexts (situated beliefs) rather than only domain-general beliefs
constraints: The article notes direct evidence on how personal and situational factors jointly shape motivational beliefs remains scarce, particularly in demanding STEM contexts
target_learners: beginning postsecondary students in math-intensive STEM programs
target_learning_goals: math-related expectancy and value beliefs in authentic achievement situations
examples: Students rated test-specific motivation after each of four test parts while working on different math content areas such as basic arithmetic, geometry, and calculus
key_sources: Benden, D. K., & Lauermann, F. (2026). The Interplay of Personal and Situational Factors in Situated Expectancy-Value Theory: Cross-Classified Analyses of Students' Situation-Specific Motivations in the Math Domain. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0001032

article_title: Testing a three-phase model of the relationship between motivational appraisals, observable engagement, and subjective engagement: Insights from combining mobile learning data and daily diaries.
citation: Breitwieser, J., Brod, G., & Malmberg, L.-E. (2026). Testing a three-phase model of the relationship between motivational appraisals, observable engagement, and subjective engagement: Insights from combining mobile learning data and daily diaries. Journal of Educational Psychology. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0001009
title: A three-phase model positioning observable engagement as the mediator between motivational appraisals and retrospective subjective engagement
description: The model integrates SEVT, engagement, and self-regulated learning process models by dividing learning into before, during, and after phases. It hypothesizes that appraisals of expectancy, value, and cost before learning drive observable behaviour during learning, and that post-learning perceptions of satisfaction, effort, and task delay are shaped by, but not identical to, that behaviour. A key contribution is "the explicit positioning of observable engagement as a mediator, highlighting the role of actual behaviour in linking motivational appraisals to retrospective perceptions of engagement." Direct effects of appraisals on subjective engagement are assumed to be tentative and subject to exploratory investigation.
requirements: Data capturing appraisals before learning, objective behaviour during learning, and subjective perceptions after learning in temporal order
constraints: Only the quantity, not the quality, of observable engagement is modelled as a mediator
Direct effects of appraisals on subjective engagement are tentative and not strong predictions
target_learners: school-aged learners in informal mobile learning settings
target_learning_goals: understanding how motivational appraisals relate to actual and perceived engagement in self-directed learning
examples: In the study, appraisals were measured in a morning diary, observable engagement as app log counts of vocabulary items studied, and satisfaction, effort, and task delay in an after-learning diary

article_title: Standardized illustrative sentences for the Springfield Spelling List.
citation: David Spence Hill. (1917). Standardized Illustrative Sentences for the Springfield Spelling List. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org
title: Standardize the administration procedure of spelling scales, including uniform illustrative sentences, before comparing achievement results
description: The article recommends that testing procedures for standard spelling scales be made uniform, because extemporized illustrative sentences may obscure or delay children's spelling responses and vary across scores of examiners. The author wrote all sentences in advance and urges that "there is considerable room for improvement in the direction of standardizing a procedure for the actual administration of standard spelling scales."
requirements: Examiners must use the same pre-written illustrative sentences for every word on the day of the test
constraints: The article notes it is possible that failure to uniformize sentences is not a very serious defect in contemporary studies
target_learning_goals: Accurate measurement of spelling achievement on standardized word lists
examples: The author administered the Springfield list in New Orleans with examiner-pronounced words followed by pre-written illustrative sentences, children writing the word only

article_title: Standardized illustrative sentences for the Springfield Spelling List.
citation: David Spence Hill. (1917). Standardized Illustrative Sentences for the Springfield Spelling List. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org

examples: Grade 3 through Grade 8 word-and-sentence pairs are printed in the article, from FILL to DECISION

article_title: The new clinical psychology and the psycho-clinicist. Part II. The psychological clinic and the public schools.
citation: J. K. W. Wallin. (1911). The New Clinical Psychology and the Psycho-Clinicist. Part II. The Psychological Clinic and the Public Schools. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journal/edu
title: Bureau of school research as a central clearing-house for educational data
description: A proposed central school department in charge of a director who is an expert in child, educational and clinical psychology with experimental pedagogy and teaching experience. The article argues investigation results are liable to run to sand unless they are "properly unified, correlated and brought to a focus", and that the bureau should gather, compile, compare, correlate, interpret and turn to practical use data from five sources: medico-dental examination records, sociological case data, pedagogical records, controlled educational experiments, and psycho-clinical records.
requirements: A director who is an expert in child, educational and clinical psychology, familiar with experimental pedagogy, with practical teaching experience and some knowledge of medical inspection work
constraints: The author frames the plan as aspirational for school systems; he notes that where a comprehensive bureau is not feasible, a clinical laboratory alone should claim first attention
target_learners: public-school pupils, particularly exceptional, retarded and delinquent children
target_learning_goals: scientific diagnosis and classification of pupils' health, development and pedagogical status
examples: The Chicago public schools' department of child study and pedagogic investigation, established in 1899, is cited as the one outstanding existing exception conducting studies and issuing annual reports
key_sources: J. K. W. Wallin. (1911). The New Clinical Psychology and the Psycho-Clinicist. Part II. The Psychological Clinic and the Public Schools. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journal/edu

article_title: The new clinical psychology and the psycho-clinicist. Part II. The psychological clinic and the public schools.
citation: J. K. W. Wallin. (1911). The New Clinical Psychology and the Psycho-Clinicist. Part II. The Psychological Clinic and the Public Schools. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journal/edu
title: Four ages of the child: chronological, physiological, pedagogical and psychical
description: Wallin's framework for analyzing retardation: a child's development can be indexed on four independent ages, so a single chronological age may mask divergent developmental status. He states that "a child has at least four ages: a chronological, a physiological, a pedagogical and a psychical," illustrating with a 15-year-old who may be physiologically, pedagogically and psychically younger. Mental age must be determined independently by serial graded age tests, since pedagogical retardation may reflect late entrance or undeserved promotion rather than mental defect.
requirements: Reliable normal norms and graded serial age tests to determine mental age independently of school progress
constraints: The framework presumes measurement instruments (such as the Binet-Simon scale) whose norms the article itself notes are not yet validated for American children
target_learners: school pupils, especially pedagogically retarded children
target_learning_goals: accurate diagnosis of the source and degree of a pupil's retardation
examples: The article's worked example of a 15-year-old who is physiologically 13, pedagogically 12, and psychically 11
key_sources: J. K. W. Wallin. (1911). The New Clinical Psychology and the Psycho-Clinicist. Part II. The Psychological Clinic and the Public Schools. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journal/edu

article_title: The new clinical psychology and the psycho-clinicist. Part II. The psychological clinic and the public schools.
citation: J. K. W. Wallin. (1911). The New Clinical Psychology and the Psycho-Clinicist. Part II. The Psychological Clinic and the Public Schools. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journal/edu
title: Five functions of the school psycho-clinical laboratory
description: The article specifies a five-part functional charter for a school clinical laboratory serving exceptional children: clinical examination of exceptional children, establishment of reliable norms for normal children, acting as a clearing-house for placing exceptional children in appropriate special schools or institutions, training teachers in psycho-clinical testing methods, and supervising special-school curricula while offering courses on the psychology of mental deficiency. Its central aim is "the scientific investigation of abnormalities of development", with examination including graded serial tests, form-board and sensory-motor tests, standardized intellectual tests, and anthropometric measures, and percentile curves plotted for each child.
requirements: Full data from the other sources (medical, sociological, pedagogical) so the laboratory can perform its clearing-house function, and reliable norms for typical normal children against which to plot percentile curves
constraints: The laboratory cannot examine all pupils needing examination in a large school system, so testing must be partly delegated to trained special-room teachers; recommendations of the director are not subject to reversal except by the board or superintendent
target_learners: exceptional children: pedagogically retarded, subnormal, supernormal and delinquent pupils
target_learning_goals: diagnosis, classification and placement of exceptional children, and establishment of developmental norms
examples: Children mentally retarded more than four years are classed as probably permanently arrested institutional cases and separated from the merely retarded or backward

article_title: Supplemental Material for Academic Buoyancy and Adaptability: A Multisample Study of Reciprocal Effects
citation: Martin, A. J., Malmberg, L.-E., Holliman, A. J., Teig, N., Putwain, D. W., Collie, R. J., Burns, E. C., Bostwick, K. C. P., Kennett, R., & Pearson, J. (2026). Academic buoyancy and adaptability: A multi-sample study of reciprocal effects—Supplementary materials. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu/
title: Reciprocal-effects account of academic buoyancy and adaptability as longitudinally interrelated constructs
description: This supplementary analysis frames academic buoyancy and adaptability as two related constructs whose longitudinal development is mutually reinforcing: estimating them as "latent constructs" with parallel multi-item factors, the analysis found that "higher buoyancy at an earlier time point is associated with adaptability gains later, and higher initial adaptability is associated with buoyancy gains over time". The account treats each construct as an antecedent of the other's later gains, with autoregressive stability paths and covariate (gender, age) paths modeled alongside.
requirements: Requires longitudinal multi-item measures of both academic buoyancy and adaptability at each time point, and parallel factors across samples so measurement invariance can be established
constraints: Applies to the subset of studies with parallel multi-item factors (Studies 1, 2, 5, 6); studies with single-item indicators of either construct were excluded
target_learners: School and university students in the pooled multi-sample dataset
target_learning_goals: Academic buoyancy in the face of academic setbacks
Adaptability to change and uncertainty in academic settings
examples: A latent cross-lagged panel model fitted to pooled data from Studies 1, 2, 5, and 6, with correlated item residuals across time, shown in Figure S1

article_title: Learning environments are associated with age-related differences in thalamocortical attention circuits in childhood
citation: Mino-Matot, T., Kebiri, H., Jorge, J., Ledoux, J.-B., Fornari, E., Bach Cuadra, M. & Denervaud, S. (2026). Learning environments are associated with age-related differences in thalamocortical attention circuits in childhood. npj Science of Learning, Article in Press. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00452-4
title: The pediatric thalamus as a set of specialized modulatory units with dissociable large-scale connectivity profiles
description: The article proposes viewing the child thalamus not as a unitary relay but as functionally differentiated territories with distinct large-scale "connectivity proﬁles". Cluster 1 couples with the visual network and anticorrelates with limbic regions; Clusters 2 and 5 jointly engage subcortical structures and the ventral attention network, a profile associated with salience detection and reorienting; Cluster 4 preferentially couples with somatomotor and dorsal attention networks. The framework grounds the study's hypothesis that pedagogy co-varies with specific attention-related thalamic channels during development.
requirements: Data-driven, pediatric-adapted functional parcellation of thalamic voxels from resting-state fMRI, with cluster quality guided by spatial coherence, hemispheric symmetry, and functional specificity criteria
constraints: The K = 8 solution is cohort-specific until externally replicated in larger developmental samples
Resting-state measures may underestimate condition-dependent dynamics
target_learners: children aged 4–15 years in school settings
target_learning_goals: attention and salience detection supporting learning
sensorimotor–attentional integration
examples: The article's K = 8 parcellation yielded dissociable, interpretable connectivity profiles across large-scale networks (Fig. 1C), supporting a view of the pediatric thalamus as "a set of specialized modulatory units rather than a unitary hub".
key_sources: Mino-Matot, T., Kebiri, H., Jorge, J., Ledoux, J.-B., Fornari, E., Bach Cuadra, M. & Denervaud, S. (2026).
