article_title: Smartphone-based study reminders can be a double-edged sword
citation: Lea Nobbe, Jasmin Breitwieser, Daniel Biedermann & Garvin Brod. (2024). Smartphone-based study reminders can be a double-edged sword. npj Science of Learning 9:40. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00253-7
title: Design study reminders to fade out and to build habits through learner-owned cues and implementation intentions rather than dependence on prompts
description: The article argues that because reminders can create reliance, interventions promoting self-regulated learning should aim for studying that persists without prompts: "Ideally, then, reminders should fade out over time, while the frequency of studying should remain the same." It recommends anchoring studying to recurring situations in students' daily lives, using plans and implementation intentions that let learners express their own timing preferences, and designing reminders "when helping to form a habit through establishing easily identi ﬁable study cues in students' daily lives rather than in their phones."
requirements: Reminders must align with students' intentions and be implemented together with them, per the article's discussion of nudging in education.
constraints: The article states its findings come from German lower secondary students aged 10–12 studying vocabulary, and that generalization to older students and other learning strategies is unclear.
target_learning_goals: distributed practice in self-study
self-regulated vocabulary learning
examples: In the study, the Reminder Group saw a screen reminding them of a video on distributed practice on 16 of 36 days, pseudorandomly assigned, while the Control Group watched the video only.
key_sources: Lea Nobbe, Jasmin Breitwieser, Daniel Biedermann & Garvin Brod. (2024). Smartphone-based study reminders can be a double-edged sword. npj Science of Learning 9:40. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00253-7

article_title: Optimizing practice scheduling requires quantitative tracking of individual item performance
citation: Luke G. Eglington and Philip I. Pavlik Jr. (2020). Optimizing practice scheduling requires quantitative tracking of individual item performance. npj Science of Learning 5:15. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00074-4
title: Optimal Efficiency Threshold (OET) framework: model-based adaptive practice scheduling guided by microeconomic efficiency
description: The OET framework treats practice scheduling as an economic problem: choose for practice the item whose predicted recall probability is closest to (but below) a threshold that maximizes learning gains per unit of time. Efficiency is defined as "the gain in retrievability at some ﬁnal test divided by the time cost of the current practice", with utility weighting correct and incorrect trial gains and costs by the probability of correctness. A computational memory model tracks each item's practice history to estimate recall probability and RT. The framework was instantiated in simulations and a vocabulary-learning experiment.
requirements: An accurate computational model of recall probability fit to prior data with variety in spacings and repetitions
Tracking of individual item practice history and predicted recall probability during learning
constraints: The exact OET value varies across learning materials and feedback types; lower OETs may be preferable when failures provide larger or faster learning gains
Tested with word-pair learning as a simplifying assumption; complete models would need to account for inter-item relations and transfer
target_learners: students learning vocabulary or independent facts in online educational systems
target_learning_goals: retention of declarative/factual material (e.g., vocabulary)
examples: Simulations of 6 conventional and 22 model-scheduled conditions; an experiment comparing OETs 0.40–0.98 against a nonadaptive S15 control
key_sources: Luke G. Eglington and Philip I. Pavlik Jr. (2020). Optimizing practice scheduling requires quantitative tracking of individual item performance. npj Science of Learning 5:15. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00074-4

article_title: Optimizing practice scheduling requires quantitative tracking of individual item performance
citation: Luke G. Eglington and Philip I. Pavlik Jr. (2020). Optimizing practice scheduling requires quantitative tracking of individual item performance. npj Science of Learning 5:15. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00074-4
title: Value practice decisions by learning gain per unit of time (efficiency), not by gain alone
description: The article argues that practice scheduling is fundamentally an economic problem: gains in learning should be valued relative to their time cost. Efficiency is "the gain in retrievability at some ﬁnal test divided by the time cost of the current practice". Considering time cost led to different conclusions than prior recommendations, because difficult items take longer and fail more often, reducing learning per second. This principle motivated the OET scheduling approach and its simulations and experiment.
requirements: A way to quantify both learning gain and time cost per trial (e.g., a model estimating recall probability and response latency)
constraints: If failures provide larger or faster learning gains, lower difficulty thresholds may be preferable; efficiency is relevant unless the gains and time costs of successes and failures are equal
target_learners: students practicing factual material in online educational systems
target_learning_goals: efficient allocation of limited practice time to maximize retention
examples: Simulations comparing schedules that valued efficiency against conventional schedules ignoring time cost; an experiment testing OET 0.40 (discrepancy reduction) against higher OETs
key_sources: Luke G. Eglington and Philip I. Pavlik Jr. (2020). Optimizing practice scheduling requires quantitative tracking of individual item performance. npj Science of Learning 5:15. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00074-4

article_title: Extracurricular music and visual arts activities are related to academic performance improvement in school-aged children
citation: Chiaki Ishiguro, Toru Ishihara and Noriteru Morita. (2023). Extracurricular music and visual arts activities are related to academic performance improvement in school-aged children. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00155-0
title: Mediated transfer of arts education to academic performance (Winner et al.'s second transfer hypothesis)
description: This framework holds that arts education affects general academic performance not directly but through artistic skills as mediating factors. The article quotes the hypothesis: "artistic skills are mediating factors in the transfer such that arts instruction can lead to the improvement of artistic skills and result in achieving certain academic outcomes". The study's structural equation models operationalized it by testing indirect effects of extracurricular music and visual arts on academic GP via art subject grades, and the authors report the mediated pattern "supported the second hypothesis of Winner et al.".
requirements: Longitudinal data capturing both art subject scores and general academic performance at two time points, plus baseline art scores and SES controls, to separate direct from mediated effects
constraints: The article states the current study shows correlational relationships and could not specify which activities within each club type drive the effect
The article notes the transfer effect size is quite small
target_learners: school-aged children in junior high school (seventh to ninth grade)
target_learning_goals: general academic performance in five major subjects (Japanese, mathematics, social studies, science, English) via music and visual arts skills
examples: The study measured music GP, visual arts GP, and ACGP of Japanese junior high students at the end of seventh and ninth grades and modeled indirect effects through art subject grades.
key_sources: Chiaki Ishiguro, Toru Ishihara and Noriteru Morita. (2023). Extracurricular music and visual arts activities are related to academic performance improvement in school-aged children. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00155-0

article_title: Transcranial direct current stimulation targeting the bilateral IFG alters cognitive processes during creative ideation
citation: Xie, C., Zhang, S., Qiao, X., & Hao, N. (2024). Transcranial direct current stimulation targeting the bilateral IFG alters cognitive processes during creative ideation. npj Science of Learning, 9, 75. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00285-z
title: Compensation account: tDCS can modify creative cognition itself rather than merely enhancing or inhibiting it
description: The article proposes that brain stimulation may not simply raise or lower a fixed creative process but can reorganize it: "the effects of tDCS might extend beyondmere enhancement or inhibition of certain cognitive functions; it could also lead to a modiﬁcation of creative cognition itself". Drawing on compensation research, it posits that if associative processes are disrupted, executive processes may compensate, weakening the correlation between associative ability and creativity without necessarily lowering creativity. The CRA and EEG-classification results are read through this lens: L+R− stimulation shifted solving toward analytical strategies and L−R+ toward remote associations, while overall performance stayed comparable across groups.
requirements: Requires a convergent-thinking task with trial-level semantic metrics (e.g., CRA with quantified relative semantic distance) plus task-related neural recording to detect process shifts that overall performance measures miss.
constraints: Demonstrated at the group level for one 15-min 1.5 mA tDCS protocol pair over F7/F8 during a Chinese-language CRA task; the authors note individual differences in tDCS effects were not analyzed.
EEG's relatively low spatial resolution and decision-tree classifiers limit inference about activation of specific brain areas, per the article's stated limitations.
target_learning_goals: convergent creative thinking
understanding how neural stimulation changes creative cognitive processes
examples: Participants were randomly assigned to L+R−, L−R+, or Sham tDCS before a Stroop task and a 20-trial Chinese CRA task with EEG recorded, and 80 functional-connectivity classification models were built per group per frequency band.
key_sources: Xie, C., Zhang, S., Qiao, X., & Hao, N. (2024). Transcranial direct current stimulation targeting the bilateral IFG alters cognitive processes during creative ideation. npj Science of Learning, 9, 75. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00285-z

article_title: The representational instability in the generalization of fear learning
citation: Kenny Yu, Wolf Vanpaemel, Francis Tuerlinckx & Jonas Zaman. (2024). The representational instability in the generalization of fear learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00287-x
title: Probabilistic dynamic framework of stimulus representation in fear generalization
description: The article proposes that behavior transfer must consider internal representational variability as well as external environmental variability, challenging static stimulus representation assumptions in generalization research. It formulates "a comprehensive system for perceptual fear generalization, which integrates error-driven learning and similarity-based generalization processes", treating perception as a dynamic, probabilistic process and perceptual memory as a separate, stable component whose mapping may shift over time.
requirements: Simultaneous measurement of perception (size estimation) and perceptual memory (size reproduction) during learning and generalization tasks
constraints: Investigated under fear contexts in a differential conditioning paradigm with size stimuli; the authors note the dynamic interplay between perceptual and memory systems remains largely unexplored beyond this setting
target_learning_goals: understanding how stimulus representations shape generalization of learned threat and safety associations
examples: A differential conditioning experiment (N = 80) with size estimation, US expectancy, and size reproduction tasks, analyzed with Bayesian state-space and mixture models
key_sources: Kenny Yu, Wolf Vanpaemel, Francis Tuerlinckx & Jonas Zaman. (2024). The representational instability in the generalization of fear learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00287-x

article_title: Neurocognitive academic training to improve symptoms executive functions and Chinese handwriting in children with ADHD
citation: Han Jiang, Stuart J. Johnstone, Yingxin Li, Jinjin Lu & Bo-Bei Mao. (2026). Neurocognitive Academic Training to Improve Symptoms Executive Functions and Chinese Handwriting in Children with ADHD. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00415-9
title: Neurocognitive-Academic Training (NAT): a low-frequency multicomponent intervention integrating NCT, teacher positive feedback, and scaffolded Chinese handwriting practice
description: NAT is a school-deliverable multicomponent intervention for children with ADHD that "integrates neurocognitive training (NCT), teacher positive feedback, and scaffolded academic tasks". Each 45-minute session combines a 5-minute warm-up, 25-30 minutes of NCT via the Focus Pocus platform with a dry-electrode EEG headset, a break, and a 3-6 minute handwriting module, delivered twice weekly over 10 weeks across three progressive phases. The 20-session protocol achieved symptom, EF, on-task, and handwriting gains despite lower frequency than conventional NCT programs.
requirements: Trained teachers delivering standardized positive feedback during NCT and around handwriting tasks
Computerized NCT platform with adaptive difficulty (Focus Pocus) and EEG-monitoring headset
Scaffolded handwriting tasks using grade-appropriate, curriculum-aligned characters with mastery criteria for phase progression
constraints: The integrated design "does not allow us to disentangle the specific contribution of each component" to outcomes
Generalizability to older children facing complex compositional tasks may be constrained since about one-third of participants were preschoolers
target_learners: Children aged 5-9 with clinically diagnosed ADHD in kindergarten Year 3 to primary school Year 2
target_learning_goals: Inhibitory control and working memory
ADHD symptom reduction
On-task behavior during academic tasks
Chinese character handwriting construction, accuracy, and directionality
examples: Sessions ran 5-minute warm-up, 25-30 minutes of NCT with real-time teacher feedback, a transition break, and a 3-6 minute handwriting module with phase-specific on-task and quality criteria

article_title: Neurocognitive academic training to improve symptoms executive functions and Chinese handwriting in children with ADHD
citation: Han Jiang, Stuart J. Johnstone, Yingxin Li, Jinjin Lu & Bo-Bei Mao. (2026). Neurocognitive Academic Training to Improve Symptoms Executive Functions and Chinese Handwriting in Children with ADHD. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00415-9
title: Cognitive-energetic model grounding of NAT: synergistic engagement of cognitive mechanisms, energetic pools, and executive functions
description: The article grounds NAT in the cognitive-energetic model, which "posits that ADHD involves deficits across three interrelated levels: cognitive mechanisms, energetic mechanisms, and EFs". NAT's efficacy is interpreted as synergistic: NCT trains core cognitive efficiency, progressively structured handwriting tasks challenge and regulate the child's arousal, activation, and effort pools, and phased teacher positive feedback modulates the effort pool via reward sensitivity. Enhanced cognitive efficiency alone is described as insufficient for transfer; it must be supported by an optimal energetic state and deployed under executive control within a meaningful academic context.
requirements: Simultaneous engagement of all three levels — cognitive training, scaffolded ecologically valid tasks, and motivational feedback — rather than EF training in isolation
constraints: The article states enhanced cognitive efficiency alone "is insufficient for far-transfer" without optimal energetic state and meaningful context
target_learning_goals: Executive function efficiency
Transfer of trained cognitive skills to academic tasks such as Chinese handwriting
examples: NAT's three components are mapped onto the model's three levels: NCT for cognitive mechanisms, scaffolded handwriting tasks for energetic pools, teacher feedback for effort regulation
key_sources: Han Jiang, Stuart J. Johnstone, Yingxin Li, Jinjin Lu & Bo-Bei Mao. (2026). Neurocognitive Academic Training to Improve Symptoms Executive Functions and Chinese Handwriting in Children with ADHD. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00415-9

article_title: Analyzing the network structure of students’ motivation to learn AI: a self-determination theory perspective
citation: Jiajing Li, Jianhua Zhang, Ching Sing Chai, Vivian W. Y. Lee, Xuesong Zhai, Xingwei Wang & Ronnel B. King. (2025). Analyzing the network structure of students' motivation to learn AI: a self-determination theory perspective. npj Science of Learning 10:48. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00339-w
title: Self-determination theory as a framework for students' AI learning motivation
description: The article applies self-determination theory (SDT) to AI education, treating motivation as having both quantity and quality. Based on degree of internalization, "SDT differentiates intrinsic motivation, identiﬁed regulation, introjected regulation, external regulation, and amotivation." SDT further posits that fulfillment of three basic psychological needs — autonomy, competence, and relatedness — fosters more internalized motivation, and that environmental factors such as social support and facilitating conditions act as catalysts. The study extends SDT into AI-infused learning and argues motivation should be studied as an intertwined dynamic system rather than as isolated variables.
requirements: Application requires measuring qualitatively distinct motivation types and basic psychological needs satisfaction, which the study did via validated multi-item Likert scales with internal consistency from 0.78 to 0.95.
constraints: The study notes its findings on need centrality refine SDT in the AI context specifically; the sample was all Chinese university students, which the authors say may explain introjected regulation's centrality.
target_learners: university students learning with and about AI
target_learning_goals: AI literacy
sustained engagement and motivation in AI learning
examples: The study operationalized the five motivation types with the AI Motivation Scale (four items per subscale) and needs satisfaction with three items each, then mapped them as network nodes.
key_sources: Jiajing Li, Jianhua Zhang, Ching Sing Chai, Vivian W. Y. Lee, Xuesong Zhai, Xingwei Wang & Ronnel B. King. (2025). Analyzing the network structure of students' motivation to learn AI: a self-determination theory perspective. npj Science of Learning 10:48. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00339-w

article_title: Self-regulated spacing in a massive open online course is related to better learning
citation: Paulo F. Carvalho, Faria Sana and Veronica X. Yan. (2020). Self-regulated spacing in a massive open online course is related to better learning. npj Science of Learning 5:2. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-0061-1
title: Use spaced study as a buffer that improves performance for lower-ability students and those who do not engage in active practice
description: This principle holds that distributing study across multiple sessions offers an alternative route to the benefits of active practice: "for those students who do not engage in as many activities during learning, they can instead space out their learning more to obtain the same benefits". The article frames spacing as working "as a buffer, improving performance for low ability students and those who do not engage in active practices". It applies to self-regulated online and course-based learning where learners control their own study schedules.
requirements: Learners must have the opportunity to return to the same unit content across multiple study sessions separated in time.
constraints: The evidence is observational, so a third variable such as motivation cannot be eliminated; those who neither space nor complete activities are likely to underperform.
target_learners: MOOC and online course students, including lower-ability students and students who complete few practice activities
target_learning_goals: Retention and quiz/exam performance of complex course material such as introductory psychology
examples: In the MOOC data, spacing was defined as the number of sessions students took to complete a unit, averaging 4.08 sessions per unit, and more sessions related to higher quiz grades within the same student.
key_sources: Paulo F. Carvalho, Faria Sana and Veronica X. Yan. (2020). Self-regulated spacing in a massive open online course is related to better learning. npj Science of Learning 5:2. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-0061-1

article_title: Enhancing mathematical learning outcomes through a low-cost single-channel BCI system
citation: Hou, Z., Li, X., Yan, J., & Xu, S. Y. (2024). Enhancing mathematical learning outcomes through a low-cost single-channel BCI system. npj Science of Learning, 9, 65. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00277-z
title: Low-Cost Single-Channel BCI neurofeedback system for math learning
description: The article proposes "a novel Low-Cost Single-Channel BCI system that can enhance mathematical learning outcomes by providing neurofeedback based on alpha rhythms". It uses a single-channel MindWave headset (NeuroSky) with a dry electrode at Fp1, sampling at 128 Hz, with MATLAB software computing alpha power (8–12 Hz) in 5-second sliding windows via Welch's method and displaying it as a color-modulated bar updated every 5 seconds. The system was delivered alongside algebra learning on Khan Academy.
requirements: A single-channel EEG headset with a dry electrode positioned at Fp1 per the international 10-20 system
Real-time software computing alpha power from sliding EEG windows and presenting visual (and auditory) feedback during the learning task
constraints: Tested only on university students learning algebra on an online platform; the authors state future studies should test other mathematical domains, age groups, and learning environments
target_learning_goals: algebra problem-solving performance
mathematics self-efficacy
self-regulation of attention and arousal via neurofeedback
examples: BCI group participants received real-time neurofeedback for 50 minutes while learning algebra on Khan Academy; controls received sham feedback not based on their brain activity
key_sources: Hou, Z., Li, X., Yan, J., & Xu, S. Y. (2024). Enhancing mathematical learning outcomes through a low-cost single-channel BCI system. npj Science of Learning, 9, 65. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00277-z

article_title: Embodied word learning in schools and sustained attention in virtual reality
citation: Rudling, M., Rumetshofer, T., Nirme, J. & Mårtensson, J. (2026). Embodied Word Learning in Schools and Sustained Attention in Virtual Reality. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00395-2
title: Embodied, grounded-cognition account of L2 word learning motivating non-parasitic word-object training
description: The article frames vocabulary learning via the grounded cognition perspective, in which "language use and language learning are both embodied, ingrained in sensorimotor experience, and situated in a learning context". It contrasts L1 experiential multimodal learning with school L2 parasitic word learning, where word-object associations are weaker under the unified competition model. To mimic L1 learning the study used the ancient farming equipment paradigm, where unknown tools necessitate "a direct visual-phonological link". The theory guided the VR assembly design and the interpretation that meaningful integration of activity and language is required.
requirements: The learning activity and linguistic content must be meaningfully integrated, with the word embedded in the task itself rather than detached from it
constraints: The study's VR task introduced words only after assembly was complete, which the authors say contradicts the meaningful-integration principle and may have limited learning potential
Participants never moved beyond object form into semantic meaning
target_learners: school-aged children (Swedish middle school, years four and six, ages 9-13)
target_learning_goals: second-language (L2) vocabulary and word-object associations
examples: Children assembled segmented 3D models of old Finnish agricultural tools in VR and were shown each word in text and speech after correct assembly
key_sources: Rudling, M., Rumetshofer, T., Nirme, J. & Mårtensson, J. (2026). Embodied Word Learning in Schools and Sustained Attention in Virtual Reality. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00395-2

article_title: Embodied word learning in schools and sustained attention in virtual reality
citation: Rudling, M., Rumetshofer, T., Nirme, J. & Mårtensson, J. (2026). Embodied Word Learning in Schools and Sustained Attention in Virtual Reality. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00395-2
title: VR object-assembly word-learning game and matched PC passive-viewing condition
description: The authors developed both training programs for this study: a VR game on Meta Quest Pro headsets, implemented in Unity 3D, in which children assembled 3D segmented ancient farming tools with hand controllers, after which the word appeared on a blackboard with a spoken recording played three times; and a matched PC condition in PsychoPy showing 15-second assembly videos without hands. The VR environment "was deliberately designed to minimize visual distractions". Each 18-word VR set took on average 19.40 minutes; each PC session took 8 minutes.
requirements: Head-mounted displays with hand controllers and inside-out movement tracking, and laptop delivery of the PC and recall tests
constraints: In this implementation the VR environment "is still richer than the very plain PC user interface", which the authors suggest may have added strain on attentional load
Words were exposed only once per learning phase and training lasted one week per condition
target_learning_goals: recognition and recall of 108 novel spoken and written word forms paired with unfamiliar objects
examples: Children assembled segmented objects from three to five pieces in VR, with pieces signalling correct connections by turning from white to green
In the PC condition children watched silent videos of objects assembling themselves from the same parts, then saw the word above a still image

article_title: Cardiovascular exercise enhances motor learning across multiple sessions in people with Parkinson’s disease: a randomized controlled pilot trial
citation: Wanner, P., Frisch, N., Rikus, S., Roig, M. & Steib, S. (2025). Cardiovascular exercise enhances motor learning across multiple sessions in people with Parkinson's disease: a randomized controlled pilot trial. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00391-6
title: Schedule a bout of moderate-intensity cardiovascular exercise immediately after motor skill practice to enhance multi-session motor learning in neurorehabilitation
description: The article recommends, based on its pilot RCT, that motor skill practice in pwPD be followed by a 30-min bout of moderate-intensity cycling. The authors write that "CVE may be an effective and low-cost tool to enhance motor learning in typical rehabilitation settings" and call it "a simpler and more cost-effective intervention to enhance motor learning compared to other currently proposed methods, such as brain stimulation".
requirements: Adequate pre-participation screening, which the authors state made the intervention safe and feasible for pwPD with mild-to-moderate disease stages
Practice must occur in close temporal proximity to the CVE bout, which was administered immediately after each practice session
constraints: Effects are preliminary pilot evidence from a small sample and require confirmation in better powered studies
Exploratory analyses suggest sedentary persons may first need to reach a critical cardiorespiratory fitness level to fully benefit
target_learners: people with mild-to-moderate Parkinson's disease in motor rehabilitation
target_learning_goals: motor skill learning and retention of a novel balance task
examples: In the trial, each of six weekly stabilometer practice sessions was followed by 30 min of moderate-intensity cycling at 60% maximal power output for the EXE group, or seated rest for the REST group.
key_sources: Wanner, P., Frisch, N., Rikus, S., Roig, M. & Steib, S. (2025). Cardiovascular exercise enhances motor learning across multiple sessions in people with Parkinson's disease: a randomized controlled pilot trial. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00391-6

article_title: Post-class naps boost declarative learning in a naturalistic school setting
citation: Thiago Cabral, Natália B. Mota, Lucia Fraga, Mauro Copelli, Mark A. McDaniel and Sidarta Ribeiro. (2018). Post-class naps boost declarative learning in a naturalistic school setting. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0031-z
title: Naturalistic in-school sleep intervention pattern: weekly randomized cross-over naps after regular teacher-led lessons
description: This pattern embeds a nap intervention in ordinary schooling: curricular content is taught by the regular class teacher, students are "randomly sorted into sleep and non-sleep sets of equal size" each week, and each student experiences all conditions. Retention is measured days later with teacher-normed multiple-choice tests. The design bypasses experimenter-novelty confounds and between-group differences that limited prior school nap studies.
requirements: A scheduled slot after a morning class, a quiet dark room with mats and eye masks, and curricular content divided into equivalent parts verified on an independent sample
constraints: The authors did not monitor rest/activity (actigraphy or EEG) and did not assess sleep inertia at awakening because the school schedule ended at 12:00
target_learners: fifth-grade students in a public school
target_learning_goals: retention of declarative curricular content in Science and History
examples: Over 6 weeks, Science and History units were split into parts A, B, C; students napped up to 60 min from 8:15 or attended another lecture or a break, with Friday multiple-choice retention tests of 10 questions per part.
key_sources: Thiago Cabral, Natália B. Mota, Lucia Fraga, Mauro Copelli, Mark A. McDaniel and Sidarta Ribeiro. (2018). Post-class naps boost declarative learning in a naturalistic school setting. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0031-z

article_title: Post-class naps boost declarative learning in a naturalistic school setting
citation: Thiago Cabral, Natália B. Mota, Lucia Fraga, Mauro Copelli, Mark A. McDaniel and Sidarta Ribeiro. (2018). Post-class naps boost declarative learning in a naturalistic school setting. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0031-z
title: Stage 2 sleep account of post-learning nap benefits for declarative school content
description: The authors interpret their results through sleep-stage composition: morning naps show low slow-wave sleep and consist mostly of Stage 2 and REM sleep. Because the tested material was declarative and involved "rote learning and the association of multiple contents, but not abstract or creative thinking", they conclude "the morning nap beneﬁts were likely related to Stage 2 sleep, not REM sleep", which they link to prior work relating Stage 2 sleep to declarative memory.
requirements: Declarative, rote-style curricular material as tested here; the mechanism is hypothesized, not measured, since no sleep recording was performed
constraints: No actigraphy or EEG was collected, so sleep-stage composition during the study naps was inferred from prior literature rather than observed
target_learners: school-age learners of declarative curricular content
target_learning_goals: declarative memory consolidation after learning
examples: The article states morning naps "are comprised mostly of Stage 2 sleep and rapid-eye-movement (REM) sleep" and attributes the observed declarative retention gains to the Stage 2 component.
key_sources: Thiago Cabral, Natália B. Mota, Lucia Fraga, Mauro Copelli, Mark A. McDaniel and Sidarta Ribeiro. (2018). Post-class naps boost declarative learning in a naturalistic school setting. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0031-z

article_title: Seeking the neural representation of statistical properties in print during implicit processing of visual words
citation: Jianyi Liu, Tengwen Fan, Yan Chen and Jingjing Zhao. (2023). Seeking the neural representation of statistical properties in print during implicit processing of visual words. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00209-3
title: Predictive coding with precision modulation explains how long-term statistical knowledge and short-term predictions interact in word processing
description: The article uses predictive coding, in which learning is "a continuous optimization of a generative model" achieved through continuous interaction between top-down predictions and bottom-up prediction errors. The system assigns different weights to real-time prediction errors according to environmental variability (prediction precision), a mechanism the authors call conceptually "a form of meta-learning". In the experiment, low-precision equal probability sequences revealed only lexical frequency representations, while high-precision oddball sequences caused inconsistent information to be evaluated as worthy of learning, yielding stronger sub-lexical consistency representations and vMMN responses.
requirements: Short-term predictions with built-in high precision (e.g., repeated standard stimuli) for sub-lexical consistency representations to become detectable
constraints: The study did not consider participants' hearing characteristics, a stated limitation for generalizability
The assumption of no long-term prediction differences between stimulus types lacks direct proof, a stated limit on explanatory power
target_learning_goals: implicit neural processing of statistical regularities in print
visual word recognition
examples: Equal probability sequences with low built-in prediction precision and three oddball sequences with high precision were used; consistent characters appeared with p = 0.75 and inconsistent deviants with p = 0.25
key_sources: Jianyi Liu, Tengwen Fan, Yan Chen and Jingjing Zhao. (2023). Seeking the neural representation of statistical properties in print during implicit processing of visual words. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00209-3

article_title: Immersive auditory-cognitive training improves speech-in-noise perception in older adults with varying hearing and working memory
citation: Vanessa Frei & Nathalie Giroud. (2025). Immersive auditory-cognitive training improves speech-in-noise perception in older adults with varying hearing and working memory. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00306-5
title: Integrated perceptual-cognitive system theory (Schneider and Pichora-Fuller) as the article's resource-allocation account of speech comprehension
description: The article adopts this theory as its explanatory framework for why combined sensory and cognitive training should work: speech comprehension succeeds through a direct link between sensory and cognitive processing that draws on shared resources. As the article states, "The theory assumes a direct link between sensory and cognitive processing, based on a shared pool of processing resources." Efficient allocation of these resources toward the sensory and cognitive demands of speech enables comprehension, whereas increased load or reduced individual capacities limit success. The authors use it to interpret why the immersive environment's extra sensory information intensified training, particularly for listeners with limited hearing or auditory working memory.
requirements: A training situation that imposes both sensory and cognitive demand so that allocation of shared processing resources must be managed
constraints: The article notes that in very favorable listening situations additional visual speech cues have been proposed to act as increased sensory load rather than support, per cited empirical works
target_learners: older adults with varying hearing acuity and cognitive capacities
target_learning_goals: speech perception in noise
efficient allocation of processing resources between sensory and cognitive demand
examples: The authors interpret the immersive session's extra redundant sensory information as provoking resource allocation between sensory information and varying memory load, potentially producing the stronger training effect
key_sources: Vanessa Frei & Nathalie Giroud. (2025). Immersive auditory-cognitive training improves speech-in-noise perception in older adults with varying hearing and working memory. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00306-5

article_title: Immersive auditory-cognitive training improves speech-in-noise perception in older adults with varying hearing and working memory
citation: Vanessa Frei & Nathalie Giroud. (2025). Immersive auditory-cognitive training improves speech-in-noise perception in older adults with varying hearing and working memory. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00306-5
title: Speech-memory paradigm: a short-term auditory-cognitive training with natural continuous speech and varying memory load, in audio-only and immersive stereoscopic VR modalities
description: The training element is a speech-memory task in which participants hear natural continuous sentences with varying memory loads (one vs two sentences, 60 items per session) and answer a verbal comprehension question after each item. As the article describes it, "The AU and IM approach used the same training task and consisted of a speech-memory task, whereby participants were presented with natural continuous sentences with varying memory loads and were required to answer a comprehension question after each sentence." The immersive version presents the speaker via a stereoscopic three-dimensional 180-degree video in an HP Reverb G2 head-mounted display; sessions lasted about 40-45 minutes, and comprehension questions after high-load items always referred to the first heard sentence, with mock items every tenth trial to prevent listening strategies.
requirements: Natural continuous speech material presented at a normalized 70 dB level with comprehension questions to enforce processing
Randomized item order and single presentation of each item to reduce repetition-based learning effects
constraints: The immersive environment predominantly increased redundant sensory information given the very favorable listening situation, per the authors' interpretation; perceived immersion was not systematically assessed
target_learners: healthy older adults (61-80) with mild to moderate hearing loss and varying cognitive capacities
target_learning_goals: speech comprehension of natural continuous speech
selective attention and working memory engagement during listening
examples: Each session contained 30 low-load (one-sentence) and 30 high-load (two-sentence) items on general-knowledge topics such as Flora, Fauna, and Swiss History, spoken by a trained actress who was also the visualized speaker
key_sources: Vanessa Frei & Nathalie Giroud. (2025). Immersive auditory-cognitive training improves speech-in-noise perception in older adults with varying hearing and working memory. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00306-5

article_title: Introducing students to neural communication: an embodied-learning classroom demonstration
citation: B. D. M. Hatin. (2020). Introducing students to neural communication: an embodied-learning classroom demonstration. npj Science of Learning 5:18. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00077-1
title: Embodied metaphor: whole-body engagement with a metaphor supports learning of abstract science concepts beyond passive engagement
description: The article frames embodied metaphors as a type of active learning especially well-suited to abstract neuroscience topics. While metaphors such as the "lock and key" metaphor for receptor activity are common, the article argues that "whole-body engagement in a learning environment supports and improves learning beyond what is observed through passive engagement with a metaphor" — e.g., acting out opening a lock with a key rather than passively hearing the metaphor. Students and foam projectiles take on roles such as soma, axon hillock, presynaptic axon terminal, post-synaptic cell, and metabotropic and ionotropic receptors.
requirements: Students physically enact the metaphor (whole-body engagement) rather than passively hearing it
constraints: Presented as especially suited to abstract topics that cannot be directly viewed, such as chemical activity at the synapse
target_learners: university students in STEM and neuroscience classrooms
target_learning_goals: understanding abstract science concepts that cannot be directly observed
examples: The article cites an earlier embodied action-potential activity in a university classroom reported to improve student understanding of the stages of an action potential.
key_sources: B. D. M. Hatin. (2020). Introducing students to neural communication: an embodied-learning classroom demonstration. npj Science of Learning 5:18. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00077-1

article_title: Introducing students to neural communication: an embodied-learning classroom demonstration
citation: B. D. M. Hatin. (2020). Introducing students to neural communication: an embodied-learning classroom demonstration. npj Science of Learning 5:18. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00077-1
title: Adapt embodied activities to class size, space and resources, and consider the socio-political context before using toy weapons
description: The article recommends customizing the activities "based on available class size, classroom space, and resources": volunteers can model each activity for the class, or activity stations with written instructions can let students try each at their own pace. For deeper critical thinking, students can figure out how the task fits each concept themselves, or devise their own metaphors. Educators should also weigh "the current socio-political climate and historical context with respect to the use of weapons" and give a discretionary warning or consider alternative activities where toy weapons are inappropriate.
requirements: Instructor judgment about class size, resources, space and the local context before staging the activities
constraints: In a large class where volunteers model the activities, passive observers are not engaged in active learning
target_learners: university students in neuroscience classrooms of varying sizes
target_learning_goals: engagement with and understanding of neural communication concepts
examples: Activity stations set up around the classroom with written instructions so students can try each activity at their own pace.

article_title: Educational App-Development needs to be informed by the Cognitive Neurosciences of Learning & Memory
citation: T. P. Reber and N. Rothen (2018). Educational App-Development needs to be informed by the Cognitive Neurosciences of Learning & Memory. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0039-4
title: Memory-related educational apps should be developed on the basis of fundamental principles from the cognitive neuroscience of memory, with theoretically motivated features varied within the app for large-scale long-term testing
description: The article proposes that educational ICT, especially memory-related apps such as foreign-language learning apps, "need to be developed on the basis of fundamental principles derived from cognitive neuroscience of memory". Theoretically motivated design features, such as the specifics of episode spacing, should be varied within the app so effects can be assessed in isolation with meaningfully comparable effect sizes, while apps collect data in real-world classroom and homework scenarios. This enables large samples in long-term real-world settings. The principle rests on the article's argument that ICT design is not informed by established memory science, which the authors give as the likely reason ICT fails to facilitate learning.
requirements: Apps must embed within-app variation of factors hypothesized to aid learning, including their interactions
Data collection must extend to real-world scenarios beyond the classroom, including homework conditions
constraints: The four learning principles are vastly underexplored in real-life educational settings
Almost all studies on these principles were restricted to relatively short time intervals of less than half a year
target_learning_goals: memory-based learning such as vocabulary acquisition
skill and knowledge outcomes measured by school grades
examples: The comment proposes varying the specifics of spacing of learning episodes within an ICT application and assessing effect sizes in isolation, with data collected in classroom and homework conditions
key_sources: T. P. Reber and N. Rothen (2018). Educational App-Development needs to be informed by the Cognitive Neurosciences of Learning & Memory. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0039-4

article_title: Retrieval practice is costly and is beneficial only when working memory capacity is abundant
citation: Yicong Zheng, Pengyuan Sun and Xiaonan L. Liu. (2023). Retrieval practice is costly and is beneficial only when working memory capacity is abundant. npj Science of Learning 8:8. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00159-w
title: Modified SAC dual-process account of the testing effect
description: The article adapts the source of activation confusion (SAC) model to explain when retrieval practice strengthens memory. It assumes retrieval practice involves two sequential processes, a retrieval attempt and a post-retrieval re-encoding process, both consuming resources from a limited WM pool. Its critical assumption is "trading" WM resources for memory strengthening, so that "successfully retrieving the item does not guarantee that the memory is more effectively strengthened than restudying the item" when resources are depleted. Item familiarity reduces WM consumption, explaining why lower-capacity learners benefit only from familiar stimuli.
requirements: Retrieval attempts must succeed for re-encoding to strengthen nodes, since re-encoding only strengthens the episode node when retrieval is successful (no feedback was provided)
constraints: The simulation simplified to Days 2 and 3, assuming Day 1 learning criteria equalized associations; the authors state the cognitive mechanisms underlying the two processes remain unclear
target_learners: undergraduate students learning novel cue-target associations
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of learned associations
examples: The authors fitted a weighting parameter for extra WM cost and individual-level mean and standard deviation parameters by minimizing root-mean-square error against observed accuracy
key_sources: Yicong Zheng, Pengyuan Sun and Xiaonan L. Liu. (2023). Retrieval practice is costly and is beneficial only when working memory capacity is abundant. npj Science of Learning 8:8. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00159-w

article_title: Is plasticity of synapses the mechanism of long-term memory storage?
citation: Wickliffe C. Abraham, Owen D. Jones and David L. Glanzman. (2019). Is plasticity of synapses the mechanism of long-term memory storage? npj Science of Learning 4:9. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0048-y
title: The synaptic plasticity and memory (SPM) hypothesis holds that experience-dependent synaptic change is a fundamental mechanism of learning and memory retention
description: The SPM hypothesis proposes that memories are stored primarily through experience-dependent changes at synapses. The review describes how this concept gained sway after electrophysiological work revealed lasting activity-dependent synaptic changes such as LTP and LTD. Martin et al.'s four evidentiary criteria (detectability, mimicry, anterograde intervention, retrograde intervention) are presented as the framework for confirming it. The review concludes the hypothesis has strong support but lacks conclusive proof that memories reside at synapses.
requirements: Confirming the hypothesis requires evidence meeting Martin et al.'s criteria: detectability, mimicry, anterograde intervention, and retrograde intervention
constraints: The review states we are still without conclusive proof that memories reside at synapses, and non-synaptic mechanisms have emerged that are also capable of acting as memory substrates
target_learners: learners across species studied in memory research (mammals and invertebrates)
target_learning_goals: long-term memory storage and retention
examples: The review cites detectability of synaptic plasticity after many forms of learning and reversal learning inducing complementary reversal of synaptic plasticity

article_title: Is plasticity of synapses the mechanism of long-term memory storage?
citation: Wickliffe C. Abraham, Owen D. Jones and David L. Glanzman. (2019). Is plasticity of synapses the mechanism of long-term memory storage? npj Science of Learning 4:9. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0048-y
title: The synaptic tag and capture (STC) hypothesis posits that weakly stimulated synapses set tags that capture plasticity-related proteins synthesized in response to strong stimulation of other inputs
description: The STC hypothesis explains how weakly and strongly stimulated synapses interact associatively over long intervals. A weakly stimulated set of synapses sets a tag that can sequester and use key proteins synthesized in response to stimulation of other synaptic inputs, generating late-phase plasticity. The review presents evidence from L-LTP and from Aplysia long-term facilitation, where a single 5-HT pulse tags a synapse that captures plasticity-inducing molecules from soma. Cross-tagging means proteins from L-LTP can promote L-LTD in neighboring synapses and vice versa.
requirements: Requires protein synthesis triggered by strong stimulation of converging inputs, and a tag set by weak stimulation whose molecular identity is not yet known
constraints: The review states the tag is "yet to be fully defined mechanistically", and for LTF the molecular identity of the tag is not yet known
target_learners: mammalian and invertebrate nervous systems studied in memory research
target_learning_goals: association of events across extended temporal intervals in long-term memory formation
examples: Martin et al. showed a synapse given one 5-HT pulse (short-term facilitation only) underwent LTF when paired with strong training of a second synapse

article_title: Is plasticity of synapses the mechanism of long-term memory storage?
citation: Wickliffe C. Abraham, Owen D. Jones and David L. Glanzman. (2019). Is plasticity of synapses the mechanism of long-term memory storage? npj Science of Learning 4:9. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0048-y
title: Cell-intrinsic memory storage via stable epigenetic marks, particularly DNA methylation, is proposed as an alternative to storage in altered synaptic weights
description: This model holds that long-term memories are stored within neuronal nuclei as thermodynamically stable epigenetic changes, chiefly DNA methylation, first proposed by Holliday. The review reports that DNMT inhibitors block memory formation or consolidation and can disrupt well-consolidated memory, that methylation patterns change over weeks after training, and that active demethylation by Tet enzymes means cytosines could in principle subserve a binary code. Synaptic changes would then be the mechanism by which stored nuclear memories are expressed.
requirements: Requires an explanation of how epigenetic changes can faithfully maintain a record of learning-induced changes across the thousands of synaptic connections a neuron maintains; no such explanation is presently at hand
constraints: The synapse specificity problem is the strongest argument against this hypothesis: it appears far more difficult to encode which specific synapses were strengthened in a cell-intrinsic model
target_learners: mammals and invertebrates studied in memory research
target_learning_goals: long-term memory storage, consolidation, and maintenance
examples: Holliday proposed that methylated or non-methylated DNA sites switch a neuron's phenotype so it responds to a previously received signal

article_title: Is plasticity of synapses the mechanism of long-term memory storage?
citation: Wickliffe C. Abraham, Owen D. Jones and David L. Glanzman. (2019). Is plasticity of synapses the mechanism of long-term memory storage? npj Science of Learning 4:9. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0048-y
title: A synthesis of the synaptic and cell-intrinsic views: memory maintained by coordinated ongoing communication between the synapse and the nucleus, potentially via transneuronal RNA exchange
description: The review proposes integrating Cajal's synaptic view with Golgi's syncytial notion: learning-related synaptic plasticity triggers epigenetic changes in neuronal nuclei, and memory is maintained by coordinated synapse-to-nucleus and nucleus-to-synapse signaling, with candidates including retrograde signaling molecules and dendritic ncRNAs. A more radical variant holds memory is entirely stored as nuclear epigenetic changes, with synaptic changes as the expression mechanism. The discovery that Arc protein, packaged in exosomes, transfers mRNA between neurons reveals an RNA-mediated thoroughfare the review says could endow somata with the capacity for recognizing one another's roles in learning.
requirements: Requires an account of how non-synaptic RNA exchange can preserve synaptic specificity of memory traces
constraints: It is not yet known how important such non-synaptic communication is for overall brain operation, nor the function of transferred Arc mRNA in recipient neurons
target_learning_goals: long-term memory storage and maintenance
examples: The review cites exosomal transfer of Arc mRNA, a retrovirus-like capsid protein, from active neurons to neighbors where it can be translated

article_title: The effect of prediction error on episodic memory encoding is modulated by the outcome of the predictions
citation: Francesco Pupillo, Javier Ortiz-Tudela, Rasmus Bruckner and Yee Lee Shing. (2023). The effect of prediction error on episodic memory encoding is modulated by the outcome of the predictions. npj Science of Learning 8:18. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00166-x
title: Hippocampal-striatal dopaminergic account of outcome-modulated prediction-error effects on encoding
description: The article proposes that interactions between the striatal and hippocampal dopaminergic systems explain why prediction error helps memory after correct predictions and harms it after incorrect ones. When "the expectation of a certain outcome was low, a correct prediction might nevertheless provide a PE signal which increases the release of dopamine in the striatum, promoting hippocampal activation, and resulting in better encoding". Conversely, when an outcome is strongly expected, an incorrect prediction corresponds to a negative PE that suppresses striatal dopamine release and hippocampal activation, resulting in impaired encoding. The article draws on evidence that dopamine enhances long-term potentiation in the hippocampus and that increased striatum-hippocampus connectivity may lead to enhanced memory encoding.
requirements: Future studies investigating the connectivity between the hippocampus and striatum at these different conditions are needed to provide support for these hypotheses, per the article
constraints: The recognition task used does not allow the authors to conclude whether recognition performance is driven by recollection or by familiarity processes, so hippocampal involvement is not established
target_learners: young adults learning probabilistic context-object associations
target_learning_goals: episodic encoding of novel items under established prior expectations
examples: The article interprets its two-experiment contingency-learning paradigm, in which prediction outcome moderated PE effects on recognition, through this dopaminergic mechanism

article_title: Uncovering subgroup heterogeneity in dyslexia intervention outcomes using explainable machine learning
citation: Tan, A.S.-C., & Ali, F. (2026). Uncovering subgroup heterogeneity in dyslexia intervention outcomes using explainable machine learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00429-3
title: Explanation-aware clustering: combining model explainers with unsupervised clustering to uncover heterogeneous subgroups within predicted classes
description: This framework pairs a model explainer with unsupervised learning to reveal heterogeneity hidden by binary classification. LIME "perturbs the input data locally around a single instance and fits a simple interpretable model" to identify predictors contributing to class membership; clustering of these LIME profiles (via K-Means, cluster number selected by lowest Davies-Bouldin Index) then identifies subgroups within each class, addressing explainer models' "tendency to overstate class homogeneity due to such local approximations". The article uses it to uncover 2 responder and 4 non-responder subgroups with distinct longitudinal outcomes.
requirements: A trained predictive model with explainer output (LIME coefficients), plus unsupervised clustering and a cluster-validity index to select subgroup count
constraints: Explainer models tend to overstate class homogeneity due to local approximations; clustered subgroups rest on predictor importance, not actual predictor values directly
target_learners: Students with dyslexia or learning difficulties in literacy intervention
target_learning_goals: Prediction of intervention responsiveness and long-term literacy development to inform personalized intervention
examples: K-Means applied to LIME coefficients from a Gaussian Naive Bayes model identified responder and non-responder subgroups whose membership predicted trajectories 68.2 months post-intervention

article_title: An ecological approach to understanding transitions and tensions in complex learning contexts
citation: Luke McCrone & Martyn Kingsbury. (2024). An ecological approach to understanding transitions and tensions in complex learning contexts. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00267-1
title: A taxonomy of spatial, pedagogic and agentic transitions and tensions between formal and informal learning spaces
description: The article defines three categories of transitions and tensions between timetabled and non-timetabled learning spaces. 'Spatial' ones "exist as a function of timetables and architectural divides between formal and informal space"; 'pedagogic' ones exist between teacher-centred transmission intent and student-centred intent, producing 'failed', hidden and postponed interactions; and 'agentic' ones occur between the fixed power dynamic of the lecture theatre and the more democratic adjacent informal space. The taxonomy emerged from mixed-methods analysis of occupancy data, ethnographic observation and field interviews, and conceptualises the spaces as interconnected ecological zones.
requirements: Requires mixed-methods data combining quantitative occupancy monitoring with ethnographic observation and field interviews to detect the transitions and tensions
constraints: Derived from one lecture theatre and adjacent breakout space in a UK STEM university chemical engineering department
target_learning_goals: supporting active learning
managing transitions between timetabled and non-timetabled learning
examples: Occupancy plots of type 1 and type 2 timetable configurations, sociograms of breakout space interaction, and field interviews with students were used to characterise on-ramp and off-ramp transitions
key_sources: Luke McCrone & Martyn Kingsbury. (2024). An ecological approach to understanding transitions and tensions in complex learning contexts. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00267-1

article_title: An ecological approach to understanding transitions and tensions in complex learning contexts
citation: Luke McCrone & Martyn Kingsbury. (2024). An ecological approach to understanding transitions and tensions in complex learning contexts. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00267-1
title: The ecotone concept: transitional zones between learning spaces as a third ecosystem of pedagogic potential
description: The article proposes the ecological concept of the 'ecotone' — a zone of overlap and transition between two ecosystems, translating etymologically to "ecologies in tension" — as a way of thinking about the space between lecture theatre and breakout space. Ecotones are "a distinct third ecosystem subject to conflicting tidal and river forces which create tensions" and, being "less encumbered by the inertia and rules of the adjoining spaces", present opportunities for transition and innovation that feedback into the core. The authors postulate this metaphor may significantly advance understanding of complex interactions between space and pedagogy, and suggest applications to diverse student groups and to 'onlife' hybrid physical-virtual learning spaces.
requirements: Requires an ecological mindset that views formal and informal spaces as interconnected rather than fixed, isolated entities
constraints: The article acknowledges the use of the ecotone concept in higher education is limited and presents challenges in applying a metaphor from nature to model social systems
target_learning_goals: understanding and enabling transitions between transmission-based and active learning
designing productive learning spaces and timetables
examples: Applying the ecotone metaphor helped recognise the formal and informal spaces as greater than the sum of their parts and facilitated institutional discussion that raised awareness of tensions

article_title: An ecological approach to understanding transitions and tensions in complex learning contexts
citation: Luke McCrone & Martyn Kingsbury. (2024). An ecological approach to understanding transitions and tensions in complex learning contexts. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00267-1
title: Highlight the pedagogic potential of informal transitional spaces adjacent to lecture theatres to support active learning before costly redesign
description: Rather than redesigning lecture theatres wholesale — which the article notes is time- and cost-intensive — institutions can use a mixed-method ecological approach to recognise the pedagogic potential of the informal spaces and periods between formal ones. The authors write that "ecotone thinking can empower teachers to reconsider their use of existing spaces", for example by inviting students to move between spaces to aid group formation and transitions between lecture segments and group-based interactions. This understanding informed student-staff partnership projects that redesigned 'transitional spaces' outside lecture theatres.
requirements: Requires recognising formal and informal spaces as interconnected ecological zones rather than isolated entities
Requires occupancy and qualitative data to identify where transitional pedagogic potential exists
constraints: Full architectural redesign aligned with active learning classrooms is time- and cost-intensive, and disproportionate capital investment in UK university education space renders broad redesign difficult
target_learners: undergraduate STEM students in lecture-based courses
target_learning_goals: facilitating group formation
connecting timetabled learning to other contexts
enabling transitions between transmission and active learning
examples: Findings informed student-staff partnership projects redesigning 'transitional spaces' just outside lecture theatres, and a 'regenerative design' approach in which spaces were redesigned more cost-effectively

article_title: Hypothesis testing governs strategic motor learning
citation: Wei Ding, Anjuli Niyogi, Jordan A. Taylor & Jonathan S. Tsay. (2026). Hypothesis Testing Governs Strategic Motor Learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00428-4
title: Hypothesis testing framework of strategic motor learning
description: A process account in which strategic adaptation operates through hypothesis testing: learners generate candidate action–outcome hypotheses about an environmental change, test them against sensory feedback, discard failures, and iteratively refine actions and hypotheses until a solution is abruptly discovered. The proposed formalization comprises 'a hypothesis space and an inference procedure', with discrete spatial transformations (rotations, mirror reflections, translations, gain changes) each carrying a prior belief, actions sampled in proportion to beliefs, and Bayesian-style belief updating favoring more specific hypotheses. Target geometry shapes which hypotheses remain viable, steering both learning speed and the diversity of adopted rules.
requirements: Feedback that lets learners evaluate candidate action–outcome hypotheses against sensory outcomes
constraints: The authors state they are 'not claiming that hypothesis testing provides a superior account across all regimes of motor learning'—state-space/Kalman models describe implicit recalibration and reinforcement learning captures skill acquisition
target_learners: adults learning new sensorimotor mappings (online participants, mean age ~25)
target_learning_goals: discovering effective movement strategies under changed sensorimotor environments
examples: Participants in the visuomotor rotation task explored the workspace to align a 60° rotated cursor to targets without being told the perturbation's nature; the framework treats their sign flips and mirror reversals as hypothesis tests rather than execution failures.
key_sources: Wei Ding, Anjuli Niyogi, Jordan A. Taylor & Jonathan S. Tsay. (2026). Hypothesis Testing Governs Strategic Motor Learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00428-4

article_title: Reading comprehension in L1 and L2 readers: neurocomputational mechanisms revealed through large language models
citation: Gu, C., Nastase, S. A., Zada, Z., & Li, P. (2025). Reading comprehension in L1 and L2 readers: neurocomputational mechanisms revealed through large language models. npj Science of Learning, 10:46. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00337-y
title: Shared computational principles between LLMs and human language processing, refined by individual differences
description: The article works within the framework that LLMs and human brains share computational principles for language processing, centered on the "principle of context-speciﬁc embedding", which "posits that preceding context is actively engaged in word comprehension during language processes". GPT-2 contextual embeddings serve as explicit linguistic features in encoding models whose alignment with brain responses indexes this shared processing. The study refines the framework by showing alignment depends on readers' linguistic, attentional, and language-experience characteristics.
requirements: LLM-based encoding models with contextual embeddings and naturalistic reading data with explicit comprehension measures
constraints: The study used only GPT-2; the authors note variations in model architecture may lead to distinct patterns of model-brain associations
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension of expository texts
examples: Encoding models built from the eighth layer of GPT-2 predicted brain responses recorded during self-paced reading of five expository texts with simultaneous fMRI and eye-tracking

article_title: The dynamics of student engagement in cooperative science learning: a multimodal approach
citation: Ido Davidesco, Yushuang Liu, Kim Chaloner, Emma Laurent, Gabriella A. Ali, Sarah C. Creider, Sean Hughes, Laura Noejovich, Henry Valk, Dana Bevilacqua, David Poeppel & Suzanne Dikker. (2026). The dynamics of student engagement in cooperative science learning: a multimodal approach. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00457-z
title: Engagement as a dynamic, multidimensional, multilevel construct that fluctuates moment by moment during cooperative learning
description: The article characterizes engagement as "a dynamic, multidimensional, and multi-level phenomenon that unfolds during real-world classroom collaboration." Building on the three-component view (behavioral, cognitive, affective) and the ICAP framework, it argues that ICAP's engagement modes "are not discrete or stable categories but ﬂuid states that learners continuously move between during learning." The framework motivates combining conversational, embodied, and neural indicators rather than relying on any single measure of engagement.
requirements: Multimodal measurement (video coding, microanalysis, and EEG) is needed because behavioral, conversational, and neural indicators do not always align.
constraints: The study was conducted at an independent school, and the authors state observed patterns may not generalize to public schools serving more diverse populations; EEG analyses collapsed across engagement states, possibly missing variability within states.
target_learners: High-school students working in small cooperative groups
target_learning_goals: Sustained engagement and participation in cooperative science learning tasks
examples: Nine groups of four high-school students collaboratively designed a model of a cell while EEG, video coding, and microanalysis were combined to track engagement states.

article_title: A systematic review of AI-driven intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) in K-12 education
citation: Létourneau, A., Martineau, M. D., Charland, P., Karran, J. A., Boasen, J. & Léger, P. M. (2025). A systematic review of AI-driven intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) in K-12 education. npj Science of Learning 10:29. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00320-7
title: Core components of effective ITS deployment: personalization, adaptivity, and immediate data-driven feedback
description: The review synthesizes the features that distinguish successful ITS deployments. It concludes that "personalization and adaptivity appear to be part of a core of ITS components, which influence their effectiveness": systems tailoring content to individual needs, prior knowledge and learning styles, and providing immediate, real-time data-driven feedback during tasks. Integrated, these components break complex concepts into individualized manageable steps and supply just-in-time hints, potentially improving engagement and retention. The synthesis draws on studies of Yixue, UZWEBMAT, Rimac and TECH8.
requirements: Immediate, real-time feedback capability
Tailoring of instructional content to individual student needs, prior knowledge, and learning styles
constraints: The review states effectiveness is maximized when features align with instructional theory under the right situational conditions (per Honebein and Reigeluth); benefits may partly reflect novelty in short interventions
target_learners: K-12 students in primary and secondary education
target_learning_goals: Subject-matter learning and performance, primarily in STEM subjects and language learning
examples: The review cites Yixue Squirrel AI and UZWEBMAT personalized learning paths and Rimac and TECH8 adaptive feedback mechanisms as instances of these core components

article_title: Electrocortical correlates of attention differentiate individual capacity in associative learning
citation: Raynal, E., Schipper, K., Brandner, C., Ruggeri, P. & Barral, J. (2024). Electrocortical correlates of attention differentiate individual capacity in associative learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00236-8
title: Trial-and-error shape–color associative learning task scored with Signal Detection Theory d'
description: A computerized associative learning task in which 12 abstract two-dimensional shapes had to be associated with one of four colors through trial-and-error feedback, with yes/no responses to target or lure color-shape pairings. Performance is scored with the Signal Detection Theory index d', which the authors chose because it "allows us to assess the impact of attentional processes on perceptual sensitivity" while minimizing response bias. The task was designed to avoid ceiling effects in non-clinical populations and permits SDT indices over classical behavioral measures.
requirements: Difficulty must be calibrated to the sample population; associations count as learned once responses within the last 48 trials exceed 95% correct
constraints: The task was demanding: 19 participants failed to reach the criterion within the 504-trial maximum
The task may exhibit a directional response bias; the authors suggest a counterbalanced response-button design could mitigate this
target_learning_goals: associative learning of shape–color pairings
examples: Participants completed a minimum of 360 trials with 1000 ms visual feedback (Correct, False, or Too slow) after each response

article_title: Electrocortical correlates of attention differentiate individual capacity in associative learning
citation: Raynal, E., Schipper, K., Brandner, C., Ruggeri, P. & Barral, J. (2024). Electrocortical correlates of attention differentiate individual capacity in associative learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00236-8
title: Attentional-efficiency account of individual differences in associative learning
description: The article's explanatory framework holds that individual differences in associative learning arise from differences in how efficiently learners engage attentional processes. Across three EEG signatures, the authors report that "better learners engage attentional processes more eﬃciently than weaker learners, making more resources available", with increased functional activity in early attentional regions (precuneus, BA 7) and decision-making regions (frontal BA 11). The framework links P1, P3b and occipital GFP effects into a proposed sequence from early attentional processing through object recognition to frontal attentional control.
requirements: EEG recording during an associative learning task, analyzed with topographic (TANCOVA), Global Field Power, and sLORETA source-estimation methods
constraints: Whether individual differences reflect differences in the timing of the same processes or in the nature of the processes themselves remains unresolved
Overlapping GFP and TANCOVA results make it challenging to pinpoint the exact sequence of neural events
Findings are from young adults on a visual associative task; generalizability to other populations, learning types and modalities is untested
target_learning_goals: associative learning performance variability
examples: The authors propose the frontoparietal network's role in top-down regulation of attention could help better learners discriminate targets from lures in the task

article_title: Interbrain neural correlates of self and other integration in joint statistical learning
citation: Zheng Zheng & Jun Wang. (2024). Interbrain neural correlates of self and other integration in joint statistical learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00280-4
title: Co-representation account of joint statistical learning
description: The article frames its findings within the co-representation account, in which people act so that "actions at another person's command are represented just as if they were at one's own command". On this view, participants implicitly represent their co-actor's task information even when no response is required, coupling self-task and other-task information, which produces the observed joint statistical learning effect. The authors argue this challenges the traditional view that task relevance is a prerequisite for statistical learning, since co-representation rendered the irrelevant co-actor's stimuli salient.
requirements: A joint action setup in which co-actors share a complementary task with pre-assigned targets so that each co-actor's task information can be co-represented
constraints: Observed with only female participants in female–female pairings, so the authors caution against generalizing to female–male or male–male pairings
target_learning_goals: implicit extraction of statistical regularities from sequences
self-other integration in joint action
examples: Dyads performed a complementary SRTT in which a fixed 12-step stimulus sequence was divided between co-actors, with all participants reporting they were unaware of any sequence or pattern

citation: Zheng Zheng & Jun Wang. (2024). Interbrain neural correlates of self and other integration in joint statistical learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00280-4
title: Joint statistical learning complementary SRTT hyperscanning paradigm with OSF data release
description: A modified serial reaction time task in which a fixed 12-location stimulus sequence is randomly divided and assigned to each co-actor for response. The experiment comprised eight blocks: Blocks 1 to 6 and 8 were "constructed from a ﬁxed sequence of locations, while the seventh block was constructed from an interference sequence". Dyads were assigned to a joint context (both respond to pre-assigned colours) or a baseline context (actor plus passive observer), with concurrent dual-EEG recording at 512 Hz. All behaviour and EEG data, and in-house scripts, are deposited on the Open Science Framework.
requirements: Dual-EEG recording system with synchronized amplifiers
Paired participants randomly assigned to joint or baseline context
constraints: Interference and main sequence assignment counterbalanced across dyads; only female participants recruited
