article_title: Cognitive training enhances growth mindset in children through plasticity of cortico-striatal circuits
citation: Lang Chen, Hyesang Chang, Jeremy Rudoler, Eydis Arnardottir, Yuan Zhang, Carlo de los Angeles and Vinod Menon. (2022). Cognitive training enhances growth mindset in children through plasticity of cortico-striatal circuits. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00146-7
title: Design cognitive training as mastery-oriented learning experiences to enhance both skills and growth mindset
description: The article's tutoring program deliberately promoted mastery-oriented rather than performance-oriented learning: "children were encouraged to learn and received positive feedback upon completion of activities, rather than being evaluated for their performance levels." Because this design was aligned with growth mindset's core concept, the training enhanced growth mindset alongside number knowledge. The authors suggest "a supportive learning environment can lead to simultaneous improvements in academic performance and growth mindset."

constraints: Effects demonstrated in a four-week one-on-one tutoring program for 7–10-year-old children focused on number knowledge
target_learners: early elementary school children ages 7–10, including children with math learning difficulties
target_learning_goals: foundational number knowledge (counting, comparing, ordering numbers)
growth mindset
examples: A one-on-one tutoring program (3 days/week, ~60 min/day, 4 weeks) using non-symbolic dot arrays and symbolic Arabic numerals, with positive feedback upon completion of activities

article_title: Cognitive training enhances growth mindset in children through plasticity of cortico-striatal circuits
citation: Lang Chen, Hyesang Chang, Jeremy Rudoler, Eydis Arnardottir, Yuan Zhang, Carlo de los Angeles and Vinod Menon. (2022). Cognitive training enhances growth mindset in children through plasticity of cortico-striatal circuits. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00146-7
title: Cortico-striatal plasticity account of growth-mindset malleability
description: The article proposes that plasticity of cortico-striatal circuitry is "a key neurobiological mechanism underlying cognitive-training-induced changes in growth mindset." In this account, the dorsal ACC supports cognitive control processes such as implementation and correction of action plans, while the striatum is implicated in value-based action selection; together they may "facilitate more effective goal-directed actions to support learning and growth mindset." The account also draws on the expected value of control framework, in which the dorsal ACC weighs effort costs against potential rewards when allocating cognitive resources.
requirements: Longitudinal training data with task-based fMRI at pre- and post-training visits to observe circuit plasticity
constraints: Neuroimaging evidence comes from the training group only; the smaller control neuroimaging sample limited specificity analysis, and the authors call for larger control samples and active control groups matched for expectation of improvement
target_learners: children ages 7–10 in early elementary school
target_learning_goals: growth mindset

citation: Gankin, K., Venkatesh, R., Khokhlovich, E., & Vyshedskiy, A. (2026). Receptive and expressive language phenotyping in over 62,000 autistic individuals. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00445-3

description: The article proposes classifying autistic language with two independent dimensions: receptive comprehension phenotypes (Command, Modifier, Syntactic) and expressive phenotypes (Nonspeaking, Single-Word, Single-Sentence, Multi-Sentence), rather than a single tripartite category. It argues the traditional system "oversimplifies the substantial heterogeneity in language abilities observed across autistic individuals" and misses rare profiles such as mute individuals with intact syntactic comprehension. The framework underpins the study's phenotyping of 62,414 individuals and its recommendations for individualized intervention.
requirements: Assessment must separately capture receptive comprehension items and expressive production items, as in the study's 15-item and 11-item caregiver questionnaires
constraints: The article states its findings are observational and descriptive and do not demonstrate that the proposed framework alters clinical decision-making

target_learning_goals: Accurate characterization of receptive and expressive language abilities to guide language therapy goal setting

citation: Wolfram, T. & Morris, D. (2023). Conventional twin studies overestimate the environmental differences between families relevant to educational attainment. npj Science of Learning 8, 24. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00173-y
title: Nuclear Twin and Family Design (NTFD) as a framework for relaxing Classical Twin Design assumptions
description: The NTFD extends the CTD by adding parents and non-twin siblings, allowing assortative mating to be modelled directly (via phenotypic assortment or social homogamy), non-additive genetic influences and shared environment to be estimated simultaneously, and the shared environment to be decomposed into sibling-shared (S), parental transmission (P), and twin-specific (T) components. The article states that "Including additional relative classes in the NTFD enables several of the assumptions in the CTD to be relaxed and more parameters to be estimated." It is used to quantify bias in CTD ACE estimates of educational attainment.

Assumptions about the source of spousal resemblance (phenotypic assortment vs social homogamy) that cannot all be estimated simultaneously
constraints: Only two of phenotypic transmission, non-additive genetic effects, and sibling-shared environments can be estimated at once, so baseline models fix one to zero
The biases reported for educational attainment will not necessarily generalise to other traits

target_learning_goals: decomposing genetic and environmental sources of variance in educational attainment
examples: Applied to 982 German TwinLife families, contrasting PA ASTE (A = 51%) with the CTD (A = 34%) on the same data

citation: Jinxi Wen, Wenjing Lyu, Jin Liu & Li Yang. (2025). Commensality and academic performance: measuring peer acceptance among college students. npj Science of Learning 10:69. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00357-8
title: Social capital account: commensality as a behavioral proxy for peer acceptance that grants bonding and bridging social capital
description: The article interprets its findings through social capital theory, proposing that "commensality serves as a behavioral proxy for peer acceptance, a social state that, in turn, grants students access to valuable social capital." Roommate commensality is aligned with bonding social capital offering emotional support through strong, trust-based ties, while commensality with more distant peers reflects bridging social capital that grants access to diverse information and perspectives. The framework is used to explain why the most physically distant peers showed the strongest associations.

constraints: The authors state the direction of causality cannot be determined from their data, so the account is interpretive rather than causally tested

target_learning_goals: academic performance (semester average scores, major ranking, failed subjects)
examples: The article proposes that interactions with more distant peers are intentional choices that bridge structural holes in the university's social network, sources of unique information and diverse perspectives

title: Universities should explore promoting environments that encourage peer commensality
description: The article suggests that "promoting environments that encourage peer commensality could be a valuable strategy for universities to explore." Because commensality values were positively correlated with academic outcomes across multiple metrics, campus dining arrangements and residential design that create opportunities for shared mealtimes — including with classmates beyond one's own dormitory — merit consideration. The authors frame this as exploratory, given that their findings are correlational rather than causal.
requirements: Institutional infrastructure the article names: a high-density residential campus, a centralized payment system, and a cultural norm of on-campus dining
constraints: The approach may not be directly transferable to non-residential or commuter models common in many Western countries; the authors note their findings are not causal due to potential self-selection bias
target_learning_goals: academic performance and peer integration
examples: The article's measurement used campus card swipe data: two students swiping in the same canteen within a 2-min interval during the same meal period counted as sharing a meal

description: The article proposes that visual working memory does not allocate resources directly to each individual item but may integrate items to some extent before storage, yielding a non-linear complexity–capacity relationship. It draws on resource theory and Gestalt grouping, and cites work suggesting both feature-based and object-based storage may exist in WM, with retention format linked to task demands. As the authors put it, "it might integrate these items to some extent before storage."

target_learning_goals: understanding the storage units and capacity limits of visual working memory

article_title: A dual-process model for cognitive training
citation: Julia Ericson and Torkel Klingberg. (2023). A dual-process model for cognitive training. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00161-2
title: Dual-process piecewise linear model of cognitive training dynamics
description: A quantitative model describing cognitive training as two simultaneous processes: a fast task-specific improvement and a slow, linear capacity improvement that transfers to untrained tasks. The learning trajectory is a piecewise linear function with two phases — phase 1 includes both task-specific and capacity improvement, phase 2 only capacity improvement — fitted to individual daily performance data via a hidden Markov model whose hidden state is the current phase, with parameters optimized by expectation maximization. The article states "training is not only task speci ﬁc or transferable but a combination of the two" and that the models "provide methods for quantifying and separating these processes".
requirements: Daily performance data from the trained task across the training period, plus repeated transfer test sessions to validate the capacity factor
Individual-level (not group-averaged) training curves, since the task-specific phase is identified only at the individual level
constraints: The transition day was constrained by CFA results to be at most day 10, which affected 4.5% of the population
A longer training period could potentially yield more than two phases
The model assumes the probability of returning from phase 2 to phase 1 is zero and that phase 1 is always the starting phase
target_learners: Children ages 9 to 11 undergoing adaptive working memory training
target_learning_goals: Working memory capacity and transfer to visuospatial, verbal working memory, and arithmetic tasks
examples: Fitted to daily Grid performance of each of the 1300 children, with the median transition day at 3.05 and parameters optimized by expectation maximization

citation: Tae Lee Lee, Hanall Lee and Nyeonju Kang. (2023). A meta-analysis showing improved cognitive performance in healthy young adults with transcranial alternating current stimulation. npj Science of Learning 8:1. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00152-9
title: Neural synchronization and LTP-plasticity account for online and offline tACS cognitive benefits
description: The article proposes that tACS delivers "weak sinusoidal oscillating electrical currents" that temporarily synchronize neural firing timing with endogenous brain oscillations. Online-tACS is described as facilitating "higher entrainment between ongoing neural oscillation and external electrical oscillations," while offline-tACS "may cause longer lasting after-effects" related to LTP-type synaptic plasticity. This mechanism account explains why timing of stimulation matters and why performance (accuracy) rather than speed improves.

constraints: The account is the authors' interpretation; the meta-analysis did not directly test entrainment or LTP mechanisms

examples: In the meta-analysis, both online- and offline-tACS significantly improved cognitive performance, which the authors interpret as supporting the synchronization or LTP proposition

title: Meta-analytic evidence base of 56 tACS studies (93 performance and 32 reaction time comparisons)
description: The evidence base is a systematically assembled corpus: after searching PubMed, Web of Science, and other resources and removing duplicates and irrelevant articles, "the remaining 56 studies that examined potential effects of tACS on cognitive functions" qualified. These included 1797 healthy young adults (mean age range 18.0–33.0 years), 9 randomized controlled trials and 46 crossover designs, yielding 93 cognitive-performance and 32 reaction-time comparisons. Protocol parameters ranged from 0.7–3 mA intensity and 2 s–48 min session durations.

constraints: Cochrane risk-of-bias assessment flagged randomization, deviations from intended interventions, and outcome measurement; 41 of 56 studies did not mention blinding of experimenters or assessors

article_title: Probing boundary conditions of Productive Failure and analyzing the role of young students’ collaboration
citation: Claudia Mazziotti, Nikol Rummel, Anne Deiglmayr and Katharina Loibl. (2019). Probing boundary conditions of Productive Failure and analyzing the role of young students' collaboration. npj Science of Learning 4:2. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0041-5
title: ICAP framework as a coding lens for collaborative engagement in Productive Failure
description: The article uses the Interactive–Constructive–Active–Passive (ICAP) framework by Chi and colleagues as a tool for aligning students' overt learning activities with underlying cognitive processes during collaborative problem solving. It "can serve as a tool for aligning different kinds of students' overt learning activities" — from passively listening to interactively co-constructing solution ideas — "to underlying cognitive processes". The framework proposes a hierarchy (I > C > A > P) in which higher engagement levels are more conducive to learning. The authors coded 5074 utterances from PF-Coll dyads using six categories derived from ICAP and broader collaborative-learning literature.
requirements: Coding requires transcripts of recorded dialogs and a coding scheme differentiating interactive, constructive, active, coordinative, back channeling, and off-task utterances
constraints: The authors found no clear superiority of interactive processes in their study, and note the ICAP categories may be too broad to capture nuances of collaborative learning
target_learners: elementary school students working in dyads
target_learning_goals: conceptual knowledge of fraction equivalence
collaborative problem-solving discourse quality
examples: Coders classified students' verbal utterances from audiotaped dyad dialogs, using a conservative approach choosing the lower code in cases of ambiguity (ICC absolute = 0.92)

article_title: Multi-stakeholder perspective on responsible artificial intelligence and acceptability in education
citation: Alexander John Karran, Patrick Charland, Joé Trempe-Martineau, Ana Ortiz de Guinea Lopez de Arana, Anne-Marie Lesage, Sylvain Sénécal & Pierre-Majorique Léger. (2025). Multi-stakeholder perspective on responsible artificial intelligence and acceptability in education. npj Science of Learning 10:44. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00333-2
title: Multi-stakeholder confidence-trust framework for AI acceptability in education
description: The article proposes that acceptance of AI in education hinges on a balance of agency, confidence, and trust underpinned by explainability and transparency. Confidence and trust are described as "inextricably linked, representing a feedback loop wherein conﬁdence builds towards trust and trust instils conﬁdence". Trust is an umbrella construct relying on transparency of AI processes, alignment with educational ethics, explainability, privacy protection, and evidence of effectiveness. The study operationalises this framework through vignette-manipulated variables (agency, transparency, explainability, privacy) and mediators (global utility, individual usefulness, justice, confidence, risk) predicting intention to use.
requirements: AI systems must exhibit reliability, assessment accuracy, and transparent and explainable decision-making, requiring robust design, testing, and ongoing monitoring
constraints: The framework was tested with vignette methodology on hypothetical AI applications not yet widely deployed; school director data were excluded from mediation analysis due to small sample size
target_learning_goals: Responsible and ethical deployment of AI in education
Stakeholder acceptance and intention to use educational AI applications
examples: Four ecologically valid vignette scenarios (Correct-AI, Answer-AI, Tutor-AI, Emotion-AI) in a 2 x 2 x 2 × 2 counterbalanced design with manipulation checks

description: The principle holds that the level of agency granted to educational AI applications must be carefully adjusted because "increased AI autonomy consistently correlates with diminished perceptions of justice, conﬁdence, and utility among stakeholders". AI applications must have sufficient agency to augment educational endeavours without superseding critical human oversight and ethical accountability. The article grounds this in mediation results across stakeholder groups showing negative indirect effects of agency on intention to use.

target_learning_goals: Responsible AI deployment in education
Preserving student agency and critical thinking

description: The article proposes that because a child's PGS is measured at the individual level rather than the family level, it "has added value to SES in predicting which children are at risk for lower EA". Children at double risk, through family background and genetic predisposition, could be targeted by policies such as extra educational programs to reduce inequality in educational outcomes.

The sample over-represented children from high SES backgrounds relative to the Dutch population

article_title: CGRP inhibition in the PBN shifts defensive strategy from freezing to active avoidance in a platform-based active avoidance paradigm
citation: Hanny Hayeon Lee, Eul Han & Yong Sang Jo. (2026). CGRP inhibition in the PBN shifts defensive strategy from freezing to active avoidance in a platform-based active avoidance paradigm. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00453-3
title: Platform-based active avoidance (PBA) paradigm
description: The PBA paradigm is an operant defensive-learning task in which an auditory tone CS predicts a footshock US and mice avoid shock by moving onto a central platform safe zone within the first 5 s of CS onset. The authors developed it because it "eliminates appetitive reinforcement", letting animals learn "to avoid shock by moving onto a permanently available platform without any competing reward demands", thereby isolating threat-driven avoidance and defensive response selection from food-motivation confounds.
requirements: A permanent safe zone (8 × 8 cm platform) continuously available in the operant chamber; an auditory CS (12 kHz, 50 dB) coterminating with a footshock US; trial-by-trial scoring of platform entry within the first 5 s of CS onset by an experimenter blind to shock intensity and group.
constraints: Continuous platform availability produces stay behaviour (conditioning stay rate: 46%; retention test stay rate: 15%), so passive occupancy must be separated from cue-evoked entries when interpreting avoidance learning.
target_learners: mice (CalcaCre/+ and C57BL/6J, approximately 3-6 months old)
target_learning_goals: cue-evoked active avoidance (stimulus-response associative learning)
defensive response selection between passive and active strategies
examples: Independent cohorts were conditioned at 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4 or 0.5 mA across four days alternating afternoon conditioning sessions (25 CS-US trials) with next-day CS-only retention tests (4 CS presentations).
key_sources: Hanny Hayeon Lee, Eul Han & Yong Sang Jo. (2026). CGRP inhibition in the PBN shifts defensive strategy from freezing to active avoidance in a platform-based active avoidance paradigm. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00453-3

article_title: CGRP inhibition in the PBN shifts defensive strategy from freezing to active avoidance in a platform-based active avoidance paradigm
citation: Hanny Hayeon Lee, Eul Han & Yong Sang Jo. (2026). CGRP inhibition in the PBN shifts defensive strategy from freezing to active avoidance in a platform-based active avoidance paradigm. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00453-3
title: CGRP neurons bias defensive response selection toward passive freezing under high threat rather than driving associative avoidance learning
description: The article proposes that parabrachial CGRP neurons regulate defensive behavioural output rather than serving as the obligatory aversive-US pathway for associative learning: in operant active avoidance, "CGRP signalling contributes les s to the associative processes underlying S-R learning than to t he regulation of defensive beha- vioural output though downstream CeA-dependent circuits." Silencing CGRP reduced freezing and nocifensive reactivity and enabled avoidance under high threat, shifting behavioural output from passive freezing toward active avoidance.
requirements: The interpretation rests on the PBA paradigm isolating threat-driven avoidance without appetitive reinforcement, so that performance changes reflect defensive response selection rather than reward-related processes.
constraints: TetTox silencing remained in effect throughout both conditioning and retention testing, preventing clear attribution of the behavioural effects to acquisition, retention, or expression of active avoidance.
The account is specific to operant active avoidance and differs from CGRP's established role in supporting associative learning in Pavlovian fear conditioning.
target_learning_goals: defensive response selection between passive freezing and active avoidance
operant avoidance learning under varying threat intensity

article_title: Disentangling sensory precision and prior expectation of change in autism during tactile discrimination
citation: Sapey-Triomphe, L.-A., Sanchez, G., Hénaff, M.-A., Sonié, S., Schmitz, C., & Mattout, J. (2023). Disentangling sensory precision and prior expectation of change in autism during tactile discrimination. npj Science of Learning, 8:54. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00207-5
title: Refined predictive-coding account of ASD: atypical perceptual learning dynamics rather than a static prior/sensory imbalance
description: The article proposes that ASD is better characterized by the dynamic adjustment of precision weights to context than by a static imbalance between prior and sensory precision. It defines the sensory precision πu, the precision ratio r = πu/πx, and a response bias parameter b in a dynamic perceptual decision-making model, and argues that "these results point to atypical perceptual learning rather than altered perceptual inference per se". The account subsumes the observed no, normal, or slower adaptation depending on context.
requirements: Combining behavioral tasks sensitive to sensory precision and the precision ratio with computational modeling of trial-to-trial responses
constraints: Findings concern autistic adults without intellectual disability in low-level tactile frequency discrimination tasks; the authors call for further empirical and computational studies to refine predictive coding theories
target_learning_goals: implicit perceptual learning of stimulus statistics
adjustment of precision weights to context

article_title: Social learning through prediction error in the brain
citation: Jessica Joiner, Matthew Piva, Courtney Turrin and Steve W. C. Chang. (2017). Social learning through prediction error in the brain. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0009-2
title: Reinforcement learning via reward prediction error as a framework for social learning
description: The review's organizing framework is reinforcement learning, in which an agent compares expected reward to actual reward and uses the discrepancy — the reward prediction error — to update value functions and policy. It argues that "Prediction-based computational principles in the brain may be strikingly conserved between self-referenced and other-referenced information", so that other-referenced (vicarious) prediction errors can mediate social learning under the same computational principles as self-referenced learning.
requirements: A reward signal, a value function, and a policy through which the agent computes expected value and updates behavior
constraints: Vicarious reinforcement in an RL framework would have to be model-based, since it is unclear how a model-free RL system could learn about another agent without modeling its potential thoughts and future actions
target_learners: humans and nonhuman animals learning from observation
target_learning_goals: learning about others' actions and reward outcomes through observation
examples: Temporal difference learning applied to observational learning of another person's stimulus-reward contingencies in the modified Q-learning studies discussed
key_sources: Jessica Joiner, Matthew Piva, Courtney Turrin and Steve W. C. Chang. (2017). Social learning through prediction error in the brain. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0009-2

citation: Jessica Joiner, Matthew Piva, Courtney Turrin and Steve W. C. Chang. (2017). Social learning through prediction error in the brain. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0009-2
title: Two developmental accounts of representing others: theory-theory and simulation theory
description: The review presents two historically competing developmental accounts of how we represent others. In theory-theory, "like small scientists testing causal relations, children are constantly gathering data from the world and testing the predictions they make using the collected data"; in simulation theory, we understand others egocentrically by using the machinery of our own mental processes and projecting it onto others' behaviors. The review notes these accounts predict different neural implementations (allocentric vs egocentric mechanisms).
requirements: A proposal for how other-referenced information is represented in the brain to distinguish the two accounts empirically
constraints: The review states its current understanding of how the brain implements these processes is not complete
target_learners: children and nonhuman animals developing representations of others
target_learning_goals: understanding and modeling other individuals' internal states
key_sources: Jessica Joiner, Matthew Piva, Courtney Turrin and Steve W. C. Chang. (2017). Social learning through prediction error in the brain. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0009-2

title: Table 1: taxonomy of prediction-error types and correlated brain areas
description: The review provides a representative table mapping prediction-error types to brain areas from primate electrophysiology or human neuroimaging, organized along an egocentric/allocentric axis. Egocentric rows cover self action, self reward outcome, self reward value, and self reward timing errors (e.g., VTA, SN, striatum, OFC); allocentric rows cover other action, other reward outcome, and other motivation errors (e.g., ACCg, dmPFC, dlPFC, TPJ, MTG, STS). It is explicitly "not a comprehensive list but rather a list to highlight the presence of predictive coding in the brain".
requirements: Evidence from primate electrophysiology or human neuroimaging to assign an area to a prediction-error type
constraints: Not comprehensive; distributions of areas are naturally constrained by the amount of research examining different types of prediction errors

article_title: An fMRI study of scientists with a Ph.D. in physics confronted with naive ideas in science
citation: Geneviève Allaire-Duquette, Lorie-Marlène Brault Foisy, Patrice Potvin, Martin Riopel, Marilyne Larose, Steve Masson. (2021). An fMRI study of scientists with a Ph.D. in physics confronted with naive ideas in science. npj Science of Learning 6:11. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00091-x
title: Coordination account of conceptual change: naive and scientific ideas coexist and must be coordinated rather than replaced
description: This account, proposed in the article's discussion, holds that learning science does not erase naive ideas: "Conceptual change might instead yield multiple ideas of each given natural phenomena, including scienti ﬁc and naive ideas, which then have to be coordinated to demonstrate appropriate conceptual understanding." Expert performance then depends on inhibitory control to suppress the dominant naive idea when the context demands a scientific judgment, framed as "a dynamic vigilance, allowing active control of thoughts when the context requires for it". The fMRI evidence shows frontal inhibitory-control activations for incongruent statements in both physics and biology among Ph.D. physicists.
requirements: Learners must have both naive and scientific ideas coexisting in memory for coordination-based conceptual change to apply
constraints: The article states its interpretation relies on reverse inference from brain activity to mental processes and recommends the findings be treated with considerable caution
target_learning_goals: conceptual change in science
overcoming naive ideas and misconceptions
examples: Physicists with a Ph.D. judging incongruent statements recruited MFG and IFG associated with inhibitory control, while congruent statements showed more focal posterior activations consistent with automatic processing

title: Pro audito computer-based speechreading training (lippenlesen.ch)

The training "contains eight lessons structured in the same way": an introductory video, flashcards, and exercises, covering vowel and consonant mouth forms, contextual information, numbers and names, and speech perception in noise. Participants trained 20 minutes on each of five days per week over three weeks, with log files recording training time.

article_title: Impact of impulsivity on the relationship of the brain structures with school performance
citation: Youngwoo Bryan Yoon & Wi Hoon Jung. (2025). Impact of impulsivity on the relationship of the brain structures with school performance. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00344-z
title: Opposing caudate and cerebellar pathways to academic performance via impulsivity and self-regulation
description: The article proposes an explanatory account in which two brain structures influence school performance through distinct, opposing routes tied to impulsivity. A larger caudate nucleus volume is associated with "heightened sensitivity to immediate rewards, making students more susceptible to distractions and less able to defer gratification for long-term academic goals", raising impulsivity and lowering GPA. A larger cerebellum supports executive functions such as working memory and attention through extensive prefrontal connections, lowering impulsivity and supporting better GPA. Impulsivity serves as the key mediator connecting structural differences to academic outcomes.
requirements: Structural differences in the caudate and cerebellum are assumed to translate to functional differences in self-regulation and decision-making, an assumption the article flags as not directly tested.
constraints: The account rests on cross-sectional correlational data; causal relationships and temporal precedence were not established.
Interpretation assumes structure-function correspondence, which the article notes is complex and not always direct.
target_learning_goals: understanding neurobiological influences on academic achievement
self-regulation
impulse control
examples: The mediation analyses showed left cerebellar GMV exerting a positive indirect effect on GPA through lower impulsivity, and right caudate GMV a negative indirect effect through higher impulsivity.

citation: Robert Fairlie and Prashant Loyalka. (2020). Schooling and Covid-19: lessons from recent research on EdTech. npj Science of Learning 5:13. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00072-6
title: Balance remote learning by intermingling work on electronic devices with traditional materials to keep students engaged
description: The article recommends a balanced approach to remote learning in which schoolchildren intermingle work on electronic devices and work with traditional materials, which the authors suggest "might be optimal". The stated purpose is to break up continuous device time, keep students engaged throughout the day, and avoid problems associated with removing the structure of classroom schedules.
requirements: Remote learning arrangements must combine work on electronic devices with work using traditional materials such as workbooks, books, at-home experiments, and art projects.
constraints: The authors caution about extrapolating from the limited technology substitution shown in their experiments to full-scale substitution during the pandemic; the balanced approach is offered as an example lesson rather than a tested design in the article.
target_learners: primary school students (ages 9–13) in remote instruction
target_learning_goals: maintaining engagement and motivation in academic subject material during remote learning
examples: Schools could mail workbooks to students or recommend that students print out exercises to break up continuous time on devices; activities such as reading books, running at-home experiments, and art projects can break up extensive technology use.

article_title: The effects of declarative learning on early and late motor skill learning
citation: Mohan W. Gupta and Timothy C. Rickard. (2025). The Effects of Declarative Learning on Early and Late Motor Skill Learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00386-3
title: Three-hypothesis framework for declarative interference with motor learning: consolidation disruption, breakdown of inhibition, and resource competition
description: The article organizes competing mechanistic accounts of why an interleaved declarative task might impair motor performance into three named hypotheses. The consolidation-disruption hypothesis holds that "a declarative task commandeers hippocampal–neocortical micro-consolidation during any break period"; the breakdown-of-inhibition hypothesis ties impairment to failed dissipation of reactive inhibition via somatosensory surround inhibition; and the resource-competition hypothesis posits a shared limited cognitive resource with declarative-linked fast learning, predicting impairment only early in training. The experiments adjudicate among them.
requirements: Distinguishing the hypotheses requires varying when the intervening declarative task occurs during training (late versus early) and the amount of reactive inhibition accrued
constraints: The article limits its conclusions to the finger-tapping task, noting the FTT is simple and learned quickly
target_learners: adult undergraduate students learning motor sequences
target_learning_goals: motor sequence skill acquisition and its interaction with declarative memory
examples: Experiment 1 and 2 placed the 4- and 14-minute intervening tasks after substantial training; Experiment 3 placed it after the first three trials to target the fast declarative-linked process

citation: Nation, K. (2017). Nurturing a lexical legacy: reading experience is critical for the development of word reading skill. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0004-7
title: The lexical legacy hypothesis: diverse, meaningful reading experiences build word-specific lexical knowledge measurable in word reading
description: The lexical legacy hypothesis holds that reading provides exposure to words in many different contexts, episodes and experiences which, over time, sum to a rich and nuanced database about each word's lexical history within an individual's experience. The article states that skilled word reading is, in part, a consequence of "experiencing words in diverse and meaningful language environments during reading experience", and that these encounters produce local variation at the word level that is measurable during word reading behaviour even in skilled adults.

constraints: The article describes the hypothesis as speculative and under-specified, with mechanisms that bring about change not yet detailed

lexical quality and word knowledge

title: The lexical quality hypothesis: word representations specify spelling, sound and meaning, and quality drives processing
description: Perfetti's lexical quality hypothesis, as presented in the article, defines lexical quality as the extent to which a word's mental representation specifies its spelling, sound and meaning. High quality representations contain "tightly bound orthographic, phonological and semantic constituents" that support efficient word identification and free cognitive resources for comprehension. The article uses it as the processing framework the lexical legacy hypothesis feeds: lexical quality is both cause and consequence of reading skill differences.

article_title: Foil type modulates developmental changes in statistical learning across childhood to adulthood
citation: Liang, F., Zhu, Y., Li, R. & Fu, Q. (2026). Foil Type Modulates Developmental Changes in Statistical Learning Across Childhood to Adulthood. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00434-6
title: Implicit-explicit competitive interaction account of developmental change in statistical learning
description: The article interprets its crossover pattern through the competitive neurocognitive networks framework, which "proposes that the interactions between implicit and explicit systems evolve across development." Implicit extraction of statistical regularities is described as most robust prior to age 12, supporting efficient discrimination of familiarized words from nonword foils, while adults' advantage on partword foils "likely involves additional involvement of explicit processes." Children may initially acquire a "fuzzy" representation of frequent patterns, with the ability to precisely delineate boundaries and suppress interference from overlapping partword foils continuing to mature into adulthood.
requirements: A 2AFC design that includes both nonword foils and partword foils, since the dissociation would be obscured if foil types were collapsed
constraints: The account is the authors' interpretation of a behavioral crossover pattern, not a directly tested mechanism; the study was behavioral-only and did not include adolescents
target_learning_goals: auditory statistical learning of word boundaries in continuous speech
examples: Grade 5 children outperformed younger children only on nonword foils, whereas adults selectively outperformed Grade 5 children on partword foils, the pattern the framework is invoked to explain
key_sources: Liang, F., Zhu, Y., Li, R. & Fu, Q. (2026). Foil Type Modulates Developmental Changes in Statistical Learning Across Childhood to Adulthood. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00434-6

article_title: Foil type modulates developmental changes in statistical learning across childhood to adulthood
citation: Liang, F., Zhu, Y., Li, R. & Fu, Q. (2026). Foil Type Modulates Developmental Changes in Statistical Learning Across Childhood to Adulthood. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00434-6
title: Include both nonword and partword foils when measuring developmental change in statistical learning
description: The article's own methodological lesson is that foil selection is critical when detecting age-related effects in statistical learning. Because the developmental pattern reversed across foil types — improvement within childhood for nonword foils but an adult advantage for partword foils — the authors state that "this crossover pattern reveals a developmental dissociation that would be obscured if foil types were collapsed." Assessments or studies that collapse foil types or use only one foil type risk missing genuine developmental change.
requirements: Use both nonword foils and partword foils in 2AFC recognition tests of statistical learning
constraints: Demonstrated for auditory statistical learning of trisyllabic nonsense words after brief exposure; the article notes broad child age ranges can also obscure age-related effects
target_learning_goals: auditory statistical learning and word segmentation
examples: In the study, partword foil accuracy was stable within childhood while nonword foil accuracy improved, and the reverse contrast appeared from late childhood to adulthood; collapsing foil types would have hidden both effects

article_title: Common health conditions in childhood and adolescence, school absence, and educational attainment: Mendelian randomization study
citation: Hughes, A., Wade, K. H., Dickson, M., Rice, F., Davies, A., Davies, N. M. & Howe, L. D. (2021). Common health conditions in childhood and adolescence, school absence, and educational attainment: Mendelian randomization study. npj Science of Learning 6:1. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00080-6
title: Mendelian randomization with polygenic scores for triangulating causal effects of health on educational outcomes
description: The article applies genetic causal inference to educational outcomes. Polygenic scores (PGSs) combine multiple SNPs associated with a condition into "a PGS representing genetic liability for a condition", improving statistical power relative to single SNPs. "In one-sample Mendelian randomization, causal influence of an exposure is estimated using the PGS as an instrumental variable for the exposure in a two-stage least-squares model." Two-sample MR instead compares SNP associations with exposure and outcome across independent GWAS samples. The article stresses triangulation across phenotypic, one-sample and two-sample MR approaches.
requirements: A polygenic score sufficiently strong to serve as an instrument (the article used first-stage F-statistics > 10 and found only the BMI PGS qualified)
constraints: Genetic results are conditional on MR assumptions; the article reports pleiotropy evidence for BMI–absenteeism and possible family-level (parental-genotype, assortative-mating) bias
Low PGS predictive power (<1% variance for ADHD, migraine, asthma; <0.1% for ASD, depression) limited genetic methods for those conditions, so nulls there should not be read as evidence of no effect
target_learners: school-age children and adolescents in an English birth cohort
target_learning_goals: educational attainment at age 16 (GCSE) and school attendance
examples: Only the BMI PGS passed instrument-strength tests in ALSPAC, so IV estimates were reported only for BMI; the study triangulated phenotypic, one-sample and two-sample MR results for the same conditions.

article_title: Morphology in children’s books, and what it means for learning
citation: Korochkina, M. & Rastle, K. (2025). Morphology in children's books, and what it means for learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00313-6
title: Print-exposure account of derivational affix learning through naturalistic reading of children's books
description: This theoretical account describes how children may learn derivational affix morphemes through real-life reading experience rather than explicit instruction. The article offers "the first concrete description of how readers may learn afﬁx morphemes through real-life text input", grounded in quantification of the CYP-LEX corpus. The account "considers the realities of morpheme presentation in natural language", including the low number of distinct words carrying each affix, the need for specialised linguistic knowledge to identify many morphemes, and misleading spelling patterns such as pseudo-affixed words.
requirements: Children must encounter affixes with a large number of distinct stems and predictable meaning shifts for learning without instruction to be feasible, as the article states as a prerequisite for affix learning in the absence of instruction.
constraints: The account is largely confined to English and its writing system; the article states its conclusions about what children may learn through reading experience are largely confined to English.
target_learners: British children aged 7–16 reading for pleasure
target_learning_goals: Acquisition of derivational morpheme knowledge supporting vocabulary growth and rapid word recognition
examples: The authors quantified type frequency, token frequency, cross-book distribution, and orthographic detectability of 48 common affixes in 1200 popular children's books to characterise the learning input.
key_sources: Korochkina, M. & Rastle, K. (2025). Morphology in children's books, and what it means for learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00313-6

article_title: Evidence for a competitive relationship between executive functions and statistical learning
citation: Pedraza, F., Farkas, B. C., Vékony, T., Haesebaert, F., Phelipon, R., Mihalecz, I., Janacsek, K., Anders, R., Tillmann, B., Plancher, G. & Németh, D. (2024). Evidence for a competitive relationship between executive functions and statistical learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00243-9
title: PFC-mediated competition model of declarative-procedural interactions: prefrontal executive functions arbitrate against model-free statistical learning
description: The article interprets its results within the interactive memory systems framework, in which learning relies on either the basal ganglia-based procedural system or the medial temporal lobe-based declarative system, with "Larger reliance on one implies a smaller reliance on the other". It focuses on indirect cross-inhibition via prefrontal control processes, proposing that procedural, model-free learning is the 'default' learner overridden by PFC control involvement. The observed negative EF–SL correlations are attributed to "the suppression of model-free, procedural learning by prefrontal EF".
requirements: Requires the assumption that implicit statistical learning taps the procedural, model-free system and that executive functions reflect prefrontal control
constraints: The article states the alternative explanation that both working memory and fluency relate to long-term memory access "needs to be validated through studies that examine long-term memory access, cognitive control, and predictive processes... within a single experimental design"
The EF battery was incomplete: for set shifting and inhibition only the BCST and GNG tasks were available
target_learning_goals: implicit statistical learning
probabilistic pattern extraction
examples: The two experiments operationalized competition as negative correlations between ASRT learning scores and EF factor scores extracted by maximum-likelihood exploratory factor analysis

article_title: Body-part specificity for learning of multiple prior distributions in human coincidence timing
citation: Yoshiki Matsumura, Neil W. Roach, James Heron & Makoto Miyazaki. (2024). Body-part specificity for learning of multiple prior distributions in human coincidence timing. npj Science of Learning 9:34. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00241-x
title: Bayesian estimation model with scalar variability for coincidence timing
description: The article adopts a Bayesian estimation account in which the brain learns the statistical distribution of target intervals and integrates it with noisy sensory input, with sensory variability scaling with the interval (scalar variability). This yields a nonlinear TR×TS function (Eq. 4) whose curves diverge between priors only when two independent priors are learned. The authors state that "the /C22TR × TS functions exhibit curves with gentler gradients in the longerTS" because bias toward the prior mean strengthens at longer intervals. Preliminary Experiments I and II verified the predictions.
requirements: Prior distributions imposed across task sessions; measurement of response time intervals across many trials to fit the model curves
constraints: Priors were assumed Gaussian in the model although uniform distributions were used experimentally; the model focuses on prior means, leaving acquired variability (σprior) and Weber fraction unspecified by the fitted curves
target_learners: healthy adult participants performing sensorimotor timing tasks
target_learning_goals: learning statistical distributions (priors) of time intervals for sensorimotor prediction
examples: Preliminary Experiment I presented a single wide prior combining the short and long distributions and confirmed the nonlinear model's predictions

article_title: Body-part specificity for learning of multiple prior distributions in human coincidence timing
citation: Yoshiki Matsumura, Neil W. Roach, James Heron & Makoto Miyazaki. (2024). Body-part specificity for learning of multiple prior distributions in human coincidence timing. npj Science of Learning 9:34. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00241-x
title: Somatotopic organisation hypothesis for body-part specific learning of multiple priors
description: The article proposes that body-part specific learning of temporal priors is organised somatotopically, drawing on the supplementary motor area (SMA), which shows both time-interval tuning, action selectivity, and somatotopic body-part mapping. The authors infer that "when the neural representations of the body parts in the SMA are identical and close, the assigned priorsare generalised. However, when those in the SMA are distant, the assigned priors are independently acquired." The cerebellum and basal ganglia, which also show somatotopy and timing-related activity, are offered as complementary possible neural bases.
requirements: Convergent neuroimaging or neurophysiological evidence to identify the actual neural bases
constraints: The neural-basis discussion is acknowledged by the authors as merely speculative; whether body-part specificity operates in nontemporal tasks remains unclear
target_learners: healthy adult participants performing sensorimotor timing tasks
target_learning_goals: concurrent learning of multiple statistical priors tied to different motor effectors
examples: Experiment 4 and 5 (hand vs foot) showed concurrent learning from the earliest trial bin, whereas adjacent-finger assignment required more trials

article_title: Persistent association between family socioeconomic status and primary school performance in Britain over 95 years
citation: Sophie von Stumm, Sophie Nicole Cave and Paul Wakeling. (2022). Persistent association between family socioeconomic status and primary school performance in Britain over 95 years. npj Science of Learning (2022) 7:4. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00120-3
title: Equity versus equality in education as competing policy orientations
description: The article distinguishes two policy orientations: equality of education means "all children enjoy the same learning opportunities" — the same curricula, pace and methods regardless of ability — whereas "equity in education aims at reducing children’s differences in educational outcomes, by distributing education resources in ways that level the playing field for all children". The authors argue Britain's persistent SES–performance association reflects prioritising equality of opportunity over equity, and recommend redistributing resources toward children's differential learning needs.
requirements: Resource redistribution must be targeted at children with the greatest learning needs, for example by allocating more teaching staff to children at risk of academic failure and behavioural misconduct
constraints: The article notes equity prescribes inequality in educational opportunity, and that well-prepared parents who tend to occupy positions of power may object to redistribution; previous policies that maximised the best students' achievement, such as ability streaming or tracking, disadvantaged low-SES subgroups
target_learners: primary school children from low SES families
primary school children at risk of academic failure
target_learning_goals: reducing SES-related differences in primary school learning outcomes
weakening the intergenerational transmission of social and economic inequality
examples: The authors point to awarding grants to schools that enroll pupils from impoverished family homes to fund extra educational resources as an example of redistribution efforts

citation: Hughes, A. M., Torvik, F. A., van Bergen, E., Hannigan, L. J., Corfield, E. C., Andreassen, O. A., Ystrom, E., Ask, H., Davey Smith, G., Davies, N. M. & Havdahl, A. (2024). Parental education and children’s depression, anxiety, and ADHD traits, a within-family study in MoBa. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00260-8
title: Genetic nurture (dynastic effects) versus direct genetic transmission as competing accounts of intergenerational associations
description: The article's organizing framework distinguishes genetic nurture — indirect effects of parents' genotypes on children via environmental pathways — from direct genetic transmission of variants from parents to children. It operationalizes this with within-family Mendelian randomization, which instruments parental education with polygenic indexes and adjusts for the child's own genotype to block bias from inherited variants. The article states: "their impact on children’s outcomes can be considered a case of genetic nurture, or dynastic effects: an indirect effect of parents’or other relatives’genotype on children’s traits via environmental pathways".
requirements: Requires genetic data on large numbers of mothers, fathers, and children to separate maternal from paternal effects, which few studies have
constraints: Within-family MR estimates were imprecise in this sample; PGI-based approaches capture only genetic liability associated with specific SNPs, unlike variance-decomposition designs
target_learning_goals: understanding environmental versus genetic origins of social gradients in children's emotional and behavioural outcomes
examples: Applied to 40,879 MoBa trios to estimate conditional effects of maternal and paternal educational attainment on children's age-8 traits

article_title: States of epistemic curiosity interfere with memory for incidental scholastic facts
citation: Keller, N. E., Salvi, C., Leiker, E. K., Gruber, M. J. & Dunsmoor, J. E. (2024). States of epistemic curiosity interfere with memory for incidental scholastic facts. npj Science of Learning 9:22. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00234-w
title: Arousal-biased competition account of curiosity's overshadowing of nearby scholastic information
description: The article interprets its findings through an arousal-biased competition model of memory allocation, in which the goal-state to resolve uncertainty about a high-curiosity trivia question competes with and overshadows encoding of other material presented close in time. The authors write that "arousal will enhance memory when there is need for selective attention toward the target information", and that arousal "can narrow the focus of attention toward stimuli that are irrelevant to the source of arousal". Because the trivia and scholastic material share a similar epistemic nature, bottom-up pop-out of incidental items may be blunted, reversing the spillover benefit seen for simple visual stimuli.
requirements: A phasic high-curiosity state elicited by specific target material, and unrelated material presented in close temporal proximity to it
constraints: The article applies the account to trial-by-trial, second-scale phasic curiosity states, not to sustained tonic curiosity
The overlap between arousal generally and curiosity specifically is, per the authors, an open question meriting further investigation
target_learning_goals: retention of complex scholastic facts (science, history, English) presented near curiosity-eliciting material
examples: The three task versions presented the scholastic fact before or after the trivia answer, and in all versions high-curiosity pairing impaired scholastic memory

citation: Gabriel, F., Kennedy, J.P., Marrone, R. & Leonard, S. (2025). Pragmatic AI in education and its role in mathematics learning and teaching. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00315-4
title: Control-Value Theory account of mathematics anxiety in learning mathematics
description: The article adopts the Control-Value Theory of Achievement Emotions as its explanatory account of maths anxiety: "anxiety in educational contexts can be understood as the feeling that arises when students place value on a subject like mathematics but perceive a lack of control over their performance in it". It uses this account to structure a conceptual model in which students' appraisals of control and value shape emotional responses and likelihood of success, and to justify individually tailored, relative measurement of these appraisals over time.
requirements: Recognition that appraisals of control and value vary significantly across individuals and situations, implying relative rather than absolute measurement
constraints: The authors state the accompanying model is not a complete representation of the process of learning and forms one sub-system in a larger process
target_learners: School students learning mathematics, including middle school students
target_learning_goals: Reducing mathematics anxiety
Supporting socio-emotional learning in mathematics
examples: The article applies the account in Figure 1, where appraisals of control and value feed success in mathematics activities and maths anxiety

description: Figure 1 presents "a much simplified and sharply focussed model of the process of learning mathematics" in which the educational goal is socio-emotional learning and mathematics activities are the means. It includes a balancing loop where emotional self-regulation dampens maths anxiety, and reinforcing loops in which success builds perceived control, and perceived control reduces anxiety, which further increases control; the authors note that perceived loss of control can also escalate anxiety. The model marks points of teacher influence and potential AI contribution.

constraints: The authors stress the model is incomplete, omitting factors such as resilience, and is not a complete representation of the process of learning

article_title: Statistical learning dynamically shapes auditory perception
citation: Luthra, S., Luor, A., Tierney, A. T., Dick, F., & Holt, L. L. (2025). Statistical learning dynamically shapes auditory perception. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00328-z
title: Distributional learning sculpts a gain function via suppression of less-likely stimuli and modest enhancement of more-likely stimuli
description: The article proposes that expectation built from distributional learning across a task-irrelevant sensory dimension sculpts a gain function characterized by "modest enhancement of more-likely stimuli, and robust suppression of less-likely stimuli." Rather than prioritizing expected input alone (Bayesian-style enhancement) or solely accentuating surprising input, the account holds that "effects of expectation are largely driven by suppression of less-probable, unexpected stimuli." Expectation establishes a selection filter—variously a dimension-selective attentional filter or an experience-driven predictive filter—that is graded by distribution shape, range, and stimulus position, and is distinct from task-utility manipulations previously attributed to attention.
requirements: Extended experience with probability distributions across a continuous sensory dimension
A task-irrelevant perceptual dimension along which distributions are defined
constraints: Effects were demonstrated on tone detection in noise and tone duration decisions across acoustic frequency; whether they generalize to other modalities or task-relevant dimensions is not established by these experiments.
target_learners: adult listeners performing online psychoacoustic tasks
target_learning_goals: implicit statistical (distributional) learning across a sensory dimension
perceptual sensitivity and decision speed modulation
examples: Exp 7 showed a five-fold probability increase conferred only an average 3.7% detection improvement at the mode, while off-center frequencies decreasing in probability lost 4.7% detection accuracy.

article_title: The mitigating effect of repeated memory reactivations on forgetting
citation: MacLeod, S., Reynolds, M. G. & Lehmann, H. (2018). The mitigating effect of repeated memory reactivations on forgetting. npj Science of Learning 3:9. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0025-x
title: Reconsolidation account of memory strengthening through reactivation
description: The article interprets its findings within reconsolidation theory: each time a memory is reactivated it "undergoes a new bout of consolidation", with cellular/synaptic plastic changes contributing to memory maintenance. The authors propose that repeated descriptive and component reactivations strengthened 28-day image memories via these reconsolidation bouts, while 1-h benefits likely reflected short-term synaptic facilitation supporting working memory. They also relate the findings to Distributed Reinstatement Theory, in which repeated reactivations extend the neural network supporting a memory beyond the hippocampus.
requirements: Reactivation content must pertain to the target memory; distractor reactivations did not enhance retention
constraints: The 1-h improvement cannot be attributed to protein-synthesis-dependent reconsolidation because the interval was too short
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of studied visual material (episodic memory)
examples: Participants received three equally spaced reactivations during retention intervals of 1 h, 9 days, or 28 days, then completed an in-lab free-recall test

citation: Zhang, Z., Katayoun, M., Tan, L., & Wei, G. (2026). Development and Validation of a Multidimensional Scale for AI Tutoring Acceptance in Higher Education. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00431-9
title: AITAQS four-dimensional framework of AI tutoring acceptance quality
description: The framework conceptualizes AI tutoring acceptance quality as a higher-order learner-perceived construct with four constitutive dimensions: "Feedback Quality", "Instructional Effectiveness", "Interaction Experience", and "User Trust". Each dimension captures a distinct domain — pedagogical, functional, interactional, relational — and none is sufficient alone; a system may be easy to use yet instructionally weak. The dimensions are treated as internal content of the construct rather than antecedents, correlates, or distal outcomes, and the construct is explicitly bounded away from satisfaction, motivation, behavioural intention, and academic achievement.
requirements: All four dimensions must be assessed together, since none is sufficient on its own to capture the construct
constraints: The scale is not intended to measure downstream outcomes such as actual academic achievement, learner motivation, behavioral intention, or global satisfaction
target_learning_goals: evaluating the perceived quality of AI tutoring as instructional support (feedback, instruction, interaction, trust)
examples: The 12-item AITAQS operationalizes the framework with three items per dimension, validated with undergraduate students at five universities in Shanxi Province, China.

article_title: Sex differences in brain correlates of STEM anxiety
citation: Ariel A. Gonzalez, Katherine L. Bottenhorn, Jessica E. Bartley, Timothy Hayes, Michael C. Riedel, Taylor Salo, Elsa I. Bravo, Rosalie Odean, Alina Nazareth, Robert W. Laird, Matthew T. Sutherland, Eric Brewe, Shannon M. Pruden and Angela R. Laird. (2019). Sex differences in brain correlates of STEM anxiety. npj Science of Learning 4:18. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0058-9
title: Tripartite network model of salience, default mode, and central executive networks as a framework for anxiety-related disruption in STEM learning
description: The article applies the tripartite network model, in which the salience network (SN), default mode network (DMN), and central executive network (CEN) interact to govern cognition and emotion. The article states that "The interactions of these three large-scale networks underlie a unifying tripartite network model that seeks to characterize the maladaptive network organization and function common across psychiatric disorders". Because hallmarks of STEM anxiety resemble those of clinical anxiety, the authors used inter-network connectivity among SN, DMN, and CEN as the neural framework for interpreting anxiety in physics students.
requirements: Resting-state fMRI data preprocessed with motion correction and censoring, with network time series extracted from a meta-analytic parcellation of the three networks
constraints: The article notes prior work reports both increased and decreased SN connectivity with anxiety in clinical and healthy populations, so the direction of network disruption is not settled
target_learners: undergraduate STEM students in gateway physics courses
target_learning_goals: understanding the neurobiological correlates of STEM anxiety during physics learning
examples: The study parcellated SN, DMN, and CEN from rs-fMRI of 101 physics students and computed pairwise inter-network Pearson correlations as edge weights

description: The article recommends that efforts to retain women in STEM target the learning climate rather than ability or interest, since female students maintained performance while reporting higher anxiety. It states: "We recommend that positive changes in favor of promoting women in STEM should focus on addressing climate issues that contribute to STEM anxiety." Recommended actions include improving parental and teacher support, increasing visible role models, revising Title IX policies, and zero-tolerance policies for harassment.

constraints: The article notes the studied course was equal but not equitable, i.e., it did not reduce sex differences in anxiety
target_learners: elementary and secondary school girls in STEM
target_learning_goals: reducing STEM anxiety and retaining women in STEM careers
examples: The authors suggest instructional techniques that build positive affect while teaching content, and improving parental and teacher support shown to impact girls' anxiety, confidence, and performance

title: Support adolescents' self-regulation of online behaviors, emotions, and self-efficacy within an emotionally secure family relationship to safeguard well-being
description: The article concludes that effective regulation of adolescents' online behaviors, emotions, and self-efficacy, "especially when combined with an emotionally secure family relationship", can ensure adolescents' well-being. It recommends equipping adolescents with self-regulatory capacity for future challenges, and states "Teachers should provide professional support to educate parents on this theme, especially in a digital context."

Adolescents' use of cognitive-emotional regulation strategies and development of online learning self-efficacy

article_title: The neurocognitive mechanism underlying math avoidance among math anxious people
citation: Jie Liu, Zhifeng Li, Jiawang Yang, Hao He & Fang Cui. (2025). The neurocognitive mechanism underlying math avoidance among math anxious people. npj Science of Learning 10:50. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00343-0
title: Expected Value of Control (EVC) account of math avoidance in high math anxiety
description: The article frames its neural findings with Expected Value of Control theory: people "integrate information about the expected reward and efﬁcacy of task performance to determine the expected value of control, and then adjust their control allocation (i.e., mental effort) accordingly". In the approach-avoid task, participants weighed their effectiveness at solving arithmetic problems against the rewards on offer. The authors propose that HMA individuals, lacking self-efficacy in mathematical ability, generate a lower expected value of cognitive control and so allocate less mental effort to accepting problems, aligning with the observed difficulty-driven avoidance.
requirements: Requires a context in which learners weigh expected reward and perceived efficacy of task performance before deciding whether to engage cognitive effort
constraints: The authors' application to HMA is an interpretation of the observed findings, not a direct test of EVC theory
examples: In the study's task, participants considered their effectiveness in solving arithmetic problems and the corresponding rewards to decide whether to accept or reject challenges

article_title: Triggers of curiosity in social constructivist classroom discourse
citation: Ali, F., Wang, Y., Wang, S. J.-W. & Zhu, G. (2025). Triggers of curiosity in social constructivist classroom discourse. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00330-5
title: Three discourse patterns sustain curiosity chains: sustained teacher-student episodes, one student's question sparking another's, and consecutive student question turns
description: This lesson-level pattern describes three qualitatively identified configurations in which curiosity chains (S:CUR4→S:CUR2→S:CUR) occur in classroom discourse. The first is a sustained dialogue between teacher and one student using probing questions, encouragement, and confirmation-seeking; the second occurs when "the teacher engages in a discussion with one student, subsequ ently stimulating the curiosity of another student regarding the same topic"; the third involves "various students posing different questions," including consecutive student question turns when the teacher refrains from interrupting.
requirements: Knowledge Building classroom discourse in which students are free to pose questions and the discourse alternates between teacher and students
constraints: Patterns were qualitatively interpreted from two KB classrooms (one per grade) in one Canadian private school
target_learning_goals: sustaining chains of student curiosity and question asking during collaborative knowledge building
examples: Qualitative examples include a second-grade student's seed-germination question sparking another student's question about planting seeds on rock, and consecutive student questions about worms and compost.
key_sources: Ali, F., Wang, Y., Wang, S. J.-W. & Zhu, G. (2025). Triggers of curiosity in social constructivist classroom discourse. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00330-5

article_title: Triggers of curiosity in social constructivist classroom discourse
citation: Ali, F., Wang, Y., Wang, S. J.-W. & Zhu, G. (2025). Triggers of curiosity in social constructivist classroom discourse. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00330-5
title: Knowledge Building as a social constructivist pedagogical model provides the discourse context in which curiosity chains emerge
description: Knowledge Building (KB) is the pedagogical model underpinning the studied classrooms: it is "underpinned by social constructivism," emphasizing "inquiry and dialog-based classroom discourse" and "collaborative engagement and knowledge creation as a learning community." A distinguishing characteristic is "students’shared responsibility for learning and propelling the discourse forward," with teachers facilitating rather than leading. The article treats KB discourse as the ideal context in which antecedents, triggers, and manifestations of curiosity can be examined.
requirements: Discourse serves as the mediator, with students constructing and expressing knowledge through dialogue
constraints: The study's curiosity findings are limited to social constructivist classrooms implementing KB; I-R-E style conventional classrooms differ in utterance types and quality
target_learners: elementary students in student-centered, inquiry-based classrooms
target_learning_goals: collaborative knowledge creation and community knowledge building through dialogue
examples: Ten-month KB courses were conducted in second grade (topic: growth and changes in animals, Atlantic salmon) and third grade (topic: soil in the environment), with books, artifacts, visiting experts, and field visits.

article_title: Short naps improve subsequent learning in a high school setting
citation: Vidal, V., Pretel, M. R., Capurro, L., Tassone, L. M., Moyano, M. D., Malacari, R. G., Brusco, L. I., Ballarini, F. M. & Forcato, C. (2025). Short naps improve subsequent learning in a high school setting. npj Science of Learning 10:15. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00307-4
title: School naps can be implemented in ordinary classrooms without specialized resting facilities, because sleeping seated at a desk suffices to boost encoding
description: A design principle holding that academic nap interventions need not require beds or dedicated rest rooms: in this study students slept "sitting in chairs, with their heads resting on their forearms on the table" in the school library, and still showed better encoding. The article states this "allows for the development of easily implementable strategies to improve academic performance without needing specialized resting places equipped with beds". This keeps the ecological character of the intervention, with lessons delivered by the regular teacher.
requirements: A quiet space such as a library with chairs and tables, plus supervision to ensure a quiet environment
constraints: Presence of experimenters may have increased sleep onset latency, per the article
Ecological school settings introduce uncontrolled variables such as timing between classes and examination days
target_learning_goals: boosting memory encoding of academic lesson content
examples: Students napped in the school library seated at large tables with heads on their forearms, with EEG recorded, then attended their regular teacher's biology lesson

Professional artists teach "90-min weekly workshops over an entire semester" covering disciplines including painting, dance, and music for students aged 14–16 in Chilean public high schools. The program aimed to improve creative skills and educational effectiveness through art.

Schoolteacher support alongside the artist in each workshop

creative behaviors and cultural appreciation

article_title: Anticipated variability increases generalization of predictive learning
citation: Hadar Ram, Guy Grinfeld & Nira Liberman. (2024). Anticipated variability increases generalization of predictive learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00269-z
title: Accuracy–applicability trade-off account of generalization breadth
description: The article explains generalization breadth via a trade-off: narrower generalization is "more likely to be accurate" but applies to fewer new objects, while broader generalization applies to more cases but is less likely to be accurate; the learner seeks a "sweet spot". The paper proposes that expecting high variability in the application context shifts this trade-off toward broader generalization, so learners "cast a wider net" by attributing the outcome to a broader range of stimuli. This is the mechanism account the three experiments were designed to test.
requirements: An anticipated application context whose variability the learner can represent, so the trade-off point can shift before generalization occurs
constraints: Derived from the notion of the trade-off (ref. 18) and supported here behaviorally; the article notes the task cannot separate perceptual non-discrimination from expecting the same outcome
target_learners: adult online experiment participants (Mechanical Turk, Prolific, Israeli panel)
target_learning_goals: broad vs narrow generalization of learned stimulus–outcome contingencies to novel, similar stimuli
examples: In Experiment 1, participants told to expect samples from labs across the world predicted "pathogenic" for more of the smaller, previously unseen rings than participants told to expect samples from the same lab
key_sources: Hadar Ram, Guy Grinfeld & Nira Liberman. (2024). Anticipated variability increases generalization of predictive learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00269-z

article_title: Anticipated variability increases generalization of predictive learning
citation: Hadar Ram, Guy Grinfeld & Nira Liberman. (2024). Anticipated variability increases generalization of predictive learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00269-z
title: Construal Level Theory link: psychological distance cues variability and abstraction
description: The article invokes Construal Level Theory (CLT), which holds that distancing an object in time, space, social distance or hypotheticality changes how we think about it, and that "distance introduces variability": distal objects are less similar to current experience, more uncertain, and therefore represented more abstractly. The paper proposes that psychological distance to the anticipated application of learning serves as a subtle cue for potential variability, eliciting more abstract, broader representations and thus broader generalization, complementing explicitly instructed variability expectations.
requirements: A perceived temporal (or other psychological) distance between the learning situation and the anticipated application context
constraints: The CLT-based hypothesis rests on the premise that distance increases the range and variability of possibilities; Experiment 2 tested only the distance–expected-variability link, using time distance
target_learners: adult learners anticipating future application of learning
target_learning_goals: abstract, broader category formation and generalization from limited learning experience
examples: Experiment 3 told participants the actual task would occur immediately or a week later, without any difference in the actual learning and generalization procedures
key_sources: Hadar Ram, Guy Grinfeld & Nira Liberman. (2024). Anticipated variability increases generalization of predictive learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00269-z
