citation: Yicong Zheng, Pengyuan Sun and Xiaonan L. Liu. (2023). Publisher Correction: Retrieval practice is costly and is beneficial only when working memory capacity is abundant. npj Science of Learning (2023) 8:36. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00185-8
title: Working-memory-resource model of retrieval practice versus restudy distinguishing consumed resources from the extra cost of testing
description: The corrected Fig. 3 depicts a resource model comparing a Retrieval Attempt path with a Re-encoding path, each shown for High WM and Low WM, against a Restudy condition. It tracks Initial Episode Node Strength to Final Episode Node Strength, with "WM Capacity Available WM Resources Consumed WM (strengthen the node) Extra cost of test (no strengthening)" as annotated components. Retrieval and re-encoding consume working memory resources to strengthen the node, while testing carries an extra cost with no strengthening; restudy rows are marked N/A for these components.
requirements: Working memory capacity must be represented as available resources to model strengthening versus non-strengthening outcomes.
constraints: The supplied text presents this model only through the corrected figure's labels and axis annotations, without derivations or parameter values.
target_learners: learners studied in the original article on retrieval practice and working memory capacity
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of studied material as indexed by episode node strength
examples: The corrected figure contrasts Retrieval Attempt and Re-encoding panels, each split by High WM and Low WM, against a Restudy panel whose cost components are marked N/A.

article_title: International perspectives on gaps and solutions for integrating research evidence into classroom practices
citation: Bowen, A. E. J., Ferreira, R. A., Tolmie, A., Thomas, M. S. C., Borst, G. & Van Herwegen, J. (2025). International perspectives on gaps and solutions for integrating research evidence into classroom practices. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00370-x
title: Adapted five-dimension research gap analysis framework for education
description: A taxonomy for structuring research agendas in education, adapted from Miles's (2017) seven-dimension research gap framework by collapsing the Knowledge and Theoretical gaps and the Empirical and Evidence gaps into single dimensions. The article states "The seven-dimension deductive research gap analysis framework proposed by Miles23 was then used as an organising structure" and that the adapted framework yields five dimensions: gaps in existing theory and knowledge, between research and practice, in research methodologies, in empirical testing and evidence verification, and in research with specific populations. It is used to organise a thematic gap analysis of international expert workshop content.
requirements: Dataset of presentation slides and discussion notes from researchers working on science of learning translation
Thematic analysis coding informed by reflexive thematic analysis methods
constraints: Adapted for this study's data; the authors note it had not previously been applied to define an education research agenda
Developed from a small expert sample without educator perspectives in the data
target_learners: Educational researchers and policymakers seeking to structure research agendas for evidence integration in education
target_learning_goals: Improving integration of research evidence into classroom practice across school subjects and learner populations
examples: Thematic analysis of a two-day workshop with five heads of science of learning labs from the UK, France, and Chile, with themes agreed between all authors

article_title: Integrating stereotypes and factual evidence in interpersonal communication
citation: Koch, S. B. J., Tyborowska, A., Niermann, H. C. M., Cillessen, A. H. N., Roelofs, K., Bašnáková, J., Toni, I., & Stolk, A. (2024). Integrating stereotypes and factual evidence in interpersonal communication. npj Science of Learning 9, 52. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00262-6
title: Dual-contributions framework: stereotypes and interaction-based evidence provide complementary, neuroanatomically and developmentally dissociable contributions to communication
description: The article proposes a summary model (Fig. 3) in which stereotype beliefs and evidence from ongoing social interactions jointly shape communicative adjustment. Stereotypes "provide initial boundaries on mutual understanding," while interaction dynamics moderate how strongly those priors are applied. The two contributions are experimentally visible on a single metric and are independently predicted by right ACCg structural integrity and early-life social exposure, yielding "complementary, yet neuroanatomically and developmentally dissociable, contributions to interpersonal communication."
requirements: A setting where stereotype-driven and interaction-driven behavioral adjustments can be separately quantified on the same behavioral metric
constraints: Demonstrated in a nonverbal communication game minimizing linguistic conventions, with stereotype beliefs manipulated only via presumed partner age
target_learning_goals: adjusting communicative behavior to an interaction partner by integrating prior beliefs with interaction-based evidence
examples: The game dissociated stereotype-driven adjustments (more time in the object square toward the presumed child) from interaction-driven convergence, with the two kinds of variance not accounting for each other.
key_sources: Koch, S. B. J., Tyborowska, A., Niermann, H. C. M., Cillessen, A. H. N., Roelofs, K., Bašnáková, J., Toni, I., & Stolk, A. (2024). Integrating stereotypes and factual evidence in interpersonal communication. npj Science of Learning 9, 52. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00262-6

article_title: Integrating stereotypes and factual evidence in interpersonal communication
citation: Koch, S. B. J., Tyborowska, A., Niermann, H. C. M., Cillessen, A. H. N., Roelofs, K., Bašnáková, J., Toni, I., & Stolk, A. (2024). Integrating stereotypes and factual evidence in interpersonal communication. npj Science of Learning 9, 52. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00262-6
title: Nonverbal communication game quantifying stereotype- and interaction-driven adjustments
description: A two-player digital game board with a 3 × 3 grid on which participants guide a partner (a role-blind confederate) to a hidden acorn by moving a bird avatar. Only the participant knows the location and only the partner can collect the object, driving dyads to "achieve mutual understanding by aligning on a limited but idiosyncratic number of strategies." Dyads solved trials well above chance (89.8 ± 11.7% against a chance level of 7.7%), indicating participants generated communicative behaviors that, despite their novelty, could be mutually understood. The game measures stereotype-driven adjustment (time spent in the object square) and interaction-driven convergence across eight blocks with alternating presumed partners.
requirements: A role-blind confederate performing both presumed-partner roles so that adjustments reflect stereotype beliefs rather than partner behavior
constraints: Minimizes linguistic conventions, so findings may not generalize to verbal communication with its prosodic and lexical cues
target_learners: adolescent participants in dyadic social interaction studies
target_learning_goals: measuring real-time communicative adjustment to partner beliefs and interaction dynamics
examples: Participants alternated between presumed child and adult partners over eight blocks of five trials, with the confederate blind to which role he performed.

article_title: An fMRI study on the generalization of motor learning after brain actuated supernumerary robot training
citation: Yuan Liu, Shuaifei Huang, Weiguo Xu, Zhuang Wang & Dong Ming. (2024). An fMRI study on the generalization of motor learning after brain actuated supernumerary robot training. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00294-y
title: Brain-machine-body account: BCI-SRF training enhances motor sequence learning generalization through functional reorganization of the sensorimotor network
description: The article's explanatory framework holds that motor sequence learning depends on the sensorimotor network, and that "BCI-SRF training enhances the generalization ability of motor sequence learning through functional reorganization of sensorimotor networks". Three properties are proposed: novel limb morphology activating broader sensorimotor neural resources, efferent and afferent pathways via EEG decoding and FES sensory feedback enhancing cortical-subcortical interactions, and sixth-finger motor imagery recruiting additional frontal resources. The framework integrates the frontal-parietal circuit and the SM_cortex-cerebellar-thalamus cortical-subcortical circuit as jointly supporting motor sequence learning.
requirements: Brain-actuated SRF system with EEG decoding of sixth-finger motor imagery and TENS sensory feedback forming an extra SRF control circuit
Sustained longitudinal training (20 sessions over 4 weeks in this study)
constraints: The authors state their data are insufficient to elucidate the exact role of each circuit effect or their combination
No direct evidence of structural plasticity effects was provided; functional plasticity was the observed basis
Sample size was not very large, and clinical patients have not yet been tested
target_learners: Healthy adults learning human-machine interaction skills
Potentially stroke patients needing motor relearning (speculated application)
target_learning_goals: Generalization of motor sequence learning to novel sequences
Functional reorganization of the sensorimotor network supporting skill acquisition
examples: Twenty healthy right-handed participants were randomly assigned to BCI-SRF or inborn finger training for 20 sessions over 4 weeks, with novel SRF-finger opposition sequences measured at pre, post, and 1-month follow-up

article_title: Grit and academic resilience during the COVID-19 pandemic
citation: Chen, D. L., Ertac, S., Evgeniou, T., Miao, X., Nadaf, A., & Yilmaz, E. (2024). Grit and academic resilience during the COVID-19 pandemic. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00265-3
title: Behavioral grit measure constructed from digital-platform setback responses
description: A behavioral, revealed-preference measure of grit computed from naturally occurring data on a digital learning platform. A day with a score at least 5 points below the previous week's average is defined as a "setback", and a student's "gritty response as an increase in effort" — more out-of-school assessment attempts on the following day — is coded 1; behavioral grit is the percentage of setbacks followed by increased effort, calculated separately for math and science for pre- and during-Covid windows. It captures the perseverance-of-effort facet of grit and is not prone to social desirability effects.
requirements: A digital learning platform recording per-activity timestamps, assessment attempts, and daily scores, including voluntary out-of-school-hours activity
Sufficient setback observations per student; grit is not defined on days without a sizable score decline
constraints: Very high-performing students (average daily scores consistently above 90) are omitted because there is little room for improvement
Results may be country- or age-dependent; weekends are excluded from attempt calculations
target_learning_goals: non-cognitive skill measurement (grit/perseverance) and prediction of academic resilience
examples: The authors report the measure is largely robust to variations such as counting effort two days after the setback or defining setbacks as bottom-20% performances
key_sources: Chen, D. L., Ertac, S., Evgeniou, T., Miao, X., Nadaf, A., & Yilmaz, E. (2024). Grit and academic resilience during the COVID-19 pandemic. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00265-3

article_title: Grit and academic resilience during the COVID-19 pandemic
citation: Chen, D. L., Ertac, S., Evgeniou, T., Miao, X., Nadaf, A., & Yilmaz, E. (2024). Grit and academic resilience during the COVID-19 pandemic. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00265-3
title: Use digital learning platform data to assess non-cognitive skills and customize learning experiences for students with heterogeneous resilience
description: Digital learning platforms can serve not only to deliver content but also to collect behavioral information that measures non-cognitive skills like grit and predicts responses to shocks. The article argues AI-based remote learning technologies can "identify not only students who are struggling in terms of comprehension but also those who lack resilience or motivation" and respond by adapting difficulty levels and sequences and providing personalized motivational feedback. Survey self-reports can be complemented with high-dimensional revealed-preference data.
requirements: A digital platform integrated into regular schooling that records behavioral activity such as clicks, content access, and time on task
constraints: The article's data cannot definitively infer causality; results may depend on how the pandemic was experienced and the platform's degree of curriculum integration
target_learners: K-12 students learning via digital platforms, including in remote-learning conditions
target_learning_goals: sustaining engagement and perseverance; academic resilience to disruptions
examples: Features promoting gritty behavior, such as growth-mindset messages, can be directly incorporated into digital learning environments to support self-regulated virtual learning

article_title: Mediational effects of reading-related intermediate phenotypes from polygenic scores to reading skills
citation: Remon, A., Mascheretti, S., Voronin, I., Feng, B., Ouellet-Morin, I., Brendgen, M., Vitaro, F., Robaey, P., Andlauer, T. F. M., Boivin, M. & Dionne, G. (2025). Mediational effects of reading-related intermediate phenotypes from polygenic scores to reading skills. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00346-x
title: Multimodal sensory-to-phonological sequence account of genetic influences on reading acquisition
description: The article advances an etiological account in which genetic susceptibility for reading is phenotypically expressed through a sequence from basic multimodal sensory processing to phonological skills to reading behavior. It states that "the genetic variation represents the first step in a multiple-layered liability that ultimately leads to behavioral phenotypes," consistent with the multiple deficits model, and that training programs targeting attentional control have improved reading. The serial mediation results are presented as supporting "one of the most robust theoretical hypothesis underlying reading acquisitions."
requirements: Longitudinal or genetically informed designs with sensitive measures of sensory processing and phonological skills to trace the sequence
constraints: The cross-sectional design cannot determine causal influences among measures over time; only a first formal test of the sequential association
target_learning_goals: Reading decoding
Reading comprehension
examples: Sequential SEM models tested RBTP enabling PA, PA underpinning decoding, and decoding supporting comprehension
key_sources: Remon, A., Mascheretti, S., Voronin, I., Feng, B., Ouellet-Morin, I., Brendgen, M., Vitaro, F., Robaey, P., Andlauer, T. F. M., Boivin, M. & Dionne, G. (2025). Mediational effects of reading-related intermediate phenotypes from polygenic scores to reading skills. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00346-x

article_title: Mediational effects of reading-related intermediate phenotypes from polygenic scores to reading skills
citation: Remon, A., Mascheretti, S., Voronin, I., Feng, B., Ouellet-Morin, I., Brendgen, M., Vitaro, F., Robaey, P., Andlauer, T. F. M., Boivin, M. & Dionne, G. (2025). Mediational effects of reading-related intermediate phenotypes from polygenic scores to reading skills. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00346-x
title: Use reading-specific polygenic scores rather than general educational-attainment or cognitive-ability scores when predicting reading skills
description: The article argues that polygenic scores specifically targeting reading are needed for accurate prediction and early identification. It states that "PGSs specifically targeting reading skills are essential for improved prediction and understanding of the complex etiology through which reading skills unfold during childhood," enabling identification of genetically susceptible children while phenotypes remain malleable. The specificity analysis, controlling for EY4-PGS and IQ3-PGS, supports the distinctiveness of reading-specific genetic effects.
requirements: Trait-specific PGSs built from GWAS summary statistics on reading rather than proxy traits
Genotyping and phenotypic reading measures in the target population
constraints: PGSs currently account for a small proportion of phenotypic variance; generalization limited by a sample of European-ancestry children from higher socioeconomic backgrounds
target_learners: Children in early primary school at genetic risk for reading difficulties
target_learning_goals: Early identification of reading (dis)ability susceptibility
examples: Reading-PGS computed with PRS-CS from the Eising et al. word-reading GWAS summary statistics, controlling for twenty principal components of genetic relatedness

article_title: Level of M1 GABAB predicts micro offline consolidation of motor learning during wakefulness
citation: Pasquale Cardellicchio & Sara Borgomaneri. (2025). Level of M1 GABAB predicts micro offline consolidation of motor learning during wakefulness. npj Science of Learning 10:10. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00299-1
title: GABAB-mediated disinhibition and excitation–inhibition balance as a mechanism account for rapid motor memory consolidation in M1
description: The article advances an account in which GABAB-mediated slow inhibition regulates M1 plasticity during consolidation: reduced GABAergic tone permits LTP-like Hebbian plasticity, and the excitation–inhibition balance stabilizes newly learned skills. It states that "greater GABA inhibitory tone could strongly stabilize the newly learned skill by protecting it from interference" and that inhibitory synaptic plasticity plays a key role in forming selective engrams. GABAB receptors, with their slower, prolonged action, are argued to be more significant for consolidation than fast GABAA receptors.
requirements: At-rest GABAB functioning in M1 must be measurable, here via LICI paired-pulse TMS protocols, before skill acquisition begins.
constraints: pp-TMS measures are indirect indices of GABA and glutamate levels, and MRS–TMS correspondence studies report mixed findings.
Neurophysiological measures were limited to a single session and restricted to the pre-skill-acquisition phase.
target_learners: healthy adults acquiring new motor skills
clinical populations with motor impairments such as post-stroke patients
target_learning_goals: consolidation of motor sequence skills during brief waking rest between practice blocks
examples: The study measured SICI, LICI, ICF and sICF at rest before learning and related them to micro-online and micro-offline gains during a 36-block finger-tapping task.
key_sources: Pasquale Cardellicchio & Sara Borgomaneri. (2025). Level of M1 GABAB predicts micro offline consolidation of motor learning during wakefulness. npj Science of Learning 10:10. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00299-1

article_title: An update on recent advances in targeted memory reactivation during sleep
citation: Julia Carbone & Susanne Diekelmann. (2024). An update on recent advances in targeted memory reactivation during sleep. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00244-8
title: Home-use TMR and dream-incubation devices (Dreem headband, Dormio, SleepStim, Ezzence)
description: The review describes a set of devices enabling TMR outside the lab: the Dreem headband delivers sounds via bone-conduction transducers during REM sleep; 'Dormio' is a wearable for targeted dream incubation during the hypnagogic period; 'SleepStim' pairs a smartwatch and smartphone with "a machine-learning model ... to identify periods of deep sleep to trigger TMR sounds"; and 'Ezzence' is a smartphone-controlled olfactometer releasing odors during specific sleep stages.
requirements: Devices must either detect target sleep stages (e.g., via EEG or movement/heart-rate machine-learning classification) or be used in procedures tolerant of unmonitored sleep.
constraints: SleepStim experiments found the memory benefit depended on sound intensity and sleep stage, with greater improvements at lower intensity and when cues were delivered in SWS; Ezzence feasibility was tested without yet validating it for TMR.
target_learning_goals: declarative spatial memory
procedural skill memory
dream content shaping
examples: social-anxiety patients used the Dreem headband for a week of REM cueing at home
a pilot found 67% of Dormio awakenings incorporated the cued word 'tree'
SleepStim was tested over three subsequent nights of object-location cueing

article_title: Delayed rewards weaken human goal directed actions
citation: Omar David Perez & Gonzalo P. Urcelay. (2025). Delayed rewards weaken human goal directed actions. npj Science of Learning 10:36. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00325-2
title: Perez and Dickinson's rate-correlation theory of goal-directed control
description: The article adopts the theory of Perez and Dickinson, in which a goal-directed system computes the correlation between response rate and outcome rate, holding responses and outcomes in contiguous working-memory slots. As the article states, "goal-directed strength is determined by subjects'experienced correlation between action and outcome rates and is directly related to instrumental performance and sensitivity to outcome revaluation." The theory explains why "Delays disrupt this experienced correlation, weakening goal- directed control", integrating the observed effects of delay on response rates, revaluation sensitivity and contingency knowledge, and it accounts for why ratio training supports higher rates than interval training.
requirements: Requires a mnemonic system keeping responses and outcomes in contiguous working-memory slots to compute the experienced rate correlation.
constraints: When rewards are delayed, empty time samples assign the context a causal relationship with the outcome, weakening goal-directed control until the contextual association is extinguished.
target_learners: Adult human participants in instrumental decision-making tasks
target_learning_goals: Formation of action-outcome (instrumental contingency) knowledge and sensitivity to changes in outcome value
examples: The authors state the framework "integrates the observed effects of delay on revaluation sensitivity, response rates, and action-outcome contingency knowledge" in their stockbroker task.
key_sources: Omar David Perez & Gonzalo P. Urcelay. (2025). Delayed rewards weaken human goal directed actions. npj Science of Learning 10:36. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00325-2

article_title: Mechanisms of offline motor learning at a microscale of seconds in large-scale crowdsourced data
citation: Marlene Bönstrup, Iñaki Iturrate, Martin N. Hebart, Nitzan Censor and Leonardo G. Cohen. (2020). Mechanisms of offline motor learning at a microscale of seconds in large-scale crowdsourced data. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-0066-9
title: Micro-offline gains as rapid within-seconds consolidation extending memory consolidation to a timescale of seconds
description: The article proposes that the short rest periods interspersed with practice allow a rapid form of consolidation: "extending the concept of consolidation to a time-scale in the order of seconds, rather than hours or days". Stabilization (resistance to retroactive interference) tested at the seconds scale, plus persistence of gains under reduced or unpredictable practice, is taken as evidence that micro-offline gains indicate rapid, within-seconds consolidation accounting for early skill learning. The theory also blurs the border between online and offline stages of memory formation, suggesting behaviorally distinct stages arise from overlapping physiological processes.
requirements: Short rest periods interspersed with practice during early skill learning, providing a state of reduced interference compared with practice
constraints: The stabilization effect in Experiment 2 was small (Cohen's d 0.15) and no microscale learning differences across interference groups were found; overnight offline learning did not correlate with micro-offline gains, suggesting different mechanisms at play
target_learners: adults learning a new sequential motor skill
target_learning_goals: early acquisition of procedural motor skills (sequential finger tapping)
examples: Experiment 2 adapted a behavioral retroactive interference protocol to the level of single trials, with interference applied immediately or 10 s after each practice period
key_sources: Marlene Bönstrup, Iñaki Iturrate, Martin N. Hebart, Nitzan Censor and Leonardo G. Cohen. (2020). Mechanisms of offline motor learning at a microscale of seconds in large-scale crowdsourced data. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-0066-9

article_title: Mechanisms of offline motor learning at a microscale of seconds in large-scale crowdsourced data
citation: Marlene Bönstrup, Iñaki Iturrate, Martin N. Hebart, Nitzan Censor and Leonardo G. Cohen. (2020). Mechanisms of offline motor learning at a microscale of seconds in large-scale crowdsourced data. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-0066-9
title: Web-based crowdsourced version of the sequential finger tapping task on Amazon Mechanical Turk
description: A web-based implementation of the well-characterized sequential finger tapping task (5-item keypress sequence, 4-1-3-2-4, with the nondominant left hand) programmed in Psytoolkit, administered on Amazon Mechanical Turk with participants using their own computers. It proved "useful to study human motor learning dynamics at a large scale", enabling samples of hundreds of participants (e.g., N = 389) with data collection averaging 16 h and 26 min per experiment, and replicated the in-lab learning-curve shape and microdynamics.
requirements: Participants with >95% MTurk approval rate, US location, right-handedness; clear definitions of correct adherence to instructions for post-hoc data quality checks
constraints: A proportion of participants did not follow instructions and had to be excluded; variability is higher than in-lab at comparable sample sizes; designs requiring prolonged task durations or longitudinal measurements need extra care; groups must be properly randomized given rapid changes in worker pool composition
target_learners: adult MTurk workers learning a motor sequence
target_learning_goals: measurement of microscale motor skill learning dynamics in early acquisition
examples: Experiment 1 recruited 389 participants via Amazon Mechanical Turk who trained over 36 trials of 10 s practice and 10 s rest for a total of 12 min on their own keyboards

article_title: Identification of loci involved in childhood visual acuity and associations with cognitive skills and educational attainment
citation: Schmitz, J., Abbondanza, F., Marianski, K., Luciano, M. & Paracchini, S. (2023). Identification of loci involved in childhood visual acuity and associations with cognitive skills and educational attainment. npj Science of Learning, 8:25. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00175-w
title: Gene-environment correlation model linking EA polygenic propensities to childhood visual acuity and adult myopia risk
description: The article proposes a gene-environment correlation model in which genetic factors associated with higher educational attainment (EA PGS) are also associated with better childhood visual acuity, given visual acuity's positive links to cognitive skills and school grades. Because EA PGS are known to be associated with myopia in adults, the model holds that "environmental exposures linked to higher EA might have detrimental effects on vision offsetting the initial positive effect", e.g. more reading and near work increasing myopia risk once educational trajectories diverge. The study tested the model's predictions: EA PGS positively associated with childhood visual acuity while myopia PGS showed a negative association.
requirements: Testing the model requires polygenic scores for EA and myopia and measures of childhood visual acuity before educational trajectories diverge, as in the ALSPAC analyses at age ~11.8
constraints: The authors state they cannot rule out residual confounding by unmeasured variables, and vision and education were assessed at only a single time point
target_learners: children in the ALSPAC longitudinal cohort (mean age 11.8 years)
target_learning_goals: understanding how genetic propensity toward educational attainment relates to sensory function and academic outcomes during childhood
examples: The study found EA PGS positively related to childhood visual acuity in ALSPAC children before the end of compulsory education, while a prior study found EA PGS was not predictive of visual function in ALSPAC mothers
key_sources: Schmitz, J., Abbondanza, F., Marianski, K., Luciano, M. & Paracchini, S. (2023). Identification of loci involved in childhood visual acuity and associations with cognitive skills and educational attainment. npj Science of Learning, 8:25. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00175-w

article_title: A micro-genesis account of longer-form reinforcement learning in structured and unstructured environments
citation: Benjamin James Dyson and Ahad Asad. (2021). A micro-genesis account of longer-form reinforcement learning in structured and unstructured environments. npj Science of Learning 6:19. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00098-4
title: Micro-genesis account: between-task win-calmness and loss-restlessness must first develop from micro-transactions within tasks
description: The article proposes that longer-form reinforcement-learning expressions described between tasks (gain-calmness as "decreased choice switching following prior tasks producing gains" and loss-restlessness as "increased tendency to switch choices following prior tasks with losses") can only manifest across tasks if they first develop from contingencies between trial triplets within a task. It operationalises calmness as two consecutive stay responses and restlessness as two consecutive shift responses, testing whether the trial n-2 outcome shapes stay-stay or shift-shift responding. The account retains win-stay and lose-shift as central mechanisms while extending the associative chain across multiple outcomes and actions.
requirements: Participants must experience reliable gains or losses different from baseline for the longer-form effects to take effect
constraints: Effects are studied within repeated zero-sum games (Rock, Paper, Scissors) against computerised opponents
target_learners: adult participants making repeated choices in competitive decision-making games
target_learning_goals: outcome-action associative learning (win-stay/lose-shift) in repeated decision-making
examples: Calmness was coded as stay-stay across trials n-2 to n-1 and n-1 to n, and restlessness as shift-shift across the same window, analysed as a function of the trial n-2 outcome
key_sources: Benjamin James Dyson and Ahad Asad. (2021). A micro-genesis account of longer-form reinforcement learning in structured and unstructured environments. npj Science of Learning 6:19. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00098-4

article_title: Exploring the potential of LLM to enhance teaching plans through teaching simulation
citation: Bihao Hu, Jiayi Zhu, Yiying Pei & Xiaoqing Gu. (2025). Exploring the potential of LLM to enhance teaching plans through teaching simulation. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00300-x
title: Refining problem chains into context-based, trap-based, and summary-based types improves LLM teaching plan design
description: The article replaces a generic numbered problem-chain output format with three distinct chain types that structure classroom questioning across a lesson. Context-based chains introduce new knowledge through scenarios, trap-based chains pose medium- to high-difficulty questions that provoke critical thinking and productive failure, and summary-based chains support review and further interest. The authors report that "this subdivision approach enhances the LLM’s understanding of the teaching process, progressing from basic to advanced levels, and leads to better outcomes when designing andimproving teaching plans."
requirements: Prompts must include the lesson's knowledge points, instructional objectives, and teaching priority and challenge, with examples supplied for each chain type
constraints: Trap-based problem chains score slightly lower in usability than the other two types, indicating LLM limits in designing deep and challenging questions
target_learning_goals: gradual understanding and mastery of mathematical concepts through sequenced problem chains
examples: In the Stratified Random Sampling lesson example (Fig. 2), GPT-4 simulated teacher-student dialogs, generated reflections, and produced the enhanced plan with the three chain types in the Statistics module
key_sources: Bihao Hu, Jiayi Zhu, Yiying Pei & Xiaoqing Gu. (2025). Exploring the potential of LLM to enhance teaching plans through teaching simulation. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00300-x

citation: Bihao Hu, Jiayi Zhu, Yiying Pei & Xiaoqing Gu. (2025). Exploring the potential of LLM to enhance teaching plans through teaching simulation. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00300-x
title: Nine-category, nineteen-dimension teaching plan evaluation framework with expert rater panel
description: The article develops an evaluation framework of 9 categories and 19 indicators covering problem chains, teaching activities, knowledge content, teaching methods and strategies, teaching evaluation, interdisciplinarity, practical value, scope, and overall score, rated on an 8-point Likert scale. Three mathematics teachers with over five years of experience scored the 480 plans, aided by two expert teachers with over ten years of experience. The pre-evaluation consistency test "had an ICC (2, 3) value of 0.716, which exceedsthe 0.6 threshold, indicating a high degree of consistency in the teachers’evaluations."
requirements: Raters review each teaching plan for at least ten minutes and receive explanations and examples of each dimension; discrepancies are resolved by consultation with the two expert teachers
constraints: The framework omits assessment of instructional objectives and teaching priorities and challenges, which were retained from prior-generation output rather than re-evaluated
target_learners: high school mathematics teachers and pre-service teachers whose plans are evaluated
target_learning_goals: comprehensive assessment of teaching plan quality across pedagogical and content dimensions
examples: Raters pre-evaluated a mixed set of 15 plans from Datasets C and D before formal evaluation of the eight datasets

article_title: Learning and navigating digitally rendered haptic spatial layouts
citation: Ruxandra I. Tivadar, Benedetta Franceschiello, Astrid Minier and Micah M. Murray. (2023). Learning and navigating digitally rendered haptic spatial layouts. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00208-4
title: Ultrasonic digital haptics tablet rendering floor plans and trajectories as friction-reduction textures
description: A tablet-based surface haptic display in which "the touchscreen of a tablet device monitors the position of the fingertip" and "localised piezoelectric actuators, in turn, vibrate at ultrasonic frequencies to dynamically change the perceived friction at the fingertip and thus give the impression of texture". In the study it rendered an apartment floor plan with four textures (walls, furniture obstacles, areas outside, and the trajectory), using square-wave ultrasonic signals for sharp sensations and a sinusoidal signal for the trajectory. It served as the sole learning medium for the 2D layout before physical reconstruction and blindfolded navigation.
requirements: Users require familiarisation and training to discriminate the haptic textures and learn exploration strategies (lateral finger sweeps) before the layout can be learned.
constraints: The haptic maps used only the two ultrasonic wave shapes provided natively in the device's Haptic Texture Library Creation Tool, limiting the textures to those the tool provides.
target_learners: sighted blindfolded adults learning unfamiliar spatial layouts; proposed for visually impaired and blind populations in rehabilitation
target_learning_goals: spatial layout learning, cognitive map formation, and navigation of real-world trajectories
examples: In the study, 25 blindfolded participants learned the apartment layout solely from the tablet's haptic rendering, reconstructed it with LEGO bricks, and navigated trained and untrained trajectories in the real space.
key_sources: Ruxandra I. Tivadar, Benedetta Franceschiello, Astrid Minier and Micah M. Murray. (2023). Learning and navigating digitally rendered haptic spatial layouts. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00208-4

article_title: EEG analysis of brain dynamics in a simulated multi-task and multi-stage learning environment
citation: Hui Xie, Chunli Jia, Yanxia Luo, Jiangshan He, Zexiao Dong, Dan Liang, Ziqi Ren, Mingzhe Jiang, Xinbo Gao & Xueli Chen. (2025). EEG analysis of brain dynamics in a simulated multi-task and multi-stage learning environment. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00376-5
title: Longitudinal multi-task, multi-stage EEG framework for monitoring learning across an entire course
description: The article establishes a framework for continuous neural monitoring across a full semester rather than short isolated tasks. As the authors state, "we established a longitudinal EEG acquisition and analysis framework within an authentic course-based learning scenario, achieving continuous neural monitoring over an entire semester." It combines time-domain amplitude, spectral (relative PSD), connectivity (PLI, entropy-based information transfer), and machine-learning analyses across three tasks and three course stages to characterize evolving brain dynamics during learning.
requirements: Participants complete repeated weekly sessions of multiple task types while wearing EEG across an entire course
Sufficient high-quality EEG data segments to survive quality screening
constraints: A small sample size may reduce statistical efficacy and increase the risk of false positives or negatives, per the authors' own power analyses
14-channel density limits source-space and complex network analyses requiring high spatial resolution
target_learners: undergraduate students in an authentic elective course
target_learning_goals: monitoring cognitive states and neural engagement during knowledge acquisition, experiential manipulation, and integrative application
examples: Twenty undergraduates completed an 11-week biology course with weekly lecture, virtual lab, and quiz sessions while wearing Emotiv EPOC+ headsets; six participants' high-quality data were retained for analysis
key_sources: Hui Xie, Chunli Jia, Yanxia Luo, Jiangshan He, Zexiao Dong, Dan Liang, Ziqi Ren, Mingzhe Jiang, Xinbo Gao & Xueli Chen. (2025). article_title: EEG analysis of brain dynamics in a simulated multi-task and multi-stage learning environment
citation: Hui Xie, Chunli Jia, Yanxia Luo, Jiangshan He, Zexiao Dong, Dan Liang, Ziqi Ren, Mingzhe Jiang, Xinbo Gao & Xueli Chen. (2025). title: Semester-long simulated-MOOC EEG dataset from an 11-lesson biology course
description: This dataset comprises weekly 14-channel EEG recordings (Emotiv EPOC+ headsets, 128 Hz sampling) from undergraduates completing an 11-week elective biology course simulating a MOOC, with lecture, virtual lab, and quiz tasks each session and three course stages. As the authors state, "the data were analyzed for stage classification using machine learning models" on 7,544 samples of 84 relative-PSD features. The dataset supports stage-wise EEG analyses and the article's machine-learning experiments.
requirements: Data must pass the article's quality screening; participants with more than two stages containing over 40% poor-quality segments were excluded
Preprocessing with EEGLAB filtering, ICA artifact removal, and segment rejection rules
constraints: Only six participants' high-quality data were ultimately retained for analysis
Some segments were excluded due to poor electrode contact and external noise interference
target_learners: undergraduate students in an engineering elective course
target_learning_goals: capturing neural activity during information acquisition, virtual experimentation, and knowledge application tasks
examples: Stage sample sizes printed in the article are 2717 (Stage 1), 2453 (Stage 2), and 2374 (Stage 3), totaling 7,544 samples

article_title: Lighting the wick in the candle of learning: generating a prediction stimulates curiosity
citation: Garvin Brod and Jasmin Breitwieser. (2019). Lighting the wick in the candle of learning: generating a prediction stimulates curiosity. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0056-y
title: Knowledge-gap relevance account: prediction generation stimulates curiosity by increasing the relevance of the knowledge gap
description: The article advances an interpretation, building on Berlyne's arousal conjecture and Loewenstein's information-gap proposal, that "generating a prediction increases the relevance of the knowledge gap, i.e., the subjective value of the soon-to-be-learned information." The increased relevance plays out as enhanced arousal in anticipation and enhanced attention to the gap. The authors speculate that a key driver is a priori committing to a specific outcome, which goes beyond merely generating a response.
requirements: Generating a prediction before receiving feedback, so learners commit to a specific outcome before seeing the correct one
constraints: The article offers this as an interpretation and speculation, not a tested mechanism; the study cannot provide causal evidence for the effects of feedback on curiosity because the curiosity rating always took place before feedback
target_learning_goals: stimulating curiosity for factual knowledge to support memory encoding
examples: The experiment compared prediction generation with matched example generation, both followed by curiosity ratings, answer anticipation, and feedback
key_sources: Garvin Brod and Jasmin Breitwieser. (2019). Lighting the wick in the candle of learning: generating a prediction stimulates curiosity. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0056-y

article_title: Enhancing children’s numeracy and executive functions via their explicit integration
citation: Scerif, G., Sučević, J., Andrews, H., Blakey, E., Gattas, S. U., Godfrey, A., et al. (2025). Enhancing children's numeracy and executive functions via their explicit integration: the ONE programme cluster randomised controlled trial. npj Science of Learning 10, 8. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00302-9
title: Mutualistic / interactive-specialisation framework of EF-mathematics co-development
description: The article grounds the ONE programme in frameworks of neurocognitive development, such as interactive specialisation and mutualistic/transactional views, in which the dynamic interplay of domain-general control functions (EFs) and domain-specific skills (numerical cognition) promotes their change. Large-scale longitudinal data are cited to show that EF does not act as a unidirectional influence on mathematics; instead, components of EF and mathematics predict change in each other across the primary school years. The mechanism hypothesis is that "practising EF challenge in the context of mathematical content provides opportunities for deeper processing and learning, thereby enhancing the co-development of EF and mathematics." The ONE programme was designed to test this integrated-intervention mechanism directly.
requirements: Interventions must embed executive challenge within mathematical content rather than training EF in isolation, so that co-developing skills are practised together
constraints: The article notes the empirical evidence for integrated interventions in very young children was limited and mixed prior to this trial
No neural or long-term longitudinal data were collected in this study
target_learners: preschool children aged 3-4 years, especially those growing up in economic disadvantage
target_learning_goals: early numeracy and executive functions (working memory, inhibitory control, cognitive flexibility) developing together
examples: The ONE programme operationalised the framework by training educators to deliver 25 activities combining EF challenge with mathematics content in preschool routines

article_title: Native learning ability and not age determines the effects of brain stimulation
citation: Maceira-Elvira, P., Popa, T., Schmid, A.-C., Cadic-Melchior, A., Müller, H., & Schaer, R. (2024). Native learning ability and not age determines the effect of brain stimulation on motor skill acquisition. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00278-y
title: Classifier-based learner stratification model predicting likelihood to benefit from atDCS from baseline task performance
description: A machine-learning framework that labels individuals as "optimal" or "suboptimal" learners of a finger-tapping task from age and baseline speed and accuracy, then projects the distance to the separating hyperplane onto a sigmoid function to estimate each person's likelihood of benefiting from stimulation. The article reports "achieving a prediction accuracy of 97% (i.e., F1 score)" on training data, and each class is split into high and low tiers by median split. It embodies the hypothesis that optimal acquisition relies on prioritizing accuracy improvement early in training.
requirements: Training data from unstimulated or placebo-stimulated participants of a prior dataset, excluding verum groups so no verum data trains the model
Baseline block and first training block measurements of speed and accuracy plus age as features
constraints: The 97% F1 score only indicates the separability of the training features, since no validation set was held aside
The model estimates the native state of the neural system indirectly, depending on relative performance between the baseline block and the first training block
target_learners: healthy young, middle-aged, and older adults learning a sequential motor task
target_learning_goals: acquisition of sequential motor skills (finger-tapping)
examples: A 2nd-degree polynomial expansion and 10-fold cross-validation selected a support-vector classifier as the best model
key_sources: Maceira-Elvira, P., Popa, T., Schmid, A.-C., Cadic-Melchior, A., Müller, H., & Schaer, R. (2024). Native learning ability and not age determines the effect of brain stimulation on motor skill acquisition. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00278-y

article_title: Native learning ability and not age determines the effects of brain stimulation
citation: Maceira-Elvira, P., Popa, T., Schmid, A.-C., Cadic-Melchior, A., Müller, H., & Schaer, R. (2024). Native learning ability and not age determines the effect of brain stimulation on motor skill acquisition. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00278-y
title: Restorative-account and task-integration biomarker interpretation of the differential atDCS effect
description: The article proposes that atDCS acts restoratively rather than enhancively: performance change between the baseline block and the first training block "may indicate the ability of an individual to rapidly integrate task-relevant information", which "would be an indirect biomarker for the state of the neural components supporting the early stages of skill acquisition". Because the two blocks use different sequences, the integrated information is sequence-unspecific, such as number-to-finger mapping and interface properties. The authors link the effect to metaplastic properties of the motor network and to streamlined construction of inverse internal models.
requirements: Prior identification of parameters related to the mechanism to be treated for clinical use
Aggregated interaction between subthreshold atDCS and motor training-derived changes in synaptic efficiency to induce LTP
constraints: The estimation is indirect and limited to the finger-tapping task context
The mechanism through which the emergence of internal models could be streamlined is not clear
target_learning_goals: early-stage acquisition of sequential motor skills
examples: The authors note the detrimental effect in high-tier optimal learners resembles observations in highly trained individuals such as pianists

It also hosts "The code written to classify individuals into the four groups of learners", enabling reuse of the stratification pipeline and access to individual likelihood estimates.

citation: Maceira-Elvira, P., Popa, T., Schmid, A.-C., Cadic-Melchior, A., Müller, H., & Schaer, R. (2024). Native learning ability and not age determines the effect of brain stimulation on motor skill acquisition. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00278-y
title: Assess an individual's likelihood of benefiting from stimulation before administering atDCS, to target those with less efficient learning mechanisms
description: The article proposes personalized clinical deployment of atDCS: "healthcare providers could assess the likelihood of an individual beneﬁting from stimulation based on a set of parameters related to the mechanism to be treated". Because stimulation benefits individuals with less efficient learning mechanisms and can harm those with optimal ones, screening baseline task performance narrows the administration scope and may increase efficacy in clinical applications. This requires identifying relevant parameters for each treated mechanism in advance.
requirements: Prior identification of parameters related to the mechanism to be treated (e.g., rehabilitation, memory)
constraints: The identified parameter set applies to a well-delimited context constituted by the finger-tapping task; additional investigations are needed for other behaviors and cognitive functions
target_learners: older and middle-aged adults undergoing motor rehabilitation or enhancement
target_learning_goals: improved acquisition of sequential motor skills through personalized neuromodulation
examples: In the article, the likelihood was assessed from a baseline block and first training block of the finger-tapping task before classifying participants into four learner tiers

article_title: Building dementia knowledge globally through the Understanding Dementia Massive Open Online Course (MOOC)
citation: Eccleston, C., Doherty, K., Bindoff, A., Robinson, A., Vickers, J. & McInerney, F. (2019). Building dementia knowledge globally through the Understanding Dementia Massive Open Online Course (MOOC). npj Science of Learning 4:3. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0042-4
title: Dementia Knowledge Assessment Scale 2.0 (DKAS 2.0)
description: The DKAS 2.0 is a reliable, validated survey used as the pre- and post-course outcome measure in this study. The article states it "comprises 25 items about the characteristics and trajectory of dementia, risk factors and aspects of caring for people with the condition", with items derived from a Delphi study of international experts. Responses are rescored 0–2 and summed to a 0–50 score, enabling objective measurement of knowledge acquisition rather than reliance on engagement or completion metrics.
requirements: Administered before any course content is delivered and again after completing the final unit, with only complete pre-post cases analysed
constraints: Score distribution post-UDMOOC was non-normal, so medians and bootstrap confidence intervals were used
target_learning_goals: Assessing essential dementia knowledge across characteristics, trajectory, risk factors and caring
examples: Used pre and post in the 2016 and 2017 UDMOOC offerings with 4894 complete respondents

citation: Eccleston, C., Doherty, K., Bindoff, A., Robinson, A., Vickers, J. & McInerney, F. (2019). Building dementia knowledge globally through the Understanding Dementia Massive Open Online Course (MOOC). npj Science of Learning 4:3. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0042-4
title: Understanding Dementia MOOC (UDMOOC)
description: The UDMOOC is a free, 9-week online course from the Wicking Dementia Research and Education Centre aiming to improve dementia knowledge in a broad international community. It covers "basic neurobiology, dementia pathophysiology, medical management and person-centred care", and its "design includes a conversational framework, video discussions, summaries and transcripts, discussion forums, games and quizzes". It was designed to maximise accessibility for non-traditional adult learners who may have low levels of previous education.
requirements: Open enrolment with no exclusion criteria; content designed for accessibility for learners with low previous education
constraints: Completion requires participants to finish the final unit before the post-test survey to be counted in the evaluation
target_learning_goals: Understanding brain pathology associated with dementia and how it affects the person, to help carers comprehend and respond to behaviour
examples: Delivered free online in 2016 and 2017, enrolling 20,061 and 29,039 participants across 117 and 132 countries respectively

citation: Eccleston, C., Doherty, K., Bindoff, A., Robinson, A., Vickers, J. & McInerney, F. (2019). Building dementia knowledge globally through the Understanding Dementia Massive Open Online Course (MOOC). npj Science of Learning 4:3. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0042-4
title: MOOCs should include objective, validated measures of knowledge acquisition rather than relying on engagement or completion metrics
description: The article argues that evidence of MOOC educational impact is limited because, as it observes, "Few MOOCs, include objective measures of knowledge acquisition, instead choosing primary outcome measures such as engagement, retention and completion as evidence of success." Building validated knowledge measures into the course itself allowed the UDMOOC evaluation to demonstrate actual knowledge gains across a broad cohort. The principle calls for embedding reliable outcome instruments in MOOC design so learning, not participation, is the success criterion.
requirements: A validated knowledge scale relevant to the course content must be administered pre- and post-course to evaluate learning outcomes
constraints: The authors note completion rates are insufficient as a measure of educational outcome
target_learners: Broad, diverse international MOOC cohorts including carers, health professionals and the general public
target_learning_goals: Demonstrating and verifying knowledge acquisition in massive open online courses
examples: The UDMOOC had the DKAS 2.0 built in as a pre-post measure, revealing gains from a median of 34.5 to 45

article_title: Differences in exam performance between pupils attending selective and non-selective schools mirror the genetic differences between them
citation: Smith-Woolley, E., Pingault, J.-B., Selzam, S., Rimfeld, K., Krapohl, E., von Stumm, S., Asbury, K., Dale, P. S., Young, T., Allen, R., Kovas, Y. & Plomin, R. (2018). Differences in exam performance between pupils attending selective and non-selective schools mirror the genetic differences between them. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0019-8
title: Gene-environment correlation (rGE) accounts for genetic differences between school types: selection on heritable traits makes school assignment genetically structured
description: The article offers gene-environment correlation as the explanatory framework for its findings: 'genetic factors are contributing to variation in educational environments'. Children are 'intentionally phenotypically selected, but unintentionally genetically selected' into school types because the traits schools select on—ability, achievement, SES—are heritable. The authors distinguish evocative rGE (being selected on genetically influenced traits) from active rGE (children selecting environments correlating with their genotype), and note that academically gifted children tend to come from academically gifted parents who 'not only provide the genes but also the environments to help them progress academically'.
requirements: A polygenic score for a heritable selection-relevant trait and measures of the selection factors schools use
constraints: The article notes the majority of variation in EduYears GPS occurs within school type, not between types (d = 0.41 implies approximately 83% distribution overlap)
target_learners: Secondary-school students in England transitioning at age 11 across state non-selective, grammar and private school types
target_learning_goals: Educational achievement at age 16 (GCSE composite of English, mathematics and science)
examples: The study found mean EduYears GPS differences between school types that vanished after controlling for heritable selection factors, which the authors interpret as unintentional genetic selection via phenotypic selection

citation: Smith-Woolley, E., Pingault, J.-B., Selzam, S., Rimfeld, K., Krapohl, E., von Stumm, S., Asbury, K., Dale, P. S., Young, T., Allen, R., Kovas, Y. & Plomin, R. (2018). Differences in exam performance between pupils attending selective and non-selective schools mirror the genetic differences between them. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0019-8
title: Attend to pupil-selection factors before attributing achievement gaps to school type: schools matter, but the type of school explains under 1% of achievement variance after controls
description: This principle holds that apparent advantages of selective schooling should be attributed to the heritable pupil characteristics used in admission rather than to school value added, since after controls 'the type of school that a child attends explains less than one percent of the individual differences in educational achievement'. The authors caution that 'by finding a small effect of school type, we are not saying schools are unimportant, or that teaching does not work'—schools matter, but school type appears less important.
requirements: Measures of prior achievement, prior ability and family SES, ideally alongside a polygenic score, available before school-type effects are estimated
constraints: The GCSE measure was a composite of only three core subjects (English, mathematics, science); for other subjects school type may have a greater influence
Grammar and private schools are unevenly distributed geographically, which the authors addressed by splitting non-selective schools by area selectivity
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement at the end of compulsory education (GCSE)
examples: The study compared unadjusted GCSE gaps (d = 1.05 vs grammar) with gaps after hierarchical regression controls, showing the advantage fell to betas of 0.03 (grammar) and 0.07 (private)

article_title: Offline consolidation mechanisms of the retrieval practice effect: an analysis based on EEG signal characteristics
citation: Jing Zhang, Xiaoning Huo, Hongbo Lv, Jiahua Xu & Xiaofeng Ma. (2025). Offline consolidation mechanisms of the retrieval practice effect: an analysis based on EEG signal characteristics. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00349-8
title: Dual-phase consolidation model of retrieval-practiced memories
description: The authors propose a model in which "memory strengthwithin this dichotomous framework develops progressively through ofﬂine processes." Under feedback-free retrieval practice, successfully retrieved items are encoded only once and form conceptually-related semantic memory networks that during sleep "are repeatedly reactivated and replayed, gradually enhancing memory strength." Conversely, restudy tasks do not trigger replay because no relevant semantic networks form during online learning, and feedback-based retrieval does not require offline reprocessing because it "achieve[s] immediate pathway correction via online monitoring mechanisms." The model aligns with the Complementary Learning Systems framework, positing that sleep enhances memory stability through post-retrieval integration and consolidation of semantic networks.
requirements: Requires an offline sleep period following encoding for the no-feedback consolidation pathway to operate
Applies to weakly encoded, feedback-free retrieval-practice memories rather than strongly encoded traces
constraints: The correlational electrophysiological evidence precludes definitive causal inferences about the role of slow wave-spindle coupling in memory
The proposed mechanism is framed within a dichotomous strength framework and rests on nap rather than full-night sleep data
target_learners: Undergraduate learners memorizing paired associative materials
target_learning_goals: Long-term retention of weakly associated verbal material
examples: The nap-vs-wake experiment assigned participants across restudy, retrieval practice with feedback, and retrieval practice without feedback conditions with 90-minute and 24-hour tests

article_title: What students do when encountering failure in collaborative tasks
citation: Rachel Lam. (2019). What students do when encountering failure in collaborative tasks. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0045-1
title: Preparation for Future Collaboration (PFC): a three-phase productive-failure design with phase-specific cognitive mechanisms
description: Preparation for Future Collaboration adapts Productive Failure by splitting exploration into two phases. As the article states, "there are three phases of activity in the PFC design: (1) individual exploration, (2) continued exploration in peer collaboration, and (3) explicit instruction by a teacher." Individual exploration activates prior knowledge and attends to critical features; collaboration engages explaining, elaboration, differentiation, and early knowledge assembly; explicit instruction supports consolidation and assembly of canonical knowledge. The article uses this design as the setting in which micro-failures were observed.
requirements: An exploratory generation task prior to formal instruction, followed by teacher-led explicit instruction presenting canonical concepts
constraints: Cognitive mechanisms engaged during collaboration are inferred; the article notes mechanisms are the same as in productive failure but distributed differently across PFC phases
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of canonical concepts (e.g., the four R's of waste reduction)
examples: The prior study implemented PFC in two fourth-grade classes: individual question items on the four R's, partner collaboration to reach joint decisions, then explicit teacher instruction on the four R's
key_sources: Rachel Lam. (2019). What students do when encountering failure in collaborative tasks. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0045-1

article_title: What students do when encountering failure in collaborative tasks
citation: Rachel Lam. (2019). What students do when encountering failure in collaborative tasks. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0045-1
title: Micro-failures: failure conceptualized as recognizable in-process iterations of uncertainty and response during learning
description: Drawing on Tawfik, Rong, and Choi, the article adopts a process view of failure rather than a static end-product view. As the article states, they "coin the term "micro-failures," which specifically refer to iterations where a learner recognizes an uncertainty while working through a task and then has the opportunity to respond to improve understanding." Student dialogs during collaboration make these iterations visible in ways end-products like solutions cannot. The framework connects failure recognition to cognitive mechanisms of assimilation, disequilibrium/cognitive conflict, an inquiry state, and mental-model restructuring, cycling at each recognition of failure.
requirements: Tasks that implicitly surface knowledge gaps so learners can overtly display awareness of impasses, and opportunities to respond to those impasses
constraints: The framework is applied in this article to dialogs from dyadic collaboration in a single environmental-sustainability topic with fourth graders
target_learning_goals: recognizing and responding to knowledge gaps during collaborative problem solving
examples: Micro-failure episodes were operationalized as moments of overtly displayed impasse: verbalized uncertainty, disagreement, questions, long pauses, or hedges
key_sources: Rachel Lam. (2019). What students do when encountering failure in collaborative tasks. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0045-1

article_title: What students do when encountering failure in collaborative tasks
citation: Rachel Lam. (2019). What students do when encountering failure in collaborative tasks. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0045-1
title: Nine-category coding scheme for dialogic behaviors within micro-failure episodes
description: The article developed and validated a coding scheme for student behaviors during micro-failure episodes in collaborative dialog. As reported, "We identified nine categories of behaviors that occurred within failure episodes in the dialogs: questioning and explaining with a partner, explaining after teacher prompts, arguing to consensus, initiating teacher help, making a quick choice without consensus, arguing without consensus, quick arguing with a dominating partner, ignoring contributions and moving forward, and going off task." Two raters independently coded 20 percent of episodes with sufficient interrater agreement (κ = 0.72, P < 0.01), and the scheme underpinned the Functional/Dysfunctional grouping and all subsequent analyses.
requirements: Verbatim transcripts of student dialogs; micro-failure episodes segmented by overt displays of impasse (uncertainty, disagreement, questioning, pauses, hedges)
constraints: Developed and applied to dyadic dialogs from a single fourth-grade environmental-sustainability task; more than one code could occur in a single episode
target_learners: primary school students working in dyads
target_learning_goals: identifying dialogic behaviors during failure episodes that relate to conceptual learning
examples: The scheme's Table 1 gives real discourse excerpts for each code, such as a dyad questioning and explaining about whether an item is refuse or reuse
key_sources: Rachel Lam. (2019). What students do when encountering failure in collaborative tasks. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0045-1

article_title: No guts, no glory: underestimating the benefits of providing children with mechanistic details
citation: Chuey, A., McCarthy, A., Lockhart, K., Trouche, E., Sheskin, M. & Keil, F. (2021). No guts, no glory: underestimating the benefits of providing children with mechanistic details. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00108-5
title: Expose young children to detailed causal mechanisms rather than omitting them, because exposure yields concrete memory plus abstract system-level knowledge that supports epistemic evaluation
description: The article argues educators should not strip mechanistic details from instruction for young children. A seven-minute adult-level video on a combustion engine gave 6–9-year-olds concrete memory for parts and, from around age 8, abstract causal patterns supporting expert detection: children "not only learned a surprising amount, but were notably engaged". Mechanistic exposure may also support relearning, generalization, categorization and induction.
requirements: Access to mechanistically rich material (e.g., a video of how a complex system works) rather than isolated facts alone
constraints: Findings come from a single mechanical system and a small subset of causal patterns; they may not generalize to biology or economics mechanisms
Classrooms should assess more than memory for details, since detail-only assessment can make complex mechanisms seem out of learners' reach
target_learning_goals: abstract causal understanding of complex systems
epistemic evaluation of informants' expertise
examples: 180 children were shown a seven-minute adult-level video about an internal combustion engine and tested immediately or one week later against a no-video control
key_sources: Chuey, A., McCarthy, A., Lockhart, K., Trouche, E., Sheskin, M. & Keil, F. (2021). No guts, no glory: underestimating the benefits of providing children with mechanistic details. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00108-5

article_title: Longitudinal markers of cognitive procedural learning in fronto-striatal circuits and putative effects of a BDNF plasticity-related variant
citation: Lena S. Geiger, Torsten Wüstenberg, Zhenxiang Zang, Mirjam Melzer, Stephanie H. Witt, Marcella Rietschel, Markus M. Nöthen, Stefan Herms, Franziska Degenhardt, Andreas Meyer-Lindenberg & Carolin Moessnang. (2024). Longitudinal markers of cognitive procedural learning in fronto-striatal circuits and putative effects of a BDNF plasticity-related variant. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00282-2
title: Adaptive Control of Thought (ACT) three-stage model of procedural learning
description: The article adopts the ACT model, a behavioral account of procedural memory in which procedural learning occurs in three main stages: an initial encoding drawing heavily on cognitive demands with rapid performance improvement, a reactivation-and-modification stage with a gradually reached performance plateau, and a transition to longer-term retention with stable, automatized performance at reduced cognitive demand. The study uses this framework to motivate hypotheses about exponential behavioral learning curves and declining fronto-striatal activation, citing reduced brain activation as the neural signature of automatization.
requirements: Repeated training across multiple sessions so that the staged transition from controlled to automatized performance can be observed longitudinally.
constraints: The article notes that most imaging evidence for reduced activation comes from pre-post designs, which do not allow modeling based on the law of practice assumption.
target_learners: healthy young adults performing verbal working memory tasks
target_learning_goals: procedural learning and automatization of cognitive skills
examples: The study tested ACT-derived hypotheses with a modified Sternberg task across five fMRI sessions, fitting linear and exponential learning curves to behavior and to activation in 246 Brainnetome parcels.
key_sources: Lena S. Geiger, Torsten Wüstenberg, Zhenxiang Zang, Mirjam Melzer, Stephanie H. Witt, Marcella Rietschel, Markus M.
