article_title: Unveiling the impact of goal types: enhancing self-efficacy in rehabilitation robotics
citation: Tsuda, A., Manalo, E., Teramae, T., & Noda, T. (2026). Unveiling the Impact of Goal Types: Enhancing Self-Efficacy in Rehabilitation Robotics. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00444-4
title: Four goal structures (process, outcome, shift, transform) adapted from Zimmerman's framework for robot-assisted motor learning
description: The study adapts Zimmerman and colleagues' goal-type framework into four manipulated conditions for exoskeleton-assisted practice. In the robot context, "outcome-goal participants focused on achieving the highest score and verbally reported their scores after each throw," process-goal participants concentrated on executing key movement components, transform-goal participants monitored outcomes and reported adjustments, and shift-goal participants began with movement execution before shifting to performance outcomes. The framework assumes skill acquisition proceeds through phases, with outcome goals suited to later, procedurally stable stages.
requirements: Learners must be able to verbalize their goal focus during practice, as all goal conditions required spoken self-reports
constraints: Derived from non-clinical, healthy, novice learners in a single session; generalizability of the stage-based ordering to clinical rehabilitation populations is untested
target_learners: adult novices learning a motor skill with assistive robotics
target_learning_goals: upper-limb motor skill acquisition
self-efficacy during robot-assisted practice
examples: The experiment assigned 100 participants to the four goal conditions or a practice-only control during 15 minutes of robot-assisted boccia practice
key_sources: Tsuda, A., Manalo, E., Teramae, T., & Noda, T. (2026). Unveiling the Impact of Goal Types: Enhancing Self-Efficacy in Rehabilitation Robotics. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00444-4

article_title: Unveiling the impact of goal types: enhancing self-efficacy in rehabilitation robotics
citation: Tsuda, A., Manalo, E., Teramae, T., & Noda, T. (2026). Unveiling the Impact of Goal Types: Enhancing Self-Efficacy in Rehabilitation Robotics. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00444-4
title: Decompose rehabilitation goals into achievable components and continually adjust them to sustain self-efficacy
description: The article argues that rehabilitation professionals should break overarching goals into manageable parts and update them as patients progress, because goal proximity and attainable standards sustain self-efficacy and motivation. It states that "physicians and other rehabilitation professionals must decompose overarching goals into achievable components and continually adjust them based on patients' progress in order to sustain self-efficacy, maintain motivation, and ultimately promote performance gains." This follows from the study's finding that high self-efficacy did not by itself produce performance gains, implying goals must remain proximal and attainable over time.
requirements: Accurate assessment of patients' current abilities so decomposed goals stay closely connected to current attainment
constraints: The article's own findings come from healthy novices in a single session; the recommendation is argued for rehabilitation contexts rather than tested clinically in this study
target_learning_goals: sustaining self-efficacy across rehabilitation
motor performance improvement through attainable goal progression
examples: The authors recommend SMART goals and structured team meetings with standardized measurements and ongoing progress monitoring as implementation practices
key_sources: Tsuda, A., Manalo, E., Teramae, T., & Noda, T. (2026). Unveiling the Impact of Goal Types: Enhancing Self-Efficacy in Rehabilitation Robotics. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00444-4

article_title: A strategic mindset predicts and promotes effective learning and academic performance
citation: Chen, P., Teo, Q.K., Foo, D.X.Y., Jiang, Y., Sun, L., Ong, X.L., Neo, D., Pereira, D.J.H., Tan, B., Chua, K.Q., Gan, J.X.F. & Ong, D.C. (2025). A strategic mindset predicts and promotes effective learning and academic performance. npj Science of Learning, 10:74. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00367-6
title: Strategic mindset: a self-prompting orientation toward strategy-eliciting questions
description: A strategic mindset is a psychological orientation in which learners frequently ask themselves questions that prompt access and use of task-appropriate methods, especially when facing difficulty or unproductivity. The article defines it as "an orientation toward asking oneself questions that elicit the access and use of task-appropriate methods." It is conceptually and empirically distinct from both growth mindset of intelligence and general metacognitive strategy use, functioning as a trigger mechanism that converts moments of difficulty into opportunities for strategy generation rather than helpless responses.
requirements: The learner must encounter moments of difficulty or unproductivity that serve as cues to trigger strategy-eliciting self-questioning
constraints: Distinct from a growth mindset of intelligence and from general metacognitive strategy use per prior factor analyses cited in the article
target_learners: Adolescent and adult students in academic settings
target_learning_goals: Self-regulated learning and effective strategy use during academic tasks
key_sources: Chen, P., Teo, Q.K., Foo, D.X.Y., Jiang, Y., Sun, L., Ong, X.L., Neo, D., Pereira, D.J.H., Tan, B., Chua, K.Q., Gan, J.X.F. & Ong, D.C. (2025). A strategic mindset predicts and promotes effective learning and academic performance. npj Science of Learning, 10:74. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00367-6

article_title: A strategic mindset predicts and promotes effective learning and academic performance
citation: Chen, P., Teo, Q.K., Foo, D.X.Y., Jiang, Y., Sun, L., Ong, X.L., Neo, D., Pereira, D.J.H., Tan, B., Chua, K.Q., Gan, J.X.F. & Ong, D.C. (2025). A strategic mindset predicts and promotes effective learning and academic performance. npj Science of Learning, 10:74. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00367-6
title: Online self-administered strategic mindset intervention for secondary school students
description: A scalable, cost-effective online exercise (~40 minutes) that adolescents can self-administer in classrooms. It involves "learning about the common challenges that Secondary school students often face; hearing other students'testimonials about how they had used the strategic mindset psychology to overcome these challenges, to make progress, and to learn better"; reading scientific evidence; identifying personal strategy-eliciting questions; and committing to more effective learning approaches. Crucially, it does not train specific strategies but teaches the value of self-prompting.
requirements: Delivery in a classroom environment with sufficient peer engagement and minimal disruption for fidelity
Students need some existing repertoire of learning strategies to benefit maximally
constraints: Did not include training in specific learning strategies; conveyed via slides rather than videos due to technical limitations in some schools
target_learners: Secondary school students (ages 13–17) in public school classrooms
target_learning_goals: Increasing use of effective learning strategies when studying for exams and improving exam performance
examples: Randomly assigned 1070 Secondary 2–4 students in 77 classes across 6 schools to the strategic mindset exercise or a similarly structured control about co-curricular activities, measuring later strategy use and final exam scores.

article_title: Developmental brain dynamics of numerical and arithmetic abilities
citation: Stephan E. Vogel and Bert De Smedt. (2021). Developmental brain dynamics of numerical and arithmetic abilities. npj Science of Learning (2021) 6:22. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00099-3
title: Dynamic interaction of domain-specific and domain-general brain networks in numerical and arithmetic development
description: The review's organizing framework holds that numerical and arithmetic development cannot be reduced to a single mechanism or brain region; instead, domain-specific functions (e.g., quantity and symbol representations) and domain-general functions (e.g., working memory, visual-spatial reasoning) interact on a continuum. The authors state that "The involved brain dynamics are, therefore, best described as an interaction of multiple brain regions/networks that vary along a functional continuum" (Fig. 1, Fig. 3). The framework underpins the review's account of typical development, dyscalculia, and education effects.
requirements: Interpretation requires considering task constraints, age, ability level, education and environmental factors the review lists as modulators of the networks
constraints: The review states the classification of domain-specific and domain-general is rather continuous than categorical
Many causal questions about these networks remain open because longitudinal evidence is lacking
target_learners: children from infancy through primary school
target_learning_goals: numerical and arithmetic abilities
examples: The review's Fig. 1 depicts the triple-code components (approximate, visual, verbal number representations) with auxiliary domain-general functions such as working memory and executive functions interacting with numerical and arithmetic abilities
key_sources: Stephan E. Vogel and Bert De Smedt. (2021). Developmental brain dynamics of numerical and arithmetic abilities. npj Science of Learning (2021) 6:22. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00099-3

article_title: DIY productive failure: boosting performance in a large undergraduate biology course
citation: Sunita G. Chowrira, Karen M. Smith, Patrick J. Dubois and Ido Roll. (2019). DIY productive failure: boosting performance in a large undergraduate biology course. npj Science of Learning 4:1. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0040-6
title: DIY productive failure cycle for large university classes: Exploration then Consolidation with pre-reading
description: A lesson-level pattern reversing conventional instruction: students attempt challenging, open-ended problems in small groups before explicit instruction, then receive consolidation built on their own solutions. Class time "contained two main phases, an Exploration phase and a Consolidation phase", preceded by the course's standard pre-reading and quiz. Student responses collected during Exploration become the raw material for Clicker-based formative feedback and an instructor-led Walkthrough that models expert problem-solving while eliciting student contributions.
requirements: Pre-reading assignments so students arrive with activated prior knowledge and basic vocabulary
Problems designed at higher Bloom's levels that are challenging but not frustrating
Moderate metacognitive prompts during Exploration to prevent frustration-driven disengagement
constraints: First iterations without moderate support led many students to give up out of frustration
target_learners: first-year university students in large-enrollment science courses
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of complex processes such as DNA replication and transcription and translation
examples: In the Transcription and Translation activity, students designed the process to mimic a cell starting from a given DNA sequence, reasoning about parts, roles, and order
key_sources: Sunita G. Chowrira, Karen M. Smith, Patrick J. Dubois and Ido Roll. (2019). DIY productive failure: boosting performance in a large undergraduate biology course. npj Science of Learning 4:1. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0040-6

article_title: DIY productive failure: boosting performance in a large undergraduate biology course
citation: Sunita G. Chowrira, Karen M. Smith, Patrick J. Dubois and Ido Roll. (2019). DIY productive failure: boosting performance in a large undergraduate biology course. npj Science of Learning 4:1. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0040-6
title: Depth of search and availability of solution as mechanisms explaining PF's advantage over active learning
description: The authors' explanatory account of why PF outperformed AL when both conditions were active. Building on Loibl et al.'s mechanisms (prior knowledge activation, awareness of knowledge gaps, recognition of deep features), they "attribute the difference in learning between conditions in our study to two factors: depth of search and availability of solution." Quick clicker feedback in AL does not give students time to fully understand problem requirements, whereas PF's extended struggle does; and having the canonical solution available in AL may encourage accepting it "at face value" without dissecting its deep structure.
requirements: Both conditions must already provide active learning support for the mechanism account to be needed
constraints: Offered as the authors' interpretation of a quasi-experiment, not a directly tested mechanism
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding and recognition of deep features of domain processes
examples: The authors note some evidence that self-generated feedback during PF's first phase may support better learning than only external feedback
key_sources: Sunita G. Chowrira, Karen M. Smith, Patrick J. Dubois and Ido Roll. (2019). DIY productive failure: boosting performance in a large undergraduate biology course. npj Science of Learning 4:1. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0040-6

article_title: DIY productive failure: boosting performance in a large undergraduate biology course
citation: Sunita G. Chowrira, Karen M. Smith, Patrick J. Dubois and Ido Roll. (2019). DIY productive failure: boosting performance in a large undergraduate biology course. npj Science of Learning 4:1. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0040-6
title: Course instructors can design and implement PF themselves (DIY PF) and still obtain gains over established active learning
description: PF's effectiveness had been shown mainly in lessons designed and taught by learning scientists; this study tested a "Do-it-Yourself" approach in which disciplinary-expert instructors designed and implemented PF with advice from a learning scientist but no activity-specific feedback. The authors argue "Implementation by instructors (disciplinary experts) is an impor tant hurdle that novel pedagogies should clear before they can be considered relevant to a wider audience," and the results support scalability and ecological validity of PF in post-secondary biology.
requirements: Iterative refinement to achieve fidelity of PF implementation
General design guidelines (e.g., from Kapur and Bielaczyc) plus advice from a learning scientist on motivation, literature, and design principles
constraints: Only one instructor taught PF; transfer to instructors with even less support remains untested
Quasi-experimental design with self-selected sections, compensated statistically
target_learners: first-year university students in large-enrollment courses
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding in discipline-specific topics
examples: The PF instructor designed activities from Kapur and Bielaczyc's guidelines with a learning scientist providing only general emphases, not activity-specific feedback
key_sources: Sunita G. Chowrira, Karen M. Smith, Patrick J. Dubois and Ido Roll. (2019). DIY productive failure: boosting performance in a large undergraduate biology course. npj Science of Learning 4:1. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0040-6

article_title: Learning to adaptively cooperate through social interactions during childhood and adolescence
citation: Zhang, R., Zhang, L., Hao, X.-M., Dreher, J.-C., & Qu, C. (2026). Learning to adaptively cooperate through social interactions during childhood and adolescence. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00423-9
title: Developmental reinforcement-learning framework of reward-based versus belief-based social learning in the Chicken game
description: The article builds a hierarchical Bayesian reinforcement-learning framework contrasting a reward-based model that updates action values from experienced payoffs via Rescorla-Wagner prediction errors, a belief-based model that tracks the opponent's probability of choosing Swerve, and a second-order belief model additionally tracking opponents' second-order beliefs. Each family had sub-models with one or two learning rates and a preference parameter θ. The framework was applied to a child-friendly Chicken game against pre-programmed high-competitive and low-competitive opponents across five age groups, with "lower values indicate better out-of-sample prediction accuracy" for LOOIC model comparison.
requirements: Repeated interaction with opponents whose behavioral tendencies can be manipulated, plus trial-by-trial choice data suitable for hierarchical Bayesian fitting
constraints: The second-order belief model did not fit the current data well in children
The authors note findings are based on a specific strategic interaction paradigm and may depend on the structure of the task and payoff matrix
target_learning_goals: adaptive social decision-making in social dilemmas
learning opponents' behavioral tendencies
examples: Study 1 used a simplified payoff matrix without negative losses for preschoolers, while Study 2 used a full matrix with losses for ages 6-17
key_sources: Zhang, R., Zhang, L., Hao, X.-M., Dreher, J.-C., & Qu, C. (2026). Learning to adaptively cooperate through social interactions during childhood and adolescence. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00423-9

article_title: Timing of reward cues alters the interaction between reward and interest on memory over time
citation: Zhongyu Hu & Jiongjiong Yang. (2025). Timing of reward cues alters the interaction between reward and interest on memory over time. npj Science of Learning 10:82. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00374-7
title: Reward-cue timing framework: controlling quality of rewards determines encoding priority and selective consolidation of reward- versus interest-associated information
description: The article proposes that manipulating the timing of reward cues "influences the controlling quality of extrinsic reward, alters the relative priority of reward and intrinsic motivation, and in turn modulates the allocation of encoding resources". Pre-clip cues make reward a controlling factor that enhances salience of rewarded stimuli, while post-clip cues preserve intrinsic motivation so high-interest stimuli guide encoding. Both patterns then depend on selective, sleep-associated consolidation, consistent with the dopaminergic memory consolidation hypothesis and the adaptive memory consolidation framework.
requirements: Reward cues must be temporally separated from encoding (before vs. after stimuli) to manipulate controlling quality
constraints: The interactive effects emerged only at the 1-day delay, not at immediate testing
Findings were obtained with film clips and intentional memory instructions; the authors note future studies could use other material types, such as trivia questions, to replicate
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of learned material
examples: Experiment 1 cued rewards before film clips and found memory enhancement for low-interest clips at 1 day; Experiment 2 cued rewards after clips and found enhancement for high-interest clips at 1 day
key_sources: Zhongyu Hu & Jiongjiong Yang. (2025). Timing of reward cues alters the interaction between reward and interest on memory over time. npj Science of Learning 10:82. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00374-7

article_title: Fragmented learning from short videos modulates neural activity and connectivity during memory retrieval
citation: Wei, M., Liu, J., Wang, H., Li, Q. & Dong, G.-H. (2026). Fragmented learning from short videos modulates neural activity and connectivity during memory retrieval. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00399-y
title: Fragmented-input deficit account: short-video format disrupts information integration, cognitive control, and semantic processing during memory retrieval
description: The article's explanatory framework holds that the fragmented, fast-paced structure of short videos — not multitasking — impairs memory by disrupting three interrelated brain systems. The authors state that "learning through short videos impairs memory by disrupting brain systems involved in information integration, cognitive control, and semantic processing": reduced claustrum activation reflects difficulty reconstructing a coherent situational representation, reduced caudate activation reflects weakened top-down control, and reduced MTG activation reflects impeded deep semantic processing. Rapid context-switching may reset event boundaries, hindering integration of continuous semantic cues even in a single-viewing context.
requirements: A memory task following video exposure, with neural measures of retrieval-phase activity and connectivity
constraints: The authors state the MTG interpretation "remains a preliminary interpretation and requires further empirical validation"
fMRI does not allow direct inference of causality or temporal dynamics
the sample was drawn from a college student population, which may limit generalizability
target_learners: university students (Mage = 20.95) learning factual video content
target_learning_goals: memory formation and retrieval of factual video content
examples: Participants watched either a single continuous 10-minute clip or 7 matched short segments (30 seconds to 2.5 minutes) before an immediate four-alternative forced-choice memory test during fMRI scanning
key_sources: Wei, M., Liu, J., Wang, H., Li, Q. & Dong, G.-H. (2026). Fragmented learning from short videos modulates neural activity and connectivity during memory retrieval. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00399-y

article_title: Target configuration determines how and what we learn during sensorimotor adaptation
citation: Villavicencio, P., Tsay, J. S. & de la Malla, C. (2025). Target configuration determines how and what we learn during sensorimotor adaptation. npj Science of Learning 10:89. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00379-2
title: Training-context determines both the learning processes engaged (implicit vs explicit) and the representations formed (gain vs translation)
description: An account in which the spatial layout of training targets biases which learning processes are engaged and what representation of the perturbation is formed. The authors propose that "an extent-based layout may naturally prime a gain-based rule" and that if implicit and explicit systems compete for error reduction, reduced residual error suppresses implicit adaptation; alternatively, extent and angle may engage different sensorimotor populations with differing plasticity. Angular layouts may require greater attentional resources, hindering strategy discovery and increasing implicit reliance.
requirements: Training context must be manipulated while holding the perturbation and shared target constant to attribute process and representation differences to target configuration.
constraints: The authors note three candidate mechanisms (selective modulation of implicit learning, of explicit learning, or of general cognitive resources) and state future studies are needed to disentangle these possibilities.
target_learners: Adult participants performing goal-directed reaching tasks
target_learning_goals: Sensorimotor adaptation to visuomotor gain perturbations, including implicit calibration and explicit strategy formation
examples: Extent training (two amplitudes, one direction) versus Angular training (two directions, one amplitude) with a shared 11 cm training target across two experiments (1.3× and 0.7× gain).
key_sources: Villavicencio, P., Tsay, J. S. & de la Malla, C. (2025). Target configuration determines how and what we learn during sensorimotor adaptation. npj Science of Learning 10:89. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00379-2

article_title: Utilizing epigenetics to study the shared nature of development and biological aging across the lifespan
citation: Raffington, L. (2024). Utilizing epigenetics to study the shared nature of development and biological aging across the lifespan. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00239-5
title: Theories of development and biological aging differ in whether aging and development are coupled or distinct processes
description: The article organizes competing biological and psychological theories of how development relates to aging (Table 1), including antagonistic pleiotropy, DOHaD, disposable soma, life history theory, the Ground Zero Model, lifespan psychology, and the pseudo-programmatic theory, under which "the ticking of epigenetic clocks reﬂects the continuation of developmental processes". These theories yield contrasting predictions for whether methylation profile scores of child development should correlate with adult biological aging. The article uses them to frame testable competing hypotheses about fast versus slow early development forecasting midlife aging.
requirements: Testing the theories empirically requires molecular quantifications of child development and longitudinal cohorts spanning childhood into adulthood
constraints: The article notes the theories have historically resided in philosophy due to lack of empirical investigation
target_learning_goals: understanding how childhood development and experience relate to later-life biological aging and plasticity
examples: The article contrasts evolutionary life history theory (children who develop faster age faster) with DOHaD (children who develop slower age faster), predicting a non-linear relation if both are true
key_sources: Raffington, L. (2024). Utilizing epigenetics to study the shared nature of development and biological aging across the lifespan. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00239-5

article_title: Utilizing epigenetics to study the shared nature of development and biological aging across the lifespan
citation: Raffington, L. (2024). Utilizing epigenetics to study the shared nature of development and biological aging across the lifespan. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00239-5
title: Generations of methylation profile scores as biomarkers of biological aging and related phenotypes
description: The article describes methylation profile scores (MPSs) computed from genome-wide DNA methylation, organized in generations: first-generation "epigenetic clocks" trained on chronological age that track it with correlation coefficients upwards of r = 0.95; second-generation measures (GrimAge, PhenoAge) trained on cross-sectional physiology and mortality; and third-generation measures such as DunedinPACE capturing longitudinal multisystem decline. Table 2 lists each measure's tissue, training criterion, and interpretation, including MPSs of inflammation, BMI, and Epigenetic-g for cognitive performance.
requirements: Genome-wide DNAm measurement technology and discovery samples large enough (thousands of individuals) to train predictive algorithms
constraints: Next-generation measures were developed in adult blood samples, so their cross-tissue and cross-age applicability must be considered
target_learning_goals: quantifying biological aging and cognitive performance as molecular readouts linking development and aging
examples: Table 2 lists DunedinPACE trained on 19 years of follow-up in 19 system-integrity biomarkers, interpreted as years of physiological decline per calendar year
key_sources: Raffington, L. (2024). Utilizing epigenetics to study the shared nature of development and biological aging across the lifespan. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00239-5

article_title: The neural and cognitive basis of expository text comprehension
citation: Keller, T. A., Mason, R. A., Legg, A. E., & Just, M. A. (2024). The neural and cognitive basis of expository text comprehension. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00232-y
title: Make instructional technical texts more cohesive by explicitly relating different types of information across sentences and paragraphs
description: Because passage difficulty was modulated by processes that bind together different types of information from distributed cortical areas, the authors recommend engineering texts so such relations are explicit. They suggest "Explicit cohesive devices that can be incorporated across sentences and paragraphs include overlap of arguments and clear indications of causal, temporal, and spatial relations that are not overtly stated." Cohesion facilitates coherence and improves discourse comprehension, consistent with prior educational research.
requirements: Texts must make relations among different types of information explicit, using argument overlap and clear causal, temporal, and spatial relation indicators.
constraints: The present study did not find reliable correlations between passage comprehension and cohesion measures; the materials were not designed to vary greatly in cohesion.
target_learners: Readers of technical instructional texts in STEM and technical education
target_learning_goals: Improved comprehensibility and retention of technical text content
examples: Passages that were harder to comprehend "inadequately interrelate different types of information, evoking additional integrative and inferential processing" in the study.
key_sources: Keller, T. A., Mason, R. A., Legg, A. E., & Just, M. A. (2024). The neural and cognitive basis of expository text comprehension. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00232-y

article_title: Constructivist developmental theory is needed in developmental neuroscience
citation: Arsalidou, M. & Pascual-Leone, J. (2016). Constructivist developmental theory is needed in developmental neuroscience. npj Science of Learning 1, 16016. https://doi.org/10.1038/npjscilearn.2016.16
title: Pascual-Leone's Theory of Constructive Operators (TCO): mental-attentional capacity as measurable maturational driver of developmental stages
description: TCO is a neo-Piagetian causal model of organismic processing that explains Piaget's descriptive stage theory from a metasubjective perspective "from within the subject's own processes". Behaviour is generated by general-purpose hidden operators modulating self-propelling schemes under "a principle of overdetermination" whereby performance is determined by the dominant set of activated compatible schemes. It offers a theory-guided measurement method quantifying mental-attention demand of tasks and capacity per stage, with capacity increasing one symbolic-processing unit every other year after age 3, reaching seven units at about 15–16 years.
requirements: Process-task analysis to quantify the mental-attention demand of tasks and the mental-attentional capacity available at each developmental stage
constraints: Capacity of seven units is obtained only when all necessary schemes, figurative and operative, and their essential parameters have been counted; adults often function mobilising at most a capacity of five unless highly motivated and challenged
target_learners: children and adolescents across developmental stages
target_learning_goals: explaining cognitive-development constraints on task performance and problem solving
examples: The article applies TCO to advise against averaging brain responses across wide age ranges and to guide age-group selection via the trade-off between task mental demand and mental-attentional capacity
key_sources: Arsalidou, M. & Pascual-Leone, J. (2016). Constructivist developmental theory is needed in developmental neuroscience. npj Science of Learning 1, 16016. https://doi.org/10.1038/npjscilearn.2016.16

article_title: Constructivist developmental theory is needed in developmental neuroscience
citation: Arsalidou, M. & Pascual-Leone, J. (2016). Constructivist developmental theory is needed in developmental neuroscience. npj Science of Learning 1, 16016. https://doi.org/10.1038/npjscilearn.2016.16
title: Five categorical modes of processing proposed as a more comprehensive alternative to dual-process theories
description: The article argues dual-process (type 1/type 2) theories are descriptively valid but neither comprehensive enough nor formulated from within the person's processing, and lack developmental data. It proposes distinguishing five categorical modes of processing: (1) the intuitive meaning-bearing experiential mode, (2) affective-motivational schemes and processes, (3) the explicit logical and linguistic mode, (4) sociocultural and sociomotivational processes, and (5) the brain's hidden operators and executive control processes. Each mode is claimed to be explicitly expressed in the brain, and distinguishing them should permit comprehensive neuroscientific interpretation.
requirements: Distinguishing the categorial modes of processing to permit comprehensive neuroscientific interpretations
constraints: Dual-process theories lack developmental data and are not organismic in a comprehensive way, discussing only two of many dimensions of variation
target_learners: children and adults whose processing is interpreted in neuroscience studies
target_learning_goals: interpreting relations between cognition, brain processes and development
examples: The article maps type-2 processing to the experiential mode and type-1 to automatised explicit linguistic processing, and links gist-versus-verbatim fuzzy-trace processing to scheme-based overdetermination
key_sources: Arsalidou, M. & Pascual-Leone, J. (2016). Constructivist developmental theory is needed in developmental neuroscience. npj Science of Learning 1, 16016. https://doi.org/10.1038/npjscilearn.2016.16

article_title: Constructivist developmental theory is needed in developmental neuroscience
citation: Arsalidou, M. & Pascual-Leone, J. (2016). Constructivist developmental theory is needed in developmental neuroscience. npj Science of Learning 1, 16016. https://doi.org/10.1038/npjscilearn.2016.16
title: Misleading versus facilitating tasks: misleading situations reliably assess effective complexity of mental attention
description: The article distinguishes misleading tasks, which activate mutually incompatible schemes competing for application (e.g., dual-task paradigms and backward span tasks), from facilitating tasks solvable with habitual automatised schemes, such as standard forward span tasks. Misleading situations "can assess effective complexity reliably — whereas facilitating situations, common in learning/memory paradigms and psychometric-intelligence tasks, do not". Effective complexity is indexed by the number of effortfully activated task-relevant schemes required, and these situations show developmental performance discontinuities subtending stages.
requirements: Attentional inhibition of misleading or irrelevant schemes concurrent with effortful mental activation of relevant schemes; ignoring this methodological prescription leads to errors in assessing effective complexity of tasks
constraints: Methods of task analysis for estimating complexity more theoretically are still undeveloped; the passing-age criterion remains a safe but relative estimate
target_learners: children of differing ages and ability levels
target_learning_goals: measuring mental-attentional capacity and effective task complexity
examples: Backwards digit span, where the automatised habit of saying digits forward competes with the instruction to say them backwards, exemplifies a misleading task
key_sources: Arsalidou, M. & Pascual-Leone, J. (2016). Constructivist developmental theory is needed in developmental neuroscience. npj Science of Learning 1, 16016. https://doi.org/10.1038/npjscilearn.2016.16

article_title: Can cognitive processes help explain the success of instructional techniques recommended by behavior analysts?
citation: Rebecca A. Markovits and Yana Weinstein. (2018). Can cognitive processes help explain the success of instructional techniques recommended by behavior analysts? npj Science of Learning 3:2. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0018-1
title: Behavior-analytic stimulus control account of response-card learning
description: According to behavior analysis, learning occurs when a stimulus or context requiring a particular response is repeatedly paired with reinforcement of correct responding and non-reinforcement of incorrect responding, so that correctness and fluency increase. The article describes this as the development of "stimulus control": once fluency and mastery are gained, the term itself triggers the correct response, such as giving the correct definition on a test. The article argues this process is promoted by the use of response cards, which structure antecedent–consequence contact during class.
requirements: Repeated presentations of the stimulus with feedback so correct responding is reinforced and incorrect responding is not
Opportunities for active student responding during instruction
constraints: This is the article's account of the mechanism from behavior analysis; the article presents it as an explanation rather than a directly tested result in this manuscript
target_learning_goals: fluency and accuracy of academic responses such as defining terms
examples: A student given a term to define receives feedback on early errorful attempts; with practice, correctness and fluency increase until the term controls the correct-definition response

article_title: Can cognitive processes help explain the success of instructional techniques recommended by behavior analysts?
citation: Rebecca A. Markovits and Yana Weinstein. (2018). Can cognitive processes help explain the success of instructional techniques recommended by behavior analysts? npj Science of Learning 3:2. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0018-1
title: Behavior analysts and cognitive psychologists should collaborate on overlapping pedagogical recommendations to explain why effective techniques work
description: The article argues that the two fields produce "remarkably similar recommendations" for improving educational outcomes yet have never come together to discuss them. It recommends open dialog between behavior analysts and cognitive psychologists on overlapping techniques—comparing behavioral techniques with the cognitive processes potentially responsible for their effectiveness—to advance both fields and extend practical applications. Understanding mechanisms is framed as crucial for developing better recommendations for teachers.
requirements: Willingness of both fields to compare techniques and theories of why they are effective
constraints: The article notes partnerships between the fields have been achieved in other domains, such as visual attention, but not in this one
target_learners: all students, as both fields target improving educational outcomes
target_learning_goals: identifying mechanisms behind effective pedagogical techniques to improve recommendations for teachers
examples: The article's own comparison of guided notes with the generation effect and response cards with retrieval practice, plus proposed exploration of mind-wandering and dual coding theory

article_title: Overemphasizing individual differences and overlooking systemic factors reinforces educational inequality
citation: Zengilowski, A., Maqbool, I., Deka, S. P., Niebaum, J. C., Placido, D., Katz, B., Shah, P. & Munakata, Y. (2023). Overemphasizing individual differences and overlooking systemic factors reinforces educational inequality. npj Science of Learning 8:13. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00164-z
title: Prioritize structural, community-participatory approaches and research-practice partnerships over individual-only interventions when addressing educational inequality
description: This principle holds that interventions addressing educational inequality should address structural and systemic barriers while ensuring community participation, rather than exporting individual-level trainings as universal solutions. The authors argue "a structural focus or combined approach may be most impactful" and that "communities are reservoirs of knowledge that can be used for supporting human ﬂourishing." They recommend research–practice partnerships that prioritize local knowledge, operationalizing constructs like executive function and well-being in ways reflecting communities' lived realities.
requirements: Programs must address structural issues while ensuring community participation, and operationalize constructs like well-being and executive function in ways that reflect the lived realities of local communities.
constraints: The authors acknowledge debates surrounding the effectiveness or continuity of some exemplary programs and explicitly do not argue for generalizability or universality of these models.
target_learners: Students facing structural and systemic barriers, including minoritized students in the U.S. and marginalized children in South Asia
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement
student well-being and social-emotional functioning
reduction of educational inequality
examples: The Child-Parent Center Program combined culturally relevant instruction, parental involvement, smaller classes and health/nutrition changes; Restorative Justice for Oakland Youth shifted a district from punitive policies to restorative practices; Delhi engaged local lay counselors for student mental health; India's Mid-Day Meal Scheme and a Pakistani school lunch program combined nutrition with community engagement.

article_title: Relation of life sciences students’ metacognitive monitoring to neural activity during biology error detection
citation: Mei Grace Behrendt, Carrie Clark, McKenna Elliott & Joseph Dauer. (2024). Relation of life sciences students' metacognitive monitoring to neural activity during biology error detection. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00231-z
title: Metacognitive calibration as a foundation for error detection, self-regulated learning, and conceptual change
description: The article frames metacognitive calibration—the match between objective performance and subjective self-assessment—as "fundamental to self-regulated learning because it forms the basis for performance monitoring". Well-calibrated learners should show high confidence when accurate and low confidence when not. Calibration is theorized as "a critical initial step in the process of conceptual change": students aware of their misconceptions detect and remedy them, while unaware students become overly secure and miss opportunities for knowledge revision. The study tests this account neurally during an authentic biology model evaluation task.
requirements: Confidence ratings must be collected so calibration can be scored against actual accuracy, ideally with bias-free signal detection metrics such as meta-d' and metacognitive efficiency
constraints: The relationship between brain activity and metacognitive calibration is described as complex and multifaceted; different metacognitive aspects may involve distinct regions, and it remains debated whether calibration is task-specific or trait-like
target_learning_goals: accurate self-assessment of performance
error detection in scientific models
conceptual change in biology
examples: The study operationalized calibration via phi coefficients, meta-d', and metacognitive efficiency computed from confidence ratings in the fMRI task
key_sources: Mei Grace Behrendt, Carrie Clark, McKenna Elliott & Joseph Dauer. (2024). Relation of life sciences students' metacognitive monitoring to neural activity during biology error detection. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00231-z

article_title: The method of educational assessment affects children’s neural processing and performance: behavioural and fMRI Evidence
citation: Howard, S. J., Burianová, H., Calleia, A., Fynes-Clinton, S., Kervin, L. and Bokosmaty, S. (2017). The method of educational assessment affects children's neural processing and performance: behavioural and fMRI Evidence. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0010-9
title: Cognitive Load Theory extends from learning and instructional design to the design of educational assessment
description: The article applies Cognitive Load Theory's distinction between intrinsic and extraneous load to standardised testing: information varies in the demands it places on learners' working memory "as a function of its inherent complexity (intrinsic load) and complexity with which information is presented (extraneous load)". It argues the mode of information delivery in a test can influence WM demands, and that its behavioural and neuroanatomical data suggest "these principles may also apply to the assessment of children's knowledge and skills" rather than only to acquisition of competencies.
requirements: Assessment items must be equated in content complexity for extraneous-load differences between methods to be interpretable
constraints: Cognitive Load Theory's foremost concern has thus far been learning and instructional design; application to assessment rests on the article's own behavioural and neuroanatomical data
target_learners: school-aged children taking standardised assessments (Grade 2, age 7-8 in the study)
target_learning_goals: accurate measurement of domain-specific competencies such as spelling, reading comprehension and numeracy
examples: The proofreading condition, modelled on Australia's NAPLAN, recruited dorsal attentional and WM-related activations, which the article maps onto increased intrinsic load via Whelan's fMRI-to-load mapping
key_sources: Howard, S. J., Burianová, H., Calleia, A., Fynes-Clinton, S., Kervin, L. and Bokosmaty, S. (2017). article_title: The method of educational assessment affects children’s neural processing and performance: behavioural and fMRI Evidence
citation: Howard, S. J., Burianová, H., Calleia, A., Fynes-Clinton, S., Kervin, L. and Bokosmaty, S. (2017). The method of educational assessment affects children's neural processing and performance: behavioural and fMRI Evidence. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0010-9
title: Design assessments to maximise variance associated with the target competencies and minimise variance from extraneous information and processing
description: A test-construction principle the article derives from its findings: because methods differ in WM demands that are peripheral to the construct, developers should prefer methods that keep WM demands essential to the target ability. The article states "it is preferable to maximise variance associated with the competencies being assessed and minimise the variance associated with any extraneous information and processing, as is the case for all test construction", so that WM exerts only its indirect effect through learning or a direct role in the target ability.
requirements: Assessment development must consider not only what to assess but also how to assess
constraints: Proofreading-type tasks may still legitimately require WM when the target ability itself requires concurrent consideration of intent, meaning and language conventions
target_learners: all test-takers of standardised educational assessments, including young children
target_learning_goals: valid and accurate indexing of competencies such as spelling, numeracy and reading comprehension
examples: The study compared three standardised spelling methods equated for word difficulty, pilot-tested with 31 Grade 2 children, showing accuracy ordering from multiple choice to proofreading

citation: Howard, S. J., Burianová, H., Calleia, A., Fynes-Clinton, S., Kervin, L. and Bokosmaty, S. (2017). The method of educational assessment affects children's neural processing and performance: behavioural and fMRI Evidence. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0010-9
title: For assessment to support tailored educational support, results must accurately reflect students' competency levels (assessment for learning)
description: The article argues that identifying student needs and providing tailored supports is a fundamental aim of assessment, necessitating that results "accurately reﬂect their levels of competency". It invokes the distinction between assessment of learning and assessment for learning, noting a student underperforming due to literacy or WM constraints rather than lacking numeracy knowledge may not benefit from mathematical remediation. Assessment methods should therefore be aligned with, and derived from, the intended learning outcomes.
requirements: Assessment must be clearly aligned with, and derived from, the intended learning outcomes
constraints: Even systematic bias preserves relative rankings across years, regions, schools and students, but undermines needs identification
target_learners: school students whose standardised assessment results inform educational support decisions
target_learning_goals: accurate diagnosis of competency levels to guide bespoke educational support
examples: The article cites findings that WM training can improve numeracy among low-numeracy children, and that children not improving with remediation show immature WM-related strategies

article_title: Metacognition: ideas and insights from neuro- and educational sciences
citation: Damien S. Fleur, Bert Bredeweg and Wouter van den Bos. (2021). Metacognition: ideas and insights from neuro- and educational sciences. npj Science of Learning 6:13. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00089-5
title: Online versus offline distinction in metacognitive processes
description: The article proposes distinguishing online metacognition — rapid, on-the-fly monitoring and control such as in EF tasks — from offline metacognition, which requires reflecting on past or future activities and developing meta-representations, as in metacognitive judgements. Within Nelson and Narens' framework, meta-knowledge is "the upward ﬂow from object-level to meta-level" and meta-control the downward flow. The authors state: "we propose to explicitly distinguish online and of ﬂine processes", noting the distinction is often not made explicitly but will help bridge cognitive neuroscience and educational sciences.
requirements: Requires clarifying which protocol assesses which construct, since it is unclear whether protocols operationalise online or offline processes
constraints: Offline metacognition is typically studied in school settings whereas EF evaluation is performed in the lab, limiting direct comparison
Educational sciences research typically does not frame metacognition in online/offline terms
target_learners: learners across educational settings studied in both disciplines, from primary schoolers to university students
target_learning_goals: metacognitive monitoring and regulation of learning
examples: The review maps brain regions associated with meta-knowledge and meta-control onto online and offline categories, e.g. MFC and ACC for online meta-knowledge and aPFC and lPFC for offline processes
key_sources: Damien S. Fleur, Bert Bredeweg and Wouter van den Bos. (2021). Metacognition: ideas and insights from neuro- and educational sciences. npj Science of Learning 6:13. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00089-5

article_title: Metacognition: ideas and insights from neuro- and educational sciences
citation: Damien S. Fleur, Bert Bredeweg and Wouter van den Bos. (2021). Metacognition: ideas and insights from neuro- and educational sciences. npj Science of Learning 6:13. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00089-5
title: Design metacognitive instruction that combines strategy instruction with strategy knowledge and extends over a longer duration
description: This design principle holds that metacognitive instruction works best when it pairs offline meta-control training with offline meta-knowledge development. The article reports interventions "lead to the highest effect sizes when they both (i) instructed a combination of metacognitive strategies with an emphasis on planning strategies" and provided knowledge about strategies, and that "The longer the duration of the intervention, the more effective they were", with the strongest academic effects in mathematics.
requirements: Instruction must combine metacognitive strategies with an emphasis on planning strategies together with knowledge about strategies, illustrating benefits of applying trained strategies
constraints: Effects of metacognitive training interventions are often difficult to evaluate due to a lack of randomised control designs in the literature
target_learning_goals: learning strategies, planning, and academic achievement
examples: Meta-analyses of direct metacognitive instruction showed the strongest effects on academic performance in mathematics, followed by reading and writing

article_title: Integrating educational knowledge: reactivation of prior knowledge during educational learning enhances memory integration
citation: Marlieke Tina Renée van Kesteren, Lydia Krabbendam and Martijn Meeter (2018). Integrating educational knowledge: reactivation of prior knowledge during educational learning enhances memory integration. npj Science of Learning 3:11. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0027-8
title: Design curricula so new learning follows reactivation of previously learned, congruent information
description: The article argues that education should actively reactivate prior knowledge while new information is studied, because reactivation during encoding strengthens the association of new material with existing knowledge networks. It stresses "the necessity for a curriculum where knowledge is slowly expanded and previously learned information is often revisited to allow strong knowledge networks to form". Reactivation helps even when new information does not match prior knowledge.
requirements: Learners must possess relevant prior knowledge (pre-experimental B–C links) that can be reactivated during new learning, as in the article's curriculum-based stimuli
constraints: The reactivation component was, by the authors' own admission, "an extreme simpli ﬁcation of reactivation in classroom learning"; effects were shown with word-picture-description stimuli, not full lessons
target_learners: first-year university students (psychology and family studies)
target_learning_goals: retention and integration of new curricular subject matter with existing knowledge
examples: Participants were instructed to reactivate the associated B-picture by generating a mental image during AC-encoding and rated their subjective reactivation strength as strong, a bit, or none

article_title: Shifting the mindset culture to address global educational disparities
citation: Hecht, C. A., Murphy, M. C., Dweck, C. S., Bryan, C. J., Trzesniewski, K. H., Medrano, F. N., Giani, M., Mhatre, P., & Yeager, D. S. (2023). Shifting the mindset culture to address global educational disparities. npj Science of Learning 8:29. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00181-y
title: Mindset classroom culture framework: messages and opportunities as two dimensions communicating a growth or fixed culture
description: This framework defines the classroom culture as "the shared system of beliefs, goals, and norms that define what it means to be a learner in that classroom," and the mindset culture as the shared beliefs about learning in a school or classroom. It holds that teachers communicate the culture through two broad, empirically identified dimensions: informal verbal messages about growth, and formal opportunities to improve such as learning-focused grading and revision for credit. The framework predicts that cultures supporting growth beliefs narrow group-based achievement disparities by providing "psychological affordances" for students' own growth mindset beliefs.
requirements: Practices must clearly and consistently lead students to perceive the teacher as endorsing a growth mindset and provide affordances for students to benefit from their own growth mindset beliefs
constraints: The article states effects of growth mindset beliefs and interventions are heterogeneous, varying across students and academic contexts, and strongest where contexts support and reinforce the intervention message
target_learners: adolescent and college students, especially those from structurally disadvantaged groups
target_learning_goals: learning-oriented behaviors, belonging, willingness to take on challenging coursework
examples: Laboratory studies manipulated teacher statements and grading policies (Table 1) and measured students' perceived culture and learning-oriented choices

article_title: Change by challenge: A common genetic basis behind childhood cognitive development and cognitive training
citation: Bruno Sauce, John Wiedenhoeft, Nicholas Judd and Torkel Klingberg. (2021). Change by challenge: A common genetic basis behind childhood cognitive development and cognitive training. npj Science of Learning 6:16. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00096-6
title: The cognitive challenge hypothesis: developmental genes rely heavily on cognitive experiences (contrasted with the maturation hypothesis)
description: The article frames two accounts of gene-environment interplay in cognitive development. Under the "maturation hypothesis (also known as experience-expectant)", genes set a "default course" of development needing only common supporting experiences. Under the "cognitive challenge hypothesis (also known as skill learning or experience-dependent)", the effect of developmental genes "relies heavily on cognitive experiences", so variation in cognitive change arises from genes interplaying with idiosyncratic cognitive challenges. The study tests the prediction that cogPGS explains WM change in both development and training.
requirements: Requires intervention designs that create deliberate and trackable cognitive experiences to distinguish it from the maturation hypothesis, because typical-development studies confound the two hypotheses
constraints: The two processes are not mutually exclusive and could coexist or dominate at different points during childhood, as the article states
target_learners: children and adolescents (ages 6–25 in the developmental sample, 7–19 in the training sample)
target_learning_goals: working memory and general cognitive abilities (reasoning, attention, learning)
examples: The study combined a longitudinal developmental sample with an intervention sample of 25-day intense WM training to contrast the two hypotheses using the same polygenic score
key_sources: Bruno Sauce, John Wiedenhoeft, Nicholas Judd and Torkel Klingberg. (2021). Change by challenge: A common genetic basis behind childhood cognitive development and cognitive training. npj Science of Learning 6:16. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00096-6

article_title: A population-wide gene-environment interaction study on how genes, schools, and residential areas shape achievement
citation: Rosa Cheesman, Nicolai T. Borgen, Torkild H. Lyngstad, Espen M. Eilertsen, Ziada Ayorech, Fartein A. Torvik, Ole A. Andreassen, Henrik D. Zachrisson and Eivind Ystrom. (2022). A population-wide gene-environment interaction study on how genes, schools, and residential areas shape achievement. npj Science of Learning 7:29. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00145-8
title: Agnostic multilevel gene-environment interaction framework for testing latent environmental moderation
description: The article advances a social-genetic research strategy that estimates total interactions between polygenic indices and environmental levels (schools, neighbourhoods, districts, municipalities) using multilevel random-slope models, "thus remaining agnostic to specific features of environments". Controlling parental EA-PGI exploits random genetic segregation to disentangle within-family genetic effects from environments selected by parents. The authors present it as a framework within which to test the interactive roles of specific school characteristics.
requirements: Requires genotype data on parent-child trios so parental PGI can be adjusted, plus linked environmental membership identifiers and standardised outcome data
constraints: Latent interactions do not identify which specific environmental features drive moderation; measured-environment approaches alone could miss the interaction
PGI based on between-family GWAS weights may leave some bias and do not capture the full genetic component
target_learning_goals: standardised academic achievement in maths, reading and English
examples: Applied to 23,471 Norwegian MoBa trios across 2578 schools and 7700 neighbourhoods, comparing 11 nested multilevel models by AIC

article_title: Preschool musicality is associated with school-age communication abilities through genes related to rhythmicity
citation: Lucía de Hoyos, Ellen Verhoef, Aysu Okbay, Janne R. Vermeulen, Celeste Figaroa, Miriam Lense, Simon E. Fisher, Reyna L. Gordon & Beate St Pourcain. (2025). Preschool musicality is associated with school-age communication abilities through genes related to rhythmicity. npj Science of Learning 10:39. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00329-y
title: MAPLE framework and Atypical Rhythm Risk Hypothesis as accounts of musicality-language links
description: The article situates its findings within two theoretical frameworks: the Musical Abilities, Pleiotropy, Language, and Environment (MAPLE) framework, "which states that musicality and language share genetic variation and therefore musicality and language are interrelated", and the Atypical Rhythm Risk Hypothesis, "which proposes that rhythm impairment is associated with delays in speech/language abilities". The study's genetic results — shared rhythmicity effects on speech-related communication — are interpreted as consistent with both accounts.
requirements: Genetic instruments (polygenic scores) for rhythmicity and longitudinal phenotypes ordered in developmental time to test directionality
constraints: PGS analyses account for only a small proportion of phenotypic variance (incremental R2: 0.004–0.01)
requires replication in an independent population-based cohort
target_learners: typically developing children from infancy through adolescence
target_learning_goals: speech-related and language communication development
examples: The mediation-style SEM in ALSPAC showing PGS-rhythmicity-shared effects on school-age speech-related communication was read as consistent with these frameworks

article_title: Harmonic memory signals in the human cerebral cortex induced by semantic relatedness of words
citation: Noguchi, Y. (2024). Harmonic memory signals in the human cerebral cortex induced by semantic relatedness of words. npj Science of Learning, 9:6. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00221-1
title: Oscillatory resonance/sharing model of semantic integration in verbal working memory
description: The article proposes that each semantic feature of a word is maintained as a neural oscillation at a specific frequency, and that memorizing words sharing a common feature "induces a resonance or sharing of the oscillatory signal across the words, generating a regular EEG waveform" with fewer spectral frequencies. This contrasts with memorizing unrelated words, which produces an irregular waveform "composed of a larger number of frequencies (like white noise)". The alpha-to-beta band (8–30 Hz) carries these harmonic signals, which the author contrasts with theta-gamma coupling models that encode item sequences while keeping items independent.
requirements: Retention of multiple word items in verbal working memory, with alpha-to-beta oscillatory activity over temporal cortex measurable during the retention period
constraints: The author states the model "might be oversimpliﬁed, given that neural underpi nnings of semantic information have been mostly unclear and controversial"

The study did not directly investigate semantic knowledge in long-term memory (mental lexicon); results are interpreted as reflecting the WM process in posterior regions rather than the anterior temporal semantic hub
Results are also consistent with more complex models in which a single feature is recalled as combined signals of multiple frequencies
target_learners: healthy adult humans performing verbal working memory tasks
target_learning_goals: retention and integration of word lists in verbal working memory
semantic chunking of related items
examples: Experiment 1 compared Sem and NonSem trials during delay 5 and found reduced IPI-SD over posterior temporal cortex; Experiment 2's animacy-judgment RSA showed semantically associated words induced similar IPI distributions

article_title: A new education agenda based on The International Science and Evidence Based Education Assessment
citation: Singh, N. C., Gilead, T., Chakraborty, A., Van Herwegen, J., van Atteveldt, N., Borst, G., Bugden, S., Jasinska, K., Kay, J., Pugh, K., & Duraiappah, A. (2025). A new education agenda based on The International Science and Evidence Based Education Assessment. npj Science of Learning 10, 24. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00288-w
title: ISEE Assessment human-flourishing framework built on Aristotle's eudaimonia
description: The ISEE Assessment's conceptual framework defines the purpose of education as human flourishing rather than economic growth, built on Aristotle's concept of "eudaimonia, loosely translated as 'flourishing.'" It defines flourishing, learning, evaluation and education through transdisciplinary review and consensual discussion, resting on the idea that education must ensure holistic development nurturing both human relationships and academic growth, aligned with Article 26 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. It contrasts this with human capital theory, traditionally considered the primary educational goal for economic growth.
requirements: Working definitions of flourishing, learning, learner advancement and education established through transdisciplinary research review and consensual discussion among working groups
constraints: The paper states it does not encompass all recommendations from the original assessment, which are detailed in the report and policy briefs
target_learners: all learners across micro, meso and macro levels of education systems
target_learning_goals: holistic development for human flourishing and well-being
peaceful and sustainable mindsets
examples: The framework underpins the paper's three findings: the CASE approach, potentiality-based assessment, and the evolving role of technology

citation: Singh, N. C., Gilead, T., Chakraborty, A., Van Herwegen, J., van Atteveldt, N., Borst, G., Bugden, S., Jasinska, K., Kay, J., Pugh, K., & Duraiappah, A. (2025). title: Multi-level model of education linking child learning outcomes to micro, meso and macro levels
description: The ISEE Assessment adopts a multi-level model, "inspired by Bronfenbrenner's ecological systems model that links learning outcomes for a child with micro, meso and macro levels of the education system." The micro level comprises child and school factors, the meso level society and family, and the macro level government factors. The assessment spans these levels to investigate linkages within education and arrive at recommendations that could inform education policy and governance.
requirements: Assessment must consider linkages across micro, meso and macro levels rather than any single level in isolation
constraints: The model is described as inspired by Bronfenbrenner's ecological systems model; the article does not report empirical validation of the model
target_learners: children and students within nested education systems
target_learning_goals: understanding how societal, family and government factors shape learning outcomes
examples: Working Group 2 assessed macro-level factors on education institutionally and individually, while Working Group 3 examined micro-level factors impacting individual learning processes

article_title: Optimising, generalising and integrating educational practice using neuroscience
citation: Robert Colvin. (2016). Optimising, generalising and integrating educational practice using neuroscience. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/npjscilearn.2016.12
title: Three aims framework: optimisation, generalisation and integration of instructional techniques via neuroscience
description: The article proposes that cross-disciplinary neuroscience-education research should target three aims: optimisation (improving an existing intervention to achieve maximal results), generalisation (adapting an effective intervention from one domain to another, also called transfer), and integration (combining complementary techniques into a more comprehensive intervention). The aims are characterised as being of practical importance, building on existing education and cognitive research, and being infeasible to address based on behavioural experiments alone. Hypotheses from biological processes must still be validated behaviourally.
requirements: Hypotheses based on biological processes must be validated by behavioural experiments
Research must build on existing education and cognitive research
constraints: The framework targets existing interventions rather than new ones
No guarantee that potential outcomes from collecting activation signatures will eventuate
target_learning_goals: improved student attainment through improved instructional techniques
examples: A hypothetical geometry intervention is used to illustrate optimisation by refocusing on visual processing bottlenecks

article_title: Optimising, generalising and integrating educational practice using neuroscience
citation: Robert Colvin. (2016). Optimising, generalising and integrating educational practice using neuroscience. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/npjscilearn.2016.12
title: Functional activation signatures as the measurement focus: brain activity before, during and after learning
description: The article defines functional activation signatures as temporally staged patterns of brain activity in which 'activity takes place mostly in sensory processing areas before becoming more dominant in areas associated with higher-order cognitive abilities'. It argues the neuroscientific focus should be on brain activity before, during and after learning a task, rather than on task performance, since learning indicates a physical change in the brain such as synaptic plasticity, neurogenesis, or changes in neurons, in grey matter, white matter or both.
requirements: Measurement technology able to capture temporal and spatial changes in brain activity across days or weeks
constraints: Neuroscientific knowledge remains limited by the complexity of the brain and technological and financial constraints of current tools
target_learning_goals: relating brain change to academic attainment
examples: Comparing activation signatures between novice and expert on a geometry task to locate bottlenecks
key_sources: Robert Colvin. (2016). Optimising, generalising and integrating educational practice using neuroscience. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/npjscilearn.2016.12

article_title: Optimising, generalising and integrating educational practice using neuroscience
citation: Robert Colvin. (2016). Optimising, generalising and integrating educational practice using neuroscience. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/npjscilearn.2016.12
title: Three-level classification of neural processes, cognitive processes and academic abilities
description: The article presents an incomplete classification of mental processes across three levels: neural processes (the basic infrastructure and subconscious processes amenable to direct neuroscientific analysis), cognitive processes (basic units of conscious cognition such as selective attention, symbol processing, working memory, pattern recognition and abstract problem solving), and academic abilities (such as critical reading, writing, higher mathematics and long-term planning). Multiple neural processes may be involved in cognitive processes, which are in turn composed into academic abilities, highlighting that academic abilities are ultimately formed from underlying neural processes.
requirements: The framework presumes academic abilities are formed from underlying neural processes, so explanation must trace through the three levels
constraints: The distinction between skills and processes through the three levels is arguable in many cases
The classification is explicitly incomplete
target_learners: learners of academic abilities such as reading, writing and mathematics
target_learning_goals: relating academic abilities to underlying neural and cognitive processes
examples: Figure 2 depicts how neural processes are composed to generate high-level academic abilities
key_sources: Robert Colvin. (2016). Optimising, generalising and integrating educational practice using neuroscience. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/npjscilearn.2016.12

article_title: Optimising, generalising and integrating educational practice using neuroscience
citation: Robert Colvin. (2016). Optimising, generalising and integrating educational practice using neuroscience. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/npjscilearn.2016.12
title: Direct neuroscience input to broad education policy matters is unlikely; focus narrowly on cognitive-level optimisation, generalisation and integration
description: The article recommends a narrow focus: neuroscience is unlikely to directly impact aspects of education such as teacher career paths, governmental policy or curriculum. Its greatest impact comes when it builds upon existing education research into effective learning and addresses the right questions, namely optimising, generalising and integrating existing interventions at the cognitive level. Interventions must remain sensitive to the social and cultural aspects of a particular learning environment.
requirements: Research must build on the existing wealth of education research into effective learning
The right questions must be addressed, at the cognitive level
constraints: Neuroscience is unlikely to directly impact teacher career paths, governmental policy or curriculum
Interventions must be sensitive to social and cultural aspects of the particular learning environment
Considerations such as class size must be balanced against financial and administrative realities
target_learning_goals: increasing the scope and benefit of effective instructional interventions
examples: The article points to Hattie's synthesis of techniques that influence learning as an ideal starting place for deeper research into effective teaching interventions
