article_title: Directed information flow during laparoscopic surgical skill acquisition dissociated skill level and medical simulation technology
citation: Anil Kamat, Basiel Makled, Jack Norfleet, Steven D. Schwaitzberg, Xavier Intes, Suvranu De, Anirban Dutta. (2022). Directed information flow during laparoscopic surgical skill acquisition dissociated skill level and medical simulation technology. npj Science of Learning 7:19. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00138-7
title: Perception-action cycle account of surgical skill acquisition via internal models, efference copy and corollary discharge
description: The article organizes its findings within a perception-action cycle framework in which motor learning "involves making sensory predictions from efferent copies of motor commands" and validating them with reafferent sensory input. Internal models (inverse and forward) support "perceptual decision-making to reduce behavioral variability", with the cerebellum providing "a substrate for error-based learning through updating a forward model, whereas the striatum underpins habit formation". Directed information flow (efference copy, corollary discharge) within the dorsal stream from PFC to SMA to PMC is used to interpret expert-novice and simulator-technology differences in fNIRS connectivity.
requirements: Learners must interact with the simulation environment so reafferent sensory feedback generated by their own actions can be compared against sensory predictions
constraints: The fNIRS montage captured only five regions (LPFC, RPFC, LPMC, RPMC, SMA); ventral-stream regions such as the VLPFC were not investigated
fNIRS has limited spatial resolution and depth sensitivity, which the authors state needs to be considered for brain-behavior analysis
target_learners: medical students (novices) and experienced surgeons (experts) training in laparoscopic surgery
target_learning_goals: acquisition of bimanual laparoscopic psychomotor skills such as FLS pattern cutting
examples: The authors propose that experts in the novel VR simulator could have used directed exploration whereas novices depended on random exploration in the initial stages of the FLS task
key_sources: Anil Kamat, Basiel Makled, Jack Norfleet, Steven D. Schwaitzberg, Xavier Intes, Suvranu De, Anirban Dutta. (2022). Directed information flow during laparoscopic surgical skill acquisition dissociated skill level and medical simulation technology. npj Science of Learning 7:19. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00138-7

article_title: Enhancing senior high school student engagement and academic performance using an inclusive and scalable inquiry-based program
citation: Davenport Huyer, L., Callaghan, N. I., Dicks, S., Scherer, E., Shukalyuk, A. I., Jou, M. & Kilkenny, D. (2020). Enhancing senior high school student engagement and academic performance using an inclusive and scalable inquiry-based program. npj Science of Learning 5:17. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00076-2
title: Discovery: a term-long inquiry-based biomedical engineering program delivered by graduate students with high school teachers
description: Discovery is "a term-long inquiry-focused learning model delivered by STEM graduate students in collaboration with high school teachers, in the context of biomedical engineering". Each 12-week term, entire class cohorts of Grade 11–12 students work in teams of 3–4 on projects modelled on an engineering capstone, iterating between classroom work and four visits to university teaching facilities, culminating in a research poster symposium. Deliverables include a background essay, client meeting, proposal, progress report, poster, and final presentation, assessed by high school teachers as 10–15% of the course grade.
requirements: Collaboration between university trainees (3–6 lead instructors per term at ~1:8 mentor-to-student ratio) and high school teachers, with instructor training via a teaching workshop
Students must be able to independently commute to campus for hands-on sessions (~40 min transit in this study)
constraints: Teachers may find the framework difficult to implement depending on resources and institutional support, particularly if post-secondary collaboration is inaccessible
Subjects where experiments are logistically or financially simpler may be more feasible adoption routes
target_learners: Senior high school students (Grades 11–12) in university-preparatory science courses at non-specialized public schools, from diverse cultural and socioeconomic backgrounds
target_learning_goals: Critical thinking and problem solving through inquiry
Application of subject-specific biology, chemistry, and physics curriculum concepts to real-world biomedical engineering problems
Familiarity with the scientific method and engineering design principles
examples: Over five terms, 268 instances of participation (170 students, participating 1–4 times) completed the program at a partner school that scores in the top decile of the board's Learning Opportunities Index
key_sources: Davenport Huyer, L., Callaghan, N. I., Dicks, S., Scherer, E., Shukalyuk, A. I., Jou, M. & Kilkenny, D. (2020). article_title: Enhancing senior high school student engagement and academic performance using an inclusive and scalable inquiry-based program
citation: Davenport Huyer, L., Callaghan, N. I., Dicks, S., Scherer, E., Shukalyuk, A. I., Jou, M. & Kilkenny, D. (2020). Enhancing senior high school student engagement and academic performance using an inclusive and scalable inquiry-based program. npj Science of Learning 5:17. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00076-2
title: Mandatory whole-class participation in partnered inquiry programming to reach reluctant high-ability students
description: Discovery's design pattern is whole-class, mandatory participation in a term-long partnered inquiry project, chosen deliberately for inclusivity: "The mandatory nature of program participation was established to reach highly capable students who may be reluctant to engage on their own initiative, as a means of enhancing the inclusivity and impact of the program." Students work as full class cohorts with their teacher and graduate mentors rather than as self-selected volunteers, which the article links to building a relevant learning community and to capturing under-engaged students.
requirements: A post-secondary partner able to provide facilities, graduate student mentors, and co-developed curriculum with teachers 1–2 months before each term
constraints: Requires institutional investment and accessible post-secondary collaboration; the second-school replication had only two terms, and the authors call for larger collections to separate SES and cohort effects
target_learners: All students in a senior science class cohort, including capable students reluctant to opt in voluntarily
target_learning_goals: STEM persistence and interest
Critical thinking and problem-solving practice within curriculum subjects
examples: Students were enrolled regardless of volunteering; teachers assessed deliverables against consistent rubrics, and the program was a mandatory course component representing 10–15% of the final grade

article_title: The impact of premature birth on auditory-visual processes in very preterm schoolchildren
citation: Marion Décaillet, Solange Denervaud, Cléo Huguenin-Virchaux, Laureline Besuchet, Céline J. Fischer Fumeaux, Micah M. Murray & Juliane Schneider. (2024). The impact of premature birth on auditory-visual processes in very preterm schoolchildren. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00257-3
title: Multisensory stimulus contexts may serve as an access point for remediating highly variable behaviour in children
description: The article proposes that presenting multisensory (simultaneous audio-visual) stimuli can reduce behavioural variability, because performance variability was significantly decreased under multisensory stimulus conditions in both full-term and preterm schoolchildren alike. As the authors put it, "Multisensory stimulus contexts ma y thus provide an access point for remediating situations where highly variable behavior may be a contributor to poorer performance and cognition". This recommendation extends the observed IQR reduction under multisensory conditions to potential remediation contexts.
requirements: Highly variable behaviour must be a contributor to the poorer performance being targeted, as the article frames the remedy
Multisensory stimulus presentation must be feasible in the setting, as in the simple detection task with simultaneous audio-visual stimuli
constraints: The recommendation is grounded in reduced interquartile ranges under multisensory conditions in schoolchildren, not in a tested intervention
The article cites variability's contribution to poorer performance in children with ADHD as an example, not a tested population here
target_learners: Schoolchildren, including very preterm children and children with highly variable behaviour
target_learning_goals: Reducing behavioural performance variability that contributes to poorer performance and cognition
examples: In the simple detection task, interquartile ranges of RTs were significantly smaller under multisensory than unisensory conditions in both VPT and FT children, despite generally slower and more variable RTs in VPT children

article_title: Executive functions as mediators of early educational disparities by SES, gender and birth month
citation: Rémeau, M., Schmitt, P., & Borst, G. (2026). Executive functions as mediators of early educational disparities by SES, gender and birth month. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00422-w
title: Promote executive function development early (e.g., through enriched structured play or targeted support) to reduce multiple forms of early academic disadvantage
description: The article proposes that because EFs mediate SES-, gender- and birth-month-related disparities, supporting EF growth from an early age is a promising equity lever. It states that "promoting EF development from an early age, through enriched structured play or targeted support, may represent a promising pathway for reducing disparities" rooted in socioeconomic disadvantage, age differences and gender-based self-regulation challenges.
requirements: EFs are characterized as a common, malleable mechanism underlying early inequalities, so interventions must target EFs specifically rather than demographic factors that cannot be changed
constraints: The article calls for future research to examine the effectiveness of such interventions; effectiveness has not been demonstrated in this study
The study is cross-sectional, limiting causal inference about EF as mechanism
target_learners: preschool children in their first year of formal schooling (age 3 in France)
target_learning_goals: early oral language and early numeracy (pre-academic) abilities; school readiness
examples: The study's own mediation modeling showed EFs accounted for 23–51% of the total effects of SES, gender and birth month on pre-academic scores, motivating the recommendation
key_sources: Rémeau, M., Schmitt, P., & Borst, G. (2026). Executive functions as mediators of early educational disparities by SES, gender and birth month. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00422-w

article_title: Executive functions as mediators of early educational disparities by SES, gender and birth month
citation: Rémeau, M., Schmitt, P., & Borst, G. (2026). Executive functions as mediators of early educational disparities by SES, gender and birth month. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00422-w
title: Three-core executive function framework as foundational for early academic learning
description: The article defines executive functions as distinct but interrelated higher-order neurocognitive processes, largely dependent on the prefrontal cortex, that regulate thought, behavior and emotion toward goal-directed outcomes. It states "Three core EFs have been identified: working memory, inhibitory control, and cognitive flexibility", and treats a general EF factor combining these three as the mediating mechanism linking sociodemographic factors to pre-academic abilities in preschoolers.
requirements: The framework presumes EFs are measurable as a one-factor latent construct; the article's one-factor CFA including inhibitory control, cognitive flexibility and working memory showed excellent fit
constraints: The study aggregated EF dimensions into a broad latent construct, so it does not identify the most influential EF subcomponent for each pre-academic sub-domain
Only cool EFs were assessed; hot EFs such as self-control and delay of gratification were not included
target_learning_goals: pre-academic abilities including early oral language and early numeracy
examples: A one-factor CFA of inhibitory control, cognitive flexibility and working memory fit the data with CFI = 1.000 and standardized loadings from .40 to .78

article_title: Do it yourself: discerning the effects of self-directed activity on conceptual learning
citation: Brod, G., Holstein, E., Weindorf, L., Colantonio, J., Bonawitz, E. & Theobald, M. (2025). Do it yourself: discerning the effects of self-directed activity on conceptual learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00364-9
title: Bayesian Yoking Procedure: a three-step computational method for personalized yoked control conditions
description: A novel methodological approach in which each yoked participant observes the responses of an "ideal Bayesian learner" personalized to have that participant's individual prior beliefs. It proceeds in three steps: (1) creating profiles of children's prior belief distributions from pretest data using a hypothesis space of four competing theories (size, material, mass, random guessing) and k-means clustering into six profiles, (2) performing trial-by-trial Bayesian posterior updating for each prototypical profile across the 34 learning trials, and (3) assigning new learners to the best-fitting profile via lowest Wasserstein distance, so yoked children see the responses they would most likely have generated themselves.
requirements: Children's prior beliefs must be assessable via a pretest and mappable to a finite hypothesis space of competing theories
The learning task must allow trial-by-trial Bayesian posterior updating from observed data
Bayesian modeling of children's belief revision in the domain must approximate children's actual responses
constraints: Profile binning was necessary for practical reasons, requiring pre-coding of only six experimental conditions rather than individual matching, which could introduce assignment inaccuracies
It is currently unclear how well the procedure generalizes beyond water displacement; the authors name chemistry, mathematics, and medical reasoning as promising candidates
The optimal Bayesian models predict only the most certain responses, while children respond with some uncertainty on close to 10% of trials, possibly following a sampling hypothesis
target_learning_goals: revision of intuitive causal misconceptions through prediction-feedback learning
examples: Children in the yoked condition observed predictions generated from one of six predefined prior-belief profiles matched via Wasserstein distance to their pretest responses, and the yoked responses matched an individualized ideal model 94.6% of the time
key_sources: Brod, G., Holstein, E., Weindorf, L., Colantonio, J., Bonawitz, E. & Theobald, M. (2025). Do it yourself: discerning the effects of self-directed activity on conceptual learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00364-9

article_title: Do it yourself: discerning the effects of self-directed activity on conceptual learning
citation: Brod, G., Holstein, E., Weindorf, L., Colantonio, J., Bonawitz, E. & Theobald, M. (2025). Do it yourself: discerning the effects of self-directed activity on conceptual learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00364-9
title: Even minimal volitional acts such as generating predictions support conceptual learning beyond the informational content of the evidence
description: This principle holds that letting learners perform a volitional act themselves—even one that does not alter the evidence they see, such as generating a prediction before feedback—enhances causal learning relative to observing another learner perform the same act. The article's experiment shows the benefit persists when evidence informativeness, timing, and physical activity are held constant via personalized Bayesian yoking, and links the benefit to increased perceived autonomy.
requirements: Learners must generate their own response before seeing the outcome
The observed evidence must be matched to the learner's own prior beliefs so the comparison is fair
constraints: Demonstrated with a computerized prediction-feedback task in 5- to 7-year-olds; generalization to other domains and to hands-on experimentation is untested
target_learning_goals: causal/conceptual learning and belief revision
examples: In the experiment, children in the active condition made their own predictions about which sphere would displace more water before seeing the outcome, while yoked children observed matched predictions, with all children seeing identical evidence

article_title: Understanding mechanisms of generalization following locomotor adaptation
citation: Cristina Rossi, Ryan T. Roemmich & Amy J. Bastian. (2024). Understanding mechanisms of generalization following locomotor adaptation. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00258-2
title: Credit assignment framework: adaptation recalibrates a shared body model that generalizes across contexts and a treadmill-specific model that does not
description: The article proposes that during split-belt adaptation the nervous system updates two distinct forward models: a shared model representing "the general movement dynamics of our body" that generalizes to overground walking, and a treadmill-specific model that does not. Partial generalization arises because only the shared portion of recalibration transfers, producing "a predeﬁned portion of forward model recalibration that generalizes across context". The framework was tested against the slow switching hypothesis using repeated context switching with sensory prediction error eliminated.
requirements: A context switch after overground washout with sensory prediction error eliminated during treadmill blocks to test model predictions
constraints: The authors note this interpretation of speed effects is speculative and that alternative candidate frameworks exist in which internal models are reused and optimized to be shared for different functions
target_learners: healthy adults adapting walking on a split-belt treadmill
target_learning_goals: motor adaptation and generalization of learned walking patterns across contexts
examples: Participants repeatedly switched between treadmill and overground contexts with extended speed match tasks; aftereffects appeared only in the first overground block
key_sources: Cristina Rossi, Ryan T. Roemmich & Amy J. Bastian. (2024). Understanding mechanisms of generalization following locomotor adaptation. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00258-2

article_title: Improving analytical reasoning and argument understanding: a quasi-experimental field study of argument visualization
citation: Simon Cullen, Judith Fan, Eva van der Brugge and Adam Elga (2018). Improving analytical reasoning and argument understanding: a quasi-experimental field study of argument visualization. npj Science of Learning 3:21. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0038-5
title: Argument visualization: tree diagrams exposing the logical structure of argumentative texts
description: Argument visualizations are tree diagrams that illustrate the logical relations in argumentative text. "Claims, the sentences contained in white boxes, are the fundamental units of argument visualizations", grouped beneath horizontal green brackets labeled "because" (reasons, which aim to raise confidence in a conclusion) or red brackets labeled "however" (objections). Their "hierarchical layout is intended to re ﬂect the hierarchical structure of real arguments", with color and grouping cues binding elements that share a common function; dashed borders mark premises that remain implicit in the text. In the seminar, students produced such visualizations of real scholarly texts as the medium for analysis, discussion, feedback, and revision.
requirements: Training uses real academic texts rather than highly simplified arguments
Timely, detailed, individualized instructor feedback on students' visualizations
Students actively generate their own representations rather than receiving explanations of the readings
constraints: The present findings do not disentangle the contribution of visualization itself from the intensive, interactive course and its explicit focus on argument analysis
target_learners: undergraduate students, primarily first-year students at a selective university
target_learning_goals: analytical reasoning
parsing argumentative texts into logical components
constructing and evaluating written arguments
examples: Students worked in groups of two or three to visualize arguments from contemporary analytic philosophy papers, then revised visualizations in response to weekly feedback before submission
Problem sets began as fill-in-the-blank exercises with progressively less scaffolding before students visualized arguments from scratch
key_sources: Simon Cullen, Judith Fan, Eva van der Brugge and Adam Elga (2018). Improving analytical reasoning and argument understanding: a quasi-experimental field study of argument visualization. npj Science of Learning 3:21. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0038-5

article_title: Generalization of procedural motor sequence learning after a single practice trial
citation: B. P. Johnson, I. Iturrate, R. Y. Fakhreddine, M. Bönstrup, E. R. Buch, E. M. Robertson and L. G. Cohen. (2023). Generalization of procedural motor sequence learning after a single practice trial. npj Science of Learning 8:45. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00194-7
title: Rapid formation of abstract parsing-event memories as a mechanism for within-seconds skill generalization
description: The article proposes that abstract structural memories, specifically shared parsing cue structures (two sequences composed of different keypresses that start and end with the same keypress), can form within seconds and generalize to new skills. It argues that "Rapid formation of a generalizable memory for such parsing event affords several behavioral advantages": compressing two keypresses into one event, parsing the sequence into chunks, and serving as a temporal marker for chunk initiation. As a possible neural substrate it points to wakeful hippocampus-neocortical replay supporting memories encoding abstract relational structure.
requirements: A shared parsing cue between the two skills (e.g., sequences that start and end with the same keypress)
constraints: The authors note they "did not ask subjects if they identi ﬁed this parsing cue consciously and thus could not dissect implicit/explicit contributions"; the neural replay account is a proposed future-research question, not a tested result in this study
target_learners: adults learning new sequential motor skills
target_learning_goals: rapid generalization of newly acquired procedural skills to related new skills
examples: Four MTurk experiments using 5-item keypress sequences (4-1-3-2-4 and variants) with 10-second practice trials and rest intervals
key_sources: B. P. Johnson, I. Iturrate, R. Y. Fakhreddine, M. Bönstrup, E. R. Buch, E. M. Robertson and L. G. Cohen. (2023). Generalization of procedural motor sequence learning after a single practice trial. npj Science of Learning 8:45. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00194-7

article_title: Generalization of procedural motor sequence learning after a single practice trial
citation: B. P. Johnson, I. Iturrate, R. Y. Fakhreddine, M. Bönstrup, E. R. Buch, E. M. Robertson and L. G. Cohen. (2023). Generalization of procedural motor sequence learning after a single practice trial. npj Science of Learning 8:45. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00194-7
title: Design early practice schedules so that successive skills share abstract parsing-rule structure, since this structure generalizes within seconds
description: The article concludes that "our results document parsing structure generalization in the very early stages of skill learning (i.e., within-seconds and after a single trial of practice)" and states "This information may be useful for improving the design of practice schedules in the context of sports, music, and physical rehabilitation." Sequencing a second skill to share abstract event cues (e.g., starting and ending with the same element) with a just-practiced first skill leverages one-trial generalization, whereas sharing only ordinal or transition structure does not.
requirements: The two skills must share a parsing rule structure (e.g., sequences starting and ending with the same keypress) for early generalization to occur
constraints: Generalization was demonstrated for 5-item keypress sequences over seconds-long timescales; the article notes the impact of sequence difficulty and sequence length on generalization remains to be addressed, and the double-tap compression effect "may be attenuated as the sequence length increases"
target_learners: adults practicing sequential motor skills in sports, music, or physical rehabilitation
target_learning_goals: accelerated learning of related new skills through generalization from prior practice
examples: Participants who practiced sequence 4-1-3-2-4 for one 10-second trial showed higher onset performance on skill B sequences sharing the start-end parsing rule than on those sharing only transitions
key_sources: B. P. Johnson, I. Iturrate, R. Y. Fakhreddine, M. Bönstrup, E. R. Buch, E. M. Robertson and L. G. Cohen. (2023). Generalization of procedural motor sequence learning after a single practice trial. npj Science of Learning 8:45. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00194-7

article_title: Creativity supports learning through associative thinking
citation: Luchini, S. A., Kaufman, J. C., Goecke, B., Wilhelm, O., Kenett, Y. N., Lei, D., Benedek, M., van Hell, J. G., & Beaty, R. E. (2025). Creativity supports learning through associative thinking. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00334-1
title: Learning Efficiency Test (LET) Lithuanian-English paired-associate paradigm with SemDis-scored verb generation for measuring associative learning and thinking
description: The LET assesses "how quickly and durably people acquire new verbal information" by having participants learn 45 Lithuanian-English word pairs over two days with iterative testing with immediate feedback and no-feedback final tests; Lithuanian was chosen to control for prior knowledge. Associative thinking was measured with a verb generation task scored for semantic distance via the SemDis platform using a GloVe model trained on a 6-billion-token corpus.
requirements: Participants must be English speakers with negligible prior Lithuanian exposure; the task is administered online on participants' personal computers
constraints: The authors state their studies employed a single word learning paradigm, and it remains unclear whether findings extend to non-language-based or visual learning or other task modalities
target_learning_goals: foreign-language vocabulary learning (paired-associate learning)
examples: Study 1 used 45 Lithuanian-English word pairs with 4 s presentation and iterative testing until all pairs were recalled; Study 2 added free and goal-directed verb generation conditions with 40 items each
key_sources: Luchini, S. A., Kaufman, J. C., Goecke, B., Wilhelm, O., Kenett, Y. N., Lei, D., Benedek, M., van Hell, J. G., & Beaty, R. E. (2025). Creativity supports learning through associative thinking. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00334-1

article_title: Strategies for remediating the impact of math anxiety on high school math performance
citation: Rachel G. Pizzie and David J. M. Kraemer. (2023). Strategies for remediating the impact of math anxiety on high school math performance. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00188-5
title: Emotion Regulation intervention using cognitive reappraisal (emotional distancing and arousal reframing)
description: The Emotion Regulation (ER) intervention was a classroom adaptation of cognitive reappraisal, "a technique for reframing an anxious situation". It taught an emotional distancing strategy in which students "view the situation from a more objective perspective" (e.g., explaining the problem to a best friend), and a reframing technique treating physiological arousal as a challenge rather than an obstacle. Like the SS intervention, it was delivered in a 20–30 minute structured small-group discussion, followed by pre-test expressive writing about thoughts and feelings about the upcoming test and reappraisal strategies, plus reminders. The article reports this intervention was less efficacious for highly math-anxious students, whose anxiety-related grade declines persisted, though low-anxiety students in this group performed better.
requirements: Delivered as a structured small-group discussion with facilitator guidance and redirects for off-topic responses
Requires pre-test writing prompts about thoughts, feelings, and reappraisal strategies before exams
constraints: The article states cognitive reappraisal is a working-memory-intensive, effortful strategy that may be difficult to implement when cognitive resources are compromised by anxiety or when learning difficult new math skills; its benefits in this study accrued to low math-anxious students rather than highly anxious ones
target_learning_goals: Downregulating anxious responses to mathematics; reframing test-related emotional reactions to support math performance
examples: Students practiced reframing statements such as viewing the situation as a challenge rather than an obstacle, and wrote before tests about the thoughts and feelings they might experience and which reappraisal strategies they would use.
key_sources: Rachel G. Pizzie and David J. M. Kraemer. (2023). Strategies for remediating the impact of math anxiety on high school math performance. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00188-5

article_title: Understanding and supporting university students’ use of distributed practice via implementation intentions
citation: David, L., Biwer, F., Crutzen, R., & de Bruin, A. (2026). Understanding and supporting university students' use of distributed practice via implementation intentions. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00448-0
title: Implementation intentions as a metacognitive planning strategy linking situational cues to goal-directed study behaviour
description: Implementation intentions are specific plans that connect a situational cue to a goal-directed behaviour, extending a goal intention with a plan specifying when, where, and how to act. The article describes them as "a metacognitive strategy in which goal-achievement is supported by extending the goal intention with a detailed plan". In this study students in the intervention group specified when and how to incorporate regular review sessions and formulated if-then obstacle plans. The authors argue this structured planning could foster effective study habits, though the empirical test found no increase in distributed practice.
requirements: Plans must be specific enough to link cues to actions; the article reports many students struggled to specify components in detail, which could weaken the cue-context link.
constraints: Effects depend on plan quality, if-then format, and motivation; the four-week course may have been too short to capture behavioural change from goal refinement cycles.
target_learners: university students in health-related undergraduate programs
target_learning_goals: self-regulated use of distributed practice and effective learning strategies
examples: Students planned review via practice-testing, summarization, or visualization (e.g., flashcards after tutorials), scheduled at home or in the library, with obstacle plans for poor time-management and distractions.
key_sources: David, L., Biwer, F., Crutzen, R., & de Bruin, A. (2026). Understanding and supporting university students' use of distributed practice via implementation intentions. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00448-0

article_title: Examining the role of civic attitudes in the link between family wealth and school dropout among tertiary vocational students
citation: Finkenauer, C., Boer, M., Spitzer, J., Weinberg, D., Visser, K., Jonker, M. & Stevens, G. W. J. M. (2023). Examining the role of civic attitudes in the link between family wealth and school dropout among tertiary vocational students. npj Science of Learning 8:38. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00189-4
title: Civic attitudes account: institutional trust as the pathway linking experienced family wealth to school dropout
description: The article proposes that adolescents' civic attitudes — their beliefs about whether institutions are fair and can be trusted — explain part of the association between family wealth and school dropout. It distinguishes two related but distinct civic attitudes: institutional trust, which "focuses on the trustworthiness of specific institutions", and system justification, which "refers to beliefs about the overall fairness and legitimacy of the social, political, and economic systems in a specific country". In this account, experiencing financial scarcity lowers trust in institutions, which in turn reduces engagement and staying in school. The account is supported by the study's mediation models and framed as underexplored in dropout research.
requirements: Assessment of both objective family wealth and adolescents' own perceptions and experiences of wealth, since subjective experience is the operative predictor
constraints: Findings are correlational, with family wealth and civic attitudes assessed at the same timepoint, and were obtained in vocational schools in the Netherlands; generalization to other levels and countries is unclear
target_learning_goals: School retention and educational attainment
examples: Path model M2c (n = 1,218) tested institutional trust and system justification as simultaneous mediators between three family wealth indicators and officially reported dropout
key_sources: Finkenauer, C., Boer, M., Spitzer, J., Weinberg, D., Visser, K., Jonker, M. & Stevens, G. W. J. M. (2023). Examining the role of civic attitudes in the link between family wealth and school dropout among tertiary vocational students. npj Science of Learning 8:38. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00189-4

article_title: Prevalence of undiagnosed dyslexia in African-American primary school children
citation: Laura Cassidy, Kayla Reggio, Bennett A. Shaywitz and Sally E. Shaywitz. (2023). Prevalence of undiagnosed dyslexia in African-American primary school children. npj Science of Learning 8:52. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00204-8
title: Shaywitz DyslexiaScreen: a brief teacher-completed dyslexia screener with high ROC AUC for grades K-2
description: The Shaywitz DyslexiaScreen is "a series of questions posed to the teachers based on age appropriate skills dealing with the interface of oral and written language (phonological processing)" and "is not a test or assessment tool requiring a response by the student." It is brief, completed independently by the teacher on a tablet, based on the teacher's observations after months with the child, and was used in this study for universal screening in two New Orleans charter schools.
requirements: Completed by the child's teacher who ideally has spent months with each child in the classroom; teachers received an intensive training session on dyslexia by a Certified Academic Language Therapist
target_learners: Children in kindergarten through second grade
target_learning_goals: Early identification of children at risk for dyslexia
examples: Used in early spring 2018 to screen 246 K-2 children in two New Orleans charter schools; 121 (49.2%) screened at risk.
key_sources: Laura Cassidy, Kayla Reggio, Bennett A. Shaywitz and Sally E. Shaywitz. (2023). Prevalence of undiagnosed dyslexia in African-American primary school children. npj Science of Learning 8:52. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00204-8

article_title: Socioeconomic and genomic roots of verbal ability from current evidence
citation: Guang Guo, Meng-Jung Lin and Kathleen Mullan Harris. (2022). Socioeconomic and genomic roots of verbal ability from current evidence. npj Science of Learning 7:22. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00137-8
title: Conceptual model of the genomic component within parental SES shaping verbal ability
description: The article proposes that parental SES, traditionally viewed as environmental, "could be decomposed into an environmental component and a genomic component," the latter originating from parental genomes that shape family education, occupation, income, neighborhood, and schools. Because 50% of each parent's alleles transmit to offspring while 100% act on parental SES, offspring genome and parental SES are correlated (path C), so regression estimates of both are upwardly biased when estimated separately. The model (Fig. 1) motivates correcting the offspring-genome effect by including parental SES and estimating the genomic component as about twice the reduction in the SES effect.
requirements: Data with both offspring genome and parental SES measures at the individual level
constraints: Without parental genomic data the non-transmitted allele effect cannot be estimated directly; the analysis capitalizes on offspring genome and parental SES
The two genomic subcomponents being about the same is a hypothesis, since each is acted upon by about 50% of total parental alleles
target_learners: Youth aged 12–18 in the United States
target_learning_goals: Verbal ability (Peabody Picture Vocabulary Test score)
examples: The article regresses verbal ability on parental SES and offspring genome in an Add Health sample of 7194 to estimate the model's paths
key_sources: Guang Guo, Meng-Jung Lin and Kathleen Mullan Harris. (2022). Socioeconomic and genomic roots of verbal ability from current evidence. npj Science of Learning 7:22. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00137-8

article_title: Socioeconomic and genomic roots of verbal ability from current evidence
citation: Guang Guo, Meng-Jung Lin and Kathleen Mullan Harris. (2022). Socioeconomic and genomic roots of verbal ability from current evidence. npj Science of Learning 7:22. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00137-8
title: Include both SES and offspring genome in the same model, and routinely collect DNA in large social-science studies, to obtain more accurate estimates of SES effects
description: The article argues that the decades-long practice of including SES in a model and interpreting its coefficients as purely environmental effects needs amendment, because about 20–30% of conventionally estimated SES coefficients are parentally genomic. It states: "A straightforward and ready solution is to include both SES and offspring genome in the same model," which corrects roughly 50% of the upward bias in SES effects and makes genetic effects more truly a reflection of children's own genomes. It further recommends routinely collecting DNA data in large social-science studies granted their primary purpose is understanding social and environmental influences.
requirements: DNA measures (polygenic scores) and rich longitudinal SES measures collected on the same individuals
constraints: Published GWAS are mostly based on individuals of European descent, so the approach does not apply as well to racial minorities; the analysis excludes African Americans, Asian Americans, Native Americans and Hispanic African Americans
target_learners: Youth aged 12–18 in longitudinal social-science studies
target_learning_goals: Verbal ability and cognitive development
examples: The Add Health analysis of 7194 individuals shows the education PGS effect reduced by more than 20% and SES effects by about 10–15% when both are modeled jointly
key_sources: Guang Guo, Meng-Jung Lin and Kathleen Mullan Harris. (2022). Socioeconomic and genomic roots of verbal ability from current evidence. npj Science of Learning 7:22. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00137-8

article_title: Neural signals gradually shift towards inferior frontal gyrus and long-term effects following facial imitation-based social learning
citation: Qi Liu, Siyu Zhu, Can Liu, Yanmiao Yang, Chunmei Lan, Xinwei Song, Benjamin Becker, Keith M. Kendrick, Xinqi Zhou & Weihua Zhao. (2025). Neural signals gradually shift towards inferior frontal gyrus and long-term effects following facial imitation-based social learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00372-9
title: Mirror neuron system information-flow account of imitation-based social learning
description: The article proposes that facial imitation-based social learning is supported by the mirror neuron system (IFG, IPL, STS), whose representational pathway reorganizes with practice: early and middle phases show bidirectional IFG–IPL, IPL–STS and STS–IFG coupling, but "by the end of the period of repetitive FISL course, the main ﬂow of representational information was directed from the IPL/STS to the IFG". The IFG is described as taking a dominant role, receiving increased sensory or visual input that lets it flexibly execute imitation goals with greater accuracy or speed. The account also holds that refined, more similar MNS representations and strengthened MNS connectivity with social-cognition regions underlie improved imitation and face-emotion perception.
requirements: Repeated imitative learning practice over multiple sessions for the representational reorganization to emerge
Neuroimaging (fNIRS/fMRI) to observe the spatiotemporal trajectory of MNS changes
constraints: Findings from male participants only; the authors state they cannot extrapolate to females
fNIRS covered only the three main cortical MNS regions, not premotor or supplementary motor regions
Deliberate conscious imitation was trained, so unconscious motor contagion contributions cannot be ruled out
target_learners: Individuals with social-cognition deficits (e.g., ASD, schizophrenia, depression), as proposed clinical applications
target_learning_goals: Imitative accuracy and speed for facial expressions
Recognition and perception of others' emotional facial expressions
examples: Eighty male participants imitated 20 validated facial expressions across 16 sessions over one month, with fNIRS in the 2nd, 9th and 16th sessions and pre/post fMRI face and scene perception tasks
key_sources: Qi Liu, Siyu Zhu, Can Liu, Yanmiao Yang, Chunmei Lan, Xinwei Song, Benjamin Becker, Keith M. Kendrick, Xinqi Zhou & Weihua Zhao. (2025). Neural signals gradually shift towards inferior frontal gyrus and long-term effects following facial imitation-based social learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00372-9

article_title: Neural computations in children’s third-party interventions are modulated by their parents’ moral values
citation: Minkang Kim, Jean Decety, Ling Wu, Soohyun Baek and Derek Sankey. (2021). Neural computations in children's third-party interventions are modulated by their parents' moral values. npj Science of Learning 6:38. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00116-5
title: Early implicit evaluation account of preschoolers' costly third-party intervention
description: This account holds that young children's costly intervention into third-party harm is driven by rapid implicit evaluation of moral norm violation rather than by late deliberative processes, impulsivity, or self-oriented distress. In it, early neural discrimination indexed by central P2 shapes later regulatory processing and the decision to intervene. The article states that "rapid implicit evaluations of norm violations are implicated in a young child 's intervention into third-party harm", and that late neural dynamics are bounded by earlier temporal dynamics.
requirements: Triangulated measurement combining EEG/ERP recordings, observed behaviour in a live transgression setting, and parent-report dispositions
constraints: The brain–behaviour relationships were drawn from group-level data
Due to the small sample size, analysis of the Protester group was underpowered
Children may have attributed power and authority to the adult transgressor, preventing protest or report
target_learning_goals: moral norm evaluation and costly third-party intervention into harm
key_sources: Minkang Kim, Jean Decety, Ling Wu, Soohyun Baek and Derek Sankey. (2021). Neural computations in children's third-party interventions are modulated by their parents' moral values. npj Science of Learning 6:38. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00116-5

article_title: Effects of context on the neural correlates of attention in a college classroom
citation: Jennie K. Grammer, Keye Xu and Agatha Lenartowicz. (2021). Effects of context on the neural correlates of attention in a college classroom. npj Science of Learning 6:15. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00094-8
title: Use portable EEG to assess student attention in classrooms because behavioral observation misses covert attentional processes
description: The article argues that portable EEG provides an objective, real-time index of classroom attention that behavioral observation and self-report cannot supply, because those methods "are each indirect and cannot pick up the dynamic changes in student engagement". In their study, neural measures revealed that looking-away during group work may coincide with attentional engagement, and the authors conclude EEG signals "offer a powerful tool for understanding differences in student cognitive states as a function of classroom instruction that are unobservable from behavior alone".
requirements: Research-grade EEG equipment to limit data loss, as used in this study
Trained reliable coders or complementary measures if behavioral comparison is desired
constraints: The approach would require further study in learning contexts dominated by auditory content, as alpha modulation in auditory attention has been less consistently assessed
Activities were not counterbalanced and students were observed in only one session
How neural measures relate to student outcomes and to self-report remains untested
target_learning_goals: sustaining attention during classroom instruction
examples: Students participated in a lesson on educational neuroscience with four 10–15-minute activities (whole-group lecture, video watching, group discussion, independent work), with two to three students per group of 4–9 wearing portable EEG.
key_sources: Jennie K. Grammer, Keye Xu and Agatha Lenartowicz. (2021). Effects of context on the neural correlates of attention in a college classroom. npj Science of Learning 6:15. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00094-8

article_title: Habituation as an adaptive shift in response strategy mediated by neuropeptides
citation: Evan L. Ardiel, Alex J. Yu, Andrew C. Giles and Catharine H. Rankin. (2017). Habituation as an adaptive shift in response strategy mediated by neuropeptides. npj Science of Learning 2:9. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0011-8
title: Habituation to noxious stimuli as a PDF-orchestrated shift in behavioral strategy from backward escape to forward dispersal
description: The article proposes that habituation is not simply response decrement but part of a coordinated shift in behavioral strategy: reversal responses are largely maintained while their duration shortens and latency increases, and forward locomotion between responses increases, promoting dispersal from a dangerous locale. It interprets this within the dual-process theory of habituation, in which "each stimulus induces both local circuit habituation and organism-wide sensitization," so that coincident habituation and sensitization form an optimal escape strategy balancing immediate threat evasion against longer-term evacuation, resonating with Bolles's species-specific defense responses.
requirements: Repeated aversive stimulation detectable by a nociceptive circuit
Multiple behavioral metrics measured in an intact, freely moving animal
constraints: The authors state this interpretation is not expected to generalize to every habituating behavior
target_learning_goals: Habituation to repeated noxious stimulation
examples: Detailed behavioral analysis during learning acquisition showed the population shifts from a backwards escape response to rapid forward acceleration away from the locus of stimulation
key_sources: Evan L. Ardiel, Alex J. Yu, Andrew C. Giles and Catharine H. Rankin. (2017). Habituation as an adaptive shift in response strategy mediated by neuropeptides. npj Science of Learning 2:9. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0011-8

article_title: Brief memory reactivations induce learning in the numeric domain
citation: Gilad Schrift, Dror Dotan and Nitzan Censor. (2022). Brief memory reactivations induce learning in the numeric domain. npj Science of Learning 7:18. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00136-9
title: Memory reactivation-reconsolidation framework as an account of reactivation-induced numeric learning
description: The article frames brief reactivations within the reconsolidation framework: as stabilized memories are reactivated, either by retrieval or by a reminder cue, they revert to a labile state and can be modified by incoming inputs during offline re-stabilization. The authors state that "the reactivation process facilitates learning associated with declarative human memory, and exists also in a mathematical context", and speculate that neural reactivations within the fronto-parietal numerical cognition network may support consolidation of hippocampus-dependent memories. The neural mechanisms remain to be determined.
requirements: Encoded, consolidated memories that can be reactivated by a brief reminder cue
constraints: The neural mechanisms underlying this form of reactivation-induced learning remain to be determined, per the article
target_learning_goals: Rote memorization and fluent retrieval of arithmetic facts
examples: Reactivations consisted of five seconds of visual-auditory presentation of each fact in random order, for a total of 40 seconds per session
key_sources: Gilad Schrift, Dror Dotan and Nitzan Censor. (2022). Brief memory reactivations induce learning in the numeric domain. npj Science of Learning 7:18. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00136-9

article_title: Brief memory reactivations induce learning in the numeric domain
citation: Gilad Schrift, Dror Dotan and Nitzan Censor. (2022). Brief memory reactivations induce learning in the numeric domain. npj Science of Learning 7:18. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00136-9
title: Number-fact retrieval task with eight arbitrary numeric facts
description: An online task (built with PsychoJs, run on Pavlovia) in which participants learn the results of 8 novel numeric facts presented with the nonexistent operator '&' (e.g., "3&8 = 29"), using only single-digit operands and 2-digit results with digits 2–9. Performance is quantified by a recall score where a correct result digit in the correct position scored 1 point and each correct digit in the incorrect position scored 0.5, scaled 0–100, plus response times and forced-choice tests with confidence ratings. It was used to mimic numeric fact learning in adults already familiar with elementary arithmetic.
requirements: Participants already familiar with elementary arithmetic; facts generated with low between-fact similarity to avoid disrupting learning
constraints: The facts are arbitrary with no systematic rule, so the task isolates rote memorization rather than conceptual or rule-based arithmetic learning
target_learning_goals: Memorization and rapid, accurate retrieval of numeric facts
examples: Encoding included 3 rounds of active-retrieval practice with feedback, a forced-choice test to determine if additional training was required, and a baseline test after a 30-minute break
key_sources: Gilad Schrift, Dror Dotan and Nitzan Censor. (2022). Brief memory reactivations induce learning in the numeric domain. npj Science of Learning 7:18. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00136-9

article_title: Applying, not ignoring: how feedback uptake and neural synchrony drive creativity
citation: Junting Yin, Zheyu Jin, Yuxuan Zhang, Xuening Li, Yangzhuo Li, Guoping Zhang & Junlong Luo. (2025). Applying, not ignoring: how feedback uptake and neural synchrony drive creativity. npj Science of Learning 10:61. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00351-0
title: Design feedback dialogues that let receivers actively respond, and include why/how content alongside emotional feedback
description: The article recommends interactive feedback environments, "such as dialogic exchanges between teachers and students or struc- tured peer collaboration", to promote cognitive alignment and divergent thinking. It further advocates that feedback should "actively guide learners in integrating and applying new input" and that providers include "why" or "how-to" feedback alongside emotional feedback, because comments and scaffolding were more likely applied and application tracked creativity gains.
requirements: Feedback must allow receivers to respond and articulate understanding, as in the IF condition's 30-second response turns
constraints: Benefits were assessed within a single session with a short interval; the article calls for testing persistence over longer periods
The AUT measure primarily reflects divergent thinking and does not capture the full range of creativity
The majority of participants were female; the article calls for more gender-diverse samples
target_learners: adult learners in workplace performance-review settings
target_learning_goals: divergent thinking and creativity acquisition and transfer
effective uptake and application of feedback
examples: In the experiment, IF dyads exchanged 30-second feedback and response turns, while OF receivers rested without responding; only IF improved both acquisition and transfer
key_sources: Junting Yin, Zheyu Jin, Yuxuan Zhang, Xuening Li, Yangzhuo Li, Guoping Zhang & Junlong Luo. (2025). Applying, not ignoring: how feedback uptake and neural synchrony drive creativity. npj Science of Learning 10:61. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00351-0

article_title: Language and nonlanguage factors in foreign language learning: evidence for the learning condition hypothesis
citation: Xin Kang, Stephen Matthews, Virginia Yip and Patrick C. M. Wong. (2021). Language and nonlanguage factors in foreign language learning: evidence for the learning condition hypothesis. npj Science of Learning 6:28. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00104-9
title: Learning condition hypothesis (LCH): similar learning conditions drive associations in language learning success
description: The LCH postulates that a primary factor determining proficiency levels of languages is the condition under which they are learned, rather than fundamentally different mechanisms for native and foreign languages. The article states: "We hypothesize that success in learning one language and the other may be linked, not due to a set of core functions for language learning, but because these languages are learned in similar conditions." It predicts that languages closer on a naturalistic-to-instructed continuum will show stronger associations of learning success.
requirements: Languages must be learned under describable conditions on a naturalistic-to-instructed continuum so that condition similarity between language pairs can be compared
constraints: The article acknowledges that age of learning covaries with the continuum of learning conditions and could be a confounding variable
target_learning_goals: multilingual proficiency across first, second, and third languages
examples: 636 Hong Kong learners whose L1 (Chinese) was naturalistic, L2 (English) mostly classroom-based, and L3 instructed, spanning the continuum
key_sources: Xin Kang, Stephen Matthews, Virginia Yip and Patrick C. M. Wong. (2021). Language and nonlanguage factors in foreign language learning: evidence for the learning condition hypothesis. npj Science of Learning 6:28. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00104-9

article_title: The effect of classroom environment on literacy development
citation: Gary Rance, Richard C. Dowell and Dani Tomlin. (2023). The effect of classroom environment on literacy development. npj Science of Learning 8:9. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00157-y
title: Cognitive resource allocation and the Irrelevant Sound Effect as explanations for open-plan learning disadvantage
description: The article draws on the theory of cognitive resource allocation, which "proposes that a ﬁnite, interactive pool of cognitive resources, including memory and attention, are ﬂexibly allocated to an activity depending on the demands of the task." When an auditory signal is masked or degraded, listeners compensate with top-down, knowledge-based processing, increasing cognitive load; comprehension may be restricted if resource limits are exceeded. The article also invokes the Irrelevant Sound Effect (ISE), whereby meaningful noise impacts non-auditory tasks such as reading through an increased attention burden, and links both accounts to its finding that children with poorer attention and speech-in-noise skills showed the greatest open-plan disadvantage.
requirements: A masked or degraded auditory signal that requires compensatory top-down listening
Meaningful (speech) noise sources competing with the target signal
constraints: The article states the present work cannot be taken as proof of the listening-effort relationship as there were no direct measures of listening effort
The lack of significant interaction between working memory and reading development suggests more than cognitive resource limitations may underlie the observed effect
target_learning_goals: Reading fluency development
Speech perception and attention in classroom listening conditions
examples: Students demonstrating the poorest listening in noise skills tended to be those with the greatest negative academic impact in the noisier open-plan study phases
key_sources: Gary Rance, Richard C. Dowell and Dani Tomlin. (2023). The effect of classroom environment on literacy development. npj Science of Learning 8:9. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00157-y

article_title: Using social and behavioral science to address achievement inequality
citation: Brummelman, E., van Atteveldt, N., Wolf, S. & Sierksma, J. (2024). Using social and behavioral science to address achievement inequality. npj Science of Learning, 9, 44. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00259-1
title: The hidden talents approach: adversity enhances some social and cognitive abilities
description: The hidden talents approach is a framework, rooted in biology, psychology, and anthropology, holding that some abilities developed under adversity are strengths rather than deficits. The editorial describes how Muskens et al. "adopted a hidden talents approach" to theorize that "some social and cognitive abilities are enhanced, rather than impaired, through adversity", such as detecting threats, finding creative solutions in scarcity, and reading others' intentions. It underpins the editorial's argument that low-SES children's attributes are specialized skills often underappreciated in academic contexts, not deficiencies to fix.
requirements: Academic contexts must recognize and value the specialized skills developed under adversity for the approach to inform intervention design.
constraints: The editorial notes the approach's prediction about real-world math items was contradicted in the TIMSS analysis it reports.
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement
accurate recognition of low-SES students' strengths
examples: Muskens et al. used the approach to hypothesize low-SES students would perform better on math items about money, food, and social relationships; the hypothesis was not supported.
key_sources: Brummelman, E., van Atteveldt, N., Wolf, S. & Sierksma, J. (2024). Using social and behavioral science to address achievement inequality. npj Science of Learning, 9, 44. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00259-1

article_title: Associations between school enjoyment at age 6 and later educational achievement: evidence from a UK cohort study
citation: Tim T. Morris, Danny Dorling, Neil M. Davies and George Davey Smith. (2021). Associations between school enjoyment at age 6 and later educational achievement: evidence from a UK cohort study. npj Science of Learning 6:18. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00092-w
title: Treat early school enjoyment as a promising, potentially modifiable intervention target and early indicator of pupils needing educational support
description: The article argues that because school enjoyment is "potentially more modi ﬁable than socioeconomic factors" it "potentially represents a promising intervention target for improving educational outcomes". It suggests a simple measure of school enjoyment at an early age may have long-term predictive value for identifying children who may need greater educational support, and that early schooling may be the most effective period for interventions since positive emotional factors decline from childhood to adolescence.
requirements: School-based interventions capable of promoting positive emotions such as enjoyment, which previous studies have demonstrated
constraints: The article explicitly states these findings should not be taken as evidence that improving school enjoyment will improve educational outcomes; replication in other settings and at other ages is required

Observational data do not allow causal evidence; lack of enjoyment may arise from health problems or social, emotional and behavioural difficulties, where upstream interventions may be more beneficial
target_learning_goals: Educational achievement at the end of compulsory schooling
examples: The study measured school enjoyment with two questionnaires at ages 6 and 6.5 in the ALSPAC cohort and linked responses to GCSE results in the UK National Pupil Database
key_sources: Tim T. Morris, Danny Dorling, Neil M. Davies and George Davey Smith. (2021). Associations between school enjoyment at age 6 and later educational achievement: evidence from a UK cohort study. npj Science of Learning 6:18. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00092-w

article_title: The challenge of explicit learning in life skill education
citation: Dominik M. Piehlmaier & Dee Warmath. (2025). The challenge of explicit learning in life skill education. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00375-6
title: Continuum of knowledge from factual through inflexible, semi-flexible, to flexible knowledge
description: The article introduces a continuum of knowledge ordering forms by transferability. Factual knowledge is memorized content the individual "struggles to apply what they know, even to decisions in the knowledge domain". Inflexible knowledge applies within a domain but not beyond it; semi-flexible knowledge (e.g., statistical methods) transcends domains but is limited to a specific method; flexible knowledge (e.g., strategic thinking) applies broadly across domains with few constraints. The continuum frames the argument that collegiate financial education over-relies on the inflexible end.
requirements: Flexible knowledge is described as developing through instruction that gives learners tacit or procedural understanding of decision processes, not just declarative content
constraints: The article notes a three-month course cannot cover all eventualities a financial decision-maker will face, limiting inflexible knowledge's transferability to ill-structured real-world decisions
target_learners: undergraduate students in collegiate life skills or financial education courses
target_learning_goals: applying knowledge to optimal real-world financial decision-making
transferring learning across domains and unfamiliar problems
examples: The RCT taught semi-flexible knowledge via an applied statistics course and flexible knowledge via a design thinking/strategic planning course, compared against an explicit personal finance course
key_sources: Dominik M. Piehlmaier & Dee Warmath. (2025). The challenge of explicit learning in life skill education. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00375-6

article_title: The challenge of explicit learning in life skill education
citation: Dominik M. Piehlmaier & Dee Warmath. (2025). The challenge of explicit learning in life skill education. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00375-6
title: Add strategic thinking instruction to explicit concept education in life skills programs to improve behavior
description: The article recommends that life skills education programs could be improved by teaching students how to frame decisions strategically rather than only delivering declarative concepts. It suggests this "might be accomplished by adding strategic thinking to the current explicit concept education (e.g., debt, budgeting, investing in the financial context)", for example lessons on conducting a situation analysis or design thinking methods. The recommendation rests on the RCT finding that strategic thinking instruction, not explicit financial education, produced more optimal intertemporal choices.
requirements: Strategic thinking content that teaches students to understand the situation, identify needs or opportunities, and consider connections between possible courses of action and desired outcomes
constraints: Effects were observed over a five-week period with one behavioral measure; the authors note longer follow-ups and other measures are needed
target_learners: undergraduates at a critical stage of financial life decisions
target_learning_goals: optimal financial decision-making
strategic framing of consequential life decisions
examples: The study's strategic thinking arm used six prerecorded lectures from a design thinking/strategic planning course covering strategic mission, design thinking, and reframing to define opportunities

article_title: Large-scale randomized experiments reveals that machine learning-based instruction helps people memorize more effectively
citation: Utkarsh Upadhyay, Graham Lancashire, Christoph Moser and Manuel Gomez-Rodriguez. (2021). Large-scale randomized experiments reveals that machine learning-based instruction helps people memorize more effectively. npj Science of Learning 6:26. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00105-8
title: Spaced selection framework: optimizing question selection probabilities under an exponential forgetting curve model
description: The article introduces a machine learning modeling framework that, rather than optimizing the rate of study, optimizes which questions to include in each study session. It represents study sessions as triplets of time, question set, and recall vector, models recall probability with the "exponential forgetting curve model with binary recalls", estimates forgetting rates via a variant of half-life regression, and derives optimal selection probabilities p*_i(t) = (1/√q)(1 − m_i(t)) using stochastic optimal control. The resulting procedure is named SELECT.
requirements: Learner review and recall data to estimate forgetting rates via half-life regression
Learners must be tested in each study session, as in the app used
constraints: The parameter q trades off recall probability upon review and study-session size; in the trial the user chose session size, so results are agnostic to q
target_learners: Adult learners (18+) studying large sets of paired-associate items, e.g., driver's permit theory questions
target_learning_goals: Long-term memorization and retention of factual paired-associate content
examples: In the randomized trial, the app presented questions in the order given by the selection probability while the user chose the size of the study session.

title: Furhat robot-assisted speech training system with simulated social interaction
description: The system uses the social robot Furhat, which "can be programmed to interact with autistic children and provide effective training", with cloud-based speech recognition (Google ASR and Microsoft Azure Cognitive Services) and speech synthesis (Amazon Polly and Acapela TTS), a back-projected face with synchronized lip movements, and face tracking. A web-application architecture (Raspberry Pi 4B web server in Golang, React.js GUI with participant and instructor modes) synchronizes image display, audio and the robot's facial expressions. Children ask the robot questions and judge whether its answers match the elicited focus type and position.

citation: Zhang, L., Li, Y., Wang, L., Zhang, X., Sun, Y., He, S. & Zhu, W. (2026). Effects of Tai Chi on attentional bias in men with methamphetamine use disorder. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00426-6
title: Prefrontal hypofrontality and functional-recovery account of Tai Chi effects in MUD
description: The article frames MUD as involving "hypofrontality", a state of insufficient prefrontal neural activation that fails to support cognitive control, leading to heightened salience attribution to drug cues. Within this framework, the better maintenance of prefrontal activation in the Tai Chi group is interpreted as functional recovery — an improved capacity to sustain task-relevant recruitment of prefrontal resources — rather than neural efficiency. The authors add a speculative motor-learning mechanism: Tai Chi's complex movement sequences may recruit fronto-striatal, dopamine-mediated plasticity pathways.
requirements: Interpretation depends on prior literature describing prefrontal hypofunction in MUD populations

inhibitory control
prefrontal cognitive control

article_title: Statistical learning occurs during practice while high-order rule learning during rest period
citation: Romain Quentin, Lison Fanuel, Mariann Kiss, Marine Vernet, Teodóra Vékony, Karolina Janacsek, Leonardo G. Cohen and Dezso Nemeth. (2021). Statistical learning occurs during practice while high-order rule learning during rest period. npj Science of Learning 6:14. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00093-9
title: Distinct temporal dynamics account: statistical learning relies on online evidence accumulation while high-order rule learning requires rest-period consolidation
description: The article proposes that apparently simultaneous learning subcomponents have different short-scale temporal dynamics: statistical learning of probabilistic regularities is evidenced online during practice, while high-order rule learning of deterministic regularities is acquired offline during short rest periods. The authors state the results "suggest that the brain mechanisms leading to statistical and high-order rule learning are fundamentally different, the former requires online evidence accumulation while the latter requires a rest consolidation period." They offer two candidate explanations: high-order rule learning may need more attentional resources, or deterministic regularities may need rest to be consolidated, possibly rehearsed or replayed.
requirements: Distinguishing the learning types requires task designs with random, probabilistic, and deterministic transitions, such as the SRT and ASRT tasks used here
constraints: Future studies must dissociate whether the dynamic difference relates to the low-order/high-order or the probabilistic/deterministic nature of the learning, or a mixture of both
target_learners: healthy young adults in laboratory sequence-learning studies
target_learning_goals: implicit sequence learning
statistical learning of probabilistic regularities
high-order deterministic rule learning
examples: Three experiments using SRT and ASRT tasks with 506 behavioral sessions decomposed learning into online and offline gains via bin-level analysis

title: SRT and ASRT task designs distinguishing general skill, statistical, and high-order rule learning
description: The serial reaction time (SRT) task presents a deterministic 12-element sequence; the alternating serial reaction time (ASRT) task interleaves four predetermined elements with four random ones, creating an eight-element probabilistic sequence. Trial types (pattern, random-high, random-low) allow the article to state that the structure "allows the distinction between (i) general skill learning, measured by a decrease in RT for all trials, (ii) statistical learning, measured by the difference in RT between the random-high trials and the random-low trials ... and (iii) high-order deterministic learning, measured by the difference in RT between pattern trials and random-high trials."
requirements: Blocks binned into five bins to compute online and offline gains; warm-up trials, repetition and trill triplets, and error trials discarded from analyses
constraints: In the SRT task with only deterministic transitions, general skill cannot be dissociated from sequence learning within each block or rest period; high-order rule learning was only observable in the long ASRT task
target_learners: healthy young adult participants in visuomotor sequence-learning experiments
target_learning_goals: implicit visuomotor sequence learning and its subcomponents
examples: Experiment 1 used the SRT task with 63 participants in two sessions 12 h apart; Experiments 2 and 3 used the ASRT task with 180 and 25 participants respectively

citation: Toru Ishihara, Noriteru Morita, Toshihiro Nakajima, Koji Yamatsu, Koichi Okita, Masato Sagawa and Keita Kamijo. (2021). Differential effects of changes in cardiorespiratory fitness on worst- and best- school subjects. npj Science of Learning 6:8. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00086-8
title: Intra-individual variability in grade points as a moderator of the physical fitness–academic performance association
description: The article proposes that the association between physical fitness and academic performance is moderated by intra-individual variability in grade points: improvements in fitness benefit a student's worst subjects selectively rather than raising all subjects uniformly. The authors state that "the longitudinal association between improvements in physical ﬁtness and academic performance is moderated by intra- individual variability in academic grades," and suggest this moderator might explain why some large-scale cluster RCTs found no overall effect of physical activity interventions on academic performance. It reframes baseline-performance moderation from an inter-individual to an intra-individual level.

The authors write that "increasing physical activities does not negatively in ﬂuence academic performance," supporting the position of the American College of Sports Medicine. This principle justifies adding physical activity to the school day without fearing academic cost.

article_title: Does pre-testing promote better retention than post-testing?
citation: Latimier, A., Riegert, A., Peyre, H., Ly, S. T., Casati, R. & Ramus, F. (2019). Does pre-testing promote better retention than post-testing? npj Science of Learning 4:15. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0053-1
title: Spend retrieval-practice time testing students after, not before, initial exposure to learning content
description: The article recommends that when a fixed amount of time is available for retrieval practice, quizzes should follow rather than precede the first exposure to content. Post-testing produced both larger retention gains and transfer to untrained questions, whereas pre-testing did not transfer. The authors state: "current evidence suggests that testing time dedicated to enhancing retention is better spent after than before the initial exposure to learning content."

Transfer to related but untested questions

title: Shared encoding mechanisms: experienced and vicarious RPE signaling influence episodic memory in comparable ways
description: The article proposes that reward prediction errors generated during one's own choices and during observation of another player's choices feed into episodic memory encoding through shared mechanisms. It reports that "positive image RPEs were associated with enhanced memory" in both learning conditions, and that gambling positively modulated the RPE-memory relationship independent of condition. The account aligns with prior work pointing to similarities in RPE signaling during learning from one's own and others' choices and feedback, while allowing that subjective memory strength still favors experiential learning.

citation: Lisa Bardach, Claudia Neuendorf, Kou Murayama, Thorsten Fahrbach, Michel Knigge, Benjamin Nagengast, and Ulrich Trautwein. (2023). title: Differentiation-polarization theory extended to students' awareness of school-track-related stereotypes
description: Differentiation-polarization theory holds that sorting students into tracks polarizes their school attitudes: higher-track belonging reflects higher status, whereas lower-track students lose status and react against the values of ability and hard work, so that an "anti-school culture" emerges in the lower tracks. The authors extend the polarization component to students' awareness of how the public perceives their track, predicting the most negative perceptions in the lowest track. The study's finding that lowest-track students reported the highest stereotype awareness in all waves is presented as supporting this extension.

constraints: The authors note the extension concerns awareness of stereotypes pertaining to a student's own track, not stereotypes about other tracks
target_learners: secondary school students in stratified (tracked) school systems
target_learning_goals: students' awareness of negative school-track-related stereotypes and its role in academic engagement, self-concept, and achievement
examples: The study applied the theory to predict mean differences in stereotype awareness between Hauptschule, Realschule, and Mittelschule students across four waves

title: Relational thinking versus relational reasoning: intuitive versus intentional pattern processing
description: The article distinguishes two coupled processes for discerning meaningful patterns in informational streams. Relational thinking is the spontaneous, in-the-moment coupling of percepts and concepts, while relational reasoning is the purposeful harnessing of pattern recognition for higher-order learning and performance. As the article puts it, relational thinking is "more fleeting, external, and rather effortless and unconscious in nature", whereas relational reasoning "has a more enduring, representational quality and which demands effort and intentionality". The two are compared on locus, temporal frame, and cognitive demands.

constraints: The boundaries between the intuitive and intentional systems may not be categorically distinct, per the article
