article_title: Relational thinking and relational reasoning: harnessing the power of patterning
citation: Patricia A Alexander. (2016). Relational thinking and relational reasoning: harnessing the power of patterning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/npjscilearn.2016.4
title: Four forms of relational reasoning: analogical, anomalous, antithetical, and antinomous
description: Drawing on reasoning, mathematical set theory, and philosophy literatures, the author's research program settled on four forms of relational reasoning encompassing key patterns of similarity and dissimilarity discernible in any informational stream. As printed, the forms "pertained to patterns of similarity (analogical reasoning), discrepancy (anomalous reasoning), opposition (antithetical reasoning), and exclusivity (antinomous reasoning)". Analogical reasoning has garnered the most empirical attention, and anomalous reasoning has focused largely on science and mathematics; antinomous and antithetical reasoning have grounding in ontological categories research and in persuasive-text and conceptual-change literatures.
requirements: Theoretical and empirical grounding within educational, psychological, and philosophical literatures
constraints: Other forms of relational reasoning likely exist beyond these four
target_learning_goals: discerning patterns of similarity, discrepancy, opposition, and exclusivity in informational streams
examples: Heraclitus's unity of opposites is cited as philosophical grounding for antithetical and antinomous reasoning

title: TORR family of relational reasoning measures (TORR, vTORR, TORRjr)
description: The article describes three psychometric measures of relational reasoning developed to move beyond the field's overreliance on the Raven's Matrices and figural analogical items. The TORR is figural and intended as a more fluid measure; the vTORR uses linguistic content and was conceived as somewhat more crystallized, though its novel items still entail flexible problem solving; and the TORRjr is an easier version for children and early adolescents paralleling the TORR in scales, items, and format. The measures can be "easily administered to children, adolescence, and adults either online or in print".

title: Embed relational reasoning training within academic domains rather than teaching it generically
description: The article recommends that efforts to foster relational reasoning not be treated as generic skills. As the author states, "relational reasoning training should not be isolated from the content with which students are typically or routinely engaged", and should instead be naturally nested within the academic domains framing students' educational experience. This rests on the strategy-training literature's finding that entirely generic efforts are less likely to have lasting effects, and on the article's argument that educators must recognize analogies, anomalies, antitheses, and antinomies in the subjects they teach.

target_learning_goals: analogical, anomalous, antithetical, and antinomous reasoning within domain content

article_title: Interleaved practice enhances memory and problem-solving ability in undergraduate physics
citation: Joshua Samani and Steven C. Pan. (2021). Interleaved practice enhances memory and problem-solving ability in undergraduate physics. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00110-x
title: Five candidate mechanisms for the interleaving benefit in physics problem-solving
description: The article proposes five non-mutually-exclusive explanatory accounts for the observed interleaving benefits, adapted from the interleaving literature to physics problem-solving: inductive learning of confusable problem categories, distributed practice via study-phase retrieval, reduced lag-to-test, relational processing of non-isomorphic problem types (described as material-appropriate processing), and practice in strategy selection. The authors state these accounts "are not necessarily mutually exclusive" and that the study was not designed to adjudicate between them.
requirements: The accounts are drawn from the interleaving literature with adaptations to problem-solving in introductory physics and remain candidates rather than tested mechanisms
constraints: The article states none of the accounts are mutually exclusive and the study did not adjudicate between them; inductive learning of problem categories alone might not be sufficient to explain the results because criterial tests also required memory retrieval of formulas
target_learning_goals: recall and application of physics formulas and principles
problem-solving with novel, multi-topic problems
examples: The article notes interleaved homework sets provided more opportunities to compare non-isomorphic problem categories than blocked sets, and that blocked assignments allowed students to bypass memory retrieval by reusing solutions held in working memory
key_sources: Joshua Samani and Steven C. Pan. (2021). Interleaved practice enhances memory and problem-solving ability in undergraduate physics. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00110-x

article_title: Interleaved practice enhances memory and problem-solving ability in undergraduate physics
citation: Joshua Samani and Steven C. Pan. (2021). Interleaved practice enhances memory and problem-solving ability in undergraduate physics. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00110-x
title: Replace conventionally blocked homework with interleaved homework when assignments contain multiple isomorphic problems per topic
description: The article recommends that instructors convert blocked homework assignments, in which one topic is practiced at a time, into interleaved assignments that switch between topics, because this simple rearrangement of the same problems fostered longer-lasting and more generalizable learning in undergraduate physics. As the authors put it, "Simply interleaving those assignments in a similar fashion may greatly enhance their effectiveness." The intervention is described as a relatively low-cost learning intervention in terms of time and equipment.
requirements: Assignments should contain multiple isomorphic or nearly isomorphic problems for each topic, as in the present study
constraints: The article cautions it is unclear whether interleaving benefits will be apparent on high-stakes exams after extensive cramming, and implementation issues such as the relative predictability of interleaving schedules and the point during learning when interleaving is introduced remain to be resolved
target_learners: students in courses where multiple topics are learned using blocked homework assignments
target_learning_goals: long-term memory for factual content
problem-solving with novel, more challenging problems
examples: In the study, only the arrangement of homework problems during normal instruction was manipulated: blocked assignments had three successive isomorphic problems per topic, whereas interleaved assignments had one problem per topic, with all students completing the same 84 total problems
key_sources: Joshua Samani and Steven C. Pan. (2021). Interleaved practice enhances memory and problem-solving ability in undergraduate physics. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00110-x

article_title: Regulation competencies and social well-being in at-risk adolescents: a systematic review of behavioral and neurophysiological research
citation: Jamaludin, A., Samyuktha, S. & Tan, A. L. (2026). Regulation competencies and social well-being in at-risk adolescents: a systematic review of behavioral and neurophysiological research. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00435-5
title: Integrative framework of regulation competencies as a multi-level, context-sensitive developmental capability linking adversity to social well-being
description: The review articulates an integrative conceptualization (Figure 3) in which structural and relational risks such as socioeconomic disadvantage and trauma exposure exert influence through regulation competencies spanning emotional (ER), metacognitive (MR), and social (SR) domains. Regulation competencies "function as proximal mechanisms that translate contextual adversity into social well-being outcomes, including empathy, belonging, distress regulation, and prosocial engagement". The framework reframes regulation from an individual-level attribute to a context-sensitive developmental capacity, with neurophysiological measures anchoring regulatory capacities in observable neural and autonomic processes.
requirements: Testing the framework as a whole requires designs that assess regulation competencies, biological processes, and social well-being outcomes within the same adolescents
constraints: The review notes the literature has largely examined individual components of this framework in isolation rather than testing the framework as a whole
target_learners: at-risk adolescents aged 10 to 18 facing socioeconomic disadvantage, trauma exposure, marginalized status, or clinical vulnerability
target_learning_goals: emotional, metacognitive, and social regulation supporting empathy, belonging, resilience, and prosocial engagement
examples: The review consolidates 45 studies into tabular matrices mapping regulation domains, designs, outcomes, and risk profiles (Supplementary Table S2)
key_sources: Jamaludin, A., Samyuktha, S. & Tan, A. L. (2026). Regulation competencies and social well-being in at-risk adolescents: a systematic review of behavioral and neurophysiological research. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00435-5

article_title: A qualitative systematic review on AI empowered self-regulated learning in higher education
citation: Min Lan & Xiaofeng Zhou. (2025). A qualitative systematic review on AI empowered self-regulated learning in higher education. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00319-0
title: Human-centered versus AI-centered self-regulation distinction with regulation through human-AI interaction as the predominant form
description: The review distinguishes two forms of self-regulation in AI-supported learning. In "human-centered self-regulation, AI serves as a facilitator by enabling learners to collect and access their learning data", whereas AI-centered self-regulation places AI in a central regulatory role generating SRL cycles from learner data. The authors argue the predominant form should be regulation through human-AI interaction, with AI engaging the human-centered SRL cycle across behavior, emotion and affect, and cognition to ensure goal alignment.
requirements: AI must engage with the human-centered SRL cycle across multiple dimensions—behavior, emotion and affect, and cognition—to enhance coherence and ensure goal alignment between AI and human learners
constraints: The review states novel theoretical developments are essential to guide optimal design and implementation of AI tools in this context
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning
examples: The review's Fig. 4 depicts AI engaging the human-centered SRL cycle across behavioral, affective, and cognitive dimensions
key_sources: Min Lan & Xiaofeng Zhou. (2025). A qualitative systematic review on AI empowered self-regulated learning in higher education. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00319-0

article_title: Recover or discover: How outcome feedback shapes response patterns within game spaces
citation: Zhang, Y., & Dyson, B. J. (2026). Recover or discover: How outcome feedback shapes response patterns within game spaces. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00414-w
title: Dice Dual zero-sum number-selection game with Pre/During/Post phase structure
description: Dice Dual is a zero-sum competitive game in which "both the participant and a computerized opponent select one number of a virtual 6-sided die on each trial", with even or odd sums determining wins, counterbalanced across participants. Each block contains Pre, During, and Post phases: exploitable opponent behaviour types (repetition, alternation) in Pre and Post, and an artificially fixed win rate in During. The authors used it across three experiments to index pattern acquisition, suppression, and reactivation via win rate and optimal behaviour rate (OBR).
requirements: A computerized opponent with exploitable behaviour types (repetition or alternation) in Pre and Post phases
A fixed win rate programmed in the During phase to simulate punishment or reinforcement
constraints: Punishment and reinforcement labels are descriptive of outcome valence, not formal operant conditioning or computational reinforcement learning mechanisms
Phase transitions were covert, with no on-screen cues marking a new phase
target_learning_goals: Strategic adaptation to opponent patterns under outcome feedback
Balancing reuse of old response patterns with acquisition of new ones
examples: Participants completed 504 trials of Dice Dual in 4 counterbalanced blocks of 126 trials, responding with 6 keys while win/lose feedback was shown as "WIN +1" or "LOSE -1"
key_sources: Zhang, Y., & Dyson, B. J. (2026). Recover or discover: How outcome feedback shapes response patterns within game spaces. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00414-w

article_title: A systematic review of AI literacy scales
citation: Tomáš Lintner. (2024). A systematic review of AI literacy scales. npj Science of Learning 9:50. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00264-4
title: Consensus core competencies of AI literacy: technical understanding, societal impact, and AI ethics, with contested creation and evaluation
description: The review synthesizes the scale authors' conceptualizations of AI literacy and finds broad agreement on three foundational competencies: "they emphasize the technical understanding of AI", "the societal impact of AI as a critical component", and "AI ethics is acknowledged as an essential aspect". The authors disagree, however, on whether higher-order skills — creating and critically evaluating AI — belong in AI literacy: MAILS found creation of AI a separate construct while AILQ includes it as core. The review suggests these skills may become core competencies of functional AI literacy in the near future.
requirements: Scale conceptualizations should specify which of the core competencies (technical understanding, societal impact, ethics) and higher-order skills (creation, evaluation) they measure
target_learning_goals: understanding AI systems
critically evaluating AI
ethical use of AI
examples: Ng et al.'s conceptualization proposes four aspects: know and understand, use, evaluate, and understanding of ethical issues related to the use of AI
key_sources: Tomáš Lintner. (2024). A systematic review of AI literacy scales. npj Science of Learning 9:50. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00264-4

article_title: A systematic review of AI literacy scales
citation: Tomáš Lintner. (2024). A systematic review of AI literacy scales. npj Science of Learning 9:50. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00264-4
title: AI literacy test: a performance-based scale of 30 multiple-choice items and one sorting item for university students
description: The AI literacy test is a performance-based scale assessing AI-related knowledge through 30 multiple-choice questions with single correct options plus one sorting question, validated with IRT on 1286 university students (mean age 23.6). It draws on Long & Magerko's conceptualization of 17 AI competencies in five areas. The review found limited evidence for content validity and high evidence for structural validity, internal consistency, and construct validity, and calls it the only performance-based scale targeting higher education students.
requirements: Available in German and English, though the English version has not yet been revalidated
constraints: The review notes some questions dealing with atypical use of AI in practice may become obsolete due to developments in AI
target_learners: professionals who encounter AI in their work
target_learning_goals: AI-related knowledge: what AI is, can do, how it works, and how it should be used
examples: Items range from specialized knowledge such as distinguishing supervised from unsupervised learning to recognizing areas of daily life where AI is used
key_sources: Tomáš Lintner. (2024). A systematic review of AI literacy scales. npj Science of Learning 9:50. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00264-4

article_title: A systematic review of AI literacy scales
citation: Tomáš Lintner. (2024). A systematic review of AI literacy scales. npj Science of Learning 9:50. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00264-4
title: SNAIL: a general-population self-report scale with the three-factor TUCAPA model of AI literacy
description: SNAIL (Scale for the Assessment of Non-experts' AI Literacy) is a 31-item general-population scale developed from a Delphi expert study, whose exploratory factor analysis yielded the three-factor TUCAPA model: "technical understanding, critical appraisal, and practical application". It has been revalidated in Turkish and in German for learning-gains use. The review rates it a promising instrument with high evidence for structural validity and internal consistency, but notes an indicated floor effect, with almost half of items having >15% lowest-score responses.
requirements: Content validity on the general population still needs to be checked, and the floor effect investigated, per the review
constraints: Only limited evidence for reliability and responsiveness due to a small longitudinal sample size
target_learning_goals: technical understanding of AI
critical appraisal of AI
practical application of AI
examples: Most participants complete the scale within 10 minutes, making it feasible for quick assessment
key_sources: Tomáš Lintner. (2024). A systematic review of AI literacy scales. npj Science of Learning 9:50. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00264-4

article_title: A systematic review of AI literacy scales
citation: Tomáš Lintner. (2024). A systematic review of AI literacy scales. npj Science of Learning 9:50. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00264-4
title: MAILS: a modular meta AI literacy scale in which creating AI emerged as a separate factor from AI literacy
description: MAILS is a 34-item general-population scale built on Ng et al.'s four AI literacy areas plus psychological competencies (self-efficacy, self-perceived competency). Its CFA found that "creating AI was found to be a separate factor", so the authors made the scale modular: AI literacy (18 items), create AI (4 items), AI self-efficacy (6 items), and AI self-competency (6 items) can each be measured independently. The review found high evidence for structural validity, internal consistency, and construct validity, and reports it is the only scale with evidence for minimal floor and ceiling effects.
requirements: Content validity on the general population still needs to be checked, per the review
constraints: Available in German and English, although the English version has not yet been revalidated
target_learning_goals: knowing and understanding AI
using and applying AI
detecting AI
AI ethics
AI self-efficacy
examples: Most participants completed the scale within 20 minutes (mean 16:05, SD 5:46 in Table 4)
key_sources: Tomáš Lintner. (2024). A systematic review of AI literacy scales. npj Science of Learning 9:50. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00264-4

article_title: Multivariate genome-wide covariance analyses of literacy, language and working memory skills reveal distinct etiologies
citation: Chin Yang Shapland, Ellen Verhoef, George Davey Smith, Simon E. Fisher, Brad Verhulst, Philip S. Dale and Beate St Pourcain. (2021). Multivariate genome-wide covariance analyses of literacy, language and working memory skills reveal distinct etiologies. npj Science of Learning 6:23. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00101-y
title: GSEM with combined Independent Pathway/Cholesky (IPC) models for multivariate genetic covariance in unrelated individuals
description: GSEM adapts multivariate twin models to genetic relationship matrices (GRMs) from genome-wide SNP data in unrelated individuals, dissecting phenotypic variance into additive genetic (A) and residual (E) factors. Beyond SNP heritabilities and genetic correlations, it identifies underlying genetic factor structures. The article introduces a novel combined IPC model, "enhancing the interpretability of genetic factor structures without a loss of model fit in residual factor structures", and shows unmodeled shared residual variation can strongly affect model fit.
requirements: Genome-wide SNP genotyping of unrelated individuals to derive GRMs
Dense phenotyping with comparable measures across participants
constraints: Population-level phenomena such as assortative mating and dynastic effects can potentially inflate genetic correlations and upward-bias SNP heritability
Lack of independent cohorts with comparable measures prevented direct replication
target_learning_goals: literacy (reading fluency, spelling)
phonological awareness
oral language comprehension
phonological working memory
examples: Applied to ALSPAC youth (N = 6453) across reading fluency, spelling, phonemic awareness, listening comprehension and non-word repetition measures
key_sources: Chin Yang Shapland, Ellen Verhoef, George Davey Smith, Simon E. Fisher, Brad Verhulst, Philip S. Dale and Beate St Pourcain. (2021). Multivariate genome-wide covariance analyses of literacy, language and working memory skills reveal distinct etiologies. npj Science of Learning 6:23. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00101-y

article_title: No significant changes in synaptic density and gray matter volume following motor learning—a pilot study
citation: Hehl, M., Toyonaga, T., Carson, R. E., Dupont, P., Van Laere, K., Swinnen, S. P. & Cuypers, K. (2026). No significant changes in synaptic density and gray matter volume following motor learning—a pilot study. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00451-5
title: Expansion-renormalization model of learning-related gray matter change
description: The article invokes the expansion-renormalization model to frame expectations about when learning-related gray matter changes should be detectable. As the article states, "This has given rise to the expansion-renormalization model which predicts an initial increase in GM volume, followed by a selection process and a partial or complete return to baseline GM volume". The model implies an inverted U-shape time course, with reported motor-related GM changes occurring within 5 days to 6 weeks and partially reverting after 2–4 months of retention or continued training beyond 4 weeks. The study's measurement schedule (MRI at baseline, 2 and 4 weeks; PET at 4 weeks) was designed around this anticipated window of maximal structural plasticity.
requirements: Measurement timing must be aligned with the expected expansion window while participants are still actively improving the skill
constraints: The article notes neuroplastic changes could have been transient and not sufficiently captured with measurements at 2 and 4 weeks, and a closer meshed measurement paradigm with a longer follow-up might help
target_learners: young healthy adults learning a new motor skill
target_learning_goals: motor skill acquisition and its neural substrates
examples: The study scheduled MRI assessments at baseline, 2 weeks and 4 weeks, and PET at 4 weeks, intended to coincide with the anticipated window of maximal structural plasticity
key_sources: Hehl, M., Toyonaga, T., Carson, R. E., Dupont, P., Van Laere, K., Swinnen, S. P. & Cuypers, K. (2026). No significant changes in synaptic density and gray matter volume following motor learning—a pilot study. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00451-5

article_title: No significant changes in synaptic density and gray matter volume following motor learning—a pilot study
citation: Hehl, M., Toyonaga, T., Carson, R. E., Dupont, P., Van Laere, K., Swinnen, S. P. & Cuypers, K. (2026). No significant changes in synaptic density and gray matter volume following motor learning—a pilot study. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00451-5
title: Bimanual tracking task (BTT) four-week motor learning paradigm
description: The bimanual tracking task is a laboratory motor-learning paradigm in which participants track a visual target moving along a target line by rotating two dials with the left and right index fingers, controlling the vertical and horizontal movements of a cursor. Performance is scored per trial as a percentage from 0–100% reflecting accuracy in speed, movement direction and distance from the target, with on-screen score feedback after each trial. In this study, "participants were stratiﬁed by sex and pseudo-randomly assigned to either a complex or a simple training group", training four sessions per week of 30 min for four weeks, with an individually adapting staircase-like level paradigm for the complex group and a standardized 18-task progress test administered six times.
requirements: The task can be adapted to participants' improving skill levels over time to secure continuing motivation and challenge; the complex group requires an individually adapting staircase-like level paradigm
constraints: The article notes the task was chosen as a novel task not part of the daily motor repertoire, and that GM changes with motor learning had not yet been examined for the BTT specifically
target_learners: young healthy adult volunteers (mean age 24.7 years)
target_learning_goals: bimanual coordination and visuomotor integration
examples: Training adherence was 99.7 ± 0.76% with no significant difference between the two training groups
key_sources: Hehl, M., Toyonaga, T., Carson, R. E., Dupont, P., Van Laere, K., Swinnen, S. P. & Cuypers, K. (2026). No significant changes in synaptic density and gray matter volume following motor learning—a pilot study. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00451-5

article_title: The distinct functions of working memory and intelligence in model-based and model-free reinforcement learning
citation: Chengyan Yang, Tongran Liu, Mengxin Wen & Xun Liu. (2025). The distinct functions of working memory and intelligence in model-based and model-free reinforcement learning. npj Science of Learning 10:72. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00363-w
title: Dual-system reinforcement learning framework: model-based versus model-free strategies
description: The article adopts the dual-system RL framework in which "the model-based strategy is characterized by its ﬂexibility and is typically driven by speciﬁc goals, taking current states into account", while "the model-free strategy is more efﬁcient and resource-conserving" and driven by habits and immediate rewards. A validated computational model estimates parameters — learning rate, eligibility trace, inverse temperature, and a mixing weight — that quantify each learner's reliance on the two systems in a two-stage task. The article uses this framework to show that WM load arbitrates between the strategies.
requirements: Estimation requires trial-level behavioral data (choices and obtained rewards) plus the task's environmental transition structure and available options.
constraints: The article notes the relationship between model-based strategy adoption and intelligence is unstable and affected by characteristics inherent in different two-stage paradigms.
target_learners: adult learners in experimental RL tasks
target_learning_goals: understanding how learners arbitrate between flexible planning and habitual responding during feedback-based learning
examples: In the study, a model-based agent who chose the pink door and received nine strawberries from the white bear would subsequently also choose the cyan door leading to that bear, whereas model-free agents relied exclusively on rewards.
key_sources: Chengyan Yang, Tongran Liu, Mengxin Wen & Xun Liu. (2025). The distinct functions of working memory and intelligence in model-based and model-free reinforcement learning. npj Science of Learning 10:72. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00363-w

article_title: Understanding the role of eye movement consistency in face recognition and autism through integrating deep neural networks and hidden Markov models
citation: Hsiao, J. H., An, J., Hui, V. K. S., Zheng, Y. & Chan, A. B. (2022). Understanding the role of eye movement consistency in face recognition and autism through integrating deep neural networks and hidden Markov models. npj Science of Learning 7:28. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00139-6
title: DNN+HMM unified learning model of visual routine development in face recognition
description: The DNN+HMM is a joint learning model in which a hidden Markov model generates sequences of fixations — location and spatial-frequency scale simulating "global/local attention" — and a multi-scale CNN plus MLP learns perceptual representations from the resulting masked inputs aggregated into a visual short-term memory. The HMM provides an interpretable summary of the model's eye movement strategy that can be compared with human data via EMHMM. Trained on the LFW-a dataset with 80 models representing simulated individuals, the model accounted for the adult eyes-focused advantage and predicted that in early learning, consistency rather than pattern predicts performance.
requirements: Fixations occur within person-specific regions of interest, with constraints of human perception such as saccade noise and retinal acuity built in
constraints: The transition matrix and prior were fixed so the ROI sequence was deterministic; the model abstracts away from biological details and may not reflect nuanced individual differences among neurodiverse populations
target_learning_goals: Development of consistent visual routines (eye movement strategies) for face recognition
examples: Trained on the 100 most frequent people in LFW-a (3651 images) for 500 epochs, with partial training at 100 epochs simulating children
key_sources: Hsiao, J. H., An, J., Hui, V. K. S., Zheng, Y. & Chan, A. B. (2022). Understanding the role of eye movement consistency in face recognition and autism through integrating deep neural networks and hidden Markov models. npj Science of Learning 7:28. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00139-6

article_title: Individual differences in the learning potential of human beings
citation: Elsbeth Stern (2017). Individual differences in the learning potential of human beings. npj Science of Learning 2:2. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-016-0003-0
title: Multi-store model of human information processing with working memory as gatekeeper to a self-organizing long-term memory network
description: The article presents a model of human information processing (developed together with Dr. Lennart Schalk, Fig. 1) in which sensory memory feeds a limited working memory, which "is responsible for temporarily maintaining and manipulating information during cognitive activity" and acts as gatekeeper to long-term memory. Long-term memory is described as "a self-organizing network, in which verbal terms, images, or procedures are represented as interlinked nodes with varying associative strength". Working memory selects incoming information, aligns it with retrieved knowledge, inhibits irrelevant input, and updates knowledge by adding nodes and altering associative strengths; procedural knowledge automates with practice and frees working-memory resources.
requirements: Appropriate learning opportunities that connect core knowledge and working memory to symbol systems
Instructional support for restructuring declarative knowledge, such as self-explanations, contrasting cases, and metacognitive questions
constraints: Working memory capacity is limited, so only a fractional amount of incoming sensory information passes into it
The full potential of working memory is not in place at birth but matures during childhood and changes until puberty
target_learning_goals: Acquisition of procedural and conceptual knowledge in academic subjects
Efficient use of working memory resources through chunking and automatization
examples: The article illustrates chunking with the digit series 91119893101990, which becomes reproducible when stored as two historical dates, freeing working memory resources
Conceptual change is illustrated by children who equate weight with being heavy and deny that a single grain of rice has weight
key_sources: Elsbeth Stern (2017). Individual differences in the learning potential of human beings. npj Science of Learning 2:2. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-016-0003-0

article_title: The neuroscience of advanced scientific concepts
citation: Robert A. Mason, Reinhard A. Schumacher and Marcel Adam Just. (2021). The neuroscience of advanced scientific concepts. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00107-6
title: Four neurosemantic dimensions underlie the neural representation of advanced physics concepts in expert physicists
description: The article proposes that physics concepts in expert brains are organized along four underlying dimensions: "relating to a measurable magnitude", "relating to a mathematical formulation", "entailing a repeated systematic change over time as in periodicity or wave-related concepts", and "relating to classical physics as opposed to post-classical intangible but consilient ideas". These factors emerged from factor analysis of consistently activated voxels and constitute "an orthogonal set of dimensions that collectively underpinned the neural representations of all of the concepts". Independent faculty ratings of the concepts along each dimension converged with the brain-derived factor scores.
requirements: Concepts must be rated along the hypothesized dimensions by independent domain experts to validate the factor interpretations
constraints: Dimensions were derived from the first four seconds of thought about each concept, capturing first-order rather than extended associations
Factor interpretations were developed by one author based on concept ordering, then validated by ratings
target_learning_goals: representation of classical and post-classical physics concepts
examples: Concepts at the extremes of the measurable magnitude dimension included frequency, wavelength, acceleration, and torque at one end and dark matter, duality, cosmology, and multiverse at the other
key_sources: Robert A. Mason, Reinhard A. Schumacher and Marcel Adam Just. (2021). The neuroscience of advanced scientific concepts. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00107-6

article_title: The neuroscience of advanced scientific concepts
citation: Robert A. Mason, Reinhard A. Schumacher and Marcel Adam Just. (2021). The neuroscience of advanced scientific concepts. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00107-6
title: Four cognitive processes characterize thinking about post-classical physics concepts, each linked to specific brain regions
description: The article proposes that post-classical concepts evoke four types of cognitive processes: "(1) Reasoning about intangibles, taking into account their separation from direct experience and their lack of direct observability; (2) Assessing consilience with other, ﬁrmer knowledge; (3) Causal reasoning about relations that are not apparent or observable ; and (4) Knowledge management of a large knowledge organization consisting of a multi-level structure of other concepts." Each process was linked to voxel clusters whose activation increased for post-classical concepts, with the process-location associations supported by independent ratings convergence, participants' reported properties, and the Neurosynth meta-analysis database. The article notes this reverse inference is uncertain on its own but is backed by converging evidence here.
requirements: Converging evidence beyond reverse inference: ratings convergence, reported concept properties, and meta-analytic location-process associations
constraints: The process attributions rest on reverse inference from activation locations, which the article calls an uncertain inferential method on its own
target_learning_goals: reasoning about intangible, post-classical scientific concepts
examples: The concept of multiverse evoked properties related to assessing consilience, such as "a hypothetical way to explain away … constants."
Thinking about a tachyon invokes a structured network of simpler concepts (mass, velocity, light, etc.), constituting a knowledge unit larger than a single concept
key_sources: Robert A. Mason, Reinhard A. Schumacher and Marcel Adam Just. (2021). The neuroscience of advanced scientific concepts. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00107-6

article_title: Structural and transcriptional signatures of arithmetic abilities in children
citation: Zhang, D., Xie, Y., Wang, L. & Zhou, K. (2024). Structural and transcriptional signatures of arithmetic abilities in children. npj Science of Learning 9, 58. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00270-6
title: OpenNeuro ds001486 public arithmetic-processing longitudinal dataset
description: A publicly deposited neuroimaging and behavioral dataset (OpenNeuro ds001486) collected by Suárez-Pellicioni et al., containing structural MRI and arithmetic and working-memory measures from students in grades 3 to 8, measured twice about two years apart. The present study used the first session cross-sectionally (n = 130 after quality exclusions) to build GMV-based predictive models. Custom code is available at the authors' GitHub repository.
requirements: Structural MRI preprocessing via the FreeSurfer recon-all pipeline and Destrieux atlas parcellation into 148 regions
constraints: The gene transcription profile data were acquired from post-mortem data in adults, not children
target_learners: children and adolescents in grades 3 to 8 (ages 8-15)
target_learning_goals: arithmetic ability (subtraction and multiplication)
working memory
examples: 132 students (mean age 11.26 years, 62 males) recruited from schools in the Chicago metropolitan area; two children removed for wrong cortical surface locations before analysis
key_sources: Zhang, D., Xie, Y., Wang, L. & Zhou, K. (2024). Structural and transcriptional signatures of arithmetic abilities in children. npj Science of Learning 9, 58. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00270-6

article_title: Instructor-learner body coupling reflects instruction and learning
citation: Yafeng Pan, Suzanne Dikker, Yi Zhu, Cuirong Yang, Yi Hu and Pavel Goldstein. (2022). Instructor-learner body coupling reflects instruction and learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00131-0
title: Body-to-Body Coupling (BtBC) via Motion Energy Analysis as a measure of pedagogical interaction
description: The article introduces BtBC as a dyadic measure derived from video-based Motion Energy Analysis, "a computer-vision method based on the assessment of differences in sequences of frames in video recordings, requiring no motion capture devices on instructors or learners". Motion in instructor and learner ROIs is cross-correlated over 30-s moving windows across 251 time lags, yielding an overall BtBC index averaged over all lags. The framework positions "the real-time interaction of teaching and learning bodies" as important for learning, with instructional approach shaping whether coupling emerges.
requirements: A high-definition video recording of the instructor-learner interaction from which motion energy can be extracted for pre-defined regions of interest
constraints: MEA uses fixed pre-defined ROIs and cannot track moving ROIs or movement details; findings are correlational, from same-gender (female-female) dyads, and require replication with larger samples
target_learners: adult learners in dyadic instructor-learner interactions
target_learning_goals: conceptual learning of psychological concepts (e.g., reinforcement and transfer)
examples: In the reported experiment, 48 female participants formed 24 instructor-learner dyads teaching reinforcement and transfer concepts under scaffolding and explanation approaches, with BtBC quantified from video using the rMEA package
key_sources: Yafeng Pan, Suzanne Dikker, Yi Zhu, Cuirong Yang, Yi Hu and Pavel Goldstein. (2022). Instructor-learner body coupling reflects instruction and learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00131-0

article_title: Abnormal brain activation during speech perception and production in children and adults with reading difficulty
citation: Yang Fu, Xiaohui Yan, Jiaqi Mao, Haibin Su & Fan Cao. (2024). Abnormal brain activation during speech perception and production in children and adults with reading difficulty. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00266-2
title: fNIRS foreign speech perception and production paradigm for detecting RD
description: A paired-task neuroimaging protocol combining a passive rapid event-related Spanish CV-syllable perception task (120 pairs varying in syllable consistency and similarity to Chinese, four runs of around 4 min) with a speech production imitation task (26 multi-syllabic Chinese pseudowords and 26 Spanish words, 156 trials), recorded with a 48-channel continuous-wave fNIRS system. The article uses it because "fNIRS is especially suitable for studying speech production, because of its relative tolerance with motion artifacts." Activation patterns from these tasks feed an SVM classifier that distinguishes RD from controls.
requirements: Participants must be native Chinese speakers who have not learned Spanish, so foreign-speech similarity to the native language can be controlled
constraints: The article notes the relatively small sample size and cross-sectional design might have limited the capability of revealing developmental changes
target_learners: Chinese children (fifth grade) and young adults with and without reading difficulty
target_learning_goals: Foreign (Spanish) speech perception and production as behavioral and neural indices of phonological processing in reading difficulty
examples: Participants listened to 120 pairs of Spanish consonant-vowel syllables and imitated 26 Chinese pseudowords and 26 Spanish words while HbO responses were recorded with a NIRSport2 system at 4.4 Hz
key_sources: Yang Fu, Xiaohui Yan, Jiaqi Mao, Haibin Su & Fan Cao. (2024). Abnormal brain activation during speech perception and production in children and adults with reading difficulty. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00266-2

article_title: Does anxiety explain why math-anxious people underperform in math?
citation: Daker, R.J., Gattas, S.U., Necka, E.A., Green, A.E. & Lyons, I.M. (2023). Does anxiety explain why math-anxious people underperform in math? npj Science of Learning, 8:6. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00156-z
title: Mechanistic heterogeneity framework for math-anxious underperformance as a function of emotion regulation capacity (HF-HRV)
description: This framework holds that the mechanisms by which trait math anxiety leads to poor math performance differ across individuals as a function of physiological emotion regulation capacity, indexed by resting HF-HRV. As the article states, "there is substantial heterogeneity in the mechanisms by which math anxiety and math performance are associated, and this heterogeneity occurs as a function of HF-HRV." For low-HF-HRV individuals, the in-the-moment anxiety account is largely correct (the indirect effect is 94% of the total effect); for high-HF-HRV individuals it is largely incomplete (14%); for average levels it is in-between (about half). The article presents this as a corrective to the dominant single-mechanism account in which state anxiety is the primary cause of math-anxious underperformance.
requirements: Measuring both trait math anxiety and an index of emotion regulation capacity (baseline HF-HRV) alongside performance, so that the realized mechanism can differ across individuals
constraints: The article notes the current design is not well-suited for state-level analyses of HF-HRV, since anticipatory/task HF-HRV was collected after the state anxiety rating it is meant to moderate
The college-aged population and the particular difficult mental math task may limit generalizability; the authors state future work is needed for younger populations and other math task forms
target_learners: college-aged students high in math anxiety
target_learning_goals: improving math performance in math-anxious learners
key_sources: Daker, R.J., Gattas, S.U., Necka, E.A., Green, A.E. & Lyons, I.M. (2023). Does anxiety explain why math-anxious people underperform in math? npj Science of Learning, 8:6. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00156-z

article_title: A working memory dependent dual process model of the testing effect
citation: Zheng, Y., Shi, A. & Liu, X. L. (2024). A working memory dependent dual process model of the testing effect. npj Science of Learning 9:56. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00268-0
title: Working-memory-dependent dual-process model of the testing effect
description: The model posits that the testing effect comprises two temporally ordered processes: retrieval attempt, the initiation of a search for the answer, and post-retrieval re-encoding, the reiteration of the correct answer in working memory after successful retrieval. The article states that "the testing effect comprises two processes: retrieval-attempt and post-retrieval re-encoding". Both processes draw from the same pool of working memory resources, enabling a trade-off between WM expenditure and memory fortification, which explains why people with different working memory capacities benefit differently from testing.
requirements: Working memory resources available during the task, linked to individual WMC and the WM demands of the material
constraints: The evidence that both processes consume the same WM pool remains indirect; direct empirical validation is still lacking, per the article
target_learners: learners varying in working memory capacity
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of studied material
examples: The model was first introduced by Zheng et al. to explain individual differences in the testing effect, with behavioral evidence from image-word pair learning
key_sources: Zheng, Y., Shi, A. & Liu, X. L. (2024). A working memory dependent dual process model of the testing effect. npj Science of Learning 9:56. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00268-0

article_title: A working memory dependent dual process model of the testing effect
citation: Zheng, Y., Shi, A. & Liu, X. L. (2024). A working memory dependent dual process model of the testing effect. npj Science of Learning 9:56. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00268-0
title: Modified SAC model quantifying WM resource trade-off
description: A modified Source of Activation Confusion model in which memory strength is delineated by base-level strength and activation level in a network of concept and episode nodes connected by associative edges. The article states the trade-off idea "has been quantitatively implemented in a modiﬁed Source of Activation Confusion (SAC) model". The model posits a limited pool of WM resources, consumed by node operations such as encoding and retrieval and replenished over time; individuals with higher WMC have greater WM resources available.
requirements: A limited pool of WM resources whose consumption and replenishment are modeled for encoding and retrieval operations
constraints: The model is a quantitative implementation rooted in the original SAC framework; the article notes direct validation of the shared-resource assumption is lacking
target_learners: learners with high or low working memory capacity
target_learning_goals: memory strengthening through retrieval practice
examples: Used to model how familiarity of memory nodes impacts WM resources consumed during encoding and retrieval
key_sources: Zheng, Y., Shi, A. & Liu, X. L. (2024). A working memory dependent dual process model of the testing effect. npj Science of Learning 9:56. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00268-0

article_title: A working memory dependent dual process model of the testing effect
citation: Zheng, Y., Shi, A. & Liu, X. L. (2024). A working memory dependent dual process model of the testing effect. npj Science of Learning 9:56. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00268-0
title: Balance learners' working memory capacity with task difficulty to unlock retrieval practice benefits
description: The model implies educational practice should match the difficulty of retrieval practice tasks to learners' working memory capacity. The article states that "achieving the right balance between an individual 's WMC and task dif ﬁculty" may be crucial for unlocking the full potential of retrieval practice for diverse students, providing a mechanistic rationale for the desirable difficulty hypothesis.
requirements: Knowledge of learners' working memory capacity and of the working memory demands of the learning materials
constraints: Tasks that significantly challenge an individual's WMC yield difficulty too high to be beneficial; overly easy testing yields limited benefits
target_learners: students varying in working memory capacity, including low-WMC learners and older adults
target_learning_goals: long-term retention through retrieval practice
examples: The optimal level of difficulty is reached when task demands moderately engage the WMC, allowing both retrieval success and additional processing
key_sources: Zheng, Y., Shi, A. & Liu, X. L. (2024). A working memory dependent dual process model of the testing effect. npj Science of Learning 9:56. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00268-0

article_title: The relationship of school performance with self-control and grit is strongly genetic and weakly causal
citation: Kevenaar, S. T., van Bergen, E., Oldehinkel, A. J., Boomsma, D. I. & Dolan, C. V. (2023). The relationship of school performance with self-control and grit is strongly genetic and weakly causal. npj Science of Learning, 8:53. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00198-3
title: Causal twin model for testing direct phenotypic effects in the presence of genetic and environmental confounding
description: The article fits a causal twin model, depicted in Fig. 2, that estimates the putatively causal regression coefficients of self-control and grit on school performance while allowing background A, D, or E correlations (dashed double-headed arrows) between the traits. The article explains that "the strongest support for the causal hypothesis would be the finding that the phenotypic regression coefficients ... are significant, while the background correlations are all zero". Because causal effects and confounding are not mutually exclusive, the model fits the phenotypic regression while permitting A, D, or E confounding, with the classical twin design supplying the decomposition into additive genetic, dominance, and environmental components.
requirements: Genetically informative twin data (MZ and DZ pairs) with the focal traits measured, plus correction for covariates such as sex, SES, and rater
constraints: The classical twin design "is a design that relies on underlying assumptions", and the article fitted only one source of confounding at a time; reverse or bidirectional causation was not ruled out
target_learners: 12-year-old twin children (11.5–12.5 years) in the Netherlands
target_learning_goals: School performance (teacher-rated math, reading, and literacy) as related to self-control and perseverance of effort
examples: Applied to Netherlands Twin Register data: teacher ratings of 8728 twins' self-control (ASEBA Achenbach Self-Control Scale), grit (three perseverance items), and school performance
key_sources: Kevenaar, S. T., van Bergen, E., Oldehinkel, A. J., Boomsma, D. I. & Dolan, C. V. (2023). The relationship of school performance with self-control and grit is strongly genetic and weakly causal. npj Science of Learning, 8:53. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00198-3

article_title: The relationship of school performance with self-control and grit is strongly genetic and weakly causal
citation: Kevenaar, S. T., van Bergen, E., Oldehinkel, A. J., Boomsma, D. I. & Dolan, C. V. (2023). The relationship of school performance with self-control and grit is strongly genetic and weakly causal. npj Science of Learning, 8:53. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00198-3
title: Netherlands Twin Register teacher-rating dataset on self-control, grit, and school performance in 12-year-old twins
description: A dataset from the Netherlands Twin Register comprising teacher ratings of grit, self-control, and school performance for 11.5–12.5-year-old twins, including 3837 complete pairs and 1054 incomplete pairs, with data on 8728 individuals (1957 MZ and 2934 DZ pairs). Self-control was measured with the 8-item Achenbach Self-Control Scale (Cronbach's alpha 0.87), grit with three teacher-rated perseverance items (alpha 0.90), and school performance as the sum of teacher ratings of math, reading, and literacy (alpha 0.84), which correlated 0.70 with the CITO standardized test.
requirements: Parental permission to contact teachers; zygosity established by DNA or blood test for 32.2% of same-sex pairs and by parental questionnaire (over 96% accuracy) otherwise
constraints: All measures are teacher ratings, which the article acknowledges may be biased by teachers' awareness of students' school performance; ceiling effects required right-censored maximum likelihood modelling
target_learning_goals: Measuring non-cognitive skills (self-control, perseverance) and academic school performance
examples: Data collection was approved by the Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam ethics committee (VCWE-2021-111) with parental written informed consent
key_sources: Kevenaar, S. T., van Bergen, E., Oldehinkel, A. J., Boomsma, D. I. & Dolan, C. V. (2023). The relationship of school performance with self-control and grit is strongly genetic and weakly causal. npj Science of Learning, 8:53. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00198-3

article_title: Faster implicit motor sequence learning of new sequences compatible in terms of movement transitions
citation: Susanne Dyck & Christian Klaes. (2025). Faster implicit motor sequence learning of new sequences compatible in terms of movement transitions. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00296-4
title: Movement-transition-based associative map for implicit motor sequence learning
description: The article proposes that in implicit motor sequence learning the memory representation underlying facilitative learning of compatible sequences is an associative map built from movement transitions between consecutive responses, rather than from ordinal positions. It situates this within dual-system accounts of MSL, in which an intra-dimensional system associates representations within one dimension and supports implicit MSL. As the authors put it, "in implicit MSL movement transitions form the basis for an associative map", contrasting with the cognitive-motor schema based on ordinal positions reported for explicit MSL. The authors prefer the expression facilitative learning or schema-like memory effect.
requirements: Extensive previous training of the original sequence (three sessions in experiment 1) before switching to the new sequence
constraints: The associative map is likely based on simple associations between consecutive movements within a single dimension, so the authors prefer the term schema-like memory effect rather than schema memory
target_learners: Healthy adults aged 18-35 learning motor sequences in an implicit serial reaction time task
target_learning_goals: Implicit motor sequence learning and transfer to new, compatible motor sequences
examples: Experiment 1 trained an original sequence for three sessions before switching to new, compatible, incompatible, or same sequences in an implicit bimanual SRTT; both compatible and incompatible sequences shared the same movement-transition overlap and were learned faster than a completely new sequence
key_sources: Susanne Dyck & Christian Klaes. (2025). Faster implicit motor sequence learning of new sequences compatible in terms of movement transitions. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00296-4

article_title: The Role of Eye Movement Consistency in Aging-Related Decline in Face Recognition
citation: Zheng, Y., Lo, T. W., Lau, E. Y., Eskes, G., Hui, L. L., & Hsiao, J. H. (2026). The Role of Eye Movement Consistency in Aging-Related Decline in Face Recognition. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00437-3
title: Eye movement consistency as an index of visual routine quality: the inverted-U lifespan account
description: The article frames face recognition as depending on visual routines — consistent, learned scanning patterns — whose quality is indexed by eye movement entropy measured with EMHMM. During development, children show decreasing entropy as routines form; adults show stable low-entropy idiosyncratic routines; and in middle-to-older adulthood entropy rises again, suggesting "an inverted U shape across the lifespan". The account holds that aging-related decline in consistency reflects difficulty executing, not forgetting, learned routines, tied to declining selective attention and inhibitory control and possibly fixation noise from sensorimotor decline.
requirements: Eye tracking during face recognition and EMHMM modeling to quantify pattern (E-N scale) and consistency (overall and C3 entropy)
Interpretation of entropy as routine quality presumes a learned visual routine from extensive face recognition experience in early adulthood
constraints: The article reports the age distribution concentrated between 50 and 70, which may affect aging-related correlations and limit generalizability outside this range
The sample was restricted to Asian participants processing Asian faces, so generalization to other cultural groups remains unclear
Younger adult faces only were used, leaving own-age bias unexamined
The study used a cross-sectional design; longitudinal work is needed to trace lifespan changes
target_learners: middle-aged and older adults (40–81 years old)
target_learning_goals: face recognition and the visual scanning and attentional strategies that support it
examples: The article suggests future work examine whether training older adults to restore earlier visual routines by enhancing eye movement consistency could mitigate face recognition decline
key_sources: Zheng, Y., Lo, T. W., Lau, E. Y., Eskes, G., Hui, L. L., & Hsiao, J. H. (2026). The Role of Eye Movement Consistency in Aging-Related Decline in Face Recognition. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00437-3

article_title: Targeted memory reactivation of face-name learning depends on ample and undisturbed slow-wave sleep
citation: Whitmore, N. W., Bassard, A. M. & Paller, K. A. (2022). Targeted memory reactivation of face-name learning depends on ample and undisturbed slow-wave sleep. npj Science of Learning, 7:1. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00119-2
title: Targeted memory reactivation (TMR) with sleep-quality moderators (N3 duration and cue-evoked arousal)
description: TMR is a procedure in which "information that people learn is associated with a sound or smell during learning" and the same sensory cue is presented during sleep without waking the learner, after which "people remember information associated with the cue stimulus better than other information that was equally well-learned." The framework holds that cues reactivate specific recent memories during sleep and thereby strengthen them. This article extends the framework by showing TMR effectiveness for face-name learning depends on two sleep-quality factors: ample N3 (slow-wave) sleep duration and absence of cue-evoked arousal or sleep disruption.
requirements: Cues must be delivered during stage N3 sleep and at a volume not causing arousal
Learned material must be associated with a sensory cue (spoken names and background music in this study) during learning
constraints: The study could not determine whether benefits were due to the spoken names, the music, or both
Only one sleep session was recorded, so whether sleep-quality differences reflect stable individual differences is unclear
target_learners: adult learners (18–31 years old) in laboratory nap settings
target_learning_goals: memory consolidation of face-name associations
examples: Participants studied 40 face-name pairs per class with distinctive background music, then during a nap half the spoken names from one class were presented at 10-s intervals with that class's music
key_sources: Whitmore, N. W., Bassard, A. M. & Paller, K. A. (2022). Targeted memory reactivation of face-name learning depends on ample and undisturbed slow-wave sleep. npj Science of Learning, 7:1. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00119-2

article_title: Targeted memory reactivation of face-name learning depends on ample and undisturbed slow-wave sleep
citation: Whitmore, N. W., Bassard, A. M. & Paller, K. A. (2022). Targeted memory reactivation of face-name learning depends on ample and undisturbed slow-wave sleep. npj Science of Learning, 7:1. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00119-2
title: Face-name TMR experimental protocol: two music-associated classes, nap cueing, and interference learning
description: A laboratory procedure in which participants learned 80 face-name pairs (40 per class, ostensibly Japanese History and Latin-American History classes), each class with a distinctive instrumental music track. Learning combined face viewing with spoken and written names, recall training with feedback, and visualization practice. Presleep tests assessed recognition (230 faces: old, rotated, new) and name recall; a mean 59-minute nap followed with manual TMR cueing during N3; interference learning of 20 new pairs preceded postsleep tests.
requirements: EEG recording to detect N3 sleep and pause cueing on transitions to other stages or wake
Spoken-name cue intensity manually controlled at 45–50 dB peak, the highest volume possible without causing arousal
constraints: Due to a technical error, the study could not test whether TMR effects differed for spoken-name-plus-music cues versus music-only cues within the cued class
target_learners: adult participants (18–31, mean age 23.38) recruited from a university population and surrounding community
target_learning_goals: face recognition and name recall for newly learned people
examples: Each to-be-learned person was presented twice, face shown once in quarter-right and once in quarter-left orientation, with a one-sentence biographical fact
key_sources: Whitmore, N. W., Bassard, A. M. & Paller, K. A. (2022). Targeted memory reactivation of face-name learning depends on ample and undisturbed slow-wave sleep. npj Science of Learning, 7:1. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00119-2

article_title: Long-term cognitive and neurophysiological effects of mental rotation training
citation: Linlin Dong, Yufeng Ke, Xiaodong Zhu, Shuang Liu & Dong Ming. (2025). Long-term cognitive and neurophysiological effects of mental rotation training. npj Science of Learning 10:16. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00309-2
title: LTP- and metaplasticity-based account of lasting mental rotation training effects
description: The article proposes that prolonged repetitive training fosters cognitive reorganization and long-term consolidation through synaptic plasticity. It states that "Long-term potentiation (LTP), a sustained enhancement of synapses driven by recent activity patterns, is a form of synaptic plasticity that underpins learning and memory processes," strengthened by repeated activation of relevant neural circuits during training. It further invokes metaplasticity — "the plasticity of synaptic plasticity" — whereby regular training increases the likelihood of synaptic strengthening, regulating and prolonging plasticity to explain continued improvements 20 days after training.
requirements: Repeated activation of relevant neural circuits over an extended training period
constraints: Proposed as a possible explanation, not directly tested in the study
target_learners: healthy college students undergoing cognitive training
target_learning_goals: spatial cognitive skill acquisition and retention
examples: The authors offer this mechanism to explain continued improvements in neurophysiological responses and behavioral performance observed 20 days after training.
key_sources: Linlin Dong, Yufeng Ke, Xiaodong Zhu, Shuang Liu & Dong Ming. (2025). Long-term cognitive and neurophysiological effects of mental rotation training. npj Science of Learning 10:16. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00309-2

article_title: Long-term cognitive and neurophysiological effects of mental rotation training
citation: Linlin Dong, Yufeng Ke, Xiaodong Zhu, Shuang Liu & Dong Ming. (2025). Long-term cognitive and neurophysiological effects of mental rotation training. npj Science of Learning 10:16. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00309-2
title: Adaptive-difficulty 10-day 3D mental rotation training protocol with concurrent HD-tDCS
description: A 10-consecutive-day training protocol in which participants completed a 30-min daily session combining 3D Shepard and Metzler mental rotation tasks with parietal HD-tDCS (2 mA, up to 25 min per day, 4×1 montage with anode at PZ). Each session "entailed one block of task at a ﬁxed diﬁculty level and four blocks with adaptively calibrated diﬁculty levels," with difficulty stepped up when the participant achieved 85% or higher average accuracy on adaptive tasks the previous day. The protocol was evaluated in 34 healthy right-handed college students tested at pre-test, post1, post2, and post3.
requirements: Daily difficulty calibration based on the participant's performance from the previous day
A minimum 60% accuracy acclimatization on a 50-degree task before formal training
constraints: Tested only in healthy right-handed college students
The HD-tDCS component showed no significant added benefit
target_learning_goals: three-dimensional mental rotation accuracy and response speed
examples: Difficulty level increased by one step the following day if the participant achieved an average accuracy of 85% or higher on the adaptive difficulty tasks.
key_sources: Linlin Dong, Yufeng Ke, Xiaodong Zhu, Shuang Liu & Dong Ming. (2025). Long-term cognitive and neurophysiological effects of mental rotation training. npj Science of Learning 10:16. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00309-2

article_title: Micro-consolidation occurs when learning an implicit motor sequence, but is not influenced by HIIT exercise
citation: Emily Brooks, Sarah Wallis, Joshua Hendrikse & James Coxon. (2024). Micro-consolidation occurs when learning an implicit motor sequence, but is not influenced by HIIT exercise. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00238-6
title: Micro-consolidation is a rapid consolidation process shared across memory systems with distinct topology, not requiring explicit sequence awareness
description: The article characterises micro-consolidation as consolidation occurring "on a more rapid scale of seconds", measurable as performance gains during brief rest periods between practice blocks. Because the effect appeared in an implicit task supported by cortico-striatal networks, whereas earlier evidence came from explicit tasks implicating hippocampal-neocortical replay, the authors propose "micro-consolidation as a process shared across memory systems with distinct topology". Explicit sequence awareness is not required for the effect to occur.
requirements: Alternating practice and rest structure (10-s epochs) with skill quantified as correct responses per second, as in the original Bonstrup paradigm
constraints: Demonstrated here for an implicit 12-item fixed sequence in healthy young adults; whether there is overlap with explicit micro-consolidation mechanisms remains open
target_learners: healthy young adults learning novel motor sequences
target_learning_goals: early-phase implicit motor sequence skill acquisition
examples: Thirty-eight adults performed an implicit serial reaction time task alternating 10-s practice and rest for 16 blocks, with micro-offline gains modelling early learning
key_sources: Emily Brooks, Sarah Wallis, Joshua Hendrikse & James Coxon. (2024). Micro-consolidation occurs when learning an implicit motor sequence, but is not influenced by HIIT exercise. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00238-6

article_title: Micro-consolidation occurs when learning an implicit motor sequence, but is not influenced by HIIT exercise
citation: Emily Brooks, Sarah Wallis, Joshua Hendrikse & James Coxon. (2024). Micro-consolidation occurs when learning an implicit motor sequence, but is not influenced by HIIT exercise. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00238-6
title: Implicit serial reaction time task with 10-s alternating practice-rest structure for measuring micro-consolidation
description: An implicit serial reaction time task (SRTT) in which "the task alternated every 10-s between task practice and rest for a total of 16 practice blocks, 320-s in total". Participants respond to visual cues with four fingers of the non-dominant left hand; undisclosed to them, cues follow a 12-item repeating sequence (2-3-1-4-3-2-4-1-3-4-2-1). Skill is conceptualised as number of correct responses per second, and micro-offline and micro-online changes are computed from block-start and block-end tapping speeds using a four-item sliding average.
requirements: Correct response required to progress to the next cue; post-task questioning to detect explicit awareness of five or more sequence items
constraints: The 12-item sequence differs from the seminal explicit 5-item micro-consolidation work and from SRTT versions using fixed-versus-random comparison, limiting direct quantification of implicit learning magnitude
target_learning_goals: implicit motor sequence learning
examples: Used with 38 participants pseudo-randomly allocated to HIIT or LOW exercise conditions before task completion
key_sources: Emily Brooks, Sarah Wallis, Joshua Hendrikse & James Coxon. (2024). Micro-consolidation occurs when learning an implicit motor sequence, but is not influenced by HIIT exercise. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00238-6

article_title: Micro-consolidation occurs when learning an implicit motor sequence, but is not influenced by HIIT exercise
citation: Emily Brooks, Sarah Wallis, Joshua Hendrikse & James Coxon. (2024). Micro-consolidation occurs when learning an implicit motor sequence, but is not influenced by HIIT exercise. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00238-6
title: De-identified behavioural data and analysis code released for the implicit micro-consolidation study
description: The article releases the study's supporting materials: "De-identiﬁed behavioural data are available at [https://osf.io/4e3xr/]" and "All code used for analysis is available at [ https://github.com/jhendrikse/micro_consolidation]". These artefacts allow reuse of the behavioural dataset and reproduction of the exponential-function learning modelling, sliding-average micro-scale decomposition, and Bayesian t-test analyses described in the statistical analysis section.
requirements: OSF repository for data; GitHub repository for the analysis code
target_learning_goals: reproducible analysis of micro-scale motor learning data
examples: Analysis code reproduces the sliding-average micro-offline/micro-online decomposition used in blocks 1-7

article_title: Mindset and perceived parental support of autonomy safeguard adolescents’ autonomous motivation during COVID-19 home-based learning
citation: Benneker, I. M. B., Lee, N. C. & van Atteveldt, N. (2023). Mindset and perceived parental support of autonomy safeguard adolescents' autonomous motivation during COVID-19 home-based learning. npj Science of Learning 8:4. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00153-2
title: Self-determination theory's three basic psychological needs as a framework for predicting autonomous motivation during home-based learning
description: The article applies self-determination theory, which "proposes that humans have three fundamental needs that must be satisfied in order to achieve complete autonomous motivation: autonomy, relatedness and competence." It operationalizes autonomy as perceived parental autonomy support, relatedness as positivity of parent-adolescent interaction, and competence as self-efficacy, and tests them as predictors of adolescents' autonomous motivation during COVID-19 school closures alongside mindset theory.
requirements: Measures of all three needs appropriate to the home-based learning context, including dyadic parent and adolescent reports
constraints: In this study only the autonomy need (parental autonomy support) was supported; relatedness and competence measures did not significantly predict motivation
Data are observational, so the framework's predictive roles were tested without causal inference
target_learners: Dutch early adolescents in secondary school (mean age ~14.45 years)

article_title: Achievement motivation modulates Pavlovian aversive conditioning to goal-relevant stimuli
citation: Yoann Stussi, Aude Ferrero, Gilles Pourtois and David Sander. (2019). Achievement motivation modulates Pavlovian aversive conditioning to goal-relevant stimuli. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0043-3
title: Relevance detection model of preferential emotional learning
description: The relevance detection model derives from appraisal theories of emotion and holds that preferential emotional learning is driven not by a threat-specific mechanism but by rapid detection of whether a stimulus is relevant to the organism's concerns—its goals, needs, motives, or values. The article frames it as asserting that "Stimuli that are detected as relevant to the organism’s concerns beneﬁt from preferential emotional learning, regardless of their valence and evolutionary status per se." The findings—facilitated conditioning to goal-relevant stimuli in high achievers—are presented as supporting this model over preparedness and fear module theories.
requirements: Requires a stimulus appraised as relevant to the organism's current concerns, which vary across individuals and contexts
constraints: In this study the goal-relevance was temporary and task-bound, and the resulting learning bias was modest and transient, with no differential resistance to extinction
target_learning_goals: preferential aversive (emotional) learning to concern-relevant stimuli
examples: Participants with high achievement motivation more readily acquired a conditioned response to neutral geometric figures that had been goal-relevant in a spatial cueing task, despite the figures holding no inherent threat value or evolutionary significance

article_title: Non-invasive peripheral nerve stimulation selectively enhances speech category learning in adults
citation: Llanos, F., McHaney, J. R., Schuerman, W. L., Yi, H. G., Leonard, M. K. and Chandrasekaran, B. (2020). Non-invasive peripheral nerve stimulation selectively enhances speech category learning in adults. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-0070-0
title: Arousal-based salience-gated neuromodulation account of paired-tVNS speech category learning
description: The article proposes that sub-threshold tVNS engages ascending brainstem neuromodulatory systems, and that "temporally precise changes to arousal can enhance the gain of perceptually salient stimuli, resulting in greater memory consolidation speci ﬁcally for these stimuli." Under arousal-biased competition (ABC) and GANE models, arousal benefits perceptually salient stimuli and not less salient ones, explaining why stimulation paired with the more salient easier-to-learn tones (cued by pitch height, a dominant dimension for English listeners) enhanced learning while hard-category pairing did not. The account is consistent with the null FFR findings, locating the effect in attention/arousal-modulated consolidation rather than sensory re-encoding.
requirements: Stimulation must be temporally paired with the to-be-learned stimuli so the arousal signal is precise rather than diffuse.
constraints: The article states the null FFR result may reflect the approximately 25 min session being too short to drive sensory plasticity, or sub-threshold intensities being suboptimal for this modality.
The article states it cannot directly link invasive cervical VNS in animal models to auricular tVNS in humans, and stimulation frequency was not manipulated.
target_learners: Adult native English speakers learning non-native speech categories
target_learning_goals: Acquisition of non-native speech sound categories (Mandarin tone categories)
examples: Stimulation paired with easier-to-learn Tone 1/3 enhanced learning while pairing with harder-to-learn Tone 2/4 did not, matching the salience-gated prediction.

title: Sub-perceptual-threshold paired-tVNS speech category training paradigm
description: A training paradigm in which transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation is delivered to the cymba concha and cymba cavum via ear-molded Ag-AgCl electrodes as 15 biphasic square-wave pulses (150 µs pulse width) at 25 Hz, beginning ~300 ms before and continuing 250 ms into each auditory stimulus. "Stimulation was delivered with a pulse amplitude of 0.2 mA below the participant's perceptual threshold", calibrated individually with a 0.1 mA-up/0.3 mA-down staircase, enabling participant blinding. The task itself is trial-based Mandarin tone categorization of 80 natural speech stimuli with visual corrective feedback, followed by a feedback- and stimulation-free Generalization block with novel talkers.
requirements: Individual staircase calibration of perceptual threshold so stimulation stays sub-perceptual and participants can be blinded.
Temporal alignment of the pulse train with auditory stimulus onset.
constraints: Amplitude was limited to no higher than 3 mA due to safety restrictions.
The article states the frequency of stimulation (25 Hz) was not manipulated and its effects cannot be assessed in this modality.

target_learning_goals: Learning to categorize non-native Mandarin tone categories by pitch contour
examples: Participants trained on 40 stimuli across six blocks with visual Correct/Wrong feedback, then categorized 40 new-talker exemplars in a Generalization block without feedback or stimulation.
