article_title: Genetics of cognitive performance, education and learning: from research to policy?
citation: Peter M. Visscher. (2022). Genetics of cognitive performance, education and learning: from research to policy? npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00124-z
title: Human genomics and polygenic scores should be fully embedded in social-science and neuroscience research designs
description: The article proposes that "human genomics, in particular the use of polygenic scores, should become fully embedded into social sciences research, including economics, sociology and psychology". The rationale is that because a substantial proportion of differences in life outcomes is due to DNA, genomic information can strengthen research: it allows more powerful experimental designs by accounting for a proportion of variation among samples, detecting biases and confounders such as genetic ancestry differences between treatment and control groups, and moving from associations to causation. The same principles are said to apply to human-subjects neuroscience, since variation in any measured trait, including brain imaging data, is partly genetic.
requirements: Availability of polygenic score data on research samples, which the article says is increasing in power over time and requires large experimental sample sizes
constraints: The article's examples rest on studies it itself qualifies as indirect (twin tracking study) or underpowered (the 131-adult learning study)
target_learning_goals: understanding the role of genetic variation in cognitive performance and educational outcomes
improving experimental design in education and learning research
examples: The commentary points to the Knigge twin study of delayed tracking and the Youn et al. 100-day learning study as snapshots of how genetics can address questions about cognitive performance, learning and social outcomes

At the same time, the author acknowledges that tracking individuals using their genetic predictor for cognitive ability — a "personalised education" approach — is clearly not endorsed widely. The principle therefore records both the proposed use and its stated social constraint.

citation: Peach, R. L., Yaliraki, S. N., Lefevre, D. and Barahona, M. (2019). Data-driven unsupervised clustering of online learner behaviour. npj Science of Learning 4:14. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0054-0
title: DTW-kernel, RMST-sparsified similarity graph with Markov Stability multiscale clustering of learner time-series
description: A three-stage unsupervised framework for analysing online learner temporal behaviour. A dynamic time warping kernel computes pairwise similarity between raw time-series: "Our method uses a dynamic time warping similarity kernel to generate a sparsified similarity graph between learners, to which we apply a multiscale graph partitioning algorithm". RMST sparsification retains strong, globally relevant edges; Markov Stability scans Markov time to find robust partitions at all resolutions without pre-imposing cluster number or type, yielding a quasi-hierarchy from 10 down to 2 clusters that the analyst can choose from.
requirements: Time-stamped interaction data (task completions or page clicks) for each learner; robustness is assessed via low VI(t) dips and persistent VI(t,t') plateaus across scales.
constraints: Temporal behaviours do not fully account for learner performance, and the authors state it is not intended as a diagnostic tool but for exploration, aid, intervention and course design.
target_learning_goals: identifying temporal engagement behaviours (distributed vs massed vs sporadic learning)
flagging learners at risk of low performance for aid and intervention
informing course design
examples: Applied to 81 learners over six online courses of a part-time management degree, yielding robust 10-, 6- and 2-cluster partitions with 'Early Birds', 'On time', 'Low Engagers', 'Crammers' and sporadic outliers.

article_title: Learning reduces ingroup bias more with perceived losses than gains across cultures
citation: Yuqing Zhou, Björn Lindström, Alexander Soutschek, Pyungwon Kang, Shihui Han, Philippe N. Tobler & Grit Hein. (2025). Learning reduces ingroup bias more with perceived losses than gains across cultures. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00362-x
title: Prediction-error learning account of intergroup impression updating
description: The article frames impression formation as continuous reinforcement learning: impressions and closeness are updated trial by trial through prediction errors. "These updates are driven by prediction errors — discrepancies between expected and actual outcomes." The rate of updating is modulated by prior uncertainty, with strong priors slowing updating. Rescorla-Wagner models with separate learning rates for positive and negative prediction errors best fit expectancy ratings, and a closeness model driven by time-discounted sums of positive and negative prediction errors best fit closeness ratings in both cultures. Negative ingroup prediction errors in the Loss frame carry the weight (Wneg_in) that links learning to bias reduction.
requirements: Formal testing requires computational reinforcement learning modeling with parameters estimated from trial-by-trial expectancy and closeness ratings.
constraints: The account was tested with all-male samples in two cultures and specific group inductions (Swiss-Middle East; Chinese-German), which the authors note may introduce context-specific confounding factors.
target_learning_goals: Formation and updating of intergroup impressions and social closeness
examples: The winning Learning Model 3 fit expectancy ratings with r2 = 0.33 ± 0.26 (Loss) and r2 = 0.38 ± 0.30 (Gain) in the Western sample, with good parameter recovery (rs > 0.88).

title: Delay school start times to mitigate the disadvantage of later chronotypes on adolescent academic success
description: The article proposes delaying school start times as a policy response to the synchrony effect: because later chronotypes show lower grades and higher grade retention mainly in morning timings, the authors argue that "delaying start times could be a possible policy to mitigate this disadvantage". They ground this in their randomised three-timing design and note the benefit is likely largest for students with later chronotypes at the start of secondary school and for older students in math.

constraints: The article calls for translational studies and more local evidence before designing educational public policies; the results are correlational, with random assignment supporting comparability but not causal claims

title: Obstacle Course (OC): a controlled-delivery rodent enrichment paradigm with an exercise-matched Control Course
description: The Obstacle Course is an enrichment paradigm delivered outside animal housing that "enables systematic control over animal engagement with enrichment stimuli". Mice run a square track filled with 12 object-based obstacles for 1 h/day, 6 days/week for 9 weeks; two new obstacles are added and three rearrangements made per session, so mice experienced 132 obstacles over the enrichment period. An exercise-matched Control Course (CC) uses 12 fixed hurdles, identical in size and run for a fixed duration, serving "as a control for physical exercise". Beam sensors and an Arduino board track lap times.

examples: In the reported study, OC, CC, EH and SH groups (n = 10 per group) were compared across six behavioral tasks; OC mice experienced 132 obstacles over 9 weeks while CC mice ran a fixed 12-hurdle course

title: Improved schema formation as an explanatory account of OC-mediated memory enhancements

Schema formation is described as "a process reliant on semanticization and abstraction of experiences and generation of internal representations which are categorically organized", which could allow items consistent with existing memories to be integrated into long-term memory more rapidly. The OC experience requires rich interactions with a wide variety of object-based obstacles, which the authors suggest may facilitate the establishment of object schemas, giving OC animals more highly diversified internal representations of the world.

constraints: The mechanisms by which OC training achieves superior effects cannot be delineated from the present study

citation: Breitwieser, J., Neubauer, A. B., Schmiedek, F. & Brod, G. (2024). Realizing the potential of mobile interventions for education. npj Science of Learning, 9, 76. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00289-9
title: Mobile interventions as a third educational use of mobile technology targeting behavioral, experiential and cognitive change
description: The article defines mobile interventions as a complement to m-learning (mobile devices as content-delivery learning tools) and mobile data collection for theory testing (research tools). Mobile interventions aim "to change students' behavior, experiences, or cognitive processes relevant to learning" across analog and digital, formal and informal contexts. Two features set them apart: "the repeated delivery of intervention prompts at shorter time intervals" and "the utilization of high-resolution data collected alongside the intervention," enabling support before or between learning sessions.
requirements: Delivery via mobile devices to exploit affordances other methods cannot easily replicate, such as multiple prompts per day and high-resolution state data
constraints: Not a delivery mechanism for educational content itself; positioned as complement, not competitor, to m-learning and experience-sampling research
target_learners: school and university students learning in and out of formal settings
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning skills
study behavior
emotional and motivational states relevant to learning

citation: Breitwieser, J., Neubauer, A. B., Schmiedek, F. & Brod, G. (2024). Realizing the potential of mobile interventions for education. npj Science of Learning, 9, 76. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00289-9
title: Time mobile prompts to support learning without becoming a distraction or increasing screen time
description: The article stresses that intervention timing must be optimized because mobile interventions can themselves cause harm: prompts could open a gateway to other apps "that are just one click away, thus increasing screen time," and interventions "could also be a distraction in themselves if prompts disrupt learning activities." It recommends identifying both optimal and suboptimal time points at which a student may be more susceptible to distraction, and combining mobile interventions with digital self-control tools such as screen time limits.
requirements: Data about a student's current context and internal state to determine when prompting is beneficial and when it is disruptive
constraints: Concerns about media multitasking, decreased attention, and excessive screen time are well documented and mobile interventions could inadvertently aggravate these challenges
target_learners: school students using mobile devices for learning
target_learning_goals: protecting attention and study focus
effective timing of supportive prompts

title: Adhere to intent-to-treat estimation and instrumented designs when prompts may not be followed
description: The article identifies adherence to prompts as a major methodological challenge in educational micro-randomized trials, since education often targets the effect of a behavior on a different outcome rather than the behavior itself. It recommends estimating the effect of randomized prompts regardless of whether the behavior was performed — analogous to an intent-to-treat analysis — and using instrumental variable estimation to recover the effect of the behavior when adherence is not perfect, noting the applicability of these approaches still remains to be thoroughly investigated.
requirements: Designs must anticipate non-perfect adherence, where participants may not engage when prompted or may engage without being prompted
constraints: Whether instrumental variable methods are useful across different applications of micro-randomized trials is an open question the article flags
target_learners: school students participating in mobile intervention studies
target_learning_goals: valid causal estimation of mobile intervention effects on learning outcomes

title: Address data protection and privacy with special safeguards for minors in mobile intervention research
description: The article argues the field "must address issues regarding data protection and privacy," because advanced JITAIs may require extensive data collection including sensitive information such as location tracking, and integrating LLMs or third-party services raises consent concerns. Educational applications involving minors require additional protections under regulations like COPPA in the U.S. or GDPR in Europe, and parental consent becomes essential but adds access-management complexity.

constraints: Best practices must integrate lessons from mHealth while considering the unique conditions of educational applications, such as the young age of participants and the involvement of parents and teachers

article_title: Lasting enhancements in neural efficiency by multi-session transcranial direct current stimulation during working memory training
citation: Yufeng Ke, Shuang Liu, Long Chen, Xiashuang Wang and Dong Ming. (2023). Lasting enhancements in neural efficiency by multi-session transcranial direct current stimulation during working memory training. npj Science of Learning 8:48. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00200-y
title: Metaplasticity account of lasting tDCS-enhanced working memory training effects
description: The article offers a metaplasticity explanation for the lasting neurobehavioral improvements observed when anodal tDCS is paired with multi-session working memory training. It defines metaplasticity as "a higher-order form of plasticity that can enable or inhibit plasticity induction, stabilize synapses, and homeostatically regulate cellular activity". When stimulation is paired with repeated cognitive training that induces synaptic plasticity, metaplasticity modulates plasticity and extends the time window for associative plasticity, increasing stimulation-induced aftereffects on cortical excitability or learning. The authors propose that anodal tDCS over the left dlPFC modulated synaptic plasticity of WM-related neural substrates this way.
requirements: Pairing brain stimulation with repeated cognitive training capable of inducing synaptic plasticity
constraints: The authors present this as a possible interpretation rather than a directly tested mechanism
target_learners: healthy young adults undergoing working memory training
target_learning_goals: working memory capacity and efficiency
examples: The study applied anodal HD-tDCS over the left dlPFC simultaneously with ten consecutive days of adaptive verbal N-back training and measured lasting EEG and behavioral aftereffects three weeks later.

article_title: Lasting enhancements in neural efficiency by multi-session transcranial direct current stimulation during working memory training
citation: Yufeng Ke, Shuang Liu, Long Chen, Xiashuang Wang and Dong Ming. (2023). Lasting enhancements in neural efficiency by multi-session transcranial direct current stimulation during working memory training. npj Science of Learning 8:48. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00200-y
title: Neural efficiency framework operationalized via task-related ERD/ERS and P300 responses
description: The article uses a neural efficiency framework in which ERD/ERS measures the amount of neural resources needed to solve a problem: "Within the theoretical framework of neural ef ﬁciency, increasing task- related alpha and beta oscillations re ﬂect the reduced amount of neural resources that need to be engaged during problem-solving". Frontal theta ERS is treated as a signature of WM manipulation and integration of cognitive resources, and P300 GFP as reflecting attentional allocation and the number of synchronously activated neuronal elements. The framework is used to interpret tDCS-augmented training gains as increased efficiency of WM-related neural circuits.
requirements: Task-related EEG recording with ERD/ERS and P300 measures during WM tasks
constraints: The article notes P300 amplitude typically decreases with increasing WM load, complicating interpretation of direction
target_learning_goals: working memory processing efficiency
examples: The article interpreted increased P300 GFP in the active group as stronger engagement of neural resources and possibly less effortful WM processing due to increased neural efficiency.

article_title: Cerebellar interpositus nucleus exhibits time-dependent errors and predictive responses
citation: Parras, G. G., Delgado-García, J. M., López-Ramos, J. C., Gruart, A., & Leal-Campanario, R. (2024). Cerebellar interpositus nucleus exhibits time-dependent errors and predictive responses. npj Science of Learning 9, 12. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00224-y
title: The cerebellar IPn operates as an active-inference (Bayesian) system that minimizes prediction errors across learning stages
description: The article proposes that the IPn functions as an active inference system linking action and perception, operating by "comparing predicted states with actual states, learning from errors, and updating its internal representations" to minimize future errors. Its firing pattern is learning-stage-dependent: long-lasting error responses before acquisition, reduced errors midway, and predictive (conditioned) responses once learning is established. The discussion states that "the ﬁring pattern of IPn neurons matches the Bayesian inference, where the response to current stimuli is based on the likelihood of the previous experience", so the IPn generates predictions of the upcoming US.
requirements: A hierarchical organization is stated as fundamental for correct inference, with CS and US information converging at the cerebellar cortex and IPn via mossy and climbing fibers
constraints: The framework is advanced here for a delay classical eyeblink conditioning paradigm in rabbits using an auditory CS; the authors note cerebellum-dependent learning and timing are more complex than previously thought
target_learners: Adult male rabbits undergoing classical eyeblink conditioning
target_learning_goals: Acquisition and timing refinement of a conditioned eyelid (motor) response through error minimization

article_title: Both individual and peer growth mindsets matter for academic resilience
citation: King, R.B., Li, J., & Wang, Y. (2026). Both individual and peer growth mindsets matter for academic resilience. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00403-z
title: Mindset-by-context framework: growth mindsets as a "seed" that grows in a social context serving as "soil"
description: The mindset-by-context framework holds that an individual's growth mindset operates within a social environment that can reinforce or undermine it. The article states that "an individual's growth mindset is like a 'seed' that grows in the social context, which serves as the 'soil'", and that "A supportive context is a prerequisite for sustaining the benefits of an individual's growth mindset". Fixed-mindset school ecologies with practices such as emphasizing performance feedback may weaken mindset effects. The study's interaction finding is offered as empirical fleshing-out of this framework.
requirements: For growth mindsets to have maximal effect, the broader environment must be congruent with the individual's beliefs
constraints: Peer mindset was operationalized only at school level; classroom-level context was not measurable in PISA
target_learning_goals: academic achievement and resilience under socioeconomic adversity
key_sources: King, R.B., Li, J., & Wang, Y. (2026). Both individual and peer growth mindsets matter for academic resilience. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00403-z

article_title: Both individual and peer growth mindsets matter for academic resilience
citation: King, R.B., Li, J., & Wang, Y. (2026). Both individual and peer growth mindsets matter for academic resilience. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00403-z
title: PISA 2018 secondary-analysis dataset and definition-driven operationalization of academic resilience
description: The study uses the publicly available PISA 2018 dataset: "the sample consists of 606,191 students nested within 21,562 schools" from 79 countries. Resilience follows the definition-driven approach: "Students are classified as academically resilient if they are in the lowest quartile of SES in their countries but are able to achieve proficiency level 3 or above in all three PISA domains". Growth mindset was measured with one reverse-coded item; peer mindset is the school-level aggregate computed with a leave-one-out approach.
requirements: SES quartiles computed within each country to address quartile bias; averaging of ten plausible values per domain
constraints: Cross-sectional data
one-item mindset measure
no classroom-level data
binary outcome prevented use of sampling weights
target_learning_goals: reading, mathematics, and science proficiency among disadvantaged students

article_title: Both individual and peer growth mindsets matter for academic resilience
citation: King, R.B., Li, J., & Wang, Y. (2026). Both individual and peer growth mindsets matter for academic resilience. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00403-z
title: Use a whole-school approach that targets both individual growth beliefs and the broader growth-oriented school environment when supporting disadvantaged students
description: Because both individual and peer growth mindsets predict academic resilience, the article argues interventions should target beliefs and context together: "educators may need to use a whole school approach that targets both individual beliefs and the broader school environment". Suggested practices include establishing growth-mindset role models, providing constructive feedback, reframing mistakes as learning opportunities, and encouraging students to embrace challenges. The authors caution that "Growth mindsets and the interventions developed to enhance them are not silver bullets".
requirements: School environment must reinforce growth-oriented beliefs, since effects depend on contextual affordances
constraints: Relying on growth mindsets alone may be ineffective or socially unjust; multi-pronged approaches addressing socioeconomic structures are needed
target_learning_goals: academic resilience and persistence despite socioeconomic adversity
examples: Multilevel logit models of PISA 2018 showed individual (β = .198), peer (β = .091), and interaction (β = .025) effects on resilience odds after covariates

article_title: Disentangling the contribution of individual and social learning processes in human advice-taking behavior
citation: Maayan Pereg, Uri Hertz, Ido Ben-Artzi and Nitzan Shahar. (2024). Disentangling the contribution of individual and social learning processes in human advice-taking behavior. npj Science of Learning 9:4. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00214-0
title: Three-process account of advice-taking: individual learning, informed advice-taking, and non-informed advice-taking
description: The article proposes and substantiates an explanatory framework in which choice behavior in repeated advice environments integrates three latent processes: "individual learning (i.e., learning the value of actions, independent of advice)", "informed advice-taking (i.e., learning the value of following advice)", and "non-informed advice-taking (i.e., a constant bias to follow advice regardless of outcome history)". Prediction-error-based Q-learning models estimate each component, with the winning mixture model assigning value to the instructed card (φ) and updating the value of following advice from outcomes (ω-weighted). The authors link the non-informed bias to social norms such as reciprocity or epistemic trust in advisors.
requirements: A repeating advice environment with interleaved revealed and concealed advice trials to disentangle the three processes
constraints: The authors note the results "do not necessarily expand to other forms of social learning that were not explicitly examined here", such as observational learning
Only prediction-error-based RL models were examined; alternative frameworks like active inference were not explored
target_learners: adult online participants (Prolific) performing value-based decision-making
target_learning_goals: disentangling how learners integrate personal experience with repeated external advice

article_title: How to capture developmental brain dynamics: gaps and solutions
citation: van Atteveldt, N., Vandermosten, M., Weeda, W. & Bonte, M. (2021). How to capture developmental brain dynamics: gaps and solutions. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00088-6
title: Example framework unifying developmental change across levels, functions, and time
description: The article proposes an example framework unifying developmental changes across three dimensions: levels of change (genes, brain function and structure, behavior, cognition, and social environment), interactively emerging functions (reading, math, executive function), and time. As the figure caption states, "During development (TIME dimension), there is continuous interaction across levels of change (LEVELS: gray bars) as well as across emerging functions (FUNCTIONS: presented as interactive networks)." Neural and cognitive correlates of functions first appear as wide, overlapping networks that gradually specialize to more focused networks with learning and maturation.
requirements: Must encompass multiple levels and functional networks and their dynamic interactions across time
Used across studies and disciplines to allow communication between experts at each level
constraints: The article presents it as an example framework, a suggestion for how such a framework could look
target_learning_goals: Reading, math, executive function development
examples: Table 1 maps each workshop speaker's research onto the framework's levels and functions
key_sources: van Atteveldt, N., Vandermosten, M., Weeda, W. & Bonte, M. (2021). How to capture developmental brain dynamics: gaps and solutions. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00088-6

article_title: How to capture developmental brain dynamics: gaps and solutions
citation: van Atteveldt, N., Vandermosten, M., Weeda, W. & Bonte, M. (2021). How to capture developmental brain dynamics: gaps and solutions. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00088-6
title: Use a common developmental framework spanning levels, functions, and time across studies and disciplines
description: The article recommends that a framework encompassing multiple levels, functional networks, and their dynamic interactions across time (illustrated by its Fig. 1) be used across studies and disciplines. It states "a common framework is essential in order to allow communication between the experts at each level", enabling researchers to specify which levels and networks their study addresses and take into account constraints and modulatory influences from other levels. It also supports exploratory research by relating findings to specific parts of the multilevel model.
requirements: Multidisciplinary, multisite studies involving researchers from different levels and disciplines
Measures comparable across studies
constraints: Studies encompassing different levels and functions at multiple time points are currently scarce

target_learning_goals: Reading, math, executive function and broader developmental outcomes
examples: Workshop participants used the framework to map each presenter's work onto levels and functions (Table 1)

article_title: A brief tablet-based intervention benefits linguistic and communicative abilities in toddlers and preschoolers
citation: Peña, M., Vásquez-Venegas, C., Cortés, P., Pittaluga, E., Herrera, M., Pino, E. J., Escobar, R. G., Dehaene-Lambertz, G., & Guevara, P. (2024). A brief tablet-based intervention benefits linguistic and communicative abilities in toddlers and preschoolers. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00249-3
title: Ludic tablet-based fast-mapping game for word-object and letter-sound associations
description: A tablet game designed by a multidisciplinary team of early childhood educators, speech therapists, game designers, and cognitive neuroscience researchers, built on the fast-mapping paradigm. The main application taught 14 letter-sound associations and 59 infrequently used word-object associations across four to eight training sessions, each word-object association trained once to evaluate fast-mapping after a single exposure. Each trial comprised an encoding phase, a recognition phase, and, for preschoolers, a vocalization phase, with "contingent interaction, delivering immediate feedback to the children's responses". A tutor application allowed remote monitoring by a supervising educator.
requirements: A supervising early childhood educator to minimally oversee sessions and evaluate preschoolers' vocalizations
Tablets secured onto soft cushion-like supports, used individually in a quiet room setting
constraints: Training concentrated on uncommon word-object associations and letter-sound associations only, not all language features with semantic and grammatical contents
target_learners: Preschoolers (~42 months old) from low-income families
target_learning_goals: New word-object (vocabulary) associations
Letter-sound (pre-reading) associations
examples: In the study, children played four to eight sessions in nursery room environments, with the Control group playing only after the intervention finished

title: Fast mapping as a word-learning process for designing early vocabulary interventions
description: Fast mapping is described as "a word-learning process that creates an initial association between a new word and its meaning". The authors adopted it to design their game because previous studies showed toddlers and preschoolers succeed in this task in the short and long term, and because fast-mapping ability is positively associated with concurrent and subsequent language development in late-talking, typically developing, and atypically developing children. The game operationalizes fast mapping by training each word-object association only once across sessions.

article_title: Comparing models of learning and relearning in large-scale cognitive training data sets
citation: Aakriti Kumar, Aaron S. Benjamin, Andrew Heathcote and Mark Steyvers. (2022). Comparing models of learning and relearning in large-scale cognitive training data sets. npj Science of Learning 7:24. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00142-x
title: Interactive two-timescale model of naturalistic learning (M4): permanent skill plus labile task-set preparedness that is lost with delay and rapidly regained with practice
description: M4 models performance as the sum of a slow learning process indexing permanent skill, based on total games played, and a fast process representing task-set preparedness whose weight depends on a context-loss function of elapsed time between sessions. The article states that "task-set preparedness is lost between sessions but is also more rapidly regained with each additional practice session", and that skill, like riding a bike, "is maintained permanently, without loss". The context loss function L(t) = 1 - e^(-γt) captures varied temporal patterns; for the fitted data, 50% of context is lost after about 450 days and close to 80% after 800 days.
requirements: Practice data spanning multiple sessions with varied between-session delays, so that context loss and relearning can be estimated
constraints: The forgetting rate parameter γ is assumed to be shared across participants because not all participants have enough data for a stable individual estimate
target_learners: adult self-directed learners on online cognitive training platforms
target_learning_goals: long-term skill acquisition and retention of cognitive tasks such as selective attention and task switching
examples: The model was fit to individual users' gameplay histories from two Lumosity games, Lost in Migration (a flanker task) and Ebb and Flow (a task switching game), and its relearning predictions plotted against empirical curves in Figs. 5 and 6

article_title: Questioning central assumptions of the ICAP framework
citation: Thurn, C. M., Edelsbrunner, P. A., Berkowitz, M., Deiglmayr, A. & Schalk, L. (2023). Questioning central assumptions of the ICAP framework. npj Science of Learning 8:49. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00197-4
title: Do not rely on the ICAP framework alone for selecting interventions or assessing learning in the classroom
description: Because overt behaviors are ambiguous with respect to underlying learning processes and the I > C > A > P hierarchy lacks a convincing empirical basis, the comment concludes that "practitioners should not be advised to rely on ICAP for selecting effective interventions and assessing learning processes in the classroom". Instead, changes in knowledge components can only be detected via deliberate assessment. Judging engagement from two susceptible sources — overt behaviors and student output — risks wrong inferences in practice.
requirements: Practitioners need evidence-based tools that are practical in everyday teaching; deliberate assessment events are necessary to gain insight into students' learning processes.
constraints: The ICAP framework itself provides no guidance on how to generate and use diagnostic information on students' covert learning processes.
target_learning_goals: Selecting effective interventions and accurately assessing students' learning processes
examples: The comment argues that relying primarily on overt behavior to plan, monitor, and judge instructional events bears the risk of distorting insights into actual covert learning processes.

citation: Louise Elffers, Eddie Denessen and Monique Volman. (2024). Combining perspectives in multidisciplinary research on inequality in education. npj Science of Learning 9:5. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00215-z
title: Three dimensions along which disciplinary perspectives on educational inequality vary
description: The article identifies a taxonomy of three dimensions on which perspectives on inequality in education differ between academic disciplines. As the authors state, "These dimensions pertain to (1) how the problem of inequality in education is framed, (2) how inequality in education is empirically evaluated, and (3) how the role of education in fostering (in)equality is conceptualized." The taxonomy organizes the article's argument that combining disciplinary insights requires awareness of these varying lenses.
requirements: Researchers combining insights across disciplines must be aware of and able to locate their work on each of the three dimensions
constraints: The authors note the brief comment "cannot do justice to all theoretical perspectives on inequality in education, nor to the rich empirical literature on the topic from all disciplines"
target_learners: Researchers studying inequality in education across academic disciplines
target_learning_goals: Understanding and addressing educational inequality through multidisciplinary research

citation: Louise Elffers, Eddie Denessen and Monique Volman. (2024). Combining perspectives in multidisciplinary research on inequality in education. npj Science of Learning 9:5. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00215-z
title: Explicate the theoretical lens through which educational inequality is studied
description: Because disciplines frame inequality differently—some problematizing unequal outcomes, others unequal treatment or unequal provision—researchers should make their framing explicit. The article states "the need to explicate the lens through which the problem of inequality in education is studied," since answering "what needs to be equal to speak of equality" makes clear whether unequal treatment and/or outcomes are problematized or strived for.
requirements: Researchers must answer what needs to be equal to speak of equality, clarifying whether unequal treatment and/or unequal outcomes are problematized or strived for
constraints: The authors note these lenses "may be very different, and therefore not self-evident"
target_learning_goals: Fruitful combining of insights and ideas from across disciplines on educational inequality
examples: The article points to review articles such as the works of Jencks and Espinoza as aids for researchers placing their work vis-à-vis the broad range of perspectives

citation: Louise Elffers, Eddie Denessen and Monique Volman. (2024). Combining perspectives in multidisciplinary research on inequality in education. npj Science of Learning 9:5. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00215-z
title: Consider the implicit norms embedded in empirical evaluations of educational inequality
description: Evaluations of inequality embed norms about which outcomes matter and for whom. The article proposes "consideration of the implicit norms that forms of evaluation set for the pursuit of equality in education," including "consideration of the potential reinforcement of inequality through the normativity of pursuing certain outcomes." Group-level indicators (e.g., explained variance by background) and individual-level learning-gain indicators embody different norms about what equality requires.
requirements: Reflection must include consideration of the potential reinforcement of inequality through the normativity of pursuing certain outcomes
constraints: The article notes a narrow focus on cognitive outcomes may in fact perpetuate or even increase inequality
target_learning_goals: Choosing and interpreting indicators of educational equality with awareness of their normative repercussions
examples: The article cites critical discussions such as the works of Au and Hogg as aids for researchers considering implicit norms embedded in particular evaluations
key_sources: Louise Elffers, Eddie Denessen and Monique Volman. (2024). Combining perspectives in multidisciplinary research on inequality in education. npj Science of Learning 9:5. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00215-z

article_title: Combining perspectives in multidisciplinary research on inequality in education
citation: Louise Elffers, Eddie Denessen and Monique Volman. (2024). Combining perspectives in multidisciplinary research on inequality in education. npj Science of Learning 9:5. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00215-z
title: Reflect on education's dual role as both producer and reducer of inequality
description: Educational interventions may remedy or aggravate inequality, sometimes both at once. The article identifies "reflection on the potential role of education as both a producer and reducer of inequality" as a third principle, noting that "Remediation and aggravation of inequality may even happen as the result of the same educational intervention." Researchers studying interventions for disadvantaged students should not assume they contribute to equality.
requirements: When studying interventions for disadvantaged or underperforming students, researchers must take into account potential negative treatment effects as well, rather than assuming interventions contribute to equality
constraints: The article notes it is difficult to determine to what extent a treatment such as tracking helped or hampered development, especially if control groups cannot be put in place
target_learning_goals: Evaluating educational interventions for their counterfactual impact and unintended effects on inequality
examples: The article cites literature such as the work of Van de Werfhorst and Mijs and Marks as informing reflections on the potential counterfactual impact or unintended effects of interventions
key_sources: Louise Elffers, Eddie Denessen and Monique Volman. (2024). Combining perspectives in multidisciplinary research on inequality in education. npj Science of Learning 9:5. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00215-z

article_title: Toward a unified vocabulary for embodiment research challenges and solutions
citation: Peng Wang, Jingming Li, Qian Yu, Liye Zou, Xia Xu, Myrto Mavilidi, Ryan S. Falck, Fabian Herold, Robert J. Schinke, Markus Raab & Fred Paas. (2026). Toward a unified vocabulary for embodiment research: challenges and solutions. npj Science of Learning 11:36. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00413-x
title: 4E cognition as an umbrella framework grouping Embodied, Embedded, Enactive, and Extended approaches
description: The article presents the 4E cognition approach as an integrative framework grouping Embodied, Embedded, Enactive, and Extended ideas under one umbrella, explicitly acknowledging the multifaceted nature of cognitive systems. It advocates that cognition is "shaped and structured by dynamic interactions between the brain, body, and both the physical and social environments". The authors use it as a broad definition many subfields can agree on, while noting fragmentation persists within 4E because its traditions diverge at the level of ontology and explanation.
requirements: A shared glossary should map terms to their core claims, typical operationalizations, and underlying commitments while noting where positions are genuinely incommensurable
constraints: The 4E umbrella brings together traditions that sometimes diverge at the level of ontology and explanation, e.g., enactivist approaches foreground autonomy and sense-making while many embodied or grounded cognition strands use representational sensorimotor simulations
target_learners: researchers and students across psychology, neuroscience, education, AI, and public health
target_learning_goals: understanding how body, brain, and environment interact in cognition and learning
examples: The article defines embodiment as an umbrella term with sub-terms like embodied (body-focused) and embedded (environment-focused), building on the 4E cognition framework
key_sources: Peng Wang, Jingming Li, Qian Yu, Liye Zou, Xia Xu, Myrto Mavilidi, Ryan S. Falck, Fabian Herold, Robert J. Schinke, Markus Raab & Fred Paas. (2026). Toward a unified vocabulary for embodiment research: challenges and solutions. npj Science of Learning 11:36. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00413-x

article_title: Toward a unified vocabulary for embodiment research challenges and solutions
citation: Peng Wang, Jingming Li, Qian Yu, Liye Zou, Xia Xu, Myrto Mavilidi, Ryan S. Falck, Fabian Herold, Robert J. Schinke, Markus Raab & Fred Paas. (2026). Toward a unified vocabulary for embodiment research: challenges and solutions. npj Science of Learning 11:36. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00413-x
title: Apply the 3 Cs—clear, concise, consistent terminology—in embodiment research communication
description: The authors propose that embodiment research language should be "clear, concise, and consistent". Clear means pairing precise scholarly terms with plain-language glosses; concise means shorter self-descriptive labels (e.g., embodiment-informed instruction) with practice-facing descriptors; consistent means defining terms at first use, aligning with established frameworks, and avoiding scope drift. They argue adopting the 3 Cs makes studies easier to line up side by side and supports cumulative knowledge generation.
requirements: Define terms at first use and align with established frameworks; when theories truly differ, give them distinct labels rather than overloading the term embodied cognition
constraints: Conciseness should not come at the expense of precision, especially when a term signals theoretical assumptions; the goal is a shared vocabulary that makes differences explicit, not a single theory of embodiment
target_learning_goals: clear cross-disciplinary scientific communication about embodiment and embodied learning
examples: The article suggests pairing a technical term such as embodied pedagogical dynamics with an explanatory gloss about how bodily action and perception are intentionally leveraged during instruction
key_sources: Peng Wang, Jingming Li, Qian Yu, Liye Zou, Xia Xu, Myrto Mavilidi, Ryan S. Falck, Fabian Herold, Robert J. Schinke, Markus Raab & Fred Paas. (2026). Toward a unified vocabulary for embodiment research: challenges and solutions. npj Science of Learning 11:36. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00413-x

article_title: Reading and writing habits compensate for aging effects in speech connectedness
citation: Malcorra, B. L. C., Mota, N. B., Weissheimer, J., Schilling, L. P., Wilson, M. A. & Hübner, L. C. (2022). Reading and writing habits compensate for aging effects in speech connectedness. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00129-8
title: Cognitive reserve: cognitively stimulating activities increase brain resilience to cope with cognitive-processing changes in typical and atypical aging
description: The article frames education and frequency of reading and writing habits under "the concept of cognitive reserve which establishes the theory that activities that stimulate the brain are linked to an increase in brain resilience to cope with changes in cognitive processing resulting from typical and atypical aging". It uses this framework to interpret its finding that RWH's coefficient compensated for the aging effect in speech connectedness, aligning with longitudinal evidence that reading activity prevents long-term cognitive decline.
requirements: The framework presumes activities that stimulate the brain, such as formal education and frequent reading and writing habits, are present across the lifespan
constraints: The article notes its own correlational design "could not be taken as a causality effect"
target_learners: typical adults and older adults, predominantly with low educational level and low to middle-low SES
target_learning_goals: maintenance of speech connectedness and cognitive efficiency in aging
examples: The study measured oral narratives of 118 healthy individuals aged 51–82 as word-graphs and found the strength of RWH's coefficient compensated for the aging effect.
key_sources: Malcorra, B. L. C., Mota, N. B., Weissheimer, J., Schilling, L. P., Wilson, M. A. & Hübner, L. C. (2022). Reading and writing habits compensate for aging effects in speech connectedness. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00129-8

article_title: Knee flexion of saxophone players anticipates tonal context of music
citation: Moura, N., Vidal, M., Aguilera, A. M., Vilas-Boas, J. P., Serra, S. & Leman, M. (2023). Knee flexion of saxophone players anticipates tonal context of music. npj Science of Learning 8:22. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00172-z
title: Embodiment account: anticipatory knee movement facilitates cognitive processing and technical execution in music performance
description: The article frames knee flexion as embodiment, "the process of transforming inner subjective experiences, ideas or intentions in a physical manifestation". Within predictive coding and active inference, the authors propose that "anticipatory knee movement facilitates the cognitive processing involved in motor adaptation, and consequently supports technical execution". The framework links modeled acoustic expectations to projected movement, drawing on short-term memory models of tonal induction.
requirements: Prior familiarity with the performed piece, as participants "had previous contact with the piece".
constraints: Findings come from standard saxophone repertoire with descendant pitch lines and low rhythmical density; the authors state other musical styles and genres should be considered.
target_learning_goals: motor learning
expressive music performance
key_sources: Moura, N., Vidal, M., Aguilera, A. M., Vilas-Boas, J. P., Serra, S. & Leman, M. (2023). Knee flexion of saxophone players anticipates tonal context of music. npj Science of Learning 8:22. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00172-z

article_title: Knee flexion of saxophone players anticipates tonal context of music
citation: Moura, N., Vidal, M., Aguilera, A. M., Vilas-Boas, J. P., Serra, S. & Leman, M. (2023). Knee flexion of saxophone players anticipates tonal context of music. npj Science of Learning 8:22. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00172-z
title: R-package for computational modeling of the auditory periphery (ANI, pitch expectation, rhythmical density)
description: The authors released "the routines for the computational modeling of the auditory periphery ... freely available as an R-package at a Github repository". It computes the auditory nerve image with CalcANI, periodicity pitch images with PeriodicityPitch, pitch expectation profiles with ContextualityIndex (Comparison), and rhythmical density with RoughnessFFT. The package implements the model used to derive pitch expectation and rhythmical density profiles from audio in this study.
requirements: Mono audio recordings of the performance, converted into a 40-channel auditory nerve image.
target_learning_goals: analyzing sensorimotor coupling in performance data
key_sources: Moura, N., Vidal, M., Aguilera, A. M., Vilas-Boas, J. P., Serra, S. & Leman, M. (2023). Knee flexion of saxophone players anticipates tonal context of music. npj Science of Learning 8:22. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00172-z

article_title: Surprise responses in the human brain demonstrate statistical learning under high concurrent cognitive demand
citation: Marta Isabel Garrido, Chee Leong James Teng, Jeremy Alexander Taylor, Elise Genevieve Rowe and Jason Brett Mattingley. (2016). Surprise responses in the human brain demonstrate statistical learning under high concurrent cognitive demand. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/npjscilearn.2016.6
title: MMN as a sensory prediction error marking implicit learning of probabilistic (non-rule-based) statistical structure
description: The framework treats the mismatch negativity — an early fronto-central response peaking at about 100–250 ms — as "a sensory prediction error and a neurophysiological marker of a learned regularity". The article extends classic oddball work to a probabilistic paradigm in which the regularity "can not be encoded as a deterministic sequence-based rule, a ﬁnite set of known stimuli, or by a categorical separation between expected and unexpected events". Learners implicitly encode the Gaussian distribution's variance, so prediction-error magnitude scales with a tone's improbability relative to its context. The article uses this framework to argue that change detection proceeds automatically even under cognitive demand.
requirements: Exposure to an auditory stream whose frequencies are sampled from a contextual distribution, with probe tones embedded to evoke prediction-error responses
constraints: Prediction-error generation likely combines release from adaptation with a second-order memory comparison mechanism; adaptation alone does not account for the responses
target_learning_goals: implicit learning of statistical regularities in the sensory environment
key_sources: Marta Isabel Garrido, Chee Leong James Teng, Jeremy Alexander Taylor, Elise Genevieve Rowe and Jason Brett Mattingley. (2016). Surprise responses in the human brain demonstrate statistical learning under high concurrent cognitive demand. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/npjscilearn.2016.6

article_title: Anterograde interference in multitask perceptual learning
citation: Jia Yang, Fang-Fang Yan, Tingting Wang, Zile Wang, Qingshang Ma, Jinmei Xiao, Xianyuan Yang, Zhong-Lin Lu & Chang-Bing Huang. (2025). Anterograde interference in multitask perceptual learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00312-7
title: Integrated reweighting account with shared and protected weight structures for multitask learning
description: The article extends the Integration Reweighting Theory to sequential multitask learning: "The Integration Reweighting Theory and related reweighting models propose thatl e a r n i n gi n v o l v es optimizing connection weights between stable stimulus representation and task decisions." The authors propose that perceptual learning engages distinct plastic sites with compatible or incompatible overlapping weight structures, and that a network preserving learned-task weights while adjusting non-overlapping nodes can yield the observed asymmetric anterograde interference. This supports a meta-plasticity strategy of reducing plasticity in previously engaged regions to protect established learning.
requirements: Models of perceptual learning would need to incorporate shared and independent hidden layers that preserve weight structures from learned tasks
constraints: The theory and models have primarily been applied to investigate perceptual learning and transfer in single tasks; extension to sequential multitask learning is the article's proposal
target_learners: adults learning multiple perceptual tasks sequentially
target_learning_goals: acquisition of multiple perceptual skills with preserved prior learning
examples: A schematic neural network in which learning task A first protects task-A weights, so task B learned via non-overlapping nodes is unaffected by sequence position, while learning task B first prevents the optimal decision boundary for task A
key_sources: Jia Yang, Fang-Fang Yan, Tingting Wang, Zile Wang, Qingshang Ma, Jinmei Xiao, Xianyuan Yang, Zhong-Lin Lu & Chang-Bing Huang. (2025). Anterograde interference in multitask perceptual learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00312-7

article_title: Using virtual reality to study spatial mapping and threat learning
citation: Marino, C. E., Rjabtsenkov, P., Sharp, C., Ali, Z., Pineda, E., Bavdekar, S. Y., Garg, T., Jordan, K., Halvorsen, M., Aponte, C., Blue, J., Zhu, X. & Suarez-Jimenez, B. (2025). Using virtual reality to study spatial mapping and threat learning. npj Science of Learning 10:14. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00305-6
title: Attentional control theory account: state anxiety disrupts spatial mapping by diverting attention toward threat
description: The article uses attentional control theory as its explanatory framework for why some participants fail contextual threat learning. Under this account, "anxiety may impair performance via increased competition among attentional resources, thereby reducing attention to the ongoing task". Applied here, transient state anxiety in uncertain situations allocates attention toward threat detection and away from the environmental context — landmarks and location cues — needed to build a cognitive map, so non-learners lack an accurate mental representation of which zones predict shock. The authors also offer a competing explanation: anxiety-driven compensatory attention to potential threats may bias attention away from the actually predictive context.
requirements: The task must require attention to contextual and spatial cues (landmarks, zones) for successful discrimination, as the VR flower-picking paradigm does.
constraints: The authors state that deficits in discrimination learning in non-learners cannot be solely explained by heightened anxiety during the task; attention allocation was not assessed in this study, and the study did not assess trauma or other potential channels of learning.
target_learners: Healthy adult students navigating virtual environments
target_learning_goals: Learning to discriminate threat from safety based on contextual location cues
Forming accurate spatial/cognitive maps of an environment
examples: The VR conditioning task required participants to use local and distal landmarks to infer which half of the environment predicted shocks; non-learners failed this discrimination while showing higher state anxiety.
key_sources: Marino, C. E., Rjabtsenkov, P., Sharp, C., Ali, Z., Pineda, E., Bavdekar, S. Y., Garg, T., Jordan, K., Halvorsen, M., Aponte, C., Blue, J., Zhu, X. & Suarez-Jimenez, B. (2025). Using virtual reality to study spatial mapping and threat learning. npj Science of Learning 10:14. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00305-6

article_title: Montessori education: a review of the evidence base
citation: Chloë Marshall. (2017). Montessori education: a review of the evidence base. npj Science of Learning 2:11. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0012-7
title: Montessori method as a triad of child, teacher and prepared environment with self-directed engagement
description: The review describes the Montessori method as organised around "the dynamic triad of child, teacher and environment", in which the teacher guides children through a prepared environment supporting development "through active exploration, choice and independent learning". Two aspects are highlighted: manipulable learning materials for sensorial and academic concepts, and a self-directed mode of engagement during a 3-h work cycle in which children choose what, where, with whom and for how long they work, free of competition and extrinsic rewards. Montessori's underlying account holds that children pass through sensitive periods and stages of development, and that self-construction is fostered by self-directed activity in the prepared environment.
requirements: Requires trained teachers who guide children based on careful observation of the children rather than a formal timetable
Requires a specially prepared environment and class rules within which freedom operates
constraints: The name is not copyrighted and implementation varies considerably across schools, with the name frequently used without full adherence
target_learners: Children aged 3–6 and 6–12 in preschool and elementary settings
target_learning_goals: Optimal development across intellectual, physical, emotional and social domains
Sensorial concepts, mathematics, literacy, science, geography and history
examples: Children build the pink tower from ten cubes differing only in dimension, choosing when to repeat the activity and tidying it away afterwards
A 3-h external work cycle in which children move freely around the classroom and select activities while the teacher guides and gives small-group lessons
key_sources: Chloë Marshall. (2017). Montessori education: a review of the evidence base. npj Science of Learning 2:11. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0012-7

article_title: Montessori education: a review of the evidence base
citation: Chloë Marshall. (2017). Montessori education: a review of the evidence base. npj Science of Learning 2:11. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0012-7
title: Montessori learning-materials design pattern: single-concept isolation, control of error, and concrete-to-abstract progression
description: The review enumerates the design principles running through Montessori's learning materials: the child learns through movement and gains a concrete foundation preparing for more abstract concepts; each material isolates just one concept, as in the pink tower where cubes "differ only in their dimensions"; and each piece contains a control of error that alerts the child to mistakes, "thereby allowing self-correction with minimal teacher support". The materials span practical life, sensorial, literacy (writing before reading, phonics), mathematics and geography, with sensorial materials such as the long rods and touchboards serving as preparation for academic materials.
requirements: Materials must isolate a single concept with no additional cues
Each material must include a control of error enabling self-correction
constraints: The review notes it offers only a brief survey of some of the most important elements, not an exhaustive treatment
target_learning_goals: Sensorial classification and naming
Literacy and mathematics foundations through concrete materials
examples: The sound boxes contain six pairs of closed cylinders varying in sound, with sound as the only usable cue for matching
Number rods divide ten rods into alternating red and blue 10 cm sections so they take the numerical values 1–10
key_sources: Chloë Marshall. (2017). Montessori education: a review of the evidence base. npj Science of Learning 2:11. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0012-7

article_title: Speed and accuracy instructions affect two aspects of skill learning differently
citation: Teodóra Vékony, Claire Pleche, Orsolya Pesthy, Karolina Janacsek and Dezso Nemeth. (2022). Speed and accuracy instructions affect two aspects of skill learning differently. npj Science of Learning 7:27. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00144-9
title: When designing learning studies, take into account the possible differences between measured competence and performance
description: The article argues that single-session measurements capture momentary performance rather than long-term acquired knowledge. It states that "the measured momentary performance is not always equivalent to the acquired knowledge (competence)" and recommends that "using only a single session to evaluate learning might be problematic" when describing long-term knowledge, since contextual factors such as fatigue, practice or overlearning can influence measured performance.
requirements: Testing in more than one instructional/measurement context, e.g. re-testing acquired knowledge under equal speed-accuracy emphasis after initial learning, as the study did with a Same Instruction Phase.
constraints: The demonstrated competence-performance dissociation concerned probability-based learning; serial-order-based learning showed no instruction effect in either phase.
target_learning_goals: procedural learning of probability-based and serial-order-based regularities
examples: Participants learned under speed or accuracy instructions and were later re-tested with equal emphasis, revealing that the speed-group advantage in probability-based learning disappeared when acquired knowledge was measured.
key_sources: Teodóra Vékony, Claire Pleche, Orsolya Pesthy, Karolina Janacsek and Dezso Nemeth. (2022). Speed and accuracy instructions affect two aspects of skill learning differently. npj Science of Learning 7:27. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00144-9

article_title: Social interaction shapes and boosts second language learning: virtual reality can show us how
citation: Ana Zappa, Mel Slater & Antoni Rodriguez-Fornells. (2025). Social interaction shapes and boosts second language learning: virtual reality can show us how. npj Science of Learning 10:90. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00381-8
title: Social L2 Learning (SL2) model: L2 learning in real-life or simulated social interaction, with context quality explaining L1–L2 differences
description: The Social L2 Learning (SL2) model, proposed by Li and Jeong, defines socially interactive L2 learning as "real-life or simulated real-life environments where learners can interact with objects and people, perform actions, receive, use, and integrate perceptual, visuospatial, and other sensorimotor information". It claims L2 learning processes differ from L1 acquisition mainly because L2 learning contexts are generally poorer, and grounds its premises in memory research, including the encoding-specificity principle: retrieval is facilitated when learners are in the context in which they first encoded the material. The review uses the model to interpret neural evidence that social encoding yields more native-like processing.
requirements: Learning environments must allow interaction with objects and people and integration of perceptual, visuospatial, and sensorimotor information so that learning and communication become embodied.
constraints: The article notes the model cannot convincingly be tested via flat-screen paradigms such as video viewing or imagined social partners that bear little resemblance to naturalistic L1 acquisition.
target_learning_goals: Second language proficiency achieved through socially embedded communication
examples: The review cites fMRI studies of social vs. translation word encoding and live vs. video sign-syntax learning as supporting the model's prediction that richer social contexts yield more native-like processing.
key_sources: Ana Zappa, Mel Slater & Antoni Rodriguez-Fornells. (2025). Social interaction shapes and boosts second language learning: virtual reality can show us how. npj Science of Learning 10:90. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00381-8

article_title: Social interaction shapes and boosts second language learning: virtual reality can show us how
citation: Ana Zappa, Mel Slater & Antoni Rodriguez-Fornells. (2025). Social interaction shapes and boosts second language learning: virtual reality can show us how. npj Science of Learning 10:90. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00381-8
title: Proposed extension of the Revised Hierarchical Model: socially enriched contexts foster more direct L2 word-to-concept links from the start of learning
description: The article builds on the Revised Hierarchical Model, in which "the L2 lexicon initially relies on L1 translations during early learning and later develops direct connections to conceptual meanings as proficiency increases". The authors propose an extension in which socially enriched, multimodal and interactive contexts facilitate "more direct links between L2 lexical items and conceptual representations compared to learning in classical non-social settings", allowing learners to bypass reliance on L1 translations from the beginning. The extension explicitly incorporates the four factors of multimodality, embodiment, interaction and social feedback, and is offered as an empirically testable target for VR-based research.
requirements: Testing requires paradigms that manipulate social-enrichment factors while controlling linguistic input, e.g., via VR with virtual agents whose gaze, gestures and object interaction can be varied.
constraints: The extension is a proposal; the article states it should be empirically tested using VR to compare word learning outcomes across socially enriched and traditional contexts, and presents it as a model to refine rather than a validated result.
target_learning_goals: Direct mapping of L2 word forms to conceptual meaning; vocabulary integration into the L2 lexicon
examples: The review's Fig. 2B depicts the extension, with stronger links between L2 wordforms and concepts under multimodal, social learning settings compared with classical non-social settings.
key_sources: Ana Zappa, Mel Slater & Antoni Rodriguez-Fornells. (2025). Social interaction shapes and boosts second language learning: virtual reality can show us how. npj Science of Learning 10:90. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00381-8

article_title: How to optimize knowledge construction in the brain
citation: van Kesteren, M. T. R. & Meeter, M. (2020). How to optimize knowledge construction in the brain. npj Science of Learning 5:5. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-0064-y
title: SLIMM framework: mPFC detects schema resonance and integrates new information while inhibiting the hippocampus
description: The SLIMM framework is a systems-level neuroscientific model of schema-mediated memory cited and described in this review. It holds that "the mPFC detects resonance from an activated schema and then acts to directly integrate newly learned information", a process usually achieved through offline processes such as (re)consolidation. The review notes the hippocampus is not related to integrating new information with existing schemas in this framework and "it is suggested to be inhibited by the mPFC" in such situations.
requirements: Applies to human, whole-brain, systems-level accounts of schema storage, access and update involving the hippocampus and mPFC
constraints: The review states specifics of consolidation processes are still up to debate, and the framework's claims are posed as proposals rather than tested conclusions
target_learning_goals: long-term declarative memory formation
schema-based knowledge integration
key_sources: van Kesteren, M. T. R. & Meeter, M. (2020). How to optimize knowledge construction in the brain. npj Science of Learning 5:5. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-0064-y

article_title: How to optimize knowledge construction in the brain
citation: van Kesteren, M. T. R. & Meeter, M. (2020). How to optimize knowledge construction in the brain. npj Science of Learning 5:5. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-0064-y
title: Memory formation proceeds through successive phases of encoding, consolidation, retrieval and reconsolidation
description: The review organizes declarative memory formation as a cycle of phases: encoding by the hippocampus and medial temporal lobe, offline consolidation (especially during sleep) that semanticizes memories, retrieval that reconstructs memories depending on present cues, and reconsolidation whereby retrieved memories are updated and integrated into existing schemas. "Memories are then suggested to become reconsolidated into existing schemas, presumably altering their features again", so schemas are continuously adjusted to optimize understanding and prediction.
requirements: Memory content moves between episodic detail and semantic organization across phases, so interventions must be matched to the relevant phase
constraints: The review chose to focus on the adult brain and acknowledges not all discussed processes might translate directly to the developing brain
target_learning_goals: understanding how long-term knowledge is built
balancing episodic detail and semantic generalization
key_sources: van Kesteren, M. T. R. & Meeter, M. (2020). How to optimize knowledge construction in the brain. npj Science of Learning 5:5. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-0064-y

article_title: How to optimize knowledge construction in the brain
citation: van Kesteren, M. T. R. & Meeter, M. (2020). How to optimize knowledge construction in the brain. npj Science of Learning 5:5. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-0064-y
title: Predictive coding account: the brain builds a world model that generates prediction errors, and very strong schemas resist change
description: The review presents predictive coding as a general theory of brain function explaining why information is organized into schemas: "our brains evolved to predict what will happen next", requiring a clear and consistent world model similar to semantic memory or schema. This model generates prediction errors when inconsistent information is encountered and supports prospection recruiting the mPFC. The review notes a drawback: "when it becomes very strong it will be resistant to change; many and large prediction errors are needed to adapt it."
requirements: A not-yet-fully-developed model for prediction errors to drive adaptation
constraints: Once the model becomes very strong, many and large prediction errors are needed to adapt it
target_learning_goals: schema-based prediction
memory generalization
key_sources: van Kesteren, M. T. R. & Meeter, M. (2020). How to optimize knowledge construction in the brain. npj Science of Learning 5:5. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-0064-y

article_title: Note-by-note predictability modulates rhythm learning and its neural components
citation: Marc Deosdad-Díez & Josep Marco-Pallarés. (2025). Note-by-note predictability modulates rhythm learning and its neural components. npj Science of Learning 10:59. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00353-y
title: IDyOM information content as a note-by-note measure of temporal predictability in rhythms
description: The Information Dynamics of Music (IDyOM) model is a computational model that captures statistical features of music; in this study it quantifies the temporal predictability of each individual note. The article states that "Information content (IC) gives a quantitative measure of the unpredictability of an event based on extracting the statistical properties of a corpus of music by which the model is trained." The model was trained on 185 chorale melodies by Bach, using onset, inter-onset interval and metrical accent viewpoints, and the authors note it "tries to simulate the process of musical enculturation and statistical learning of musical features of humans".
requirements: A predefined training corpus from which onset, inter-onset interval and metric accent probabilities are extracted
constraints: IC reflects statistics of the training corpus and the experimental rhythms; in this study the corpus was 185 Bach chorale melodies
target_learning_goals: temporal prediction and accurate timing of rhythmic production
examples: The nine experimental rhythms were selected according to their information content (Table 1 reports mean, SD, min and max IC per rhythm)
key_sources: Marc Deosdad-Díez & Josep Marco-Pallarés. (2025). Note-by-note predictability modulates rhythm learning and its neural components. npj Science of Learning 10:59. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00353-y

article_title: Note-by-note predictability modulates rhythm learning and its neural components
citation: Marc Deosdad-Díez & Josep Marco-Pallarés. (2025). Note-by-note predictability modulates rhythm learning and its neural components. npj Science of Learning 10:59. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00353-y
title: Represent rhythm timing explicitly as spatial distance between visual markers to reduce asynchrony and support rhythm learning
description: This principle recommends presenting temporal intervals in a rhythm-learning task as distances between vertical lines, so that visual space directly encodes time between sounds. The authors report that the graphical group's manipulation yielded "a global reduction of the asynchrony and, on the other, a reduction in the effect of learning, supporting the effectiveness of this procedure to reduce the uncertainty in rhythm templates and enhancing performance." In the study, each sound was marked with a vertical line, with greater distances standing for longer intervals, contrasted against categorical shape cues and meaningless dots.
requirements: Visual cues must correspond meaningfully to the temporal structure of the rhythm rather than being arbitrary shapes or unrelated marks
constraints: The study did not include a group without any visual information, so the authors state they cannot determine whether the graphical procedure improved accuracy compared to the absence of a visual aid
target_learning_goals: accurate timing and synchronization in rhythm production
examples: Participants in the graphical group saw vertical lines whose spacing represented inter-onset intervals while listening, synchronizing and reproducing nine rhythms
key_sources: Marc Deosdad-Díez & Josep Marco-Pallarés. (2025). Note-by-note predictability modulates rhythm learning and its neural components. npj Science of Learning 10:59. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00353-y

article_title: The impact of classroom soundfield systems on reading fluency in normal-hearing students
citation: Shiels, L., Carew, P., Tomlin, D. & Rance, G. (2025). The impact of classroom soundfield systems on reading fluency in normal-hearing students. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00350-1
title: Cognitive Resource Allocation theory as an explanation for greater SFA benefit among lower-IQ students
description: The article invokes Cognitive Resource Allocation theory to explain why lower-IQ children gained more reading fluency benefit from sound field amplification. The theory "proposes a limited pool of resources that are flexibly allocated depending on task demands". Under poor listening conditions, perception of the acoustic signal requires more resources, compromising the cognitive processing left for the task; individuals with higher intelligence can allocate more resources to demanding tasks, explaining the observed IQ–benefit relationship in this study.
requirements: Applies to listening tasks where degraded acoustic conditions increase the perceptual resource requirement, as stated in the article's account.
constraints: The article presents it as a proposed explanation for the observed IQ–SFA benefit relationship, not as a directly tested mechanism.
target_learning_goals: reading fluency development under degraded classroom listening conditions
key_sources: Shiels, L., Carew, P., Tomlin, D. & Rance, G. (2025). The impact of classroom soundfield systems on reading fluency in normal-hearing students. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00350-1

article_title: The impact of classroom soundfield systems on reading fluency in normal-hearing students
citation: Shiels, L., Carew, P., Tomlin, D. & Rance, G. (2025). The impact of classroom soundfield systems on reading fluency in normal-hearing students. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00350-1
title: Front Row Juno sound field amplification system used in mainstream classrooms
description: The Front Row Juno is a classroom sound field amplification (SFA) system in which the teacher's voice, "recorded via a lanyard-worn microphone", is sent to loudspeakers arranged around the classroom. It elevates instructions above ambient noise and evenly distributes auditory information so the teacher need not raise their voice; typical amplification is 8–10 dB. In this study one Juno system was installed per classroom, with gain calibrated from measured teacher voice levels at six seating positions.
requirements: Classroom eligibility required an enclosed classroom with no existing SFA in use.
constraints: The study's mean 7 dB SNR improvement (from approximately −7 dB to 0 dB) fell short of the recommended +15 dB minimum for optimal learning.
target_learners: mainstream primary school students, including normal-hearing grade 3–4 children
target_learning_goals: improved access to the teacher's spoken instruction in noisy classrooms
examples: Twenty-three Victorian grade 3–4 classes each received one Front Row Juno system, alternating On and Off across three school terms.
key_sources: Shiels, L., Carew, P., Tomlin, D. & Rance, G. (2025). The impact of classroom soundfield systems on reading fluency in normal-hearing students. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00350-1

article_title: The impact of classroom soundfield systems on reading fluency in normal-hearing students
citation: Shiels, L., Carew, P., Tomlin, D. & Rance, G. (2025). The impact of classroom soundfield systems on reading fluency in normal-hearing students. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00350-1
title: Consider sound field amplification important support in classrooms that do not meet recommended acoustic standards
description: The authors conclude that, although SFA did not produce measurable reading fluency gains for the general student body in this study, "SFA should be considered important support in classrooms that do not meet recommended acoustic standards". Amplification advanced fluency development for students with lower intellectual abilities while having no negative consequences for other students, and it improves access to the teacher's voice and reduces teacher voice strain.
requirements: Classrooms whose occupied noise levels and SNRs fall below recommended acoustic standards, such as the +15 dB minimum the article cites.
