constraints: Reading fluency benefits were not demonstrated for the general 8–10-year-old student population in this study; translational academic impact is suggested to apply particularly to younger year levels.
target_learners: mainstream primary school students, particularly those with lower cognitive abilities or listening difficulties
target_learning_goals: protecting reading fluency development and access to spoken instruction in noisy classrooms
examples: In this study, 23 Victorian classrooms with occupied noise levels around 65 dBA used Front Row Juno systems, alternating between SFA-On and SFA-Off terms.
key_sources: Shiels, L., Carew, P., Tomlin, D. & Rance, G. (2025). The impact of classroom soundfield systems on reading fluency in normal-hearing students. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00350-1

article_title: Time of day and sleep effects on motor acquisition and consolidation
citation: Charlène Truong, Célia Ruffino, Jérémie Gaveau, Olivier White, Pauline M. Hilt and Charalambos Papaxanthis. (2023). Time of day and sleep effects on motor acquisition and consolidation. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00176-9
title: Schedule motor practice sessions in the evening, close to sleep, when consolidation is the goal
description: This principle holds that the timing of practice, not just its amount, determines how well a newly trained motor skill survives to the next day. The article reports that "the timing of practice is an important factor for motor consolidation, which is better after training in the evening than in the morning". Because acquisition did not differ across times of day but consolidation did, scheduling near the night of sleep is the lever trainers control. The authors state the finding "may help in planning effective interventions in sports and rehabilitation".
requirements: A training session ending in the evening so that a night of sleep follows soon after practice
constraints: The conclusion applies primarily to individuals with an intermediate chronotype, as the majority of participants belonged to this type
New investigations are necessary to generalize the results and understand the underlying neural mechanisms
target_learners: Adults learning fine motor skills, e.g., athletes and patients in rehabilitation
target_learning_goals: Motor skill consolidation and retention between practice sessions
examples: Participants who trained at 8 p.m. improved skill 24 h later (12/12 increased), while morning-trained participants deteriorated (9/12 decreased)
key_sources: Charlène Truong, Célia Ruffino, Jérémie Gaveau, Olivier White, Pauline M. Hilt and Charalambos Papaxanthis. (2023). Time of day and sleep effects on motor acquisition and consolidation. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00176-9

article_title: Time of day and sleep effects on motor acquisition and consolidation
citation: Charlène Truong, Célia Ruffino, Jérémie Gaveau, Olivier White, Pauline M. Hilt and Charalambos Papaxanthis. (2023). Time of day and sleep effects on motor acquisition and consolidation. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00176-9
title: Sleep-proximity account of motor consolidation: sleep shortly after training protects the new motor memory from interference and forgetting
description: The article proposes that consolidation of a newly trained motor skill depends on the temporal proximity between training and sleep rather than on time of day per se. Training close to a night of sleep enables offline learning, while a full waking day between training and sleep exposes the labile memory to retroactive interference and forgetting. The authors state that "a training session close to sleep could protect against memory deterioration induced by additional memories (retroactive interferences)" and that "the morning group, spending more time awake than the afternoon and evening groups, could be more exposed to interferences". Alternative explanations are acknowledged but not resolved.
requirements: Training that ends close enough to sleep for the night of sleep to occur soon after acquisition
constraints: The authors state it remains to be determined whether it is the time of day or the proximity between training and sleep that influences consolidation, suggesting nap designs as a test
Sleep stages were not quantified in the study; only the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index was used
target_learners: Adults practicing fine motor skills, including sports and rehabilitation populations
target_learning_goals: Long-term retention and offline consolidation of newly acquired motor skills
examples: G8sleep retested 2 h after waking matched G8pm's offline gain, while G8awake retested before sleep showed none
key_sources: Charlène Truong, Célia Ruffino, Jérémie Gaveau, Olivier White, Pauline M. Hilt and Charalambos Papaxanthis. (2023). Time of day and sleep effects on motor acquisition and consolidation. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00176-9

article_title: Addressing the theory crisis in statistical learning research
citation: Conway, C. M., Jenkins, H. E., Milne, A. E., Singh, S. & Wilson, B. (2025). Addressing the theory crisis in statistical learning research. npj Science of Learning 10, 68. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00359-6
title: Data–phenomena–theory framework with a bottom-up, phenomenon-driven approach to theory building in statistical learning
description: The article adopts Eronen and Bringmann's distinction between data, phenomena, and theories: "Data are the raw measurements collected in psychology experiments" and "Phenomena are a description of the effects compiled across the observed data", with theories created to explain and be constrained by phenomena. It advocates a "bottom-up" stance: before building theories, researchers should establish which phenomena are robust, validly measured, and causally understood, so that theories encapsulate only robust findings and avoid explaining unrobust ones.
requirements: Robust phenomena must first be identified using criteria of consistency, replicability, and detectability by several independent methods and observation approaches.
constraints: The article notes that development of any new theory of statistical learning is likely to be less clear and much noisier than the evolution example, and it is yet to be determined whether the reviewed phenomena are sufficiently robust for inclusion in an eventual theory.
target_learners: Researchers and theorists in statistical learning and the psychological sciences
target_learning_goals: Theory building grounded in robust, validly measured, causally understood empirical phenomena
examples: The article uses the theory of evolution as a model: Darwin's disparate observations (data) gave rise to general phenomena such as adaptation, competition, and heritability, which the theory of evolution by natural selection then explained and unified while remaining open to falsification.
key_sources: Conway, C. M., Jenkins, H. E., Milne, A. E., Singh, S. & Wilson, B. (2025). Addressing the theory crisis in statistical learning research. npj Science of Learning 10, 68. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00359-6

article_title: Math items about real-world content lower test-scores of students from families with low socioeconomic status
citation: Marjolein Muskens, Willem E. Frankenhuiss & Lex Borghans. (2024). Math items about real-world content lower test-scores of students from families with low socioeconomic status. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00228-8
title: Scarcity mindset and attention capture as an explanatory account of content-induced performance bias
description: The article adopts a scarcity-mindset account, in which "poverty capturing attention and/or generating intrusive and distracting thoughts, reducing an individual 'sc o g n i t i v e resources", with financially salient content in particular causing "attention capture" that interferes with immediate and later performance. The authors apply this account to their finding that money, food, and social-relationship content hinders low-SES performance, assuming attention capture extends to content associated with negative thoughts and feelings. The account is presented as an interpretation aligned with prior monetary-salience findings, not as tested in this study.
requirements: The account is invoked as an interpretation of observational patterns; the article states experimental research is needed to test the mechanisms.
constraints: The article notes its data are observational, so attention capture is a proposed, not demonstrated, mechanism; spill-over evidence is attributed to a prior study by Duquennois.
target_learners: low-SES students in grades 4 and 8 taking standardized math tests
target_learning_goals: fair and unbiased measurement of mathematics achievement
examples: The authors reference a prior study using TIMSS and other datasets showing low-SES students perform worse on money-content items, with spill-over effects on subsequent non-financial items attributed to attention capture.
key_sources: Marjolein Muskens, Willem E. Frankenhuiss & Lex Borghans. (2024). Math items about real-world content lower test-scores of students from families with low socioeconomic status. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00228-8

article_title: Math items about real-world content lower test-scores of students from families with low socioeconomic status
citation: Marjolein Muskens, Willem E. Frankenhuiss & Lex Borghans. (2024). Math items about real-world content lower test-scores of students from families with low socioeconomic status. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00228-8
title: The hidden talents approach: adversity may enhance rather than impair specific cognitive abilities
description: The hidden talents approach "proposes that adaptive developmental processes might result in certain cognitive abilities being enhanced, rather than impaired, by adversity". A general pattern in prior studies is that performance of people living in poverty or adversity "bene ﬁts more from ecologically relevant materials than the performance of people from more favorable environments does", including working-memory tasks where achievement gaps nearly closed with ecologically relevant content. The article notes evidence for most hidden talents is currently mixed, and this study's results were unexpected from this approach.
requirements: Prior studies supporting the approach focused on executive-function components developed in home environments without formal schooling.
constraints: The article states evidence for most hidden talents is currently limited and mixed; the approach did not predict this study's test-performance findings.
target_learners: children and youth living in poverty or adverse conditions
target_learning_goals: understanding how adversity shapes cognitive abilities relevant to assessment and instruction
examples: The article cites executive-functioning studies where youth exposed to poverty and violence scored lower on abstract working-memory updating tasks but the gap nearly closed with ecologically relevant content, and market-selling studies showing math abilities untapped by formal tests.
key_sources: Marjolein Muskens, Willem E. Frankenhuiss & Lex Borghans. (2024). Math items about real-world content lower test-scores of students from families with low socioeconomic status. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00228-8

article_title: Counting days is a spacing incentive that unlocks the potential of low GPA students
citation: Iman YeckehZaare & Paul Resnick. (2025). Counting days is a spacing incentive that unlocks the potential of low GPA students. npj Science of Learning 10:35. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00322-5
title: Counting Days grading incentive in the Runestone retrieval practice tool
description: A grade-based incentive implemented in a retrieval practice tool built into the Runestone online textbook platform. In the treatment condition, "students earn a ﬁxed increment of points for every day on which they correctly answer at least ten practice questions, thereby promoting spaced learning", whereas the control condition awards points per question without any distribution requirement. The tool uses an adaptive spacing algorithm inspired by the SuperMemo 2 algorithm, presenting multiple-choice and active-code questions from a topic-based bank. The design rewards spaced activity so that an equivalent amount of activity massed near exams earns fewer course points.
requirements: Activity must be measurable and delivered and tracked through a course management system so days of activity can be counted
A set of practice questions per day (ten in the within-class experiment) as the threshold for earning the day's points
Points capped so students can earn the maximum with about 40 days of activity, roughly three days per week
constraints: Results may be specific to the domain and level of introductory programming
Impact may depend on using similar question types for assessing learning outcomes as those used in the practice activity
May depend on students having internalized the norm of doing activities the instructor assigns points for, so it may be more effective in more elite institutions
Does not provide complete autonomy, since students do not set their own goals for how much practice to do on how many days
target_learners: high school and college students in introductory programming courses
target_learning_goals: spaced retrieval practice
long-term retention of course material
examples: In the within-class experiment, 10% of the course grade (100 points) was based on the practice tool; treatment students earned 2.5 points per day for correctly answering ten practice questions, for up to 40 days
In the between-instructor experiment, 71 instructors teaching 97 courses to 1,648 students randomized at the instructor level configured the points per day and questions per day themselves
key_sources: Iman YeckehZaare & Paul Resnick. (2025). Counting days is a spacing incentive that unlocks the potential of low GPA students. npj Science of Learning 10:35. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00322-5

article_title: A RCT for assessment of active human-centred learning finds teacher-centric non-human teaching of evolution optimal
citation: Buchan, L., Hejmadi, M., Abrahams, L. & Hurst, L. D. (2020). A RCT for assessment of active human-centred learning finds teacher-centric non-human teaching of evolution optimal. npj Science of Learning 5:19. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00078-0
title: Test lesson plans in series rather than in parallel, because serial designs expose interaction effects between teaching modes that parallel designs miss
description: The article argues that teaching happens in series while methodology tests are typically done in parallel, implicitly assuming no interaction effects. Its replicated 2×2 serial trial found a replicable interaction effect, leading the authors to state that "parallel modes of testing, even in an RCT format, might mislead and that lessons plans in series should be considered for fuller testing".
requirements: Requires large sample sizes, since detecting interaction effects between lessons in series demands more power, as with drug interaction trials
Requires adherence to prescribed lesson sequences, which the authors achieved through teacher training and recently-introduced curriculum topics
constraints: The 2×2 serial design used here excludes temporal effects because simultaneous delivery of the schemes was not feasible
The cause of the interaction effect could not be identified by the study
target_learning_goals: Understanding of evolution, including natural selection, variation, geological time and homology/common ancestry
examples: The study randomised whole classes to four four-lesson schemes in a 2×2 design modelled on drug interaction trials such as CHARIMMA, with pre, post and delayed retention testing in situ by trained classroom teachers
key_sources: Buchan, L., Hejmadi, M., Abrahams, L. & Hurst, L. D. (2020). A RCT for assessment of active human-centred learning finds teacher-centric non-human teaching of evolution optimal. npj Science of Learning 5:19. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00078-0

article_title: Social interaction and conceptual change pave the way away from children’s misconceptions about the Earth
citation: Diego Pablo de la Hera, Mariano Sigman and Cecilia Ines Calero. (2019). Social interaction and conceptual change pave the way away from children 's misconceptions about the Earth. npj Science of Learning 4:12. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0051-3
title: Framework theory account of conceptual change from naive flat-earth models to a scientific spherical Earth
description: The article adopts the knowledge-as-theory / Framework Theory approach, under which children hold coherent mental models of the Earth constrained by naive presuppositions, and conceptual change proceeds "through the gradual revision of framework theories 'presuppositions". The developmental path runs from rectangular flat-earth models, through disc and dual-earth synthetic models formed "by accretion of new scientific information", to suspended-earth and finally spherical models in which people live all around a planet held by gravity. The study uses this framework to interpret peer interaction as catalyzing revision of the support presupposition, shifting children from dual to non-dual models.
requirements: Assumes children's prior conceptions form coherent theories that constrain interpretation of new information
constraints: The article notes learning pathways are complex and not linear or hierarchical
target_learners: children in early elementary school (around 7 years old, second grade)
target_learning_goals: observational astronomy and cosmology: shape of the Earth, its position in space, location of people and objects on it
examples: Dyads were paired so a less knowledgeable child interacted with a more knowledgeable peer on Earth-shape concepts, and gains clustered on the dual/not-dual axis
key_sources: Diego Pablo de la Hera, Mariano Sigman and Cecilia Ines Calero. (2019). Social interaction and conceptual change pave the way away from children 's misconceptions about the Earth. npj Science of Learning 4:12. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0051-3

article_title: Interpersonal neural synchronization underlies interactive concept learning in older adults
citation: Zi-Wei Liang, Zhi-Jun Zhan, Ying-Chen Liu, Hong-Zhou Xu & Jing Yu. (2025). Interpersonal neural synchronization underlies interactive concept learning in older adults. npj Science of Learning 10:75. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00368-5
title: Interpersonal neural synchronization as a dyadic neural mechanism of interactive learning, examined via fNIRS hyperscanning, INS, and IS-RSA
description: The article frames interactive learning as a joint action whose effectiveness is underwritten by "interpersonal neural synchronization (INS), the coupling of neural processes across brains", which "supports dyadic interaction through shared attention, mutual prediction, and co-regulation". It operationalizes this with fNIRS hyperscanning (wavelet transform coherence between instructor and learner HbO signals), permutation tests against pseudo dyads, Granger causality for directional coupling, and IS-RSA to link inter-individual performance similarity with neural similarity, focusing on the prefrontal cortex.
requirements: Simultaneous dual-brain recording (fNIRS hyperscanning) of both instructor and learner during real interaction
constraints: The fNIRS setup captured only frontal cortical activity, leaving other cortical and subcortical regions unexplored
The one-to-one laboratory setting does not fully reflect real-world lifelong learning contexts where group instruction and peer interactions are common
target_learners: Older adults (55+) in lifelong-learning settings, with younger-adult comparison groups
target_learning_goals: Concept learning (social psychology concepts) in interactive instructor-led settings
examples: Study 1 and Study 2 recorded dyads with a Shimadzu FORE3000 fNIRS system over the PFC, computing instructor-learner INS via wavelet transform coherence and validating against 1000 pseudo dyads
key_sources: Zi-Wei Liang, Zhi-Jun Zhan, Ying-Chen Liu, Hong-Zhou Xu & Jing Yu. (2025). Interpersonal neural synchronization underlies interactive concept learning in older adults. npj Science of Learning 10:75. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00368-5

article_title: Biologically based neural circuit modelling for the study of fear learning and extinction
citation: Nair, S. S., Paré, D. and Vicentic, A. (2016). Biologically based neural circuit modelling for the study of fear learning and extinction. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/npjscilearn.2016.15
title: Biologically based neural circuit modelling as a multi-level framework integrating biological information to study fear and anxiety networks
description: The review advocates biologically based computational modelling as a framework for understanding fear/anxiety networks, arguing these are complex dynamical systems that defy intuition. The authors state that "biologically based modelling can be used to integrate biological information at different levels of organisation", allowing study of emergent properties and rapid quantitative testing of hypotheses difficult to address experimentally. The framework spans neuronal (Hodgkin–Huxley ionic channels), synaptic (reversal potential, rise/decay times, facilitation/depression, plasticity), and network levels, and envisions "a reciprocal interaction" between models and experiments in which observations constrain models and verify predictions.
requirements: Experimental data to constrain single-cell and network parameters; where data are lacking, parameters are varied within reasonable bounds until network behaviour replicates prior experimental findings.
Output measures such as the magnitude of neuronal responses to the CS as a proxy for the intensity of emotional responses.
constraints: Output measures used so far "will not sufﬁce when studying more complex and realistic behavioural paradigms" beyond classical fear conditioning.
The paper focuses on the synaptic, cellular and systems levels, leaving molecular-level and cognitive-level modelling to other reviews.
Network models typically cannot incorporate all cell types and compensate by adjusting proportions and synaptic strengths.
target_learners: Neuroscience researchers studying fear and anxiety circuits
target_learning_goals: Understanding neural circuit mechanisms of fear learning and extinction
Linking circuit dysfunction to maladaptive fear responses in mental disorders
examples: The Kim et al. biophysical lateral amygdala network with 800 principal cells and 200 fast-spiking interneurons, built from experimental data on cell properties, connectivity and neuromodulation.
key_sources: Nair, S. S., Paré, D. and Vicentic, A. (2016). Biologically based neural circuit modelling for the study of fear learning and extinction. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/npjscilearn.2016.15

article_title: Biologically based neural circuit modelling for the study of fear learning and extinction
citation: Nair, S. S., Paré, D. and Vicentic, A. (2016). Biologically based neural circuit modelling for the study of fear learning and extinction. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/npjscilearn.2016.15
title: Biophysically realistic lateral amygdala network model (Kim et al.) with 800 principal cells and 200 fast-spiking interneurons
description: A biophysically realistic computational model of the lateral amygdala described in the review. The number of LA neurons was scaled down 30 to 1, "including 800 principal cells and 200 fast-spiking interneurons", distributed randomly in a realistic tri-dimensional representation of the horn-shaped LAd. Principal cells had three compartments with multiple voltage-dependent currents; the large network contains roughly 1,000 neurons and ~40,000 synapses, so individual low-level aspects cannot be tuned to achieve particular impacts on high-level behaviour.
requirements: Experimentally constrained passive and active membrane properties, probabilistic gradients of intrinsic connectivity matched to observed spatial heterogeneity, thalamic and shock inputs, and dopaminergic and noradrenergic neuromodulatory inputs adjusted to experimental observations.
constraints: Scaling down 30 to 1 means such large networks (~1,000 neurons, ~40,000 synapses) cannot have individual low-level aspects tuned to achieve particular impacts on high-level model behaviour.
Connections set with probabilistic gradients of connectivity because quantitative data on spatial distributions of inputs and outputs are typically unavailable.
target_learning_goals: Understanding mechanisms of fear memory formation and storage in the lateral amygdala
examples: The model reproduced the continuum of spike frequency adaptation by varying Ca2+-dependent K+ current density, and reproduced the formation of two distinct types of tone-responsive principal cell populations observed experimentally.
key_sources: Nair, S. S., Paré, D. and Vicentic, A. (2016). Biologically based neural circuit modelling for the study of fear learning and extinction. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/npjscilearn.2016.15

article_title: Interplay of socioeconomic status, cognition, and school performance in the ABCD sample
citation: Langensee, L., Rumetshofer, T. & Mårtensson, J. (2024). Interplay of socioeconomic status, cognition, and school performance in the ABCD sample. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00233-x
title: Educators and policy makers should work to ensure that academic success chances are not determined by parental wealth and education, and should provide learning resources outside the home where home stimulation is limited
description: The article closes with a design recommendation for learning environments: teachers, policy makers, and educational researchers are called upon "to continue to strive towards creating school environments in which a child's chances at distinguishing themselves academically are controlled entirely by them." Because the study shows SES gradients in self-reported grades that persist over time and across levels of cognitive capacity, it recommends that anyone involved in children's schooling be mindful of possible systematic socioeconomic disadvantage and create optimal learning conditions suited to each child's situation.
requirements: Awareness of possible systematic socioeconomic disadvantage among those involved in children's schooling
constraints: The supporting evidence is observational, from self-reported grades, in a sample skewed toward higher-SES families, limiting conclusions about disadvantaged children.
target_learners: Children and adolescents in primary and secondary school, particularly those from socioeconomically disadvantaged backgrounds
target_learning_goals: Equitable academic achievement regardless of socioeconomic background
examples: The authors recommend that "resources need to be readily available outside children's homes and children should actively be encouraged to take advantage of them" where home intellectual stimulation may be limited.
key_sources: Langensee, L., Rumetshofer, T. & Mårtensson, J. (2024). Interplay of socioeconomic status, cognition, and school performance in the ABCD sample. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00233-x

article_title: Effects of described demonstrator ability on brain and behavior when learning from others
citation: Selbing, I., Becker, N., Pan, Y., Lindström, B., & Olsson, A. (2025). Effects of described demonstrator ability on brain and behavior when learning from others. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00292-0
title: Two-form framework of observational learning: copying versus observational outcome learning
description: The article organizes social learning by distinguishing two forms of learning from observation. The authors write that learning about others' actions is "commonly divided into two forms of learning: 1) learning by observing the action of the demonstrator, and 2) learning by observing the outcome of a demonstrator's actions", referred to as "copying" and "observational outcome learning" respectively. The framework structures their hypotheses and RL models: copying is modeled as a tendency to make the same choice as the demonstrator, while observational outcome learning is modeled as Q-value updating from observed outcomes. In this study the framework guided which parameters could vary with described demonstrator ability.
requirements: Requires that both the demonstrator's action and the outcome of that action are available to the observer, as in the article's task, for both forms of learning to be possible
constraints: The authors note that for observational outcome learning the link between demonstrator ability and learning efficiency is less straightforward, since observers can also learn from the outcomes of poor decisions
target_learners: Adult university students learning probabilistic avoidance tasks through observation
target_learning_goals: Learning which of two choice options is optimal from observing another person's choices and their outcomes
examples: Fifty Q-learning-based RL models were generated varying whether copying and/or observational outcome learning were included and whether their parameters were description-sensitive
key_sources: Selbing, I., Becker, N., Pan, Y., Lindström, B., & Olsson, A. (2025). Effects of described demonstrator ability on brain and behavior when learning from others. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00292-0

article_title: Who’s learning? Using within-family studies to understand personalized learning
citation: von Stumm, S. & Wertz, J. (2021). Who's learning? Using within-family studies to understand personalized learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00082-4
title: Aptitude–treatment interaction paradigm as framework for matching instruction to learner characteristics
description: The article describes the aptitude–treatment interaction (ATI) paradigm as the concept that some learning environments are more or less effective for particular individuals depending on their learning abilities and needs. As printed: "The concept that some learning environments are more or less effective for particular individuals, depending on their learning abilities and needs, is known as 'aptitude– treatment interaction' or 'ATI paradigm'". The 'treatment' refers to the environment available to the learner, while 'aptitude' refers to individual differences forecasting success under a given treatment.
requirements: Testing aptitude–treatment effects requires assessing how various degrees of (mis)match between instruction and learner characteristics affect learning outcomes
constraints: The article states aptitude–treatment interactions "have not been conclusively demonstrated" and that testing them in classrooms requires extremely large sample sizes because effect sizes are likely to be small
target_learners: children in formal and informal educational settings
target_learning_goals: optimizing fit between instruction and learner characteristics to maximize learning
key_sources: von Stumm, S. & Wertz, J. (2021). Who's learning? Using within-family studies to understand personalized learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00082-4

article_title: Computational markers show specific deficits for dyslexia and ADHD in complex learning settings
citation: Gabay, Y., Jacob, L., Mansour, A. & Hertz, U. (2025). Computational markers show specific deficits for dyslexia and ADHD in complex learning settings. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00323-4
title: Hybrid reinforcement learning / Bayesian inference model of multidimensional learning
description: A computational model combining reinforcement learning with a statistically optimal Bayesian approach to explain choices in multidimensional reward learning. It updates feature values of the chosen stimulus with learning rate η, decays unchosen features with rate ηk, weights dimensions via δ, and balances RL versus Bayesian attention weights via a free parameter alpha, then maps values to choices through a softmax with inverse temperature β. "Prior research indicates that the hybrid reinforcement learning/Bayes model was the model with the best ﬁt in explaining participants' strategies on the same experimental paradigm." The article uses it to derive computational markers distinguishing ADHD and dyslexia learning dynamics.
requirements: Trial-by-trial choice and reward data from each participant; parameters β, η, ηk, δ, α are fit individually by minimizing the negative log likelihood of choices.
constraints: The Bayesian part assumes complete memory of all stimulus-reward observations, an assumption the model itself makes about the learner.
target_learning_goals: Multidimensional reinforcement learning under uncertain dimension relevance
Discovering which stimulus dimension predicts reward
examples: Parameters were fit individually per participant using the R optim package, estimating the joint likelihood of all choices in each task separately.
key_sources: Gabay, Y., Jacob, L., Mansour, A. & Hertz, U. (2025). Computational markers show specific deficits for dyslexia and ADHD in complex learning settings. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00323-4

article_title: Learning: One definition to rule them all?
citation: Martin Lövdén, Isabelle Hansson & Toms Voits. (2026). Learning: One definition to rule them all? npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00441-7
title: Umbrella definition of learning as environment-informed information processing that changes system properties and behavioral potential
description: The article proposes a unifying definition: "a system's processing of information from its environment, resulting in a change of system properties that alter its behavioral potential and reactions to this information." It combines structural and functional perspectives: the structural aspect is acknowledged but not specified, while the functional component guides operational definitions. It is intended to apply across disciplines, organisms, machines, and groups, with discipline-specific operationalizations of information and behavior.
requirements: Requires discipline-specific definitions of the terms information and behavior to reach acceptable precision
constraints: Excludes maturation and senescence to the extent these are not based on processing of information from the environment
target_learners: Organisms, artificial systems, groups, and cellular networks, as systems that learn
target_learning_goals: Theorizing and cross-disciplinary communication about what learning is
examples: The article evaluates the definition against desiderata for a good cross-disciplinary concept and contrasts it with prior definitions such as Barron's structured-updating formulation
key_sources: Martin Lövdén, Isabelle Hansson & Toms Voits. (2026). Learning: One definition to rule them all? npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00441-7

article_title: Gender similarities in the brain during mathematics development
citation: Kersey, A. J., Csumitta, K. D., & Cantlon, J. F. (2019). Gender similarities in the brain during mathematics development. npj Science of Learning 4:19. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0057-x
title: Gender Similarities Hypothesis as applied to early childhood mathematical cognition
description: The Gender Similarities Hypothesis argues that boys and girls function similarly in most areas of cognition. This study tests it neurally in early childhood mathematics and reports that the data are consistent with it: "gender similarities in early childhood mathematics show, as proposed in the domain of spatial cognition, that gender differences in STEM fields in adults are not derived from intrinsic differences in children's brains but likely from a complex environmental origin." The theory treats male and female brains as one heterogeneous population rather than two categorical groups, supported here by equivalence testing, Bayes factors, and null variance and interaction tests.
requirements: Testing similarities, not just differences, requires statistical equivalence tests and Bayesian analyses rather than reliance on null t tests
constraints: The article notes gender differences in STEM may emerge later in development or from interactions with puberty-related hormone changes, which these childhood data do not address
target_learners: children aged 3–10 in early mathematics development
target_learning_goals: early mathematics and numerical cognition development
examples: The study measured 104 children's neural maturity during mathematics education videos and found equivalence rather than difference across all five whole-brain analyses
key_sources: Kersey, A. J., Csumitta, K. D., & Cantlon, J. F. (2019). Gender similarities in the brain during mathematics development. npj Science of Learning 4:19. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0057-x

article_title: Dissociable sensory, motor, and visuomotor predictive functions
citation: Inmaculada Márquez & Mario Treviño. (2025). Dissociable sensory, motor, and visuomotor predictive functions. npj Science of Learning 10:85. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00377-4
title: Compartmentalized, context-dependent predictive control in human sensorimotor function
description: The article proposes that predictive processing in sensorimotor control is not a unified hierarchical architecture but a set of specialized, task-specific computations. As the authors state, "predictive control relies on specialized, context-dependent mechanisms, in which task-speci ﬁc computations adaptively integrate context and internal state dynamics". The framework holds that sensory detection, motor execution, and visuomotor adaptation operate as loosely coupled, domain-specific subsystems, with angular and speed errors engaging distinct control policies. It is supported by the study's weak cross-task associations and dominant within-subject variability, and is offered as useful for understanding adaptive control in real-world behaviors such as sports, driving, or human–machine interaction.
requirements: Within-task performance must be measured with task-specific metrics; the framework was built from a within-subject, multi-task battery in the same participants.
constraints: The design emphasized rapid, trial-level corrections to transient perturbations rather than long-term adaptation.
With only 54 participants, statistical power may have been insufficient to detect small cross-domain effects.
target_learning_goals: sensorimotor prediction and adaptation
perceptual detection of prediction errors
motor consistency
examples: The study combined a visuomotor interception task with angular or speed perturbations, a sensory detection task, and a no-feedback motor variability task in the same 54 participants.
key_sources: Inmaculada Márquez & Mario Treviño. (2025). Dissociable sensory, motor, and visuomotor predictive functions. npj Science of Learning 10:85. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00377-4

article_title: Dissociable sensory, motor, and visuomotor predictive functions
citation: Inmaculada Márquez & Mario Treviño. (2025). Dissociable sensory, motor, and visuomotor predictive functions. npj Science of Learning 10:85. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00377-4
title: Three-task sensorimotor prediction battery (interception, detection, motor variability)
description: A battery of three joystick- and keyboard-based tasks administered to the same participants to quantify distinct components of predictive processing. As the authors write, "we developed a battery of three tasks targeting distinct com- ponents of predictive processing, all of which were performed by the same group of participants": (1) a visuomotor adaptation task with angular and speed perturbations during target interception; (2) a sensory detection task requiring judgments about brief changes in target direction or speed; and (3) a motor variability task assessing directional consistency during blindfolded joystick movements. Performance was quantified using eye movements, interception accuracy, detection accuracy, response times, and movement variability.
requirements: A calibrated computer and joystick, an eye tracker for gaze recording, and counterbalanced task order with a minimum 1-day interval between sessions.
constraints: Task sessions occurred on different days, leaving performance susceptible to shifts in internal states such as arousal or fatigue.
target_learners: adults aged 19–30 with normal or corrected-to-normal vision
target_learning_goals: measuring sensory detection, motor execution, and visuomotor adaptation
examples: Angular discrepancies were imposed by rotating joystick output by ±30° to ±180°; speed discrepancies scaled velocity to 50%–150% of joystick input.
key_sources: Inmaculada Márquez & Mario Treviño. (2025). Dissociable sensory, motor, and visuomotor predictive functions. npj Science of Learning 10:85. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00377-4

article_title: Dissociable sensory, motor, and visuomotor predictive functions
citation: Inmaculada Márquez & Mario Treviño. (2025). Dissociable sensory, motor, and visuomotor predictive functions. npj Science of Learning 10:85. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00377-4
title: Analyze behavioral variability as a functional signal rather than noise, using single-trial modeling
description: Because within-subject trial-to-trial fluctuations dominated behavior across all three tasks, the article recommends treating variability as informative state-dependent dynamics rather than measurement noise. The authors recommend that "Future studies should adopt single-trial modeling (e.g., Hidden Markov or state-space models) to capture latent state transitions and nonlinear interactions", since trial-averaged analyses may obscure rapid state-dependent fluctuations central to predictive control.
requirements: Single-trial data collection with dense trial repetition per condition, since trial-averaged analyses risk masking dynamic processes.
constraints: The recommendation arises from a sensorimotor task setting with 54 participants and may not transfer directly to other learning domains.
target_learning_goals: understanding trial-to-trial behavioral variability in adaptive control
examples: The authors found within-subject variability exceeded between-subject variability by roughly an order of magnitude across all tasks and proposed Hidden Markov or state-space models for future work.
key_sources: Inmaculada Márquez & Mario Treviño. (2025). Dissociable sensory, motor, and visuomotor predictive functions. npj Science of Learning 10:85. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00377-4

article_title: Eye gaze patterns reveal how reasoning skills improve with experience
citation: Belén C. Guerra-Carrillo and Silvia A. Bunge. (2018). Eye gaze patterns reveal how reasoning skills improve with experience. npj Science of Learning 3:18. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0035-8
title: Gaze metrics operationalizing visual search, relational thinking, and relational integration as probes of reasoning mechanisms
description: The article develops an eyetracking framework for pinpointing the cognitive mechanisms behind improved reasoning. It operationalizes "efﬁciency of visual search as the number of ﬁxations needed to identify the relevant relations in a stimulus array, relational thinking as the total duration spent ﬁxating the relevant relations, and relational integration as the number of transitions between these relations." The metrics were refined after fixation-pattern analysis showed no clear-cut processing stages, and were defined on first-time-point data collapsed across groups to remain unbiased with respect to instruction effects.
requirements: Eyetracking data on a transitive inference task with defined areas of interest (relevant scales, irrelevant scales, question area), with metrics computed per trial on an individual subject basis
constraints: The initially planned three-stage decomposition (visual search, relational encoding, relational integration) was not supported; the data showed a gradual transition from search to integration, so the encoding metric was renamed relational thinking
target_learners: Young adults preparing for the LSAT
target_learning_goals: Relational reasoning and transitive inference
examples: Participants made a median of 22 fixations on accurately solved transitive inference problems, and the metrics were computed after marking the point in each trial where fixations preferentially shifted to the relevant scales.
key_sources: Belén C. Guerra-Carrillo and Silvia A. Bunge. (2018). Eye gaze patterns reveal how reasoning skills improve with experience. npj Science of Learning 3:18. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0035-8

article_title: Impaired audio-visual associations in dyslexia: evidence beyond linguistic processing
citation: Pasqualotto, A., Cochrane, A., Venuti, P. et al. (2025). Impaired audio-visual associations in dyslexia: evidence beyond linguistic processing. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00382-7
title: Gamified non-linguistic audio-visual associative learning task for children
description: A gamified task, adapted from an adult paradigm, in which children learn associations between pairs of unfamiliar environmental sounds and novel visual symbols (Bamum-alphabet bears) across 6 blocks of 12 trials (72 total). The article states "The task was presented as a game to engage children, with a storyline involving three bears building a balloon for their journey around the world." Stimuli were "deliberately selected to be non-linguistic, difficult to label verbally" to minimize phonological and familiarity confounds, and pairings were scaffolded across blocks.
requirements: Two familiarization phases (passive auditory and 1-back visual) precede the learning task; children start at the a priori guessing rate of 1/3
Bear locations change across trials to prevent spatial learning; feedback follows each response
constraints: The asymmetry between auditory (passive) and visual (active 1-back) familiarization may have led to stronger encoding of visual inputs; individual differences in familiarity or affective associations with the sounds may have introduced variability
target_learners: Italian-speaking children aged 8-12, including children with developmental dyslexia
target_learning_goals: Audio-visual associative learning through repeated exposure
Adaptation to novel associations and updating of the mapping state space
examples: Children listened to two sounds presented back to back and selected the visual symbol (bear) associated with that sound pair; four sound combinations mapped to three symbols, with two combinations requiring attention to both sounds
key_sources: Pasqualotto, A., Cochrane, A., Venuti, P. et al. (2025). Impaired audio-visual associations in dyslexia: evidence beyond linguistic processing. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00382-7

article_title: Impaired audio-visual associations in dyslexia: evidence beyond linguistic processing
citation: Pasqualotto, A., Cochrane, A., Venuti, P. et al. (2025). Impaired audio-visual associations in dyslexia: evidence beyond linguistic processing. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00382-7
title: Mutualistic developmental account of audio-visual associative learning and reading
description: The article proposes that AV associative learning and reading develop mutually: children with stronger reading skills tended to reach higher asymptotic accuracy, and the mechanisms supporting AV learning develop alongside reading expertise. The authors state this "could align with a mutualistic model of cognitive development, wherein advances in the acquisition of one ability, such as reading, may support and interact with other learning processes". They further propose a developmental transition: in pre-readers AV learning relates to phonological awareness, while in proficient readers it is associated with domain-general skills, particularly working memory capacity.
requirements: Capturing short-term learning trajectories across multiple stages, as in the dynamic framework of reading acquisition, to characterize the learning process rather than a single outcome point
constraints: The correlational findings offer insights but should be interpreted with caution given small sample sizes and multiple uncorrected associations; further research with larger samples is needed to validate these patterns
target_learners: Children across reading-development stages, from pre-readers to proficient readers, including children with dyslexia
target_learning_goals: Reading acquisition
Formation and consolidation of cross-modal (audio-visual) associations
examples: Reading-matched controls (younger children) still outperformed children with DD despite being younger, suggesting AV learning difficulties in DD are not simply a byproduct of reading skill
key_sources: Pasqualotto, A., Cochrane, A., Venuti, P. et al. (2025). Impaired audio-visual associations in dyslexia: evidence beyond linguistic processing. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00382-7

article_title: Impaired audio-visual associations in dyslexia: evidence beyond linguistic processing
citation: Pasqualotto, A., Cochrane, A., Venuti, P. et al. (2025). Impaired audio-visual associations in dyslexia: evidence beyond linguistic processing. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00382-7
title: Subprocess account of audio-visual associative learning as a candidate locus of dyslexia difficulty
description: The article motivates reinterpreting AV learning difficulties in dyslexia in terms of the subprocesses that could be affected: forming clear unimodal representations, binding newly associated auditory and visual information in working memory, and consolidating bound representations in long-term memory. The authors state that forming AV pairs "could be considered to rely on the process of binding in working memory, that is the integration of a number of isolated characteristics into a compound representation". Any of these subprocesses could potentially be impaired in children with DD, and domain-general skills such as attentional resources are likely candidates supporting them.
requirements: Clear representations of both auditory and visual stimuli must be available; the binding must be coded and maintained first in working memory before consolidation in long-term memory
constraints: The article notes poorer nonspeech-sound discrimination in DD has been reported in the past but with mixed evidence; further characterization of auditory processing difficulties and of the domain-general skills involved in each subprocess is needed
target_learners: Children with developmental dyslexia and typically-developing readers
target_learning_goals: Forming durable audio-visual associations through repeated exposure
examples: The article cites prior hypotheses of a failure to deploy attentional resources in cross-modal binding in developmental dyslexia, and an adult study linking learning performance to verbal working memory across two language groups
key_sources: Pasqualotto, A., Cochrane, A., Venuti, P. et al. (2025). Impaired audio-visual associations in dyslexia: evidence beyond linguistic processing. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00382-7

article_title: The influence of task and interpersonal interdependence on cooperative behavior and its neural mechanisms
citation: Zijun Yin, Bin Xuan, Chengchi Liu, Jingchao Yi, Xiaoyan Zheng & Mingming Zhang. (2025). The influence of task and interpersonal interdependence on cooperative behavior and its neural mechanisms. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00303-8
title: Three-dimensional structural model of social interaction behaviors (goal, interactive, and task structure)
description: The article adopts a three-dimensional structural model for dissecting social interaction behaviors, "delineating it into goal structure (cooperation versus competition), interactive structure (synchronous versus turn-based), and task structure (interdependent versus independent)". The study fixes goal structure at cooperation and interactive structure at synchronous, and varies the task-structure subdimension by contrasting high and low task interdependence within cooperation key-pressing tasks. The model thus provides the design axis along which the experimental tasks were refined.
requirements: Prior three-dimensional SIB conceptualization (Liu & Pelowski) is used to classify tasks along the three structures
constraints: The study examines only the cooperative, synchronous, interdependent subdimensions
target_learning_goals: cooperative behavior and inter-brain coordination
examples: Cooperation key-pressing tasks refined into HICT (synchronous key presses scored for response-time similarity) and LICT (individual speed against standard times)
key_sources: Zijun Yin, Bin Xuan, Chengchi Liu, Jingchao Yi, Xiaoyan Zheng & Mingming Zhang. (2025). The influence of task and interpersonal interdependence on cooperative behavior and its neural mechanisms. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00303-8

article_title: The influence of task and interpersonal interdependence on cooperative behavior and its neural mechanisms
citation: Zijun Yin, Bin Xuan, Chengchi Liu, Jingchao Yi, Xiaoyan Zheng & Mingming Zhang. (2025). The influence of task and interpersonal interdependence on cooperative behavior and its neural mechanisms. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00303-8
title: Adapted cooperation key-pressing paradigm distinguishing HICT and LICT with fNIRS hyperscanning
description: A two-task experimental element adapted from a prior cooperation key-pressing paradigm and administered under fNIRS hyperscanning. In HICT, "if |RTleft − RTright |<| R Tleft + RTright |/8, they could receive 1 point" rewarding synchronous key-pressing; in LICT, each participant pressed faster than a personally calibrated standard time derived from practice trials. Each round comprised 20 formal trials with per-trial fast/slow feedback, and neural data were collected from 21 channels covering PFC.R, DLPFC.L, DLPFC.R and TPJ.R.
requirements: Two NIRSport fNIRS systems; E-prime 3.0 stimulus control; participants refrained from verbal or non-verbal communication
constraints: The fNIRS device's limited channel capacity conﬁned the study to the PFC and the TPJ.R, and the authors note the generalizability of the ﬁndings may be limited because real-world cooperative situations are often more complex.
target_learning_goals: cooperative behavior and neural coordination during joint tasks
examples: The HICT scoring rule awarded 1 point when response times were close; the LICT awarded 1 point when both participants pressed faster than their respective standard times
key_sources: Zijun Yin, Bin Xuan, Chengchi Liu, Jingchao Yi, Xiaoyan Zheng & Mingming Zhang. (2025). The influence of task and interpersonal interdependence on cooperative behavior and its neural mechanisms. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00303-8

article_title: Extracellular and intracellular cleavages of proBDNF required at two distinct stages of late-phase LTP
citation: Pang, P. T., Nagappan, G., Guo, W. & Lu, B. (2016). Extracellular and intracellular cleavages of proBDNF required at two distinct stages of late-phase LTP. npj Science of Learning 1, 16003. https://doi.org/10.1038/npjscilearn.2016.3
title: Two-stage BDNF account of L-LTP: extracellular tPA/plasmin cleavage at induction, intracellular furin/PC1 cleavage of newly synthesized proBDNF at maintenance
description: The article proposes that TBS-induced L-LTP in hippocampal CA1 comprises two temporally distinct, BDNF-dependent stages: "an induction stage (I) that depends on extracellular cleavage of secreted proBDNF by the tPA/plasmin system, and a maintenance stage (II) in which proBDNF is cleaved intracellularly by FIN/PC1 before its secretion." Stage I signaling is mainly MAPK, while stage II additionally requires PLC-gamma and PI3K. A tentative mechanistic connection proposes BDNF secretion at stage I creates a protein synthesis-independent TrkB synaptic tag captured by soma-derived BDNF at stage II.
requirements: BDNF secretion and processing at both stages; the model is grounded in pharmacological rescue and inhibition experiments in hippocampal slice and cultured neuron preparations
constraints: Applies to TBS-induced, BDNF-sensitive L-LTP; the article notes previous work established that BDNF is required for TBS-induced L-LTP, but not for L-LTP induced by multiple sets of tetanic stimulation
The synaptic tag model connecting the two stages is explicitly tentative: "Further investigations are necessary to validate this model"
target_learners: basic neuroscience researchers studying memory mechanisms
target_learning_goals: understanding molecular mechanisms of long-lasting synaptic plasticity underlying long-term memory
examples: Stage I was defined by sensitivity to tPA/plasmin inhibition and stage II by sensitivity to protein synthesis inhibition and intracellular cleavage blockade; the authors suggest division of L-LTP into multiple stages may facilitate mechanistic studies
key_sources: Pang, P. T., Nagappan, G., Guo, W. & Lu, B. (2016). Extracellular and intracellular cleavages of proBDNF required at two distinct stages of late-phase LTP. npj Science of Learning 1, 16003. https://doi.org/10.1038/npjscilearn.2016.3

article_title: Spatiotemporal predictions guide attention throughout the adult lifespan
citation: Nir Shalev, Sage Boettcher & Anna C. Nobre. (2024). Spatiotemporal predictions guide attention throughout the adult lifespan. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00281-3
title: Dynamic visual search task with spatiotemporally predictable targets
description: An online task in which participants search for eight upward-pointing triangle targets that fade in and out among sixteen downward-pointing distractors over roughly fourteen-second trials. Four targets per trial are "spatially and temporally predictable", appearing at fixed onsets within fixed quadrants, while four appear at unpredictable times and locations; participants are not informed of the manipulation. Data, and the experimental code (PsychoPy, hosted on Pavlovia), are available at OSF (DOI: 10.17605/OSF.IO/8UPY5).
requirements: Participants used a personal computer; the experiment did not support phones or tablets
Normal or corrected-to-normal vision and no diagnosed psychiatric or neurological condition
constraints: A well-controlled artificial environment used to maximize trial-by-trial learning of regularities, rather than realistic scenes
Cognitive issues were not controlled for in remote testing
target_learning_goals: Learning and using spatiotemporal regularities to guide attention during dynamic visual search
examples: 300 Prolific participants each completed ten practice trials and one block of 30 experimental trials with 240 targets; predictable target onsets were drawn one per time bin and assigned to distinct quadrants for each participant.
key_sources: Nir Shalev, Sage Boettcher & Anna C. Nobre. (2024). Spatiotemporal predictions guide attention throughout the adult lifespan. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00281-3

article_title: Spatiotemporal predictions guide attention throughout the adult lifespan
citation: Nir Shalev, Sage Boettcher & Anna C. Nobre. (2024). Spatiotemporal predictions guide attention throughout the adult lifespan. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00281-3
title: Integrate spatiotemporal regularities into dynamic, realistic search scenes to enhance ecological validity
description: The authors recommend extending dynamic search paradigms beyond well-controlled artificial environments by embedding spatiotemporal regularities in realistic scenes. They note that in real life some regularities are stored in long-term memory, such as expectations about traffic lights, and that such designs "would not only enhance ecological validity but also enable exploration of whether spatiotemporal regularities guide attention across adulthood based on long-term expectations."
requirements: Prior experience with realistic stimuli as a meaningful source of attentional guidance
constraints: The influence of prior experience with spatiotemporal regularities has not been tested with dynamic objects and scenes, per the authors
target_learners: Adults across the adult lifespan, including older adults
target_learning_goals: Proactive attentional guidance using learned temporal and spatial regularities
examples: The current study used a controlled artificial display with fixed quadrant-onset pairings to maximize trial-by-trial learning; the authors propose realistic scenes as the next step.
key_sources: Nir Shalev, Sage Boettcher & Anna C. Nobre. (2024). Spatiotemporal predictions guide attention throughout the adult lifespan. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00281-3

article_title: Visual perceptual learning of feature conjunctions leverages non-linear mixed selectivity
citation: Behnam Karami & Caspar M. Schwiedrzik. (2024). Visual perceptual learning of feature conjunctions leverages non-linear mixed selectivity. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00226-w
title: Global pooling strategy for conjunction learning: pure color, pure orientation, and mixed selectivity neurons are jointly read out, enabled by global feedback
description: The article proposes that conjunction learning is best explained by a global pooling readout in which "pure color, pure orientation, and mixed selectivity neurons are combined to give rise to choice information", rather than precision pooling of only the most diagnostic neurons. Global (conjunction-level) feedback permits consistent credit assignment to mixed selectivity representations, whereas feature-specific feedback leaves their credit ambiguous. The framework distinguishes three neuronal resources and two pooling regimes, and predicts faster learning and non-linear task transfer when all resources are engaged.
requirements: Feedback must be delivered at the conjunction level so that credit can be consistently assigned to mixed selectivity representations
constraints: The benefit of global feedback was demonstrated for a linearly separable conjunction task; mixed selectivity was not strictly required to solve the task
The readout-versus-encoding question (whether learning changes encoding or downstream readout) was not resolved in this behavioral study
target_learners: adult human subjects learning visual feature conjunctions
target_learning_goals: discrimination of conjunctive visual features (orientation and color)
examples: Experiment 1 trained subjects with conjunction-level feedback and produced faster learning, larger non-linear mixing, and an XOR transfer advantage relative to feature-specific feedback
key_sources: Behnam Karami & Caspar M. Schwiedrzik. (2024). Visual perceptual learning of feature conjunctions leverages non-linear mixed selectivity. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00226-w

article_title: Divergent effects of mindsets on performance trajectories
citation: Melody M. Chao, Allen H. Huang, Anirban Mukhopadhyay & Janghoon Shon. (2025). Divergent effects of mindsets on performance trajectories. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00355-w
title: Growth versus fixed mindset as opposite ends of a continuum within an achievement-motivation model
description: The article treats mindsets as beliefs about the malleability of personal attributes arranged on a continuum, with "the fixed and growth mindsets conceptualized as opposite ends of a continuum, ranging from a relatively rigid and immutable view of personal attributes to a dynamic view of change". The growth mindset "is built on a model of achievement motivation", premised on beliefs shaping how individuals respond to challenges and setbacks, motivating persistence. The study tests this framework's implicit linearity assumption and finds it fails.
requirements: A mindset measure capturing endorsement of beliefs in growth and change along the continuum, as the article's 3-item scale did
constraints: The article's own data contradict the framework's assumed linear positive association between growth mindset strength and performance
target_learning_goals: academic achievement and persistence through challenge
key_sources: Melody M. Chao, Allen H. Huang, Anirban Mukhopadhyay & Janghoon Shon. (2025). Divergent effects of mindsets on performance trajectories. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00355-w

article_title: Dissecting the role of adult hippocampal neurogenesis towards resilience versus susceptibility to stress-related mood disorders
citation: Katherine L. Jones, Mei Zhou and Dhanisha J. Jhaveri. (2022). Dissecting the role of adult hippocampal neurogenesis towards resilience versus susceptibility to stress-related mood disorders. npj Science of Learning 7:16. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00133-y
title: Neurogenic theory of anxiety/depression
description: The neurogenic theory of anxiety/depression posits, as the review states, that "stress-induced impairment in neurogenesis is an important causal factor in the aetiology of anxiety/depression and that restoration of neurogenesis is necessary for the therapeutic effects of antidepressants". It framed two decades of ablation and enhancement experiments appraised in this review. The review concludes the theory "has fallen short in providing a unified mechanism that links stress to affective behaviour", since subtracting or adding adult-born neurons alone is not sufficient to produce the predicted behavioural changes.
requirements: Causal testing requires ablation or enhancement of adult neurogenesis with behavioural outcome measures under baseline and stressed conditions
constraints: Simple addition or subtraction of adult-born neurons is not sufficient to produce anxiety/depression or antidepressant-like effects; off-target ablation effects and compensatory mechanisms confound tests of the theory
target_learners: rodent models in translational neuropsychiatric research
target_learning_goals: understanding the causal role of adult hippocampal neurogenesis in stress response, recovery and mood regulation
examples: The review's appraisal of ablation and gain-of-function rodent studies testing the theory's predictions
key_sources: Katherine L. Jones, Mei Zhou and Dhanisha J. Jhaveri. (2022). Dissecting the role of adult hippocampal neurogenesis towards resilience versus susceptibility to stress-related mood disorders. npj Science of Learning 7:16. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00133-y

article_title: Dissecting the role of adult hippocampal neurogenesis towards resilience versus susceptibility to stress-related mood disorders
citation: Katherine L. Jones, Mei Zhou and Dhanisha J. Jhaveri. (2022). Dissecting the role of adult hippocampal neurogenesis towards resilience versus susceptibility to stress-related mood disorders. npj Science of Learning 7:16. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00133-y
title: Critical-period properties hypothesis: immature adult-born neuron excitability and connectivity link chronic stress to mood behaviour
description: The review's working hypothesis is that "the unique properties of adult-born hippocampal neurons during their critical period of maturation are functionally important and causally link chronic stress to altered mood-related behaviour". It posits that chronic stress alters the cellular and physiological properties of these neurons and their pattern of connectivity, producing a dysfunctional hippocampal circuit, and that antidepressants act in part by modulating distinct properties of immature adult-born neurons. Immature neurons exhibit "a critical period of heightened intrinsic excitability and synaptic plasticity" at approximately 4–6 weeks of neuron age, giving them capacity to influence dentate gyrus circuit activity and behaviour.
requirements: Future studies must monitor and manipulate stress-induced changes in molecular, cellular and physiological properties of adult-born neurons, map their connectome, and use spatially and temporally controlled manipulations during behavioural tasks
constraints: The hypothesis is a proposal for future work, not a tested result; prior evidence rests on manipulations with off-target effects and brain-wide ablation that preclude determining the precise role of adult-born hippocampal neurons
target_learners: rodent models in translational neuropsychiatric research
target_learning_goals: understanding mechanisms linking stress-induced changes in adult hippocampal neurogenesis to affective behaviour
examples: The review proposes two posits: chronic stress alters properties and connectivity of immature adult-born neurons, and antidepressants modulate distinct properties of these immature neurons
key_sources: Katherine L. Jones, Mei Zhou and Dhanisha J. Jhaveri. (2022). Dissecting the role of adult hippocampal neurogenesis towards resilience versus susceptibility to stress-related mood disorders. npj Science of Learning 7:16. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00133-y

citation: Smith, D. D., Bartley, J. E., Peraza, J. A., Bottenhorn, K. L., Nomi, J. S., Uddin, L. Q., Riedel, M. C., Salo, T., Laird, R. W., Pruden, S. M., Sutherland, M. T., Brewe, E., & Laird, A. R. (2025). Dynamic reconﬁguration of brain coactivation states associated with active and lecture-based learning of university physics. npj Science of Learning (2025) 10:55. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00348-9
title: Embodied cognition framework for physics learning
description: Embodied cognition posits that "cognitive processes are deeply rooted in the body 's interactions with the world" and that "conceptual knowledge is grounded in sensory and motor experiences". The article uses it to predict and interpret instructional-method-specific neural dynamics: active learning students preferentially engaged a somatomotor state at rest, while lecture-based students engaged visual states. The authors also invoke Hebbian learning to explain how repeated activation produces intrinsic cortical restructuring.
requirements: Instructional contexts must differ in sensorimotor versus observational engagement for the framework to predict differential neural recruitment.
constraints: The article reports it as an interpretive framework; behavioral differences between instructional groups were not observed, so neural findings did not translate to behavior.
target_learners: Undergraduate students in introductory physics courses
target_learning_goals: Physics conceptual reasoning and physics knowledge retrieval
examples: The study used modeling instruction (model building, collaborative group activities) as its active learning condition and traditional lecture-based instruction as its comparison.

article_title: Reading experience reveals shared and idiosyncratic neural patterns during text comprehension
citation: Song, M., Li, L., He, D. & Cai, Q. (2025). Reading experience reveals shared and idiosyncratic neural patterns during text comprehension. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00390-7
title: Topicalized Author Recognition Test (tART)
description: The tART is a new instrument the authors developed to measure reading experience as a distribution across topics rather than only an overall quantity of print exposure. It included "135 author names spanning 9 topics/genres", with "Each topic comprised 10 real author names and 5 foils", and five response options scored 0 to 4 covering recognition and books read. Topic distributions were converted with a SoftMax transform into probability distributions, whose pairwise KL divergence quantified dissimilarity in reading experience among participants. In this study the maximum exposure score was 360, the sample's mean was 45.844 (SD = 24.975), and scores were validated against self-reported reading frequency (Spearman r = 0.744).
requirements: Topics must have at least 10 authors specialized in the domain who have each published at least three books, to allow reliable topic profiling
A pilot phase to select author names spanning a wide range of recognition difficulty, and a false-alarm-rate scaling factor to correct overclaiming
constraints: The tART covered only nine topics within the participants' native language, omitting science, technology and some social-science categories, biasing it toward literary and humanities-related author knowledge
ART-based measures cannot fully account for individual variability in attention to or memory for author names
It assesses the quantitative amount of exposure rather than qualitative dimensions such as depth of engagement
target_learners: Adult native-language readers (college students aged 18–24 in this study)
target_learning_goals: Profiling reading experience across topics and genres for research on language and reading processing
examples: Author names were drawn from categories on popular Chinese online book stores and reading apps (Jingdong Books, Dangdang, Weixin), with foreign translated authors excluded to limit assessment to the native language
key_sources: Song, M., Li, L., He, D. & Cai, Q. (2025). Reading experience reveals shared and idiosyncratic neural patterns during text comprehension. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00390-7

article_title: Reading experience reveals shared and idiosyncratic neural patterns during text comprehension
citation: Song, M., Li, L., He, D. & Cai, Q. (2025). Reading experience reveals shared and idiosyncratic neural patterns during text comprehension. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00390-7
title: Design reading interventions that account for both the quantity and the diversity of learners' reading materials
description: The article proposes that its neurocognitive link between cumulative reading experience and real-time comprehension has implications for education. The authors recommend "designing reading interventions that take into account the quantity and diversity of reading materials", and suggest that "customizing reading experiences to align with individual exposure levels may enhance cognitive engagement, improve comprehension efficiency, and foster critical thinking and empathy development." The principle treats reading experience as an experiential index shaping how shared or individualized readers' neural processing of texts will be.
requirements: Assessment of learners' print exposure quantity and topical distribution, e.g. with an instrument like the tART
constraints: The supporting evidence is correlational; factors such as IQ, socioeconomic status, personal interests and cognitive traits may have modulated the association, limiting causal interpretation
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension efficiency, critical thinking, and empathy development
examples: The study profiled 39 college students' reading across nine topics with the tART and linked topic distributions to precuneus/DMN activity during narrative reading
