article_title: Language experience matters for the emergence of early numerical concepts
citation: Stacee Santos, Hiram Brownell, Marie Coppola, Anna Shusterman and Sara Cordes. (2023). Language experience matters for the emergence of early numerical concepts. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00202-w
title: Language access, rather than vocabulary ability, as the catalyst for the development of numerical abilities
description: The article proposes that the duration of a child's access to fluent linguistic input, indexed by Hearing Age, drives the emergence of both symbolic number knowledge and non-symbolic numerical discrimination. The authors state that "these ndings support our contention that language access (as measured by Hearing Age), rather than language ability (as measured by vocabulary), is a catalyst for re ning the development of numerical abilities." Possible mechanisms discussed include more number talk promoting attention to number (Spontaneous Focus on Number), while vocabulary alone did not capture the relevant experience.
requirements: A measure of cumulative duration of auditory access to spoken language, such as Hearing Age computed from hearing technology onset
Comparison samples differing in language access duration to test whether group effects persist
constraints: Hearing Age is a proxy that "only provides an estimate of the child's language access since birth but does not take into account the reduced access oral DHH children using auditory technology may experience on a day-to-day basis"
The sample was small, reflecting the low prevalence of congenital hearing loss, and could not explore how different hearing devices or levels of hearing account for performance
target_learners: preschool children (ages 3–6) acquiring early number concepts
oral deaf and hard-of-hearing children born to non-signing hearing parents
target_learning_goals: symbolic number knowledge (counting, number word knowledge via Give-N)
non-symbolic numerical discrimination acuity
understanding of comparative quantity language (the word "more")
examples: The study computed a Hearing Age for each DHH child from the hearing questionnaire and replaced chronological age with it in regression models, finding group differences in the three numerical measures disappeared while vocabulary differences persisted
key_sources: Stacee Santos, Hiram Brownell, Marie Coppola, Anna Shusterman and Sara Cordes. (2023). Language experience matters for the emergence of early numerical concepts. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00202-w

article_title: Benefits of classroom remote microphone technology for inattentive children
citation: Shiels, L., Tomlin, D., Payne, J.M. et al. (2026). Benefits of classroom remote microphone technology for inattentive children. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00427-5
title: Consider referral to audiologists for remote microphone fitting when listening difficulties accompany childhood inattention
description: The article recommends remote microphone technology as a non-pharmacological classroom support for children whose inattention carries listening difficulties. It argues RMT "requires only the teacher and student to wear devices, avoiding disruption to other students' learning", and concludes that referral to audiologists for RMT fitting should be considered when LiD is a concern for inattentive or hyperactive children.
requirements: Audiologist fitting of ear-level receivers with individualized comfort-level volume adjustment
Teacher willingness to wear the transmitter and caregivers to perform daily listening checks and overnight charging
constraints: Benefits were demonstrated for auditory but not visual attention measures
Long-term use did not improve auditory processing, memory or attention skills beyond the typical trajectory
Uptake barriers such as comfort, sound quality and peer perception were not systematically documented
target_learners: Primary school children aged 6-12 with inattention or ADHD and listening difficulties
target_learning_goals: Access to verbal instruction and classroom listening
Attention during listening tasks
Reading fluency and academic progress
examples: In the trial, participants were fit bilaterally with Phonak Roger Focus II-312 receivers wirelessly connected to a Phonak Roger Touchscreen Microphone transmitter worn by the teacher

article_title: Benefits of classroom remote microphone technology for inattentive children
citation: Shiels, L., Tomlin, D., Payne, J.M. et al. (2026). Benefits of classroom remote microphone technology for inattentive children. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00427-5
title: Phonak Roger Focus II remote microphone system for classroom use
description: The trialed intervention is a teacher-worn Phonak Roger Touchscreen Microphone transmitter wirelessly connected to ear-level Roger Focus II-312 receivers worn bilaterally by the student. Unlike hearing aids, "these receivers exclusively obtain wireless signals from the Roger Touchscreen Transmitter at safe, comfortable and adjustable (-8 to +8 dB) volumes", fitted with open domes to minimize occlusion and adjusted in 2 dB increments to individual comfort.
requirements: Caregiver overnight charging and daily morning listening checks
Educator guidance on classroom use emailed prior to trial commencement
Individualized volume fitting by an audiologist
constraints: Transmits only the teacher's wireless signal rather than amplifying environmental sound
No data logging in the trialed devices, so compliance relied on teacher estimates
target_learners: Children aged 6-12 with normal hearing, inattention and listening difficulties
target_learning_goals: Improved speech understanding and access to teacher instructions in noisy classrooms
examples: In phase one, the transmitter was positioned 20 cm from the loudspeaker presenting the target signal to replicate recommended distance from the educator's mouth, with volume standardized to 0 dB for simulated classroom assessments

article_title: The dynamics of state math anxiety vary by paradigm and timing during arithmetic
citation: Yao, X., Huber, J.F., Li, Z., Findik, Y., Nuerk, H.-C. & Artemenko, C. (2026). The dynamics of state math anxiety vary by paradigm and timing during arithmetic. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00398-z
title: Reciprocal theory of math anxiety and performance
description: The article presents a reciprocal theory integrating cognitive disruption, reduced competency, and interpretation accounts of math anxiety. Rather than treating these as mutually exclusive, it states that "a bidirectional relationship between math anxiety and math performance" exists, so that anxiety and performance influence each other and create a vicious cycle. The study's data are interpreted against this backdrop: trait math anxiety shapes state anxiety responses and performance, while lower performance may in turn feed higher state and eventually trait anxiety.
requirements: The theory presupposes that both trait and state math anxiety are assessed to capture the bidirectional relation between anxiety and performance over time.
constraints: The article states the assumption that lower performance induces higher state math anxiety over time requires further investigation, as state math anxiety was not assessed at the trial level in the current study.
target_learning_goals: arithmetic performance
managing math anxiety during mathematics learning
examples: The study tested trait and state math anxiety simultaneously while participants performed arithmetic, and interpreted the replicated anxiety-complexity effect via the disruption account's working-memory mechanism.

article_title: Personalized and gamified auditory-cognitive training improves naturalistic speech-in-noise comprehension in older adults with hearing loss
citation: Ockelmann, J., Scherpiet, S., Stropahl, M. & Giroud, N. (2025). Personalized and gamified auditory-cognitive training improves naturalistic speech-in-noise comprehension in older adults with hearing loss. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00369-4
title: Ease of Language Understanding (ELU) model alignment: cognitive resources become increasingly critical as auditory input degrades
description: The article interprets its findings through the Ease of Language Understanding (ELU) model, "which posits that cognitive resources become increasingly critical as auditory input becomes degraded." In this account, when auditory input quality falls, top-down cognitive capacity compensates, so training cognitive abilities should support speech-in-noise comprehension even without changing sensory fidelity. The study's dissociation — comprehension improved while OLSA intelligibility thresholds did not — is presented as consistent with this framework.
requirements: Applicable to listening situations where auditory input is degraded, making cognitive compensation load-bearing.
constraints: The article states the findings align with the ELU model rather than testing it directly.
target_learners: older adults with mild-to-moderate hearing loss
target_learning_goals: speech-in-noise comprehension supported by cognitive (top-down) processing
examples: The RCT's finding that SIN comprehension improved without corresponding changes in speech intelligibility thresholds (OLSA) is cited by the authors as supporting the ELU model.
key_sources: Ockelmann, J., Scherpiet, S., Stropahl, M. & Giroud, N. (2025). Personalized and gamified auditory-cognitive training improves naturalistic speech-in-noise comprehension in older adults with hearing loss. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00369-4

article_title: Personalized and gamified auditory-cognitive training improves naturalistic speech-in-noise comprehension in older adults with hearing loss
citation: Ockelmann, J., Scherpiet, S., Stropahl, M. & Giroud, N. (2025). Personalized and gamified auditory-cognitive training improves naturalistic speech-in-noise comprehension in older adults with hearing loss. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00369-4
title: ActivEar: a gamified, personalized mobile auditory-cognitive training app on the CogniFit platform
description: ActivEar is a mobile ACT application used as the experimental intervention, delivered via the CogniFit research platform with training contents "drawn from the ActivEar mobile application." After installation, the CogniFit cognitive assessment battery (CAB™) established baseline performance, which "informed the automated synthesis of a personalized training plan" prioritizing each participant's lowest-scoring abilities and updating after every training unit. Units comprised two training tasks and a concluding assessment task, with gamification elements such as adaptive difficulty and reward systems.
requirements: Daily training of at least 20 minutes, five days a week, over four weeks, logged via the CogniFit platform.
constraints: Sensory aspects were integrated into broader cognitive tasks rather than trained separately.
target_learners: older adults with mild-to-moderate hearing loss, with or without hearing aids
target_learning_goals: working memory, phonological short-term memory, selective attention, divided attention, and speech-in-noise comprehension
examples: Experimental-group participants completed four weeks of home-based ActivEar training, with activity automatically logged by the application.

article_title: Comparing feedback learning and arousal responses in Down, Fragile X, and Williams syndromes
citation: Hallman, A. E. Z., Willfors, C., Frick, M. A., Nordgren, A. & Kleberg, J. L. (2026). Comparing feedback learning, pupil dilation, and gaze allocation in intellectual disability. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00438-2
title: Simplified reward contingency reversal task with eye tracking for feedback learning in intellectual disability
description: This is a simplified deterministic reinforcement learning paradigm combined with eye tracking, designed to be feasible for individuals with intellectual disability in the mild to moderate range. Each trial presented "a pair of pictures, and participants were required to choose one of the options", with win feedback indicated by a thumbs up and a sound and loss feedback by a thumbs down and a matched sound. "After four consecutive correct responses (wins), the reward contingency reversed without warning, resulting in a loss", and the task included five achievable blocks with a maximum of 25 trials. The authors state the paradigm "support[s] the use of this paradigm in ID populations and provide[s] a robust foundation for examining syndrome-specific differences in physiological feedback processing."
requirements: Instructions were given both in written and oral form and "adjusted based on the participant's receptive language skills", with two practice trials before the task.
constraints: The task was intentionally simplified; the authors note the lack of observable adaptation difficulties likely reflects this simplicity rather than the absence of cognitive flexibility difficulties, and recommend more complex paradigms for future work.
target_learners: Individuals with intellectual disability in the mild to moderate severity range, including Down, Fragile X, and Williams syndromes, aged 6 to 60 years
target_learning_goals: Reinforcement learning: associating choices with rewards and losses from deterministic feedback
examples: Participants completed up to 25 two-alternative trials while a Tobii eye tracker recorded pupil dilation and gaze; those with a proportion of optimal choices below 0.6 were excluded.
key_sources: Hallman, A. E. Z., Willfors, C., Frick, M. A., Nordgren, A. & Kleberg, J. L. (2026). Comparing feedback learning, pupil dilation, and gaze allocation in intellectual disability. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00438-2

article_title: Knowledge reshapes inquiry by changing question asking ability and impacting academic assessment
citation: Tuval Raz & Yoed N. Kenett. (2026). Knowledge Reshapes Inquiry: Changes in Question Asking Ability and its Impact on Academic Assessment. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00402-0
title: Question-Asking in Information Seeking (QuInS) framework
description: The QuInS framework portrays question-asking as a multi-stage cognitive process rather than a single request for information. As the article describes it, "people detect a knowledge gap, express curiosity, formulate and define a question, evaluate the reply, and refine their understanding across repeated cycles". The framework highlights how even a single question reflects a broader sequence of cognitive stages aimed at reducing uncertainty. The present study builds on this view in examining how question-asking changes as domain knowledge accumulates over a semester.
requirements: Question asking is understood as embedded in an information-seeking process rather than an isolated act
constraints: The framework is presented in the article as background theory from prior work, not tested directly in this study
target_learning_goals: question-asking and inquiry skills
knowledge acquisition and information seeking
examples: The study uses the framework to motivate examining how domain-specific question-asking evolves as knowledge accrues during a course

article_title: Mnemonic-trained brain tuning to a regular odd-even pattern subserves digit memory in children
citation: Yafeng Pan, Ning Hao, Ning Liu, Yijie Zhao, Xiaojun Cheng, Yixuan Ku and Yi Hu. (2023). Mnemonic-trained brain tuning to a regular odd-even pattern subserves digit memory in children. npj Science of Learning 8:27. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00177-8
title: Encoding-pattern versus processing-efficiency hypotheses of mnemonic training, instantiated as four theoretical models of neural change
description: The article contrasts two accounts of why mnemonic training works: the processing-efficiency hypothesis holds that "the cognitive processing of to-be- memorized materials consumes less cognitive resource after training", while the encoding-pattern hypothesis proposes altered encoding patterns, inferred from mnemonists mapping digit pairs to images at even positions. These are instantiated as four models (A–D) predicting post- versus pre-training neural activity by digit position odd versus even. The results, conforming to Model B, support the encoding-pattern account.
requirements: EEG measurement of encoding-phase neural responses (ERP and oscillatory power) to digits presented sequentially at known positions, before and after training
constraints: The authors note their analyses were insufficient to completely exclude processing-efficiency, which may involve efficient neural networks not detected in ERP and oscillatory power analyses
target_learners: developing children (primary or middle school students, mean age ~13 years)
target_learning_goals: short-term digit memory via the digit-image mnemonic
examples: Model B predicted differential neural activity between odd and even digit positions at post-training but not pre-training; the observed P200 and theta odd-even effects matched this prediction
key_sources: Yafeng Pan, Ning Hao, Ning Liu, Yijie Zhao, Xiaojun Cheng, Yixuan Ku and Yi Hu. (2023). Mnemonic-trained brain tuning to a regular odd-even pattern subserves digit memory in children. npj Science of Learning 8:27. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00177-8

article_title: Neural activations associated with feedback and retrieval success
citation: Wiklund-Hörnqvist, C., Andersson, M., Jonsson, B. & Nyberg, L. (2017). Neural activations associated with feedback and retrieval success. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0013-6
title: Fronto-striatal gating account of test-enhanced learning
description: The article proposes that repeated testing with feedback strengthens memory via fronto-striatal interactions, in which "the striatum acts as a gating mechanism that regulates input of task-relevant information to the prefrontal cortex (PFC)". On this account, feedback induces updating of memory representations mediated via the striatum, and the first successful retrieval demands executive control and selective updating that become less demanding once irrelevant representations are filtered out, explaining the observed activity reduction across tests.
requirements: Feedback with the correct answer during initial testing, when knowledge level is low, to support updating of memory representations
constraints: The account is offered as a suggestion from this single fMRI study; T3 was excluded from the fMRI ANOVAs and only high-confidence 'know and correct' responses were analyzed
target_learners: young healthy adults learning foreign vocabulary
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of paired-associate vocabulary
examples: Participants learned 60 Swahili–Swedish word-pairs across three consecutive cued-recall tests with feedback during event-related fMRI scanning
key_sources: Wiklund-Hörnqvist, C., Andersson, M., Jonsson, B. & Nyberg, L. (2017). Neural activations associated with feedback and retrieval success. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0013-6

article_title: Fostering inclusion in EEG measures of pediatric brain activity
citation: Fostering inclusion in EEG measures of pediatric brain activity. (2024). npj Science of Learning 9, 27. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00240-y
title: Employ research staff who identify similarly to the participant population, or involve community members in reviewing materials and protocols
description: The review argues that hair-related conversations are not replacements for lived experience: “It is essential that labs employ research staff, both for participant-facing data collection, as well as for data analysis and study design, w ho identify similarly to the demo- graphic of the participant population.” This increases the cultural appropriateness of protocols, participant experiences, and interpretation and communication of findings. When such staffing is not possible, community members and leaders should review study materials and protocols.
requirements: When staff matching is not possible, community members and leaders should review study materials and protocols.
constraints: The authors caution that their observations and recommendations may not be appropriate for all participants, since cultural groups are not monolithic.
target_learners: Black and/or Latinx children and families participating in developmental neuroscience research
target_learning_goals: Reducing biases in participation and data acquisition in neuroscience research through culturally appropriate protocols
examples: The authors chose the terms ‘Latin’ and ‘Latinx’ in consultation with authorship team members who identify as Latina, and honor participant preferences for other terms where possible.
key_sources: Fostering inclusion in EEG measures of pediatric brain activity. (2024). npj Science of Learning 9, 27. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00240-y

article_title: Fostering inclusion in EEG measures of pediatric brain activity
citation: Fostering inclusion in EEG measures of pediatric brain activity. (2024). npj Science of Learning 9, 27. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00240-y
title: Modified and emerging EEG hardware for dense, curly, and styled hair, including caps with elongated pedestals and dry comb electrodes
description: The review describes hardware accommodations for hair diversity: Magstim EGI “now allows for ordering caps with elongated pedestals, which allow for more space for hair between the cap and scalp,” and dry comb electrodes entering the market penetrate hair — including long-lasting styles like braids and locs — without post-visit washing. Etienne and colleagues designed a novel electrode for reliable EEG recordings on coarse and curly hair, and analytical efforts are underway to account for hair texture and volume differences.
requirements: Novel electrodes are not currently available for most pediatric EEG systems and require a specific braiding pattern.
constraints: The review notes it is unclear how specialized electrodes, increased pedestal lengths, and increased scalp oils from not pre-washing hair may impact the EEG signal.
target_learners: Infants and young children with dense, curly, or styled hair participating in EEG research
target_learning_goals: Enabling high-quality EEG data collection across hair types so developmental findings generalize across racial and ethnic groups

article_title: A transient memory lapse in humans 1–3 h after training
citation: Beverly A. Wright & Ruijing Ning. (2024). A transient memory lapse in humans 1–3h after training. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00272-4
title: Transient memory lapses as a fundamental facet of memory formation, explained by transitions between memory phases or by fluctuating internal retrieval cues
description: This account holds that retention curves can be U-shaped because memory lapses "reflect periods of transition between different memory phases" (STM, ITM, LTM) with distinct kinetics and molecular requirements, or because lapses "reflect temporary failures in memory retrieval" when internal cues present during training fluctuate in the first hours after training. The article extends this account to human perceptual learning, proposing at least three perceptual memory phases: one ending ~1 h after training, one from ~3 h after training until sleep, and one beginning with sleep. It also suggests lapses may mark memory vulnerability to retrograde interference and may serve stability-plasticity balance functions.
requirements: Memory must be evaluated at a minimum of three post-training time points, with timings that straddle the lapse, for a lapse to be detectable
constraints: Nearly all documented lapses, including the present perceptual-learning cases, are attributed to the nondeclarative memory system, with only a few declarative examples reported
target_learners: human adults learning perceptual discrimination tasks
target_learning_goals: retention of learned perceptual skills over the hours following training
examples: The authors interpreted the human perceptual-learning lapses as consistent with a transition between forms of perceptual memory 1–3 h after training, aligning with STM, ITM, and LTM phases identified in non-human species
key_sources: Beverly A. Wright & Ruijing Ning. (2024). A transient memory lapse in humans 1–3h after training. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00272-4

article_title: Insights from 200+ years of personalized learning
citation: David Dockterman. (2018). Insights from 200 + years of personalized learning. npj Science of Learning 3:15. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0033-x
title: The Lancasterian (Monitorial) System as an early competency-based, self-paced, peer-learning model
description: The article describes the early-nineteenth-century Monitorial System created by John Lancaster as a scalable instructional organization predating modern personalized learning. Children were placed along learning progressions per domain, with student monitors delivering "scripted lessons to develop skills and assessments to move each student to the next level in the sequence as soon as he demonstrated mastery." The author writes, "Today we might call what Lancaster devised 200 years ago a self-paced, mastery-based, peer-learning instructional system," noting its similarity to current competency-based visions.
requirements: A scalable, accountable mechanism for organizing masses of students with an affordable cadre of teachers, as the article states drove its creation
constraints: The article states the competency-based organizing principle "turned out to be too much of an organizational burden for urban schools" as populations grew
target_learners: mass public school students in the early nineteenth century
target_learning_goals: foundational reading, writing, and math mastery
examples: Lancaster published books guiding uniform implementation, and the system spread across the United States and other nations in the early nineteenth century
key_sources: David Dockterman. (2018). Insights from 200 + years of personalized learning. npj Science of Learning 3:15. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0033-x

article_title: Insights from 200+ years of personalized learning
citation: David Dockterman. (2018). Insights from 200 + years of personalized learning. npj Science of Learning 3:15. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0033-x
title: Aptitude–Treatment Interaction (ATI) as a framework for matching instruction to learner variability
description: The article presents ATI, launched by Cronbach and Snow in the 1970s, as a research approach bringing rigor to studying the intersection of learner and instruction. It recognizes that learners differ cognitively, psychologically, and environmentally, so individuals respond differently to tasks and instruction forms, and "the same learner might respond to the same intervention differently under different environmental or psychological conditions." ATI laid foundations for computer-based adaptive learning by organizing efforts to match treatment to student need under optimal conditions.
requirements: Methodological techniques for determining the most effective match for each student, as ATI is said to have described
constraints: The article states the combinations of potential variables and treatments were, according to Cronbach and Snow, "virtually inexhaustible"
target_learners: all learners, across cognitive, psychological, and environmental difference dimensions
target_learning_goals: matching instructional methods to individual learner aptitudes and conditions
examples: The article credits ATI's expansive view of learner aptitudes with elevating psychological needs, such as social-emotional competencies, to central instructional considerations
key_sources: David Dockterman. (2018). Insights from 200 + years of personalized learning. npj Science of Learning 3:15. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0033-x

article_title: Insights from 200+ years of personalized learning
citation: David Dockterman. (2018). Insights from 200 + years of personalized learning. npj Science of Learning 3:15. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0033-x
title: Design learning environments proactively around anticipated learner variability, not exceptions to a group lesson
description: A personalization-based pedagogy, the article argues, starts from the assumption that each student differs across multiple dimensions, not just domain knowledge and skill. Rather than constructing lessons for the group and differentiating for outliers, "learning environments and related tasks, often supported by technology, can be constructed to remove expected barriers and bolster supports to address anticipated needs, including affective and behavioral ones, and both proactively and reactively." Design and materials should focus on the variability within the target population that matters most for learning and demonstrating competence.
requirements: Instructional design and materials informed by data and learning science about the target population's anticipated variability
constraints: Teaching and learning in this system "won't be uniform," so it conflicts with infrastructure built on same-content-same-pace assumptions
target_learners: all K-12 learners, including those with affective, behavioral, and executive-function needs
target_learning_goals: academic competence alongside motivation, mindset, and self-regulated learning
examples: The article argues research should identify under what conditions each intervention works with different learner characteristics, matching an instructional action with the right learner at the right time
key_sources: David Dockterman. (2018). Insights from 200 + years of personalized learning. npj Science of Learning 3:15. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0033-x

article_title: Genetic associations with mathematics tracking and persistence in secondary school
citation: K. Paige Harden, Benjamin W. Domingue, Daniel W. Belsky, Jason D. Boardman, Robert Crosnoe, Margherita Malanchini, Michel Nivard, Elliot M. Tucker-Drob and Kathleen Mullan Harris. (2020). Genetic associations with mathematics tracking and persistence in secondary school. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-0060-2
title: Polygenic scores as a molecular tracer for studying flows of students through the STEM pipeline
description: The article proposes using the education polygenic score (education-PGS), a composite of genetic variants associated with completing more years of school, as a "molecular tracer" of students through the high school math pipeline. Because genetic sequence is fixed at conception and cannot be changed by educational experiences, comparing students equivalent in education-PGS but attending different schools can illuminate how achievement depends on contextual factors, complementing research on school-based factors such as instructional practices. The authors visualize genetically stratified flows using a river plot of course sequences by year.
requirements: Requires a genome-wide association study summary (the cited 1.1-million-person GWAS) to construct the education-PGS, plus linked genetic and official transcript data for the same students.
constraints: Polygenic scores are valid only within shared ancestry; the article states validity of education GWAS results has been established only for people of European ancestry, and results may not generalize to other populations.
The genetic predictor captures only a fraction of genotypic variation relevant for education, and up to half of the PGS association may operate indirectly through parental genotypes.
target_learners: U.S. secondary school students (Add Health cohort, 9th-12th grade)
target_learning_goals: Understanding how students flow through the secondary school math pipeline and how school context shapes advanced mathematics coursetaking
examples: The authors analyzed genetic and transcript data from 3,635 European-ancestry Add Health students, visualizing flows with a river plot whose river shading represents average education-PGS per course path.
key_sources: K. Paige Harden, Benjamin W. Domingue, Daniel W. Belsky, Jason D. Boardman, Robert Crosnoe, Margherita Malanchini, Michel Nivard, Elliot M. Tucker-Drob and Kathleen Mullan Harris. article_title: Prior text-based learning enhances the benefits of simulation-based learning on confidence and long-term recall
citation: Angélique Lebert & Óscar Vilarroya. (2025). Prior text-based learning enhances the benefits of simulation-based learning on confidence and long-term recall. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00380-9
title: SBL benefits arise from immersive, embodied, and interactive engagement that supports sensorimotor internal simulation and internal feedback
description: The article proposes that SBL's benefits stem from its "immersive, interactive, and embodied design" which enhances sensorimotor engagement and internal simulation, fostering "a robust internal feedback mechanism that reinforces both prediction and its verification." Drawing on the Integrated Model of Text–Picture Comprehension, the authors treat SBL as a depictive, embodied route and text as a descriptive route converging on a single mental model. This account is used to interpret both the memory advantages and the confidence–accuracy calibration observed in the SBL condition.
requirements: Learning material must be representable through bodily movements and realistic encounters, as with clinical cases
constraints: The study operationalized SBL narrowly as standardized-patient encounters, excluding feedback, decision-making, and iterative practice components
Findings pertain to the embodied-interactive bundle relative to text, not to SBL writ large
target_learners: naïve adult learners without medical or psychological background
target_learning_goals: acquisition and long-term retention of novel structured clinical information
examples: Participants interviewed a professional actor portraying a fictitious clinical case, touching the actor to feel symptom manifestations, over two spaced 10–12 minute sessions
key_sources: Angélique Lebert & Óscar Vilarroya. (2025). Prior text-based learning enhances the benefits of simulation-based learning on confidence and long-term recall. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00380-9

article_title: Prior text-based learning enhances the benefits of simulation-based learning on confidence and long-term recall
citation: Angélique Lebert & Óscar Vilarroya. (2025). Prior text-based learning enhances the benefits of simulation-based learning on confidence and long-term recall. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00380-9
title: Sequence structured text-based learning before immersive embodied simulation to scaffold later embodied encoding
description: The article reports that beginning with text-based learning improved subsequent simulation-based performance, while starting with simulation did not benefit later text learning. The authors suggest "initial symbolic structuring can scaffold later embodied encoding" and "underscores that sequencing effects are conditional." This principle recommends placing structured, low-to-high complexity text-based instruction before immersive embodied sessions, consistent with the authors' proposal of "a sequential, low-to-high complexity approach that progressively builds learners' long-term memory stores."
requirements: Applies when learning sessions are content-matched and temporally spaced, as in the study's "content-matched, temporally spaced sessions with distinct cases"
constraints: The authors note the order effect, while intriguing, requires further validation and may not generalize to other educational contexts
The mechanism (cognitive flexibility, engagement shifts, or proactive interference) remains speculative
target_learners: naïve adult learners acquiring novel structured knowledge
target_learning_goals: improving subsequent simulation-based learning accuracy through instructional sequencing
examples: In the study, participants who completed the text condition first showed enhanced subsequent performance in the simulation condition, whereas starting with simulation did not benefit the control condition

article_title: The practical utility of genetic screening in school settings
citation: Shero, J., van Dijk, W., Edwards, A., Schatschneider, C., Solari, E. J., & Hart, S. A. (2021). The practical utility of genetic screening in school settings. npj Science of Learning, 6:12. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00090-y
title: Two-predictor screener ShinyApp (two_predictor_screener)
description: A web application released by the authors to accompany the simulation analyses. The article states that "a ShinyApp ( https://jshero.shinyapps.io/two_predictor_screener/) was developed allowing any combination of correlations among the variables to be tested as a screener for any cutoff in the same ways presented in this paper." It extends the paper's fixed grid of progress-monitoring correlations, PGS effectiveness values, and learning-disability cutoffs to arbitrary combinations, and was designed so schools can test screener cut-off choices and usage patterns beyond those analyzed. It operationalizes the paper's probability-density approach for practitioners.
requirements: Requires knowable or able-to-be-estimated correlations between the screeners and the outcome of interest, as the Methods state.
constraints: Its outputs rest on the same multivariate normality and additive-prediction assumptions the paper's models make.
target_learners: Educators and researchers evaluating screening systems for K-12 students
target_learning_goals: Predicting academic achievement and identifying students at risk of learning disabilities
examples: The paper used it to test cutoffs or PGS/progress-monitoring values not represented in its tables.
key_sources: Shero, J., van Dijk, W., Edwards, A., Schatschneider, C., Solari, E. J., & Hart, S. A. (2021). The practical utility of genetic screening in school settings. npj Science of Learning, 6:12. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00090-y

article_title: The practical utility of genetic screening in school settings
citation: Shero, J., van Dijk, W., Edwards, A., Schatschneider, C., Solari, E. J., & Hart, S. A. (2021). The practical utility of genetic screening in school settings. npj Science of Learning, 6:12. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00090-y
title: Genetically informed personalized education framework (precision medicine analogy)
description: The article describes a framework, imported from precision medicine, in which educators would use various tools and screeners — potentially including a polygenic score — to understand individual students and tailor instruction. The authors "define personalized education as differentiated and targeted instruction at the individual level." Under this framework PGS results are treated as probabilistic, non-deterministic information to be combined with other data to predict general trends in achievement. The paper's simulations were designed to quantify whether this framework's genetic component adds incremental value over existing screening in schools.
requirements: Educators would need to use PGS alongside other tools and screeners, and communicate that results are risk probabilities rather than diagnoses.
constraints: The framework faces ethical concerns (genetic essentialism, scientific racism risks), inequitable effectiveness across ancestry groups, and the article concludes the evidence does not support individual-level genetic personalization at current technology levels.
target_learners: School-age students, particularly those at academic risk
target_learning_goals: Personalizing instruction and identifying academic risk at the individual (or group) level
examples: The authors conclude the best path to using PGS may be as a learning-disability screener rather than individual-level personalization, though group-level (quartile-level) differentiation could have some utility.
key_sources: Shero, J., van Dijk, W., Edwards, A., Schatschneider, C., Solari, E. J., & Hart, S. A. (2021). The practical utility of genetic screening in school settings. npj Science of Learning, 6:12. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00090-y

article_title: The practical utility of genetic screening in school settings
citation: Shero, J., van Dijk, W., Edwards, A., Schatschneider, C., Solari, E. J., & Hart, S. A. (2021). The practical utility of genetic screening in school settings. npj Science of Learning, 6:12. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00090-y
title: Use PGS alongside progress monitoring as a strategic learning-disability screener, choosing either- or both-cutoff rules according to the school's priority
description: The article recommends polygenic scores be considered not for individualized instruction but as an inexpensive, time-efficient additional screening tool within universal screening systems. Schools "could be strategically used to increase either positive or NPV": allowing identification by either measure reduces false negatives, while requiring both measures reduces false positives. The choice depends on the values of the school or locality, and the authors stress results must be communicated as probabilistic risk, not diagnosis.
requirements: Combination with existing progress monitoring tools; accurate communication to teachers and parents that results are not diagnostic; the article also recommends comprehensive cost-benefit analyses before implementation and genetic-counseling-like educational outreach.
constraints: Current PGS effectiveness (~2% for specific measures) limits value; reference samples are predominantly European ancestry, so results apply mainly to students of European ancestry and would likely be greatly decreased for other ancestries; ethical concerns including genetic essentialism and potential misuse against marginalized groups must be addressed first.
target_learners: K-12 students being universally screened for academic risk, especially in early grades
target_learning_goals: Early, accurate identification of students at risk of learning disabilities to guide supplemental intervention
examples: The simulations quantified NPV gains of 0.3–3.4% under the either-cutoff rule and PPV gains of 3.9–13.4% under the both-cutoffs rule, and the authors suggest the either-cutoff approach may be especially beneficial in earlier grades.

article_title: Cognitive neuroepigenetics: the next evolution in our understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying learning and memory?
citation: Paul Marshall and Timothy W Bredy. (2016). Cognitive neuroepigenetics: the next evolution in our understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying learning and memory? npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/npjscilearn.2016.14
title: Neuroepigenetic model of memory: dynamic, reversible, state-dependent modifications to DNA, RNA and protein form a parallel and distributed system for consolidation, storage and retrieval
description: The article proposes that memory arises from bidirectional and reversible modifications operating at all levels of cellular control. It states that "DNA, RNA and protein each inﬂuence one another to produce a holistic cellular state that contributes to the formation and maintenance of memory, and predicts a parallel and distributed system for the consolidation, storage and retrieval of the engram". This contrasts with the serial, protein-centric view derived from the central dogma. The model is illustrated in Figure 2 as dynamic modifications occurring across consolidation, storage and retrieval.
requirements: Evidence linking nucleic-acid mechanisms to memory behaviour requires specific measurement, specific manipulation and functional validation, per the article's stated three requirements
constraints: The article notes more evidence is required to establish the generalized nature of the Figure 2 model across all phases of learning and memory; the role of DNA editing in gene-expression regulation related to learning and memory remains to be explored further
target_learners: not applicable to human learners; the framework concerns molecular mechanisms of memory in animals and humans at the cellular level
target_learning_goals: molecular and cellular mechanisms underlying memory formation, consolidation, storage and retrieval
examples: Figure 2 presents a neuroepigenetic model of memory with cytosine/5-methylcytosine, adenosine/N6-methyladenosine and acetylated/deacetylated histone state changes across consolidation, storage and retrieval
key_sources: Paul Marshall and Timothy W Bredy. (2016). Cognitive neuroepigenetics: the next evolution in our understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying learning and memory? npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/npjscilearn.2016.14

article_title: Cognitive neuroepigenetics: the next evolution in our understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying learning and memory?
citation: Paul Marshall and Timothy W Bredy. (2016). Cognitive neuroepigenetics: the next evolution in our understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying learning and memory? npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/npjscilearn.2016.14
title: Post-translational modification of protein hypothesis: memory quasi-stored in dynamic, consistently similar post-translational modifications without requiring active protein synthesis
description: The review presents, from Routtenberg and Rekart, the post-translational modification of protein hypothesis, which it states "memory can also be quasi-stored in dynamic, but consistently similar, post-translational modi ﬁcations of proteins, which can affect subsequent processing of stimuli without the need to be in an active state". The authors expand this idea to include DNA and RNA alongside traditional protein-synthesis views. Prion-like conformational state changes of proteins, which self-perpetuate, are noted as another way proteins may overcome molecular turnover.
requirements: Application of this hypothesis requires conceiving of memory storage as distributed across DNA, RNA and protein, not protein synthesis alone, per the authors' expanded framing
constraints: The review labels this idea intriguing without presenting direct evidence; it presents classic examples of the necessity of protein synthesis for memory, such as habituation in Aplysia and fear learning in mice, alongside it
target_learners: not applicable to human learners; the framework concerns molecular memory mechanisms in animal and human nervous systems
target_learning_goals: molecular mechanisms of long-term memory storage and maintenance
examples: The review cites Kandel's examples of intracellular signalling cascades in Aplysia habituation and mouse fear learning as classic cases of protein-synthesis necessity that should not be overlooked

article_title: Does splitting sleep improve long-term memory in chronically sleep deprived adolescents?
citation: Cousins, J. N., van Rijn, E., Ong, J. L., Wong, K. F., & Chee, M. W. L. (2019). Does splitting sleep improve long-term memory in chronically sleep deprived adolescents? npj Science of Learning 4:8. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0047-z
title: For chronically sleep-restricted learners, scheduling a daytime nap as part of a split sleep schedule can harness afternoon learning without impairing morning learning
description: This principle holds that when adolescents cannot obtain adequate nocturnal sleep, dividing the available sleep between a shortened night and a mid-afternoon nap supports memory better than concentrating the same total sleep at night, particularly for afternoon learning. The article states that "a split sleep schedule appears to be preferable for harnessing the cognitive functions that underpin learning in the afternoon, without negatively impacting upon morning learning", and that "facilitating naps in schools may be an effective measure to improve learning outcomes". It is grounded in the experimental comparison of split versus continuous restricted sleep on picture encoding and factual knowledge.
requirements: A mid-afternoon nap opportunity (1.5 h in the study, chosen to allow a full cycle of N2, SWS and REM sleep) in addition to nocturnal sleep
constraints: The evidence applies under sleep restriction below the recommended 8–10 h; whether splitting sleep advantages adolescents with adequate habitual sleep was not tested
The 90-min nap "is toward the upper limits of nap durations that may be practical to implement in schools"; shorter naps of 30–60 min have shown benefits but were not tested in this schedule
Splitting sleep reduced total sleep time and REM sleep, and REM-linked faculties (procedural memory, creative problem solving, emotional regulation) may have been affected
target_learning_goals: Long-term memory for school learning material encoded across the school day (factual knowledge and picture recognition)
examples: In the simulated school week, the split group's 1.5 h nap at 14:00–15:30 followed afternoon learning blocks about amphibian species, and the group remembered more of that material after recovery sleep

This dataset covers the behavioural data from the three within-subjects experiments reported in the article, enabling reuse and reanalysis of the associative recognition and story recall/recognition findings.

constraints: No proprietary code was written for these studies.

article_title: On the promise of personalized learning for educational equity
citation: Hanna Dumont and Douglas D. Ready. (2023). On the promise of personalized learning for educational equity. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00174-x
title: Adequacy conception of educational equity as the framework under which personalized learning serves equity
description: The article distinguishes three conceptions of educational equity as an analytic lens: "equality of outcomes", "equality of inputs", and "suffcientarianism" or "adequacy". Under adequacy, "the inputs provided should ensure that all students reach a minimum level of educational outcomes", and inequality beyond that minimum is no longer problematic. The authors argue personalized learning by definition cannot provide equality of inputs, may exacerbate outcome inequality because high-ability students advance faster, but aligns with adequacy if it equips all students with basic competencies to participate in society.
requirements: Implementation must ensure at-risk students receive the resources necessary to develop basic competencies, since inequality of inputs is appropriate only to that extent
constraints: Requires deep normative discussion of how basic competencies are conceptualized and defined, as there may not be shared definitions of basic or consensus on complex future skills
Personalized learning is unlikely to yield equality of outcomes and by definition does not provide equality of inputs
target_learners: K-12 students, particularly those from disadvantaged socioeconomic backgrounds
target_learning_goals: Basic competencies needed to participate in society as active members and live meaningful lives
examples: The article notes U.S. whole-school reform programs such as Success for All and the University of Chicago Charter School, whose key element is that teachers adapt instruction to students' needs, improved learning for disadvantaged students
key_sources: Hanna Dumont and Douglas D. Ready. (2023). On the promise of personalized learning for educational equity. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00174-x

article_title: Sex differences in motivational biases over instrumental actions
citation: Luigi A. E. Degni, Sara Garofalo, Gianluca Finotti, Francesca Starita, Trevor W. Robbins & Giuseppe di Pellegrino. (2024). Sex differences in motivational biases over instrumental actions. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00246-6
title: Two-bias framework of motivational cue effects on instrumental actions: direction bias and intensity bias
description: The article organizes motivational cue effects on value-based decisions into two distinct biases. The direction bias (outcome-specific transfer) occurs when an outcome-predictive cue favors actions congruent with the outcome it predicts, and is related to a cognitive top-down strategy exploiting the cue's informative value. The intensity bias (general transfer) describes how outcome-predictive cues "generally enhance or energize instrumental responses, even if directed toward different (but motivationally similar) outcomes", attributed to a general cue-induced increase of motivation. The two biases are measured with different dependent variables (percentage of congruent responses versus vigor) and, per the article, show a double dissociation across measures.
requirements: Separately trained Pavlovian stimulus-outcome and instrumental response-outcome associations, and distinct trial types and dependent measures to disentangle the two biases
constraints: The article notes the direction bias has been reported to require high-level cognitive abilities such as working memory and conscious perception of the cues, and that the intensity bias is detectable through vigor measures rather than number of responses
target_learners: adult human participants in decision-making and motivational research
target_learning_goals: understanding how motivational cues bias the direction and intensity of instrumental actions
examples: Experiment 1 used an appetitive slot-machine PIT task with tailored food rewards; Experiment 2 used an aversive space-war PIT task with 100 dB aversive noises and grip-force measurement
key_sources: Luigi A. E. Degni, Sara Garofalo, Gianluca Finotti, Francesca Starita, Trevor W. Robbins & Giuseppe di Pellegrino. (2024). Sex differences in motivational biases over instrumental actions. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00246-6

article_title: Growth mindset and academic outcomes: a comparison of US and Chinese students
citation: Xin Sun, Shaylene Nancekivell, Susan A. Gelman and Priti Shah. (2021). Growth mindset and academic outcomes: a comparison of US and Chinese students. npj Science of Learning 6:21. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00100-z
title: Mindset interventions can target the malleability of school performance and effort attribution rather than the malleability of intelligence
description: The article proposes an alternative route to motivation intervention: rather than increasing beliefs about the malleability of intelligence, interventions "can focus on the malleability of mastering school subjects and directly promoting a more effort-oriented attribution to school performance." This rests on the finding that students in both cultures view effort as more important than ability for school-level achievement, so students can be motivated to invest effort even without a growth view of intelligence. A related suggested message is that school success is only modestly related to intelligence per se.
requirements: Students must already view effort as more important than ability for school-level achievement, as both samples in the article did
constraints: The classic mindset intervention paradigm was reported as not effective on a sample of N = 624 Chinese students, cited as consistent with the current investigation
The article notes this alternative is a theoretical proposal ('in theory, could be more impactful'), not a tested intervention
target_learners: Middle-school and college students in US and Chinese educational contexts
target_learning_goals: Academic motivation and effort investment in school mathematics achievement
examples: Study 2 measured effort-ability attributions for school-level achievements such as achieving an A in a middle-school algebra course, where both samples rated effort above ability
