article_title: Exploring the genetic prediction of academic underachievement and overachievement
citation: Kaito Kawakami, Francesca Procopio, Kaili Rimfeld, Margherita Malanchini, Sophie von Stumm, Kathryn Asbury, Robert Plomin. (2024). Exploring the genetic prediction of academic underachievement and overachievement. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00251-9
title: GPAΔ: a continuous genomically predicted achievement discrepancy index (observed achievement minus GPS)
description: GPAΔ (Genomically-Predicted Achievement Discrepancy) is a continuous difference score created by subtracting a standardized genome-wide polygenic score (EA4, based on educational attainment) from standardized observed achievement. The authors state they "devised an index called Genomically-Predicted Achievement Discrepancy (GPAΔ) by subtracting a GPS for adult educational attainment from educational achievement at age 7." Negative scores indicate underachievement and positive scores overachievement, spanning a continuum rather than dichotomizing students. Domain-specific versions (English–GPS, Mathematics–GPS) were also constructed.
requirements: Requires genotyping and creation of a genome-wide polygenic score, plus assessed early school achievement to compute the difference
constraints: Until a GWA study is done on GPAΔ per se, GPAΔ requires that early school achievement is assessed so the difference between GPS and observed achievement can be obtained
GPS predictive power is attenuated in populations with different ancestries; the study included only participants of European ancestry
target_learners: children in the early school years (age 7)
target_learning_goals: identifying academic underachievement and overachievement for personalized educational support
examples: In the TEDS cohort, GPAΔ at age 7 was computed for 4175 genotyped participants and correlated with achievement slopes across ages 7, 9, 12, and 16
key_sources: Kaito Kawakami, Francesca Procopio, Kaili Rimfeld, Margherita Malanchini, Sophie von Stumm, Kathryn Asbury, Robert Plomin. (2024). Exploring the genetic prediction of academic underachievement and overachievement. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00251-9

article_title: Exploring the genetic prediction of academic underachievement and overachievement
citation: Kaito Kawakami, Francesca Procopio, Kaili Rimfeld, Margherita Malanchini, Sophie von Stumm, Kathryn Asbury, Robert Plomin. (2024). Exploring the genetic prediction of academic underachievement and overachievement. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00251-9
title: Use genomic discrepancy indices as an early-warning system to target underachievers early, pending intervention tests
description: The article proposes GPAΔ screening as an early-warning system: because GPS are stable from conception, they can flag likely underachievers before achievement falls far behind, when interventions are most likely to succeed. The authors argue "Targeting GPAΔ underachievers might prove cost-effective because such interventions seem more likely to succeed by going with the genetic ﬂow rather than swimming upstream." This remains an explicitly untested hypothesis requiring intervention research.
requirements: Intervention research testing whether GPAΔ underachievers respond better to intervention than other underachievers
Early school achievement must be assessed to compute the GPS–achievement difference
constraints: Interventions effective for GPAΔ underachievers might be less effective in preventing the decline of GPAΔ overachievers
GPAΔ currently requires DNA, genotyping, and GPS creation; predictive power represents an upper bound for European-ancestry samples
target_learners: children in the early school years, particularly those underachieving relative to genomic prediction
target_learning_goals: early identification of underachievement to personalize education and maximize achievement toward individual potential
examples: The study screened 4175 TEDS participants at age 7 and charted trajectories showing underachievers regressing about one-third toward genomic prediction by age 16
key_sources: Kaito Kawakami, Francesca Procopio, Kaili Rimfeld, Margherita Malanchini, Sophie von Stumm, Kathryn Asbury, Robert Plomin. (2024). Exploring the genetic prediction of academic underachievement and overachievement. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00251-9

article_title: Trajectories of performance change indicate multiple dissociable links between working memory and fluid intelligence
citation: Aaron Cochrane and C. Shawn Green. (2021). Trajectories of performance change indicate multiple dissociable links between working memory and fluid intelligence. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00111-w
title: Three-account framework for why aggregated WM performance correlates with fluid intelligence
description: The article frames three candidate explanations for observed links between WM and Gf: (1) Gf shares "processing constraints with WM", predicting stationary correlations; (2) Gf reflects "the ability to learn", predicting correlations with the rate of change; (3) Gf relates to performing novel tasks well "from the very ﬁrst attempt", predicting correlations with initial performance. All three, the authors note, are confounded by aggregation of performance over time.
requirements: Requires time-sensitive modeling of task performance to dissociate the three accounts, since aggregation over trials confounds them
constraints: The possibilities are described as neither exhaustive nor necessarily independent
target_learning_goals: understanding individual differences in cognitive task performance and fluid intelligence
examples: The 87-participant study tested all three accounts by modeling WM trajectories into initial accuracy, rate of change, and final accuracy components
key_sources: Aaron Cochrane and C. Shawn Green. (2021). Trajectories of performance change indicate multiple dissociable links between working memory and fluid intelligence. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00111-w

article_title: Trajectories of performance change indicate multiple dissociable links between working memory and fluid intelligence
citation: Aaron Cochrane and C. Shawn Green. (2021). Trajectories of performance change indicate multiple dissociable links between working memory and fluid intelligence. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00111-w
title: Avoid discarding trials as practice trials; use time-sensitive analyses instead
description: The article recommends that researchers "should avoid discarding trials whenever possible", because removing early trials as practice replaces one stationarity assumption with another unprincipled one and, as the results show, is "actually discarding signal, not noise". Instead, time-sensitive analyses of pilot data can identify timescales of change and what amount of practice would leave participants at reasonably stable performance.
requirements: Time-sensitive (trajectory) modeling of performance, or pilot data analyzed with time-sensitive methods to establish stable-performance timescales
constraints: Where practice-trial removal is still implemented, the article notes it is unclear how many trials should be removed to ensure the remaining sample is stationary
target_learning_goals: accurate measurement of cognitive constructs in experimental and individual-differences research
examples: The study modeled all 68 spatial-span trials fully disaggregated (every mouse click a data line) rather than dropping early trials
key_sources: Aaron Cochrane and C. Shawn Green. (2021). Trajectories of performance change indicate multiple dissociable links between working memory and fluid intelligence. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00111-w

article_title: Trajectories of performance change indicate multiple dissociable links between working memory and fluid intelligence
citation: Aaron Cochrane and C. Shawn Green. (2021). Trajectories of performance change indicate multiple dissociable links between working memory and fluid intelligence. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00111-w
title: Nonlinear mixed-effects Bayesian regression model of WM trajectory components
description: A fully disaggregated nonlinear Bayesian mixed-effects model, implemented in the R package brms, estimating each participant's initial accuracy, rate of change (a time constant), and asymptotic accuracy as a continuous function of trial number, with an exponential change curve bounded via logistic-regression link functions. Fixed effects of task order and feedback were included and found not reliable on their own. The authors state it "prevents the conﬂation of components of learning inherent in many other forms of learning estimates".
requirements: Estimation via brms with 4 chains, 5,000 iterations per chain, first 3,000 discarded as warm-up; Bernoulli family; data fully disaggregated per mouse click
constraints: Rate parameters included an additive offset of 2 on a binary log scale to avoid impossibly small time constants, assisting model convergence
target_learning_goals: quantifying individual differences in within-task learning dynamics
examples: Applied to 68 trials of a digitized forward spatial span task, with set size mean-centered at 6.5
key_sources: Aaron Cochrane and C. Shawn Green. (2021). Trajectories of performance change indicate multiple dissociable links between working memory and fluid intelligence. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00111-w

article_title: Nudging parents and teachers to improve learning and reduce child labor in Cote d’Ivoire
citation: Sharon Wolf and Guilherme Lichand. (2023). Nudging parents and teachers to improve learning and reduce child labor in Cote d'Ivoire. npj Science of Learning 8:37. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00180-z
title: Eduq+ message-based nudge program
description: Eduq+ is a low-cost message-based nudge intervention implemented by Movva with the Ivorian Ministry of Education, sending "two SMS-messages per week in simpli ﬁed French" to parents and/or teachers of primary students. Each two-week core module follows a behavioral-economics-based sequence: "a motivating fact (message 1), a suggested activity (message 2), an interactive message (message 3), and a growth message (message 4)". Parent messages addressed social-emotional development and educational engagement; teacher messages included pedagogical tips and motivational support. Costs were 796 USD per school or 6.68 USD per student.
requirements: requires a message-delivery platform and mobile access for parents or teachers; enrollment of schools and parents
constraints: tested only in two regions of Cote d'Ivoire in cocoa-growing communities; text in simplified French and audio in local language for parents, text only for teachers
target_learners: second and fourth grade students in rural cocoa-growing communities, via their parents and teachers
target_learning_goals: literacy and numeracy outcomes, parental engagement, teacher motivation, and reduced child labor
examples: Parent messages included activities like making a list with the child of things they like and dislike in school; teacher messages suggested small group activities within large class sizes and discouraged corporal punishment
key_sources: Sharon Wolf and Guilherme Lichand. (2023). Nudging parents and teachers to improve learning and reduce child labor in Cote d'Ivoire. npj Science of Learning 8:37. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00180-z

article_title: Physical embodiment and anthropomorphism of AI tutors and their role in student enjoyment and performance
citation: Ackermann, H., Henke, A., Chevalère, J., Yun, H. S., Hafner, V. V., Pinkwart, N., & Lazarides, R. (2025). Physical embodiment and anthropomorphism of AI tutors and their role in student enjoyment and performance. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00293-z
title: HRIES: Human-Robot Interaction Evaluation Scale with four anthropomorphism subdimensions
description: The HRIES is a questionnaire assessing the anthropomorphism of a robot using a multicomponent approach based on dehumanization theory and psychosocial theory. As the article states, "It measures the anthropomorphism of a robot using four dimensions: perceived sociability, animacy, agency, and disturbance." Each dimension is a four-item subscale (e.g., sociability: warmth, trustworthy, likable, friendly; disturbance: scary, creepy, uncanny, weird), and the study used it in post-test questionnaires in which students rated the tutor agent. The article reports it has repeatedly shown good psychometric reliability and structural validity.
requirements: Students complete post-test self-report ratings of the robotic agents after interaction, evaluating each agent separately with pictures presented in randomized order
target_learning_goals: perception and evaluation of robotic tutor agents during AI-supported learning
examples: In this study the HRIES was administered after a 60-minute learning session with the emotionally-adaptive ITS Betty's Brain, yielding the sociability, animacy, agency, and disturbance scores used in four separate path models
key_sources: Ackermann, H., Henke, A., Chevalère, J., Yun, H. S., Hafner, V. V., Pinkwart, N., & Lazarides, R. (2025). Physical embodiment and anthropomorphism of AI tutors and their role in student enjoyment and performance. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00293-z

article_title: Physical embodiment and anthropomorphism of AI tutors and their role in student enjoyment and performance
citation: Ackermann, H., Henke, A., Chevalère, J., Yun, H. S., Hafner, V. V., Pinkwart, N., & Lazarides, R. (2025). Physical embodiment and anthropomorphism of AI tutors and their role in student enjoyment and performance. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00293-z
title: Evaluate anthropomorphism of pedagogical agents by subdimension and balance human-like traits against potential negative perceptions
description: The article recommends that designers of robotic tutors not treat anthropomorphism as uniformly beneficial. As the authors put it, "our results suggest that high anthropomorphism– negative as well as positive human-like traits– might not always be beneﬁcial for learning and should be evaluated with respect to different subdimensions." Perceived sociability was linked to lower task performance and perceived disturbance to lower enjoyment, so designs should balance human-like traits with mitigating negative perceptions, considering learners' individual prerequisites such as language proficiency.
requirements: Assessment instruments that distinguish subdimensions of anthropomorphism (e.g., sociability, animacy, agency, disturbance) rather than a single anthropomorphism score
constraints: Findings are based on a specific sample and experimental setup with 56 students and a 1-hour interaction; the authors call for validation with diverse participant groups and longer interactions
target_learners: school-aged students learning with AI-based tutoring systems and social robots
target_learning_goals: maintaining on-task enjoyment and task performance when learning with robotic tutor agents
examples: The study measured sociability, animacy, agency, and disturbance separately with the HRIES and found only sociability (negatively predicting performance) and disturbance (negatively predicting novelty-phase enjoyment) significant
key_sources: Ackermann, H., Henke, A., Chevalère, J., Yun, H. S., Hafner, V. V., Pinkwart, N., & Lazarides, R. (2025). Physical embodiment and anthropomorphism of AI tutors and their role in student enjoyment and performance. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00293-z

article_title: What we learned from creating one of the world’s most popular MOOCs
citation: Barbara A. Oakley and Terrence J. Sejnowski. (2019). What we learned from creating one of the world's most popular MOOCs. npj Science of Learning 4:7. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0046-0
title: Mayer's principles of multimedia learning as a foundation for effective instructional video
description: Mayer's framework comprises some 30 principles describing how to convey ideas while respecting the limits of working memory, defined as learning "from both pictures and words". The article reproduces the video-relevant subset in Table 1, including multimedia, coherence, signaling, spatial and temporal contiguity, pre-training, segmenting, modality, personalization, voice, embodiment, animation, and the image principle. The authors treat these principles as the theoretical basis explaining LHTL's video design choices and its popularity.
requirements: Application to video requires attending to working-memory limitations when combining words and pictures
constraints: The principles are presented as "technologically agnostic," applying regardless of the technology used to convey information
target_learners: online learners in MOOCs, predominantly 25-34-year-old working adults
target_learning_goals: effective conveyance of learning concepts through video while managing cognitive load
examples: LHTL's videos were designed to satisfy the signaling, segmenting, coherence, personalization, voice, and embodiment principles via green-screen integration, pre-planned scripts, and motion
key_sources: Barbara A. Oakley and Terrence J. Sejnowski. (2019). What we learned from creating one of the world's most popular MOOCs. npj Science of Learning 4:7. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0046-0

article_title: What we learned from creating one of the world’s most popular MOOCs
citation: Barbara A. Oakley and Terrence J. Sejnowski. (2019). What we learned from creating one of the world's most popular MOOCs. npj Science of Learning 4:7. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0046-0
title: Green-screen instructor integration into on-screen visuals for MOOC video production
description: A video production pattern in which the instructor is filmed against green screen and seamlessly inserted into the slides or animations being taught, allowing the instructor to point at and interact with the visuals. The authors report that this "instructor inserted into an animation" approach takes advantage of every one of Mayer's principles (save the animation and image principles), avoiding split attention between a boxed talking head and on-screen imagery while enabling signaling, coherence, segmenting, and embodied presence.
requirements: Green screen filming and editing software to make the green background transparent and replace it with instructional imagery
Careful pre-planning of both visuals and script
constraints: The approach was simple and low cost, although time consuming; the bulk of filming was done in a home basement and raw footage edited by one co-instructor
target_learners: MOOC learners across 200 countries, core age 25-34
target_learning_goals: integrating instructor signaling and presence with visual explanations to reduce cognitive load
examples: In LHTL, the instructor points to the portion of an illustration as it is described, with the background replaced by a PowerPoint slide with animation
key_sources: Barbara A. Oakley and Terrence J. Sejnowski. (2019). What we learned from creating one of the world's most popular MOOCs. npj Science of Learning 4:7. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0046-0

article_title: The inherence bias in preschoolers’ explanations for achievement differences: replication and extension
citation: Renoux, M., Goudeau, S., Alexopoulos, T., Bouquet, C. A. & Cimpian, A. (2024). The inherence bias in preschoolers' explanations for achievement differences: replication and extension. npj Science of Learning 9:10. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00218-w
title: The inherence bias: a cognitive account of why explanations overweight inherent factors and underweight extrinsic ones
description: The inherence bias is the tendency to explain observations by appealing to factors inherent to the entities involved (e.g., intelligence, personality) rather than extrinsic contextual factors. The article presents it as "a general version of the so-called correspondence bias" and links it to psychological essentialism. It arises from attentional spotlight effects, memory accessibility differences, and working-memory limitations, with cultural context amplifying or attenuating these factors. The studies here test its operation in preschoolers' explanations of achievement differences.
requirements: Explanations must be elicited about observations with both inherent and extrinsic candidate causes available
constraints: The article states the degree of deviation from a perfectly rational thinker "will vary from case to case depending on the reasoner, the context, and the observation being explained"; it is not an inescapable deterministic pattern
target_learning_goals: children's explanations and perceptions of academic achievement differences among peers
examples: Study 1 vignettes about a peer called on more often or talking longer in class discussions; Study 2 scenarios in which the child does better or worse than a peer on a math exercise
key_sources: Renoux, M., Goudeau, S., Alexopoulos, T., Bouquet, C. A. & Cimpian, A. (2024). The inherence bias in preschoolers' explanations for achievement differences: replication and extension. npj Science of Learning 9:10. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00218-w

article_title: Trends in testing effect research: from lab to classroom, but not yet for all learners
citation: Wilschut, T., Sense, F. & van Rijn, H. (2026). Trends in testing effect research: from lab to classroom, but not yet for all learners. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00400-2
title: Design retrieval practice environments inclusively by reducing decoding and orthographic demands, e.g., spoken prompts, verbal responses, and auditory feedback
description: The article recommends adapting computerized retrieval practice applications to the needs of learners with SLDs. It states that "adjustments—such as providing spoken prompts, accepting verbal responses, or integrating audi-313 tory feedback—can help reduce demands from decoding and orthographic processing and better314 support neurodiverse learners." Further suggested customizations include balancing verbs and nouns in study sets, pacing/pausing options, scaffolding, and adapting repetition schedules, with systematic analysis of each feature's effects on learners' motivational, affective, cognitive, and perceptual needs.
requirements: Learning environments whose input format, difficulty, and pacing can be adjusted to individual learners' needs
constraints: The article presents these as design recommendations grounded in limited evidence; the underlying empirical base for SLD learners is very small
target_learners: Learners with specific learning disabilities, including dyslexia and DLD
Neurodiverse learners in educational and digital learning contexts
target_learning_goals: Long-term retention of learned material via retrieval practice
Accessible and effective word learning
examples: Wilschut et al.'s adaptive retrieval practice paradigm compared typing-based and speech-based response modes in dyslexic and typically developing learners
Balancing the proportion of verbs and nouns in a study set to manage task difficulty for learners with DLD
key_sources: Wilschut, T., Sense, F. & van Rijn, H. (2026). Trends in testing effect research: from lab to classroom, but not yet for all learners. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00400-2

article_title: Children’s neurodevelopment of reading is affected by China’s language input system in the information era
citation: Zhou, W., Kwok, V. P. Y., Su, M., Luo, J., & Tan, L. H. (2020). Children's neurodevelopment of reading is affected by China's language input system in the information era. npj Science of Learning, 5:3. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-0062-0
title: Restrict pinyin input use and promote orthography-based input methods including handwriting to preserve visuo-orthographic encoding of Chinese characters
description: The authors recommend that, to protect intermediate Chinese readers' character learning, frequent use of the pronunciation-based pinyin input method should be limited and orthography-based input such as handwriting should be encouraged. They write: "To preserve visuo-orthographic encoding of Chinese characters, we would recommend to restrict the use of pinyin input, and promote orthography-based input methods including handwriting." The recommendation rests on the study's associations between pinyin typing and weaker reading-network activation, connectivity, gray matter, and character reading fluency.
requirements: Learners must be intermediate Chinese readers (around ages 9-11) who have moved past initial pinyin-supported decoding, since the authors hold that beginning readers rely on pinyin to bridge spoken and written language.
constraints: The supporting evidence is cross-sectional, showing associations between pinyin typing frequency and brain/behavioral measures rather than experimentally established causal effects.
target_learners: Chinese elementary school children in grades 4-6 (intermediate readers, ages 9-11)
target_learning_goals: Chinese character recognition and reading fluency
visuo-orthographic analysis of Chinese characters
examples: The study grouped 45 children by daily pinyin typing time (more or less than 15 min per day) and found more frequent typists showed weaker cortical activations, weaker functional connections, less gray matter in the left middle frontal region, and lower character reading fluency.
key_sources: Zhou, W., Kwok, V. P. Y., Su, M., Luo, J., & Tan, L. H. (2020). Children's neurodevelopment of reading is affected by China's language input system in the information era. npj Science of Learning, 5:3. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-0062-0

article_title: M1 recruitment during interleaved practice is important for encoding, not just consolidation, of skill memory
citation: Taewon Kim, Hakjoo Kim, Benjamin A. Philip & David L. Wright. (2024). M1 recruitment during interleaved practice is important for encoding, not just consolidation, of skill memory. npj Science of Learning 9, 77. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00290-2
title: M1 plays a broad role in motor skill memory, supporting encoding during interleaved practice as well as offline consolidation
description: The article proposes that primary motor cortex contributes to "multiple mechanisms inﬂuencing both online and ofﬂine behavioral outcomes" in motor skill learning. Traditionally, M1's role in interleaved practice was ascribed to offline consolidation; this study shows inhibiting M1 during interleaved practice instead impedes "the construction of a novel motor memory yet preserves effective consolidation". The account holds that M1 and dorsal premotor cortex are both important for developing motor sequence representations across training, even though M1 may not itself store the post-learning representations.
requirements: Interleaved practice with frequent switching between to-be-learned skills during training, so that M1 is engaged during encoding of sequence knowledge
constraints: The article notes tDCS montage might have inadvertently affected PMd or SMA, so the disruption could reflect inhibiting PMd or SMA–M1 connectivity rather than an independent effect at M1
The inhibitory effects of ctDCS on M1 might diminish over time as the motor system adapts by recruiting non-M1 sensorimotor areas such as PMd
target_learners: Adults learning novel motor sequences (right-handed undergraduate students in the study)
target_learning_goals: Retention and encoding of novel motor skill memory
examples: Fifty-four participants practiced three 6-item discrete sequence production tasks in RP-Sham, IP-Sham, or IP-ctDCS groups, with retention tests at 5 min, 6 h, and 24 h
key_sources: Taewon Kim, Hakjoo Kim, Benjamin A. Philip & David L. Wright. (2024). M1 recruitment during interleaved practice is important for encoding, not just consolidation, of skill memory. npj Science of Learning 9, 77. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00290-2

article_title: Evaluating large language models for criterion-based grading from agreement to consistency
citation: Da-Wei Zhang, Melissa Boey, Yan Yu Tan & Alexis Hoh Sheng Jia. (2024). Evaluating large language models for criterion-based grading from agreement to consistency. npj Science of Learning 9:79. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00291-1
title: Use LLM criterion-based grading to track learning growth against criteria rather than relying on one-time absolute grades
description: Because LLM grading showed good interrater consistency with benchmarks but significantly lower absolute grades than examiners, the authors recommend that "responsible use should focus not on one-time grades but on tracking learning growth against desired criteria". This uses criterion-based grading as meaningful educational feedback for learning, exploiting LLMs' reliable adherence to grading standards while avoiding their biased absolute score levels.
requirements: Detailed knowledge of criteria (e.g., band descriptors) must be provided to the LLM in the prompt
The LLM must demonstrate reliable interrater and intrarater consistency with the chosen criteria
constraints: Absolute grades from LLMs such as ChatGPT and Claude were significantly lower than official examiner grades, so one-time LLM grades should not be trusted
target_learners: Learners receiving writing feedback, e.g., IELTS / English-language learners
target_learning_goals: Criterion-based writing assessment and feedback identifying gaps between current performance and desired outcomes
examples: In the study, ChatGPT 3.5 with detailed band descriptors achieved good interrater consistency (ICC = 0.77) with official IELTS grades while grading significantly lower than examiners (d = 0.71)
key_sources: Da-Wei Zhang, Melissa Boey, Yan Yu Tan & Alexis Hoh Sheng Jia. (2024). Evaluating large language models for criterion-based grading from agreement to consistency. npj Science of Learning 9:79. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00291-1

article_title: Structured human-LLM interaction design reveals exploration and exploitation dynamics in higher education content generation
citation: Pablo Flores Romero, Kin Nok Nicholas Fung, Guang Rong & Benjamin Ultan Cowley. (2025). Structured human-LLM interaction design reveals exploration and exploitation dynamics in higher education content generation. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00332-3
title: Structured prompt-template and keyword-card interaction design for human-LLM co-creation
description: A novel interaction protocol for studying human-LLM foraging: six editable prompt templates divided into Exploration and Exploitation types, plus a shared pool of keyword cards contributed by course participants and categorized into concepts such as 'Actors', 'AI tools', 'Environments', and 'Subjects'. The templates "facilitated the exploration-exploitationbehavioral modes of IFT, standardized the interaction between participants, guided those without prior experience, and enabled systematic analysis of their foraging behavior". Participants crafted prompts by combining templates with guide or GPT-sourced keywords in 45-minute facilitated ChatGPT sessions.
requirements: Prompt templates and keyword cards derived from participants' reported interests gathered before the course
A researcher-mediated 45-minute session protocol with setup, introduction, execution, and conclusion phases
constraints: The structured design intentionally limits free-form prompting, so results do not reflect typical ChatGPT use
The specific task complicates comparisons with previous web search studies that formally assess IFT principles
target_learners: Doctoral-level educational scientists in an AI in Education course
target_learning_goals: Pedagogical content creation and study-design scenario development with generative AI
examples: In the study, exploration prompts opened new ChatGPT conversations to remove context carryover, while exploitation prompts elaborated an already generated scenario with one or two keywords
key_sources: Pablo Flores Romero, Kin Nok Nicholas Fung, Guang Rong & Benjamin Ultan Cowley. (2025). Structured human-LLM interaction design reveals exploration and exploitation dynamics in higher education content generation. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00332-3

article_title: Multiple timescales of learning indicated by changes in evidence-accumulation processes during perceptual decision-making
citation: Cochrane, A., Sims, C. R., Bejjanki, V. R., Green, C. S., & Bavelier, D. (2023). Multiple timescales of learning indicated by changes in evidence-accumulation processes during perceptual decision-making. npj Science of Learning 8:19. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00168-9
title: Two-process account of perceptual learning: gradual perceptual sensitivity change versus fast, variable decision-criterion modulation
description: The article proposes that perceptual learning reflects two processes with different dynamics: drift rate indexes a continuous, gradual tuning of perceptual sensitivity accumulating with training, while response boundary indexes a faster, more variable process describing the threshold of evidence needed to act, associated in the authors' account with inhibitory processes. They write that "the speed at which inhibitory processes can be upregulated or downregulated may be much faster than the speed at which perceptual processes are modifiable". This account unifies continuous improvement with between-day discontinuities, each occurring at its own timescale.
requirements: Joint modeling of RT and accuracy with an evidence-accumulation model, since process-level decomposition is needed to see the two timescales
constraints: The source of large across-day and across-participant RB heterogeneity remains poorly understood per the authors; bias and non-decision time were held constant, so the account covers only DR and RB dynamics
target_learners: young adult learners in perceptual discrimination tasks
target_learning_goals: perceptual sensitivity improvement in visual motion direction discrimination
examples: Four days of dot-motion training in which drift rate followed a cumulative-trial exponential while response boundary reset and varied idiosyncratically between days
key_sources: Cochrane, A., Sims, C. R., Bejjanki, V. R., Green, C. S., & Bavelier, D. (2023). Multiple timescales of learning indicated by changes in evidence-accumulation processes during perceptual decision-making. npj Science of Learning 8:19. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00168-9

article_title: Multiple timescales of learning indicated by changes in evidence-accumulation processes during perceptual decision-making
citation: Cochrane, A., Sims, C. R., Bejjanki, V. R., Green, C. S., & Bavelier, D. (2023). Multiple timescales of learning indicated by changes in evidence-accumulation processes during perceptual decision-making. npj Science of Learning 8:19. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00168-9
title: Model learning with joint RT-and-accuracy diffusion models at the trial level rather than accuracy-only aggregated analyses
description: The article recommends analyzing learning with by-trial evidence-accumulation models fit to the joint distributions of response time and accuracy, rather than aggregating across sessions or relying on accuracy alone. It argues that "using only impoverished discrete-choice behavioral data could prevent or bias possible inferences regarding learning trajectories". The approach provides a clear justification for using the diffusion model's drift rate parameter as an index of perceptual learning as a function of each training trial.
requirements: Access to trial-level RT and accuracy data and Bayesian estimation tools such as brms/Stan; extensive computational resources, as the article notes at least several weeks of computer time per model
constraints: The article notes the models tested represent only a small portion of possible models of change, and interpretability of the response boundary parameter is more complex due to within-day and between-day dynamics
target_learners: adult learners in perceptual and cognitive training contexts
target_learning_goals: accurate inference about learning trajectories and underlying decision processes
examples: Fitting six candidate DDM parameterizations by trial across four days of dot-motion training, with the continuous DR flexible RB model winning the comparison
key_sources: Cochrane, A., Sims, C. R., Bejjanki, V. R., Green, C. S., & Bavelier, D. (2023). Multiple timescales of learning indicated by changes in evidence-accumulation processes during perceptual decision-making. npj Science of Learning 8:19. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00168-9

article_title: Optimized collusion prevention for online exams during social distancing
citation: Mengzhou Li, Lei Luo, Sujoy Sikdar, Navid Ibtehaj Nizam, Shan Gao, Hongming Shan, Melanie Kruger, Uwe Kruger, Hisham Mohamed, Lirong Xia and Ge Wang. (2021). Optimized collusion prevention for online exams during social distancing. npj Science of Learning 6:5. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00083-3
title: Grouping-based anti-collusion scheme (GAS): grouping students by competence, optimizing inter-group question overlap, and augmenting the question pool to control collusion gain below any desired level
description: The GAS is the article's core anti-collusion design for distanced online testing. It consists of three elements the article enumerates: "Grouping: Students with similar competences are grouped together to receive the same sequence of questions in an exam"; Optimization, which aggressively reduces the number of questions that can be copied between groups, even to zero; and Augmentation, enlarging the pool beyond M1 questions. It works because cyclic sequences can reduce maximum question leakage to zero when M2 - M1 + 1 >= C, grouping reduces the equivalent number of students, and similar-competence students gain little from intra-group collusion. Competences can be estimated from GPA, earlier quizzes, or a first portion of the exam via dynamic programming.
requirements: Prior knowledge of students' competences, estimated from GPA, earlier quizzes, or a first portion of the exam
constraints: The analysis is a first-order approximation of an idealized DOT scenario; intra-group collusion is facilitated because group members share the same sequence
target_learners: undergraduate students in math or fact-based courses
target_learning_goals: valid measurement of learning outcomes in remote online exams
examples: The final exam assigned M1 = 40 questions from a pool of M2 = 60 using greedy algorithms with a heuristically constructed colluding matrix P.
key_sources: Mengzhou Li, Lei Luo, Sujoy Sikdar, Navid Ibtehaj Nizam, Shan Gao, Hongming Shan, Melanie Kruger, Uwe Kruger, Hisham Mohamed, Lirong Xia and Ge Wang. (2021). Optimized collusion prevention for online exams during social distancing. npj Science of Learning 6:5. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00083-3

article_title: Optimized collusion prevention for online exams during social distancing
citation: Mengzhou Li, Lei Luo, Sujoy Sikdar, Navid Ibtehaj Nizam, Shan Gao, Hongming Shan, Melanie Kruger, Uwe Kruger, Hisham Mohamed, Lirong Xia and Ge Wang. (2021). Optimized collusion prevention for online exams during social distancing. npj Science of Learning 6:5. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00083-3
title: DOT platform: a web application delivering individualized, synchronized question sequences for distanced online testing, with publicly released source code
description: The DOT platform is a web application the authors developed and applied to a real undergraduate final exam. It "incorporat[es] the anti-collusion techniques as well as other complementary techniques for online exams", presenting each student their own set of M1 questions one by one in predetermined time slots without revisiting previous questions, with a WebEx session available during the exam for instructor support. The source codes and simulation data are publicly available on Github (https://github.com/edward1001001/Anticheating_in_DOT).
requirements: A question pool of M2 questions and estimates of student competences to construct the colluding matrix and optimize assignments
constraints: Mainly designed for math or fact-based courses; illustrated with multiple-choice questions, though compatible with most question types except easy-writing-type tests
target_learners: undergraduate students taking remote online exams
target_learning_goals: valid remote assessment of learning outcomes
examples: Used for the final exam of an undergraduate imaging course on 28 April 2020 with 78 of 85 students participating.
key_sources: Mengzhou Li, Lei Luo, Sujoy Sikdar, Navid Ibtehaj Nizam, Shan Gao, Hongming Shan, Melanie Kruger, Uwe Kruger, Hisham Mohamed, Lirong Xia and Ge Wang. (2021). Optimized collusion prevention for online exams during social distancing. npj Science of Learning 6:5. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00083-3

article_title: Optimized collusion prevention for online exams during social distancing
citation: Mengzhou Li, Lei Luo, Sujoy Sikdar, Navid Ibtehaj Nizam, Shan Gao, Hongming Shan, Melanie Kruger, Uwe Kruger, Hisham Mohamed, Lirong Xia and Ge Wang. (2021). Optimized collusion prevention for online exams during social distancing. npj Science of Learning 6:5. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00083-3
title: Use optimized individualized question sequences so that a question pool of only about 1.5 times the test length suffices to suppress collusion gain, instead of maintaining huge question pools
description: The article argues that conventional randomization from large pools requires impractically large banks (e.g. a 300-question pool for 30-question tests), whereas with its optimization method "a pool of size 1.5 times the number of questions in a test is found to be sufficient to suppress collusion gain to an insignificant level". The substantially smaller required pool lets educators devise intellectually demanding questions and update them frequently rather than relying on published question banks, encouraging better compliance with best practices.
requirements: Optimization of question-sequence assignments using the DOT framework with competence information
constraints: Targets collusion specifically; other misconduct such as accessing unauthorized sources or contract cheating requires complementary techniques
target_learners: students in online or distanced courses
target_learning_goals: academic integrity in remote assessment
examples: The DOT final exam used a pool of 60 questions for 40-question tests, and only 19 questions were assigned to all students.
key_sources: Mengzhou Li, Lei Luo, Sujoy Sikdar, Navid Ibtehaj Nizam, Shan Gao, Hongming Shan, Melanie Kruger, Uwe Kruger, Hisham Mohamed, Lirong Xia and Ge Wang. (2021).
