article_title: Prior math achievement and inventive production predict learning from productive failure
citation: Manu Kapur, Janan Saba and Ido Roll. (2023). Prior math achievement and inventive production predict learning from productive failure. npj Science of Learning 8:15. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00165-y
title: Productive Failure: problem-solving before instruction as a subset of PS-I designs
description: Productive Failure is an instructional sequence in which "students generate representations and solutions to a novel problem that targets a concept they have not learned yet prior to receiving instruction on the same topic." It comprises a generation and exploration phase, where students in groups generate multiple Representations and Solution Methods (RSMs) without scaffolds, followed by a consolidation and knowledge assembly phase in which the teacher compares student-generated RSMs with canonical solutions. PF is "a subset of the PS-I design" and is "intentionally designed to result in failure in problem-solving" so that failure prepares students to learn the target concepts.
requirements: A generation and exploration phase in which students generate multiple RSMs in groups before instruction
A consolidation phase where the teacher contrasts student-generated RSMs with canonical solutions
constraints: Most student-generated solutions are not complete in mathematical validity, efficiency, or generalizability; failure is expected by design
target_learning_goals: Deep conceptual understanding of challenging math concepts such as average speed and standard deviation
examples: In both studies, students worked in triads on a complex problem for two periods with no scaffolds, then received whole-class consolidation instruction and practiced isomorphic problems.
key_sources: Manu Kapur, Janan Saba and Ido Roll. (2023). Prior math achievement and inventive production predict learning from productive failure. npj Science of Learning 8:15. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00165-y

article_title: Prior math achievement and inventive production predict learning from productive failure
citation: Manu Kapur, Janan Saba and Ido Roll. (2023). Prior math achievement and inventive production predict learning from productive failure. npj Science of Learning 8:15. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00165-y
title: Facilitate learning environments that give space to inventive production, since generating more solution methods promotes learning regardless of prior achievement
description: The article's pedagogical recommendation is to design PF environments that "emphasize and give more space to inventive production to encourage students to activate their prior knowledge and create more RSMs for the problems." Because the number of generated RSMs was the strongest measured predictor of learning in both topics, while prior achievement mattered little, the authors argue this emphasis "may significantly contribute to promoting math learning" for students of diverse backgrounds.
requirements: A problem-solving phase before instruction in which students can generate multiple representations and solution methods, individually or in groups
constraints: Evidence comes from two Singapore math topics (average speed, standard deviation) in schools at the high and medium end of the achievement spectrum; the authors do not claim the findings hold more generally
target_learners: Secondary mathematics students across achievement levels
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding and transfer of challenging mathematical concepts
examples: In the studies, groups designed solutions to a complex problem over two periods with no scaffolds or homework, then the teacher consolidated student-generated RSMs against canonical solutions.
key_sources: Manu Kapur, Janan Saba and Ido Roll. (2023). Prior math achievement and inventive production predict learning from productive failure. npj Science of Learning 8:15. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00165-y

article_title: Exams at classroom have bidirectional effects on the long-term memory of an unrelated graphical task
citation: P. Lopes da Cunha, D. Ramirez Butavand, L. B. Chisari, F. Ballarini and H. Viola (2018). Exams at classroom have bidirectional effects on the long-term memory of an unrelated graphical task. npj Science of Learning 3:19. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0036-7
title: Schedule exams attentively relative to other teaching, since exams modulate retention of temporally adjacent content
description: The authors recommend that educators consider when exams fall within the school day, because an exam can improve or impair retention of unrelated content learned up to about one hour before or after it. As they conclude, "educators should be attentive to their student's exams' schedule, as this will modulate the retention of the contents of previous or later teaching." The recommendation follows directly from the bidirectional timing effects observed.
requirements: Knowledge of when exams and other learning activities occur within the same school day
constraints: Effects were observed for exams occurring within about one hour before or after the unrelated learning; exams 4 h before or after showed no effect
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of curricular content learned in the classroom
examples: Students who took an exam 1 h after copying a figure showed improved 24-h retention if their retention was weak, and impaired retention if it was strong
key_sources: P. Lopes da Cunha, D. Ramirez Butavand, L. B. Chisari, F. Ballarini and H. Viola (2018). Exams at classroom have bidirectional effects on the long-term memory of an unrelated graphical task. npj Science of Learning 3:19. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0036-7

article_title: Exams at classroom have bidirectional effects on the long-term memory of an unrelated graphical task
citation: P. Lopes da Cunha, D. Ramirez Butavand, L. B. Chisari, F. Ballarini and H. Viola (2018). Exams at classroom have bidirectional effects on the long-term memory of an unrelated graphical task. npj Science of Learning 3:19. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0036-7
title: Behavioral tagging / synaptic tagging and capture account for the temporal-window interaction between exams and unrelated learning
description: The authors invoke the hypothesis of synaptic tagging and capture and its behavioral counterpart, behavioral tagging, to explain why exam effects on unrelated graphical memory occur only within a temporal window of up to about one hour around learning. As they write, "One cellular mechanism proposed to explain this late associative effect among stimuli or events is provided by the hypothesis of synaptic tagging and capture and its behavioral counterpart, the behavioral tagging." Weak or strong memory traces are presumed to interact with exam-induced arousal within this window.
requirements: Temporal proximity (within about one hour) between the arousing event and the learning event for the two processes to interact
constraints: Proposed as a possible explanation; the study did not test cellular mechanisms directly
target_learning_goals: long-term memory formation of classroom content
examples: Exams 4 h before or after copying did not affect retention, consistent with a limited temporal interaction window
key_sources: P. Lopes da Cunha, D. Ramirez Butavand, L. B. Chisari, F. Ballarini and H. Viola (2018). Exams at classroom have bidirectional effects on the long-term memory of an unrelated graphical task. npj Science of Learning 3:19. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0036-7

article_title: “You did incredibly well!”: teachers’ inflated praise can make children from low-SES backgrounds seem less smart (but more hardworking)
citation: Schoneveld, E., & Brummelman, E. (2023). "You did incredibly well!": teachers' inflated praise can make children from low-SES backgrounds seem less smart (but more hardworking). npj Science of Learning, 8:31. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00183-w
title: Attribution-theory account of inflated praise as an inequality-reinforcing mechanism
description: The article builds on attribution theory, in which attributions reflect locus, stability, and controllability, and ability and effort are compensatory internal causes of success. It theorizes that teachers, influenced by negative stereotypes about low-SES children's abilities, attribute low-SES students' successes to "hard work" and thus give them more inflated praise, which children in turn interpret as a sign of low ability. The article identifies "effort attributions as a possible mechanism" linking teacher bias to inequality-reinforcing feedback.
requirements: Teachers must perceive a student's success as particularly praiseworthy due to presumed high effort for inflated praise to be dispensed
constraints: The mechanism was tested with hypothetical vignettes rather than real teacher-student interactions
Effects were probably larger than they would be in real life, per the authors
target_learning_goals: Academic ability perceptions and motivation in classroom feedback contexts
examples: Study 1 measured teachers' open-ended attributions of student success after vignettes; Study 2 measured children's smartness and effort inferences after praise vignettes
key_sources: Schoneveld, E., & Brummelman, E. (2023). "You did incredibly well!": teachers' inflated praise can make children from low-SES backgrounds seem less smart (but more hardworking). npj Science of Learning, 8:31. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00183-w

article_title: Explaining forgetting at different timescales requires a time-variant forgetting function
citation: Maarten van der Velde, Florian Sense, Jelmer P. Borst & Hedderik van Rijn. (2026). Explaining forgetting at different timescales requires a time-variant forgetting function. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00447-1
title: Time-variant forgetting parameters within ACT-R as an explanatory framework for retention across timescales
description: The article proposes letting ACT-R declarative-memory parameters vary with the between-session interval instead of assuming one fixed forgetting function. Three candidate mechanisms are offered: a retrieval threshold (τ) governing the minimum activation needed for retrieval, a decay rate (d) quantifying how quickly traces weaken, and a scaling factor (h) capturing contextual interference by shrinking between-session time. The authors note that "the same observations of response accuracy on a retrieval task can be explained through any one of these three mechanisms," and that a declining threshold suggests increasing retrieval effort, time-variant decay fits consolidation accounts, and decreasing h reflects declining interference.
requirements: A behavioural measure of response accuracy on retrieval trials across a wide range of between-session intervals to fit the parameters per interval bin
constraints: Response accuracy alone cannot identify which of the three parameters drives the fit; including response time would be needed to separate activation-related parameters (d and h) from the threshold (τ)
ACT-R makes no explicit predictions about whether or how each parameter should vary across timescales
target_learners: undergraduate students using adaptive fact-learning systems
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of factual course material through retrieval practice
examples: Fitting threshold, decay, and scaling parameters separately to logarithmically spaced interval bins of naturalistic fact-learning data
key_sources: Maarten van der Velde, Florian Sense, Jelmer P. Borst & Hedderik van Rijn. (2026). Explaining forgetting at different timescales requires a time-variant forgetting function. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00447-1

article_title: Explaining forgetting at different timescales requires a time-variant forgetting function
citation: Maarten van der Velde, Florian Sense, Jelmer P. Borst & Hedderik van Rijn. (2026). Explaining forgetting at different timescales requires a time-variant forgetting function. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00447-1
title: Naturalistic fact-learning dataset from an adaptive learning system (25,843 sequences, 218 learners)
description: A naturalistic dataset collected through an adaptive fact-learning system used in an undergraduate cognitive psychology course, in which learners self-initiated retrieval-practice sessions on glossary terms. The analysed subset "contained a total of 171,219 trials, making up 25,843 learning sequences from 218 learners," with between-session intervals varying naturally from seconds to multiple weeks (median about 20 hours). Data and analysis code are available on OSF at https://doi.org/10.17605/osf.io/mzd6s.
requirements: Written informed consent from participants; ethical approval by the Ethical Committee Psychology at the University of Groningen (ID: 18072-O)
constraints: Only the first trial of each second session was predicted; subsequent repetitions were discarded, and 3,650 sequences (14.1%) were excluded from cross-validation evaluation
target_learners: undergraduate students in a cognitive psychology course
target_learning_goals: retention of course-related facts through open-answer retrieval practice
examples: Learning sequences of three or more practice trials in one session followed by at least one trial in the next session, each containing exactly one between-session interval
key_sources: Maarten van der Velde, Florian Sense, Jelmer P. Borst & Hedderik van Rijn. (2026). Explaining forgetting at different timescales requires a time-variant forgetting function. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00447-1

article_title: Explaining forgetting at different timescales requires a time-variant forgetting function
citation: Maarten van der Velde, Florian Sense, Jelmer P. Borst & Hedderik van Rijn. (2026). Explaining forgetting at different timescales requires a time-variant forgetting function. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00447-1
title: Adaptive learning systems need memory models that are accurate both within and between learning sessions to make useful scheduling recommendations
description: The article argues that adaptive scheduling of practice should rest on a memory model that predicts retention correctly on both short (seconds to minutes) and long (hours to weeks) timescales. A model calibrated within a single session "will already systematically underestimate retention" after an hour or more, "hampering its ability to make useful scheduling recommendations in a subsequent learning session." A time-variant forgetting function is the proposed remedy, enabling a single model to tailor predictions to a wide range of intervals.
requirements: A theoretically grounded model with meaningful parameters (not a purely measurement-oriented model) so counterfactual scheduling scenarios can be simulated
Parameter estimates that remain valid across the interval range encountered in deployment, e.g., via time-variant parameters
constraints: A single fixed parameter value for the interference scaling factor h may work in settings with a limited range of intervals but is suboptimal for more general educational applications
target_learners: learners using adaptive practice systems across K-12 and higher education
target_learning_goals: optimising the timing of retrieval practice within and across sessions to improve retention
examples: Using a within-session-fitted ACT-R model to schedule a second study session would systematically underestimate retention after an hour or more, per the article's analysis of the naturalistic dataset
key_sources: Maarten van der Velde, Florian Sense, Jelmer P. Borst & Hedderik van Rijn. (2026). Explaining forgetting at different timescales requires a time-variant forgetting function. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00447-1

article_title: A visual generalization gradient of conceptual stimuli based on fear acquisition in visual and auditory modalities
citation: Xin Liu, Benjamin Becker, Ya Jie Wang, Ying Mei, Haoran Dou & Yi Lei. (2025). A visual generalization gradient of conceptual stimuli based on fear acquisition in visual and auditory modalities. npj Science of Learning 10:37. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00318-1
title: Hierarchical network model of conceptual fear generalization
description: The article invokes the hierarchical network model to explain why conceptually similar stimuli elicit stronger generalized fear. Concepts are "stored as nodes within a network, with connections to other related concepts (e.g., orioles, ﬁsh) varying by similarity and relevance". During concept processing a distance effect emerges: greater conceptual distance makes categorization and generalization harder, so stimuli with higher conceptual similarity are perceived as analogous threat sources and elicit stronger fear responses. The authors state their gradient findings support this framework for crossmodal fear generalization.
requirements: Stimuli must share conceptual (not merely perceptual) similarity with the conditioned stimulus for the network-distance account to apply
constraints: The article presents the model as an interpretive framework supported by its gradient findings, not as a directly tested mechanism; fNIRS could not distinguish prelimbic and infralimbic mPFC functions
target_learners: adult learners in laboratory fear-conditioning studies
individuals with anxiety-related disorders (as discussed by the authors)
target_learning_goals: understanding how learned threat responses generalize across conceptually related stimuli
examples: The study's GSs were drawn from conceptual categories related to the sparrow CS+ (e.g., Pigeon as GS1, Duck as GS2, Goat as GS3), with fear responses weakening as conceptual distance increased
key_sources: Xin Liu, Benjamin Becker, Ya Jie Wang, Ying Mei, Haoran Dou & Yi Lei. (2025). A visual generalization gradient of conceptual stimuli based on fear acquisition in visual and auditory modalities. npj Science of Learning 10:37. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00318-1

article_title: Double training promotes retinotopic transfer of category learning
citation: Zhu, J.-P., Xie, X.-Y., Yu, C. & Zhang, J.-Y. (2026). Double training promotes retinotopic transfer of category learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00396-1
title: COVIS dual-systems framework and its continuum refinement for category learning
description: The article describes the Competition between Verbal and Implicit Systems (COVIS) framework, which "posits two partially distinct systems: an explicit, prefrontal-dependent rule-based (RB) system and an implicit, basal ganglia-dependent information-integration (II) system". RB learning engages verbalizable rules on a single dimension and depends on working memory and executive attention; II learning combines multiple incommensurable dimensions implicitly via striatal-based feedback learning. The article argues recent evidence refines rather than refutes this view, supporting a continuum of partially overlapping explicit and implicit processes.
requirements: Distinguishing rule-based from information-integration category structures, as the framework's predictions concern these two learning types
constraints: The article states the separation between systems is relative rather than absolute, with partially overlapping neural activations
target_learners: Adults learning perceptual categories in laboratory visual tasks
target_learning_goals: Implicit information-integration category learning and explicit rule-based category learning
examples: The study used a four-category II structure defined by spatial frequency and orientation (categories F, D, K, J) with trial-by-trial feedback
key_sources: Zhu, J.-P., Xie, X.-Y., Yu, C. & Zhang, J.-Y. (2026). Double training promotes retinotopic transfer of category learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00396-1

article_title: Double training promotes retinotopic transfer of category learning
citation: Zhu, J.-P., Xie, X.-Y., Yu, C. & Zhang, J.-Y. (2026). Double training promotes retinotopic transfer of category learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00396-1
title: To promote transfer of location-specific learning, expose the transfer context concurrently with or after primary training, not before
description: The article's double-training principle holds that pairing primary training with passive or interleaved exposure to the transfer context enables generalization, but only when that exposure is "concurrently with or after II learning", not before it. In the experiments, an irrelevant contrast discrimination task at the mirror-symmetric location reduced location specificity when interleaved with or following the II category task, but abolished transfer when it preceded category training. The authors extend this to practice design: "varying stimulus presentation and incorporating spaced, multi-context practice can strengthen abstract memory traces, reduce context dependence, and foster flexible knowledge transfer".
requirements: A primary task trained at one location plus an irrelevant task providing exposure at the transfer location, with the transfer-location exposure occurring during or after primary learning
constraints: Transfer was markedly weaker when exposure to the transfer location preceded category learning; all experiments ran within a single 1-1.5-hour session, so the authors caution the similarity to perceptual learning principles should be interpreted cautiously
target_learners: Adult learners in perceptual and category-learning training, including clinical rehabilitation populations
target_learning_goals: Generalization of trained categorization or discrimination skill to untrained locations and contexts
examples: Experiment 2 interleaved eight blocks of contrast discrimination at the transfer location with the II category task; Experiment 4 placed the II task first and the contrast task second; both showed comparable post-test accuracy across locations, whereas Experiment 3's reversed order left a large deficit
key_sources: Zhu, J.-P., Xie, X.-Y., Yu, C. & Zhang, J.-Y. (2026). Double training promotes retinotopic transfer of category learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00396-1

article_title: First-year students’ math anxiety predicts STEM avoidance and underperformance throughout university, independently of math ability
citation: Daker, R.J., Gattas, S.U., Sokolowski, H.M., Green, A.E., & Lyons, I.M. (2021). First-year students' math anxiety predicts STEM avoidance and underperformance throughout university, independently of math ability. npj Science of Learning 6:17. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00095-7
title: Macro-avoidance vs. micro-avoidance framework for math anxiety's academic consequences
description: The authors propose distinguishing two forms of math avoidance: macro-avoidance, the high-level decision to avoid STEM courses, majors, and careers, and micro-avoidance, "small-scale decisions about how much attention to pay in math class, how much effort to exert on math homework, and so on". Because their models controlled for % STEM Courses, macro-avoidance could not explain the grades effect, so they propose micro-avoidance as a candidate mechanism linking math anxiety to STEM achievement independently of math ability. The framework extends Ashcraft and colleagues' local vs. global avoidance distinction to academic behaviors like paying less attention in class, skipping class, and studying less.
requirements: Future research must directly measure micro-avoidance behaviors in real educational contexts to test the hypothesis
constraints: The micro-avoidance mechanism is a hypothesis the present data cannot directly confirm; the article states its data cannot fully rule out the in-the-moment working-memory account either
target_learning_goals: STEM participation
STEM achievement
examples: The study showed math anxiety predicted STEM Grades even with % STEM Courses as a covariate, ruling out macro-avoidance as the explanation for the grades effect
key_sources: Daker, R.J., Gattas, S.U., Sokolowski, H.M., Green, A.E., & Lyons, I.M. (2021). First-year students' math anxiety predicts STEM avoidance and underperformance throughout university, independently of math ability. npj Science of Learning 6:17. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00095-7

article_title: First-year students’ math anxiety predicts STEM avoidance and underperformance throughout university, independently of math ability
citation: Daker, R.J., Gattas, S.U., Sokolowski, H.M., Green, A.E., & Lyons, I.M. (2021). First-year students' math anxiety predicts STEM avoidance and underperformance throughout university, independently of math ability. npj Science of Learning 6:17. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00095-7
title: Interventions aiming to boost university STEM outcomes should target math anxiety specifically, not only math ability
description: Because first-semester math anxiety predicted both STEM participation and achievement over four years independently of math ability, and math anxiety accounted for roughly 40% of the math ability–STEM outcome associations, the authors argue that "future interventions developed with the aim of boosting STEM outcomes would do well to focus on math anxiety as a key leverage point". Focusing on math ability alone may fail to optimally boost STEM outcomes.
requirements: Interventions must be developed and tested empirically; the article provides impetus but does not itself test an anxiety intervention
constraints: The evidence is correlational/longitudinal, not an intervention trial; causal efficacy of anxiety-targeted interventions is not established in this article
target_learning_goals: STEM course participation
STEM academic achievement
examples: The study measured math anxiety at university entry and tracked four years of transcript data, showing unique predictive effects over and above math ability
key_sources: Daker, R.J., Gattas, S.U., Sokolowski, H.M., Green, A.E., & Lyons, I.M. (2021). First-year students' math anxiety predicts STEM avoidance and underperformance throughout university, independently of math ability. npj Science of Learning 6:17. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00095-7

article_title: Teaching resources for the European Open Platform for Prescribing Education (EurOP2E)—a nominal group technique study
citation: Bakkum, M. J. et al. (2022). Teaching resources for the European Open Platform for Prescribing Education (EurOP2E)—a nominal group technique study. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00141-y
title: EurOP²E — the European Open Platform for Prescribing Education
description: EurOP²E is a platform that "seeks to improve and harmonize European clinical pharmacology and therapeutics (CPT) education by facilitating international collaboration and sharing problem-based, online, open educational resources." It was set up to address the EACPT Education Working Group's recommendation 6, that schools utilize more online learning resources and share them nationally and internationally. Depending on the theme, its function will vary from supporting international communication and collaboration to providing teach-the-teacher materials and initiating collaborative production of ready-to-use teaching materials.
requirements: Open (free to re-use, adapt, and redistribute) distribution of resources
Teacher participation and collaboration across countries
constraints: Must be dynamic as educators' resource needs change with growing collaboration
Local/national differences in electronic prescribing systems must be accounted for when making such resources available for international use
target_learners: Medical and pharmacy students in European CPT education
target_learning_goals: Safe, effective and responsible prescribing
Clinical pharmacology and therapeutics knowledge, skills and attitudes
examples: Participants proposed and ranked 35 teaching materials across four online meetings to inform what the platform should host
key_sources: Bakkum, M. J. et al. (2022). Teaching resources for the European Open Platform for Prescribing Education (EurOP2E)—a nominal group technique study. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00141-y

article_title: Quantifying two-dimensional and three-dimensional stereoscopic learning in anatomy using electroencephalography
citation: Anderson, S. J., Jamniczky, H. A., Krigolson, O. E., Coderre, S. P. & Hecker, K. G. (2019). Quantifying two-dimensional and three-dimensional stereoscopic learning in anatomy using electroencephalography. npj Science of Learning 4:10. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0050-4
title: ERP components (N250 and reward positivity) as quantitative neural markers of perceptual expertise and feedback-based learning
description: The article builds on a framework in which two event-related potential components track learning in reinforcement-based paradigms. The N250, measured over posterior scalp, "reflects the acquisition of long-term memory for perceptual categorization expertise at the subordinate (more detailed) level", while the reward positivity, measured at FCz, represents prediction error in response to positive feedback, and "the reduction in reward positivity amplitude re ﬂects an underlying learning process". The study applies these markers to anatomy learning to compare 2D, 3D, and interleaved stereoscopic conditions.
requirements: EEG recording during a reinforcement-based learning task with trial-and-error feedback, with enough error trials early in learning for difference-wave confirmation of the reward positivity
constraints: The authors note a possible threshold below which expertise cannot be distinguished by N250 amplitude, and that modules of 300 or fewer trials were too short to observe N250 increases with learning
target_learning_goals: identification and localization of neuroanatomical structures; perceptual expertise in object recognition
examples: Difference-wave analysis confirmed the reward positivity at peak latencies of 284 ms (2D), 296 ms (3D), and 284 ms (2D/3D), all p < 0.001
key_sources: Anderson, S. J., Jamniczky, H. A., Krigolson, O. E., Coderre, S. P. & Hecker, K. G. (2019). Quantifying two-dimensional and three-dimensional stereoscopic learning in anatomy using electroencephalography. npj Science of Learning 4:10. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0050-4

article_title: Quantifying two-dimensional and three-dimensional stereoscopic learning in anatomy using electroencephalography
citation: Anderson, S. J., Jamniczky, H. A., Krigolson, O. E., Coderre, S. P. & Hecker, K. G. (2019). Quantifying two-dimensional and three-dimensional stereoscopic learning in anatomy using electroencephalography. npj Science of Learning 4:10. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0050-4
title: Teach with both 2D and 3D models interleaved rather than 3D models exclusively, to promote generalization between dimensions
description: Based on the neural findings, the authors recommend that stereoscopic 3D models aid visual recognition but should not be used alone: "exclusive use of 3D models should be avoided. Instead, teaching that includes both 2D and 3D models is likely the most advantageous, as it promotes generalization of knowledge by forcing students to practice moving ﬂuidly between dimensions." The interleaved 2D/3D group's decreased reward positivity during retention and transfer supports this recommendation.
requirements: Access to both 2D and stereoscopic 3D representations of the same anatomical content, presented in an interleaved fashion
constraints: The authors caution educators should be conscious of overall cognitive load when designing curricula, since stereopsis adds complexity and real educational settings may add further load
target_learning_goals: spatial understanding of anatomical structures; retention and transfer of anatomical knowledge
examples: Participants in the combined group viewed models randomly as 2D or 3D on a trial-by-trial basis, each 50% of the time, during the first module
key_sources: Anderson, S. J., Jamniczky, H. A., Krigolson, O. E., Coderre, S. P. & Hecker, K. G. (2019). Quantifying two-dimensional and three-dimensional stereoscopic learning in anatomy using electroencephalography. npj Science of Learning 4:10. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0050-4

article_title: Improving online and offline gain from repetitive practice using anodal tDCS at dorsal premotor cortex
citation: Taewon Kim, John J. Buchanan, Jessica A. Bernard and David L. Wright. (2021). Improving online and offline gain from repetitive practice using anodal tDCS at dorsal premotor cortex. npj Science of Learning 6:31. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00109-4
title: Left PMd plays a proprietary role in motor sequence learning and sleep-related consolidation of novel skill memories
description: The article advances and tests the account that left dorsal premotor cortex is specifically (propriately) involved in motor sequence learning and in sleep-related consolidation of novel skill memory. The authors state their data "are consistent with the proposed proprietary role of left PMd for motor sequence learning and the more recent claim that PMd is central to sleep-related consolidation of novel skill memory." The account explains why left- but not right-PMd stimulation during repetitive practice produced overnight offline gains matching interleaved practice.
requirements: Exogenous upregulation (anodal tDCS) targeted at left PMd during practice of novel motor sequences
constraints: Evidence concerns three novel six-element sequences practiced with the left index finger by right-handed young adults; the account is tested only for stimulation delivered during repetitive practice
target_learners: right-handed young adults (19–23 years) learning novel motor sequences
target_learning_goals: acquisition and sleep-related consolidation of novel motor sequence skills
examples: Anodal tDCS at left PMd during 20 min of repetitive practice produced overnight skill memory enhancement congruent with the IP-sham condition, while right-PMd stimulation did not
key_sources: Taewon Kim, John J. Buchanan, Jessica A. Bernard and David L. Wright. (2021). Improving online and offline gain from repetitive practice using anodal tDCS at dorsal premotor cortex. npj Science of Learning 6:31. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00109-4

article_title: Improving online and offline gain from repetitive practice using anodal tDCS at dorsal premotor cortex
citation: Taewon Kim, John J. Buchanan, Jessica A. Bernard and David L. Wright. (2021). Improving online and offline gain from repetitive practice using anodal tDCS at dorsal premotor cortex. npj Science of Learning 6:31. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00109-4
title: Supplement repetitive practice of multiple motor skills with anodal tDCS at left PMd to gain sleep-related offline consolidation otherwise seen only after interleaved practice
description: The article's central design recommendation is that neuromodulation of targets beyond M1 during practice can improve outcomes of a low-retention practice schedule. The authors state that "neuromodulation of targets beyond M1, via application of anodal tDCS during practice, can facilitate not just the acquisition and retention of a single novel motor skill but also multiple skill memories developed simultaneously." Applying anodal tDCS at left PMd throughout repetitive practice produced an overnight offline gain matching interleaved practice.
requirements: 2 mA anodal stimulation via a 25 cm2 anode placed 2.5 cm anterior to M1 (FC3/FC4) with supraorbital reference, applied for the entire 20-min practice period
constraints: The overnight gain emerged only for left-PMd stimulation and only following overnight sleep; no early 6-h consolidation was induced, and blinding was not formally evaluated
target_learners: adult learners practicing novel motor sequences (right-handed undergraduates in the study)
target_learning_goals: retention and sleep-related consolidation of novel motor sequence skills
examples: Participants in the L-PMd condition received 2 mA anodal tDCS throughout 20 min of repetitive practice of three six-key sequences and showed overnight gain congruent with the IP-sham condition
key_sources: Taewon Kim, John J. Buchanan, Jessica A. Bernard and David L. Wright. (2021). Improving online and offline gain from repetitive practice using anodal tDCS at dorsal premotor cortex. npj Science of Learning 6:31. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00109-4

article_title: Brain activity links performance in science reasoning with conceptual approach
citation: Bartley, J. E., Riedel, M. C., Salo, T., Boeving, E. R., Bottenhorn, K. L., Bravo, E. I., Odean, R., Nazareth, A., Laird, R. W., Sutherland, M. T., Pruden, S. M., Brewe, E. & Laird, A. R. (2019). Brain activity links performance in science reasoning with conceptual approach. npj Science of Learning 4:20. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0059-8
title: Resource framework: physics cognition as dual knowledge-structure and control-structure processes along an axis of knowledge compilation
description: The article adopts a resource framework in which physics cognition relies on dual "knowledge structure" and "control structure" processes: students apply executive functions to select or inhibit associational patterns grounding their physical reasoning. Knowledge structures are "flexible, contextually primed collections of linked knowledge elements called 'resources'" activated to scaffold reasoning. Differences among students are described along an axis of compilation or memory chunking: students without precompiled structures must assemble associations during reasoning, whereas experts access well-developed associational patterns. The authors use this framework to interpret their neuroimaging findings, mapping CEN/DAN activity to control structures and DMN involvement to associational mappings in semantic or episodic memory.
requirements: Students must learn to activate stable associations between physical laws to support long deductive chains during problem solving
constraints: The authors acknowledge results may be specific to the FCI questions used, and that additional brain dynamics may be relevant for different kinds of physics problem solving
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of Newtonian mechanics
physics problem-solving proficiency
examples: Groups A and B were interpreted as applying predominantly Newtonian (compiled) thinking, while Group C utilized multiple modules characterized by simple, vague, or confused ideas that differed across problems
key_sources: Bartley, J. E., Riedel, M. C., Salo, T., Boeving, E. R., Bottenhorn, K. L., Bravo, E. I., Odean, R., Nazareth, A., Laird, R. W., Sutherland, M. T., Pruden, S. M., Brewe, E. & Laird, A. R. (2019). Brain activity links performance in science reasoning with conceptual approach. npj Science of Learning 4:20. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0059-8

article_title: Brain activity links performance in science reasoning with conceptual approach
citation: Bartley, J. E., Riedel, M. C., Salo, T., Boeving, E. R., Bottenhorn, K. L., Bravo, E. I., Odean, R., Nazareth, A., Laird, R. W., Sutherland, M. T., Pruden, S. M., Brewe, E. & Laird, A. R. (2019). Brain activity links performance in science reasoning with conceptual approach. npj Science of Learning 4:20. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0059-8
title: Instruction should attend to how students select, link, and reorganize resources, and leverage rather than overwrite incorrect conceptions
description: Based on their neuroimaging findings, the authors recommend that physics instruction explicitly address resource selection and organization rather than focusing on accuracy alone. They state that "instruction that explicitly attends to how students select, link, and reorganize resources may be critical in developing appropriately compiled knowledge to map back onto control processes." They further argue instructors should leverage students' incorrect conceptions to facilitate conceptual change, transitioning existing resources into stable and accessible knowledge structures, because a focus on accuracy alone oversimplifies the complex processes engaged during physics reasoning.
requirements: Instructors must attend to the conceptual foundations of wrong answers, which reveal more about students' ability to succeed than simple accuracy measures
constraints: The authors caution it is a long path between brain imaging and the potential development of lesson plans
target_learning_goals: conceptual change in Newtonian mechanics
developing stable, coherently compiled physics knowledge structures
examples: The study used module analysis of FCI answer distributions to distinguish subgroups of similarly responding students and showed their conceptual approaches manifest as measurable brain differences during reasoning
key_sources: Bartley, J. E., Riedel, M. C., Salo, T., Boeving, E. R., Bottenhorn, K. L., Bravo, E. I., Odean, R., Nazareth, A., Laird, R. W., Sutherland, M. T., Pruden, S. M., Brewe, E. & Laird, A. R. (2019). Brain activity links performance in science reasoning with conceptual approach. npj Science of Learning 4:20. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0059-8

article_title: Children perpetuate competence-based inequality when they help peers
citation: Sierksma, J. (2023). Children perpetuate competence-based inequality when they help peers. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00192-9
title: Empowerment vs. non-empowerment help framework
description: The article distinguishes two types of peer help: empowerment help, operationalized as hints that teach strategies, and non-empowerment help, operationalized as giving correct answers. As the article states, "Such so-called empowerment help enables the development of skills and leads to improvement in performance", whereas non-empowerment help "does not provide an opportunity to practice and improve" and "undermines feelings of autonomy and competence in recipients". The framework organizes the three studies' measures and hypotheses about who receives which type of help.
requirements: Recipients must be able to practice and use hints for skill development to occur
constraints: In this work the types were restricted to hints and answers; the article notes children might provide other types of help or none at all
target_learning_goals: skill development through practice
peer-supported learning
examples: Study 2 and 3 operationalized empowerment help as hints and non-empowerment help as correct answers in quizmaster cover-story experiments
key_sources: Sierksma, J. (2023). Children perpetuate competence-based inequality when they help peers. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00192-9

article_title: Children perpetuate competence-based inequality when they help peers
citation: Sierksma, J. (2023). Children perpetuate competence-based inequality when they help peers. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00192-9
title: Structure cooperative and collaborative learning so that low-competence peers are not denied practice opportunities
description: Because children differentiate help by perceived competence, the article argues that educators should structure peer-to-peer helping and collaborative learning so that all children receive opportunities to practice and improve. The article states such insight "could, for example, inform how to best structure educational practices that involve cooperative and collaborative learning" so that "all children pro ﬁt from the education they receive regardless of their background". Without such structuring, peer helping may reinforce competence-based disparities rather than reduce them.
requirements: Awareness that peer helpers may give less empowering help to peers perceived as incompetent
constraints: The studies were lab-based with forced-choice measures and a within-subjects design; the article notes effects might be smaller when contrasts are less salient and classroom evidence is still needed
target_learners: students in cooperative and collaborative learning arrangements
target_learning_goals: equal opportunities to practice and improve skills
reducing competence-based educational inequality
examples: The article's quizmaster experiments showed children gave fewer hints to peers they overheard were not good at puzzles or math, despite endorsing that those peers could improve
key_sources: Sierksma, J. (2023). Children perpetuate competence-based inequality when they help peers. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00192-9

article_title: Measuring and forecasting progress in education: what about early childhood?
citation: L.M. Richter et al. (2021). Measuring and forecasting progress in education: what about early childhood? npj Science of Learning 6:27. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00106-7
title: Nurturing Care Framework for early childhood environments
description: The Nurturing Care Framework (NCF), developed following the 2017 Lancet series on early childhood development, is a framework describing the qualities of environments that support young children's early learning and development. The article states it "describes the qualities of holistic environments that promote, support and protect young children 's health, nutrition, safety, and early learning, and satisfy the need for warm and affectionate responsiveness from others." It is used in the article to articulate why child-directed speech, emotional attunement and predictable adult responsiveness are foundations of children's learning from birth.
requirements: Environments must provide health, nutrition, safety and early learning supports together with warm and affectionate responsiveness from caregivers
target_learners: Young children from before birth through the preschool years
target_learning_goals: Early cognitive, language and socioemotional development; readiness for primary education
examples: The article cites the NCF as articulating the importance of child-directed speech, caregiver emotional attunement and predictable adult responsiveness as foundations of children's learning.
key_sources: L.M. Richter et al. (2021). Measuring and forecasting progress in education: what about early childhood? npj Science of Learning 6:27. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00106-7

article_title: High-intensity acute exercise impacts motor learning in healthy older adults
citation: Eleanor M. Taylor, Claire J. Cadwallader, Dylan Curtin, Trevor T.-J. Chong, Joshua J. Hendrikse & James P. Coxon. (2024). High-intensity acute exercise impacts motor learning in healthy older adults. npj Science of Learning 9:9. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00220-2
title: U-shaped arousal and dose-response intensity account for exercise effects on motor learning in older adults
description: The article offers an explanatory account in which acute exercise benefits motor learning depend on intensity and task cognitive demands. It notes the arousal–cognition relationship "is thought to be U-shaped" so higher intensity may harm complex cognition, while a dose-response relationship favours higher intensity for consolidation, possibly via catecholamines, lactate, and BDNF. This framework organises why exercise hurt acquisition yet preserved retention in older adults.
requirements: Exercise intensity and timing must be characterised relative to the learning task's cognitive demands
constraints: The account is the authors' interpretation; the study tested only one high-intensity protocol immediately before learning in older adults
target_learning_goals: motor skill acquisition and consolidation
examples: The study used a 20-minute HIIT protocol reaching up to 90% HRR, contrasting with moderate-intensity protocols in prior older-adult studies that found no behavioural effect
key_sources: Eleanor M. Taylor, Claire J. Cadwallader, Dylan Curtin, Trevor T.-J. Chong, Joshua J. Hendrikse & James P. Coxon. (2024). High-intensity acute exercise impacts motor learning in healthy older adults. npj Science of Learning 9:9. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00220-2

article_title: High-intensity acute exercise impacts motor learning in healthy older adults
citation: Eleanor M. Taylor, Claire J. Cadwallader, Dylan Curtin, Trevor T.-J. Chong, Joshua J. Hendrikse & James P. Coxon. (2024). High-intensity acute exercise impacts motor learning in healthy older adults. npj Science of Learning 9:9. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00220-2
title: Cognitively demanding variant of the sequential visual isometric pinch task (SVIPT) with three sequences
description: A computer-based force pinch task in which participants squeeze a transducer to move a cursor to five coloured targets in a specified sequence, with target orders pseudorandomly shuffled among 3 different orders. The article describes it as "a more cognitively challenging version of the SVIPT that requires the trial-to-trial recall, planning, execution, and learning of multiple sequences," engaging both explicit sequence learning and implicit force-to-cursor mapping. Skill was scored via a speed-accuracy trade-off function.
requirements: A force transducer, on-screen cursor display, and per-block skill feedback to encourage improvement
constraints: Force target set at 45% of each participant's maximum voluntary pinch contraction; retention tested same-day after a 6-hour delay without sleep
target_learning_goals: explicit and implicit motor sequence learning
examples: 10 blocks of 12 acquisition trials, then a warm-up and four retention blocks after the delay
key_sources: Eleanor M. Taylor, Claire J. Cadwallader, Dylan Curtin, Trevor T.-J. Chong, Joshua J. Hendrikse & James P. Coxon. (2024). High-intensity acute exercise impacts motor learning in healthy older adults. npj Science of Learning 9:9. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00220-2

article_title: Mechanisms of interactive specialization and emergence of functional brain circuits supporting cognitive development in children
citation: Christian Battista, Tanya M. Evans, Tricia J. Ngoon, Tianwen Chen, Lang Chen, John Kochalka and Vinod Menon. (2018). Mechanisms of interactive specialization and emergence of functional brain circuits supporting cognitive development in children. npj Science of Learning 3:1. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0017-2
title: Interactive specialization model of functional brain circuit development, refined by longitudinal evidence
description: The interactive specialization (IS) model posits that cognitive development depends on selective strengthening of inter-regional connections over time, giving rise to specialized functional systems. This study tests and refines IS at the level of functional brain circuits, summarizing four features: "selective strengthening of some functional brain circuits, and corresponding weakening of others"; increased local intra- and inter-hemispheric connectivity in posterior task-relevant regions; strengthening of dorsal–ventral stream interactions (IPS–VTOC); and decreasing engagement of fronto–parietal circuits over childhood. The authors argue regional specializations emerge from dynamic changes in inter-regional connectivity rather than domain-specific regional specialization alone.
requirements: Longitudinal task-based fMRI with behavioral and cognitive data at multiple time points in the same children
constraints: The article states a strong IS interpretation predicting matching activation changes was not supported; how circuit changes contribute to regional specialization remains a significant challenge for future studies.
target_learners: Children and adolescents ages 7–14 developing arithmetic skills
target_learning_goals: Numerical problem solving and arithmetic skill acquisition
examples: In the study, left IPS connectivity with right IPS, SPL and FG increased with age while connectivity with dlPFC, vlPFC and insula decreased, in a 30-child longitudinal cohort over 6 years.
key_sources: Christian Battista, Tanya M. Evans, Tricia J. Ngoon, Tianwen Chen, Lang Chen, John Kochalka and Vinod Menon. (2018). Mechanisms of interactive specialization and emergence of functional brain circuits supporting cognitive development in children. npj Science of Learning 3:1. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0017-2

article_title: Steady-state EEG captures how elementary classroom instruction drives plasticity for novel visual words
citation: Fang Wang, Elizabeth Y. Toomarian, Radhika S. Gosavi, Blair Kaneshiro, Anthony M. Norcia & Bruce D. McCandliss. (2025). Steady-state EEG captures how elementary classroom instruction drives plasticity for novel visual words. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00371-w
title: Contrasting Dual-Route and computational multi-grain-size accounts of the negative brain-behavior correlation in new vocabulary learning
description: The article presents two theoretical frameworks that interpret the negative correlation between learning-sprint SSVEP amplitudes and decoding skill. From a Dual-Route perspective, the pattern reflects "a race between a lexical route and a sublexical decoding route", where weaker decoders show larger learning effects as practice strengthens the lexical route. A computational alternative posits no distinct lexical versus sublexical mechanisms, applying the same learning principles across multiple grain sizes, so less skilled readers rely on larger grain-size mappings that accentuate learned-versus-novel differences. The authors note the data cannot distinguish the frameworks but that they generate testable predictions.
requirements: Future studies contrasting well-formed versus poorly formed nonword strings, or learned versus novel words at various grain sizes such as rime units, to distinguish the two accounts
constraints: The current data cannot directly distinguish the contrasting frameworks, as the article states
target_learners: early readers in kindergarten through second grade
target_learning_goals: visual word recognition and vocabulary learning
examples: The article derives that a Dual-Route reading implies no comparable oddball effect for well-formed versus poorly formed nonword strings, whereas the computational framework predicts oddball effects for learned versus novel words at various grain sizes
key_sources: Fang Wang, Elizabeth Y. Toomarian, Radhika S. Gosavi, Blair Kaneshiro, Anthony M. Norcia & Bruce D. McCandliss. (2025). Steady-state EEG captures how elementary classroom instruction drives plasticity for novel visual words. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00371-w

article_title: Steady-state EEG captures how elementary classroom instruction drives plasticity for novel visual words
citation: Fang Wang, Elizabeth Y. Toomarian, Radhika S. Gosavi, Blair Kaneshiro, Anthony M. Norcia & Bruce D. McCandliss. (2025). Steady-state EEG captures how elementary classroom instruction drives plasticity for novel visual words. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00371-w
title: Two-week classroom learning sprint with counterbalanced word-to-class assignment
description: A reusable instructional-research pattern in which a fixed list of uncommon vocabulary words is semi-randomly divided among classrooms, each class teaching its assigned words for a short intensive period (~15-20 min per day, 5 days per week, two weeks) while other classes' words serve as counterbalanced controls. Activities focus on phonemic awareness, phonics, and writing, designed to help students attend to grapheme-phoneme relationships rather than rote visual memorization. Display boards and progress trackers support engagement; the word lists are matched on unigram, bigram, and trigram frequencies and orthographic neighborhood size.
requirements: Word lists matched across classes on sublexical properties; counterbalanced assignment of words to classes; daily instruction embedded in authentic classroom routines
constraints: The sprint teaches very low-frequency words (<1 per million); the article notes the design does not allow distinguishing among candidate explanations for the brain-behavior pattern
target_learners: early readers in mixed first- and second-grade classrooms
target_learning_goals: acquisition of novel written vocabulary and attention to grapheme-phoneme structure
examples: Teachers used laminated velcro display cards, vocabulary flashcards, spelling games, memory exercises, poetic exploration, Kahoot quizzes, and creative writing, all organic to the students' learning environment
key_sources: Fang Wang, Elizabeth Y. Toomarian, Radhika S. Gosavi, Blair Kaneshiro, Anthony M. Norcia & Bruce D. McCandliss. (2025). Steady-state EEG captures how elementary classroom instruction drives plasticity for novel visual words. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00371-w
grain_size: unit (two weeks of daily instruction across three classrooms)

article_title: Steady-state EEG captures how elementary classroom instruction drives plasticity for novel visual words
citation: Fang Wang, Elizabeth Y. Toomarian, Radhika S. Gosavi, Blair Kaneshiro, Anthony M. Norcia & Bruce D. McCandliss. (2025). Steady-state EEG captures how elementary classroom instruction drives plasticity for novel visual words. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00371-w
title: SSVEP oddball paradigm with reliable components analysis for school-based EEG measurement of word learning
description: A measurement element combining steady-state visual evoked potentials with Reliable Components Analysis (RCA) over a 128-sensor array, recorded in a laboratory inside the school. Word oddballs are presented at 1 Hz within a 3 Hz base stream across three conditions (learned-vs-unlearned low-frequency words, high-frequency words vs pseudowords, medium-frequency words vs pseudowords). The article notes the paradigm elicits much higher signal-to-noise responses than other EEG paradigms, enabling reliable measurement with just 10 trials of 10 s each, and that RCA produces component topographies more closely resembling underlying cortical sources than PCA or Common Spatial Patterns.
requirements: A dedicated EEG recording space within the school; brief practice session; a repetition detection task young readers can sustain; RCA spatial filtering with permutation tests and FDR correction
constraints: Signals above 10 Hz are very weak, so analyses were restricted to frequencies and harmonics within 10 Hz; catch trials were excluded due to movement artifacts from button presses
target_learners: children aged roughly 6.75 to 8.89 years in early elementary grades
target_learning_goals: measuring cortical discrimination of learned versus novel visual word forms
examples: Each participant completed 30 trials total across three conditions in about 40 minutes including setup, practice, and breaks; 8 of 10 trials per condition were used for analysis
key_sources: Fang Wang, Elizabeth Y. Toomarian, Radhika S. Gosavi, Blair Kaneshiro, Anthony M. Norcia & Bruce D. McCandliss. (2025). Steady-state EEG captures how elementary classroom instruction drives plasticity for novel visual words. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00371-w

article_title: A tailored small group instruction intervention in mathematics benefits low achievers
citation: Rosholm, M., Tonnesen, P. B., Rasmussen, K., Overgaard, S., Færch, J. V., Malm, S. G. & Harder, J. (2025). A tailored small group instruction intervention in mathematics benefits low achievers. npj Science of Learning 10, 18. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00310-9
title: Tailored small-group mathematics intervention with screening, dialog-based teaching and an adaptive learning path
description: A 12-week small-group mathematics instruction intervention for the 20% lowest achievers, inspired by Math Recovery but with an adaptive learning path and assessment by the intervention teachers themselves. "Common to all of them was that they began with an investigative screening-test and -conversation, mapping pupils' understanding of mathematics, deficiencies (math holes) and their emotional perception of mathematics." Teaching was dialog-based, in 25–35 minute sessions four times per week, using specially developed materials, with teachers working to fill math holes and improve vocabulary, motivation and desire for learning.
requirements: Teachers participated in a four-day preparation course; coached arms added a three-day coaching course for the school mathematics coordinator
constraints: Only around 50% of the intended 48 sessions were actually held, particularly in grade 8 due to cancellations
target_learners: Low-achieving pupils in mathematics, the 20% lowest scorers in grades 2 and 8 in Danish public schools
target_learning_goals: Mathematics competencies across curriculum areas, including filling individual math holes, mathematical vocabulary, and motivation for learning
examples: Three variants were tested: 1-group (one teacher, 3–4 pupils), 1-group with coaching, and 1-1 with coaching; 1-1 without coaching had been tested in an unpublished 2014 intervention
key_sources: Rosholm, M., Tonnesen, P. B., Rasmussen, K., Overgaard, S., Færch, J. V., Malm, S. G. & Harder, J. (2025). A tailored small group instruction intervention in mathematics benefits low achievers. npj Science of Learning 10, 18. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00310-9

article_title: Protection of savings by reducing the salience of opposing errors
citation: Javidialsaadi, M., Albert, S. T., Al Mutairi, B. M. S., & Wang, J. (2025). Protection of savings by reducing the salience of opposing errors. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00352-z
title: Error-sensitivity account of savings with a proposed suppressive learning property opposing the memory-of-errors model
description: The article explains savings via a state-space model in which adaptation is "a recursive process controlled by two parameters: an error sensitivity (controls the amount of learning from error) and a retention factor". Savings after gradual learning reflects upregulated error sensitivity, which large oppositely signed washout errors reverse. The authors propose errors produce two effects: increased sensitivity to similar errors and suppression of sensitivity to opposite errors, challenging the locality property of the memory-of-errors model.
requirements: Requires fitting state-space models with both a retention parameter and an error-sensitivity parameter; the complete model was superior by AIC in 55 of 60 participants.
constraints: Implicit and explicit contributions were not measured, so the authors call their process-level hypothesis speculative and limited.
target_learners: healthy young adults performing visuomotor reaching tasks
target_learning_goals: sensorimotor adaptation and re-learning rate
examples: State-space model fits to exposure-2 learning curves showed error sensitivity elevated in the no-feedback washout group and not in the abrupt washout group.
key_sources: Javidialsaadi, M., Albert, S. T., Al Mutairi, B. M. S., & Wang, J. (2025). Protection of savings by reducing the salience of opposing errors. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00352-z

article_title: Question asking practice fosters aspects of curiosity in science content in young children
citation: Park, A.T., Colantonio, J., Delgado Reyes, L., Sharp, S.D.S., Koepp, A.E., Bonawitz, E., & Mackey, A.P. (2025). Question asking practice fosters aspects of curiosity in science content in young children. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00384-5
title: Use encouraging question asking as a simple, scalable pedagogical component to foster valuation of new science information in young learners
description: The article recommends encouraging children to ask questions during science lessons, with teachers modeling question asking and praising children's questions, as an "efficient, scalable teaching method to bolster curiosity". The authors state that "Encouraging question asking is simple, allowing teachers and parents to use the strategy with minimal training" and that it "can be applied to diverse content domains in diverse settings". It is positioned as one component of interventions supporting academic development, especially for children with weaker academic foundations.
requirements: Teachers model question asking throughout the lesson and children are encouraged to ask questions themselves; questions are followed by praise and an answer from the teacher
The goal of becoming a good question asker is stated and reaffirmed at the start of each lesson
constraints: Effects were relatively small in a constrained, two-week paradigm; real-world interventions with multiple active ingredients might produce bigger effects
Training may not transfer to other domains such as basic math facts or reading skills
The sample included few children from low socioeconomic backgrounds and was recruited online during the pandemic, limiting generalization
target_learners: Children ages 5-7 in Kindergarten through 2nd grade
target_learning_goals: Valuing new science information
Curiosity-driven question asking
Science learning
examples: Over eight one-on-one virtual lessons, children in the question-asking condition were told the purpose was to get really good at asking questions, teachers modeled questions, and questions were praised and answered
key_sources: Park, A.T., Colantonio, J., Delgado Reyes, L., Sharp, S.D.S., Koepp, A.E., Bonawitz, E., & Mackey, A.P. (2025). Question asking practice fosters aspects of curiosity in science content in young children. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00384-5

article_title: Attenuated conflict self-referential information facilitating conflict resolution
citation: Li, Z., Wang, J., Chen, Y., Li, Q., Yin, S. & Chen, A. (2024). Attenuated conflict self-referential information facilitating conflict resolution. npj Science of Learning 9, 47. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00256-4
title: Control account of self-referential facilitation of conflict processing via early identification and active inhibition of task-irrelevant dimensions
description: The article substantively describes a control-hypothesis mechanism account in which self-referential information is "readily retrieved with reduced top-down cognitive resource consumption". Early identification of self-relevance frees resources for active inhibition of the task-irrelevant (word-meaning) dimension, which the authors say binds more easily to self-referential information via semantic processing. Early processing weakens competition between task-relevant and task-irrelevant dimensions, yielding earlier conflict monitoring (earlier decoding) and lower conflict intensity at resolution (smaller SP). The article presents this as the first neurophysiological evidence for the account, combining ERP and MVPA time courses.
requirements: Self-referential information must be identifiable early in processing; the account presupposes self-referential content has a processing advantage over other-referential information
constraints: The CE reduction appears in block designs but not in event-based designs, which the authors attribute to insufficient time to mobilize attentional resources per trial

The study used a single Chinese possessive pronoun ('wo de') to represent self; the authors recommend incorporating varied stimuli (names, faces, handwriting) and third-person terms to avoid stimulus-property confounds
EEG has inherent limitations in precisely localizing brain activity; the leftward bias should be checked with fMRI
target_learners: adult participants in cognitive-control tasks (mean age 20.84 years)
target_learning_goals: efficient cognitive control and interference resolution in conflict tasks
examples: In the modified Stroop task, participants named ink colors of carrier words carrying 'my' (self-reference) or 'the' (non-self-reference) across 6 blocked sessions of 97 trials, with an ABBA block-order procedure
key_sources: Li, Z., Wang, J., Chen, Y., Li, Q., Yin, S. & Chen, A. (2024). Attenuated conflict self-referential information facilitating conflict resolution. npj Science of Learning 9, 47. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00256-4

article_title: Curious behaviors in times of uncertainty: dynamics of student question-posing in online educational discussion
citation: Ali, F., Yang, Y., & Poh, J.-H. (2026). Curious behaviors in times of uncertainty: dynamics of student question-posing in online educational discussion. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00440-8
title: Four-category taxonomy of question types crossing open-closed with possibility-non-possibility dimensions
description: Building on Acar and colleagues' framework, the article proposes crossing two dimensions — open versus closed questions and possibility versus non-possibility thinking — to yield four categories: open non-possibility (O-NP), open possibility (O-P), closed non-possibility (C-NP), and closed possibility (C-P). The article states possibility thinking questions "explicitly invite speculation, imagination, or the consideration of alternatives via words such as '…might…' and '…could…'". Because the taxonomy is grounded in lexical features, it was implemented as an automated rule-based classifier with weighted F1 = 0.896 against human labeling of 1,807 sentences, enabling large-scale analysis of question-posing intent in naturalistic data.
requirements: Reliance on lexical cues in question starters, which the authors note does not fully capture nuances of intent and tone
constraints: Past question categorizations were limited to specific domains; this taxonomy is offered as working assumptions needing further validation with additional psychological measures
target_learning_goals: question-posing as curious behavior
information-seeking stance
examples: Applied to the SGExams corpus, sentences were classified by starter words and modals, e.g., open non-possibility questions begin with interrogatives without possibility modals, closed possibility questions start directly with modal verbs.
key_sources: Ali, F., Yang, Y., & Poh, J.-H. (2026). Curious behaviors in times of uncertainty: dynamics of student question-posing in online educational discussion. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00440-8

article_title: Curious behaviors in times of uncertainty: dynamics of student question-posing in online educational discussion
citation: Ali, F., Yang, Y., & Poh, J.-H. (2026). Curious behaviors in times of uncertainty: dynamics of student question-posing in online educational discussion. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00440-8
title: Distinction between domain-relevant task-proximal and domain-irrelevant task-distal uncertainty
description: The article proposes that uncertainty is not monolithic and can be categorized by domain relevance and task proximity. Domain-relevant, task-proximal uncertainties "directly implicate students' goals", while domain-irrelevant, task-distal uncertainties, "while strong, may not readily translate into curious behaviors within the educational sphere". This account explains why seasonal exam uncertainty consistently elevated question-posing across topics while COVID-19 uncertainty did not. The authors argue future researchers should differentiate among forms of uncertainty rather than assuming uniform links with curious behaviors.
requirements: Future studies differentiating forms of uncertainty by domain relevance and task proximity
constraints: The two dimensions were not independently isolated in this study — educational periods and the COVID-19 pandemic differed on both simultaneously, so their independent contributions cannot be definitively identified
target_learners: adolescent students in online learning communities
target_learning_goals: understanding how situational uncertainty shapes curious behaviors
examples: Exam periods represent structured, predictable, academically consequential uncertainty; the COVID-19 pandemic represented unstructured, unpredictable global disruption without clear links to students' immediate needs.
key_sources: Ali, F., Yang, Y., & Poh, J.-H. (2026). Curious behaviors in times of uncertainty: dynamics of student question-posing in online educational discussion. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00440-8

article_title: Curious behaviors in times of uncertainty: dynamics of student question-posing in online educational discussion
citation: Ali, F., Yang, Y., & Poh, J.-H. (2026). Curious behaviors in times of uncertainty: dynamics of student question-posing in online educational discussion. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00440-8
title: SGExams multi-year Reddit dataset of student discussions
description: A large-scale corpus of posts and comments from r/SGExams, Singapore's most active youth forum, collected via a custom PRAW pipeline from Jan 2019 to Oct 2023. After filtering post flairs, "a total of 33,291 posts and 571,091 comments from 55,011 users, spanning 12 post flairs remained", consolidated into five broader topics. Validation included a 99.8% retrieval rate against manual counts, demographic verification showing 93.7% of age-indicative users were adolescents aged 13-25, and lexical-semantic uncertainty quantification (weighted F1 = 0.82, κ = 0.91). The raw dataset is shared in the authors' institutional repository with the author field withheld.
requirements: IRB approval with waiver of consent for deidentified, publicly available data; responsible sharing with author field withheld
constraints: Topic labeling relied on the community's initial post flairs, with potential for discussions to drift across topics; diverse flairs lacking commonality were excluded
target_learners: adolescent students in Singapore (secondary school to college)
target_learning_goals: studying curious behaviors and question-posing in naturalistic settings
examples: The dataset supported both macro-level monthly time-series modeling and micro-level parent-child conversational analyses across hours.

article_title: Alpha neurofeedback training improves visual working memory in healthy individuals
citation: Zhou, W., Nan, W., Xiong, K., & Ku, Y. (2024). Alpha neurofeedback training improves visual working memory in healthy individuals. npj Science of Learning 9, 32. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00242-w
title: WM-system account of neurofeedback transfer: alpha NF benefits tasks relying on the visuospatial sketchpad but not tasks relying on the phonological loop
description: The article proposes that contradictory outcomes of alpha NF studies arise because WM tasks engage different storage systems. "alpha activity tends to occur during tasks that require maintenance of simultaneously presented visual or spatial information that involves visuospatial sketchpad." It explains its own pattern—the Sternberg task's letters activated the phonological loop through subvocal rehearsal, whereas the color-recall and Corsi tasks involved the visuospatial sketchpad. This account organizes the study's task-specific training effects.
requirements: Tasks must be classifiable by which WM storage system (visuospatial sketchpad vs phonological loop) they engage
constraints: The account is the authors' interpretation offered to explain their null Sternberg result and prior contradictory findings; the article calls for future work on how alpha NF influences neural activity during the color-recall task
target_learning_goals: visual working memory capacity and precision
examples: The article contrasts its letter-based modified Sternberg task (phonological loop) with the color-recall and Corsi-block tasks (visuospatial sketchpad) and with Zoefel et al.'s mental-rotation task
key_sources: Zhou, W., Nan, W., Xiong, K., & Ku, Y. (2024). Alpha neurofeedback training improves visual working memory in healthy individuals. npj Science of Learning 9, 32. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00242-w

article_title: Alpha neurofeedback training improves visual working memory in healthy individuals
citation: Zhou, W., Nan, W., Xiong, K., & Ku, Y. (2024). Alpha neurofeedback training improves visual working memory in healthy individuals. npj Science of Learning 9, 32. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00242-w
title: Neurofeedback training protocols should use engaging feedback interfaces and enough sessions to support long-term learning
description: Based on their finding of within-session but not across-session alpha learning, the authors argue that feedback design and training dose matter. "Motivational factor is one predictor of NF success, and the learning eﬃciency of NF training will be improved by the participant ’s t r o n g motivation." They note most studies up-regulate alpha via visual feedback (e.g., a face changing to smiling or crying) and that successful long-term NF learning could be obtained by more than five training sessions.
requirements: An engaging feedback interface to sustain participant motivation
More than five training sessions to obtain successful long-term NF learning
constraints: In this study a blue-bar feedback interface and five sessions yielded short-term but not across-session alpha enhancement; the article also notes a fixed 8–12 Hz band did not account for inter-individual alpha-frequency differences
target_learning_goals: self-regulation of EEG alpha activity for cognitive enhancement
examples: Participants kept a blue bar high via real-time alpha amplitude at Pz; after the experiment some participants reported feeling bored during NF training, and five daily sessions were delivered
