article_title: A methodological perspective on learning in the developing brain
citation: van Duijvenvoorde, A. C. K., Whitmore, L. B., Westhoff, B. & Mills, K. L. (2022). A methodological perspective on learning in the developing brain. npj Science of Learning 7:12. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00127-w
title: Use longitudinal intervention designs to disentangle maturational change from experience-dependent learning in the brain
description: The review recommends repeatedly measuring the same individuals over time, ideally with an intervention and matched comparison, when studying learning in a brain that is simultaneously maturing. It argues that "longitudinal intervention designs are one possible method to disentangle maturational and experience-dependent processes in the brain", because concurrent behavioral and neuroimaging measures reveal whether brain change is coupled or uncoupled with behavioral change. This design lets researchers compare the magnitude of experience-dependent learning against the magnitude of developmental change.
requirements: Repeated measurement of the same individuals over time, with concurrent behavioral and neuroimaging measures
A comparison or control group to estimate maturational change absent the intervention
constraints: The review notes these designs "might incur higher costs and burden on participants"
Longitudinal studies are time-consuming and dependent on long-lasting research funding
target_learning_goals: disentangling maturational versus experience-dependent contributions to skill learning, e.g., reading
examples: The review describes a study that measured white matter integrity four times across an intensive 8-week reading intervention and compared children to a matched-age control group
key_sources: van Duijvenvoorde, A. C. K., Whitmore, L. B., Westhoff, B. & Mills, K. L. (2022). A methodological perspective on learning in the developing brain. npj Science of Learning 7:12. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00127-w

article_title: A methodological perspective on learning in the developing brain
citation: van Duijvenvoorde, A. C. K., Whitmore, L. B., Westhoff, B. & Mills, K. L. (2022). A methodological perspective on learning in the developing brain. npj Science of Learning 7:12. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00127-w
title: Three-fold taxonomy of brain plasticity: experience-independent, experience-expectant, and experience-dependent plasticity
description: The review organizes brain plasticity into three types: "experience-independent", in which brain changes unfold relatively independently of experience; "experience-expectant", in which neural sensitivity is attuned to particular environmental stimuli during specific developmental windows (sensitive periods); and "experience-dependent", which reflects individual-varying experiences and supports learning throughout life. The review grounds experience-expectant plasticity in ocular dominance work on the visual cortex and states that its discussion of learning focuses on experience-dependent learning across childhood and adolescence.
requirements: Relevant environmental input during sensitive periods for experience-expectant plasticity to unfold
constraints: The review's developmental cognitive neuroscience discussion focuses on experience-dependent learning rather than the other two types
target_learning_goals: understanding how experience shapes brain development and skill learning
examples: Depriving visual input to one eye produced ocular dominance in the visual cortex of the eye receiving input, demonstrating sensitive-period dependence of visual cortex development
key_sources: van Duijvenvoorde, A. C. K., Whitmore, L. B., Westhoff, B. & Mills, K. L. (2022). A methodological perspective on learning in the developing brain. npj Science of Learning 7:12. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00127-w

article_title: Phonological awareness mediates the relationship between DCDC2 and reading performance with home environment
citation: Li, M., DeMille, M. M. C., Lovett, M. W., Bosson-Heenan, J., Frijters, J. C., Gruen, J. R. & the GRaD Study Consortium. (2024). Phonological awareness mediates the relationship between DCDC2 and reading performance with home environment. npj Science of Learning 9, 36. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00247-5
title: Moderated mediation model of gene effects on reading via phonological awareness conditioned on home environment
description: The article proposes and tests a model in which "The relationship between RU2-Short and reading outcomes was mediated by the phonological awareness. And this relationship was moderated by different values of parental education and SES." Phonological awareness (CTOPP Elision and Blending composite) transmits the effect of the DCDC2-READ1 RU2-Short risk variant to word reading accuracy, fluency, and comprehension, while parental education and SES condition the strength of the indirect effect. The model was estimated with PROCESS OLS regression with bootstrapped indirect effects.
requirements: Genotyping of the READ1 allele partitioned into functional groups, including the RU2-Short risk alleles
Measures of phonological awareness and reading outcomes, and home environment indicators (parental education and SES)
constraints: Tested with a single genetic risk variant, RU2-Short, and two demographic groups (African-American and Hispanic-American children)
Cross-sectional design; the authors state a longitudinal design would have been more appropriate to test mediation
target_learners: Children ages 8-15 from African-American and Hispanic-American family backgrounds
target_learning_goals: English word reading accuracy, word reading fluency, and reading comprehension
examples: Analysis of GRaD Study data in which conditional indirect effects were estimated at the mean and plus/minus one SD of parental education (Mean = 13 years, SD = 3 years) and at two SES levels

Phonological awareness mediates the relationship between DCDC2 and reading performance with home environment. npj Science of Learning 9, 36. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00247-5

article_title: When scientific paradigms lead to tunnel vision: lessons from the study of fear
citation: Paré, D. & Quirk, G. J. (2017). When scientific paradigms lead to tunnel vision: lessons from the study of fear. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0007-4
title: Behavioral engagement model: the amygdala opposes engagement with stimuli or situations rather than coding threat
description: The article proposes replacing the threat-coding account of amygdala function with the claim that "BL activity does not promote motor inhibition per se but regulates something more general, which we refer to as behavioral engagement" — whether mammals engage with or disengage from stimuli or situations. The amygdala provides a continuous engagement-regulating signal and lets prior experience enter the decision, through plasticity affecting reinforcer value and memory consolidation. It is one of many nodes weighting motivational, contextual and mnemonic factors.
requirements: Naturalistic paradigms allowing a larger repertoire of spontaneous and learned behaviors, since paradigms restricting behavior range cannot reveal what amygdala neurons code
constraints: The term behavioral inhibition was rejected because disengaging sometimes requires motor output; whether the engagement process is deliberative in all species and conditions is unclear, per the article
target_learners: mammals in ethologically significant situations (foraging, conspecific interactions, predator confrontation)
target_learning_goals: deciding whether to engage with or disengage from stimuli and situations
examples: The model reinterprets Choi and Kim's post-inactivation risk taking as reproducing the Type-1 firing suppression required to initiate foraging, and macaque lesion effects as loss of engagement regulation
key_sources: Paré, D. & Quirk, G. J. (2017). When scientific paradigms lead to tunnel vision: lessons from the study of fear. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0007-4

article_title: When scientific paradigms lead to tunnel vision: lessons from the study of fear
citation: Paré, D. & Quirk, G. J. (2017). When scientific paradigms lead to tunnel vision: lessons from the study of fear. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0007-4
title: Sensory-to-behavioral-response transformation: a response-selection network between lateral amygdala and downstream nuclei
description: The article argues that between LA and its targets there is "a shift in the nature of the representation, from a sensory code to a behavioral response code". In downstream nuclei (BL, CeA) CS-elicited firing parallels the time course of conditioned responses, unlike the transient LA responses. A network of interconnected structures — BL, basomedial nucleus, mPFC and hippocampal formation — selects an appropriate response from alternatives (freezing, fleeing, attack, approach, reward-seeking), executed via descending projections to CeA, striatum, VMH or BNST. The authors state models based solely on potentiated LA sensory responses cannot account for behavioral flexibility when threatened.
requirements: Behavioral paradigms allowing trial-to-trial variation in the subject's decisions under fixed CS–US contingency to reveal the behavior-dependent coding
constraints: Models of fear learning solely based on potentiated sensory responses of LA neurons cannot account for behavioral flexibility such as freezing, fleeing, or attack depending on threat proximity, per the article
target_learners: mammals (rats, cats, monkeys) in aversive and appetitive conditioning
target_learning_goals: selection of appropriate defensive or appetitive responses to conditioned stimuli
examples: Figure 3 contrasts the fear-conditioning schema (LA potentiation driving freezing via CeA) with a broader network in which arbitrary CS–US pairings feed a response-selection network
key_sources: Paré, D. & Quirk, G. J. (2017). When scientific paradigms lead to tunnel vision: lessons from the study of fear. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0007-4

article_title: When scientific paradigms lead to tunnel vision: lessons from the study of fear
citation: Paré, D. & Quirk, G. J. (2017). When scientific paradigms lead to tunnel vision: lessons from the study of fear. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0007-4
title: Observe behavior in naturalistic conditions before adopting tightly controlled laboratory paradigms for studying a brain system
description: The article's methodological lesson: a research community "can be biased by relying on an attractive, controlled laboratory paradigm". When a rat faces one threatening stimulus allowing a single reflexive response, one is bound to find neuronal responses tightly linked to the CS. Only when the situation allows behavioral flexibility can one examine the relation between stimuli, neuronal activity, decisions and responses. It echoes O'Keefe and Nadel's recommendation that "observational studies in naturalistic conditions should be performed prior to using controlled laboratory paradigms".
requirements: Experimental situations that allow behavioral flexibility, and parallel measurements of autonomic responses such as pupil dilation, gastric motility, heart and respiration rate
constraints: Naturalistic tasks are harder to interpret: movement-related correlates may or may not reflect decision processes about food and threats, unlike the simpler study of tone-evoked activity followed by reflexive freezing, per the article
target_learners: researchers designing studies of neural systems underlying learning and behavior
target_learning_goals: choosing research paradigms that reveal what neurons code for across a large behavioral repertoire
examples: The article contrasts fear conditioning's single reflexive response with foraging and platform-mediated avoidance tasks where animals express avoidance, feeding and hesitation
key_sources: Paré, D. & Quirk, G. J. (2017). When scientific paradigms lead to tunnel vision: lessons from the study of fear. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0007-4

article_title: Neurophysiological prediction of competitive orientation via EEG during outcome evaluation in gamified learning
citation: Hiroki Watanabe, Ayato Tabata, Chikara Ishii & Yasushi Naruse. (2026). Neurophysiological prediction of competitive orientation via EEG during outcome evaluation in gamified learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00420-y
title: Match competitive gamification elements to learners' competitive orientation instead of implementing them uniformly
description: This principle holds that competitive game elements in gamified learning should be selected flexibly according to individual differences in competitive orientation, because the article finds these elements "can undermine motivation for individuals with low competitive orientation". The article argues results "highlight the importance of considering individual differences among learners and designing competitive elements flexibly according to competitive orientation, rather than implementing them uniformly for all learners", and proposes EEG-based assessment during learning as an objective complement to self-report questionnaires such as BrainHex.
requirements: An objective or subjective measure of learners' competitive orientation, such as the BrainHex questionnaire or EEG-derived ERP features, must be available before or during learning.
constraints: The article states its sample of 28 adults was small, limiting statistical power and generalizability, and that prediction performance was moderate; the motivation incongruence effect was detected for low-COS learners while task performance showed no congruence effect.
target_learners: adult learners in gamified digital learning environments
target_learning_goals: sustaining motivation and engagement in goal-structured gamified learning tasks
examples: Twenty-eight adults completed a gamified mental arithmetic task under competitive and self-referential goal conditions while P300, FRN and RewP responses to outcome feedback were recorded.
key_sources: Hiroki Watanabe, Ayato Tabata, Chikara Ishii & Yasushi Naruse. (2026). Neurophysiological prediction of competitive orientation via EEG during outcome evaluation in gamified learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00420-y

article_title: Evidence for a unitary structure of spatial cognition beyond general intelligence
citation: Malanchini, M., Rimfeld, K., Shakeshaft, N. G., McMillan, A., Schofield, K. L., Rodic, M., Rossi, V., Kovas, Y., Dale, P. S., Tucker-Drob, E. M. & Plomin, R. (2020). Evidence for a unitary structure of spatial cognition beyond general intelligence. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-0067-8
title: Spatial Spy: a gamified virtual-reality battery assessing six spatial orientation skills
description: Spatial Spy is a novel gamified online battery set in a virtual city, developed in Unity by ETT Solutions, assessing six spatial orientation skills: map reading, route memory, navigation by directions, navigation by landmarks, large-scale scanning and large-scale perspective taking. Participants "solve a mystery by collecting clues while orienting and navigating around the streets of a virtual environment". Tasks combine accuracy and reaction-time scores equally weighted; the battery took 35–60 minutes (median 43) and was validated in 2,660 TEDS twins.
requirements: A web browser on a desktop or laptop computer with mouse or trackpad and keyboard; a training session and practice trials precede testing
constraints: Assessment in a computer-simulated environment may capture spatial orientation less well than real-life settings; the authors propose VR orientation may reflect an allocentric approximation of egocentric real-life orientation
target_learning_goals: spatial orientation and navigation skills (map reading, route memory, wayfinding, scanning, perspective taking)
examples: TEDS twins completed the battery online in web browsers, pausing with the 'P' key; test–retest reliability was estimated in a 100-participant pilot completing the battery twice over two months

article_title: The effect of low-intensity exercise on emotional and cognitive engagement in the classroom
citation: Ayame Tamura, Kou Murayama, Ryo Ishii, Michiko Sakaki and Ayumi Tanaka. (2022). The effect of low-intensity exercise on emotional and cognitive engagement in the classroom. npj Science of Learning 7:9. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00125-y
title: Monoamine/locus coeruleus arousal account of exercise effects on classroom mood and cognition
description: The article frames its intervention with a physiological mechanism account in which "engaging in physical exercise triggers changes in neurotransmitter levels, especially monoamines", improving mood, and in which exercise-activated locus coeruleus norepinephrine release supports alertness, arousal, and attention to task-relevant stimuli. It uses this account to predict improved mood and reduced mind-wandering and sleepiness in class, though no physiological measures were collected in the study.
requirements: Future research incorporating physiological measures (plasma measures, pupil diameters, saliva alpha-amylase) to test the proposed pathway
constraints: The study itself assessed no arousal or physiological measures, so the mechanism remains untested in this data
target_learning_goals: classroom motivation and emotional engagement
attention during lessons
examples: The authors hypothesised that exercise during a university lecture would positively influence emotional and cognitive engagement on the basis of this account

article_title: The effect of low-intensity exercise on emotional and cognitive engagement in the classroom
citation: Ayame Tamura, Kou Murayama, Ryo Ishii, Michiko Sakaki and Ayumi Tanaka. (2022). The effect of low-intensity exercise on emotional and cognitive engagement in the classroom. npj Science of Learning 7:9. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00125-y
title: Three-minute slow aerobics programme (expert-created DVD)
description: The specific exercise artifact used in the intervention: a short slow-aerobics routine developed by experts, delivered via DVD with music. The article describes slow aerobics as combining upper limb, lower limb and trunk movements at an intensity that does not cause average heart rate to exceed 110 bpm, and notes the three-minute version was developed to encourage reasonable and habitual exercise and is practicable for people with low physical strength.
requirements: DVD and music; brief practice of body movements in initial lessons
constraints: Low-intensity by design (heart rate not exceeding 110 bpm); selected for classroom practicality rather than maximal physiological stimulus
target_learners: university students (designed also for people with relatively low physical strength)
target_learning_goals: classroom motivation and emotional engagement
examples: Participants followed the DVD through three movements (arm extensions, hip and hand shaking with overhead extension, and body-wrapping twists) in time with music

article_title: Alpha sensory stimulation modulates theta phase during speech-print associative learning
citation: Zhijun Liao, Xiya Ao, Yulu Sun, Manli Zhang & Xiangzhi Meng. (2024). Alpha sensory stimulation modulates theta phase during speech-print associative learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00263-5
title: Cross-frequency account: alpha and theta oscillations are temporally coordinated mechanisms for learning versus memory of speech-print mappings
description: The article proposes that alpha oscillations regulate attentional/cognitive resources during the establishment of speech-print associations, while theta oscillations support memory storage and maintenance. It interprets its cross-frequency phase-resetting finding as suggesting "α and θ oscillations as temporally coordinated mechanisms associated with different subprocesses, i.e., the learning (α) and memory (θ), of speech-print mappings." This account aligns the observed alpha-driven 4 and 7 Hz phase resetting in early learning with prior work linking prestimulus alpha to cross-sensory integration and theta to associative memory.
requirements: Future mechanistic tests, for which the authors recommend transcranial magnetic/current stimulation combined with online EEG recording, given the "limited efﬁciency and signal-to-noise ratio of sensory entrainment".
constraints: The phase-resetting evidence was limited to early exposure, congruent trials, and alpha-rate stimulation; theta-rate stimulation showed no behavioral effect in this study.
target_learners: adult learners acquiring novel speech-print associations
target_learning_goals: learning cross-modal associations between speech sounds and written symbols
examples: The authors note the phase-resetting effect was "most evident in the initial stage of learning" and interpret alpha-rate stimulation as possibly suppressing task-irrelevant processing and supporting sustained attention to new information.
key_sources: Zhijun Liao, Xiya Ao, Yulu Sun, Manli Zhang & Xiangzhi Meng. (2024). Alpha sensory stimulation modulates theta phase during speech-print associative learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00263-5

article_title: Alpha sensory stimulation modulates theta phase during speech-print associative learning
citation: Zhijun Liao, Xiya Ao, Yulu Sun, Manli Zhang & Xiangzhi Meng. (2024). Alpha sensory stimulation modulates theta phase during speech-print associative learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00263-5
title: Time-resolved Paired Associative Learning paradigm with rhythmic tone-flash sensory entrainment
description: A novel PAL paradigm in which each trial begins with 16 transient task-irrelevant tone-flash stimuli presented "brieﬂy (30 ms) and isochronously at a rate of 5 Hz ... or 10 Hz" before a novel speech-print pair, followed by dense sampling of stimulus onset asynchronies (200–980 ms, 20 ms steps) so that frequency-dependent behavioral effects of rhythmic stimulation can be measured. Five pseudo-phones crossed with five Korean characters generated the learning stimuli, learned via feedback over 10 blocks of 80 trials. A null-stimulation control task replaced entrainment with a single salient visual stimulus.
requirements: A unimodal familiarization phase ensuring successful recognition (> 70%) of the learning materials before associative learning.
constraints: Studied with right-handed native Chinese speakers with no Korean experience; the design does not include EEG, which the authors say is needed for fine-grained temporal dynamics.
target_learners: healthy adults learning novel speech-print mappings
target_learning_goals: paired associative learning of speech sounds and written symbols
examples: Thirty-six participants were randomly assigned to one stimulation condition; a separate group of 25 completed the Null-stimulation control task.

article_title: Hierarchical event segmentation of episodic memory in virtual reality
citation: Yue Li, Mikael Johansson & Andrey R. Nikolaev. (2025). Hierarchical event segmentation of episodic memory in virtual reality. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00321-6
title: Event segmentation theory: hierarchical perceptual and conceptual boundaries structure episodic memory, with top-down processes dominating bottom-up ones
description: Event segmentation theory holds that episodic memory is structured by event boundaries arising from contextual shifts. "Changes in motion, location, color, and sound result in perceptual boundaries", delineating lower-level sub-events, while "Changes in expectations, goals, and task sets formconceptualboundaries" delineating higher-level events; together they shape a hierarchical temporal structure. Contextual shifts disrupt predictions, generate prediction errors, and establish boundaries that segment continuous experience into event models, which serve as anchors for temporal order memory. The article applies the theory to predict and interpret differential effects of mission versus spatial boundaries in a VR task.
requirements: Contextual shifts during encoding that can be distinguished into perceptual and conceptual types
A memory measure sensitive to whether items fall within or across event models, such as recency discrimination
constraints: The relative prominence of one boundary type over the other may shift dynamically depending on the nature of the ongoing activity and individual goals
target_learners: healthy adult volunteers in episodic memory experiments
target_learning_goals: temporal order memory for sequentially encountered events
examples: In the VR salesperson task, mission boundaries defined by customer identity impaired sequence memory accuracy while booth-defined spatial boundaries did not
key_sources: Yue Li, Mikael Johansson & Andrey R. Nikolaev. (2025). Hierarchical event segmentation of episodic memory in virtual reality. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00321-6

article_title: Hierarchical event segmentation of episodic memory in virtual reality
citation: Yue Li, Mikael Johansson & Andrey R. Nikolaev. (2025). Hierarchical event segmentation of episodic memory in virtual reality. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00321-6
title: Interactive VR salesperson paradigm for studying event segmentation of episodic memory
description: A custom-built VR environment (Unreal Engine 4.26, HTC Vive Pro 2) in which participants "acted as salespersons interacting with customers across different booths", delivering objects while remembering the order in which objects appeared. Mission boundaries were defined by customer identity and spatial boundaries by distinct booths, yielding a 2 x 2 design of within/across boundary conditions. Memory was assessed afterwards with a recency discrimination test on a computer, with confidence ratings. Datasets, 3D models and analysis code are openly released.
requirements: VR hardware and the custom Unreal Engine environment with distinct booths and customer characters
A recency discrimination test administered outside VR after each encoding block
constraints: Current VR environments often rely on simplified settings and artificial characters, which may limit generalizability to everyday memory processes
The salesperson task inherently emphasized customer-related goals, potentially making conceptual boundaries more salient
target_learning_goals: temporal order memory for object sequences encountered during interactive encoding
examples: Six blocks of encoding with 13 customers, 13 booths, and 25 unique objects per block, followed by desktop recency discrimination tests

article_title: Mathematics interest, self-efficacy, and anxiety predict STEM career choice in emerging adulthood
citation: Ferdinand, R., Malanchini, M. & Rimfeld, K. (2024). Mathematics interest, self-efficacy, and anxiety predict STEM career choice in emerging adulthood. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00275-1
title: Prioritise nurturing maths interest in adolescence to support STEM career pathways, over focusing only on reducing maths anxiety or raising self-efficacy
description: The article argues that because maths interest was the only construct that significantly and independently predicted actual STEM career choice for both sexes — remaining significant after adjusting for achievement and SES — educational effort should prioritise "enhancing maths interest in adolescence over merely reducing maths anxiety and increasing self-efficacy". It recommends developing targeted interventions fostering STEM participation aligned with the UK's need for STEM expertise.
requirements: Interventions target adolescence, when maths interest is measured and developing; effect sizes are modest (ORs 1.63–1.88).
constraints: The study design does not allow causal inference, so interventions rest on longitudinal associations, not tested causal effects.
target_learning_goals: Sustaining maths interest to support later STEM career participation
examples: The TEDS cohort study measured maths interest at age 16 with a three-item PISA-adapted scale (α = 0.93) and linked it to self-reported degree/apprenticeship choices at age ~21.

article_title: Mathematics interest, self-efficacy, and anxiety predict STEM career choice in emerging adulthood
citation: Ferdinand, R., Malanchini, M. & Rimfeld, K. (2024). Mathematics interest, self-efficacy, and anxiety predict STEM career choice in emerging adulthood. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00275-1
title: Social Cognitive Career Theory (SCCT) as a framework for maths-related motivational influences on STEM career choice
description: Social cognitive career theory is described as "a theory of motivation concerned with explaining the socio-cognitive processes behind career-related intentions and choices", highlighting "self-efficacy and interest as key motivational attitudes influencing career-related behaviour". The study used SCCT to motivate hypotheses that self-efficacy and interest would independently predict STEM career choice; results partially contradicted it, since self-efficacy did not predict independently.
requirements: Requires measures of domain self-efficacy and interest, and longitudinal designs linking motivational attitudes to later career behaviour.
constraints: Support is not always consistent: prior studies report differential effects per construct, and this study found self-efficacy did not independently predict career choice.
target_learners: Adolescents and emerging adults making educational and career choices
target_learning_goals: Understanding socio-cognitive drivers of STEM career-related intentions and choices
examples: The authors pre-registered predictions from SCCT that self-efficacy and interest would each positively and independently predict STEM career choice.

citation: Ferdinand, R., Malanchini, M. & Rimfeld, K. (2024). Mathematics interest, self-efficacy, and anxiety predict STEM career choice in emerging adulthood. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00275-1
title: Twins Early Development Study (TEDS) longitudinal cohort and STEM career choice measure
description: TEDS is a UK longitudinal twin cohort born 1994–1996, representative of England and Wales in ethnicity and SES, with a 76.5% response rate by early adulthood. The study used waves at ~1.5 years, ~16, ~18–21 and ~21–24, randomly selecting one twin per pair. STEM career choice was self-reported degree/apprenticeship choices at age 21, classified via the HESA HECoS coding system and coded dichotomously.
requirements: Data available to researchers upon request under the TEDS data access policy; informed consent obtained at each wave.
constraints: Missingness showed MNAR patterns: missing data came from individuals with lower SES, with SES absence accounting for 43–44% of variance in maths achievement and STEM career choice missingness; career data limited to degree and apprenticeship decisions.
target_learners: UK adolescents and emerging adults (twins born 1994–1996)
target_learning_goals: Linking adolescent maths attitudes and achievement to adult STEM career participation
examples: 5.1% (117) of the 2254 participants with career data reported an apprenticeship choice and 29.4% (662) reported a STEM career choice.

article_title: Mindfulness training enhances face working memory: evidence from the drift-diffusion model
citation: Kou, H., Luo, W., Li, X. et al. (2025). Mindfulness training enhances face working memory: evidence from the drift-diffusion model. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00389-0
title: Drift-diffusion model decomposition of working-memory decision processes
description: The drift-diffusion model (DDM) is a perceptual decision-making framework that separates components hidden in raw accuracy and reaction-time data by modeling stochastic evidence accumulation from a starting point to a decision boundary. The article fits four parameters: drift rate (v, average evidence accumulation speed), decision boundary (a, response caution), bias (z, starting point), and nondecision time (t). The article states that "The DDM provides a robust framework for decomposing decision processes into distinct components," and uses it here to identify which component of working-memory performance mindfulness training changes.
requirements: Response-time and accuracy data from each participant and condition to fit the Bayesian hierarchical model (dockerHDDM, 10000 samples, 5000 burn-ins)
constraints: The article notes behavioral indicators "include components beyond cognition," which is the motivation for decomposition; parameter interpretation depends on task structure (the DMTS task here)
target_learning_goals: decomposing working-memory decision processes into processing efficiency, response caution, bias, and nondecision components
examples: The study fitted v, a, z, and t per condition and subject, finding training effects on v but stable a and z.
key_sources: Kou, H., Luo, W., Li, X. et al. (2025). Mindfulness training enhances face working memory: evidence from the drift-diffusion model. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00389-0

article_title: Beware the myth: learning styles affect parents’, children’s, and teachers’ thinking about children’s academic potential
citation: Xin Sun, Owen Norton and Shaylene E. Nancekivell. (2023). Beware the myth: learning styles affect parents', children's, and teachers' thinking about children's academic potential. npj Science of Learning 8:46. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00190-x
title: Be wary of describing children as hands-on or visual learners because these descriptions trigger unwarranted inferences about ability
description: The article recommends caution in labeling students by learning style. It argues that "these categories, similar to other social categories, are likely to trigger incorrect thinking about children's abilities by educators, parents, and their peers", even when descriptions are used with good intentions. The recommendation follows directly from the three experiments showing such descriptions shape judgments of intelligence, sportiness, effort, and predicted grades.
requirements: Describing a child to parents, teachers, or peers using a learning style category such as visual or hands-on is sufficient to trigger the inferred ability differences shown in the experiments.
constraints: The evidence comes from American, predominately white samples of parents, teachers, and 6–12-year-old children; the authors state the effect's real-world magnitude may differ because surveys used forced-choice decisions.
How labels versus descriptions influence the effects is an open question for future work.
target_learners: elementary school students (grades K–12, children 6–12 years studied)
target_learning_goals: accurate adult and peer judgments of children's academic potential and subject-specific abilities
examples: In Experiment 3, parents and teachers given descriptions of a Grade-5 visual and a hands-on learner predicted the visual learner would earn higher grades in math, language arts, and social studies, and the hands-on learner higher grades in art, gym, and music.

article_title: Targeted memory reactivation with sleep disruption does not weaken week-old memories
citation: Nathan W. Whitmore, Erika M. Yamazaki & Ken A. Paller. (2024). Targeted memory reactivation with sleep disruption does not weaken week-old memories. npj Science of Learning 9, 64. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00276-0
title: Time-dependent memory resilience account: TMR-SD weakens memories only when consolidation has not yet transformed them
description: The article proposes that sleep-based consolidation progressively makes memories resistant to the harm caused by reactivation combined with sleep disruption. Reactivation via cue sounds is described as involving selection of a memory followed by modification of storage, and the authors write that "sleep disruption weakens memories specifically by interfering with consolidation that would otherwise transpire." On this account, week-old memories survive TMR-SD whereas newly formed memories are degraded, aligning with amnestic-drug and electroconvulsive-therapy findings of temporally graded vulnerability, which the authors call "one of the main hallmarks of systems consolidation."
requirements: A memory reactivation procedure (auditory cues linked during learning) and a sleep period during which cues can be delivered at arousal-provoking intensity
constraints: Findings derive from afternoon naps; the authors state further research is needed to determine generalization beyond afternoon naps, and they did not examine TMR without sleep disruption for week-old memories directly
target_learners: adult learners (undergraduate and community participants aged 18-33)
target_learning_goals: declarative spatial memory for object locations
examples: The article compares a 1-hour-delay study where TMR-SD weakened spatial memories with the present 1-week-delay study where it did not, using identical procedures aside from the delay

article_title: An fMRI study of error monitoring in Montessori and traditionally-schooled children
citation: Denervaud, S., Fornari, E., Yang, X.-F., Hagmann, P., Immordino-Yang, M. H., & Sander, D. (2020). An fMRI study of error monitoring in Montessori and traditionally-schooled children. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-0069-6
title: Pedagogical experience shapes the development of error monitoring and its neural correlates
description: The article proposes that daily pedagogical experience modulates how children detect and respond to their own errors. Traditional pedagogy provides direct correctness feedback, while Montessori pedagogy avoids direct correctness information and encourages children "to notice their own incorrect thinking" and to help peers identify incorrect thinking pro-socially. The framework predicts different neural and behavioral error-monitoring patterns by pedagogy, which the fMRI study tests via activation and PPI connectivity in a math proofreading task.
requirements: Children must be enrolled long-term in a consistent pedagogical system (from Kindergarten on, or at least 3 years for the youngest children in this study)
constraints: Groups were not randomly assigned, so family-related or motivation-related factors could drive effects; modest sample size and cross-sectional design; conclusions drawn from a single math task
target_learners: children aged 8–12 in Montessori or traditional schools
target_learning_goals: error monitoring and self-regulated learning from incorrect responses
examples: Comparing 32 Swiss Montessori and traditionally-schooled children on a math proofreading fMRI task with feedback
key_sources: Denervaud, S., Fornari, E., Yang, X.-F., Hagmann, P., Immordino-Yang, M. H., & Sander, D. (2020). An fMRI study of error monitoring in Montessori and traditionally-schooled children. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-0069-6

article_title: Education shapes the structure of semantic memory and impacts creative thinking
citation: Denervaud, S., Christensen, A. P., Kenett, Y. N. & Beaty, R. E. (2021). Education shapes the structure of semantic memory and impacts creative thinking. npj Science of Learning 6:35. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00113-8
title: Cognitive network science framework of flexible semantic memory structure
description: The article applies a cognitive network science framework in which semantic memory is represented as a network of concept nodes and similarity edges, characterized by clustering coefficient (CC), average shortest path length (ASPL), and modularity (Q). A "flexible" structure has "high connectivity (higher CC, lower Q) and short path lengths between concepts (lower ASPL)" and is thought to support creative thinking by keeping remotely associated concepts closer. The study uses this framework to test whether educational experience shapes children's knowledge representation.
requirements: Verbal fluency data processed into binary response matrices with identical node sets across groups (TMFG filtering retains 3n–6 edges) so network measures are comparable.
constraints: Modularity in semantic networks is stated to be inversely related to a network's flexibility; the framework's application here is group-based and could not link individual network metrics to creativity scores.
target_learning_goals: concept learning and knowledge representation in semantic memory
creative thinking
examples: The study estimated semantic networks from 60-second animal-category verbal fluency data of Montessori and traditionally schooled children and compared CC, ASPL and Q between groups.

article_title: Profiles of mathematical deficits in children with dyslexia
citation: B. Pedemonte, C. W. Pereira, V. Borghesani, M. Ebbert, I. E. Allen, P. Pinheiro-Chagas, J. De Leon, Z. Miller, B. L. Tee & M. L. Gorno-Tempini. (2024). Profiles of mathematical deficits in children with dyslexia. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00217-x
title: Four-domain taxonomy of mathematical cognition with distinct cognitive and neural correlates
description: The article organizes mathematical cognition into four domains — number processing, arithmetical procedures, arithmetic facts retrieval, and geometrical abilities — each grounded in a distinct body of cognitive and neuroscience research. It states that "These four domains, which affect mathematical cognition and differ in their cognitive and neural correlate s, can be differentially impacted by neurological processes and environmental factors." Number processing rests on subitizing and the approximate number system; procedures rely on fronto-parietal networks; facts retrieval on hippocampal and angular gyrus structures; geometry on occipito-temporal, temporo-parietal, and parietal visuospatial systems.
requirements: Assessment must cover each domain with dedicated subtests, including formats (digits, dots, words), timed and untimed calculation, and 2D/3D geometry tasks
constraints: The article presents this as a preliminary classification; e.g., transcoding and magnitude understanding may subdivide number-processing deficits further
target_learners: children in grades 2–8 with dyslexia or mathematical learning difficulties
target_learning_goals: diagnosis of mathematical cognitive deficits across number processing, calculation, fact retrieval, and geometry

citation: B. Pedemonte, C. W. Pereira, V. Borghesani, M. Ebbert, I. E. Allen, P. Pinheiro-Chagas, J. De Leon, Z. Miller, B. L. Tee & M. L. Gorno-Tempini. (2024). Profiles of mathematical deficits in children with dyslexia. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00217-x
title: UCSF Mathematical Cognition Battery (MCB)
description: The UCSF MCB is an experimental battery developed at the UCSF Dyslexia Center to identify and differentiate mathematical difficulties in children with dyslexia. "It spans number processing, arithmeti cal procedures, arithmetic facts retrieval, and geometrical abilities, allowing for personalized educational practices and interventions based on individual proﬁles." It has seven grade-specific forms for grades 2–8 and "encompasses a total of 19 subtests, including 4 computer-based subtests and 15 paper-based subtests", plus subtests for complex skills and teaching exposure, with completion times recorded to assess fluency.
requirements: Administration with recording of both accuracy and completion time; grade-appropriate form selection
constraints: The MCB has not yet been standardized; criteria currently rely on clinical and qualitative evaluations, and some subtests may be redundant or unnecessary
target_learners: children in grades 2–8 referred for dyslexia evaluation
target_learning_goals: identifying individual mathematical strengths and weaknesses across four domains

title: Large multimodal foundation models (LMFMs) as LLM-enabled multimodal AI middleware for education
description: LMFMs are foundation models that, building on the LLM-as-middleware idea demonstrated by Shen and colleagues, process inputs and outputs not only via written text but also via spoken text, images, and videos, with examples ChatGPT-4-Turbo and Gemini. The review frames them as advancing personalized learning, engagement, and research tooling, while raising accuracy, bias, privacy, and access concerns. It characterizes them as representing "a significant advancement in this field due to its multimodality, boosted accuracy, faster response times". The framework organizes the article's four-audience analysis of opportunities and challenges.
requirements: Requires LLMs fine-tuned to the specifications of connected AI tools to generate correct inputs, per the middleware account.
Educational use requires reevaluation of teaching methods, curricula, and new competencies among educators and students, per the review.
constraints: Accuracy and reliability of outputs remain concerns; biases may be intensified by processing multiple input modalities.
The digital divide and resource limits of educational institutions constrain equitable implementation, per the review.

representational competence
language learning
computational thinking

description: Custom GPTs are pre-prompted LMFM applications introduced by OpenAI for ChatGPT Plus users that turn educators and students into developers of specialized software without programming. The review states that "These custom GPTs enable educators to rapidly create tools tailored for specific lessons", while students can build apps for exam preparation, and that uploading files with exercises and solutions ensures the precision of the GPT's responses, a feature the review calls critical in educational environments. They support personalized learning assistants offered at scale in classrooms.

personalized learning assistants

title: LMFM-supported learning mechanisms for learners: multimedia feedback, barrier-free interaction, scaffolded visual and code generation, collaboration support
description: The review enumerates a set of learning mechanisms LMFM applications can facilitate for students: multimodal formative feedback combining text and images, barrier-free interaction via speech-to-text and translation, real-time scaffolding during image, handwritten-solution, and code generation, representational competence training, animation of phenomena, targeted support during experimentation, collaborative learning via peer feedback models, and interpretation of behavioral and physiological data. It notes that "text in combination with images leads to better understanding than text alone". The pattern is a learner-facing ensemble of multimodal support functions around one LMFM application.
requirements: Effective preprompting to integrate animation principles and prevent hallucinations.
Domain-specific content provided to fine-tuned LMFMs for individualized applications.
Students need sufficient representational competence to critically reflect on LMFM-generated visual representations.
constraints: Benefits for complex or abstract concepts are framed as potential; the review states LMFMs 'could' and 'may' provide these supports rather than reporting tested gains.
target_learners: students with visual or auditory impairments or difficulties in writing or reading
target_learning_goals: understanding of complex or abstract concepts
representational competence
language skills
feedback during graph and code generation
self-regulated learning
examples: The review describes LMFMs analyzing images of experimental setups, generating artificial measurement data to reduce extraneous cognitive load during experimentation, and acting as conversational partners in history role-play as characters like Napoleon.

title: Keep the human in the loop: treat LMFMs as supplementary tools that complement rather than replace human teaching
description: The review's concluding design principle is that AI must complement rather than replace human teachers, developers, and researchers, who remain central to understanding, communicating, and mitigating LMFM risks. It states that "Emphasizing AI as a supplementary tool in teaching is paramount, ensuring it complements rather than replaces human teaching", and that researchers should view AI as a supportive tool enhancing rather than substituting the indispensable skills they contribute. The principle applies across learners, educators, researchers, and developers.
requirements: Awareness among students and educators of LMFM challenges and risks for effective integration and risk mitigation.
Human oversight to verify output accuracy and trace sources.
constraints: The review warns of a risk of developing an overreliance on LMFMs, creating a dependency that could leave researchers ill-equipped without AI support; it also notes human skills must be decided upon for curriculum retention or reduction.
target_learning_goals: responsible and ethical AI integration in education
preservation of human competencies alongside AI-supported learning
examples: The review concludes that LMFMs should be understood as tools enabling interactive, tailored, and efficient educational environments that teachers and students can personalize without programming skills, while keeping the human in the loop as a responsible teacher or increasingly self-directed learner.

article_title: Longitudinal associations between sedentary behavior types and mathematics ability mediated by externalizing and internalizing problems
citation: Guan, K., Zhang, Z., Liu, Z. et al. (2026). Longitudinal associations between sedentary behavior types and mathematics ability mediated by externalizing and internalizing problems. npj Sci. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00424-8
title: Mentally active versus mentally passive sedentary behavior classification
description: The study adopts a framework that classifies sedentary behavior by level of cognitive engagement rather than treating it as a uniform construct. The article notes that "research classified SB into passive and active categories based on the level of cognitive engagement, offering a framework to clarify their effects on psychological health and cognitive functions". In this study, "listening to music was considered mentally passive SB, whereas playing e-games and reading for leisure were classified as mentally active SB", while Internet use was left unclassified "due to ongoing debate about its categorization". The framework motivates the study's differentiation of SB types.
requirements: Classification of individual sedentary behavior types by cognitive engagement level, which the authors note requires finer-grained approaches (e.g., differentiating leisure- from learning-oriented Internet use)
constraints: Internet use for leisure "was not classified as either type of SB due to ongoing debate about its categorization"
target_learning_goals: mathematics ability and cognitive development
examples: In the study, listening to music was mentally passive; playing e-games and reading for leisure were mentally active; TV viewing and homework durations were reported by caregivers

article_title: Dynamic, continuous multitasking training leads to task-specific improvements but does not transfer across action selection tasks
citation: Angela D. Bender, Hannah L. Filmer, Claire K. Naughtin and Paul E. Dux. (2017). Dynamic, continuous multitasking training leads to task-speciﬁc improvements but does not transfer across action selection tasks. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0015-4
title: Task-specific coordination account: dual-task gains arise from learning concrete stimulus-response associations for the practiced tasks
description: The article's explanatory framework holds that dual-task training benefits arise when the brain learns "how two speciﬁc tasks can be coordinated eﬃciently", via strengthened stimulus-response associations rather than generalized executive enhancement. The authors contrast this with the neuronal overlap theory, which predicts transfer when trained and transfer tasks share neural substrates; their null transfer results are described as inconsistent with the overlap account and in keeping with improved resource allocation in the practiced situation.
requirements: Exposure to the component tasks practiced in combination, so coordination of the two specific tasks can be learned
constraints: Gains do not generalize to action control tasks using new stimuli or different input modalities; the article notes its paradigm differs from video action games requiring intentional task-priority switching
target_learners: Healthy adults aged 18–40 in cognitive training studies
target_learning_goals: Multitasking and response selection under dual-task interference
examples: Participants trained on combined tracking plus discrimination for six sessions; gains stayed confined to the practiced dual-task condition

article_title: Dynamic, continuous multitasking training leads to task-specific improvements but does not transfer across action selection tasks
citation: Angela D. Bender, Hannah L. Filmer, Claire K. Naughtin and Paul E. Dux. (2017). Dynamic, continuous multitasking training leads to task-speciﬁc improvements but does not transfer across action selection tasks. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0015-4
title: Cognitive training interventions should include active controls, randomization, theory-targeted outcomes, and related transfer tasks
description: Drawing on recent reviews of cognitive training, the article states that "a gold standard cognitive intervention should (1) employ outcome measures with a clear targeted theoretical construct; (2) minimize potential placebo effects... by including an active control group", (3) randomize participants, and (4) restrict transfer tasks to theoretically related ones. The study applied these by using a single-task active control, randomization, and a factor-analytically grounded transfer battery.
requirements: An active control group ensuring equal task engagement and enjoyment
Random allocation of participants to treatment or control
Outcome measures with a clear targeted theoretical construct
Transfer tasks restricted to tasks related to the trained construct
constraints: A no-contact control group was deliberately not included because such groups often differ in motivation and expectancy effects
target_learners: Healthy adult participants in cognitive training research
target_learning_goals: Multitasking and executive control of action
examples: The study told both groups the same cover story, matched enjoyment ratings (t(37) = 1.70, p = .10), and randomized 39 analyzed participants across multitasking and single-task training

article_title: The control of movement gradually transitions from feedback control to feedforward adaptation throughout childhood
citation: Malone, L. A., Hill, N. M., Tripp, H., Zipunnikov, V., Wolpert, D. M. & Bastian, A. J. (2025). The control of movement gradually transitions from feedback control to feedforward adaptation throughout childhood. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00304-7
title: Percentile reference curves for motor adaptation and overall performance in children aged 3–17
description: The article established smooth percentile curves (1st through 99th percentiles) for the mean initial angle (adaptation) and mean final angle (overall performance) at the end of learning, for the whole sample and by sex, from Push ball data of children aged 3–17. The article states these "are designed to be used as a reference, indicating how a child performed compared to other children aged 3–17 years on the Push ball task". The adaptation measure "increased gradually across age for the overall group, with males and females showing similar patterns".
requirements: Requires the remote Push ball visuomotor rotation task data from a large cross-sectional sample of children aged 3–17
constraints: The article states the reference percentile curves "should not yet be used as standards, adding value judgements and detailing how a child should adapt and perform"
target_learning_goals: Motor adaptation and sensorimotor learning development
examples: Supplementary Fig. 10 compares two 4-year-olds and two 10-year-olds showing different individual patterns of adaptation and overall performance relative to age-matched percentiles

article_title: What data and analytics can and do say about effective learning
citation: Jason M. Lodge and Linda Corrin. (2017). What data and analytics can and do say about effective learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0006-5
title: Interpret learning analytics data with reference to the learning design of the activities that produced it
description: The commentary argues that meaning-making from data in real educational settings requires reference to how learning activities are designed: just as experimental design licenses inference in the lab, learning design gives meaning to classroom behavioural data. Examining behaviour "with reference to a particular learning design helps teachers to see if students engaged with activities in the way they expected", and mismatches signal that the design may need review. This positions analytics as a bridge between laboratory and classroom.
requirements: Teachers or designers must know the pedagogical intent of the learning activities against which behaviour patterns are interpreted
constraints: Data without reference to learning design cannot support inferences about learning, as the article states the conditions give meaning to the data
target_learners: higher education students learning in online and blended environments
target_learning_goals: understanding and improving how students engage with designed learning activities
examples: The article describes teachers checking whether student behaviour patterns match the pedagogical reasons an activity should lead to learning, and reviewing the design if they do not
key_sources: Jason M. Lodge and Linda Corrin. (2017). What data and analytics can and do say about effective learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0006-5

article_title: What data and analytics can and do say about effective learning
citation: Jason M. Lodge and Linda Corrin. (2017). What data and analytics can and do say about effective learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0006-5
title: Determine what you want to know and how it relates to design before identifying which learning data are needed
description: The commentary recommends that before collecting analytics, practitioners determine what they want to know, what is already known, and how this relates to design; only then can the needed data be identified. It stresses that "Identifying the right data is crucial to getting learning analytics right", noting some data are easy to access, some unavailable, and some available but not useful. Both big data and small data about individuals and particular tasks matter.
requirements: Explicit determination of the questions to be answered and their relation to learning design before data collection
constraints: Some needed data may not be available, and some available data are not useful, as the article states
target_learners: students in online and blended learning environments across education levels
target_learning_goals: monitoring and supporting student learning through appropriately chosen data
examples: The article contrasts mass collection of behavioural data with the need for small data about individuals and particular learning tasks
key_sources: Jason M. Lodge and Linda Corrin. (2017). What data and analytics can and do say about effective learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0006-5

article_title: What data and analytics can and do say about effective learning
citation: Jason M. Lodge and Linda Corrin. (2017). What data and analytics can and do say about effective learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0006-5
title: Learning analytics and the science of learning as mutually reinforcing fields bridging laboratory and classroom
description: The commentary proposes that learning analytics—"the integration and analysis of data from multiple sources to inform action", built on data science, psychology, business analytics and the science of learning—can form a fruitful collaboration with the science of learning. Psychology provides options for inferring learning from behavioural data; analytics supplies new tools to assess those options in real digital environments and helps verify laboratory patterns under controlled conditions against real-life observations. This positions analytics as bridging education, psychology and neuroscience through a common focus on behaviour.
requirements: Care about the inferences being made on the basis of data; strategies for use grounded in outcomes of education and psychology research
constraints: Learning analytics may not provide the ultimate answer to improving learning; behavioural data alone do not holistically capture student learning
target_learners: students in online and blended higher education environments
target_learning_goals: understanding and predicting learning processes in real-life digital settings
examples: The article cites automated feedback provision and curriculum design as areas where learning analytics studies have been conducted, and notes potential for computational neuroscience to help refine predictive models
key_sources: Jason M. Lodge and Linda Corrin. (2017). What data and analytics can and do say about effective learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0006-5

article_title: Neural patterns reflect conceptual grasp of novice students following first class learning in physics
citation: Cetron, J.S., Hillis, M.E., Diamond, S.G., May, V.V. & Kraemer, D.J.M. (2026). Neural patterns reflect conceptual grasp of novice students following first class learning in physics. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00394-3
title: Multivariate neural measures can serve as an additional data modality for examining learning in applied curriculum development research
description: The authors propose that multivariate pattern analysis of neural activity — deriving individual neural scores from the decodability of concept-relevant categories — can complement traditional behavioral assessments. As they write, such methods may provide "an additional modality with which to examine learning for applied curriculum development research." The recommendation rests on their finding that neural scores after one hour of instruction predicted quiz and near-transfer performance in novices.
requirements: fMRI data collection during a task engaging the learned concepts
stimuli organized into expert-defined concept-relevant categories not explicitly taught to learners
behavioral knowledge assessments against which neural scores can be validated
constraints: the authors frame this as future-oriented; benefits of hands-on instruction over longer timescales remain unexplored
evidence is a single correlational study with brief (one-hour) instruction
target_learners: novice STEM learners with no advanced physics or engineering experience
target_learning_goals: abstract concept knowledge in static mechanics (linear forces, moments)
examples: The article's authors suggest the decodability demonstrated in this study "would suggest that these methods could be well-suited to such comparisons of longer-term classroom interventions."
key_sources: Cetron, J.S., Hillis, M.E., Diamond, S.G., May, V.V. & Kraemer, D.J.M. (2026). Neural patterns reflect conceptual grasp of novice students following first class learning in physics. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00394-3

article_title: Growth mindsets are less endorsed and less associated with academic performance in non-WEIRD cultures
citation: Wang, Y., Tang, X., Wu, S., & Sun, X. (2026). Growth mindsets are less endorsed and less associated with academic performance in non-WEIRD cultures. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00406-w
title: Cultural variation account of the growth mindset framework
description: The article proposes that the growth mindset of intelligence is culturally ingrained rather than universal: it argues that "the growth mindset of intelligence is not a universal belief system that uniformly characterizes individuals' motivation to learn and predicts academic achievement". The account unifies prior null and negative findings in non-WEIRD samples (e.g. Chinese students' "fixed mindset, high performer" pattern) with the stronger mindset–achievement links observed in WEIRD countries, using Cultural and Psychological Distance from the US as the organizing axis.
requirements: Requires a quantified index of cultural WEIRDness (Cultural and Psychological Distance from the US, calculated from World Values Survey responses via a fixation index measure)
constraints: Indexed relative to the US as reference culture; index range 0.026 to 0.234
Based on 15- to 16-year-old students in PISA 2018; mindset measured with a single self-report item
target_learning_goals: Academic motivation and beliefs about the malleability of intelligence
key_sources: Wang, Y., Tang, X., Wu, S., & Sun, X. (2026). Growth mindsets are less endorsed and less associated with academic performance in non-WEIRD cultures. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00406-w

article_title: Growth mindsets are less endorsed and less associated with academic performance in non-WEIRD cultures
citation: Wang, Y., Tang, X., Wu, S., & Sun, X. (2026). Growth mindsets are less endorsed and less associated with academic performance in non-WEIRD cultures. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00406-w
title: Consider culture-specific factors when applying the growth mindset framework
description: The article recommends that "culture-specific factors should be considered when applying the growth mindset framework", because both mindset endorsement and the mindset–achievement association vary systematically with cultural distance from the US. This means educators and researchers should not assume that growth mindset beliefs, or their motivational and achievement benefits, transfer uniformly to non-WEIRD contexts, and should adapt mindset-based approaches to local cultural understandings of intelligence.
requirements: Assessment of the target population's cultural distance from WEIRD norms, or local evidence on mindset endorsement and its achievement correlates
constraints: Evidence base is correlational PISA data; the math moderation was only marginal (p = .066)
target_learners: Students in non-WEIRD countries and cultures
target_learning_goals: Learning motivation and academic achievement
examples: Large-scale mindset interventions in Argentina and South Africa showed increases in mindset endorsement but null effects on academic performance, as the article reports from prior studies
