article_title: The differential role of cortical protein synthesis in taste memory formation and persistence
citation: Levitan, D., Gal-Ben-Ari, S., Heise, C., Rosenberg, T., Elkobi, A., Inberg, S., Sala, C. & Rosenblum, K. (2016). The differential role of cortical protein synthesis in taste memory formation and persistence. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/npjscilearn.2016.1
title: Differential-role theory: increased cortical protein synthesis promotes LTM formation whereas decreased protein synthesis promotes LTM persistence
description: An explanatory account of long-term memory phases in which protein synthesis plays different, stage-specific roles in the gustatory cortex. The article proposes that "an increase in protein synthesis promotes LTM formation, whereas reduced protein synthesis promotes LTM persistence", so that LTM remains sensitive to protein synthesis inhibition in cortex at least 3 days after acquisition. Building on this and related hippocampal findings, it further suggests "LTM persistence has at least two different time phases, each with a different underlying molecular mechanism".
requirements: Stereotactic drug infusion targeting the cortical region storing the memory trace, with delayed memory testing to unmask persistence effects
constraints: Evidence is from the CTA paradigm and the gustatory cortex in rats; the authors state additional experiments are needed to reveal the extent of generalization to other learning paradigms and brain regions
target_learners: male Wistar Hola rats undergoing conditioned taste aversion learning
target_learning_goals: formation and persistence of long-term associative taste memory
examples: Anisomycin before acquisition impaired CTA LTM formation, while the same drug 3 days after acquisition enhanced persistence tested at 14 days, and APV failed to recapitulate the enhancement
key_sources: Levitan, D., Gal-Ben-Ari, S., Heise, C., Rosenberg, T., Elkobi, A., Inberg, S., Sala, C. & Rosenblum, K. (2016). The differential role of cortical protein synthesis in taste memory formation and persistence. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/npjscilearn.2016.1

article_title: Home numeracy experiences are associated with number-related brain activity and connectivity in early childhood
citation: Girard, C., Longo, L., Chesnokova, H., Epinat-Duclos, J., & Prado, J. (2026). Home numeracy experiences are associated with number-related brain activity and connectivity in early childhood. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00419-5
title: Experience-dependent tuning account: richer home numeracy experience reduces local activity while increasing inter-regional connectivity
description: The authors propose that richer early home numeracy experiences tune the developing number-processing network, so that regions communicate more and each works less locally. They note that "a pattern of reduced local activity coupled with increased inter-regional connectivity has been described as a hallmark of experience-induced optimization in cortical networks." On this account, greater communication between regions may decrease local processing demands, explaining why higher home numeracy predicts lower digit-specific activity but stronger left-IPS connectivity. They caution the account "remains speculative given the lack of observed relation between brain activity and numerical performance."
requirements: A measure of the home numeracy environment (practice frequency, games at home) and task-based fMRI in children around school entry
constraints: Cross-sectional design cannot establish whether connectivity precedes activity or draw causal conclusions
Efficiency interpretation remains speculative without brain-behavior correlations; reduced activation may partly reflect shallower attention during passive viewing
Interpretations cannot be disentangled within the current passive paradigm
target_learners: Five-year-old children at the start of formal schooling
target_learning_goals: Symbolic number processing and foundational numeracy
examples: PPI analyses showed positive associations between home numeracy practices and left-IPS connectivity, while whole-brain regressions showed negative associations with digit-specific activity in the same sample
key_sources: Girard, C., Longo, L., Chesnokova, H., Epinat-Duclos, J., & Prado, J. (2026). Home numeracy experiences are associated with number-related brain activity and connectivity in early childhood. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00419-5

article_title: Structured interaction between teacher and student in the flipped classroom enhances learning and interbrain synchrony
citation: Qi Li, Die Wang, Weilong Xiao, Yingying Tang, Qi Sun, Binghai Sun & Zhishan Hu. (2024). Structured interaction between teacher and student in the flipped classroom enhances learning and interbrain synchrony. npj Science of Learning 9:73. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00286-y
title: Design teacher-student interaction in flipped classrooms as a structured, planned sequence rather than leaving it spontaneous
description: The article concludes that a well-planned interaction schedule, in which students summarize content, receive feedback, ask and answer questions, and hear a teacher summary, is the active ingredient of flipped classroom learning gains. It states that "a well-planned, structured interaction is crucial for achieving positive teaching outcomes" and that "carefully planned interaction schedules can signiﬁcantly beneﬁte d u c a t i o n a l content delivery." Spontaneous interaction offered lower educational benefits in the experiment.
requirements: The teacher arranges the interaction process step by step before class, building on prior knowledge acquired from pre-class lecture videos
constraints: Demonstrated in one-on-one, laboratory-simulated flipped classes with declarative management-psychology content; the authors note it is unknown whether structured interaction after a face-to-face lecture works as well
target_learning_goals: declarative conceptual knowledge (management psychology theories)
examples: In the FT condition, students summarized the teaching contents, the teacher gave feedback, encouraged questions, asked questions, and summarized the knowledge concisely
key_sources: Qi Li, Die Wang, Weilong Xiao, Yingying Tang, Qi Sun, Binghai Sun & Zhishan Hu. (2024). Structured interaction between teacher and student in the flipped classroom enhances learning and interbrain synchrony. npj Science of Learning 9:73. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00286-y

article_title: Structured interaction between teacher and student in the flipped classroom enhances learning and interbrain synchrony
citation: Qi Li, Die Wang, Weilong Xiao, Yingying Tang, Qi Sun, Binghai Sun & Zhishan Hu. (2024). Structured interaction between teacher and student in the flipped classroom enhances learning and interbrain synchrony. npj Science of Learning 9:73. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00286-y
title: Interbrain synchrony as the neural foundation of structured teacher-student interaction in flipped classrooms
description: The article proposes that enhanced teacher-student interbrain synchrony (IBS), the temporal coupling of neural systems between individuals in social interaction, underlies the learning benefits of structured interaction. FT alone showed enhanced IBS in left DLPFC, STG, and S1; IBS was higher in the interaction phase of FT; and IBS correlated with learning improvements. The authors state that "IBS serves as its neural foundation" and that the findings "provide neurobiological evidence for the ICAP theory", framing synchrony as reflecting convergence in teacher-student understanding of knowledge.
requirements: fNIRS-based hyperscanning of teacher-student dyads during teaching to measure synchrony
constraints: Preliminary laboratory study with one teacher and one-on-one dyads; the authors encourage future studies to increase the sample size and test real-world classrooms
target_learning_goals: declarative conceptual knowledge
examples: FT condition dyads showed significantly enhanced class-related IBS in left DLPFC, STG, and S1, while LT and CT conditions did not
key_sources: Qi Li, Die Wang, Weilong Xiao, Yingying Tang, Qi Sun, Binghai Sun & Zhishan Hu. (2024). Structured interaction between teacher and student in the flipped classroom enhances learning and interbrain synchrony. npj Science of Learning 9:73. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00286-y

article_title: Behavioral and eye-tracking investigation of event segmentation following short video watching
citation: Li, H., Li, J., Hao, X., & Liu, W. (2025). Behavioral and eye-tracking investigation of event segmentation following short video watching. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00378-3
title: Segment-and-refresh habituation account of short-video effects on event segmentation
description: The article proposes an explanatory account, extending Event Segmentation Theory, in which frequent rapid context shifts during short-video watching habituate the cognitive system to a high-frequency "segment-and-refresh" processing mode. This habituation is said to lower the threshold for perceiving event boundaries, causing over-segmentation of continuous streams, and to impair sustained attention as a downstream consequence. When viewers later watch a continuous narrative, the habituated state persists, so minor fluctuations are over-interpreted as event boundaries, disrupting the formation of coherent event models needed for durable memory encoding.
requirements: Exposure to a rapid, fragmented stream of context shifts in the manipulation phase
A subsequent continuous encoding task that depends on event segmentation
constraints: The authors note the observed effects are limited to the acute effects of short-video exposure, since the memory encoding task was administered immediately after the manipulation phase, and the persistence of these cognitive alterations remains an open question
target_learners: University students who are typical daily short-video users
Adolescents and other heavily engaged age groups (suggested extension)
target_learning_goals: Memory encoding of continuous, temporally unfolding information
Event segmentation of continuous experience
examples: Study 1 exposed four groups (Short-R, Short-P, Long, Schema) to 25 minutes of video manipulation before encoding a ~20-min BBC Sherlock episode with eye-tracking and a free recall test
key_sources: Li, H., Li, J., Hao, X., & Liu, W. (2025). Behavioral and eye-tracking investigation of event segmentation following short video watching. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00378-3

article_title: Behavioral and eye-tracking investigation of event segmentation following short video watching
citation: Li, H., Li, J., Hao, X., & Liu, W. (2025). Behavioral and eye-tracking investigation of event segmentation following short video watching. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00378-3
title: Habitual exposure to short-form media may hinder students' ability to build structured mental representations from extended learning materials
description: The article draws an educational implication from its event-segmentation findings: effective learning from extended materials such as a lecture or textbook relies on segmenting continuous information into a coherent structure, and the segmentation impairment observed after short-video exposure suggests that habitual exposure to short-form media may interfere with building these structured mental representations, potentially affecting comprehension and long-term retention. The authors state this as a caution for educational contexts rather than a tested instructional manipulation.
requirements: Learning tasks that require segmenting a continuous flow of information (e.g., lectures, textbooks)
constraints: The study tested university students immediately after acute exposure; persistence of the effect and generalization to classroom learning remain untested
target_learning_goals: Comprehension and long-term retention of extended, continuous learning materials
examples: The authors propose future research use more emotionally neutral and educationally relevant video clips, such as recordings from real-life educational lectures, as memory encoding material
key_sources: Li, H., Li, J., Hao, X., & Liu, W. (2025). Behavioral and eye-tracking investigation of event segmentation following short video watching. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00378-3

article_title: Genetics and educational attainment
citation: David Cesarini and Peter M. Visscher. (2017). Genetics and educational attainment. npj Science of Learning 2:4. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0005-6
title: Evaluate education policies on intervention benefits and costs, not on the heritability of educational attainment
description: Interpretive principle for education policy: heritability estimates describe a population variance decomposition, and "the heritability of educational attainment per se is not relevant for evaluating the likely consequences of some change to education systems or policy". The article illustrates with human height, heritability around 80%, which nonetheless showed huge secular changes since industrialization, and argues what matters is whether interventions generate benefits that justify their costs.
requirements: Policy and intervention evaluation must rest on whether interventions generate benefits that can justify their costs, not on the trait's heritability.
target_learners: education researchers and policymakers evaluating schooling systems
target_learning_goals: educational attainment and scholastic outcomes
examples: The article notes schooling systems already use heritable characteristics to assign environments: children with poor eyesight are supplied with glasses and children with low grades are more likely to be required to retake a grade level.
key_sources: David Cesarini and Peter M. Visscher. (2017). Genetics and educational attainment. npj Science of Learning 2:4. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0005-6

article_title: Using a willingness to wait design to assess how readers value text
citation: Amrita Bains, Carina Spaulding, Jessie Ricketts and Saloni Krishnan. (2023). Using a willingness to wait design to assess how readers value text. npj Science of Learning 8:17. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00160-3
title: Willingness-to-wait paradigm for situational reading enjoyment
description: An online task in which participants read forty synopses of unfamiliar books taken verbatim from an online book merchant, rate enjoyment on a 1–9 scale, answer one literal and one inferential comprehension question, and then choose to "wait" 3–6 s or "skip" to see the book cover. The authors present it as "a paradigm to measure situational enjoyment during reading", giving "an elegant experimental means of exploring the factors that influence our enjoyment and motivation for reading".
requirements: Synopses must be unfamiliar to participants (previously read items are excluded) and span varied genres, with word counts of 60–200
constraints: Delays are counterbalanced across synopses so delay does not specifically affect decisions; participants who wait on all forty trials are excluded as not understanding the task
target_learning_goals: Situational reading enjoyment and motivation
Reading comprehension of synopses
examples: Both experiments ran the task online via Gorilla.sc with a fixed £5.10 participation fee and attention-check trials
key_sources: Amrita Bains, Carina Spaulding, Jessie Ricketts and Saloni Krishnan. (2023). Using a willingness to wait design to assess how readers value text. npj Science of Learning 8:17. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00160-3

article_title: Using a willingness to wait design to assess how readers value text
citation: Amrita Bains, Carina Spaulding, Jessie Ricketts and Saloni Krishnan. (2023). Using a willingness to wait design to assess how readers value text. npj Science of Learning 8:17. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00160-3
title: Liking/wanting decomposition of reward as applied to reading motivation
description: The article adopts the neuroscientific reward framework in which "motivation involves at least two separable components: 'liking', or the experience of enjoyment or reward, and 'wanting', the desire to obtain a reward", and links it to situated expectancy-value theory, in which subjective task value is influenced by "task enjoyment, self-schema, later utility, and perceived costs". Unlike most reading motivation questionnaires that measure only liking, the paradigm operationalises wanting as willingness to incur a temporal cost, testing whether enjoyment indexes reward.
requirements: Measurement of both a liking component (enjoyment ratings) and a wanting component (cost-bearing decisions)
constraints: Costs used are temporal (and indirectly financial), not monetary or physical costs directly
target_learning_goals: Understanding and measuring moment-to-moment motivation to read
examples: The study offered no extrinsic motivator, so waiting reflected wanting driven by enjoyment alone
key_sources: Amrita Bains, Carina Spaulding, Jessie Ricketts and Saloni Krishnan. (2023). Using a willingness to wait design to assess how readers value text. npj Science of Learning 8:17. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00160-3

article_title: Action video games normalise the phonemic awareness in pre-readers at risk for developmental dyslexia
citation: Bertoni, S., Andreola, C., Mascheretti, S., Franceschini, S., Ruffino, M., Trezzi, V., Molteni, M., Sali, M. E., Salandi, A., Gaggi, O., Palazzi, C., Gori, S. & Facoetti, A. (2024). Action video games normalise the phonemic awareness in pre-readers at risk for developmental dyslexia. npj Science of Learning 9, 25. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00230-0
title: Sluggish attentional shifting as slow multisensory accumulation of evidence: the AVG mechanism account
description: The article frames phonological deficits in dyslexia as arising from a sluggish attentional shifting equivalent to a slow "accumulation of multisensory evidence". AVGs, with high-speed, spatiotemporally unpredictable stimuli and strong reward signals, are hypothesised to accelerate evidence accumulation and place the brain in a more plastic state, thereby improving phonemic discrimination in at-risk pre-readers. The account links right-lateralised attentional networks (alerting, ventral stimulus-driven control, the "When" pathway, salience network) to phonemic awareness development.
requirements: Training targeting stimulus-driven and goal-directed attentional control with reward signals, as AVGs provide
constraints: The neural account is a hypothesis; the study collected no neural-correlate data, and the authors state future studies are needed to test this neurobiological hypothesis
target_learners: Pre-readers (kindergarten) at risk for developmental dyslexia
target_learning_goals: Phonemic awareness and reading-development predictors
examples: At-risk pre-readers played the commercial action game Space Invaders Extreme 2 for at least 20 sessions of 45 min over 1.5 months
key_sources: Bertoni, S., Andreola, C., Mascheretti, S., Franceschini, S., Ruffino, M., Trezzi, V., Molteni, M., Sali, M. E., Salandi, A., Gaggi, O., Palazzi, C., Gori, S. & Facoetti, A. (2024). Action video games normalise the phonemic awareness in pre-readers at risk for developmental dyslexia. npj Science of Learning 9, 25. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00230-0

article_title: Deliberately making miskates: Behavioural consistency under win maximization and loss maximization conditions
citation: Yajing Zhang, Thi Kim Truc Huynh and Benjamin James Dyson. (2023). Deliberately making miskates: Behavioural consistency under win maximization and loss maximization conditions. npj Science of Learning 8:55. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00206-6
title: Goal-incongruent feedback account of performance disruption after wins and losses
description: The article proposes that the disruptive effect of negative feedback is not inherent to its valence but arises from a mismatch between feedback and the learner's current goal, termed goal-incongruent feedback. Drawing on consistency theory and goal-directed learning, it argues that "the traditional disruption generated by losses is the result of incongruity with the goal (implicit or explicit) of win maximization", and that wins disrupt behaviour equivalently when the goal is losing. Learners can thus flexibly redefine 'success'. The account reframes loss-related performance costs as goal-state mismatches rather than intrinsic properties of negative outcomes.
requirements: The learner's goal (win or loss maximization) must be established, implicitly or explicitly, so feedback can be evaluated as congruent or incongruent with it.
constraints: The study used abstracted points-based feedback with the visually presented words 'win' and 'lose'; the authors note that "the use of points system represents abstracted rather than concrete forms of feedback" and question whether consistency remains isomorphic with more tangible rewards and punishments.
target_learners: Adult participants in competitive decision-making games (university students)
target_learning_goals: Flexible interpretation of performance feedback; adaptive goal-directed adjustment of outcome-action strategies
examples: Participants instructed to "Just try to do as BADLY as you can! Try to get the most negative score." showed behavioural disruption following wins, mirroring disruption following losses under win maximization.
key_sources: Yajing Zhang, Thi Kim Truc Huynh and Benjamin James Dyson. (2023). Deliberately making miskates: Behavioural consistency under win maximization and loss maximization conditions. npj Science of Learning 8:55. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00206-6

article_title: Deliberately making miskates: Behavioural consistency under win maximization and loss maximization conditions
citation: Yajing Zhang, Thi Kim Truc Huynh and Benjamin James Dyson. (2023). Deliberately making miskates: Behavioural consistency under win maximization and loss maximization conditions. npj Science of Learning 8:55. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00206-6
title: Feedback valence should be interpreted relative to the learner's goal rather than assumed universally negative for losses
description: This principle holds that putatively positive ('win') and negative ('lose') feedback are malleable in interpretation, and disruption arises from mismatch with the learner's goal, not from valence itself. The authors state that "our data show that people are ﬂexible in de ﬁning ‘success’ speciﬁcally via the malleable interpretation of putatively positive ( win) and negative (lose) forms of feedback". Designers and educators should therefore consider what goal a learner holds when predicting reactions to success and failure feedback.
requirements: The learner's goal state must be known or set so feedback congruency can be established.
constraints: Evidence comes from abstracted points-based games with university samples; the authors caution about generalization to tangible rewards and punishments.
The article notes the historical emphasis on win-stay/lose-shift and loss-related disruption reflects "our implicit focus on win maximization" in the behavioural sciences.
target_learners: Adult learners in game-based or competitive learning settings
target_learning_goals: Interpretation of performance feedback; emotion and motivation following success and failure
examples: The article links the flexibility to deliberately seek loss to the principle of 'fun failure' in games and to acts of intentional self-sabotage demonstrating cognitive proficiency.
key_sources: Yajing Zhang, Thi Kim Truc Huynh and Benjamin James Dyson. (2023). Deliberately making miskates: Behavioural consistency under win maximization and loss maximization conditions. npj Science of Learning 8:55. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00206-6

article_title: The precision of attention selection during reward learning influences the mechanisms of value-driven attention
citation: Oudeng Jia, Qingsong Tan, Sihan Zhang, Ke Jia & Mengyuan Gong. (2025). The precision of attention selection during reward learning influences the mechanisms of value-driven attention. npj Science of Learning 10:49. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00342-1
title: Precision-of-selection account of value-driven relational attention
description: This account holds that how reward-associated stimuli are represented during learning depends on the precision of attentional selection the training task demands. The article states that "when the learning task required only coarse selection (e.g., singleton search or feature search among dissimilar items), a relational code for reward-associated feature was formed. However, whenﬁne selection was necessary (e.g., feature search among similar items), a more precise feature code was utilized." Search mode and stimulus similarity jointly determine selection precision, so neither alone explains whether learned value generalizes via feature relationships or exact feature values. The account links value-driven attention theories with visual search theories in which relational coding is a typical guidance format.
requirements: A training task whose selection demands (search mode plus target-distractor similarity) determine whether coarse or fine selection is required
A subsequent test task able to dissociate feature-value matching from feature-relationship matching of distractors
constraints: Findings were obtained in simplified visual search contexts; the authors state generalizability to naturalistic viewing conditions requires further investigation
No direct, continuous measure of attentional precision was used; the article calls for future work employing such measures
The specific neural mechanisms by which reward modulates relation-based attention remain unclear
target_learners: Adult participants in visual search and reward-learning experiments
target_learning_goals: Value-driven attentional priority for reward-associated stimuli and generalization of learned reward contingencies to novel stimuli
examples: Experiments 1a and 1b (singleton search) and Experiment 2a (feature search among dissimilar items) showed relational reward effects, while Experiment 2c (feature search among similar items) did not
key_sources: Oudeng Jia, Qingsong Tan, Sihan Zhang, Ke Jia & Mengyuan Gong. (2025). The precision of attention selection during reward learning influences the mechanisms of value-driven attention. npj Science of Learning 10:49. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00342-1

article_title: Investigating epistemic emotions experienced while reading refutation texts through a fine-grained measure of emotion
citation: Jheng, Y.-L., Catrysse, L., Van de Cruys, S., Kendeou, P., Poels, K. & Gijbels, D. (2025). Investigating epistemic emotions experienced while reading refutation texts through a fine-grained measure of emotion. npj Science of Learning 10, 30. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00324-3
title: DynamicEmo: an online sentence-by-sentence emoji measure of epistemic emotions during reading
description: DynamicEmo is a computer-based online measure developed by the authors in which participants "select an emoji to indicate their emotional experience for each sentence of the refutation text". It covers seven epistemic emotions from the Epistemically-Related Emotion Scales (surprise, curiosity, enjoyment, confusion, anxiety, frustration, boredom) plus a neutral option, allowing dynamics of emotions to be gauged across a single text and analysis at text, paragraph, and sentence levels. In this study it served as the online emotion measure during reading of eight vaccine texts, and the authors suggest it could also support real-time emotion monitoring and scaffolding in educational settings.
requirements: Participants read the full text on screen and report an emoji per sentence; single-item emoji indicators are used, which the authors justify as psychometrically sound alternatives to multi-item scales under time constraints.
constraints: The article notes different measures may capture different facets of the phenomenon; in this study the vaccine hesitancy scale was administered post-reading and excluded from analysis to avoid priming.
target_learners: adult learners (ages ~18–65, diverse educational levels, Prolific participants)
target_learning_goals: knowledge revision of vaccine misconceptions; tracking in-the-moment epistemic emotions during reading
examples: Participants read eight randomly assigned refutation/non-refutation texts about vaccine misconceptions while selecting an emoji for each sentence; emotion counts were then analyzed with Poisson GLMMs at text and paragraph levels.
key_sources: Jheng, Y.-L., Catrysse, L., Van de Cruys, S., Kendeou, P., Poels, K. & Gijbels, D. (2025). Investigating epistemic emotions experienced while reading refutation texts through a fine-grained measure of emotion. npj Science of Learning 10, 30. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00324-3

article_title: Mapping the Montessori mathematics curriculum to Dehaene’s four pillars of learning
citation: Marshall, C., Livingston, L., & Van Herwegen, J. (2026). Mapping the Montessori Mathematics Curriculum to Dehaene's Four Pillars of Learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00436-4
title: Four key design principles of the Montessori maths curriculum: concrete-to-abstract, simple-to-complex, repetition, and control of error
description: The article enumerates four principles underpinning the Montessori maths curriculum. Concrete representations are always the starting point, with subsequent materials becoming "increasingly less concrete"; sequences are logical with each new challenge isolated so children explore something simple before elaboration; repetition is offered in many ways, with parallel and less-concrete materials, so children can deep-mine understanding at their own pace; and most materials have in-built control of error so children find mistakes themselves and repeat as needed.
requirements: Children need controlled and coordinated hand movements, perceptual discrimination, and self-discipline from the practical life and sensorial curricula before starting the maths materials
constraints: Abstraction is the result of individual experience, so children vary in how long they take, requiring freedom to work at their own pace
target_learners: 3- to 6-year-old children in Montessori early-years settings
target_learning_goals: Abstract mathematical concepts including number, the decimal system, arithmetic operations, and fractions
examples: The Group 1 sequence moves from Number Rods embodying quantities 1-10, to Sandpaper Numerals, to the Spindle Box, to Numbers and Counters where children create the sequence themselves and recall quantities from memory.
key_sources: Marshall, C., Livingston, L., & Van Herwegen, J. (2026). Mapping the Montessori Mathematics Curriculum to Dehaene's Four Pillars of Learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00436-4

article_title: Mapping the Montessori mathematics curriculum to Dehaene’s four pillars of learning
citation: Marshall, C., Livingston, L., & Van Herwegen, J. (2026). Mapping the Montessori Mathematics Curriculum to Dehaene's Four Pillars of Learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00436-4
title: Dehaene's Four Pillars of Learning: attention, active engagement, error feedback, and consolidation
description: The article's organizing framework, drawn from Dehaene's 2020 book 'How we learn': four evidence-based pillars that must be in place for learning to succeed. Attention is "the mechanism by which the brain selects, amplifies, and channels information for processing and encoding as memory"; active engagement requires effortful involvement so experience enables building mental models; error feedback arises when predicted expectations are violated; consolidation is a shift from slow, conscious, effortful processing to fast, automatic expertise.
requirements: All four pillars must be in place for the learning process to be successful, per Dehaene as the article summarizes
constraints: The framework concerns learning rather than pedagogy; the article extends it to pedagogy by mapping a curriculum onto it
target_learners: 3- to 6-year-old children learning mathematics, as applied in this article
target_learning_goals: Acquisition of abstract mathematical knowledge
examples: The article maps each Group 1 Montessori material onto a pillar: single-quality isolation for attention, fetch-and-match activities for active engagement, the Spindle Box for error feedback, and cumulative sequences for consolidation.
key_sources: Marshall, C., Livingston, L., & Van Herwegen, J. (2026). Mapping the Montessori Mathematics Curriculum to Dehaene's Four Pillars of Learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00436-4

article_title: Enhancing learning and retention with distinctive virtual reality environments and mental context reinstatement
citation: Joey Ka-Yee Essoe, Nicco Reggente, Ai Aileen Ohno, Younji Hera Baek, John Dell'Italia and Jesse Rissman. (2022). Enhancing learning and retention with distinctive virtual reality environments and mental context reinstatement. npj Science of Learning 7:31. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00147-6
title: Context-dependence harnessing account: distinctive contexts, contextual crutch, and mental reinstatement jointly optimise learning of interference-prone material
description: The article proposes that learning protocols can harness context-dependence by pairing distinctive encoding contexts with mental reinstatement at retrieval. Distinctive contexts provide unique cues bound to each information set, "reducing interference between the sets", while the "contextual crutch" phenomenon accelerates acquisition but risks context-dependent forgetting, which cued mental reinstatement mitigates because it "can be nearly as effective as physically returning to the learning context". The fMRI results supply a mechanism: neural pattern similarity to the encoding context during retrieval indexes contextually supported recall.
requirements: Participants must subjectively experience the VR-based contexts as environments they inhabit (high sense of presence) for context effects to emerge
constraints: Context-to-content relationship was arbitrary in this study; benefits were evaluated only immediately and at one week, so the time course of the advantage remains undetermined
target_learners: Adult monolingual or bilingual English speakers learning foreign vocabulary
target_learning_goals: Retention and transfer of interference-prone paired-associate material such as foreign vocabulary
examples: Participants learnt Swahili and Chinyanja words in two custom VR contexts (Fairyland Garden and Moon Base), with expanding retrieval practice and cued mental reinstatement before each recall trial
key_sources: Joey Ka-Yee Essoe, Nicco Reggente, Ai Aileen Ohno, Younji Hera Baek, John Dell'Italia and Jesse Rissman. (2022). Enhancing learning and retention with distinctive virtual reality environments and mental context reinstatement. npj Science of Learning 7:31. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00147-6

article_title: Enhancing learning and retention with distinctive virtual reality environments and mental context reinstatement
citation: Joey Ka-Yee Essoe, Nicco Reggente, Ai Aileen Ohno, Younji Hera Baek, John Dell'Italia and Jesse Rissman. (2022). Enhancing learning and retention with distinctive virtual reality environments and mental context reinstatement. npj Science of Learning 7:31. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00147-6
title: Two custom first-person desktop VR learning contexts (Fairyland Garden and Moon Base) with cued mental reinstatement test protocol
description: The study built two custom, first-person desktop VR environments as learning contexts: "Fairyland Garden" was "bright, verdant, visually open", while "Moon Base" was "dark, rocky, closed-in", each containing nine named rooms. Learners navigated with mouse and keyboard, encountered 40 concrete objects per language along predetermined paths, and heard each translation three times. The contexts were created with the open source OpenSimulator platform, and a cued mental-reinstatement protocol prompted participants to imagine a specified room before each recall trial.
requirements: Measure of participants' sense of presence to confirm contexts are subjectively experienced as real environments
Control of experimenter-related cues (single audio speaker for both languages, no verbal contact during procedures)
constraints: Desktop rather than head-mounted display, which may have limited some participants' sense of presence
target_learners: Adult English speakers learning foreign vocabulary in controlled settings
target_learning_goals: Retention, transfer, and interference reduction for paired-associate foreign vocabulary learning
examples: Participants navigated Fairyland Garden and Moon Base along predetermined paths with pedestals holding objects such as a rooster labelled with its Swahili translation jogoo, tested outside VR in a laboratory, MRI scanner, and surprise telephone test
key_sources: Joey Ka-Yee Essoe, Nicco Reggente, Ai Aileen Ohno, Younji Hera Baek, John Dell'Italia and Jesse Rissman. (2022). Enhancing learning and retention with distinctive virtual reality environments and mental context reinstatement. npj Science of Learning 7:31. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00147-6

article_title: Frontal midline theta transcranial alternating current stimulation enhances early consolidation of episodic memory
citation: Limor Shtoots, Asher Nadler, Roni Partouche, Dorin Sharir, Aryeh Rothstein, Liran Shati & Daniel A. Levy. (2024). Frontal midline theta transcranial alternating current stimulation enhances early consolidation of episodic memory. npj Science of Learning 9:8. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00222-0
title: Theta oscillatory upregulation inherently benefits early episodic memory consolidation, independent of mental-state strategies
description: The article proposes that theta-band oscillatory activity is intrinsically beneficial to early consolidation of newly formed episodic memories, likely via cortico-hippocampal communication during waking replay. Because tACS entrains neural firing "not linked with particular cognitive/affective strategies," finding a theta advantage under tACS indicates the benefit is not attributable to relaxation or attentional strategies used in prior neurofeedback work. The authors speculate that "theta entrainment might lead to greater waking replay of an encoding-related pattern of neural activity," strengthening memory representations.
requirements: Theta-frequency stimulation applied during the post-learning consolidation window, following encoding of the material to be consolidated
constraints: The study could not measure hippocampal activity, so whether effects arose from hippocampal or cortico-hippocampal modulation or other processes remains unknown
The authors acknowledge the alternative that frontal theta stimulation relaxed participants, and a quiet mind rather than direct circuit modulation benefited memory
target_learning_goals: episodic memory for studied object pictures
examples: Four groups received frontal theta, parietal theta, frontal beta, or sham stimulation for 20 min after three study-test cycles, then completed recall tests after 2 h, 24 h, and 1 week
key_sources: Limor Shtoots, Asher Nadler, Roni Partouche, Dorin Sharir, Aryeh Rothstein, Liran Shati & Daniel A. Levy. (2024). Frontal midline theta transcranial alternating current stimulation enhances early consolidation of episodic memory. npj Science of Learning 9:8. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00222-0

article_title: Frontal midline theta transcranial alternating current stimulation enhances early consolidation of episodic memory
citation: Limor Shtoots, Asher Nadler, Roni Partouche, Dorin Sharir, Aryeh Rothstein, Liran Shati & Daniel A. Levy. (2024). Frontal midline theta transcranial alternating current stimulation enhances early consolidation of episodic memory. npj Science of Learning 9:8. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00222-0
title: Insert a washout period between post-learning stimulation and memory assessment to attribute benefits to consolidation rather than retrieval
description: When assessing whether a post-learning intervention benefits consolidation, the article recommends delaying the first memory test long enough for stimulation aftereffects to dissipate. The 2-h break "was implemented as a washout period in order to separate the effects of stimulation on early consolidation from the lingering effects of such stimulation on retrieval." The rationale draws on reports that alpha-band tACS aftereffects washed out once 70 min had passed, so testing at 120 min provided added caution.
requirements: Knowledge of how long stimulation aftereffects persist, so the washout duration exceeds the reported persistence window
constraints: The article notes reports of persistent theta increase following tACS are rarer than for alpha, so the 120-min delay is a precaution rather than a proven boundary
target_learning_goals: episodic memory for studied object pictures
examples: Participants were tested 120 min after stimulation ended, by which time theta stimulation aftereffects would arguably have washed out, so benefits could be attributed to consolidation
key_sources: Limor Shtoots, Asher Nadler, Roni Partouche, Dorin Sharir, Aryeh Rothstein, Liran Shati & Daniel A. Levy. (2024). Frontal midline theta transcranial alternating current stimulation enhances early consolidation of episodic memory. npj Science of Learning 9:8. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00222-0

article_title: Frontal midline theta transcranial alternating current stimulation enhances early consolidation of episodic memory
citation: Limor Shtoots, Asher Nadler, Roni Partouche, Dorin Sharir, Aryeh Rothstein, Liran Shati & Daniel A. Levy. (2024). Frontal midline theta transcranial alternating current stimulation enhances early consolidation of episodic memory. npj Science of Learning 9:8. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00222-0
title: Frontal midline HD-tACS protocol delivering 3 Hz theta stimulation at Fz with a 4x1 ring montage
description: The stimulation apparatus is a battery-driven constant-current generator connected to a passive 4 × 1 HD-tDCS distributor delivering alternating current via five small circular electrodes in a ring montage, which "can stimulate the target region more intensively than the classical bipolar electrode montage." For the frontal theta group the central electrode was Fz, chosen for the implicated role of midline frontal theta in memory; ring electrodes were AF4, AF3, FC2, and FC1. Stimulation was 3 Hz at 1.5 mA peak-to-peak for 20 min, with 30-s ramps; sham used ramp-up/ramp-down only to preserve blinding.
requirements: Conductive gel applied under electrodes with impedance kept under 1 quality unit per electrode to maintain contact quality
constraints: Current-flow modeling estimated relatively low electric field changes (0.12 mV/mm frontal, 0.28 mV/mm parietal), lower than intensities usually required to induce neural entrainment (~0.3–0.4 mV/mm)
target_learning_goals: episodic memory for studied object pictures
examples: Electrode sites were selected using HD-Targets software, which uses a finite-element model of a template adult brain to estimate current distribution

article_title: Human learning dynamics during teleoperation of surgical robots
citation: Yinqi Huang, Yilin Cai, Mengyao Li, Yue Chen & Robert C. Wilson. (2026). Human learning dynamics during teleoperation of surgical robots. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00442-6
title: LQG controller with an updated internal motion-scaling estimate as a baseline model of human teleoperation learning
description: The article models the human teleoperator as a linear-quadratic-Gaussian (LQG) controller that "explicitly separates state estimation from feedback control" and carries "an internal estimate of the motion scaling ratio that is updated over training". The Kalman gain provides an interpretable parameter governing how internal state estimates are updated across training, retention, and transfer. Humans and the model showed qualitatively similar improvement and generalization patterns, so the authors position the model as "a baseline model for rail-tracking behavior, rather than as a full perceptual model of teleoperation".
requirements: System dynamics must be defined; the model targets continuous closed-loop sensorimotor control under sensory noise rather than reward-driven sequential decision problems.
constraints: The model does not incorporate strategic exploration, fatigue, or attention, and was given the rail centerline rather than stereo endoscopic visual feedback; it intentionally simplifies human kinematics and omits cognitive-load mechanisms.
target_learning_goals: motor skill acquisition and generalization in surgical robot teleoperation
examples: The controller was initialized with an incorrect motion-scaling estimate, completed 12 training trials in four blocks, and was tested on a transfer trial at g = 0.4, mirroring the human experiment.
key_sources: Yinqi Huang, Yilin Cai, Mengyao Li, Yue Chen & Robert C. Wilson. (2026). Human learning dynamics during teleoperation of surgical robots. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00442-6

article_title: High-intensity cardiovascular exercise facilitates online motor skill learning, with no effect of BDNF genotype
citation: Brooks, E., Hawi, Z., Hosler, J. et al. (2026). High-intensity cardiovascular exercise facilitates online motor skill learning, with no effect of BDNF genotype. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00432-8
title: Exercise-induced physiological cascade account: HIIT primes motor learning by creating an environment conducive to neuroplasticity
description: The article explains the HIIT benefit via a mechanistic account in which "Exercise, particularly performed at higher intensities, causes a cascade of physiological effects" — increased cerebral blood flow, oxygen, metabolites, neurotransmitters and neurotrophins such as BDNF — "which ultimately creates an environment conducive for neuroplasticity, and therefore learning and memory". Increased arousal from noradrenaline and cortisol may improve focus, and exercise modulates cortical excitability to facilitate LTP-like plasticity. Within-session gains are attributed to a generalised influence rather than specific online or offline processes.
requirements: Higher-intensity exercise appears central: the account ties facilitation to intensity-dependent upregulation of neurotrophins and plasticity responses.
constraints: The authors state the exercise influence on consolidation may be relatively specific to retention hours-days after training rather than brief rest periods within a session; the mechanism account is interpretive, not directly tested in this study.
target_learners: Healthy young adults learning novel motor skills
target_learning_goals: Motor skill acquisition (visuomotor accuracy and speed)
examples: Participants cycled 20 minutes of HIIT (alternating two-minute high-intensity up to 90% HRR and three-minute moderate intervals) 10 minutes before SVIPT practice.
key_sources: Brooks, E., Hawi, Z., Hosler, J. et al. (2026). High-intensity cardiovascular exercise facilitates online motor skill learning, with no effect of BDNF genotype. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00432-8

article_title: High-intensity cardiovascular exercise facilitates online motor skill learning, with no effect of BDNF genotype
citation: Brooks, E., Hawi, Z., Hosler, J. et al. (2026). High-intensity cardiovascular exercise facilitates online motor skill learning, with no effect of BDNF genotype. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00432-8
title: Schedule skill practice closely after exercise cessation to exploit the exercise priming window
description: The article operationalised exercise priming by timing "Motor skill training on the SVIPT 62 was timed to commence 10-minutes after exercise, in line with previous studies reporting a maximal priming effect when there is a close temporal coupling between exercise and learning". It also cites evidence that facilitative physiological effects are prominent 15–30 minutes after HIIT and that closer coupling yields greater benefit. Skill learning was detected in the HIIT group from about 16.5 minutes after exercise cessation.
requirements: Practice must follow exercise within the priming window; this study used a 10-minute delay between exercise cessation and task commencement.
constraints: The observed facilitation was for a task with a protracted learning trajectory (SVIPT); prior work with a rapidly plateauing task (SRTT) practised on average 35 minutes post HIIT and found no benefit, so timing and task demands jointly matter.
target_learners: Healthy young adults in motor skill training
target_learning_goals: Enhancing acquisition of novel motor skills
examples: Participants completed a 20-minute HIIT bout followed by a 1–2-minute cool down, with SVIPT practice beginning 10 minutes after exercise.
key_sources: Brooks, E., Hawi, Z., Hosler, J. et al. (2026). High-intensity cardiovascular exercise facilitates online motor skill learning, with no effect of BDNF genotype. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00432-8

article_title: Differences in spatiotemporal brain network dynamics of Montessori and traditionally schooled students
citation: Zanchi, P., Mullier, E., Fornari, E., Guerrier de Dumast, P., Alemán-Gómez, Y., Ledoux, J.-B., Beaty, R., Hagmann, P., & Denervaud, S. (2024). Differences in spatiotemporal brain network dynamics of Montessori and traditionally schooled students. npj Science of Learning, 9, 45. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00254-6
title: The spatiotemporal connectome framework characterizes brain dynamics via system diversity (integration) and spatiotemporal diversity (stability)
description: The spatiotemporal connectome is an analytical framework that characterizes resting-state functional connectivity with a structural prior: neural activity is chunked into time windows, connectivity matrices (506 × 506 regions) constrained by structural connectivity are translated into connected components (CCs), and CCs are classified by the eight functional systems of Yeo's atlas plus the cerebellar system. From these, two group-level metrics are derived: "system diversity (SD) and spatiotemporal diversity (STD)", where SD informs about "integration and segregation" and STD about "temporal stability". The article uses these metrics to compare Montessori- and traditionally schooled students at global and functional-system scales.
requirements: SD and STD require a sufficient number of connected components for a reliable outcome, so they are computed at group level rather than individually
constraints: SD and STD are group-level measures, which prevents correlating brain metrics with individual behavioral measures in this study
target_learners: students aged 4 to 18 in Montessori or traditional schools
target_learning_goals: characterizing how pedagogical experience relates to brain network integration and temporal stability
examples: The article applied the framework to 87 students' resting-state fMRI and diffusion MRI, comparing SD and STD at global and functional-system scales between pedagogy groups.
key_sources: Zanchi, P., Mullier, E., Fornari, E., Guerrier de Dumast, P., Alemán-Gómez, Y., Ledoux, J.-B., Beaty, R., Hagmann, P., & Denervaud, S. (2024). Differences in spatiotemporal brain network dynamics of Montessori and traditionally schooled students. npj Science of Learning, 9, 45. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00254-6

article_title: Delayed tracking and inequality of opportunity: Gene-environment interactions in educational attainment
citation: Antonie Knigge, Ineke Maas, Kim Stienstra, Eveline L. de Zeeuw and Dorret I. Boomsma. (2022). Delayed tracking and inequality of opportunity: Gene-environment interactions in educational attainment. npj Science of Learning 7:6. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00122-1
title: Defer definite track placement until partway through secondary school, or reassess track level during secondary school, to reduce inequality of opportunity
description: The article proposes that educational systems with early tracking avoid fixing track level at the end of primary school. If the observed associations reflect a causal effect of delayed tracking, the authors advise that systems seeking to combat inequality of opportunity "delay deﬁnite tracking to a later age", and suggest it may be more logical to "assess, or at least reassess, the track level of a child at some point in secondary school" so talents and track level do not mismatch early.
requirements: A school system in which secondary schools offer both immediate single-track placement and combined heterogeneous classes, so that definitive tracking can be postponed while students are observed.
constraints: The authors state the design is not experimental: whether children delay tracking is not exogenously controlled, other confounders cannot be ruled out, and the advice is conditional on the findings reflecting a causal effect.
target_learners: Students transitioning from primary to secondary education in tracked systems
target_learning_goals: Realizing students' genetic potential and reducing dependence of track placement on family background
examples: In Dutch secondary schools, some students are placed in a class combining two or more levels for 1–3 years before teachers decide the definitive track, and the study compared these delayed-tracking twins with immediately tracked twins.
key_sources: Antonie Knigge, Ineke Maas, Kim Stienstra, Eveline L. de Zeeuw and Dorret I. Boomsma. (2022). Delayed tracking and inequality of opportunity: Gene-environment interactions in educational attainment. npj Science of Learning 7:6. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00122-1

article_title: Delayed tracking and inequality of opportunity: Gene-environment interactions in educational attainment
citation: Antonie Knigge, Ineke Maas, Kim Stienstra, Eveline L. de Zeeuw and Dorret I. Boomsma. (2022). Delayed tracking and inequality of opportunity: Gene-environment interactions in educational attainment. npj Science of Learning 7:6. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00122-1
title: Transactional models of gene–environment interplay applied to tracking age
description: The article uses transactional models of development to explain why delayed tracking allows greater realization of genetic potential. These models hold that children "select and are selected into different environments partly based on their genetic predispositions, and these environments in turn have an impact on their development", through active and evocative gene–environment correlation. Applied here, delaying definitive tracking gives children more autonomy and time, so their learning environment fits their genetic predispositions better.
requirements: A wider environment that gives children autonomy in shaping their direct environment, so genetic differences can be expressed in developmental differences.
constraints: The authors note heritability should be read as variance explained, not as genetic determination, and that genetic influence may also express negative potential; the shared environment is a broad 'black box' indicator of family background.
target_learners: Children and adolescents in educational systems with ability tracking
target_learning_goals: Alignment of learning environments with students' genetic predispositions to support realizing potential
examples: The article cites evidence that shared-environmental variance in cognitive ability decreases from around 60% in infancy to virtually none in adolescence while genetic variance increases, as children gain autonomy in selecting peer groups and academic courses.
key_sources: Antonie Knigge, Ineke Maas, Kim Stienstra, Eveline L. de Zeeuw and Dorret I. Boomsma. (2022). Delayed tracking and inequality of opportunity: Gene-environment interactions in educational attainment. npj Science of Learning 7:6. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00122-1

article_title: Growth mindset and socioeconomic inequality in academic achievement across seventy-three PISA countries
citation: Madia, J. E., Gruijters, R. J., Raabe, I. J. & Hübner, N. (2025). Growth mindset and socioeconomic inequality in academic achievement across seventy-three PISA countries. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00365-8
title: Four-way decomposition framework separating the total SES effect into controlled direct, reference interaction, mediated interaction, and pure indirect effects
description: The article applies VanderWeele's four-way decomposition within a counterfactual (potential outcomes) framework to disentangle mediation and interaction. The "TE is the sum of all four components": the Controlled Direct Effect (effect of SES net of mindset), the Reference Interaction (interaction when SES does not affect mindset), the Mediated Interaction (interaction operating through SES-influenced mindset), and the Pure Indirect Effect (SES operating through mindset). The authors argue this avoids overcontrolling bias and misleading coefficient comparisons that plague standard regression approaches in the mindset literature.
requirements: Assumes relationships between SES, growth mindset, and achievement are unconfounded and no reverse causality is present, per the article's stated assumptions
constraints: Estimates are upper bounds of the true causal effect because sequential ignorability may be violated in observational data
target_learners: 15-year-old students assessed in PISA 2022 across 73 countries
target_learning_goals: Mathematics, reading, and science achievement as measured by PISA test scores
examples: Applied to PISA 2022 data from 73 countries using the Stata Med4way package, with the mediator fixed at levels 0, 0.2, 0.4, and 0.6 plus a closing-gap specification
key_sources: Madia, J. E., Gruijters, R. J., Raabe, I. J. & Hübner, N. (2025). Growth mindset and socioeconomic inequality in academic achievement across seventy-three PISA countries. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00365-8

article_title: Growth mindset and socioeconomic inequality in academic achievement across seventy-three PISA countries
citation: Madia, J. E., Gruijters, R. J., Raabe, I. J. & Hübner, N. (2025). Growth mindset and socioeconomic inequality in academic achievement across seventy-three PISA countries. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00365-8
title: Interventions targeting individual mindsets alone are unlikely to reduce socioeconomic achievement gaps; systemic factors deserve greater emphasis
description: Based on the finding that growth mindset mediates only about 2.9–3.2% of the SES effect, the article recommends that "interventions solely focused on cultivating this individual-level trait may have a limited impact on reducing educational inequalities". It argues greater emphasis and resources should be directed toward systemic factors such as school resources, teacher quality, and parental involvement, which the study implies may play a more substantial role in equitable outcomes.
requirements: Policy goals of reducing socioeconomic achievement gaps, per the article's framing
constraints: The article notes growth mindset interventions may still provide meaningful benefits for individual students' motivation and engagement, even though their capacity to reduce systemic inequalities appears limited
target_learners: Socioeconomically disadvantaged students across diverse national contexts
target_learning_goals: Reducing socioeconomic disparities in academic achievement
examples: The study's decomposition across 73 PISA 2022 countries showed the direct SES effect accounts for about 98% of the total effect, supporting the recommendation to prioritize systemic levers
key_sources: Madia, J. E., Gruijters, R. J., Raabe, I. J. & Hübner, N. (2025). Growth mindset and socioeconomic inequality in academic achievement across seventy-three PISA countries. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00365-8

article_title: Mixing problems increases performance of all students but especially of low-achieving ones in college calculus
citation: Steve Bennoun, Veronica X. Yan, & Alice Xu. (2026). Mixing problems increases performance of all students but especially of low-achieving ones in college calculus. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00450-6
title: Discriminative-contrast account of the interleaving effect: interleaved practice trains identifying which concept or approach is relevant to solve a given problem
description: This account explains why mixing problems supports learning: on exams students are tested on determining "which concept or approach is relevant to solve a given problem", a skill blocked homework never practices. Interleaving "draws learners’attention away from similar surface features and toward key structural features that deﬁne and distinguish concepts". The article also notes interleaved sets distribute topics over time, adding spacing benefits that protect learning from forgetting. The authors use this account to predict, and to explain, larger benefits for students with weaker prior knowledge.
requirements: Requires topics that can be distinguished so students can practice identifying which concept or approach applies to each problem
constraints: Interleaving benefits are reduced when discriminative contrast is disrupted by introducing spacing (fillers) between examples, per cited experiments
target_learners: Learners with lower prior knowledge or weaker mathematics preparation
target_learning_goals: Selecting the appropriate concept or problem-solving approach for a given problem
Long-lasting retention of learned concepts
examples: The study's interleaved homework sets mixed problems on different topics across assignments so students practiced both individual skills and approach identification
key_sources: Steve Bennoun, Veronica X. Yan, & Alice Xu. (2026). Mixing problems increases performance of all students but especially of low-achieving ones in college calculus. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00450-6

article_title: Mixing problems increases performance of all students but especially of low-achieving ones in college calculus
citation: Steve Bennoun, Veronica X. Yan, & Alice Xu. (2026). Mixing problems increases performance of all students but especially of low-achieving ones in college calculus. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00450-6
title: Reorder homework sets so problems on each topic are distributed across multiple assignments — a low-cost restructuring that requires no extra time, technology, or curricular change
description: The article recommends implementing interleaved-and-spaced homework by identifying key topics of each lecture and redistributing questions on the same topic across assignments, e.g. through cumulative assignments or a structure like Fig. 1. It emphasizes that "it is simple to set up and has virtually no cost— it does not require extra instructional time, it does not require reorganizing curricula, nor does it require any technology". The study shows this works even in a course already using active-learning practices supporting low-achieving students.
requirements: Identifying the key topics of each lecture
Rearranging questions so problems on the same topic appear across assignments
constraints: The study could not disentangle interleaving from spacing effects, and the results do not establish whether interleaving is the optimal homework organization; some authors argue starting with a small number of blocked exercises then interleaving may be optimal
target_learners: Undergraduate students in large-enrollment mathematics courses
target_learning_goals: Improving high-stakes exam performance
Reducing achievement gaps between student groups
examples: In the study, topics presented in class appeared on the next three homework sets in the interleaved condition, while blocked sets grouped problems by topic in class order, with all students completing the same 40 problems per phase
key_sources: Steve Bennoun, Veronica X. Yan, & Alice Xu. (2026). Mixing problems increases performance of all students but especially of low-achieving ones in college calculus. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00450-6

article_title: The effect of language on performance: do gendered languages fail women in maths?
citation: Tamar Kricheli-Katz and Tali Regev. (2021). The effect of language on performance: do gendered languages fail women in maths? npj Science of Learning 6:9. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00087-7
title: Grant test takers the choice of being addressed in the feminine or the masculine in exams
description: Because address form causally affects performance in gendered languages, the article recommends that learners be allowed to choose their form of address. As the authors put it, "to improve women’s performance, women and men should be granted the right to choose whether they wish to be addressed in the feminine or in the masculine in exams." This follows from their finding that feminine address helps women but can modestly hurt men in some contexts, so a blanket switch is not optimal for everyone.
requirements: Assessment instructions written in a gendered language must offer both masculine and feminine address forms to test takers.
constraints: Effects of feminine address on men were negative in some contexts, although smaller than the effects on women and marginally significant; effects were established in an online, individually taken test setting, not a classroom.
target_learners: Adult and adolescent test takers in gendered-language settings
target_learning_goals: Mathematics achievement test performance
examples: In the main experiment, a representative sample of Hebrew-speaking adults took an SAT-type maths test online, randomly addressed in the feminine or the masculine; women addressed in the feminine scored higher and the gender gap shrank.
key_sources: Tamar Kricheli-Katz and Tali Regev. (2021). The effect of language on performance: do gendered languages fail women in maths? npj Science of Learning 6:9. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00087-7

article_title: Keep it simple: streamlining book illustrations improves attention and comprehension in beginning readers
citation: Eng, C. M., Godwin, K. E., & Fisher, A. V. (2020). Keep it simple: streamlining book illustrations improves attention and comprehension in beginning readers. npj Science of Learning, 5:14. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00073-5
title: Limit extraneous illustrations in reading materials for beginning readers to support attention and comprehension
description: The article recommends optimizing instructional reading materials by removing illustration details unrelated to the story text while retaining relevant illustrations. It reports that "extraneous illustrations promoted attentional competition and hindered reading comprehension", and the authors state they are "not advocating for the removal of illustrations from books" but for considering children's developing attention regulation in design. The principle is grounded in the Streamlined-versus-Standard comparison and the control experiment.
requirements: Relevant illustrations that reinforce the text should be retained; only extraneous details are removed
Illustration relevance should be determined systematically, as in the adult calibration study with over 90% agreement
constraints: The comprehension assessment primarily focused on recall of key story events, assessing both understanding and memory
The effect of removing extraneous illustrations on children's engagement and motivation was not measured
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension
Attention to text during independent reading
examples: Half of a commercially available first-grade book (Good Job Dennis) was presented with extraneous illustrations removed after an adult calibration study classified details as relevant or extraneous
key_sources: Eng, C. M., Godwin, K. E., & Fisher, A. V. (2020). Keep it simple: streamlining book illustrations improves attention and comprehension in beginning readers. npj Science of Learning, 5:14. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00073-5

article_title: The International Science and Evidence-based Education Assessment
citation: Duraiappah, A., van Atteveldt, N., Asah, S., Borst, G., Bugden, S., Buil, J. M., Ergas, O., Fraser, S., Mercier, J., Restrepo Mesa, J. F., Mizala, A., Mochizuki, Y., Okano, K., Piech, C., Pugh, K., Ramaswamy, R., Singh, N. C. & Vickers, E. (2021). The International Science and Evidence-based Education Assessment. npj Science of Learning 6:7. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00085-9
title: ISEE Assessment conceptual framework linking contexts, policies and the What, Where, How and When of learning
description: The ISEE Assessment is guided by a conceptual framework (Fig. 1) that maps inter-linkages within the education system: societal and environmental contexts influence educational policies and practices, which in turn influence what, where, how and when we learn. The article states that "The conceptual framework presented in Fig. 1 captures the key inter-linkages within the education system, which will be assessed, and will guide the assessment." The framework uses learning success benchmarks that feed into human flourishing and the 17 Sustainable Development Goals.
requirements: Requires a multi-perspective, multicultural and multidisciplinary team of independent experts interacting with education stakeholders
constraints: The assessment draws primarily on peer-reviewed scientific literature but also includes credible grey literature
target_learners: learners of all backgrounds and stages of life, from infancy to old age
target_learning_goals: rethinking the purpose and organization of education for the 21st century
examples: The framework guided the assessment's four questions on what, how, where and when we learn

title: Four pillars of education as benchmarks for evaluating learning success
description: The framework adopts UNESCO's four pillars of education — Learning to Know, Learning to Do, Learning to Be, and Learning to Live Together — as benchmarks for evaluating learning success, which the article links to human flourishing and the Sustainable Development Goals. The article states: "Second, we will use the four pillars of education: (i) learning to Know, (ii) learning to Do, (iii) learning to Be, and learning to Live Together19 as benchmarks to analyze how contextual factors have in ﬂuenced and been in ﬂuenced by the educational aims and practices that these pillars encompass". The pillars are used in Box 4 of the conceptual framework.
