article_title: Does tapping in sync reflect cognitive control? Links between sensorimotor synchronization, social context, and executive function in early childhood
citation: Yunhee Kim, Doyeon Chae, Jaehwan Jang, Kyeong Taek Oh, Byeong-Sun Park & Min-gu Kim. (2026). Does tapping in sync reflect cognitive control? Links between sensorimotor synchronization, social context, and executive function in early childhood. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00443-5
title: Sensor-embedded bongo drum platform with DTW-based synchronization measurement
description: A custom bongo drum platform embedded with thin-film pressure sensors was used to measure preschoolers' tapping. The article states this "intuitive and child-friendly interface facilitated consistent participation among young children and ensured reliable measurement across conditions". Synchronization was quantified with the Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) algorithm, which "flexibly compar[es] the overall flow and shape of the sequences", making it robust to occasional missed strikes unlike strict onset-to-onset asynchrony measures.
requirements: Requires pressure-sensor bongo drums recording strike data in real time and DTW analysis of tapping sequences against reference rhythms.
constraints: Hand dominance was not directly assessed; data and code are available only upon request from the corresponding author because public repository consent was not obtained.
The study's design and analysis were not preregistered.
target_learners: Children aged 4-5 years in preschool settings
target_learning_goals: Sensorimotor synchronization to rhythmic stimuli
examples: Four drums (two for the child and two for the experimenter) equipped with thin-film pressure sensors; reference signals generated from the exact temporal structure of the auditory stimuli.
key_sources: Yunhee Kim, Doyeon Chae, Jaehwan Jang, Kyeong Taek Oh, Byeong-Sun Park & Min-gu Kim. (2026). Does tapping in sync reflect cognitive control? Links between sensorimotor synchronization, social context, and executive function in early childhood. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00443-5

article_title: Personalized targeted memory reactivation enhances consolidation of challenging memories via slow wave and spindle dynamics
citation: Check, G.-H., Kweon, Y.-S., Oh, S., & Lee, S.-W. (2025). Personalized targeted memory reactivation enhances consolidation of challenging memories via slow wave and spindle dynamics. npj Science of Learning 10:47. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00340-3
title: Personalized TMR protocol: response-contingent cue repetition schedule (1/2/4 PRES by difficulty and accuracy)
description: A sleep-based intervention in which auditory cues for 104 semantically related word pairs are replayed during stable NREM 2/NREM 3 sleep, with the number of presentations (PRES) adjusted by learners' prospective difficulty ratings and pre-sleep recall accuracy: "1 PRES for correct responses at L2, 2 PRES for incorrect responses at L2, and 4 PRES for any response at L3"; no cues were delivered for L1 items. Unlike fixed TMR, cue frequency tracks individual memory trace strength and task difficulty. Prospective three-level difficulty self-ratings (L1–L3) taken after each retrieval trial drive the schedule.
requirements: A sleep expert monitoring EEG in real-time to deliver cues during stable NREM 2 or NREM 3 for at least 10 consecutive 30-s epochs
Prospective difficulty self-ratings and pre-sleep retrieval accuracy for each word pair
Cue-to-cue spacing of approximately 5 s exceeding the spindle refractory period
constraints: Manual administration of auditory stimuli by sleep experts poses challenges for real-world applications
The small sample per group may limit generalizability of the findings
target_learners: Healthy young adults learning semantically related word pairs (mean age 26.57)
target_learning_goals: Long-term retention and error correction of paired-associate verbal memories over a 12-hour sleep interval
examples: 12 participants received cues tailored to difficulty: 6.8 ± 4.1 cues in the 1-PRES condition, 39.7 ± 66.4 in 2-PRES, and 877.0 ± 299.5 in 4-PRES, totaling 923.4 ± 318.2 cues over 67.1 ± 23.3 min
key_sources: Check, G.-H., Kweon, Y.-S., Oh, S., & Lee, S.-W. (2025). Personalized targeted memory reactivation enhances consolidation of challenging memories via slow wave and spindle dynamics. npj Science of Learning 10:47. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00340-3

article_title: Personalized targeted memory reactivation enhances consolidation of challenging memories via slow wave and spindle dynamics
citation: Check, G.-H., Kweon, Y.-S., Oh, S., & Lee, S.-W. (2025). Personalized targeted memory reactivation enhances consolidation of challenging memories via slow wave and spindle dynamics. npj Science of Learning 10:47. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00340-3
title: System consolidation framework: NREM slow waves and spindles support sleep-dependent transfer and stabilization of memory traces
description: The article operates within a system consolidation framework in which "memories are gradually transferred from hippocampal to neocortical storage sites" during sleep, supported by two NREM oscillatory dynamics: slow waves, which "promote widespread cortical synchrony and maintains synaptic homeostasis", and sleep spindles generated by thalamocortical circuits, which "enhance hippocampal-cortical communication and facilitate robust memory consolidation". These oscillations synchronize neural activity across distributed regions, reinforcing memory reactivation and integration into cortical networks. External interventions like TMR aim to synchronize with and enhance these mechanisms.
requirements: Stable NREM 2 and NREM 3 sleep stages for effective cueing, with stimulation paused during wake, REM, or NREM 1
constraints: The framework concerns NREM-based consolidation; REM and NREM 1 epochs are excluded from stimulation and analysis
target_learners: Adult learners consolidating newly encoded declarative material during overnight sleep
target_learning_goals: Sleep-dependent memory consolidation and long-term retention of newly learned information
examples: ERPAC analysis showed enhanced SW-spindle coupling in both cueing groups relative to CNT, interpreted as improved coordination between thalamocortical and hippocampal networks
key_sources: Check, G.-H., Kweon, Y.-S., Oh, S., & Lee, S.-W. (2025). Personalized targeted memory reactivation enhances consolidation of challenging memories via slow wave and spindle dynamics. npj Science of Learning 10:47. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00340-3

article_title: Three mechanisms of language comprehension are revealed through cluster analysis of individuals with language deficits
citation: Vyshedskiy, A., Venkatesh, R., Khokhlovich, E. & Satik, D. (2024). Three mechanisms of language comprehension are revealed through cluster analysis of individuals with language deficits. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00284-0
title: Prefrontal Synthesis (PFS), Prefrontal Modification (PFM), and memory recall as the neurological mechanisms underlying the three language-comprehension clusters
description: The article proposes that the three empirically-derived clusters map onto three neurologically distinct mechanisms. Prefrontal Synthesis (PFS), mediated by the LPFC via frontoposterior connections such as the arcuate fasciculus, deliberately juxtaposes two or more mental objects and underlies the syntactic mechanism. The mechanism of modifying color or size of a single mental object is called "Prefrontal Modification or PFM", limited to the ventral pathway's control of a single object's appearance, and underlies the modifier mechanism. Command comprehension relies only on recalling existing object-encoding neuronal ensembles from memory. The article reports that all seven sentence types requiring combination of two or more mental objects clustered into the syntactic mechanism, "This prediction was borne out of data".
requirements: Interpretation of the clusters depends on the cognitive-neuroscience account linking abilities to PFS, PFM, and memory recall; without defining these subcomponents of symbolic thinking the authors state they could not interpret the clusters
constraints: PFM and PFS are voluntary and deliberate, LPFC-dependent; involuntary imagination and spontaneous insight (vmPFC-dependent) are too slow to mediate comprehension, per the authors
Routinization offers an additional PFS-independent route to interpreting syntactic sentences
target_learners: children and adolescents with language comprehension deficits
target_learning_goals: language comprehension of commands, modifiers, and syntactic structures
examples: Sentences with spatial prepositions, flexible syntax, stories, fairy tales, explanations, possessive pronouns, and verb tenses clustered together as predicted for PFS-mediated types
Understanding "give me the short blue pencil" was interpreted as PFM: recall of the pencil followed by LPFC modification of size and color

article_title: Three mechanisms of language comprehension are revealed through cluster analysis of individuals with language deficits
citation: Vyshedskiy, A., Venkatesh, R., Khokhlovich, E. & Satik, D. (2024). Three mechanisms of language comprehension are revealed through cluster analysis of individuals with language deficits. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00284-0
title: Refinement of the Merge hypothesis: a split into simple Merge (PFM-mediated) and complex Merge (PFS-mediated)
description: The article engages the linguistics hypothesis that unbounded Merge — a cognitive operation taking two linguistic units (e.g., 'blue' and 'cat') and forming a set — is the uniquely human generative engine of infinite expression. It argues the clustering data refine this hypothesis by distinguishing two subcomponents. The article reports that "25% of participants in our study acquired the modi ﬁer mechanism without developing the syntactic mechanism", which suggests "a division within the Merge operation": "simple Merge", underling comprehension of color, size, and number modifiers and mediated by PFM, and "complex Merge", underling syntactic structures and mediated by PFS. The finding of a large command-limited cluster also supports Merge by confirming command abilities are mediated by a separate mechanism.
requirements: Interpretation rests on the empirical dissociation of modifier from syntactic abilities in the phenotype data, which requires the PFM/PFS neurological account
constraints: Merge is positioned as a separator between modifier and syntactic abilities on one hand and command abilities on the other; command structures are limited by definition to comprehension of single words
target_learners: children and adolescents with language comprehension deficits
target_learning_goals: comprehension of modifiers and syntactic linguistic structures
examples: The modifier phenotype's possession of modifier abilities without syntactic abilities was taken as evidence for the simple-Merge/complex-Merge division

article_title: Context-based learning for Inhibition of alternative conceptions: the next step forward in science education
citation: Alexandra Renouard and Yves Mazabraud. (2018). Context-based learning for Inhibition of alternative conceptions: the next step forward in science education. npj Science of Learning 3:10. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0026-9
title: Interaction-centered context-based learning model for inhibiting alternative conceptions
description: The article proposes a synthetic learning model in which learning is driven by interactions between individuals and their contextual elements. Context "designates each element with which we interact specifically, such as the people around us, media, teaching and learning resources, or our living environment". Rather than the classical transformist tradition of conceptual change, the approach "focuses on the learning context rather than on conceptions themselves", aiming to act on brain inhibition processes by identifying environmental factors that impede scientific learning.
requirements: Individual contexts must be describable, requiring survey of teacher, student, media, textbook and environment interactions
constraints: The model is a proposal in a perspective article; no empirical test of the model is reported in the article
target_learning_goals: acquisition of scientific conceptions
scientific literacy
examples: The authors thank students and parents who accepted to participate to the testing of the model, though no test results are reported

title: Student profile atlas for context-based science teaching
description: An atlas of student profiles built from quantified learner-context interactions. Parameters defining each interaction are "its nature (human-human, human-object, technological, verbal, peer-to-peer, or hierarchical relationship), as well as its intensity", its stability and its resistance, quantified by criteria chosen per study. The number of profile types, their percentage and repartition "define an atlas that may be taken into account to either change the curriculum or to design temporary pedagogical projects".
requirements: Data collected via interviews or Multiple Choice Questions for small samples, or online questionnaires with automated processing for large populations
constraints: Quantification criteria need to be chosen for each study; the atlas requires an entry per individual or a statistically representative group
target_learning_goals: targeted design of science instruction
curriculum adaptation
examples: The article describes example student profiles with weak to strong interaction links and matched targeted actions in its Figure 2

article_title: The gendered effects of the COVID-19 pandemic on adolescent literacy and schooling outcomes in India
citation: Nandi, A., Haberland, N., Kozak, M., & Ngô, T. D. (2023). The gendered effects of the COVID-19 pandemic on adolescent literacy and schooling outcomes in India. npj Science of Learning, 8, 42. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00193-8
title: Target remedial education programs toward poor and marginalized students to recover pandemic learning losses
description: This principle holds that after large-scale learning disruptions, remedial education programs should be directed especially toward poor and marginalized students, who bear the largest losses. The authors state that "Remedial education programs, especially for poor and marginalized students, are necessary for improving learning levels and reducing the longer-term risk of dropping out of school." The recommendation follows directly from their finding that literacy losses were concentrated among the poorest-quintile, rural, and disadvantaged-caste girls, and is reinforced by cited evidence that targeted after-school recovery programs in Tamil Nadu were highly cost-effective.
requirements: Governments must allocate more resources and improve the quality of education delivery to support learning recovery after school closures
constraints: The authors' own evidence is limited to 15–17-year-olds in India; unobserved differences between pre- and post-COVID groups may bias the estimates, and subgroup findings for boys may reflect inadequate statistical power
target_learners: Adolescents aged 15–17 in India, especially girls in poor, rural, and socioeconomically disadvantaged caste households
target_learning_goals: Foundational literacy (ability to read a complete sentence)
Schooling attainment and reduced dropout risk
examples: A Tamil Nadu state education recovery program of after-school learning sessions covering 3.3 million students recovered 28% of language and 21% of mathematics learning loss at a cost of US$7.6 per child per year

article_title: Psychological proximity improves reasoning in academic aptitude tests
citation: Britt Hadar, Maayan Katzir, Sephi Pumpian, Tzur Karelitz and Nira Liberman. (2023). Psychological proximity improves reasoning in academic aptitude tests. npj Science of Learning 8:10. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00158-x
title: Test developers should pre-test question materials so content is not psychologically closer to some examinees than to others
description: The article recommends that cognitive-test developers treat the psychological distance of question content as a designable property rather than a neutral one. It argues that "some differences in a person 's distance to test items may also depend on social group", since culture-specific entities feel close to some examinees and alien to others. Developers should therefore "take into account the demographic and socioeconomic characteristics of examinees" and "try to construct questions that do not create or amplify differences in level of achievement that are based on these differences", via pre-testing and tailoring content.
requirements: Access to examinee demographics or pre-test panels to judge whether items invoke proximal or distal content for the target population
constraints: Psychological distance to test items is idiosyncratic, depending on familiarity, knowledge and exposure, so calibration is population-specific
target_learners: Examinees taking high-stakes academic aptitude and cognitive assessment tests
target_learning_goals: Accurate measurement of verbal reasoning ability without distance-based cultural bias
examples: The authors propose pre-testing materials and tailoring content to avoid making it psychologically closer to some examinees than to others, noting the bias would impact low-scoring examinees in particular.
key_sources: Britt Hadar, Maayan Katzir, Sephi Pumpian, Tzur Karelitz and Nira Liberman. (2023). Psychological proximity improves reasoning in academic aptitude tests. npj Science of Learning 8:10. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00158-x

article_title: Psychological proximity improves reasoning in academic aptitude tests
citation: Britt Hadar, Maayan Katzir, Sephi Pumpian, Tzur Karelitz and Nira Liberman. (2023). Psychological proximity improves reasoning in academic aptitude tests. npj Science of Learning 8:10. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00158-x
title: Construal level theory account of opposing distance/proximity predictions for reasoning
description: The article organizes its hypotheses with construal level theory (CLT), which "proposes that objects that are distal in time, space, or social perspective or are uncertain (i.e., distant on the dimension of hypotheticality), are mentally represented (i.e., construed) on a higher level of abstraction". It uses CLT to derive two opposing predictions: distance fosters abstraction that filters irrelevant details and groups information, reducing working-memory load, while proximity yields concrete, vivid, detailed representations that are processed with more attention, each plausibly aiding reasoning. The three studies test these competing accounts empirically.
requirements: Reasoning problems whose extraneous content (objects, people, times, places) can be rewritten as psychologically proximal or distal while retaining logical structure
constraints: Prior knowledge activated by proximity or distance is superfluous to solving the problems correctly, by the article's design
target_learners: Examinees solving verbal reasoning problems on aptitude assessments
target_learning_goals: Correct solution of verbal reasoning problems requiring accurate representation of parameters and mapping onto a logical structure
examples: Studies 1–3 contrasted proximal versions (objects and places in participants' culture, ingroup members, recent past) against distal versions (distant cultures, unfamiliar groups, distant past).

article_title: A practical implementation science framework for education
citation: Allen, S. E., Bardach, L., Jirout, J., Mackey, A., McCoy, D., Pesando, L. M., & Kizilcec, R. F. (2026). A practical implementation science framework for education. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00430-w
title: A four-phase implementation framework for education adapted from the EPIS Framework
description: The article presents a simplified protocol for implementing evidence-based pedagogical practices and technologies in real-world educational settings. It breaks the process into four milestones, each of which must be fully met before advancing: "Exploration Phase: Selecting the right intervention requires forming partnerships with students and teachers"; a Preparation Phase for developing a revisable Theory of Change; an Implementation Phase of small-scale testing; and a Sustainment Phase assimilating the intervention into regular operations. The authors chose the EPIS delineation because "it has two planning phases, one for exploration and another for preparation, whereas other process-based frameworks have only one planning phase."
requirements: Each milestone must be achieved and evaluated before moving to the next, using the supplementary checklist to evaluate progress
Successful implementation requires a level of time-consuming, resource-intensive planning that exceeds what can be expected in advance of submitting most grant proposals
constraints: The framework is a simplification: the supplementary tools do not include a list of every factor to consider, and the authors state the protocols should be viewed as a foundation rather than a definitive or exhaustive manual
target_learners: School students in K-12 and higher education settings where evidence-based practices and technologies are being implemented
target_learning_goals: Improving learning outcomes and student well-being through faithful implementation of research-validated pedagogical practices and technologies
examples: The four phases are mapped onto the Milpitas School District technology initiative, which used small-scale pilot tests and ongoing feedback as part of regular operations

article_title: A practical implementation science framework for education
citation: Allen, S. E., Bardach, L., Jirout, J., Mackey, A., McCoy, D., Pesando, L. M., & Kizilcec, R. F. (2026). A practical implementation science framework for education. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00430-w
title: Thorough Inquiry: implementation projects should continually deepen understanding of learners' needs and monitor for unforeseen issues
description: One of three complementary principles for success the article offers as a positive reframing of the failure modes. Thorough Inquiry holds that "Successful projects continually strive to gain a deep understanding of students' needs, explore multiple possible ways to meet those needs, consider the unique constraints in the local context, and closely monitor for unforeseen issues." It requires committing time and resources to understanding the problem before committing to a solution.
requirements: An intentional allocation of time and resources to understand the problem before committing to a solution
constraints: The authors state the three failure modes are more likely where time and resources are not specifically allocated in those areas
target_learners: Students and teachers in schools undergoing implementation of new practices or technologies
target_learning_goals: Selecting and sustaining interventions that genuinely meet local student learning needs
examples: The Milpitas superintendent opened the initiative by asking teachers and principals what the school of the future would look like, rather than negotiating with vendors first as the LAUSD did

article_title: A practical implementation science framework for education
citation: Allen, S. E., Bardach, L., Jirout, J., Mackey, A., McCoy, D., Pesando, L. M., & Kizilcec, R. F. (2026). A practical implementation science framework for education. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00430-w
title: Teamwork & Communication: clear roles and shared decisions with students and teachers across all organizational levels
description: The second principle for success: "Successful projects have clear team member roles, make all important decisions in partnership with students and teachers, and openly share setbacks and successes." The article grounds this in Implementation Science consensus that any implementation project must consider both individual-level behavioral factors and systemic organizational factors, and that all levels of the organization have essential contributions to make. Budgets should actively build a team with clear lines of communication and formal roles for stakeholders, co-investigators, project staff, and leadership.
requirements: A budget allocated to actively build a team with clear lines of communication and formal stakeholder roles
constraints: The article notes many efforts fail by not engaging with stakeholders at all levels of the organization
target_learners: Students, teachers, administrators, and families as implementation stakeholders
target_learning_goals: Sustained adoption of evidence-based pedagogical practices through genuine stakeholder partnership
examples: In high-engagement postsecondary pedagogy implementations, the most common feature of successful projects was meaningful collaboration between instructors and departmental leadership, especially support amid early setbacks

article_title: A practical implementation science framework for education
citation: Allen, S. E., Bardach, L., Jirout, J., Mackey, A., McCoy, D., Pesando, L. M., & Kizilcec, R. F. (2026). A practical implementation science framework for education. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00430-w
title: Iterative Revision: iterate within each phase and adapt plans in response to new information
description: The third principle for success: "Successful projects iterate within each phase until meeting the milestones to a high standard, set flexible timelines and budgets, and adapt their plan in response to new information." The article argues that because implementation is an ill-structured problem, where the best strategy cannot be anticipated in advance, the plan must anticipate challenges and the need for ongoing revision. Iterative revision complements thorough planning rather than replacing it.
requirements: Flexible timelines and budgets, plus explicit budgeting of time, resources, and personnel to continuously revise strategies based on ongoing feedback
constraints: Iteration only works alongside meticulously achieved concrete milestones; the article warns it is possible to have the proper mindset while inadvertently setting the project up for failure
target_learners: Education researchers, administrators, teachers, and students partnering on school change initiatives
target_learning_goals: Maintaining intervention effectiveness as unforeseen challenges emerge during real-world implementation
examples: The Milpitas initiative's phased roll-out with small-scale pilot tests revealed the need for adaptations to the original plan before full scale

title: Supplementary implementation toolkit: one-page overview, milestone checklist, SWOT-based Theory of Change brainstorming aid, and case studies
description: A set of simplified planning tools provided in the article's supplementary information, designed to avoid jargon and integrate existing frameworks. It includes "a one-page summary of the principles, processes, and pitfalls," "a checklist for planning and conducting an implementation project that is patterned after familiar pre-registration protocols" providing criteria for advancing between stages, "a brainstorming aid to help craft a Theory of Change" based on SWOT Analysis, and brief accounts of three well-documented case studies. The tools deliberately do not itemize every possible factor, instead ensuring planning is sufficiently thorough in finding factors to consider.
requirements: Used as a basis to ensure sufficiently thorough planning, with users expected to engage the broader Implementation Science literature or consult specialists for more complex issues
constraints: The authors state the simplification necessary to increase accessibility omits depth and nuance present in more comprehensive frameworks, and the toolkit should be viewed as a foundation rather than a definitive or exhaustive manual

target_learning_goals: Planning and conducting implementation projects that avoid the three common failure modes

article_title: Reading ability conflates SES creativity gaps
citation: Guilherme Lichand, Lêticia Lopes, Sachin Allums. (2026). Reading ability conflates SES creativity gaps. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00404-y
title: Assessments of higher-order skills should account for limitations in foundational skills, e.g., by administering oral exams or non-verbal measures
description: The article recommends that creativity and other higher-order-skill assessments better account for limitations in foundational skills such as reading, which are disproportionately concentrated among low-income students. Concretely, it suggests that "assessors might consider administering oral exams or even non-verbal measures of creativity or other higher-order skills in order to accurately capture underlying skills." This follows from the experimental finding that removing reading requirements eliminates or reverses SES gaps. The authors also warn that unfair test design "might end up reinforcing deficit narratives that mischaracterize the potential of disadvantaged students."
requirements: Assessment items must otherwise be answerable verbally or non-verbally, as in the trials where students responded aloud and enumerators recorded responses
constraints: The article notes it remains unclear whether the findings extend to convergent thinking, form-first vs function-first divergent tasks, or figural creativity; reading instructions aloud in figural tasks might help but this cannot be said for certain
target_learners: K-12 students, particularly low-SES students with limited reading proficiency
target_learning_goals: Accurate assessment of creative thinking and other higher-order skills
examples: In Studies 2 and 3, enumerators read question prompts aloud in the treatment condition and typed students' spoken answers in both conditions, isolating creativity from reading and writing ability

article_title: A Bayesian perspective on observers’ inference of group norms
citation: Duan, J., Guo, X., Zheng, L. & Yin, J. (2026). A Bayesian perspective on observers' inference of group norms. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00405-x
title: Bayesian inference model of group norm inference
description: The article's computational account treats observers as "lay Bayesians" who integrate observed group behavior with prior beliefs to update the probability that a group norm exists. The model derives posterior probabilities from the number or proportion of norm-consistent behaviors and was compared against a frequency-tracking baseline that relies exclusively on the cumulative tally of observed evidence. In all three experiments its outputs positively predicted participants' judgments, and it captured fine-grained variability that the baseline clustered away.
requirements: Requires manipulation of the number or proportion of norm-consistent behaviors and participants' prior and posterior probability judgments about norm existence.
constraints: The study examines injunctive normative constraints in novel group situations; boundary conditions under which observed behaviors are taken as norm evidence could not be determined in the current study.
target_learners: Adult volunteers judging computer-animated group events
target_learning_goals: Inferring latent group norms from observed behavior patterns in novel social situations
examples: Model-derived posteriors predicted judgmental posteriors (β = 0.69 in Experiment 1; β = 0.87 in Experiment 2) in Bayesian hierarchical regressions with random participant effects.

article_title: Neural mechanisms underpinning the association between visual arts education and creativity
citation: Jing Teng, Xinuo Qiao, Kelong Lu, Tuo Liu, Xinyue Wang, Zhenni Gao, Tingting Yu & Ning Hao (2025). Neural mechanisms underpinning the association between visual arts education and creativity. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00388-1
title: Incorporate design-related visual arts practices such as sketching, visual imagination, and visual-spatial problem solving into general curricula as elective or supplementary courses
description: This principle holds that elements of design-related visual arts education — practices such as sketching, visual imagination, and visual-spatial problem solving — can be incorporated into general curricula as elective or supplementary courses. The article argues these practices "directly engage cognitive processes such as flexibility, imagination, and problem-solving, which are essential for success in various fields". It is grounded in the study's findings that design majors showed higher creative performance and more efficient, flexible neural processing, though the authors note further research is needed before policy conclusions.
requirements: The recommended practices are design-related ones the study links to creative engagement: sketching, visual imagination, and visual-spatial problem solving, offered as elective or supplementary courses.
constraints: The article states the findings are quasi-experimental, may reflect pre-existing differences, and should not be generalized beyond the design-major context; further research is needed.
target_learning_goals: domain-general creativity
divergent thinking
flexibility, imagination, and problem-solving
examples: The study compared design majors with propensity-score-matched non-design majors and found the design group performed better across creative tasks and showed more efficient, flexible brain network engagement.

article_title: Longitudinal changes in cortical responses to letter-speech sound stimuli in 8–11 year-old children
citation: Romanovska, L., Janssen, R. & Bonte, M. (2022). Longitudinal changes in cortical responses to letter-speech sound stimuli in 8–11 year-old children. npj Science of Learning 7:2. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00118-3
title: Expansion-renormalisation / inverted-U account of reading-skill automatisation in the developing speech-language network
description: The article proposes that non-linear, inverted-U developmental trajectories in cortical responses to letter-speech sound stimuli reflect a gradual switch from effortful to automatised processing. It states that "skill learning in general is thought to re ﬂect an expansion-renormalisation pattern, with an initial increase in cortical activation/volume in the key areas involved in the acquisition of a speci ﬁc skill, followed by a decrease once pro ﬁciency is reached". Applying this to reading, the observed left STG and pre-CG changes "may re ﬂect changes during the proposed prolonged time-course of letter-speech sound automatisation", paralleling reported inverted-U trajectories in VWFA/ventral occipito-temporal cortex. The account integrates active explicit mapping strategies early in learning with passive associative mechanisms as proficiency increases.
requirements: Longitudinal measurement spanning the developmental period in which letter-speech sound mappings become automatised
Tasks that engage the letter-speech sound mapping regions being tracked
constraints: The authors state the pattern must be verified in larger samples and that it "may re ﬂect" rather than demonstrates the mechanism
No significant ventral occipito-temporal session differences were found, possibly because the simple "aba"/"ada" text stimuli "do not provide optimal engagement of the VWFA"
target_learners: Typically reading children aged 8–11 in the first years of reading instruction
target_learning_goals: Automatisation of letter-speech sound mappings supporting word decoding

title: Text-based recalibration paradigm for probing letter-speech sound mappings
description: An audio-visual perceptual-learning paradigm in which "aba"/"ada" text is combined with an individually determined ambiguous /a?a/ speech sound during exposure blocks, shifting later auditory-only perception of the ambiguous sound toward the text. In this study children completed four runs with 24 exposure blocks and post-test trials on /a?a/ and its two flanking sounds, inside fMRI across three yearly sessions. The paradigm was "speci ﬁcally designed to investigate reading-induced changes in the left posterior STC" and avoided the working-memory demands of congruency paradigms.

MR-compatible audio presentation in silent gaps between volume acquisitions

The simple two-word text stimuli may not optimally engage the VWFA

target_learning_goals: Short-term perceptual learning of letter-speech sound associations; probing automatisation of audio-visual letter-speech integration

article_title: Self-perceptions as mechanisms of achievement inequality: evidence across 70 countries
citation: Hofer, S. I., Heine, J.-H., Besharati, S., Yip, J. C., Reinhold, F., & Brummelman, E. (2024). Self-perceptions as mechanisms of achievement inequality: evidence across 70 countries. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00211-9
title: Psychological affordances account: environments act as 'fertile soil' determining whether self-perceptions translate into achievement
description: The article draws on the psychological affordances account, in which self-perceptions are 'seeds' that only influence behavior in environments that afford that behavior — 'a fertile soil in which these seeds can grow'. Self-perceptions are defined as children's mental representations and evaluations of themselves, often taking the form of personal theories that structure experience. The account explains why the competency and fear-of-failure associations with achievement were stronger in higher-social-mobility countries, with environments that 'afford' growth mindsets conveying that children can improve through effort and dedication.
requirements: A country context that affords acting in line with beneficial self-perceptions (higher social mobility in this study's analyses)
constraints: The account was tested with cross-sectional, correlational PISA 2018 data; causal conclusions are not permitted and b-path estimates may contain reverse effects from achievement to self-perceptions
target_learning_goals: Reading achievement
reduction of socioeconomic achievement inequality

title: Three-step design model for GAI-powered characters in IVR
description: The article's Pedagogical Design answer to RQ2 is a three-step design model integrating pedagogy with GAI and VR: "selecting the applicable reference framework, identifying the learning objectives and the instructional methods that could be feasible in IVR, and designing the GAI characters." It was applied in a sustainability education context, grounding character design in the refined sustainability competence framework and producing the Tero and Madida use cases. The authors present it as how AI technologies, learning content, and pedagogical approaches "can be integrated having the form of a pedagogical GAI character in IVR."

article_title: Applying the science of learning to EdTech evidence evaluations using the EdTech Evidence Evaluation Routine (EVER)
citation: Natalia Kucirkova, Garvin Brod and Nadine Gaab. (2023). Applying the science of learning to EdTech evidence evaluations using the EdTech Evidence Evaluation Routine (EVER). npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00186-7
title: The EdTech Evidence Evaluation Routine (EVER) as a framework for evaluating EdTech evidence
description: EVER is a simple guide proposed by the authors to evaluate the evidence base of existing EdTech solutions and to help companies grow their products' evidence base. It is a matrix crossing evaluation approaches (conceptual, qualitative, quantitative, validation) with quality assurance aspects, with each cell rated. The authors state it "can be used as a prompt for reflection when evaluating the evidence portfolio of diverse EdTech products, processes and initiatives" and is best used as part of formative evaluations.
requirements: Criteria for assigning scores differ across evaluation method types, so users must apply type-appropriate criteria
constraints: EVER is best used as part of formative evaluations; it is not intended to determine good or bad solutions
It should be supplemented with other frameworks targeting cost-effectiveness, data privacy and teachers' usability evaluations
target_learning_goals: Literacy and math foundational skills
Behaviour change
Assessment combined with intervention
examples: Applied to EdTech for assessment, intervention or edutainment in K-12 education, at lifecycle stages from pre-company accelerator stage to mature companies seeking funding
key_sources: Natalia Kucirkova, Garvin Brod and Nadine Gaab. (2023). Applying the science of learning to EdTech evidence evaluations using the EdTech Evidence Evaluation Routine (EVER). npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00186-7

article_title: Applying the science of learning to EdTech evidence evaluations using the EdTech Evidence Evaluation Routine (EVER)
citation: Natalia Kucirkova, Garvin Brod and Nadine Gaab. (2023). Applying the science of learning to EdTech evidence evaluations using the EdTech Evidence Evaluation Routine (EVER). npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00186-7
title: Four quality assurance aspects for judging EdTech evidence: methodological quality, outcome strength, generalizability, ethics and transparency
description: EVER organizes evidence quality along four aspects. Methodological quality asks whether methods are appropriately executed, described and justified. Outcome strength concerns sizable impact or predictive value, quantified via effect size or sensitivity/specificity. Generalizability is the extension of findings from one sample to the target population, requiring representativeness. Ethics and transparency ensure ethical design, users' well-being, culturally-responsive approaches and transparent data use.
requirements: Each criterion's strength is rated on a 0–5 point-scale for each cell, including cells where the company has no activity
constraints: A larger sample typically comes with higher generalizability but still needs to match the target population in demographic characteristics, socio-cultural values, skills and abilities
target_learning_goals: Evaluating whether EdTech works, for whom, and ethically
examples: The aspects answer stakeholder questions such as whether the tool works for my students, how much of an effect it has, and whether users know which personal data are collected
key_sources: Natalia Kucirkova, Garvin Brod and Nadine Gaab. (2023). Applying the science of learning to EdTech evidence evaluations using the EdTech Evidence Evaluation Routine (EVER). npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00186-7

title: EVER's Table 1 matrix of four evaluation approaches by four quality assurance aspects
description: Table 1 outlines the evidence base and evaluation approaches employed to test an EdTech product (rows: conceptual, qualitative, quantitative, validation) crossed with quality assurance aspects (columns: methodological quality, outcome strength/predictive value, generalizability, ethics and transparency), each cell marked for rating. The authors note criteria can differ by method type, e.g. methodological quality criteria for conceptual studies can differ from generalisability criteria in quantitative or qualitative studies.
requirements: Each of the cells is rated on the 0–5 point-scale

examples: The matrix is applied in conjunction with local quality assurance assessments at district or school level and by EdTech developers in iterative product development

title: Embrace methodological plurality when evaluating EdTech evidence rather than positioning RCTs as best for all
description: The authors argue that EdTech evaluation should recognise the value of all types of research. They state it is important "to embrace methodological plurality that recognises the value of all types of research, without positioning RCT evidence as the best evidence for all EdTech", because different designs and methods answer different research questions and there is no universally applicable hierarchy of research methods.
requirements: A match between the method and the question being asked
target_learners: All learners served by EdTech products
target_learning_goals: Sound evaluation of EdTech impact on learning
examples: EVER rates conceptual, qualitative, quantitative and validation approaches side by side rather than ranking them

article_title: Non-linear development in statistical learning of visual orthographic regularities
citation: Duan, R., Sun, Q., & Tong, X. (2025). Non-linear development in statistical learning of visual orthographic regularities. npj Science of Learning 10, 6. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00298-2
title: iMINERVA memory-based account of consistency-dependent statistical learning development
description: The article invokes the iMINERVA model, "a computational model accounting for distributional statistical learning" proposed by Thiessen and Pavlik Jr., which emphasizes long-term memory via "memory-based principles of similarity-based comparison, decay, integration, and abstraction". Under this account, learners compare prior and current pseudocharacters and integrate them into a consistent positional representation when consistency passes a threshold; integration facilitates learning at high and moderate consistency but is weakened at 60% consistency, and memory development with age yields different trajectories for more consistent levels.
requirements: Learners must encode and retain prior items in long-term memory to compare them with current input
constraints: The article presents this as an interpretation; it states the interplay of statistical learning development, memory, and prior language experience requires further tests to prove
target_learning_goals: acquisition of visual orthographic positional regularities
distributional statistical learning
examples: The article uses iMINERVA to explain why high (100%) and moderate (80%) consistency showed developmental change while low (60%) consistency showed none, attributing the latter to constrained memory retrieval of conflicted representations

article_title: Speech connectedness predicts reading performance three months in advance: a longitudinal experiment
citation: Bárbara Malcorra, Marina Ribeiro, Giovanna Jensen, Tamara Meletti & Natália Bezerra Mota. (2024). Speech connectedness predicts reading performance three months in advance: a longitudinal experiment. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00248-4
title: Word-recurrence graph analysis of oral narratives as a measure of speech connectedness
description: The article represents transcribed oral narratives as directed graphs in which "each node represents a word, and each directed edge represents the temporal order of consecutive words." Three connectedness attributes are computed: repeated edges (RE), largest connected component (LCC), and largest strongly connected component (LSC), using a 30-word moving window to control verbosity. The graphs "are not based on meaning but on recurrence patterns," which the authors argue lets them "reveal patterns of connectedness from the earliest stages of language acquisition because they do not rely on meaning or linguistic rules." Developmentally, RE decreases while LCC and LSC increase as children advance in schooling.
requirements: Audio-recorded, transcribed oral narratives (three 30-second narratives per session, concatenated)
constraints: Metrics reflect word recurrence patterns rather than semantic content or linguistic relationships
target_learners: first- and second-grade elementary school children (ages 5–8)
target_learning_goals: oral narrative structure
reading acquisition
phonological awareness
reading comprehension
examples: Three positive-affect IAPS images (a baby, a dog, a dessert) each viewed for 15 seconds, with narratives limited to 30 seconds and analyzed via a 30-word moving window

title: Scalable AI-based narrative collection and screening application
description: The authors describe a narrative collection application that displays three positive-content images, records children's spoken stories, and "transcribed automatically using an AI-based algorithm." Each narrative is converted into a word recurrence graph analyzed to determine academic development, and results can be plotted "on a normative curve representing the evolution of oral narrative complexity throughout the school years" to compare a child's communication-skill development with peers. The article presents this as "a safe and scalable way to evaluate public educational policies" and "a valuable, language-independent tool for education professionals."

constraints: Graph attributes indicate academic development in children without signs or symptoms of mental distress, per the cited prior work
target_learners: elementary school children in large-scale school settings, e.g., public education systems in Brazil
target_learning_goals: monitoring oral narrative development and reading acquisition on a large scale
examples: The study's own protocol: five 15-minute individual sessions across the 2022 school year, with storytelling tasks and reading performance tasks administered in regular class hours

article_title: Helping children with reading difficulties: some things we have learned so far
citation: Genevieve McArthur and Anne Castles. (2017). Helping children with reading difficulties: some things we have learned so far. npj Science of Learning (2017) 2:7. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0008-3
title: Proximal and distal causal schema for reading difficulties
description: The article proposes organising the causes of reading difficulties along a proximal/distal axis. A proximal cause is "a component of the cognitive system that directly and immediately produces that reading behaviour", while "a distal cause has a distant (i.e., an indirect or delayed) impact on a reading behaviour". The schema is used to categorise comorbidities as proximal or distal, to clarify reciprocal causal relationships between reading and self-concept, and to divide interventions into proximal (e.g., phonics, vocabulary training) and distal (e.g., coloured lenses) types.
requirements: Causal hypotheses generated by the schema must ultimately be tested through experimental training studies, as the authors state.
constraints: The authors present the schema as a simplifying tool for "almost overwhelming complexity", not as established causal knowledge.
target_learning_goals: word reading accuracy
reading fluency
reading comprehension
examples: The article uses the schema to explain how a history of poor vocabulary understanding may reduce motivation to read (distal), impairing letter-sound learning (proximal) and word reading.
key_sources: Genevieve McArthur and Anne Castles. (2017). Helping children with reading difficulties: some things we have learned so far. npj Science of Learning (2017) 2:7. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0008-3

article_title: Helping children with reading difficulties: some things we have learned so far
citation: Genevieve McArthur and Anne Castles. (2017). Helping children with reading difficulties: some things we have learned so far. npj Science of Learning (2017) 2:7. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0008-3
title: Multi-component cognitive models of reading as a roadmap of proximal causes
description: The article draws on several theoretical and computational models of reading which, despite varying in some respects, all include cognitive components representing letter and word recognition, recognition and production of speech sounds and spoken words, access to stored word meanings, and links between these components. Impairment in any component or link directly impairs reading behaviour. The article uses these models as "a useful roadmap, providing an explicit account of the key processes directly underpinning successful reading behaviour" when assessing poor readers.
requirements: Standardized tests of potential proximal causes, such as vocabulary and letter-sound knowledge tests, are needed to apply the roadmap in assessment.
constraints: The models vary in some respects, as the article notes, so the component list is a common core rather than a single settled architecture.
target_learning_goals: reading accuracy and comprehension
examples: The article cites the dual route cascaded model, the simple view of reading, the CDP+ model, and connectionist models as examples of this model family.
key_sources: Genevieve McArthur and Anne Castles. (2017). Helping children with reading difficulties: some things we have learned so far. npj Science of Learning (2017) 2:7. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0008-3

article_title: Helping children with reading difficulties: some things we have learned so far
citation: Genevieve McArthur and Anne Castles. (2017). Helping children with reading difficulties: some things we have learned so far. npj Science of Learning (2017) 2:7. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0008-3
title: Assess reading behaviours, proximal causes, and comorbidities before designing an individualised intervention
description: The article recommends a three-step assessment sequence that exploits heterogeneity rather than despairing of it. Practitioners first assess different aspects of reading (word reading accuracy, fluency, comprehension) with standardized tests, then test potential proximal causes using cognitive models as a roadmap, and finally assess comorbid spoken language, attention, anxiety, depression, and self-concept problems. The resulting profile makes it possible to design an intervention matched to the child's needs, targeting proximal impairments while accommodating comorbidities.
requirements: Teachers need appropriate training in administering the standardized reading and cognitive tests, and specialists (speech and language therapists, neuropsychologists, clinical psychologists) are needed for comorbidity assessment.
constraints: The article bases this approach on evidence "thus far", describing it as tentative and requiring coordinated efforts of teachers, specialists and parents.
target_learning_goals: word reading accuracy
reading fluency
reading comprehension
examples: The article names commercially available and free tests for each step, including the York Assessment for Reading Comprehension, the Castles and Coltheart Word Reading Test (CC2), the Peabody Picture Vocabulary Test, and the Letter-Sound Test available at www.motif.org.au.

article_title: Spatial thinking as the missing piece in mathematics curricula
citation: Katie A. Gilligan-Lee, Zachary C. K. Hawes and Kelly S. Mix. (2022). Spatial thinking as the missing piece in mathematics curricula. npj Science of Learning 7:10. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00128-9
title: Spatial visualization skills taxonomy: mental rotation, mental transformation, perspective taking, and spatial scaling
description: The article organizes target spatial skills under the umbrella of spatial visualization, defined as "the ability to generate and mentally manipulate objects or images". As shown in its Fig. 1, activities targeting spatial visualization include mental rotation (mentally turning objects/shapes by degrees of rotation), mental transformation (mentally combining or deconstructing shapes within or across planes), perspective taking (imagining scenes from different points of view), and spatial scaling (mentally mapping between spaces of different scales). The article uses this taxonomy to show which skills are absent from mathematics curricula.
requirements: Curriculum designers must attend to the dynamic and imaginative types of spatial thinking, not just naming shapes or verbal recall of properties
constraints: The article notes these activities are seldom referenced in mathematics curricula and none are mentioned in the Common Core State Standards for Mathematics
target_learners: school-age children from early years through secondary mathematics
target_learning_goals: spatial visualization supporting mathematical problem solving
using spatial visualization as a mental blackboard to model and manipulate mathematical problems and relations
examples: Fig. 1 presents sample spatial tasks: mental rotation, mental transformation, spatial scaling, and perspective taking items used to assess different spatial skills
key_sources: Katie A. Gilligan-Lee, Zachary C. K. Hawes and Kelly S. Mix. (2022). Spatial thinking as the missing piece in mathematics curricula. npj Science of Learning 7:10. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00128-9

It argues educators should "leverage their inherently spatial properties" and "promote both spatial and mathematical thinking simultaneously", noting that shape-naming tasks currently call mostly on memory and verbal recall rather than dynamic spatial skills.

article_title: Investigating lexical categorization in reading based on joint diagnostic and training approaches for language learners
citation: Benjamin Gagl & Klara Gregorová. (2024). Investigating lexical categorization in reading based on joint diagnostic and training approaches for language learners. npj Science of Learning 9:29. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00237-7
title: Lexical Categorization Model (LCM): pre-lexical word-likeness-based filtering in the left-ventral occipitotemporal cortex
description: The LCM holds that the left-ventral occipitotemporal cortex, including the visual word form area, implements a lexical categorization process: "This process is assumed to ﬁlter non-words from further consideration for lexical or semantic processing." Categorization is easy for highly word-like words and word-unlike non-words but difficult when their word-likeness distributions overlap, producing an inverted-U relationship between categorization uncertainty and word likeness. The model has no free parameters, making simulations transparent, and word-likeness is estimated from a lexicon of all German words (SUBTLEX).
requirements: Requires a lexicon-based word-likeness estimate (OLD20 based on all German five-letter uppercase words from SUBTLEX-DE) to compute lexical categorization uncertainty.
Requires explainable machine learning methods and meaningful model-derived features for the individualized diagnostics built on it.
constraints: Prior extensive model comparisons with native German readers identified the LCM as adequate for lvOT activation; the article notes alternative approaches can simulate visual word recognition entirely, which the neuro-cognitive approaches currently cannot.
target_learners: adult non-native German language learners who are slow readers
potentially other slow-reader groups such as dyslexics and illiterates
target_learning_goals: reading speed
visual word recognition
lexical categorization ability
examples: The training procedure was motivated directly from the model: a lexical decision task with feedback trains the categorization process assumed in the left-ventral occipitotemporal cortex.
key_sources: Benjamin Gagl & Klara Gregorová. (2024). Investigating lexical categorization in reading based on joint diagnostic and training approaches for language learners. npj Science of Learning 9:29. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00237-7

article_title: Investigating lexical categorization in reading based on joint diagnostic and training approaches for language learners
citation: Benjamin Gagl & Klara Gregorová. (2024). Investigating lexical categorization in reading based on joint diagnostic and training approaches for language learners. npj Science of Learning 9:29. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00237-7
title: Three-session feedback-based lexical decision training with pre-post reading-speed diagnostics
description: The training pattern comprises three daily sessions of a lexical decision task — 1600 five-letter stimuli per week, including 800 SUBTLEX-DE words, 400 pseudowords, and 400 consonant strings — with immediate feedback (green/red squares after each response), preceded and followed by a standardized SLS reading speed assessment. Only the pre-test and first session data are used for outcome prediction. This task structure trains lexical categorization while monitoring general reading speed change at the sentence level.
requirements: Stimuli drawn randomly from a lexicon to represent natural variation in word characteristics, increasing feature generalizability.
A standardized sentence-level reading speed test (adult SLS) for pre-post diagnostics.
In control comparisons, at least 14 days between the two randomized training weeks.
constraints: The post-test placement differed across experiments (day 3 in Experiment 1, day 4 in Experiments 2 and 3), which the authors handled with a design-change variable in the predictive model.
target_learning_goals: lexical categorization skill
reading speed
examples: In the font-change variant, the visual appearance of letter strings changed every 32 trials across 50 blocks, training adaptation of visual-orthographic representations alongside lexical categorization.
