article_title: Disrupting links between poverty, chronic stress, and educational inequality
citation: Madeline B. Harms and Sherona D. Garrett-Ruffin. (2023). Disrupting links between poverty, chronic stress, and educational inequality. npj Science of Learning 8:50. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00199-2
title: Poverty-related stress framework: chronic early-life stress from poverty alters neurocognitive development in ways that hinder academic performance
description: The article defines "poverty-related stress" as "this overall context of poverty" in which poverty-level income produces multiple contextual stressors while reducing families' ability to cope. It proposes that cumulative risk exposure produces chronic stress that alters neuroendocrine and neural development—biasing the nervous system toward reactive, defensive responding rather than a reflective, regulated state—and that executive function and threat/reward circuits likely mediate the link between SES and achievement.
requirements: Chronic, severe stress experienced during heightened-susceptibility developmental periods (early childhood and adolescence)
constraints: Policy recommendations focus on the United States; low- and middle-income countries face additional challenges not covered
target_learners: children living in poverty in the United States
target_learning_goals: executive function and self-regulation
academic learning and school readiness
examples: The article links childhood poverty to increased threat-detecting circuitry activity and decreased self-regulatory circuitry activity, explaining reduced classroom focus
key_sources: Madeline B. Harms and Sherona D. Garrett-Ruffin. (2023). Disrupting links between poverty, chronic stress, and educational inequality. npj Science of Learning 8:50. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00199-2

article_title: Early reading at first grade predicts adult reading at age 42 in typical and dyslexic readers
citation: Emilio Ferrer, Bennett A. Shaywitz, John M. Holahan and Sally E. Shaywitz. (2023). Early reading at first grade predicts adult reading at age 42 in typical and dyslexic readers. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00205-7
title: Do not require periodic retesting of adults with childhood-identified dyslexia seeking accommodations
description: The article argues that standardized testing agencies requiring applicants requesting accommodations to be retested every three or five years is not supported by longitudinal evidence. Because early reading level and the grade 1-5 trajectory strongly predict adult reading, "once a person is identified as dyslexic in the early grades, he or she is very likely to be dyslexic as an adult at age 42." This principle applies to accommodation policy for adult dyslexic readers.
requirements: Dyslexia identification must have occurred in the early grades with documented reading assessment
constraints: Findings come from one epidemiologic US cohort of primary English speakers followed to age 42
target_learning_goals: reading proficiency
access to accommodations for reading tasks
examples: The longitudinal data show dyslexic readers identified via WJ Reading Cluster and WISC-R criteria in grades 2 or 4 still showed substantial adult reading differences at age 42 on all ART-2 measures.
key_sources: Emilio Ferrer, Bennett A. Shaywitz, John M. Holahan and Sally E. Shaywitz. (2023). Early reading at first grade predicts adult reading at age 42 in typical and dyslexic readers. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00205-7

article_title: Effects of videos with whole-body movements on young children’s geography learning
citation: Mavilidi, M.F., Paas, F., Zou, L., Lubans, D.R., Mokhtari, L., Schmidt, M., Castro Alonso, J.C., Ng, R., & Bennet, S. (2026). Effects of Videos with Whole-Body Movements on Young Children's Geography Learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00408-8
title: Online movement-based geography video intervention for young children (embodied cognition condition)
description: A digital learning session in which children watched a world-map video with animated cartoon animals and "engage in simple full-body movements, mimicking the animal movements shown in the video", such as jumping like a kangaroo or walking like an elephant while moving between continents, while verbally repeating continent names. Each 5-min video was played twice, covering three continents (Oceania, Asia, America) with content on location, animal, favourite food and climate; sessions lasted 10-15 min in small groups of up to four children at a science museum. The seated control group watched the identical videos without movements.
requirements: Children verbally assenting plus written parental consent; quiet room at the museum; trained research assistants delivering pre-test, activity and post-test in order
constraints: Single learning session only; content limited to an introductory subset of geography competencies (naming continents and animals, locating them on a map)
conducted in small groups with a maximum of four children per session
target_learning_goals: Early geography knowledge: continent names, animals of each continent, and continent locations on a map
examples: Both conditions watched each 5-min video twice for repeated exposure; the intervention group received additional opportunities to practise the animal movements
key_sources: Mavilidi, M.F., Paas, F., Zou, L., Lubans, D.R., Mokhtari, L., Schmidt, M., Castro Alonso, J.C., Ng, R., & Bennet, S. (2026). Effects of Videos with Whole-Body Movements on Young Children's Geography Learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00408-8

article_title: Effects of videos with whole-body movements on young children’s geography learning
citation: Mavilidi, M.F., Paas, F., Zou, L., Lubans, D.R., Mokhtari, L., Schmidt, M., Castro Alonso, J.C., Ng, R., & Bennet, S. (2026). Effects of Videos with Whole-Body Movements on Young Children's Geography Learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00408-8
title: Integration of cognitive load theory and embodied cognition for digital movement-based learning
description: The article combines an evolutionary upgrade of cognitive load theory with embodied cognition to design and interpret digital movement-based learning. Physical actions are treated as a form of biologically primary knowledge serving as "cognitive offloading" mechanisms that may reduce working memory burden, while sensorimotor, multimodal representations are held to convey object properties and support memory encoding. In the study, movements also "fulfilled an analogous role of 'segmentation'", consolidating transient video information. The authors state that no measures were included to test the proposed mechanisms, so the mechanistic interpretation remains speculative.
requirements: Movements should be relevant to and temporally connected with the goal-directed learning task; complementary information presented across modalities without repetition
constraints: No cognitive load measures were included, so whether cognitive load was induced or alleviated in the embodied group cannot be inferred; overly cognitive or coordinatively demanding movements can impede learning
target_learners: Young children learning via digital environments
target_learning_goals: Knowledge acquisition in STEM domains such as geography through digitally supported embodied activity
examples: The game-based geography task was designed on cognitive load theory, embodied and experiential learning principles, with movements segmenting transient spoken text and animations
key_sources: Mavilidi, M.F., Paas, F., Zou, L., Lubans, D.R., Mokhtari, L., Schmidt, M., Castro Alonso, J.C., Ng, R., & Bennet, S. (2026). Effects of Videos with Whole-Body Movements on Young Children's Geography Learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00408-8

article_title: Effects of videos with whole-body movements on young children’s geography learning
citation: Mavilidi, M.F., Paas, F., Zou, L., Lubans, D.R., Mokhtari, L., Schmidt, M., Castro Alonso, J.C., Ng, R., & Bennet, S. (2026). Effects of Videos with Whole-Body Movements on Young Children's Geography Learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00408-8
title: Balance the cognitive demands of motor and learning tasks in digital movement-based learning
description: The article concludes that combining whole-body movement with digital instruction requires deliberately balancing the cognitive load of the motor task against the learning task. It states that "Balancing out the cognitive load demands of the motor and learning tasks is important for facilitation of learning outcomes, as too complex motor tasks may impede learning", and cites the proposal that physically demanding or poorly connected actions can impede learning. The null result is interpreted as consistent with the embodied condition introducing additional dual-task demands rather than reducing extraneous load.
requirements: Designers must calibrate movement complexity and temporal/meaningful connection to the learning task; movement should segment transient information without adding dual-task interference
constraints: The study could not verify the mechanism because cognitive load was not measured; null differences should be interpreted cautiously given the single brief session and simple content
target_learners: Young children in digital learning environments
target_learning_goals: Knowledge acquisition supported, rather than impeded, by concurrent physical activity
examples: In the study, whole-body movements were intended to act like segmentation of the transient video, but the authors note the dual-task performance may have been too complex, causing interference
key_sources: Mavilidi, M.F., Paas, F., Zou, L., Lubans, D.R., Mokhtari, L., Schmidt, M., Castro Alonso, J.C., Ng, R., & Bennet, S. (2026). Effects of Videos with Whole-Body Movements on Young Children's Geography Learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00408-8

article_title: Effects of videos with whole-body movements on young children’s geography learning
citation: Mavilidi, M.F., Paas, F., Zou, L., Lubans, D.R., Mokhtari, L., Schmidt, M., Castro Alonso, J.C., Ng, R., & Bennet, S. (2026). Effects of Videos with Whole-Body Movements on Young Children's Geography Learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00408-8
title: Open dataset and paired geography knowledge assessment materials (OSF release)
description: The study released its data and analyses publicly on OSF (https://osf.io/qr2un/overview), with analyses conducted on SPSS Statistics v29.0. Its learning measure assessed geography knowledge (naming continents and animals living in each continent, continents' location on the map) with a 1-minute free pre-test and an immediate post-test combining free-recall and cued-recall map-placement tasks, each worth a maximum of 6 points (12 total). The reliability coefficient (Cronbach's alpha) was .79 in the present study, aligning with a previous study using the same testing materials.
requirements: Pre-test scores were expected to be low in this age group; the pre-test is acknowledged as a coarse indicator of prior knowledge with limited sensitivity
constraints: The maximum possible post-test score was 12, and uniformly low pre-test scores mean floor effects could be a plausible explanation; the task captures only an introductory subset of geography competencies
target_learners: Children around age 5-6 in informal science-museum settings
target_learning_goals: Assessing early geography knowledge acquisition (continent names, animals, map locations)
examples: The cued-recall task presented an A3 printed map with toy animal figurines, and children matched animals to continents with a spoken prompt
key_sources: Mavilidi, M.F., Paas, F., Zou, L., Lubans, D.R., Mokhtari, L., Schmidt, M., Castro Alonso, J.C., Ng, R., & Bennet, S. (2026). Effects of Videos with Whole-Body Movements on Young Children's Geography Learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00408-8

article_title: Choice-making in an adaptive learning system with motivational pedagogical agents
citation: Man Su, Belle Dang, Andy Nguyen & Tomohiro Nagashima. (2025). Choice-making in an adaptive learning system with motivational pedagogical agents. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00366-7
title: Choice-making operationalized as a measurable, temporal facet of self-regulated learning
description: The article defines choice-making as an SRL component that bridges Zimmerman's performance and self-reflection phases, measured as the frequency of engagement with optional tasks in an adaptive system. It positions choice-making as broader than goal-setting, self-monitoring, help-seeking, or task selection, encompassing "persisting independently, switching strategies mid-task, or engaging with different resources within or across tasks". Process mining and LSA are used to capture it in situ over time.
requirements: Optional-task choice opportunities embedded in the learning system so engagement decisions are loggable
Fine-grained process data (e.g., logs amenable to LSA and process mining) rather than only aggregated metrics
constraints: Measured here only as task-level engagement decisions within clearly defined scenarios, not all forms of SRL choice such as goal-setting or help-seeking
target_learning_goals: Self-regulated learning and strategic choice-making during adaptive algebra practice
key_sources: Man Su, Belle Dang, Andy Nguyen & Tomohiro Nagashima. (2025). Choice-making in an adaptive learning system with motivational pedagogical agents. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00366-7

article_title: Enhancing learning and retrieval of new information: a review of the forward testing effect
citation: Chunliang Yang, Rosalind Potts and David R. Shanks. (2018). Enhancing learning and retrieval of new information: a review of the forward testing effect. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0024-y
title: Eight-mechanism theoretical framework for the forward testing effect, classified by locus (encoding vs retrieval) and motivational role
description: The review organizes candidate explanations of the forward testing effect along two dimensions: whether the mechanism acts at encoding or retrieval, and whether it is motivational. Non-motivational accounts are the release from PI, encoding reset, activation facilitation, encoding strategy, and retrieval strategy theories; motivational accounts are the test expectancy, failure-encoding-effort, and retrieval effort theories, the latter two attributing effort to "retrieval failures in prior interim tests" inducing dissatisfaction. Mechanisms are not mutually exclusive and may operate in parallel; which dominates depends on material, e.g. release from PI matters for single items while activation facilitation matters for complex materials.
requirements: Direct testing of key predictions made by different theoretical accounts, which the review says few have received
constraints: The review states most accounts are at a preliminary stage of development and few have been directly tested
Mechanisms need not be mutually exclusive and may produce overlapping forward testing effects
target_learners: College students and other learners studied in forward testing experiments
target_learning_goals: Learning and retrieval of new information following interim testing on prior material
examples: The review cites Yang et al.'s Experiment 3 measuring classification time as an index of retrieval effort, which affirmed the retrieval effort theory's prediction
Weinstein et al. had participants report test-expectancy before each list and found the Interim Test group's expectancy increased across lists while the Distractor group's decreased
key_sources: Chunliang Yang, Rosalind Potts and David R. Shanks. (2018). Enhancing learning and retrieval of new information: a review of the forward testing effect. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0024-y

article_title: Inter-brain coupling reflects disciplinary differences in real-world classroom learning
citation: Jingjing Chen, Penghao Qian, Xinqiao Gao, Baosong Li, Yu Zhang and Dan Zhang. (2023). Inter-brain coupling reflects disciplinary differences in real-world classroom learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00162-1
title: Inter-brain coupling framework distinguishing student-class coupling (hard disciplines) from student-top coupling (soft disciplines)
description: A framework in which individual students' inter-brain coupling to others during real classroom learning indexes the learning process without needing parametric task designs. Student-class coupling (to all other classmates) is proposed to reflect engagement with course content, whereas student-top coupling (to top-performing peers) captures alignment with exemplars of personal construction. The article argues the two serve as "potential neural correlates for successful learning in hard and soft disciplines correspondingly", with distinct dominant frequency bands (theta vs alpha) for the two disciplines.
requirements: Wearable EEG recording from an entire class during regular lessons across a semester
Final exam scores as outcome measures and both Pearson and permutation tests for significance
constraints: Findings rest on uncorrected p values for two disciplines in one class; effect sizes were relatively small (r2 = 0.187 for Chinese, r2 = 0.115 for Math) and the hard-soft dimension itself is described as contentious
target_learning_goals: successful classroom learning in hard disciplines (Math) and soft disciplines (Chinese)
examples: Thirty-four grade-10 students wore two-electrode headband EEG devices during 18 Chinese and 20 Math sessions over 4 months, with total interdependence (TI) used to compute pairwise inter-brain couplings
key_sources: Jingjing Chen, Penghao Qian, Xinqiao Gao, Baosong Li, Yu Zhang and Dan Zhang. (2023). Inter-brain coupling reflects disciplinary differences in real-world classroom learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00162-1

article_title: Inter-brain coupling reflects disciplinary differences in real-world classroom learning
citation: Jingjing Chen, Penghao Qian, Xinqiao Gao, Baosong Li, Yu Zhang and Dan Zhang. (2023). Inter-brain coupling reflects disciplinary differences in real-world classroom learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00162-1
title: Wearable dual-channel EEG headband setup for real-classroom brain recording
description: A portable EEG data-collection setup in which students wore "a dual-channel headband with dry electrodes... to record EEG at Fp1 and Fp2 over the forehead at a sampling rate of 250 Hz" during regular Math and Chinese lessons. Headbands were fitted before and removed after each 40-minute session, enabling EEG acquisition from an entire class across a full semester (39 sessions over 4 months). An eye-closed/open validation task confirmed signal quality via the expected alpha-range spectral peak in the eye-closed condition.
requirements: Trained experimenters to help fit headbands before each session
Artifact preprocessing (saturation, drift, and ocular artifact rejection) yielding 57.2 ± 1.85% retained epochs per student
constraints: Only two frontal electrodes (Fp1/Fp2) with limited frontal coverage, which the authors list among factors behind the relatively small effect sizes
target_learning_goals: monitoring students' classroom learning processes in real-world settings
examples: Used to record 34 students for one semester, with a separate eye-closed/open task validating signal quality in the classroom environment
key_sources: Jingjing Chen, Penghao Qian, Xinqiao Gao, Baosong Li, Yu Zhang and Dan Zhang. (2023). Inter-brain coupling reflects disciplinary differences in real-world classroom learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00162-1

article_title: The social brain of language: grounding second language learning in social interaction
citation: Ping Li and Hyeonjeong Jeong. (2020). The social brain of language: grounding second language learning in social interaction. npj Science of Learning 5:8. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-0068-7
title: Social L2 Learning (SL2) framework: grounding adult L2 learning in real-life or simulated social interaction
description: The SL2 framework argues that adult second-language learning should be grounded in social interaction, defined as "learning through real-life or simulated real-life environments where learners can interact with objects and people, perform actions, receive, use, and integrate perceptual, visuospatial, and other sensorimotor information". It draws on the New Science of Learning, the Competition Model, encoding-specificity, and embodied cognition theories, and combines neurocognitive bases with social cognition. The article presents SL2 both as a theoretical hypothesis and a practical model for technology-based learning.
requirements: Learning contexts must permit interaction with objects and people and integration of perceptual, visuospatial, and sensorimotor information so that learning becomes embodied
constraints: The proposed SL2 brain network hypothesis of dynamic connection to the theory-of-mind network "needs to be examined carefully by comparing learning with social interaction versus without"
target_learning_goals: L2 vocabulary learning
native-like lexico-semantic representation
communicative competence
key_sources: Ping Li and Hyeonjeong Jeong. (2020). The social brain of language: grounding second language learning in social interaction. npj Science of Learning 5:8. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-0068-7

article_title: The social brain of language: grounding second language learning in social interaction
citation: Ping Li and Hyeonjeong Jeong. (2020). The social brain of language: grounding second language learning in social interaction. npj Science of Learning 5:8. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-0068-7
title: SL2 neural network: a right-heavy IPL–IFG–CN loop plus visual cortex for social L2 learning
description: The article proposes a brain network underlying social L2 learning comprising the inferior parietal regions (SMG, AG), IFG, caudate nucleus, and visual regions (LG). It stresses that "this network highlights the stronger role of the right-hemisphere brain regions as compared with the typical left-lateralized language networks", with IFG handling lexical-semantic processing bilaterally and the right-hemisphere cortical and subcortical regions participating in social learning. The authors hypothesize this network dynamically connects to mPFC and TPJ of the theory-of-mind network.
requirements: Understanding how the areas collaborate during learning and memory requires a network-science analysis of functional/structural brain patterns
constraints: The hypothesized dynamic connection to the ToM network "needs to be examined carefully by comparing learning with social interaction versus without"; how the left frontal IFG and right parietal IPL form a dynamic network "remains to be understood"
target_learning_goals: neurocognitive mechanisms of socially grounded L2 vocabulary learning
key_sources: Ping Li and Hyeonjeong Jeong. (2020). The social brain of language: grounding second language learning in social interaction. npj Science of Learning 5:8. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-0068-7

article_title: Stable, flexible, common, and distinct behaviors support rule-based and information-integration category learning
citation: Casey L. Roark and Bharath Chandrasekaran. (2023). Stable, flexible, common, and distinct behaviors support rule-based and information-integration category learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00163-0
title: Taxonomy of category-learning behaviors: learning success, strategy, strategy consistency, learning speed, and learning stability
description: The article introduces a taxonomy of behaviors during category learning that decomposes individual differences into five measurable components: learning success (maximum cumulative accuracy), learning strategy (how a learner "uses underlying stimulus information to make decisions about category identity"), strategy consistency (the proportion of responses accounted for by the best-fitting strategy), learning speed (trials to reach a group-median performance benchmark), and learning stability (longest streak of correct responses normalized by total correct in a moving window of 50 trials). The taxonomy enables asking which behaviors are stable traits of an individual and which are flexibly modulated by the task, and which commonly or distinctly support success in RB versus II category learning.
requirements: Supervised category-learning tasks with feedback, so strategy models can be fit and cumulative accuracy, speed, and stability computed over trial windows
constraints: Consistency cannot be calculated for learners using random strategies; speed is undefined for learners who never reach the group median; stability is measured against modest overall accuracy in these tasks
target_learning_goals: Perceptual category learning
individual-differences analysis of learning behavior
examples: Experiment 1 illustrated the taxonomy with representative learners differing in maximum cumulative accuracy (92% vs 46%), consistency (92% vs 46%), speed (0 vs 282 trials), and stability (0.61 vs 0.32)
key_sources: Casey L. Roark and Bharath Chandrasekaran. (2023). Stable, flexible, common, and distinct behaviors support rule-based and information-integration category learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00163-0

article_title: Dissipation of reactive inhibition is sufficient to explain post-rest improvements in motor sequence learning
citation: Mohan W. Gupta and Timothy C. Rickard. (2022). Dissipation of reactive inhibition is sufficient to explain post-rest improvements in motor sequence learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00140-z
title: Reactive inhibition accrual-and-dissipation model of motor sequence learning
description: The model assumes that "learning is concurrent with performance", that reactive inhibition (RI) builds during continuous performance and slows RT, and that RI dissipates during breaks. It predicts the largest post-rest improvement when long trials are paired with short breaks, without invoking any offline facilitating consolidation. The article argues this account is sufficient to explain post-rest improvements after a 300 s rest and that facilitating consolidation "does not appear to be necessary".
requirements: Within-trial and across-break RI dynamics must be measured or controlled when inferring offline gains from post-rest improvements
constraints: The study was not designed to estimate RI accrual and dissipation rates; the article notes more research is needed on the exact relative rate and whether it is constant across on-task durations
target_learners: adults learning motor sequences with the non-dominant hand
target_learning_goals: motor sequence skill learning
examples: Four groups trained 360 s on a finger-tapping task with trial lengths of 10 s or 30 s and breaks of 10 s or 30 s, then rested 300 s before a 60 s test
key_sources: Mohan W. Gupta and Timothy C. Rickard. (2022). Dissipation of reactive inhibition is sufficient to explain post-rest improvements in motor sequence learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00140-z

article_title: Dissipation of reactive inhibition is sufficient to explain post-rest improvements in motor sequence learning
citation: Mohan W. Gupta and Timothy C. Rickard. (2022). Dissipation of reactive inhibition is sufficient to explain post-rest improvements in motor sequence learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00140-z
title: Control for reactive inhibition when inferring offline consolidation from post-rest improvements in motor learning studies
description: Because RI builds during continuous performance and dissipates during breaks, post-rest RT improvements can be illusory learning rather than offline consolidation. The article argues RI "is clearly a necessary factor in understanding motor performance, whereas facilitating consolidation does not appear to be necessary". Studies comparing practice schedules should equate or manipulate break-to-trial ratios before attributing gains to consolidation.
requirements: Manipulation or measurement of on-task trial time and break time, as in the 2×2 design used here
constraints: Findings concern short breaks and rest periods (10–300 s); the article notes RI is a short-lasting phenomenon
target_learning_goals: accurate attribution of motor skill gains to online versus offline processes
examples: The 10 s trial, 10 s break group—analogous to groups in two recent studies—showed RI both within trial and across the rest, raising the possibility that inferred consolidation reflects solely RI dissipation
key_sources: Mohan W. Gupta and Timothy C. Rickard. (2022). Dissipation of reactive inhibition is sufficient to explain post-rest improvements in motor sequence learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00140-z

article_title: Towards AI-powered personalization in MOOC learning
citation: Yu, H., Miao, C., Leung, C. and White, T. J. (2017). Towards AI-powered personalization in MOOC learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0016-3
title: Allow learners to personalize learning paths in courses where topic dependencies are weak, using knowledge representation tools
description: The article proposes that when topic dependencies are not clearly defined, learners should be given freedom to access content without following the pre-defined sequence. It argues this is advantageous "based on their personal situations (e.g. background knowledge, time constraints)". Learning paths are to be built from finely grained, well-labelled knowledge units via backward design, and analysed with machine learning against background information and outcomes.
requirements: Learning contents must first be refined into finely grained and well labelled knowledge units
Easy-to-use software tools are needed to construct and modify learning paths
constraints: For courses with clearly defined topic dependencies (e.g. mathematics), letting all students follow the same learning path is advantageous
Learning outcomes are often hard to define and hard to measure; without a learning outcome objective function machine learning cannot compute optimized personal learning paths
target_learners: university-level MOOC learners, including working professionals with fragmented time
target_learning_goals: flexible sequencing of course content to fit learners' backgrounds and needs
examples: An Introduction to Human-Computer Interaction course was modelled in Goal Net with topics such as 'Universal Usability' and '8 Golden Rules' that can be taken in different orders
key_sources: Yu, H., Miao, C., Leung, C. and White, T. J. (2017). Towards AI-powered personalization in MOOC learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0016-3

article_title: Towards AI-powered personalization in MOOC learning
citation: Yu, H., Miao, C., Leung, C. and White, T. J. (2017). Towards AI-powered personalization in MOOC learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0016-3
title: Goal Net methodology and MADE: AI knowledge representation tool for modelling learning paths
description: Goal Net, with its associated Multi-Agent Development Environment (MADE), is an AI knowledge representation tool designed to model logic flows guiding software agents visually without lengthy code. Based on goal setting theory, it "allows users to express a complex process (e.g. organizing a set of learning tasks) as a network of goals and activities", tracking transitions and goal achievement. The authors illustrate it with a learning path for an HCI course built from micro-MOOCs, quizzes and forum discussions.
requirements: Finely grained, well-labelled knowledge units as building blocks
The tool must express a process as a network of goals and activities with trackable transitions
constraints: The article presents Goal Net as a candidate tool for learning-path construction, not as an evaluated intervention
target_learning_goals: constructing and tracking personalized sequences of learning activities and goals
examples: Figure 1 shows a learning path of learning activities (rounded rectangles) and learning goals (circles) in the Introduction to HCI course
key_sources: Yu, H., Miao, C., Leung, C. and White, T. J. (2017). Towards AI-powered personalization in MOOC learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0016-3

article_title: Towards AI-powered personalization in MOOC learning
citation: Yu, H., Miao, C., Leung, C. and White, T. J. (2017). Towards AI-powered personalization in MOOC learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0016-3
title: Micro-MOOCs: short topical micro-lectures under five minutes as building blocks of flexible learning paths
description: Micro-MOOCs are a form of MOOC in which course content is delivered as micro-lectures: "short videos on speci ﬁc topics, typically no longer than 5 min each, along with concise textual explanations." The article positions them as potential building blocks of personalized learning paths, notes providers such as Curious, Everpath and Pathwright attracting learners with short, fragmented study time, and states they make backward design more convenient.
requirements: Course instructors apply backward design: decide objectives, determine evaluation criteria, then choose learning activities
constraints: Suited to learners with short and fragmented time for MOOC learning, such as working professionals
target_learners: working professionals and other MOOC learners with short and fragmented study time
target_learning_goals: modular learning of specific topics supporting personalized path construction
examples: New MOOC service providers such as Curious, Everpath and Pathwright use micro-MOOCs as the main form of learning content delivery
key_sources: Yu, H., Miao, C., Leung, C. and White, T. J. (2017). Towards AI-powered personalization in MOOC learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0016-3

article_title: Towards AI-powered personalization in MOOC learning
citation: Yu, H., Miao, C., Leung, C. and White, T. J. (2017). Towards AI-powered personalization in MOOC learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0016-3
title: Virtual learning companions with human traits for large-scale interactive learning support
description: Virtual learning companions (VLCs) are AI software agents with human-like characteristics proposed to provide interactive learning experience at scale in MOOCs. The article describes a curious companion that monitors progress and "identiﬁes learning contents that can potentially arouse the learner 's curiosity"; a remembrance companion helping learners recall previously acquired knowledge through progressively more explicit hints; and Betty's Brain, a teachable companion based on learning-by-teaching theories. VLCs also generate behaviour data for learning skill analytics.
requirements: VLCs need to be equipped with human-like characteristics to provide believable interactions
VLCs need to be able to hold meaningful conversations to facilitate learning of complex topics
Informed consent mechanisms from learners are needed in MOOC platforms using VLCs
constraints: The article states VLCs are not yet ready for MOOCs: AI conversational interaction remains an open research challenge, and ethical issues must be carefully deliberated
Limiting what VLCs can do to comply with ethical guidelines may not prevent learners from gaming them

article_title: Toward an understanding of when prior knowledge helps or hinders learning
citation: Garvin Brod. (2021). Toward an understanding of when prior knowledge helps or hinders learning. npj Science of Learning 6:24. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00103-w
title: A hierarchical three-determinant framework of when prior knowledge helps or hinders learning
description: The article proposes that whether and how prior knowledge affects learning depends on three determinants: whether it is activated, whether it is relevant, and whether it is congruent with the to-be-learned content. These are arranged hierarchically in Figure 1, so relevance only matters once knowledge is activated, and congruency only once knowledge is activated and relevant. The determinants are dichotomies meant as "the extreme ends of one scale/dimension", all acting at an intra-individual level.
requirements: Prior knowledge must be activated (retrieved from memory) before it can affect learning at all
constraints: The determinants are intra-individual; inter-individual and environmental determinants such as age or intervention duration are not considered
The dichotomies are the extreme ends of one scale/dimension, not true categories
target_learners: school and adult learners generally, as discussed across cited memory and conceptual-change research
target_learning_goals: acquisition of new domain knowledge in instruction
examples: Figure 1 maps combinations: not activated → negligible effects; activated but irrelevant → negligible or hindering via intrusions; activated, relevant, incongruent → mostly hindering; only activated, relevant, congruent knowledge reliably helps

article_title: Toward an understanding of when prior knowledge helps or hinders learning
citation: Garvin Brod. (2021). Toward an understanding of when prior knowledge helps or hinders learning. npj Science of Learning 6:24. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00103-w
title: Assess a learner's prior knowledge before teaching new content
description: Because prior knowledge steers learning in ways that depend on activation, relevance, and congruency, the article concludes that assessing what a learner already knows remains essential before instruction. The author writes "it remains of outmost importance to assess a learner ’s prior knowledge before teaching her some new content", while noting that how that knowledge steers learning is a matter for future research. Unraveling these systematics is explicitly flagged as unfinished work.
requirements: Determine not only the amount of prior knowledge but also whether it will be activated, is relevant, and is congruent with the to-be-learned content
constraints: The article offers no tested procedure for how assessment should capture activation, relevance, or congruency; the meta-analysis studies it reviews did not report correlations of misconceptions with learning gains
target_learners: students receiving domain-specific instruction at any level
target_learning_goals: improving learning gains from instruction by anticipating how existing knowledge will interact with new content
examples: The commentary recommends assessment in the context of the meta-analysis finding that pretest knowledge predicted outcomes but not gains, and notes the meta-analysis included misconception measures whose correlation with gains was not reported

title: Exam Playbook: a scalable, self-administered online version of the Strategic Resource Use intervention
description: The Exam Playbook is an online app adaptation of the previously validated Strategic Resource Use intervention, delivered through ECoach to 14 large introductory STEM and Economics classes. It prompts pre-exam self-reflection: "It prompted students to anticipate the format and demands of their upcoming exam, provided a comprehensive checklist of learning resources available in the class, and asked students to select which would be useful". Students then explain each choice and plan when, where, and how to use the resources, and receive a printable summary of their responses.

article_title: Understanding the effects of education through the lens of biology
citation: H. Moriah Sokolowski and Daniel Ansari. (2018). Understanding the effects of education through the lens of biology. npj Science of Learning 3:17. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0032-y
title: Gene–environment interplay framework explaining persistent individual differences in educational outcomes
description: The review organizes biological mechanisms underlying individual differences under the umbrella of "gene– environment interplay", which "incorporates the effect of genetics, gene – environment correlations, and gene – environment interactions". It argues that additive G + E models are insufficient because genes and experiences modify each other's effects. Scarr and McCartney's account that genotypes direct experience grounds the framework, and it is used to explain why rank orders of ability persist after intervention and why intervention gains fade.
requirements: Genes and environment must be treated as dynamically interdependent rather than as a nature-versus-nurture dichotomy
constraints: The gene–environment interaction field is criticized for sample sizes, varying assessments, and inconsistent statistical methods
Scarr and McCartney's theory is noted as not without criticism and counterarguments
target_learners: children in educational systems across development
target_learning_goals: explaining individual differences in educational attainment and response to intervention

article_title: Understanding the effects of education through the lens of biology
citation: H. Moriah Sokolowski and Daniel Ansari. (2018). Understanding the effects of education through the lens of biology. npj Science of Learning 3:17. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0032-y
title: Aim educational interventions at maximizing each child's individual potential across many outcome measures rather than equalizing performance
description: The article recommends abandoning the twin goals of shifting the mean and narrowing the distribution of a single attainment measure, because biological mechanisms generate individual differences even under equitable conditions. It argues "the goal of educational interventions should be to maximize potential at the individual level" across "a kaleidoscope of educational outcomes" on which individuals occupy different rank positions. Policy should offer diverse educational opportunities so children find niches fitting their predispositions.
requirements: Educational attainment must be reconceptualized as an umbrella term spanning many distinct measurable outcome distributions
constraints: True equity in the sense of equal outcomes is described as unattainable even in a perfectly equitable system
target_learners: all children across development, including those from impoverished environments
target_learning_goals: maximizing individual potential across cognitive and emotional educational outcome measures
examples: The Abecedarian follow-up showed mean gains of 5–7 points with unchanged variance, illustrating why mean-shift goals should replace gap-narrowing goals

citation: Xiaodong Xu, Cheng Jia, Kang Chen & Lijuan Chen. (2025). Unveiling the neural mechanisms of supernatural fiction comprehension using fNIRS. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00327-0
title: The simulation account of fiction comprehension
description: The simulation account holds that readers comprehend actions and events that cannot occur in reality by mentally simulating them with perceptual, motor and mentalizing resources. As the article puts it, "The simulation theory positsthat individuals engage their sensorimotor system and associated brain networks (e.g., IFG) to mentally simulate events that they cannot physically enact". The study tests this account against a cognitive-difficulty alternative and interprets its sensorimotor activation, connectivity and mediation findings as direct evidence for simulation during supernatural reading.
requirements: Readers must engage their sensorimotor system and associated networks such as the IFG to mentally simulate events they cannot physically enact.
constraints: The article notes it did not explicitly measure the extent to which participants mentally simulated characters' actions, and cannot entirely rule out a world-knowledge-inconsistency explanation.
target_learning_goals: Comprehension and interpretation of fictional and supernatural narratives
examples: The study contrasted supernatural Harry Potter excerpts (SF), the same scenarios with realistic names (SR), and realistic versions (RR), using a within-item design drawn from the HP Collection.

article_title: Recurrent individual treatment assignment: a treatment policy approach to account for heterogeneous treatment effects
citation: Ilja Cornelisz and Chris van Klaveren. (2022). Recurrent individual treatment assignment: a treatment policy approach to account for heterogeneous treatment effects. npj Science of Learning 7:3. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00117-4
title: Recurrent Individual Treatment Assignment (RITA) algorithm: sequential RCTs with rank-based probability updating that avoids explicit ITE estimation
description: RITA is a longitudinal individual assignment algorithm based on sequential RCTs or A/B-tests. Rather than estimating ITEs, it ranks each individual's observed treatment response each period, updates individual mean ranks per intervention, and adjusts assignment probabilities using an exponential learning parameter. The article states RITA 'refrains from attempting to estimate ITE and focuses on individual treatment response and assignment instead.' It maintains a minimum exploration level to allow for dynamic treatment effects.
requirements: Sequential RCT or A/B-test setting with recurrent assignment decisions over multiple periods
Observed treatment response variation across periods for each individual
Pre-specified upper and lower exploration bounds on assignment probabilities
constraints: Maintaining exploration leads to sub-optimal performance if no dynamic treatment effects exist
Performance depends on hyperparameter settings (learning parameter form, Bayesian updating modeling, number of interaction terms allowed)
Asymptotic properties, convergence, and optimality remain uninvestigated
target_learners: individuals in high-iterative educational or clinical settings
students in online adaptive practicing environments
target_learning_goals: optimizing which intervention, feedback, or adaptive practicing algorithm is assigned to each individual learner over time
examples: In the simulation study, RITA was applied to 1000 individuals across 60 periods with assignment probabilities initialized at 0.5 and exploration bounds set at 0.05/0.95

A caliper can be built in to mitigate undesirable oscillating behavior

article_title:
Common oscillatory mechanisms across multiple 
memory systems
citation: Drew B. Headley and Denis Paré. (2017). Common oscillatory mechanisms across multiple memory systems. npj Science of Learning 2:1. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-016-0001-2
title: Slow/fast mode framework of oscillatory dynamics across memory systems
description: The review organizes oscillatory dynamics in the hippocampus, cortex, and striatum into two brain states: a slow mode during quiet rest or SWS, characterized by hippocampal large irregular activity plus cortical and striatal delta, and a fast mode during active waking and REM, typified by theta in the hippocampus and its targets and gamma in the rest of cortex. It proposes that "The fast mode is associated with the ef ﬁcacious encoding and retrieval of both declarative and procedural memories" while the slow mode regulates offline declarative consolidation. The framework explains why different memory types depend on different sleep stages.
requirements: Shared low-level circuit constraints across hippocampal, cortical, and striatal networks that generate comparable delta, theta, and gamma rhythms
constraints: The review notes most supporting evidence is correlational and REM consolidation physiology is less well understood than SWS consolidation
target_learners: adults and animals forming declarative and procedural memories
target_learning_goals: memory encoding
memory retrieval
memory consolidation across declarative and procedural systems
examples: The review maps SWS delta and SWR reactivation onto declarative consolidation and REM hippocampal-amygdala theta onto emotional memory consolidation

article_title:
Common oscillatory mechanisms across multiple 
memory systems
citation: Drew B. Headley and Denis Paré. (2017). Common oscillatory mechanisms across multiple memory systems. npj Science of Learning 2:1. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-016-0001-2
title: Three shared oscillations (delta, theta, gamma) span hippocampal, cortical, and striatal memory circuits
description: The review defines three rhythms it treats as common across memory systems: "delta (0.5 – 2 Hz), theta (6– 9 Hz), and gamma (35– 100 Hz)" recordable from or influencing the cortex, hippocampus, and striatum. It explains their generation mechanisms: cortical intrinsic circuitry for delta, medial septum pacing for hippocampal theta, and pyramidal-interneuron recursion for gamma, with gamma nested under and modulated by the slower rhythms. This shared substrate is presented as a general-purpose coordination mechanism largely blind to information content.
requirements: Afferent excitatory drive and reciprocal pyramidal-interneuron connectivity for gamma; MS-DBB and entorhinal inputs for theta; intrinsic cortical circuitry for delta
constraints: Nested phenomena such as spindling (7–14 Hz) and faster delta (2–4 Hz) are explicitly excluded from the review's scope
target_learners: adults and animals across declarative and procedural memory tasks
target_learning_goals: neural coordination of memory encoding, consolidation, and retrieval
examples: The review's Fig. 1–3 depict delta propagation, MS-DBB theta pacing, and PING gamma generation across the three regions

article_title:
Common oscillatory mechanisms across multiple 
memory systems
citation: Drew B. Headley and Denis Paré. (2017). Common oscillatory mechanisms across multiple memory systems. npj Science of Learning 2:1. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-016-0001-2
title: PING mechanism: gamma oscillations generated by pyramidal-interneuron reciprocal interaction
description: The review describes two candidate gamma generation mechanisms, interneuron-network gamma (ING) and pyramidal-ING (PING), regarding PING as the in vivo mechanism. In PING, "the excitatory drive is supplied by local pyramidal cells" whose spiking activates inhibitory interneurons that silence the network before pyramidal cells regain excitability, producing rhythmic winner-take-all-like selection each cycle. Hippocampal and cortical microcircuit connectivity (~50–60% between neighboring pyramidal cells and interneurons) is described as suited to PING, with PV basket cells most strongly entrained.
requirements: Reciprocal connectivity between local pyramidal cells and inhibitory interneurons, with excitatory drive sufficient to recruit interneurons each cycle
constraints: ING alone is generally not considered to generate gamma in the intact brain; striatal gamma origin (intrinsic versus cortically imposed) remains unresolved
target_learners: adults and animals with intact hippocampal, cortical, and striatal circuits
target_learning_goals: local coordination of spiking for information processing during memory tasks
examples: The review notes optogenetically silencing PV basket cells reduces gamma evoked by principal cell activation

article_title: The two-faced process of learning and the importance of Janus-faced solutions
citation: Robin Samuelsson. (2023). The two-faced process of learning and the importance of Janus-faced solutions. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00210-w
title: Janus-faced learning: a unified account combining social transmission and individual construction
description: The article proposes a conciliatory theoretical framework named after the metaphor of a Janus face, which 'considers how learning centrally involves taking what is known and using this for future actions as the double-faced view for understanding human learning'. It argues that the dichotomy between individually constructed (Piagetian constructivist) and socially transmitted (Vygotskian sociocultural) learning is unnecessary, and that learning is 'a process pendulating between exploration and exploitation, between individual and social learning mechanisms'. Learners may rely on instructed material at one stage while constructing their own conceptions at other stages.
requirements: A complete account of learning must contain both individual-construction and social-transmission dimensions, so theories and environments must incorporate both modes
constraints: The article is a theoretical perspective, not an empirical test of the framework
target_learners: children in early childhood and primary education
target_learning_goals: understanding human learning as both individual and social; balanced educational design
examples: Guided play scenarios, Montessori schools, and Tools-of-the-Mind programmes are described as pedagogical alternatives that incorporate both poles in balanced learning environments
key_sources: Robin Samuelsson. (2023). The two-faced process of learning and the importance of Janus-faced solutions. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00210-w

citation: Robin Samuelsson. (2023). The two-faced process of learning and the importance of Janus-faced solutions. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00210-w
title: Balanced learning environments that are knowledge-rich, materially and socially engaging
description: The article describes a recurring design pattern in successful pedagogical alternatives: environments that 'powerfully incorporate both these poles in balanced learning environments that are knowledge-rich, materially and socially engaging'. Such environments reconcile accumulated knowledge with children's joy of learning, balancing playful exploratory discovery with the teaching of what is known. The pattern operationalises the Janus-faced view at the level of the whole learning environment rather than a single activity.
requirements: Environments must draw on accumulated cultural and scientific knowledge while also engaging children as active explorers
constraints: The article notes the interplay of exploration and exploitation in learning sciences literature 'has not been suf ﬁciently uncovered'
target_learners: children in preschool and school education
target_learning_goals: both transmission of accumulated knowledge and fostering of exploration, creativity and innovation
examples: Montessori preschools promoting active hands-on learning with select tools and scaffolding, and Tools-of-the-Mind programmes using cultural tools in play-based, teacher-scaffolded activity
key_sources: Robin Samuelsson. (2023). The two-faced process of learning and the importance of Janus-faced solutions. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00210-w

citation: Long, Y., Luo, H. & Zhang, Y. (2024). Evaluating large language models in analysing classroom dialogue. npj Science of Learning 9:60. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00273-3

citation: Long, Y., Luo, H. & Zhang, Y. (2024). Evaluating large language models in analysing classroom dialogue. npj Science of Learning 9:60. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00273-3
title: Productive classroom dialogue framework: Alexander's five characteristics, exploratory talk, and accountable talk
description: The article organises classroom dialogue research around socio-cultural views of learning as socially mediated, and identifies consensus features of productive dialogue. Alexander's characteristics hold that classroom dialogue should be "collective, with participants reaching a shared understanding", "reciprocal", "supportive", "cumulative" and "purposeful". Littleton and Mercer distinguish disputational, cumulative and exploratory student–student talk, with exploratory talk regarded as most educationally effective, and accountable talk encompasses accountability to the learning community, standards of reasoning, and knowledge.
requirements: A generally participative ethos with participants respecting and listening to all ideas, making discourse norms accessible to all
target_learning_goals: higher-order thinking, reasoning, collaborative problem-solving through dialogic pedagogy
examples: The authors drew on these frameworks, especially Hennessy et al.'s coding scheme, when constructing their revised 15-category coding scheme

article_title: Regular rhythmic primes improve sentence repetition in children with developmental language disorder
citation: Fiveash, A., Ladányi, E., Camici, J., Chidiac, K., Bush, C. T., Canette, L.-H., Bedoin, N., Gordon, R. L. & Tillmann, B. (2023). Regular rhythmic primes improve sentence repetition in children with developmental language disorder. npj Science of Learning 8:23. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00170-1
title: Shared rhythm–grammar processing mechanisms account for rhythmic priming effects
description: The article frames rhythmic priming within the hypothesis that "engaging the beat-based rhythm processing system impacts subsequent language processing via shared underlying mechanisms". It draws on dynamic attending theory — endogenous neural oscillations synchronize with a regular beat and persist after the rhythm stops — and on the Processing Rhythm in Speech and Music (PRISM) framework, which posits that rhythm and language share facets of neural and cognitive processing. The sentence repetition benefit after regular primes, together with the null on a non-grammatical task, is treated as consistent with this account.
requirements: Priming effects require rhythmic stimulation before a language task with a grammar component
constraints: The exact mechanisms remain open: the authors call for research with other language tasks and neural methods to better understand the mechanisms underlying the priming phenomenon
target_learners: Children aged 5.4–13 years with developmental language disorder
target_learning_goals: Syntactic processing and complex sentence repetition
examples: Regular 32-s musical primes with a 500-ms inter-beat interval in 4/4 meter preceded spoken sentences with subject- and object-relative clauses
key_sources: Fiveash, A., Ladányi, E., Camici, J., Chidiac, K., Bush, C. T., Canette, L.-H., Bedoin, N., Gordon, R. L. & Tillmann, B. (2023). Regular rhythmic primes improve sentence repetition in children with developmental language disorder. npj Science of Learning 8:23. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00170-1

article_title: Effect of cognitive control strategies on young children’s attention and emotion during coding learning
citation: Chanjuan Fu, Xiaoxin Hao, Xinyue Shi, Hanxin Qian, Shanyun He & Fengji Geng. (2025). Effect of cognitive control strategies on young children’s attention and emotion during coding learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00360-z
title: Dual-mechanism framework of cognitive control integrated with Zimmerman's cyclical phase model of self-regulated learning
description: The article organizes its intervention around two frameworks: the dual-mechanism framework, which "dissociates cognitive control into proactive and reactive modes based on temporal dynamics", and Zimmerman's cyclical phase model, in which self-regulated learning proceeds through forethought, performance and self-reflection phases. It maps proactive control onto each phase—planning in forethought, real-time monitoring in performance, goal evaluation in self-reflection—and argues proactive control should be fostered to enhance self-regulated learning in young children whose control is still reactive by default.
requirements: Learners are old enough (around five to six years) to be able to use proactive control when prompted by educational strategies
constraints: The article notes this alignment with proactive strategies had not been empirically tested in real learning settings before this study
target_learning_goals: Sustained attention during learning
Emotional regulation during learning
Early coding/computational skills
examples: The coding course embedded planning (mini-map planning), monitoring (role-based checking of commands) and reflecting (evaluating wrong commands) into lesson phases for the experimental group

article_title: Brain dynamics of (a)typical reading development—a review of longitudinal studies
citation: Chyl, K., Fraga-González, G., Brem, S. & Jednoróg, K. (2021). Brain dynamics of (a)typical reading development—a review of longitudinal studies. npj Science of Learning 6:4. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00081-5
title: Interactive account of ventral occipito-temporal function in reading development
description: The review presents the interactive account of vOT function as an explanatory framework for the inverted U-shaped development of visual specialization to print. It "emphasizes the dynamic contribution of top-down predictions from other language areas (involved in phonology and semantics) across reading development". According to the review, "vOT activation is the highest during learning, when the stimulus is recognized as potentially meaningful, but with a high prediction error", and the prediction error decreases with expertise, leading to a decline in vOT activation with higher reading skill.
requirements: Longitudinal sensitivity data across reading stages to observe the rise and decline of vOT activation
constraints: The account is motivated by ERP evidence of inverted U-shape development; the review notes testing similar inverted U-shapes in language-network regions beyond second/third grade would require further studies
target_learning_goals: development of visual word recognition and reading fluency
examples: The review uses the account to interpret longitudinal N1 print-sensitivity data that emerge at reading onset and level off with practice

article_title: Producing concept-motivated signs supports learning of STEM in American Sign Language
citation: Rachel Sortino, Christina Kim, Thalia Guettler, Katie McClyman, Lorna Quandt, Alicia Wooten & Rachel Pizzie. (2026). Producing concept-motivated signs supports learning of STEM content in American Sign Language. npj Science of Learning 11:37. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00418-6
title: English-motivated versus concept-motivated ASL signing styles for STEM signs
description: The article distinguishes two ASL signing styles for STEM vocabulary. English-motivated (EM) signs connect concepts through English words and "generally fall into three categories" of borrowed signs, initialized signs, and fingerspelling. Concept-motivated (CM) signs use visuospatial depiction; the article states "the iconicity of CM signing is more closely matched to the scientiﬁc or technical meaning of STEM signs". In the lessons, CM videos used three-dimensional, visuospatial depictions of content while EM videos used a more linear signing style with more fingerspelled terms. The article situates both on an embodied-learning spectrum, treating sign production by learners as more embodied than observation.
requirements: Fluent ASL signers with sufficient knowledge of ASL and STEM content to perceive the visuospatial information conveyed in CM signs
constraints: The CM style relies on more conceptual knowledge to understand the added visuospatial information in the signs, which the EM style does not
target_learners: deaf and hard of hearing (DHH) students learning STEM through ASL
target_learning_goals: STEM conceptual understanding
accessible language of instruction in ASL
examples: Study 1 created four STEM topics (acids and bases, normal distribution, graphing derivatives, stress and strain curves) as paired video lessons in both styles

article_title: Neural correlates of video game empathy training in adolescents: a randomized trial
citation: Kral, T. R. A., Stodola, D. E., Birn, R. M., Mumford, J. A., Solis, E., Flook, L., Patsenko, E. G., Anderson, C. G., Steinkuehler, C. & Davidson, R. J. (2018). Neural correlates of video game empathy training in adolescents: a randomized trial. npj Science of Learning 3:13. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0029-6
title: Crystals of Kaydor: a story-based iPad game with mechanics for emotion recognition, intensity gauging, empathic responding, and helping quests
description: Crystals of Kaydor is a story-based iPad game in which players control a robot crash-landed on an alien planet who must understand and collaborate with inhabitants. Players "learn to recognize six basic emotions (anger, fear, happiness, surprise, disgust and sadness)" via avatar facial expressions built on the Facial Action Coding System, gauge emotion intensity with a slider, choose empathic responses, and complete helping quests. In-game telemetry recorded via ADAGE provided engagement measures.
requirements: Players engage with the emotion recognition, intensity rating, and empathic responding mechanics that provide feedback and rehearsal opportunities
constraints: The article notes the game's relatively low difficulty produced ceiling effects in accuracy on the empathy training mechanics
target_learning_goals: Emotion recognition and emotion intensity identification
Empathic responding and perspective taking
examples: In the trial, participants played Crystals daily for 2 weeks, averaging 217 min total (range 98–334 min)

Neural correlates of video game empathy training in adolescents: a randomized trial. npj Science of Learning 3:13. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0029-6

article_title: Neural correlates of video game empathy training in adolescents: a randomized trial
citation: Kral, T. R. A., Stodola, D. E., Birn, R. M., Mumford, J. A., Solis, E., Flook, L., Patsenko, E. G., Anderson, C. G., Steinkuehler, C. & Davidson, R. J. (2018). Neural correlates of video game empathy training in adolescents: a randomized trial. npj Science of Learning 3:13. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0029-6
title: Design empathy training games so that engagement with empathy-specific mechanics, not generic playtime, drives the targeted learning processes
description: The article's results indicate that neural change tracked engagement with mechanics that directly target empathy processes (emotion recognition and intensity gauging), while total playtime and generically pro-social mechanics did not predict RTPJ activation change. The authors conclude that video games can improve empathy-related brain function "through skillful use of game mechanics that tap into processes underlying empathy". This supports designing mechanics around the specific underlying processes rather than relying on exposure time.
requirements: Game mechanics must directly target the processes underlying the trained skill (here, perspective taking and emotion regulation)
Telemetry or other measures of engagement with those mechanics are needed to link engagement to outcomes
constraints: The authors note additional research with clinical populations and/or participant-adaptive game difficulty is needed to elucidate whether such training leads to improvements in empathic behavior
target_learning_goals: Empathic accuracy
Perspective taking
Emotion regulation
examples: Crystals mechanics required emotion recognition, emotion intensity ratings, and empathic responding, while a taser minigame and quest completion did not predict RTPJ activation change
