article_title: Training on multiple days results in better learning in embedded eyeblink conditioning in young human adults
citation: Robert Winton, Meenam Pious & Anders Rasmussen. (2025). Training on multiple days results in better learning in embedded eyeblink conditioning in young human adults. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00347-w
title: Embedded eyeblink conditioning protocol: the US is embedded within CS duration without co-termination
description: The embedded protocol is a variant of Pavlovian conditioning in which, per the article, "the US is embedded within the duration of the CS" so that the CS and US overlap without co-terminating, unlike delay (co-terminating) or trace (stimulus-free gap) protocols. Its advantage is that learned responses can be attributed to the anticipated US onset rather than the cessation of the CS. Prior animal work cited in the article suggests it is robust to interfering intertrial USs, but its neurocognitive mechanisms in humans remain underexplored.
requirements: A CS and US whose durations overlap without co-terminating, with the US onset occurring within the CS duration
constraints: Little is known about the neurocognitive mechanisms underlying embedded eyeblink conditioning; extracerebellar regions such as the hippocampus cannot be excluded
target_learning_goals: cerebellar associative motor learning (conditioned eyeblink response acquisition)
examples: In this study a 1000 Hz, 1000 ms tone CS was paired with a corneal air puff US embedded within the CS at a 500 ms ISI, 100 trials per day across 3 non-consecutive days
key_sources: Robert Winton, Meenam Pious & Anders Rasmussen. (2025). Training on multiple days results in better learning in embedded eyeblink conditioning in young human adults. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00347-w

article_title: Effects of targeted memory reactivation during sleep at home depend on sleep disturbances and habituation
citation: Göldi, M. & Rasch, B. (2019). Effects of targeted memory reactivation during sleep at home depend on sleep disturbances and habituation. npj Science of Learning 4:5. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0044-2
title: Real-life TMR applications should use supervised methodology with sleep monitoring and automatic stopping of stimulation at signs of awakening
description: The article concludes that unsupervised home TMR with a plain mp3 player cannot control sleep stage, arousal, or volume, so its memory effects depend strongly on sleep disturbances and habituation. It recommends that "future studies should use supervised TMR methodology", including sleep monitoring, automatic sleep-stage detection, automatic stopping of stimulation at signs of awakening, and brain-signal-based volume control, mirroring closed-loop slow-wave stimulation approaches.
requirements: Sleep monitoring with automatic sleep stage detection during cueing
Automatic stopping of stimulation when signs of awakenings are detected
Brain-signal based volume control of the sounds
constraints: The memory benefits shown in this study were limited to night 3 and to undisturbed sleepers; awakenings by the played words selectively impaired cued-word memory in a home setting.
target_learning_goals: Vocabulary learning and memory consolidation during sleep
examples: In the reported home study, participants played an mp3 file with 60 Dutch words nightly without any experimenter control of sleep or awakenings, and only undisturbed sleepers benefited.
key_sources: Göldi, M. & Rasch, B. (2019). Effects of targeted memory reactivation during sleep at home depend on sleep disturbances and habituation. npj Science of Learning 4:5. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0044-2

article_title: Student teacher inter brain coupling forecast cross semester academic fluctuation in real world classrooms
citation: Xiaomeng Xu, Dan Zhang & Yu Zhang. (2026). Student teacher inter brain coupling forecast cross semester academic fluctuation in real world classrooms. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00421-x
title: Inter-brain coupling as a process-level signature of interpersonal alignment during classroom instruction
description: The article advances an account in which inter-brain coupling, quantified as total interdependence (TI) of student-teacher EEG coherence, is "a process-level signature of interpersonal alignment during communication, reflecting coordinated attention, shared task engagement, and mutual adaptation in moment-to-moment information processing." It further proposes that high-beta coupling indexes deeper, effortful, top-down engagement while theta synchrony reflects moment-to-moment responsiveness to instruction. The account underpins the paper's use of coupling dynamics as a longitudinal marker of effective pedagogy in ecologically valid classrooms.
requirements: Requires wearable dual-channel EEG (Fp1/Fp2) recorded simultaneously from teachers and students during regular lessons, with TI computed per frequency band and averaged within waves
constraints: The authors state the contribution is primarily empirical and that the precise theoretical meaning and underlying mechanisms of inter-brain coupling remain to be specified and tested in future work
target_learners: junior and senior secondary school students (aged 12-15)
target_learning_goals: academic achievement in Chinese and math
examples: The study measured TI across broadband, delta, theta, alpha, low-beta and high-beta bands in 393 regular classes over three semesters
key_sources: Xiaomeng Xu, Dan Zhang & Yu Zhang. (2026). Student teacher inter brain coupling forecast cross semester academic fluctuation in real world classrooms. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00421-x

article_title: Student teacher inter brain coupling forecast cross semester academic fluctuation in real world classrooms
citation: Xiaomeng Xu, Dan Zhang & Yu Zhang. (2026). Student teacher inter brain coupling forecast cross semester academic fluctuation in real world classrooms. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00421-x
title: Longitudinal wearable-EEG hyperscanning dataset from 393 authentic classroom sessions
description: A longitudinal observational dataset of classroom inter-brain coupling: "a total of 4,175 longitudinal EEG recordings were collected from 107 junior and senior students across 393 regular Chinese and math classes" over three semesters (six waves), using dual-channel dry-electrode headbands at Fp1/Fp2 sampled at 250 Hz. Outcomes are rank-based normalized half-semester exam scores. The dataset supports student-teacher, student-class and student-excellence coupling analyses with lag-0 validated by a bootstrapped mismatched-pairing baseline.
requirements: Student-teacher pairs required at least six valid matched epochs per session, and students with valid sessions below 20% within a wave were omitted
constraints: Devices were limited to two channels to minimize disruption; the recorded lessons reflect routine, non-intervention instruction
target_learners: junior and senior secondary school students in Beijing, China
target_learning_goals: Chinese and math academic achievement
examples: Lag coupling analysis compared matched TI against 148,593 non-matched pairings, with TI reliably higher only at lag 0 (t = 2.247, p = 0.024) and lag +1
key_sources: Xiaomeng Xu, Dan Zhang & Yu Zhang. (2026). Student teacher inter brain coupling forecast cross semester academic fluctuation in real world classrooms. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00421-x

article_title: Nurture might be nature: cautionary tales and proposed solutions
citation: Hart, S. A., Little, C. & van Bergen, E. (2021). Nurture might be nature: cautionary tales and proposed solutions. npj Science of Learning 6:2. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00079-z
title: Gene–environment correlation framework: passive, evocative, and active types produce genetic confounds in environment–outcome research
description: Gene–environment correlation describes "the process by which a person's genotype inﬂuences their exposure to the environment". The article distinguishes "three types of gene–environment correlations that can result in genetic confounds": passive (association between inherited genotype and the rearing environment), evocative (a genetically influenced trait elicits responses from others), and active (genetically influenced traits shape which environments people select). Genes act indirectly through personality, behaviors and cognitions, not directly. The article focuses on passive gene–environment correlation because it is theorized to have greater effect in childhood.
requirements: Interpreting environment–outcome associations requires considering that genotypes shape exposure to environments via personality, behaviors, and cognitions
constraints: The article focuses on passive gene–environment correlation as the confound of interest for rearing-environment studies, theorized to be stronger in childhood
target_learners: children in family-based developmental and educational research
target_learning_goals: interpreting causal claims about home environments and children's academic and behavioral outcomes
examples: Examples given: home environments less chaotic for children with high effortful control (passive); genes associated with being rated as "more likeable" (evocative); childhood socialization associated with adolescent exposure to risky environments (active)
key_sources: Hart, S. A., Little, C. & van Bergen, E. (2021). Nurture might be nature: cautionary tales and proposed solutions. npj Science of Learning 6:2. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00079-z

article_title: Nurture might be nature: cautionary tales and proposed solutions
citation: Hart, S. A., Little, C. & van Bergen, E. (2021). Nurture might be nature: cautionary tales and proposed solutions. npj Science of Learning 6:2. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00079-z
title: Classical twin design partitions trait variance into additive genetic, shared environmental, and non-shared environmental influences
description: The classical twin design exploits that "twins share either all (identical or monozygotic twins) or half (non-identical or dizygotic twins) of their genes". Comparing monozygotic and dizygotic twin correlations partitions variance into additive genetic influences (A/heritability), shared environmental influences (C), and non-shared environmental influences (E). Heritability is indicated when the monozygotic correlation exceeds the dizygotic correlation; shared environment is estimated by subtracting heritability from the monozygotic correlation, and non-shared environment by subtracting the monozygotic correlation from one.
requirements: Samples of related individuals differing in genetic relatedness (monozygotic vs dizygotic twins) or environmental exposure (monozygotic twins reared apart)
constraints: Classical twin studies are limited for disentangling genetic confounds because both twin types commonly share their rearing environment, so monozygotic and dizygotic resemblance cannot be compared for shared environmental measures like home library or household income
target_learners: children and adolescents in behavioral-genetics twin research
target_learning_goals: estimating sources of individual differences in traits such as reading ability and school achievement
examples: In Grade-2 word-reading fluency data from van Bergen et al., monozygotic and dizygotic twin correlations were 0.84 and 0.46, yielding Falconer-formula estimates A = 0.76, C = 0.08, E = 0.16
key_sources: Hart, S. A., Little, C. & van Bergen, E. (2021). Nurture might be nature: cautionary tales and proposed solutions. npj Science of Learning 6:2. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00079-z

article_title: Nurture might be nature: cautionary tales and proposed solutions
citation: Hart, S. A., Little, C. & van Bergen, E. (2021). Nurture might be nature: cautionary tales and proposed solutions. npj Science of Learning 6:2. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00079-z
title: Familial Control Method: parental traits as covariates proxy-controlling for genetic transmission in rearing-environment studies
description: The Familial Control Method is defined as "Using a measure of the same trait in the parent as the child as a covariate in models estimating the effect of the rearing environment"; the covariate "serves as a proxy control for the genetic transmission effect". The authors advise assessing the trait in both parents, because the child shares all their genes with both parents but only 50% with one. It is designed for traits transmitted mostly through genes, like reading ability, and is currently the most feasible proxy genetic control for most behavioral researchers, requiring neither twin/adoption samples nor DNA.
requirements: Both parents should be assessed to best tag the child's genetic liability
The trait measured in parents should be the same or highly similar to the child's trait, reasonably measurement invariant and genetically stable across cohorts and lifespan
constraints: If parent–child resemblance also reflects environmental transmission, the method can be too conservative, removing some true environmental variance
Correlations are attenuated by measurement error; structural equation modeling with multiple indicators reduces this
target_learners: children and their parents in family-based educational research
target_learning_goals: testing direct environmental effects (e.g., home literacy/numeracy environments) on children's academic outcomes free of genetic confounding
examples: Van Bergen et al. used step-wise regression with parents' reading ability as covariates for home-literacy indicators; Hart et al. applied it to the home numeracy environment and children's math ability
key_sources: Hart, S. A., Little, C. & van Bergen, E. (2021). Nurture might be nature: cautionary tales and proposed solutions. npj Science of Learning 6:2. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00079-z

article_title: Nurture might be nature: cautionary tales and proposed solutions
citation: Hart, S. A., Little, C. & van Bergen, E. (2021). Nurture might be nature: cautionary tales and proposed solutions. npj Science of Learning 6:2. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00079-z
title: When genetic confounding cannot be controlled, researchers must state it as a limitation and hedge environmental causal claims to avoid parent blaming
description: The article's renewed call for reporting standards: when none of the genetic-control options are possible, researchers should "clearly mention the possible genetic confounding as a limitation", and be cautious with environmental causal statements, which "could lead to unnecessary parent blaming" or wasted interventions. This principle exists because prior reviews' calls failed by not offering actionable correlational design solutions to researchers outside behavior genetics, so researchers published confounded work rather than doing nothing.
requirements: Awareness of the passive gene–environment correlation mechanism and of the available control designs (genetically sensitive, PGS, Familial Control Method)
constraints: Observational genetically sensitive designs cannot establish causality or its absence; they can only strongly infer it above typical observational studies
target_learners: behavioral and educational researchers; journal editors and reviewers
target_learning_goals: improving causal inference standards in research on parenting and home environments
examples: The article notes reviews have asked editors and reviewers "to insist that manuscripts adhere to these standards", yet conference talks and press coverage still present uncontrolled causal claims
key_sources: Hart, S. A., Little, C. & van Bergen, E. (2021). Nurture might be nature: cautionary tales and proposed solutions. npj Science of Learning 6:2. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00079-z

article_title: Deciding for others diminishes model-based decision-making but depends on individual prosociality
citation: Yangchu Huang, Xinyi Du & Shanshan Zhen. (2026). Deciding for others diminishes model-based decision-making but depends on individual prosociality. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00397-0
title: Reinforcement learning drift-diffusion modelling as a framework for decomposing prosocial decision-making into latent cognitive computations
description: The reinforcement learning drift-diffusion model (RLDDM) formalises value-based decisions as evidence accumulation processes in which noisy evidence favouring one option accumulates until it hits a decision boundary. Per the article, "The strength of RLDDM is its ability to identify the specific cognitive computation affected by an experimental effect of interest". In this study it decomposed self-other differences into model-based weights, model-free weights, model-free learning rates, stickiness parameters, decision boundary and non-decision time, disentangling mechanisms that choices alone cannot separate.
requirements: Choices and response times must both be recorded so the drift-diffusion process can be fitted jointly
Task structure must be learnable so model-based and model-free value estimates can be computed separately
constraints: The article notes the dual-system distinction may not capture the full spectrum of strategies, and the eligibility trace decay parameter showed relatively poor parameter recovery, so λ was fixed at 1
target_learning_goals: understanding reinforcement learning (model-based vs model-free) in value-based decision-making
examples: Applied to a 92-participant two-step task, the RLDDM isolated reduced model-based weights, a slower model-free learning rate, and shorter non-decision time for others
key_sources: Yangchu Huang, Xinyi Du & Shanshan Zhen. (2026). Deciding for others diminishes model-based decision-making but depends on individual prosociality. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00397-0

article_title: Motor sequences resist automatization as attentional demands increase with sequence learning
citation: Dahm, S. F., Kraft, V., Martini, M., Krause, D. & Hermsdoerfer, J. (2026). Motor sequences resist automatization as attentional demands increase with sequence learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00412-y
title: Parallel-Neural-Network-Model account: attentional demands increase in the transition from the reacting mode to the associative mode during sequence learning
description: The article applies the Parallel-Neural-Network-Model, in which a fast-learning, attention-dependent spatial system and a slow-learning motor system operate in parallel, and sequence execution proceeds through a reacting mode, an associative mode, and a chunking mode. The authors interpret their counterintuitive finding that dual-task costs increased for the practiced sequence within this framework: "sequence production based on explicit internal sequence representations (i.e., associative mode) requires more attentional resources than reacting to external stimulus information (i.e., reacting mode)". They also invoke the Triarchic Theory of Learning, predicting automaticity develops only after a temporary increase in attentional demands.
requirements: Extensive practice of a fixed sequence before automatization is expected
Assessment of automatization via comparison of dual-task and single-task performance
constraints: The article states progression to the automatic mode may require even more extensive practice than the ten sessions used
Sequence complexity may moderate automatization effects, with shorter sequences automatized after relatively little practice
target_learners: Adults learning motor sequences (participants aged 19 to 35)
target_learning_goals: Automatization of motor sequences and reduction of attentional demands during skilled performance
examples: The study contrasted a ten-session practiced sequence against an unpracticed structurally matched control sequence under single- and dual-task conditions
key_sources: Dahm, S. F., Kraft, V., Martini, M., Krause, D. & Hermsdoerfer, J. (2026). Motor sequences resist automatization as attentional demands increase with sequence learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00412-y

article_title: Semantic relatedness and the efficacy of retrieval practice
citation: Gupta, M.W., Pan, S.C., & Rickard, T.C. (2026). Semantic relatedness and the efficacy of retrieval practice. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00416-8
title: Dual-memory model of test-enhanced learning
description: The dual-memory framework holds that restudy strengthens the retrieval route formed during initial study (study memory), whereas "a test with feedback trial both strengthens study memory and forms a separate memory of the test event (test memory), yielding two independent retrieval routes for the tested items on the final test." A parameter-free quantitative instantiation predicts test-condition accuracy from restudy accuracy (PCT-predicted = 2*PCR − PCR²), with predicted TE = PCR − PCR². The model has closely fit cued-recall testing-effect data across word pairs, triplets, and history and biology facts, retention intervals of 1, 2, and 7 days, and feedback and no-feedback conditions.
requirements: Testing trials must provide correct-answer feedback so that a test memory forms regardless of retrieval accuracy
Cued-recall training design with one test trial per item for the parameter-free predictions
constraints: The three simplifying assumptions (identical study-memory distributions, identical study and test memory distributions, stochastic independence) are made "on the basis of simplicity and we do not necessarily expect them to hold in the general case"
The model does not anticipate the absent testing effect reported for non-linguistic materials with apparent zero relatedness
target_learners: Adult learners in laboratory cued-recall experiments
target_learning_goals: Long-term retention and recall of paired verbal materials
examples: Rickard and Pan (2018) demonstrated close model fits to mean PCT across 512 participants from multiple cued-recall experiments; Rickard (2020) showed the predictions hold for cumulative proportion-correct distributions

article_title: Semantic relatedness and the efficacy of retrieval practice
citation: Gupta, M.W., Pan, S.C., & Rickard, T.C. (2026). Semantic relatedness and the efficacy of retrieval practice. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00416-8
title: Correlated-strengths account of reduced testing efficacy for highly related materials
description: The article proposes that for highly related cue–target pairs, "study and test memories are formed by partially overlapping features drawn from pre -existing semantic associations between the cue and target," so that study and test memory strengths become positively correlated across items rather than independent. This shared representational substrate is captured by a single free parameter ρ in a simulated extension of the dual-memory model. The account explains why the independent-routes model overpredicts testing efficacy for high relatedness while remaining adequate for low relatedness materials.
requirements: A sufficiently high degree of cue–target semantic relatedness so that study and test memories recruit overlapping semantic features
constraints: The article states the account is one interpretation consistent with the model; ρ acts as a scaling parameter for mean predictions, so only distribution fits are informative
It is plausible that for low relatedness pairs ρ is ≤ .1, making the extension empirically indistinguishable from the independence case there
target_learners: Adult learners studying verbal paired materials
target_learning_goals: Understanding when retrieval practice enhances long-term retention
examples: The authors predict that neural pattern similarity between study and test, and item-level embedding cosine similarity, should track the model-estimated ρ

article_title: Semantic relatedness and the efficacy of retrieval practice
citation: Gupta, M.W., Pan, S.C., & Rickard, T.C. (2026). Semantic relatedness and the efficacy of retrieval practice. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00416-8
title: Do not infer whether a factor moderates testing efficacy from an ANOVA interaction on proportion correct; use a process model plus distribution matching instead
description: When both restudy and test condition means shift in the same direction across levels of another factor, an ANOVA interaction on proportion correct is theoretically uninterpretable, because the mapping from latent memory strength to accuracy is non-linear and unknown. The article instead evaluates an empirically supported process model as a yardstick and applies a matching strategy via cumulative proportion-correct distributions. This revealed a real relatedness × testing-efficacy interaction that "a traditional ANOVA interaction" masked.
requirements: A process model whose quantitative mapping from the psychological construct to the dependent measure has empirical support for at least one level of the moderator
Sufficiently large samples to minimize sampling variability in cumulative distributions
constraints: The article limits the interpretation problem to cases where both condition means change in the same direction across factor levels, and notes special cases such as crossover interactions are interpretable
target_learners: Researchers and practitioners evaluating when retrieval practice is effective
target_learning_goals: Accurate theoretical and applied inference about the moderators of the testing effect
examples: In the present experiment the null ANOVA interaction coexisted with a significant Data Type × Relatedness interaction in the model-based comparison and with distribution-wide overprediction for the high relatedness group

article_title: Individual differences in frontoparietal plasticity in humans
citation: Boroshok, A. L., Park, A. T., Fotiadis, P., Velasquez, G. H., Tooley, U. A., Simon, K. R., Forde, J. C. P., Delgado Reyes, L. M., Tisdall, M. D., Bassett, D. S., Cooper, E. A. & Mackey, A. P. (2022). Individual differences in frontoparietal plasticity in humans. npj Science of Learning 7:14. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00130-1
title: Proxy measures of neural plasticity potential: VTA resting-state connectivity for dopamine system connectivity and T1w/T2w myelin maps for myelination
description: This framework treats neuroplasticity as a potential to change rather than a process, and operationalizes it in living humans with two MRI-based proxies. As the article states, "As a proxy for dopamine system connectivity, we analyzed resting-state functional connectivity between the VTA and task-active regions", drawing on animal work showing VTA stimulation enhances plasticity while myelination constrains it. Myelination is proxied by myelin map values, the ratio of T1-weighted to T2-weighted signal intensities in task-active regions. The framework predicts that stronger VTA-frontoparietal connectivity and lower myelin map values at baseline forecast greater learning from short-term training.
requirements: Baseline MRI scanning (structural T1w/T2w and resting-state fMRI) plus a task localizer to define task-active regions of interest before training begins
constraints: The article notes resting-state fMRI cannot distinguish top-down from bottom-up connectivity directions or dopamine from other transmission, and that only five minutes of resting-state data were collected, which may limit reliability
target_learning_goals: predicting individual differences in learning gains from short-term cognitive training (working memory)
examples: In the study, five frontoparietal ROIs were identified with a 2-back > 1-back fMRI localizer contrast, and VTA rsFC and T1w/T2w ratios were extracted from each ROI to predict accuracy and response-time gains
key_sources: Boroshok, A. L., Park, A. T., Fotiadis, P., Velasquez, G. H., Tooley, U. A., Simon, K. R., Forde, J. C. P., Delgado Reyes, L. M., Tisdall, M. D., Bassett, D. S., Cooper, E. article_title: The rational use of causal inference to guide reinforcement learning strengthens with age
citation: Alexandra O. Cohen, Kate Nussenbaum, Hayley M. Dorfman, Samuel J. Gershman and Catherine A. Hartley. (2020). The rational use of causal inference to guide reinforcement learning strengthens with age. npj Science of Learning 5:16. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00075-3
title: Bayesian reinforcement learning with hidden-cause discounting of value updates
description: A family of Bayesian reinforcement learning models in which the learning rate is "dynamically modulated by the posterior probability that an outcome was caused by a hidden agent on each trial", so participants "update their value estimates to a lesser extent when they believe a trial 's outcome can be attributed to the agent". Priors on intervention probability are derived from participants' attribution judgments (empirical Bayesian), estimated from experience (adaptive), or allow impossible interventions (noisy). The study used these models, alongside one-, two-, and three-learning-rate models, to test whether causal structure guides learning across age groups.
requirements: Participants must be able to form beliefs about hidden-agent intervention, measured here via trial-wise attribution judgments used to derive model priors.
constraints: In the task, external causes were invisible and ambiguous; participants could not know with certainty whether any specific outcome was agent-caused.
target_learning_goals: value-based decision making and credit assignment in causally complex probabilistic environments
examples: The empirical Bayesian model reduces value updates proportionally to the participant's belief the agent caused an outcome, e.g., a rock outcome in Robber territory is discounted while a gold outcome is not.
key_sources: Alexandra O. Cohen, Kate Nussenbaum, Hayley M. Dorfman, Samuel J. Gershman and Catherine A. Hartley. (2020). The rational use of causal inference to guide reinforcement learning strengthens with age. npj Science of Learning 5:16. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00075-3

article_title: The rational use of causal inference to guide reinforcement learning strengthens with age
citation: Alexandra O. Cohen, Kate Nussenbaum, Hayley M. Dorfman, Samuel J. Gershman and Catherine A. Hartley. (2020). The rational use of causal inference to guide reinforcement learning strengthens with age. npj Science of Learning 5:16. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00075-3
title: Three-territory gold-mining reinforcement learning task with hidden agents
description: A developmental adaptation of the Dorfman et al. task in which participants choose between two mines with fixed reward probabilities (80% vs 20% gold) across three 50-trial blocks. Each block occurs in a territory visited by a hidden agent that intervenes on 30% of trials: a Millionaire who adds gold, a Robber who replaces gold with rocks, or a Sheriff who intervenes randomly. After each outcome participants report whether the agent caused it. The task measures learning via optimal choice and causal attribution via forced judgments, supporting computational model comparison across ages.
requirements: Participants must understand task instructions; piloting indicated age 7 was the youngest age at which children reliably understood the instructions, and experimenter corrections occurred only during practice trials.
constraints: The exact intervention probability (30%) was not told to participants; intervention was invisible and ambiguous on each trial.
target_learning_goals: reinforcement learning from positive and negative feedback
causal attribution of outcomes to external agents
examples: Ninety participants (ages 7–25, M age = 15.89) completed three blocks of 50 trials; 12 additional participants were excluded for selecting the better option on fewer than 60% of trials.

article_title: Shared and distinct neural correlates of first and second language morphological processing in bilingual brain
citation: Fei Gao, Lin Hua, Paulo Armada-da-Silva, Juan Zhang, Defeng Li, Zhiyi Chen, Chengwen Wang, Meng Du, Zhen Yuan. (2023). Shared and distinct neural correlates of first and second language morphological processing in bilingual brain. npj Science of Learning 8:33. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00184-9
title: Unified competition model of bilingual development applied to morphological processing
description: The unified competition model holds that for language structures shared between L1 and L2, bilinguals employ common cognitive resources and strategies drawn from L1. The article frames its findings as supporting this account: "the current results support a uni ﬁed competition model for bilingual development, where bilinguals would primarily employ L1 neural resources for L2 morphological representation and processing." Shared ELAN, P250 and LAN patterns across L1 and L2, plus quantitative (not qualitative) L1–L2 frontal differences, are cited as evidence of L1-to-L2 resource transfer.
requirements: L1 and L2 must share the linguistic structure under investigation (here derivational morphology)
constraints: The article notes it cannot completely rule out the proficiency confounding effect on current results, since participants' English proficiency was below Chinese by no means addressed with monolingual controls
Evidence comes from late bilinguals with intermediate-to-high English proficiency, so generalization to early bilinguals is open
target_learners: late bilinguals at intermediate to advanced L2 proficiency
target_learning_goals: L2 morphological representation and processing
cross-language transfer of morphological parsing strategies
examples: Chinese-English bilinguals performed a visual derivational morphological priming task while EEG and fNIRS were recorded simultaneously; L1 and L2 shared early and late structural parsing processes
The study did not find dissociable brain regions for L1 and L2 morphological processing, only quantitative left-frontal differences

article_title: The Power of Voice to Convey Emotion in Multimedia Instructional Messages
citation: Lawson, A. P., & Mayer, R. E. (2022). The Power of Voice to Convey Emotion in Multimedia Instructional Messages. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00282-y
title: Cognitive-affective model of e-learning: emotion recognition as the first link in a chain from instructor tone to learning outcome
description: The cognitive-affective model of e-learning is the authors' framework, derived from CATLM and consistent with ICAMLM, for how emotional elements in online lessons affect learners. As printed, "the model posits that learners recognize the emotional tone displayed by the instructor (i.e., first link in Fig. 3), which triggers an emotional response within the learner such as feeling the same emotion as the instructor (i.e., second link in Fig. 3)", which then primes cognitive effort and better learning outcomes. The present study tests only the first link, whether the instructor's voice alone suffices for the learner to recognize emotional tone, which the authors call crucial for initiating the chain of affective and cognitive processes.
requirements: The first link requires that emotional cues in the instructional message, such as the instructor's voice, are calibrated so learners can recognize the emotional tone
constraints: The study examined only the first link and did not examine effects on learning processes and outcomes
target_learners: adult online learners in multimedia instructional settings
target_learning_goals: recognizing the emotional tone of an instructor during online multimedia learning
key_sources: Lawson, A. P., & Mayer, R. E. (2022). The Power of Voice to Convey Emotion in Multimedia Instructional Messages. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00282-y

article_title: The Power of Voice to Convey Emotion in Multimedia Instructional Messages
citation: Lawson, A. P., & Mayer, R. E. (2022). The Power of Voice to Convey Emotion in Multimedia Instructional Messages. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00282-y
title: Russell's core affect model maps the four instructor emotions onto positive–negative and active–passive dimensions
description: The article adapts Russell's model of core affect as the taxonomy underlying its four instructor emotions. As printed, "Russell's (1980, 2003) model of core affect represents human emotion along two orthogonal dimensions: a positive–negative dimension and an active–passive dimension." The animated instructor was designed to convey the emotion of each of the four quadrants, "which we have labeled as happy (positive/active), content (positive/passive), frustrated (negative/active), and bored (negative/passive)", a classification the authors note is similar to Pekrun and Perry's taxonomy of achievement emotions. The positivity hypothesis tested in the study focuses on the positive–negative dimension of this space.
requirements: Classifying an instructor's emotional display requires locating it on both the positive–negative and the active–passive dimensions
constraints: The study's predictions focus on the positive–negative dimension rather than the full two-dimensional space
target_learners: adult online learners in multimedia instructional settings
target_learning_goals: recognizing instructor emotional tone along valence and activity dimensions

citation: Lawson, A. P., & Mayer, R. E. (2022). The Power of Voice to Convey Emotion in Multimedia Instructional Messages. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00282-y
title: When the goal is to convey positive emotion, narrated slides with voice-over can substitute for an embodied onscreen agent
description: This design principle holds that for positive emotional tone, the instructor's recorded voice carries enough affective information that an embodied onscreen agent adds no measurable benefit in emotion recognition. The article states that "when the goal is to convey positive emotion, instructional designers may be able to present narrated slides with voice-over rather than to go to the expense of also adding onscreen embodied agents." It rests on the finding that voice alone matched voice plus agent for happy, content, and bored instructors, and it can lower production cost since many existing videos, such as Khan Academy's, already use disembodied voice.
requirements: A recorded human voice conveying the intended emotional tone in the narrated slideshow
constraints: When the goal is to convey more nuanced or unexpected emotions, such as frustration, the article states "it may be necessary to present both voice and embodiment cues"
The clips studied were all under a minute, so generalization to longer lessons is untested
target_learners: adult online learners in multimedia instructional settings
target_learning_goals: recognizing the positive or negative emotional tone of an instructor in instructional video
examples: Participants in the experiment rated the emotional tone of 16 short clips from a statistics lesson, half with the animated instructor on screen and half with voice-over only

title: Learning-by-modeling framework: knowledge acquisition through model building, simulation, analysis, evaluation and revision subprocesses
description: The framework (Fig. 1, adapted from the Common Core Mathematics Standards) characterizes computational modeling as multifaceted subprocesses of "building, evaluating, and revising of models based on the learners' underlying understanding of the domain theory and relations that govern the behavior of the model". It matches NGSS "Developing and Using Models" practices and defines the key processes an educational DSML must support; the authors investigate selected starred subprocesses in their case studies.

computational thinking concepts and practices
examples: The authors map students' five documented difficulty categories onto the Fig. 1 subprocesses to motivate DSML design.

description: The article's design framework rests on three principles the authors name explicitly: "An evidence-centered design approach ... to ensure coherence and coverage of domain concepts, relations, and practices in the design of the DSML constructs"; opportunities "for exploratory learning of dynamic processes by creating a discrete-time step-by-step model of continuous dynamic processes"; and "A block-based programming language ... to lessen programming difficulties among novice learners". citation: Vania Dimitrova & Paul Brna. (2016). From Interactive Open Learner Modelling to Intelligent Mentoring: STyLE-OLM and Beyond. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:332–349. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0087-3
title: STyLE-OLM framework for interactive open learner modelling
description: STyLE-OLM is a computational framework in which learners and the system jointly construct, inspect, discuss and alter the learner model through structured diagnostic dialogue. The article states: "The main contribution of this work is the holistic framework for interactive open learner modelling which addresses the three main issues – providing a suitable communication means, managing a diagnostic dialogue, and maintaining a jointly constructed learner model." It combines Conceptual Graphs-based representation, a dialogue-game planner with strategies and tactics, and a belief modal operator mechanism for agreements and conflicts, and was instantiated in programming and finance domains.

A dialogue framework giving learner and system symmetric power to negotiate the learner model
A mechanism for accommodating different beliefs about the learner's domain knowledge
constraints: Evaluation evidence came from carefully designed user studies within university conditions focusing on selected aspects, limiting broader applicability across domains and contexts
target_learning_goals: domain terminology and concept knowledge
metacognitive self-awareness and reflection
examples: Instantiated in STyLE-OLM for finance concepts in the LARFLAST project and for programming concepts
Adopted in OWL-OLM, PORML, SAIC and the Perico agent

citation: Vania Dimitrova & Paul Brna. (2016). From Interactive Open Learner Modelling to Intelligent Mentoring: STyLE-OLM and Beyond. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:332–349. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0087-3
title: STyLE-OLM communication medium: diagrammatic Conceptual Graphs with sentence openers
description: The communication medium combines a graphical construction area for propositions representing learner model beliefs with sentence openers expressing illocutionary acts. The article says it "exploited the diagrammatic external representation of Conceptual Graphs for designing a communication medium which provided a structured interface combining a graphical construction area for propositions representing beliefs from the LM." Sentence openers scaffolded the discourse structure, and the controlled expression of domain statements enabled conversion of propositions into logical axioms. The same medium was reused in OWL-OLM with OWL-based learner models.
requirements: A controlled way of expressing domain statements so propositions can be converted into logical axioms
constraints: The article notes the drawback of "the rather limited way of constructing domain propositions with the graphical apparatus provided"
target_learning_goals: articulating and inspecting domain knowledge statements
engaging in diagnostic dialogue about the learner model
examples: OWL-OLM implemented the same communication medium using UML-like diagrammatic expressions and sentence templates

article_title: Automated Assessment of Non-Native Learner Essays: Investigating the Role of Linguistic Features
citation: Sowmya Vajjala. (2016). Automated assessment of non-native learner essays: Investigating the role of linguistic features. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/1612.00729
title: CAF-based six-group taxonomy of linguistic features for L2 essay scoring
description: The article organizes its automatically extractable features around the SLA notions of Complexity, Accuracy and Fluency (CAF), stating that "L2 writing proﬁciency in SLA research has been discussed in the context of the notions of Complexity, Accuracy and Fluency (CAF)". Concretely, "the features are classiﬁed into 6 groups: word level, parts of speech, syntactic characteristics, discourse properties, errors, and others", with lexical richness and syntactic complexity encoding complexity, error features encoding accuracy, and discourse coherence features encoding fluency. All representations are computed with open-source NLP tools (Stanford Parser/CoreNLP, LanguageTool).
requirements: Automatically extractable features computed from learner text using NLP preprocessing (tagging, parsing, coreference)
constraints: Prompt is used only as a categorical feature without prompt-specific vocabulary features
Ngram features were deliberately excluded as sparse, hard to interpret, and topic-specific
target_learners: non-native English speakers writing exam essays
target_learning_goals: second language writing proficiency assessment
examples: Feature extraction code was hosted at bitbucket for the paper; features were computed with Stanford Parser, Stanford CoreNLP, and LanguageTool

article_title: Including Learning Analytics in the Loop of Self-Paced Online Course Learning Design
citation: Hongxin Yan, Fuhua Lin & Kinshuk. (2021). Including Learning Analytics in the Loop of Self-Paced Online Course Learning Design. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education (2021) 31:878–895. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00225-z
title: The Learning Design-Analytic (LDA) model: course learning design and learning analytics mutually support each other in self-paced online learning
description: The LDA model is a proposed model of learning design interacting with learning analytics, suggested mainly for STEM disciplines in self-paced online learning. In it, course learning design builds learning activities which generate learning data; learning analytics uses those data to mitigate SPOL learning barriers, and its results feed back to improve the design. The article states that 'course learning design that aims for learning success builds learning activities, which generate the learning data' and that analytics results 'can, in turn, empower the course learning design by facilitating a data-driven approach.'
requirements: Sufficient and meaningful data-collection points must be embedded in the course by designing certain learning activities, such as check-point activities like quizzes, posting, and reflecting
constraints: The model is suggested mainly for STEM disciplines in self-paced online learning in higher formal education
target_learners: adult learners in self-paced online higher education courses
target_learning_goals: learning success in STEM disciplines, including conceptual development, inquiry-based and problem-solving skills
examples: The COMP272 Data Structures and Algorithms course revision at Athabasca University follows the LDA model by planning a diagnostic test, a learner profile survey, and unit-level formative assessment.
key_sources: Hongxin Yan, Fuhua Lin & Kinshuk. (2021). Including Learning Analytics in the Loop of Self-Paced Online Course Learning Design. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education (2021) 31:878–895. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00225-z

article_title: Including Learning Analytics in the Loop of Self-Paced Online Course Learning Design
citation: Hongxin Yan, Fuhua Lin & Kinshuk. (2021). Including Learning Analytics in the Loop of Self-Paced Online Course Learning Design. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education (2021) 31:878–895. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00225-z
title: List of learner and learning data sources for LA applications in STEM SPOL courses
description: For STEM disciplines in SPOL, the article enumerates the data sources relevant to its LA applications, to be considered during course design: academic background (SIS), prior knowledge (diagnostic test), learning interest and approach (survey or log), knowledge state (assessment), attempts of and time spent on formative assessment (log), assessment grade (log), access to recommended learning materials (log), study schedule plan (LMS database), study pace (log), social interactions (log), social style (survey), and help-seeking frequency (log). The article states that 'students' knowledge state (or knowledge and skill proficiency) is the most critical input variable for the LA applications.'
requirements: The survey should be considered in the course learning design stage to determine the questions that can generate the genuine learner data required by the LA applications
constraints: The data sources are those the study recognizes as relevant for STEM disciplines in SPOL in higher formal education
target_learners: students in STEM self-paced online higher education courses
target_learning_goals: estimating knowledge state and supporting learning awareness, struggling-student identification, and academic intervention
examples: The COMP272 revision plans a diagnostic test for prior knowledge, a beginning-of-course survey for academic profiles, and log data from unit self-quizzes.

article_title: Including Learning Analytics in the Loop of Self-Paced Online Course Learning Design
citation: Hongxin Yan, Fuhua Lin & Kinshuk. (2021). Including Learning Analytics in the Loop of Self-Paced Online Course Learning Design. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education (2021) 31:878–895. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00225-z
title: Embedding check-point activities in a course so learning data are generated regardless of how and where students learn
description: This course-level design pattern addresses SPOL's data-generation problem: students who learn offline or log in irregularly leave little learning data. If a course embeds a series of check-point activities (e.g., quizzes, posting, reflecting) in the learning system, students will periodically return and interact with it, so their learning progress, study pace, and knowledge and skill state can be consistently scanned and recorded. The article states that 'by purposefully designing check-points activities, course instructors can pre-determine what, when, where and how learning data are generated and recorded during a student's learning journey.'
requirements: Check-point activities cannot be placed randomly and arbitrarily; guidelines must be followed so that necessary learning data are generated and pedagogical needs are met
target_learners: self-paced online learners, especially adult learners with work and family commitments
target_learning_goals: consistent recording of learning progress, study pace, and knowledge and skill state for learning analytics
examples: COMP272 embeds unit-level auto-graded self-quizzes as check-point activities, with a small portion of course grade awarded for participation.

article_title: Literature Review on the Integration of Generative AI in Programming Education
citation: Jemimah Nathaniel, Solomon Sunday Oyelere, Jarkko Suhonen, Matti Tedre. (2025). Literature Review on the Integration of Generative AI in Programming Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00524-3
title: GenAI-Ped framework for integrating GenAI in programming education
description: The GenAI-Ped framework is a structured four-phase approach to guide GenAI integration in programming education while preserving foundational programming principles and higher-order thinking skills. The article states it is designed "to guide GenAI integration in programming education and ensure that foundational programming principles and higher-order thinking skills are preserved and enhanced." It adapts a self-regulated learning framework, Bloom's taxonomy, needs analysis, an AI-Lab prompt-engineering framework, and Universal Design for Learning principles across four phases: learner needs analysis and objective development, GenAI tool analysis, teaching/assessment/prompt engineering methods, and lesson-level GenAI integration.
requirements: Requires learner needs analysis, SMART objectives grounded in Bloom's taxonomy, evaluated and configured GenAI tools, and formative plus summative assessment aligned with learning objectives
constraints: Adapted from prior frameworks (Prasad et al. SRL, Roth et al. UDL, Dickey et al. AI-Lab); presented as a proposal built from review findings, not empirically validated in this article
target_learning_goals: foundational programming logic
higher-order thinking skills
prompt engineering competence
examples: Phase 3 describes hybrid pedagogical models such as live code-along demonstrations where instructor and class co-develop a function using ChatGPT's suggestions while critiquing output and refining prompts
key_sources: Jemimah Nathaniel, Solomon Sunday Oyelere, Jarkko Suhonen, Matti Tedre. (2025). Literature Review on the Integration of Generative AI in Programming Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00524-3

article_title: To Advance AI Use in Education, Focus on Understanding Educators
citation: René F. Kizilcec. (2023). To Advance AI Use in Education, Focus on Understanding Educators. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00351-4
title: Technology Acceptance Model: perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use as malleable determinants of technology acceptance
description: The Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), introduced by Davis (1989), explains how an individual's perceptions of a technology influence attitudes and behavioral intentions, which in turn affect actual use. It treats "the perceived usefulness of a technology and its perceived ease of use" as fundamental determinants of acceptance, and holds that these perceptions are malleable through presentation, framing, design, and marketing. The article positions TAM as a foundation for a psychology of technology in education and calls for experimental tests of how framing, transparency, training, and context causally shape acceptance.
requirements: The model presupposes that user perceptions of usefulness and ease of use can be measured and influenced by how the technology is presented and framed.
constraints: The article states TAM does not account for the strong emotional responses that new technologies, especially AI-powered ones, can trigger among educators.
target_learning_goals: Understanding and shaping educator adoption of AI-powered education technology
examples: The article proposes using TAM to experimentally investigate causal effects of framing, presentation, transparency, training, and context on education technology acceptance, since prior education applications relied almost exclusively on structural equation modeling of survey data.
key_sources: René F. Kizilcec. (2023). To Advance AI Use in Education, Focus on Understanding Educators. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00351-4

article_title: To Advance AI Use in Education, Focus on Understanding Educators
citation: René F. Kizilcec. (2023). To Advance AI Use in Education, Focus on Understanding Educators. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00351-4
title: Academic Resistance Model: cognitive, emotional, and intentional attitudes toward organizational change complement TAM
description: The Academic Resistance Model (ARM), introduced by Piderit (2000), accounts for cognitive, emotional, and intentional attitudes about an organizational change, complementing the Technology Acceptance Model's focus on usefulness and ease of use. The article cites Rienties (2014) as an illustration: educators cognitively appreciated the usefulness of a new student evaluation system yet felt strong negative emotional attitudes and resisted the change due to anxiety and mistrust. ARM is offered as a lens for understanding educators' resistance to AI-powered systems.
requirements: Applying the model requires attending to emotional and intentional attitudes toward change, not only cognitive perceptions of usefulness.
target_learners: Educators facing organizational adoption of new education technology
target_learning_goals: Understanding and addressing educator resistance to education technology adoption
examples: Rienties (2014) found educators who cognitively appreciated a new student evaluation system's usefulness still resisted it due to anxiety and mistrust.
key_sources: René F. Kizilcec. (2023). To Advance AI Use in Education, Focus on Understanding Educators. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00351-4

article_title: To Advance AI Use in Education, Focus on Understanding Educators
citation: René F. Kizilcec. (2023). To Advance AI Use in Education, Focus on Understanding Educators. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00351-4
title: Design AI education tools around educators' existing workflows, with clear value propositions for their time investment
description: Because implementing AI in education is a sociotechnical challenge, technology designers need to understand the status quo of educators' environment, workflow, schedule, and resources to find entry points with a clear value proposition for educators' return on time investment. Tools that fit seamlessly into ubiquitous systems like learning management systems and help with effortful tasks such as grading or summarizing student responses are more likely to be adopted; cost and reliability of hardware and software also matter, reliability being especially salient for educators who have encountered issues during class time.
requirements: Designers must understand educators' existing environment, workflow, schedule, and resources before introducing a new tool.
constraints: Educators have limited time and flexibility to engage in new activities.
target_learners: Educators in schools and higher education
target_learning_goals: Effective integration and adoption of AI tools in teaching practice
examples: The article notes educators' familiarity with gradual AI feature introductions in tools like Google Docs (e.g., rephrasing suggestions) as easy-to-integrate models.

article_title: Using Ontological Engineering to Overcome AI-ED Problems: Contribution, Impact and Perspectives
citation: Mizoguchi, R., & Bourdeau, J. (2015). Using Ontological Engineering to Overcome AI-ED Problems: Contribution, Impact and Perspectives. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0077-5
title: Distinction between light-weight and heavy-weight ontologies
description: The article distinguishes two kinds of ontology. Light-weight ontologies are vocabulary-oriented, used as metadata for semantic searches in the Semantic Web; heavy-weight ontologies are "concept-oriented. They are conceptual artifacts that intend to explicate the underlying conceptual structure of the target world" and are sometimes required to have philosophical validity. The authors concentrate on heavy-weight ontologies, arguing a heavy-weight ontology can serve as vocabulary but not the reverse. This distinction frames their entire AIED program.
requirements: Heavy-weight ontologies may need philosophical validity and grounding in a top-level ontology
constraints: The article is concerned mainly with heavy-weight ontology, which the authors state is not a matter of how ontologies are represented in computers
target_learners: AIED system developers and instructional designers
target_learning_goals: Building AIED systems on shared, theory-compliant conceptual foundations
examples: The OBO foundry biomedical ontologies compliant with the BFO top-level ontology are given as examples of heavy-weight ontology work
key_sources: Mizoguchi, R., & Bourdeau, J. (2015). Using Ontological Engineering to Overcome AI-ED Problems: Contribution, Impact and Perspectives. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0077-5

article_title: Using Ontological Engineering to Overcome AI-ED Problems: Contribution, Impact and Perspectives
citation: Mizoguchi, R., & Bourdeau, J. (2015). Using Ontological Engineering to Overcome AI-ED Problems: Contribution, Impact and Perspectives. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0077-5
title: OMNIBUS: an ontology of learning/instructional theories as ways of goal decomposition
description: OMNIBUS is an ontology of learning/instructional theories built with the Hozo editor, capturing theories "as a set of ways of decomposing a goal into a sequence of sub-goals". The article reports that "OMNIBUS has 99 ways of goal decomposition extracted from 11 theories/models", for example decomposing 'to help learners learn' differently under behaviorist versus constructivist approaches. It is described as the framework able to include any theory compliant with its specifications of theory and model.
requirements: Theories and models must comply with the specification of the concepts of theory and of model to be included
constraints: Building on OMNIBUS requires mastering a high-complexity system and the Hozo editor, which the authors name as obstacles to adoption
target_learners: Authors of intelligent tutoring systems and instructional designers
target_learning_goals: Designing theory-compliant learning/instructional scenarios
examples: A behaviorist way of instruction is modeled as decomposing the goal into giving stimuli, observing the response, and repeating
key_sources: Mizoguchi, R., & Bourdeau, J. (2015). Using Ontological Engineering to Overcome AI-ED Problems: Contribution, Impact and Perspectives. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0077-5

article_title: Using Ontological Engineering to Overcome AI-ED Problems: Contribution, Impact and Perspectives
citation: Mizoguchi, R., & Bourdeau, J. (2015). Using Ontological Engineering to Overcome AI-ED Problems: Contribution, Impact and Perspectives. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0077-5
title: SMARTIES: a theory-aware authoring system running on OMNIBUS
description: SMARTIES is an intelligent interactive authoring system that helps authors decompose the goal of supporting learners into an executable sequence of learning/instructional actions. At every decision point it offers decompositions suggested by theories stored in OMNIBUS, so authors build a tree of sub-goals whose decompositions are all theory-supported. It also "can translate the decomposition tree into IMS LD code executable by IMS LD compliant tools". The article calls it a next-generation intelligent system running without heuristic knowledge.
requirements: Runs completely on the basis of the OMNIBUS ontology, without heuristic knowledge
target_learners: Authors of intelligent tutoring systems and instructional designers
target_learning_goals: Producing theory-compliant learning/instructional scenarios
examples: Authors repeatedly choose among theory-suggested decompositions until they obtain a full decomposition tree, then export it as IMS LD code

article_title: Using Ontological Engineering to Overcome AI-ED Problems: Contribution, Impact and Perspectives
citation: Mizoguchi, R., & Bourdeau, J. (2015). Using Ontological Engineering to Overcome AI-ED Problems: Contribution, Impact and Perspectives. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0077-5
title: I_L event: a concept unifying learning and instructional events, formed 'in the wild'
description: During collaborative ontology engineering for OMNIBUS, the authors lacked a concept for what happens when a learning agent and an instruction agent act and interact together. They created the I_L event, "which integrates a 'Learning_event' with an 'Instructional_event' in one entity, and represents interaction between the learner and the instructional agent, as well as the activity on each respective side". The article frames this as an instance of Engeström and Sannino's concept formation in the wild, and notes the term itself needs improvement for human sharing.
requirements: Connection to a top-level ontology, which constrained concept formation during its creation
constraints: The authors state the term 'I_L event' needs improvement to be shared effectively among humans
target_learners: Ontology engineers and AIED system builders
target_learning_goals: Representing learning and instruction jointly in ontologies for authoring systems
examples: The authors also created the What_to_learn concept out of necessity, to express anything being learned intentionally or not

citation: Mizoguchi, R., & Bourdeau, J. (2015). Using Ontological Engineering to Overcome AI-ED Problems: Contribution, Impact and Perspectives. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0077-5
title: Three-level ontology engineering methodology anchored in a top-level ontology (YAMATO)
description: The article's methodology evolved from a three-layer model (common vocabulary, formal definition of concepts, operational building blocks such as task ontology) into an approach anchored on YAMATO, a top-level ontology released in 2010. Anchoring ensures specification of the most abstract basic concepts such as event, process and system, and the authors claim it "provides a common vocabulary, and on the scientific level, it allows for refutation or discussion at the most abstract and even philosophical level". OMNIBUS was reoriented under this constraint.
requirements: Ontologies must be related to a top-level ontology
target_learning_goals: Building interoperable, refutable conceptual foundations for AIED systems
examples: Mizoguchi's YAMATO top-level ontology and the later MAUOC ontology of culture were both built with reference to this anchoring principle

article_title: Creating a Team Tutor Using GIFT
citation: Gilbert, S. B., Slavina, A., Dorneich, M. C., Sinatra, A. M., Bonner, D., Johnston, J., Holub, J., MacAllister, A., & Winer, E. (2017). Creating a Team Tutor Using GIFT. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0151-2
title: An object-oriented terminology ontology for describing team tutors
description: The article proposes a standardized vocabulary for team tutors, conceptualized "as an ontology, analogous to an object-oriented hierarchy in programming context." Terms include Team, Member, Role, Task, Team Task, Action, Skill, Skill Requirement, and Team Skill Requirement, plus a second set distinguishing action performance, performance state, task performance, and performance metric. The ontology lets authors map which skill requirements a team possesses through its members' roles and tasks, and is intended to ease planning and cross-platform comparison of team tutors.
requirements: Applied during initial tutor planning to map the tutor's purpose and functioning before authoring
constraints: Proposed terminology, adopted to ease internal communication; the article does not report validation with other teams
target_learners: teams of learners in team-training contexts
target_learning_goals: team skills such as communication and coordination
examples: In the Surveillance Scenario the ontology was instantiated as two members with roles whose tasks were Transfer, Acknowledge, and Identify, each with skill requirements
key_sources: Gilbert, S. B., Slavina, A., Dorneich, M. C., Sinatra, A. M., Bonner, D., Johnston, J., Holub, J., MacAllister, A., & Winer, E. (2017). Creating a Team Tutor Using GIFT. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0151-2

article_title: Creating a Team Tutor Using GIFT
citation: Gilbert, S. B., Slavina, A., Dorneich, M. C., Sinatra, A. M., Bonner, D., Johnston, J., Holub, J., MacAllister, A., & Winer, E. (2017). Creating a Team Tutor Using GIFT. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0151-2
title: The Surveillance Scenario: a scalable two-person military surveillance team task in VBS2
description: The Surveillance Scenario is a team task in Virtual Battlespace 2 (VBS2) in which "The Surveillance Scenario requires a team of two. Each member stands atop a building and is responsible for surveillance of a 180-degree zone." Members scan for enemies, verbally and by keypress alert each other to crossings (Transfer), acknowledge alerts (Acknowledge), and identify transferred enemies (Identify); unannounced identification counts as backup behavior. It follows an Event-Based Approach to Training model, is scalable in difficulty by changing enemy numbers, and was designed as an open-ended research platform agnostic of tutoring approach.
requirements: A task requiring tutorable skills and enabling assessment; communication implemented through structured language or keypresses so it can be measured
constraints: The current tutor "was not developed to use contextual markers to distinguish between true backup behavior and a fortuitous identification"
target_learners: two-person teams in military surveillance training
target_learning_goals: observation, communication, acknowledgment, identification, and backup behavior
examples: Task mechanics: Alice presses the 1 key and says 'Person crossing at the 1'; Bob presses E to acknowledge and spacebar to identify; only keys 1, 2, space, and E are used
key_sources: Gilbert, S. B., Slavina, A., Dorneich, M. C., Sinatra, A. M., Bonner, D., Johnston, J., Holub, J., MacAllister, A., & Winer, E. (2017). Creating a Team Tutor Using GIFT. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0151-2

article_title: Creating a Team Tutor Using GIFT
citation: Gilbert, S. B., Slavina, A., Dorneich, M. C., Sinatra, A. M., Bonner, D., Johnston, J., Holub, J., MacAllister, A., & Winer, E. (2017). Creating a Team Tutor Using GIFT. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0151-2
title: A seven-dimension design space of feedback choices for team tutoring testbeds
description: The article organizes feedback design as seven dimensions realizable in the Surveillance testbed: subject (individual vs. team), target (public vs. private), timing (immediate, after, omitted), type (proactive vs. reactive), specificity (generic vs. specific), tone (positive vs. negative), and style (collaborative vs. competitive). "Table 1 illustrates different dimensions of feedback that can be explored." The pattern lets researchers vary feedback systematically, since feedback at too high a frequency could be overwhelming and ignored, while immediate delivery has been reported effective under higher cognitive load.
requirements: A task testbed in which feedback can be delivered and varied along these dimensions without interrupting training
constraints: How much feedback is too much "may depend on the team members themselves"
target_learners: teams of two or more learners in real-time team tasks
target_learning_goals: team communication and task performance under feedback variation
examples: Specific feedback example from Table 1: 'You missed an OPFOR located at 7 o'clock'; collaborative style: 'Slow down scanning to help the team'

article_title: Training the Body: The Potential of AIED to Support Personalized Motor Skills Learning
citation: Olga C. Santos. (2016). Training the Body: The Potential of AIED to Support Personalized Motor Skills Learning. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:730–755. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0103-2
title: Two AIED research directions for personalized motor skills learning: modelling psychomotor interaction and providing personalized psychomotor support
description: The paper organizes its forward-looking agenda in Table 2 around two AIED directions: modelling psychomotor interaction (detecting the learner's physical interaction, modelling expert movements, diagnosing the learner-expert mismatch) and providing personalized psychomotor support (modelling the intervention, deciding the intervention strategy and timing, delivering the intervention). The author argues these "pose familiar AIED problems, but in novel and challenging new forms" and maps them to novel approaches: wearable devices, big data processing, 3D modelling, TORMES methodology, ambient intelligence, and 3D printing.
requirements: Detecting physical interaction requires collecting movement data via wearable sensors and processing data streams with big data mining to extract movement indicators in time for just-in-time feedback.
constraints: The agenda is a proposal for future AIED research, not a tested system.
target_learners: Learners training motor skills, e.g., musical instrument, handwriting, surgery, sports and martial arts, sign language, dance
target_learning_goals: Acquisition and automatization of motor skills through practice
examples: Table 2 maps each research issue to a challenge and a novel approach, e.g., diagnosing mismatch between learner and expert movements is addressed with 3D modelling.
key_sources: Olga C. Santos. (2016). Training the Body: The Potential of AIED to Support Personalized Motor Skills Learning. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:730–755. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0103-2

article_title: Training the Body: The Potential of AIED to Support Personalized Motor Skills Learning
citation: Olga C. Santos. (2016). Training the Body: The Potential of AIED to Support Personalized Motor Skills Learning. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:730–755. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0103-2
title: Four-aspect analytical lens for motor skills learning systems: sensing, modelling, designing, and delivering feedback
description: The paper reviews 17 motor skills learning systems along four numbered aspects: 1) sensing the learner's corporal movement and context, 2) modelling interactions to compare learner movement against the accurate movement, 3) designing the feedback (what support, and when and how), and 4) delivering feedback "in an effective non-intrusive way to advice the learner on how the body and limbs should move". Personalization issues within each aspect are flagged as places where AIED research can contribute.
requirements: Each aspect requires its own design decision: sensor choice, comparison model, feedback design, and non-intrusive delivery channel.
target_learning_goals: Motor skills acquisition with personalized feedback
examples: Applied in Table 1 to systems from karate training with accelerometers to vibrotactile violin bowing feedback (MusicJacket).
key_sources: Olga C. Santos. (2016). Training the Body: The Potential of AIED to Support Personalized Motor Skills Learning. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:730–755. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0103-2

article_title: Training the Body: The Potential of AIED to Support Personalized Motor Skills Learning
citation: Olga C. Santos. (2016). Training the Body: The Potential of AIED to Support Personalized Motor Skills Learning. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:730–755. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0103-2
title: Build accurate-movement models from recordings of several experts, since no one performs a movement identically each time
description: When modelling expert movements for comparison, the article recommends building the model from several recordings — repeated movements by the same expert and by other experts — and extrapolating the "accurate" movement in terms of relevant parameters. Because "it is not possible for any person to perform a given movement in the same exact way each time", a single recording would misrepresent the target. This supports diagnosing the mismatch between learner and expert movements.
requirements: Movements for which support is provided must be identified and isolable; accurate movements are recorded from experts with physical capabilities similar to the learner.
constraints: Whether movements are domain-defined or must be extracted from domain experts depends on the kind of activity.
target_learners: Learners practising specific motor skills against expert reference models
target_learning_goals: Correcting and refining movement technique toward expert performance
examples: Comparison is usually done against the movement carried out by an expert, with a threshold triggering feedback when overcome.

article_title: Title: Assessing Quality of Scenario-Based Multiple-Choice Questions in Physiology: Faculty-Generated vs. ChatGPT-Generated Questions among Phase I Medical Students
citation: Chauhan, A., Khaliq, F., & Nayak, K. R. (2025). Assessing Quality of Scenario-Based Multiple-Choice Questions in Physiology: Faculty-Generated vs. ChatGPT-Generated Questions among Phase I Medical Students. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 35, 2315–2344. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00471-z
title: Van der Vleuten's five-criteria utility framework for assessment-tool quality
description: The article adopts van der Vleuten's criteria as its framing model for assessment quality, outlining "five key criteria that collectively define the utility of an assessment tool": validity (accuracy in measuring intended targets), reliability (consistency over repeated administrations), educational impact (contribution to learning outcomes), acceptability (stakeholder perceptions of fairness, transparency, relevance), and cost (financial, time, and effort resources). The study applies this lens by evaluating SBMCQ quality through item analysis and stakeholder (faculty) perceptions.
requirements: Assessment tools should balance reliability, validity, acceptability, feasibility, and educational impact, per the framework the article cites
constraints: Presented in the article as a conceptual framework drawn from prior work (Baartman et al., 2007), not tested empirically in this study
target_learners: Medical educators designing and evaluating assessments
target_learning_goals: Evaluating quality and utility of assessment tools in medical education
examples: The study operationalizes quality via difficulty index, discrimination index, and distractor effectiveness, plus faculty focus group perceptions of fairness and relevance
