citation: Käser, T., & Alexandron, G. (2023). Simulated Learners in Educational Technology: A Systematic Literature Review and a Turing-like Test. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00337-2
title: Taxonomy of purposes for simulated learners in educational technology
description: The review organizes the applications of simulated learners into several purposes: teacher training, hypothesis generation and evaluation about human learning, adaptive learning algorithm development, collaborative virtual worlds, and testing learning environments. As the abstract states, simulated learners can be used "for teacher training, for generating and evaluating hypotheses on human learning, for developing adaptive learning algorithms". This taxonomy frames the trends the review traces over 2010-19.

constraints: Simulated learner models tend to represent only narrow aspects of student learning
target_learners: teacher trainees working with simulated students
target_learning_goals: teacher training practice
hypothesis testing about human learning
adaptive learning algorithm development
collaboration skills practice
examples: The review lists teacher training, hypothesis evaluation, adaptive algorithm development, virtual worlds with simulated pals, and testing learning environments as uses

title: A Turing-like test as a standard validation criterion for simulated learners
description: The review proposes a universal validation criterion for simulated learners modeled on Turing's Test. To validate simulated learner models, the authors "suggest a standard and universal criterion, which is based on the lasting idea of Turing's Test". They discuss the properties of this test and its potential to move the field of simulated learners forward, addressing the observed lack of validity evidence.
requirements: Simulated learner models must be developed and then validated against the criterion
constraints: The proposal is intended for future research rather than an established practice in the reviewed decade

target_learning_goals: establishing validity of simulated learner models
examples: The authors propose and discuss the test's properties in the concluding part of the review

article_title: An Intelligent Tutoring System for Entity Relationship Modelling
citation: Pramuditha Suraweera, Antonija Mitrovic. (2004). An Intelligent Tutoring System for Entity Relationship Modelling. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197310
title: KERMIT: a problem-solving environment for practising conceptual database design with the Entity-Relationship data model
description: KERMIT is a "Knowledge-based Entity Relationship Modelling Intelligent Tutor" described as "a problem-solving environment for the university-level students, in which they can practise conceptual database design using the Entity-Relationship data model". The system observes students' actions, adapts to their knowledge and learning abilities, and was deployed within genuine teaching activities in database courses.
requirements: University-level students practising conceptual database design with the Entity-Relationship data model
target_learning_goals: conceptual database design using the Entity-Relationship data model
examples: The paper describes the system's architecture and functionality and evaluates it in the context of genuine teaching activities.

article_title: An Intelligent Tutoring System for Entity Relationship Modelling
citation: Pramuditha Suraweera, Antonija Mitrovic. (2004). An Intelligent Tutoring System for Entity Relationship Modelling. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197310
title: Constraint-Based Modelling as a domain-modelling and student-modelling approach extended to design tasks
description: The article uses "Constraint-Based Modelling (CBM) to model the domain knowledge and generate student models". The authors had previously applied CBM in tutors teaching SQL and English punctuation rules, and present KERMIT as evidence that CBM "can be used to support students learning design tasks, which are very different from domains we dealt with in earlier tutors". CBM thus functions in the paper as a reusable framework for domain and student modelling across qualitatively different task types.
requirements: A domain whose knowledge can be represented as constraints, with system observation of students' actions to generate student models
target_learning_goals: conceptual database design skills
examples: KERMIT applies CBM to Entity-Relationship modelling; earlier tutors applied it to SQL and English punctuation rules.

article_title: The Civic Mission of MOOCs: Engagement across Political Differences in Online Forums
citation: Yeomans, M., Stewart, B. M., Mavon, K., Kindel, A., Tingley, D., & Reich, J. (2018). The Civic Mission of MOOCs: Engagement across Political Differences in Online Forums. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 28, 553–589. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0161-0
title: Discourse: a software tool for human coding of MOOC forum posts in context
description: Discourse is a software tool the authors built to handle forum data formats and to let coders "read and rate within the context of the other posts in the thread that preceded it". A team of coders (at least two per post) classified 24,556 posts from both courses by writers' intent; over 90% agreement with trace metadata supported using raw trace data in the reported analyses.
requirements: Requires a team of at least two human coders per post to classify writers' intent in conversational context
constraints: Validated against trace data in these two courses; coder consensus agreed with the metadata structure over 90% of the time
target_learners: MOOC forum participants in politically-themed courses
target_learning_goals: Measuring peer interaction and deliberative engagement across political differences
examples: Coders labelled each reply and comment as substantive, a short yes, or off-topic; off-topic posts (0.5% of all posts) were removed and 64% of on-topic comments counted as substantive

article_title: Research-Based Design of Pedagogical Agent Roles: a Review, Progress, and Recommendations
citation: Kim, Y., & Baylor, A. L. (2015). Research-Based Design of Pedagogical Agent Roles: a Review, Progress, and Recommendations. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0055-y
title: Three systematically operationalized pedagogical agent roles: Expert, Motivator, and Mentor
description: Baylor and Kim (2005) designed three instructional agent roles grounded in social-cognitive perspectives of learning. The Expert provided accurate information with authoritative speech and deictic gestures; the Motivator modeled coping strategies as a peer with emotional expressions; the Mentor combined both functions. Table 1 operationalized each role by "Appearance (image), Animation, Voice, Affect and messaging (script)." The roles were instantiated through pre-scripted agents with controlled gender, lip synchronization, and script length.
requirements: Learners must perceive the agent as intended; role instantiations require coordinated appearance, animation, voice, affect, and script
constraints: Agent-learner interactions were pre-scripted so each learner received all guidance, which limited the intelligence of the agents
target_learning_goals: computer literacy skills
instructional design skills
examples: Experiment 1 with 78 undergraduates learning computer literacy; Experiment 2 with 71 pre-service teachers learning instructional design skills

article_title: Narrative Balance Management in an Intelligent Biosafety Training Application for Improving User Performance
citation: Alvarez, N., Sanchez-Ruiz, A., Cavazza, M., Shigematsu, M., & Prendinger, H. (2014). Narrative Balance Management in an Intelligent Biosafety Training Application for Improving User Performance. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25, 35–59. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0022-z
title: Narrative Balance Management: drama management via Balance, Global Balance, Impact and Intensity parameters
description: The Narrative Balance Management account models a training session's dramatic flow with four parameters adapted from dimensions of conflict: Balance (how good or bad an event is for the user), Impact (its dramatic load), and the dynamic Global Balance and Intensity maintained by the system. When invoked, the manager "selects an event from the Task Trees which maximizes Impact, with the current Intensity as the upper boundary, and with the Balance most similar to the current Global Balance, but with opposite value". Global Balance attenuates toward zero over time, and empty events from a timer (set to 15 s in the system) raise Intensity so that difficulty escalates when the user is comfortable and assistance appears when the user struggles.
requirements: A domain expert must assign static Balance and Impact values to each event node when designing the scenario's task trees
A Task Model Database for the domain must be defined so the manager can be assembled into other training systems
constraints: The article notes Balance and Impact values are static and quite subjective, since they depend on expert judgment of dramatic quality
target_learners: Medical students training biohazard laboratory procedures
target_learning_goals: Biohazard spill-cleaning protocols
Handling unexpected laboratory accidents
examples: In the sample session, the manager selected a spill overflow when Intensity reached 5, and triggered a new broken-bottle spill when a fast user bumped a table
key_sources: Alvarez, N., Sanchez-Ruiz, A., Cavazza, M., Shigematsu, M., & Prendinger, H. (2014). Narrative Balance Management in an Intelligent Biosafety Training Application for Improving User Performance. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25, 35–59. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0022-z

article_title: Narrative Balance Management in an Intelligent Biosafety Training Application for Improving User Performance
citation: Alvarez, N., Sanchez-Ruiz, A., Cavazza, M., Shigematsu, M., & Prendinger, H. (2014). Narrative Balance Management in an Intelligent Biosafety Training Application for Improving User Performance. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25, 35–59. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0022-z
title: Task Trees: hierarchical knowledge representation for task recognition and event selection
description: Task Trees are the knowledge structure used by both the Task Model Reasoner and the Narrative Manager in the Bio-safety Lab. A tree's root represents the whole task, intermediate nodes are subtasks, and leaves are Task-Level Events; sibling nodes relate through AND, OR and SEQ conditions, and leaf nodes marked as errors let the system recognize plausible but incorrect actions. The article states "A Task Tree is a hierarchical model which has a root node representing the whole task to perform on the top of the tree and child nodes being the subtasks in which it can be divided". Narrative Manager trees additionally mark system nodes with Balance, Impact and Closure parameters.
requirements: The spill-clearing task tree contains more than 250 nodes, so building one requires detailed protocol knowledge and expert annotation of error nodes
constraints: The article contrasts this with Death Kitchen's Danger Matrix, which allowed only one constraint (partial order) for event selection
target_learning_goals: Recognition and correction of user errors during protocol execution
Real-time monitoring of multi-step laboratory procedures
examples: The spill accident tree models bordering, covering, disinfecting, and waste disposal, with incorrect border-placement nodes that trigger warnings
key_sources: Alvarez, N., Sanchez-Ruiz, A., Cavazza, M., Shigematsu, M., & Prendinger, H. (2014). Narrative Balance Management in an Intelligent Biosafety Training Application for Improving User Performance. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25, 35–59. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0022-z

article_title: Narrative Balance Management in an Intelligent Biosafety Training Application for Improving User Performance
citation: Alvarez, N., Sanchez-Ruiz, A., Cavazza, M., Shigematsu, M., & Prendinger, H. (2014). Narrative Balance Management in an Intelligent Biosafety Training Application for Improving User Performance. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25, 35–59. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0022-z
title: Integrate narrative with learning content so that narrative events generate the training tasks themselves
description: The article argues that narrative elements should not be an independent layer added on top of training mechanics, but should be the mechanism that generates events and tasks: "we use narrative techniques to generate the events in the scenario, giving to the user new tasks to solve or helping him", so the events directly determine the type and number of training contents experienced. This follows the article's reading of prior work that engagement raises knowledge acquisition when educational content and narrative are motivationally and tightly integrated. Balancing difficulty is also framed as a route toward psychological flow, keeping learners interested.
requirements: A task model database mapping domain tasks so narrative-triggered events correspond to genuine training content
constraints: The article notes prior work found off-task possibilities within narratives can hinder user performance, and results on engagement-to-learning links have been controversial
target_learners: Students in virtual training environments for procedural protocols
target_learning_goals: Engagement and persistence in training
Learning outcomes for safety protocols
examples: In Bio-safety Lab the Narrative Manager creates new spills, hides tools, or gives hints, and these events are themselves the practice content the user must resolve

article_title: The Future Trajectory of the AIED Community: Defining the ‘Knowledge Tradition’ in Critical Times
citation: Rebecca Eynon. (2024). The Future Trajectory of the AIED Community: Defining the ‘Knowledge Tradition’ in Critical Times. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 34, 105–110. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00354-1
title: AIED as a knowledge tradition characterised by an engineering view of education
description: Eynon characterises AIED as a distinctive knowledge tradition whose work “tends to be broadly characterised by a desire to use technology as the primary way to address perceived problems in education”. She calls this an “engineering view of education” in which AI systems are seen as relatively neutral tools designed to achieve specific learning outcomes, typically tested with randomised control trials and other experimental designs. The underlying belief that appropriately designed technology can make learning more efficient and effective persists even as learning theories and AI techniques have shifted.
requirements: Researchers and systems explicitly framed within this tradition, with technology treated as a designed means to specified learning outcomes
constraints: The author notes it is highly risky for an outsider to capture the tenets of a field and offers the characterisation as a short-essay representation
target_learners: Researchers and practitioners in artificial intelligence in education
target_learning_goals: Understanding the epistemological framing of AIED research and its methods
examples: The author points to the typical use of randomised control trials and other experimental designs to test causal models as the tradition's most typical research methods
key_sources: Rebecca Eynon. (2024). The Future Trajectory of the AIED Community: Defining the ‘Knowledge Tradition’ in Critical Times. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 34, 105–110. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00354-1

article_title: The Future Trajectory of the AIED Community: Defining the ‘Knowledge Tradition’ in Critical Times
citation: Rebecca Eynon. (2024). The Future Trajectory of the AIED Community: Defining the ‘Knowledge Tradition’ in Critical Times. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 34, 105–110. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00354-1
title: AIED should articulate its implicit visions of education and clarify its contribution to education, not only learning
description: The article argues that AIED largely concerns theories and practices of learning, not education, which are related but distinct. It recommends the community make explicit “what people in this field believe education “is” and how it should be”, addressing questions such as what vision of education AIED supports, whose vision it represents, and whether it should work across cultures and the globe.
requirements: The community should be clearer about what its work contributes to the wider domain of education and what it does not
constraints: The author states it is perhaps not the role of AIED researchers to focus on these wider questions of education in depth
target_learners: AIED researchers; teachers and education systems using AIED systems
target_learning_goals: Clarifying how AIED learning systems fit within education systems and teachers' professional practice
examples: The article notes augmentation of teaching is usually explored through usability and outcomes, while implications for teachers' identity and professional practice are less often explored

citation: Rebecca Eynon. (2024). The Future Trajectory of the AIED Community: Defining the ‘Knowledge Tradition’ in Critical Times. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 34, 105–110. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00354-1
title: Broaden AIED's core issues and connect to other knowledge traditions rather than radically rethinking its tenets
description: Responding to critique, the article suggests broadening the issues the AIED community deems central, rather than rethinking its central tenets, especially if the broadening “also means stronger connections with other knowledge traditions”. The community should take a clear position on aspects currently in flux — such as the balance between learning and computational science, the learning–education connection, and the commercial relationship — while recognising the strength and longstanding nature of the field.

constraints: The two knowledge traditions cannot be straightforwardly bridged because their philosophical foundations are quite different

examples: The author frames the special issue prompt as either a call for rethinking AIED's tenets or broadening its core focus, and argues the latter is more feasible and productive

article_title: Adaptive Intelligent Support to Improve Peer Tutoring in Algebra
citation: Walker, E., Rummel, N., & Koedinger, K. R. (2014). Adaptive Intelligent Support to Improve Peer Tutoring in Algebra. Int J Artif Intell Educ 24, 33–61. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0001-9
title: APTA: the Adaptive Peer Tutoring Assistant for high school algebra
description: APTA is an adaptive collaborative learning support environment built on the literal equation solving unit of the Cognitive Tutor Algebra. One student, the tutee, solves equations while the peer tutor watches, marks steps right or wrong, and chats; the system adds adaptive help-giving prompts addressed to the tutor. As the article states, "a second student (the peer tutor) marks the problem steps right or wrong and discusses the problems with the tutee in a chat window." Prompts are visible to both students and posed as non-critical questions to protect the tutor's authority.
requirements: Peer tutors and tutees interact through separate interfaces connected by a central control module
Sentence classifiers must be selected before utterances are typed in the chat window
constraints: In the reported version, prompts were always addressed to the peer tutor, not the tutee
The evaluation retained fixed roles rather than the designed reciprocal role swap
target_learners: High school algebra students in grades 7-12
target_learning_goals: Literal equation solving
Peer tutoring help-giving skills
examples: Students received an average of one prompt in the chat window for every three peer tutor actions after piloting tuning
key_sources: Walker, E., Rummel, N., & Koedinger, K. R. (2014). Adaptive Intelligent Support to Improve Peer Tutoring in Algebra. Int J Artif Intell Educ 24, 33–61. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0001-9

article_title: Adaptive Intelligent Support to Improve Peer Tutoring in Algebra
citation: Walker, E., Rummel, N., & Koedinger, K. R. (2014). Adaptive Intelligent Support to Improve Peer Tutoring in Algebra. Int J Artif Intell Educ 24, 33–61. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0001-9
title: Taxonomy of collaboration-support systems: mirroring, metacognitive tools, and guiding systems
description: The article organizes prior systems supporting collaboration using a three-way distinction it attributes to Soller et al.'s review: "mirroring systems that reflect the state of students'collaboration back to the students, metacognitive tools that provide information about the current and desired state of the interaction, and guiding systems that propose remedial actions in response to perceived collaborative weaknesses." APTA belongs to guiding systems providing peer interaction support, which the article further distinguishes, citing Magnisalis et al., from group formation and domain-specific support. Guiding systems must handle ambiguity in assessment, modeling, and support phases.
requirements: Assessment of student dialogue as it occurs
A model of ideal collaborative interactions
A support mechanism that intervenes when weaknesses are perceived
constraints: The article notes ACLS systems are rarely sufficiently developed to be deployed in natural context because producing relevant support from uncertain information is difficult
target_learners: Collaborating students in classroom learning environments
target_learning_goals: Collaborative interaction quality
Domain learning through collaboration
examples: LeCS prompts non-participating students; GroupLeader uses 46 sentence starters; APTA prompts peer tutors based on assessed help-giving skills

article_title: Adaptive Intelligent Support to Improve Peer Tutoring in Algebra
citation: Walker, E., Rummel, N., & Koedinger, K. R. (2014). Adaptive Intelligent Support to Improve Peer Tutoring in Algebra. Int J Artif Intell Educ 24, 33–61. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0001-9
title: Four peer tutor help-giving skills as targets for adaptive support
description: APTA's adaptive support targets an enumerated set of tutor competencies: "our goal was to target four peer tutor skills that exemplify good help in our context." These are timely help (responding to tutee errors and help requests), appropriate help (prompting self-explanation and giving error feedback), conceptual help (explaining steps with domain concepts), and use of classifiers (accurately labeling utterances). Each skill maps to a subset of the production rules and to its own knowledge-traced skill estimate that drives feedback selection.
requirements: Sentence classifiers in the chat interface so classifier use can be assessed
Access to tutee problem-solving step evaluations from the domain tutor
constraints: The skill set is specific to the peer tutoring context and literal equation solving domain
target_learners: High school students acting as peer tutors
target_learning_goals: Giving timely, appropriate, and conceptual help during peer tutoring
examples: When a tutor gives an instrumental hint after a tutee error, the system may ask in chat, "Tutor, why do you say that? Can you explain more?"
key_sources: Walker, E., Rummel, N., & Koedinger, K. R. (2014). Adaptive Intelligent Support to Improve Peer Tutoring in Algebra. Int J Artif Intell Educ 24, 33–61. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0001-9

article_title: Adaptive Intelligent Support to Improve Peer Tutoring in Algebra
citation: Walker, E., Rummel, N., & Koedinger, K. R. (2014). Adaptive Intelligent Support to Improve Peer Tutoring in Algebra. Int J Artif Intell Educ 24, 33–61. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0001-9
title: Four-valence production rule model of peer tutor help-giving with adapted knowledge tracing
description: APTA models peer tutoring with 19 production rules divided into four valence levels rather than correct/buggy: "rules were divided into four types: effective, somewhat effective, somewhat ineffective, and ineffective behaviors. These four levels allowed us to represent ambiguity in the model." Rules cover four skills (timely, appropriate, conceptual help, classifier use) and fire on tutor inaction as well as action. An algorithm based on Bayesian knowledge tracing maintains a mastery probability per skill, and rule firings update it; unmodeled behavior is treated as correct, as in constraint-based tutoring.
requirements: Multiple assessment channels: CTA step classifications, student self-classifications, and machine dialogue classifications
A configurable xml rule representation so the rule set can be modified without recompiling
constraints: The approach violates knowledge-tracing assumptions: a student can transfer from a learned to an unlearned state, and more than one skill maps to a given action
Skill estimates are tuned to trigger feedback rather than to accurately estimate collaborative skills
target_learners: High school peer tutors in algebra
target_learning_goals: Peer tutoring help-giving skills
examples: A tutor's nonconceptual next-step hint after a tutee error fired rules 2, 13, 15, and 16, raising timely-help and classifier estimates while lowering appropriate-help and conceptual-help estimates

article_title: Supporting Literacy Assessment in West Africa: Using State-of-the-Art Speech Models to Assess Oral Reading Fluency
citation: Henkel, O., Horne-Robinson, H., Hills, L., Roberts, B., & McGrane, J. (2025). Supporting Literacy Assessment in West Africa: Using State-of-the-Art Speech Models to Assess Oral Reading Fluency. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00435-9
title: Ghana ORF Dataset: publicly available oral reading fluency recordings from Ghanaian students
description: The University of Oxford & Rising Academies Ghanaian Student Oral Reading Fluency Dataset contains the results from ORF tasks administered in a Ghanaian school network, including original passages, audio recordings of students reading, and high-quality human transcriptions. The authors state it addresses a gap because "there are no publicly available datasets of children's voices speaking English that (a) focus on students' oral reading rather than speaking and (b) are from countries other than the United States, Canada, or the United Kingdom." Passages came from PrePIRLS, designed for LMICs.
requirements: Human transcriptions were produced by careful relistening, estimated at approximately 5 min per story, to faithfully preserve added or repeated words
constraints: Recordings come from students of one school network on the peri-urban periphery of Accra, so the sample is regionally specific
target_learners: Students aged 9-18 in Ghana, grades spanning primary to secondary
target_learning_goals: Oral reading fluency assessment
examples: 130 readers (of 162 screened, 32 nonreaders) read short passages aloud; 239 recordings total; 35 of 130 students (15%) reported speaking English at home
key_sources: Henkel, O., Horne-Robinson, H., Hills, L., Roberts, B., & McGrane, J. (2025). Supporting Literacy Assessment in West Africa: Using State-of-the-Art Speech Models to Assess Oral Reading Fluency. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00435-9

article_title: Supporting Literacy Assessment in West Africa: Using State-of-the-Art Speech Models to Assess Oral Reading Fluency
citation: Henkel, O., Horne-Robinson, H., Hills, L., Roberts, B., & McGrane, J. (2025). Supporting Literacy Assessment in West Africa: Using State-of-the-Art Speech Models to Assess Oral Reading Fluency. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00435-9
title: Use free, publicly available, unmodified large-scale speech models to scale oral reading fluency assessment in lower-resource contexts
description: Because top open-source models now transcribe children's oral reading accurately without fine-tuning, ORF assessment can be automated where one-on-one assessment is too costly. The authors argue the combination of "accurate transcription, ability to handle diverse accents, and production of reliable ORF scores" could enhance literacy assessment where regular individualized assessment has been blocked by resource constraints, enabling more frequent progress monitoring.
requirements: Recordings of students reading passages aloud, plus the original story text and audio duration to compute WCPM
Model transcripts must be evaluated against the original text to capture student reading errors, not normalized away
constraints: Findings rest on only two specific ASR models, a relatively small sample from two datasets (Ghana and the United States), and English-only assessment
Automated WCPM does not match expert scores exactly; the authors frame ORF as a formative or diagnostic measure where small measurement errors are unlikely to hurt practical use
target_learners: Beginning and intermediate readers in lower-resource, linguistically diverse education contexts, particularly the Global South
target_learning_goals: Formative assessment and monitoring of oral reading fluency
examples: The study used Whisper V2 and wav2vec 2.0 out-of-the-box on classroom recordings from Ghana and validated automated WCPM against expert human raters on 165 assessments
key_sources: Henkel, O., Horne-Robinson, H., Hills, L., Roberts, B., & McGrane, J. (2025). Supporting Literacy Assessment in West Africa: Using State-of-the-Art Speech Models to Assess Oral Reading Fluency. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00435-9

article_title: From the Lab to the Wild: Examining Generalizability of Video-based Mind Wandering Detection
citation: Bühler, B., Bozkir, E., Goldberg, P., Sümer, Ö., D'Mello, S., Gerjets, P., Trautwein, U., Kasneci, E. (2025). From the Lab to the Wild: Examining Generalizability of Video-based Mind Wandering Detection. Int J Artif Intell Educ 35, 823–857. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00412-2
title: Transfer-learning pipeline using AffectNet-pretrained ResNet50 latent features for video-based mind wandering detection
description: A detection pipeline in which the article uses transfer learning, where the feature extraction part of a ResNet50 CNN pre-trained on the AffectNet facial expression recognition dataset is applied to webcam video. Faces are detected frame-wise with RetinaFace, aligned, cropped, and fed to the CNN without its classification layer, producing a 2048-digit latent feature vector passed to downstream classifiers including SVMs, XGBoost, DNNs, and LSTM/BiLSTM temporal models, with an optional fine-tuned end-to-end CNN-LSTM variant.
requirements: Learner facial video from consumer-grade webcams with faces detectable across all frames; the article removed instances where no face could be detected across all frames
Ground-truth mind wandering self-reports (self-caught or probe-caught) for supervised training or evaluation
constraints: The in-the-wild dataset used for cross-dataset evaluation is modest in size (N = 15 participants), so it was used solely for evaluation purposes
target_learners: university students in online learning settings such as reading scientific text or watching video lectures
target_learning_goals: continuous, non-intrusive assessment of learners' attentional state (mind wandering) during learning tasks
examples: Within the lab study, latent features reached F1 up to 0.459 (LSTM); in cross-dataset prediction, BiLSTM on latent features reached F1 0.352, comparable to the state-of-the-art
key_sources: Bühler, B., Bozkir, E., Goldberg, P., Sümer, Ö., D'Mello, S., Gerjets, P., Trautwein, U., Kasneci, E. (2025). From the Lab to the Wild: Examining Generalizability of Video-based Mind Wandering Detection. Int J Artif Intell Educ 35, 823–857. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00412-2

article_title: Another 25 Years of AIED? Challenges and Opportunities for Intelligent Educational Technologies of the Future
citation: Niels Pinkwart. (2016). Another 25 Years of AIED? Challenges and Opportunities for Intelligent Educational Technologies of the Future. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:771–783. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0099-7
title: Utopian and dystopian future scenarios as an analytic device for envisioning AIED's future
description: The paper constructs two contrasting narrative scenarios—students Ana and Ben in a utopian future and Dan and Eve in a dystopian one—as a deliberation device. The author states the scenarios, which are admittedly extreme, may "serve as a means for thinking about possible futures of AIED and about decisions that AIED researchers and developers might be faced with in the future." The device grounds the derivation of the seven challenges and frames them as risks and opportunities rather than predictions.
requirements: External trends in technology, education, and educational technology must first be listed as relatively stable states or development trends
constraints: The author notes there is no way any of these visions can be right or wrong in a scientific way, and no way to prove or falsify them now
target_learners: secondary school students nearing graduation as depicted in the scenarios
target_learning_goals: anticipating future directions of AIED research and deployment
examples: A dialogue-based utopia with privacy-respecting lifelong tutors and a dystopia with commercial data-selling tutors and teacher layoffs
key_sources: Niels Pinkwart. (2016). Another 25 Years of AIED? Challenges and Opportunities for Intelligent Educational Technologies of the Future. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:771–783. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0099-7

article_title: Another 25 Years of AIED? Challenges and Opportunities for Intelligent Educational Technologies of the Future
citation: Niels Pinkwart. (2016). Another 25 Years of AIED? Challenges and Opportunities for Intelligent Educational Technologies of the Future. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:771–783. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0099-7
title: Seven-challenge framework for the future of AIED
description: The paper's central organizing framework is a set of seven challenges derived by comparing the utopian and dystopian visions: intercultural and global dimensions, practical impact, privacy, interaction methods, collaboration at scale, effectiveness in multiple domains, and the role of AIED in educational technology. The author writes that a comparison of the two visions "leads to seven challenges that AIED might have to face in the future" and discusses each as both a risk and an opportunity depending on how the field positions itself.
requirements: Interpretation of the external trends and the two contrasting scenarios together
constraints: The challenges are speculative; the author states they cannot be proven or falsified now
target_learning_goals: strategic orientation of artificial intelligence in education research
examples: Each challenge is elaborated in the Discussion section, e.g., privacy best practices for stakeholders and moving beyond Constraint Based Modeling comfort zones
key_sources: Niels Pinkwart. (2016). Another 25 Years of AIED? Challenges and Opportunities for Intelligent Educational Technologies of the Future. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:771–783. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0099-7

article_title: Another 25 Years of AIED? Challenges and Opportunities for Intelligent Educational Technologies of the Future
citation: Niels Pinkwart. (2016). Another 25 Years of AIED? Challenges and Opportunities for Intelligent Educational Technologies of the Future. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:771–783. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0099-7
title: PSLC DataShop as a long-term learner-data collection for a data-driven science of learning
description: PSLC DataShop is a long-term data collection referenced as an underexploited asset of the field. The paper states that "the field is probably just beginning to understand the larger value of long-term data collections such as the PSLC DataShop (Koedinger et al.,2010) in order to contribute to a data driven science of learning and the related adaptive educational technologies." It exemplifies the broader trend of increasing importance of data, whose value lies in aggregation and analysis for building student models.
requirements: Aggregation and analysis practices that turn collected interaction data into insights for adaptive educational technologies
constraints: The field is described as only beginning to understand the larger value of such collections
target_learners: researchers building student models and adaptive educational technologies
target_learning_goals: data-driven understanding of student learning and improvement of tutoring systems
examples: The paper cites DataShop alongside Big Data trends as evidence of data's growing value in AIED

article_title: An Extended Learning Analytics Framework Integrating Machine Learning and Pedagogical Approaches for Student Performance Prediction and Intervention
citation: Alalawi, K., Athauda, R., & Chiong, R. (2024). An Extended Learning Analytics Framework Integrating Machine Learning and Pedagogical Approaches for Student Performance Prediction and Intervention. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00429-7
title: SPPA: Student Performance Prediction and Action framework
description: SPPA is a web-based Learning Analytics Intervention framework covering the full course life cycle: Course Design, Course Delivery, and Course Evaluation. It lets academics generate course-specific predictive models from historical continuous assessment data, run predictions after each assessment, identify at-risk students via dashboards, and deliver personalised interventions. The article states that "SPPA is implemented as a web application and is accessible by course instructors (also called academics in this paper) and students via a web browser." It integrates pedagogical principles such as constructive alignment and Hattie and Timperley's feedback model, and is released as an open-source project.
requirements: Academics need access to the course's historical continuous assessment data to build predictive models
constraints: Prediction and intervention are only possible after students submit at least the first continuous assessment task
target_learning_goals: early identification of at-risk students
improved pass rates and grades through targeted interventions
examples: Deployed in six courses at a tertiary institution with four academics piloting learning analytics interventions
key_sources: Alalawi, K., Athauda, R., & Chiong, R. (2024). An Extended Learning Analytics Framework Integrating Machine Learning and Pedagogical Approaches for Student Performance Prediction and Intervention. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00429-7

article_title: An Extended Learning Analytics Framework Integrating Machine Learning and Pedagogical Approaches for Student Performance Prediction and Intervention
citation: Alalawi, K., Athauda, R., & Chiong, R. (2024). An Extended Learning Analytics Framework Integrating Machine Learning and Pedagogical Approaches for Student Performance Prediction and Intervention. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00429-7
title: Course-specific predictive models built from continuous assessment data using five ML algorithms
description: SPPA automates creation of student performance predictive models from a course's own historical continuous assessment scores rather than institution-wide integrated data. It "implements five well-known machine learning (ML) algorithms (Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machine, Decision Tree, k-Nearest Neighbours, and Naive Bayes)" and evaluates them with accuracy, precision, recall and F-measure using a 70–30 train-test split and fivefold cross-validation. Models come in binary (likely to pass/fail) and multi-class (fail/borderline/pass) forms, and the best model is selected by highest accuracy followed by F-measure, recall and precision.
requirements: Historical continuous assessment data for the course
Prediction is only meaningful after at least one continuous assessment is submitted
constraints: Using only continuous assessment data means predictions and interventions cannot occur before the first assessment task
target_learning_goals: early identification of at-risk students
examples: Course A used 2019–2021 records (147 student records) to create predictive models; Course B used 306 student records from 2017 to 2021
key_sources: Alalawi, K., Athauda, R., & Chiong, R. (2024). An Extended Learning Analytics Framework Integrating Machine Learning and Pedagogical Approaches for Student Performance Prediction and Intervention. citation: Alalawi, K., Athauda, R., & Chiong, R. (2024). An Extended Learning Analytics Framework Integrating Machine Learning and Pedagogical Approaches for Student Performance Prediction and Intervention. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00429-7
title: CA Mapping Model linking course learning outcomes, assessment tasks and teaching-learning activities
description: The CA Mapping Model operationalises Biggs' Constructive Alignment inside SPPA: instructors map Course Learning Outcomes (CLOs) to Assessment Tasks (ATs) and Teaching and Learning Activities (TLAs) at coarse or fine granularity. The article notes that "Instructors specify the course's CLOs and map them to ATs and TLAs in the CA Mapping Model." This mapping is then used to identify students' knowledge gaps and to auto-generate personalised study/revision plans for interventions, and to locate course areas for improvement during course evaluation. Finer-grained mappings yield more detailed feedback and evaluation information.
requirements: Instructors create and maintain the mapping; finer granularity is expected to be developed over multiple course iterations
constraints: Feedback detail depends on mapping granularity; coarse mappings provide less specific revision guidance
target_learning_goals: identifying knowledge gaps
personalised revision planning
aligned course design
examples: In an example mapping, CLO1 on peer-to-peer networks is split into CLO1a and CLO1b mapped to practical tests, a final exam, lectures and labs

article_title: Exploring the Long-Term Effects of the Statewide Implementation of an Automated Writing Evaluation System on Students’ State Test ELA Performance
citation: Yue Huang, Joshua Wilson, & Henry May. (2024). Exploring the Long-Term Effects of the Statewide Implementation of an Automated Writing Evaluation System on Students' State Test ELA Performance. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00443-9
title: Utah Compose (UC), a statewide automated writing evaluation system with the PEG scoring engine and interpretable partially connected neural networks
description: Utah Compose is a web-based AWE system developed by Measurement Incorporated, implemented statewide in Utah from Fall 2014, providing "unlimited access to pre-designed prompts aligned with different grade levels and writing genres" plus automated scores and instant revision feedback. It uses the PEG scoring engine built on "800 + linguistic variables" and trains models for six writing traits across three genres and five grade bands, with human-machine agreement reported at a quadratic weighted kappa of 0.835 (SD = 0.026). For interpretability, UC "employs neural networks with selectively connected hidden nodes" matching pre-classified linguistic feature groups so revision improves scores, plus peer review, tutorials, and graphic organizers.
requirements: Trained on a diverse sample of essays scored by well-trained human raters, with generalization evaluated on a separate held-out test dataset
constraints: Implementation was naturalistic: no state-mandated usage and no uniform professional development for teachers
target_learning_goals: Writing proficiency and improvement through practice, immediate feedback, and guided instructional support
examples: State-contracted tool of the Utah State Board of Education starting Fall 2014; the Utah-branded equivalent of MI Write
key_sources: Yue Huang, Joshua Wilson, & Henry May. (2024). Exploring the Long-Term Effects of the Statewide Implementation of an Automated Writing Evaluation System on Students' State Test ELA Performance. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00443-9

article_title: Reflections on Andes’ Goal-free User Interface
citation: VanLehn, K. (2015). Reflections on Andes' Goal-free User Interface. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0067-7
title: Goal-free vs. goal-aligned user interfaces for step-based tutoring systems
description: A goal-aligned user interface displays relevant goals as blank boxes or constrained entry locations that scaffold problem-solving steps; a goal-free user interface is "essentially a blank canvas, with no visual indications of the goals that should be attempted next". Andes implemented the goal-free vision so users could enter steps anywhere and in any order, like paper, while the system still recognized goals and correctness. The design requires the system to do plan recognition, interpret composite steps, and support assessment without location-based goal cues.
requirements: The tutoring system must provide goal scaffolding on demand via next-step and what's-wrong hint buttons
The system must decompose large composite steps into primitive physics rules
Immediate feedback keeps students on a recognizable solution path
constraints: Plan recognition works poorly because users often have no recognizable plan
Embedded assessment (assignment of blame) is much harder because an incorrect step's location provides no information about the user's intended goal
target_learning_goals: physics problem solving
examples: Andes3, released around 2010, looked and acted like MS PowerPoint, with tools for text, equations, arrows and coordinate axes, and offered text auto-completions when defining variables
key_sources: VanLehn, K. (2015). Reflections on Andes' Goal-free User Interface. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0067-7

article_title: ToTCompute: A Novel EEG-Based TimeOnTask Threshold Computation Mechanism for Engagement Modelling and Monitoring
citation: Ghergulescu, I. & Muntean, C. H. (2016). ToTCompute: A Novel EEG-Based TimeOnTask Threshold Computation Mechanism for Engagement Modelling and Monitoring. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0111-2
title: ToTCompute mechanism for automatic computation of task-dependent TimeOnTask engagement thresholds
description: ToTCompute is a mechanism that automatically computes TimeOnTask threshold values for various game tasks using game-playing logs and EEG engagement data collected during an initial testing session. It computes "the relative engagement changes for all participants every second (i.e., every TimeOnTask iteration)" and applies a time series linear model with an autocorrelation test, returning NA when data is random or the trend is not negative. Thresholds represent upper limits above which engagement decreases by a predefined relative change (e.g., 5, 10, 15%).
requirements: An initial testing session with at least 30 participants playing while wearing the Emotiv EPOC headset
The game creator must identify independent game tasks within the game
constraints: The algorithm returns NA when the autocorrelation test indicates random data or when the time series linear model is not statistically significant or lacks a negative trend
target_learning_goals: engagement monitoring and modelling during game-based learning
key_sources: Ghergulescu, I. & Muntean, C. H. (2016). ToTCompute: A Novel EEG-Based TimeOnTask Threshold Computation Mechanism for Engagement Modelling and Monitoring. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0111-2

article_title: ToTCompute: A Novel EEG-Based TimeOnTask Threshold Computation Mechanism for Engagement Modelling and Monitoring
citation: Ghergulescu, I. & Muntean, C. H. (2016). ToTCompute: A Novel EEG-Based TimeOnTask Threshold Computation Mechanism for Engagement Modelling and Monitoring. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0111-2
title: Emotiv EPOC headset Affectiv Suite engagement measure
description: The Emotiv EPOC is a wireless brain computer interface device recording EEG through 14 electrodes; its Affectiv Suite provides real-time detection of emotional state including engagement, excitement, frustration and meditation. The article operationalises engagement as "the engagement measure provided by the Affectiv Suite of the Emotiv EPOC headset", citing third-party validation studies showing reliable engagement and excitement measures. It was chosen after a comparative review rated it highest in usefulness for research among low-cost EEG equipment.
requirements: Emotiv API access for retrieving engagement values
Good signal from all sensors at setup
constraints: Only raw EEG signals can be saved as binary .edf files through the proprietary software, so custom Java programs were needed to save affective data
target_learning_goals: engagement detection during game-play
key_sources: Ghergulescu, I. & Muntean, C. H. (2016). ToTCompute: A Novel EEG-Based TimeOnTask Threshold Computation Mechanism for Engagement Modelling and Monitoring. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0111-2

article_title: ToTCompute: A Novel EEG-Based TimeOnTask Threshold Computation Mechanism for Engagement Modelling and Monitoring
citation: Ghergulescu, I. & Muntean, C. H. (2016). ToTCompute: A Novel EEG-Based TimeOnTask Threshold Computation Mechanism for Engagement Modelling and Monitoring. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0111-2
title: Non-disturbing engagement monitoring via game-play interaction logging and physiological sensing
description: The article distinguishes disturbing methods (questionnaires interrupting game-play) from non-disturbing methods that monitor engagement "without interrupting the game-play and game flow". Non-disturbing methods log player behaviour automatically and may add physiological equipment such as EEG or eye-tracking. ToTCompute exemplifies this pattern by combining game-playing event logs (task start/stop timestamps) with continuous EEG-based engagement recording during game-play.
requirements: Automatic logging embedded in the game to record task start and stop timestamps
Clear, independent game tasks for which metrics can be computed
constraints: Additional equipment such as EEG adds cost and is harder to incorporate in everyday game-based e-learning scenarios
target_learning_goals: continuous engagement monitoring during learning games
examples: The Fire Protocol case study embedded automatic logging in the game and recorded EEG with the Emotiv EPOC headset while participants played.

article_title: Transforming Driver Education: A Comparative Analysis of LLM-Augmented Training and Conventional Instruction for Autonomous Vehicle Technologies
citation: Murtaza, M., Cheng, C.-T., Fard, M., & Zeleznikow, J. (2024). Transforming Driver Education: A Comparative Analysis of LLM-Augmented Training and Conventional Instruction for Autonomous Vehicle Technologies. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00407-z
title: A dual-focus framework for preparing ChatGPT prompts for training, distinguishing general LLM prompting principles from application-specific pedagogical principles
description: The article introduces a framework for structuring ChatGPT prompts used as training tools, built on "a dual focus, incorporating general LLM prompting principles, which apply universally across multiple contexts, and application-specific (pedagogical) principles tailored to particular training scenarios". The general principles cover goal and scene setting, structured instruction, and regular reiteration of objectives to counter token-limit context loss. The pedagogical principles cover personalised responses, proactive knowledge checking via follow-up questions, and phrasing of output format such as bullet points. The framework was demonstrated by equipping ChatGPT with an AV user manual for conversation-based driver training.
requirements: ChatGPT must be instructed to base responses solely on the provided training material and not draw from external knowledge sources, to avoid inconsistent or invented information
constraints: The article notes the brief ~1100-word manual "does not adequately represent the complexities of processing larger documents", which could challenge ChatGPT's token capacity and increase the risk of inaccurate or invented information
target_learners: adult licensed drivers learning ADAS and AV functions
target_learning_goals: accurate operation of advanced driver assistance functions
formation of accurate mental models of complex systems
examples: In the driver-training demonstration, ChatGPT was given the AV manual contents and instructed to teach via an interactive, conversation-based approach, with participants asking on average seven questions and receiving responses averaging approximately 124 words per question
key_sources: Murtaza, M., Cheng, C.-T., Fard, M., & Zeleznikow, J. (2024). Transforming Driver Education: A Comparative Analysis of LLM-Augmented Training and Conventional Instruction for Autonomous Vehicle Technologies. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00407-z

article_title: Transforming Driver Education: A Comparative Analysis of LLM-Augmented Training and Conventional Instruction for Autonomous Vehicle Technologies
citation: Murtaza, M., Cheng, C.-T., Fard, M., & Zeleznikow, J. (2024). Transforming Driver Education: A Comparative Analysis of LLM-Augmented Training and Conventional Instruction for Autonomous Vehicle Technologies. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00407-z
title: ChatGPT-based interactive user manual for training drivers on ADAS and AV functions
description: An LLM-based instructional tool in which the text content of a conventional vehicle user manual (~1100 words) is delivered through ChatGPT as a conversational, interactive medium on a simulator screen. Participants received "a ChatGPT-based interactive user manual, with training conducted directly on a simulator screen", within a 15-minute session with no limit on the number or length of questions. ChatGPT provided personalised guidance, clarified queries, and verified understanding through follow-up questions, while being restricted to the manual's data to avoid external information.
requirements: Learners need an introductory video defining learning objectives, introducing ADAS context and vocabulary, and giving an interaction kickstarting example before using the tool
constraints: The article reports no false responses during the experiment but notes the brief manual does not represent the complexities of processing larger documents, which could challenge ChatGPT's token capacity
target_learners: adult licensed drivers aged 20 to above 40 with varied driving experience
target_learning_goals: correct activation and deactivation of ADAS functions
understanding ADAS functionality and limitations
examples: Participants asked on average seven questions per session, and ChatGPT answered accurately on existing functions, non-existing functions, and complex conditional scenario-based inquiries

article_title: The Affective Experience of Novice Computer Programmers
citation: Bosch, N., & D'Mello, S. (2017). The Affective Experience of Novice Computer Programmers. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0069-5
title: Updated model of affect dynamics and co-occurrence during complex learning, adding a boredom→engagement re-engagement link and co-occurrence arcs
description: The article tests the D'Mello and Graesser affect dynamics model, in which engagement, confusion, frustration, and boredom interact through impasse detection and resolution, and proposes a revision based on its findings. The revised model (Fig. 7) keeps the impasse-driven cycle but, as the authors state, "Figure 7 presents an updated theoretical model incorporating the new affect transition as well as co-occurrences" — replacing the boredom→frustration link with a boredom→engagement re-engagement link and adding arcs for the confusion+frustration and curiosity+engagement co-occurrence pairs, plus a curiosity (novelty) state.
requirements: Applies to complex learning situations with impasses, tested here for novice computer programming with fine-grained (15-s interval) affect judgments
constraints: The predicted boredom→frustration transition was not significant in this data; the boredom→engagement transition, though observed, was attributed to the fast-paced, hint-supported nature of this particular learning environment
target_learners: novice computer programming students without prior programming experience
target_learning_goals: learning fundamentals of computer programming in Python
examples: The study tested the original model against affect transition likelihoods from 99 novices and found five of six predicted transitions significant, motivating the revised model in Fig. 7
key_sources: Bosch, N., & D'Mello, S. (2017). The Affective Experience of Novice Computer Programmers. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0069-5

article_title: Intelligent Tutoring Systems by and for the Developing World: A Review of Trends and Approaches for Educational Technology in a Global Context
citation: Benjamin D. Nye. (2015). Intelligent Tutoring Systems by and for the Developing World: A Review of Trends and Approaches for Educational Technology in a Global Context. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0028-6
title: Ecological system model for intelligent tutoring systems (Bronfenbrenner-based)
description: The article conceptualizes the stakeholders surrounding an ITS as an ecological system, modeled on Bronfenbrenner (1992). Students receive direct influences through microsystems (family, peers, teachers, local administrators), indirect influences through the mesosystem, and macrosystem factors such as infrastructure, governmental policies, and cultures. Developers have their own ecosystem of collaborators, funding agencies, and cultures, and cultural divides can exist between technology sponsors, developers, host governments, and end-users. The model frames why adoption barriers in the developing world extend beyond the technology itself.
requirements: Availability and perceptions of appropriate educational technology must be communicated across cultural divides between sponsors, developers, host governments, and end-users
constraints: The article notes the developing world is highly diverse, not a monolith, and every educational technology should ideally be tuned to the specific intended learners and educational ecosystem
target_learners: students in developing countries using educational technology
target_learning_goals: successful adoption and fit of tutoring systems within local educational ecosystems
examples: Figure 1 of the article diagrams this ecological system for ITS, used to organize the review's barrier analysis

article_title: Intelligent Tutoring Systems by and for the Developing World: A Review of Trends and Approaches for Educational Technology in a Global Context
citation: Benjamin D. Nye. (2015). Intelligent Tutoring Systems by and for the Developing World: A Review of Trends and Approaches for Educational Technology in a Global Context. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0028-6
title: Inner-loop/outer-loop adaptivity criterion defining intelligent tutoring systems
description: The article defines ITS via VanLehn's (2006) two types of adaptivity: an outer loop that determines the next learning task, typically keeping tasks within the learner's zone of proximal development, and an inner loop that helps the learner while working on a given task. The inner loop provides step-specific scaffolding such as hint sequences, error-correction feedback, and cues toward important parts of the problem state. The article uses this inner-loop criterion as its inclusion test for the mapping study, with an 'adaptive learning systems' category for outer-loop-only fringe systems.
requirements: Inclusion requires step-based tutoring, i.e., adaptive support while working on a task, providing hints and/or feedback intelligently
constraints: The article notes the search was not designed to comprehensively cover adaptive learning systems, which were analyzed only to consider the fringe of inclusion criteria
target_learning_goals: step-specific scaffolding, hints, and error-correction feedback during problem solving
examples: The review cites a meta-analysis (VanLehn 2011) finding that systems with step-based adaptivity produced higher learning gains than those with only an outer loop

article_title: Intelligent Tutoring Systems by and for the Developing World: A Review of Trends and Approaches for Educational Technology in a Global Context
citation: Benjamin D. Nye. (2015). Intelligent Tutoring Systems by and for the Developing World: A Review of Trends and Approaches for Educational Technology in a Global Context. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0028-6
title: Three stakeholder patterns for developing-world ITS: transferred, home-grown, and new systems designed for a target region
description: The article observes three patterns among reviewed papers, depending on stakeholders. In the first, an established ITS from a higher-income country is transferred and localized for less developed countries; these tend to be mature with numerous evaluations. The second is a home-grown system developed by researchers in a developing region targeting local or national needs. The third is a new system designed predominantly in a most-developed country but intended for a less developed area, grouped with transfers due to low numbers.
requirements: Transferred and collaborative systems depend on stakeholders from both a high-income country and a lower-income country
constraints: The review found collaborations and transfers addressed mobile platforms and data costs in none of the reviewed papers, while home-grown ITS more often addressed mobile platforms, data costs, and student basic ICT skills
target_learners: learners in developing regions served by transferred or locally developed tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: delivery of adaptive tutoring suited to local infrastructure, language, and culture
examples: Examples of transferred/collaborative ITS were Cognitive Tutor in Latin America, the LISTEN Reading Tutor in Africa, the Single Display Groupware system, and the Braille Tutor; home-grown ITS were most strongly represented by China, India, and Mexico

article_title: AI as a Methodology for Supporting Educational Praxis and Teacher Metacognition
citation: Kaśka Porayska-Pomsta. (2016). AI as a Methodology for Supporting Educational Praxis and Teacher Metacognition. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:679–700. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0101-4
title: AI as a methodology: knowledge representation and elicitation as a front-end technology for educators' metacognition in praxis
description: The article proposes viewing AI not only as back-end functionality of educational technology but as a "front-end technology-of-the-mind" through which educators represent, experiment with and compare their practices at fine-grained detail. AI's knowledge representation acts as a surrogate of the world, forcing ontological commitments that expose multiple perspectives, and as a medium of human expression that leaves a trace of one's views over time. Knowledge elicitation engages teachers in externalising tacit knowledge, which the exemplar projects (LeAM, TARDIS) show scaffolds critical reflection on their own practices.
requirements: Educators must make a conscious effort to represent the what, the why and the how of their thinking; methods, tools and common knowledge representation standards are needed so practitioners can generate evidence independently of researchers
constraints: Neither exemplar project evaluated the effectiveness of these methods, so no objective measures can be offered; existing systems such as ASSISTments and Learning Designer lack explicit support for teachers' metacognitive enquiry or fine-grained reflection on momentary decisions
target_learners: teachers, tutors, coaches and other front-line educational practitioners
target_learning_goals: adaptive metacognitive skills in praxis
evidence-based practice and pedagogical innovation
reflective practice and continuous professional development
examples: LeAM used Wizard-of-Oz studies where tutors talked aloud about feedback decisions and selected situational factors, directly implementing a Bayesian network; TARDIS used knowledge elicitation across three stages to build practitioners' self-observation skills culminating in an annotation schema
key_sources: Kaśka Porayska-Pomsta. (2016). AI as a Methodology for Supporting Educational Praxis and Teacher Metacognition. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:679–700. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0101-4

article_title: Reducing Workload in Short Answer Grading Using Machine Learning
citation: Rebecka Weegar · Peter Idestam-Almquist. (2024). Reducing Workload in Short Answer Grading Using Machine Learning. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00322-1
title: Review all automated grading output to ensure fair and correct grading, particularly in high-stakes exams
description: The article argues that even a very accurate automated grader cannot fully replace manual grading, because disagreement with a human grade may be spurious and graders can be sensitive to manipulation. It therefore evaluates a setup in which "the output of the classifier was manually reviewed and corrected when needed", measuring workload including this full review. This makes fairness for students a design requirement rather than an optional check.
requirements: A workflow must budget time for reviewing every automatically scored answer, not only suspected errors
constraints: Even with a very accurate classifier, fully replacing manual grading is not yet possible in high-stakes exams
target_learners: higher education students in large introductory courses
target_learning_goals: correct and fair assessment of short-answer exam responses
examples: In the evaluated exam grading, all classifier output was reviewed in clusters using a spreadsheet program, and the overall workload reduction of 64-74% was achieved with this complete review in place
key_sources: Rebecka Weegar · Peter Idestam-Almquist. (2024). Reducing Workload in Short Answer Grading Using Machine Learning. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00322-1

article_title: Reducing Workload in Short Answer Grading Using Machine Learning
citation: Rebecka Weegar · Peter Idestam-Almquist. (2024). Reducing Workload in Short Answer Grading Using Machine Learning. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00322-1
title: Modular spreadsheet-based grading setup combining clustering, sampled manual grading, classification, and full review
description: A reusable grading workflow in which student answers are clustered (k-means on lemmatized unigrams), a sample is manually graded as training data, per-question classifiers score the remaining answers, and all scores are reviewed in cluster order. The authors propose "a modular and reusable grading setup that can be used in a course setting without the need for specifically developed interfaces for grading"; a spreadsheet program displayed answers, scores, and comments.
requirements: Clustering must allow manually setting the number of clusters and provide a measure of representativeness for selecting training answers
constraints: Evaluated on short answers (average 13 tokens) from one introductory computer science exam, mainly in Swedish
target_learners: higher education students in comparatively large courses
target_learning_goals: efficient and correct grading of short-answer exam questions
examples: The ordinary exam (438 students, 64 questions) and a retake exam (73 students) were graded with this setup; the graders reported clustering made grading more efficient and supported consistent scoring

article_title: In Sync or Out of Sync? Understanding Stress and Learning Performance in Collaborative Healthcare Simulations through Physiological Synchrony and Arousal
citation: Lixiang Yan · Dragan Gašević · Vanessa Echeverria · Linxuan Zhao · Yueqiao Jin · Xinyu Li · Roberto Martinez-Maldonado. (2025). In Sync or Out of Sync? Understanding Stress and Learning Performance in Collaborative Healthcare Simulations through Physiological Synchrony and Arousal. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00475-9
title: Embodied cognition theory grounds the use of physiological indicators in embodied collaborative learning analytics
description: Embodied cognition holds that cognitive processes are deeply influenced by the body's interactions with and responses to the surrounding environment, extending learning beyond purely intellectual activity. The article uses this framework to justify collecting physiological data — heart rate, EDA, pupil dilation — during embodied collaborative learning, treating bodily responses as integral to understanding learning experiences. It further stresses that bodily experiences are socially situated, so physiological measures should be read alongside cognitive and behavioural processes in collaborative settings.
requirements: Physiological data must be interpreted in relation to the specific learning activity and context, since heart rate reflects both sympathetic and parasympathetic activity
constraints: In dynamic embodied settings, frequent movement compromises EDA sensor reliability, so heart rate is preferred
Simple interpretations of heart rate are complicated by its dual autonomic regulation
target_learners: students in co-located, physically active collaborative learning environments such as healthcare simulation
target_learning_goals: understanding stress, engagement, and affective states during embodied collaborative learning
examples: The article applies the theory in high-fidelity nursing simulations where students physically interact with peers and patient manikins, modelling heart-rate synchrony and arousal with LMMs
key_sources: Lixiang Yan · Dragan Gašević · Vanessa Echeverria · Linxuan Zhao · Yueqiao Jin · Xinyu Li · Roberto Martinez-Maldonado. (2025). In Sync or Out of Sync? article_title: A Large Language Model Approach to Educational Survey Feedback Analysis
citation: Michael J. Parker, Caitlin Anderson, Claire Stone, YeaRim Oh. (2024). A Large Language Model Approach to Educational Survey Feedback Analysis. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00414-0
title: Eight-tag course feedback classification system suitable for varied course types and amenable to customization
description: A set of eight generalizable tags (course logistics and fit, curriculum, teaching modality, teaching, assessment, resources, peer and teacher interaction, other) developed by the authors for multi-label classification of open-ended course feedback. Each tag carries "A one to three sentence description of each tag" so humans or LLMs can apply it, and the same descriptions served as LLM prompt context. The set was reduced from 71 initial labels after low inter-rater agreement, then iteratively tested on sets of 100 responses.
requirements: Tag descriptions must be adapted or kept current so tags can be applied appropriately by annotators or prompts; the intent is that others can adapt the tags by modifying the description portion for their own purposes.
constraints: Developed and validated on online biomedical science course feedback; the article presents it as also intended for other educational offerings but reports testing on this program's data.
target_learners: higher education / online biomedical science course students (whose feedback the tags classify)
target_learning_goals: analysis of student feedback to guide course improvement and quality assurance
examples: Four authors independently labeled 2,500 survey responses with the final tag set; inter-rater agreement was evaluated with Jaccard similarity averaged across rater pairs.

article_title: A Large Language Model Approach to Educational Survey Feedback Analysis
citation: Michael J. Parker, Caitlin Anderson, Claire Stone, YeaRim Oh. (2024). A Large Language Model Approach to Educational Survey Feedback Analysis. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00414-0
title: Biomedical science end-of-course survey comment dataset (2,500 evaluation comments; 2,000-comment development set)
description: An evaluation corpus of "2,500 survey responses (625 for each of four open-ended questions)" drawn at random from 50,525 responses to a uniform end-of-course survey across 365 course iterations of 15 online biomedical science courses (e.g., Pharmacology, Genetics, Immunology). A further 2,000 comments served as a development set for prompt tuning. Responses were collected via Qualtrics, cleaned with Pandas, and screened manually and via named entity recognition so that no private or sensitive information was transmitted to publicly available LLMs.
requirements: Pre-processing removed leading and trailing white space and automated removal of responses with no content; responses were inspected for private or sensitive information before transmission to publicly available LLMs.
constraints: Drawn from one online biomedical science program; on average learners answered approximately two of the four questions, and response lengths ranged from one word to several paragraphs.
target_learning_goals: course evaluation and qualitative feedback analysis for course improvement

article_title: A Large Language Model Approach to Educational Survey Feedback Analysis
citation: Michael J. Parker, Caitlin Anderson, Claire Stone, YeaRim Oh. (2024). A Large Language Model Approach to Educational Survey Feedback Analysis. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00414-0
title: Educational survey analysis goals achieved by chaining composable LLM-performed NLP tasks into workflows
description: A framework treating educational survey analysis goals as sequences of natural language processing tasks — multi-label, multi-class, and binary classification, extraction, inductive thematic analysis, and sentiment analysis — each performed by an LLM in zero-shot mode. High-level analysis proceeds bottom-up via inductive thematic analysis or top-down via multi-label classification with predefined labels; focused analysis chains extraction followed by classification or thematic analysis, with sentiment analysis as a final step. The authors demonstrate these "composable building blocks" on real end-of-course survey comments, with quantification supported by classification counts.
requirements: Workflows require clear specification of the analysis goal in prompts, label definitions as context, and batching of comments to fit the model's context window when deriving themes.
constraints: Demonstrated on end-of-course feedback from online biomedical science courses; inductive thematic analysis lacks an accepted evaluation method, per the article.
target_learners: higher education and online course providers analyzing student feedback
target_learning_goals: deriving insights from qualitative survey feedback to improve courses and teaching
examples: Example workflows included deriving themes from Q1 comments, finding suggestions for improvement via extraction plus multi-class classification, and identifying content gaps in immunology courses.

citation: Kennel, K., Ishimaru, S., Küchemann, S., Steinert, S., Kuhn, J., & Ruzika, S. (2025). title: Gaze-based diagnosis of content-related student difficulties for misconception-driven adaptive feedback
description: An adaptive educational system framework in which eye tracking data collected during problem solving is used to diagnose not only that a learner needs help but which specific content-related difficulty they have, enabling misconception-driven feedback during the solution process. The article states that "to the best of our knowledge, there is no system that makes diagnosis about the problem-solving strategy and that is able to predict specific content-related student difficulties on the basis of gaze data." The framework rests on the eye-mind hypothesis linking gaze direction to cognitive processing.
