citation: H. Chad Lane. (2023). Commentary for the International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education Special Issue on K-12 AI Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00359-w
title: The Five Big Ideas of AI framework organizes K-12 AI instruction around five ideas with grade-band progressions
description: The AI4K12 initiative's Five Big Ideas framework structures what should be taught in K-12 AI education. As the commentary describes, "The Big Five Ideas (perception, representation and reasoning, learning, natural interaction, and societal impact) act as the basis for their approach," with grade band progressions split as K-2, 3-5, 6-8, and 9-12. The commentary endorses the framework as intuitive and influential across the special issue, while stressing that classroom testing is needed to validate the developmental appropriateness of the grade bands.
requirements: Classroom testing is needed; the commentary calls to "conduct testing in classrooms" to confirm vocabulary appropriateness across grade bands
constraints: The commentary notes AI lacks convergence on agreed foundational ideas compared with older fields like mathematics and physics
target_learners: K-12 students across grade bands K-2, 3-5, 6-8, and 9-12
target_learning_goals: AI awareness, knowledge, skills, and ethics
examples: A deep dive into machine learning (Big Idea 3) demonstrates grade-band-relevant instruction, carving ML into sub-concepts such as training a model, neural networks, and reasoning

title: Erasmus+ two-year high school AI curriculum combining AI with Python programming
description: Bellas et al. present a European Erasmus+ effort defining an AI curriculum for high school students and teachers with no previous AI knowledge. The commentary describes a 2-year sequence organized around an expanded version of the Five Big Ideas with 8 key ideas, using teaching units implemented as needed and mobile learning to keep costs manageable. It highlights attention to math prerequisites and integration so learners "learn Python and AI at the same time." Initial evaluation via teacher feedback and student technical questionnaires was encouraging.

constraints: Whether the specific teaching units are effective "will only become clear with time and research"

title: ARIN-561 game teaching core AI techniques with AI Consumer/Operator/Developer role distinctions
description: ARIN-561 is a game described by Leitner et al. for teaching Search, Bayesian Networks, Decision Trees, Clustering, and Linear Regression to high school learners, built around an escape-from-an-alien-planet narrative with AI concepts woven into game mechanics (e.g., applying breadth-first search to find a companion robot). The commentary also highlights the paper's role taxonomy: "they use AI Consumer to refer to someone who simply uses AI-based technologies, AI Operator to refer to one who applies AI techniques to solve problems, and AI Developer for people who implement and improve AI algorithms."
requirements: The commentary suggests far more in-game scaffolding support will likely be needed if the game is released publicly
constraints: The prototype has been pilot tested but larger scale studies are the next step; the current version prioritizes consumer and operator roles over developer interactions

examples: Learners apply a breadth-first search algorithm and visualize its execution in game; subsequent activities add depth-first and greedy search for algorithm comparison

article_title: A Multimedia Adaptive Tutoring System for Mathematics that Addresses Cognition, Metacognition and Affect
citation: Arroyo, I., Woolf, B. P., Burelson, W., Muldner, K., Rai, D., & Tai, M. (2014). A Multimedia Adaptive Tutoring System for Mathematics that Addresses Cognition, Metacognition and Affect. Int J Artif Intell Educ 24:387–426. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0023-y
title: Effort-based tutoring (EBT): adaptive problem selection and pedagogical moves inferred from correctness, help requests and time
description: EBT is Wayang Outpost's pedagogical decision-making model. It "adapts problem selection depending on the effort exerted by a student on a practice activity based on three different dimensions of student behavior: attempts to solve a problem, help requested, and time to answer". It defines a region of expected behavior per problem from historical log data, infers a most-likely student state (e.g., mastery without effort, hint abuse, low effort), and selects pedagogical and affective/motivational moves accordingly (Table 1). The authors contrast it with BKT and IRT, claiming it models cognitive, affective and metacognitive states together and captures inherent item difficulty beyond the required procedure.
requirements: Expected values E(Ii), E(Hi), E(Ti) and delta thresholds per problem estimated from accumulated student-problem interaction data across years
Content availability and classroom-management constraints such as minimum problems and maximum review time per topic
constraints: The authors state they do not claim a non-Bayesian approach is superior to Bayesian knowledge tracing, as further studies would be needed
EBT is used for decisions within a knowledge unit, while BKT-style mastery estimation is used at the topic level
target_learners: middle and high school mathematics students
target_learning_goals: mathematics problem solving on standardized-test items
self-regulation and effort
examples: Table 1 maps nine observed behavior patterns (incorrect answers, hints, time) to decisions such as increase, maintain or reduce problem difficulty and affective responses like praising effort or deemphasizing immediate success

citation: Arroyo, I., Woolf, B. P., Burelson, W., Muldner, K., Rai, D., & Tai, M. (2014). A Multimedia Adaptive Tutoring System for Mathematics that Addresses Cognition, Metacognition and Affect. Int J Artif Intell Educ 24:387–426. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0023-y
title: Wayang Outpost / MathSpring multimedia mathematics tutoring system
description: Wayang Outpost, now called MathSpring, is a multimedia-based intelligent tutoring system for mathematics built on cognitive apprenticeship theory. It models solutions "via worked-out examples with the use of sound and animation, and provides practice opportunities on math word problems", mostly released MCAS and SAT items clustered into coarse-grained knowledge units so students must classify problem types. It provides multimedia hints implementing Mayer's principles, adaptive difficulty selection, animated affective learning companions, and teacher tools reporting progress per skill mapped to Common Core standards.
requirements: Content organized as clustered high-stakes test items within knowledge units
Log data from past students to estimate item difficulty and expected behavior
constraints: Knowledge units are more coarse-grained than most other math tutoring systems, with only pairs or triplets of problems highly similar and parameterized
There is no explicit scaffold-fading procedure; help fading happens naturally through transfer to similar-difficulty problems
target_learners: middle and high school students preparing for standardized mathematics tests
target_learning_goals: mathematics problem solving
problem-type identification and classification
test readiness
examples: Students preparing to retake the 10th grade MCAS test used Wayang in regular math classes before the statewide exam

citation: Arroyo, I., Woolf, B. P., Burelson, W., Muldner, K., Rai, D., & Tai, M. (2014). A Multimedia Adaptive Tutoring System for Mathematics that Addresses Cognition, Metacognition and Affect. Int J Artif Intell Educ 24:387–426. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0023-y
title: Open student model (Student Progress Page) scaffolding self-regulation through reflection and informed choice
description: The Student Progress Page (SPP) is Wayang's open student model, which "allows students to inspect their progress and the tutor's assessment of their work". It lists mathematics topics, displays effort as a blooming plant, shows a BKT-based mastery bar, offers tutor comments, and provides buttons to continue, review or challenge. It is designed to encourage reflection on progress, greater control and responsibility over learning, and increased trust through transparency, supporting self-assessment and goal setting at moments of boredom.
requirements: Students must be able to view topic-level effort and mastery assessments and choose next steps (continue, review, challenge, switch topics)
constraints: Currently students cannot modify the student model or dispute the assessment of their own knowledge
target_learners: middle and high school mathematics students
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning
reflection on progress
goal setting
examples: In one experimental condition the tutor suggested visiting the SPP when it detected boredom or lack of excitement, while controls had the same page available via a button without suggestions

citation: Arroyo, I., Woolf, B. P., Burelson, W., Muldner, K., Rai, D., & Tai, M. (2014). A Multimedia Adaptive Tutoring System for Mathematics that Addresses Cognition, Metacognition and Affect. Int J Artif Intell Educ 24:387–426. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0023-y
title: Emotion-phase mapping: prospective emotions in forethought, activity emotions in performance, retrospective emotions in self-evaluation
description: Combining Pekrun's control-value theory of achievement emotions with Zimmerman and Moylan's cyclical self-regulation model (forethought, performance, self-reflection), the authors propose that "prospective emotions are more likely to occur in the forethought phase, activity emotions in the performance phase, and retrospective emotions in the self-evaluation phase". This mapping guides when Wayang delivers affective and metacognitive support, on the premise that negative-valence emotions in any phase can disengage students, degrade performance and make them quit the self-regulatory loop.
requirements: A tutoring environment that detects or elicits emotions at different phases of the self-regulatory cycle
constraints: The authors state this mapping "is still an issue that deserves further investigation"
target_learners: middle and high school mathematics students
target_learning_goals: self-regulation of learning
emotional regulation during problem solving
examples: Wayang's affective learning companions and progress reports are delivered when the system infers disengagement, aiming to re-engage students in the next problem

article_title: Preface to the Special Issue on K-12 AI Education
citation: Ning Wang · James Lester. (2023). Preface to the Special Issue on K-12 AI Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00363-0
title: K-12 AI education as a distinct emerging field, analogous to science or history education
description: The editors frame "AI Education for K-12" as a field distinct from "AI in Education": whereas AIED has long built technologies to support human learning, this field educates K-12 students about AI itself. They write that "in a manner that is analogous to how we educate K-12 students about science or history, we now must develop curricula, pedagogies, and learning technologies" for K-12 AI education. The special issue is presented as a first step toward crystallizing this nascent research field.
requirements: Curricula, pedagogies, and learning technologies must be developed to support K-12 AI education, as the article states
target_learning_goals: Understanding artificial intelligence
AI literacy
key_sources: Ning Wang · James Lester. (2023). Preface to the Special Issue on K-12 AI Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00363-0

article_title: Preface to the Special Issue on K-12 AI Education
citation: Ning Wang · James Lester. (2023). Preface to the Special Issue on K-12 AI Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00363-0
title: AI4K12 Five Big Ideas in AI as an organizing framework for K-12 AI learning progressions
description: The preface identifies the AI4K12 initiative's Five Big Ideas in AI as an organizing framework for K-12 AI learning progressions, used by Touretsky et al. with a focus on machine learning. The editors write that "Based on the AI4K12 initiative, they discuss how the Five Big Ideas in AI provide an organizing framework for K-12 AI learning progressions with a focus on machine learning." The framework thus structures how machine learning is sequenced for K-12 learners.
requirements: Learning progressions must be developed around the Five Big Ideas, adapted to grade bands
target_learning_goals: Understanding machine learning
AI concept progressions
key_sources: Ning Wang · James Lester. (2023). Preface to the Special Issue on K-12 AI Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00363-0

article_title: How to Improve the Explanatory Power of an Intelligent Textbook: a Case Study in Legal Writing
citation: Sovrano Francesco, Ashley Kevin, Brusilovsky Peter Leonid, Vitali Fabio. (2024). How to Improve the Explanatory Power of an Intelligent Textbook: a Case Study in Legal Writing. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00399-w
title: Illocutionary theory of explanation: explaining means answering an explicit question together with relevant implicit archetypal questions
description: Grounded in Achinstein's Ordinary Language Philosophy account, the article defines explaining as an illocutionary act: "Explaining is an illocutionary act that provides answers to an explicit question on some topic along with answers to several other implicit or unformulated questions deemed necessary for the explainee to understand the topic properly." Implicit questions are instances of archetypes such as why, how, what, who, when, where, drawn from AMR and PDTB discourse theories. YAI4Edu operationalizes this by organizing textbook content as clusters of archetypal question-answer pairs.
requirements: A collection of texts that adequately answers a set of archetypal questions about the explanandum
In the generic case with no assumptions about the explainee, only archetypal questions can be exploited for illocution
constraints: Illocution was considered too abstract to implement directly; the article notes the computer-friendly interpretation relies on pre-defined archetypes
target_learners: English-speaking university students learning legal writing
target_learning_goals: Understanding complex textbook topics through question-driven explanations
examples: The article contrasts the non-explanatory answer "I am fine" with an answer that also addresses archetypal questions, which becomes an explanation
key_sources: Sovrano Francesco, Ashley Kevin, Brusilovsky Peter Leonid, Vitali Fabio. (2024). How to Improve the Explanatory Power of an Intelligent Textbook: a Case Study in Legal Writing. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00399-w

article_title: How to Improve the Explanatory Power of an Intelligent Textbook: a Case Study in Legal Writing
citation: Sovrano Francesco, Ashley Kevin, Brusilovsky Peter Leonid, Vitali Fabio. (2024). How to Improve the Explanatory Power of an Intelligent Textbook: a Case Study in Legal Writing. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00399-w
title: YAI4Edu: a pipeline that converts static e-books into interactive intelligent textbooks with open-ended questioning and overviewing
description: YAI4Edu is an extension of YAI4Hu that automatically transforms static educative e-books in PDF, XML or HTML format into interactive intelligent textbooks. Interaction is given by "i) word glosses that can be clicked to open an overview; ii) a special kind of search box that allows the reader to get answers to any open-ended English question." It extracts a knowledge graph of template-triplets formatted as RDF from a collection of texts and retrieves answers via embedding similarity using a MiniLM-based model. Source code and anonymized evaluation data are released under MIT license at https://github.com/Francesco-Sovrano/YAI4Edu.
requirements: A collection of texts integrating the textbook (e.g., an encyclopedia) from which to extract the knowledge graph
Hyper-parameters for the Intelligent Explanation Generator (k=10, p=.57, L=50, s=.95, q=4, a=2 in the case study)
constraints: The extracted knowledge graph is imperfect because of the adopted extraction procedure and may contain mistakes from wrongly identified grammatical dependencies
target_learners: University students in an interdisciplinary legal analytics and AI course
target_learning_goals: Learning how to write a legal memorandum in the U.S. legal system
examples: Applied to 22 textbook pages, 5,407 legal-encyclopedia web pages, and 11,198 BVA legal cases, producing an interactive annotated version of the textbook
key_sources: Sovrano Francesco, Ashley Kevin, Brusilovsky Peter Leonid, Vitali Fabio. (2024). How to Improve the Explanatory Power of an Intelligent Textbook: a Case Study in Legal Writing. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00399-w

article_title: How to Improve the Explanatory Power of an Intelligent Textbook: a Case Study in Legal Writing
citation: Sovrano Francesco, Ashley Kevin, Brusilovsky Peter Leonid, Vitali Fabio. (2024). How to Improve the Explanatory Power of an Intelligent Textbook: a Case Study in Legal Writing. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00399-w
title: Intelligent Explanation Generator: an algorithm selecting questions best answered by the whole text collection
description: The Intelligent Explanation Generator is the component of YAI4Edu responsible for selecting pedagogically useful implicit questions. It computes the Degree of Explainability (DoX) of text snippets about an explanandum, takes the top k snippets, extracts archetypal questions from them with a fine-tuned T5 model, and filters pertinent answers through sub-steps that remove over-long questions, correct grammar via Gramformer, drop overly similar questions, and keep the top q questions sorted by answer pertinence. It operationalizes Hypothesis 1: the most useful implicit questions are those best answered by the collection as a whole, neither too detailed nor too general.
requirements: A fine-tuned T5 question-extraction model and a pre-trained answer-retrieval language model
Hyper-parameters: pertinence threshold p, question length threshold L, similarity threshold s, and caps q and a
constraints: Questions extracted by the T5 model can be imperfect, containing errors that could propagate to the Intelligent Explanation Generator
target_learning_goals: Retrieving helpful explanations efficiently from large text collections
examples: In the case study it was configured with k=10, p=.57, L=50, s=.95, answer lengths 150–1000, q=4 questions and a=2 answers per overview question
key_sources: Sovrano Francesco, Ashley Kevin, Brusilovsky Peter Leonid, Vitali Fabio. (2024). How to Improve the Explanatory Power of an Intelligent Textbook: a Case Study in Legal Writing. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00399-w

article_title: How to Improve the Explanatory Power of an Intelligent Textbook: a Case Study in Legal Writing
citation: Sovrano Francesco, Ashley Kevin, Brusilovsky Peter Leonid, Vitali Fabio. (2024). How to Improve the Explanatory Power of an Intelligent Textbook: a Case Study in Legal Writing. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00399-w
title: Legal-writing case study corpus: over 16,000 documents yielding a knowledge graph of over 55 million RDF triplets
description: The case study applied YAI4Edu to 22 pages excerpted from the textbook "United States Legal Language and Culture" (Brostoff & Sinsheimer, 2013), 5,407 open access web pages from the Legal Information Institute encyclopedia and Wikipedia, and 11,198 legal cases on PTSD disability claims from the Board of Veterans' Appeals. Altogether 16,606 documents yielded 1,309,463 extracted questions and a knowledge graph whose total size was 55,046,923 RDF triplets (Table 1). The material supports teaching how to write a legal memorandum for a veteran's PTSD disability claim.
requirements: About ten manually added RDF triplets were needed to fill identified knowledge gaps such as "memo" being a synonym for "memorandum"
constraints: The whole extracted RDF graph was not thoroughly analyzed, so other knowledge gaps may yet emerge
target_learners: Students in the University of Pittsburgh course Applied Legal Analytics and AI
target_learning_goals: Writing legal memoranda, using statutes, reading and synthesizing cases, and making arguments with concrete cases
examples: The textbook is actively used in a University of Pittsburgh course co-taught by instructors from the School of Law and Carnegie Mellon's Language Technologies Institute
key_sources: Sovrano Francesco, Ashley Kevin, Brusilovsky Peter Leonid, Vitali Fabio. (2024). How to Improve the Explanatory Power of an Intelligent Textbook: a Case Study in Legal Writing. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00399-w

article_title: Early prediction of writing quality using keystroke logging
citation: Rianne Conijn, Christine Cook, Menno van Zaanen, Luuk Van Waes. (2022). Early prediction of writing quality using keystroke logging. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00268-w
title: Five-category taxonomy of keystroke features for writing-process analysis
description: The article organizes keystroke-log features drawn from prior literature into five groups: "features related to timings of pauses, revisions, typing bursts, verbosity, and other (non-typing) events". Pause features include IKI metrics and long-pause percentages; revision features cover backspaces and leading-edge versus in-text revisions; fluency features capture bursts; verbosity features count keystrokes and words plus 30-s variability measures; other-event features include focus shifts and cut/paste/jump durations. The study extracted 54 features in these categories from Inputlog raw logs for prediction modeling.
requirements: Keystroke logs with per-keystroke event records, plus a baseline copy task to set individual pause and IKI thresholds, as the article required for feature extraction.
constraints: The authors state keystroke logging data are indirect observation, so they make no theoretical claims about cognitive subprocesses; their approach is explicitly data-driven.
target_learners: ESL students in higher education academic writing courses
target_learning_goals: Academic summarization and writing quality
examples: 54 features were extracted from raw Inputlog logs of a 30-minute timed academic summary task written by 126 ESL premaster students.
key_sources: Rianne Conijn, Christine Cook, Menno van Zaanen, Luuk Van Waes. (2022). Early prediction of writing quality using keystroke logging. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00268-w

article_title: Can Multi-Label Classifiers Help Identify Subjectivity? A Deep Learning Approach to Classifying Cognitive Presence in MOOCs
citation: Yuanyuan Hu. (2023). Can Multi-Label Classifiers Help Identify Subjectivity? A Deep Learning Approach to Classifying Cognitive Presence in MOOCs. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00310-6
title: Multi-label, fine-tuned BERT classifier architecture of five binary BERT classifiers with sigmoid outputs
description: The article builds a multi-label classifier by revising "the standard BERT model from a class-independent model to five binary BERT classifiers for each category", one per cognitive presence category. Messages are pre-processed (emojis and URLs replaced, abbreviations expanded, stop words removed), tokenised with BertTokenizer, and passed through a bert-base-uncased model with 12 transformer layers and 768 dimensions, followed by a linear classification layer and a sigmoid function outputting five probability scores between 0 and 1. Because the sigmoid layer "can allow more than one phase to reach a score of over 0.5", multiple labels may attach to one message; predictions above a 0.33 threshold, chosen because a human coder's weight over three coders' decisions was equivalent to around 0.33, become labels. Training used tenfold cross-validation with data augmentation and over-sampling performed after the dataset splits, Binary Cross-Entropy loss, batch size 8, 10 epochs, and a learning rate of 2 × 10−5.
requirements: Requires pre-trained BERT weights (bert-base-uncased) fine-tuned on manually labelled discussion messages where expert coders agreed without confusion
Requires data augmentation and over-sampling of minority categories applied after the training-test split to avoid over-optimistic results
constraints: Trained and tested on discussion messages from one introductory Philosophy MOOC on the FutureLearn platform
The data augmentation method might deepen the confusion between Exploration and Integration, where most coder disagreements occurred
target_learners: MOOC learners in an introductory Philosophy course on FutureLearn
target_learning_goals: Automatic identification of phases of cognitive presence (critical discourse and knowledge construction) in learners' online discussion messages
examples: Applied to 1,917 discussion messages sampled from 16 tasks of the Logical and Critical Thinking MOOC, with the AgreementSet used for training and the DisagreementSet for validation
key_sources: Yuanyuan Hu. (2023). Can Multi-Label Classifiers Help Identify Subjectivity? A Deep Learning Approach to Classifying Cognitive Presence in MOOCs. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00310-5

article_title: Preface for the Special Issue on Culturally Aware Educational Technologies
citation: Amy Ogan & W. Lewis Johnson. (2015). Preface for the Special Issue on Culturally Aware Educational Technologies. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0036-1
title: Modeling culture as a collection of influences and affiliations to cultural groups (Mohammed & Mohan's ICON approach)
description: The editorial describes an approach in which culture is "modeled as a collection of influences and affiliations to cultural groups," which "ma[kes] it possible to model cultural diversity within national learner populations." Rather than assuming national culture, the system gives learners control over contextual specificity while dynamically generating feedback, hints, problem descriptions, and images with matching grammar and vocabulary.
requirements: The learner must be given the ability to adjust the level of contextual specificity of generated content.
constraints: It avoids making assumptions about learner background and preferences that may be unwarranted, per the article; detailed model structure is not described in this editorial.
target_learners: learners in culturally diverse national populations
target_learning_goals: culturally tailored instructional content and feedback
examples: The special-issue system dynamically generates feedback, hints, problem descriptions, and images whose grammar and vocabulary match the learner's cultural preference.
key_sources: Amy Ogan & W. Lewis Johnson. (2015). Preface for the Special Issue on Culturally Aware Educational Technologies. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0036-1

article_title: Preface for the Special Issue on Culturally Aware Educational Technologies
citation: Amy Ogan & W. Lewis Johnson. (2015). Preface for the Special Issue on Culturally Aware Educational Technologies. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0036-1
title: Kinect-sensor environment for young children to learn and practice Chinese (Si, 2014)
description: An environment described by Si (2014) for "young children to learn and practice Chinese," using a Kinect sensor that allows a wider variety of input than AIED systems have typically used. The editors expect this sensing technology to appear more frequently in future AIED systems, particularly for domains such as culture where verbal and non-verbal skills like proximity or gestures are teaching targets.
requirements: Sensor input must support a wider variety of input modalities than typical AIED systems used.
constraints: The editorial describes the system's purpose and technology but reports no evaluation results.
target_learning_goals: Chinese language and culture, including non-verbal skills such as proximity and gestures
examples: The system lets children practice Chinese with input beyond keyboard or mouse, capturing gesture and proximity relevant to cultural instruction.
key_sources: Amy Ogan & W. Lewis Johnson. (2015). Preface for the Special Issue on Culturally Aware Educational Technologies. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0036-1

article_title: Preface for the Special Issue on Culturally Aware Educational Technologies
citation: Amy Ogan & W. Lewis Johnson. (2015). Preface for the Special Issue on Culturally Aware Educational Technologies. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0036-1
title: Experiential learning environment with virtual agents representing synthetic cultures for cultural conflict competence (Hall et al., 2014)
description: An experiential learning environment in which "children learn cultural conflict competence by exploring the interactions between virtual agents representing synthetic cultures." Built by an interdisciplinary multinational European team, it extends Bennett's Developmental Model of Intercultural Sensitivity into a learning framework. The editors report that its results indicate synthetic cultural environments can promote intercultural competence when combined with suitable classroom instruction.
requirements: Suitable classroom instruction must be combined with the synthetic cultural environment for competence gains, per the reported results.
constraints: The approach is theoretical rather than sensor-based; gains are conditioned on combined classroom instruction.
target_learning_goals: cultural conflict competence and intercultural competence
examples: Children explored interactions between virtual agents representing synthetic cultures as the core learning activity.
key_sources: Amy Ogan & W. Lewis Johnson. (2015). Preface for the Special Issue on Culturally Aware Educational Technologies. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0036-1

article_title: Preface for the Special Issue on Culturally Aware Educational Technologies
citation: Amy Ogan & W. Lewis Johnson. (2015). Preface for the Special Issue on Culturally Aware Educational Technologies. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0036-1
title: AIED developers should make designs culturally aware and adaptable to a variety of cultural contexts
description: The editors recommend that developers of AI in education systems be culturally aware so their designs do not "incorporate implicit cultural assumptions that will impede adoption in other cultural contexts," and that designs should be adaptable to a variety of cultural contexts. This arises from evidence that instructional methods' effects vary across contexts and that cross-cultural models may not transfer.
requirements: Developers must examine architectures and approaches underlying current learning technologies for implicit cultural assumptions.
constraints: Cultural issues are fluid and diverse, involving complex factors such as geographic location, religion, class, and individual personality.
target_learners: learners in diverse global cultural contexts
target_learning_goals: effective learning across cultural contexts; cultural awareness and tolerance of diversity
examples: The special issue solicited work on representing culture and its influence across AIED subfields including user modeling, instructional design, and serious games.
key_sources: Amy Ogan & W. Lewis Johnson. (2015). Preface for the Special Issue on Culturally Aware Educational Technologies. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0036-1

article_title: Special Issue on Intelligent Support for Learning in Groups
citation: Rohit Kumar & Jihie Kim. (2013). Special Issue on Intelligent Support for Learning in Groups. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 24. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0013-5
title: The four-dimension framework defining the field of Intelligent Support for Learning in Groups (ISLG)
description: The editors define ISLG as a field of interest within AIEd characterized by four dimensions named for the abbreviation's letters: intelligent technologies, support offered, learning applications, and group characteristics. They argue the combination is broad rather than narrow: "While at first look, it may be seem that the scope of this field is extremely narrow, due to the constraints of combining these four dimensions, it is in fact the contrary." Each dimension is elaborated as an axis for characterizing any ISLG work.
requirements: Work must involve intelligent technologies that differentiate it from work conducted by CSCL researchers
constraints: The editors state the characterization of the learning application is critical to describing work in ISLG to understand its generalizability
target_learners: learners in groups including dyads, small groups and teams
target_learning_goals: group learning across academic and professional domains
examples: The four special-issue articles are each characterized along the four dimensions, e.g. Walker and colleagues' work described as dyads of high school students in an Algebra domain
key_sources: Rohit Kumar & Jihie Kim. (2013). Special Issue on Intelligent Support for Learning in Groups. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 24. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0013-5

article_title: Special Issue on Intelligent Support for Learning in Groups
citation: Rohit Kumar & Jihie Kim. (2013). Special Issue on Intelligent Support for Learning in Groups. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 24. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0013-5
title: Support in ISLG is characterized by stakeholder supported and form of support
description: The editors propose characterizing forms of support offered to learning in groups by identifying the stakeholders being supported: "some of the stakeholders include learners, teachers, mentors, content creators, administrators and researchers." They list common forms of support — "interactive feedback, assessment, engagement, content recommendation, customizability and authoring/development tools" — each applicable to one or more stakeholders, and note that personalized-support conventions raise questions about capturing individual contributions and distributing learning tasks among group members.
requirements: Existing educational tools and support can be revisited in the context of ISLG
constraints: Group contexts require attention to the types of individual contributions captured and monitored and the distribution of learning tasks among individuals
target_learning_goals: collaborative learning supported by intelligent systems
examples: The special-issue articles offer support to educators (group assessment), learners acting as peer-tutors, and small groups in language learning
key_sources: Rohit Kumar & Jihie Kim. (2013). Special Issue on Intelligent Support for Learning in Groups. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 24. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0013-5

article_title: Special Issue on Intelligent Support for Learning in Groups
citation: Rohit Kumar & Jihie Kim. (2013). Special Issue on Intelligent Support for Learning in Groups. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 24. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0013-5
title: Group characteristics as a defining axis of ISLG work
description: The editors treat group composition, size, evolution and construction as a dimension researchers must consider when choosing technologies and supports. Groups range "from set of individuals with homogenous characteristics, to participants that have various roles assigned to them (e.g. peer, tutor, mentor, observer, teacher)" with varying skills such as expert and novice. Groups may be fixed or constantly evolving, and their construction "maybe ad-hoc or carefully crafted."
requirements: The characteristics of the group are closely tied to those of the learning application
target_learning_goals: collaborative learning
examples: The special-issue groups typically comprise two or three students in Yoo and Kim's dataset, and dyads and triads in Rosé and colleagues' work
key_sources: Rohit Kumar & Jihie Kim. (2013). Special Issue on Intelligent Support for Learning in Groups. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 24. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0013-5

article_title: Special Issue on Intelligent Support for Learning in Groups
citation: Rohit Kumar & Jihie Kim. (2013). Special Issue on Intelligent Support for Learning in Groups. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 24. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0013-5
title: MentorChat: a domain-independent architecture for conversational-agent-supported group learning
description: Tegos et al.'s MentorChat is described as "a domain-independent system architecture for building group learning applications that are supported by conversational agents." A focus is "the development of tools that allow educators to customize and control agent behaviour based on their own expert knowledge." In the article it is customized for a language learning application used by small groups of 2 to 3 students, exploring "directed prompts to elicit a higher degree of pedagogically beneficial responses from the learners."
requirements: Tools must allow educators to customize and control agent behaviour based on their own expert knowledge
constraints: Customized in the article for a language learning application used by small groups of 2 to 3 students
target_learners: small groups of 2 to 3 students in language learning
target_learning_goals: productive dialogue in group language learning
examples: Used for a language learning application where directed prompts elicit pedagogically beneficial responses
key_sources: Rohit Kumar & Jihie Kim. (2013). Special Issue on Intelligent Support for Learning in Groups. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 24. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0013-5

article_title: Special Issue on Intelligent Support for Learning in Groups
citation: Rohit Kumar & Jihie Kim. (2013). Special Issue on Intelligent Support for Learning in Groups. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 24. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0013-5
title: Bazaar: a modular architecture for developing collaboration-support agents
description: Adamson et al.'s Bazaar is presented as an architecture that, in contrast to MentorChat, "focuses on agent development instead of end-to-end learning applications." Its modular design "allows these agents to be integrated with a variety of learning environments while being composed of a collection of reusable behavioural components." It delivers domain-independent interventions to promote academically productive collaboration among learners in dyads and triads.
requirements: Agents must be composable from a collection of reusable behavioural components
constraints: Unlike the other articles, results discussed come from use across different Engineering and Science domains and learner age groups
target_learners: small homogeneous groups of learners (dyads and triads) in Engineering and Science domains
target_learning_goals: academically productive collaboration
examples: Similar support interventions used across different Engineering and Science domains and learner age groups, which the editors read as indicating readiness for applicability outside the laboratory
key_sources: Rohit Kumar & Jihie Kim. (2013). Special Issue on Intelligent Support for Learning in Groups. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 24. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0013-5

article_title: Using Sequence Analysis to Determine the Well-Functioning of Small Groups in Large Online Courses
citation: H. Ulrich Hoppe, et al. (2021). Using Sequence Analysis to Determine the Well-Functioning of Small Groups in Large Online Courses. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00229-9
title: Sequence alignment and clustering as an analytic method ('microscope') for characterizing collaboration quality in asynchronous group work
description: The article adapts sequence alignment from bioinformatics: group action logs are human-coded into contribution types — "coordination, monitoring, minor contribution, and major contribution" — plus a "gap" code for more than 24 hours of inactivity. Pairwise edit distances (a Levenshtein variant, with gap operations costed 2) form a similarity matrix that is clustered with partitioning around medoids (PAM), with k chosen by silhouette analysis. The authors claim this method "can serve as a kind of microscope to capture differences in the underlying collaboration processes", and distinguish it from sequential pattern mining, which finds recurring subsequences rather than whole-string similarity.
requirements: Human coding of action types (coordination and monitoring depend on human judgement; inter-rater Cohen's Kappa of 0.79 was considered sufficient)
constraints: Encoded collaboration actions are attributed to the group as a whole, not to individual group members
The method is data-driven but based on sequence alignments, not sequential patterns; hypothesis-driven pattern approaches require predefined patterns and miss unexpected behavior
target_learners: higher education students in large online courses
target_learning_goals: collaborative knowledge building and coordination in small-group online tasks
examples: Study 1 aligned and clustered action sequences of 65 groups into three clusters (19, 17, 29 sequences); Study 2 replicated this with two clusters (19 and 10 sequences)
key_sources: H. Ulrich Hoppe, et al. (2021). Using Sequence Analysis to Determine the Well-Functioning of Small Groups in Large Online Courses. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00229-9

article_title: Using Sequence Analysis to Determine the Well-Functioning of Small Groups in Large Online Courses
citation: H. Ulrich Hoppe, et al. (2021). Using Sequence Analysis to Determine the Well-Functioning of Small Groups in Large Online Courses. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00229-9
title: IKARion system architecture: learning analytics backend with group model and rule-based adaptive scaffolding in Moodle
description: IKARion extends the Moodle platform with a dedicated learning analytics backend connected to an expert system for generating potentially adaptive scaffolds. "This architecture contains an analytics backend that analyzes the action logs received from the learning platform (Moodle) to generates a group model." The group model represents the current context of each learning group and instantiates variables such as inactivity (gaps), imbalance and productivity (word count), including a semantic word count based on a dictionary extracted from learning materials. The group model feeds a rule-based component that steers feedback and adaptation in Moodle; the learned decision tree provides "indicators for critical situations". Two consecutive versions were used in parallel with two versions of the CmC course and other smaller courses.
requirements: Connection to the Moodle learning platform supplying action logs in real time; the architecture "complies with the real-time requirement of the course settings"
constraints: The experiments with this architecture "did not exploit the potential of flexible adaptation"; scaffolds were triggered by clearly controlled and fixed conditions
target_learners: higher education students working in small groups in large online courses
target_learning_goals: improving collaboration and interaction in small-group work through timely feedback and scaffolding
examples: The IKARion architecture was used with two versions of the CmC course and other smaller courses, with scaffolds triggered by fixed conditions rather than flexible adaptation
key_sources: H. Ulrich Hoppe, et al. (2021). Using Sequence Analysis to Determine the Well-Functioning of Small Groups in Large Online Courses. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00229-9

article_title: The Future of Adaptive Learning: Does the Crowd Hold the Key?
citation: Heffernan, N. T., Ostrow, K. S., Kelly, K., Selent, D., Van Inwegen, E. G., Xiong, X., & Williams, J. J. (2016). The Future of Adaptive Learning: Does the Crowd Hold the Key? Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:615–644. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0094-z
title: Crowdsourcing as a knowledge base building model with three primary design issues
description: The article organizes crowdsourced content creation using the taxonomy of Saxton et al. (2013), placing ASSISTments' approach in the knowledge base building model, where "information- or knowledge-generation processes are outsourced to community users" with incentives and quality control. It distinguishes crowdsourcing from the 'wisdom of crowds' and separates teachersourcing from learnersourcing. Three issues structure the design space: what is outsourced, crowd collaboration, and managerial control over quality.
requirements: Incentive measures and quality control mechanisms to elicit quality knowledge from the crowd
constraints: Managerial control over contribution quality is described as one of the greater challenges of crowdsourcing in general
target_learners: K-12 students using online learning platforms
target_learning_goals: Mathematics problem solving supported by elaborated feedback
examples: Stack Overflow ranks users by the value of their answers; Wikipedia allows open authorship; ASSISTments plans algorithmic promotion of explanations that produce the greatest learning

title: Bangert-Drowns et al. (1991) iterative model of learning from feedback
description: The article presents a well-established model in which students begin at an initial knowledge state, practice information retrieval to form a response, receive feedback, evaluate their response, and adjust their knowledge, iterating with each question. The authors present it "because the type of feedback supplied after each item will affect the learning process considerably", and use it to argue that incorrect or low-quality learnersourced contributions must not be shown as feedback.
requirements: Feedback supplied after each item that students can use to evaluate and adjust their knowledge
constraints: Incorrect or extremely low quality learnersourced contributions should not be presented to other students as feedback

target_learning_goals: Adjusting knowledge states in response to feedback on practice items
examples: Depicted as Fig. 3 with an initial dashed-circle knowledge state cycling through item, response, feedback, and adjustment

citation: Heffernan, N. T., Ostrow, K. S., Kelly, K., Selent, D., Van Inwegen, E. G., Xiong, X., & Williams, J. J. (2016). The Future of Adaptive Learning: Does the Crowd Hold the Key? Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:615–644. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0094-z
title: ASSISTments online learning platform and its experiment infrastructure
description: ASSISTments is a free online learning platform of Worcester Polytechnic Institute providing "students with assistance while offering teachers assessment", currently used by hundreds of teachers and over 50,000 students with over 10 million problems solved last year. It supports randomized controlled experiments with student-level randomization at low cost, has enabled over 18 peer-reviewed articles since 2002, and provides feedback types including correctness feedback, mistake messages, hints, and scaffolds, plus actionable item reports surfacing common wrong answers.
requirements: Teachers or researchers author or select content; students work problems online with feedback settings chosen by the content designer
constraints: The framework set forth may or may not be generalizable to other platforms
target_learning_goals: Mathematics skill practice with elaborated feedback and teacher assessment
examples: Item reports show percent correct and common wrong answers (e.g., 27% correct on one problem, about half of wrong answers sharing the misconception 1/9^10) with a +feedback link for writing mistake messages

title: Scale down the crowdsourced task and relabel feedback creation as self-explanation to make learnersourcing viable
description: Because learners are 'experts-in-training', the article argues learnersourcing is acceptable only if the requested task is simplified: "By scaling down the task requested of each learner, the process of learnersourcing becomes much more viable." ASSISTments does this by "relabeling feedback creation as 'self-explanation'" and diluting content creation into elements common to traditional mathematics homework, such as showing work on nightly problems.
requirements: Task complexity matched to learner ability; anonymous collection to avoid social strife from downvoting
constraints: Complexity of self-explanations varies drastically with content, e.g., perimeter problems versus logarithmic functions
target_learners: K-12 students contributing explanations of their own solution paths
target_learning_goals: Self-explanation and producing worked examples that benefit future students
examples: Students are asked to 'show their work' on homework problems; existing commenting infrastructure with sentence-starter menus collected 80,000 comments over five years

article_title: Introduction to IJAIED Special Issue, FATE in AIED
citation: Beverly Woolf, Kaska Porayska-Pomsta, Wayne Holmes, Ken Holstein. (2022). Introduction to IJAIED Special Issue, FATE in AIED. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00299-x
title: A sufficient ethics framework for AIED must be flexible and draw on the learning sciences and related fields
description: This is the editorial's normative account of what an ethics framework for AI in education requires. It argues that "any sufficient framework for ethics of AIED needs to include insights from the learning sciences, cognitive and educational neuroscience" and from fields whose impact has not yet been felt in education technology. The framework must also support flexibility to incorporate new knowledge as science, socio-cultural norms, values and educational systems emerge and adapt, because AIED is a design discipline, not solely an empirical science. The editorial presents this as an argued position, not a tested result.
requirements: Must include insights from the learning sciences, cognitive and educational neuroscience, and other fields not yet felt in education technology
constraints: The editorial states designing such a framework is challenging, requires many years of focus, and must accommodate unknown unknowns as well as known unknowns
target_learners: AIED researchers and practitioners designing AI-based educational technologies
target_learning_goals: Ethical design, development and deployment of AI-supported instructional systems
key_sources: Beverly Woolf, Kaska Porayska-Pomsta, Wayne Holmes, Ken Holstein. (2022). Introduction to IJAIED Special Issue, FATE in AIED. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00299-x

article_title: A Closer Look into Recent Video-based Learning Research: A Comprehensive Review of Video Characteristics, Tools, Technologies, and Learning Effectiveness
citation: Navarrete, E., Nehring, A., Schanze, S., Ewerth, R., & Hoppe, A. (2025). A Closer Look into Recent Video-based Learning Research: A Comprehensive Review of Video Characteristics, Tools, Technologies, and Learning Effectiveness. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00481-x
title: Eight-category taxonomy of video characteristics and contextual aspects for video-based learning
description: The review derives a taxonomy that organizes video characteristics and contextual aspects into eight categories: audio features, visual features, textual features, instructor behavior, learners' activities, interactive features, production style, and instructional design. Each category is populated with sub-categories and example features drawn from the 257 reviewed articles, such as transcripts, metadata, and on-screen text under textual features, and quizzes, annotations, and navigation interface elements under interactive features. The authors state the taxonomy "provides a holistic view and allows to systematically consider the critical components of a learning video" and can support assessment, optimization, and customization of educational video content.
requirements: Articles must concern video-based learning materials with specific video characteristics that can be classified into the taxonomy's categories
constraints: Derived from computer science databases for the period 2016 to 2021, excluding work influenced by large language models and generative AI that emerged after the review period
target_learners: Researchers and designers of video-based learning environments and intelligent educational systems
target_learning_goals: Systematic consideration of video characteristics when designing, assessing, or customizing learning videos
examples: Table 3 of the review lists sub-categories per category, e.g. audio records and representation cues under audio features, and Khan-style, dialogue-style, and slide-based videos under production style
key_sources: Navarrete, E., Nehring, A., Schanze, S., Ewerth, R., & Hoppe, A. (2025). A Closer Look into Recent Video-based Learning Research: A Comprehensive Review of Video Characteristics, Tools, Technologies, and Learning Effectiveness. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00481-x
title: Tools supporting video-based learning: information extraction, interactive tools, recommenders, classifiers, and navigation/segmentation tools
description: The review identifies eight types of tools and methods supporting video-based learning: information extraction methods, interactive tools, recommendation systems, classifiers and predictors, video navigation and segmentation tools, video analysis tools and methods, video summarization, and others. The review states "The first five tool types amount to 80% of the reviewed papers". Tools commonly exploit textual and visual features, using low-level tasks such as optical character recognition, keyword extraction, natural language processing, word embeddings, slide transition detection, and speech recognition to generate transcripts.
requirements: Tools typically rely on extracted video elements such as transcripts, video frames, images, and metadata as input
constraints: Coverage limited to computer science databases and the 2016–2021 period; excludes post-2021 generative AI developments
target_learners: Learners using educational videos in formal or informal settings
target_learning_goals: Improved access, navigation, recommendation, and support for learning with videos
examples: Interactive tools include in-video annotations, in-video quizzes, and feedback mechanisms to prevent mind wandering, such as systems that detect distraction and pause the video

Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00481-x
title: Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning as the evidence-based framework underlying effective video design
description: The review situates video-based learning design within the Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning, which it describes as an evidence-based framework explaining how learners process information from videos and identifying principles for optimizing cognitive load. The review reports that research applying this framework established that "videos incorporating principles such as segmentation, coherence, and signaling, signiﬁcantly outperform those lacking these design elements". It also notes frameworks addressing motivational aspects and social presence have further refined understanding of effective educational videos, and states these theoretical foundations inform the technological features examined in the review.
requirements: Video design decisions should be grounded in the framework's principles for optimizing cognitive load
constraints: The review attributes these findings to prior work (e.g., Mautone & Mayer; Moreno & Mayer; Mayer et al.) rather than testing them itself
target_learners: Learners watching educational videos across formal and informal settings
target_learning_goals: Effective design of learning videos that manages cognitive load and supports knowledge retention
examples: The review cites segmentation, coherence, and signaling as multimedia learning principles that videos incorporating significantly outperform videos lacking

article_title: Socio-Cultural Imbalances in AIED Research: Investigations, Implications and Opportunities
citation: Blanchard, E. G. (2015). Socio-Cultural Imbalances in AIED Research: Investigations, Implications and Opportunities. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0027-7
title: WEIRD subjects as outliers: the generalization-risk account of imbalanced psychology samples
description: The article adopts Henrich et al.'s (2010a) account that WEIRD populations are not representative of humankind: members of industrialized societies "frequently score as outliers" on basic psychological functions, and WEIRD subjects "may often be the worst population from which to make generalizations". The account distinguishes four levels of comparison (industrialized vs small-scale, WEIRD vs non-WEIRD, Americans vs other WEIRD, American students vs other Americans) and holds that universal learning processes exist but their outputs depend on socio-cultural features. The article uses it to argue that AIED findings generalized from WEIRD samples carry untested assumptions.
requirements: comparative studies across populations, since the account calls for consideration of human diversity to become more systematic
constraints: exclusive reliance on WEIRD samples may be adequate when seeking existential proofs that a process exists
target_learners: learners from WEIRD and non-WEIRD populations
target_learning_goals: valid generalization of learning-research findings across cultures

article_title: Ontology-Based Generation of Medical, Multi-term MCQs
citation: J. Leo, G. Kurdi, N. Matentzoglu, B. Parsia, U. Sattler, S. Forge, G. Donato, W. Dowling. (2019). Ontology-Based Generation of Medical, Multi-term MCQs. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-018-00172-w
title: EMCQG: a modular ontology-based system for generating case-based medical MCQs
description: EMCQG (EMMeT Multiple Choice Question Generator) is a modular system built on EMMeT-OWL that fills question-template skeletons with content from the ontology. It comprises a templating system plus modules for stems, options, exclusions, explanations, difficulty, and question text: "the remaining main modules act as engines to fill in and structure the template skeletons with content from EMMeT-OWL". Templates encode rules over ranked clinical relations (e.g., distractor ranks must not exceed the key's), and OWL reasoning validates candidate terms against patient demographics.
requirements: A large medical ontology with clinical terms, ranked semantic relations, and POC relation attributes (EMMeT-OWL)
Expert-identified question templates representative of board-examination questions
constraints: EMCQG is not open source, and thus not available for public review
Only four medical question templates are implemented in the current version
target_learners: medical residents preparing for board examinations
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning and diagnosis
drug-of-choice and differential-diagnosis knowledge
examples: For the What is the most likely diagnosis template, EMCQG built a question whose key Urethritis had stronger ranked hCF and hRF relations to the stem entities than the distractors Dysmenorrhea and HIV Infection
key_sources: J. Leo, G. Kurdi, N. Matentzoglu, B. Parsia, U. Sattler, S. Forge, G. Donato, W. Dowling. (2019). Ontology-Based Generation of Medical, Multi-term MCQs. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-018-00172-w

article_title: Ontology-Based Generation of Medical, Multi-term MCQs
citation: J. Leo, G. Kurdi, N. Matentzoglu, B. Parsia, U. Sattler, S. Forge, G. Donato, W. Dowling. (2019). Ontology-Based Generation of Medical, Multi-term MCQs. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-018-00172-w
title: EMMeT-OWL: an OWL translation of the Elsevier Merged Medical Taxonomy used as the question-generation knowledge base
description: EMMeT v4.4 is a large clinical knowledge base encoded in SKOS and translated automatically into an OWL 2 ontology, EMMeT-OWL, which serves as the knowledge source for EMCQG. It "contains over 900 K concepts covering clinical areas such as anatomy, clinical findings, drugs, organisms, procedures, and symptoms" plus over 350K custom ranked clinical semantic relations and approximately 8K POC relations with demographic attributes. A reliable OWL class hierarchy was built by aligning over 100K concepts to SNOMED-CT classes, adding over 1M subclass relations.
requirements: Quarterly expert curation of custom semantic relationships with second-editor QA review
External vocabularies (SNOMED-CT, UMLS) for concept verification
constraints: SKOS hierarchical assertions are not OWL subclass relations, so the hierarchy required external SNOMED-CT alignment
Rank usage is less granular than the 0-100 definition, ranging only from 6-10
target_learning_goals: diagnosis and clinical management knowledge assessed via generated MCQs
examples: A rank of 10.0 for hasClinicalFinding means a most common clinical finding, e.g., urethritis's most common clinical finding is hemorrhage of urethra
key_sources: J. Leo, G. Kurdi, N. Matentzoglu, B. Parsia, U. Sattler, S. Forge, G. Donato, W. Dowling. (2019). Ontology-Based Generation of Medical, Multi-term MCQs. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-018-00172-w

article_title: Ontology-Based Generation of Medical, Multi-term MCQs
citation: J. Leo, G. Kurdi, N. Matentzoglu, B. Parsia, U. Sattler, S. Forge, G. Donato, W. Dowling. (2019). Ontology-Based Generation of Medical, Multi-term MCQs. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-018-00172-w
title: EMCQG's difficulty model: question difficulty computed from stem indicativeness and distractor-key rank differences
description: EMCQG's difficulty calculator estimates question difficulty from the ranked strength of relations rather than axiomatic concept similarity. Stem indicativeness (stemInd, from sympInd and histInd) measures how strongly stem entities indicate the key; option difference (optDiff, from squared distractor differences disDiff) measures how close distractors are to the key. "The question difficulty is based on an average of the stem entities’ difficulty and the option entities’ difficulty." Squaring distractor differences weights very-similar distractors more heavily, in the absence of an empirically validated coefficient.
requirements: Ranked and POC-annotated relations in EMMeT-OWL
constraints: The authors state: "we do not provide a formal evaluation of the effectiveness of our difficulty measure"; a formal investigation of how well the models capture real difficulty is future work
target_learners: users of EMCQG generating questions for different levels of expertise
target_learning_goals: categorising generated questions as easy, medium, or hard
examples: For example question Q11, stemInd was computed as .17 and optDiff as .015, giving an overall question difficulty of .092
key_sources: J. Leo, G. Kurdi, N. Matentzoglu, B. Parsia, U. Sattler, S. Forge, G. Donato, W. Dowling. (2019). Ontology-Based Generation of Medical, Multi-term MCQs. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-018-00172-w

title: Four expert-derived case-based question templates for medical MCQ generation
description: Elsevier medical experts identified four question templates representative of board-examination preparation questions: What is the most likely diagnosis?, What is the drug of choice?, What is the most likely clinical finding?, and What is the differential diagnosis?. "Four medical question templates have been implemented in the current implementation of E MCQG." Each template specifies stem entities (patient demographic, history, symptoms), option-entity rules over ranked relations, and validity rules ensuring distractors are weaker than or unrelated to the key.
requirements: Templates require clinical semantic relations (hCF, hRF, hD, hDDx) with rankings, and POC attributes for patient demographics
constraints: Each template is structurally different, so each has its own difficulty calculator and explanation generator
target_learners: medical residents preparing for board examinations
target_learning_goals: most likely diagnosis
drug of choice
clinical findings
differential diagnosis
examples: Template rules require that for any distractor, the sum of its relations' ranks to all stem entities is strictly less than the key's sum

article_title: Debiasing Education Algorithms
citation: Jamiu Adekunle Idowu. (2024). Debiasing Education Algorithms. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00389-4
title: Two-category taxonomy of algorithmic fairness: individual fairness and group fairness
description: The review organizes algorithmic fairness into two broad categories. Individual fairness holds that "similar individuals should receive similar outcomes", with measures including fairness through awareness, fairness through unawareness, and counterfactual fairness. Group fairness "focuses on ensuring equal statistical outcomes across distinct groups partitioned by protected attributes", with measures such as equal opportunity, demographic parity, and equalized odds. The review uses this taxonomy to frame which metrics education studies adopt.
requirements: Choosing a fairness definition requires contextualizing it to the application, as the review notes definitions may not align with real-world applications
constraints: The review notes that pursuing demographic parity will harm equalized odds, so multiple fairness measures cannot be satisfied simultaneously
target_learners: students affected by predictive models in educational settings
target_learning_goals: equitable treatment of students by educational prediction and recommendation algorithms
key_sources: Jamiu Adekunle Idowu. (2024). Debiasing Education Algorithms. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00389-4

article_title: Debiasing Education Algorithms
citation: Jamiu Adekunle Idowu. (2024). Debiasing Education Algorithms. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00389-4
title: ABROCA: Absolute Between-ROC Area fairness metric
description: ABROCA is a fairness metric proposed by Gardner et al. (2019) and adopted by several reviewed studies. "This metric measures the absolute value of the area between the baseline group ROC curve ROCb and the comparison group(s) ROCc. The lower the ABROCA value, the less unfair the algorithm." Unlike threshold-dependent metrics such as equalized odds, ABROCA evaluates model discrimination across all thresholds and can be computed directly from prediction modeling results with minimal computational requirement.
requirements: Requires ROC curves for a baseline group and comparison group(s) from a prediction modeling task
constraints: The review notes ABROCA might not be as effective in scenarios where specific decision thresholds are crucial
target_learners: student subgroups evaluated by predictive models (e.g., MOOC learners, dropout-prediction students)
target_learning_goals: measuring subgroup discrimination in student dropout, performance, and forum post classification models
examples: S6 (Sha et al., 2021) used ABROCA to assess fairness of students' forum post classification; S2 (Sha et al., 2022) used it for dropout prediction, performance prediction, and forum post classification
key_sources: Jamiu Adekunle Idowu. (2024). Debiasing Education Algorithms. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00389-4

article_title: Debiasing Education Algorithms
citation: Jamiu Adekunle Idowu. (2024). Debiasing Education Algorithms. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00389-4
title: Evaluate the fairness of data and features before algorithmic fairness
description: The review recommends that developers assess the fairness of data and features used in educational algorithms before addressing algorithmic fairness itself, to "prevent algorithms from receiving discriminatory inputs". Biased data and features reflect historical prejudices, demographic inequalities, and cultural stereotypes, and feature unfairness is difficult to detect later in model implementation. The review notes limited work has addressed this aspect despite its importance.
requirements: Evaluation of distribution and hardness bias in datasets, and extraction of fairer features with feature-fairness evaluation, before model training
constraints: The review notes limited work has been done in evaluating bias in data and feature engineering
target_learners: students in educational settings whose data feeds predictive algorithms
target_learning_goals: preventing discriminatory inputs to dropout, performance, and classification models
examples: S2 found all three datasets (Moodle, KDDCUP 2015, OULA) exhibited distribution and hardness bias, and class-balancing techniques reduced this bias
key_sources: Jamiu Adekunle Idowu. (2024). Debiasing Education Algorithms. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00389-4

article_title: Data-Related Ethics Issues in Technologies for Informal Professional Learning
citation: Pammer-Schindler, V. & Rosé, C. (2021). Data-Related Ethics Issues in Technologies for Informal Professional Learning. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00259-x
title: KnowSelf activity logging and reflection prototype
description: KnowSelf is a Windows activity-log application that "collects time-stamped PC activity data, linked to web or file resources, identifies idle times, and visualizes the fragmentation of worktime". It supports manual time labeling into user-meaningful categories, note-taking, visualizations supporting reflection-on-action, and proactive prompts triggered at predetermined times or by user behavior such as long idleness. It was positively evaluated in two field studies with senior IT and strategy consultants.
requirements: Manual time labeling to sort automatically logged data into categories meaningful to the user
constraints: Centralized multi-device logging with centralized storage was strongly rejected by target users due to data sensitivity
target_learners: knowledge workers and consultants in workplace settings
target_learning_goals: time management reflection and improvement
examples: Two field studies in a German medium-sized company with reasonably senior IT and strategy consultants positively evaluated KnowSelf and regular review of time use
key_sources: Pammer-Schindler, V. & Rosé, C. (2021). Data-Related Ethics Issues in Technologies for Informal Professional Learning. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00259-x

article_title: Data-Related Ethics Issues in Technologies for Informal Professional Learning
citation: Pammer-Schindler, V. & Rosé, C. (2021). Data-Related Ethics Issues in Technologies for Informal Professional Learning. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00259-x
title: MoodMap App for self-tracked mood and team awareness
description: The MoodMap App is a mood self-tracking prototype whose interface follows Russell's two-dimensional model of affect along valence and arousal, with mood captured by clicking a bi-dimensional mood map based on Itten's colour system. Users can attach free-text notes and context information; moods, notes and context are aggregated and visualized at individual and collaborative levels, including a Compare Me View and a Collaborative View showing others' current mood. It was tested in two field studies, in virtual team meetings and in call-center teams.
requirements: User-centered design iterations adapted the app to each study setting, including configuration of whether contextual information to mood was mandatory
constraints: In the virtual team meeting setting the collaborative view anonymized user names, which impacted usefulness because knowing the author of a mood entry is necessary to react ad personam
target_learners: professionals in collaborative and team-based workplace settings
target_learning_goals: reflection on salient work issues, awareness of own emotions, team communication
examples: Case 4 in four business-2-business call-center teams showed positive impact for those two of the four teams who accepted the intervention

article_title: Speech Enabled Reading Fluency Assessment: a Validation Study
citation: van der Velde, M., Harmsen, W., Veldkamp, B. P., Feskens, R., Keuning, J., & Swart, N. (2025). Speech Enabled Reading Fluency Assessment: a Validation Study. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00480-y
title: SERDA: Speech Enabled Reading Diagnostics App for Dutch oral reading fluency
description: SERDA is a Dutch oral reading fluency assessment instrument for primary school, administering word decoding (150 words in three 50-word subtasks with progressive demasking) and passage reading tasks on a tablet while recording children's speech. The article states that "Through the incorporation of speech recognition, speech-based diagnostics, and their conversion into didactic suggestions for practitioners, SERDA allows for the provision of individualized feedback on children's oral word and passage reading performance". It extracts item-, subtask- and person-level accuracy, speed and WCPM measures and derives LNIRT ability and speed estimates, with short administration duration and automatic scoring intended to reduce testing burden.
requirements: Administered individually on a tablet with microphone recording; the ASR requires optimization for children's speech before high-stakes use
constraints: Excludes prosody metrics; the ASR only produces speed scores for correctly read words; recommended for formative rather than high-stakes settings
target_learners: Children in Grades 2 and 3 of Dutch primary education
target_learning_goals: Oral reading fluency: word decoding accuracy, speed and automaticity (WCPM)

article_title: Computing of Learner’s Personality Traits Based on Digital Annotations
citation: Omheni, N., Kalboussi, A., Mazhoud, O., & Hadj Kacem, A. (2017). Computing of Learner’s Personality Traits Based on Digital Annotations. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 27, 241-267. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0124-x
title: i-Read online reading environment with personality profiling from annotations
description: i-Read is an online reading environment where learners upload reading materials, annotate them, and share annotated documents. Its architecture includes a user annotation interface, an annotation analyzer module, a profile constructor module, and three databases with two servers. The analyzer computes six annotation features (total, average, graphical, textual, reference, and compounding annotation counts), and the profile constructor applies multivariate linear regression to estimate Big Five trait scores. The system "offers, besides the traditional annotation functionalities of creation, archiving and sharing, the functionality of readers' personality modeling based on their digital annotation traces."
requirements: Learners must annotate reading materials within the system so that annotation traces can be captured and analyzed.
constraints: The system's regression coefficients were derived from pen-and-paper experiment data, and evaluation focused on conscientiousness and neuroticism only.
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension
learner profiling for personalization

title: Big Five personality model as framework for learner profiling
description: The Big Five model describes personality as five traits: openness to experience, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, and neuroticism. The article adopts it as the target framework for learner profiling, using the NEO-IPIP inventory as the reference measure. The model is described as "the best accepted and the most commonly used scientific measure of personality", discovered through factor analysis of natural-language adjectives. The article maps each trait to annotation behavior patterns.
