article_title: Reciprocal Tutoring: Design with Cognitive Load Sharing
citation: Chih-Yueh Chou & Tak-Wai Chan. (2015). Reciprocal Tutoring: Design with Cognitive Load Sharing. International Artificial Intelligence in Education Society. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0083-7
title: Cognitive Load Sharing (CLS) approach for designing reciprocal tutoring systems
description: CLS is a design approach for reciprocal tutoring systems in which a complex learning task is decomposed into sub-tasks that are distributed to various agents (human students, virtual tutors or tutees) and computer scaffolding tools, so each learner focuses on an assigned sub-task while others handle the rest. The authors state its rationale is to Bdivide and conquer^ and which entails distributing sub-tasks to computer scaffolding tools or various agents. From the perspective of cognitive load theory, the objective of CLS is to alter the intrinsic cognitive load of students by adaptively dividing learning tasks among various agents.
requirements: A learning task must be analyzable and partitionable into sub-tasks that different agents can complete
constraints: The benefit of cognitive load reduced by sharing should be greater than the damage of the increased effort resulting from sharing sub-tasks and collaboration among agents
Other agents must be able to complete their sub-tasks
target_learners: Students in one-to-one classrooms learning with personal computing devices
target_learning_goals: Complex learning tasks such as solving problems and writing programs
examples: In the Distributed Reciprocal Tutoring system, a Petal-Like-System tool assisted tutees constructing recursive Lisp programs and a Diagnosis-Hint-Tree assisted tutors in locating errors and providing hints
key_sources: Chih-Yueh Chou & Tak-Wai Chan. (2015). Reciprocal Tutoring: Design with Cognitive Load Sharing. International Artificial Intelligence in Education Society. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0083-7

article_title: Reciprocal Tutoring: Design with Cognitive Load Sharing
citation: Chih-Yueh Chou & Tak-Wai Chan. (2015). Reciprocal Tutoring: Design with Cognitive Load Sharing. International Artificial Intelligence in Education Society. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0083-7
title: Six design dimensions with 12 research questions for the RTS design space
description: The paper organizes the design space of reciprocal tutoring systems into six dimensions, each posing research questions that assist developers in adopting the CLS approach. The dimensions are task partition, social scaffolding, scaffolding tools, scaffolding and fading, student modeling, and benefit-cost-tradeoffs. The authors state: They are divided into six design dimensions: task partition (questions #1 and #2), social scaffolding (questions #3 and #4), scaffolding tools (questions #5 and #6), scaffolding and fading (questions #7, #8, and #9), student modeling (questions #10 and #11), and benefit-cost-tradeoffs (question #12). Although focused on reciprocal tutoring, they note the questions and principles can be applied to other learning activities.
requirements: Designers must analyze how the learning task is decomposed, which brain performs which part of the learning task, and how these brains should interact
constraints: Involving as many CLS mechanisms as possible may not lead to a good RTS
target_learners: Students in reciprocal tutoring arrangements in one-to-one classrooms
target_learning_goals: Learning-by-tutoring and learning-by-being-tutored
examples: Table 1 compares the designs of related RTSs according to the design space, listing configurations, companions, tasks, reciprocity, and scaffolding tools of systems from Integration-Kid to OPAL

title: Reciprocal tutoring as peer tutoring with alternating tutor and tutee roles
description: Reciprocal tutoring is defined as a form of cooperative learning in which a task is partitioned into tutoring and tuteeing sub-tasks distributed among agents, with dyads taking turns in the two roles. The authors define it: BReciprocal tutoring is a form of cooperative learning by adopting the 'divide and conquer 'strategy. A learning task is partitioned into sub-tasks of tutoring and 'tuteeing'where tuteeing is learning by working on the solution while being tutored.^ They phrase the scenario as the tutor's tutor tutors the tutor who tutors the tutee, making it a type of peer tutoring that enables peer students to tutor other students.
requirements: A protocol is required to assist agents in playing their roles to complete their sub-tasks and to collaborate in completing the entire learning task
constraints: The scope is designing protocols and computer supports for reciprocal tutoring, such as sub-task partition, roles of agents, virtual agents, and computer scaffolding tools
target_learners: Peer students acting as tutors and tutees
target_learning_goals: Learning-by-tutoring and learning-by-being-tutored
examples: Figure 6 illustrates a scenario where a student tutors a tutee while the system plays the role of the tutor's tutor

title: Fade scaffolding at an appropriate pace so students do not over-depend on it or become frustrated
description: In the CLS approach, when students become proficient in their assigned sub-tasks, tools should be removed or more sub-tasks distributed to maintain appropriate difficulty. The article warns that pacing matters in both directions: fading too slowly might hinder students from learning sub-tasks whereas fading too rapidly might frustrate students. An appropriate fading of scaffolding guides students to learn and prevents them from excessively depending on scaffolding. Scoring mechanisms based on tutees' help requests have been used to prevent over-dependence on tutors and tools.
requirements: Establishing student models of student knowledge and behavior is crucial in appropriately fading scaffolding
constraints: Fading too slowly hinders learning of sub-tasks; fading too rapidly frustrates students
target_learners: Students progressing from scaffolded tuteeing and tutoring toward independent task completion
target_learning_goals: Completing all sub-tasks of a learning task independently after scaffolding is removed
examples: Table 3 presents an example of scaffolding and fading mechanisms across four learning stages for a novice student, from tuteeing with a tuteeing tool and virtual tutor to serving as tutee and tutor by themselves

article_title: Help Helps, But Only So Much: Research on Help Seeking with Intelligent Tutoring Systems
citation: Aleven, V., Roll, I., McLaren, B. M., & Koedinger, K. R. (2016). Help Helps, But Only So Much: Research on Help Seeking with Intelligent Tutoring Systems. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0089-1
title: Executable production-rule model of help seeking with a taxonomy of maladaptive help-seeking behaviors
description: The article's central theoretical artifact is a knowledge-engineered, rule-based, executable model of help seeking during tutored problem solving, built through cognitive task analysis guided by tutor log and pre/post-test data. Unlike prior descriptive models, it is detailed and executable and can drive tutoring via model tracing. "In its final incarnation, the model comprised approximately 80 production rules. It included a taxonomy of maladaptive help-seeking behaviors with broad categories such as Help Abuse, Help Avoidance, Try-step Abuse, and more detailed subcategories." Recent findings suggest revisions: the model should prescribe help use in a narrower range of circumstances and account for bottom-out hints aiding learning when self-explained.
requirements: Requires knowledge engineering guided by theories of help seeking and supported by classroom observations and mined log and pre/post-test data
constraints: Narrower in scope than prior models, focusing only on help seeking in the context of tutored problem solving
Does not capture that bottom-out hints may aid learning when self-explained, and needs narrower prescriptions about when help use is appropriate
target_learners: Students learning with step-based intelligent tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: Effective (adaptive) help seeking as a self-regulated learning skill
examples: The Help Tutor applied the model with the standard model-tracing algorithm, saying, e.g., 'Try to take more time to read the hint' when a student clicked through hint levels quickly
key_sources: Aleven, V., Roll, I., McLaren, B. M., & Koedinger, K. R. (2016). Help Helps, But Only So Much: Research on Help Seeking with Intelligent Tutoring Systems. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0089-1

article_title: Help Helps, But Only So Much: Research on Help Seeking with Intelligent Tutoring Systems
citation: Aleven, V., Roll, I., McLaren, B. M., & Koedinger, K. R. (2016). Help Helps, But Only So Much: Research on Help Seeking with Intelligent Tutoring Systems. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0089-1
title: KLI-based theoretical analysis: hints aid learning only when students make sense of them
description: The article uses the Knowledge-Learning-Instruction (KLI) framework to argue that a limited but non-negligible role exists for principle-based tutor hints. Under KLI, instruction must match the complexity of targeted knowledge: conceptual knowledge requires sense-making processes such as self-explanation, while procedural knowledge is best built through induction and refinement during problem-solving practice. "In short, the theoretical analysis suggests that help helps, but only so much." Hints may aid conceptual learning and may help procedural learning indirectly, for example by helping students identify relevant problem features. This analysis marks a shift from the authors' 2006 viewpoint by foregrounding the sense-making processes required for hints to work.
requirements: Students must self-explain the hints or otherwise make sense of them for the beneficial effects to occur
constraints: Takes a strong cognitive perspective without addressing social, motivational, and metacognitive aspects of help seeking, which could change the analysis
target_learners: Novice students learning complex domains such as geometry with step-based tutors
target_learning_goals: Conceptual knowledge of principles and procedural problem-solving skill
examples: The analysis predicts hints are not directly useful for acquiring procedural knowledge, since verbal sense making cannot influence non-verbal learning directly

title: Evaluation framework distinguishing 16 possible effects of SRL interventions
description: The article proposes a framework for evaluating interventions supporting self-regulated learning, built on four distinctions: targeted SRL processes versus domain-level learning; current versus future learning; same versus a new learning environment; same versus a different domain. "These four items define a space of 16 possible effects on learning that interventions to support SRL may have." It relates the Help Tutor studies to this space and argues future research should test additional cells, such as effects on future domain-level learning. The authors see measuring SRL both during and after an intervention as key to moving the field forward.
requirements: Researchers must operationalize and measure SRL outcomes both during and after the intervention to evaluate lasting effects
constraints: Only a sampling of the 16 possibilities was addressed in the Help Tutor studies; transfer to other environments cannot be taken for granted
target_learners: Students using advanced learning technologies with SRL support
target_learning_goals: Self-regulated learning skills and domain-level learning
examples: The Help Tutor studies measured current domain learning, and current and future help-seeking behavior via logs, hypothetical scenarios, and post-test items with embedded help

article_title: A Planning Algorithm to Support Learning in Open-ended, Unstructured Environments
citation: Stephanie Frost · Gord McCalla. (2020). A Planning Algorithm to Support Learning in Open-ended, Unstructured Environments. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00221-3
title: CFLS planner: collaborative filtering on learning sequences for open-ended pedagogical planning
description: The CFLS planner is a pedagogical planning algorithm designed for open-ended, unstructured learning environments based on the ecological approach architecture. It builds a neighbourhood of learners who followed a similar sequence of the b most recent learning objects as a target learner, then recommends the most successful forward path of f learning objects drawn from those neighbours' subsequent histories. Success is judged through analysis of interaction data (average P[learned] on the forward path) rather than external metadata. The planner requires no externally engineered metadata about learning objects and no structured learner model in advance, since all relationships are derived from learner behaviour traces captured on learning objects.
requirements: Accumulated usage data from prior learners in the environment to enable neighbourhood formation
constraints: Suffers a cold start problem when insufficient usage data is available
Neighbourhood matching approach (exact sequence match, set match, or partial order) depends on the density of data available
target_learners: self-directed learners in open-ended, unstructured learning environments
target_learning_goals: personalized guidance on learning goal setting and achievement through recommended learning object sequences
examples: In the simulation, the CFLS planner matched learners using a set match with pass/fail outcome correspondence and recommended the path with the highest average P[learned] among neighbours.

article_title: A Planning Algorithm to Support Learning in Open-ended, Unstructured Environments
citation: Stephanie Frost · Gord McCalla. (2020). A Planning Algorithm to Support Learning in Open-ended, Unstructured Environments. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00221-3
title: Base learning-path recommendations on learner interaction traces rather than externally engineered metadata
description: In open-ended, unstructured learning environments where learning objects lack prerequisite annotations or other metadata, a planner can still generate effective personalized learning sequences by mining patterns from the interaction traces learners leave on learning objects. The article's simulation demonstrated that such a trace-based planner could match or exceed a prerequisite-informed planner, showing that learner behaviour data implicitly encodes relationship information that would otherwise require knowledge engineering. This principle is realized by the CFLS planner's use of collaborative filtering over learning sequences.
requirements: A learning environment that captures usage data (learner identifier, learning outcome value, timestamp) attached to learning objects
Accumulated interaction data from prior learners
constraints: Requires the environment to have been in operation long enough to accumulate sufficient data
Cold start problem when little data is available
target_learners: self-directed learners in open-ended learning environments
target_learning_goals: personalized sequence recommendations for learning object consumption
examples: The simulation captured P[learned] values and timestamps on each learning object as learners interacted, and the CFLS planner used only this captured data to form neighbourhoods and rank candidate paths.

citation: Kochmar, E., Vu, D. D., Belfer, R., Gupta, V., Serban, I. V., & Pineau, J. (2022). International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 32, 323–349. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00267-x
title: Three-tier personalization architecture for feedback selection in a dialogue-based ITS
description: The article organizes feedback selection as three increasingly personalized Random Forest models: a BASELINE model using only "linguistic features" assessing hint quality in isolation (14 features), a SHALLOW PERSONALIZATION model adding 8 "performance-based features" such as past attempts and correctness proportions (22 total), and a DISCOURSE PERSONALIZATION model that also analyzes up to 4 previous interaction turns with keyword, topic-overlap, and perplexity features (49 total). Models are trained in a binary classification setting to predict whether a student will correctly solve the exercise on the next attempt given a hint. This architecture lets an ITS choose pedagogical interventions without hand-crafted rules.
requirements: A database of expectations (reference solutions) from which hints are generated, and recorded historical student–system interactions for training
constraints: The number of previous dialogue turns (up to 4) was selected to maximize coverage of interactions available on the platform at the time of the experiments
target_learners: adult online learners of machine learning and data science
target_learning_goals: problem-solving exercises in data science and machine learning
examples: The three models were compared on 50-fold cross-validation and in the live pilot, with the discourse model winning in both

title: Harrow's taxonomy as the review's chosen framework for classifying skill proficiency levels in ITS
description: Harrow's taxonomy (1972) classifies psychomotor skills in six levels of increasing performance capability: "Reflex Movements, Basic Fundamental Movements, Perceptual Abilities, Physical Abilities, Skilled Movements, Non-discursive Communication". The review selected it over Dave's, Simpson's, Thomas's, and Ferris and Aziz's taxonomies because it includes physical and non-discursive elements; its Physical Activities level accommodates stretching, strength, flexibility, complex sports movements, and expressive movements. The review applies it as a checklist at task level to reveal how mastery of psychomotor skills is promoted in existing ITS.
requirements: Application at task level, checking whether a task's execution corresponds to a taxonomy level, with similar tasks grouped to account for class imbalances
constraints: Dave's, Simpson's, and Ferris and Aziz's taxonomies give no possibility to classify physical or motor abilities; Thomas's taxonomy focuses on learning outcomes, making it less straightforward to apply
target_learners: Learners using ITS to develop psychomotor skills
target_learning_goals: Psychomotor skill proficiency across Harrow's levels
examples: The review classifies following basic salsa steps as covering all levels except Physical Activities, since the implemented dancing task does not require fitness despite its importance for dancing

citation: Richard Cox & Paul Brna. (2015). Twenty Years on: Reflections on "Supporting the Use of External Representations in Problem Solving". Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:193–204. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0054-z
title: AIED systems for external-representation reasoning: switching, synchrony, selection guidance and effective use
description: The article articulates a framework of roles that AIED systems can play in supporting learners who reason with external representations. The roles are: enabling learners to "move easily from one ER to a different one (switching ERs)"; using AI to keep several forms of ER in synchrony as the student works on one of them; guiding the student to the ER form most likely to be of use; and helping the student use an ER effectively. The switchER2 system embodied these roles, providing feedback on errors of omission and commission during representation building.
requirements: Empirical results were needed to determine factors that help learners select, construct and make use of an ER, as the authors state.
constraints: The authors note that systems that intelligently parse and respond to input graphics or support ER switching remain relatively rare.
target_learning_goals: Selecting, constructing, using and switching between external representations during problem solving
examples: switchER2 provided feedback on errors of omission (leaving part of a problem unrepresented) and errors of commission (mistakes in the diagram), plus attention-drawing, hinting and suggesting interventions.

article_title: Towards Designing Profitable Courses: Predicting Student Purchasing Behaviour in MOOCs
citation: Alshehri, M., Alamri, A., Cristea, A. I., & Stewart, C. D. (2021). Towards Designing Profitable Courses: Predicting Student Purchasing Behaviour in MOOCs. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 31, 215–233. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00246-2
title: FutureLearn multi-run MOOC dataset (23 runs, 5 courses, 245,255 learners) with clickstream and demographic features
description: A large-scale dataset of 23 runs spread over 5 University of Warwick courses delivered via FutureLearn between 2013 and 2017, spanning literature, psychology, computer science and business. It combines system-logged clickstream activity (3,007,789 materials accessed; 2,794,578 steps declared completed) with optional survey demographics (gender, age group, education level, country, employment status and area). The derived time-spent feature is computed as the difference between first visit and last completion timestamps per step. The authors state it covers "a total of 23 runs spread over 5 MOOC courses, on 4 distinct topic areas".
requirements: Learners' optional demographic survey responses and system logs correlating unique IDs and timestamps to learner activities
constraints: Analysing a single platform, FutureLearn, which the authors state limits the work
target_learners: MOOC learners on FutureLearn, predominantly professional, highly educated adults from developed nations
target_learning_goals: Predicting certificate purchasing decisions and course revenue in online courses
examples: Courses analysed: Shakespeare and his World (10 weeks), The Mind is Flat (6 weeks), Babies in Mind (4 weeks), Big Data (9 weeks), Supply Chains (6 weeks)
key_sources: Alshehri, M., Alamri, A., Cristea, A. I., & Stewart, C. D. (2021). Towards Designing Profitable Courses: Predicting Student Purchasing Behaviour in MOOCs. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 31, 215–233. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00246-2

article_title: Towards Designing Profitable Courses: Predicting Student Purchasing Behaviour in MOOCs
citation: Alshehri, M., Alamri, A., Cristea, A. I., & Stewart, C. D. (2021). Towards Designing Profitable Courses: Predicting Student Purchasing Behaviour in MOOCs. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 31, 215–233. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00246-2
title: Increasing learners' time spent on the MOOC platform is a desirable design target for course designers
description: Because time spent on each step proved a powerful predictor of purchasing behaviour, the article recommends that course designers treat increasing time spent on the platform as a design goal. The authors write that "increasing time spent on the MOOC platform is a desirable target for course designers" and that this can be refined "by targeting different adaptive strategies based on the learners' characteristics". The finding rests on predictive accuracy rather than a tested causal intervention.
requirements: Step-level time-spent logging, computed from first-visit and last-completion timestamps
constraints: Time as a prediction variable is controversial on online platforms due to potential influence by external variables; the study did not experimentally test whether increasing time spent causes purchasing
target_learning_goals: Course design that supports purchasing behaviour and platform sustainability
examples: The predictive models achieved accuracies of 0.82–0.91 using time spent per step only, supporting time spent as a usable indicator
key_sources: Alshehri, M., Alamri, A., Cristea, A. I., & Stewart, C. D. (2021). Towards Designing Profitable Courses: Predicting Student Purchasing Behaviour in MOOCs. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 31, 215–233. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00246-2

article_title: Autograding Mathematical Induction Proofs with Natural Language Processing
citation: Zhao, C., Silva, M., & Poulsen, S. (2025). Autograding Mathematical Induction Proofs with Natural Language Processing. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 35, 3202–3232. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00498-2
title: LLM-embedding autograding pipeline for freeform mathematical proofs
description: The paper describes an automated grading process in which a student-written proof is first run through a pretrained large language model to obtain embeddings, and a custom classification model is then applied to those embeddings to calculate accuracy on various rubric points. Embedding selection and grading-model fitting are decoupled so the expensive semantic feature extraction is reused and a simple classifier (e.g., linear regression) suffices for the downstream grading task.
requirements: Requires a labeled corpus of student proofs graded against a shared rubric to train the per-rubric-point classifiers
constraints: Model accuracy is not guaranteed and misgrading cases were observed in user feedback; classifier is trained per rubric point and per problem, so generalization to new problems is not established
target_learners: Undergraduate students in discrete mathematics or proof-based courses
target_learning_goals: Writing correct proof-by-induction arguments
examples: Embeddings from GPT-3, MathBERT, and Llama-based models were used with a simple classifier over rubric points to grade freeform induction proofs
key_sources: Zhao, C., Silva, M., & Poulsen, S. (2025). Autograding Mathematical Induction Proofs with Natural Language Processing. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 35, 3202–3232. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00498-2

article_title: Autograding Mathematical Induction Proofs with Natural Language Processing
citation: Zhao, C., Silva, M., & Poulsen, S. (2025). Autograding Mathematical Induction Proofs with Natural Language Processing. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 35, 3202–3232. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00498-2
title: Labeled corpus of student induction proofs graded against a 7-point rubric
description: A dataset of student-written induction proofs collected from pretests and posttests, graded by a research team against a 7-point rubric covering base cases, the inductive hypothesis, and the inductive step. Grades were collapsed from a 0/1/2 scale to a binary correct/incorrect label per rubric point for training autograding models.
requirements: Proofs must be graded against a consistent rubric by multiple raters to provide usable training labels
constraints: Grades were collapsed to binary per rubric point, limiting the granularity of feedback compared to a multi-level scale
target_learning_goals: Identifying and correcting common misconceptions in proof by induction
examples: Proofs from four distinct induction problems were labeled and used to train and evaluate the autograding models
key_sources: Zhao, C., Silva, M., & Poulsen, S. (2025). Autograding Mathematical Induction Proofs with Natural Language Processing. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 35, 3202–3232. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00498-2

article_title: Autograding Mathematical Induction Proofs with Natural Language Processing
citation: Zhao, C., Silva, M., & Poulsen, S. (2025). Autograding Mathematical Induction Proofs with Natural Language Processing. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 35, 3202–3232. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00498-2
title: Rubric-point-decomposed automated feedback for iterative proof revision
description: A lesson-level pattern in which a submitted proof is decomposed by rubric points and the student receives targeted feedback identifying which specific step of the proof is problematic, then revises and resubmits. The rubric was designed so that each point addresses a known misconception about induction proofs, allowing errors to be localized rather than reported as a single holistic score.
requirements: A rubric whose points align with documented misconceptions in the target proof technique, and a grading model accurate enough per point to avoid misleading feedback
constraints: Feedback identifies the failing rubric point but does not explain how to fix the error, which some students found insufficiently elaborated
target_learners: Undergraduate students learning proof by induction
target_learning_goals: Producing a complete and logically correct induction proof
examples: Students in the study submitted proofs and received rubric-point-level feedback indicating which parts of their proof were incorrect, then revised their proofs
key_sources: Zhao, C., Silva, M., & Poulsen, S. (2025). Autograding Mathematical Induction Proofs with Natural Language Processing. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 35, 3202–3232. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00498-2

article_title: Moving-Target Intelligent Tutoring System for Marksmanship Training
citation: Vladimir Zotov & Eric Kramkowski. (2023). Moving-Target Intelligent Tutoring System for Marksmanship Training. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00308-z
title: MT-ITS: embedded moving-target marksmanship tutoring system
description: MT-ITS is a software-based tutor embedded into the digital sight of an instrumented rifle, operating in the Virtual Immersive Soldier Simulator. Its two feedback mechanisms are "a real-time correction of aiming" delivered by the Smart Sight System, which presents the optimal point of aim as a red rectangle on the target, and an after-action feedback showing each shot sequentially plus a statistical summary. It incorporates domain, tutor, and user-interface components of a standard ITS; its learner model is largely undeveloped, and the system is tuned for novice shooters.
requirements: Requires the VBS2 simulation environment and instrumented rifle tracking to compute and deliver point-of-aim cues and record shot data
constraints: Limited by poverty of sensor inputs, restrictions of the simulation environment, and deficiencies of instrumentation, placing it in a category of an advanced feedback training system with some AI elements rather than a fully-fledged ITS
Applicability was limited to novice shooters because the learner model is not well-elaborated
target_learners: novice shooters from Reserve Canadian Army units with little to no firearms experience
target_learning_goals: engaging moving targets: estimating distance and speed, adjusting point of aim, analyzing missed shots, and learning tracking techniques
examples: In the experiment, MT-ITS trainees alternated cued and non-cued trials and received after-action feedback with per-shot diagrams and a summary slide; in the second training block the target dropped after three hits to emphasize engagement speed.
key_sources: Vladimir Zotov & Eric Kramkowski. (2023). Moving-Target Intelligent Tutoring System for Marksmanship Training. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00308-z

article_title: Moving-Target Intelligent Tutoring System for Marksmanship Training
citation: Vladimir Zotov & Eric Kramkowski. (2023). Moving-Target Intelligent Tutoring System for Marksmanship Training. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00308-z
title: Four-component architecture of intelligent tutoring systems
description: The article defines an ITS as "a computer-based system that provides customized and immediate feedback to trainees" and, citing Sottilare et al. (2014), describes four major components: a domain model with expert knowledge and typical errors, a learner model representing the user's current knowledge state, a tutor model that decides how to teach from the other two models, and a user interface converting student inputs between forms. The article also classifies ITS by AI structure into simple reflex, goal-based, model-based, and learning systems, positioning MT-ITS as combining simple reflex with goal-based mechanisms.
requirements: The tutor model takes inputs from domain and learner models in order to customize its feedback to trainees
constraints: Depending on AI structure, only the simple reflex type can be built without elaborate task representations or cognitive architectures, per the article's classification
target_learning_goals: acquisition of motor-cognitive skills such as marksmanship through customized immediate feedback
examples: MT-ITS maps to the architecture: its domain module holds optimal-performance metrics, its tutor model drives both feedback forms, and VBS2 scripts serve as the user interface, while the learner model is largely undeveloped.
key_sources: Vladimir Zotov & Eric Kramkowski. (2023). Moving-Target Intelligent Tutoring System for Marksmanship Training. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00308-z

article_title: Moving-Target Intelligent Tutoring System for Marksmanship Training
citation: Vladimir Zotov & Eric Kramkowski. (2023). Moving-Target Intelligent Tutoring System for Marksmanship Training. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00308-z
title: Alternating cued and non-cued practice trials with blocked after-action feedback
description: MT-ITS training alternates cued trials, on which the optimal point of aim is shown, with non-cued trials, and delivers feedback in blocks rather than after every trial. The cued presentations are justified by the Instance Theory of Automatization, which "assumes that practice leads to storing of multiple instances of trained material in memory, thus increasing the speed of retrieval and contributing to effortless performance." Cued and non-cued trials were interleaved to avoid fostering reliance on the cue, and after-action feedback was summarized per trial rather than per shot.
requirements: Requires a system able to compute and display the optimal point of aim and to record per-shot performance for the after-action summary
constraints: The article notes that presenting feedback on only the immediately preceding trial might overwhelm trainees and foster heavy reliance and dependence on this form of feedback
target_learners: novice military shooters training on moving-target engagement
target_learning_goals: automating point-of-aim adjustment for moving targets and reducing dependence on external cues
examples: MT-ITS presented the same target types with and without the aiming cue sequentially, repeating the combination for all target types, and gave after-action feedback as a sequential shot-by-shot presentation plus a statistical summary.
key_sources: Vladimir Zotov & Eric Kramkowski. (2023). Moving-Target Intelligent Tutoring System for Marksmanship Training. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00308-z

article_title: Automatic Classification of Online Discussions and Other Learning Traces to Detect Cognitive Presence
citation: Dornauer, V., Netzer, M., Kaczkó, É., Norz, L.-M., & Ammenwerth, E. (2024). Automatic Classification of Online Discussions and Other Learning Traces to Detect Cognitive Presence. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00335-4
title: Community of Inquiry framework with cognitive presence as the four-phase Practical Inquiry Model
description: The Community of Inquiry framework describes how to achieve meaningful educational experiences in collaborative online learning through three presences: cognitive, social, and teaching. Cognitive presence, developed by Garrison et al. (2001) from Dewey's Practical Inquiry Model, "comprises four phases a student goes through in the critical thinking process": triggering event, exploration, integration, and resolution. The article uses this construct as its target of automatic measurement, coding student posts into these phases to build a classifier for a future teacher dashboard.
requirements: Manual coding of posts or meaningful units into the four phases (via a CoI codebook) to ground automatic measurement
Asynchronous forum discussion data from a collaborative online course
constraints: The phases are not always sequential; students may move back and forth through them (Garrison, 2017)
Triggering events may be rare in a given course: in this study the triggering phase appeared in only one post and was excluded from analysis
target_learning_goals: critical thinking and construction of meaning through sustained reflection and discourse
examples: The study coded 1,521 meaningful units from 1,147 German-language posts into the phases to train and evaluate automatic classifiers
key_sources: Dornauer, V., Netzer, M., Kaczkó, É., Norz, L.-M., & Ammenwerth, E. (2024). Automatic Classification of Online Discussions and Other Learning Traces to Detect Cognitive Presence. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00335-4

article_title: A Measurement Model of Microgenetic Transfer for Improving Instructional Outcomes
citation: Pavlik Jr, P. I., Yudelson, M., & Koedinger, K. R. (2015). A Measurement Model of Microgenetic Transfer for Improving Instructional Outcomes. International Artificial Intelligence in Education Society. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0039-y
title: CPFA: a contextual performance factors analysis model of learning and transfer
description: CPFA is a mixed-effect logistic regression model that crosses source practice contexts with target performance contexts, estimating separate coefficients for learning and transfer given prior successes (gamma) and failures (rho), for a total of eight learning and transfer parameters. Unlike Q-matrix approaches, it 'explicitly assumes asymmetric (one-way) transfer may occur and does not presume any latent factors exist'. It supports a microgenetic, trial-by-trial analysis of change and can summarize complex transfer patterns 'within a small table of numbers'.
requirements: Randomized item sequences and random-effect intercepts for students and items, since without random effects 'the models estimates of learning and transfer will be confounded'
constraints: In this paper the scope was 'kept... limited to item-types and performance categories', though the mixed-effect form could include other hierarchical factors
target_learning_goals: Pre-algebra skills such as least common multiple and fraction addition
examples: Applied to two pre-algebra warm-up lessons delivered in the Carnegie Learning Bridge to Algebra tutor, each of 16 randomly selected items from sets of 24
key_sources: Pavlik Jr, P. I., Yudelson, M., & Koedinger, K. R. (2015). A Measurement Model of Microgenetic Transfer for Improving Instructional Outcomes. International Artificial Intelligence in Education Society. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0039-y

article_title: AIED—Coming of Age?
citation: Wayne Holmes. (2024). AIED—Coming of Age?. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00352-3
title: Six challenges for the AIED community's coming of age
description: The author enumerates six challenges the AIED community should engage: generative AI, researcher responsibility for misuse, AI literacy, openness to other fields, ethics and human rights, and anthropomorphic language. He frames them as provocation, not criticism: 'raising these challenges is not a criticism of the work to date of the AIED community. Instead, it is a recognition of the successes of the AIED community alongside the fact that the world has changed.'
requirements: The community must debate and engage with each challenge rather than continue its traditional focus unchanged
constraints: The author raises the challenges 'although (because of space) not explore in enough detail'
target_learners: AIED researchers and the AIED research community
target_learning_goals: Responsible and ethical research practice in AI in education
examples: The Special Issue's fifteen opinion pieces from inside and outside the AIED community respond to the Durham panel provocation
key_sources: Wayne Holmes. (2024). AIED—Coming of Age?. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00352-3

article_title: AIED—Coming of Age?
citation: Wayne Holmes. (2024). AIED—Coming of Age?. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00352-3
title: AI literacy curricula should give the human dimension of AI equal billing with the technological dimension
description: The author argues AI curricula typically focus on how AI works and how to create it while treating ethics as an afterthought. He argues 'the human dimension of AI should be given equal billing to the technological dimension of AI, and that the two dimensions should be interwoven throughout any course', for example studying emotion detection's impact on people alongside how it works.
requirements: Interweaving must occur throughout any course, not as a separate ethics unit
constraints: Existing curricula such as AI4K12 and MIT's DAILy Workshop currently emphasise the technological dimension
target_learning_goals: Understanding AI's impact on humans and society, including ethical questions of power and political motivation
examples: If a student studies how emotion detection works, they should simultaneously study its potential impact on people, including surveillance in classrooms
key_sources: Wayne Holmes. (2024). AIED—Coming of Age?. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00352-3

article_title: AIED—Coming of Age?
citation: Wayne Holmes. (2024). AIED—Coming of Age?. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00352-3
title: Teachers need AI literacy in both dimensions to support students and evaluate AIED tools
description: The author argues teachers in every discipline should develop AI literacy in both the human and technological dimensions of AI, for two reasons: 'so that they can best support their students' developing AI Literacy, and so that they are empowered to evaluate whether an AIED tool might be useful, effective, and ethical in their specific context.' Teachers should also be supported to teach about AI within their own discipline.
requirements: Support must extend to teachers from every discipline, not only computing teachers
target_learning_goals: Evaluating commercial AIED tools for usefulness, effectiveness and ethics; supporting students' AI literacy
examples: The author asks what the implications of generative AI are for literature and art, and how these technologies affect what it is to be human
key_sources: Wayne Holmes. (2024). AIED—Coming of Age?. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00352-3

article_title: AIED—Coming of Age?
citation: Wayne Holmes. (2024). AIED—Coming of Age?. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00352-3
title: Educational technologies should be thoroughly tested before classroom availability, on the medical clinical-trials model
description: Drawing on a Council of Europe project, the author argues that because society insists medical interventions are thoroughly tested before wide availability due to safety and efficacy implications for the human body, 'we should insist on educational technologies being thoroughly tested before being made available in classrooms (because of their safety and efficacy implications for the developing human mind)'. The project also works toward a recommendation that teaching about AI include both human and technological dimensions.
requirements: A legal instrument to govern the application of AI in educational settings is being developed to operationalise this
constraints: The work is situated in a Council of Europe project addressing teaching with AI and teaching about AI
target_learning_goals: Ensuring safety and efficacy of AI tools used in education
examples: The Council of Europe project is drawing on the medical model of clinical trials for a legal instrument governing AI in education

article_title: Can Online Discussion Participation Predict Group Project Performance? Investigating the Roles of Linguistic Features and Participation Patterns
citation: Jaebong Yoo & Jihie Kim. (2014). Can Online Discussion Participation Predict Group Project Performance? Investigating the Roles of Linguistic Features and Participation Patterns. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0010-8
title: A framework for predicting project performance from online discussion participation features
description: The article presents a procedural framework in which online student activity data is collected from discussion platforms, pre-processed (noise removal, normalization), transformed into predictive variables, and analyzed against project grades. "Predictive V ariable Generation in Fig. 7 mainly consists of four modules: Role (Sink/Source) classifiers, Linguistic Tools (LIWC and Coh-Metrix), Work Patterns, and Degree of Participation." Its purpose is instructional assessment: alerting instructors about students who may need assistance.
requirements: Discussion data must be pre-processed with noise reduction and normalization before role classifiers and linguistic tools can run
Human-annotated training data is needed to build the automatic role classifiers
constraints: The presented work focused on a computer science course; the authors plan to apply the approach to other engineering courses
Discussion was optional and not graded in the studied course
target_learners: undergraduate engineering students in project-based computer science courses
target_learning_goals: predicting group project performance from collaboration behaviors
identifying students needing assistance
examples: Eight semesters of phpBB and Moodle data from an Operating Systems course were transformed into a consistent XML format and analyzed with the framework

article_title: Investigating the Impact of a Collaborative Conversational Agent on Dialogue Productivity and Knowledge Acquisition
citation: Adelson de Araujo, Pantelis M. Papadopoulos, Susan McKenney, Ton de Jong. (2025). Investigating the Impact of a Collaborative Conversational Agent on Dialogue Productivity and Knowledge Acquisition. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00469-7
title: Academically Productive Talk framework with the Four Goals of Productive Discussion
description: The Academically Productive Talk (APT) framework, also known as Accountable Talk, "encourages student interaction and reasoning to ultimately foster a deeper understanding of the subject matter through the strategic use of 'talk moves'", i.e., reflective prompts. It describes dialogue productivity through the Four Goals of Productive Discussion: sharing thoughts; orienting and listening to one another; deepening the reasoning; and engaging with each other's reasoning. The article uses these goals both to design Clair's talk moves and to measure guidance effectiveness.
requirements: Guidance must attend to student dialogue and pose talk moves in a timely manner to help students across aspects of dialogue productivity
constraints: APT talk moves are content-independent, though the article's What-if talk move marks a deviation by directly addressing content
target_learners: secondary school students (14-16-year-old) working in dyads
target_learning_goals: productive collaborative dialogue during inquiry learning
knowledge acquisition in science (digestive system)
examples: Clair's interventions were designed and evaluated against the four goals, with pattern-mining measures per goal
key_sources: Adelson de Araujo, Pantelis M. Papadopoulos, Susan McKenney, Ton de Jong. (2025). Investigating the Impact of a Collaborative Conversational Agent on Dialogue Productivity and Knowledge Acquisition. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00469-7

article_title: Investigating the Impact of a Collaborative Conversational Agent on Dialogue Productivity and Knowledge Acquisition
citation: Adelson de Araujo, Pantelis M. Papadopoulos, Susan McKenney, Ton de Jong. (2025). Investigating the Impact of a Collaborative Conversational Agent on Dialogue Productivity and Knowledge Acquisition. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00469-7
title: Clair, a CCA with six APT-based talk moves triggered via dialogue variables and a fuzzy expert system
description: Clair is a Collaborative Conversational Agent integrated into the Go-Lab chat tool that guides student-student dialogue using APT principles. It uses six talk moves (Checking-in, Peer questioning, Reorienting, Peer coordination, What-if, Press for reasoning), two of which are proactive rather than reactive. Talk moves are triggered from fifteen automatic 'dialogue variables' based on ConSent classifiers built on the multilingual Universal Sentence Encoder, interpreted by "a fuzzy expert system designed to interpret whether a talk move could be used" with fuzzy sets (high, medium, low) and one inference rule per talk move.
requirements: Student dyads must use the chat tool for collaboration so interventions can reach the intended audience; classifiers depend on the pre-trained mUSE encoder
constraints: Dyads with one or zero Clair interventions were excluded from analysis; some dyads excessively focused on asking questions to Clair rather than engaging their peer
target_learners: secondary school students (14-16-year-old, HAVO/VWO) in dyads
target_learning_goals: dialogue productivity via APT goals
collaborative inquiry learning about enzymes and digestion
examples: The What-if talk move poses hypothetical variations of nine standard statements from the orientation phase, e.g., what would happen if the enzyme in saliva was exposed to very high temperatures
key_sources: Adelson de Araujo, Pantelis M. Papadopoulos, Susan McKenney, Ton de Jong. (2025). Investigating the Impact of a Collaborative Conversational Agent on Dialogue Productivity and Knowledge Acquisition. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00469-7

article_title: Examining Student Teachers’ Agency in an AI-Supported Learning Environment: Q Methodology Research
citation: Chaaban, Y., Jung, S.-G., Medina, J., Azem, J. Y., Salminen, J., & Jansen, B. J. (2025). Examining Student Teachers' Agency in an AI-Supported Learning Environment: Q Methodology Research. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00529-y
title: Cipherbot: an instructor-curated RAG-based educational GenAI chatbot
description: Cipherbot is an educational chatbot that "bases its answers to student questions on learning material uploaded by the instructor". It operates on OpenAI's ChatGPT 4o and integrates Redis Queue, Celery, Azure Storage, Azure Cognitive Search and Azure OpenAI Chat Completions. Unlike commercial systems, "Cipherbot grounds its responses in the content curated by the course instructor to mitigate the ethical issues of accuracy and relevance", and it tackles hallucination "by employing a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) approach" that reveals resources as references. It also generates engagement analytics for the instructor.
requirements: Instructor uploads and curates course learning material on the platform before use
constraints: The article notes Cipherbot remains a technology that requires intentional and purposeful use
target_learners: University student teachers in a classroom management course
target_learning_goals: Clarifying concepts, reviewing learning materials, scenario practice, and preparing for assessments in classroom management
examples: The instructor uploaded 117 resources ahead of the semester; students role-played with Cipherbot as teacher or student and compared group responses with the chatbot's
key_sources: Chaaban, Y., Jung, S.-G., Medina, J., Azem, J. Y., Salminen, J., & Jansen, B. J. (2025). Examining Student Teachers' Agency in an AI-Supported Learning Environment: Q Methodology Research. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00529-y

article_title: Examining Student Teachers’ Agency in an AI-Supported Learning Environment: Q Methodology Research
citation: Chaaban, Y., Jung, S.-G., Medina, J., Azem, J. Y., Salminen, J., & Jansen, B. J. (2025). Examining Student Teachers' Agency in an AI-Supported Learning Environment: Q Methodology Research. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00529-y
title: Socio-cognitive three-dimension framework of student agency in AI-supported learning environments
description: The study draws on Bandura's socio-cognitive perspective, which views agency as a dynamic interplay between personal capacities and environmental resources rather than purely individual or socially determined. The authors state: "we draw on socio-cognitive perspectives in exploring the perceptions of student agency within AI-supported learning environments along three dimensions: intrapersonal, behavioral and environmental." The intrapersonal dimension covers beliefs, self-efficacy, motivation, interest, attitude and knowledge; the behavioral dimension covers self-directed learning including goal setting, monitoring, self-reflection and ethical evaluation; the environmental dimension covers learning atmosphere, interdependence, student-instructor relations, resources, criticality and authorship. The Q sample of 37 statements was categorized across these three dimensions.
requirements: Q sample statements categorized across the three dimensions based on the literature-based conceptualization
constraints: The framework was adapted from existing literature on student agency in a university context and served as a departure point for this study
target_learning_goals: Understanding and enacting student agency while using GenAI systems for academic work
examples: The 37-statement Q sample was split into 13 intrapersonal, 11 behavioral and 13 environmental statements
key_sources: Chaaban, Y., Jung, S.-G., Medina, J., Azem, J. Y., Salminen, J., & Jansen, B. J. (2025). Examining Student Teachers' Agency in an AI-Supported Learning Environment: Q Methodology Research. article_title: Generation and Use of Hints and Feedback in a Hilbert-Style Axiomatic Proof Tutor
citation: Josje Lodder, Bastiaan Heeren, Johan Jeuring, Wendy Neijenhuis. (2021). Generation and Use of Hints and Feedback in a Hilbert-Style Axiomatic Proof Tutor. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 31:99-133. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00222-2
title: LOGAX e-learning tool for Hilbert-style axiomatic proofs
description: LOGAX is an interactive tutoring tool in which students stepwise construct Hilbert-style axiomatic proofs in propositional logic using axioms a, b, c, Modus Ponens and the deduction theorem. As the article states, "LOGAX provides feedback, hints at different levels, next steps, and complete solutions." A dialog box lets students choose a rule and fill in line numbers while the software performs the step, and students can formulate their own exercises and ask for hints, a next step, or a complete proof at any moment.
requirements: Students must already have extensive training in writing syntactically correct formulae, since the tool does not focus on teaching formula syntax
constraints: The current version does not employ a student model, so fading strategies cannot be applied
target_learners: premaster and bachelor computer science students at the Open University of the Netherlands
target_learning_goals: construct simple axiomatic proofs in propositional logic
examples: Students choose an exercise or formulate their own, add proof lines via a dialog box, and can request hints, next steps, or a full proof; the target statement is labelled 1000 until the proof is renumbered.
key_sources: Josje Lodder, Bastiaan Heeren, Johan Jeuring, Wendy Neijenhuis. (2021). Generation and Use of Hints and Feedback in a Hilbert-Style Axiomatic Proof Tutor. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 31:99-133. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00222-2

article_title: Generation and Use of Hints and Feedback in a Hilbert-Style Axiomatic Proof Tutor
citation: Josje Lodder, Bastiaan Heeren, Johan Jeuring, Wendy Neijenhuis. (2021). Generation and Use of Hints and Feedback in a Hilbert-Style Axiomatic Proof Tutor. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 31:99-133. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00222-2
title: Dynamic recalculation of the solution space for hints in open solution domains
description: For domains like axiomatic proofs where not all solutions can be calculated upfront, the article proposes generating proofs automatically and extending them dynamically. As the authors put it, "If a student takes a step outside the current solution space, LOGAX dynamically recalculates the solution space, taking the student step as a starting point." The new solution space then serves as the source for hints and feedback, so the tutor can always respond even to diverging student steps. The authors present this dynamic approach as central to their solution and suggest similar techniques would be useful for ITSs in other multi-solution domains.
requirements: An algorithm that can generate proofs and extend partial proofs from an arbitrary student step as starting point
constraints: Needed because not all possible solutions can be calculated upfront or algorithmically in such domains
target_learning_goals: constructing formal proofs
examples: When a student introduces Axiom b in the exam exercise, LOGAX builds a new DAM from the student solution and uses it to recognize and hint on solution paths absent from the initial DAM.
key_sources: Josje Lodder, Bastiaan Heeren, Johan Jeuring, Wendy Neijenhuis. (2021). Generation and Use of Hints and Feedback in a Hilbert-Style Axiomatic Proof Tutor. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 31:99-133. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00222-2

title: Dialog-box interface that lets the software perform rule steps
description: LOGAX uses a dialog box in which the student chooses which rule to apply and fills in step numbers or formula parameters, while the software performs the step. The article explains: "The reason to use a dialog box in LOGAX to add new proof lines is that a student can concentrate on proof construction." Grounded in scaffolding theory on reducing degrees of freedom, this design lets students focus on steps closely related to the learning goal and reduces syntax errors, since only small formulae still need to be entered by hand.
requirements: Students should already have extensive training in writing syntactically correct formulae before using the interface
constraints: Students can still make syntax errors in the smaller formulae entered when adding, for example, an axiom instantiation
target_learners: students in logic courses who already write correct formulae
target_learning_goals: concentrating on proof construction strategies rather than formula syntax
examples: To add a Modus Ponens the student fills in at least two of the three line numbers and LOGAX performs the step automatically, adding a forward or backward step to the proof.

article_title: Fully Individualized Curriculum with Decaying Knowledge, a New Hard Problem: Investigation and Recommendations
citation: Lebis, A., Humeau, J., Fleury, A., Lucas, F., & Vermeulen, M. (2024). Fully Individualized Curriculum with Decaying Knowledge, a New Hard Problem: Investigation and Recommendations. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00376-9
title: FIC/DK-P: a formal framework modeling fully individualized curricula with decaying knowledge
description: FIC/DK-P models the problem of selecting, for a student, a sequence of courses such that the student becomes qualified for a stated objective while mastery values decay over time. It represents mastery continuously in [0;1], courses as macro entities with prerequisites, credits and temporal availability, and student profiles with per-knowledge decay functions, so that "it becomes essential to predict and mitigate this decay effect to determine the optimal sequence of courses."
requirements: Institutions must catalog courses with the knowledge taught, prerequisites, credit values and temporal availability; a knowledge decomposition into the [0;1] mastery interval must be agreed upon.
constraints: The study makes four stated hypotheses: no logistical constraints, a complete course catalog, courses confined to a single academic term, and perfect learning (no probabilistic learning models).
target_learners: university and engineering school students building individualized curricula toward professional objectives
target_learning_goals: sequencing courses so prerequisites and objective requisites remain satisfied despite knowledge decay
examples: Instantiated with an Ebbinghaus-inspired decay function on simulated datasets from a French engineering school master's program (catalog size C between 300 and 500 courses, K between 200 and 600 knowledge).
key_sources: Lebis, A., Humeau, J., Fleury, A., Lucas, F., & Vermeulen, M. (2024). Fully Individualized Curriculum with Decaying Knowledge, a New Hard Problem: Investigation and Recommendations. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00376-9

article_title: Fully Individualized Curriculum with Decaying Knowledge, a New Hard Problem: Investigation and Recommendations
citation: Lebis, A., Humeau, J., Fleury, A., Lucas, F., & Vermeulen, M. (2024). Fully Individualized Curriculum with Decaying Knowledge, a New Hard Problem: Investigation and Recommendations. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00376-9
title: Identify students' knowledge profiles, including decay functions, before proposing curriculum customization
description: Because the student profile strongly affects solving FIC/DK-P, institutions should assess not only current mastery but how each student forgets before individualizing curricula. The authors recommend that "institutions must therefore be careful to identify the precise profile of their students before proposing customization," warning that otherwise the risk is "to propose sequences of courses irrelevant to students' needs."
requirements: Regular assessment instruments capable of estimating and refining per-student decay functions over the years.
constraints: Cluster-based assignment of predefined decay functions is described as possibly less efficient than individual self-positioning testing.
target_learners: students entering individualized curriculum tracks at universities and engineering schools
target_learning_goals: accurate prediction of knowledge decay to keep personalized curricula relevant to student needs
examples: The authors propose conducting self-positioning tests to regularly test and compare the evolution of students' knowledge, or clustering students by features such as grades and high school specialties and assigning predefined decay functions.

article_title: A Configurable Conversational Agent to Trigger Students’ Productive Dialogue: A Pilot Study in the CALL Domain
citation: Tegos, S., Demetriadis, S., & Tsiatsos, T. (2013). A Configurable Conversational Agent to Trigger Students' Productive Dialogue: A Pilot Study in the CALL Domain. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0007-3
title: MentorChat configurable domain-independent conversational agent architecture
description: MentorChat is a cloud-based dialogue-based ITS whose architecture consists of three core modules: student, conversational agent, and teacher. The agent module rests on three models — peer interaction, domain, and intervention — where the "peer interaction model analyses and stores the most important aspects of students' interactions" and the domain model comes from teacher-authored concept maps or rules. The design deliberately avoids hardwiring an explicit domain model, instead enabling teacher-led configuration of agent behavior, which the authors argue lowers development cost and increases reusability and teacher acceptance.
requirements: Teacher-led domain modeling via concept maps or event-condition-intervention rules
System dictionaries for stemming, synonyms and antonyms to support pattern matching
constraints: The system does not enable identification of multiple dialogue acts in a single student's utterance
The automatic concept-mapping modeling method is a work in progress not yet assessed
target_learning_goals: productive transactive peer dialogue
explicit reasoning about domain concepts
examples: In the pilot, the teacher configured agent behavior via rules consisting of a key word or phrase and a relevant reflective-question intervention

title: MentorChat system
description: MentorChat is a cloud-based, web-technology application (MySQL, PHP, AJAX, HTML5, CSS3) available in English and Greek for synchronous text-based collaborative activities. Students discuss open-ended domain questions in phases and submit joint answers, while an animated two-dimensional avatar agent with Text-To-Speech tracks dialogue and delivers teacher-defined prompts. Teacher panels cover user management, activity structure, domain modeling, and real-time monitoring with interaction analysis indicators.

constraints: Requires teacher-defined key words/phrases to trigger interventions
target_learning_goals: collaborative discussion of open-ended domain questions
examples: Pilot installation used in a third-year English language course at Taurida National University of Ukraine

description: The authors argue the agent "should not be designed as teacher replacement, but should serve as an intelligent tool enhancing the impact of the collaboration strategies employed by the teacher, who always remains responsible for the orchestration and scaffolding of the educational activity." This 'teacher-as-activity-designer' perspective motivates teacher-led configuration of domain models and intervention rules, aiming for broader teacher acceptance and reusability across domains.

article_title: Preface to the Special Issue on Creating and Improving Adaptive Learning: Smart Authoring Tools and Processes
citation: Andrew M. Olney, Stephen B. Gilbert, Kelly Rivers. (2021). Preface to the Special Issue on Creating and Improving Adaptive Learning: Smart Authoring Tools and Processes. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education (2022) 32:1–3. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00277-9
title: Two-axis taxonomy classifying adaptive authoring systems by whether authoring is adaptive and whether content is adaptive
description: The editorial organizes smart authoring approaches with a two-way classification. Systems building adaptive tutors via teachable agents are characterized as "adaptive authoring of adaptive content", a dashboard tool orchestrating mixed activities is "an adaptive authoring system", and an adaptive-testing authoring system is "authoring adaptive content". The editorial states "The comparison between these four systems can be seen in Table 1", which crosses adaptive/non-adaptive authoring with adaptive/non-adaptive content.

constraints: Derived from the four papers accepted in this one special issue, not from a broader survey of adaptive systems
target_learners: teachers and trainers who are not programmers
target_learning_goals: authoring and improving adaptive learning environments
examples: Matsuda's teachable-agent paper and MacLellan and Koedinger's Apprentice Learner paper are placed in the adaptive-authoring/adaptive-content cell; Barrett et al. in non-adaptive authoring/adaptive content; Albó et al. in adaptive authoring/non-adaptive content

description: The editorial invokes Feigh et al. (2012)'s characterization of adaptive systems generally, not just in educational contexts. In this framework, "a successful adaptive system has to be able to react to triggers arising from actions or new information from the user, the external environment, the task state, the system itself, and from historical patterns over time." The editorial uses it to interpret the teachable-agent papers as building adaptive tutors that are themselves adaptive.

article_title: Intelligent Augmented Reality Training for Motherboard Assembly
citation: Giles Westerfield, Antonija Mitrovic & Mark Billinghurst. (2015). Intelligent Augmented Reality Training for Motherboard Assembly. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25:157–172. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0032-x
title: MAT: Motherboard Assembly Tutor combining a constraint-based ITS with a spatially-registered AR interface
description: MAT is an intelligent AR system that trains users to identify and install components (memory, processor, graphics card, TV tuner card, heatsink) on a computer motherboard. A communication module relays information between the AR interface and the ITS over "XML remote procedure calls over a TCP/IP network connection"; the AR interface uses a head-mounted display, camera-based marker tracking, spatially-registered 3D models, animations, and a screen-aligned HUD with color-coded text and text-to-speech. The architecture is designed to be modular so it can be adapted to new assembly and maintenance tasks.
requirements: The display elements and the domain model must be customized for each type of task, while the underlying architecture and scaffolding algorithms remain the same
constraints: The fiducial marker-based tracking approach has limited accuracy, poor resistance to occlusion and obtrusive markers
target_learners: novice users with minimal computer hardware assembly experience
target_learning_goals: identifying motherboard components and installing memory, processors, and heat sinks
examples: A prototype taught 16 university students to install five motherboard components through an HMD, with tracking via eight markers around the motherboard and ARToolkit marker tracking

article_title: Intelligent Augmented Reality Training for Motherboard Assembly

title: ASPIRE constraint-based tutor authoring process applied to a procedural AR assembly task
description: ASPIRE is an authoring system and deployment environment for constraint-based tutors. For MAT the authors followed the standard ASPIRE procedure with no changes to the authoring system: describing task characteristics (an 18-step procedural assembly task), composing a domain ontology of 14 concepts with properties and relationships, specifying problem/solution structures (with multiple correct solutions accepted where several configurations are valid), and generating a domain model of 275 constraints. ASPIRE-Tutor then performs student modelling, feedback and problem selection, matching every student action to constraints and providing progressively more detailed feedback as the student struggles.
requirements: Feedback messages generated automatically from templates must be re-written by the author in some cases to be more understandable to students
constraints: ASPIRE generates text-based interfaces automatically, and supporting an external interface such as AR requires its remote procedure call protocol
target_learners: novice users learning procedural assembly skills
target_learning_goals: correctly performing multi-step procedural assembly with adaptive feedback
examples: The ITS used the Boolean isOpen property of the MemorySlot concept to determine whether a memory slot had been successfully opened, with the value set via the AR interface

article_title: Review on Neural Question Generation for Education Purposes
citation: Said Al Faraby, Adiwijaya Adiwijaya, Ade Romadhony. (2024). Review on Neural Question Generation for Education Purposes. Int J Artif Intell Educ 34:1008–1045. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00374-x
title: Neural Question Generation: deep-learning-based automatic question generation from an input context
description: The review defines Neural Question Generation (NQG) as a form of Automatic Question Generation that utilizes neural network-based models such as sequence-to-sequence models and transformers, which automatically learn patterns and relationships in the input context. QG has three essential components: context, question, and answer. The review contrasts NQG with rule-based methods, which produce controlled question patterns but struggle with diverse and complex contexts.
requirements: Neural-based models require extensive training on large datasets of human-generated questions to work as described
constraints: The review states training and execution of NQG models can be computationally expensive
Controlling the types of questions generated is challenging due to the black-box nature of these models
target_learners: students in education settings using teacher- or self-generated questions
target_learning_goals: question generation supporting knowledge construction, comprehension assessment, and critical thinking
examples: The review surveys NQG applications including data augmentation for question-answering systems, drafting quizzes for educational purposes, and conversational agents

title: Taxonomy of educational question types from Graesser's sixteen types, Bloom's taxonomy, and comprehension levels
description: The review organizes question types for education using three categorizations: Graesser and Person's sixteen common question types in education distinguished by expected answer type; Bloom's taxonomy cognitive processes; and comprehension levels of literal, inferential, and evaluative questions. Each type is classified into three difficulty levels: low, medium, and high, mapping question types such as concept completion (low) through comparison (medium) to judgmental (high).
requirements: The taxonomy rests on cognitive science and educational psychology literature reviewed by the authors (Graesser and Person, 1994; Bloom, 1956; Basaraba et al., 2013)
constraints: The authors note the table displays question types and difficulty levels rather than directly equating individual question types between Graesser and Bloom
target_learners: students across K-12 and higher education
target_learning_goals: generating questions that recall prior knowledge, test comprehension, and hone critical thinking
examples: Table 2 lists low-level types such as verification, disjunctive, and concept completion, and high-level types such as causal antecedent, judgmental, and evaluation

citation: Filippo Sciarrone, Pierpaolo Vittorini, Christothea Herodotou, Elvira Popescu, Nuno Palmero Otero, Chee-Kit Looi, Marcelo Milrad. (2025).
