title: Responsible GAI integration framework: balancing innovation with pedagogical intent, ethics and human oversight
description: The editorial frames effective GAI integration in TEL as requiring a balance of innovation with responsibility. It states that "Effective implementation also requires a fundamental rethinking of educational frameworks, pedagogical strategies, and assessment methods to maximize GAI's benefits while minimizing potential drawbacks", and that ethical issues, data privacy and algorithmic bias must be addressed so systems remain "inclusive, equitable, and centered on human needs". The framework positions human oversight as essential to GAI's educational effectiveness.
requirements: Educational frameworks, pedagogical strategies and assessment methods must be rethought for GAI integration; ethical issues, data privacy and algorithmic bias must be addressed.
constraints: GAI's effectiveness hinges on thoughtful integration with human oversight; unchecked adoption risks perpetuating algorithmic bias.
target_learners: learners and educators across educational sectors
target_learning_goals: personalized learning, feedback, assessment, and equitable access to high-quality educational resources
examples: The editorial surveyed special-issue studies across architecture, literacy, computer science, data science, primary mathematics, biology assessment and teacher education as instances of this balancing act.
key_sources: Filippo Sciarrone, Pierpaolo Vittorini, Christothea Herodotou, Elvira Popescu, Nuno Palmero Otero, Chee-Kit Looi, Marcelo Milrad. (2025). Guest Editorial: Special Issue on “Bridging Futures: The Convergence of Technology Enhanced Learning and Generative AI”. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00516-3

article_title: The Evolution of Research on Digital Education
citation: Pierre Dillenbourg. (2016). The Evolution of Research on Digital Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0106-z
title: Six fundamental trends structure the evolution of AIED and learning technologies
description: The article organizes 25 years of AIED research around six trends: more physical, less semantic, more social, less design, more open, and more teachers. The author states: "I deconstruct the evolution of learning technologies into six fundamental trends." Each trend traces a shift in what learning environments are and who participates in them, and together they "form a beam of evolution vectors" rather than isolated changes.
requirements: Analysis takes a broad perspective covering communities around AIED, including Intelligent Tutoring Systems, CSCL, Learning Sciences, Learning Analytics, Education Data Mining and MOOC communities
constraints: The six trends are artificially segmented from each other; in reality they form a beam of evolution vectors
The 25-year span is an arbitrary time span defined by the journal anniversary
target_learners: researchers and designers of learning technologies
target_learning_goals: understanding the historical evolution of AI in education research
examples: The trends are used to structure the whole article, one section per trend, from physicality to teacher orchestration
key_sources: Pierre Dillenbourg. (2016). The Evolution of Research on Digital Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0106-z

article_title: The Evolution of Research on Digital Education
citation: Pierre Dillenbourg. (2016). The Evolution of Research on Digital Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0106-z
title: Reflect table: an interactive furniture display supporting participation balance
description: The Reflect table is furniture-based ambient output designed to help teams balance participation: "LEDS embedded in the table in front of team members display the amount of speech produced by each of them." It illustrates 'modest computing', in which displayed information is not the focus of attention, resolution is low, and no interpretation is proposed. It supports self-awareness that triggers reflection and self-regulation at the team level.
requirements: A physical team workspace in which the table's low-resolution display can be seen peripherally rather than attended directly
constraints: It displays simply a level of noise without any intelligence, which the author notes can hardly be considered aligned with the goals of AIED
target_learning_goals: balanced participation and team-level self-regulation in collaborative learning
examples: Used as the example of self-awareness ('group mirrors') contrasted with Lantern's awareness of others
key_sources: Pierre Dillenbourg. (2016). The Evolution of Research on Digital Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0106-z

article_title: The Evolution of Research on Digital Education
citation: Pierre Dillenbourg. (2016). The Evolution of Research on Digital Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0106-z
title: The shift from semantic learner modelling to behavioural particles interpreted by machine learning
description: Early AIED assumed a domain model, student model and tutor model gave actions semantics. New approaches capture "behavioural fragments or behavioural particles that, considered individually, do not convey very many semantics", such as gaze, posture, typing patterns and prosody, and process large data sets with machine learning. The author argues this drift from interpreting correct/wrong answers to interpreting behavioural dust is a fundamental evolution of the field.
requirements: Availability of cheap, small, non-intrusive sensors and algorithms able to process massive amounts of data
Careful selection of features, i.e. abstractions of raw data, since machine learning does not work well without them
constraints: Capturing anything that can be captured and running black box predictive algorithms may seem a caricature of science
target_learners: researchers in learning analytics and educational data mining
target_learning_goals: modelling learner states from low-semantic behavioural signals
examples: Raca et al. estimated lecture-room attention from the ratio of students' near-synchronous head co-movements
key_sources: Pierre Dillenbourg. (2016). The Evolution of Research on Digital Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0106-z

article_title: The Evolution of Research on Digital Education
citation: Pierre Dillenbourg. (2016). The Evolution of Research on Digital Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0106-z
title: Probabilistic approaches to pedagogical decision-making replace declarative tutoring knowledge
description: Tutoring knowledge, once stored in declarative formats such as production rules, evolved towards probabilistic approaches that represent what the system needs to choose between learning activities, following Self's slogan 'do not diagnose what you cannot treat'. The article notes these approaches take advantage of MOOC participant numbers and that Markov models capture learning-process dynamics. It asks whether empirically acquired pedagogical expertise is more effective than symbolically elicited laws such as aptitude-treatment interactions.
requirements: A sufficient number of learners must have used the system for the algorithms to become reliable
constraints: The cold start problem: these algorithms only become reliable when a sufficient number of learners have used the system
Whether probabilistic expertise is more effective than elicited pedagogical knowledge is posed as an open question
target_learning_goals: adaptive instructional decisions at run time
examples: Bayesian networks for learner modelling appeared in the early nineties and continued to grow
key_sources: Pierre Dillenbourg. (2016). The Evolution of Research on Digital Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0106-z

article_title: The Evolution of Research on Digital Education
citation: Pierre Dillenbourg. (2016). The Evolution of Research on Digital Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0106-z
title: Design learning technologies around classroom orchestration and teachers' practical constraints
description: The article argues that the design of learning technologies must take teachers' practical constraints into consideration more than before. "Orchestration is the real time management of multi-plane activities", covering individual, team and class-wide activities, and emphasises classroom-life constraints such as time, space, visibility and safety. As systems became more open, they created greater need and more opportunities for teacher interventions at runtime.
requirements: Designers must consider the whole context: login requirements, darkening the room, homework generation, grades produced
A graph of individual, team and classroom activities distributed over the classroom ecosystem needs to be orchestrated
constraints: Some activities can run in autonomous environments, but the whole graph needs orchestration
target_learning_goals: effective real-time management of multi-plane learning activities
examples: Paper components in digital environments were valued because they facilitated orchestration by making the workflow visible, e.g. collecting or distributing sheets
key_sources: Pierre Dillenbourg. (2016). The Evolution of Research on Digital Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0106-z

article_title: The Evolution of Research on Digital Education
citation: Pierre Dillenbourg. (2016). The Evolution of Research on Digital Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0106-z
title: Two-phase meta-trend: novel approaches are first opposed, then integrated for complementarity
description: The article's second meta-trend is that most reported trends followed a two-phase pattern: new approaches emerge because they differ clearly from existing ones, then the duality fades. "Different approaches are first perceibed as mutually exclusive but then integrated for their complementarity." The author estimates this cycle takes between 5 and 10 years, so a few more should occur in the coming decade.
requirements: Time for researchers to bypass the sterile opposition between ideas and the resulting litany of overstatements
constraints: The cycle is estimated, not measured, at between 5 and 10 years
target_learning_goals: anticipating how oppositions in the field resolve over time
examples: Individual versus social views of cognition, and digital versus physical, each first opposed then integrated
key_sources: Pierre Dillenbourg. (2016). The Evolution of Research on Digital Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0106-z

citation: Tom Murray. (2003). MetaLinks: Authoring and Affordances for Conceptual and Narrative Flow in Adaptive Hyperbooks. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 13, pp.199-233. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197317
title: MetaLinks: an authoring tool and web server for adaptive hyperbooks
description: MetaLinks is an authoring tool and web server for producing adaptive hyperbooks that provide textbook-like content in a flexible manner. The abstract describes it as supporting "opportunistic processes of active reading and learning", so that "a single on-line artifact can address the diverse needs of a variety of user goals and backgrounds" through adaptive methods.
requirements: Requires an authoring tool and web server infrastructure as described in the article
target_learners: learners using adaptive hyperbooks with diverse goals and backgrounds
target_learning_goals: inquiry, exploratory, or curiosity-driven learning in richly interconnected material
examples: The system is designed to support inquiry, exploratory, or curiosity-driven learning in richly interconnected material.

citation: Tom Murray. (2003). MetaLinks: Authoring and Affordances for Conceptual and Narrative Flow in Adaptive Hyperbooks. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 13, pp.199-233. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197317
title: Interface features of narrative smoothing, custom depth control, and thematic links address discontinuous flow in open-ended hyperbook learning
description: The article reports that its goals are addressed through interface features and adaptive methods "including narrative smoothing, custom depth control, and thematic links". These respond to the usability problem that flexible, idiosyncratic navigation through hyperbook content risks discontinuous conceptual and narrative flow for learners exploring open-ended material.
requirements: Adaptive hyperbook content richly interconnected enough to support flexible navigation
constraints: Targets usability issues arising in open-ended learning environments where users navigate flexibly and idiosyncratically

target_learning_goals: maintaining conceptual and narrative coherence during self-directed reading
examples: MetaLinks implements narrative smoothing, custom depth control, and thematic links as adaptive methods in its hyperbooks.

title: Conceptual and narrative flow as a design concern for open-ended hyperbook learning

It treats learner reading as opportunistic and active, so the system must supply adaptive smoothing and linkage structures to keep a coherent storyline and concept structure intact across non-linear paths through richly interconnected material.

article_title: WhatsApp Discourse Throughout COVID-19: Towards Computerized Evaluation of the Development of a STEM Teachers Professional Learning Community
citation: Zahava Scherz · Asaf Salman · Giora Alexandron · Yael Shwartz. (2023). WhatsApp Discourse Throughout COVID-19: Towards Computerized Evaluation of the Development of a STEM Teachers Professional Learning Community. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00320-3
title: A three-category coding scheme for assessing PLC WhatsApp discourse (Community Development, Knowledge Development, Administrative Issues)
description: The article synthesizes a coding scheme for assessing PLC discourse, built on teacher-knowledge frameworks (CK, PCK, TK) and PLC characteristics. It classifies each WhatsApp message into "three main categories": Community Development (building community, cooperation, sharing, positive feedback), Professional Knowledge Development (CK/PCK/TK and matching ASK- subcategories), and Administrative Issues, plus Media and Not Applicable tags. Messages are multi-labeled, discursive sequences are delimited into threads, and tags serve as indications of teachers' learning or PLC development.
requirements: Annotation by trained experts with joint training and consolidation sessions; validity requires both annotators agreeing on a tag (achieved IRR above 95%).
constraints: PK without content knowledge was not used as a separate category because the authors found it does not exist without content knowledge; Media tags were annotated automatically and excluded from reliability analysis.
target_learners: in-service STEM teacher leaders in professional learning communities
target_learning_goals: professional knowledge development (content, pedagogical-content, technological knowledge) and community development
examples: Example annotations include CK ('I checked with a physicist: the particles move by force of inertia...') and ASK-TK ('How do I assign students to separate zoom rooms?')

article_title: Dynamic Cultural Contextualisation of Educational Content in Intelligent Learning Environments using ICON
citation: Phaedra Mohammed & Permanand Mohan. (2015). Dynamic Cultural Contextualisation of Educational Content in Intelligent Learning Environments using ICON. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 25:249–270. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0033-9
title: ICON system: dynamic intracultural contextualisation architecture for ILEs
description: ICON (Instructional Cultural cONtextualisation) models conceptual and linguistic variations across the subcultures in a student's background and generates culturally adapted educational content dynamically. Its architecture comprises four components: "a Contextual Student Model, Contextual Element Repository, Cultural Linguistics Adapter, and a Controller". The CSM estimates metacultural competence via weighted rule-based membership scores; the repository selects culturally appropriate images and terms using the CERA ontology; the adapter varies formality (acrolect/mesolect/basilect) and substitutes localized vocabulary measured as sentence distortion; the Controller links ICON to the host ILE.
requirements: Requires detailed student demographic data plus national-level census and statistical data organised into an ontological structure to estimate cultural group membership strengths.
Requires ontological structures and Semantic Web techniques for meaningful semantic contextualisation, as the authors concur with prior work.
constraints: The Cultural Linguistics Adapter's formality variation is limited to English-based Creoles and to grammatical transformation rules.
In the reported work the modelling range was fully developed for only Trinidadian culture.
target_learners: students from diverse subcultures within a society, exemplified by Trinidadian university students
target_learning_goals: adapting educational content (problem descriptions, images, feedback, hints) to students' cultural backgrounds while preserving the learning context
examples: For a sample student with a strong Roman Catholic background and mixed ancestry, ICON recommended references like 'bake and shark', 'doubles' and 'Angostura bitters', and transformed 'John gave away free biscuits' into 'John gave away free Angostura bitters'.
key_sources: Phaedra Mohammed & Permanand Mohan. (2015). Dynamic Cultural Contextualisation of Educational Content in Intelligent Learning Environments using ICON. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 25:249–270. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0033-9

article_title: Dynamic Cultural Contextualisation of Educational Content in Intelligent Learning Environments using ICON
citation: Phaedra Mohammed & Permanand Mohan. (2015). Dynamic Cultural Contextualisation of Educational Content in Intelligent Learning Environments using ICON. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 25:249–270. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0033-9
title: Give students control over the extent of cultural contextualisation in ILEs via student-initiated controls such as a cultural density slider
description: Because system-initiated determination of cultural formality and references was not unanimously accepted and preferences fluctuate by content type, the article argues that student-initiated control should be featured in ILEs. In CRITS, "movement of the cultural density slider triggers the contextualisation changes" so that language formality, cultural references and images adjust in real time, with 0% restoring original content. The study's finding that students tolerated different densities for different content types further supports this principle.
requirements: Requires a dynamic contextualisation approach that can modify content in real time, such as the ICON architecture with a Contextual Student Model and Cultural Linguistics Adapter.
Requires an interface mechanism, such as a density slider mapped to a formality scale, through which students express their preferred level of contextualisation.
constraints: The article's supporting evidence comes from one small study (37 participants) in a Computer Science domain with content modelled only for Trinidadian culture, so the authors call the threshold findings preliminary.
Informal dialect at high densities risked perceptions of lacking professionalism and pedagogical expertise.
target_learners: students from diverse cultural subcultures, exemplified by Trinidadian university programming students
target_learning_goals: adapting problem descriptions, images, hints and instructional feedback to students' preferred level of cultural contextualisation
examples: In the CRITS study, participants moved the slider in fixed increments of 20% from 0% to 100% and rated content at each level; one student left the slider at 20% because hints at 40% were too comical and distracted her.
key_sources: Phaedra Mohammed & Permanand Mohan. (2015). Dynamic Cultural Contextualisation of Educational Content in Intelligent Learning Environments using ICON. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 25:249–270. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0033-9

article_title: Preschoolers’ Understanding of a Teachable Agent-Based Game in Early Mathematics as Reflected in their Gaze Behaviors – an Experimental Study
citation: Gulz, Agneta; Londos, Ludvig & Haake, Magnus. (2020). Preschoolers' Understanding of a Teachable Agent-Based Game in Early Mathematics as Reflected in their Gaze Behaviors – an Experimental Study. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education (2020) 30:38–73. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00193-4
title: Learning-by-teaching with a teachable agent in three successive pedagogical modes
description: Magical Garden implements the learning-by-teaching pedagogy: the child instructs a digital tutee (the teachable agent) and learns by doing so. Each scenario is, in the article's words, "always repeated in three successive pedagogical modes": the child practices the task alone, then demonstrates it to the watching TA, then supervises the TA's attempt, accepting or correcting the TA's proposal with happy/unhappy smileys. The design yields two stated pedagogical gains: repeated, non-repetitive task practice, and the chance to evaluate someone else performing the task, which is more feasible for young children than reflecting on their own actions under cognitive load.
requirements: The child must be able to ascribe some knowledge to the TA that can differ from and be influenced by their own, and perceive the TA's behavior as goal-directed for meaningful instruction
constraints: Full benefit requires understanding that the TA has agency; the article questions whether preschoolers' less developed theory of mind supports this
target_learning_goals: early mathematics and number sense within the number range 1–9
examples: In mode three the TA proposes a button shown in a thought bubble and the child accepts or corrects it; after the three modes child and TA receive water droplets to grow the garden
key_sources: Gulz, Agneta; Londos, Ludvig & Haake, Magnus. (2020). Preschoolers' Understanding of a Teachable Agent-Based Game in Early Mathematics as Reflected in their Gaze Behaviors – an Experimental Study. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education (2020) 30:38–73. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00193-4

article_title: Preschoolers’ Understanding of a Teachable Agent-Based Game in Early Mathematics as Reflected in their Gaze Behaviors – an Experimental Study
citation: Gulz, Agneta; Londos, Ludvig & Haake, Magnus. (2020). Preschoolers' Understanding of a Teachable Agent-Based Game in Early Mathematics as Reflected in their Gaze Behaviors – an Experimental Study. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education (2020) 30:38–73. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00193-4
title: Magical Garden: a teachable agent-based play-&-learn game for early math with a state-machine adaptation logic
description: Magical Garden is a research-based play-&-learn game for 4- to 6-year-olds targeting number sense and basic math skills within the number range 1–9. It comprises "60 scenarios, ordered by difficulty defined by number range (1–4, 1–6, or 1–9), representation (none, fingers, dots, dice, number symbols) and method (counting, proto-addition/subtraction, 'true' addition/subtraction)". A state machine tracks each child's progress, steering different paths: children who master a scenario move on, while children who struggle repeat scenarios through varying sub-games or drop back half or entire difficulty levels.
requirements: Children play individually on their own tablet with a personal log-in and their own digital friend (the TA)
constraints: The game deliberately keeps each child working just beyond current mastery, so repetition amounts differ substantially among individual children
target_learning_goals: number sense: connecting number words, magnitudes, and iconic, semi-symbolic and symbolic number representations
examples: Sub-games feature distinct narratives, e.g., a nearsighted bumblebee needing help finding the right flower or a treasure hunter reaching a cave by attaching balloons to her basket
key_sources: Gulz, Agneta; Londos, Ludvig & Haake, Magnus. (2020). Preschoolers' Understanding of a Teachable Agent-Based Game in Early Mathematics as Reflected in their Gaze Behaviors – an Experimental Study. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education (2020) 30:38–73. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00193-4

article_title: Preschoolers’ Understanding of a Teachable Agent-Based Game in Early Mathematics as Reflected in their Gaze Behaviors – an Experimental Study
citation: Gulz, Agneta; Londos, Ludvig & Haake, Magnus. (2020). Preschoolers' Understanding of a Teachable Agent-Based Game in Early Mathematics as Reflected in their Gaze Behaviors – an Experimental Study. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education (2020) 30:38–73. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00193-4
title: Dynamic assessment in a game: state-machine steering toward the zone of proximal development
description: Magical Garden integrates assessment and instruction through its state-machine progression logic. The article states that "Magical Garden relies on dynamic assessment, i.e., integrating assessment and instruction (Vygotskij 1978), to address a 'potential for learning' rather than a 'static levels of achievement'", with the goal of keeping each child working at a level just beyond current mastery — the zone of proximal development — to maximize learning. Repetition is embedded without monotony by varying the sub-game narrative while keeping the pedagogical challenge constant.
requirements: Continuous logging of each child's performance to decide progression, repetition, or stepping back in difficulty
constraints: The amount and placement of repetition vary among individual children, so different children receive substantially different amounts of training on the same task type
target_learning_goals: number sense and basic math skills
examples: When a child's performance remains low, the system goes back a half or entire level in difficulty so the child can practice and prepare for a new attempt on the higher level
key_sources: Gulz, Agneta; Londos, Ludvig & Haake, Magnus. (2020). Preschoolers' Understanding of a Teachable Agent-Based Game in Early Mathematics as Reflected in their Gaze Behaviors – an Experimental Study. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education (2020) 30:38–73. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00193-4

article_title: Preschoolers’ Understanding of a Teachable Agent-Based Game in Early Mathematics as Reflected in their Gaze Behaviors – an Experimental Study
citation: Gulz, Agneta; Londos, Ludvig & Haake, Magnus. (2020). Preschoolers' Understanding of a Teachable Agent-Based Game in Early Mathematics as Reflected in their Gaze Behaviors – an Experimental Study. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education (2020) 30:38–73. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00193-4
title: Malfunction events in the experimental Bird Rescue sub-game as a probe of number sense processing
description: The researchers implemented an event named a malfunction in an experimental version of the Bird Rescue sub-game: when the correct button is pressed, the elevator passes the correct branch and gets stuck in the treetop, where a service bird repairs it. The design rationale is that "there are no bottom-up salient stimuli present that can indicate malfunction when the elevator passes the branch that corresponds to the button pressed, only previous knowledge or understanding on the part of the child – in this case understanding that relates to number sense". Responses to malfunctions were predicted to differ between children who connect the feather set, elevator buttons, and vertically ordered branches and children who do not.
requirements: A mixture of standard (functioning) and manipulated (malfunctioning) trials, with correct branches in number range 1–6 for experimental trials so children can notice the malfunction before the treetop
constraints: Randomized branch assignments and bird colors prevent colors from serving as cues for noticing a malfunction
target_learning_goals: connecting multiple number representations: feather sets, iconic button representations, and vertical branch ordering
examples: Each round of the experimental sub-game contained four trials in fixed order: standard child-in-charge, manipulated child-in-charge, standard TA-in-charge, manipulated TA-in-charge

article_title: Recent Meta-reviews and Meta–analyses of AIED Systems
citation: Benedict du Boulay. (2015). Recent Meta-reviews and Meta-analyses of AIED Systems. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0060-1
title: Step-based tutoring: evaluating and reacting to each learner step in problem-solving, as the organizing distinction in ITS effectiveness research
description: The letter uses a granularity-of-feedback account to organise ITS effectiveness findings: step-based tutors "evaluates and reacts to each step that the learner makes in a problem-solving session as opposed to evaluating only the final answer given by the learner". This distinction frames which systems the surveyed meta-analyses cover. It serves as the letter's working characterisation of the ITS class whose effectiveness the reviews compare against human tutoring and conventional instruction.
requirements: Applies to problem-solving tutors whose granularity of evaluation is per-step rather than final-answer only, as the letter's definition states.
constraints: The letter uses the definition to characterise surveyed systems; it does not test whether step granularity itself causes effectiveness differences.
target_learners: Learners using intelligent tutoring systems in the surveyed studies (school pupils and university students)
target_learning_goals: Problem-solving skill in tutored domains
examples: The letter applies the definition to the ITSs surveyed by VanLehn (2011) and the step-based ITSs in the Ma et al. (2014) meta-analysis.
key_sources: Benedict du Boulay. (2015). Recent Meta-reviews and Meta-analyses of AIED Systems. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0060-1

article_title: Integrating Generative AI into Programming Education: Student Perceptions and the Challenge of Correcting AI Errors
citation: Kohen-Vacs, D., Usher, M., & Jansen, M. (2025). Integrating Generative AI into Programming Education: Student Perceptions and the Challenge of Correcting AI Errors. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00496-4
title: Pair instructor-designed programming tasks with LLM-generated debugging challenges in a scaffolded curriculum
description: This principle holds that programming education should combine AI-augmented learning with traditional instruction so students build both fluency and error-correction skill. The article states that "pairing instructor-designed tasks with LLM-generated debugging challenges can help students gradually build their analytical and error-correction abilities," alongside reflective exercises and critical evaluation of AI outputs. It arises directly from the finding that students underperformed on LLM-generated debugging tasks in high-stakes exams without prior training.
requirements: Programming curricula must include both traditional instructor-designed coding exercises and LLM-generated debugging tasks so that core skills such as debugging, logic development, and algorithmic thinking are preserved alongside AI-augmented practice.
constraints: Study 2 was conducted in high-stakes summative exams without prior instruction or training; the article notes task origin was confounded with distinct cognitive demands (debugging versus algorithmic development).
target_learning_goals: Debugging and error correction of AI-generated code
Algorithmic thinking and foundational programming competencies
Critical evaluation of AI outputs
examples: The Study 2 exams included flawed Java code generated by an LLM, such as an RSA implementation with intentionally embedded errors, alongside instructor-designed tasks like implementing a modular inverse method and a Feistel network.
key_sources: Kohen-Vacs, D., Usher, M., & Jansen, M. (2025). Integrating Generative AI into Programming Education: Student Perceptions and the Challenge of Correcting AI Errors. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00496-4

article_title: Enhancing Procedural Writing Through Personalized Example Retrieval: A Case Study on Cooking Recipes
citation: Mejia-Domenzain, P., Frej, J., Neshaei, S. P., Mouchel, L., Nazaretsky, T., Wambsganss, T., Bosselut, A., & Käser, T. (2025). Enhancing Procedural Writing Through Personalized Example Retrieval: A Case Study on Cooking Recipes. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00405-1
title: RELEX: an adaptive learning system for personalized example-based procedural writing feedback
description: RELEX (REcipe Learning through EXamples) is a learning system for procedural writing that provides each learner with a tailored example recipe, personalized in-text highlighting, explanatory suggestions, and a reflection space. Its stated purpose is to "facilitate procedural writing by providing students with tailored examples, accompanied by relevant annotations and reflective prompts". It targets structure, clarity, and specificity, retrieves examples from over 180,000 rated recipes, and was evaluated in a 2x2 controlled study with 200 participants.
requirements: A database of rated recipes (RELEXset) and a fine-tuned quality predictor (RELEXset-Predictor) to select higher-quality examples in real time
constraints: Instantiated in the cooking-recipe domain, chosen for familiarity and relevance to culinary students and chef apprentices
target_learners: Chef apprentices and culinary students; recruited study participants aged 18-30 with at least an undergraduate degree
target_learning_goals: Procedural writing quality: structure, clarity, and specificity of recipes
examples: A learner requesting feedback on a chicken recipe is shown the similar, higher-quality "Louisiana Chicken" recipe with missing structural elements highlighted and reflection questions posed
key_sources: Mejia-Domenzain, P., Frej, J., Neshaei, S. P., Mouchel, L., Nazaretsky, T., Wambsganss, T., Bosselut, A., & Käser, T. (2025). Enhancing Procedural Writing Through Personalized Example Retrieval: A Case Study on Cooking Recipes. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00405-1

article_title: Enhancing Procedural Writing Through Personalized Example Retrieval: A Case Study on Cooking Recipes
citation: Mejia-Domenzain, P., Frej, J., Neshaei, S. P., Mouchel, L., Nazaretsky, T., Wambsganss, T., Bosselut, A., & Käser, T. (2025). Enhancing Procedural Writing Through Personalized Example Retrieval: A Case Study on Cooking Recipes. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00405-1
title: Double-content examples in heuristic domains: examples must be processed on a learning-domain and an exemplifying-domain level
description: The article frames example-based learning in heuristic domains (where no algorithmic solution exists, such as cooking recipes) through the notion of double-content examples. Learners must process two content levels: "(1) the learning domain (i.e., how to structure the solution) and (2) the exemplifying domain (i.e., the topic)". In structural domains examples are annotated with solution steps, whereas double-content examples are enriched with self-explanation prompts and instructional explanations. RELEX instantiates this framing in procedural writing.
requirements: Examples in heuristic domains must be enriched, e.g., with self-explanation prompts or instructional explanations, because learners process two content levels
constraints: Applies to heuristic domains with no single correct solution; prior work noted static examples and explanations can be redundant or not timely
target_learners: Learners composing procedural texts in heuristic domains, e.g., culinary students
target_learning_goals: Acquiring heuristics for structuring and writing high-quality procedural texts
examples: A cooking-recipe learner must understand procedural text structure (learning domain) while being familiar with cooking (exemplifying domain)
key_sources: Mejia-Domenzain, P., Frej, J., Neshaei, S. P., Mouchel, L., Nazaretsky, T., Wambsganss, T., Bosselut, A., & Käser, T. (2025). Enhancing Procedural Writing Through Personalized Example Retrieval: A Case Study on Cooking Recipes. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00405-1

article_title: Enhancing Procedural Writing Through Personalized Example Retrieval: A Case Study on Cooking Recipes
citation: Mejia-Domenzain, P., Frej, J., Neshaei, S. P., Mouchel, L., Nazaretsky, T., Wambsganss, T., Bosselut, A., & Käser, T. (2025). Enhancing Procedural Writing Through Personalized Example Retrieval: A Case Study on Cooking Recipes. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00405-1
title: Five-function personalized example feedback pattern: on-demand analysis, similar better example, colored highlighting, dismissible suggestions, reflection space
description: RELEX operationalizes personalized example-based feedback through five interface functionalities: F1 an Analyze button requesting feedback and new examples on demand; F2 a better, similar recipe retrieved per learner; F3 colored highlighting of missing structure, clarity, and specificity aspects; F4 short, deletable explanation tips on highlighted elements; and F5 a Reflection Space prompting self-explanation and comparison. "The five design functionalities of RELEX (see Table 1) are based on design requirements derived from user interviews as well as from literature."
requirements: Each functionality must trace to at least one user requirement (U1-U5 from ten user interviews) or literature requirement (L1-L5 from example-based learning design principles)
constraints: Explanations should be short and minimalist and should not tell learners things they already know, per the cited design principles
target_learners: Learners writing procedural texts, including culinary students and study participants aged 18-30
target_learning_goals: Improving structure, clarity, and specificity of procedural texts through active example processing
examples: F3 highlights missing elements such as "List each ingredient separately" in the example recipe with separate colors; F5 poses the questions "What aspects of this example recipe do you find interesting, useful, convincing, and which not?" and "What deficiencies does your recipe have compared to the example recipe on the right?"

article_title: How to Optimize Student Learning Using Student Models That Adapt Rapidly to Individual Differences
citation: Eglington, L.G., Pavlik, P.I. (2022). How to Optimize Student Learning Using Student Models That Adapt Rapidly to Individual Differences. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00296-0
title: Prior Error Valence (PEV) feature for learner models
description: PEV is a model feature the authors introduce for adaptive instructional systems: "PEV is a recency-weighted cumulative moving average of the signed model error on all prior trials for the student". Signed error is the model's predicted correctness probability minus the student's binary response, and errors are downweighted with an exponential smoothing kernel using a decay parameter. Unlike the proportional-decay feature it adapts from Galyardt and Goldin, PEV takes model error rather than binary correctness as input and does not require ghost attempts.
requirements: Requires prior correctness outcomes and prior learner model predictions, data the authors note is frequently available in AIS already
constraints: PEV tracks systematic error from any source, including possible model misspecification, which the authors say makes its effects differ from proportional decay
target_learners: students in adaptive instructional systems without prior individual parameter estimates
target_learning_goals: accurate estimation of student knowledge and mastery for practice sequencing
examples: Implemented as EPFA, a PFA model plus PEV, and evaluated on six datasets with student-stratified 10-fold cross-validation
key_sources: Eglington, L.G., Pavlik, P.I. (2022). How to Optimize Student Learning Using Student Models That Adapt Rapidly to Individual Differences. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00296-0

article_title: How to Optimize Student Learning Using Student Models That Adapt Rapidly to Individual Differences
citation: Eglington, L.G., Pavlik, P.I. (2022). How to Optimize Student Learning Using Student Models That Adapt Rapidly to Individual Differences. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00296-0
title: Student-level recency-weighted proportional correctness feature (RKC,SPFA)
description: This feature extends Galyardt and Goldin's KC-level proportional decay measure by tracking the recency-weighted proportion of correct responses at the level of the student across KCs. The authors hypothesized this additional feature "could stand in for student learning differences as well as learning transfer across KCs". It requires two ghost attempts (one incorrect, one correct) to center the measure at .5 so it can adapt upward or downward, and the authors have implemented a version in a running system.
requirements: Requires appending two ghost attempts (one failure, one success) to practice sequences so proportions are defined from the first attempt
constraints: The version computes the recency-weighted average across KCs, so it partially reflects transfer rather than pure student learning rate
target_learning_goals: tracking individual student performance differences for mastery estimation
examples: Fit as RKC,SPFA and RKC,SEPFA variants across six datasets; a version is implemented in a running system
key_sources: Eglington, L.G., Pavlik, P.I. (2022). How to Optimize Student Learning Using Student Models That Adapt Rapidly to Individual Differences. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00296-0

article_title: How to Optimize Student Learning Using Student Models That Adapt Rapidly to Individual Differences
citation: Eglington, L.G., Pavlik, P.I. (2022). How to Optimize Student Learning Using Student Models That Adapt Rapidly to Individual Differences. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00296-0
title: Adaptive instructional systems should include online mechanisms that adjust for systematic learner-model error
description: The article's central design recommendation: because individual student parameters are frequently unavailable, learner models assuming equal learning rates will make systematic errors, so AIS should "include mechanisms to adjust predictions to account for them". The recommended mechanisms adjust online in a running system using data already present in most AIS — prior correctness and prior learner model predictions — rather than requiring pretests or student clustering.
requirements: Prior correctness outcomes and prior learner model predictions must be logged and available in the running system
constraints: The authors do not claim the suggested model adjustments completely resolve the issue and state experiments are needed to verify tractability in practice
target_learners: students in adaptive instructional systems, especially new students with no prior data
target_learning_goals: efficient practice sequencing and accurate mastery decisions
examples: The authors implemented PEV and student-level proportional decay adjustments that improved model accuracy in all six tested datasets

article_title: Designing a Knowledge Representation Approach for the Generation of Pedagogical Interventions by MTTs
citation: Luc Paquette, Jean-François Lebeau, Gabriel Beaulieu & André Mayers. (2015). Designing a Knowledge Representation Approach for the Generation of Pedagogical Interventions by MTTs. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 25:118–156. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0030-z
title: Astus's knowledge-based system: a knowledge representation approach in which each type of knowledge unit has a clearly defined semantic on which the MTT's pedagogical module can rely
description: Astus is a model-tracing tutor (MTT) framework whose knowledge-based system models the task as the teacher's instructions rather than as the procedural knowledge of an ideal learner. The article states this is "achieved by designing a knowledge representation approach in which each type of knowledge unit has a clearly defined semantic on which the MTT 's pedagogical module can rely on." Its procedural knowledge uses goals and procedures organized in a procedural graph comparable to hierarchical task networks; its declarative knowledge uses concepts, relations and functions accessed through a fixed task-independent query interface. This lets the pedagogical module "automatically generate interventions as well as the pedagogical content used to instantiate them."
requirements: The task model must be authored with goals, procedures, concepts, relations and functions whose semantics are known to the MTT, with task-specific manipulations done through Astus's fixed query interface
constraints: Astus does not have the capability to interpret how the requested information is produced, since instantiation through task-specific processes cannot be explained by the MTT
target_learning_goals: well-defined procedural tasks such as AVL tree element insertion and subtraction
examples: The article illustrates hint generation using MTTs for the insertion of elements into an AVL tree and for subtraction, e.g. the totally ordered sequence procedure PInsert achieving the goal GInsert.
key_sources: Luc Paquette, Jean-François Lebeau, Gabriel Beaulieu & André Mayers. (2015). Designing a Knowledge Representation Approach for the Generation of Pedagogical Interventions by MTTs. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 25:118–156. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0030-z

article_title: Designing a Knowledge Representation Approach for the Generation of Pedagogical Interventions by MTTs
citation: Luc Paquette, Jean-François Lebeau, Gabriel Beaulieu & André Mayers. (2015). Designing a Knowledge Representation Approach for the Generation of Pedagogical Interventions by MTTs. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 25:118–156. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0030-z
title: Sierra's impasse-and-repair theory of the origin of learners' procedural errors
description: Sierra, as presented in the article, is "a theory to explain the origin of learners' procedural errors (VanLehn 1990)" proposing "plausible cognitive processes that could lead learners to execute incorrect steps." Errors arise when learners face impasses — situations in which their current knowledge is insufficient — and apply one of three repair strategies: no-op, back-up and barge-on. The article reports the theory was validated by a computational model of learning applied to subtraction that successfully modeled the acquisition of multiple errors observed in learners' behavior, and Astus takes inspiration from it to diagnose errors.
requirements: Modeling errors via impasse and repair requires a hierarchical goal structure that meets Sierra's criterion for a hierarchical goal structure
constraints: Little effort has been made to incorporate elements of the Sierra theory into ITSs, according to the article
target_learning_goals: understanding and diagnosing learners' procedural errors
examples: The article describes how a no-op repair ignores an unachievable goal, a back-up repair returns to a previously unfinished goal, and a barge-on repair modifies procedural knowledge to resolve the impasse.
key_sources: Luc Paquette, Jean-François Lebeau, Gabriel Beaulieu & André Mayers. (2015). Designing a Knowledge Representation Approach for the Generation of Pedagogical Interventions by MTTs. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 25:118–156. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0030-z

article_title: Designing a Knowledge Representation Approach for the Generation of Pedagogical Interventions by MTTs
citation: Luc Paquette, Jean-François Lebeau, Gabriel Beaulieu & André Mayers. (2015). Designing a Knowledge Representation Approach for the Generation of Pedagogical Interventions by MTTs. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 25:118–156. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0030-z
title: A taxonomy of error types an MTT can diagnose via impasse-and-repair interpolation, organized by knowledge unit, repair type and observed error
description: The article enumerates the error types Astus can diagnose in a table listing, for each error, "1) the knowledge unit that might have been incorrectly executed, 2) the possible sources of the error (repair types) and 3) a description of the observed error." The taxonomy includes path disruption, relation/function swap, relation/function place/parameter swap, incorrect condition, violated order constraint, incorrect object order, incomplete for-each procedure, loop early stop, continued loop and no loop. The article states "Table 1 contains a list of all the different types of error that Astus can diagnose."
requirements: Each error type is tied to a specific procedural knowledge unit type (query, conditional, sequence, for-each or loop procedure) whose semantics the MTT knows
constraints: Some error types can be associated with many repair types; when an error involves executing the wrong sub-goal, the article states it is not possible to accurately identify what caused the incorrect sub-goal to be executed
target_learning_goals: negative feedback on errors in well-defined procedural tasks
examples: A violated order constraint error can be caused by an incorrect knowledge of the order constraint (barge-on), or by the learner avoiding the correct sub-goal via no-op or back-up.

article_title: Care - Making the Affective Leap: More Than a Concerned Interest in a Learner's Cognitive Abilities
citation: Bridget Cooper. (2003). Care - Making the Affective Leap: More Than a Concerned Interest in a Learner's Cognitive Abilities. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 13, pp.3-9. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197311
title: An elaborate definition of 'care' in intelligent learning systems that includes the affective aspects of learning
description: The commentary develops a definition of 'care' for intelligent learning systems that goes beyond a merely cognitive concern for learners. It explicitly 'elaborat[es] and extend[s] the definition to include recent research from neuroscience and education on the affective aspects of learning'. Care is treated as tied to profound empathy rather than as detached monitoring of cognitive ability, and the article argues that current systems fall short of this elaborate definition, which limits their capacity to reproduce care.
requirements: The definition must incorporate affective-aspect research from neuroscience and education, not only learner cognition
constraints: The commentary itself concludes existing systems 'tend to focus more heavily on the cognitive rather than the affective nature of care'
target_learning_goals: affective as well as cognitive dimensions of learning
examples: The commentary evaluates the systems described in the same journal issue against this extended definition of care and profound empathy
key_sources: Bridget Cooper. (2003). Care - Making the Affective Leap: More Than a Concerned Interest in a Learner's Cognitive Abilities. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 13, pp.3-9. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197311

citation: Bridget Cooper. (2003). Care - Making the Affective Leap: More Than a Concerned Interest in a Learner's Cognitive Abilities. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 13, pp.3-9. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197311
title: Profound empathy as the affective core of care in learning systems
description: The article proposes profound empathy as the construct through which care should be understood in intelligent learning systems. It 'reflects on the association of profound empathy with care and in what ways the systems described in this issue illustrate features of profound empathy'. The construct functions as a benchmark: systems can be examined for whether they exhibit the features of profound empathy that caring human educators display, and the article uses it to diagnose what the issue's systems achieve and what they lack.
requirements: Assessment of a system's care requires examining it against the features of profound empathy
constraints: The systems reviewed only partially instantiate the construct, showing 'some features of profound empathy'
target_learners: learners interacting with intelligent tutoring and learning systems
target_learning_goals: affective engagement and caring relationships in learning
examples: The commentary reviews the intelligent learning systems in the same journal issue for features of profound empathy

title: Design intelligent learning systems for care that goes beyond concerned interest in learners' cognitive abilities
description: The principle, stated in the article's title and argument, is that care in intelligent learning systems must be 'More Than a Concerned Interest in a Learner's Cognitive Abilities'. Because the commentary links profound empathy with care and finds the issue's systems reproduce care only in a limited way, designers should aim for systems that address learners' affect as well as their cognition when emulating caring educational relationships.

constraints: Without that definition, the article argues, a system's 'ability to reproduce it is limited'

article_title: Lab4CE: a Remote Laboratory for Computer Education
citation: Julien Broisin, Rémi Venant & Philippe Vidal. (2017). Lab4CE: a Remote Laboratory for Computer Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 27:154–180. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0079-3
title: Scaffolding capacities required for an educational-oriented remote laboratory
description: The article defines a set of pedagogical capabilities that remote laboratory environments must provide to effectively support practical learning: a common view of the experiment, shared control over remote experiments, synchronous communication tools, social/artifact awareness tools, learning analytics for tutoring, and a user-friendly authoring tool. The authors motivate this with the claim that "the scaffolding around the lab may be at least as important as the lab itself" and with a survey where students pointed to help and support and engagement. They use the framework to evaluate six existing remote lab projects, concluding they "do not focus on pedagogical concerns".
requirements: The remote lab environment should give learning actors access to a common view of the experiments and shared control, plus synchronous communication, awareness, learning analytics and authoring capacities
constraints: Existing projects studied (iLab, LiLa, LabShare, WebLab-Deusto, Lab2Go, Go-Lab) partially or fully lack most of these capacities, and none takes experiment instructional design into account
target_learners: distant learners in STEM higher education
target_learning_goals: inquiry skills and practical disciplinary skills through remote laboratory work
examples: Table 1 rates iLab, LiLa, Labshare, WebLab, Lab2Go and Go-Lab against each requirement, e.g. authoring tool is not supported by any of the six projects
key_sources: Julien Broisin, Rémi Venant & Philippe Vidal. (2017). Lab4CE: a Remote Laboratory for Computer Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 27:154–180. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0079-3

article_title: Lab4CE: a Remote Laboratory for Computer Education
citation: Julien Broisin, Rémi Venant & Philippe Vidal. (2017). Lab4CE: a Remote Laboratory for Computer Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 27:154–180. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0079-3
title: Lab4CE remote laboratory environment
description: Lab4CE is a remote laboratory for computer education built on a "three-layered architecture inspired from the iLab shared architecture": a laboratory layer implementing OpenStack for virtual machine management at scale, a middleware layer with RESTful core services and an Elasticsearch-based learning analytics store, and a learning layer hosting rich pedagogical interfaces. It distinguishes an experiment (a teacher-defined specification of virtual resources and pedagogical objectives) from a practical session (a learner-owned instantiation), and integrates scaffolding tools intended to increase engagement in remote practical activities.
requirements: Existing virtualization tools (OpenStack as IaaS) plus middleware services mapping experiments and practical sessions onto OpenStack artifacts with role-based access control
constraints: The web Terminal control interface restricts practice to computer science topics that do not require a graphical interface
target_learners: undergraduate computer science students and their tutors
target_learning_goals: system and network administration, programming, database management skills
examples: In the study, a simple experiment with a single Linux computer let each of 139 students access their own virtual machine from anywhere
key_sources: Julien Broisin, Rémi Venant & Philippe Vidal. (2017). Lab4CE: a Remote Laboratory for Computer Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 27:154–180. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0079-3

article_title: Lab4CE: a Remote Laboratory for Computer Education
citation: Julien Broisin, Rémi Venant & Philippe Vidal. (2017). Lab4CE: a Remote Laboratory for Computer Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 27:154–180. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0079-3
title: Lab4CE micro authoring tool for experiment design
description: An authoring tool for instructors that addresses the micro learning design capacity the authors find lacking in other remote labs such as Go-Lab's Graasp.eu. Designers first fill a form specifying learning metadata (name, description, pedagogical objective, availability period), then design the experiment's topology at two granularity levels by dragging Computer, Router and Switch components, each with adaptable default software configurations. Publication translates the configuration into OpenStack format, guaranteeing "independence between the authoring tool and the virtualization software".
requirements: Virtual resources must be configurable to the specific discipline taught, e.g. a programming language must be installed and configured on the remote lab
constraints: Experiments are specifications only; the authoring tool does not deploy resources, which are created on demand when learners start a practical session
target_learners: instructors and instructional designers of remote computer science experiments
target_learning_goals: configuration and re-engineering of online experiments aligned with pedagogical objectives
examples: The illustrated scenario designed an IP-configuration experiment with four computers, two switches and one router, and constraints such as Stations 1 & 2 in the same subnet
key_sources: Julien Broisin, Rémi Venant & Philippe Vidal. (2017). Lab4CE: a Remote Laboratory for Computer Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 27:154–180. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0079-3

article_title: Lab4CE: a Remote Laboratory for Computer Education
citation: Julien Broisin, Rémi Venant & Philippe Vidal. (2017). Lab4CE: a Remote Laboratory for Computer Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 27:154–180. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0079-3
title: Artifact-awareness tool for shared practical sessions
description: A component of Lab4CE's rich learning interface operationalizing artifact awareness, defined in the article as "one person's up-to-the-moment knowledge of the artifacts and tools that other distributed people are using as they perform their individual, ongoing work". It shows users involved in an experiment with role and connection status icons, supports inviting peers or tutors into a practical session, displays partners' Terminals as live-feed thumbnails, and highlights with a light red line when another user performs an action on a shared resource. The middleware proxies and broadcasts interactions in real time to the session's owner and guests.
requirements: The middleware layer must act as a proxy between users and virtual resources so interactions can be captured and broadcast in real time
constraints: Unlike VNC-based or video-based solutions, it requires no additional software on users' hosts; in computer education audio/video feeds are worthless since no physical changes occur on the computer
target_learners: learners and tutors engaged in collaborative remote practical sessions
target_learning_goals: awareness of who is working on what during collaborative practical work
examples: In the illustrated scenario, Julien and Rémi working on Station 2 see each other's Terminal thumbnails and the red line marking a guest's action

article_title: Lab4CE: a Remote Laboratory for Computer Education
citation: Julien Broisin, Rémi Venant & Philippe Vidal. (2017). Lab4CE: a Remote Laboratory for Computer Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 27:154–180. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0079-3
title: Lab4CE learning analytics tool and management dashboard
description: Two analytics artifacts for tutors. The learning analytics tool visualizes, per virtual resource, a timeline of all recorded activities — commands with date, string and output, and chat posts from public and private rooms — with color-coded nodes, filters and zoom; it supports "monitoring of students' activities, (a)synchronous guidance and assistance, evaluation of learners' performances, or identification of learners who face challenges". The management dashboard built on Horizon monitors the computational status and configuration of each learner's virtual resources so tutors can initiate a chat if something seems wrong.

constraints: The ready-to-use Horizon dashboard is designed for cloud monitoring and does not provide fine-grained information such as the software embedded in a virtual resource or network routing tables; a learning-oriented dashboard is work in progress

examples: Tutors can record a near-perfect session into the store and reuse it to demonstrate the best solution for a given experiment

article_title: Ensemble Learning for Estimating Individualized Treatment Effects in Student Success Studies
citation: Beemer, J., Spoon, K., He, L., Fan, J., & Levine, R.A. (2018). Ensemble Learning for Estimating Individualized Treatment Effects in Student Success Studies. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 28, 315–335. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0148-x
title: Individualized treatment effects (ITE) as a framework for student success analytics
description: Individualized treatment effects, borrowed from the personalized medicine literature, quantify for each student the predicted difference in an outcome between experiencing an intervention and not, even though each student experiences only one modality. The article computes ITE by training separate ensemble learners on treatment and control groups and using each to predict the counterfactual outcome for the other group. It states the ensemble learner serves "as a best guess of the outcome for the treatment (control) group students if they had experienced the control (treatment)". ITE then support evaluating interventions, characterizing benefiting subgroups, and advising individual students.
requirements: Data on students who did and did not experience the intervention, with covariates available in student information system or learning management system databases
A trained predictive ensemble learner for each group to estimate the counterfactual outcome
constraints: Randomized experiments or crossover designs are typically not an option in education settings, so non-randomized assignment may leave unobserved confounders unadjusted; the method was illustrated without direct measures of attitudes, behavior, or motivation
target_learners: higher education students in large enrollment bottleneck courses
at-risk student subgroups such as URM, EOP, and first-generation students
target_learning_goals: evaluating the impact of instructional interventions on course success, retention, and graduation outcomes
examples: Applied to a supplemental instruction section in STAT 119 at SDSU, producing average ITE of 9.3 exam points and 0.45 grade points and example-student profiles of predicted grade-letter improvements
key_sources: Beemer, J., Spoon, K., He, L., Fan, J., & Levine, R.A. (2018). Ensemble Learning for Estimating Individualized Treatment Effects in Student Success Studies. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 28, 315–335. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0148-x

title: STAT 119 supplemental instruction section (STAT 119A) at San Diego State University
description: A one-credit supplemental instruction course attached to the large-enrollment STAT 119 introductory statistics course, enrolling 20–30 students per section meeting twice weekly for one hour. Sections are led by statistics graduate teaching assistants trained to develop "an active problem solving environment in the classroom", with students working through problems rather than watching solutions and TAs facilitating group discussion of conceptual difficulties. It deviates from the traditional UMKC SI model by using graduate students rather than near-peers and requiring enrollment in STAT 119A.
requirements: Students voluntarily enroll for one additional credit unit; students scoring below 70% on the first-week algebra assessment are strongly encouraged to enroll
Instructors are trained prior to the semester and regularly evaluated by a course coordinator
constraints: Differs from the UMKC SI model: instructors are graduate students rather than near-peers, and attendance is effectively required via enrollment and encouragement rather than voluntary drop-in
target_learners: undergraduates in a large enrollment introductory statistics bottleneck course
students scoring below 70% on an initial algebra assessment
target_learning_goals: improving final exam scores, course grades, and non-repeatable grades (C or better) in introductory statistics
examples: The Fall 2013 offering enrolled 17% of STAT 119 students; enrollees averaged 83% pass rate versus 72% for non-enrollees

article_title: Against Personalised Learning
citation: Caroline Pelletier. (2023). Against Personalised Learning. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education (2024) 34:111–115. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00348-z
title: Three political-philosophical questions AI education research should answer about personalisation
description: The commentary proposes that AI research in education should provide 'nuanced, thoughtful and empirically-grounded responses' to three historically central educational questions: what the purpose of education is; what vision of a better world education sustains; and how education practises equality as a political claim, understood as self-determination rather than indoctrination. It argues AI has been treated as a mere technique, which 'has the effect of de-politicising education'.
requirements: Researchers and teachers treating questions of purpose as within their remit, since teaching or research invokes a sense of purpose.
constraints: The author does not claim everyone should have clear and categorical answers; the questions are offered to trouble assumptions and open possibilities.
target_learners: teacher educators and MA students in education and technology
target_learning_goals: critical examination of the purposes and political commitments of educational technology research
examples: The commentary returns to the three standard claims about personalised learning to illustrate how each question troubles their assumptions.

article_title: Algorithmic Fairness in Automatic Short Answer Scoring
citation: Nico Andersen, Julia Mang, Frank Goldhammer, Fabian Zehner. (2025). Algorithmic Fairness in Automatic Short Answer Scoring. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00495-5
title: Eight-stage machine-learning pipeline for automatic scoring with stage-specific bias vulnerabilities
description: The article describes a machine-learning pipeline for automatic short-answer scoring comprising eight stages: data collection, scoring/labeling, preprocessing, feature engineering, model selection, data split, model training, and model evaluation. For each stage it names a characteristic bias vulnerability, e.g. unrepresentative samples create "representation bias", human labeling creates "annotation bias", and unstratified data splits can induce "sampling bias". It is used to explain where unfairness can enter automatic scoring systems before it surfaces at model evaluation.
requirements: Data collected representatively with respect to demographic characteristics
Scoring according to precise scoring guidelines
Features relating to construct-relevant information
constraints: Statistical models can be difficult or impossible to reconstruct and understand, especially with many interdependent parameters as in deep learning
target_learning_goals: Fair and accurate automatic scoring of constructed reading-comprehension responses
examples: The article walks through each pipeline stage with a concrete bias example, such as text-length features disadvantaging boys who tend to write shorter texts in reading comprehension tasks
key_sources: Nico Andersen, Julia Mang, Frank Goldhammer, Fabian Zehner. (2025). Algorithmic Fairness in Automatic Short Answer Scoring. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00495-5

title: PISA 2015 German reading constructed-response dataset for fairness analysis
description: A dataset of n = 38,722 text responses to reading-comprehension items from the 2015 German PISA assessment, written by n = 4,060 students (49% girls). From 43 reading literacy items, 37 dichotomously scored (correct/incorrect) items were selected; booklet design meant each student responded to between one and 15 items. The OECD-reported interrater agreement for reading literacy in Germany is 94.8%. Blank responses were excluded.
requirements: Dichotomous scoring to allow examination of false positives and negatives at the item level
constraints: Tasks and text responses cannot be disclosed for reasons of confidentiality
Language use at home had 11% missing values and serves only as a proxy for language proficiency
target_learning_goals: Examining demographic disparity in automatic versus human scoring of constructed responses
examples: Group performance differed by membership: girls scored Y = .74 versus boys' Y = .68; native speakers Y = .73 versus foreign-language speakers' Y = .61

article_title: Going Beyond the Problem Given: How Human Tutors Use Post-Solution Discussions to Support Transfer
citation: Sandra Katz, David Allbritton, John Connelly. (2003). Going Beyond the Problem Given: How Human Tutors Use Post-Solution Discussions to Support Transfer. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 13, pp.79-116. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197313
title: A framework for describing distributed plans for reflection spanning problem solving and post-solution discussion
description: The article proposes a framework describing how reflective activity is distributed across problem-solving discussion and post-solution dialogue in tutoring. It was induced from Study 1 analyses that identified "several tutorial strategies that are distributed between problem solving and post-solution reflection." The framework organizes these strategies as plans for reflection rather than as isolated post-hoc activities, grounded in the observed roles of post-solution dialogues such as explaining conceptual knowledge and integrating it with strategic knowledge.
requirements: Applicable to tutoring contexts where problem-solving dialogue and post-solution reflection both occur, as observed in Andes tutoring sessions
constraints: Proposed based on analyses of a small set of tutors (seven tutors, 15 students) in one physics tutoring domain
target_learners: physics students working with human tutors in the Andes tutoring system
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding and transfer in physics problem solving
examples: Study 1 tutors guided 15 students through Andes problems, and transcript analysis identified tutorial strategies distributed between problem solving and reflection

article_title: A Novel Framework for the Generation of Multiple Choice Question Stems Using Semantic and Machine-Learning Techniques
citation: Praveen Kumar, A., Nayak, A., Shenoy K., M., Chaitanya, & Ghosh, K. (2024). A Novel Framework for the Generation of Multiple Choice Question Stems Using Semantic and Machine-Learning Techniques. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00333-6
title: Hybrid OBT+MBT framework combining ontology-based and machine-learning-based generation of heterogeneous MCQ stems
description: The article proposes a hybrid automatic question generation framework in which an Ontology-Based Technique (OBT) generates Wh-type question stems from DL and SWRL rules built over a domain ontology, while a Machine-Learning Based Technique (MBT) generates Cloze stems from unstructured textbook text. As the article states, it "describes a technique for combining semantic-based and machine-learning-based techniques to generate grammatically correct MCQ stems of various types for a technical domain." The two pipelines run simultaneously on a preprocessed text file, and the resulting stems are evaluated against Bloom's Taxonomy cognitive levels.
requirements: An ontology for the technical domain must be built (via Protégé) and a Topic_list of relevant topics must be manually created by a subject expert before generation proceeds
constraints: The reported system targets single-response MCQs for one technical domain (Operating Systems), with Wh-type stems produced only by OBT and Cloze stems only by MBT
target_learners: students in technical/engineering courses assessed with MCQs
target_learning_goals: assessing cognitive skills across Bloom's Taxonomy levels in a technical domain
examples: The framework was instantiated on the Operating Systems course: OBT generated Wh-type stems from a built OS ontology while MBT generated Cloze stems from preprocessed textbook sentences
key_sources: Praveen Kumar, A., Nayak, A., Shenoy K., M., Chaitanya, & Ghosh, K. (2024). A Novel Framework for the Generation of Multiple Choice Question Stems Using Semantic and Machine-Learning Techniques. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00333-6

article_title: A Novel Framework for the Generation of Multiple Choice Question Stems Using Semantic and Machine-Learning Techniques
citation: Praveen Kumar, A., Nayak, A., Shenoy K., M., Chaitanya, & Ghosh, K. (2024). A Novel Framework for the Generation of Multiple Choice Question Stems Using Semantic and Machine-Learning Techniques. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00333-6
title: Mapping ontology rule consequent types onto Wh-type stem types (odd-one-out, T/F, synonym, definition, one-word)
description: Each DL or SWRL rule is first transformed into an Instance Tree (ITree); traversal then selects a stem template based on the consequent's variable type. The article specifies, for example, that "If the consequent is a 'Type variable', then the odd one out question stem generated is 'Which among the following is not a 'Type Variable'?'", while a 'theEquivalentNameOf' antecedent yields a synonym stem, a single property/class antecedent yields a definition stem, and multiple class variables yield a one-word stem. This pattern makes the ontology's rule structure directly determine which cognitive-level stem type is produced.
requirements: DL/SWRL rules must follow the article's naming conventions for classes and properties so the transformation algorithm can parse them
constraints: Stem variety is bounded by the consequent/antecedent configurations the article enumerates; question words map to specific Bloom cognitive skills per its Table 2
target_learners: students in technical domain courses (e.g., Operating Systems)
target_learning_goals: generating heterogeneous Wh-type MCQ stems assessing different cognitive levels
examples: For SWRL Example 1 the ITree traversal produced 'WHAT IS A/AN HARDWARE THAT HAS CONTROL OVER INPUT OUTPUT DEVICES?'; for DL Example 2 it produced the odd-one-out stem 'WHICH AMONG THE FOLLOWING IS NOT A/AN OPERATING SYSTEM?'
