citation: Praveen Kumar, A., Nayak, A., Shenoy K., M., Chaitanya, & Ghosh, K. (2024). A Novel Framework for the Generation of Multiple Choice Question Stems Using Semantic and Machine-Learning Techniques. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00333-6
title: MBT three-stage Cloze generation pipeline (sentence selection, key-sentence classification, Naive Bayes keyword selection)
description: MBT converts preprocessed textbook sentences into Cloze stems in three stages. A subject expert's Topic_list filters sentences; then five classifiers pick key sentences — the article notes that "the five classifiers- SVM, K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Decision Tree (DT), Gaussian Naive Bayes (GNB), and Logistic Regression (LR) are trained, and the classification is done", using features Sentence Length, Nouns, Abbreviations, and Appendix Words, with a 75%-25% train-test split over cross-validation. Finally a Naive Bayes classifier ranks candidate words by blank-substitution probability, and the top three words per key sentence become Cloze blanks.
requirements: A manually created Topic_list from a subject expert; training data with the Feature_set (SL 100–200 characters, NN, ABR, AW)
constraints: Only the first three ranked words per key sentence become blanks, so n key sentences yield three Cloze stems each
target_learners: students assessed with Cloze MCQs in technical courses
target_learning_goals: automated generation of grammatically correct Cloze assessment items
examples: In the sample run, sentence S1 was selected (SL criteria met, AW present) and produced three Cloze stems blanking 'binding', 'swapped', and 'addresses'

title: Operating Systems ontology built for OBT (344 classes, 57 object properties, 10 data properties)
description: Because no existing ontology was available for the Operating Systems course, one of the authors hand-built the domain ontology in Protégé over 25 to 30 days; "In terms of size, this OS ontology comprises 57 object properties, 10 data properties, and 344 classes." It models concepts such as 'Computer', 'Hardware', 'OperatingSystem', and 'Interrupt', with TBox axioms (subset and equivalence, e.g., 'MainMemory ≡ PhysicalMemory') and ABox axioms feeding the ITree-to-question transformation.
requirements: Semi-automatic construction in Protégé with DL/SWRL rules added to extend semantics; a naming convention for classes and properties
constraints: Building the ontology took 25 to 30 days of expert effort, illustrating the semantic approach's upfront cost
target_learners: students of the Operating Systems course
target_learning_goals: Wh-type MCQ stem generation grounded in domain semantics
examples: Sample axioms include the SWRL constraint 'Interrupt(?i), Software(?s), isTriggeredBy(?i, ?s) → SystemCalls(?i)' representing a domain fact as a rule

title: Cap Cloze questions per key sentence at the three highest-probability candidate words to reduce manual evaluation burden
description: The article limits blank selection to the top-ranked words from the Naive Bayes probability list, because generating every candidate would make human evaluation prohibitive: "the number of Cloze questions generated from each key sentence is limited by choosing only the first three words from the Word_prd list." This keeps expert evaluation of usefulness tractable while retaining the highest-probability blanks.
requirements: A sorted Word_prd list of words with computed blank-substitution probabilities
constraints: The article presents this cap as an evaluation-burden trade-off; it does not report testing whether three blanks per sentence is optimal

target_learning_goals: practical scale-up of automatically generated Cloze items for drills and practice
examples: For sample sentence S1, only 'binding', 'swapped', and 'addresses' — the first three entries of the sorted Word_prd — were replaced by blanks

article_title: Examining AI Use in Educational Contexts: A Scoping Meta-Review and Bibliometric Analysis
citation: Yao Fu, Zhenjie Weng, Jiaxi Wang. (2024). Examining AI Use in Educational Contexts: A Scoping Meta-Review and Bibliometric Analysis. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00442-w
title: Thematic map of AIED organized around AI's impact on learning, teaching, and administration
description: The article's thematic analysis of the 126 systematic reviews generated "three major themes and nine subthemes related to AI's impact on learning, teaching, and administration", presented as a thematic map (Fig. 10) capturing relationships between themes and subthemes. The learning theme covers domains of learning, adaptive and personalized learning, and AI-based assessments; the teaching theme covers instructional pedagogies and instructor role recalibration, curriculum design, and teacher professional development; the administration theme covers student performance analysis and support, administrative efficiency, and research priorities. The map serves as the organizing framework for the meta-review's synthesis of the AIED field.
requirements: Built from systematic reviews of AI use in educational contexts, coded inductively via thematic analysis with a codebook and inter-rater agreement of 91.6%
constraints: The authors note selected reviews on AIED emphasize more on the strengths of AI use in education, with limited reviews mentioning negative or neutral impact
target_learners: learners across PreK-12 and higher education
target_learning_goals: understanding the state of AI integration across learning, teaching, and administration in education

article_title: Not Fade Away?
citation: Devedzic, V. (2016). Not Fade Away? Commentary to paper Education and The Semantic Web (IJAIED Vol.14, 2004). International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26, 378–386. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0051-2
title: Hype-cycle model of enthusiasm for Semantic Web in education
description: The article organizes its retrospective with a diagram that is "a variant of the Gartner's Hype Cycle", plotting how enthusiasm for Semantic Web in education changed over time from a technology trigger through a peak of inflated expectations, a trough of disillusionment (which the author locates around 2011), a slope of enlightenment, and a plateau of productivity. The author uses the diagram's phases to structure the commentary's narrative sections and to hold not only for Semantic Web but for other technologies in education.
requirements: A timeline of community enthusiasm and adoption for a technology to be mapped onto the cycle's phases
constraints: The author presents it as a variant of Gartner's Hype Cycle, an interpretive diagram rather than a tested model
target_learners: researchers and developers of Web-based education technology
target_learning_goals: understanding the trajectory of educational technology research programs
examples: The commentary's sections (Wishing Well, Expecting to Fly, Waiting for Godot, Down to the Crossroads) each correspond to a phase of the Fig. 1 diagram

title: New-generation Personal Learning Environments integrating Web 2.0 and Semantic Web practices
description: The article describes a new generation of PLEs that merge Web 2.0 practices with Semantic Web ones (the Social Semantic Web). Traditionally a PLE is "a set of lightweight services and tools controlled by individual learners" not integrated into a centralized system; the new generation emphasizes learners' social interaction and collaborative exchange, creating new meaning through annotation, linking and aggregation with existing resources, informal learning, use of existing vocabularies and services such as Linked Open Data and DBpedia Spotlight for annotation, and openness, contextualized learning, and ubiquitous data access.

target_learners: individual learners in informal and formal Web-based learning

title: Wrap Semantic Web infrastructure into valued learning products rather than selling it as infrastructure
description: The article's central design recommendation: "Linked Data can only be the infrastructure, and infrastructure never sells as such." The way to sell Semantic Web in education is to follow the Google Knowledge Graph and Facebook Open Graph Protocol approach — enrich another valued idea, technology, or category of learning systems and resources (PLEs, OERs, MOOCs, learning analytics) with ontologies, semantic search and Web of data, so the technologies work in the background.
requirements: A valued learning system, product or resource category to enrich with Semantic technologies
constraints: The commentary warns Linked Data still poses practical challenges in education: data quality/correctness/completeness, community agreement on vocabularies, source stability, and annotation difficulty
target_learners: developers and researchers building educational systems
target_learning_goals: adoption and practical impact of Semantic technologies in education

title: GIFT: a generalized framework for building intelligent tutoring systems with authoring, instructional management, and evaluation functions
description: GIFT is a research prototype ITS framework sponsored by the US Army Research Laboratory, described as a 'generalized framework for building ITSs' in the shell-tutor tradition. It ties together models of learners, instruction, and knowledge/skill domains through three functions: authoring, instructional management, and evaluation. Its stated design goals are to lower authoring skills/time, deliver adaptive instruction tailored to individual learners or teams, and provide tools to evaluate ITS effectiveness. The framework is grounded in learning, tutoring, and motivational theory and is released as free software.
requirements: Software, documentation, and technical papers are accessed via www.GIFTtutoring.org; the framework supports integration of external environments through a standardized gateway
constraints: Described as a research prototype rather than a production system; its design goals are stated as aspirations being realized progressively
target_learners: Individual learners and teams of learners in military and civilian training domains
target_learning_goals: Adaptive instruction across cognitive, affective, psychomotor, and social domains
examples: GIFT authoring tools interface with games (e.g., Virtual BattleSpace, Virtual Medic), simulations, applications, and physiological/behavioral sensors via a standard gateway specification

title: GIFT authoring tools with standard gateway for external environments and drag-and-drop course objects
description: GIFT's authoring function provides policies, tools, and methods enabling authors (instructional designers, developers, instructors, course managers, and subject matter experts) to create ITSs without programming knowledge, curate content across cognitive, affective, psychomotor, and social domains, and sequence it by hierarchical or dependency relationships. A 'standard gateway specification for interacting with all types of external environments' lets course objects interface with games, simulations, applications, and sensors, and course objects 'require no programming and may be added to a GIFT-based tutor through a simple drag and drop.' GIFT is also LTI compliant for MOOC delivery platforms.

constraints: Adding new external environments beyond existing interfaces requires minor programming to define enumerations

target_learning_goals: Lowering the skills and time required to author ITSs in a variety of task domains
examples: Course objects interface with Virtual BattleSpace, Virtual Medic, an excavator simulator, Microsoft PowerPoint, Zephyr Bioharness, Microsoft Kinect, and Emotiv Epoc EEG

title: GIFT evaluation testbed methodology for experimentally assessing ITS technologies
description: GIFT's evaluation function serves as a testbed, derived from Hanks et al. (1993), supporting manipulation of the learner model, instructional strategies, and domain-specific knowledge within GIFT. It enables researchers to experimentally assess ITS components, tools, and methods and their effect on engagement, knowledge or skill acquisition, retention, reasoning, and transfer of skills. The methodology supports observation and classification of agent behaviors in an exploratory phase using educational data mining, stricter hypothesis-testing comparisons in a confirmatory phase, and replication of conditions and measurement to generalize results.

constraints: Generalization of results requires replication of conditions and associated measurement to be possible
target_learners: ITS researchers evaluating adaptive instructional methods and technologies
target_learning_goals: Evaluating effects of instructional tools, models, and methods on engagement, learning, performance, retention, reasoning, and transfer
examples: Figure 1 illustrates the analysis testbed methodology implemented in GIFT to support experimentation

title: Four-way typology of group-oriented tutoring: team taskwork, teamwork, collaborative learning, and collaborative problem solving
description: The article distinguishes four group-oriented tutoring capabilities that GIFT is being extended to support through intelligent, computer-guided instruction. Team taskwork tutoring develops proficiency in tasks requiring more than one member; teamwork tutoring enhances coordination, cooperation, and communication toward a shared goal; collaborative learning is defined as 'a situation in which two or more people learn or attempt to learn something together'; and collaborative problem solving involves agents pooling knowledge, skills, and efforts to reach a solution. The typology draws on Salas (2015), Dillenbourg (1999), and the PISA 2015 collaborative problem solving framework.
requirements: Validation of team models requires experimentation via the GIFT testbed across a variety of domains to generalize results
constraints: Team taskwork is domain-dependent, with learner models, team models, measures, and interventions potentially unique to each domain; teamwork tutoring is distinguished as targeting team processes rather than specific domains
target_learners: Teams and collaborative groups in military and civilian training
target_learning_goals: Team taskwork proficiency, teamwork processes (communication, coaching, conflict management, cooperation), collaborative learning, and collaborative problem solving
examples: Gilbert et al. (2017) extended the GIFT data structure to represent team taskwork domain knowledge in a simple surveillance mission involving two team members

title: Validate literature-derived tutoring relationships experimentally across domains before generalizing them
description: The article argues that although meta-analyses can identify the significance and impact of tutoring mechanisms, context and conditions differ for each reported effect size, so 'it is still necessary to validate these relationships across a variety of domains in order to generalize the results.' It proposes the GIFT testbed as the vehicle for such validation, including validation of collaborative learning, collaborative problem solving, and team tutoring functions in both AIED and CSCL tutors. This principle applies to any instructional relationship imported from prior literature into a new tutoring system.

title: AWA: a web application providing rhetorical-move highlighting as formative feedback on draft legal writing
description: AWA is a web application developed at UTS that accepts pasted plain text, invokes NLP services on the Open Xerox server, and renders output in multiple forms including highlighting of rhetorically salient sentences, move-frequency statistics, a wordcloud, and key concepts, places and people. It adopts "the metaphor of receiving feedback from a colleague who has used different coloured highlighters". Version 1 was implemented in PHP with version 2 under development in Ruby-on-Rails.

constraints: The system is presently available only for internal use
Designed as a prototype; students are told to be critical of its output

critical analysis
self-assessment of writing quality

title: Rhetorical move typology of salient sentences for analytical writing analytics
description: The XIP rhetorical parser detects sentences conveying rhetorical moves in analytical texts, building on Swales' concept of rhetorical moves as communicative functions in scholarly argumentation. AWA labels salient sentence types: Summarizing issues (S), Background knowledge (B), Contrasting ideas (C), Emphasizing important ideas (E), Novel ideas (N), Surprising facts (S), open Questions (Q), and research Trends (T). Detection relies on "syntactically related words and expressions that convey constituent concepts", e.g. a pair conveying 'contrast' plus 'idea/mental operation' signals a Contrasting idea sentence.
requirements: Dedicated lexicons listing words and expressions associated with constituent concepts
Pattern-matching rules selecting sentences with syntactic dependencies instantiating concept pairs
constraints: The typology is designed to be modified if a new domain establishes the need for additional rhetorical moves
The parser does not yet analyse or provide feedback above the sentence-level

target_learning_goals: recognising rhetorical structure in academic argumentation
self-assessment of analytical writing
examples: Sentences containing 'challenge...identify', 'highlights...need', and 'demonstrating...failure' are all labelled 'C' because bold words match the contrast + idea/mental operation pattern

title: Confusion-matrix annotation by a domain expert as a rapid parser-refinement methodology
description: A practical methodology for refining analytics tools with time-poor domain experts: the lecturer annotates AWA output pasted into Word using signal detection theory codes (True/False Positives/Negatives) in a 2×2 confusion matrix, with margin comments; the linguist responds in the shared document. The article describes this as "a rapid version of the more systematic coding that a qualitative data analyst would normally perform on a large corpus". The structured exchange builds a corpus from which precision, recall and F1 could in principle be calculated.

A familiar tool (Word) and simple 2×2 representation requiring no training
constraints: The corpus from this exercise is not yet large enough to calculate precision, recall and F1 reliably

article_title: Disparities in Students’ Propensity to Consent to Learning Analytics
citation: Warren Li, Kaiwen Sun, Florian Schaub, Christopher Brooks. (2022). Disparities in Students' Propensity to Consent to Learning Analytics. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 32:564–608. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00254-2
title: Providing students agency over learning analytics consent is necessary but insufficient; institutions and instructors must build trust and transparency to prevent biased data collection
description: The article argues that offering students a consent choice alone will not produce representative participation, because subpopulations differ in trust and comfort. Students' "comments corroborate these findings and suggest that agency alone is insufficient; institutional leaders and instructors also play a large role in alleviating the issue of bias." The authors suggest instructors can bolster comfort "by being more transparent regarding who data is used and who has access to it."
requirements: Consent mechanisms must be paired with institutional and instructor actions that build student trust in how data is used and who has access to it.
constraints: The study was conducted at a single institution (University of Michigan) with a predominantly White, higher-socioeconomic-status student body, and used a hypothetical broad consent prompt rather than a live system.
target_learning_goals: Equitable participation in learning analytics data collection and unbiased predictive modeling of student outcomes
examples: The study sent an email-based one-question consent prompt to 4,000 stratified students and found Black students underrepresented (−40%) and White students overrepresented (31%) among respondents despite stratified recruitment.

title: Simulated Student architecture for detecting and avoiding negative situations in collaborative learning
description: The Simulated Student architecture is a model of a simulated peer agent that monitors collaborative learning interactions to detect and avoid situations that decrease the benefits of learning in collaboration. It targets three named situations: off-topic conversations, students with passive behaviour, and problems related to students' learning. The article presents it as a model whose features are instantiated in an agent added to a real collaborative system, and evaluates whether the model is adequate in the avoidance of negative situations.

article_title: ELM-ART – An Interactive and Intelligent Web-Based Electronic Textbook
citation: Gerhard Weber & Peter Brusilovsky. (2016). ELM-ART – An Interactive and Intelligent Web-Based Electronic Textbook. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0066-8
title: The interactive and intelligent textbook paradigm combining intelligent tutoring and adaptive hypermedia
description: ELM-ART introduced a paradigm in which a Web-based textbook looks like a traditional programming textbook with sections of text, program examples and problems, but all content is interactive and the book is intelligent, using AI technologies such as intelligent program analysis, concept-based hyperspace organization, intelligent links between examples and problems, and adaptive navigation support. The article calls it "a winning approach to combine intelligent tutoring and adaptive hypermedia technologies into a consistent design that matches the hypertext nature of the Web". This paradigm served as a blueprint for later systems and authoring tools.

title: ELM-ART adaptive and intelligent Web-based LISP textbook
description: ELM-ART is a Web-based interactive and intelligent electronic textbook for introductory LISP programming, built on the CL-HTTP LISP web server. It offers adaptive navigation support and curriculum sequencing using a traffic light metaphor, interactive questions evaluated by the server, example-based problem solving with ELM cognitive diagnosis and detailed feedback, an inspectable and modifiable open learner model, learner-set preferences, an interactive LISP interpreter, and communication tools (discussion list, chat, tutor contact). Server-side interaction logging supported experiments with navigation support and sequencing. The system remained in use for more than 15 years.

citation: Goldberg, B., Amburn, C., Ragusa, C., & Chen, D. (2018). Modeling Expert Behavior in Support of an Adaptive Psychomotor Training Environment: a Marksmanship Use Case. Int J Artif Intell Educ 28:194–224. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0155-y
title: GIFT-based methodology for building generalized expert models of psychomotor skill for adaptive tutoring
description: The article presents a methodology for extending intelligent tutoring systems into psychomotor domains, using GIFT (Generalized Intelligent Framework for Tutoring) to sync sensor data from a marksmanship simulator and a wearable breathing sensor. It holds that a psychomotor ITS requires, at a minimum, "data types at a granular enough level to inform appropriate assessments", "established models of expert performance to inform performance state determinations", and "a pedagogical model that guides practice and accelerates skill acquisition through formative feedback and adaptive sequencing". Expert models are built bottom-up from sensor data to complement top-down doctrinal task descriptions, and serve as AI assessment criteria driving a self-regulated training environment.

Expert performance data from top performers to build models
A pedagogical model for formative feedback and adaptive sequencing
constraints: Models in this work cover only trigger squeeze, breath control, and body stability; aiming assessment is deferred to future work
Validation of the approach in psychomotor domains requires further work to confirm diagnostic sensitivity
target_learning_goals: Psychomotor skill acquisition in rifle marksmanship fundamentals
examples: Eight U.S. Army Marksmanship Unit Service Rifle Team members fired five-shot groups in four stance/gear conditions while GIFT logged time-synced simulator and breathing sensor data

article_title: Modeling Expert Behavior in Support of an Adaptive Psychomotor Training Environment: a Marksmanship Use Case
citation: Goldberg, B., Amburn, C., Ragusa, C., & Chen, D. (2018). Modeling Expert Behavior in Support of an Adaptive Psychomotor Training Environment: a Marksmanship Use Case. Int J Artif Intell Educ 28:194–224. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0155-y
title: Instrumented FATS M100 marksmanship simulator with BioHarness breathing sensor and GIFT data logging
description: The data-collection apparatus combines Meggitt's FATS M100 Advanced Reality Simulator—a simulated M4 carbine with embedded sensors—with a Zephyr BioHarness BT wireless breathing strap, all logged through GIFT on a synced timestamp. The weapon was "designed with embedded sensors, including: point of aim through an infrared laser mounted in the barrel at a 6 Hz sampling rate, a trigger sensor that measures displacement during the execution of a shot, butt-stock pressure, and the weapon's cant angle". A custom GIFT Gateway plug-in received simulator data over TCP, and a GIFT plug-in received BioHarness data wirelessly via Bluetooth at approximately 18 Hz.
requirements: Time-synced logging across sensor channels via GIFT for post-hoc merging
Mechanical and digital zeroing of the weapon before data collection
constraints: Weapon cant and butt-stock pressure were not analyzed in this work
Recoil was approximately 70% of a real weapon's intensity
Automatic dispersion and wind effects were disabled
target_learners: Soldiers training on rifle marksmanship in simulators
target_learning_goals: Behavioral measurement of marksmanship functional elements (stability, trigger control, breath control)
examples: Eight experts fired five-shot groups on a 25 m zeroing target in Camo-Prone, Camo-Kneeling, Gear-Prone, and Gear-Kneeling conditions while all sensor streams were logged on a single synced timestamp

citation: Jingwan Tang, Xiaofei Zhou, Xiaoyu Wan, Michael Daley, Zhen Bai. (2023). ML4STEM Professional Development Program: Enriching K-12 STEM Teaching with Machine Learning. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00292-4
title: ML4STEM: a two-session professional development framework for integrating machine learning into K-12 STEM teaching
description: ML4STEM is a professional development framework that prepares K-12 STEM teachers to use machine learning as a scientific discovery tool. It is "composed of two sessions: Teachers-as-Learners (TaL) and Teachers-as-Designers (TaD)", grounded in the TPACK framework with focus on TK, TCK, TPK, and TPCK, and operationalizes five principles: "learning by design, hands-on experience with technology, modeling of technology use, collaborative participation, and reflection". TaL builds initial technical and pedagogical understanding through an example activity, while TaD develops integrative TPCK through collaborative lesson-plan design.
requirements: An accessible ML learning platform suited to learners with limited math and computing skills, exemplified by SmileyDiscovery
constraints: The framework targets basic and accessible ML technologies (k-means clustering) before more in-depth ML concepts and methods

Pedagogical knowledge for ML-supported inquiry-based learning
Positive attitudes toward applying ML in class teaching
examples: Implemented in two 75-minute online classes across two consecutive weeks with 18 K-12 in-service STEM teachers in a teacher education course

It "utilizes visual reasoning of face-based data visualization, which maps multidimensional data features to facial features", and supports k-means clustering through three ML components: multidimensional data exploration, similarity computation, and pattern recognition (manual and automatic clustering with centroid generation).

Evidence-based scientific inquiry in STEM topics

description: ML4STEM adopts five pedagogical principles drawn from the technology-integration PD literature. article_title: Intelligent Textbooks
citation: Sergey Sosnovsky, Peter Brusilovsky, Andrew Lan. (2025). Intelligent Textbooks. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00451-9
title: Five-generation taxonomy of intelligent textbook research: engineered, integrated, extracted, datamined, and generated intelligence
description: The article organizes the history of intelligent textbook research into five generations defined by their source of intelligence. Generation 1 relied on human domain experts to engineer domain models for closed-corpus adaptive systems; Generation 2 used open architectures and Semantic Web ontologies to integrate external resources; Generation 3 applied ML and NLP to extract knowledge from textbook content; Generation 4 data-mined student interaction logs; and Generation 5 incorporates large language models. The article states that "the first and second generations were driven by classical AI approaches for symbolic knowledge representation and logic-based knowledge inference, the third generation employed Machine Learning (ML) and Natural Language Processing (NLP) methods focusing on knowledge extraction."
requirements: Digital textbook content whose structure and text can be processed by the generation's chosen AI methods
constraints: First-generation systems were closed-corpus environments with limited collections of instructional texts
Second-generation closed-box systems were impossible to extend, modify, and scale once designed
target_learners: students reading digital textbooks across subject domains
target_learning_goals: improved access to, interaction with, and mastery of textbook content
examples: Figures 1–5 illustrate each generation: engineered domain models, ontology-based integration, content analysis pipelines, interaction-data mining, and generative AI interfaces
key_sources: Sergey Sosnovsky, Peter Brusilovsky, Andrew Lan. (2025). Intelligent Textbooks. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00451-9

article_title: Intelligent Textbooks
citation: Sergey Sosnovsky, Peter Brusilovsky, Andrew Lan. (2025). Intelligent Textbooks. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00451-9
title: Design intelligent textbook technology around an effective instructional approach, not technology-driven innovation alone
description: The article argues that pedagogical research on intelligent textbooks is underrepresented yet essential: technology must enable an effective instructional approach to yield a useful educational tool. It notes that although the technology side progresses rapidly, "empirically proven recipes for effective use of these technologies are still in short supply," and warns that "excessive focus on technology-driven innovation without considering whether or not a developed technology can enable an effective instructional approach is unlikely to produce a useful educational tool." Designers should therefore ground textbook features in established didactic approaches.
requirements: Evaluation of whether the developed technology enables an effective instructional approach
constraints: Pedagogy-focused work has not been among the most popular directions of reported research
target_learners: students using intelligent textbooks in any subject domain
target_learning_goals: effective use of intelligent textbook technologies for learning
examples: Workshop papers explored organizing interaction with digital textbooks according to programmed instruction, orchestrating lessons around textbooks, and interacting with causal concept maps to understand textbook material
key_sources: Sergey Sosnovsky, Peter Brusilovsky, Andrew Lan. (2025). Intelligent Textbooks. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00451-9

article_title: Intelligent Textbooks
citation: Sergey Sosnovsky, Peter Brusilovsky, Andrew Lan. (2025). Intelligent Textbooks. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00451-9
title: Mutually beneficial cycle between intelligent textbook tool development and learner-data extraction
description: The article proposes that new learner-support tools and data extraction reinforce each other: new tools open new modes of learner-textbook interaction, which generate new types of data that in turn power further tool development. The authors observe that "new tools open up new ways of learner-textbook interaction, which generates new types of data that can, in turn, power the development of new tools." They note this cycle existed before in intelligent educational systems but has accelerated and become more evident with new AI technologies, and that chatbots need calibration based on real teacher-learner interaction data.
requirements: Large-scale data extracted from textbooks and learner interactions to power new tools
constraints: LLM context length is limited and not enough to cover long documents
target_learning_goals: personalized learner experiences and better understanding of learner behavior
examples: Richer learning interfaces increased the volume of collected learner data, which enabled new personalization approaches
key_sources: Sergey Sosnovsky, Peter Brusilovsky, Andrew Lan. (2025). Intelligent Textbooks. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00451-9

article_title: Intelligent Textbooks
citation: Sergey Sosnovsky, Peter Brusilovsky, Andrew Lan. (2025). Intelligent Textbooks. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00451-9
title: Smart content: interactive assessable activities embedded in intelligent textbooks
description: Smart content items are interactive activities embedded in online textbooks that engage students in learning by doing rather than just reading, typically exercises with automatic assessment that let students check understanding and receive feedback. The article emphasizes their data value: "'smart content' activities produce a much richer volume of learning data that is crucial for both student modeling and knowledge extraction." Key research issues are infrastructure (connecting an interactive item while maintaining authentication and data collection) and content matching (assigning an item to its proper place in the textbook).
requirements: Infrastructure connecting interactive items to textbooks while maintaining authentication and data collection
Content matching to assign each smart content item to its proper place within the textbook
constraints: Only a fraction of smart content activities could be intelligent by themselves, i.e., ITS problems with intelligent scaffolding
target_learners: students in computer science textbooks, where smart content is increasingly popular
target_learning_goals: learning by doing, checking understanding, and receiving performance feedback
examples: Workshop papers on smart content focused especially on computer science textbooks, grouped with intelligent interfaces as the first large research theme of textbook enrichment

article_title: Teaching a Conversational Agent using Natural Language: Effect on Learning and Engagement
citation: Rachel Love, Edith Law, Philip R. Cohen, Dana Kulić. (2025). Teaching a Conversational Agent using Natural Language: Effect on Learning and Engagement. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00461-1
title: Curiosity Notebook with extended natural language teaching modality and mixed-initiative interaction
description: The Curiosity Notebook is "a highly conﬁgurable, learning-by-teaching web application, which supports a natural language teaching dialog on a range of classiﬁcation tasks". This work extends it with a Snips NLU model parsing free-form teaching inputs into intents and slot values mapped to 30 rock features, and adds a mixed-initiative model where the agent initiates 25% of teaching actions and selects the focus rock 50% of the time. Users teach via Describe, Explain, and Compare buttons, check the agent's notebook, quiz it, and correct errors.
requirements: A domain-specific NLU model mapping intents and slot values to known feature IDs in the platform database
constraints: The language model was developed by hand using source material and pilot utterances, and remained fixed for all participants
target_learners: adult learners in a learning-by-teaching interaction
target_learning_goals: domain knowledge acquisition through teaching a classification task (rock classification)
examples: Participants taught two virtual agents (Alpha via sentence-selection, Gamma via natural language) about rock classification with six rocks per condition and 30 features

title: Protégé Effect framing for teachable agents
description: The Protégé Effect is "a pedagogical phenomenon in which the student is likely to invest more in learning the material when it is for the beneﬁt of the agent". When a teachable agent occupies the novice role, students synthesise information better and adapt teaching based on the tutee's performance, which may lead to positive cognitive outcomes. Teachable agents additionally offer unlimited attention and tolerate incorrect teaching without harm to their own outcomes.
requirements: An agent framed as a novice learner for the student to teach
target_learners: students in classroom or remote settings
target_learning_goals: increased engagement and investment in learning material through teaching
examples: The Curiosity Notebook study framed teaching as helping agents Alpha and Gamma prepare for a test to establish motivation to teach well

article_title: Automated Gaze-Based Identification of Students’ Strategies in Histogram Tasks through an Interpretable Mathematical Model and a Machine Learning Algorithm
citation: Boels, L., Garcia Moreno-Esteva, E., Bakker, A., & Drijvers, P. (2024). Automated Gaze-Based Identification of Students' Strategies in Histogram Tasks through an Interpretable Mathematical Model and a Machine Learning Algorithm. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 34, 931-973. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00368-9
title: Attentional anchors as perceptual forms of gaze patterns that facilitate task-specific strategies
description: The article draws on enactivism and embodied cognition to interpret students' gaze patterns as attentional anchors (AAs). An AA is "a real or imagined object, area, or other behavior of the perceptual manifold that emerges to facilitate motor-action coordination." In this study, stable horizontal or vertical scanpaths on the graph area are interpreted as AAs that facilitate students' imagined actions for finding the mean from a histogram, regardless of strategy correctness. The AA concept is used both to ground the theoretical interpretation of gaze patterns and to guide the construction of the IMM.
requirements: The AA concept requires that gaze patterns form a stable scanpath with multiple aligned fixations and saccades that students themselves recognize as relevant to their strategy
constraints: The relationship between eye movements and cognitive processes is not straightforward, and not every eye movement is part of a student's strategy
target_learning_goals: Estimating the arithmetic mean from histogram representations
Correct interpretation of histograms versus case-value plots
examples: Student L10 described chopping and flattening bars (compensation) while gaze data showed a stable horizontal scanpath interpreted as an AA for an incorrect case-value plot strategy

Automated Gaze-Based Identification of Students' Strategies in Histogram Tasks through an Interpretable Mathematical Model and a Machine Learning Algorithm. citation: Boels, L., Garcia Moreno-Esteva, E., Bakker, A., & Drijvers, P. (2024). Automated Gaze-Based Identification of Students' Strategies in Histogram Tasks through an Interpretable Mathematical Model and a Machine Learning Algorithm. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 34, 931-973. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00368-9
title: Interpretable mathematical model (IMM) algorithm for classifying gaze strategies from saccade properties
description: The IMM is an algorithm that transforms sequences of saccades on the graph area into classifications of horizontal or vertical scanning. It maps saccades to values based on length (200-pixel cutoff) and slope (0.875 cutoff), removes short saccades, counts runs of consecutive long horizontal or vertical scans, and outputs a binary classification. The authors state "The best model we found relies on the following algorithm, which is based on saccade lengths and angles." Cut-off values were found empirically by testing values close to a slope of 1.
requirements: Raw gaze data (x-y coordinates of fixations and saccades) on the graph area AOI
Prior qualitative identification of attentional anchors to set the starting point for slope cutoffs
constraints: The 200-pixel saccade length cutoff was fixed and not scaled to the width and height of the graph area
The model was constructed as one general model for all five histogram items based on similar attentional anchors across items
target_learning_goals: Automated identification of students' task-specific strategies for estimating the mean from histograms
examples: The algorithm maps saccades to -1, 0, or 1 values, splits into subsequences, removes duplicates and short saccades, and sums to determine predominantly horizontal or vertical scanning

International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 34, 931-973. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00368-9
title: Prefer interpretable models over black-box machine learning when strategy identification must be transparent to educational researchers
description: The article argues that when automated classification must be understood by educational researchers, an interpretable model built directly from the data is preferable to a black-box MLA. The authors note that "the disadvantage of many MLAs is that they are effectively like black boxes that do not reveal how they identify the results from the data," whereas an interpretable model "captures the most important characteristics of the strategy, in a way that can be understood by human beings and that is transparent." They used the MLA only as a baseline for the IMM.
requirements: Prior qualitative or theoretical insight into the task-specific strategies to guide model construction
Sufficient data quality for the model to classify strategies from raw gaze data
constraints: A white-box model built a priori risks relevant information in the eye-movement data being overlooked because it is based on human assumptions, not on data
target_learning_goals: Automated identification of students' task-specific strategies for estimating the mean from histograms
examples: The authors compared a random forest MLA baseline with their interpretable mathematical model and reported the IMM was transparent, performed well, and was theoretically meaningful

article_title: Web Delivery of Adaptive and Interactive Language Tutoring: Revisited
citation: Trude Heift. (2016). Web Delivery of Adaptive and Interactive Language Tutoring: Revisited. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:489–503. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0061-0
title: E-Tutor: a web-delivered ILTS for German with modular NLP answer processing, adaptive learner modeling, and curriculum-aligned activities
description: E-Tutor (renamed from German Tutor in 2003, expanded 2009) is an Intelligent Language Tutoring System for learners of German as a foreign language, used in regular university classroom instruction. It uses a modular answer-processing architecture in which "if any error checking module detects an error, further processing is blocked", so only one error at a time is displayed. It implements "10 different activity types for each of the 15 chapters", covering vocabulary, grammar, listening/reading comprehension, culture, pronunciation and writing, and follows the sequence of the textbook Deutsch: Na klar!
requirements: Must process and analyze learner input with a linguistically sophisticated system equipped with a grammar and parser that detects grammatical errors
Must keep a record of student work and performance shareable with instructors and follow the course book's grammatical and vocabulary sequence
constraints: The initial system was limited to content commonly taught in the first semester of university language instruction
Client-end Java applets caused compatibility issues, leading to a rewrite in plain-vanilla HTML 4.0 with frames and Javascript
target_learners: University learners of German as a foreign language at beginner and intermediate proficiency levels
target_learning_goals: German grammar (e.g., subject-verb agreement, article usage, relative clauses, passive constructions)
vocabulary, pronunciation, listening and reading comprehension, cultural knowledge, and writing skills
examples: The 2003 upgrade rewrote the Prolog grammar in Java with JSP pages and servlets, yielding a significant (10:1) improvement in system responsiveness and load handling
A context-sensitive help function links grammatical errors to runtime-constructed inflectional paradigms geared at the specific learner mistake

article_title: Web Delivery of Adaptive and Interactive Language Tutoring: Revisited
citation: Trude Heift. (2016). Web Delivery of Adaptive and Interactive Language Tutoring: Revisited. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:489–503. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0061-0
title: E-Tutor's dynamic learner model: skill-specific scores and phrase descriptors modulate feedback and remediation
description: E-Tutor's learner model provides a dynamic assessment of each learner by considering past and current performance and behavior. The grammar and parser generate phrase descriptors, frame structures modeling grammatical phenomena (e.g., subject-verb agreement, noun gender) with values correct, error, or absent, which "correspond to structures in the learner model and are the interface medium between the learner model and the grammar". For each grammar constraint the model keeps a per-student score that increases or decreases with evidence of successful or unsuccessful use; feedback wording and amount depend on the learner's rank (novice vs. expert) per skill, and remedial exercises target individual weaknesses.
requirements: A fully specified lexicon and a grammar and parser that generate phrase descriptors for each grammatical constraint
Separation of feedback generation from linguistic analysis and learning activity so feedback messages can be adjusted per exercise
constraints: Scores for each grammar skill are tracked independently, so a student may be expert at one skill and novice at another
target_learners: University learners of German as a foreign language
target_learning_goals: Individualized error-contingent feedback and remediation across German grammar skills
examples: The system might change the order in which errors are displayed depending on the learner's past performance or the focus of the learning activity
Session summaries group mistakes into categories such as Article Inflection and Verb Inflection set by a parameter file

citation: Trude Heift. (2016). Web Delivery of Adaptive and Interactive Language Tutoring: Revisited. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:489–503. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0061-0
title: E-Tutor learner corpus with comparative error profiles and exercise-specific preemptive hints
description: In 2009 the authors created a learner corpus of "several million responses submitted by roughly 5000 previous learners who had completed the activity types of E-Tutor between 2003 and 2008". An interface lets learners examine interlanguage and task-specific phenomena and compare their error patterns to thousands of previous users of the same exercises. Statistical analysis of the corpus produced ranked error lists per exercise, activity type and chapter, from which the system generates exercise-specific preemptive hints displayed when students start an exercise; the number of hints can be adjusted based on prior learner performance.
requirements: The linguistic analysis of user input and the system log constructed from all user inputs, accumulated over years of classroom use
constraints: The hint ranking is based on prior student performance during 2003–2008 only
target_learners: University learners of German as a foreign language using E-Tutor in classroom instruction
target_learning_goals: Exploratory data-driven learning about interlanguage phenomena and one's own error patterns in German
examples: Fig. 5 shows comparative performance reports where a student performed much better on word order than the 4378 previous users while making more grammar and less spelling mistakes
Research (e.g., Ellis et al. 2001) is cited that preemptive feedback may lead to more successful task completion and reduce frustration

title: Classroom-integrated CALL systems must align with the course curriculum and keep shareable records of student work
description: The article argues that an ILTS intended for regular classroom instruction differs from self-study software: "Any application used in a real language learning classroom, however, needs to keep a record of the student’s work and performance that can be shared with instructors and its lexical and grammatical content must follow the same or, at least, a similar sequence as the one reflected by the remaining class materials". E-Tutor follows the grammatical and vocabulary sequence of Deutsch: Na klar! so it can be used alongside face-to-face instruction.

target_learning_goals: Foreign language learning aligned with a graded university curriculum
examples: E-Tutor follows the grammatical and vocabulary sequence of Deutsch: Na klar! (Vansant et al. 2011), lending itself to use with regular face-to-face instruction

annotated training data with ground-truth performance metrics from the ResusciAnne manikin SimPad

citation: Di Mitri, D., Schneider, J., & Drachsler, H. (2022). KeepMeInTheLoop: Real-Time Feedback with Multimodal Data. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education (2022) 32:1093–1118. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00281-z
title: Multimodal Pipeline: a five-step framework for collection, storing, annotation, processing and exploitation of multimodal data
description: The Multimodal Pipeline is a framework proposed by Di Mitri et al. for handling data from multiple modalities in learning systems. The CPR Tutor architecture implements its five steps — collection, storing, annotation, processing and exploitation — organised into a Presentation Layer interfacing with the user, an Application Layer implementing the tutor logic, and a Data Layer. The article presents it as the basis for closing the feedback loop with real-time multimodal feedback.
requirements: sensor applications assigning Recording Objects with timestamps for synchronised data collection
annotation tooling (Visual Inspection Tool) to label time intervals
constraints: The article states this was the first complete implementation of the pipeline, in the CPR Tutor context
target_learning_goals: real-time feedback for psychomotor skill acquisition
examples: The CPR Tutor realised the five steps with Kinect and Myo recording, MLT-JSON session storage, VIT annotation, SharpFlow processing, and real-time audio feedback

title: SharpFlow: open-source Python tool for offline training and real-time classification of chest compressions
description: SharpFlow is a Python script developed by the authors for data processing in the CPR Tutor, with code available on GitHub. It is "used for offline training and validation of the mistake detection classifiers and the real-time classification of the single CCs", loading MLT-JSON sessions into Pandas data frames, resampling and scaling sensor data, and running a TCP server that feeds data chunks to the stacked LSTM models.
requirements: min-max scaler and LSTM models loaded from memory
TCP connection with the CPR Tutor client
constraints: Classification relies on batch data chunks pushed at the end of each chest compression rather than continuous streaming
target_learning_goals: detecting CPR training mistakes from multimodal sensor data
examples: The authors released SharpFlow on GitHub (https://github.com/dimstudio/SharpFlow) and used it to classify chest compressions in about 70 milliseconds

title: Limit real-time feedback to one message at a time with sufficient intervals to avoid overloading the learner
description: In real-time multimodal feedback systems, feedback should be fired one message at a time with sufficient lags between messages to prevent cognitive overload. The CPR Tutor assessed every chest compression but set its feedback frequency to 10 seconds, choosing audio as the least occupied sensory channel during CPR. This design was inspired by the Presentation Trainer, where the authors found it "more beneficial and less confusing for the user to fire one feedback message at a time".
requirements: a prioritisation mechanism deciding which single feedback message to fire when multiple mistakes are detected
constraints: The 10-second interval was chosen based on prior evidence and manual tuning, not optimised empirically in this study
target_learners: learners practising psychomotor skills with real-time feedback
target_learning_goals: correcting performance mistakes without cognitive overload
examples: The CPR Tutor fired audio feedback at most once every 10 seconds, sequencing five rule-based thresholds by mistake class

article_title: A Multi-Temporal Context-aware System for Competences Management
citation: João H. Rosa, Jorge L. V. Barbosa, Marcos Kich, Lucas Brito. (2015). A Multi-Temporal Context-aware System for Competences Management. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25:455–492. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0047-y
title: Multi-temporal context awareness: joint use of workers' present and past contexts to assist competence development
description: The article names and defines multi-temporal context awareness as an organizing concept for competence-management systems. It observes that context-aware applications 'usually use data only from the users' current situations (i.e. the present) and do not consider the previous contexts observed during a period (i.e. the past)'. The framework holds that combining the present dimension (current location, events, people, resources) with the past dimension (contexts histories or trails) gives applications 'an additional and more complete information source' for decisions, enabling automatic detection of competence advances and personalized services.
requirements: Storage of observed contexts over time (contexts history/trail mechanism) in addition to sensing the current context
constraints: The past dimension is defined as contexts as per Dey et al.'s definition, which includes location data; the article states Trail Management is considered only as this use of the past dimension
target_learners: knowledge workers in organizations developing professional competences
target_learning_goals: development and advancement of professional competences
examples: MultCComp operationalizes the framework: the present dimension suggests nearby events, resources and experienced people; the past dimension records development activities in trails and detects competence improvements automatically
key_sources: João H. Rosa, Jorge L. V. Barbosa, Marcos Kich, Lucas Brito. (2015). A Multi-Temporal Context-aware System for Competences Management. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25:455–492. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0047-y

article_title: A Multi-Temporal Context-aware System for Competences Management
citation: João H. Rosa, Jorge L. V. Barbosa, Marcos Kich, Lucas Brito. (2015). A Multi-Temporal Context-aware System for Competences Management. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25:455–492. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0047-y
title: MultCComp: a multi-temporal context-aware system for competences management
description: MultCComp is a context-aware system that applies proficiency levels to competences and uses present and past context information to help workers develop competences. Its present-dimension architecture has 'seven components': three modules (Profile, Competence, Context), three agents (Personal Assistant, Relationship Agent, Competences Agent) and an Administrative Website. The Competences Agent makes recommendations about people, events and resources triggered by context changes, and the past dimension uses the UbiTrail model to record development activities and automatically detect users' advances in their competences.
requirements: Users authorize their location; workers inform the system about activities they performed to develop their competences; a mapped set of location contexts and an organization-wide competence map
constraints: Design decisions were based on consulting in an ERP vendor in Southern Brazil; the system tolerates loss of wireless connectivity only through a local buffer with limited functionalities
target_learners: workers in organizations undertaking competence management
target_learning_goals: identifying and closing competence gaps; advancing proficiency levels
examples: The prototype was evaluated in two experiments in an evaluation environment: a functionality demonstration with two evaluation scenarios followed by two users, and an acceptance scenario followed by 21 users
key_sources: João H. Rosa, Jorge L. V. Barbosa, Marcos Kich, Lucas Brito. (2015). A Multi-Temporal Context-aware System for Competences Management. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25:455–492. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0047-y

article_title: A Multi-Temporal Context-aware System for Competences Management
citation: João H. Rosa, Jorge L. V. Barbosa, Marcos Kich, Lucas Brito. (2015). A Multi-Temporal Context-aware System for Competences Management. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25:455–492. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0047-y
title: UbiTrail model for generic trails management, chosen over Life Annotation, PELEP and Hong et al.'s mechanism
description: UbiTrail (Silva et al. 2010) is the trail-management model MultCComp adopts for its past dimension. A trail is a sequence of ptrail registers with attributes entity, resources, event, extension and location, based on the UbiTrail ontology; its architecture comprises a UbiTrailServer storing trails and providing basic and specialized services, and a UbiTrailClient running on users' mobile devices. The article compares it with three alternatives: 'Life Annotation ... does not standardize the trails information, which makes it difficult to query them'; PELEP 'does not support generic trails management'; and Hong et al.'s mechanism 'does not support the creation of services to query the trails'.
requirements: Applications must specify the ontology for their domain before using UbiTrail
constraints: UbiTrail assumes external providers of context and location data
target_learners: workers and learners in context-aware environments whose activity histories are managed
target_learning_goals: recording and querying learners'/workers' past activities to support personalized services
examples: MultCComp uses UbiTrail to store ptrail records whenever workers perform competence-development activities, and the Competences Agent queries the trails to infer developed competences
key_sources: João H. Rosa, Jorge L. V. Barbosa, Marcos Kich, Lucas Brito. (2015). A Multi-Temporal Context-aware System for Competences Management. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25:455–492. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0047-y

article_title: A Multi-Temporal Context-aware System for Competences Management
citation: João H. Rosa, Jorge L. V. Barbosa, Marcos Kich, Lucas Brito. (2015). A Multi-Temporal Context-aware System for Competences Management. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25:455–492. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0047-y
title: Four event types in the competence ontology: resource use, event participation, interaction with a person, and accomplishment of an evaluation test
description: MultCComp specifies its competence-domain ontology by instantiating the Event class with the activities workers can perform to advance competences: '(1) Resource Use', '(2) Participation of Event', and '(3) Interaction with Person' with a higher-level-competence user. Because recorded activity alone cannot establish that a competence improved, a fourth instance was added: '(4) Accomplishment of Evaluation Test'. Each activity performed registers a ptrail on the worker's trail; without a passed test the proficiency level is marked as partially developed rather than developed.
requirements: Each of the five proficiency levels may have an evaluation test associated with it; a person in charge applies tests and informs grades via the Administrative Website
constraints: The authors state they 'have no concrete data to affirm that the tests will enable a viable approach' to confirm competence development, and note alternatives such as peer or supervisor review
target_learners: workers developing professional competences in organizations
target_learning_goals: validating attainment of proficiency levels in competences
examples: Interaction with Person is confirmed by asking the interacted person whether they really helped; if they respond no, the information is not registered in the trail
key_sources: João H. Rosa, Jorge L. V. Barbosa, Marcos Kich, Lucas Brito. (2015). A Multi-Temporal Context-aware System for Competences Management. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25:455–492. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0047-y

article_title: A Multi-Temporal Context-aware System for Competences Management
citation: João H. Rosa, Jorge L. V. Barbosa, Marcos Kich, Lucas Brito. (2015). A Multi-Temporal Context-aware System for Competences Management. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25:455–492. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0047-y
title: Trigger recommendations from context changes and always inform users when a contextualized opportunity is detected
description: MultCComp's Competences Agent triggers its recommendation capability only when one of the user's contexts changes, dividing recommendation into capabilities initiated by different perceptions (events update, resources update, locations update, profile update, competences update). The authors 'adopted this strategy because we believe that the contextualized opportunities are very dynamic and must be mapped continuously', since 'the opportunities may arise at anytime and anywhere'. When several recommendations match the same context, all options are shown so users can choose.
requirements: Continuous monitoring of context changes (events, resources, locations, profiles, competences map) feeding the agent's perceptions
constraints: The authors report applying this approach in prior context-aware systems in Commerce, Health and Education that 'received good evaluation of users' acceptance', but the article prints no direct test of this design choice in MultCComp
target_learners: mobile workers in organizations using context-aware systems
target_learning_goals: taking advantage of contextualized learning opportunities to develop competences
examples: A locations-update perception triggers filtering of users in the same location by complementary competences, messaging selected users about the newly arrived person who can assist them

article_title: The Eras and Trends of Automatic Short Answer Grading
citation: Steven Burrows, Iryna Gurevych, Benno Stein. (2015). The Eras and Trends of Automatic Short Answer Grading. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0026-8
title: Five-era historical taxonomy of ASAG systems: four methodology eras plus an evaluation era
description: The review organizes 35 identified ASAG systems into five thematically consistent time periods it calls eras. As the article states, "The five eras are concept mapping, information extraction, corpus-based methods, and machine learning, and evaluation"; the first four are method-based while the fifth is evaluation-based, reflecting a movement toward reproducibility, standardized corpora, and permanent evaluation. Each era is defined, then each system receives its own section with an ID cross-referenced to component tables.
requirements: Systems are assigned to their dominant era when they overlap multiple eras, keeping activities as disjoint as possible
constraints: Era time periods may overlap with others
The historical review covers 35 systems and 2 competitions as identified by the authors
target_learners: students assessed with short answer questions in educational settings
target_learning_goals: automatic assessment of short natural-language responses to objective questions
key_sources: Steven Burrows, Iryna Gurevych, Benno Stein. (2015). The Eras and Trends of Automatic Short Answer Grading. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0026-8

article_title: The Eras and Trends of Automatic Short Answer Grading
citation: Steven Burrows, Iryna Gurevych, Benno Stein. (2015). The Eras and Trends of Automatic Short Answer Grading. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0026-8
title: Three swim-lane taxonomy situating short answer questions among gradable question types
description: The review defines short answer questions within a hierarchical view of question types organized under three swim lanes: depth of learning, question category, and question type. Depth of learning separates recognition from recall questions; question category separates natural language from structured text and speech; question type distinguishes short answers from fill-the-gap and essay questions using the dimensions of length, focus, and openness. The figure is explicitly not exhaustive but shows common examples to differentiate ASAG questions from others.
requirements: Short answer questions must meet five criteria including natural-language responses recalling external knowledge, content-focused assessment, and restricted openness with objective question design
constraints: Graphical questions are omitted because the review's interest extends only to text-modeled recall questions
Reading comprehension questions do not fully comply with the recall lane despite inclusion of key papers
target_learners: students answering short answer, fill-the-gap, or essay questions
target_learning_goals: distinguishing question types suitable for automatic grading
key_sources: Steven Burrows, Iryna Gurevych, Benno Stein. (2015). The Eras and Trends of Automatic Short Answer Grading. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0026-8

article_title: The Eras and Trends of Automatic Short Answer Grading
citation: Steven Burrows, Iryna Gurevych, Benno Stein. (2015). The Eras and Trends of Automatic Short Answer Grading. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0026-8
title: SemEval '13 Task 7 shared-task corpus and grading scheme for ASAG
description: SemEval '13 Task 7, the Joint Student Response Analysis and Eighth Recognizing Textual Entailment Challenge, was the first large-scale and non-commercial ASAG competition. Its corpora draw from a tutorial dialog system for high school physics (Beetle) and primary school science questions from grades 3-6 (SciEntsBank); "Approximately 8,000 student answers are included across all questions." A 5-way categorical grading scheme uses labels "correct", "partially correct incomplete", "contradictory", "irrelevant", and "non domain", with collapsed 3-way and 2-way variants.
requirements: Solutions must handle a degree of domain adaptation, with test data spanning unseen answers, unseen questions in the same domain, and questions in unseen domains
constraints: The review concentrates on the 5-way task, unseen domains, and macro-averaged F1 because accuracy and micro-averaged F1 lack a mechanism for accommodating class imbalance
There is no notion of an overall winner in the competition
target_learners: high school physics students and primary school students in grades 3-6
target_learning_goals: 5-way categorical grading of student responses to objective questions
examples: The review identifies SoftCardinality, UKP-BIU, and ETS as the best performing systems by its stated definition, with Dzikovska '12 as the strongest baseline
key_sources: Steven Burrows, Iryna Gurevych, Benno Stein. (2015). The Eras and Trends of Automatic Short Answer Grading. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0026-8

article_title: The Eras and Trends of Automatic Short Answer Grading
citation: Steven Burrows, Iryna Gurevych, Benno Stein. (2015). The Eras and Trends of Automatic Short Answer Grading. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0026-8
title: ASAP '12 SAS Kaggle competition dataset for short answer scoring
description: The Automated Student Assessment Prize (ASAP) short answer scoring competition was hosted on Kaggle in 2012, covering ten questions of varied high-school-level subject matter from arts to science. "The participants were given 1,800 student answers for training, which were randomly taken from a pool of 3,000." A further 6,000 student answers were used for testing, and agreement between predicted and human-judge-resolved scores was evaluated with quadratic weighted kappa. The review examines the top three systems from a modified ranking: Tandella '12, Zbontar '12, and Conort '12.
requirements: Each student answer is associated with the score to predict and a confidence score
constraints: A few participants kept their code and methodology private, forcing a modified top-5 ranking that excluded the original 1st, 5th, and 6th submissions
target_learners: high school students across arts and science subjects
target_learning_goals: predicting scores for short answers with agreement to human judges
examples: Zbontar '12 used stacking to combine ridge regression, support vector regression, gradient boosting, random forests, and k-nearest-neighbor base learners into a final ridge regression model

article_title: The Negotiation of Meaning in Epistemic Situations
citation: Michael J. Baker. (2015). The Negotiation of Meaning in Epistemic Situations. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0050-3
title: NTD model of negotiation in teaching-learning dialogues
description: The NTD model represents negotiation between tutor and learner as movement from initial to final states in which agents share the goal of reaching agreement on 'negotia', the objects of negotiation. Parties make offers that are successively refined, and the refine strategy was defined in terms of two main elements: "communicative acts of negotiation, and transformation functions". Crucially, communicative acts are proposals with acceptances or rejections, not assertions, so participants express what they are willing to accept rather than their beliefs. The article presents this as the retained core of a research programme later extended to argumentation, affect and CSCL.
requirements: Dialogue participants who make proposals that can be accepted, rejected or refined rather than asserted as beliefs
constraints: The published model detailed only the refine strategy; the argue strategy was deferred to later work, so it addressed knowledge refinement processes in negotiation rather than full negotiation
target_learners: students in tutorial dialogue with a computer tutor
target_learning_goals: reaching shared agreement on task-level knowledge such as problem solutions and their justifications
examples: The KANT prototype engaged students in negotiative dialogue about musical structure analysis and justifications
key_sources: Michael J. Baker. (2015). The Negotiation of Meaning in Epistemic Situations. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0050-3

article_title: The Negotiation of Meaning in Epistemic Situations
citation: Michael J. Baker. (2015). The Negotiation of Meaning in Epistemic Situations. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0050-3
title: Paradigm shift from cognitivist belief-models to dialogue as collective thinking
description: The article argues that the theory underlying the negotiation model was radically changed over 20 years: "from a cognitivist model of thoughts underlying dialogue, to a view of dialogue itself as one manifestation of collective thinking". Methodologically this means "the group rather than individuals is taken as the unit of cognitive analysis", focusing on co-elaboration of the discursive object using the communicative acts and transformation operators of the original model. The shift followed the 1990s situated cognition debate and the move to computer-mediated group communication, and it reframes collaborative learning as the relation between acceptance in dialogue and what students believe.
requirements: Analysis of interaction corpora at the group level rather than attribution of underlying individual beliefs
constraints: The author concluded the original NTD model was not, in all its elements, a basis for analysing significant bodies of interaction corpus data
target_learning_goals: co-elaboration of knowledge in and by dialogue
examples: An attempted beliefs-desires-intentions analysis of a 40-minute physics dialogue transcript was abandoned as empirically unfeasible
key_sources: Michael J. Baker. (2015). The Negotiation of Meaning in Epistemic Situations. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0050-3

article_title: The Negotiation of Meaning in Epistemic Situations
citation: Michael J. Baker. (2015). The Negotiation of Meaning in Epistemic Situations. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0050-3
title: Tension-relaxation analysis of interpersonal relations in collaborative argumentation
description: Extending Bales' division of social interaction into a task zone and a socio-emotional zone, the author and Andriessen developed a formal analysis method aimed at studying "the 'interaction' between deepening of a conflict (extending down into an argument chain) and fluctuations in tension-relaxation". The expectation was that deepening conflicts raise tension up to a threshold supportable by the interpersonal relation. They also elaborated the notion of a collaborative working relation, which develops over time and acts as a buffer mediating the mutual regulation of tensions.
requirements: Analysis of both the depth of argumentative conflict and fluctuating tension levels in the same interaction data
constraints: Early results are described as preliminary; systematic analysis of interpersonal relations and affects in collaborative learning is described as very recent
target_learners: students in collaborative argumentation and problem-solving
target_learning_goals: sustaining productive argumentative collaboration while regulating interpersonal tension
examples: Early results showed a lag in tension lowering after a local conflict, which could raise tension levels for subsequent conflicts
