article_title: Investigating the Effect of Agency on Learning from Worked Examples, Erroneous Examples and Problem Solving
citation: Xingliang Chen & Antonija Mitrovic & Moffat Mathews. (2019). Investigating the Effect of Agency on Learning from Worked Examples, Erroneous Examples and Problem Solving. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education (2019) 29:396–424. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-019-00179-x
title: Cognitive Efficiency-based adaptive strategy for selecting preparatory learning activities in SQL-Tutor
description: The article describes an adaptive strategy that selects each preparatory task (worked example, 1- or 2-error erroneous example, problem, or skip) based on the student's Cognitive Efficiency: "CE is computed as the quotient between the problem-solving score on the most recent problem (P) and the self-reported mental effort score (R), CE = P ÷ R". Performance P is derived from constraint violations per SQL clause, and CE thresholds, combined with prior-knowledge level (LPK/HPK), determine the next preparation task. The strategy extends Kalyuga and Sweller's (2005) cognitive efficiency measure to activity selection in an ITS.
requirements: Per-problem performance scoring based on violated vs relevant constraints, and a self-reported mental effort rating after each task
constraints: Performance is computed from the first submission only, so students could ask for feedback by submitting an empty solution initially; the strategy does not consider how well the student knows each constraint
target_learners: Second-year university database students with low or high prior SQL knowledge
target_learning_goals: SQL query writing: conceptual, procedural, and debugging knowledge
examples: For HPK students CE > 1 led to skipping the preparation task; for LPK students CE below 0.25 led to a worked example
key_sources: Xingliang Chen & Antonija Mitrovic & Moffat Mathews. (2019). Investigating the Effect of Agency on Learning from Worked Examples, Erroneous Examples and Problem Solving. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education (2019) 29:396–424. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-019-00179-x

article_title: Investigating the Effect of Agency on Learning from Worked Examples, Erroneous Examples and Problem Solving
citation: Xingliang Chen & Antonija Mitrovic & Moffat Mathews. (2019). Investigating the Effect of Agency on Learning from Worked Examples, Erroneous Examples and Problem Solving. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education (2019) 29:396–424. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-019-00179-x
title: Select preparatory learning activities adaptively, since adaptive selection matched or beat free student choice for both low- and high-prior-knowledge students
description: The article recommends letting a performance-based adaptive strategy choose preparatory tasks (worked examples, erroneous examples, or problems) before problem solving. Its findings "suggest that the adaptive strategy in the Low-Agency condition was efficient in selecting learning activities for both LPK and HPK students": Low-Agency students improved significantly, HPK students improved only under Low-Agency, and LPK students learned equally well whether the system or they themselves selected activities. This supports pairing tutored problem solving with adaptively chosen worked or erroneous examples rather than unrestricted student choice.
requirements: A measure of recent problem-solving performance with mental-effort ratings (cognitive efficiency) to drive selection, and classification of students by prior knowledge
constraints: The study's small sample (40 completers) and confound with activity-type mix mean conclusions are not solely due to agency, as the authors state
target_learners: University students in introductory database courses, both low and high prior knowledge
target_learning_goals: Database querying (SQL) conceptual, procedural and debugging knowledge
examples: SQL-Tutor presented WE or ErrEx to LPK students and ErrEx, PS, or skip to HPK students based on cognitive efficiency thresholds, before each of ten fixed problems

article_title: Authoring Effective Embedded Tutors: An Overview of the Extensible Problem Specific Tutor (xPST) System
citation: Stephen B. Gilbert, Stephen B. Blessing, Enruo Guo. (2015). Authoring Effective Embedded Tutors: An Overview of the Extensible Problem Specific Tutor (xPST) System. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25:428–454. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0045-0
title: The xPST architecture: a model-tracing-like tutor engine overlaid on third-party software via TutorLink plug-ins and a plain-text instruction file
description: xPST is an authoring system that produces tutors behaving like model-tracing tutors without a formal cognitive model: authors write an xPST Instruction File with Mappings, Sequence, and Feedback sections, and the xPST Tutor Engine checks each learner action and returns hints, just-in-time messages, or error marking. TutorLink plug-ins mediate between the engine and third-party applications, with a Listener Module that "eavesdrops on user 's actions" and a Presentation Module that displays feedback in the host interface. The article presents this as a way to let instructional designers build embedded tutors on existing software.
requirements: For each new third-party interface, a TutorLink plug-in (driver) must be written to mediate between the application and the xPST Engine
constraints: The xPST tutor "cannot generalize to novel problems" because instruction is problem-specific with no cognitive model
target_learners: instructional designers and instructors authoring tutors
students learning software tasks and domain procedures
target_learning_goals: step-by-step task performance on existing software with hints and just-in-time error feedback
examples: Implementations on Paint.NET, the Firefox browser (Web xPST), and the Torque Game Engine Advanced, including the Evacuate 3D scenario
key_sources: Stephen B. Gilbert, Stephen B. Blessing, Enruo Guo. (2015). Authoring Effective Embedded Tutors: An Overview of the Extensible Problem Specific Tutor (xPST) System. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25:428–454. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0045-0

article_title: Authoring Effective Embedded Tutors: An Overview of the Extensible Problem Specific Tutor (xPST) System
citation: Stephen B. Gilbert, Stephen B. Blessing, Enruo Guo. (2015). Authoring Effective Embedded Tutors: An Overview of the Extensible Problem Specific Tutor (xPST) System. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25:428–454. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0045-0
title: Web xPST: a web-based authoring and delivery environment for tutors on third-party websites
description: Web xPST is the refined second-phase Firefox plug-in implementation through which authors "sign into an account and create xPST -based tutors for web-based content". It has an embedded text editor for creating and saving xPST Instruction Files, a side pane for problem instructions, and a toolbar for requesting help. It was used to build the AP Biology NIH NCBI tutor and the xSTAT statistics tutor evaluated with students.
requirements: A TutorLink Firefox plug-in to interact with browser widgets; common web widgets are accommodated and others added by extending the Listener Module and checktypes
target_learners: high-school and college students using web-based tools
target_learning_goals: completing multi-step web-based tasks such as bioinformatics searches and statistics homework
examples: xSTAT statistics tutor built with JotForm forms; AP Biology tutor on NIH NCBI Bioinformatics tools

article_title: Authoring Effective Embedded Tutors: An Overview of the Extensible Problem Specific Tutor (xPST) System
citation: Stephen B. Gilbert, Stephen B. Blessing, Enruo Guo. (2015). Authoring Effective Embedded Tutors: An Overview of the Extensible Problem Specific Tutor (xPST) System. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25:428–454. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0045-0
title: Grant learners bounded exploration in embedded tutors, guiding them back on path quickly and blocking only unrelated actions
description: When tutoring on an existing interface, the article recommends a "middle-of-the-road" approach: learners keep freedom to explore, since exploration "is a natural part of learning", but are guided back on path as quickly as possible and blocked when necessary. In the Paint.NET tutor, users could explore drop menus a limited number of times, feedback was planned for plausible related errors, and unrelated menu items were blocked with a reminder of the current goal.
requirements: The tutor must detect which learner actions are related versus unrelated to the current goal
Movable hint windows so feedback does not obscure needed interface parts
constraints: More flexibility generally equates to more complicated tutors; Paint.NET students reported the system allowed too much freedom to explore
target_learners: novice learners using authentic software applications
target_learning_goals: staying on the solution path while retaining exploratory freedom in the target application
examples: Paint.NET tutor allowed 7–10 menu explorations, gave feedback on plausible related errors, and blocked unrelated menu items with a goal reminder

article_title: Three Algorithms for Grouping Students: A Bridge Between Personalized Tutoring System Data and Classroom Pedagogy
citation: Lechuga, C. G., & Doroudi, S. (2023). Three Algorithms for Grouping Students: A Bridge Between Personalized Tutoring System Data and Classroom Pedagogy. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00309-y
title: Within-module grouping method: k-means clustering of students by items still needed for a teacher-assigned ALEKS module
description: A group-formation method for ALEKS classes with teacher-defined modules that builds a |Q|+1-dimensional binary feature vector per student indicating membership in M\K (items needed to complete the module, including prerequisites) plus a count feature of module items in the outer fringe. The article states "We apply the k-means algorithm to cluster students based on what students still need to learn in order to complete the module," with "k = 5 to form our groups," producing possibly unequal-sized homogeneous groups by module readiness.
requirements: An ALEKS class set up with pre-defined modules, so each student's set of items still needed for the module (including prerequisites) can be computed
ALEKS student-model data on each student's state and outer fringe across course items
constraints: Designed for classes with modules; the article notes two students can overlap substantially in M\K yet have very different module outer fringes, which the added count feature only helps eliminate
target_learners: K-12 students in ALEKS Algebra 1 classes with modules
target_learning_goals: Differentiated instruction matched to students' prior knowledge relative to a module
examples: Class 1 (27 students) was grouped at the start of each of 11 modules (first module and three review modules removed) and compared against random and score-based grouping of fixed size 5.
key_sources: Lechuga, C. G., & Doroudi, S. (2023). Three Algorithms for Grouping Students: A Bridge Between Personalized Tutoring System Data and Classroom Pedagogy. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00309-y

article_title: Three Algorithms for Grouping Students: A Bridge Between Personalized Tutoring System Data and Classroom Pedagogy
citation: Lechuga, C. G., & Doroudi, S. (2023). Three Algorithms for Grouping Students: A Bridge Between Personalized Tutoring System Data and Classroom Pedagogy. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00309-y
title: Curriculum-wide grouping method: equal-size homogeneous groups each tied to a spot in the curriculum they are ready to learn
description: A grouping method for ALEKS classes without pre-determined modules, where students work at their own pace across the curriculum. The article states the method "simultaneously identifies (1) homogenous groups of students in that they are all ready to work on a specific spot in the curriculum, and (2) the spot in the curriculum that each group of students should work on." Groups are "intended to be of equal size of n ≥ 3 , which is the only parameter needed to form the groups," making it suited to remediation or self-directed learning.
requirements: An ALEKS class configured without modules, so students may work on ready-to-learn items from anywhere in the curriculum
A group size parameter n ≥ 3 supplied by the teacher
constraints: Best applied in classes without pre-determined modules; the article positions it as likely useful for remediation or self-directed learning
target_learners: K-12 students in self-paced ALEKS classes without modules
target_learning_goals: Remediation and self-directed learning with teacher-led small-group instruction matched to curriculum readiness
examples: The article describes its use for classes where students work on content spread over the entire curriculum, with the method placing greater emphasis than the within-module method on identifying appropriate content per group.
key_sources: Lechuga, C. G., & Doroudi, S. (2023). Three Algorithms for Grouping Students: A Bridge Between Personalized Tutoring System Data and Classroom Pedagogy. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00309-y

article_title: Three Algorithms for Grouping Students: A Bridge Between Personalized Tutoring System Data and Classroom Pedagogy
citation: Lechuga, C. G., & Doroudi, S. (2023). Three Algorithms for Grouping Students: A Bridge Between Personalized Tutoring System Data and Classroom Pedagogy. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00309-y
title: Reciprocal pairing method: greedy pairing of students with complementary knowledge for reciprocal peer tutoring
description: A pairing method supporting Reciprocal Peer Tutoring in ALEKS classes without modules. It simultaneously forms pairs where "Complementary knowledge refers to when each student in the pair possesses some knowledge that the other does not," and identifies the content each pair should focus on, aiming for exchanges in the tutee's zone of proximal development. Pairing uses a greedy rank-based approach because "such an optimal solution for a typical class size of 15–25 is extremely expensive computationally and perhaps impossible."
requirements: An ALEKS class without pre-determined modules, so individual strengths can be drawn from the entire curriculum
Student-model knowledge states over hundreds of skills to identify complementary knowledge
constraints: Uses a greedy approach rather than an optimal pairing configuration due to computational expense; the article notes such a greedy approach could be run many times to yield better solutions
target_learners: K-12 students in ALEKS classes without modules
target_learning_goals: Reciprocal peer tutoring in which students interchange tutor and tutee roles on content each is ready to learn
examples: The article positions the method as the first study interested in forming reciprocal pairs with complementary knowledge, avoiding student-developed questions and one-sided tutoring exchanges.
key_sources: Lechuga, C. G., & Doroudi, S. (2023). Three Algorithms for Grouping Students: A Bridge Between Personalized Tutoring System Data and Classroom Pedagogy. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00309-y

article_title: Three Algorithms for Grouping Students: A Bridge Between Personalized Tutoring System Data and Classroom Pedagogy
citation: Lechuga, C. G., & Doroudi, S. (2023). Three Algorithms for Grouping Students: A Bridge Between Personalized Tutoring System Data and Classroom Pedagogy. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00309-y
title: Knowledge Space Theory and the outer fringe as a multidimensional readiness construct underlying ALEKS grouping
description: ALEKS's domain model is based on Knowledge Space Theory, a combinatoric and probabilistic model of knowledge assessment in which a student's knowledge state is the set of items the student can complete correctly unaided, and a knowledge structure captures prerequisite relationships among items. The outer fringe is defined conceptually as "the set of items the student is ready to learn," tracked over hundreds of discrete items; the article notes the inner and outer fringes are "somewhat related to Vygotsky's (1930–1934/1978) notion of Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD)." The outer fringe serves as a pillar for all three grouping methods.
requirements: An adaptive assessment that identifies each student's state, unknown items, and outer fringe from a course structure of typically 300 to 600 items
constraints: Unlike Vygotsky's ZPD, ALEKS assumes two students with the same exact knowledge state always have the same outer fringe and does not predict differences in learning pace
target_learners: K-12, higher education, and independent learners using ALEKS courses in mathematics, chemistry, statistics, and accounting
target_learning_goals: Determining student knowledge and readiness to learn individual course items for individualized learning paths and grouping
examples: The article uses outer fringes with respect to a module as the basis of the overlap metrics evaluating the within-module grouping method.
key_sources: Lechuga, C. G., & Doroudi, S. (2023). Three Algorithms for Grouping Students: A Bridge Between Personalized Tutoring System Data and Classroom Pedagogy. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00309-y

article_title: Three Algorithms for Grouping Students: A Bridge Between Personalized Tutoring System Data and Classroom Pedagogy
citation: Lechuga, C. G., & Doroudi, S. (2023). Three Algorithms for Grouping Students: A Bridge Between Personalized Tutoring System Data and Classroom Pedagogy. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00309-y
title: Use multidimensional learning data from personalized tutoring systems to form student groups with content recommendations, bridging personalized instruction and classroom pedagogy
description: Because teachers struggle to integrate adaptive tutoring systems into pedagogical practice, the article proposes using the systems' fine-grained learning data as a bridge: "Our proposed solution is to use ALEKS learning data to form homogenous or heterogeneous groups of students along with providing teachers with content recommendations that each group could focus on." Viewing ability as multidimensional over hundreds of skills, rather than a fixed unidimensional score, supports differentiated instruction, collaborative problem solving, inquiry learning, and conceptual teacher-led lessons, with flexible regrouping at any time.
requirements: Access to fine-grained multidimensional student ability data (student model over several hundred skills) from the tutoring system
Teacher willingness to use system data for lesson planning and small-group formation
constraints: The article states the algorithms must ultimately be tested in actual classroom settings and that it cannot make claims about improved outcomes such as higher academic achievement
target_learners: K-12 students in blended learning classrooms using intelligent tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: Teacher-led differentiated instruction and collaborative learning aligned with personalized tutoring data
examples: The three methods were devised for distinct use cases: module-based differentiation, self-paced curriculum-wide grouping, and reciprocal peer tutoring pairs, each also identifying content for the group or pair to focus on.
key_sources: Lechuga, C. G., & Doroudi, S. (2023). Three Algorithms for Grouping Students: A Bridge Between Personalized Tutoring System Data and Classroom Pedagogy. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00309-y

article_title: Carelessness and Affect in an Intelligent Tutoring System for Mathematics
citation: Maria Ofelia Z. San Pedro, Ryan S. J. d. Baker, & Ma. Mercedes T. Rodrigo. (2014). Carelessness and Affect in an Intelligent Tutoring System for Mathematics. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0015-y
title: Contextual Slip model of carelessness within Bayesian Knowledge Tracing
description: The Contextual Slip model operationalizes carelessness as the probability that an incorrect action is a slip rather than a knowledge failure. Built on Bayesian Knowledge Tracing, it "contextually estimates the probability that a specific student action indicates a slip/carelessness, whenever the student reaches a problem step requiring a specific skill, but answers incorrectly". First-step slip estimates using future actions train a linear regression model that predicts slip in real time from action features such as action speed, help-seeking history, and p-know. The article applies it to a Cognitive Tutor for scatterplots.
requirements: Requires BKT parameter estimates per skill and log features of each student action to compute slip probabilities
constraints: First-step estimates use future information (actions N+1, N+2), making them unusable in real time; the regression approximation is needed for real-time use
target_learners: middle school and high school mathematics students
target_learning_goals: reducing careless errors in mathematics problem-solving
examples: Detectors trained per condition achieved cross-validated correlations of r=0.886 (NoScooter) and r=0.836 (Scooter) with training labels
key_sources: Maria Ofelia Z. San Pedro, Ryan S. J. d. Baker, & Ma. Mercedes T. Rodrigo. (2014). Carelessness and Affect in an Intelligent Tutoring System for Mathematics. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0015-y

article_title: BEETLE II: Deep Natural Language Understanding and Automatic Feedback Generation for Intelligent Tutoring in Basic Electricity and Electronics
citation: Dzikovska, M., Steinhauser, N., Farrow, E., Moore, J., & Campbell, G. (2014). BEETLE II: Deep Natural Language Understanding and Automatic Feedback Generation for Intelligent Tutoring in Basic Electricity and Electronics. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 24, 284–332. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0017-9
title: Conceptual change instructional approach for countering naïve science conceptions
description: The conceptual change method is a science-instruction framework the article adopts as the organizing approach for its electricity curriculum. It has two key processes: students are "presented with unavoidable and incontrovertible evidence that explicitly contradicts their existing na¨ıve conception(s)" and are then "guided just enough to allow them to generate an accurate conceptualization" of the domain. BEETLE II implements it with simulation exercises that contradict misconceptions followed by reflective dialogue, leveraging Socratic tutoring and self-explanation research.
requirements: Instruction must present evidence that directly contradicts students' existing naïve conceptions
A guided reflection stage must help students generate accurate new conceptualizations
constraints: The article applies it to the sub-topic of electricity and electric circuits
target_learners: students with no prior knowledge of electronics and electricity
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of basic electricity and electric circuits
overcoming common physics misconceptions
examples: BEETLE II curriculum exercises use varied circuit configurations designed to show that sequential circuit analysis fails and global reasoning is required
key_sources: Dzikovska, M., Steinhauser, N., Farrow, E., Moore, J., & Campbell, G. (2014). BEETLE II: Deep Natural Language Understanding and Automatic Feedback Generation for Intelligent Tutoring in Basic Electricity and Electronics. article_title: BEETLE II: Deep Natural Language Understanding and Automatic Feedback Generation for Intelligent Tutoring in Basic Electricity and Electronics
citation: Dzikovska, M., Steinhauser, N., Farrow, E., Moore, J., & Campbell, G. (2014). International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 24, 284–332. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0017-9
title: Predict-Verify-Evaluate (PVE) cycle combining prediction, simulation testing, and reflective explanation
description: PVE is the lesson-level instructional pattern used across most of the BEETLE II curriculum. Students predict a circuit's behavior and explain the prediction, test it in the simulator, compare outcome to prediction, and when predictions fail they are "asked to try and generate an explanation for the behavior of the circuit that they just observed" — a flow the authors call the "“Predict-Verify-Evaluate” strategy (PVE)". It is designed to encourage deep thinking about observed phenomena and inference of underlying explanatory principles, rather than misconception-specific remediation dialogues.
requirements: A simulation environment in which students can build circuits and observe behavior
Tutorial dialogue support for the prediction and reflection steps
constraints: Most, not all, of the curriculum is set up in this manner
target_learners: students learning basic electricity and electronics concepts
target_learning_goals: self-explanation of observed phenomena
conceptual change away from naïve circuit misconceptions
examples: For each topic students predict, build and observe circuits in the simulator, evaluate whether results matched predictions, and complete a reflection dialogue when predictions were not realized
key_sources: Dzikovska, M., Steinhauser, N., Farrow, E., Moore, J., & Campbell, G. (2014). BEETLE II: Deep Natural Language Understanding and Automatic Feedback Generation for Intelligent Tutoring in Basic Electricity and Electronics. citation: Dzikovska, M., Steinhauser, N., Farrow, E., Moore, J., & Campbell, G. (2014). BEETLE II: Deep Natural Language Understanding and Automatic Feedback Generation for Intelligent Tutoring in Basic Electricity and Electronics. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 24, 284–332. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0017-9
title: BEETLE II intelligent tutoring system with deep NLP and dynamic feedback generation
description: BEETLE II is an intelligent tutoring system for basic electricity and electronics combining a simulated circuit workbench (integrated with the open-source GNUCAP simulator) with a tutorial dialogue capability. Its dialogue component "supports context-specific interpretation and diagnosis of natural language student explanations, and implements a set of generic tutoring tactics that can be instantiated in different problem-solving contexts". The pipeline runs deep parsing (TRIPS), contextual interpretation, domain reasoning and diagnosis, tutorial planning, and natural language generation, allowing feedback to be produced on the fly without authoring messages for every anticipated answer.
requirements: Symbolic NLP infrastructure: parser, domain ontology and mapping rules
A domain reasoner with an ontology of on-screen objects, properties and relations
constraints: Curriculum is presented in a fixed sequence; adaptive curriculum planning is only contemplated for future work
The symbolic approach may fail on domain-related terms not labeled synonymous in the domain-independent ontology
target_learners: university students with no prior knowledge of electronics and electricity
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of open and closed paths, voltage, series and parallel circuits, and fault finding with a multimeter
examples: Students type explanations such as answers to "Why was bulb C off when switch Z was open?" and the system restates correct parts, gives hints, or bottoms out with the answer
key_sources: Dzikovska, M., Steinhauser, N., Farrow, E., Moore, J., & Campbell, G. (2014). BEETLE II: Deep Natural Language Understanding and Automatic Feedback Generation for Intelligent Tutoring in Basic Electricity and Electronics. article_title: BEETLE II: Deep Natural Language Understanding and Automatic Feedback Generation for Intelligent Tutoring in Basic Electricity and Electronics
citation: Dzikovska, M., Steinhauser, N., Farrow, E., Moore, J., & Campbell, G. (2014). BEETLE II: Deep Natural Language Understanding and Automatic Feedback Generation for Intelligent Tutoring in Basic Electricity and Electronics. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 24, 284–332. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0017-9
title: Symbolic NLP approach enabling dynamic adaptive feedback generation in simulation-based tutoring
description: The article advances a symbolic (rule-based, deep-parsing) approach to natural language understanding in tutoring systems, in contrast to statistical answer-matching approaches. The authors note symbolic methods are "more brittle to unexpected student input than statistical approaches", but argue that "the structured semantic representations they produce offer particular advantages for integrating tutoring with simulation-based environments". A domain-independent parser and ontology adapted via ontology-mapping rules lets one mapping rule handle synonyms (e.g., "linked" and "connected" map to the same domain concept), supporting generic tutoring tactics instantiated on the fly rather than pre-authored messages.
requirements: Upfront investment in parsing and interpretation infrastructure
Hand-written ontology mapping rules and domain-specific interpretation rules
constraints: More brittle to unexpected student input than statistical approaches
The BEETLE II domain was chosen more restricted than AutoTutor domains so symbolic domain reasoners could be built
target_learners: students interacting with dialogue-based intelligent tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: context-appropriate feedback on natural-language explanations during simulation-based learning
examples: BEETLE II handles paraphrases like "The bulb is contained in a closed path" and "There is a closed path containing a bulb" and resolves ellipsis such as "all off"
key_sources: Dzikovska, M., Steinhauser, N., Farrow, E., Moore, J., & Campbell, G. (2014). BEETLE II: Deep Natural Language Understanding and Automatic Feedback Generation for Intelligent Tutoring in Basic Electricity and Electronics. title: Error recovery policy for non-interpretable student utterances
description: When the interpreter cannot understand a student utterance (for example, a term related in the domain but not synonymous in the domain-independent ontology, like "a broken path" for "an open path"), the tutorial planner follows an error recovery policy: "the tutorial planner attempts to produce a message that describes the problem but without giving away the answer", naming the unrecognized terms, and accompanies the message with a hint at an appropriate level. The method, drawn from task-oriented spoken dialogue systems, is intended to help students learn to phrase answers the system can understand.
requirements: Ontology information from which the content of the help message is computed automatically
A hint-selection mechanism considering numbers of previous incorrect and non-interpretable answers
constraints: Interpretation may still fail when domain-similar terms are not synonyms in the broader ontology
target_learners: students typing free-form natural language explanations to a tutor
target_learning_goals: recovery from interpretation failures without revealing the correct answer
learning phrasings the system can interpret
examples: If a student refers to a damaged path, the system responds that it does not understand "paths are damaged" because batteries or bulbs can be damaged, but not paths, then gives a hint

article_title: How Can I Get It Right? Using GPT to Rephrase Incorrect Trainee Responses
citation: Jionghao Lin, Zifei Han, Danielle R. Thomas, Ashish Gurung, Shivang Gupta, Vincent Aleven, Kenneth R. Koedinger. (2024). How Can I Get It Right? Using GPT to Rephrase Incorrect Trainee Responses. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.00970
title: GPT-4-based explanatory feedback system for tutor training
description: An automated feedback system built on the GPT-4 model that identifies trainees' responses in binary form (correct/incorrect) and provides template-based feedback with incorrect responses rephrased by GPT-4. The system targets novice tutors in scenario-based training lessons on an online learning platform. As the authors state, "our study employed the GPT-4 model to build an explanatory feedback system", integrating the classifier and rephrasing results into real-time feedback during training sessions.
requirements: Requires a binary classifier (the 5-shot GPT-4 classifier) to pinpoint incorrect responses before rephrasing
Requires lesson-specific principles and scenario text as prompt inputs
constraints: Evaluated only on three lessons; the authors call for broader evaluation on other lessons
Binary correct/incorrect classification may be overly simplistic for real-world applications, per the authors
target_learners: novice tutors (trainees), including community volunteers, retired individuals, and college students
target_learning_goals: effective praise
reacting to student errors
determining what students know
examples: The system presents template-based suggestions such as "AI-generated feedback suggests that your response could focus more on praising the student for their efforts in the learning process."
key_sources: Jionghao Lin, Zifei Han, Danielle R. Thomas, Ashish Gurung, Shivang Gupta, Vincent Aleven, Kenneth R. Koedinger. (2024). How Can I Get It Right? Using GPT to Rephrase Incorrect Trainee Responses. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.00970

article_title: How Can I Get It Right? Using GPT to Rephrase Incorrect Trainee Responses
citation: Jionghao Lin, Zifei Han, Danielle R. Thomas, Ashish Gurung, Shivang Gupta, Vincent Aleven, Kenneth R. Koedinger. (2024). How Can I Get It Right? Using GPT to Rephrase Incorrect Trainee Responses. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.00970
title: Framework for determining the quality of rephrased responses (accuracy × responsiveness)
description: A two-dimensional framework the authors propose from their evaluation results for judging the quality of rephrased feedback responses. Accuracy measures whether the rephrased response is a better example of the lesson's target practice; responsiveness measures how selectively words are changed while preserving the trainee's original words and ideas. Responses rated 1 or 2 in accuracy are acceptable; the "optimal rephrased responses should be high in both accuracy and responsiveness (i.e., Excellent area in Fig. 6)", while low-accuracy responses (≤ 0) are undesirable regardless of responsiveness.
requirements: Expert ratings on both dimensions using a five-point Likert scale (Strongly Disagree to Strongly Agree)
constraints: Low responsiveness may indicate major structural and semantic changes that are harder for trainees to learn and retain, per the authors
target_learning_goals: improving quality of automated explanatory feedback
recognizing desired forms of tutoring responses
examples: A rephrasing rated accuracy 2 but responsiveness 0 (e.g., "I see you're making good progress with your efforts. Keep it up!") falls in the Good area; a human rephrasing rated accuracy -1 with high responsiveness is undesirable.
key_sources: Jionghao Lin, Zifei Han, Danielle R. Thomas, Ashish Gurung, Shivang Gupta, Vincent Aleven, Kenneth R. Koedinger. (2024). How Can I Get It Right? Using GPT to Rephrase Incorrect Trainee Responses. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.00970

article_title: An Analysis of Student Model Portability
citation: Valdés Aguirre, B., Ramírez Uresti, J. A., & du Boulay, B. (2016). An Analysis of Student Model Portability. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0113-0
title: A four-dimension classification for grading student model portability
description: The article introduces a classification that grades student models in terms of portability. Portability is measured across four dimensions — accessibility, complexity, architecture, and popularity — each composed of factors such as open source status, availability, inputs, types of data, input formats, computational techniques, data mining use, model origin, implementation, modularity, server/client architecture, and re-implementation. Each factor is graded 1 to 4 (low, mid, high restrictions, or no information), dimension grades are normalized sums mapped to 1–4, and the overall grade is the sum of the dimensions, where a grade of 4 represents "the models with least types restrictions we found (Very Low)". The authors intend it "to be used by researchers both as a methodology to measure the portability of a student model and as a guide to find existing reusable models".
requirements: Grades are calculated from questions answerable from published literature without access to source code, so published documentation of the model's inputs, implementation, and availability is required.
constraints: The authors normalize each dimension equally, which they acknowledge "is a strong assumption to make and may bias our analysis".
The classes are coarse, so "there might be considerable differences between some models that fall in the same class".
A domain independence factor was excluded because it could not be measured in a practical way.
target_learners: Researchers and developers building or reusing student models in ITSs and ILEs
target_learning_goals: Selection and reuse of existing student models when building adaptive learning systems
examples: The classification was applied to 70 student models identified from full papers at AIED 2013, EDM 2014 and ITS 2014, graded and grouped into tables from low to very high portability restrictions.
key_sources: Valdés Aguirre, B., Ramírez Uresti, J. A., & du Boulay, B. (2016). An Analysis of Student Model Portability. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0113-0

article_title: A Comparison of Model-Tracing and Constraint-Based Intelligent Tutoring Paradigms
citation: Viswanathan Kodaganallur, Rob R. Weitz, David Rosenthal. (2005). A Comparison of Model-Tracing and Constraint-Based Intelligent Tutoring Paradigms. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197305
title: A comparative framework contrasting the model-tracing and constraint-based intelligent tutoring paradigms
description: The article contrasts two approaches to building intelligent tutoring systems: the "well-established model-tracing paradigm" and "the relatively newer constraint-based paradigm". It evaluates the proponents' claim that constraint-based tutors "afford performance at levels comparable to that of model-tracing tutors, but with significantly less development effort", and organizes the comparison around remediation quality, domain feasibility, and development effort.
requirements: The comparison presumes building both types of tutor for the same problem domain, as the authors did for statistical hypothesis testing
target_learning_goals: statistical hypothesis testing skills supported by intelligent tutoring
examples: The authors built both a model-tracing and a constraint-based tutor for statistical hypothesis testing and compared the paradigms directly.

article_title: How Personalization Affects Motivation in Gamified Review Assessments
citation: Rodrigues Luiz, Palomino Paula T., Toda Armando M., Klock Ana C. T., Pessoa Marcela, Pereira Filipe D., Oliveira Elaine H. T., Oliveira David F., Cristea Alexandra I., Gasparini Isabela, Isotani Seiji. (2023). How Personalization Affects Motivation in Gamified Review Assessments. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00326-x
title: Gamification Science framework: gamification affects motivation, which affects behavior and cognitive outcomes, with moderators on each link
description: The article uses the Gamification Science framework (Landers et al., 2018) as its explanatory account of how gamification operates in education. It states the framework "claims gamification affects motivation; motivation affects behavior; behavior affects cognitive outcomes; and moderators affect each of those connections". The authors use this causal chain to argue that gamification studies must prioritize measuring motivational outcomes aligned to gamification's goals, since improved motivation might not lead to the desired behavior, and to motivate testing personalization's effect on autonomous motivation as a mediator of learning gains.
requirements: Gamification studies should measure motivational outcomes aligned to gamification's goals to prevent misleading conclusions from behavior-only or cognition-only analyses
constraints: The framework is presented as a claim of prior work (Landers et al., 2018) motivating this study's design, not as something tested in this article
target_learners: students completing assessments for learning in virtual learning environments
target_learning_goals: autonomous motivation to engage with educational assessments
examples: The authors justify H1 by noting autonomous motivation is known to mediate improvements in learning outcomes according to empirical evidence and the Gamification Science framework

article_title: Constructive Criticism? Working with (Rather than Against) the AIED Back-Lash
citation: Neil Selwyn. (2023). Constructive Criticism? Working with (Rather than Against) the AIED Back-Lash. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00344-3
title: A seven-position matrix of interests and agendas structures AIED debates in the 2020s
description: The article proposes that AIED controversies cannot be reduced to informed proponents versus uninformed critics. Instead it offers "a loose matrix of interests and agendas" (Fig. 1) distinguishing at least seven positions: technical, educational, corporate and social proponents, and social, educational and technical critics, each framing AI in education through its own values, from an engineering mindset to critical pedagogy.
requirements: Understanding any given AIED debate requires identifying which of the distinct stakeholder positions are speaking, since each frames AI issues differently
constraints: The article presents this as a broad guide rather than an exhaustive classification
target_learners: AIED researchers, developers, and education stakeholders engaging with AI debates
target_learning_goals: Understanding the structure of controversies around AI in education
key_sources: Neil Selwyn. (2023). Constructive Criticism? Working with (Rather than Against) the AIED Back-Lash. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00344-3

article_title: Constructive Criticism? Working with (Rather than Against) the AIED Back-Lash
citation: Neil Selwyn. (2023). Constructive Criticism? Working with (Rather than Against) the AIED Back-Lash. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00344-3
title: Engage AIED criticism constructively rather than defensively
description: The article argues proponents should resist instinctive responses to fix, dismiss, or rebut critics, and instead "engage with what these criticisms are telling us about AIED". This means treating critics as raising points "worth unpacking in further detail", examining the specific applications, motivations and values behind the backlash rather than presuming critics lack technical understanding or educational vision.
requirements: Willingness to treat criticism as informative about AIED rather than as misinformation to be corrected
Reflection on one's own positionality and the values driving one's work
constraints: The article explicitly recommends against proposing quick solutions or chiding critics for negativity
target_learning_goals: Constructive engagement with critique of educational AI
examples: The author recounts an AIED reviewer dismissing his book because he had not built an AI system, as an example of the defensive 'you cannot critique AI until you have built AI' posture

title: Approach AIED as a political project and make underpinning values explicit
description: The article contends critics remind the field that "AIED needs to be approached as a political project", since AI in education is entangled with power, disadvantage and marginalisation, and tends toward centralisation of power. Everyone working in AIED should be ready to examine and make explicit the values and ideologies driving debates, reflect on their own positionality, and reject claims that AI is non-political and neutral.

Acknowledgement that claiming neutrality tacitly supports the status quo
constraints: The article notes these political issues rarely drive discussions in technical venues such as IJAIED

target_learning_goals: Political awareness of how educational AI is designed and deployed

article_title: Avoiding Help Avoidance: Using Interface Design Changes to Promote Unsolicited Hint Usage in an Intelligent Tutor
citation: Mehak Maniktala, Christa Cody, Tiffany Barnes, Min Chi. (2020). Avoiding Help Avoidance: Using Interface Design Changes to Promote Unsolicited Hint Usage in an Intelligent Tutor. https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.13371
title: Assertions: unsolicited hint steps presented in the workspace as partially-worked example steps
description: Assertions are a hint delivery mechanism in the Deep Thought logic tutor: "Assertions are partially-worked example steps designed to appear within a student workspace, and in the same format as student-derived steps, to show students a possible subgoal leading to the solution." Each Assertion adds a cyan node with the hint content, labels it "Subgoal", marks it unjustified with a question mark, and asks the student to justify it before using it. They appear automatically after about 40% of steps, and their design draws on contiguity, attention, expectation, and persuasion principles to reduce help avoidance.
requirements: Requires data-driven hint content, generated in this tutor by the Hint Factory from prior students' transaction log data.
Assertions must be justified by the student before the hint content can be used in the solution.
constraints: Assertions were evaluated in a single domain (propositional logic proofs) with undergraduate engineering students.
Only one unsolicited hint may be present at a time and the hint content is not updated based on new student work.
target_learners: undergraduate engineering students learning propositional logic
target_learning_goals: multi-step problem-solving strategies
efficient proof construction
domain rule application
examples: In the Deep Thought tutor, students in the treatment condition received Assertions after about 40% of their steps, resulting in 3-4 hints per problem given the mean 9-step training solutions.
key_sources: Mehak Maniktala, Christa Cody, Tiffany Barnes, Min Chi. (2020). Avoiding Help Avoidance: Using Interface Design Changes to Promote Unsolicited Hint Usage in an Intelligent Tutor. https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.13371

article_title: Avoiding Help Avoidance: Using Interface Design Changes to Promote Unsolicited Hint Usage in an Intelligent Tutor
citation: Mehak Maniktala, Christa Cody, Tiffany Barnes, Min Chi. (2020). Avoiding Help Avoidance: Using Interface Design Changes to Promote Unsolicited Hint Usage in an Intelligent Tutor. https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.13371
title: Workspace-integrated, format-isomorphic hint placement to reduce help avoidance
description: This pattern delivers unsolicited help by embedding it inside the student's problem-solving workspace rather than in a separate message area. The article's rationale: "placing Assertions contiguously within the area of student attention would make unsolicited hints more noticeable," and formatting them like student-derived steps leverages visual expectation to speed interpretation. Persuasive labelling ("Subgoal", "Try to justify the added goal") frames the help as part of normal tutor workflow, circumventing autonomy preferences that drive help avoidance.
requirements: Hint content must be renderable in the same visual format as student-produced steps.
The learner's attention must be reliably focused on the workspace where the help appears.
constraints: The article argues the pattern applies where help and workspace are otherwise physically separated; Message-style hints in this study often went unnoticed, possibly due to change blindness.
Only studied with unsolicited next-step hints whose content is identical to the control's.
target_learning_goals: help usage
efficient problem solving
productive persistence
examples: Assertions added a cyan, question-marked 'Subgoal' node in the Deep Thought workspace; Messages appeared as text below the workspace after one minute of inactivity.
key_sources: Mehak Maniktala, Christa Cody, Tiffany Barnes, Min Chi. (2020). Avoiding Help Avoidance: Using Interface Design Changes to Promote Unsolicited Hint Usage in an Intelligent Tutor. https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.13371

article_title: Avoiding Help Avoidance: Using Interface Design Changes to Promote Unsolicited Hint Usage in an Intelligent Tutor
citation: Mehak Maniktala, Christa Cody, Tiffany Barnes, Min Chi. (2020). Avoiding Help Avoidance: Using Interface Design Changes to Promote Unsolicited Hint Usage in an Intelligent Tutor. https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.13371
title: Cluster-based method combining performance, effort, and hint usage to discover productive persistence
description: The article proposes "a new cluster-based method that combines posttest performance, eﬀort (to quantify persistence), and unsolicited hint usage to discover productive persistence." It defines productive persistence as "persistent (high) eﬀorts that result in higher posttest performance", building on work distinguishing productive persistence from wheel-spinning. Effort is operationalised through two research-based measures: time spent on unsolved (skipped) training problems and the number of restarts on eventually-solved problems. Students are clustered on five features spanning productivity, effort, and unsolicited hint usage.
requirements: Log data capturing hint usage, problem-solving time, solution lengths, skips, and restarts across training and posttest.
A prior proficiency measure to interpret cluster patterns by student subgroup.
constraints: Effort measures rely on this tutor's specific affordances (skipping up to three problems per level, restarts), so transfer to other systems requires equivalent logging.
The article's stated productive-persistence clustering results concern students with low prior proficiency.
target_learning_goals: persistence
productive help usage
problem-solving mastery
examples: The authors report that students with low prior proficiency who received Assertions exhibit productive persistence, based on these clusters.

article_title: Towards Trustworthy AutoGrading of Short, Multi-lingual, Multi-type Answers
citation: Johannes Schneider, Robin Richner, Micha Riser. (2023). Towards Trustworthy AutoGrading of Short, Multi-lingual, Multi-type Answers. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00289-z
title: Similarity-threshold autograding architecture with teacher-controlled error constraints and a human-deferred uncertainty zone
description: The article proposes an autograding framework in which fine-tuned multilingual transformer models embed question-answer pairs and score similarity to the correct answer. "Using two thresholds on the score, we can place a question-answer pair into one of three categories" — likely correct, uncertain, or likely incorrect — with uncertain pairs deferred to a human. Teachers specify minimum accuracy levels (maximum false-negative and false-positive rates), from which thresholds are computed to maximize the fraction of samples autograded while honoring the constraints. A validation procedure then compares accuracy on manually and automatically graded answers per exam.
requirements: A dataset of question-answer pairs with teacher-provided correct/incorrect marks as ground truth
Teachers must specify minimum accuracy thresholds for answers classified as correct and incorrect
Difficult samples within the threshold range must be graded manually by a human
constraints: Restricted to questions whose answers can be marked as correct or incorrect
Accuracy of about 90% on autograded samples is deemed insufficient for fully automatic grading of high-stake exams
Relying only on semantic similarity may not suffice because an autograder cannot reason logically
target_learners: students studying at home for exam preparation
target_learning_goals: accurate assessment of short free-text and numeric answers across subjects and languages
examples: The system was trained and evaluated on about 10 million answers and 990000 questions from Classtime, covering languages including Ukrainian, English, Russian and German

article_title: The Intertwined Histories of Artificial Intelligence and Education
citation: Shayan Doroudi. (2022). The Intertwined Histories of Artificial Intelligence and Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00313-2
title: Information-processing psychology (Newell and Simon's symbolic approach to cognition and learning)
description: Newell and Simon's information-processing psychology laid foundations for both cognitive psychology and symbolic AI, positing that problem solving uses processes resembling human ones, studied via think-aloud protocols. Learning is framed as "gradually accumulating the various production rules necessary to solve a problem," where each production has "a bipartite form, consisting of a condition and an action." Simon and Newell argued this theory of problem solving "gives us a new basis for attacking the psychology of education and the learning process," positioning it as the basic science education lacked.
requirements: Detailed models of the information and programs skilled performers possess, developed by studying human problem-solving data such as think-aloud protocols
constraints: Newell and Simon themselves judged that studying performance must take precedence over learning "in the present state of the art" of the 1970s
target_learning_goals: problem solving
skill acquisition
examples: The 1971 Simon and Newell paper included a section on The Practice of Education; the approach informed Carnegie Mellon tutoring systems and the ACT theory of skill acquisition

article_title: Student Modeling Based on Problem Solving Times
citation: Pelánek, R., & Jarušek, P. (2015). Student Modeling Based on Problem Solving Times. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0048-x
title: Log-linear model of problem solving times analogical to the IRT three-parameter model
description: A generative student model for interactive problem solving that specifies the distribution of problem solving times rather than correctness probability. It assumes, in the article's words, "a linear relationship between a problem solving skill and a logarithm of time to solve a problem": tsp = bp + apθs + N(0, cp²), where b is basic difficulty, a a discrimination factor, and c a randomness factor. The notation is deliberately chosen to mirror the IRT three-parameter logistic model, and the model is also related to k=1 collaborative filtering. It supports prediction of solving times and estimation of problem and student parameters.
requirements: Times are log-transformed and only successfully completed problems are modeled; normalization sets mean skill 0 and mean discrimination -1 to resolve scale indeterminacy
constraints: Applicable to well-structured problems where the solution cannot be guessed and solving time is a sufficient performance measure
target_learners: university and high school students practicing programming, mathematics, and logic puzzles
target_learning_goals: problem solving skill estimation and problem difficulty calibration in adaptive practice
examples: Used in the Problem Solving Tutor to predict solving times and recommend problems of suitable difficulty
key_sources: Pelánek, R., & Jarušek, P. (2015). Student Modeling Based on Problem Solving Times. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0048-x

article_title: Student Modeling Based on Problem Solving Times
citation: Pelánek, R., & Jarušek, P. (2015). Student Modeling Based on Problem Solving Times. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0048-x
title: Problem Solving Tutor — web-based adaptive practice system recommending problems by predicted solving time
description: A free web-based tutoring system (tutor.fi.muni.cz) providing computerized adaptive practice focused on the outer loop of tutoring. "The tutor contains 30 types of problems (more than 1400 specific problem instances) mainly from areas of programming, mathematics, and logic puzzles." It estimates each student's skill from past attempts, predicts solving times, and recommends two problems per step — one harder, one easier — using a linear scoring function over expected time, randomness, and prior attempts. Students see personalized time predictions and post-solution comparisons with peers, adding a game-like competitive element. The system is used in more than 20 schools with more than 10 000 registered users and data from more than 400 000 solved problems.
requirements: A gradual-start approach with initial difficulty estimates added as artificial users to handle the cold start problem, running a simplified model until richer models predict better
constraints: The system focuses solely on the outer loop of tutoring (problem ordering), not on within-problem hints or step-level tutoring
target_learners: university and high school students in more than 20 schools
target_learning_goals: problem solving practice in programming, mathematics, and logic puzzles at suitable difficulty
examples: Problem types include graphs and functions, linear transformations, robot programming, standard programming, finite automata, and logic puzzles such as Sudoku and Sokoban
key_sources: Pelánek, R., & Jarušek, P. (2015). Student Modeling Based on Problem Solving Times. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0048-x

article_title: Student Modeling Based on Problem Solving Times
citation: Pelánek, R., & Jarušek, P. (2015). Student Modeling Based on Problem Solving Times. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0048-x
title: Use model parameters — difficulty, discrimination, and randomness — as feedback for content authors and to filter and sequence problems
description: Beyond predicting solving times, the fitted parameters give insight into pedagogical properties of problems. The article notes that "Problems with small discrimination and large randomness clearly depend more on luck than on skill and thus are probably not a very good pedagogical problems, so we may want to filter out such problems." Early in a session, when the skill estimate is weak, problems with small discrimination and variance give more reliable time estimates; later, higher-discrimination problems tune selection to the individual student. Parameter discrepancies also helped detect cheating and misbehaving problems.
requirements: Sufficient solved-problem data per problem to estimate discrimination and variance reliably
constraints: At session start, when skill estimates are weak, prefer low-discrimination, low-variance problems; the boundary guidance follows the article's recommendation, not an optimized optimum
target_learners: students in computerized adaptive practice systems
target_learning_goals: selecting problems of appropriate difficulty and discriminating power for adaptive practice
examples: In the Problem Solving Tutor, the linear scoring function for recommendations combines expected solving time, problem randomness, and prior attempts, and parameters are given as feedback to content authors

article_title: Towards Understanding How to Assess Help-Seeking Behavior Across Cultures
citation: Amy Ogan, Erin Walker, Ryan Baker, Ma. Mercedes T. Rodrigo, Jose Carlo Soriano, Maynor Jimenez Castro. (2015). Towards Understanding How to Assess Help-Seeking Behavior Across Cultures. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0034-8
title: Hofstede's cultural dimensions as a post-hoc framework for interpreting cross-cultural help-seeking differences
description: The article applies Hofstede's cultural dimensions—Masculinity, Individualism, and Power Distance—to interpret why effective help seeking diverged across sites. It suggests Philippine and U.S. students may have "viewed work on the ITS as a competition" consistent with their higher Masculinity scores, while lower Power Distance may have let Costa Rican students informally collaborate despite instructions to work individually. The authors emphasize these are post-hoc speculations not directly tested.
requirements: Empirical research across a larger number of sites is stated as necessary to determine whether these dimensions best explain the results
constraints: The article states it did not test the relationship between Hofstede's dimensions and student behaviors directly; Philippines respondents scored similarly to Costa Rica on Individualism yet behaved differently, so that dimension alone could not explain the results
target_learners: Students aged 12-14 using intelligent tutoring systems in Costa Rica, the Philippines, and the United States
target_learning_goals: Help seeking as a cross-curricular self-regulation skill in mathematics learning
examples: The article links Hofstede survey scores for the three countries to observed classroom behaviors, e.g., Philippine students heeding teacher directions and working silently and alone
key_sources: Amy Ogan, Erin Walker, Ryan Baker, Ma. Mercedes T. Rodrigo, Jose Carlo Soriano, Maynor Jimenez Castro. (2015). Towards Understanding How to Assess Help-Seeking Behavior Across Cultures. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0034-8

article_title: Towards Understanding How to Assess Help-Seeking Behavior Across Cultures
citation: Amy Ogan, Erin Walker, Ryan Baker, Ma. Mercedes T. Rodrigo, Jose Carlo Soriano, Maynor Jimenez Castro. (2015). Towards Understanding How to Assess Help-Seeking Behavior Across Cultures. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0034-8
title: Seventeen log-derived help-seeking features for assessing help seeking in intelligent tutors
description: A set of 17 behavioral features distilled from tutor log files and normalized as a percentage of total student actions, designed to "encompass a wide array of possible help-seeking behaviors". Features include help avoidance (NHP), help abuse (HPQ), self-explanation pauses after help use (HPL), help non-use on well-known skills (NHW), pauses before and after hints and bug messages, and first-encounter hint requests, each labeled with a predicted positive, negative, or ambiguous relationship to help seeking.
requirements: Threshold parameters for each feature (time or Bayesian Knowledge Tracing knowledge probability) are optimized by brute-force grid search with leave-one-out cross-validation per dataset
constraints: The article notes the feature set was generated based on U.S.-focused research, so indicators of successful help seeking in other contexts may not be captured
target_learners: Middle-school mathematics students (ages 12-14) using the Cognitive Tutor
target_learning_goals: Assessing effective versus ineffective help seeking within intelligent tutoring systems
examples: Features were operationalized with Bayesian Knowledge Tracing and used in forward-selection regression models in all three countries

article_title: Mapping Artificial Intelligence in Education Research: a Network-based Keyword Analysis
citation: Shihui Feng & Nancy Law. (2021). Mapping Artificial Intelligence in Education Research: A Network-based Keyword Analysis. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 31, 277–303. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00244-4
title: Three-step multi-scale (macro, meso, micro) framework for analyzing keyword co-occurrence networks of a research field
description: The article proposes a network-based review method that analyzes keyword co-occurrence networks at three levels: macro-level distribution of keyword structural importance, meso-level community detection of knowledge clusters, and micro-level identification of trending and bridging keywords. As the authors state, "A novel three-step approach in the analysis of the keyword co-occurrence networks (KCN) is proposed to identify the knowledge structure, knowledge clusters and trending keywords within AIED over time." Temporal KCNs on two-year windows support evolution analysis. The authors argue the framework generalizes beyond AIED.
requirements: A corpus of keyworded articles from a field, standardized keywords, and construction of undirected weighted KCNs with fast-greedy modularity clustering
constraints: Applied and demonstrated on the AIED literature from 2010 to 2019
target_learners: researchers mapping the development of a scientific field
target_learning_goals: understanding knowledge structure, clusters, and trends of a research field
examples: Applied to 1830 AIED articles from five publication sources, with five temporal KCNs each covering a two-year window

title: Dataset of 1830 AIED articles from five major publication sources, 2010–2019
description: The corpus comprises all available research articles from five prominent AIED publication venues: AIEDC, IJAIED, EDM, L@S and ITS conferences/journal, from 2010 to 2019. "In total, there are 1830 articles in the final dataset for analyzing the research topics and their evolution within the AIED field." article_title: Reasoning Mind Genie 2: An Intelligent Tutoring System as a Vehicle for International Transfer of Instructional Methods in Mathematics
citation: Khachatryan, G. A., Romashov, A. V., Khachatryan, A. R., Gaudino, S. J., Khachatryan, J. M., Guarian, K. R., & Yufa, N. V. (2014). Reasoning Mind Genie 2: An Intelligent Tutoring System as a Vehicle for International Transfer of Instructional Methods in Mathematics. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0019-7
title: Genie 2: a knowledge-engineered intelligent tutoring system delivering an entire national curriculum tradition
description: Genie 2 is an intelligent tutoring system for grades 2–6 mathematics that "represents and delivers an existing curriculum in its entirety — i.e., as a system of interconnected pedagogical practices". Its behavior was created by interviewing a panel of expert Russian mathematics teachers and codifying their practices into a decision system plus student model, instructional data structures, and detailed scripts. Unlike Cognitive Tutor's paper-and-pencil curriculum companion, in Genie 2 the intelligent tutoring system is "the primary vehicle for the introduction and discussion of new material".
requirements: A panel of expert teachers from the source tradition must be interviewed and must also participate in software design decisions and content authoring
Iterative design-research cycles of development, piloting, and analysis in destination-country schools
constraints: Core 5th and 6th grade curricula take about 120 h each; grades 2–4 curricula take 70 h each
Online Tutoring mode saw limited use since few schools are willing to pay for online tutoring
target_learners: United States students in grades 2–6 mathematics
target_learning_goals: School mathematics curriculum content and procedures aligned with the Russian mathematics tradition
examples: Students work at their own computers at their own pace while the teacher monitors and works with individuals or small groups; the system's modes include Guided Study, Homework, Review Mode, and Wall of Mastery

International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0019-7
title: Russian mathematics instruction principles: a set of shared salient practices extracted from expert teachers
description: Interviews with the expert teacher panel surfaced numerous shared methods, leading the authors to speak of a single "Russian mathematics education tradition". The article enumerates its salient aspects: guided instruction rather than pure discovery; fading from worked examples to independent problem solving; motivating new constructs before formal definitions; organizing knowledge around mathematically meaningful structures (e.g., treating decimals as a special case of fractions); explicit rules and definitions; mathematical precision; explanatory feedback referring back to definitions and rules; automaticity through spaced practice; breaking difficult concepts into constituent components; and an overriding "anti-principle" placing the accumulated content-specific experience of practitioners above any general principles.
requirements: The practices are content-specific and were held together by a community of teachers whose accumulated experience governs pedagogical decisions
constraints: The article contrasts these with United States practices as observed in this project and cited literature, not as a controlled comparison
target_learners: School mathematics students, especially struggling or average students in guided instruction
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding, procedural fluency and automaticity, mathematical precision, and coherent knowledge structures in mathematics
examples: Before defining factors, students solve: among how many children can 18 apples be divided evenly? The meaningful list of divisors then motivates the term

title: Wall of Mastery: a mastery-based mode for advancing through difficulty levels on covered objectives
description: Wall of Mastery is a Genie 2 mode added "as a systematic way for students to learn to solve level B and C problems on each objective presented in Guided Study". After an objective is covered, the level A cell in its row becomes enabled; completing a cell's problem sequence with high accuracy marks it complete and enables the next difficulty cell. The article describes it as "a rudimentary open learner model", noting learner control is likely more appropriate for advanced problem solving over previously studied topics than for basic instruction.
requirements: The corresponding objective must first be covered in Guided Study
Students must complete problems with high accuracy to unlock the next difficulty level
constraints: Positioned for advanced problems over previously studied topics rather than first-time instruction
target_learners: Grades 2–6 students using Genie 2 who have completed objectives in Guided Study
target_learning_goals: Mastery of more advanced (level B and C) problems on previously studied objectives

title: Detailed lesson scripts capturing expert teachers' instructional decision-making
description: For each objective, an expert Russian teacher writes a detailed script describing how they would present it, including material presented to students plus bracketed instructions for which questions to ask and how to respond to different answers. An early failure led to redesign: initial textbook-style Theory content involved little student activity, so the system was changed to ask students questions on every screen, or roughly every half minute. Curriculum developers then revise scripts for cultural fit while a lead teacher reviews to ensure the mathematical and pedagogical structure is preserved.
requirements: Expert teacher authors, translation to English, curriculum developer revision, and lead-teacher review
Scripts must preserve the mathematical and pedagogical structure through revision
constraints: The level of detail of the scripts varies considerably from teacher to teacher, especially in the degree of interactivity
target_learners: Grades 2–6 students studying mathematics through Genie 2
target_learning_goals: Delivery of content-specific expert teaching practices, including questioning, explanations, and misconception handling
examples: A script excerpt shows solving 12 + _ = 83, with branching on whether the student identifies it as an equation with an unknown summand

title: Design intelligent tutoring systems for cross-cultural transfer by knowledge-engineering expert teachers from the source tradition
description: The article proposes a methodology for developing intelligent tutoring systems that transfer curriculum between countries: interview a panel of expert teachers from the source tradition, codify their practices into system algorithms and detailed scripts, iteratively pilot in destination-country classrooms, and use the system to deliver instructional experiences directly to students while scaffolding destination teachers' learning. The authors argue this is promising precisely because professional knowledge is voluminous and cultural, making conventional translation of textbooks prohibitively difficult: "the curriculum should properly be considered not just as the books... as the sequence of instructional experiences intended to be delivered to students".
requirements: Access to a panel of expert teachers from the source tradition
Iterative design-research cycles with development, piloting, and analysis in destination schools
Multiple information sources: teacher interviews and feedback, qualitative classroom observations, and quantitative log data
constraints: Developed and demonstrated for mathematics curriculum transfer from Russia to the United States; the article proposes these as general principles based on this single case
target_learners: Students in the destination country studying the imported curriculum (here, US grades 2–6 mathematics students)
target_learning_goals: Learning the source country's curriculum content and instructional methods in the destination country
examples: The panel's feedback on warm-up activities led to a new element type, speed games — timed sequences of mental math items in an appealing visual form replacing untimed, undifferentiated problem sequences

article_title: Jim Greer’s and Mary Mark’s Reviews of Evaluation Methods for Adaptive Systems: a Brief Comment about New Goals
citation: du Boulay, B. (2021). Jim Greer's and Mary Mark's Reviews of Evaluation Methods for Adaptive Systems: a Brief Comment about New Goals. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 31, 622–635. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00198-z
title: A taxonomy of learner-focused evaluable goals extending outcome, efficiency, transfer, retention and short-term motivation measures
description: The article proposes that evaluation of adaptive systems should extend beyond Mark and Greer's goals to "a new range of evaluative goals which go beyond the quality of learning outcomes, learning efficiency, transfer, retention, and short-term motivation." Table 1 lists learner-focused evaluable goals a-n, adding metacognitive understanding and regulatory skill, meta-affective awareness and regulation of feelings, pleasure in learning for its own sake, participation in learning activities, and cooperation between learners, each with suggested measures such as think-aloud problem-solving, self-reports, open learner models and long-delayed post-questionnaires.
requirements: Evaluation designs must add measures such as think-aloud problem-solving, self-reports, open learner models, long-delayed post-questionnaires or long-term cohort studies to capture these goals
constraints: The rows a-g of Table 1 are those already covered by Mark & Greer; only h-n are new
target_learners: school and university learners using AIED and computer-based learning systems
target_learning_goals: metacognitive understanding and regulatory skill
meta-affective awareness and regulation
longer-term motivation and appetite for further learning
examples: Table 1 lists goals including "Meta-cognitive understanding of the learning outcome, e.g. via think aloud problem-solving, observation of future learning" and "Increased pleasure in the act of learning for its own sake, e.g. via long-delayed post-questionnaires or interviews."

article_title: Jim Greer’s and Mary Mark’s Reviews of Evaluation Methods for Adaptive Systems: a Brief Comment about New Goals
citation: du Boulay, B. (2021). Jim Greer's and Mary Mark's Reviews of Evaluation Methods for Adaptive Systems: a Brief Comment about New Goals. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 31, 622–635. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00198-z
title: Orchestration systems fall into three broad types and bring new teacher-focused evaluable goals
description: The article argues that the centrality of the human teacher in classrooms using AIED systems has led to "orchestration" systems (Dillenbourg 2013) that assist teachers to manage the added complexity. "These orchestration systems fall into three broad types": systems for classes where all learners work with an AIED system and the teacher needs help targeting extra help; systems helping teachers track learners using more standard technology; and systems working directly with learners while offering the teacher a dashboard of general difficulties. They open new evaluable goals, e.g. "the degree to which the human teacher's time is being used effectively", changes in the division of labour, better diagnosis of difficulties, and reification of orchestration for teacher reflection.
requirements: Such systems assume a human teacher in the loop, with learners exposed to individual or small-group work with the AIED system, interaction with the teacher, and whole-class teaching
constraints: Orchestration systems were not yet built when Mark and Greer (1993) wrote, and were not strongly in evidence at Greer's 2016 retrospective
target_learners: school students in classes where the teacher deploys AIED systems
target_learning_goals: effective use of scarce teacher time
teacher awareness of learner difficulties
teacher reflection on planned versus actual orchestration
examples: ASSISTments is described as a system students use for homework which "also provides, the next day, an analysis for the teacher of their common and individual difficulties to help the teacher choose what issues to focus on."
