title: Treat interest and engagement as necessary but not sufficient for learning, preserving room for reflection
description: The article warns of "a tension between capturing interest and provoking engagement as against fostering effective learning, in that interest and engagement are (mostly) necessary but not sufficient conditions for learning." Learning other than rote needs a reflective component that can be drowned out if engagement and fun leave no room for it. Designs that capture interest should therefore protect space for reflection, since individual differences in self-regulation and cognitive load affect how much is learned in game-based environments.
requirements: Learning designs must include a reflective component alongside interest-capture and engagement mechanisms
constraints: In game-based learning, individual differences in self-regulation ability and cognitive load capacity affect how much is actually learned
target_learners: learners in game-based or highly engaging learning environments
target_learning_goals: effective learning beyond engagement
reflection on learned material
examples: The article cites reviews of the positive and negative attributes of game-based learning and notes that many questions about games' effectiveness remain unresolved.

title: MEWS corpus of L2 argumentative essays with analytic trait scores (content, organization, language quality)
description: The MEWS corpus (Measuring Writing Skills in English as a Second Language) contains "argumentative essays written by German and Swiss L2 upper secondary school students". article_title: From Small Seeds Grow Fruitful Trees: How the PHelpS Peer Help System Stimulated a Diverse and Innovative Research Agenda over 15 Years
citation: Vassileva, J., McCalla, G. I., & Greer, J. E. (2015). From Small Seeds Grow Fruitful Trees: How the PHelpS Peer Help System Stimulated a Diverse and Innovative Research Agenda over 15 Years. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0073-9
title: PHelpS peer help system matching ready, willing and able helpers via inspectable user models
description: PHelpS helped Correctional Service Canada workers find peer helpers when stuck while using the OMS database. It relied on two minimalist AI methodologies: a knowledge representation scheme capturing authentic tasks at many levels of detail, and user models overlaying task hierarchies recording which tasks each worker had carried out and how well. The system recommended peers who were "ready (were online at the time of the help request), willing (were logged into PHelpS and had indicated availability to help), and able (who knew how to accomplish that step and had proved able to help others in the past)". Help seekers and helpers could inspect user models and choose or refuse help, an early use of open learner modelling.
requirements: Task hierarchies capturing the organization's authentic tasks, which need verification, updating and consistency maintenance across units
User models capturing which tasks workers had carried out and how well
constraints: The sponsoring organization ended the project because the cost of implementing PHelpS, especially the intensive task modelling, was too high
Management could misuse individual user models to monitor workers, raising privacy concerns
target_learners: Workplace employees learning to use a complex database system
target_learning_goals: Just-in-time task-oriented learning in the workplace
examples: A proof-of-concept test with real workers at the Saskatoon Regional Psychiatric Centre of CSC using a limited number of simulated but realistic tasks

International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0073-9
title: Active user modelling paradigm: user model as a context-based computation, not a knowledge structure
description: The active user modelling paradigm arose when the authors observed that in their distributed MAGALE architecture each user held up to 20 fragmented models stored across many agents, so that in a real sense the user model ceased to be an object. It views user modelling as a process, "a computation (function) over a space of four major dimensions: subjects, objects, purposes and resources", where the subject does the modelling, the object is modelled, the purpose is the adaptation served, and the resources contribute information. It shifts focus from representation issues to the process of collecting, interpreting and utilising user data for a particular purpose, making it a procedural rather than declarative approach.
requirements: A purpose for which the model is being created, plus defined subject, object and contributing resources for each modelling activity
Ability to interpret multi-modal information from multiple heterogeneous sources and integrate it into a user model of appropriate granularity
constraints: When user models are fragmented in a decentralized architecture there is no single user model at all, only the subset of user characteristics important to the task at hand
target_learners: Learners and workers in distributed help and learning systems
target_learning_goals: Context-appropriate helper recommendation and adaptation
examples: A multi-agent recommender system for investment portfolio management built on a library of purpose-based user modelling processes combined at run time depending on context and resource availability

citation: Vassileva, J., McCalla, G. I., & Greer, J. E. (2015). International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0073-9
title: Ecological approach architecture: learning object repositories storing fragmented learner models whose interaction patterns are mined for pedagogical goals
description: The ecological approach (EA) abstracts learning environments as learning object repositories that include learning material, learning technology and other learners, later activated as agents. All interactions between learners and learning objects are recorded at a fine-grained level and stored with the object, "constituting fragmented learner models (as in I-Help) distributed throughout the repository". Over time this data can be mined for patterns fulfilling pedagogical goals such as recommending the next learning object by comparing a learner's interaction patterns with those of similar learners, recommending helpful peers, or inferring traditional learner models.
requirements: Fine-grained recording of learner-object interactions (even keystrokes) stored with each learning object
Large accumulated interaction data over many learners pursuing many learning goals
constraints: The article notes simulation will never replace human testing; the EA has been tested largely through low-fidelity simulation experiments
target_learners: Learners in technology-saturated, lifelong learning contexts
target_learning_goals: Just-in-time contextualized learning support; recommending next learning objects; recommending helpful peers
examples: The EA platform (EAP) simulation explored strategies for recommending learning objects to determine which strategy worked best; other simulations examined peer-performance observation and data-driven instructional planning

article_title: Towards a Tutoring System to Support Robotics Activities in Classrooms – Two Wizard-of-Oz Studies
citation: Sandra Schulz · Bruce M. McLaren · Niels Pinkwart. (2023). Towards a Tutoring System to Support Robotics Activities in Classrooms – Two Wizard-of-Oz Studies. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 33. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00305-2
title: Taxonomy of students' problems during robotics activities with four main categories
description: A taxonomy of the problems students encounter during robotics activities, developed from existing literature and a prior qualitative analysis by Schulz and Pinkwart (2017). It organizes problems into the main categories “hardware”, “software”, “environment” and “math/physics”, each with subcategories such as construction, sensor malfunction, program code, interference from humans, and determining a threshold (Table 1). The authors use the taxonomy as the basis for the cognitive model that governs when and how the wizards give feedback.
requirements: Derived from existing literature and a prior qualitative analysis of students' problems; intended to categorize problems so that support can target the appropriate category.
constraints: Wizards reported the taxonomy did not cover handling the tools and suggested more subcategories were needed; task configuration in WOZ I made software problems dominant.
target_learners: secondary school students in robotics and computer science activities
target_learning_goals: problem-solving and debugging during robotics tasks
examples: Table 1 lists main categories with subcategories such as Hardware: Construction, Malfunction of sensor, Broken sensor; Software: Program code, Programming environment, Firmware from robot.
key_sources: Sandra Schulz · Bruce M. McLaren · Niels Pinkwart. (2023). Towards a Tutoring System to Support Robotics Activities in Classrooms – Two Wizard-of-Oz Studies. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 33. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00305-2

article_title: Towards a Tutoring System to Support Robotics Activities in Classrooms – Two Wizard-of-Oz Studies
citation: Sandra Schulz · Bruce M. McLaren · Niels Pinkwart. (2023). Towards a Tutoring System to Support Robotics Activities in Classrooms – Two Wizard-of-Oz Studies. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 33. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00305-2
title: Give robotics feedback through a four-layer escalation from general problem category to concrete solution
description: Feedback during robotics problem-solving should escalate through four layers: naming the main problem category, then the subcategory, then a situation-specific description of the problem without revealing the solution, and only in the fourth layer the concrete problem and a solution. Wizards “go[] always from the 1st layer to the 4th layer and only providing more detailed help if needed”, so students are led toward the solution without being handed it, and each new independent problem restarts at layer 1.
requirements: Wizards trained in the model and its feedback rules, with standardized wording, continuous observation of students' interaction, body language and progress, and support only when help is needed.
constraints: Wording on layers 3 and 4 may vary slightly by wizard; timing of further hints varies with students' motivation and self-efficacy; one wizard reported needing to jump directly to layer 4 when earlier layers were not understood.
target_learners: secondary school students (grades 7–11) working in pairs on robotics programming tasks
target_learning_goals: problem-solving, debugging, and troubleshooting strategy during robotics activities
examples: In the worked example, the wizard tells students the problem lies in the software (layer 1), in the program code (layer 2), that the robot should not drive so close to the box (layer 3), and finally to program the ultrasonic threshold to at least 15 cm (layer 4).

article_title: Teaching Responsible Data Science: Charting New Pedagogical Territory
citation: Lewis Armanda; Stoyanovich Julia. (2021). Teaching Responsible Data Science: Charting New Pedagogical Territory. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00241-7
title: Objects-to-interpret-with: representational devices targeting metacognition of interpretation and representation
description: The article proposes objects-to-interpret-with as a methodological notion for RDS education, inspired by Papert's constructivist objects-to-think-with. They are "representational devices that aid learners in developing heuristic knowledge and understanding contextual knowledge, with a focus on the metacognitive aspects of interpretation and representation." Instances include model cards, datasheets, and nutritional labels, which present information multimodally, support active learning, and develop metacognition while revealing the partiality and latent mechanisms of algorithms and platforms.
requirements: Specifying the intended audience and purpose of interpretability is essential, as is articulating the desired balance between model performance and model interpretability.
constraints: The article focuses the framework on a population whose technical sophistication lies in the middle — students of data science.
target_learners: graduate and advanced undergraduate data science students
target_learning_goals: interpretability of data and machine learning models
metacognition involving interpretation and representation
examples: The course project has students develop nutritional labels for Automated Decision Systems as an object-to-interpret-with, serving as an end-to-end auditing device for the entire ADS.
key_sources: Lewis Armanda; Stoyanovich Julia. (2021). Teaching Responsible Data Science: Charting New Pedagogical Territory. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00241-7

article_title: Teaching Responsible Data Science: Charting New Pedagogical Territory
citation: Lewis Armanda; Stoyanovich Julia. (2021). Teaching Responsible Data Science: Charting New Pedagogical Territory. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00241-7
title: Nutritional label for Automated Decision Systems as the RDS course's object-to-interpret-with project deliverable
description: In the RDS course project, students design an original object-to-interpret-with in the form of a nutritional label for an Automated Decision System. "Adhering to constructivist principles, students develop nutritional labels for ADS." The label combines textual explanations and graphic information, requires students to distill the most important information about a model and adapt it for non-technical audiences, and functions as an end-to-end auditing device for the entire ADS.
requirements: Students are expected to have basic familiarity with the python programming language, which is used in labs and assignments.
constraints: The authors state the nutritional label is not the singular way to communicate a model to diverse audiences, since it does not make a model definitively interpretable to all stakeholders and for all purposes.
target_learners: graduate and advanced undergraduate data science students
target_learning_goals: making Automated Decision Systems interpretable
identifying intended audiences and non-transparent aspects of ADS
examples: The final course project combines elements of a replication study, process analysis, design and deployment, and nutritional label design; students replicate a model with an existing dataset and algorithm and identify transparency flaws.
key_sources: Lewis Armanda; Stoyanovich Julia. (2021). Teaching Responsible Data Science: Charting New Pedagogical Territory. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00241-7

article_title: Teaching Responsible Data Science: Charting New Pedagogical Territory
citation: Lewis Armanda; Stoyanovich Julia. (2021). Teaching Responsible Data Science: Charting New Pedagogical Territory. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00241-7
title: Ranking Facts: an open-source tool that automatically constructs a nutritional-label summary of algorithmic rankers
description: Ranking Facts is an existing instance of an object-to-interpret-with in the RDS space. It "automatically constructs a user friendly summary of several important properties of algorithmic rankers, including stability, statistical parity, and diversity." Its Fairness pane supports intuitive understanding of statistical parity at top ranks without requiring knowledge of the fairness metric's mathematical properties, and its Diversity pane signals how item categories are represented at top ranks versus the overall dataset.
requirements: Constructed automatically by the open-source web-based tool, per the Fig. 3 caption.
constraints: Ranking Facts reveals that rankings may be highly sensitive to inputs and can hide disparate impacts on subsets of data.
target_learners: lay audiences and data science students
target_learning_goals: understanding fairness, diversity, and stability of algorithmic rankings
examples: Fig. 3 shows the Ranking Facts nutritional label for a dataset of university department rankings, from the demo at dataresponsibly.com.
key_sources: Lewis Armanda; Stoyanovich Julia. (2021). Teaching Responsible Data Science: Charting New Pedagogical Territory. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00241-7

article_title: Teaching Responsible Data Science: Charting New Pedagogical Territory
citation: Lewis Armanda; Stoyanovich Julia. (2021). Teaching Responsible Data Science: Charting New Pedagogical Territory. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00241-7
title: Dataset Nutrition Label: a manually constructed framework of modules for dataset transparency
description: Developed by a second team (Holland et al., 2018), the Dataset Nutrition Label is a framework using the nutritional-label paradigm for algorithmic transparency. It "provides modules that display metadata and source information, textual descriptions and summary statistics of variables, as well as graphs visualizing more complex information like probabilistic models and ground truth correlations." It contributes to transparency by taking a descriptive snapshot of a dataset's inherent qualities and introducing interpretable features such as keywords.
requirements: The Probabilistic Modeling pane requires knowledge of a model's properties, though a highly visual presentation facilitates understanding.
constraints: In contrast to Ranking Facts, which is computed automatically, the Dataset Nutrition Label prototype shown in Fig. 4 is manually constructed.
target_learners: dataset creators and dataset consumers, technical and non-technical
target_learning_goals: understanding dataset creation, usage, and maintenance, including emergent and pre-existing bias
examples: Fig. 4 shows the Dataset Nutrition Label prototype representing the COMPAS Recidivism Risk Score Dataset.
key_sources: Lewis Armanda; Stoyanovich Julia. (2021). Teaching Responsible Data Science: Charting New Pedagogical Territory. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00241-7

article_title: Teaching Responsible Data Science: Charting New Pedagogical Territory
citation: Lewis Armanda; Stoyanovich Julia. (2021). Teaching Responsible Data Science: Charting New Pedagogical Territory. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00241-7
title: A table of nine pedagogical activities for teaching interpretability, each paired with an assessment method
description: Table 1 of the article lays out pedagogically-sound activities mapping learning-science best practices to RDS interpretability practice, including replicating an existing study, reverse engineering a platform, diagnostic learning logs, problem recognition tasks, process analysis, peer review, before-after iteration, design and deploy, and creating a nutritional label for a machine learning platform. "Table 1 showcases several pedagogically-sound activities that map to best practices in the learning sciences and to RDS interpretability practices." Each activity is paired with an assessment method such as metrics evaluation, open coding, cognitive walkthroughs, or A/B testing.
requirements: Activities should be offered through multiple presentation modes and levels of interactivity to maximize engagement and promote heuristics development.
constraints: The authors state that future iterations of the course will tie in further pedagogical principles.
target_learners: diverse groups of students with varying technical and theoretical prior knowledge, from varied disciplinary backgrounds, and with different learning goals
target_learning_goals: interpretability of data and models
transitioning from novice to expert level knowledge
examples: In Table 1, replicating an existing study has students reconstruct a (portion of a) published study and highlight any replication issues, assessed via metrics evaluation and content analysis.
The RDS course incorporates some of these activities; its final project combines replication study, process analysis, design and deployment, and nutritional label design.
key_sources: Lewis Armanda; Stoyanovich Julia. (2021). Teaching Responsible Data Science: Charting New Pedagogical Territory. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00241-7

article_title: Teaching Responsible Data Science: Charting New Pedagogical Territory
citation: Lewis Armanda; Stoyanovich Julia. (2021). Teaching Responsible Data Science: Charting New Pedagogical Territory. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00241-7
title: Teach ethics and responsibility early in the data science program and keep prerequisites minimal to enroll a diverse student group
description: The RDS course requires only an introductory data science or computer science course, deliberately excluding machine learning as a prerequisite. "This is a deliberate choice that reflects our goals to (1) educate data science students on ethics and responsibility early in their program of study, and (2) to enroll a diverse group of students." The semester-long course is structured as six thematic modules combining case studies, algorithmic and statistical insights, and hands-on exercises with open-source datasets and software libraries.
requirements: Students are expected to have basic familiarity with the python programming language, which is used in labs and assignments.
constraints: The authors faced a lack of a textbook offering comprehensive coverage of RDS balancing case studies, social-science concepts, and statistical and algorithmic techniques, so the course has no required textbook.
target_learners: graduate and advanced undergraduate data science students, including first-year students
target_learning_goals: ethics and responsibility in data science
algorithmic fairness, privacy, transparency, and interpretability
examples: The six modules span introduction, the data science lifecycle with profiling and cleaning, algorithmic fairness and diversity, privacy and data protection, transparency and interpretability, and ethical, legal, and regulatory frameworks.
Students are encouraged to attend public hearings of the New York City Committee on Technology on regulation of Automated Decision Systems and reflect on them in discussion.
key_sources: Lewis Armanda; Stoyanovich Julia. (2021). Teaching Responsible Data Science: Charting New Pedagogical Territory. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00241-7

article_title: Data-Driven Hint Generation in Vast Solution Spaces: a Self-Improving Python Programming Tutor
citation: Kelly Rivers & Kenneth R. Koedinger. (2015). Data-Driven Hint Generation in Vast Solution Spaces: a Self-Improving Python Programming Tutor. International Artificial Intelligence in Education Society. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0070-z
title: ITAP: data-driven hint generation via state abstraction, path construction, and state reification
description: ITAP (Intelligent Teaching Assistant for Programming) is a self-improving data-driven tutoring system that generates personalized next-step hints for code-writing problems. It combines algorithms for "state abstraction, path construction, and state reification to fully automate the process of hint generation", building a solution space graph from student states and constructing paths even for never-seen states. It requires only a reference solution and an automatic test method, and updates the solution space every time a student attempts a solution.
requirements: At least one reference solution to the problem (e.g. a teacher exemplar)
A test method that can automatically score code (e.g. pairs of expected input and output)
constraints: ITAP currently recognizes correct solutions and provides hints on semantically or algorithmically incorrect programs; it is not implemented to handle syntactically incorrect programs
States with more than 15 edits are given a simple path directly to the original goal due to the exponential nature of power sets
target_learners: Novice programmers in introductory programming courses
target_learning_goals: Writing correct Python code for code-writing problems
Moving from incorrect program states to correct solutions via next-step hints
examples: The article demonstrates the full process on an isWeekend problem, where a student's lowercase-string error is canonicalized, a two-edit macro path is constructed, reification locates the edit in the original code, and a bottom-out hint template is filled out
key_sources: Kelly Rivers & Kenneth R. Koedinger. (2015). Data-Driven Hint Generation in Vast Solution Spaces: a Self-Improving Python Programming Tutor. International Artificial Intelligence in Education Society. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0070-z

article_title: Modelling Human Teaching Tactics and Strategies for Tutoring Systems: 14 Years On
citation: Benedict du Boulay & Rosemary Luckin. (2015). Modelling Human Teaching Tactics and Strategies for Tutoring Systems: 14 Years On. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0053-0
title: INSPIRE framework characterising expert one-to-one tutors
description: The INSPIRE framework (Intelligent, Nurturant, Socratic, Progressive, Indirect, Reflective, Encouraging) provides an empirically observed account of expert human teachers working one-to-one. The review reports that it characterises expert behaviour, compared to less expert teachers, along dimensions including "their use of questions rather than didactic statements", attention to motivating and encouraging students, and fostering learner reflection on process. The review uses it as a benchmark of expert teaching richness and as a design source for the GURU tutor.
requirements: Requires empirical observation of expert tutors working one-to-one to ground the framework's dimensions
constraints: The review notes both the meta-analysis and meta-review underplay the motivational aspects of expert teaching that INSPIRE emphasises
target_learning_goals: domain learning supported alongside student motivation
examples: GURU embodied the INSPIRE framework of Lepper and Woolverton (2002) alongside expert-teacher coding to provide conversational teaching in Biology
key_sources: Benedict du Boulay & Rosemary Luckin. (2015). Modelling Human Teaching Tactics and Strategies for Tutoring Systems: 14 Years On. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0053-0

article_title: Modelling Human Teaching Tactics and Strategies for Tutoring Systems: 14 Years On
citation: Benedict du Boulay & Rosemary Luckin. (2015). Modelling Human Teaching Tactics and Strategies for Tutoring Systems: 14 Years On. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0053-0
title: Akhras and Self's four properties of constructivist learning interaction sequences
description: Under Akhras and Self's view of Constructivism, teaching emphasises "the process rather than the product of learning", and intelligent learning environments evaluate learning according to four properties of constructivist learning processes: cumulativeness, constructiveness, self-regulatedness, and reflectiveness. These properties describe sequences of learning interactions and inform decisions about the learning opportunities provided to learners, taking into account the affordances of learning situations. The review presents this as an example of teaching strategies derived from epistemological learning theories.
requirements: Learning environments must be able to evaluate learning interactions according to the four properties to make decisions about learning opportunities
constraints: The framework is presented as one constructivist view among several overlapping theory-derived strategies in the review
target_learning_goals: constructivist learning processes including self-regulation and reflection
examples: Cumulativeness involves the same entity being experienced more than once in a sequence; constructiveness involves entities experienced earlier being related to new entities the learner generates later
key_sources: Benedict du Boulay & Rosemary Luckin. (2015). Modelling Human Teaching Tactics and Strategies for Tutoring Systems: 14 Years On. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0053-0

article_title: Spendency: Students’ Propensity to Use System Currency
citation: Snow, E. L., Allen, L. K., Jackson, G. T., & McNamara, D. S. (2015). Spendency: Students' Propensity to Use System Currency. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 25, 407–427. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0044-1
title: iSTART-ME: game-based intelligent tutoring system with iBucks currency and unlockable features
description: iSTART-ME is the motivationally enhanced, game-based version of the iSTART reading-strategy tutor, in which earned points double as spendable currency: "The points that students earn throughout their interactions with iSTART serve as a form of currency (iBucks) and can be used to unlock game-based features within the system." Students spend iBucks on avatar and theme personalization and on strategy mini-games, and advance through levels ranging from 0 to 25 that unlock additional features.
requirements: Students must earn iBucks through practice interactions before features can be purchased; "Each of these system features requires either 300 or 450 iBucks."
constraints: The system "uses an unlocking scaffolding with these personalizable features, thus, as students advance within the system they are rewarded with the opportunity to buy more game-based features."
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension through self-explanation strategy training
examples: In the study, 40 high school students interacted with the full game-based selection menu across eight training sessions, earning and spending iBucks on personalizable features and mini-games.
key_sources: Snow, E. L., Allen, L. K., Jackson, G. T., & McNamara, D. S. (2015). Spendency: Students' Propensity to Use System Currency. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 25, 407–427. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0044-1

article_title: Spendency: Students’ Propensity to Use System Currency
citation: Snow, E. L., Allen, L. K., Jackson, G. T., & McNamara, D. S. (2015). Spendency: Students' Propensity to Use System Currency. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 25, 407–427. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0044-1
title: Spendency: the construct of students' propensity to spend in-game currency
description: Spendency is the construct this article introduces for students' propensity to use system currency: "Students'propensity to use system currency as a way to engage with the game-based features was defined as their spendency." It is operationalized as a proportion, "total points spent / total points earned," indexing how much of a student's available iBucks was spent on mini-games and personalizable features rather than hoarded. The authors state the term "can be applied to any system that utilizes a gamification technique where in-game currency is applicable."
requirements: Requires logged process data recording the currency each student earned and the currency each student spent within the system.
target_learners: high school students using game-based learning systems
target_learning_goals: understanding how engagement with game-based currency features relates to learning outcomes
examples: In the study, spendency ranged from 0.0 to 0.99 (M=0.49, SD=0.26), revealing that some students never spent iBucks while others spent them as soon as they were earned.
key_sources: Snow, E. L., Allen, L. K., Jackson, G. T., & McNamara, D. S. (2015). Spendency: Students' Propensity to Use System Currency. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 25, 407–427. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0044-1

article_title: Spendency: Students’ Propensity to Use System Currency
citation: Snow, E. L., Allen, L. K., Jackson, G. T., & McNamara, D. S. (2015). Spendency: Students' Propensity to Use System Currency. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 25, 407–427. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0044-1
title: Include game-based currency features with caution so they do not interfere with the learning goal relative to the system's timeframe
description: The article recommends that developers treat currency-backed game features as a potential cost to performance: "These initial results should warn developers to ensure that the inclusion of features does not interfere with the learning goal relative to the timeframe of the system." Because higher spendency harmed immediate and transfer outcomes while enjoyment and motivation stayed high, the appropriateness of game-based features depends on the system's learning goal and timeframe.
requirements: The system's learning goal and timeframe must be specified before deciding whether and how to include game-based currency features.
constraints: The article notes that "if the learning goal of a system is to show immediate gains in domain knowledge, the inclusion of game-based features may be detrimental to that goal," whereas in a system designed for long-term practice the immediate effects may matter less.
target_learners: high school students using game-based intelligent tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: protecting target skill acquisition and transfer when gamification elements are added
examples: In the iSTART-ME study, students with higher spendency showed lower in-system achievement, lower daily self-explanation quality, and lower transfer comprehension despite reporting high enjoyment and motivation.
key_sources: Snow, E. L., Allen, L. K., Jackson, G. T., & McNamara, D. S. (2015). Spendency: Students' Propensity to Use System Currency. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 25, 407–427. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0044-1

article_title: Technology Support for Discussion Based Learning: From Computer Supported Collaborative Learning to the Future of Massive Open Online Courses
citation: Carolyn Penstein Rosé & Oliver Ferschke. (2016). Technology Support for Discussion Based Learning: From Computer Supported Collaborative Learning to the Future of Massive Open Online Courses. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0107-y
title: Quick Helper: peer help recommendation in a MOOC using context-aware matrix factorization
description: The Quick Helper is a discussion-focused intervention integrated with DALMOOC to support help seeking and increase the chance that help requests receive satisfactory responses. Students click a button, are guided to formulate a help request posted to the MOOC discussion board, and "a context-aware matrix factorization model selects three potential help providers from the pool of student peers" based on features of students, questions, and student connections. Selected helpers receive an automatic email invitation to the thread.
requirements: Requires a context-aware matrix factorization model built from students' help-request text and metadata rather than large-scale knowledge engineering about learners
constraints: The article states it attempts to attract help to requests as formulated but does not support the process of asking for help effectively, nor does it directly address reticent help seekers
target_learners: MOOC participants in the Data, Analytics, and Learning course
target_learning_goals: Effective help seeking and peer help exchange in online discussion forums
examples: Deployed in DALMOOC on the edX platform as an example of integrating learning interventions with current MOOC platforms
key_sources: Carolyn Penstein Rosé & Oliver Ferschke. (2016). Technology Support for Discussion Based Learning: From Computer Supported Collaborative Learning to the Future of Massive Open Online Courses. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0107-y

article_title: Technology Support for Discussion Based Learning: From Computer Supported Collaborative Learning to the Future of Massive Open Online Courses
citation: Carolyn Penstein Rosé & Oliver Ferschke. (2016). Technology Support for Discussion Based Learning: From Computer Supported Collaborative Learning to the Future of Massive Open Online Courses. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0107-y
title: Bazaar Collaborative Reflection: agent-supported synchronous chat in a MOOC
description: Bazaar Collaborative Reflection makes synchronous collaboration opportunities available to students in a MOOC context, importing agent-supported collaborative learning technology in which "conversational computer agents can serve as effective automated facilitators of synchronous collaborative learning". A Lobby program matches waiting students with a random conversational partner; matched pairs receive a link to a chat room where they interact with each other and with a conversational agent appearing as a regular user.
requirements: Requires a Lobby matching mechanism and a MOOC platform integration providing chat rooms with an embedded conversational agent
constraints: Typical MOOC providers do not offer opportunities for synchronous collaboration, which the technology requires
target_learners: MOOC participants in the Data, Analytics, and Learning course
target_learning_goals: Collaborative reflection and discussion-based learning at scale
examples: Integrated into DALMOOC by means of a Lobby program where students wait to be matched, then chat with a partner and an agent in a private chat room
key_sources: Carolyn Penstein Rosé & Oliver Ferschke. (2016). Technology Support for Discussion Based Learning: From Computer Supported Collaborative Learning to the Future of Massive Open Online Courses. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0107-y

article_title: Technology Support for Discussion Based Learning: From Computer Supported Collaborative Learning to the Future of Massive Open Online Courses
citation: Carolyn Penstein Rosé & Oliver Ferschke. (2016). Technology Support for Discussion Based Learning: From Computer Supported Collaborative Learning to the Future of Massive Open Online Courses. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0107-y
title: Micro-script support: integrating text mining and conversational agents for dynamic collaborative learning support
description: The article's central explanatory account is that support for collaborative learning has evolved from static scripted collaboration (structured interfaces, prompts, scripted roles) toward adaptive, context-sensitive support. This "novel type of micro-script support for productive discussion processes" is "enabled by an integration of text mining and conversational agents". Automatic analysis of collaborative processes enables real-time assessment, dynamically triggered interventions during sessions, and efficient analysis of collaborative learning interactions.
requirements: Requires on-line monitoring of collaborative learning processes via automatic analysis of discussion behavior
constraints: So far, automated collaborative learning process analysis has focused on text-based interactions and key-click data; audio analysis has only begun and automated video analysis remains future work
target_learners: collaborative learning groups in online courses
target_learning_goals: Productive discussion processes and knowledge building in collaborative learning
examples: The Quick Helper and Bazaar interventions in DALMOOC instantiate dynamic support triggered by automated analysis of discussion behavior

article_title: Statistical Techniques to Explore the Quality of Constraints in Constraint-Based Modeling Environments
citation: Gálvez, J., Conejo, R., & Guzmán, E. (2013). Statistical Techniques to Explore the Quality of Constraints in Constraint-Based Modeling Environments. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0008-2
title: The IRT+CBM framework treats constraints as psychometric items, enabling data-driven assessment of constraint quality
description: The article proposes a framework that combines Constraint-Based Modeling with Item Response Theory, based on an analogy between constraints and items: both are 'measurement instruments that, though in different environments, collect evidence of knowledge.' A Constraint Characteristic Curve is defined for each constraint, representing the probability of satisfying it as a function of knowledge, allowing IRT mechanisms such as calibration and information analysis to be applied in CBM tutors. The framework replaces heuristic estimates of constraint mastery with a well-founded probabilistic technique.
requirements: A calibration process with prior data from students' performance is needed to estimate CCC parameters before IRT mechanisms can be applied
constraints: If a constraint is always violated or never violated by any student, the information it provides is not relevant for assessment and it only introduces noise
target_learners: students in problem solving learning environments
target_learning_goals: domain principle mastery assessed via constraint satisfaction and violation
key_sources: Gálvez, J., Conejo, R., & Guzmán, E. (2013). Statistical Techniques to Explore the Quality of Constraints in Constraint-Based Modeling Environments. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0008-2

article_title: Statistical Techniques to Explore the Quality of Constraints in Constraint-Based Modeling Environments
citation: Gálvez, J., Conejo, R., & Guzmán, E. (2013). Statistical Techniques to Explore the Quality of Constraints in Constraint-Based Modeling Environments. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0008-2
title: PIPSE: a project investment problem solving environment with CBM+IRT assessment
description: PIPSE is a web-based problem solving environment developed for a Project Management course, focused on 'the study of the profitability of starting up a project given a series of variables associated with the costs and benefits'. Students apply indexes such as Net Present Value and Internal Rate of Return, building solutions in a datasheet-like table whose formulas the system interprets automatically. The interface 'tries to reduce the cognitive overload' so that inherent calculus does not burden working memory. Student solutions are sent via Web Services to assessment subsystems, including the CBM+IRT component, making the system suitable for both assessment and learning.
requirements: External assessment subsystems communicate with PIPSE through Web Services and can be dynamically replaced, added, or removed
constraints: The domain is well-defined with a small domain model of 17 constraints categorized into three subsets
target_learning_goals: project investment profitability analysis using NPV and IRR
examples: In the experiments, student exam solutions were introduced into PIPSE, which sent them to CBM-Engine for constraint checking and calibration
key_sources: Gálvez, J., Conejo, R., & Guzmán, E. (2013). Statistical Techniques to Explore the Quality of Constraints in Constraint-Based Modeling Environments. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0008-2

article_title: Statistical Techniques to Explore the Quality of Constraints in Constraint-Based Modeling Environments
citation: Gálvez, J., Conejo, R., & Guzmán, E. (2013). Statistical Techniques to Explore the Quality of Constraints in Constraint-Based Modeling Environments. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0008-2
title: CBM-Engine: a service-oriented assessment component implementing CBM with IRT
description: The CBM-Engine is 'a Service Oriented Architecture-based component' that implements CBM with IRT assessment, designed so its services 'can be used to apply the previously explained methodology in any external system/tutor'. It uses a three-layered architecture: a top services layer offering Web Services, a business logic layer where inferences are carried out, and a persistence layer storing data structures. External systems communicate through three SOA entry points — management, session, and IRT — each with an internal module handling incoming information and returning violated constraints or IRT results.
requirements: External systems or tutors must be registered using an authoring tool that defines constraints and the data structures providing solution information
constraints: Its Web interface exists only for basic administrative tasks and is not part of the relevant architecture
target_learners: students in problem solving environments connected to the engine
target_learning_goals: assessment of domain knowledge via constraint violation and satisfaction
examples: PIPSE communicates only with the top services layer, sending external structures through the three entry points
key_sources: Gálvez, J., Conejo, R., & Guzmán, E. (2013). Statistical Techniques to Explore the Quality of Constraints in Constraint-Based Modeling Environments. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0008-2

article_title: Data-driven Exploration of Engagement with Workplace-based Assessment in the Clinical Skills Domain
citation: Alicja Piotrkowicz, Kaiwen Wang, Jennifer Hallam, Vania Dimitrova. (2021). Data-driven Exploration of Engagement with Workplace-based Assessment in the Clinical Skills Domain. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 31:1022–1052. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00264-0
title: Multi-faceted data-driven assessment analytics approach for workplace learning
description: A computational framework combining three analytical channels applied to workplace-based assessment data: "(i) a set of features for analysing clinical skills WBA data, (ii) analysis of the temporal aspects of that data using process mining, and (iii) utilising text analytics to compare student reflections on WBA". It is aimed at programme design and evaluation, helping instructors compare cohorts and assess the effectiveness of clinical settings, in contrast to student-centred analytics. The approach treats engagement with formative workplace assessment as a proxy for aspects of self-regulated learning.
requirements: Digitally recorded workplace-based assessment data with timestamps, categorical skill, entrustability level, assessor role, location, and free-text feedback and reflection fields
Stakeholder engagement from clinical education tutors and curriculum designers to identify key challenges and needs
constraints: Findings are from an exploratory case study of Year 1 medical students in one UK institution across three academic years
Short free-text fields (average 25 tokens for student reflection) limited the available text analysis

article_title: Adaptive Learning is Hard: Challenges, Nuances, and Trade-offs in Modeling
citation: Pelánek, R. (2025). Adaptive Learning is Hard: Challenges, Nuances, and Trade-offs in Modeling. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00400-6
title: Adaptive learning environments require three interlocking models: a student model, a domain model, and a pedagogical model
description: The article describes a basic architecture for personalization consisting of three models. A student model is "an abstraction of a student that serves as a basis for adaptive decisions"; a domain model abstracts the domain into learning units and their relations; a pedagogical model specifies the personalization strategy translating model information into system actions. The author notes the terminology varies widely and that any adaptive learning environment needs these three components in some form, illustrating them with a mathematics realization using knowledge components, prerequisite relations, Bayesian Knowledge Tracing, and mastery learning.
requirements: Any adaptive learning environment must realize all three model components in some form for personalization to occur.
constraints: Terminology varies widely across educational technology; the pedagogical model is often described with other terms such as instructional strategy or recommendation algorithm.
target_learners: students in mathematics, programming, and language learning domains
target_learning_goals: adaptive guidance and feedback appropriate to current student knowledge
examples: A mathematics realization maps tasks to knowledge components, defines prerequisite relations, uses Bayesian Knowledge Tracing for the student model, and drives mastery learning and recommendations from those estimates.

article_title: Adaptive Learning is Hard: Challenges, Nuances, and Trade-offs in Modeling
citation: Pelánek, R. (2025). Adaptive Learning is Hard: Challenges, Nuances, and Trade-offs in Modeling. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00400-6
title: Make design trade-offs in adaptive learning environments explicit, and favor easily realizable approaches when gains are small
description: The article argues designers must weigh cost-effectiveness under limited time, money, and people, since "it is not possible to avoid the issue of trade-offs" and making them explicit is beneficial. Because published research asks only whether an approach improves learning, it cannot tell designers that a slightly weaker but far more easily realizable approach Y should often get priority over X. The principle calls for research that explicitly takes trade-offs into account and for developers to state their compromises openly.
requirements: Awareness of resource constraints (time, money, people) and of the relative realizability of candidate approaches.
constraints: Existing research on whether an approach improves learning does not by itself provide guidance for practical trade-off decisions.
target_learners: designers and developers of adaptive learning environments
target_learning_goals: realistic design decisions for adaptive behavior in practical learning environments
examples: The article contrasts approach X with a smaller-improvement but much more easily realizable approach Y that should often get priority.
The article recommends more research explicitly taking trade-offs such as predictive accuracy versus computational requirements into account.

article_title: Different Topics, Similar Patterns: The Consistency of Learners and Learning Across Interactive STEM Simulations
citation: Jade Mai Cock · Ido Roll · Käser Tanja. (2025). Different Topics, Similar Patterns: The Consistency of Learners and Learning Across Interactive STEM Simulations. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00512-7
title: Three-paradigm feature-abstraction framework with spectral clustering for cross-topic inquiry-pattern analysis
description: The article presents a clustering framework to analyze log data from interactive simulations under three levels of topic abstraction: variable (simulation-specific qualification by independent variable), relationship (qualification by the nature of the variable–outcome relationship, generalizable across isomorphic simulations), and focus (simulation-agnostic qualification by number of involved variables). Sequences are transformed into Markov transition matrices and clustered with spectral clustering, which handles non-convex data. The framework aims to "identify productive inquiry patterns without relying on predefined behavior assumptions" and to offer insight into the trade-offs between topic-agnostic and context-rich representations.
requirements: Log data retaining timestamps and the simulation elements learners interact with, so interactions can be extracted into chronological action sequences.
Sufficient interaction log coverage per learner to build a transition matrix for each simulation activity.
constraints: The relationship paradigm is only generalizable across isomorphic simulations with similar types of relationships between independent and dependent variables.
The focus paradigm is very coarse and mainly captures context switching between variables.
Break thresholds were data driven (3s merge, 20s break) for these two labs and may not transfer to other environments.
target_learning_goals: Scientific inquiry skills such as forming hypotheses, collecting and interpreting data, and uncovering relationships between variables in interactive simulations
examples: Applied to Beer's Law Lab and Capacitor Lab logs: sequences were encoded per paradigm, transformed into transition matrices, and clustered with spectral clustering using k-means, yielding two clusters per lab with optimal nc = 2 and gamma = 10^-4.

It states that "Progress from Scholar to the present day has progressed along seven broad dimensions, as evidenced here largely through AIED citations", presenting each dimension with indicative citations rather than a complete review.

target_learning_goals: understanding how AI-based educational systems have developed in pedagogy, cognition, and social context

The notice explains that the article "was published due to a clerical error" and that it was retracted by the editorial team and authors. It supplies the DOI of the retracted online version and a Springer link to the correct published article chapter.

citation: Fabian Santiago-Muñoz, Mikel Larrañaga, Jon A. Elorriaga, Ana Arruarte. (2025). Identification of Patterns to Prevent the Failure of Engineering Students. Int J Artif Intell Educ 35:3356–3405. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00502-9
title: Exploratory unsupervised clustering methodology for identifying at-risk student profiles from pre-admission data
description: The article develops an exploratory, unsupervised methodology that applies clustering to university pre-admission data to find latent structures without predefined labels. "The process involves three main phases (see Fig. 1): Data Preparation, Experimentation and Analysis of the Selected Models." Model selection combines internal validation (Silhouette, Davies-Bouldin, Calinski-Harabasz), association with outcomes (Cramér's V), and cluster quality (purity, entropy) via a composite score. It is positioned as an alternative to deductive, theory-driven and supervised approaches.
requirements: Requires the necessary educational data to be available, as the article states the methodology is applicable to other subjects as long as such data exist
Requires sequential filtering with explicit thresholds (Silhouette > 0; Cramér's V > 0.3)
constraints: Applicable to other subjects only as long as the necessary educational data are available
Results depend on the choice of normalization technique

article_title: Advancing the Design and Implementation of Artificial Intelligence in Education through Continuous Improvement
citation: Bhimdiwala, A., Neri, R. C., & Gomez, L. M. (2022). Advancing the Design and Implementation of Artificial Intelligence in Education through Continuous Improvement. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00278-8
title: FATE in AIEd conceptualized as four interwoven, inseparable dimensions
description: The article defines FATE in AIEd as four interwoven dimensions: fairness attends to discrimination based on contextual and temporal student characteristics; accountability provides mechanisms for teacher knowhow and institutional resources; transparency discloses design rationale to practitioners; and ethics keeps "values of fairness, local voice, and agency in view". The authors state the dimensions are "interwoven and inseparable from one other", so a fairness issue entails transparency, ethics, or accountability problems.
requirements: Design, development, and implementation processes must address all four dimensions together rather than in isolation
constraints: The conceptualization was derived from literature within AI and AIEd communities, not empirically tested in this article
target_learning_goals: Fair and equitable algorithmic decision-making in educational technology

title: Six principles of Improvement Science as a framework for pursuing FATE in AIEd
description: The article presents Improvement Science (Bryk et al., 2015) as a continuous-improvement framework for AIEd, stating that "Improvement Science is guided by the following six principles": making work problem-specific and user-centered, treating variation in performance as the core problem, seeing the system that produces current outcomes, embedding measures of key outcomes, anchoring improvement in disciplined inquiry through PDSA cycles, and accelerating improvement through networked communities. It argues these principles develop user ownership needed to adapt AIEd to local contexts and address FATE issues that arise in practice.
requirements: Engagement of diverse stakeholders (teachers, developers, researchers) across all stages from design to deployment
Organizational contexts that can sustain iterative cycles of inquiry
constraints: The article is an argumentative illustration of the framework's promise; it reports no empirical test of IS applied to AIEd in the text provided
target_learners: K-12 teachers and learners using AIEd systems
target_learning_goals: Reliable, fair, locally adaptable implementation of AIEd systems

title: Driver diagrams as a collaborative tool for building working theories of AIEd improvement
description: A driver diagram is a visual IS tool the article recommends for AIEd improvement work: "Driver diagrams include a measurable aim, primary drivers that directly impact the aim, and secondary drivers that localize change to specific parts of a system of practice." Primary drivers are described as "a representation of a community's hypothesis about the main areas of influence necessary to advance the improvement aim"; secondary drivers serve as starting points for developing, testing, and refining change ideas.

A measurable aim, primary drivers, and secondary drivers
constraints: Drivers are hypotheses built from research and context-specific data, and primary drivers are often too general to lead to focused change ideas

target_learning_goals: Building working theories of practice improvement for AIEd systems

title: Embed practical measures into daily practice to assess AIEd adaptations
description: The article recommends practical measures—"metrics of process data about what happens in a classroom" (e.g., transitions, instructional shifts, class discussion)—aligned to a driver diagram, to indicate whether changes and adaptations are driving the improvement aim. Because teachers are overburdened, "practical measures are interwoven into daily practice to support teachers' efforts to assess if and how adaptations to the system result in improvement," opening the black box of AIEd systems for users.

Measures that do not overburden teachers, since they "rarely have the time needed" for extra measurement work
constraints: The article notes measurement has too often been used to forge inequality; in an improvement context it becomes a tool for iterative progress

citation: Duong Ngo, Andy Nguyen, Belle Dang, Ha Ngo. (2024). Facial Expression Recognition for Examining Emotional Regulation in Synchronous Online Collaborative Learning. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 34:650–669. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00378-7
title: FER analysis pipeline combining img2pose facial localization and Residual Masking Network emotion detection for synchronous online learning video
description: The article's analytical pipeline processes session recordings through a two-shot detector: img2pose pre-trained on the Wider face dataset performs facial localization, and Residual Masking Network classifies emotion into seven classes (Anger, Disgust, Fear, Happiness, Sadness, Surprise, Neutral). The authors chose a two-step approach because a recent survey suggested it "achieves better performance on out-of-sample data", and relied on pre-trained models because small collaborative-learning datasets (< 100 examples per class) preclude training domain-specific models. Residual Masking Network achieved 73.28% accuracy on FER2013, above reported human recognition accuracy of 65.5%.
requirements: Video recordings of learners with cameras on, suitable for pre-trained facial localization and emotion models
constraints: The pipeline uses publicly available pre-trained models because the dataset scope (< 100 examples per class) makes training or fine-tuning domain-specific models impractical
target_learners: Higher education students in synchronous online collaborative courses
target_learning_goals: Understanding and supporting socially shared regulation of learning and emotional regulation in group work
examples: Applied to 14 group videos (mean participant time around 13 min) recorded during online English speaking tasks on Microsoft Teams

article_title: Calibration Discrepancy Predicts Students’ Subsequent Metacognitive Strategy Use in Computer-based Learning Environments
citation: HaeJin Lee · Nigel Bosch. (2025). Calibration Discrepancy Predicts Students’ Subsequent Metacognitive Strategy Use in Computer-based Learning Environments. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00514-5
title: Coherence analysis (CA) as a theory-driven measure of metacognitive strategy use from trace data
description: Coherence analysis is a method that evaluates metacognitive strategies by examining the sequential alignment of students' learning actions within online learning contexts. The article states CA "examines how learning activities are sequentially connected in a way that indicates metacognitive strategies such as self-reflection and planning". In this study, the authors use CA to quantify coherent reading (reviewing material after a quiz) and coherent quiz (preparatory engagement before a quiz) as metacognitive strategies, counting time devoted to related content within a five-minute window.
requirements: Trace data recording each interaction with timestamps at activity and page levels
A defined time window limiting the gap between learning activities (five minutes in this study)
constraints: Suited to short-term, online learning environments with constrained task scope and duration, as in this study
target_learners: College students in computer-based learning environments
target_learning_goals: Metacognitive strategy use (planning, monitoring, reflection) during self-paced learning
examples: Coherent reading was measured by summing time spent reviewing material related to missed quiz questions within five minutes after the quiz; coherent quiz summed reading-related time in the five minutes before attempting quizzes.

title: Six SRL-relevant learning patterns identified by constrained sequential pattern discovery in online learning
description: The article presents an enumerated set of frequent learning sequences mined with cSPADE and mapped to Zimmerman and Pons's SRL strategies, e.g., "Read → Quiz" indicating "Seeking evaluation". Table 1 lists six patterns (Read → Quiz, Quiz → Read, Quiz → Quiz, Quiz → Examples, Read → Examples, Quiz → Summary) with support proportions ranging from 0.450 (n = 9 5) to 0.850 (n = 179) among the 210 students, and these were used as SRL constructs in the regression analyses.

A literature-grounded mapping from learning sequences to SRL strategies

title: Metacognitive experience as a distinct element in models of metacognition (Flavell, Pintrich, Efklides)
description: The article reviews models of metacognition and highlights that "metacognitive experience is identified as a separate and distinct element" in the frameworks of Flavell, Pintrich, and Efklides. In Efklides's model, metacognitive experiences manifest as "metacognitive judgments/estimates, feelings, and task-specific knowledge in real-time", serving as a bridge between cognitive and emotional regulation, and are distinguished from metacognitive knowledge and from metacognitive skills (intentional application of strategies for cognitive control).
requirements: Distinguishing momentary judgments and feelings from relatively static metacognitive knowledge when measuring metacognition
constraints: Brown's (1987) and Schraw and Dennison's (1994) models do not identify metacognitive experience as a separate main component, treating it instead as a skill within monitoring

target_learning_goals: Metacognitive monitoring, judgment accuracy, and self-regulated learning
examples: In this study, students' pretest and posttest retrospective judgments (estimated scores 0–100%) operationalize metacognitive judgments as instances of metacognitive experience.

article_title: Redefining Literature Education: The Role of ChatGPT in Undergraduate Courses
citation: Andrea Roxana Bellot, Mar Gutiérrez-Colón Plana, Katarzyna Agnieszka Baran. (2025). Redefining Literature Education: The Role of ChatGPT in Undergraduate Courses. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00497-3
title: Educators integrating AI into literature teaching should account for AI's Western-centric cultural bias and deliberately include diverse global perspectives
description: The article argues that because ChatGPT's training data comes largely from English-language and Western sources, its outputs may reinforce Western ideas, values and storytelling traditions and limit students' exposure to non-Western literary traditions. It advises that "educators need to be aware of these cultural limitations when integrating AI into the literature classroom and intentionally include diverse, global perspectives." The principle rests on cited reviews of AI bias (Messeri and Crockett; Resnik and Hosseini; Roe) rather than on data from this study.
requirements: Educator awareness of training-data origins of the AI tool in use
Curricular effort to bring in non-Western texts and perspectives alongside AI-generated material
constraints: Evidence for the bias is drawn from prior literature the article cites, not from the study's own data
target_learning_goals: critical engagement with a diverse range of literary texts
examples: The authors propose future studies on AI's cultural biases in students' understanding of different literary traditions and on applying AI to non-Western traditions and non-English literature

article_title: The Birth of IJAIED
citation: John Self. (2015). The Birth of IJAIED. Int J Artif Intell Educ (2016) 26:4–12. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0040-5
title: AIED's two distinctive characteristics: precision in describing vague educational terms, and real-time analysis of learner interaction to adapt it
description: The author describes what he considered the two distinctive characteristics of the AIED field. The first is "the striving towards some kind of precision, derived from AI or computation generally, in the description of otherwise vague terms (such as metacognition, collaboration, even learning itself)" of importance to educationalists. The second is that AIED systems carry out significant real-time analysis of interaction with learners in order to adapt that interaction, responding in ways that are not pre-specified, which the author calls the essential difference between AI programs and general computer programs. The account is the author's own later characterization of the field.
requirements: The account presumes AIED research involves computational or AI-derived descriptions of educational phenomena, as the author frames the field's identity.
constraints: The author states he has no idea whether his 1997 'scope and standards' wording applies to today's field, doubting that it does.
target_learners: learners interacting with AIED (intelligent tutoring) systems
target_learning_goals: adaptation of instructional interaction based on real-time analysis of learner interaction
examples: The author cites his 'scope and standards' webpage for JAIED as his best attempt to pin down the field's AI flavour.

citation: Matt Dennis, Judith Masthoff, Chris Mellish. (2016). Adapting Progress Feedback and Emotional Support to Learner Personality. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0059-7
title: Validated personality trait stories for conveying learner personality at a polarised level
description: Short stories about fictional learners, adapted from IPIP-NEO self-report questionnaire items (Goldberg et al. 2006), describe one Big Five trait at a high or low polarised level. They were used instead of simplistic labels "such as 'John is an extrovert'" so participants could identify and empathise with the learner. A validation experiment had participants rate each story with the Mini-Markers scale (Saucier 1994), and stories were adjusted and re-validated as needed.
requirements: Stories must express the intended trait and not inadvertently express another trait at the same time, verified via validation with the Mini-Markers scale
target_learners: adult online participants taking the role of a teacher giving feedback
target_learning_goals: tailoring progress feedback and emotional support to learner personality
examples: Stories were created for each of the five traits (e.g. high and low conscientiousness 'Josh'), validated, and used in five between-subjects experiments on Amazon Mechanical Turk

citation: Matt Dennis, Judith Masthoff, Chris Mellish. (2016). Adapting Progress Feedback and Emotional Support to Learner Personality. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0059-7
title: Validated categories of emotional support statements (praise, emotional reflection, reassurance, advice)
description: A set of emotional support categories was built from a brainstorming exercise with three teachers followed by a card sorting exercise to group related statements, which were then labelled as categories (Praise, Emotional Reflection, Reassurance, Advice). "A validation experiment was implemented which showed participants each emotional support statement in turn and asked them to place it into one of the categories." Statements not reliably categorised were discarded, leaving validated example statements per category.
requirements: Statements must be reliably categorised by participants in the validation experiment; unreliable statements are discarded
target_learners: learners receiving progress feedback in digital educational systems
target_learning_goals: providing emotional support (reassurance, encouragement, praise, empathy) alongside progress feedback
examples: Example statements include praise ('Well done'), emotional reflection ('I know what you're feeling'), reassurance ('You will get the hang of it eventually'), and advice ('Just keep practising')

title: Algorithm for adapting emotional support and slant to learner personality and performance
description: Based on the five experiments, the authors created algorithms describing how feedback should be adapted to learner personality and performance. "Two algorithms were created using different methods to describe the adaptations and evaluated on how well they described the experimental data using DICE scores", and a refined algorithm was created from the results. It recommends slant (positive, neutral, negative) and emotional support types and quantities for given trait levels and scores. A qualitative study with teachers and trainee teachers was run to evaluate and further refine the algorithm.
requirements: Experimental data on which emotional support types and slant participants use for each trait level and score, with recommendations derived from homogeneous subset means (e.g. subset mean ≥ 0.5 for recommending an emotional support type)
target_learners: learners of conversational agents and intelligent tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: motivating learners through tailored progress feedback and emotional support
examples: For slant, a subset mean ≤ −0.5 led to a recommended negative slant and ≥ 0.5 to a positive slant; otherwise a neutral slant was recommended

title: Five Factor Model of personality as an axis for adapting learning feedback
description: The Five Factor Model (Big 5) describes personality via five traits: Extraversion, Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, Emotional Stability (vs neuroticism), and Openness to Experience, with nomenclature and definitions adopted from John and Srivastava (1999). The authors adopt it because it "is considered robust by most psychologists", trait levels remain relatively stable over time, and validated questionnaires measure it with as few as 10 to 300 items. It serves as the organising framework for the paper's five feedback-adaptation experiments.
requirements: Validated questionnaires (e.g. IPIP-NEO, Mini-Markers) to identify or convey an individual's trait levels
constraints: Psychologists agree on five traits but not on their names
In this paper the model is used via polarised trait-level stories rather than measured trait scores
target_learners: learners in digital educational systems whose personality can be represented via the five traits
target_learning_goals: adapting progress feedback and emotional support to learner personality and performance
examples: Each experiment addressed one trait, using validated high/low stories and six possible scores (10% to 90%) on a mock test

article_title: Preface to the IJAIED 25th Anniversary Issue
citation: Monique Grandbastien, Rosemary Luckin, Riichiro Mizoguchi, Vincent Aleven. (2016). Preface to the IJAIED 25th Anniversary Issue. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0092-6
title: IJAIED 25th anniversary issue of 35 invited retrospective articles by authors of highly-cited papers
description: The 25th anniversary issue of IJAIED comprises invited short articles in which authors of the journal's most impactful original research papers reflect on their classic article, including subsequent developments and future directions. The editors write that they "approached the authors of highly-cited articles from the journal's history to write a new, short article that presented a new outlook on the line of work featured in their historic article". The 35 resulting articles went through the journal's regular peer review process.

Each invited article had to address the seven questions posed by the editors

target_learning_goals: understanding the intellectual history and state of the art of AI in education research
examples: 35 invited retrospective articles compiled for the journal's 25th year of operation, each reviewed under the journal's stringent peer review process

article_title: Preface to the IJAIED 25th Anniversary Issue

title: Seven-question reflection framework used to structure the anniversary articles
description: The editors structured each invited retrospective around seven questions: motivation, approach, core contributions, practical impact, core limitations, subsequent research, and future directions. They state: "We asked the reviewers to evaluate not only whether the article met the regular review criteria, but also whether it addressed the seven questions above." This framework turns classic papers into structured accounts of a research programme's motivation, impact, limitations and trajectory.
requirements: Reviewers evaluated whether invited articles addressed all seven questions in addition to regular review criteria

target_learning_goals: documenting the motivation, contributions, limitations and future directions of a research line

article_title: Preface to the IJAIED 25th Anniversary Issue
citation: Monique Grandbastien, Rosemary Luckin, Riichiro Mizoguchi, Vincent Aleven. (2016). Preface to the IJAIED 25th Anniversary Issue. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0092-6
title: AIED as a mature research community whose history shapes future research directions
description: The preface frames Artificial Intelligence in Education as a research community with a traceable history: the journal's early years "coincided with the coalescing of the research community in Artificial Intelligence and Education", alongside the start of the International Conference on AI in Education (first held in 1987) and the Intelligent Tutoring Systems conference (first held in 1988). The editors emphasize the staying power of featured projects, which "often over many years reached a state of substantial maturity and produced sharable and reusable results, surviving— often capitalizing on— rapid changes in the underlying technologies used". They hold that a research field needs a sense of its history, and that this history influences current exploration of new ways technology can impact education.
requirements: A research field needs a sense of its history, which the anniversary issue provides
constraints: The editors explicitly declined to synthesize general trends and lessons from the set of articles, judging that too daunting a scholarly task
target_learners: researchers new to the AIED field
target_learning_goals: understanding the historical development, milestones and future directions of AI in education as a research field
examples: The journal was titled the Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education from 1989 to 1995, renamed in 1995 with volume numbers continuing in sequence; John Self's article on the birth of IJAIED in this issue records the Society's history
