article_title: Computer-Based Interaction Analysis with DEGREE Revisited
citation: B. Barros & M. F. Verdejo (2015). Computer-Based Interaction Analysis with DEGREE Revisited. Int J Artif Intell Educ (2016) 26:113–123. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0063-y
title: Activity Theory-based declarative methodology for defining collaborative learning scenarios (dialogue, task, outcome template)
description: The project's first core contribution is a methodology based on Activity Theory that provides declarative mechanisms for specifying collaborative scenarios. An intermediate language creates a generic template with three elements (dialogue, task, and outcome) used to build a scenario-instance from a taxonomy of values; a framework then interprets the instance to launch an interactive online learning environment. The authors situate this approach within the later development of collaborative scripts and collaborative learning flow patterns. It was implemented in DEGREE and re-implemented in subsequent system versions.
requirements: A fully integrated configuration program and a framework that provides a common platform, gives the scenario-instance semantics, manages users, and stores processes and results as learning objects
target_learners: distance-learning students with no previous experience of collaboration
target_learning_goals: collaborative learning process design and analysis
examples: The template approach evolved as a research field within CSCL, scripts (Dillenbourg 2002), and collaborative learning flow patterns (CLFPs), and lay within the scope of educational modelling languages such as IMS and PALO

title: DEGREE collaborative learning tool with semi-structured communication, experiment configuration, interaction analysis, and interventions
description: DEGREE is a collaborative learning tool that "uses semi-structured communication (with sentence openers, tagged dialogs)" and offers tools to configure a collaborative experiment, provide an analysis of the collaboration process, and offer interventions to improve the interaction. The authors report that its sentence-opener model of facilitating collaborative interaction was re-implemented in a collaborative version of the SIETTE system for collaborative small-group assessment and interaction analysis. The community also cited DEGREE as an integrated approach to designing, conducting, and analysing a collaborative experiment.
requirements: Teachers' criteria for indicator values must be modelled when the learning activity is designed; the technological setup of activities and monitoring was deliberately undertaken to avoid increasing teachers' workload
constraints: The authors decided not to address automated tagging of discourse units because NLP technology at the time would not have yielded a result sufficiently reliable for use in the system

description: The article presents a taxonomy of indicators for characterizing group and individual behaviour in CSCL, based on three perspectives: the group in relation to similar groups, an individual in relation to his/her colleagues, and the group itself. The authors describe this taxonomy as the first step in building a CSCL ontology for analysing collaborative learning tasks. The experience was later shared in the Kaleidoscope NoE, and conclusions on indicators for collaborative processes were summarized in a joint article.

description: The article organizes the evolution of computer-based interaction analysis into three stages shown in Fig. 3: 1995–2005 (small groups, one data source, purpose-built systems, logs and visualization/awareness tools), 2000–2010 (large groups and small learning communities, e-learning platforms as data sources, social network analysis, statistical and Bayesian methods, machine learning), and 2005–2015 (an explosion of data from social networks, MOOCs and open, non-structured text sources, with information retrieval, classification, visualization, and learning analytics). citation: Andrea Horbach, Joey Pehlke, Ronja Laarmann-Quante, Yuning Ding. (2024). Crosslingual Content Scoring in Five Languages Using Machine-Translation and Multilingual Transformer Models. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00370-1
title: Multilingual ASAP content scoring datasets in five languages with three newly collected variants, publicly released
description: The article presents language variants of the ASAP short-answer content scoring dataset covering Chinese, English, French, German and Spanish for three science-related prompts. Three variants were newly collected via crowdsourcing (ASAPen, ASAPes, ASAPfr, about 300 usable answers per prompt), alongside ASAPde and a Chinese dataset from high school students. Each was double-annotated by native speakers using the original scoring guidelines, with inter-annotator agreement in QWK reported per prompt (e.g. .83-.69 for ASAPen). The article states the data "is publicly available under https://github.com/andreahorbach/CrosslingualScoring/".
requirements: Answers double-annotated by native speakers trained on the original English ASAP scoring guidelines
constraints: Crowdsourced datasets show higher amounts of low-scoring answers and lower inter-annotator agreement than the original ASAP data
target_learners: high school students (Chinese and original ASAP data)
target_learning_goals: automated scoring of conceptual correctness of short written answers to science prompts
examples: The French data was collected via platforms including Facebook and Amazon Mechanical Turk, yielding 1,070 answers of which 672 were usable

title: Do not use crosslingual automated content scoring for high-stakes assessment at present
description: The article's ethical considerations argue that crosslingual scoring exposes learners to different model biases depending on their answer language, since "learners will be scored by different models depending on their choice of language and thus be subjected to different model biases". Translating all answers into one language is suggested as more advisable, but the article cautions that machine translation quality varies by source language and that multilingual transformer models work differently well for different languages and combinations. It therefore concludes crosslingual scoring is not currently suitable for high-stakes assessment.
requirements: If used, awareness that per-language models or translation steps introduce language-dependent bias
constraints: The article states crosslingual scoring is at the moment not suitable for high-stakes assessment
target_learners: non-native speaking students answering in a language they are proficient in
target_learning_goals: fair automated scoring of content in short written answers
examples: The article recommends automatic translation of all learner answers into the same language in which a model has been trained as a more advisable scenario, while noting its caveat about minority-language quality

article_title: Uncovering Measurement Biases in LLM Embedding Spaces: The Anna Karenina Principle and Its Implications for Automated Feedback
citation: Abigail Gurin Schleifer, Beata Beigman Klebanov, Giora Alexandron. (2025). Uncovering Measurement Biases in LLM Embedding Spaces: The Anna Karenina Principle and Its Implications for Automated Feedback. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00485-7
title: The Anna Karenina Principle in Automated Short Answer Scoring
description: The Anna Karenina (AK) principle in ASAS is the authors' explanatory account of why embeddings-based clustering of student responses favors correct answers: correct responses ('happy families') are densely and similarly represented, whereas incorrect responses ('unhappy families') "tend to differ from each other", increasingly so the more severe the error. The strong version adds that incorrect responses sit closer to correct ones than to their own profile, so correct responses are "the center of the universe". Lower density and non-convexity of poor-knowledge profiles are proposed as inhibitors of downstream discoverability, yielding a measurement bias against lower-knowledge learners.
requirements: Pre-trained LLM embeddings of student responses and a theory-driven profile labeling to diagnose the geometry
constraints: Demonstrated in the context of ASAS with LLM embeddings on Hebrew biology explanation responses; the authors note it may be fundamental to educational assessment but call for dedicated study
target_learning_goals: constructing scientific explanations
diagnosis of error patterns for formative feedback
examples: Within-KP cosine similarity medians fell monotonically with KP index across three embedding models; incorrect responses' nearest high-density region was KP1
key_sources: Abigail Gurin Schleifer, Beata Beigman Klebanov, Giora Alexandron. (2025). Uncovering Measurement Biases in LLM Embedding Spaces: The Anna Karenina Principle and Its Implications for Automated Feedback. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00485-7

article_title: Uncovering Measurement Biases in LLM Embedding Spaces: The Anna Karenina Principle and Its Implications for Automated Feedback
citation: Abigail Gurin Schleifer, Beata Beigman Klebanov, Giora Alexandron. (2025). Uncovering Measurement Biases in LLM Embedding Spaces: The Anna Karenina Principle and Its Implications for Automated Feedback. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00485-7
title: Validate and adjust pre-trained LLM embeddings before using them for task-specific formative assessment
description: The article argues that because pre-trained embeddings may not capture the nuances that matter in science education assessment, LLM-based formative assessment systems need "adjustments and validation on the specific task" before deployment. Without careful validation, significant information loss in the embedding representation may be overlooked, leading to suboptimal educational decisions. This follows directly from the demonstrated discoverability bias, in which learners with less complete knowledge are represented less faithfully in embedding space and risk receiving less appropriate feedback.
requirements: Task-specific validation of the embedding representation against pedagogically meaningful labels before the embeddings are relied on for assessment decisions
constraints: Shown for three embedding models and two clustering algorithms on Hebrew biology explanation responses; the authors state results may be LLM- and clustering-method-specific
target_learners: high school biology students receiving automated feedback on written explanations
target_learning_goals: accurate diagnosis of student error patterns for personalized formative feedback
examples: The study compared theory-driven KPs with KMeans and HDBSCAN clusters over AlephBERT, OpenAI text-embedding-3-large, and Llama3.1-8B embeddings of 669 students' responses to two biology items

citation: Jill-Jêenn Vie, Fabrice Popineau, Éric Bruillard, Yolaine Bourda. (2018). Automated Test Assembly for Handling Learner Cold-Start in Large-Scale Assessments. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0163-y
title: General Diagnostic Model for learner ability estimation over knowledge components
description: The General Diagnostic Model (GDM) is a cognitive-diagnosis student model in which learners carry ability vectors with one component per knowledge component and questions carry discrimination vectors and an easiness parameter, combined through a logistic probability of a correct answer. The article states it "choose[s] to calibrate a General Diagnostic Model, because it predicts student performance better than other cognitive diagnosis models", citing its prior work, and assumes the learner's level does not change during the initial question bundle. Estimated ability components can be interpreted as degrees of mastery per knowledge component.
requirements: An expert-specified q-matrix mapping each question to the knowledge components involved in its resolution
A history of dichotomous learner responses over the item bank for calibration
constraints: Assumes the learner's level does not change across the initial bundle of questions
Discrimination components are fixed at zero for knowledge components a question does not involve
target_learning_goals: diagnosing mastery of knowledge components in mathematics assessment
examples: The model was calibrated with the mirt R package using a Metropolis-Hastings Robbins-Monro algorithm, and its ability estimates fed the prediction of remaining question outcomes in the cold-start experiments
key_sources: Jill-Jêenn Vie, Fabrice Popineau, Éric Bruillard, Yolaine Bourda. (2018). Automated Test Assembly for Handling Learner Cold-Start in Large-Scale Assessments. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0163-y

article_title: Automated Test Assembly for Handling Learner Cold-Start in Large-Scale Assessments
citation: Jill-Jêenn Vie, Fabrice Popineau, Éric Bruillard, Yolaine Bourda. (2018). Automated Test Assembly for Handling Learner Cold-Start in Large-Scale Assessments. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0163-y
title: InitialD: DPP-based diverse question sampling for cold-start assessment
description: InitialD (for Initial Determinant) is an automated test-assembly algorithm that "samples k questions from the item bank according to a determinantal point process, using the question feature vectors", so that the selected questions measure different knowledge components and minimize redundancy in learner answers. It selects the first bundle of questions before any adaptation is possible, supports feedback naming knowledge components needing further work, and randomizes across newcomers, which the authors note is "interesting for security purposes" and helps calibrate various items. Sampling 10 questions from a bank of 10,000 takes about 10 million operations after preprocessing.
requirements: Question feature vectors (e.g., discrimination vectors from a calibrated student model) from which pairwise similarities can be computed
A preprocessed kernel matrix over the item bank
constraints: Exact DPP sampling was tested here only on item banks of up to 23 questions; exact best-subset search is NP-hard and intractable at scale
Complexity is O(nk3) after a preprocessing step in O(n3)
target_learning_goals: rapid initial diagnosis of learner knowledge
low-stakes formative assessment
examples: Applied to the TIMSS 2003 (757 learners, 23 questions) and Fraction subtraction (536 students, 20 questions) datasets in a stratified 80/20 cross-validation protocol

title: Wayang Outpost (MathSpring): intelligent tutoring system for middle-school mathematics combining cognitive apprenticeship, multimedia learning and multidimensional personalization
description: Wayang Outpost, later MathSpring, is an intelligent tutoring system for middle-school mathematics described in this special issue. It "combines principles of cognitive apprenticeship and multimedia learning to implement a range of coaching and scaffolding approaches helping students develop problem-solving skills." It adapts in both the outer loop (problem selection, informing students of their learning state) and the inner loop (instructional videos, elaborate feedback, step-by-step worked-out examples of similar problems). The system has been used in mathematics classrooms since 2003 and the accompanying paper presents extensive empirical evidence for its effectiveness.
requirements: Tracking of learner cognitive, metacognitive and affective states to drive adaptive pedagogical decisions
target_learning_goals: mathematical problem-solving skills
examples: Used in mathematics classrooms since 2003; outer-loop adaptation selects problems of appropriate difficulty and inner-loop adaptation provides videos, elaborate feedback and worked-out examples.

description: ASSISTments is a mathematics learning system whose special-issue contribution focuses on its mission and lessons learned rather than a study summary. It outlines "the entire 'ASSISTments ecosystem' that enables collecting usage data and conducting research studies, while ensuring that the normal learning process is not compromised in any way." Its design is very teacher-centric, involving teachers from content authoring to planning experiments. Each year tens of thousands of school children use it to learn math. It deliberately follows a minimalist approach to intelligence and adaptivity, with no strong student model and no sophisticated adaptation procedure.

description: The preface argues that math and science classes require teachers to promote general problem-solving skills, self-regulation strategies, and coping with negative affective traits like boredom, frustration and anxiety. Therefore, "to be maximally effective in these domains, Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS) and other AIED technologies need to address a wide range of student characteristics and adapt to various categories of students by being cognitively, metacognitively, and motivationally aware." citation: Ulrike Padó, Yunus Eryilmaz, Larissa Kirschner. (2024). Short-Answer Grading for German: Addressing the Challenges. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00383-w
title: ASYST: an easy-to-use automated grading system with local processing and Excel-based workflow
description: ASYST (Automated Grading System) is a graphical user interface wrapping the German Transformer SAG model (and an English model) so that teachers without programming skills can generate automated grade suggestions. It "takes as input an Excel sheet containing student answers and correct reference answers", optionally accepts existing manual grades for reliability analysis, and runs grading locally: "Automated grading is fully local, which precludes data protection issues because the student answers never leave the teacher's computer." Results are saved as an Excel sheet for teacher review. It is released as a compiled Windows 11 executable with open-source Python code.
requirements: An Excel sheet containing student answers and correct reference answers as input
constraints: The tool covers only the languages supported by its wrapped SBERT models; an evaluation mode for model performance on one's own data is a future development goal
target_learners: teachers grading short-answer tests in German universities and schools
target_learning_goals: efficient and trustworthy automated short-answer grading support
examples: Six experienced teachers generated grade suggestions with ASYST in individual test runs and saved results in a new Excel sheet, with 100% task completion and SUS 88.8

title: Three-challenge framework for broad-scale adoption of automated short-answer grading: technical, usability, and trust
description: The article organizes the barriers to classroom adoption of automated short-answer grading into three challenges: "A technical challenge regarding the need for high-quality models, which is exacerbated for languages with fewer resources than English; a usability challenge in adapting high-quality research prototypes to the needs of non-expert users, and a trust challenge in communicating the abilities and limitations of the tools." The framework draws on the Technology Acceptance Model and usability research, and structures the paper's contributions: a German Transformer model, the ASYST interface, and a hybrid human-machine grading workflow.
requirements: Meeting the trust challenge requires users' understanding of tool capabilities and preserved teacher agency, per Nazaretsky et al. as the article reports
constraints: Technical quality is harder for languages with fewer training resources than English
target_learners: teachers using automated grading tools in classrooms
target_learning_goals: adoption of reliable, usable, and trusted automated grading support
examples: The paper addresses each challenge in turn with German data as the instantiation: model training and evaluation, the ASYST GUI, and the automated grading workflow

title: Deep Thought logic tutor with backward worked examples and backward problem solving proof types
description: Deep Thought (DT) is an intelligent logic-proof tutor organized into 7 levels in which students apply logic rules to premises to reach a conclusion. For this study two new proof types were added: Backward Worked Examples, where “the tutor constructs an entire proof by using BW derivation only as students click on the > button,” and Backward Problem Solving, where “forward derivations are disabled” and students refine the conclusion into unjustified subgoal nodes until all connect to premises. Problem scores combine accuracy, time function and solution size equally.

constraints: There are no backward hints in DT, and BPS problems are restrictive by design, requiring proofs entirely in the backward direction

target_learning_goals: Logic proof construction
Subgoaling and problem-solving strategy learning
examples: The training session contained 20 problems across levels 2-6, with BPSs distributed only in the first half so T2 could independently master backward strategy later; students spent around 6 hours on training on average

title: BasqueARA, Agrega2-Es and Agrega2-En+ graded science-text corpora for secondary education
description: The article compiles and releases three independent, document-level, grade-annotated science corpora for ESO secondary education: BasqueARA (329 documents), Agrega2-Es (401 documents) and Agrega2-En+ (251 documents), with English texts written for non-native learners. Texts were extracted from the Agrega2 repository and other sources, split by headings into self-contained reading passages, and 'each document was assigned a level 1-4 according to the original ESO grade for which the material was developed.'
requirements: Documents must be self-contained science reading passages divided by a unit's headings and subheadings, with exercises discarded

title: Scientific discourse differs cognitively and linguistically from general-domain text, complicating generic readability assessment
description: The article draws on prior characterizations of scientific texts to argue that generic ARA approaches, developed mostly on general-domain corpora, may not transfer to science textbooks. Scientific texts are said to have 'a more rigid structure, a higher presence of terminology' and be 'consistently formal', and their informative-argumentative core is harder to understand than narrative text despite simpler syntax, because they relate complex events requiring higher abstraction and linguistic competence. This motivates testing domain-specific corpora and models.
requirements: Readability assessment for science classrooms should account for genre, type and topic rather than relying on generic approaches
constraints: Most readability studies of science textbooks have assumed the accuracy of existing approaches with little investigation of performance in this distinct scenario
target_learning_goals: selecting science texts of appropriate difficulty for disciplinary learning
examples: The article notes Ehara (2022) found 10%-30% of scientific texts are not readable to intermediate ESL learners

citation: R. Charles Murray, Kurt Vanlehn, Jack Mostow. (2004). Looking Ahead to Select Tutorial Actions: A Decision-Theoretic Approach. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197308
title: Decision-theoretic framework for selecting tutorial actions by looking ahead to their anticipated effects
description: The article proposes a framework in which an intelligent tutoring system selects tutorial actions by anticipating their consequences for the student and the tutorial state before acting. It is stated to "use a dynamic decision network to consider the tutor's uncertain beliefs and objectives in adapting to and managing the changing tutorial state". The framework treats action selection as decision making under uncertainty rather than fixed rule following.
requirements: A model of the tutorial state including student attributes and task and discourse state, as instantiated in the article's prototype engines
constraints: The abstract does not report results from a complete integrated intelligent tutoring system

examples: Prototype action selection engines for calculus and elementary reading illustrate the approach

title: Dynamic decision network for managing the changing tutorial state
description: A dynamic decision network is the computational mechanism the article proposes for tutorial action selection. It represents "the tutor's uncertain beliefs and objectives" so the tutor can adapt to and manage a changing tutorial state over time. It combines uncertain belief representation with the tutor's objectives to choose among possible tutorial actions.
requirements: Uncertain beliefs about the student and objectives must be representable in the network

target_learning_goals: adaptive selection of tutorial actions

article_title: Coordinating the Complexity of Tools, Tasks, and Users: On Theory-based Approaches to Authoring Tool Usability
citation: Tom Murray. (2015). Coordinating the Complexity of Tools, Tasks, and Users: On Theory-based Approaches to Authoring Tool Usability. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:37–71. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0076-6
title: Complexity-matching framework for authoring tool usability
description: The article proposes that ITS authoring tool design should be grounded in coordinating three kinds of complexity: tool complexity, task complexity, and user complexity capacity. As the article states, "one way to do this is to match the complexity of tool design to the complexity of authoring tasks and the complexity capacity of users and user communities". This entails estimating the complexity of the mental models users must build to use a tool as intended, with the goal of designing tools that meet realistic user audiences rather than maximizing power.
requirements: Designers must estimate the complexity of the mental models a user is expected to build to use the tool as intended
constraints: The framework is explicitly exploratory and speculative; the author notes the suggestions are preliminary and many details remain to be worked out beyond the paper
target_learners: authoring tool user communities (teachers, domain experts, instructional designers, knowledge engineers)
target_learning_goals: usable design of complex educational authoring tools
key_sources: Tom Murray. (2015). Coordinating the Complexity of Tools, Tasks, and Users: On Theory-based Approaches to Authoring Tool Usability. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:37–71. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0076-6

article_title: Coordinating the Complexity of Tools, Tasks, and Users: On Theory-based Approaches to Authoring Tool Usability
citation: Tom Murray. (2015). Coordinating the Complexity of Tools, Tasks, and Users: On Theory-based Approaches to Authoring Tool Usability. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:37–71. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0076-6
title: Three-source taxonomy of system complexity: structural, dynamic, and perspectival
description: Adapting Campbell (1988), the article generalizes a scheme of complexity sources into three categories shown in Fig. 2. Structural complexity concerns parts, part types, properties, and relationships (one-to-one mappings simplest, many-to-many most complex); dynamic complexity concerns systems whose properties and relationships change over time; and perspectival complexity is defined as "complexity due to multiplicity and uncertainty, including conflicting goals or subtasks", diverse stakeholder perspectives, stochastic indeterminacy, and vagueness.
requirements: Measuring these factors would require enumerating or estimating components, relationships, and dynamic behaviors of the system
constraints: The article notes perspectival factors would be measured more heuristically than the other two types, and that complexity has a quasi-subjective component involving human context and purpose
target_learning_goals: characterizing and comparing the complexity of tools, tasks, and user mental models
key_sources: Tom Murray. (2015). Coordinating the Complexity of Tools, Tasks, and Users: On Theory-based Approaches to Authoring Tool Usability. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:37–71. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0076-6

article_title: Coordinating the Complexity of Tools, Tasks, and Users: On Theory-based Approaches to Authoring Tool Usability
citation: Tom Murray. (2015). Coordinating the Complexity of Tools, Tasks, and Users: On Theory-based Approaches to Authoring Tool Usability. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:37–71. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0076-6
title: Activity Theory framing of tool, task, user, and community of practice
description: The article borrows Activity Theory as an orientation and vocabulary for authoring tool usability, because it "stresses the mediating role of tools (artifacts) and their usage rules in collective human activity". It frames usability as the interaction between users, tools, rules, and tasks, and asks whether a tool and its rules of use afford a particular task for a particular class of users, including socio-cognitive complexity of the community of practice and division of labor.
requirements: Users must be considered in particular roles, since complexity capacity is role- and experience-dependent rather than a measure of innate intellectual sophistication
constraints: The article assumes tool feature complexity stands as a fair indication of task complexity for software tools, which it acknowledges is not strictly true
target_learning_goals: matching tools to user roles and communities of practice
key_sources: Tom Murray. (2015). Coordinating the Complexity of Tools, Tasks, and Users: On Theory-based Approaches to Authoring Tool Usability. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:37–71. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0076-6

article_title: Coordinating the Complexity of Tools, Tasks, and Users: On Theory-based Approaches to Authoring Tool Usability
citation: Tom Murray. (2015). Coordinating the Complexity of Tools, Tasks, and Users: On Theory-based Approaches to Authoring Tool Usability. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:37–71. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0076-6
title: Epistemic Forms and Games as complexity classes of authoring interface features
description: Drawing on Collins and Ferguson, the article uses Epistemic Forms (and Epistemic Games) to classify authoring tool interface components and procedures into epistemic classes that can be roughly ordered by complexity. As the article puts it, "filling in a text form or setting a slider level are examples of simple tasks, while filling in a table or hierarchy have medium complexity, and creating and debugging formal procedures has much complexity". These classes partially address the dimensionality problem of combining different complexity types into a holistic assessment.
requirements: Tool features must be classifiable into epistemic classes so they can be matched to user complexity capacity
constraints: The article states that Epistemic Forms only partially solves the dimensionality (apples vs. oranges) challenge of integrating various types of complexity
target_learning_goals: ordering authoring tasks and interface features by cognitive complexity

title: Match authoring tool complexity to the complexity capacity of the intended user community
description: The article's central design recommendation is that authoring tools should be designed for realistic user audiences by matching tool complexity to task complexity and user complexity capacity, rather than pursuing maximal power. It recommends a qualitative, comparative approach: "we can categorize system complexity and cognitive capacity qualitatively roughly into types or groupings that will provide sufficient insight" into matching decisions, using rough low/medium/high categories with more precise frameworks when needed.
requirements: Designers must assess the complexity capacity of intended users, weigh investment risk, and make usability/power tradeoffs appropriate to realistic use contexts
constraints: The article states effortful quantitative complexity analysis is not necessary for these goals, and that the frameworks are a beginning step pointing to additional operationalization work
target_learning_goals: authoring and customizing intelligent tutoring systems
examples: The article presents Table 1 as an example mapping of author roles to low, medium, and high complexity capacity levels

article_title: Perceived Task-Difficulty Recognition from Log-file Information for the Use in Adaptive Intelligent Tutoring Systems
citation: Ruth Janning, Carlotta Schatten, Lars Schmidt-Thieme. (2016). Perceived Task-Difficulty Recognition from Log-file Information for the Use in Adaptive Intelligent Tutoring Systems. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0097-9
title: Generalised classification plait: a layered stacking ensemble that feeds previous classifiers' decisions back as additional inputs to improve multi-class recognition with small noisy datasets
description: The generalised classification plait is an ensemble structure in which classifiers such as SVM, DCT or KNN "are i enough.nterweaved within a plait structure by combining the classification decisions of classifiers in previous plait layers with the feature vectors and feeding these combined new feature vectors into further classifiers". It generalises the earlier SVM plait to other classification models and multi-class problems, and "Different from plain stacking, the presented plait consists of several layered stackings with different additional inputs". It has three hyper-parameters: the number of plait layers, the number of classifiers per layer, and the number of features per classifier.
requirements: The original feature vector must be splittable into s input vectors of n features each; if l is too small, input vectors may overlap to ensure enough feature values per classifier.
constraints: Experiments used 3 classifiers per layer, 4 features per classifier and 20 layers, with error converging after at most 7 layers; the article states additional tests and experiments with larger data should be conducted for generalisability.
target_learners: students practicing mathematics in intelligent tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: recognition of students' perceived task-difficulty to support adaptivity and task sequencing
examples: The experiments split the 11 per-task log-file features into 3 input vectors of 4 features and retrained classifiers over 7 layers, then fed the seventh-layer outputs to a second stage classifier for the final decision.

title: Self-labelling tutoring tool dataset: 7 students, 40 fraction/arithmetic tasks, 280 self-labelled tasks with log-file recording
description: A dataset from a study in which "7 students in the age of 21 – 28 each had to solve 40 mathematical tasks and to label at the end of a task the perceived task-difficulty themselves by means of the small offline self-labelling tutoring java tool". "Each of the 7 students has seen all 40 tasks resulting in 280 labelled tasks", distributed as 40 too hard, 20 hard, 93 appropriate, 121 easy and 6 too easy. The tool is a drill-and-practice math system that does not model student knowledge but provides only the log-file data and labels; every action was written with a time stamp into a log file.

article_title: C3-IoC: A Career Guidance System for Assessing Student Skills using Machine Learning and Network Visualisation
citation: Adán José-García, Alison Sneyd, Ana Melro, Anaïs Ollagnier, Georgina Tarling, Haiyang Zhang, Mark Stevenson, Richard Everson, Rudy Arthur. (2023). C3-IoC: A Career Guidance System for Assessing Student Skills using Machine Learning and Network Visualisation. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00317-y
title: C3-IoC career guidance system (three-module architecture)
description: C3-IoC is an online AI-based career guidance system helping undergraduates and high school students explore IT job roles. As the article states, "The system consists of three modules: (1) a novel knowledge base covering the full range of skills, both technical and non-technical...; (2) a user skill profiling module in which students' technical skills are collected using a CV parser and non-technical skills are self-assessed through a questionnaire; and (3) a job role matching and visualisation module". It supports self-evaluation of skills and exploration of emerging IT jobs via a personalised job network visualisation.
requirements: Users upload a PDF CV and complete a 24-question non-technical skills questionnaire, of which four questions are mandatory
A knowledge base of skills and job roles built from the IT job corpus and the O*NET general job corpus is required for matching
constraints: The article notes the accuracy of job role prediction is highly dependent on the information in the user profile, in particular the minimum number of questionnaire questions answered
The system primarily focuses on the IT sector, incorporating other job roles only at a coarse resolution
target_learning_goals: Career exploration in the IT sector
Self-evaluation and awareness of technical and non-technical skills
examples: Users progress through a three-stage journey: CV parser and questionnaire, radar-chart skill refinement, and a network map of the user's placement in the IT job role space

citation: Adán José-García, Alison Sneyd, Ana Melro, Anaïs Ollagnier, Georgina Tarling, Haiyang Zhang, Mark Stevenson, Richard Everson, Rudy Arthur. (2023). title: C3-IoC knowledge base built from the IT job corpus and the O*NET general job corpus
description: The C3-IoC knowledge base combines two complementary datasets. From the UK 'Find a job' website, crawled weekly from October 2018 to December 2019, "Duplicated jobs were removed, resulting in a corpus of 22,359 jobs"; text mining with a Word2Vec model extended a 100-skill seed list to 902 terms, manually cleaned to "an IT skill dictionary consisting of 195 unique skills", and 26 job roles were identified. From O*NET 2019 (version db_24), "we considered a total of 142 skills and 381 job roles", restricted to roles over 50% of respondents ranked as requiring a Bachelor's degree or higher.

Manual cleaning and peer revision to merge synonyms and match non-technical skills between the two datasets
constraints: ESCO and O*NET lack up-to-date IT sector skills and roles, and ESCO does not consider discrete levels of importance of skills for specific job roles
The O*NET restriction to degree-level roles removed a large number of job roles, most described as 'physical' or 'manual'
Five IT job corpus non-technical skills could not be matched to O*NET questions and were excluded
target_learning_goals: Understanding which technical and non-technical skills are relevant for emerging IT jobs
examples: Each job role was represented as a weighted list of skills, where the weighting is the proportion of ads in that role containing that skill (Table 2 lists the 26 roles, e.g. software developer with 2374 jobs)

citation: Adán José-García, Alison Sneyd, Ana Melro, Anaïs Ollagnier, Georgina Tarling, Haiyang Zhang, Mark Stevenson, Richard Everson, Rudy Arthur. (2023). C3-IoC: A Career Guidance System for Assessing Student Skills using Machine Learning and Network Visualisation. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00317-y
title: Job role network method: skill-level-aware similarity metric, RCA weighting, and Louvain community detection for projecting users into a job role space
description: The article proposes representing job roles and users as weighted skill vectors and matching them with a similarity metric in which "the distance between u and j does not increase if the user has at least the requisite skill level for the job role", so Sim(u,j) in [0,1] favours roles the user can meet. Job role networks are built with "the revealed comparative advantage index (RCA), which denotes the relative importance of a skill for a job role after accounting for skills which are common across many job roles" and a force-directed layout, with "the Louvain community detection algorithm" identifying job role types. This places students within communities of job roles, visualised for the IT job corpus and the general job corpus.
requirements: Skill importance ratings normalised in the range [0, 5] for both databases
A user skill profile with weighted technical and non-technical skills
constraints: The absence of an edge between nodes indicates job roles have no skills with effective needs in common
The general corpus was restricted to degree-level job roles, so the network shows only those roles
target_learning_goals: Understanding how one's skillset relates to communities of job roles
Exploring related career fields and the skills associated with specific occupations
examples: In the Bioinformatician example projection (Fig. 6), the top job role matches included Bioinformatic Scientist (96%) and Molecular and Cellular Biologist (91%), with the user located in the Science and Technology community
The general job corpus network has 11 communities and the IT job corpus network has 4 communities (Figs. 4 and 5)

description: The study organizes findings around a conceptual framework in which the Master's thesis journey is divided into three procedures: proposal development, tools development, and thesis report writing, mapped onto Creswell's (2012) six steps of conducting research. Each procedure contains enumerated steps (e.g., introduction and background, literature review, research design and methodology; developing, piloting, finalizing tools; abstract through references). The authors state these actions were "employed as the pre-established themes for analysis and data presentation," structuring how ChatGPT use and non-use were compared.
requirements: Thesis procedures must be decomposable into the three processes and their enumerated steps for the framework to structure analysis
constraints: Developed for University of Dhaka Master's science education thesis students; findings themes follow the framework's pre-established themes

target_learning_goals: Research methodology competence
Academic thesis writing

article_title: Automated Analysis of Reflection in Writing: Validating Machine Learning Approaches
citation: Thomas Daniel Ullmann. (2019). Automated Analysis of Reflection in Writing: Validating Machine Learning Approaches. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education (2019) 29:217–257. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-019-00174-2
title: Model for reflection detection: eight categories synthesized from 24 reflective writing models
description: The article synthesizes 24 reflective writing models into a "model for reflection detection" combining depth and breadth qualities. "In total, the model consists of eight categories": the depth dimension Reflection (reflective vs. non-reflective) and seven breadth categories — Experience, Feeling, Belief, Difficulty (critical stance), Perspective, Learning (retrospective outcomes), and Intention (prospective outcomes). The synthesis deliberately used a general model rather than one specific model, so the evaluation covers categories "common to many models" used in manual content analysis of reflective writing.
requirements: Categories are operationalized as indicator questions rated by coders sentence by sentence, e.g. "The writer describes an experience he or she had in the past"
constraints: No widely agreed definition of reflection exists; the article adopts its own working definition for the purpose of the study
target_learners: higher education students writing reflective essays
target_learning_goals: reflective thinking
reflective writing
examples: Example annotated sentences per category, e.g. for Feeling: "Although I was a bit anxious about the lesson, I kept on top of the feelings."
key_sources: Thomas Daniel Ullmann. (2019). Automated Analysis of Reflection in Writing: Validating Machine Learning Approaches. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education (2019) 29:217–257. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-019-00174-2

title: Annotated reflective-writing sentence dataset of 5080 sentences from 76 student essays
description: The study built labeled data sets from a text collection of 77 student writings, 67 drawn by relevance sampling from the BAWE corpus (largely health, business, and engineering students, mostly second- and third-year) and ten from the reflective writing literature. A sentence splitter produced "a total of 5080 sentences (116,633 words)", which crowdsourced workers rated with indicator questions for each of the eight categories; each data set was split 80% training / 20% test.
requirements: Crowd-worker annotation with per-category indicator questions and majority-vote aggregation
constraints: Relevance sampling was used because reflective texts are relatively rare, so the corpus over-represents reflective content relative to random sampling
target_learners: higher education students in health, business, engineering, tourism, and linguistics
target_learning_goals: automated assessment of reflective writing
examples: BAWE corpus texts awarded merit (40) or distinction (24) grades were included

article_title: Example-Tracing Tutors: Intelligent Tutor Development for Non-programmers
citation: Aleven, V., McLaren, B. M., Sewall, J., van Velsen, M., Popescu, O., Demi, S., Ringenberg, M., & Koedinger, K. R. (2016). Example-Tracing Tutors: Intelligent Tutor Development for Non-programmers. International Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0088-2
title: Cognitive Tutor Authoring Tools (CTAT)
description: CTAT is a set of authoring tools for building example-tracing tutors without programming. It supports a six-part authoring process including cognitive task analysis, interface building via drag-and-drop, recording and generalizing behavior graphs, annotating with hints and knowledge components, and mass production of problems via templates and spreadsheets. The article states "Using CTAT, example-tracing tutors can be built and deployed entirely without programming".
requirements: Authors must define a KC model by annotating links of a behavior graph with KC labels.
constraints: Example-tracing tutors support tutoring only for problems with a moderately branching solution space or problems for which the similarity among different solution paths can be expressed using formulas.
target_learning_goals: domain-specific problem-solving skills

citation: Aleven, V., McLaren, B. M., Sewall, J., van Velsen, M., Popescu, O., Demi, S., Ringenberg, M., & Koedinger, K. R. (2016). title: Tutorshop
description: Tutorshop is a web-based content management and learning management system created for deploying CTAT tutors in classrooms and other settings. It is implemented in Ruby on Rails and provides management of class lists, student and teacher accounts, assignments, and reports on student progress. The article notes "Tutorshop has been used in many research projects" and functions as the backbone of the Mathtutor website and the Genetics Tutor.
requirements: Tutorshop is used as the deployment environment for CTAT tutors.
constraints: Tutorshop has not been used to deliver non-CTAT tutors.
target_learning_goals: domain-specific problem-solving skills

citation: Aleven, V., McLaren, B. M., Sewall, J., van Velsen, M., Popescu, O., Demi, S., Ringenberg, M., & Koedinger, K. R. (2016). Example-Tracing Tutors: Intelligent Tutor Development for Non-programmers. International Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0088-2
title: Example-tracing tutors as intelligent tutoring systems
description: The article argues that example-tracing tutors should be viewed as ITS based on VanLehn's criterion that ITSs have an inner loop providing step-level guidance. The authors update this argument, offering an alternative definition of adaptivity with three factors: empirical grounding in learner understanding, individualization across psychological dimensions, and appropriate interactivity. They argue "example-tracing tutor technology supports the building of tutors that exhibit all three factors that make up this definition".
requirements: The tutor must exhibit adaptive behavior grounded in empirical understanding of learners, individualization, and interactivity.
constraints: Example-tracing tutors currently do not have features for responding adaptively to student self-regulation, metacognition, or affect.
target_learning_goals: domain-specific problem-solving skills

article_title: Teaching the Teacher: Tutoring SimStudent Leads to More Effective Cognitive Tutor Authoring
citation: Matsuda, N., Cohen, W. W., & Koedinger, K. R. (2015). Teaching the Teacher: Tutoring SimStudent Leads to More Effective Cognitive Tutor Authoring. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0020-1
title: SimStudent: a machine-learning agent that learns an expert model through tutored problem solving
description: SimStudent is a domain-general machine-learning agent that learns an expert model of a target task through tutored problem solving, using the same tutor interface crafted for the target cognitive tutor. It learns production rules representing individual cognitive skills, with an if-part (information retrieval path and preconditions) and a then-part (operator function sequence). Three machine-learning techniques are combined: version spaces for the information retrieval path, FOIL inductive logic programming for preconditions, and iterative-deepening depth-first search for the operator function sequence. The domain dependency is implemented as background knowledge comprising a WME structure, feature predicates, and operator functions.
requirements: Background knowledge including a WME structure, feature predicates, and operator functions must be provided prior to learning.
constraints: SimStudent does not learn strategic knowledge to select among equally available productions, so accuracy reflects both correct and incorrect production applications.
target_learning_goals: Authoring expert models for cognitive tutors
key_sources: Matsuda, N., Cohen, W. W., & Koedinger, K. R. (2015). Teaching the Teacher: Tutoring SimStudent Leads to More Effective Cognitive Tutor Authoring. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0020-1

article_title: Teaching the Teacher: Tutoring SimStudent Leads to More Effective Cognitive Tutor Authoring
citation: Matsuda, N., Cohen, W. W., & Koedinger, K. R. (2015). Teaching the Teacher: Tutoring SimStudent Leads to More Effective Cognitive Tutor Authoring. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0020-1
title: Cognitive Tutor Authoring Tools (CTAT) with integrated SimStudent for intelligent authoring
description: CTAT is a suite of software tools that helps authors build Tutoring Interfaces with virtually no programming effort and demonstrate solutions stored as model solutions in a behavior graph. When SimStudent is integrated into CTAT, it learns to solve problems and generates an expert model from the author's tutoring or demonstrations using the Tutoring Interface. The system supports two authoring strategies, Authoring by Tutoring and Authoring by Demonstration, and also allows authors to demonstrate incorrect steps so SimStudent learns buggy production rules.
requirements: An author must provide a Tutoring Interface and demonstrate or tutor solution steps for SimStudent to learn an expert model.
target_learning_goals: Creating expert models and tutoring interfaces for cognitive tutors

article_title: Automated Scoring of Constructed Response Items in Math Assessment Using Large Language Models
citation: Morris, W., Holmes, L., Choi, J. S., & Crossley, S. (2025). Automated Scoring of Constructed Response Items in Math Assessment Using Large Language Models. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00418-w
title: Balance class distributions through targeted filtering and augmentation before finetuning scoring models on constructed response items
description: The article recommends addressing data imbalance before training scoring models. Targeted filtering removes easily classified low-scoring responses, and generative data augmentation paraphrases under-represented high-scoring responses. The authors state that "class balance and the distribution of the data are more important than the overall number of samples collected."
requirements: A pre-trained generative language model that can run locally for privacy-protected data augmentation
constraints: Datasets may remain imbalanced even after augmentation, especially with high prevalence of low-scored responses
target_learners: K-12 students taking standardized math assessments
target_learning_goals: Accurate automated scoring of constructed response math items
examples: SGD classifiers on document-term matrices filtered up to 78.14% of 1-scoring responses while retaining over 98% of 2s and 3s; Coedit-XL generated up to 8 paraphrases per authentic high-scoring response with injected spelling errors and lowercasing.
key_sources: Morris, W., Holmes, L., Choi, J. S., & Crossley, S. (2025). Automated Scoring of Constructed Response Items in Math Assessment Using Large Language Models. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00418-w

article_title: Automated Scoring of Constructed Response Items in Math Assessment Using Large Language Models
citation: Morris, W., Holmes, L., Choi, J. S., & Crossley, S. (2025). Automated Scoring of Constructed Response Items in Math Assessment Using Large Language Models. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00418-w
title: NAEP 2023 Automated Math Scoring Challenge dataset and competition
description: The NAEP 2023 Automatic Math Scoring Challenge provided a training dataset of 251,370 responses from 10 items (five grade 4, five grade 8) and a test dataset of 27,930 responses with withheld scores. Items required short or extended constructed responses with maximum scores between 2 and 5. The competition goal was to predict scores within QWK 0.05 of human inter-rater reliability without demographic bias (pairwise SMD > 0.10).
requirements: Researchers must request dataset access through https://www.researchdatagov.org/product/15704
constraints: The dataset is not publicly available
target_learners: Grade 4 and grade 8 students in U.S. schools
target_learning_goals: Automated scoring of constructed response math assessment items
examples: The ten items spanned algebraic representations, patterns and functions, mathematical reasoning, probability, geometry, properties of numbers, and number operations.
key_sources: Morris, W., Holmes, L., Choi, J. S., & Crossley, S. (2025). Automated Scoring of Constructed Response Items in Math Assessment Using Large Language Models. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00418-w

article_title: Automated Scoring of Constructed Response Items in Math Assessment Using Large Language Models
citation: Morris, W., Holmes, L., Choi, J. S., & Crossley, S. (2025). Automated Scoring of Constructed Response Items in Math Assessment Using Large Language Models. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00418-w
title: Transformer attention-based semantic representation for automated constructed response scoring
description: The article describes how transformer LLMs such as BERT generate sentence-level embeddings through attention layers where "each embedding in the sequence is compared with and modified by each other embedding based on their similarity." This allows word meanings to be contextually influenced, producing a classification token representing the semantic meaning of the entire sequence. After finetuning, this token predicts human scores for constructed response items, capturing relationships that bag-of-words approaches miss.
requirements: Labeled training data for finetuning on specific scoring tasks
constraints: Bag-of-words approaches consider words individually outside syntactic context, limiting generalizability
target_learners: Students producing constructed responses in math assessments
target_learning_goals: Automated prediction of human scores for open-ended responses
examples: DeBERTa-v3-large was finetuned as a pseudo-regression task with MSE loss, with predicted scores rounded to the nearest integer during post-processing.
key_sources: Morris, W., Holmes, L., Choi, J. S., & Crossley, S. (2025). Automated Scoring of Constructed Response Items in Math Assessment Using Large Language Models. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00418-w

article_title: Learning Analytics to Reveal Links Between Learning Design and Self-Regulated Learning
citation: Yizhou Fan, Wannisa Matcha, Nora’ayu Ahmad Uzir, Qiong Wang, Dragan Gašević. (2021). Learning Analytics to Reveal Links Between Learning Design and Self-Regulated Learning. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 31, 980–1021. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00249-z
title: Learning analytics method combining cluster analysis, process mining, and epistemic network analysis to link learning design and learning tactics
description: The article proposes "a novel learning analytic method that combines three data analytic techniques, including a cluster analysis, a process mining technique, and an epistemic network analysis". Clustering detects learning tactics within sessions using the EM algorithm; process mining examines tactic usage across sessions; ENA visualises and statistically analyses connections between tactics and learning-design units for each performance group. The combination is offered as a new methodological approach for studying links between learning design and learning tactics.
requirements: Trace data from an online learning environment, course design metadata, and performance data; a learning design that varies across units so tactic–design links can be observed
constraints: Applied to one MOOC (Flipped Classroom) with adult teacher-learners on a Chinese platform; learners active for more than three sessions and three weeks were included
target_learners: pre-service and in-service teachers in a MOOC
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning
use of learning tactics aligned with learning design
examples: Applied to a flipped-classroom MOOC with 97,475 registrants, analysing 4,664,214 unique events split into 201,038 learning sessions

title: Flipped Classroom MOOC with diverse unit-level learning designs as research context
description: A seven-week MOOC developed by a Chinese university in 2014 and offered on the iCourse 163 platform, targeting in-service and pre-service teachers. Each unit followed a different design: "Unit 1 followed a traditional lecture-based design", Unit 2 case-based learning, Unit 3 project-based, Unit 4 case-based with reading activities, and Unit 5 problem-based. The article states that "it is precisely this variety and diversity of the learning design that made this MOOC unique and provided a suitable research context to address the research questions".

constraints: No unit quiz and peer review were offered for unit 0 and unit 6; the study used offerings from the 4th to the 16th round, after the curriculum structure stabilised

target_learning_goals: understanding and applying the flipped classroom pedagogy in daily teaching practice
examples: Unit 2 asked learners to write their own teaching plan, graded through peer review; Unit 3 required learners to produce a teaching video

article_title: Applying Large Language Models to Enhance Dialogue and Communication Analysis for Adaptive Team Training
citation: Spain, R., Min, W., Kumaran, V., Pande, V., Saville, J., & Lester, J. (2024). Applying Large Language Models to Enhance Dialogue and Communication Analysis for Adaptive Team Training. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-4565500/v1
title: Team Communication Analysis Framework using transformer-based LLMs for dialogue act recognition with limited training data
description: The article presents a team communication analysis framework that leverages transformer-based LLMs, particularly GPT models, for dialogue act recognition in scenarios with limited training data. Speech uttered by team members is collected by the learning environment and converted into transcripts using automatic speech recognition; the framework then analyzes the transcripts to recognize dialogue acts, and these insights are passed to an adaptation engine that provides adaptive scaffolding to each team member. The framework is designed to support adaptive team training by enabling instructors and researchers to gain insights into team actions and processes that impact team coordination.
requirements: Speech uttered by team members is collected by the learning environment and converted into transcripts using automatic speech recognition
An adaptation engine component receives the analysis insights to provide adaptive scaffolding to team members
constraints: The article focuses on evaluating the Team Communication Analysis Framework component, specifically addressing dialogue act recognition in scenarios with limited training data
target_learners: team members in military squad training exercises
target_learning_goals: team communication behaviors
team coordination
dialogue act recognition for adaptive feedback
examples: The framework was evaluated with labeled transcripts from a U.S. Army training event where squads completed a 45-minute live training exercise involving observing and maintaining overwatch of a village
key_sources: Spain, R., Min, W., Kumaran, V., Pande, V., Saville, J., & Lester, J. (2024). Applying Large Language Models to Enhance Dialogue and Communication Analysis for Adaptive Team Training. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-4565500/v1

article_title: Applying Large Language Models to Enhance Dialogue and Communication Analysis for Adaptive Team Training
citation: Spain, R., Min, W., Kumaran, V., Pande, V., Saville, J., & Lester, J. (2024). Applying Large Language Models to Enhance Dialogue and Communication Analysis for Adaptive Team Training. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-4565500/v1
title: Zero-shot LLMs refined through prompt engineering offer a promising means for supporting dialogue act recognition with minimal training data
description: The article concludes that zero-shot LLMs, refined through prompt engineering, offer a promising means for supporting dialogue act recognition, and that prompt refinements—particularly those addressing confusion between dialogue acts—can lead to superior recall rates for challenging labels. This principle supports incorporating these capabilities into future training systems to provide learners and instructors with tailored feedback to support and improve team communication behaviors. The article states this approach "paves the way for developing AI-enabled training systems that can adapt to the dynamic communication styles of different teams".
requirements: Access to a proprietary LLM such as GPT-4 or an open-source alternative such as T5
Iterative prompt refinement targeting label confusions identified through error analysis
constraints: T5 remains a viable option because it is open-source, whereas GPT-4 is proprietary; this distinction becomes more critical as implementation scales up in training settings with multiple sessions where the costs of model deployment are significant
In a training environment where T5 models have not been trained with data from that specific training, GPT-4 with zero-shot or few-shot learning might significantly outperform T5
target_learners: team members in military squad training exercises
instructors and researchers using adaptive team training systems
target_learning_goals: team communication behaviors
team coordination
adaptive feedback on teamwork skills
examples: The article reports that GPT-4 achieved 77.30% accuracy on the held-out test set without requiring fine-tuning with training data or extensive hyperparameter optimization

title: Three recurrence indicators (gaze synchronization, language conformance, emotional matching) as a system-based index of collaborative synchronization
description: The article proposes a system-based index for measuring learners' collaborative processes built on the degree of behavior recurrence of each speaker. It focuses on "three indicators—gaze synchronization, language conformance, and emotional matching through facial expression" to establish an index of synchronization during PCA-mediated collaborative learning. The indicators are quantitative metrics derived from qualitative investigations of joint activity, intended for real-time detection of coordination quality by tutoring systems.

constraints: Indicators detected process measures but not learning performance in the reported experiment

citation: Nygren, T., Samuelsson, M., Hansson, P.-O., Efimova, E., & Bachelder, S. (2025). AI Versus Human Feedback in Mixed Reality Simulations: Comparing LLM and Expert Mentoring in Preservice Teacher Education on Controversial Issues. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00484-8
title: Combine AI feedback with human expert insight when using AI in teacher training simulations
description: The study concludes that AI can help scale mixed reality simulations for teacher education, but AI-generated feedback should be balanced by human expertise. It finds "it should be carefully evaluated and balanced by human expertise in teacher education", since AI misses missed opportunities and contextual understanding that experts provide. AI mentoring is preferable to no feedback but should complement rather than replace expert mentoring.
requirements: AI feedback should be paired with human expert review to catch missed teaching opportunities and contextual nuances the AI does not identify
constraints: AI systems in the study did not identify missed opportunities unless directly instructed and lacked contextual understanding of preservice teachers' development
target_learning_goals: teaching controversial issues
receiving feedback on classroom discussion facilitation
examples: The study compared AI and expert feedback on the same simulation transcripts and found AI useful for structure, respect/discussion rules, and pupil misconceptions but not for missed opportunities

citation: Pierpaolo Vittorini, Stefano Menini, Sara Tonelli. (2021). An AI-Based System for Formative and Summative Assessment in Data Science Courses. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00230-2
title: AI-based automated grading system for R assignments with NLP comment classification
description: A tool that automatically grades assignments consisting of R commands and Italian-language comments. It performs static code analysis to extract commands, outputs, and comments, then uses a Python NLP server (fastText embeddings, 300 dimensions) and an R classification engine (CARET/E1071 SVM) to judge comment correctness. The distance calculator module combines missing commands, differing outputs, and comment correctness into a final grade converted to the Italian 0–31 scale.
requirements: Requires a professor-provided correct solution with commands, outputs, and gold standard comments
Requires a set of sentence pairs from previous exams to tune the classifier for each specific topic
constraints: Developed and tested only for statistical analysis of health data in R with Italian-language comments
Can return false pass/fail outcomes, especially near the pass threshold
target_learners: Master's degree students in Medicine and Surgery, Prevention Sciences, and Nursing Sciences
target_learning_goals: Statistical analysis of health data in R
Correct interpretation of statistical test results
examples: Used for formative assessment during homework and for summative assessment in exams, with exams randomly corrected manually or through the automated system
key_sources: Pierpaolo Vittorini, Stefano Menini, Sara Tonelli. (2021). An AI-Based System for Formative and Summative Assessment in Data Science Courses. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00230-2

citation: Matsuda, N., Yarzebinski, E., Keiser, V., Raizada, R., Stylianides, G. J., & Koedinger, K. R. (2013). Studying the Effect of a Competitive Game Show in a Learning by Teaching Environment. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0009-1
title: SimStudent as a machine-learning teachable agent with high cognitive fidelity, including incorrect learning
description: SimStudent is "a machine-learning architecture that learns procedural skills inductively from examples", integrated into APLUS where students tutor it with yes/no feedback, hints, quizzes, and self-explanation prompts. Its unique characteristic is the ability "to model both correct and incorrect learning": given prior knowledge based on surface features, it makes induction errors from correct examples, producing overly specific or general productions mirroring common algebra errors. The authors hypothesize such "high cognitive fidelity" teachable agents offer better learning-by-teaching opportunities.
requirements: Students provide feedback, demonstrations, and explanations during tutored problem-solving
constraints: SimStudent does not understand students' free-text responses; question answering is designed to promote reflective thinking
target_learning_goals: procedural skill in solving linear equations
conceptual understanding of algebraic equivalence

title: 2×2 framework organizing attentional states by direction of attention and content of thoughts
description: The article proposes a 2×2 (direction of attention × content of thoughts) framework to organize attentional states during learning with technology. It distinguishes overt attention (sustained, focused, alternating, divided), covert attention, covert inattention (mind wandering, tune outs, zone outs), and overt inattention (off-task, distracted). The framework is intended to guide diagnosis and redirection of attention in attention-aware learning environments.
requirements: The framework requires distinguishing whether attention appears directed towards the learning environment or elsewhere, and whether thoughts are content-related or content-unrelated.

description: The article defines an attention-aware learning environment as one that can "detects and (re)directs the learner’s attention in near real-time in order to achieve some desired outcome". citation: Olatinwo, S. O., & Demmans Epp, C. (2025). Predicting Tags for Learner Questions on Stack Overflow. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00441-x
title: BERT-CBA architecture: BERT embeddings combined with CNN, BiLSTM, highway, and attention layers for tag recommendation
description: BERT-CBA is a stacked deep learning architecture for multi-label tag recommendation on Stack Overflow posts. BERT generates contextual word embeddings, a CNN layer extracts "local semantic features", a BiLSTM layer fuses these with contextual features, a highway layer refines features and reduces overfitting, and an attention layer selects important words before sigmoid classification. The article positions it as addressing limitations of prior statistical and neural methods that lack bidirectional context and interpretability.

title: A classification framework for CSCL interaction-management systems distinguishes mirroring, metacognitive, and coaching systems
description: The article proposes a classification framework built on a simple model of coaching for systems that support the management of collaborative interaction. The framework distinguishes between mirroring systems, which display basic actions to collaborators; metacognitive tools, which represent the state of interaction via a set of key indicators; and coaching systems, which offer advice based on an interpretation of those indicators. citation: Soroush Sabbaghan, & Sarah Elaine Eaton. (2025). Navigating the Ethical Frontier: Graduate Students' Experiences with Generative AI-Mediated Scholarship. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00454-6
title: COREI: a seven-application GenAI-powered research support suite for graduate students
description: COREI (Collaborative Research Environment and Intelligence) is a suite of seven GenAI-powered tools developed to support academic research: LEO (literature exploration and research-gap identification), NORA (research-plan guidance with pre-set methodologies), OMAR (manuscript outline generation), SARA (citation-backed literature search), VIDA (web-based information retrieval), SADI (context-aware document interaction), and CESAR (APA 7th edition-compliant copyediting). Built with Python and OpenAI's GPT-4o and deployed via Streamlit, it integrates external APIs including Elsevier Scopus, SerpAPI, and Crossref. The authors describe it as "a comprehensive suite of GenAI-powered tools developed by the first author to support various aspects of academic research."

constraints: Pre-set methodologies in NORA are "not meant to be viewed as a one-size-fits-all solution"; automated tools like SADI and CESAR may not fully capture the nuances of documents or academic writing.
target_learning_goals: academic research skills
academic writing
literature review
examples: Participants used LEO to find research questions, OMAR for personalized suggestions, and CESAR to polish writing in APA 7th edition style, logging 13,122 total interactions across the seven applications.

title: Bayesian Knowledge Tracing for task-loop adaptivity in mixed-reality learning
description: The article applies Bayesian Knowledge Tracing, which "models student knowledge growth as a latent variable using a two-state Hidden Markov Model", to select tasks in an Intelligent Science Station. Each knowledge component has four parameters (p(L0), p(T), p(S), p(G)), and mastery is declared when prediction and explanation Ln scores both exceed 0.95. Task selection implements a "gentle slope" of improvement, picking the unmastered category closest to mastery.

citation: Susan Bull & Judy Kay. (2016). SMILI☺: a Framework for Interfaces to Learning Data in Open Learner Models, Learning Analytics and Related Fields. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0090-8
title: SMILI☺ framework: core questions for designing and describing open learner models
description: The SMILI☺ (Student Models that Invite the Learner In) framework provides a systematic way to describe, compare and critique open learner models by answering a set of core questions: how the OLM fits into the overall interaction, how it was evaluated, why it was created, what aspects of the learner model are open, how they are presented, and who controls access. The revised version reformats these as "the set of essential questions which designers should consider and which can be used to describe OLMs". It is offered as a guide for designers of interfaces for OLMs, learning analytics and related fields.
requirements: Designers must identify the purposes relevant to their OLM and describe how each core question is addressed, with sufficient detail to allow the OLM to be fully understood by others and compared with other OLMs.
constraints: The original full-table version was found to be too complicated for routine use in publications; the revised framework offers a lightweight version that calls for identification of purposes in text without the full table breakdown.
target_learners: learners using intelligent tutoring systems and adaptive learning environments
target_learning_goals: metacognitive processes such as reflection, planning and monitoring of learning

title: Purposes for opening the learner model: a taxonomy of why OLMs are created
description: The article organises the reasons for creating an OLM into a set of purposes that form the columns of the SMILI☺ tables and the third core question of the revised framework. Purposes include improving learner model accuracy, supporting metacognitive processes of planning, monitoring and reflection, facilitating collaboration or competition, facilitating navigation, respecting the learner's right to access and control their personal data, and using the learner model as an assessment of the learner. The revised version adds three new purposes: facilitating communication with interface agents, promoting positive affective states, and presenting data aggregated from multiple sources.
requirements: Authors describing an OLM should indicate which of these purposes apply, marking those that are critical, contentious or not relevant, so that differences between OLMs can be highlighted with reference to the various elements.

title: Offering a choice of learner model visualisations to suit purpose, competency-set size and user preference
description: The Next-TELL OLM offers five visualisations of the same underlying learner model — skill meters, table, treemap, competency network and word clouds — that can be selected according to the user's preferred way of accessing the data. The treemap is "particularly useful for displaying large, hierarchically structured learner models", while the network visualisation gives a clearer overview in a smaller space but "can sometimes be hard to read". The word cloud provides "a clear and quick overview of the extremes (strengths and weaknesses)", useful for teachers' on-the-spot classroom decision-making.
requirements: The system must support multiple visualisations of the same underlying learner model so that users can select the one best suited to their purpose and preference.
constraints: The table and skill meters require scrolling if the competencies do not all fit onto the screen, so are less usable in large learner models; the treemap makes it harder to compare competencies from different parts of the tree.

title: Three classes of learner model: cognitive, pragmatic and data-intensive
description: The article identifies three important classes of learner model. The earliest days saw a dichotomy between cognitive and pragmatic learner models; more recently a third class of data-intensive, automatically generated models has emerged that harnesses large bodies of learning data. Despite this diversity, there is "a consistent view of the learner model as a dynamic representation of the learner's knowledge (lack of it, misconceptions and similar) as it evolves through the learning interactions". The representation requires two key elements: an ontology for the aspects to be modelled, and a means to use learning data to infer what the learner knows.
requirements: A learner model representation requires an ontology for the aspects to be modelled and a means to use learning data, as it becomes available, to infer what the learner knows.
