The framework underpins the study's AI-based open schooling activities and its self-report instrument.

title: CONNECT transversal skills self-report instrument
description: The CONNECT transversal skills instrument is a validated self-report questionnaire with a Likert scale and an open-ended question, distributed via Qualtrics. It was "validated by international educators, ensuring content, face and construct validity, with ethical adherence to the AERA, APA, and NCME standards" and met International Test Commission translation standards. The instrument produced automated, personalized feedback reports reflecting geographic, age, and gender insights.

target_learners: Secondary school students aged 15 to 17 in public state schools
target_learning_goals: Assessment of transversal skills in science education
examples: Used with 330 students across the UK, Greece, and Brazil

description: Thesis Writer is described as "a domain-specific, online learning environment for the scaffolding of student academic writing, combined with an online editor optimized for producing academic text." It targets theses and research article writing using the IMRD scheme rather than the essay genre, and unlike automated essay scoring tools it focuses on "instruction, planning, and genre mastery" rather than feedback. It was evaluated with first-year business administration students writing research proposals.

article_title: Ask-Elle: an Adaptable Programming Tutor for Haskell Giving Automated Feedback
citation: Gerdes, A., Heeren, B., Jeuring, J., & van Binsbergen, L. T. (2016). Ask-Elle: an Adaptable Programming Tutor for Haskell Giving Automated Feedback. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0080-x
title: Ask-Elle: a strategy-based model tracing and property-based testing tutor for Haskell
description: Ask-Elle is a web-based intelligent tutoring system for the functional programming language Haskell that supports the stepwise development of programs by verifying the correctness of incomplete programs and providing hints. Its main functionality is obtained by means of "strategy-based model tracing and property-based testing": a programming strategy derived from teacher-specified model solutions is used to trace a student's refinement steps, and QuickCheck properties are tested when no model solution can be recognised. Teachers add exercises by providing a task description, model solutions, and properties, and can annotate these with feedback messages and adjust the flexibility allowed in student solutions.
requirements: Teachers must provide a task description, one or more model solutions, and a configuration file with QuickCheck properties for each exercise
constraints: The tutor cannot give feedback on student programs that deviate from a path towards one of the model solutions
target_learners: first-year computer science students learning Haskell
target_learning_goals: incremental development of correct, well-designed functional programs
key_sources: Gerdes, A., Heeren, B., Jeuring, J., & van Binsbergen, L. T. (2016). Ask-Elle: an Adaptable Programming Tutor for Haskell Giving Automated Feedback. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0080-x

article_title: Ask-Elle: an Adaptable Programming Tutor for Haskell Giving Automated Feedback
citation: Gerdes, A., Heeren, B., Jeuring, J., & van Binsbergen, L. T. (2016). Ask-Elle: an Adaptable Programming Tutor for Haskell Giving Automated Feedback. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0080-x
title: Class 3 programming exercises with teacher-configurable feedback and flexibility
description: Ask-Elle offers class 3 programming exercises, which can be solved by applying alternative solution strategies, in contrast to class 1 exercises with a single correct solution and class 2 exercises with different implementation variants of a fixed strategy. Teachers add exercises by providing model solutions and a configuration file, and can use annotations (DESC, FB, MUSTUSE, ALT) to adapt feedback and control which implementations are accepted. This design allows teachers to accept or reject solutions based on different model solutions, such as an inefficient but simple recursive solution.
requirements: Teachers must specify model solutions and a configuration file with properties for each exercise
constraints: The tutor cannot give feedback on programs that deviate from a path towards a model solution
target_learning_goals: independent program design using alternative solution strategies
key_sources: Gerdes, A., Heeren, B., Jeuring, J., & van Binsbergen, L. T. (2016). Ask-Elle: an Adaptable Programming Tutor for Haskell Giving Automated Feedback. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0080-x

article_title: Evaluating a Persuasive Intervention for Engagement in a Large University Class
citation: Orji, F. A., Greer, J., & Vassileva, J. (2021). Evaluating a Persuasive Intervention for Engagement in a Large University Class. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00260-4
title: Socially-oriented persuasive strategies implemented as social visualizations of student performance data in a learning support system.
description: This design pattern implements persuasive strategies (social learning, social comparison, competition) as social visualizations showing students' assessment grades inside a learning support system. The article states "The persuasive strategy defines what information is visualized, e.g. whether the student can see just the score of the group (social learning) or also their own score to easily compare it with that of the group (social comparison) and or with specific peers (competition)." The visualizations update dynamically and include emoji feedback, and the authors note they "use familiar designs and can be implemented in any domain to represent various measures of student performance."
requirements: Access to student assessment grade data to populate the visualizations
Pseudonymized display of peers' grades and points to protect privacy while letting each viewer see their own real ID
A learning support system into which the visualizations can be integrated
constraints: The article notes it was not possible to make the behaviour of others directly observable due to the asynchronous nature of the online activities and privacy considerations, so the social learning strategy was implemented as aggregated performance of other students
target_learners: University students in large blended undergraduate courses
target_learning_goals: Increased engagement in online learning activities
examples: The article implemented three versions: a social comparison visualization showing the class average and the grades of five random higher-performing students, a social learning visualization showing grade ranges and the number of students within each range, and a competition visualization awarding points and ranking students on a leaderboard.
key_sources: Orji, F. A., Greer, J., & Vassileva, J. (2021). Evaluating a Persuasive Intervention for Engagement in a Large University Class. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00260-4

article_title: Evaluating a Persuasive Intervention for Engagement in a Large University Class
citation: Orji, F. A., Greer, J., & Vassileva, J. (2021). Evaluating a Persuasive Intervention for Engagement in a Large University Class. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00260-4
title: SARA (Student Advice Recommender Agent) personalized learning support system.
description: SARA is a learning support system that "provides personalized advice" and "directs the student to appropriate learning supports and resources by mining data from student academic history, personal history (including demographics), and current activity." It uses "a predictive model of student academic success in specific courses" and was introduced in the Introduction to Biology course alongside the MindTap platform. In this study, SARA served as the delivery vehicle for the persuasive social visualizations, and the persuasive intervention was placed into SARA's general advice-giving system to trigger reflection and inspire engagement in MindTap activities.
requirements: Student academic history, personal history, and current course activity data to feed the predictive model
constraints: The article notes the persuasive visualization could not be integrated into MindTap itself, so it was placed in SARA instead
target_learners: Undergraduate students in large blended courses
target_learning_goals: Directing students to appropriate learning supports and resources
Increasing engagement with course learning activities
examples: The article reports that students who regularly read the weekly SARA advice scored significantly higher — by 4.6 percentage points — than the predicted score after the midterm exam.
key_sources: Orji, F. A., Greer, J., & Vassileva, J. (2021). Evaluating a Persuasive Intervention for Engagement in a Large University Class. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00260-4

article_title: Evaluating a Persuasive Intervention for Engagement in a Large University Class
citation: Orji, F. A., Greer, J., & Vassileva, J. (2021). Evaluating a Persuasive Intervention for Engagement in a Large University Class. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00260-4
title: Socially-oriented persuasive strategies: social learning, upward social comparison, and competition.
description: The article defines "socially-oriented strategies" as "a class of persuasive strategies that provoke an intentional or unintentional change in an individual attitude or behaviour due to the influence of other people," drawing on social influence theory and Social Learning Theory. The three examined strategies are upward social comparison, in which people "compare themselves to similar others who are performing well"; social learning, where "the user learns through observation, imitation, and modelling the behaviour of others"; and competition, typically implemented as a leaderboard where users "can see their position relative to that of their peers." These strategies come from the Persuasive Systems Design Model's "social support" category of seven strategies.
requirements: A mechanism for informing users of the actions or performance of other users, such as social visualization, so that users can compare with, align with, or compete with others
constraints: The article notes these three strategies are commonly used in persuasive technology and have been shown successful at encouraging users in performing specific tasks, which is why they were chosen
target_learners: Students in blended and online higher-education courses
target_learning_goals: Motivating students to engage actively in learning activities

article_title: Plug-in Tutor Agents: Still Pluggin’
citation: Ritter, S. (2016). Plug-in Tutor Agents: Still Pluggin'. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26, 405–415. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0062-z
title: Tool-tutor architecture: separating tool from tutor via semantic messaging
description: The tool-tutor architecture separates the tool (which supports real work with its own computational capabilities) from the tutor (which understands the student's aim and provides feedback). Communication occurs at the semantic level using a selection-action-input triple, with the tutor focusing on feedback content and the tool handling display details. The author notes that "Semantic messaging standardized the method of describing an action (as a selection-action-input triple)."
requirements: A clear messaging protocol between tool and tutor
Tools with inherent computational capabilities distinct from educational context
constraints: Purpose-built tools needed modification to support tutoring in practice
target_learning_goals: problem-solving in tool-based contexts

citation: Jim Reye. (2004). Student Modelling based on Belief Networks. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197306
title: Belief networks as a framework for representing and reasoning about uncertainty in student modelling
description: The article presents belief networks as a way to represent and reason about uncertainty, which it identifies as a significant factor in modelling students. The framework structures student models and allows a system to use a systematic approach when gathering information about the scope of the student's knowledge. It serves as the organizing framework for the article's discussion of student modelling.

article_title: How Should Intelligent Tutoring Systems Sequence Multiple Graphical Representations of Fractions? A Multi-Methods Study
citation: Rau, M. A., Aleven, V., Rummel, N., & Pardos, Z. (2014). How Should Intelligent Tutoring Systems Sequence Multiple Graphical Representations of Fractions? A Multi-Methods Study. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0011-7
title: Instructional materials should provide interleaved practice with multiple graphical representations to promote robust learning, especially for conceptual knowledge.
description: The article concludes that "instructional materials should provide interleaved practice with multiple graphical representations in order to promote students' robust learning, in particular if the goal is to promote the acquisition of conceptual knowledge that transfers to novel tasks." This principle is grounded in the classroom experiment showing qualified support for interleaving over blocking. The benefit was most evident for conceptual transfer at the delayed posttest.
requirements: The learning materials must employ multiple graphical representations of the same content, such as circle diagrams, rectangles, and number lines.
constraints: The advantage of interleaving depends on students' prior knowledge and the type of target knowledge; blocked practice may be effective early in the learning sequence.
target_learning_goals: Conceptual knowledge of fractions that transfers to novel tasks
examples: The classroom experiment contrasted blocked, moderately interleaved, fully interleaved, and increasingly interleaved practice schedules using the Fractions Tutor.

citation: Conati, C. (2016). Commentary on: “Toward Computer-Based Support of MetaCognitive Skills: a Computational Framework to Coach Self Explanation”. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0074-8
title: SE-Coach: an ILE combining a solution-graph representation, incremental scaffolding interface tools, and a probabilistic student model to coach self-explanation
description: The SE-Coach is an intelligent learning environment designed to help students self-explain worked-out example solutions in introductory physics. It leverages "An explicit representation of what it means to understand an example solution" (the solution graph dependency network), "Interface tools to scaffold the target self-explanations" delivered via three levels of scaffolding, and "A probabilistic student model" that uses interface actions to assess which parts of the example have been correctly explained. It was designed to integrate with the Andes physics problem-solving ILE.
requirements: Requires a solution graph dependency network modeling how each solution step derives from previous steps and physics knowledge
Requires interface tools providing incremental scaffolding so as to interfere as little as possible with spontaneous student behaviors
Requires a probabilistic student model leveraging the solution graph and observed interface actions
constraints: Initially self-explanation is voluntary; more direct tutorial interventions are reserved for students with low tendency to self-explain
target_learning_goals: self-explanation of worked-out examples
Newtonian physics knowledge

citation: Conati, C. (2016). Commentary on: “Toward Computer-Based Support of MetaCognitive Skills: a Computational Framework to Coach Self Explanation”. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0074-8
title: Three-level incremental scaffolding for self-explanation: masking interface, uncovered-step prompts, and menu-based explanation tools
description: The SE-Coach delivers "incremental guidance" via "three levels of scaffolding": (i) a masking interface requiring students to mouse over each solution step to see it, helping focus attention; (ii) explicit self-explain prompts next to each uncovered step; and (iii) menu-based tools offering "constructive but controllable ways to generate the different types of explanations relevant for a solution step". The philosophy is to provide guidance to self-explanation incrementally, interfering as little as possible with spontaneous behaviors.
requirements: Menu-based tool explanations are evaluated for correctness against the information contained in the solution graph
constraints: Students with low tendency for self-explanation may not be receptive to interface scaffolding alone and may need more direct tutorial interventions

description: Betty's Brain, described by the commentary citing Tan et al. (2006), "is an environment that uses teachable agents to help students learn both domain and self-regulatory skills". article_title: Preface to the IJAIED 25th Anniversary Issue, Part 2
citation: Lane, H. C., McCalla, G., Looi, C., & Bull, S. (2016). Preface to the IJAIED 25th Anniversary Issue, Part 2: The Next 25 Years: How Advanced Interactive Learning Technologies will Change the World. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26, 539–543. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0109-9
title: AIED as an interdisciplinary research community combining AI with education and the learning sciences
description: The editorial characterizes AIED as a fundamentally interdisciplinary field in which the journal's creation 25 years ago corresponded with the formal emergence of the field itself. It states that "A good AIED research project was seen to be one in which both the technological frontier and the pedagogical frontier were being challenged in novel and interesting ways." The framework holds that AIED research draws on AI together with data mining, personalization, human-computer interaction, the semantic web, recommender systems, multi-agent systems, information visualization, computational linguistics, and simulation, and uses social-science methods for theoretical insight and empirical validation. It is used in the preface to frame the special issue's forward-looking papers.
requirements: AIED research must engage both the technological frontier and the pedagogical frontier
target_learners: learners supported by advanced learning technologies across the AIED field
target_learning_goals: interdisciplinary design of advanced learning technologies
examples: The preface cites the wide diversity of IJAIED papers spanning affective computing, collaborative learning, educational games, and immersive technologies as evidence of the field's interdisciplinary scope.

Preface to the IJAIED 25th Anniversary Issue, Part 2: The Next 25 Years: How Advanced Interactive Learning Technologies will Change the World. article_title: Preface to the IJAIED 25th Anniversary Issue, Part 2
citation: Lane, H. C., McCalla, G., Looi, C., & Bull, S. (2016). International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26, 539–543. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0109-9
title: Three core characteristics of AIED research with a learner-first core value
description: The editorial identifies three key characteristics that have emerged in AIED research over its first 25 years: "(i) aggressiveness in asking hard and deep questions; (ii) openness to an eclectic range of ideas; and (iii) a learner-first perspective." It further states that the most defining core value of AIED research is placing the learner at the focus of the field's work, driven by important problems for which AI and other perspectives create advanced learning technologies that "care" for the learner (Self 1998). This framework frames the special issue's vision papers.
requirements: Research problems must be important to learners, with AI used in conjunction with other disciplines to create technologies that care for the learner
target_learning_goals: design of learning technologies centered on learner needs
examples: The preface invokes Self's (1998) call for systems that care for the learner as the field's defining core value.

citation: Uto, M., Miyazawa, Y., Kato, Y., Nakajima, K., & Kuwata, H. (2020). Time- and Learner-Dependent Hidden Markov Model for Writing Process Analysis Using Keystroke Log Data. Int J Artif Intell Educ, 30, 271–298. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-019-00189-9
title: Time- and learner-dependent Gaussian hidden Markov model for estimating writing-process sequence patterns from keystroke logs
description: The article proposes an extension of the Gaussian hidden Markov model that "incorporates parameters representing temporal change in a subtask appearance distribution for each learner," so that writing-process sequence patterns can be estimated from keystroke log data. The model treats the writing process as a sequence of subtasks such as planning, formulation, and revision, and is intended to relieve instructors of analyzing sequence patterns for all learners manually.

Parameter estimation via the proposed collapsed Gibbs sampling algorithm

development of writing skills

article_title: Reflections on the Ecolab and the Zone of Proximal Development
citation: Rosemary Luckin & Benedict du Boulay. (2016). Reflections on the Ecolab and the Zone of Proximal Development. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0072-x
title: Zone of Available Assistance (ZAA) and Zone of Proximal Adjustment (ZPA) as an operationalization of Vygotsky's ZPD
description: The article introduces the ZAA and ZPA as two additional concepts introduced to clarify the ZPD for software implementation. The ZAA describes the variety of resources available within a learner's world, while the ZPA is created from a sub-set of the resources from the ZAA and should represent the resources that most accurately match a learner's needs. A More-Able Partner works with the learner to select optimal resources from the ZAA to create the learner's ZPA. Assistance must be flexible, quantifiable, and capable of being increased and decreased.
requirements: Assistance offered to a learner must be flexible and capable of being increased and decreased, and must therefore be quantifiable.
constraints: The ZPD concept as originally introduced lacked specificity about the type of assistance that should be offered to learners, how it should be quantified and how it should be provided and withdrawn.
target_learning_goals: Food webs and food chains (science curriculum)
key_sources: Rosemary Luckin & Benedict du Boulay. (2016). Reflections on the Ecolab and the Zone of Proximal Development. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0072-x

article_title: Reflections on the Ecolab and the Zone of Proximal Development
citation: Rosemary Luckin & Benedict du Boulay. (2016). Reflections on the Ecolab and the Zone of Proximal Development. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0072-x
title: The Ecolab Interactive Learning Environment
description: The Ecolab is an Interactive Learning Environment built to explore how an interpretation of the ZPD could support learners. It offers a simulated environment where learners place organisms and explore relationships between them to form food webs, with the metaphor of an Ecology Laboratory. The learning environment operates in 4 phases of relationship complexity, from simple two-organism relationships to complex food webs, and can be viewed in World, Web, or Energy views.
requirements: The underlying knowledge of food chains and webs used by the software was organized to reflect educational requirements about which concepts might be particularly problematic.
constraints: The curriculum covered was small, which was acceptable for a research tool but would be a serious limitation for a commercial system.
The design did not encompass people acting in the role of a More-Able Partner; it was designed for a single learner to use independently.
target_learning_goals: Food webs and food chains (science curriculum)

article_title: Reflections on the Ecolab and the Zone of Proximal Development
citation: Rosemary Luckin & Benedict du Boulay. (2016). Reflections on the Ecolab and the Zone of Proximal Development. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0072-x
title: Ecology of Resources model of context
description: The Ecology of Resources is a specification and a method for modelling a learner's context, developed from the ZAA and ZPA concepts. It is grounded on the definition that a learner has a single context that is their lived experience of the world, a 'phenomenological gestalt' reflecting their interactions with multiple people, artefacts and environments. The role of the More-Able Partner is to work with learners to select the optimal resources from a learner's ZAA, which extends beyond a single piece of software to include peers, home environment and wider school resources. Associated with the model is a design framework with a three-phase process for working with educators to develop context sensitive technologies.
requirements: Associated with the Ecology of Resources model is a design framework with a three-phase process for working with educators to develop context sensitive technologies and technology applications.
constraints: The Ecology of Resources extends the ZAA and ZPA concepts beyond learners' interactions with the Ecolab to their learning context more generally.
target_learning_goals: Context-sensitive design of educational technology

article_title: Complexity and Difficulty of Items in Learning Systems
citation: Pelánek, R., Effenberger, T., & Čechák, J. (2022). Complexity and Difficulty of Items in Learning Systems. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00252-4
title: Pragmatic distinction between complexity and difficulty measures based on data source
description: The article proposes a pragmatic distinction between complexity and difficulty measures for well-structured problems in learning systems: "a complexity measure is based only on the item description, it does not use any data about student performance; a difficulty measure is based only on data about student performance". Complexity is "an intrinsic item characteristic" concerned with the structure of the item, while difficulty describes how hard the item is for students. The authors acknowledge that context, biases, and scaffoldings make the distinction "more convoluted", so measures "end up lying on a spectrum rather than at two clear poles".
requirements: Items must be well-structured problems with clear instructions and an objective solution that can be checked algorithmically
constraints: The distinction is a pragmatic simplification; aspects like the role of context, biases, and scaffoldings make the distinction between complexity and difficulty more convoluted
target_learning_goals: Appropriate sequencing of learning items
Accurate student modeling

article_title: Evaluating the Impact of Learner Control and Interactivity in Conversational Tutoring Systems for Persuasive Writing
citation: Wambsganss, T., Benke, I., Maedche, A., Koedinger, K., & Käser, T. (2025). Evaluating the Impact of Learner Control and Interactivity in Conversational Tutoring Systems for Persuasive Writing. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00409-x
title: WritingTutor: a conversational tutoring system for persuasive essay writing with learner control features.
description: WritingTutor is a web-based conversational tutoring system that guides students through persuasive essay-writing exercises via dialog-based interaction, providing theory input and adaptive feedback on essay objectivity, polarity, and text quality. It comprises a learner-centered conversational user interface, distinct learner control features (content navigation buttons and an interface appearance panel for avatar, name, color scheme, and background), and an NLP/ML back end using a Naive Bayes classifier with semantic similarity matching for intent classification and the textblob library for polarity and objectivity feedback.
requirements: A Naive Bayes classifier trained on labeled user intents (62 intents) with a confidence threshold of 0.70, plus textblob for polarity/objectivity scoring.
constraints: Designed and evaluated for persuasive essay writing with university students; the article notes findings indicate limitations of learner control embedded in CTS.
target_learning_goals: persuasive essay writing
essay quality assessment

title: Learner control in CTS instantiated as deep-level content navigation plus surface-level interface appearance customization.
description: The article operationalizes learner control in a conversational tutoring system as two feature clusters derived from a literature review of 65 papers: deep-level control via "a sequence of pre-defined buttons, where students could skip certain learning steps" (content, pace, and sequence control), and surface-level control via an interface design panel giving students control over "the 1) avatar, 2) name, 3) general color scheme, and 4) background picture".

constraints: The article reports these features did not yield significant learning-outcome or experience differences after pair-wise comparison.

title: Deep learning model for automatic detection of hand-over-face gestures in learning contexts.
description: The authors proposed a novel deep learning approach for automatic detection of hand-over-face gestures in images, achieving "a classification accuracy of 86.87%". This model enables automated, non-intrusive monitoring of learner nonverbal behavior using a low-cost webcam, supporting integration with intelligent tutoring systems.

title: Nonverbal behavior monitoring via webcam can inform personalized interventions in intelligent tutoring systems.
description: Because learner nonverbal behaviors such as head movements, eye gaze, and hand-over-face gestures vary systematically with task type and difficulty, tutoring systems can use webcam-based monitoring of these signals to detect disengagement or difficulty and adapt instruction accordingly. The proposed method "uses a low-cost webcam and can easily be integrated with modern tutoring technologies", enabling personalized education without specialized sensors.
requirements: A standard laptop with an inbuilt webcam positioned to capture the learner's head-and-shoulders.
target_learning_goals: personalized support and adaptive instruction based on learner engagement

title: A data-driven cause-effect framework links learning context to nonverbal behavior via hidden affective states.
description: The authors propose a framework in which task difficulty (cause) influences hidden affective or mental states, which in turn produce observable nonverbal behaviors such as gestures and movements (effect). They "propose a data-driven cause-effect approach (difficulty → affect → gestures)" that capitalizes on digital learning environments and advances in computer vision. By varying the cause and measuring the effect, the relationship between learning context and behavior can be established without directly measuring affect, enabling inference of learner states from observable behavior.
requirements: Observable and measurable learning context (task type and difficulty) and observable gestures or body movements.
constraints: Hidden affective or mental states are not explicitly measured; the approach is speculative and context-specific.
target_learning_goals: inferring learner engagement and affective states from nonverbal behavior

article_title: AI Curriculum for European High Schools: An Embedded Intelligence Approach
citation: Bellas, F., Guerreiro-Santalla, S., Naya, M., & Duro, R. J. (2023). AI Curriculum for European High Schools: An Embedded Intelligence Approach. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00315-0
title: Embedded Intelligence Approach to AI Education Using Smartphones
description: The curriculum centers on programming real-world devices that interact with real environments, using smartphones as the central technological element. The article states that 'Current smartphones have the technological level required for AI teaching in terms of sensors, actuators, computing power and communications.' This approach reduces cost and makes AI education feasible at schools with limited budgets.
requirements: Students must have access to smartphones with adequate sensors, actuators, computing power and communications
constraints: Relies on Android smartphones; budget limitations may arise if students cannot use their own devices
target_learners: High school students aged 15-18 in scientific programmes
target_learning_goals: Understanding AI working principles through programming embedded intelligence systems
examples: Students implement smartphone apps through App Inventor, use Robobo robot for autonomous robotics, and Home Assistant framework for IoT tasks

citation: Bellas, F., Guerreiro-Santalla, S., Naya, M., & Duro, R. J. (2023). AI Curriculum for European High Schools: An Embedded Intelligence Approach. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00315-0
title: Intelligent Agent Framework for AI Curriculum Organization
description: The curriculum is organized around the concept of an intelligent agent situated in an environment, cycling through sensing and actuation stages. Five internal processes are identified: motivation, representation, learning, reasoning, and memory. The article states that 'the agent is continuously interacting with its environment in a cycle' and that 'the agent can learn from its experience in order to improve the action selection process.'
requirements: The framework requires that all five operational blocks be present in any intelligent agent implementation, though their complexity can vary
constraints: Memory is excluded as a dedicated topic because 'a proper implementation of a memory system is out of the scope of this education level'
target_learners: High school students aged 15-18 in scientific programmes
target_learning_goals: Understanding the fundamental components and processes of intelligent agents
examples: The framework is presented to students in the introductory teaching unit and structures all eight AI topics in the curriculum

article_title: Impact of an Artificial Intelligence Research Frame on the Perceived Credibility of Educational Research Evidence
citation: Mutlu Cukurova & Rosemary Luckin & Carmel Kent. (2020). Impact of an Artificial Intelligence Research Frame on the Perceived Credibility of Educational Research Evidence. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-019-00188-w
title: The in-credible AI effect: disciplinary framing as a peripheral cue in credibility judgements
description: The article proposes that perceived credibility of unfamiliar research evidence is processed via a peripheral route, where "the perceived credibility is shaped by peripheral cues or heuristic rules, the subject frame in which the evidence is presented, for example". Within this framework, the discipline framing of identical evidence acts as a heuristic that biases credibility judgements, producing what the authors name "the in-credible AI effect". The framework draws on the Heuristic Systematic Model and the elaboration likelihood model of persuasion, and explains why AI-framed evidence is judged less credible than neuroscience- or educational-psychology-framed evidence.
requirements: Unfamiliar research evidence that recipients process via peripheral cues rather than central scrutiny
constraints: The effect applies to perceived credibility, not to the veracity of the evidence, which is held constant across frames
target_learning_goals: critical evaluation of educational research evidence
understanding of framing effects in credibility judgements
examples: The experiment presented identical educational research evidence in AI, neuroscience, and educational psychology frames and measured five credibility dimensions
key_sources: Mutlu Cukurova & Rosemary Luckin & Carmel Kent. (2020). Impact of an Artificial Intelligence Research Frame on the Perceived Credibility of Educational Research Evidence. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-019-00188-w

article_title: Are MOOC Learning Analytics Results Trustworthy? With Fake Learners, They Might Not Be!
citation: Alexandron, G., Yoo, L. Y., Ruipérez-Valiente, J. A., Lee, S., & Pritchard, D. E. (2019). Are MOOC Learning Analytics Results Trustworthy? With Fake Learners, They Might Not Be! International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 29, 484–506. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-019-00183-1
title: Learning analytics research in MOOCs should adopt more robust techniques for evaluating and validating results, including large-scale replication research and advanced verification techniques.
description: The article argues that because fake learners introduce noise that can bias learning analytics, the community should "adopt more robust techniques for evaluating and validating learning analytics research". It recommends "encouraging and facilitating replication research at scale" and "developing advanced verification techniques", drawing on the hardware verification industry and verification of autonomous vehicles. It also calls for developing detection methods that generalize across platforms and course designs.
requirements: Detection algorithms capable of identifying fake learners must be available, since filtering requires detection and such algorithms are currently not available as off-the-shelf tools.
constraints: The article states that current detection algorithms detect only a subset of fake learners, and there might be more types of fake learners who currently sneak under the radar.
target_learning_goals: valid inference about effective learning strategies and resource use in MOOCs
examples: The article replicates two highly-cited learning analytics studies with and without fake learners' data and compares the results, following Replication Research and Sensitivity Analysis methodology.
key_sources: Alexandron, G., Yoo, L. Y., Ruipérez-Valiente, J. A., Lee, S., & Pritchard, D. E. (2019). Are MOOC Learning Analytics Results Trustworthy? With Fake Learners, They Might Not Be! citation: Alexandron, G., Yoo, L. Y., Ruipérez-Valiente, J. A., Lee, S., & Pritchard, D. E. (2019). Are MOOC Learning Analytics Results Trustworthy? With Fake Learners, They Might Not Be! International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 29, 484–506. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-019-00183-1
title: Fake-learner detection algorithms for CUMA and unauthorized collaboration in MOOCs.
description: The article uses dedicated algorithms to identify two types of fake learners: "Copying Using Multiple Accounts (CUMA)", where a master account receives credit while harvesting accounts collect correct answers, and unauthorized "Collaborators" who submit assignments together, detected using dissimilarity metrics on submission timing. In the 8.MReVx course, the CUMA algorithm detects 65 master accounts out of 478 certificate earners (a lower bound), and the collaborator algorithm identifies 20 (~4%) of certificate earners.
requirements: Detection requires sophisticated algorithms that are currently not available as off-the-shelf tools for cleaning data.
constraints: The CUMA algorithm is designed to provide a lower bound on the true number of master accounts, and the algorithms detect only a subset of fake learners; other fake learning methods may exist.
target_learning_goals: identifying non-learning behavior that biases analytics of learning in MOOCs
examples: In the MITx 8.MReVx Summer 2014 course, the algorithms identified 65 CUMA master accounts and 20 collaborators among certificate earners, with 11 accounts using both methods.

citation: Goodman, B., Linton, F., & Gaimari, R. (2016). Encouraging Student Reflection and Articulation Using a Learning Companion: A Commentary. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26, 474–488. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0041-4
title: Learning companion roles taxonomy: Weak Peer, Strong Peer, Expert, Motivator, Mentor, Teachable Agent, Facilitator, and Distributed Leader
description: The article organizes simulated pedagogical agents by the roles they can play: "Weak Peer, Strong Peer, Expert, Motivator, Mentor, Teachable Agent, Facilitator, and Distributed Leader." Each role carries distinct pedagogical support, from domain expertise to small-group dynamics, with pros and cons summarized in the authors' Table 3. For example, a Facilitator "requires knowledge about group dynamics to best support a group of learners." The taxonomy guides designers choosing a companion role for an ITS or CSCL environment.
requirements: The learning companion's pedagogical support depends on the pedagogical knowledge available to reason about learners' state and how to engage them
constraints: Each role carries stated cons, e.g., a weak peer's comments could confuse or frustrate the learner
target_learning_goals: domain learning through peer reflection and articulation
effective group collaboration skills

article_title: Encouraging Student Reflection and Articulation Using a Learning Companion: A Commentary
citation: Goodman, B., Linton, F., & Gaimari, R. (2016). Encouraging Student Reflection and Articulation Using a Learning Companion: A Commentary. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26, 474–488. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0041-4
title: Simulated peer in an ITS ensures collaborator availability while retaining individualized tutoring
description: The article describes a design pattern in which "[a] simulated learning companion, acting as a peer in an intelligent tutoring environment ensures the availability of a collaborator and encourages the student to learn collaboratively, while drawing upon the instructional advantages that ITSs provide." This blends ITS individualized coaching with CSCL peer learning, avoiding the need for a second human participant. The companion's role and knowledge extent are defined by the instructional designer and controlled at runtime, adapting behavior to individual student needs — an advantage over human collaborators.
requirements: A differentiated peer role, since students have higher expectations for communication from a tutor than from a peer
constraints: Menu-based dialogues made the interaction unnatural and not always the most appropriate
target_learning_goals: reflection on problem-solving actions
articulation of reasoning
examples: LuCy in the PROPA ITS prompted students to explain reasoning behind actions and justify decisions via menu-driven dialogue

article_title: Active Grade Estimator on Short Answer Assessment
citation: Mohammad Iqbal, Tsamara Rana Nugraha and Hsing-Kuo Pao. (2024). Active Grade Estimator on Short Answer Assessment. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-5651820/v1
title: Active Grade Estimator (AGE): a pool-based active learning model for automated short answer grading with two-stage sampling, assessment voting, and grading estimation modules
description: AGE is a pool-based active learning model for automated grading systems (AGSs) that integrates LLMs and regression models. It consists of three major modules: "two-stage sampling, assessment voting, and grading estimation modules". The two-stage query first selects the most contextually similar student answer via cosine similarity, then rewrites it via LLM canonicalization and simplification before teacher annotation. A voting mechanism based on minimum error grading estimation reduces annotation bias from multiple teachers, and a regression model estimates grades for remaining ungraded answers.
requirements: Requires a pool set of ungraded student answers, a set of answer keys, and teacher(s) to grade selected answers iteratively until a stopping condition is met.
constraints: The composition function must apply canonical construction before simplification, as the reverse order may lose information.
target_learners: students in online courses with short-answer assessments
target_learning_goals: automated grading of short answers
examples: The model was demonstrated on the UNT and SciC datasets with different grading tasks (regression and classification).
key_sources: Mohammad Iqbal, Tsamara Rana Nugraha and Hsing-Kuo Pao. (2024). Active Grade Estimator on Short Answer Assessment. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-5651820/v1

article_title: Utilizing a Pretrained Language Model (BERT) to Classify Preservice Physics Teachers’ Written Reflections
citation: Wulff, P., Mientus, L., Nowak, A., & Borowski, A. (2023). Utilizing a Pretrained Language Model (BERT) to Classify Preservice Physics Teachers' Written Reflections. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 33, 439–466. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00290-6
title: Reflection-supporting model with five elements (circumstances, description, evaluation, alternatives, consequences) for structuring preservice teachers' written reflections
description: The article uses a reflection-supporting model developed by Nowak et al. (2019), based on the ALACT-model by Korthagen and Kessels (1999), which "defines a reflection to include the elements: circumstances of the teaching situation, description of the teaching situation, evaluation of students' and teacher actions, devising of alternatives, and derivation of consequences." Preservice teachers were instructed to produce written reflections following this five-element scaffold during teaching placements. The authors state "the simplicity of the model makes it accessible to teachers at various degrees of expertise."
requirements: Preservice teachers receive explicit instruction on what is expected in each element of the reflection
constraints: The model was employed with preservice physics teachers at two mid-sized German universities

professional development through structured written reflection
examples: Preservice teachers wrote reflections on self-taught lessons or on lessons observed in a 16-minute video vignette

title: Transfer learning with pretrained language models for educational text classification
description: The article describes transfer learning as training "a general language representation from large language datasets" during pretraining, followed by fine-tuning on a downstream task. BERT uses a masked-token prediction objective (similar to a cloze task) and a next-sentence-prediction task during pretraining. The authors explain that "pretrained model weights in language models can form a solid backbone that provides structure for further downstream tasks", reducing the amount of task-specific training data needed.

A fine-tuning phase where pretrained weights are adjusted to the target classification task

examples: The study adopted a pretrained German BERT model by deepset AI with a vocabulary of 30,000 tokens, fine-tuned on labeled reflection segments

article_title: The Impact of Looking Further Ahead: A Comparison of Two Data-driven Unsolicited Hint Types on Performance in an Intelligent Data-driven Logic Tutor
citation: Christa Cody, Mehak Maniktala, Nicholas Lytle, Min Chi, Tiffany Barnes. (2021). The Impact of Looking Further Ahead: A Comparison of Two Data-driven Unsolicited Hint Types on Performance in an Intelligent Data-driven Logic Tutor. https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.05741
title: Hint Factory: data-driven Next-Step hint generation via Markov Decision Process
description: The Hint Factory is a data-driven method for generating hints by transforming historical student problem-solving attempts into a Markov Decision Process, using observed frequencies as transition probabilities. It estimates the expected value of each previously-observed problem state by "assigning rewards to complete solutions, small negative rewards (i.e. costs) to steps to positively reward more eﬃcient solutions, and large negative rewards to errors." Individual student attempts are represented as states with transitions when students add or delete nodes or make errors. The method selects a target state with the highest expected value and uses the latest statement derived there as a pointing hint.
requirements: Historical student data from prior correct solutions to the same problem, combined into an interaction network
constraints: Requires well-defined domains with multiple valid solutions; the process can be done offline with a simple table for real-time hint provision
target_learners: undergraduate students in a discrete mathematics course
target_learning_goals: solving formal logic proofs efficiently in time and steps
examples: Used in the Deep Thought logic tutor to generate Next-Step hints, and previously applied in tutors for logic and linked lists
key_sources: Christa Cody, Mehak Maniktala, Nicholas Lytle, Min Chi, Tiffany Barnes. (2021). The Impact of Looking Further Ahead: A Comparison of Two Data-driven Unsolicited Hint Types on Performance in an Intelligent Data-driven Logic Tutor. https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.05741

article_title: The Impact of Looking Further Ahead: A Comparison of Two Data-driven Unsolicited Hint Types on Performance in an Intelligent Data-driven Logic Tutor
citation: Christa Cody, Mehak Maniktala, Nicholas Lytle, Min Chi, Tiffany Barnes. (2021). The Impact of Looking Further Ahead: A Comparison of Two Data-driven Unsolicited Hint Types on Performance in an Intelligent Data-driven Logic Tutor. https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.05741
title: Waypoint hints: data-driven subgoal hints 2-3 steps ahead
description: Waypoints are a new hint type created by modifying the Next-Step hint generator to select target statements 2-3 steps away from the student's current state, among which the state with higher frequency within prior correct solutions is chosen. They are intended to serve as near-term subgoals, giving students more room to explore the solution space and develop their own problem-solving strategies without expert labelling. Expert review of a random sample verified this simple algorithm produces hints similar to those from data-driven Approach Maps.
requirements: A Hint Factory-style interaction network built from historical correct student solutions
constraints: Waypoints take longer to justify and resulted in fewer hints by design; the authors note more scaffolding may be needed to help students follow them

title: Deep Thought logic proof tutor with unsolicited Assertions hint delivery
description: Deep Thought is a propositional logic tutoring system used in a discrete mathematics course, with four phases: introduction, pretest, training (18 problems), and posttest (four harder, non-isomorphic problems). It provides immediate error feedback on justifications and derived statements, automated proof-completion detection, and node coloring based on necessity and frequency in historical correct solutions. Unsolicited hints are delivered as Assertions — "unsolicited, tutor-initiated steps inserted into the student workspace" — which prior work showed resulted in better performance than text-based messages.

constraints: No bottom-out hints: only level 1 pointing hints were used, with hint levels 2-4 disabled; hints are not necessarily provided when most needed

target_learning_goals: efficient logic proof solving in time, steps, and accuracy
examples: Students solved 18 training problems with data-driven hints and took a four-problem posttest without any assistance

citation: Ning Wang · James Lester. (2023). K-12 Education in the Age of AI: A Call to Action for K-12 AI Literacy. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00358-x
title: AI literacy defined as the ability to readily engage with AI by leveraging AI tools, systems, and frameworks to effectively and ethically solve problems in a wide range of sociocultural contexts
description: The article defines AI literacy as "the ability to readily engage with AI by leveraging AI tools, systems, and frameworks to effectively and ethically solve problems in a wide range of sociocultural contexts." It frames this as a component-based definition with three key parts: understanding AI capabilities, utilizing AI for problem solving, and applying AI in sociocultural contexts. This definition serves as the organizing framework for the article's call for K-12 AI literacy curricula and research.
requirements: AI literacy education should not require all students to engage with advanced concepts or mathematical foundations of AI
constraints: The definition is a conceptual framing by the authors, not an empirically tested construct

understanding AI capabilities

article_title: Adaptive and Intelligent Web-based Educational Systems
citation: Peter Brusilovsky, Christoph Peylo. (2003). Adaptive and Intelligent Web-based Educational Systems. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197315v1
title: Five groups of AIWBES technologies classified by their field of origin
description: The article organizes the variety of adaptive and intelligent Web-based educational systems into five technology groups: adaptive hypermedia, adaptive information filtering, intelligent class monitoring, intelligent collaborative learning, and intelligent tutoring. It states that "An earlier review (Brusilovsky, 1999) identified five major technologies used in AIWBES" and that these technologies have roots in Adaptive Hypermedia and Intelligent Tutoring Systems, with newer Web-inspired technologies subdivided into the other three groups. Table 1 lists technologies and sample systems for each group.
requirements: The taxonomy requires distinguishing technologies by their field of origin, as the article groups them according to whether they originated in Adaptive Hypermedia, Intelligent Tutoring Systems, Information Retrieval, CSCL, or Machine Learning/Data Mining.
constraints: The article notes that at the time of the earlier review, the lack of examples of Web-inspired technologies did not allow further classification, and that the borders between intelligent and non-intelligent systems are not clear-cut.

target_learning_goals: understanding the landscape of adaptive and intelligent educational technologies

citation: Peter Brusilovsky, Christoph Peylo. (2003). Adaptive and Intelligent Web-based Educational Systems. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197315v1
title: Three major AI-Ed development paradigms: AI-CAI, ITS, and AIWBES
description: The article distinguishes three major development paradigms in AI-Ed since 1970, compared in Table 2 across time span, goal, context, learning material, technologies, system completeness, and platform. The AI-CAI paradigm (1970s) aimed to replace primitive CAI in transferring knowledge; the ITS paradigm (1980s-1990s) aimed to "Support problem solving"; and the AIWBES paradigm (late 1990s-2000s) aims at "Comprehensive support" in a context of independent self-study with rich on-line learning material.
requirements: The paradigm comparison requires analyzing systems across multiple dimensions including goal, application context, learning material, technologies, system completeness, and platform.
constraints: The article states that "If we analyze the variety of adaptive and intelligent educational systems developed since the birth of the AI-Ed field in 1970, we can distinguish at least three major development paradigms."

article_title: ITS, The End of the World as We Know It: Transitioning AIED into a Service-Oriented Ecosystem
citation: Nye, B. D. (2016). ITS, The End of the World as We Know It: Transitioning AIED into a Service-Oriented Ecosystem. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0098-8
title: Four-Loop User Adaptation model extends traditional ITS adaptation at grain sizes above the outer loop and below the inner loop
description: The article proposes a four-loop model of user adaptation built on VanLehn's (2006) inner loop/outer loop framing. Beyond macro-adaptivity (problem selection) and step-based adaptivity (hints and feedback), it adds meta-adaptivity, where "the system adapts to the user by shifting the learner to an entirely different ITS system," and micro-adaptivity, which fine-tunes interactions below the problem step level. The paper states: "This implies a four-loop model for user adaptation, as shown in Fig.1." It holds that system, activity, and step boundaries "are likely to remain key decision points for adaptive systems."
requirements: Adaptation loops at meta and micro grain sizes require sufficient user data and mature AIED technology to be feasible
constraints: The article notes other loops of interest may exist and that VanLehn (2015) framed ITS behavior more generally as regulatory loops
target_learners: learners using adaptive learning technologies in formal and self-directed settings
target_learning_goals: adaptive selection of problems, feedback, systems, and event-level interactions matched to learner needs
examples: Fig. 1 depicts the four-loop model spanning system handoffs, problem selection, step-level help, and event-level optimization

citation: Nye, B. D. (2016). ITS, The End of the World as We Know It: Transitioning AIED into a Service-Oriented Ecosystem. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0098-8
title: Service-oriented AIED ecosystem decomposes the four-component ITS architecture into reusable, composable web services
description: The article argues AIED is reaching a juncture where systems split "into an ecosystem of reusable infrastructure and platforms" that may be "hosted across many different servers or institutions." It questions the traditional four-component ITS architecture (Domain, Pedagogy, Student, Communication modules from Woolf, 2010), stating "there is no reason to think that any given ITS must contain all these components, in the sense of building them, controlling them, or owning them." Instead, each piece could be "used as a web-service for many different learning systems," enabling deep specialization while remaining widely applicable through integration with platforms that have large sustained user bases.
requirements: Composing and coordinating specialized AIED services requires greater standardization and focus on data sharing between systems
constraints: Moving toward services carries costs: asynchronous service-oriented programming expertise, risk that a key service may fail or be discontinued, and collaboration investment to understand others' work
target_learners: learners across K-12 and higher education using adaptive learning platforms
target_learning_goals: enabling user adaptation and large-scale experimentation in education
examples: The author analogizes to web applications that integrate log-in services, cloud-based ads, and embedded media from many providers

citation: Nye, B. D. (2016). ITS, The End of the World as We Know It: Transitioning AIED into a Service-Oriented Ecosystem. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0098-8
title: Meta-adaptation transfers learners between systems (or to humans) based on needs and performance, via distributed or brokered adaptation
description: Meta-adaptation is described as "transferring the learner between different systems based on their needs and performance," the maximum possible grain size of adaptation, allowing learners to benefit from complementary strengths of multiple systems and potentially mitigating wheel spinning. It can also mean referring a learner to a human instructor, tutor, or peer. The article distinguishes distributed adaptation, where individual systems decide referrals, from brokered adaptation, which "would require a new type of service whose purpose is to monitor student learning across all systems (i.e., a student model integrator)" consulted as part of each system's outer loop.
requirements: Gains from system transitions must exceed the overhead costs of introducing learners to a new system, activity, or interface
constraints: Handoffs raise technical and societal issues: what data to share, which stakeholders (systems, teachers, students) control handoffs, and privacy/data-ownership concerns
target_learners: learners moving between multiple adaptive learning systems, individually or in cohorts
target_learning_goals: routing learners to the system, activity, or human support best suited to their current needs and performance
examples: First steps toward meta-adaptation cited include ONR STEM Grand Challenge integrations of Wayang Outpost with ASSISTments and AutoTutor with ALEKS, and integration of a version of AutoTutor with the ARL GIFT architecture.

title: AI-controlled experimental sampling: multi-armed bandit and adaptive design optimization methods for running education experiments at scale
description: The article frames the experimental process itself as an efficient search problem that AI can play a major role in. It notes that educational data mining research "has already started looking at dynamically assigning subjects to different learning conditions based on multi-armed bandit models," that cognitive model-comparison experiments have used adaptive design optimization, and that adaptive sampling is common in medical research. In the long term, automated experimentation may compare the effectiveness of different services or content modules by randomly selecting them from open repositories, allowing direct comparison of theories and exploration of interactions between theoretically-grounded constructs.
requirements: Methods must output interpretable statistics grounded in theories and concepts comparable across systems; efficient-search problems in AIED experiments need fundamental framing and solution
constraints: Trace- and path-based models are often too granular to generalize and may tailor instruction so tightly to specific problems that theoretical implications are hard to infer; model-comparison approaches require pre-existing hypothesized models; integrating expert knowledge with statistically-sampled information (e.g., as Bayesian priors) remains an open problem
target_learners: researchers studying learning on large-scale online platforms
target_learning_goals: estimating relative importance and boundary conditions of learning principles across contexts
examples: Multi-armed bandit models treat each treatment condition like a slot machine with different payout distributions, e.g., student learning gains

article_title: How Does Prior Knowledge Influence Eye Fixations and Sequences of Cognitive and Metacognitive SRL Processes during Learning with an Intelligent Tutoring System?
citation: Taub, M., & Azevedo, R. (2019). How Does Prior Knowledge Influence Eye Fixations and Sequences of Cognitive and Metacognitive SRL Processes during Learning with an Intelligent Tutoring System? Int J Artif Intell Educ (2019) 29:1-28. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-018-0165-4
title: Winne and Hadwin's information processing theory of SRL: four cyclical phases shaped by cognitive conditions such as prior knowledge
description: The article adopts Winne & Hadwin's information processing theory of SRL, in which "learning occurs through a series of four cyclical phases, where SRL is an event that unfolds over time". The phases are task understanding, goal setting and planning, enacting learning strategies, and adapting goals, plans, and strategies; they are cyclical, not necessarily sequential, and can run simultaneously. The model also posits cognitive conditions, including prior domain knowledge, that impact how students progress through the phases. The authors use it to frame their investigation of prior knowledge effects on SRL during MetaTutor learning.
requirements: SRL is treated as an event that temporally unfolds during learning, examined with process data rather than self-report
constraints: Phases are cyclical and not necessarily sequential; students may engage multiple phases simultaneously
target_learners: college students learning complex science topics
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning during learning with intelligent tutoring systems
examples: The study tested the model's claim that prior domain knowledge, a cognitive condition, impacts SRL phases during learning with MetaTutor.

title: MetaTutor: hypermedia-based ITS with four SRL-specialized pedagogical agents and an SRL palette
description: MetaTutor is "a hypermedia-based intelligent tutoring system that teaches participants about the human circulatory system", containing 47 pages of text and static diagrams with a 90-minute learning session. It was "designed specifically to foster SRL processes during learning": a timer, table of contents, learning goal and sub-goals, an SRL palette for self-initiating cognitive and metacognitive processes, and "four pedagogical agents where each agent is responsible for a different aspect of SRL" (Gavin the Guide, Pam the Planner, Sam the Strategizer, Mary the Monitor). In this study it was used with prompt-and-feedback and control conditions.
requirements: A sub-goal setting phase prior to the 90-minute session, in which participants set two sub-goals with Pam the Planner
constraints: In the control condition the agents did not prompt or provide feedback, acting only as minimal external regulation

planning, cognitive strategy use, and metacognitive monitoring
examples: Participants were randomly assigned to a prompt-and-feedback condition (n = 95) or a control condition (n = 99) during the 90-minute learning session.

title: Four-code scheme for coding self-initiated SRL processes by type (cognitive vs. metacognitive) and accuracy (high vs. low)
description: For sequence mining, the authors coded every self-initiated SRL behavior from log files into "separate codes (see Table 1) of behaviors, which contained two separate elements, with four codes in total (2 × 2)": cognitive-high accuracy, cognitive-low accuracy, metacognitive-high accuracy, metacognitive-low accuracy. Accuracy was defined per strategy: notes scored via Latent Semantic Analysis against content (50% similarity threshold), summaries by key words and length on first attempt, judgments of learning and feelings of known via a coding scheme relating ratings to page-quiz performance, and monitoring progress toward goals via a 60% quiz threshold. This allowed sequences to be analyzed by both process type and accuracy.
requirements: Log files recording user-initiated SRL palette clicks and strategy artifacts (notes, summaries, judgment responses, quiz scores)
constraints: Only self-initiated processes were coded, so externally prompted behaviors from pedagogical agents were excluded
target_learners: college students learning with an intelligent tutoring system
target_learning_goals: measuring sequences of cognitive and metacognitive self-regulated learning processes
examples: Notes were compared to content pages with Latent Semantic Analysis, with scores of 50% similarity and higher coded as accurate.

title: Design adaptive intelligent tutoring systems that individualize scaffolding and feedback based on learner prior knowledge
description: The authors conclude that their multichannel findings "have implications for designing adaptive intelligent tutoring systems that provide individualized scaffolding and feedback based on individual differences, such as levels of prior knowledge". Because high and low prior knowledge students engaged in different SRL process sequences and AOI-pair fixations despite identical interfaces, an ITS should detect the learner's prior knowledge level and tailor which SRL processes it scaffolds and prompts accordingly, rather than offering uniform support to all learners.

title: Viacocrea prototype: multi-user collaborative platform structuring cocreative problem-solving in six phases with digital creative techniques
description: The Viacocrea prototype is a multi-user collaborative digital platform used to support small-group cocreative problem-solving in real classroom PBL. It offers "a multi-user collaborative platform, a graphic representation of cocreative phases, and creative techniques aimed at structuring, supporting, enriching, and orchestrating small group cocreative problem-solving endeavours". In this study, five groups of secondary students followed six Viacocrea phases (Starting up, Defining, Designing, Building Up, Concluding, Communicating), performing two digital creative techniques per phase. title: Use reliable pre-trained sentence embedding models to provide real-time novelty feedback that helps teachers and students regulate collaborative ideation
description: The article argues that automatic novelty scores from reliable sentence embedding models can be translated into actionable, real-time feedback for teachers and student groups during cocreation. article_title: AutoTutor and Family: A Review of 17 Years of Natural Language Tutoring
citation: Nye, B. D., Graesser, A. C., & Hu, X. (2014). AutoTutor and Family: A Review of 17 Years of Natural Language Tutoring. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0029-5
title: Expectation-misconception tailored discourse framework with the 5-step tutoring frame
description: AutoTutor's core explanatory framework stores anticipated correct answers (expectations) and frequent invalid answers (misconceptions), and uses semantic matching to evaluate student input against them. Dialogs follow a 5-step frame in which the tutor poses a question, the student answers, the tutor gives brief feedback, collaboration improves the answer, and the tutor checks understanding. Discourse moves such as pumps, hints, prompts, assertions, and summaries guide students to cover each expectation, with assertions as a bottom-out response. The review presents this framework as the shared design inherited across the AutoTutor family.
requirements: Authoring of expectations, misconceptions, and discourse moves per main question via curriculum scripts or authoring tools
Semantic analysis techniques (e.g., LSA, regular expressions, word-overlap, logical entailment) to match student input to expectations and misconceptions
constraints: Finding good misconception coverage often requires multiple design iterations because even experts have trouble anticipating misconceptions
Dialogs for a full physics problem can last 30 to 100 turns before all expectations are covered
target_learners: learners across domains including computer literacy, physics, biology, and critical thinking
target_learning_goals: constructing explanations and answers to deep reasoning questions
remedying misconceptions in subject-matter content
examples: A sample physics dialog in Table 1 shows the tutor using a main question, pump, hint, answer, prompt, and short feedback to help a learner explain that two objects in free fall have the same acceleration
