citation: Mei Si. (2015). A Virtual Space for Children to Meet and Practice Chinese. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25:271–290. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0035-7
title: Four Kinect-enabled multiplayer virtual Chinese practice environments
description: A Unity-based multi-user system with a central server and Kinect-equipped clients, plus a mouse-and-keyboard fallback, in which users control virtual characters with body movements and talk via integrated voice chat. Four environments were built: Cao Chung Weighing an Elephant, The Elephant and the Blind Men, a school café, and a chat room, each embedding narratives and puzzles. The environments were "designed as supplementary materials to the learners' regular Chinese classes" and support different levels of open-ended conversation with an emphasis on social interaction.
requirements: Clients need a Kinect camera, a microphone and a speaker; a central server handles most computation
Integrated voice chat so users need no special operations to talk with each other
constraints: Environment 3 and 4 conversation and movement-coordination demands were too advanced for the 6–8 age group in the evaluation
Configuration of Environment 2's object set is not fully automated; the game must be rebuilt after adding new materials
target_learners: children aged 6 to 8 learning Mandarin Chinese in afterschool programs
target_learning_goals: Mandarin Chinese vocabulary, sentences, directions and movements
culture-related gestures and non-verbal behaviors
examples: In the evaluation, Environment 1 was used for three classes and Environment 2 for three classes; teachers led the class in reciting action and object names while two students played
key_sources: Mei Si. (2015). A Virtual Space for Children to Meet and Practice Chinese. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25:271–290. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0035-7

article_title: A Virtual Space for Children to Meet and Practice Chinese
citation: Mei Si. (2015). A Virtual Space for Children to Meet and Practice Chinese. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25:271–290. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0035-7
title: Embodied cognition as rationale for gesture-based language learning environments
description: The article draws on theories of embodied cognition, which "highlight the tight relationship between our body, mind, and the environment", arguing that physical movements help thinking and that memory can be offloaded to body-environment relationships. Citing gesture research showing gesturing plays an active role in learning and recall, the authors hypothesize that embodied interactive environments affording natural gestures and body movements will benefit language learning. This motivates the Kinect-based hands-free interface, though the evaluation did not test it against mouse and keyboard.
requirements: Environments must provide affordance for natural use of gestures and body movements
constraints: The evaluation "does not provide a concrete answer" on whether the Kinect interface enhances learning outcomes compared to mouse and keyboard
target_learners: children and young adults learning a foreign language
target_learning_goals: second language vocabulary and sentence practice
recall of learned concepts through gesture
examples: The system maps users' body movements to a character's movements so learners practice phrases such as picking up and dropping down while performing the corresponding actions
key_sources: Mei Si. (2015). A Virtual Space for Children to Meet and Practice Chinese. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25:271–290. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0035-7

article_title: A Collaborative Case Study System for Distance Learning
citation: Marta C. Rosatelli, John Self. (2004). A Collaborative Case Study System For Distance Learning. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 14, pp.97-125. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197307
title: LeCS: a web-based collaborative case study system for distance learning
description: LeCS (Learning from Case Studies) is a web-based system supporting collaboration between distant learners on case study activities. The article states that "LeCS is a web-based collaborative case study system that can be applied to any domain in which the learning from case studies method is used." It "provides a set of tools for geographically dispersed students working collaboratively on the case study solution," and its design was informed by an empirical qualitative study of paired distance collaboration.
requirements: Learners must be geographically dispersed and working on a case study activity suited to the learning from case studies method
target_learners: distance learning students working in pairs or small groups
target_learning_goals: solving case studies collaboratively at a distance
examples: The article describes LeCS's user interface, implementation, and agent-based architecture, and how it addresses recommendations derived from the empirical study.
key_sources: Marta C. Rosatelli, John Self. (2004). A Collaborative Case Study System For Distance Learning. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 14, pp.97-125. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197307

article_title: A Collaborative Case Study System for Distance Learning
citation: Marta C. Rosatelli, John Self. (2004). A Collaborative Case Study System For Distance Learning. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 14, pp.97-125. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197307
title: Collaborative case study work at a distance as a learning design
description: The pattern is distance learning from case studies: two or more learners at a distance collaborate on a case study activity using a shared web-based environment. The article frames it as "enabling collaboration between two or more learners at a distance on a case study activity," with learners "required to collaborate in order to solve a case study." LeCS instantiates this pattern with collaboration tools and learning-process support.
requirements: A collaborative learning environment must be provided so that distant learners can work together on the case study solution
target_learning_goals: case study problem solving through collaboration
examples: The empirical study simulated a scenario in which a pair of subjects at a distance collaborated on a case study, and LeCS was built to support such scenarios.
key_sources: Marta C. Rosatelli, John Self. (2004). A Collaborative Case Study System For Distance Learning. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 14, pp.97-125. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197307

article_title: A Collaborative Case Study System for Distance Learning
citation: Marta C. Rosatelli, John Self. (2004). A Collaborative Case Study System For Distance Learning. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 14, pp.97-125. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197307
title: Agent-based architecture for a collaborative case study system
description: LeCS is described as having an agent-based architecture in which software agents accomplish the system's support functions. The article announces a general description of LeCS covering "its user interface, implementation, and agent-based architecture," and states that the system "accomplishes functions regarding the learning process that together give real-time support to the distant learners." The architecture thus underpins both the collaboration tools and the real-time learning-process support.
requirements: Agents must implement the functions that provide real-time support to distant learners during case study solution
target_learning_goals: collaborative case study solution supported by software agents
examples: The paper describes how LeCS addresses the recommendations derived from the empirical study through its agent-based architecture.
key_sources: Marta C. Rosatelli, John Self. (2004). A Collaborative Case Study System For Distance Learning. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 14, pp.97-125. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197307

article_title: Creating Terminological Correspondence Recognition Tests with GPT-4: A Case Study in English-to-Turkish Translations in the Engineering Domain
citation: Marina Sánchez-Torrón, Egemen Ipek, Vanessa Enríquez Raído. (2024). Creating subject competence translation tests with GPT-4: A case study in English-to-Turkish translations in the engineering domain. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-4187415/v1
title: GPT-4-generated English-to-Turkish subject competence MCQ tests
description: An artifact of five automatically generated multiple-choice subject competence tests for assessing translators' knowledge of engineering terminology in English-to-Turkish translation. "We generated ve subject-area assessment tests, each composed of 20 questions." Each question presents an English sentence containing an engineering term and four Turkish answer options, generated via a zero-shot prompt in OpenAI Playground with specified sampling settings. The tests were evaluated by one expert translator but, per the authors, "are not t for direct implementation without further rement".
requirements: Requires detailed prompts specifying format, cognate avoidance, distractor similarity, and CSV output
constraints: Not fit for direct implementation without further refinement
Proprietary GPT-4 makes results non-reproducible
Findings may vary across domains and language pairs
target_learners: Professional translators and post-editors in human-in-the-loop translation workflows
target_learning_goals: Subject (domain-specific) competence in engineering terminology for post-editing machine translation output
examples: Five tests of 20 questions each were generated in July 2023 via an iterative zero-shot prompt refined over 18 iterations and about 6 hours
key_sources: Marina Sánchez-Torrón, Egemen Ipek, Vanessa Enríquez Raído. (2024). Creating subject competence translation tests with GPT-4: A case study in English-to-Turkish translations in the engineering domain. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-4187415/v1

article_title: Supporting Effective Collaboration: Using a Rearview Mirror to Look Forward
citation: McManus, M. M., & Aiken, R. M. (2015). Supporting Effective Collaboration: Using a Rearview Mirror to Look Forward. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26, 365–377. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0068-6
title: Group Leader Tutor: an ITS component that monitors and teaches collaborative skills in networked Jigsaw teams
description: The Group Leader (GL) Tutor was the software heart of the Intelligent Collaborative Learning System (ICLS), a client-server system on an Ethernet LAN using a shared FoxPro database. The authors state that 'The GL Tutor, a software process and the key contribution of our research, monitored and taught the effective use of collaborative skills.' It traced discussions through a finite state machine, compared used skills against optimal skills in the Collaborative Skills Network, assessed mastery by comparing successful uses to missed uses, and generated tutoring feedback based on previously stored feedback in a historical database.
requirements: A networked environment where students communicate by selecting sentence openers from menus and typing their own sentence closers, plus a shared multi-user database with record locking to avoid concurrent writing
constraints: The system was scripted and menu driven, and synchronous chat via files on the LAN yielded slow response time, which the authors call a major drawback
target_learners: undergraduate students in introductory computer science courses
target_learning_goals: effective use of collaborative skills such as communication, trust, leadership and creative conflict while working on group programming projects
examples: In two experiments undergraduate students used the ICLS to write statistics and database programs in C, working synchronously through expert and home group phases guided by the GL Tutor
key_sources: McManus, M. M., & Aiken, R. M. (2015). Supporting Effective Collaboration: Using a Rearview Mirror to Look Forward. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26, 365–377. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0068-6

article_title: Supporting Effective Collaboration: Using a Rearview Mirror to Look Forward
citation: McManus, M. M., & Aiken, R. M. (2015). Supporting Effective Collaboration: Using a Rearview Mirror to Look Forward. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26, 365–377. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0068-6
title: Collaborative Skills Network: mapping sentence openers to collaborative skills and subskills
description: The Collaborative Skills Network was a conceptualization of collaborative skills, their subskills, and the sentence openers that signal them, grounded in Johnson and Johnson's collaborative learning framework. As the authors explain, 'Each sentence opener in a discussion was related to a particular CL skill (Communication, Trust, Leadership and Creative Conflict) or subskill (Openness for the Communication skill) as defined by Johnson and Johnson (1991).' Selecting the opener 'I think' indicated openness of the sending subskill of communication, letting the GL Tutor interpret which skill a student was using and compare it to the optimal skills defined in the network.
requirements: Sentence openers whose association with particular skills and subskills is predefined in the network, so the tutor can trace discussion through a finite state machine
constraints: The network was operationalized through scripted, menu-driven sentence openers, a later-recognized insufficiency for identifying and guiding collaborative skills
target_learners: students working collaboratively in networked group projects
target_learning_goals: developing collaborative skills and subskills during group discussion
examples: A student's opener 'I think' was interpreted as the openness attribute of the sending subskill of the communication skill, as in 'I think that the counter needs to be set to zero.'
key_sources: McManus, M. M., & Aiken, R. M. (2015). Supporting Effective Collaboration: Using a Rearview Mirror to Look Forward. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26, 365–377. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0068-6

article_title: Supporting Effective Collaboration: Using a Rearview Mirror to Look Forward
citation: McManus, M. M., & Aiken, R. M. (2015). Supporting Effective Collaboration: Using a Rearview Mirror to Look Forward. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26, 365–377. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0068-6
title: Monitor and guide collaborative skills by connecting sentence openers with sentence closers, not openers alone
description: This principle states that identifying, monitoring, guiding, and assessing collaboration should combine the sentence opener a student selects with the free-form sentence closer they write, since the closer provides context the opener lacks. Reflecting on later systems, the authors write that 'we recognize that the use of sentence openers alone for identifying, monitoring, and guiding collaborative skills is insufficient.' Israel's ICSS demonstrated that coupling openers with closer text enabled more accurate classification of skills and discussion types.
requirements: A mechanism (e.g., agents or natural language processing) that can couple each sentence opener with text from the corresponding sentence closer to classify the skill and discussion type
constraints: The ICLS itself relied on openers alone given the resources of its era; the principle emerged from the authors' retrospective assessment informed by later research
target_learners: students collaborating in networked or online group learning environments
target_learning_goals: accurate monitoring, guidance and assessment of collaborative skills during group discussion
examples: Israel's ICSS coupled sentence openers with text from sentence closers using agents, achieving correct classification whenever a closer keyword was recognized
key_sources: McManus, M. M., & Aiken, R. M. (2015). Supporting Effective Collaboration: Using a Rearview Mirror to Look Forward. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26, 365–377. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0068-6

article_title: Evolution Is not enough: Revolutionizing Current Learning Environments to Smart Learning Environments
citation: Kinshuk, Chen, N.-S., Cheng, I.-L., & Chew, S. W. (2016). Evolution Is not enough: Revolutionizing Current Learning Environments to Smart Learning Environments. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0108-x
title: Smart Learning Environments: fusion of technology and pedagogy with full context awareness, big data/learning analytics, and autonomous decision making
description: The paper defines smart learning environments (SLEs) as ecosystems that fuse technology and pedagogy, in which "smart learning environments engage and integrate formal and informal learning in order to create autonomous adaptive learning environments for supporting individual learners with real-time and seamless learning experiences in ubiquitous settings." SLEs are distinguished from other technology advances by three features the paper elaborates: full context awareness (via IoT and sensing devices), big data and learning analytics to infer individual learning needs in real time, and autonomous decision making that recommends activities, locations, problems, learning objects and group compositions based on life learning profiles.
requirements: Learning technologies combined with IoT/ubiquitous sensing devices for context awareness
Big data and learning analytics techniques to collect, combine and analyze individual learning profiles
constraints: Providing each learner with just-in-time adaptive support through full context awareness is described as "still a challenge for TEL"
target_learners: learners in formal and informal learning settings, K-12 through higher education and lifelong learners
target_learning_goals: seamless, personalized, adaptive learning support across formal and informal contexts
examples: The paper describes smart cloud services (pull, prospect, content, push) from Boulanger et al. (2015) as an enabling framework
key_sources: Kinshuk, Chen, N.-S., Cheng, I.-L., & Chew, S. W. (2016). Evolution Is not enough: Revolutionizing Current Learning Environments to Smart Learning Environments. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0108-x

article_title: Evolution Is not enough: Revolutionizing Current Learning Environments to Smart Learning Environments
citation: Kinshuk, Chen, N.-S., Cheng, I.-L., & Chew, S. W. (2016). Evolution Is not enough: Revolutionizing Current Learning Environments to Smart Learning Environments. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0108-x
title: Flipped classroom as a student-centered blended learning environment in smart learning settings
description: The flipped classroom is presented as a popular method for enhancing teaching quality and improving learners' outcomes, particularly gaining interest in K-12 education (Chen et al. 2014). The paper states that "By integrating various learning technologies in the classroom, the flipped classroom approach has shifted the instruction from a teacher centered physical classroom, to a student centered blended learning environment." It enables interactive learning activities inside and outside the physical classroom and combines formal and informal learning approaches to increase student engagement.
requirements: Integration of various learning technologies in the classroom
target_learners: K-12 students (where the approach has gained particular interest)
target_learning_goals: increased student engagement and improved learning outcomes through student-centered blended learning
examples: Students take a vital role through collaborative activities while course content is delivered interactively both inside and outside class
key_sources: Kinshuk, Chen, N.-S., Cheng, I.-L., & Chew, S. W. (2016). Evolution Is not enough: Revolutionizing Current Learning Environments to Smart Learning Environments. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0108-x

article_title: Evolution Is not enough: Revolutionizing Current Learning Environments to Smart Learning Environments
citation: Kinshuk, Chen, N.-S., Cheng, I.-L., & Chew, S. W. (2016). Evolution Is not enough: Revolutionizing Current Learning Environments to Smart Learning Environments. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0108-x
title: Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs) enabling free, self-paced, self-directed online learning at scale
description: MOOCs are described as an online course format providing free access to open education with vast intakes over the Internet: "They allow everyone across the globe to pursue more knowledge with no limitation on the number of student intake and enrollment period." Learners can complete courses at their own pace, and MOOCs "enable self-directed learning where learners can achieve their own learning needs and goals by applying appropriate personal learning strategies." Both asynchronous and synchronous modes are supported to increase learner and instructor interaction.
requirements: Interactive video lectures and learning activities to engage learners in the learning process
target_learners: anyone across the globe pursuing more knowledge, with no enrollment limitation
target_learning_goals: self-directed learning at the learner's own pace and schedule
examples: The paper notes MOOCs force educators to rethink delivery, with revenue from certification, advertisement and profiling, despite high dropout rates and lack of personalization
key_sources: Kinshuk, Chen, N.-S., Cheng, I.-L., & Chew, S. W. (2016). Evolution Is not enough: Revolutionizing Current Learning Environments to Smart Learning Environments. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0108-x

article_title: Evolution Is not enough: Revolutionizing Current Learning Environments to Smart Learning Environments
citation: Kinshuk, Chen, N.-S., Cheng, I.-L., & Chew, S. W. (2016). Evolution Is not enough: Revolutionizing Current Learning Environments to Smart Learning Environments. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0108-x
title: Education-as-a-Service and Learning-as-a-Service: a federated reorganization of academia into modular, provider-specialized functional units
description: Facing a global, open education market with competition from free MOOC-based models, the paper introduces Education-as-a-Service (EaaS): "A new concept of BEducation-as-a-Service^ is emerging as an approach to deal with the challenges of global and open market." EaaS reengineers academia's structure, "which embeds all functions in one environment, to a federated approach where many different providers provide different functional education units, according to their unique expertise" — lectures, assessment by third parties, and social-interaction monitoring being separable. Learning-as-a-Service takes the learner's viewpoint, with self-directed knowledge maps and service choices at different learning stages.
requirements: Configurable and modularized functional units that can be identified, divided, remixed, reused and rearranged
Multiple providers each contributing according to unique expertise
constraints: Traditional schools that do not adapt risk being diminished from the global and open market
target_learners: global learners acting as consumers of educational services
target_learning_goals: flexible, aggregated learning paths at learners' own pace across multiple providers
examples: A learner may take Introduction to Calculus at one school known for fun teaching, Differential Calculus at another known for rigorous examples, then obtain a certificate from a separate assessment organization
key_sources: Kinshuk, Chen, N.-S., Cheng, I.-L., & Chew, S. W. (2016). Evolution Is not enough: Revolutionizing Current Learning Environments to Smart Learning Environments. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0108-x

article_title: Text-based Question Difficulty Prediction: A Systematic Review of Automatic Approaches
citation: Samah AlKhuzaey, Floriana Grasso, Terry R. Payne, Valentina Tamma. (2023). Text-based Question Difficulty Prediction: A Systematic Review of Automatic Approaches. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00362-1
title: Taxonomy of item difficulty prediction approaches: expert-driven versus machine-driven
description: The review introduces a classification (its Fig. 1) that distinguishes two families of item difficulty prediction approaches. Expert-driven approaches are qualitative, resting on "an expert consensus that exploits their domain knowledge and experience" and on pre-defined features from educational taxonomies or experts' difficulty perceptions. Machine-driven approaches quantify difficulty using statistical or data-driven prediction models to enhance scalability and minimise human intervention. The review uses this taxonomy to organise the field and to motivate its focus on automatic, text-based, a priori prediction.
requirements: Applies to a priori prediction of textual assessment items; the review excludes post-administration estimation and non-textual items
constraints: The review restricts scope to difficulty sources intrinsic to the question text, excluding learner knowledge and performance factors
target_learners: test-takers in traditional classrooms, eLearning platforms, CAT systems and ITSs
target_learning_goals: accurate a priori estimation of assessment item difficulty for item calibration and sequencing
examples: The review's Fig. 1 presents the taxonomic decomposition of item difficulty prediction approaches into expert-driven and machine-driven branches
key_sources: Samah AlKhuzaey, Floriana Grasso, Terry R. Payne, Valentina Tamma. (2023). Text-based Question Difficulty Prediction: A Systematic Review of Automatic Approaches. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00362-1

article_title: Text-based Question Difficulty Prediction: A Systematic Review of Automatic Approaches
citation: Samah AlKhuzaey, Floriana Grasso, Terry R. Payne, Valentina Tamma. (2023). Text-based Question Difficulty Prediction: A Systematic Review of Automatic Approaches. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00362-1
title: Four-task architecture of difficulty prediction models: ground truth labelling, pre-processing, feature extraction, prediction
description: The review characterises difficulty prediction models as sharing four architectural components representing four fundamental tasks: "1) Ground truth labelling, 2) pre-processing, 3) feature extraction and 4) prediction." Ground truth is labelled via psychometric theories (CTT, IRT) or expert rating; pre-processing applies standard NLP techniques such as stemming, POS tagging and lemmatisation; feature extraction operates at syntactic (surface) or semantic levels; and prediction is overwhelmingly supervised. The review uses this structure to organise its findings sections.
requirements: A dataset of questions with ground-truth difficulty labels, obtained via psychometric testing theories or manual labelling
constraints: Feature extraction is limited in the review's scope to features intrinsically derived from item structure, not student performance data
target_learners: students taking pedagogical assessments in classroom, CAT, ITS and AQG settings
target_learning_goals: predicting question difficulty to support item calibration, item sequencing and evaluation of generated questions
examples: The review's subsections Ground Truth Labelling, Pre-processing, Feature Extraction and Prediction each treat one of the four tasks
key_sources: Samah AlKhuzaey, Floriana Grasso, Terry R. Payne, Valentina Tamma. (2023). Text-based Question Difficulty Prediction: A Systematic Review of Automatic Approaches. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00362-1

article_title: Domain-General Tutor Authoring with Apprentice Learner Models
citation: Christopher J. MacLellan & Kenneth R. Koedinger. (2022). Domain-General Tutor Authoring with Apprentice Learner Models. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00214-2
title: Apprentice Learner Architecture: a modular framework of knowledge, performance, and learning components for interactive learning from tutors
description: The Apprentice Learner Architecture is a modular framework positing the knowledge structures, performance components, and learning mechanisms needed for apprentice learning—computational models that learn interactively from examples and feedback. It posits four knowledge structures (working memory, relational knowledge, overly-general operators, and skills), three performance components (relational inference, how search, and skill execution), and four learning mechanisms (how-, where-, when-, and which-learning). The architecture is designed to interact with tutoring systems, where agents receive steps, attempt them or request demonstrations, and receive feedback. It unifies mechanisms from prior systems such as ACM, CASCADE, STEPS, and SIMSTUDENT.
requirements: Requires interaction with a tutoring system that can provide steps, demonstrations, and correctness feedback
constraints: The architecture remains intentionally abstract on implementation specifics for each component, as different implementations may be preferable in different circumstances
target_learners: tutor authors and non-programmers building intelligent tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: authoring expert models for tutoring systems across domains
examples: The architecture was used to create two models: the Decision Tree model, which non-incrementally learns skills, and the Trestle model, which learns incrementally
key_sources: Christopher J. MacLellan & Kenneth R. Koedinger. (2022). Domain-General Tutor Authoring with Apprentice Learner Models. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00214-2

article_title: Domain-General Tutor Authoring with Apprentice Learner Models
citation: Christopher J. MacLellan & Kenneth R. Koedinger. (2022). Domain-General Tutor Authoring with Apprentice Learner Models. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00214-2
title: Decision Tree model: a non-incremental apprentice learner model within the Apprentice Learner Architecture
description: The Decision Tree model is one of two apprentice learner models built within the Apprentice Learner Architecture. It uses a non-incremental decision tree learner for when-learning, meaning it reprocesses all experienced training examples each time it updates its learned classifier. Like the Trestle model, it draws on the same small set of prior knowledge (six operators and three types of relational knowledge) to support expert model authoring. The model was used to author a novel experimental design tutor and evaluated across seven additional tutoring domains.
requirements: Needs access to a relational representation of each step in the tutor interface, which CTAT can automatically generate from drag-and-drop authored interfaces
constraints: Non-incremental approaches are less efficient to train because they reprocess all examples after each new example
target_learning_goals: learning expert models for tutoring systems from demonstrations and feedback
examples: Used to author an experimental design tutor via interactive training on 20 problems
key_sources: Christopher J. MacLellan & Kenneth R. Koedinger. (2022). Domain-General Tutor Authoring with Apprentice Learner Models. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00214-2

article_title: Domain-General Tutor Authoring with Apprentice Learner Models
citation: Christopher J. MacLellan & Kenneth R. Koedinger. (2022). Domain-General Tutor Authoring with Apprentice Learner Models. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00214-2
title: Trestle model: an incremental apprentice learner model within the Apprentice Learner Architecture
description: The Trestle model is the second apprentice learner model built within the Apprentice Learner Architecture. It uses Trestle, an incremental concept learning algorithm based on psychological studies of how humans learn concepts, for when-learning. Incremental algorithms efficiently update their classification tree in response to each new datum without reprocessing all previous training examples. Like the Decision Tree model, it draws on the same small set of prior knowledge (six operators and three types of relational knowledge).
requirements: Requires tutor interactions providing steps, demonstrations, and feedback
constraints: Incremental approaches learn less accurate classifiers than non-incremental approaches because they do not reconsider all data during each update
target_learning_goals: learning expert models for tutoring systems from demonstrations and feedback
examples: Evaluated across seven additional tutoring domains alongside the Decision Tree model
key_sources: Christopher J. MacLellan & Kenneth R. Koedinger. (2022). Domain-General Tutor Authoring with Apprentice Learner Models. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00214-2

article_title: Domain-General Tutor Authoring with Apprentice Learner Models
citation: Christopher J. MacLellan & Kenneth R. Koedinger. (2022). Domain-General Tutor Authoring with Apprentice Learner Models. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00214-2
title: Apprentice learner models enable non-programmers to author tutors for complex domains where existing approaches struggle
description: Apprentice learner models provide a means for non-programmers to build expert models by training computational agents through demonstrations and feedback, similar to how human apprentices learn. Domain experts train models by providing examples and feedback, and these models translate instruction into expert models that can power tutoring systems. This approach generalizes from training, unlike Example-Tracing which does not perform any generalization, making it viable for domains where demonstrating all correct solutions is impractical.
requirements: Requires a tutor interface with a relational representation that the agent can perceive
Requires interactive training with demonstrations and feedback
constraints: Particulars of how the interface was authored impact the agent's learning and performance
target_learners: teachers and other non-programmers building educational technologies
target_learning_goals: authoring pedagogically effective tutoring systems
examples: The Decision Tree model was used to author a novel experimental design tutor, and both models were applied across eight tutor domains
key_sources: Christopher J. MacLellan & Kenneth R. Koedinger. (2022). Domain-General Tutor Authoring with Apprentice Learner Models. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00214-2

article_title: MArCo: Building an Artificial Conflict Mediator to Support Group Planning Interactions
citation: Patricia Azevedo Tedesco. (2003). MArCo: Building an Artificial Conflict Mediator to Support Group Planning Interactions. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 13, 117-155. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197314
title: Model of strategic changes describing what types of changes happen to a group plan and how changes to one strategy component impact the others
description: The article builds "a model of strategic operations, which describes what types of changes happen to a plan as well as how changes to one component of the strategy (beliefs, intentions, ordering relations, context beliefs and goals) impact the other ones." It serves to diagnose which changes are happening to the group plan during interaction. Together with a model of the group and the history of the interaction, it supplies the inputs the conflict mediator uses to detect and mediate meta-cognitive conflicts.
requirements: Requires a model of strategic changes, a model of the group, and the history of the interaction as inputs to diagnose changes to the group plan
constraints: Addressed to meta-cognitive conflicts arising in group planning interactions

description: MArCo is the article's prototype system: "MArCo, our prototype embedding the artificial conflict mediator, shows how our conceptual framework has been put to practical use." It operationalises the framework for detecting and mediating meta-cognitive conflicts, drawing on the model of strategic changes, the model of the group, and the history of the interaction. title: Design collaborative environments so that conflicts inherent to group problem solving are mediated rather than suppressed, because well-employed conflicts refine solutions
description: The article motivates its framework by noting that the emphasis on building co-operative/collaborative environments has highlighted "the issue of conflicts, inherent to group problem solving." Rather than treating conflict as a failure to eliminate, it treats well-employed conflict as a resource: mediation should trigger articulation and reflection so the group's solution is refined. Designers of collaborative learning systems should therefore build in conflict detection and mediation.

citation: Jennifer K. Olsen & Nikol Rummel & Vincent Aleven. (2021). Designing for the co-Orchestration of Social Transitions between Individual, Small-Group and Whole-Class Learning in the Classroom. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 31:24–56. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00228-w
title: Transition taxonomy: pragmatic and pedagogical social transitions organized by activity impact, group-size direction, and fluidity
description: The article presents a transition taxonomy that outlines the range of social transitions occurring in classrooms, distilled from prior literature and printed as Table 1. It distinguishes two top-level types: pragmatic transitions, which are 'not based in learning theory but still are practical considerations that add to the teacher's load', and pedagogical transitions that are part of the learning design and often inspired by learning theory. Each transition is characterized by activity impact (whole activity, between activities, within an activity), direction of group-size impact (increase, decrease, same), and fluidity (synchronous vs. asynchronous). The taxonomy structured the scenarios used in both studies.
requirements: To develop technology that supports social transitions within a lesson, the range of possible social transitions must first be understood
constraints: The taxonomy was applied to primary-school technology-enhanced classrooms and the study scenarios covered all taxonomy types except transitions between activities at the same social level
target_learning_goals: supporting classroom orchestration of learning activities across individual, small-group and whole-class social levels
examples: Table 1 maps each of the 14 transition types to the Study 1 and Study 2 scenarios that elicited them, e.g. absence, late arrival, early dismissal, rotating activities, and within-activity group-size changes

title: Six design desires for shared control of co-orchestrated social transitions between teacher and system
description: The article formulates six design desires (Table 2) for balancing teacher and system responsibilities when orchestrating fluid social transitions. They specify that 'Teachers are the instigators of the lesson-designing process', that the system carries out real-time orchestration decisions within the confines of the teacher's lesson design, that teachers can make real-time changes and override system decisions, that the system provides monitoring with visible decisions and explanations, that teachers handle behavior, help-giving and reviewing system decisions, and that the system communicates transition information to students. Desires 4 and 5 were updated after Study 2.
requirements: Co-orchestration must be designed according to the teacher's values and classroom culture for the technology to be adopted in the long term
constraints: The desires were derived from primary-school teachers' perspectives; involving students is left for future work
target_learning_goals: fluid social transitions between individual, small-group and whole-class learning in technology-enhanced classrooms
examples: The desires were implemented in a mid-fidelity prototype of an orchestration system for specific social transition scenarios used in Study 2

title: Divide orchestration control by planning phase: teachers design the lesson and may override; the system executes real-time transition decisions within that design
description: The article recommends splitting co-orchestration control around social transitions by phase. Teachers act as 'the instigators of the lesson-designing process', specifying when and how students transition between social levels, while 'the system is responsible for carrying out real-time orchestration decisions around social transitions within the confines of the teacher's lesson design'. This automation contrasts with systems that remain at the mirroring, alerting, or advising level, and frees teacher time for one-on-one support. Teachers retain the ability to make any real-time changes and override system decisions, which the authors say gives a sense of autonomy and control.

The system's decisions must remain within the bounds of what the teacher has planned
constraints: If roles are not well distributed, the technology can lead to greater orchestration load rather than a reduction
target_learners: primary school students in technology-enhanced classrooms
target_learning_goals: managing transitions between social levels without consuming teacher time needed for student support
examples: In the design sessions teachers asked for an 'override button' to adjust to what is currently occurring in the classroom, and the desires were realized in a mid-fidelity prototype

title: System monitors students and makes its decisions visible and explainable; system communicates transition information directly to students
description: Two linked design desires assign awareness and communication work to the system. The system should provide 'monitoring of the students', make all system decisions visible to teachers and some to students, and provide explanations for decisions made, since teachers 'always want to know why [the system is making a decision]'. Additionally, 'the system is responsible for the communication of information to the students' around their transitions, so students are not constantly interrupting the teacher and can take more charge of their own learning. Desires 4 and 5 were refined after teachers reviewed prototype scenarios in Study 2.

System decisions and their reasoning must be visible to the teacher

citation: Ningyu Zhang, Gautam Biswas, Nicole Hutchins. (2022). Measuring and Analyzing Students' Strategic Learning Behaviors in Open-Ended Learning Environments. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 32, 931–970. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00275-x
title: Task-oriented strategy framework for OELEs: strategies as conscious, controllable action sequences mapped to IA, SC, and SA cognitive processes
description: The framework defines strategies as "students’ conscious and controllable sequences of actions to facilitate and enhance task performance", making them measurable from log data. A hierarchical task model maps logged, time-stamped actions to three primary cognitive processes: Information Acquisition, Solution Construction, and Solution Assessment. Coherence Analysis plus sequence mining identify common action sequences interpreted as strategies, and differential sequence mining compares their use across performance groups. The authors state the framework generalizes prior Betty's Brain work and is applicable to other open-ended tasks that employ similar cognitive processes.
requirements: Learning environments must log students' activities in the context of the tasks they are performing for the analysis methods to be applied
constraints: The use of strategies is latent and cannot be observed or measured directly; it is only reflected in students' action sequences
target_learners: middle school students working in open-ended learning environments
target_learning_goals: science content learning
computational thinking practices
self-regulated learning strategies
examples: In the classroom study, students' logged actions were represented using a pre-defined <action,view> scheme, and sequence mining used an s-support threshold of 0.7 and a gap threshold of 6 minutes

title: CTSiM: a learning-by-modeling OELE for synergistic science and computational thinking learning
description: Computational Thinking using Simulation and Modeling (CTSiM) is an open-ended learning environment in which middle school students learn science by building conceptual and computational models. Students perform five primary tasks: reading a hypertext resource library, building conceptual models, constructing executable models with a block-based language, running simulations to debug behaviors, and comparing their model's behaviors to an expert reference model. Students have access to all interfaces at all times, which the authors say supports the open-ended nature of the approach. Units include kinematics, dynamics, diffusion, and ecology (fish tank).
requirements: Students compare their models against an expert reference model; students never see the code for the expert model
constraints: The study omitted the collision unit from analyses because it served as preparation for the diffusion unit
target_learners: middle school students (sixth grade in the reported study)
target_learning_goals: science concepts such as Newton's laws, conservation of momentum, and diffusion
computational thinking concepts and practices such as variables, loops, conditionals, decomposition, and debugging
examples: In the diffusion unit, students model random particle motion, particle-particle collisions, and particle-wall collisions, and study the aggregated emergent behaviors

title: Measure strategy use from logged activity traces rather than relying solely on self-report instruments
description: The article argues that strategy measurement should be grounded in students' observable action sequences from system logs, complementing self-reports, think-aloud protocols, and interviews. It notes that self-report methods suffer from problems: self-report items "often do not form an internally consistent category", interviewers interpret responses "through their own heuristics lenses", and learners report perceived rather than actual learning processes. Trace-based methods treat students' observable behaviors in an OELE as outward criteria providing information about their strategy use.
requirements: The learning environment must collect detailed, time-stamped logs of students' interactions that can be linked to outcomes
constraints: Aggregated behavior descriptions such as time spent on activities can mask actual strategies because of loss of contextual information
target_learners: students working in computer-based learning environments
target_learning_goals: measuring and evaluating learning strategy use
self-regulated learning assessment
examples: The authors apply coherence analysis and sequence mining to CTSiM log data to detect and interpret effective and ineffective strategies

article_title: Exploring Brazilian Teachers’ Perceptions and a priori Needs to Design Smart Classrooms
citation: Ferreira, A., Lima, D. A., Oliveira, W., Bittencourt, I. I. B., Dermeval, D., Reimers, F., Isotani, S. (2024). Exploring Brazilian Teachers’ Perceptions and a priori Needs to Design Smart Classrooms. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00410-4
title: Four-aspect taxonomy of smart classrooms: Smart Content, Smart Interaction, Smart Assessment, and Smart Physical Environment
description: The article adopts a taxonomy organizing smart classrooms around four aspects of the teaching and learning experience. As printed, "A useful taxonomy of smart classrooms is based on four signiﬁcant aspects of the teaching and learning experience: Smart Content, Smart Interaction, Smart Assess- ment, and Smart Physical Environment". Smart Content covers digital multimedia materials; Smart Interaction covers real-time communication, collaboration, and engagement monitoring; Smart Assessment covers digital and AI-supported evaluation with personalized feedback; Smart Physical Environment covers sensor-based climate and lighting adjustment. The article uses this taxonomy as background framing for why teachers' needs should inform each aspect.
requirements: Each aspect presupposes integration of advanced technologies (IoT, AI, sensors) into the physical classroom space rather than isolated devices.
constraints: The article notes the widely used definition by Huang et al. (2019) coexists with "other interpretations and models of what constitutes a smart classroom".
target_learners: K-12 and higher-education students in technology-integrated classrooms
target_learning_goals: personalized, engaging, and efficient teaching and learning supported by smart classroom technologies
examples: The article describes sensor-monitored lighting and automated climate control as Smart Physical Environment features, and IoT-based exam integrity systems as Smart Assessment features.

citation: Ferreira, A., Lima, D. A., Oliveira, W., Bittencourt, I. I. B., Dermeval, D., Reimers, F., Isotani, S. (2024). Exploring Brazilian Teachers’ Perceptions and a priori Needs to Design Smart Classrooms. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00410-4
title: Smart classroom distinguished from a merely technology-equipped classroom by holistic, adaptive integration
description: The article defines the smart classroom concept by contrast with ordinary technology presence: "it is essential to differentiate a smart classroom from one equipped with technology". A smart classroom integrates devices holistically and interactively so that its intelligence lies in adaptively and responsively using technology to meet individual student needs, including personalization of teaching, real-time analysis of student engagement, and adapting the physical environment. The article also cites Huang et al.'s acronym in which the term "stands for Showing, Manageable, Accessible, Real-time Interactive, and Testing". This distinction frames the study's argument that design should respond to teachers' needs, not only hardware.
requirements: Integration of technologies (IoT and AI) so everyday objects can communicate and share data that teachers can transform into informed decisions.
constraints: The concept is recent and the article acknowledges multiple competing interpretations and models.
target_learners: teachers and students in smart learning environments
target_learning_goals: making learning more engaging, personalized, and efficient while fostering collaboration, innovation, and inclusivity
examples: The article contrasts adaptive, sensor-driven environments with classrooms that merely have computers, projectors, and internet access.

title: Online superpowers questionnaire and 410-teacher response dataset
description: The study's instrument is a mixed online questionnaire built in Google Forms (November 2021), with 12 multiple-choice demographic items and seven open-ended questions on teachers' needs and smart-classroom perceptions; the analysis focused on two questions about desired superpowers and their classroom application. Released December 1st, 2021, it received 467 responses in 31 days, "of which 410 were deemed suitable for analysis". Inductive thematic analysis produced 20 codes and four themes; Table 3 lists sub-themes such as Assessment Activities, School Bureaucracy, Cognitive Abilities, and Immersive Learning. Most respondents were higher education teachers (60.2%) and over 40 years old (56.1%).
requirements: Responses had to specify one or more superpowers relevant to the educational context and their practical utility in a classroom session.
constraints: 57 responses were excluded as off-topic or ambiguous; participants were not required to have prior smart-classroom experience, so responses capture a priori desires rather than experience-based evaluations.
target_learners: Brazilian teachers across basic, professional, and higher education
target_learning_goals: eliciting teacher needs to inform smart classroom and educational technology design
examples: Sample exclusion rationale given in the article: "It would exterminate the SARS-CoV -2 virus and its variants" lacked direct relevance to pedagogical practice.

article_title: Intelligent Feedback on Hypothesis Testing
citation: Tacoma, S., Heeren, B., Jeuring, J., & Drijvers, P. (2020). Intelligent Feedback on Hypothesis Testing. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00218-y
title: Combining model tracing and constraint-based modeling to generate feedback on multistep reasoning
description: This framework combines two ITS design paradigms so that constraints check the internal consistency of a (partial) solution — identifying missing elements and inconsistencies — while model-tracing elements provide hints on appropriate next steps and diagnose specific common errors via buggy rules. In this article the combination was implemented in a domain module for hypothesis testing with 36 expert rules, 16 buggy rules, and 49 constraints. The authors found "constraints to be very useful for identifying missing elements and inconsistencies in students’ solutions", while model tracing allowed addressing specific errors and providing hints. Unlike prior systems (ActiveMath, Invention Lab) where the paradigms reasoned about separate domain aspects, this design integrates them to cooperatively reason about the domain as a whole.
requirements: A domain module containing expert rules, buggy rules, and constraints, with a reasoning engine that prioritizes rules and constraints when more than one is applicable
constraints: In this implementation no distinction was made between rules following the expert strategy and rules not following it
The possibility of generating worked-out solutions was not exploited
target_learners: first-year university social sciences students in introductory statistics
target_learning_goals: carrying out hypothesis tests and understanding the logic of hypothesis testing
examples: The domain module used constraints to flag a rejection region without hypotheses, and buggy rules to distinguish a t-test for independent groups from other test-type errors
key_sources: Tacoma, S., Heeren, B., Jeuring, J., & Drijvers, P. (2020). Intelligent Feedback on Hypothesis Testing. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00218-y

title: Hypothesis-testing construction tasks in the Digital Mathematics Environment with ITS feedback
description: Six hypothesis-testing construction tasks delivered in the Digital Mathematics Environment, in which students freely select steps from a drop-down menu called "Action", complete them in answer boxes, and state an overall conclusion. Two versions existed: an experimental version with intelligent feedback on steps and logic, plus a hint button, and a control version providing only verification feedback on individual answer boxes. The domain module was built on the Ideas framework, expanded to support constraints, and its software is available at http://hackage.haskell.org/package/ideas-statistics. A pilot with five students informed improvements to feedback formulation and prioritization.
requirements: A domain module added to the Digital Mathematics Environment enabling intelligent feedback on hypothesis-testing construction tasks
constraints: Assessment criteria for correct solutions were stricter in the experimental condition, requiring four essential steps, than in the control condition, which required only a correct conclusion about the null hypothesis
target_learners: first-year psychology students at a Dutch university
target_learning_goals: proficiency in carrying out hypothesis tests
examples: In the final two tasks the test statistic was given, so fewer steps were needed for a complete solution than in earlier tasks

article_title: Teaching Database Design with Constraint-Based Tutors
citation: Antonija Mitrovic & Pramuditha Suraweera. (2016). Teaching Database Design with Constraint-Based Tutors. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:448–456. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0084-6
title: Constraint-Based Modeling with ideal solutions for tutoring ill-defined design tasks
description: The article describes the constraint-based approach used by KERMIT and EER-Tutor for teaching conceptual database design, an ill-defined task with huge solution spaces. Instead of requiring a problem solver, the tutor checks whether the student's schema is correct by matching it to constraints and a pre-specified ideal solution: "The ideal solution captures the semantics of the problem without the need for a problem solver". Syntactic constraints check ER-model syntax while semantic constraints compare the solution to the problem requirements, recognizing alternative correct solutions by looking for equivalent ways of specifying ER components.
requirements: A pre-specified ideal solution per problem, supplied by the human teacher
A constraint set distinguishing syntactic and semantic constraints
constraints: KERMIT stored only one correct solution per problem, although several correct solutions may exist for all but the simplest problems
target_learners: university students in introductory relational database courses
target_learning_goals: conceptual database design using the ER/EER models
examples: KERMIT matched submitted solutions to a constraint set of 92 constraints plus the ideal solution; EER-Tutor contains 57 problems and over 200 constraints
key_sources: Antonija Mitrovic & Pramuditha Suraweera. (2016). Teaching Database Design with Constraint-Based Tutors. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:448–456. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0084-6

title: EER-Tutor: a Web-enabled constraint-based tutor for Enhanced Entity Relationship modeling
description: EER-Tutor is a Web-enabled re-implementation of KERMIT, developed in the WETAS authoring shell, supporting the Enhanced Entity Relationship model with specializations and categories. Its interface shows requirements at the top, an EER toolbar, a drawing area where incorrect parts are highlighted in red, and a feedback pane. It is one of three tutors available on Addison-Wesley's DatabasePlace portal, "used by more than 10,000 students worldwide", and its code was the foundation for COLLECT-UML and research on metacognitive skills, affect-sensitive agents, and tutorial dialogues.
requirements: Developed in WETAS, the authoring shell for constraint-based ITSs
constraints: The current version contains 57 problems and over 200 constraints
target_learners: students learning database design worldwide via the DatabasePlace portal
target_learning_goals: Enhanced Entity Relationship modeling and database design
examples: An affect-sensitive agent tracked students' facial features and problem-solving actions and responded with affect-sensitive feedback such as encouraging a struggling student to try simpler problems

title: Require students to name diagram components using words or phrases from the problem text
description: In KERMIT, when a student creates a new diagram component, its name must be a word or phrase from the problem text. The authors defend this naming policy as beneficial for learning: it mirrors how students underline words in requirements, lets colour-coding show how much of the problem text is covered, aligns with Software Engineering's encouragement of "the use of the customer's language", prevents uninterpretable invented labels, and makes interpretation of students' solutions easier while avoiding natural language understanding problems.
requirements: The problem text is shown in full to the student alongside the diagram tools
constraints: Some have criticized the decision as being overly restrictive
target_learning_goals: conceptual database design (ER modeling)
examples: Using different colours for different component types makes it easier for the student to see how much of the problem text is already covered and what is still outstanding

title: Distinction between instructional domains and instructional tasks in analyzing ill-definedness
description: The article applies Mitrovic and Weerasinghe's (2009) distinction between instructional domains and instructional tasks when discussing ill-definedness. The ER model itself is well-defined, with a handful of constructs with well-defined syntax, but conceptual database design using the ER model is an ill-defined task: requirements are underspecified and ambiguous, there is no algorithm to produce ER schemas, the stopping criterion is unclear, and there is no best solution but "rather a family of solutions for each problem". These features are typical of design tasks in general.
requirements: Understanding the application domain, common sense and background knowledge to interpret requirements
constraints: Checking semantic correctness requires ensuring the schema covers requirements completely and is of high quality, which is much harder than checking syntactic correctness
target_learners: students learning design tasks such as database modeling
target_learning_goals: conceptual database design; understanding ill-defined problem solving
examples: The article contrasts ER modeling with SQL query writing, where solutions are more structured because queries consist of six clauses
key_sources: Antonija Mitrovic & Pramuditha Suraweera. (2016). Teaching Database Design with Constraint-Based Tutors. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:448–456. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0084-6

article_title: Automated Essay Writing: An AIED Opinion
citation: Mike Sharples. (2022). Automated Essay Writing: An AIED Opinion. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00300-7
title: Transformer AI as a general-purpose language machine ungrounded in world experience
description: The article characterises Transformer AI systems such as GPT-3 as "a general-purpose language machine" that works like a highly trained text completer, attending to the previous 750 words to continue text. Because "Transformers are models of language not experiential knowledge", they can produce plausible text yet invent references and studies. The article uses this account to explain both the assessment threat and the fake-reference problem.
requirements: Access to a pretrained Transformer language model such as GPT-3 via a prompt interface
constraints: The article states such systems have no internal inspectable model of how the world works to check accuracy or scholarship
target_learning_goals: academic writing
understanding capabilities and limits of generative AI
examples: The author generated an entire 2,200-word academic paper with GPT-3 in under five minutes from a real IJAIED paper title
key_sources: Mike Sharples. (2022). Automated Essay Writing: An AIED Opinion. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00300-7

article_title: Stupid Tutoring Systems, Intelligent Humans
citation: Ryan S. Baker. (2016). Stupid Tutoring Systems, Intelligent Humans. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0105-0
title: Intelligence amplification as an alternate paradigm for AIED
description: The article proposes reframing AIED around intelligence amplification rather than artificial intelligence: AI technology derives important information about an online learning system, but action is taken by a human, not the system. As the author puts it, "The learning system is not itself intelligent; the human intelligence that surrounds the system is supported and leveraged." Designers are informed to support redesign, and instructors are informed so they can support students right away. The author frames this as what leading systems at scale already do, distilling information with sophisticated algorithms while placing "the ultimate decisions in the hands of a human being."
requirements: Data mining and reporting methods to inform humans, since humans cannot sift through large amounts of information quickly
constraints: Human beings vary in quality, so not all human responses to reporting are equally effective
target_learners: online learners across K-12 and higher education
target_learning_goals: improving learning outcomes through informed human decision-making rather than automated personalization
examples: ASSISTments uses simple interactions with hints, scaffolds, and three-in-a-row mastery, with data from hundreds of A/B tests analyzed by humans; Course Signals predicts risk and provides information to instructors who decide on action.
key_sources: Ryan S. Baker. (2016). Stupid Tutoring Systems, Intelligent Humans. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0105-0

article_title: Cross-prompt Pre-finetuning of Language Models for Short Answer Scoring
citation: Funayama, H., Matsubayashi, Y., Asazuma, Y., Mizumoto, T., & Inui, K. (2025). Cross-prompt Pre-finetuning of Language Models for Short Answer Scoring. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00474-w
title: Expanded RIKEN SAS dataset with 10,000 new annotations
description: The RIKEN SAS dataset is a publicly available Japanese collection of annotated high school students' answers to reading comprehension questions, with rubrics, prompts, and analytic-criterion scores. The authors "added 10,000 new data annotations (20 prompts with 500 answers each)" to it, yielding 34 prompts treated as 109 independent analytic-criterion prompts. It served as the testbed for all cross-prompt pre-finetuning experiments, with six prompts (21 analytic criteria) as targets and 28 prompts (88 criteria) as cross-prompt pre-finetuning data.
requirements: Rubrics with key phrases and human-annotated gold scores for each prompt
constraints: Limited to Japanese reading-comprehension questions from high school students
target_learning_goals: Japanese reading comprehension short-answer writing
examples: Six target prompts were split into 200 train, 50 development, and 250 test answers per prompt
key_sources: Funayama, H., Matsubayashi, Y., Asazuma, Y., Mizumoto, T., & Inui, K. (2025). Cross-prompt Pre-finetuning of Language Models for Short Answer Scoring. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00474-w

article_title: Cross-prompt Pre-finetuning of Language Models for Short Answer Scoring
citation: Funayama, H., Matsubayashi, Y., Asazuma, Y., Mizumoto, T., & Inui, K. (2025). Cross-prompt Pre-finetuning of Language Models for Short Answer Scoring. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00474-w
title: Two-phase cross-prompt pre-finetuning approach for automated short answer scoring
description: A training framework in which an SAS model is first pre-finetuned on already annotated prompts using rubric key phrases concatenated with each answer, so it learns "the task's general property (i.e., a principle of scoring): an answer receives a high score if it contains the information speciﬁed by the rubric." The pre-finetuned model is then finetuned on a new target prompt without requiring access to the cross-prompt data, resolving data accessibility because the second phase "needs access to only the parameters of the pre-ﬁnetuned model." The approach was instantiated with both a BERT regression model and open-source LLMs.
requirements: Predefined rubrics or reference expressions (key phrases) for each prompt
A pool of already annotated prompts with gold scores for the pre-finetuning phase
constraints: Gains are concentrated in low-resource settings; no significant benefit with 200 in-prompt answers
Validated only on Japanese reading-comprehension data
target_learning_goals: automated scoring of short answers against rubrics
examples: BERT and Llama-3-Swallow models were pre-finetuned on 28 prompts (42,240 rubric-answer pairs) and then finetuned on target prompts with 10-200 annotated answers
key_sources: Funayama, H., Matsubayashi, Y., Asazuma, Y., Mizumoto, T., & Inui, K. (2025). Cross-prompt Pre-finetuning of Language Models for Short Answer Scoring. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00474-w

article_title: Natural Language Generation Using Deep Learning to Support MOOC Learners
citation: Chenglu Li & Wanli Xing. (2021). Natural Language Generation Using Deep Learning to Support MOOC Learners. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00235-x
title: Social support theory as a three-category framework for analyzing forum support
description: The article adopts social support theory, defined as exploring "the resources exchanged by individuals with the perception by the provider or the receiver that such exchange would be beneficial to the receiver". It distills the theory into three categories: informational support (advice, suggestions, useful information), emotional support (empathy, concern, acceptance, encouragement), and community support (a sense of belonging through shared social activities). The authors use this framework both to code human and machine-generated replies on a 0-3 scale and to structure the validation survey.
requirements: Coders or participants need definitions and examples of the three support types to rate texts reliably
constraints: Applied in the article to text-based discussion forum exchanges in MOOCs, extending the theory from physical to digital environments
target_learning_goals: Engagement and persistence in online discussion forums through informational, emotional, and community support
examples: The authors manually rated 150 original and 150 generated replies for each support type on a none (0) to strong (3) scale before MANOVA/ANOVA testing
key_sources: Chenglu Li & Wanli Xing. (2021). Natural Language Generation Using Deep Learning to Support MOOC Learners. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00235-x

article_title: Natural Language Generation Using Deep Learning to Support MOOC Learners
citation: Chenglu Li & Wanli Xing. (2021). Natural Language Generation Using Deep Learning to Support MOOC Learners. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00235-x
title: Deep-learning NLG reply-generation pipeline (RNN and GPT-2) trained on MOOC forum post-reply pairs
description: A three-stage pipeline for generating forum replies: data preprocessing, model training, and quantitative evaluation. After cleaning (removing unreplied posts, stripping HTML, UTF-8 encoding, masking links), "there were 13,850 entries of post-reply pairs left", split 0.6/0.2/0.2 into training, validation, and testing sets. An LSTM-based RNN and a medium GPT-2 pretrained model (24 layers, 345 million parameters) were trained; generated replies were evaluated with word perplexity, Flesch-Kincaid grade level, and BERT-embedding cosine similarity against posts.
requirements: Posts paired with at least one human reply for supervised training
Sufficient computational power (the authors cite GPU limits in choosing the medium GPT-2 model)
constraints: Trained and evaluated on one creative thinking MOOC's forum data; web links are masked with a [LINK] token rather than generated
target_learning_goals: Automatic provision of supportive, contextually coherent replies to learner posts
examples: The testing set's 2770 posts were used as prompts, with model replies compared against original replies' readability and coherence metrics
key_sources: Chenglu Li & Wanli Xing. (2021). Natural Language Generation Using Deep Learning to Support MOOC Learners. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00235-x

article_title: Uncovering Blind Spots in Education Ethics: Insights from a Systematic Literature Review on Artificial Intelligence in Education
citation: Ana Mouta, Ana María Pinto-Llorente, Eva María Torrecilla-Sánchez. (2023). Uncovering Blind Spots in Education Ethics: Insights from a Systematic Literature Review on Artificial Intelligence in Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00384-9
title: Dialogic ethics framework for AIED recognising AI as a non-neutral tool
description: The review frames AIED ethics through dialogic ethics that reflect participation from diverse educational communities, and argues for recognising AI as a non-neutral tool. It proposes that "Ethical reasoning seems to be able to offer such considerations and possible transitions a sustainable conceptual support", asking how ethical frameworks can incorporate dialogic ethics reflecting diverse communities' participation. The framework spans data ownership, equity, emotions, and training, aiming to strengthen debates on the ethics of education itself.
requirements: Ethical frameworks must incorporate dialogic ethics reflecting the principles of participation from diverse educational communities
constraints: The review limits its evidence base to peer-reviewed publications from 2011–2022 in English, French, Portuguese, and Spanish
target_learners: K-12 and higher education stakeholders including teachers, governance bodies, technology industry, and policy-makers
target_learning_goals: Ethical use and design of AI in education
Ethical development of educational stakeholders
examples: The review synthesises 107 papers mapping applications, cultural inclusion, emotions, capacity building, and regulations to identify blind spots in AIED ethics

title: Artemisa chatbot for sexual harassment support at Peruvian university
description: The European project ACACIA (Restrepo et al., 2019), funded in part by Erasmus+, features a chatbot named Artemisa designed to address sexual harassment and recruit volunteers to promote diversity and tolerance at the Peruvian National University of San Marcos. The review lists it as a cultural and inclusive AIED feature providing support to victims of sexual harassment, ensuring anonymity, accessibility, and responsiveness valuable in sensitive and emotionally challenging situations. Like other chatbots, it presents accessibility challenges for users.
requirements: Training in accessibility, tolerance, and diversity acceptance to mitigate biases
constraints: Like other chatbots, it presents accessibility challenges for users
