article_title: Different Futures of Adaptive Collaborative Learning Support
citation: Rummel, N., Walker, E., & Aleven, V. (2016). Different Futures of Adaptive Collaborative Learning Support. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0102-3
title: Adaptive collaborative learning support (ACLS): intelligent technologies that assess collaborative interaction and deliver tailored pedagogical interventions
description: ACLS is defined as the intersection of CSCL and AIED research: "ACLS involves the use of intelligent technologies to improve student collaboration and learning by assessing the current state of the interaction and providing a tailored pedagogical intervention". Unlike typical intelligent tutoring, its goals are to improve collaboration between two or more students rather than support an individual learner. Support can focus on group formation, domain knowledge, or peer interaction, produced with natural language processing, machine learning, and user modelling techniques.
requirements: Assessment of the current state of the interaction to tailor interventions
constraints: Differs from individual intelligent tutoring because its goal is improving collaboration between students, not individual learning
target_learners: students working in small collaborative groups
target_learning_goals: domain learning and collaboration skills during computer-supported collaborative learning
examples: The APTA system provides peer tutors with reflective prompts, using an integrated cognitive model and machine classifier to diagnose domain errors and ineffective tutoring approaches
key_sources: Rummel, N., Walker, E., & Aleven, V. (2016). Different Futures of Adaptive Collaborative Learning Support. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0102-3

article_title: Different Futures of Adaptive Collaborative Learning Support
citation: Rummel, N., Walker, E., & Aleven, V. (2016). Different Futures of Adaptive Collaborative Learning Support. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0102-3
title: Taxonomy of ACLS support dimensions: timing, psychological realm, mode, locus, target, and type of support
description: The article organizes ACLS research around dimensions drawn from prior taxonomies: "identify dimensions such as the timing of support (whether it is provided immediately or with some delay during the collab- oration, or before or after the collaboration), the psychological realm of support (cognitive, social, metacognitive, motivational, affective)". Further dimensions are the mode of support (explicit or implicit), the locus of support (direct or indirect), the target of support (group formation, domain knowledge, peer interaction, social skill), and the type of support (guiding, challenging reflection, mirroring). The paper uses these dimensions to structure its research agenda and to diagnose the Dystopian system's uncoordinated support.
requirements: Research within each individual support dimension before coordinated decision-making across dimensions is possible
constraints: The taxonomies describe properties of support but fall short of an integrated instructional framework
target_learning_goals: design of adaptive support for collaborative learning
examples: The paper's Fig. 1 design space combines the mode and locus dimensions into four delivery quadrants
key_sources: Rummel, N., Walker, E., & Aleven, V. (2016). Different Futures of Adaptive Collaborative Learning Support. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0102-3

article_title: Different Futures of Adaptive Collaborative Learning Support
citation: Rummel, N., Walker, E., & Aleven, V. (2016). Different Futures of Adaptive Collaborative Learning Support. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0102-3
title: Design space of ACLS delivery combining mode and locus of support into four quadrants
description: The article presents a design space (Fig. 1, from Walker et al. 2009a) crossing mode of support (explicit or implicit) with locus of support (direct or indirect). "In many existing ACLS approaches, modelled after individual intelligent tutoring systems, support is explicit and direct (see lower right quadrant of Fig. 1)." The other quadrants are Peer-Mediated Feedback (indirect, explicit, prompting partners to co-regulate), Adaptive Resources (direct, implicit, resources provided when needed), and Adaptive Opportunities (indirect, implicit, modifying the learning environment such as adaptive problem assignment). The article states there is not yet a principled way of choosing among these possibilities in a given learning context.
requirements: Coordination across dimensions requires a comprehensive instructional framework
constraints: At this point in time the authors know no principled way of choosing from among the quadrant possibilities in any given learning context
target_learning_goals: delivery of adaptive support for collaboration
examples: Peer-Mediated Feedback prompts a partner to ask What do you mean by that? rather than asking the first student to expand their explanation
key_sources: Rummel, N., Walker, E., & Aleven, V. (2016). Different Futures of Adaptive Collaborative Learning Support. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0102-3

article_title: Different Futures of Adaptive Collaborative Learning Support
citation: Rummel, N., Walker, E., & Aleven, V. (2016). Different Futures of Adaptive Collaborative Learning Support. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0102-3
title: Comprehensive instructional framework for ACLS integrating collaborative learning theory, instructional theory, and instructional design principles
description: The article's central proposal is a comprehensive instructional framework, rooted in educational theory, to guide nuanced and flexible ACLS and prevent the Dystopian future. Its development "encompasses three components: 1. The integration of theories of collaborative learning to create a comprehensive framework that, alongside data-driven models, can inform support; 2. The derivation of principles of when, how, and what support to provide...; 3. The derivation of methods for balancing adaptivity and adaptability within support." Such a framework would orchestrate support across the multiple dimensions (timing, realm, mode, locus, target, type) in a coordinated and transparent manner, and its explainable models would underpin system transparency and shared control.
requirements: Rigorous empirical research and theory-building within each support dimension
Coordination of decision-making across all support dimensions
constraints: The authors expect that by 2040 the field will likely not yet have a comprehensive and actionable instructional framework, though substantial progress is possible
target_learning_goals: domain-level learning and learning of collaboration skills
examples: In the Utopian scenario, the framework lets the system coordinate motivational and social support (a break suggestion) with the goal of helping students progress at the domain level
key_sources: Rummel, N., Walker, E., & Aleven, V. (2016). Different Futures of Adaptive Collaborative Learning Support. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0102-3

article_title: Choice Architecture for Nudges to Support Constructive Learning in Active Video Watching
citation: Vania Dimitrova & Antonija Mitrovic. (2021). Choice Architecture for Nudges to Support Constructive Learning in Active Video Watching. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00263-1
title: Choice architecture framework for personalised nudges to promote active video watching
description: The paper proposes what it calls the first choice architecture framework for personalised nudges in learning environments, defining target behaviours (e.g. making comments, noticing important segments, reflecting, linking to personal experience), observed behaviours to correct (e.g. watching without commenting, shallow comments), and nudges as interaction games. It adopts the Münscher et al. nudge taxonomy of decision information, decision structure and decision assistance, and adopts Michie et al.'s behaviour-change principles of capability, motivation and opportunity. The authors state: "Our work is the first attempt to devise choice architecture for personalised nudges to improve learning", using a data-driven, learner-sourcing approach where past learners' behaviour shapes future learning experiences.
requirements: A learner model to detect observed behaviours where nudges may be needed, since the framework states that detecting unhelpful situations "requires a learner model"
constraints: The framework is outlined within the context of video-based informal learning and was operationalised in AVW-Space for pitch presentation skills
target_learners: university students (undergraduate, Master and PhD) learning transferable skills from videos
target_learning_goals: transferable skills such as delivering pitch presentations, including noticing key skill elements and reflecting on personal experience
examples: Example interaction games include DI_visible (heatmap of high-attention intervals), DS_increase-effort (prompting unused aspects), and DA_reminder (prompting a summary after watching without commenting)
key_sources: Vania Dimitrova & Antonija Mitrovic. (2021). Choice Architecture for Nudges to Support Constructive Learning in Active Video Watching. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00263-1

article_title: Choice Architecture for Nudges to Support Constructive Learning in Active Video Watching
citation: Vania Dimitrova & Antonija Mitrovic. (2021). Choice Architecture for Nudges to Support Constructive Learning in Active Video Watching. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00263-1
title: ICAP-based operationalisation of learner engagement categories in AVW-Space
description: The article operationalises the ICAP framework (Chi & Wylie, 2014) for video-based learning, classifying overt learner behaviours into Passive, Active, Constructive and Interactive modes, with learning effectiveness increasing from passive to interactive. Because AVW-Space did not support collaboration, the Interactive mode was excluded, yielding categories of Passive learners (watch but write no comments), Active learners (watch and write comments), and Constructive learners (comments add something new). The article quotes the underlying evidence: "as students become more engaged, starting from the passive mode to the interactive mode, the learning effectiveness increases; i.e. Passive < Active < Constructive < Interactive". In the reported studies Active and Constructive learners were not distinguished because the system could not analyse comment text.
requirements: Interaction logs and comments that allow overt behaviours to be classified into ICAP categories
constraints: AVW-Space did not support collaboration, so the Interactive mode was not considered; AL and CL were not distinguished in the reported studies
target_learners: university students watching videos in self-study settings
target_learning_goals: increasing cognitive engagement during video-based learning of presentation skills
examples: Passive learners log on and watch videos but write no comments; Active learners write comments on points in the videos; Constructive learners' comments or aspect use add something new, such as reflecting on past experience
key_sources: Vania Dimitrova & Antonija Mitrovic. (2021). Choice Architecture for Nudges to Support Constructive Learning in Active Video Watching. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00263-1

article_title: Choice Architecture for Nudges to Support Constructive Learning in Active Video Watching
citation: Vania Dimitrova & Antonija Mitrovic. (2021). Choice Architecture for Nudges to Support Constructive Learning in Active Video Watching. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00263-1
title: AVW-Space active video watching platform
description: AVW-Space is a controlled video watching learning environment designed for self-study, in which teachers select publicly available videos and define aspects that serve as micro-scaffolds for learning. It comprises a Private Space, where students individually watch videos and write comments linked to a video timestamp and an aspect, and a Social Space, where teacher-approved anonymised comments can be browsed and rated using reflection-promoting categories. The article states: "AVW-Space fosters active learning via interactive note taking and by providing micro-scaffolds for reflection", and students can also rate comments written by others, providing opportunities for social learning. The instantiation for pitch presentations included eight YouTube videos (four tutorials and four example pitch presentations).
requirements: Teacher effort to select videos and define aspects; teacher approval of comments before sharing in the Social Space
constraints: The version used in the reported studies could not analyse comment text, so Active and Constructive learners were not distinguished
target_learning_goals: transferable skills, specifically delivering pitch presentations
examples: Aspects for tutorials included reflective triggers such as "I didn't realize I wasn't doing this" and "I did/saw this in the past"; example-video aspects were Delivery, Speech, Structure and Visual aids
key_sources: Vania Dimitrova & Antonija Mitrovic. (2021). Choice Architecture for Nudges to Support Constructive Learning in Active Video Watching. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00263-1

article_title: Choice Architecture for Nudges to Support Constructive Learning in Active Video Watching
citation: Vania Dimitrova & Antonija Mitrovic. (2021). Choice Architecture for Nudges to Support Constructive Learning in Active Video Watching. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00263-1
title: High attention intervals derived from past learners' comments
description: High attention intervals are a learner-sourcing mechanism that aggregates comments made by past learners into continuous stretches of video, using a time-gap parameter θ (set to 4 seconds for tutorials and 6 seconds for examples) and an aggregation predicate. The intervals indicate areas in a video where users have noted something and are used to trigger interactive prompts and visualisations such as heat maps. The article states: "The high attention intervals are used for identifying situations that could trigger interactive prompts", implementing nudging as signposting through interactive visualisations and personalised prompts in AVW-Space.
requirements: A corpus of timestamped comments from past learners, and a chosen time-gap parameter θ that gives a reasonable interval partitioning
constraints: Larger values of θ will aggregate almost all comments into one interval, limiting the granularity of the partitioning
target_learners: future learners watching videos in AVW-Space
target_learning_goals: noticing important segments in videos and making comments at high-attention points
examples: Interval aggregation was computed for the eight videos of the pitch presentation instantiation based on comments from students in the two initial studies
key_sources: Vania Dimitrova & Antonija Mitrovic. (2021). Choice Architecture for Nudges to Support Constructive Learning in Active Video Watching. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00263-1

article_title: Equality of Learning Opportunity via Individual Fairness in Personalized Recommendations
citation: Mirko Marras, Ludovico Boratto, Guilherme Ramos, Gianni Fenu. (2022). Equality of Learning Opportunity via Individual Fairness in Personalized Recommendations. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00271-1
title: Seven curriculum-design principles operationalized as measurable properties of recommendation lists
description: The paper derives from curriculum-design literature a set of seven principles intended to be equalized in educational recommendations: familiarity, validity, learnability, variety, quality, manageability, and affordability. Instructional designers traditionally organize learning opportunities relying on "a range of principles coming from the curriculum design field, including significance, self-sufficiency, validity, interest, utility, learnability, feasibility". Each principle is operationalized as a function over a recommended list returning a value in [0,1] computed from platform data such as course categories, last-update timestamps, instructional levels, asset types, learner ratings, enrolment counts, and fees. The set is explicitly not claimed to be unique or universal.
requirements: Principles are operationalized only from data typically available on an online course platform, so not all curriculum-design principles or guidelines can be directly operationalized
constraints: The authors do not argue these are the only principles, as they depend on educational context and fairness auditing; some operationalizations are simplified (e.g., recency of updates as a proxy for validity)
target_learning_goals: equality of recommended learning opportunities consistent with platform educational principles
examples: The exploratory analysis characterized recommendations from ten algorithms against these seven principles using the COCO dataset.
key_sources: Mirko Marras, Ludovico Boratto, Guilherme Ramos, Gianni Fenu. (2022). Equality of Learning Opportunity via Individual Fairness in Personalized Recommendations. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00271-1

article_title: Equality of Learning Opportunity via Individual Fairness in Personalized Recommendations
citation: Mirko Marras, Ludovico Boratto, Guilherme Ramos, Gianni Fenu. (2022). Equality of Learning Opportunity via Individual Fairness in Personalized Recommendations. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00271-1
title: Fairness metric combining consistency (complement of weighted Manhattan distance) and equality (complement of Gini index) across learners
description: The paper formalizes consistency as the similarity between the targeted degree p_u(m) each platform sets for each principle m and the degree q(m) achieved in a learner's recommended list, measured as the complement of a weighted Manhattan distance. It then defines equality as "the complement of the Gini index over the consistencies across learners", where a value of 1 means the recommender is perfectly equal across learners in terms of consistency. Unlike prior individual-fairness work, learners count as positively treated when they achieve high consistency regardless of their past interactions, and no sensitive demographic attributes are used.
requirements: The targeted degree for each principle for each learner must be set by or known by the educational platform, requiring stakeholders empowered with decision-making capabilities to configure the platform
constraints: The notion assumes principles are context-sensitive and may provide different target degrees per learner or time period; quantifying student-specific target degrees from training-set preferences may be unreliable because preferences may have been biased by the recommender itself
target_learning_goals: monitoring and ensuring equality of recommended learning opportunities across learners
examples: The metric is computed locally on each ranked list so it can be optimized on a pre-computed recommended list through a post-processing function.

title: COCO educational dataset from an online course platform
description: COCO (Dessì et al., 2018) is, to the authors' knowledge, the widest educational dataset carrying all attributes required to model the proposed principles. "Collected from an online course platform, it includes 43,045 courses and 4,123,127 learners who gave 6,564,870 ratings." The authors note other educational datasets generally include only (learner, course, rating) triplets. For evaluation, a fixed-timestamp split at 2017-06-08 "led to 43,021 learners, 24,321 courses, and 529,857 interactions".
requirements: Requires course attributes such as category, last update timestamp, instructional level, enrolment counts, price, and asset types to model the principles
target_learning_goals: evaluating equality and personalization of course recommendations
examples: Used to evaluate ten recommendation algorithms and the post-processing equality approach.

title: Post-processing re-ranking mechanism applicable to any recommender's output
description: A novel post-processing approach that re-ranks courses originally suggested and optimized for personalization, so that recommended lists meet desirable principles of course recommendations equally across learners. The authors state that "our post-processing mechanism can be applied to the output of any recommender system to arrange recommendations that meet a range of properties", decoupling beyond-accuracy aspects from the underlying recommendation strategy. It supports optimizing different combinations of the principles of equality under individual learner preferences.
requirements: Pre-computed top-k recommendation lists from an underlying recommender, plus platform-defined target degrees and weights for the principles
target_learning_goals: balancing personalization with equality of recommended learning opportunities
examples: Evaluated on the COCO dataset against ten underlying recommendation algorithms, reported to yield higher equality with negligible loss in personalization.

article_title: Preface to Special Issue on User Modelling to Support Personalization in Enhanced Educational Settings
citation: Olga C. Santos, Milos Kravcik, Jesus G. Boticario. (2016). Preface to Special Issue on User Modelling to Support Personalization in Enhanced Educational Settings. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:809–820. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0114-z
title: Three-aspect taxonomy of user modelling research for personalization in learning environments
description: The article organizes personalization research in learning environments into three main areas, derived from analysing 39 PALE workshop contributions: "1) modelling learners and their performance to provide engaging learning experiences, 2) designing adaptive support, and 3) building standards-based models to cope with interoperability and portability". The first area covers modelling affective states, confusion, self-regulation, reputation and open learner models; the second covers adaptive study plans, hints, recommendations and educator involvement; the third covers standards such as IMS LIP, IMS RDCEO and IMS AFA. The four special-issue papers are each situated within one of these aspects.
requirements: Suitable user models that deal with the evolving nature of learner's current needs
target_learners: learners in technology-enhanced educational settings across formal and informal contexts
target_learning_goals: effective, active, efficient and satisfactory learning through personalization
examples: The special issue maps Ghergulescu and Muntean and Janning et al. to aspect 1, Dennis et al. to aspect 2, and Valdés Aguirre et al. to aspect 3.

description: The Personalization Approaches in Learning Environments (PALE) workshop series has been "run each year at the UMAP conference ever since 2011". The article analyses "A total of 39 contributions" from the first five editions (2011 to 2015) in terms of the three research aspects, covering intelligent tutoring systems, educational recommender systems, learning management systems, personal learning environments, educational games, agent-based environments, multi-user virtual environments and ad-hoc approaches. It served as the catalyst for this special issue.

citation: Kenneth R. Koedinger & Vincent Aleven. (2016). An Interview Reflection on “Intelligent Tutoring Goes to School in the Big City”. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 26, 13–24. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0082-8
title: PUMP Algebra Cognitive Tutor curriculum with embedded intelligent tutoring system
description: The PUMP (Pittsburgh Urban Mathematics Project) Algebra curriculum embedded the Algebra Cognitive Tutor into a complete redesigned course. The authors “would redesign the whole course from the bottom up including replacements for the textbook, new kinds of assessments, use of collaborative learning in the classroom portion of the curriculum, and new teaching approaches.” The recommended structure was non-technology text materials and classroom practices for 3 days a week and tutor use in the computer lab the other 2 days a week. It was evaluated in the 1993–94 school year in three city schools with a high proportion of low income and low performing students.
requirements: Integration of the tutor technology with other teaching practices and the existing social context of schools
constraints: In the first study there was not quite enough tutor material to reach the 3-day classroom / 2-day lab goal

target_learning_goals: practical and general understanding of algebra

title: Use multiple kinds of assessment — both standardized tests and curriculum-aligned open-ended items — when evaluating learning interventions
description: Following Ann Brown's suggestion, the 1997 study measured outcomes with both standardized test items and items designed to reflect curriculum goals of practical, general algebra understanding. The authors argue the debate over standardized versus open-ended assessment is best answered by “to include both kinds of assessments,” because a single standardized measure may lack validity and “is likely to miss (or underestimate) all of the learning that may be resulting from an intervention.” They express frustration that this practice, and multiple-assessment designs in randomized field trials generally, has not caught on.
requirements: Assessments must include both standardized items and items designed to reflect the intervention's curriculum goals
constraints: The idea has not caught on in practice; the What Works Clearinghouse stuck to single standardized tests as its only outcome measure
target_learners: K-12 and higher-education students in evaluated learning interventions
target_learning_goals: valid measurement of intervention learning outcomes, including complex problem solving and use of representations
examples: The 1997 study used standardized test items plus items measuring complex problem solving and use of representations

title: The Holodeck: an experiential supercomputer integrating visual, audio, physical, biometric, social, and infrastructure components for cyberlearning
description: The Holodeck is the article's central envisioned artifact: a networked software/hardware instrument for integrated education, research, and innovation. The article states it is 'a software/hardware instrument that seamlessly integrates visual, audio, and physical (haptics, objects, real-time fabrication) components with novel technologies.' It supports capture of behavioural, physiological, affective, and cognitive data, real-time analysis, scenario modeling, and human-human, human-agent, and human-robot interaction, linked to facilities such as the ASU Decision Theater and UCSB AlloSphere.
requirements: Networked infrastructure linking local and central nodes with low-latency, on-demand scaling, plus field kits for remote sites

target_learning_goals: transdisciplinary collaboration
creativity and innovation
wicked-problem deliberation
examples: The initial NYU Holodeck balanced small group, cross-site collaboration with incremental equipment costs and included field kits for global distributed support

title: Learning to Be and Learning to Live: lifelong, lifewide learning as the modus operandi of living
description: The article's organizing vision, drawing on UNESCO's 1972 'Learning to Be' treatise, frames learning as spanning the entire spectrum of life rather than age-bounded stages. It defines 'Learning to Live' as 'referring to both learning how to thrive in a new and evolving range of contexts and circumstances, as well as providing the modus operandi for living as learning.' Blended formal and informal environments, passion-based pursuits, mentoring in both directions, and the dissolution of retirement and life-stage boundaries underpin this framework, which the Holodeck is meant to serve.

constraints: Articulated as a utopian projection circa 2041, not an evaluated design
target_learners: learners of all ages and stages
target_learning_goals: self-actualization
thriving across evolving contexts
passion-based learning

title: Low thresholds, high ceilings, wide walls: an access pattern for learning ecosystems
description: The article adopts Resnick et al.'s design pattern for learning ecosystems as a quality of its envisioned cyberlearning environments: 'This eco-system provides low thresholds (lower barriers to entry), high ceilings (growth and impact potential), and wide walls (broad explorations and broad participation).' The pattern holds that entry barriers should be minimal, growth and impact potential large, and the space of explorations and participants broad, supporting universal access for individuals, teams, and communities to learning and innovation resources.

developing individual and collective expertise

title: Four primary qualities of cyberlearning environments: rich stories, open streaming content, shared contribution, and re-solvable challenges
description: The article enumerates the primary qualities of its envisioned cyberlearning environments: personal stories and interactive experiences that 'make it rich'; open streaming content that 'make it real and compelling'; contributions that 'make it yours, together'; and wicked challenges that can be iteratively 're-solved'. Each quality pairs an experiential feature with a learning function—dreams and storytelling for ethical understanding, multimodal simulation for visceral understanding of implications, active ownership of learning trajectories for expertise and collaboration, and iterative re-solving for societal progress.

deep collaborations
strong communication skills

The table lists interface capabilities and their 2030 vision: affect and emotion recognition with 'Strong recognition, fluent expression highly personalized'; embodied interactions with full body capture everywhere; learning companions (virtual + robotic) that seamlessly switch between virtual and physical settings; brain-computer interfaces; physiological in-body monitoring; augmented reality; and enhanced haptics.

article_title: LECTOR: Summarizing E-book Reading Content for Personalized Student Support
citation: Erwin Daniel López Zapata, Cheng Tang, Valdemar Švábenský, Fumiya Okubo, Atsushi Shimada. (2025). LECTOR: Summarizing E-book Reading Content for Personalized Student Support. Int J Artif Intell Educ 35. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00478-6
title: LECTOR: discourse-based attention model estimating Slide-Topic relationships
description: LECTOR (Lecture slides and TOpic Relationships) is an attention-based model that estimates a Matrix of Slide-Topic relationships M from lecture slides. "LECTOR extracts a set of topic candidates from the lecture slides and assigns a unique score to each slide-topic pair"; the score is "a linear combination of two scores, one based on the words’ importance (Importance score) and the other on the similarity between the topic and the slide embeddings (Similarity score)". It uses a domain-specific pre-trained BERT model and leverages the hierarchical structure of slides, assuming the main title introduces the main discourse and each slide title introduces the slide's discourse. Multiplying M with slide-wise reading logs yields topic-based reading characteristics such as student topic preferences.
requirements: A corpus of lecture slides with textual content (extracted via BookRoll's OCR) for domain-specific BERT pre-training
Topic candidates defined as single nouns and 2-gram noun sequences extracted with a Bi-LSTM pretrained model for Japanese slides
constraints: Slides written in Japanese motivated a Bi-LSTM noun extractor because grammatical categories are harder to find; n was limited to 2 because longer noun phrases in Japanese tend to represent multi-topic ideas
target_learners: university engineering students in a programming theory course
target_learning_goals: contextualizing reading behavior with slide content to support at-risk student prediction and personalized support
examples: The model was applied to 2,255 slides from 70 e-book materials of a Programming Theory course (2019-2023) and its output matrix M was multiplied with l1-normalized reading-time vectors to derive topic preference vectors
key_sources: Erwin Daniel López Zapata, Cheng Tang, Valdemar Švábenský, Fumiya Okubo, Atsushi Shimada. (2025). LECTOR: Summarizing E-book Reading Content for Personalized Student Support. Int J Artif Intell Educ 35. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00478-6

article_title: LECTOR: Summarizing E-book Reading Content for Personalized Student Support
citation: Erwin Daniel López Zapata, Cheng Tang, Valdemar Švábenský, Fumiya Okubo, Atsushi Shimada. (2025). LECTOR: Summarizing E-book Reading Content for Personalized Student Support. Int J Artif Intell Educ 35. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00478-6
title: Multimodal integration of reading activity and content data via matrix M
description: The article formalizes the integration of reading activity data and reading content data as a matrix multiplication between traditional reading logs and a matrix M encoding topic distributions across pages of the reading material. The article interprets "this multimodal integration ... as a matrix multiplication between traditional reading logs and a matrix M that encodes topic distributions across pages of the reading material". This reframes non-contextualized reading logs as an optimization problem of accurately estimating topic distributions across educational materials, enabling topic-based reading characteristics such as student topic preference vectors derived from l1-normalized reading time.
requirements: An accurate estimate of the matrix M of Slide-Topic relationships, since the integration's value depends on the quality of that estimate
constraints: The article states this multimodal integration had not been formally defined prior to this work; prior exploratory studies used simplified models (binary scores, co-occurrence graphs) without validating technical NLP performance
target_learners: university students using e-book reading systems
target_learning_goals: interpreting student reading behavior at the topic level to inform at-risk prediction and personalized interventions
examples: LECTOR's output M was multiplied with slide-wise reading logs to derive vectors of topic preferences used in Experiment 2
key_sources: Erwin Daniel López Zapata, Cheng Tang, Valdemar Švábenský, Fumiya Okubo, Atsushi Shimada. (2025). LECTOR: Summarizing E-book Reading Content for Personalized Student Support. Int J Artif Intell Educ 35. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00478-6

article_title: Beyond Predictive Learning Analytics Modelling and onto Explainable Artificial Intelligence with Prescriptive Analytics and ChatGPT
citation: Teo Susnjak. (2024). Beyond Predictive Learning Analytics Modelling and onto Explainable Artificial Intelligence with Prescriptive Analytics and ChatGPT. Int J Artif Intell Educ 34:452–482. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00336-3
title: Prescriptive Learning Analytics Framework (PLAF): an eight-step framework unifying predictive modelling, XAI transparency, and counterfactual prescriptive feedback
description: PLAF is a step-by-step framework with two key components, predictive and prescriptive phases, for identifying at-risk learners and generating evidence-based remedial advice. The article states that "The framework assumes that the data identification and acquisition steps have already been completed" and proceeds through feature engineering, model development, global interpretability (Step 4), local explainability (Step 5), counterfactual modelling (Step 6), natural-language conversion (Step 7), and intervention initiation (Step 8). It maps each step to specific technologies (SHAP, Anchors, DiCE, ChatGPT) and demonstrates practicality with use case scenarios on programme-completion prediction.
requirements: Data identification and acquisition steps must already be completed before the framework's steps begin
Counterfactual modelling must use actionable, mutable features constrained to feasible and realistic ranges
constraints: The framework was demonstrated on programme/qualification completion prediction at one Australasian HEI; the prescriptive phase's remaining evaluation is qualitative, using two hypothetical students
target_learners: at-risk undergraduate students at higher education institutions
target_learning_goals: timely identification of learners at risk of qualification non-completion and initiation of effective interventions
examples: The framework was demonstrated using programme/qualification completion predictive models built on a dataset of ~7000 learners, with two hypothetical-student case studies carried through the explainability and prescriptive steps
key_sources: Teo Susnjak. (2024). Beyond Predictive Learning Analytics Modelling and onto Explainable Artificial Intelligence with Prescriptive Analytics and ChatGPT. Int J Artif Intell Educ 34:452–482. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00336-3

article_title: Beyond Predictive Learning Analytics Modelling and onto Explainable Artificial Intelligence with Prescriptive Analytics and ChatGPT
citation: Teo Susnjak. (2024). Beyond Predictive Learning Analytics Modelling and onto Explainable Artificial Intelligence with Prescriptive Analytics and ChatGPT. Int J Artif Intell Educ 34:452–482. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00336-3
title: Cohort-relative z-score feature engineering converts raw academic and behavioural features into course-agnostic values for predictive modelling
description: This design pattern transforms raw behavioural and academic performance features (e.g., average grade, VLE resource access counts) into z-score standardised values relative to the learner's cohort, making them "more generic, contextually meaningful and comparable across different cohorts." The article states this conversion "converted the learner's absolute and mean values for a given feature into a form that captures the degree to which it deviates from the learner's cohort." The pattern increases descriptive power and model accuracy but trades off interpretability, which matters when features feed prescriptive feedback.
requirements: Access to cohort-level distributions of each feature to compute means and standard deviations
Domain knowledge to guide creation of derived features that amplify signal in the data
constraints: Z-score values possess greater descriptive power but come with the cost of lower interpretability, complicating Step 7's conversion back to raw values
target_learners: undergraduate learners across different cohorts and programmes
target_learning_goals: accurate prediction of programme completion outcomes across heterogeneous courses and programmes
examples: Engineered features marked in Table 1 include Grade Mark Deviation From Class Mean, Online Learning Pages Viewed Count Zscore, and Online Learning On Time Submission Count Zscore, all relativised to cohort totals

citation: Teo Susnjak. (2024). Beyond Predictive Learning Analytics Modelling and onto Explainable Artificial Intelligence with Prescriptive Analytics and ChatGPT. Int J Artif Intell Educ 34:452–482. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00336-3
title: DiCE-based counterfactual modelling configured with mutable, range-constrained features to generate feasible prescriptive pathways
description: DiCE (Diverse Counterfactual Explanations) is used in Step 6 to simulate what-if scenarios and generate candidate prescriptive feedback suggestions by treating counterfactual generation as an optimisation problem. The article notes that "counterfactual modelling needs to be performed using features upon which actionable steps can be taken," so a new model was trained on predominantly mutable features, with immutable demographics removed and features constrained to feasible and realistic ranges. Several candidate pathways are generated, unrealistic ones filtered and discarded, and the most realistic selected for feedback generation.
requirements: A separate predictive model trained on an alternative, predominantly mutable feature set, with some compromise in accuracy expected
Features constrained within feasible and realistic value ranges to generate feasible pathways
constraints: Use of only actionable features tended to produce weaker models, so stabilising features like Age Description were retained
target_learners: at-risk learners for whom tailored remedial advice is generated
target_learning_goals: identifying minimal changes in learning behaviour (engagement, assignment marks, on-time submissions) that would flip the prediction to successful completion
examples: Target features included engagement levels with the VLE, average assignment marks, and total number of on-time assignment submissions; immutable features like learner age were removed from counterfactual variation

citation: Teo Susnjak. (2024). Beyond Predictive Learning Analytics Modelling and onto Explainable Artificial Intelligence with Prescriptive Analytics and ChatGPT. Int J Artif Intell Educ 34:452–482. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00336-3
title: SHAP and Anchors as complementary XAI tools for global interpretability and local-level explainability of at-risk predictions
description: SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanation), based on Shapley values from game theory, generates both global interpretability (Step 4) and local explainability (Step 5), addressing the "how" and "why" questions around model behaviour. Anchors complements it at local level: "Anchors reduces a black-box model into a human-readable set of predicates resembling a degenerate decision tree." The article describes SHAP's advantage as detailed quantification of each feature's effect on predictions, while Anchors produces succinct, human-readable rule-based approximations of the underlying complex model's behaviour.
requirements: A trained black-box predictive model whose behaviour the surrogate tools approximate
Both techniques construct surrogate or proxy models simulating the primary model's behaviour
constraints: Both are approximations of the underlying model rather than exact accounts of its mechanics
target_learners: stakeholders including academic advisors, student support teams, and institutions using at-risk predictions
target_learning_goals: validating specific predictions before interventions and explaining to students how and why they were identified as at-risk
examples: Local explainability was demonstrated with two hypothetical students (Student A and Student B) predicted non-completion with probabilities of 97% and 90% respectively, using SHAP force-style plots interpreted as a tug-of-war

article_title: The Impacts of Domain-General vs. Domain-Specific Diagramming Tools on Writing
citation: Barstow, B., Fazio, L., Lippman, J., Falakmasir, M., Schunn, C. D., & Ashley, K. D. (2017). The Impacts of Domain-General vs. Domain-Specific Diagramming Tools on Writing. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 27, 671–693. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0130-z
title: Argument diagrams as hybrid spatial-symbolic tools: salience plus relative writing difficulty explain framework effects
description: The article proposes that argument diagramming works through two mechanisms: the spatial structure of diagrams makes some argument aspects salient (relevance of citations, presence or absence of opposition), while the detailed textual fields within diagram components make other aspects salient (such as validity, which varied across frameworks). A complementary account holds that harder writing challenges, like writing about validity, require the more direct scaffolding of a domain-specific framework. The authors state that "argument diagrams are importantly a hybrid spatial-symbolic tool for supporting thinking and reasoning" and offer these explanations as a starting point, noting prior studies lack theoretical explanations for diagramming effects.
requirements: Diagrams must combine spatial connections between argument elements with detailed textual fields within nodes and links for the two-part mechanism to operate
constraints: The authors state both explanations lack a strong prediction for why the domain-general framework increased supporting-evidence inclusion, and a combination of the ideas may be needed
target_learners: undergraduate students in psychology research methods courses
target_learning_goals: argumentative writing in science, including citation relevance, opposing evidence, and writing about validity

title: Integrate argument diagramming into college-level science course curricula to improve students' research writing
description: The article recommends that argument diagramming be embedded in course assignments rather than treated as an add-on: "the results of this study indicate that diagramming is a useful practice to employ in college-level psychology courses to improve students ' writing, and should be integrated into curricula." In the study, diagramming was woven into existing lab assignments via training, diagram creation, blind peer review of diagrams, revision based on feedback, and use of the diagram in drafting, without adding total lab time. The recommendation rests on the observed gains in citation relevance and opposing-evidence inclusion.
requirements: Time for diagramming activities must be reallocated from other course activities, as the study did not increase total lab or paper-writing time
constraints: Effects were demonstrated in a naturalistic system where training, peer review, and feedback were inseparable from diagram creation, so which element drives gains is unknown

target_learning_goals: writing research paper introductions with relevant citations and opposing evidence
examples: Students created argument diagrams for their hypotheses, peer reviewed three other diagrams in SWoRD, revised their diagrams from feedback, and used TF feedback to draft introductions

title: LASAD-based argument diagramming intervention with SWoRD peer review for research paper introductions
description: The intervention used LASAD, "an online diagramming tool that allows users to create visual representations of arguments, including both the elements of an argument and their relationships," customized with two frameworks (domain-general and psychology-specific). Students trained on a model diagram in pairs, built diagrams justifying their hypotheses, received blind peer review of their diagrams through the SWoRD system from four reviewers, revised, and used TF feedback to draft introductions. Survey data showed most students found LASAD easy to use and used their diagrams and peer comments when writing, but found peer ratings much less useful.

article_title: Implementation of Motivational Tactics in Tutoring Systems: 20 years on
citation: du Boulay, B., & del Soldato, T. (2016). Implementation of Motivational Tactics in Tutoring Systems: 20 years on. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26, 170-182. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0052-1
title: MORE's characterisation of motivation as effort, confidence and independence monitored on thresholded linear scales
description: MORE characterised motivation indirectly via three associated factors: "effort, confidence and independence". Each was conceived as a linear scale, seeded halfway, incremented or decremented by learner and system activities, with a threshold below which the system switched on tactics to raise the value — "the model was essentially a motivational thermostat". Confidence here meant confidence in tackling the next task, not stable self-efficacy, and the three scales interacted, e.g. providing help could raise effort but lower independence.
requirements: Continuous monitoring of learner actions such as perseverance, help requests and menu choices, rather than one-off pre-lesson measurement
constraints: The authors state this notion of motivation was a huge simplification, omitting academic emotions, engagement, goal setting and learner values
target_learners: learners in problem-solving tutoring, e.g. Prolog debugging
target_learning_goals: maintaining and improving motivation during a single lesson
examples: Effort was measured via perseverance when facing difficulties; confidence and independence via help requests and menu choices about perceived problem difficulty

article_title: Implementation of Motivational Tactics in Tutoring Systems: 20 years on
citation: du Boulay, B., & del Soldato, T. (2016). Implementation of Motivational Tactics in Tutoring Systems: 20 years on. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26, 170-182. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0052-1
title: MORE (Motivational Reactive Plan): a Prolog-debugging tutor with separate domain and motivational planners plus an arbitration mechanism
description: MORE was a 1990s teaching system for Prolog debugging that "incorporated two kinds of pedagogic reasoning": a domain planner sequencing problems by prerequisites and difficulty, and a production-system motivational reasoner maintaining or improving the learner's motivational state. Because the two planners could disagree about the next action, "a third mechanism (a set of rules) was implemented which arbitrated about how to deal with such disparities". Its defining feature was making micro-adaptive motivational pedagogy explicit and adjustable.
requirements: Explicit, adjustable representations of motivational strategy and tactics so rules can be revised in light of new theory or evidence
constraints: The system was not developed and maintained, so the motivational reasoning component was never integrated into a large-scale domain-based tutor
target_learning_goals: domain mastery alongside maintained motivation
examples: When the planners disagreed, e.g. offering a harder problem versus one of the same difficulty, the arbitration rules decided the action

citation: du Boulay, B., & del Soldato, T. (2016). Implementation of Motivational Tactics in Tutoring Systems: 20 years on. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26, 170-182. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0052-1
title: Motivational strategy as ordered production rules mapping student state to goals and tactics
description: MORE expressed its motivational pedagogy as an ordered production system (Table 1) whose rules matched student-model and history items such as "effort-valu < medium", "help-state = rejected" or "problem-state = failed" to top-level goals (increase confidence, increase effort, respect control) and tactics (provide specific help, praise performance, stimulate challenge, avoid intervention). The first matching rule fired. The grain size is the lesson-level strategy layer sitting beside domain sequencing.
requirements: A student model with motivational, behavioural and problem-outcome variables for rules to match against
constraints: The authors note an ambiguity between goals and tactics sharing the same term, and that the rules were the same for all learners and initial values were set arbitrarily at the halfway point
target_learners: individual learners in a tutoring system
target_learning_goals: effort, confidence and independence maintenance during problem solving
examples: If problem-state = given-up, goals were increase effort and increase confidence with tactics encourage effort and facilitate success, e.g. providing help about the next step

article_title: Implementation of Motivational Tactics in Tutoring Systems: 20 years on
citation: du Boulay, B., & del Soldato, T. (2016). Implementation of Motivational Tactics in Tutoring Systems: 20 years on. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26, 170-182. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0052-1
title: Nine-cell taxonomy of motivational tactics in advance of learner action: values, expectancies and feelings crossed with appeals to the positive, fear of the negative, and changing outlook
description: Following Pintrich (2003), the authors divide motivation into values, expectancies and feelings, and divide motivational strategies addressing these into "appeals to the positive, appeals to the fear of the negative, and attempts to change some aspect of the learner 's assessment of the situation" (Table 3). Each cell illustrates the broad focus of a tactic stated in advance of learner action, e.g. cell 6: "Understanding is as much a result of effort as it is of innate talent." Cells 3, 6 and 9 aim to change the learner's outlook so that appeal tactics may work in future.
requirements: Ideally the system ascertains the specific causes of a learner's lack of motivation, since different causes need different approaches, and models reactions to first versus n'th use of a tactic
constraints: The table illustrates tactic focus rather than actual tutor wording or non-verbal reactions such as switching topic or changing the task
target_learners: learners including those unmotivated or demotivated
target_learning_goals: effort investment, realistic goal setting, and reframed beliefs about learning
examples: Cell 1 urges effort so the learner achieves a valued goal; cell 8 urges effort so the learner avoids unpleasant affective outcomes such as shame

citation: Pareto, L. (2014). A Teachable Agent Game Engaging Primary School Children to Learn Arithmetic Concepts and Reasoning. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0018-8
title: Teachable agent game environment combining learning-by-doing and learning-by-teaching for arithmetic
description: A digital learning game environment of 48 two-player card and board games where "the mathematical content is intrinsically interwoven with the game idea". Students play games based on a graphical model of arithmetic and can teach an agent to play via show-mode and try-mode. The agent asks situation-specific multiple-choice questions organized into five categories reflecting progression in mathematical thinking, from game idea to advanced strategic thinking. The design combines the motivational power of games with the reflective power of a teachable agent posing deep questions.
requirements: Students must be able to play the games and respond to the agent's multiple-choice questions during regular math classes
constraints: Question difficulty follows the agent's knowledge level; progression requires satisfactory answers
The agent looks ahead at most two steps to simulate human rather than optimal play
target_learners: students with difficulties in mathematics grades 7-8
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of the base-10 number system
arithmetic operations and their connections
causal and strategic mathematical reasoning
examples: In a Pack-Many game, adding 4 squares to 6 triggers a packing operation where 10 squares are packed into an orange square-box, mirroring carrying in the decimal system

title: Teaching scheme based on cognitive-apprentice model with three scaffolding steps
description: The student tutor teaches the agent through a cognitive-apprentice model (Collins et al. 1989) with three steps: 1) show how to play while the agent observes, 2) let the agent try playing while providing corrective feedback, or 3) let the agent play by itself. These steps correspond to gradual withdrawal of support, where scaffolding is temporary and removed as the apprentice masters more of the task. This design was chosen because formulating general explanations of good choices would be too difficult for primary school students.
requirements: The tutor must have the option to show, provide corrective feedback, or step back
Scaffolding should be temporary and gradually removed
target_learning_goals: learning-by-teaching of arithmetic reasoning
examples: In try-mode the agent selects a card and the tutor has the final decision via go and stop signs; if rejected the tutor must provide an alternative card

title: Teachable agent questioning system with five question categories
description: The agent asks the tutor situation-specific multiple-choice questions at the moment a card is chosen but before the computation is executed, to encourage mental calculation and reasoning. Questions are organized into five categories: game idea, graphical model, scoring, basic strategic thinking, and advanced strategic thinking. Question difficulty follows the agent's knowledge level, aligned with Vygotskij's zone of proximal development. Questions are posed every 3rd turn on average, about three questions per game.
requirements: Multiple-choice format with a don't-know option
Important questions are checked several times with different surface formulations
Progression requires 75% of previous questions answered satisfactorily
constraints: Questions are text-based and appear in a dialogue window
The youngest children are not good at writing, motivating the multiple-choice format
target_learning_goals: self-explanation
transfer of tacit game knowledge to articulated language
mathematical reasoning
examples: A question template compares two choices with respect to points, asking whether one card is better than another given the current game state

citation: Pareto, L. (2014). A Teachable Agent Game Engaging Primary School Children to Learn Arithmetic Concepts and Reasoning. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0018-8
title: Graphical model of arithmetic with packing and unpacking of squares
description: Cards and the game board represent positive or negative integers modelled by groups of coloured squares. Moving squares from a card to the board represents addition, the opposite direction subtraction. Packing 10 squares into a square-box corresponds to carrying, unpacking to borrowing. The graphical model enforces all mathematical rules so that all possible actions represent valid computations, and provides children with visual cues and more familiar vocabulary for mathematical discussions.
requirements: The graphical representation must emphasize position by colour and make transitions between positions explicit
constraints: Square-boxes are viewed from above so they look just like squares, mimicking the visual similarity of digits
target_learning_goals: understanding the base-10 positioning system
understanding integer behaviour under arithmetic operations
examples: The Find-Pair category illustrates the difference 96−23=73 with 9 orange and 6 red squares representing 96

citation: Fang, Y., Lippert, A., Cai, Z., Chen, S., Frijters, J. C., Greenberg, D., & Graesser, A. C. (2021). Patterns of Adults with Low Literacy Skills Interacting with an Intelligent Tutoring System. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00266-y
title: Graesser and McNamara's multilevel theoretical framework of reading comprehension
description: The article organizes AutoTutor lessons around a multilevel framework identifying "Six levels of comprehension": word, syntax, the explicit textbase, the referential situation model, the genre/rhetorical structure, and the pragmatic communication level. Word and syntax represent basic reading components; textbase, situation model, and rhetorical structure cover higher-level semantic and discourse components. The pragmatic communication level was not directly implemented in AutoTutor because it is highly constrained by contexts difficult to stage reliably in a computer environment.
requirements: Lessons and questions must be categorizable by theoretical level (via a Q-matrix with primary, secondary, tertiary, or no relevance codes)
constraints: The pragmatic communication level was not directly implemented because it is highly constrained by contexts difficult to stage reliably in the computer environment
target_learners: adults with low literacy skills reading between 3rd and 8th grade levels
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension across word, textbase, situation model, and rhetorical structure levels
examples: AutoTutor's 29 lessons were coded by primary theoretical level (word, textbase, situation model, or rhetorical structure) using an expert-assigned Q-matrix

title: AutoTutor for CSAL: trialogue-based intelligent tutoring system for adult reading comprehension
description: AutoTutor for CSAL is a web-based conversation-based ITS in which two computer agents (a teacher agent and a peer agent) hold trialogue conversations with adult learners. The three-way conversations are designed to provide instruction on reading comprehension strategies, help adults apply strategies to texts, assess performance, and guide computer use. Lessons begin with a 2–3 min video reviewing a comprehension strategy, then agents scaffold learning by asking questions, providing short feedback, explaining answers, and giving correct responses. Game-like competitions between the student and peer agent are programmed so the human student never loses.

Lessons aligned with a comprehension-strategy curriculum (PACES)
constraints: The pragmatic communication level of comprehension was not directly implemented in the system

examples: In a game-mode lesson, the peer agent gives a wrong answer so the tutor agent directs corrective feedback to the peer rather than the human student

article_title: Navigating Ethical Benefits and Risks as AIED Comes of Age
citation: Ken Koedinger. (2024). Navigating Ethical Benefits and Risks as AIED Comes of Age. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00350-5
title: Frame AI in education as replacing unsupported homework with deliberate practice at the edge of competence, not as replacing teachers
description: This principle holds that the productive framing of AI in education is not replacing teachers but replacing doing homework without any available support. It works by using AI to automate assessment of where a student's competence is, select an appropriate next task, and provide feedback and instruction just when needed, grounding this in the author's statement that "A key principle of effective learning and expertise development is deliberate practice." The article uses this framing to answer criticism that AI aims to replace human workers, arguing instead that active learning with a guide on the side can be scaled with a technology component.
requirements: Assessment of where the student's competence is, so that tasks can be selected at the edge of that competence
Feedback and reactive instruction so students can learn from failure
constraints: The author frames this as a framing and argument, not a tested result; the article reports no data on it
target_learners: K-12 and college students doing homework assignments
target_learning_goals: Deliberate practice at the edge of competence
Active learning with just-in-time feedback and instruction
examples: The author describes homework assignments becoming more interactive than a passive piece of paper, with interaction data informing teachers and parents about progress and needs
key_sources: Ken Koedinger. (2024). Navigating Ethical Benefits and Risks as AIED Comes of Age. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00350-5

article_title: Navigating Ethical Benefits and Risks as AIED Comes of Age
citation: Ken Koedinger. (2024). Navigating Ethical Benefits and Risks as AIED Comes of Age. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00350-5
title: Build AI models designed for explainability and interpretation from the start, around theoretical constructs, rather than probing black boxes after the fact
description: This principle directs AIED developers to design models for explainability and ease of interpretation from the beginning, built around a theoretical understanding of the relevant constructs — the psychological domain, content and motivational constructs, the social need, and the interaction constructs. The article argues that "We need to build models that are designed for explainability and ease of interpretation from the start, not as an after-the-fact attempt to poke into a complex black-box model after it has been built." It is used in the commentary to respond to datafication criticisms, stressing that interpretation of data, a human collaborative thing, should drive decisions.
requirements: Relevant theoretical constructs built in from the start of model design
Human collaborative interpretation of data to drive decisions
constraints: The author states much current explainable AI effort consists of great big Band-Aids not addressing the fundamental issues; post-hoc labeling moves construct development from beginning to end and does not save time
target_learners: All learners served by AIED systems, since model decisions affect them
target_learning_goals: Valid interpretation of learner data to support instructional decisions
examples: The author warns that otherwise researchers must figure out by labeling example clusters what drives a deep learning model's predictions, opening the door to right predictions for wrong reasons via indicator variables spuriously correlated with true causal variables

citation: Ken Koedinger. (2024). Navigating Ethical Benefits and Risks as AIED Comes of Age. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00350-5
title: From prediction to causal models: AIED research should move from diagnosis to remedy rather than stopping at prediction
description: This account explains a perceived failure mode of current AIED research and prescribes its remedy. Its core claim is that "Real problems bring up causal inference which none of these machine learning systems do, they just do correlation." The framework holds that biases inherent in data sets processed in a correlational way get reflected in system decisions, and that opening up the black box to build better causal models lets research move from diagnosis to remedy — from identifying injustices and inequities to moving forward toward justices. The article uses it to argue that papers stopping at prediction mean the field has lost its way.
requirements: New research on causal inference and attention to bias in a deep way
Community support for work that takes the next steps beyond prediction
constraints: The author acknowledges some progress has been made on building systems that make inferences about cause, but says there is still much to be found in that area
target_learners: Students and schools meant to benefit from AIED research moving to remedies
target_learning_goals: Improving education by moving from diagnosing learner states to selecting and acting on remedies
examples: The author cites John Self's statement that a key theme of AI in education is to build systems that care, and recalls 1990s work in highly diverse urban schools motivated by social justice concerns

citation: Martin, P. P., Kranz, D., & Graulich, N. (2025). title: Computational grounded theory: a three-step framework integrating unsupervised ML pattern detection, human refinement, and quantitative confirmation for rubric development
description: Computational grounded theory integrates qualitative research with computational techniques to analyze large datasets systematically for theory development, addressing grounded theory's subjective interpretation and replication difficulties. The article describes it as outlining "a three-step process to guide researchers in rubric design and application": pattern detection (unsupervised ML converts text into interpretable, data-driven categories), pattern refinement (human experts interpret and refine the data-driven categories via thematic content analysis, merging or adding categories), and pattern confirmation (computational methods such as supervised ML test reliability and generalizability). This study examines the validity of the first two steps.
requirements: Human experts must interpret the data-driven categories, since pattern detection only assigns numerical labels to responses
constraints: The article examines the validity of only the first two steps; developing an automatic ML classifier is beyond its scope
target_learning_goals: mechanistic reasoning about reaction rates in organic chemistry
examples: The authors applied HDBSCAN to extract categories from student reasoning, interpreted the categories via the concepts students integrated, and quantitatively compared the resulting rubric with a research-informed one

citation: Martin, P. P., Kranz, D., & Graulich, N. (2025). Revealing Rubric Relations: Investigating the Interdependence of a Research-Informed and a Machine Learning-Based Rubric in Assessing Student Reasoning in Chemistry. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 35, 1465–1503. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00440-y
title: Research-informed rubric of mechanistic reasoning comprising multivariate, comparative, and electronic reasoning categories
description: The research-informed rubric evaluates whether a student reasons in a multivariate, comparative, and electronic way. Multivariate reasoning identifies multiple chemical properties and explains how their interactions impact reaction plausibility (coded present if at least two chemical properties were outlined for at least one reaction). Comparative reasoning contrasts molecules or their reactivity to focus on similarities and differences. Electronic reasoning considers the movement and distribution of electrons, incorporating effects such as resonance, hyperconjugation, or inductive effects. Author DK binary-coded all responses; inter-rater reliability on a 20% subset reached Cohen's κ of 0.84 (95% CI [0.78, 0.91]) after discussion, described as almost perfect agreement.
requirements: Coders with domain expertise; the article reports binary coding of each category with inter-rater reliability checking on a randomly selected 20% subset
constraints: The productive code evaluating correctness rather than complexity was removed; the rubric captures complexity of reasoning, not correctness
target_learning_goals: multivariate, comparative, and electronic mechanistic reasoning
examples: Applied to student responses to two SN1 case comparisons prompting students to explain which of two contrasted reactions occurs at a higher rate

title: ML-based rubric pipeline: BERT-base-German-cased embeddings, UMAP dimensionality reduction, and HDBSCAN clustering yielding a fifteen-category holistic rubric
description: This pipeline inductively develops a holistic rubric from open-ended student responses. Stopwords are removed (a final list of 586 words), BERT-base-German-cased converts responses into contextualized embeddings, UMAP reduces the 768-dimensional vectors to five dimensions, and HDBSCAN groups data points into compact, mutually exclusive clusters while extracting noise points. The authors evaluated 37 HDBSCAN solutions varying minimum cluster size, minimum sample size, and dimension number, selecting a fifteen-cluster solution (minimum cluster size nine, minimum sample size six) using qualitative criteria rather than statistical measures. The clusters encompass reasoning types such as structural, energetic, phenomenological, and electronic reasoning.
requirements: Qualitative evaluation of multiple hyperparameter settings; the selected solution required minimum cluster size nine, minimum sample size six, and five dimensions
constraints: Noise points representing non-normative or mixed ideas are excluded from clusters; the analysis was conducted on German-written responses
target_learning_goals: categorizing students' open-ended mechanistic reasoning for formative assessment
examples: Applied to 454 German-written responses collected in four courses across three German universities; a step-by-step implementation guide is available in Grootendorst (2020)

title: Pair computational clustering with human subject-matter expertise so categorizations capture context-specific nuances
description: The article argues that data-driven categories require human interpretation to capture the specifics of a context, and that interpreting the clusters in this study required significant subject matter expertise. The authors frame this as human-machine collaboration that augments human analytic power: "Computational techniques offer breadth, reproducibility, and scalability in data analysis, while human expertise ensures that categorizations accurately capture the underlying nuances specific to the context." The principle guides rubric development in which ML pre-structures categories and experts refine them.
requirements: Human experts with subject matter expertise to interpret data-driven clusters using research-informed thematic content analysis
constraints: The authors hypothesize that subject matter expertise will remain necessary to interpret data-driven clusters in the future
target_learning_goals: valid formative assessment of open-ended mechanistic reasoning
examples: The authors qualitatively evaluated 37 HDBSCAN solutions against two criteria: clusters should avoid merging conceptually distinct reasoning types and additional clusters should introduce new reasoning types

The editors state the issue shows AIED in MOOCs as an emerging research field and addresses assessment in science courses, human simulated responses and drop-out prediction.

article_title: Understanding Visitors’ Curiosity in a Science Centre with Deep Question Processing Network
citation: Zhaozhen Xu, Amelia Howarth, Nicole Briggs, Nello Cristianini. (2024). Understanding Visitors' Curiosity in a Science Centre with Deep Question Processing Network. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00377-8
title: WTC corpus of 8,600 curated open-domain questions from We The Curious
description: The WTC corpus is a dataset of open-domain questions collected by the Bristol science centre We The Curious through Project What If between January 2017 and October 2019 via four methods: the Project What If Cube, Curious Cube outings, staff-facilitated question gathering, and online input. After manual moderation and automated pre-processing removing duplicates and questions shorter than three words, "the filtered WTC dataset contains 8,600 questions". The corpus has 5,732 vocabulary items, question lengths of 3-55 words, and an average length of 7.15 words, and is used in this article to demonstrate QBERT's applicability to real-world question data.
requirements: Questions were collected verbatim and moderated by We The Curious staff, with identifying information and inappropriate content removed before analysis.
constraints: The anonymised and moderated WTC dataset is available from We The Curious on reasonable request for research purposes, not released openly; personal data is not shared with other parties, including the analysis team.
target_learners: Science centre visitors and members of the public of all ages and backgrounds in Bristol
target_learning_goals: Understanding community curiosity to inform exhibitions and educational content
examples: Questions collected include "Are all babies born with blue eyes?" and counterfactual questions such as "How long will the earth and humans last if we carry on damaging it and nothing changes?"

citation: Hall, L., Tazzyman, S., Hume, C., Endrass, B., Lim, M.-Y., Hofstede, G., Paiva, A., Andre, E., Kappas, A., & Aylett, R. (2014). Learning to Overcome Cultural Conflict through Engaging with Intelligent Agents in Synthetic Cultures. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0031-y
title: eCUTE Intercultural Competence Learning Framework
description: A three-stage framework (Beginner, Journeyman, Expert) extending Bennett's Developmental Model of Intercultural Sensitivity by focusing on the intercultural competencies that facilitate or moderate the development of intercultural sensitivity. Each stage pairs an attitude (e.g. "Conscious incompetence") with emotional, cognitive and behavioural goals, from observing and recognising emotions about another group's strange behaviours, through relating and experimenting, to adapting and belonging through empathy. MIXER's learning goals and evaluation measures were structured around the Beginner and Journeyman stages of this framework.
requirements: Learning activities must map emotional, cognitive and behavioural goals to the learner's stage, as MIXER does via its rule-set game scenario
constraints: MIXER targets the Beginner and Journeyman stages for 9–11 year olds and does not attempt the Expert stage
target_learning_goals: intercultural conflict competence
recognising emotions in intercultural encounters
understanding other groups' practices and values
examples: MIXER's evaluation defined emotional, cognitive and behavioural learning goals drawn from the framework's Beginner stage
key_sources: Hall, L., Tazzyman, S., Hume, C., Endrass, B., Lim, M.-Y., Hofstede, G., Paiva, A., Andre, E., Kappas, A., & Aylett, R. (2014).
