citation: Hall, L., Tazzyman, S., Hume, C., Endrass, B., Lim, M.-Y., Hofstede, G., Paiva, A., Andre, E., Kappas, A., & Aylett, R. (2014). Learning to Overcome Cultural Conflict through Engaging with Intelligent Agents in Synthetic Cultures. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0031-y
title: MIXER experiential learning application
description: MIXER (Moderating Interactions for Cross-Cultural Empathic Relationships) is a computer-based learning experience for 9–11 year olds set in a virtual summer camp where two teams of six intelligent agents play Werewolves with different rule sets representing two synthetic cultures or moral circles. The child user acts as an invisible friend advising the protagonist Tom via a tablet-based Pictorial Interaction Language of over 70 graphics, learning by observing and advising rather than playing. The scenario ends with Tom resolving the conflict by discussing the rule differences, reinforcing that apparent unfairness may reflect simple differences that can be resolved.
requirements: Delivery as part of a whole learning experience with teacher-led classroom discussion to reinforce the message that difference is acceptable
constraints: Does not attempt to create believable cultural differences between the groups other than the rule sets, given the target group's age and experience
target_learning_goals: intercultural conflict competence
willingness to include out-group members in one's moral circle
examples: Children interacted with MIXER on a laptop with headphones and the Pictorial Interaction Language on an iPad, in small groups leaving the classroom
key_sources: Hall, L., Tazzyman, S., Hume, C., Endrass, B., Lim, M.-Y., Hofstede, G., Paiva, A., Andre, E., Kappas, A., & Aylett, R. (2014). citation: Hall, L., Tazzyman, S., Hume, C., Endrass, B., Lim, M.-Y., Hofstede, G., Paiva, A., Andre, E., Kappas, A., & Aylett, R. (2014). Learning to Overcome Cultural Conflict through Engaging with Intelligent Agents in Synthetic Cultures. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0031-y
title: FAtiMA cognitive appraisal agent architecture with cultural Theory of Mind
description: FAtiMA (Fearnot AffecTIve Mind Architecture) is a cognitive appraisal architecture in which events are assessed in relation to agent goals and generate an affective outcome, used in reactive action-tendency rules and a deliberative planning system generating coping behaviours based on hope and fear. For MIXER it was extended with a 1-level Theory of Mind consisting of a collection of Models of Others forming a recursive hierarchical tree, encoding equivalents to Baron-Cohen's Eye-Direction Detection and Shared-Attention Mechanism capabilities. Making the utility of goals depend on cultural values establishes a link between culture and behaviour, so agents' appraisal and action generation are culturally dependent.
requirements: Authoring of each agent's goals, actions, inference rules, emotional reactions and action tendencies, with appraisal variable values authored beforehand
constraints: A 1-level Theory of Mind is modelled, with Models of Others recursing one level
target_learning_goals: experiencing believable intercultural conflict between synthetic cultures
examples: In MIXER, agents choose options to maximise expected utility, e.g. to not be 'killed' out of the Werewolves game

article_title: Modelling and Optimizing Mathematics Learning in Children
citation: Käser, T., Busetto, A.G., Solenthaler, B., Baschera, G.-M., Kohn, J., Kucian, K., von Aster, M., Gross, M. (2013). Modelling and Optimizing Mathematics Learning in Children. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0003-7
title: Dynamic Bayesian network student model of mathematical skills with prerequisite dependencies
description: The student model represents mathematical knowledge as a dynamic Bayesian network: "a directed acyclic graphical model representing different mathematical skills and their dependencies", where a connection means mastering one skill is a prerequisite for another. Skills cannot be observed directly, so the system infers them from task performance, updating posteriors after each solved task with the sum-product algorithm and a memory of the last five time steps. The net contains 100 skills ordered hierarchically by number range and difficulty, designed with experts' advice and inspired by knowledge space theory, allowing movements along all edges including backward movements to model forgetting and knowledge gaps.
requirements: Each skill is assigned to exactly one task, and the net structure was designed using experts' advice and incorporates domain knowledge
constraints: Posteriors are calculated over the last five time steps (memory of 5)
All probabilities are initialized to 0.5 in accordance with the principle of maximum entropy
target_learners: Elementary school children (grades 2–5) with developmental dyscalculia or difficulties in learning mathematics
target_learning_goals: Number representation and understanding
Arithmetic operations and procedures (addition and subtraction)
key_sources: Käser, T., Busetto, A.G., Solenthaler, B., Baschera, G.-M., Kohn, J., Kucian, K., von Aster, M., Gross, M. (2013). Modelling and Optimizing Mathematics Learning in Children. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0003-7

article_title: Modelling and Optimizing Mathematics Learning in Children
citation: Käser, T., Busetto, A.G., Solenthaler, B., Baschera, G.-M., Kohn, J., Kucian, K., von Aster, M., Gross, M. (2013). Modelling and Optimizing Mathematics Learning in Children. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0003-7
title: Calcularis adaptive computer-based training system for numerical cognition
description: Calcularis is a computer-based training system for enhancing numerical cognition in children with developmental dyscalculia or mathematics difficulties, composed of multiple games in a hierarchical structure grouped into Part A (number representations and understanding, e.g. the LANDING game) and Part B (cognitive operations and procedures with numbers, e.g. the PLUS-MINUS game). The article states it provides "a fully adaptive learning environment" in which the student model and controlling algorithm optimize learning by providing an ideal level of cognitive stimulation. Its curriculum is structured on the natural, hierarchical development of number processing, with specific numerical stimulus design and training of operations and procedures.
requirements: Children trained with the program for a period of 6 weeks with a frequency of five times per week, during sessions of 20 min
constraints: The article notes existing computer-based approaches for children with mathematics difficulties lack user adaptation, which this system addresses; analyses included only children with at least 24 complete training sessions
target_learners: Children with developmental dyscalculia or difficulties in learning mathematics in grades 2–5 of public elementary schools
target_learning_goals: Number understanding across representations (verbal, Arabic, concrete, number line)
Automation of addition and subtraction procedures
examples: In the LANDING game children indicate the position of a displayed number on a number line by steering a falling cone with a joystick; in the PLUS-MINUS game children solve addition and subtraction tasks using blocks of tens and ones

article_title: Adding Communicative and Affective Strategies to an Embodied Conversational Agent to Enhance Second Language Learners’ Willingness to Communicate
citation: Emmanuel Ayedoun, Yuki Hayashi, Kazuhisa Seta. (2018). Adding Communicative and Affective Strategies to an Embodied Conversational Agent to Enhance Second Language Learners' Willingness to Communicate. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-018-0171-6
title: DiMaCA: a dialogue management model combining communication strategies and affective backchannels to foster WTC-friendly agent conversations
description: DiMaCA is a dialogue management model specifying rules for when an embodied conversational agent deploys communication strategies (CS) and affective backchannels (AB) during L2 conversations. Its rationale is 'increasing L2 learners' confidence via CSs and reducing their level of anxiety towards communication via ABs', in line with MacIntyre's WTC model. The model is implemented as a strategies management module that detects six conversation states (e.g., learner silent, learner NUNA, agent NUNA) and triggers adapted CS and AB accordingly, with CS chosen in a heuristically predefined order and AB chosen stochastically.
requirements: A dialogue script defining the conversation domain, intent detection via external speech recognition services, and databases of CS and AB options per conversation state
constraints: The Guessing strategy is only an approximation: the agent does not perform dynamic reasoning about learner intention from a wide range of possibilities but relies on a narrow range of expected answers specified in advance in the dialogue script
target_learners: Japanese undergraduate and graduate EFL learners
target_learning_goals: Willingness to communicate in English as a second language
examples: In a restaurant scenario, when the learner is NUNA the system first uses Repetition, then Simplification, then Code-switching across successive turns to make it progressively easier for the learner to overcome the difficulty
key_sources: Emmanuel Ayedoun, Yuki Hayashi, Kazuhisa Seta. (2018). Adding Communicative and Affective Strategies to an Embodied Conversational Agent to Enhance Second Language Learners' Willingness to Communicate. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-018-0171-6

citation: Emmanuel Ayedoun, Yuki Hayashi, Kazuhisa Seta. (2018). Adding Communicative and Affective Strategies to an Embodied Conversational Agent to Enhance Second Language Learners' Willingness to Communicate. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-018-0171-6
title: Embodied conversational agent Jack for restaurant-context English conversation practice
description: The system is an embodied conversational agent, personified as Jack, implemented with the Unity game engine front-end and Node.js back-end, built on the authors' previous work. It supports spoken dialogues in a restaurant context where learners are welcomed, guided to a table, order drinks and dishes, and request the bill. Speech recognition is performed by external services (Wit.ai and Dialogflow) that turn utterances into intents and entities with confidence scores. Jack also uses non-verbal backchannels like gaze, head nods, smiles, and blinking.
requirements: Intents for the conversation domain must be defined beforehand on the Wit.ai or Dialogflow platform so they can be identified from learner utterances
constraints: The conversation is domain-specific (restaurant scenario); the dialogue script is written in XML and can be modified to target a different conversation context
target_learners: Japanese EFL learners at a university
target_learning_goals: Practicing daily English conversation and increasing willingness to communicate in L2
examples: Learners interacted individually with the system in a prepared room and could take the initiative to ask questions or make orders

citation: Emmanuel Ayedoun, Yuki Hayashi, Kazuhisa Seta. (2018). Adding Communicative and Affective Strategies to an Embodied Conversational Agent to Enhance Second Language Learners' Willingness to Communicate. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-018-0171-6
title: Nine communication strategies and four categories of affective backchannels implemented in DiMaCA
description: The authors selected nine communication strategies from Dörnyei and Scott's taxonomy (including Simplification/Approximation, Code-switching, Asking clarification, Suggesting AP, Asking confirmation, Asking repetition, Expressing NU, Guessing, Repetition) chosen for probable WTC-friendliness and technical feasibility. They also introduce four categories of affective backchannels — Congratulatory, Encouraging, Sympathetic, and Reassuring AB — 'to enable ECAs to explicitly convey thoughtful support to learners by congratulating them, cheering them up, or showing sympathy in accordance with the interaction state'.
requirements: CS selection follows a heuristically predefined order per state; AB selection is stochastic within the triggered category
constraints: Response reject was excluded because it cannot be considered a WTC-friendly strategy, illustrating the selection criteria applied
target_learners: L2 learners with low willingness to communicate
target_learning_goals: Overcoming communication pitfalls and reducing anxiety during L2 conversation
examples: When the learner remains silent, the system first applies a Reassuring or Encouraging AB and then conducts a comprehension check to determine whether the learner is NUNA or UNA

title: Design conversational agents for L2 learners to resolve communication pitfalls on the learner's behalf rather than leaving repair to the learner
description: Because L2 communication breakdowns occur more often than in L1 and too much difficulty may cause learners to abort their attempts, the article argues that an agent intended to increase WTC should itself handle conversational trouble. By enabling the ECA to use communication strategies, the authors aim 'to enhance its own strategic competence to release learners from the challenging and WTC-inhibiting burden of resolving communication pitfalls by themselves', hypothesizing that learners who can rely on a supportive agent develop a sense of security that increases confidence.
requirements: The agent needs a repertoire of communication strategies (e.g., repetition, simplification, code-switching) triggered by detected conversation states
constraints: The article notes that for learners with low WTC, mastering such strategies themselves does not guarantee they will use them when facing trouble
target_learners: L2 learners, especially those at lower proficiency levels who experience difficulty communicating in the target language
target_learning_goals: Willingness to communicate and confidence in L2 conversation
examples: In the dialogue excerpt of Fig. 3, successive agent interventions using AB and CS helped the learner gradually overcome an initial breakdown and finally produce the answer 'non-smoking please'

citation: Hossain, Z., Bumbacher, E., Brauneis, A., Diaz, M., Saltarelli, A., Blikstein, P., & Riedel-Kruse, I. H. (2018). Design Guidelines and Empirical Case Study for Scaling Authentic Inquiry-based Science Learning via Open Online Courses and Interactive Biology Cloud Labs. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0150-3
title: Provide both free-form live experimentation and pre-programmed batch mode to support exploration and controlled investigation
description: The article recommends that course layouts and UIs "should allow students to both “play” with the biology in a free form manner using simple and intuitive interfaces in live mode, but also provide the possibility for programming experiments in batch mode." Live mode helps students intuitively calibrate to the system's scales, while batch mode enables controlled experiments and mitigates low-bandwidth challenges. This dual approach was implemented across the course and supported by usage data showing students mainly used live experiments.
requirements: Simple and intuitive live interfaces for free-form exploration
Batch mode scripting capability for controlled experiments
constraints: Live mode requires sufficient internet bandwidth (above 5 Mbps reported as unworkable below that threshold)
target_learning_goals: scientific inquiry practices
experimentation skills
examples: Students mainly used live experiments (2255 live compared to 69 batch), and hierarchical clustering of joystick trajectories revealed six dominant exploration clusters

title: Present real experiments and modeling side by side so students can compare and recognize divergences
description: The article recommends that "real experiments and modeling should be presented to the student side by side, where the correspondence between both should be easily understandable." This bifocal modeling approach helps students understand key properties of the real system through the model while recognizing its subtleties by seeing how real and model behavior diverge. Even simple models capturing only overall tendencies can provide powerful lenses for understanding complex biological systems.
requirements: Equivalent symbolism between model and real experiment representations
Mechanistic models that capture overall behavioral tendencies
constraints: Even simple models may not capture all real-system behaviors such as light-intensity-dependent variability
target_learning_goals: model-based reasoning
understanding biological mechanisms
examples: Students compared a parameter-fitting simulation of Euglena to real experiment videos and reported differences in light-intensity sensitivity, spinning behavior, and reaction lag

article_title: A Festschrift to Honour Jim Greer: Guest Editors’ Introduction, Part 2
citation: Gord McCalla, Julita Vassileva. (2021). A Festschrift to Honour Jim Greer: Guest Editors' Introduction, Part 2 — A Special Issue of the International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00284-w
title: Five-topic organization of the Festschrift tracking Jim Greer's changing research interests
description: The guest editors organize the Festschrift's 24 papers into a five-topic taxonomy that, in their words, has each paper "slotted into one of five topics that roughly track Jim's changing research interests during his long career". The topics move from Greer's early interests in learner modelling, personalization and evaluation to his later interests in peer learning, collaboration, the social dimension, privacy, and learning analytics and educational data mining. The taxonomy serves as the special issue's organizing framework rather than as an empirically tested model.
requirements: Papers are assigned by their principal focus, so the taxonomy requires that each contribution have one identifiable main focus
constraints: The editors state the topics only roughly track Greer's changing research interests, so the grouping is approximate
target_learners: AIED researchers and practitioners reading the special issue

citation: Jessica L. Parker, Veronica M. Richard, Alexandra Acabá, Sierra Escoffier, Stephen Flaherty, Shannon Jablonka, Kimberly P. Becker. (2025). title: Three-step AI discussion prompt (original response, AI interaction, comparison and revision decision)
description: A discussion-board structure created by the professor in which step one is the original pre-AI discussion task, step two asks students to "Interact with an LLM like ChatGPT to check your responses", and step three asks students to compare their observations with the AI's insights and decide whether to change their original responses, explaining why. Steps two and three were not graded to encourage honesty. The prompt frames AI as "a tool to facilitate self-reflection and critical thinking" rather than an authority.

constraints: Steps two and three were ungraded in this course to encourage honesty and transparency

title: Graduated levels of AI integration aligned with Bloom's taxonomy and the AI Assessment Scale
description: The course organized AI use into five levels—"No AI", "AI-Assisted Idea Development", "AI Collaboration", "Full AI Integration", and "Advanced AI Integration"—mapped onto Bloom's Taxonomy levels and AI mastery levels from none/novice to expert (Table 1). Levels ranged "from 'no AI' to 'advanced AI' integration, depending on the level of AI mastery required to complete an assigned task" and align with Perkins et al.'s AI Assessment Scale (2023). Higher levels require deeper ethical understanding and critical evaluation of AI output.

description: The study grounds itself in Knox's (2019) postdigital education—where digital technology is "an integrated and intrinsic part of the educational ecosystem" rather than an external force—and Eaton's (2023) postplagiarism era, in which "hybrid human-AI writing may become the norm". In hybrid writing, AI "is not just a tool but a collaborator in the writing process, reshaping how writing is approached, executed, and evaluated". The authors use this framing to interpret their finding that the doctoral writing process became a continuous human-AI flow, and to argue academic integrity conceptions must evolve.

article_title: Implementing CBM: SQL-Tutor After Fifteen Years
citation: Mitrovic, A., & Ohlsson, S. (2015). Implementing CBM: SQL-Tutor After Fifteen Years. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0049-9
title: Constraint-based modelling (CBM): student modelling via constraints on correct solutions
description: CBM is a student modelling approach proposed by Ohlsson as a way to overcome limitations of earlier approaches such as bug libraries. The article states that "A constraint-based tutor only needs a set of constraints that describe features of correct solutions", eliminating the need for bug libraries and for a runnable domain module. Because CBM does not require a problem solver, it "can be applied to open-ended tasks for which there is no algorithmic solution or executable expert model". SQL-Tutor was built to test whether CBM was as promising as it seemed, and the approach was later adopted by many researchers beyond the authors' group.
requirements: A set of constraints describing features of correct solutions, with relevance and satisfaction conditions
constraints: The constraint formalism is difficult to grasp and, per the authors, is the aspect of CBM most often misunderstood, including the mistaken idea of buggy constraints
target_learning_goals: SQL querying and other well-defined and ill-defined tasks modelled with constraints
examples: SQL-Tutor operationalized CBM with syntax and semantic constraints, all problem-independent, so new problems require only problem text and one correct solution

title: SQL-Tutor, the first constraint-based tutor for SQL querying
description: SQL-Tutor is an intelligent tutoring system for the SQL Select statement, designed as a complement to database courses that assumes students have some knowledge from lectures and labs. "The system provides numerous problem-solving opportunities in the context of various databases", which students can freely choose among. Its interface reduces working memory load by displaying the database schema and problem text, and it provides feedback at several levels of specificity, from simple correctness flags to hints and full solutions. The system has been in regular use in university database courses since the late 1990s.
requirements: Students should already have acquired some knowledge via lectures, labs and demonstrations
constraints: The system covers only the SQL Select statement, more precisely a subset of its language constructs
target_learners: university students learning SQL in database courses
target_learning_goals: writing correct SQL Select queries

title: Bridge the theory-technology gap: keep talking across research and implementation communities
description: From the SQL-Tutor experience the authors draw the lesson that theoretical concepts and implementation efforts must be brought together deliberately. They write that "The first lesson of SQL-Tutor in particular and the CBM approach in general for ITS researchers is thus simple to state but sometimes hard to execute: Keep talking." Basic inquiry into cognitive skills and willingness of technologists to implement systems jointly revealed the weaknesses of bug-library tutoring and enabled the CBM alternative. They note institutional disincentives often get in the way of such gap-bridging.
requirements: Willingness of researchers on both sides of the theory-technology gap to reach out to each other
constraints: Institutional disincentives to gap-bridging all too often get in the way, per the authors

examples: The two authors, one a theorist and one a system builder, collaborated after a 1998 sabbatical visit, producing SQL-Tutor and the CBM line of tutors

article_title: The SIETTE Automatic Assessment Environment
citation: Conejo, R., Guzmán, E., & Trella, M. (2016). The SIETTE Automatic Assessment Environment. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26, 270–292. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0078-4
title: Siette: a domain-independent web-based automatic assessment environment
description: Siette is a web-based automatic assessment system developed over 16 years at the University of Málaga. It supports classical test theory, item response theory, and computer adaptive testing, and integrates them with multidimensional student models used by intelligent educational systems. The system is designed as "a web-based assessment component that can be semantically integrated with intelligent systems or with large LMSs, such as Moodle." Teachers use an authoring tool to create large item pools of multiple-choice, open answer, generative, and complex task items.

Interoperability with other systems via web services and APIs
constraints: Not an open-source project; free academic use granted upon request
Designed mainly for higher education
target_learning_goals: accurate measurement of learner knowledge
formative and summative assessment across multiple skills
examples: Integrated with Moodle at the University of Málaga virtual campus serving 2500 staff and 35000 students per year
Used for botany assessment in a laboratory using QR codes attached to dried plant sheets

title: Multi-unidimensional approach to bridging psychometric and ITS learner models
description: Siette addresses the mismatch between the fine-grained multidimensional learner models of ITSs and the single-latent-trait focus of CTT and IRT through a multi-unidimensional approach. Rather than using true multidimensional IRT models, the system "developed a mechanism that assumes that multiple independent traits are assessed simultaneously." This allows a CAT component to produce separate knowledge estimates for each domain topic in a hierarchical learner model, supporting adaptive question selection across multiple nodes. The domain model uses part-of relationships with topics and subtopics, and items can be attached to one or more sibling nodes.
requirements: A hierarchical domain model that can be overlaid with an ITS domain model
Item pools calibrated per trait under the assumption of independent traits
constraints: Currently does not support true multidimensional items
Classic multidimensional IRT models are complex and more than two or three dimensions are rarely used

adaptive question selection
examples: Adaptive question-selection algorithm selects the next question according to which domain nodes require higher precision

title: Systems should encapsulate and automatise complex processes to reduce the teacher's cognitive load
description: Based on their analysis of why innovative features of Siette are rarely adopted, the authors recommend that intelligent educational systems should hide complexity from teachers. They state: "These challenges could be overcome if the system encapsulates and automatizes some processes to reduce the cognitive load of the teacher." This includes automating item calibration, misconception handling, and analysis. They further recommend that "the final users (teachers) should be able to access the system in a simple way at the beginning and discover advances features as needed."

article_title: A Manifesto for a Pro-Actively Responsible AI in Education
citation: Kaśka Porayska‑Pomsta. (2024). A Manifesto for a Pro-Actively Responsible AI in Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 34, 73–83. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00346-1
title: AIED as a human-centred sub-discipline of AI whose technologies aim to strengthen, not substitute, human capacities
description: The article characterises AIED as a distinctive sub-field of AI: rather than compensating for or bypassing user abilities, its technologies are interventions "to enhance and change human thinking and behaviour" and "to emphasise, help train and strengthen the capacities with which we are biologically endowed." Because of this, fidelity to human cognition is central: AIED applications must support learning "in cognitively congruent, efficacious and socio-culturally desirable ways." The theory explains why AIED cannot be evaluated only by task performance but must consider user experience, context, culture, affect and motivation as integral to learning, and why the field is intertwined with wider social, cultural, economic and political contexts.
requirements: Fidelity of AIED applications to human cognition and behaviour, so support is cognitively congruent and socio-culturally desirable
constraints: The account is the author's characterisation of the field's ambitions and does not report empirical tests
target_learners: all learners addressed by AIED technologies
target_learning_goals: strengthening learners' innate cognitive and behavioural capacities
human-centred learning support
examples: The article cites the field's early adoption of participatory, user-centred design and action research integrated with engineering as reflecting this human-centred perspective

article_title: A Manifesto for a Pro-Actively Responsible AI in Education
citation: Kaśka Porayska‑Pomsta. (2024). A Manifesto for a Pro-Actively Responsible AI in Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 34, 73–83. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00346-1
title: The standard model of AI: a fully autonomous agent that single-mindedly maximises a pre-set objective irrespective of user needs
description: The article describes, drawing on Russell (2019), a standard model of AI in which "AI is a fully autonomous agent whose job is to single-mindedly find ways that maximise the achievement of a pre-set objective, irrespective of the users' real-time or long-term needs or contexts," with full and difficult-to-track or challenge control of the interaction. Russell's critique locates its problems in rigid insistence on local optima of limited contexts and in human fallibility in specifying objectives guaranteed to be ethical and beneficial to all stakeholders. He proposes replacing it with a flexible model "open to manipulation and personalisation by their users" that gives data back to users and whose objectives can be negotiated. The article uses this framing to position AIED's Open Learner Models as pre-eminent existing examples relevant to new forms of human-centred AI design.
requirements: A shift toward models sensitive to human needs and contextualised preferences, open to user manipulation and personalisation, whose objectives can be negotiated
constraints: Presented as the author's summary of Russell (2019)'s argument and her application of it to AIED, not as an empirical finding of this article
target_learners: all users of AI systems, including learners
target_learning_goals: human agency in human-AI interaction
AI for human good
examples: The article contrasts this standard model with AIED approaches that give users degrees of agency, control and ownership over system-generated data and over their learning processes
key_sources: Kaśka Porayska‑Pomsta. (2024). A Manifesto for a Pro-Actively Responsible AI in Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 34, 73–83. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00346-1

article_title: A Manifesto for a Pro-Actively Responsible AI in Education
citation: Kaśka Porayska‑Pomsta. (2024). A Manifesto for a Pro-Actively Responsible AI in Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 34, 73–83. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00346-1
title: Build AIED systems with user control over system operation as critical to their adaptive potential
description: The article argues that exposure to differently abled learners and non-mainstream contexts spotlights "the necessity to extend our field of view" and "to consider certain dimensions, such as user control over the operation of the systems we build, as critical to the adaptive potential of those systems." The principle directs designers to build learner agency, control and ownership — as instantiated in Open Learner Models — into AIED systems, because typicality-based overlay models can produce inflexible designs where users must adapt to the technology rather than the reverse. The article cites Bull & Kay (2016) for an AIED-centric perspective on user control.
requirements: Designs must give users degrees of agency, control and ownership over system-generated data and learning processes, as in Open Learner Models
constraints: The extent to which qualitative and interpretivist methods alone can inform generalisable conclusions and standardised approaches remains, by the article's own statement, an open question

target_learning_goals: learner agency and self-regulation
adaptive pedagogical support
examples: The article points to AIED supports that facilitate pro-active help-seeking by students and students' self-reporting on their emotional states in collaborative or exploratory settings as ways tailoring can give learners greater agency

title: Voice-Based Synthetic Assistant (VBSA): a cloud-based Alexa-powered pedagogical agent for real-time monitoring and error correction in emergency care training
description: The VBSA is a task-specific, voice-only synthetic assistant built on the AWS cloud using Alexa Voice Service, DynamoDB, and Lambda. It monitors each step of a trainee's treatment process in real time, creates error variables when a mistake occurs, and speaks corrective recommendations back to the trainee, while a web-based dashboard lets one trainer monitor all trainees simultaneously. The article describes it as "a pedagogical agent without a computer avatar, effectively a scaled-down version," and reports that it was developed for the full MARCHE protocol though tested only on the massive hemorrhage scenario. Its architecture comprises nine functional blocks including interface, process monitoring, goal recognition, and dynamic task allocation.

citation: H. Ulrich Hoppe. (2015). A Framework System for Intelligent Support in Open Distributed Learning Environments—a Look Back from 16 Years Later. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26, 504–511. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0058-8
title: ODLE framework: multi-agent architecture and component engineering for open distributed learning environments
description: The 1998 paper introduced a framework system for open distributed learning environments combining intelligent support with interactive learning environments. It was, per Fidas et al. as quoted here, characterized by "the combination of intelligent support with interactive learning environments, by the provision of reusable components and by a distributed multi-agent architecture." Openness meant embedding intelligent support into existing face-to-face classrooms and group settings rather than closed-loop private-tutor ITS scenarios, requiring the system to give up full understanding and control of the learning process.

constraints: Openness entails giving up full understanding and control of the learning process on the part of the intelligent system
target_learners: school students in face-to-face classrooms and group learning settings
target_learning_goals: collaborative group learning in mathematics and general problem solving
examples: The approach was exemplified with several applications in mathematics and general problem solving, and applied in EU projects including NIMIS, SEED, COLDEX and Argunaut

title: Multiple student modelling to configure and inform group learning situations
description: Multiple student modelling is an approach to configuring and informing group learning situations based on individually assessed learner models. As characterized by Greer et al. in this commentary, Hoppe's COSOFT was "the first ambitious project to address several issues related to the use of student modelling in order to parameterize human-human collaboration," including group composition, peer-helper selection, problem identification and task selection. The 1998 paper took this up and Mühlenbrock et al. pursued it further.

constraints: Precise learner modelling on an individual level is not possible when the system is not in full control of task specification and credit assignment
target_learners: students in collaborative group learning settings
target_learning_goals: forming learning groups and selecting tasks and peer helpers suited to group learning
examples: The idea was taken up in the Intelligent IntraNet Peer Help-Desk (later I-Help) at the University of Saskatchewan

title: NIMIS ubiquitous computing classroom for early learning
description: NIMIS (Networked Interactive Media in Schools, 1998–2000) was a ubiquitous computing classroom featuring a large interactive display and pen-based tablets at student desks, targeting early learning in the first years of primary school. Installations existed in Germany, Portugal and the UK with different curricular orientations. The German environment supported initial reading and writing skills based on the "reading through writing" approach, with an action log recording learner activity.

article_title: The Impact of Contextualized Emotions on Self-Regulated Learning and Scientific Reasoning during Learning with a Game-Based Learning Environment
citation: Michelle Taub, Robert Sawyer, James Lester, Roger Azevedo. (2019). The Impact of Contextualized Emotions on Self-Regulated Learning and Scientific Reasoning during Learning with a Game-Based Learning Environment. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-019-00191-1
title: Contextualizing learner emotions within in-game action outcomes
description: This framework defines emotional context in terms of the outcomes of specific in-game actions rather than general session-level affect. The article states: "we define context in terms of different in-game outcomes (i.e., a relevant vs. irrelevant book for solving the mystery, a positive vs. negative scan outcome, a correct vs. incorrect final diagnosis)". Emotions are measured as duration proportions in a five-second window after feedback (or during reading) using facial detection software, then compared across positive and negative outcomes. The approach addresses prior methods (e.g., BROMP) that produced instantaneous rather than continuous measures not tied to specific gameplay events.
requirements: Facial detection software capable of continuous emotion measurement, and in-game actions that produce identifiable positive or negative feedback outcomes
constraints: The study excluded the temporal component of context and could not detect engagement or boredom due to facial-detection software restrictions, using joy as a proxy for positive state
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning
scientific reasoning
microbiology content learning
examples: In CRYSTAL ISLAND, emotions were contextualized around scanning food items, reading books, and submitting diagnosis worksheets, with outcomes dichotomized as positive or negative

title: CRYSTAL ISLAND game-based learning environment
description: CRYSTAL ISLAND is a narrative-centered game-based learning environment in which students solve the mystery of an illness affecting island inhabitants. Students "gather clues by navigating to the five different locations", read books about illnesses, scan food items for pathogenic substances, and complete a diagnosis worksheet indicating illness type, transmission source, and treatment plan. The game fosters self-regulated learning through strategic planning, monitoring, and adaptation, and fosters scientific reasoning through hypothesis generation and testing. Overall game score is an expert-defined, validated performance measure positively correlated with post-test score (r(59) = 0.32, p = 0.012).

constraints: The game does not allow students to explicitly state their hypotheses, which the authors suggest could be addressed with a new design tool

self-regulated learning
scientific reasoning and hypothesis testing

article_title: Evaluation of Parsons Problems with Menu-Based Self-Explanation Prompts in a Mobile Python Tutor
citation: Fabic, G. V. F., Mitrovic, A., & Neshatian, K. (2019). Evaluation of Parsons Problems with Menu-Based Self-Explanation Prompts in a Mobile Python Tutor. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 29, 507–535. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-019-00184-0
title: PyKinetic: a mobile Python tutor with Parsons problems with incomplete LOCs and menu-based SE prompts
description: PyKinetic is "a mobile tutor developed using Android SDK to teach Python 3.x programming", designed for novices as a complement to traditional lectures. It presents Parsons problems whose lines of code (LOCs) are randomly ordered with correct indentation; learners drag and drop LOCs and complete incomplete LOCs by selecting from menu options instead of typing. The study version contained 15 Parsons problems across six Python topics, with 22 menu-based SE prompts (14 conceptual, 8 procedural) given after solving incomplete LOCs. The experimental version added SE prompts; the control version was identical apart from the SE prompts.
requirements: Learners use Android devices (version 4.0 and higher); problems are presented in portrait mode, a change made after the pilot study
constraints: Problems limited to a maximum of 16 LOCs; a maximum of 3 incomplete LOCs per problem; SE prompts cannot be skipped and allow only a single attempt
target_learning_goals: Python syntax and conceptual knowledge
code writing and code execution (procedural knowledge)
examples: In the evaluation study, 63 participants from two universities used PyKinetic for about an hour between a 15-min pre-test and 15-min post-test

citation: Fabic, G. V. F., Mitrovic, A., & Neshatian, K. (2019). Evaluation of Parsons Problems with Menu-Based Self-Explanation Prompts in a Mobile Python Tutor. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 29, 507–535. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-019-00184-0
title: Parsons problems design for smartphones: single combined area, pre-indented single LOCs, incomplete LOCs with menu-based SE prompts
description: The article's Parsons problems differ from common implementations in four ways the authors enumerate. First, students solve problems "in the same area where the LOCs are presented", with no separation between problem and solution space, making better use of limited smartphone screen space. Second, all lines are provided with correct indentation as scaffolding for novices. Third, all blocks contain only single LOCs, encouraging students to think about each individual line. Fourth, the problems contain incomplete LOCs accompanied by menu-based SE prompts that learners must answer upon solving them, targeting both procedural and conceptual knowledge.
requirements: Menu-based SE prompts require feedback on incorrect choices so learners with misconceptions receive guidance
constraints: Combining problem and solution areas might overwhelm learners because all LOCs are displayed at once, though the authors did not observe this as an issue given the 16-LOC limit
target_learning_goals: code sequencing and writing skills
declarative and procedural Python knowledge
examples: The study version contained 15 Parsons problems across six Python topics, given in a fixed order of increasing difficulty, with 22 SE prompts

article_title: Examining the Effect of Assessment Construct Characteristics on Machine Learning Scoring of Scientific Argumentation
citation: Haudek, K. C., & Zhai, X. (2024). Examining the Effect of Assessment Construct Characteristics on Machine Learning Scoring of Scientific Argumentation. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00385-8
title: Three-dimensional framework of assessment construct characteristics for ML-based science assessment: Complexity, Diversity, and Structure
description: The article adopts and empirically tests a framework abstracting three fundamental features of the assessment construct for ML-based science assessments. "Complexity" captures the cognitive processes students must engage in, from identifying provided information to evaluating multiple pieces of data. "Diversity" reflects the combinations of different cognitive demands, specifically the number of dimensions of three-dimensional science learning engaged. "Structure" reflects cognitive developmental features, operationalized as alignment to levels of a validated learning progression for scientific argumentation. The framework was used to code 19 assessment items and examine associations with ML scoring accuracy.
requirements: Assessment items must be codable on all three dimensions by trained human raters using a defined coding scheme
constraints: The three characteristics were not independent in this sample of items (all pairwise Fisher's exact tests p < .01), preventing combination into a single statistical model
target_learning_goals: scientific argumentation competence
examples: Items were coded on all three dimensions: e.g., item S4 was coded Complexity level 4, Diversity level 3, Structure level 3; item G1 was coded level 1 on all three characteristics
key_sources: Haudek, K. C., & Zhai, X. (2024). Examining the Effect of Assessment Construct Characteristics on Machine Learning Scoring of Scientific Argumentation. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00385-8

article_title: Examining the Effect of Assessment Construct Characteristics on Machine Learning Scoring of Scientific Argumentation

title: When developing ML scoring models, consider assessment construct characteristics—particularly for higher complexity and multidimensional items
description: The article recommends that developers of ML scoring models for science assessments should attend to the Complexity, Diversity, and Structure of assessment constructs. The authors state these findings "highlight the importance of considering these construct characteristics when developing ML models for scoring assessments, particularly for higher complexity items and multidimensional assessments." Lower-level items (level 1 on any characteristic) consistently achieved substantial agreement, while higher-level items showed decreased and more variable performance.
requirements: Awareness of the cognitive complexity, number of learning dimensions, and learning progression level of assessment items before ML model development
constraints: The study used a consistent set of ML parameters across all models; tuning parameters might improve performance for mid-level constructs more than higher-level ones, as the authors note
target_learning_goals: scientific argumentation competence
examples: The study held training set size constant at 361 responses and used identical text processing parameters across all 17 models to isolate the role of construct characteristics

description: A processing pipeline that takes learner-uploaded PDF essays and produces automated content feedback. The article describes "a pipeline composed of four components. These are 1) Preprocessing, 2) Segmentation, 3) Analytic scoring and 4) Feedback generation": text extraction and sentence tokenisation, sentence-level sliding-window classification into learning-tip sections, multilabel prediction of lecture-topic codes per segment against a ground truth table, and rule-triggered feedback texts displayed in a custom Moodle plugin. article_title: First-Year Engineering Students’ Strategies for Taking Exams
citation: Jakub Kuzilek, Zdenek Zdrahal, Jonas Vaclavek, Viktor Fuglik, Jan Skocilas, Annika Wolff. (2023). First-Year Engineering Students' Strategies for Taking Exams. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00303-4
title: Layered Markov chain method transforming exam attempt logs into probabilistic graphs
description: The article introduces "the method - which transforms the student exam attempt log into a probabilistic graphical representation". Exam attempts are aggregated to six exam-period weeks, encoded as quaternary states over three courses (64 states per week, state space of 384), and used to build non-homogeneous layered Markov chains with absorbing final-week states. Graph complexity is measured with a polynomial-based average complexity measure, and graphs are compared with a normalized shortest-path kernel. Edges taken by more than 10% of a group are extracted to reveal predominant patterns.
requirements: Exam attempt logs with dates, courses and outcomes for each student
A predefined exam period divided into weeks and a fixed set of exam courses
constraints: The Markov property means the model works with no memory and cannot provide more complex information about the process
Complexity comparison across graphs with different state sets requires a simulation study the authors did not carry out
target_learning_goals: exam planning and time management during exam periods
examples: The method is demonstrated on 311 FME students in 2017/2018, e.g. example student 15456106's log transforming to the state sequence <1, 1, 1, 3, 15, 63>

citation: Matayoshi, J., Cosyn, E., & Uzun, H. (2021). Are We There Yet? Evaluating the Effectiveness of a Recurrent Neural Network-Based Stopping Algorithm for an Adaptive Assessment. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00240-8
title: Combining deep learning with existing AIED models rather than replacing them
description: The article proposes augmenting rather than replacing established AIED models with deep learning. Rather than directly comparing RNNs with other models, the authors "are instead interested in the results when deep learning is used in combination with one of these models." Specifically, they augment the KST-powered ALEKS assessment with the classification strengths of an RNN model, motivated by evidence that deep learning models are not guaranteed to outperform existing educational models. This approach leverages the complementary strengths of knowledge-structure-based assessment and sequence-based prediction.

Sufficient sequential data to train the deep learning component
constraints: The article notes deep learning models are by no means guaranteed to outperform other educational models, citing Wilson et al. (2016)
The approach is demonstrated specifically for a placement assessment where coarse category prediction suffices rather than full knowledge state identification

target_learning_goals: accurate course placement recommendation
examples: The authors combine an RNN classifier with the ALEKS PPL assessment to predict final course placement from partial assessment data, enabling a stopping algorithm that reduces average assessment length by over 26%

article_title: The Use of Large Language Models in Education
citation: Wanli Xing, Nia Nixon, Scott Crossley, Paul Denny, Andrew Lan, John Stamper, Zhou Yu. (2025). The Use of Large Language Models in Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00457-x
title: Three-strand framework for research on LLMs in education
description: The editorial organizes special-issue research on LLMs in education into three strands. The first applies open-source and proprietary LLMs to streamline educational tasks "such as feedback analysis and automated grading, mainly through diverse prompting strategies"; the second focuses on fine-tuning and pretraining LLMs for specific educational environments; the third focuses on enhancing adaptive digital learning environments with LLMs. The framework maps how LLM integration moves from off-the-shelf prompting toward domain adaptation and adaptive learning support.

citation: Gowda, S. M., Baker, R. S., Corbett, A. T., & Rossi, L. M. (2013). Towards Automatically Detecting Whether Student Learning is Shallow. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0006-4
title: Genetics Cognitive Tutor three-factor cross dataset with transfer, PFL and problem-solving post-tests
description: A dataset from 71 Carnegie Mellon undergraduates using the Genetics Cognitive Tutor's three-factor cross module, first published in Baker et al. (2011a, b). Students completed "a total of 22,885 problem-solving actions across 10,966 problem steps in the tutor" during two 1-h laboratory sessions, followed by a problem-solving post-test, a transfer test, and a PFL test. Average post-test performance was 0.81 (SD=0.18), transfer 0.85 (SD=0.18), and PFL 0.89 (SD=0.15). The dataset supports training and cross-validating shallowness detectors.
requirements: Paper-and-pencil post-tests measuring problem-solving, transfer, and PFL to generate ground-truth shallowness labels
constraints: Data come from a single tutor module (three-factor cross) at one university; the retention test administered 7 weeks later was not analyzed in detail
target_learners: college undergraduates in genetics or introductory biology
target_learning_goals: three-factor cross gene mapping problem solving, transfer of genetics reasoning, preparation for future learning
examples: Students averaged pre-test performance of 0.31 (SD=0.19) and post-test performance of 0.81 (SD=0.18); 18 students achieved a perfect post-test score

article_title: Towards Automatically Detecting Whether Student Learning is Shallow
citation: Gowda, S. M., Baker, R. S., Corbett, A. T., & Rossi, L. M. (2013). Towards Automatically Detecting Whether Student Learning is Shallow. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0006-4
title: Operational distinction between shallow learning, robust learning, and no learning
description: The article proposes that failure to achieve robust learning takes two distinct forms: no learning at all, or shallow learning—"learning that applies only to the current skill, and does not support transfer or PFL". Shallow learners "may learn the exact skills presented in the tutor, but who do not learn in a robust fashion". The construct is operationalized as the difference between a student's problem-solving post-test score and their transfer or PFL test score, with higher problem-solving performance indicating shallow learning. This distinction matters because the two groups need different interventions: students not yet robust may need more practice, while shallow learners need support building conceptual understanding.
requirements: Tests of both the exact tutor material and of robust learning (transfer or PFL) to compute the score difference used as the ground-truth label
constraints: The operational definition assumes approximately equal average performance across tests so percent-correct scores can be compared directly
target_learners: college students learning genetics problem solving in an intelligent tutoring system
target_learning_goals: distinguishing shallow from robust learning to enable differentiated support
examples: 25 of 71 students were labeled no-transfer-shallow learners, with an average 0.11 point difference between problem-solving and transfer scores

article_title: Supporting Coordination and Peer Editing in Students’ Online Collaborative Writing Processes
citation: Maya Usher, Ido Roll, Orly Fuhrman, Ofra Amir. (2025). Supporting Coordination and Peer Editing in Students’ Online Collaborative Writing Processes. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 35. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00450-w
title: SITU: a minimalist group awareness tool embedded in Google Docs
description: SITU is a Google Docs add-on group awareness (GA) tool designed to "support productive coordination and encourage peer editing in the context of OCW tasks". It has two functionalities: a traffic-light color rating (red/yellow/green, with three 'S' logo shapes) letting students anonymously mark paragraph readiness, and a to-do list of up to 200 words of written feedback about required editing. Anonymity is intended to reduce the guilt and anxiety of editing a co-author's work, and the document itself serves as the organizing mechanism for interactions rather than an external dashboard.
requirements: Deployed as a Google Docs add-on within a shared OCW document; relies on students rating paragraph readiness and providing written feedback to co-authors
constraints: The article states the to-do list did not provide specific suggestions or instructions on how or what to revise, leaving decisions to students
target_learning_goals: online collaborative writing
peer editing
task coordination in asynchronous group work
examples: In the main study, experimental-group documents contained six pre-rated paragraphs (two red, two yellow, two green) and students could re-rate paragraphs or rate new ones
key_sources: Maya Usher, Ido Roll, Orly Fuhrman, Ofra Amir. (2025). Supporting Coordination and Peer Editing in Students’ Online Collaborative Writing Processes. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 35. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00450-w

title: Embed coordination and feedback mechanisms directly within the shared writing environment rather than in external dashboards
description: The article's implications section recommends that educators and tool designers "consider integrating tools that allow for non-intrusive coordination and feedback naturally within the writing environment". SITU demonstrates this by using the document itself as the organizing mechanism: color ratings appear beside paragraphs and the to-do list appears in a side bar, keeping the document organized and navigable. The principle holds that support should be situated in time (immediate, real-time) and in space (within the task itself).
requirements: Tools must be user-friendly and seamlessly embedded into the writing space without disrupting workflow
constraints: The article's evidence comes from a non-academic writing task and about 40-minute sessions with unknown peers, so transfer to formal academic assignments is untested
target_learners: undergraduate students working on asynchronous online collaborative writing tasks
target_learning_goals: coordination of collaborative writing activities
peer editing of co-authors' text
examples: SITU's color-coded rating system provided visual cues about paragraph status with minimal distraction, and its to-do list kept the document itself fairly organized

citation: J. D. Fletcher & Robert A. Sottilare. (2018). Shared Mental Models in Support of Adaptive Instruction for Teams Using the GIFT Tutoring Architecture. Int J Artif Intell Educ 28:265–285. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0147-y
title: Shared mental models as organized knowledge structures enabling team prediction, explanation, and coordination
description: The article defines shared mental models as the descriptions, explanations, and predictions of team behavior held in common by team members, drawing on Rouse and Morris and Cannon-Bowers et al. It presents them as dynamic cognitive activities rooted in team member interactions rather than static products. The article proposes that ITSs augment individual learner models with these shared models to enable adaptive team instruction, listing seven functions they serve, including "Timing functions that influence how activity is paced" and "Systems-monitoring functions that enable the adjustment of team and member activities in response to errors and omissions".
requirements: Team members must hold models in common; the article states success of interdependent teams "depends on the extent to which this model sharing occurs"
constraints: The article focuses on cognitive factors in small teams and leaves non-cognitive factors and teams of teams for separate consideration

target_learning_goals: team coordination and communication
shared understanding of roles and responsibilities
team task performance

citation: J. D. Fletcher & Robert A. Sottilare. (2018). Shared Mental Models in Support of Adaptive Instruction for Teams Using the GIFT Tutoring Architecture. Int J Artif Intell Educ 28:265–285. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0147-y
title: GIFT (Generalized Intelligent Framework for Tutoring) adapted for team tutoring via hierarchical DKFs and team models
description: GIFT is an open-source architecture for authoring, delivering, managing, and evaluating ITS, composed of modules (Sensor, Learner, Pedagogical, Domain) that interact through standardized messages. The article describes modifications needed for team tutoring: authoring tools that define "team concepts, conditions, scenarios, individual roles, responsibilities, and assessments", hierarchical Domain Knowledge Files (one DKF per team member and one for the team), and a Team Model assessing team states such as performance, cohesion, and coaching/leadership. Its distributed architecture allows each learner's tutor to share individual state changes with other tutoring agents, supporting both team-level and individual learner models.
requirements: The article states the current GIFT structure (version 2016-1) "cannot provide collective tutoring sufficiently without significant modification"
A method must be developed to link responsibilities to individual team members or subgroups and define assessments for each responsibility
constraints: The authors caution the approach "is not just plug-and-play" and "requires large amounts of data"
target_learners: interdependent teams in military and civilian training settings
target_learning_goals: collective task performance
team coordination
individual competencies within team contexts

title: The 7C's taxonomy of teamwork competencies
description: The article presents teamwork competencies summarized by Salas et al. (2015) and Sottilare et al. (2015) as the "7C's": Cooperation, Coordination, Communication, Cognition, Coaching, Conflict Resolution, and Conditions (Context, Composition, Culture). Each is defined behaviorally — for example, Coordination covers "mutual performance monitoring, back-up and support, adaptability, and task-related assertiveness". The article proposes these competencies as behavioral markers from which GIFT team models, as antecedents of learning and performance, may be derived.

article_title: Detecting and Addressing Frustration in a Serious Game for Military Training
citation: DeFalco, J. A., Rowe, J. P., Paquette, L., Georgoulas-Sherry, V., Brawner, K., Mott, B. W., Baker, R. S., & Lester, J. C. (2018). Detecting and Addressing Frustration in a Serious Game for Military Training. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0152-1
title: Theory-based motivational feedback design for addressing learner frustration in military training
description: The article designs frustration interventions using motivationally designed feedback messages grounded in three theoretical constructs chosen for the military population: control-value theory (indicating the value of the activity), social identity theory (targeting military identity), and self-efficacy theory (supporting learners' ability to achieve goals through effort). Grounded in Amsel's frustration theory, the approach favors helping learners "recover, manage, and persist" through frustration rather than removing its source or giving explicit corrective feedback. Messages were also designed to be fail-soft, minimizing negative impact if triggered by a detector false positive.
requirements: Messages should be meaningful, relevant, and support goal-oriented efforts
Interventions selected with the goal of being fail-soft against detector false positives
constraints: Theoretical constructs were selected to reflect the unique profile of the target population, USMA cadets
target_learners: US Army combat medics and combat lifesavers in tactical combat casualty care training
target_learning_goals: Tactical combat casualty care skills including hemorrhage control and care under fire
Persisting through frustration during game-based training
examples: Experiment 2 tested control-value, social identity, self-efficacy, non-motivational, and no-message conditions with 124 cadets in TC3Sim via GIFT
key_sources: DeFalco, J. A., Rowe, J. P., Paquette, L., Georgoulas-Sherry, V., Brawner, K., Mott, B. W., Baker, R. S., & Lester, J. C. (2018). Detecting and Addressing Frustration in a Serious Game for Military Training. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0152-1

article_title: Detecting and Addressing Frustration in a Serious Game for Military Training
citation: DeFalco, J. A., Rowe, J. P., Paquette, L., Georgoulas-Sherry, V., Brawner, K., Mott, B. W., Baker, R. S., & Lester, J. C. (2018). Detecting and Addressing Frustration in a Serious Game for Military Training. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0152-1
title: TC3Sim combat medic training simulation integrated with GIFT
description: TC3Sim (also known as vMedic) is a serious game used to train US Army combat medics and combat lifesavers on tactical combat casualty care tasks, including care under fire. It presents linearly structured scenarios with fixed event sequences while allowing learners to freely navigate 3D environments and choose how to administer casualty care. TC3Sim is integrated with the Generalized Intelligent Framework for Tutoring (GIFT), which managed sensors, delivered pre-tests, training materials, post-tests, and run-time motivational feedback triggered by affect detectors. A downloadable version has been made publicly available.
requirements: GIFT integration for sensor management, assessment administration, and feedback delivery
constraints: Training scenarios are structured linearly, presenting a fixed series of events regardless of the learner's actions
target_learners: US Army combat medics and combat lifesavers
target_learning_goals: Tactical combat casualty care: hemorrhage control, care under fire, tactical field care, casualty evacuation
examples: Scenarios included a leg amputation/tourniquet task, a village scenario with enemy fire, and the Kobayashi Maru scenario where the soldier expires regardless of actions

citation: DeFalco, J. A., Rowe, J. P., Paquette, L., Georgoulas-Sherry, V., Brawner, K., Mott, B. W., Baker, R. S., & Lester, J. C. (2018). Detecting and Addressing Frustration in a Serious Game for Military Training. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0152-1
title: Interaction-based frustration detector model for TC3Sim
description: A logistic regression detector of frustration induced from 39 features of learner interaction with TC3Sim, synchronized to BROMP field observations and validated with 10-fold participant-level cross-validation (Kappa = 0.105, A' = 0.692). Detection of player frustration was a function of enemy action affecting the player, patient status such as dangerously high heart rate and worsening condition, and the player's diagnostic actions, which were associated with less frustration. The detector was integrated into GIFT to trigger motivational feedback messages in later experiments.
requirements: Synchronization of trainee actions with BROMP field observations via the HART application
Feature engineering specific to the TC3Sim user interface and scenario events
constraints: Much of the creation of interaction-based detectors is specific to the system for which the detectors are created and must be replicated for new learning environments
target_learners: US Army combat medics and combat lifesavers in TC3Sim training
target_learning_goals: Detecting trainee frustration during tactical combat casualty care training to trigger supportive feedback
examples: The detector's weights included Sum of Systolic Change (1.08), Max of Heart Rate (1.04), and Total Number of Blood Sweep Actions (−0.07) over a 20 s time window

article_title: Regulative Loops, Step Loops and Task Loops
citation: VanLehn, K. (2015). Regulative Loops, Step Loops and Task Loops. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0056-x
title: Regulative loop framework: systems that repeatedly compare performance to a gold standard and act to close the gap
description: The article proposes that tutoring and CSCL systems be seen as instances of a single negative-feedback, goal-seeking loop. In it, students apply knowledge to a task, producing a performance that is "a comparison of the performance against some gold standard and an adjustment to the students' knowledge that brings their performance closer to the gold standard." Computer systems can take over varying amounts of this loop, yielding self-regulation, mirroring, formative assessment or coaching. The framework unifies ITS and regulative CSCL systems.
requirements: A task on which students produce an observable performance, a gold standard to compare it against, and a mechanism for adjustment
constraints: The class probably includes most ITS but only some CSCL systems, namely those taking a regulative rather than a structural approach
target_learners: individual students and small groups in ITS and CSCL settings
target_learning_goals: domain skills, self-regulation, collaboration, motivation, depending on the knowledge type addressed
examples: Fig. 1 depicts the regulative loop based on the one in Soller et al. 2005, with terminology changed by the present author
key_sources: VanLehn, K. (2015). Regulative Loops, Step Loops and Task Loops. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0056-x

article_title: Regulative Loops, Step Loops and Task Loops
citation: VanLehn, K. (2015). Regulative Loops, Step Loops and Task Loops. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0056-x
title: Four-way classification of regulative activity: self-regulation, mirroring, formative assessment, coaching
description: The article classifies regulative approaches by how much of the loop the system executes. If students execute the whole loop themselves, the activity is self-regulation; if the system monitors performance and presents it back, mirroring; if it also compares to a gold standard and reports the comparison, formative assessment; if it additionally generates advice or modifies the task or context, coaching. Coaching is "just what an intelligent tutoring system typically does."
requirements: A regulative loop with a monitorable student performance and a gold standard
constraints: Although Soller et al. intended the classification for collaborative learning, the article argues it applies equally to single-student activities
target_learning_goals: improving performance toward a gold standard across cognitive, meta-cognitive, collaborative and motivational knowledge
examples: Mirroring characterizes reflective debriefing and open learner modeling, where the system presents a display of the student's performance, often as a timeline
key_sources: VanLehn, K. (2015). Regulative Loops, Step Loops and Task Loops. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0056-x

article_title: Regulative Loops, Step Loops and Task Loops
citation: VanLehn, K. (2015). Regulative Loops, Step Loops and Task Loops. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0056-x
title: Four dimensions for classifying regulative loop systems: knowledge type, recipient, change process, granularity
description: Beyond the main classification, the article augments it with four independent dimensions, summarized in Table 1: "Type of knowledge: Cognitive, meta-cognitive, collaborative skill, motivations; Recipient: Student, teacher, activity structure (interventions only); Type of change process: Reminding, persuasion, teaching, remediation; Granularity: Step, task, module." Knowledge type distinguishes cognitive knowledge, meta-cognitive knowledge addressed by meta-tutors, collaboration skill, and motivations. Recipient covers whether information goes to the student directly, to a teacher, or restructures the activity.
requirements: A regulative loop system to which the dimensions are applied
constraints: The type of change process in students' minds is unobservable; designers often have such a process in mind when designing advice
target_learners: students in ITS and CSCL environments, individually or in groups
target_learning_goals: classifying and designing regulative support across cognitive, meta-cognitive, collaborative and motivational goals
examples: MTDashboard monitors students and small groups and presents information to the teacher on a handheld dashboard, who may choose which groups to visit

article_title: Regulative Loops, Step Loops and Task Loops
citation: VanLehn, K. (2015). Regulative Loops, Step Loops and Task Loops. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0056-x
title: Four knowledge-change processes for advice: reminding, persuasion, teaching, remediation
description: The third dimension names the change process the regulative loop is intended to produce. Reminding modifies retrieval cues when the student has merely forgotten to apply knowledge; persuasion assumes the student possesses the knowledge and needs convincing to use it; teaching assumes the student lacks the knowledge but knows its prerequisite concepts; remediation is needed when "the students lack pre-requisite knowledge." The Why2-Atlas physics tutor's hints assumed students knew vectors; when used with students who did not, it was less effective than human tutors who could teach the required remedial concepts.
requirements: Diagnosis of whether the student lacks the knowledge, possesses it unused, or lacks prerequisites
constraints: Remediation requires teaching prerequisite concepts; a simple statement of knowledge will not suffice in that case
target_learners: students receiving advice from tutoring or CSCL systems
target_learning_goals: applying, adopting, acquiring or rebuilding knowledge targeted by system advice
examples: Pointing hints described in Behavior of Tutoring Systems are advice intended to cause reminding; persuasive hints assume students already possess the knowledge
key_sources: VanLehn, K. (2015). Regulative Loops, Step Loops and Task Loops. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0056-x

article_title: Regulative Loops, Step Loops and Task Loops
citation: VanLehn, K. (2015). Regulative Loops, Step Loops and Task Loops. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0056-x
title: Granularity of regulative loops: step, task, and module grain sizes
description: The fourth dimension is the grain size at which performance and knowledge are analyzed. "A step is the smallest user interface action for which it makes sense to call it correct or incorrect." A task is the smallest unit of user activity that is logically and informationally independent of preceding and following units; a complete physics problem solution is a task, but a single equation is not. A module, chapter or unit is a larger grain size of learning activities addressing the same topic.
requirements: User activity that can be segmented into units at the chosen grain size
constraints: Entering the first character of an equation is too small to be a step; entering a single equation is not a task because it depends on variable definitions and other equations
target_learners: students working on step-based tasks in tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: correcting performance at the appropriate grain of analysis
examples: In physics, typing in an equation is a step; a complete solution of a physics problem is a task
key_sources: VanLehn, K. (2015). Regulative Loops, Step Loops and Task Loops. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0056-x

article_title: Regulative Loops, Step Loops and Task Loops
citation: VanLehn, K. (2015). Regulative Loops, Step Loops and Task Loops. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0056-x
title: Regulative loop systems: a class spanning ITS and regulative CSCL systems
description: The article proposes the name "regulative loop systems" for instructional systems conforming to Fig. 1. This class "probably includes most ITS but only some CSCL systems, namely those that take a regulative approach instead of a structural one." Structural work explores novel tasks whose structure elicits improved learning, while regulative work augments existing tasks with regulatory mechanisms interacting with students as activity occurs. A CSCL script system becomes regulative if it also checks whether students followed the scripts and mirrors, assesses or intervenes.
requirements: Monitoring of student performance against a gold standard with mirroring, assessment or intervention
constraints: Excludes purely structural CSCL systems that do not monitor whether students followed scripts
target_learners: students in ITS and regulative CSCL environments
target_learning_goals: bringing student performance closer to a gold standard during learning activities
examples: A CSCL system that asks students to follow scripts would be structural, yet becomes a regulative loop system if it determines whether students followed the scripts

article_title: Evaluation Methods for Intelligent Tutoring Systems Revisited
citation: Jim Greer & Mary Mark. (2015). Evaluation Methods for Intelligent Tutoring Systems Revisited. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:387–392. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0043-2
title: Six emerging evaluation approaches for intelligent tutoring and adaptive learning environments
description: The article organizes its survey around six approaches that "hold great promise for evaluating educational environments": using the open web and crowd sourcing, comparing decisions of adaptive environments with human experts, using simulated learners, washing out selection bias, examining learning curves, and performing evaluations derived from mega quantities of micro measurements. Each is presented as an expansion of the 1993 survey, enabled by increases in computer speed, storage, and connectivity. The framework spans formative and summative evaluation of smart, intelligent, or adaptive educational environments.
