title: Special issue collection on Artificial Intelligence for Higher Education in the COVID-19 era (International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 2024)
description: This element is the special issue collection announced by the journal's editor's note, titled "Special Issue on Artificial Intelligence for Higher Education in the COVID-19 era: Emerging Technologies, Challenges, and Pedagogy-informed Applications". The note states the special issue "features 2 papers" which were "rigorously reviewed according to journal standards", and that the papers are available via the journal homepage's Collections link. article_title: Measuring the Quality of Test-based Exercises Based on the Performance of Students
citation: Josu Arruarte, Mikel Larrañaga, Ana Arruarte & Jon A. Elorriaga. (2021). Measuring the Quality of Test-based Exercises Based on the Performance of Students. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 31, 585–602. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00208-0
title: TEA – a Visual Learning Analytics tool for analyzing the quality of test-based exercises
description: TEA (test ariketen aztertzailea, "Test Exercises Examiner") is a teacher-oriented tool that uses Visual Learning Analytics to help instructors determine the appropriateness of test-based exercises. It analyzes performance at two granularity levels, each item and the whole test, using bar charts, circular charts and boxplots, and incorporates an alert mechanism highlighting suspicious tests or items. It can be used to supervise resource quality throughout a course or for retrospective analysis, and includes a guide describing each metric and plot for teachers who are not proficient in statistics.
requirements: For retrospective analysis, TEA requires additional information such as the final marks of the students, which could be considered their ground-truth knowledge level.
constraints: So far, TEA has only been used to evaluate manually created exercises.
Although TEA has been evaluated only on a single subject, giving satisfactory results.

target_learning_goals: validity and quality of test-based assessment exercises measuring student knowledge
examples: Instructors of the Fundamentals of Computer Science module used TEA with Moodle-recorded answers and final grades to identify tests and items to improve or replace.

article_title: Measuring the Quality of Test-based Exercises Based on the Performance of Students
citation: Josu Arruarte, Mikel Larrañaga, Ana Arruarte & Jon A. Elorriaga. (2021). Measuring the Quality of Test-based Exercises Based on the Performance of Students. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 31, 585–602. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00208-0
title: Four-aspect classification of metrics and statistics for measuring the quality of test-based exercises
description: The article classifies the metrics and statistics usable to measure the quality of test-based exercises from student performance data according to four aspects: whether the results of the exercise are consistent (CIC via Cronbach's alpha, True Weight), whether undesired situations can be inferred (mean, median, standard deviation, skewness, kurtosis), whether the exercise meets the student's level of knowledge (Ease Index, Item Difficulty), and whether the exercise can determine the student's knowledge level (Error Ratio, Standard Error, Random Guess Score, Discrimination Index, Discrimination Efficiency, Item Discrimination Index). This classification, building on Peña (2014), structures both the tool and the evaluation questions.
requirements: The analysis assumes students have only one attempt to answer each question and that all the students have already answered.
constraints: Some metrics are valid only at the item level (e.g., CIC, true weight, error ratio, standard error), others only at the test level (e.g., standard deviation, skewness, kurtosis).
target_learners: teachers and developers of educational material
target_learning_goals: evaluating the quality and validity of test-based exercises and items
examples: TEA implements these metrics and statistics and presents them through visualizations and alerts.

The categories are explicitly not mutually exclusive, and the classification extends and re-organises the scheme of Yao et al. (2012) as extended by Alsubait (2015).

article_title: The Social life of AI in Education
citation: Williamson, B. (2024). The Social life of AI in Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 34. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00342-5
title: The social life of AI in education: AI in education as a socially and historically specific result of technical, commercial and political convergences
description: This framework holds that AI in education "is not just a bundle of technologies but is the socially and historically specific result of an accumulation of technical developments, scientific practices, institutional applications, and power struggles". It treats current interest in AIED as the result of convergences: decades of academic R&D, growing commercial concerns, and political enthusiasm for digital transformation. The framework directs attention both to how AI is produced and framed by different actors and to its social effects, including unintended consequences.
requirements: Researchers and designers must attend to the specific companies, government centres and human actors responsible for developing and using the technology, rather than treating AI as a monolithic category

citation: Adamson, D., Dyke, G., Jang, H., & Rosé, C. P. (2014). Towards an Agile Approach to Adapting Dynamic Collaboration Support to Student Needs. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0012-6
title: Academically Productive Talk (APT) framework of facilitation moves for eliciting transactive discussion
description: Academically Productive Talk is a classroom discussion facilitation approach comprising core moves (Revoicing, Press for Reasoning, Challenge, Restate, Add More, Agree/Disagree, Explain Other) that teachers and agents employ to encourage discussions in which students make reasoning public and interact with it transactively. The article maps each move onto three transact dimensions (self/other-oriented, representational/transformational, consensus/conflict-oriented) and proposes these moves as content-independent building blocks for dynamic collaborative learning support. The framework posits a logical ordering of move demand, from self-oriented representational moves to other-oriented transformational conflict-oriented ones.
requirements: Students must receive instruction on APT moves prior to online interaction so agent moves can model and facilitate the discussion style
constraints: The preconditions for successful use of specific APT moves and which learners benefit most from which moves remain unexplored in prior classroom literature
target_learning_goals: articulate and monitor own reasoning
evaluate and challenge peers' reasoning
build deep understanding of causal mechanisms
examples: The article maps eight APT moves onto transact categories in Table 1, with example teacher utterances such as 'Explain your thinking' and 'Do you agree or disagree, and why?'

title: Transactivity construct: 18 types of transactive moves along three dimensions
description: Transactivity is a construct from a Piagetian framework formalized as 18 types of transactive moves that characterize each student's conversational turn as an explicit reasoning display connecting with previously articulated reasoning. The article draws on three dimensions for motivating experimental studies: self-oriented versus other-oriented (whether the contribution operates on the speaker's own or a partner's reasoning), representational versus transformational (whether the original idea is restated or transformed), and consensus-oriented versus conflict-oriented. The authors propose these dimensions create a logical ordering of demand that applies to corresponding APT facilitation moves.

constraints: Alternative frameworks (Inter-subjective Meaning Making, Productive Agency) privilege subtly different formulations of similar behaviors

mutual examination and integration of mental models

title: Bazaar: modular architecture for dynamic collaboration support with conversational agents
description: Bazaar is a publicly available, event-driven architecture for designing multi-party collaborative agents that builds upon the earlier Basilica architecture. It hosts a library of reusable behavioral components, uses a two-stage event-processing flow (Preprocessors analyse the event stream for triggers; Reactors propose tutor actions), and features an Output Coordinator that manages sequencing and timing of potentially clashing interventions using a priority-based proposal system extending Lison's concurrent mode approach. The architecture enabled the series of APT agent studies reported in the article across multiple content domains and grade levels.
requirements: Coordination between simple support behaviors is necessary even when only one APT facilitation strategy is being used
constraints: Experiencing clashes between macro-level and micro-level support behaviors is distracting and confusing for students
target_learners: high school students in collaborative chat environments
undergraduate students in collaborative chat environments

eliciting transactive conversational behavior
examples: The Output Coordinator assigns each Proposal a timed window of relevance and a priority between 0 and 1, periodically re-evaluating priorities and enacting the highest-priority proposal

title: Adapt the dynamic support strategy to the contextual needs of different student populations (agile support)
description: Agile support for collaborative learning means adapting the facilitation strategy taken by the support technology to the specific contextual needs of different student populations, rather than applying the same context-sensitive rules for all groups. The article proposes that the choice of facilitation strategy can be adapted in response to an automated assessment of interaction patterns indicating whether a successful intervention is occurring. title: ARCS-guided question-triggering mechanism linking five reading interaction types to motivational dimensions
description: IRead's question-triggering mechanism operationalizes Keller's ARCS model (Attention, Relevance, Confidence, Satisfaction) by connecting its "four dimensions of the ARCS model with five typical types of interactions in reading, designing specific question-triggering mechanisms for each interaction type." The five interaction types are highlighting, note-taking, concept query, term searching, and inactivity, each with its own trigger, question presentation, and LLM customization prompt (Table 2). Questions are individualized from the reader's highlighting, note-taking, and other interaction behaviors following constructivist learning theory, and the overall approach implements guided discovery learning by posing questions without providing answers.

title: IRead interactive textbook reading tool
description: IRead is an interactive tool for textbook reading that "uses LLMs with visualization and interaction techniques, to enhance students' reading and learning experiences." It comprises an enhanced textbook reader with highlighting, note-taking, minimap, and search; a hierarchical concept tree visualization with information cards generated by an LLM and refined through human oversight; and Question Wiz, an AI-driven question bot presenting interaction-specific questions. A fuzzy concept mapping technique using sentence-transformer embeddings and cosine similarity links concepts to text terms exceeding a predefined similarity threshold. Its content is produced by a one-time textbook data processing workflow per imported textbook.

title: Psychometric multiple-membership ordinal logistic regression model of course effects on soft skills
description: The framework builds on a model in which each course has an effect on each soft skill, decomposed into a fixed average course effect plus random course deviations, with random student effects capturing initial proficiency differences. The article states that "Pinos Ullauri et al. (2024) modelled soft skills proficiency with multiple-membership ordinal logistic regression", predicting the log odds of being assessed at or below category k on a 4-point Likert scale. The trained ensemble predicts expected soft skill proficiency given any proposed course set, which is what allows the recommender to score candidate course sets.

Course history data per student per stage, with course indicators and course counts
constraints: Course effects are modelled as random effects via multiple membership because the sparse, imbalanced data is insufficient for fixed-effect estimation
The dataset required multiple imputation of missing stage-0 values to reach convergence
target_learning_goals: soft skill proficiency development across 10 soft skills such as Problem Solving and Leadership
examples: Applied to 884 students from three cohorts (2021–2023) at IMT Nord Europe, with 1,660 data instances expanded to 1,910 via multiple imputation

title: MIRT-inspired fitness aggregation: compensatory average and partially compensatory product over per-skill scores
description: To turn the multi-objective problem of optimising 10 per-skill scores into a mono-objective one, the article proposes two aggregation methods inspired by Multidimensional Item Response Theory. The compensatory method averages the scores, allowing "compensation between surpluses or deficits of soft skill proficiency"; the partially compensatory method multiplies them, requiring each score to be as high as possible. The article states this approach is "inspired from Multidimensional Item Response Theory (MIRT)", which allows treating the problem as mono-objective and potentially diminishing optimisation complexity.

A targeted soft skill profile defining the thresholds against which discrepancies are scored
constraints: Percentage increases are not comparable across aggregation methods because of their different mathematical definitions
target_learning_goals: balancing proficiency across multiple soft skills relative to targets
examples: With compensatory aggregation a 10% increase in each of 10 scores conveys a 10% fitness increase, whereas in partially compensatory aggregation it translates to 159.4%

citation: Stevenson, C. E. (2017). Role of Working Memory and Strategy-Use in Feedback Effects on children's Progression in Analogy Solving: an Explanatory Item Response Theory Account. Int J Artif Intell Educ 27:393–418. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0129-5
title: Multilevel explanatory IRT based on Embretson's Multidimensional Rasch Model for Learning and Change
description: The article applies an item response theory approach based on Embretson's Multidimensional Rasch Model for Learning and Change, extended with multilevel and explanatory components, to model children's pretest-to-posttest change in analogy solving. Ability is built up in a summation term over testing occasions, with an initial ability factor and modifiabilities representing change. Person covariates such as age and working memory are entered with regression parameters on the latent scale, and nested models are compared with likelihood ratio tests. The authors state this "allowed for reliable estimates of learning from feedback" where classical gain scores are unreliable.

constraints: The article notes results are likely similar to those using classical test theory sum scores with standard linear regression; the advantages are reliable change scores, equating across datasets, and accounting for random school and experiment differences
target_learners: primary school children (kindergarten through fourth grade)
target_learning_goals: figural analogical reasoning
examples: Models M0–M3 were estimated successively with lme4 in R, adding item difficulty, age, session, condition, working memory, and strategy-use effects, each tested with likelihood ratio tests

citation: Lenat, D. B., & Durlach, P. J. (2014). Reinforcing Math Knowledge by Immersing Students in a Simulated Learning-By-Teaching Experience. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0016-x
title: BELLA: a simulated learning-by-teaching architecture in which the tutee avatar is a puppet controlled by a super-agent that models the user
description: BELLA is a sixth-grade mathematics learning-by-teaching system in which the user tutors an avatar, Elle, who appears to learn but never does. The article states that "Elle is just a puppet controlled by BELLA, a diagnostic instrument BELLA manipulates the way a doctor manipulates a stethoscope." BELLA observes the user's corrections and inactions, builds a symbolic user model, and uses it Socratically to select Elle's mental model — its gaps, bugs and exaggerated errors — so as to target the user's own confusions. It was built by extending the Cyc AI platform's ontology, knowledge base, inference engine and NLG subsystem.
requirements: Requires a large symbolic AI knowledge base (Cyc) with domain content, inference engine and natural language generation already in place
constraints: Elle never actually learns anything directly from the human tutor; all changes to the Elle model are made by BELLA, not by the user
target_learning_goals: Reinforce and deepen conceptual and procedural understanding of pre-algebra and pre-geometry
examples: BELLA runs an avatar Elle with an ablated version of the student model, exaggerating each knowledge gap so the user notices, corrects, and thereby refreshes their own understanding
key_sources: Lenat, D. B., & Durlach, P. J. (2014). Reinforcing Math Knowledge by Immersing Students in a Simulated Learning-By-Teaching Experience. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0016-x

article_title: Reinforcing Math Knowledge by Immersing Students in a Simulated Learning-By-Teaching Experience
citation: Lenat, D. B., & Durlach, P. J. (2014). Reinforcing Math Knowledge by Immersing Students in a Simulated Learning-By-Teaching Experience. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0016-x
title: The hypothesis that pretending to be taught may prove more powerful than actually being taught by the user
description: The article's central conjecture is that a tutee that only pretends to learn — while a super-agent selectively feigns ignorance based on a user model — can better target the user's specific difficulties than a true LBT system that must believe its user and start from a tabula rasa. The authors write that "this very distinction — pretending to be taught versus 'really' directly being taught by the user — may prove useful and powerful." A true LBT system must obey its user; BELLA can instead role-play an intelligently selected set of foibles.
requirements: Requires a user model accurate enough to select pedagogically advantageous Elle models
constraints: As of the article, only a small sample of anecdotal results exists; rigorous data to test the central conjecture were planned for the coming year
target_learning_goals: Overcoming current confusions and misconceptions in pre-algebra
examples: BELLA is compared to a parent who feigns ignorance very selectively, role-playing someone with an intelligently-selected set of foibles
key_sources: Lenat, D. B., & Durlach, P. J. (2014). Reinforcing Math Knowledge by Immersing Students in a Simulated Learning-By-Teaching Experience. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0016-x

citation: Lenat, D. B., & Durlach, P. J. (2014). Reinforcing Math Knowledge by Immersing Students in a Simulated Learning-By-Teaching Experience. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0016-x
title: BELLA student model: about 150 tuples covering Common Core concepts, skills, bugs and missing heuristics, each scored 0–100 with full change history
description: BELLA models each student's domain knowledge as a set of about 150 tuples, each corresponding to a Common Core concept, skill, or specific type of bug or missing heuristic. Each element is summarized as a number from 0 to 100, and BELLA stores the entire history of every model element — every action or inaction that caused the number to change. The teacher can drill down through a UI to see the exact historical in-game events that caused each revision. The authors estimate the model will grow to about 200 tuples when the sixth-grade Common Core curriculum is fully covered.
requirements: Model initialization method not yet settled: options include pretesting, a normative 6th-grade model, interviewing the teacher or student, or starting with a very incompetent Elle
constraints: The authors hypothesize but have not tested that this set of about 150 elements suffices for the BELLA task
target_learning_goals: Diagnosing and tracking specific Common Core concepts, skills, bugs and heuristics in pre-algebra
examples: A user model element was initially set to 0.84, then raised to 0.89 after the user selected a piece of advice about reordering addends

title: BELLA adventure game context: math problems emerge naturally from a 3D sandbox role-playing game rather than as isolated exercises
description: BELLA embeds all math problems in an engaging adventure game in which Elle's spacecraft has crash-landed and she faces challenges requiring mathematical help. The article emphasizes that "we have worked hard to make all the math problems emerge naturally in the course of that adventure, rather than being disembodied, isolated game show questions." For example, adding mixed numbers arises because Elle needs to find the shortest route on a map. Users who guess or bypass problems see consequences over time in wasted resources.
requirements: Game, UI and Cyc run as separate components (Unity 3D, Firefox, Java) that communicate
constraints: An earlier storyline (shopping, cooking, construction) was rejected by students, who wanted futuristic sci-fi, robots, and aliens
target_learning_goals: Applying pre-algebra skills to situated problem-solving scenarios
examples: Elle must place the correct linear combination of batteries into slots to sum to the voltage needed to open an electromagnetically locked door
key_sources: Lenat, D. B., & Durlach, P. J. (2014). Reinforcing Math Knowledge by Immersing Students in a Simulated Learning-By-Teaching Experience. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0016-x

title: Microtheory-based representation of interaction contexts enabling temporal reasoning about user and tutee models
description: BELLA represents each step of the user–Elle dialogue as a new reified context (microtheory) that snapshots the user model, the Elle model, and the problem state at that moment. As the article describes, "a growing graph of interaction contexts is built" that provides a way to refer to past states, back up a step, and serve as grist for BELLA to induce conclusions about the user. Several mt-types are distinguished: Elle-belief mts, user-model snapshot mts, time-point mts, process mts, math belief mts, quantitative relationship mts, problem interpretation mts, tactician mts and strategist mts.
requirements: Requires pre-creating and caching a large resource pool of microtheories to keep up with proliferation in real time
constraints: Keeping up with the proliferation of dozens of new microtheories in real time was a challenge to Cyc's inference engine in early 2013
target_learning_goals: Tracking the temporal evolution of student and tutee knowledge states during problem solving
examples: Each step creates a named interaction context (e.g., 'Step37') that snapshots the state of the problem, Elle's model, and the user model
key_sources: Lenat, D. B., & Durlach, P. J. (2014). Reinforcing Math Knowledge by Immersing Students in a Simulated Learning-By-Teaching Experience. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0016-x

citation: Lenat, D. B., & Durlach, P. J. (2014). Reinforcing Math Knowledge by Immersing Students in a Simulated Learning-By-Teaching Experience. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0016-x
title: Exaggerated-mirror tutee modeling: giving the teachable agent the user's own errors amplified to prompt noticing and correction
description: BELLA's core instructional pattern is to give Elle the same types of deficiencies as the user but more exaggerated, so the user notices, corrects, and in doing so refreshes their own understanding. The article explains that if the user evaluates operations left to right, "Elle will be given that same tendency with an even higher likelihood to the same sort of operator-precedence error, so Elle will make even more egregious and obvious such errors which the user will have a good chance of noticing, correcting." When the user corrects Elle, BELLA both learns about the user and gives them a small esteem-building experience.
requirements: Requires an accurate user model to identify which errors to exaggerate
constraints: If the user does not notice Elle's mistake, BELLA may keep or worsen Elle's model to make the error more obvious, or have Elle self-reflect
target_learning_goals: Noticing and repairing one's own misconceptions by correcting a tutee's errors
examples: Elle's model is kept slightly behind the user's; as the student learns, BELLA improves Elle's model so it makes fewer mistakes

article_title: Analysing Student Programs in the PHP Intelligent Tutoring System
citation: Weragama, D. & Reye, J. (2014). Analysing Student Programs in the PHP Intelligent Tutoring System. Int J Artif Intell Educ 24:162–188. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0014-z
title: PHP ITS knowledge base: first-order logic predicates, rules and actions for program analysis
description: The PHP ITS models program analysis as an AI state-space problem using "a set of predicates based on First Order Logic, and a set of rules and actions based on AI approaches". Student programs are converted to Abstract Syntax Trees, walked node by node to create facts, and the resulting final state is compared against an Overall Goal to determine correctness. Hierarchical planning concepts handle user-defined functions and loops. Missing facts identify specific errors for feedback.
requirements: Each exercise requires an Overall Goal specified in terms of the knowledge base predicates
Adding exercises requires technical knowledge of the ITS representations
constraints: Does not cover advanced PHP topics such as classes and objects
Cannot handle all types of loops; only definite loops and collection-iteration loops, which account for over 50% of real-world loops
target_learners: novice programmers learning PHP web development
target_learning_goals: PHP programming constructs including selection structures, loops, functions, arrays and HTML form processing
examples: Gap exercises where students complete supplied code
Grade-display exercise demonstrating flattened nested selection structures
key_sources: Weragama, D. & Reye, J. (2014). Analysing Student Programs in the PHP Intelligent Tutoring System. Int J Artif Intell Educ 24:162–188. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0014-z

title: PHP Intelligent Tutoring System with web interface and four-level help system
description: The PHP ITS is a web-based tutoring system containing 27 exercises covering 34 topics. Students select exercises, enter solutions, and receive feedback. If incorrect, students can request "four further levels of help regarding the error" — two levels of 'What is wrong?' and two of 'How do I fix it?'. A Bayesian Belief Network student model tracks topic-level knowledge and suggests the next best exercise based on Zone of Proximal Development principles.
requirements: Exercise authors must be familiar with the knowledge base predicate representations
constraints: Adding new exercises is time consuming and cannot be done without technical knowledge of the ITS
target_learning_goals: basic PHP programming for dynamic web page development
examples: Main interface with exercise description, code entry pane, feedback pane, and rendered web page display

article_title: Transforming EFL Teaching with AI: A Systematic Review of Empirical Studies
citation: Arnab Kundu, Tripti Bej. (2024). Transforming school EFL teaching with AI: A Systematic Review of Empirical Studies. Research Square preprint. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-4805086/v1
title: Eight-category functional taxonomy of AI technologies in school EFL teaching
description: The review categorizes the AI tools used across the 22 studies into eight functionality-based classes: NLP, chatbots and virtual tutors, gamification, adaptive learning platforms, speech and pronunciation tools, content creation and management tools, AI-powered assessment tools, and VR/AR. It reports that "NLP appears as a popular and e cient AI technology in EFL education, providing tailored, interactive experiences for students," supporting grammar correction, pronunciation feedback, and vocabulary building. The taxonomy organizes which tool types serve which language-learning aspects.
requirements: Tools must be matched to specific EFL learning aspects and functionalities as the review's categorization does
constraints: The review's data are concentrated in Southeast Asian school contexts rather than global
target_learning_goals: EFL vocabulary, grammar, speaking, listening, reading, and writing skills
examples: Google Assistant, ChatGPT, and Google Dialogflow are classified under NLP or chatbots/virtual tutors; Jungle Animals Game under gamification

title: Four-component conceptual framework for AI-enabled language learning: technology, pedagogy, linguistic, and learning components
description: The review proposes a conceptual framework (Fig. 1) examining AI-enabled language learning at the intersection of four components. As the article states, "It examines AI-enabled language learning by examining the intersection of technology, pedagogy, linguistic, and learning components." The technology component covers AI tools' capabilities, limitations, and data privacy; the language component covers phonetics, morphology, syntax, semantics, and pragmatics; the learning component covers learner interaction with AI tools and outcomes. The framework structures the review's analysis of the included studies.
requirements: Combining insights across all four components to develop effective AI-enabled EFL learning solutions
target_learning_goals: EFL language acquisition across linguistic subsystems
examples: Tables 2 and 3 of the review classify each included study by technology component, linguistic component, and pedagogical component

title: Eight pedagogical approaches evolving in AI-enabled school EFL teaching
description: The review identifies eight pedagogical approaches that evolved in AI-enabled EFL teaching: "personalized learning, blended learning, gami cation, project-based learning, collaborative learning, inquiry-based learning, competency-based learning, and task-based language teaching (Table 5)." Each is instantiated with AI-specific practices, e.g., adaptive difficulty levels in gamification, AI-driven research assistants in project-based learning, and AI-driven role-playing and simulation environments in task-based language teaching. The pattern describes how AI capabilities support these approaches in school EFL classrooms.
requirements: Teachers need pedagogical expertise in using AI tools for approaches such as collaborative learning with ChatGPT
constraints: The review notes these approaches shift practice from traditional teacher-centered methods toward student-centered, adaptive pedagogy
target_learning_goals: Communicative competence and engagement in EFL learning
examples: Table 5 lists nuanced practices such as learning analytics to monitor progress and adjust instruction under personalized learning

title: ActiveMath: a web-based adaptive mathematics tutoring environment
description: ActiveMath, begun in 2000 by Erica Melis, is a web-based system for tutoring students in mathematics topics ranging from fractions to calculus. According to the preface, it "employs a variety of AI techniques to model students and support their learning by providing feedback during problem solving, planning personalized curricula and generating navigational cues to help students find the best topics to study." It uses open standards to semantically represent mathematical content with rich metadata, and Melis's 2001 paper on it is the journal's tenth highest cited paper of all time.

The preface describes how Melis recognized "around 2004 or 2005 that this type of instructional material, in which students are presented with one or more errors in worked solutions and are prompted to find and fix the errors, could be an important instructional technique that could be integrated with interactive software." This launched a collaboration between Melis and McLaren and an ongoing line of inquiry in web-based mathematics learning.

article_title: An Intelligent Support System to Help Teachers Plan Field Trips
citation: Noemi Mauro, Liliana Ardissono, Federica Cena, Livio Scarpinati, Gianluca Torta. (2024). An Intelligent Support System to Help Teachers Plan Field Trips. Int J Artif Intell Educ 34, 793–824. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00366-x
title: FieldTripOrganizer web application for teacher-led field trip planning
description: FieldTripOrganizer is a web-based, mobile-accessible application that helps teachers design custom field trips by filtering Points of Interest and activities by geographical area, domain of interest, school level, and type, and by incrementally building an itinerary. The article proposes "a field trip planner based on the mixed-initiative approach aimed at increasing teachers' autonomy and motivation in designing educational tours". While the user designs the trip, the application keeps the spare time visible, invokes the VROOM solver to re-estimate the optimal schedule after each addition or removal, and graphically annotates items with a green or red semaphore indicating whether they fit the time constraints. It was instantiated on science field trips in the Ivrea area of Piedmont, Italy, and evaluated with 18 science teachers.
requirements: Domain experts must populate the external data source (Omeka-S CMS) with places and activities at setup time
constraints: Budget constraints are not handled; administrative aspects such as paying services are out of scope
target_learners: Student classes from preschool to high school visiting cultural and natural sites
target_learning_goals: Out-of-school learning through science field trips complementing in-class work
examples: In the user study, participants organized a science field trip for a class of students in two geographical areas (Ivrea City and Alice Lake), once per application

article_title: An Intelligent Support System to Help Teachers Plan Field Trips
citation: Noemi Mauro, Liliana Ardissono, Federica Cena, Livio Scarpinati, Gianluca Torta. (2024). An Intelligent Support System to Help Teachers Plan Field Trips. Int J Artif Intell Educ 34, 793–824. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00366-x
title: Mixed-initiative interaction for field trip planning: user control combined with delegated scheduling support
description: The article's organizing framework applies Horvitz's mixed-initiative interaction to field trip organization: the teacher leads every design step and selects places and activities, while the system takes over burdensome computations such as consistency checks and itinerary optimization. Unlike most personalized tour planners that autonomously generate optimized itineraries and let users only critique complete solutions, this approach combines information filtering with automated scheduling so that "the user [is] in full control of the design process, delegating the system to manage difficult and burdensome tasks such as consistency checks and itinerary optimization". The framework treats PoIs as complex entities aggregating activities, and separates information filtering from itinerary optimization, which is solved as a Travelling Salesman Problem rather than a utility-maximizing Tourist Trip Design Problem.
requirements: An underlying itinerary generation service that computes the schedule taking the shortest time, so feasibility annotations rest on an optimized partial schedule
constraints: The approach excludes automated planning where the system leads the construction of the itinerary, and does not focus on fine-grained routing or reactive itinerary adaptation during trip execution
target_learners: Teachers of any school level organizing field trips for whole classes
target_learning_goals: Design of out-of-school learning itineraries aligned with didactic objectives and time constraints
examples: Free-text comments showed participants appreciated the mixed-initiative model, e.g., liking "the automatic planning function, so that you don't have to build the itinerary manually, but still have the ability to select the activities to do"
key_sources: Noemi Mauro, Liliana Ardissono, Federica Cena, Livio Scarpinati, Gianluca Torta. (2024). An Intelligent Support System to Help Teachers Plan Field Trips. Int J Artif Intell Educ 34, 793–824. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00366-x

title: Visual feasibility annotation of options against the itinerary's time constraints
description: This lesson/task-level design pattern keeps the planner constantly aware of the temporal feasibility of each candidate item while an itinerary is built incrementally. Each PoI and activity is annotated with "a green or red semaphore depending on whether the item can be included in the itinerary without exceeding the available time or not", alongside a continuously updated display of spare time. If the user disregards the indication and causes a scheduling error, the application explains the problem. In the study's thematic analysis, most participants considered awareness of the remaining time very useful, and some missed this functionality in the baseline planner.
requirements: An itinerary generator invoked after each item addition or removal so the next feasibility estimate relies on a refreshed, optimized schedule
constraints: The heuristic feasibility estimation may generate false negatives because it does not optimize the schedule of the revised itinerary and may overestimate displacement time
target_learners: Teachers planning multi-stop itineraries under fixed time budgets
target_learning_goals: Informed selection of places and activities that fit the trip's temporal constraints
examples: The interface shows spare time (e.g., 2 hours and 20 minutes) in the left section and per-item visit and setup times (e.g., 30 minutes execution + 10 minutes setup) next to each semaphore

title: Generic ontology-based domain data model for places, activities, and objects
description: FieldTripOrganizer's domain knowledge is expressed as an OWL ontology (Fig. 1) stored in the Omeka-S content management system, which domain experts populate at setup time. The model defines "Items" representing places (PoIs), activities, or objects, related through is-a, use_in, and is_in relations, so that a PoI can aggregate one or more activities — unlike the atomic elements of typical tourist applications. Activities carry attributes for school levels (difficulty), type (laboratory or outdoors), and setup time (10 minutes by default). The generic data model abstracts from entity details and specifies only "Domains of interest", making the application suitable for tours on different topics such as science and arts.

article_title: A Survey of Current Machine Learning Approaches to Student Free-Text Evaluation for Intelligent Tutoring
citation: Xiaoyu Bai · Manfred Stede. (2023). A Survey of Current Machine Learning Approaches to Student Free-Text Evaluation for Intelligent Tutoring. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education (2023) 33:994–1032. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00323-0
title: Taxonomy of student free-text evaluation: automatic essay evaluation (holistic and aspect-based) and automatic short-answer scoring (with or without reference answers)
description: The survey organises the field of student free-text evaluation — the automatic evaluation of students' free-text production including short answers and essays — along two axes. By text type, it distinguishes automatic essay evaluation (AEE), where the survey uses "evaluation instead of scoring to emphasise that our survey is not limited to models that predict scores", and automatic short-answer scoring (ASAS). By method, it distinguishes feature-based models, neural architectures (RNN/LSTM, CNN, pre-trained BERT), and hybrid combinations. AEE is further split into holistic essay grading and evaluation of specific aspects of essays; ASAS into evaluation without and based on reference answers. The survey presents state-of-the-art model performance on popular datasets within this structure.
requirements: Supervised ML training data labelled for the target evaluation task, since the survey frames the task as supervised learning where the model outputs a score or correctness judgement
constraints: The survey excludes grammatical error correction in essays, assessment of students' written reflection, and students' interaction data from computer-supported collaborative learning, which it states are beyond its scope
target_learners: students producing free-text answers and essays across middle school, high school, and college levels, including second-language learners
target_learning_goals: accurate automated evaluation of student free-text answers and essays to support feedback and tutoring in intelligent tutoring systems
examples: The survey's Table 1 lists recent works grouped under holistic essay scoring, evaluation of specific aspects of essays, short-answer evaluation without reference answers, and short-answer evaluation based on reference answers

title: AITS: An Intelligent Tutoring System for Teaching Search Algorithms
description: AITS is an intelligent tutoring system developed to help students learn and tutors teach search algorithms, a fundamental AI topic. It consists of six main units: Student Interface, Tutor Interface, Automatic Assessment, Test Generator, Learning Analytics, and Domain Knowledge & Learning Objects. Learning is achieved through a wide range of learning activities including theory, examples, visualizations, interactive exercises, and tests. The system adapts test difficulty to individual students using a rule-based expert system.

title: Interactive Step-Based Algorithm Visualizations Following Active Learning Principles
description: Algorithm visualizations in AITS are developed according to the essence of student active learning. During an animation demonstrating an algorithm, the system can stop at a random step and ask the student to specify the next action or justify why an action was made, using multiple choice questions. The principles of active learning postulate that the more users directly manipulate and act upon the learning material, the higher the mental efforts and psychological involvement and therefore the better the learning outcome.

Multiple choice questions for interaction
Immediate corrective feedback on erroneous answers

title: Automatic Assessment Mechanism with Four-Stage Framework
description: The automatic assessment mechanism evaluates student answers to search algorithm exercises in four stages: (1) calculating similarity between student and correct answer using edit distance, (2) categorizing the answer type based on completeness and accuracy, (3) identifying types of errors including carelessness, and (4) automatically marking via an automated marker based on answer type, edit distance, and error types. It consists of three main parts: Error Detection Mechanism, Automatic Marking Mechanism, and Feedback Mechanism.

Requires a correct answer for comparison
Requires domain-specific error categorization scheme
constraints: Answers must be strings or transformable into strings for generalization to other domains

title: Five-Category Answer Categorization Scheme Based on Completeness and Accuracy
description: A student's answer is characterized in terms of completeness and accuracy, yielding five categories: Incomplete-Accurate (IncAcc), Incomplete-Inaccurate (IncIna), Complete-Inaccurate (ComIna), Complete-Accurate (ComAcc), and Superfluous (SF). An answer is complete if all nodes of the correct answer appear in the student's answer; it is accurate when all its nodes are correct. The Superfluous category is further split into SF-LG (last node is the goal node) and SF-LNG (last node is not the goal node). This categorization is influenced by the scheme proposed in Fiedler and Tsovaltzi (2003), enriched in terms of superfluity.
requirements: Answers must be representable as sequences of nodes
Requires edit distance calculation to determine completeness and accuracy
constraints: Designed for sequence-based answers to search algorithm exercises
target_learning_goals: Correct application of search algorithms
examples: Example: SA = <A B D E M H> and CA = <A C D E Z H> categorized as ComIna

title: Error Importance Model Accounting for Carelessness in Automated Assessment
description: Not all errors students make are of the same importance, and not all are due to lack of knowledge. Some are due to carelessness or inattention. The system distinguishes two types of single-error answers: Type I (only one operation required to achieve matching) and Type II (only one node relabeling operation for two consecutive nodes that have been switched). Special edit operations (Second_Node_Insertion, Second_Node_Relabeling, Goal_Node_Relabeling) carry a cost of 2 versus 1 for basic operations, reflecting that errors in selecting the second node or goal node are considered more serious.
requirements: Edit distance calculation with weighted special-case operations
Empirically set weights w1=0.6 and w2=0.8 based on tutors' experience
constraints: Weights set empirically based on two tutors' experience
Simple/complex distinction (≤6 nodes vs >6 nodes) based on empirical data
target_learning_goals: Correct application of search algorithms
examples: Carelessness defined as giving the wrong answer despite having the needed skills for answering correctly

title: Automated Marking Algorithm for Search Algorithm Exercises
description: The automated marking algorithm calculates student scores based on answer type, edit distance, and error types. For simple answers (≤6 nodes), the score is calculated via a formula using edit distance and the number of nodes. For complex answers, the algorithm branches on the answer category (ComIna, IncAcc, IncIna, SF-LG, SF-LNG) and single-error type, applying different weight parameters. The marking scale is 0 to 100 points. The algorithm is based on empirical estimation and evaluation results as well as the principle of simulating tutor marking.

Answer categorization from the error detection mechanism
Empirically set parameters w1=0.6 and w2=0.8

title: General Assessment Framework for Automated Marking Across Domains
description: The authors specify a general framework for the assessment process consisting of four stages: (1) specify similarity between student answer and correct answer, (2) categorize student answer according to the answer categorization scheme, (3) check for important errors, and (4) calculate the mark via the automated marker. The framework can be used in different domains by proper instantiations of three elements: similarity metric, answer categorization scheme, and automated marking algorithm. As implemented in AITS, it could easily be used for domains where answers are strings or could be transformed into strings.

citation: Leitner, M., Greenwald, E., Wang, N., Montgomery, R., & Merchant, C. (2023). Designing Game-Based Learning for High School Artificial Intelligence Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 33, 384–398. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00327-w
title: Three-category taxonomy of K-12 AI learners: AI Consumers, AI Operators, and AI Developers
description: The article organizes high school AI learners into three categories drawn from the K-12 AI education research community: "those who will be AI end-users in their everyday lives and careers, those who will need to implement AI algorithms, and those who will research and advance AI algorithms." AI Consumers (all students) need to learn what is possible with AI and its impact; AI Operators need to understand algorithm varieties, strengths and weaknesses to make informed decisions; AI Developers need deep algorithmic understanding including estimating space and time complexity. ARIN-561's design targets appropriate takeaways for each category.
requirements: Designs must provide takeaways appropriate to each learner category, as the article's game does by exposing algorithm tradeoffs for Operators and step-by-step algorithm mechanics for Developers
target_learning_goals: understanding what AI can accomplish
selecting appropriate AI algorithms for tasks
understanding how search algorithms work in detail
examples: ARIN-561 gives Consumers a glimpse of how task-specific information enables more efficient approaches, Operators comparisons of algorithms on memory usage and runtime, and Developers introductory ways to calculate time and space complexity

title: ARIN-561: a game-based learning environment teaching classical search algorithms to high school students
description: ARIN-561 is a game-based learning environment in which students play a scientist who crash-lands on an alien planet and solves problems by learning and applying AI knowledge. Its first prototype focuses on classical search algorithms: "how each algorithm works and what its suitable applications are." Students learn Breadth First Search, Depth First Search, and Greedy Search through map-based pathfinding tutorials, sliding 8-puzzle circuit tasks, and a color code puzzle, with in-the-moment scaffolding for time and space complexity analysis. The design has not yet been evaluated in studies with students.

constraints: the design has not yet been evaluated in any studies with students
target_learning_goals: learning classical search algorithms
applying math knowledge
building computational thinking skills
examples: the BFS tutorial has students track down a lost robot companion on a labeled map, translating map areas and paths into nodes and edges of a search tree

title: Spatial-map-first tutorial progression scaffolds search-tree abstraction before abstract puzzle tasks
description: Each algorithm tutorial in ARIN-561 begins with a spatial search task on a map with labeled areas and walking paths, which readily translate to nodes and edges in a search tree. The article states this "provides a more accessible entry point for students to begin thinking about search and serves as a familiar reference while trying to interpret and understand the novel and abstract tree representation." Only after this foundation do students encounter puzzle tasks like sliding puzzles or code cracking that less closely resemble searching a tree, transferring understanding from moving between areas via paths to moving between puzzle configurations via piece moves.
requirements: an initial problem domain whose structure maps directly onto the abstract representation being taught
target_learning_goals: interpreting and constructing search trees
parsing problems in terms AI systems can operate on
examples: the Depth First Search tutorial uses a map designed to produce an extremely wide tree, exposing that Breadth First Search can run out of memory, then links memory growth to linear and exponential functions from math class

title: Integrate narrative, educational content, and gameplay tightly and calibrate narrative complexity to align engagement with learning in educational games
description: Drawing on the success of Crystal Island, the article adopts the principle that "tight integration between educational content, narrative, and gameplay, along with properly calibrated narrative complexity are two factors that can lead to a positive relationship between learning and engagement." ARIN-561 builds its narrative around tasks commonly solved by search algorithms (pathfinding, puzzle solving, password cracking), so students only advance the story through gameplay that teaches search algorithms. The narrative uses a straightforward escape-the-planet premise with embedded mystery to spark curiosity without distracting from learning.

title: Stochastic simulated student module for testing learning-styles modelling approaches
description: A software module implemented as an expert system that encapsulates knowledge about how learning styles affect student performance. It receives the student's real learning styles and a selected learning style combination, and stochastically infers session performance via P = M − (D × K × α), where difficulty D depends on the amount of unmet learning styles plus random terms for strong and moderate unmet preferences. It is uncoupled from any educational system, so it "can be easily adapted and reused for testing other student modelling approaches based on LS."

constraints: Performance inference is stochastic and considers that inadequately adapted content may contribute to failure but cannot determine it

examples: Used to compare three reinforcement strategies over simulated courses of 30 concepts × 6 levels (at least 180 learning sessions)

title: Probabilistic learning styles model based on FSLSM dimensions
description: The article treats FSLSM learning-style tendencies as probabilities, called student's probabilistic learning styles (LSp), representing "the probability of preference for each learning style by a specific student." Each of the four FSLSM dimensions (processing, perception, input, understanding) holds a probability pair summing to 1; learning style combinations are stochastically selected per session via roulette wheel selection, and LSp is updated by reinforcement learning as the process evolves. The model can be initialized by cold start (0.50) or from Index of Learning Styles Questionnaire results divided by 11.
requirements: LSp values must maintain consistent probability distributions within each dimension when updated
constraints: The student model is restricted to learning styles and based on FSLSM, though the article notes it could have been realized with other learning styles theories

description: Because experiments showed that starting with a student model already consistent with the learner's actual learning styles produced fewer learning problems and greater average performance, the article argues that "the reuse of student models in new courses is essential." It proposes that emerging patterns could enable sharing student models between different platforms, including learning styles characteristics, so that different adaptive educational systems collaboratively and continuously evolve the student model over time.

article_title: Instructing a Teachable Agent with Low or High Self-Efficacy – Does Similarity Attract?
citation: Betty Tärning, Annika Silvervarg, Agneta Gulz, Magnus Haake. (2019). Instructing a Teachable Agent with Low or High Self-Efficacy – Does Similarity Attract? International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-018-0167-2
title: Design teachable agents to express low self-efficacy
description: The article proposes, as a preliminary conclusion from its experimental results, that teachable agents should preferably be designed to have low self-efficacy. Students teaching a low-SE digital tutee showed better in-game performance, and low-SE students matched with a low-SE tutee significantly increased their own self-efficacy. The principle directs designers of teachable-agent (digital tutee) software to give the tutee chat feedback expressing uncertainty and modesty about its knowledge and performance rather than confidence.
requirements: The agent must be a teachable agent/digital tutee where the student takes a teacher role, with a channel (here, chat feedback after each round) through which the tutee expresses its self-efficacy
constraints: The authors label this a preliminary conclusion on the basis of this single study with 10- to 11-year-olds in a place-value math game
the effect on high-SE students may be hidden behind a ceiling effect
target_learning_goals: place value and base-ten number system skills
math self-efficacy
examples: In the study, the tutee Lo's chat feedback was manipulated to express either high or low SE, e.g. upon losing: "We lost … But that might not be so strange, it feels like I don ’t remember anything of what you just taught me."

title: Educational cobots: robots designed to support human teachers in classrooms
description: The paper proposes 'Educational Cobots' as a future direction for AIED: 'a cobot is a robot co-worker that works alongside humans to help them perform their work, so an educational cobot is a robot designed to support human teachers'. With AIED capabilities, cobots could monitor learners in Intelligent Learning Environments, flag learners needing extra help, keep learners engaged, and answer learner questions. The concept is framed as a way to help teachers differentiate instruction in classes of 25 or more students.

Robots able to navigate a dynamic classroom and use standard classroom equipment

description: The article introduces a framework placing four online platforms along two axes: how much subject-matter expertise the average content creator has, and whether the content-creation decision is made individually or by groups/departments. Stack Overflow sits toward the novice/individual side, Udemy toward expert/small-team, and Stack Overflow Jobs at the extreme expert/group corner. The framework underpins the hypothesis that "more novice-driven and individual-driven platforms are more agile" in manifesting new topics.

description: The article uses Stack Overflow tags — user-created words or phrases describing question topics — as the representation of new topics/skills in the software domain. Tens of new tags are created weekly, and moderators curate them via synonym-marking and deletion polls, making them "a set of precise and specific community-curated topics." The authors chose tags over topic modelling (e.g. LDA) for three reasons: crowdsourced manual curation, fine-grained specificity, and exact-match semantics.

article_title: Problem Order Implications for Learning
citation: Nan Li, William W. Cohen, Kenneth R. Koedinger. (2013). Problem Order Implications for Learning. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0005-5
title: SimStudent as a computational model of skill learning with where, when, and how learners
description: SimStudent is a machine-learning agent that inductively learns skills to solve problems from demonstrated solutions and problem-solving experience, using a variation of the version space algorithm, inductive logic programming, and iterative-deepening depth-first search. It learns production rules with three parts — perceptual information (where), precondition (when), and operator function sequence (how) — each acquired by a corresponding learning mechanism. The article uses SimStudent as a precise, unambiguous computational model of the problem-order question, tutoring it with automatic tutors on problems previously used with human students. The authors report it has been shown to find high-quality models of student learning across domains and to discover student models that predict human student behavior better than human-generated models.
requirements: Requires a perceptual hierarchy, a set of feature predicates, and a set of operator functions provided as prior knowledge before learning
constraints: Does not assume a memory limitation, which differs from human students
Presents a bias towards more generalized skills over specific ones without considering computational cost
Does not model aspects of human learning such as motivation
target_learners: Simulated students modeling human learners in math and science domains
target_learning_goals: Acquisition of problem-solving skills (production rules) in domains such as fraction addition, equation solving, and stoichiometry
examples: In the equation solving domain, SimStudent was tutored on problems such as −3x + 2 = 8 and learned production rules like the divide rule with perceptual information, precondition, and operator sequence parts

article_title: Co-producing AIED Ethics Under Lockdown: an Empirical Study of Deliberative Democracy in Action
citation: Teresa Swist, Simon Buckingham Shum, Kalervo N. Gulson. (2024). Co-producing AIED Ethics Under Lockdown: an Empirical Study of Deliberative Democracy in Action. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 34:670–705. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00380-z
title: Deliberative Democracy and the Deliberative Mini-Public framework
description: Deliberative Democracy emerged around 1990 as a "deliberative turn" in democratic theory, responding to a crisis of confidence in how typical democratic systems engage citizens. It operates by convening a Deliberative Mini-Public (DMP) with three core features: "Influence", "Inclusion", and "Deliberation", the latter providing "open dialogue, access to information, respect, space to understand and reframe issues, and movement to toward consensus". Random or stratified selection delivers the mini-public aspect; neutral facilitation, balanced expert witnesses, and senior-leadership sanction are further key features. The article applies DD as an organisational consultation on AI ethics in higher education.
requirements: Sanction by senior leadership with commitment that the DMP's recommendations matter, so the process is not tokenistic
Neutral facilitation by a person or team with no stake in the outcome
Random or stratified sampling to deliver the mini-public aspect and mitigate bias
constraints: The use of DD for an organisational rather than citizen consultation, and for AI ethics, is novel, so established practice evidence is limited
Who sets the DMP's purpose/agenda may be contentious; arm's-length conduct is advised if framing bias is feared
target_learning_goals: understanding ethical issues of analytics/AI educational technology
deliberative decision-making and consensus skills
examples: The UTS consultation convened a DMP of 20 recruited from 131 applicants via stratified sampling, running five Zoom sessions over seven weeks with external DD facilitation
key_sources: Teresa Swist, Simon Buckingham Shum, Kalervo N. Gulson. (2024). Co-producing AIED Ethics Under Lockdown: an Empirical Study of Deliberative Democracy in Action. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 34:670–705. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00380-z

title: UTS EdTech Ethics Deliberative Democracy consultation
description: A university-wide DD consultation at the University of Technology Sydney, run under pandemic lockdown, co-producing ethical principles to govern Analytics/AI-enabled Educational Technology (AAI-EdTech). The brief asked: "What principles should govern UTS use of analytics and artificial intelligence to improve teaching and learning for all, while minimising the possibility of harmful outcomes?" External DD facilitator working with an institutional planning team

Recruitment mitigates but does not eliminate sampling bias, with an inherent response bias towards people willing to engage
target_learning_goals: co-producing ethical principles for AAI-EdTech

description: eBanshu is a web-based learning system released in 2013 and used by more than 20 universities in China with over 33,000 students enrolled on 100 courses. It equips online classes with synchronous tools — a text chat room, a hands-up facility for asking instructors questions, and note-taking and note-sharing facilities — and asynchronous tools including a discussion forum, a materials-sharing facility, and an assignment submission facility. In this study the communication tools were "provided for students to freely use, not counted in their final assessment", and the system automatically logged students' behavior and messages for analysis.

Behavioral logs are automatically recorded for analysis

article_title: An Intelligent Tutor for Planning in Large Partially Observable Environments
citation: Heindrich, L., Consul, S., & Lieder, F. (2025). An Intelligent Tutor for Planning in Large Partially Observable Environments. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 35, 3095–3127. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00493-7
title: Meta-level MDP framework for modeling planning under uncertainty
description: The article formalizes human planning in partially observable environments as a meta-level Markov Decision Process that separates "an object-level component, which models the interaction with the real world, and a meta-level component, which models the (often internal) planning operations." Belief states are multivariate Normal distributions updated via Bayesian conjugate priors when noisy observations arrive. Computations can be repeated arbitrarily many times, iteratively increasing belief accuracy. This extends prior fully observable meta-level MDP models by incorporating observation noise, making the belief state reflect uncertainty rather than precise knowledge.
requirements: A model of the planning task as a directed acyclic graph with ground-truth rewards drawn from known distributions
Specification of observation precision and planning cost parameters
constraints: Assumes rewards are drawn from multivariate Normal distributions
Assumes computations produce Gaussian-noisy samples rather than deterministic revelations
target_learning_goals: planning under uncertainty
resource-rational decision-making
examples: The framework was applied to a flight-planning task where learners route an airplane over a network of airports with uncertain profitability
key_sources: Heindrich, L., Consul, S., & Lieder, F. (2025). An Intelligent Tutor for Planning in Large Partially Observable Environments. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 35, 3095–3127. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00493-7

article_title: An Intelligent Tutor for Planning in Large Partially Observable Environments
citation: Heindrich, L., Consul, S., & Lieder, F. (2025). An Intelligent Tutor for Planning in Large Partially Observable Environments. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 35, 3095–3127. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00493-7
title: Intelligent cognitive tutor for planning in partially observable environments
description: An intelligent tutoring system that teaches MGPO-discovered planning strategies through interactive practice with metacognitive feedback. "To teach people the planning strategies discovered by MGPO, we developed a cognitive tutor" that presents learners with highlighted planning-action choices, provides feedback on suboptimal selections with delay penalties proportional to the VOC difference, and demonstrates the optimal strategy through step-by-step videos. Unlike prior tutors using dynamic programming with cached Q-values, this tutor computes VOC values online via MGPO, enabling application to large, partially observable environments where pre-computing feedback is infeasible.
requirements: The MGPO algorithm for online VOC computation
A set of precomputed observation samples for the environment
constraints: Delay penalty uses a fixed 0.05 VOC threshold rather than exact Q-value differences
Premature termination triggers a delay penalty rather than actual termination when MGPO would continue planning
target_learning_goals: planning strategies
metacognitive skill
resource-rational information search
examples: Used in a flight-planning scenario where participants route an airplane over 60 airports, inspecting nodes to reveal stochastic observations of profitability
key_sources: Heindrich, L., Consul, S., & Lieder, F. (2025). An Intelligent Tutor for Planning in Large Partially Observable Environments. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 35, 3095–3127. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00493-7

article_title: An Intelligent Tutor for Planning in Large Partially Observable Environments
citation: Heindrich, L., Consul, S., & Lieder, F. (2025). An Intelligent Tutor for Planning in Large Partially Observable Environments. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 35, 3095–3127. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00493-7
title: Shaping method for teaching cognitive strategies through graduated task complexity
description: A training curriculum inspired by Skinner's method of successive approximations in which "the training starts with a minimal version of the planning task, and as the training progresses, the planning task becomes increasingly more similar to the scenario in which people's planning strategies shall be improved." Complexity increases along two dimensions simultaneously: the number of planning operations the learner chooses between and the size of the environment. This prevents the slow, frustrating learning that occurs when learners face many possible actions in large environments from the start, reducing errors and delay penalties during early learning.
requirements: Smaller versions of the target environment that preserve its structural properties
A mechanism for selecting meaningful choices with different VOC values
constraints: The choice set must always include the optimal planning operation
The number of offered choices is limited (2–4 in the experiment)
target_learning_goals: planning in complex environments
metacognitive strategy acquisition
examples: Training progressed from an 8-node environment with 2 choices, through 16-node (3 choices) and 30-node (4 choices), to the full 60-node environment over 12 trials

article_title: Automated Essay Scoring and the Deep Learning Black Box: How Are Rubric Scores Determined?
citation: Kumar, V. S., & Boulanger, D. (2020). Automated Essay Scoring and the Deep Learning Black Box: How Are Rubric Scores Determined? International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00211-5
title: Rubric-level prediction as a route to interpretable, trustable AES with human-in-the-loop assessment
description: The article's organizing account holds that predicting constituent rubric scores (Ideas, Organization, Style, Conventions) rather than only holistic scores "reveals the reasoning behind AIED-based AES systems". Because rubric scales are narrower (0–6 vs 0–24), each rubric score offers more training examples per competence, and feature-importance analysis per rubric model provides high-level explanations of predicted scores. The framework ties interpretability to trustworthiness and to human-in-the-loop verification of machine grading.
requirements: Hand-graded essays with rubric-level labels (as in ASAP D7)
Sufficient samples per rubric score for model training
constraints: The article states it is beyond the scope of the study to verify whether holistic prediction through rubric scores is more accurate, and that less accurate models may be more interpretable
target_learning_goals: Writing quality across ideas, organization, style, and conventions
examples: The study trained six MLP architectures on 397 SALAT-derived writing features to predict D7's four rubric scores and used permutation importance to rank features per rubric

title: AES research should report thorough and transparent performance protocols to enable fair comparison and replication
description: The article advocates that AES studies describe methodologies and report outcomes under proper protocols, because present reports "commonly – and perhaps inadvertently – lack transparency", hindering performance evaluation and comparison of techniques. Transparent reporting should include agreement metrics computed by consistent procedures, per-dataset (per writing task) results, and disclosure of which data splits were used, permitting fairer comparisons among AES systems and study replication.
requirements: Consistent agreement metrics (e.g., QWK) computed by the same procedure across studies
Disclosure of training/testing data availability and splits
constraints: Some prior work (e.g., SAGE) seemingly used original labeled ASAP testing sets no longer available, preventing fair comparison
target_learning_goals: Automated scoring of student writing
examples: The article reports its own models' performance as five-iteration averages on the testing set rather than the highest kappa, to avoid overfitting to the testing set

citation: Kumar, V. S., & Boulanger, D. (2020). Automated Essay Scoring and the Deep Learning Black Box: How Are Rubric Scores Determined? International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00211-5
title: SALAT NLP tool suite extracting 1592 writing features for rubric scoring models
description: The study processed 1567 essays with the Suite of Automatic Linguistic Analysis Tools (SALAT) — GAMET, SEANCE, TAACO, TAALED, TAALES, and TAASSC — yielding "a total of 1592 writing features" covering grammar/mechanics errors, sentiment and cognition, text cohesion, lexical diversity, lexical sophistication, and syntactic complexity. After filter methods (variance pruning, correlation pruning at |r| > 0.9, removal of word/token counts) features were reduced to 397, with Lasso/Ridge (ElasticNet) regularization performing customized per-rubric selection during training.
requirements: Feature normalization before variance-based pruning
Per-tool correlation pruning to ensure fair representation among tool families
constraints: Features directly counting words or tokens were pruned to reduce model dependence on word counts, following Perelman's adversarial-essay critique
target_learning_goals: Rubric-level writing quality assessment
examples: GAMET flags a subset of 324 spelling, style, and grammar errors classified into six macrofeatures; TAASSC computes 367 syntactic indices grouped into four categories

article_title: Formative Feedback on Student-Authored Summaries in Intelligent Textbooks Using Large Language Models
citation: Morris, W., Crossley, S., Holmes, L., Ou, C., Dascalu, M., & McNamara, D. (2025). Formative Feedback on Student-Authored Summaries in Intelligent Textbooks Using Large Language Models. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 35, 1022–1043. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00395-0
title: iTELL summary feedback pipeline with pre-scoring filters
description: iTELL (Intelligent Textbook for Enhanced Language Learning) is a computational framework that converts machine-readable textbooks into interactive web-apps in which students write end-of-section summaries that are scored automatically by the study's LLMs. Before scoring, summaries pass a filter component: "The filter ensures that the summary is between 50 and 200 words, and the summary is passed through a semantic similarity measure using Doc2Vec (Le & Mikolov, 2014) that assesses whether the summary is on topic." Summaries that heavily borrow from the source or contain offensive language are rejected without LLM analysis, which the authors say ensures only effortful summaries reach the models and reduces computational load.
requirements: Students produce summaries directly in the application; cut-and-paste is not allowed
Summaries must pass the length, topic-similarity, source-borrowing, and offensive-language filters before LLM scoring
constraints: The article notes the models need to be tested on intelligent textbook users to ensure the feedback leads to increased learning
target_learners: students using intelligent textbooks in higher education and secondary education
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension through end-of-section summarization
examples: Within iTELL, students below a score threshold are encouraged to revisit the section and rewrite their summary before moving on; KeyBART supplies key phrases from the source not present in the summary to guide revision

title: Use hybrid ML, LSA and Coh-Metrix approaches for detecting student understanding
description: The article recommends combining machine learning, LSA and Coh-Metrix approaches rather than relying on any single automated method, as "the results demonstrate the benefits of using a machine learning approach for detecting content, but also highlight the promise of hybrid methods that combine ML, LSA and Coh-Metrix approaches for detecting student understanding." article_title: Advancing understanding of learning experience design: refining and clarifying definitions using an eDelphi study approach
citation: Tawfik, A., Schmidt, M., Payne, L., & Huang, R. (2024). Advancing understanding of learning experience design: refining and clarifying definitions using an eDelphi study approach. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10355-z
title: Learning experience design (LXD) as a human-centered, transdisciplinary approach to designing learning experiences
description: The article defines LXD as a perspective on learning design that goes beyond content development to consider the broader human experience of interacting with learning environments. Building on Schmidt and Huang (2022), LXD is characterized as "a human-centric, theoretically-grounded, and socio-culturally sensitive approach to learning design, intended to propel learners towards identified learning goals, and informed by UXD methods". The eDelphi findings refine this definition, situating LXD alongside instructional design rather than as a separate field, and emphasizing transdisciplinarity across HCI, UXD, and learning design.
requirements: Consensus among practitioners about the elements that comprise LXD, established through systematic and collaborative approaches such as eDelphi studies
constraints: Experts did not agree that LXD is a discrete field of study or a unique phenomenon with its own characteristics, methods, and processes; LXD is positioned as an emergent perspective within the existing field of instructional design
target_learners: All learners in technology-mediated learning environments
target_learning_goals: Knowledge construction through human-centered design of learning experiences
