article_title: A systematic review of educational online peer-review and assessment systems: charting the landscape
citation: Babik, D., Gehringer, E., Kidd, J., Sunday, K., Tinapple, D., & Gilbert, S. (2024). A systematic review of educational online peer-review and assessment systems: charting the landscape. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10349-x
title: Four-layer OPRA classification framework (user needs, use cases, features, design options)
description: The article constructs a framework organizing educational online peer-review and assessment systems into hierarchically organized layers: user needs, use cases, features, and design options. The top layers are implementation-independent (problem domain), the bottom layers implementation-dependent (solution domain). It was validated by applying the multi-case method with a questionnaire to originators of existing systems, receiving 15 usable responses from 23 contacted, and reaching saturation after detailed analysis of 16 systems.
requirements: A system is not an OPRA system unless it accommodates the identified user needs and use cases
constraints: The list of features and design options is not exhaustive; the framework is extensible as OPRA systems evolve
target_learners: higher education students in STEM, liberal arts, and business courses
target_learning_goals: peer review and assessment skills
providing and receiving formative feedback

article_title: A systematic review of educational online peer-review and assessment systems: charting the landscape

title: Compendium of six primary categories of OPRA user needs
description: The article identifies six primary categories of user needs accommodated in OPRA systems: (1) eliciting submissions, (2) structuring the peer assessment process (workflow), (3) eliciting evaluations and critiques, (4) aggregating results, (5) communicating/presenting results, and (6) improving review value/quality. Each is decomposed into use cases, features, and design options with named system implementations (e.g., Aropä, CrowdGrader, Expertiza, Mobius SLIP, Peerceptiv).

description: The Go-Lab ecosystem is a two-platform architecture supporting teacher design of inquiry-based science learning. The sharing and support platform (Golabz) presents digital resources including over 600 online laboratories, while the authoring and learning platform (Graasp) enables co-creation and implementation of Inquiry Learning Spaces. The ecosystem was developed following "participatory design, respon-sive design, and privacy–by–design methodologies" and is fully GDPR compliant. It aggregates labs from multiple third-party repositories under one umbrella, offering a one-stop portal for STEM inquiry learning resources.

constraints: Students do not need to register to use ILSs

title: Small-group joint drawing followed by discussion in a larger multimedia group

Classroom work in small groups of maximum 3–6 participants produced 12 drawings in Exercise I and 8 in Exercise II, which were then shared and discussed at the whole-class and online level. title: HeDiCom framework for higher education teachers' digital competence
description: The HeDiCom (Higher Education Digital Competence) framework is a generic framework of digital competencies for teachers in higher education, developed by Tondeur and colleagues through a review of digital competence research and comparison of existing frameworks, expert meetings with policy makers, and validation with practitioners. The preface states it "provides guidance and clearer expectations of higher education teachers' digital competency which can guide innovation in practice beyond the GOT." It extends pedagogical and technical knowledge domains to include empowering students.

title: AI digital competencies framework extending DigCompEdu and revising P21
description: A concept paper by Tsz Kit Ng, Ka Lok Leung, Jiahong Su, Chi Wui Ng, and Kai Wah Chu addresses AI digital competencies for higher education teachers. It explores opportunities and challenges of employing AI systems for teaching, learning, and assessment, and "complemented the DigCompEdu framework and revised the P21's framework to accommodate AI technologies in order to provide an overview of the necessary AI digital competencies." The framework aligns AI-specific competencies with generic digital competence frameworks.

description: In a future-oriented conceptual paper, Markauskaite, Carvalho and Faws consider teachers' digital competencies in relation to postdigital capabilities at three levels of the educational ecosystem: global developments, teachers' local practices, and daily activities. The authors "argue that there is a need to move beyond person-centric theorisations of teacher digital competencies towards more holistic, ecological conceptualisations." This requires teachers' agency and critical engagement with a future-oriented, sustainable university mission that is postdigital at its core.

title: Feedback as a multidimensional, dialogic process encompassing cognitive and socio-emotional domains
description: The article presents feedback as "by its nature multidimensional and encompasses both the cognitive and socio-emotional domains", associated with engagement, achievement, motivation, behaviour, self-regulation and satisfaction. With student-centered pedagogy, feedback has expanded "towards a dialogic framework" rather than one-way transmission, establishing continuous interaction that facilitates knowledge construction. The article identifies two main functions: corrective feedback verifying correctness and exploratory feedback elaborating on performance after feedback is received.
requirements: Feedback interactions require teacher strategies and skills for utilizing writing, oral exposition, or video-based media
Teachers' knowledge includes understanding how feedback is perceived and received by students and how students act on it
constraints: Feedback interactions are highly culturally sensitive, employing different cultural norms and codes of written or spoken communication
target_learning_goals: learning improvement
student engagement
self-regulation

title: Design online learning environments that address the multidimensional nature of feedback rather than favoring one medium
description: The article argues that learning design should select technology affordances according to learning principles rather than comparing media. It states that "the specific context of learning design requires the selection of learning technology affordances according to the principles of learning (e.g., the authenticity of learning and learners' characteristics and needs)". Following Mayer (2001), the focus should be a learner-centered approach on "how to integrate media to enhance human learning".

constraints: Comparing textual-based and video-based feedback is inconclusive

authentic learning

Video-based feedback and instructional video provide ground for contextualized, situated learning

title: Community of Inquiry (CoI) framework as organizing framework for online learning relationships
description: The study applies the community of inquiry (CoI) framework, in which learning occurs through the intersection of teaching presence, cognitive presence, and social presence. The authors define cognitive presence as "the extent to which learners are able to construct and confirm meaning through sustained reflection and discourse in a critical community of inquiry" and treat teaching presence as the "binding" element of CoI. It is structured in two stages: a diagnostic stage using multiple-choice questions with hint and NA options, and a reinforcement stage of sequenced exercises of increasing difficulty with immediate explanatory feedback. The model is designed to be replicable by instructors lacking programming skills on free platforms such as Genially.com or Canva.

Instructor-authored content: diagnostic questions, theory explanations, exercise sequences, and feedback

Question type should be adapted depending on target students' needs (age, special educational needs, gifted students)

foundational mathematics and statistics knowledge

title: Diagnostic-then-reinforcement flow with hint and No Answer options as metacognitive axis
description: The article's core pedagogical pattern is a flow chart in which a first diagnostic multiple-choice question (correct answer, at least three incorrect answers, a NA option, and a hint option) routes students: correct answers advance to the next concept; incorrect or NA answers trigger a tutoring process with theory and exercises of progressive difficulty; the hint option displays a theoretical orientation followed by a second diagnostic question of similar difficulty. Built in Articulate Rise 360 and embedded within the existing on-campus orientation platform (Monash Essentials), it comprises eight sections, including six content sections: Welcome to MOLH, Start Here, Learn Online, Study Effectively, Stay Well & Connected, and Graduation & Beyond. citation: Ormel, B. J. B., Pareja Roblin, N. N., McKenney, S. E., Voogt, J. M., & Pieters, J. M. (2012). Research–practice interactions as reported in recent design studies: still promising, still hazy. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-012-9261-6
title: Three sources of knowledge inform the design of instructional solutions: literature, project data, and practical knowledge
description: The article distinguishes "three sources of knowledge that we see are commonly used to inform the design of solutions, often in combination with one another: literature, project data, practical knowledge". Literature-based design builds upon theory and/or evidence found in literature; data-driven design is steered by empirical findings from field investigation during project development; and practical knowledge-informed design incorporates the wide range of insights and knowledge about research, design, teaching, learning and schooling. This framework is used to map all 18 reviewed projects in a Venn diagram according to the sources said to have informed the (re)designed product.
requirements: Sources must be said to have informed the (re)designed product, not merely gathered as research data
constraints: The sources in Fig. 1 do not represent all the data gathered in the studies but only those sources which were said to have informed the (re)designed product
target_learning_goals: designing instructional solutions informed by research
examples: Only two projects clearly indicated that they used all three sources of knowledge to inform their work: Flannery and Pragman (2008) and Gu et al. (2009).
key_sources: Ormel, B. J. B., Pareja Roblin, N. N., McKenney, S. E., Voogt, J. M., & Pieters, J. M. (2012). Research–practice interactions as reported in recent design studies: still promising, still hazy. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-012-9261-6

article_title: Research–practice interactions as reported in recent design studies: still promising, still hazy
citation: Ormel, B. J. B., Pareja Roblin, N. N., McKenney, S. E., Voogt, J. M., & Pieters, J. M. (2012). Research–practice interactions as reported in recent design studies: still promising, still hazy. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-012-9261-6
title: Knowledge produced by design research may be declarative, procedural, or observable
description: Building on previous work (Edelson 2002; Van den Akker 1999), the article indicates that "the nature of knowledge produced by design research may be one or more of the following: declarative (describing products, concepts or theories); procedural (informing how to take action); or observable (empirical findings or experiences)". Each of these has the potential to contribute to theory building, and knowledge produced may also be characterized by its focus, for example on teaching, learning and/or resources. This typology is used to code the public knowledge produced in each of the 18 reviewed projects.
requirements: Knowledge produced must be classifiable as declarative, procedural, or observable for coding
constraints: This study aims to identify and describe immediate interactions between research and practice and does not explicitly aim to portray broader dissemination and use of the research findings
target_learning_goals: characterizing knowledge outputs of design research
examples: Observable knowledge was found in all 18 studies, including students' comments, learning gains, and teachers' opinions.

title: MOVES-NL: a technology-enhanced inclusive embodied design for learning integer arithmetic
description: MOVES-NL is a novel, technologically enabled classroom design for learning basic arithmetic procedures through coordinating full-body and manual interactions centered on navigating the number line. It includes three activities supporting an egocentric-to-allocentric enactive progression: walking a floor-projected number line, walking with a wall-projected avatar mimicking the student's actions, and reenacting movements with a handheld figurine on a tablet. Per the SpEED framework, it employs "Both interactive projections and mirrored/tangible avatars as media; ambulatory (embodied), visual, auditory and haptic modalities; and NLs as semiotic modes."
requirements: A motion-sensing camera, projectors, and a mini-PC housed in a portable structure (MOVES), plus the SENSEi software for the avatar interaction
constraints: The current design is restricted to individual usage by the chosen media, posing challenges for scaling to full-class instruction
target_learners: middle-school students with and without cognitive disabilities
target_learning_goals: integer addition and subtraction on the number line
examples: Students stood on the number line, turned toward the positive or negative side, and took steps equal to the absolute value of the second operand, moving forward for positives and backward for negatives

title: SpEED: Special Education Embodied Design framework extended with an egocentric-perspective conjecture
description: Special Education Embodied Design (SpEED) is a pedagogical design framework grounded in enactivist theories which seeks to cater to learners' diverse sensorimotor strengths. It guides designers in catering to sensorimotorically diverse students' needs respecting choices of media, modalities, and semiotic modes. This article extends SpEED with a general conjecture that multimodal experiences designed for grounding mathematical concepts should preferably be egocentric, and that "mathematics learning activities are most effective when students have opportunities to coordinate their egocentric, embodied experience with allocentric semiotic displays."
requirements: Learning activities should stage perspectival coordination as an integral aspect of the activity rather than separating doing and representing
constraints: The authors state that if corroborated through future research, SpEED could bear broadly across instructional contexts and concepts
target_learning_goals: grounding symbolic mathematical procedures in sensorimotor experience
examples: The MOVES-NL design instantiated the framework by having students walk a floor-based number line while an avatar mirror-walked their action on its own number line

citation: Ma, H. (2021). Empowering digital learning with open textbooks. Education Tech Research Dev, 69, 393–396. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09916-9
title: Faculty adoption of high-quality open textbooks strengthens credibility and yields savings when teachers are willing to develop and use them
description: The commentary argues that open textbook use in higher education is credible and beneficial, but that its benefits are conditional on teacher engagement: "only if teachers are willing to develop and use open textbooks can millions be saved for students and higher performance be achieved by students." It therefore recommends encouraging faculty to utilize high-quality open textbooks, particularly in a post-pandemic world.
requirements: Teacher willingness to develop and use open textbooks
target_learning_goals: affordable access to learning materials
maintaining learning outcomes with open textbooks

article_title: Missed opportunities in mixed methods EdTech research? Visual joint display development as an analytical strategy for achieving integration in mixed methods studies
citation: Peters, M., & Fàbregues, S. (2024). Missed opportunities in mixed methods EdTech research? Visual joint display development as an analytical strategy for achieving integration in mixed methods studies. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10234-z
title: Joint display analysis as an iterative process for identifying connections between qualitative and quantitative constructs and generating meta-inferences
description: The article defines joint display analysis, following Fetters and Guetterman (2021), as "an iterative process in which researchers use the joint display structure to identify connections between qualitative and quantitative constructs and generate meta-inferences" based on the fit of the two data types. This allows researchers to acquire new insights beyond those provided by each component individually. The article positions this as a tool for the "cognitive process of merging, comparing, relating, and linking qualitative and quantitative data or results" during study execution, supporting integration and inferential transparency.
requirements: Requires rigorous intra-method analysis of both strands as a first step before mixed analysis begins.
constraints: The article notes that meaningful integration of qualitative and quantitative data remains elusive and needs further development, citing Guetterman et al. (2015).
target_learning_goals: Conducting rigorous mixed methods integration in EdTech research
key_sources: Peters, M., & Fàbregues, S. (2024). Missed opportunities in mixed methods EdTech research? Visual joint display development as an analytical strategy for achieving integration in mixed methods studies. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10234-z

citation: Peters, M., & Fàbregues, S. (2024). Missed opportunities in mixed methods EdTech research? Visual joint display development as an analytical strategy for achieving integration in mixed methods studies. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10234-z
title: A radial meta-joint display integrating five analytical levels to model student learning ecologies in online higher education
description: The article presents a final meta-joint display, chosen as a radial display, that integrates findings at five distinct levels: LE core components, MMR pillar building sub-components, learner profile solutions from qualitized data, the LE matrix representing four conceptual zones of learning, and traits of a connected academic curriculum. Learner activity was placed at the centre and curriculum traits at the outer border as a mediating factor. The radial form was chosen to represent the ecological, dynamic process of learning across multiple contexts and to link information while avoiding complexity.
requirements: Requires rigorous intra-method analysis and identification of a logical framework for organizing the two types of data together before constructing the display.
constraints: The article notes that constructing novel meta-joint displays is complex and iterative, often requiring uncertain design decisions and reliance on established methodological guidelines.
target_learning_goals: Representing student learning ecologies across formal and informal contexts
examples: The final integrated model was developed through four distinct iterations, from pre-publication initial model to ETR&D methodological article, with mixed analysis procedures added between iterations.

title: Assess joint display effectiveness using organizational intent, analytic intent, and effectiveness of the visual presentation
description: Following Haynes-Brown and Fetters (2021), the article states that "joint display effectiveness can be assessed on three criteria, namely, organizational intent, analytic intent, and the effectiveness of the visual presentation". In the illustrative study, organizational intent was to depict the ecological and integrated nature of learner experiences, analytic intent was to examine interconnections by evaluating the extent to which quantitative data supported qualitative findings, and effectiveness was evaluated by aiming for a display that was self-explanatory and avoided unnecessary complexity.
requirements: Requires iterative design review across publishing stages to improve organizational and analytical intent.
target_learning_goals: Designing and evaluating visual joint displays for mixed methods integration
examples: The authors piloted the meta-joint display in research seminars and conferences to infer whether the display was appealing and easily understood.

title: Learning Ecology sensitizing model with learner activities, digital resources, and relationship interactions as core components
description: The article describes a Learning Ecology (LE) sensitizing model, derived from the literature on lifelong learning, online higher education, and human development and informed by Barron's (2006) ontological definition. It identifies "learner activities, material resources, and social relationships as the core components of an individual's learning ecology". Built prior to data collection following a sensitizing model technique, it served as a guiding heuristic to prepare lines of inquiry, develop research questions and interview protocols, and guide hybrid theory-driven thematic analysis.

examples: The LE sensitizing model was used to develop the survey instrument through the MMR integration strategy of building at the design level.

citation: Lehesvuori, S., Urrutia, F., Heilala, V., Araya, R., & Hämäläinen, R. (2026). Discovering technology-aided possibilities for automatic analysis of science teacher questions. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10545-3
title: Prompt engineering techniques for LLM-based classroom discourse analysis
description: The article describes a framework of prompting techniques — Vanilla, Chain of Thought, and Self-Ask — applied with zero-shot and few-shot strategies to detect teacher questions from ASR outputs. "Recent advancements have introduced techniques to enhance response quality, such as Chain of Thought (CoT) (Lee et al., 2024) and Self-Ask (SA) (Press et al., 2023)." Self-Ask "explicitly introduces intermediate sub-questions that guide the model through each reasoning step." The framework frames prompt engineering as "designing effective prompts to elicit desired responses from LLMs, crucial for instructing models in specific tasks."

constraints: The number of shots was set to five, as research suggests that using more examples leads to only limited improvements in performance

examples: Vanilla zero-shot and Self-Ask prompts tested on Finnish ASR outputs with context sentences before and after the target sentence

citation: Morel, G. M. (2021). Student-centered learning: context needed. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09951-0
title: Own It, Learn It, Share It framework for student-centered learning
description: Lee and Hannafin's design framework "intersects constructivist, constructionist, and self-determination theories to address student-centered learning." It has three parts: "Own It involves students developing ownership over the process and achieving personally meaningful learning goals," Learn It involves autonomous learning "through metacognitive, procedural, conceptual, and strategic scaffolding," and Share It involves students generating "artifacts aimed at authentic audiences beyond the classroom assessment." The framework also includes "ten discrete design guidelines for the instructional design process."
requirements: The framework is described as combining constructivist, constructionist, and self-determination theories
constraints: Cheng notes it is a time-consuming, general approach rather than an efficient, customizable approach in times of restricted resources
target_learners: students in digital and online learning contexts
target_learning_goals: student engagement
ownership of learning
autonomous learning
examples: Baird applied the framework as a blueprint to a flexible assignment designed to promote intrinsic motivation and engagement

title: Distinguish autonomy from independence when designing student-centered digital learning
description: In shifting to digital learning, designers are "cautioned when incorporating the notion of" autonomy, because "autonomy is not synonymous with independence, but rather involves how self-determination reflects one's will." Designers should therefore build autonomy support as volitional self-determination rather than as unsupervised independence. During major disruption, learners may find voluntary action toward external expectations especially difficult.
requirements: Designers must treat autonomy as self-determination reflecting one's will, not as independence
constraints: In times of major disruption, learners may find evoking actions voluntarily toward external expectations, rules, and pressures especially difficult

title: M3 evaluation framework (Micro, Meso, Macro) for mobile learning interventions
description: The study adopts Vavoula and Sharples' (2011) M3 evaluation framework, which provides a "structured format to assess usability, educational and organisational impact and their inter-relationships". Micro-level evaluates individual user experience of the technology via end-activity evaluations; meso-level examines student experience via group and teacher interviews; macro-level evaluates effects on attitudes and performance via pre-post designs with experimental and control groups. The authors report it was "valuable for data validation and triangulation".

mathematics achievement
examples: The study evaluated tablet usability (micro), student and teacher perceptions (meso), and attitude and test-score effects (macro)

description: The article concludes that "it is the teacher not just the technology that drives the change in the classroom". Technical breakdowns, student characteristics and learning design are all seen as teacher responsibilities, and the authors argue it would be worthwhile addressing how teachers are trained to target those issues as well as being trained to use new technologies. The teacher in this study anticipated glitches, worked around a failed sharing facility, and adapted undifferentiated lesson plans to challenge advanced students and those who struggle.

article_title: The positivity principle: do positive instructors improve learning from video lectures?
citation: Lawson, A. P., Mayer, R. E., Adamo-Villani, N., Benes, B., Lei, X., & Cheng, J. (2021). The positivity principle: do positive instructors improve learning from video lectures? Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-10057-w
title: The positivity principle: people learn better from instructors who display positive emotions rather than negative emotions.
description: The positivity principle states that "people learn better from instructors who display a positive emotional tone rather than from instructors who display a negative emotional tone." It is derived from the cognitive-affective model of e-learning, a four-step chain in which learners recognize the instructor's emotional stance, feel a social partnership, work harder to learn, and perform better on outcome tests. The article tests it with two video-lecture experiments on binomial probability.
requirements: Instructors must display a positive emotion during a lesson for the model's chain to begin.
constraints: The authors note the model is linear and affective interactions are more complex; subject matter and learning context may elicit emotional responses independent of the instructor.
target_learners: university students in psychology subject pools
target_learning_goals: statistics content, specifically binomial probability

article_title: The positivity principle: do positive instructors improve learning from video lectures?
citation: Lawson, A. P., Mayer, R. E., Adamo-Villani, N., Benes, B., Lei, X., & Cheng, J. (2021). The positivity principle: do positive instructors improve learning from video lectures? Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-10057-w
title: The cognitive-affective model of e-learning: a four-step model linking instructor emotion to learning outcomes.
description: The cognitive-affective model of e-learning proposes that "there are 4 steps that lead from the emotion displayed by an instructor to an effect on learning outcome." First the learner recognizes the instructor's emotional stance (step 1), then feels a social partnership with the instructor (step 2), then works hard to learn the lesson (step 3), and thus performs better on learning outcome tests (step 4). The article describes it as a set of to-be-tested steps rather than an established set of findings.
requirements: The instructor must display a positive emotion during the lesson as the model's first step.
constraints: The authors acknowledge affective interactions between student and teacher are more complex than this linear model, and the study is a preliminary step in establishing basic relations.
target_learners: university students learning from video lectures
target_learning_goals: improved learning outcomes from computer-based instruction

citation: Lawson, A. P., Mayer, R. E., Adamo-Villani, N., Benes, B., Lei, X., & Cheng, J. (2021). The positivity principle: do positive instructors improve learning from video lectures? Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-10057-w
title: Adapted core-affect framework: instructor emotions classified along valence and activity dimensions.
description: The study adapts Russell's model of core affect, which displays "two orthogonal dimensions: valence (which runs from positive to nega- tive) and arousal, or what we have called activity (which runs from active to passive)." These dimensions create four quadrants represented as happy (positive/active), content (positive/passive), frustrated (negative/active), and bored (negative/passive), which are the four emotions displayed by instructors in the study's videos.
requirements: Emotions must be portrayed so learners can perceive differences along both the valence and activity dimensions.
constraints: The authors prefer the term activity over arousal because they focus on the instructor's portrayed emotion; cultural background can affect how learners interpret displayed emotion, which the study did not address.

article_title: Embracing discomfort in active learning and technology-rich higher education settings: sensemaking through reflexive inquiry
citation: McLay, K. F., Thomasse, L., & Reyes, V. C., Jr. (2023). Embracing discomfort in active learning and technology-rich higher education settings: sensemaking through reflexive inquiry. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10192-6
title: Bakhtinian dialogism, ideological becoming and chronotope as a framework for sensemaking of teaching discomfort
description: The article deploys Bakhtin's concepts of dialogism, 'ideological becoming' and the chronotope as an explanatory framework for teacher educators' sensemaking. Ideological becoming occurs in 'contact zones' where authoritative discourse (assumed true, "passed down through time as traditional knowledge") meets internally persuasive discourse, which is "neither imposed nor fixed but changeable". Chronotopes are "time–space contexts for an individual's developing ideologies", invoked in professional conversations as 'chunks of history'. The authors use this framework to reconceive discomfort and student resistance as a necessary 'worthwhile struggle' rather than failure.
requirements: Professional conversations with colleagues, in a safe collegial environment, to enable dialogic rather than solitary exploration of discomfort
constraints: The framework is applied to teacher educators' sensemaking in a technology-rich active-learning course; the authors note stressors on higher education can constrain such dialogic engagement
target_learning_goals: Professional identity development
Sensemaking of pedagogical discomfort and failure
examples: The three authors' reflexive 'snapshots' of teaching an educational technology course, analysed through ideological becoming and chronotope
key_sources: McLay, K. F., Thomasse, L., & Reyes, V. C., Jr. (2023). Embracing discomfort in active learning and technology-rich higher education settings: sensemaking through reflexive inquiry. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10192-6

article_title: Embracing discomfort in active learning and technology-rich higher education settings: sensemaking through reflexive inquiry
citation: McLay, K. F., Thomasse, L., & Reyes, V. C., Jr. (2023). Embracing discomfort in active learning and technology-rich higher education settings: sensemaking through reflexive inquiry. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10192-6
title: Five design principles for a technology-rich active-learning teacher education course
description: The redesigned educational technology course followed five design principles embedding active-learning strategies across curriculum, pedagogy and assessment: flipped learning via short (under ten minutes) online videos; course staff as "critical friends" and co-explorers rather than experts; "cyclical tutorials linked to assessment" following a three-wave 'Sandpit–Synergy–Showcase' structure; group assessment with a shared mark in three of four tasks; and formal critical reflection. Together these scaffolded four target competencies: curation, collaboration, creation and critical reflection.
requirements: Tutors willing to act as co-explorers rather than digital-tool experts
Assessment tasks aligned with the Sandpit–Synergy–Showcase tutorial cycle
constraints: The authors report the course evoked student resistance, anxiety and polarised evaluations, so the pattern does not guarantee satisfaction
target_learning_goals: Twenty-first century skills: curation, collaboration, creation, critical reflection
examples: Approximately 270 (2017) and 300 (2018) students experienced the redesigned course in tutorials of about 20 students

article_title: Closed circuit video recording for a fine music program
citation: Palmer, W. A. (1953). Closed Circuit Video Recording for a Fine Music Program. Journal of the Society of Motion Picture and Television Engineers.
title: Closed circuit video recording of TV music concerts on 16mm film
description: A production method in which six standard hour television concerts were recorded on 16mm film using closed circuit video recording combined with prescoring of music. The article reports this "provided the flexibility of live TV camera technique, with the editing and selection advantages of motion pictures." Four standard TV cameras picked up pictures, recorded off a monitor with a special video recording camera, and sound was edited in later.
requirements: Prescored music played during takes while musicians and singers performed along with it, with actual sound edited in later
constraints: Recording was done off a monitor with a special video recording camera
target_learning_goals: audio-visual production technique for educational and cultural programming
examples: Each unit involved four days of shooting, during which enough material for one and a half programs was obtained
key_sources: Palmer, W. A. (1953). Closed Circuit Video Recording for a Fine Music Program. Journal of the Society of Motion Picture and Television Engineers. https://doi.org/10.1007/bf02713329

article_title: Virtual reality and gamification in education: a systematic review
citation: Lampropoulos, G., & Kinshuk. (2024). Virtual reality and gamification in education: a systematic review. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10351-3
title: Gamified virtual reality learning environments as an effective educational tool
description: The review concludes that "gamified virtual reality emerged as an effective educational tool that can improve learning at all educational levels, subjects, and contexts". This framework positions the integration of virtual reality and gamification as a means to enrich and transform traditional teaching and learning, supporting immersion, social presence, knowledge acquisition, and material comprehension through realistic and interactive experiences.
requirements: Integration of virtual reality and gamification elements in conjunction within an educational context
target_learning_goals: improved learning outcomes, motivation, engagement, and self-efficacy
key_sources: Lampropoulos, G., & Kinshuk. (2024). Virtual reality and gamification in education: a systematic review. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10351-3

article_title: Context and agency: complementarity and interactivity
citation: Elen, J. (2021). Context and agency: complementarity and interactivity. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09850-w
title: Context and agency as complementary and interacting perspectives on educational technology research
description: In this reaction to Joo, Kim and Kim's study of mobile learning management system use, Elen argues that "their study can be approached from to complementary and interacting perspectives: context and agency." The framework treats contextual factors and learner agency as two lenses that jointly explain technology use rather than competing accounts. It is offered as a way of interpreting research on technology acceptance and continuance intention in learning settings.
requirements: Research on technology use in learning should be interpreted through both contextual and agency perspectives
target_learning_goals: use of mobile learning management systems
examples: The reaction reads Joo, Kim and Kim's finding that perceived usefulness plays a pivotal role in m-LMS use through the lenses of context and agency
key_sources: Elen, J. (2021). Context and agency: complementarity and interactivity. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09850-w

article_title: Sense of promisingness: towards creative expertise through knowledge-building discourse in online graduate education
citation: Huang-Yao Hong, Mei-Ju Chen, Bodong Chen, Chao-Yu Guo, Li-Ting Tseng (2025). Sense of promisingness: towards creative expertise through knowledge-building discourse in online graduate education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10483-0
title: Hong and Sullivan's idea-centered discourse framework: sharing-, argument-, and integration-oriented discourse
description: The article applies Hong and Sullivan's (2009) framework for sustained idea improvement, which "proposes three idea-centered discourse processes: idea-generation/diversification (sharing-oriented discourse), idea-argumentation/justification (argument-oriented discourse), and idea-integration/synthesis (integration-oriented discourse)". The study used this framework as the coding scheme for discourse moves and as the pedagogical structure for cultivating sense of promisingness in thesis-proposal development.
requirements: Discourse moves coded from connected note pairs (a note and its build-on note) in Knowledge Forum
target_learning_goals: judging promising thesis ideas
sustained idea improvement through discourse
key_sources: Huang-Yao Hong, Mei-Ju Chen, Bodong Chen, Chao-Yu Guo, Li-Ting Tseng (2025). Sense of promisingness: towards creative expertise through knowledge-building discourse in online graduate education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10483-0

article_title: Sense of promisingness: towards creative expertise through knowledge-building discourse in online graduate education
citation: Huang-Yao Hong, Mei-Ju Chen, Bodong Chen, Chao-Yu Guo, Li-Ting Tseng (2025). Sense of promisingness: towards creative expertise through knowledge-building discourse in online graduate education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10483-0
title: Sense of promisingness operationalized as knowing-what, knowing-how, and knowing-why
description: The article operationalizes sense of promisingness in graduate education as a student's ability to identify relevant literature (knowing-what), utilize appropriate research methods (knowing-how), and articulate study significance (knowing-why) to generate promising thesis proposals. It defines the concept as "an ability to discern or judge what may be effective in uncertain conditions", drawing on Bereiter's promisingness knowledge, and treats knowing-why as especially essential because it justifies relevance and feasibility.
requirements: Content analysis of online discourse notes coded for theoretical relevance, methodological feasibility, and study importance
target_learning_goals: developing promising thesis proposals
judging idea promise under uncertainty
key_sources: Huang-Yao Hong, Mei-Ju Chen, Bodong Chen, Chao-Yu Guo, Li-Ting Tseng (2025). Sense of promisingness: towards creative expertise through knowledge-building discourse in online graduate education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10483-0

article_title: Instructor presence in instructional videos in higher education: three field experiments in university courses
citation: Steffi Heidig, Maik Beege, Günter Daniel Rey, Sascha Schneider. (2024). Instructor presence in instructional videos in higher education: three field experiments in university courses. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10391-9
title: Social Cues Hypothesis
description: The Social Cues Hypothesis proposes that presenting the instructor in instructional videos next to slides leads to increased social presence, higher affective and motivational ratings, and more generative processing of learning material, resulting in better learning outcomes. It draws on social agency theory, which holds that social cues activate social responses and motivate deeper engagement. The article tests this hypothesis across three field studies.
requirements: Social cues such as voice, image, facial expression, eye gaze, and gestures must be provided to activate social schemata in learners.
constraints: The hypothesis was only partially supported: positive effects on some affective measures occurred but not consistently across studies or affective variables.
target_learning_goals: affective engagement
social presence
learning outcomes
key_sources: Steffi Heidig, Maik Beege, Günter Daniel Rey, Sascha Schneider. (2024). Instructor presence in instructional videos in higher education: three field experiments in university courses. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10391-9

article_title: Instructor presence in instructional videos in higher education: three field experiments in university courses
citation: Steffi Heidig, Maik Beege, Günter Daniel Rey, Sascha Schneider. (2024). Instructor presence in instructional videos in higher education: three field experiments in university courses. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10391-9
title: Interference Hypothesis
description: The Interference Hypothesis proposes that presenting a visible instructor next to slides increases extraneous processing and may harm learning. The additional visual information from the instructor's video overloads the visual/spatial channel and causes split attention between slides and instructor, reducing resources available for generative processing. The article tests this hypothesis across three field studies.
requirements: The visible instructor must add visual information that competes for limited working memory capacity alongside the slide content.
constraints: The hypothesis was not supported: no effects on extraneous processing or learning outcomes were found across three field studies.
target_learning_goals: extraneous processing management
learning outcomes
key_sources: Steffi Heidig, Maik Beege, Günter Daniel Rey, Sascha Schneider. (2024). Instructor presence in instructional videos in higher education: three field experiments in university courses. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10391-9

article_title: Fostering integrated mental models of different professional knowledge domains: instructional approaches and model-based analyses
citation: Lehmann, T., Pirnay-Dummer, P., & Schmidt-Borcherding, F. (2019). Fostering integrated mental models of different professional knowledge domains: instructional approaches and model-based analyses. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09704-0
title: T-MITOCAR as an automated model-based assessment tool for knowledge integration
description: T-MITOCAR (Text-Model Inspection Trace of Concepts and Relations) is an automated computer-based diagnostic tool that uses natural language expressions as input data to generate graph-based representations of learners' mental models. It measures structural and semantic similarities of verbally externalized mental models compared to a reference (expert) model using measures such as GAMMA (structural density) and BSM (balanced semantic matching). The tool relies on "the dependence of syntax and semantics within natural language" and works with a comparably small amount of text (350 words+).
requirements: Requires learners to externalize their mental models in natural language written formulations of at least 350 words
constraints: The reference model configuration may influence results; the authors note their reference model was not an argumentative text
target_learning_goals: knowledge integration across domains
mental model assessment
key_sources: Lehmann, T., Pirnay-Dummer, P., & Schmidt-Borcherding, F. (2019). Fostering integrated mental models of different professional knowledge domains: instructional approaches and model-based analyses. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09704-0

article_title: Using gesture recognition with the memory strategy to improve preschoolers’ learning performance, motor skills, and executive function
citation: Hsien-Sheng Hsiao, I-Hsiung Chang, Yi-Hsuan Chen, & Jyun-Chen Chen. (2025). Using gesture recognition with the memory strategy to improve preschoolers’ learning performance, motor skills, and executive function. Education Tech Research Dev, 73, 1791–1809. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10471-4
title: Four-step language learning memory strategy integrated into gesture-based physical learning activity
description: The study structures its learning activity around Oxford's (1990) memory strategy, whose "four steps of this memory strategy are: (1) creating mental linkages; (2) applying images and sounds; (3) reviewing; and (4) employing actions." Each step was implemented as a stage of the "Save the Prince/Princess" game, in which children used English knowledge, body movements, and memory to pass levels. The strategy was given to both the experimental and control groups, so the comparison isolates the gesture-recognition component.
requirements: An instructor delivering the four steps within themed English vocabulary lessons (Numbers, Fruits, Colors, and Animals)
constraints: The article states the four steps are suitable for integration into an interactive learning environment with gesture recognition
target_learners: preschoolers aged five to six learning English as a second language
target_learning_goals: English vocabulary learning
gross motor skills (stability and movement)
working memory
examples: While teaching the word "Bird," the children were asked to discuss their image of birds and to perform like a bird

Education Tech Research Dev, 73, 1791–1809. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10471-4
title: Orbbec Astra Pro gesture-based interactive interface for preschool learning
description: The study built four sets of gesture-based computing devices using the Orbbec Astra Pro, chosen for its depth and spatial resolution. The device "uses infrared to measure distance, projects a 19-jointed human skeleton image, and offers real-time motion-sensing controller technology that captures the body movements of users," letting teachers observe and improve children's gross motor skills with direct screen feedback. Children answered questions by controlling gestures and body postures, passing levels on correct answers.
requirements: Enough space per device, about 1.2–3 m, to avoid interference between equipment
Each device best used by three to four children to provide enough training and rest time
constraints: The article notes the traditional approach had one instructor and one assistant for 10 to 15 students, whose management time interrupted learning and motion behaviors

gross motor skills
executive function
examples: Four sets of gesture-based computing devices were built so preschoolers could learn at the same time

article_title: The effect of programming on primary school students’ mathematical and scientific understanding: educational use of mBot
citation: Sáez-López, J.-M., Sevillano-García, M.-L., & Vazquez-Cano, E. (2019). The effect of programming on primary school students’ mathematical and scientific understanding: educational use of mBot. Education Tech Research Dev, 67, 1405–1425. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09648-5
title: mBot robot with mBlock visual programming environment
description: The mBot is an inexpensive educational robot built on an Arduino UNO board, programmed through mBlock, "a variant adapted to Scratch 2.0" that adds a 'robots' block category. It includes brightness, proximity and line-following sensors, two RGB LEDs, a buzzer and a button. The study used it in sixth-grade math and science units for engine-control and ultrasonic-sensor activities with immediate feedback.
requirements: Visual block programming environment (mBlock, adapted from Scratch 2.0) so primary students can program intuitively
constraints: Authors position it as suitable from levels 3–4 of primary education onwards; science-area integration showed no significant learning gains
target_learning_goals: computational concepts such as sequences, loops and conditionals
integer and coordinate understanding in mathematics
examples: Keyboard arrow-key engine-control activity with speeds 50, 100 and 255
Ultrasonic-sensor obstacle-avoidance activity using a conditional and a loop
key_sources: Sáez-López, J.-M., Sevillano-García, M.-L., & Vazquez-Cano, E. (2019). The effect of programming on primary school students’ mathematical and scientific understanding: educational use of mBot. Education Tech Research Dev, 67, 1405–1425. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09648-5

article_title: The effect of programming on primary school students’ mathematical and scientific understanding: educational use of mBot
citation: Sáez-López, J.-M., Sevillano-García, M.-L., & Vazquez-Cano, E. (2019). The effect of programming on primary school students’ mathematical and scientific understanding: educational use of mBot. Education Tech Research Dev, 67, 1405–1425. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09648-5
title: Constructionist rationale for robotics and programming in primary education
description: The article grounds its design in Papert's constructionist theory, which "holds that when children work with materials that allow them to design and construct meaningful artifacts, they learn better", alongside meaningful learning and sociocultural-constructivist foundations. Learning occurs through creating and sharing meaningful artifacts with tools such as robots and computers, in opposition to passive instruction. This frames the project-based, learning-by-doing activities with the mBot.
requirements: Active methodologies and student participation rather than traditional passive instruction
constraints: The authors note robotics have not been found to statistically improve academic outcomes in some prior work (Fagin and Merkle 2003)
target_learning_goals: computational thinking
problem solving and logical-mathematical understanding
examples: mBot activities in which students program motion and sensors within math and science didactic units

article_title: Informing designs for learning when shifting to digital
citation: Hrastinski, S. (2021). Informing designs for learning when shifting to digital. Education Tech Research Dev, 69, 285–288. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09894-y
title: Design for learning as an informed practice
description: The article proposes understanding design for learning as an informed practice: "Teachers could be informed by 'what is known', such as theories, research, evidence, best and good practices, and previous experiences". Being informed also involves "applying professional judgment to reflect and act on analyses and evaluations of teaching and learning". This extends Bennett et al.'s descriptive model of teachers' design work toward improvement.
requirements: Teachers must have access to what is known, such as theories, research, evidence, best and good practices, and previous experiences
constraints: The article notes teachers' design practice has been given limited attention regarding how it could be improved
target_learning_goals: designing for learning
improving teaching quality
key_sources: Hrastinski, S. (2021). Informing designs for learning when shifting to digital. Education Tech Research Dev, 69, 285–288. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09894-y

article_title: Informing designs for learning when shifting to digital
citation: Hrastinski, S. (2021). Informing designs for learning when shifting to digital. Education Tech Research Dev, 69, 285–288. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09894-y
title: Encourage teachers to inform their designs for learning and iteratively improve them through reflection and evaluation
description: The article recommends that "teachers should be encouraged to inform their designs for learning and iteratively improve their designs based on reflection and evaluation". Teachers should look into what is known and deliberately learn through reflection and evaluation rather than relying solely on implicit assumptions. This is framed as especially important when rapidly shifting to digital.
requirements: Teachers must take time to look into what is known and deliberately learn through reflection and evaluation
constraints: In times requiring a pivot to online learning with a short timeline, a 'quick' design might be tempting
target_learning_goals: designing for learning
improving course designs
examples: Teachers conducted different types of evaluations, such as unit evaluations and questionnaires, verbal and written reflections from students, data from digital platforms, and assessment data

article_title: A multimodal representation framework for collaborative knowledge-building in an immersive astronomy simulation: using transmodal ordered network analysis
citation: Zhou, Y., Kang, J., Wang, Y., & Ashiq, M. (2025). A multimodal representation framework for collaborative knowledge-building in an immersive astronomy simulation: using transmodal ordered network analysis. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10510-0
title: A multimodal framework for knowledge representation across virtual, conceptual, and physical spaces in AR-enhanced CSCL.
description: The article proposes a multimodal framework that examines knowledge representations across three interconnected spaces in immersive environments: virtual, conceptual, and physical spaces. Virtual Space refers to the digital environment (the simulation platform), Conceptual Space includes abstract thought and internal knowledge representation, and Physical Space refers to the tangible environment where gestures and hands-on activities help learners ground abstract concepts. The framework synthesizes collaborative knowledge-building, distributed cognition, and multiple representations in science education. It provides a structured way to analyze multimodal knowledge construction in immersive environments and is "adaptable to various technology-rich CSCL contexts."
requirements: Requires an environment with multiple forms of representation across digital, verbal, and embodied modes.
constraints: The application of the framework may be limited in environments that rely predominantly on verbal or non-digital interactions.
target_learners: College students in introductory science courses
target_learning_goals: Collaborative knowledge construction of complex scientific concepts
key_sources: Zhou, Y., Kang, J., Wang, Y., & Ashiq, M. (2025). A multimodal representation framework for collaborative knowledge-building in an immersive astronomy simulation: using transmodal ordered network analysis. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10510-0

article_title: An empirical longitudinal study of AI integration in transforming teachers’ pedagogical content knowledge: insights from language educators in rural China
citation: Gretchen Geng · Junyu Chen. (2026). An empirical longitudinal study of AI integration in transforming teachers' pedagogical content knowledge: insights from language educators in rural China. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10602-5
title: DST-informed Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK) model specifying five knowledge domains
description: The article introduces the DST-informed PCK model, which specifies AI-empowered PCK by detailing the five domains of knowledge teachers draw upon: teaching practice and scaffolding, curriculum knowledge, subject content knowledge, student diversity and inclusive education, and educational contexts. Grounded in Dynamic Systems Theory, it treats PCK as emergent, adaptive, and context-sensitive rather than static, informing teaching practice and scaffolding strategies for personalised student learning.
requirements: Teachers must draw on all five PCK domains for the model to inform teaching practice and scaffolding strategies
constraints: Developed from a small longitudinal study of eight rural language teachers in one Chinese school
target_learning_goals: AI-integrated pedagogical content knowledge
key_sources: Gretchen Geng · Junyu Chen. (2026). An empirical longitudinal study of AI integration in transforming teachers' pedagogical content knowledge: insights from language educators in rural China. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10602-5

citation: Gretchen Geng · Junyu Chen. (2026). An empirical longitudinal study of AI integration in transforming teachers' pedagogical content knowledge: insights from language educators in rural China. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10602-5
title: AI-in-PCK stage framework mapping AI adoption trajectory
description: The AI-in-PCK stage framework maps the trajectory of AI adoption, illustrating how teachers' concerns and practices evolve from initial exploration and experimentation to strategic integration and ongoing learning while responding to classroom realities and student feedback. It applies the Concern-Based Adoption Model as a conceptual lens, capturing shifts from self-oriented considerations to task-related and impact-driven concerns across seven concerns-based stages.
requirements: Sustained exposure to AI tools and relevant professional development opportunities over time
constraints: Trajectory observed over an 18-week period in one rural school context
target_learners: Rural language teachers adopting AI tools
target_learning_goals: Staged adoption of AI in pedagogical practice

article_title: What does it mean to be “career ready”? A study of competencies important for instructional designers and educational technologists
citation: Exter, M., & Ashby, I. (2026). What does it mean to be “career ready”? A study of competencies important for instructional designers and educational technologists. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10727-7
title: Taxonomy of ID/ET professional competencies spanning domain knowledge and skills, cross-disciplinary skills, and dispositions
description: The article presents a taxonomy of professional competencies for instructional design and educational technology roles, organized into three themes: domain knowledge and skills, professional/cross-disciplinary skills, and dispositions. Each theme is broken into sub-themes and categories, with frequency counts by role and context. The authors state they “decided to combine knowledge and skills, and break up into two logical themes: “domain knowledge & skills” and “cross-disciplinary knowledge and skills””, with dispositions as a separate theme.
requirements: Competency definitions must be grounded in what professionals report as important on the job, using an operational definition of ID and ET roles to determine inclusion.
constraints: The taxonomy reflects competencies reported by 31 professionals across K12, higher education, and corporate contexts; it is not a validated universal standard.
target_learners: Instructional design and educational technology professionals
Current and future ID/ET graduate students
target_learning_goals: Career readiness
Professional competency development

article_title: Enhancing literacy and numeracy through teacher dashboards and digital personalised learning: an A/B/C test in Kenyan early years education
citation: Sun, C., Major, L., Daltry, R., Obradovic, L., & Friedberg, A. (2026). Enhancing literacy and numeracy through teacher dashboards and digital personalised learning: an A/B/C test in Kenyan early years education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10703-1
title: Three DPL implementation models: supplementary, substitute, and integrative
description: The article identifies three models for implementing Digital Personalised Learning: 'supplementary (DPL outside regular instruction such as additional technology-led sessions or afterschool programmes)', 'substitute (DPL replaces traditional teaching with all instruction delivered through technology)', and 'integrative (featuring both teacher and technology, integrating teacher, learner, and classroom interactions, with technology supporting teaching and learning)'. The study notes supplementary models are most common in LMICs, with UNICEF identifying 35 of 40 personalised learning tools used for supplemental learning, resulting in limited teacher involvement.
requirements: Implementation requires consideration of how DPL is aligned with teachers' daily classroom routines and curriculum content.
constraints: The article acknowledges Van Schoors et al.'s caution against oversimplifying classifications of DPL implementation.
target_learners: Early-years and primary learners in low- and middle-income countries
target_learning_goals: Foundational literacy and numeracy competencies
key_sources: Sun, C., Major, L., Daltry, R., Obradovic, L., & Friedberg, A. (2026). Enhancing literacy and numeracy through teacher dashboards and digital personalised learning: an A/B/C test in Kenyan early years education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10703-1

citation: Sun, C., Major, L., Daltry, R., Obradovic, L., & Friedberg, A. (2026). Enhancing literacy and numeracy through teacher dashboards and digital personalised learning: an A/B/C test in Kenyan early years education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10703-1
title: EIDU DPL tool with LSTM-based personalised learning sequence
description: The study was built on an existing DPL tool developed by EIDU, 'pre-installed as an application on low-cost Android devices purchasable for less than $50'. The tool offers learner-facing content aligned to the Kenyan national curriculum, structured by literacy and numeracy domains covering 25 literacy and 23 numeracy substrands across 2,239 units. 'The sequence of these learning units is personalised to support each learner's progression using a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network', which functions offline to mitigate low-connectivity issues.
requirements: Learners interact with a collection of learning units personalised to their predicted current competency level, with teachers able to align digital content with classroom teaching by selecting specific substrands.
constraints: The algorithm functions offline to mitigate low-connectivity issues, and the intended usage time is 5 minutes per session using up to two devices shared per class.
target_learners: Early-years learners (pre-primary to Grade 2) in Kenya
target_learning_goals: Foundational literacy and numeracy competencies
key_sources: Sun, C., Major, L., Daltry, R., Obradovic, L., & Friedberg, A. (2026). Enhancing literacy and numeracy through teacher dashboards and digital personalised learning: an A/B/C test in Kenyan early years education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10703-1

title: Prescriptive grouped dashboard design with action-oriented category labels
description: The Grouped Dashboard categorised learners into three groups based on the same ranking calculation as the List Dashboard, using labels designed to adopt 'prescriptive' language which prompts specific pedagogical action: 'practised enough', 'keep going' and 'need more practice'. The category labels echoed categorisations made by teachers themselves, identified in prior design-based research as 'fast learners', 'time-takers' and those in between. Both dashboard designs featured brief explanatory text and a clean user interface following guidelines for low visualisation-literate users.
requirements: Dashboard design should strike an effective balance between supporting teachers' awareness in their classroom and informing their decision-making more directly.
constraints: The pedagogical purpose of the dashboard was limited to the digital learning environment, specifically supporting teachers' distribution of the DPL tool amongst learners rather than directly informing classroom teaching practices.
target_learners: Teachers of early-years learners in low- and middle-income countries
target_learning_goals: Supporting teachers' pedagogical decision-making in distributing DPL tools

article_title: Model-based support for teaching practice and self-efficacy in artificial intelligence-enhanced virtual reality teaching simulation
citation: Chih-Pu Dai · Fengfeng Ke. (2026). Model-based support for teaching practice and self-efficacy in artificial intelligence-enhanced virtual reality teaching simulation. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10592-4
title: A three-stage design framework for model-based support in VR simulation-based teacher education
description: The article proposes a design framework for model-based support in simulation-based teacher education that integrates Grossman et al.'s teaching practice components, Kavanagh et al.'s pedagogical reasoning model, and Kolb's experiential learning theory. The framework structures support across three stages: "support at the pretraining stage, support during in-situ (or in-simulation) practice, and support at the post-simulation stage." Its aim is to guide preservice teachers in making pedagogical decisions when facing dilemmas while interacting with AI-powered virtual students.
requirements: Support should be integrated across pretraining, in-simulation, and post-simulation stages of the VR experience.
target_learning_goals: Teaching knowledge and skills
Teaching self-efficacy
key_sources: Chih-Pu Dai · Fengfeng Ke. (2026). Model-based support for teaching practice and self-efficacy in artificial intelligence-enhanced virtual reality teaching simulation. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10592-4

citation: Chih-Pu Dai · Fengfeng Ke. (2026). Model-based support for teaching practice and self-efficacy in artificial intelligence-enhanced virtual reality teaching simulation. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10592-4
title: EVETeach: an AI-enhanced VR teaching simulation with a generative AI virtual student agent
description: EVETeach (Enactive Virtual Environment for teaching) is a VR simulation-based learning environment built on the open-source OpenSimulator platform. Its core element is an AI-powered virtual student agent, called Evelyn, created by refining a generative AI model with a localized dataset of ambitious teaching classroom videos and TIMSS video clips, so that the agent "can question, respond and interact with the preservice teachers in an authentic and domain-specific manner."
requirements: A localized dataset of classroom transcripts is used to refine the generative AI model for domain-specific interaction.
target_learning_goals: Ambitious teaching practices
Classroom discussion facilitation

article_title: Promoting preservice teachers’ multiperspective professional vision in virtual learning environments – On the effects of modeling videos and prompts during video-based lesson analysis
citation: Janeczko, J. M., Lehmkuhl, A., Junker, R., Zucker, V., Meschede, N., & Holodynski, M. (2026). Promoting preservice teachers' multiperspective professional vision in virtual learning environments – On the effects of modeling videos and prompts during video-based lesson analysis. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10546-2
title: Teacher education programs should use video-based virtual learning environments for individualized promotion of professional vision
description: The article recommends that teacher education programs adopt video-based virtual learning environments that provide individualized learning paths, immediate feedback, and adaptive progression to promote professional vision. The VLE enables learners to progress at their own pace, with each learning unit requiring a defined level of competence before advancing. The study showed that such environments improved multiperspective professional vision compared to untreated controls.
requirements: The VLE must provide preprogrammed feedback based on expert assessments and adaptive learning paths based on preservice teachers' learning progress.
constraints: The content of the VLE must be adapted to the subject and school type, including knowledge input, classroom video selection, analysis tasks, master ratings, and feedback.
target_learners: preservice teachers in elementary science education
target_learning_goals: multiperspective professional vision of classroom management and instructional support
examples: The study's VLE consisted of five modules with increasing complexity, combining knowledge input via animated videos and quizzes with video analyses using closed and open response formats with automated feedback.

Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10546-2
title: Professional vision as a situation-specific skill mediating between professional knowledge and teaching actions
description: The article defines professional vision (PV) as teachers' ability to notice and reason about relevant classroom events based on their professional knowledge. According to the model of competence as a continuum, PV is a situation-specific skill that mediates between teachers' professional knowledge and their teaching actions. The article identifies four facets of PV: description, interpretation, evaluation, and generation of alternative teaching actions.
requirements: PV development requires structured opportunities to apply professional knowledge to authentic classroom situations, such as through video-based analysis.
target_learning_goals: noticing and reasoning about relevant classroom events

title: Cognitive apprenticeship approach as a didactic framework for designing digital support tools in video-based learning
description: The article draws on the cognitive apprenticeship approach, which focuses on learning through guided experience and describes support activities including modeling, scaffolding, and coaching. Modeling means that an expert performs an exemplary task while verbalizing their perceptions, thoughts, and strategies. Scaffolding and coaching can be embodied in prompts that stimulate cognitive, metacognitive, volitional, or cooperative activities during learning.
requirements: Support tools derived from this approach must be designed according to multimedia learning principles to avoid increasing extraneous cognitive load.
constraints: Scaffolding types with high levels of guidance, such as modeling, are particularly effective for less advanced learners, and combined scaffolds may not be supportive for everyone.
target_learners: preservice teachers with diverse entry levels
target_learning_goals: effective video-based lesson analysis
examples: The study implemented modeling videos showing an expert's screencast thinking aloud during video analysis, and written prompts guiding planning and conducting of analyses.

article_title: Evidence-based development of an instrument for the assessment of teachers’ self-perceptions of their artificial intelligence competence
citation: Delcker, J., Heil, J., & Ifenthaler, D. (2025). Evidence-based development of an instrument for the assessment of teachers' self-perceptions of their artificial intelligence competence. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10418-1
title: AICO_edu questionnaire for teachers' perceived AI competence
description: AICO_edu (AI Competence Educators) is a self-report questionnaire developed to assess teachers' perceived AI competence. "Each dimension was captured through six to eight items (TH: 8; LF: 6; IP: 8; AT: 8; TL: 8; PF: 7), which were answered on a five-point Likert scale." It focuses on perceived AI competence rather than general digital competence, and is intended for use by school leaders and educators in teacher training.
requirements: Items answered on a five-point Likert scale from strongly disagree to strongly agree
constraints: Measures perceived competence, not performance-task results; the authors note "there is a clear difference between perceived competences and the actual competences of a person"
target_learners: Pre-service and in-service vocational school teachers
target_learning_goals: Self-assessment of artificial intelligence competence across six dimensions
key_sources: Delcker, J., Heil, J., & Ifenthaler, D. (2025). Evidence-based development of an instrument for the assessment of teachers' self-perceptions of their artificial intelligence competence. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10418-1

article_title: Evidence-based development of an instrument for the assessment of teachers’ self-perceptions of their artificial intelligence competence
citation: Delcker, J., Heil, J., & Ifenthaler, D. (2025). Evidence-based development of an instrument for the assessment of teachers' self-perceptions of their artificial intelligence competence. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10418-1
title: Six-dimension model of teachers' AI competence
description: Based on a systematic literature review and qualitative interviews with 35 stakeholders, the article identifies six dimensions of AI competence for teachers: Theoretical Knowledge about AI, Legal Framework and Ethics, Implications of AI, Attitude toward AI, Teaching and Learning with AI, and Ongoing Professionalization. The article states that "AI competence in the context of education is a set of skills that enable teachers to ethically responsible develop, apply, and evaluate AI for learning and teaching processes." The model is holistic and multidimensional, distinguishing itself from frameworks that focus on a single construct.
requirements: Ongoing teacher professionalization and training to maintain the competence set
constraints: The PF and AT dimensions did not fit the final single-factor measurement model in their current form
target_learning_goals: Developing AI competence for ethical and responsible use of AI in teaching
key_sources: Delcker, J., Heil, J., & Ifenthaler, D. (2025). Evidence-based development of an instrument for the assessment of teachers' self-perceptions of their artificial intelligence competence. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10418-1

article_title: Evidence-based development of an instrument for the assessment of teachers’ self-perceptions of their artificial intelligence competence
citation: Delcker, J., Heil, J., & Ifenthaler, D. (2025). Evidence-based development of an instrument for the assessment of teachers' self-perceptions of their artificial intelligence competence. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10418-1
title: Design AI competence instruments as holistic and multidimensional rather than single-construct
description: The article argues that AI competence measurement should cover multiple constructs rather than a single one. "Furthermore, the instrument covers various constructs associated with perceived AI competence instead of focusing on a single construct." This responds to prior instruments that were either too general, producing extensive questionnaires, or too narrow, capturing only attitudes or anxiety toward AI.
requirements: Item wording must be explicit enough to guarantee valid answers, as ambiguous items had to be removed during validation
constraints: The authors note that creating a manageable scale conflicts with fully specifying the PF and AT dimensions, which would require more items
target_learners: Teachers in vocational education and training
target_learning_goals: Measuring holistic perceived AI competence for reflection and professional development
examples: The AICO_edu questionnaire operationalizes this principle with six subscales covering theoretical knowledge, legal and ethical awareness, implications, attitudes, teaching with AI, and professionalization.
