article_title: Integration of ICTs in teaching practices: propositions to the SAMR model
citation: Rute Nogueira de Morais Bicalho, César Coll, Anna Engel, Maria Cláudia Santos Lopes de Oliveira. (2023). Integration of ICTs in teaching practices: propositions to the SAMR model. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10169-x
title: SAMR model: a four-level hierarchical taxonomy of ICT integration (Substitution, Augmentation, Modification, Redefinition)
description: The SAMR model, developed by Puentedura, classifies ICT integration into four hierarchical formative levels: "Substitution, Augmentation, Modification and Redefinition". The first two levels form an improvement range and the last two a transformation range involving structural changes in teaching performance. The article uses the model to scale ICT contributions in teachers' practices while noting it has been "repeatedly criticized for its lack of theoretical foundation and empirical evidence".
requirements: Teachers are expected to be able to describe and categorize the uses they make of ICTs using the four-level taxonomy.
constraints: The article notes the model has been criticized for weak theoretical foundation, lack of empirical evidence in peer-reviewed studies, absence of context, emphasis on technology as product rather than process, and a hierarchical linear structure.
target_learning_goals: integration of ICTs into teaching practices
key_sources: Rute Nogueira de Morais Bicalho, César Coll, Anna Engel, Maria Cláudia Santos Lopes de Oliveira. (2023). Integration of ICTs in teaching practices: propositions to the SAMR model. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10169-x

article_title: Integration of ICTs in teaching practices: propositions to the SAMR model
citation: Rute Nogueira de Morais Bicalho, César Coll, Anna Engel, Maria Cláudia Santos Lopes de Oliveira. (2023). Integration of ICTs in teaching practices: propositions to the SAMR model. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10169-x
title: New learning ecology: a multiplicity of educational scenarios, resources and agents dispersed in time and space
description: The article characterizes the new learning ecology as "a multiplicity of educational scenarios, resources and agents dispersed in time and space, allowing for alternative and varied ways for the teaching and learning process and human development". ICT ubiquity helped alter the parameters of human learning: where, with whom, what, for what and how people learn. Recognizing and enhancing this ecology means planning more student-centered teaching practices that recognize emerging learning spaces and integrate students' interests into school content.
requirements: Educational intentionality in thinking, planning and executing student-centered teaching practices.
target_learning_goals: personalization of learning
connecting learning across contexts
key_sources: Rute Nogueira de Morais Bicalho, César Coll, Anna Engel, Maria Cláudia Santos Lopes de Oliveira. (2023). Integration of ICTs in teaching practices: propositions to the SAMR model. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10169-x

article_title: Integration of ICTs in teaching practices: propositions to the SAMR model
citation: Rute Nogueira de Morais Bicalho, César Coll, Anna Engel, Maria Cláudia Santos Lopes de Oliveira. (2023). Integration of ICTs in teaching practices: propositions to the SAMR model. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10169-x
title: Treat SAMR levels as fluid and non-hierarchical rather than a ladder to climb
description: The article proposes "a more flexible, non-hierarchical understanding of the SAMR model", arguing each level "does not need to be understood as better or worse or refer to a ladder on which teachers advance to higher levels". Teachers can move between levels depending on context, intentions, objectives and learning outcomes, with clarity confirmed by pedagogical intentionality and self-evaluation.
requirements: Pedagogical intentionality and (self) evaluation by the teacher when defining the level of ICT use.
constraints: The linear reading of the model is described as problematic because it treats a complex and dynamic process in a linear way.
target_learning_goals: integrating ICTs into teaching practices
examples: A teacher with good command of technologies may use a device at the Substitution level because it is the best strategy for a given time and objective.
key_sources: Rute Nogueira de Morais Bicalho, César Coll, Anna Engel, Maria Cláudia Santos Lopes de Oliveira. (2023). Integration of ICTs in teaching practices: propositions to the SAMR model. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10169-x

article_title: Integration of ICTs in teaching practices: propositions to the SAMR model
citation: Rute Nogueira de Morais Bicalho, César Coll, Anna Engel, Maria Cláudia Santos Lopes de Oliveira. (2023). Integration of ICTs in teaching practices: propositions to the SAMR model. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10169-x
title: Consider sociocultural context when integrating ICTs to avoid prescriptive, decontextualized uses of SAMR
description: The article warns that "A decontextualized reading of the SAMR model could lead to prescriptive uses of ICTs, only at the Substitution or Augmentation level". It argues that historical, institutional and cultural events must be considered in ICT integration, and that what mattered during remote teaching was not the use of ICTs per se but "the opening of teachers to the heterogeneous needs of students".
requirements: Considering the historical, institutional and cultural events surrounding ICT integration.
constraints: A purely technical appropriation of the model leaves teachers susceptible to consumption of technologies to the detriment of pedagogical value.
target_learning_goals: effective integration of ICTs in teaching practices

article_title: Immersive virtual reality–based manual therapy training: a mixed-methods trial
citation: Trinidad-Fernández, M., Bossavit, B., Fuentes-Abolafio, I. J., García-Conejo, C., Mayorga-Vega, D., Díaz-Balboa, E., & Cuesta-Vargas, A. (2026). Immersive virtual reality–based manual therapy training: a mixed-methods trial. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10620-3
title: iVR application for femorotibial mobilization training on Meta Quest 2
description: An immersive virtual reality application developed for the Meta Quest 2 head-mounted display to teach the femorotibial mobilization technique. Users are immersed "with a first-person perspective" in a virtual clinician's room with an articulated supine patient avatar, interacting with the patient's left leg through controllers represented as virtual hands. The application includes a tutorial phase with step-by-step visual guidance and a practice phase with feedback on cadence, aiming to provide "a safe and controlled environment where users can learn and practice the Femorotibial mobilization technique".
requirements: Requires a Meta Quest 2 headset with two manual controllers, whose position and orientation data are used to compute movements following physical principles.
constraints: The application provides no haptic feedback, so tissue deformation and limb weight cannot be felt in the virtual experience.
target_learning_goals: Performing the femorotibial mobilization technique with coordinated angulation and translation movements

article_title: Design principles to develop digital innovation skills: a design-based research approach
citation: van den Berg, C., & Bozalek, V. (2024). Design principles to develop digital innovation skills: a design-based research approach. Education Tech Research Dev, 72, 947–972. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10308-y
title: Nine design principles for teaching digital innovation skills through authentic learning
description: A pattern for designing learning environments that develop digital business innovation skills, refined over three DBR iterations at a South African university. The final principles are: "Ensure collaboration takes place", "Provide opportunities for students to find their own solutions", "Implement a working digital innovation in a business", "Incorporate a design-thinking ethos", "Ensure that students utilise interdisciplinary skills", "Implement a formal process of reflection", "Allow for experimentation", "Ensure that tasks culminate in a capstone project", and "Partner with entrepreneurs". Each principle is mapped to authentic learning elements (A1–A9) and skill sets (S1–S8) from the Kereluik et al. framework.
requirements: Industry partners willing to host student digital innovation projects
A blended learning environment supporting online and face-to-face collaboration
Assessment rubrics covering the entire process, not just the end product
constraints: Conducted at a single university, limiting generalisability of the findings
The study's design and approach may not apply to other contexts or disciplines
target_learners: Information Systems students in higher education
target_learning_goals: Digital innovation skills
Collaboration
Design thinking
Interdisciplinary problem-solving
examples: Students worked in groups of five with industry partners to design and implement digital innovations such as eCommerce websites using design thinking and agile methods
key_sources: van den Berg, C., & Bozalek, V. (2024). Design principles to develop digital innovation skills: a design-based research approach. Education Tech Research Dev, 72, 947–972. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10308-y

article_title: Design principles to develop digital innovation skills: a design-based research approach
citation: van den Berg, C., & Bozalek, V. (2024). Design principles to develop digital innovation skills: a design-based research approach. Education Tech Research Dev, 72, 947–972. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10308-y
title: Capstone project with agile methodology funnelling all course tasks into one digital innovation artefact
description: An instructional element added after iteration 1 in which "a new principle was added to allow all tasks to be funnelled into a comprehensive capstone project that applies agile methods". Students work in teams with industry partners to design and implement a working digital innovation such as a mobile application or website, using open-source software. "The application of Agile allows changes to group formation, regular feedback and the assessment of the overall process and not merely the end solution."
requirements: Clear team roles and regular feedback opportunities
Assessments measuring outcomes per week so teams can make improvements
constraints: Interpersonal issues in teams and requirement limitations with industry partners could not be pre-empted
target_learners: Final-year and postgraduate Information Systems students
target_learning_goals: Implementing a working digital innovation in a business
Collaboration and project management
examples: Iteration 3 teams built websites and eCommerce platforms for a guest house, a hair salon, a fashion designer, a recruitment agency, a quantity surveyor and a winemaker
key_sources: van den Berg, C., & Bozalek, V. (2024). Design principles to develop digital innovation skills: a design-based research approach. Education Tech Research Dev, 72, 947–972. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10308-y

article_title: Design principles to develop digital innovation skills: a design-based research approach
citation: van den Berg, C., & Bozalek, V. (2024). Design principles to develop digital innovation skills: a design-based research approach. Education Tech Research Dev, 72, 947–972. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10308-y
title: Authentic learning environment framework for cultivating digital innovation skills
description: The article applies the Herrington et al. (2010) authentic learning framework as the theoretical basis for teaching digital innovation skills, arguing that developing 21st-century skills "can be enhanced by an authentic learning environment in which students must be engaged in an inventive and realistic task that provides opportunities for complex collaborative activities". The framework comprises nine elements coded A1–A9: authentic contexts, authentic tasks, expert performances and modelling, multiple roles and perspectives, collaborative learning, reflection, articulation, coaching and scaffolding, and authentic assessment. Table 1 maps each element to concrete course-design implementations such as NGO partnerships, blogs, peer review and a semester-long capstone project.
requirements: Real-world tasks with industry or community partners
Assessment that evaluates the whole collaborative process
constraints: Group work and collaboration require ongoing monitoring to facilitate conflict resolution
target_learning_goals: 21st-century skills including critical thinking, creativity, collaboration and digital innovation capability
examples: Authentic contexts were implemented by forming working partnerships with NGOs and community organisations to implement real digital solutions such as websites and mobile applications
key_sources: van den Berg, C., & Bozalek, V. (2024). Design principles to develop digital innovation skills: a design-based research approach. Education Tech Research Dev, 72, 947–972. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10308-y

article_title: The efficacy of animation and visualization in teaching data structures: a case study
citation: Kogan, G., Chassidim, H., & Rabaev, I. (2024). The efficacy of animation and visualization in teaching data structures: a case study. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10382-w
title: AVDS: a free online animation and visualization tool for data structures
description: The AVDS tool is a free online animation and visualization tool developed to complement an undergraduate Data Structures course, covering "a classic set of algorithms and data structures commonly studied in the undergraduate data structures course." It provides interactive visualization of algorithm execution, including AVL tree rotations. Source code is available on GitHub, and the tool provides usage reports for teaching staff showing analytics per topic.
requirements: Requires JavaScript, HTML, and CSS programming experience to understand the source code
constraints: At the time of the experiment, the system did not show the steps of the algorithm, but did provide a final answer only
target_learners: undergraduate computer science and software engineering students
target_learning_goals: understanding data structures and algorithms, including AVL tree operations
examples: Used during a 20-minute performance test on AVL trees; students could use it to solve questions or verify answers
key_sources: Kogan, G., Chassidim, H., & Rabaev, I. (2024). The efficacy of animation and visualization in teaching data structures: a case study. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10382-w

article_title: The efficacy of animation and visualization in teaching data structures: a case study
citation: Kogan, G., Chassidim, H., & Rabaev, I. (2024). The efficacy of animation and visualization in teaching data structures: a case study. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10382-w
title: Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) applied to learning-tool adoption
description: The study applies the Technology Acceptance Model, which measures three key factors related to acceptance of a learning technology: perceived usefulness (PU), perceived ease of use (PEOU), and attitude toward usage (ATU). These factors are measured "to determine the level of acceptance and adoption of the AVDS tool and to provide insights into areas that need improvement." The model was tested via structural equation modeling with weight constraints across experimental conditions.
requirements: Multiple questionnaire items per construct with validity and reliability evaluation (Cronbach's alpha, AVE, composite reliability)
constraints: A minimum sample size of 200 to 300 observations is often recommended for SEM, but this study had 78 participants
target_learning_goals: understanding factors influencing adoption of learning technology
examples: TAM administered before and after the performance test to the experimental group and once to the control group

title: Structure VR learning activities with scaffolded interaction and reflective explanation to support learning efficiency and learner confidence
description: The article recommends structuring VR learning activities as a sequenced instructional design that integrates exploration of a virtual system, scaffolded interaction tasks, and a reflective self-explanation activity. The authors conclude that "structuring VR learning activities with scaffolded interaction and reflective explanation may support learning efficiency and learner confidence in engineering contexts." This sequencing pairs generative learning strategies with interactive simulation rather than treating VR as a standalone medium.

article_title: Effects of an automated corrective feedback-based peer assessment approach on students’ learning achievement, motivation, and self-regulated learning conceptions in foreign language pronunciation
citation: Chen-Chen Liu, Gwo-Jen Hwang, Peng Yu, Yun-Fang Tu, Youmei Wang. (2025). Effects of an automated corrective feedback-based peer assessment approach on students' learning achievement, motivation, and self-regulated learning conceptions in foreign language pronunciation. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10484-z
title: The ACF-PA learning model: a four-stage foreign language speech learning cycle combining AI technology with corrective feedback
description: The article proposes a four-stage foreign language speech learning model based on the corrective feedback learning loop (Hattie & Timperley, 2007), comprising "acquisition, correction, reflection, and application." In the acquisition stage, learners receive lectures on pronunciation rules; in the correction stage, the AI tool "French Assistant" provides immediate automated corrective feedback using automatic speech recognition; in the reflection stage, peer assessment is adopted after courses using rubrics covering vowel, consonant, stress, intonation, and fluency; in the output stage, learners complete pronunciation exercises and peer assessment across five learning tasks. The model integrates AI technology with corrective feedback strategies to provide timely, personalized guidance.
requirements: An AI learning app with automatic speech recognition capability (French Assistant) that provides immediate automated corrective feedback on pronunciation
constraints: The study was conducted over only 5 weeks, which the authors note was not enough to form long-term learning habits
target_learners: College students learning foreign language pronunciation
target_learning_goals: French pronunciation accuracy
Self-regulated learning
Intrinsic motivation
examples: Students used the French Assistant app to search for French words, upload pronunciation audio, and receive immediate feedback with detailed information about wrongly pronounced syllables and scores

article_title: Weaving in: shifts in youth mathematical engagement through weaving
citation: Thompson, N. (2024). Weaving in: shifts in youth mathematical engagement through weaving. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10316-y
title: Three instantiations of mathematics in weaving: arithmetic and calculations, image and shape transformations, and multiple embedded patternings
description: A taxonomy from the author's prior work with experienced weavers, describing three simultaneous, overlapping mathematical instantiations that emerge through weaving practice. The article states: "These instantiations are (1) arithmetic and calculations, (2) image and shape transformations, and (3) multiple embedded patternings." Image and shape transformations deal with designing with regard to space, shape, proportion, symmetry, while multiple embedded patternings encompasses invention and experimentation with patterns, sequences, and structure. The current study operationalizes two of these instantiations to analyze youth artifacts.
requirements: Prior work with experienced weavers (Thompson, 2022) that identified the three instantiations
constraints: The current study operationalizes only two of the three instantiations: image and shape transformations and multiple embedded patternings
target_learning_goals: mathematical engagement through making
pattern and shape reasoning

article_title: Weaving in: shifts in youth mathematical engagement through weaving
citation: Thompson, N. (2024). Weaving in: shifts in youth mathematical engagement through weaving. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10316-y
title: Six-session weaving workshop with graduated math goals from shape recognition to sequence exploration
description: A reusable instructional design at the unit level: six one-hour sessions during the school day in which youth use laser-cut frame looms and grid paper to plan and create woven artifacts. Sessions progress from introducing weaving designs and warping looms, through planning on grid paper and completing initial projects, to a second project exploring relationships between materials, number, shape, and sequence, ending with reflection on connections to math. Youth were encouraged to make at least two projects and to try new techniques and styles in their second design.
requirements: Frame looms laser-cut from an open-source pattern
Grid paper for planning designs
Yarn in multiple colors and thicknesses, string for warping, scissors, pencils, tapestry needles
constraints: Youth sometimes created small projects, abandoned projects, or wanted to continue working beyond the scope of the workshop
target_learners: middle-school youth (grades 6-8) in a mixed-age classroom
target_learning_goals: recognize how shapes, patterns, motifs emerge on grid structure
reason about how sequence and shape intersect
explore relationships between materials, number, shape, sequence
examples: Youth used an over one, under one sequence in first projects and progressed to over two, under two or over three, under two sequences in second projects

citation: Thompson, N. (2024). Weaving in: shifts in youth mathematical engagement through weaving. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10316-y
title: Recognize and validate mathematical engagement expressed through crafting as a legitimate form of doing math
description: A design recommendation grounded in epistemological pluralism: educators should recognize performing mathematical ideas through crafting as a form of doing math, even when youth do not verbalize their understanding in traditional academic ways. The article states: "If we commit to epistemological pluralism and to validating multiple ways of knowing and doing, we can come to recognize performing mathematical ideas through crafting as a form of doing math." This principle reframes what counts as mathematical engagement and may help make math more accessible and welcoming to more diverse learners.
requirements: A commitment to epistemological pluralism as a theoretical stance
Willingness to broaden definitions of what counts as math
constraints: This form of mathematical doing may not result in increased test scores or traditional academic discussion of math
target_learners: youth from traditionally minoritized backgrounds in mathematics
target_learning_goals: mathematical engagement
epistemological pluralism in STEM
examples: Youth crafters did not always verbalize their mathematical understanding in traditional academic ways, and often not at all

article_title: Educational theories and computer game design: lessons from an experiment in elementary mathematics education
citation: Es-Sajjade, A., & Paas, F. (2020). Educational theories and computer game design: lessons from an experiment in elementary mathematics education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09799-w
title: MATHERIAL game design based on CLT and GDT
description: MATHERIAL is a two-player interactive math game in which players solve and create mathematical equations while competing in parallel games. The design drew on cognitive load theory to minimize extraneous load and maximize intrinsic load, and on game design theory principles (identity, immersion, interactivity, increased complexity, informed teaching, and instruction). The game avoided animations to draw more on working memory capacity and used player status development instead of sophisticated avatars.

title: Include student voice in developing learning analytics policy
description: The commentary argues that policy governing the ethical use of student data in learning analytics must be developed with student input, not imposed on students. It states it is "equally important that the student voice be included in the development of such policy". This positions students as stakeholders whose understanding of data sharing purposes and benefits must be built through consultative processes around systems implementation.

constraints: Building a shared understanding and vocabulary with students about the possibilities and ethical implications of learning analytics is difficult

title: Use instructor cues such as pointing gestures and gaze shifts when teaching complex content
description: The article concludes that "instructor cues such as pointing gestures and gaze shifts may be particularly helpful when teaching complex relationships, abstract constructs, or procedural content." This principle directs educators to incorporate instructor signaling when content complexity is high, as the study found a significant three-way interaction showing instructor signaling improved knowledge acquisition as perceived difficulty increased.

title: Design online mathematics courses with self-check buttons, prior knowledge sections, and chunked scaffolding to support competence
description: The article recommends three design features for improving competence in online mathematics courses: self-check buttons with informative and correctness feedback, prior knowledge explanations with self-check practice, and content chunking with scaffolding. These features are grounded in both quantitative and qualitative findings and are being integrated into the school's new Algebra 1 course.

constraints: Recommendations should be considered in light of specific context variations and requirements due to limited purposive sampling

title: Self-determination theory as a framework for online course design
description: Self-determination theory is an organismic theory of motivation holding that satisfaction of three psychological needs—autonomy (self-regulation), competence (self-efficacy), and relatedness (belonging)—creates conditions for integrated extrinsic and intrinsic motivation to thrive. The article applies this framework to design an online Algebra 2 unit, mapping specific design components to each need.
requirements: Social factors that support rather than undermine the three psychological needs
constraints: Motivation varies in strength and orientation along a continuum from amotivation through controlled and autonomous extrinsic motivation to intrinsic motivation
target_learners: Online learners in secondary and higher education
target_learning_goals: Supporting autonomous and intrinsic motivation for learning

title: Instructional theory as a prescriptive collection of methods that best fit a design situation
description: The article defines an instructional theory as a prescriptive collection of methods that best fit a design situation, drawing on Gibbons and Rogers' (2009) concept of method layers: content, strategy, message, control, representation, media-logic, and data management. It uses this lens to critique the Giannakas et al. (2018) review of mobile game-based learning.

title: Designers should embrace multiple learning theories in mGBL designs
description: The article argues that mGBL designers should embrace multiple learning theories in their designs, drawing on previous ideas about eclectic instructional design. It emphasizes that what is more important is identifying the foundational instructional theories, models, and/or methods that provide a design foundation for mGBL solutions.

article_title: In-between worlds: Chilean university lecturers’ experiences of teaching transition between face-to-face and virtual reality contexts during the COVID-19 pandemic
citation: Dai, K., Garcia, J., & Olave-Encina, K. (2023). In-between worlds: Chilean university lecturers' experiences of teaching transition between face-to-face and virtual reality contexts during the COVID-19 pandemic. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10217-0
title: In-betweenness: a theoretical lens for educators' transitions between face-to-face and virtual teaching contexts.
description: Drawing on Bhabha's (1994) 'in-between space' and social constructivism, the article proposes 'in-betweenness' as the status of continuously shifting between face-to-face and virtual online teaching environments. In this inter-space, lecturers' identity, agency, and digital competencies are reshaped through agentic responses as they move back and forth between contexts. The authors offer it as a unique theoretical lens for exploring instructors' transitions from traditional to technology-mediated settings.
requirements: Applicable when educators transition between two distinct teaching contexts, such as face-to-face and virtual-world-based settings.
constraints: Findings from the underlying qualitative study may not generalise to other cases, as stated by the authors.
target_learning_goals: Professional identity and agency development in technology-mediated teaching

citation: Hale Ilgaz. (2021). The role of mobile technologies in shifting to digital. Education Tech Research Dev 69, 189–190. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09945-y
title: Define the unique functions and affordances of mobile learning environments and tools before designing for them
description: For a successful learning process, the editorial holds that researchers and practitioners should first define what mobile learning environments and tools uniquely do. It cites Grant (2019) on difficulties in defining mobile learning, analysis, design characteristics and implications. The principle treats mobile learning as distinct from other digital learning rather than a smaller version of it, so design should start from the tool's own affordances.
requirements: Researchers and practitioners must analyze the specific mobile learning environment or tool rather than assuming generic features
target_learning_goals: effective design of mobile learning environments
examples: The editorial cites Grant (2019), 'Difficulties in defining mobile learning: Analysis, design characteristics, and implications,' as the basis for defining affordances before design

title: Consider design issues alongside accessibility, ease of use, and speed when shifting education to mobile and digital technologies
description: The editorial argues that in today's world speed, accessibility and mobility are important themes, and that mobile devices and mobile-compatible applications play an important role in the educational digital shift. However, it states that "In addition to the accessibility, ease of use, and speed features, design issues should also be considered." citation: Hyeonjin Kim and Michael J. Hannafin. (2008). Grounded design of web-enhanced case-based activity. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-006-9010-9
title: Case-based reasoning (CBR) theory as an account of how expertise emerges through experience
description: CBR theory posits that individuals think, reason, and act based on experiences stored as cases. When facing a problem, people retrieve prior cases considered relevant to the new situation, generate a first-approximation solution, and evaluate results. Personal case libraries are indexed, which serves to structure individual case knowledge. The article uses CBR as the grounding theory for designing case-based activity learning environments.
requirements: Learners need access to exemplary expert cases because novices lack their own case knowledge
constraints: The article notes few longitudinal studies exist on how novices become experts through CBA or CBR approaches
target_learning_goals: domain knowledge and expertise development
problem solving
examples: Chess experts retrieving memories of chess positions and appropriate playing methods

article_title: Grounded design of web-enhanced case-based activity
citation: Hyeonjin Kim and Michael J. Hannafin. (2008). Grounded design of web-enhanced case-based activity. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-006-9010-9
title: Case-based activity (CBA) five-phase activity structure
description: CBA is an instructional pattern consisting of five phases: scenario work, what's the story, planning, doing, and telling your story. Scenario work establishes task context; what's the story supports analysis of expert cases; planning involves situation assessment and first-approximation solutions; doing is reflective action on plans; and telling your story supports reflection and transfer through constructing and sharing stories. The phases are designed to scaffold novices through authentic tasks with expert case support.
requirements: Access to expert case libraries
Instructor support and peer review
constraints: Novices tend to develop superficial scenarios without scaffolding
target_learning_goals: authentic problem solving
professional reasoning
transfer of learning
examples: A web-enhanced CBA course for preservice teachers learning to teach with technology, structured from a simple graphing program to WebQuest lesson planning
key_sources: Hyeonjin Kim and Michael J. Hannafin. (2008). Grounded design of web-enhanced case-based activity. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-006-9010-9

citation: Hyeonjin Kim and Michael J. Hannafin. (2008). Grounded design of web-enhanced case-based activity. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-006-9010-9
title: Grounded design: base design decisions on established theory and research in human learning
description: Grounded design is the systematic implementation of processes and procedures rooted in established theory and research in human learning. The article applies this principle by deriving its web-enhanced CBA framework from CBR theory across psychological, pedagogical, technological, and pragmatic foundations, ensuring that design processes and pedagogical activities are informed by available research and theory.
requirements: Designers must identify the theoretical foundations (psychological, pedagogical, technological, pragmatic) relevant to their environment
constraints: The article notes the design foundations are interdependent in practice and cannot be fully isolated

title: Web-based case library as computer-facilitated apprenticeship
description: A web-based case library is a collection of indexed expert (and peer) exemplary cases that reflect the presence of experts, including their situated knowledge and perspectives that function to advise or guide. Multimedia cases present contextual information to increase authenticity and meaningfulness, and web affordances such as hypertext links and search engines allow rapid access to expert cases and resources. Tools help simulate the retrieving of memories in personal case libraries during problem solving.

article_title: Learning critical thinking skills online: can precision teaching help?
citation: Ramasamy, S. (2011). An Analysis of Informal Reasoning Fallacy and Critical Thinking Dispositions among Malaysian Undergraduates. Asia e University. https://www.aeu.edu.my
title: Informal Reasoning Fallacy Instrument (IRFI)
description: The IRFI is a 50-item multiple-choice instrument developed by the author to measure whether someone exhibits strong reasoning by being non-fallacious, covering five fallacies (ad hominem, slippery slope, hasty generalization, post hoc, false analogy). It "functions as a Likert scale" via a scoring rubric adopted from Ricco (2007), Neuman (2003) and Weinstock et al (2004): 0 points for falling into the fallacy trap with poor reasoning, 1 for avoiding the trap with reasonable reasoning, and 2 for strong non-fallacious reasoning, giving a 0-100 range with sub-scales of 0-20. Distracters were compiled from students' most frequently generated poor reasoning in an open-ended first phase, and two critical-thinking experts validated content, choices, rubric and language. Overall Cronbach's alpha was .802, though sub-scale reliabilities ranged from .306 (False Analogy) to .593.
requirements: Expert validation of scenarios, response choices, scoring rubric and language by two critical-thinking experts
A scoring rubric distinguishing poor, reasonable and strong reasoning
constraints: Sub-scale reliabilities were low, including .306 for False Analogy and .476 for Hasty Generalization
target_learning_goals: identifying informal reasoning fallacies
critical thinking
examples: Administered online via surveymonkey.com with no time limit to 259 volunteers, yielding a final sample of 189 after excluding 70 incomplete cases

title: Seven-construct model of critical thinking disposition
description: The article presents the Facione, Facione and Giancarlo (2000) account in which "the dimension of critic al thinking disposition has seven conceptually non -discrete constructs which emphasizes on developing the habitual intention to be truth- seeking, open-minded, systematic, analytical, inquisitive, confident in reasoning, and maturity in making judgments." Dispositions are thought of as a critical spirit and probing inquisitiveness that weak critical thinkers generally lack, and a person may be positively or negatively disposed toward some dispositions but not all equally. The article defines each construct (e.g., truth-seeking as intellectual integrity and a courageous desire for best possible knowledge even against one's beliefs) and operationalises the model through the CCTDI's seven sub-scales, each scored 10-60 with interpretive bands for negative, ambivalent and positive disposition.
requirements: Measurement via the CCTDI's seven sub-scales, each scored 10-60 with interpretive guidelines
constraints: The constructs are conceptually non-discrete
A person can be positively or negatively disposed toward certain thinking skills but not toward all dispositions equally
target_learning_goals: critical thinking dispositions
reflective formation of reasoned judgments
examples: The study used the CCTDI, a 75-item attitudinal measure with 6-point Likert response format, obtaining overall Cronbach's alpha of .843

article_title: The impact of high-immersion virtual reality on anatomy learning, enjoyment, presence, and cognitive load
citation: Kaplan-Rakowski, R., Norton, S., & Wojdynski, T. (2026). The impact of high-immersion virtual reality on anatomy learning, enjoyment, presence, and cognitive load. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10676-1
title: Cognitive affective model of immersive learning (CAMIL)
description: CAMIL is a theoretical framework describing affective and cognitive factors influencing learning within VR, with constructivist foundations. The article states that "CAMIL states that the instructional methods, specifically effective interaction and immersion, enrich the learning experience, thus increasing academic gains rather than the medium of VR." It explains how technological factors such as immersion, control dimensions, and representational fidelity impact presence and agency, subsequently influencing interest, motivation, self-efficacy, embodiment, cognitive load, and self-regulation. The study uses CAMIL to interpret why presence and enjoyment rose while learning fell.
requirements: Instructional methods must channel immersion toward productive cognitive activity for proximal affective benefits to translate into learning
constraints: The article notes that in the absence of carefully aligned instructional methods, proximal benefits may not translate into superior performance on factual knowledge tests
target_learning_goals: factual and spatial knowledge of anatomy and other STEM content
examples: The study used CAMIL to interpret that higher immersion and presence do not guarantee improved learning when the instructional goal is primarily factual and spatial recall of anatomical structures

title: Awake Heart VR anatomy tutorial
description: Awake Heart is a free educational VR application used as the instructional treatment in the study, covering names of heart components, heart functions, and potential medical conditions such as tachycardia and heart murmurs. In it, "study participants explored a highly detailed, anatomically accurate 3D model of the human heart. The treatment combined guided narration with interactive elements that required participants to identify anatomical structures." The video group watched a screencast of the identical tutorial on a standard class projector, with no pausing or rewinding.
requirements: A VR headset (Oculus Quest 2 in the study) for the immersive condition; approximately 16 minutes of session time
constraints: The article notes the intervention was a single 16-minute session, limiting inferences about sustained or cumulative learning outcomes
target_learners: college students without prior medical training
target_learning_goals: heart anatomy: component names, heart functions, and related medical conditions
examples: VR participants moved a virtual hand to study the holographic heart from all directions and clicked labels to receive lectures on heart components

citation: Kaplan-Rakowski, R., Norton, S., & Wojdynski, T. (2026). The impact of high-immersion virtual reality on anatomy learning, enjoyment, presence, and cognitive load. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10676-1
title: Channel VR immersion toward productive cognitive activity aligned with learning goals
description: The article argues that immersion alone does not produce learning; instructional design must direct it. It states that "instructional methods should channel immersion toward productive cognitive activity (e.g., guided manipulation, prompts for self-explanation)" and that improved VR designs "may therefore need to structure interaction more explicitly around core learning goals rather than around free exploration alone." This principle follows from the finding that VR learners enjoyed the lesson more yet learned less than video learners.
requirements: Explicit alignment between interactive VR features and subject-specific learning goals; structured interaction rather than free exploration
constraints: The article frames this as needed for factual, recall-oriented tasks such as anatomy labeling; VR may show advantages for other task types
target_learning_goals: factual and spatial STEM knowledge
examples: The study's VR condition allowed free exploration of a holographic heart, and the authors suggest that designs structured around guided manipulation and self-explanation prompts may better support learning

article_title: How do teachers engaging messages affect students? A sentiment analysis
citation: Samuel Falcon, Jaime Leon. (2023). How do teachers engaging messages affect students? A sentiment analysis. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10230-3
title: Teachers' engaging messages conceptualised through Message Framing Theory and Self-Determination Theory
description: Teachers' engaging messages (TEM) are messages that push pupils to engage in school tasks, characterised by focusing on positive consequences and highlighting the benefits of engaging in a task or warning students if the task is not carried out. The article contextualises TEM with two theories: Message Framing Theory and Self-Determination Theory, the latter distinguishing extrinsic, introjected, identified and intrinsic forms of motivation the messages can appeal to. The study measures TEM with the introjected-benefits subscale of the Teachers' Engaging Messages Scale and tests whether TEM predict students' sentiment and motivation to learn.
requirements: Measured via student reports on the Teachers' Engaging Messages Scale, here the introjected messages focused on benefits subscale (McDonald's Omega 0.91)
constraints: The study analysed only the introjected-benefits subscale rather than all message types
target_learners: secondary school students (mean age 16.39) in mathematics classes
target_learning_goals: students' motivation to learn
students' sentiment about teacher communication
examples: Example TEM quoted in the article: 'If you work hard, you will feel fulfilled' and 'Unless you work hard, you will be disappointed with yourself'

article_title: An editorial on replication studies and scaling up efforts
citation: J. Michael Spector, Tristan E. Johnson, Patricia A. Young. (2015). An editorial on replication studies and scaling up efforts. Education Tech Research Dev 63:1–4. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-014-9364-3
title: Typologies of replication studies (Lykken's three types; Schmidt's direct vs. conceptual)
description: The editorial presents two classifications of replication studies. Lykken (1968) identified three types: literal, operational, and constructive replications. Schmidt (2009) re-categorized them into direct and conceptual replications, "with direct replications being the preferred path by many as they preserve the original instrumentation and approach." ETR&D accepts both direct and conceptual replications.
requirements: Replication studies require access to the original study's instruments and procedures, which the editorial says researchers often withhold
constraints: Literal replication is described as nearly impossible to conduct and may suffer the same experimental biases as the original
target_learning_goals: improving the scientific rigor and generalizability of educational technology research
examples: ETR&D issued a call for papers reporting replication studies following the 2014 National Technology Leadership Summit
key_sources: J. Michael Spector, Tristan E. Johnson, Patricia A. Young. (2015). An editorial on replication studies and scaling up efforts. Education Tech Research Dev 63:1–4. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-014-9364-3

article_title: An editorial on replication studies and scaling up efforts
citation: J. Michael Spector, Tristan E. Johnson, Patricia A. Young. (2015). An editorial on replication studies and scaling up efforts. Education Tech Research Dev 63:1–4. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-014-9364-3
title: Replication studies should be conducted to make educational technology research more scientific and ground large-scale implementation
description: The editorial argues that replications add confidence in findings, enable generalization beyond the original setting, and can identify biases in the original study. ETR&D "urges researchers to conduct such studies so as to make educational technology research more scientific and provide a firm and convincing foundation for large-scale implementations and impact studies."
requirements: Researchers need willingness to conduct replications and access to original instruments and procedures
constraints: Direct replications are preferred by many because they preserve original instrumentation, but the journal accepts conceptual replications too

enabling generalization of educational technology findings
examples: ETR&D welcomes meta-analytic studies that analyze and synthesize experimental findings across related studies

article_title: Unlocking the Everdoor: analyzing the serious game Spiritfarer
citation: Noah Glaser, Lucas Jensen, Tina Riedy, Maggie Center, Jim Shifflett, Joseph Griffin. (2024). Unlocking the Everdoor: analyzing the serious game Spiritfarer. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10357-x
title: Emergent grounded theory: Spiritfarer's game design embodiment elicits personal connections and emotional responses that yield educational and therapeutic benefits
description: The article's central theoretical contribution is a conjecture map (Fig. 1) articulating an emergent theory of the Spiritfarer player experience. As the authors state, "The emergent theory is that Spiritfarer, as a serious game, elicits strong personal connections and emotional responses from players." The theory links game design embodiment (cozy vibes, hand-drawn aesthetics, relaxing music, crafting mechanics, hugging mechanic) to player responses (personal connection, emotional response, long sessions and sharing), then to educational benefits (perceptions on death, palliative care, diverse grieving) and therapeutic benefits (addressing personal loss, emotional acceptance, letting go), culminating in changed outlooks, compassion, and empathy. It was developed through iterative open and axial coding with constant comparison.
requirements: Grounded in LED data analyzed via open coding, axial coding, and constant comparative process until theoretical saturation
constraints: The conjecture map's arrows represent theoretical progression and interrelations, not strict causal links
target_learners: Spiritfarer players aged 15 to 66 in the study's sample
players of commercially available narrative games
target_learning_goals: understanding grief and loss
empathy development
emotional acceptance
examples: The research team mapped codes in a shared Google Drawing and formulated testable propositions from the theory

article_title: Unlocking the Everdoor: analyzing the serious game Spiritfarer

title: Design serious games about difficult topics with cozy, low-stress mechanics and no fail states so emotional engagement is sustained without frustration
description: The article's design recommendation, drawn from participant responses and discussion, is that games addressing heavy themes benefit from comforting, forgiving mechanics. The article reports that "There was no fail state or possibility of losing, and even mistakes were rewarded through crafting," and that the absence of punishment created "a low-stress, forgiving environment that encourages experimentation and exploration." Participants said this ensured engagement without the frustration of potential failure, and that relaxing everyday tasks like farming, crafting, and fishing balanced the emotional weight of the narrative.
requirements: Game mechanics and tasks must remain engaging without overwhelming players
aesthetic and audio elements that convey emotion and comfort
constraints: Derived from one commercially available game and a qualitative player sample; the article presents it as an emergent theory rather than a tested causal design principle
target_learners: players engaging with serious topics such as grief and loss
target_learning_goals: emotional processing of grief and loss
empathy for others' experiences
examples: Spiritfarer downplayed grinding for materials so resource management became enjoyable, and rewarded mistakes through crafting

article_title: From avoidance to ownership: preschool teachers learn to teach code—a case study
citation: Avia Ben-Ari, Tess Gavrielle Levinson, Jessica Blake-West, Marina Umaschi Bers, Rinat B. Rosenberg-Kima. (2025). From avoidance to ownership: preschool teachers learn to teach code—a case study. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10548-0
title: Coding as Another Language (CAL) framework: coding as a literacy acquired through five consecutive stages
description: Coding as Another Language (CAL; Bers, 2019) is a pedagogical approach that "recognizes coding as a form of literacy—as a language like any other", bridging computer science powerful ideas with language arts via the ScratchJr block platform. It stems from three theoretical frameworks: the Curriculum Research Framework, Constructionism, and Positive Technological Development. Bers proposes "five consecutive coding stages"—Emergent, Coding and Decoding, Fluency, New Knowledge, and Purposefulness—corresponding to the accumulative consolidation of traditional literacy, with the Fluency stage marking the shift from learning to read/write/code to using these skills for learning.
requirements: Implementation uses the ScratchJr block-programming platform and the CAL curriculum's 24 lessons combining unplugged and screen-based activities
constraints: The curriculum was originally designed for the U.S. context and aligned to American educational standards, requiring cultural adjustments when implemented outside the U.S.
target_learners: preschool and kindergarten children, including non-writing children
target_learning_goals: basic coding concepts and computational thinking
socio-emotional aspects of learning
creative self-expression
examples: In this study the CAL-ScratchJr curriculum consisted of 45-min long 24 sessions including songs, games, scaffolded coding instruction, exploration and creation, read-aloud story time, and literacy activities, translated into Hebrew

title: Invite teachers to critically adapt a new curriculum and provide accessible support, since agency plus support can dismantle resistance even after brief training
description: The article finds that inviting teachers to adjust a new curriculum where they believe needed, while requiring each modification to be articulated and justified to a research team, helped dismantle initial resistance and fostered ownership. citation: Hengtao Tang, Yu-Ju Lin, & Yingxiao Qian. (2021). Improving K-12 Teachers' Acceptance of Open Educational Resources by Open Educational Practices: A Mixed Methods Inquiry. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-10046-z
title: Technology Acceptance Model (extended TAM 2/TAM 3) as a framework for K-12 teachers' OER acceptance
description: The article frames teachers' OER acceptance using the technology acceptance model, in which perceived ease (PE) and perceived usefulness (PU) determine intention (IN) with attitudes (AT) mediating. It extends this with TAM 2's social influence and cognitive instrumental processes — subjective norm (SN) and job-fit (JF) — and TAM 3's addition of self-efficacy (SE) as a determinant for PE. The article states PE "is also the most fundamental determinant of teachers' IN since it predicts PU and AT." The seven factors structured both the survey instrument and the deductive qualitative coding template.

constraints: The article cautions teacher perception might be influenced by other factors, such as alignment with standards, grades, and subjects

examples: The study measured PE, PU, AT, SE, SN, JF, and IN before and after a renewable-assignment intervention and used TAM theories as the a priori coding template for qualitative analysis

citation: Ronimus, M., Eklund, K., Pesu, L., & Lyytinen, H. (2019). Supporting struggling readers with digital game-based learning. Education Tech Research Dev, 67, 639–663. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09658-3
title: GraphoLearn (GL) adaptive digital reading game
description: GraphoLearn is a serious game for children aged 6–8 that trains phoneme discrimination and grapheme–phoneme correspondence. The player hears a speech sound and clicks the matching letter among alternatives, receiving immediate feedback; trials are short and fast-paced, and content is organized into three difficulty categories chosen by an adaptation mechanism based on previous responses. Engagement is supported by "a labyrinth-like fantasy world and an avatar", with rewards of virtual accessories for completing learning tasks. Difficulty adapts dynamically, with typical success rates of 80–90%.

constraints: The version used trains early reading skills only up to decoding single words

children aged 6–8 at risk for dyslexia

phoneme discrimination
word-level decoding

article_title: Supporting struggling readers with digital game-based learning
citation: Ronimus, M., Eklund, K., Pesu, L., & Lyytinen, H. (2019). Supporting struggling readers with digital game-based learning. Education Tech Research Dev, 67, 639–663. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09658-3
title: Three-component engagement framework (behavioral, cognitive, emotional) applied to game-based learning
description: The article applies Fredricks et al.'s (2004) three-component engagement framework to game-based reading training. Behavioral engagement is defined as observable behaviors such as attentiveness and persistence; cognitive engagement covers "internal investment in learning, that is, the learner's efforts and persistence in attempting to understand and master the given tasks"; emotional engagement refers to positive and negative emotions experienced during the activity. In this study, behavioral engagement was operationalized as exposure time from game logs, cognitive and emotional engagement were measured via child self-reports and parent/teacher evaluations, and in-game success rate was used as a potential mediator between engagement and learning.
requirements: Because self-report measures are problematic with young children, the study used both self-report measures and teachers' and parents' evaluations
constraints: Engagement was assessed only at posttest in a small intervention sample
target_learning_goals: word reading
reading fluency

article_title: Metacognition research in education: topic modeling and bibliometrics
citation: Xieling Chen, Xinyue Li, Di Zou, Haoran Xie, & Fu Lee Wang. (2025). Metacognition research in education: topic modeling and bibliometrics. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10451-8
title: Dataset of 2568 education-category metacognition articles from Web of Science (2000–2023)
description: The study assembled a corpus for bibliometric and topic-modeling analysis by searching WoS with the terms "metacognition*" or "metacognitive*" or "meta-cognitive*" in title, abstract, or keywords, confined to the education category. Two subject matter experts screened 3,801 retrieved publications against inclusion criteria (explicit metacognition focus in education settings, empirical study), achieving an inter-rater reliability score of 96% on 200 randomly chosen articles, yielding 2,568 qualifying publications spanning 2000 to 2023.
requirements: Articles must explicitly mention metacognition or metacognitive components as research focus in education settings and be empirical studies
constraints: Restricted to English-language journal articles in the WoS education category
target_learning_goals: mapping the research landscape of metacognition in education
examples: Two experts independently assessed 200 randomly chosen articles, resulting in an inter-rater reliability score of 96%

article_title: Metacognition research in education: topic modeling and bibliometrics
citation: Xieling Chen, Xinyue Li, Di Zou, Haoran Xie, & Fu Lee Wang. (2025). Metacognition research in education: topic modeling and bibliometrics. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10451-8
title: 19-topic structural topic model of metacognition research in education
description: The article applies a structural topic model (STM) to the abstracts and titles of 2,568 metacognition articles, running 26 candidate models with topic numbers from 5 to 30 and selecting the 19-topic model based on semantic coherence, exclusivity (FREX), and expert verification. The 19 labeled topics include "self-regulated learning", "judgments of learning and memory accuracy", "assessment and feedback", "creative and critical thinking", and "nursing, medical, clinical, and healthcare education". The article states this "marks the inaugural application of topic modeling technology to the field of metacognition". Topics were labeled by two domain experts through a three-step procedure of interpreting discriminating terms, examining representative articles, and unifying labels.
requirements: Optimal model selection based on exclusivity and semantic coherence measures alongside human verification by two experts
constraints: Topics derived from titles and abstracts of WoS education-category articles only
target_learning_goals: identifying prevailing research themes in metacognition
examples: For the topic "creative and critical thinking", experts inspected discriminating terms such as "creative", "creativity", "thinking", "critical", and "divergent" and analyzed representative articles before naming the topic
key_sources: Xieling Chen, Xinyue Li, Di Zou, Haoran Xie, & Fu Lee Wang. (2025). Metacognition research in education: topic modeling and bibliometrics. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10451-8

article_title: Metacognition research in education: topic modeling and bibliometrics
citation: Xieling Chen, Xinyue Li, Di Zou, Haoran Xie, & Fu Lee Wang. (2025). Metacognition research in education: topic modeling and bibliometrics. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10451-8
title: Five correlation-based thematic groups organizing the 19 metacognition research topics
description: Using STM's assumption that documents are mixtures of correlated topics, the article estimated and visualized topic correlations with the "huge" package, plotting a graph where nodes represent topics and shorter connected lines indicate higher positive correlation. The analysis discovered five groups (G1–G5): G1 pairs "self-regulated learning" with "statistical analysis of gender differences"; G2 links collaborative learning/CSCL, digital and online learning, assessment and feedback, healthcare education, and metacognitive models; G3 links epistemic belief revision, scientific inquiry, reflective pedagogy, and teacher education; G4 pairs special/early childhood education with problem-solving; G5 links second language writing with listening/speaking and reading comprehension. The article states these correlations "reveal potential interdisciplinary thematic areas or emerging subfields where further research might be fruitful".
requirements: Topic correlation estimation requires the document–topic proportion distributions from the fitted STM
constraints: Positive correlations (> 0) suggest likelihood of co-occurrence in one article; negatively correlated topics show no connections
target_learning_goals: identifying interdisciplinary thematic areas for future metacognition research
examples: The article suggests metacognition instruction for developing language skills as one direction, evidenced by the close connections among reading and language comprehension, L2 writing and motivation, and listening and speaking

article_title: The handwriting programming language for primary school: aligning computer science education with established teaching practices
citation: Brender, J., El-Hamamsy, L., Giang, C., Mathex, L., Käser, T., & Mondada, F. (2025). The handwriting programming language for primary school: aligning computer science education with established teaching practices. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10503-z
title: The handwriting programming language (HPL) system
description: The HPL system is a computer-vision-based interface that lets students write handwritten program instructions on paper, take a picture with a web-app, and send the decoded commands to a virtual or physical agent (the Thymio robot) for execution. It uses the Google Cloud Vision API to convert handwriting into strings, then maps them to commands via Levenshtein edit distance, with a set of 17 pre-defined instructions that can be expanded. It was designed following the educational robotics learning systems (ERLS) framework and constructive alignment principles, with special attention to aligning with existing primary school classroom practices.
requirements: Requires a device with a camera and web access to run the web-based application
Requires the Google Cloud Vision API for handwriting character recognition
Requires an agent (virtual or physical) to execute the decoded commands
constraints: Implemented for use with the Thymio robot and a syntax resembling Scratch
The mapping was implemented in French and in English but can be adapted to any language decodable by Google Cloud Vision's API
target_learning_goals: Computer science concepts including sequences, loops, and conditional statements
Programming an educational robot
examples: Students write their solution, one line per instruction, in a box in the activity book, then photograph it with the web-app

title: Align new programming tools with teachers' existing classroom practices to increase acceptance
description: The article argues that new CS programming modalities for primary school should be designed to be close to teachers' existing practices, because generalist primary teachers "are generally reluctant to adopt instructional or curricular innovations, specifically those related to technology". HPL embodies this principle by being paper-based rather than tablet-based, requiring no devices beyond those already in classrooms, and using handwriting, a skill already taught. citation: Tim Coughlan. (2020). The use of open data as a material for learning. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09706-y
title: A six-category, 28-theme conceptual framework of open data use in learning
description: The article's conceptual framework organises early-adopter practice into six categories: Characteristics for Learning, Teaching Approach, Open Data in Society, Creating and Sharing, Skills and Knowledge, and Making Data Usable. It was derived from thematic analysis of ten educator interviews, in which "The final refined analysis described below has 6 categories that contain 28 themes". The framework maps perceived strengths of open data, activity designs, societal interactions, collaborative practices, literacy requirements, and the preparation work needed for learning activities, and is offered to support greater use of open data by educators.

citation: Greenhalgh, S. P., Nnagboro, C., Kaufmann, R., & Gretter, S. (2021). Academic, social, and cultural learning in the French #bac2018 Twitter hashtag. Education Tech Research Dev, 69, 1835-1851. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-10015-6
title: The #bac2018 Twitter hashtag as an informal learning context around the French baccalauréat exams
description: The #bac2018 hashtag is a Twitter-based, self-organized space used in the month leading up to the 2018 baccalauréat exams. The article documents "use of the #bac2018 Twitter hashtag in the month leading up to the 2018 baccalauréat exams", where exam-takers and others tweeted practices ranging from sharing notes to joking. The bac itself is described as "significant not only for their role in the French educational system but also for their connections with broader French society and culture", giving the hashtag ties to both schooling and wider culture. It functions here as a data source and an instance of learning in a digital, non-formal context.

other Twitter users engaging with bac-related content

title: A broadened conception of learning encompassing academic, social, and cultural manifestations in digital contexts
description: The article advances a conception of learning that goes beyond academic performance to include social and cultural practices. It argues that skepticism about educational social media reflects "an overly narrow conception of learning that focuses on academic performance and disregards other manifestations". Its analysis of #bac2018 is offered as a demonstration that hashtag practices carry academic, social, and cultural significance simultaneously. The authors conclude that these findings "underline the complexity and richness that characterizes learning—especially in digital contexts".

constraints: The framework is developed from one hashtag around one national exam and is presented as an argument rather than a tested model

target_learning_goals: Recognizing social and cultural learning alongside academic learning

description: This principle holds that judgments about whether a platform like Twitter contributes to learning should account for social and cultural practices as well as academic outcomes. The article argues that narrow, performance-based evaluation produces unwarranted skepticism, since #bac2018 practices "were associated with not only academic learning but also social and cultural practices". title: Video Enhanced Rubric (VER): a digital multimedia application combining video-modeling examples with analytic rubrics
description: The Video Enhanced Rubric is a digital multimedia application that delivers video-modeling examples combined with rubrics to the learner. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09668-1
title: Four-step Roles-Functions-Methods-Guidelines framework for prioritizing and selecting among conflicting design guidelines
description: The article introduces a step-by-step framework to address dilemmas between contradicting design guidelines when fostering complex skill development with multimedia. Designers "propose four steps to prioritize the methodological guidelines over the multimedia guidelines": first identify the role(s) of the artifact, second identify and rank its function(s) per role, third identify the method(s) needed to implement those functions given the target audience, and fourth derive the guideline(s) from the chosen methods in order of importance. Applied to the Viewbrics VER, this yielded two designs: an orientation role prioritizing motivation, and a Preparation, Evaluation and Selection role prioritizing feedback. The authors expect the approach to decrease design tensions for researchers and practitioners.
requirements: The artifact's roles, functions and methods must be identified and prioritized from top to bottom in order of importance before guidelines are selected
constraints: The framework was illustrated with a single use case (the Viewbrics VER in Dutch pre-university education)
target_learners: Educational researchers and practitioners designing multimedia for complex skill development
target_learning_goals: Design of technology-enhanced formative assessment supporting complex skill mastery
examples: In the Viewbrics use case, role 1 (orientation) prioritized motivation via ARCS, while role 2 (Preparation, Evaluation and Selection) prioritized feedback via the FA cycle and 4C/ID

title: Threefold typology of Chinese public opinion profiles toward online education across pandemic phases: affirmative, achievement-based, and critical users
description: The article proposes a typology of public opinion profiles derived from LDA topic modeling of Weibo microblogs across the three pandemic phases. Before the pandemic, users were profiled as "affirmative" because the positive tone in both topics confirmed online education's power to help level up life standards. During the pandemic, when online education became a dominant mode, users were profiled as "achievement-based", concerned with curriculum design and learning effectiveness. After the pandemic, users were profiled as "critical", attending to socio-political consequences, life impacts, and technological aspects.
requirements: LDA topic modeling with perplexity-based selection of the optimal number of topics per phase (2, 4, and 7 topics respectively)
constraints: The authors caution that topics obtained through LDA might not be optimal and that different hyperparameters could have generated more coherent topics
target_learners: Chinese general public discussing online education on Weibo
K-12 and higher education students and their families
target_learning_goals: Understanding public perceptions and acceptance of online learning modes during emergency remote teaching
examples: LDA analysis identified 2 topics pre-pandemic, 4 amid-pandemic, and 7 post-pandemic, with the top 15 tokens per topic translated and thematically integrated into the three profiles
key_sources: Mingming Zhou, Hao Mou. (2022). Tracking public opinion about online education over COVID-19 in China. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10080-5

article_title: Tracking public opinion about online education over COVID-19 in China
citation: Mingming Zhou, Hao Mou. (2022). Tracking public opinion about online education over COVID-19 in China. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10080-5
title: Large-scale Weibo corpus of online-education microblogs spanning pre-, amid-, and post-pandemic phases
description: A dataset of Sina Weibo microblogs about online education collected with a self-developed algorithm using Chinese search terms, filtered to remove zombie and commercial accounts, with user identity details removed. The final dataset included 212,335 microblogs by 87,100 users pre-pandemic, 1,048,575 microblogs by 538,021 users amid-pandemic, and 561,004 microblogs by 287,963 users post-pandemic. Gender information was retrieved from user profiles.
requirements: Gender and other user attributes depend on self-reported Weibo profile information, which the authors note might suffer from unintentional or intentional errors
constraints: The authors argue the sample may be insufficient to generalize observed trends because many netizens voiced opinions on private WeChat Moments instead

article_title: Digital competence for emergency remote teaching in higher education: understanding the present and anticipating the future
citation: Henry Cook, Tiffani Apps, Karley Beckman, Sue Bennett. (2023). Digital competence for emergency remote teaching in higher education: understanding the present and anticipating the future. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10194-4
title: Conceptual frame of eight normative statements characterising university teachers' ERT digital competence
description: The article derives a conceptual frame from a thematic review of 15 empirical studies of teachers' digital competence during the COVID-19 ERT period. The frame comprises eight normative statements grouped under three themes: technologies, preparedness, and experience. As the authors state, "Eight normative statements were derived from the reviewed research literature which applied in Phase 2." The statements range from selecting appropriate technologies to assessing the time demand and value of digital technology integration, and were used as an analytic lens for university framework documents.
requirements: Derived from peer-reviewed empirical studies of teacher digital competency published during the ERT period (2020 through November 2022)
constraints: Characterises digital competence specifically for the ERT period; the authors note the review likely omitted contextual arrangements not yet published
target_learning_goals: Digital competence for teaching and learning in emergency remote contexts
examples: Applied in Phase 2 to code ten Australian university teaching and digital capability frameworks for explicit reference to each normative statement

article_title: Factors contributing to teachers’ acceptance intention to gamified EFL tools: a scale development study
citation: Zhanni Luo. (2024). Factors contributing to teachers' acceptance intention to gamified EFL tools: a scale development study. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10249-6
title: Six-factor framework of teachers' acceptance intention toward gamified learning tools
description: A conceptual framework synthesised from TAM, TAM2, TAM3, UTAUT and related models using grounded-theory grouping of TAM-expanding factors. As the article states, "attitude consists of four constructs: perceived enjoyment, perceived usefulness (PU), perceived ease of use (PEoU), and perceived risks", with PU containing four sub-constructs (relatedness, PU on engagement, PU on academic outcomes, social influence), PEoU containing four sub-constructs (accessibility, compatibility, complexity, user control), plus facilitating conditions and control variables. It served as the basis for item generation in the scale development.
requirements: Intended for measuring or studying teacher acceptance of gamified learning tools; the article notes it can be used or adapted for future studies in gamified learning
constraints: The EFA in this study retained only PU and PEoU, so the full six-construct structure was not statistically supported in this context
target_learning_goals: acceptance intention toward gamified EFL learning tools
examples: Framework factors were regrouped from Table 2 of prior TAM-expanding frameworks, with each factor treated as a code in a grounded-theory process

The final PU scale contains five items and the PEoU scale six items, all on a 7-point Likert format. The article reports the PU scale reached "the value of the internal consistency of 0.899" and both constructs showed AVE above the 0.5 cut-off criterion.

article_title: From sources of self-efficacy to technology integration intentions: a new social cognitive model
citation: Serkan Perkmen, Sara Dexter. (2026). From sources of self-efficacy to technology integration intentions: a new social cognitive model. Educational technology research and development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10623-0
title: Social Cognitive Model of Technology Integration (SCCT adapted for preservice teachers' technology integration intentions)
description: The article adapts a portion of social cognitive career theory (Lent et al., 1994) into a new model extending the Intrapersonal Technology Integration Scale by adding the four sources of self-efficacy (mastery experiences, vicarious information, verbal persuasion, emotional arousal) upstream of self-efficacy, outcome expectations, interests, and intentions. The article states that "SCCT further models that interests form from self-efficacy and outcome expectations, which SCCT models assume are developed because of the learning experiences that provided the four sources of self-efficacy". Path analysis with 144 preservice teachers supported the model, which explained 55% of intention variance.
requirements: Requires measures of sources of self-efficacy, self-efficacy, outcome expectations, interests, and intentions, as provided by SETSES and ITIS
constraints: Tested cross-sectionally with a convenience sample of 144 Turkish preservice teachers in one introductory educational technology course; RMSEA (0.12) exceeded the threshold value
target_learners: preservice teachers in introductory educational technology courses
target_learning_goals: technology integration intentions
self-efficacy for educational technology
