title: Sources of Educational Technology Self-Efficacy Scale (SETSES)
description: A 29-item scale (final 23-item version) developed by the first researcher to measure preservice teachers' perceptions of the four sources of self-efficacy within educational technology coursework: Mastery Experiences (10 items), Vicarious Information (7 items), Verbal Persuasion (5 items), and Emotional Arousal (7 items). Items were drawn from mathematics self-efficacy scales, a qualitative educational technology study, and the researcher's own items. The article reports that "The Cronbach's alpha of the overall scale was found to be 0.90, indicating a high reliability" for the retained 23-item version, and suggests it "can serve as a diagnostic tool for instructors".
requirements: Administered as a 5-point Likert instrument; negative items reverse-scored before analysis
constraints: Discriminant validity only partially established: mastery experiences were not distinct from vicarious information (HTMT 0.91)
target_learners: preservice teachers in educational technology courses
target_learning_goals: measuring sources of self-efficacy for educational technology
examples: Pilot tested with 35 preservice teachers and reviewed by two experts for face validity before the main study

title: Intrapersonal Technology Integration Scale (ITIS)
description: An existing four-subscale measure (self-efficacy, outcome expectancy, interests, intentions) developed by Niederhauser and Perkmen (2008) and validated with 92 U.S. preservice teachers, translated into Turkish by Sahin (2008). Each subscale uses a 5-point Likert scale with scores from 1 to 5; the article reports original alphas of 0.90, 0.93, 0.89, and 0.85. In this study the ITIS provided the downstream components that the new SETSES extends, and the article notes ITIS "did not include sources of self-efficacy" and "truncates at the right-hand side with intentions and goals".

constraints: Leaves off SCCT's activity selection, practice, and performance outcomes, and omits sources of self-efficacy

examples: Combined with SETSES in the path analysis and hierarchical regression reported in this study

citation: Bijl, A., Veldkamp, B. P., Wools, S., & de Klerk, S. (2024). Serious games in high-stakes assessment contexts: a systematic literature review into the game design principles for valid game-based performance assessment. Education Tech Research Dev, 72, 2041–2064. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10362-0
title: Four validity threats framework for traditional high-stakes performance assessment
description: The review organizes its analysis around four validity threats that traditional high-stakes performance assessments pose: test anxiety among candidates, the restricted linearity resulting from combining standardization with construct-relevant tasks, a lack of assessment authenticity, and inconsistencies between raters in scoring performance. It states that "The first validity threat associated with high-stakes performance assessments is the prevalence of test anxiety among candidates", and evaluates serious-game mechanics by their potential to mediate each threat. The framework structures the review's extraction of game mechanics and its design principles.
requirements: Game mechanics selected for game-based performance assessment should be evaluated for their potential to mediate the validity threats and avoid introducing construct-irrelevant variance
constraints: The framework is developed for high-stakes performance assessment of professional competencies in vocational and higher education settings
target_learners: candidates in secondary vocational education, higher education, or vocational settings
target_learning_goals: professional competencies specific to a work setting
examples: The review discusses each threat in turn and maps game mechanics (authenticity, unobtrusive data collection, adaptivity, progress feedback, freedom of gameplay) against them

citation: Weeldenburg, G., Slingerland, M., Borghouts, L. B., Kromkamp, L., van Dijk, B., van der Born, E., & Vos, S. (2024). Evaluation of the digital teacher professional development TARGET-tool for optimizing the motivational climate in secondary school physical education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10379-5
title: TARGET-tool: online teacher dashboard plus mobile student scans guiding a ten-step professional development process
description: The TARGET-tool is a digital CPD tool supporting PE teachers in building an optimal motivational learning climate in secondary school PE. It comprises an online teacher dashboard and student scans on mobile devices, embedding evidence-based TARGET-framework teaching strategies across the task, authority, recognition, grouping, evaluation, and time dimensions as printable cards. Teachers follow predefined steps: profile setup, dimension selection with an optional 62-item SELF-scan, baseline TARGET-scan, strategy selection, experimentation, optional two-item QUICK-scan, and a second TARGET-scan. It was developed via a 14-month participatory design process with researchers, designers, and PE teachers.
requirements: Teachers work with the tool individually and independently; high-quality support materials such as the landing page and introductory video support uptake
constraints: Scheduling student scans and generating passwords was experienced as highly complex
The abundance of motivating strategies was perceived as overwhelming by some teachers
target_learning_goals: Optimizing the motivational PE climate
Building inclusive PE learning environments
examples: Ten PE teachers from 10 Dutch secondary schools implemented the tool with 18 PE classes (399 students) for 4 to 6 weeks

title: Interconnected Model of Professional Growth (IMPG) as a framework for understanding technology-supported teacher professional development
description: The Interconnected Model of Professional Growth (Clarke & Hollingsworth, 2002) is the theoretical framework this study uses to understand how teachers develop skills and knowledge over time. It proposes teachers as active learners who shape their professional development through reflective participation in professional development programs and day-to-day practice. Professional development results from reflection and enactment across four interrelated domains: the external domain (external sources of information or support), the domain of practice (professional experimentation), the domain of consequences (salient outcomes such as student learning or motivation), and the personal domain (teacher knowledge, beliefs, and attitudes). Learning and growth occur when changes in one domain lead to changes in another through reflection and enactment.
requirements: Change in one domain must mediate to another through the processes of reflection and enactment
target_learning_goals: Understanding and supporting teacher professional development processes
examples: The study mapped teachers' TARGET-tool experiences onto the four domains, e.g., experimentation in the evaluation dimension producing an assessment rubric

title: Digital CPD tools should align with CPD prerequisites—active teacher involvement, practice applicability, critical reflection, and iterative experimentation—to support professional growth
description: The article argues that for digital tools to be effective in continuing professional development, they should meet literature-based CPD prerequisites: being evidence-informed, facilitating active teacher involvement, addressing teachers' needs and interests, being aligned with and applicable in professional practice, stimulating critical reflection, supporting iterative cycles of experimentation and reflection within a safe environment, and focusing on student outcomes. The TARGET-tool was designed around these prerequisites, and the evaluation suggests that a tool engaging teachers as active, reflective participants can induce changes across all IMPG domains.

examples: The TARGET-tool operationalizes these prerequisites via student scans for objective data, strategy experimentation in practice, and reflection prompts

citation: Chubko, N., Morris, J. E., McKinnon, D. H., Slater, E. V., & Lummis, G. W. (2020). Digital storytelling as a disciplinary literacy enhancement tool for EFL students. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09833-x
title: DST as a multimodal middle ground that facilitates community-of-practice formation and shared knowledge construction for EFL students
description: The article frames digital storytelling as an educational technology that "establishes a meaningful and inclusive multimodal learning context" in which EFL students with different life experiences, sociocultural backgrounds and proficiencies negotiate concepts. Drawing on communities-of-practice theory, the authors argue the videomaking process encourages students to construct shared knowledge, gives them autonomy, and creates a context for collaboration, with DST serving as a tool for adapting prior beliefs about STEM-A to a video format. In this study the framework explains why video-producing groups showed the largest disciplinary literacy gains.

Teachers should be ready to enter a community of practice with their students and co-construct disciplinary knowledge
constraints: The mechanism account is the authors' interpretation of a small-sample case study; time spent on video production and group composition varied across groups

article_title: The crucial role of theoretical scholarship for learning design and technology
citation: Richard E. West, Peg Ertmer, Susan McKenney. (2020). The crucial role of theoretical scholarship for learning design and technology. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09770-9
title: Two-dimension framework of quality theoretical scholarship: originality and utility
description: The editorial adopts Corley and Gioia's framework for judging theoretical contributions in borrower disciplines. It states that "The authors delineated two key dimensions of quality theoretical scholarship: originality and utility." Originality means contributing new ideas through original synthesis, applications to practice, methodological development, or wholly new conceptual understandings about teaching and learning. Utility means theory matters "to the degree that it is useful and can have an actual impact on the world". The editorial applies this framework to learning design and technology, a field that likewise borrows from many disciplines and speaks to both academics and practitioners.
requirements: Theoretical work must contribute new ideas to the academic discourse, per the originality dimension
constraints: The framework was synthesized for business management, a field the editorial says similarly self-identifies as a borrower discipline
target_learners: education researchers and journal reviewers in learning design and technology
target_learning_goals: evaluating the quality of theoretical scholarship
examples: The editorial used this framework, together with Whetten's practical considerations, to inspire its special-issue review rubric

citation: Richard E. West, Peg Ertmer, Susan McKenney. (2020). The crucial role of theoretical scholarship for learning design and technology. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09770-9
title: Five-criterion rubric for evaluating theoretical scholarship: instructive, scholarly, practical, logical, writing quality
description: The guest editors created an evaluative rubric for reviewers of theoretical papers, rating each criterion on a scale of 1 to 3. The five criteria are that "The article should be… INSTRUCTIVE", SCHOLARLY, PRACTICAL, LOGICAL, and of high WRITING QUALITY. Instructive asks whether the theoretical framework expands current perspective and makes a genuine contribution; scholarly asks whether it suggests new research and/or development directions; practical asks whether it suggests new recommendations for Learning, Design, and Technology practice; logical asks whether the article provides a strong, logical argument using existing literature or evidence; and writing quality covers clarity of expression, flow, and effective use of headings and visuals.
requirements: Reviewers rate each paper on a scale of 1 to 3 for each criterion
constraints: The editors state they do not argue this is the perfect set of criteria, but offer it as a useful start
target_learners: journal reviewers and editors in learning design and technology
target_learning_goals: assessing the rigor and quality of theoretical scholarship
examples: The rubric was offered to the reviewers of the special issue and used to select the articles published in it

description: Peterson's monograph organizes graphs used in instructional materials into seven types. The abstract states: "In general, there are seven types of graphs: multiple bars; divided bar; divided circle; line graph; cosmograph; composite bars; and pictograph." This taxonomy serves as the organizing framework for the monograph's recommendations about matching chart types to common graphic problems in teaching materials.

title: Three thematic clusters organise assistive technology research: enabler of inclusion, barriers to effective use, and possibilities and benefits
description: The review's keyword co-occurrence analysis (VOSviewer) of 45 Key Words Plus from the 31 studies identifies three thematic clusters structuring the field: "AT as an enabler of inclusion and participation" (cluster 1), "barriers to effective use of AT" (cluster 2) and "possibilities and benefits of AT" (cluster 3). Cluster 1 includes terms such as assistive technology, inclusion, software, web, tablet and robotic; cluster 2 highlights teacher training, education, higher education and school; cluster 3 highlights autonomy, participation, social skill, access and motivation. A bibliometric density map places student, disability, assistive technology and teacher in the central yellow zone of highest co-occurrence.
requirements: Keyword co-occurrence analysis using VOSviewer on the automatically extracted keywords of the reviewed studies
constraints: Derived from the 31 studies included in this review, limited to four databases and 2009–2020

target_learning_goals: inclusion and accessibility of the curriculum for students with disabilities

article_title: Assistive technology for the inclusion of students with disabilities: a systematic review
citation: José María Fernández-Batanero, Marta Montenegro-Rueda, José Fernández-Cerero, Inmaculada García-Martínez. (2022). Assistive technology for the inclusion of students with disabilities: a systematic review. Educational technology research and development, 70, 1911–1930. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10127-7
title: Systematic review corpus of 31 empirical studies on assistive technology for students with disabilities (2009–2020)
description: A PRISMA-guided corpus of 31 peer-reviewed empirical studies (2009–2020) on AT for inclusion of students with disabilities, identified from Web of Science, Scopus, ERIC and PsycINFO plus manual reference-list searching. From 216 initially selected articles, duplicates and ineligible items were removed through double screening using inclusion–exclusion criteria (publication date, type, focus, method), yielding the final 31. A data extraction table coded authors, participants, methodological design, results and AT included, citations and country. The review reports that "The sample consists of 31 articles that met the inclusion criteria of this review, out of a total of 216 identified."
requirements: Peer-reviewed journal articles focused on assistive technology in special education, published 2009–2020, using quantitative, qualitative or mixed empirical methods
constraints: Selection restricted to the four databases chosen by the authors, which the authors state as a limitation of the paper
target_learners: students with disabilities in primary, secondary, university and preschool education
target_learning_goals: inclusion, accessibility and participation of students with disabilities
examples: Appendix 1 presents the 31 studies with method, results, citation counts and country, e.g. Bouck, Park & Stenzel (2020) on virtual manipulatives supporting mathematics problem solving
key_sources: José María Fernández-Batanero, Marta Montenegro-Rueda, José Fernández-Cerero, Inmaculada García-Martínez. (2022). Assistive technology for the inclusion of students with disabilities: a systematic review. Educational technology research and development, 70, 1911–1930. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10127-7

article_title: The use of learning analytics and the potential risk of harm for K-12 students participating in digital learning environments
citation: Beerwinkle, A. L. (2021). The use of learning analytics and the potential risk of harm for K-12 students participating in digital learning environments. Education Tech Research Dev, 69, 327–330. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09854-6
title: Local education agencies should establish a clear oversight framework for digital learning analytics before using them
description: The article recommends that before K-12 agencies use the analytics generated by digital learning, they must first put an oversight framework in place. As printed: "local education agencies must first make sure they have a clear framework for oversight of how digital learning analytics will be used." The framework is a precondition for using analytics to improve student learning outcomes.
requirements: Local education agencies must have a clear framework for oversight of how digital learning analytics will be used before employing them.
target_learners: K-12 students in digital learning environments
target_learning_goals: Ethical oversight of student data use in learning analytics
examples: The author urges this step because the 2020 pandemic move to digital learning produced a wealth of digital learning analytics available for improving student learning outcomes.
key_sources: Beerwinkle, A. L. (2021). The use of learning analytics and the potential risk of harm for K-12 students participating in digital learning environments. Education Tech Research Dev, 69, 327–330. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09854-6

article_title: The use of learning analytics and the potential risk of harm for K-12 students participating in digital learning environments
citation: Beerwinkle, A. L. (2021). The use of learning analytics and the potential risk of harm for K-12 students participating in digital learning environments. Education Tech Research Dev, 69, 327–330. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09854-6
title: Willis, Slade, and Prinsloo's typology of ethical approaches to learning analytics
description: The article describes a typology derived from a cross-continental, cross-institutional perspective on ethical oversight of student data in learning analytics. The author writes that the typology "provides different ways to view learning analytics as well as the type of approval(s) possibly needed for each view." It is presented as a starting point that K-12 institutions can use when reviewing their ethical oversight of student data analysis.
requirements: The typology maps views of learning analytics to the type of approval possibly needed for each view.
constraints: The article notes the typology was published before the Covid-19-mandated shift to digital, limiting its support for that shift.
target_learners: K-12 students whose data are analyzed
target_learning_goals: Ethical oversight of student data in learning analytics
examples: The author responds to the typology from a K-12 educational environment perspective.
key_sources: Beerwinkle, A. L. (2021). The use of learning analytics and the potential risk of harm for K-12 students participating in digital learning environments. Education Tech Research Dev, 69, 327–330. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09854-6

article_title: Developing educational materials about risks on social network sites: a design based research approach
citation: Vanderhoven, E., Schellens, T., Vanderlinde, R., & Valcke, M. (2015). Developing educational materials about risks on social network sites: A design-based research approach. Ghent University. https://biblio.ugent.be
title: Four context-sensitive design principles for educational materials about SNS risks
description: Through reflection on all eight studies, the authors revised their initial design principles into four contextually sensitive principles: individual reflection is critical; simulated environments are sufficient; involving parents is beneficial; and a short-term intervention is sufficient. Table 5 maps each revised principle to the initial principle it reinterprets, e.g. collaborative learning becomes "Individual reflection is critical" and authentic setting becomes "Simulated environments are sufficient".
requirements: Materials should build in time for individual reflection before peer discussion
A homework task completed in collaboration with parents is proposed to involve all parents
constraints: The authors acknowledge the principles are context-specific, which jeopardizes external validity; generalizability to other behaviors and cultures requires future research
target_learning_goals: awareness of contact risks on SNSs
safer attitudes and behavior regarding privacy and cyberbullying
examples: The final package combined a one-hour course with a homework task done together with parents, which appeared sufficient to obtain the proposed goals
key_sources: Vanderhoven, E., Schellens, T., Vanderlinde, R., & Valcke, M. (2015). Developing educational materials about risks on social network sites: A design-based research approach. Ghent University. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-015-9415-4

article_title: Developing educational materials about risks on social network sites: a design based research approach
citation: Vanderhoven, E., Schellens, T., Vanderlinde, R., & Valcke, M. (2015). Developing educational materials about risks on social network sites: A design-based research approach. Ghent University. https://biblio.ugent.be
title: Design-based research as a four-step iterative methodology for developing educational materials
description: The article operationalises Reeves' (2006) design-based research model, in which "a design-based approach involves four sequential steps: (1) analysis of practical problems, (2) development of solutions based on existing knowledge, (3) evaluation research of the solutions in practice, and (4) reflection on the produced design principles", with iterative cycles of testing and refinement. The authors applied all four steps with researchers collaborating with practitioners throughout, and argue the full-process demonstration contributes to the design-based research literature.
requirements: Close cooperation between researchers and practitioners, such as educational publishers, developers, teachers and headmasters
Flexibility in methods across iterations to meet newly revealed needs
constraints: The authors note design-based research is very time consuming (three consecutive years for eight studies) and it is difficult to know when the design is good enough to finalize
target_learning_goals: safe behavior on social network sites
media literacy regarding online risks
examples: The study's eight studies were mapped onto the four steps: three exploratory studies, five intervention iterations, and a final reflection producing four design principles
key_sources: Vanderhoven, E., Schellens, T., Vanderlinde, R., & Valcke, M. (2015). Developing educational materials about risks on social network sites: A design-based research approach. Ghent University. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-015-9415-4

article_title: Developing educational materials about risks on social network sites: a design based research approach
citation: Vanderhoven, E., Schellens, T., Vanderlinde, R., & Valcke, M. (2015). Developing educational materials about risks on social network sites: A design-based research approach. Ghent University. https://biblio.ugent.be
title: One-hour SNS contact-risks educational package with syllabus, teacher manual, and parental homework task
description: The developed intervention is a package for secondary education focusing on contact risks (privacy risks, cyberbullying, sexual solicitation), consisting of a pupil syllabus and a teacher manual, with every course lasting one hour. Its fixed structure includes an introduction, an individual exercise on a simulated worst-case SNS profile, class discussion, a voting-cards game, and theory with real-life examples, applying the prevention and constructivist principles in Table 3.
requirements: A teacher manual with learning goals
Materials kept clear, concise and not time-consuming, as stakeholders requested
constraints: The simulated worst-case profile contained so many risks that pupils found it less realistic and could dissociate from it
target_learning_goals: heightened awareness of contact risks on SNSs
decreased unsafe attitudes and behavior on SNSs
examples: Pupils answered questions about a simulated worst-case scenario SNS profile, discussed answers in class, and responded to statements with green or red voting cards
key_sources: Vanderhoven, E., Schellens, T., Vanderlinde, R., & Valcke, M. (2015). Developing educational materials about risks on social network sites: A design-based research approach. Ghent University. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-015-9415-4

article_title: A meta-analysis of technology-delivered literacy instruction for elementary students
citation: Dahl-Leonard, K., Hall, C., & Peacott, D. (2024). A meta-analysis of technology-delivered literacy instruction for elementary students. Education Tech Research Dev (2024) 72:1507–1538. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10354-0
title: ABRACADABRA web-based literacy program
description: ABRACADABRA (A Balanced Approach for Children Designed to Achieve Best Results for All) is a publicly available, web-based literacy program that was the most frequently evaluated program in this meta-analysis's corpus, used in 12 of the 50 publicly available treatment conditions. The article states it "was developed based on the recommendations of the NRP (2000) report and targets a range of skills, including phonological awareness, phonics, vocabulary, comprehension, fluency" and that its "Activities in ABRACADABRA can be customized to a student's specific abilities and challenges." The article cites a meta-analysis of 17 ABRACADABRA studies estimating a weighted average effect of g = 0.26.
requirements: Delivered on a technological device as technology-delivered instruction; in this corpus it was implemented in school settings on computers/laptops
constraints: The g = 0.26 figure is attributed to Abrami et al. (2020), a separate meta-analysis, not computed in this article
target_learners: Students with or at risk for reading difficulties
target_learning_goals: Phonological awareness
Phonics/decoding/word reading
Vocabulary
Comprehension
Fluency
examples: 12 of the 50 publicly available treatment conditions in the corpus used ABRACADABRA, with total instructional hours ranging from 6 to 33 in Table 4
key_sources: Dahl-Leonard, K., Hall, C., & Peacott, D. (2024). A meta-analysis of technology-delivered literacy instruction for elementary students. Education Tech Research Dev (2024) 72:1507–1538. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10354-0

article_title: A meta-analysis of technology-delivered literacy instruction for elementary students
citation: Dahl-Leonard, K., Hall, C., & Peacott, D. (2024). A meta-analysis of technology-delivered literacy instruction for elementary students. Education Tech Research Dev (2024) 72:1507–1538. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10354-0
title: Multicomponent technology-delivered literacy instruction
description: The dominant design pattern in this corpus of technology-delivered elementary literacy programs is multicomponent instruction: almost all programs (90%) addressed multiple literacy skills, averaging four of the seven coded domains (phonological awareness, phonics/decoding/word reading, encoding/spelling, text reading/fluency, vocabulary, comprehension, writing). The article states this finding "is in alignment with recommendations from prior systematic reviews of reading research, such as the NRP (2000) report and the WWC practice guide on effective early reading instruction." Typical dosage averaged 36 minutes a day, 4 days per week, for 18 weeks (about 37 total hours).
requirements: Instruction delivered primarily on a technological device in English
Coverage of multiple literacy domains within one program
constraints: The pattern describes the corpus; the moderator analysis found no statistically significant effect difference associated with any single literacy domain
target_learners: Elementary students in Grades K-5, primarily K-2
target_learning_goals: Reading and writing-related literacy skills including phonics, fluency, phonological awareness, and comprehension
examples: Programs such as ABRACADABRA, Lexia, and Fast ForWord addressed an average of four literacy domains per treatment condition
key_sources: Dahl-Leonard, K., Hall, C., & Peacott, D. (2024). A meta-analysis of technology-delivered literacy instruction for elementary students. Education Tech Research Dev (2024) 72:1507–1538. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10354-0

article_title: Report of three experiments in the use of television in instruction, 1958–59
citation: Cincinnati Public Schools; Holmes, Presley D., Jr. (1959). Report of Three Experiments in the Use of Television in Instruction, 1958-59; Television Research in the Teaching-Learning Process. https://eric.ed.gov
title: Holmes's classification system for organizing television research on the teaching-learning process
description: Holmes developed a classification system for television research information relating to the teaching-learning process. Research information was organized and coded so that it "would be readily and meaningfully available," to identify what is now known and what is not known, thus permitting suggestions for future research. The system is the thesis's organizing artifact and the basis for its trend findings.
requirements: Research information must be organized and coded according to the classification system
target_learning_goals: organizing and synthesizing research on television in the teaching-learning process
examples: The thesis coded research information from television studies to identify what is known and unknown and suggest future research.
key_sources: Cincinnati Public Schools; Holmes, Presley D., Jr. (1959). Report of Three Experiments in the Use of Television in Instruction, 1958-59; Television Research in the Teaching-Learning Process. https://doi.org/10.1007/bf02713451

article_title: Impact of an educational robot-based intervention on second-graders computational thinking skills: experimental evaluation of the Irûmi program in Paraguay
citation: Emma Näslund-Hadley, Juan Manuel Hernández-Agramonte, Humberto Santos, Pablo Zoido. (2026). Impact of an educational robot-based intervention on second-graders computational thinking skills: experimental evaluation of the Irûmi program in Paraguay. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10675-2
title: Irûmi educational robot-based CT program for second graders
description: Irûmi ("companion" in Guaraní) is an educational program developed by OMAPA, Paraguay's MEC, and the IDB to develop CT skills in second-grade students. It combines "a curriculum of 18 classroom activities, supported by a technological kit featuring a robot", with teacher training through four workshops and monthly tutor visits. Activities span Disconnected Activities, Familiarization Activities, and Reinforcement and New Topics, using the Smart Robot Albert, 56 coding cards, and erasable navigation boards.
requirements: A second-grade teacher leading activities with support from student assistants, robots distributed at up to three students per robot, and teacher training workshops plus monthly tutor follow-up visits
constraints: Implementation varied across schools: only 69 percent of teachers attended all four workshops, the average number of activities completed was 14.7 of 18, and 25 percent of schools received materials with delay
target_learners: Second-grade students in Paraguayan public primary schools
target_learning_goals: Computational thinking skills including abstraction, algorithmic thinking, and evaluation
examples: Students create a sequence of instructions for the robot, then scan coding cards using the robot's sensors to execute the sequence on a navigation board; classes ran up to three 40-min sessions per week over 11 weeks
key_sources: Emma Näslund-Hadley, Juan Manuel Hernández-Agramonte, Humberto Santos, Pablo Zoido. (2026). Impact of an educational robot-based intervention on second-graders computational thinking skills: experimental evaluation of the Irûmi program in Paraguay. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10675-2

article_title: I have to go online next week?! Practical suggestions based on Ke (2016)
citation: Nagurney, A. (2021). I have to go online next week?! Practical suggestions based on Ke (2016). Education Tech Research Dev, 69, 149–151. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09870-6
title: When transitioning a course online quickly, design around activation, context/narrative, reflection, and feedback
description: The article's organizing principle is that a fast transition to online teaching should be guided by the themes elucidated by Ke's (2016) systematic review: activation of known material, context and narrative, reflection, and appropriate feedback. It states these are "all major issues to be taken into consideration when designing online courses" and discusses them "from a practical perspective aimed at assisting course instructors when making a fast transition to an online teaching modality."
requirements: Instructors must consider all four themes when transitioning a course to an online format
constraints: The suggestions are framed for instructors making a fast transition to online teaching
target_learners: course instructors making a fast transition to online teaching
target_learning_goals: effective online course design
examples: The article discusses the four themes from a practical perspective for instructors transitioning a course online next week
key_sources: Nagurney, A. (2021). I have to go online next week?! Practical suggestions based on Ke (2016). Education Tech Research Dev, 69, 149–151. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09870-6

article_title: Do teaching staff trust stakeholders and tools in learning analytics? A mixed methods study
citation: Asma Shannan Alzahrani, Yi-Shan Tsai, Naif Aljohani, Emma Whitelock-wainwright, Dragan Gasevic. (2023). Do teaching staff trust stakeholders and tools in learning analytics? A mixed methods study. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10229-w
title: Two-form framework of trust in learning analytics: trust in stakeholders and trust in LA tools
description: The article organises trust in learning analytics by the target of trust, distinguishing "trust in stakeholders" (HEIs and third parties such as technology vendors) from "trust in LA tools". It further treats trust as multidimensional, drawing on dimensions such as competence, privacy and ethics, transparency and consent, usefulness, data accuracy, and prediction precision. The framework structures both the survey items and the interview analysis, and is operationalised via the SHEILA framework's ideal vs predicted expectation approach, where "low predicted expectations indicate that respondents were less confident in LA tools or the ability of their HEIs".
requirements: Measuring trust requires distinguishing the referent of trust (stakeholder vs tool) and comparing ideal against predicted expectations
constraints: The framework was examined with teaching staff in Saudi higher education, an early-stage LA adoption context
target_learning_goals: adoption and trustworthy use of learning analytics for data-informed teaching decisions
examples: The survey measured ideal and predicted expectations across 15 SHEILA items, and interviews were coded into four themes including teaching staff perceptions of trust and distrust in LA tools or stakeholders
key_sources: Asma Shannan Alzahrani, Yi-Shan Tsai, Naif Aljohani, Emma Whitelock-wainwright, Dragan Gasevic. (2023). Do teaching staff trust stakeholders and tools in learning analytics? A mixed methods study. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10229-w

article_title: Enhancing inhibition ability through situational training games: effectiveness, motivation and experience
citation: Sora Chi-Fang Huang, Zhi-Hong Chen, Yu-Tzu Lin. (2026). Enhancing inhibition ability through situational training games: effectiveness, motivation and experience. Education Tech Research Dev 74. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10593-3
title: Situational cognitive training game framework
description: The article proposes a three-component framework for designing cognitive training games that balances training effectiveness, motivation, and context. As printed, "this study proposes a situational cognitive training game framework that integrates cognitive training foundation, motivational design framework, and human–computer interaction framework". The cognitive foundation adopts classic inhibition trainings (Simon and Stroop tasks); the motivational design framework draws on Keller's ARCS model and Yee's gameplay motivation framework, using game elements to enhance challenge, confidence, and satisfaction; the human–computer interaction framework incorporates authentic contexts to promote immersion and engagement.
requirements: Classic inhibition trainings as the cognitive design basis to ensure training effectiveness
Game elements aligned with ARCS factors and Yee's achievement and immersion components
Authentic real-life contexts grounded in the human–computer interaction framework
constraints: Developed and evaluated for inhibition ability, one EF sub-skill, with university students
target_learning_goals: inhibition ability (executive function)
examples: Four games were built on the framework: two button-selection games based on the Simon task and two voice-recognition games based on the Stroop task, set in soccer, baseball, sushi-eating, and pet-training situations
key_sources: Sora Chi-Fang Huang, Zhi-Hong Chen, Yu-Tzu Lin. (2026). Enhancing inhibition ability through situational training games: effectiveness, motivation and experience. Education Tech Research Dev 74. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10593-3

article_title: Enhancing inhibition ability through situational training games: effectiveness, motivation and experience
citation: Sora Chi-Fang Huang, Zhi-Hong Chen, Yu-Tzu Lin. (2026). Enhancing inhibition ability through situational training games: effectiveness, motivation and experience. Education Tech Research Dev 74. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10593-3
title: Situational training game design pattern: authentic scenarios plus progressive challenge and real-time feedback
description: A reusable lesson/game-level design pattern for cognitive training games: embed classic cognitive tasks in authentic real-life situations and layer motivational game elements. The article states that "the game integrated key design elements, including authentic scenarios, sound effects, animations, progressive difficulty stages, time limits, and scoring mechanisms". Progressive stages, timers and scoring serve achievement-oriented motives, while authentic contexts such as restaurants and apartments with animated transitions and sound effects foster presence, relatedness and autonomy.
requirements: Tasks must target a specific EF sub-skill based on classic cognitive assessments
Staged progression with selectable difficulty levels
Immediate feedback via sound effects and animations
constraints: Evaluated in 15-minute single-session training; long-term effects unknown
target_learning_goals: inhibition ability
training motivation
examples: The sushi-eating game is based on the Stroop task, requiring participants to inhibit the interference of color words; the baseball game adds a third-stage rule change requiring response inhibition of previous habitual actions
key_sources: Sora Chi-Fang Huang, Zhi-Hong Chen, Yu-Tzu Lin. (2026). Enhancing inhibition ability through situational training games: effectiveness, motivation and experience. Education Tech Research Dev 74. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10593-3

article_title: Enhancing inhibition ability through situational training games: effectiveness, motivation and experience
citation: Sora Chi-Fang Huang, Zhi-Hong Chen, Yu-Tzu Lin. (2026). Enhancing inhibition ability through situational training games: effectiveness, motivation and experience. Education Tech Research Dev 74. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10593-3
title: Four situational inhibition training games (button-selection and voice-recognition)
description: A series of four digital inhibition training games developed with Construct 3 per the situational cognitive training game framework. As printed, "the game system comprises two types of games: button-selection and voice-recognition games". Button-selection games are based on the Simon task and require suppressing automatic responses across three difficulty stages; voice-recognition games are based on the Stroop task and require verbally responding while inhibiting conflicting visual and textual information. Situations include soccer, baseball, sushi-eating, and pet training, and the system provides immediate feedback and accurate response-time recording.
requirements: Built with Construct 3 for digitalized delivery with precise response-time recording
Tasks derived from classic inhibition trainings (Simon and Stroop tasks)
constraints: Voice recognition accuracy was noted by participants as needing improvement
target_learning_goals: inhibition ability (executive function)
examples: In the baseball button-selection game, the third stage introduces a new rule so that when the pitcher faces right and lowers his leg, the correct response is the left button, opposite from the prior rule
key_sources: Sora Chi-Fang Huang, Zhi-Hong Chen, Yu-Tzu Lin. (2026). Enhancing inhibition ability through situational training games: effectiveness, motivation and experience. Education Tech Research Dev 74. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10593-3

article_title: Conceptualizing a pedagogical model for immersive virtual reality safety training: pedagogical practices in trainer interviews
citation: Lehikko, A., Nykänen, M., & Ruokamo, H. (2025). Conceptualizing a pedagogical model for immersive virtual reality safety training: pedagogical practices in trainer interviews. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10490-1
title: Pedagogical model for IVR safety training with four phases plus trainer pre- and post-training activities
description: A multidisciplinary pedagogical model combining a simulation learning framework, IVR scenarios, and elements of the Cognitive Affective Model for Immersive Learning, framed socioculturally. It proposes "four essential training phases: introduction, IVR briefing, IVR scenario, and debriefing", with facilitated discussions before and after the individually performed IVR scenario enacting social learning. Based on the trainer interviews, the authors "include the trainers' pre- and post-activities in the pedagogical model to encourage the practitioners to strive for a good fit between the training goals, the learners' work tasks, and the organizational safety culture." The model considers learners' sense of agency, presence, body ownership, embodiment, and cognitive load.
requirements: Trainers must be provided with sufficient training and facilitation materials beforehand; some may need coaching and support to create positive learner–facilitator interaction
constraints: The IVR environment used in the interventions only accommodates individual learning; the model has not yet been empirically tested in this study
target_learners: vocational and higher education learners in practice-based learning
target_learning_goals: safety knowledge
safety attitudes and motivation
self-efficacy
procedural and psychomotor skills
examples: Pre-training activities include organizing training programs, choosing pedagogies, and adapting the training to the learners' work context; post-training activities encompass feedback collection and outcome evaluation
key_sources: Lehikko, A., Nykänen, M., & Ruokamo, H. (2025). Conceptualizing a pedagogical model for immersive virtual reality safety training: pedagogical practices in trainer interviews. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10490-1

article_title: Conceptualizing a pedagogical model for immersive virtual reality safety training: pedagogical practices in trainer interviews
citation: Lehikko, A., Nykänen, M., & Ruokamo, H. (2025). Conceptualizing a pedagogical model for immersive virtual reality safety training: pedagogical practices in trainer interviews. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10490-1
title: Align IVR safety training with learners' work context and the organization's safety culture rather than relying on immersive technology alone
description: The article recommends that IVR safety training design begin with the organization's training needs and the learners' immediate work context, followed by carefully formulated objectives and method selection. "Establishing clear, well-formulated goals is fundamental", and "IVR safety training should be aligned with the organization's safety culture." Selecting the scenario topic from the learners' direct work context and using practical examples creates better premises for training transfer, and technological limitations should be considered when designing IVR scenarios and setting goals.
requirements: Identifying the organization's training needs and the learners' immediate work context should be prioritized before formulating objectives and selecting methods
constraints: It is advisable to consider possible technological limitations when designing IVR scenarios and setting goals
target_learning_goals: declarative and procedural safety knowledge
training transfer to daily work
examples: The interviews highlighted selecting the scenario topic from the learners' direct work context and using practical examples; aligning training concepts with safety practices and operating procedures supports declarative and procedural goals
key_sources: Lehikko, A., Nykänen, M., & Ruokamo, H. (2025). Conceptualizing a pedagogical model for immersive virtual reality safety training: pedagogical practices in trainer interviews. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10490-1

article_title: Analyzing learners’ engagement and behavior in MOOCs on programming with the Codeboard IDE
citation: Gallego-Romero, J.M., Alario-Hoyos, C., Estévez-Ayres, I. et al. (2020). Analyzing learners' engagement and behavior in MOOCs on programming with the Codeboard IDE. Education Tech Research Dev 68, 2505–2528 (2020). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09773-6
title: Codeboard web-based IDE integrated into MOOCs via IMS LTI
description: Codeboard is an open-source, web-based development environment that lets learners "code directly in Codeboard without installing any additional software locally", supporting multiple languages (Java, C, C++, Python). Teachers provide base code and test cases; activities integrate into MOOC learning sequences through the IMS LTI standard and scale to thousands of concurrent learners. In this study a modified local instance collected compilation, execution, access and code data across 117 activities in three Java MOOCs on edX.
requirements: A local installation with code modifications is needed for low-level data collection, as Codeboard has no API for data collection
IMS LTI support in both platform and tool for seamless integration
constraints: Activity logs originally lack compilation/execution results, requiring an added description field
target_learners: MOOC learners on introductory Java programming
target_learning_goals: Learning-by-doing programming skills in Java
examples: Three 5-week Java MOOCs on edX used 38, 25 and 54 Codeboard activities respectively, all formative, with base code and weekly solutions provided
key_sources: Gallego-Romero, J.M., Alario-Hoyos, C., Estévez-Ayres, I. et al. (2020). Analyzing learners' engagement and behavior in MOOCs on programming with the Codeboard IDE. Education Tech Research Dev 68, 2505–2528 (2020). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09773-6

article_title: Analyzing learners’ engagement and behavior in MOOCs on programming with the Codeboard IDE
citation: Gallego-Romero, J.M., Alario-Hoyos, C., Estévez-Ayres, I. et al. (2020). Analyzing learners' engagement and behavior in MOOCs on programming with the Codeboard IDE. Education Tech Research Dev 68, 2505–2528 (2020). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09773-6
title: Balance seamless anonymous access to external MOOC tools against requiring learner commitment in exchange for additional features
description: The article's main design implication is that integrating external tools in MOOCs involves a trade-off: the most seamless design lets learners use the tool anonymously with no extra registration, while requiring registration (an extra commitment step) unlocks persistence features such as saved progress. The authors "suggest the need for a trade-off between designing MOOCs that allow a very easy and anonymous access to external tools aimed for a more active learning, and forcing learners to give a step forward in terms of commitment in exchange for benefitting from additional features".
requirements: The external tool must offer additional features (e.g., saved progress) that only registered users can access
constraints: The study is observational; registration self-selection means the engagement gap cannot be attributed causally to registration
target_learners: MOOC learners, including those unwilling to complete extra registrations
target_learning_goals: Active learning and learning-by-doing activities within MOOCs
examples: In the three Java MOOCs, learners could either work anonymously (base code reset each visit) or register in Codeboard to keep their latest modified code across activities

article_title: Development and implementation of an IVR-based assessment system for student teachers’ professional vision
citation: Liu, T.-C., & Lin, Y.-C. (2025). Development and implementation of an IVR-based assessment system for student teachers' professional vision. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10463-4
title: IVR-based PVAS: an immersive virtual reality assessment system for student teachers' professional vision
description: The IVR-based PVAS is an IVR technology-based professional vision assessment system built in Unity 3D that simulates a middle school classroom with 20 virtual students. Participants act as the instructor, look around freely from a first-person perspective via an HMD, click on students whose behaviour concerns them (perception subtask), and select multiple-choice reasons for misbehaviour while optionally consulting a virtual tablet of student backgrounds (interpretation subtask). The system records fields of view, clicking actions, and log data, and administers a mental effort rating scale after each event. The article states it was developed 'through a design-based research (DBR) approach' across four phases with an expert group.
requirements: An HMD and two Oculus Touch controllers; a backend script editing system for positioning virtual students and editing classroom events
constraints: The classroom scenario represents only one relatively representative type among many possible classroom situations rather than encompassing all types of classroom settings
target_learning_goals: professional vision: perceiving and interpreting student misbehaviour for classroom management
examples: Twenty-four student teachers were assessed on seven classroom events involving three distraction-related misbehaviours, two instructional situations, five seat positions, and four student backgrounds
key_sources: Liu, T.-C., & Lin, Y.-C. (2025). Development and implementation of an IVR-based assessment system for student teachers' professional vision. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10463-4

article_title: Development and implementation of an IVR-based assessment system for student teachers’ professional vision
citation: Liu, T.-C., & Lin, Y.-C. (2025). Development and implementation of an IVR-based assessment system for student teachers' professional vision. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10463-4
title: Four-phase design-based research process for developing an IVR-based assessment system
description: The article organises the development of the IVR-based PVAS as a design-based research process combining scientific investigation with systematic solution development, emphasising iterative design, development, and evaluation with researcher–practitioner collaboration. The four phases are: (1) problem analysis and potential solution, (2) needs assessment and identification of design criteria via focus group interviews with an expert group, (3) design and construction of classroom events, assessment environment, and assessment task, and (4) evaluation and improvement with in-service teachers. The article states 'The development of the IVR-based PVAS included four phases,' and that the approach enabled continuous improvement and deep insight into student teachers' professional vision.
requirements: Collaboration between researchers and an expert group of practitioners (here: two IVR/e-assessment experts, three expert teachers, one classroom management specialist)
target_learning_goals: assessment of professional vision for classroom behaviour management
examples: Phase 2 used two two-hour focus group interviews yielding design criteria for the assessment environment, misbehaviour characteristics, and assessment task features; Phase 4's evaluation led to adding chair-rocking sounds and participant instructions

article_title: Development of software to support argumentative reading and writing by means of creating a graphic organizer from an electronic text
citation: Mochizuki, T., Nishimori, T., Tsubakimoto, M., Oura, H., Sato, T., Johansson, H., Nakahara, J., & Yamauchi, Y. (2019). Development of software to support argumentative reading and writing by means of creating a graphic organizer from an electronic text. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09676-1
title: Argumentative reading and writing software with Document, Knowledge Map, and Essay Editor panes and dynamic quotation nodes
description: The software supports argumentative reading and writing for novice students through three linked panes: "the Document pane, where a user reads, underlines, highlights and annotates a text; the Knowledge Map pane, where a learner generates a knowledge map based on the text"; and an Essay Editor pane. Dragging underlined or highlighted text onto the map automatically creates quotation nodes that copy the portion and its color, and these update dynamically when the underline changes. Learners add personal idea nodes, link them to quotation nodes, and drag nodes into the Essay Editor to create uneditable quotations carrying source information, word count, and quotation ratio to discourage plagiarism and distortion of the author's ideas.
requirements: Students need instruction in a simplified Toulmin's model and a training text before using the software for argumentative reading and writing
A stylus and tablet PC environment, since none of the evaluated students had prior experience reading digital texts with a stylus
constraints: Color meanings are not fixed; the learner or teacher adjusts definitions to the appropriate school level or purpose
The essay quotation function intentionally prevents direct editing of quoted content
target_learners: Novice undergraduate students with no prior argumentative reading and writing education
target_learning_goals: Argumentative reading: identifying an author's claims and grounds
Argumentative writing: building constructive opinions on a text's argument
examples: In the classroom study, the knowledge-mapping class created knowledge maps from underlined and/or highlighted portions of the target text and wrote essays while viewing the maps, while the non-knowledge-mapping class wrote essays after underlining without maps

citation: Akinkuolie, B., & Shortt, M. (2021). Applying MOOCocracy learning culture themes to improve digital course design and online learner engagement. Education Tech Research Dev, 69, 369–372. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09936-5
title: MOOCocracy learning culture themes as a framework for understanding MOOC learning culture
description: The MOOCocracy themes, drawn from Loizzo and Ertmer's (2016) study of "the learning culture of massive open online courses", serve as an organizing framework for thinking about MOOC design. In this response commentary, the authors use the themes as the lens through which "key ideas, value, and future research implications are addressed in relation to MOOC design". The framework treats MOOCs as having a distinctive learning culture that designers should attend to when building digital courses and seeking to engage online learners.
requirements: The framework is applied to MOOC design contexts, as in the source commentary's relation of the themes to digital course design
constraints: The framework derives from Loizzo and Ertmer's (2016) MOOCocracy study; this article is a response commentary and reports no new empirical data
target_learners: online learners in massive open online courses
target_learning_goals: engagement and learning in massive open online courses
examples: The commentary addresses key ideas, value, and future research implications of the MOOCocracy study for MOOC design using its themes

article_title: DUDA: a digital didactic learning unit based on educational escape rooms and multisensory learning activities for primary school children during COVID-19 lockdown
citation: Walter Setti, Rebecca Tarello, Erica Volta, Lucia Ferlino, Monica Gori, Gualtiero Volpe. (2025). DUDA: a digital didactic learning unit based on educational escape rooms and multisensory learning activities for primary school children during COVID-19 lockdown. Education Tech Research Dev 73. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10407-4
title: D-UDA: a digital didactic learning unit combining an escape room with multisensory games for fifth-grade mathematics
description: D-UDA (unità didattica di apprendimento digitale) is a website-based digital learning unit for fifth-grade mathematics, offered during the first Italian COVID-19 lockdown. The article states that "The D-UDA experience was divided into two parts: the virtual classroom and the virtual archeological site." The first part contains logic puzzles aligned with INVALSI national test frameworks; the second contains multisensory Scratch games, a Domus escape room, and a robot-programming activity in OpenRoberta. It was integrated into the curriculum in agreement with teachers.
requirements: Built only with freely available technologies such as Scratch and G-Suite to foster the inclusion of children with economic difficulties
Conducted under supervision of at least one teacher and the experimenter who intervened in case students encountered difficulties
constraints: Tools used are very basic and not easily usable on all browsers
target_learners: Fifth-grade primary school children, including those with sensory impairments or economic difficulties
target_learning_goals: Fifth-grade mathematics (numbers; space and figures; relations, data and forecasts)
Transversal competencies such as cooperation and engagement
examples: Fifty-four fifth graders from four classrooms in the Dimensione L'UDA project tested D-UDA in June 2020 during lockdown

title: Sequential educational escape room structure for a digital learning unit
description: The unit adopts the escape room model, relying on the EscapED theoretical framework and Nicholson's puzzle-organization typology. The authors state: "We applied the sequential structure, where players must solve the puzzles one at a time, and the final puzzle allows them to win the game." In D-UDA, solving classroom riddles yields a code linking to Scratch games, whose completion yields puzzle pieces composing a feather that unlocks the final Domus escape room. A narrative character, a cycling-traveler archaeologist, links the enigmas.
requirements: A narrative link connecting all enigmas
Puzzles organized so each solved puzzle yields access to the next stage
target_learning_goals: Logical-mathematical problem solving within a game narrative
examples: Four classroom enigmas (e.g., a Caesar's cipher puzzle about Emperor Titus) unlock a code leading to the virtual archaeological site games

title: Three-dimensional construct of student engagement (behavioral, emotional, cognitive)
description: The article adopts the framework that engagement is a multidimensional construct underpinning academic success. As printed: "Scholarly discourse further delineates engagement as a complex construct, comprising three essential dimensions: behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement (Fredricks et al., 2004)." Behavioral engagement covers participation in academic, social, or extracurricular pursuits; emotional engagement covers attitudes toward teachers, peers, academics, and school; cognitive engagement entails thoughtful effort with intricate concepts. D-UDA's multisensory group activities were designed to enhance behavioral engagement and teamwork.

target_learning_goals: Behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement in learning activities
examples: D-UDA's cooperative multisensory games were chosen to highlight effects on teamwork and potential to enhance students' behavioral engagement

article_title: A large-scale implementation of predictive learning analytics in higher education: the teachers’ role and perspective
citation: Herodotou, C., Rienties, B., Boroowa, A., Zdrahal, Z., & Hlosta, M. (2019). A large-scale implementation of predictive learning analytics in higher education: the teachers' role and perspective. Education Tech Research Dev, 67, 1273–1306. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09685-0
title: OU Analyse (OUA) predictive learning analytics system and dashboard
description: OUA is a PLA system built at the Open University UK that "uses a range of advanced statistical and machine learning approaches to predict students at-risk so that cost-effective interventions can be made." It combines four predictive models (Naïve Bayes, CART, k-NN with demographic data, k-NN with VLE data) via voting to predict whether students will submit their next teacher-marked assessment and complete the course. Teachers access predictions through a dashboard showing cohort comparisons, per-student predictions, and nearest-neighbour views; contact with students happens outside the dashboard.
requirements: Machine learning models are trained on legacy data from the previous presentation of the same course
Weekly VLE interaction data and student demographics must be recorded and available
constraints: Predictions target only students who have not yet submitted the next TMA
Accuracy is relatively stable across presentations but increases toward the end of a course presentation
target_learners: distance learning higher education students in Level 1 undergraduate courses
target_learning_goals: assignment submission
course completion and retention
examples: Predictions are computed weekly from static (demographic) and behavioural (VLE activity types such as forum, content, resource, glossary, wiki) data, with precision, recall, F-measure and accuracy tracked per week (Fig. 1)

title: Technology Acceptance Model and Academic Resistance Model as combined lenses on teachers' PLA adoption
description: The article uses the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Academic Resistance Model (ARM) together to explain why some teachers engage with predictive learning analytics. TAM explains usage via "perceived usefulness" and "perceived ease of use"; ARM explains resistance through three attitude dimensions: cognitive (beliefs about PLA accuracy), emotional (feelings about being monitored or replaced), and intentional (plans to use or resist the technology). The authors argue the models complement each other, with perceived usefulness overlapping cognitive attitudes and anxiety about complexity spanning both models.
requirements: Both models are needed because TAM focuses on technology design and use while ARM addresses attitudes to organisational change
constraints: The article applies these lenses interpretively to interview data from six self-selected teachers, not as a tested model
target_learners: teachers and associate lecturers in distance higher education
target_learning_goals: adoption and effective use of predictive learning analytics in teaching practice
examples: Interview questions were organised around TAM pillars (impact on teaching, ease of use) and ARM pillars (concerns and feelings, future intentions)

citation: Elaish, M. M., Al-Azawei, A., Yadegaridehkordi, E., Hussein, M. H., Hwang, G.-J., Majoul, B., Ouchaouka, L., & Alaaraj, S. (2026). A comparative study of students' adoption and usage of mobile learning in developing countries: Tunisia, Morocco, and Libya. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10613-2
title: Extended UTAUT model integrating Hofstede's cultural dimensions, Trust, and Compatibility for m-learning acceptance
description: The study proposes an acceptance model grounded in UTAUT — whose constructs are Performance Expectancy, Effort Expectancy, Social Influence, Facilitating Condition, Behavioural Intention, and Use Behaviour — extended "by also drawing on Hofstede's Cultural Dimension theory (Hofstede, 1980), Trust (TR), and Compatibility (COMP)". The model posits thirteen hypotheses linking these constructs to behavioural intention and use behaviour, and was tested with SEM on student samples from three developing countries. It provides a context-sensitive framework for studying technology acceptance where cultural and economic factors matter.
requirements: Measurement of UTAUT, Hofstede, Trust, and Compatibility constructs via validated questionnaire items adapted from prior studies
Sample size following the rule of at least 10 times the number of indicators or structural paths
constraints: Developed and tested for m-learning acceptance among university students in developing countries (Tunisia, Morocco, Libya)
Data collected only from selected regions within each country
target_learning_goals: Acceptance and adoption of mobile learning technologies
examples: The model was tested on 588 respondents (147 Tunisia, 243 Morocco, 198 Libya) using SmartPLS, with country and academic year as control variables

article_title: Developing a quality curriculum in a technological era
citation: Twining, P., Butler, D., Fisser, P., Leahy, M., Shelton, C., Forget-Dubois, N., & Lacasse, M. (2021). Developing a quality curriculum in a technological era. Education Tech Research Dev, 69, 2285–2308. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09857-3
title: A sociocultural framework of educational alignment spanning national, local school and classroom levels
description: The article introduces a sociocultural framework for understanding curriculum change. As the abstract states, it "introduces a sociocultural framework that highlights the complexity of achieving alignment between policies and practice spanning the national to local school to classroom levels." The framework treats alignment as a multi-level problem: policies set at national level must be realised in local schools and ultimately in classrooms, and misalignment across these levels explains why curriculum reforms fail. It frames the three key issues the paper explores as underpinning this alignment.
requirements: Alignment must be achieved across national policy, local school and classroom levels simultaneously
constraints: The framework is presented as highlighting complexity rather than prescribing a single implementation mechanism
target_learners: education system stakeholders, from national policy makers to classroom teachers
target_learning_goals: designing and implementing national curricula that reflect changes in the world outside school
examples: The paper uses the framework to organise its expert-based exploration of stakeholder engagement, teacher professionalism and summative assessment
key_sources: Twining, P., Butler, D., Fisser, P., Leahy, M., Shelton, C., Forget-Dubois, N., & Lacasse, M. (2021). Developing a quality curriculum in a technological era. Education Tech Research Dev, 69, 2285–2308. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09857-3

article_title: An educational model of equity and computing: a study of marginalized student experience during COVID pandemic
citation: Li, Q., Moallem, M., Boettinger, J., Cai, Q., & Levi, M. (2024). An educational model of equity and computing: a study of marginalized student experience during COVID pandemic. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10443-0
title: Equity-5C (E-5C) model for computing education
description: The E-5C model is a prescriptive model aiming to achieve equity in computing education, grounded in social cognitive theory and social cohesion theory. The article states that "the model depicts five key elements (5Cs), communication, collaboration, confidence, curriculum, and career pathways, each represented by a circle," with computing equity at the center. The circular design reflects no hierarchy or fixed order, and double-arrowed lines indicate the elements may overlap and influence each other. The model guided the design of the Girls Who Code clubs and served as an advanced organizer for the ideas included.
requirements: Careful curriculum design grounded in evidence-based theoretical perspectives
Continued communication and interactions amongst stakeholder groups such as teachers/facilitators, students, and parents
constraints: The article states the model can be adapted for a virtual environment only with a slight modification of each element
target_learners: K-12 students, particularly girls and other underserved or underrepresented groups
target_learning_goals: Develop interest in computer science
Develop computational thinking skills
Promote equity in computing education
examples: The model was implemented in two Girls Who Code clubs (grades 3–5 and 6–12) on a university campus, using project-based learning with Scratch and later VexGo robotics

title: Hilton's (2016) 16-study review of OER efficacy and perceptions
description: The reviewed artifact is Hilton's (2016) review in Educational Technology Research and Development, which "synthesized findings of 16 studies that investigated the academic outcomes of open educational resources (OER) and perceptions of college students and instructors." The commentary uses it as the evidence base for international perspectives on OER in online learning, examining its value, implications, and limitations.
requirements: The review synthesizes studies of OER academic outcomes and of student and instructor perceptions
constraints: The review addresses college textbook choices and college students and instructors, per the article's account
target_learning_goals: academic outcomes when using OER instead of traditional textbooks
examples: The commentary examines the review from international perspectives and suggests future directions

article_title: Instructional design students’ design judgment development
citation: Muruvvet Demiral-Uzan, Elizabeth Boling. (2024). Instructional design students’ design judgment development. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10361-1
title: Nelson and Stolterman's typology of design judgment, operationalized for instructional design practice
description: This framework conceptualizes design judgment as the ability to gain subconscious insights abstracted from experience and reflection in complex, indeterminate situations, and identifies multiple forms of judgment exercised across design situations. The article operationalizes the types for ID as a coding framework: "framing, deliberated off hand, default, core, instrumental, appearance, appreciative, connective, compositional, navigational, and quality." Table 1 defines each type with sample actions in the ID process, and the framework was extended as new actions were identified in interview data.
requirements: Coding requires an operationalization of each judgment type with sample actions in the ID process, as provided in Table 1
Identifying judgments requires access to design documents and interviews about students' thinking at moments of judgment
constraints: The article notes students might not know the constructs, so judgments were inferred from accounts of thinking processes rather than direct reports
The study did not aim to generalize findings across ID students or courses
target_learning_goals: exercising and developing design judgment in real-world instructional design projects
examples: Table 4 demonstrates coding of one interview excerpt in which a single material-selection moment was coded as framing, connective, instrumental, appreciative, navigational, and quality judgments
key_sources: Muruvvet Demiral-Uzan, Elizabeth Boling. (2024). Instructional design students’ design judgment development. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10361-1

article_title: Instructional design students’ design judgment development
citation: Muruvvet Demiral-Uzan, Elizabeth Boling. (2024). Instructional design students’ design judgment development. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10361-1
title: Reflection-in-action as the lens for explaining design judgment development
description: Drawing on Schön (1983), the article treats reflection-in-action—reflection made while designing—as the mechanism through which design judgment develops. The article states that reflections "can be made while designing (reflection- in-action), and that these are key to development of design judgment." In the analysis, each coded judgment was re-coded for whether reflection was employed, using indicators such as whether consequences of choices were considered, moves were tried out, and inquiry was involved, linking reflective practice to judgment development over the semester.
requirements: Indicators for coding reflection: consideration of consequences of choices, trying out design moves, and inquiry in the design situation
Data must allow reconstruction of students' thinking at moments of judgment, e.g., interviews prompted by design documents
constraints: Because experienced students may have reflected previously, it can be difficult to capture whether a judgment was made with reflection, as reported for Husain
target_learners: master's-level instructional design students in introductory ID courses
target_learning_goals: developing design judgment through reflective design practice
examples: Segments where students deeply considered and questioned what they had done and why were coded as design judgment made with reflection; statements without these indicators were coded as lacking reflection

article_title: Using social media affordances to support Ill-structured problem-solving skills: considering possibilities and challenges
citation: Adrie A. Koehler, Daniela Rezende Vilarinho-Pereira. (2023). Using social media affordances to support Ill-structured problem-solving skills: considering possibilities and challenges. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-10060-1
title: Five prominent educational affordances of social media: association, visibility, persistence, searchability, and identity creation
description: The article synthesizes prior affordance frameworks (e.g., Treem and Leonardi; Boyd; Xue and Churchill) and identifies the affordances named at least three times across articles. It states: "we identified five prominent affordances: association, visibility, persistence, searchability, and identity creation." Affordances are treated as relations between agent abilities and environment features rather than tool properties, and the article maps how each affordance is embodied differently across applications (wikis, blogs, Instagram, Snapchat, Facebook) and how each can support problem finding and solution generation in problem-centered learning.
requirements: Affordances exist only in relation to a user's abilities and a specific context, so tool selection must connect to the context and audience
constraints: Social media applications are constantly being created, updated, and discontinued, so affordance-based analysis rather than tool-specific analysis is needed
target_learners: K-12, undergraduate, and graduate learners in problem-centered learning
target_learning_goals: Ill-structured problem-solving skills, including problem finding and solution generation
examples: Table 4 compares how wiki, blog, Instagram, Snapchat, and Facebook embody association, visibility, persistence and searchability, and identity

article_title: Theory-driven design and validation of a tool to enhance academic focus
citation: Michael D. Mrazek, Dustyn S. Ransom, Amy R. Texter, Calvin V. Tower, Bryce A. Rutila, Thomas F. Kennedy, Elijah J. Woodson, Jonathan W. Schooler, Alissa J. Mrazek. (2026). Theory-driven design and validation of a tool to enhance academic focus. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10730-y
title: Focus Coach digital study tool
description: The Focus Coach is a no-cost, publicly available digital study tool that students keep open on their phone or computer while completing a separate academic assignment. It supports attention training through customizable sessions, real-time self-monitoring via periodic check-ins asking “Just then, how focused were you?”, and progress tracking via an end-of-session graph of focus. It occupies the full phone screen to block unrelated apps, offers curated ambient soundtracks, and lets teachers view engagement patterns while individual responses remain private. It complements a brief online course teaching anchoring, focusing, and releasing distractions.
requirements: Used during real academic work (independent work or homework), typically alongside the online attention-training course; students customize session duration, check-in frequency, check-in sound, and optional ambient soundtrack.
constraints: The article notes it is not possible to assess focus trajectories without the tool, and the tool and course were delivered together, so unique component effects cannot be disentangled.
target_learners: adolescent middle and high school students in public schools
target_learning_goals: sustaining attention and self-regulating focus during academic work
examples: In Study 1 students completed an average of 6.4 Focus Coach sessions (SD = 3.9) averaging 20.4 minutes, answering 2.6 check-ins per session; in Study 2, 5.3 sessions averaging 16.3 minutes.
