Theory-driven design and validation of a tool to enhance academic focus. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10730-y

article_title: Theory-driven design and validation of a tool to enhance academic focus
citation: Michael D. Mrazek, Dustyn S. Ransom, Amy R. Texter, Calvin V. Tower, Bryce A. Rutila, Thomas F. Kennedy, Elijah J. Woodson, Jonathan W. Schooler, Alissa J. Mrazek. (2026). Theory-driven design and validation of a tool to enhance academic focus. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10730-y
title: Eleven-principle theory-driven design framework for attention-training interventions
description: The article organizes intervention design around 11 scientific insights and corresponding design strategies drawn from educational psychology and cognitive science: seamless classroom integration, reduced need for transfer, motivation-enhancing framing, strong attentional sets, self-monitoring of attention, external accountability, positive reinforcing feedback, distraction recovery, environmental constraints on distraction, an optimal auditory environment, and shaping classroom culture and shared norms. The authors state that “Effective interventions are rarely built from a single insight; they succeed by combining multiple, mutually reinforcing design choices,” and that no existing attention-training intervention had integrated these principles into a single tool. The framework guided the Focus Coach's two-year iterative development.
requirements: Principles are individually supported by prior research; the framework assumes students value attention as a skill worth developing and that interventions minimize teacher burden to be sustainable.
constraints: The article notes restrictive strategies such as device bans can fail, and that the framework was developed and evaluated in K-12 settings with adolescents.
target_learners: K-12 students across grade levels and subject areas
target_learning_goals: attentional focus and self-regulated learning during academic tasks
examples: Principle 5 and 6 were implemented as intermittent check-ins that prompt self-monitoring and create accountability; Principle 9 as full-screen phone display; Principle 10 as curated looping ambient soundtracks.

article_title: Supporting school teachers’ rapid engagement with online education
citation: Abaci, S., Robertson, J., Linklater, H., & McNeill, F. (2021). Supporting school teachers' rapid engagement with online education. Education Tech Research Dev, 69, 29-34. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09839-5
title: Philipsen et al.'s framework of six synthesized findings as important components of TPD for online and blended learning
description: The framework, from a systematic meta-aggregative review of 15 published studies based on Desimone's (2009) model, is composed of six synthesized findings (SF1-SF6), each leading to an action recommendation presented as "important components" in a framework model. The components cover designing a supportive TPD programme and environment, acknowledging the existing OBL context, addressing teacher change, determining goals and relevance, acknowledging TPD strategies, and disseminating knowledge and evaluating the TPD. The authors apply it as a reflection tool for their emergency remote teaching support and find it "a useful reflection tool to guide professional learning for teachers beyond the emergency situations".
requirements: A systematic review with credible qualitative data underlies the framework; applying it requires mapping local support activities to its six synthesized findings
constraints: All but one of the reviewed studies were situated in a higher education context, so the framework is biased toward higher education settings
target_learners: course developers of teacher professional development
target_learning_goals: professional learning for online and blended teaching
pedagogical skills relevant to online teaching
examples: The authors structured online seminars mixing peer presentations by fellow teachers with theoretical ideas, mapping this to SF5 on TPD strategies
key_sources: Abaci, S., Robertson, J., Linklater, H., & McNeill, F. (2021). Supporting school teachers' rapid engagement with online education. Education Tech Research Dev, 69, 29-34. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09839-5

article_title: Supporting school teachers’ rapid engagement with online education
citation: Abaci, S., Robertson, J., Linklater, H., & McNeill, F. (2021). Supporting school teachers' rapid engagement with online education. Education Tech Research Dev, 69, 29-34. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09839-5
title: Future versions of the TPD-for-OBL framework should differentiate between school and higher education settings
description: Because schools and higher education institutions operate within different parameters, the authors suggest "future versions of the framework should differentiate between these settings". The differing parameters they name include institutional autonomy, in-house resources and staff for professional development, and student engagement and parental involvement in online learning. This recommendation follows directly from their application of the framework to primary and secondary teacher support during emergency remote teaching.
requirements: Framework developers should account for operational differences between educational levels when synthesizing TPD components
constraints: Derived from one team's reflection on a single emergency support effort in Scotland; the authors state evaluation of the webinar series is still to be undertaken
target_learning_goals: design of teacher professional development for online and blended learning
examples: The authors recommend policy makers, initial teacher education institutions, and professional bodies develop a clear vision of teaching that includes capacity to practice outside physical classrooms

article_title: Critical events and pivotal factors as tools for analyzing the sustainability of online study programs
citation: Jarkko Suhonen · Erkki Sutinen. (2022). Critical events and pivotal factors as tools for analyzing the sustainability of online study programs. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10133-9
title: Four-pillar sustainability model for online study programs
description: The article applies a four-pillar sustainability model in which "The model consists of four sustainability pillars: economic, social, environmental, and ethical." The economic pillar covers resources and funding, the social pillar internal dynamics and community, the environmental pillar the physical, technical, cultural and psychological contexts, and the ethical pillar the values behind goals and working principles. The pillars are mutually interrelated and can be traded off; the authors use the model to analyze critical events and pivotal factors of an online doctoral program.
requirements: Analysis requires identifying pivotal factors connected to critical events from the perspective of each pillar
constraints: The authors note relying too heavily on a single pillar or even two could be potentially problematic for the sustainability of the program
target_learners: doctoral students in online study programs
target_learning_goals: sustainable design and continuation of online study programs
examples: The authors analyzed six critical events of the IMPDET online doctoral program using the model, labeling factors Eco+, Eco-, Env+, Env-, So+, So-, Et+, Et-.

title: IMPDET online doctoral study program
description: IMPDET (International Multidisciplinary PhD Studies in Educational Technology) is an international online doctoral study program hosted in Finland since 2004, originally designed for applicants from emerging and transitional countries. Its pedagogical components include independent research experience with two to four supervisors, a mixed-model teaching approach (online, campus, or mixed), and course work of 30 or 50 ECTS credits. The authors report that "A total of 93 students have been admitted to the program by end of 2021, 32 (34%) of whom graduated and 17 (18%) officially quit their studies between 2004 and 2021."

constraints: At the end of studies the completed course work should fulfill the minimum requirements set by the students' faculty
target_learners: doctoral students, primarily from emerging and transitional countries
target_learning_goals: doctoral degrees in computer science or education
examples: During 2012–2021 the majority of admitted students were from Africa, and a doctoral studies hub was launched in Tanzania in 2014.

article_title: Could virtual reality be the next approach for international students learning Maltese?
citation: Jacqueline Żammit. (2024). Could virtual reality be the next approach for international students learning Maltese? Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10375-9
title: Teachers should test and experience VR first, limit student VR time, and balance VR with traditional teaching techniques
description: From the study's recommendations: teachers need to first test and experience VR before offering it to students, limit the time that VR is used by students, and be ready to answer student questions not covered by the VR application. The article states that following these recommendations makes teachers highly likely to find and maintain an optimal balance when applying VR during lessons, and that VR should be combined with traditional teaching techniques rather than replace real-life teachers.
requirements: Teacher training and continuous professional development for successful VR integration
constraints: The study's results cannot be generalized, as they depend on subjective, untested teacher comments from a small sample
target_learning_goals: Maltese as a second language proficiency
balanced technology integration in language lessons
examples: Teacher 1 stated VR cannot replace real-life teachers, but combining VR with traditional teaching techniques is a hybrid strategy that can modify the learning process

article_title: Could virtual reality be the next approach for international students learning Maltese?
citation: Jacqueline Żammit. (2024). Could virtual reality be the next approach for international students learning Maltese? Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10375-9
title: VR's immersive environment aligns with constructivist, situated, and multimodal accounts of language learning
description: The article interprets VR's potential for ML2 through several frameworks: its immersive and interactive environment aligns with the constructivist theory of learning, in which learners construct knowledge based on their experiences; real or virtual tours align with situated learning, where learning is most effective when embedded in meaningful, real-world contexts; and combining VR with traditional methods aligns with the multimodal theory of learning, which posits that different modes of communication can complement and enhance each other. Acceptance of VR is interpreted through the Technology Acceptance Model and the Theory of Diffusion of Innovations.
requirements: Further empirical investigations to clarify the practical implications of integrating VR tools into language teaching methodologies
constraints: The specific mechanisms through which VR influences language acquisition and proficiency levels are not yet fully elucidated
target_learning_goals: second language acquisition
engagement and motivation in language learning
examples: The discussion links VR tours to situated learning and the teaching-plus-entertainment theme to edutainment and gamification concepts

article_title: Orchestrating iVR technology in an authentic classroom setting and its effects on factual knowledge, comprehension and transfer
citation: P. Spangenberger, N. Matthes, F. Kapp, L. Kruse, J. L. Plass. (2025). Orchestrating iVR technology in an authentic classroom setting and its effects on factual knowledge, comprehension and transfer. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10409-2
title: MARLA: a curriculum-aligned iVR serious game for offshore wind energy troubleshooting
description: MARLA is an immersive VR serious game developed for Meta Quest in which apprentices take the role of a service technician who must "diagnose an error in the hydraulic brake pressure system and repair it". It was built over three years (2019–2022) by an interdisciplinary team using the ADDIE model, and includes a pedagogical agent (Alex), three miniature wind energy plant models, a help view with hypotheses and an interactive hydraulic plan, and game-based feedback. It implements a cognitive apprenticeship approach across a training level (~45 min) and a mission level (~25 min).
requirements: Developed in line with curricula from German vocational education in electrical engineering and two stated learning objectives (structural troubleshooting procedure; factual knowledge about offshore wind energy plants)
constraints: Design required close cooperation with stakeholders (researchers, game designers, teachers, technicians) and approximately 1.5 years of prototyping, testing and adapting scenarios
target_learners: apprentices in electrical engineering at German vocational schools
target_learning_goals: structural troubleshooting procedure
factual knowledge about offshore wind energy plants
sustainability-related learning objectives
examples: Players are accompanied by the pedagogical agent Alex in the training level and operate more independently in the mission level, reflecting modeling, coaching and exploration phases

article_title: Orchestrating iVR technology in an authentic classroom setting and its effects on factual knowledge, comprehension and transfer
citation: P. Spangenberger, N. Matthes, F. Kapp, L. Kruse, J. L. Plass. (2025). Orchestrating iVR technology in an authentic classroom setting and its effects on factual knowledge, comprehension and transfer. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10409-2
title: Hybrid teaching setting pairing iVR phases with classroom modules across the six cognitive apprenticeship phases
description: The article's lesson design combines an individual iVR learning situation with teacher-led classroom learning. "For the individual learning sessions, six learning modules were created, of which three modules were mandatory and three optional." Three cognitive apprenticeship phases (modeling, coaching, scaffolding) take place in iVR and require actions, while three phases (articulation, reflection, exploration) take place in the classroom with learning material and require cognitive processing; the modules are arranged so the phases complement each other.
requirements: iVR application designed in line with relevant learning objectives and curricula
teacher-led classroom sessions with accompanying learning modules
constraints: Requires organizational preparation of space, equipment and supervisors in the authentic school setting
target_learning_goals: complex technical troubleshooting procedures
applying technical knowledge in concrete situations
examples: In the evaluation, apprentices had 75 min for the training level plus modules 1–3 on day one, and 45 min for the mission level plus modules 4–6 one week later

article_title: Orchestrating iVR technology in an authentic classroom setting and its effects on factual knowledge, comprehension and transfer
citation: P. Spangenberger, N. Matthes, F. Kapp, L. Kruse, J. L. Plass. (2025). Orchestrating iVR technology in an authentic classroom setting and its effects on factual knowledge, comprehension and transfer. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10409-2
title: Align iVR affordances with the learning objectives when designing instructional iVR experiences
description: The article argues that iVR is more effective when its specific affordances (presence, agency, interaction with 3D objects, representing inaccessible or unsafe systems) are matched to the learning objectives rather than used for their own sake. As the authors state, "this medium can be more effective than other media if the learning materials take advantage of the affordances of iVR, that is, where the affordances of iVR are aligned with the learning objectives." Their MARLA design operationalizes this by targeting complex cognitive and motor troubleshooting tasks that benefit from agency.
requirements: Learning objectives derived from relevant curricula before media selection
design features (e.g., pedagogical agent, miniature models, help view) chosen to support those objectives
constraints: The authors note high organizational effort is still required to embed iVR in classrooms, and effects may stem from the combination of iVR and the cognitive apprenticeship approach
target_learners: vocational apprentices learning complex technical systems
target_learning_goals: factual knowledge
troubleshooting comprehension
transfer of technical procedures
examples: MARLA's two learning objectives (structural troubleshooting procedure; factual knowledge about offshore wind plants) guided the inclusion of the pedagogical agent, miniature models, help view and game-based elements

article_title: A systematic review of using tablet games to promote early math learning in preschool settings: effectiveness and influencing factors
citation: Jing Chen. (2026). A systematic review of using tablet games to promote early math learning in preschool settings: effectiveness and influencing factors. Educational technology research and development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10626-x
title: Four-level model of factors influencing tablet-based DGBL effectiveness
description: The review organizes influencing factors, adapted from Outhwaite et al. (2020b), into four levels: "app-level factors, individual-level factors, school-level factors, and macro-level factors". App-level factors include self-adaptation, multi-level content, and a parental involvement module; individual-level factors include demographic, developmental, environmental, and experience-related variables; school-level factors cover time on task and integration mode; macro-level factors cover device accessibility and educational philosophy. The review concludes effectiveness "is not determined by a single factor but by the interplay among four-level factors", shifting focus from whether DGBL works to under what conditions it works.
requirements: Requires coding of intervention studies across all four levels to give a comprehensive picture of implementation conditions
constraints: Some identified factors may not show influences in the reviewed studies; macro-level factors' influence has not yet been explored
target_learning_goals: early mathematics learning (numeracy, shapes, spatial abilities, measurement)
examples: The review coded each included study's discussion sections against the four-level framework, producing Tables 8 and 9 of factors with example studies

It states that "Understanding these common design practices is critical to effectively and efficiently support faculty with transferring their instruction online," especially when many institutions face large numbers of inexperienced faculty needing such support.
requirements: Institutions must first understand common faculty design practices before designing support

examples: The article frames this principle in the context of institutions supporting a large number of inexperienced faculty with moving instruction online.

article_title: Concept-guided development of technology in ‘traditional’ and ‘innovative’ schools: quantitative and qualitative differences in technology integration
citation: Sandra de Koster, Monique Volman, Els Kuiper. (2017). Concept-guided development of technology in 'traditional' and 'innovative' schools: quantitative and qualitative differences in technology integration. Education Tech Research Dev 65:1325–1344. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-017-9527-0
title: Concept-guided development of technology use: a pedagogy-driven approach taking the school's educational concept as the starting point for developing technology use
description: The article proposes concept-guided development of technology use, in which school teams develop and implement forms of technology use in line with the school's educational concept, encompassing both pedagogical practices and the beliefs and perspectives motivating them. It is "a pedagogy-driven approach that aims to promote this ﬁt" between proposed technology use and the school's educational concept. The approach calls for a definition of technology integration that gives room to a variety of educational concepts and encompasses teachers' perceptions, so that integration depends on fit with existing or desired classroom practices rather than on the school's pedagogy type.
requirements: A team of teachers supported to reflect on the school's educational concept and design learning arrangements as they see best fit
A definition of technology integration that encompasses the perceptions of the teachers who carry out the concepts
constraints: The labeling of school types as 'traditional' or 'innovative' is indicative rather than conclusive
To what extent achieved integration can be attributed to the approach cannot be concluded from the exploratory study
target_learning_goals: integration of technology use into classroom practice in line with the school's educational concept
examples: Five Dutch primary schools each designed and realized up to four technology-supported learning arrangements over two school years, coached by external educational counsellors
key_sources: Sandra de Koster, Monique Volman, Els Kuiper. (2017). Concept-guided development of technology in 'traditional' and 'innovative' schools: quantitative and qualitative differences in technology integration. citation: Sandra de Koster, Monique Volman, Els Kuiper. (2017). Concept-guided development of technology in 'traditional' and 'innovative' schools: quantitative and qualitative differences in technology integration. Education Tech Research Dev 65:1325–1344. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-017-9527-0
title: Use a teacher-as-designer approach with voluntary participation to foster ownership and support implementation of technology-supported learning arrangements

target_learning_goals: successful implementation and integration of school-designed technology use

article_title: Designing electronic collaborative learning environments
citation: Paul A. Kirschner, Jan Willem Strijbos, Karel Kreijns, Pieter Beers. (2004). Designing electronic collaborative learning environments. Educational Technology Research and Development, 52(3), pp.47-66. https://hal.science/hal-00703892
title: An affordance framework for electronic collaborative learning environments
description: The article presents what it calls an affordance framework for electronic collaborative learning environments for learning and working. The framework is offered as a shared lens because designers currently build such environments according to their own constructivist interpretations, educators employ them in diverse situations, and researchers comparing them find no conclusive evidence about whether, where, when or why they work. The framework is intended to structure the design and evaluation of these environments.

constraints: Motivated by the article's observation that researchers studying such environments find no conclusive evidence as to whether, where, when and why they work
target_learners: Students using electronic collaborative learning environments
target_learning_goals: Collaborative learning in electronic environments
examples: The article presents the framework alongside an interaction design procedure and an educational affordance approach to tasks, with results of three projects dealing with these three issues.

article_title: Designing electronic collaborative learning environments
citation: Paul A. Kirschner, Jan Willem Strijbos, Karel Kreijns, Pieter Beers. (2004). Designing electronic collaborative learning environments. Educational Technology Research and Development, 52(3), pp.47-66. https://hal.science/hal-00703892

The approach is elaborated in one of the article's three projects.

article_title: Television in army training: Evaluation of television in army basic training
citation: Kanner, Joseph H.; Runyon, Richard P.; and Desiderato, Otello. (1955). Television in Army Training: Evaluation of Television in Army Basic Training. Technical Report No. 14, Human Resources Research Office, The George Washington University, Washington 7, D. C.
title: Mass-medium television instruction can replace regular instruction with no loss in learning effectiveness
description: The report draws an applied design conclusion from its experimental comparisons: instruction of the types studied could be delivered by television as a mass medium without sacrificing learning. It states the results "suggest that, should conditions require the Army to adopt a mass medium of instruction such as television", the instruction types used in the study could be presented "with the strong assurance that there would be no loss in learning effectiveness". The principle is grounded in the study's comparisons of television, kinescope, and regular instruction with the same instructors.

article_title: A framework for designing and developing multimedia-based performance assessment in vocational education
citation: Sebastiaan de Klerk, Bernard P. Veldkamp, Theo J. H. M. Eggen. (2018). A framework for designing and developing multimedia-based performance assessment in vocational education. Education Tech Research Dev (2018) 66:147–171. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-017-9559-5
title: A two-stage framework for MBPA design and development in vocational education
description: The article introduces a comprehensive framework for designing and developing multimedia-based performance assessment, uniting assessment development and multimedia development theory with a sole focus on vocational education. As printed: "The framework therefore comprises two general stages: analysis and design and development and administration , both involving different processes." The first stage, guided by assessment and subject matter experts, proceeds through seven steps from determining purposes and constructs to constructing the measurement model; the second stage, guided by multimedia experts, covers ICT development, task building, implementation, pretesting, and fitness-for-purpose evaluation. Unlike ECD, it offers a step-by-step approach while remaining iterative.
requirements: A multidisciplinary team including assessment experts, subject matter experts, psychometricians, and multimedia experts working across both stages
constraints: The framework was developed for and focuses solely on vocational education, though the authors state it can be used in other settings
target_learning_goals: procedural and manual skills currently measured by performance-based assessment
examples: The framework was used to rebuild a pilot MBPA for confined space guards in Dutch vocational education
key_sources: Sebastiaan de Klerk, Bernard P. Veldkamp, Theo J. H. M. Eggen. (2018). A framework for designing and developing multimedia-based performance assessment in vocational education. Education Tech Research Dev (2018) 66:147–171. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-017-9559-5

article_title: A framework for designing and developing multimedia-based performance assessment in vocational education
citation: Sebastiaan de Klerk, Bernard P. Veldkamp, Theo J. H. M. Eggen. (2018). A framework for designing and developing multimedia-based performance assessment in vocational education. Education Tech Research Dev (2018) 66:147–171. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-017-9559-5
title: Multimedia-based performance assessment (MBPA)
description: MBPA is an innovative assessment type that blends computer-based testing and performance-based assessment. Using multimedia such as animation, video, and virtual reality, students are immersed in a virtual environment in which they complete tasks or achieve objectives while navigating that environment. The article states: "MBPA includes a whole range of new response types for logging actual student behavior in the tasks—for example, speed, clicking behavior, navigational behavior through the virtual environment, typing, eye-tracking, and accuracy." MBPA is used to measure vocational skills currently measured by performance-based assessment, offering an alternative with more interaction between student and computer than other CBT.
requirements: An ICT infrastructure able to incorporate and present multimedia and innovative items, including a virtual interface that can incorporate movies, animations, and avatars
constraints: The article emphasizes this need not refer to immersive virtual environments as in serious games or simulations
target_learners: vocational education students, such as confined space guards in training
target_learning_goals: procedural and manual skills, higher-order cognitive skills
examples: A pilot MBPA measured the vocational skills of confined space guards, capturing all tasks of the existing PBA using multimedia and interactive tasks

article_title: A framework for designing and developing multimedia-based performance assessment in vocational education
citation: Sebastiaan de Klerk, Bernard P. Veldkamp, Theo J. H. M. Eggen. (2018). A framework for designing and developing multimedia-based performance assessment in vocational education. Education Tech Research Dev (2018) 66:147–171. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-017-9559-5
title: Iterative, parallel assessment design with backward loops to the original purpose
description: In response to expert feedback, the final framework replaced a sequential structure with a dynamic, parallel process. The authors report: "we have tried to make the framework more dynamic and ﬂuid by transforming the sequential form of the framework into a more parallel form and by adding more backward loops between steps and stages." Backward loops connect each step to the original purpose determination so progress is constantly monitored against the assessment's intended purpose, and observations in the development stage can send developers back to the design stage. Steps were also unnumbered to emphasize the fluid nature.
requirements: ICT experts involved in the design stage as well as the development stage, otherwise the gap between design and development becomes too large
target_learning_goals: valid, reliable measurement of vocational competencies
examples: Experts stated the framework needs to incorporate more loops (80%) and more balance between the first and second stages (100%), and the final framework added backward loops between steps and stages

article_title: From digital literacy to digital competence: the teacher digital competency (TDC) framework
citation: Garry Falloon. (2020). From digital literacy to digital competence: the teacher digital competency (TDC) framework. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09767-4
title: The Teacher Digital Competence (TDC) framework integrates curriculum, personal-ethical and personal-professional competencies
description: The TDC framework is a conceptual framework depicting broadly-based teacher digital competence as three integrated competency sets. It extends TPACK-aligned curriculum competencies (technical, technological, discipline/content, pedagogical/learning design) with personal-ethical pillars (digital citizenship, safety and data security, health and wellbeing, impacts on people, society and environment) and personal-professional pillars (information literacy, strategic professional networking, commitment to continuous professional learning). The article states the framework 'represents diagrammatically a broadly-based conceptualisation of teacher digital competence', with double-headed arrows indicating the interrelated nature of the pillars. It is intended to inform curriculum and programme design in teacher education rather than prescribe content.
requirements: All teaching faculty must have a consistent understanding of the breadth and definition of the competencies for successful implementation
Targeted TDC elements should be made explicit to students via course outlines, integrated into course content, and reflected in assessment tasks
constraints: The article states conceptual frameworks are not intended to act as a formula or prescription detailing universally-applicable curricula; content must be tailored by expert professionals to context
The discussion and suggestions for use specifically focus on applicability to teacher education, though it could equally inform practicing teachers
target_learners: pre-service teachers in initial teacher education programmes
target_learning_goals: digital competence for using digital technologies safely, ethically and productively in teaching
examples: Health education faculty integrating personal-ethical (wellbeing/safety) competencies by requiring students to research effects of prolonged device use; science education courses aligning with information access competencies through scientific networks
key_sources: Garry Falloon. (2020). From digital literacy to digital competence: the teacher digital competency (TDC) framework. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09767-4

article_title: From digital literacy to digital competence: the teacher digital competency (TDC) framework
citation: Garry Falloon. (2020). From digital literacy to digital competence: the teacher digital competency (TDC) framework. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09767-4
title: Janssen et al.'s twelve-element digital competence model organises core, supportive and dispositional competencies as building blocks
description: Janssen et al.'s (2013) Delphi study of 95 experts from academic, education, government/policy and IT business sectors identified twelve elements essential to broadly-based digital competence, summarised in the article's Table 1 (e.g., functional, integrative, specialised, communication and collaboration, information management, privacy and security, legal and ethical, technology and society, learning with and about technology, informed decision making, coherence/self-efficacy, dispositional). The article reports they conceptualised each element as a 'building block', with core competencies enhanced by networking and information management capabilities and parallel supportive competencies covering legal/ethical, societal-impact and dispositional factors. The TDC framework builds directly on this model by positioning its general competencies within teacher education.
requirements: Digital competence should be understood as a pluralistic concept, viewed from a plurality of angles, with balance struck between over-inclusive and too-restrictive common denominators
constraints: The authors signal limitations to direct application to specific contexts: development and display of digital competence differs across contexts
target_learners: teacher educators designing digital capability programmes
target_learning_goals: holistic digital competence spanning technical, ethical, societal and dispositional elements
examples: The article's Table 1 explains each of the twelve competency areas with the knowledge and understanding it covers

article_title: Implementation of the flipped classroom and its longitudinal impact on improving academic performance
citation: Torres-Martín, C., Acal, C., El-Homrani, M., & Mingorance-Estrada, Á. C. (2022). Implementation of the flipped classroom and its longitudinal impact on improving academic performance. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10095-y
title: Flipped classroom implementation requires sustained access to a fully equipped technology classroom
description: The article's longitudinal data show that the flipped classroom methodology depends on reliable access to a "fully equipped classroom with technological resources". In the one academic year (2017/2018) when such a classroom was only occasionally available, a mixed methodology had to be used and average grades declined. The authors state this reinforces "the connection between the usual use of technological resources and the flipped classroom methodology".
requirements: A technology classroom with a computer for each student must be available for regular use during face-to-face sessions.
constraints: When a fully equipped technology classroom is unavailable, the methodology degrades into a mixed approach and the performance benefit is reduced.
target_learners: university students in a first-year education degree subject
target_learning_goals: academic performance in subject grades
examples: In 2017/2018, when "there was not a fully equipped classroom with technological resources", a mixed methodology was carried out and grades declined.

title: Prepare for student resistance and unequal technological readiness when introducing the flipped classroom
description: The article identifies three limitations when starting the flipped classroom: "resistance to change, technological aspects and teaching perspectives". Students accustomed to traditional methodology face a period of progressive familiarization, and "not all students have basic skills in the use of technological resources". The authors recommend a progressive adaptation period and inviting a former student to share their experience.
requirements: A process of progressive familiarization and successive adaptation, which can last the first month of the course.
constraints: Not all students have basic technological skills or the same resources at home, so previous teaching work must be adapted to available resources.
target_learners: university students accustomed to traditional teaching methodology
target_learning_goals: adaptation to active learning methodologies
examples: The authors suggest inviting "a student from the previous course to explain the experience to the students of the new course".

article_title: Trends, tensions, and futures of maker education research: a 2025 vision for STEM+ disciplinary and transdisciplinary spaces for learning through making
citation: Ioannou, A., & Gravel, B. E. (2024). Trends, tensions, and futures of maker education research: a 2025 vision for STEM+ disciplinary and transdisciplinary spaces for learning through making. Education Tech Research Dev, 72, 1–14. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10334-w
title: Four clusters structure the current state of maker education research
description: The editors organize the special issue's eighteen papers into four thematic clusters: STEM+ disciplinary and transdisciplinary learning spaces; digital technologies in making; assessment practices and frameworks; and representation, inclusion, and tensions around maker-centered initiatives. They state that "these clusters reflect the current state-of-the-art in the field as well as significant questions to guide near future research." The taxonomy serves as a map of the maker education research landscape.
requirements: The taxonomy reflects the editors' perceived dominant focus of each manuscript, as papers often span multiple clusters
target_learners: K-20 students in formal and informal maker contexts
target_learning_goals: Learning through making and design across STEM+ disciplines

article_title: Trends, tensions, and futures of maker education research: a 2025 vision for STEM+ disciplinary and transdisciplinary spaces for learning through making
citation: Ioannou, A., & Gravel, B. E. (2024). Trends, tensions, and futures of maker education research: a 2025 vision for STEM+ disciplinary and transdisciplinary spaces for learning through making. Education Tech Research Dev, 72, 1–14. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10334-w
title: Adopt an ecological lens on maker education rather than a technocentric focus
description: The editors recommend that research and practice treat technologies as tools that mediate cultural practices, skills, and social organizations rather than as the primary focus. They argue that "a technocentric approach with an agenda to promote the use of technology per se... should be de-stressed as the primary focus in future research." Instead, the deliberate integration of specific tools and materials into the overall context of maker activities should be stressed.
requirements: Teachers should not be expected to design maker-oriented learning experiences without support; ample time working with maker technologies and some technical proficiency are necessary before incorporation into lessons
constraints: An overly technocentric approach may lead to a decrease in students' and teachers' interest in making
target_learning_goals: Learning through making and design

title: Assessment in maker education requires new forms and tools suited to heterogeneous contexts
description: The editors argue that because makerspaces differ inherently in learning opportunities, processes, and challenges, traditional one-size-fits-all assessment is inadequate. They state that "a traditional, one-size-fits-all assessment tool or practice of assessment is unlikely to fulfill the expectation of capturing learning and skill development in these dynamic learning spaces." New forms of assessment and tools are needed to document learning outcomes.

constraints: Heterogeneity in intended outcomes makes assessment difficult and makes context inseparable from findings

article_title: AI-assisted data extraction for systematic reviews in education
citation: Schroeder, N. L., Jaldi, C. D., Zhang, S., & Yamoah, K. (2025). AI-Assisted Data Extraction for Systematic Reviews in Education. https://osf.io/nraxf/?view_only=879654690be249cc9237525ed7f86ec2
title: AIDE: AI-Assisted Data Extraction tool (R package and web version)
description: AIDE is a free, open-source tool for human-in-the-loop LLM-based data extraction in systematic reviews, available as an R package (https://github.com/noah-schroeder/AIDE) and a web version (https://noah-schroeder.github.io/AIDE-Web/). It sends a PDF's full text and coding-form prompts to an LLM API, auto-populates responses in a user interface, shows the LLM's reasoning and source page, and requires the user to press Record after reviewing or editing each answer. The web version stores API keys in sessionStorage and uses structured JSON response parsing.
requirements: Requires an API key from Google AI Studio, Mistral AI, or Open Router, or a local model via Ollama
constraints: The R-based pilot version runs locally and should not be hosted on an external-facing website because API keys would not be secure
target_learning_goals: Accurate, efficient data extraction for research synthesis
examples: The analysis page presents the PDF on the left and LLM answers, source text, and record buttons on the right
key_sources: Schroeder, N. L., Jaldi, C. D., Zhang, S., & Yamoah, K. (2025). AI-Assisted Data Extraction for Systematic Reviews in Education. https://osf.io/nraxf/?view_only=879654690be249cc9237525ed7f86ec2

article_title: AI-assisted data extraction for systematic reviews in education

title: Enforce human-in-the-loop validation of every LLM-extracted data point in research synthesis
description: The article recommends that LLM-assisted data extraction in research synthesis should only proceed with mandatory human validation of every data point before it is recorded into a coding form. The authors argue that because LLM decision-making is opaque and probabilistic, "human validation of LLM-extracted data remains a mandatory step at this time." They built AIDE specifically to enforce this validation step rather than allow bulk recording.
requirements: A program must require every data point to be validated by a human coder before it is recorded into a coding form
constraints: The authors found no empirical support yet for time savings, only anecdotes
target_learners: Education researchers conducting systematic reviews and meta-analyses
target_learning_goals: Maintaining accuracy and integrity of data extraction in research synthesis
examples: AIDE requires the user to press Record after reviewing or editing each LLM-extracted answer, and the authors declined to implement a "record all" function

article_title: Computer vision versus human vision: analyzing middle school teachers’ construct restructuring following computer vision professional development
citation: Kurz, T. L., Jayasuriya, S., Swisher, K., Mativo, J., Pidaparti, R., & Robinson, D. T. (2026). Computer vision versus human vision: analyzing middle school teachers' construct restructuring following computer vision professional development. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10594-2
title: ImageSTEAM computer vision PD intervention using free online tools (pixlr, Teachable Machine, GauGAN, Tinkercad) with teachers co-creating and delivering lessons to middle school students
description: The intervention was a two-to-three-week professional development experience in which in-service middle school teachers from Title I schools learned computer vision technologies and then taught lessons to middle school students. Tools used were free, browser-based, and required no programming: "pixlr (an image editing software)", "Google's Teachable Machine (a tool which allows students to capture image or audio data, define a class for the data, and train a classification-based neural network)", NVIDIA's GauGAN, and Tinkercad, plus custom Google Colaboratory notebooks demonstrating vision algorithms. Curricular materials are freely available at https://www.imagesteam.org.
requirements: Tools must be free to use, require no custom installation, and need no programming knowledge, which "helped ensure the accessibility of the lessons to wider audience."
constraints: The PD varied across states: three weeks face-to-face in Arizona versus two weeks hybrid in Georgia, with flexibility built into the curriculum design.
target_learners: Middle school in-service teachers from Title I schools
Middle school students in Arizona and Georgia
target_learning_goals: Understanding computer vision concepts and technologies
Ability to integrate computer vision lessons into middle school instruction
examples: Sample lessons included detecting water damage in satellite images after a hurricane, training an algorithm to recognize American Sign Language, and exploring visual illusions using image editing software.

article_title: Computer vision versus human vision: analyzing middle school teachers’ construct restructuring following computer vision professional development
citation: Kurz, T. L., Jayasuriya, S., Swisher, K., Mativo, J., Pidaparti, R., & Robinson, D. T. (2026). Computer vision versus human vision: analyzing middle school teachers' construct restructuring following computer vision professional development. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10594-2
title: Personal Construct Theory with repertory grids and hierarchical cluster analysis as a method for mapping teachers' cognitive restructuring
description: Personal Construct Theory (Kelly, 1955) frames the study's methodology: constructs are elicited directly from participants through pairwise comparisons of elements (here, computer vision and human vision), avoiding researcher-imposed survey instruments. The authors note it "can provide unique insight because it has the potential to show how cognitive structures changes through the analysis of dendrograms using hierarchical cluster analysis." Repertory grids serve as cognitive mapping tools whose cluster membership reveals how participants perceive constructs as similar or dissimilar, enabling pre-post comparison of cognitive structure.
requirements: Constructs must come directly from participants via pairwise comparisons to reduce researcher bias
Sample sizes of no more than 20 are recommended due to the intense nature of data collection
constraints: Construct language generated by one subgroup may not represent all participants; here constructs came only from Arizona participants, skewing results
Personal Construct Theory is more reliant on cognition than emotion
Participants may lack the framework (language and concepts) needed to elicit meaningful constructs
target_learning_goals: Mapping changes in teachers' conceptual understanding of computer vision
examples: The study elicited 18 constructs from pairwise comparisons of computer vision and human vision and analyzed pre/post repertory grids using Ward's Method with squared Euclidean distances.

article_title: Roversa: A low-cost, multilingual robotics platform for K-12 computer science integration
citation: Bredder, E., Wilkens, K., Espinal, A., Vieira, C., Harris, P., Bailey, J., & Chiu, J. (2026). Roversa: A low-cost, multilingual robotics platform for K-12 computer science integration. Educational technology research and development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10628-9
title: Roversa: a low-cost, multilingual, customizable educational robot for K-8 CS integration
description: Roversa is an educational robot built on the BBC micro:bit platform, designed to be inexpensive, multilingual, and adaptable across grade levels. The article states it is "a new educational robot specifically designed to be low-cost, multilingual (e.g., uses multiple languages), and versatile for K-8 levels." It features push-button directional programming, a calibration menu, English-Spanish language switching, a MakeCode extension, LEGO-compatible laser-cut wooden chassis, and swappable aesthetic costumes. Four prototype iterations refined movement accuracy, assembly, and circuit-board integration.
requirements: Requires the micro:bit platform, which many schools already own, lowering cost
constraints: The initial study examined only two US school districts; Latin American usability testing is planned for future research
target_learners: K-8 students, including multilingual learners and students with disabilities
target_learning_goals: Computer science concepts such as sequencing, loops, and directional programming
examples: Prototype 3 added evenly spaced holes fitting LEGO connectors and a template students can use to create their own robot exterior with paper and tape

citation: Bredder, E., Wilkens, K., Espinal, A., Vieira, C., Harris, P., Bailey, J., & Chiu, J. (2026). Roversa: A low-cost, multilingual robotics platform for K-12 computer science integration. Educational technology research and development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10628-9
title: ERA Framework focal principles guiding educational robot design
description: The Educational Robot Applications (ERA) Framework (Catlin & Blamires) guides the design of educational robots by identifying areas to consider surrounding the technology, the teachers, and the students. The article states that "ERA is a framework to help guide the design of educational robots by identifying areas to consider surrounding the technology, the teachers, and the students." The authors focused on five principles: technology intelligence and interaction, student engagement, and teacher equity and practicality. These served both as design goals for Roversa and as a priori codes for analyzing educator feedback.
requirements: Designers must align robot intelligence with specific learning outcomes and consider teacher learning and curricular planning time
constraints: The article focuses only on the five selected principles rather than the full framework
target_learning_goals: Design and evaluation of educational robots for CS learning
examples: The Roversa team used the five principles to justify design choices such as multilingual interfaces (equity) and on-the-fly calibration (practicality)

article_title: Designing and using digital platforms for 21st century learning
citation: Meier, E. B. (2021). Designing and using digital platforms for 21st century learning. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09880-4
title: Theory of change perspective for evaluating online learning design heuristics
description: The article applies a "theory of change" lens to review the Nacu et al. heuristic for educator learning-support roles in networked technologies. It frames the heuristic as one component within a larger system: platforms must address twenty-first century learning goals and support equitable access, and a theory of change could identify the critical variables needed for teachers and designers to transition to student-centered online learning. The framework positions online learning as a knowledge-building environment rather than a delivery channel.
requirements: A holistic approach that repositions online learning as a knowledge-building environment
constraints: Heuristics alone do not prepare designers or teachers to enact this work
target_learning_goals: pursue their interests and take ownership of their learning

citation: Meier, E. B. (2021). Designing and using digital platforms for 21st century learning. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09880-4
title: Design online platforms that give learners equitable access and support interest-driven ownership of learning
description: The article endorses the aim, drawn from Nacu et al., of designing network platforms that give learners "equitable access to systems that inspire young people 'to pursue their interests and take ownership of their learning'." It argues such design became especially important when platforms assumed a central role during the Covid-19 pandemic. The principle is presented as a design orientation rather than an empirically tested recommendation.
requirements: Platforms designed and implemented to address twenty-first century learning goals

citation: Gloria Natividad Beltrán del Río. (2021). The importance of always bearing in mind students' privacy, consent, vulnerability, and agency issues. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09954-x
title: Willis et al.'s heuristic typology of ethical approaches to student data in learning analytics
description: A heuristic typology derived from analyzing three higher education institutions on three continents (University of South Africa; Open University, UK; Indiana University, US), offered as "a starting point for discussion about the policy frameworks and processes of ethical review". It summarizes four common ethical issues: invasive techniques, surveilling students' activities, questionable interventions, and storing and interpreting data for different purposes.
requirements: Derived from cross-institutional analysis of three higher education institutions
constraints: Intended as a starting point for discussion, not a final framework
target_learning_goals: ethical use of student data in learning analytics

citation: Gloria Natividad Beltrán del Río. (2021). The importance of always bearing in mind students' privacy, consent, vulnerability, and agency issues. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09954-x
title: Always bear in mind students' privacy, consent, vulnerability, and agency when using educational data
description: The editorial's central principle: educational researchers and institutions should remain "aware of and vigilant against all possible risks" when collecting, mining, and analyzing student data, because such vigilance protects "learners, students, and teachers". It frames ethical oversight as an ongoing duty across virtual teaching and learning analytics.
requirements: Awareness and vigilance against all possible risks in educational data mining
constraints: Legislation related to educational-data privacy across countries is not likely to be harmonized in the near future
target_learning_goals: ethical learning analytics
student data privacy

(2017) study of medical students' emotions in computer-based learning environments. It frames emotions as theoretically and empirically linked to engagement and learning outcomes across many domains and settings. The theory anchors the special issue's call to explore whether emotions are malleable factors that can be harnessed to support engagement, persistence, and achievement.

title: Systems view of faculty design work in the digital learning era
description: The commentary adopts a systems view of findings and implications of research on university teachers' design work. It treats obtaining faculty design talent for digital learning as a system-level question, asking "Build, buy, or rent?" — i.e., whether to develop faculty capacity, hire for it, or otherwise acquire it. article_title: Human–machine knowledge building: reconceptualising knowledge building partnerships in the age of artificial intelligence
citation: Falloon, G., & Jones, M. (2026). Human–machine knowledge building: reconceptualising knowledge building partnerships in the age of artificial intelligence. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10605-2
title: Three-zone model for human–GenAI knowledge building partnerships
description: The article proposes a conceptual model of three overlapping Zones—Reckoning, Collaboration and Judgement—aligned with Krathwohl's revision of Bloom's cognitive domain, describing how humans and GenAI might partner in collaborative knowledge construction. It states the model identifies "a possible 'division of labour' within and across Zones" while arguing "the primacy of innately human capabilities operating in the Judgement Zone". The zones interact iteratively rather than hierarchically, with circular arrows between the Collaboration and Judgement zones representing continuous human evaluation of AI-human outputs.
requirements: Human evaluation of GenAI outputs and reasoned judgement about their use, supported by human domain and tacit knowledge
constraints: The article states the model is not intended as a hierarchy or linear process, and that zone boundaries and activities may change as the technology evolves
target_learners: learners and professionals in educational institutions, businesses, service industries, and government and non-government agencies
target_learning_goals: collaborative knowledge building with GenAI
reasoned judgement and ethical decision-making about AI-generated information

citation: Lee, J., Lim, C., & Kim, H. (2017). Development of an instructional design model for flipped learning in higher education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-016-9502-1
title: A design model for flipped learning in higher education that integrates online and face-to-face sessions
description: The article develops a prescriptive instructional design model for flipped learning (FL) that guides designers through analysis, design, development, implementation, and evaluation of both online and face-to-face components. The model treats online lectures and F2F activities as "core complementary constituents of the learning experience as a coherent whole" rather than as supplementary additions. It was validated through expert review, usability testing, and field evaluation.
requirements: Requires a design team or instructor able to create and curate online video lectures and facilitate interactive F2F sessions
constraints: Designed for higher education contexts; the authors note that FL design involves "considerable intricacy" and "practically infinite design variability in diverse contexts"

problem solving

article_title: Development of an instructional design model for flipped learning in higher education
citation: Lee, J., Lim, C., & Kim, H. (2017). Development of an instructional design model for flipped learning in higher education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-016-9502-1
title: Design online and face-to-face components as core complementary constituents rather than supplementary additions
description: The article argues that effective flipped learning requires treating online and face-to-face components as equally essential, not layering one on top of the other. It states that "neither component has a supplementary role, but rather each is a core complementary constituent of the learning experience as a coherent whole." This principle guides the allocation of content between modes in the model's analysis phase.
requirements: Requires analysis of which content is best suited to online delivery versus F2F interaction before design begins
constraints: The article notes that blending "does not mean simply combining the two or laying one on top of the other" and that typical mixes fail to achieve the benefits of either mode
target_learning_goals: integrated learning experiences across modalities
examples: The model's analysis step allocates basic concepts to online portions and difficult materials requiring peer or teacher help to F2F sessions

title: Flipped learning course structure with online lectures before F2F collaborative problem-solving sessions
description: The article describes a recurring lesson structure in which students watch online lectures individually before class and then engage in group problem-solving activities during F2F sessions. article_title: Exploring groups’ affective states during collaborative learning: what triggers activating affect on a group level?
citation: Törmänen, T., Järvenoja, H., & Mänty, K. (2021). Exploring groups’ affective states during collaborative learning: what triggers activating affect on a group level? Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-10037-0
title: Group-level affective states can be captured by combining video observation of emotional expressions with EDA measures of physiological activation
description: The article presents a multimodal approach in which group affective valence is coded from video-observed emotional expressions and physiological activation is measured with electrodermal activity, segmented into commensurable 30-s units. The authors argue that "by combining different process data modalities revealing the different components of affect, it might be possible to track emotionally meaningful situations that shape the course of the collaborative learning process." The approach treats valence and activation as complementary dimensions of group-level affect.

Manual video coding of group valence with interrater reliability checking
constraints: Generalizable conclusions cannot be made from the results due to the small sample size
Poor quality EDA data from some students limited the sample; one individual's data loss excluded the whole group
target_learning_goals: understanding affective processes in collaborative learning

article_title: Reflections on educational technology research and development
citation: Jonathan Michael Spector. (2017). Reflections on educational technology research and development. Educational Technology Research and Development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-017-9545-y
title: Write and talk to be understood: use simple, descriptive language
description: The author argues, from 15 years as ETR&D Development Editor and his philosophy training, that the basic goal of communication is to be understood, and that simple, descriptive language promotes understanding. He cites Nielsen's 'A Game of India' as an example of 'a complex story using only the simplest, descriptive language'. He offers the 4 Cs of effective communication: compelling, clear, coherent and concise.
requirements: The communication should have something of interest and value to say, told as a compelling story with evident purpose and scope
constraints: The author notes some remarks may seem disconnected and unnecessarily personal
target_learning_goals: effective scholarly communication
examples: The author shared Nielsen's 'A Game of India' with students as an example of good writing

article_title: Reflections on educational technology research and development
citation: Jonathan Michael Spector. (2017). Reflections on educational technology research and development. Educational Technology Research and Development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-017-9545-y
title: Focus on the goal of helping people learn, not on accumulating papers or models
description: The author's central message, attributed to Gagné, is that 'our job is to help people learn' rather than to pile up papers or build reputations. He extends this to instructional design models: 'one ought not focus on the model itself. It is how the model is used that might have an impact on learning.' He warns that researchers 'spend more time devising new models than paying careful attention to what counts—namely, helping to improve learning.'
requirements: Learning improvements should be the indicator of success for instructional design
constraints: Indicators of learning improvement are difficult to collect and analyze except for the simplest of learning tasks, as the author states
target_learning_goals: improving learning outcomes
examples: The author recalls Gagné and his wife tutoring disadvantaged inner-city kids in math

title: Measure attainment rather than guessing: WYMIWYG and challenging goals
description: The author proposes WYMIWYG—'what you measure ... is what you will know you have attained'—arguing one should 'collect and analyze indicators and measures' rather than guess. Because students 'will perform only to the indicated measure', he recommends challenging goals with associated indicators. This connects measurement to goal-driven instruction.

constraints: Students are often busy with many other interests and may perform only to the indicated measure

title: CADDIE: Cyclic ADDIE model of instructional design
description: The author proposes CADDIE (Cyclic ADDIE), 'a simplification of Tennyson's 4th generation ISD model that emphasizes the notion that design is essentially a dynamic and iterative process that sometime starts in the middle'. The C stands for cyclic, with 'cycles within a particular aspect of instructional design as well as between various aspects'. The designer is analogous to a golf caddie whose main task is to help the learner have a successful experience.

citation: Jonathan Michael Spector. (2017). Reflections on educational technology research and development. Educational Technology Research and Development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-017-9545-y
title: GAIDA and XAIDA expert systems for instructional design
description: Two systems designed and implemented under the Air Force AIDA project: 'Guided Approach to Instructional Design Advising (GAIDA) was based on Gagné's (1985) events of instruction and was aimed at extending the abilities of a novice instructional designer', and was 'later adopted for use in Air Force technical training'. title: Humility and open-minded inquiry are essential for learning and instruction

description: The article describes concept network analysis (aka knowledge structure analysis) as a method for measuring multiple document integration by converting students' learning products, such as summary essays, into networks with nodes representing core concepts and edges representing semantic relationships. Quantity of integration is the proportion of integrative links, semantic quality is the similarity of integrative links to an expert referent network, and structural quality is graph centrality similarity (GCsim) to the expert network form. The article uses this approach to evaluate how reading purpose and expert networks influence integration.

article_title: An exploratory study of a new concept macrostructure measure when learning history in middle school
citation: Chen, X., Wang, W., Peng, C., Guo, W., & Clariana, R. B. (2025). An exploratory study of a new concept macrostructure measure when learning history in middle school. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10536-4
title: Text knowledge structure at two grain sizes: microstructure and macrostructure
description: The article frames the knowledge structure (KS) of history lesson materials at two grain sizes: a microstructure of details, event sequences, and memorizable facts, and a macrostructure consisting of the structure of the text's macropropositions. Macropropositions are defined as "propositions that contain onlytop-level 'gist' information" and span across pages, so the topic structure must often be implicitly inferred while reading. The article argues many students cannot go beyond the microstructure, and that KS measures using only topic-level concepts provide a measure of macrostructure.
requirements: Elicitation tasks must use topic-level terms rather than sentence- or paragraph-level terms to capture macrostructure
constraints: Over time, text macrostructure is weighted more heavily than microstructure, so concurrent validity results may not generalize to macrostructure measured immediately after learning
target_learning_goals: organized conceptual understanding of history text content
examples: Study 1 used 43 topic-level key terms from an expert network of the Qin Dynasty lesson; Study 2 used 23 topics from the American Revolution text

title: Use sorting-task macrostructure measures as a low-cost complement to traditional multiple-choice tests for formative and summative assessment
description: The article recommends supplementing multiple-choice tests with a topic-level sorting task whose term-term distances are converted to Pathfinder networks and compared to an expert network for percent overlap. It describes this as "a low-cost and easy to use complement to traditional multiple-choice tests for multidimensionally detecting learning performance", usable for both formative and summative purposes, including group-level network maps for classroom formative use.
requirements: An expert network of the lesson's key topics as the referent; sorting software such as jRate and Pathfinder analysis; topic-level key terms selected by a content expert
constraints: The sorting task may have influenced immediate posttest performance, alternately accounting for some correlation variance; findings apply to topic-level macrostructure and may not generalize to microstructure sorting or to macrostructure measured immediately after learning; validity may be less pronounced in domains that disregard chronology
target_learning_goals: diagnosing conceptual knowledge structure of lesson content alongside achievement
examples: Study 1 students sorted 43 Qin Dynasty terms one month after the unit exam; Study 2 students sorted 23 American Revolution terms immediately after self-directed reading

title: jRate sorting task software with Pathfinder network analysis for eliciting conceptual macrostructure
description: jRate (Schuelke, 2012) is the computer sorting task software used in both studies: participants drag topic-level key terms around a screen to form clusters according to their understanding, and the software converts the sorting into a proximity file of term-term distances in screen pixels. These files are analyzed by Pathfinder software (Schvaneveldt, 2020) with Minkowski r = infinity and q = n−1 to produce networks compared to an expert referent network by percent overlap and Freeman's graph centrality.
requirements: A computer per participant with jRate installed; an expert referent network of topic-level key terms; Pathfinder software to convert proximity files into networks
constraints: The measure was validated here only for topic-level (macrostructure) terms in history content with explicit chronology, one month after learning
target_learning_goals: eliciting and measuring students' conceptual macrostructure of lesson content
examples: Study 1 used a 43 × 43 proximity array of the Qin terms; Study 2 used a 23 × 23 array of the American Revolution terms

description: The article synthesizes child development, intercultural communication theory, and culturally sustaining pedagogy into a framework for designing robot-mediated collaborative interaction. The framework guided both the design of loosely structured fantasy play, personalized invitations, familiar contexts, and bilingual communication, and the interpretation of the qualitative data.

article_title: Increasing the immersivity of 360° videos facilitates learning and memory: implications for theory and practice
citation: Peney, T., & Skarratt, P. A. (2024). Increasing the immersivity of 360° videos facilitates learning and memory: implications for theory and practice. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10402-9
title: Arousal-attention account of IVR facilitation effects
description: The article proposes that IVR's facilitative effect on memory may operate through physiological arousal and its attentional consequences. Novelty of IVR increases arousal relative to the same content on other devices, and, drawing on the Yerkes-Dodson inverted-U and Easterbrook's cue-utilization model, moderate arousal maintains optimal attentional focus while high or low arousal narrows attention, modulating what is encoded, stored and retrieved. This framework is offered as a candidate mechanism for the observed recall advantage, not as a tested result.
requirements: Requires measurement or manipulation of arousal to test the mechanism, which the present study did not do
constraints: The article states it was not possible to determine if results occurred solely due to increased arousal from novelty, which the authors argue is likely short-term
target_learning_goals: incidental learning and recall memory

description: An incidental learning assessment comprising 20 questions about a three-minute 360° film, administered as a surprise after viewing. Fifteen questions targeted events at specific timepoints and five were foils concerning events that did not occur, with negative responses coded as correct. Questions were presented in a unique random order for each participant on the same device on which they viewed the film. The paradigm measures "basic memory processes in the absence of instruction provided by the experimenter".

constraints: The article notes some responses required subjective judgement to ascertain their accuracy

article_title: Causal reasoning with causal graphs in educational technology research
citation: Weidlich, J., Hicks, B., & Drachsler, H. (2024). Causal reasoning with causal graphs in educational technology research. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10241-0
title: Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) as a graphical formalism for reasoning about causality and bias in educational technology research
description: The paper introduces DAGs as a visual, non-parametric tool for encoding causal assumptions and tracing sources of bias. It distinguishes DAGs from structural equation models, noting that "DAGs are non-parametric" and that "DAGs are conceptual tools" used for identification rather than estimation. The framework rests on three elemental configurations: forks (confounding), chains (mediation), and inverted forks (colliders).
requirements: Researchers must supply explicit causal assumptions from domain knowledge, since "there are no causal conclusions without causal assumptions".
constraints: DAGs are identification tools only; estimation is methodologically decoupled and requires separate statistical machinery.
target_learning_goals: drawing valid causal inferences from observational and experimental research designs
examples: The paper contrasts a DAG with a SEM: in a DAG, an arrow from X to Y asserts a causal effect without specifying functional form, whereas a SEM imposes parametric assumptions such as linearity and multivariate normality.
key_sources: Weidlich, J., Hicks, B., & Drachsler, H. (2024). Causal reasoning with causal graphs in educational technology research. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10241-0

article_title: Causal reasoning with causal graphs in educational technology research
citation: Weidlich, J., Hicks, B., & Drachsler, H. (2024). Causal reasoning with causal graphs in educational technology research. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10241-0
title: Make causal assumptions explicit before data analysis to expose and prevent bias
description: The paper argues that researchers should articulate their causal assumptions graphically before collecting or analyzing data, because "there are no causal conclusions without causal assumptions". Explicit assumptions make it possible to trace whether a proposed causal effect is identified given the assumed structure, and to detect confounding, overcontrol, and collider bias before they distort estimates.
requirements: Researchers must commit to a causal structure (which arrows are present and which are absent) prior to estimation.
constraints: The value of the exercise depends on the plausibility and completeness of the assumed graph; a misspecified DAG can itself mislead.
target_learning_goals: bias identification
valid causal inference
examples: The paper's running example of an intervention X and outcome Y shows how adding a confounder Z as a fork immediately reveals a non-causal back-door path that would otherwise contaminate the estimate.
key_sources: Weidlich, J., Hicks, B., & Drachsler, H. (2024). Causal reasoning with causal graphs in educational technology research. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10241-0

article_title: Causal reasoning with causal graphs in educational technology research
citation: Weidlich, J., Hicks, B., & Drachsler, H. (2024). Causal reasoning with causal graphs in educational technology research. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10241-0
title: Control for confounders but not for mediators or colliders
description: The paper derives three configuration-specific recommendations: for a fork (confounder), "control for Z"; for a chain (mediator), "do not control for Z" because doing so blocks the causal pathway and induces overcontrol bias; and for an inverted fork (collider), "do not control for Z" because conditioning opens a spurious path and induces endogenous selection bias. These rules follow directly from the graphical structure of each configuration.
requirements: Researchers must classify each third variable as a confounder, mediator, or collider within the assumed DAG before deciding whether to adjust for it.
constraints: The recommendations hold only under the assumed causal structure; if the true graph differs, the classification and the resulting adjustment decision may be wrong.
target_learning_goals: choosing covariates for statistical adjustment
avoiding overcontrol and collider bias
examples: The paper's mediator example shows that controlling for a mediator blocks the path X → Z → Y and can yield a false-negative; its collider example shows that conditioning on a collider opens the path X ← Z → Y and can yield a false-positive.
key_sources: Weidlich, J., Hicks, B., & Drachsler, H. (2024). Causal reasoning with causal graphs in educational technology research. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10241-0
