citation: Tani, M., Manuguerra, M., & Khan, S. (2022). Can videos affect learning outcomes? Evidence from an actual learning environment. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10147-3
title: Cognitive load theory as a framework for multimedia learning effects
description: The article uses cognitive load theory to explain how multimedia presentations affect knowledge acquisition. Its tenets include that "learners can only process a limited amount at any one time" and that learners handle knowledge construction "through at least two processors, depending on whether the form of representation is verbal or pictorial". Offloading cognitive demands via cues such as textbooks, instructor feedback, and multimedia is associated with better retention and transfer, freeing capacity to detect distinctions and coordinate ideas with evidence.
requirements: Materials should be designed with instructor awareness of "the impacts of instructional tasks on students' cognitive load".
constraints: The theory's basic model has remained constant for 20 years, with emphasis shifting toward cognitive processes and longer-term outcomes.
target_learning_goals: Acquisition of declarative, conceptual, procedural, and evaluative knowledge

description: The article's innovation followed seven principles for multimedia learning, including that "Students learn better from words and pictures than from words alone" (multimedia principle), spatial and temporal contiguity, coherence, modality, redundancy, and individual differences principles. The presentation used images and words rather than full sentences, linked images and words simultaneously, and used narration with storytelling linking abstract concepts to historical contexts.
requirements: Presentations should avoid extraneous sounds beyond narration and should not introduce new information beyond face-to-face lectures.
constraints: Design effects are stronger for low-knowledge learners than for high-knowledge learners (individual differences principle).

citation: Liang, M., Lim, C. P., Park, J., & Mendoza, N. B. (2023). A review of ICT-enabled learning for schoolgirls in Asia and its impacts on education equity. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10178-w
title: Gender Analysis Framework (GAF) as a lens for reviewing ICT-enabled learning for schoolgirls
description: The review adopts the Gender Analysis Framework (GAF; Jhpiego, 2020) as its organizing lens, a "multidimensional framework that systematically examines how ICT-enabled learning influences schoolgirls". GAF comprises four interrelated dimensions: access to assets, practice and participation, belief and perception, and institutions, laws and policies. The review narrows GAF to primary and secondary education and uses it to code and synthesize the 30 included studies.
requirements: The framework requires organizing data on gender differences across social contexts, as the article states GAF "offers a mechanism to organize data on gender differences in a variety of social contexts".
constraints: The review narrows GAF to primary and secondary education, and the article notes the review "only focuses on evidences from empirical research without further analyzing context-related elements" such as GDP, religion, and geographical location.

article_title: Transforming student engagement in COVID-19 remote instruction: a research perspective
citation: Dave Edyburn. (2021). Transforming student engagement in COVID-19 remote instruction: a research perspective. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09919-6
title: OLSit three-stage model of student-centered engagement (Own It, Learn It, Share It)
description: The OLSit model is a three-stage design framework for student-centered learning built from a literature synthesis of research on student engagement, autonomy, scaffolding, motivation, and meta-cognition. In the Own It phase, "students define their purpose and create a learning plan with the assistance of the teacher"; in the Learn It phase the student engages in learning activities operationalized through a learning plan; in the Share It phase the student identifies channels for sharing learning with an authentic audience. Edyburn re-examines the model as applicable to COVID-19 remote instruction.
requirements: Teacher guidance during the Own It phase, since the model distinguishes itself from pure discovery learning where the student is left floundering
constraints: The literature has yet to see replications of the OLSit model, per the article
target_learning_goals: student engagement
self-directed learning

title: Three quality criteria for digital formative assessment of deep conceptual understanding: relevance, validity, and in-depth informativity
description: The article proposes that a DFA for deep conceptual understanding must fulfill three criteria: relevance (focusing on the most relevant components of a topic), validity (appropriateness of inferences, including actionable diagnostic information for teachers), and in-depth informativity (combining in-depth insights into student thinking with automatable analysis). These criteria structure the four-step design process and are summarized in Fig. 5.
requirements: Prior to item construction, epistemological and empirical research in the subject-matter area is required to unpack topics into the most relevant concept elements
constraints: The digital assessment of deep conceptual understanding is more challenging to realize than the digital assessment of procedural skills

description: The article suggests four steps to ensure the validity, relevance, and in-depth informativity of DFAs: Step 1, selection of relevant topics by identifying basic concepts; Step 2, unpacking selected basic concepts into concept elements, representations, language means, and valid indicators; Step 3, optimizing validity and in-depth informativity of DFA items; and Step 4, enhancing in-depth informativity by exploiting additional digital potentials such as log data and speech-to-text.

constraints: The four-step design process can help to identify technical limitations of digital platforms

It uses closed formats (multiple-choice, single-choice, drag-and-drop) automatically coded regarding typical assets and misconceptions, plus open-ended items manually coded by teachers with item-specific categories. Evaluation outcomes are displayed on dashboards with varying degrees of detail.

title: Identification-relevance account of learning from mental-health films
description: The article's findings organize around viewer identification and perceived relevance as the mechanisms linking film viewing to learning and self-disclosure about mental health. Viewers differ in identification by psychological status and sex, and identification relates to talking about personal problems, suggesting relevance and acceptability as central conditions for film-based mental-health instruction.

title: Critical pedagogy defined from a post-colonial framework focused on liberation
description: The article defines critical pedagogy "from a post-colonial framework focused on liberation," positioning it as an explanatory lens for teacher professional development in online and blended learning. It argues that liberatory ideas are already implicitly embedded in professional development frameworks, and that an explicit critical framework is needed to surface questions of power and equity in the shift to digital learning.

article_title: Digital learning innovation: engineering students’ learning motivation for AI scaffolding
citation: Jung Sun Sung · Wenhao David Huang. (2026). Digital learning innovation: engineering students’ learning motivation for AI scaffolding. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10576-w
title: ARCS model as a framework for designing and evaluating AI-featured scaffolding activities in STEM
description: The ARCS model (Keller, 1987) classifies motivation into four categories—Attention, Relevance, Confidence, and Satisfaction—each with three subcategories. The article applies this model as a design framework for AI-featured scaffolding activities and as an analytical lens for measuring motivational differences between conventional and AI methods. The article finds that the nature and meaning of subcategories under each category should be carefully reconsidered when applying AI features in instruction, and that the designing process emphasizes the Relevance category as it relates to the other three.
requirements: The nature and meaning of sub-categories under each of the four categories should be carefully reconsidered when applying AI features in instruction.
constraints: The designing process requires not only a deeper investigation of learners' characteristics but also reconceptualizing the genuine learning objectives and outcome criteria through AI scaffoldings.
target_learning_goals: Motivational design of AI-featured scaffolding activities in STEM
examples: The study used the ARCS model to design four scaffolding activities and to structure both the survey instrument (modified IMMS) and the interview protocol.

article_title: Understanding and managing the complexities in situated learning in immersive virtual environments
citation: Wang, M., Dede, C., Grotzer, T. A., & Chen, J. (2025). Understanding and managing the complexities in situated learning in immersive virtual environments. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10519-5
title: Framework of three complexity types surrounding situated learning
description: The article presents a conceptual framework delineating "the complexities of real-world problems, the complexities in exploring real-world problems, and the complexities in reflecting on problem exploration experience." It argues that real-world problems are ill-structured, involving "incomplete information and the lack of well-determined algorithms," and that exploration and reflection each pose distinct difficulties. The framework is intended as "a guide for designing situated learning curricula, evaluating situated learning practices, and addressing situated learning challenges."
requirements: A holistic understanding of complexities is needed so that scaffolding does not undermine the open-ended nature of situated learning
constraints: The authors state a limitation: "a lack of a systematic review of relevant studies before proposing the framework"

citation: Connolly, C., & Hall, T. (2021). Designing for emergency remote blended and online education: a response to Bennett et al. (2017). Education Tech Research Dev, 69, 281–284. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09892-0
title: Bennett et al.'s descriptive model of university teachers' design processes, framed by the 3P model and Approaches to Teaching framework
description: The commentary describes a "descriptive model illustrating university teachers' design processes, and the commonalities in the experience of university teachers as educational designers" produced by Bennett et al. (2017). The model is said to "assist university educators who require heuristics to evaluate the impact of their designs for teaching on the learning experience of their students". Its conceptual framing rests on the 3P model (presage–process–product) (Biggs 1993) and the Approaches to Teaching framework (Prosser and Trigwell 1997). The commentary calls it "a useful, replicable descriptive model" that is "especially salient in the current situation" for creating or modifying courses.
requirements: University educators require heuristics to evaluate the impact of their designs for teaching on the learning experience of their students
constraints: The study underpinning the model is solely focused on the Australian university sector
target_learning_goals: educational design of units of learning and courses
examples: The commentary suggests the model "should be immediately useful for those now creating units of learning anew and or modifying existing courses" during emergency remote teaching.

article_title: A feedback learning and mental models perspective on strategic decision making
citation: Capelo, C., & Dias, J. F. (2009). A feedback learning and mental models perspective on strategic decision making. Educational Technology Research and Development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-009-9123-z
title: Dynamic model of decision-making process based on feedback loops and mental models
description: The article presents a dynamic model of the decision-making process in which managers make decisions and learn in the context of feedback loops. In single-loop learning, managers compare information about the state of a real system to pre-established goals and make decisions without changing their mental models. In double-loop learning, information about the business system also feeds back to modify the managers' mental models, which they then use to anticipate and evaluate the consequences of alternative strategic choices. Cognitive limitations and quality of feedback information are identified as key factors that impact the effectiveness of double-loop learning.
requirements: Managers must have access to feedback information about the state of the business system to compare against goals
constraints: Due to cognitive limitations, the mental models that managers use for decision making are necessarily imperfect, making a flawless assessment of the dynamic behavior of the business system nearly impossible
target_learners: Managers making strategic decisions in dynamically complex business contexts
target_learning_goals: Improving strategic decision making through better understanding of business system structure and behaviour
key_sources: Capelo, C., & Dias, J. F. (2009). A feedback learning and mental models perspective on strategic decision making. Educational Technology Research and Development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-009-9123-z

title: Use intentional self-reflection practices to strengthen theoretical understanding and expertise development
description: The article recommends that learners use intentional self-reflection practices such as "journals, blogs, informal conversations, concept maps" to strengthen skills and knowledge in developing individual expertise. Self-reflection deepens theoretical understanding and strengthens metacognitive skills and problem solving.
requirements: Learners must engage in reflective practices such as journals, blogs, informal conversations, or concept maps
constraints: Expertise development takes time, practice, and awareness of experts' thought processes

article_title: Instructional design learners make sense of theory: a collaborative autoethnography
citation: Fiock, H., Meech, S., Yang, M., Long, Y., Farmer, T., Hilliard, N., Koehler, A. A., & Cheng, Z. (2022). Instructional design learners make sense of theory: a collaborative autoethnography. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-10075-8
title: Sensemaking approaches to theoretical understanding in instructional design
description: The article organizes its findings around a framework of sensemaking approaches ID learners use: deconstructing theory, distinguishing terminology, integrating concepts with previous knowledge, maintaining openness to multiple perspectives, personalizing understanding, and applying theory. The authors describe how learners move from basic, perfunctory understanding through awareness of insufficient knowledge toward constructed understanding, with struggle as an integral emotional and intellectual component. The framework draws on Weick et al.'s (2005) sensemaking concept and Meyer and Land's (2006) threshold concepts and liminality.
requirements: Learners must encounter complex, abstract theory with inconsistent terminology to trigger the sensemaking process
constraints: Findings stem from a single collaborative autoethnography of six learners in one course and may not generalize to other settings
target_learning_goals: developing deep theoretical understanding of ID theory

article_title: Design considerations in emergency remote teaching during the COVID-19 pandemic: a human-centered approach
citation: Karakaya, K. (2021). Design considerations in emergency remote teaching during the COVID-19 pandemic: a human-centered approach. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09884-0
title: Design ERT with humanizing pedagogy and pedagogy of care to prioritize student needs, feelings, and challenges
description: The article recommends that during emergency remote teaching, university instructors foreground students' needs, feelings, and challenges by adopting humanizing pedagogy and pedagogy of care. Humanizing pedagogy involves "pushing beyond purely cognitive approaches" and "addressing issues of power, access, and representation," while pedagogy of care attends to the feeling of caring and being cared for. The article argues this helps teachers build empathy and tailor supportive designs during crisis transitions.
requirements: University teachers have autonomy in deciding what and how to teach, enabling them to adopt a human-centered design approach
constraints: Intended for emergency remote teaching contexts during crisis, not routine course design
target_learners: university students in emergency remote teaching
target_learning_goals: student well-being and support
inclusive online learning experiences
examples: The article recommends ERT designs coach learners on how to learn online, discuss expectations with the learning community, and offer flexible deadlines to accommodate learners' lived experiences.

article_title: Development and validation of a learning analytics rubric for self-regulated learning
citation: de Barba, P. G., Oliveira, E. A., & English, N. (2025). Development and validation of a learning analytics rubric for self-regulated learning. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10521-x
title: Learning Analytics SRL Rubric for Canvas LMS
description: A learning analytics rubric developed to measure students' self-regulated learning processes within learning management systems in a scalable, consistent, and explainable manner. It maps items from validated SRL scales (MSLQ, OSLQ, MAI, A-SRL) onto Canvas LMS trace data indicators, using three key analytics features: materials and source type, study sessions, and lead-up versus normal days. The rubric employs an analytic structure with criteria based on the five-stage model of skill acquisition, and was validated with postgraduate students comparing self-assessments against system-generated scores.
requirements: Requires an LMS (Canvas) that logs page accesses with timestamps and resource type
Requires ungraded quizzes or similar identifiable extra activities in the LMS
constraints: Only 10 of 211 SRL scale items were feasible to map to LMS data (less than 5%)
Motivational and emotional/affective aspects of SRL and help-seeking behavior are under-represented
Thresholds for indicators were mostly arbitrarily defined due to lack of specific research
Indicator 8 (checking feedback on past assessments) was deemed not feasible because the software could not reliably identify when students were accessing feedback
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning processes including planning, monitoring, time and effort regulation, and learning strategies
examples: Indicator 1 reviews content across the semester to understand relationships between materials
Indicator 3 follows a weekly study schedule measured by average study sessions per week
key_sources: de Barba, P. G., Oliveira, E. A., & English, N. (2025). Development and validation of a learning analytics rubric for self-regulated learning. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10521-x

citation: de Barba, P. G., Oliveira, E. A., & English, N. (2025). Development and validation of a learning analytics rubric for self-regulated learning. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10521-x
title: Zimmerman's cyclical three-phase model of self-regulated learning
description: The socio-cognitive perspective on self-regulated learning, primarily advanced by Zimmerman (2002), conceptualizes SRL as a cyclical process involving three phases: forethought, performance, and self-reflection. During the forethought phase, students engage in task analysis and activate self-motivational beliefs. The performance phase involves self-control and self-observation. In the self-reflection phase, students evaluate their performance and make attributions about causes of results. This model emphasizes that self-regulated learning is not a fixed trait but rather a context-specific set of processes that students can develop over time.
requirements: Assessment should capture the temporal and contextual dimensions of regulatory processes rather than treating them as static attributes
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning across forethought, performance, and self-reflection phases
examples: The article maps its eight indicators onto Zimmerman's cyclical model, with indicators 5 and 7 reflecting forethought phase activities
key_sources: de Barba, P. G., Oliveira, E. A., & English, N. (2025). Development and validation of a learning analytics rubric for self-regulated learning. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10521-x

article_title: Development and validation of a learning analytics rubric for self-regulated learning
citation: de Barba, P. G., Oliveira, E. A., & English, N. (2025). Development and validation of a learning analytics rubric for self-regulated learning. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10521-x
title: Winne and Hadwin's four-phase cognitive information processing model of SRL
description: Winne and Hadwin's (2013) model conceptualizes SRL as involving four loosely sequential phases: task definition, goal setting and planning, enacting tactics and strategies, and adaptation. This model emphasizes metacognition—thinking about one's thinking—as a central mechanism through which students monitor and control their cognitive processes during learning. This cognitive approach complements the socio-cognitive perspective and has shaped measurement approaches in the field, including instruments like the Metacognitive Awareness Inventory.
requirements: Students must accurately monitor their understanding and learning processes to make appropriate adjustments to their strategies
target_learning_goals: metacognitive monitoring and control during learning
examples: The Metacognitive Awareness Inventory focuses specifically on students' knowledge of cognition and regulation of cognition
key_sources: de Barba, P. G., Oliveira, E. A., & English, N. (2025). Development and validation of a learning analytics rubric for self-regulated learning. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10521-x

article_title: Measuring learning in serious games: a case study with structural assessment
citation: Wouters, P., van der Spek, E. D., & van Oostendorp, H. (2011). Measuring learning in serious games: A case study with structural assessment. Educational Technology Research and Development, 59(6), 741–763. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-010-9183-0
title: Structural assessment measures learning by comparing a learner's knowledge organization with a referent structure
description: Structural assessment is defined as measuring the learners' knowledge organization and comparing this with a referent structure. It rests on the assumption that knowledge is organized in structures containing important concepts and the relations among them. The article proposes it as an alternative to verbal assessment for serious games, arguing that effective knowledge structures enable faster problem solving and integration of new information.
requirements: A domain analysis must identify the important concepts of the domain or task
Experts in the domain must agree about the essential concepts and relations
constraints: Agreement on essential concepts is more likely in 'hard' domains with a central body of theory than in 'soft' domains
target_learners: Novices and advanced learners in domains requiring complex skills
target_learning_goals: Knowledge organization and understanding of domain concepts
key_sources: Wouters, P., van der Spek, E. D., & van Oostendorp, H. (2011). Measuring learning in serious games: A case study with structural assessment. Educational Technology Research and Development, 59(6), 741–763. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-010-9183-0

article_title: Measuring learning in serious games: a case study with structural assessment
citation: Wouters, P., van der Spek, E. D., & van Oostendorp, H. (2011). Measuring learning in serious games: A case study with structural assessment. Educational Technology Research and Development, 59(6), 741–763. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-010-9183-0
title: Pathfinder network technique for structural assessment
description: Pathfinder is a graph-theoretic distance technique that represents a proximity matrix in a graphical network structure (PFnet). It uses the distance measured by the minimum number of links connecting two nodes in a graph. The algorithm removes direct links if a shorter, indirect path connects both concepts. Pathfinder was adopted because it does not force a hierarchical structure on the data and identifies meaningful links between concepts.
requirements: A proximity matrix of relatedness ratings between concept pairs
A scaling procedure to transform ratings into a network representation
constraints: When participants use many extreme relatedness ratings, Pathfinder includes all links when there are tied distances, producing networks with many more links than expected
target_learning_goals: Representing and evaluating knowledge organization
key_sources: Wouters, P., van der Spek, E. D., & van Oostendorp, H. (2011). Measuring learning in serious games: A case study with structural assessment. Educational Technology Research and Development, 59(6), 741–763. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-010-9183-0

article_title: Measuring learning in serious games: a case study with structural assessment
citation: Wouters, P., van der Spek, E. D., & van Oostendorp, H. (2011). Measuring learning in serious games: A case study with structural assessment. Educational Technology Research and Development, 59(6), 741–763. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-010-9183-0
title: Three-step structural assessment process: elicitation, representation, evaluation
description: The article distinguishes three consecutive steps to implement a structural approach to measure and interpret knowledge structures. Knowledge elicitation captures the underlying organization of knowledge through methods such as card sorting or rating relatedness between concept pairs. Knowledge representation transforms ratings into a graphical network. Knowledge evaluation compares the learner's structure with a referent knowledge structure using similarity or coherence measures.
requirements: Selection of important domain concepts through cognitive task analysis, instructional material analysis, or expert interviews
A referent knowledge structure derived from an instructor, an expert, or an analysis of instructional material
target_learning_goals: Assessment of knowledge organization in complex-skill domains

article_title: Systematic design of a learning environment for domain-specific and domain-general critical thinking skills
citation: Tiruneh, D. T., Weldeslassie, A. G., Kassa, A., Tefera, Z., De Cock, M., & Elen, J. (2016). Systematic design of a learning environment for domain-specific and domain-general critical thinking skills. Education Tech Research Dev, 64, 481–505. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-015-9417-2
title: First Principles of Instruction model as a framework for designing CT-embedded subject matter instruction
description: The article draws on Merrill's First Principles of Instruction model, which "abstracted five interrelated prescriptive instructional design principles: activation, demonstration, application, integration and problem-centeredness". The model holds that learning is promoted when learners acquire knowledge and skills in the context of real-world problems, and that instruction designed on these principles can result in effective, efficient and engaging learning. The authors used it as the design framework for the experimental E&M learning environment, translating each principle into concrete classroom activities: whole-task problems, prior-knowledge activation, instructor modelling, coached application, and peer presentation and defence of solutions.
requirements: Design requires identifying desired CT outcomes and splitting them into sub-skills before designing instruction
Instructors need training and involvement in the design process to implement lessons as designed
constraints: No previous study, to the authors' knowledge, had tested the efficacy of this model in designing interventions targeting CT skill development
target_learning_goals: domain-specific critical thinking skills in electricity and magnetism
domain-general critical thinking skills
examples: The experimental learning environment gave students whole-task problems such as explaining why lightning-strike charge stays on the exterior of an aircraft, before instruction on the chapter began.
key_sources: Tiruneh, D. T., Weldeslassie, A. G., Kassa, A., Tefera, Z., De Cock, M., & Elen, J. (2016). Systematic design of a learning environment for domain-specific and domain-general critical thinking skills. Education Tech Research Dev, 64, 481–505. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-015-9417-2

article_title: Systematic design of a learning environment for domain-specific and domain-general critical thinking skills
citation: Tiruneh, D. T., Weldeslassie, A. G., Kassa, A., Tefera, Z., De Cock, M., & Elen, J. (2016). Systematic design of a learning environment for domain-specific and domain-general critical thinking skills. Education Tech Research Dev, 64, 481–505. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-015-9417-2
title: Immersion-based embedding of CT skills in systematically designed subject matter instruction
description: The article contrasts the Infusion approach, in which students are explicitly trained on how to apply CT skills as part of subject matter instruction, with the Immersion approach, which "aims to help students acquire the desired CT skills as they construct knowledge and skills of a subject matter domain, without explicit instruction about desired CT skills". The study's intervention followed the Immersion approach: CT skills (reasoning, argument analysis, hypothesis testing, likelihood and uncertainty analysis, and problem solving and decision-making) were embraced as part of regular domain-specific classroom activities rather than taught separately. The pattern operated through whole-task problems, demonstrations, coached group application, and tutorial sessions where students defended solutions.
requirements: Subject matter instruction must be systematically designed so that domain-specific activities implicitly target the desired CT skills
constraints: The Immersion-based intervention improved domain-specific CT but did not yield a significantly greater domain-general CT gain than regular instruction
target_learning_goals: critical thinking skills embedded within domain-specific instruction
examples: Students were divided into 10 groups of 4 or 5 and worked on contextually relevant E&M problems requiring collaboration.
key_sources: Tiruneh, D. T., Weldeslassie, A. G., Kassa, A., Tefera, Z., De Cock, M., & Elen, J. (2016). Systematic design of a learning environment for domain-specific and domain-general critical thinking skills. Education Tech Research Dev, 64, 481–505. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-015-9417-2

article_title: Systematic design of a learning environment for domain-specific and domain-general critical thinking skills
citation: Tiruneh, D. T., Weldeslassie, A. G., Kassa, A., Tefera, Z., De Cock, M., & Elen, J. (2016). Systematic design of a learning environment for domain-specific and domain-general critical thinking skills. Education Tech Research Dev, 64, 481–505. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-015-9417-2
title: Design subject matter instruction to implicitly target CT skills through systematically structured domain-specific activities rather than teaching general CT skills separately
description: The article argues that "the design of CT instructional interventions should be supported by the principles of instructional design research" and tested an alternative method to address CT development through the systematic design of subject matter instruction rather than explicit instruction on general CT skills. The principle holds that meaningful subject matter learning inherently involves developing relevant CT skills, so instruction should be designed so that CT is an implicit goal of domain-specific activities. The study's evidence supports this principle for domain-specific CT outcomes.
requirements: Instructional design must be based on valid principles from instructional design research, such as the First Principles of Instruction model
constraints: The approach produced domain-specific CT gains but no significant domain-general CT advantage over regular instruction
target_learners: higher education students in domain-specific courses
target_learning_goals: domain-specific critical thinking skills
domain-general critical thinking skills
examples: In the experimental condition, students worked in small groups on contextually relevant E&M problems, observed instructor demonstrations modelling reasoning procedures, and defended solutions in tutorial sessions, while the control condition solved traditional end-of-chapter computation problems.

article_title: Connecting sustainability and computer science curricula through website learning projects embedding different types of student-generated content
citation: Blanco, J. M., Domínguez, C., Jaime, A., & Usandizaga, I. (2024). Connecting sustainability and computer science curricula through website learning projects embedding different types of student-generated content. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10376-8
title: A three-project progression (video → channel → website) where students create, review, and reuse peer-generated content about SDG topics.
description: The article describes a "series of three learning projects whose outcome is content addressing the computer engineering profession and its relationship to SDGs". Students first create a video on a specific SDG, then create derivative videos in a shared channel, and finally build a multilingual website integrating content from previous projects and peers. The design embeds "the exchange of information and the sharing of opinions" through teamwork and progressive content building.
requirements: Instructor-provided presentation documents and materials
Video channel and website hosting infrastructure
Team-based work with 3–8 members per project
constraints: SDG-related content is "not assessed in exams or other tests, and is used purely for formative assessment"
Time-constrained: video and channel projects last 3 weeks each, website project lasts 8 weeks
target_learning_goals: Project management skills
Understanding of the impact of ICT on Sustainable Development Goals
examples: Teams of three or four students produced a video on one SDG in three weeks; later teams of six to eight built a multilingual website with videos, web articles, and self-assessment questionnaires organised by SDG.
key_sources: Blanco, J. M., Domínguez, C., Jaime, A., & Usandizaga, I. (2024). Connecting sustainability and computer science curricula through website learning projects embedding different types of student-generated content. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10376-8

article_title: A classification tool to foster self-regulated learning with generative artificial intelligence by applying self-determination theory: a case of ChatGPT
citation: Chiu, T. K. F. (2024). A classification tool to foster self-regulated learning with generative artificial intelligence by applying self-determination theory: a case of ChatGPT. Education Tech Research Dev, 72, 2401–2416. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10366-w
title: Classification tool of 20 ChatGPT learning activities with descriptions and consensus mappings to SDT needs and SRL phases
description: The article's main artifact is a classification tool listing 20 ChatGPT-based learning activities, each with a description and a consensus rating of which SDT need and SRL phase it serves (Tables 1 and 2). Activities include when students "search information, get examples, check their answers, generate review questions to check for their understanding, create new problems for practice, create challenging problems, get insight into complex problems, ask ideas for their improvement, make lists or outlines," and more. It is intended to help researchers replicate intervention studies and help teachers adapt activities.
requirements: Activities carry consensus-established labels, descriptions, and explanations of their impact on needs and phases, refined across three Delphi rounds.
constraints: The authors note many activities are not typical or less common teaching practices, so teachers would need to modify them for their own teaching.
target_learners: School students in Hong Kong across primary and secondary academic levels
target_learning_goals: Self-regulated learning across forethought, performance, and self-reflection phases
SDT needs satisfaction (autonomy, competence, relatedness)
examples: Teachers and researchers can use the tool to conduct intervention research on whether ChatGPT fosters the SRL process, and developers may use the activities to improve educational ChatGPT development.
key_sources: Chiu, T. K. F. (2024). A classification tool to foster self-regulated learning with generative artificial intelligence by applying self-determination theory: a case of ChatGPT. Education Tech Research Dev, 72, 2401–2416. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10366-w

article_title: A classification tool to foster self-regulated learning with generative artificial intelligence by applying self-determination theory: a case of ChatGPT
citation: Chiu, T. K. F. (2024). A classification tool to foster self-regulated learning with generative artificial intelligence by applying self-determination theory: a case of ChatGPT. Education Tech Research Dev, 72, 2401–2416. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10366-w
title: SDT-based digital needs support framework crossed with the three-phase SRL cycle for designing ChatGPT learning activities
description: The article organizes ChatGPT-based learning design around self-determination theory, which "suggests three innate needs: autonomy, relatedness, and competence," crossed with the social cognitive SRL model of three iterative phases: forethought, performance, and self-reflection. Digital needs support means designing digital learning environments to satisfy these needs; the study applies the framework to classify which ChatGPT activities satisfy which need and foster which SRL phase from a teacher perspective.
requirements: Learning activities must be classified so each maps to one SDT need and one SRL phase, with consensus on impact established among qualified teachers.
constraints: The article states digital support, particularly in AI, has not been extensively studied in SDT-based research, and the panel's perspective is eastern (Hong Kong) rather than western.
target_learners: School students in blended and technology-enhanced learning settings
target_learning_goals: Motivation and needs satisfaction
Self-regulated learning process
examples: The framework structured the Delphi survey: teachers indicated which SDT needs and SRL phases each candidate ChatGPT activity primarily impacted.
key_sources: Chiu, T. K. F. (2024). A classification tool to foster self-regulated learning with generative artificial intelligence by applying self-determination theory: a case of ChatGPT. Education Tech Research Dev, 72, 2401–2416. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10366-w

article_title: A classification tool to foster self-regulated learning with generative artificial intelligence by applying self-determination theory: a case of ChatGPT
citation: Chiu, T. K. F. (2024). A classification tool to foster self-regulated learning with generative artificial intelligence by applying self-determination theory: a case of ChatGPT. Education Tech Research Dev, 72, 2401–2416. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10366-w
title: Pair ChatGPT-based activities with teacher needs support, since ChatGPT alone cannot satisfy every student need at every SRL phase
description: Because the consensus mappings show ChatGPT activities leave relatedness and autonomy unsatisfied in some SRL phases, the article recommends combining digital and teacher support: "To fully utilize each student’s SRL potential, ChatGPT and the teacher should collaborate." Teachers provide direction and guidance for school children who are still developing, complementing the instant, tailored feedback ChatGPT offers.
requirements: Teachers with well-researched needs-support practices who can provide direction and guidance alongside ChatGPT activities.
constraints: The article states the classification may not simply apply to classroom instruction because the aims and contexts differ, since the study looked only at digital support rather than blended learning.
target_learners: School students, including young students still developing self-regulation
target_learning_goals: Full use of each student's SRL potential
SDT needs satisfaction across all three phases
examples: The discussion recommends collaboration for young students' SRL, noting teachers must provide direction and guidance because school children are still developing.

article_title: The relation of the social situation of contact to the media in mass communication
citation: Audio-Visual Communication Review. (1953). Audio-Visual Communication Review, 158. https://eric.ed.gov/
title: Social situation of contact as a factor in audience response to mass media
description: The digest presents the construct of the social situation of contact, defined as "the immediate social setting of contact with content and medium; that is, the people who are immediately involved in the individual's interactions when he is a member of the audience." Three basic situations were investigated: the child socially alone, the peer situation with friends, and the family situation with parents, grandparents, and much younger or older siblings. The study uses this construct to argue that audience response is shaped by the social setting of contact, not only by demographic attributes.
requirements: Investigation must distinguish the three basic social situations of contact: alone, peer, and family
constraints: Evidence came from a limited audience that is not representative of the general population
target_learners: children in kindergarten through sixth grade
target_learning_goals: understanding how the social setting of media contact shapes audience response
examples: The study interviewed 79 boys across kindergarten, second, fourth, and sixth grades about television, movies, and comic books
key_sources: Audio-Visual Communication Review. (1953). Audio-Visual Communication Review, 158. https://eric.ed.gov/

article_title: Profile analysis and its effect on learning when used to shorten recorded film commentaries
citation: Fletcher, Richard M. (1955). Profile Analysis and Its Effect on Learning When Used To Shorten Recorded Film Commentaries. Technical Report SDC Z69-7-55, Instructional Film Research Program, Pennsylvania State University. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Fletcher+profile+analysis+film+commentaries
title: Employ profile analysis before production to eliminate commentary material that does not contribute to learning
description: The report recommends that writers of film commentaries use profile analysis of viewer learning reports to identify and remove material that does not support learning before production, freeing time for material that does. As the report states, "profile analysis be employed by writers of film commentaries to eliminate material prior to production that does not contribute to learning so that it can be replaced with material that does." It rests on the finding that learning was equal for a much shorter profile version.
requirements: Four groups of about 32 recruits each providing continuous learning profiles by turning a knob during the commentary
constraints: Demonstrated at the commentary stage of instructional films; the report notes "It is at the commentary stage that it is most feasible to make any desired modification."
target_learners: military recruits in instructional film training
target_learning_goals: learning of information presented in instructional film commentaries
examples: The Human Reproduction commentary was shortened by judges with profiles and by judges without profiles, and the shortened versions were tested on each bit of information contained in the commentaries.
key_sources: Fletcher, Richard M. (1955). Profile Analysis and Its Effect on Learning When Used To Shorten Recorded Film Commentaries. Technical Report SDC Z69-7-55, Instructional Film Research Program, Pennsylvania State University. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Fletcher+profile+analysis+film+commentaries

article_title: Profile analysis and its effect on learning when used to shorten recorded film commentaries
citation: Fletcher, Richard M. (1955). Profile Analysis and Its Effect on Learning When Used To Shorten Recorded Film Commentaries. Technical Report SDC Z69-7-55, Instructional Film Research Program, Pennsylvania State University. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Fletcher+profile+analysis+film+commentaries
title: Profile technique with knob-response learning reports for shortening instructional material
description: The profile technique, developed by Twyford, collects moment-by-moment learning judgments from a viewing audience: "Each recruit turned a knob to indicate whether he was learning nothing, little, average, much, or the most he could." These profiles, obtained from four groups of 32 recruits each, guide judges in shortening film commentaries, and the report describes the technique as "much simpler and quicker to use in making an evaluation than the established method of measuring learnings with tests."
requirements: A recorded instructional material whose commentary can be modified, and a group of audience members providing knob-based learning ratings during presentation
constraints: Report notes the commentary stage is where modification is most feasible
target_learners: military recruits (profile providers); learners of instructional films
target_learning_goals: identifying which instructional material contributes to learning
examples: Four profiles were obtained from four groups of 32 recruits each for the commentaries of The Weather and Human Reproduction.

article_title: An exploration of instructional designers' prioritizations for integrating ChatGPT in design practice
citation: Fan Yang · Jill E. Stefaniak. (2025). An exploration of instructional designers' prioritizations for integrating ChatGPT in design practice. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10509-7
title: Instructional designers integrating GenAI should critically evaluate outputs and retain formative design practices such as team reviews and pilot testing
description: The article recommends that instructional designers approach GenAI use with intentionality rather than adopting it naively. It states that "Instructional designers should still be held to the same standards that predate GenAI, including designing and presenting content that is accurate, credible, and poses no harm to the learner." Designers should cross-reference ChatGPT content with reliable sources, engage SMEs to review generated content, and continue formative design practices.
requirements: Designers must be prepared to critically evaluate GenAI outputs against accuracy and credibility standards
constraints: The article notes no specific standards yet govern how GenAI should be used in instructional design
target_learners: instructional designers in higher education and industry
target_learning_goals: accurate and credible instructional content development
examples: The article recommends cross-referencing ChatGPT content with textbooks, research reports, and professional bodies, and pilot-testing new content with a subset of learners
key_sources: Fan Yang · Jill E. Stefaniak. (2025). An exploration of instructional designers' prioritizations for integrating ChatGPT in design practice. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10509-7

article_title: Social robots for education: a global analysis of deployments in real scenarios
citation: Ferrer, I., & Aymerich-Franch, L. (2026). Social robots for education: a global analysis of deployments in real scenarios. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10611-4
title: Taxonomy of six roles performed by social robots in education
description: The article classifies the roles social robots perform in educational deployments into six categories: "teacher, teaching assistant, tutor, psychological assistant, peer, and patient simulator." Each role is defined in Table 4, e.g., a teacher delivers "subjects' content, answering questions according to the learning program," while a peer acts "as a learning companion with no authoritative role." Roles can coexist or alternate within the same deployment and vary with subject and pedagogical objectives.
requirements: Robots must be placed in a real scenario to perform the tasks for which they were designed to count as a deployment
constraints: Roles are not mutually exclusive; some robots fulfill one or more roles within the same case
target_learning_goals: subject-matter instruction
social and emotional skills
programming skills
key_sources: Ferrer, I., & Aymerich-Franch, L. (2026). Social robots for education: a global analysis of deployments in real scenarios. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10611-4

article_title: Social robots for education: a global analysis of deployments in real scenarios
citation: Ferrer, I., & Aymerich-Franch, L. (2026). Social robots for education: a global analysis of deployments in real scenarios. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10611-4
title: Documentary database of 206 social robot education deployments
description: A documentary research database compiled from over 1,000 reviewed sources (papers, media, developer websites, and personal communications) in which the authors traced and analyzed "206 cases of social robot deployments" across 28 countries and 43 robot models. Cases are classified by robot name, manufacturer, institution, area and sub-area of deployment, country, type of educational content delivery, role performed, and specific tasks carried out.
requirements: Cases must meet the article's inclusion criteria: robots with social features, physical embodiment, minimal anthropomorphic features, verbal and/or non-verbal communication, mostly autonomous or semi-autonomous operation, at least minimum movement capacity, and deployments aimed at educational provision
constraints: Data collection took place from May 2020 to May 2021; the strategic non-probabilistic sampling method means the resulting sample is not representative
target_learning_goals: mapping real-world deployments of social robots for education
informing integration strategies and design practices
examples: Data will be made available on request, per the article's data availability statement

article_title: Cheating in the second year of generative AI chatbots: a follow-up study on high school student cheating behaviors
citation: Ruishi Chen, Victor R. Lee, Annie Camey Kuo, Denise Clark Pope, Sarah Miles. (2026). Cheating in the second year of generative AI chatbots: a follow-up study on high school student cheating behaviors. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10587-1
title: Academic integrity as a long-standing coevolutionary negotiation between student practices and educator expectations, with generative AI as a new iteration rather than a new pattern
description: The article frames cheating not as a new AI-driven phenomenon but as part of a "long-standing coevolutionary pattern in education, in which students continually explore new ways to gain academic advantage while educators respond by developing new norms, policies, and instructional strategies to maintain academic integrity." Under this lens, generative AI represents "a new iteration of an ongoing negotiation between students' practices and educators' expectations" rather than a novel form of dishonesty. The framework draws on prior scholarship (McCabe et al., 2001; Whitley, 1998; Stephens & Wangaard, 2013) and is used to interpret the finding that cheating rates remained stable while AI use grew.
requirements: Self-report survey instrumentation that tracks specific dishonest behaviors over time, enabling comparison against historical baselines
constraints: The article notes specific technologies change over time, so the framework addresses the general negotiation pattern rather than predicting effects of any single technology
target_learning_goals: academic integrity
appropriate technology use norms
examples: The authors apply this lens to interpret stable cheating rates alongside increasing AI chatbot exposure and use in the 2023-24 survey
key_sources: Ruishi Chen, Victor R. Lee, Annie Camey Kuo, Denise Clark Pope, Sarah Miles. (2026). Cheating in the second year of generative AI chatbots: a follow-up study on high school student cheating behaviors. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10587-1

article_title: Comparing perceptions of the school librarian using the future ready school—librarian framework
citation: Felicia Warden · Andrew A. Tawfik. (2026). Comparing perceptions of the school librarian using the future ready school—librarian framework. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10670-7
title: Future Ready Schools—Librarian Framework (FRS-LF) three meta-constructs of school librarianship
description: The Future Ready Schools—Librarian Framework (FRS-LF), developed by the U.S. Department of Education's Office of Educational Technology and the American Institutes for Research, guides schools to "apply digital resources for effective learning outcomes." It organizes school librarianship into three meta-constructs: pedagogy (Use of Space and Time; Literacy; Curriculum, Instruction, and Assessment), collaboration (Community Partnerships; Collaborative Leadership; Personalized Professional Development), and systems and policies (Robust Infrastructure; Budget and Resources; Data and Privacy). The article uses it as the lens for surveying stakeholder alignment.
requirements: Requires collaboration among administrators, teachers, and librarians as stakeholders within the K-12 ecosystem
constraints: The study notes the framework was applied in a Tennessee public-school context aligned with state librarian guidelines
target_learners: K-12 administrators, teachers, and school librarians
target_learning_goals: Stakeholder alignment on librarian roles supporting digital learning, literacy, and technology integration

article_title: Validation of a peer observation and evaluation tool for online teaching in the U.S.
citation: Jia, Y., Spagnolo, A. B., Barrett, N., Murphy, A. A., Basto, P. M., Rothpletz-Puglia, P., & Luther, S. (2025). Validation of a peer observation and evaluation tool for online teaching in the U.S. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10428-z
title: Peer Observation and Evaluation Tool-Online (POET-O)
description: The POET-O is a peer observation and evaluation instrument for single online lessons, created by "modifying and adapting the POET (Trujillo et al., 2008) by adding selected items from the Quality Matters rubric." The final instrument has 32 items across five sections: Presentation and Activities (7 items), Use of Technology (5), ADA Compliance/Accessibility (4), Assessment (3), and Instructor (13), each rated on a 4-point scale from "Not Present" to "Accomplished Well" with a "Not Applicable" option. The complete tool includes pre-observation, observation, general reviewer comments, post-observation, and faculty reflection and action plan sections.
requirements: Requires standardized training and/or debriefing of faculty reviewers to ensure reliable and consistent assessment
Requires lesson submitters to provide course materials, syllabus, and assessment items for review
constraints: Validated only for online synchronous and asynchronous lessons; the authors state it "should be further evaluated" for in-person lab/practice-based lessons
Does not include peer assessment of the use of learning theory or teaching philosophy

title: Three models of teaching observation: evaluation, developmental, and collaborative
description: The article describes "three models of teaching observation—evaluation, developmental, and collaborative—are commonly recognized in the literature (Yiend et al., 2014)." The evaluation model is managerial and judgmental, overseeing teaching quality for compliance. The developmental model is less judgmental and more formative, involving an educational expert as observer. The collaborative model, also formative, entails mutual observation between academic colleagues. The POET-O assumes the collaborative model with the purpose of improving teaching through constructive dialogue.
constraints: The article notes the collaborative model "in nature has a greater chance of ongoing success" per Fletcher (2018)

citation: Fink, M. C., Radkowitsch, A., Bauer, E., Sailer, M., Kiesewetter, J., Schmidmaier, R., Siebeck, M., Fischer, F., & Fischer, M. R. (2020). Simulation research and design: a dual-level framework for multi-project research programs. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09876-0
title: A dual-level framework describes simulation research and design programs as a research committee plus subordinate projects moving through four phases
description: The article proposes a framework describing a research program as "a dual-level, multi-project system consisting of one research committee and two or more research projects". It passes through four program/project phases: creating a foundation, constructing and adapting simulations and research materials, conducting empirical investigations, and analyzing data and communicating results. Members take on consultant, researcher, designer, and content expert roles, and phases can overlap and iterate. The framework was derived from theory on multi-team systems, Sonnenwald's program stages, and the multi-center simulation research model, and is illustrated with the COSIMA program.
requirements: Applies to research programs with a research committee and multiple subordinate research projects focusing on the assessment and facilitation of knowledge and competences
constraints: Scope limited to programs developing simulations as complex scientific artifacts; phases may overlap and iterate rather than run strictly linearly
target_learners: higher education students in medical and teacher education (the program's research populations)
target_learning_goals: diagnostic competences facilitated through simulation-based learning
examples: The COSIMA program: a research committee of twelve professors coordinating eight projects, seven empirical and one meta-analysis, investigating scaffolding in simulation-based learning environments

title: Simulations can be classified by modality (live, role-play, digital) and purpose (assessment, facilitation, research)
description: The article defines simulations as "authentic models of professional situations that can be manipulated by participants", distinguished from simulators as the technical devices used to conduct them. It classifies simulations by modality into live simulations with trained standardized persons, role-play simulations with briefly prepared participants, and digital simulations run on computers, and by purpose into assessment, facilitation, or research. The framework offers specific recommendations for these two critical features.
requirements: Design processes should consider modality and purpose as critical features; simulations and simulators are distinct artifacts that have to be designed separately
constraints: The framework targets simulations that assess and train knowledge and competences, excluding simulations emphasizing skills such as motor skills
target_learners: learners in medical education and teacher education
target_learning_goals: knowledge and competence acquisition and assessment in simulated professional situations
examples: COSIMA 4 simulated a medical interview using live simulations with professional actors, digital simulations, and role-play simulations

title: Simulation components: learning and testing environments, simulation scenarios, case vignettes, briefings, and debriefings
description: The article classifies the simulation components typically developed in simulation research programs (Table 2). Learning environments "pursue the goal of facilitating knowledge and competence acquisition and include instructional support", while testing environments assess without instructional support. Simulation scenarios are professional situations in which an agent can demonstrate competences; case vignettes depict persons with specific characteristics and a task; briefings include a familiarization and fiction contract; debriefings let learners compare their solution to the designated solution.
requirements: Components must be designed separately and embedded in the learning and testing environment according to the experimental procedure
target_learners: higher education learners in simulated professional situations
target_learning_goals: facilitation and assessment of knowledge and competences in simulations
examples: COSIMA 4 created case vignettes from a blueprint specifying critical features, with an expert workshop evaluating their accuracy and difficulty

title: Research materials for simulation studies: assessment instruments, educational intervention, and experimental procedure
description: Table 1 of the article classifies the materials developed for research purposes in simulation-based studies. Instruments that assess knowledge treat it as a prerequisite of performance, while competence instruments "operationalize this construct as observable results and processes in simulations", including computer-based tests, coding schemes, and rating scales. The educational intervention is the treatment condition examined, such as instructional support like prompts, and the experimental procedure consists of the measurement procedure and an experimenter's guide.

title: An interdisciplinary framework differentiates diagnostic competences into professional knowledge base, epistemic-diagnostic activities, and diagnostic quality
description: The article adopts the framework by Heitzmann et al. (2019), shown in its Fig. 2, for facilitating diagnostic competences with simulations. Knowledge and competences are differentiated "according to types of knowledge (i.e., the structure of knowledge) as well as content-related facets of knowledge". The framework links individual learning prerequisites, instructional support (scaffolding such as prompting, role-taking, and reflection phases), epistemic-diagnostic activities like generating hypotheses and evaluating evidence, and diagnostic quality comprising accuracy and efficiency, within a learning-process and test-performance loop.

constraints: Serves simulations assessing and training knowledge and competences in medical education and teacher education

target_learning_goals: diagnostic competences, including diagnostic accuracy and efficiency

article_title: Collaborative note-taking affects cognitive load: the interplay of completeness and interaction
citation: Jamie Costley, Mik Fanguy. (2021). Collaborative note-taking affects cognitive load: the interplay of completeness and interaction. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09979-2
title: Implement collaborative note-taking because germane-load gains outweigh extraneous-load costs
description: The article recommends adopting collaborative note-taking in online and flipped courses despite the confusion cost it imposes. The authors state that "considering this conflict, the authors of present study suggest it is still beneficial to implement collaborative note-taking", because reported gains in understanding outweigh the drawbacks of higher extraneous load. The recommendation rests directly on the study's finding that collaborative note-takers reported both higher germane and higher extraneous load.

schema development from lecture videos

article_title: How pictures and graphs aid learning from print
citation: How Pictures and Graphs Aid Learning From Print. (1953). Audio-Visual Communication Review. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Audio-Visual+Communication+Review
title: For maximum learning results, pictures should be relevant, large, simple, well reproduced, realistic, and integrated with the text
description: This principle, drawn from the University of Illinois review of over 50 experimental studies, states that "for maximum results, pictures should be relevant, large enough to be read easily in detail, simple, reproduced well, realistic rather than stylized, and integrated with the text." It guides the design of graphic materials accompanying printed learning materials. The review also notes evidence that colored pictures attract more attention than black-and-white, with attention-attraction power varying with sex, age, and personality.
requirements: Pictures must be relevant to the text and large enough to be read easily in detail
constraints: The review notes the attention findings concern attention attraction, not retention, since questions about retention had not been faced by the research it reviewed
target_learning_goals: learning from print-supported instruction
examples: The review abstracted over 50 studies bearing on pictures and graphs as aids to learning from print

title: SCY pedagogical scenarios: reusable blueprints assembled from activity-ELO-tool triplets, LASs, and scenario templates
description: Pedagogical scenarios are the SCY project's formalized instructional design method for building technology-enhanced learning environments. A scenario "presents the learning process as an organized assembly of elementary learning processes, each associated with a specific learning object and a tool for creating this learning object." Designers select a scenario and then add domain content; the SCY technical infrastructure instantiates it without programming.

title: Scenario-based design pattern: select a scenario, adapt it to context, then add domain content
description: The SCY design pattern treats instructional design as selecting a reusable pedagogical scenario blueprint, adapting it, and adding domain content. The original two-step process (select scenario, instantiate with content) was extended in practice with an intermediate adaptation stage: "the initial two-step design process (select scenario, instantiate with content) was extended with an intermediate stage in which designers adapted a scenario by leaving out LASs" or specific ELOs that did not fit their context. Designers first decide target group and learning goals, select one of the 12 scenarios, then specify assignments, resources, and ELO-specific information. The scenario functions as an overall framework from which elements can be omitted while its character and structure are preserved.

title: Reuse programmed instructional-design scenarios to reduce development time and assure quality
description: Because designing technology-enhanced learning environments is costly and time-consuming — the article cites estimates "of the number of hours required to produce 1 h of instruction have ranged from 100 (Tannenbaum 2001) to 300 (Merrill & ID2 Research Group 1998)" — reuse of the instructional design supports time efficiency and quality assurance. SCY implements this by providing re-usable scenarios already programmed in the learning environment, so "no programming is required from the instructional designer," while an authoring system lets designers set parameters such as scaffolding level or create new scenarios. The approach balances ready-made structures with adaptability, echoing Murray's point that customization, extensibility, and scriptability characterize proficient authoring systems.

title: SCY design approach relative to ADDIE: collapsed phases with scenario selection early and infrastructure-driven implementation
description: The article positions the SCY instructional design approach against traditional sequential ISD models labeled ADDIE (Analysis, Design, Development, Implementation, Evaluation). It states that "All components of the ADDIE model are incorporated in the SCY approach, with defining learning goals in the beginning and implementation at the end," but with different emphases and collapsed steps: an existing pedagogical scenario is chosen quickly, learning goals are completed early partly from what the scenario offers, parts of design, development, and implementation are done together, the infrastructure takes care of implementation, and evaluation is realized formatively through rapid prototyping and summatively through ongoing experimental and field studies. The approach is characterized as providing templates or blueprints that designers adapt and fill with content, resembling ADAPT IT and the SimQuest authoring approach at a more detailed level.

constraints: Design for ill-structured problems such as SCY missions creates a set of specific challenges the article attributes to Jonassen (1997)

title: Waves taxonomy of emerging learning technologies: extended, connected, and repeated waves
description: The article organizes decades of emerging learning technologies into a three-part taxonomy of waves. Some waves persist over long periods (extended), some link to earlier or later technologies (connected), and some recur cyclically as they go in and out of favor (repeated). The authors state that "some waves are extended over time whereas some are connected to other waves and still others are repeated in cycles as they go in and out of favor," and use this framework to structure their historical account of collaborative writing tools, videoconferencing, blended learning, and open content.

constraints: The taxonomy is a reflective organizing lens offered by the authors, not an empirically tested classification

examples: Collaborative writing tools as an extended wave; synchronous videoconferencing as a connected wave; blended learning and open content as repeated waves

title: Awareness-Ask-Action (AAA) cybersecurity framework for K-12 educational technology
description: The AAA framework is a three-level adaptation of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's five-aspect framework (identify, protect, detect, respond, recover), tailored for an Edtech cybersecurity and privacy PD. The "Action" level supports personnel as they detect, respond to, and recover from attacks. The PD's four modules were mapped onto this framework.

constraints: Adapted specifically for Edtech cybersecurity and privacy PD for K-12 school personnel rather than for general cybersecurity training

examples: The PD's first two modules covered educational technology and data types and frequent cyber attacks (Awareness); the third covered communicating with software providers (Ask); the fourth covered steps to take proper action (Action)

description: The study applies Zimmerman's Self-Regulated Learning theory, which presents learning as a self-initiated process across emotional, motivational, behavioral, and (meta)cognitive dimensions. The (meta)cognitive dimension "encompasses three cyclical phases: forethought, performance, and reflection", and the authors used these phases to organize the benefit and challenge themes learners reported about ethics board games. The framework functioned as an organizational tool rather than determining category substance.

article_title: Machine learning for human learners: opportunities, issues, tensions and threats
citation: Webb, M. E., Fluck, A., Magenheim, J., Malyn-Smith, J., Waters, J., Deschênes, M., & Zagami, J. (2021). Machine learning for human learners: opportunities, issues, tensions and threats. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09858-2
title: Taxonomy of machine learning types by the inputs systems learn from
description: The article organizes machine learning into four types classified by the inputs the system learns from, stating that "Machine learning can be classified according to the inputs that it learns from". The four types are supervised learning (training data plus correct answers), unsupervised learning (learning from a dataset on its own), semi-supervised learning (learning from incomplete data) and reinforcement learning (based on feedback from the environment). Deep learning is presented as a major current research focus within machine learning, itself a subset of artificial intelligence. This taxonomy frames which ML approaches may appear in educational applications.
requirements: Distinguishing the types requires attending to what input data each system learns from, whether correct answers, incomplete data, or environmental feedback
constraints: The article notes most educational ML applications are still being developed so specific algorithms in use are still under consideration
target_learning_goals: understanding the nature of machine learning systems

article_title: Machine learning for human learners: opportunities, issues, tensions and threats
citation: Webb, M. E., Fluck, A., Magenheim, J., Malyn-Smith, J., Waters, J., Deschênes, M., & Zagami, J. (2021). Machine learning for human learners: opportunities, issues, tensions and threats. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09858-2
title: Deep learning as back-propagation through weighted multi-layer neural networks
description: The article characterizes machine deep learning via LeCun et al.'s account, in which "Deep learning discovers intricate structure in large data sets by using the back-propagation algorithm". Back-propagation occurs during training: predictions are compared with known target values and the weights of links between adjacent layers are adjusted backwards to minimize error, making the systems non-deterministic and adaptive through experience. Because of the complexity and probabilistic nature of these multi-layered networks, deep learning typically operates as a black box, which grounds the article's later explainability arguments.
requirements: Depends on weighted neural networks trained with datasets, learning rate parameters and a training regime chosen by system engineers
constraints: Typically trained on static datasets, and incorporating new data requires retraining which can result in catastrophic forgetting of existing knowledge
target_learning_goals: understanding how machine learning systems work and their limits

title: Design machine learning systems used in education with explainability built in from the outset
description: The article argues that because "learning and assessment of learning are problems that can never be completely formalised", some level of interpretability and explainability is necessary for machine learning systems used in education, unless incorrect results have no significant consequences. The capability to explain decisions should be programmed in during design, using explanation types from rationale to impact, each comprehensible to the decision's recipient without exposing commercially protected algorithms. This serves fairness, bias minimization, user trust and legal compliance such as GDPR.
requirements: Explainability mechanisms must be incorporated during system design, not added post hoc
Explanation methods must be matched to domain, use case and type of user
constraints: Where systems are used only informally or as adjuncts with no severe consequences for incorrect results, explainability requirements are lower
target_learners: all learners affected by educational machine learning systems
target_learning_goals: fair and interpretable decisions about learning and assessment
examples: Industry guidance distinguishing six explanation types from rationale to impact explanation

title: Accountability as the reverse of explainability, with a three-layer accountability model
description: The article distinguishes the two central issues directionally: "Accountability is the reverse of explainability. Explainability flows through the system from inputs to output (decision) whereas accountability flows backwards, from a decision to the person taking responsibility for it." It presents Kroll's three-layer accountability model: a bottom recording layer tracking what the system does, a middle analytical layer matching records with output performance, and a top responsibility layer determining who made which change. Applied to the USA visa lottery this required only a .12% computational overhead, suggesting accountability mechanisms can be built in at design time.
requirements: Accountability mechanisms need to be built in during system design
Layers must reconcile accountability with protecting commercially confidential algorithms or trained model weights
constraints: When machine learning systems must operate very quickly, immediate accountability is impractical and post-facto accountability is what remains
target_learners: teachers held accountable for learning achievements
target_learning_goals: responsible and traceable deployment of machine learning in education

title: Six explanation types for machine learning systems in industry guidance
description: Initial industry guidance on AI explainability, cited in the article, identifies six main types of explanation. As printed, "This guidance identifies six main types of explanation (Itransition 2019; ICO and Turing 2019, p. 19) as follows." They are: rationale explanation (the reasons behind a decision in accessible terms), responsibility explanation (who is involved and who to contact for human review), data explanation (what data was used and how), fairness explanation (steps ensuring unbiased, equitable decisions), safety and performance explanation (accuracy, reliability, security, robustness steps), and impact explanation (effects on individuals and wider society).
requirements: Explanations must be delivered in a form accessible and non-technical to the recipient
constraints: There are no agreed metrics for the quality of explanation methods, so comparisons across contexts are difficult
