article_title: Learning during a pandemic: an Activity Theory analysis of the challenges experienced by Aotearoa/New Zealand university students
citation: Dilani Gedera · Dianne Forbes · Cheryl Brown · Maggie Hartnett · Ashwini Datt. (2023). Learning during a pandemic: an Activity Theory analysis of the challenges experienced by Aotearoa/New Zealand university students. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10284-3
title: Activity Theory as an analytical framework for online learning challenges, with revised terminology and four levels of contradictions
description: The article applies Engeström's Activity Theory, in which "Engeström's (1987) expanded Activity Theory comprises elements forming an activity system" — subject/participant, tools, objective, rules, community, roles and outcome. It adopts revised terminology (e.g., participant instead of subject, objective instead of object) to avoid confusion in educational contexts, and uses contradictions — imbalances within, between elements of, or between activity systems — as the analytical lens, classifying them as primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary. Contradictions manifest as obstacles, interruptions, conflicts, tensions and gaps but are treated as a driving force for change and development.
requirements: The activity system is used as the minimal meaningful unit of analysis, with Activity Theory elements serving as coding buckets for qualitative data.
constraints: Engeström's original terminology does not easily translate to educational contexts, requiring the revised terms adopted in this article.
target_learning_goals: understanding and improving students' online learning experiences during disrupted teaching

It builds in heuristics such as 'vary one thing at a time' by restricting varied variables to one, offers simple values via sliders, gives pop-up feedback on actions, and automatically assigns control-variable values across trials. title: Pedagogical roles educators could consider in remote learning environments, adapted from Nacu et al.'s online learning support roles
description: The article proposes a set of pedagogical roles that educators can enact when facilitating remote learning, extending the online learning support roles framework of Nacu et al. (2018). As the abstract states, "this paper introduces pedagogical roles educators could consider in remote environments and a heuristic evaluation method to focus on how those moves might relate to the technologies they are using." The framework is offered as a practical lens for educators adapting their instructional practice during pandemic-driven school closures.

description: The article recommends that educators and researchers distinguish remote learning from online learning when adapting instructional practice. Design guidance for remote learning should therefore cover non-device-mediated formats such as worksheet packets as well as online formats.

article_title: Designing and delivering representation-focused science lessons in a digital learning environment
citation: Cirkony, C., Tytler, R., & Hubber, P. (2022). Designing and delivering representation-focused science lessons in a digital learning environment. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10094-z
title: Socio-semiotic theory underpinning the Representation Construction Approach
description: The article grounds RCA in socio-semiotics, in which meaning is made with signs within social and cultural contexts and is distributed across representational forms and modes. It states that "socio-semiotic theory considers meaning to be distributed across different representational forms (e.g., dialogue, written text, drawings, graphs, role-plays) and modes (i.e., verbal, written, visual, action) (Bezemer & Kress, 2016), each of which offers partial access to meaning." The study applies this perspective analytically to assess how the STILE platform facilitated students' meaning-making through generating and coordinating digital and non-digital multimodal representations.
requirements: A learning environment must provide a range of representations and modes, and the tools and activities available to generate and integrate them
constraints: No single representation can fully convey conceptual meaning, and there is no ideal representation
target_learners: K-12 science students, exemplified by Grade 9 students
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding of science ideas such as energy transfer and the particle model
Representational competence and disciplinary literacy in science
examples: The study analysed Grade 9 students' drawings, role-plays, written responses, and annotated diagrams through a socio-semiotic lens across two STILE modules on heat transfer

title: STILE online learning platform with interactive canvas and written response applications
description: STILE (Student Teacher Interactive Learning Environment) is a customisable, cloud-based interactive online platform for K-12 science units, freely available to Victorian government secondary schools. In this study its modules embedded multimedia resources, assessments with automated feedback, and open-ended tools: "the interactive canvas allowed students to draw and annotate diagrams and integrate multiple media; and the written response application provided an infinitely expanded ruled pad allowing students to construct text-based responses." The platform also served as a repository for student work that teachers could access to guide discussion and refinement.

Students need individual device access; in this study laptops with removable keyboard, Active-Pen technology, and built-in camera
constraints: Issues with internet connectivity in one lesson meant students responded in their project books instead of the platform
target_learners: K-12 science students, exemplified by Grade 9 students
target_learning_goals: Constructing and refining multimodal representations of science concepts
Inquiry-based knowledge building in blended science lessons
examples: A customised 12-module energy-transfer unit with pre- and post-test and a summative inquiry task was designed on STILE and implemented with face-to-face and online interactions

article_title: Designing and delivering representation-focused science lessons in a digital learning environment
citation: Cirkony, C., Tytler, R., & Hubber, P. (2022). Designing and delivering representation-focused science lessons in a digital learning environment. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10094-z
title: Sequence representational challenges before introducing scientific explanations in online representation-focused units
description: The article's findings indicate that the ordering of student-generated representational work relative to expert scientific representations shapes the quality of students' uptake. In the Temperature module, students explored their own ideas first and then refined them after a video explanation, whereas in the Convection module the early video seemed to lock students into a procedural interpretation. The authors conclude that "grappling with the representational problem before being introduced to scientific ideas better prepared students for generative uptake," and recommend embedding multimodal formative representation-focused activities early in the learning sequence.
requirements: Online units must be carefully planned to embed multimodal formative representation-focused activities early in the learning sequence
Teachers need to refine the planned sequence in response to students' representations
constraints: If scientific resources are presented too late, students may not understand the principles well enough to translate them to another activity, per prior studies the article cites
target_learners: K-12 science students, exemplified by Grade 9 students
target_learning_goals: Generative uptake of scientific ideas through representation construction and refinement
Conceptual understanding of energy transfer and the particle model
examples: In the Temperature module students engaged in open-ended exploratory activities before viewing the first scientific video and showed steady uptake across modes; in the Convection module the video preceded the challenges and students copied its conventions inappropriately

description: The article develops a mobile CT framework built on Brennan and Resnick's (2012) CT framework, redefining its three dimensions for mobile app development in mathematics. Mobile CT concepts include 'screen interface, component abstraction, public web services, data persistence, loops, conditionals, operators, and procedural abstraction'; practices add modeling and algorithmic thinking; perspectives add socializing. The framework scaffolds design and evaluation of mobile app development activities in primary mathematics lessons.

title: 5E instructional model structuring mobile app development mathematics lessons in five stages
description: The article uses the 5E instructional model (engagement, exploration, explanation, elaboration, evaluation) as the instructional design framework for mobile CT-integrated mathematics lessons. Each stage maps to app development activities: engagement reviews prior area knowledge and arouses interest in calculation games; exploration has students design game interfaces on paper; explanation asks students to explain designs; elaboration extends to complex cases like null values; evaluation involves testing games and reflecting. The article states the model 'could be suitable for the instructional design of primary school CT-integrated mathematics curriculum.'

A mobile app development platform such as App Inventor

problem-solving skills

This design activity raised students' interest and motivation as they became designers rather than formula appliers, addressing the problem that students 'may merely recall formulas and apply them'. The article proposes a set of design principles for integrating CT into mathematics curriculum from this approach.

article_title: Rubric formats for the formative assessment of oral presentation skills acquisition in secondary education
citation: Rob J. Nadolski, Hans G. K. Hummel, Ellen Rusman, Kevin Ackermans. (2021). Rubric formats for the formative assessment of oral presentation skills acquisition in secondary education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-10030-7
title: Viewbrics online tool integrating video-modelling examples with analytic text-based rubrics and a progress dashboard
description: The Viewbrics tool is a dedicated online tool supporting formative assessment of oral presentation skills with analytic rubrics in text-based and video-enhanced versions. Video-modelling examples "contain question prompts that illustrate behavior associated with (sub)skills performance levels in context, and are presented by young actors the target group can identify with". It supports teacher, peer, and self-assessment, reflection, goal-setting, and a dashboard visualizing per-subskill progress (green improving, blue constant, red declining) with emoticon feedback. The tool was "incrementally developed and validated with teachers and students to structure the formative assessment method in classroom settings". Its rubrics cover eleven subskills scored on four-point scales, organized under logos, ethos, and pathos.
requirements: Teachers and students must be trained and motivated in rubric usage before instruction
Rubrics must be tailored to the specific learning objectives and target groups
constraints: Designed for formative assessment only, not summative assessment purposes
Developing video-enhanced rubrics is more costly than text-based rubrics
target_learners: First-year secondary school students (12–13 years) in the Netherlands
target_learning_goals: Oral presentation skills (informative presentations)
examples: Both experimental groups used the Viewbrics tool with teacher-, peer-, and self-feedback; after Project 2 students saw visualized progress in the dashboard and set personal learning goals shown under 'Mijn leerdoelen' [My learning goals]

citation: Rob J. Nadolski, Hans G. K. Hummel, Ellen Rusman, Kevin Ackermans. (2021). Rubric formats for the formative assessment of oral presentation skills acquisition in secondary education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-10030-7
title: Six-step formative assessment method for oral presentation skills with analytic rubrics
description: The article's formative assessment method structures classroom rubric use into a recurring cycle applied around each oral presentation. As printed, "The formative assessment method consisted of six steps: (1) study the rubric; (2) practice and conduct an oral presentation; (3) conduct a self-assessment; (4) consult feedback from teacher and peers; (5) Reflect on feedback; and (6) select personal learning goal(s) for the next oral presentation". The method is embedded in project-based education and repeated across two projects, with advice on the second presentation targeting subskills performed insufficiently in the first. It was applied with twelve- to thirteen-year-old students in Dutch secondary schools.
requirements: Analytic rubrics validated for the domain and target group must be available in a digital tool supporting self-, peer-, and teacher-assessment
Teachers and students require condition-specific workshops on rubric usage and feedback provision

description: The editorial frames embodied cognition as the view that the mind is closely connected to sensorimotor experience, in contrast to the traditional view that the body plays a small role in cognition. It argues that "the cognitive process develops when a tightly coupled system emerges from interactions between organisms and their environment, with the interactions being real-time and goal-directed." The special issue applies this framework to language learning in virtual environments, where avatar-based motion may originate internal mediation.

article_title: Assessing multiple object tracking in young children using a game
citation: Kimiko Ryokai, Faraz Farzin, Eric Kaltman, Greg Niemeyer. (2013). Assessing multiple object tracking in young children using a game. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-012-9278-x
title: TrackFX: the first game-based MOT task on a touch tablet for children as young as 30 months
description: TrackFX is a touch-tablet game transferring the classic MOT paradigm to children under 5 in non-experimental settings. Players track ladybug targets among spider distractors hidden under leaf occluders that move randomly at "a normalized velocity of 540 px/sec for 10 s" before the player selects the leaf covering each target. Levels follow a 2-up-1-down psychophysical staircase, advancing at or above 66% correct twice in a row and dropping otherwise, with a 66% tracking threshold estimated from each session.

constraints: Levels 1–3 are introductory acclimation levels, not included in data analyses

title: TEACCH Structured Teaching and the individual work system as a visually organized framework for independent practice
description: The TEACCH approach (Structured Teaching) organizes time, space and sequences of events to support autistic individuals in understanding and executing learning activities; it is a framework, not a curriculum. Its individual work system (IWS) is "a visually organized space where children practice acquired skills", a low-tech instructional technology using furniture, printed images and Velcro or magnets. A work system visually communicates four pieces of information: the tasks to do, how much work there is, how the student knows they are finished, and what to do when finished. The article implements this framework in immersive VR to promote independent learning.
requirements: Customization to each student's skills and needs, since one size does not fit all for autistic students
constraints: Effectiveness of comprehensive TEACCH programs is difficult to demonstrate because they comprise multiple components deployed in natural settings

target_learning_goals: Independent learning, skill practice, generalization of skills across settings, and access to the curriculum
examples: The VR-IWS implements the four information elements virtually, with trays on an input shelf, completion at a work table, and storage on an output shelf

article_title: Design, development, and evaluation of an individual digital study assistant for higher education students
citation: Karrenbauer, C., Brauner, T., König, C. M., & Breitner, M. H. (2023). Design, development, and evaluation of an individual digital study assistant for higher education students. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10255-8
title: Individual digital study assistants (IDSA) as online student support tools that strengthen self-regulation, goal achievement, and study organization
description: The article defines an IDSA as "an efficient online student support tool that strengthens self-regulation skills, goal achievement, and study organization through suitable functionalities". Unlike pedagogical conversational agents, an IDSA does not directly assist in learning content; instead it provides individual study structuring, situation-specific guidance, and recommendations based on individual goals, interests, and competencies. It accesses information from student dialogs, campus and learning management systems, completed modules, and external resources such as OER platforms.
requirements: Must access information sources including student-provided details, campus and learning management system data, and external resources such as OER platforms to generate individualized support and recommendations
constraints: Contrary to a pedagogical conversational agent, an IDSA is not directly involved in the different facets of the learning process and handles learning content only on a reflective level
target_learners: Higher education students in their early study phase
target_learning_goals: Self-regulated learning
study organization
goal setting and achievement

title: Student life cycle as a three-phase organizing structure for designing student support functionalities
description: The article uses the student life cycle (Sprenger et al., 2010) as an organizational structure for developing support and functionalities. The article states that "The study process comprised three phases (see Table 1), which included structured sub-dimensions that can be used to structure the development and implementation of IDSAs": before university study (recruitment to enrollment), during university study (examinations, organization, re-registration), and after university study (graduation, alumni activities). Transition phases such as arriving at a university require intensive support.
requirements: Phase-specific focus translating requirements into practical information, e.g., addressing beginning-student needs such as student financing or finding locations on campus
constraints: The structure and focus of a student life cycle may differ in terms of teaching, quality management, and campus management system cost
target_learners: Higher education students across study phases, with emphasis on early-phase students
target_learning_goals: Study organization and phase-appropriate individual support

title: Five quality domains from the literature as the theoretical framework underlying IDSA requirements
description: The literature review provided the theoretical framework for the requirements and the basis for prototype development. The article states that "Five domains were identified: (a) user satisfaction, (b) pedagogical domain, (c) service quality, (d) perceived information quality, and (e) perceived system quality." The pedagogical domain was grounded in the ICAP framework, whose criteria are "specifically adapted to online teaching and learning", while the technological domains cover service quality, information quality, and system quality variables mapped onto the derived requirements.
requirements: Requirements must be mapped onto the five domains, with net-benefit variables such as content completeness, knowledge acquisition, and performance improvement assigned to the pedagogical domain
constraints: The framework was derived from a literature review of information-systems success research rather than tested directly in this study

target_learning_goals: User acceptance and effective use of digital study support for self-regulated learning

title: Multi-functionality in a digital study assistant must not come at the expense of the depth and content of individual functionalities
description: Drawing on the field-test feedback that functionalities were rated only slightly above the satisfaction level and that students "only perceived limited added value from certain functionalities", the article advises that "Multi-functionality must not be achieved at the expense of the depth and content of individual functionalities". It further suggests the need to critically evaluate an IDSA prototype's maturity before its deployment, and that functionalities can be individually adapted to address student groups within different life cycle phases.
requirements: An intensive test phase with student feedback incorporation before rollout, so weaknesses are identified and corrected
constraints: Usability and user-friendliness may be limited when the assistant is integrated into an existing learning management or campus management system that predefines frontend structure and navigation
target_learners: Higher education students, particularly those in their early study phase
target_learning_goals: Self-regulated learning, study organization, and goal achievement through digital study support
examples: The prototype offered eight functionalities including To-do, Personality, Organization of Learning, Get-Together, OER, Interests, Evaluation, and Data Sovereignty, and was field-tested for three months in three German higher education institutions

title: The AI-GFCA learning model: four scaffolding stages (generalization, formulation, correction, appreciation) supported by an AI speaking app
description: The AI-GFCA learning model is a four-stage scaffolding framework for technology-supported role-play in L2 learning. As the article states, "the study employed generalization, formulation, correction, and appreciation strategies by integrating AI speaking learning by proposing the AI-GFCA learning model to scaffold students' performance in role-play tasks, English speaking skills, L2 errors, and interaction mindset." Generalization clarifies task goals and success criteria from O'Donnell and Topping's objectives-and-criteria approach; formulation builds collaborative readiness; correction conducts intergroup corrective feedback with internal and external monitoring; appreciation fosters positive appraisal to reduce tension. The model was tested against AI-supported conventional learning lacking the pedagogical theory.

target_learning_goals: L2 role-play performance
English speaking skills

article_title: Improving workplace-based assessment and feedback by an E-portfolio enhanced with learning analytics
citation: van der Schaaf, M., Donkers, J., Slof, B., Moonen-van Loon, J., van Tartwijk, J., Driessen, E., Badii, A., Serban, O., Ten Cate, O. (2016). title: Probabilistic student model (MEBN) translating E-portfolio data into personalized feedback
description: The article's student model is a probabilistic representation of a learner's state and context: "A student model is a statistical model that translates the existing E-portfolio performance scores into the progress state of the learner" to predict future performance on workplace tasks. It is built on multi-entity Bayesian networks (MEBN), fed with numerical data (entrustment scores) and narrative data (sentiment analysis of written comments), and must support prediction of entrustability, selection of feedback, and selection of the topic of interest. One knowledge fragment implements a frustration alert based on portfolio consistency, score drops and feedback-seeking strategy.
requirements: The student model database must contain data about the learner's actual internal state, the learning context, and pedagogical knowledge in knowledge fragments to translate state and context into just-in-time messages and visualizations
Building the MEBN knowledge fragments requires that pedagogical knowledge about learning at the workplace is made explicit and translated into probabilistic terms
constraints: Probabilistic student models often require a lot of data points to generate reliable feedback messages, so programs of different duration gather different amounts and types of data
Combining numerical and narrative data requires text mining and natural language processing techniques whose usefulness the article says is still scarce
target_learners: students in professional education (medical, veterinary, teacher education)
target_learning_goals: development of professional competencies and entrustment for workplace tasks
examples: A level-1 (below level) assessment for EPA 1 is processed through assessment outcome, narratives, EPA level, domain competency level, interest selector and feedback decision blocks to generate improvement feedback and a timeline update

description: The E-portfolio environment is enhanced with "a feedback module providing personalized improvement feedback (JIT module)" and "a visualization module that visualizes the feedback in terms of the personal development over time (VIZ module)". Feedback is provided at two granularity levels: aggregated messages (improvement, positive/negative, supervisor, trend, cohort, gaps) and detailed feedback with concrete improvement suggestions accessible by clicking. The interactive graph is a timeline with coloured trend lines per EPA, assessment dots placed by date and aggregated score, with pop-up boxes for assessment summaries and narrative JIT feedback.

constraints: Experts noted it was not always clear when elements in the VIZ module are interactive, and suggested options for colour blindness and black-and-white printing

title: Entrustable professional activities (EPAs) with five entrustment levels as assessment anchor
description: Workplace-related tasks are operationalized as units of professional practice: "These so-called entrustable professional activities (EPAs) appeared to provide a valid and useful anchor for assessment of learners in medical education-training programs." EPAs are independently executable within a time frame, observable and measurable in process and outcome, making them suitable for entrustment decisions. Learners send competency requests per EPA; supervisors rate entrustment on five levels, from not allowed to practice (level 1) to being able to give the supervision task (level 5), with level four equating to the graduation requirement. EPAs are mapped against competency domains (e.g., CanMEDS roles) via job analysis.

constraints: In medical curricula, EPAs are interrelated: some EPAs are more important in some clerkships or not assessed at all, so entrustment scores in one clerkship can affect scores in another

target_learning_goals: professional competency development and readiness for unsupervised practice

description: The article develops the enhanced E-portfolio through "An iterative design approach with a central role for the user" matching the information system development life cycle. "Our approach consists of five iterative phases": making pedagogical knowledge about workplace learning explicit (phase 1, Delphi studies and seven focus groups with 78 participants), translating it into probabilistic student models (phase 2), developing personalized feedback and visualization (phase 3), implementing the prototype in professional education (phase 4), and evaluating perceived usefulness (phase 5), with findings fed back to preceding phases.

title: Design learning-analytics feedback through the eyes of the users, with privacy safeguards
description: The article concludes that analytics-enhanced assessment design succeeds only when developed and implemented through the eyes of the users: "Only a close cooperation between the community of practitioners and technical partners will ensure a sound implementation of an easy accessible E-portfolio environment" with personalized feedback modules. Because E-portfolio data is multi-sourced, ethical safeguards are required: learners as data owners must grant access via informed consent procedures, and "the E-portfolio data has to be anonymized before analysing it in the student model". When the human factor is neglected, personalized feedback may be incorrect or misinterpreted, with undesirable and unethical impact.

constraints: The article warns that improper attention to the human factor can lead to incorrect or easily misinterpreted feedback with unethical impact on the user

target_learning_goals: trustworthy, ethically sound personalized feedback and assessment at the workplace

citation: Twyford, L., abstractor. (1955). Audio-Visual Communication Review research abstracts: training device effectiveness studies. Audio-Visual Communication Review. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Audio-Visual+Communication+Review
title: Use inexpensive mockups in place of actual equipment when the training objective does not require actual participation
description: This principle holds that a low-cost mockup of an instrument panel and controls can substitute for the real machine when the objective is procedural or nomenclature learning. The tank hull trainer study found the mockup "a better training aid than the tank hull trainer" for starting and stopping, and equal to the hull trainer and tank for nomenclature, concluding that on cost grounds the mockup is preferable.
requirements: The training objective must be one for which actual participation is not required, as the study found actual participation was not required for starting and stopping procedures and nomenclature learning.
constraints: For track and suspension information the hull trainer, not the mockup, was better than the tank itself, so substitution is objective-specific.
target_learners: military trainees learning vehicle operation and controls
target_learning_goals: procedural skills such as starting and stopping procedures
nomenclature and location of instruments and controls
examples: Trainees were taught starting and stopping procedures and driver's instruments and controls using a mockup of the M47 instrument panel and driver's controls instead of practicing on the actual tank.

article_title: Validating student AI competency self-efficacy (SAICS) scale and its framework
citation: Thomas K. F. Chiu, Murat Çoban, Ismaila Temitayo Sanusi, Musa Adekunle Ayanwale. (2025). Validating student AI competency self-efficacy (SAICS) scale and its framework. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10512-y
title: Eight-dimension AI competency framework for K-12 students grounded in teacher perspectives
description: The framework defines student AI competency as the capacity "to use AI to support their learning ethically, healthily, and productively" across eight dimensions: Interdisciplinary Learning with AI (ILAI), Assessment with AI (ASAI), Decision Making with AI (DMAI), Data, Ethics, and AI (DEAI), Designing AI (DGAI), Multimedia Creation with AI (MCAI), Human-Centric Learning (HCLG), and Confidence with AI (CFAI). It was derived from teacher panelists via Delphi consensus and extends UNESCO's four-component framework by adding learning-activity dimensions such as interdisciplinary learning, assessment, and multimedia creation. Each dimension is elaborated with example competencies, e.g., judging AI-generated essays (DMAI) and protecting personal data (DEAI).
requirements: Delphi panel of experienced K-12 AI education professionals to establish dimension consensus
constraints: The article states the framework "focuses mostly on the level of AI competency" and does not incorporate data, mathematics, science, and computation literacies
target_learners: K-12 students (grades 7–12 in the validation sample)
target_learning_goals: student AI competency: using AI ethically, safely, healthily, and productively in learning
examples: The Delphi panel renamed dimensions such as changing "Support for learning" to "Interdisciplinary learning with AI" and integrated "Comfort with AI", "Perceived ease to use", and "Engagement in self-reflection" into "Confidence with AI"
key_sources: Thomas K. F. Chiu, Murat Çoban, Ismaila Temitayo Sanusi, Musa Adekunle Ayanwale. (2025). Validating student AI competency self-efficacy (SAICS) scale and its framework. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10512-y

article_title: Validating student AI competency self-efficacy (SAICS) scale and its framework
citation: Thomas K. F. Chiu, Murat Çoban, Ismaila Temitayo Sanusi, Musa Adekunle Ayanwale. (2025). Validating student AI competency self-efficacy (SAICS) scale and its framework. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10512-y
title: SAICS scale: a validated 32-item, eight-dimension student AI competency self-efficacy instrument
description: The SAICS scale is a 32-item self-report instrument measuring student AI competency self-efficacy across eight dimensions, with four items per dimension (Table 6). Items are rated "on a 5-point Likert scale from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree)" and include examples such as "I can use AI to check whether my solutions are correct" (ASAI) and "I know how to protect my personal data when using AI" (DEAI). The instrument was developed through three Delphi rounds and validated with 448 students via CFA and gender-invariance testing.
requirements: Administration to K-12 students with the 5-point Likert response format; validation evidence currently rests on the Hong Kong secondary sample
constraints: The article states the scale "lacks specificity across disciplines" and "may not be appropriate for a non-Chinese population, as the participants were Chinese students"
target_learning_goals: assessing student self-efficacy for AI competency in learning
examples: Validation used 448 students from six Hong Kong secondary schools chosen from three school-university partnership programs

article_title: Taking educational games seriously: using the RETAIN model to design endogenous fantasy into standalone educational games
citation: Gunter, G.A., Kenny, R.F. & Vick, E.H. (2008). Taking educational games seriously: using the RETAIN model to design endogenous fantasy into standalone educational games. Education Tech Research Dev, 56, 511–537. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-007-9073-2
title: RETAIN design and evaluation model for educational games
description: RETAIN is a design and evaluation model for educational games developed by the authors to judge how well academic content is integrated with game play. Per the abstract, it was developed "to aide in the evaluation of how well academic content is endogenously immersed and embedded within the game's fantasy and story context". It also addresses transfer of knowledge and repeated use of content so it becomes automatic. The article positions it as the new design paradigm for standalone educational games.
requirements: Academic content must be endogenously immersed and embedded within the game's fantasy and story context for the model's evaluation to apply
target_learning_goals: academic skills and knowledge acquisition
transfer of knowledge
automatic availability of learned content
examples: The article discusses RETAIN as a model for designing endogenous fantasy into standalone educational games

article_title: Taking educational games seriously: using the RETAIN model to design endogenous fantasy into standalone educational games
citation: Gunter, G.A., Kenny, R.F. & Vick, E.H. (2008). Taking educational games seriously: using the RETAIN model to design endogenous fantasy into standalone educational games. Education Tech Research Dev, 56, 511–537. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-007-9073-2
title: Embed academic content endogenously within a game's fantasy and story context rather than housing it inside the game superficially
description: The principle holds that academic learning in games occurs when content is woven into the game's own fantasy and narrative rather than appended to it. The abstract states RETAIN evaluates "how well academic content is endogenously immersed and embedded within the game's fantasy and story context". This contrasts with the ad hoc practice of placing content inside a game and expecting motivation to follow. The article offers this as part of its proposed design paradigm.
requirements: A game fantasy and story context into which the academic content can be immersed endogenously
target_learning_goals: academic skills and knowledge acquisition
examples: RETAIN is proposed as the evaluation model for how endogenously content is embedded in a game's fantasy and story context

title: Design educational games so repetitive usage makes academic content available for automatic use and supports transfer
description: The article holds that educational game design should encourage repeated engagement with academic content until it can be used automatically, and should promote transfer of knowledge. The abstract says the RETAIN model addresses games that "promoters transfer of knowledge, and encourages repetitive usage to that content becomes available for use in an automatic way". Repetition within the game's fantasy context is thus treated as a mechanism for fluent, transferable learning.

citation: AlNajdi, S.M. (2022). The effectiveness of using augmented reality (AR) to enhance student performance: using quick response (QR) codes in student textbooks in the Saudi education system. Education Tech Research Dev, 70, 1105–1124. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10100-4

description: The iEN portal is Saudi Arabia's national education portal, built by the Ministry of Education to integrate technology into the educational system. From its home page "users can log in and access all the benefits in the portal, it has three sub-portals: books and lessons, iEN revisions, and additional resources". It offers AR experiments, e-textbooks, learning games, video clips, and TV channels, and offers role-based accounts for students, teachers, principals, and parents.

article_title: Supporting motivation, task performance and retention in video tutorials for software training
citation: Hans van der Meij, Jan van der Meij, Tessa Voerman, Evert Duipmans. (2018). Supporting motivation, task performance and retention in video tutorials for software training. Education Tech Research Dev 66, 597–614. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-017-9560-z
title: Theoretical model combining demonstration-based training (DBT) and multimedia learning theory for video tutorial design
description: The model organizes video tutorial design around Bandura's four observational learning processes (attention, retention, production, motivation) and connects instructional features to them. Features include signaling, preview, pace, user control, practice, practice timing, practice files, anchoring in the task domain, conversational style, music, length, and the retention features segmentation, labels, simple-to-complex sequencing, pauses, and review. The article states the "instructional features in the model also connect to multimedia learning theory" with its "empirically tested principles for instructional design". All features except labels and music were incorporated in the study's tutorial.
requirements: Design features are tied to the four observational learning processes and should be selected according to which process they support
constraints: The model does not mention instructor-led support, since the prototypical context is an individual user working alone at a computer
Design features effective for novices may not work for more knowledgeable users due to the expertise reversal principle
target_learners: novice software users, e.g., upper elementary students
target_learning_goals: procedural software skills such as document formatting
examples: The study's tutorial taught six Microsoft Word formatting tasks with previews, demonstrations, and reviews, segmented into three chapters sequenced simple-to-complex, with videos capped at 3 minutes
key_sources: Hans van der Meij, Jan van der Meij, Tessa Voerman, Evert Duipmans. (2018). Supporting motivation, task performance and retention in video tutorials for software training. Education Tech Research Dev 66, 597–614. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-017-9560-z

article_title: Supporting motivation, task performance and retention in video tutorials for software training
citation: Hans van der Meij, Jan van der Meij, Tessa Voerman, Evert Duipmans. (2018). Supporting motivation, task performance and retention in video tutorials for software training. Education Tech Research Dev 66, 597–614. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-017-9560-z
title: Interleave modeling and production by keeping videos accessible during practice
description: The article argues, citing Bandura, that "modeling and production should be interleaved": practice immediately after observing a model reveals where imitation fails and prompts learners to replay video segments, addressing retention gaps and solidifying acquired knowledge. In the study, video access was blocked once participants started practicing, which the authors identify as a situational variable that likely limited learning and consolidation compared to earlier studies with unlimited access.
requirements: Learners must be able to replay video segments when practice reveals gaps in understanding
constraints: In this study access was blocked during practice tasks, which the authors say limited participants' opportunity for learning
target_learners: novice software learners, including elementary students
target_learning_goals: retention and consolidation of demonstrated procedures
examples: Participants in this study could view videos until they felt sure of the task but could not look back during practice; earlier studies with unlimited access found higher post-test scores and a review advantage

article_title: How research informs educational technology decision-making in higher education: the role of external research versus internal research
citation: Hollands, F., & Escueta, M. (2020). How research informs educational technology decision-making in higher education: the role of external research versus internal research. Education Tech Research Dev, 68, 163–180. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09678-z
title: Australian university's streamlined alpha-launch process for piloting and scaling educational technology
description: A multi-step institutional process for acquiring educational technology, developed by an Academic Director at an Australian university. It combines a prioritized list of technology initiatives informed by external research (Horizon and Gartner reports), a market scan, and a time-boxed pilot: "An alpha launch runs for 6 weeks, or half a semester, with the idea that if it yields positive results, the technology can be in place campus-wide by the beginning of the following semester." During the launch the Office of Learning and Teaching tracks five metrics including student evaluations, grades, engagement, faculty evaluation, and longer-term student resilience. The term alpha launch signals no guarantee of continued licensing, countering pilots that inevitably led to long-term use.
requirements: Leadership by a designated faculty member (the Academic Director) to spearhead the process
Regular stakeholder feedback mechanisms, including a showcase every 6 weeks and a technology list re-prioritized every 6 months
constraints: The article states the alpha-launch study design is not sufficiently rigorous to allow causal inferences
Recommendations about scaling up may be made before some important results (end-of-course grades, longer-term resilience metrics) are available
target_learners: Higher education students at a university implementing educational technology campus-wide
target_learning_goals: Improving pedagogy and student outcomes through vetted educational technology adoption
examples: An online polling initiative that underwent an alpha launch and was subsequently implemented university-wide
key_sources: Hollands, F., & Escueta, M. (2020). How research informs educational technology decision-making in higher education: the role of external research versus internal research. Education Tech Research Dev, 68, 163–180. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09678-z

article_title: How research informs educational technology decision-making in higher education: the role of external research versus internal research
citation: Hollands, F., & Escueta, M. (2020). How research informs educational technology decision-making in higher education: the role of external research versus internal research. Education Tech Research Dev, 68, 163–180. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09678-z
title: Interrogate the theory of change for an educational technology tool or strategy before expending resources on high-quality implementation
description: Before investing in careful implementation of an educational technology, decision-makers should first examine whether there is a plausible mechanism by which the technology can produce the intended outcomes. The article recommends this because many interviewees assumed "educational technology will improve student outcomes if it is implemented correctly" and that repeated tinkering would eventually produce success — beliefs that "may preclude serious examination of the underlying mechanism by which technology use is expected to affect learning." After implementation, periodic reassessment of efficacy is warranted to check whether the theory of change holds up in practice.
requirements: A stated theory of change linking the technology's use to the intended learning outcomes
Periodic reassessment of efficacy once the tool or strategy is implemented
constraints: The article frames this as a recommendation arising from observed decision-maker beliefs, not a tested intervention
target_learners: Higher education students affected by educational technology acquisition decisions
target_learning_goals: Ensuring educational technology investments plausibly improve academic outcomes
examples: The article's Example 1 institution presumed its educational technology strategy could improve outcomes if implementation were perfected, an approach the authors say does not rigorously vet effectiveness before scale-up

title: Technological Readiness Index as a framing lens for investigating institutional needs of the sudden online-teaching uptake
description: The study employs the Technological Readiness Index (TRI) as its analytical lens "to investigate the institutional needs necessitated by the sudden uptake of online teaching and how these needs could be funded" in a developing country. The lens frames the analysis of what universities in Zimbabwe required when online teaching became suddenly necessary during COVID-19, organising needs around readiness for technology-mediated teaching.

constraints: Applied here to one developing-country case (Zimbabwean universities)

article_title: Understanding the educators’ practices in makerspaces for the design of education tools
citation: Turakhia, D., Ludgin, D., Mueller, S., & Desportes, K. (2024). Understanding the educators' practices in makerspaces for the design of education tools. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10305-1
title: A codebook framework of educators' competencies, strategies, and challenges in makerspaces
description: The article's thematic analysis of interviews with seven educators across five makerspaces produced a codebook organized into three macro-themes. The authors state that the analysis 'resulted in a codebook consisting of six sets of competencies that educators valued most, five sets of strategies they deployed, and three sets of challenges that educators encountered'. They offer it 'as a potential framework for further studying makerspace learning', with sub-themes linking strategies to the competencies they build.
requirements: Derived from semi-structured interviews with educators in makerspaces serving middle and high school students; the authors note it is 'not exhaustive or identical across educators or makerspaces'.
constraints: The authors caution the codebook 'gives an overview of the educators' perspectives and experiences and is possibly indicative of more prominent themes', not a complete taxonomy.
target_learners: middle and high school students in makerspaces
target_learning_goals: maker competencies including technical skills, communication, creative mindset, agency, and contextual reflection
examples: Six rounds of coding on over 240 response quotes from Zoom interviews, using Braun and Clarke's six-phase thematic coding process with inter-rater agreement over 80%.

article_title: Understanding the educators’ practices in makerspaces for the design of education tools
citation: Turakhia, D., Ludgin, D., Mueller, S., & Desportes, K. (2024). Understanding the educators' practices in makerspaces for the design of education tools. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10305-1
title: Scaffolding learning through problem scoping, project stages, concept progression, adapted support, and metaphors
description: The most prominent strategy theme in educators' interviews was scaffolding learning. The codebook lists five sub-strategies: widening project scope over time, incrementally teaching skills through project stages, introducing complex concepts over time, providing more support early and more autonomy as students learn, and teaching complex concepts using analogies familiar to individual learners instead of a one-size-fits-all approach.
requirements: Educators adapt scaffolding to project complexity and learner familiarity, e.g. starting with simple circuits before computer and laser cutter work.

target_learning_goals: technical skills and design concepts built incrementally
examples: One educator described a two-week skill-building phase with cardboard, glue, and paper before moving to digital fabrication and CAD, then 3D printing and games.

article_title: Managing large classes in virtual teaching: experiences of university teachers in Ghana during COVID-19
citation: Inusah Salifu · Usman Kojo Abonyi. (2023). Managing large classes in virtual teaching: experiences of university teachers in Ghana during COVID-19. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10151-7
title: Moore's Theory of Transactional Distance (dialogue, structure, learner-autonomy)
description: The study's theoretical framework is Moore's Theory of Transactional Distance, which holds that distance in distance education is "transactional, not spatial or temporal" — a psychological and communication space between learner and teacher. Success of virtual teaching depends on three transactions: dialogue (quality interactions creating knowledge), course structure (rigidity or flexibility of objectives, assessment modes, teacher- versus learner-centredness), and learner-autonomy, which is determined by the first two. The theory provided the framework for analysing teacher-student-environment interplay and framed interview questions and observation memos.
requirements: Virtual teaching programmes must attend to dialogue, course structure, and learner autonomy for success
constraints: The theory posits a contrary relationship among the three transactions: an increase in one may cause a corresponding decrease in the other two
target_learners: university students in virtual large classes
target_learning_goals: effective instructor-learner interaction
self-directed learning
well-structured course content
examples: The study used the TTD's dialogue, structure and learner-autonomy elements to code interview data and structure classroom observations
key_sources: Inusah Salifu · Usman Kojo Abonyi. (2023). Managing large classes in virtual teaching: experiences of university teachers in Ghana during COVID-19. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10151-7

article_title: How do enhanced videos support generative learning and conceptual understanding in individuals and groups?
citation: Ruf, A., Zahn, C., Roos, A.-L., & Opwis, K. (2023). How do enhanced videos support generative learning and conceptual understanding in individuals and groups? Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10275-4
title: FrameTrail enhanced video-based learning environment with annotation and hyperlink tools
description: FrameTrail is the enhanced video-based environment used in the experiment, in which a 3:56-minute instructional video on synaptic plasticity was embedded together with "topic-related in-depth information in form of prepared text snippets directly available below the video". Annotation-condition participants read the snippets and wrote self-written summaries into the video; hyperlink-condition participants dragged the predefined snippets into the video at appropriate places; display time of both could be manually changed. The environment also provided log-file protocols of micro- and macro-actions used as process measures.
requirements: Enhanced tools must be clearly instructed and included as a necessary part of the learning task, as the authors state optional tools may not be used effectively
constraints: The hyperlink condition could only be evaluated via information structuring and overall impression, since not all HPQ categories could be addressed in both tool conditions
target_learners: university students in a controlled laboratory setting
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of a complex natural science topic (synaptic plasticity)
generative learning through creating own hypervideo information structures
examples: Participants in the annotation condition wrote own summaries into the video; participants in the hyperlink condition added predefined text snippets per drag and drop; the control group simply watched the video and read the text snippets

title: Super Cyber Kids framework: a 30-field matrix crossing adapted NIST dimensions with six child cybersecurity categories
description: The framework organizes children's cybersecurity skills in a matrix whose X-axis holds the five adapted NIST dimensions (Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover) and whose Y-axis holds six categories extracted from the literature: malicious code, frauds, abusive content, preventing technologies, data privacy and awareness, and safety. article_title: BE COOL! a digital learning environment to challenge and socially include gifted learners
citation: Tessa H. S. Eysink, Alieke M. van Dijk, Ton de Jong. (2020). BE COOL! a digital learning environment to challenge and socially include gifted learners. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09754-9
title: The ability-adjusted jigsaw method: combining heterogeneous design groups with ability-matched expert groups
description: The ability-adjusted jigsaw method unites learning by design, learning together, and inquiry learning. Children of varying ability levels work in heterogeneous design groups on a complex, open-ended problem; each child is responsible for one topic, with topic assignment depending on ability level. Members split into homogeneous expert groups of similar ability who "are responsible for becoming experts about the same topic" via inquiry assignments matched to their level, then return to share and integrate knowledge in the design group. The method is adapted from the original jigsaw procedure of Aronson et al. (1978) and is intended to serve both cognitive and socio-emotional needs of gifted and non-gifted children.
requirements: A complex, open-ended design problem requiring knowledge of multiple topics
Topic assignment matched to children's ability levels
Homogeneous expert groups with inquiry assignments matched to ability level
constraints: The article notes elementary school children may experience problems with knowledge sharing and integration, which may be amplified when children differ in knowledge level and pace of learning, hence the worksheet support
target_learners: Gifted, average-ability, and low-ability children in grades 4 to 6 of primary education
target_learning_goals: Science inquiry skills (light and heat, oxygen, water, nutrition)
Design and justification of a solution to an authentic problem
Collaborative knowledge sharing across ability levels
examples: A seven-week science lesson series for grades 4–6 in which children design a liveable house on the moon for a family of four

title: BE COOL! digital learning environment with personal learner and teacher sections
description: BE COOL! is a digital learning environment implementing the ability-adjusted jigsaw method for a seven-week moon-house lesson series in grades 4–6. Children log into a personal learning environment showing the learning-by-design steps and group members; inquiry assignments include learning goals with self-judgment before and reflection after, Resources and Help tabs, and a core assignment of six core questions per topic. A teacher section enables registration and grouping (using CITO scores and the Dutch Digital Action Protocol for Giftedness), monitoring of progress via five status symbols, and feedback pages with a response model and rating options; a teacher manual provides technical, practical, and worksheet information.

constraints: The article reports the environment was developed and studied for Dutch primary education grades 4–6 on the moon-house topic

title: Seven-step learning-by-design cycle with three group-composition phases
description: BE COOL! structures the lesson series as a seven-step learning-by-design cycle: problem statement, orientation, gathering information, designing, testing and improving, developing a prototype, and reporting. These steps are organized into three phases with different group compositions: a heterogeneous prior-knowledge phase (steps 1–2), a homogeneous expert phase (step 3, containing the five inquiry-cycle phases of orientation, investigation, drawing conclusions, evaluating, and broadening), and a heterogeneous design phase (steps 4–7). The cycle is meant to engage learners in designing a solution for an authentic problem so they achieve understanding of complex systems.

constraints: The inquiry learning is embedded specifically in the third step of the design cycle, in which children work in homogeneous groups

article_title: Applying collaborative cognitive load theory to computer-supported collaborative learning: towards a research agenda
citation: Jeroen Janssen, Paul A. Kirschner. (2020). Applying collaborative cognitive load theory to computer-supported collaborative learning: towards a research agenda. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09729-5
title: Collaborative Cognitive Load Theory (CCLT)
description: CCLT extends cognitive load theory to (computer-supported) collaborative learning by treating groups of collaborative learners as information processing systems. Its core concepts are collective working memory (individuals "share the burden of information processing"), mutual cognitive interdependence (group members learn about and depend on each other's expertise), and transaction costs (the working-memory burden of communication and coordination). The article uses CCLT to formulate testable hypotheses and design guidelines for CSCL.
requirements: Effectiveness depends on the balance between the distribution advantage and the transaction costs incurred by transactive activities
constraints: Whether CSCL is effective depends on the balance struck between distribution advantage and transaction costs; when transaction costs exceed the distribution advantage, individual learning is more effective
target_learners: students in computer-supported collaborative learning settings
target_learning_goals: domain-specific knowledge acquisition through collaboration
examples: The article applies CCLT to hypothesize about student, group, task, and technological characteristics affecting CSCL

title: Antecedents–processes–consequences framework for CSCL research
description: The article argues that fundamental understanding of CSCL requires simultaneously studying antecedents (student-, group-, task-, and technological characteristics), processes (descriptions and qualities of interactions and individual learning activities during collaboration), and consequences (e.g., individual achievement, group performance, perceived efficacy) of collaboration, and whether processes mediate antecedents' effects on consequences. Table 2 enumerates the antecedent elements, such as prior knowledge, group size, task complexity, and availability of collaboration scripts, scaffolds, and awareness tools.
requirements: Research must simultaneously study processes of collaboration, how antecedents affect them, and how they affect consequences
constraints: Most prior research has focused on the relation between antecedents and consequences, neglecting the process of collaboration itself
target_learning_goals: understanding and improving collaborative learning processes and outcomes
examples: The article's Fig. 1 depicts the relationship between antecedents, processes, and consequences of collaboration

citation: Jeroen Janssen, Paul A. Kirschner. (2020). Applying collaborative cognitive load theory to computer-supported collaborative learning: towards a research agenda. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09729-5
title: CCLT-based design guidelines for CSCL environments: strengthen the collective working memory effect while minimizing transaction costs
description: The article offers guidelines (Table 3) for instructional design of CSCL environments based on the principle that effective collaboration requires strengthening the collective working memory effect while keeping transaction costs to a minimum. Guidelines cover student characteristics (e.g., "Students with low prior knowledge may obtain new knowledge from group members with high prior knowledge"), group characteristics (familiarity, optimal group size, optimal heterogeneity), task characteristics (sufficiently complex tasks, interdependence), and technological characteristics (scripts, scaffolds, awareness tools).
requirements: Tasks must be sufficiently complex to justify the additional mental effort required by transactive activities
A minimum of prior knowledge must be secured, as too little prior knowledge will overload students' working memories
constraints: Further exploration and research is necessary to refine these guidelines for optimal application by instructional designers
Optimal group size in a given CSCL situation requires additional investigation
target_learning_goals: effective and efficient collaborative knowledge acquisition
examples: The guidelines recommend groups neither too large (to limit transactive activities) nor too small (to benefit from the collective working memory effect)

article_title: How mindful and mindless online searching affects curiosity and information recall
citation: Ju Ae Kim, Jiwon Kim, Sung-il Kim, Mimi Bong. (2026). How mindful and mindless online searching affects curiosity and information recall. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10570-2
title: Information gap theory of curiosity as the mechanism linking answer generation to mindful search and better retention
description: The article anchors its intervention in Loewenstein's information gap theory: "Curiosity emerges when the focus shifts to a gap in one's knowledge, creating a sense of deprivation", motivating information-seeking to resolve the gap, with resolution serving as a reward in a cyclical process. Combined with transactive memory system theory—where the internet acts as a new transactive memory partner—the framework explains why generating answers first makes knowledge gaps salient, induces curiosity, and buffers the metacognitive costs of mindless searching. The authors use it to interpret their finding that pre-search curiosity was elevated only in the answer-first group.
requirements: Learners must recognize a gap between what they know and what they need to know before searching
constraints: The hypothesized mechanism linking answer generation to recall via curiosity was only partially supported, since post-search curiosity and metacognitive judgments did not differ between groups
target_learning_goals: information recall from online searching
metacognitive awareness of knowledge gaps
examples: Participants in the thinking-before-googling condition spent three minutes generating or guessing answers to three broad brainstorming questions about modern pentathlon before searching

citation: Joshua M. Rosenberg, K. Bret Staudt Willet. (2021). Balancing' privacy and open science in the context of COVID-19: a response to Ifenthaler & Schumacher (2016). Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09860-8
title: Lundberg et al.'s (2019) decision-making model for balancing privacy risk to respondents with societal (science) benefits
description: A decision-making model for balancing privacy and open science developed by Lundberg et al. (2019) in the context of the Fragile Families Challenge. Rather than prescribing a recipe, the model is "deeply contextualized" in a project's discipline and risks to participants, and it operationalizes balance as "a tiered system of sharing some data publicly and other data through a gated application system." The commentary presents it as a way to move forward with open science values while respecting participants' privacy and rights, and suggests future work may extend it.
requirements: Sharing decisions must be contextualized in the project, discipline, and understanding of risks to participants rather than following a fixed recipe
constraints: Minimizing participants' risks may require sharing no data while maximizing open science requires sharing all data; the commentary states neither extreme is tenable in many cases
target_learning_goals: ethical data sharing and protection of participant privacy in research and learning analytics
examples: The commentary's authors applied a similar tiered approach in their own work: a carefully anonymized Twitter dataset plus an application process for access to the original data, and Reddit data shared in original form

title: Treat open science and privacy as values that must be balanced, beginning with deep understanding of the specific context
description: The commentary's key implication is that educational technology designers and researchers should consider open science and privacy as values needing balance in their work. Balancing "begins with a deep understanding of the specifics of the context," including what students think of the specific data being collected. The tension parallels that between the utility of learning analytics and student privacy noted by Chen and Zhu (2019).
requirements: Deep understanding of the specifics of the context, including student perceptions of the specific data being collected
constraints: The commentary states these recommendations are likely more stringent than FERPA or an IRB may require, and adherence should be considered a necessary-but-insufficient step in protecting participants' privacy
target_learning_goals: ethical design and conduct of learning analytics and educational research
examples: The authors ground the principle in Ifenthaler and Schumacher's (2016) finding that student comfort varies by data type, and in Lundberg et al.'s (2019) tiered sharing model

citation: Enrico Gandolfi · Richard E. Ferdig. (2025). Exploring the relationship between motivation and augmented reality presence using the augmented reality presence scale (ARPS). Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10446-5
title: Four-phase continuum of AR presence from control-focused to merging presence
description: Rasch construct key map and Wright map results yielded a continuum of AR presence composed of four phases: control-focused presence (−1.50 logits or below), realism-focused presence (−1.49 to −0.25 logits), human-focused presence (−0.24 to 0.50 logits), and merging presence (0.50 logits or above). Low presence reflects a need to "control, assess, and supervise the experience", while high presence involves embodiment and blending of AR and reality. The article uses this construct map to define what presence means in AR settings and to connect low/low-medium presence to withdrawn presence and medium–high/high presence to mesmeric presence found in prior XRPS work.

constraints: Derived from a mobile, geolocated AR tour with college students; the authors note the methods should be replicated with additional AR applications
target_learners: undergraduate students in educational technology and human computer interaction courses
target_learning_goals: measuring and understanding presence in augmented reality learning experiences
examples: Table 4 maps each phase to example items, e.g., merging presence is exemplified by "During the AR experience, I felt like my real body was there".

Emma's design was restricted by the available Elckerlyc models

target_learning_goals: science motivation, specifically task relevance and self-efficacy in physics inquiry learning

citation: Haifang Liu. (2026). AI-enhanced legal pedagogy: a case study of generative AI integration in property law courses. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10698-9

description: The article proposes an integrated framework in which constructivist learning theory, the Technology Acceptance Model, and the TPACK framework are not parallel layers but "constrain and inform one another at specific theoretical junctures". article_title: Open educational resources: undertheorized research and untapped potential
citation: David A. Wiley. (2021). Open educational resources: undertheorized research and untapped potential. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09907-w
title: The access hypothesis of OER benefits
description: The access hypothesis, named by Grimaldi, Basu Mallick, Waters, and Baraniuk (2019), is an explanatory mechanism for OER effects: "OER benefits learning by providing access to critical course materials, and therefore predicts that OER should only benefit students who would not otherwise have access to the materials." It reframes OER outcome questions as questions about the impact of the price of required course materials, since many OER are available at no or low cost. The commentary presents it as a current direction toward stronger theorization of OER research.
requirements: Researchers must account for students who would have had access to required course materials even had they been expensive when estimating OER effects
constraints: Predicts benefits only for students who would not otherwise have access to the materials
target_learners: higher education students, including Pell-eligible and other cost-burdened students
target_learning_goals: improving student outcomes such as final grades and success metrics through affordable access to course materials
examples: Grimaldi et al. (2019) used simulation analysis to show that failing to account for students with prior access likely prevents detecting any OER effect

article_title: The added value of game elements: better training performance but comparable learning gains
citation: Manuel Ninaus, Rodolpho Cortez, Izabel Hazin, Kristian Kiili, Silke M. Wortha, Elise Klein, Elisabeth M. Weiss, Korbinian Moeller. (2023). The added value of game elements: better training performance but comparable learning gains. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10263-8
title: Intrinsic integration of learning content into game core mechanics
description: Intrinsic integration is a game design approach in which the game's core mechanics are directly tied to the learning content, so that players process essential learning content through game actions. The article states it "refers to the general idea that there must be an intrinsic association between the game's core mechanics and the learning content or learning mechanic". The study applied it by implementing number line estimation as the game's walkable platform, letting learners experience fraction magnitudes as walking distances.
requirements: An intrinsic association between the game's core mechanics and the learning content or learning mechanic
constraints: The article notes the concept of intrinsic integration has not been studied extensively yet, and that to what extent it interacts with essential processing needs well-controlled experimental manipulations
target_learning_goals: fraction magnitude understanding
examples: The game-based training embedded number line estimation as a walkable path on Mount Olympos where the avatar Semideus recovered hidden gold coins marked by fractions

title: Semideus game-based fraction number line estimation training
description: A digital training environment in which the number line from 0 to 1 is visualized as a walkable platform; participants control the character Semideus recovering gold coins stolen by a goblin on Mount Olympos. The article states it "was already successfully utilized in previous studies for evaluating fraction knowledge in Finnish and German schoolchildren". It includes game fiction, visual aesthetics, coins, life points, and a 3-star end-of-level rating.
requirements: Participants estimate fraction positions within 10 s and repeat trials until correct; correct answers earn coins scaled to precision
constraints: In this study it was compared against a stripped, minimalistic non-game version with identical items and task, isolating the game elements
target_learning_goals: fraction magnitude estimation on a 0-to-1 number line
examples: In the study, 41 adults trained five consecutive days, 15–20 min per session, on 96 trials of fraction number line estimation

article_title: The added value of game elements: better training performance but comparable learning gains
citation: Manuel Ninaus, Rodolpho Cortez, Izabel Hazin, Kristian Kiili, Silke M. Wortha, Elise Klein, Elisabeth M. Weiss, Korbinian Moeller. (2023). The added value of game elements: better training performance but comparable learning gains. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10263-8
title: When investigating game elements, study the actual learning process, not only pretest–posttest outcomes
description: The article argues that effects of game elements can appear during the learning process even when pre-post learning outcomes do not differ, so research should measure performance during training. It states this "underscores the importance of studying the actual learning process when investigating the effects of game elements rather than analyzing learning outcomes alone (i.e., pretest–posttest differences)". In the study, only the training-phase measures revealed the accuracy and speed differences between conditions.
requirements: Behavioral performance measures (accuracy and response duration) collected during the training sessions themselves
constraints: In this study the interpretation that higher accuracy reflects increased cognitive engagement needed to be treated with caution because only behavioral indicators were available
target_learners: adult university students in game-based learning studies
target_learning_goals: fraction magnitude understanding
examples: The study compared game-based and non-game-based training conditions on PAE and response duration across five sessions, revealing condition differences invisible in the pre-post measure
