article_title: Role-playing monument exploration: an online educational game with a role-playing mechanism and multi-dimensional scaffolding for monument tours
citation: Shu-Wei Liu, Hung-Yu Chan, & Huei-Tse Hou. (2025). Role-playing monument exploration: an online educational game with a role-playing mechanism and multi-dimensional scaffolding for monument tours. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10480-3
title: 1946 Base Exploration: a Gather Town role-playing game-based monument guide with multi-dimensional scaffolding
description: An online educational game built in Gather Town that reconstructs a real military monument in northern Taiwan, in which three-learner teams role-play 1946 officers completing three timed mission stages (arranging facilities, planning guard paths, determining attack location) with guides playing the commander, soldiers, and invaders. The article states it was built "using Gather Town as the main game platform to construct an authentic virtual space based on the topography and appearance of a real military monument in northern Taiwan". Learners draw solutions on an in-game whiteboard and receive merits-based scoring for task correctness, communication attitude, and alertness to invaders.
requirements: Guides who role-play historical characters and provide dynamic scaffolding during play
An authentic virtual space based on the monument's real topography and appearance
constraints: The study used a single military monument in northern Taiwan with teams of three learners
target_learners: adult learners aged 20–55 in online monument guide activities
target_learning_goals: history and background of military monuments
application of military strategies (attacking directions and guarding routes)
examples: In the quasi-experiment, the experimental group explored the base in Gather Town for 60 minutes while guides played the commander, soldier, and invaders
key_sources: Shu-Wei Liu, Hung-Yu Chan, & Huei-Tse Hou. (2025). Role-playing monument exploration: an online educational game with a role-playing mechanism and multi-dimensional scaffolding for monument tours. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10480-3

article_title: Role-playing monument exploration: an online educational game with a role-playing mechanism and multi-dimensional scaffolding for monument tours
citation: Shu-Wei Liu, Hung-Yu Chan, & Huei-Tse Hou. (2025). Role-playing monument exploration: an online educational game with a role-playing mechanism and multi-dimensional scaffolding for monument tours. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10480-3
title: Multi-dimensional scaffolding framework for game-based monument education
description: The article proposes a framework in which game-based monument education provides learners with simultaneous support from five scaffold types: cognitive, procedural, emotional, and strategic scaffolds embedded in the game, plus peer scaffolding among learners. The authors write that learners "can obtain complete and immediate learning support through the cognitive, procedural, emotional, and strategic scaffolds within the game, as well as peer scaffolds among learners", with the aims of enhancing interactivity, maintaining flow, and generating motivation. Guides role-playing historical characters act as dynamic scaffolds that observe learners and give immediate, situation-dependent assistance, while static scaffolds (buildings, observation spots, whiteboard tips) provide fixed knowledge and task structure.
requirements: Guides available to observe learner performance and provide immediate dynamic scaffolding
Game-embedded static scaffolds (buildings, observation spots, game space, whiteboard tips)
Group collaboration among learners for peer scaffolding
constraints: The authors note the challenge of whether instructors can provide the same level of scaffolding at different times and the guiding-manpower cost issue
target_learners: adult learners in online monument guide activities
target_learning_goals: monument history knowledge
strategic planning and problem solving
sustained flow and motivation
examples: Table 1 details each scaffold type: cognitive scaffolding via buildings, observation spots and game space; procedural scaffolding via whiteboard tips; emotional scaffolding via guides' in-character tone and costume; strategic scaffolding via the whiteboard and commander feedback
key_sources: Shu-Wei Liu, Hung-Yu Chan, & Huei-Tse Hou. (2025). Role-playing monument exploration: an online educational game with a role-playing mechanism and multi-dimensional scaffolding for monument tours. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10480-3

The article states that "the guides who role-played the soldier and commander could interact with learners according to the game situation and provide dynamic scaffolding to help learners solve task problems immediately", combining cognitive, procedural, emotional, and strategic support in character. This keeps support contextualized and immediate rather than delivered as out-of-character instruction.

A game situation that calls for different scaffold types at different moments
constraints: The authors note it was a challenge whether instructors could provide the same level of scaffolding at different times, and the cost of guiding manpower

historical context understanding
motivation and engagement

article_title: Exploring expert perceptions of creativity in instructional design: a phenomenographic study
citation: Carolina Cuesta-Hincapie. (2025). Exploring expert perceptions of creativity in instructional design: a phenomenographic study. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10560-4
title: Outcome space of expert ways of experiencing creativity in ID: two dimensions with progression from understanding creativity to perceiving pedagogical challenge
description: The article's organizing framework is an outcome space in which the four categories of description form a progression from less to more comprehensive ways of experiencing creativity in ID. The article states the "outcome space was two-dimensional", with one dimension covering how participants understood and enacted creativity and one covering how they perceive creativity in the ID field. Progression from Category 1 to Category 4 "represents increasingly comprehensive ways of experiencing and conceptualizing creativity in ID".
requirements: Categories must be generated from collective participant experience rather than individual meaning, per the phenomenographic method the article follows
constraints: Derived from six purposefully selected experts; the article presents the categories as relative, experiential, and context-orientated rather than judging their accuracy
target_learners: instructional design graduate students and educators
target_learning_goals: understanding and fostering creativity in instructional design practice and education
examples: Category 1: creativity is a skill requiring intentionality; Category 2: creativity is fundamental in ID but not acknowledged; Category 3: creativity relates to the designer's character; Category 4: creativity as a pedagogical challenge in ID education

article_title: Exploring expert perceptions of creativity in instructional design: a phenomenographic study
citation: Carolina Cuesta-Hincapie. (2025). Exploring expert perceptions of creativity in instructional design: a phenomenographic study. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10560-4
title: Treat creativity as a core, explicitly integrated competency in ID education rather than an optional add-on
description: The article advocates reevaluating how creativity is fostered within instructional design programs. It argues that because creativity is developed alongside the designer's character and is needed to translate any process model into a design, ID education programs should make it "a core component of the IDer's work rather than an optional add-on". This aligns with prior work cited in the article holding that creativity should be a built-in rather than an add-on competency.
requirements: A shared understanding or vocabulary of creativity in the field, which participants report is currently lacking
constraints: The experts do not give a specific definition of creativity for the field; the article calls for a more contextual and adaptive definition aligned with individual educators' and students' needs
target_learning_goals: creative competency development in instructional design practice
examples: Boling notes all process models require human enactment and creativity is needed to translate a model into a design, so designers who have developed their creative responses will be creative in using ID process models

article_title: “A design framework for enhancing engagement in student-centered learning: own it, learn it, and share it” by Lee and Hannafin (2016): an international perspective
citation: Kevin M. Wong. (2021). “A design framework for enhancing engagement in student-centered learning: own it, learn it, and share it” by Lee and Hannafin (2016): an international perspective. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09842-w
title: Cultural-context sensitivity as a lens for interpreting student-centered learning principles internationally
description: The commentary advances the view that design principles which appear universal, such as owning, learning, and sharing knowledge, carry culture-dependent meanings. It states that "owning, learning, and sharing are principles that can be appreciated by systems of education around the globe," yet their "definitions and understandings" must be reconsidered across cultures. This lens frames international adoption of student-centered design frameworks as an interpretive, context-sensitive task rather than direct transfer.
requirements: Consideration of local cultural definitions of owning, learning, and sharing knowledge before adopting the framework in a new context
constraints: The commentary does not specify how cultural differences should be operationalized in design; it calls for future research on this question
target_learners: educators and designers implementing student-centered learning across international contexts
target_learning_goals: culturally appropriate implementation of student-centered learning designs
examples: The commentary applies this lens to Lee and Hannafin's own-it, learn-it, share-it framework when considering international adoption

article_title: Using electronic technology in the dynamic testing of young primary school children: predicting school achievement
citation: Kirsten W. J. Touw, Bart Vogelaar, Merel Bakker, Wilma C. M. Resing. (2019). Using electronic technology in the dynamic testing of young primary school children: predicting school achievement. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09655-6
title: Computerized tablet-administered dynamic series completion test with graduated prompts
description: A newly developed computerized visual-spatial series completion test for 6–8-year-olds, administered on an Acer Aspire Switch 10 tablet and programmed in GM:Studio. Each item presents a row of six boxes with geometric figures and an empty seventh box; children drag figures into the empty box. The tablet delivers "general verbal instructions", auditory feedback (a high 'pling' for correct answers), visual effects, and a four-step graduated prompts sequence from general metacognitive prompts to item-specific cognitive prompts, and automatically scores performance via log files.
requirements: Administered individually in a quiet room by trained examiners
Items piloted with children of the same age for suitability
constraints: The article notes the 18-item pre- and post-tests were relatively long for some children
Internal consistency of the item set was modest (alpha 0.64)
target_learners: Grade-2 primary school children aged 6–8 years
target_learning_goals: Inductive reasoning: detecting pattern transformations and periodicity in geometric series
examples: In the study, 80 trained children completed two tablet-based training sessions with graduated prompts while 84 controls solved paper-and-pencil mazes and dot-to-dot tasks

article_title: Using electronic technology in the dynamic testing of young primary school children: predicting school achievement
citation: Kirsten W. J. Touw, Bart Vogelaar, Merel Bakker, Wilma C. M. Resing. (2019). Using electronic technology in the dynamic testing of young primary school children: predicting school achievement. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09655-6
title: Dynamic testing as a test–train–test format revealing learning potential beyond static ability
description: Dynamic testing is an assessment framework using a test-training-test format that incorporates feedback and training into the testing phases, providing information about an individual's progression in performance and cognitive functioning. Derived from Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development, it "focuses on the individual's potential for growth and learning abilities" rather than relying on previous learning experiences as conventional static tests do. In this study the framework was implemented computerized on a tablet, with the number of prompts needed serving as a dynamic measure of the child's need for instruction.
requirements: Multiple assessment points (pre-test, training, post-test)
Standardized graduated prompts procedure ranging from general to specific instruction
constraints: Administering multiple assessment points can be time-consuming and difficult to apply in practice
target_learners: Primary school children in the early grades
target_learning_goals: Insight into individual cognitive strengths, instructional needs and potential for learning
examples: The study operationalized dynamic testing as a tablet-delivered series completion test with two training sessions using graduated prompts between pre- and post-test

article_title: Teachers’ experiences of teaching online during COVID-19: implications for postpandemic professional development
citation: Carlos González, Daniel Ponce, Violeta Fernández. (2023). Teachers' experiences of teaching online during COVID-19: implications for postpandemic professional development. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10200-9
title: Five-dimension framework of higher education teachers' digital competencies for post-GOT online and blended teaching
description: The article organizes teachers' digital competencies around the four dimensions proposed by Esteve-Mon et al. (2020)—basic digital skills, the pedagogical application of digital technologies, the use of technology to support continuous professional development, and the ability to further the digital competencies of higher education students—extended with Villarroel and Bruna's (2017) transversal competencies. The authors state: "We organized our results around these five dimensions to converge the analysis of teachers' experiences with teachers' digital competency development needs for post-GOT online and blended teaching." The framework structures both the interview analysis and the professional development recommendations.
requirements: The framework was applied to higher education teachers teaching undergraduate courses online due to COVID restrictions in Chile
constraints: The article notes existing competency frameworks were not initially developed for use in higher education
target_learning_goals: digital competencies for online and blended teaching
examples: The results section presents themes under each of the five dimensions, with interview excerpts from 151 teachers and full excerpt tables in an appendix

article_title: The research we have is not the research we need
citation: Thomas C. Reeves, Lin Lin. (2020). The research we have is not the research we need. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09811-3
title: Educational technology research should be reoriented toward making a difference in the lives of learners
description: The article closes its analysis with a values-oriented recommendation: research on emerging learning technologies should be judged by whether it makes a difference for learners. The authors write that readers should be “always striving to make a difference in the lives of learners around the world,” framing learner impact as the ultimate aim of the research program the special issue represents.
requirements: Research efforts should be framed around serious problems related to teaching, learning, and performance rather than technologies alone
target_learning_goals: improving teaching, learning, and performance outcomes
examples: The concluding commentary of the special issue on systematic review research on emerging learning environments and technologies delivers this recommendation to its readers.

article_title: “We are too dumb for this”: a critical discourse analysis of stereotypical attributions to struggle with computational thinking
citation: Lucas Vasconcelos. (2025). “We are too dumb for this”: a critical discourse analysis of stereotypical attributions to struggle with computational thinking. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10532-8
title: Attribution theory's three dimensions (locus, stability, controllability) as a framework for analyzing struggle discourse in computational thinking
description: Attribution theory describes how individuals interpret and explain the causes of events and behaviors. The article uses its three dimensions — locus (dispositional vs. situational), stability (permanent vs. temporary), and controllability — as the coding framework for preservice teachers' attributions during struggle with computational thinking. The article states that "Attributions can differ in three fundamental aspects: locus (origin), stability, and controllability", and that attributions influence motivation, emotional responses, and subsequent behavior, making them a lens for identifying stereotypical versus non-stereotypical explanations of struggle.
requirements: Analysis requires discourse data captured as attributions occur, which the article argues minimizes self-report biases such as memory lapses.
constraints: The article frames its critical discourse analysis through a Western lens on computer science stereotypes, noting stereotypes differ in Eastern countries.
target_learners: K-12 learners in computer science education
target_learning_goals: understanding causal attributions during productive struggle
promoting growth-oriented attributions
examples: The study coded 27 discourse episodes in NVivo by locus, stability, and controllability, classifying statements like "Neither of us know computers" as dispositional, uncontrollable, and permanent.
key_sources: Lucas Vasconcelos. (2025). “We are too dumb for this”: a critical discourse analysis of stereotypical attributions to struggle with computational thinking. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10532-8

article_title: “We are too dumb for this”: a critical discourse analysis of stereotypical attributions to struggle with computational thinking
citation: Lucas Vasconcelos. (2025). “We are too dumb for this”: a critical discourse analysis of stereotypical attributions to struggle with computational thinking. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10532-8
title: Two-week Scratch-based computational thinking module with water filter simulation tasks
description: The study's instructional element was a two-week computational thinking module in a science teaching methods course in which participants learned block-based programming in Scratch, created and tested a water filter, and coded science simulations analogous to the water filter. Tasks followed the computational thinking subskills: participants "decomposed the problem by coding the outcomes of using different purification media, applied abstraction skills by connecting code blocks to science concepts", designed algorithmic steps, applied patterns, and debugged code errors. This element generated the struggle episodes analyzed in the study.
requirements: Participants had no prior training on computational thinking or block-based programming; the module was embedded in an existing course to circumvent curriculum overload.
constraints: The article notes the limited scope of data was due to restricted time allocated for computational thinking activities within the teacher education course.
target_learners: preservice science teachers in secondary education methods courses
target_learning_goals: computational thinking subskills: decomposition, abstraction, algorithmic thinking, pattern recognition, debugging
examples: Participants coded simulations where a wait block represented filtration time, and visual feedback alerted them when code was inadequate, making struggle tangible.

article_title: Learning analytics in inquiry-based learning: a systematic review
citation: Fan Chen, Gaowei Chen. (2025). Learning analytics in inquiry-based learning: a systematic review. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10507-9
title: Dual-role account of learning analytics in inquiry-based learning
description: The review frames LA in IBL as playing two complementary roles. First, LA provides "data-supported analysis to uncover student engagement and performance during inquiry activities", including assessing engagement levels, identifying learning patterns or challenges, and evaluating inquiry skills like formulating testable hypotheses. Second, "LA-driven insights serve as supportive tools that provide real-time feedback and targeted intervention" for students while assisting teachers in improving IBL design and implementation. The review uses this dual-role framing to organise its analysis of how LA both understands inquiry processes and supports students and teachers across inquiry stages.
requirements: LA in IBL requires process data collection and analysis, such as behaviour logs, discussion transcripts, and multimodal data, to generate actionable insights for students and teachers.
constraints: The review notes limited understanding of how LA has been used to understand students' inquiry processes at specific stages, and limited research on the effectiveness of LA tools as interventions.
target_learning_goals: scientific inquiry skills
collaborative knowledge building
evidence-based reasoning
examples: The review cites Dickler et al. (2021) employing teacher-facing dashboards to scaffold students' inquiry through discursive supports, and de Araujo et al. (2024) using LA-based conversational agents to foster productive discourse during IBL tasks.
key_sources: Fan Chen, Gaowei Chen. (2025). Learning analytics in inquiry-based learning: a systematic review. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10507-9

description: A framework for teacher professional development (PD) for online and blended learning (OBL) derived from a systematic meta-aggregative review. The article reports that it "resulted from the analysis of 15 research papers published between 2004 and 2015" and "introduced six interrelated components", spanning supportive program design, acknowledging context, teacher change, goals, PD strategies, and dissemination and evaluation.

constraints: Derived from analysis of 15 research papers published between 2004 and 2015, so its evidence base is bounded by that literature
target_learners: teachers transitioning to online and blended learning
target_learning_goals: teacher capability for online and blended learning instruction
examples: The special issue responses apply the framework to crisis-driven rapid shifts to online delivery across practice, design, research, international, critical pedagogy, and K-12 perspectives

citation: Gloria Natividad Beltrán del Río. (2021). A useful framework for teacher professional development for online and blended learning to use as guidance in times of crisis. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09953-y
title: Special-issue table of seven responses to Philipsen et al.'s TPD-for-OBL review

It organizes the special issue's contributions, noting for example that "The findings can be clearly applied to guide an appropriate TPD for the recovery as well as for a resilient education system".

title: EATS: an Emotion and Attention Tracking System for live online classes
description: EATS is a platform built on the BigBlueButton live classroom system that measures students' emotion and attention in real time via image processing technology for students with cameras activated. As the article describes it, "the platform developed on the BigBlueButton live classroom system displays emojis corresponding to users’ facial expressions, allowing the instructor to monitor students’ emotions in real time." article_title: Expanding conceptual evidence-building with the science of learning: integrating evidence weights, alignment estimates and iterative updates for educational innovations
citation: Natalia Kucirkova, Phil Vahey, David Patterson, David Dockterman. (2026). Expanding conceptual evidence-building with the science of learning: integrating evidence weights, alignment estimates and iterative updates for educational innovations. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10732-w
title: A five-step systematic methodology for building the conceptual evidence base of educational innovations
description: The article introduces a structured methodology for evaluating educational innovations' conceptual foundations, developed through practice at the International Centre for EdTech Impact. It proceeds from evidence identification to interpretation and application: "We followed five systematic steps. First, we conducted a rapid literature review, guided by the principle of methodological plurality. Second, we evaluated the identified studies using the criterion of weight of evidence." The sequence was designed to reduce the risk of retrospectively selecting evidence to justify existing product features, and culminates in a theory of change shared with the company to inform its research roadmap.
requirements: A rapid literature review guided by the innovation's learning goals and instructional approach, with predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria
Weight-of-evidence appraisal of identified studies across multiple disciplines
Alignment analysis relating evidence to the innovation's specific features and assumptions
Discussion of findings with representatives of the organization that designed the innovation
Development of a theory of change integrating the literature with a logic model
constraints: The authors describe it as "a conceptually grounded, practice-informed methodological proposal and not an application of grounded theory in the strict methodological sense"
Rapid reviews "may not provide the same depth as a full systematic review"
target_learners: developers and researchers of educational innovations
school districts and procurement teams evaluating educational tools
target_learning_goals: evaluating and strengthening the conceptual research foundations of educational innovations
examples: The methodology was applied to two case studies: the I Can Read early childhood literacy product from Asia and the entirely digital SplashLearn math and reading platform from the USA

As printed: "This includes seven quality parameters - transparency, accuracy, accessibility, specificity, purposivity, utility and propriety - used to rank studies and establish a weighted evidence base for the underlying assumptions behind a theory of change." In the case studies, studies were marked high, medium or low quality by two independent researchers applying these criteria.

Recognition that a study's rating may differ across innovations because specificity, purposivity and utility vary by context

title: ESSA Tier IV evidence standard requiring a well-defined logic model and planned research
description: ESSA Tier IV is the lowest of four statutory evidence levels in the US Every Student Succeeds Act framework, relating to a research-informed rationale. Per the What Works Clearinghouse definition quoted in the article: "the product demonstrates a rationale if the study design follows a well-defined logic model and related research or evaluation is planned or underway". The article focuses on Tier IV for early-stage interventions, where empirical impact evidence may not yet exist, and observes that certification providers apply the guidance with considerable flexibility.
requirements: A well-defined logic model with related research or evaluation planned or underway
constraints: Certification providers differ widely in requirements: Digital Promise demands at least five empirical citations, an annotated bibliography, a qualitative study and a FERPA letter, while others demand only a logic model and rapid review
The article states there is currently no systematic methodology or detailed guidance for conducting the foundational research required for the lowest Tier

title: Embed evidence-informed mechanisms from the earliest stages of product development rather than treating research as post hoc validation
description: The article argues that research should shape educational innovations from the start, not merely validate them afterwards. As the authors state: "rather than treating research as an afterthought or a post hoc validation tool, we argue that evidence-informed mechanisms should be embedded from the earliest stages of product development." This includes using empirical findings to define and frame the educational problems a product addresses, and integrating Science of Learning principles at each stage rather than prioritizing efficacy studies over conceptual alignment.

A structured review process connecting research to product design before efficacy studies
constraints: The authors note that retroactively aligning existing products with research risks superficial or selective use of evidence

citation: Inka Sara Hähnlein, Pablo Pirnay-Dummer. (2024). Promoting pre-service teachers' knowledge integration from multiple text sources across domains with instructional prompts. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10363-z
title: Two-order definition of knowledge integration: first-order constructive structuring and second-order cross-domain transfer
description: The article adopts Lehmann's (2020a) two-part definition of knowledge integration that organises its study of pre-service teachers' multiple-document comprehension. "First-order knowledge integration, as a form of constructive learning, is the active linking, merging, distinguishing, organizing, and structuring of knowledge structures into a coherent model." "Second-order knowledge integration, as a form of knowledge application, is the simultaneous transfer of knowledge from different domains with the goal of reaching a suitable problem solution." The experiment targets both orders through reading and a transfer-oriented writing task.
requirements: Integration requires multiple document comprehension building on single-text comprehension (Construction-Integration Model and Document Model Framework), including an integrated mental model and an intertext model of sources
constraints: The article notes teacher education is hardly designed to link subject areas, so learners' professional knowledge tends to be fragmented and poorly integrated
target_learning_goals: knowledge integration across domains
multiple-document comprehension
transfer of integrated knowledge to instructional problems
examples: The study's writing task on a fictional scenario required integrating knowledge from four texts from educational science, educational psychology, didactics, and policy-making to derive implications for lesson planning

title: T-MITOCAR computer-linguistic technology for modeling and comparing semantic knowledge structures of texts
description: T-MITOCAR (Text-Model Inspection Trace of Concepts and Relations) is a computational linguistic heuristic technology "developed as a means of automatically analyzing, modeling, visualizing, and comparing the semantic knowledge structure of texts." It builds graphs of concepts linked by association strengths from propositional relations, grounded in mental model theory, and compares texts quantitatively via four structural measures (SUR, GRA, GAMMA, STRU) and three semantic measures (CONC, PROP, BSM) yielding similarity values between zero and one. The study used it to compare student texts with a reference model of the four source texts.
requirements: A reference model built from the source texts against which learner texts are compared using the seven similarity measures
constraints: The article states the similarity indices measure different features and "can therefore not be treated like a subsuming scale (e.g., on a test)"
target_learning_goals: assessing semantic knowledge structure of learner-produced texts
knowledge integration across domains
examples: The four source texts were combined into one document and modelled with T-MITOCAR to generate the reference model against which all 109 student texts were compared

citation: Dirk Ifenthaler, Jane Yin-Kim Yau. (2020). Utilising learning analytics to support study success in higher education: a systematic review. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09788-z
title: Three-method taxonomy of learning analytics: descriptive, predictive and prescriptive analytics
description: The review organises learning analytics methodologies into three types. "Descriptive analytics use data obtained from sources such as course assessments, surveys, student information systems, learning management system activities and forum interactions mainly for reporting purposes." Predictive analytics use similar data to measure onward learning success or failure, while prescriptive analytics deploy algorithms mainly to predict study success and course completion and to recommend immediate interventions. The review uses this taxonomy to characterise the diversification of early trace-data approaches into broader educational applications.
requirements: Data from sources such as course assessments, surveys, student information systems, learning management system activities and forum interactions
target_learning_goals: study success, course completion, and dropout prevention
examples: The review's Table 1 classifies the 46 key publications' data analytics methods, including binary logistic regression, decision tree analysis, and support vector machines, with main predictions on course completion, grades, and dropout rates.

citation: Kyungmee Lee. (2018). Everyone already has their community beyond the screen: reconceptualizing online learning and expanding boundaries. Educational Technology Research and Development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-018-9613-y
title: Double-layered CoP model of online learning
description: The double-layered CoP model conceptualizes online learning as "interlinked processes of participation and socialization in multiple communities across online- and ofﬂine-''layers'' of learners' lives". It was originally developed by incorporating CoP principles into an online teacher education course addressing divisions between teachers' online learning and their classroom teaching. The model guides online course designers to expand the perceived boundaries of the course environments they design to include learners' offline learning contexts, rather than focusing exclusively on building a single community within an online course.
requirements: The course must explicitly guide students to choose and develop one of their existing communities into a supportive CoP, as a student-driven process
constraints: The author states the suggested principles are more relevant and applicable to online course design than face-to-face course design
target_learners: adult online learners in higher education, particularly in-service teachers and working professionals
target_learning_goals: authentically constructivist learning through participation and socialization in communities of practice
examples: Jane's 12-week online course required structured CoP journal entries reflecting on developing external CoPs and connecting course ideas to practices in them

title: Four-phase development of an internal course CoP paired with sequenced external CoP development tasks
description: In the double-layered CoP model, "an online course itself is nurtured and developed into an internal CoP through four interdependent learning phases; i.e., course preparation, foundation building, interactive learning, and knowledge transfer". In parallel, each student develops an existing community in their teaching context into an external CoP through sequenced sub-tasks: community selection, membership development, knowledge sharing, and collaborative practice. Students write CoP journal entries reflecting on these experiences and connecting course ideas to practice.
requirements: Course preparation must explicitly explain the double-layered CoP structure and emphasize the value of learning in CoPs before the course starts
constraints: The external CoP development task is described as rather challenging and needs to be structured as small sub-tasks in a sequence

citation: Audio-Visual Communication Review, digest items abstracted by E. G. Sherburne, Jr. and Edmund Faison. (1955). Audio-Visual Communication Review. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=audio-visual+communication+review
title: Two-ladder classification of readability: easy-difficult and interesting-dull parameters
description: The University of Illinois readability survey organizes readability measurement around two principal parameters. The easy-difficult ladder covers vocabulary difficulty, word length, sentence length and complexity, and parts-of-speech difficulty; the interesting-dull ladder covers references to people, verb-adjective ratios, image-bearing and human-interest words, and early-learned words and localisms. The survey reports that "Readability measures, for the most part, classify writing on two principal parameters", making this the organizing framework of the reviewed literature.
requirements: Applying the framework requires measuring stylistic elements such as vocabulary difficulty, sentence length and complexity, and human-interest word counts as listed in the survey
constraints: The survey notes the formulas deal with stylistic qualities of prose rather than with its meaning
target_learners: adult readers of printed instructional material
target_learning_goals: comprehension of written text
engagement with written material
examples: The survey lists the easy-difficult elements as vocabulary difficulty, length of words, length and complexity of sentence, and difficulty related to parts of speech

article_title: Invisible borders in educational technology research? A comparative analysis
citation: Marín, V. I., Buntins, K., Bedenlier, S., & Bond, M. (2023). Invisible borders in educational technology research? A comparative analysis. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10195-3
title: Cultural clusters and national research traditions as an explanatory framework for EdTech research topics
description: The article frames country differences in EdTech research using Ronen and Shenkar's eco-cultural clustering, which "consider[s] three main variables (religion, language and geography)" and identifies 11 global clusters, with Germany in the Germanic, Spain in the Latin European and the UK in the Anglo cluster. It layers this over Biesta's distinction between the Anglo-Saxon tradition from curriculum studies and the continental tradition from Pädagogik, attributing Germany and Spain to the continental tradition and the UK to the Anglo-Saxon tradition. The framework explains why topical clusters persist despite a shared publication language.

constraints: The article notes the three clusters are similar in economic terms (high GDP-PPP), so economic aspects may influence EdTech research development and were not closely considered in the study
target_learning_goals: Understanding how national research traditions shape EdTech research topics and terminology
examples: Germany's Medienpädagogik divided into Medienerziehung and Mediendidaktik; Spain's Tecnología Educativa framed within Didáctica; the UK's shift toward technology enhanced learning as lingua franca

citation: Marianthi Grizioti. (2025). Computational thinking beyond coding: exploring student computational practices while playing and modifying a socio-scientific simulation game with integrated computational tools. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10477-y
title: Three-axis framework for CT in socio-scientific contexts: computational tools, engagement process and content
description: The article proposes a framework organizing the development of computational literacy around three axes. The first concerns the representational tools provided to learners, where the study introduced "multiple interconnected representations" combining data handling, map-based interface and coding. The second concerns the engagement process and learner roles, scaffolded by the three-stage PFO model. The third concerns content, integrating societal and scientific aspects of the simulated issue to support critical computational thinking. The themes and codes are offered as guidelines for designing CT activities and evaluation instruments.
requirements: Tools must interconnect multiple computational affordances beyond coding, such as databases, map editors and block-based programming
constraints: The article states the results cannot be applied to the general population without validation with a larger number of students with different backgrounds
target_learning_goals: computational thinking practices (abstraction, pattern recognition, automation)
critical engagement with socio-scientific issues
systems thinking
examples: The CT-Chef game in ChoiCo was used across Play, Focused Modifications and Open design stages in a 7-week school project

title: PFO model of progressive engagement: Play, Focused Modifications, Open Modifications & Design
description: The PFO model adapts the Use-Modify-Create model for game-based learning, structuring student engagement with a digital game through "layered structural access" to game elements. In the first layer students play the game with access only to its interface; in the second they access and modify certain elements such as a database without making major changes; in the third they access complex functionalities for open modifications or creating a new game. The article reports this scaffolding enabled evolution from micro-level to macro-level computational reasoning.
requirements: Activities must be sequenced across the three layers with progressively deeper access to game structure
constraints: The article notes students struggled in prior UMC research with the transition from Modify to Create, and this study was limited by restricted time for open modifications
target_learners: middle school students with little game design experience
target_learning_goals: progressive development of complex CT practices
system-based thinking about simulations
examples: Students first played CT-Chef repeatedly to improve scores, then made focused modifications such as changing an ending condition, then created new game versions with added rules, choices and attributes

title: ChoiCo environment and CT-Chef socio-scientific simulation game
description: ChoiCo (Choices with Consequences) is a web-based open access game authoring environment with a Play Mode for choice-driven simulation games and a Design Mode offering three interconnected computational tools: an editable database of game fields and choices, a map editor connected to the database, and three block-based coding workspaces for game mechanics. CT-Chef is a game created for this study dealing with managing a sustainable, health-promoting restaurant, where choices affect five game fields including money, healthy food and customers per day.
requirements: Design Mode access to the database, map editor and coding workspaces for modification and creation activities
constraints: Student games had to maintain the initial game mechanics of surviving as long as possible via map-based choices
target_learning_goals: CT practices through game play, modification and design
data editing and systems reasoning
examples: The game extends an older game called Eating Out used in a prior pilot study, and was played in a school computer laboratory by 7 groups

article_title: Developing computational thinking in teacher education: a brief experience with coding, robotics, and machine learning
citation: Susana Sánchez Castro, Mª Ángeles Pascual Sevillano, Rogelio Buceta Otero, Javier Fombona Cadavieco. (2026). Developing computational thinking in teacher education: a brief experience with coding, robotics, and machine learning. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10744-6
title: Creative Computational Problem Solving (CCPS) model: five interactive phases structuring computational thinking development through creative problem solving with programming and robotics
description: The CCPS model (Chevalier et al., 2020, 2021) is a framework for structuring the development of computational thinking in educational settings, described by the article as "one of the most comprehensive and validated frameworks" in this area. It organizes learning through creative problem solving and integrates programming and educational robotics as central tools. It is structured around five interactive phases: Understanding, Idea Generation, Formalization, Implementation/Programming, and Evaluation, in which outcomes are analyzed, errors debugged, and processes improved iteratively. This study operationalized the five phases through a two-hour workshop with rotating stations and guided creative challenges.
requirements: Operational frameworks are needed to guide educational practice in specific contexts; the phases must be operationalized through concrete activities such as rotating stations and guided creative challenges
constraints: The article notes TPACK lacks a specific operational guide for structuring the teaching of CT or machine learning and needs complementing by more concrete, situated models; CCPS is applied here only as a two-hour initial-exposure microintervention, not sustained competency development
target_learning_goals: computational thinking
creative problem solving
programming and robotics familiarity
examples: The workshop operationalized the five phases: students understood proposed challenges, generated ideas, formalized solutions using mental diagrams or programming blocks, implemented tasks in Scratch, micro:bit, or Makey Makey, and reviewed outcomes to refine proposals

citation: Susana Sánchez Castro, Mª Ángeles Pascual Sevillano, Rogelio Buceta Otero, Javier Fombona Cadavieco. (2026). Developing computational thinking in teacher education: a brief experience with coding, robotics, and machine learning. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10744-6
title: Two-hour station-based microintervention workshop with Scratch, Makey Makey, and micro:bit–Maqueen including an introductory machine-learning component
description: A two-hour face-to-face workshop in the ICT course of the Bachelor's Degree in Primary Education, designed as a feasible microintervention within regular teacher education timetables. It featured three hands-on stations with teacher guidance: programming with Scratch (sequences, loops, conditionals, debugging), interaction with Makey Makey boards (conductivity and physical-digital interaction), and controlling Maqueen robots with micro:bit (sensor-based control including a line-following challenge). An introductory machine-learning component provided "an initial conceptual approximation to machine learning, rather than to develop operational ML skills," explaining how data classify patterns and how models are trained from examples. A total of 105 students participated in four groups of 25–30.
requirements: Teacher guidance to introduce the tools and the logic underlying each challenge; rotating stations with specific objectives and tasks aligned with different aspects of computational thinking
constraints: The machine-learning component did not involve technical development or training of machine learning models; the study design does not isolate whether differences are attributable to the intervention content or to any structured active-learning experience
target_learning_goals: computational thinking concepts (sequencing, loops, conditionals, abstraction, debugging)
algorithmic logic and parallelism
perseverance in iterative problem solving
examples: In the micro:bit–Maqueen station, students examined how the robot interpreted sensor values associated with light and dark surfaces and how these inputs determined wheel movement and trajectory correction

title: Use asynchronous discussion forums as a low-bandwidth interactive e-learning design, optionally coupled with podcasts where bandwidth allows
description: The article recommends that instructors in higher education in low-bandwidth contexts design e-courses around asynchronous discussion forums, because "effective use of discussion forums can produce important learning effects and is a low-bandwidth strategy". Coupling podcasts with forums may further enhance learning effects, but podcasts are "not a low-bandwidth addition" and require more bandwidth and additional instructor effort. The article suggests distributing podcast materials offline where live streaming is infeasible.

Students and instructors develop expertise in using forums and podcasts effectively

The HIL design requires more bandwidth and additional instructor effort

Higher-order thinking (cognitive and metacognitive)
Academic achievement in chemistry
examples: In the study, 102 undergraduates were randomly assigned to tutorial sections using NIL, MIL (discussion forums added) or HIL (podcasts plus forums) designs across three chemistry topics, with achievement measured by pre- and post-tests per unit

article_title: Generative AI as a cognitive partner: personalised GPTs and differentiated learning in undergraduate teacher education
citation: Jason Zagami. (2026). Generative AI as a cognitive partner: personalised GPTs and differentiated learning in undergraduate teacher education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10746-4
title: Prompt–Reflect–Refine cycle as a model for AI-mediated dialogic learning
description: The Prompt–Reflect–Refine cycle is the study's structured pedagogical routine for AI-mediated learning: students formulate a prompt, evaluate the AI response against pedagogical frameworks (TPACK and AITSL Standards), then modify their artefact or prompt and document reasoning. The article states "the prompt initiates cognitive activation, reflection triggers evaluation, and refinement consolidates learning". It operationalises dialogic metacognition, constrains interaction away from one-shot querying, and creates analysable traces of metacognitive regulation across successive prompts and artefacts.
requirements: Students must explicitly evaluate AI outputs against nominated pedagogical frameworks rather than accept them
Weekly tasks structured around the three-cycle steps with documented reasoning
constraints: Replication should focus on reproducing the pedagogical workflow rather than an immutable underlying language model, since OpenAI periodically updates foundation models
target_learners: pre-service secondary teachers in Initial Teacher Education
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of Digital Technologies curriculum
pedagogical reasoning and lesson design
metacognitive regulation
critical AI literacy
examples: Students completed weekly Prompt–Reflect–Refine tasks within the Canvas LMS, with reflection prompts requiring evaluation against TPACK and AITSL Standards

title: Lexia English Language Development: a CALL tool for oral academic English in grades K-6
description: Lexia English is a computer-assisted language learning program for Emergent Bilinguals in grades K-6, released July 2020, intended to supplement rather than replace English language development instruction at 30-60 minutes weekly. It emphasizes oral language via speaking and listening activities, with 17 Emergent Bilingual characters guiding learners through scaffolded conversational interactions. A built-in Speech Recognition Engine measures correct usage of grammatical structures and provides instant corrective feedback by visually highlighting incorrect sentence segments, and an auto-placement tool suggests one of 19 starting levels.
requirements: Students are expected to use the online program between 30 and 60 min per week
Scripted teacher-led lesson plans are recommended for pre-teaching or reteaching skills
constraints: The program is intended to supplement, rather than replace, English language development instruction for ELs

target_learning_goals: Academic English oral language skills (speaking and listening)
English grammar and vocabulary
Discourse functions for discussing academic content
examples: A speaking activity in the lesson 'Evaluating with Esther using prepositions' focuses on the multi-word preposition 'in addition to' under the speaking purpose 'Evaluate' and the theme 'Protecting Earth's Resources'.

citation: Nicholas Feroce, Jenny Liu, Rajendra Chattergoon. (2025). Exploring the impact of a CALL tool for emergent bilinguals. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10462-5
title: Interaction-approach SLA design: scaffolded output, comprehensible input, and corrective feedback in a CALL program
description: The program's linguistic components were intentionally developed based on theories within the interaction approach to second language acquisition. Speaking activities are framed as scaffolded conversational interactions implementing the Output Hypothesis, while language frames serve as comprehensible input under the Input Hypothesis. Program characters first model the sentence, followed by joint repetition, then independent student production, supporting purposeful repetition for fluency and automaticity. A Speech Recognition Engine with instant corrective feedback is intended to trigger learners' metalinguistic awareness as they hypothesize utterance formulation and test out sentences.
requirements: Speaking activities must be framed as scaffolded conversational interactions with program characters
Corrective feedback must be provided so learners can test sentences and receive feedback on whether they were understood
constraints: The program is not intended to replace real-life conversational interactions; its affordances lie in complementing classroom instruction
target_learners: K-6 Emergent Bilinguals learning academic English
target_learning_goals: Production of complete sentences with target vocabulary and grammar
Fluency and automaticity in oral academic language
Metalinguistic awareness of utterance form
examples: Program characters model a sentence, the character and student repeat together, then the student produces it independently.

title: GenAI-RP Scale: a validated survey instrument measuring GenAI readiness, benefits, and challenges for both faculty and students in higher education
description: The GenAI-RP Scale is a survey instrument comprising three subscales: Readiness, Benefit, and Challenge, with parallel but role-tailored items for students and instructors. The article states the scale 'comprises three distinct subscales: a) Readiness scale, b) Benefit scale, and c) Challenge scale,' with items adapted from prior instruments and reviewed by three content experts. It was validated via EFA and CFA on data from 460 students and 132 faculty collected in spring 2024.

title: GenAI readiness conceptualized as three components: comprehension, ethical awareness, and utilization/proficiency
description: The article defines readiness to use GenAI for education as 'the perceived state of preparedness of an individual (student or instructor) in terms of cognitive understanding, ethical consideration, and practical skills regarding the use of generative artificial intelligence for teaching or learning.' Unlike Wang et al.'s four-factor AI readiness framework (Cognition, Ability, Vision, Ethics), this study conceptualized readiness with three components — GenAI Comprehension, Ethical Awareness of GenAI, and GenAI Utilization and Proficiency — merging Cognition and Vision, with factor definitions differentiated for learners and instructors.
requirements: Factor definitions were revised after content and factor-structure validation to ensure accuracy
constraints: The conceptualization was developed for GenAI specifically rather than general AI technologies, targeting both students and instructors across diverse disciplines in higher education

ethical awareness of GenAI
proficiency in using GenAI for learning or teaching
examples: The final readiness scale comprises Factor 1 GenAI Comprehension (six items), Factor 2 Ethical Awareness of GenAI (three items), and Factor 3 GenAI Utilization and Proficiency (three student items, seven faculty items)

citation: Aleksandra Bereznikova, Emily Theophilou, Davinia Hernández-Leo. (2026). The influence of socratic dialogue within GenAI on critical thinking and technology perception. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10693-0
title: Two-phase Socratic GenAI workshop activity with outside-domain and within-domain prompts
description: A workshop activity in which participants interact with ChatGPT in two six-minute phases: first with a general out-of-domain Socratic prompt ("Teach me about the principles of generative AI through a Socratic dialogue using a simple, non-AI topic"), then with a within-domain prompt on a topic of their expertise, completing questionnaires after each phase. The prompt uses "probing, indirect questions and relatable analogies". It was refined iteratively after early trials produced didactic monologues.
requirements: Participants receive a brief introduction to the Socratic Method before the two phases
Participants paste the prompt directly into the conversational AI interface

understanding of genAI principles

article_title: Factors shaping faculty online teaching competencies during the Covid-19 pandemic
citation: Trevisan, O., De Rossi, M., Christensen, R., Knezek, G., & Smits, A. (2023). Factors shaping faculty online teaching competencies during the Covid-19 pandemic. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10197-1
title: Faculty online-teaching competence as dispositions and environmental conditions framed by the Theory of Planned Behavior and the Integrated Model of Behavior Prediction
description: The article frames faculty competence for online teaching as a multifaceted attribute combining knowledge, skills, pedagogical expertise and "sound pedagogical-technological dispositions including motivation and confidence in one's competence, or self-efficacy". It uses the socio-psychological Theory of Planned Behavior combined with the Integrated Model of Behavior Prediction, which "describes behavior through an antecedent of intentions that vary with attitude, perceived norms, and self-efficacy". Internal factors (dispositions, enthusiasm, resolutions) and external factors (institutional support, training) are treated as antecedents of competent online-teaching behavior, and the study's cluster factors map onto this framework.
requirements: Competent online-teaching behavior is understood as requiring both internal dispositions and external environmental conditions to be addressed together
constraints: The framework is applied to higher education faculty in education departments during the Covid-19 pandemic transition
target_learning_goals: competence for online teaching and technology integration
examples: The study measured Enthusiasm (ease/usefulness of OT), Resolutions to use OT, and perceived institutional Support as observable indicators of the framework's internal and external factors

title: Professional development for online teaching should be strength-based, embedded in daily practice, and responsive to faculty's self-identified needs
description: The article argues that developing faculty competencies for online teaching incorporates behavioral, intellectual, and attitudinal components, and that professional development "could benefit from an appreciative approach that is strength-based rather than deficiency-based, incorporated into the daily teachers' practices, and responsive to their self-identified needs and interests". Because faculty characteristics vary by profile, needs for professional support vary as well, so training pathways should be tailored to faculty's approaches and needs and support them at their own level of readiness.

article_title: Design, development, and evaluation of a virtual reality game-based application to support computational thinking
citation: Friday Joseph Agbo, Solomon Sunday Oyelere, Jarkko Suhonen, Markku Tukiainen. (2023). Design, development, and evaluation of a virtual reality game-based application to support computational thinking. Education Tech Research Dev 71:505–537. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10161-5
title: iThinkSmart VR game-based application with three CT mini games
description: iThinkSmart is an educational VR game-based application built in Unity (free software, deployable on students' existing smart devices with a low-cost HMD of about 5 US Dollars) to support CT knowledge in Nigerian higher education. As printed, "The mini games contained in iThinkSmart application include (i) River Crossing, (ii) Mount Patti Treasure Hunt (MoPaTH), and (iii) Tower of Hanoi." Each mini game targets CT knowledge units through visualization, and the application computes learners' CT competency in real time using the objective distance model. Table 1 maps each game to algorithmic thinking, recursive thinking, problem decomposition, problem abstraction, and pattern recognition.
requirements: Runs on students' smartphones with a low-cost Google Cardboard-style HMD and an internet connection for real-time learning-log recording
constraints: Some participants reported the application did not run smoothly on all phones; movement was limited to walking mode with no running mode
target_learners: computer science students in higher education institutions in Nigeria
target_learning_goals: computational thinking concepts: algorithmic thinking, recursive thinking, problem decomposition, problem abstraction, pattern recognition
examples: The experimental group solved CT puzzles via River crossing and MoPaTH mini games in VR; the control group solved identical quizzes on Kahoot! blended with a PowerPoint lecture
key_sources: Friday Joseph Agbo, Solomon Sunday Oyelere, Jarkko Suhonen, Markku Tukiainen. (2023). Design, development, and evaluation of a virtual reality game-based application to support computational thinking. Education Tech Research Dev 71:505–537. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10161-5

article_title: Design, development, and evaluation of a virtual reality game-based application to support computational thinking
citation: Friday Joseph Agbo, Solomon Sunday Oyelere, Jarkko Suhonen, Markku Tukiainen. (2023). Design, development, and evaluation of a virtual reality game-based application to support computational thinking. Education Tech Research Dev 71:505–537. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10161-5
title: Objective distance (OD) model for computing learners' CT competency during gameplay
description: The study adapts Chaichumpa and Temdee's (2018) objective distance model to compute learners' CT competency in real time during iThinkSmart gameplay. As the article states, "OD measures the distance between the expected/satisfactory learner's score ( S i) and the current learner's score ( C i ), mainly used to provide personalized support and intelligent feedback to a learner." The formula uses the satisfactory score, current score, and total score for each instance of a learning object. In this study, the total weighted score and satisfactory score were defined in the system while the player's current score was obtained during gameplay, and control-group Kahoot! data were manually computed with the same formula.
requirements: A defined satisfactory score and total weighted score per learning-object instance, plus the player's current score captured during gameplay
constraints: The model was proposed for evaluating students' competency while learning in a smart learning environment to enhance digital literacy, as attributed to Chaichumpa and Temdee (2018) and Temdee (2021)
target_learners: computer science students in higher education
target_learning_goals: measuring computational thinking competency during game-based learning
examples: Experimental-group test scores were assessed and computed using the OD model during gameplay; control-group CSV data from Kahoot! were manually computed with the OD formula

title: Participatory online co-design cycle embedded in design science research
description: The study embeds participatory design into the design science research methodology as the driver of the design, development, and demonstration phases. The article prints that "the online co-design process cycle involves planning, exploring, designing, discussing, and evaluating stages", which are iterative and strengthen research rigor within DSR. Online co-design was adopted because face-to-face meetings were not feasible during the Covid-19 pandemic, and it engages users and researchers to conceptualize, create, and prototype an artefact through an online environment.
requirements: Engagement of users and researchers in iterative online stages of planning, exploring, designing, discussing, and evaluating
constraints: Adopted to suit situations where face-to-face meetings between participants and researchers are not feasible
target_learners: higher education students co-designing educational games
target_learning_goals: computational thinking knowledge through co-designed mini games
examples: Mount Patti Treasure Hunt was conceptualized through a co-design process with students, building on a prior online co-design of mini games (Agbo et al., 2021a)

title: Visualize abstract CT concepts through game-based approaches rather than theoretical instruction alone
description: The article argues that teaching CT concepts abstractly may not build comprehension, so a visualized approach helps students. As printed, "When students learn CT concepts through a theoretical approach, they can gain abstract knowledge that may not enhance their comprehension, hence a visualized approach to teaching CT concepts could be helpful to students." The study operationalizes this by co-designing mini games with students and refining them into a VR application that visualizes CT concepts such as recursion via the Tower of Hanoi. It leverages experiential learning theory (Kolb, 2014) in doing so.
requirements: Mini games targeted at specific CT knowledge units, using visualization of introductory programming concepts
constraints: The study addresses abstract CT concepts (e.g., recursion) that students find difficult to comprehend through mathematical functions alone
target_learners: novice computer science students in higher education without prior programming experience
target_learning_goals: computational thinking concepts and problem-solving skills supporting programming education
examples: The Tower of Hanoi mini game was integrated to facilitate CT skills through visualization of recursion while experiencing gameplay in VR

article_title: Developing a digital tutor as an intermediary between students, teaching assistants, and lecturers
citation: Sebastian Hobert, Florian Berens. (2023). Developing a digital tutor as an intermediary between students, teaching assistants, and lecturers. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10293-2
title: Digital tutors as intermediaries between students, teaching assistants, and lecturers
description: The article proposes the concept of a chatbot-based digital tutor that acts as an intermediary among the three actors of large-scale lecture settings. It addresses three identified communication flaws through three mediated communications: students interact with the tutor in "simulated one-to-one tutoring settings based on the computers are social actors paradigm", teaching assistants get feedback about student progress, and lecturers get access to feedback about students' learning progress and state of knowledge. The concept targets long-term support across a whole lecture period rather than short-term chatbot use.
requirements: The tutor must provide a natural language and social interaction interface (R1) and be available all the time on common student devices (DP2)
constraints: Designed for large-scale formal educational settings where one-to-one instruction cannot be achieved due to resource constraints such as the lack of lecturers and teaching assistants
target_learners: students in large-scale university lecture courses
target_learning_goals: individualized learning support and feedback during a full lecture period, including practicing content and formative assessment
examples: The concept was implemented as a progressive web app and evaluated in an introductory statistics lecture at a large German university over a four-month field study
key_sources: Sebastian Hobert, Florian Berens. (2023). Developing a digital tutor as an intermediary between students, teaching assistants, and lecturers. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10293-2

citation: Sebastian Hobert, Florian Berens. (2023). Developing a digital tutor as an intermediary between students, teaching assistants, and lecturers. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10293-2
title: Seven design principles for chatbot-based digital tutors in long-term formal learning settings
description: From ten requirements derived from an expert workshop, the ICAP framework, and the CASA paradigm, the authors deduced seven design principles in three categories: DP1, a natural language-based conversational user interface; DP2, availability all the time on common devices; DP3, a Q&A component based on a (learning) object database; DP4, provision of a formative assessment component; DP5, provision of learning content; DP6, a learning analytics component; and DP7, functionalities for collecting input and feedback. The principles were implemented and evaluated in the field.
requirements: A natural language processing component to enable communication, access to databases or a knowledge base containing learning objects and organizational information, and storage of messages and learning actions for analytics
constraints: DP6 is not visible to students and therefore could not be evaluated by them in the survey
target_learning_goals: answering knowledge and organizational questions, formative assessment with automatic feedback, provision of learning content, and collection of student feedback
examples: The digital tutor app implemented all seven principles, including an audience response system for DP7 and a discourse storage and learning action log feeding the learning analytics component for DP6

title: Chatbot-based digital tutor app (progressive web app) for large-scale lectures
description: The developed artifact is a fully-functional progressive web app with a chat-based student interface, content overlays, and a sidebar, built with the Bootstrap framework and AJAX calls to RESTful web services, with a separate AdminLTE-based interface for teaching assistants and lecturers. Message processing uses the NLP.js library, with the natural language processing classifier "trained with approximately 3000 dialog entries". It integrates a learning object data storage, a micro content database, formative quiz question storage, an audience response system, and a learning action log.

constraints: The tutor can deliver materials such as lecture slides or recordings only as files (e.g., PDFs or videos) rather than conversing about their content
target_learners: students in an introductory statistics lecture
target_learning_goals: question answering, formative practice with instant feedback, learning content provision, and feedback collection across a lecture period
examples: In the field study the app collected over 9100 audience response responses in in-class sessions and approximately 1100 during self-study times

article_title: Inter-brain coupling analysis reveals learning-related attention of primary school students
citation: Jingjing Chen, Bing Xu & Dan Zhang. (2022). Inter-brain coupling analysis reveals learning-related attention of primary school students. bioRxiv. https://doi.org/10.1101/2022.06.08.495411
title: Inter-brain attention coupling framework: class-average attention dynamics represent learning-related attention
description: The framework holds that learning-related attention follows the structure of course contents, so attention dynamics shared across students reflect course-content-driven processing. It defines "the degree to which an individual student’s attention dynamics match the attention dynamics averaged across classmates" as inter-brain attention coupling, computed with Pearson correlation over 30-s epochs. Comparing a student to the class average is expected to "filter out idiosyncratic dynamics responsive to distractors", capturing attention intended by the course contents even when a student's raw attention level is high but off-task.
requirements: Students must be engaged in the same learning task or course content so a meaningful class-average attention dynamic exists; the article builds on the inter-subject correlation framework applied to students situated in the same learning task.
constraints: Validated only in a grade-3 classroom with a single-channel EEG device and one neuroscience lecture topic; the authors note further validation with larger samples, other educational stages, and more kinds of courses is needed.
target_learners: primary school students (grade 3, ages 8-9 in the study)
target_learning_goals: monitoring learning-related attention and the learning process during classroom instruction
examples: Students wore EEG headbands through five ~20-minute sessions alternating a 2-minute meditation task with teacher lectures on introduction to neuroscience; coupling was computed per 30-s epoch against the class-average (all other students).
key_sources: Jingjing Chen, Bing Xu & Dan Zhang. (2022). Inter-brain coupling analysis reveals learning-related attention of primary school students. bioRxiv. https://doi.org/10.1101/2022.06.08.495411

article_title: Inter-brain coupling analysis reveals learning-related attention of primary school students
citation: Jingjing Chen, Bing Xu & Dan Zhang. (2022). Inter-brain coupling analysis reveals learning-related attention of primary school students. bioRxiv. https://doi.org/10.1101/2022.06.08.495411
title: Wearable single-channel EEG headband (NeuroSky-based) for continuous classroom attention monitoring
description: A single-channel headband (Cusoft, China) with dry electrodes and a NeuroSky EEG biosensor recording at Fpz at 512 Hz, with a reference on the left ear lobe. The biosensor "can calculate every second’s attention level  based on their patented algorithm from EEG signals", with values from 1 to 100 indicating "very distracted" to "very focused". The article uses it because it monitors attention continuously and non-intrusively, and notes its high portability and low cost make findings readily applicable in educational practice.
requirements: Students wear the headband during sessions with experimenter help; the detected attention level was previously validated and was quality-tested here with a meditation control task.
constraints: Single-channel recording; the authors link the null EEG-power coupling results partly to "the limited single-channel EEG recordings".
target_learners: primary school students in regular classrooms
target_learning_goals: continuous, non-intrusive monitoring of attention levels during learning
examples: Twenty-eight grade-3 students wore the headbands during five regular classroom sessions of about 20 minutes, each combining a meditation task with a teacher lecture on introduction to neuroscience.

article_title: Teachers enacting a technology-rich curriculum for emergent literacy
citation: Amina Cviko, Susan McKenney, Joke Voogt. (2012). Teachers enacting a technology-rich curriculum for emergent literacy. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-011-9208-3
title: PictoPal: a technology-rich emergent literacy curriculum linking on-computer writing with off-computer authentic use
description: PictoPal is "a technology-rich curriculum for emergent literacy with learning activities both on the computer and off the computer", designed to teach children about the communicative functions of written language. Children compose texts on the computer and use their printed products in meaningful classroom contexts, such as broadcasting a weather forecast to classmates. A module centered on the theme of springtime consisted of eight activities exposing children to different text types.
requirements: Teachers make the connection between computer activities and classroom activities by introducing, organizing and arranging classroom applications; a teacher manual supports the teacher with suggestions for the classroom activities.
constraints: The curriculum focuses on a selection of national attainment goals: functional reading and writing, function of written language, relationship between spoken and written language, and language consciousness.
target_learners: kindergarten pupils ages 4-6 (junior and senior classes)
target_learning_goals: emergent literacy, specifically the communicative functions of written language
examples: During the eight-week implementation teachers ran three inter-linked activities a week: an introductory activity, an on-computer activity, and an off-computer activity.
key_sources: Amina Cviko, Susan McKenney, Joke Voogt. (2012). Teachers enacting a technology-rich curriculum for emergent literacy. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-011-9208-3

The article describes it as "a visual word processor with voice output": the lower portion consists of a grid with cells containing words and images, and the upper portion is a writing window. Clicking on cells lets children put words and images in the writing window and hear the words spoken aloud, and children can print their resulting written products for authentic classroom use.
requirements: Children click on cells to place words and images in the writing window and hear words spoken aloud; printed products are used in off-computer classroom activities.

examples: In one on-computer activity children co-created the script for a weather forecast, which they then broadcast to classmates in the off-computer activity.
