article_title: Approaches to illuminate content-specific gameplay decisions using open-ended game data
citation: Rosenheck, Louisa; Cheng, Meng-Tzu; Lin, Chen-Yen; Klopfer, Eric. (2021). Approaches to illuminate content-specific gameplay decisions using open-ended game data. Springer US. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09989-0
title: Game Learning Analytics guiding questions for illuminating content-specific gameplay decisions
description: The article proposes that its three approaches — looking at "actions and tool use, play patterns and player types, and tool input patterns" — could ground "a set of more generalized guiding questions in the GLA field that could be adopted by learning games designers and data scientists". The framework organizes analytics around identifying content-specific gameplay decisions, i.e. methods of completing game tasks related to a domain, so that designers and data scientists can convey information about how students think within a game's subject matter.

A game context open-ended enough for students to make choices that demonstrate their thinking
constraints: Developed and illustrated in the context of one selected game quest in a genetics domain
target_learning_goals: Mendelian genetics inquiry and problem solving within a learning game
examples: The study analyzed student exploration of high school level Mendelian genetics in The Radix Endeavor using the three approaches

article_title: An investigation of blended learning to support reading instruction in elementary schools
citation: Paul Macaruso, Shani Wilkes, Jen Elise Prescott. (2020). An investigation of blended learning to support reading instruction in elementary schools. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09785-2
title: Lexia Core5 Reading: a fully-blended learning program for elementary reading instruction
description: Core5 is described as "a fully-blended learning program which synchronizes the use of digital technology and offline materials employed by teachers in delivering their lessons." Its digital component targets six strands of reading—phonological awareness, phonics, structural analysis, automaticity/fluency, vocabulary, and comprehension—organized into 18 levels aligned to the Common Core State Standards. Students are placed by an embedded assessment, must complete units at 90%–100% accuracy, and struggling students receive adaptive branching to scaffolded tasks and then explicit direct instruction. Offline materials include Lexia Lessons for teacher-led small-group work and Lexia Skill Builders for independent practice.
requirements: Teachers track students' daily progress in the online component via the implementation dashboard and use these data to drive instructional plans such as administering Lexia Lessons
constraints: Students must complete each unit with 90%–100% accuracy before moving to subsequent units
target_learners: elementary school students in kindergarten through fifth grade, including at-risk and low-SES readers
target_learning_goals: reading skills across phonological awareness, phonics, structural analysis, automaticity/fluency, vocabulary, and comprehension
examples: In this study Core5 was incorporated into the ELA curriculum of three treatment charter schools alongside Wonders, with teachers offered Lexia's Implementation Support Service Package training modules
key_sources: Paul Macaruso, Shani Wilkes, Jen Elise Prescott. (2020). An investigation of blended learning to support reading instruction in elementary schools. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09785-2

In this study, teachers were encouraged to track daily online progress via an implementation dashboard and deliver Lexia Lessons to small groups accordingly.

article_title: Young children’s embodied interactions with a social robot
citation: Yanghee Kim · Michael Tscholl. (2021). Young children's embodied interactions with a social robot. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09978-3
title: Minimalistic design: tap into children's natural way of embodied interaction rather than assigning tasks or giving direct instructions
description: The authors propose a form of minimalistic design for young children that aligns with a child's world and habitual way of embodied interaction. In their triadic activity, the robot introduced itself as a newbie from another planet who needed help, and its simple remarks such as "I like that" and "I'm confused" functioned as powerful feedback prompting children to discuss and redo the activity. The design demonstrated that intense embodied engagement was elicited without direct instructions or task assignment.
requirements: The robot's embodied social behavior must trigger task-related behavior and relevant feedback, as in the newbie persona and simple evaluative remarks
constraints: The authors frame this from observations of children aged three to six interacting freely over time; current natural language processing is not sufficiently mature to manage natural conversations, so a Wizard of Oz method controlled the robot's utterances
target_learners: young children in early childhood and kindergarten settings
target_learning_goals: early literacy and arithmetic skills
collaborative communication skills
early science concepts
examples: The robot being new to earth signaled to children that they had to help it; its remark "I'm confused" when children conflicted prompted them to re-do the activity and agree on one answer
key_sources: Yanghee Kim · Michael Tscholl. (2021). Young children's embodied interactions with a social robot. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09978-3

article_title: Young children’s embodied interactions with a social robot
citation: Yanghee Kim · Michael Tscholl. (2021). Young children's embodied interactions with a social robot. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09978-3
title: Embodied cognition as a framework for designing robot-mediated learning for young children
description: Embodied cognition posits that cognition is grounded in bodily interactions with social, cultural, and physical environments rather than confined to amodal symbolic structures. The article applies this lens to child-robot interaction, analyzing how children access, assemble, and use bodily, social, and physical resources during problem-solving, guided by Wilson and Golonka's questions. The authors conclude the perspective proved useful for identifying a robot's affordances and describing how embodiments come about in physical and social contexts.
requirements: Environments must be designed so the complex interrelations between cognition, the body, and the environment can be observed in situ
Effective designs must allow learners to enact their full behavioral repertoire rather than limiting them to a certain range of actions and gestures
constraints: The authors note the various ways the body is implicated in cognition and learning have not yet been sufficiently explored, and current social robotics research typically studies only one or two robotic features and narrowly defined discrete skill acquisition
target_learners: young children aged three to six
target_learning_goals: foundational academic skills and concepts
holistic intellectual, social, emotional, and physical development
examples: Study One elicited bodily movement and haptic interaction intentionally through the robot's sensors and movements; Study Two observed spontaneous embodiment while children helped the robot solve problems
key_sources: Yanghee Kim · Michael Tscholl. (2021). Young children's embodied interactions with a social robot. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09978-3

article_title: Analyzing properties of success for assessment development in maker-based learning
citation: Kailea Saplan · Sam Abramovich · Peter Wardrip. (2024). Analyzing properties of success for assessment development in maker-based learning. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10286-1
title: The five Properties of Success framework for unpacking definitions of success in maker-based learning
description: The Properties of Success framework decomposes any definition of success in maker-based learning into five underlying properties: Subject of Success, Guiding Metaphor of Success, Timescale for Success, Data for Success, and Audience for Success. It emerged when the authors realized their five interview themes were "not an exhaustive list of overarching categories of success, but rather underlying features within a definition of success." Each property carries design assertions, such as that many different stakeholders can be the subject of success, not just the participating patron.
requirements: Educators articulate a definition of success for their program before selecting or designing an assessment
constraints: Derived from a small qualitative sample of 17 staff and educators in two public library systems; the tools built on it have not undergone extensive testing
target_learners: library staff and maker educators in public library makerspaces
target_learning_goals: assessment design and evaluation of maker-based learning programs
examples: The framework's properties structure the petal diagram at the center of the Properties of Success Analysis Tool
key_sources: Kailea Saplan · Sam Abramovich · Peter Wardrip. (2024). Analyzing properties of success for assessment development in maker-based learning. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10286-1

article_title: Analyzing properties of success for assessment development in maker-based learning
citation: Kailea Saplan · Sam Abramovich · Peter Wardrip. (2024). Analyzing properties of success for assessment development in maker-based learning. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10286-1
title: Properties of Success Analysis (PSA) Tools: a three-part toolkit linking definitions of success to assessment features
description: The PSA Tools consist of three tools: the Properties of Success Analysis Tool (a graphic organizer with a petal diagram for articulating a definition of success across the five properties), the Success and Assessment Table (which defines each property, gives examples, and links properties to assessment development decisions), and the Reflection Prompts (for describing the most appropriate assessment type and reflecting on affordances and constraints). They invite educators to "reflect on and unpack their definitions of success in order to identify what features a relevant assessment tool should have."
requirements: Used together, ideally before assessment development, so educators can articulate their understanding of success and establish a common language for discussing success and assessment
constraints: The tools have not undergone extensive testing, which the authors name as the next step; they were designed with public library makerspaces in mind
target_learners: library staff and maker educators in public library makerspaces
educators in other informal learning environments such as youth arts organizations
target_learning_goals: selecting or designing assessments aligned with definitions of success in maker-based learning
examples: Educators fill out the petal diagram, use the Success and Assessment Table to link properties to assessment decisions, then complete the Reflection Prompts; the tools can also be used in reverse to break down current assessment practices
key_sources: Kailea Saplan · Sam Abramovich · Peter Wardrip. (2024). Analyzing properties of success for assessment development in maker-based learning. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10286-1

article_title: Teachers’ role in digitalizing education: an umbrella review
citation: Olivia Wohlfart, Ingo Wagner. (2022). Teachers' role in digitalizing education: an umbrella review. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11023-022-10166-0
title: TPACK framework as the dominant theoretical lens in reviews of teachers' digitalization role
description: The Technological-Pedagogical-Content-Knowledge (TPACK) model, introduced by Mishra and Koehler, acknowledges the complexity of teaching by "differentiating seven knowledge domains in the interplay of technological, pedagogical, and content knowledge." In this umbrella review it was the most applied framework: eight of the 23 reviews based their work specifically on TPACK, and 10 of the 14 reviews focused on digital literacy applied it. The reviews examined TPACK's publication development, knowledge-domain delineation, measurement, context, and model development.
requirements: Clear definitions and operationalization of the individual knowledge domains, which the reviewed reviews find rare, for further developing the model and survey instruments
constraints: Four of the TPACK-focused reviews acknowledge that clear definition and delineation of individual knowledge domains is rare and nearly impossible
Context is treated mostly marginally, as a limitation or area for further research
target_learning_goals: teachers' digital literacy
technology integration knowledge
examples: Eight reviews specifically focus on the TPACK framework, examining publication development, distinction of knowledge domains, measurement, context, and model development (Table 2).
key_sources: Olivia Wohlfart, Ingo Wagner. (2022). Teachers' role in digitalizing education: an umbrella review. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10166-0

article_title: The critical, relational practice of instructional design in higher education: an emerging model of change agency
citation: The Critical, Relational Practice of Instructional Design in Higher Education: An Emerging Model of Change Agency. (2007).
title: Agentic model of instructional design: four types of agency with intentional and operational dimensions
description: The article proposes a "complex and reflexive" agentic model of instructional design in which designers act as moral, political agents of change. Narrative data from twenty designers at six Canadian universities revealed four types of agency that "appeared to fit into four categories: interpersonal, professional, institutional and societal." The model carries intentional dimensions (values, principles) and operational dimensions (concrete actions), and designers move in and out of a zone of moral coherence across projects.
requirements: Agency types must be understood as grounded in designers' narratives of practice rather than frequency counts
constraints: The categories were not mutually exclusive, nor equally represented in the data
The model is explicitly tentative and emerging
target_learning_goals: professional identity development
change agency in instructional design practice
examples: The model was developed from post hoc thematic analysis of research conversations, focus groups and story circles using Atlas Ti
key_sources: The Critical, Relational Practice of Instructional Design in Higher Education: An Emerging Model of Change Agency. (2007). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-007-9061-6

article_title: The critical, relational practice of instructional design in higher education: an emerging model of change agency
citation: The Critical, Relational Practice of Instructional Design in Higher Education: An Emerging Model of Change Agency. (2007).
title: Zone of moral coherence as the alignment condition for agentic instructional design practice
description: The article contends instructional design should be understood as a moral practice and proposes a zone of moral coherence: when the values of designers, clients, institutions and the profession align, agency operates coherently and with greater impact. "In cases where there is agreement among agencies concerning the values, ethical and functional dimensions of agency, we suggest that the overall agency is operating in a zone of moral coherence." Where agencies conflict, the effect of agency is tempered and potentially negated, producing dissonance that may lead designers to question staying in the profession.
requirements: Alignment among the values of designers, clients, organizations and learners
constraints: Designers are at times required to practice outside the zone, causing moral incoherence and dissonance
target_learning_goals: ethical professional practice
navigating value conflicts in design work
examples: A designer left a position after repeated contradictory supervisor instructions in a rigid, cookie-cutter environment, illustrating moral incoherence
key_sources: The Critical, Relational Practice of Instructional Design in Higher Education: An Emerging Model of Change Agency. (2007). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-007-9061-6

article_title: Addressing students’ emotional needs during the COVID-19 pandemic: a perspective on text versus video feedback in online environments
citation: Regina Kaplan-Rakowski. (2021). Addressing students' emotional needs during the COVID-19 pandemic: a perspective on text versus video feedback in online environments. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09897-9
title: During times of crisis, educators should prioritize emotional support and wellness over instructional efficiency, shifting to a more affective approach such as video for communication and feedback
description: The article argues that although teaching and learning efficiency should always be a concern, the pandemic increased the importance of emotional learning, mental health, and wellness, so instructors should reevaluate priorities. Its key message is that "educators should shift to a more affective approach during times of crisis, and one way to do this is by implementing video for communication and feedback". This may come at the expense of instructional efficiency.
requirements: Instructors must recognize crisis conditions such as social isolation and mental stress that accompany a pandemic
constraints: The article states video feedback is not a panacea for any learning scenario and feedback type should be selected with respect to situational principles
target_learning_goals: emotional support and mental wellness
social presence in online learning
examples: The article recommends implementing synchronous and asynchronous video for communication and feedback, noting asynchronous video allows flexibility in timing and longer reflection on assignments
key_sources: Regina Kaplan-Rakowski. (2021). Addressing students' emotional needs during the COVID-19 pandemic: a perspective on text versus video feedback in online environments. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09897-9

article_title: Addressing students’ emotional needs during the COVID-19 pandemic: a perspective on text versus video feedback in online environments
citation: Regina Kaplan-Rakowski. (2021). Addressing students' emotional needs during the COVID-19 pandemic: a perspective on text versus video feedback in online environments. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09897-9
title: Feedback modality should be selected with respect to situational principles rather than treated as universally superior
description: The article cautions against treating video feedback as universally appropriate: "video feedback is not panacea for any learning scenario. Instead, the type of feedback should be selected with respect to situational principles". It illustrates that video feedback may suit an assignment in a computer graphics course but may not be pertinent for feedback on a multiple-choice quiz.
requirements: Instructors must judge the fit between feedback modality and the specific assignment or learning scenario
constraints: Video feedback may not be pertinent for feedback on a multiple-choice quiz
target_learning_goals: effective instructor feedback
examples: The article contrasts video feedback for a computer graphics course assignment with feedback on a multiple-choice quiz

article_title: Uniting epistemological perspectives to support contextualized knowledge development
citation: Sara van der Linden, Susan McKenney. (2020). Uniting epistemological perspectives to support contextualized knowledge development. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09772-7
title: United reflection model combining deliberate and aware epistemological perspectives
description: The article proposes a united reflection model in which six reflective processes are derived by crossing three types of reflection (on, for, in action) with two epistemological perspectives. The deliberate perspective involves "Knowledge-based processing by focusing on evidence-based norms" while the aware perspective involves "Context-based processing by focusing on salient moments". Uniting them is claimed to yield better sense-making, better instructional planning, and more responsive teaching, with each reflection type producing a complete picture to guide understanding, planning, or in-the-moment adjustment.
requirements: Teachers engage in reflection activities spanning both deliberate analysis against standards and explication of practical awareness
Reflection is structured across retrospective, anticipatory, and in-action temporal foci
constraints: The model is a theoretical proposal; the article presents no empirical test of it
target_learning_goals: Contextualized knowledge of how to teach
Reflective practice
Instructional planning
examples: The article maps RoA, RfA, and RiA onto Bloom's revised taxonomy complexity levels and summarizes the six processes in Fig. 2
key_sources: Sara van der Linden, Susan McKenney. (2020). Uniting epistemological perspectives to support contextualized knowledge development. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09772-7

article_title: Uniting epistemological perspectives to support contextualized knowledge development
citation: Sara van der Linden, Susan McKenney. (2020). Uniting epistemological perspectives to support contextualized knowledge development. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09772-7
title: Zones of Proximal Performance and Implementation as reflection outcomes
description: The article defines two constructs building on Vygotsky's zone of proximal development and McKenney's zone of proximal implementation. The Zone of Proximal Performance targets "the difference between the pre-determined, explicated teaching behaviors individual teachers can execute on their own, and those they could identify and perform with guidance". The Zone of Proximal Implementation targets the analogous difference for learner, classroom, and school-related insights. Deliberate reflection informs the ZPP; aware reflection informs the ZPI; comparing both guides action.
requirements: Reflection activities that surface both performance relative to standards and situated contextual insights
constraints: The zones are conceptual constructs derived from prior theory, not measured in this article
target_learning_goals: Understanding gaps between current and potential teaching performance and implementation
examples: Conclusion drawing in the reflection procedure is framed as determining considerations within the ZPP (deliberate) or ZPI (aware)
key_sources: Sara van der Linden, Susan McKenney. (2020). Uniting epistemological perspectives to support contextualized knowledge development. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09772-7

article_title: Uniting epistemological perspectives to support contextualized knowledge development
citation: Sara van der Linden, Susan McKenney. (2020). Uniting epistemological perspectives to support contextualized knowledge development. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09772-7
title: Video coaching blueprint for early career teachers organized around activities, materials, and participation
description: The blueprint operationalizes united reflection in video coaching, defined as a professional development approach in which "teachers and coaches record instances of teaching and engage in video-based discussions in a sustained manner". It is organized around a skeleton design with three components: activities and tasks (six reflective processes), materials and resources (priming tools, examples of practice, artifacts of practice), and participation and practices (coach and learner roles). Tasks within task classes are executed sequentially, after which conclusions are compared.
requirements: Recording of teaching instances and sustained video-based discussions
Coach roles of coordinator, facilitator, and curator
Materials including priming tools, examples of practice, and artifacts of practice
constraints: The blueprint is a design proposal requiring further operationalization; the article states further operationalization is needed to apply the ideas in practice
target_learning_goals: Reflection on, for, and in action
Developing effective teaching practices in context
Professional identity development
examples: During RoA a coach and teacher select a relevant framework and go through preparation, image forming, and conclusion drawing to analyze videotaped practice
key_sources: Sara van der Linden, Susan McKenney. (2020). Uniting epistemological perspectives to support contextualized knowledge development. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09772-7

article_title: Uniting epistemological perspectives to support contextualized knowledge development
citation: Sara van der Linden, Susan McKenney. (2020). Uniting epistemological perspectives to support contextualized knowledge development. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09772-7
title: 4C/ID as the underlying instructional design model for video coaching
description: The article positions the Four Components Instructional Design model as well-suited to the complex learning of united reflection during video coaching. It states this holistic approach "has been shown to stimulate the integration of knowledge, skills and attitudes", mitigating compartmentalization of learning tasks or fragmentation of constituent skills. The four components applied are whole learning tasks (RoA, RfA, RiA as task classes of increasing complexity), procedural information (the three reflection steps), supportive information, and part-task practice.
requirements: Authentic learning tasks that increase in complexity and are meaningful to learners
Procedural information to automate recurrent aspects of reflection
Supportive information bridging what learners know and need to know
target_learners: Early career teachers in video coaching programs
target_learning_goals: Complex learning integrating reflection perspectives and applying insights to practice
examples: RoA is classified as least complex, RfA medium complex, and RiA most complex because it combines all cognitive processes in the moment
key_sources: Sara van der Linden, Susan McKenney. (2020). Uniting epistemological perspectives to support contextualized knowledge development. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09772-7

article_title: Uniting epistemological perspectives to support contextualized knowledge development
citation: Sara van der Linden, Susan McKenney. (2020). Uniting epistemological perspectives to support contextualized knowledge development. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09772-7
title: Three-step reflection procedure: preparation, image forming, conclusion drawing
description: As the procedural (recurrent) aspect of united reflection, the article adopts a generic three-step procedure from Reymen et al. in the context of engineering design: preparation, image forming, and conclusion drawing. Preparation requires practitioners "to detail the reflective question and to collect facts related to it"; image forming investigates the identified phenomena using the framing to interpret or anticipate the teaching situation; conclusion drawing contrasts findings and considers implications for practice, determining the ZPP or ZPI.
requirements: A detailed reflective question and collected facts in the preparation step
Framing that guides interpretation, whether framework-driven or context-driven
constraints: The procedure was originally described in the context of engineering design and is here adapted to teaching
target_learning_goals: Structured reflection on teaching practice
examples: Table 1 cross-tabulates the three steps with deliberate and aware perspective variants, plus comparing perspectives
key_sources: Sara van der Linden, Susan McKenney. (2020). Uniting epistemological perspectives to support contextualized knowledge development. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09772-7

article_title: Uniting epistemological perspectives to support contextualized knowledge development
citation: Sara van der Linden, Susan McKenney. (2020). Uniting epistemological perspectives to support contextualized knowledge development. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09772-7
title: Coach roles of coordinator, facilitator, and curator in video coaching for ECTs
description: The article distinguishes three roles for coaches supporting early career teachers, plus the learner role. "The coordinator is responsible for organizing learning opportunities and determines the appropriate task complexity." The facilitator stimulates learning, scaffolds support, prompts thinking, and provides cognitive feedback. The curator "is responsible for selecting relevant and high-quality learning materials and determines the authenticity of the task". Learners manage their own learning behavior and may act as co-facilitators.
requirements: Individual approaches to coaching to meet teachers' personal development needs
Coordination among the three roles so tasks, support, and materials align
target_learning_goals: Professional development through scaffolded video-based reflection
examples: The facilitator may detail their own framing, interpretation and conclusion drawing, or invite peers to share reflections for comparison
key_sources: Sara van der Linden, Susan McKenney. (2020). Uniting epistemological perspectives to support contextualized knowledge development. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09772-7

article_title: The effect of cumulative eye movements’ guidance of experts on transition from novice to expert
citation: Neslihan Yondemir Çalişkan, Emine Şendurur. (2025). The effect of cumulative eye movements' guidance of experts on transition from novice to expert. Education Tech Research Dev, 73:59–89. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10414-5
title: Cumulative multi-expert EMME instructional videos for Photoshop
description: Eight weekly instructional videos built from the cumulative eye movements of seven professional graphic-designer experts, plus screen, voice, and mouse recordings. Signals included "red rectangular shapes (sometimes with red arrows) around highly ranked AOI", red lines, red stars, yellow highlights, zoom-in, and text-based shortcut reminders. Unlike most prior EMME work using one expert, seven experts' fixations were cumulatively ranked on AOIs to decide when signals appeared.
requirements: Eye-tracking data from multiple experts recorded while demonstrating the target tasks, analyzed with OGAMA on defined AOIs
Video production aligned with multimedia design principles and cognitive load theory guidelines
constraints: Participants were not informed of the roots or aims of the provided signals
The intervention ran weekly over eight weeks, longer than typical one-shot EMME studies
target_learners: novice graphic design students (university associate-degree students)
target_learning_goals: procedural use of Adobe Photoshop tools and interface
examples: Week 1 introduced the workspace and experts' fixations were heavily located within the toolbox AOI, so a red rectangular frame frequently appeared around the toolbox as a signal
key_sources: Neslihan Yondemir Çalişkan, Emine Şendurur. (2025). The effect of cumulative eye movements' guidance of experts on transition from novice to expert. Education Tech Research Dev, 73:59–89. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10414-5

article_title: The effect of cumulative eye movements’ guidance of experts on transition from novice to expert
citation: Neslihan Yondemir Çalişkan, Emine Şendurur. (2025). The effect of cumulative eye movements' guidance of experts on transition from novice to expert. Education Tech Research Dev, 73:59–89. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10414-5
title: Backward fading of expert guidance signals as novices gain expertise
description: A video-series design in which signaling elements derived from experts' eye movements are gradually reduced to prevent the expertise reversal effect. "The guidance on the basic elements of the content faded gradually toward the end of the training": the first four episodes included all signals, text-based signaling was removed in episodes five and six, and in the last two episodes important signals remained but their duration of appearance was reduced.
requirements: A multi-episode sequence ordered so learners first gain familiarity with the interface
Expert eye movement, voice recording, and observation data used to decide which elements to keep or release
constraints: Fading began after the fourth video; the article reports the pattern for an eight-week procedural Photoshop sequence
target_learners: novices transitioning toward expertise in a complex software interface
target_learning_goals: procedural skill acquisition and growing independence from guidance
examples: Text-based signaling was removed in episodes five and six while visual representations and durations remained the same
key_sources: Neslihan Yondemir Çalişkan, Emine Şendurur. (2025). The effect of cumulative eye movements' guidance of experts on transition from novice to expert. Education Tech Research Dev, 73:59–89. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10414-5

article_title: The effect of cumulative eye movements’ guidance of experts on transition from novice to expert
citation: Neslihan Yondemir Çalişkan, Emine Şendurur. (2025). The effect of cumulative eye movements' guidance of experts on transition from novice to expert. Education Tech Research Dev, 73:59–89. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10414-5
title: Design EMME guidance videos using multimedia learning and cognitive load principles together with expert eye-movement data
description: The article produced its guided videos by combining expert eye-movement rankings with principles adapted from Mayer (2021) and Sweller et al. (2019): signaling, temporal and spatial contiguity, modality, redundancy, coherence, pre-training, and segmenting. For example, "The signaling elements were temporally and spatially closed to prevent the split attention effect", and the video automatically paused when a notification signal appeared to prevent the modality effect.
requirements: Expert eye-tracking data identifying which interface areas and actions matter for each task
Signal location, time, and duration decided from fixation counts on defined AOIs and verified by two researchers
constraints: The article states a risk that as knowledge and skills develop, certain elements might become redundant for learners, motivating fading
target_learners: novice learners of complex graphical software
target_learning_goals: managing extraneous cognitive load while learning procedural software skills
examples: The first week's video was the longest (21 min. 55 s.) and the last week's the shortest (2 min. 50 s.) following the segmenting principle

article_title: Temporary instructor presence in lecture slides does not enhance online learning
citation: Tim Kühl, Felicia Teske, Martin Merkt, Christina Sondermann. (2025). Temporary instructor presence in lecture slides does not enhance online learning. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10435-0
title: Interference and social-cue hypotheses as competing accounts of instructor presence in online lecture slides
description: The article frames instructor presence in online lecture slides with two competing lines of reasoning, both empirically supported. The interference hypothesis holds that the instructor acts as a seductive detail and induces split attention, raising extraneous cognitive load; the social-cue hypothesis, traced to Social Agency Theory, holds that the instructor "elicits a social response in learners that in turn triggers them to process the content more deeply", raising germane load. The study tested whether temporary presence could keep the benefit while avoiding the cost.
requirements: Both lines of reasoning are assumed to operate simultaneously, so their drawbacks and advantages may cancel each other out
constraints: The empirical evidence on instructor presence is described as equivocal, with the latest meta-analysis showing a small retention effect but no transfer effect
target_learning_goals: retention of lecture content
transfer of lecture content to new problems
examples: The two experiments operationalized temporary presence as showing the instructor only on introductory and transitional slides with hardly any content, about 10 of 16 slides lasting about three minutes
key_sources: Tim Kühl, Felicia Teske, Martin Merkt, Christina Sondermann. (2025). Temporary instructor presence in lecture slides does not enhance online learning. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10435-0

article_title: Beyond boundaries: leveraging technology for differentiated professional development with lesson study video club
citation: Yuzhu Xia, Adria Patthoff, Liana Balloffet, Marco A. Bravo, Kip Téllez. (2025). Beyond boundaries: leveraging technology for differentiated professional development with lesson study video club. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10524-8
title: LSVC hybrid professional development model
description: LSVC is a year-long hybrid teacher PD model that integrates Lesson Study and Video Club principles, using technology (live videoconferencing, teacher-recorded videos, facilitator-selected video content, online asynchronous collaboration tools) to connect teachers across geographies and experience levels. Activities include "whole group workshops, individual self-study, semi-structured conversations with partners, and small group reflective seminars." It was implemented with 71 dual language elementary teachers over three cohorts, and the fully remote format was retained after its benefits became evident.
requirements: Sustained, year-long delivery with cycles of collaborative reflection, full-group discussion, and instructional coaching
Widely available technology for synchronous and asynchronous collaboration
constraints: Delivery varied across the studied years to accommodate COVID-19 pandemic requirements
The model was mediated by shifting district distance-learning requirements during the study period
target_learners: in-service elementary dual language teachers across the career span, from first-year to 27 years of experience
target_learning_goals: integrating language, literacy, and mathematics instruction in dual language settings
bilingual instructional practices and mentoring capability
examples: Three year-long cohorts of 71 DLP teachers in 31 schools across 11 districts in California and Texas participated; 57 completed both pre- and post-surveys.
key_sources: Yuzhu Xia, Adria Patthoff, Liana Balloffet, Marco A. Bravo, Kip Téllez. (2025). Beyond boundaries: leveraging technology for differentiated professional development with lesson study video club. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10524-8

article_title: Beyond boundaries: leveraging technology for differentiated professional development with lesson study video club
citation: Yuzhu Xia, Adria Patthoff, Liana Balloffet, Marco A. Bravo, Kip Téllez. (2025). Beyond boundaries: leveraging technology for differentiated professional development with lesson study video club. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10524-8
title: Career-span differentiation framework for teacher PD (three experience categories)
description: The study reframes the expert/novice binary into an extended learning progression, grouping teachers by "less than five years, five to ten years, and over ten years" of experience and treating experience differences as assets rather than deficits. Grounded in situated perspectives of learning and communities of practice (Lave & Wenger), it holds that teacher learning unfolds in iterative cycles across the career continuum, so a single PD initiative should differentiate support by career stage. The framework motivated the study's second research question on whether perceived growth differs by career experience group.
requirements: PD structures that center the spectrum of teachers' years of experience and specialized contexts
constraints: The trajectory of teacher learning is recognized as non-linear (Feiman-Nemser)
target_learners: novice, mid-career, and veteran in-service teachers in specialized contexts such as dual language programs
target_learning_goals: differentiated professional growth across career stages
examples: The authors initially framed analysis around an expert/novice distinction and refined it into the three-category career-span grouping used in the survey analysis.

title: Teacher PD should center teachers' specialized contexts and experience spectrum rather than one-size-fits-all delivery
description: The article argues that school- or district-wide, one-size-fits-all PD delivery should be minimized in teachers' regular PD experiences because teaching is specialized by grade level, content area, experience, and programmatic structures. It states that "Teacher PD structures, as such, should center the spectrum of teachers' years of experience as well as other specialized and contextualized nature of teaching," requiring developers to cater to individual needs while enabling collaborative learning. This aligns with the study's finding that growth patterns differed by career stage.
requirements: Recognition of individual teachers' distinct challenges and differentiated support structures
constraints: Traditional PD with outside experts delivering skills and leaving is described as not substantively effective

title: A descriptive framework of university teachers' design work enabling co-design of authentic meaning-making experiences through culturally relevant pedagogy
description: The review treats the descriptive framework from Bennett et al. (2017) as a roadmap for expert instruction that is flexible across interdisciplinary higher education fields. It states that the framework "allows educators and students opportunities to co-design authentic meaning making experiences given cultural relevant pedagogy". The review reads this framework from a learning design perspective focused on culturally relevant educational ecosystems and interactive media during the COVID-19 era.

culturally relevant instruction

article_title: Responses to the televised kefauver hearings: Some social psychological implications
citation: Wiebe, G. D. (1952). Responses to the Televised Kefauver Hearings: Some Social Psychological Implications. Public Opinion Quarterly, 16, 179-200. https://www.jstor.org/stable/2745943
title: Alternative leadership as a mechanism converting social impotence into political participation
description: The article proposes that an alternative leadership channel can absorb citizen dissatisfaction that would otherwise remain a feeling of "social impotence" in dealing with a problem. The author states the Halley election "illustrates the function of an alternative leadership which converts the particular dissatisfaction characteristic of social impotence into a benefit of membership without depriving members of their prior benefits of membership." It is an interpretive account of how aroused feelings become political action.

An alternative leadership figure or channel must be available outside the two major party candidates
constraints: The account rests on a single observed election outcome interpreted by the author, not on a tested comparison

converting concern about social problems into action
examples: The election of Rudolf Halley, chief counsel to the Kefauver Committee, as president of the New York City City Council over both major party candidates

article_title: Pedagogical AI conversational agents in higher education: a conceptual framework and survey of the state of the art
citation: Habeeb Yusuf, Arthur Money, Damon Daylamani-Zad. (2025). Pedagogical AI conversational agents in higher education: a conceptual framework and survey of the state of the art. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10447-4
title: Conceptual framework of pedagogical AI conversational agents organised by pedagogical applications and technological functions
description: The article develops a conceptual framework from thematic analysis of 92 studies, organising pedagogical AI conversational agents into two overarching themes. As the article states, "pedagogical AI conversational agents can primarily be considered in terms of their pedagogical applications and their pedagogical purposes, which include pastoral, instructional and cognitive", further considered in terms of mode of study and intent, and technological functions in terms of embodiment, functional type and features. The two themes complement each other: increased technological functions enable wider pedagogical applications, and specified applications require specialised functions.
requirements: Serves as an interpretative visual representation of how themes from the literature analysis may be organised conceptually
constraints: Derived from literature published between 2014 and 2022 within a pre-defined set of search criteria in higher education settings
target_learning_goals: teaching and learning support across instructional, pastoral and cognitive purposes
examples: Figure 2 presents the resulting conceptual framework; Tables 4–7 map each category to the surveyed literature

article_title: A proposed methodology for investigating student-chatbot interaction patterns in giving peer feedback
citation: Michael Pin-Chuan Lin, Daniel H. Chang, Philip H. Winne. (2025). A proposed methodology for investigating student-chatbot interaction patterns in giving peer feedback. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10408-3
title: A methodology for investigating student-chatbot interaction patterns via coded pathway logs
description: The article proposes a methodology in which student-chatbot exchanges are logged, coded into a 2×2 matrix of guidance acceptance (reject/accept) by revision correctness (correct/incorrect), and mapped onto possible interaction paths whose counts reveal where chatbot instruction succeeds or fails. It extends Winne and Nesbit's critique of snapshot between-group designs by tracing each participant's conversational trajectory. The authors state they "propose a new methodology to identify where improvements can be made in conversation patterns in educational chatbots", enabling progressive redesign of chatbot scripts.
requirements: Chat histories must be automatically stored (e.g., in Rasa's backend server) and coders must resolve discrepancies to produce a final matrix per participant
constraints: The article states the small sample size constrains understanding of specific interaction pathways, and the method was piloted on one task (thesis statements, arguments and counterarguments)
target_learning_goals: giving effective peer feedback on draft essays
examples: Participants' self-judgements were coded 0/1 and combined with CCQ correctness and revision outcomes into paths A–L (Tables 2–5), then visualized across both chatbot sessions (Fig. 7)
key_sources: Michael Pin-Chuan Lin, Daniel H. Chang, Philip H. Winne. (2025). A proposed methodology for investigating student-chatbot interaction patterns in giving peer feedback. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10408-3

citation: Michael Pin-Chuan Lin, Daniel H. Chang, Philip H. Winne. (2025). A proposed methodology for investigating student-chatbot interaction patterns in giving peer feedback. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10408-3
title: Chatbot DD: a Rasa-based, CAM-grounded chatbot for coaching peer feedback on essay outlines
description: DD is a task-oriented chatbot built on the open-source Rasa framework (rasa_core 0.11.12, rasa_core_sdk 0.11.5, rasa_nlu 0.13.7) with a web chatroom interface in which students mainly interacted by clicking buttons. The authors state: "We developed the chatbot based on the four components of CAM: content, methods, sequence, and sociology (Collins et al., 1991)." DD teaches four feedback types (constructive suggestions, positive comments, negative comments, questions for improvement), checks understanding with comprehension-checking questions, praises correct answers, then guides revision of fabricated feedback on a sample outline.
requirements: A fallback action for unprocessable input, participatory refinement with the course instructor and teaching staff, and training data for the NLU (about 200 thesis statements)
constraints: The article states the small training set limited NLU accuracy and the chatbot still sometimes failed to identify intents; students mainly used buttons rather than natural language
target_learning_goals: understanding and giving the four types of effective peer feedback
examples: In a 50-minute tutorial, each participant was randomly assigned one of five fabricated outlines and its substandard feedback sheet, learned about feedback types with DD, then revised the sheet with DD's guidance

article_title: Leading the AI transformation in schools: it starts with a digital mindset
citation: Marcus Pietsch · Dana-Kristin Mah. (2025). Leading the AI transformation in schools: it starts with a digital mindset. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10439-w
title: Ambidextrous leadership: simultaneous opening and closing behaviors for leading innovation under paradox
description: Ambidextrous leadership holds that organizational transformation requires two leadership behaviors simultaneously: opening behavior that unleashes creativity and experimentation, and closing behavior that reduces variance and secures implementation. The article applies it to schools, mapping transformational leadership onto opening and digital instructional leadership onto closing behavior, and tests their interaction as a predictor of AI integration. As Rosing and Zacher describe it, "Opening leader behavior comprises, for example, to encourage followers to experiment with new ideas, to give room for independent thinking and acting, and to allow for learning from errors."
requirements: Leaders must demonstrate a high level of both opening and closing behaviors, operationalized methodically as an interaction of the two
constraints: The article notes a paucity of studies empirically investigating such integrative leadership approaches in schools
target_learning_goals: leading digital and AI transformation
fostering innovation in schools
examples: In the school context, a leader gives teachers freedom to experiment with digital tools (opening) while monitoring whether tool use improves instruction and achievement (closing).
key_sources: Marcus Pietsch · Dana-Kristin Mah. (2025). Leading the AI transformation in schools: it starts with a digital mindset. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10439-w

article_title: Leading the AI transformation in schools: it starts with a digital mindset
citation: Marcus Pietsch · Dana-Kristin Mah. (2025). Leading the AI transformation in schools: it starts with a digital mindset. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10439-w
title: Digital mindset of school leaders as a four-dimensional belief system: empathy, innovativeness, openness, agility
description: A digital mindset is a multidimensional combination of beliefs activated in the context of digitalization, divided into self-oriented and situation-oriented components. Drawing on Pabst von Ohain's expert-based study of prototypical digital transformation leaders, the article characterizes it in four dimensions: "empathic, innovative, open, and agile." The article measures one facet per dimension (perspective taking, technology orientation, openness to change, proactivity) and models these facets as antecedents of leadership practices and, indirectly, AI integration.
requirements: Measurement requires domain- and context-specific scales; the article adapted existing seven-point scales for each facet
constraints: Empirical research on what constitutes a digital mindset and how to measure it is scarce, as the article notes
target_learning_goals: leading digital transformation
implementing AI in schools
examples: The survey measured perspective taking with three items from Davis' interpersonal reactivity index, e.g. "When I'm upset at someone, I usually try to 'put myself in his shoes' for a while."

article_title: E-learning with multiple-try-feedback: Can hints foster students’ achievement during the semester?
citation: Jakob Schwerter, Franz Wortha, Peter Gerjets. (2022). E-learning with multiple-try-feedback: Can hints foster students' achievement during the semester? Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10105-z
title: Provide elaborative hints within multiple-try feedback as supportive information during practice for novices acquiring complex skills
description: The article interprets its findings through instructional design frameworks such as 4C/ID, arguing that "the additional hints in the feedback messages served as supportive information during practice, which is particularly effective for novice learners who are still acquiring schemata". Hints after a first incorrect answer give just-in-time procedural information that helps learners correct errors and acquire schemas applicable to subsequent interrelated tasks. The principle is grounded in a semester-long randomized experiment in statistics education.
requirements: Feedback must be immediate, task-related, and given in a situation where learners need help, following the conditions the article cites from Shute (2008)
constraints: The study did not incorporate fading of support, which the authors suggest may explain the lack of immediate-testing gains; learners might not have sufficiently internalized newly acquired schemas without support
target_learners: undergraduate social science students in introductory statistics courses
target_learning_goals: applying statistical knowledge and skills to problems, including higher-order outcomes such as hypothesis testing
examples: In the experiment, students in the MCR + H condition received one hint after a first incorrect answer, e.g., a note explaining how the estimated variance fits into the formula for calculating the standard deviation

article_title: An international perspective for ‘Improving teacher professional development for online and blended learning: a systematic meta-aggregative review’
citation: Portillo, J., Lopez de la Serna, A. (2021). An international perspective for ‘Improving teacher professional development for online and blended learning: a systematic meta-aggregative review’. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09851-9
title: Meta-aggregative review methodology as an extensible synthesis allowing new evidence to be added without reinterpreting original findings
description: The article characterises the systematic meta-aggregative review approach adopted by Philipsen et al. (2019) as an accumulating synthesis structure: "As far as the authors adopted the approach of a systematic meta-aggregative review, new data supported by unequivocal or credible evidence can be conveniently incorporated without reinterpreting the original findings." This makes the review's TPD findings extendable to new contexts, such as frugal-technology use in international remote education.

constraints: The original findings are not reinterpreted when new data are added
target_learners: Education researchers and policy-makers designing TPD programs
target_learning_goals: Synthesising and updating evidence on teacher professional development for online and blended learning
examples: The authors propose incorporating recent discoveries in frugal-technology use into the existing meta-aggregation as new aggregated components.

title: Three emerging themes of shifting to digital: datafication, convergence and personalized learning

article_title: Instructors’ perceptions of a large language model framework for generating automated multiple-choice questions from video transcripts
citation: Giacomo Cassano, Daniel Ebbert, Negin Mirriahi, Nicoletta Di Blas. (2026). Instructors’ perceptions of a large language model framework for generating automated multiple-choice questions from video transcripts. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10646-7
title: LLM-based framework generating MCQs from video transcripts with the IWF checklist embedded in the generation prompt
description: A four-step pipeline that processes a video into a transcript (Whisper), segments the transcript into topics, extracts and classifies concepts as Essential, Supporting, or Organizational, and generates one MCQ per essential concept using GPT-4o. Unlike most prior approaches, which apply quality guidelines primarily for post-hoc evaluation, "the framework explicitly integrates the Item-Writing Flaws (IWF) checklist directly into the generation prompt". Each item includes a self-contained stem, one correct answer, three plausible distractors, and LLM-generated formative feedback per option.
requirements: Uses GPT-4o via structured prompts and explicit task constraints in LangChain; the model was not trained or fine-tuned by the authors
constraints: Relies exclusively on transcript-based representations, so visually or multimodally conveyed content was not captured
Evaluated on short, carefully scripted videos averaging 7 minutes with clean transcripts, described as an ideal case
target_learners: MOOC learners in higher education across disciplines including humanities, architecture, and engineering
target_learning_goals: Formative and summative assessment of comprehension of video lesson content
examples: Across 45 videos averaging 7.01 minutes, the framework generated a mean of 5.77 MCQs per video (SD = 2.65), all reviewed by the originating instructor
key_sources: Giacomo Cassano, Daniel Ebbert, Negin Mirriahi, Nicoletta Di Blas. (2026). Instructors’ perceptions of a large language model framework for generating automated multiple-choice questions from video transcripts. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10646-7

article_title: Instructors’ perceptions of a large language model framework for generating automated multiple-choice questions from video transcripts
citation: Giacomo Cassano, Daniel Ebbert, Negin Mirriahi, Nicoletta Di Blas. (2026). Instructors’ perceptions of a large language model framework for generating automated multiple-choice questions from video transcripts. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10646-7
title: Embed pedagogical quality principles directly into LLM generation prompts rather than applying them only for post-hoc evaluation
description: The article argues that item-writing quality criteria should constrain generation itself, not just evaluation afterwards. Its conclusion states that "embedding pedagogical quality principles directly into LLM prompting represents a viable and promising direction for assessment automation". Operationalizing the IWF checklist within the generation stage produced items that met recognized quality standards in the majority of cases, though the authors call for continued refinement of concept extraction and linguistic control mechanisms.
requirements: Structured prompts and explicit task constraints guiding the LLM, since reliability is addressed at the level of use
constraints: The framework still produced unfocused stems, occasional loss of contextual specificity, and misclassification of illustrative examples as essential concepts
target_learners: Instructors creating MCQ assessments from instructional videos
target_learning_goals: Automated generation of pedagogically sound assessment items aligned with item-writing quality standards
examples: The framework embedded the IWF checklist into the MCQ-generation prompt, constraining the model to avoid ambiguous stems, implausible distractors, multiple correct answers, unintended cues, and negative or overly complex wording

article_title: Empathy in the shift to digital
citation: Gwendolyn M. Morel. (2021). Empathy in the shift to digital. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09952-z
title: Empathic design requires designers to predict how learners will feel while engaging with the final design solution
description: Empathic design is an instructional design approach in which the designer anticipates the learner's cognitive and emotional experience of the designed activity. The article quotes its definition: empathic design requires the designer "to predict how the person impacted by the design (in this case the learner) will feel while engaging with the final design solution". It was revisited during the rapid shift to digital learning, when time and infrastructure for thoughtful design were disrupted.
requirements: Designers must undertake learner analysis to imagine learners' cognitive and emotional experiences of the final design
constraints: The article notes the approach depends on time and infrastructure that can be stripped away or disrupted during unforeseen circumstances such as a rapid pivot to remote teaching
target_learners: learners in digital and remote learning environments
target_learning_goals: meaningful learning experiences designed around learners' cognitive and emotional states
examples: Tracey and Hutchinson (2019) used the framework to investigate the association between designers' imagined cognitive and emotional experiences of their learners and the actual learners' representation of the final designed activity

title: Reconsider empathy as a design approach in favor of humanizing pedagogy to expand the dimensions for understanding learners

citation: Gwendolyn M. Morel. (2021). Empathy in the shift to digital. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09952-z
title: Prioritize holistic design elements, including learners' emotional responses and states, as a regular part of learner analysis and evaluation
description: The editorial concludes that the pivot to remote delivery reinforced the need for efficient yet holistic design approaches. It argues for "prioritizing elements of holistic design as a regular part of learner analysis and evaluation", so that learners' emotional responses and states are treated as a critical component of the learning experience, maintaining connection with learners even when learning situations change.
requirements: Learner analysis and evaluation must routinely include emotional and holistic design elements, not only cognitive ones
constraints: Socioemotional traumatic times paired with limited educational infrastructure make performing learner analysis of any type difficult
target_learners: learners in changing or disrupted learning situations, including remote delivery
target_learning_goals: maintaining connection with learners and designing inclusive learning experiences
examples: The editorial recommends holistic design as regular practice, citing Goodyear and Ellis (2008) on learner analysis and evaluation, and notes empathic design, humanizing pedagogy, and culturally responsive pedagogy share meaningful implications for inclusive design

title: Learner-Generated Context (LGC) framework: learners as creators of their own learning contexts
description: The LGC framework holds that learning is constructed across a continuum of contexts, and that the preferred form is one in which "learners become the creators of their learning contexts and construct knowledge autonomously by interacting with or creating resources (e.g., people, technology, and learning contents) with self-defined learning goals". The article uses LGC to define LGC-based learning and to derive design guidance for digital tools, categorizing facilitation into designing technology for learners' contexts, personalized learning support, and assisting interactions with resources.
requirements: Digital technology must be designed so learners can generate and control their own learning context rather than receive unilaterally imposed contexts
constraints: The framework assumes learners have self-defined learning purposes; the article notes prior LGC studies assumed the presence of human instructors capable of timely feedback
target_learning_goals: autonomous knowledge construction
self-directed English language learning
examples: The study applied the framework to design an AI English learning support system for Korean secondary students

description: The VAS framework structures each course Activity as a five-step sequence: work on a mathematical activity, review what research says, research-informed reflection on the activity, engagement with modelled mentor–mentee interactions, and reflection connecting to one's own mentoring practice. The authors adapted Wilkerson et al.'s (2018) vignette approach, writing that "The VAS framework structured each Activity within the themed weeks, guiding participants through a five-step process". It is put forward as a model for designing online research-informed short PD courses.

citation: Richard E. West, Gregory S. Williams. (2017). 'I don't think that word means what you think it means': A proposed framework for defining learning communities. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-017-9535-0
title: Four-boundary framework for defining learning communities: access, relationships, vision, and function
description: The article proposes that learning communities be defined by four boundaries that serve as limits for what counts as a community: access (who is present physically or virtually), relationships (emotional ties), vision (shared purpose), and function (what members do together). The authors state that "learning community boundaries often defined in terms of participants' sense that they share access, relationships, vision, or function", and that these boundaries "sometimes overlap but often represent distinctive features". The framework is offered to guide research and practice.

constraints: The authors state the boundaries "are not finalized indicators" and recommend further research to verify or adapt the framework

improving research on social learning
examples: The authors apply the boundary strategy to freshman learning communities, virtual communities, and classroom-based K-16 student communities identified in their literature review

article_title: Dual empowerment in VR-based technical training: longitudinal evidence of developmental dynamics in learning outcomes and skill transfer
citation: Min Jou, Yungwei Hao. (2026). Dual empowerment in VR-based technical training: longitudinal evidence of developmental dynamics in learning outcomes and skill transfer. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10654-7
title: Dual Empowerment (DE) framework: staged instructional integration of VR-based cognitive precision and authentic physical practice
description: Dual Empowerment is a developmental instructional design framework in which "Dual Empowerment (DE) refers to the deliberate instructional integration of VR-based simulation and authentic physical practice to support both learning outcomes (LO) and skill transfer/retention (STR)". VR empowerment supplies data-driven feedback, scenario simulation, and safe trial-and-error for precision-oriented learning; physical empowerment reintroduces authenticity, sensory calibration, and practical application under ecological constraints. DE treats the two modalities as interdependent empowerment pathways whose structured, staged coordination—not immersion alone—supports durable competence, extending experience-centered immersive learning models such as CAMIL toward a design model for blended vocational training.
requirements: Both modalities must be structurally coupled rather than loosely connected; the design assumes neither modality alone is sufficient and competence is stabilized only when simulation-informed strategies withstand authentic constraints
constraints: The framework targets skill-intensive vocational domains; the article notes existing frameworks like TPACK, CoI, and Activity Theory do not fully specify how immersive and physical modalities should be coupled over time, which DE addresses
target_learners: vocational education and training (VET) learners in skill-intensive technical domains
target_learning_goals: procedural skill acquisition, durable skill transfer and retention in welding and comparable technical trades
examples: A five-stage welding program operationalized DE with 216 learners, combining real-time performance feedback, visualized learning traces, and structured VR–hands-on transitions

title: Five-stage dual-empowerment blended learning sequence alternating VR and physical empowerment
description: The instructional sequence is a staged progression in which "The instructional sequence followed a five-stage progression aligned with experiential and spiral learning principles", with each stage systematically integrating VR and physical empowerment. Stage 1 introduces concepts and safety; Stage 2 familiarizes basic flat-welding skills with real-time parameter display and short hands-on sessions; Stage 3 applies horizontal welding with seam inspection against VR metrics; Stage 4 adds high-difficulty vertical tasks under authentic constraints; Stage 5 reviews longitudinal skill charts and conducts final real-condition performance tests that operationalize the transfer criterion.
requirements: Task complexity increases across stages while psychological regulation is maintained through feedback continuity between VR and physical practice
constraints: Developed and evaluated for welding training in a semester-long vocational course; transferability to other skill-intensive domains is proposed by the authors but not tested in this study
target_learners: vocational students without prior welding certification in a semester-long welding course
target_learning_goals: progressive welding skill acquisition across flat, horizontal, and vertical butt-joint tasks, culminating in transfer validation under real welding conditions
examples: Stage 5 compared longitudinal simulation data with real-world performance to assess consistency, closing the feedback loop between LO and STR

citation: O'Neill, E. J., Fulton, C., Matthews, J., & Hensey, C. (2026). Metacognition design framework to aid metacognitive skill development in university students supported by the virtual learning environment. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10574-y
title: Metacognition Design Framework: a blended learning design placing the student learning journey centrally, aligned with learning outcomes
description: The Metacognition Design Framework is a learning design framework that scaffolds metacognitive skill development in blended higher-education settings. "The student's learning journey, comprising activities and tasks, is centrally placed within the Metacognition Design Framework (Fig. 2), constructively aligned with the learning outcomes." Core student activities are an authentic, complex project or assignment and a critical reflection on learning, with learning resources and supports arranged around this pathway; delivery mode (online/face-to-face, synchronous/asynchronous) is indicated by spatial arrangement. It builds on and adapts Oliver and Herrington's task, resources and supports classification and targets knowledge, regulation and social components of metacognition.

Requires VLE tools and blended delivery with linkage between online and face-to-face components

title: I-SEE learning strategies: Introducing, Signposting, Enabling and Evaluating organized as recursive quadrants of the framework
description: The framework groups its learning resources and supports into four overarching I-SEE learning strategies delivered predominantly asynchronously online via the VLE: "we broadly grouped the learning resources and supports outlined within the Metacognition Design Framework into four overarching 'I-SEE' learning strategies". Introducing builds metacognitive knowledge through resources and teaching; Signposting communicates expectations via guidance, rubrics and exemplars; Enabling lets students plan, monitor and assess learning through quizzes, checklists and reusable learning objects; Evaluating uses feedback in varied formats so students learn to assess progress and adjust approaches. Though presented sequentially, the strategies are applied collectively as recursive elements throughout the learning journey, depicted as interlocking quadrants of a jigsaw cog.

article_title: Emotion theory in education research practice: an interdisciplinary critical literature review
citation: Eliot, J. A. R., & Hirumi, A. (2019). Emotion theory in education research practice: an interdisciplinary critical literature review. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-018-09642-3
title: Three-approach taxonomy of emotion theory: basic, multidimensional, and academic emotion theory
description: The review classifies the dominant taxonomies of emotion into three approaches. Basic emotion theory relies on "a small number of discrete, discontinuous states" with plausible evolutionary facial expressions; multidimensional theories (Plutchik's cone, the Geneva Emotional Wheel, Damasio's primary/secondary scheme) map emotions onto geometric axes; academic emotion theory is Pekrun's control-value schema, distinguished by its separate intellectual history and focus on school learning. The review uses this taxonomy to weigh each approach's value for empirical research on emotion and learning.
requirements: The taxonomy is a classificatory scheme for comparing operational definitions across disciplines, not a novel conceptual scheme; the authors state the paper is a qualitative critique refining definitions rather than developing a new theory
constraints: The review excludes emotional intelligence theory, fear/stress/test anxiety research, and evolutionary-psychology work on emotion and intelligence as beyond scope
target_learners: education researchers studying emotion and learning
target_learning_goals: selection of operational definitions of emotion constructs for empirical studies of emotion and learning
examples: The review organizes the literature into the three groups and traces their intellectual histories in Fig. 3, a taxonomy of emotion taxonomies

citation: Eliot, J. A. R., & Hirumi, A. (2019). Emotion theory in education research practice: an interdisciplinary critical literature review. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-018-09642-3
title: Achievement Emotions Questionnaire (AEQ) and its derivative instruments
description: The AEQ is the self-report instrument paralleling academic emotion theory, operationalizing Pekrun's taxonomy of achievement, epistemic, and social emotions arranged around positive/negative, activity/outcome-focused, and activating/deactivating axes. The review notes it "has generated variants for use in different age groups, subject areas, and languages in addition to the original English." Studies using academic emotions as a research construct overwhelmingly adopt the AEQ or a derivative, making the instrument central to the review's critique of measurement practice in education research.
requirements: Requires self-report administration, most frequently as a posttest questionnaire, which the review argues captures memories of emotions rather than real-time emotional states during instruction
constraints: The review questions its validity as a sole instrument, especially for adolescent subjects whose self-concept is developmentally fluid
target_learners: secondary school students in online courses
target_learning_goals: measuring academic emotions as variables in research on emotion and learning
examples: The Pekrun et al. (2011) validation study used a convenience sample of N = 389 undergraduates volunteering for extra credit, relying predominantly on structural equation modeling

article_title: Emotion theory in education research practice: an interdisciplinary critical literature review
citation: Eliot, J. A. R., & Hirumi, A. (2019). Emotion theory in education research practice: an interdisciplinary critical literature review. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-018-09642-3
title: Syntactic model of academic emotions as combinations of basic emotions and propositional beliefs
description: The review proposes modeling supposed academic emotions as sentence-like structures: many emotions found in multidimensional theories "may be explicable as complex constructs of basic emotions combined with each other and/or with propositional beliefs that are not necessarily emotional"—for example, anger at a task plus fear of consequences plus metacognitive awareness yielding confusion. The model retains the intuitive appeal of larger natural-language vocabularies while avoiding risks to statistical significance and power from reifying academic emotions. The review links it to Harley et al.'s (2012) promising work with co-occurring basic emotions.
requirements: Requires retaining basic emotion constructs as the compositional primitives, with propositional beliefs as non-emotional components
constraints: The review presents it as a potential approach with continuity, though not identity, with philosophical models by de Sousa (1987) and Rorty (1980), not as a tested instrument
target_learners: education researchers studying emotion and learning
target_learning_goals: operationalizing complex emotional states such as confusion and curiosity in empirical learning research
examples: Harley, Bouchet and Azevedo (2012) found most subjects were best described as experiencing multiple co-occurring basic emotions using Ekman's set; Grafsgaard, Boyer and Lester (2012) achieved significant results modeling complex emotions as simultaneous incidence of specific basic emotions on the face
