citation: Patricia A. Young. (2021). The ever evolving MOOC. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09959-6
title: MOOCocracy: MOOCs as a social learning democracy comprising place and space
description: MOOCocracy is the account, proposed by Loizzo and Ertmer and discussed in this editorial, that MOOCs function as a social learning democracy with two components. The editorial states that "MOOCocracy's comprise both place and space": adult learners participate from the places where they live worldwide, while the space represents "digital learning cultures on a massive scale" (p. 1016). Interactions are asynchronous with little formal oversight or personal contact.
requirements: Adult learners participate asynchronously from their own locations, requiring little formal oversight
constraints: Interactions require little formal oversight and even less personal contact, as stated in the editorial
target_learners: adult learners worldwide taking MOOC courses
target_learning_goals: topic-driven knowledge attainment and self-directed learning in massive open online courses
examples: The special section offers four responses critiquing and examining Loizzo and Ertmer's (2016) MOOCocracy study
key_sources: Patricia A. Young. (2021). The ever evolving MOOC. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09959-6

article_title: The ever evolving MOOC
citation: Patricia A. Young. (2021). The ever evolving MOOC. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09959-6
title: Three generations of MOOCs: cMOOCs, xMOOCs, and hybrid MOOCs
description: The editorial organizes MOOC development into a three-generation taxonomy, citing Bozkurt et al. (2018): "the basic MOOC has transformed into cMOOCs (first generation); xMOOCs (second generation) and third generation Hybrid MOOCs". This framework frames the special section's discussion of how the platform's educational function is merging with social and political functions.
requirements: Understanding of the lineage from the first connectivist courses, which the editorial traces to Downes and Siemens' 2008 course
constraints: The taxonomy is attributed to Bozkurt et al. (2018) and presented as a historical framing rather than a tested model
target_learners: MOOC participants and designers of massive open online courses
target_learning_goals: understanding the evolution and design of massive open online courses
examples: The editorial cites Sebastian Thrun and Peter Norvig's 2011 Stanford MOOC on Artificial Intelligence, which attracted 160,000 participants, as a milestone in this evolution

article_title: Putting learning back into learning analytics: actions for policy makers, researchers, and practitioners
citation: Dirk Ifenthaler, David Gibson, Doreen Prasse, Atsushi Shimada, Masanori Yamada. (2021). Putting learning back into learning analytics: actions for policy makers, researchers, and practitioners. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09909-8
title: Four themes of learning analytics challenges: data literacy, guiding principles and policies, ethical standards, and flexible user-centred design
description: The article organises the issues and challenges facing educators linked to learning analytics into four themes developed by an international expert panel. As printed, "The four themes are 1. development of data literacy in all stakeholders, 2. updating of guiding principles and policies of educational data, 3. standards needed for ethical practices with data quality assurance, and 4. flexible user-centred design for a variety of users of analytics, starting with learners and ensuring that learners and learning is not harmed." The themes frame both the Delphi findings and the research agenda.
requirements: The themes emerged from expert panel discussion and are offered as provocations to organise researcher, policymaker and practitioner dialogs
constraints: The themes are outcomes of expert panel discussion rather than tested empirical results
target_learning_goals: supporting learning processes and educational decision-making with learning analytics
ethical and effective use of educational data
examples: The expert panel agreed there is a widespread lack of knowledge and understanding regarding learning analytics and the need to select and use learning analytics systems to support learning, teaching and assessment

article_title: Taking adaptive learning in educational settings to the next level: leveraging natural language processing for improved personalization
citation: Mathias Mejeh, Martin Rehm. (2024). Taking adaptive learning in educational settings to the next level: leveraging natural language processing for improved personalization. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10345-1
title: studybuddy: an adaptive learning technology platform supporting learners' self-regulated learning
description: studybuddy is a digital platform available as both a website and an app, designed to promote SRL by providing learners with tailored and timely regulation strategies. It gathers SRL-related data over time via a brief daily survey on motivation, emotion, cognition, metacognition, and resource management, and offers feedback through prompts, strategy recommendations, a dashboard, and a planning tool. "Figure 2 depicts studybuddy's four components: an automated prompting system, a digital dashboard, personalized strategies, and a planning tool." The article focuses on the prompting system and personalized strategy delivery.
requirements: Learners respond to daily questionnaire items on a standardized 7-point Likert scale so thresholds can trigger regulation strategies
constraints: During the initial two co-design phases the authors found that although already highly adaptive, it required further development to increase its adaptiveness
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning, including motivation, emotion, cognition, metacognition, and resource management
examples: In the context of self-efficacy, learners are asked whether they feel optimistic about making progress, and selecting one of the four lowest values on the 7-point scale automatically suggests a regulation strategy
key_sources: Mathias Mejeh, Martin Rehm. (2024). Taking adaptive learning in educational settings to the next level: leveraging natural language processing for improved personalization. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10345-1

article_title: Taking adaptive learning in educational settings to the next level: leveraging natural language processing for improved personalization
citation: Mathias Mejeh, Martin Rehm. (2024). Taking adaptive learning in educational settings to the next level: leveraging natural language processing for improved personalization. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10345-1
title: Threshold-triggered automated prompting combined with personalized strategy delivery in a daily feedback loop
description: This pattern divides learning into episodes that proceed cyclically, with a feedback loop in which preceding phases influence subsequent phases. Learners answer brief daily surveys (morning and afternoon); "If a student does not exceed a specific threshold, the app automatically prompts them with an appropriate regulation strategy." Personalized strategy recommendations are then grounded in personal motivation, emotion, cognition, metacognition, and resource management data, delivered as short videos using pictographs and text, and adjusted after each data collection before and after tasks.
requirements: A questionnaire-based mechanism that systematically gathers SRL-related data from learners over time
Strategy content; the majority of strategies are based on the German version of the Learning and Study Strategies Inventory (LASSI)
constraints: When learners receive adaptive feedback depends on which learning episodes are defined and how long they are
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning strategy use and reflection on the learning process
examples: Example strategies include creating a sense of achievement for motivation, expressive writing for emotion, the slow down strategy for cognition, task management for metacognition, and the flow place strategy for resource management
key_sources: Mathias Mejeh, Martin Rehm. (2024). Taking adaptive learning in educational settings to the next level: leveraging natural language processing for improved personalization. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10345-1

article_title: Taking adaptive learning in educational settings to the next level: leveraging natural language processing for improved personalization
citation: Mathias Mejeh, Martin Rehm. (2024). Taking adaptive learning in educational settings to the next level: leveraging natural language processing for improved personalization. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10345-1
title: Three-tier NLP analysis pipeline: opinion mining, part-of-speech tagging, and sentiment analysis
description: To analyze how integrating NLP into an ALT could provide just-in-time SRL support, the authors "employed a three-tier approach, namely using opinion mining, POS, and sentiment analysis." Opinion mining compares learner lexicons against reference lexicons built from SRL components of the MSLQ and LASSI using cosine similarity (0 to 1); POS tagging assigns syntactic tags to contextualize word pairs; sentiment analysis uses the DE-LIWC2015 dictionaries covering positive and negative emotions. The approach is explicitly informed by qualitative interview data from the co-design process.
requirements: Reference lexicons grounded in identified (meta-)cognitive, motivational, and emotional SRL components
Qualitative research and sound theoretical considerations informing the quantitative NLP configurations
constraints: In its current form the word network remains somewhat unclear from a purely descriptive standpoint, per the authors
target_learners: high school students whose interview and verbal input is analyzed
target_learning_goals: identifying learners' SRL-related terminology, context, and emotional disposition to tailor adaptive support
examples: Analysis was performed in R using the textstem, udpipe, and quanteda libraries, with LIWC software for sentiment analysis
key_sources: Mathias Mejeh, Martin Rehm. (2024). Taking adaptive learning in educational settings to the next level: leveraging natural language processing for improved personalization. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10345-1

article_title: Exploratory studies in the use of pictures and sound for teaching foreign language vocabulary
citation: Kale, S. V., and Grosslight, J. H. (1955). Exploratory Studies in the Use of Pictures and Sound for Teaching Foreign Language Vocabulary. Technical Report SDC 269-7-53, Instructional Film Research Program, Pennsylvania State University.
title: Use still pictures instead of motion pictures for film-based vocabulary instruction to avoid production expense
description: The report recommends that, because still pictures appear to be as effective as motion pictures for teaching foreign vocabulary under a written criterion, "the expense of producing motion pictures be avoided by using still pictures". It is a cost-saving design recommendation grounded in the null value the studies found for motion in pictures.
requirements: Learning goal is foreign vocabulary with a criterion of writing the foreign words
constraints: Applies where still and motion pictures were found equally effective; motion showed no value in these studies
target_learners: college students learning foreign language vocabulary
target_learning_goals: foreign language vocabulary learning measured by written word production
examples: Study 1 prepared five versions of motion pictures, including still pictures with English and Russian words, and taught Russian words to 409 college students

article_title: Learning design for short-duration e-textile workshops: outcomes on knowledge and skills
citation: Ioannou, A., Miliou, O., Georgiou, Y., Timotheou, S., Barkhuus, L., & Rode, J. (2025). Learning design for short-duration e-textile workshops: outcomes on knowledge and skills. Education Tech Research Dev, 73, 443–463. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10411-8
title: Computational making framework (Rode et al., 2015) with five dimensions as an analytical lens for children's e-textile projects
description: The framework describes the child as "the artifact creator who makes autonomous judgments and applies nonlinear processes when constructing artifacts" and organizes computational making into five dimensions: aesthetics, creativity, constructing, visualizing multiple representations, and understanding materials. This study adopted it as the analytical lens for coding facilitators' fieldnotes, triangulated with artifacts and video, and reported findings under each of the five dimensions.
requirements: Coding of qualitative fieldnotes against the five dimensions, triangulated with artifacts and video data
constraints: The article notes the framework stems from Rode et al. (2015) and that computational making "needs further investigation to develop effective educational practices"
target_learners: young children (around age 11-16) novices to e-textiles and microprocessors
target_learning_goals: computational making skills including aesthetics, creativity, constructing, visualizing multiple representations, and understanding materials
examples: Facilitators' fieldnotes from four facilitators were coded by two researchers independently (nearly 90% agreement), then triangulated with final e-textile projects and per-group video recordings around pivotal moments
key_sources: Ioannou, A., Miliou, O., Georgiou, Y., Timotheou, S., Barkhuus, L., & Rode, J. (2025). Learning design for short-duration e-textile workshops: outcomes on knowledge and skills. Education Tech Research Dev, 73, 443–463. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10411-8

article_title: Learning design for short-duration e-textile workshops: outcomes on knowledge and skills
citation: Ioannou, A., Miliou, O., Georgiou, Y., Timotheou, S., Barkhuus, L., & Rode, J. (2025). Learning design for short-duration e-textile workshops: outcomes on knowledge and skills. Education Tech Research Dev, 73, 443–463. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10411-8
title: In short-duration e-textile workshops with young novices, include some direct instruction and in-situ scaffolding and facilitation, which is not incompatible with the making ethos
description: The article argues that under limited time, novice learners, and novice educators, "some direct instruction and in-situ scaffolding and facilitation may be required for the objectives to be achieved." Although this may be in tension with openness in the making ethos, teachable moments and just-in-time instruction let learners pursue their own projects while receiving support on identified knowledge gaps. The detailed four-hour workshop design—preparation and hands-on practice followed by project development—is offered as a model other educators can use.
requirements: Facilitators need to be well-informed about the properties and limitations of available e-textile materials and ready to assist
Novice educators need workshop models and examples explaining how to handle the variety of e-textile tools and materials
constraints: Recommended under specific circumstances: limited time, novice learners with respect to e-textiles and microprocessors, novice educators regarding STEAM or making practices, and lack of workshop models
target_learners: young children with no prior e-textile or microprocessor experience
target_learning_goals: circuitry knowledge and computational making skills in short STEAM-oriented workshops
examples: The workshop demonstrated micro:bit basics, practiced button-trigger actions and LED control, covered Ohm's Law with practical activities, and used the 2D circuit diagram discussion before crafting as an example of direct facilitation that worked very well
key_sources: Ioannou, A., Miliou, O., Georgiou, Y., Timotheou, S., Barkhuus, L., & Rode, J. (2025). Learning design for short-duration e-textile workshops: outcomes on knowledge and skills. Education Tech Research Dev, 73, 443–463. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10411-8

article_title: Teachers’ use of data from digital learning platforms for instructional design: a systematic review
citation: Alina Hase, Poldi Kuhl. (2024). Teachers’ use of data from digital learning platforms for instructional design: a systematic review. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10356-y
title: Data use for teaching: a five-step circular process model
description: The review adopts Mandinach and Gummer's circular process of data use for teaching, in which teachers move from identifying problems and framing questions, through collecting and analyzing data, to deriving decisions and evaluating outcomes. As the review states, "We are following the data use for teaching process consisting of five steps: (1) the identification of problems and framing questions, (2) the use of data, (3) the transformation of data into information, (4) the transformation of information into decisions, and (5) the evaluation of outcomes." The review uses this model to frame how teachers turn platform data into instructional actions.
requirements: Data should not be collected without a specific goal; the process starts with identifying problems and formulating leading questions
constraints: The review notes transforming information into decisions seems to be difficult for teachers and is therefore often neglected
target_learning_goals: Using student data to inform instructional design and adapt teaching to student needs
examples: The review applies the model to interpret how teachers in the included studies moved from consulting dashboards to differentiation and individualization actions
key_sources: Alina Hase, Poldi Kuhl. (2024). Teachers’ use of data from digital learning platforms for instructional design: a systematic review. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10356-y

article_title: Teachers’ use of data from digital learning platforms for instructional design: a systematic review
citation: Alina Hase, Poldi Kuhl. (2024). Teachers’ use of data from digital learning platforms for instructional design: a systematic review. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10356-y
title: Learning analytics process model: awareness, reflection, sensemaking, impact
description: The review introduces Verbert et al.'s learning analytics process model as a framework for teachers' dashboard use. It comprises four stages: "(1) awareness, (2) reflection, (3) sensemaking, and (4) impact", in which people become aware of data, ask questions to reflect on it, answer questions to create new insights, and deduce consequences for their behavior. The review applies the stages to dashboards, noting few address the impact stage of actual behavioral consequence.
requirements: People need to be aware of the data, ask questions to reflect on the data, answer the questions and create new insights, and deduce consequences for their behavior
constraints: Few, if any, dashboards address Stage 4 of actual impact, per the review's quoted application
target_learners: K-12 teachers using learning analytics dashboards
target_learning_goals: Interpreting learning analytics data to improve teaching and enable individualized learning processes
examples: The review maps teachers' dashboard consultation during and after lessons onto the model's stages
key_sources: Alina Hase, Poldi Kuhl. (2024). Teachers’ use of data from digital learning platforms for instructional design: a systematic review. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10356-y

article_title: Virtual virtuoso: a systematic literature review of immersive learning environments for psychomotor skill development
citation: Khaleel Asyraaf Mat Sanusi, Deniz Iren, Nardie Fanchamps, Mai Geisen, Roland Klemke. (2025). Virtual virtuoso: a systematic literature review of immersive learning environments for psychomotor skill development. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10449-2
title: Four-dimension framework for analyzing ILEs for psychomotor skill training
description: The review organizes ILE-based psychomotor training research around four interconnected dimensions: "motor skills, ILE technologies, feedback components, and design characteristics of virtual environments". Each dimension is grounded in principles that can enhance training effectiveness, and synthesizing them "enables a comprehensive analysis of utilizing ILEs in the context of psychomotor skill training". The framework structures the review's research questions, frequency analysis, and correlation analysis.
requirements: Studies must address at least one of the four dimensions (motor skills, technologies, feedback, design characteristics) to be analyzed within the framework
constraints: The framework was applied to a corpus of 39 peer-reviewed studies published from 2013 onwards
target_learners: learners training psychomotor skills in immersive learning environments
target_learning_goals: psychomotor skill development and acquisition
examples: The review coded 39 articles with one-hot encoding across the four dimensions and ran frequency and Pearson correlation analyses on the resulting variables
key_sources: Khaleel Asyraaf Mat Sanusi, Deniz Iren, Nardie Fanchamps, Mai Geisen, Roland Klemke. (2025). Virtual virtuoso: a systematic literature review of immersive learning environments for psychomotor skill development. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10449-2

article_title: Design and effects of representational scripting on group performance
citation: B. Slof, G. Erkens, P. A. Kirschner, J. G. M. Jaspers. (2010). Design and effects of representational scripting on group performance. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-010-9148-3
title: Representational scripting: sequencing phase-related part-tasks with ontologically congruent external representations
description: Representational scripting integrates scripting and representational tools so that the phase-related part-tasks of a problem-solving process are made explicit and sequenced, evoking specific problem representations. The article defines a script as "a set of instructions regarding to how the group members should interact, how they should collaborate and how they should solve the problem". It structures complex tasks into problem orientation, problem solution and solution evaluation phases, each matched to a zero-, first- or second-order external representation whose expressiveness and processability supply the required representational guidance.
requirements: The representational guidance of a specific ER must be congruent (matched) with the part-task demands and activities of a specific problem phase
Students must be made aware of the different problem phases and their required problem representations
constraints: An ER is seldom effective for all part-task demands and activities
The effect of the design does not automatically apply to all complex learning-tasks
target_learners: non-expert secondary education students carrying out complex learning-tasks collaboratively
target_learning_goals: carrying out complex learning-tasks
creating qualitative and quantitative problem representations
examples: In the study, the complex business-economics task was divided into three phases and groups in the match condition received a conceptual ER, then a causal ER, then a simulation ER, each matched to its phase
key_sources: B. Slof, G. Erkens, P. A. Kirschner, J. G. M. Jaspers. (2010). Design and effects of representational scripting on group performance. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-010-9148-3

article_title: Design and effects of representational scripting on group performance
citation: B. Slof, G. Erkens, P. A. Kirschner, J. G. M. Jaspers. (2010). Design and effects of representational scripting on group performance. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-010-9148-3
title: VCRI CSCL environment augmented with representational scripting
description: Virtual Collaborative Research Institute (VCRI) is a groupware application for supporting the collaborative performance of complex learning-tasks, inquiry-tasks and research projects. For this study five tools were augmented with representational scripting: a chat tool for synchronous communication, an Assignment menu with the task description and information sources, a shared Co-writer text processor, an individual Notes tool, and a Status bar awareness tool. Groups had to close each finished phase in the assignment menu, which opened the next phase and delivered the next external representation.
requirements: All students in all conditions had access to these tools and information sources, and were information equivalent
constraints: Only in the matched condition did students receive a new ER matched to the demands of each phase; in the three mismatch conditions the ER did not change
target_learners: secondary education students working in triads
target_learning_goals: collaborative solution of a complex business-economics problem
examples: When group members agreed a part-task was finished they closed that phase, received a new part-task, entered answers in a different Co-writer window, and received an ER
key_sources: B. Slof, G. Erkens, P. A. Kirschner, J. G. M. Jaspers. (2010). Design and effects of representational scripting on group performance. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-010-9148-3

article_title: Design and effects of representational scripting on group performance
citation: B. Slof, G. Erkens, P. A. Kirschner, J. G. M. Jaspers. (2010). Design and effects of representational scripting on group performance. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-010-9148-3
title: Make phase-related part-tasks explicit and sequenced and provide part-task-congruent external representations for each phase
description: The article's design implication is that complex learning-task completion is facilitated when the different phase-related part-tasks are made explicit and properly sequenced, and part-task congruent ERs are provided. Using multiple ERs can provide different perspectives of the knowledge domain and, when properly matched to the task demands and activities, their complementary function can gradually increase student understanding and phase-related part-task activity. The study's match condition implemented this by delivering a conceptual, causal and simulation ER in phased order.
requirements: Part-task congruent ERs (i.e., domain specific content schemes) must be provided for each phase-related part-task
The part-tasks must be made explicit and properly sequenced
constraints: The effect of the design of representational scripting does not automatically apply to all complex learning-tasks; it depends on the characteristics of the problem and the involved knowledge domains
target_learners: non-expert students collaboratively carrying out complex learning-tasks in CSCL environments
target_learning_goals: successful completion of complex learning-tasks
better complex learning-task performance
examples: Groups in the match condition received the conceptual ER for problem orientation, the causal ER for problem solution and the simulation ER for solution evaluation, and outperformed the conceptual and simulation mismatch conditions on total task performance
key_sources: B. Slof, G. Erkens, P. A. Kirschner, J. G. M. Jaspers. (2010). Design and effects of representational scripting on group performance. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-010-9148-3

article_title: Reflective comments on shifting to digital
citation: J. Michael Spector, Phil Harris. (2021). Reflective comments on shifting to digital. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09961-y
title: Use prior published research, rather than a particular pedagogical or technological approach, to inform responses to rapid shifts to digitally intensive learning
description: The article describes a deliberate, well-reasoned editorial process in which scholars examined recently published research from multiple perspectives and contexts to identify what might be applied when educators must make a sudden shift to digitally-based learning. Its focus was "on what has been established by prior research that can help in this situation and similar situations that might arise in the future", rather than on COVID-19 or any single approach. The article uses this principle to organize a special issue of reflective commentaries on flexible learning.
requirements: Identify and examine recently published research applicable to the shift situation, gathered from multiple countries, cultures, perspectives, and situations
constraints: The article states the focus was not on COVID-19 and not on a particular pedagogical or technological approach
target_learners: educators required to make a sudden shift to digitally-based learning and instruction
target_learning_goals: informing practice and improving instruction during rapid shifts to digitally-based learning
examples: The editors and editorial boards of a special issue on flexible learning asked a group of scholars to examine selected recently published papers from various points of view to identify what might be applied in the current situation and what might inform future research.
key_sources: J. Michael Spector, Phil Harris. (2021). Reflective comments on shifting to digital. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09961-y

article_title: Enhancing middle school students’ computational thinking competency through game-based learning
citation: Yanjun Pan, Elizabeth L. Adams, Leanne R. Ketterlin-Geller, Eric C. Larson, Corey Clark. (2024). Enhancing middle school students' computational thinking competency through game-based learning. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10400-x
title: Factory Craft: a Minecraft-based game-based learning system for middle school computational thinking
description: Factory Craft is a "first person, three-dimensional, multi-level role-player game that aims to enhance CT competency for middle school students." It integrates an adapted Mineplex Lumberjack Tycoon mod, a node-based Minecraft Factory Planner (MFP), and the Canvas LMS so teachers can monitor learning. Students act as engineers building automated factories and contraptions on a planet named Tiny Town, with content focused on Data and Analysis, Algorithms and Programming, and Impacts of Computing.
requirements: Teachers use the integrated Canvas learning management system to monitor students' learning
constraints: The study used only three game levels targeting the CSTA Data and Analysis standards (2-DA-07, 2-DA-08, 2-DA-09) for grades 6-9
target_learning_goals: computational thinking competency aligned to CSTA K-12 standards, including data collection, encoding, and computational model refinement
examples: In the study, students played a Tutorial plus three lessons (Data Collection, Data Encoding, Data Sorting) individually for 40 minutes per session, with approximately 160 minutes of total gameplay across six 50-minute sessions.
key_sources: Yanjun Pan, Elizabeth L. Adams, Leanne R. Ketterlin-Geller, Eric C. Larson, Corey Clark. (2024). Enhancing middle school students' computational thinking competency through game-based learning. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10400-x

article_title: Enhancing middle school students’ computational thinking competency through game-based learning
citation: Yanjun Pan, Elizabeth L. Adams, Leanne R. Ketterlin-Geller, Eric C. Larson, Corey Clark. (2024). Enhancing middle school students' computational thinking competency through game-based learning. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10400-x
title: CSTA-aligned game levels that embed CT facets (decomposition, abstraction, debugging) in crafting and modeling tasks
description: Each Factory Craft game level was designed by aligning game objectives, learning objectives, CSTA standards, and CT facets. For example, Lesson 2 asks students to "build various models of contraptions to produce objects and explore ways to build objects more efficiently with minimal waste," requiring data collection, analysis, pattern recognition, and modeling that reflect abstraction. The MFP lets students drag and drop inputs and outputs to construct contraption models used in Minecraft.
requirements: Alignment of game objectives, learning objectives, CSTA standards, and CT facets for each level, as displayed in Table 1
constraints: The pattern was implemented and evaluated only in a one-group exploratory summer-camp study with 31 students
target_learning_goals: CT facets of decomposition, abstraction (data collection and analysis, pattern recognition, modeling), and debugging
examples: Lesson 2's chest contraption model required 20 logs per hour as input to produce 80 planks as output, which could subsequently be used to craft 10 chests per hour.

article_title: Academics’ (Re) construction of teacher identities in the context of technology integration at a South African university
citation: Folabit, N. L., & Jita, L. C. (2026). Academics’ (Re) construction of teacher identities in the context of technology integration at a South African university. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10708-w
title: Integrated identity theory and TPACK framework for analysing teacher identity reconstruction in technology integration
description: The article integrates Stryker and Burke's identity theory with the TPACK framework as a combined analytical lens. Identity theory explains how academics interpret and negotiate roles through "role salience, role conflict, and identity tension," while TPACK explains how these processes are enacted through technological, pedagogical, and content knowledge. The authors state identity theory "foregrounds the dynamics of self-reconstruction, and TPACK illustrates the pedagogical mechanism through which academics’ reconstruction of their teacher identity is materialised."
requirements: Analysts must map inductive codes to TPACK constructs (TK, PK, CK) and identity theory constructs (role identity, salience, conflict) to keep analysis conceptually coherent
constraints: The article notes TPACK does not fully address socio-structural challenges academics face, such as workload and infrastructure limitations
target_learners: University academics integrating technology into teaching
target_learning_goals: Professional identity reconstruction
Technology-integrated pedagogical practice
examples: The study applied the integrated framework in hybrid inductive-deductive thematic analysis of interviews with 12 academics, coding gamification and multimedia use under TPK and role conflict under identity reconstruction

article_title: The iBuddy experience: A digital simulation-based approach to enhance secondary school students’ privacy awareness
citation: Luca Botturi, Tiffany Fioroni, Chiara Beretta, Davide Andreoletti, Alessandro Ferrari, Felipe Cardoso, Anna Picco-Schwendener, Suzanna Marazza, Silvia Giordano. (2024). The iBuddy experience: A digital simulation-based approach to enhance secondary school students' privacy awareness. Education Tech Research Dev 72. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10309-x
title: iBuddy simulation system (app, local server, browser client)
description: iBuddy is a 2-hour class simulation in which students install an app to configure a fictional android classmate; the system collects personal data (gallery pictures, contacts, installed apps and usage time) on a local server and generates custom questions displayed to the class to produce a wow effect. The functional architecture is "composed by three parts": a Mobile Client, a local Server, and a Browser Client. The local network is isolated from the internet and all data are deleted during the session.
requirements: An overhead projector is the only required classroom technology beyond the system itself
A presenter and an operator (usually at the local server) run the session
Students without smartphones work in pairs with a classmate
constraints: Data are kept on a local server with no internet connection and deleted about 30 minutes after collection
Without explicit consent the system cannot collect photos or contacts
The operator must exclude embarrassing or illegal content from custom questions
target_learning_goals: awareness that apps access personal data
naming data processes such as customization and advertising
taking specific actions to protect personal data
examples: Between March 2021 and March 2022, 52 sessions were carried out with 978 students in 17 schools; the first 12 sessions tested and fine-tuned the system
key_sources: Luca Botturi, Tiffany Fioroni, Chiara Beretta, Davide Andreoletti, Alessandro Ferrari, Felipe Cardoso, Anna Picco-Schwendener, Suzanna Marazza, Silvia Giordano. (2024). title: Two-phase session design: playful narrative simulation followed by modular debriefing
description: The iBuddy session is designed in two phases: (a) a highly engaging narrative-based playful simulation playable with all age groups, and (b) a flexible modular debriefing adjustable to the age group and to questions emerging in each session. The debriefing has two steps: behind-the-scenes modules (what happened, emotions, technical features, data deletion) and real-life modules (how the internet works, personalization, advertising, data value, profiles, terms of use, alternatives), combined usually 3 or 4 at a time.
requirements: Half of the session time is devoted to debriefing
Cliffhangers or pointers to the debriefing are integrated during the simulation design
A presenter leads and an operator prepares safe custom questions
constraints: The debriefing path depends on participants' questions, age group and available time
The debriefing is less interactive and engaging than the simulation
target_learners: students aged 11–20 in secondary, high school and university classes
target_learning_goals: privacy awareness
understanding of data collection and processing
uptake of privacy-safe behaviors
examples: Debriefing part 1 always includes modules 1.1, 1.3 and 1.4 with optional 1.2; part 2 offers modules M2.0–M2.6 from which the presenter combines 3 or 4

The iBuddy experience: A digital simulation-based approach to enhance secondary school students' privacy awareness. Education Tech Research Dev 72. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10309-x
title: Three interpretations of the privacy paradox guiding instructional design
description: Drawing on Kokolakis (2017), the article organizes the privacy paradox—the inconsistency between stated privacy concerns and observed behavior—into three interpretations: (1) surveys are the wrong methodology and most people have only vague concerns, so behavior should be monitored; (2) users lack information about how their data are captured, stored and used, so invisible data flows should be made visible; (3) the paradox exists as a positive privacy vs. utility trade-off. The authors used these interpretations to determine their instructional approach, translating them into letting participants experience first-hand the exposure of data they were unaware of having exposed.
requirements: Awareness interventions should address factual knowledge of how technologies operate, not only lists of do's and don'ts
Relevance must be tied to personal situations where sensitivity and visibility of data are at stake
constraints: The theoretical debate on the existence of the privacy paradox is still open; different interpretations may explain different users
Conceptualizing privacy risks is inherently challenging, depending on technical, cultural and subjective factors
target_learning_goals: privacy awareness
informed decisions about personal data disclosure
examples: The iBuddy wow effect was designed by provoking students with data that are highly sensitive, difficult to extract, and not frequently exposed

description: Within the MAPAW project, a set of 4 short digital stop-motion video clips (duration 2–3 minutes) was developed and released under Creative Commons license, presenting Emma, a girl, and her use of a social network called Momentum. The videos address personal data collection, personalized advertising, the technical network infrastructure involved in data collection, and legal aspects, and can be used to wrap up discussion. All original materials are available at www.protectyourdata.ch in Italian and other Swiss national languages, along with pointers to other online privacy education resources.

title: Robot-assisted digital storytelling system for hospitalized children's health education
description: A robot with a screen face that shows emotional expressions such as happiness, sadness and anger, plays videos, and accepts touch and voice input. Children interact by clicking the screen or speaking keywords to select story sessions or answer comprehension questions embedded at specified story periods. Two digital stories (Duck Abel and an IV story) were presented as cartoon animations simulating the treatment process, each for 20 minutes.

constraints: The cost of the robots and the additional time required to prepare the health education materials are stated as the biggest challenge

The design aims to distract attention and reduce anxiety during nursing care.

cartoon animation to simulate the treatment process
interaction points for selection and question answering

title: Treat learning content as integral to gameplay, rules, and actions when designing learning games
description: Walkington's response focuses on intrinsic integration—the notion that in learning games the content to be learned should be integral to the gameplay, game rules, and game actions. The editorial calls this "very timely when educators seek to select games to use in their classrooms, but these games are hard to design."

constraints: The editorial notes such games are hard to design

title: Generalize game design elements beyond game-based learning to other interactive learning designs
description: Gibson's design perspective suggests Ke's (2016) review offers an opportunity to re-imagine digital learning design. The editorial states Gibson "attempts to generalize from the five game design elements presented by Ke and discuss how these elements extend beyond game-based learning to other interactive learning designs" such as team-based projects and project-based learning.

article_title: Understanding student engagement in online learning environments: the role of reflexivity
citation: Peter Kahn, Lucy Everington, Kathleen Kelm, Iain Reid, Francine Watkins. (2017). Understanding student engagement in online learning environments: the role of reflexivity. Education Tech Research Dev, 65, 203-218. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-016-9484-z
title: Student engagement theorised as the exercise of agency, underpinned by reflexivity
description: This framework theorises student engagement as the exercise of intentional human action, or agency, drawing on Archer's staged model in which agents configure concerns in structural settings and translate them into projects and practices. Reflexivity is the internal deliberation underpinning this: "the ordinary mental capacity to consider oneself in relation to one's social setting". The study applies the framework to online postgraduate environments, extending it with collective reflexivity, and finds it helps explain engagement while revising the single-dominant-mode claim.
requirements: Analysis must attend to both the individual student's deliberations and the structural setting in which action is conducted
constraints: The study examined engaged postgraduate students in fully online Masters programmes, and the methodology tended to select engaged rather than disengaged participants
target_learners: postgraduate students in fully online higher education
target_learning_goals: student engagement in online learning
examples: Interviews probed reflexivity with questions such as whether students paused to think about tasks, and discussion postings were coded for concerns and actions

title: Social practices of mutual understanding in asynchronous online discussion
description: A recurring set of six social practices that students used in asynchronous discussion boards to develop mutual understanding towards shared goals: invitation, provocation, identifying a common interest, reaching out, defending, and encouragement. The most common was identifying common interests (29 instances), followed by provocation (18). The authors note "The most commonly applied strategy was to seek to identify common interests", with students drawing out each other's interests through mutual self-disclosure or selectivity in the postings to which one responds.
requirements: Discussion boards must allow students freedom in which posts they respond to with follow-up posts, so interests can overlap
constraints: The genesis of these social practices, such as whether students first saw them modelled by a tutor, lies beyond the scope of this study
target_learners: postgraduate students in fully online higher education
target_learning_goals: development of mutual insight through online discussion
examples: Table 3 lists the six practices with frequencies, e.g. provocation (f = 18) and reaching out to students who receive fewer responses (f = 3), each with a student quotation

The authors state the course was designed "by applying instructional design factors as well as teaching and facilitation strategies derived from the learning by design (LBD) framework." The study examined the effects of these design factors via action research.
requirements: The framework requires instructional design factors and teaching and facilitation strategies derived from LBD to be implemented in the course design, as the article states it did.
constraints: The article examines LBD as implemented in one synchronized online robotics course for inservice teachers; effectiveness evidence comes from that single action-research study.

target_learning_goals: robotics content knowledge
self-efficacy in robotics
problem-solving and collaboration strategies
confidence in teaching robotics

robotics teaching confidence and self-efficacy
problem-solving and collaboration strategies

title: Online survey instrument measuring teacher interest, self-efficacy, strategies, and confidence for the robotics course

article_title: Creative intention and persistence in educational robotic
citation: Anaïs Leroy, Margarida Romero. (2022). Creative intention and persistence in educational robotic. Educational technology research and development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10128-6
title: Dual-process model of the creative process with two inhibitory-control stages
description: The article proposes a model of the creative process based on dual process models, in which achieving a creative solution requires two stages of inhibitory control: first inhibiting the conservative intention to reuse an already known solution, then persisting in the inhibition of familiar associations while searching for a new solution. As the article states, "Being creative is an effortful choice which requires a regulatory process from the creative intention to the creative solution." The study's results are interpreted as coherent with this model, with inhibitory control possibly influencing both creative intention and creative behavior persistence.
requirements: The model presupposes a prior successful solution exists that can be repeated conservatively, as in a repeated task
constraints: The article states the model should also be engaged on other creative tasks to observe if the results apply beyond the educational robotic task
target_learning_goals: sustaining creative behavior in repeated problem-solving tasks
examples: In the CreaCube study, conservative intention relied on the fast system building on prior knowledge, while creative intention required inhibiting fixation on the newly learned solution.
key_sources: Anaïs Leroy, Margarida Romero. (2022). Creative intention and persistence in educational robotic. Educational technology research and development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10128-6

article_title: Creative intention and persistence in educational robotic
citation: Anaïs Leroy, Margarida Romero. (2022). Creative intention and persistence in educational robotic. Educational technology research and development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10128-6
title: CreaCube task: a repeated creative problem-solving activity with modular robotic cubes
description: CreaCube (Romero, David & Lille, 2018) is a manipulative robotic cube task in which participants build, with four Cubelets modular cubes (white wheel cube, blue battery cube, black sensor cube, red inverse cube), a vehicle that moves independently between two points. Eighteen figures can be created, twelve of which complete the task successfully. The article uses it twice in succession to observe creative intention, creative behavior persistence, and creative solution, supported by video recording and a CreaCube learning analytics platform.
requirements: Participants must explore and manipulate the cubes to discover their affordances, which are not directly visible
constraints: The use of a specific set of modular robotics material (Cubelets) requires considering the need for further studies using other interactive technologies to transfer these results
target_learners: adults (in this study, aged M = 27.7 years)
target_learning_goals: creative problem solving with educational robotics
examples: Participants first built a vehicle from a red starting point to a black finishing point, then repeated the same task with no instruction to solve it the same or a different way.
key_sources: Anaïs Leroy, Margarida Romero. (2022). Creative intention and persistence in educational robotic. Educational technology research and development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10128-6

article_title: Creative intention and persistence in educational robotic
citation: Anaïs Leroy, Margarida Romero. (2022). Creative intention and persistence in educational robotic. Educational technology research and development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10128-6
title: Four-profile classification of creative intention versus effective solution in repeated tasks
description: The article classifies participants along two axes — creative versus conservative intention, and creative versus conservative effective solution — yielding four profiles: the creatives, the conservatives, the non-intentional creatives and the non-intentional conservatives. Non-intentional creatives intended to repeat their solution but failed and adopted a creative behavior, while non-intentional conservatives include participants whose creative intention collapsed into conservative behavior. This pattern lets an observer diagnose where in a repeated task creative pursuit is lost or accidentally achieved.
requirements: Video analysis of both task occurrences to code the first figure tested in activity 2 and the successful final figures
constraints: Profiles were identified in one educational robotic task with adult participants
target_learning_goals: diagnosing creative intention and persistence in repeated tasks
examples: A participant reproducing a train figure by only swapping two cubes was coded as the same figure; assembling the four cubes in a square was coded as a different figure.

article_title: Exploring learning in classic African board games: a review of recent literature
citation: Rebecca Y. Bayeck. (2026). Exploring learning in classic African board games: a review of recent literature. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10733-9
title: Sociocultural learning theory as the framework for understanding learning in classic African board games
description: The review draws on sociocultural learning theory (Vygotsky) to interpret learning in classic African board games. The theory holds that "humans are not isolated entities shaped by the context, but part of a social and cultural context they cannot be separated from". From this perspective, engagement and participation in activity and practice implies learning, so learning is always occurring and is not restricted to structured teaching. The review uses this lens to treat gameplay interactions, tool mediation, and problem solving with games as learning, framing classic African board games as analog technologies that mediate learning.
requirements: Learning is analyzed through participation in activities such as gameplay and through tools, artifacts, or others used to address local problems
constraints: The framework treats learning as socially mediated and culturally embedded, so it interprets learning broadly rather than measuring instructional outcomes
target_learners: players of classic African board games across class, age, and gender, including adult Songo players and school children in African communities
target_learning_goals: mathematics
computational thinking
literacies
cultural knowledge
AI understanding
examples: The review interprets Songo gameplay literacies (Bayeck 2019) and AI agent development for Ayo, Awale, and Ntxuva as instances of learning mediated by these games
key_sources: Rebecca Y. Bayeck. (2026). Exploring learning in classic African board games: a review of recent literature. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10733-9

article_title: Backward design as a mobile application development strategy
citation: Kantorski, B., Sanford-Dolly, C. W., Commisso, D. R., & Pollock, J. A. (2019). Backward design as a mobile application development strategy. Education Tech Research Dev, 67, 711–731. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09662-7
title: Wiggins and McTighe's three-stage backward design framework as a guiding strategy for educational app development
description: Backward design is a curriculum design methodology in which learning goals and assessment are established before instruction is planned. McTighe and Wiggins "formalized the backward design process into three consecutive stages": Stage I identify desired results, Stage II determine acceptable evidence, and Stage III plan learning experiences and instruction. The authors applied all three stages to develop the CityHacks app, arguing it ties learning-goal identification, assessment design, and app feature design into one coherent process.
requirements: Learning goals and acceptable evidence of understanding must be established before learning experiences and instruction are planned
constraints: The authors note design should also involve evaluation and other research theories and practices, so backward design alone is beneficial only "to a certain extent"

title: Narrative-based educational app pattern combining branching story, embedded performance-task assessment, and supplementary interactive features
description: The BiblioTech platform is a user-centered, reading-based app in which users "craft their own story by choosing where characters go and what they learn" through a branching, build-your-own-adventure narrative. Features such as mini-games, infographics, interactive diagrams, video interviews, and a digital notebook supplement the story, while a built-in debate assessment functions as "a complex, authentic performance task that contextualizes learning by requiring users to make key decisions that affect the story's outcome." Mini-games act like quizzes that build vocabulary familiarity without affecting the story outcome.

title: Adaptive Reader technology with three selectable reading levels in CityHacks: In Search of Sleep
description: Adaptive Reader is an in-app feature that lets users choose among three reading levels while keeping scientific content constant. It "converts the reading level of the text from a story suitable for 5th grade level to either a 3rd/4th grade level or up to an 8th grade level, depending on the option chosen by the user." Text was leveled using Flesch–Kincaid (finished narrative scored 4.8), Lexile, and the New Dale–Chall vocabulary-based method, analyzed section-by-section so each section sits one tier up and one tier down from the medium text. Peers read at appropriate levels but access the same content for full participation.
requirements: Readability must be checked with both length-based tools (Flesch–Kincaid, Lexile) and a vocabulary-based tool (Dale–Chall), because Lexile has no semantic component
constraints: Simply lowering the Lexile level would not have changed true readability given the app's challenging concepts and vocabulary
target_learners: children at risk of learning or behavioral disabilities
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension
access to identical science content across reading abilities
examples: A pop-up box at the end of selected chapters lets users continue at the same level or choose an easier or more difficult one

article_title: Supporting interdisciplinary collaborative concept mapping with individual preparation phase
citation: Esther Tan, Jacob Gerolf de Weerd, Slavi Stoyanov. (2021). Supporting interdisciplinary collaborative concept mapping with individual preparation phase. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09963-w
title: Epistemic and social process framework for collaborative knowledge co-construction and transactivity
description: The article organises collaborative knowledge co-construction along two dimensions. The epistemic dimension uses Beers et al.'s (2006) 'primitives of negotiation' — contribution, clarification, verification, elaboration — plus the authors' added positioning. The social dimension uses Weinberger and Fischer's (2006) five social modes: "externalisation, elicitation, quick-consensus building, integration-oriented consensus building and conflict-oriented consensus building", which represent different levels of transactivity, with conflict-oriented consensus building the highest. The study applies this framework as coding schemes to audio-recorded collaborative discourse.
requirements: Discourse data coded by trained independent raters with sufficient inter-rater reliability (Cohen's Kappa κ = 0.79 epistemic, κ = 0.88 social)
constraints: Transactivity levels are inferred from nominal-level coded discourse categories rather than direct measures
target_learners: third-year university students in interdisciplinary minors
target_learning_goals: interdisciplinary knowledge integration
collaborative knowledge co-construction
examples: Audio recordings of eight groups' collaborative concept mapping were coded into the epistemic categories and the five social modes, then compared across WIP and WOIP with chi-square tests.

article_title: Spatial versus normal audio guides in exhibitions: Cognitive mechanisms and effects on learning
citation: Manuela Glaser, Laura Hug, Stephan Werner, Stephan Schwan. (2025). Spatial versus normal audio guides in exhibitions: Cognitive mechanisms and effects on learning. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10424-3
title: The Model of Audio-Visual Cognitive Processing (MAVCP) extends multimedia learning theory with a non-verbal auditory representation built from acoustic and spatial codes
description: The MAVCP is the authors' own integration of auditory perception theories (auditory scene analysis, the association model) with multimedia learning theories (CTML, CATLM, ICALM). It posits three attentionally selected bases — sound base, word base and image base — organized into acoustic, verbal and visual mental representations that are integrated into a single mental model with prior knowledge. As the authors state, "this model emphasizes the integration not only of audio-textual (word base) and visual information (image base) but also of acoustic spatial codes (sound base) as a relevant aspect of multimedia learning." Learning quality depends on how clearly content is presented, extractable by attention, and attributable across bases.
requirements: Auditory and visual learning content must be clearly presented, extractable from surrounding information by attentional processes, and easily attributable to each other
constraints: The authors note the CTML mainly refers to two-dimensional learning material, and the MAVCP is proposed as a further development for spatial acoustic information
target_learning_goals: integration of audio explanations with exhibited visual content
memory of audio-explained exhibit content
examples: The MAVCP (Fig. 1) was used to derive the prediction that the spatial contiguity principle should extend to spatial acoustic information in exhibitions, tested in two experiments with a spatial audio guide

description: The article proposes a conceptual framework that extends Davis's Technology Acceptance Model by adding three external constructs — self-efficacy, educational quality, and technological complexity — as antecedents of perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness, which in turn drive behavioral intention. The model "adopts constructs drawn from the TAM and the motivational factors of e-learning adoption" and was tested with PLS-SEM on 299 Nigerian instructors. It addresses the gap that no prior Nigerian study had examined "the motivational factor of the instructor’s efficacy, technological complexity, and educational quality" together.

It was administered to instructors of three private schools across three geopolitical zones in Nigeria; "299 respondents (90.60%) were included in this study". citation: Rotem Israel-Fishelson, David Weintrop. (2026). Authenticity in a high school data science curriculum. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10622-1
title: Thick Authenticity framework (Shaffer & Resnick, 1999) as the organizing lens for analyzing curriculum authenticity
description: The study operationalizes Shaffer and Resnick's (1999) 'thick authenticity' framework, which the article describes as "a comprehensive view of authentic learning, defined as 'thick authenticity.'" It comprises four interconnected dimensions: personal authenticity (alignment with interests, values, goals), real-world authenticity (tasks mirroring professional contexts), disciplinary authenticity (thinking in the modes of a discipline), and authentic assessment (assessment reflecting real-world knowledge application). The researchers coded 108 relevant interview segments against these four dimensions to assess student perceptions.
requirements: Coding requires segments assignable to one or more dimensions, as instances of authenticity are not always mutually exclusive
constraints: The framework is applied to a single interest-driven high school data science curriculum context
target_learning_goals: data science practices
perceiving authenticity and relevance of learning activities
examples: Two researchers independently coded 350 interview segments, identified 108 authenticity-related segments, and achieved Cohen's Kappa of 0.79 (relevancy) and 0.89 (dimension coding)

As the article states, "The curriculum's flexibility boosted Personal Authenticity by enabling students to pursue data exploration activities and projects that resonated with their diverse interests." Each characteristic maps to one of the four thick-authenticity dimensions.

title: API Can Code: an interest-driven high school data science curriculum using RapidAPI, EduBlocks, and CODAP

It comprises three units of six lessons each: data impact and evaluation, programmatic data retrieval and manipulation from public APIs via EduBlocks, and data analysis and visualization with CODAP, culminating in an open-ended final project. Students query RapidAPI repositories, work with datasets on themes like music, sports, and earthquakes, and present findings to peers with structured slides.
