article_title: Co-designing a pedagogical framework and principles for a hybrid STEM learning environment design
citation: Mäkelä, T., Fenyvesi, K., Kankaanranta, M., Pnevmatikos, D., & Christodoulou, P. (2022). Co-designing a pedagogical framework and principles for a hybrid STEM learning environment. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10114-y
title: Consider a wide range of design principles rather than singular ones when designing learning environments
description: The article's closing recommendation is that learning environment design should draw on the full breadth of the framework rather than isolated principles. As the authors write, "Instead of focusing on singular design principles, we recommend considering a wide range of different design principles in order to support multiple ways of teaching and learning and to develop both subject-related and cross-curricular competencies". The framework's five categories operationalise this breadth.
requirements: Access to a framework organising principles into categories spanning cognitive, socio-emotional, subject-related and cross-curricular dimensions
constraints: Recommendation arises from this co-design study; no comparative test of singular versus wide-range approaches is reported
target_learners: designers and educators of STEM and other learning environments
target_learning_goals: multiple ways of teaching and learning
subject-related and cross-curricular competencies
examples: The STIMEY project employed the full set of design principles in developing its hybrid STEM learning environment
key_sources: Mäkelä, T., Fenyvesi, K., Kankaanranta, M., Pnevmatikos, D., & Christodoulou, P. (2022). Co-designing a pedagogical framework and principles for a hybrid STEM learning environment. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10114-y

article_title: Structured or unstructured educational robotics curriculum? A study of debugging in block-based programming
citation: Chrysanthos Socratous, Andri Ioannou. (2021). Structured or unstructured educational robotics curriculum? A study of debugging in block-based programming.
title: Structured versus unstructured educational robotics curriculum comparison design for block-based programming
description: The study implements a quasi-experimental comparison of two educational robotics curricula for young learners working in block-based programming: "a structured ER curriculum group and an unstructured one". Within the quasi-experiment, "both qualitative and quantitative data are collected", covering error frequency and type, debugging ability, and engagement in the learning process.
requirements: Two comparison groups, one following a structured ER curriculum and one an unstructured ER curriculum
constraints: Quasi-experimental design with two comparison groups (n = 35), not a randomized experiment
target_learners: young learners in block-based programming contexts
target_learning_goals: debugging programs
reducing programming errors
engagement in the learning process
examples: The study compared a structured ER curriculum group with an unstructured one (n = 35), collecting qualitative and quantitative data on errors, debugging, and engagement.
key_sources: Chrysanthos Socratous, Andri Ioannou. (2021). Structured or unstructured educational robotics curriculum? A study of debugging in block-based programming. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-10056-x

article_title: Measuring presence in virtual world teacher education: validation of the eXtended Reality Presence Scale
citation: Gandolfi, E., Soyturk, I., Kosko, K. W., Ferdig, R. E., & Clements, R. (2026). Measuring presence in virtual world teacher education: validation of the eXtended Reality Presence Scale. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10619-w
title: eXtended Reality Presence Scale (XRPS)
description: The XRPS is a 17-item Likert survey (1 = Never to 5 = Always) measuring presence in XR experiences, built on Lee's (2004) construct and scored via Rasch analysis into three subscales: emotional connectivity, co-presence, and awareness of self. Example items include "I felt like I was with actual students in the classroom." This study validated it for immersive videos of gaming environments such as Minecraft.edu.
requirements: Requires polytomous Rasch modeling with a minimum of 50 participants for precise item calibrations, per the article's cited guidance
constraints: Item 4 of the co-presence subscale misfit in this context and was excluded; the article notes twitches-based attention measures are context-dependent
target_learning_goals: measuring presence in immersive video-based teacher education
examples: Administered after each of two 360-degree videos (real classroom and Minecraft.edu) watched by 91 PSTs in sequence
key_sources: Gandolfi, E., Soyturk, I., Kosko, K. W., Ferdig, R. E., & Clements, R. (2026). Measuring presence in virtual world teacher education: validation of the eXtended Reality Presence Scale. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10619-w

article_title: Measuring presence in virtual world teacher education: validation of the eXtended Reality Presence Scale
citation: Gandolfi, E., Soyturk, I., Kosko, K. W., Ferdig, R. E., & Clements, R. (2026). Measuring presence in virtual world teacher education: validation of the eXtended Reality Presence Scale. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10619-w
title: Three-dimension framework of presence in XR (physical, social, and self-oriented presence)
description: The article adopts Lee's (2004) framework in which presence—the sensation of 'being there' in a technologically mediated environment—is examined from three angles: physical presence (interaction with physical elements, mediated by technology in XR), social presence (interaction with social actors and virtual characters), and self-presence (how users see and feel themselves, including identification with avatars). The article states these dimensions "collectively offer a holistic framework for designing, fostering, and measuring presence in XR environments" and reports the study's results support this framework.
requirements: Measurement instruments operationalizing the framework should capture emotional connectivity, co-presence, and self-awareness as distinct but related subscales
constraints: The article notes presence is one possible construct among alternatives such as immersion or engagement for evaluating mediated experiences
target_learning_goals: understanding and measuring presence in XR learning experiences
examples: The XRPS subscales used in this study map onto the framework's social and self-oriented dimensions
key_sources: Gandolfi, E., Soyturk, I., Kosko, K. W., Ferdig, R. E., & Clements, R. (2026). Measuring presence in virtual world teacher education: validation of the eXtended Reality Presence Scale. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10619-w

article_title: Integrating cognition, self-regulation, motivation, and metacognition: a framework of post-pandemic flipped classroom design
citation: Yan Shen, Dan Spencer, Jennifer Tagsold, Hyunsong Kim. (2025). Integrating cognition, self-regulation, motivation, and metacognition: a framework of post-pandemic flipped classroom design. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10485-y
title: Integrated flipped classroom design framework combining FL cycles, SRL cycles, and metacognitive FC orientation
description: The article proposes a conceptual framework of FC design with three main aspects: Flipped Learning (FL) Cycle, Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) Cycle, and Metacognitive FC Orientation. It is founded on interconnected theories — First Principles of Instruction, Self-Regulated Learning, the MUSIC Model of Academic Motivation, and Metacognition — because "a successful flipped classroom requires not only effective and engaging instructions and activities, but also self-regulated and motivated learners with metacognitive awareness." The FL cycle comprises online, in-class, and after-class stages; SRL cycles run in parallel with Proactive Planning, Performance Monitoring, and Learning Reflection stages; and orientation develops students' metacognitive knowledge about FC tasks, strategies, and themselves as learners.
requirements: Requires integration of the three SRL phases with recurring pre-class, in-class, and after-class learning activities to develop students' self-regulation skills required in FC
Requires effective FC design guided by a robust instructional design framework grounded in learning theories
constraints: The authors state there are no existing FC studies that have fully implemented the entire framework; supporting evidence comes from three studies that incorporated one or multiple design aspects
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning skills
metacognitive knowledge
academic motivation
active learning and higher-order thinking skills
key_sources: Yan Shen, Dan Spencer, Jennifer Tagsold, Hyunsong Kim. (2025). Integrating cognition, self-regulation, motivation, and metacognition: a framework of post-pandemic flipped classroom design. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10485-y

article_title: Integrating cognition, self-regulation, motivation, and metacognition: a framework of post-pandemic flipped classroom design
citation: Yan Shen, Dan Spencer, Jennifer Tagsold, Hyunsong Kim. (2025). Integrating cognition, self-regulation, motivation, and metacognition: a framework of post-pandemic flipped classroom design. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10485-y
title: Flipped learning cycle design pattern: defined cycles with gradually increasing challenge and regular specific feedback across online, in-class, and after-class steps
description: A repeatable lesson-level pattern in which each flipped learning cycle encompasses online, in-class, and after-class learning steps. Cycles should be "as consistent in length and steps as possible", with tasks designed by selectively applying the First Principles of Instruction; challenge levels should gradually increase along the cycle, from introductory online tasks to less structured in-class whole problems to after-class problems at sustained or increased complexity with reduced support; and regular, specific intrinsic and corrective feedback should be provided throughout the cycle steps to sustain students' self-perception of competence.
requirements: Defining the FL cycle length based on a regular class schedule makes the FL cycles easier to plan
Individual assistance should be offered when the challenge levels are likely to be above any particular student's abilities
constraints: Although there are mixed findings about whether the reduction of class time affects learning outcomes, the decision should be made based on the benefits of reduced class size, the students' existing SRL skills, and the amount of SRL support available
target_learning_goals: active learning
problem-centered application
student motivation and perceived competence
examples: Spencer et al. (2022) created flipped learning cycles guiding students through online lessons and assessments, in-class small-group problem solving, and independent after-class problems
key_sources: Yan Shen, Dan Spencer, Jennifer Tagsold, Hyunsong Kim. (2025). Integrating cognition, self-regulation, motivation, and metacognition: a framework of post-pandemic flipped classroom design. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10485-y

article_title: Revisiting Kuo and Belland’s exploratory study of undergraduate students’ perceptions of online learning: minority students in continuing education
citation: Beth Beschorner. (2021). Revisiting Kuo and Belland’s exploratory study of undergraduate students’ perceptions of online learning: minority students in continuing education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09900-3
title: Design online coursework through an asset lens that considers students' cultural and racialized experiences
description: The principle holds that instructors designing online coursework should treat students' cultural and racialized experiences as assets rather than deficits. The article states that instructors "might consider the cultural and racialized experiences of their students through an asset lens as they design online coursework." It frames this as a design orientation for equitable online instruction.
requirements: Instructors must attend to students' experiences when planning online coursework
constraints: Offered as a commentary recommendation during COVID-19 emergency online teaching, not a tested design
target_learners: undergraduate students in continuing education, including minority students
target_learning_goals: equitable participation and success in online courses
examples: The article describes how instructors might apply the asset lens when planning how students interact with content, instructor, and peers in online coursework
key_sources: Beth Beschorner. (2021). Revisiting Kuo and Belland’s exploratory study of undergraduate students’ perceptions of online learning: minority students in continuing education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09900-3

article_title: Revisiting Kuo and Belland’s exploratory study of undergraduate students’ perceptions of online learning: minority students in continuing education
citation: Beth Beschorner. (2021). Revisiting Kuo and Belland’s exploratory study of undergraduate students’ perceptions of online learning: minority students in continuing education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09900-3
title: Three types of online interaction: content, instructor, and other learners
description: The article organizes online course design around three interaction types, following the interaction framework it attributes to Moore (1989) and Kuo and Belland (2016): learners' interaction "with the content, with the instructor, and with other learners." Instructors are advised to determine, for each type, how students will interact when designing online coursework. The framework serves as the organizing structure for the article's equity recommendations.
requirements: Instructors must plan for each of the three interaction types when designing online courses
constraints: Applied here to undergraduate online courses in the context of the COVID-19 shift to online delivery
target_learning_goals: designing equitable online learning experiences across content, instructor, and peer interaction
examples: The commentary uses the three interaction types to structure its advice on creating more equitable online courses
key_sources: Beth Beschorner. (2021). Revisiting Kuo and Belland’s exploratory study of undergraduate students’ perceptions of online learning: minority students in continuing education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09900-3

article_title: Improving metacognition through self-explication in a digital self-regulated learning tool
citation: Eelco Braad, Nick Degens, Wolmet Barendregt, Wijnand IJsselsteijn. (2022). Improving metacognition through self-explication in a digital self-regulated learning tool. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10156-2
title: Conceptual model of metacognition during self-regulated learning combining SRL phases with five facets of learning
description: The article derives a conceptual model of metacognition during SRL from the COPES model (Winne & Hadwin, 1998), combining the preparatory, performance, and appraisal phases with five facets: conditions, operations, (meta)cognitive products, evaluations, and standards. It defines two adaptation routes: "metacognitive monitoring and control lead to adaptations of the current task definition, goals and performance expectations, and plans (local update)" and reflection leading to a global update of metacognitive knowledge. The model structures the tool's design rationale of encouraging informed local and global updates via self-explication.
requirements: Learners must be able to inspect their metacognitive processes through self-explication so belief-based judgments can be replaced by experience-based ones
constraints: The model is a metacognitive perspective that the article says must be seen within the broader construct of SRL
target_learning_goals: metacognitive knowledge and skills for self-regulated learning
examples: The tool's five prompt categories (ideas about learning, goals, plans, checks, improvements) map onto the model's phases and facets
key_sources: Eelco Braad, Nick Degens, Wolmet Barendregt, Wijnand IJsselsteijn. (2022). Improving metacognition through self-explication in a digital self-regulated learning tool. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10156-2

article_title: Improving metacognition through self-explication in a digital self-regulated learning tool
citation: Eelco Braad, Nick Degens, Wolmet Barendregt, Wijnand IJsselsteijn. (2022). Improving metacognition through self-explication in a digital self-regulated learning tool. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10156-2
title: Detached digital self-explication SRL tool with five prompt categories, refined prompt cards, and strategy cards
description: A web-application offering detached, domain-general or domain-specific metacognitive support in parallel to ongoing learning. It prompts learners to make implicit metacognition concrete via five main prompt categories (ideas about learning, goals, plans, checks, improvements to learning), each with 6–9 refined prompt cards and one metacognitive strategy card providing direct instruction. Learners "could freely navigate through the different categories as available and add, review, or update their responses as desired", with responses saved automatically. Materials were reviewed in a student focus group and by two educational experts.
requirements: Support must be made progressively available so as not to overwhelm learners or preclude self-initiated metacognitive processing
constraints: The domain-specific configuration requires designers to have some knowledge of the subject matter, limiting when and where the tool can be used
target_learners: 1st-year higher-education students in a multimedia design program
target_learning_goals: metacognitive awareness across all phases of self-regulated learning
examples: In the evaluation, the most frequently requested feature was an option to receive reminders to check up on learning within the tool
key_sources: Eelco Braad, Nick Degens, Wolmet Barendregt, Wijnand IJsselsteijn. (2022). Improving metacognition through self-explication in a digital self-regulated learning tool. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10156-2

article_title: Efficacy of a blended learning approach to elementary school reading instruction for students who are English Learners
citation: Elizabeth R. Kazakoff, Paul Macaruso, Pam Hook. (2018). Efficacy of a blended learning approach to elementary school reading instruction for students who are English Learners. Education Tech Research Dev 66:429–449. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-017-9565-7
title: Lexia Reading Core5 blended learning reading program
description: Core5 is a personalized, adaptive digital reading program for preschool through grade five, providing "a structured (i.e., explicitly teaches word identification and decoding), sequential approach" across phonological awareness, phonics, structural analysis, automaticity/fluency, vocabulary, and comprehension. It contains 18 levels subdivided into 89 activities and 1,243 units of 4-8 minutes, with an adaptive auto placement tool, scaffolded guided-practice steps, immediate corrective feedback, individualized Prescriptions of Intensity (20–80 min per week), teacher reports, and offline Lexia Lessons and Skill Builders. In this study it was integrated into standard ELA instruction via station or lab rotation models.
requirements: Students must meet usage fidelity, i.e., their Prescriptions of Intensity, for the program to work as studied
constraints: Mastery of 90–100% accuracy within a level is required to advance to the next level
target_learners: elementary students in grades K-5, including English Learners and at-risk readers
target_learning_goals: phonological awareness
phonics
structural analysis
fluency
vocabulary
reading comprehension
examples: Students began Core5 through an adaptive auto placement tool placing them at their actual skill level; 70% of each matched group began below grade level
key_sources: Elizabeth R. Kazakoff, Paul Macaruso, Pam Hook. (2018). Efficacy of a blended learning approach to elementary school reading instruction for students who are English Learners. Education Tech Research Dev 66:429–449. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-017-9565-7

article_title: Designing biomimetic robots: iterative development of an integrated technology design curriculum
citation: Debra Bernstein, Gillian Puttick, Kristen Wendell, Fayette Shaw, Ethan Danahy, Michael Cassidy. (2022). Designing biomimetic robots: iterative development of an integrated technology design curriculum. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-10061-0
title: BioRobots design conjecture: studying biological organisms supports understanding of structure–function relationships, which supports engineering design and CT practices
description: The BioRobots project rests on a design conjecture (Sandoval, 2014) that "studying biological organisms will support student understanding of structure–function relationships," and that using this understanding to design a robot will support student practices in engineering design and computational thinking. Conjectured embodiments and mediating processes follow from this conjecture, and the conjecture map was revised in Y3 to reflect evolving thinking about alignment of science, engineering, and CT practices.
requirements: A design task that requires students to create a conceptual model of the animal structure–function relationship by decomposing the animal system and extracting relevant principles
constraints: The conjecture was tested in 3- to 4-week middle school implementations in science, engineering, enrichment, and after-school settings
target_learners: middle school students in science, engineering, enrichment, and after-school programs
target_learning_goals: understanding of structure–function relationships in biology and engineering
engineering design practices
computational thinking practices such as decomposition, abstraction, and algorithmic thinking
examples: Students study animals such as pangolins, gophers, mole rats, and moles, then design digging robots using craft materials and the Hummingbird robotics kit programmed in Scratch or MakeCode
key_sources: Debra Bernstein, Gillian Puttick, Kristen Wendell, Fayette Shaw, Ethan Danahy, Michael Cassidy. (2022). Designing biomimetic robots: iterative development of an integrated technology design curriculum. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-10061-0

article_title: Designing biomimetic robots: iterative development of an integrated technology design curriculum
citation: Debra Bernstein, Gillian Puttick, Kristen Wendell, Fayette Shaw, Ethan Danahy, Michael Cassidy. (2022). Designing biomimetic robots: iterative development of an integrated technology design curriculum. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-10061-0
title: Biomimetic design task pattern: study animal structure–function, then design and build a robot inspired by that analysis
description: In this pattern, students first study the natural world to learn how animals accomplish tasks, then engineer a robot inspired by what they learned. The design challenge (a biomimetic search-and-rescue robot) requires students to decompose the animal system, extract relevant principles to create a conceptual model, use the model as a basis for conceptualizing their robot design, and build a functional robot, engaging science, engineering, and CT practices across a 3- to 4-week unit.
requirements: Biology resources (text and curated videos about animal structures and functions)
Engineering resources (mechanism examples, design worksheets)
Robotics kit and programming environment
constraints: Y1 experience showed an open-ended version of this pattern led to a wide range of outcomes; a narrowed task with targeted resources better enabled discipline-driven design
target_learning_goals: animal structure–function relationships
engineering design practices
computational thinking practices
examples: Y2 students designed pangolin-inspired digging robots with cable-drive then claw mechanisms, testing in a bin of shredded paper more than 20 times
key_sources: Debra Bernstein, Gillian Puttick, Kristen Wendell, Fayette Shaw, Ethan Danahy, Michael Cassidy. (2022). Designing biomimetic robots: iterative development of an integrated technology design curriculum. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-10061-0

article_title: Shifting to open education in our digital learning
citation: Kimmons, R. (2021). Shifting to open education in our digital learning. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09949-8
title: Diffusion of innovations explains slow OER adoption by lack of established relative advantage
description: The editorial applies Rogers' diffusion of innovations model to OER adoption, treating relative advantage as the primary driver of uptake. It argues that "lack of relative advantage is the primary reason for slow or limited adoption," so OER's relative advantage must be established in the literature and made clear to faculty and administrators for adoption to increase. The special issue's responses then complicate this account.
requirements: For OER adoption to increase, their relative advantage must be firmly established in the literature and made clear to faculty and administrators
constraints: The editorial argues relative advantage alone will not lead to rapid adoption if it is merely conceptualized as cost savings
target_learning_goals: adoption of open educational resources in course design
examples: The editorial frames Hilton's efficacy and perceptions reviews as instrumental in establishing OER's relative advantage in the literature.
key_sources: Kimmons, R. (2021). Shifting to open education in our digital learning. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09949-8

article_title: Editors’ introduction to the special issue on cognition & learning technology
citation: Dirk Ifenthaler, Pedro Isaías, J. Michael Spector, Kinshuk, Demetrios Sampson. (2009). Editors' introduction to the special issue on cognition & learning technology. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-009-9127-8
title: ALA-Reader with Pathfinder network analysis for capturing knowledge structures in student essays
description: ALA-Reader is a technology, used together with Pathfinder network analysis, that the special issue's first paper applied to student essays. According to the editors, it was used "to explore an automated procedure to capture and represent knowledge structures in student essays", making essay-based knowledge structure elicitation automated rather than manual.
requirements: Requires student essays as the input text from which knowledge structures are derived
constraints: Described by the editors as an exploration of an automated procedure, not as a validated method in this introduction
target_learning_goals: knowledge structure representation and assessment
examples: The first special issue paper by Clariana, Wallace and Godshalk applied ALA-Reader and Pathfinder network analysis to essays

article_title: Editors’ introduction to the special issue on cognition & learning technology
citation: Dirk Ifenthaler, Pedro Isaías, J. Michael Spector, Kinshuk, Demetrios Sampson. (2009). Editors' introduction to the special issue on cognition & learning technology. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-009-9127-8
title: HIMATT: highly integrated model assessment technology and tools
description: HIMATT is a suite of three integrated tools for assessing the development of skill and knowledge in challenging problem-solving domains. As the editors describe it, "HIMATT, elicits text and annotated concept maps, and then provides a set of automated analysis techniques to compare representations to a reference model (e.g., an expert model), to a prior representation by the problem solver, or to representations of other problem solvers."
requirements: Elicits text and annotated concept maps as input representations
Requires a comparison target such as an expert reference model, a prior representation, or other problem solvers' representations
constraints: The editors note its creators are still cross-validating the methods to determine areas of convergence and divergence
target_learners: problem solvers in challenging problem-solving domains
target_learning_goals: assessment of skill and knowledge development over time
examples: The second special issue paper by Pirnay-Dummer, Ifenthaler and Spector presents the HIMATT suite; MITOCAR is described as one of the tools now integrated in HIMATT

article_title: The recording of audience reactions by infra-red photography
citation: Greenhill, L. P. (1955). The Recording of Audience Reactions by Infra-Red Photography. Technical Report SDC 269-7-56, Instructional Film Research Program, Pennsylvania State University, for the Special Devices Center, Office of Naval Research. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=The+Recording+of+Audience+Reactions+by+Infra-Red+Photography
title: Infrared time-lapse photography apparatus for recording audience reactions to film
description: The report developed a practical means of recording audience reactions in a darkened room using infrared photographs, so that reactions can be related to film content. The technique "made use of high speed infrared film, time lapse photography on 16 mm films at one frame a second, infrared reflector heat lamps with ruby glass, mirror reflection of the picture on the screen for synchronization purposes, and a special projector for analyzing the scenes." Counting persons watching the screen yields a measure presumably related to a sequence's effectiveness, replacing time-consuming test administration.
requirements: Permit relatively continuous records of reactions
Records easily synchronized with the film
Economical
Portable
Permit recordings at very low levels of illumination
target_learning_goals: assessing audience attention and reaction to film sequences as an indicator of learning from films
examples: The procedure was demonstrated with children watching puppets, and its application is described in A. E. Siegel's 1955 Stanford PhD dissertation on film-mediated fantasy aggression.
key_sources: Greenhill, L. P. (1955). The Recording of Audience Reactions by Infra-Red Photography. Technical Report SDC 269-7-56, Instructional Film Research Program, Pennsylvania State University, for the Special Devices Center, Office of Naval Research. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=The+Recording+of+Audience+Reactions+by+Infra-Red+Photography

article_title: The recording of audience reactions by infra-red photography
citation: Greenhill, L. P. (1955). The Recording of Audience Reactions by Infra-Red Photography. Technical Report SDC 269-7-56, Instructional Film Research Program, Pennsylvania State University, for the Special Devices Center, Office of Naval Research. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=The+Recording+of+Audience+Reactions+by+Infra-Red+Photography
title: Design audience-reaction recording methods to be continuous, synchronized, economical, portable, and usable at very low illumination
description: Before selecting equipment, the report analyzed needs for infrared photography of audiences and derived five requirements: the method "should permit relatively continuous records of reactions," records "should be easily synchronized with the film," it "should be economical," "portable," and "permit the making of recordings at very low levels of illumination." These needs then guided equipment selection and method development. The principle generalizes as requirements analysis preceding instrument design for classroom observation.
requirements: Needs analysis should precede equipment selection for recording methods
constraints: Prior infrared photography methods were generally too expensive to use and difficult to apply
target_learners: school children in darkened viewing rooms
target_learning_goals: measuring audience reactions to instructional film content
examples: Based on the five needs the report selected equipment and developed methods for making film records of audience reaction, demonstrated with children watching puppets.

Technical Report SDC 269-7-56, Instructional Film Research Program, Pennsylvania State University, for the Special Devices Center, Office of Naval Research. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=The+Recording+of+Audience+Reactions+by+Infra-Red+Photography

article_title: Online discussion compensates for suboptimal timing of supportive information presentation in a digitally supported learning environment
citation: Noroozi, O., Busstra, M. C., Mulder, M., Biemans, H. J. A., Tobi, H., Geelen, A., van't Veer, P., Chizari, M. (2012). Online discussion compensates for suboptimal timing of supportive information presentation in a digitally supported learning environment. Education Tech Research Dev (2012) 60:193-221. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-011-9217-2
title: Cognitive load theory as the explanatory framework for timing of information presentation in IDLM
description: The article uses cognitive load theory to explain why the timing of supportive information matters: 'Total cognitive load comprises intrinsic, extraneous, and germane cognitive load.' Intrinsic load is fixed by learner expertise and material nature; extraneous load stems from inappropriate design and should be minimized, for example by optimally timing information presentation; germane load is the working-memory resources devoted to elaboration that constitutes actual learning. The study applies this framework to predict and interpret the effects of information-before versus information-during presentation in interactive digital learning materials.
requirements: Instructional designs should minimize extraneous load (e.g. avoiding temporal and spatial split attention) and optimize germane load
constraints: The article notes that making learning too easy may reduce elaborative deep processing, invoking the desirable difficulty perspective as a counterweight
target_learners: higher education students in life sciences
target_learning_goals: knowledge construction in complex, high element interactivity tasks such as designing evaluation studies
examples: The IDLM task clusters on evaluation-study design contained supportive information modules whose timing (before vs. during each cluster) was manipulated between conditions
key_sources: Noroozi, O., Busstra, M. C., Mulder, M., Biemans, H. J. A., Tobi, H., Geelen, A., van't Veer, P., Chizari, M. (2012). title: Taxonomy of information types and their timing of presentation in digital learning materials
description: The article organizes instructional information into types with distinct preferred timing: 'The literature points out that various types of information such as supportive, procedural, declarative, prerequisite, etc. require different timing of presentation (information before ''IB'' or information during ''ID'' the learning task) in IDLM.' Supportive information (conceptual, mental and causal models, theories, clues to be understood rather than memorized) suits high element interactivity tasks; procedural information provides step-by-step rules for recurrent task aspects; declarative information helps connect new information to existing knowledge structures. The study focuses on the timing of supportive information, where prior findings were mixed.
requirements: Timing decisions should take into account the load a task imposes on the learner's cognitive system
constraints: Prior studies on supportive information timing reported mixed findings, with evidence favoring both before-task and during-task presentation
target_learners: higher education students working with interactive digital learning materials
target_learning_goals: meaningful learning through elaboration and connection of new information to existing cognitive structures
examples: Kester et al.'s studies reviewed in the framework found supportive-before favored in one exploratory study but supportive-during formats yielded better efficiency in others

The CSCL platform Drewlite, a simplified version of Drew developed within the Scale project, 'comprises different tools for communication, collaboration, and argumentation such as chat, graph, text board, view board, and multi modules.' Its graph module let students build box-and-arrow knowledge maps with comment fields for tests 1 and 2, and its chat module supported the online discussion condition.

constraints: Drewlite is less elaborate in managing sessions and traces than the full Drew platform, which the authors judged irrelevant for their study

title: SOLO-based coding scheme for quality of knowledge construction
description: Knowledge construction quality was operationalized with a content analysis coding scheme based on Veldhuis-Diermanse (2002), itself grounded in the SOLO taxonomy of Biggs and Collis. 'The original coding scheme consists of ﬁve hierarchical levels (after Biggs and Collis 1982; Biggs 1999) from basic to advanced': E prestructural, D unistructural, C multistructural, B relational, and A extended abstract. Contributions in the Drewlite comment screens were segmented into meaningful units, coded with level-specific verbs, scored 1-5 points, and averaged per student. Inter-rater Cohen's kappa was 0.78 for test 1 and 0.81 for test 2, with 85% identical scores on intra-coder retest.

constraints: Scores of three inactive students were excluded due to limited contributions, leaving 84 students in the analysis

target_learning_goals: assessing quality of knowledge construction regardless of content area

article_title: Automated assessment system for programming courses: a case study for teaching data structures and algorithms
citation: Andre L. C. Barczak, Anuradha Mathrani, Binglan Han, Napoleon H. Reyes. (2023). Automated assessment system for programming courses: a case study for teaching data structures and algorithms. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10277-2
title: Bespoke automarker for C++ DSA coursework with test-case marking, resubmission, tolerance intervals and infinite-loop timer
description: A purpose-built client–server automated assessment tool for C++ programming exercises in a second-year DSA course, written in PHP with MySQL storage under Apache/Linux, separate from the institutional LMS. Students upload code from a template; the server compiles with GCC and "executes the code over 10 test cases, while referencing a model solution supplied by the teacher", marking 0–10 with endless resubmission until the deadline. A parser tolerates text variation, tolerance intervals handle approximate answers, and a timer flags possible infinite loops.
requirements: Students access the stand-alone server via the institutional network or the institution's VPN
A well-defined code template is crucial since assignments are directly handled by the machine
constraints: The tool cannot analyse code directly to give a specific clue why code fails
It is not possible to know if a program is truly in an infinite loop due to the undecidability of the halting problem
target_learning_goals: programming and algorithmic reasoning skills in data structures and algorithms
examples: The queue assignment sets a tolerance value because correct answers may vary with the initial state and order of updates of multiple queues; assignments with a single correct answer have tolerance set to zero
Normally half of the test inputs are known to students while the other half are kept hidden to avoid hard-coding results
key_sources: Andre L. C. Barczak, Anuradha Mathrani, Binglan Han, Napoleon H. Reyes. (2023). Automated assessment system for programming courses: a case study for teaching data structures and algorithms. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10277-2

citation: Andre L. C. Barczak, Anuradha Mathrani, Binglan Han, Napoleon H. Reyes. (2023). Automated assessment system for programming courses: a case study for teaching data structures and algorithms. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10277-2
title: Activity Theory six-element framework framing automarker-mediated formative learning
description: The article uses Activity Theory as the pedagogical lens aligning the automarker with DSA coursework. "AT extends the three elements of the Vygotskian triangle (1934–1987) into six elements that together realize the final outcomes": subject (instructor), tool (automarker), object(ives) (building algorithmic reasoning and programming skills), learning community (instructor and students), rules and regulations (prescribed coursework), and division of labour (teacher and learner roles). Ongoing interactions among the six elements transfer into final outcomes such as programming practice and instructor workaround strategies.
requirements: The core of AT is the proposed learning activity, emphasizing how ongoing interactions take place between the six elements
Community members have clearly defined responsibilities specific to their role and must comply with set rules and regulations
constraints: The framework is applied to one DSA course context at a tertiary institution
target_learning_goals: know-what, know-how and know-why competencies in programming
examples: Figure 1 (A) and (B) maps the AT elements to this study's context, with the automarker as tool and the DSA coursework rules governing activities

title: Seven progressive DSA coursework activities spanning linked-list, stack, queue, list, tree, graph and heap
description: The DSA coursework was organised into seven distinct topics forming learning activities that gradually extended in complexity of programmatic concepts. "The DSA coursework was organised into seven distinct topics related to the different data structures, namely linked-list, stack, queue, list, tree, graph and heap." Table 1 details each activity's task (e.g., adding sparse matrices, evaluating RPNs, Dijkstra shortest path, heap sorting) and the automarker functionality for marking it, including stress tests, infinite-loop checks and tolerance-based verification.
requirements: Activities must be pertinent to each topic since different programming skills apply to different topics/sub-topics
Exercises need a justified pedagogical foundation formalizing skills and notions pertinent to the algorithmic field
constraints: Activities gradually extended in complexity to challenge students within one second-year course
target_learning_goals: algorithmic reasoning and programming practice across core data structures
examples: Activity 6 asks students to find the shortest path from a source node to every other node in a graph using Dijkstra's algorithm, with the automarker verifying minimum distances and using graphs with islands to stress the code

title: Allow repeated code resubmission with automated feedback to encourage practice and build coding competencies
description: The article recommends an assessment design in which students may resubmit code repeatedly and receive automated feedback, so that practice drives competency building. As the authors state, "the strategy of allowing students to resubmit codes multiple times and provide them with automated feedback encourages them to practice and build their coding competencies". In the DSA course this was implemented by the automarker, which marked each submission against test cases and gave clues for debugging before the deadline.
requirements: An automated assessment tool that evaluates submissions against test cases and returns feedback clues
Assignments with a deadline within which resubmissions are permitted
constraints: The article notes students may otherwise rely on numerous trial-and-error submissions rather than leverage the tool for critical thinking
target_learners: undergraduate computer science students in practice-oriented programming courses
target_learning_goals: building programming and coding competencies through sustained practice
examples: Students were given endless opportunities to resubmit their codes multiple times until the assignment deadline, with the automarker displaying marks and clues after each attempt

article_title: Safeguarding student privacy in an age of analytics
citation: Royce Kimmons. (2021). Safeguarding student privacy in an age of analytics. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09950-1
title: Start learning analytics with data types that introduce minimal risk to students and are well-connected to the system's intended learning objectives
description: The article recommends that ethical learning analytics design should not treat all data uniformly but begin by selecting data types that pose little risk to students while serving the system's purpose. It states that professionals "should start by identifying and using data types that introduce minimal risk to students" that are also "reasonably well-connected to the intended purpose and learning objectives of the system."
requirements: Student voices should be involved in decision making regarding learning analytics systems.
constraints: An omnibus approach wherein all types of data are treated with equal levels of privacy consideration is overly simplistic.
target_learners: students whose data are used in learning analytics systems
target_learning_goals: ethical use of student data in learning analytics systems
examples: The recommendation is drawn from Ifenthaler and Schumacher's (2016) survey findings on differing student privacy sensitivity across data types.
key_sources: Royce Kimmons. (2021). Safeguarding student privacy in an age of analytics. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09950-1

article_title: Safeguarding student privacy in an age of analytics
citation: Royce Kimmons. (2021). Safeguarding student privacy in an age of analytics. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09950-1
title: Professional standards for student privacy in learning analytics remain nebulous and require ongoing leadership, thoughtfulness, and sensitivity
description: The article frames the ethical governance of learning analytics as an immature, unsettled domain: technological development outpaces responsible policy and ethics, and the collected responses show "a unified call for researchers, practitioners, and policy makers to be more aware of and responsive to student privacy." It underscores that "professional standards in this space remain somewhat nebulous at present" and require ongoing leadership and sensitivity to ensure ethical behavior.
requirements: Ongoing leadership, thoughtfulness, and sensitivity from researchers, practitioners, and policy makers to ensure ethical behavior.
constraints: Learning analytics systems introduce concomitant potentials for harm alongside their potential to benefit students.
target_learners: students whose behaviors are tracked, analyzed, and studied in educational settings
target_learning_goals: ethical engagement in learning analytics and related activities with student data
examples: The editorial synthesizes three responses (research, policy, practitioner perspectives) as evidence of a collective call for privacy-responsive practice.

article_title: Chaos: exploring an engaging online model for rapid application during the pandemic
citation: Joshua W. Tabor. (2020). Chaos: exploring an engaging online model for rapid application during the pandemic. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09878-y
title: The Own it, Learn it, Share it framework structures student-centered online learning in three steps
description: Tabor describes Lee and Hannafin's framework as a three-step student-centered course design built on self-determination theory, constructivism, and constructionism. In 'own it', students set their own goals; in 'learn it', teachers support them through direct instruction, tools, resources or discourse; in 'share it', students present a completed artifact to a selected group for feedback. Each step is designed to provide support as students explore topics interesting to them with a tangible product evaluated upon completion.
requirements: Teachers must understand the rationale behind each step of the framework, which the authors support with multiple examples explaining the 'why'
constraints: Applying the outline may be difficult due to a possible lack of understanding of student-centered learning techniques, lack of time to train teachers, and possibly teacher apathy towards online education
target_learning_goals: Student engagement and lifelong learning in digital, student-centered environments
examples: Tabor proposes schools let teachers practice with the framework and set expectations that some, if not all, of it be followed when planning for the upcoming year

article_title: Insights on identifying potential types of guidance for supporting student inquiry when using virtual and remote labs in science
citation: Gamor, K.I. (2021). Insights on identifying potential types of guidance for supporting student inquiry when using virtual and remote labs in science. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09928-5
title: Taxonomy of guidance types for supporting student inquiry in virtual and remote labs
description: The article engages with a taxonomy of potential types of guidance for supporting student inquiry when using virtual and remote labs in science, drawn from the Zacharia et al. (2015) literature review it responds to. The article's keyword list names the guidance types covered: "Process constraints", "Performance dashboard", "Prompts", "Heuristics", "Scaffolds", "Direct presentation of information", "Automated guidance", "Automated tutoring", and "Adaptive feedback". The framework describes how and when to apply these guidance types across inquiry phases for optimal effect.
requirements: Guidance must be matched to the relevant phase of inquiry to achieve optimal effect, per the reviewed framework
target_learners: students conducting science inquiry with virtual and remote labs
target_learning_goals: science inquiry skills supported by guidance in computer-supported inquiry learning environments
examples: The article indexes the taxonomy's guidance types as keywords: process constraints, performance dashboards, prompts, heuristics, scaffolds, direct presentation of information, automated guidance, automated tutoring, and adaptive feedback.
key_sources: Gamor, K.I. (2021). Insights on identifying potential types of guidance for supporting student inquiry when using virtual and remote labs in science. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09928-5

article_title: Insights on identifying potential types of guidance for supporting student inquiry when using virtual and remote labs in science
citation: Gamor, K.I. (2021). Insights on identifying potential types of guidance for supporting student inquiry when using virtual and remote labs in science. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09928-5
title: Apply guidance types matched to the inquiry phase and to how and when they are used for optimal effect
description: The principle holds that guidance in inquiry learning should be selected not only by type but by timing: the appropriate type of guidance should be leveraged during the relevant phase of inquiry. The article credits the reviewed framework with aptly describing "how and when to apply the types of guidance for optimal effect", making phase-matching a condition of optimal guidance effect.
requirements: Designers must know which guidance type is appropriate for each phase of inquiry before deploying it
constraints: Optimal effect depends on applying guidance at the right phase; mis-timed guidance is not addressed as beneficial
target_learners: students conducting inquiry with virtual and remote labs in science
target_learning_goals: effective support of student inquiry through appropriately timed guidance
examples: The reviewed framework describes how and when to apply guidance types such as prompts, heuristics, scaffolds, process constraints, and direct presentation of information across inquiry phases.

article_title: Student engagement profiles in a mobile app: Links to self-regulated learning and performance
citation: Wong, J., Khalil, M., Suschevskiy, V., Baars, M., de Koning, B., & Paas, F. (2026). Student engagement profiles in a mobile app: Links to self-regulated learning and performance. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10586-2
title: Mobile study app for retrieval practice with practice, test, compete, and battle modes
description: A mobile study app developed by a university lecturer, developer, and programmer, designed to enhance learning by facilitating SRL through retrieval practice with instructor-provided multiple-choice questions and feedback. Students could use it in "practice, test, compete, and battle" modes: practice gives immediate feedback per item, test gives feedback at the end of a set, compete is a timed competition with a leaderboard, and battle is a peer or instructor challenge. Use in the Law course was optional.
requirements: The course instructor must provide a set of multiple-choice questions along with answers and explanations for the app to be used in a course.
constraints: The app provides only MCQs, which the authors note face arguments about whether they can assess higher-order cognition.
target_learning_goals: retrieval practice and reinforcement of key course information
familiarization with multiple-choice exam questions
examples: In the nine-week Law course, 60% of final exam grades were based on MCQ scores, and app use was an optional study tool during self-study time.

article_title: Exploring the role of synchrony in asynchronous, synchronous, and quasi-synchronous online learner engagement
citation: Duncan Culbreth · Florence Martin. (2025). Exploring the role of synchrony in asynchronous, synchronous, and quasi-synchronous online learner engagement. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10504-y
title: Bichronous online learning framework extended to position MIM quasi-synchronicity as supporting BOL
description: Bichronous online learning (BOL) is "a framework that considers synchrony as a spectrum with three categories: Asynchronous, synchronous, and bichronous", blending asynchronous and synchronous modalities within one learning environment. This study extends BOL by framing mobile instant messaging (MIM) as a quasi-synchronous modality, and proposes that "quasi-synchronicity may be considered a subset of BOL", since a single service can support a range of synchronies through secondary features.
requirements: A modality must demonstrate both asynchronous and synchronous qualities, as MIM does via notifications allowing students to read messages after posting
constraints: Research on instructional design for BOL is described as nascent
The proposition rests on one course-based mixed-method study
target_learners: graduate and upperclassman undergraduate students in online courses
target_learning_goals: online discussion and debate skills
engagement in online learning environments
examples: Debates in an online graduate course were run via Moodle forum, Zoom video call, and Discord MIM across three consecutive weeks, with one student describing MIM as striking "a nice middle ground between the forum (almost completely asynchronous) and the zoom call (almost completely synchronous)"

citation: Schmid, R., Pauli, C., & Petko, D. (2023). Examining the use of digital technology in schools with a school-wide approach to personalized learning. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10167-z
title: Three types of digital technology integration in schools with school-wide personalized learning
description: The article systematizes its three case analyses into a taxonomy of how schools integrate digital tools into daily practices under a school-wide personalized learning policy. As the authors state, "A systematization of our analyses resulted in three different types in terms of how schools integrate digital tools into their daily practices": selective use according to individual teacher preference, selective use according to individual student preference, and structural use in accordance with a school-wide strategy. The taxonomy is derived from qualitative content analysis of interviews, observations, and documents in three contrasting Swiss lower-secondary schools.
requirements: Derived from multiple-case analysis of schools that have implemented personalized learning school-wide, with data triangulated across student questionnaire, interviews, observations, and curriculum documents
constraints: Based on three cases selected as the schools with the most frequent digital technology use among 31 Swiss lower-secondary schools; the authors present the types as indications for future research and practice rather than a validated typology
target_learners: lower-secondary students (8th grade) in schools with personalized learning concepts
target_learning_goals: implementation of personalized learning through digital technology use
examples: The three case-study schools each exemplified one type: School A (teacher preference), School B (student preference), and School C (school-wide strategy)

title: Self-developed learning platform with barcode-based assignment tracking in a personalized learning school
description: School C uses a self-developed learning platform that is crucial to organizing its personalized teaching, especially during self-directed learning phases. Teachers record each assignment on the platform, where "Every assignment receives a barcode, which is needed for the administration of completed assignments"; missed deadlines turn assignments red, requiring students to attend in-depth lessons. The platform "primarily helps the teachers administrate the individual tasks and further serves as 'file manager' for the teaching materials," though assignments are still printed weekly because providing every student a device is not financially possible.
requirements: Teachers record every assignment on the platform with a barcode; maintenance resources are limited (ICT supporters had only four hours per year), so all devices share the same interface
constraints: Assignments are printed out for students because providing each student a device is currently financially not possible, per the ICT supporter

target_learning_goals: organization and administration of individualized assignments and learning plans

title: Regular self-directed learning phases with personal learning plans as the structural core of school-wide personalized learning
description: Across the Swiss perLen schools, personalized learning was implemented through a common structural pattern: regular scheduled time slots in which students learn autonomously following individual learning plans, with teachers providing adaptive support. As the article states, "they have integrated regular time slots in the schedule in which the students learn autonomously according to a personal learning plan." During these phases students have more voice and choice about what, how, and when they learn, and digital technology use is concentrated in them (e.g., computer workstations in learning landscapes and learning studios).
requirements: Schedule slots for self-directed learning; personal learning plans per student; teachers reoriented toward adaptive support during these phases
constraints: Observed in German-speaking Swiss lower-secondary schools with explicitly implemented personalized learning concepts; implementations differed in details across schools
target_learners: lower-secondary students in heterogeneous learning groups
target_learning_goals: student self-direction, student voice and choice, adaptive individual support
examples: School A students spend one third of their time in self-directed learning phases in mixed classes, working in a learning landscape; School C runs learning studios of about 50 students

article_title: Interaction analysis of learning objects in online courses: What are their interactive characteristics and design intent behind them?
citation: Victoria Abramenka-Lachheb, Gamze Ozogul. (2025). Interaction analysis of learning objects in online courses: What are their interactive characteristics and design intent behind them? Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10556-0
title: Window of Interaction framework: eight dimensions defining the interactive potential of an artifact
description: The Window of Interaction (WoI) framework, drawn from HCI by Janlert and Stolterman, provides "an analytical and descriptive approach to understanding how technology is designed to foster interaction." It analyzes interactivity as a property of designed artifacts rather than user experience, rating eight dimensions from low to high: agency, independence, receptivity, predictability, freedom of action, pace/time, attention demand, and awareness level. This study reports the first empirical application of WoI in Instructional Design and Technology, prioritizing agency, receptivity, freedom of action, pace, and attention demand.
requirements: The framework is non-prescriptive: it "does not attempt to prescribe what a highly interactive environment is,or how it should be designed," allowing continuous reinterpretation
constraints: The framework "does not offer quantifiable measurements akin to hard sciences but rather is subject to individual judgments that are subjective by nature"
target_learning_goals: supporting authentic learning tasks through human-technology interaction
examples: The authors operationalized five WoI dimensions into interview questions and artifact-analysis rubrics (Table 1), rating each of 19 learning objects low/medium/high on each dimension

article_title: Interaction analysis of learning objects in online courses: What are their interactive characteristics and design intent behind them?
citation: Victoria Abramenka-Lachheb, Gamze Ozogul. (2025). Interaction analysis of learning objects in online courses: What are their interactive characteristics and design intent behind them? Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10556-0
title: Corpus of 19 demonstrated learning objects rated on WoI dimensions
description: Participants presented 19 learning objects: "13 shared one each, while two shared three each." Table 2 categorizes them as videos, simulations, eLearning sites, graphics, and LMS assignments, rating each on agency, receptivity, freedom of action, pace/time, and attention demand. Coding allowed finer-grained distinctions, with some objects falling between levels (e.g., between middle and high), visualized along a continuum in Fig. 4.
requirements: Analysis excluded default features of the technology resources, focusing on "what the participants created and how they made their learning objects interactive"
constraints: Ratings rest on designers' self-reported descriptions of their objects rather than direct measurement of user interaction behavior
target_learning_goals: interactive engagement with course content
examples: Object 15, a course site designed as a game on an LMS, was rated high agency, low receptivity, high freedom of action, high pace, middle attention demand
key_sources: Victoria Abramenka-Lachheb, Gamze Ozogul. (2025). Interaction analysis of learning objects in online courses: What are their interactive characteristics and design intent behind them? Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10556-0

article_title: Interaction analysis of learning objects in online courses: What are their interactive characteristics and design intent behind them?
citation: Victoria Abramenka-Lachheb, Gamze Ozogul. (2025). Interaction analysis of learning objects in online courses: What are their interactive characteristics and design intent behind them? Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10556-0
title: Treat low receptivity as an intentional pedagogical choice rather than a design shortcoming
description: The article recommends that designers deliberately limit receptivity — for example, requiring learners to complete all content before advancing — when the goal is to guide learners through critical content in a controlled sequence before complex authentic tasks. Low receptivity "should not be interpreted as a shortcoming, but rather, it reflects intentional decisions to support specific pedagogical goals through interaction design."
requirements: Designers must tie the level of receptivity to specific learning goals and prerequisite knowledge needs rather than to interactivity for its own sake
constraints: Grounded in designers' self-reported intent from a small qualitative sample, not in measured learner outcomes
target_learning_goals: prerequisite knowledge building before authentic learning tasks
examples: Forced interaction sequences requiring learners to complete all components before advancing were used to focus attention and ensure prerequisite understanding
key_sources: Victoria Abramenka-Lachheb, Gamze Ozogul. (2025). Interaction analysis of learning objects in online courses: What are their interactive characteristics and design intent behind them? Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10556-0

article_title: Interaction analysis of learning objects in online courses: What are their interactive characteristics and design intent behind them?
citation: Victoria Abramenka-Lachheb, Gamze Ozogul. (2025). Interaction analysis of learning objects in online courses: What are their interactive characteristics and design intent behind them? Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10556-0
title: Minimize attention demand of interactive learning objects so learners can focus on authentic tasks
description: Because authentic learning tasks inherently require higher-order thinking, the article recommends that interactive learning objects minimize unnecessary cognitive strain: "Designers should focus on making navigation and interaction intuitive so that learners can fully engage with the content and tasks rather than being burdened by complex interface mechanics." Most analyzed objects were rated low on attention demand.
requirements: Navigation and interaction must be intuitive; external coders advised that attention demand should remain low from a technology perspective so students focus on the authentic task itself
constraints: Recommendation arises in the context of authentic learning tasks in online higher education courses
target_learning_goals: higher-order thinking in authentic learning tasks
examples: External coders pointed out that attention demand should remain low so students can focus on the authentic task rather than figuring out how to use the technology, prompting reanalysis of all artifacts
key_sources: Victoria Abramenka-Lachheb, Gamze Ozogul. (2025). Interaction analysis of learning objects in online courses: What are their interactive characteristics and design intent behind them? Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10556-0

article_title: An experimental comparison of conclusion-drawing by the communicator and by the audience
citation: Hovland, Carl I., and Mandell, Wallace. (1952). An Experimental Comparison of Conclusion-Drawing by the Communicator and by the Audience. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 47, 581-88. https://psycnet.apa.org
title: Resistance-to-acceptance account of post-communication opinion change
description: The abstract's general conclusion offers a mechanism account of delayed opinion change: content is learned equally from trustworthy and untrustworthy sources, but an "initial resistance to the acceptance of the material presented by an untrustworthy source" suppresses immediate agreement. If this resistance diminishes with time while the content is forgotten more slowly, agreement with the untrustworthy source increases after the communication. The abstract presents this as an explanatory assumption for the observed data rather than a separately tested model.
requirements: Applies to communications where the content itself provides the basis for the opinion, so that content is retained longer than the resistance to accepting it
constraints: Presented by the abstractor as an explanatory assumption accounting for the post-communication opinion changes, not as a directly tested prediction
target_learning_goals: opinion change and retention of communicated factual content
examples: The abstracted four-week follow-up showing equal retention but increased agreement with the untrustworthy source
key_sources: Hovland, Carl I., and Mandell, Wallace. (1952). An Experimental Comparison of Conclusion-Drawing by the Communicator and by the Audience. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 47, 581-88. https://doi.org/10.1007/bf02716997

article_title: Understanding students’ game experiences throughout the developmental process of the number navigation game
citation: Phuong Bui, Gabriela Rodríguez-Aflecht, Boglárka Brezovszky, Minna M. Hannula-Sormunen, Samuli Laato, Erno Lehtinen. (2020). Understanding students' game experiences throughout the developmental process of the number navigation game. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09755-8
title: Poels et al.'s multidimensional game experience framework, extended with a positive value dimension
description: The study models students' gaming experience using Poels et al.'s (2007) framework of core game experience dimensions, extended with a positive value dimension measuring students' belief that the game helps them. The article states the framework consists "of seven dimensions of game experience as (a) flow, (b) (sensory and imaginative) immersion, (c) competence, (d) challenge, (e) positive affect, (f) negative affect, and (g) tension". The Game Experience Questionnaire operationalizes these plus positive values in eight subscales used to compare NNG versions.
requirements: The GEQ subscales require adequate reliability; the article removed Challenge and Tension from NNG 3 analysis due to low alpha (0.38)
constraints: The questionnaire was simplified in language and length for the age of participants, with 15 of 42 original items removed and 4 items added
target_learning_goals: whole-number arithmetic flexibility and adaptivity
student engagement and motivation in mathematics learning
examples: The GEQ was answered by different student groups after playing four NNG versions from 2014 to 2016, with eight separate factors found via principal component analysis
key_sources: Phuong Bui, Gabriela Rodríguez-Aflecht, Boglárka Brezovszky, Minna M. Hannula-Sormunen, Samuli Laato, Erno Lehtinen. (2020). Understanding students' game experiences throughout the developmental process of the number navigation game. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09755-8

article_title: Understanding students’ game experiences throughout the developmental process of the number navigation game
citation: Phuong Bui, Gabriela Rodríguez-Aflecht, Boglárka Brezovszky, Minna M. Hannula-Sormunen, Samuli Laato, Erno Lehtinen. (2020). Understanding students' game experiences throughout the developmental process of the number navigation game. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09755-8
title: Number Navigation Game (NNG), an intrinsically integrated mathematics game for primary students
description: NNG is a mathematical game-based learning environment for primary school students focusing on flexibility and adaptivity with whole-number arithmetic. Players navigate a ship on a 100-square map by entering arithmetic operations to collect materials and return to harbor, with moves and energy scoring modes. The article describes it as having "an 'intrinsically integrated' design (Habgood and Ainsworth 2011a, b) in which the core gaming mechanism is integrated directly to the educational content of the game". It evolved through four versions from 2D simple graphics to a 3D Unity3D version with extrinsic motivational features.
requirements: Development demanded continuous testing and development activities, a multidisciplinary team of researchers, educators and programmers, and extensive research funding
constraints: The article notes intrinsically integrated games "can be more expensive and difficult to develop", and that funding limits hinder application of research-based games in the real world
target_learners: fourth to sixth grade primary school students
target_learning_goals: adaptive number knowledge
flexibility and adaptivity with whole-number arithmetic
maintaining interest in mathematics learning
examples: Across versions the game added a number pad, visual cues, pirate ships and hidden operations, a Shop, a Lighthouse Island, tutorial and hint options, and customization features
key_sources: Phuong Bui, Gabriela Rodríguez-Aflecht, Boglárka Brezovszky, Minna M. Hannula-Sormunen, Samuli Laato, Erno Lehtinen. (2020). Understanding students' game experiences throughout the developmental process of the number navigation game. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09755-8

article_title: Understanding students’ game experiences throughout the developmental process of the number navigation game
citation: Phuong Bui, Gabriela Rodríguez-Aflecht, Boglárka Brezovszky, Minna M. Hannula-Sormunen, Samuli Laato, Erno Lehtinen. (2020). Understanding students' game experiences throughout the developmental process of the number navigation game. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09755-8
title: Serious game designers should prioritize usability and interface clarity, and design reward systems so players can see and own their transformations
description: Based on the NNG developmental evidence, the article recommends that designers focus effort on usability and clarity of the user interface in addition to educational content, and that reward mechanisms be designed so players visibly construct and own their game world. The article concludes that "improvement in game's usability and clarity in the user interface were effective in providing more positive, smooth and immersive game experiences for players". It also stresses paying attention to "the integration of meaningful use of extrinsic game elements" to maintain players' interest and motivation.
requirements: Designers must attend to how reward systems and motivating mechanisms are designed, since the same functional rewards produced different experiences depending on whether players could see and take part in the transformation
constraints: The article notes that not all motivating elements have the intended impacts on students' gaming experiences, and that further work is needed to investigate the exact value extrinsic elements add
target_learning_goals: sustained engagement and motivation in mathematics game-based learning
examples: NNG 2 added a number pad, visual cues, a materials bar and per-material saving, which improved game experience; NNG 4's Lighthouse Island let students construct buildings and buy ships with earned materials and coins, which students described as owning something
key_sources: Phuong Bui, Gabriela Rodríguez-Aflecht, Boglárka Brezovszky, Minna M. Hannula-Sormunen, Samuli Laato, Erno Lehtinen. (2020). Understanding students' game experiences throughout the developmental process of the number navigation game. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09755-8

article_title: Prioritizing teacher emotions: shifting teacher training to a digital environment
citation: Owens, J.K., Hudson, A.K. (2021). Prioritizing teacher emotions: shifting teacher training to a digital environment. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09921-y
title: Prioritize teachers' emotional well-being and provide intervention support to increase teacher self-efficacy during the shift to digital learning
description: The commentary argues that Jarrell et al.'s findings could be "a starting place for educational stakeholders to prioritize teachers' emotional well-being and offer an opportunity to provide intervention support in order to increase teacher self-efficacy in the shift to digital and possibly reduce teacher burnout." The principle holds that emotional well-being should be treated as a priority during technology-driven changes in teaching, with intervention support offered proactively rather than after burnout or attrition occurs.
requirements: Educational stakeholders must treat teachers' emotional well-being as a priority during the digital shift
Intervention support must be available to increase teacher self-efficacy
constraints: The commentary states the reduction in burnout is possible rather than demonstrated, using the hedge "possibly reduce teacher burnout"
target_learning_goals: teacher self-efficacy
teacher emotional well-being
reduced teacher burnout
examples: The commentary frames Jarrell et al.'s findings as a starting place for stakeholders to prioritize teacher emotional well-being and offer intervention support during the shift to digital learning.
key_sources: Owens, J.K., Hudson, A.K. (2021). Prioritizing teacher emotions: shifting teacher training to a digital environment. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09921-y
