article_title: Quiz-based inquiry: embedding incrementally sequenced questions to enhance engagement and learning in synchronous online lectures
citation: Zamzami Zainuddin, Michael Sailer, Shurui Bai, Madziatul Churiyah, Agung Winarno. (2026). Quiz-based inquiry: embedding incrementally sequenced questions to enhance engagement and learning in synchronous online lectures. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10614-1
title: Quiz-Based Inquiry (QBI) framework integrating Gagné's instructional events with inquiry-based learning phases
description: QBI is an instructional architecture in which formative assessment is the organising mechanism of synchronous online lectures. It uses "Gagné's events as scaffolds to organise inquiry throughout lectures, ensuring instructional structure provides coherence while inquiry processes add epistemic depth". Each lecture cycle runs question, response, peer comparison, instructor feedback, and conceptual consolidation, so questioning acts as a temporal scaffold regulating attention, dialogue, and conceptual development. The framework claims instruction and inquiry are not mutually exclusive.
requirements: Quiz prompts must be distributed across content segments and aligned with key conceptual shifts rather than administered as a single end-of-session block
Feedback must be immediate and integrated within the instructional cycle to support real-time adaptation
constraints: The article states IBL frameworks often give limited guidance on the timing of inquiry phases within lecture-based instruction, which QBI addresses
Effects were demonstrated in one course with three intact sections; the article notes possible novelty effects
target_learners: undergraduate students in synchronous online lectures
target_learning_goals: sustained attention and inquiry
conceptual understanding and consolidation
engagement and interaction
examples: The study operationalised QBI in 150-min sessions across three phases: orientation and cognitive activation, guided inquiry and collaborative exploration, and consolidation and formative evaluation
key_sources: Zamzami Zainuddin, Michael Sailer, Shurui Bai, Madziatul Churiyah, Agung Winarno. (2026). Quiz-based inquiry: embedding incrementally sequenced questions to enhance engagement and learning in synchronous online lectures. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10614-1

article_title: Quiz-based inquiry: embedding incrementally sequenced questions to enhance engagement and learning in synchronous online lectures
citation: Zamzami Zainuddin, Michael Sailer, Shurui Bai, Madziatul Churiyah, Agung Winarno. (2026). Quiz-based inquiry: embedding incrementally sequenced questions to enhance engagement and learning in synchronous online lectures. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10614-1
title: Dual-quiz architecture: discussion-oriented prompts during instruction plus evaluative prompts at transition points
description: This lesson-level pattern distributes two kinds of quiz prompts across a lecture session. As the article states, "A defining characteristic of QBI is its dual-quiz architecture: discussion-oriented prompts regulate inquiry during instruction, whereas evaluative prompts consolidate learning at key transition points". Discussion prompts trigger individual response, aggregated display, peer discussion, and instructor clarification; evaluative prompts emphasise retrieval, transfer, and application with immediate feedback. Together they integrate participation, feedback, and assessment into a recursive cycle.
requirements: Both prompt types must be distributed throughout the session rather than confined to the end
Real-time response visibility and structured peer discussion must follow responses
constraints: Designed for synchronous online lecture settings of about 150 minutes
Requires an interactive presentation platform or equivalent real-time response mechanism
target_learning_goals: attention regulation
dialogic reasoning
retrieval and application of concepts
examples: Sessions were organised into three phases: orientation and cognitive activation (30 minutes), guided inquiry and collaborative exploration (80 minutes), and consolidation and formative evaluation (40 minutes)
key_sources: Zamzami Zainuddin, Michael Sailer, Shurui Bai, Madziatul Churiyah, Agung Winarno. (2026). Quiz-based inquiry: embedding incrementally sequenced questions to enhance engagement and learning in synchronous online lectures. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10614-1

article_title: Integrating augmented reality into inquiry-based learning approach in primary science classrooms
citation: Wen, Y., Wu, L., He, S., Ng, N. H.-E., Teo, B. C., Looi, C. K., & Cai, Y. (2023). Integrating augmented reality into inquiry-based learning approach in primary science classrooms. Education Tech Research Dev, 71, 1631–1651. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10235-y
title: QIMS: an inquiry-based learning framework for leveraging the affordances of AR
description: QIMS is an inquiry-based learning framework proposed by the authors to leverage the affordances of augmented reality in teaching and learning. The article states that "In leveraging the affordances of AR, an inquiry-based learning framework, referred to as QIMS, was proposed in this study." It was operationalised into a learning package on plant reproduction for primary 5 students and evaluated against non-QIMS conditions.
requirements: Implementation requires a learning package designed on the QIMS framework, as the study developed its lessons on the topic of plant reproduction based on QIMS
constraints: Evaluated in primary science lessons with students aged 11–12; the article notes many existing studies neglected pedagogy and instructional models when implementing AR
target_learning_goals: Science learning (plant reproduction)
21st-century skills: self-directed learning, creative thinking, critical thinking, knowledge creation efficacy
examples: A learning package on plant reproduction for primary 5 students was developed based on the QIMS framework and tested in a three-condition quasi-experiment

article_title: Actualization of teaching conceptions in lesson design: how teaching conceptions shape TPACK regarding spherical video-based virtual reality-supported writing instruction
citation: Mengyuan Chen, Ching-sing Chai, Morris Siu-Yung Jong. (2023). Actualization of teaching conceptions in lesson design: how teaching conceptions shape TPACK regarding spherical video-based virtual reality-supported writing instruction. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10295-0
title: RAT framework: Replacement, Amplification, and Transformation as levels of technology integration
description: The RAT framework categorizes teachers' technology integration by pedagogical purpose into three levels. The article states "The Replacement category involves technology use to replace existing teaching activities and resources without changing established instructional practices, student learning processes, or content goals", Amplification enhances current practices with increased efficiency and productivity, and Transformation transforms instructional method, learning processes, and subject-matter understanding. In this study RAT provides the dimension for analyzing the level of SVVR integration in teachers' TPACK.
requirements: Teachers' rationales or pedagogical purposes for technology use must be analyzable to classify integration level
constraints: The article notes researchers need to explore teachers' rationales at the Transformation level to promote deep integration
target_learning_goals: technology-integrated writing instruction
examples: Teachers' TPACK segments were classified: 26 (10.88%) Replacement, 126 (52.72%) Amplification, 87 (36.40%) Transformation

Actualization of teaching conceptions in lesson design: how teaching conceptions shape TPACK regarding spherical video-based virtual reality-supported writing instruction. citation: Mengyuan Chen, Ching-sing Chai, Morris Siu-Yung Jong. (2023). Actualization of teaching conceptions in lesson design: how teaching conceptions shape TPACK regarding spherical video-based virtual reality-supported writing instruction. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10295-0
title: Three orientations of teaching conceptions for SVVR-supported writing: skill, community, and identity
description: The article adopts a three-orientation taxonomy of teachers' conceptions of VRWI. As it states, prior phenomenographic analysis "established three orientations of conceptions as "skill-oriented," "community-oriented," and "identity-oriented"". Skill-oriented conceptions focus on writing skills measurable by examination; community-oriented conceptions include collaborative and autonomous learning in the writing process; identity-oriented conceptions, the most sophisticated, emphasize developing writer identity through personal meaning-making and self-conscious choice from diverse cultural resources.
requirements: Conceptions must be actualized in specific knowledgeable actions for classroom teaching
constraints: The taxonomy was established for first-language composition teaching contexts
target_learners: secondary school teachers of first-language writing
target_learning_goals: writing instruction conceptions and TPACK construction
examples: Interview segments were coded by orientation: 78 skill-oriented (31.84%), 110 community-oriented (44.89%), 57 identity-oriented (23.27%)
key_sources: Mengyuan Chen, Ching-sing Chai, Morris Siu-Yung Jong. (2023). Actualization of teaching conceptions in lesson design: how teaching conceptions shape TPACK regarding spherical video-based virtual reality-supported writing instruction. citation: Mengyuan Chen, Ching-sing Chai, Morris Siu-Yung Jong. (2023). Actualization of teaching conceptions in lesson design: how teaching conceptions shape TPACK regarding spherical video-based virtual reality-supported writing instruction. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10295-0
title: SVVR-supported writing learning system built with EduVenture VR
description: The SVVR learning system used in the study was developed with EduVenture VR, which, as the article states, "consists of an SVVR composer for teachers and a user interface for students". Teachers filmed local Hong Kong places with a panoramic camera and built SVVR environments in the composer, adding human-computer interactions such as voice prompts, tags, portals, single/multiple-choice questions, and voice memos to guide students' exploration and stimulate thinking. The system immersed students in an authentic field trip experience for writing.
requirements: Teachers use the SVVR composer to film places with a panoramic camera and edit videos with interactive elements
constraints: Images are filmed in the real world and viewed through a simple headset such as Google cardboard glasses
target_learning_goals: Chinese-language reading and writing instruction
examples: Each teaching unit lasted 14-18 periods (45 minutes each): eight to ten periods of reading comprehension, four to six periods of SVVR-assisted writing, and two periods of evaluation and feedback

article_title: Shooting live television shows on film
citation: Sherburne, E. G., Jr. (1953). Research Abstracts 77. https://eric.ed.gov
title: Limit television instruction to small viewing groups, bounded daily totals, and short continuous viewing periods
description: The summarized army TV research sets concrete operating limits for instructional television: group size, daily curriculum time, and continuous viewing time are each capped. The abstract states "Not more than 20 students should view one TV screen" and that "no more than 30 minutes of continuous viewing should be attempted", with a four-hour daily curriculum ceiling. These limits function as design parameters for classroom TV use.
requirements: A TV receiver screen adequate for the group size; the abstract separately sets a 16-inch minimum screen for 20 viewers.
constraints: Limits are stated for army training contexts with the receiver technology of the period; the abstract prints no test statistics supporting the thresholds.
target_learners: Army trainees in classroom television instruction
target_learning_goals: Delivery of curriculum content via television without overloading viewers
examples: The abstract's conclusions specify caps of 20 students per screen, four hours of total curriculum per day, and 30 minutes of continuous viewing.
key_sources: Sherburne, E. G., Jr. (1953). Research Abstracts 77. https://eric.ed.gov

article_title: Shooting live television shows on film
citation: Sherburne, E. G., Jr. (1953). Research Abstracts 77. https://eric.ed.gov
title: Prefer informal, extemporaneous instruction on television; special TV-specific instructions are not required
description: Among the summarized conclusions on educational television, the abstract reports that "Best instruction is informal and extemporaneous" and that "Special instructions for TV are not required". That is, ordinary instructional practice carried over to TV outperformed specially scripted TV instruction, and instructors did not need TV-specific preparation beyond the presentation behaviors listed elsewhere.
requirements: An instructor willing to teach informally and extemporaneously on camera.
constraints: Stated for army training television; the abstract offers no supporting statistics for this conclusion.
target_learning_goals: Effective delivery of instruction over television
examples: The abstract lists conclusions (c) that best instruction is informal and extemporaneous and (d) that special instructions for TV are not required.
key_sources: Sherburne, E. G., Jr. (1953). Research Abstracts 77. https://eric.ed.gov

article_title: Shooting live television shows on film
citation: Sherburne, E. G., Jr. (1953). Research Abstracts 77. https://eric.ed.gov
title: Three-camera film technique for shooting live television shows on film
description: Freund's abstracted article describes producing the weekly half-hour program "I Love Lucy" on film with three motion picture cameras shooting simultaneously: the middle camera on a long shot and the two side cameras on closeups. This "provides more flexibility in editing, and better photographic quality than in kinescope recording", placing the technique at an intermediate point on the film-to-kinescope continuum described on the page.
requirements: Three motion picture cameras with a crew of four men per camera, plus roughly four days of rehearsal and shooting per weekly show.
constraints: Editing time is approximately four weeks and shows seen on screen were shot six weeks previously; the method was used for a weekly half-hour program with a live studio audience of approximately 300 people.
target_learners: Television production personnel learning film-based TV production methods
target_learning_goals: Producing television programs on film with editing flexibility and high photographic quality
examples: The abstract describes the middle camera on a long shot, side cameras on closeups, two days of dry rehearsals and two days of rehearsals with camera, and about one and one-half hours of actual shooting for a half-hour show.

article_title: Co-designing, developing, and implementing multiple learning analytics dashboards for data-driven decision-making in education: a design-based research approach

title: EasyVis dashboards within the MLADs framework
description: The EasyVis dashboards are the learning analytics dashboards developed for primary teachers in three Swedish municipalities, each integrating DLM activity data from an EdTech company with attendance and final grades from municipalities. "All three dashboards in our MLADs included a secure login system and three tabs: Class level, Student level and Help." The Class level tab shows classroom statistics, weekly DLM performance, attendance tables, comparisons against an adjustable class-average benchmark, and predictive risk alerts; the Student level tab shows per-student detail; the Help tab explains data origins and visualizations.

Data source labels in each dashboard section to build user trust

Early identification of struggling students
Differentiated instruction and formative assessment support

article_title: Fostering self-regulation in training complex cognitive tasks
citation: Ludo W. van Meeuwen, Saskia Brand-Gruwel, Paul A. Kirschner, Jeano J. P. R. de Bock, Jeroen J. G. van Merriënboer. (2018). Fostering self-regulation in training complex cognitive tasks. Education Tech Research Dev 66, 53–73. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-017-9539-9
title: Development portfolio combining task metadata and regulation prompts
description: A development portfolio supports SRL and continuous learning by combining metadata about all available learning tasks with regulation prompts, giving students insight into their performance status. The article states that "the development portfolio can foster the accurate selection of learning tasks that match the students' learning needs" and is expected to support increases in self-efficacy. In the study it comprised learning task worksheets, learning task self-reports, and progression self-reports, with metadata covering task complexity, support, supportive information, and trainable competences.

Regulation prompts at the right moments, prior to and after learning tasks

Domain-specific ATC competences
Self-efficacy for learning
examples: Process worksheets with metadata and pre- and post-task regulation prompts were provided to students in the integrated condition across 50 radar simulator tasks in 7 weeks

article_title: Fostering self-regulation in training complex cognitive tasks
citation: Ludo W. van Meeuwen, Saskia Brand-Gruwel, Paul A. Kirschner, Jeano J. P. R. de Bock, Jeroen J. G. van Merriënboer. (2018). Fostering self-regulation in training complex cognitive tasks. Education Tech Research Dev 66, 53–73. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-017-9539-9
title: Gradually shift control over task selection from coach to student to foster SRL skills and self-efficacy
description: In a shared control learning environment, the student and the coach share responsibility for future learning, and responsibility gradually shifts from coach to student. The article argues this gives students positive mastery experiences with tasks that fit their learning needs: "Shared control in which the responsibility of the control gradually shift from coach to student will have a positive effect not only on the SRL skills of the students, but will also beneﬁt students' self-efﬁcacy". The study operationalized this through portfolio-based worksheets and coaching meetings.
requirements: Students must be given the opportunity to take initiative in regulating their learning
Learning tasks must be selected that optimally fit individual learning needs
SRL skills must be developed before full control is handed over
constraints: In this study students did not experience freedom in task selection; the authors recommend future research on shared control task-selection designs with feedback
target_learners: Vocational and professional trainees in complex cognitive domains

Self-efficacy
Preparation for continuous learning
examples: Worksheets and self-reports prepared students for briefings and progression report meetings so they could contribute from their own point of view and experience control over their learning process

article_title: Precision diagnosis in virtual learning contexts: a predict-observe-explain-diagnose-based approach to scientific inquiry
citation: Kuan‑Fu Chen, Gwo‑Jen Hwang, Mei‑Rong Alice Chen. (2025). Precision diagnosis in virtual learning contexts: a predict‑observe‑explain‑diagnose‑based approach to scientific inquiry. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10527-5
title: POED strategy: extending POEE with a two-tier diagnostic test phase that diagnoses misconceptions and guides knowledge reconstruction
description: The POED strategy extends the Predict-Observe-Explain-Evaluate (POEE) strategy by replacing the evaluation phase with a two-tier test-based diagnosis phase. The article states that "a two-tier test-based learning diagnosis strategy was adopted to replace the evaluation in POEE to diagnose learners' misconceptions and guide them to construct correct knowledge and concepts". In the implemented VR system, students progress through prediction, observation, explanation, and evaluation scenes, then take a two-tier test whose first tier verifies factual knowledge and second tier requires conceptual justification; incorrect answers prompt a choice between retrying or reading supplementary learning materials, and progression is contingent on passing both tiers.
requirements: A two-tier test database with teacher-designed diagnostic questions and supplementary learning materials, plus a learning process database recording student behavior
constraints: The article notes the two-tier test questions were limited to multiple-choice questions only, which it says cannot diagnose some misconceptions
target_learners: eighth-grade junior high school natural science students
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of factors affecting chemical reaction rate
diagnosis and correction of science misconceptions
examples: The system was implemented with UPTALENT SVVR for the natural science course topic of factors influencing the chemical reaction rate, with 10 two-tier diagnostic questions developed by teachers with 10 years of experience
key_sources: Kuan‑Fu Chen, Gwo‑Jen Hwang, Mei‑Rong Alice Chen. (2025). Precision diagnosis in virtual learning contexts: a predict‑observe‑explain‑diagnose‑based approach to scientific inquiry. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10527-5

citation: Kuan‑Fu Chen, Gwo‑Jen Hwang, Mei‑Rong Alice Chen. (2025). Precision diagnosis in virtual learning contexts: a predict‑observe‑explain‑diagnose‑based approach to scientific inquiry. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10527-5
title: POED-based VR learning system built on UPTALENT SVVR with two-tier diagnostic testing
description: A spherical video-based virtual reality (SVVR) learning system implemented with UPTALENT for a junior high school natural science course. The article states the system "consisted of a POEE database, a two-tier test database, a learning material database, an SVVR scene database, and a learning process database". Students predict experimental results, watch experiment videos, explain principles via microphone, and take a two-tier test; the system "automatically determined whether the answer was correct or incorrect, and then proceeded with the corresponding instructional action".
requirements: Teacher-designed two-tier diagnostic questions and supplementary learning materials stored in the system databases
constraints: The article notes traditional VR application in basic education remains limited due to high development costs and technical complexity, which SVVR addresses as a more accessible alternative
target_learning_goals: learning the factors affecting chemical reaction rate through inquiry-based VR activities
examples: Students answered 10 diagnostic questions; after incorrect answers a cue tone reminded them to read supplementary learning materials, and they had to pass the two-tier test before proceeding to subsequent VR scenes

title: Embed misconception diagnosis with targeted feedback in inquiry-based learning rather than answer-only evaluation
description: The article argues that inquiry-based evaluation should go beyond judging answers to diagnosing the misconceptions behind wrong judgments. It states that without analysis and feedback on learners' misconceptions, "the learning effects of inquiry-based learning activities may be worse than expected", and that diagnosing possible misconceptions from wrong judgments makes it possible "to provide learning guidance" that helps students construct accurate knowledge.
requirements: Diagnostic questions that probe both factual knowledge and conceptual understanding, plus supplementary learning materials students can consult when diagnosed with misconceptions
constraints: The article's evidence comes from a small sample of 55 eighth graders in one science topic over six weeks, so it cautions the results may not generalize to other groups or subjects
target_learning_goals: accurate conceptual understanding in science
metacognitive self-assessment of understanding
examples: The study replaced the POEE evaluation phase with a two-tier diagnostic test in VR, and behavioral analysis showed experimental students read supplementary materials after errors and then answered correctly

article_title: Writing for the greater good: what do educators think about using Wikipedia as a teaching tool?
citation: Shani Evenstein Sigalov, Piotr Konieczny. (2025). Writing for the greater good: what do educators think about using Wikipedia as a teaching tool? Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10505-x
title: Wikipedia writing assignments as a service-learning form of Open Educational Practice (Renewable Assignment)
description: The article frames the Wikipedia writing assignment—students research a topic and expand or create an article—as an Open Educational Practice that contributes to the public domain, called a Renewable Assignment or Non-Disposable Assessment (Wiley & Hilton, 2018). It aligns with service-learning, and the article lists six key elements of service-learning found within Wikipedia assignments, from "contributing to society" to contributions that "can be easily assessed by the community". This framing underpins educators' motivations, particularly the service-learning aspect that motivated both students and instructors.
requirements: Assignments must be connected to the course's objectives and allow for self-reflection, per the article's six service-learning elements
constraints: The article notes absence of adequate university support and recognition may limit skill development, yielding outcomes comparable to traditional assignments
target_learning_goals: research, critical thinking, writing, and source citation skills
digital, information, and academic literacies
examples: Educators substituted traditional tests or papers, typically read only by faculty, with assignments contributing to the greater good beyond the classroom

article_title: Exploring the structure of digital literacy competence assessed using authentic software applications
citation: Frank Reichert, Nancy W. Y. Law, Gary K. W. Wong, Jimmy de la Torre. (2020). Exploring the structure of digital literacy competence assessed with authentic software applications. Education Tech Research Dev, 68, 2991–3013. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09825-x
title: Use multiple digital tools in learning and assessment, and avoid relying on a single tool when assessing DL, because tool-specific performance may not correlate highly
description: The article recommends that educators treat DL as comprehensive across tools while using several applications for learning and assessment, since the study found tool-specific performance dimensions. It states that "reliance on only one specific tool is particularly likely to provide biased results of students' DL and should be avoided unless the assessment of a tool-specific competence is the explicit goal". Teachers and assessment developers should consider tool dependencies when analyzing and interpreting results.
requirements: Assessment or learning designs must incorporate multiple software applications rather than a single tool
constraints: Reliance on one tool is acceptable when assessing a tool-specific competence is the explicit goal
target_learning_goals: digital literacy competence
examples: The ILPA technical DL module required students to search the Internet, edit a Word document, create a PowerPoint presentation, and discuss in an online forum, spanning multiple applications
key_sources: Frank Reichert, Nancy W. Y. Law, Gary K. W. Wong, Jimmy de la Torre. (2020). Exploring the structure of digital literacy competence assessed with authentic software applications. Education Tech Research Dev, 68, 2991–3013. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09825-x

article_title: Exploring the structure of digital literacy competence assessed using authentic software applications
citation: Frank Reichert, Nancy W. Y. Law, Gary K. W. Wong, Jimmy de la Torre. (2020). Exploring the structure of digital literacy competence assessed with authentic software applications. Education Tech Research Dev, 68, 2991–3013. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09825-x
title: Bifactor model of digital literacy competence: a general DL dimension supplemented by tool-specific dimensions
description: The article proposes that DL as assessed through authentic software is best modeled as a hierarchical bifactor structure: a general dimension measured by all items representing the "essence" of DL, plus specific residual dimensions capturing commonality not accounted for by the general dimension. In the ILPA data these specific dimensions were defined by the software applications used (online information seeking, knowledge-based information seeking, word processing, digital presentation), challenging frameworks that depict DL as a generic, tool-independent competence.
requirements: Assessment data collected with authentic software applications and items detailed enough for multidimensional IRT modeling
constraints: The specific dimensions do not map well onto existing DL frameworks; the structure was established on 2007 ILPA data from Hong Kong using Microsoft Office applications
target_learning_goals: digital literacy competence
examples: The bifactor model fit the ILPA data better (RMSEA = .052, CFI = .978) than a four-dimensional model without a general dimension

article_title: Activity-Centred Analysis and Design (ACAD): Core purposes, distinctive qualities and current developments
citation: Peter Goodyear. (2015). Teaching as design. HERDSA Review of Higher Education. https://www.herdsa.org.au/herdsa-review-higher-education-vol-2/27-50
title: Activity-centered design model: design shapes learning indirectly through epistemic, physical and social structures
description: The article's Figure 1 (adapted from Goodyear & Ellis, 2008) portrays an activity-centric view in which teaching-as-design affects student learning activity only indirectly. Design works "through the specification of worthwhile tasks (epistemic structures), the recommendation of appropriate tools, artefacts and other physical resources (structures of place), and recommendation of divisions of labour etc. (social structures)". The model prioritises what students do, think, feel and say, treating everything else as stimulus or scaffold for their activity.
requirements: Teachers must design good learning tasks and communicate task specifications clearly to students
constraints: Design works indirectly; students adapt, interpret and customise what is designed
target_learning_goals: effective engagement in designed learning activities
examples: The article uses the model to argue teachers are obliged to help students locate, access and configure physical resources and find good ways of working with peers
key_sources: Peter Goodyear. (2015). Teaching as design. HERDSA Review of Higher Education. https://www.herdsa.org.au/herdsa-review-higher-education-vol-2/27-50

citation: Peter Goodyear. (2015). Teaching as design. HERDSA Review of Higher Education. https://www.herdsa.org.au/herdsa-review-higher-education-vol-2/27-50
title: Science of design partition: epistemology, phenomenology and praxiology as three areas for studying teachers' design work
description: The article adopts Nigel Cross's partitioning of the science of design to structure research relevant to building design capability in universities: "design epistemology (the study of 'designerly ways of knowing'), design phenomenology (the study of the form and configuration of designed artefacts), and design praxiology (the study of the practices and processes of design)". Each area is treated in its own section with examples and identified research gaps.
requirements: Managers and staff need a sharper, shared understanding of what is special about design
constraints: Design phenomenology is extended beyond Cross's original definition to identify the scope of what can and should be designed in higher education
target_learning_goals: understanding and improving design for learning
examples: Section 6 treats actionable knowledge for design; section 7 asks what gets designed; section 8 reviews empirical studies of what designers do

citation: Peter Goodyear. (2015). Teaching as design. HERDSA Review of Higher Education. https://www.herdsa.org.au/herdsa-review-higher-education-vol-2/27-50
title: Three design components: learning tasks, supportive environments, and social organisation
description: An activity-centered approach focuses on "three main classes of things which can be designed: (i) good learning tasks, (ii) properly supportive physical and digital environments, and (iii) forms of social organisation and divisions of labour". The components entangle in students' actual learning activity but are best kept conceptually distinct during design, which allows shifting elements between components, e.g. offloading an over-complicated task specification to scaffolding in digital tools.
requirements: Each component must be designed and managed at multiple scale levels by people in different roles
constraints: Learning, activity and experience cannot be designed, only designed for (Wenger, 1998)
target_learning_goals: productive learning activity at learntime
examples: If a groupwork design may go awry, the teacher-designer can supplement the social design with additional instructions about how to co-ordinate work

article_title: Activity-Centred Analysis and Design (ACAD): Core purposes, distinctive qualities and current developments
citation: Peter Goodyear. (2015). Teaching as design. HERDSA Review of Higher Education. https://www.herdsa.org.au/herdsa-review-higher-education-vol-2/27-50
title: Conceptions of learning (acquisition, participation, knowledge creation) change the design relation between tools and student activity
description: The article argues that writing on design for learning mostly adopts Sfard's 'acquisition' metaphor, and that the relation between what is designed and students' situated activity differs substantially across conceptions of learning. "If learning is seen as a matter of acquiring knowledge, then tools which are set in place for students are there to help them acquire that knowledge: they are solely a means to that end"; under participation, tools are there to be mastered; under knowledge creation, students design new tools as a legitimate outcome of their work.
requirements: Teachers need an expansive, nuanced conception of students' engagement in design
target_learning_goals: designing for one's own learning as part of graduating as a lifelong learner
examples: The article states all three metaphors are valuable and cites Paavola et al. (2004) on knowledge creation

title: LAMS and pedagogical design patterns as promising approaches to reusable designs for learning

article_title: Teachers’ AI digital competencies and twenty-first century skills in the post-pandemic world
citation: Davy Tsz Kit Ng, Jac Ka Lok Leung, Jiahong Su, Ross Chi Wui Ng, Samuel Kai Wah Chu. (2023). Teachers' AI digital competencies and twenty-first century skills in the post-pandemic world. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10203-6
title: Four-domain conceptual framework for teachers' AI competency
description: The article proposes a new framework extending DigCompEdu, P21's framework, and Ng et al.'s four cognition domains model, organizing teachers' AI competency into four domains: "Teacher professional engagement", "Instructional design", "Content choices" across disciplines, and "Learning competencies". It frames AI competency as "a non-technical, critical and complex competency that young people need to learn to manipulate AI technologies ethically, safely and wisely", not merely technological skill. constraints: Conceptual paper using research examples as evidence; the framework is proposed rather than empirically validated

twenty-first century skills
AI literacy

title: Four cognition domains of AI competency based on Bloom's taxonomy
description: Drawing on Ng et al. (2021b), the article describes a model categorizing AI competencies into four cognition domains: "know and understand; use and apply; evaluate and create; and ethical issues", ordered from lower to higher thinking skills and inspired by Bloom's Taxonomy. For example, recognizing and understanding AI maps to know and understand, critically interpreting data to evaluate and create, and societal impacts to ethical issues. The model helps teachers design instruction and assessment around students' AI competencies.

AI knowledge from low to high thinking skills

article_title: Combining exploratory learning with structured practice educational technologies to foster both conceptual and procedural fractions knowledge
citation: Mavrikis, M., Rummel, N., Wiedmann, M., Loibl, K., & Holmes, W. (2022). title: iTalk2Learn adaptive digital learning platform combining an ELE and an ITS
description: The iTalk2Learn platform is an adaptive digital learning platform developed in the EU-funded iTalk2Learn project that sequences content from two types of systems, an ELE and an ITS. It "was configured in two parallel versions, English and German, both of which combined an ELE delivering exploratory tasks and an ITS delivering structured tasks." A Student Needs Assessment component uses inputs such as screen/mouse actions, feedback-message counts, and speech to decide whether to keep a student in the ELE or switch to structured ITS practice.
requirements: A Student Needs Assessment component drawing on interaction inputs including speech to sequence activities between ELE and ITS
constraints: In the reported studies the platform was configured with Fractions Lab as the ELE and either Maths Whizz (UK) or Fractions-Tutor (Germany) as the ITS
target_learners: Primary and secondary school students aged 8–12 beginning formal fractions instruction
target_learning_goals: Conceptual and procedural knowledge of equivalent fractions
examples: In the studies, students spent about 40 minutes on the platform; ELE time averaged 19.85 minutes (SD 0.004) with 5 to 9 ITS tasks

Combining exploratory learning with structured practice educational technologies to foster both conceptual and procedural fractions knowledge. Education Tech Research Dev, 70, 691–712. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10104-0
title: Fractions Lab exploratory learning environment with adaptive task-dependent support
description: Fractions Lab is the ELE developed by the iTalk2Learn project, used in both the German and UK studies. "It provides exploratory tasks that aim to help the student develop conceptual knowledge of fractions." Students manipulate graphical fraction representations (number lines, rectangles, sets, liquid measures) to solve tasks such as finding equivalent fractions. Task-Dependent Support varies along two dimensions — six feedback purposes and four feedback levels from Socratic questioning to a didactic-procedural backstop — with delivery mode (low- or high-interruptive) chosen by a Bayesian network predicting affective benefit.
requirements: Rule-based Task-Dependent Support operationalized by feedback purpose and feedback level to ameliorate the cognitive demands of exploration
constraints: The article notes exploration without guidance may not foster learning because it places high cognitive demands on learners
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding of fractions, including equivalence across representations
examples: Feedback purposes include Polya-style prompts, next-step instruction, affirmation, and reflection prompts such as "Please explain why you made the denominator 12."

citation: Mavrikis, M., Rummel, N., Wiedmann, M., Loibl, K., & Holmes, W. (2022). Combining exploratory learning with structured practice educational technologies to foster both conceptual and procedural fractions knowledge. Education Tech Research Dev, 70, 691–712. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10104-0
title: iTalk2Learn pedagogical intervention model: exploratory task first, then adaptive switching to structured practice
description: The pedagogical intervention model of iTalk2Learn specifies an exploratory-first sequencing in which "students begin their session in the ELE, where they engage with an exploratory task." While students work, the Student Needs Assessment component judges whether the student is under-, over-, or appropriately challenged; an appropriately challenged student is switched to the ITS for a structured practice task mapped to the fine-grain goal of the completed ELE task. Students complete a fixed ITS sequence (up to five tasks) before returning to the ELE. The model aligns with problem-solving-before-instruction approaches the authors cite (Sinha & Kapur, 2021).
requirements: A Student Needs Assessment component with expert-rated task difficulty and rules to decide when to switch between ELE and ITS tasks
constraints: The first ITS task is mapped as closely as possible to the fine-grain goal of the completed ELE task; students return to the ELE after five structured tasks or when under-challenged
target_learners: Primary and secondary students learning equivalent fractions
target_learning_goals: Joint development of conceptual and procedural fractions knowledge
examples: If a student receives several supportive feedback messages, the system infers they are overly challenged and assigns a less challenging exploratory task on the same concept

article_title: The impact of visual aid displays showing a manipulative task
citation: Lasser, S. (1954). The Impact of Visual Aid Displays Showing a Manipulative Task. The Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 6: Part 3, 95-106.
title: Lasser's account: visual-aid presentations are not stored as memory-images and do not furnish ready-made meanings
description: The author theorizes, from the subjects' comments during the repair task, that film and filmstrip presentations are not stored as memory-images and cannot furnish ready-made meanings, even though "fragmentary imagery did occur during the performance task." This account frames learning from visual perception as something the learner must construct during subsequent performance rather than receive as stored pictures. It is offered as the author's interpretation of the experiment, motivating further research.
requirements: Further research is proposed to investigate how learning from visual perception becomes available to the learner during subsequent performance.
constraints: The account is theorized from the subjects' comments, not directly tested in the experiment.
target_learners: RAF members learning a manipulative task
target_learning_goals: performing a manipulative repair task from visual instruction
examples: Subjects' comments collected during performance of the 23-suboperation sash-cord repair task served as the basis for the theorizing.

article_title: Team design communication patterns in e-learning design and development
citation: Rapanta, C., Maina, M., Lotz, N., & Bacchelli, A. (2013). Team design communication patterns in e-learning design and development. Educational Technology Research and Development, 61(4), 581-605. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-013-9306-5
title: Team e-learning design as a socio-cognitive activity analyzed at micro, meso, and macro levels
description: The article frames team design as a socio-cognitive activity rooted in Bucciarelli (1984), in which any design task effort must be made explicit as a communication message and any communication task must relate to the design task. It operationalizes this with a three-level interaction analysis coding scheme: "(a) The micro level, which refers to how each person behaves as part of the team; (b) the meso level, which refers to emerging structures as behaviors of two or more participants; and (c) the macro level, which refers to the shared subject focus of the team." Design objects, moves, and sequences are coded in parallel with communication moves and sequences.
requirements: Both a design-task analysis of problem space exploration and a communication-task analysis of the management space must be conducted in parallel
constraints: A main difficulty is the identification and separation of the cognitive from the social aspects of discourse in highly interdisciplinary teams
target_learners: instructional designers working in e-learning project teams
target_learning_goals: understanding and guiding team design decision-making in e-learning development
examples: The scheme was applied to 15 video-recorded meetings (25.7 transcribed hours) from two European distance university course teams
key_sources: Rapanta, C., Maina, M., Lotz, N., & Bacchelli, A. (2013). Team design communication patterns in e-learning design and development. Educational Technology Research and Development, 61(4), 581-605. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-013-9306-5

article_title: Team design communication patterns in e-learning design and development
citation: Rapanta, C., Maina, M., Lotz, N., & Bacchelli, A. (2013). Team design communication patterns in e-learning design and development. Educational Technology Research and Development, 61(4), 581-605. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-013-9306-5
title: Extended verbal protocol dataset of 15 e-learning design team meetings
description: The study's empirical corpus consists of video-recorded project meetings from two interdisciplinary e-learning course teams at well-established European distance universities. "In total, 15 project meetings (10 from Team A and 5 from Team B) were video-recorded and 25.7 meeting hours were totally transcribed." Team A was observed for one year during a 60-credit Bachelor course on Design Thinking; Team B for half a year during a 6-credit Masters course on Instructional Design Models. Meetings were situated in the development phase of design.
requirements: Meetings were situated in the development phase, after course structure and objectives had been decided
constraints: Only interaction moments with reflective decision-making formed the final dataset, segmented into topic-based episodes, sequences, and moves
target_learners: interdisciplinary e-learning design team members in higher education
target_learning_goals: describing and improving team instructional design processes
examples: Team A won a quality award for its course, supporting the teams' representativeness of high-quality design

article_title: “How Did I Do?”: Giving learners effective and affective feedback
citation: Howard, N. R. (2021). "How Did I Do?": Giving learners effective and affective feedback. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09874-2
title: Design digital feedback experiences so they are efficient and offer affective benefits to students and instructors
description: The article argues that future efforts should "ensure students and instructors are engaged in an efficient feedback experience that offers affective benefits in digital learning spaces". It treats feedback in digital learning as something that should serve both efficiency and affect, positioning Borup et al.'s work as "a critical anchor" for such efforts. The principle is stated as a design goal rather than tested here.
requirements: Feedback delivery in digital learning spaces must attend to both efficiency and affective benefits for students and instructors, as the article states.
target_learning_goals: effective and affective feedback experiences in online and blended learning
examples: The article offers this as a goal for future efforts building on Borup et al.'s (2015) examination of feedback perceptions in blended learning.
key_sources: Howard, N. R. (2021). "How Did I Do?": Giving learners effective and affective feedback. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09874-2

citation: Howard, N. R. (2021). "How Did I Do?": Giving learners effective and affective feedback. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09874-2
title: Borup et al.'s (2015) blended-course feedback study as an anchor for future feedback research and practice
description: The article treats Borup et al.'s (2015) study of teacher candidate and instructor feedback perceptions in blended learning as a foundational reference point, calling it "a critical anchor to support future efforts". The study, published in Educational Technology Research and Development, is used to ground the commentary's strategies and design goals for digital feedback experiences.
requirements: Serves as a grounding reference for efforts to improve feedback experiences in digital learning spaces.

examples: The commentary builds its feedback delivery strategies for educators directly on this study.

article_title: Designing AI-powered learning: adult learners’ expectations for curriculum and human-AI interaction
citation: Jinhee Kim, Seongryeong Yu, Rita Detrick, Xi Lin, Na Li. (2025). Designing AI-powered learning: adult learners' expectations for curriculum and human-AI interaction. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10549-z
title: Three-type learner-AI interaction framework: cognitive, socio-emotional, and artifact-mediated interaction
description: The article organizes human-AI interaction in learning into three multifaceted types: "cognitive, socio-emotional, and artifact-mediated interactions" (Kim, 2024; Kim et al., 2022). Cognitive interactions are task-focused exchanges supporting content comprehension, thinking, reasoning, and knowledge construction. Socio-emotional interactions involve expression and regulation of emotions within collaboration, shaping the emotional and social dynamics of learning. Artifact-mediated interactions focus on how learners engage with AI through its interface, whose design characteristics shape the learning experience. The study uses this framework to structure its research questions and findings on supports adult learners need.
requirements: Learners need supports specific to each interaction type: metacognition and question-crafting for cognitive, ethical norms for socio-emotional, and interface design for artifact-mediated interaction
constraints: The article warns reliance on AI outputs may result in passive learning behaviors or reduce learners' critical evaluation skills, and poorly designed AI systems may frustrate users and reduce trust
target_learners: working adult learners in higher education
target_learning_goals: content mastery
lifelong learning habits
effective learner-AI interaction
examples: The study's interview guiding questions (Appendix A) were structured around cognitive, socio-emotional, and artifact-mediated interaction, and findings were organized into these three interaction themes

article_title: Impact of learning analytics-based personalized feedback: an experimental study on student behavior in a large introductory STEM course
citation: Jae-Eun Russell, Anna-Marie Smith, Salim George, Adam Brummett. (2026). Impact of learning analytics-based personalized feedback: an experimental study on student behavior in a large introductory STEM course. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10728-6
title: Excel-based if/then template system for generating personalized feedback emails from learning analytics data
description: The intervention used a scalable personalization pipeline: "Feedback messages were generated from structured templates using predefined if/then decision rules implemented in Excel." Analytics variables such as practice problems completed and homework start times were evaluated against thresholds (e.g., ≤ 20 practice problems, exam score < 60%) that flagged behaviors and populated standardized text blocks, rather than assigning students to pre-defined groups. Generated emails were reviewed by the course instructor before distribution via mail merge.
requirements: Instructor review of generated messages prior to distribution to ensure the combination of feedback elements was appropriate and coherent
constraints: The article notes the degree or specificity of personalization implemented may not have been sufficient to generate performance gains beyond generic messages
target_learners: undergraduate students in a large introductory chemistry course
target_learning_goals: initiating homework early
engaging with optional practice problems
examples: Four personalized emails were sent to the experimental group at key points (after Exams 1 and 2, before Exam 3, and before the final), while the control group received two generic emails emphasizing the same behaviors
key_sources: Jae-Eun Russell, Anna-Marie Smith, Salim George, Adam Brummett. (2026). Impact of learning analytics-based personalized feedback: an experimental study on student behavior in a large introductory STEM course. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10728-6

article_title: Role of organisational readiness and stakeholder acceptance: an implementation framework of adaptive learning for higher education
citation: Mirata, V., & Bergamin, P. (2023). Role of organisational readiness and stakeholder acceptance: an implementation framework of adaptive learning for higher education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10248-7
title: ALIF: an empirically supported implementation framework for adaptive learning linking determinants, strategies, and outcomes
description: ALIF is an implementation framework for adaptive learning built from qualitative data linking three core elements: determinants, strategies, and outcomes. The article states it "consists of three core elements, namely, (a) determinants that prevent or enable implementation, (b) specific strategies that address these determinants, and (c) expected proximal and distal outcomes". Elements are categorised into technological, pedagogical, and organisational dimensions, differentiated across two implementation stages, with societal and global dimensions as outer context.
requirements: Relationships between determinants, strategies, and outcomes must be empirically supported by qualitative data from the implementing context
constraints: Derived from expert panels at two universities in Switzerland and South Africa; the article notes implementation occurs in unique institutional conditions
target_learning_goals: scaled implementation of adaptive learning in higher education institutions
examples: The framework's Table 3 maps determinants such as lack of leadership commitment to strategies such as aligning the adaptive learning strategy with broader institutional goals
key_sources: Mirata, V., & Bergamin, P. (2023). Role of organisational readiness and stakeholder acceptance: an implementation framework of adaptive learning for higher education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10248-7

article_title: Role of organisational readiness and stakeholder acceptance: an implementation framework of adaptive learning for higher education
citation: Mirata, V., & Bergamin, P. (2023). Role of organisational readiness and stakeholder acceptance: an implementation framework of adaptive learning for higher education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10248-7
title: Build stakeholder acceptance of adaptive learning by communicating its advantages and presenting evidence-based results
description: Because acceptability by all stakeholders was the most frequently mentioned outcome and was strongly connected to recognition of adaptive learning's advantages, the article supports communicating advantages and presenting evidence-based results as implementation strategies. Participants suggested "the communication of the advantages and presentation of evidence-based results on the influence of adaptive learning on the success and drop-out rate of students and the satisfaction of stakeholders" as the most effective strategies, alongside didactically sound course design, skilled staff, and favourable working conditions.
requirements: Strategies must address the determinant of insufficient recognition of the advantages of adaptive learning for students, instructors, and the institution
constraints: The connection was identified from qualitative expert statements, particularly salient for the Swiss university panel
target_learning_goals: stakeholder acceptability of adaptive learning
scaled implementation of adaptive learning
examples: The implementation team communicates the advantages and added value of adaptive learning among all stakeholders, and the research team presents intermediate research results demonstrating effects on student success, dropouts, satisfaction, and inclusiveness

article_title: Cultivating inclusive mindsets exploring faculty’s and students’ perspectives on using online simulations for inclusive pedagogy in teacher education
citation: Hoda Harati, Gretchen McAllister, Yingying Liu. (2026). Cultivating inclusive mindsets exploring faculty's and students' perspectives on using online simulations for inclusive pedagogy in teacher education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10662-7
title: Building Inclusive Classrooms simulation (SchoolSims platform)
description: An online, story-based simulation hosted on the SchoolSims platform with 3rd-grade and 6th-grade versions, in which candidates role-play a teacher responding to a parent complaint about LGBTQ+-related book-commercial content. It "uses recorded real actors, branching decisions, and reflective prompts" in a "mistake-friendly learning environment where candidates can replay scenarios to understand the consequences of their decisions." Candidates interact with stakeholders including administrators, colleagues, librarians, students, parents, and external experts, and receive a summary of choices with feedback at the conclusion.
requirements: Integration into a course topic with structured debriefs and reflection activities, which TEs described as essential for maximizing impact
constraints: Decision options felt too binary to some students; the simulation could not fully replicate the complexities of real-life classroom situations
target_learners: elementary teacher candidates in literacy methods courses
target_learning_goals: inclusive pedagogy for LGBTQ+ topics
stakeholder communication
decision-making in contested classroom contexts
examples: In the scenarios, a student submits a book report video on a book featuring same-gender penguins (3rd grade) or a story about a transgender student (6th grade), and a parent leaves a voicemail requesting a discussion.
key_sources: Hoda Harati, Gretchen McAllister, Yingying Liu. (2026). Cultivating inclusive mindsets exploring faculty's and students' perspectives on using online simulations for inclusive pedagogy in teacher education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10662-7

article_title: Cultivating inclusive mindsets exploring faculty’s and students’ perspectives on using online simulations for inclusive pedagogy in teacher education
citation: Hoda Harati, Gretchen McAllister, Yingying Liu. (2026). Cultivating inclusive mindsets exploring faculty's and students' perspectives on using online simulations for inclusive pedagogy in teacher education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10662-7
title: Situated learning plus simulation-based learning as a framework for simulation-supported inclusive pedagogy preparation
description: The study grounds its simulation design in two complementary frameworks. Situated learning holds that "professional knowledge develops through participation in socially and contextually meaningful activity rather than through abstract instruction alone" (Lave & Wenger, 1991), while simulation-based learning provides "structured opportunities for rehearsal, reflection, and decision-making in low-risk environments that approximate the complexity of real practice" (Levin & Frei-Landau, 2023). Together they position the simulation as a pedagogical space where candidates test responses, reflect on consequences, and develop readiness for inclusive practice in contested contexts.
requirements: Realistic dilemmas, stakeholder perspectives, and reflective opportunities within the simulation to support professional reflection and decision-making
constraints: The article frames the frameworks as interpretive lenses for perception data, not as tested mechanisms; findings reflect self-reported perceptions rather than observed practice
target_learning_goals: enacting inclusive pedagogy
professional decision-making
reflective practice
examples: The discussion interprets candidates' movement from abstract to practical strategies through legitimate peripheral participation and features of a community of practice.

article_title: Promoting computational thinking of both sciences- and humanities-oriented students: an instructional and motivational design perspective
citation: Katai, Z. (2020). Promoting computational thinking of both sciences- and humanities-oriented students: an instructional and motivational design perspective. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09766-5
title: Design-principle framework for CT-promoter e-learning environments: sequenced multiple representation, genuine active involvement, selective hiding, and pattern-recognition orientation
description: The article organizes its learning environment around four research-based design principles for promoting computational thinking. Sequenced multiple representations exploit complementarity and redundancy: "We use four different representations of the number sequence to be sorted: embodied by a dancer-sequence, stored in a white-box array, stored in a black-box array and illustrated as a color-scale bar." Active involvement follows the meta-study conclusion that "AV's promote effective learning when users are engaged actively in the visualization process (instead of passively viewing it)", selective hiding forces learners to perform comparison operations explicitly, and a pattern-recognition strategy moves from carefully selected sample inputs to orchestration on random inputs. The framework is grounded in constructivist learning theory.
requirements: Attentive and thoughtful design of the constructivist learning environment, as the article states such an environment assumes
constraints: The article notes such a learning experience is only a first step in developing students' CT, since cultivating the skill implies devising procedures, not only assimilating ready-made ones
target_learning_goals: computational thinking
algorithmic thinking
understanding sorting algorithms
examples: The AlgoRythmics environment visualizes algorithms via videotaped folk-dancer performances wearing the numbers to be sorted, animated white-box and black-box arrays students reconstruct and orchestrate, and a parallel simulation of six algorithms on color-scale bars.
key_sources: Katai, Z. (2020). Promoting computational thinking of both sciences- and humanities-oriented students: an instructional and motivational design perspective. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09766-5

article_title: Promoting computational thinking of both sciences- and humanities-oriented students: an instructional and motivational design perspective
citation: Katai, Z. (2020). Promoting computational thinking of both sciences- and humanities-oriented students: an instructional and motivational design perspective. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09766-5
title: Six-stage hearing–seeing–doing e-learning session with interleaved motivation questionnaires
description: A lesson-level sequence that alternates motivational phases with measurement points: a hearing introduction, a dance-performance phase to arouse curiosity, an animation phase supporting abstracting, three doing phases (reconstruction, white-box orchestration, black-box orchestration) implementing active involvement and progressive challenge, and a closing parallel simulation arousing aesthetic emotions. Nine questionnaires (Q1–9) are interleaved between stages to track emotions, challenge, and involvement. The article states that during the doing phases "students are invited to actively participate in the animations (Mayer and Chandler 2001) according to the principle of moderate-progressive challenge".
requirements: Help-buttons indicating the next operation, and repeatable tasks on randomly generated inputs until solved correctly without help, to reduce anxiety and promote a sense of achievement
constraints: The article notes that if e-learning materials are interesting only because they are novel, they may lose their appeal as learners become accustomed to them
target_learning_goals: computational thinking
understanding how sorting algorithms work
examples: In the reported experiment both groups followed the session Q1–2, s1, Q3, s2, Q4, s3, Q5, s4, Q6, s5, Q7, s6, Q8–9 in computer labs with individual access to the online tool.

article_title: Bridging strategy gaps in programming: the role of visual scaffolding for learners with low cognitive ability
citation: Huang, S. C.-F., Chen, Z.-H., Lin, Y.-T., & Yeh, M. K. (2026). Bridging strategy gaps in programming: the role of visual scaffolding for learners with low cognitive ability. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10684-1
title: Real-time visual scaffolding programming system with color-coded blocks and synchronized visual output
description: Two custom-built programming systems were developed using the Unity engine and Google Blockly, with an interface divided into task description, programming tool, and top-down and bottom-up tracking windows. The experimental system adds real-time visual scaffolding: "the results of the programming blocks were displayed in real time on the left side of the interface, within both top-down and bottom-up tracking windows." Each code block was color-coded to match arrows and lines in the visual output, serving as signaling cues that guide attention and reduce the need to mentally simulate program execution.
requirements: Learners solve block-based programming tasks (loops, conditions, functions) in the system so the tracking windows and real-time output can guide strategy use
constraints: The intervention period in the study was relatively short, and learner performance may depend on their familiarity with the system
target_learners: Adult novice programmers with at least six months of programming learning experience, including low-EF learners
target_learning_goals: Programming strategy use (top-down versus bottom-up) and problem-solving during block-based programming tasks
examples: Participants solved three tasks—loops, conditions, and functions—moving a target through checkpoints with as few blocks as possible, with the experimental group seeing color-coded real-time program output
key_sources: Huang, S. C.-F., Chen, Z.-H., Lin, Y.-T., & Yeh, M. K. (2026). Bridging strategy gaps in programming: the role of visual scaffolding for learners with low cognitive ability. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10684-1

article_title: Bridging strategy gaps in programming: the role of visual scaffolding for learners with low cognitive ability
citation: Huang, S. C.-F., Chen, Z.-H., Lin, Y.-T., & Yeh, M. K. (2026). Bridging strategy gaps in programming: the role of visual scaffolding for learners with low cognitive ability. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10684-1
title: Top-down and bottom-up programming strategy framework
description: The article adopts a two-strategy framework from behavioral theory (Brooks, 1983; Storey, 2006) in which "The top-down strategy involves building plans from the whole picture and then delving deeper into the details, while the bottom-up strategy integrates individual programming concepts, gradually constructing the whole picture." The study operationalizes these strategies through top-down and bottom-up tracking windows whose fixation and visit data reveal which strategy a learner uses. Experienced learners are reported to often prefer the top-down strategy.
requirements: Eye-tracking indicators (fixation duration, fixation count, visit count) on strategy-aligned areas of interest to infer which strategy a learner is using
constraints: The article notes that while beginners' behavior shows some bottom-up strategies, it remains difficult to draw definitive conclusions about beginners' strategy use
target_learning_goals: Programming problem-solving strategy and program comprehension
examples: The study's two systems provided top-down and bottom-up tracking windows offering a macro-perspective and a micro-perspective aligned with the two strategies
key_sources: Huang, S. C.-F., Chen, Z.-H., Lin, Y.-T., & Yeh, M. K. (2026). Bridging strategy gaps in programming: the role of visual scaffolding for learners with low cognitive ability. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10684-1

article_title: Is too much help an obstacle? Effects of interactivity and cognitive style on learning with dynamic versus non-dynamic visualizations with narrative explanations
citation: Marta M. Koć-Januchta, Tim N. Höffler, Helmut Prechtl, Detlev Leutner. (2020). Is too much help an obstacle? Effects of interactivity and cognitive style on learning with dynamic versus non-dynamic visualizations with narrative explanations. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09822-0
title: Expertise reversal account of the self-paced static pictures disadvantage for highly developed visualizers
description: The article offers two hypothetical explanations for why highly developed visualizers learned poorer with self-paced static pictures and narration. The first invokes the expertise reversal effect: "Highly developed visualizers experience self-paced static pictures with narration as providing too much external support, which hinders them from constructing their own mental representations of processed information." The second proposes that generating mental images of spoken words while processing pictures overloaded the visual channel. Both are stated as speculation requiring further research.
requirements: Further research is required, including measuring interactive intensity of learner-control button usage and eye-tracking of attention processes
constraints: The article labels both explanations hypothetical and speculative; neither was tested in the study
target_learning_goals: understanding primary reactions of photosynthesis from multimedia environments

article_title: Towards emotion awareness tools to support emotion and appraisal regulation in academic contexts
citation: Elise Lavoué, Maedeh Kazemitabar, Tenzin Doleck, Susanne P. Lajoie, Rubiela Carrillo, et al.. (2019). Towards emotion awareness tools to support emotion and appraisal regulation in academic contexts. Educational Technology Research and Development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09688-x
title: Emotion-reporting grid for university students based on daily experienced emotions
description: The article describes an emotion-reporting grid created for university students, grounded in the emotions students actually experienced day to day. As the abstract states, "This study created an emotion-reporting grid for university students based on the emotions they experienced daily." Students then used the grid as the basis for retrospective interviews: "Students were interviewed based on their self-reported grid." The grid serves as the data-collection instrument that makes daily emotions and their antecedents visible for later analysis.
requirements: Students self-report the emotions they experience daily on the grid
constraints: Designed for university-level academic contexts
target_learning_goals: emotion awareness
emotion regulation in academic learning

title: Pekrun's control-value theory of achievement emotions as an analytic framework for emotion awareness data
description: The study uses Pekrun's control-value theory of achievement emotions as the framework for a quantitative descriptive analysis of students' retrospective emotion interviews. The abstract states: "A quantitative descriptive analysis of these retrospective interviews was conducted based on Pekrun's control-value theory of achievement emotions." Within this framework, transcripts are coded along three axes: the focus of emotions, the causes students attribute, and their appraisals of value and control. The theory thus organizes both the emotional experience and the situational appraisals that antecede it.

constraints: Applied to university-level academic emotion episodes in this study
target_learning_goals: understanding achievement emotions
appraisal of value and control in learning situations

article_title: Impact of an instructional guide and examples on the quality of feedback: insights from a randomised controlled study
citation: George Gyamfi, Barbara E. Hanna, Hassan Khosravi. (2024). Impact of an instructional guide and examples on the quality of feedback: insights from a randomised controlled study. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10346-0
title: RiPPLE learnersourcing platform with embedded feedback guide
description: RiPPLE is a teaching and research platform developed at the University of Queensland in which students create learning resources (multiple-choice questions, multi-answer questions, worked examples, and open-ended "notes") and moderate peers' resources before release to a shared bank. In this study the platform housed the intervention: "The guide, housed on RiPPLE, popped up the first time students began to provide feedback" and remained accessible thereafter. It also supports large-scale experimental research designs such as RCTs.
requirements: Students create and peer-moderate learning resources; a resource must be evaluated at least 3 times with an average of at least 3.5/5 to pass moderation
constraints: The study's guide was customisable to course contexts; the article notes limited understanding of the extent to which students re-consulted the guide after it first popped up
target_learning_goals: evaluative judgement
peer feedback quality
creation of learning resources
examples: 195 postgraduate applied linguistics students produced weekly reflection notes and completed 7231 moderations over 13 weeks

citation: George Gyamfi, Barbara E. Hanna, Hassan Khosravi. (2024). Impact of an instructional guide and examples on the quality of feedback: insights from a randomised controlled study. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10346-0
title: Adapted S.P.A.R.K. model for coding peer feedback quality
description: The S.P.A.R.K. mnemonic, from Gardner (2019), presents five recommended traits of feedback: "it should be Specific, Prescriptive, Actionable, Referenced, Kind." Because the original points were memorization suggestions rather than a coding scheme, the authors adapted the definitions — revising the overlapping "prescriptive" and "actionable" criteria for a tighter distinction — and used the adapted scheme in NVIVO to code sampled comments. Double coding of 30% of comments per group yielded a Cohen's Kappa of 0.83 with 95.2% inter-rater agreement.
requirements: Independent criteria distinct from the feedback guide's own tips, to avoid exaggerating differences between trained and untrained groups
Double coding to establish clarity, replicability and validity of adapted definitions
constraints: The original definitions of prescriptive and actionable overlapped and were difficult to differentiate consistently, requiring revision for coding
target_learners: postgraduate peer reviewers in higher education
target_learning_goals: evaluative judgement of feedback quality
examples: Sample coded comments include a prescriptive comment suggesting hedge words and an actionable comment asking the author to explain the relationship between UG and L1 acquisition

article_title: Students’ preferences with university teaching practices: analysis of testimonials with artificial intelligence
citation: Carmen Álvarez-Álvarez & Samuel Falcon. (2023). Students' preferences with university teaching practices: analysis of testimonials with artificial intelligence. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10239-8
title: Nine-category taxonomy of university teaching practices adapted from Smith and Baik (2021)
description: The study classifies student testimony using nine categories of teaching practices drawn from a systematic review: Clarity, Investigation, Application, Experience (Experiential), Challenges, Importance (Relevance), Interaction and relationships, Consolidation, and Self-regulation, plus an added category "0" for "none". Each category has stated characteristics; for example, Clarity covers curriculum design, lesson design and delivery, and Interaction and relationships covers collaborative learning, dialogue, student–teacher relationship and peer tutoring. The article uses the taxonomy as the GPT-3 classification rubric so responses can be coded "at a level that can be easily understood by both teachers and students".
requirements: A shared rubric with definitions per category so that coders (human or AI) classify each response into a single category
constraints: The categories capture Smith and Baik's (2021) findings "at a general level of abstraction"
target_learning_goals: identifying and categorising students' preferences for university teaching practices
examples: Responses such as "Classroom debate, in which we all participate" were classified as Interaction and relationships; "The slides and the teacher's good method of explanation" as Clarity.

title: When adopting mobile game-based learning, draw on systematic review findings to guide effective utilisation of mGBL approaches
description: The article recommends that decisions about using mobile game-based learning be grounded in the accumulated findings of review scholarship rather than ad hoc choices. It presents its response as "highlighting how practitioners, scholars and designers can use their findings to effectively utilise mobile Game Based Learning (mBGL) approaches to support and enhance learning", treating the 13-year review as a practical resource for designing and deploying mGBL.

constraints: The article addresses utilisation of mGBL approaches specifically; it does not claim the review findings transfer to non-mobile or non-game contexts
target_learners: practitioners, scholars and designers of mobile game-based learning
target_learning_goals: effective utilisation of mobile game-based learning to support and enhance learning
examples: The article structures its response around the key ideas of the Giannakas et al. (2018) review, read from a practical perspective for mGBL use
