description: The editorial centers the special issue on Nacu et al. (2018)'s framework of "10 educator roles that can cultivate autonomy and encourage learners as creative producers with 21st-century skills." The framework functions as a heuristic evaluation tool: "a heuristic evaluation of educator roles can provide guidance for designing these environments." All seven responses take this evaluation as their reference point.

title: Design online learning environments to support educators as well as learners
description: The editorial's closing recommendation is that online learning design attend to educators, not only learners: "Online learning designers should pay attention to not only the experiences of learners but also to how educators are enabled to support their learning." Environments used to train individuals with 21st-century skills "should also support the educators in this regard," and defining educator roles and tasks is presented as important for an effective learning process.

constraints: Stated in the context of environments aiming to cultivate 21st-century skills

article_title: Learning teamwork through a computer game: for the sake of performance or collaborative learning?
citation: Elina Riivari, Marke Kivijärvi, Anna-Maija Lämsä. (2021). Learning teamwork through a computer game: for the sake of performance or collaborative learning? Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-10009-4
title: Novicraft computer-based awareness simulation game for team, leadership, and management training
description: Novicraft is, in the article's words, "a computer-based awareness game, designed particularly for team, leadership, and management training", developed by a multidisciplinary research-based team and informed by learning and motivation theories. Played in real time in teams of three to five on an island-escape scenario, it uses scripts to assign members different resources so that "there is no possibility of free riding to escape from the island as a team". Its five tasks each target different teamwork, collaboration, and leadership skills, and its theoretical basis is Belbin's nine team roles and Kogler Hill's team leadership model.
requirements: Played in teams of three to five with each participant at their own computer, following the developers' recommendation of a maximum of 12 students per session
Trained facilitators who set up the game and act as passive instructors and observers
constraints: Used as a mandatory component of an undergraduate HRM course at a Finnish business school; the game was played in a co-located computer classroom, and the article notes it is no longer available because of technical changes
target_learners: undergraduate university students in a human resource management course
target_learning_goals: teamwork skills
team roles
internal team leadership actions
decision making in teams
examples: In the studied course, teams completed five sequential island-escape tasks, such as negotiating ingredient combinations for burner oil and coordinating fence-building to pass a dog-guarded field

article_title: Relational topologies in the learning activity spaces: operationalising a sociomaterial approach
citation: Linda Castañeda, Victoria I. Marín, Daniel Villar-Onrubia. (2024). Relational topologies in the learning activity spaces: operationalising a sociomaterial approach. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10296-z
title: Three relational topologies for sociomaterial analysis of learning spaces
description: The article proposes a methodological framework built on three sequential topologies for the sociomaterial analysis of teaching and learning spaces. As the authors state, the approach is based on "three different topologies: (1) Topologies of influence and activity in the learning space, focused on the use of tools; (2) Topologies for the multi-spatial learning context... and (3) Entanglements in multi-spatial contexts". The first topology is described as "the seed of the second one, and so on", so they were developed iteratively. Each topology starts from a guiding question (who introduces tools; where learning happens; how devices, interfaces and spaces entangle) and is operationalised through concrete data-collection and visualisation procedures.
requirements: Combination of "topologies of digital data practices" with the three ACAD design dimensions (set, epistemic, social)
Mixed qualitative and quantitative data collection with participants' self-reports
constraints: Applying topologies can be challenging due to their complex, non-linear, and heterogeneous nature
Specialised software is required to visualise and analyse the multiple data layers
target_learning_goals: Understanding technology-mediated learning activity across spaces, tools and devices
examples: The three topologies were developed and illustrated sequentially using data from the RICT course case study
key_sources: Linda Castañeda, Victoria I. Marín, Daniel Villar-Onrubia. (2024). Relational topologies in the learning activity spaces: operationalising a sociomaterial approach. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10296-z

title: ACAD framework's three design dimensions as relational conditions for learning
description: The Activity-Centred Analysis and Design (ACAD) framework (Goodyear & Carvalho, 2014) provides a holistic and relational understanding of design for learning. The article states that ACAD defines three main aspects to analyse when intentionally designing situations for learning: "(1) the set design, (2) the epistemic design, and (3) the social design", while recognising that "learning activity is always emergent and cannot be predefined". The article uses ACAD as the anchoring framework that its topologies operationalise, with particular emphasis on the under-studied set design.
requirements: Analysis must treat the three design aspects relationally rather than in isolation
constraints: Less attention has been given to the 'set design' in prior ACAD literature
target_learning_goals: Design and analysis of situations for learning
examples: The RICT case study analyses the course structure through the ACAD lens, with special emphasis on the set design component

title: Decuypere's IUDE toolbox of four topologies of data practices
description: The article draws on Decuypere's (2021) methodological framework of topologies of digital data practices, defined as "the actions, performances, and the resulting consequences of introducing data-producing technologies in everyday situations". Decuypere presents "four topologies of data practices... Interface (on), Usage (with), Design (behind) and Ecology (beyond)", together constituting the IUDE-toolbox. The framework uses topologies as the basic unit of analysis to study the qualitative qualities of relations between actors, and is explicitly non-one-size-fits-all and adaptable.
requirements: Focus on actions and consequences of data-producing technologies rather than the technologies themselves
Use of topologies as the basic unit of analysis
constraints: Presented as a non-one-size-fits-all and adaptable solution
target_learning_goals: Studying digital data practices in educational processes
examples: The article's first topology falls between the user and interface categories as classified by Decuypere

citation: Linda Castañeda, Victoria I. Marín, Daniel Villar-Onrubia. (2024). Relational topologies in the learning activity spaces: operationalising a sociomaterial approach. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10296-z
title: RICT case study: pre-service teacher-training course as testbed for the topologies
description: The RICT case is an on-campus pre-service teacher-training course, "Educational Resources and ICT for Primary School", at a Spanish university, taught in English to first-year students over 12 weeks (5 h per week) with 6 ECTS credits and an estimated workload of 150 h. The cohort included 50 students organised into eight stable working groups. The course is designed around a formal cooperative learning model with cooperative base groups, weekly trialogical learning tasks, and pre-established scripted roles. Data were collected in the academic year 2021-2022, starting at week 6, over 2 weeks, anonymously.
requirements: Group discussions, brainstorming dynamics, and online questionnaires for tool, space and device reporting
constraints: No identification or personal data were collected; supporting data is unavailable because participants did not agree to public sharing

examples: Students discussed tools in three categories (compulsory, discovered during tasks, pre-existing) and voted on the spaces they used most often

title: Use multidimensional topology analyses to inform institutional infrastructure and edtech decisions
description: The article argues that the topological approach can inform institutional planning of digital infrastructures and pedagogical design. It states that "Multidimensional analyses can help universities make informed decisions about infrastructure and technology resources", giving examples such as evaluating the need for plugs and WIFI connections, classroom furnishings, and mobile-friendly versions of virtual learning environments, and whether investing in other edtech tools and platforms is necessary. constraints: Relying on self-reported data might be perceived as a limitation, though the authors contend participants' subjective experiences provide valuable insights

citation: Jere-Folotiya, J., Chansa-Kabali, T., Munachaka, J. C., Sampa, F., Yalukanda, C., Westerholm, J., Richardson, U., Serpell, R., & Lyytinen, H. (2014). title: GraphoGame ciNyanja cellphone-based phonics game with adaptive trials and performance logging
description: GraphoGame is a computer-mediated online environment for learning letter-sound correspondences, developed in Finland and mounted here in ciNyanja on cellphones with headphones for supervised small-group play. "GraphoGameTM is based on repeated trials in which the player must choose from 2 to 8 alternatives, the letter that corresponds to the phoneme s/he hears from headphones." It adapts to keep the success rate high (about 80%), progresses from easy to difficult phonemes to larger units, and records session duration and per-trial choices as time-series data, generating daisy-graph performance profiles.
requirements: Requires cellphone handsets with headphones and supervised small-group administration at schools
constraints: The intervention time in this research was too short (under 100 min) to go beyond letter sounds
target_learners: Grade one students in Zambian Government public schools in Lusaka
target_learning_goals: Letter-sound correspondence knowledge and initial literacy (decoding/spelling) in ciNyanja
examples: A ciNyanja version was mounted on Nokia phone handsets and played by grade one students in small supervised groups at their schools

citation: Lin Lin, Tristan Johnson. (2021). Shifting to digital: informing the rapid development, deployment, and future of teaching and learning. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09960-z
title: Four-aspect commentary framework: Impact/Value, Application, Limitations and Constraints, Future Suggestions
description: The editors established review criteria asking responding authors to structure their commentary pieces around four aspects: 'Impact/Value', 'Application', 'Limitations and Constraints', and 'Future Suggestions'. Each aspect is phrased as a question the respondent answers from their own perspective, e.g., 'What impact or value does the paper have on "Shift to Digital" from your specific perspective?' This pattern turns a review of prior work into practice-oriented dialogue.
requirements: Respondent authors identify 2–3 manuscripts of interest and specify the perspective they will focus on
A defined context of need, here flexible learning, online learning, and learning disruptions with limited resources
constraints: Essays were 500–1000 words and situated the 17 previously published articles within COVID-19 learning needs
target_learning_goals: applying published research to rapid digital shifts
examples: Responding authors were asked to focus on Impact/Value, Application, Limitations and Constraints, and Future Suggestions when writing their commentary pieces

article_title: Improving the transfer of inquiry strategies by using short instructional videos
citation: Ana Saavedra · Daniel L. Schwartz. (2026). Improving the transfer of inquiry strategies by using short instructional videos. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10648-5
title: Internal psychological cue account of inquiry-strategy transfer
description: The article proposes that transfer of effortful inquiry strategies requires not only recognizing external situational cues but also attending to internally generated psychological cues. Because students' natural default strategy (difference reduction) feels easy at the outset, alerting students to the feelings that draw them to it — cognitive ease and later frustration — can help them inhibit it and switch to the more demanding means-ends strategy. The article states: "If we can help alert students to the internal cues associated with this natural tendency, we may be able to help them inhibit the default strategy and switch to the more cognitively demanding base-unit strategy." It blends cognitive and behavior-change approaches to transfer.
requirements: Students must have a well-worn default strategy that feels natural and effortless, generating recognizable internal cues
constraints: Tested for one inquiry strategy (base-unit) in simulation-based inquiry; the authors note it is unknown whether increasing instruction dosage improves transfer
target_learning_goals: self-directed inquiry strategies
transfer of learning strategies to new science simulations
examples: The Expanded video told students the default strategy feels easiest but makes things more complicated, and that effort at the beginning pays off
key_sources: Ana Saavedra · Daniel L. Schwartz. (2026). Improving the transfer of inquiry strategies by using short instructional videos. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10648-5

article_title: Improving the transfer of inquiry strategies by using short instructional videos
citation: Ana Saavedra · Daniel L. Schwartz. (2026). Improving the transfer of inquiry strategies by using short instructional videos. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10648-5
title: Expanded instructional video treatment
description: The Expanded video was the most complete of five instructional video treatments, lasting 4′58″. It demonstrated the base-unit strategy, explained why it works, contrasted it with the ineffective default piling-on strategy, and — uniquely — alerted students to the feelings that draw them to the default strategy and to internal cues for switching. As the article describes it, "The Expanded treatment includes the Contrast + Explain content and further alerts students to the feelings that draw them to the default strategy (i.e., cognitive ease)." It was compared against ablated variants and a no-video control across five experiments.
requirements: Delivered after students explored the Balancelet simulation, which set up the video's relevance
constraints: The key instructional message occurred in a mere few sentences embedded in the video, which the authors note as a possible reason for small between-video differences
target_learners: eighth- and ninth-grade students in Colombian public and private schools
target_learning_goals: adopting an effective inquiry strategy
inhibiting an ineffective default strategy
transfer of inquiry strategies
examples: Experiment 1 compared Show and Expanded; Experiment 5 included all five video treatments plus Control with a larger, more diverse sample

article_title: Video feedback: is it worth the effort? A response to Borup et al.
citation: Lowenthal, P. R. (2021). Video feedback: is it worth the effort? A response to Borup et al. Education Tech Research Dev, 69, 127-131. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09872-4
title: Weigh the effort of video feedback against its communication benefits and user preferences
description: The article's title poses the question "is it worth the effort?" about video feedback, and its abstract sets up the trade-off: video feedback is now easy to produce and can increase conversational and affective communication, yet research suggests instructors and students might prefer text-based feedback. The principle is that adopters should weigh production effort against these communication benefits and stated preferences rather than assuming video is automatically better.
requirements: Instructors must have the means to produce video feedback, since the article notes it is easier than ever to provide
constraints: Users might prefer text-based feedback despite video's benefits
target_learners: higher education students in blended and online courses
target_learning_goals: instructor feedback on student work
social presence and communication in online courses
examples: The article responds to Borup, West, and Thomas's (2015) study of text versus video communication for instructor feedback in blended courses, discussing the value of that research and how it can be applied.

article_title: The role of teachers in a sustainable university: from digital competencies to postdigital capabilities
citation: Lina Markauskaite, Lucila Carvalho, Tim Fawns. (2023). The role of teachers in a sustainable university: from digital competencies to postdigital capabilities. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10199-z
title: Postdigital teaching capabilities: an ecological, distributed and relational framework
description: The article proposes that teaching capabilities in a postdigital university are "distributed and relational", extending across an activity system that includes other people, culture, environment and the embodied self. It draws on theories of cognition that see human capabilities as "extended, enacted, embedded, enculturated and embodied", arguing that what teachers know cannot be separated from their feelings, material and digital environments, and social others. The framework situates capabilities at macro (global), meso (local practices) and micro (daily activities) levels of the educational ecosystem.
requirements: Conceptualisations must describe capabilities that extend across an activity system rather than properties inherent in an individual
constraints: The article presents this as a conceptual proposal offered as an entry point, not an empirically validated model
target_learning_goals: teaching with digital technologies in sustainable, future-oriented universities
examples: The article grounds the framework in ecopedagogies, pedagogies of care and pedagogies of self-care as complementary postdigital pedagogies at macro, meso and micro levels
key_sources: Lina Markauskaite, Lucila Carvalho, Tim Fawns. (2023). The role of teachers in a sustainable university: from digital competencies to postdigital capabilities. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10199-z

article_title: The role of teachers in a sustainable university: from digital competencies to postdigital capabilities
citation: Lina Markauskaite, Lucila Carvalho, Tim Fawns. (2023). The role of teachers in a sustainable university: from digital competencies to postdigital capabilities. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10199-z
title: Sen's capability approach applied to university teachers' digital capabilities
description: The article adopts Sen's capability approach to broaden thinking about teachers' digital capabilities. Capabilities are connected to people's freedoms to be and to do what they value, and are "more than a person's individual abilities, or the absence of constraints, instead as encompassing the actual opportunities that help people to achieve their values". This view emphasises relational agency to make choices appropriate for oneself, other people and the environment, and requires reconciling personal, professional and societal values through teaching practices.
requirements: Recognition of the diversity of values and the complexity of contexts that teachers navigate
constraints: Requires moving beyond individually situated and profession-referenced conceptualisations of capability
target_learning_goals: exercising relational agency in teaching with digital technologies
examples: The article contrasts Sen's relational, opportunity-centred view with person-centred definitions of competence adopted in psychology
key_sources: Lina Markauskaite, Lucila Carvalho, Tim Fawns. (2023). The role of teachers in a sustainable university: from digital competencies to postdigital capabilities. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10199-z

article_title: The role of teachers in a sustainable university: from digital competencies to postdigital capabilities
citation: Lina Markauskaite, Lucila Carvalho, Tim Fawns. (2023). The role of teachers in a sustainable university: from digital competencies to postdigital capabilities. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10199-z
title: Ecopedagogies as a macro-level postdigital pedagogy for sustainability
description: Ecopedagogies are education models rooted in transformation-based teaching and critical theory, aimed at ending socio-environmental injustices, including those in the digital infosphere. They invite combinations of multiple perspectives and knowledges (e.g., indigenous and western), ask for a shift from local to planetary perspectives, and involve teachers unpacking hidden assumptions about development and sustainability. The article positions them at the macro (planetary) level of the educational ecosystem, with digital technologies playing a crucial role in enabling connections and knowledge co-creation.
requirements: Teachers and students being open and flexible, searching for the value of multiple perspectives and disciplinary stances
constraints: Teachers must consider not only pedagogical benefits of power-intensive technologies such as videoconferencing and AI but also their consumption of natural resources and environmental impact
target_learning_goals: critical literacy about sustainability and development
transforming societal structures
examples: The article notes ecopedagogies may include helping students learn when not to use technology or when to find alternatives

article_title: The role of teachers in a sustainable university: from digital competencies to postdigital capabilities
citation: Lina Markauskaite, Lucila Carvalho, Tim Fawns. (2023). The role of teachers in a sustainable university: from digital competencies to postdigital capabilities. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10199-z
title: Pedagogies of care and self-care as meso- and micro-level postdigital pedagogies
description: The article discusses pedagogies of care, founded on Noddings' reciprocal relations of listening, receptiveness and presence, and pedagogies of self-care, arguing that caring for the self is only possible through caring for others and that collective caring requires sufficient resources. Distributed care involves "attending to the relations between all elements in a learning ecology", requiring collective action at micro, meso and macro levels. The article notes these pedagogies can be in tension with neoliberal institutional priorities focused on job-market-ready graduates.
requirements: A system that allows space, time and energy to care, and individuals knowing their own limits and values
constraints: Care in higher education is particularly challenging in relation to AI and automatic technology, such as learning analytics that constrain legitimate behaviour or knowledge
target_learning_goals: enacting ethics, empathy and social justice in teaching
teacher wellbeing
examples: During Covid-19, enacting an ethic of care included considering differences in students' technological access and home infrastructures, and what happens with students' data

title: Activity systems view of teaching capabilities as distributed activity
description: The article takes an activity systems view to foreground teaching as a distributed activity enacted collectively by people and technologies, including students, learning designers, IT staff, librarians, policymakers and accreditors. It focuses on 'teaching capabilities' rather than 'teacher capabilities' to acknowledge distributed agency, influenced by curricula, policies, leadership, disciplines, resources and socio-political contexts. Capabilities span global (macro), local (meso) and individual (micro) levels of the educational ecosystem.
requirements: Widening thinking beyond the individual teacher to the broader distributed activity system
constraints: The article states most existing literature takes a person-centred view that this framework deliberately departs from
target_learners: educational stakeholders in distributed teaching systems
target_learning_goals: collective enactment of teaching towards a sustainable university mission
examples: The article lists elements influencing distributed teaching capabilities, including educational policies, leadership, joint goals and visions, and physical and digital resources

title: Four dimensions of epistemic fluency for postdigital teaching
description: Drawing on Markauskaite and Goodyear (2017), the article identifies four key dimensions of fluency: "(1) combination and integration of different kinds of knowledge; (2) coordination and weaving different ways of knowing; (3) creating tools and assembling productive environments; and (4) constructing a conscientious and conscious self". These dimensions connect to postdigital pedagogies and underpin capabilities for teaching in hybrid environments, including knowing when to design, when to practise skills, when to learn from colleagues, and when to outsource decisions to learning analytics tools.
requirements: Teachers engaging in different kinds of expert practices, not explicit professional learning alone, to develop recognition of what makes teaching productive in a situation
constraints: The article states this recognition cannot be achieved through explicit professional learning alone
target_learning_goals: integrating diverse knowledge and ways of knowing in hybrid teaching
co-designing tools and environments
examples: The article describes empathic design of digital learning environments and engaging learners in co-design as practices connected to the third dimension

article_title: Multimodal analysis of interaction data from embodied education technologies
citation: Walkington, C., Nathan, M. J., Huang, W., Hunnicutt, J., & Washington, J. (2024). Multimodal analysis of interaction data from embodied education technologies. Education Tech Research Dev, 72, 2565–2584. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10254-9
title: MAET: multimodal analysis for embodied technologies as a research method
description: MAET is a research method adapted from multimodal analysis for embodied, interactive educational technologies where learners collaborate. It tracks "learners' gestures, actions on physical and virtual objects, whole body movements and positions, and their talk moves" over time and space. Its distinguishing affordance is alignment with embodied cognition theories, valuing action itself as a conceptual tool, unlike social semiotics, conversation analysis, or multimodal (inter)action analysis approaches.
requirements: A networked system of audio, motion, and video data capture technologies are necessary for MAET to rigorously examine interactions across modalities
Video recordings, screen recordings, and motion capture data synced across perspectives
constraints: Relies on video camera feeds rather than automatic multimodal learning analytics such as automatic gesture detection
Syncing and coding video data from multiple perspectives for micro-interactions can be quite time-consuming
Cost, technical expertise, and setup may be prohibitive in some cases
target_learners: Learners using collaborative immersive educational technologies (K-12 students, teacher-learners)
target_learning_goals: Understanding embodied and collaborative mathematical reasoning
examples: Applied to a motion capture game (The Hidden Village), a shared VR environment for mathematics teachers, and shAR hologram conjecture tasks

title: Embodied and extended cognition as the theoretical framework for immersive learning technologies
description: The paper grounds MAET in embodied cognition (Wilson, 2002)—the idea that all thoughts are grounded in perception, action, and spatial systems—and in extended/distributed cognition, where knowledge is stretched over people, places, and objects. Enactivism holds that "learning is moving in new ways." The framework explains why gesture, body position, and collaborative action matter for learning in shAR, VR, and MC environments.
requirements: Technologies that capture embodied interactional information beyond speech or writing
constraints: Research on embodied learning has not broadly embraced the collaborative nature of learning environments, per the authors
target_learners: Mathematics learners and teachers in technology-enhanced environments
target_learning_goals: Mathematical reasoning and conceptual understanding through embodied action
examples: Used to interpret collaborative gesture sequences and joint attention in the three technology cases

title: The Hidden Village motion capture geometry game with Conjecture Builder
description: The Hidden Village is a motion capture video game in the visual novel genre where high school students crash-land on an alien planet and perform arm motions captured by a Kinect camera to make poses matching geometry conjectures they must prove true or false. The Conjecture Builder feature "allows the students to determine how different physical motions mighty correspond to geometry ideas" by creating and programming their own arm motions.
requirements: Motion capture via Kinect camera (a current version uses a laptop camera) to determine if players make the desired poses
target_learning_goals: Proving or disproving geometry conjectures (e.g., similar triangles, parallelogram area, rectangle diagonals, vertical angles)

article_title: Each discipline is different: teacher capabilities for future-focussed digitally infused undergraduate programmes
citation: Louise Starkey, Anne Yates, Mairead de Roiste, Karsten Lundqvist, Adreanne Ormond, John Randal, Allan Sylvester. (2023). Each discipline is different: teacher capabilities for future-focussed digitally infused undergraduate programmes. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10196-2
title: Disciplinary-culture-centred account of digital-era pedagogical change in Higher Education
description: The article frames educational systems as dynamic and emergent, using complexity thinking and appreciative inquiry to explain how digital technologies alter disciplines and teaching. It argues that "Disciplinary culture is the basis of Higher Education teacher identity and underpins pedagogical practice and use of digital technology", which in turn determines the digital capabilities teachers need. Disciplines are described as evolving rather than static, with digital technology superimposed on older disciplines and central to newer ones.
requirements: Teachers' capability development must be understood within each discipline's culture, traditions, skills and knowledge
constraints: Findings derive from five disciplines in one New Zealand university and the first three phases of an appreciative inquiry
target_learning_goals: Discipline-appropriate pedagogical practice and digital capability development
examples: Case studies of Information Systems, Geography, Statistics for Business, Critical Indigenous Studies and Computer Science written by disciplinary experts

citation: Mutluhan Yilmaz, Andrea Gauthier, Mutlu Cukurova. (2026). Supporting online learners' regulation skills with the help of learning analytics and generative artificial intelligence. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10595-1
title: RefleXED tutor-support tool for LA-driven feedback provision
description: RefleXED is a practical tool developed in this study to support tutor-generated feedback. It "displays each student’s standardised SRLs proxy scores, cluster information based on the result of RQ1, and comprehensive insights into the SRLs pillars used in the study", while automatically retrieving the student's first name from the database. Tutors see only IDs, cluster membership and proxy scores, with tooltips explaining each proxy's behavioural variables and calculations, helping them craft tailored feedback regardless of familiarity with statistical terms. It was used by the control-condition tutor in the quasi-experiment.
requirements: Requires LMS log data processed into standardised SRLs proxy scores and cluster labels per student
constraints: Tutors access only student ID, cluster, and standardised proxy scores, without visibility of student names
target_learners: higher education students in online courses
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning skills (goal setting, task strategies, time management, help-seeking, self-evaluation)
examples: The study's single tutor used RefleXED's feedback creation interface to compose personalised messages for the control group across two intervention weeks

title: Ye and Pennisi's framework for modelling SRL from LMS behavioural traces
description: The study adopts Ye and Pennisi's (2022) theory-based framework that integrates Pintrich's SRL model (forethought, planning, activation, monitoring, control, reflection) with the Online Self-Regulated Learning Questionnaire as a lens for collecting and modelling LMS log data. The authors chose it because "the SRL skills indicators it provides are aligned with behavioural traces that can be captured from online learning platforms", enabling assessment across all SRL cycle phases. It maps SRL phases to LMS behavioural data and OSLQ indicators, and the study operationalised it into five proxies: goal setting, task strategies, time management, help-seeking, and self-evaluation.
requirements: Course resources must closely correspond to the framework's indicators so data sources align conceptually and practically with the measurement model
constraints: The study's course lacked Optional Self-Assessments and bonus quiz completion indicators, so these two were excluded from proxy computation
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning skills
examples: Raw MOODLE log events were extracted, normalised and z-score standardised, then aggregated into the five SRL proxies used for clustering and feedback generation

title: Embed effective learning strategies, knowledge construction tools or educational theories when developing educational computer games
description: The editorial's central design principle: educational computer games should be developed by taking effective learning strategies, knowledge construction tools or educational theories into account, because effectiveness may fall short otherwise. It states that "merely applying digital games to educational settings might be insufﬁcient" and that learning objectives and contents need to be well-integrated into gaming missions and scenarios.

target_learning_goals: subject-domain knowledge and skills supported by game-based learning

article_title: Determining mobile learning acceptance outside the classroom: an integrated acceptance model
citation: Chenxi Liu, Ana-Paula Correia, Young Min Kim. (2025). Determining mobile learning acceptance outside the classroom: an integrated acceptance model. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10514-w
title: Integrated m-learning acceptance model combining TAM with the updated DeLone and McLean IS Success Model
description: The article proposes a novel acceptance model that imports the three quality dimensions of the updated DL&ML into the TAM belief-intention structure. As printed: "The proposed model includes seven quality-related constructs. Among them, content quality and content design quality correspond to the information quality dimension; mobility, compatibility, interface design, and interactivity correspond to the system quality dimension; and service quality corresponds to the service quality dimension." These seven exogenous quality constructs are hypothesized to influence perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness, which in turn drive behavioral intention. The model was tested with SEM and supported eight of thirteen hypotheses.
requirements: Quality constructs must have clearly defined components; the article notes prior studies left components underdefined and inconsistent
constraints: Attitude was excluded from the instrument based on prior studies; content quality and interface design constructs were removed from the final analysis for discriminant validity
target_learners: Adult learners in the U.S., both students and non-students, using m-learning apps outside the classroom
target_learning_goals: Understanding and predicting learners' acceptance of mobile learning applications
examples: Tested via a two-step SEM strategy (measurement model then structural model) on 639 valid MTurk survey responses; structural model fit: RMSEA = 0.06, SRMR = 0.06, CFI = 0.91, TLI = 0.90
key_sources: Chenxi Liu, Ana-Paula Correia, Young Min Kim. (2025). Determining mobile learning acceptance outside the classroom: an integrated acceptance model. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10514-w

article_title: An exploratory case study of the use of a digital self-assessment tool of 21st-century skills in makerspace contexts
citation: Ourania Miliou, Maria Adamou, Aekaterini Mavri, Andri Ioannou. (2024). An exploratory case study of the use of a digital self-assessment tool of 21st-century skills in makerspace contexts. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10314-0
title: Assessmake21 digital self-assessment tool for 21st-century skills in makerspaces
description: Assessmake21 is a web-based digital self-assessment tool, developed as an expansion of SkillsTrack, that supports self-assessment of 21st-century skills in makerspace contexts. Students tag a skill they are using during making, which triggers reflection challenges such as building a visual portfolio with uploaded photos; completing challenges progresses them through levels, and educators award badges. It offers a Definitions feature with conceptual and operational definitions drawn from frameworks such as P21, and an educator's dashboard showing individual and classroom progress. The article reports it offers tagging of five skills: Collaboration, Creativity, Problem-solving, Life/Social Skills, and Communication.
requirements: A teacher sets up and manages a virtual classroom on the educator's dashboard, registering students with a unique login code and choosing one of three self-assessment approaches (parallel, parallel tapping with challenges at the end, or at-the-end).
constraints: The tool offered limited options for skills that could be tagged, and teachers recommended expansion to a broader skills repertoire; tablet use posed typing and multi-tab difficulties.
The vocabulary of the skill conceptualisations was difficult for some 12-year-old students.
target_learners: K-12 students aged 12-18 in makerspace contexts
target_learning_goals: Self-assessment and reflection on 21st-century skills (collaboration, creativity, problem-solving, life/social skills, communication) during making activities
examples: Six teachers used the tool across formal and non-formal makerspaces for 6-7 months, with activities including programming, digital fabrication, robotics, circuitry, and arts and crafts.

article_title: Augmented reality for area measurement reasoning of elementary students
citation: Eunhye Flavin, Moon Chung, Sunghwa Flavin, Matthew T. Flavin. (2025). Augmented reality for area measurement reasoning of elementary students. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10502-0
title: Clements and Sarama's eight-phase learning trajectory for area measurement
description: The article adopts Clements and Sarama's (2020) learning trajectory, which "explains how children conceptually understand and calculate area according additive and multiplicative reasoning" across eight phases, from Area Senser to Array Structurer. Each phase is defined by observable behaviors and hypothesized mental actions, e.g., Phase 6 children identify "a square unit as both a unit and a component of a larger unit of units such as a row and column". The study used the trajectory both to design MeoGeo activities toward phase 8 and to code students' reasoning development across tests.
requirements: Instructors assess and understand the developmental phases of their students to provide appropriate support through each phase
target_learning_goals: spatial structuring of 2D area
additive and multiplicative reasoning for area
examples: Students' written and verbal test responses were coded into trajectory phases, e.g., additive reasoning classified as level 5
key_sources: Eunhye Flavin, Moon Chung, Sunghwa Flavin, Matthew T. Flavin. (2025). Augmented reality for area measurement reasoning of elementary students. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10502-0

article_title: Augmented reality for area measurement reasoning of elementary students
citation: Eunhye Flavin, Moon Chung, Sunghwa Flavin, Matthew T. Flavin. (2025). Augmented reality for area measurement reasoning of elementary students. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10502-0
title: MeoGeo: marker-less AR app for area measurement with resizable virtual units on a regular grid
description: MeoGeo is an iOS AR app, built with Swift, ARKit and RealityKit using LiDAR sensors, that lets students tap the screen to place virtual unit squares superimposed on the camera feed and resize them by dragging a side length. It "employs real-time marker-less AR technology", and it "discretizes the physical space of the user into a regular grid, enforcing placement of virtual units", eliminating the gaps and overlaps common with physical manipulatives. Virtual objects stay anchored to physical locations and computational occlusion hides parts behind physical objects.
requirements: an iPad with ARKit-capable sensors (students used a 6th-generation iPad Pro)
constraints: the app enforces grid placement, so free-form unit placement is not possible
target_learning_goals: area measurement reasoning for basic and composite shapes
spatial structuring with units of varying sizes
examples: Activity 1 had students measure a 600 cm2 rectangle using 10 cm × 10 cm and 10 cm × 20 cm unit sizes
key_sources: Eunhye Flavin, Moon Chung, Sunghwa Flavin, Matthew T. Flavin. (2025). Augmented reality for area measurement reasoning of elementary students. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10502-0

article_title: Augmented reality for area measurement reasoning of elementary students
citation: Eunhye Flavin, Moon Chung, Sunghwa Flavin, Matthew T. Flavin. (2025). Augmented reality for area measurement reasoning of elementary students. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10502-0
title: Sequenced AR tiling activities progressing from basic rectangles to composite shapes with increasing unit-size variety
description: The intervention used four weekly AR activities, each about 60 minutes, sequenced from measuring a rectangle with two unit sizes, to L-shapes with two and then three unit sizes, to a large rectangle with four unit sizes. The design rests on the premise that "Understanding the same area can be tiled with different shapes and measured using various unit squares is essential for developing area measurement competency", so the authors "intentionally instructed students to use different unit sizes when measuring the area of shapes". Later activities pushed students toward efficient strategies such as covering more area with fewer, larger units.
requirements: an instructor present as a social scaffolder to explain each activity and guide reasoning
constraints: activities were implemented over four weekly sessions in a summer program setting
target_learners: elementary students with weak area measurement reasoning
target_learning_goals: decomposition and recomposition of composite shapes
multiplicative reasoning with rows and columns
examples: Activity 3 asked students to measure a 700 cm2 L-shape using 10 cm × 10 cm, 10 cm × 20 cm, and 10 cm × 30 cm units
key_sources: Eunhye Flavin, Moon Chung, Sunghwa Flavin, Matthew T. Flavin. (2025). Augmented reality for area measurement reasoning of elementary students. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10502-0

article_title: Teacher dashboard design for self-regulated learning: a participatory approach
citation: Susan Verbunt-Janssen, Carolien A. N. Knoop-van Campen, Martine Baars, Inge Molenaar. (2026). Teacher dashboard design for self-regulated learning: a participatory approach. Educational technology research and development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10632-z
title: COPES model of self-regulated learning as the organizing framework for SRL teacher dashboard indicators
description: The COPES model (Winne & Hadwin, 1998) frames SRL as unfolding in four phases: task definition, goal setting, enactment, and adaptation. The article states "in the enactment phase, students execute their plans, monitor, and control their progress". The study used COPES as the theory-driven coding scheme for focus group data, compared teacher-generated indicators against it to identify gaps, and structured the dashboard prototype's widgets around its phases.
requirements: Metacognitive indicators must be mapped to specific COPES phases to structure dashboard information
constraints: Teachers in this study did not spontaneously mention task definition indicators, creating a gap between teacher needs and the theory-based indicator set
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning
metacognition
examples: The prototype dashboard has five widgets, one per COPES phase, including a task definition widget with prior knowledge and motivation indicators teachers did not request
key_sources: Susan Verbunt-Janssen, Carolien A. N. Knoop-van Campen, Martine Baars, Inge Molenaar. (2026). Teacher dashboard design for self-regulated learning: a participatory approach. Educational technology research and development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10632-z

article_title: Teacher dashboard design for self-regulated learning: a participatory approach
citation: Susan Verbunt-Janssen, Carolien A. N. Knoop-van Campen, Martine Baars, Inge Molenaar. (2026). Teacher dashboard design for self-regulated learning: a participatory approach. Educational technology research and development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10632-z
title: Detect-diagnose-act framework for adaptive learning technologies
description: The article explains the functioning of adaptive learning technologies through the detect-diagnose-act framework (Molenaar, 2022). As printed: "Detect represents the input data, such as answers to questions to measure students' current knowledge". Diagnosis assesses current knowledge and predicts future progress, and diagnoses are translated into pedagogical-didactical actions that either inform the teacher or are taken adaptively by the ALT. The framework contextualizes where teacher dashboards sit within ALTs.
requirements: Input data on student responses must be collected before diagnosis and action can occur
constraints: Current ALT dashboards mostly present cognitive progress indicators rather than metacognitive ones
target_learning_goals: monitoring student progress
adaptive instruction
examples: Dutch primary education context where 60% of students use an ALT daily (Kennisnet, 2019)
key_sources: Susan Verbunt-Janssen, Carolien A. N. Knoop-van Campen, Martine Baars, Inge Molenaar. (2026). Teacher dashboard design for self-regulated learning: a participatory approach. Educational technology research and development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10632-z

article_title: Teacher dashboard design for self-regulated learning: a participatory approach
citation: Susan Verbunt-Janssen, Carolien A. N. Knoop-van Campen, Martine Baars, Inge Molenaar. (2026). Teacher dashboard design for self-regulated learning: a participatory approach. Educational technology research and development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10632-z
title: Prototype SRL teacher dashboard with COPES-phase widgets and teacher-prioritized interface features
description: A prototype teacher dashboard presenting students' metacognitive indicators organized by COPES phase in five widgets: task definition (prior knowledge, motivation), goal setting (self-determined and ALT-determined goals), enactment monitoring (assignment count, progress versus self-set goals), enactment control (planned and executed actions), and adaptations (learning curves). The design "aims to alleviate their cognitive load" while implementing prioritized interface features such as saved settings, color-coded data streams, information buttons, and a unified quick overview.
requirements: Teachers' interface priorities (quick overview, personalization, few clicks) must be implemented for usability
constraints: Currently tailored for single-lesson use; additional data representations such as growth per grade will be incorporated upon classroom deployment
target_learners: primary school students in grades 5 and 6
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning
metacognitive feedback
examples: Fig. 1 shows the dashboard with widgets a through e, each associated with one COPES phase
key_sources: Susan Verbunt-Janssen, Carolien A. N. Knoop-van Campen, Martine Baars, Inge Molenaar. (2026). Teacher dashboard design for self-regulated learning: a participatory approach. Educational technology research and development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10632-z

article_title: Teacher dashboard design for self-regulated learning: a participatory approach
citation: Susan Verbunt-Janssen, Carolien A. N. Knoop-van Campen, Martine Baars, Inge Molenaar. (2026). Teacher dashboard design for self-regulated learning: a participatory approach. Educational technology research and development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10632-z
title: Involve teachers as partners in participatory design when building teacher-facing learning analytics tools
description: The study argues that participatory design, which actively engages users as partners influencing design choices and trade-offs, produces educational tools grounded in teachers' needs, abilities, and classroom contexts. The article states that "participatory design enhances both the technical soundness and pedagogical strength of educational tools, supporting successful adoption". The study operationalized this through iterative focus groups and a KANO questionnaire feeding directly into prototype design decisions.
requirements: Iterative cycles of investigating, reflecting, and learning collaboratively with teachers through activities such as focus groups and structured evaluation
constraints: Rigor in participatory design is defined by teachers' goals and expressed as internal validity of a well-structured process account rather than experimental standards
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning support
usable teacher tools
examples: Two design rounds: five focus groups (19 participants) generating indicators and features, then a KANO questionnaire (45 teachers) refining priorities that guided the prototype

article_title: NASA-TLX for predictability and measurability of instructional design models: case study in design methods
citation: Christopher Nikulin, Gabriela Lopez, Eduardo Piñonez, Luis Gonzalez, Pia Zapata. (2019). NASA-TLX for predictability and measurability of instructional design models: case study in design methods. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09657-4
title: Instructional design model for product development structured as 11 measurable modules across four design phases
description: The article proposes a prescriptive instructional design model for the Product Development Process, built on the design phases of Pahl et al. and split so each phase can be measured with NASA-TLX. The authors state: "We divide the design method into 11 modules to represent all the phases of product creation", with each module containing a minimum of three measurable activities. The four phases are clarification of the task, conceptual design, design embodiment, and detailed design and final product, spanning activities from data collection and sketching through CAD modelling to prototype manufacture and validation.
requirements: Design phases must be split into modules with specific, measurable tasks so NASA-TLX can be applied to each activity
constraints: The initial design methods need modification to have clear tasks measurable in practice; instructional design methods must have specific outcomes to be measurable and predictable
target_learning_goals: understanding and executing the product development design process phases
examples: In the case study, four young designers followed the 11 modules over more than 40 working hours to create a working surface attachable to a wheelchair, validated with handicapped teenagers from TELETON
key_sources: Christopher Nikulin, Gabriela Lopez, Eduardo Piñonez, Luis Gonzalez, Pia Zapata. (2019). NASA-TLX for predictability and measurability of instructional design models: case study in design methods. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09657-4

article_title: NASA-TLX for predictability and measurability of instructional design models: case study in design methods
citation: Christopher Nikulin, Gabriela Lopez, Eduardo Piñonez, Luis Gonzalez, Pia Zapata. (2019). NASA-TLX for predictability and measurability of instructional design models: case study in design methods. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09657-4
title: NASA-TLX multidimensional workload questionnaire used as a common measurement instrument across design activities
description: NASA-TLX is a multi-dimensional rating procedure that assigns a total workload score based on a weighted average of six sub-scales: mental demand, physical demand, temporal demand, performance, effort, and frustration level. Its application has two sequential phases: weighing, consisting of 15 binary comparisons among the six dimensions after task execution, and estimation, in which the individual rates each dimension on a scale from 0 to 100 immediately after task completion. In this study it was adopted as an outcome evaluation instrument for comparing different design phases and activities, with 133 questionnaires delivered.
requirements: Tasks must be represented as specific measurable activities so the questionnaire can be framed per module activity
constraints: The workload index is not an intrinsic feature of the task but results from interaction among task requirements, circumstances, capacities, and individual perceptions and behaviors
target_learning_goals: monitoring and comparing designer workload across design process activities
examples: Questionnaires were administered in Spanish at the end of each module, three per module framed for each activity, yielding 133 questionnaires across 11 modules
key_sources: Christopher Nikulin, Gabriela Lopez, Eduardo Piñonez, Luis Gonzalez, Pia Zapata. (2019). NASA-TLX for predictability and measurability of instructional design models: case study in design methods. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09657-4

article_title: Forum posts, communication patterns, and relational structures: A multi-level view of discussions in online courses
citation: Poquet, O., Trenholm, S., & Santolini, M. (2024). Forum posts, communication patterns, and relational structures: A multi-level view of discussions in online courses. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10262-9
title: Multi-level framework separating posting activity, communication structures, and emergent relational structures in online discussions
description: The framework holds that analysis of digital learner interactions should differentiate three overlapping processes: posting activity at the individual level, communication structures as learner-to-learner projections, and emergent relational structures as filtered backbones of communication networks. The article proposes that "posting activity gives rise to communication patterns and emergent relational structures," operationalizing the levels as interdependent so that statistical modeling of lower levels affords inference about higher ones. It supplies level-specific units of analysis, comparison methods, and example research questions (Table 1), demonstrated on twenty courses.
requirements: The analyst must specify a generative (conceptual) model of the fundamental principles for how participation and communication emerge
constraints: The example includes no self-report or learning-gain data to triangulate inferences about outcome nature and quality
The framework presents the three processes as static, not dynamically interacting over a course
The example null model is limited; further work is needed to integrate temporal aspects and discourse properties
target_learners: university students in online and blended courses
target_learning_goals: participation in discussion forums
communication and relationship formation among learners
examples: Applied to twenty Moodle courses using PCA grouping, null-model simulation of posting networks, edge-weight filtering, and ERGM analysis
key_sources: Poquet, O., Trenholm, S., & Santolini, M. (2024). Forum posts, communication patterns, and relational structures: A multi-level view of discussions in online courses. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10262-9

article_title: Forum posts, communication patterns, and relational structures: A multi-level view of discussions in online courses
citation: Poquet, O., Trenholm, S., & Santolini, M. (2024). Forum posts, communication patterns, and relational structures: A multi-level view of discussions in online courses. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10262-9
title: Twenty-course Moodle forum dataset from an Australian university (August–December 2016)
description: The empirical basis of the study is forum data from twenty courses on a Moodle platform in Social Sciences and Humanities at one Australian university, taught by different instructors and including blended and fully online offerings. The article states "Data were collected from the Moodle platform in twenty courses" and that courses were selected for high forum-post volume per administrative records. Courses enrolled on average some 44 students (M = 84, SD = 111), lasted typically 13 weeks, and post-to-post reply networks were constructed per course for analysis.
requirements: Courses were selected due to the high number of forum posts as per the administrative records
constraints: The authors do not differentiate between the courses as blended and online, which they call an important limitation of the insights
target_learners: university students in Social Sciences and Humanities courses
target_learning_goals: participation in course discussion forums
examples: Post-to-post networks built from Moodle reply buttons; one course (D) placed learners in fixed small groups with weekly group assignments
key_sources: Poquet, O., Trenholm, S., & Santolini, M. (2024). Forum posts, communication patterns, and relational structures: A multi-level view of discussions in online courses. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10262-9

article_title: Forum posts, communication patterns, and relational structures: A multi-level view of discussions in online courses
citation: Poquet, O., Trenholm, S., & Santolini, M. (2024). Forum posts, communication patterns, and relational structures: A multi-level view of discussions in online courses. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10262-9
title: Design forum tasks that combine individual participation and interactivity to create conditions for learner relationship formation
description: The article's synthesis argues that forum designs eliciting both individual posting and engagement with others were most likely to foster relational structures. It reports that "courses with high participation and high interactivity were more likely to create conditions for relationship formation among learners," whereas courses focusing only on interactivity without individual participation were less successful at developing relational structures. The principle guides instructors choosing forum task designs when relationship formation is a goal.
requirements: Forum tasks must elicit both individual participation and engagement with others
constraints: Inference rests on log data without self-reports to verify whether frequent pairs experienced social presence
Only one course (D, with fixed small groups and weekly group tasks) showed the full group-formation pattern
target_learners: university students in online and blended courses
target_learning_goals: relationship formation among learners
participation in discussion forums
examples: Course D assigned learners to fixed small groups with weekly group tasks and showed the highest participation, interactivity, and the only significant Simmelian-tie pattern

article_title: Impact of using authentic online learning environments on students’ perceived employability
citation: María-Jesús Martínez-Argüelles, Dolors Plana-Erta, Àngels Fitó-Bertran. (2023). Impact of using authentic online learning environments on students' perceived employability. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10171-3
title: Herrington and Oliver's nine critical characteristics of authentic learning environments
description: The article adopts the framework of Herrington and Oliver (2000), which identifies nine critical characteristics of an authentic learning environment: authentic context, authentic activities, access to expert performances, multiple roles and perspectives, collaborative construction of knowledge, reflection, articulation, coaching and scaffolding, and authentic assessment within tasks. The authors state that "environments that include these elements are more suited to facilitating authentic learning" and use the nine criteria both to redesign a fully online finance course and to measure its perceived authenticity via a 16-question instrument. The study's results support the framework's applicability to asynchronous online higher education.
requirements: Learning must be designed with a holistic vision beyond teaching discipline knowledge, enabling student inculturation in a relevant context
constraints: Implementing all nine elements in a single course can be especially complex for the teacher and involve higher student dedication than the course credit-load
target_learners: higher education students in fully online degree programs
target_learning_goals: general employability competencies such as analytical thinking, problem-solving, and decision-making
examples: The Financial Statement Analysis course was redesigned so students acted as assistant finance managers producing a financial report for a board meeting, with six videos, four activities, and access to the SABI database.
key_sources: María-Jesús Martínez-Argüelles, Dolors Plana-Erta, Àngels Fitó-Bertran. (2023). Impact of using authentic online learning environments on students' perceived employability. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10171-3

article_title: Impact of using authentic online learning environments on students’ perceived employability
citation: María-Jesús Martínez-Argüelles, Dolors Plana-Erta, Àngels Fitó-Bertran. (2023). Impact of using authentic online learning environments on students' perceived employability. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10171-3
title: ALS-redesigned online Financial Statement Analysis course with role-play, embedded videos, and professional database access
description: A compulsory advanced course in the fully online BA degree at UOC was redesigned around a realistic job scenario: students, as recently hired assistant finance managers, produce a professional financial report for their superior, the financial manager (the instructor), to present at a board of directors meeting. "Students were required to conduct four learning activities individually; these activities would provide the theoretical and practical basis for completing the last activity, the final financial report." Six roughly 3-minute videos embedded in the virtual classroom recreated supervisor meetings every 18–20 days, and students used the professional SABI database for sector comparison. Assessment was continuous with personalized feedback at each stage.
requirements: An LMS integrating activities, resources, communication spaces, and evaluation into a virtual classroom, plus instructor availability for continuous feedback
constraints: The learning environment is online and asynchronous, with no synchronous moments; meetings are recreated through videos
target_learners: part-time online bachelor's students in Business and Administration, most combining work with study
target_learning_goals: financial diagnosis of company statements; generating economic knowledge from data; managing a company considering its competitive situation
examples: In Activity 1 the financial manager asks the assistant to analyze a credit insurance proposal for a forecasted sales rise of 30,000,000 euros a year and justify a choice.
key_sources: María-Jesús Martínez-Argüelles, Dolors Plana-Erta, Àngels Fitó-Bertran. (2023). Impact of using authentic online learning environments on students' perceived employability. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10171-3

article_title: Impact of using authentic online learning environments on students’ perceived employability
citation: María-Jesús Martínez-Argüelles, Dolors Plana-Erta, Àngels Fitó-Bertran. (2023). Impact of using authentic online learning environments on students' perceived employability. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10171-3
title: Use technology as a means of providing authenticity, not an end in itself
description: The article argues that communication, visualization, and simulation technologies can give online students opportunities to experience and solve real-world problems, but that tools alone do not create authenticity. As the authors put it, "Technological tools are a means of providing authenticity, not an end in themselves. The effectiveness of authentic learning scenarios depends on how the learning process is designed." The course redesign illustrates this: videos and the virtual classroom served a holistic, integrated design for cognitive authenticity rather than substituting for it.
requirements: A holistic and integrated vision of the student learning process within which the technologies are deployed
constraints: Technologies are not sufficient to ensure the quality of authenticity on their own
target_learning_goals: cognitive authenticity connecting learning to real-world work practice
examples: The redesign used six embedded videos and the SABI database as supports within an integrated role-play scenario, not as standalone innovations.
key_sources: María-Jesús Martínez-Argüelles, Dolors Plana-Erta, Àngels Fitó-Bertran. (2023). Impact of using authentic online learning environments on students' perceived employability. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10171-3

article_title: Impact of using authentic online learning environments on students’ perceived employability
citation: María-Jesús Martínez-Argüelles, Dolors Plana-Erta, Àngels Fitó-Bertran. (2023). Impact of using authentic online learning environments on students' perceived employability. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10171-3
title: Apply ALS attributes selectively and favor advanced courses close to labor-market entry
description: The authors recommend that faculty judge how deeply each of the nine authenticity attributes should be present in a given course, since fulfilling all attributes in one course can be complex and demand more student dedication than its credit-load. They also observe from the teachers' perspective that "creating ALS is easier in advanced courses and closer to the insertion to the labor market of students," because those students have a solid conceptual background and the course can more easily recreate a real work environment with cognitive authenticity.
requirements: Faculty assessment of the appropriate depth of each Herrington and Oliver attribute per course
constraints: Trying to fulfill all ALS attributes within a single course can be especially complex for the teacher and involve higher student dedication than the course credit-load
target_learners: advanced undergraduate students in online professional degrees
target_learning_goals: authentic work-related competencies linked to course learning outcomes
examples: The redesigned course was a compulsory advanced course whose learning outcomes map directly onto the assistant finance manager professional profile.

article_title: Learners and learning contexts: international perspectives on new alignments for the digital age
citation: Joke Voogt, Gerald Knezek. (2021). Learners and learning contexts: international perspectives on new alignments for the digital age. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09985-4
title: Three clusters of needed alignments: learning and learning contexts, technology integration and teachers, and partnerships
description: The editorial organizes the special issue's twelve papers into three thematic clusters where new alignments are needed for technology to foster learning. As the authors state, "The papers in this special issue identified three clusters where new alignments are needed in order to make technology work in the practice of education." The clusters span what is worth learning, teacher technology integration, and stakeholder partnerships, with recommendations at macro, meso and micro levels.
requirements: Papers addressing the theme from research, policy and practice perspectives
target_learning_goals: effective technology-supported learning across formal and non-formal contexts
examples: Ten Thematic Working Groups from EDUsummIT 2019 published in the special issue, plus two additional accepted papers
key_sources: Joke Voogt, Gerald Knezek. (2021). Learners and learning contexts: international perspectives on new alignments for the digital age. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09985-4

article_title: Learners and learning contexts: international perspectives on new alignments for the digital age
citation: Joke Voogt, Gerald Knezek. (2021). Learners and learning contexts: international perspectives on new alignments for the digital age. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09985-4
title: Cross-cultural alignment model for responsive teaching and learning in networked digital environments
description: Shonfeld and colleagues propose, from a social justice point of view, a cross-cultural alignment model to foster cross-cultural responsive teaching and learning. The editorial states the model "discusses the interactions and alignments that are needed between the educational system, digital environments, learners and educators for effective cross-cultural projects." It responds to the observation that cross-cultural projects can develop twenty-first century skills but technologies often contribute to inequality, ethical issues and well-being concerns.
requirements: Digital learning environments offering opportunities for learners from different cultures to be connected
constraints: Cross-cultural projects are not always easy to realize; technologies may contribute to inequality and ethical issues
target_learning_goals: digital, collaboration, inter-cultural and lifelong learning skills
examples: The model is positioned within a social justice perspective on technology use in networked society
key_sources: Joke Voogt, Gerald Knezek. (2021). Learners and learning contexts: international perspectives on new alignments for the digital age. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09985-4

article_title: Learners and learning contexts: international perspectives on new alignments for the digital age
citation: Joke Voogt, Gerald Knezek. (2021). Learners and learning contexts: international perspectives on new alignments for the digital age. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09985-4
title: Connected learning reframes learning in the digital age through self-driven action across formal and non-formal contexts
description: Prestridge and colleagues describe connected learning environments facilitated by digital technologies. Core to connected learning is that it "emphasizes self-driven actions and interactions for learning with a diversity of (digital) tools, people and ways of knowing." It spans formal and non-formal contexts and is examined through three concepts: open and bounded context, prescribed and emergent curriculum, and the rise of a new class of influencer.
requirements: Diversity of digital tools, people and ways of knowing for self-driven learning
constraints: Complexities around open versus bounded contexts and prescribed versus emergent curriculum
target_learners: learners in formal and non-formal digital contexts
target_learning_goals: self-driven learning in the digital age
examples: The authors envision connected learning as a new alignment for learning in the digital age

title: Model visualizing dynamic relationships between organization, innovation, research and new contexts for sustainability and scalability of technology innovations
description: Howard and colleagues present a model to visualize the dynamic relationship between organization, innovation, research and new contexts, starting from the assumption that "dynamic and iterative processes are needed to make technological innovations sustainable and scalable." Organization sits at the core of the model, representing collaboration between stakeholders, schools and research. The model's utility is illustrated in three cases from different parts of the world.
requirements: Collaboration between stakeholders, schools and research, with organization at the core of the model
constraints: The model's utility is illustrated in three cases; broader validation is not reported in the editorial
target_learners: learners in schools implementing digital technology innovations
target_learning_goals: sustainable and scalable technology-supported learning innovations
examples: The model is illustrated in three cases from different parts of the world

article_title: Toward a framework of uncertainty in ill-structured problem solving
citation: Rebecca Clark-Stallkamp, Barbara B. Lockee. (2026). Toward a framework of uncertainty in ill-structured problem solving. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10680-5
title: A framework of uncertainty in ill-structured problem solving: a subjective locus plus seven intersecting sources
description: The framework defines uncertainty as a subjective, metacognitive and psychological experience — the locus of uncertainty, "a psychological response or subjective state of unknowingness" — arising as learners interpret problems, make judgments, and regulate action under incomplete, conflicting, or changing information. Around this locus it delineates seven intersecting sources: problem context/space, outcomes, sociocultural, epistemological, environmental, dynamicity, and complexity. Complexity and dynamicity act as overarching amplifiers, and all sources are situated within the problem context, which serves as the foundation for how uncertainty manifests. The framework was derived from thematic and taxonomic coding of 74 peer-reviewed articles.
requirements: Articles in the underlying corpus had to describe a problem or decision-making context, connect to learning or knowledge construction, and explicitly reference uncertainty or evidence of it manifesting
constraints: Derived from literature coded by the first author with second-author auditing rather than dual coding; intended for ill-structured problem-solving and learning contexts
target_learning_goals: problem solving
metacognitive regulation of uncertainty
argumentation and justification of solutions
examples: Taxonomic coding of the 74-article corpus produced the seven source categories and the locus of uncertainty, with code examples tabulated for each component

article_title: Look at me! Can a pedagogical agent facilitate orientation and support learning in VR?
citation: Daniela Decker, Martin Merkt. (2025). Look at me! Can a pedagogical agent facilitate orientation and support learning in VR? Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10531-9
title: Cognitive Affective Model of Immersive Learning (CAMIL)
description: CAMIL is an explanatory framework for learning in immersive VR, built in part on Cognitive Load Theory's assumption of limited working-memory capacity. The article states that "CAMIL extends this perspective by identifying three key technical factors that shape learning in VR: immersion, control, and representational fidelity". All three factors influence presence, the feeling of being there, which the article treats as a prerequisite for learning in VR; only control factors determine agency. The study uses CAMIL to motivate expectations that cueing could raise presence and that reduced representational fidelity from non-diegetic cues could lower it.
requirements: Presence and agency as psychological prerequisites for learning in VR
constraints: The article notes CAMIL suggests highly immersive VR may be particularly beneficial for procedural knowledge, while this study tested declarative memory
target_learners: adult learners in immersive VR environments
target_learning_goals: declarative factual knowledge
spatial representation of a learning environment
examples: The experiment operationalized CAMIL's factors by comparing a diegetic-style light cue and a human-like agent cue against no cueing in a virtual workshop
key_sources: Daniela Decker, Martin Merkt. (2025). Look at me! Can a pedagogical agent facilitate orientation and support learning in VR? Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10531-9
