citation: Daniela Decker, Martin Merkt. (2025). Look at me! Can a pedagogical agent facilitate orientation and support learning in VR? Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10531-9
title: Carefully calibrate a pedagogical agent's level of realism and pre-test its design elements and animations before deployment
description: Because the highly embodied pedagogical agent reduced physical and self-presence in the VR experiment, the article recommends calibrating agent realism carefully. The authors state that "the pedagogical agent reduced physical and self-presence, underscoring the importance of carefully calibrating its level of realism. Pre-testing both the design elements and their animations is therefore advisable." They suggest possible causes include an uncanny valley effect and disruptive repositioning between tasks, and propose more fluid repositioning, such as the agent walking to its new position, in future designs.
requirements: Pre-testing of agent design elements and animations before use
constraints: The agent's negative presence effects were observed in a short (~5 minute) passive-listening laboratory setting
target_learners: adult learners in immersive VR learning environments
target_learning_goals: maintaining presence during VR learning
examples: The agent was designed with Character Creator 3.3 and iClone 7.8, featured conversational gestures, idle positions, breathing movements, and facial expressions, and was pilot-tested for credibility

It has twelve components and treats sustainability as dynamic: "AI technology enables sustainability to be treated as a dynamic and evolving concept of sustainability, and learners are able to study the nature and rate of anthropogenic environmental change, identify likely future challenges and opportunities, and make decisions". It serves as a methodological guide for designing AI-supported activities.

constraints: Designed for the formal school geography curriculum context

understanding anthropogenic environmental change

article_title: Digital distractions in education: a systematic review of research on causes, consequences and prevention strategies
citation: Florence Martin, Siyu Long, Katy Haywood, Kui Xie. (2025). Digital distractions in education: a systematic review of research on causes, consequences and prevention strategies. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10550-6
title: Technology-Personal-Environment (TPE) framework for organizing digital distraction research
description: The TPE framework, adapted from the Technology-Organization-Environment (TOE) framework for individual-level technology adoption, organizes digital distraction into three dimensions: technological factors (device access, affordances, alerts), personal factors (traits, motives, boredom, physical conditions), and environmental factors (classroom setting, instructor behavior, instructional activities). The review uses it as its coding structure, mapping causes, consequences, and prevention strategies onto the three dimensions, stating that "the TPE framework provides a comprehensive structure for examining the causes, consequences, and potential intervention strategies for addressing digital distraction in educational settings."
requirements: Studies must code distraction factors into technological, personal, and environmental dimensions for the framework to structure analysis
constraints: The framework was adapted from the organization-level TOE framework, and the review notes only 6 of 26 primary studies used any theoretical or conceptual framework
target_learning_goals: sustained attention during academic tasks
reduction of off-task technology use
examples: The review coded all 26 studies' causes, consequences, and prevention strategies into TPE-based categories and presents Fig. 2 as a visual summary mapping findings to the framework
key_sources: Florence Martin, Siyu Long, Katy Haywood, Kui Xie. (2025). Digital distractions in education: a systematic review of research on causes, consequences and prevention strategies. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10550-6

title: Instruments for measuring digital distraction, including self-developed Digital Distraction Scales and the Internet Addiction Test
description: This element covers the measurement instruments used across the 26 reviewed studies. Fourteen studies utilized instruments to measure digital distraction, nine of which reported self-developed instruments. Three studies designed a Digital Distraction Scale (DDS) with contextual purpose, and the Internet Addiction (IA) Test was another commonly included measurement. The review tabulates these instruments study by study (Table 3), noting that "Three of the studies specifically designed a Digital Distraction Scale (DDS) with contextual purpose."
requirements: Empirical studies of digital distraction require a defined instrument, and the review's inclusion criteria required a clearly defined methods section
constraints: Most instruments were self-developed rather than validated external scales, and 12 of 26 studies reported no instrument for measuring digital distraction
target_learning_goals: measuring digital distraction and off-task device use
examples: Göl et al. (2023) used a Digital Distraction Scale (DDS) with DD components questionnaires; Chen et al. (2020) used DD intensity items with the Internet Addiction Test and Barratt Impulsiveness Scale

article_title: Effects of fear-arousing communications
citation: Janis, Irving L., and Feshbach, Seymour. (1953). Effects of Fear-Arousing Communications. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology 48: 78-92.
title: Emotional-tension/reassurance account of fear appeal effectiveness
description: The authors' explanatory framework holds that a persuasive communication's overall effectiveness "will tend to be reduced by the use of a strong fear appeal, if it evokes a high degree of emotional tension without adequately satisfying the need for reassurance." It comprises two hypotheses: a strong appeal, compared with a milder one, increases the likelihood the audience is left in emotional tension not fully relieved by rehearsing the recommendations; and when strongly aroused fear is not fully relieved, the audience becomes motivated to ignore or minimize the threat. The framework explains the experiment's pattern of equal learning but poorer attitude and behavior change under the strong appeal.
requirements: The communication must contain reassuring recommendations that can potentially relieve the aroused fear for the mechanism to operate as described
constraints: The account is offered as consistent with, not proven by, the single experiment: the authors write that the evidence "appears to be consistent with" the two hypotheses
target_learning_goals: adoption of recommended health practices (dental hygiene) in response to persuasive communications
examples: The 15-minute illustrated dental hygiene lecture was prepared in three forms differing only in fear-appeal intensity, each recorded with its own set of slides and presented by the same speaker
key_sources: Janis, Irving L., and Feshbach, Seymour. (1953). Effects of Fear-Arousing Communications. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology 48: 78-92. https://doi.org/10.1007/bf02713264

article_title: Effects of fear-arousing communications
citation: Janis, Irving L., and Feshbach, Seymour. (1953). Effects of Fear-Arousing Communications. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology 48: 78-92.
title: Matching fear-appeal intensity to reassurance in persuasive health instruction
description: A design pattern for persuasive communications in which the intensity of threat content is calibrated against the reassurance provided. The experiment varied a 15-minute illustrated lecture across strong, moderate, and minimal appeal forms that "contained the same information about tooth decay and the same recommendations concerning oral hygiene practices," differing only in how threats were emphasized. The pattern that emerged favors milder appeals: the minimal appeal yielded the greatest conformity and resistance to counterpropaganda, while the strong appeal, which raised emotional tension without adequate reassurance, reduced overall effectiveness.
requirements: Threat content must be paired with recommendations the audience can rehearse to relieve aroused tension
constraints: Evidence comes from one experiment on dental hygiene with high-school students; the authors state effectiveness is reduced when tension is not adequately relieved, not that strong appeals are always ineffective
target_learning_goals: adopting recommended oral hygiene practices
retaining persuasive message content against counterpropaganda
examples: Three recorded lecture forms with different slide sets were presented by the same speaker to three experimental groups and a control group of 200 Connecticut high-school students
key_sources: Janis, Irving L., and Feshbach, Seymour. (1953). Effects of Fear-Arousing Communications. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology 48: 78-92. https://doi.org/10.1007/bf02713264

article_title: Designing research to inform sustainability and scalability of digital technology innovations
citation: Howard, S. K., Schrum, L., Voogt, J., & Sligte, H. (2021). Designing research to inform sustainability and scalability of digital technology innovations. Educational Technology Research and Development, 69(4). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09913-y
title: Four-loop causal model of technological innovation: Organization, Innovation, Research, New Contexts
description: The article presents an adapted causal loop model drawing on systems thinking, in which 'loops' represent components of a system of technology innovation in education and arrows represent effects between components. The four loops are Organization (L1) at the core, Innovation (L2), Research (L3), and New Contexts (L4). It was developed by a thematic working group of educational technology experts at EDUsummIT 2019 and refined against literature on educational change, and is used to analyze three international case studies.
requirements: Research must be led by participants and co-constructed with researchers, and outputs aimed at practitioners, for the Research loop to be meaningful
constraints: The authors state this is only an initial testing of the model and considerable work is needed to validate the key factors and relationships among the loops
target_learners: teachers and teacher educators involved in technology integration
target_learning_goals: understanding and designing sustainable and scalable technology innovations
examples: The model was applied as a coding structure to three case studies from the Netherlands, United States and Australia, with results mapped to the framework in Figs. 2, 3 and 4

article_title: Online professional development to support K-12 teachers’ computer science integration
citation: Lauren E. Margulieux · Brendan D. Calandra · Bryan Cox. (2026). Online professional development to support K‑12 teachers' computer science integration. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10640-z
title: Project MICRO micro-courses and ISTE integrated-CT micro-credential badges
description: Project MICRO (Micro-credentials for Integrating Computing Responsibly into Other Domains) is a set of three free, online, self-paced micro-courses of about one college credit hour each, co-created by Georgia State University, the Georgia Department of Education, and ISTE. Courses cover everyday computing, information literacy, cybersecurity, data, CT concepts (abstraction, algorithms, automation, decomposition, debugging), block-based programming, and teaching methods. Teachers can submit assignments, including lesson plans, to earn ISTE badges aligned to the Integrated CT Endorsement: "CT learner", "CT designer", and "CT facilitator".
requirements: Courses were adapted from a 3-credit-hour digital literacy and CT course in a CS endorsement program and aligned to ISTE's CT Competencies and CSTA standards, with instructions added to highlight activities that satisfy badge requirements.
constraints: Personalized support of participants was not feasible at this scale, and teachers engaged independently, potentially without social or intellectual support from peers.
target_learners: preservice and in-service K-12 teachers outside of computer science
target_learning_goals: integrating computational thinking and CS concepts into non-CS content-area instruction
examples: 215 teachers completed pre- and post-surveys; a subset of 15 teachers submitted 17 lesson plans, which were scored with a 0–3 rubric for CT and CS concepts.

article_title: Online professional development to support K-12 teachers’ computer science integration
citation: Lauren E. Margulieux · Brendan D. Calandra · Bryan Cox. (2026). Online professional development to support K‑12 teachers' computer science integration. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10640-z
title: SAMR framework for levels of technology-enhanced learning activities
description: The Substitution, Augmentation, Modification, Redefinition (SAMR) framework describes differences in the quality of activities afforded by technological tools. In the first two levels, activities are "fundamentally the same as the original activities": Substitution uses technology for the same activity, perhaps more efficiently, while Augmentation adds something that could not have been done without it. In Modification and Redefinition, technology qualitatively changes the activity, with Redefinition incorporating new tasks that would have been impossible without technology. The MICRO PD drew its example activities primarily from the last two levels, framing programming as teaching the computer to complete a task.
requirements: No level of SAMR is right or wrong; the appropriate level depends on a teacher's teaching and learning goals.
constraints: The authors did not expect that teachers' applications of the PD would necessarily always align with the higher levels of SAMR.
target_learners: K-12 teachers integrating computing into non-CS classrooms
target_learning_goals: designing technology-enhanced learning activities at appropriate integration levels
examples: The PD framed creating a computer program as teaching the computer to complete a task, which the authors say pushes activities to at least the Modification level.

citation: Chungsoo Na, Soojeong Jeong, Jody Clarke-Midura, Youngin Shin. (2024). Linking self-regulated learning to community of inquiry in online undergraduate courses: A person-centered approach. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10380-y
title: Extended Community of Inquiry framework incorporating self-regulated learning as a learning presence
description: The article extends the CoI framework (social, cognitive, teaching presence) by situating SRL as a fourth, 'learning presence' construct, following Shea and Bidjerano (2010). In the extended conceptual model, SRL comprises seven sub-constructs including goal setting, environmental structuring, task strategies, help-seeking, time management, and two forms of self-evaluation, and is hypothesized to relate to all three original presences. The study's empirical findings support that 'SRL skills as a learning presence are critical components under the framework of the community of inquiry.'
requirements: Empirical measurement of SRL strategy use (e.g., OSLQ) alongside CoI perceptions to test the extended model
constraints: Theoretical controversy on integrating a new presence into CoI still exists (Akyol & Garrison, 2011a; Garrison & Akyol, 2013), as the article notes

title: CTML explains multimedia learning via active processing, limited capacity, and dual-channel assumptions
description: The Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning is a theoretical framework guiding design of online multimedia lessons. The article states that "CTML is based on three main assumptions": learners actively select, organize, and integrate information; working-memory capacity is limited (about four chunks); and verbal and nonverbal information are processed in two independent channels. Over a dozen tested learning principles derive from these assumptions.

article_title: Thy word is a lamp unto my feet: A study via metaphoric perceptions on how online feedback benefited Chinese learners
citation: Ding, S. L., & Chew, E. (2019). Thy word is a lamp unto my feet: A study via metaphoric perceptions on how online feedback benefited Chinese learners. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09651-w
title: Delayed-uptake: learners' delayed reflective responses to asynchronous online feedback as an indicator of the learning developmental process
description: Delayed-uptake is the authors' term for students' delayed or 'soon after responses' of reflective thoughts following asynchronous online feedback, gathered after students had time to form thoughts. Whereas uptake research examines immediate learner responses after feedback, this concept captures perceptions expressed later, here as metaphors. The authors argue that "online feed -back creates a more profound delaye d-uptake" and that this delayed-uptake "is deemed an indicator of the learning developmental process". It extends uptake analysis to technology-mediated written feedback contexts.
requirements: Asynchronous online feedback must give learners time to reflect before responses are collected
constraints: The article states it is far from sufficient to claim the 'effectiveness' of online tools in contributing to conclusive outcomes for language learning
target_learning_goals: second-language writing improvement and reflective awareness of feedback
examples: Students who received GradeMark feedback completed an open-ended questionnaire days later and expressed perceptions as metaphors such as footprints on the beach, showing reflection after the feedback event.
key_sources: Ding, S. L., & Chew, E. (2019). Thy word is a lamp unto my feet: A study via metaphoric perceptions on how online feedback benefited Chinese learners. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09651-w

article_title: Thy word is a lamp unto my feet: A study via metaphoric perceptions on how online feedback benefited Chinese learners
citation: Ding, S. L., & Chew, E. (2019). Thy word is a lamp unto my feet: A study via metaphoric perceptions on how online feedback benefited Chinese learners. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09651-w
title: Adapt feedback modes and strategies to learners' cultural, educational and personality differences rather than assuming one strategy fits all
description: The article argues that because learners differ in cultural background, educational history and personality (e.g., introversion), educators should be context-sensitive when choosing feedback modes. It states: "Strategies need to be adapted for different learn ers in various learning situations" and that "no one strategy is applicable to all learners". The study's metaphoric method itself exemplifies adapting elicitation to restrained expressers.
requirements: Educators need to build their skills and be flexible and open-minded, and academic training should attend to student differences, learning outcomes, and contextual realities
constraints: Findings from a Confucian-influenced background may not be applicable to learners from different backgrounds, per the authors' own limitation
target_learners: introverted or culturally reticent higher-education language learners
target_learning_goals: effective uptake of feedback on second-language writing
examples: The study used metaphoric elicitation in Mandarin instead of direct questioning because participants were restrained in open expression; online feedback was chosen to avoid public embarrassment.
key_sources: Ding, S. L., & Chew, E. (2019). Thy word is a lamp unto my feet: A study via metaphoric perceptions on how online feedback benefited Chinese learners. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09651-w

article_title: Thy word is a lamp unto my feet: A study via metaphoric perceptions on how online feedback benefited Chinese learners
citation: Ding, S. L., & Chew, E. (2019). Thy word is a lamp unto my feet: A study via metaphoric perceptions on how online feedback benefited Chinese learners. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09651-w
title: GradeMark: Turnitin's online assessment and feedback tool providing in-text, overall written and voice comments with rubrics
description: GradeMark is a feature of the Turnitin platform enabling language educators to assess students' written work online and provide feedback with a rubric. In this study it delivered three types of feedback comments — in-text and overall (written) as well as voice (audio) — posted online within two weeks of submission. The article cites its strength as "the quality of the feedback provided" and its "facility for direct annotation with quick marking".
requirements: Students need access to read and listen to the posted comments (they were given 1–2 days in this study)
constraints: The study reported some initial technical obstacles for first-time users
target_learners: undergraduate second-language writers in higher education
target_learning_goals: improving writing through individualized online feedback on assignments
examples: For four consecutive years, GradeMark was used to give respondents in-text, overall and voice feedback on writing assignments, with feedback posted within 2 weeks of submission.

article_title: Assessing the impact of substituting interaction types: an empirical study of the interaction equivalency theory
citation: Hauert, S., Luo, T., & Yen, C.-J. (2026). Assessing the impact of substituting interaction types: an empirical study of the interaction equivalency theory. Education Tech Research Dev, 74, 1–27. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10563-1
title: Interaction equivalency theory (Anderson's substitutivity thesis)
description: Anderson's (2003a) interaction equivalency theory is this study's theoretical foundation. Its first thesis posits that "Deep and meaningful formal learning is supported as long as one of the three forms of interaction (student–teacher; student–student; student–content) is at a high level," with the other two offered at minimal levels or eliminated without degrading the educational experience. At its core, the theory argues a well-designed course can substitute one interaction type for another without significantly impacting performance. The study provides the first experimental test with random assignment of this substitutive prong, distinguishing it from the well-studied additive second thesis.
requirements: At least one of the three interaction forms must be at a high level for deep and meaningful formal learning to be supported
constraints: The theory's substitutive prong had not previously been tested; this study tested it only for learner–content substituting for learner–learner, with explicit declarative knowledge, in one week-long episode with adult undergraduates
target_learning_goals: knowledge acquisition of explicit, declarative content in formal distance education
examples: The study operationalized the theory by randomly assigning students to an interactive multimedia lecture with adjunct questions or to vignette-based peer discussion, then comparing summative assessment scores
key_sources: Hauert, S., Luo, T., & Yen, C.-J. (2026). Assessing the impact of substituting interaction types: an empirical study of the interaction equivalency theory. Education Tech Research Dev, 74, 1–27. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10563-1

article_title: Assessing the impact of substituting interaction types: an empirical study of the interaction equivalency theory
citation: Hauert, S., Luo, T., & Yen, C.-J. (2026). Assessing the impact of substituting interaction types: an empirical study of the interaction equivalency theory. Education Tech Research Dev, 74, 1–27. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10563-1
title: Paired treatment materials: interactive adjunct-question lecture versus vignette peer-discussion lecture
description: The study operationalized the two interaction types with matched multimedia lectures on automobile insurance hosted on Knowmia.com with closed captions and sign-in tracking. The learner–content group viewed an interactive version with "adjunct questions with confirmatory or corrective feedback" inserted throughout; the learner–learner group viewed a non-interactive version with mandatory check-ins at the same timeline locations and engaged in discussion by responding to vignette prompts, creating their own vignette, and critiquing at least one peer's vignette. Both groups could interact with the instructor via an Ask-the-instructor thread or private message, and groups were partitioned from each other in the LMS.
requirements: Lectures required sign-in and disabled fast-forwarding to confirm attendance; check-ins were placed at the same timeline locations as the adjunct questions to keep the versions matched
constraints: The content covered explicit, declarative knowledge (automobile insurance) in a single week-long instructional episode in a paralegal studies program
target_learners: adult undergraduate community-college students in a paralegal studies program
target_learning_goals: understanding and application of automobile insurance concepts measured by a 10-item, 50-point summative assessment
examples: Figure 4 and Figure 5 show an adjunct question on liability coverage with corrective and confirmatory feedback; Figure 7 shows a sample vignette students critiqued
key_sources: Hauert, S., Luo, T., & Yen, C.-J. (2026). Assessing the impact of substituting interaction types: an empirical study of the interaction equivalency theory. Education Tech Research Dev, 74, 1–27. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10563-1

article_title: Assessing the impact of substituting interaction types: an empirical study of the interaction equivalency theory
citation: Hauert, S., Luo, T., & Yen, C.-J. (2026). Assessing the impact of substituting interaction types: an empirical study of the interaction equivalency theory. Education Tech Research Dev, 74, 1–27. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10563-1
title: Substitute learner–content interaction for learner–learner interaction when interpersonal interaction is not required by the instructional objective
description: Based on the trial's findings, the article recommends that designers first determine whether a learning experience requires interpersonal interaction for an instructional objective or ancillary purpose such as community building. If not, learner–content interactions "impose a lower perceived workload and a higher perceived level of learning" while correlating to higher measured performance, and can be substituted for learner–learner interactions without impacting performance. This relieves instructors of moderation workload and frees capacity for interpersonal interactions where they matter.
requirements: Front-end analysis must first determine whether interpersonal interaction is needed to accomplish an instructional objective or ancillary purpose such as building a sense of community or collaboration
constraints: Evidence comes from adult learners in one undergraduate, law-related occupational program with explicit, declarative content over one week; results may not generalize to other populations, knowledge types, or contexts
target_learners: adult distance-education students in formal online undergraduate programs
target_learning_goals: knowledge acquisition of explicit, declarative content without degrading measured performance
examples: In the study, designers should also evaluate which tools and methods best operationalize each interaction type; the authors note interactive multimedia with real-time feedback can enhance timely assessment while creating instructor capacity
key_sources: Hauert, S., Luo, T., & Yen, C.-J. (2026). Assessing the impact of substituting interaction types: an empirical study of the interaction equivalency theory. Education Tech Research Dev, 74, 1–27. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10563-1

article_title: Development of a participation style scale for online instructional discussions
citation: Pala Ferhat Kadir, Erdem Mukaddes. (2020). Development of a participation style scale for online instructional discussions. Educational Technology Research and Development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09817-x
title: Participation style in online instructional discussions as a two-dimensional construct of participation reasons (Why) and participation forms (How)
description: The article defines participation style as the sum of individualistic characteristics explaining participation in online discussions, structured in two dimensions. The Why dimension comprises the main motivators of participation, while the How dimension comprises items expressing participation behaviors or forms. The authors state: "The Why dimension comprises the main motivators of the participants' participation in online instructional environments, whereas the How dimension comprises items expressing participation behaviors or forms." This mirrors Kolb's learning-style inventory logic of pairing a preference for receiving information with a preference for transforming it, applied here to online discussion participation.
requirements: The scale is intended for individuals who have actually participated in online instructional discussions; participants who stated they had never participated were excluded from both study groups
constraints: The study groups consisted of undergraduate and graduate students at Turkish universities, mainly in Computer Education and Instructional Technologies departments
target_learners: undergraduate and graduate students participating in online instructional discussions
target_learning_goals: identifying learners' participation styles in online discussion environments to support more effective learning
examples: The scale was applied to undergraduate and graduate students at 15 and 24 Turkish universities across two datasets
key_sources: Pala Ferhat Kadir, Erdem Mukaddes. (2020). Development of a participation style scale for online instructional discussions. Educational Technology Research and Development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09817-x

article_title: Development of a participation style scale for online instructional discussions
citation: Pala Ferhat Kadir, Erdem Mukaddes. (2020). Development of a participation style scale for online instructional discussions. Educational Technology Research and Development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09817-x
title: Four participation styles in online instructional discussions: To Socialize/Connective, To Get Information/Analytical, To Discuss/Innovative, To Fulfill Requirements/Practical
description: The article identifies four participation styles formed by pairing each Why factor with its parallel How factor. The authors state: "The participation styles were accordingly defined as 'To Socialize/Connective,' 'To Get Information/Analytical,' 'To Discuss/Innovative,' and 'To Fulfill Requirements/Practical.'" Each style pairs a motivation (e.g., socializing, information seeking, discussing, fulfilling requirements) with a characteristic behavior pattern (connective, analytical, innovative, or practical participation). The styles are determined by the factor on which a student scores highest.
requirements: Scores are calculated per factor, and the predominant style is the one with the most points; when dimensions are used together, the predominant style is determined by averaging item points
constraints: The article notes there may be other styles beyond these four; the styles were validated with Turkish undergraduate and graduate student samples
target_learners: undergraduate and graduate students in online instructional discussions
target_learning_goals: categorizing learners' participation styles to guide discussion environment design and self-aware learning management
examples: Instructors and researchers can determine learners' participation styles before organizing discussion environments
key_sources: Pala Ferhat Kadir, Erdem Mukaddes. (2020). Development of a participation style scale for online instructional discussions. Educational Technology Research and Development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09817-x

article_title: Army television research activities
citation: Joseph H. Kanner. (1951). Army Television Research Activities. https://eric.ed.gov
title: Signal Corps experimental mobile color television unit
description: An experimental production unit built for Army television research on color instruction. The article states: "The Signal Corps operates an experimental mobile color unit which consists of three color cameras and associated equipment mounted in an air-conditioned van." Transistor use makes the cameras lighter than predecessors though bulkier than standard image orthicons. It supported the color-versus-monochrome teaching study at Fort Monmouth and Huntsville.
requirements: Requires the mobile van with three color cameras and associated equipment to conduct color TV instruction studies in the field
constraints: The cameras remain bulkier than standard image orthicons despite being lighter due to extensive use of transistors
target_learners: Army trainees at the Signal School and the Ordnance Guided Missile School
target_learning_goals: Military teaching and training delivered over television
examples: Used at the Signal School, Fort Monmouth, and the Ordnance Guided Missile School, Huntsville, Alabama, across a wide variety of subject matter

article_title: Usage of augmented reality (AR) and development of e-learning outcomes: An empirical evaluation of students’ e-learning experience
citation: Baabdullah, Alsulaimani, Allamnakhrah, Alalwan, Dwivedi & Rana. (2021). Usage of Augmented Reality (AR) and Development of e-Learning Outcomes: An Empirical Evaluation of Students' e-Learning Experience. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Usage+of+Augmented+Reality+AR+and+Development+of+e-Learning+Outcomes+An+Empirical+Evaluation+of+Students+e-Learning+Experience
title: UGT-based conceptual model of students' e-learning experience with augmented reality learning applications
description: The article adapts Uses and Gratifications Theory (Katz et al., 1974) into a conceptual model in which four UGT benefit dimensions — "personal integrative benefits (PIB); cognitive benefits (CGB); social integrative benefits (SIB); and affective benefits (AB)" — act as antecedents of students' e-learning experience with AR learning applications, which in turn drives e-learning performance. The model extends UGT with telepresence as an additional antecedent and technostress as a moderator of all four benefit-experience paths. It was operationalised as a two-stage SEM model with 34 scale items across eight latent constructs and tested on 325 valid survey responses.
requirements: Respondents must be actively engaged in using AR learning applications for the experience constructs to be meaningful
constraints: Tested with undergraduate students at four large Saudi universities in science, computer science, engineering and medicine disciplines; the article does not claim generalisation beyond this context
target_learning_goals: positive e-learning experience with augmented reality learning applications
improved e-learning performance
examples: The model was validated via a questionnaire survey of 500 approached undergraduates (325 valid, 65% response rate) using seven-point Likert scales, with measurement and structural model fit indices reported
key_sources: Baabdullah, Alsulaimani, Allamnakhrah, Alalwan, Dwivedi & Rana. (2021). article_title: Mapping student-AI interaction dynamics in multi-agent learning environments: Supporting personalized learning and reducing performance gaps
citation: Hao, Z.; Cao, J.; Li, R.; Yu, J.; Liu, Z.; Zhang, Y. (2025). Mapping Student-AI Interaction Dynamics in Multi-Agent Learning Environments: Supporting Personalised Learning and Reducing Performance Gaps. https://osf.io/preprints/eduRxiv
title: MAIC: a massive AI-empowered course system with an AI teacher, four AI peer roles, and analytical back-end agents
description: MAIC is an online learning platform that constructs LLM-driven agents to support teaching and learning. Interface agents include a teacher and four AI peer types — "Sparker, Questioner, Thinker and Notetaker" — each with distinct functions, while back-end analytical agents (Classroom Situation Analysis, Learning Situation Analysis, Classroom Director) decide pacing and which agent appears. Students can choose observation or interaction mode and adjust discussion intensity, speech intervals, and text display speed.
requirements: Instructors upload course materials so agents can draft teaching slides and lecture scripts using multimodal understanding and knowledge structure extraction
constraints: The study used one introductory course, Towards Artificial General Intelligence, at a single elite university in China
target_learners: university students from various academic disciplines
target_learning_goals: understanding of artificial general intelligence topics
interactive and personalized learning
examples: Students begin by selecting a course, customize classroom participants, and can interchange observation and interaction modes anytime

article_title: The NISPI framework: Analysing collaborative problem-solving from students' physical interactions
citation: Cukurova, M., Luckin, R., Millán, E., & Mavrikis, M. (2017). The NISPI framework: Analysing collaborative problem-solving from students' physical interactions. Preprint submitted to Computers and Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.03.004
title: NISPI framework: nonverbal indexes of students' physical interactivity for interpreting CPS competence
description: The NISPI (Nonverbal Indexes of Students' Physical Interactivity) framework codes students' states in 30-second windows as passive (0), semi-active (1) or active (2) based on hand activity with objects and head direction, then derives group-level indexes for synchrony, individual accountability, equality and intra-individual variability. The article states the coding scheme "is simple enough to be automated with existing learning analytics systems" and comprehensive enough to interpret key CPS aspects. It was applied to high school and university groups in practice-based learning and validated against human observers' CPS rankings.
requirements: Video data of group work collected with a multimodal learning analytics system, coded in 30-second windows by trained coders with reliability checks
constraints: The evaluation through these concepts is only one part of understanding CPS quality; results derive from a relatively small sample and validity and automation at larger scale remain future work
target_learning_goals: collaborative problem-solving competence
examples: Three-student groups building interactive toys and motor artefacts with the TALKOO physical computing kit were coded and their index values compared with human observers' high/medium/low CPS rankings
key_sources: Cukurova, M., Luckin, R., Millán, E., & Mavrikis, M. (2017). The NISPI framework: Analysing collaborative problem-solving from students' physical interactions. Preprint submitted to Computers and Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2017.08.007

article_title: The NISPI framework: Analysing collaborative problem-solving from students' physical interactions
citation: Cukurova, M., Luckin, R., Millán, E., & Mavrikis, M. (2017). The NISPI framework: Analysing collaborative problem-solving from students' physical interactions. Preprint submitted to Computers and Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.03.004
title: TALKOO Arduino-based physical computing kit with multimodal learning analytics system
description: The TALKOO kit comprises pluggable hardware modules, a visual IDE and prototyping material, requiring no soldering or prior electronics knowledge; components "have the ability to talk back to the visual IDE and to a learning analytics system". Students combined the kit with craft materials to build interactive toys and motor-driven artefacts. The accompanying LAS collects ambient sensor data (colour and depth cameras with audio) and live human interaction data around an integrated screen and standing round table designed to foster collaboration.
requirements: A multimodal learning analytics environment with computer vision sensors and workstation furniture supporting shared group work
constraints: Complete description of the LAS architecture is out of the scope of the paper and is documented elsewhere (Spikol et al., 2016)
target_learning_goals: collaborative problem-solving
physical computing and prototyping skills
examples: High school students worked in pairs or groups of three across two sessions, including open-ended activities to build an interactive toy and a motor-based artefact

article_title: A study of the relationship between institutional policy, organisational culture and e-learning use in four South African universities
citation: Czerniewicz, L. & Brown, C. (2009). A study of the relationship between institutional policy, organisational culture and elearning use in four South African universities. Computers & Education, 53, 121-131. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2009.01.006
title: McNay's four-type organisational culture taxonomy combined with Structured/Unstructured elearning policy types as an analytic framework
description: The study frames institutional elearning contexts using two axes: an elearning policy typology (Structured versus Unstructured, defined by policy document, formal support unit and institution-wide LMS) and McNay's (1995) taxonomy of organisational cultures. The article describes the four cultural types: the collegium has "loose institutional policy definition, informal networks and decision arenas, and innovation at the level of the individual or department"; the bureaucracy has loose policy but strong regulation; the corporation has tight policy and tight implementation with top-down directives; the enterprise has a well-defined policy framework with students as clients. Institutions are classified by combining both axes.
requirements: Classification requires evidence on leadership style, institutional approach to ICT integration, and organisational style of policy implementation, drawn from key-informant interviews and prior research
constraints: The article notes no institution falls neatly into one grouping and institutions may change classification over time
The study does not cover all permutations; Structured Collegium and Structured Enterprise types were missing
target_learning_goals: understanding how institutional context shapes elearning adoption and use
examples: Four institutions were classified: A-S-Corp and B-S-Corp as Structured Corporations, C-U-Coll as Unstructured Collegium, D-U-Bur as Unstructured Bureaucracy
key_sources: Czerniewicz, L. & Brown, C. (2009). A study of the relationship between institutional policy, organisational culture and elearning use in four South African universities. Computers & Education, 53, 121-131. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2009.01.006

article_title: A study of the relationship between institutional policy, organisational culture and e-learning use in four South African universities
citation: Czerniewicz, L. & Brown, C. (2009). A study of the relationship between institutional policy, organisational culture and elearning use in four South African universities. Computers & Education, 53, 121-131. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2009.01.006
title: Institutional elearning policies should be supportive, flexible and non-restrictive so as to frame staff innovation while sustaining a culture that fosters varied pedagogical practices
description: The article concludes that policies are needed but must enable rather than compel: "supportive, flexible, non-restrictive institutional policies would be the most useful frames for staff innovation in the classroom". It argues successful, embedded and innovative ICT-teaching practices are likely the product of both enabling institutional policies and conducive collegium or enterprise cultures, suggesting a Structured Collegium or Structured Enterprise type as closest to the needed coalescence.
requirements: Policy understood as allocation of goals, values and resources, including centralised support structures and institution-wide systems
constraints: The article warns top-down corporate approaches may not be consultative enough and may be resented or resisted, with staff perceiving ICTs as forced
Neither the Structured Collegium nor Structured Enterprise type was found among the four institutions studied, so the recommendation is extrapolated
target_learning_goals: effective and innovative elearning use in teaching and learning
examples: The study found Structured Corporate types achieved critical mass while the Unstructured Collegium fostered staff variety of use, motivating the call for policies that support and enable while sustaining innovation
key_sources: Czerniewicz, L. & Brown, C. (2009). A study of the relationship between institutional policy, organisational culture and elearning use in four South African universities. Computers & Education, 53, 121-131. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2009.01.006

article_title: A study of the relationship between institutional policy, organisational culture and e-learning use in four South African universities
citation: Czerniewicz, L. & Brown, C. (2009). A study of the relationship between institutional policy, organisational culture and elearning use in four South African universities. Computers & Education, 53, 121-131. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2009.01.006
title: 2007 South African ICT access and use survey with 26 ICT-mediated activities categorised by Laurillard's Conversational Framework
description: A questionnaire survey of ICT access and use in six diverse South African universities, comprising access, use and demographics parts. Use was categorised into "26 ICT - mediated activities in four of the media form groupings in Laurillard's Conversational Framework (2002)", linking ICT use to the teaching and learning events of acquisition, discovery, dialogue, practice and creation. Respondents reported courses using ICTs, frequency of use for the 26 activities, and satisfaction with management, technical and pedagogical support.
requirements: Print surveys handed out on campus, as online response was very poor
constraints: Realised response rates were 27% for students (3533 usable responses) and 16% for staff (216 usable responses); representativeness of respondent views cannot be known and smaller campuses were under-represented
target_learning_goals: measuring ICT use for teaching and learning across communicative, interactive, adaptive and productive media forms
examples: The four-institution subset analysed here comprised 101/760, 34/296, 21/564 and 36/419 staff/student respondents respectively
