article_title: Children's engagement with digital technology in educational spaces: A scoping review
citation: J. Harverson, C. Zomer, C. Chu, S. Horwood, M. Horwood, M. Nicholas, L. Paatsch. (2026). Children's engagement with digital technology in educational spaces: A scoping review. Computers & Education 240 (2026) 105454. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2025.105454
title: A 14-theme taxonomy of children's digital engagement conceptualisations
description: Through inductive thematic analysis of definitions and measures of engagement across the 88 included studies, the review developed a taxonomy of engagement themes: effort, interpersonal skills or behavior, attention, enjoyment, participation, skills, interest, usability, motivation, valuing, and miscellaneous themes (belonging, responsibility, tension). The review states "This resulted in the identification of 14 themes (see Table 4; Clarke & Braun, 2017)", each with related terms and example definitions and measures. The taxonomy shows engagement's multidimensional nature in children's digital learning contexts.
requirements: Applicable to studies of children's engagement with digital technology in formal or semi-formal educational settings
constraints: The abstract refers to ten key themes while the results section reports 14 themes identified through thematic analysis
Definitions referring broadly to behavioural, emotional and cognitive components were not included in the theme table
target_learning_goals: characterising and measuring children's engagement with digital technology in play and learning
examples: Table 4 lists example definitions such as Attard's (2018) 'individual thoughts that are projected outwards in terms of a person's investment and effort towards learning' under effort, and example measures such as time-on-task observation under participation
key_sources: J. Harverson, C. Zomer, C. Chu, S. Horwood, M. Horwood, M. Nicholas, L. Paatsch. (2026). Children's engagement with digital technology in educational spaces: A scoping review. Computers & Education 240 (2026) 105454. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2025.105454

article_title: Children's engagement with digital technology in educational spaces: A scoping review
citation: J. Harverson, C. Zomer, C. Chu, S. Horwood, M. Horwood, M. Nicholas, L. Paatsch. (2026). Children's engagement with digital technology in educational spaces: A scoping review. Computers & Education 240 (2026) 105454. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2025.105454
title: Theoretical foundations of children's digital engagement draw primarily from motivational theories spanning educational and digital disciplines
description: The review synthesised nine theories or models of engagement referenced across the eight theorising studies, classifying them as education-only (BSCS 5E Instructional Model, ARCS model, Guthrie and Wigfield's reading engagement), digital-only (Immersion Theory, Positive Technological Development framework), both (Malone and Lepper's intrinsic motivation theory, CAMIL), or context-general (Flow Theory, Self Determination Theory). The review states these theoretical foundations were "primarily rooted in motivational theories", noting Flow Theory and Self Determination Theory are "widely used to understand motivational processes in a variety of settings, including education".
requirements: An explicit link between engagement and a well-established theory, framework, or model was required for a study to count as theorising engagement
constraints: References to Fredricks and colleagues' (2004) categorisation were excluded because it is a meta-construct drawing on a multitude of theories rather than a single theory
target_learning_goals: conceptualising children's engagement with digital technology in educational settings
examples: Table 3 maps each theory to studies: Flow theory (Csikszentmihalyi, 1988) referenced by Jingili et al. (2024) and Barreto et al. (2017); CAMIL (Makransky & Petersen, 2021) referenced by Molloy and Farrell (2024)
key_sources: J. Harverson, C. Zomer, C. Chu, S. Horwood, M. Horwood, M. Nicholas, L. Paatsch. (2026). Children's engagement with digital technology in educational spaces: A scoping review. Computers & Education 240 (2026) 105454. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2025.105454

article_title: Generic service integration in adaptive learning experiences using IMS learning design
citation: Luis de-la-Fuente-Valentín, Abelardo Pardo, Carlos Delgado Kloos. (2011). Generic service integration in adaptive learning experiences using IMS learning design. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2010.12.007
title: Generic Service Integration (GSI): a bidirectional bridge between IMS LD course engines and external Web 2.0 services
description: GSI is an extension of the IMS Learning Design specification that allows conventional third-party Web 2.0 tools to be included in courses defined with IMS LD. The article states it "allows the inclusion of conventional Web 2.0 services (third party tools) in the context of courses defined with IMS LD, and to bidirectionally exchange information among the course flow engine and the third party tools". A GSI layer built on top of an IMS LD-compliant platform offers a fixed API to the engine, while per-service adapters translate the generic vocabulary into each tool's access method. Services are described functionally at authoring time, matched to a catalogue at deployment, and instantiated cleanly per course offering.
requirements: The UoL must contain a GSI description of the third party service in the IMS manifest
The run-time environment must be compliant with both IMS LD and GSI
A GSI adapter module specific to the requested external tool must be installed in the run-time environment
constraints: Services are assumed to behave passively: an event must occur within the course before the engine requests data from the service
Privacy considerations of the data exchange are deferred to other work by the authors
target_learning_goals: adaptive orchestration of learning flows using external Web 2.0 tools
examples: A workshop Unit of Learning adapted its second act based on a questionnaire hosted in Google Forms, with responses mapped to IMS LD properties
key_sources: Luis de-la-Fuente-Valentín, Abelardo Pardo, Carlos Delgado Kloos. (2011). Generic service integration in adaptive learning experiences using IMS learning design. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2010.12.007

article_title: Generic service integration in adaptive learning experiences using IMS learning design
citation: Luis de-la-Fuente-Valentín, Abelardo Pardo, Carlos Delgado Kloos. (2011). Generic service integration in adaptive learning experiences using IMS learning design. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2010.12.007
title: Four requirements for integrating external services into reusable adaptive learning flows
description: The article enumerates four requirements that service-integration extensions should fulfil to preserve the spirit of IMS Learning Design: self-containment, adaptability, reusability and interoperability. Self-containment means "All the information required to deploy and enact a learning flow must be included in the Unit of Learning", interpreted as instructions to find and instantiate the service rather than the service itself. Adaptability extends flow adaptation to third-party services in both directions; reusability requires clean per-instance service instantiation; interoperability forbids proprietary protocols.
requirements: Service descriptions must be packaged in the UoL so deployment does not depend on a specific vendor tool
External services must be configurable by course events and must serve as sources of property values
constraints: The current version of IMS LD only supports a simplified mechanism to include external tools, with orchestration independent of events in the external resource
target_learning_goals: designing interoperable, reusable adaptive learning experiences with third-party tools
examples: In the pilot, each course instantiation created a clean Google Forms instance so all students started under the same circumstances
key_sources: Luis de-la-Fuente-Valentín, Abelardo Pardo, Carlos Delgado Kloos. (2011). Generic service integration in adaptive learning experiences using IMS learning design. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2010.12.007

article_title: Generic service integration in adaptive learning experiences using IMS learning design
citation: Luis de-la-Fuente-Valentín, Abelardo Pardo, Carlos Delgado Kloos. (2011). Generic service integration in adaptive learning experiences using IMS learning design. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2010.12.007
title: Three-type taxonomy of adaptive learning schemes: content, flow and interface adaptation
description: The article adopts, citing He, Kinshuk and Patel (2002), a taxonomy of adaptive learning schemes by the element modified: "content adaptation, where the same learning activity is presented to all the students but with different material; flow adaptation, where a different set of activities is chosen for each student; and interface adaptation, where the same information is presented to all the students but with different layouts". It uses this taxonomy to argue, following Burgos, Tattersall and Koper (2007), which types IMS LD supports: flow and content via properties, conditions and visibility attributes, but not interface modification inside a Unit of Learning.
requirements: Any adaptation type must be generalizable to one of the three described types
constraints: Interface modifications are not supported by adaptation inside a UoL, since IMS LD says nothing about how compliant players present information
target_learning_goals: classifying and implementing adaptation in learning experiences
examples: The workshop UoL used flow adaptation: the second act depended on questionnaire results gathered in the first act
key_sources: Luis de-la-Fuente-Valentín, Abelardo Pardo, Carlos Delgado Kloos. (2011). Generic service integration in adaptive learning experiences using IMS learning design. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2010.12.007

article_title: Accessibility and emotionality of online assessment feedback: Using emoticons to enhance student perceptions of marker competence and warmth
citation: Moffitt, RL; Padgett, C; Grieve, R. (2020). Accessibility and emotionality of online assessment feedback: Using emoticons to enhance student perceptions of marker competence and warmth. Computers and Education, 143. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.103654
title: Use positively valenced emoticons in written online assessment feedback to add warmth without sacrificing perceived quality or professionalism
description: The article concludes that instructors can use positively valenced emoticons to inject emotionality into written online assessment feedback. As the authors put it, instructors can use emoticons "to inject some fun, warmth, and emotionality in written online assessment feedback without sacrificing feedback quality or professional integrity." The recommendation rests on the experiment showing warmth and competence benefits for happy emoticons with null effects on quality and professionalism.
requirements: Feedback is written and delivered online in a higher education assessment context
constraints: Benefits were demonstrated for positively valenced emoticons; negatively valenced emoticons lowered perceived warmth and competence
Perceived competence advantage was reported specifically for 3 happy face emoticons
target_learning_goals: student perceptions of feedback accessibility, emotionality, and marker warmth and competence
examples: Undergraduates (N = 241) read a faux essay with written feedback identical except for emoticon frequency (none, 1, 3, or 6) and valence (happy, sad, or confused) in a between-groups experiment
key_sources: Moffitt, RL; Padgett, C; Grieve, R. (2020). Accessibility and emotionality of online assessment feedback: Using emoticons to enhance student perceptions of marker competence and warmth. Computers and Education, 143. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.103654

article_title: ICT integration in the classroom: Challenging the potential of a school policy
citation: Tondeur, J., van Keer, H., van Braak, J., & Valcke, M. (2008). ICT integration in the classroom: Challenging the potential of a school policy. Computers & Education, 51, 212-223. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2007.05.003
title: Five areas of local ICT policy from a school improvement approach
description: The article organises local ICT school policy around five areas derived from the school improvement movement: an ICT policy plan with clear goals and strategies, leadership directing ICT integration, support and training for implementation, evaluation to monitor ICT use and guide planning, and between-school cooperation for disseminating ICT knowledge. The article states that "Table 1 distinguishes ﬁve key factors from the school improvement approach and links these concretely to school policies fostering ICT integration in the classroom." It uses this framework to structure both the principal interviews and the multilevel analysis of classroom ICT use.
requirements: Development of a local school policy guaranteeing conditions supporting continuous change processes, with clear goals and systematic strategies
constraints: The article notes this list of school factors cannot depict the complexity of school improvement
target_learning_goals: integration of ICT into teaching and learning practices
examples: Principals were interviewed about each of the five areas; 75% of schools developed partnerships with other schools to share an ICT coordinator
key_sources: Tondeur, J., van Keer, H., van Braak, J., & Valcke, M. (2008). ICT integration in the classroom: Challenging the potential of a school policy. Computers & Education, 51, 212-223. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2007.05.003

article_title: Assessing aspects of children's written grammar: automating the process
citation: C.E. Holdich, R.G. Holdich and P.W.H. Chung. (2002). Assessing aspects of children's written grammar: automating the process. Computers and Education, Vol 39, pp37-50. http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/2.5/
title: Check Text program: a Visual Basic Script text-analysis tool measuring ten grammar indicators in children's writing
description: The Check Text program, written in Visual Basic Script, supplies statistical information about children's story texts across ten indicators covering vocabulary, syntax and punctuation, including total story length, type-token ratio of the first 100 words, common verbs, words over five letters, adverbs, 'and' and other basic connectives, simple sentence starters, mean sentence length, and commas relative to sentence length. It was created because existing text analysis programs 'are targeted at the way adults write rather than children'. The program's output was compared to examiners' written interpretations of each story.
requirements: Features analysed must be made specifically relevant to children's writing and presented in a way that is meaningful to teachers and children
constraints: A complete linguistic analysis was not undertaken; information about subordinate clause types and adjectival expansion is absent
The formative study used only 12 publicly available examiner-commented stories
target_learning_goals: written grammar: sentence construction, vocabulary and punctuation development
examples: Applied to 12 SATs stories spanning National Curriculum levels 2c to 5+, the computer successfully distinguished positive and negative grammar features within these texts
key_sources: C.E. Holdich, R.G. Holdich and P.W.H. Chung. (2002). Assessing aspects of children's written grammar: automating the process. Computers and Education, Vol 39, pp37-50. http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/2.5/

article_title: Impact of the provision of PowerPoint slides on learning
citation: Samuel P. León, Inmaculada García-Martínez. (2021). Impact of the provision of PowerPoint slides on learning. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2021.104283
title: Do not assume that providing teacher slides before class benefits learning; provision can harm performance and attendance
description: The article's findings caution against routine pre-class distribution of teacher-made slides. In its within-subject study, "access to slides developed by teachers had a negative impact on student performance and attendance to classes", and the authors suggest the dilemma of whether to provide slides may require a change of focus toward the material itself and students' own note-making.
requirements: Slides, if provided, should be created by the module lecturer who understands their purpose, as the article states the ideal author is the module lecturer.
constraints: The study examined concise outline slides that could not directly answer exam questions; results may not generalise to slides designed as complete study documents.
target_learners: university students in an Early Childhood Education degree
target_learning_goals: subject-matter exam performance
class attendance
examples: Slides were concise outlines created by the teacher; exam questions were designed so correct responses could not be literally extracted from any of the slides.
key_sources: Samuel P. León, Inmaculada García-Martínez. (2021). Impact of the provision of PowerPoint slides on learning. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2021.104283

article_title: Creative use of podcasting in higher education and its effect on competitive agency
citation: Lazzari, Marco. (2009). Creative use of podcasting in higher education and its effect on competitive agency. COMPUTERS & EDUCATION. http://hdl.handle.net/10446/22717
title: University podcasting service with students as both users and creators of podcasted lessons
description: The article describes an academic podcasting experience built on the university's podcasting service, in which students of a course on multimedia communication and human-computer interaction "acted both as users of the university's podcasting service, and as creators of podcasted lessons." This dual role is the core design element of the experience evaluated in the paper.
requirements: Students must have access to the university's podcasting service and be positioned as creators of podcasted lessons, not only as consumers.
target_learners: higher education students in a multimedia communication and human-computer interaction course
target_learning_goals: understanding of theoretical issues of the course
practical skills in podcasting and multimedia communication
examples: Students of the course co-produced podcasted lessons while also using the service as listeners.
key_sources: Lazzari, Marco. (2009). Creative use of podcasting in higher education and its effect on competitive agency. COMPUTERS & EDUCATION. http://hdl.handle.net/10446/22717

article_title: Experiences of using a public key infrastructure for the preparation of examination papers
citation: David W Chadwick, Rana Tassabehji and Andrew Young. (1999). Experiences of Using a Public Key Infrastructure for the Preparation of Examination Papers. IT Institute, University of Salford. http://www.salford.ac.uk/its024/X500.htm
title: Three user types — Supporter, Potential Supporter and Resister — profile how staff adopt an electronic process
description: From questionnaire and interview profiling of pilot participants, the authors derive "a profile of 3 types of user". The Supporter is enthusiastic, needs no post-implementation support and actively counters problems; the Potential Supporter is enthusiastic but needs practice, training, documentation and an assisting infrastructure; the Resister prefers established paper processes, sees new processes as extra burden, and treats technical hiccups as an excuse to delay or abandon the system. Each type is characterised by course tenure, age, attitudes and thoughts scores, home Internet access and security-software knowledge.
requirements: A full assessment of the types and profiles of users in the organisation before change is attempted, so implementation can be tailored to their differing needs
constraints: Derived from an admittedly small sample of computer-literate departments; the authors state further study is needed for less computer-frequent departments
target_learners: university lecturers and administrators adopting new electronic processes
target_learning_goals: understanding and adopting a new secure electronic work process
examples: Profiling distinguished ITI lecturers (technology oriented, mostly supporters) from CMS staff, where one respondent with markedly low thoughts-about-computers scores predicted resistance that materialised mid-pilot
key_sources: David W Chadwick, Rana Tassabehji and Andrew Young. (1999). Experiences of Using a Public Key Infrastructure for the Preparation of Examination Papers. IT Institute, University of Salford. http://www.salford.ac.uk/its024/X500.htm

article_title: Experiences of using a public key infrastructure for the preparation of examination papers
citation: David W Chadwick, Rana Tassabehji and Andrew Young. (1999). Experiences of Using a Public Key Infrastructure for the Preparation of Examination Papers. IT Institute, University of Salford. http://www.salford.ac.uk/its024/X500.htm
title: Before introducing an electronic process, profile user types and design a tailored implementation with training and education
description: The article recommends that organisational change begins with user profiling: "Before any kind of change can take place, a full assessment of the types of user in an organisation must be made." By identifying types and profiles, an implementation process can be tailored to differing needs, and stakeholders can be educated in a way that builds commitment, without which no project can succeed. Users need both software training and an appreciation of how the encryption works to avoid mistakes.
requirements: A consultative stage involving all parties, since views of the existing process differed (50% of CMS staff found it satisfactory while others found it inconvenient, slow and antiquated)
constraints: Derived from a small pilot in two computer-literate departments; results may differ in computer-naïve departments
target_learners: university staff adopting new administrative technology
target_learning_goals: commitment to and effective use of a new electronic process
examples: The pilot used in-depth interviews, questionnaires at start and end, and semi-structured observations during training to profile participants before and during rollout
key_sources: David W Chadwick, Rana Tassabehji and Andrew Young. (1999). Experiences of Using a Public Key Infrastructure for the Preparation of Examination Papers. IT Institute, University of Salford. http://www.salford.ac.uk/its024/X500.htm

article_title: Touch Arithmetic: A process-based Computer-Aided Assessment approach for capture of problem solving steps in the context of elementary mathematics
citation: Adesina, A., Stone, R., Batmaz, F., & Jones, I. (2014). Touch Arithmetic: A process‐based Computer‐Aided Assessment approach for capture of problem solving steps in the context of elementary mathematics.
title: MuTAT: a multi-touch arithmetic assessment tool capturing solution steps via trace links
description: MuTAT (Multi-Touch Arithmetic Tool) is a tablet-based prototype for process-based computer-aided assessment in elementary mathematics. Its interface has a problem pane with draggable numeric values and a solution pane; a touch-and-hold gesture activates arithmetic operators, and interactions are recorded with timestamps and coordinates so that "visual representations of the process data is constructed" from traces of problem-solving actions.
requirements: An interactive interface that provides problem-solvers opportunities to explicitly enter their solutions, with integrated problem text and solution workspace so trace links can be created between solution items and their origins
constraints: The tool presents stepwise information horizontally, which may disadvantage students who prefer vertical sums especially with carry-over digits
The 9.7-inch tablet screen may affect problems that require three or more stages
target_learning_goals: multi-digit addition in arithmetic word problems
arithmetic strategy use and number bonds understanding
examples: In the observational study, 39 children answered 390 questions on MuTAT and 156 on paper, producing a log file of 8,221 records
key_sources: Adesina, A., Stone, R., Batmaz, F., & Jones, I. (2014). Touch Arithmetic: A process‐based Computer‐Aided Assessment approach for capture of problem solving steps in the context of elementary mathematics. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2014.06.015

article_title: Touch Arithmetic: A process-based Computer-Aided Assessment approach for capture of problem solving steps in the context of elementary mathematics
citation: Adesina, A., Stone, R., Batmaz, F., & Jones, I. (2014). Touch Arithmetic: A process‐based Computer‐Aided Assessment approach for capture of problem solving steps in the context of elementary mathematics.
title: Trace-based capture of problem-solving process for process-level assessment and feedback
description: The article proposes using structured trace information, analogous to on-line requirement traceability in software engineering, to capture problem-solving steps. As students perform interactive actions on an integrated problem text and solution space, dependency links are created between solution items and their origins, allowing an answer's life to be followed "in both forward and backward directions". This makes the thinking behind a solution visible and supports process-level feedback, which the article cites Hattie and Timperley as arguing is most effective in assessment situations.
requirements: Interactive problem-solving tasks that reduce inconsistencies and ambiguities in the representation of solution steps
Integration of the problem text/scenario with the solution space so interactive actions are executed between them
constraints: Fewer prior studies had explored dependencies and relationships in the problem-solving process in ways they can be unambiguously represented, motivating this approach
target_learners: primary school children learning elementary mathematics
target_learning_goals: diagnosis of strengths and weaknesses in problem solving
process-level feedback on strategies and intermediate steps
examples: The MuTAT prototype implements the approach: dragging numbers from problem pane to solution pane creates trace links, and a diagrammatic representation of solution steps is generated from the recorded traces
key_sources: Adesina, A., Stone, R., Batmaz, F., & Jones, I. (2014). Touch Arithmetic: A process‐based Computer‐Aided Assessment approach for capture of problem solving steps in the context of elementary mathematics. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2014.06.015

article_title: Touch Arithmetic: A process-based Computer-Aided Assessment approach for capture of problem solving steps in the context of elementary mathematics
citation: Adesina, A., Stone, R., Batmaz, F., & Jones, I. (2014). Touch Arithmetic: A process‐based Computer‐Aided Assessment approach for capture of problem solving steps in the context of elementary mathematics.
title: Assess the problem-solving process, not only the final product, to enable richer feedback in elementary mathematics
description: The article argues that computer-aided assessment should extend beyond scoring final answers to capturing steps and dependencies, because considering "the whole steps and actions during the problem‐solving process provides useful information". Process-level feedback addresses what strategies the learner used and why an answer was wrong, which the article (citing Hattie and Timperley) treats as more effective than task-level feedback. Teachers, parents and practitioners can use such process data to improve feedback processes.
requirements: Tools or techniques that reveal the problem-solving process, including detailed steps and the final answer, so strategies can be accurately assessed
constraints: Traditional paper-and-pencil capture of detailed steps suffers from the absence of consistent notation for representing solution steps and the difficulty in enforcement
target_learners: primary school children in elementary mathematics
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of arithmetic
strategic problem solving
examples: MuTAT allowed intermediate steps such as use of correct operations and intermediate answers to be scored independently of final answers, so assessors can assign partial credit
key_sources: Adesina, A., Stone, R., Batmaz, F., & Jones, I. (2014). Touch Arithmetic: A process‐based Computer‐Aided Assessment approach for capture of problem solving steps in the context of elementary mathematics. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2014.06.015

article_title: Facilitating professional mobile learning communities with instant messaging
citation: Pimmer, Christoph; Brühlmann, Florian; Odetola, Titilayo Dorothy; Oluwasola, Deborah Olusola; Dipeolu, Oluwafemi; Ajuwon, Ademola J. (2019). Facilitating professional mobile learning communities with instant messaging. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.09.005
title: Moderated mobile instant messaging groups as a vehicle for professional mobile learning communities during school-to-work transition
description: The article frames Mobile Instant Messaging as "a genuine form of mobile learning" and uses moderated WhatsApp groups—in which moderators shared knowledge and stimulated professional discussions—to engage young professionals in mobile learning communities during the school-to-work transition. This transition is described as "one of the most central but also challenging developmental phases marked by the experience of knowledge gaps and a lack of belonging." The framework links moderated knowledge sharing to both knowledge and socio-professional outcomes.
requirements: Moderators who share knowledge and stimulate professional discussions in the messaging groups
constraints: Effects examined in a developing context marked by a lack of alternative support structures
target_learners: Newly graduated nurses in Nigeria during school-to-work transition
target_learning_goals: Professional knowledge
Professional identity and connectedness
Transfer of school knowledge to work practice
examples: Newly graduated nurses participated in WhatsApp groups over a period of 6 months with moderators sharing knowledge and stimulating professional discussions
key_sources: Pimmer, Christoph; Brühlmann, Florian; Odetola, Titilayo Dorothy; Oluwasola, Deborah Olusola; Dipeolu, Oluwafemi; Ajuwon, Ademola J. (2019). Facilitating professional mobile learning communities with instant messaging. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.09.005

article_title: Facilitating professional mobile learning communities with instant messaging
citation: Pimmer, Christoph; Brühlmann, Florian; Odetola, Titilayo Dorothy; Oluwasola, Deborah Olusola; Dipeolu, Oluwafemi; Ajuwon, Ademola J. (2019). Facilitating professional mobile learning communities with instant messaging. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.09.005
title: Six-month moderated WhatsApp group intervention for newly graduated nurses
description: An intervention element in which newly graduated nurses from Nigeria participated in WhatsApp groups where "moderators shared knowledge and stimulated professional discussions over a period of 6 months." It was evaluated within "a quasi-experimental, survey-based approach with an intervention and control condition (n = 114)", with data collected via online surveys and knowledge tests.
requirements: Moderators who share knowledge and stimulate professional discussions
Sustained participation over a period of 6 months
constraints: Evaluated against a control group which was not subject of any treatment
target_learning_goals: Professional knowledge
Reduced professional isolation
Professional identification
examples: Data were collected via online surveys and knowledge tests in an international research project setting
key_sources: Pimmer, Christoph; Brühlmann, Florian; Odetola, Titilayo Dorothy; Oluwasola, Deborah Olusola; Dipeolu, Oluwafemi; Ajuwon, Ademola J. (2019). Facilitating professional mobile learning communities with instant messaging. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.09.005

article_title: Adolescent user behaviors on short video application, cognitive functioning and academic performance
citation: Ziyan Xu, Xinqiao Gao, Jun Wei, Huiqin Liu, & Yu Zhang. (2022). Adolescent user behaviors on short video application, cognitive functioning and academic performance. https://www.statista.com/statistics/1095186/tiktok-us-users-age/
title: Adolescence as a developmental window of susceptibility to media effects
description: The article organizes its age-comparison findings with the account that "adolescence is often proposed as a window of susceptibility to various types of media effects and behavioral addictions". It holds that media-use impact is conditional upon differential susceptibility due to different developmental levels, with mid-adolescence a watershed in cognitive-developmental trajectories. The study uses this framework to predict and interpret why 12-13-year-olds show SVA effects on working memory and verbal ability while 15-16-year-olds largely do not.
requirements: Comparing age cohorts that differ in developmental stage, since susceptibility is hypothesized to vary with developmental level
constraints: The article notes the study is cross-sectional, so reverse directions between variables may not be ruled out and causal links cannot be drawn
target_learning_goals: Self-regulation and academic delay of gratification
Working memory and verbal ability supporting academic performance
examples: The study compared 454 younger and 368 older adolescents from one Beijing middle school using two-group SEM with nested model comparison to test whether each path differed between cohorts.
key_sources: Ziyan Xu, Xinqiao Gao, Jun Wei, Huiqin Liu, & Yu Zhang. (2022). Adolescent user behaviors on short video application, cognitive functioning and academic performance. https://www.statista.com/statistics/1095186/tiktok-us-users-age/

article_title: Investigating social vulnerability in children using computer mediated role-play
citation: Fallon, T. L., Aylett, R., Minnis, H. and Rajendran, G. (2018). Investigating social vulnerability in children using computer mediated role-play. Computers and Education, 125, pp. 458-464. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.06.027
title: Theme-matched DSE vignette and Kar2ouche computer role-play assessment tasks
description: A newly created set of 22 theme-matched measures: 11 paper-pencil vignettes and 11 computer-mediated role-play scenarios built in the Kar2ouche story-boarding tool, in which "the child and the researcher role-play by typing into the speech bubbles". Items were independently validated by an expert against DSM-V DSE symptoms on a 5-point rating scale, and both formats were matched on themes and scoring (0–2 per item). Inter-rater reliability was r = .82 for vignettes and r = .99 for the computer task.
requirements: Items must be validated against the specific DSM-V symptoms of Disinhibited Social Engagement Disorder
Paper-pencil and computer versions must be matched on themes and scoring to be comparable
constraints: Complete materials are available only by contacting the first author
Scoring of justification questions requires subjective judgement by trained raters
target_learners: typically developing children aged 6, 8 and 10 years
children in middle childhood being assessed for social vulnerability
target_learning_goals: measuring disinhibited social engagement and social vulnerability
assessing social safety awareness and theory of mind
examples: Children completed the tasks individually with a researcher in a quiet room at school, with testing approximately 1 hour per child; presentation order was counterbalanced and pseudo-randomised.
key_sources: Fallon, T. L., Aylett, R., Minnis, H. and Rajendran, G. (2018). Investigating social vulnerability in children using computer mediated role-play. Computers and Education, 125, pp. 458-464. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.06.027

article_title: The effect of competition on learning in games
citation: Nergiz Ercil Cagiltay, Erol Ozcelik, Nese Sahin Ozcelik. (2015). The effect of competition on learning in games. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2015.04.001
title: Serious game designers should incorporate competition to facilitate learning
description: The article concludes that adding competition as a game design element improves learning outcomes and motivation. Based on their experiment, the authors state that "game designers should incorporate the element 'competition' to the games they created to facilitate learning." The competition was implemented as a real-time panel showing other players' scores, ranking and nick names.
requirements: A competition environment among human players, with visible scores, ranking and nick names in real time
constraints: The authors note some studies show cooperation is more effective than competition, and results need validation in larger samples and other domains and age groups
target_learners: undergraduate students in computer-related engineering departments
target_learning_goals: conceptual database modeling with entity-relationship diagrams
examples: In the study, half of 142 randomly assigned participants played a game version showing all current players' scores, ranking and nick names in real time, while the control version left that list empty.
key_sources: Nergiz Ercil Cagiltay, Erol Ozcelik, Nese Sahin Ozcelik. (2015). The effect of competition on learning in games. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2015.04.001

article_title: Pedagogical agents communicating and scaffolding students' learning: High school teachers' and students' perspectives
citation: Sikström, P., Valentini, C., Sivunen, A., & Kärkkäinen, T. (2024). Pedagogical Agents Communicating and Scaffolding Students' Learning : High School Teachers' and Students' Perspectives. Computers and Education, 222, Article 105140. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105140
title: Human–machine communication in instruction: applying human communication scripts and the relational/task-related framework to pedagogical agents
description: The article extends human–machine communication (HMC) theory to the instructional context, arguing that teachers and students apply human-to-human communication scripts when evaluating PAs, and that instructional communication's two dimensions — relational and task-related — structure expectations for PA behavior. It builds on the computers are social actors (CASA) paradigm, under which "people tend to apply the same social scripts to both computers and humans." The framework organizes PA design around communicational, pedagogical, and technological considerations.
requirements: PA communication should be adaptive, adequate, relational, and logical, as the article states
constraints: Findings derive from Finnish high school teachers' and students' expectations, not from observed PA use
target_learning_goals: scaffolding student learning
instructional communication with learning technology
key_sources: Sikström, P., Valentini, C., Sivunen, A., & Kärkkäinen, T. (2024). Pedagogical Agents Communicating and Scaffolding Students' Learning : High School Teachers' and Students' Perspectives. Computers and Education, 222, Article 105140. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105140

article_title: Interaction during online classes fosters engagement with learning and self-directed study both in the first and second years of the COVID-19 pandemic
citation: Gherghel, C., Yasuda, S., & Kita, Y. (2023). Interaction during online classes fosters engagement with learning and self-directed study both in the first and second years of the COVID-19 pandemic. Computers & Education, 200, 104795. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104795
title: Design online classes with deliberate opportunities for social interaction, because interactivity fosters engagement and spillovers into self-directed study
description: The article's core design recommendation is that online lecturers should structure classes to include social interaction opportunities such as group work, discussions, and presentations. The study found that "participants who reported that the classes they had attended had more group work, discussions, and presentations (social interaction), also reported that they enjoyed the classes more" and put in more effort, with indirect effects on out-of-class self-directed study. Because what happens during online classes can affect learning outside class, lecturers should be aware that class structure influences students' broader learning behavior.
requirements: Online course delivery must include activities that create opportunities for interaction among students and between students and instructors, such as group work, discussions, and presentations.
constraints: The article cautions that "the more the better" is not always the case, that interaction quality matters, and that introverted or socially anxious students may find interactive courses burdensome.
target_learners: First-year university students in online courses
target_learning_goals: Learning engagement with online classes
Self-directed learning skills
examples: The study measured perceived opportunities for social interaction during online classes with five items including pair work and group work, and found interactivity predicted engagement and self-directed study time in both 2020 and 2021.
key_sources: Gherghel, C., Yasuda, S., & Kita, Y. (2023). Interaction during online classes fosters engagement with learning and self-directed study both in the first and second years of the COVID-19 pandemic. Computers & Education, 200, 104795. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104795

article_title: Virtual and remote labs in education: A bibliometric analysis
citation: Ruben Heradio, Luis de la Torre, Daniel Galan, Francisco Javier Cabrerizo, Enrique Herrera-Viedma, Sebastian Dormido. (2016). Virtual and remote labs in education: A bibliometric analysis. Computers & Education, Volume 98, Pages 14-38. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2016.03.010
title: Virtual and remote labs as educational alternatives to conventional hands-on labs
description: Virtual and remote labs are web-based alternatives to conventional hands-on laboratories in engineering and science education. The review describes them as reducing the costs of "required equipment, space, and maintenance staff" while providing additional educational benefits. They serve as the review's central object of study across the literature from the field's beginnings to 2015.
requirements: Web-based experimentation infrastructure is needed so that laboratory activities can be delivered without conventional hands-on equipment.
target_learners: engineering and science students in higher education
target_learning_goals: experimental and laboratory skills in engineering and science education
examples: The review analyzes the literature on virtual and remote labs gathered from ISI Web of Science, Scopus, and GRC2014.
key_sources: Ruben Heradio, Luis de la Torre, Daniel Galan, Francisco Javier Cabrerizo, Enrique Herrera-Viedma, Sebastian Dormido. (2016). Virtual and remote labs in education: A bibliometric analysis. Computers & Education, Volume 98, Pages 14-38. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2016.03.010

article_title: Virtual and remote labs in education: A bibliometric analysis
citation: Ruben Heradio, Luis de la Torre, Daniel Galan, Francisco Javier Cabrerizo, Enrique Herrera-Viedma, Sebastian Dormido. (2016). Virtual and remote labs in education: A bibliometric analysis. Computers & Education, Volume 98, Pages 14-38. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2016.03.010
title: Bibliometric analysis of educational literature via science mapping combined with performance analysis
description: The article uses two prominent bibliometric approaches to analyze a research field: science mapping and performance analysis. The authors state they "examined" bibliographical data "using two prominent bibliometric approaches: science mapping and performance analysis". Science mapping structures the literature by topics and their evolution, while performance analysis assesses publications; together they let the review identify influential publications and research topics from large bibliographical datasets.
requirements: Bibliographical data gathered from bibliographic databases, here ISI Web of Science, Scopus, and GRC2014, is needed as input to the analysis.
target_learning_goals: understanding the state and evolution of research on a learning technology
examples: The review applied these approaches to literature on virtual and remote labs from the field's beginnings to 2015.

article_title: ‘Pretty Lights’ and Maths! Increasing student engagement and enhancing learning through the use of electronic voting systems
citation: Samuel O. King and Carol Robinson. (2008). 'Pretty Lights' and Maths! Increasing student engagement and enhancing learning through the use of electronic voting systems. Mathematics Education Centre, Loughborough University. https://dspace.lboro.ac.uk/
title: Turning Point electronic voting system with PowerPoint-embedded MCQs for large undergraduate Mathematics lectures
description: The article describes a radio-frequency EVS comprising handsets, a receiver and operating software, with Turning Point's "enabling software is embedded in Microsoft PowerPoint". Lecturers prepare multiple-choice questions as PowerPoint slides; students respond via handsets and responses are displayed as charts, letting the lecturer address misconceptions such as a common error on double integrals. At Loughborough, handsets are collected and returned lecture-by-lecture and purchased centrally by the department.
requirements: Handsets, a receiver and operating software must be procured; in the UK a handset costs between £30-£50 and receivers £200-£300, with departments typically purchasing the handsets
constraints: Infra-red EVS variants are limited to classes of under about 100 students, whereas radio systems scale beyond 1000; some handsets fail in use (26 students, 18%, reported a handset had failed)
target_learners: second-year undergraduate Engineering students in large Mathematics lectures
target_learning_goals: formative checking of mathematical understanding
increasing in-class participation and engagement
examples: At the Mathematics Education Centre, lecturers used Turning Point handsets with MCQ slides; Figure 2 shows a response chart exposing a common student misconception about double integrals
key_sources: Samuel O. King and Carol Robinson. (2008). 'Pretty Lights' and Maths! Increasing student engagement and enhancing learning through the use of electronic voting systems. Mathematics Education Centre, Loughborough University. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2009.01.012

article_title: ‘Pretty Lights’ and Maths! Increasing student engagement and enhancing learning through the use of electronic voting systems
citation: Samuel O. King and Carol Robinson. (2008). 'Pretty Lights' and Maths! Increasing student engagement and enhancing learning through the use of electronic voting systems. Mathematics Education Centre, Loughborough University. https://dspace.lboro.ac.uk/
title: Use EVS primarily in formative-assessment mode so instant feedback empowers students and informs lecturers' pedagogical adjustments
description: The paper argues the value of EVS lies in formative feedback: it is instant, acts as "a barometer for personal understanding of study", lets students gauge the class, and gives staff knowledge of what needs correcting or reinforcing. The authors state that "The formative feedback that the use of EVS engenders is pivotal in the learning process", enabling lecturers lacking a week-by-week sense of student assimilation to make pedagogical changes addressing gaps.
requirements: Lecturers must act on the response displays, elaborating on issues arising and addressing identified misconceptions and gaps in understanding
constraints: Feedback's benefit depends on lecturers having and using a means of gauging student assimilation; without it, necessary pedagogical changes cannot be made
target_learners: large undergraduate classes, particularly Engineering students studying Mathematics
target_learning_goals: self-assessment of understanding
identification of problem areas
lecturer awareness of class-wide misconceptions
examples: Students ranked 'Checks whether I'm understanding course material as I thought I was' first and 'Allow learners to identify problem areas' second among seven benefits

article_title: Factors influencing students’ perceived impact of learning and satisfaction in Computer Supported Collaborative Learning
citation: Pablo-César Muñoz-Carril, Nuria Hernández-Sellés, Eduardo-José Fuentes-Abeledo, Mercedes González-Sanmamed. (2021). Factors influencing students' perceived impact of learning and satisfaction in Computer Supported Collaborative Learning. Computers & Education, 174. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2021.104310
title: Integrated TAM–ECM–Flow research model of satisfaction and perceived impact on learning in CSCL
description: The article develops a research model combining seven constructs from three theories: "the Expectation-Confirmation Model (ECM) (Bhattacherjee, 2001), the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) (Davis, 1989) and Flow Theory (Csikszentmihalyi, 1997)". It links confirmation, perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, attitude, perceived enjoyment, and satisfaction to perceived impact on learning, tested via PLS-SEM. The model explained 84% of the variance of perceived impact on learning and 86.3% of satisfaction, and all 13 hypothesised paths were supported.
requirements: Questionnaire scales previously validated in prior studies, reviewed by a panel of 5 international experts and pre-tested with 30 students
constraints: The article states the research was carried out in a single University and focuses only on student perception in a CSCL context
target_learners: university master's students in virtual courses
target_learning_goals: satisfaction with technology-mediated collaborative learning
perceived impact on learning in CSCL
examples: PLS-SEM with SmartPLS 3.2.7 on questionnaire data from 701 master's students; bootstrapping with 5000 subsamples; SRMR of 0.05
key_sources: Pablo-César Muñoz-Carril, Nuria Hernández-Sellés, Eduardo-José Fuentes-Abeledo, Mercedes González-Sanmamed. (2021). Factors influencing students' perceived impact of learning and satisfaction in Computer Supported Collaborative Learning. Computers & Education, 174. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2021.104310

citation: Pablo-César Muñoz-Carril, Nuria Hernández-Sellés, Eduardo-José Fuentes-Abeledo, Mercedes González-Sanmamed. (2021). title: Five-phase online collaborative learning experience with projects and case studies
description: The studied courses embedded "online collaborative working processes using project and case-study based methodologies" across five phases: pre-group identification of classmates, self-formed groups of 4 or 5 members via forums and Google Sheets, intra-group agreements on roles and communication tools, development of collaborative learning activities, and online self-assessment and peer-assessment of process and results. Teachers created virtual spaces, facilitated debates, gave feedback, and assessed group processes and products.
requirements: Virtual campus spaces, forums, and Google Sheets for group formation and communication
target_learners: master's students in four-month, 6-ECTS online courses
target_learning_goals: collaborative project and case-study learning
self- and co-evaluation of collaborative processes
examples: Phase 5 included online self-assessment and peer-assessment of process and results, plus a self-reflection of the learning process

Factors influencing students' perceived impact of learning and satisfaction in Computer Supported Collaborative Learning. Computers & Education, 174. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2021.104310
title: Plan and monitor social interaction during CSCL design, since it does not arise spontaneously
description: The article holds that successful CSCL requires deliberately designing its social dimension: collaboration "must be planned in the design phase and monitored so that it happens properly during implementation". Designers should define social relationship aspects together with the cognitive aspects of task completion, foster a positive, socially accepting atmosphere, and attend to intra-group emotional support, motivation, and a sense of belonging to the community.
requirements: Detailed planning of pedagogical, curricular, social, and technological aspects before implementation
Teacher feedback and monitoring of interaction during implementation
constraints: The article warns that poor planning risks poor learning experiences and individual or group failures
target_learners: university students working in virtual collaborative groups
target_learning_goals: knowledge construction through collaboration
satisfaction with collaborative learning
examples: The studied courses required groups to agree on internal rules, member roles, communication tools, and how to act when a member was not committed to the task

article_title: Effectiveness of flip teaching on engineering students' performance in the physics lab
citation: Gómez-Tejedor, J. A., Vidaurre, A., Tort-Ausina, I., Molina-Mateo, J., Serrano, M.-A., Meseguer-Dueñas, J. M., Martínez Sala, R. M., Quiles, S., & Riera, J. (2020). Effectiveness of flip teaching on engineering students’ performance in the physics lab. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.103708
title: First-principles-based flip teaching design for laboratory sessions: pre-class videos for activation, in-class demonstration and integration phases.
description: The article describes an FT laboratory design in which students study documents and screencast videos before the session on the institution's online platform, so the session begins directly with experimental work. The learning design was based on the “first principles of instruction” following Lo, Lie, and Hew (2018): videos serve the activation phase, in-class measuring with teacher supervision serves the demonstration phase, and in-class organising, discussing and defending results serves the integration phase. Teacher explanations were reduced to answering doubts about out-of-class learning.
requirements: Students must study the pre-class documents and videos in advance; the article notes students realized after the first session that they needed to read and watch the materials beforehand.
constraints: The article could not trace how resources had been used in the FT courses, as no tracking tool was available on the platform at that time.
target_learners: undergraduate engineering students in technical degree courses
target_learning_goals: laboratory experimental skills
understanding of theoretical contents and experimental procedures
discussion and defence of results
examples: Videos were screencasts explaining the lab work and equipment, e.g. a video introducing the free fall practice; groups of six uploaded a spreadsheet after each two-hour session and a report within ten days.
key_sources: Gómez-Tejedor, J. A., Vidaurre, A., Tort-Ausina, I., Molina-Mateo, J., Serrano, M.-A., Meseguer-Dueñas, J. M., Martínez Sala, R. M., Quiles, S., & Riera, J. (2020). Effectiveness of flip teaching on engineering students’ performance in the physics lab. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.103708

article_title: Effectiveness of flip teaching on engineering students' performance in the physics lab
citation: Gómez-Tejedor, J. A., Vidaurre, A., Tort-Ausina, I., Molina-Mateo, J., Serrano, M.-A., Meseguer-Dueñas, J. M., Martínez Sala, R. M., Quiles, S., & Riera, J. (2020). Effectiveness of flip teaching on engineering students’ performance in the physics lab. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.103708
title: Analogous-students method for computing individual normalized gains across non-overlapping cohorts.
description: Because the same students did not experience both methodologies, the authors introduced the “analogous students” concept: students in the FT and TM groups occupying the same position in a lab-grade ranking within low/high grade subgroups are paired, and the individual normalized gain gi is computed for each FT student from the paired TM student's grade. The introduction of the concept allowed the authors “to associate confidence intervals with the results of the gain and perform a more robust statistical study.” Random exclusion balanced unequal subgroup sizes, giving a final sample of 613 students.
requirements: Two-step procedure: divide groups into low and high levels by total course grade, then rank by laboratory grades within each subgroup for each course and pair same-position students.
constraints: When subgroup sizes differed between methodologies, some students were excluded randomly from the subgroup with most members; the method assumes grade ranks are comparable across cohorts.
target_learners: higher education students in courses where methodological changes cannot be tested on the same students
target_learning_goals: measuring knowledge gained between teaching methodologies
examples: Applied to Physics (299 students) and Electricity (314 students) cohorts from 2013-2017, producing individual gains gi mostly between 0 and 0.2.

citation: Gómez-Tejedor, J. A., Vidaurre, A., Tort-Ausina, I., Molina-Mateo, J., Serrano, M.-A., Meseguer-Dueñas, J. M., Martínez Sala, R. M., Quiles, S., & Riera, J. (2020). Effectiveness of flip teaching on engineering students’ performance in the physics lab. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.103708
title: Introduce flip teaching progressively, starting with laboratory practices.
description: The article recommends that institutions adopting flip teaching begin with laboratory sessions rather than lectures, because the lab offers the clearest gain: pre-class videos free session time from long teacher explanations for discussion and experimental work. The authors state that as a general conclusion FT “works very well for lab sessions in technical degree courses” and that “For a progressive application of FT, we recommend starting the experience with the laboratory practices.”
requirements: Pre-class documents and videos must be available on an online platform, and lab-work design should be directly related in content and timing to the rest of the subject's learning activities.
constraints: Evidence comes from Physics and Electricity courses in one engineering degree; the authors advise caution in extrapolating the results to non-STEM disciplines.
target_learning_goals: laboratory performance
autonomous learning
academic results in practical sessions
examples: At the Universitat Politècnica de València, FT was introduced into lab sessions from the first day of class, with teachers' explanations reduced to answering doubts about out-of-class learning.

article_title: Using Bayesian networks to improve knowledge assessment
citation: Millán-Valldeperas, E.; Descalço, L.; Castillo, G.; Oliveira, P.; Diogo, S. (2013). Using Bayesian networks to improve knowledge assessment. Elsevier. http://hdl.handle.net/10630/7068
title: Generic Bayesian student model (GBSM) integrated into the PMatE computerized testing system
description: The GBSM is an existing generic Bayesian student model that was integrated into an existing computerized testing system within the Mathematics Education Project (PmatE) of the University of Aveiro. In this work it "had been used" to define Bayesian Student Models (BSMs) "for a concrete domain: first degree equations", with separate BSMs built for the computer test and the written exam. Its diagnosis capabilities were then evaluated against expert grading.
requirements: Requires definition of a domain-specific Bayesian student model from the generic model for the target domain
constraints: The article reports low agreement between the computer-test BSM diagnosis and the expert average
target_learners: students learning first degree equations in the PMatE system
target_learning_goals: diagnosing student knowledge of 12 concepts related to first degree equations
examples: Two BSMs were developed, one for the computer test and another for the written exam, and used to estimate students' knowledge on the same 12 concepts

article_title: Using Bayesian networks to improve knowledge assessment
citation: Millán-Valldeperas, E.; Descalço, L.; Castillo, G.; Oliveira, P.; Diogo, S. (2013). Using Bayesian networks to improve knowledge assessment. Elsevier. http://hdl.handle.net/10630/7068
title: PMatE computerized testing system (Mathematics Education Project, University of Aveiro)
description: PMatE (Projecto Matemática Ensino) is an existing computerized testing system within the Mathematics Education Project of the University of Aveiro. In this study it served as the platform into which the generic Bayesian student model was integrated, delivering the computerized test that 152 students took alongside a written exam covering the same 12 concepts on first degree equations. Its test results fed a BSM whose diagnosis was compared with expert averages.
requirements: An existing testing platform delivering domain tests whose results can feed a Bayesian student model
constraints: Diagnosis from the computer-test BSM showed low agreement with the expert average in this evaluation

target_learning_goals: assessing student knowledge of first degree equations
examples: 152 students each took a computerized test within PMatE and a written exam designed to measure knowledge in 12 concepts related to first degree equations

article_title: Immersive virtual reality serious games for evacuation training and research: A systematic literature review
citation: Zhenan Feng, Vicente A. González, Robert Amor, Ruggiero Lovreglio, Guillermo Cabrera-Guerrero. (2018). Immersive Virtual Reality Serious Games for Evacuation Training and Research: A Systematic Literature Review. https://www.scopus.com
title: Conceptual framework for developing and implementing IVR serious games for evacuation research
description: The review's main outcome is a conceptual framework (Figure 4) integrating the factors identified across the 15 reviewed papers: expected pedagogical and behavioral outcomes, IVR equipment selection (HMD or PBD) and navigation solutions, development elements (simulated hazards, narrative methods, senses stimulation, NPCs), and an implementation phase in which outcomes and participation experience are measured. The framework "integrates critical aspects and provides connections between them, including pedagogical and behavioral impacts, gaming environment development, and outcome and participation experience measures". It prescribes iterating improvement until measured results meet expectations.
requirements: Researchers need to identify expected outcomes and impacts before the development process
The IVR SGs development needs to include data recording function if such data is necessary for learning measures
Appropriate navigation solution should be designed thoroughly in accordance with the available IVR equipment
constraints: The framework was derived from only 15 eligible papers, twelve of which were rated 6 or over on the review's quality scale
target_learners: building occupants training for indoor emergencies such as fire and earthquake
target_learning_goals: evacuation best practices
self-protection skills
spatial knowledge for evacuation
examples: The framework connects teaching-method selection to participants' background and game narrative method, and links static hazards to the surroundings-driven narrative method
key_sources: Zhenan Feng, Vicente A. González, Robert Amor, Ruggiero Lovreglio, Guillermo Cabrera-Guerrero. (2018). Immersive Virtual Reality Serious Games for Evacuation Training and Research: A Systematic Literature Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.09.002

article_title: Immersive virtual reality serious games for evacuation training and research: A systematic literature review
citation: Zhenan Feng, Vicente A. González, Robert Amor, Ruggiero Lovreglio, Guillermo Cabrera-Guerrero. (2018). Immersive Virtual Reality Serious Games for Evacuation Training and Research: A Systematic Literature Review. https://www.scopus.com
title: Four narrative methods structure IVR serious game storylines: action-driven, instruction-driven, performance-driven, and surroundings-driven
description: The review identifies four narrative methods for encouraging participants to follow and complete IVR SG storylines: "there were four narrative methods recognized by this review, namely action-driven method (Chittaro & Buttussi, 2015) , instruction-driven method (Andrée et al., 2016; Aoki et al., 2007; Burigat & Chittaro, 2016; Cosma et al., 2016; Meng & Zhang, 2014; Smith & Ericson, 2009; Zou et al., 2016) , performance-driven method (Li et al., 2017), and surrounding -driven method". Action- and surroundings-driven methods restrict movement so participants must follow the storyline, while instruction- and performance-driven methods keep the open world, relying on participants' ability and willingness to complete the game.
requirements: A narrative method is needed because an IVR environment can often be simulated as an open world where participants may get lost or wander around out of curiosity
constraints: Narrative method choice should account for participants' background, expected outcomes, and the IVR environment
target_learners: building occupants training for indoor emergencies
target_learning_goals: following and completing evacuation training storylines
achieving expected learning and behavior outcomes
examples: Li et al. (2017) introduced a scoring system generating scores based on gaming performance; Duarte et al. (2014) and the Kinateder and Ronchi studies filled the environment with simulated hazards so participants had no choice but to follow the storyline pathway
key_sources: Zhenan Feng, Vicente A. González, Robert Amor, Ruggiero Lovreglio, Guillermo Cabrera-Guerrero. (2018). Immersive Virtual Reality Serious Games for Evacuation Training and Research: A Systematic Literature Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.09.002

article_title: Immersive virtual reality serious games for evacuation training and research: A systematic literature review
citation: Zhenan Feng, Vicente A. González, Robert Amor, Ruggiero Lovreglio, Guillermo Cabrera-Guerrero. (2018). Immersive Virtual Reality Serious Games for Evacuation Training and Research: A Systematic Literature Review. https://www.scopus.com
title: Static and dynamic simulated hazards in IVR evacuation serious games
description: The review categorizes simulated hazards in IVR SGs into two levels. Static hazards do not interact with participants and are used to "increase fear perception, trigger events, constrain moving area , and improve environment al realism", such as a burning vehicle blocking an evacuation way or an engine failure triggering evacuation. Dynamic hazards interact with participants and provide negative experience, such as losing visibility in smoke, blood-spattered eyes after a head hit, or falling and fragile objects hurting virtual bodies during an earthquake simulation. Participants face these realistic hazards in a completely safe environment.
requirements: IVR SGs need to integrate corresponding functions to carry out analysis for pre-defined behavior outcomes
constraints: Dynamic hazards should be chosen depending on the research purposes and participants' backgrounds
target_learners: building occupants training for indoor emergencies
target_learning_goals: hazard perception and risk awareness
self-protection strategies such as crawling under smoke
examples: Smith and Ericson (2009) suggested participants crawl on the floor to get under the smoke as the correct behavior; Li et al. (2017) used falling and fragile objects so participants needed a self-protection strategy
key_sources: Zhenan Feng, Vicente A. González, Robert Amor, Ruggiero Lovreglio, Guillermo Cabrera-Guerrero. (2018). Immersive Virtual Reality Serious Games for Evacuation Training and Research: A Systematic Literature Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.09.002

article_title: Instagram as a platform for teacher collaboration and digital social support
citation: Eric Richter, Jeffrey P. Carpenter, André Meyer, Dirk Richter. (2022). Instagram as a platform for teacher collaboration and digital social support. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2022.104624
title: Three-form conceptualization of teacher collaboration on social media (information seeking, information sharing, co-creating)
description: The article develops a multi-faceted, theory-driven conceptualization of teacher collaboration on social media, distinguishing "information seeking, information sharing, co-creating". It builds on Gräsel et al.'s (2006) forms of teacher collaboration and the low-cost/high-cost distinction, positioning seeking and sharing as lower-cost activities and co-creating as a higher-cost form requiring greater investment. The study operationalizes the framework in a 10-item survey instrument and validates it via CFA on Instagram users.
requirements: The framework assumes collaboration activities can be self-reported via Likert-scale items and differentiated as latent factors, as operationalized in the study's instrument.
constraints: The instrument was developed and validated for Instagram use among German teachers; the article calls for replication on other platforms and more balanced samples.
target_learners: in-service teachers using social media for professional collaboration
target_learning_goals: teacher professional development through peer collaboration and digital social support
examples: The study measured the three forms with items such as "I use Instagram to look for teaching related information" and "I prepare lessons together with my colleagues on Instagram."
key_sources: Eric Richter, Jeffrey P. Carpenter, André Meyer, Dirk Richter. (2022). Instagram as a platform for teacher collaboration and digital social support. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2022.104624

article_title: The mediating role of digital informal learning in the relationship between students' digital competence and their academic performance
citation: Mehrvarz, Mahboobe; Heidari, Elham; Farrokhnia, Mohammadreza; Noroozi, Omid. (2021). The mediating role of digital informal learning in the relationship between students' digital competence and their academic performance. Computers & Education 167 (2021) 104184. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2021.104184
title: Digital informal learning as a three-aspect construct (cognitive, metacognitive, social-motivational)
description: The article treats digital informal learning (DIL) as unstructured, technology-mediated learning outside formal settings. It defines it as "the unstructured technology-mediated learning opportunities in informal learning settings", in which learners control what, when and how they learn. Following He and Li (2019), the article structures DIL into three measured aspects: "cognitive learning (CL), metacognitive learning (MCL), and social and motivational learning (SML)", each operationalised with a four-item questionnaire subscale in the study. The Discussion adds that the article attributes a self-determination-theory basis to DIL via He and Li (2019).
requirements: Learners need access to digital technologies in informal, out-of-class contexts for DIL to occur
DIL demands proper digital competence to form optimal learning and behavior in such a digital-based learning environment
constraints: Measured here by self-report questionnaires only; no empirical intervention was used
target_learning_goals: self-directed learning with digital technologies
academic performance

description: Because the study found digital competence directly improves academic performance and DIL carries an additional indirect effect, the authors recommend dual support. They state that higher education institutions, educators and curriculum designers "should not only improve the students' digital competence through extra-curricular programs", but also "should provide opportunities for students to learn outside the formal classes through digital environments". title: Three self-report questionnaires measuring digital competence, digital informal learning, and perceived academic performance
description: The study's measurement battery comprises three validated self-report instruments. Digital competence was measured with He and Zhu's (2017) questionnaire based on Calvani's framework, with three dimensions: technical skills (11 items), cognitive skills (12 items), and ethical knowledge (6 items) on 5-point Likert scales; six low-loading items were removed and overall Cronbach's alpha was 0.90. DIL was measured with He and Li's (2019) questionnaire with CL, SML, and MCL subscales of four items each (alpha 0.89). Academic performance was measured by students' self-perception with Yu et al.'s (2010) four-item questionnaire (alpha 0.86).

citation: Koskinen, A., McMullen, J., Hannula-Sormunen, M., Ninaus, M., & Kiili, K. (2023). The strength and direction of the difficulty adaptation affect situational interest in game-based learning. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2022.104694
title: Strength and direction of difficulty adaptation as two dimensions affecting motivational outcomes in adaptive digital learning environments
description: The article proposes that motivational outcomes of adaptive learning environments depend on two under-examined dimensions of difficulty adaptation: strength (how much difficulty is adjusted) and direction (upwards or downwards). It operationalizes this as five adaptation levels applied via estimation-accuracy thresholds, and argues that examining only overall adaptation effects can mask these dimensions, since "the non-significant main effect between difficulty conditions on situational interest indicates that without examining the effects of strength and direction of adaptation, our results would have indicated that adaptation of difficulty does not affect motivational outcomes."
requirements: Adaptive systems must log or assign adaptation strength and direction so their separate effects can be analyzed
Manipulation checks must confirm the adaptation mechanism worked as designed before motivational effects are interpreted
constraints: Findings come from one game-based fraction-learning context with fifth-graders
target_learning_goals: Conceptual fraction knowledge (number line estimation)
examples: In the Number Trace game, basic-game level performance assigned participants to six levels of adaptation, and motivational outcomes were compared across content-matched level pairs.

article_title: The effectiveness of brain-compatible blended learning material in the teaching of programming logic
citation: van Niekerk, J.F. (2015). The effectiveness of brain-compatible blended learning material in the teaching of programming logic. Nelson Mandela Metropolitan University.
title: Brain-compatible learning: a principles-based educational approach grounded in neuroscience and educational psychology
description: The dissertation frames brain-compatible learning as an educational approach stemming from neuroscience and educational psychology, made possible by 1990s brain-imaging advances. It is explicitly not a formalised recipe for teachers; it provides a "set of principles and a base of knowledge and skills upon which we can make better decisions about the learning process". The approach is based on the underlying "biology of learning" rather than traditional practice, and underpins the study's intervention design.
requirements: Designers need some insight into how learning works at a biological level to understand the reasons for the principles
constraints: Not a formalised education approach or recipe for teachers; no single authoritative list of principles exists
target_learning_goals: learning of algorithms and problem-solving skills in programming

article_title: The effectiveness of brain-compatible blended learning material in the teaching of programming logic
citation: van Niekerk, J.F. (2015). The effectiveness of brain-compatible blended learning material in the teaching of programming logic. Nelson Mandela Metropolitan University.
title: A synthesized set of brain-compatible learning principles for instructional design
description: The dissertation synthesises principles reported across multiple authors (Fogarty, Jensen, Materna, Sousa, Craig, Smilkstein, Caine and Caine) into a summary table, noting that "Currently, no single authoritative list or taxonomy exists that describes and encompasses all known brain-compatible learning principles". The set includes no retention without rehearsal, short focused activities, challenge without threat, emotions affecting learning, multifaceted experiences, parts-and-wholes processing, implicit and explicit memory systems, uniqueness of each brain, innate search for meaning, patterning, real-life context, and immediate feedback.
requirements: Principles are drawn from overlapping lists by multiple authors rather than a single taxonomy
constraints: Some principles (e.g. healthy lifestyle, unique brains) are difficult for an instructional designer to control for in a blended or classroom environment
target_learning_goals: retention and meaningful learning of new subject material
examples: The table lists principles such as "Short, focused learning activities are best" and "Immediate feedback amplifies learning" with the authors endorsing each

description: The intervention is an e-learning package delivered via Moodle lessons augmenting lectures, containing an "Interactive sorting algorithm presentation", an "Interactive question during fizzbuzz code execution", and "Example of immediate interactive feedback during fizzbuzz task" (Figures 3.4-3.6). It "incorporated several brain-compatible learning principles" and was "administered as a controlled experiment intervention" to a sample group whose performance was compared to a control group of the rest of the class.

constraints: Designed to augment, not replace, the lecturer's function
