title: Purpose-designed qualitative instrument organised around six experience themes
description: The study used a purpose-designed qualitative research instrument (Appendix A) whose thematic organisation is summarised in Table 3.1. The results chapter analyses six themes: whether the e-learning material differed from "normal" classes, whether it was engaging (enjoyable), whether students preferred it, whether learning was a positive experience, whether the material was "rich" enough (multimedia), and whether students felt they had learned. Closed-question responses are reported in Tables 4.4-4.9 and Figures 4.1-4.12, plus open-ended questions.

article_title: The effectiveness of brain-compatible blended learning material in the teaching of programming logic
citation: van Niekerk, J.F. (2015). The effectiveness of brain-compatible blended learning material in the teaching of programming logic. Nelson Mandela Metropolitan University.
title: Pair practice with constant, consistent, specific and immediate feedback so that practice makes correct learning permanent
description: The dissertation argues that practice alone does not guarantee learning: "Practice does not make perfect. Practice makes permanent" (Sousa, 2006). For practice to improve learning, learners must analyse results and know what to change, so "Practice should thus be accompanied by feedback that is constant, consistent, and specific" and the effect of feedback "is also amplified if it is immediate". This principle directly shaped the intervention's interactive feedback design.
requirements: Feedback must be constant, consistent and specific to the learner's performance; immediacy amplifies its effect
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of algorithm and problem-solving skills
examples: The intervention included an "Example of immediate interactive feedback during fizzbuzz task" (Figure 3.6)

article_title: The effectiveness of brain-compatible blended learning material in the teaching of programming logic
citation: van Niekerk, J.F. (2015). The effectiveness of brain-compatible blended learning material in the teaching of programming logic. Nelson Mandela Metropolitan University.
title: Connect new content to learners' existing knowledge patterns, since new neural patterns only grow as extensions of existing ones
description: Drawing on Smilkstein, the dissertation states that "dendrites, synapses, and neural networks grow only from what is already there", so new knowledge must connect to learners' past experiences and prior learning. Every time prior learning is activated, the brain is more likely to connect to the new material, increasing comprehension; linking to something familiar acts as a foundation for new knowledge. Irrelevant connections are pruned.
requirements: Instruction must activate learners' relevant prior knowledge before presenting new material
constraints: What is considered meaningful depends on the learner's own perspective
target_learners: higher education students entering programming courses
target_learning_goals: comprehension and understanding of new algorithmic concepts
key_sources: van Niekerk, J.F. (2015). The effectiveness of brain-compatible blended learning material in the teaching of programming logic. Nelson Mandela Metropolitan University. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2016.09.008

article_title: The effectiveness of brain-compatible blended learning material in the teaching of programming logic
citation: van Niekerk, J.F. (2015). The effectiveness of brain-compatible blended learning material in the teaching of programming logic. Nelson Mandela Metropolitan University.
title: Present learning as short, focused activities within a challenging but non-threatening environment
description: The dissertation reports the primacy-recency effect, whereby material presented first is remembered best and the middle of a lesson least, and recommends "limiting cognitive activities to periods of 5 to 10 minutes each" to minimise low-impact middle-of-lesson learning. It also holds that "Learning is enhanced by challenge and inhibited by threat": perceived threat triggers downshift and a fight-or-flight response that closes connections to the prefrontal cortex and impairs logical thinking.
requirements: Content must be challenging enough to engage curiosity but delivered non-threateningly, with learners feeling secure
constraints: What constitutes a threat differs from person to person; a problem challenging for one learner may threaten another
target_learners: higher education students in large programming classes
target_learning_goals: attention, engagement and logical thinking during lessons
key_sources: van Niekerk, J.F. (2015). The effectiveness of brain-compatible blended learning material in the teaching of programming logic. Nelson Mandela Metropolitan University. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2016.09.008

article_title: The effectiveness of brain-compatible blended learning material in the teaching of programming logic
citation: van Niekerk, J.F. (2015). The effectiveness of brain-compatible blended learning material in the teaching of programming logic. Nelson Mandela Metropolitan University.
title: Use rich, multi-sensory and multifaceted learning experiences that engage emotion and multiple memory pathways
description: The dissertation argues that learning involves both focused attention and peripheral perception, and that "Experiences that provide rich sensory input well beyond the capacity of a book or a worksheet have the greatest chance of sparking dendritic growth and increased synaptic connections" (McGeehan, 2001). Emotions are crucial because they focus attention and drive learning and memory; Materna is cited recommending engaging multiple memory pathways through multi-sensory formats combining discussion, visuals and hands-on activities.
requirements: Designers should engage both visual and verbal faculties and consider the entire context in which teaching occurs
constraints: Motivation for the e-learning material depends on students finding it meaningful and engaging
target_learners: higher education students with varied learning styles and preferences
target_learning_goals: long-term retention and meaningful engagement with subject content
examples: Theme 5 of the qualitative instrument asked whether the e-learning material was "rich" enough (multimedia), with responses reported in Table 4.8

article_title: Preparing preservice teachers to teach with digital technologies: An update of effective SQD-strategies
citation: Jo Tondeur, Ottavia Trevisan, Sarah K. Howard, Johan van Braak. (2025). Preparing preservice teachers to teach with digital technologies: An update of effective SQD-strategies. Computers & Education 232. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2025.105262
title: SQD2: an updated Synthesis of Qualitative Data model of strategies for preparing preservice teachers to teach with digital technologies
description: SQD2 is a revised evidence-based model structuring strategies for developing preservice teachers' digital competencies across micro, meso and macro levels, updating the original 2012 SQD model. It consolidates 28 sub-categories into 10 categories and six synthesised statements, including familiarisation, reflective practice, collaborative design, a cycle of authentic experiences and feedback, an affective dimension, and institutional vision. The authors report that "new categories and most importantly new relationships among them emerged through the current study", with exploration foregrounded and the meso level reframed around pedagogy, commitment and the affective dimension.
requirements: Strategies must address both micro-level preparation of preservice teachers and meso-level institutional conditions, with attention to relationships among categories rather than treating them separately
constraints: Derived from a meta-aggregation of 28 qualitative studies published between 2012 and 2024, so the model reflects qualitative evidence from that window only
target_learners: preservice teachers in teacher training institutions
target_learning_goals: digital competence for integrating digital technologies in teaching and learning
examples: The review aggregated 28 sub-categories into 10 categories and six synthesised statements, presented in Figs. 3–8 and consolidated into the SQD2 model in Fig. 9

article_title: Preparing preservice teachers to teach with digital technologies: An update of effective SQD-strategies
citation: Jo Tondeur, Ottavia Trevisan, Sarah K. Howard, Johan van Braak. (2025). Preparing preservice teachers to teach with digital technologies: An update of effective SQD-strategies. Computers & Education 232. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2025.105262
title: Structure teacher training programs to afford opportunities for preservice teachers to experience and experiment with digital technologies and different approaches to learning
description: The review's institutional-level finding holds that teacher training programs should be deliberately designed so preservice teachers encounter and try out digital technologies and varied pedagogical approaches, including stand-alone ICT courses and modelled delivery modes such as online, hybrid and blended learning. As the article states, "Teacher training programs need to be structurally designed to afford opportunities for preservice teachers to experience and experiment with digital technologies and different approaches to learning." This underpins the SQD2 institutional vision synthesis.
requirements: Institutional guidance on expectations for different modes of delivery, and teaching courses that model desired approaches and learning designs
constraints: Grounded in qualitative evidence aggregated across 15 countries; the review notes the optimal combination of strategies depends on each teacher's unique profile

target_learning_goals: digital competence and technology-integrated pedagogical design
examples: Eutsler (2022) designed learning tasks modelling the gradual release of responsibility — Teacher as Control, Teacher as Facilitator and Problem-based learning — and the review reports the value of stand-alone ICT courses (Dewa & Ndlovu, 2022; Şen & Hava, 2020)

article_title: The learner centric ecology of resources: A framework for using technology to scaffold learning
citation: Rosemary Luckin. (2008). The Learner Centric Ecology of Resources: A Framework for using Technology to Scaffold Learning. Computers & Education 50, 449-462. https://www.veselproject.net
title: Learner Centric Ecology of Resources model of context
description: The model describes a learning context as "a set of inter-related resource elements, including people and objects, the interactions between which provide a particular context". The learner sits at the centre, with Knowledge/Skills filtered through Curriculum, Resources filtered through Administration, and Environment filtered through Organisation. Bi-directional arrows link Knowledge, Resources and Environment and link Curriculum, Administration and Organisation, while learner-to-Knowledge and learner-to-Environment arrows are uni-directional. It is offered as a design tool, an evaluation framework, and a lens for reconceptualising the learning-teaching process.
requirements: Requires mapping the elements present in an existing context, the links between them and potential barriers
constraints: Uni-directional learner arrows reflect the article's observation that learners' activity has little impact upon the nature of knowledge, curricula and environment organisation

citation: Rosemary Luckin. (2008). The Learner Centric Ecology of Resources: A Framework for using Technology to Scaffold Learning. Computers & Education 50, 449-462. https://www.veselproject.net
title: ZAA and ZPA as constructs relating the ZPD to educational technology
description: The article defines two constructs that clarify the relationship between the ZPD and educational technology. "The ZAA is used to describe the types of resources, both human and artifact, that are available within a particular context"; the ZPA is "a selected subset of the ZAA that are the resources that are the most appropriate form of assistance for a given learner at a particular moment in time". The article stresses that a rich ZAA alone does not create a ZPD: a more able partner must organise and activate resources, or make existing assistance obvious, so the learner can select appropriately.
requirements: A more able partner must organise and activate the available resources appropriately for the learner to form a ZPA
constraints: The existence of a rich set of resources within the ZAA is not sufficient to ensure the interactions necessary to create a ZPD
target_learners: learners working with more able partners, including teachers, parents and software
target_learning_goals: receiving appropriately challenging activities with the right quantity and quality of assistance
examples: In earlier software scaffolding work the ZAA was within the software, with scaffolding techniques making timely interventions to draw the learner's attention to available assistance, thus creating a ZPA

citation: Rosemary Luckin. (2008). The Learner Centric Ecology of Resources: A Framework for using Technology to Scaffold Learning. Computers & Education 50, 449-462. https://www.veselproject.net
title: HOMEWORK system: tablet-PC-based integrated learning across home and school
description: The HOMEWORK system supports integrated learning across home and school contexts for Key Stage 1 maths. It "consists of components for lesson planning, control and home use" with multimedia numeracy resources; teachers link resources into lesson plans, use an interactive whiteboard for whole-class work, and allocate activities and homework to children's individual tablet PCs. At home the tablet gives access to class resources, learning-objective information for parents, fun activities and a parent-teacher messaging system.

constraints: Developed for the UK school organisational context; the home organisational context is far more variable and the system needed to recognise these variations

Analysis showing that for a limited curriculum and resources the system addresses all the links between the model's elements

citation: Rosemary Luckin. (2008). The Learner Centric Ecology of Resources: A Framework for using Technology to Scaffold Learning. Computers & Education 50, 449-462. https://www.veselproject.net
title: Learner Generated Contexts as a future direction for technology-supported learning
description: The article proposes that growing tools for capturing and publishing materials extend the capacity to create learning contexts beyond teachers, academics, designers and policy makers. "a Learner Generated Context is one in which a learner or group of learners marshall the resources available to them to create an ecology that meets their needs"; its key aspect is creation "through the enterprise of those who would previously have been consumers in a context created for them". The author identifies scaffolding learners to generate their own contexts as the key future challenge.
requirements: Increased understanding of how to scaffold learners to effectively generate their own learning contexts
constraints: Proposed as a future research agenda; the article offers a hypothetical community environmental centre example rather than an implemented system
target_learners: learners and communities acting as creators rather than consumers of learning contexts, e.g. community environmental centre volunteers
target_learning_goals: self-directed, collaborative learning around common, self-defined goals
examples: A sketched scenario in which community centre members collect and publish pollution data, maintain an environmental wiki, discuss local issues, attract politicians' attention and ground a volunteer course

citation: Rosemary Luckin. (2008). The Learner Centric Ecology of Resources: A Framework for using Technology to Scaffold Learning. Computers & Education 50, 449-462. https://www.veselproject.net
title: Design technology-mediated learning for reciprocal teacher-learner relationships around different expertise
description: Because learners may know more about technologies that could act as learning tools than the experts who know the subject matter, the article argues that "It should be a collaborative relationship where the more able partner is both the teacher and the learner, but with respect to different expertise". New educational theories are needed to encompass situations where the balance between learner and teacher or mentor control is constantly changing. The article links this to Bruner's notion of learning by transaction and the inadequacy of translating obuchenie simply as instruction.
requirements: Teachers and experts need to know enough about learning technologies to scaffold learning, while learners need to know how to use these tools to learn subject matter
constraints: The article presents this as an observation suggesting the need for further exploration, not a tested finding
target_learners: learners and teachers/experts in technology-mediated settings
target_learning_goals: subject or skill learning supported through mutually beneficial collaboration
examples: The cited e-Science work by Underwood, Smith, Luckin & Fitzpatrick on enabling educational e-Science communities to grow and build contexts to share and exploit resources

article_title: Monitoring student progress using virtual appliances: A case study
citation: Romero-Zaldivar, V.-A., Pardo, A., Burgos, D., & Delgado Kloos, C. (2012). Monitoring student progress using virtual appliances: A case study. Computers & Education, 58(4), 1058–1067. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2011.12.003
title: Coverage measure (covs) quantifying the extent of monitoring per student
description: The coverage measure covs is a per-student figure of merit computed from version control server logs as 1 − UPf/(UPe + UPf), where UPe is the number of event upload operations and UPf the number of file update operations. The article states "a coverage value of 0.5 denotes a fully monitored user environment" and values above 0.5 are possible. It is used both to answer the feasibility question and to select the students included in the correlation and regression analyses. A copy of recorded events is kept in the student's own folder so students may review, amend or delete collected events.
requirements: A version control system (Subversion) whose server logs record event-upload and file-update operations separately per user
constraints: Students may disable monitoring at any time, so coverage varies from student to student; the article reports a significant number of students with covs below 0.5
target_learning_goals: monitoring student engagement with course practical activities to predict academic achievement
examples: In the Fall 2010 course, only students with covs ≥ 0.40 (79 students) were included in the correlation and regression analyses

article_title: Monitoring student progress using virtual appliances: A case study
citation: Romero-Zaldivar, V.-A., Pardo, A., Burgos, D., & Delgado Kloos, C. (2012). Monitoring student progress using virtual appliances: A case study. Computers & Education, 58(4), 1058–1067. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2011.12.003
title: Virtual appliances as self-contained, instrumentable environments for learning analytics
description: The approach packages a course's full tool set in a virtual machine distributed to students, exploiting virtualization's isolation, compatibility and encapsulation so that "a multi-level comprehensive monitoring scheme can be deployed" inside the appliance. Rather than forcing activities onto a generic platform, the design places "generic 'sensors' closer to the environment in which students interact" — instrumenting applications with wrapper programs and relaying events through the Subversion client to a central server. This trades a tool-embedding approach (high specialization, partial coverage) for generic monitoring with broad coverage of the student's actual workspace.
requirements: All course tools must be installed in the appliance; each tool to be recorded must be instrumentalized individually (wrapper programs or log harvesting); a central collection server and version control channel must be configured
constraints: Monitoring must comply with data protection legislation (EU Directive 1995/46/EC, Spanish LOPD), so students must be informed and can disable monitoring; if the tool set changes, the monitoring module must be modified unless recording is moved to the operating system level
target_learners: students in face-to-face or distance settings
target_learning_goals: predicting academic achievement
instructor monitoring and adjustment of course activities
examples: A second-year engineering course appliance configured with compiler, debugger, memory profiler, editor, browser and command interpreter, with events relayed via a Subversion wrapper

title: Give students control over the monitoring mechanism to comply with data protection rules
description: The article's deployment treated compliance with data protection legislation as a design requirement: students were shown an explanatory page before downloading the appliance, could disable monitoring, and a machine without monitoring was offered as an alternative. Recorded events were also kept in plain text in the student's own folder so students "may exercise the right to review, amend or delete any of the collected events". The authors state that this compliance "translates basically into giving students total control over the monitoring mechanism".
requirements: Students must be informed explicitly, precisely and unequivocally of the data file's existence, purpose, recipients, the voluntary nature of monitoring, and their rights of access, rectification, erasure and objection
constraints: The policy may have a significant impact on the amount of data collected, since students can disable monitoring at any point
target_learners: university students whose course activities are monitored
target_learning_goals: ethical, legally compliant collection of learning interaction data for analytics
examples: Before downloading the virtual machine, students saw a web page explaining the monitoring mechanism and had to agree; a non-monitored machine was also available

citation: Zhao Yu, Pinto Llorente Ana María, Sánchez Gómez María Cruz. (2021). Digital competence in higher education research: A systematic literature review. Computers & Education, 168, 104212. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2021.104212
title: DigComp five-component framework of digital competence
description: The European Commission's Digital Competence Framework (DigComp), established to identify and support EU citizens' digital competence, presents five components: information and data literacy, communication and collaboration, digital content creation, safety, and problem solving. It was updated into Digcomp 2.1 in 2017 with the same key dimensions, and sub competences can be evaluated across different levels of proficiency. In this review it is the most-used basis for assessment instruments in higher education.
requirements: Assessment instruments built on it operationalize its five dimensions across proficiency levels
constraints: The review reports only 27% of reviewed publications applied assessment based on Digcomp
target_learning_goals: digital competence
examples: Nine reviewed publications followed and established instruments on the basis of the Digcomp dimensions

title: DigCompEdu six-area framework of educators' digital competence
description: Within the DigCompEdu project of the European Commission, digital competence is considered the ability of users to make safe, critical and creative use of ICT to satisfy different objectives. Redecker (2017) categorized an educator's digital competence into six areas: professional engagement, digital resources, teaching and learning, assessment, empowering learners, and facilitating learners' digital competence. The review reports this framework has been consolidated and spread internationally, and the Spanish Common Digital Competence Framework for Teachers (INTEF) adapts DigComp and DigCompEdu into five competence areas including 21 competencies.
requirements: Built on the basis of DigComp; used for training, evaluation, certification and accreditation purposes
constraints: Addresses educators' digital competence specifically, not students'

professional development
examples: Cabero-Almenara et al. (2020) measured the reliability and validity of the DigCompEdu Check-In questionnaire covering these six areas

description: The article proposes an integrated framework (Figure 1) linking levels of actual parental resistance (no, passive, active) to four resistance factors — social, environmental, economic and pedagogical — plus parenting styles and demographic variables. It builds on the "Three Pillars of Technological Rejection" model, whose "model contains three types of reasons for rejecting technologies: social, economic and environmental", adding the pedagogical factor. "The study introduced and empirically tested an integrated framework for the examination of parental resistance to the educational use of smartphones".

In it, “evaluators' ratings produce evidence in the form of a graph, presenting estimated proportion of users who effectively use the interface versus the time they had to work with it in order to succeed effectiveness.” The article develops the method and applies it to an educational simulation interface.

article_title: Battling bias: Effects of training and training context
citation: Poos, J., van den Bosch, K. & Janssen, C.P. (2017). Battling bias: Effects of training and training context. Computers & Education, vol. 111, pp. 101-113. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2017.04.004
title: Use engaging narrative text rather than expensive immersive games for bias-mitigation training when resources are scarce
description: This principle holds that when training content is held equal, a well-written narrative text can achieve bias-mitigation training outcomes comparable to an interactive game. The article found that "embedding training in the context of a game provides no additional performance bene ﬁts" compared with text-based narratives, and that equal immersion scores suggest "a narrative is suf ﬁcient to engage students in immersive learning". For organizations with scarce resources, the authors recommend dedicating resources to other aspects of training success rather than to a potentially expensive game.
requirements: The training content and narrative must be identical or comparable across media for the text alternative to be considered equivalent
The narrative must be engaging, as narrative has been found to increase learning and engagement
constraints: The article's evidence covers two specific biases (the fundamental attribution error and confirmation bias) and a single detective-game context
The authors state more research is needed to understand what aspects of a learning environment provide the best context for bias-mitigation training
target_learners: Adult learners in professional bias-mitigation training, such as the student and recruited adult participants in this study
target_learning_goals: Reducing cognitive biases in judgment and decision making through critical-reflective thinking
examples: Participants read text scripts of the same murder-case narratives as the game group, and trained and untrained text groups performed equivalently to their game counterparts on in-context and out-context bias measures

citation: Wachs, S., Costello, M., Wright, M. F., Flora, K., Daskalou, V., Maziridou, E., Kwon, Y., Na, E.-Y., Sittichai, R., Biswal, R., Singh, R., Almendros, C., Gámez-Guadix, M., Görzig, A., & Hong, J. S. (2021). Computers and Education, 160, 104026. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2020.104026
title: Routine Activity Theory as a framework for cyberhate victimization
description: Routine Activity Theory (RAT) is an ecological criminological framework applied here to cyberhate victimization among adolescents. It holds that victimization risk rises at the confluence of three elements: a motivated offender, a suitable target, and lack of capable guardianship. In this study, exposure to motivated offenders is operationalized as witnessing cyberhate, capable guardianship as parental mediation of Internet use, and target suitability as online disclosure of private information. The article states that "RAT asserts that the likelihood of criminality increases at the confluence of a motivated offender, a suitable target, and a lack of capable guardianship."
requirements: All three RAT elements must be measurable in the online context: exposure to offenders (witnessing cyberhate), guardianship (parental mediation), and target suitability (online disclosure)
constraints: RAT was originally developed for physical-world victimization and must be modified for cyberspace, where offenders and victims converge in virtual rather than physical space
The article notes that RAT only considers target suitability (risk factors) but not 'unsuitability' (resilience factors)
target_learners: Adolescents aged 12-18 using the Internet and social media
target_learning_goals: Understanding online risk factors for cyberhate victimization
Developing safe online routines and disclosure habits
examples: The study operationalized RAT components as witnessing cyberhate, parental mediation (instructive and restrictive), and online disclosure, testing them in a structural equation model across eight countries

description: Kaligo is a digital workbook developed in the IntuiScript project that gives children realtime extrinsic feedback (knowledge of results) each time they write a letter, digit or word. Basic feedback covers "shape, direction, order of the strokes and continuity", shown as a colored horseshoe gauge with a star when production is sufficiently like the model. Its AI analyzes spatiotemporal handwriting features, adapts pedagogical scenarios automatically, and stores productions in a dashboard teachers use to program personalized exercises.

target_learners: kindergarten beginning writers (5–6 year olds) learning cursive writing
target_learning_goals: acquisition of legible, fluent cursive handwriting (letter shape, stroke order, direction, size)
examples: Nine kindergarten teachers used Kaligo's "I write in capitals" and "I write in cursive" modules for about 20 minutes per child per week over 12 weeks, supplementing with paper or whiteboard writing activities

article_title: Can tablet apps support the learning of handwriting? An investigation of learning outcomes in kindergarten classroom
citation: Nathalie Bonneton-Botté, Sylvain Fleury, Nathalie Girard, Maëlys Le Magadou, Anthony Cherbonnier, Mickaël Renault, Eric Anquetil, Eric Jamet. (2020). Can Tablet Apps Support the Learning of Handwriting? An Investigation of Learning Outcomes in Kindergarten Classroom. Computers and Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2020.103831
title: Deliver augmented handwriting feedback on completion of each trial so it does not interrupt the writing movement
description: In motor learning of handwriting, knowledge of results should be delivered at the end of a trial rather than the moment an error occurs, so that feedback does not break the child's writing gesture or encoding process. The Kaligo app operationalizes this: feedback "was systematically delivered on completion of each letter, so as not to interrupt the child's activity". The authors contrast this with a prior app that gave feedback as soon as an error was made, which they believed may have disrupted encoding, and with teachers' typically delayed feedback.
requirements: Automatic analysis of the written product (shape, direction, stroke order, continuity) so feedback can be computed and delivered immediately after each trial
constraints: The article states the medium-level benefit cannot be attributed to any single factor; real-time feedback is one candidate among several (one-to-one instruction, dynamic model, appeal of tablets)
target_learners: kindergarten beginning writers learning cursive handwriting
target_learning_goals: legibility and kinematic quality of cursive letter production, transferable to paper
examples: Kaligo displayed a colored horseshoe gauge with size feedback (pink rectangles) immediately after each completed letter or word

article_title: The effect of a computer-based cartooning tool on children’s cartoons and written stories
citation: M. Madden, P.W.H. Chung, C.W. Dawson. (2007). The Effect of a Computer-Based Cartooning Tool On Children's Cartoons and Written Stories. Loughborough University Institutional Repository. http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/2.5/
title: The kineikonic mode: filming and editing as the two defining characteristics of moving image texts
description: The article adopts Burn and Parker's account of the moving image as a mode defined by two characteristics: filming (framing and composing a scene into actual or notional camera shots) and editing (ordering shots so juxtapositions create meaning). It quotes the definition that the mode "operates as a combinatorial mode which assembles and integrates other modes (speech, image, gesture, music) through its own 'grammar' of filming and editing", and notes it extends to comic strips, storyboards and games, which grounds the design of the study's cartooning tools.
requirements: Interpreting an artefact as a moving image text requires identifiable shot framing and some form of shot sequencing or ordering
constraints: The article warns, citing Burn and Leach, of over-using language analogies since the moving image is not precisely a language
target_learners: primary school children in Years 5 and 6 (ages 9 to 11)
target_learning_goals: moving image literacy alongside print literacy
storytelling and narrative concepts such as characterisation, setting and pace
examples: The study operationalises filming as a camera point-of-view control with shot distances and editing as an explicit left-to-right sequence bar for ordering shots
key_sources: M. Madden, P.W.H. Chung, C.W. Dawson. (2007). The Effect of a Computer-Based Cartooning Tool On Children's Cartoons and Written Stories. Loughborough University Institutional Repository. http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/2.5/

article_title: The effect of a computer-based cartooning tool on children’s cartoons and written stories
citation: M. Madden, P.W.H. Chung, C.W. Dawson. (2007). The Effect of a Computer-Based Cartooning Tool On Children's Cartoons and Written Stories. Loughborough University Institutional Repository. http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/2.5/
title: Computer-based cartooning tool with posable characters, camera controls and visual storytelling prompts
description: The tool lets users build sequences of still shots from backgrounds, clipart and character artwork; characters can be "'posed' via one interaction mode which allows limbs in a skeleton to be dragged with the mouse, and 'warped' via another interaction mode which allows simple manipulation of vector control points". It provides camera point-of-view controls, a sequence bar with undo/redo and a full-screen slide show, and optional "visual storytelling prompts" offering ideas, character and camera help per story stage. No typing interface for captions is provided, deliberately emphasising purely visual communication.
requirements: Pre-supplied character artwork created by the investigator, since the character-creation framework was judged unsuitable for novice users
An ICT suite with shared computers, since storywriting was done on paper in class
constraints: The current version probably made depicting emotion harder than on paper
No side views of characters were provided, making some poses such as bowing difficult
The visual storytelling prompts were too low-key and rarely accessed
target_learning_goals: visual storytelling
preparation for storywriting
moving image literacy techniques
examples: Used in two sub-studies to prepare retellings of The Ramayana and The Visitor before written versions were collected

article_title: Utilizing virtual reality to assist social competence education and social support for children from under-represented backgrounds
citation: Xining Wang, Gareth W. Young, Adéla Plechatá, Conor Mc Guckin, Guido Makransky. (2023). Utilizing virtual reality to assist social competence education and social support for children from under-represented backgrounds. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104815
title: Floreo VR and Google Arts & Culture platforms used as the VR social competence education materials
description: The intervention combined two VR applications across eight sessions. Floreo VR "teaches children social, behavioral, communication, and life skills through a range of simulations concerning children's daily life scenarios", delivered via Cardboard VR with instructor guidance; the research team selected only inclusive-learning modules since some are designed for children with autism spectrum disorder. Sessions 5–8 used Google Arts & Culture with Meta Quest 2 and Tablet VR for 360-degree videos, virtual museum tours, and cooperative games.
requirements: Affordable VR gear (Cardboard VR, Meta Quest 2, Tablet VR) and an instructor who guides and interacts with the child while watching the same session on a tablet
constraints: Some Floreo VR modules are designed for children with autism spectrum disorder, so only relevant inclusive-learning modules were selected
target_learners: Rural elementary and middle school children aged 9–15 in Southwest China
target_learning_goals: Social competence: social skills, communication, and social knowledge in school and public settings
examples: Eight 25–45 min VR sessions with 3–5 lessons each; virtual scenarios in classroom, playground, canteen, and library settings
key_sources: Xining Wang, Gareth W. Young, Adéla Plechatá, Conor Mc Guckin, Guido Makransky. (2023). citation: Xining Wang, Gareth W. Young, Adéla Plechatá, Conor Mc Guckin, Guido Makransky. (2023). Utilizing virtual reality to assist social competence education and social support for children from under-represented backgrounds. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104815
title: Cognitive Affective Model of Immersive Learning (CAMIL) as the framework for VR-assisted social competence education
description: The article draws on immersive learning theories to explain why VR supports social competence education. CAMIL "highlights presence and agency as the fundamental affordances of using immersive technology in learning", facilitating learning through cognitive and affective factors such as interest, intrinsic motivation, and self-efficacy. The article also invokes the immersion principle of multimedia learning, under which people "learn better with VR than with standard media when immersive lessons are designed according to instructional design principles", and Experiential Learning Theory, situating VR exploration as active experimentation.
requirements: Immersive lessons designed according to instructional design principles and the affordances of the technology
target_learners: School-age learners in immersive VR learning environments
target_learning_goals: Social competence development through presence, agency, and embodiment in simulated social scenarios
examples: The Study 2 VR condition combined embodied avatar interaction, gesture practice, and instructor-guided social norms instruction
key_sources: Xining Wang, Gareth W. Young, Adéla Plechatá, Conor Mc Guckin, Guido Makransky. (2023). Utilizing virtual reality to assist social competence education and social support for children from under-represented backgrounds. article_title: Utilizing virtual reality to assist social competence education and social support for children from under-represented backgrounds
citation: Xining Wang, Gareth W. Young, Adéla Plechatá, Conor Mc Guckin, Guido Makransky. (2023). Utilizing virtual reality to assist social competence education and social support for children from under-represented backgrounds. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104815
title: Use affordable Cardboard VR solutions to bring immersive social competence education to under-resourced rural schools
description: The article recommends low-budget VR hardware as a route to social competence education in regions with limited resources. Cardboard VR is described as "a low-budget, easy assembly, and stereoscopic viewer that can be used with most smartphone devices", and the authors report that some children experienced discomfort despite the controller-free interaction. This made the intervention feasible in rural schools where field trips and advanced technology are unaffordable.
requirements: A smartphone and low-cost stereoscopic viewer; instructor-guided sessions
constraints: A few children reported discomfort with Cardboard VR; rural teachers may resist applying cutting-edge technology
target_learners: Rural children in underdeveloped countries and regions with limited educational resources
target_learning_goals: Social competence education and access to diverse educational experiences such as virtual museum visits
examples: The studies provided three device types (Cardboard VR, Meta Quest 2, Tablet VR) so children could experience different VR functions

article_title: Show and ‘tool’: How lecture recording transforms staff and student perspectives on lectures in higher education
citation: MacKay, J. R. D. (2018). Show and ‘Tool’: How lecture recording transforms staff and student perspectives on lectures in higher education. University of Edinburgh.
title: Recording a lecture transforms the act occurring in the teaching space, affecting proximate and ultimate concerns differently for staff and students
description: The constructivist grounded theory generated in this study holds that 'the act of recording a space was considered transformative, creating a digital artefact'. The analysis separated concerns into proximate issues occurring within the lecture space (lectures as tool versus stage show) and ultimate issues outside it (canonicity versus safety net). The theory is that 'recording a lecture transforms the act occurring within that teaching space into something else', disrupting both concern types differently for each group. Recordings act as digital objects that may commodify the teaching act.
requirements: Findings derive from constructivist grounded theory analysis with participant checking via mixed engagement committees; replication requires qualitative data from staff and students in the implementing institution
constraints: The author states the findings 'may not be entirely generalisable' and 'can only be applied in the context of this specific institute', and the student sample was first-year undergraduates only
target_learning_goals: understanding how lecture recording changes the lecture space and its use for learning
examples: The study analysed 13 staff interviews and 159 student free-text survey responses during a 2018 institute-wide lecture recording rollout at a Russell Group university
key_sources: MacKay, J. R. D. (2018). Show and ‘Tool’: How lecture recording transforms staff and student perspectives on lectures in higher education. University of Edinburgh. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.05.019

citation: Jara, I., Claro, M., Hinostroza, J. E., San Martin Gutiérrez, E., Rodríguez, P., Cabello, T., Ibieta, A., & Labbé, C. (2015). Understanding factors related to Chilean students' digital skills: A mixed methods analysis. Computers & Education, 88, 387-398. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2015.07.016
title: National standardized digital skills test for Chilean 10th-grade students
description: The study measured students' digital skills with a national standardized test administered to 10th-grade Chilean students. The abstract states the study aimed "to identify and characterize factors related to the digital skills of 10th grade Chilean students, as measured by a national standardized test." The test provided the quantitative outcome for the hierarchical linear model and the basis for selecting high- and low-performing students for the case study.
requirements: Administered as a national standardized test to 10th-grade students to yield comparable digital skills scores.
target_learning_goals: Digital literacy and digital skills
examples: Used as the outcome measure in the hierarchical linear model analysis of factors explaining student performance.

citation: Jara, I., Claro, M., Hinostroza, J. E., San Martin Gutiérrez, E., Rodríguez, P., Cabello, T., Ibieta, A., & Labbé, C. (2015). title: Exploratory case study protocol comparing high- and low-performing digital skills students
description: The qualitative component was an exploratory case study that took "a more in-depth look at the characteristics of high and low-performing students on the digital skills test" by "analyzing their activities, perceptions and motivations when using technology." It complemented the statistical analysis by characterizing how students at the extremes of the test-score distribution actually behave with technology.
requirements: Students selected as high and low performers on the national digital skills test; analysis of their technology activities, perceptions, and motivations.
target_learning_goals: Understanding behaviours and motivations linked to digital skill development
examples: The case study analyzed students' Internet use during school assignments, revealing concentration and strategy differences between high and low performers.

article_title: Learning analytics and the Universal Design for Learning (UDL): A clustering approach
citation: Marvin Roski, Ratan Sebastian, Ralph Ewerth, Anett Hoppe, Andreas Nehring. (2024). Learning analytics and the Universal Design for Learning (UDL): A clustering approach. Computers & Education 214 (2024) 105028. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105028
title: I3Learn web-based learning platform for inclusive ion-bonding chemistry
description: I3Learn is a WordPress-based web learning platform on ion bonding for 9th and 10th-grade inclusive chemistry teaching in Lower Saxony, Germany, designed for 180 minutes of remote, independent learning. Its development was guided by the UDL framework: learners can choose between texts and videos, work on tasks with or without help, and use self-assessments (star ratings), plus a customizable interface, read-aloud function, glossary, simple language, and device-independent access.
requirements: Internet-connected device; the platform is designed for independent learning from home
constraints: Only three UDL-guided elements (multiple representations, tasks with/without help, self-assessment) are measurable in the log files; other elements such as simple language cannot be differentiated in the logs
target_learners: 9th and 10th graders in integrated comprehensive schools and high schools in inclusive chemistry education
target_learning_goals: Understanding ion bonding, including minimum goals (brittleness, ion bonding, ratio formula) and extended goals (nomenclature, salts in everyday life)
examples: 384 learners used at least one of the analyzed UDL-guided elements; almost 500,000 log files were generated during the first half of 2022.
key_sources: Marvin Roski, Ratan Sebastian, Ralph Ewerth, Anett Hoppe, Andreas Nehring. (2024). Learning analytics and the Universal Design for Learning (UDL): A clustering approach. Computers & Education 214 (2024) 105028. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105028

article_title: Learning analytics and the Universal Design for Learning (UDL): A clustering approach
citation: Marvin Roski, Ratan Sebastian, Ralph Ewerth, Anett Hoppe, Andreas Nehring. (2024). Learning analytics and the Universal Design for Learning (UDL): A clustering approach. Computers & Education 214 (2024) 105028. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105028
title: Universal Design for Learning (UDL) framework
description: UDL is a framework developed by CAST that aims to shape learning environments to be accessible and challenging for all learners, focusing on changing the environment rather than the learners. Its guidelines are structured according to three principles: "Provide multiple means of engagement", "Provide multiple means of representation", and "Provide multiple means of action and expression", operationalized through nine guidelines and 31 checkpoints with optional concrete suggestions such as audio and visual information, customizable interfaces, or glossaries.
requirements: Intentional design of the learning environment to minimize barriers; UDL suggestions are optional and require implementation decisions by designers
constraints: Experts' perceptions and interpretations of the guidelines vary due to the complexity of UDL, and the article notes implementations often lack sufficient detail, complicating the evidence base
target_learners: All learners in inclusive settings, including learners with disabilities or impairments
target_learning_goals: Accessible, meaningful and challenging learning experiences for all students; cultivating autonomous, self-responsible learners
examples: The I3Learn platform implements UDL checkpoints 1 (options for perception), 8.2 (vary demands and resources), and 9.3 (self-assessment and reflection), among others.
key_sources: Marvin Roski, Ratan Sebastian, Ralph Ewerth, Anett Hoppe, Andreas Nehring. (2024). Learning analytics and the Universal Design for Learning (UDL): A clustering approach. Computers & Education 214 (2024) 105028. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105028

article_title: The nature, reception, and use of online peer feedback in higher education
citation: van der Pol, J, van den Berg, B A M, Admiraal, W F & Simons, P R J 2008, 'The nature, reception, and use of online peer feedback in higher education', Computers & Education, vol. 51, no. 4, pp. 1804-1817. https://dspace.library.uu.nl/handle/1874/29790
title: Three-variable model linking the nature, evaluation (reception), and consecutive use of peer feedback
description: The article organizes peer feedback research around a link among three variables: the nature of students' feedback, the way it is "evaluated by the receiver," and its "consecutive use for the revision of students' products." It treats successful uptake of feedback as "an important aspect" and investigates the link between these three variables "across different educational contexts and tools."
requirements: Educational settings in which students produce peer feedback, receive and evaluate it, and revise products based on it, so all three variables can be observed.
constraints: Investigated in higher education contexts and with the specific tools studied (Annotation system and Blackboard discussion forum); findings reported for these settings.
target_learning_goals: improving students' products through uptake and use of peer feedback for revision
examples: Two separate studies were conducted to investigate the link between feedback nature, receiver evaluation, and use for product revision across educational contexts and tools.
key_sources: van der Pol, J, van den Berg, B A M, Admiraal, W F & Simons, P R J 2008, 'The nature, reception, and use of online peer feedback in higher education', Computers & Education, vol. 51, no. 4, pp. 1804-1817. https://dspace.library.uu.nl/handle/1874/29790

article_title: The nature, reception, and use of online peer feedback in higher education
citation: van der Pol, J, van den Berg, B A M, Admiraal, W F & Simons, P R J 2008, 'The nature, reception, and use of online peer feedback in higher education', Computers & Education, vol. 51, no. 4, pp. 1804-1817. https://dspace.library.uu.nl/handle/1874/29790
title: Support peer feedback with tools and practices that elicit concrete suggestions, because concreteness predicts uptake
description: Because feedback containing concrete suggestions was significantly related to successful uptake, peer feedback activities should be arranged so that feedback givers produce concrete suggestions. The article's tool comparison shows concreteness depends on the medium: concrete suggestions were "more often produced in the Annotation system than in the Blackboard discussion forum," while the forum showed "more evaluative forms of feedback."
requirements: A peer feedback setting in which students give feedback that receivers evaluate and use to revise products; a tool or task structure that affords annotating or concrete commenting.
constraints: The tool difference was observed between the Annotation system and the Blackboard discussion forum in the studied higher-education contexts; the general principle rests on the studies' significant relationships.
target_learning_goals: producing and using peer feedback that leads to revision of student products
examples: Students used an Annotation system and a Blackboard discussion forum to exchange peer feedback; the annotation tool was associated with more concrete suggestions and the forum with more evaluative feedback forms.
