article_title: Efficacy of a map on search, orientation and access behaviour in a hypermedia system
citation: Stanton, N., Correia, A. P. and Dias, P. (1997). Efficacy of a map on search, orientation and access behaviour in a hypermedia system. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Efficacy+of+a+map+on+search+orientation+and+access+behaviour+in+a+hypermedia+system
title: Critique of the spatial metaphor in hypertext and hypermedia navigation
description: The article argues that hypertext disorientation was treated by importing navigation ideas from geographical space, but that "electronic environments present intrinsic characteristics that do not permit a linear transfer" of geographical-environment characteristics. Maps help in physical space yet "the use of maps in an electronic environment seem not provide the expected benefits". The article thus treats the spatial metaphor as an unexamined design assumption that led to navigational aids being added to poorly designed systems.
requirements: Designers should not assume that a map aiding orientation in spatial tasks will also aid hypermedia navigation
constraints: The article states navigation is most effective when information spaces are small enough to be covered exhaustively and familiar to users, so navigation is most effective when it is least needed
target_learners: secondary and higher-education students using hypermedia learning environments
target_learning_goals: searching for, orienting to and accessing task-relevant information in non-linear learning environments
examples: The empirical study found greater map use correlated with less relevant search, consistent with Stanton et al. (1992) where maps impaired search performance
key_sources: Stanton, N., Correia, A. P. and Dias, P. (1997). Efficacy of a map on search, orientation and access behaviour in a hypermedia system. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Efficacy+of+a+map+on+search+orientation+and+access+behaviour+in+a+hypermedia+system

article_title: Efficacy of a map on search, orientation and access behaviour in a hypermedia system
citation: Stanton, N., Correia, A. P. and Dias, P. (1997). Efficacy of a map on search, orientation and access behaviour in a hypermedia system. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Efficacy+of+a+map+on+search+orientation+and+access+behaviour+in+a+hypermedia+system
title: Design hypermedia for fundamental usability rather than adding map-based navigational aids
description: The article recommends that designers of non-linear learning environments address usability rather than navigation: designers "should be addressing the usability of their systems" instead of seeking more complex navigational information. It argues navigational aids are "a symptom of poor design" and that simplicity of interface plus tools supporting users' actions, such as bookmarks and simple forward, back and home buttons, may serve learners better than map-based navigation built on the spatial metaphor.
requirements: Hypermedia environments should provide users with appropriate cues at the decision points within the interaction
constraints: Navigational aids are characterized as symptoms of the current ills of hypertext rather than cures
target_learning_goals: efficient and purposeful access to task-relevant information in non-linear learning environments
examples: The study concluded that greater map use led to less relevant searching behaviour and less effective search effort, prompting the recommendation to focus on fundamental usability
key_sources: Stanton, N., Correia, A. P. and Dias, P. (1997). Efficacy of a map on search, orientation and access behaviour in a hypermedia system. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Efficacy+of+a+map+on+search+orientation+and+access+behaviour+in+a+hypermedia+system

article_title: Are emotional e-competencies a protective factor against habitual digital behaviors (media multitasking, cybergossip, phubbing) in Spanish students of secondary education?
citation: Ana Cebollero-Salinas, Jacobo Cano-Escoriaza, Santos Orejudo. (2022). Are socio-emotional e-competencies protective factors against habitual digital behaviors (media multitasking, phubbing, cybergossip) in Spanish secondary students?. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2022.104464
title: Socio-emotional e-competencies model: five sub-competencies specific to online interaction
description: The article adopts a model of "socio-emotional e-competencies", competencies developed specifically for online interaction rather than transferred from face-to-face contexts. It comprises five sub-competencies: emotional e-awareness ("the capacity to identify and understand one's own emotions in a virtual context"), emotional e-regulation, e-self-control of impulsiveness, emotional e-independence, and social e-competency. The model is grounded in the argument that virtual environments differ from face-to-face ones in pace, anonymity, and disinhibition, so online emotion perception and expression need differentiated evaluation. In this study the five sub-competencies, measured with the e-COM questionnaire (25 items, five subscales), serve as exogenous predictors of the habitual digital behaviors factor in a structural equation model.
requirements: Measurement requires the e-COM questionnaire or an equivalent instrument assessing the five sub-competencies in online settings
constraints: The article argues competencies evaluated outside the online environment cannot simply be treated as equivalent to online socio-emotional competencies, since virtual encounters occur under a different spatio-temporal set of circumstances
target_learning_goals: Socio-emotional competencies in digital interaction, including emotion regulation, impulse control, and independence from virtual reputation
examples: The e-COM questionnaire operationalises the model with 25 items on an 11-point Likert scale, e.g., 'Before making a joke about someone on social media, I am capable of imagining how they are going to feel' for emotional e-regulation
key_sources: Ana Cebollero-Salinas, Jacobo Cano-Escoriaza, Santos Orejudo. (2022). Are socio-emotional e-competencies protective factors against habitual digital behaviors (media multitasking, phubbing, cybergossip) in Spanish secondary students?. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2022.104464

article_title: Explicit video-based instruction enhanced students’ online credibility evaluation skills: Did storifying instruction matter?
citation: Kiili, C., Kiili, K., Räikkönen, E., & Coiro, J. (2025). Explicit Video-Based Instruction Enhanced Students' Online Credibility Evaluation Skills: Did Storifying Instruction Matter?. Computers and Education, 229, Article 105252. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2025.105252
title: Bidirectional model and CORE framework of online credibility evaluation strategies
description: The article organizes online credibility evaluation through two frameworks: the bidirectional model of first- and second-hand evaluation strategies, which "distinguishes content and source evaluation strategies", and the CORE framework, which "extends the bi-directional model by adding the strategy focusing on evaluation of context". Together they frame credibility evaluation as reciprocal and iterative use of content strategies (knowledge-based, discourse-based, corroboration), source strategies (expertise, benevolence), and context strategies. The study's instruction targeted content and source strategies—author's expertise, author's intentions, and quality of evidence—and its outcome task incorporated knowledge-based and contextual evaluation.
requirements: Instruction and assessment must operationalize the distinct evaluation strategies (content, source, context) so learners can practice them one at a time
constraints: The bidirectional model was developed for readers evaluating conflicting multiple scientific texts; the CORE framework situates evaluation within the internet environment
target_learning_goals: online credibility evaluation skills
justifying credibility evaluations
examples: The study's videos taught author's expertise, author's intentions, and quality of evidence strategies, and the evaluation task measured confirming, questioning, and justifying credibility
key_sources: Kiili, C., Kiili, K., Räikkönen, E., & Coiro, J. (2025). Explicit Video-Based Instruction Enhanced Students' Online Credibility Evaluation Skills: Did Storifying Instruction Matter?. Computers and Education, 229, Article 105252. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2025.105252

article_title: Psychological effects of gamified didactics with exergames in Physical Education at primary schools: Results from a natural experiment
citation: Quintas, A., Bustamante, J.-C., Pradas, F., & Castellar, C. (2020). Psychological effects of gamified didactics with exergames in Physical Education at primary schools: results from a natural experiment. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2020.103874
title: Mechanics-Dynamics-Aesthetics (MDA) framework adapted to educational gamification
description: The article uses the Mechanics-Dynamics-Aesthetics framework (Hunicke et al., 2004) as its organising gamification model, adapted to the education field. It defines mechanics as "the system's set of constituent elements, the relation linking between them, and the way in which a system can routinely function", dynamics as how the player-student interacts with the mechanics, and aesthetics as the perceptions and sensations-emotions experienced by students while playing. The authors chose MDA over the Points-Badges-Leaderboards system because PBL "only fits one player type: 'achievers'", whereas MDA was used "to achieve an inclusive gamified atmosphere for all student-player types".
requirements: Design must attend to dynamic and aesthetic spheres in class, and not only to gamification mechanics such as the PBL system, per the authors' discussion.
constraints: The authors argue the PBL gamification system only fits one player type (achievers), which motivated the use of MDA instead.
target_learners: Primary school students (Year 6 and Year 7) in Physical Education classes
target_learning_goals: Motivation, dispositional flow, basic psychological needs, rhythmic motor skill, and commitment to learning in PE
examples: Mechanics used in the study included a system of positive points, rewards, classifications, levels of difficulty, challenges, achievements, badges, cooperative and competitive teams, virtual avatars, and avatar personalisation; aesthetics drew on the Just Dance Now exergame and the ClassDojo application.
key_sources: Quintas, A., Bustamante, J.-C., Pradas, F., & Castellar, C. (2020). Psychological effects of gamified didactics with exergames in Physical Education at primary schools: results from a natural experiment. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2020.103874

article_title: Improving children's written grammar and style: revising and editing with HARRY
citation: C.E. Holdich, P.W.H. Chung and R.G. Holdich. (2004). Improving children's written grammar and style: revising and editing with HARRY. Computers & Education, Vol 42, pp1-23. https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/2.5/
title: HARRY: a three-stage computer tutor for children's narrative writing
description: HARRY is a web-based computer tutor that helps children improve narrative writing in grammar and style. "HARRY separates the writing process into three stages": stage one prompts revision during composition via a flexible story strategy table and help pop-up boxes (ideas, sentence help, word help, check); stage two detects grammar and style weaknesses and suggests edits; stage three handles spelling and technical errors in MS Word. Prompts are stored in Access databases and randomly presented so each child receives a different set.
requirements: Story themes and prompt databases (four themes; each category contains 4-15 guiding prompts plus associated help prompts)
A Windows NT web server with ASP scripts and Microsoft Access databases; children access it via a standard web browser
constraints: A cookie-based session tracker means the child must use the same computer to continue a story
target_learners: 8/9-year-old primary school children of mixed ability
target_learning_goals: Narrative writing grammar and style
Revision and editing skills
Vocabulary variety and sophistication
Sentence construction variety
examples: In the evaluation, each of four case-study children wrote a control story and a HARRY-assisted story on the same theme over five weeks
key_sources: C.E. Holdich, P.W.H. Chung and R.G. Holdich. (2004). Improving children's written grammar and style: revising and editing with HARRY. Computers & Education, Vol 42, pp1-23. https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/2.5/

article_title: Improving children's written grammar and style: revising and editing with HARRY
citation: C.E. Holdich, P.W.H. Chung and R.G. Holdich. (2004). Improving children's written grammar and style: revising and editing with HARRY. Computers & Education, Vol 42, pp1-23. https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/2.5/
title: CHECK TEXT: a utility tool quantifying twelve aspects of children's written grammar and style
description: CHECK TEXT is a utility tool that "calculates and interprets quantitative data" on children's stories. A previous study demonstrated that it "distinguishes strengths and weaknesses in 12 aspects of children's written grammar and style", covering story length, punctuation (full stops and commas), sentence construction (basic connectives, simple sentence starters, sentence length) and vocabulary (variety and sophistication). Scores are mapped onto three assessment categories - poor, fair and good - using boundaries set from an earlier sample of stories.
requirements: Assessment boundaries calibrated against the original sample stories from Holdich, Holdich and Chung (2002), since the significance of scores is not obvious without that reference
constraints: Story length is capped in practice by lesson time in the evaluation; the article reports thresholds (e.g. basic connectives above 0.8% of total words) as empirically determined for HARRY's detection rather than for CHECK TEXT
target_learners: Primary school children (8-11 years) writing narratives
target_learning_goals: Quantitative assessment of written grammar and style features
examples: CHECK TEXT scored each control story and each of the three stages of the HARRY-assisted stories in the four case studies
key_sources: C.E. Holdich, P.W.H. Chung and R.G. Holdich. (2004). Improving children's written grammar and style: revising and editing with HARRY. Computers & Education, Vol 42, pp1-23. https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/2.5/

article_title: Improving children's written grammar and style: revising and editing with HARRY
citation: C.E. Holdich, P.W.H. Chung and R.G. Holdich. (2004). Improving children's written grammar and style: revising and editing with HARRY. Computers & Education, Vol 42, pp1-23. https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/2.5/
title: Revision-support systems for children must explain how to make improvements, not just identify weaknesses
description: Drawing on earlier systems, the article argues that flagging weaknesses is insufficient for young writers: "The main limitation of both CATCH and StoryStation was that although the systems encouraged revision and identified weaknesses, neither system made it clear to children how to make improvements." HARRY therefore pairs detection of weaknesses with conversational prompts suggesting concrete improvement techniques, implementing teaching activities such as synonym substitution and sentence combining. This principle shapes the design of editing feedback in children's writing tools.
requirements: Prompts must be explicit about how to make effective changes and highlight significant features whose correction yields improvements
constraints: The article's supporting evidence for this principle comes from reported failures of two prior systems (CATCH largely unsuccessful; StoryStation pupils confused by mixed positive/negative feedback)
target_learners: Children and young adolescent writers learning to revise and edit
target_learning_goals: Effective revision strategies such as debating word choice and varying sentence constructions
examples: CATCH's prompts, such as 'the highlighted words may not be necessary. Do you want to make changes?', did not produce improvements; HARRY instead suggests e.g. replacement synonyms for the word [nice]
key_sources: C.E. Holdich, P.W.H. Chung and R.G. Holdich. (2004). Improving children's written grammar and style: revising and editing with HARRY. Computers & Education, Vol 42, pp1-23. https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/2.5/

article_title: Media multitasking, online vigilance and academic performance among students in three Southern African countries
citation: le Roux, D.B., Parry, D.A., Totolo, A., Iyawa, G., Holloway, J., Prenter, A., Botha, L. (2021). Media Multitasking, Online Vigilance and Academic Performance among Students in three Southern African Countries. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2020.104056
title: Online vigilance as a construct of psychological connectedness to online content
description: Online vigilance, as proposed by Reinecke et al. (2018) and adopted by this article, "describes individual diﬀerences in users’ cognitive orientation to online connectedness, their attention to and integration of online-related cues and stimuli, and their prioritisation of online communication". It is measured with the Online Vigilance Scale, comprising salience, monitoring and reactivity subscales. Its key property is distinguishing technological from psychological connectedness: some users develop higher vigilance despite comparable media use. The article tests it as a predictor of academic performance alongside media use behaviours.
requirements: Assessed with the 12-item Online Vigilance Scale (salience, monitoring, reactivity subscales), responses averaged across items
constraints: The article distinguishes online vigilance from Internet or technology addiction, describing it as involvement that does not necessarily impair functioning or mental health
No prior studies had investigated its relationship with academic performance before this study
target_learners: University undergraduate students in South Africa, Botswana and Namibia
target_learning_goals: Understanding how students' psychological orientation to online connectedness relates to academic performance
examples: The survey administered the Online Vigilance Scale to 1445 undergraduates and regressed academic performance on it together with media use variables
key_sources: le Roux, D.B., Parry, D.A., Totolo, A., Iyawa, G., Holloway, J., Prenter, A., Botha, L. (2021). Media Multitasking, Online Vigilance and Academic Performance among Students in three Southern African Countries. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2020.104056

article_title: Virtual vs. traditional learning in higher education: A systematic review of comparative studies
citation: Santilli T.; Ceccacci S.; Mengoni M.; Giaconi C. (2025). Virtual vs. traditional learning in higher education: A systematic review of comparative studies. COMPUTERS & EDUCATION. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105214
title: Multidimensional framework for analysing comparative VR-vs-traditional studies in higher education
description: The review proposes an organizing framework for systematically analysing studies that compare VR-based and traditional teaching in higher education. It states: "The analysis focuses on a set of dimensions including the adopted research design, participants' characteristics, disciplinary field of application, VR technological features (i.e., immersivity, interactivity, operability, commercial availability, and presence of VR training), adopted teaching methodologies, assessed VR impact on learning outcomes and presence of studies involving students with disabilities or Specific Learning Disorders (SpLDs)." The framework structures the review's coding of 71 studies and offers a multidimensional perspective for educators, researchers and policymakers.
requirements: Systematic identification of comparative VR-vs-traditional studies in higher education contexts to which the dimension set can be applied
constraints: The framework is stated for comparative studies in higher education contexts, not for other levels of education or non-comparative VR studies
target_learning_goals: Evaluating the effectiveness of VR-based teaching on learning outcomes
examples: The framework was applied to code a corpus of 71 VR-in-higher-education studies across research design, participants, discipline, technology features, methodology and outcomes
key_sources: Santilli T.; Ceccacci S.; Mengoni M.; Giaconi C. (2025). Virtual vs. traditional learning in higher education: A systematic review of comparative studies. COMPUTERS & EDUCATION. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105214

article_title: Refining qualitative ethnographies using Epistemic Network Analysis: A study of socioemotional learning dimensions in a Humanistic Knowledge Building Community
citation: Hod, Yotam; Eagan, Brendan; Katz, Shir. (2020). Refining qualitative ethnographies using Epistemic Network Analysis: A study of socioemotional learning dimensions in a humanistic knowledge building community. Journal article. https://zenodo.org
title: Epistemic Network Analysis as a methodology for producing quantitative ethnographies of complex learning environments
description: Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA) is described as "a methodology for producing quantitative ethnographies based on complex learning environments." The study uses ENA to analyze data collected during a semester of studies in a classroom learning community, applying it to socioemotional facets of learning, which the article notes ENA "has only begun to examine." ENA is positioned as complementary to deep, qualitative ethnography rather than a replacement for it.
requirements: Data collected from a complex learning environment over time, as in the semester of studies analyzed here
constraints: The article states ENA has only begun to examine socioemotional facets of learning in classrooms
target_learning_goals: socioemotional dimensions of learning
sociocognitive development in knowledge building communities
examples: The authors employed ENA to analyze a semester of data from a humanistic knowledge building community, in parallel with a stage developmental qualitative analysis.
key_sources: Hod, Yotam; Eagan, Brendan; Katz, Shir. (2020). Refining qualitative ethnographies using Epistemic Network Analysis: A study of socioemotional learning dimensions in a humanistic knowledge building community. Journal article. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2020.103943

article_title: Refining qualitative ethnographies using Epistemic Network Analysis: A study of socioemotional learning dimensions in a Humanistic Knowledge Building Community
citation: Hod, Yotam; Eagan, Brendan; Katz, Shir. (2020). Refining qualitative ethnographies using Epistemic Network Analysis: A study of socioemotional learning dimensions in a humanistic knowledge building community. Journal article. https://zenodo.org
title: Humanistic knowledge building community studied over one semester with parallel ENA and qualitative analyses
description: The study's empirical site is a classroom learning community studied during "a semester of studies," characterized as a humanistic knowledge building community. Data collected there were analyzed twice: with Epistemic Network Analysis and with a stage developmental analysis using qualitative methods. The case serves to investigate what and how ENA can contribute to socioemotionally-focused ethnographies of classroom learning communities.
requirements: Data collected across a semester of studies in the community
constraints: Findings pertain to a single humanistic knowledge building community
target_learning_goals: socioemotional dimensions of learning
community connectedness and stage advancement
examples: The researchers analyzed the same semester of community data with ENA and with qualitative stage developmental methods.
key_sources: Hod, Yotam; Eagan, Brendan; Katz, Shir. (2020). Refining qualitative ethnographies using Epistemic Network Analysis: A study of socioemotional learning dimensions in a humanistic knowledge building community. Journal article. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2020.103943

article_title: An e-health platform for the elderly population: The butler system
citation: Etchemendy, E.; Baños, RM.; Botella, C.; Castilla López, DV.; Alcañiz Raya, ML.; Rasal, P.; Farfallini, L. (2011). An e-health platform for the elderly population: The butler system. Computers and Education. 56(1):275-279. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2010.07.022
title: Butler system: an e-health platform for the elderly population with diagnostic, therapeutic and playful applications
description: The Butler system is an interactive e-health platform designed to improve the elderly population's quality of life. It "has three applications diagnostic, therapeutic and playful", and users select which technological resources to use in each session. The article uses the platform in four sessions with elderly users to assess mood-state change and acceptance. Its purpose as stated is an e-health platform "designed to improve the elderly population's quality of life".
requirements: Users interact with the platform across multiple sessions (four in the reported study) and can choose which technological resources they use in each session.
constraints: The reported evaluation concerns elderly users (58 to 79 years old) using the platform for mood-state and acceptance outcomes.
target_learning_goals: improving emotional state and quality of life
examples: Seventeen users aged 58 to 79 completed four sessions with the system, choosing which technological resources they used in each session, with mood and acceptance measured before and after use.
key_sources: Etchemendy, E.; Baños, RM.; Botella, C.; Castilla López, DV.; Alcañiz Raya, ML.; Rasal, P.; Farfallini, L. (2011). An e-health platform for the elderly population: The butler system. Computers and Education. 56(1):275-279. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2010.07.022

article_title: Relationships between critical thinking dispositions and evaluation of videos with variation in the level of expertise of the source among middle and high school students
citation: Brivael Hémon, Kevin de Checchi, Amaël Arguel, Bastien Trémolière, & Franck Amadieu. (2025). Relationships Between Critical Thinking Dispositions and Evaluation of Videos with Variation in the Level of Expertise of the Source Among Middle and High School Students. Computers and Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2025.105274
title: Four fictitious interview videos and adapted French critical thinking disposition scales for adolescents
description: The study material comprises four 45–55-second fictitious interview videos on meat consumption reduction, in which the interviewee's position and expertise (expert vs layperson) varied, with expertise signaled by a banner and interview location. Students rated source and information trustworthiness on nine-point scales, then completed adapted French questionnaires measuring self-efficacy, epistemic justification, intellectual humility, and reasoning style. As the authors note, "The four videos had been produced for an earlier research project on students' evaluation of conflicting videos".
requirements: Item comprehension was checked with a pretest among 11-12 year-old students (N = 14) and teacher review, since scales were translated and adapted for a young audience.
constraints: The authors state their work "does not allow us to claim French validations of the questionnaires and their adaptation to another population"; the video material was purpose-built for research and may be at odds with videos adolescents actually encounter online.
target_learning_goals: Critical evaluation of sources and information in online videos
examples: In the 2x2 within-group design, experts were interviewed in an office and laypersons while shopping in a supermarket, and students evaluated source, information quality, and whether they would use the video for a class presentation after each video.
key_sources: Brivael Hémon, Kevin de Checchi, Amaël Arguel, Bastien Trémolière, & Franck Amadieu. (2025). Relationships Between Critical Thinking Dispositions and Evaluation of Videos with Variation in the Level of Expertise of the Source Among Middle and High School Students. Computers and Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2025.105274

article_title: Lessons learned from the design of situated learning environments to support collaborative knowledge construction
citation: Pérez-Sanagustín, M., Muñoz-Merino, P. J., Alario-Hoyos, C., Soldani, X., & Delgado Kloos, C. (2015). Lessons Learned from the Design of Situated Learning Environments to Support Collaborative Knowledge Construction. Computers & Education, 87, 70-82. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2015.03.019
title: Bidirectional SLE built on etiquetAR bidirectional QR codes
description: An indoor situated learning environment in which each industrial machine carries a "bidirectional" QR code generated with etiquetAR, an authoring tool whose tags "provide information (as do tradition al QR codes )" but "also collect user -generated content". Each code links to a machine video, an image of main components, and a question; answers left by teams become visible to anyone scanning later, opening a cross-team collaboration channel. Students answer via their own smartphones or teacher-provided tablets, then peer-evaluate classmates' answers.
requirements: Mobile devices (students' smartphones or teacher-provided tablets) with QR readers
A reliable technological setting with adequate Internet connectivity for loading videos
constraints: Teachers reported the SLE "is not  designed to operate in settings with slow or limited Internet connectivity"
Answers are removed after each session, so teams see only answers from their own laboratory session
target_learners: post-secondary mechanical engineering students in laboratory sessions
target_learning_goals: knowledge of machine pieces, functionality and usage
collaborative knowledge construction and reflection on peer answers
examples: In the lab session, a bidirectional QR code was attached to each of five machines (Hydraulic Press, Punch Press, Numerical Control Lathe, Machining Center, Vertical Drilling Machine)
key_sources: Pérez-Sanagustín, M., Muñoz-Merino, P. J., Alario-Hoyos, C., Soldani, X., & Delgado Kloos, C. (2015). Lessons Learned from the Design of Situated Learning Environments to Support Collaborative Knowledge Construction. Computers & Education, 87, 70-82. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2015.03.019

article_title: Lessons learned from the design of situated learning environments to support collaborative knowledge construction
citation: Pérez-Sanagustín, M., Muñoz-Merino, P. J., Alario-Hoyos, C., Soldani, X., & Delgado Kloos, C. (2015). Lessons Learned from the Design of Situated Learning Environments to Support Collaborative Knowledge Construction. Computers & Education, 87, 70-82. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2015.03.019
title: Herrington and Oliver's nine-element framework for situated learning environments
description: The article adopts, as its organizing framework, the nine SLE characteristics that "Herrington and Oliver (2000) proposed": "a framework made up of nine elements to define the characteristics SLEs should include to support SL". The elements cover authentic context, authentic activities, expert performances, multiple roles and perspectives, collaborative construction of knowledge, reflection, articulation, coaching and scaffolding at critical times, and integrated assessment. The paper's Table 1 maps how each element is instantiated in the technological and educational dimensions of the Bidirectional SLE.
requirements: An SLE design should address all nine characteristics, with collaborative knowledge construction given particular attention
constraints: The article reports that most existing mobile-SLE implementations, especially GPS-based outdoor ones, lack collaborative knowledge construction support and have not implemented all nine characteristics indoors
target_learners: learners in authentic physical settings such as labs, museums and libraries
target_learning_goals: situated knowledge construction
reflection and articulation of tacit knowledge
examples: Table 1 instantiates each of the nine elements in the Bidirectional SLE, e.g. authentic context via tags expanding the physical lab, and integrated assessment via teachers' real-time access to team answers through the etiquetAR web interface
key_sources: Pérez-Sanagustín, M., Muñoz-Merino, P. J., Alario-Hoyos, C., Soldani, X., & Delgado Kloos, C. (2015). Lessons Learned from the Design of Situated Learning Environments to Support Collaborative Knowledge Construction. Computers & Education, 87, 70-82. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2015.03.019

article_title: Lessons learned from the design of situated learning environments to support collaborative knowledge construction
citation: Pérez-Sanagustín, M., Muñoz-Merino, P. J., Alario-Hoyos, C., Soldani, X., & Delgado Kloos, C. (2015). Lessons Learned from the Design of Situated Learning Environments to Support Collaborative Knowledge Construction. Computers & Education, 87, 70-82. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2015.03.019
title: Design indoor SLEs for collaborative knowledge construction using bidirectional tags and open questions
description: From the cross-analysis of quantitative results and teacher opinions, the article derives lessons for designing SLEs that support collaborative knowledge construction indoors. Its core recommendation is that "providing a technological setting based on  bidirectional tags and learning activities based on open questions is recommendable for teachers" who want such SLEs, because open questions better support the exchange of different perspectives and bidirectional tags enable cross-team collaboration and awareness of the collaborative process.
requirements: Reliable technology that does not interfere with the learning process
Open (higher-order) questions rather than closed ones
A script to organize teamwork at each machine
Activities that explicitly push students to reflect on and evaluate classmates' answers
constraints: Teachers observed that "Sometimes students accept erroneous answers from others; they do not reflect on others' answers  enough", so the collaboration channel alone is insufficient for reflection
Slow or limited Internet connectivity hampers the design
target_learners: post-secondary students in lab sessions and similar indoor authentic settings
target_learning_goals: collaborative knowledge construction
higher-order thinking such as analysis and evaluation
examples: The article's lesson (4) grounds the recommendation in the validation of H1, H2 and H3; lesson (6) calls for exercises that inspire students to better evaluate peer answers; lesson (9) recommends technology allowing teachers to monitor activity and assess in real time
key_sources: Pérez-Sanagustín, M., Muñoz-Merino, P. J., Alario-Hoyos, C., Soldani, X., & Delgado Kloos, C. (2015). Lessons Learned from the Design of Situated Learning Environments to Support Collaborative Knowledge Construction. Computers & Education, 87, 70-82. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2015.03.019

article_title: The longitudinal association between engagement and achievement varies by time, students’ profiles, and achievement state: A full program study
citation: Mohammed Saqr, Sonsoles López-Pernas, Satu Helske, Stefan Hrastinski. (2023). The longitudinal association between engagement and achievement varies by time, students' profiles, and achievement state: A full program study. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104787
title: Multi-channel sequence analysis with mixture hidden Markov models for longitudinal engagement-achievement trajectories
description: The article offers a detailed methodology for studying how engagement and achievement evolve together across a full program: two chronologically ordered state sequences (engagement and achievement channels) are aligned per course, and a Mixture Hidden Markov Model — "a combination of LCA and HMM" — clusters multichannel trajectories jointly while estimating transition probabilities between hidden states. The method models "several variables evolving in parallel" and reveals for whom and when engagement-achievement relations change across a program.
requirements: Multi-channel longitudinal data with chronologically ordered, synchronized state sequences per channel (e.g., LMS indicators per course plus course grades)
Model selection and estimation repeated with many random starting values; the article estimated MHMMs with varying hidden states and clusters, repeated 1000 times, selecting by BIC
constraints: Online trace data can only capture behavioral and cognitive engagement; the article does not explicitly operationalize emotional engagement
The article's framing model treats contextual factors as time-invariant and therefore excludes them from the longitudinal model
target_learners: higher education students in online/blended programs
target_learning_goals: understanding longitudinal student engagement and achievement trajectories for monitoring and support
examples: The method was applied to 106 students over 15 courses of a problem-based learning healthcare program, yielding three trajectory clusters: Engaged high-achieving starters, Average starters, and Disengaged starters
key_sources: Mohammed Saqr, Sonsoles López-Pernas, Satu Helske, Stefan Hrastinski. (2023). The longitudinal association between engagement and achievement varies by time, students' profiles, and achievement state: A full program study. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104787

article_title: Split-attention and redundancy effects on mobile learning in physical environments
citation: Liu, T.-C., Lin, Y.-C., Tsai, M.-J., & Paas, F. (2011). Split-attention and redundancy effects on mobile learning in physical environments. Computers & Education. https://ro.uow.edu.au/edupapers/784
title: Cognitive load theory applied to mobile learning: split-attention and redundancy effects from combining texts, pictures, and real objects
description: The article extends cognitive load theory to mobile learning in rich physical environments, where at least three visual media co-occur: texts, pictures on the mobile device, and real objects outside it. It argues that "Split-attention effects may result from the difficult integration of physically separated media" and that "Redundancy effects may result from the similarity of the pictures and objects, which may force students to process the same information more than once." Because all media are visual, both effects compete for the same visual/pictorial channel capacity.
requirements: Learning must occur in a rich physical environment with multiple visual media whose combination can be varied (texts and/or pictures on a mobile device, plus real objects).
constraints: The study's test of these effects applies to the specific media configurations used (texts, pictures, real objects) with primary-school children learning leaf morphology; the authors note other media configurations "need to be investigated before reliable conclusions can be drawn".
target_learners: Elementary school students (fifth grade, about 11 years old)
target_learning_goals: Science content knowledge, specifically plant leaf morphology (venation, margin, phyllotaxy)
examples: The study operationalized the theory with three material versions: TP (text and picture on the tablet), TO (text on tablet plus real plants), and TPO (text, picture, and real plants).
key_sources: Liu, T.-C., Lin, Y.-C., Tsai, M.-J., & Paas, F. (2011). Split-attention and redundancy effects on mobile learning in physical environments. Computers & Education. https://ro.uow.edu.au/edupapers/784

article_title: Split-attention and redundancy effects on mobile learning in physical environments
citation: Liu, T.-C., Lin, Y.-C., Tsai, M.-J., & Paas, F. (2011). Split-attention and redundancy effects on mobile learning in physical environments. Computers & Education. https://ro.uow.edu.au/edupapers/784
title: Provide complementary rather than similar information when combining media in mobile learning environments
description: When designing mobile learning in rich physical environments, media combined with necessary real objects should convey different, complementary information rather than similar information. The article states that "providing students with complementary learning information is the recommended method to avoid this effect," because redundant media oblige students "to invest extra effort to process similar information from different media," harming comprehension and efficiency.
requirements: Mobile learning settings where objects and texts are necessary media, so additional on-device media must be selected deliberately.
constraints: The authors caution the results "can only be subscribed to the specific configuration of different media" and that many media configurations in mobile learning still need investigation before reliable guidelines can be formulated.
target_learners: Primary school children using mobile devices in physical learning environments
target_learning_goals: Comprehension of observable object characteristics (e.g., plant morphology) and efficient acquisition of that knowledge
examples: In the experiment, the TPO condition combined pictures on the device with highly similar real plants and produced the lowest comprehension (7.22) and efficiency (1.44), illustrating the redundancy the principle avoids.
key_sources: Liu, T.-C., Lin, Y.-C., Tsai, M.-J., & Paas, F. (2011). Split-attention and redundancy effects on mobile learning in physical environments. Computers & Education. https://ro.uow.edu.au/edupapers/784

article_title: Learning in serious virtual worlds: Evaluation of learning effectiveness and appeal to students in the E-Junior project
citation: Wrzesien, M., & Alcañiz Raya, M. (2010). Learning in serious virtual worlds: Evaluation of learning effectiveness and appeal to students in the E-Junior project. In Computers & Education (Vol. 55, Issue 1, pp. 178–187). Elsevier BV. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2010.01.003
title: E-Junior: a serious virtual world for teaching children natural science and ecology about the Mediterranean Sea
description: E-Junior is a serious virtual world (SVW) designed "according to pedagogical theories and curricular objectives to help children learn about the Mediterranean Sea and its environmental issues while playing." It targets elementary education and combines a gaming aspect with curricular content. In its evaluation, a class taught in the SVW was compared with a traditional class with identical learning objectives and contents.
requirements: Designed according to pedagogical theories and aligned with curricular objectives
target_learning_goals: Natural science and ecology knowledge about the Mediterranean Sea and its environmental issues
examples: Evaluated with 48 children by comparing a virtual group taught in the SVW with a traditional group covering identical content without a gaming aspect
key_sources: Wrzesien, M., & Alcañiz Raya, M. (2010). Learning in serious virtual worlds: Evaluation of learning effectiveness and appeal to students in the E-Junior project. In Computers & Education (Vol. 55, Issue 1, pp. 178–187). Elsevier BV. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2010.01.003

article_title: Learning in serious virtual worlds: Evaluation of learning effectiveness and appeal to students in the E-Junior project
citation: Wrzesien, M., & Alcañiz Raya, M. (2010). Learning in serious virtual worlds: Evaluation of learning effectiveness and appeal to students in the E-Junior project. In Computers & Education (Vol. 55, Issue 1, pp. 178–187). Elsevier BV. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2010.01.003
title: Serious virtual worlds as a class format matched to traditional classes with identical learning objectives and contents
description: The study's evaluation pattern holds content constant while varying the class format: a virtual group learned in a serious virtual world while a traditional group received "a traditional type of class that contained identical learning objectives and contents but lacked a gaming aspect." This design isolates the gaming/virtual-world aspect as the difference between conditions. It was applied to elementary natural science and ecology content about the Mediterranean Sea.
requirements: The two class formats must contain identical learning objectives and contents
target_learning_goals: Natural science and ecology content
examples: E-Junior evaluation: 48 children assigned to a serious-virtual-world class versus a traditional class with the same objectives and content
key_sources: Wrzesien, M., & Alcañiz Raya, M. (2010). Learning in serious virtual worlds: Evaluation of learning effectiveness and appeal to students in the E-Junior project. In Computers & Education (Vol. 55, Issue 1, pp. 178–187). Elsevier BV. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2010.01.003

article_title: What seams do we remove in mobile-assisted seamless learning? A critical review of the literature
citation: Lung-Hsiang Wong, Chee Kit Looi. (2011). What seams do we remove in mobile assisted seamless learning? A critical review of the literature. Computers and Education. https://hal.science/hal-00696239
title: Seamless learning as integration of experiences across formal/informal, individual/social, and physical/cyberspace dimensions
description: The article defines seamless learning as the integration of learning experiences across several dimensions. It states that "Seamless learning refers to the seamless integration of the learning experiences across various dimensions including formal and informal learning contexts, individual and social learning, and physical world and cyberspace." The construct frames the review of mobile-assisted seamless learning and serves as the organizing idea for identifying the seams that MSL designs aim to remove.
requirements: A design must address integration across at least some of the stated dimensions (formal/informal contexts, individual/social learning, physical world/cyberspace) to count as seamless learning
target_learners: learners in settings using one or more mobile device per learner
target_learning_goals: connecting formal and informal learning experiences
integrating individual and social learning
bridging physical-world and cyberspace learning
examples: The review uses this definition to investigate "the meaning of seamless learning and the potential ways to put it in practice" through academic papers on MSL
key_sources: Lung-Hsiang Wong, Chee Kit Looi. (2011). What seams do we remove in mobile assisted seamless learning? A critical review of the literature. Computers and Education. https://hal.science/hal-00696239

article_title: What seams do we remove in mobile-assisted seamless learning? A critical review of the literature
citation: Lung-Hsiang Wong, Chee Kit Looi. (2011). What seams do we remove in mobile assisted seamless learning? A critical review of the literature. Computers and Education. https://hal.science/hal-00696239
title: Ten-dimension framework characterizing mobile-assisted seamless learning
description: The review proposes a framework of ten dimensions that characterize MSL, derived from a review of recent academic papers on mobile-assisted seamless learning. The authors state, "Through a thorough review of recent academic papers on mobile-assisted seamless learning (MSL), we identify ten dimensions that characterize MSL." They argue the framework "allows us to identify research gaps in the stated area," positioning the dimensions as an analytic lens over MSL research and designs.
requirements: The dimensions are meant to be used together to map the dimensional space of an MSL design problem
constraints: The framework was derived from a review of recent academic papers on MSL and is presented as identifying research gaps rather than as a tested instructional design
target_learners: researchers and designers of mobile-assisted seamless learning environments
target_learning_goals: characterizing and situating MSL designs across dimensions
identifying research gaps in mobile-assisted seamless learning
examples: The authors apply the ten-dimension analysis to reviewed MSL systems so practitioners can locate related designs and their research-based evidence
key_sources: Lung-Hsiang Wong, Chee Kit Looi. (2011). What seams do we remove in mobile assisted seamless learning? A critical review of the literature. Computers and Education. https://hal.science/hal-00696239

article_title: What seams do we remove in mobile-assisted seamless learning? A critical review of the literature
citation: Lung-Hsiang Wong, Chee Kit Looi. (2011). What seams do we remove in mobile assisted seamless learning? A critical review of the literature. Computers and Education. https://hal.science/hal-00696239
title: One-or-more-mobile-device-per-learner setting supporting seamless learning
description: The article situates its work relative to a proposed seamless learning model supported by equipping each learner with one or more mobile device. It states it is "Inspired by the exposition by Chan, Roschelle, Hsi, Kinshuk, Sharples, Brown, et al. (2006) on the seamless learning model supported by the setting of one or more mobile device per learner." This per-learner device setting is the technological basis the review takes as the context for mobile-assisted seamless learning practice.
requirements: One or more mobile devices per learner to support the seamless learning model
constraints: The article presents this setting as an inspiration from prior work (Chan et al., 2006), not as its own empirical finding
target_learners: learners equipped with one or more mobile devices each
target_learning_goals: supporting seamless integration of learning experiences across contexts
examples: The review investigates how to put seamless learning into practice under this per-learner mobile device setting

article_title: EmoFindAR: Evaluation of a mobile multiplayer augmented reality game for primary school children
citation: López-Faican, L.; Jaén Martínez, FJ. (2020). EmoFindAR: Evaluation of a mobile multiplayer augmented reality game for primary school children. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2020.103814
title: EmoFindAR: a markerless multiplayer mobile augmented reality game for practicing emotion recognition and social skills
description: EmoFindAR is a multiplayer MAR game in which pairs of primary school children find 3D characters in a scanned physical space that display emotions such as "anger, sadness or joy", and throw objects to move the characters toward a desired emotional state. It runs on iOS smartphones using Unity, Photon Unity Networking and the Placenote AR SDK, needing no fiducial markers. The game supports both competitive and collaborative capture mechanics and was evaluated for usability, communication and motivation in a primary school study.
requirements: A pre-scanned physical location, which the authors note is an essential Placenote requirement done before the sessions
Networked multiplayer infrastructure synchronizing 3D positions and character emotional states in real time across all players' devices
constraints: The evaluation used a limited physical space and sessions of an estimated 15 minutes per pair
A single game level with no higher complexity levels for more skilled children
target_learning_goals: recognition of basic emotions and actions based on perception, assimilation, understanding and regulation of emotions
communication, coordination and collaboration skills
examples: In the evaluation, 38 fifth-grade children in 19 pairs played both modes in random order and answered Likert questionnaires, while two observers scored mood, physical activity, social interaction, tool use and satisfaction
key_sources: López-Faican, L.; Jaén Martínez, FJ. (2020). EmoFindAR: Evaluation of a mobile multiplayer augmented reality game for primary school children. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2020.103814

article_title: EmoFindAR: Evaluation of a mobile multiplayer augmented reality game for primary school children
citation: López-Faican, L.; Jaén Martínez, FJ. (2020). EmoFindAR: Evaluation of a mobile multiplayer augmented reality game for primary school children. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2020.103814
title: Design framework for healthy-competition and collaborative MAR games grounded in flow theory and conditions for successful collaborative learning
description: The article grounds EmoFindAR in three interlocking accounts: Shindler's "healthy competition" (symbolic prizes, short duration, a chance to win for all, visible value of the learning process), Szewkis et al.'s six conditions for successful collaborative learning (common goal, coordination and communication, positive interdependence, awareness of peers' work, individual accountability, joint rewards), and Csikszentmihalyi's flow theory, which the game contemplates "to get the participants to be completely immersed in the activity they perform, avoiding frustration or boredom" through balanced challenges such as spatial-orientation, concept-mapping and mixed-reality challenges.
requirements: Collaborative mechanics that require joint intervention, such as a character needing impacts from two different players within a time window
A challenge level balanced with children's abilities to avoid apathy, boredom or anxiety
constraints: The competitive mode as implemented follows healthy-competition principles: short activities with symbolic prizes focused on learning rather than final rankings
target_learning_goals: emotional intelligence skills
collaboration and communication
intrinsic motivation and engagement
examples: EmoFindAR's collaborative mode implements the six conditions via a shared augmented space in which individual actions are visible in real time and rewards are joint, and its competitive mode follows the five healthy-competition principles
key_sources: López-Faican, L.; Jaén Martínez, FJ. (2020). EmoFindAR: Evaluation of a mobile multiplayer augmented reality game for primary school children. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2020.103814

article_title: Teachers’ computational thinking content knowledge: Development of a measurement instrument
citation: Monteyne S., Struyve C., Gesquière N., Neutens T., Wyffels F., van Braak J. & Aesaert K. (2024). Teachers’ computational thinking content knowledge: Development of a measurement instrument. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105181
title: ICILS 2023 Flanders instrument measuring teachers’ computational thinking content knowledge (16 multiple-choice and short constructed response items)
description: A direct, conventional-format test of lower secondary teachers’ computational thinking content knowledge developed as part of ICILS 2023 in Flanders. The final tool consists of “16 multiple-choice and short constructed response questions”, deliberately excluding items requiring familiarity with a particular programming language. It covers the five aspects of the Fraillon et al. (2023) framework and was calibrated on 352 pre-service teachers, yielding “favorable item and overall instrument characteristics”.
requirements: Administration with a test administrator under equal testing conditions; responses binary coded correct (1) and incorrect (0); 45 minutes completion time as administered in the calibration study
constraints: Deliberately a conventional format rather than performance-based, so it may not fully capture real-world performance compared to performance-based assessments; developed for the Flemish educational context and lower secondary (grade 7-8) teachers’ content knowledge
target_learners: Lower secondary school teachers (grade 7-8) and senior pre-service teachers in teacher training programs
target_learning_goals: Computational thinking content knowledge: conceptualizing problems and operationalizing solutions
examples: Administered online through Qualtrics to 352 senior pre-service teachers from nine of the fifteen Flemish teacher training institutes
key_sources: Monteyne S., Struyve C., Gesquière N., Neutens T., Wyffels F., van Braak J. & Aesaert K. (2024). Teachers’ computational thinking content knowledge: Development of a measurement instrument. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105181

article_title: Teachers’ computational thinking content knowledge: Development of a measurement instrument
citation: Monteyne S., Struyve C., Gesquière N., Neutens T., Wyffels F., van Braak J. & Aesaert K. (2024). Teachers’ computational thinking content knowledge: Development of a measurement instrument. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105181
title: Fraillon et al. (2023) two-strand framework of computational thinking (conceptualizing problems; operationalizing solutions)
description: The organizing framework for the instrument defines computational thinking as two strands. “According to Fraillon et al. (2023), the construct of computational thinking consists of two strands: conceptualizing problems and operationalizing solutions.” Conceptualizing problems comprises knowing about and understanding digital systems, formulating and analyzing problems, and collecting and representing relevant data; operationalizing solutions comprises planning and evaluating solutions and developing algorithms, programs and interfaces. The article maps its test items onto these five aspects.
requirements: Serves as the conceptual foundation to which instrument content is aligned; in this study its elements were cross-tabled with Flemish attainment targets to ensure comprehensive coverage
constraints: Chosen for consistency with ICILS 2023; the article notes there is no universally accepted definition of the computational thinking construct
target_learning_goals: Computational thinking: problem decomposition, pattern recognition and generalization, abstraction, algorithm, modeling, testing and debugging, data representation
examples: Table 1 of the article assigns each of the twenty initial items to one framework aspect, e.g. items 1,6,12,16,20 to knowing about and understanding digital systems

article_title: Investigating the use of innovative mobile pedagogies for school-aged students: A systematic literature review
citation: Burden, K, Kearney, M, Schuck, S & Hall, A (2019). Investigating the use of innovative mobile pedagogies for school-aged students: A systematic literature review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.04.008
title: Feasible innovation in school mobile learning
description: The review proposes the notion of feasible innovation as a framework for understanding realistic degrees of innovation in mobile learning within schools. It emerges from the finding that "low to medium degrees of innovation in most studies" predominated, with only 3 articles showing radical disruption. Feasible innovation positions the innovation spectrum of mobile pedagogies against the practical constraints of traditional school structures and practices, guiding educators toward attainable innovation rather than radical disruption.
requirements: Designers must consider the practical constraints of traditional school structures and practices when aiming for innovation in mobile learning
constraints: The notion is proposed in the specific context of mobile learning in schools, not technology-enhanced learning generally
target_learning_goals: effective and appropriately innovative learning through mobile pedagogies
examples: The review discusses illustrative examples across its innovation spectrum, from conventional to radically disruptive practices
key_sources: Burden, K, Kearney, M, Schuck, S & Hall, A (2019). Investigating the use of innovative mobile pedagogies for school-aged students: A systematic literature review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.04.008

article_title: Investigating the use of innovative mobile pedagogies for school-aged students: A systematic literature review
citation: Burden, K, Kearney, M, Schuck, S & Hall, A (2019). Investigating the use of innovative mobile pedagogies for school-aged students: A systematic literature review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.04.008
title: Innovation spectrum of mobile learning pedagogies
description: The review organizes mobile learning pedagogies along an innovation spectrum ranging from low to radically innovative and disruptive practices. Illustrative examples are discussed "across this innovation spectrum", distinguishing ordinary technology-augmented practice from the radical, structurally disruptive end achieved by very few studies. This spectrum serves as the review's organizing axis for characterizing the degree to which mobile approaches disrupt traditional school structures and practices.
requirements: Classification of studies requires criteria distinguishing degrees of innovation, as instantiated in the review's content and thematic analysis
constraints: Applied to mobile learning pedagogies for school-aged students in the 2010-2017 literature
target_learning_goals: understanding and designing innovative mobile learning practices
examples: The review discusses illustrative examples across the spectrum, including the 3 articles identified as radically innovative and disruptive

article_title: Online exams for blended assessment. Study of different application methodologies
citation: Ardid Ramírez, M.; Gómez-Tejedor, JA.; Meseguer Dueñas, JM.; Riera Guasp, J.; Vidaurre, A. (2015). Online exams for blended assessment. Study of different application methodologies. Computers and Education. 81:296-303. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2014.10.010
title: In blended assessment, treat the administration mode of online exams as a design decision that changes scores
description: The study uses online exams "in three different situations: in an evaluation-proctored exam, in an evaluation-unproctored exam and as a training-homework task" within blended assessment. Because marks clearly differ by mode, and unproctored results are biased toward higher ratings with greater dispersion, instructors designing blended assessment should select and interpret online exam administration modes deliberately rather than treating online scores as mode-independent.
requirements: The same online exam instrument must be applied under explicitly chosen administration conditions (proctored, unproctored, or as homework).
constraints: The article's comparison covers the three studied situations; unproctored results carry a stated bias towards higher ratings and greater dispersion.
target_learners: university students in physics-related engineering coursework
target_learning_goals: valid assessment of student performance in blended courses
examples: The article studied online exams as a proctored evaluation exam, an unproctored evaluation exam, and a training-homework task, finding marks depend on the mode.
key_sources: Ardid Ramírez, M.; Gómez-Tejedor, JA.; Meseguer Dueñas, JM.; Riera Guasp, J.; Vidaurre, A. (2015). Online exams for blended assessment. Study of different application methodologies. Computers and Education. 81:296-303. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2014.10.010

article_title: Online exams for blended assessment. Study of different application methodologies
citation: Ardid Ramírez, M.; Gómez-Tejedor, JA.; Meseguer Dueñas, JM.; Riera Guasp, J.; Vidaurre, A. (2015). Online exams for blended assessment. Study of different application methodologies. Computers and Education. 81:296-303. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2014.10.010
title: Online exams as a component of blended assessment
description: Online exams are used "as part of the evaluation process in the context of blended assessment," complementing conventional evaluation. The article studies their deployment in three situations: evaluation-proctored, evaluation-unproctored, and training-homework use. The element's outcomes depend on administration mode, making mode specification a necessary part of its design.
requirements: A specified administration mode (proctored, unproctored, or homework) must accompany any use of the online exam for evaluation.
constraints: Unproctored application introduces a bias towards higher ratings and greater dispersion of results compared with proctored application.
target_learning_goals: course evaluation and training through online assessment
examples: Online exams were deployed in the studied course in an evaluation-proctored exam, an evaluation-unproctored exam, and as a training-homework task.

article_title: To capture the research landscape of lecture capture in university education
citation: Banerjee, S. (2021). To capture the research landscape of lecture capture in university education. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2020.104032
title: Explicitly tell students about the benefits and drawbacks of lecture capture so they use it as a supplement rather than an alternative
description: The review recommends that instructors and educators raise awareness among students that lecture capture needs to be utilised as a supplementary resource rather than an alternative to face-to-face lectures. "Students should be explicitly told about the benefits and the drawbacks of lecture capture." This ensures students make the most of the technology while obviating its drawbacks.
requirements: Instructors and educators take responsibility for raising student awareness of best practice
constraints: One cannot assume students to be aware of the best practice by default
target_learning_goals: effective use of lecture capture as a learning resource
examples: The review urges instructors to reflect on why students should attend face-to-face sessions and thereafter also watch the recorded lectures.
key_sources: Banerjee, S. (2021). To capture the research landscape of lecture capture in university education. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2020.104032

article_title: To capture the research landscape of lecture capture in university education
citation: Banerjee, S. (2021). To capture the research landscape of lecture capture in university education. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2020.104032
title: Constructivist framing of lecture capture as a technology-enhanced learning design
description: The review conceptualises lecture capture through the lens of learning theories, positioning behaviourism and constructivism as "the two key paradigms that lie at opposite ends of the spectrum." According to constructivism, students who are self-regulated actively construct their own understanding of reality by linking new information to their prior experiences. The paper argues that watching lecture capture after attending face-to-face lectures is likely to help students in knowledge building from half-baked notions.
requirements: Students attend the face-to-face sessions and use recordings to build knowledge afterwards
constraints: The scope is trained on in vivo lecture capture, where live face-to-face lectures in front of students are captured in real time
target_learning_goals: knowledge building and complex problem solving
key_sources: Banerjee, S. (2021). To capture the research landscape of lecture capture in university education. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2020.104032

article_title: Towards reliable generative AI-driven scaffolding: Reducing hallucinations and enhancing quality in self-regulated learning support
citation: Qian, K., Liu, S., Li, T., Raković, M., Li, X., Guan, R., Molenaar, I., Nawaz, S., Swiecki, Z., Yan, L., & Gašević, D. (2025). Towards Reliable Generative AI-Driven Scaffolding: Reducing Hallucinations and Enhancing Quality in Self-Regulated Learning Support. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.05929
title: COPES model of self-regulated learning as a framework for parsing SRL processes in scaffolds
description: The COPES model (Conditions, Operations, Products, Evaluations, Standards) from Winne and Hadwin provides a detailed depiction of the learning process that underscores the significance of SRL. The article uses COPES to derive a process library of 15 SRL processes that could be explicitly scaffolded, which forms the basis for evaluating whether LLM-generated scaffolds target the correct SRL processes. Two indistinguishable SRL processes (C.STR.2 and C.MTR.2) were merged during expert coding, reducing the final count to 14.
requirements: A process library derived from COPES that maps SRL processes to observable trace action patterns
constraints: Two SRL processes (C.STR.2 and C.MTR.2) were indistinguishable from trace data and had to be merged into a single category
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning processes including goal setting, self-monitoring, and strategic planning
examples: The article constructed a process library of 15 SRL processes derived from the COPES model, following principles proposed by Fan et al. (2022), to evaluate scaffold reliability.
key_sources: Qian, K., Liu, S., Li, T., Raković, M., Li, X., Guan, R., Molenaar, I., Nawaz, S., Swiecki, Z., Yan, L., & Gašević, D. (2025). Towards Reliable Generative AI-Driven Scaffolding: Reducing Hallucinations and Enhancing Quality in Self-Regulated Learning Support. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.05929

article_title: Towards reliable generative AI-driven scaffolding: Reducing hallucinations and enhancing quality in self-regulated learning support
citation: Qian, K., Liu, S., Li, T., Raković, M., Li, X., Guan, R., Molenaar, I., Nawaz, S., Swiecki, Z., Yan, L., & Gašević, D. (2025). Towards Reliable Generative AI-Driven Scaffolding: Reducing Hallucinations and Enhancing Quality in Self-Regulated Learning Support. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.05929
title: GenAI-enabled SRL scaffolding system with pre-delivery reliability and quality evaluation
description: A system that uses LLMs to generate personalised SRL scaffolds from student trace data, then evaluates them through a multi-agent reliability evaluation (checking whether scaffolds target the correct SRL processes) and an LLM-as-a-Judge quality evaluation (selecting the most helpful scaffold from pairs) before delivery to students. The system aims to automatically screen out low-quality and hallucinated scaffolds, trigger LLM regeneration, and select high-quality scaffolds from multiple candidates.
requirements: Access to student trace data from a learning task
A process library mapping SRL processes to trace action patterns
At least one LLM for scaffold generation and one for evaluation
constraints: Even GPT-4-Turbo as a Judge achieved only moderate alignment with human expert labels, suggesting room for improvement in eliminating hallucinations entirely
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning during reading-writing tasks
examples: The system was tested on a dataset of 594 scaffolds generated by three LLMs (GPT-4-Turbo, GPT-3.5-Turbo, and Gemini-Pro) for 66 secondary school students at three time points during a reading-writing task.

article_title: Mood-affect congruency. Exploring the relation between learners’ mood and the affective charge of educational videos
citation: Maik Beege. (2019). Parasocial Learning – The Impacts of Social Entities in Learning with Educational Videos. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.05.001
title: Social Agency Theory and the CASA Paradigm explain why social cues in multimedia trigger social responses
description: The thesis describes social agency theory (Mayer, Sobko, & Mautone, 2003) and the Computers-Are-Social-Actors (CASA) paradigm as the framework explaining how social cues in multimedia learning trigger social responses. "Social cues in a multimedia environment (e.g., eye contact, voice, gestures) prime a social activation schema, which triggers processes of human-to-human communication." The CASA paradigm holds that "Social responses to computers are commonplace, unavoidable, and easy to generate." This framework underpins the thesis's expectation that design features of social entities in instructional videos influence learning.
requirements: A multimedia environment must contain social cues such as eye contact, voice, or gestures to prime a social activation schema
target_learning_goals: deep cognitive processing of multimedia learning material
key_sources: Maik Beege. (2019). Parasocial Learning – The Impacts of Social Entities in Learning with Educational Videos. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.05.001

article_title: Mood-affect congruency. Exploring the relation between learners’ mood and the affective charge of educational videos
citation: Maik Beege. (2019). Parasocial Learning – The Impacts of Social Entities in Learning with Educational Videos. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.05.001
title: Cognitive Load Theory and Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning view social entities as extraneous load
description: The thesis outlines cognitive load theory (CLT) and the cognitive theory of multimedia learning (CTML) as purely cognitive frameworks. Within these frames, "Social entities are additional visual materials which must be processed but are not necessary for understanding the basic learning material." The thesis notes "social cues can be viewed as extraneous material which induces unnecessary cognitive load and can lead to cognitive overload." CTML similarly warns additional entities can overload the visual channel, inhibiting construction of a complete pictorial model.
requirements: Instructional design must minimize extraneous load, especially when intrinsic load is high
constraints: CLT and CTML do not include affective, motivational, metacognitive, and social factors, limiting design recommendations for social entities
target_learning_goals: schema construction and integration of learning content
key_sources: Maik Beege. (2019). Parasocial Learning – The Impacts of Social Entities in Learning with Educational Videos. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.05.001

article_title: Mood-affect congruency. Exploring the relation between learners’ mood and the affective charge of educational videos
citation: Maik Beege. (2019). Parasocial Learning – The Impacts of Social Entities in Learning with Educational Videos. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.05.001
title: CASTLM and ICALM frame social and affective processes as providing cognitive resources for learning
description: The thesis presents the cognitive-affective-social theory of learning with media (CASTLM; Schneider, Beege, Nebel, & Rey, 2018b) and the Integrated Cognitive Affective Model of Learning with Multimedia (ICALM; Plass & Kaplan, 2016) as frameworks countering purely cognitive accounts. "According to CASTLM and aCLT, social entities in instructional videos can foster learning." ICALM "postulates a solid connection between emotions and cognition," and holds "emotional experiences during learning influence the learner's ability to self-regulate." These frameworks motivate the thesis's experimental manipulation of social and affective cues.
requirements: Affective and social stimulation must be considered alongside cognitive load, since mental models have cognitive as well as affective components
target_learning_goals: cognitive activation and resource allocation during multimedia learning
key_sources: Maik Beege. (2019). Parasocial Learning – The Impacts of Social Entities in Learning with Educational Videos. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.05.001

article_title: Mood-affect congruency. Exploring the relation between learners’ mood and the affective charge of educational videos
citation: Maik Beege. (2019). Parasocial Learning – The Impacts of Social Entities in Learning with Educational Videos. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.05.001
title: Parasocial interaction is an asymmetrical, multidimensional process during media reception
description: The thesis describes the theory of parasocial interaction (PSI; Horton & Wohl, 1956; Hartmann, Schramm, & Klimmt, 2004b) as a framework for how social entities influence learners during video reception. PSI is "described as the conversational give and take between a persona (i.e. the social entity) and a recipient," and "the interaction is asymmetrical, since the persona acts independently from the cognitions, emotions, and behavior of the learner." The Two-Level Model holds PSI strength depends on characteristics of the personae and recipients, with perceptive-cognitive, affective, and behavioral facets.
requirements: A persona presented medially with no return channel; recipient characteristics and persona characteristics determine PSI strength
constraints: Only processes during media consumption are relevant; parasocial relationships are treated as separate constructs and not described further
target_learning_goals: attention, evaluation processes, and engagement with learning material
key_sources: Maik Beege. (2019). Parasocial Learning – The Impacts of Social Entities in Learning with Educational Videos. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.05.001

article_title: Mood-affect congruency. Exploring the relation between learners’ mood and the affective charge of educational videos
citation: Maik Beege. (2019). Parasocial Learning – The Impacts of Social Entities in Learning with Educational Videos. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.05.001
title: Design social entities so benefits of social cues outweigh added cognitive costs
description: The thesis derives a design principle from the tension between cognitive load and social agency perspectives: "Social entities need to be integrated in such a way that the benefits at least outweigh the costs." Because "designing an instructor, filming instructional videos or programming, and designing pedagogical agents increase production cost, design recommendations should be specified." The principle calls for deliberate integration of social entities rather than blanket inclusion or exclusion.
requirements: Social entities must be integrated deliberately so that benefits of social cues at least outweigh the added processing costs
constraints: Studies report negative effects, positive effects, and zero effects of social cues on learning, so effects are moderated by entity appearance, voice, gesture, recipient characteristics, learning disciplines, and pacing
target_learners: designers of instructional videos and multimedia learning environments
target_learning_goals: optimizing learning processes with social entities in video-based instruction
