article_title: An interactive multimedia learning environment for VLSI built with COSMOS
citation: Angelides, M. C. & Agius, H. W. (2001). An interactive multimedia learning environment for VLSI built with COSMOS. https://www.brunel.ac.uk/~cssthwa/
title: COSMOS: Content Oriented Semantic Modelling Overlay Scheme
description: COSMOS is a content-modelling scheme for multimedia that uses the multimedia frame (m-frame) as its basis, a 'slot-and-filler' type structure with perspectives and instances. It defines three m-frame types: syntactic m-frames (SYMs) for spatial relationships, semantic m-frames (SEMs) for events, actions and object properties, and temporal m-frames (TEMs) for temporal relationships using Allen's 13 primitives. It has been used to develop several educational multimedia systems.
requirements: A formal definition language (COSMOS-DL) and query language (COSMOS-QL) support creation, population and querying of the model
target_learning_goals: understanding of VLSI products and processes

article_title: An interactive multimedia learning environment for VLSI built with COSMOS
citation: Angelides, M. C. & Agius, H. W. (2001). An interactive multimedia learning environment for VLSI built with COSMOS. https://www.brunel.ac.uk/~cssthwa/
title: Bigger Bits: interactive multimedia learning environment for VLSI
description: Bigger Bits is an interactive multimedia learning environment built with COSMOS that teaches VLSI within the context of a fictitious computer electronics manufacturer called Bigger Bits Ltd. It uses an intelligent tutoring system architecture with domain, remedial, tutoring and student knowledge, with COSMOS forming the domain knowledge and SEMs forming the basis of the rest of the architecture. Domain knowledge was based on textbooks and advanced handbooks, with media drawn from educational videos, promotional videos and specially filmed footage.
requirements: COSMOS as the domain knowledge component
target_learning_goals: application of theoretical knowledge of VLSI product and process
key_sources: Angelides, M. C. & Agius, H. W. (2001). An interactive multimedia learning environment for VLSI built with COSMOS. https://www.brunel.ac.uk/~cssthwa/

citation: Angelides, M. C. & Agius, H. W. (2001). An interactive multimedia learning environment for VLSI built with COSMOS. https://www.brunel.ac.uk/~cssthwa/
title: Uniform component-based ITS architecture using SEMs for all knowledge types
description: The article describes using SEMs to form the basis of the remedial, tutoring and student knowledge as well as the domain knowledge, yielding a 'uniform, consistent, and flexible component-based architecture'. This approach represents both procedural and non-procedural, and content-based and non-content-based information within a consistent framework.
requirements: SEMs must maintain the perspective and instances structure across all knowledge types
target_learning_goals: domain content mastery

title: Student knowledge components: overlay SEMs, misconception SEMs and bugs library
description: Student knowledge is constructed during interaction as overlay knowledge of the domain and diagnosed misconceptions, complemented by a bugs library. Student overlay SEMs record the instance name, strength of acquired knowledge rated between 0 and 1, the successful tutoring strategy used, and media segments used. Student misconception SEMs record incorrect answers with seriousness rated between -1 and 0, and the bugs library contains mal SEMs with common misconceptions.

description: The article argues that multimedia offers significant benefits for VLSI education because it enables products and processes to be demonstrated 'in action', affording better understanding than text alone. article_title: Body in motion, attention in focus: A virtual reality study on teachers' movement patterns and noticing
citation: Yizhen Huang, Eric Richter, Thilo Kleickmann, Katharina Scheiter, Dirk Richter. (2023). Body in motion, attention in focus: A virtual reality study on teachers' movement patterns and noticing. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104912
title: Three-pattern taxonomy of preservice teacher movement in classrooms
description: The article proposes a three-category taxonomy of preservice teachers' classroom body movement patterns derived from K-means clustering of spatial point-pattern statistics. Immobile teachers "restricted their movement to the area behind the teacher's desk"; anchored teachers visited different locations but stayed mostly at the front; dynamic teachers dispersed their presence more evenly throughout the classroom, moving frequently to distant locations and spending less time in any one place. The taxonomy emerged from unsupervised clustering rather than being predefined.
requirements: Requires concurrent tracking of body and eye movements during teaching, which the article achieves with IVR technology
constraints: Identified within a standardized IVR classroom with a short teaching task and a small sample of preservice teachers
target_learning_goals: Teacher noticing of classroom events
Classroom management
key_sources: Yizhen Huang, Eric Richter, Thilo Kleickmann, Katharina Scheiter, Dirk Richter. (2023). Body in motion, attention in focus: A virtual reality study on teachers' movement patterns and noticing. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104912

title: Immersive virtual reality classroom with concurrent motion and eye tracking
description: A standardized IVR classroom environment with 30 virtual student agents arranged in five rows and three columns, programmed to display on-task and off-task behaviors. Participants taught through an HTC Vive Pro Eye headset that records eye movements at 120Hz and tracks participant location each second. The article states IVR allows researchers to "track their movement and eye movement unobtrusively and accurately" while maintaining "a balance between realism and standardization of the classroom environment."
requirements: Requires IVR hardware capable of concurrent body and eye movement tracking
constraints: Environmental influences are controlled by standardization, limiting generalizability to real-life classrooms
target_learning_goals: Teacher visual attention to classroom events

article_title: Teachers' acceptance and use of an educational portal
citation: Pynoo, B., Tondeur, J., Van Braak, J., Duyck, W., Sijnave, B. & Duyck, P. (2012). Teachers' acceptance and use of an educational portal. Computers & Education, 58(4), 1308-1317. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2011.12.026
title: Provide training, resources and safeguard ease of use to support perceived behavioral control and ease of use
description: The article recommends that policymakers and school boards introducing a voluntary educational technology address perceived behavioral control by providing training and support, and by safeguarding ease of use. It states that "Skills and knowledge can be addressed by providing training and support, but also by safeguarding the ease of use of the portal". Resources such as sufficient internet-connected computers at school and home access initiatives are also recommended.
requirements: Training and support provision to build skills and knowledge
Sufficient internet-connected computers at school
constraints: Applies to voluntary technologies that cannot be imposed on users
target_learners: Teachers in primary and secondary education
target_learning_goals: Effective use of educational technology portals for professional development
examples: The Belgian federal government's "Internet for all" and "Start to surf" initiatives providing discounted computers and internet connections
key_sources: Pynoo, B., Tondeur, J., Van Braak, J., Duyck, W., Sijnave, B. & Duyck, P. (2012). Teachers' acceptance and use of an educational portal. Computers & Education, 58(4), 1308-1317. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2011.12.026

article_title: Teachers' acceptance and use of an educational portal

title: Provide content and stimulate contribution to sustain perceived usefulness
description: Because most teachers use the portal to search and download, the article recommends that policymakers and school boards provide interesting content through the portal and stimulate teachers to contribute. It notes that "policymakers/school boards could stimulate teachers to contribute, or could even provide additional interesting (yet non-essential as long as use of the portal is not mandatory) information themselves exclusively through the portal".
requirements: A critical mass of useful, relevant content available through the portal
constraints: Content should remain non-essential as long as use of the portal is not mandatory

examples: KlasCement's resource-based model where members gain download points by uploading information

description: The article observes that downloading requires one click while uploading requires completing a form with file type, language, course, education level, viewing permissions, title, description, keywords and copyright information. It recommends that "Easing and shortening the procedure for uploading in this case should increase the likeliness of uploading information by non-heavy users, who form the majority of the users."

constraints: Applies to resource-sharing platforms where the majority of users are consumers rather than contributors

title: Differentiate support and functionality by user type
description: The article recommends that portal administrators differentiate between user types when planning support and functionality. It states that "portal administrators should consider introducing advanced functionalities from time to time, to stimulate these users" referring to heavy users who are valuable as "feeders" of the portal and could serve as promoters. Differentiating between users makes sense and could benefit technology acceptance.
requirements: Identification of user types through observed usage data
constraints: Based on a voluntary-use portal; generalisation to mandatory technologies requires further research

examples: Heavy users of KlasCement contributed most uploads and reactions and browsed advanced functionalities

article_title: Teachers' acceptance and use of an educational portal
citation: Pynoo, B., Tondeur, J., Van Braak, J., Duyck, W., Sijnave, B. & Duyck, P. (2012). Teachers' acceptance and use of an educational portal. Computers & Education, 58(4), 1308-1317. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2011.12.026
title: C-TAM-TPB: Combined Technology Acceptance Model and Theory of Planned Behavior
description: The C-TAM-TPB framework combines the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) to explain technology acceptance through five determinants: perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, subjective norms, perceived behavioral control, and attitude. These predict behavioral intention, which in turn predicts self-reported frequency of use and observed use. The article states that "This combined model incorporates the five determinants" and applies it per user type to explain portal acceptance among teachers.
requirements: Questionnaire measurement of all five determinants plus behavioral intention and self-reported frequency of use
constraints: Developed for voluntary-use settings; the article notes that findings may differ from business settings because educational institutions serve different goals and teachers have autonomy in technology choice
target_learners: Teachers in primary and secondary education
target_learning_goals: Understanding and predicting teachers' acceptance and use of educational technology
examples: Applied to explain KlasCement portal acceptance among 919 Flemish and Dutch teachers

article_title: Examining the use of instructional video clips for teaching macroeconomics

title: Use instructional videos as complementary materials in blended-learning environments
description: The article recommends producing instructional videos as complementary teaching materials integrated with face-to-face lectures in a blended-learning environment. The videos "are designed to serve as a complement to other materials (e.g., books and notes taken in face-to-face classes), thus being used in a blended-learning environment." Videos were indexed to the subject's syllabus and produced in the participants' native language.

article_title: From evaluation to learning: Some aspects of designing a cyber-university
citation: Anna Helga Jonsdottir, Gunnar Stefansson. (2014). From evaluation to learning: Some aspects of designing a cyber-university. https://arxiv.org/abs/1310.5552
title: The tutor-web: an open AIWBES drilling system designed for learning rather than evaluation
description: The tutor-web is "an open and freely accessible AIWBES system, available to students and instructors at no cost", built on open source code with material under the Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike License. Material is modular: departments contain courses, courses contain tutorials, tutorials contain lectures with slides and multiple-choice drills. Students may continue requesting drill items until a satisfactory grade is obtained; the grade is currently the average of the last 8 questions per lecture.
requirements: Drill items and an item allocation algorithm suited to individual students
constraints: Currently uses the average of the last 8 questions per lecture as the grade
target_learners: university students of mathematics and statistics
students in low-income areas such as Kenya
target_learning_goals: mathematics
statistics
examples: Used for introductory statistics, mathematical statistics, earth sciences, fishery science, linear algebra and calculus in Iceland and Kenya, with some 2000 users to date

article_title: From evaluation to learning: Some aspects of designing a cyber-university
citation: Anna Helga Jonsdottir, Gunnar Stefansson. (2014). From evaluation to learning: Some aspects of designing a cyber-university. https://arxiv.org/abs/1310.5552
title: Design drill systems for learning rather than evaluation, since classical statistical models for mere evaluation do not apply
description: The article argues that because students improve their knowledge while using the system, "the usual IRT models do not apply to the present setup, nor do any conceptual models or frameworks designed only for testing purposes". Item selection methods from computerized adaptive testing were developed to measure abilities and do not account for learning in a dynamic environment.
requirements: Item allocation and grading methods that account for learning in a dynamic environment
constraints: Applies to on-line learning environments where knowledge changes during use, not to static testing settings

target_learning_goals: knowledge acquisition through drill practice
examples: The tutor-web permits students to continue requesting drill items until the system reports a grade satisfactory to the student

article_title: Examining supervising field instructors’ reporting and assessment of technology use by pre-service teachers on school placement
citation: McGarr, O., & Gallchóir, C. Ó. (2020). Examining supervising field instructors' reporting and assessment of technology use by pre-service teachers on school placement. Computers & Education, 146, 103753. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.103753
title: Self-sustaining cycle of presentation-focused technology use in school placement
description: The article proposes that a self-sustaining cycle maintains the dominance of presentation-type technology use on school placement. Field instructors expect pre-service teachers to use technology for presentations, and the feedback they provide focuses on improving the clarity and quality of PowerPoint slides, which "maintains almost exclusive attention to this type of technology use." This cycle operates within a broader context where the dominant use of technology in host schools aligns with field instructors' expectations, leaving pre-service teachers with little impetus to experiment with alternative, more student-centred uses. The article argues this cycle cannot be addressed through tutor professional development alone, as it reflects systemic practices in schooling.
requirements: A school placement context where field instructors assess and provide feedback on pre-service teachers' technology use
constraints: The article frames this as specific to the Irish school placement model, where school-university partnerships are not formalised
target_learning_goals: developing pedagogically informed technology integration practices
key_sources: McGarr, O., & Gallchóir, C. Ó. (2020). Examining supervising field instructors' reporting and assessment of technology use by pre-service teachers on school placement. Computers & Education, 146, 103753. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.103753

article_title: Examining supervising field instructors’ reporting and assessment of technology use by pre-service teachers on school placement
citation: McGarr, O., & Gallchóir, C. Ó. (2020). Examining supervising field instructors' reporting and assessment of technology use by pre-service teachers on school placement. Computers & Education, 146, 103753. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.103753
title: Formalise school-university partnerships to align technology expectations on placement
description: The article argues that without formal school-university partnerships, pre-service teachers are caught between differing school and university expectations regarding technology use. It states that "Until stronger and more formalised school-university partnerships are achieved, this problem is unlikely to be addressed adequately, regardless of the level of professional mentoring provided to supervising field instructors." Formal partnerships would enable professional conversations between cooperating teachers and supervising field instructors, allowing both parties to interrogate dominant teacher-centred technology practices and align expectations for pre-service teachers.
requirements: Institutional policy commitment to developing formal school-university partnership structures
constraints: The article notes this applies to the Irish context where such partnerships are currently lacking and informal dialogue does not extend beyond conversations about how the pre-service teacher is getting on
target_learning_goals: developing student-centred technology-enhanced teaching practices

article_title: Understanding validity criteria in technology-enhanced learning: A systematic literature review
citation: Haastrecht, M. A. N. van, Haas, M., Brinkhuis, M. J. S., & Spruit, M. R. (2024). Understanding validity criteria in technology-enhanced learning: a systematic literature review. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105128
title: Taxonomy of 27 validity criteria for technology-enhanced learning with synonyms
description: The review assembles a taxonomy of validity criteria considered in TEL research, including effectiveness, statistical validity, external validity, rigour, authenticity, fairness, trustworthiness, usability and usefulness, each paired with synonyms observed in the literature (e.g., generalisability for external validity). Rather than prescribing definitions, the authors "take author's claims of assessing particular criteria at face value" and pair each criterion with a quote from the relevant study to document implicit definitions. The taxonomy structures the review's data extraction and analysis.
requirements: studies must report at least one clearly defined validity criterion for inclusion
constraints: criteria reported under different terminology are mapped to the taxonomy where possible, rather than defined prescriptively
target_learners: learners and educators in TEL intervention studies
target_learning_goals: validity and evaluation of technology-enhanced learning interventions
key_sources: Haastrecht, M. A. N. van, Haas, M., Brinkhuis, M. J. S., & Spruit, M. R. (2024). Understanding validity criteria in technology-enhanced learning: a systematic literature review. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105128

article_title: Re-thinking physics teaching with web-based learning
citation: Chandra, Vinesh & Watters, James J. (2012). Re-thinking physics teaching with web-based learning. Computers and Education, 58(1), 631-640. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2011.09.010
title: Electronic cognitive apprenticeship as a design framework for web-based physics learning
description: The study draws on the cognitive apprenticeship model, which proposes that learners should be exposed to "a variety of methods that systematically encourage student exploration and independence" while teachers scaffold and gradually fade support. Its instructional methods — modelling, coaching, scaffolding, articulation, reflection, exploration, questioning, and performance feedback — were each embedded in the Getsmart website (Table 1). The framework framed both the design of web-based lessons and the interpretation of results.
requirements: Teachers or designers embed each instructional method (modelling, coaching, scaffolding, articulation, reflection, exploration, questioning, feedback) in the web environment
constraints: Chat sessions required a teacher moderator to be present
target_learning_goals: conceptual knowledge of physics topics such as electronics and atomic physics
examples: Table 1 maps each method to its Getsmart implementation, e.g. scaffolding via emails, chats, online quizzes, and hypertext
key_sources: Chandra, Vinesh & Watters, James J. (2012). Re-thinking physics teaching with web-based learning. Computers and Education, 58(1), 631-640. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2011.09.010

article_title: Re-thinking physics teaching with web-based learning
citation: Chandra, Vinesh & Watters, James J. (2012). Re-thinking physics teaching with web-based learning. Computers and Education, 58(1), 631-640. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2011.09.010
title: Reflexive pedagogies: dialogue, task options, feedback loops, and mixed knowledge processes in blended delivery
description: Getsmart's learning activities were "driven by reflexive pedagogies" comprising four design characteristics: "a) activities which encouraged dialogue and group collaboration; b) a range of task options which catered for learner diversity; c) a feedback loop to facilitate learning, and d) activities which represented a mix of knowledge acquisition processes." The discussion maps these onto cognitive apprenticeship methods such as coaching, scaffolding, and articulation through online chat.
requirements: Web-based lessons, tests, online chats, and interactive activities must be linked to the four reflexive design characteristics
target_learning_goals: physics concept understanding and complex reasoning
examples: Online chats encouraged dialogue and group collaboration; web pages and real-world links catered for learner diversity
key_sources: Chandra, Vinesh & Watters, James J. (2012). Re-thinking physics teaching with web-based learning. Computers and Education, 58(1), 631-640. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2011.09.010

article_title: The role of planning in complex problem solving
citation: Eichmann, B., Goldhammer, F., Greiff, S., Pucite, L., & Naumann, J. (2019). The role of planning in complex problem solving. Computers & Education, 128, 1-12. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.08.004
title: Three behavioral process indicators for operationalizing planning in complex problem solving from log data
description: The article introduces three behavioral indicators extracted from computer-generated log data to operationalize planning in complex problem solving: "the duration of the longest interval between two successive interactions (duration indicator)", "the delay of the longest interval between two successive interactions from the beginning of the process (delay indicator)", and "the variance of times between each two successive interactions (variance indicator)". These indicators capture planning behavior occurring in the time between interactions, which the authors take to include understanding, representing, formulating, monitoring, and reflecting processes from the PISA framework.
requirements: Computer-based assessment tasks that generate log data recording the timing of each interaction with the task
constraints: The operationalization relies only on time between interactions, so it is not certain that students actually spent this time planning; students could have been reading the task or engaging in task-irrelevant behavior
target_learning_goals: complex problem solving
key_sources: Eichmann, B., Goldhammer, F., Greiff, S., Pucite, L., & Naumann, J. (2019). The role of planning in complex problem solving. Computers & Education, 128, 1-12. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.08.004

article_title: AI assistance in peer feedback provision: Pedagogically sound, but minimally adopted
citation: Pozdniakov, S., Brazil, J., Banihashem, S. K., Noroozi, O., Gašević, D., Sadiq, S., & Khosravi, H. (2026). AI assistance in peer feedback provision: Pedagogically sound, but minimally adopted. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2026.105591
title: Design AI assistance in peer feedback platforms to preserve student autonomy by positioning AI as a guide rather than a replacement for student voice
description: The article recommends that AI assistance in peer feedback should act as a guide, offering advice students can adopt, revise, or ignore, rather than replacing the student voice. This human-led approach scaffolds students' evaluative judgment and feedback literacy in real-time. The article states that "Rather than replacing the student voice, AI-A acts as a guide, offering advice students can adopt, revise, or ignore."
requirements: Students must first write peer feedback before receiving AI assistance (human-led model)
constraints: Grades did not depend on whether students incorporated suggestions from AI assistance
target_learning_goals: evaluative judgment
feedback literacy
examples: Students could submit their initial peer review without making any changes; AI-A was provided for every peer feedback instance before submission but revision was not required.

article_title: Look at me and pay attention! A study on the relation between visibility and attention in weblectures
citation: Korving, H., Hernández, M. & De Groot, E. (2016). Look at me and pay attention! A study on the relation between visibility and attention in weblectures. Computers and Education, vol. 94, pp. 151-161. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2015.11.011
title: Use a large lecturer video for weblectures longer than 15 minutes; use large slides for shorter weblectures
description: Based on the finding that the effect of visibility on reported attention depends on watching duration, the article recommends that for weblectures longer than 15 minutes a large video of the lecturer supports attention, while for shorter weblectures a large image of the slides is preferable. The authors state: "students report more attention after watching a large video of a lecturer and a small image of slides when listening to a lecture for more than 15 min. For weblectures shorter than 15 min students report more attention when the image of the PowerPoint-slides is large and easy to read".
requirements: Weblecture presentation must allow configuring the relative size of the lecturer video and the slide image.
constraints: The effect was demonstrated with 7.5-minute clips, and the authors note results might not be similar for full-length weblectures.
target_learning_goals: maintaining attention during weblectures
key_sources: Korving, H., Hernández, M. & De Groot, E. (2016). Look at me and pay attention! A study on the relation between visibility and attention in weblectures. Computers and Education, vol. 94, pp. 151-161. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2015.11.011

article_title: Look at me and pay attention! A study on the relation between visibility and attention in weblectures
citation: Korving, H., Hernández, M. & De Groot, E. (2016). Look at me and pay attention! A study on the relation between visibility and attention in weblectures. Computers and Education, vol. 94, pp. 151-161. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2015.11.011
title: Multiple resource model of attention as an explanation for visibility effects in weblectures
description: The article draws on the theory of cross-modalities for multiple attentional resources to explain why a visible lecturer might aid attention. The human information-processing system is thought to have two main input-channels, an auditory/verbal channel and a visual/pictorial channel. Dividing input over these two modalities minimises the risk of overloading one channel. The article states: "A lecturer's face changes constantly and will keep attracting visual attention", unlike static slide content, which may explain why a visible lecturer supports attention.
requirements: The explanation assumes that dividing input across auditory and visual channels reduces cognitive load on either channel alone.
constraints: The article notes this is a theoretical explanation; the moderator analysis found no effect of lecturer appeal, and the visibility effect was found only for the second weblecture.
target_learning_goals: maintaining attention during weblectures
key_sources: Korving, H., Hernández, M. & De Groot, E. (2016). Look at me and pay attention! A study on the relation between visibility and attention in weblectures. Computers and Education, vol. 94, pp. 151-161. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2015.11.011

article_title: Teaching and learning with children: Impact of reciprocal peer learning with a social robot on children’s learning and emotive engagement
citation: Chen, Huili; Park, Hae Won; Breazeal, Cynthia. (2020). Teaching and learning with children: Impact of reciprocal peer learning with a social robot on children's learning and emotive engagement. Computers and Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/J.COMPEDU.2020.103836
title: Active role-switching (ARS) policy for educational agents
description: The article presents "a novel active role-switching (ARS) policy trained using reinforcement learning, in which the agent is rewarded for adapting its tutor or tutee behavior to the child's knowledge mastery level." Rather than fixing an agent in a single role, the ARS policy adaptively switches between tutor and tutee behavior during interaction, making the agent peer-like. The authors frame this as contributing "a new dimension of designing educational agents — actively adapting roles based on the student's engagement and learning needs."
requirements: The agent must be able to estimate the child's knowledge mastery level to adapt its role behavior
target_learning_goals: vocabulary acquisition
affective engagement
examples: In the experiment, children completed a collaborative word-learning activity with the peer agent, which adaptively switched between tutor and tutee roles.
key_sources: Chen, Huili; Park, Hae Won; Breazeal, Cynthia. (2020). Teaching and learning with children: Impact of reciprocal peer learning with a social robot on children's learning and emotive engagement. Computers and Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/J.COMPEDU.2020.103836

article_title: Teaching and learning with children: Impact of reciprocal peer learning with a social robot on children’s learning and emotive engagement
citation: Chen, Huili; Park, Hae Won; Breazeal, Cynthia. (2020). Teaching and learning with children: Impact of reciprocal peer learning with a social robot on children's learning and emotive engagement. Computers and Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/J.COMPEDU.2020.103836
title: Design educational agents to adaptively switch between tutor and tutee roles based on the student's engagement and learning needs
description: The article recommends that educational agents not be fixed in a single role but actively adapt roles to the learner. It states this work "contributes to an important new dimension of designing educational agents — actively adapting roles based on the student's engagement and learning needs." The recommendation is grounded in the experiment showing the adaptive peer agent brought the most benefit to children's vocabulary learning and affective engagement.
requirements: The agent must be able to assess the student's engagement and learning needs to decide when to act as tutor or tutee
target_learning_goals: vocabulary learning
emotive engagement
examples: In the study, a reinforcement-learning-trained agent was rewarded for adapting its tutor or tutee behavior to the child's knowledge mastery level during a collaborative word-learning activity.

article_title: The effects of online peer-facilitated learning and distributed pair programming on students’ learning
citation: Tsai Chia-Wen, Lin Michael Yu-Ching, Cheng Yih-Ping, Lee Lan-Yu, Chyr Wen-Li, Lin Chih-Hsien, Lin Jian-Wei, Tsai Meng-Chuan. (2023). The effects of online peer-facilitated learning and distributed pair programming on students’ learning. Computers & Education, 203, 104849. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104849
title: Seven-phase peer coaching facilitator process for online peer-facilitated learning
description: The article describes a structured seven-phase peer coaching facilitator process adapted from Schaefer, Fabian and Kopp (2020) and Wolf et al. (2018) for implementing peer-facilitated learning online. The phases are: start and problem selection, problem and situation, vision and resource, collecting further resources, setting goals, solution and next step, and feedback. Each phase defines specific roles for team members and the peer facilitator in guiding collaborative system development.
requirements: A facilitator must be selected for each team based on observed programming performance and interest
constraints: Designed for first-year undergraduates without prior programming experience in teams of six
target_learning_goals: programming skills
collaboration
problem-solving

title: Microsoft Teams as a distributed pair programming platform
description: The study used Microsoft Teams as the primary platform enabling distributed pair programming, providing a shared editor, support for the roles of the driver and navigator and their role changing, a chat tool for communication, and remote code highlighting. Students used it to discuss, conduct video conference, share documents, co-edit or co-program, and share and see each other's screens outside of class hours.
requirements: Students submit weekly screenshots of their pair discussions as group homework
constraints: Used in a setting where all teachers and students are standardized on Microsoft Teams for online education
target_learning_goals: programming skills
remote collaboration
examples: Students remotely solved assigned programming tasks using Microsoft Teams, TeamViewer, or video conference via LINE or Facebook outside of class hours.

article_title: Describing increasing proficiency in teachers’ knowledge of the effective use of digital technology
citation: Saubern R., Urbach D., Koehler M. & Phillips M. (2020). Describing increasing proficiency in teachers’ knowledge of the effective use of digital technology. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.103784
title: TPACK Confidence and TPACK Usefulness construct maps describing increasing proficiency
description: The article develops two construct maps — one for TPACK Confidence and one for TPACK Usefulness — that qualitatively describe increasing proficiency in teachers' knowledge of effective technology use. Each map divides the Rasch-derived scale into five bands of equal length (two logits each, starting at -2.0 logits) and describes what teachers in each band typically believe or feel confident about regarding using ICT to support student learning of content. The maps provide 'an inferred typical order of acquisition' of aspects of the construct as respondents move from low to high proficiency.
requirements: Data from a TPACK survey tool analyzed via partial credit Rasch analysis to generate person-item maps
constraints: Based on self-report survey data from a single instrument (TTF TPACK Survey), which the authors note takes a particular approach to measuring TPACK
target_learning_goals: Understanding what it means to have more or less TPACK Confidence and TPACK Usefulness
examples: The TPACK Confidence map describes teachers in Band 5 as extremely confident supporting students to 'actively construct knowledge that integrates curriculum areas' while Band 1 teachers are only moderately confident about some aspects and less confident about others

article_title: The effect of uncertainty on learning in game-like environments
citation: Ozcelik, E., Ercil Cagiltay, N., & Sahin Ozcelik, N. (2013). The effect of uncertainty on learning in game-like environments. Computers & Education, 67, 12–20. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2013.02.009
title: Mission 336: a game-like learning environment for Entity-Relationship Diagrams with an uncertain and a certain version
description: Mission 336 is a computer-based game-like learning tool developed to teach Entity-Relationship Diagram concepts in higher education software engineering programs. Players "collect 336 points" by answering true–false questions about ER diagrams across seven conceptual doors, earning "ten points and the total value of the dice" for correct answers. Two versions were built: an uncertain version with random dice values and a certain version yielding double 3, identical otherwise in content and interface.
requirements: A computer-based application presenting ER diagram statements with feedback, dice rolls, and point scoring
constraints: The two versions differ only in dice values; the certain version yields a fixed double-3 throw with no randomness
target_learners: undergraduate students in computer engineering, software engineering, and information systems engineering
target_learning_goals: Entity-Relationship Diagram concepts including entities, attributes, keys, cardinality, participation, and relationship types
examples: Participants rolled two dice, answered true–false statements about ER diagrams, and received feedback with points gained or lost
key_sources: Ozcelik, E., Ercil Cagiltay, N., & Sahin Ozcelik, N. (2013). The effect of uncertainty on learning in game-like environments. Computers & Education, 67, 12–20. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2013.02.009

article_title: The effect of uncertainty on learning in game-like environments
citation: Ozcelik, E., Ercil Cagiltay, N., & Sahin Ozcelik, N. (2013). The effect of uncertainty on learning in game-like environments. Computers & Education, 67, 12–20. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2013.02.009
title: Research model linking uncertainty, motivation, accuracy, response time, and learning outcomes
description: The article proposes a hypothesized causal model (Fig. 2) of relationships between uncertainty, motivation, accuracy, response time, and post-test performance, operationalized in seven hypotheses (H1–H7). The model holds that "uncertainty is positively related to motivation", motivation relates to accuracy and response time during learning, and all four relate positively to the post-test. A path analysis using LISREL 8.8 tested the model with adequate fit (GFI = 0.95, CFI = 0.92, SRMR = 0.05), and the model accounted for 20% of the variance in the post-test.
requirements: Testing requires behavioral measures (accuracy, response time), motivation scores, and post-test scores collected during game play
constraints: The model was tested in a single game-like environment teaching Entity-Relationship Diagram concepts in higher education
target_learners: undergraduate students in computer engineering, software engineering, and information systems engineering
target_learning_goals: database design concepts (Entity-Relationship Diagrams)
examples: The path analysis with LISREL 8.8 showed adequate model-to-data fit with GFI = 0.95, CFI = 0.92, and SRMR = 0.05

article_title: Improving hybrid brainstorming outcomes with computer-supported scaffolds: Prompts and cognitive group awareness
citation: Farrokhnia, M., Noroozi, O., Baggen, Y., Biemans, H., & Weinberger, A. (2024). Improving hybrid brainstorming outcomes with computer-supported scaffolds: Prompts and cognitive group awareness. Computers & Education 227 (2025) 105229. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105229
title: Ideation Hub online brainstorming platform
description: The Ideation Hub is an online platform built for this study to run structured hybrid brainstorming sessions. It "provides task instructions for both individual and group phases, enforces time limits, and presents the necessary rules before and during each phase". It delivers condition-specific scaffolds: SCAMPER question prompts with principle descriptions and examples in the experimental conditions, and condition-dependent display or hiding of individually generated ideas during the group phase to manipulate cognitive group awareness.
requirements: An online platform able to deliver timed phase instructions, display prompts, and control visibility of individually generated ideas across group members
constraints: The platform was designed specifically for this study and its scaffolds were implemented for a business-idea generation task on sustainable development
target_learners: higher education students, mostly master's level, in agriculture and food sciences programs
target_learning_goals: generating original business ideas addressing sustainability issues through divergent thinking
examples: In experimental 1 and 2 conditions participants could view their previously generated ideas and were encouraged to apply SCAMPER principles using built-in question prompts with a description and example of each principle
key_sources: Farrokhnia, M., Noroozi, O., Baggen, Y., Biemans, H., & Weinberger, A. (2024). Improving hybrid brainstorming outcomes with computer-supported scaffolds: Prompts and cognitive group awareness. Computers & Education 227 (2025) 105229. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105229

article_title: Improving hybrid brainstorming outcomes with computer-supported scaffolds: Prompts and cognitive group awareness
citation: Farrokhnia, M., Noroozi, O., Baggen, Y., Biemans, H., & Weinberger, A. (2024). Improving hybrid brainstorming outcomes with computer-supported scaffolds: Prompts and cognitive group awareness. Computers & Education 227 (2025) 105229. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105229
title: Dual pathways to creativity model (DPCM)
description: The DPCM, proposed by Nijstad et al. (2010), is the explanatory framework this study uses to design and interpret brainstorming scaffolds. It "identifies two cognitive pathways for generating high-quality ideas: persistence and flexibility". Persistence involves deep, systematic exploration within a few idea categories, while flexibility involves exploring broad cognitive categories. The article adapts CSCL scaffolds to target each pathway: SCAMPER prompts for persistence and cognitive group awareness for flexibility, and notes support may strongly stimulate one pathway while weakly or negatively affecting the other.
requirements: Specific process constraints or support such as rules, task structures, and instructions to foster mental engagement in the pathways
constraints: Support mechanisms may strongly stimulate one pathway while weakly or even negatively affecting the other, requiring careful design
target_learners: higher education students performing creative idea-generation tasks
target_learning_goals: generating high-quality, original ideas in individual and group brainstorming
examples: The study operationalized persistence as comprehensible ideas divided by flexibility score, and flexibility as the number of UN Sustainable Development Goal categories covered by a participant's ideas
key_sources: Farrokhnia, M., Noroozi, O., Baggen, Y., Biemans, H., & Weinberger, A. (2024). Improving hybrid brainstorming outcomes with computer-supported scaffolds: Prompts and cognitive group awareness. Computers & Education 227 (2025) 105229. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105229

article_title: The influences of lecturer charismatic leadership and technology use on student online engagement, learning performance, and satisfaction
citation: Hazzam, J., & Wilkins, S. (2023). The influences of lecturer charismatic leadership and technology use on student online engagement, learning performance, and satisfaction. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104809
title: Three-dimensional model of student online engagement (cognitive, emotional, behavioral)
description: The article adopts Sun and Rueda's (2012) conceptualization that "student online engagement has three dimensions": cognitive engagement (effort and investment in learning, such as reading extra materials), emotional engagement (feelings about the online learning experience, such as excitement), and behavioral engagement (observable behavior, such as completing online tasks or following classroom rules). This taxonomy structures the study's measurement and hypotheses, with each dimension measured by validated scales and hypothesized to relate to lecturer characteristics and outcomes.
requirements: Measured with validated multi-item scales (Sun and Rueda's cognitive, emotional, and behavioral engagement scales)
constraints: The article focuses on the learning aspect of self-efficacy rather than other efficacies such as computer self-efficacy
target_learners: higher education students in online courses
target_learning_goals: student engagement in online learning
key_sources: Hazzam, J., & Wilkins, S. (2023). The influences of lecturer charismatic leadership and technology use on student online engagement, learning performance, and satisfaction. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104809

article_title: The influences of lecturer charismatic leadership and technology use on student online engagement, learning performance, and satisfaction
citation: Hazzam, J., & Wilkins, S. (2023). The influences of lecturer charismatic leadership and technology use on student online engagement, learning performance, and satisfaction. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104809
title: Lecturer technology use as three-dimensional practice: delivery, enrichment, and transformation
description: Drawing on Lai and Jin (2021) and Ertmer et al. (2012), the article defines lecturer technology use as "the ability of the lecturer to use technology to deliver, enrich, and transform teaching and learning," measured via three sub-scales: technology use for delivery (presenting content effectively), for enrichment (engaging students in collaborative and interactive learning that fosters excitement), and for transformation (implementing new methods that enhance students' strategies and skills). This framework underpins the study's measurement of lecturer technology use and its hypothesized effects on engagement.
requirements: Lecturer knowledge about technology is described as "a crucial factor influencing the design of learning activities that engage students" — availability of technology alone is not sufficient
target_learners: higher education students in online courses
target_learning_goals: online engagement
effective use of educational technology in teaching

article_title: Digital innovations in teacher recruitment: An experimental study
citation: Klassen, Robert Mark, Wang, Hui, Cutting, Joe, Thompson-Lee, Sophie, Snell, Rebecca J.S., See, Beng Huat, Saiger, Michael. (2025). Digital innovations in teacher recruitment: An experimental study. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2025.105450
title: Four psychosocial dimensions of user experience in persuasive game design: meaning, immersion, mastery, and autonomy
description: The article draws on Abeele et al. (2020) to identify "four psychosocial dimensions related to user experience ... especially relevant in the design of persuasive games: meaning, immersion, mastery, and autonomy." Meaning connects to a game's purpose, immersion to cognitive absorption, mastery to competence-building from challenging experiences, and autonomy to perceived choice during gameplay. These dimensions were measured with the PXI and used as mediators in the study's latent change models.
requirements: Measured using the PXI user experience instrument with four 3-item domains rated 0–6
target_learning_goals: increase teaching interest
increase teaching self-efficacy
increase perceived person-vocation fit

article_title: Digital innovations in teacher recruitment: An experimental study
citation: Klassen, Robert Mark, Wang, Hui, Cutting, Joe, Thompson-Lee, Sophie, Snell, Rebecca J.S., See, Beng Huat, Saiger, Michael. (2025). Digital innovations in teacher recruitment: An experimental study. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2025.105450
title: TeachQuest: a visual novel-style persuasive game for teacher recruitment
description: TeachQuest is "a visual novel-style game designed to encourage reflection while informing and persuading players about teaching." Participants take on the persona of a newly qualified teacher navigating their first half-term at a UK secondary school across five one-week sessions, interacting with students, teachers, parents, and friends. The game includes pedagogy events and core events, with mentor feedback and a follow-up student message upon completion.
requirements: Developed through a year-long collaboration including researchers, experienced teachers, a game designer, software engineer, graphic artist, and script writer
target_learning_goals: increase teaching interest
increase teaching self-efficacy
increase perceived person-vocation fit

title: Realistic job preview (RJP): four animated classroom scenarios with response rating and expert feedback
description: The RJP intervention consisted of "four animated classroom scenarios" presenting balanced, authentic depictions of workplace situations. For each scenario, participants viewed a video-based classroom scenario, rated the appropriateness of three possible responses to a dilemma, wrote a reflective rationale, and read real-time feedback comparing their ratings with experienced teachers' ratings. Participants then received one of four fit messages based on score congruence with experts.

A scoring key established through previous work with subject matter experts

article_title: Computer-supported collaborative learning: An analysis of the relationship between interaction, emotional support and online collaborative tools
citation: Hernández-Sellés, N., Muñoz-Carril, P.-C., & González-Sanmamed, M. (2019). Computer-supported collaborative learning: An analysis of the relationship between interaction, emotional support and online collaborative tools. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.04.012
title: A validated PLS-SEM model of CSCL linking interaction, emotional support, tools, and collaborative learning
description: The article proposes and validates a structural model for computer-supported collaborative learning comprising five constructs: teacher-student interaction, student interaction in work groups, intra-group emotional support, online collaborative tools, and collaborative learning. The model explains 53.3% of the variance in collaborative learning and 47.7% of the variance in intra-group emotional support. All six hypothesized paths were supported, positioning emotional support as a central mediating construct. The model is grounded in the Community of Inquiry framework, connecting cognitive, social, and teaching presence.
requirements: Survey data from students engaged in structured online collaborative projects, analyzed using PLS-SEM.
constraints: Results derive from a cross-sectional survey, so causal relationships should be interpreted with caution.
The sample comes from five subjects in a single Spanish university, limiting generalizability.
target_learners: Higher education students in online courses
target_learning_goals: Collaborative learning skills
Knowledge co-construction

title: Design online collaborative learning to intentionally build intra-group emotional support, not just cognitive interaction.
description: Because intra-group emotional support is the strongest predictor of collaborative learning, instructors should deliberately design activities and structures that build emotional bonds within work groups, including personal links, mutual encouragement, and a sense of belonging. The article emphasizes that social interaction does not happen spontaneously and must be actively scaffolded by the teacher, especially in the early phases of collaboration.
requirements: Teacher presence in early phases to scaffold group formation and socio-emotional bonding.
constraints: Social interaction should not be assumed to occur naturally; it requires deliberate design.
target_learners: Higher education students working in online groups
target_learning_goals: Collaborative learning
Social presence
examples: The study's subjects used a structured eight-phase collaboration script including group agreements, teacher feedback, and self- and peer-assessment.

citation: Reynolds, R., Walker, K., & Speight, C. (2010). Web-based museum trails on PDAs for university-level design students: Design and evaluation. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2010.04.010
title: Allow learners' own devices for museum mobile learning to reduce cognitive load of unfamiliar interfaces
description: The article recommends that mobile learning in museums allow learners' own devices rather than unfamiliar loaned hardware. Because technical problems were "partly due to an unfamiliar device (88.9 percent of students surveyed had never used a PDA)", the authors argue the problems "might be addressed by allowing learners'own devices, thus reducing cognitive load needed to learn the interface".
requirements: Devices must support the required connectivity and applications for the trails.
constraints: Based on a project using loaned Jasjar PDAs with brief visits; the authors note distraction would likely lessen with more use.
target_learning_goals: object-based learning in museums
independent research skills
examples: The project distributed 23 iMate Jasjar PDAs that students had not used before; 88.9 percent of surveyed students had never used a PDA.

article_title: Web-based museum trails on PDAs for university-level design students: Design and evaluation
citation: Reynolds, R., Walker, K., & Speight, C. (2010). Web-based museum trails on PDAs for university-level design students: Design and evaluation. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2010.04.010
title: Socio-constructivist evaluation framework combining Falk and Dierking's Contextual Model with activity theory
description: The article's summative evaluation used a hybrid analytical model based on Falk and Dierking's Contextual Model, which considers personal, physical, and sociocultural contexts of museum learners, augmented with activity theory focusing on how tools mediate visitors' experience with artefacts. The overall framework drew from socio-constructivist perspectives, in which learners become collaborative meaning makers within a community of shared practice. The authors note the Contextual Model was applied mainly to informal family visits and science centres, hence the augmentation.
requirements: Analysis of trail structure and content, student-generated data, prior findings, and interviews with project personnel.
constraints: The Contextual Model has been applied mainly to informal family visits and primarily to science centres.
target_learning_goals: meaning making with museum collections
examples: The summative stage analysed data using this hybrid model, carried out independently by one of the authors.

article_title: Web-based museum trails on PDAs for university-level design students: Design and evaluation
citation: Reynolds, R., Walker, K., & Speight, C. (2010). Web-based museum trails on PDAs for university-level design students: Design and evaluation. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2010.04.010
title: iGuides web-based museum trail system on PDAs at the Victoria and Albert Museum
description: The iGuides system, created by StreetAccess in 2004, links museum-created or external web pages into trails containing audio, text, video and images; users can input their own responses via photographs, voice recordings or text, creating personalised trails accessible on the web after the visit. Twenty trails were developed for HE design students at the V&A, hosted on the StreetAccess website and accessed via handheld PDAs over wireless networks installed in nine galleries.
requirements: Wireless network connectivity; handheld devices; the system relies on Internet connectivity to retrieve and store content.
constraints: When the network was not available the trails could not be used at all; image resolution was too low to study object details.
target_learning_goals: exploring museum collections
object-based learning
examples: Twenty trails were developed collaboratively with design tutors, students, designers and curators, including the 'thrill trail' and 'Break Into the V&A'.
