article_title: Students' perceptions of Facebook for academic purposes
citation: Arteaga Sánchez, R., Cortijo, V., & Javed, U. (2015). Students' perceptions of Facebook for academic purposes. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2013.08.012
title: The Mazman & Usluel (2010) structural model explains educational usage of Facebook through adoption and purposes of usage.
description: A structural equation model relating three latent variables — adoption, purposes of usage, and educational use of Facebook. Adoption is measured by usefulness, ease of use, social influence, facilitating conditions and community identity; purposes by social relations, work related and daily activity; educational use by communication, collaboration and resource/material sharing. The article states "educational use of Facebook is explained directly by purposes of Facebook usage and indirectly by Facebook adoption" and validates the model on a Spanish sample.
requirements: Survey measurement of the model's 11 observed variables using Likert-scale items adapted from Mazman & Usluel (2010)
constraints: Validated on a single-institution sample of business students at one Spanish university; the authors note the sample limitation and call for multi-institution and cross-country replication
target_learning_goals: adoption of social network tools for educational purposes
educational use of social networking sites
key_sources: Arteaga Sánchez, R., Cortijo, V., & Javed, U. (2015). Students' perceptions of Facebook for academic purposes. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2013.08.012

article_title: Analysis and discovery of procrastination patterns in a language learning MOOC
citation: Vázquez Mendoza, J. A., Ferri Ramírez, C., & Monserrat Aranda, C. (2024). Analysis and discovery of procrastination patterns in a language learning MOOC. Computers & Education, 223, 105154. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105154
title: A taxonomy of two forms of procrastination in online learning environments: intra-session and extra-session procrastination.
description: The article identifies two forms of procrastination in online learning environments. "Intra-session procrastination" is "Characterised by intervals of inactivity during learning that are not wide enough to be considered as a threshold of inactivity between different study sessions." "Extra-session procrastination" is "characterised by being an excessively wide interval of inactivity time between the end of one session and the beginning of another." Extra-session procrastination is further subdivided into expected rest (25 min to 48 h), ordinary procrastination (48 h to 10 weeks), and extraordinary procrastination (more than 10 weeks).
requirements: Event logs from a learning platform that allow the calculation of inactivity intervals between and within study sessions
constraints: The thresholds used (e.g., a 25-minute inactivity threshold for session boundaries) are specific to the analysed course's material durations.
target_learners: Learners in self-paced online courses such as MOOCs
target_learning_goals: Understanding and detecting procrastination behaviours that affect learning outcomes
examples: The study applies this taxonomy to the 'Basic Spanish 1' MOOC to classify user inactivity intervals.
key_sources: Vázquez Mendoza, J. A., Ferri Ramírez, C., & Monserrat Aranda, C. (2024). Analysis and discovery of procrastination patterns in a language learning MOOC. Computers & Education, 223, 105154. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105154

article_title: Analysis and discovery of procrastination patterns in a language learning MOOC
citation: Vázquez Mendoza, J. A., Ferri Ramírez, C., & Monserrat Aranda, C. (2024). Analysis and discovery of procrastination patterns in a language learning MOOC. Computers & Education, 223, 105154. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105154
title: Process mining methodology (adapted PM2) applied to MOOC event logs for discovering procrastination patterns.
description: The study employs an adapted version of the Process Mining Methodology (PM2) with seven steps, from definition of objectives to evaluation of process models, using the Disco Fluxicon software tool with an adapted Fuzzy Minner algorithm. Process mining is described as "a family of techniques based on the areas of data science and process management that provide tools to support the analysis of operational processes based on event logs." The authors note it has advantages including real-time modelling of events, modelling without a base model, easy comparison of process models, and clear visualization of behaviour.
requirements: Event logs generated by the learning platform
Software tool such as Disco Fluxicon for process model discovery
constraints: The authors note that process mining techniques remain conspicuously underutilised within the education domain despite their advantages.
target_learners: Researchers and instructors analysing MOOC user behaviour
target_learning_goals: Identifying behavioural patterns associated with course success or failure
examples: The methodology was applied to event logs from the 'Basic Spanish 1' MOOC with 96,815 active users.
key_sources: Vázquez Mendoza, J. A., Ferri Ramírez, C., & Monserrat Aranda, C. (2024). Analysis and discovery of procrastination patterns in a language learning MOOC. Computers & Education, 223, 105154. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105154

article_title: RDU Model dedicated to evaluate needed counsels for Serious Game projects
citation: Julian Alvarez, Jean-Yves Plantec, Mathieu Vermeulen, Christophe Kolski. (2017). RDU Model dedicated to evaluate needed counsels for Serious Game projects. Computers and Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2017.06.007
title: RDU model classifies counsels for Serious Game projects into Realization, Dissemination and Use
description: The RDU model is a classification framework for the counsels (accompaniments) needed across the lifecycle of Serious Game projects. The article states: "We propose to classify all these counsels in three main categories: R for Realization, D for Dissemination, and U for Use. By this way, we obtain a model named RDU." Its purpose is to support ownership adoption and appropriate use of a Serious Game within a dedicated ecosystem such as a school or hospital.
requirements: Projects need counsels addressed to Realization, Dissemination and Use in order to achieve adoption and intended use
constraints: The model addresses Serious Game projects deployed in dedicated ecosystems such as schools or hospitals
target_learners: learners using Serious Games in dedicated ecosystems such as schools and hospitals
target_learning_goals: appropriate use of Serious Games as intended by their designers
key_sources: Julian Alvarez, Jean-Yves Plantec, Mathieu Vermeulen, Christophe Kolski. (2017). RDU Model dedicated to evaluate needed counsels for Serious Game projects. Computers and Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2017.06.007

article_title: Automatic summary assessment for intelligent tutoring systems
citation: Automatic Summary Assessment for Intelligent Tutoring Systems. (2009). Preprint submitted to Elsevier February 26, 2009
title: Summary assessment system with eight components implementing the ensemble approach
description: A summary assessment system developed from the proposed ensemble approach, comprising "eight main components": a Main User Interface, Summary Concept Interface, Summary Writing Concepts web pages, Summary Exercise Interface, Summary Exercise practice set, Pre-processing Module, Ensemble System, and Exercise Result Interface. The Exercise Result Interface "informs the user which content points had been left out in the user's solution". The system targets secondary education English summary writing.
requirements: Reference summaries from the Cambridge O-Level English Language Examination and pre-processing with WordNet and a Glasgow stop word list
constraints: Mainly targeted for secondary education and for assessment of summary writings in English only
target_learners: secondary school students preparing for O-Level English examinations
target_learning_goals: summary writing content skills
examples: Students select summary types via drop-boxes, submit solutions for assessment, and view results with a sample summary containing all content points
key_sources: Automatic Summary Assessment for Intelligent Tutoring Systems. (2009). Preprint submitted to Elsevier February 26, 2009. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2009.05.008

article_title: Automatic summary assessment for intelligent tutoring systems
citation: Automatic Summary Assessment for Intelligent Tutoring Systems. (2009). Preprint submitted to Elsevier February 26, 2009
title: Scaffolding-based pedagogical model with adaptive feedback grounded in Zone of Proximal Development
description: The article's pedagogical model is "a 'scaffolding' model which is able to give students adaptive feedbacks based on their previous learning experience". It draws on Vygotsky's socio-cultural theory and the Zone of Proximal Development, where scaffolding provides "individualized support based on the learner's ZPD". A dynamically updated student model stores knowledge skill levels and learning records, and the system adapts its interactivity based on performance in practice exercises. The authors argue that combining adaptive feedback with the scaffolding teaching strategy provides a better learning experience.
requirements: A student model updated dynamically to reflect current learning capabilities, storing personal information and learning records
constraints: Assumes summary writing performance can be measured by assessment results
target_learners: secondary school students learning English summary writing
target_learning_goals: summary writing content skills
examples: Difficulty-graded exercise sequences let students build confidence on easy exercises before progressing to harder ones
key_sources: Automatic Summary Assessment for Intelligent Tutoring Systems. (2009). Preprint submitted to Elsevier February 26, 2009. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2009.05.008

article_title: Combating effort avoidance in computer adaptive practicing: Does a problem-skipping restriction promote learning?
citation: Savi, A.O., van Klaveren, C., & Cornelisz, I. (2023). Combating effort avoidance in computer adaptive practicing: Does a problem-skipping restriction promote learning? Computers and Education, 206, 104908. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104908
title: Problem-skipping restrictions may require a longer-lasting implementation to accumulate the desired effect.
description: The article concludes that problem-skipping restrictions may require a longer-lasting implementation to accumulate the desired effect, cautioning that the precise null finding "should not be interpreted as evidence of no effect." This principle frames the design of effort-restriction features in computer adaptive practice systems.
requirements: A computer adaptive practice system with a problem-skipping option that can be delayed.
constraints: The precise null finding should not be interpreted as evidence of no effect.
target_learning_goals: Improving learning outcomes by limiting effort avoidance
key_sources: Savi, A.O., van Klaveren, C., & Cornelisz, I. (2023). Combating effort avoidance in computer adaptive practicing: Does a problem-skipping restriction promote learning? Computers and Education, 206, 104908. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104908

article_title: Performance analysis of GAME: A generic automated marking environment
citation: Blumenstein, Michael; Green, Steve; Fogelman, Shoshana; Nguyen, Ann; Muthukkumarasarny, Vallipuram. (2008). Performance analysis of GAME: A generic automated marking environment. Computers and Education, 50(4). https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2006.11.006
title: GAME: generic automated marking environment for programming assignments
description: GAME is a system that "automatically assess programming assignments written in a variety of languages based on the "structure" of the source code and the correctness of the program's output." It currently marks Java, C++ and C programs. Instructors supply a "marking schema" specifying file locations and the model solution for each assessment item.
requirements: Instructors must provide a marking schema for each assessment item, including the location of files and the model solution.
constraints: Currently able to mark programs written in Java, C++ and C only.
target_learning_goals: programming correctness and code structure
key_sources: Blumenstein, Michael; Green, Steve; Fogelman, Shoshana; Nguyen, Ann; Muthukkumarasarny, Vallipuram. (2008). Performance analysis of GAME: A generic automated marking environment. Computers and Education, 50(4). https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2006.11.006

article_title: Immersive virtual reality as a tool to learn problem-solving skills
citation: Araiza-Alba, P., Keane, T., Chen, W. S., & Kaufman, J. (2021). Immersive virtual reality as a tool to learn problem-solving skills. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chb.2021.107025
title: Embodied cognition and interest theory explain IVR learning advantages
description: The article draws on embodied cognition theory, which holds that physical interactions and bodily cues can lighten cognitive load and improve task completion, and interest theory, which links engagement and motivation to positive learning outcomes. IVR is proposed to situate learners inside the environment, providing agency and presence that support these mechanisms. The authors state that "Physical interactions and bodily cues can lighten the cognitive load required in the learning process".
requirements: An IVR system that allows interaction through physical gestures or movements
constraints: The cognitive theory of multimedia learning suggests sensory information in IVR could increase extraneous cognitive load and hinder learning
target_learning_goals: Problem-solving skills
key_sources: Araiza-Alba, P., Keane, T., Chen, W. S., & Kaufman, J. (2021). Immersive virtual reality as a tool to learn problem-solving skills. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2020.104121

article_title: Immersive virtual reality as a tool to learn problem-solving skills
citation: Araiza-Alba, P., Keane, T., Chen, W. S., & Kaufman, J. (2021). Immersive virtual reality as a tool to learn problem-solving skills. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chb.2021.107025
title: IVR River Crossing Game for problem-solving practice
description: An IVR adaptation of the River Crossing Game created for the study using an HTC Vive head-mounted display and handheld controllers. The participant becomes the farmer in the game, controlling the boat directly, unlike the board game and tablet versions where the participant directs the game from outside. The authors state "the participant becomes the farmer in the game, allowing the participant to control the boat and making him or her part of the game".
requirements: An HTC Vive headset with handheld controllers and a dedicated physical space of 4 m × 4 m
constraints: Only one control was used to enable the participant to interact with the environment
target_learning_goals: Problem-solving skills
key_sources: Araiza-Alba, P., Keane, T., Chen, W. S., & Kaufman, J. (2021). Immersive virtual reality as a tool to learn problem-solving skills. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2020.104121

article_title: Pixels and pedagogy: MISTT's insights into evolving teacher identities when technology comes to play
citation: Trevisan, Ottavia; Marcato, Filippo; Christensen, Rhonda. (2026). Pixels and Pedagogy: MISTT's Insights into Evolving Teacher Identities When Technology Comes to Play. COMPUTERS & EDUCATION. https://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2026.105601
title: MISTT instrument for exploring student-teachers' professional identities with and without digital tools
description: The Multiple Contexts Influencing Student Teachers' Identities with Technology (MISTT) instrument is a survey tool designed to explore how student-teachers perceive their professional identities across four contexts — personal, university, internship school, and school system — with and without digital tools. It uses semantic differential items to capture these perceptions. The article introduces it as a new instrument for research on teacher identity and technology integration.
requirements: Administered to student-teachers in a teacher preparation program using semantic differential items
target_learning_goals: professional identity development with and without digital tools
key_sources: Trevisan, Ottavia; Marcato, Filippo; Christensen, Rhonda. (2026). Pixels and Pedagogy: MISTT's Insights into Evolving Teacher Identities When Technology Comes to Play. COMPUTERS & EDUCATION. https://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2026.105601

article_title: Pixels and pedagogy: MISTT's insights into evolving teacher identities when technology comes to play
citation: Trevisan, Ottavia; Marcato, Filippo; Christensen, Rhonda. (2026). Pixels and Pedagogy: MISTT's Insights into Evolving Teacher Identities When Technology Comes to Play. COMPUTERS & EDUCATION. https://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2026.105601
title: Four-context framing of teacher identity: personal, university, internship school, and school system
description: The article frames student-teachers' professional identities as spanning four contexts — "personal, university, internship school, and school system" — each perceivable with and without digital tools. This multi-context framing underpins the MISTT instrument's design and reflects the view that teacher identity is shaped by multiple nested environments rather than a single setting.
requirements: Perception of identity must be elicited separately for each of the four contexts and for with- and without-technology conditions
target_learning_goals: understanding professional identity formation across contexts
key_sources: Trevisan, Ottavia; Marcato, Filippo; Christensen, Rhonda. (2026). Pixels and Pedagogy: MISTT's Insights into Evolving Teacher Identities When Technology Comes to Play. COMPUTERS & EDUCATION. https://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2026.105601

article_title: Pixels and pedagogy: MISTT's insights into evolving teacher identities when technology comes to play
citation: Trevisan, Ottavia; Marcato, Filippo; Christensen, Rhonda. (2026). Pixels and Pedagogy: MISTT's Insights into Evolving Teacher Identities When Technology Comes to Play. COMPUTERS & EDUCATION. https://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2026.105601
title: Attend to teacher identity when designing technology integration efforts
description: Because technology's impact on learning depends heavily on teachers' skills, values, and dispositions — core elements of teacher identity — integration efforts should attend to how teachers perceive their professional identities with and without digital tools. The article's finding of identity expectation mismatches suggests integration initiatives should diagnose and address these mismatches rather than assume technology access alone drives change.
requirements: Diagnosis of identity perceptions across contexts, e.g. using an instrument like MISTT
constraints: The link between identity mismatches and hindered technology integration is stated as a possibility, not a tested causal result
target_learning_goals: effective technology integration in education
examples: The study administered the MISTT instrument to 621 student-teachers to diagnose identity perceptions across four contexts
key_sources: Trevisan, Ottavia; Marcato, Filippo; Christensen, Rhonda. (2026). Pixels and Pedagogy: MISTT's Insights into Evolving Teacher Identities When Technology Comes to Play. COMPUTERS & EDUCATION. https://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2026.105601

article_title: A cognitive definition of computational thinking in primary education
citation: Tsarava, K., Moeller, K., Román-González, M., Golle, J., Leifheit, L., Butz, M. V., & Ninaus, M. (2022). A Cognitive Definition of Computational Thinking in Primary Education. Computers & Education, 179, 104425. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2022.104425
title: Developmental framework of CT's cognitive correlates across educational levels
description: The article proposes a developmental account (visualized in its Fig. 5) of how CT's cognitive correlates change across education levels. It states that "basic numerical abilities (like addition, subtraction, and multiplication) seem to be prerequisites for developing CT at the primary school level", that verbal abilities are relevant along primary and secondary education, and that non-verbal reasoning abilities are essential from primary education to university and beyond, possibly reflecting pattern recognition and abstraction. The study grounds this in its own primary-school data plus reviewed evidence from other age groups.
requirements: Requires empirical association studies of CT with cognitive abilities across multiple educational levels to substantiate the age-differential pattern.
constraints: The article notes the cognitive abilities evaluated are not exhaustive, and that creativity, working memory, and non-cognitive factors like personality or self-efficacy may also be involved.
target_learners: primary school children (eight to ten years old)
target_learning_goals: computational thinking as a cognitive ability
key_sources: Tsarava, K., Moeller, K., Román-González, M., Golle, J., Leifheit, L., Butz, M. V., & Ninaus, M. (2022). A Cognitive Definition of Computational Thinking in Primary Education. Computers & Education, 179, 104425. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2021.104425

article_title: Framework for the evolution of acquiring knowledge modules to integrate the acquisition of high-level cognitive skills and professional competencies: Principles and case studies
citation: Warin, B., Kolski, C., & Sagar, M. (2011). Framework for the evolution of acquiring knowledge modules to integrate the acquisition of high-level cognitive skills and professional competencies. Computers and Education, 57(2), 1595-1614. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2011.02.013
title: Framework for evolving disciplinary course modules to integrate high-level cognitive skills and professional competencies
description: The article proposes a methodological framework destined to force disciplinary course modules to evolve in order to integrate high-level cognitive skills and professional competencies. The framework is analyzed in terms of the primary currents in educational psychology: behaviorism, cognitivism, constructivism and social constructivism. It provides a structured pathway for transforming traditional knowledge-transmission modules into learning environments that develop professional competencies alongside disciplinary knowledge.
requirements: Higher education institutions must be willing to revise existing disciplinary course modules rather than only adding new courses
Alignment with employer expectations regarding professional competencies
constraints: The framework was developed and tested in the context of higher education disciplinary modules
The framework's application is demonstrated through case studies in specific disciplinary contexts
target_learning_goals: high-level cognitive skills
professional competencies
disciplinary knowledge
key_sources: Warin, B., Kolski, C., & Sagar, M. (2011). Framework for the evolution of acquiring knowledge modules to integrate the acquisition of high-level cognitive skills and professional competencies. Computers and Education, 57(2), 1595-1614. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2011.02.013

article_title: Framework for the evolution of acquiring knowledge modules to integrate the acquisition of high-level cognitive skills and professional competencies: Principles and case studies
citation: Warin, B., Kolski, C., & Sagar, M. (2011). Framework for the evolution of acquiring knowledge modules to integrate the acquisition of high-level cognitive skills and professional competencies. Computers and Education, 57(2), 1595-1614. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2011.02.013
title: Analyzing pedagogical frameworks through four educational psychology paradigms
description: The article examines its framework in terms of the primary currents in educational psychology: behaviorism, cognitivism, constructivism and social constructivism. This four-paradigm analysis serves as an organizing pattern for evaluating how a pedagogical design aligns with established learning theories. Each paradigm provides a different lens on how the framework supports knowledge acquisition and competency development.
requirements: The designer must be able to characterize the pedagogical design's mechanisms in terms of each paradigm's assumptions about learning
constraints: The analysis is limited to these four primary currents in educational psychology
target_learning_goals: high-level cognitive skills
professional competencies

citation: Warin, B., Kolski, C., & Sagar, M. (2011). Framework for the evolution of acquiring knowledge modules to integrate the acquisition of high-level cognitive skills and professional competencies. Computers and Education, 57(2), 1595-1614. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2011.02.013
title: Three case studies of disciplinary module evolution
description: The article presents and analyzes three case studies showing the evolution of three disciplinary course modules. Each case study documents how a module was transformed using the framework and what learning outcomes resulted. The case studies serve as concrete demonstrations of the framework applied in different disciplinary contexts, providing the empirical grounding for the article's claims about motivation, efficiency, and employer alignment.
requirements: Each case study requires a disciplinary module that has undergone evolution using the framework
constraints: The case studies are limited to three specific disciplinary modules in higher education
target_learning_goals: disciplinary knowledge
professional competencies

article_title: Computer-game construction: A gender-neutral attractor to Computing Science
citation: Carbonaro, M., Szafron, D., Cutumisu, M., & Schaeffer, J. (2008). Computer-game Construction: A Gender-neutral Attractor to Computing Science. Informing Science? No—venue not printed. https://doi.org/10.28945/60
title: Computer game construction as a gender-neutral attractor to Computing Science.
description: The article presents computer game construction using ScriptEase and the Aurora Toolset as a pedagogical pattern for introducing Computing Science concepts through narrative artifact creation. Students select patterns, set options, and adapt encounters to build interactive stories, learning programming concepts without writing traditional code. The article argues this is "a viable gender-neutral approach to teaching Computing Science". The pattern leverages constructionist learning theory, positioning students as authors of shareable computational artifacts.
requirements: Access to the ScriptEase tool and Aurora Toolset within the Neverwinter Nights game infrastructure
A workshop or classroom context with supervision for learning the tools
constraints: Scripting time was limited to 0-2 hours out of 6 total hours in the study
The study was conducted with Grade 10 English students in suburban middle-class schools in Edmonton, Canada
target_learning_goals: Computing Science abstraction skills
Higher-order thinking skills
examples: 50 Grade 10 English students constructed interactive game adventures over two six-hour sessions using ScriptEase and the Aurora Toolset

article_title: Design fictions for learning: A method for supporting students in reflecting on technology in Human-Computer Interaction courses
citation: Rapp A. (2020). Design fictions for learning: A method for supporting students in reflecting on technology in Human-Computer Interaction courses. COMPUTERS & EDUCATION, 145, 1-18. https://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.103725
title: Design fiction as a reflective learning framework in HCI education
description: The article frames design fiction as an approach that leverages speculative scenarios to provoke reflection on technology's social and ethical dimensions. It positions this within HCI education as a way to move beyond technical skills toward critical engagement. The framework connects fiction-making with learning through imagination and critique.
requirements: Requires engagement with speculative scenarios that students can critically analyze
target_learning_goals: critical reflection on technology
understanding social implications of computing

article_title: Exploring the impacts of interactions, social presence and emotional engagement on active collaborative learning in a social web-based environment
citation: Molinillo, S., Aguilar-Illescas, R., Anaya-Sánchez, R., & Vallespín-Arán, M. (2018). Exploring the impacts of interactions, social presence and emotional engagement on active collaborative learning in a social web-based environment. Computers & Education, 123, 41-52.
title: Research model of antecedents of active learning in social web-based collaborative learning
description: The article proposes and tests a parsimonious model in which "social presence, emotional engagement, teacher-student interactions and, to a lesser degree, student-student interactions (in that order)" act as antecedents of active learning in SWBCL. The model posits direct paths from social presence, teacher-student interaction and student-student interaction to active learning and emotional engagement, plus a path from emotional engagement to active learning. It was evaluated with PLS-SEM on survey data from 416 undergraduates.
requirements: Validated multi-item scales for the five constructs
Social web tools supporting interaction among group members
constraints: Causal relationships should be interpreted with caution because data are cross-sectional
Only four antecedents of active learning are considered
target_learning_goals: active collaborative learning in social web-based environments

article_title: Exploring the impacts of interactions, social presence and emotional engagement on active collaborative learning in a social web-based environment
citation: Molinillo, S., Aguilar-Illescas, R., Anaya-Sánchez, R., & Vallespín-Arán, M. (2018). Exploring the impacts of interactions, social presence and emotional engagement on active collaborative learning in a social web-based environment. Computers & Education, 123, 41-52.
title: Social web tool set (blogs, social networks, file sharing, forums, Skype, wikis) for collaborative case study work
description: The article describes a set of social web tools used by student groups: blogs used as learning diaries, social networks for synchronous and asynchronous communication, shared file storage, forums for coordination and announcements, Skype for voice and video calls, and wikis for collaborative write-up of the case analysis. Tools were accessed through the Moodle 2.5 platform over one semester.

constraints: Some very recent technologies were not included in the study

knowledge co-production

citation: Hewitt, J., & Brett, C. (2007). The relationship between class size and online activity patterns in asynchronous computer conferencing environments. Computers & Education, 49, 1258-1271. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2006.12.003
title: Three-hypothesis explanatory account of why students write more but shorter notes in larger online classes
description: The article proposes three non-exclusive hypotheses to explain its counterintuitive note-production findings. Hypothesis 1 attributes the pattern to increased discussion opportunities: "there is simply more going on in large classes than in small classes", so students find more topics of interest but compensate by writing shorter notes. Hypothesis 2 ties increased note-writing to insecurity and competition in large classes, where it is hard to judge one's standing when participation is graded. Hypothesis 3 suggests both enrollment and productivity reflect instructor skill and course quality, though the authors note this would predict more total words, which was not observed.
requirements: The account is offered as untested hypotheses; the article states it should be straightforward to test each one
constraints: The hypotheses are not mutually exclusive and other explanations may exist; the article states the precise nature of the relationship is unclear

academic writing in computer conferencing environments

title: Recommended online class size limits of roughly 8 to 30 students rest on practitioner experience, not empirical evidence
description: The article's background review reports that online-learning researchers have proposed upper and lower limits on class size: Hiltz, Rovai, and Aragon propose thirty as an upper limit, Turoff proposes a need for critical mass, and Rovai suggests 8-10 students are required minimally for good interactions. The article states "the ideal class size appears to be somewhere between 8 and 30 students, depending on the type of course", representing a tradeoff between lively discussion and feeling overwhelmed. However, it emphasizes these recommendations are based on the researchers' own teaching experiences rather than formal research.

constraints: The article states these claims and recommendations appear to be based on researchers' own online teaching experiences, with little formal research conducted in this area

title: ICAP hypothesis applied to digital distance teaching
description: The study applies the Interactive Constructive Active Passive (ICAP) hypothesis (Chi & Wylie, 2014) to operationalize student-observed learning activities in digital distance teaching. The framework predicts that "as students become more engaged with the learning materials, from passive to active to constructive to interactive, their learning will increase." The study used a slider with four anchor points corresponding to ICAP levels to capture student-observed learning activities across 14 technology types, weighted by frequency of use.

title: Providing opportunities for cognitively activating instruction matters more than device familiarity for quality digital distance teaching
description: The study concludes that "infrastructural measures, such as equipping schools with digital devices so that teachers and students can familiarize themselves with technology, do not seem to be decisive for high-quality digital (distance) teaching." Instead, the quality of technology integration—whether students perceive teaching as cognitively activating—drives effort in learning. This suggests that instructional design for cognitive activation should be prioritized over mere device provision.
requirements: Teachers must design instruction that students perceive as cognitively activating, using technologies to initiate higher-level learning activities
constraints: This finding applies to short-term change from face-to-face to digital distance teaching, as occurred during the COVID-19 pandemic

Cognitive engagement

article_title: Detecting and preventing “multiple-account” cheating in massive open online courses
citation: Northcutt, C. G., Ho, A. D., & Chuang, I. L. (2015). Detecting and Preventing “Multiple-Account” Cheating in Massive Open Online Courses. https://doi.org/10.1145/2724660.2728663
title: CAMEO: a MOOC cheating strategy using harvester and master accounts
description: CAMEO (Copying Answers using Multiple Existences Online) is a cheating strategy in which a user creates at least two accounts: "harvester" accounts used to acquire correct answers by guessing at test answers and then accessing instructor-provided solutions via a "Show Answer" button, and "master" accounts used to submit these solutions as correct test answers. The strategy is internally sufficient (copying from oneself), exploitable in asynchronous courses for every question, and unrestricted in open-admission settings, making it a course-level threat to certificate validity.
requirements: At least two accounts in a MOOC with a "show answer" option available after submission
constraints: Unique to MOOC-style platforms with immediate solution feedback and open enrollment
target_learning_goals: Course certification of proficiency
examples: The authors illustrate two prototypical CAMEO users, each with two accounts, alternating or clustering harvest-and-submit sequences (Fig. 1).
key_sources: Northcutt, C. G., Ho, A. D., & Chuang, I. L. (2015). Detecting and Preventing “Multiple-Account” Cheating in Massive Open Online Courses. https://doi.org/10.1145/2724660.2728663

article_title: Detecting and preventing “multiple-account” cheating in massive open online courses
citation: Northcutt, C. G., Ho, A. D., & Chuang, I. L. (2015). Detecting and Preventing “Multiple-Account” Cheating in Massive Open Online Courses. https://doi.org/10.1145/2724660.2728663
title: Five-filter CAMEO detection algorithm using clickstream timestamp distributions
description: A detection algorithm that considers all ordered pairs of accounts as candidate harvester–master pairs and applies five conjunctive filters: a Bayesian criterion requiring 90% confidence that the proportion of positive Δt values exceeds 0.9; a 90th-percentile Δt cutoff of 5 minutes; certified master with uncertified harvester; shared IP address via transitive closure of modal IPs and usernames; and exclusion of groups with 10 or more accounts sharing a modal IP. The algorithm "is comprised of five filters with highly conservative cutoffs intended to reduce false positives."
requirements: Clickstream server logs recording "show answer" clicks and correct-answer submissions with timestamps
constraints: Provides a lower-bound estimate; the authors concede no ground-truth validation of individual classifications
target_learning_goals: Valid certification of course completion
examples: Filter 2's 5-minute cutoff sits at an "elbow" in the cumulative distribution of identified CAMEO users (Fig. 3).

description: VirtuVox is a voice-related prevention program representing "a mixed approach combining (1) an indirect intervention including a group information session on voice functioning and vocal hygiene, and (2) a direct intervention consisting of three individual vocal training sessions" with VR immersion. title: Train oral communication skills in situations as close as possible to professional reality using VR
description: The article's findings suggest that "practicing oral communication skills in situations as close as possible to their professional reality – by using VR – can improve (trainee) teachers' belief in their ability to implement these skills in real-life situations". A virtual classroom constitutes a safe environment to practice communication skills by controlling task complexity, with stepwise training that could begin with restless pupils and progressively increase their agitation level to replicate the complexity of real school situations. This principle supports designing training that embeds skill practice in representative environmental and communicative conditions rather than decontextualized exercises.
requirements: A virtual environment representative of the professional setting, with adjustable noise and pupil agitation levels
constraints: Training in actual school situations is challenging for ethical and logistical reasons, which motivates the VR-based alternative
target_learning_goals: oral communication skills in noise
transfer of trained skills to real-life teaching situations
examples: The VirtuVox program immersed trainee teachers in a virtual classroom with 16 pupils, with noise set at 70 dBA and pupils' agitation increasing from 30% to 70% across the three sessions.

description: The review draws on embodied cognition theory, which holds that "cognitive processes are not isolated brain activities but involve the whole body and environment", to explain why IVR may particularly benefit procedural training. article_title: How does students' general academic achievement moderate the implications of social networking on specific levels of learning performance?
citation: James Wakefield & Jessica K. Frawley. (2020). How does students’ general academic achievement moderate the implications of social networking on specific levels of learning performance? Computers & Education. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0360131519302477?via%3Dihub
title: Consider students' general academic achievement as a moderator when embedding social networking in course delivery
description: The article recommends that using social networking sites in teaching and learning interventions must be carefully considered in light of students' general academic achievement. It states efforts must ensure that "educational embedding of SNS technologies does not inadvertently disadvantage weaker students", since lower achievers are further distracted by Facebook while higher achievers are not significantly impacted.
requirements: Educators need baseline evidence of social networking effects on learning before incorporating SNS use in course delivery.
constraints: The article states findings are unique to introductory accounting and similar equation and problem based subjects, and should not be generalised to wider student populations.
target_learners: post-secondary students in compulsory first-year business and STEM subjects
target_learning_goals: introductory accounting performance across Bloom's taxonomy learning difficulty levels
examples: The study split the sample at the median WAM and found only low achievers significantly negatively affected by Facebook use.
key_sources: James Wakefield & Jessica K. Frawley. (2020). How does students’ general academic achievement moderate the implications of social networking on specific levels of learning performance? Computers & Education. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0360131519302477?via%3Dihub

article_title: How does students' general academic achievement moderate the implications of social networking on specific levels of learning performance?
citation: James Wakefield & Jessica K. Frawley. (2020). How does students’ general academic achievement moderate the implications of social networking on specific levels of learning performance? Computers & Education. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0360131519302477?via%3Dihub
title: Distraction-conflict theory as an account of social networking's disruptive effect on learning performance
description: The article draws on distraction-conflict theory to explain how social networking use may harm learning performance. Within the stimuli-intensive environment of students' studies and SNS use, the authors note "there is the strong possibility of conflicts in students’ attention and additional cognitive load, that is not relevant to students’ studies". This framework frames Facebook use as imposing attentional conflict and extraneous cognitive load that disrupts performance, particularly for lower-achieving students.
requirements: The account assumes social networking use occurs concurrently with, or in proximity to, study activities where attention is divided.
constraints: The article states it assumes social networking use has linear performance implications and did not explore possible non-linear implications.
target_learning_goals: academic performance in equation and problem solving centric subjects
key_sources: James Wakefield & Jessica K. Frawley. (2020). How does students’ general academic achievement moderate the implications of social networking on specific levels of learning performance? Computers & Education. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0360131519302477?via%3Dihub

article_title: Multivariate characterization of university students using the ICT for learning
citation: Vega-Hernández, M.-C., Patino-Alonso, M.-C., & Galindo-Villardón, M.-P. (2018). Multivariate characterization of university students using the ICT for learning. Computers & Education, 121, 124–130. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.03.004
title: REATIC questionnaire measuring learning styles and ICT use in university students
description: The REATIC questionnaire (De Moya Martínez et al., 2011) is a 60-item instrument rated on a Likert scale from 1 (Nothing) to 4 (Much), used here to "measure the relationship between learning styles and ICT in university student education". Its items fall into four blocks: knowledge about ICT, use of ICT, consideration of ICT, and use of ICT according to learning style, the last grouped into active, reflective, theoretical and pragmatic styles following Alonso, Gallego and Honey.
requirements: Respondents rate 60 items on a Likert scale of 1 (Nothing) to 4 (Much)
constraints: Validated with Spanish university students at the University of Salamanca
target_learning_goals: ICT use for learning
learning styles
examples: Used with 2117 University of Salamanca students in the 2013–2014 academic year
key_sources: Vega-Hernández, M.-C., Patino-Alonso, M.-C., & Galindo-Villardón, M.-P. (2018). Multivariate characterization of university students using the ICT for learning. Computers & Education, 121, 124–130. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.03.004

article_title: Identity profile of young people experiencing a sense of risk on the internet: A data mining application of decision tree with CHAID algorithm
citation: Muñoz-Rodríguez, J. M., Patino Alonso, C., Pessoa, T., & Martín-Lucas, J. (2023). Identity profile of young people experiencing a sense of risk on the internet: A data mining application of decision tree with CHAID algorithm. Computers & Education, 197, 104743. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104743
title: Onlife experience as the theoretical frame for young people's internet-related identity and risk
description: The article adopts Floridi's (2015) notion of onlife experience, living, and identity, arguing that a large part of a young person's life takes place online and that the boundary between online and offline worlds is becoming blurred. Within this frame, the internet is not a mere tool but the spatiotemporal setting where young people occupy and act, relate, move and communicate, making identity-building processes vulnerable to risks young people often do not perceive. The study's findings are read as corroborating that the cohort lives onlife and lacks critical thinking and sense when acting online.
requirements: Research on young people's internet use should treat online experience as an everyday setting for coexisting, acting and relating rather than contrasting online and offline lives.
constraints: The article notes its conclusions are subject to an obvious risk of obsolescence in the medium run due to rapid technological change.
target_learning_goals: Developing critical awareness of risks associated with internet use
Building a healthy and responsible relationship with technologies
key_sources: Muñoz-Rodríguez, J. M., Patino Alonso, C., Pessoa, T., & Martín-Lucas, J. (2023). Identity profile of young people experiencing a sense of risk on the internet: A data mining application of decision tree with CHAID algorithm. Computers & Education, 197, 104743. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104743

Computers & Education, 197, 104743. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104743
title: Educate for critical thinking and healthy technology relationships rather than restricting time and usage
description: The article contends that education should go beyond a pedagogy of limits based on restricting time and sites accessed. It argues it would be more expedient to further generate critical thinking among young people and furnish them with strategies enabling a healthy and responsible relationship with technologies such as the internet, developing a critical mediatic education that fosters responsible and unfettered identity with critical and civic online autonomy.
requirements: Educational interventions should adopt a positive attitude towards technology use, since future generations already live onlife.
constraints: The article states that overcoming the mechanisms of digital literacy that have proven to be insufficient is required.
target_learning_goals: Critical thinking about internet-related risks
Establishing a healthy and responsible relationship with technologies
examples: The study identifies the profile of young people who do not perceive online risk as a channel for proposing educational measures suited to this type of profile.

article_title: Young children's use of touch screen tablets for writing and reading at home: Relationships with emergent literacy
citation: Neumann, Michelle M. (2016). Young children's use of touch screen tablets for writing and reading at home: Relationships with emergent literacy. Computers & Education, 97. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2016.02.013
title: Emergent literacy framework linking home digital and print experiences to print awareness, print knowledge and sound knowledge
description: The article organises early literacy development around emergent literacy skills — print awareness, print knowledge and sound knowledge — shaped by home literacy experiences including digital tools. It frames touch screen tablets as home literacy environments in which different activities (writing with tablets, e-book reading, app access) relate differently to these skills. The study operationalises the framework by relating parent-reported tablet practices to directly assessed emergent literacy skills in 57 children aged 2–4 years.
requirements: Assessment of children's emergent literacy skills and parent report of home tablet practices.
constraints: Findings are correlational and specific to children aged 2–4 years in home settings.
target_learning_goals: print awareness
print knowledge
sound knowledge
examples: The study examined relationships between children's emergent literacy skills and home use of tablets for writing and reading.
key_sources: Neumann, Michelle M. (2016). Young children's use of touch screen tablets for writing and reading at home: Relationships with emergent literacy. Computers & Education, 97. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2016.02.013

article_title: What is “technology integration” and how is it measured in K-12 education? A systematic review of survey instruments from 2010 to 2021
citation: Tessa Consoli, Juliette D´esiron, Alberto Cattaneo. (2023). What is “technology integration” and how is it measured in K-12 education? A systematic review of survey instruments from 2010 to 2021. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104742
title: Technology integration (TI) as a construct lacking a shared definition, encompassing views ranging from mere technology use to transformation of teaching and learning practices.
description: The article synthesizes existing definitions of technology integration, noting that some researchers use the term as a synonym for technology use while others refer to "a far more complex phenomenon, such as the transformation or enhancement of teaching and learning practices through the use of technology." The review adopts a definition emphasizing pedagogical quality over mere frequency of use, framing TI as the instructional use of digital technologies to support pedagogical goals. This construct serves as the organizing framework for the systematic review of survey instruments.
requirements: A shared understanding of TI as involving pedagogical quality rather than mere frequency of technology use
constraints: The term TI is used inconsistently across the field, with no single accepted definition
target_learning_goals: Integration of technology into teaching and learning practices
key_sources: Tessa Consoli, Juliette D´esiron, Alberto Cattaneo. (2023). What is “technology integration” and how is it measured in K-12 education? A systematic review of survey instruments from 2010 to 2021. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104742

article_title: What is “technology integration” and how is it measured in K-12 education? A systematic review of survey instruments from 2010 to 2021
citation: Tessa Consoli, Juliette D´esiron, Alberto Cattaneo. (2023). What is “technology integration” and how is it measured in K-12 education? A systematic review of survey instruments from 2010 to 2021. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104742
title: Content analysis coding scheme for evaluating technology integration survey instruments.
description: The authors developed a coding scheme to systematically extract information from the 35 instruments, covering general information (number of items, dimensions, validity, reliability, theoretical underpinnings), dimensions of TI (teacher-related, student-related, and school-related aspects), and aspects related to the quality of TI in instructional practices. Two coders reached "an overall inter-rater agreement of 96.54%" on a random subsample of instruments.
requirements: Trained coders applying a structured coding scheme to instrument documentation
constraints: Only instruments with full documentation available in English were analyzed
target_learning_goals: Systematic evaluation of technology integration measurement instruments

article_title: Using multi-platform learning analytics to compare regional and global MOOC learning in the Arab world
citation: Ruipérez-Valiente, José A; Halawa, Sherif; Slama, Rachel; Reich, Justin. (2020). Using multi-platform learning analytics to compare regional and global MOOC learning in the Arab world. Computers and Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/J.COMPEDU.2019.103776
title: Multi-platform learning analytics procedure with common data format and script
description: The article documents a "multi-platform learning analytics procedure, where we establish a common data format and script that enables an 'apples-to-apples' comparison without exchanging data". The procedure allows comparing learner behavior across MOOC platforms while avoiding data exchange, which the authors identify as "a common privacy and data security concern".
requirements: Access to platform data from each provider to map into the common data format
constraints: Designed so that raw data need not be exchanged between platforms, addressing privacy and data security concerns
target_learning_goals: Understanding learner behavior and preferences across MOOC platforms
examples: Applied to compare edX and Edraak learner demographics and behavior

article_title: Cartoons beyond clipart: A computer tool for storyboarding and storywriting
citation: M. Madden, P.W.H. Chung and C.W. Dawson. (2007). Cartoon beyond clipart: a computer tool for storyboarding and storywriting. Loughborough University. https://dspace.lboro.ac.uk/
title: Prototype storyboarding and storywriting software with enhanced-frontal-orientation character posing
description: A Java prototype computer tool for story visualisation prior to storywriting, implementing an "enhanced-frontal-orientation" approach in which 2D vector characters are mapped to a 3D skeleton so they can be posed and warped. Users create pictures, place them on stage view screens, and enter text for each picture. The tool was trialled with Year 5 children (ages 9-10) in a school-based study.
requirements: Requires pre-supplied characters, as learners could not create their own posable characters in the prototype
constraints: Exhibits the 'constant background effect' where backgrounds are unaffected by zoom, translation or tilt
target_learning_goals: Narrative writing
Visual storytelling
Point-of-view story writing
key_sources: M. Madden, P.W.H. Chung and C.W. Dawson. (2007). Cartoon beyond clipart: a computer tool for storyboarding and storywriting. Loughborough University. https://dspace.lboro.ac.uk/

article_title: Cartoons beyond clipart: A computer tool for storyboarding and storywriting
citation: M. Madden, P.W.H. Chung and C.W. Dawson. (2007). Cartoon beyond clipart: a computer tool for storyboarding and storywriting. Loughborough University. https://dspace.lboro.ac.uk/
title: Content-centred versus build-centred software taxonomy for visual story tools
description: The article proposes a taxonomy distinguishing 'content-centred' software, whose defining feature is "a primary reliance on pre-supplied characters and artwork", from 'build-centred' software providing tools for user-created content to take an equal or dominant role. Content-centred tools offer low range and high support; build-centred tools offer high range and low support. The review found no tool offering both range and support.
requirements: Analysis criteria include characterisation flexibility and the camera's role in shot distances and types
constraints: The boundary between categories is described as blurred
target_learning_goals: Moving image production
Visual storytelling
key_sources: M. Madden, P.W.H. Chung and C.W. Dawson. (2007). Cartoon beyond clipart: a computer tool for storyboarding and storywriting. Loughborough University. https://dspace.lboro.ac.uk/

article_title: A systematic literature review on serious games evaluation: An application to software project management
citation: Calderón, A., & Ruiz, M. (2015). A systematic literature review on serious games evaluation: An application to software project management. Computers & Education, 87, 396-422. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2015.07.011
title: Six-category taxonomy of serious game application domains for evaluation studies
description: The review classifies the application domains of evaluated serious games into six categories: health & wellness, culture, professional learning & training, social, support, and education. Each category is defined by the purpose of the games it contains, e.g. health & wellness "includes serious games developed to improve people's quality life regarding their health." The taxonomy underpins the review's answer to RQ1 and its distribution analysis of evaluated games per domain.
requirements: Primary studies must report the application domain of the evaluated serious game (QA5)
constraints: Classification derived from the 102 primary studies published until March 2015
target_learners: learners across formal education, professional training, and health contexts
target_learning_goals: domain-specific knowledge and skills addressed by serious games

article_title: Instructor presence effect: Liking does not always lead to learning
citation: Wilson, K. E., Martinez, M., Mills, C., D'Mello, S., Smilek, D., & Risko, E. F. (2018). Instructor presence effect: Liking does not always lead to learning. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.03.011
title: Instructor Presence Effect: instructor visuals in video lectures act as seductive details that impair learning while increasing enjoyment and perceived learning
description: The Instructor Presence Effect names the dissociation between objective learning (comprehension) and subjective evaluation (enjoyment, interest, perceived learning) when visuals of the instructor are added to online lectures. The authors propose a seductive details mechanism: attention captured by the instructor's visual features is devoted to irrelevant processing rather than lecture content, impairing comprehension without increasing mind wandering. The article states that "visuals of the instructor potentially impairs comprehension, but learners prefer and believe they learn most effectively with this format."
requirements: Requires a comprehensive assessment comparing attention (mind wandering), learning (comprehension), and subjective evaluations across matched lecture formats
constraints: Demonstrated in online learning environments with adult participants; the authors note that laboratory studies may yield different attentional patterns due to differing sources of distraction
target_learning_goals: instructional design for online video lectures
key_sources: Wilson, K. E., Martinez, M., Mills, C., D'Mello, S., Smilek, D., & Risko, E. F. (2018). Instructor presence effect: Liking does not always lead to learning. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.03.011

article_title: Instructor presence effect: Liking does not always lead to learning
citation: Wilson, K. E., Martinez, M., Mills, C., D'Mello, S., Smilek, D., & Risko, E. F. (2018). Instructor presence effect: Liking does not always lead to learning. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.03.011
title: Do not assume that learner enjoyment or perceived engagement indicates effective learning in online lecture design
description: Because learners systematically prefer and believe they learn best from formats that objectively impair comprehension, instructional designers should not rely on learner preference or enjoyment ratings as proxies for learning effectiveness. The article shows that "learners not only find online lectures with visuals of the instructor more enjoyable and interesting, they believe this format most facilitates their learning" even as comprehension suffers. Objective comprehension measures are needed alongside subjective evaluations.
requirements: Requires objective learning measures (e.g., comprehension tests) collected alongside subjective evaluations
constraints: Demonstrated specifically for instructor visuals in online lectures; may not extend to other multimedia design decisions
target_learning_goals: evaluating multimedia lecture design
key_sources: Wilson, K. E., Martinez, M., Mills, C., D'Mello, S., Smilek, D., & Risko, E. F. (2018). Instructor presence effect: Liking does not always lead to learning. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.03.011

article_title: Teacher-led robot intervention in early primary school classrooms improves pupil and teacher outcomes
citation: Hughes, A., Gerson, S. A., & van Schaik, J. E. (2026). Teacher-led robot intervention in early primary school classrooms improves pupil and teacher outcomes. Computers & Education, 242: 105510. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2025.105510
title: Pair classroom robot curricula with concise hands-on teacher education for significant impact
description: The article recommends embedding programming with robots in primary education alongside targeted teacher education, underscoring "the importance of teacher education for significant impact". A 3-h workshop covering programming concepts, hands-on robot practice, and curriculum integration discussion, delivered before classroom implementation, was associated with significant pupil and teacher gains that the robot curriculum alone did not produce. The authors state these findings "offer practical guidance for embedding programming with robots in primary education".
requirements: Teachers attend a hands-on education workshop covering programming concepts, robot practice, and curriculum integration before implementing the robot curriculum
constraints: The workshop effect was demonstrated with a 3-h session paired with a 6-week Cubetto curriculum in Welsh early primary classrooms; the article notes unequal teacher sample sizes across conditions may limit generalisability
target_learners: Early primary school teachers (of pupils aged 4–7)
target_learning_goals: Teaching programming and computational thinking with educational robots
examples: Teachers in Intervention+ attended a 3-h robot workshop led by two researchers including a presentation on programming concepts, hands-on Cubetto practice, and discussions on incorporating programming into existing curricula
key_sources: Hughes, A., Gerson, S. A., & van Schaik, J. E. (2026). Teacher-led robot intervention in early primary school classrooms improves pupil and teacher outcomes. Computers & Education, 242: 105510. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2025.105510

article_title: Enhancing peer feedback provision through user interface scaffolding: A comparative examination of scripting and self-monitoring techniques
citation: Lahza, H. F., Demartini, G., Noroozi, O., Gašević, D., Sadiq, S., & Khosravi, H. (2025). Enhancing peer feedback provision through user interface scaffolding: A comparative examination of scripting and self-monitoring techniques. Computers & Education, 230, 105260. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2025.105260
title: Script theory of guidance (SToG) for computer-supported collaborative learning
description: The script theory of guidance (SToG) for CSCL, built upon dynamic memory theory, distinguishes between internal and external collaboration scripts. An internal script is "an existing configuration of knowledge components in students' minds that shapes their comprehension and actions in collaborative practice". An external script is a scaffold that can trigger internal script components, usually presented by an external source such as a graphical user interface, targeted towards those who lack experience with collaborative practice.
requirements: Students typically have a low level of interaction with each other and often fail to apply their existing knowledge
target_learning_goals: collaborative learning
peer feedback

Computers & Education, 230, 105260. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2025.105260
title: Winne and Hadwin's four-phase self-regulated learning model
description: Winne and Hadwin (1998) proposed a loosely coupled SRL model consisting of two main processes (control and self-monitoring) that operate iteratively over each of three main phases and an optional fourth phase: (1) definition of task, (2) goals and plans, (3) studying tactics and learning strategies, and (4) adaptations. In each phase, a student produces products that they monitor to generate internal feedback through an evaluation operation against standards. These products can further contribute to generating external feedback from the environment.
requirements: Students monitor products against standards identified by past experiences or knowledge and information provided by the task
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning
peer feedback

title: RiPPLE learning platform
description: RiPPLE is a discipline-agnostic learning platform operating at the course level, utilised to facilitate a student-centred, interactive, and collaborative learning environment. The platform incorporates learnersourcing, learning analytics, and adaptive learning mechanisms. Students generate learning resources (MCQs, worked examples, flashcards, slides, notes) and review peers' resources, which upon approval become accessible to the entire class for educational purposes.
requirements: Students are tasked with generating various types of learning resources and reviewing peers' resources
target_learning_goals: content creation
peer feedback

citation: Lahza, H. F., Demartini, G., Noroozi, O., Gašević, D., Sadiq, S., & Khosravi, H. (2025). Computers & Education, 230, 105260. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2025.105260
title: Design peer feedback interfaces based on scripting scaffolds for superior short-term feedback quality
description: The study's findings suggest that scripting interfaces, which scaffold feedback provision through structured prompts, lead to longer and higher-quality peer feedback compared to self-monitoring interfaces in the short term. The article states that "Students in the scripted condition provided longer and superior-quality feedback" than the self-monitoring condition. This principle supports designing feedback interfaces with structured prompts.
requirements: Interface design should avoid over-scripting to prevent overwhelming students
constraints: The scripting condition may restrict students' freedom, as it offers a step-by-step user interface
target_learning_goals: peer feedback provision
examples: The study randomly assigned 149 students to either a scripting interface with structured prompts or a self-monitoring interface with checkboxes for providing peer feedback.

article_title: Women and computers. Effects of stereotype threat on attribution of failure
citation: Koch, S. C., Müller, S. M., & Sieverding, M. (2008). Women and computers. Effects of stereotype threat on attribution of failure. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2008.05.007
title: Stereotype threat theory applied to the computer domain links threat to maladaptive attribution patterns
description: The article applies stereotype threat theory (Steele, 1997) to the computer domain, proposing that when a negative task-relevant stereotype about one's ingroup becomes salient, performance impairments and maladaptive attributions follow. The authors state that "maladaptive attribution patterns can be caused by stereotype threat in the minority group (in our study, women), and can be a point of reference for their future performance." The study bridges attribution theory and stereotype threat theory in the computer domain.
requirements: Conditions for stereotype threat include domain identification, task difficulty, and stereotype relevance to the situation
constraints: The effect was demonstrated only in the negative threat condition; no significant gender differences emerged in the positive or control conditions
target_learning_goals: computer self-efficacy
attribution patterns after failure
key_sources: Koch, S. C., Müller, S. M., & Sieverding, M. (2008). Women and computers. Effects of stereotype threat on attribution of failure. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2008.05.007

article_title: Evaluating a tactile and a tangible multi-tablet gamified quiz system for collaborative learning in primary education
citation: García Sanjuan, F.; El Jurdi, S.; Jaén Martínez, FJ.; Nácher-Soler, VE. (2018). Evaluating a tactile and a tangible multi-tablet gamified quiz system for collaborative learning in primary education. Computers & Education. 123:65-84. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.04.011
title: Quizbot: A Multi-Tablet Gamified Quiz System for Collaborative Learning
description: Quizbot is a tablet-based multi-display environment designed as a gamified board-shaped quiz setting where students jointly control a robot to reach correct answers. The board contains keys, walls, and bombs, and the four movement commands are split among participants so that "no single child could make progress alone". Teachers define questions beforehand through a web app, supporting three question styles: single/multiple choice, ordering, and accumulation.
requirements: Requires four participants per group, each controlling one movement command of the robot
Requires a web app for teachers to define questions beforehand
constraints: Points, badges, and leaderboards were deliberately left out of the design to avoid pointification
target_learning_goals: Collaborative learning across language, natural science, history, and geography
examples: Used with eighty children in groups of four in a summer school activity in Valencia, Spain

title: Six Conditions for Successful Collaborative Learning in Quizbot
description: The article designs Quizbot to meet six conditions for successful collaborative learning identified by Szewkis et al.: common goal, coordination and communication between peers, positive interdependence, awareness of peers' work, individual accountability, and joint rewards. The system enforces these by splitting robot controls among participants, placing tablets publicly, and rewarding or punishing the team alike, so that "they get rewarded or punished alike, which makes them constantly try to improve their collaboration".
requirements: All six conditions must be met simultaneously for collaboration to emerge
constraints: Activities that are only competitive promote negative interdependence, so cooperation must be built into the activity design
target_learners: Primary school children working in small groups
target_learning_goals: Collaboration skills including negotiation, planning, communication, and organization
examples: Quizbot distributes one movement command per student and keeps the distribution of commands publicly visible to support individual accountability

article_title: Digital support for academic writing: A review of technologies and pedagogies
citation: Strobl, Carola; Ailhaud, Emilie; Benetos, Kalliopi; Devitt, Ann; Kruse, Otto. (2019). Digital support for academic writing : a review of technologies and pedagogies. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.12.005
title: Review framework mapping writing-support technologies across writing processes, pedagogical approaches, feedback modalities and technological specifications
description: The review organises the field of digital writing-support technologies using a framework of 26 quantitative and qualitative features spanning four axes: writing processes, pedagogical approaches, feedback modalities and technological specifications. It applies this framework to a systematic analysis of 44 tools supporting first and second language writers in secondary and higher education, focusing on "instructional affordances based on their technological specifications". The framework also distinguishes micro-level revision support from macro-level strategy support, enabling the review to locate gaps in the state of the art.
requirements: Applies to technologies designed to support writing instruction in secondary and higher education, for first and second language writers
constraints: Previous studies centred on Automated Writing Evaluation, Automated Essay Scoring and rarer Intelligent Tutoring Systems, addressing mainly essay writing needs in US secondary school instruction
target_learners: secondary and higher education students, first and second language writers
target_learning_goals: academic writing
revision
writing strategies

article_title: Educators' open educational collaboration online: The dilemma of emotional ownership
citation: Educators' Open Educational Collaboration Online: The Dilemma of Emotional Ownership. (2016). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1115784
title: Model of educators' intention to engage in open educational collaboration in virtual communities
description: The article validates a data-driven model explaining educators' behavioral intention to engage in open educational collaboration in virtual communities. It comprises seven personal-level influencing factors — intention (INTOE), emotional ownership (OWN), outcome expectations (OE), preference for exchanging ideas online (PEI), affective community commitment (ACC), previous experience (EXP), and preference for collaborative OER development (ENJ) — plus two organizational control variables. The model was tested with structural equation modelling on survey data from 100 educators.
requirements: Survey measurement of all constructs using adapted or newly developed scales validated through exploratory factor analysis
constraints: Organizational innovativeness and OER awareness control paths showed no significant effects
target_learners: educators in higher education and other educational institutions
target_learning_goals: collaborative development of open educational resources and practices

title: Model of exposure to collaborative OER development at the moment of engagement
description: Figure 3 presents a synthesis model positioned at the moment of exposure when the educator discovers the opportunity to engage in collaborative OER development. The context and setting revealed during exposure set the conditions against which the educator weighs whether to engage; the critical issue is the expected level of openness and transparency, and for contribution behaviors, trust, comfort and familiarity with the practice are strong predictors.

constraints: Engagement-related behavior is not constant or linear; motivating factors may change over time, and the analysis does not indicate that moving from closed to open is a process or sequence of events

target_learning_goals: deciding whether to contribute to or dismiss opportunities for collaborative OER development

title: Idea-sharing platform for collaborative development of educational ideas

citation: Gutiérrez-Páez, N. F., Santos, P., Hernández-Leo, D., & Carrió, M. (2023). A study of motivations, behavior, and contributions quality in online communities of teachers: A data analytics approach. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104829
title: ILDE+ platform for online communities of pre-service teachers sharing learning designs
description: ILDE+ is a customized version of the Integrated Learning Design Environment supporting an online community of pre-service teachers who explore, share, discuss, and co-create learning designs. It implements six main functionalities including an LD creation template with metadata, commenting, design duplication preserving authorship, co-design via shared authorship, and social features such as "a like button for the designs, counters of visualizations and comments, or follow button for the members of the community." The platform logs user actions for analytics.

constraints: The platform was studied in the early stages of the community, when comments and likes were rarely used

description: The Analytics Layers for Learning Design framework proposes "three layers of data analytics to support and inform decision-making in learning design: learning experience (learning analytics), learning design elements (design analytics) and community of educators (community analytics)." This study's cross-case analysis of motivations, behavior, and contribution quality contributes to the community analytics layer, using data to inform stakeholders in online communities of teachers.

article_title: Investigating L2 listening comprehension and experience in immersive and interactive virtual reality: An experimental study
citation: Liang, Y., & Hu, G. (2026). Investigating L2 listening comprehension and experience in immersive and interactive virtual reality: An experimental study. Computers & Education, 248, 105593. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2026.105593
title: Four-dimensional flow model (Heutte et al., 2021) distinguishing cognitive and affective components
description: The article applies Heutte et al.'s (2021) refined four-dimensional flow model, restructured from Csikszentmihalyi's original dimensions because "not all original flow dimensions were consistently observed" in educational settings. The first three dimensions — cognitive control, immersion and time transformation, and loss of self-consciousness — collectively measure the cognitive component (absorption), while the fourth dimension, autotelic experience, measures the affective component. The study operationalizes listening experience as state flow using the EduFlow-2 scale based on this model.
requirements: Measured via the validated EduFlow-2 scale with 12 statements rated on a seven-point Likert scale
constraints: Developed specifically for educational settings where some original flow dimensions were not consistently observed
target_learning_goals: L2 listening comprehension
Flow experience during learning tasks
