title: Design VR learning environments to align interactive features with cognitive demands of the learning task
description: The article emphasizes "the importance of careful VR design to ensure that immersive features support, rather than distract from, cognitive engagement." Misalignment between VR's interactive elements and the cognitive demands of the task can induce extraneous processing that consumes resources needed for meaningful learning. Instructional design should mitigate cognitive overload while leveraging VR's affective benefits.
requirements: VR interactive elements must be congruent with the primary learning task to avoid extraneous cognitive load
constraints: Rich contextual details in VR can divert attention away from the listening task and cause learners to miss key information
target_learning_goals: L2 listening comprehension
examples: Over half of VR interviewees reported that rich contextual elements diverted attention from the listening task, causing them to miss key details

title: Design adaptive learning activities to foster quality of learner-content interaction rather than time on task
description: The article recommends intentional design and personalisation of learning activities using adaptive learning technology to enhance student-content interaction. It concludes that "the quality of study time matters, using a well-conceived instructional design that encourages deep engagement with learning", challenging the assumption that more time on task indicates deeper learning.

Instructor flexibility to select topics, depth of coverage and duration of assignments
constraints: Impact is modulated by learner diversity
Cannot infer direct causal relationship from observational data

student engagement with course content
examples: LearnSmart was used to create five weekly adaptive reading assignments over a six-week period in a first-year Macroeconomics course

title: LearnSmart adaptive learning tool on McGraw-Hill Connect platform
description: LearnSmart is an adaptive learning tool on McGraw-Hill Connect, a web-based assignment and assessment platform. It "allows content to be actively tailored to students' needs", assessing answers to practice questions, identifying struggling topics and adapting accordingly. A reading assignment is not marked complete until the student demonstrates adequate understanding, with immediate feedback and confidence rating options.

title: Learner-content interaction as a theoretical lens for adaptive learning effects on performance
description: The article uses learner-content interaction — "time spent with course content such as textbooks and class notes" — as a theoretical lens to explain how adaptive learning affects performance. It distinguishes learner-content interaction from learner-instructor, learner-learner and student-LMS interaction types, and measures it through two indicators: time spent and number of completed adaptive assignments. The lens frames assignment completion as capturing both adaptive learning use and cognitive engagement.

constraints: Generalisability is recognised as a challenge of using online traces to measure self-regulated learning

article_title: Analyzing the educational design, use and effect of spatial games for cultural heritage: A literature review
citation: Malegiannaki, I. & Daradoumis, T. (2017). Analyzing the educational design, use and effect of spatial games for cultural heritage: a Literature Review. Computers & Education, 108. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2017.01.007
title: Taxonomy of spatial games for cultural heritage by genre, context of use, social relationships and reported outcomes
description: The review organizes 34 spatial games for cultural heritage along the axes of its five research questions: game genre and plot (RQ1/RQ2), context of use (RQ3), number of players and social relationships (RQ4), and reported outcomes (RQ5). It classifies games as "action, puzzle, trivia, role-playing, simulation and adventure games", noting that "Pure strategy games were not traced, but elements of this genre are mentioned when found in games of other genres". It also distinguishes exploration and narration as content-handling dimensions.
requirements: Games reviewed must enable a physical or virtual interaction with a cultural place; papers with solely historical or intangible cultural content, non-digital games, and games not yet implemented were excluded
constraints: The review covers 2000–2016 literature found via Scopus and is not based on the game experience itself, which the authors state as a limitation; commercial and unpublished educational games were excluded
target_learning_goals: knowledge acquisition of cultural content
comprehension of cultural contexts
procedural knowledge of past roles and practices
examples: Genre categorization of 34 games from 41 papers selected via Scopus searches between 2000 and 2016

citation: Norbert Pachler, Caroline Daly, Yishay Mor, Harvey Mellar. (2009). Formative e-assessment: practitioner cases. Computers and Education. https://hal.science/hal-00592754
title: Design pattern methodology for developing cases of formative e-assessment with practitioners
description: The article documents a design pattern methodology in which cases of formative e-assessment were developed iteratively with the UK education practitioner community. Practitioners from a range of post-16 education contexts collaboratively developed cases of practice, from which patterns were extracted to inform future software design. The methodology aimed to scope the 'domain' of formative e-assessment by developing cases and identifying key formative processes within them that are affected by the use of technologies.

examples: Cases of formative e-assessment developed iteratively with the UK education practitioner community from June 2008 to January 2009

citation: Boelens, R., Voet, M., & De Wever, B. (2018). The design of blended learning in response to student diversity in higher education: Instructors' views and use of differentiated instruction in blended learning. Computers & Education, 120, 197–212. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.02.009
title: Typology of three instructor profiles for designing blended learning in response to student diversity: disregard, adaptation, and transformation
description: The article introduces a typology of three profiles of instructors' beliefs about designing blended learning to address student diversity, which "emerged from the data". Instructors with a disregard profile "offered no specific ideas about how to design blended learning arrangements to meet the needs of these students"; an adaptation profile limits support to "adjustments to existing learning arrangements"; a transformation profile holds that arrangements "should be designed in a completely different way". The typology nuances prior work treating tailored instruction as one-dimensional.
requirements: Instructors' beliefs are elicited through interviews about designing blended learning for students with different prior educational experiences
constraints: The typology emerged from a small qualitative sample in two adult education centers and its generalizability is limited by the article's own account

responding to student diversity
examples: The study classified 20 instructors: four disregard, six adaptation, ten transformation profiles

article_title: The potential of 360-degree virtual reality videos to teach water-safety skills to children
citation: Araiza-Alba, P., Keane, T., Matthews, B., Simpson, K., Strugnell, G., Chen, W. S., & Kaufman, J. (2020). The potential of 360-degree Virtual Reality videos to teach water-safety skills to children. https://www.lsv.com.au/vr
title: Cognitive theory of multimedia learning and interest theory as frameworks for predicting learning from 360° VR
description: The article draws on two frameworks to predict that compelling 360° VR experiences facilitate learning. CTML "posits that students learn best when they engage in active cognitive processing which can be facilitated by students connecting the new information with existing knowledge", while interest theory holds that "learning is best achieved when the learner is sufficiently interested in the material". The study tested whether VR's engaging, immersive qualities would enhance learning, finding support for interest-theory predictions about engagement but not for CTML predictions of superior learning outcomes.
requirements: An immersive virtual environment designed to emulate familiar real-world settings to support connections with existing knowledge
constraints: The study found no learning advantage for 360° VR over traditional media, so CTML-based predictions of superior outcomes were not supported
target_learning_goals: Water-safety knowledge and hazard identification
key_sources: Araiza-Alba, P., Keane, T., Matthews, B., Simpson, K., Strugnell, G., Chen, W. S., & Kaufman, J. (2020). The potential of 360-degree Virtual Reality videos to teach water-safety skills to children. https://www.lsv.com.au/vr

article_title: The potential of 360-degree virtual reality videos to teach water-safety skills to children
citation: Araiza-Alba, P., Keane, T., Matthews, B., Simpson, K., Strugnell, G., Chen, W. S., & Kaufman, J. (2020). The potential of 360-degree Virtual Reality videos to teach water-safety skills to children. https://www.lsv.com.au/vr
title: Use 360° VR videos to teach safety skills for hazardous situations without exposing learners to real danger
description: The article recommends 360° VR videos as a safe way to teach skills for hazardous situations: "it can expose trainees to simulated hazardous situations without putting them in any actual physical danger". The water-safety study demonstrated this by letting children experience beach rip-current hazards virtually. The authors extend this to other hazards children may encounter and to organizations such as museums and water-safety bodies.
requirements: Content designed to address specific hazards relevant to learners, with realistic first-person experience
constraints: The 360° videos used were passive experiences where participants were limited to the role of observers, which the authors note may limit learning benefits relative to more interactive VR
target_learning_goals: Safety knowledge and hazard identification
examples: Children watched four 360° beach videos on reading safety signs, spotting a rip current, surviving a rip current, and asking for help, using cardboard headsets and headphones

citation: Granić, A., Mifsud, C., & Ćukušić, M. (2009). Design, implementation and validation of a Europe-wide pedagogical framework for e-Learning. Computers & Education, 53, 1052–1081. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2009.05.018

description: The article presents a pedagogical framework (PF) developed within the Europe-wide UNITE project for secondary schools. It "consists of five components": pedagogical framework context, pedagogical approaches, assessment techniques, teacher education, and current pedagogical practices implemented in national curricula and national specifics. These components "produce the set of parameters which drive and guide the production of learning scenarios", making the learning scenario the mechanism that holds together the pedagogical and technical sides of development.

constraints: Designed for secondary schools in a Europe-wide network of 14 schools

title: Provide supports for change at pedagogical design, administrative, resource and professional-development levels
description: The article states that teachers who make the most changes in the classroom are those with the greatest level of support, and that supports need to be at the levels of "pedagogical design, coordinator support, administrative support" and "the provision of the required resources and appropriate continuing professional development". The UNITE project sought to create this support structure to ensure maximal benefits of the e-/m-Learning system for teaching and learning.
requirements: Supports must span pedagogical design, coordinator and administrative support, resources, and continuing professional development
constraints: Support needs are greatest where teacher change is expected
target_learning_goals: effective integration of e-Learning into teaching
examples: The project put supports for change in place at the levels of pedagogical design, administrative support and the provision of the required resources and appropriate continuing professional development.

title: Four key pedagogical approaches (constructivist, blended, collaborative, active learning) derived from user requirements
description: User requirements collected across the 14-school network established that "teachers want to use the system while applying autonomous and active learning principles in both individual and collaborative contexts". Consequently, "principles of constructivist theory, blended, collaborative and active learning (all derived from user requirements) are the four key pedagogical principles" representing one PF component, integrated into the learning scenarios and promoted in the implementation phase.

constraints: Approaches were derived from the specific user requirements of the participating schools

article_title: Storyboarding: A method for bootstrapping the design of computer-based educational tasks
citation: Jones, I. (2008). Storyboarding: A method for bootstrapping the design of computer-based educational tasks. https://dspace.lboro.ac.uk/
title: PowerPoint storyboarding tool and procedures
description: The tool used was Microsoft PowerPoint, chosen because it was already installed and easy to use. Copy and paste tools allowed new slides to be cloned with minor stepwise adjustments, and the "click to add notes" facility allowed slides to be annotated and date-stamped to build a time-line of evolving ideas. Files were shared with a colleague who added date-stamped comments as feedback.
requirements: Copy and paste tools for cloning slides
Manual dating and formatting of comments, since PowerPoint lacks a Reviewing mode
constraints: PowerPoint does not offer a Reviewing mode and comments had to be manually dated and formatted
Drawing tools are constrained to basic shapes and text
target_learning_goals: design of computer-based learning tasks
key_sources: Jones, I. (2008). Storyboarding: A method for bootstrapping the design of computer-based educational tasks. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2008.01.002

article_title: Storyboarding: A method for bootstrapping the design of computer-based educational tasks
citation: Jones, I. (2008). Storyboarding: A method for bootstrapping the design of computer-based educational tasks. https://dspace.lboro.ac.uk/
title: Storyboard design elements to maintain: abstracted interfaces, participant icons, imported data, peer feedback, test plans
description: The article enumerates elements to maintain when repeating the exercise: "Abstracted interfaces" with functionality in a black box, "Participant icons and call outs" capturing assumptions about collaborative learning, "Imported classroom data" from pupils' written strategies, "Peer feedback", and "Storyboards as test plans" for the first prototype.
requirements: Peer feedback channels must be opened through sharable storyboard documentation
target_learning_goals: collaborative mathematics learning
examples: A black box marked TOOLS reminded the designer to keep interface functionality shut; C and R icons with call outs captured hypothesised interactions
key_sources: Jones, I. (2008). Storyboarding: A method for bootstrapping the design of computer-based educational tasks. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2008.01.002

article_title: Storyboarding: A method for bootstrapping the design of computer-based educational tasks
citation: Jones, I. (2008). Storyboarding: A method for bootstrapping the design of computer-based educational tasks. https://dspace.lboro.ac.uk/
title: Storyboarding pitfalls to avoid: hidden assumptions, proceduralism, inefficiency
description: The article also lists elements to avoid: "Hidden assumptions", since an interface assumption grounded in the Equivalence Calculator haunted the early storyboards despite abstraction attempts; "Proceduralism", because overcoming an implementation impasse involves exposing hidden assumptions rather than following a smooth process; and "Inefficiency", as many slides were created over six months.
requirements: Awareness that interface assumptions may persist implicitly even when not represented
constraints: Storyboarding continued for six months with many slides created before guidelines were identified
target_learning_goals: robust learning task design
key_sources: Jones, I. (2008). Storyboarding: A method for bootstrapping the design of computer-based educational tasks. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2008.01.002

article_title: Storyboarding: A method for bootstrapping the design of computer-based educational tasks
citation: Jones, I. (2008). Storyboarding: A method for bootstrapping the design of computer-based educational tasks. https://dspace.lboro.ac.uk/
title: Storyboards as virtual data from thought experiments
description: The article frames the storyboards produced as "virtual data" captured from thought experiments about imagined learning tasks. Thought experiments draw on the educational literature, the curriculum domain and the designer's professional intuitions, and the storyboards make their outcomes analysable and sharable: "analysable, sharable thought experiments about notational activity, pupil discourse and the role of R in imagined trials". This responds to Papert's call for a more developed culture of disciplined thought experiment.
requirements: Sharable documentation so that peers can review the thought experiments
constraints: Thought experiments have been acknowledged to lack the rigour and systematicity of actual experiments
target_learning_goals: relational understanding of the equals sign
key_sources: Jones, I. (2008). Storyboarding: A method for bootstrapping the design of computer-based educational tasks. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2008.01.002

article_title: Storyboarding: A method for bootstrapping the design of computer-based educational tasks
citation: Jones, I. (2008). Storyboarding: A method for bootstrapping the design of computer-based educational tasks. https://dspace.lboro.ac.uk/
title: Diagnostic computer-based arithmetical puzzle task implemented in Imagine Logo
description: The outcome of the bootstrapping process was a diagnostic computer-based task for investigating mathematical thinking, in which pupils solve provided puzzles using provided equalities to transform an arithmetical sum into its answer. The software was programmed in Imagine Logo, which "lends itself to the fast proto-typing of microworlds". Implementation occurred rapidly and little re-programming or debugging has proved necessary despite substantial trialing in a variety of primary schools.
requirements: Two keypads for entering notation, based on the Equivalence Calculator
Researcher (R) interventions as a central element of the task
target_learning_goals: distinguishing compositional, commutative and partitional notation
examples: A sequence of puzzles was created for trialing with pairs of Year 5 pupils in a cross-section of schools
key_sources: Jones, I. (2008). Storyboarding: A method for bootstrapping the design of computer-based educational tasks. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2008.01.002

article_title: Motivating factors in online language teacher education in southern Argentina
citation: Banegas, D.L., & Manzur Busleimán, G. (2014). Motivating factors in online language teacher education in southern Argentina. Computers & Education, 76, 131–142. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2014.03.014
title: Do not make forum participation or group-work tasks mandatory in online teacher education
description: The authors argue that because trainees may not value collaborative learning, "forum participation or group-work tasks should not be mandatory." They recommend trainees be allowed to choose collaborative processes and instances, for example by starting their own forum threads and posing their own questions. Building a learning community, they argue, should be democratic and participatory rather than imposed.
requirements: Online course developers should not assume all trainees enjoy collaborative learning or prefer an interpersonal learning style
constraints: Based on one specific programme where most participants were practicing teachers in a region with no f2f alternatives
target_learners: practicing teachers in online pre-service teacher education
target_learning_goals: teacher qualification
professional development
examples: Trainees created a closed Facebook group to mitigate forum deficiencies, exchanging opinions, tips, and materials and arranging study groups.
key_sources: Banegas, D.L., & Manzur Busleimán, G. (2014). Motivating factors in online language teacher education in southern Argentina. Computers & Education, 76, 131–142. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2014.03.014

article_title: Motivating factors in online language teacher education in southern Argentina
citation: Banegas, D.L., & Manzur Busleimán, G. (2014). Motivating factors in online language teacher education in southern Argentina. Computers & Education, 76, 131–142. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2014.03.014
title: Dynamic and processual view of motivation with future selves in online teacher education
description: The study adopts Ushioda's (2009) dynamic and processual view of motivation and a holistic approach integrating possible selves and future self-guides as conceptualised in Dörnyei (2009). The authors interpret participants' initial motivation through "future selves which contain elements of who they want to be and what they ought to be", with ideal and ought-to-be selves in dialogical relationship. This framework explains why the extrinsic degree goal coexisted with genuine interest in learning.
requirements: Motivation research should contemplate mixed methods and instruments investigating both personal and interpersonal factors
constraints: Findings derive from one programme in a specific regional context
target_learning_goals: motivation to enrol and persist in online teacher education
examples: Participants' future selves included feared selves as teachers without a degree, surveyed via items on ideal identities and career prospects.
key_sources: Banegas, D.L., & Manzur Busleimán, G. (2014). Motivating factors in online language teacher education in southern Argentina. Computers & Education, 76, 131–142. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2014.03.014

title: Visualization tool for exploring trainees' trace data in VR training systems
description: The article describes a visualization tool used to explore trainees' trace data from the virtual reality training system. It was used to "pose nonobservable behavioral variables related to displayed errors", supporting the identification of error patterns associated with misconceptions and confusion when combined with human expert aid.

citation: Denis Pasco, Erik Gustafsson, Lucas Burget, Thibault Asselborn, Pierre Dillenbourg, Consortium Lamue, Marie Mazerolle. (2025). Rapid in-class assessment of handwriting using a digital tablet: Multidimensional analysis of gender and socioeconomic status. Computers & Education: X Reality, 232, 105311. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2025.105311
title: Dynamilis digital application for rapid in-class handwriting assessment
description: Dynamilis is a digital application that assesses the handwriting of 5–12 year old children using a consumer tablet and digital pen, scoring static, kinematic, pressure and tilt components from high-frequency pen data normalized by age and combined via PCA into a weighted total score clipped between 0 and 100. The article demonstrates its use for "rapid and in-class" assessment with 1361 second graders, capturing dynamics "not directly observable by teacher through simple observation".

article_title: Tracking e-learning through published papers: A systematic review
citation: Rodrigues, H., Almeida, F., Figueiredo, V. & Lopes, S. L. (2019). Tracking e-learning through published papers: a systematic review. Computers and Education. 136, 87-98. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.03.007
title: Four-dimension conceptual framework of e-learning research
description: The review organizes e-learning research into four dominant themes identified through Leximancer concept mapping: "education (314 hits)", "learning (208 hits)", "student (119 hits)" and "use (109 hits)". These dimensions group the literature's concepts into a holistic map that the authors argue outperforms other systematic reviews for understanding e-learning. The framework serves as the article's organizing taxonomy for the e-learning construct.
requirements: Requires a corpus of peer-reviewed articles on e-learning and education and qualitative text-analysis software such as Leximancer
constraints: Analysis is qualitative; the authors note limitations due to the qualitative nature of the analysis and propose meta-analysis with other databases as future work
target_learning_goals: understanding the e-learning construct across academic areas
examples: The concept map in Fig. 1 groups concepts (grey dots) into the four topics with hit counts
key_sources: Rodrigues, H., Almeida, F., Figueiredo, V. & Lopes, S. L. (2019). Tracking e-learning through published papers: a systematic review. Computers and Education. 136, 87-98. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.03.007

article_title: Tracking e-learning through published papers: A systematic review
citation: Rodrigues, H., Almeida, F., Figueiredo, V. & Lopes, S. L. (2019). Tracking e-learning through published papers: a systematic review. Computers and Education. 136, 87-98. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.03.007
title: Align e-learning usability with pedagogical quality and learner needs
description: The review's literature synthesis argues that usability in e-learning must be learner-centered: "The focus must be on the pedagogical aspects and not the technology in order to develop useful and functional tools." Usability is described as vital because it mitigates high dropout rates, low satisfaction, and staff workload. The review recommends aligning ease of use with pedagogical quality when developing e-learning tools.
requirements: Usability evaluation must place the user/learner at the center of the design process
constraints: The review notes there is still no consolidated evaluation methodology for e-learning applications
target_learning_goals: effective use of e-learning systems
reduced dropout and improved satisfaction
examples: The review cites usability features such as navigating and organizing educational contents according to individual cognitive styles
key_sources: Rodrigues, H., Almeida, F., Figueiredo, V. & Lopes, S. L. (2019). Tracking e-learning through published papers: a systematic review. Computers and Education. 136, 87-98. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.03.007

article_title: Tracking e-learning through published papers: A systematic review
citation: Rodrigues, H., Almeida, F., Figueiredo, V. & Lopes, S. L. (2019). Tracking e-learning through published papers: a systematic review. Computers and Education. 136, 87-98. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.03.007
title: Leximancer text-analysis software for systematic review coding
description: Leximancer is the qualitative data-analysis software the review used to extract meaning from the 99 retrieved articles. The article describes it as "a tool that adopts a quantitative approach, to conduct a qualitative analysis", using "Bayesian measurements that record the event of a word and associates it to the event of a progression of different words", coding fragments of content from one sentence to groups of sentences. It produced the concept map underlying the review's four-dimension framework.
requirements: Requires a corpus of text documents to analyze and produces concept maps from word co-occurrence
constraints: The article notes limitations due to the qualitative nature of the analysis
target_learning_goals: coding and synthesizing large bodies of educational literature
examples: The software produced the concept map in Fig. 1 grouping concepts into the four dominant topics

article_title: Unpacking the relationship between screen use and educational outcomes in childhood: A systematic literature review
citation: Caballero-Julia, D., Martín-Lucas, J., & Andrade-Silva, L. E. (2024). Unpacking the relationship between screen use and educational outcomes in childhood: A systematic literature review. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105049
title: Promote digital literacy from a young age and digital awareness and education among parents to ensure healthy childhood screen use.
description: The review concludes that children's healthy screen use depends largely on parents and teachers having the right tools to circumvent the risks of overexposure. It states it is "vitally important to promote digital literacy from a young age" and, on the other hand, digital awareness and education among parents. This responds to findings that children lack critical approaches to screens despite handling devices easily.
requirements: Teacher training in appropriate classroom screen use
Family education schemes guiding parents and children toward healthier coexistence
constraints: Research into parental guidelines and digital literacy mentoring schemes is reported as contradictory and inconsistent
target_learning_goals: digital literacy
critical and civic online mindset
responsible technology use
examples: The review cites studies concluding that proper teacher training is extremely important for correct classroom screen use
key_sources: Caballero-Julia, D., Martín-Lucas, J., & Andrade-Silva, L. E. (2024). Unpacking the relationship between screen use and educational outcomes in childhood: A systematic literature review. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105049

article_title: Unpacking the relationship between screen use and educational outcomes in childhood: A systematic literature review
citation: Caballero-Julia, D., Martín-Lucas, J., & Andrade-Silva, L. E. (2024). Unpacking the relationship between screen use and educational outcomes in childhood: A systematic literature review. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105049
title: Tri-phasic periodisation of childhood screen research as an organising framework for the field.
description: This framework organises the scientific literature on childhood screen use into three publication periods identified through MANOVA-Biplot analysis of a lexical matrix built from 158 article abstracts. The review states that "the first period (pre-2016) corresponds to the beginning of concerns over addictive effects" and healthy use of devices, the second (2016–2020) combines educational applications and the role of families, and the third centres on negative effects on identity building, health, wellbeing and behaviour involving smartphones. The framework provides a historical perspective intended to guide future research.
requirements: A corpus of article abstracts retrieved from Scopus and processed with IRaMuTeQ lemmatisation and a frequency matrix
constraints: Based exclusively on the Scopus database; exclusion of other databases could limit the breadth of the literature reviewed
target_learning_goals: understanding trends in research on childhood screen use
key_sources: Caballero-Julia, D., Martín-Lucas, J., & Andrade-Silva, L. E. (2024). Unpacking the relationship between screen use and educational outcomes in childhood: A systematic literature review. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105049

article_title: SpeakApp-Kids! Virtual reality training to reduce fear of public speaking in children – A proof of concept
citation: Sülter, R.E., Ketelaar, P.E., & Lange, W.G. (2022). SpeakApp-Kids! Virtual reality training to reduce fear of public speaking in children: A proof of concept. Computers & Education, 178, article 104384. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2021.104384
title: SpeakApp-Kids! VR prototype for public speaking practice
description: The SpeakApp-Kids! prototype is a virtual reality application that embeds repeated brief exposures to a virtual audience for children practising public speaking. The article describes it as "a prototype of the Virtual Reality (VR) SpeakApp-Kids!" used across three public speaking practice sessions before an actual presentation. It was evaluated in children aged 9-12 years as a proof of concept, with the aim of reducing state anxiety during practice and during the actual presentation, and reducing general public speaking anxiety.
requirements: Requires repeated brief exposures to a virtual audience embedded in the VR application across practice sessions.
constraints: The article presents it as a proof of concept and notes limitations were taken into account.
target_learning_goals: reduce public speaking anxiety during practice and actual presentations
key_sources: Sülter, R.E., Ketelaar, P.E., & Lange, W.G. (2022). SpeakApp-Kids! Virtual reality training to reduce fear of public speaking in children: A proof of concept. Computers & Education, 178, article 104384. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2021.104384

article_title: SpeakApp-Kids! Virtual reality training to reduce fear of public speaking in children – A proof of concept
citation: Sülter, R.E., Ketelaar, P.E., & Lange, W.G. (2022). SpeakApp-Kids! Virtual reality training to reduce fear of public speaking in children: A proof of concept. Computers & Education, 178, article 104384. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2021.104384
title: Use VR-based speech practice as an educational tool to reduce public speaking anxiety in children.
description: This principle recommends embedding VR-based speech practice with a virtual audience into education so that children can rehearse presentations before facing a real audience. The article concludes that "this VR SpeakApp-Kids! is a promising tool to be developed further as it has potential to serve as an educational tool for speech practice and thereby reducing public speaking anxiety". It further suggests the tool can prevent public speaking anxiety from developing in the first place, making it suitable for preventive use in classrooms.
requirements: Requires access to the VR SpeakApp-Kids! application and practice sessions with a virtual audience before the actual presentation.
constraints: The article states this holds taking limitations into account, as a proof of concept rather than a fully validated intervention.
target_learning_goals: reduce public speaking anxiety
prevent public speaking anxiety from developing
examples: Children practised presentations with the SpeakApp-Kids! VR prototype across three practice sessions before delivering an actual presentation, and were compared with control children preparing at home.

article_title: Mobile virtual reality for musical genre learning in primary education

article_title: The impact of an iPad-supported annotation and sharing technology on university students' learning
citation: Wakefield, J., Frawley, J. K., Tyler, J., & Dyson, L. E. (2018). The impact of an iPad-supported annotation and sharing technology on university students’ learning. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.03.013
title: Exercise caution in how instructor tablet use affects the classroom environment and what students learn
description: The article recommends that educators critically examine how tablet technology is implemented, especially in equation-centred subjects. The authors suggest that instructors "may decide to put the tablet aside and discuss the extended responses" after facilitating initial participation, and that care is needed to avoid letting the tablet dominate class time. This principle arises directly from the finding that tablet use benefited procedural learning at the expense of theoretical learning.
requirements: Instructors must monitor which types of questions and learning activities the tablet-supported interaction favours
constraints: The finding arises in a compulsory introductory first-year subject where student motivation and self-regulation may be low
target_learning_goals: procedural and theoretical disciplinary knowledge
key_sources: Wakefield, J., Frawley, J. K., Tyler, J., & Dyson, L. E. (2018). The impact of an iPad-supported annotation and sharing technology on university students’ learning. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.03.013

article_title: The impact of an iPad-supported annotation and sharing technology on university students' learning
citation: Wakefield, J., Frawley, J. K., Tyler, J., & Dyson, L. E. (2018). The impact of an iPad-supported annotation and sharing technology on university students’ learning. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.03.013
title: Affordances of tablet technology can introduce a bias towards some kinds of learning interactions over others
description: The article argues that the affordances of a technology, in the Norman (1988) sense, shape but do not dictate its educational use. The tablet's size, mobility and stylus input lend themselves to fast, structured, handwritten equation-based feedback, which "introduces a preferential bias for these types of questions over others that are less aligned". Because educators cannot fully anticipate how a tool will be appropriated in the classroom, ongoing evaluation of learning outcomes is needed rather than blanket adoption.
requirements: Deliberate, theoretically informed pedagogical design of how the technology is used in class
constraints: Neither educators nor educational technologists can know precisely how a given tool will be appropriated by instructors and students
target_learning_goals: understanding how technology affordances shape learning outcomes
key_sources: Wakefield, J., Frawley, J. K., Tyler, J., & Dyson, L. E. (2018). The impact of an iPad-supported annotation and sharing technology on university students’ learning. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.03.013

article_title: Scripting the role of assessor and assessee in peer assessment in a wiki environment: Impact on peer feedback quality and product improvement
citation: Gielen, M. & De Wever, B. (2015). Scripting the role of assessor and assessee in peer assessment in a wiki environment: Impact on peer feedback quality and product improvement. Computers & Education, 88, 370-386. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2015.07.012
title: Structure the roles of both assessee and assessor in peer assessment with a PFB request and content checklist to boost quality at the initial stage
description: The study recommends providing additional structure in peer assessment by giving the assessee a peer feedback request form and the assessor a content checklist, alongside a structured PFB template. The authors conclude that "providing additional structure, such as a content checklist for the assessor and a PFB request for the assessee is a useful approach to actively engage students in writing and assessment activities". The effect is strongest in the initial phase of performance.
requirements: a structured peer feedback template with feedback and feed forward on pre-specified criteria, and evaluation of received feedback to close the feedback loop
constraints: the effect of the additional structure diminishes over time after multiple practice occasions
target_learning_goals: academic abstract writing
peer feedback quality
examples: The study assigned 125 first-year students across control, request, content, and combination conditions over three wiki abstract-writing cycles.

article_title: Enhancing goal attainment in higher education with a scripted conversational agent: Effects of monitoring and reflection support in digital learning
citation: Martins van Jaarsveld, G., Wong, J., Baars, M., Specht, M., & Paas, F. (2025). Enhancing goal attainment in higher education with a scripted conversational agent: Effects of monitoring and reflection support in digital learning. Computers and Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2025.105441
title: Prioritize goal-monitoring activities in SRL interventions to support the transition from goal setting to goal striving
description: The article recommends that educators developing SRL supports prioritize goal-monitoring activities, because monitoring resulted in significant improvements in goal attainment while reflection alone did not. Implementing regular progress monitoring mechanisms is presented as an effective means of helping students remain engaged with their learning goals and supporting the transition to goal striving behaviours.
requirements: Requires a mechanism for regular progress-monitoring prompts, such as weekly check-in sessions
constraints: Reflection alone showed no immediate benefit in the short five-week intervention and may require longer periods
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning
goal attainment
examples: Participants in the MO and MO+RF conditions received weekly Thursday/Friday check-in prompts asking them to discuss their progress on the goal they set earlier that week

article_title: E-learning success determinants: Brazilian empirical study
citation: Cidral, W. A., Oliveira, T., Di Felice, M. & Aparicio, M. (2018). E-learning success determinants: Brazilian empirical study. Computers and Education, 122, 273-290. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2017.12.001
title: Integrated e-learning success model combining D&M IS success theory with e-learning satisfaction theory
description: The article proposes a research model integrating DeLone & McLean IS success theory with e-learning satisfaction theory (Sun et al.) and collaboration quality (Urbach et al.). It comprises 11 constructs: collaboration quality, service quality, information quality, system quality, learner computer anxiety, instructor attitude toward e-learning, diversity in assessment, learner perceived interaction with others, user satisfaction, use, and individual impact. The model was "empirically validated in higher education institutions and university centers in Brazil through a quantitative method of structural equation modeling."
requirements: Validated scales from prior IS success and e-learning studies for each construct
constraints: Studied only in higher education institutions in Brazil
target_learners: undergraduate and graduate university students in Brazil

user satisfaction
individual impact

article_title: Impact of ICT on students with high abilities. Bibliographic review (2008–2018)
citation: Fernández Batanero, José María; Reyes Rebollo, Miguel María; Montenegro Rueda, Marta. (2019). Impact of ICT on students with high abilities. Bibliographic review (2008–2018). Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.04.007
title: ICT with high-ability students: a bibliographic review of 2008–2018 research
description: The article is a bibliographic review of research on the impact of ICT on students with high abilities published between 2008 and 2018. It organizes the literature around how ICT is deployed with gifted learners, the outcomes reported, and the methods used, providing a structured map of a scattered field. The review frames ICT as a resource that can enrich learning for high-ability students while noting uneven evidence quality.
requirements: Access to published research on ICT and high-ability students from the 2008–2018 period
constraints: The review is limited to literature published between 2008 and 2018
target_learning_goals: Enrichment and extension of learning through ICT

citation: Pilli, Olga; Aksu, Meral. (2013). The effects of computer-assisted instruction on the achievement, attitudes and retention of fourth grade mathematics students in North Cyprus. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2012.10.010
title: Frizbi Mathematics 4 educational software
description: Frizbi Mathematics 4 is an educational software package for fourth-grade mathematics that was used as the experimental treatment in this study, covering three units: Multiplication of Natural Numbers, Division of Natural Numbers, and Fractions. The article describes it as "an effective tool" for "learning and teaching mathematics at the primary school level in North Cyprus." It was compared against lecture-based traditional instruction in a two-group quasi-experimental design.
requirements: Fourth-grade mathematics content matching the three units covered in the study
constraints: Evidence of effectiveness comes from a single primary school in Gazimagusa, North Cyprus

Division of natural numbers
Fractions

citation: Pilli, Olga; Aksu, Meral. (2013). The effects of computer-assisted instruction on the achievement, attitudes and retention of fourth grade mathematics students in North Cyprus. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2012.10.010
title: Use educational software such as Frizbi Mathematics 4 as an effective tool for primary school mathematics learning and teaching
description: The article concludes that "Frizbi Mathematics 4 for learning and teaching mathematics at the primary school level in North Cyprus is an effective tool." This principle recommends adopting computer-assisted instruction software as a substitute for or complement to lecture-based traditional instruction in primary mathematics, based on the measured achievement, retention, and attitude advantages reported in the study.
requirements: Educational software aligned with the curriculum units being taught
constraints: Evidence base is a single quasi-experimental study in one state primary school in North Cyprus

examples: The experimental group was taught using educational software, namely Frizbi Mathematics 4, while the control group was taught using lecture-based traditional instruction.

title: The Radix Endeavor: an MMOG with a genetics quest analyzed via back-end gameplay data
description: The Radix Endeavor is a massively multiplayer online game (MMOG) used by high school students, containing a genetics quest whose back-end data the study analyzed. The article describes collecting "back-end data from high school students as they played an MMOG called The Radix Endeavor." The game offers players multiple tools and pathways for quest completion.

constraints: Analysis focused on a specific genetics quest within the game

title: Trait examiner and trait decoder tools in the Radix genetics quest
description: Within the Radix genetics quest, players can use tools including the trait examiner and the trait decoder. The study found that "use of the trait examiner tool was most likely to lead to success, though a greater number of trait decoder tool uses could also lead to success." These tools support different pathways to quest completion.

title: Gameplay data analysis as a feedback loop in a learning ecosystem
description: The article frames gameplay data analysis as part of a feedback loop within a learning ecosystem: results of analyzing back-end data feed back to stakeholders to improve learning. It states the purpose is "to explore some of the ways in which gameplay data can be analyzed to yield results that feed back into the learning ecosystem." Data mining techniques such as classification trees generate results that inform game design validation and feedback to students and teachers.

article_title: Teachers' emphasis on developing students' digital information and communication skills (TEDDICS): A new construct in 21st century education
citation: Siddiq F., Scherer R. & Tondeur J. (2015). Teachers’ Emphasis on Developing Students’ Digital Information and Communication Skills (TEDDICS): A New Construct in 21st Century Education. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2015.10.006
title: TEDDICS scale — a multidimensional self-report instrument for teachers' emphasis on students' digital skills
description: The TEDDICS scale measures the degree to which teachers emphasize developing students' skills of accessing, evaluating, and sharing and communicating digital information, rated from "0 = no emphasis" to "3 = strong emphasis". It comprises 12 items across three subscales (3, 4, and 5 items) and showed very good reliability (ω = .92) with no ceiling or floor effects. The article proposes it as a qualitative component of ICT use in future research on technology acceptance and integration.
requirements: Teachers rate the degree to which they emphasize developing students' digital skills in their lessons on a 0–3 scale
constraints: Based on teacher self-reports, which may differ from actual classroom practice
target_learning_goals: developing students' digital information and communication skills
examples: Administered within the ICILS 2013 teacher questionnaire in Norwegian secondary schools

article_title: Teachers' emphasis on developing students' digital information and communication skills (TEDDICS): A new construct in 21st century education
citation: Siddiq F., Scherer R. & Tondeur J. (2015). Teachers’ Emphasis on Developing Students’ Digital Information and Communication Skills (TEDDICS): A New Construct in 21st Century Education. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2015.10.006
title: TEDDICS construct — teachers' emphasis on developing students' digital information and communication skills as a qualitative facet of ICT use
description: TEDDICS is a goal-oriented construct describing "a qualitative rather than a quantitative facet of ICT use", combining curricular demands, teaching practice, and teachers' beliefs about which digital skills matter. It is conceptualized around three interwoven but distinct factors — accessing, evaluating, and sharing and communicating digital information — mirroring frameworks of students' digital competence. The construct differs from frequency-of-use reports and from beliefs such as self-efficacy and perceived usefulness, providing a link between classroom practice and students' digital skills.
requirements: Validation evidence via ESEM measurement modeling and invariance testing across groups
constraints: Self-report measure; no direct link to students' actual digital skills in ICILS 2013
target_learning_goals: fostering students' digital information and communication skills

citation: Siddiq F., Scherer R. & Tondeur J. (2015). Teachers’ Emphasis on Developing Students’ Digital Information and Communication Skills (TEDDICS): A New Construct in 21st Century Education. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2015.10.006
title: Use ESEM with cross-loadings when measuring constructs whose factors plausibly overlap
description: The article argues that when construct factors are conceptually interwoven, ESEM provides "a better representation of the factorial structure than models without cross-loadings". Loosening the assumption of perfect item-factor links yields more robust measurement models that do not overestimate factor correlations. In this study ESEM outperformed CFA on all fit indices for TEDDICS.
requirements: Large samples and software supporting ESEM estimation (Mplus 7.2 was used)
constraints: CFA may remain adequate when perfect item-factor links genuinely hold
target_learning_goals: valid measurement of multidimensional teaching constructs
examples: The study applied target rotation within ESEM, allowing cross-loadings approximating zero rather than fixing them at zero

article_title: Between the lines: documenting the multiple dimensions of computer-supported collaborations
citation: Luckin, Rosemary (2003). Between the lines: documenting the multiple dimensions of computer-supported collaborations. Computers & Education, 41 (4). http://sro.sussex.ac.uk/id/eprint/1366/
title: Ecolab software learning environment
description: The Ecolab is a software environment with an underlying design metaphor of an Ecology Laboratory into which children aged 9-11 place organisms and explore food-web relationships. It operates in build and run modes, offers four phases of relationship complexity, and provides World, Web and Energy views. The system scaffolds learners through graded help and adjustable activity difficulty, and Ecolab II adds metacognitive scaffolding for planning and help-seeking skills.
requirements: The software is designed for use by a single learner, with collaboration taking place between the system and that learner
constraints: The learning environment can operate in 4 several phases of relationship complexity, so not all possible methods of activating the Ecolab are available all the time
target_learning_goals: food web relationships between organisms
examples: A child specifies that a sparrow hawk will eat a thrush and observes whether the action is possible

citation: Luckin, Rosemary (2003). Between the lines: documenting the multiple dimensions of computer-supported collaborations. Computers & Education, 41 (4). http://sro.sussex.ac.uk/id/eprint/1366/
title: Galapagos CD-ROM multimedia learning resource
description: The Galapagos CD-ROM was built as a research tool to explore the implications of narrative for group collaborations with multimedia. It describes Darwin's visit to the Galapagos islands and his resultant theory of evolution in eight sections of content material. Learners use on-screen resources including a Notepad, a Model Answer accessible after writing 50 words, and a script window to construct an explanation of wildlife variation on the islands.
requirements: Learners are set the task of using the resources provided on the CD-ROM to construct an explanation of the variations in the wildlife on the islands using an on-line Notepad
constraints: The Model Answer could only be accessed when they had written 50 words in the Notepad
target_learners: students aged 15-21 years studying for a national examination in Biology
target_learning_goals: Darwin's theory of evolution and species variation
examples: A session using Galapagos and completing the task to their own satisfaction typically took about 45 minutes

title: Digital toy technology from the CACHET project
description: The CACHET project uses freestanding electronic soft toys that can move, speak and respond to a child's touch, and can be linked wirelessly to a PC running compatible software. The toys respond through body sensors, gesture with programmed motion, and speak with a digitised vocabulary of more than 4,000 words, extended by the software to 10,000 words. The child interacts with the toy, the software, and the toy-software link, which mediates the child's actions.
requirements: A special unit transmits information between the toy and the computer, and compatible software enables further interaction through educational games
constraints: The toys can receive radio signals more than 3 metres away from the transmitter at the PC
target_learning_goals: basic language and number skills
examples: Some children used the toy simply as a pretend item, making it walk and pretending that it spoke to them

title: Annotated log documentation technique for single-learner collaboration
description: The documentation of collaborations between child and computer took the shape of an annotated user log represented graphically, first developed for evaluating Ecolab I. Each line in the chart represents a type of event, with blocks annotated by letters and numbers specifying activity type, curriculum node, difficulty level and help level. From these logs the Amount of support and Depth of support provided by the system were extracted to differentiate collaborative styles into Collaboration Profile groups.
requirements: A summary record of each child's interactions must be produced from the detailed logs maintained during their sessions of system use

citation: Luckin, Rosemary (2003). Between the lines: documenting the multiple dimensions of computer-supported collaborations. Computers & Education, 41 (4). http://sro.sussex.ac.uk/id/eprint/1366/
title: CORDFU chart for two-dimensional collaboration documentation
description: The Chronologically Ordered Dialogue & Features Used (CORDFU) chart is the development of the original annotated user log from the Ecolab evaluation for group use of multimedia. Its vertical axis records CD-ROM features above a bold horizontal line and categories of talk below it, while the horizontal axis records the amount of attention paid to a feature or dialogue category in text units of up to 24 characters. For each X recording a CD-ROM feature there is a O indicating the type of talk that occurred whilst this feature was in use.
requirements: Interactions were captured via two video sources, one of the computer screen and the other of the learners, and the video data was then transcribed and coded

examples: In the example CORDFU extract the group of learners used the notepad in conjunction with the introductory section whilst discussing their reactions to the multimedia

citation: Luckin, Rosemary (2003). Between the lines: documenting the multiple dimensions of computer-supported collaborations. Computers & Education, 41 (4). http://sro.sussex.ac.uk/id/eprint/1366/
title: CFFD chart for multi-dimensional collaboration documentation
description: The CFFD chart provides a Chronologically ordered record of Features in use, Focus of interactivity and Dialogue, extending CORDFU to four dimensions of collaboration: software features and on-screen dialogue, dialogue between children or researcher and children, children's use of toy features and dialogue with the toy, and interactions between toy and software. Each horizontal line shows one of the categories of speech and action performed by the researcher, the children, the toy and the software, and the links between the horizontal lines indicate the interactions between the participants along these dimensions.

article_title: A framework for teachers’ integration of ICT into their classroom practice
citation: Donnelly, D., McGarr, O. and O'Reilly, J. (2011). A Framework for Teachers' Integration of ICT Into Their Classroom Practice. Computers and Education;57(2), 1469-1483. https://hdl.handle.net/10344/2340
title: Teacher ICT Integration Model: four teacher types positioned on two intersecting conflict continuums
description: The article proposes a Teacher ICT Integration Model (Figure 2) that identifies four types of teachers in relation to ICT integration: a Contented Traditionalist, a Selective Adopter, an Inadvertent User and a Creative Adapter. These four types are positioned in terms of two main teacher conflict areas emerging from the research: empowerment versus fatalism and a learning focus versus an assessment focus. The two conflict areas are represented as two continuums intersecting, with assessment-focused teachers aligned with teacher-centred approaches and learning-focused teachers aligned with student-centred approaches. The model acknowledges different teacher stances on technology integration while highlighting significant boundaries between these stances.
requirements: The model is based on findings from initial interviews with teachers and stakeholders and a follow-on case study of five practising chemistry teachers using the VCL, combined with relevant literature.
constraints: The model is built on a small qualitative sample; the article notes it is difficult from this research to say exactly which teachers would fall into the Contented Traditionalist group.
target_learning_goals: effective integration of ICT resources such as virtual laboratories into classroom practice
examples: The model was developed from observations of five teachers using the Virtual Chemistry Laboratory and follow-up interviews, coded against Ertmer's first- and second-order barriers.

article_title: A peer assessment method to provide feedback, consistent grading and reduce students' burden in massive teaching settings
citation: Luaces, O., Díez, J., & Bahamonde, A. (2018). A peer assessment method to provide feedback, consistent grading and reduce students’ burden in massive teaching settings. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.08.006
title: Matrix factorization model of peer assessment with ordinal preference learning
description: The article proposes representing peer assessment as a sparse three-dimensional matrix (graders × answers × labels) and completing it via matrix factorization. Answers are encoded as bag-of-words vectors and graders and labels as one-hot vectors, all embedded in a shared k-dimensional Euclidean space. The model is trained using stochastic gradient descent on a maximum-margin loss over preference judgments (pairs of answers where one grader rated one higher than another), rather than by regression on raw grade values, reflecting an ordinal rather than cardinal view of grading.
requirements: Instructors must provide a rubric and a list of aspects (labels) to be assessed, with each label scored on an ordinal range of values.
constraints: The approach assumes an unknown relationship between grades given to different labels and relies on ordinal preference judgments rather than exact grade values.
target_learners: higher education students in massive courses
target_learning_goals: open-response assessment and feedback

article_title: Using Internet videos to learn about controversies: Evaluation and integration of multiple and multimodal documents by primary school students
citation: Salmerón, L., Sampietro, A., & Delgado, P. (2020). Using Internet videos to learn about controversies: Evaluation and integration of multiple and multimodal documents by primary school students. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2020.103907
title: Shallowing hypothesis as an account of modality effects on integration
description: The shallowing hypothesis holds that interactions with digital media are "quick episodes driven by immediate rewards", so processing becomes superficial and constructing coherent representations of complex information is difficult. The article applies it to Internet videos, predicting that "learning from Internet videos will result in lower comprehension and integration than when reading textual pages" because students consume videos mainly for entertainment. The study's inference contrast between two texts and two videos is offered as support.
requirements: Students must have habitual, entertainment-oriented experience with the digital medium for shallow processing to be expected
constraints: The article frames the hypothesis around quick, reward-driven interactions with digital media rather than all digital use
target_learning_goals: integrated understanding of controversial socio-scientific topics from multiple documents
examples: The study compared two-text and two-video conditions with equal exposure time and found the inference advantage for texts
key_sources: Salmerón, L., Sampietro, A., & Delgado, P. (2020). Using Internet videos to learn about controversies: Evaluation and integration of multiple and multimodal documents by primary school students. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.103796

article_title: Using Internet videos to learn about controversies: Evaluation and integration of multiple and multimodal documents by primary school students
citation: Salmerón, L., Sampietro, A., & Delgado, P. (2020). Using Internet videos to learn about controversies: Evaluation and integration of multiple and multimodal documents by primary school students. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2020.103907
title: Mode affordance and the humanizing voice account of source evaluation in videos
description: The article draws on social semiotics to define "mode affordance" as "the ability of each mode to easily convey a particular information aspect", noting videos visually present the author and provide "additional credibility cues conveyed by particular modes". The humanizing voice hypothesis holds that voice and the author's visible presence make sources seem more human and trustworthy, so students adopt views conveyed in videos more than those in texts. The study's belief-shift results are read as supporting this account over the persuasiveness of print hypothesis.
requirements: Videos must make the source visually salient (e.g., the author on camera) for the credibility cues to operate
constraints: The article notes the humanizing effect was demonstrated for sources depicted on video, and the persuasiveness-of-print effect may fade as students gain broader reading experience
target_learning_goals: evaluating source credibility in multimodal documents
examples: In the video-against-bottled-water condition, students shifted toward the view expressed in the video by the expert author
key_sources: Salmerón, L., Sampietro, A., & Delgado, P. (2020). Using Internet videos to learn about controversies: Evaluation and integration of multiple and multimodal documents by primary school students. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.103796

article_title: The impact of primary school teachers’ educational beliefs on the classroom use of computers
citation: Hermans, R., Tondeur, J., van Braak, J., & Valcke, M. (2008). The impact of primary school teachers’ educational beliefs on the classroom use of computers. Computers & Education, 51(4), 1499–1509. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2008.02.001
title: Teacher educational beliefs as antecedents of ICT adoption
description: The article frames teachers' educational beliefs — constructivist versus traditional orientations toward teaching and learning — as determinants of whether teachers adopt computers in the classroom, extending a literature that focused on technology-related variables. It argues "teachers’ classroom use of computers cannot be fully understood without taking their underlying educational beliefs into consideration". Beliefs are defined as "the individual conceptions about desirable ways of teaching and conceptions about how students come to learn", grounded in personal belief systems and relatively stable and resistant to change.
requirements: Measuring beliefs with validated scales (here the Constructivist and Traditional Beliefs scales of Woolley, Benjamin, and Woolley) alongside technology-related and demographic controls
constraints: Evidence concerns Flemish primary teachers; the article notes the interplay between school-level and teacher-level variables is not yet clear and calls for further research
target_learning_goals: classroom integration of computers to support teaching and learning
key_sources: Hermans, R., Tondeur, J., van Braak, J., & Valcke, M. (2008). The impact of primary school teachers’ educational beliefs on the classroom use of computers. Computers & Education, 51(4), 1499–1509. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2008.02.001

title: A network perspective is relevant for the study of online learning.
description: The study supports the relevance of a network perspective for studying online learning, proposing that learning in digital environments is mediated by personal online networks rather than residing solely at the individual level.

article_title: Training pre-service teachers to deal with cyberbullying: Collective intelligence as a mode of learning
citation: Bautista Alcaine, P., Vicente Sánchez, E., Orejudo Hernández, S., & Cano Escoriaza, J. (2024). Training pre-service teachers to deal with cyberbullying: Collective intelligence as a mode of learning. Computers & Education, 220, 105123. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105123
title: Collective Learning online platform
description: Collective Learning is an online collective intelligence tool developed by the Institute for Biocomputation and Physics of Complex Systems (BIFI) and Kampal Data Solutions, "designed to apply collective intelligence to certain problems or tasks with the aim of achieving high-quality solutions through a model of successive social interactions". It deploys actions such as edit, view, copy, permutation of users, modifying responses and response deletion across seven phases, with an AI acting as moderator selecting Top 10 answers.
requirements: An initial individual response phase followed by six successive interaction phases, with each user seeing responses of four randomized anonymized "neighbours" in phases 2–5
constraints: The popularity or prestige effect can lead to "responses of lower quality or diversity that have been endorsed by less competent leaders"
target_learning_goals: complex problem resolution
moral dilemmas
mathematics and physics problems
examples: Used with 221 pre-service teachers working on an adolescent sexting case across seven phases
key_sources: Bautista Alcaine, P., Vicente Sánchez, E., Orejudo Hernández, S., & Cano Escoriaza, J. (2024). Training pre-service teachers to deal with cyberbullying: Collective intelligence as a mode of learning. Computers & Education, 220, 105123. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105123

article_title: Training pre-service teachers to deal with cyberbullying: Collective intelligence as a mode of learning
citation: Bautista Alcaine, P., Vicente Sánchez, E., Orejudo Hernández, S., & Cano Escoriaza, J. (2024). Training pre-service teachers to deal with cyberbullying: Collective intelligence as a mode of learning. Computers & Education, 220, 105123. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105123
title: Collective intelligence as a construct for group performance on complex tasks
description: The article describes collective intelligence as "the shared effort of a large group of people confronted with diverse complex tasks", where "it is presumed that the average performance of the individual is lower than the performance achieved by the group as a whole". Building on Woolley et al. (2010), the article distinguishes top-down analysis (interaction processes such as group heterogeneity, diversity of responses, order of turns) from bottom-up analysis (gender, emotional intelligence, individual intelligence, cognitive diversity, social sensitivity).
requirements: A facilitator or moderator role to manage interaction and control the prestige effect
constraints: Conditions that lead to quality results remain open to debate, and online environments face dispersal of answers, lack of collaboration, and lack of originality
target_learning_goals: collaborative problem resolution
complex task performance
examples: Applied via the Collective Learning platform to a cyberbullying case with pre-service teachers
key_sources: Bautista Alcaine, P., Vicente Sánchez, E., Orejudo Hernández, S., & Cano Escoriaza, J. (2024). Training pre-service teachers to deal with cyberbullying: Collective intelligence as a mode of learning. Computers & Education, 220, 105123. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105123

article_title: Understanding higher education learners' acceptance and use of mobile devices for language learning: A Rasch-based path modeling approach
citation: Vo, H. N. (2020). Understanding higher education learners' acceptance and use of mobile devices for language learning: A Rasch-based path modeling approach. Computers and Education, 146, Article 103761. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.103761
title: Modified UTAUT model as a framework for examining MALL acceptance.
description: The modified UTAUT model (Dwivedi et al., 2019) adds attitude as an additional construct to the original UTAUT and drops all moderating variables. It proposes that performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, and facilitating condition predict attitude and behavioral intention, which in turn predict use behavior. The study found the model fit the data well and concluded it is "an appropriate model for examining MALL acceptance" in the Vietnamese context.
requirements: Measurement of all seven UTAUT constructs via survey scales
constraints: Cross-sectional design; changing attitudes and behavior over time were not modeled
target_learning_goals: acceptance and use of mobile assisted language learning

article_title: Learning analytics in European higher education—Trends and barriers
citation: Tsai, Yi-Shan, et al. (2020). Learning Analytics in European Higher Education – Trends and Barriers. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2020.103933
title: Ground LA in learning sciences and include students as key stakeholders in design and implementation
description: The article argues that LA adoption should be grounded in learning sciences and that students should be included as key stakeholders in the design and implementation of LA. The authors highlight "the importance of grounding LA in learning sciences and including students as a key stakeholderinthedesignandimplementationofLA", noting that the lack of engagement with students is notable given LA's ultimate goal to support learners and optimise learning.
requirements: A mechanism to ensure that LA aligns with learning theories and pedagogical practice
constraints: The absence of strategy specific for LA among consulted institutions makes it unclear to what extent LA practices have been informed by pedagogical expertise
target_learning_goals: Self-regulated learning skills
Data literacy
examples: The article reports that teaching and support staff were indicated as the main users by most institutions (n=36), followed by students (n=23) and senior managers (n=11).

title: Learning analytics adoption frameworks and models address stakeholder engagement, ethics and privacy, resource demand, and pedagogical grounding challenges
description: The article reviews existing LA adoption frameworks and models, mapping them against four challenges: stakeholder engagement and buy-in, weak pedagogical grounding, resource demand, and ethics and privacy. The authors observe that "stakeholder involvement is an area most frequently highlighted. article_title: Myartspace: Design and evaluation of support for learning with multimedia phones between classrooms and museums
citation: Vavoula, G., Sharples, M., Rudman, P., Meek, J., & Lonsdale, P. (2009). Myartspace: Design and evaluation of support for learning with multimedia phones between classrooms and museums. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2009.02.007
title: M3 evaluation framework for mobile learning across micro, meso and macro levels
description: The M3 evaluation framework structures evaluation of mobile learning technology at three levels: micro (usability and utility of individual activities), meso (the learning experience as a whole, including learning breakthroughs and breakdowns), and macro (longer-term impact on established educational and learning practice). It operates through a three-stage process of capturing user expectations, capturing reality through observation, and examining gaps between them. The article applies it throughout the Myartspace project lifecycle, from requirements analysis through design, implementation and deployment.
requirements: Evaluation must be integrated throughout the technology development lifecycle rather than conducted as a final 'success or failure' test
constraints: Macro-level evaluation requires that the technology is deployed long enough to assess its impact on practice
target_learning_goals: inquiry learning connecting museum and classroom
examples: Applied to evaluate Myartspace at three pilot sites: the Study Gallery in Poole, Urbis in Manchester, and the D-Day museum in Portsmouth
key_sources: Vavoula, G., Sharples, M., Rudman, P., Meek, J., & Lonsdale, P. (2009). Myartspace: Design and evaluation of support for learning with multimedia phones between classrooms and museums. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2009.02.007

article_title: Myartspace: Design and evaluation of support for learning with multimedia phones between classrooms and museums
citation: Vavoula, G., Sharples, M., Rudman, P., Meek, J., & Lonsdale, P. (2009). Myartspace: Design and evaluation of support for learning with multimedia phones between classrooms and museums. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2009.02.007
title: Myartspace mobile service for inquiry-led learning across museum and classroom
description: Myartspace is a service using mobile phones and a website to support inquiry learning between classrooms and museums. Students collect photos, audio recordings, text comments, and objects via two-letter exhibit codes during a museum visit; content is automatically sent by GPRS to personal online stores. In post-visit lessons students create personal galleries synthesising collected evidence to answer inquiry questions set in a pre-visit lesson.
requirements: Museums must digitise content for the museum store
Teachers receive a Teacher's Pack and Lesson Plans and customise the three-lesson sequence
constraints: Phones are locked to the Myartspace application and cannot be used for calls
Audio and text comments made when a photograph is taken are not linked to the photograph
target_learners: secondary school students (Key Stage 3, ages 13-14 in the trial)
target_learning_goals: inquiry-based collecting, selection and synthesis of museum evidence
examples: Students at the D-Day museum were set the question 'Was D-Day a triumph or disaster for Britain?'

article_title: Teacher agency and learner agency in teaching and learning a new school subject, Leaving Certificate Computer Science, in Ireland: Considerations for teacher education
citation: Scanlon, D & Connolly, C. (2021). Teacher agency and learner agency in teaching and learning a new school subject, Leaving Certificate Computer Science, in Ireland: Considerations for teacher education. Computers and Education, 174, 104291. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2021.104291
title: Figurational sociology lens on teacher and learner agency as interdependent, fluctuating processes
description: The article uses figurational sociology to frame teacher agency and learner agency not as individual possessions but as processes emerging within figurations of interdependent relationships. It argues that achieving agency is 'a combination of the teacher and the students and the other interdependent relationships within their figurations, alongside contextual factors, and educational social processes'. This framework explains why agency fluctuates rather than being a stable product.
requirements: Analysis of agency must attend to interdependent relationships within figurations, not only individual teachers or students
constraints: Developed and illustrated in the context of a newly introduced Irish school subject, Leaving Certificate Computer Science
target_learners: Post-primary students studying Leaving Certificate Computer Science in Ireland
target_learning_goals: Understanding how teacher and learner agency develop in classroom figurations
