article_title: IDR: A participatory methodology for interdisciplinary design in technology enhanced learning
citation: Niall Winters, Yishay Mor. (2007). IDR: a participatory methodology for interdisciplinary design in technology enhanced learning. Computers and Education. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00190043
title: IDR: a participatory methodology for interdisciplinary techno-pedagogical design
description: IDR is a participatory methodology for interdisciplinary techno-pedagogical design in technology enhanced learning. It draws on the design patterns tradition and the design research paradigm, and was developed iteratively by a pan-European project team of educational researchers, software developers and teachers. The article presents it as a response to design processes that 'often lack true interdisciplinarity' despite the multi-dimensional nature of designing technology for learning.

article_title: A comparison of structured and unstructured navigation through a CBT package
citation: Stanton, N. A. and Stammers, R. B. (1990). A comparison of structured and unstructured navigation through a CBT package. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ414518
title: Cognitive style taxonomy of serialist, holist, top-down and bottom-up navigation strategies
description: The article organizes trainee navigation behaviour through cognitive style classifications drawn from Pask's distinction between a "serialist" (a step-by-step approach in a linear fashion, increasing understanding by small increments) and a "holist" (a more global approach, involving testing assumptions of the overall structure of the task). Because the task under investigation had a hierarchical structure, the authors add two further styles: a "top down" strategy (starting with higher-order procedures, moving down to lower-order procedures) and a "bottomup" strategy (starting with lower-order procedures, moving up to higher-order procedures). These styles were used to classify unstructured-condition trainees and interpret differences in modules viewed.
requirements: Classification of trainee styles relied on self-report of navigation approach, for example "I looked at the most important things first" (top down)
constraints: The taxonomy was applied only to trainees in the unstructured condition, who were measured using the Embedded Figures Test
target_learning_goals: navigation and sequencing of instruction in hierarchical computer-based training tasks
key_sources: Stanton, N. A. and Stammers, R. B. (1990). A comparison of structured and unstructured navigation through a CBT package. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ414518

article_title: A comparison of structured and unstructured navigation through a CBT package
citation: Stanton, N. A. and Stammers, R. B. (1990). A comparison of structured and unstructured navigation through a CBT package. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ414518
title: Match navigation structure to trainee cognitive style rather than imposing one structure for all
description: The article concludes that the unstructured condition may be a better training environment for some individuals, whilst others may do better in the structured condition, dependent on the individual's own learning style and abilities. It recommends that further investigations should have the emphasis upon advice rather than control, as too much structure may make the environment inflexible and tedious. This principle supports offering learner-controlled sequencing with guidance rather than fixed pre-sequencing for all trainees.
requirements: Trainees must be able to relate the task goals to the learning environment clearly enough to organize a suitable learning environment of their own
constraints: A dislike of the lack of structure was reported by some subjects, and non-sequential presentation may be inappropriate for learning procedural skills
target_learning_goals: acquisition of procedural knowledge in hierarchical process-control tasks
examples: The unstructured group selected the modules to be viewed via an overview screen and returned to it after each module to select the next, while the structured group were presented with each of the modules in a fixed order
key_sources: Stanton, N. A. and Stammers, R. B. (1990). A comparison of structured and unstructured navigation through a CBT package. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ414518

article_title: The benefits and challenges of large-scale deployment of electronic voting systems: University student views from across different subject groups
citation: Marija Cubric, and Amanda Jefferies. (2015). The benefits and challenges of large-scale deployment of electronic voting systems: University student views from across different subject groups. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2015.04.004
title: Focus on the formative benefits of EVS rather than summative use to gain the promised rewards of the technology
description: The article concludes that institutions deploying EVS at scale should maintain focus on formative benefits rather than shifting toward summative assessment. It states that only through formative focus, regardless of disciplinary differences, can the promised rewards of the technology be gained. This principle emerged from findings that summative-only use was associated with lower learning benefits and higher challenges.
requirements: Deployment should prioritise formative uses of EVS over summative assessment uses
target_learning_goals: Student engagement and learning benefits from classroom response technology

title: Four-dimension framework of student perceptions of EVS: learning benefits, classroom-related benefits, usability, and student-centered challenges
description: The article proposes that students' views on EVS in large-scale institutional deployments are organised around four distinct dimensions derived through non-linear PCA: learning benefits, classroom-related benefits, usability, and student-centered challenges. Satisfaction items loaded positively on learning benefits, ease of use, and classroom benefits, and negatively on challenges. This framework extends prior small-scale EVS research to the institutional context.
requirements: Requires survey instruments covering learning, classroom, usability, and challenge dimensions
constraints: Derived from a single UK post-92 university context with large-scale deployment

article_title: A multilevel analysis of what matters in the training of pre-service teacher's ICT competencies
citation: Tondeur, Jo; Aesaert, Koen; Prestridge, Sarah; Consuegra, Els. (2018). A multilevel analysis of what matters in the training of pre-service teacher's ICT competencies. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.03.002
title: A multilevel model integrating background characteristics, ICT profile and institutional strategies to explain pre-service teachers' perceived ICT competencies
description: The article proposes and tests a model to explain pre-service teachers' perceived ICT competencies that integrates three levels: background characteristics (age and gender), their ICT profile (e.g., attitudes towards ICT), and the multiple strategies experienced in the teacher training institution. The model was tested with multilevel analyses on a survey of 931 final-year pre-service teachers in Flanders (Belgium), motivated by the observation that prior research is "generally limited to the impact of one single strategy".

constraints: Tested with final-year pre-service teachers in Flanders (Belgium); outcomes are perceived ICT competencies

citation: Tondeur, Jo; Aesaert, Koen; Prestridge, Sarah; Consuegra, Els. (2018). A multilevel analysis of what matters in the training of pre-service teacher's ICT competencies. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.03.002
title: Six strategies of the teacher training institution for preparing pre-service teachers' ICT competencies
description: The article enumerates six strategies pre-service teachers experience in their teacher training institution: "1) using teacher educators as role models, 2) reflecting on the role of technology in education, 3) learning how to use technology by design, 4) collaboration with peers, 5) scaffolding authentic technology experiences, and 6) continuous feedback." These strategies together form the institutional component of the tested model and were measured as perceived occurrences in the survey of 931 pre-service teachers.
requirements: Teacher training institutions must deliberately enact all six strategies so pre-service teachers perceive their occurrences
constraints: Studied in the context of Flemish final-year teacher education; effects are on perceived ICT competence
target_learners: pre-service teachers in teacher training institutions
target_learning_goals: competence to use ICT for learning processes and to strengthen instructional practice

article_title: A multilevel analysis of what matters in the training of pre-service teacher's ICT competencies
citation: Tondeur, Jo; Aesaert, Koen; Prestridge, Sarah; Consuegra, Els. (2018). A multilevel analysis of what matters in the training of pre-service teacher's ICT competencies. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.03.002
title: Combine multiple institutional strategies, rather than a single strategy, when preparing pre-service teachers for ICT integration
description: Because the study found that the more strategy occurrences pre-service teachers perceive, the higher their perceived ICT competence, the article recommends that results "can provide guidance for the preparation of pre-service teachers for the 21st century learning environments with new technologies". It motivates this by noting prior research is generally limited to the impact of one single strategy, whereas the model integrates multiple strategies simultaneously.
requirements: Institutional strategies must be experienced by pre-service teachers during their teacher education programme
constraints: Evidence base is a cross-sectional survey of perceived competence among final-year pre-service teachers in Flanders
target_learning_goals: ICT integration in learning processes and instructional practice
examples: The survey measured the six strategies — role models, reflection, learning technology by design, peer collaboration, scaffolding authentic experiences, and continuous feedback — as perceived occurrences among 931 final-year pre-service teachers

article_title: Variability of teachers’ technology integration in the classroom: A matter of utility!
citation: Backfisch, I., Lachner, A., Stürmer, K., & Scheiter, K. (2021). Variability of teachers’ technology integration in the classroom: A matter of utility!. Computers & Education, 166, 104159. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2021.104159
title: Technology integration quality conceptualized on two dimensions: technology exploitation and teaching quality (task-specific and task-general)
description: The article conceptualizes the quality of technology integration on two dimensions: technology exploitation (teachers' capability to implement the distinct potential of educational technologies, drawing on hierarchical frameworks like SAMR and RAT) and teaching quality (comprising task-specific strategies of cognitive activation and individual learning support, and task-general strategies of classroom management). The authors operationalize these dimensions for coding lesson documentations, with subcategories scored 0-3 yielding a maximum of 12 points per dimension. This framework extends prior models that "only focus on the types of technology use and ignore the potential impact on learning processes".
requirements: Trained raters coding lesson documentations using the four subcategories per dimension
constraints: Relies on teachers' self-reported lesson documentations rather than direct observations
target_learning_goals: technology integration quality
teaching quality

article_title: The use of video technology for providing feedback to students: Can it enhance the feedback experience for staff and students?
citation: Crook, A., Mauchline, A., Maw, S., Lawson, C., Drinkwater, R., Lundqvist, K., Orsmond, P., Gomez, S., and Park, J. (2012). The use of video technology for providing feedback to students: can it enhance the feedback experience for staff and students? Computers & Education, 58(1), 386-396. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2011.08.025
title: ASSET: a Web 2.0 platform for storing and sharing staff-created video feedback with tiered access.
description: ASSET was an online, interactive resource developed using Web 2.0 approaches of interactivity and user-generated content, built on proprietary CORE software, and designed as a platform for storing digital video files created by staff. It offered a search facility and controlled access via university logins, with videos available at University, Module, and personalised 'My playlist' levels. The resource was piloted at the University of Reading during 2009-10 and later embedded in the institution's virtual learning environment.
requirements: Staff required webcams, recording equipment, screen-capture software, and training and technical support provided by the project team to create videos.
constraints: Users encountered technical problems during the pilot, including slow video downloads, navigation difficulties, and poor video or sound quality.
target_learners: University of Reading undergraduate and postgraduate students across Arts, Humanities, Business, Law, Life Sciences and Science faculties
target_learning_goals: Improving student engagement with feedback
Making feedback clearer and more accessible
Supporting feed-forward into future student work
examples: Staff uploaded brief 2-3 minute videos of generic feedback, mostly in a 'talking head' style, with some screencasts.

title: Deliver generic video feedback promptly so students can act on it before starting their next assignment.
description: The article recommends that staff provide a rapid, generic response to all students, for example in a brief video, so students can use the information before completing their next assignment. This 'enough for now' feedback summarises what was done well and badly across the cohort while staff undertake the more time-consuming task of individual feedback. The approach addresses staff concerns about engagement, efficiency, timeliness, and quality identified in the pre-use survey.
requirements: Staff need to quickly skim-read the cohort's work to identify key points done well or badly before recording.
constraints: Generic feedback does not replace the need for individual, tailored feedback, which remains more time-consuming.

Providing feed-forward information in a timely manner

article_title: Improving the quality of teaching by utilising written student feedback: A streamlined process
citation: Hujala, M., Knutas, A., Hynninen, T., & Arminen, H. (2020). Improving the quality of teaching by utilising written student feedback: A streamlined process. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2020.103965
title: Streamlined four-step process for systematic analysis of written student feedback
description: The article proposes a repeatable mixed-methods pipeline that "combines text mining to pre-sort the open-ended feedback" with thematic analysis and multilevel modelling. It consists of four main steps: data collection, LDA topic model generation, evaluation of topic-model outcomes (qualitative via thematic analysis and quantitative via multilevel modelling), and reporting. The process is intended for programme- or institution-wide analysis of open-ended feedback rather than for an individual lecturer, and it connects qualitative findings to existing SET literature and quantitative feedback data.
requirements: Requires student feedback surveys that include both Likert-scale and open-ended questions, so that topic-model outcomes can be evaluated against numerical SET dimensions.
Requires large masses of open-ended text responses to distinguish meaningful themes within the feedback.
constraints: The authors state the process is novel and requires further evaluation to establish its full validity.
The process is aimed at programme- or institution-level analysis, not at an individual lecturer extracting topics from their own course feedback.
target_learning_goals: evaluation of teaching quality
quality assurance of degree programmes
key_sources: Hujala, M., Knutas, A., Hynninen, T., & Arminen, H. (2020). Improving the quality of teaching by utilising written student feedback: A streamlined process. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2020.103965

article_title: Improving the quality of teaching by utilising written student feedback: A streamlined process
citation: Hujala, M., Knutas, A., Hynninen, T., & Arminen, H. (2020). Improving the quality of teaching by utilising written student feedback: A streamlined process. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2020.103965
title: Combine topic modelling with thematic analysis to make qualitative analysis of large feedback datasets practical
description: The article argues that large-scale analysis of written student feedback is easily dismissed as too time-consuming when done purely by hand, and that purely automatic methods lose richness. Combining the two addresses both problems: "Topic modelling allows pre-sorting large document sets into topic categories and finding most characteristic documents from each category", while thematic analysis assigns expert human themes to those categories. This makes thematic analysis practical in larger datasets and speeds up the analysis.
requirements: Requires a corpus of open-ended feedback large enough that manual analysis alone would be impractical.
constraints: The authors note that the drawback of automated text mining compared to manual analysis is loss in the richness of the data.
For small datasets, the authors agree the automated step can be skipped in favour of a fully manual thematic analysis.
target_learning_goals: evaluation of teaching quality
quality assurance of degree programmes
examples: In the article's demonstration, the authors coded the 12 most characteristic feedback texts per topic (72 total) rather than the full corpus, requiring about 70 coded rows to achieve beneficial results.

article_title: Automated multimodal visual analytics of social and epistemic dimensions in team communication for reflective practice in healthcare simulation
citation: Zhao, L., Echeverria, V., Gašević, D., Yan, L., Alfredo, R., Li, X., & Martinez-Maldonado, R. (2026). Automated multimodal visual analytics of social and epistemic dimensions in team communication for reflective practice in healthcare simulation. Computers & Education, 252, 105655. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2026.105655
title: MMLA system generating social and epistemic network visualisations of team communication in healthcare simulation
description: The article describes an AI-powered multimodal learning analytics system deployed in a nursing simulation space that captures audio and spatial data and automatically generates visualisations of team communication. The system "employs spatial analytics and a transformer-based language model (i.e., BERT) to process learners' physical positioning and speech data, enabling the visualisation of communication dynamics as Social and Epistemic Networks". Educators access a timeline and network interface on a tablet during debriefing and can select time spans to generate networks for specific phases.
requirements: Requires headset microphones, a Pozyx positioning toolkit for spatial coordinates and body orientation, and automated transcription with a fine-tuned BERT classifier for coding communication behaviours
constraints: The classifier was validated on a subset of the 2023 data (five sessions, approximately 10% of the data) with all Cohen's κ > 0.61
target_learners: Undergraduate nursing learners in simulation-based clinical courses
target_learning_goals: Team communication skills
Reflection on collaboration and closed-loop communication
examples: Deployed across 63 simulations involving 252 learners in a third-year undergraduate clinical course, with five clinical educators leading debriefings

Computers & Education, 252, 105655. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2026.105655
title: Co-designed network visualisation design decisions for debriefing evidence
description: The article enumerates design decisions for the social and epistemic networks established through co-design with nursing educators: role-based colour coding of learner nodes, fixed node sizes and hidden edges for non-learners, absolute speech duration and absolute co-occurrence frequency for node and edge sizes, and an abstracted content view that summarises dialogue without raw transcripts. These choices were made "to highlight the communication among learners by reducing unnecessary information and cognitive load" and to allow comparison of communication across phases.
requirements: Co-design with educators to select relevant codes and visual encodings
Use of absolute rather than normalised metrics so educators can compare durations and co-occurrences across phases
constraints: Reducing the epistemic network from seven to four behaviours focused the debriefing on closed-loop communication and escalation, although it also reduced the network's informational richness
target_learning_goals: Reflecting on team communication roles, engagement and closed-loop communication strategies
examples: Educators suggested refining the epistemic network by dropping and merging behaviours, leaving four codes: task allocation, questioning, acknowledging, and escalation

Computers & Education, 252, 105655. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2026.105655
title: Network visualisations as metacognitive mirrors supporting cognitive offloading and reflection
description: The article conceptualises social and epistemic network visualisations as metacognitive mirrors that externalise learners' interaction and knowledge construction to support awareness and reflection on collaboration. Functioning as external cognitive representations, they serve "as visual anchors that cue recall of concrete communicative episodes and participation patterns", supporting cognitive offloading by reducing reliance on memory prone to decay and bias and freeing cognitive resources for higher-order reflective processes. This mechanism underpins the system's use in educator-guided debriefing.
requirements: Comprehensibility: if the networks are difficult to comprehend, they risk increasing extrinsic cognitive load, thereby obstructing effective debriefing
constraints: Comprehensibility does not guarantee pedagogical utility; the networks may be easy to comprehend yet fail to trigger deeper reflection
target_learners: Undergraduate nursing learners in team-based simulation
target_learning_goals: Recall and reflection on team communication experiences
examples: Educators displayed the networks on a projector during debriefing to help learners recall their experiences

article_title: Student academic performance stochastic simulator based on the Monte Carlo method
citation: Caro Huertas, Eduardo; González Fernández, María Camino; Mira McWilliams, José Manuel. (2014). Student academic performance stochastic simulator based on the Monte Carlo method. Computers & Education, v. 76, pp. 45-54. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2014.03.007
title: A Monte Carlo stochastic simulator of student academic performance along a university curriculum
description: A computer-based tool developed to analyze student performance along a given curriculum. It "makes use of historical data to compute passing/failing probabilities and simulates future student academic performance based on stochastic programming methods (MonteCarlo) according to the specific university regulations." The tool was adapted to the curriculum characteristics of the Bachelor in Engineering Technologies at the Technical University of Madrid (UPM).

University-specific academic regulations that govern progression through the curriculum
constraints: Adapted to the curriculum characteristics of the Bachelor in Engineering Technologies at the Technical University of Madrid (UPM)

target_learning_goals: Institutional analysis of student academic performance and progression along a curriculum

The article uses this framework to structure the simulator's outputs for curriculum analysis.

article_title: FLoRA: An advanced AI-powered engine to facilitate hybrid human-AI regulated learning
citation: Li, X., Li, T., Yan, L., Li, Y., Zhao, L., Raković, M., Molenaar, I., Gašević, D., & Fan, Y. (2025). FLoRA: An Advanced AI-Powered Engine to Facilitate Hybrid Human-AI Regulated Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.07362
title: FLoRA Engine
description: The FLoRA Engine is an AI-powered learning platform that integrates generative AI and learning analytics to detect, measure, and facilitate self-regulated learning (SRL). It provides instrumentation tools such as collaborative writing, multi-agent chatbots, and detailed learning trace logging to support dynamic, adaptive scaffolding of self-regulation tailored to individual needs in real time. The engine is designed to support hybrid human-AI regulated learning (HHAIRL) by providing targeted, timely scaffolding while preserving learners' role as active decision-makers.
requirements: Integration with a learning management system (Moodle)
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning
academic writing
clinical reasoning

title: Hybrid Human-AI Regulated Learning (HHAIRL)
description: HHAIRL is a balanced approach in which AI provides targeted, timely scaffolding while preserving the learners' role as active decision-makers and reflective monitors of their learning process. Regulation is treated as a shared responsibility that can fluidly shift between learners and intelligent systems, with a dynamic handover of control calibrated to learners' needs. The framework emphasizes human agency and oversight even when using AI assistance.
requirements: AI systems must be designed to dynamically share control with human learners and educators
target_learners: all learners using AI-supported learning environments
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning
metacognitive monitoring

title: Design scaffolding that incorporates both real-time SRL processes and evolving learning conditions
description: The article recommends incorporating both learners' real-time SRL processes and evolving conditions in scaffold design. Learning analytics detect dynamic conditions (e.g., time awareness via trace data) and static conditions (e.g., domain knowledge via pre-task surveys), which are converted into predefined statements added to the GenAI prompt. This allows scaffolds to adapt not only to learners' real-time SRL processes but also to dynamic learning conditions that shift throughout the task.

article_title: A network analysis on digital media use, reading enjoyment, and orthography precision in a highly educated sample
citation: Miccoli, L., Arias, M. Á. P., & Santiago, J. (2023). A network analysis on digital media use, reading enjoyment, and orthography precision in a highly educated sample. Computers & Education, 207, 104932. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104932
title: Partial correlation network analysis as a data-driven method for examining multifactorial relations between variables
description: The article relies on regularized partial correlation network analysis (graphical LASSO, EBICglasso), "a recently emerging tool that can reveal both the direct and indirect relations between variables". It is data-driven, does not require hypothesizing latent factors, and provides a graphical display of relations and association strengths. Centrality measures (strength, closeness, betweenness) describe node importance, and bootstrapping assesses network accuracy and stability via CS-coefficients.
requirements: Sample size estimations (power analysis) are pivotal to maximize sensitivity and reduce false negatives given LASSO regularization favors specificity over sensitivity
constraints: The article states there is no consensus on a unique way to assess network goodness of fit
target_learning_goals: written language skills (orthography)

Participants read 56 sentences (54 after exclusions), half correctly written and half containing an orthographic error not detectable by autocorrect, judging correctness and fixing errors. article_title: Effects of Manipulative Use on PK-12 Mathematics Achievement: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Amy B. Holmes, Vanderbilt University. (2013). Effects of Manipulative Use on PK-12 Mathematics Achievement: A Meta-Analysis. SREE Spring 2013 Conference Abstract. https://www.sree.org
title: Constructivist account of manipulatives as concrete objects supporting progression to abstract mathematical thinking
description: The article frames manipulatives through constructivist theories of learning, which postulate that students build increasingly complex knowledge through active engagement with concrete materials. Manipulatives are defined as "objects that appeal to several senses and that can be touched, moved about, rearranged, and otherwise handled by children", including physical items and virtual applets. The framework holds that manipulating such objects supports students' progression from concrete to increasingly abstract ways of thinking about diverse mathematical ideas, motivating the meta-analysis of manipulative interventions.
requirements: Manipulative use must introduce or reinforce mathematical concepts and be accompanied by instruction supporting model-based reasoning, which the article says necessitates extensive teacher preparation and professional development
constraints: Critics cited in the article note that simple provision of manipulative materials is not likely to result in learning without specific supporting instruction
target_learning_goals: conceptual and procedural understanding of mathematics
examples: The meta-analysis operationalized this framework by including interventions with physical or virtual manipulative materials during school-based mathematics instruction compared to nonuse or business-as-usual controls

article_title: What Works to Improve Reading Outcomes in Latin-America? A Systematic Review of the Evidence
citation: de Hoop, T., Klochikin, E., & Stone, R. (2016). What Works to Improve Reading Outcomes in Latin-America? A Systematic Review of the Evidence. SREE Spring 2016 Conference Abstract Template, American Institutes for Research. https://www.air.org
title: Simple View of Reading as the theoretical framework for appraising non-intervention reading research
description: The review adopts the Simple View of Reading (attributed to Gough & Tunmer, 1986) as its theoretical lens for appraising studies that focus on reading outcomes but are not tied to a specific intervention. In this framework, "reading success is contingent upon two main abilities: language ability and decoding abilities, and the sub-skills of each of these". The reviewers will determine the extent to which non-intervention studies take this approach into consideration, then narratively synthesize that evidence.
requirements: Applied to critically appraising non-intervention studies of reading outcomes, which are then narratively synthesized
target_learners: Children from birth through grade 3 in the Latin-American and Caribbean region
target_learning_goals: Early grade reading outcomes, including language ability and decoding sub-skills
examples: The review plans to judge how far non-intervention quantitative and qualitative studies consider the two-abilities framework before narrative synthesis
