article_title: What Works to Improve Reading Outcomes in Latin-America? A Systematic Review of the Evidence
citation: de Hoop, T., Klochikin, E., & Stone, R. (2016). What Works to Improve Reading Outcomes in Latin-America? A Systematic Review of the Evidence. SREE Spring 2016 Conference Abstract Template, American Institutes for Research. https://www.air.org
title: Adapted Hombrados & Waddington risk-of-bias tool with four bias categories
description: A risk-of-bias assessment instrument adapted from a tool developed by Hombrados & Waddington (2012), used to code and critically appraise the quality of quantitative effectiveness studies before meta-analysis. The tool "specifically focuses on the likelihood of 1) selection bias, 2) bias from spillovers, 3) outcome and analysis reporting bias, and 4) other biases such as relying on recall data or not accounting for clustering in the standard errors". Studies are rated high, medium, or low risk for each of the four categories.
requirements: Coding and critical appraisal of included quantitative studies before pooling, because findings from low-quality evaluation studies may be biased
target_learners: Children from birth through grade 3 in the LAC region
target_learning_goals: Early grade reading outcomes
examples: The reviewers plan to use the four-category ratings in an iterative analysis of potential bias from pooling RCTs and quasi-experimental studies of low, medium, and high risk
key_sources: de Hoop, T., Klochikin, E., & Stone, R. (2016). What Works to Improve Reading Outcomes in Latin-America? A Systematic Review of the Evidence. SREE Spring 2016 Conference Abstract Template, American Institutes for Research. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED567508

article_title: Meta-Analysis of Jelajah Alam Sekitar (JAS) Approach Implementation in Learning Process
citation: S. Ngabekti, S. Ridlo, E. Peniati, R. Martanto. (2017). META-ANALYSIS OF JELAJAH ALAM SEKITAR (JAS) APPROACH IMPLEMENTATION IN LEARNING PROCESS. Jurnal Pendidikan IPA Indonesia. https://doi.org/10.15294/jpii.v6i1.8490
title: Jelajah Alam Sekitar (JAS) approach with six defining characteristics
description: JAS is a learning approach that "uses the student's nature environment, whether the physical, social, technology, or culture environment as the learning object in biology" whose phenomena are learned through scientific work. It is characterized by six components — exploration, constructivism, science process, learning community, edutainment, and authentic assessment — integrated into indoor and outdoor learning. Developed by the Biology Department of FMIPA UNNES since 2005, it spread to eight Indonesian provinces and has been studied from primary school to college.
requirements: The six components (exploration, science process, constructivism, learning community, and authentic assessment) should be integrated into both indoor and outdoor learning for JAS to be well implemented
constraints: Users noted JAS needs clearer criteria distinguishing it from CTL so it is not just another name for contextual learning
target_learners: primary school to university students in Indonesia
target_learning_goals: biology learning outcomes
science process skills
environment care behavior
examples: Implemented with role playing in an Islamic boarding school ecosystem subject, in Biostatistics, and in Animal Ecology, using environments such as grass fields, the UNNES educational tour garden, and soy sauce fermentation observation
key_sources: S. Ngabekti, S. Ridlo, E. Peniati, R. Martanto. (2017). META-ANALYSIS OF JELAJAH ALAM SEKITAR (JAS) APPROACH IMPLEMENTATION IN LEARNING PROCESS. Jurnal Pendidikan IPA Indonesia. https://doi.org/10.15294/jpii.v6i1.8490

article_title: Meta-Analysis of Jelajah Alam Sekitar (JAS) Approach Implementation in Learning Process
citation: S. Ngabekti, S. Ridlo, E. Peniati, R. Martanto. (2017). META-ANALYSIS OF JELAJAH ALAM SEKITAR (JAS) APPROACH IMPLEMENTATION IN LEARNING PROCESS. Jurnal Pendidikan IPA Indonesia. https://doi.org/10.15294/jpii.v6i1.8490
title: JAS approach development and tracer study at UNNES Biology Department
description: The Biology Department of FMIPA UNNES has developed the Jelajah Alam Sekitar learning approach since 2005. A tracer study by Ridlo (2005) and Ridlo et al. (2016) shows that "since 2006 to 2016, JAS has been spread in eight provinces in Indonesia although most of it are in Central Java especially in Semarang", and that JAS has been researched from elementary school to university, tracked mostly with quantitative pre- and quasi-experiment designs.
requirements: Departmental commitment to analyzing JAS characteristics and publishing research results
constraints: Information about JAS is still rare in printed and electronic media, per the user survey
target_learners: Indonesian students from primary school to college
target_learning_goals: biology learning through direct experience of the natural environment
examples: Tracer studies documentary and online; 106 research titles analyzed in the meta-analysis from UNNES, UPGRIS, and internet library sources
key_sources: S. Ngabekti, S. Ridlo, E. Peniati, R. Martanto. (2017). META-ANALYSIS OF JELAJAH ALAM SEKITAR (JAS) APPROACH IMPLEMENTATION IN LEARNING PROCESS. Jurnal Pendidikan IPA Indonesia. https://doi.org/10.15294/jpii.v6i1.8490

article_title: Writing Instruction Improves Students' Writing Differentially Depending on Focal Instruction and Children: A Meta-Analysis for Primary Grade Students
citation: Young-Suk Grace Kim, Dandan Yang, Marcela Reyes, Carol Connor. (2021). Writing instruction improves students' writing skills differentially depending on focal instruction and children: A meta-analysis for primary grade students. Educational Research Review 34. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2021.100408
title: Direct and indirect effects model of writing (DIEW)
description: The DIEW is the theoretical framework guiding this meta-analysis's moderation questions. It posits that writing quality draws on "a comprehensive set of skills and knowledge such as domain-general cognitions (e.g., working memory), language skills (e.g., vocabulary), transcription skills (spelling and handwriting/keyboarding), higher order cognitions and regulations (e.g., inferencing, perspective taking, monitoring, goal setting), topic and discourse knowledge, and socio-emotions." Crucially, it holds that relative contributions of these skills differ dynamically by composition dimension and developmental phase: productivity relies more heavily on transcription, while quality requires a broader skill set, and transcription's constraining role is largest early in development.
requirements: Instruction targeting writing quality must address a more comprehensive set of skills and knowledge than single-skill instruction
constraints: The dynamic relations hypothesis concerns the initial versus later phases of writing development
target_learning_goals: written composition skills including quality, productivity, and fluency
examples: The meta-analysis tested DIEW-derived predictions that multi-component instruction (SRSD) would outperform single-skill transcription instruction on writing quality
key_sources: Young-Suk Grace Kim, Dandan Yang, Marcela Reyes, Carol Connor. (2021). Writing instruction improves students' writing skills differentially depending on focal instruction and children: A meta-analysis for primary grade students. Educational Research Review 34. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2021.100408

article_title: Augmentative and Alternative Communication Intervention Targets for School-Aged Participants with ASD and ID: A Single-Case Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
citation: Ganz, J. B., Pustejovsky, J. E., Reichle, J., Vannest, K. J., Foster, M., Fuller, M. C., Pierson, L. M., Wattanawongwan, S., Bernal, A. J., Chen, M., Haas, A. N., Skov, R., Smith, S. D., & Yllades, V. (2022). Augmentative and Alternative Communication Intervention Targets for School-Aged Participants with ASD and ID: a Single-Case Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Review Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40489-022-00326-6
title: Report standardized participant characteristics and prior communication modes so AAC interventions can be individualized
description: The article recommends that single-case researchers provide richer baseline descriptions of participants so future AAC interventions can be matched to learner profiles. It argues that "more detailed participant descriptions" could identify skills mediating intervention success and enable customization of modes and functions. Without such reporting, moderators of outcome cannot be determined.
requirements: Studies must describe standardized diagnostic, cognitive, and social-communication assessment information, joint attention and imitation mastery, and prior communication mode use.
constraints: The article notes most standardized and normed assessments lack standards for modification for individuals who use AAC.
target_learners: school-aged learners with ASD and/or ID and complex communication needs
target_learning_goals: social-communication skills via AAC
examples: The meta-analysis found pre-intervention comprehension skills and word use were seldom reported, preventing determination of which participant characteristics predict better outcomes with particular modes.
key_sources: Ganz, J. B., Pustejovsky, J. E., Reichle, J., Vannest, K. J., Foster, M., Fuller, M. C., Pierson, L. M., Wattanawongwan, S., Bernal, A. J., Chen, M., Haas, A. N., Skov, R., Smith, S. D., & Yllades, V. (2022). Augmentative and Alternative Communication Intervention Targets for School-Aged Participants with ASD and ID: a Single-Case Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Review Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40489-022-00326-6

article_title: Individual Participant Data Meta-Analysis of the Impact of EEF Trials on the Educational Attainment of Pupils on Free School Meals: 2011-2019
citation: Bilal Ashraf, Akansha Singh, Germaine Uwimpuhwe, Tahani Coolen-Maturi, Jochen Einbeck, Steve Higgins and Adetayo Kasim. (2021). Individual participant data meta-analysis of the impact of EEF trials on the educational attainment of pupils on Free School Meals: 2011 - 2019. Education Endowment Foundation. https://www.educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk
title: Simplified IPD meta-analysis model (sIPD) for educational trials with heterogeneous outcome scales
description: The sIPD model is a three-level Bayesian individual participant data meta-analysis model adapted for educational trials, where pupils are nested within schools and schools within trials. Because outcome scales differ across trials, the authors "first eliminate heterogeneity between trials by scaling the post-test and pre-test outcome data to a unit variance of 1 per trial", then fit a model with fixed intercept and pre-test gradient, trial-specific treatment effects, and school and pupil random effects, pooling via inverse-variance weights. Attainment gaps are estimated by adding a treatment-by-FSM interaction term.
requirements: Outcome and pre-test data must be standardised within each trial to unit variance before pooling
Bayesian fitting with vague priors and MCMC convergence checking (three chains, 200,000 iterations, Rhat and trace plots)
constraints: The scaling approach is described as statistically not the most desirable, offering a trade-off between model challenges and meaningful results
It may distort outcome distributions if outcomes do not come from a common underlying construct
Shrinkage of trial-specific effects may disadvantage less heterogeneous trials
target_learners: pupils eligible for Free School Meals in English primary and secondary schools
target_learning_goals: literacy attainment
mathematics attainment
examples: Applied to 88 EEF trials from 2011-2019 with over half a million pupils, estimating pooled effects on FSM pupils and FSM-non-FSM attainment gaps in literacy and mathematics.
key_sources: Bilal Ashraf, Akansha Singh, Germaine Uwimpuhwe, Tahani Coolen-Maturi, Jochen Einbeck, Steve Higgins and Adetayo Kasim. (2021). Individual participant data meta-analysis of the impact of EEF trials on the educational attainment of pupils on Free School Meals: 2011 - 2019. Education Endowment Foundation. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED625398

article_title: Training Individuals to Implement Discrete Trials with Fidelity: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Joelle Fingerhut and Mariola Moeyaert. (2022). Training Individuals to Implement Discrete Trials with Fidelity: A Meta-Analysis. Focus on Autism and Other Developmental Disabilities. https://doi.org/10.1177/10883576221081076
title: Behavioral skills training as a four-component training package
description: Behavioral skills training (BST) is a training package that "includes the four training methods of feedback, instruction, modeling, and rehearsal delivered together and/or sequentially." The article defines each component operationally: feedback is performance feedback from an observer, instruction is verbal, digital, or print information, modeling is a live or video demonstration, and rehearsal is structured role-play with a trainer in the presence of a trainer. The meta-analysis uses these dummy-coded components as moderators of DTT implementation fidelity gains.
requirements: For the meta-analysis definition, BST occurred when instruction, modeling, rehearsal, and feedback were implemented simultaneously or sequentially during the training
constraints: Instruction could not be isolated as a variable because 96% of studies included it; feedback could not be isolated because only 11% of studies included it separate from BST
target_learning_goals: accurate implementation of discrete trial training with fidelity
examples: In the meta-analysis, 130 (58%) of 224 participants received BST as their training, and BST recipients reached 96.06% average implementation fidelity
key_sources: Joelle Fingerhut and Mariola Moeyaert. (2022). Training Individuals to Implement Discrete Trials with Fidelity: A Meta-Analysis. Focus on Autism and Other Developmental Disabilities. https://doi.org/10.1177/10883576221081076

article_title: Training Individuals to Implement Discrete Trials with Fidelity: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Joelle Fingerhut and Mariola Moeyaert. (2022). Training Individuals to Implement Discrete Trials with Fidelity: A Meta-Analysis. Focus on Autism and Other Developmental Disabilities. https://doi.org/10.1177/10883576221081076
title: Use complete behavioral skills training to teach discrete trial implementation
description: The article concludes that because BST is statistically significantly effective for raising DTT implementation fidelity, "behavior skills training is recommended for discrete trial training implementation instruction." BST combines feedback, instruction, modeling, and rehearsal, and the meta-analysis shows complete BST outperforms trainings using only some components. The recommendation applies across implementers, since 69% of participants had no prior DTT experience.
requirements: Training should include all four BST components (feedback, instruction, modeling, rehearsal) delivered together and/or sequentially
constraints: More research is needed to determine BST effectiveness for teaching DTT in home environments and to parents, who were only 13% of participants
target_learning_goals: implementing discrete trial training with fidelity
examples: The meta-analysis of 46 SCED studies found BST-trained participants implemented DTT with 96.06% fidelity on average, above the 90% mastery threshold used in prior studies
key_sources: Joelle Fingerhut and Mariola Moeyaert. (2022). Training Individuals to Implement Discrete Trials with Fidelity: A Meta-Analysis. Focus on Autism and Other Developmental Disabilities. https://doi.org/10.1177/10883576221081076

article_title: Effects of Integrated Literacy and Content-Area Instruction on Vocabulary and Comprehension in the Elementary Years: A Meta-Analysis
citation: HyeJin Hwang, Sonia Q. Cabell & Rachel E. Joyner (2021). Effects of Integrated Literacy and Content-area Instruction on Vocabulary and Comprehension in the Elementary Years: A Meta-analysis. Scientific Studies of Reading. https://doi.org/10.1080/10888438.2021.1954005
title: Integrated literacy and content-area instruction as mutually enhancing literacy-content teaching
description: The article defines integrated instruction between literacy and the content areas as "instruction in which literacy activities (reading and/or writing) serve as a tool to cultivate content knowledge (science and/ or social studies) while, at the same time, content teaching serves as a lever to facilitate literacy skills". It is operationalized through connected texts sequenced to reflect content connections, repeated encounters with content-related words taught in relation to content rather than in isolation, and motivating purposes for literacy activities. The meta-analysis tests whether this mutually enhancing design improves vocabulary, comprehension, and content knowledge in K-5.
requirements: The approach blends ideas and skills in different subjects with balanced attention to each subject, rather than focusing on one subject with the other only used as a tool
constraints: The literature contains varied definitions of integrated models of instruction without a clear consensus
target_learners: Students in kindergarten through fifth grade
target_learning_goals: Vocabulary learning of content-related words
Reading comprehension
Science and social studies content knowledge
examples: Included interventions sequenced multiple coherently connected texts around science or social studies content and had students encounter and use content-related words repeatedly while reading and writing to learn the content
key_sources: HyeJin Hwang, Sonia Q. Cabell & Rachel E. Joyner (2021). Effects of Integrated Literacy and Content-area Instruction on Vocabulary and Comprehension in the Elementary Years: A Meta-analysis. Scientific Studies of Reading. https://doi.org/10.1080/10888438.2021.1954005

article_title: Effects of Integrated Literacy and Content-Area Instruction on Vocabulary and Comprehension in the Elementary Years: A Meta-Analysis
citation: HyeJin Hwang, Sonia Q. Cabell & Rachel E. Joyner (2021). Effects of Integrated Literacy and Content-area Instruction on Vocabulary and Comprehension in the Elementary Years: A Meta-analysis. Scientific Studies of Reading. https://doi.org/10.1080/10888438.2021.1954005
title: Present connected content ideas explicitly and cumulatively, and revisit content-related words across sessions
description: In integrated literacy and content-area instruction, the logical organization of the science or social studies content guides design: "Connected ideas from science or social studies content are presented to students explicitly and cumulatively within and across class sessions." Text sequences reflect connections among content ideas, and content-related words appear repeatedly within and across sessions, with meanings taught in relation to content rather than in isolation. The article presents this organization as the mechanism leveraged by the interventions it meta-analyzes.
requirements: Students regularly interact with multiple texts coherently connected to one another around science or social studies content
target_learners: Elementary students in kindergarten through fifth grade
target_learning_goals: Building content knowledge through text
Vocabulary learning of content-related words
Comprehension of connected texts
examples: The article gives the example of a text explaining the process of pollination followed by a text about animals assisting with plant pollination, with words like pollen, flower, and bees recurring across sessions
key_sources: HyeJin Hwang, Sonia Q. Cabell & Rachel E. Joyner (2021). Effects of Integrated Literacy and Content-area Instruction on Vocabulary and Comprehension in the Elementary Years: A Meta-analysis. Scientific Studies of Reading. https://doi.org/10.1080/10888438.2021.1954005

article_title: The Impact of Guided Notes on Post-Secondary Student Achievement: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Larwin, K. H., & Larwin, D. A. (2013). The Impact of Guided Notes on Post-Secondary Student Achievement: A Meta-Analysis. International Journal of Teaching and Learning in Higher Education, 25(1), 47-58. http://www.isetl.org/ijtlhe/
title: Use guided notes as a low-cost, low-tech means of increasing engagement and achievement in lecture-based post-secondary courses
description: Guided notes are "teacher-prepared handouts that 'guide' a student through a lecture with standard cues and prepared space in which to write key facts, concepts, and/or relationships". The article recommends them as a "low-tech" inclusion that can significantly impact post-secondary achievement, based on its meta-analytic finding of a moderate overall effect. They are provided as handouts, electronically, or as PowerPoint slides with prompts and blank space.
requirements: Provided during lecture as an alternative to no notes, full lecture notes, or student-generated notes
Studies must use cues with prepared space for students to complete key content
constraints: Negative effects were found in single studies from mathematics and dentistry
All available research included undergraduate students only; no graduate-level studies were available
target_learning_goals: academic achievement in lecture-based courses
student engagement during lectures
examples: The meta-analysis included 12 studies across psychology, physics, mathematics, education, and dentistry, calculating 27 independent effect sizes from 1,529 participants
key_sources: Larwin, K. H., & Larwin, D. A. (2013). The Impact of Guided Notes on Post-Secondary Student Achievement: A Meta-Analysis. International Journal of Teaching and Learning in Higher Education, 25(1), 47-58. http://www.isetl.org/ijtlhe/

article_title: The Effectiveness Level of Material Use in Classroom Instruction: A Meta-Analysis Study
citation: Zeynel KABLAN, Beyda TOPAN, Burak ERKAN. (2013). The Effectiveness Level of Material Use in Classroom Instruction: A Meta-analysis Study. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice. https://doi.org/10.12738/estp.2013.3.1692
title: Typology of classroom instructional materials by material type
description: The article organizes the materials used in the reviewed studies into five types: "computer presentations, hands-on materials, cartoons, concept maps, and combination of different materials". Computer presentations were in PowerPoint or animation format; hands-on materials are "materials that can be touched and moved around easily by students"; cartoons reveal important information about specific content; concept maps are two-dimensional diagrams showing relationships among concepts; and a combination category was used when more than one material was used. The typology served as a coding variable in the meta-analysis.
requirements: Studies must be classifiable into one of the five material categories for moderator coding
constraints: Distance learning, computer-based learning, and worksheet studies were excluded from the analysis
target_learning_goals: academic achievement across subject matters
examples: The 57 included studies were coded into these material categories, with computer presentations most frequent (29.8%) and hands-on materials least frequent (14%)
key_sources: Zeynel KABLAN, Beyda TOPAN, Burak ERKAN. (2013). The Effectiveness Level of Material Use in Classroom Instruction: A Meta-analysis Study. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice. https://doi.org/10.12738/estp.2013.3.1692

article_title: The Effectiveness Level of Material Use in Classroom Instruction: A Meta-Analysis Study
citation: Zeynel KABLAN, Beyda TOPAN, Burak ERKAN. (2013). The Effectiveness Level of Material Use in Classroom Instruction: A Meta-analysis Study. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice. https://doi.org/10.12738/estp.2013.3.1692
title: Meta-analysis corpus of 57 Turkish experimental studies on instructional material use (2000–2012)
description: A corpus of 57 experimental and quasi-experimental studies investigating the effectiveness of educational materials on academic achievement, drawn from national journal articles, theses and dissertations in the YÖK national thesis/dissertation centre, and conference papers. Studies were selected by explicit criteria, including that "Quasi-experimental and experimental studies that used educational materials in the experiment groups were included in this meta-analysis". Each study was coded on eight summary categories plus statistical information such as sample sizes, means and standard deviations.
requirements: Studies must report the statistical information necessary to calculate effect sizes
constraints: Limited to studies conducted in Turkey and published between 2000 and 2012; distance learning, computer-based learning and worksheet studies excluded; for studies with multiple experiment groups only the material-using group was included
target_learning_goals: academic achievement
examples: Data collection covered academic articles, YÖK thesis/dissertation records, and conference proceedings; 57 studies met all criteria and entered the analysis
key_sources: Zeynel KABLAN, Beyda TOPAN, Burak ERKAN. (2013). The Effectiveness Level of Material Use in Classroom Instruction: A Meta-analysis Study. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice. https://doi.org/10.12738/estp.2013.3.1692

article_title: Effectiveness of Computer-Assisted Mathematics Education (CAME) over Academic Achievement: A Meta-Analysis Study
citation: Demir, S., & Başol, G. (2014). Effectiveness of Computer-Assisted Mathematics Education (CAME) over Academic Achievement: A Meta-Analysis Study. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice, 14(5), 2026-2035. http://www.edam.com.tr/estp
title: Use computer-assisted education in mathematics at every level of the education system, given the pooled positive effect
description: The authors draw a design recommendation from their meta-analytic finding that CAME has a large positive effect on mathematics achievement. They write that because "The usage of specialized software increased the positive effect of CAE on mathematics achievements", "it is possible to propose the usage of CAE in every level of the education system". The recommendation is grounded in the pooled ES = .8999 result from 40 Turkish studies.
requirements: Studies included should be experimental or quasi-experimental and contain sufficient data (means, standard deviations, group sizes) for effect size calculation
constraints: The recommendation rests on studies mostly sampled from large cities, which the authors note may limit generalizability
Some included studies reported no significant effect of CAME on academic achievement
target_learners: preschool, primary, secondary, high-school, and college students in Turkey
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement
geometry achievement
examples: The meta-analysis combined 40 studies (4 PhD theses, 16 master's theses, 17 articles, and 3 technical/congressional/symposium reports) with a total sample of 5623 students, 3002 experimental and 2621 control.
key_sources: Demir, S., & Başol, G. (2014). Effectiveness of Computer-Assisted Mathematics Education (CAME) over Academic Achievement: A Meta-Analysis Study. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice, 14(5), 2026-2035. http://www.edam.com.tr/estp

article_title: The Effects of Problem Posing on Student Mathematical Learning: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Roslinda Rosli, Mary Margaret Capraro & Robert M. Capraro. (2014). The Effects of Problem Posing on Student Mathematical Learning: A Meta-Analysis. International Education Studies, 7(13). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/ies.v7n13p227
title: Review student performance in the four learning outcome areas before adopting a problem-posing program
description: The article recommends that school leaders ground adoption decisions in baseline performance across the four coded outcome areas: knowledge-based, ability-based, skill-based, and attitude-beliefs. By reviewing how students perform in each area, leaders can customize the program to student needs and set reasonable expectations. The article states leaders "should consider the four learning outcomes" before deciding on a problem-posing program.
requirements: Baseline information on student performance in knowledge, problem solving skill, problem posing ability, and attitude areas
constraints: Effect estimates rest largely on quasi-experimental designs; a one-group design tends to inflate effect sizes
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement
problem solving skills
problem posing ability
attitudes toward mathematics
examples: The meta-analysis pooled 14 datasets from 13 studies (approximately 1,316 participants) and reported mean effect sizes ranging from .76 to 1.31 across the four outcome areas.
key_sources: Roslinda Rosli, Mary Margaret Capraro & Robert M. Capraro. (2014). The Effects of Problem Posing on Student Mathematical Learning: A Meta-Analysis. International Education Studies, 7(13). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/ies.v7n13p227

article_title: A Comparative Meta-Analysis of 5E and Traditional Approaches in Turkey
citation: Özgür Anil, Veli Batdi. (2015). A Comparative Meta-Analysis of 5E and Traditional Approaches in Turkey. Journal of Education and Training Studies. https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v3i6.1038
title: Meta-analytic corpus of 14 Turkish 5E studies (2008-2014) analysed with CMA and MetaWin
description: A corpus of studies and theses on the 5E instructional model published in Turkey between 2008 and 2014, screened from 161 accessed publications (118 articles and 43 theses) down to 14 included studies. The article states "a review undertaken of the studies and theses (N=14) executed in Turkey over the period 2008-2014 on the 5E model", with academic achievement N:13, retention N:5 and attitude N:8. Effect sizes were computed as Hedges' d using the Comprehensive Meta-Analysis (CMA) program, MetaWin and Microsoft Excel 2010, and intercoder reliability between two encoders was calculated as 100%.
requirements: Studies had to contain statistical values such as sample size, arithmetic means and standard deviations, and use a pretest-posttest and control group model
constraints: Some studies were excluded because they did not reflect the relevant nature of experimental research
target_learners: students in Turkish schools and universities taught with the 5E model
target_learning_goals: academic achievement
retention
attitude toward lessons
examples: The article reports 336, 149 and 225 students in experimental groups for achievement, retention and attitude respectively, with control group sizes of 324, 137 and 211
key_sources: Özgür Anil, Veli Batdi. (2015). A Comparative Meta-Analysis of 5E and Traditional Approaches in Turkey. Journal of Education and Training Studies. https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v3i6.1038

article_title: A Comparative Meta-Analysis of 5E and Traditional Approaches in Turkey
citation: Özgür Anil, Veli Batdi. (2015). A Comparative Meta-Analysis of 5E and Traditional Approaches in Turkey. Journal of Education and Training Studies. https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v3i6.1038
title: The 5E instructional model as a five-stage constructivist learning cycle
description: The 5E instructional model, developed by Bybee at the Biological Science Curriculum Study, is a constructivist teaching sequence grounded in the view that knowledge is constructed by the individual rather than passively transmitted. The article states "This model is based on 5 different stages of learning: Engage, Explore, Explain, Elaborate and Evaluate." In this model the student plays an active role, the teacher acts as a guide, and learning is focused on process rather than product, associating the learning environment with the world outside the classroom. The meta-analysis treats this model as the intervention whose effects on achievement, retention and attitude are pooled across studies.
requirements: Instruction designed within the model engages students at every stage so they make their own conceptualizations
constraints: The article reports that teachers needed more time for classroom preparation in order to implement the 5E instructional model
target_learners: school and university students in science and other subjects
target_learning_goals: science concept learning
conceptual change
scientific processing skills
attitude toward lessons
examples: Studies in the corpus applied the model across subjects including physics, biology, geography, mathematics and social studies
key_sources: Özgür Anil, Veli Batdi. (2015). A Comparative Meta-Analysis of 5E and Traditional Approaches in Turkey. Journal of Education and Training Studies. https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v3i6.1038

article_title: A Meta-Analysis of the Relationship between E-Learning and Students' Academic Achievement in Higher Education
citation: Gloria Mothibi. (2015). A Meta-Analysis of the Relationship between E-Learning and Students' Academic Achievement in Higher Education. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.9. https://www.iiste.org
title: Provide adequate ICT infrastructure to facilitate e-learning in higher education, because the meta-analytic effect size indicates this can substantially improve learning and achievement
description: The article argues that because e-learning's success depends on the quality of ICT, higher education institutions should invest in adequate, well-managed ICT facilities. It states that "Considering the effect size of 0.712, it can statis tically be inferred that provision of adequate ICT infrastructure towards facilitating use of e-learning can substant ially lead improved learning and students' academic achievement." It also identifies adequate provision and better management of available ICT facilities as means to improve utilization.
requirements: Adequate supply of computer hardware and software, reliable power, teacher training opportunities, and funding and maintenance, which the article identifies as constraints on ICT utilization
constraints: The article notes many colleges lack well-equipped computer laboratories and are constrained by inadequate ICT facilities
target_learning_goals: overall academic achievement across disciplines
examples: The meta-analysis of 15 studies reported a mean effect size of 0.712 for e-learning's impact on academic achievement, which the article uses to ground the infrastructure recommendation.
key_sources: Gloria Mothibi. (2015). A Meta-Analysis of the Relationship between E-Learning and Students' Academic Achievement in Higher Education. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.9. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1082408

article_title: A Meta-Analysis of the Relationship between E-Learning and Students' Academic Achievement in Higher Education
citation: Gloria Mothibi. (2015). A Meta-Analysis of the Relationship between E-Learning and Students' Academic Achievement in Higher Education. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.9. https://www.iiste.org
title: E-learning as ICT-enabled teaching and learning that changes teacher and learner roles and fosters learner autonomy
description: The article frames e-learning as the use and application of information and communication technologies — websites, PCs, tablet PCs, cell phones, learning management systems, TVs and radios — to improve teaching and learning processes. It defines e-learning as "a network-enabled expression associated with functions that facilitate teaching and learning in an efficient manner" (citing Cooke). It holds that ICT features "change the role of the teacher and th e learner, facilitate learning, and lead to interactive learni ng, learner autonomy, self-sufficiency, and self-co nfidence", shifting teachers from mere sources of material to supervisors of the learning process.
requirements: ICT infrastructure of adequate quality, since the article states the success of e-learning depends on the quality of ICT
constraints: The article notes e-learning and online learning are regarded to have different meanings, and terminology varies
target_learning_goals: academic achievement, learner autonomy, self-sufficiency and self-confidence
examples: E-learning programs include web-based learning, computer-based learning, virtual classrooms and electronic activity, with content delivered via web, intranet or extranet, audio or video MP3s, satellite televisions and CD-ROMs.
key_sources: Gloria Mothibi. (2015). A Meta-Analysis of the Relationship between E-Learning and Students' Academic Achievement in Higher Education. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.9. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1082408

article_title: The Effect of 7E Learning Cycle on Learning in Science Teaching: A Meta-Analysis Study
citation: Balta, N., & Sarac, H. (2016). The Effect of 7E Learning Cycle on Learning in Science Teaching: A meta-Analysis Study. European Journal of Educational Research, 5(2), 61-72. https://doi.org/10.12973/eu-jer.5.2.61
title: The 7E learning cycle: a seven-phase constructivist instructional model for science teaching
description: The 7E learning cycle is a constructivist, student-centered instructional model consisting of seven phases: "elicit, engage, explore, explain, elaborate, evaluate, and extend". It expands the 5E model by splitting engage into elicit and engage, emphasizing prior understanding and misconceptions, and by adding an extend phase so students "transfer their learning to a new context". Each phase has described activities: concept cartoons and demonstrations in elicit, discrepant events in engage, questioning and worksheets in explore, teacher explanation with concept maps in explain, application to new areas in elaborate, formative and summative evaluation in evaluate, and transfer to everyday life in extend.
requirements: Teachers carry out each phase; the article notes the model "can be time-consuming because of the fact that each phase should be carried out meticulously"
constraints: The article notes the model can be time-consuming when each phase is carried out meticulously
target_learning_goals: science conceptual achievement
transfer of learning to new contexts
addressing misconceptions
examples: The meta-analysis synthesized 24 primary studies that implemented the 7E cycle in biology, chemistry, physics and science courses across middle school, high school and university levels
key_sources: Balta, N., & Sarac, H. (2016). The Effect of 7E Learning Cycle on Learning in Science Teaching: A meta-Analysis Study. European Journal of Educational Research, 5(2), 61-72. https://doi.org/10.12973/eu-jer.5.2.61

article_title: The Effects of Mathematical Modelling on Students' Achievement-Meta-Analysis of Research
citation: Andrzej Sokolowski. (2015). The Effects of Mathematical Modelling on Students’ Achievement-Meta-Analysis of Research. The IAFOR Journal of Education, Volume III - Issue I - Winter 2015. https://journals.iafor.org/index.php/joe
title: Modelling cycles: staged structure of mathematical modelling activity
description: The article describes mathematical modelling as an activity with a staged structure called modelling cycles, citing Blum and Leiss (2007). The stages are "understanding the problem (constructing), simplifying (structuring), mathematizing, working mathematically, interpreting, validating and exposing", with transitions involving observations, measurements, and interactions described as data. The meta-analysis uses this framing to characterize what treatment groups experienced, and notes models—the products—are simplified but accurate representations of aspects of the real world.
requirements: Learners progress through the stages with teacher guidance rather than direct solutions, consistent with the constructivist paradigm the article attributes to Hussmann (2007)
constraints: Conducting real experiments is difficult in mathematics classrooms traditionally not designed for that purpose, so supports such as computerized experiments may be needed
target_learning_goals: applying mathematics to extra-mathematical situations
constructing and validating mathematical models
examples: The 13 meta-analyzed studies all placed students in student-centered settings deriving models for given problems, using teachers' expertise only when needed
key_sources: Andrzej Sokolowski. (2015). The Effects of Mathematical Modelling on Students’ Achievement-Meta-Analysis of Research. The IAFOR Journal of Education, Volume III - Issue I - Winter 2015. https://journals.iafor.org/index.php/joe

article_title: The Effectiveness of Multiple Intelligence Applications on Academic Achievement: A Meta-Analysis=Çoklu Zekâ Ögretim Uygulamalarinin Akademik Basari Üzerindeki Etkisi: Bir Meta-Analiz Çalismasi
citation: Eyüp Yurt & Seyat Polat. (2015). The Effectiveness of Multiple Intelligence Applications on Academic Achievement: A Meta-Analysis. Journal of Social Studies Education Research 6(1), 84-122. http://www.sosyalbilgiler.org
title: Meta-analytic dataset of 73 Turkish multiple-intelligence experimental studies (2000-2014)
description: The article assembles a coded corpus of Turkish experimental studies of multiple intelligence based instructional practices published between 2000 and 2014, drawn from the Council of Higher Education Thesis Center, Dergi Park, Akademia Social Sciences and Araştirmax indexes. After applying four inclusion criteria, "66 thesis and seven articles fit for the criteria", yielding 73 studies (81 comparisons) analyzed in CMA 2.0. Coder agreement was 85%.
requirements: Studies must use pre-test post-test with control group experimental design and report participant numbers, means and standard deviations
constraints: Limited to studies conducted in Turkey between 2000 and 2014 that were accessible
target_learning_goals: academic achievement across multiple school courses
examples: Descriptively, 65,8% of studies were elementary level, 27,4% secondary, 6,8% university; 79,5% were master's thesis
key_sources: Eyüp Yurt & Seyat Polat. (2015). The Effectiveness of Multiple Intelligence Applications on Academic Achievement: A Meta-Analysis. Journal of Social Studies Education Research 6(1), 84-122. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1105368

article_title: Does Hands-On Science Practices Make an Impact on Achievement in Science? A Meta-Analysis
citation: Caglak, S. (2017). Does hands-on science practices make an ımpact on achievement in science? A meta-analysis. Journal of Education in Science, Environment and Health (JESEH), 3(1), 69-87. https://www.jeseh.net
title: Use hands-on activities as an effective strategy for teaching science
description: The article's implication is that hands-on science activities, in which students actively manipulate materials while learning science, should be employed in science teaching to support achievement and scientific literacy. The author states "Our findings also suggest that hands-on activities be used for effective science teaching" and that educators are responsible to employ or encourage their use during science teaching. The recommendation rests on the meta-analytic overall effect estimate, which the author himself flags as possibly inflated by publication bias.
requirements: Activities must involve students actively manipulating objects and variables, performing experiments, making observations, collecting and recording data, reasoning, and sharing findings, as the included interventions did
constraints: The evidence base is limited to Turkish studies between 2000 and 2015 meeting the inclusion criteria; the author states "This analysis was limited with studies conducted only in Turkey"
Some previous studies found no advantage of hands-on over virtual materials or paper-and-pencil tasks, and the author notes cognitive manipulation of variables may be the crucial ingredient
target_learners: Middle school, high school and college/university students in science courses
target_learning_goals: Science achievement (conceptual understanding and performance in science sub-disciplines)
Scientific literacy and scientific inquiry skills
examples: The meta-analysis pooled 15 Turkish experimental studies in which hands-on activities were the intervention compared against teacher-centered or lecture-based instruction, with achievement tests as the outcome measure
key_sources: Caglak, S. (2017). Does hands-on science practices make an ımpact on achievement in science? A meta-analysis. Journal of Education in Science, Environment and Health (JESEH), 3(1), 69-87. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1125775

article_title: Impact of Mobile Assisted Language Learning (MALL) on EFL: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Imtiaz Hassan Taj, Norrihan Binti Sulan, Muhammad Aslam Sipra, Waqar Ahmad. (2016). Impact of Mobile Assisted Language Learning (MALL) on EFL: A Meta-Analysis. Advances in Language and Literary Studies 7(2). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.7n.2p.76
title: MALL as a ubiquitous, multimodal platform for EFL instruction fitting the PPP paradigm
description: The article frames Mobile Assisted Language Learning as instruction delivered through mobile phones, whose "user friendly interfaces, ubiquitous access and improved data storage and retrieval capacities offer a good platform for learning". It holds that MALL fits the Presentation–Practice–Production paradigm, that phones can present rich material in multimodal ways, and that instructors can provide initial scaffolding and gradually withdraw support, allowing learners to take charge of their learning.
requirements: Mobile devices with connectivity and data storage/retrieval capacity as the delivery platform
constraints: The article notes MALL is a relatively young field, only a couple of decades old, with no dedicated journal and much literature in conference proceedings
target_learners: EFL learners from fifth grade through undergraduate level
target_learning_goals: English vocabulary acquisition
English as a foreign language instruction
examples: The meta-analysis included 13 studies in which content was delivered via mobile phones (12 studies) or a PDA (1 study), mostly through SMS or dedicated applications
key_sources: Imtiaz Hassan Taj, Norrihan Binti Sulan, Muhammad Aslam Sipra, Waqar Ahmad. (2016). Impact of Mobile Assisted Language Learning (MALL) on EFL: A Meta-Analysis. Advances in Language and Literary Studies 7(2). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.7n.2p.76

article_title: A Meta-Analysis of School-Based Interventions Aimed to Prevent or Reduce Violence in Teen Dating Relationships
citation: Lisa De La Rue, Joshua R. Polanin, Dorothy L. Espelage, Terri D. Pigott. (2017). A Meta-Analysis of School-Based Interventions Aimed to Prevent or Reduce Violence in Teen Dating Relationships. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654316632061
title: Dating violence prevention programs should explicitly incorporate skill-building components to promote behavior change
description: The article recommends that future dating violence prevention interventions explicitly include skill-building components, because knowledge and attitude change alone are unlikely to change behavior. It argues that "without a skill-building component that integrates specific training to modify behavior and develop competencies, it is unlikely that behavior change will be accomplished." Of the included studies, only two clearly described a skill-building component.
requirements: Programs aiming to change perpetration or victimization behavior must include explicit skill-building training, such as practicing how to discuss disagreements and how to leave an abusive relationship or seek support.
constraints: The review found only two included studies clearly described a skill-building component, and the small number of studies limited the ability to differentiate intervention types or components.
target_learners: middle and high school students in Grades 6 to 12, ages 11 to 18
target_learning_goals: recognizing abusive dating behaviors
negotiating conflict in relationships
seeking support or assistance
examples: The Safe Dates program includes activities intended to shift dating violence and gender role norms as well as to increase conflict management skills; the Fourth R and Safe Dates studies were the two included studies that clearly described a skill-building component.
key_sources: Lisa De La Rue, Joshua R. Polanin, Dorothy L. Espelage, Terri D. Pigott. (2017). A Meta-Analysis of School-Based Interventions Aimed to Prevent or Reduce Violence in Teen Dating Relationships. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654316632061

article_title: The Influence of Student-Centered Methods in Turkish Language Instruction on Academic Success: A Meta-Analysis Study
citation: Nurşat Biçer. (2017). The Influence of Student-centered Methods in Turkish Language Instruction on Academic Success: A Meta-analysis Study. Universal Journal of Educational Research 5(4). https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2017.050419
title: Corpus of 96 identified studies with 22 included in the meta-analysis
description: The article's evidence base is a literature review of experimental studies on student-centered methods in Turkish language instruction published between 2000 and 2016. The review "revealed that there are 96 studies available on student -centered methods based on multiple intelligences, creative drama, collaboration and games", of which 22 qualified for meta-analysis after exclusions for missing statistical data. Included studies spanned multiple intelligences-based learning (f=5), creative drama-based learning (F=6), collaborative learning (F=6) and game-based learning (f=5), mostly master's theses (11) and mostly at primary education level (17).
requirements: Studies must be experimental or quasi-experimental with experimental-control groups and report sample size, arithmetic mean and standard deviation for effect size calculation
At least five studies must be available for each method, as a minimum of five comparisons is required for the reliability of Hedges' d
constraints: Only studies conducted between 2000 and 2016 in Turkish language instruction were included; studies lacking total data, standard deviation or sample size were excluded
target_learning_goals: academic success in Turkish language instruction (reading, writing, vocabulary, grammar, speaking)
examples: Data were searched via the Council of Higher Education thesis center, EBSCO, ERIC, ASOS Index, ULAKBIM and Google Scholar, with keywords in Turkish and English
key_sources: Nurşat Biçer. (2017). The Influence of Student-centered Methods in Turkish Language Instruction on Academic Success: A Meta-analysis Study. Universal Journal of Educational Research 5(4). https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2017.050419

article_title: Functional Technology for Individuals with Intellectual Disabilities: Meta-Analysis of Mobile Device-Based Interventions
citation: Jemma Kim & Christina H. Kimm. (2017). Functional Technology for Individuals with Intellectual Disabilities: Meta-Analysis of Mobile Device-Based Interventions. The Journal of Special Education Apprenticeship, 6(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Functional+Technology+for+Individuals+with+Intellectual+Disabilities+Meta-Analysis+of+Mobile+Device-Based+Interventions
title: Functional Technology (FT) as a new paradigm beyond assistive technology for people with intellectual disabilities
description: The article proposes functional technology as a paradigm in which people with intellectual disabilities proficiently use mainstream technology, including mobile devices, in daily activities and various environments, beyond specialized assistive technology. It defines FT as "the process of implementing any assistive technology in daily routines, managing and navigating the network, and manipulating software that addresses the specific needs of individual with disabilities" (Kimm, 2016). The authors argue FT supports social integration and normalization because mobile devices' universal handheld design minimizes focus on the user's disability.
requirements: Access to mainstream mobile devices and appropriate apps and internet resources
Support for people with ID to become active agents in learning and implementing functional technology rather than passive recipients of instruction
constraints: Research on mobile device effectiveness beyond instructional technology in the classroom is described as being in a beginning stage
target_learning_goals: daily living and functional skills
communication
social integration and community participation
technology literacy
examples: Uphold et al. (2016) instructed six adults with ID to schedule exercising routines using an ePAS app on an iPod Touch; Kelley et al. (2013) used picture prompts on iPod to teach four young adults with ID campus navigation, with generalization to various locations
key_sources: Jemma Kim & Christina H. Kimm. (2017). Functional Technology for Individuals with Intellectual Disabilities: Meta-Analysis of Mobile Device-Based Interventions. The Journal of Special Education Apprenticeship, 6(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1149575

article_title: Effect of 5E Learning Model on Academic Achievement, Attitude and Science Process Skills: Meta-Analysis Study
citation: Nevin Kozcu Cakır. (2017). Effect of 5E Learning Model on Academic Achievement, Attitude and Science Process Skills: Meta-analysis Study. Journal of Education and Training Studies, 5(11). https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v5i11.2649
title: The 5E learning model: a five-phase constructivist instructional sequence for science courses
description: The 5E learning model is a constructivist instructional model for science courses comprising five phases: introduction (engagement), discovery (exploration), description (explanation), expanding (elaboration), and assessment (evaluation). The article describes it as a way "to design science courses based on structural approach and cognitive psychology" (Bybee, 1997), in which prior knowledge is identified, a research question is posed, first-hand experience is gained under teacher guidance, and the concept is transferred to a new field and evaluated.
requirements: Studies applying the model in the synthesized corpus used it in the experimental group while the control group received traditional teaching
constraints: The article's synthesis is limited to studies applied in science and technology courses in Turkey between 2006 and 2016 with semi-experimental designs
target_learners: university students and pre-service teachers in science courses
target_learning_goals: science conceptual understanding
science process skills
attitudes toward science
examples: The article describes each phase, e.g. in the introduction step "a short demonstration, problem situation or event is given in order to evaluate and reveal the preliminary knowledge of students".
key_sources: Nevin Kozcu Cakır. (2017). Effect of 5E Learning Model on Academic Achievement, Attitude and Science Process Skills: Meta-analysis Study. Journal of Education and Training Studies, 5(11). https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v5i11.2649

article_title: A Meta-Analysis of Video Modeling Interventions for Children and Adolescents with Emotional/Behavioral Disorders
citation: Elias Clinton. (2016). A Meta-Analysis of Video Modeling Interventions for Children and Adolescents with Emotional/Behavioral Disorders. Educational Research Quarterly, 40(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?q=A+Meta-Analysis+of+Video+Modeling+Interventions+for+Children+and+Adolescents+with+Emotional%2FBehavioral+Disorders
title: Video modeling taxonomy: video modeling other (VMO) versus video self-modeling (VSM), grounded in Bandura's social learning theory
description: The article organizes video modeling interventions along one axis: VMO uses footage of an adult or peer (not the learner) engaging in a target behavior, while VSM uses "footage of the learner his/herself engaging in a target behavior in order to promote future occurrences of that target beh avior." VM applies Bandura's social learning theory, in which individuals learn skills through observation and vicarious reinforcement. The review indexes all 19 studies into these two categories and further classifies them by paired components, age, gender, and dependent measures.
requirements: Video footage of a model (other or self) engaging the target behavior, presented so the learner can observe and imitate it
constraints: Both variations have been found successful where other interventions have failed, per studies the review cites; the review does not rank VMO above VSM given the skewed study distribution
target_learning_goals: increase pro-social and on-task behaviors
decrease disruptive and aggressive behaviors
examples: The review classified 3 studies as VMO (e.g., Blood et al., 2011) and 16 as VSM (e.g., Clare, Jenson, Kehle, & Bray, 2000), with paired components including token economy, teacher feedback, and self-monitoring.
key_sources: Elias Clinton. (2016). A Meta-Analysis of Video Modeling Interventions for Children and Adolescents with Emotional/Behavioral Disorders. Educational Research Quarterly, 40(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1166705

article_title: The Effect of Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics-STEM Educational Practices on Students' Learning Outcomes: A Meta-Analysis Study
citation: Saraç, H. (2018). The Effect of Science, Technology, Engin eering and Mathematics-Stem Educational Practices on Students’ Learning Outcomes: A Meta-Analysis Study. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 17(2). https://www.tojet.net
title: STEM education as an integrated, engineering-design-based approach bridging science, technology, engineering and mathematics
description: The article frames STEM education as an approach that integrates the four disciplines rather than teaching them separately: "The aim of STEM education is to achieve an approach that focuses on the integration of learning by establishing a relationship between the disciplines, rather than being separate from each other". It describes technology and engineering design-based STEM as integrating knowledge and skills across the areas in teaching mathematics and science, and as a method by which students approach problems from a multidisciplinary point of view while gaining twenty-first century skills such as critical thinking, problem solving, co-operation, and communication.
requirements: Teaching that establishes relationships between the STEM disciplines, e.g. by connecting a unit or lesson to real-life problems
constraints: The article notes STEM integration had not yet become widespread in Turkey at the time of writing, with work in the area still in its infancy
target_learning_goals: interdisciplinary knowledge integration
twenty-first century skills such as problem solving, creativity and scientific thinking
examples: The reviewed STEM practices were applied across science (23 effect sizes), mathematics (17), technology (3), and other areas, at primary/secondary, high school, and university levels
key_sources: Saraç, H. (2018). The Effect of Science, Technology, Engin eering and Mathematics-Stem Educational Practices on Students’ Learning Outcomes: A Meta-Analysis Study. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 17(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1176176

article_title: The Effects of Extensive Reading on English Vocabulary Learning: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Liu, J., & Zhang, J. (2018). The Effects of Extensive Reading on English Vocabulary Learning: A Meta-analysis. English Language Teaching, 11(6). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n6p1
title: Design extensive reading instruction for EFL vocabulary learning with Graded Readers, comprehension questions and vocabulary exercise over about one semester
description: Based on the meta-analysis's moderator results, the authors recommend specific instructional specifications for extensive reading aimed at EFL vocabulary learning. They state that "teachers should adopt Graded Readers as extensive reading materials and apply both comprehension questions and vocabulary exercise as teaching methods", and that one semester (less than three months) is the most appropriate instruction length. The recommendation is grounded in the pooled subgroup effect sizes reported in the study.
requirements: Instruction uses extensive reading with vocabulary outcomes measured by pre- and posttests
constraints: The comprehension-questions subgroup estimate rests on a single study (k = 1)
Studies longer than one year were not included in the synthesis
target_learning_goals: English vocabulary acquisition
examples: The meta-analysis coded 21 studies in which Graded Readers were used in 18 studies (86%) and book report was the most common treatment (71%), then pooled subgroup effect sizes to identify the most effective specifications.
key_sources: Liu, J., & Zhang, J. (2018). The Effects of Extensive Reading on English Vocabulary Learning: A Meta-analysis. English Language Teaching, 11(6). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n6p1

article_title: A Meta-Analysis: Improvement of Students' Algebraic Reasoning through Metacognitive Training
citation: Yujin Lee, Mary M. Capraro, Robert M. Capraro & Ali Bicer. (2018). A Meta-Analysis: Improvement of Students’ Algebraic Reasoning through Metacognitive Training. International Education Studies, 11(10). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v11n10p42
title: Metacognitive training as small-group self-questioning built on metacognitive regulation
description: Metacognitive training is a practical teaching method that adopts the concept of metacognition — students' thought processes and beliefs that regulate learning. The article describes that "Metacognitive training provides small group activities for students to ask and answer questions by themselves", using self-addressed metacognitive questions about connections between prior and new knowledge and appropriate problem-solving strategies. In this meta-analysis it is the intervention whose pooled effect on algebraic reasoning is estimated, appearing in varied forms across the included studies.
requirements: Requires students to exert initial extra effort and prolonged training to guarantee smooth and maintained application of metacognitive activity, as the article quotes Veenman, Van Hout-Wolters, and Afflerbach
constraints: The degree of improvement might vary depending on the type of metacognitive training methods employed, per the article's discussion
target_learning_goals: algebraic reasoning
mathematical problem solving
examples: Included interventions ranged from metacognitive strategy instruction and IMPROVE method to computer-assisted interventions and self-explanation with game-reward strategies, across grades K through high school
key_sources: Yujin Lee, Mary M. Capraro, Robert M. Capraro & Ali Bicer. (2018). A Meta-Analysis: Improvement of Students’ Algebraic Reasoning through Metacognitive Training. International Education Studies, 11(10). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v11n10p42

article_title: The Effects of Learning Stations Technique on Academic Achievement: A Meta-Analytic Study
citation: Mevlut AYDOGMUS & Cihad SENTURK. (2019). THE EFFECTS OF LEARNING STATIONS TECHNIQUE ON ACADEMIC ACHIEVEMENT: A META-ANALYTIC STUDY. Research in Pedagogy, Vol.9, No.1. https://doi.org/10.17810/2015.87
title: Learning stations technique
description: The learning stations technique is a form of course processing in which students, divided into heterogeneous groups, rotate through pre-prepared learning and activity areas, working individually or in groups under teacher guidance. The article defines it as "a series of learning activities in specific areas created in the learning-teaching process" undertaken to learn or review a topic. It is presented as a student-centered, cooperative technique rooted in Montessori, Dewey, Piaget and Vygotsky, supported by multiple intelligences theory, and used in Turkish curricula since the 2005 constructivist reforms.
requirements: Stations are pre-prepared according to the feature of the subject
Students are divided into heterogeneous groups considering interest, dominant intelligence, learning profile, and classroom
target_learning_goals: academic achievement across disciplines such as science, mathematics, social studies and Turkish
examples: In the included studies the technique was applied for 2 weeks in 30.8% of studies, 3-4 weeks in 38.5%, and 5 weeks or more in 30.8%, mostly in science and technology classes at primary level.
key_sources: Mevlut AYDOGMUS & Cihad SENTURK. (2019). THE EFFECTS OF LEARNING STATIONS TECHNIQUE ON ACADEMIC ACHIEVEMENT: A META-ANALYTIC STUDY. Research in Pedagogy, Vol.9, No.1. https://doi.org/10.17810/2015.87

article_title: Does the Flipped Classroom Improve Student Learning and Satisfaction? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
citation: Torstein Låg, Rannveig Grøm Sæle. (2019). Does the Flipped Classroom Improve Student Learning and Satisfaction? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. AERA Open. https://doi.org/10.1177/2332858419870489
title: Working definition of the flipped classroom as moving teacher-centered instruction out of the classroom to free time for student-centered activities
description: The article proposes a deliberately theory-neutral definition: "The flipped classroom is a teaching model that moves most of the teacher-centered instruction out of the classroom to free up time in the classroom for more student-centered learning activities." Unlike definitions requiring social activities or mandatory pre/postclass tasks, it prescribes no particular pedagogy, aiming to describe the model's general effect rather than prescribe practice. Traditional teaching is defined as predominantly teacher-centered, lecture-based information transfer.
requirements: For inclusion in the meta-analysis, most information transfer had to be moved outside and prior to class, most in-session teaching had to involve active learning, and the control condition had to be predominantly teacher centered and lecture based
constraints: The theory-neutrality may lead to a lack of pedagogical rationale on which to design intervention specifics, leaving teachers and students to a trial-and-error approach, as the article notes citing Bishop and Verleger (2013) and Lundin et al. (2018)
target_learners: students at any level of education, primary through further education
target_learning_goals: academic achievement on exams, tests, and grades; pass rates; student satisfaction with teaching
examples: Studies were included only if published 2010 or later, when interventions were explicitly labeled as flipped classrooms
key_sources: Torstein Låg, Rannveig Grøm Sæle. (2019). Does the Flipped Classroom Improve Student Learning and Satisfaction? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. AERA Open. https://doi.org/10.1177/2332858419870489

article_title: A Meta-Analytic Synthesis: Examining the Academic Impacts of Feedback on Student Achievement
citation: Nalline S. Baliram & Jeffrey J. Youde. (2018). A Meta-analytic Synthesis: Examining the academic impacts of feedback on student achievement. International Dialogues on Education, 5(2), 76-90. https://portal.issn.org/resource/ISSN/2198-5944
title: Effective feedback should be clear, age-appropriate, content-specific, timely, and of high quality
description: The article adopts Brookhart's (2008) criteria for effective feedback: it "should be clear, age -appropriate, content specific, timely, and of high quality." Effective feedback focuses on the task, process, and self-regulation, is descriptive, and includes praise along with constructive criticism. The meta-analysis results align with these recommendations, with content-specific feedback showing the largest moderator effect.
requirements: Feedback must be relevant to the students' reflection and learning process, and teachers must be aware of students' abilities, learning needs, and interests when deciding how and what feedback to give.
constraints: Feedback that is no longer relevant to current or future content may have diminished effectiveness; timely feedback within minutes of task completion may be unrealistic in larger classrooms.
target_learning_goals: academic achievement across subject disciplines
examples: The article's moderator coding classified data sets as content-specific, praise, or objective feedback; content-specific examples included written comments related to the task and visual and oral performance feedback.
key_sources: Nalline S. Baliram & Jeffrey J. Youde. (2018). A Meta-analytic Synthesis: Examining the academic impacts of feedback on student achievement. International Dialogues on Education, 5(2), 76-90. https://portal.issn.org/resource/ISSN/2198-5944

article_title: Meta-Analysis on the Effects of Teaching Methods on Academic Performance in Chemistry
citation: Sugano, S. G. C., & Nabua, E. B. (2020). Meta-Analysis on the Effects of Teaching Methods on Academic Performance in Chemistry. International Journal of Instruction, 13(2), 881-894. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2020.13259a
title: Nine-category taxonomy of chemistry teaching methods contrasted with traditional instruction
description: The article organizes chemistry education interventions into nine treatment categories used as the independent variable of the meta-analysis: inquiry-based learning; manipulative, models and multiple representations; cooperative learning; technology-aided instruction; individualized instruction; problem-based learning; project-based learning; combination learning; and multicultural education. Identified teaching methods were "cast into treatment categories that act as the independent variable of this study", with academic performance as the dependent variable. The taxonomy frames innovative methods collectively against "the traditional teaching method".
requirements: Qualified primary studies must report effect sizes or statistical details sufficient to compute them (means, standard deviations, sample sizes, t, f, p values, ANOVA tables, degrees of freedom)
constraints: Studies limited to secondary chemistry, conducted in the Philippines, completed 2005–2016, with experimental or quasi-experimental designs
target_learners: secondary chemistry students in the Philippines
target_learning_goals: academic performance in secondary chemistry
examples: The 51 qualified studies were coded and plotted into mapping matrices by treatment category, and category mean effect sizes were ranked to identify the most influential methods
key_sources: Sugano, S. G. C., & Nabua, E. B. (2020). Meta-Analysis on the Effects of Teaching Methods on Academic Performance in Chemistry. International Journal of Instruction, 13(2), 881-894. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2020.13259a

article_title: The Effect of Digital Story Applications on Students' Academic Achievement: A Meta-Analysis Study
citation: Nurullah Sahin and İsmail Coban. (2020). The effect of digital story applications on students' academic achievement: A meta-analysis study. African Educational Research Journal, Special Issue 8(3), S62-S75.
title: Digital storytelling and its seven components
description: Digital storytelling is defined in the article as "short, individual and multimedia stories that share information using multimedia tools or resources", resulting from integrating traditional storytelling with technology. The Center for Digital Storytelling stated that digital storytelling has 7 components: Perspective, A Dramatic Question, Emotional Content, Economy, Voice, Music, and Pacing/Rhythm. Robin and Pierson added Story Purpose, Image Quality, and Good Grammar and Language Use for educational purposes.
requirements: In educational use, digital story is used to present specific course content as teaching material and for students learning content, telling stories, motivation, and presentation
target_learners: students of all ages and all levels
target_learning_goals: academic achievement across course content areas
digital literacy and related 21st-century skills
examples: The meta-analysis included 94 effect sizes from 45 studies in which the experimental group was taught with digital story and the control group with other teaching techniques

article_title: The Meta-Analysis of the Studies about the Effects of Flipped Learning on Students' Achievement
citation: Aydin, M., Okmen, B., Sahin, S., & Kilic, A. (2021). The Meta-Analysis of the Studies About the Effects of Flipped Learning on Students' Achievement. Turkish Online Journal of Distance Education-TOJDE, 22(1), Article 3. https://tojde.anadolu.edu.tr
title: The F-L-I-P framework of flipped learning: flexible environment, learning culture, intentional content, professional educators
description: The article presents the Flipped Learning Network's 2014 framework of four basic components forming the acronym F-L-I-P: "1) Flexible environment, 2) Learning culture, 3) Intentional content, and 4) Professional educators". Flexible environments can be regulated by educators and students at will; the educator stops being the source of information and guides student-centered exploration; content is designed around learning objectives and points of difficulty; and educators continuously observe, give feedback, and evaluate students. The article uses this framework as the theoretical background for defining the flipped learning model whose achievement effects it meta-analyzes.
requirements: Lessons are transferred to students by means of videos outside of class, with in-class time spent on problem-solving and individual or group studies
Educators must observe students continuously, give feedback, and evaluate them
constraints: The framework is presented as background definition, not tested in this study's meta-analysis
target_learners: students at primary, secondary, high school, associate, and undergraduate levels
target_learning_goals: academic achievement in experimental and social science lessons
examples: The 25 meta-analyzed studies implemented flipped learning across science and social science lessons with pretest/posttest experimental control group designs
key_sources: Aydin, M., Okmen, B., Sahin, S., & Kilic, A. (2021). The Meta-Analysis of the Studies About the Effects of Flipped Learning on Students' Achievement. Turkish Online Journal of Distance Education-TOJDE, 22(1), Article 3. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1283687

article_title: Effect of Web 2.0 Technologies on Academic Performance: A Meta-Analysis Study
citation: Ergul Sonmez, E., & Cakir, H. (2021). Effect of Web 2.0 technologies on academic performance: A meta-analysis study. International Journal of Technology in Education and Science (IJTES), 5(1), 108-127. https://doi.org/10.46328/ijtes.161
title: Classification of Web 2.0 learning environments by characteristic, technology type, and synchronization
description: The article organizes Web 2.0 learning environments along three axes: characteristic (online reflection, online collaboration, audible discussion board, social areas, storage), technology type (weblog, wiki, voice boards, social networks, video sharing, podcast, social bookmarking, three-dimensional virtual worlds), and synchronization (mostly asynchronous, with social networks and virtual worlds synchronous). Drawing on Churchill (2011), Bower et al. (2010), and Hew and Cheung (2013), the article states that "Among the most used web 2.0 learning environments, blog, wiki, podcast and social networking can be specified" and presents examples such as Blogger, Pbwiki, Voicethread, YouTube, and Second Life. It also distinguishes Web 2.0 by users becoming "an active participant of content creation process in their learning experience".
requirements: Users must be able to collaborate, contribute content, and make changes without needing coding knowledge, as the article describes Web 2.0 environments
constraints: The classification is presented as background from prior work (Hew and Cheung, 2013), not as a tested framework in this study
target_learners: students across schooling levels, from primary school to university
target_learning_goals: academic performance in writing, reading, and subject-matter courses
examples: Table 1 classifies wikis as asynchronous online collaboration tools (Pbwiki, Wetpaint) and weblogs as asynchronous online reflection tools (Blogger, Edublogs)
key_sources: Ergul Sonmez, E., & Cakir, H. (2021). Effect of Web 2.0 technologies on academic performance: A meta-analysis study. International Journal of Technology in Education and Science (IJTES), 5(1), 108-127. https://doi.org/10.46328/ijtes.161

article_title: Effect of Web 2.0 Technologies on Academic Performance: A Meta-Analysis Study
citation: Ergul Sonmez, E., & Cakir, H. (2021). Effect of Web 2.0 technologies on academic performance: A meta-analysis study. International Journal of Technology in Education and Science (IJTES), 5(1), 108-127. https://doi.org/10.46328/ijtes.161
title: Encourage frequent use of Web 2.0 technologies in education, attending to course fit and learner age level
description: Based on the pooled positive, moderate effect of wikis and blogs on academic performance, the authors recommend that "it is important to encourage the frequent use of web 2.0 in education", while noting that "technical factors, such as in which web 2.0 can be used in which course, should be considered". They further argue the education level of students is a determinant of the positive effect, since older students show greater technology proficiency, so age level should be considered when selecting these technologies.
requirements: Selection of an age level that can use these technologies effectively, which the article says is important
constraints: Negative effect sizes in the included studies occurred in higher education contexts, and five of nineteen studies showed negative effects
target_learning_goals: academic performance across subject areas, especially foreign language writing and reading
examples: The meta-analysis pooled 19 quasi-experimental studies in which wikis or blogs were used in the experimental group and compared with control groups on final test performance
