article_title: The Impact of Flipped Classroom on College Students' Academic Performance: A Meta-Analysis Based on 20 Experimental Studies
citation: Zhang, Q., Cheung, E.S.T., & Cheung, C.S.T. (2021). The impact of flipped classroom on college students’ academic performance: A meta-analysis based on 20 experimental studies. Science Insights Education Frontiers, 8(2):1059-1080. https://doi.org/10.15354/sief.21.re019
title: Flipped classroom as a blended learning model that moves knowledge transfer before class and internalization into class
description: The article defines the flipped classroom as a teaching model in which students study instructional videos or other electronic materials before class and use class time for cooperative, interactive learning and knowledge internalization. It describes it as "a brand-new, deep-level blended learning model" integrating traditional classroom teaching and online learning, reversing teacher and student roles from lecturer/passive to instructor/active. The meta-analysis evaluates this model's impact on college academic performance.
requirements: Knowledge transfer must be completed before class via learning resources so classroom time can be used to guide internalization
Students must be able to choose learning resources and self-pace according to their learning situation
constraints: The article notes it places higher demands on teachers, who must build a learning support system and a virtual learning environment suitable for independent learning
target_learning_goals: academic performance across subject areas
independent learning skills
examples: The article cites early implementations from Lage, Platt, and Treglia (2000) in introductory economics and Bergmann and Sams' screen-recorded chemistry lectures at Woodland Park High School

article_title: The Meta-Analysis of Climate Resilience Education in Higher Education for Transformation Based on Experiential Learning Models
citation: Utomo, H. D.; Aliman, M. (2021). The meta-analysis of climate resilience education in higher education for transformation based on experiential learning models. Review of International Geographical Education (RIGEO), 11(2), 302-316. https://doi.org/10.33403rigeo.754200
title: Climate resilience education as a framework for preparing, anticipating and strengthening student responses to climate change
description: The article defines climate resilience education as an effort to prepare, anticipate and strengthen student responses to climate change and its impacts, directed at increasing adaptation capacity through understanding, changing habits, and developing practical skills. It incorporates social science and behavioral principles into climate science and offers students the opportunity to identify possible interventions with direct and long-lasting impacts. In higher education it is positioned as a transformer of society, building disaster response attitudes and adaptability that students transfer to communities.
requirements: Objectives adjusted to the standards of learning outcomes in meteorology-climatology or hydrometeorology courses
constraints: Materials are mostly science concepts, so the framework must accommodate various fields of science or simplify physics concepts recognizable in student life
target_learners: university students in geography and climatology courses
target_learning_goals: understanding climate change and its impacts
adaptation and mitigation capacity
caring attitudes toward the environment
examples: The article applies the framework to Indonesian hydro-meteorological disasters such as floods, landslides and droughts, using GIS mapping of disaster-prone areas
key_sources: Utomo, H. D.; Aliman, M. (2021). The meta-analysis of climate resilience education in higher education for transformation based on experiential learning models. Review of International Geographical Education (RIGEO), 11(2), 302-316. https://doi.org/10.33403rigeo.754200

article_title: The Meta-Analysis of Climate Resilience Education in Higher Education for Transformation Based on Experiential Learning Models
citation: Utomo, H. D.; Aliman, M. (2021). The meta-analysis of climate resilience education in higher education for transformation based on experiential learning models. Review of International Geographical Education (RIGEO), 11(2), 302-316. https://doi.org/10.33403rigeo.754200
title: Experiential learning pattern for climate resilience education with disaster experts and GIS mapping
description: The article prescribes an experiential learning pattern for climate resilience education in which students actively discuss their understanding, practice actions with concepts, and engage with relevant local examples of climate change impacts. The appropriate learning model is applied to students especially in areas affected by climate change using experiential learning by presenting hydro meteorological disaster experts and utilizing GIS for mapping disaster-prone areas. Learning media are real media that can be seen and touched or audio-visual media.
requirements: Presentation of hydro meteorological disaster experts
GIS applications for mapping disaster-prone areas
real or audio-visual learning media
constraints: intended for students especially in areas affected by climate change such as floods, landslides, droughts, tornadoes
target_learning_goals: understanding of vulnerable areas
disaster response and preparedness
21st-century skills such as critical thinking, communication, collaboration, and creativity
examples: Field visits and data collection methods; analysis of geographic information systems resulting in mapping of hydro meteorological vulnerable areas
key_sources: Utomo, H. D.; Aliman, M. (2021). The meta-analysis of climate resilience education in higher education for transformation based on experiential learning models. Review of International Geographical Education (RIGEO), 11(2), 302-316. https://doi.org/10.33403rigeo.754200

article_title: The Meta-Analysis of Climate Resilience Education in Higher Education for Transformation Based on Experiential Learning Models
citation: Utomo, H. D.; Aliman, M. (2021). The meta-analysis of climate resilience education in higher education for transformation based on experiential learning models. Review of International Geographical Education (RIGEO), 11(2), 302-316. https://doi.org/10.33403rigeo.754200
title: Embed climate resilience education in climatology or hydrometeorology courses based on experiential learning models
description: The article recommends that climate resilience education be included in climatology or hydrometeorology courses in Indonesian universities so students can transform educational outcomes in society. The climate resilience education model can apply experiential learning models such as problem-based learning, project-based learning, and discovery-inquiry learning, within a life-based curriculum that provides space for implementation in the context of life in society.
requirements: a life-based curriculum with SCPL and CPMK learning-outcome standards
courses in meteorology-climatology or hydrometeorology
constraints: positioned for universities in Indonesia
target_learners: university students in climatology or hydrometeorology courses
target_learning_goals: solving climate-related problems in society
positive response to impacts of climate change
examples: The Universitas Negeri Malang life-based curriculum is cited as providing space for implementation of climate resilience education

article_title: Effectiveness of Problem-Based Learning on Secondary Students' Achievement in Science: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Funa, A. A., & Prudente, M. S. (2021). Effectiveness of problem-based learning on secondary students’ achievement in science: A meta-analysis. International Journal of Instruction, 14(4), 69-84. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2021.1445a
title: PBL implementations in secondary science most commonly combine collaboration, probing questions, student choice of solution path, and essay-form problem solving
description: Across the 11 pooled studies, the article identifies the recurring instructional configuration of PBL in secondary science: collaboration among students, probing questions during lecture, freedom to choose how to solve the problem, and qualitative problem solving in essay form. The article reports these "strategies were included in the core elements of incorporating PBL in teaching", while quantitative problem solving, reflection, concept cartoon integration, and mind mapping were least used. ICT, multimedia, and graphic organizers were integrated during lectures and presentation of investigation results.
requirements: Problems must be at the heart of the instructional material and drive students’ curiosity and learning, per the article’s definition of PBL
constraints: The reflexive part of PBL (self-assessment and collaborative reflection) was not emphasized by the analyzed studies, which the authors attribute to the quasi-experimental designs focused on quantitative effectiveness
target_learning_goals: science achievement
problem solving
self-directed learning
examples: All 11 studies (100%) used collaboration, probing questions during lecture, and choice on how to solve the problem; 91% used qualitative problem solving in essay form (Table 6).
key_sources: Funa, A. A., & Prudente, M. S. (2021). Effectiveness of problem-based learning on secondary students’ achievement in science: A meta-analysis. International Journal of Instruction, 14(4), 69-84. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2021.1445a

article_title: Effectiveness of Problem-Based Learning on Secondary Students' Achievement in Science: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Funa, A. A., & Prudente, M. S. (2021). Effectiveness of problem-based learning on secondary students’ achievement in science: A meta-analysis. International Journal of Instruction, 14(4), 69-84. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2021.1445a
title: Maastricht Seven Step Model of PBL process
description: The article identifies the Maastricht Seven Step Model (Schmidt, 1983; Clouston et al., 2010) as "the best known and widely used process of PBL". Its steps are: clarifying the text and explaining unclear terms and concepts; defining the key problem; analyzing the problem and suggesting possible solutions; elaborating, testing, reviewing, and refining; formulating learning objectives; self-study; and integrating and testing new information. The article states most of the pooled studies used these processes along with the identified teaching strategies.
requirements: Implementation includes self-assessment and collaborative reflection alongside teachers’ evaluation, which the article calls important parts of PBL to evaluate students’ learning
constraints: The reflexive part of PBL was not given emphasis by the analyzed studies, possibly due to their quasi-experimental, quantitative research designs
target_learning_goals: problem solving
self-directed learning
science concept understanding
examples: Most studies obtained in this meta-analysis used the Maastricht Seven Step Model processes along with collaboration, probing questions, and student choice of solution method.
key_sources: Funa, A. A., & Prudente, M. S. (2021). Effectiveness of problem-based learning on secondary students’ achievement in science: A meta-analysis. International Journal of Instruction, 14(4), 69-84. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2021.1445a

article_title: Effectiveness of Problem-Based Learning on Secondary Students' Achievement in Science: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Funa, A. A., & Prudente, M. S. (2021). Effectiveness of problem-based learning on secondary students’ achievement in science: A meta-analysis. International Journal of Instruction, 14(4), 69-84. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2021.1445a
title: Use PBL as a supplemental approach with the teacher acting as guide, tutor, and facilitator
description: Based on the meta-analytic finding that PBL produces a large positive effect on secondary science achievement, the article recommends that "PBL be used as a supplemental approach to the existing teaching methods and strategies in science". It further states that "the presence of teacher as guide, tutor, and facilitator is integral" when applying PBL in science teaching, and that teachers may combine different teaching strategies with PBL to target particular skills. The article also recommends developing teachers’ skills in delivering PBL approaches.
requirements: The presence of the teacher as guide, tutor, and facilitator during PBL application
Teachers’ understanding that students learn in different ways
constraints: PBL has limitations that may hinder meaningful utilization, most especially its application in enhancing academic performance of younger students, per the article’s conclusion
target_learning_goals: science achievement
21st century skills
examples: The article recommends future studies venture into teachers’ capacity to implement PBL in their classes and integration of PBL with newly emerged innovative teaching strategies.

article_title: A Meta-Analysis of the Last Two Decades of Realistic Mathematics Education Approaches
citation: Juandi, D., Kusumah, Y. S., & Tamur, M. (2022). A Meta-Analysis of the Last Two Decades of Realistic Mathematics Education Approaches. International Journal of Instruction, 15(1), 381-400. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2022.15122a
title: Realistic Mathematics Education (RME) as a teaching theory grounded in realistic situations
description: RME is described in the article as "a unique teaching theory for the mathematical domain" whose peculiarity is that it gives rich and "realistic" situations a prominent position in learning activities. These situations act as an entry point to explore students' initial knowledge and gradually become more formal. The meta-analysis treats RME as an instructional treatment whose effect on mathematical abilities is estimated across experimental studies, and notes game-based learning is one of its characteristics without equating the two.
requirements: Implementation uses realistic situations as the starting point of learning, from which learning gradually becomes more formal
constraints: The article notes RME's framework offers students problem situations they can imagine, which university students may no longer need
target_learning_goals: mathematical ability
problem solving
mathematical reasoning and representation
examples: Included studies applied RME across topics such as geometry, algebraic thinking, linear programming, and mathematical literacy, sometimes combined with mathematics software or e-learning tools
key_sources: Juandi, D., Kusumah, Y. S., & Tamur, M. (2022). A Meta-Analysis of the Last Two Decades of Realistic Mathematics Education Approaches. International Journal of Instruction, 15(1), 381-400. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2022.15122a

article_title: Meta-Analysis on the Effectiveness of Using the Drama Approach in Social Studies Course
citation: Yildirim, E., Tikman, F., & Senturk, M. (2022). Meta-analysis on the effectiveness of using the drama approach in social studies course. International Journal on Social and Education Sciences (IJonSES), 4(1), 17-33. https://doi.org/10.46328/ijonses.301
title: Use the drama approach as an effective method for teaching social studies
description: Based on the meta-analytic finding of a strong positive effect of drama on social studies achievement, the authors conclude that drama is an effective teaching method in this domain. They state that "teachers and researchers should make use of this method for teaching in social studies lessons". The recommendation rests on the pooled effect of drama versus traditional teaching across 31 studies.
requirements: Experimental or quasi-experimental use of drama within the social studies course, as in the included studies
constraints: Evidence base is limited to primary and secondary school students in the Turkish sample (1999–2021); only 2 of the 31 studies were PhD theses
target_learners: Primary and secondary school students in social studies courses
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement in social studies
examples: The meta-analysis pooled 38 effect sizes from 31 studies in which experimental groups were taught with the drama approach and control groups with traditional methods
key_sources: Yildirim, E., Tikman, F., & Senturk, M. (2022). Meta-analysis on the effectiveness of using the drama approach in social studies course. International Journal on Social and Education Sciences (IJonSES), 4(1), 17-33. https://doi.org/10.46328/ijonses.301

article_title: A Meta-Analysis Study on the Effectiveness of a Cooperative Learning Model on Vocational High School Students' Mathematics Learning Outcomes
citation: M. Rais Ridwan, Samsul Hadi, Jailani Jailani. (2022). A meta-analysis study on the effectiveness of a cooperative learning model on vocational high school students' mathematics learning outcomes. Participatory Educational Research, 9(4). http://dx.doi.org/10.17275/per.22.97.9.4
title: Implement cooperative learning in vocational high school mathematics with attention to grade level and class size
description: The article directs its findings at Indonesian teachers choosing when to use cooperative learning in vocational high school mathematics. It states the meta-analysis "provides information to teachers in Indonesia to implement cooperative learning based on the level and number of students in the class to improve the mathematics learning outcomes of vocational high school students." Effectiveness was higher in grade 11 than grade 10 and in classes of 1-30 students than larger classes, so implementation should attend to these moderators.
requirements: Implementation should be based on the level and number of students in the class, as the article recommends.
constraints: The evidence base is 22 Indonesian quasi-experimental studies from 2013-2021 indexed in Google Scholar, SINTA, and GARUDA; effectiveness depends on grade level and sample size.
target_learners: Vocational high school students in Indonesia, grades 10 and 11
target_learning_goals: Mathematics learning outcomes
examples: The meta-analysis pooled 22 quasi-experimental studies using cooperative models in experimental classes and conventional learning in control classes, with moderator analyses by grade level and sample size.
key_sources: M. Rais Ridwan, Samsul Hadi, Jailani Jailani. (2022). A meta-analysis study on the effectiveness of a cooperative learning model on vocational high school students' mathematics learning outcomes. Participatory Educational Research, 9(4). http://dx.doi.org/10.17275/per.22.97.9.4

article_title: Blended Learning and Student Mathematics Ability in Indonesia: A Meta-Analysis Study
citation: Setiawan, A. A., Muhtadi, A., & Hukom, J. (2022). Blended Learning and Student Mathematics Ability in Indonesia: A Meta-Analysis Study. International Journal of Instruction, 15(2), 905-916. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2022.15249a
title: Blended learning as integration of face-to-face and online learning environments
description: The article treats blended learning as a model combining traditional face-to-face instruction with e-learning: 'Blended learning combines traditional face -to-face models with e -learning models, so as to create a richer learning experience'. Its basic principle is that face-to-face and online 'activities are optimally integrated into a unique learning experience consistent with the context and learning objectives'. The model is used in the meta-analysis as the treatment condition whose effect on Indonesian students' mathematical ability is synthesized, and is described as increasing interaction, participation, and access anytime and anywhere.
requirements: Suitable media for application, such as an LMS, since blended learning 'requires suitable me dia for its application'
constraints: The article's synthesis is limited to studies with Indonesian authors published 2012-2021 with an experimental blended-learning class and a control class
target_learners: Indonesian school and university students learning mathematics
target_learning_goals: mathematical ability
problem solving
concept understanding
examples: Included primary studies implemented blended learning via platforms such as Moodle and Edmodo in mathematics classes compared with conventional classes
key_sources: Setiawan, A. A., Muhtadi, A., & Hukom, J. (2022). Blended Learning and Student Mathematics Ability in Indonesia: A Meta-Analysis Study. International Journal of Instruction, 15(2), 905-916. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2022.15249a

article_title: Blended Learning and Student Mathematics Ability in Indonesia: A Meta-Analysis Study
citation: Setiawan, A. A., Muhtadi, A., & Hukom, J. (2022). Blended Learning and Student Mathematics Ability in Indonesia: A Meta-Analysis Study. International Journal of Instruction, 15(2), 905-916. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2022.15249a
title: Moodle and Edmodo as LMS media supporting blended learning in mathematics
description: The article names two learning management systems as media supporting blended learning. Moodle is described as 'one of the Learning Management System (LMS) applications that are widely used in online learning', into which text, graphics, animation, simulation, audio and video can be entered. Edmodo is described as a secure social networking community and multi-platform LMS that lets teachers and students communicate through messages and share knowledge, giving students freedom of time and place to study. Both are cited in the literature review as media through which included blended-learning implementations were delivered.
requirements: Internet access for use outside face-to-face sessions, since the model can be carried out 'at school, at home, or at other places with internet access'
target_learners: Indonesian school and university students learning mathematics
target_learning_goals: mathematics learning
online class management
student-teacher communication
examples: The article reports Edmodo-assisted blended learning in a study of mathematical problem-solving ability (Yanti et al., 2019) and Moodle-based implementations among included primary studies

article_title: The Effect of STEM Education Integrated into Teaching-Learning Approaches (SEITLA) on Learning Outcomes: A Meta-Analysis Study
citation: Mustafa Çevik, Büşra Bakioğlu. (2022). The Effect of STEM Education Integrated into Teaching-Learning Approaches (SEITLA) on Learning Outcomes: A Meta-Analysis Study. International Journal of Progressive Education, 18(2). https://doi.org/10.29329/ijpe.2022.431.8
title: Integrate STEM activities with teaching-learning approaches such as mastery learning, evidence-based learning and blended learning for greater effectiveness
description: The article recommends that educators deliberately pair STEM activities with teaching-learning approaches whose pooled effects were largest. It states that "A STEM activity integrated especially with teaching-learning approaches like mastery learning, evidence-based learning and blended learning can be more effective", and that selection should also consider curriculum, student readiness, school administration and parents' situations.
requirements: Educators need teaching knowledge and skills beyond subject matter knowledge to select and implement appropriate approaches.
constraints: In STEM activities with intensive technology use, teacher competencies and readiness of infrastructure are of great importance.
Findings are limited to 33 studies meeting the inclusion criterion, with self-reported measurement tools and no standard sought for study groups.
target_learners: K-12 and higher education students in STEM subjects
target_learning_goals: STEM learning outcomes and academic achievement
examples: The meta-analysis pooled 33 experimental studies (2015-2021, 3822 participants) comparing SEITLA experimental groups with control groups using traditional learning.

article_title: A Meta-Analysis of the E-Learning Influence on Vocational Education and Training (VET): Preliminary Study of Virtual to Actualization
citation: Daryanto, E., Siregar, B., & Januariyansah, S. (2022). A meta-analysis of the e-learning influence on Vocational Education and Training (VET): Preliminary study of virtual to actualization. International Journal of Education in Mathematics, Science, and Technology (IJEMST), 10(3), 710-721. https://doi.org/10.46328/ijemst.2509
title: Virtual actualization: combining e-learning with performance learning so students actualize virtual learning outcomes into concrete projects
description: Virtual actualization is the authors' proposed concept for VET, in which e-learning providing innovative features such as video tutorials is combined with performance (practical) learning. Students "will be able to actualize their learning outcomes in virtual form into concrete projects". The article presents this as a preliminary study of a model development research project, arguing the combination is expected to be effective because e-learning and practical learning complement each other.
requirements: E-learning must be combined with, not replace, practical VET learning, since e-learning cannot fully be used in conventional practical learning
constraints: The article reports this only as a preliminary study and a proposal for future research, not as a tested model
target_learners: VET students in vocational high schools and higher education in Indonesia
target_learning_goals: Technical and practical job competencies
Theoretical learning outcomes in vocational subjects
examples: The authors propose that VET learning use virtual/e-learning types with innovative features such as video tutorials combined with performance learning, based on the meta-analytic finding that e-learning supports theory and computer-media practical learning
key_sources: Daryanto, E., Siregar, B., & Januariyansah, S. (2022). A meta-analysis of the e-learning influence on Vocational Education and Training (VET): Preliminary study of virtual to actualization. International Journal of Education in Mathematics, Science, and Technology (IJEMST), 10(3), 710-721. https://doi.org/10.46328/ijemst.2509

article_title: A Meta-Analysis of the E-Learning Influence on Vocational Education and Training (VET): Preliminary Study of Virtual to Actualization
citation: Daryanto, E., Siregar, B., & Januariyansah, S. (2022). A meta-analysis of the e-learning influence on Vocational Education and Training (VET): Preliminary study of virtual to actualization. International Journal of Education in Mathematics, Science, and Technology (IJEMST), 10(3), 710-721. https://doi.org/10.46328/ijemst.2509
title: Use e-learning in VET as a complement to practical learning rather than a replacement for conventional machine-tool practice
description: Because the meta-analysis found e-learning cannot accommodate conventional practical learning using machine tools, the article recommends combining e-learning to support practical VET learning. The authors state e-learning "can be combined to support practical VET learning, which is expected to be effective due to the complementary combination". This positions e-learning as enrichment and support for hands-on learning rather than the primary form of instruction in conventional practical subjects.
requirements: Practical learning must retain real media such as machine tools; e-learning components should target theoretical content and computer-media practical work
constraints: Applies to conventional practical learning such as welding and painting; e-learning can be primary only for computer- and internet-media practical learning such as digital simulation and web programming
target_learners: Vocational high school and college VET students
target_learning_goals: Practical and performance skills in vocational trades
Theoretical understanding of vocational subjects
examples: The meta-analysis of 18 Indonesian VET studies found e-learning effective for theoretical learning and computer-media practical learning, while conventional machine-tool practice was not accommodated by e-learning
key_sources: Daryanto, E., Siregar, B., & Januariyansah, S. (2022). A meta-analysis of the e-learning influence on Vocational Education and Training (VET): Preliminary study of virtual to actualization. International Journal of Education in Mathematics, Science, and Technology (IJEMST), 10(3), 710-721. https://doi.org/10.46328/ijemst.2509

article_title: Can Educational Robots Improve Student Creativity: A Meta-Analysis Based on 48 Experimental and Quasi-Experimental Studies
citation: Hou, H., Zhang, X., & Wang, D. (2022). Can educational robots improve student creativity: A meta-analysis based on 48 experimental and quasi-experimental studies. Best Evidence in Chinese Education, 11(1):1449-1454. https://doi.org/10.15354/bece.22.ab001
title: Robotics laboratory with tangible and soft conditions for creative robotics teaching
description: The article describes a laboratory environment for robotics education composed of tangible conditions — equipment for conception (multimedia devices, drawing tools, electronic whiteboards), designing equipment (modeling software, robot making software, online robot simulation platform), operation facilities (LEGO robots, Arduino robots, assembly welding equipment), and presentation facilities — plus soft conditions such as "teaching program making, case demonstration, information resources, cognitive tools, dialogue and collaboration instruments, and social network support".
requirements: Effective integration of tangible and soft conditions to create an environment facilitating robotic experimental teaching
constraints: The laboratory advantage over ordinary classrooms is based on moderator analysis (SMD = 0.578 vs 0.485), not an experimental manipulation of laboratory construction
target_learners: primary and secondary students in robotics courses
target_learning_goals: innovation thinking
hands-on creation
teamwork skills
examples: The article lists LEGO robots, Arduino robots, and assembly welding equipment as operation facilities, and online robot simulation platforms as designing equipment
key_sources: Hou, H., Zhang, X., & Wang, D. (2022). Can educational robots improve student creativity: A meta-analysis based on 48 experimental and quasi-experimental studies. Best Evidence in Chinese Education, 11(1):1449-1454. https://doi.org/10.15354/bece.22.ab001

article_title: Training Individuals to Implement Discrete Trials with Fidelity: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Joelle Fingerhut, & Mariola Moeyaert. (2022). Training Individuals to Implement Discrete Trials with Fidelity: A Meta-Analysis. Focus on Autism and Other Developmental Disabilities, 37(4), 239–250. https://doi.org/10.1177/10883576221081076
title: Three-level hierarchical linear modeling for meta-analyzing single-case experimental design data
description: The article uses a three-level hierarchical linear model in which DTT implementation fidelity observations (Level 1) are nested within participants (Level 2) within studies (Level 3). Phase is dummy-coded, time is centered on the last training session, and a moderator term tests BST or individual components. The authors state "HLM is able to analyze clustered data, or observations within participants and participants within studies", allowing effect sizes to vary across participants and studies while estimating one overall intervention effect. Lag 1 autocorrelation was modeled to control Type I error and improve power.
requirements: Raw single-case data retrievable in graphical or tabular form (via WebPlot Digitizer 2.0) so observations can be modeled at each level of nesting
constraints: HLM carries distributional assumptions, for example the assumption of homogeneous residuals, which the authors list as a potential limitation
Ignoring the natural hierarchy of data can lead to an underestimate of the standard error and an increase in Type I errors, per the authors
target_learners: Meta-analysts and researchers synthesizing single-case experimental design studies
target_learning_goals: Quantitative synthesis of intervention effects from clustered single-case data
examples: The model was fit in RStudio to 46 studies with 224 participants, with four models (BST, modeling, rehearsal, no moderator) and a Bonferroni correction of α = .05/4 = .0125.
key_sources: Joelle Fingerhut, & Mariola Moeyaert. (2022). Training Individuals to Implement Discrete Trials with Fidelity: A Meta-Analysis. Focus on Autism and Other Developmental Disabilities, 37(4), 239–250. https://doi.org/10.1177/10883576221081076

article_title: Training Individuals to Implement Discrete Trials with Fidelity: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Joelle Fingerhut, & Mariola Moeyaert. (2022). Training Individuals to Implement Discrete Trials with Fidelity: A Meta-Analysis. Focus on Autism and Other Developmental Disabilities, 37(4), 239–250. https://doi.org/10.1177/10883576221081076
title: Meta-analytic dataset of 46 single-case experimental design studies of DTT training (224 participants)
description: The compiled corpus for this meta-analysis: 46 SCED studies of trainings for DTT implementation fidelity, selected via PRISMA procedures from four databases plus an ancestry search, with raw data extracted using WebPlot Digitizer 2.0. The article reports that "The number of participants across all 46 studies was 224" and that "A total of 130 (58%) participants received BST as their training." Studies met WWC (2020) standards with or without reservations, and interobserver agreement for coding was 100% on a 30% subset.
requirements: Included studies needed DTT fidelity directly observed on a percentage scale, an SCED with three demonstrations of intervention effectiveness, and WWC-compliant data points per phase
constraints: Studies pairing DTT training with training for another teaching method were excluded to avoid confounding
Duplicate data (e.g., dissertations later published) were excluded
target_learners: Special education teachers, paraprofessionals, parents, clinicians, and other DTT implementers across school, clinic, university, and home settings
target_learning_goals: Implementing discrete trial training with fidelity
examples: Table 1 lists 13 training combinations across studies and participants, with complete BST the most common (20 studies, 76 participants).
key_sources: Joelle Fingerhut, & Mariola Moeyaert. (2022). Training Individuals to Implement Discrete Trials with Fidelity: A Meta-Analysis. Focus on Autism and Other Developmental Disabilities, 37(4), 239–250. https://doi.org/10.1177/10883576221081076

article_title: A Meta-Analysis of Instructional Management Model for Students' Creative Thinking Development: An Application of Propensity Score Matching
citation: Itsarangkul Na Ayutthaya, T., & Damrongpanit, S. (2022). A Meta-Analysis of Instructional Management Model for Students’ Creative Thinking Development: An Application of Propensity Score Matching. European Journal of Educational Research, 11(4), 2429-2444. https://doi.org/10.12973/eu-jer.11.4.2429
title: Taxonomy of five instructional management models for developing students' creative thinking
description: The article organizes 400 Thai studies on creative thinking development into five instructional management model groups: all-round creative thinking development (n=80), creative thinking skills stimulation (n=25), knowledge integration based on creative environment through technology media usage (n=68), self-knowledge construction with technology media (n=124), and creative learning activities and situations management (n=103). Each group bundles named instructional methods, e.g. the knowledge integration group includes "Science Technology Engineering and Math ematics Education (STEM Education)" and blended learning. The taxonomy structures the meta-analysis and the propensity score comparison of model effectiveness.
requirements: Studies must be experimental research with instructional management style as the primary variable and creative thinking as the dependent variable, reporting statistics sufficient for effect size calculation
constraints: Derived from graduate theses and research articles conducted in Thailand between 1971 and 2020, searched via ThaiLIS Digital Collection and university e-libraries
target_learners: primary and secondary school students in Thailand
target_learning_goals: creative thinking development
examples: Table 1 lists each model's instructional methods and frequencies, e.g. 45 art activities studies in the creative learning activities group and 42 programmed/online learning studies in the self-knowledge construction group
key_sources: Itsarangkul Na Ayutthaya, T., & Damrongpanit, S. (2022). A Meta-Analysis of Instructional Management Model for Students’ Creative Thinking Development: An Application of Propensity Score Matching. European Journal of Educational Research, 11(4), 2429-2444. https://doi.org/10.12973/eu-jer.11.4.2429

article_title: The Effect of Student-Centred Methods and Techniques on Primary School Students' Mathematics Achievement: A Meta-Analysis Study
citation: Hakan Ulum, Songül Tümkaya. (2022). The effect of student-centred methods and techniques on primary school students' mathematics achievement: A meta-analysis study. Malikussaleh Journal of Mathematics Learning (MJML). https://ojs.unimal.ac.id/mjml/index
title: Use meta-analytic moderator results to help teachers choose student-centred strategies, methods, or techniques for primary school mathematics outcomes
description: The article positions its synthesis as a resource for practice: teachers selecting among student-centred strategies, methods, and techniques, and curriculum developers setting teaching principles, can use the pooled effect size and moderator results when choosing an approach for primary school mathematics. The authors state that "Teachers can adopt the results of this study as an important source to help them choose a strategy, method, or technique in a course that is appropriate for the outcomes". The moderator analysis identifying application approach as the only significant moderator is the key input for such choices.
requirements: Access to the effect-size and moderator-analysis results when selecting a strategy, method, or technique for primary mathematics outcomes
constraints: The research is limited by its inclusion criteria (studies from 2008-2018, experimental, primary school samples, non-longitudinal)
Only the application approach moderator showed a statistically significant difference between levels
target_learners: Primary school students in mathematics courses
target_learning_goals: Primary school mathematics academic achievement
examples: The meta-analysis compared nine application approaches (e.g., ABMI d = 1.334, Educational Games d = 1.280, PBL d = 0.356) to identify which student-centred approaches showed the largest effects
key_sources: Hakan Ulum, Songül Tümkaya. (2022). The effect of student-centred methods and techniques on primary school students' mathematics achievement: A meta-analysis study. Malikussaleh Journal of Mathematics Learning (MJML). https://ojs.unimal.ac.id/mjml/index

article_title: Effects of Worksheets on Problem-Solving Skills: Meta-Analytic Studies
citation: Widodo, S. A., Wijayanti, A., Irfan, M., Pusporini, W., Mariah, M., & Rochmiyati, S. (2023). Effects of worksheets on problem-solving skills: Meta-analytic studies. International Journal of Educational Methodology, 9(1), 151-167. https://doi.org/10.12973/ijem.9.1.151
title: Worksheets as learning tools and media that guide students through tasks
description: A worksheet is defined in the article as "a guide for students to learn a concept so that they can solve a problem" and as a learning tool providing instructions on tasks a student needs to complete. Worksheets can serve as a primary learning resource alongside the teacher, become learning centers in the classroom, and function as learning media conveying information. They may contain material, summaries, and tasks such as sample questions or guided practice questions.
requirements: Worksheets must be prepared before learning to be used during teaching and learning activities in the classroom
target_learning_goals: problem-solving skills
concept understanding
critical thinking
examples: The analyzed studies used worksheets combined with approaches and models such as problem-based learning, guided inquiry, POGIL, discovery learning, and realistic mathematics teaching.

article_title: The Effect of Problem-Based Learning in Science Education on Academic Achievement: A Meta-Analytical Study
citation: Ufuk Uluçınar. (2022). The Effect of Problem-Based Learning in Science Education on Academic Achievement: A Meta-Analytical Study. Science Education International, 34(2), 72-85. https://doi.org/10.33828/sei.v34.i2.1
title: Problem-based learning as a constructivist, student-centered instructional model structured around ill-structured authentic problems
description: PBL is described as "a student-centered, active learning approach" in which students construct knowledge "through peer interaction and collaborative research or inquiry". Its essential component is an ill-structured authentic real-life problem scenario, and a PBL sequence consists of seven stages, from clarifying terms and defining the problem through constructing learning objectives to integrating and controlling newly acquired knowledge. The teacher facilitates rather than presents information, helping students learn cognitive skills for problem-solving and collaboration. This meta-analysis treats PBL as the independent variable and science academic achievement as the dependent variable.
requirements: An ill-structured authentic real-life problem scenario as the essential component of learning
Teacher facilitation of cognitive and collaboration skills instead of presenting information
target_learning_goals: academic achievement in science
problem-solving skills
self-regulated learning
teamwork skills
intrinsic motivation
key_sources: Ufuk Uluçınar. (2022). The Effect of Problem-Based Learning in Science Education on Academic Achievement: A Meta-Analytical Study. Science Education International, 34(2), 72-85. https://doi.org/10.33828/sei.v34.i2.1

article_title: A Meta-Analysis of the Effectiveness of Digital Technology-Assisted STEM Education
citation: Feyyaz Öztop. (2023). A Meta-Analysis of the Effectiveness of Digital Technology-Assisted STEM Education. Journal of Science Learning. https://doi.org/10.17509/jsl.v6i2.52316
title: Corpus of 34 Turkish postgraduate theses yielding 38 effect-size comparisons of digital technology-assisted STEM education
description: The study's data corpus is 34 experimental pre-test/post-test studies drawn in November 2022 from the "Databases of National Thesis Center of the Council of Higher Education", from which "Thirty-eight effect sizes (comparison) from these identified studies were examined". Studies had to state digital technology use (computer, interactive board, internet, smartphone, video, digital game, digital education platform), include required statistics, and involve typically developing students. Coding reliability was reported as a coefficient of agreement of 1.0.
requirements: studies must be experimental with pre-test and post-test and report statistical information required for meta-analysis
constraints: limited to postgraduate theses in Turkey
only academic achievement was examined as an outcome
target_learners: typically developing students from primary school through university in Turkey
target_learning_goals: academic achievement in science and mathematics within STEM education
examples: Included studies used digital tools such as the Scratch game-design program, interactive-board videos, and online simulations within STEM activities
key_sources: Feyyaz Öztop. (2023). A Meta-Analysis of the Effectiveness of Digital Technology-Assisted STEM Education. Journal of Science Learning. https://doi.org/10.17509/jsl.v6i2.52316

article_title: Realistic Mathematics Education and Mathematical Literacy: A Meta-Analysis Conducted on Studies in Indonesia
citation: Amelia Defrianti Putri, Dadang Juandi, Turmudi. (2024). Realistic mathematics education and mathematical literacy: a meta-analysis conducted on studies in Indonesia. Journal of Education and Learning (EduLearn), Vol. 18, No. 4. https://doi.org/10.11591/edulearn.v18i4.21650
title: Use realistic mathematics education to improve students' mathematical literacy proficiency
description: The article recommends that mathematics educators adopt RME as a means of improving students' proficiency in mathematical literacy. RME involves students beginning learning by "engaging with authentic scenarios and real-world challenges" and reconstructing mathematical concepts with the teacher's assistance. The recommendation rests on the meta-analysis's pooled large positive effect (g = 1.031) across seventeen Indonesian experimental studies.
requirements: RME is implemented as an intervention contrasted with conventional learning, as in the included experimental studies
constraints: Evidence base is limited to Indonesian studies published 2014–2023 using experimental designs with control groups
target_learners: primary, middle, and high school students in Indonesia
target_learning_goals: mathematical literacy proficiency
examples: The meta-analysis pooled seventeen studies in which RME classes were compared with conventionally taught control classes on mathematical literacy measures.
key_sources: Amelia Defrianti Putri, Dadang Juandi, Turmudi. (2024). Realistic mathematics education and mathematical literacy: a meta-analysis conducted on studies in Indonesia. Journal of Education and Learning (EduLearn), Vol. 18, No. 4. https://doi.org/10.11591/edulearn.v18i4.21650

article_title: The Strategies in Teaching isiXhosa Semantics in Foundation Phase: A Systematic Review
citation: Gobodwana, A., 2024, 'The strategies in teaching isiXhosa semantics in Foundation Phase: A systematic review', Reading & Writing 15(1), a493. https://doi.org/10.4102/rw.v15i1.493
title: Translanguaging as a practical theory of language for multilingual classrooms
description: Translanguaging is presented as a broader understanding of bilingualism and multilingualism that departs from traditional approaches to language learning. The article distinguishes it from code-switching: "while code-switching involves adhering to unique grammatical rules for each language, translanguaging revolves around the practical use of language in multilingual communication". Following Wei (2018), its primary goal is to foster bilingualism and multilingualism rather than replacing children's first language, and it values the unique resources of multilingual speakers by blurring boundaries between languages.
requirements: A multilingual classroom context in which learners enter school with proficiency in more than one language
constraints: The article states translanguaging is not an official pedagogical approach to learning in South African classrooms
target_learners: Foundation Phase learners (Grades R–3) in multilingual South African classrooms
target_learning_goals: Reading home language (isiXhosa) with semantic understanding
Bilingual and multilingual language development
examples: The review reports teachers use translanguaging in multilingual classrooms to break communication barriers, based on Gobodwana (2023)
key_sources: Gobodwana, A., 2024, 'The strategies in teaching isiXhosa semantics in Foundation Phase: A systematic review', Reading & Writing 15(1), a493. https://doi.org/10.4102/rw.v15i1.493

article_title: The Strategies in Teaching isiXhosa Semantics in Foundation Phase: A Systematic Review
citation: Gobodwana, A., 2024, 'The strategies in teaching isiXhosa semantics in Foundation Phase: A systematic review', Reading & Writing 15(1), a493. https://doi.org/10.4102/rw.v15i1.493
title: Vygotskian mediation and behaviourist habit-formation framework for home-language learning
description: The article adopts two interchangeable theoretical frameworks as informants for home-language learning: Vygotsky's theory of child development centred on mediation, and Skinner's behaviourism. Vygotsky holds that mental processes are mediated by psychological tools such as language, acquired through interaction with the cultural environment; the article states "It should be easy for children to learn a second language, especially if their first language is well developed". Skinner views language learning as habit formation through reinforcement, with imitation of caregivers rewarded positively and divergence corrected by negative feedback.
requirements: Interaction with the cultural environment and interpersonal dialogue with adults or more experienced peers for tool acquisition
Reinforcement from the immediate surroundings for habit formation
constraints: The article notes a notable limitation of the mediation paradigm is Vygotsky's partial elucidation of the role of children's actions in the process of mediation
target_learners: Children from Grade R (aged 5–6 years) entering formal schooling
target_learning_goals: Home-language (isiXhosa) acquisition
Second-language learning built on a developed first language
examples: The article uses the two frameworks to explain why children transition from their native language repertoire to a second language on exposure to speakers of other languages
key_sources: Gobodwana, A., 2024, 'The strategies in teaching isiXhosa semantics in Foundation Phase: A systematic review', Reading & Writing 15(1), a493. https://doi.org/10.4102/rw.v15i1.493

article_title: Effects of the 5E Instructional Model: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
citation: Polanin, J. R., Austin, M., Taylor, J. A., Steingut, R. R., Rodgers, M. A., & Williams, R. (2024). Effects of the 5E Instructional Model: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. AERA Open. https://doi.org/10.1177/23328584241269866
title: The BSCS 5E Instructional Model and its 3E and 7E variants
description: The BSCS 5E Instructional Model is a constructivist framework for organizing and sequencing science instruction through five stages—engagement, exploration, explanation, elaboration, and evaluation—in which "the teacher serves as a facilitator, guiding students through each 'E' stage of the learning process". The 3E variant retains only explore, explain, and elaborate, while the 7E variant adds elicit and extend stages to make evocation of prior conceptions and far transfer more explicit. All three build on constructivist learning theory and incorporate the How People Learn findings on engaging prior knowledge and metacognition.
requirements: Requires a curricular enactment of at least five class periods or 4 hours, not a single 5E lesson, per the review's eligibility definition
constraints: The 3E model lacks an overt engage/elicit stage and an evaluation stage, which the authors hypothesize explains its smaller effects
target_learners: pre-K through grade 12 students in school-based STEM settings
target_learning_goals: science conceptual understanding and skills
mathematics achievement
STEM motivation
examples: The review included 61 RCTs of curricular enactments: 45 studies of the 5E model (74%) and 8 studies each of the 3E and 7E models (13% each), with an average implementation duration of 7.7 weeks
key_sources: Polanin, J. R., Austin, M., Taylor, J. A., Steingut, R. R., Rodgers, M. A., & Williams, R. (2024). Effects of the 5E Instructional Model: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. AERA Open. https://doi.org/10.1177/23328584241269866

article_title: The Effect of Vocabulary Development Interventions on Cognitive Outcomes of Vocabulary: A Meta-Analysis Study
citation: Kansızoğlu, N. & Bekiroğlu, N. (2025). The effect of vocabulary development interventions on cognitive outcomes of vocabulary: A meta-analysis study. Journal of Pedagogical Research, 9(1), 123-148. https://doi.org/10.33902/JPR.202532083
title: Adapt vocabulary teaching to individual students' needs and learning styles rather than rejecting traditional methods outright
description: The article recommends adapting vocabulary instruction to learners rather than discarding traditional methods, stating that "adapting vocabulary teaching to the individual needs and learning styles of students may be a more effective strategy". It argues traditional methods can work for some students but may not suit all, and that teaching should be adapted to individual differences and create learning environments that increase vocabulary depth.
requirements: Instruction should attend to students' individual differences and learning styles, as the article states the teaching process should be adapted to address individual differences among students.
constraints: The article notes traditional methods can be effective for some students, so adaptation rather than wholesale replacement is recommended.
target_learners: Primary and secondary school students (2nd to 8th grades) learning Turkish vocabulary
target_learning_goals: Vocabulary knowledge and vocabulary-related cognitive outcomes
examples: The article contrasts traditional practices such as using a dictionary to learn word definitions, writing sentences, and relying on teacher explanations with innovative, student-centered interventions pooled in the meta-analysis.
key_sources: Kansızoğlu, N. & Bekiroğlu, N. (2025). The effect of vocabulary development interventions on cognitive outcomes of vocabulary: A meta-analysis study. Journal of Pedagogical Research, 9(1), 123-148. https://doi.org/10.33902/JPR.202532083

article_title: Innovative Teaching Models and Critical Thinking in Mathematics and Statistics Education: A Meta-Analytical Review
citation: Sa’idah, N., Jailani, Sudiyatno, & Retnawati, H. (2026). Innovative teaching models and critical thinking in mathematics and statistics education: A meta-analytical review. International Journal of Research in Education and Science (IJRES), 12(1), 140-157. https://doi.org/10.46328/ijres.5054
title: Coded dataset of 19 studies comparing innovative versus conventional instruction on mathematical and statistical critical thinking
description: The article assembles a coded dataset of "a total of 19 studies" published 2017–2024, retrieved from ERIC, Scopus, and Google Scholar under PRISMA standards. Each record holds experimental and control group N, mean, and SD, the dependent variable (mathematical or statistical critical thinking), the independent variable (e.g., group investigation, blended learning, problem-based learning, metaverse technology), and educational level from elementary to tertiary. Table 1 summarizes the coding and Table 2 the computed Hedges' g values.
requirements: Studies must report critical thinking in mathematics or statistics as the dependent variable with experimental and control group sample size, mean, and standard deviation
constraints: Only two included studies measured statistical critical thinking; publications span 2017 to 2024
target_learning_goals: mathematical critical thinking
statistical critical thinking
examples: Table 1 codes studies such as Gaspersz & Salamor (2021, group investigation, college) and Rachmadtullah et al. (2023, metaverse technology applications, elementary) with group N, means, and SDs
key_sources: Sa’idah, N., Jailani, Sudiyatno, & Retnawati, H. (2026). Innovative teaching models and critical thinking in mathematics and statistics education: A meta-analytical review. International Journal of Research in Education and Science (IJRES), 12(1), 140-157. https://doi.org/10.46328/ijres.5054

article_title: Does Service-Learning Increase Student Learning?: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Jami L. Warren. (2012). Does Service-Learning Increase Student Learning?: A Meta-Analysis. Michigan Journal of Community Service Learning. https://quod.lib.umich.edu/m/mjcsl
title: Engagement-motivation account of why service-learning increases learning outcomes
description: The article reports an untested theoretical account, attributed to Warren and Sellnow (2010), explaining service-learning's learning benefits through a chain: service-learning increases student engagement, engaged students are more motivated to study, and motivated students learn more both cognitively and affectively. The author states that "research suggests that service-learning increases student engagement" and that engaged students "are more motivated to study," citing Rockquemore and Schaffer (2000), Flournoy (2007), Shulman (1995), and Frymier, Shulman, and Houser (1996). The article explicitly notes this theory has not yet been tested and recommends future researchers flesh out and test it.
requirements: Requires empirical testing; the article states the proposed theory has not yet been tested
constraints: The article states it is not clear why service-learning influences learning of course concepts beyond a traditionally taught course
target_learning_goals: cognitive and affective learning of course concepts
examples: The article cites existing findings on engagement (Rockquemore & Schaffer, 2000) and motivation to study (Flournoy, 2007) as the empirical basis from which Warren and Sellnow drew theoretical conclusions
key_sources: Jami L. Warren. (2012). Does Service-Learning Increase Student Learning?: A Meta-Analysis. Michigan Journal of Community Service Learning. https://quod.lib.umich.edu/m/mjcsl

article_title: Does Service-Learning Increase Student Learning?: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Jami L. Warren. (2012). Does Service-Learning Increase Student Learning?: A Meta-Analysis. Michigan Journal of Community Service Learning. https://quod.lib.umich.edu/m/mjcsl
title: Service-learning as a pedagogical strategy with four success criteria
description: Service-learning is defined in the article as "a pedagogical strat- egy in which students engage in community service that will enhance their understanding of course con- cepts and enable them to make contributions to their communities" (citing Rhodes & Davis, 2001). Drawing on Eyler and Giles (1999), the article states a service-learning experience needs to satisfy four criteria to be considered successful: personal and interpersonal development, understanding and applying knowledge learned in class, perspective transformation, and a developed sense of citizenship. The pattern is used across disciplines, including communication courses.
requirements: Community service must be integrated so as to enhance understanding of course concepts and enable contributions to communities
constraints: The four success criteria are attributed to Eyler and Giles (1999) as a definitional framework, not tested in this article
target_learning_goals: understanding and applying course concepts
personal and interpersonal development
perspective transformation
citizenship
examples: The 11 meta-analyzed studies spanned education, English, mass communication, pharmacy, political science, psychology, rehabilitation services, and sociology disciplines
key_sources: Jami L. Warren. (2012). Does Service-Learning Increase Student Learning?: A Meta-Analysis. Michigan Journal of Community Service Learning. https://quod.lib.umich.edu/m/mjcsl

article_title: Replicating the Moderating Role of Income Status on Summer School Effects across Subject Areas: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Quinn, D. M., Lynch, K., & Kim, J. S. (2014). Replicating the Moderating Role of Income Status on Summer School Effects across Subject Areas: A Meta-analysis. SREE Spring 2014 Conference Abstract. https://www.sree.org
title: Summer counterfactual account: income moderation flipped after 1998 because the higher-income summer counterfactual changed
description: An explanatory framework the authors propose for why Cooper et al.'s (2000) review found higher-income students benefited more from summer school while their 1998–2011 reviews find the opposite. They hypothesize that rising returns to family income reflect increased parental investment in cognitive development, so "the summer counterfactual for the average higher income student may have changed" between review periods. Because treatment/control contrasts depend on nonparticipants' summer loss or gain, the higher-income contrast may be weaker today. The article also acknowledges chance, given small numbers of studies, as an alternative explanation.
requirements: Requires comparison of summer treatment/control contrasts across historical periods with differing out-of-school counterfactuals for higher-income students
constraints: Offered as "one hypothesis"; the authors note the discrepancy could be "due simply to chance, particularly when sample sizes... are small"
target_learners: Kindergarten to Grade 8 students in the United States and Canada
target_learning_goals: Math and reading achievement over the summer vacation months
examples: The authors contrast Cooper et al.'s 1966–1998 review window with their 1998–2011 window and note migrant workers' children showed some of the largest effect sizes in Cooper et al.'s review
key_sources: Quinn, D. M., Lynch, K., & Kim, J. S. (2014). Replicating the Moderating Role of Income Status on Summer School Effects across Subject Areas: A Meta-analysis. SREE Spring 2014 Conference Abstract. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED562949

article_title: Replicating the Moderating Role of Income Status on Summer School Effects across Subject Areas: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Quinn, D. M., Lynch, K., & Kim, J. S. (2014). Replicating the Moderating Role of Income Status on Summer School Effects across Subject Areas: A Meta-analysis. SREE Spring 2014 Conference Abstract. https://www.sree.org
title: Offer summer academic programs primarily to low-income students, who benefit more from them
description: This principle recommends directing summer math and reading programs toward low-income student populations, because recent meta-analytic evidence shows they derive larger benefit from such programs than higher-income peers. The article reports that low-income students benefit more "in both math and reading," reversing the pattern in Cooper et al.'s (2000) earlier review. It extends the authors' prior reading-only meta-analysis (Kim & Quinn, 2013) to math and supports the policy use of summer school as a compensatory lever for disadvantaged students.
requirements: Classroom- or home-based summer reading or school-based math interventions in the United States or Canada, assessed with standardized tests
Sufficient information to compute Cohen's d and a treatment/control comparison
constraints: The math evidence base is thin: "the number of studies on the effects of math summer school is low," limiting moderator analyses and statistical power
target_learners: Kindergarten to Grade 8 students in the United States and Canada
target_learning_goals: Math and reading achievement over the summer vacation months
examples: In the within-study analyses, low-income students in the same programs outperformed their higher-income peers in both math and reading; the between-study math moderator showed low-income samples at d=0.11 versus mixed-income samples at d=-0.02

article_title: The Effectiveness of Computer-Mediated Communication on SLA: A Meta-Analysis and Research Synthesis
citation: Lin, H. (2012). The Effectiveness of Computer-Mediated Communication on SLA: A Meta-Analysis and Research Synthesis. In L. Bradley & S. Thouësny (Eds.), CALL: Using, Learning, Knowing, EUROCALL Conference, Gothenburg, Sweden, Proceedings. Research-publishing.net. https://research-publishing.net
title: Six-variable moderator framework for the effectiveness of CMC in SLA
description: The article organizes its meta-analysis around substantive and methodological features that may condition how effective CMC interventions are for L2 learning. Twelve study-level features were coded for each of the 56 studies, and the results section states that "task type, group size, participants' educational level, CMC mode, CMC tool and outcome measures were potential moderators that would affect the overall effectiveness of CMC intervention". The framework treats CMC effectiveness not as fixed but as contingent on instructional and methodological design choices, guiding how future CMC studies and implementations should be described and compared.
requirements: Primary studies must report adequate quantitative information for effect sizes to be calculated, and each study must use some form of CMC either exclusively or with other instructional tools.
constraints: Detailed moderator analysis results were not included in the paper due to space limitations, so the framework's moderator effects are reported as tentative findings without magnitudes.
Eligible studies were limited to those published between 2000 and 2011 with L2 or foreign language learners and experimental or quasi-experimental designs.
target_learners: L2 and foreign language learners in middle school, primary school, and university/college settings
target_learning_goals: Second/foreign language skills: listening, speaking, reading, and writing
examples: The meta-analysis coded 56 primary studies at two levels — study-feature coding and effect-size coding — reaching a final inter-rater reliability of 98%.

citation: Wanzek, J., Vaughn, S., Scammacca, N., Gatlin, B., Walker, M. A., & Capin, P. (2016). Meta-analyses of the effects of tier 2 type reading interventions in grades K-3. Educational Psychology Review, 28, 551-576.
title: Implement early-grade Tier 2 reading support as less extensive interventions delivered 1:1 or in small groups of five or fewer students, by varied implementers.
description: The meta-analysis supports delivering supplemental (15-99 session) reading intervention to K-3 students with or at risk for reading difficulties either one-on-one or in small groups of five or fewer, since effects did not differ across these group sizes and school personnel implemented interventions as effectively as researchers. The summary states "the research supports intervention provided 1:1 and in small groups of five or fewer students," and that interventions "can be feasibly implemented by a variety of implementers."

constraints: Only one-to-one and small groups (2-3 or 4-5 students) could be examined; only three studies used larger groups, so no conclusion covers groups larger than five.

language and reading comprehension

citation: Pyle, K. K., & Fabiano, G. A. (2017). Daily Report Card Intervention and Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder: A Meta-Analysis of Single-Case Studies. Manuscript submitted to Exceptional Children October 2016; accepted March 2017.
title: Daily Report Card (DRC) as a stand-alone behavioral intervention for students with ADHD
description: The DRC is a behavioral intervention in which "The DRC is an operationalized list of a child's target behaviors (e.g., interrupting, noncompliance, academic productivity)" with "specific criteria for meeting each behavioral goal". Teachers "provide immediate feedback to the child regarding target behaviors on the DRC, and typically some reward is provided contingent on the child's performance." This meta-analysis evaluated the DRC alone (not within multi-modal packages) for students with ADHD across 14 single-case studies.

Teachers provide feedback on the DRC and rewards are typically contingent on performance
Must be implemented in a school or primarily academic setting as studied here

title: HLM-based meta-analysis of single-case design studies as a method for quantifying intervention evidence
description: The article develops and demonstrates a three-level hierarchical linear modeling approach to meta-analyzing single-subject design studies, where "Level 1 represents the data points, or repeated measures within persons", Level 2 represents students, and Level 3 represents studies. HLM was chosen because "HLM analyses can account for complex data structures (missing data, varying intervention lengths) likely to be found in single-case-design studies". The authors argue this method shows promise for addressing criticisms of statistical analysis of single-subject designs and supports continued inclusion of such designs in meta-analyses.

Data points are coded for phase and reversal order, and outcomes converted to common percentage metrics
constraints: The authors note the number of studies and participants was small, which may limit generalizability of study-level moderator findings

description: A standard-nomenclature taxonomy developed for IES with input from early literacy experts and intervention developers, piloted by the synthesis team to code what interventions implemented. "The component taxonomy defines four levels of intervention components," with "component type" at the highest level identifying "the broad strategy used by the intervention"; five component types (instructional practices, non-academic supports, organizational structures, educator supports, and assessment and placement) contain "the 15 component domains", which break down into 81 components and additional component approaches. article_title: A Meta-Analysis of Teachers' Provision of Structure in the Classroom and Students' Academic Competence Beliefs, Engagement, and Achievement
citation: Patall, E. A., Yates, N., Lee, J., Chen, S., Bhat, P., Lee, K., Beretvas, S. N., Guan, S., Cohen, M., Zhai, F., Brecht-Heitz, S., DeLorenzo, D., & Gonzales, K. (2023). A meta-analysis of teachers’ provision of structure in the classroom and students’ academic competence beliefs, engagement, and achievement. Educational Psychologist.
title: Classroom structure as a multifaceted set of teacher practices distinct from control, with chaos as its logical opposite
description: The article defines classroom structure as "teachers’ attempts to create an organized and predictable environment that helps students effectively achieve desired outcomes", drawing on self-determination theory, instructional quality, and classroom management literatures that use largely synonymous definitions under different labels. Structure comprises practices such as communicating clear expectations, rules, and goals; framing activity with directions, routines, or schedules; organizing space and materials; monitoring progress; and giving encouragement and feedback about accomplishing desired outcomes. The construct is explicitly distinguished from control: whereas control constrains students to act in teacher-determined ways, structure provides competence-relevant information that supports self-regulation, and its logical opposite is chaos, in which teachers are confusing, contradictory, or disorganized.
requirements: Structure must be implemented as practices providing clarity of information and ongoing guidance rather than demands and sanctions that pressure students to act in teacher-determined ways
constraints: The benefits of structure can be constrained when teachers compliment structure with controlling practices or apply structure in a controlling manner
target_learning_goals: Academic engagement, competence beliefs, and achievement
key_sources: Patall, E. A., Yates, N., Lee, J., Chen, S., Bhat, P., Lee, K., Beretvas, S. N., Guan, S., Cohen, M., Zhai, F., Brecht-Heitz, S., DeLorenzo, D., & Gonzales, K. (2023). citation: Patall, E. A., Yates, N., Lee, J., Chen, S., Bhat, P., Lee, K., Beretvas, S. N., Guan, S., Cohen, M., Zhai, F., Brecht-Heitz, S., DeLorenzo, D., & Gonzales, K. (2023). A meta-analysis of teachers’ provision of structure in the classroom and students’ academic competence beliefs, engagement, and achievement. Educational Psychologist.
title: Dual process model of engagement within self-determination theory
description: The article draws on the dual process model within a self-determination theory framework, which asserts a differentiated view of teacher practice, student motivation, and student engagement. According to the model, "supportive practices like structure are theorized to be most strongly linked with desirable outcomes, including higher competence beliefs and engagement, rather than undesirable outcomes like disengagement", while thwarting practices that define chaos are expected to be most predictive of undesirable outcomes. Structure supports the psychological need for competence—the need to experience efficacy in one's behavior—whose satisfaction is theorized as necessary for optimizing motivation and learning.
requirements: Teacher practice must remain supportive rather than controlling for the model's predicted benefits to emerge
constraints: The article does not examine chaos or thwarting practices in this synthesis, so the model's predictions about chaos are not tested here
target_learning_goals: Academic engagement, disengagement, competence beliefs, and achievement

A meta-analysis of teachers’ provision of structure in the classroom and students’ academic competence beliefs, engagement, and achievement. Educational Psychologist.
title: Classroom structure intervention programs targeting teacher training
description: The article identifies several classroom structure interventions that combine effective structure strategies into teacher training programs, including the Good Behavior Game (Barrish et al., 1969), Classroom Organization and Management Program (Evertson et al., 1989), Consistency Management & Cooperative Discipline (CMCD) program (Freiberg et al., 2009), and Incredible Years Teacher Classroom Management (Reinke et al., 2014). These programs train teachers to implement structure practices in authentic classrooms, with some emphasizing that teachers should establish a caring climate and include students in decision-making about rules and expectations as they implement classroom structure. Evidence suggests many are effective for supporting students' engagement and achievement, though inconsistent results have sometimes emerged.
requirements: Teacher training that directs or trains teachers to implement structure practices, compared against teachers who were not trained or directed to use structure
constraints: Inconsistent results have sometimes emerged across these intervention programs
target_learners: Preschool through high school students in authentic classrooms

A meta-analysis of teachers’ provision of structure in the classroom and students’ academic competence beliefs, engagement, and achievement. Educational Psychologist.
title: Classroom structure practices combine anticipatory, organizational, monitoring, feedback, and involvement components at lesson and unit level
description: The article describes classroom structure as a lesson-level instructional pattern in which teachers use a diverse assortment of practices in combination to organize and guide students' school-relevant behavior during learning. These practices include communicating and maintaining clear expectations, rules, and goals; framing students' activity with explicit directions, guidance, routines, or schedules; creating an organized space and materials; providing clear, organized activities; monitoring progress; and giving encouragement and feedback about how students can accomplish desired outcomes. The pattern can be implemented with or without accompanying autonomy or emotional support, which moderates its effects.
requirements: Practices must be implemented by the teacher in an authentic classroom setting and aimed at organizing and guiding students' school-relevant behavior
constraints: The particular combination of practices has varied across studies, and some responsive strategies (rewards, intervention, punishment) carry caveats about lower effectiveness and greater potential to be experienced as controlling

title: Use research methods that center teachers' and students' experiences and align with the nature of the focal outcome when studying structure
description: The methodological moderator analyses highlighted "the importance of using methods that center teachers’ and students’ experiences and align with the nature of the focal outcome". Because personal perception is central to psychological experiences of motivation and engagement, survey measures and student respondents may yield stronger correlations for engagement and competence beliefs, while observation and teacher reports may align better with achievement outcomes. Researchers designing studies of classroom structure should match the measurement approach to the outcome's perceptual nature.
requirements: Studies must carefully consider whether structure is measured by survey or observation and who provides the report about structure or outcomes
constraints: The pattern may differ for achievement outcomes, which do not reflect personal perception, so student-report methods may not strengthen achievement correlations
