article_title: The Meta-Analytic Rain Cloud Plot: A New Approach to Visualizing Clearinghouse Data
citation: Kaitlyn G. Fitzgerald and Elizabeth Tipton. (2022). The Meta-Analytic Rain Cloud Plot: A New Approach to Visualizing Clearinghouse Data. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness. https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2022.2031366
title: Normative four-criterion framework for visualizing meta-analytic clearinghouse evidence for decision-making
description: The article proposes that visualizations of clearinghouse meta-analytic data should be judged against four normative goals derived from meta-analytic decision theory: they "ought to visually emphasize: 1. Precise studies over imprecise studies, 2. Summary effects over individual effects, 3. The magnitude of the summary effect, and 4. The uncertainty of the summary effect via a range of plausible values." The framework holds that decision-making should rest on the inverse-variance weighted average effect, judged against a user-defined magnitude threshold and communicated with uncertainty that gives intuition about the range of plausible true effects. It motivates the MARC plot's design choices, such as omitting individual-study confidence intervals to discourage vote-counting.
requirements: Because practitioners cannot be expected to know meta-analytic methods, visualizations must intuitively guide them toward normative meta-analytic thinking without requiring training
constraints: The framework focuses on decisions about the average treatment effect, because the current evidence landscape does not yet allow locally contextualized predictive decision-making
target_learning_goals: accurate interpretation of meta-analytic evidence (effect magnitude, precision, uncertainty) for adoption decisions
examples: The authors used the criteria to critique WWC bar plots, forest plots, and rainforest plots, noting bar plots draw attention to large but imprecise effects and forest plots give imprecise studies undue visual attention
key_sources: Kaitlyn G. Fitzgerald and Elizabeth Tipton. (2022). The Meta-Analytic Rain Cloud Plot: A New Approach to Visualizing Clearinghouse Data. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness. https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2022.2031366

article_title: The Meta-Analytic Rain Cloud Plot: A New Approach to Visualizing Clearinghouse Data
citation: Kaitlyn G. Fitzgerald and Elizabeth Tipton. (2022). The Meta-Analytic Rain Cloud Plot: A New Approach to Visualizing Clearinghouse Data. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness. https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2022.2031366
title: Meta-Analytic Rain Cloud (MARC) Plot
description: The MARC Plot is a visualization for clearinghouse meta-analytic evidence in which study weights are "encoded directly — as y-axis position, as dot size, and with a label for the actual study weight," with the summary effect placed at the top with weight 1.0. Individual studies appear as dots without confidence intervals to avoid encouraging vote-counting, while the summary effect's precision is shown as a cloud of values "created by generating random values from a normal distribution with mean and standard deviation equal to the mean and standard error of the summary effect." Annotations such as red/blue shading of negative/positive values and a 'More certain → Less certain' legend guide interpretation. R code and the 16 experimental visualizations were released in supplementary material.
requirements: Underlying meta-analytic data with per-study effect estimates, sampling variances, and an inverse-variance weighted summary effect
Uses the metaviz and ggplot2 packages in R (adapted source code) to render plots
constraints: Effect sizes were displayed as standardized mean differences; the article states that empirically determining which metric (e.g., Improvement Index, months of learning) best communicates to lay audiences is outside the scope of the present study
target_learners: education practitioners and policy-makers using clearinghouse evidence
target_learning_goals: correctly identifying study weights, certainty, summary effect magnitude, and uncertainty in meta-analytic evidence
examples: In the experiment, 16 visualizations (4 data sets × 4 plot types) with randomized study order were shown to participants randomized to blocks of four visualizations each

article_title: Understanding Quality Characteristics of EdTech Interventions and Implementation for Disadvantaged Pupils. Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis
citation: Björn Haßler, Bethany Huntington, Christopher Klune, Jennie Lester, Aditi Bhutoria, Hassan Mansour. (2025). Understanding Quality Characteristics of EdTech Interventions and Implementation for Disadvantaged Pupils: Systematic review with meta-analysis. Education Endowment Foundation. https://doi.org/10.53832/opendeved.1170
title: Four-level conceptual framework of EdTech mechanisms, mechanism clusters, building blocks, and higher-order constructs
description: The review proposes a multi-level conceptual framework in which "mechanisms (Level 1), mechanism clusters (Level 3), and higher-order constructs, such as EdTech interventions (Level 4)" sit within a causal flow. Mechanisms are defined as the "entities and activities organised in such a way that they are responsible for the phenomenon", with the phenomenon being improved student attainment. Mechanism clusters form when similar mechanisms are grouped by shared entities (e.g., a digital game) or activities (e.g., teacher guidance), and their composition activates processes contributing to intermediate outcomes defined as building blocks. The framework was iterated across three project phases and underpins the consolidated mechanisms map.
requirements: Mechanism clusters must be grounded in identified entities and activities from intervention studies
constraints: The study does not attempt to evaluate higher-order constructs (Level 4) themselves; impacts may vary by contextual factors of the larger intervention in which clusters are implemented
target_learning_goals: Improved attainment outcomes across curriculum subjects
examples: Fifty-six mechanisms were synthesised into nine mechanism clusters and refined with 58 practitioners in the structured community review

title: Consolidated mechanisms map of EdTech implementation
description: The review's principal output is a consolidated mechanism map: "a conceptual synthesis of our framework that maps all the synthesised mechanisms (Level 1) grouped in each of the nine mechanism clusters (Level 2) with their associated building blocks (Level 3)". Each of the 56 synthesised mechanisms is "labelled with an indicator of the extent of evidence underpinning it", highlighting alignment and differences between research evidence and practitioner perspectives. The map is intended as "a practical tool for practitioners" for educators, school leaders, policymakers, and EdTech developers.

constraints: Must be viewed within the limitations of the study, including high heterogeneity in the underlying meta-analysis
target_learning_goals: Supporting effective and equitable EdTech implementation to improve attainment
examples: The Phase 3 community review with 58 practitioners revised the nine mechanism clusters, e.g. renaming Cluster 1 to 'Grounding technology in pedagogical processes'

Understanding Quality Characteristics of EdTech Interventions and Implementation for Disadvantaged Pupils: Systematic review with meta-analysis. Education Endowment Foundation. https://doi.org/10.53832/opendeved.1170

article_title: Determination of Critical Success Factors Affecting Mobile Learning: A Meta-Analysis Approach
citation: Muasaad Alrasheedi and Luiz Fernando Capretz. (2015). Determination of Critical Success Factors Affecting Mobile Learning: A Meta-Analysis Approach. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 14(2). https://www.tojet.net/
title: Classification of m-Learning CSFs into four categories (technology, management support, teaching pedagogy, learning approach) and three stakeholder perspectives
description: The article organizes the 21 discovered CSFs using a classification adapted from Teoh (2011). It states the "variables, i.e., the CSFs, can be divided into four categories – technology, management support, teach ing pedagogy, and learning  approach," and further divides them into student, instructor, and management perspectives. Some factors such as assimilation with curriculum fall into multiple categories, reflecting overlap among the people influencing each variable. The authors observe that the factors are fairly evenly distributed across categories, implying m-Learning success depends on more than technical factors.
requirements: Applied to CSFs identified from prior m-Learning studies in higher education; factors may appear in multiple categories
constraints: The classification is based on Teoh (2011) and reflects the specific studies included in the meta-analysis
target_learning_goals: successful adoption and use of mobile learning platforms in higher education
examples: Table 3 assigns each of the 21 CSFs to its category, e.g., availability and cross-platform capability under technology, learner perceptions and user friendly design of content under learning approach

article_title: Examining the Effects of Teacher-Directed Opportunities to Respond on Student Outcomes: A Systematic Review of the Literature
citation: MacSuga-Gage, A. S., & Simonsen, B. (2015). Examining the Effects of Teacher-Directed Opportunities to Respond on Student Outcomes: A Systematic Review of the Literature. Education and Treatment of Children, 38(2), 211-240.
title: Teacher-directed opportunities to respond (TD-OTR): antecedent-response-feedback framework with individual and unison modalities
description: The review organizes TD-OTR research around a behavioral definition: "teacher behaviors (i.e., antecedent stimuli) that occasion student responses", followed by teacher feedback contingent on the response. The framework distinguishes two categories of TD-OTRs — teacher-directed individual responses and teacher-directed unison responses (choral, gestural, written, or clicker-based) — and the review uses it to code each included study's modality and delivery rate.
requirements: Requires a teacher delivering prompts during direct instruction and providing feedback contingent on student responses
constraints: Applies to teacher-directed response opportunities only; peer tutoring and other non-teacher-directed OTRs are excluded from the framework's scope
target_learners: K-12 students with and without disabilities in general and special education classrooms
target_learning_goals: Increased academic achievement and positive classroom behavior through active engagement
examples: The review coded all 15 included studies' independent variables using this framework, distinguishing modality comparisons (e.g., response cards, choral responding, SRS) from rate-increasing interventions.
key_sources: MacSuga-Gage, A. S., & Simonsen, B. (2015). Examining the Effects of Teacher-Directed Opportunities to Respond on Student Outcomes: A Systematic Review of the Literature. Education and Treatment of Children, 38(2), 211-240. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1070193

article_title: Comparing Effects of Different Applications on Pre-Service Teachers: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Şenel Elaldı, Veli Batdı. (2016). Comparing Effects of Different Applications on Pre-Service Teachers: A Meta–Analysis. Journal of Education and Training Studies. http://dx.doi.org/10.11114/jets.v4i7.1456
title: Transformative Learning Theory as an adult learning framework centered on critical reflection on experience
description: Transformative Learning Theory, introduced by Jack Mezirow in 1975, frames learning as making meaning of experience through critical reflection, and the article uses it both as a reviewed application and as one of four focal teaching methods. The article quotes Mezirow: "learning is understood as the process of using a prior interpretation on construe a new or revised interpretation of the meaning of one’s experience". It also distinguishes informative from transformative learning, citing Kegan: "informative learning changes what we know; transformative learning cha nges how we know". In the meta-analysis it produced the highest attitude effect size (d=1,4760) for Biology pre-service teachers.
requirements: Adult learners' experience as a central element, since the article states that "it is through experience that learning occurs"
Critical reflection on assumptions, which the article says can occur "either in group interaction or independently"
constraints: The article describes it as "a uniquely adult form of metacognitive reasoning", so the framework is scoped to adult learners
The article notes assumptions "can be changed only after critical reflection"
target_learning_goals: Changes in understanding of self
Revision of belief systems
Changes in lifestyle
examples: The reviewed study by Çimen (2013) applied a transformative learning model based on environmental education with pre-service biology teachers
key_sources: Şenel Elaldı, Veli Batdı. (2016). Comparing Effects of Different Applications on Pre-Service Teachers: A Meta–Analysis. Journal of Education and Training Studies. http://dx.doi.org/10.11114/jets.v4i7.1456

article_title: Comparing Effects of Different Applications on Pre-Service Teachers: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Şenel Elaldı, Veli Batdı. (2016). Comparing Effects of Different Applications on Pre-Service Teachers: A Meta–Analysis. Journal of Education and Training Studies. http://dx.doi.org/10.11114/jets.v4i7.1456
title: In teacher education, select teaching methods appropriate to learners' social and cultural context to develop the process of learning to teach
description: The article concludes that no single instructional approach dominates once learner dispositions and classroom interaction are considered, recommending that teacher educators match methods to context. It states that "in teacher education, providing appropriate selection of teaching methods within their socia l and cultural context, teachers will enable students to develop and refine the process of learning to teach". This rests on its finding that effect sizes varied widely across applications and that pre-service teachers' prior beliefs filter new methodologies.
requirements: Knowledge of pre-service teachers' predispositions toward subject matter, which the article says include beliefs about how a subject should be taught and learned
constraints: The article states "the impact of a certain classroom instructional approach on pre -service teachers’ retention and attitude scores is outweighed by teachers’ preferences or the nature of the interactions occurring in the classrooms"
The article notes pre-service teachers are drawn to "perceived practicality", which may constrain receptiveness to methods they see as impractical
target_learners: Pre-service teachers in education faculties in Turkey
target_learning_goals: Retention of learning
Attitudes toward teaching and their subject areas
examples: The meta-analysis compared nine retention applications and fourteen attitude applications, finding effect sizes ranged from d=2,0606 to d=-0,3949, supporting the claim that no single method dominates across contexts
key_sources: Şenel Elaldı, Veli Batdı. (2016). Comparing Effects of Different Applications on Pre-Service Teachers: A Meta–Analysis. Journal of Education and Training Studies. http://dx.doi.org/10.11114/jets.v4i7.1456

article_title: The Effectiveness of Feedback for L1-English and L2-Writing Development: A Meta-Analysis. TOEFL iBT™ Research Report. TOEFL iBT-14. ETS RR-11-05
citation: Douglas Biber, Tatiana Nekrasova, and Brad Horn. (2011). The Effectiveness of Feedback for L1-English and L2-Writing Development: A Meta-Analysis. ETS Research Report RR-11-05. https://www.ets.org/toefl
title: A 16-variable coding rubric characterizing feedback by source, mode, focus, type, and tone, plus outcome measures
description: The report develops an explicit coding rubric that itemizes all important factors varying across feedback studies, developed inductively by reading a wide sample of studies. It includes 16 variables covering research paradigm, design type, target language and population, writing-task genre and length, and five feedback dimensions — the article states that "feedback can be described with respect to five variables: type, focus, tone, mode, and source" — plus outcome measures. The rubric was applied to categorize all studies in the 306-article corpus and to code the subset entering the statistical meta-analysis, providing the basis for subsequent effect-size comparison.
requirements: Studies must be codable on all rubric variables, with values such as teacher/peer/tutor/self/computer for source and oral/written/computer-mediated for mode
constraints: Proficiency level applies to L2 studies only; some variables such as tone were unreported in most studies
Qualitative studies cannot be included in a quantitative meta-analysis
target_learners: L1-English and L2-English writing students from K-12 through graduate levels
target_learning_goals: Writing proficiency development, including grammatical accuracy, holistic quality, revision behavior, and attitudes toward feedback
examples: Table 1 itemizes variables and values, e.g., type of feedback coded as location of error, comment, direct correction, editing codes, and multiple types
key_sources: Douglas Biber, Tatiana Nekrasova, and Brad Horn. (2011). The Effectiveness of Feedback for L1-English and L2-Writing Development: A Meta-Analysis. ETS Research Report RR-11-05. https://www.ets.org/toefl

article_title: The Effect of Multiple Intelligences Theory-Based Education on Academic Achievement: A Meta-Analytic Review
citation: Baş, G. (2016). The effect of multiple intelligences theory-based education on academic achievement: A meta-analytic review. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice, 16, 1833–1864. https://doi.org/10.12738/estp.2016.6.0015
title: Multiple Intelligences Theory (MIT) as a pluralistic account of intelligence and a method of instruction
description: Gardner's theory of multiple intelligences defines intelligence as "a psychobiological information processing capacity to solve problems or fashion products that are valued in at least one community and culture", rejecting a single IQ-measured general intelligence. It posits at least eight modalities of intelligence — verbal-linguistic, logical-mathematical, visual-spatial, bodily-kinesthetic, musical-rhythmic, social-individual, personal-intrapersonal, and natural-naturalist — processed autonomously and localized in different brain areas. The article treats MIT not just as an intelligence theory but "as a method of instruction", providing a template for valuing individual differences in curriculum and teaching.
requirements: Teachers shift continuously between intelligence modalities in MIT-based classrooms and expand their repertoire of techniques beyond typical linguistic and logical ones
constraints: The article records criticisms that the eight potentials may not form abilities or mental domains, that MIT has not been subjected to strong experimental tests, and that it may be too broad for curriculum planning and present a static view of student competence
target_learners: students at elementary, high school, and university levels in Turkey
target_learning_goals: academic achievement across course types through instruction matched to multiple intelligence modalities
examples: In 2005 MIT was implemented into Turkey's elementary curriculum, after which the number of studies based on it increased significantly
key_sources: Baş, G. (2016). The effect of multiple intelligences theory-based education on academic achievement: A meta-analytic review. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice, 16, 1833–1864. https://doi.org/10.12738/estp.2016.6.0015

article_title: A Meta-Analytic Review of Tactile-Cued Self-Monitoring Interventions Used by Students in Educational Settings
citation: McDougall, D., Ornelles, C., Mersberg, K., & Amona, K. (2015). A Meta-Analytic Review of Tactile-Cued Self-Monitoring Interventions Used by Students in Educational Settings. JAASEP. https://jaasep.org
title: Four-component model of behavioral self-management, with self-monitoring as its first two components
description: The review situates TCSM within the behavioral self-management (BSM) framework Glynn, Thomas, and Shee proposed in 1973, grounding it in the cognitive-behavioral modification principle of reactivity: when people become cognitively aware of their behavior and the environment, they are better positioned to change their behavior. As printed, "The first two components of their model, self-assessment plus self-recording, constitute self-monitoring." The remaining components are self-determination of reinforcement and self-administration of reinforcement, and the review notes BSM has since evolved to add techniques such as self-evaluation, video self-modeling, and self-graphing. The review uses this framework to organize its background and to define where tactile cues enter the self-assessment step.
requirements: Participants must use a tactile cue that prompts periodic self-assessment and self-recording of then-current behavior, not merely an initial behavior prompt
constraints: The review applies the model to students in educational settings, mostly students with disabilities aged 10 to 15
target_learners: students with disabilities in elementary, middle, and high school educational settings
target_learning_goals: self-directed behavior change and academic engagement through self-assessment and self-recording
examples: The nine qualifying studies operationalized self-assessment questions such as "Am I working quickly?" with tactile cues from a MotivAider or vibrating wristwatch, followed by self-recording on paper forms
key_sources: McDougall, D., Ornelles, C., Mersberg, K., & Amona, K. (2015). A Meta-Analytic Review of Tactile-Cued Self-Monitoring Interventions Used by Students in Educational Settings. JAASEP. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1134294

article_title: A Meta-Analysis of Educator Training to Improve Implementation of Interventions for Students with Disabilities
citation: Matthew E. Brock and Erik W. Carter. (2017). A Meta-Analysis of Educator Training to Improve Implementation of Interventions for Students With Disabilities. Remedial and Special Education. https://doi.org/10.1177/0741932516653477
title: Measure professional development reach by observable change in educator behavior, not training hours
description: The article recommends that administrators and training programs evaluate professional development by observing classroom implementation rather than counting hours, because increased training time alone showed no relation to fidelity. They state "the reach of professional development programs should be measured not in terms of the number of training hours, but in terms of observable change in educator behavior," suggesting existing observation tools to identify educators needing further support.
requirements: Classroom observation tools for documenting implementation of evidence-based practices must be available to program evaluators.
constraints: Recommendation is made cautiously given the small number of studies and identified threats to internal validity; increased training time alone did little to change educator behavior.
target_learning_goals: Implementation fidelity of evidence-based interventions for students with disabilities
examples: The article suggests practical observation tools (e.g., Neitzel & Wolery, 2009) could be used to measure training success and identify educators who would benefit from further training and support.
key_sources: Matthew E. Brock and Erik W. Carter. (2017). A Meta-Analysis of Educator Training to Improve Implementation of Interventions for Students With Disabilities. Remedial and Special Education. https://doi.org/10.1177/0741932516653477

article_title: Unpacking TPACK in Mathematics Education Research: A Systematic Review of Meta-Analyses
citation: Young, J.R. (2016). Unpacking TPACK in Mathematics education research: A systematic review of meta-analyses. International Journal of Educational Methodology, 2(1), 19-29. https://doi.org/10.12973/ijem.2.1.19
title: TPACK framework as an analytic lens for technology-enhanced mathematics instruction
description: The Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework, an extension of Shulman's PCK, holds that technological, pedagogical, and content knowledge afford and constrain one another at their intersections; the article states that "Mishra and Koehler (2008) suggest that the intersection of PCK, TCK, and TPK is TPACK." The review uses TPACK to interpret the most salient moderators of effects across meta-analyses and concludes the framework functions as "an analytic tool to identify and categorize moderator variables in meta-analysis of technology -enhanced mathematics learning." It also notes the framework may not apply one-to-one within mathematics.
requirements: Teacher knowledge must integrate technological, pedagogical, and content considerations rather than treating the technology tool as the primary catalyst
constraints: The article states that within mathematics the TPACK framework "may not be applied in a one -to-one fashion" and that the constructs most salient in a given context should be assessed; TPACK is reported as the least stable construct to measure across in-service and pre-service teachers
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement through technology-enhanced instruction
teacher capacity for technology integration
examples: The review categorized the 13 meta-analyses' technologies by didactical functionality and mapped the five emergent moderators onto TPK, TCK, and TPACK
key_sources: Young, J.R. (2016). Unpacking TPACK in Mathematics education research: A systematic review of meta-analyses. International Journal of Educational Methodology, 2(1), 19-29. https://doi.org/10.12973/ijem.2.1.19

article_title: Unpacking TPACK in Mathematics Education Research: A Systematic Review of Meta-Analyses
citation: Young, J.R. (2016). Unpacking TPACK in Mathematics education research: A systematic review of meta-analyses. International Journal of Educational Methodology, 2(1), 19-29. https://doi.org/10.12973/ijem.2.1.19
title: Three didactical functionalities of digital technology in mathematics classrooms
description: Drawing on Drijvers, Boon, and Van Reeuwijk (2010), the review organizes mathematics technology by three didactical functionalities: "(1) doing mathematics, (2) practicing skills, and (3) conceptual understanding." Doing mathematics uses technology to complete tasks that could be done by hand, enhancing computational efficiency; practicing skills supports repetitive tasks with immediate feedback for procedural or instrumental understanding; conceptual understanding involves building deeper understandings and making connections, similar to relational understanding. The review maps calculators to computational efficiency, CAI/CBI to instrumental understanding, and mathematics-specific software to relational understanding, then shows effect sizes vary across these functions.
requirements: Categories are applied "based on the primary functionality as established in the literature," so tools with complex, multiple functions must be classified by their primary use
constraints: The article states the didactical functionalities "are not exhaustive nor mutually exclusive, as many of the tools have complex functions and multiple adaptations"
target_learners: postsecondary statistics students in some included meta-analyses
target_learning_goals: computational efficiency
procedural or instrumental understanding
conceptual or relational understanding of mathematics
examples: Calculators were categorized as computational enhancement devices; CAI/CBI as instructional delivery tools supporting practice; mathematics-specific software and virtual manipulatives as tools for relational understanding
key_sources: Young, J.R. (2016). Unpacking TPACK in Mathematics education research: A systematic review of meta-analyses. International Journal of Educational Methodology, 2(1), 19-29. https://doi.org/10.12973/ijem.2.1.19

article_title: The Effect of Augmented Reality Applications in the Learning Process: A Meta-Analysis Study
citation: Ozdemir M., Sahin C., Arcagok S., & Demir M. K. (2018). The effect of augmented reality applications in learning process: A meta-analysis study. Eurasian Journal of Educational Research, 74, 165-186. https://doi.org/10.14689/ejer.2018.74.9
title: Augmented reality as an educational technology encompassing image-based and location-based types displayed on mobile, projection, or head-mounted devices
description: Augmented reality (AR) is defined in the article as "a technology enabling virtual objects produced by computers to be placed on physical objects in real time." It has two types: image-based AR, which uses markers matched with 3D models or animations that a camera perceives, and location-based AR, which uses GPS or Wi-Fi-based positioning from users' mobile devices. AR objects can be displayed on mobile devices, projection systems, or head-mounted screens, and the article treats AR's display device as a moderator of its achievement effects.
requirements: Hardware or software able to present virtual objects overlaid on real-world objects, using one of the two AR types (marker-based or location-based positioning)
constraints: The article's effect-size synthesis covers experimental studies published October 2007 to February 2017 in SSCI-indexed journals in English only
target_learning_goals: academic achievement across natural sciences and social sciences content
examples: Included studies spanned contexts such as electromagnetism experimentation, weather simulations, solid geometry learning, and astronomical observation instruction
key_sources: Ozdemir M., Sahin C., Arcagok S., & Demir M. K. (2018). The effect of augmented reality applications in learning process: A meta-analysis study. Eurasian Journal of Educational Research, 74, 165-186. https://doi.org/10.14689/ejer.2018.74.9

article_title: The Effects of Cooperative Learning on Mathematics Achievement in Turkey: A Meta-Analysis Study
citation: Turgut, S., & Gülşen Turgut, İ. (2018). The Effects of Cooperative Learning on Mathematics Achievement in Turkey: A Meta-Analysis Study. International Journal of Instruction, 11(3), 663-680. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.11345a
title: Five essential elements define whether a group activity is cooperative learning
description: The article presents cooperative learning as small-group work in which students help each other's learning, and states that not every group activity qualifies: "An activity should include five main elements as positive interdependence, individual responsibility, supportive face-to-face communication, social skills and evaluation of group process in order to be cooperative." It then describes each element — positive interdependence created through task design, personal responsibility for one's own work, mutual support and encouragement, taught social skills such as leadership and communication, and evaluation of how well the group met its objectives and maintained relationships. The meta-analysis operationalizes cooperative learning through named techniques implementing this model.
requirements: Group members need to have acquired certain social skills to study together efficiently; the article says skills like leadership, communication, decision making and trust building should be taught to group members.
constraints: The meta-analysis covers studies done in Turkey between 2000 and 2017 comparing cooperative learning techniques with traditional teaching in mathematics; the article notes only Turkish studies were examined and more extended results could come from international studies.
target_learners: Elementary, middle school, high school and undergraduate mathematics students
target_learning_goals: Mathematics achievement (mathematics and geometry domains)
examples: The synthesized studies implemented named techniques such as learning together, teams-games-tournaments, jigsaw, student teams achievement divisions and team-assisted individualization in experimental groups.
key_sources: Turgut, S., & Gülşen Turgut, İ. (2018). The Effects of Cooperative Learning on Mathematics Achievement in Turkey: A Meta-Analysis Study. International Journal of Instruction, 11(3), 663-680. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.11345a

article_title: A Meta-Analysis on the Effect of Duration, Task, and Training in Peer-Led Learning
citation: Zha, Shenghua; Estes, Michele D.; and Xu, Ling. (2019). A meta-analysis on the effect of duration, task, and training in peer-led learning. Journal of Peer Learning, 12. https://ro.uow.edu.au/ajpl/vol12/iss1/2
title: Peer-led learning as small-group learning guided by similar-status student leaders, organised around task type, training, and session duration
description: The article frames peer-led learning (PLL) as a design space defined by three characteristics: the tasks student leaders perform, the training student leaders receive, and the duration of an average session. It defines PLL as "a type of small group learning activity where student leaders, of similar status to the learners, guide or facilitate learning within a group." The framework is grounded in social learning, social identity, and social congruence theory, and was operationalised in a two-level random-effects meta-regression of 28 post-secondary studies.
requirements: Student leaders must take distinct facilitation, tutoring, or coaching roles, and activities must occur regularly across a course period
constraints: The meta-analysis included only face-to-face post-secondary studies; online PLL was excluded
target_learning_goals: Cognitive achievement in regular course contexts
examples: Supplemental Instruction and Peer-Led Team Learning are named as widely adopted PLL program models that fit this framework
key_sources: Zha, Shenghua; Estes, Michele D.; and Xu, Ling. (2019). A meta-analysis on the effect of duration, task, and training in peer-led learning. Journal of Peer Learning, 12. https://ro.uow.edu.au/ajpl/vol12/iss1/2

article_title: A Meta-Analysis of the Cognitive, Affective, and Interpersonal Outcomes of Flipped Classrooms in Higher Education
citation: Hwan Young Jang and Hye Jeong Kim. (2020). A Meta-Analysis of the Cognitive, Affective, and Interpersonal Outcomes of Flipped Classrooms in Higher Education. Educ. Sci. 2020, 10, 115. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci10040115
title: Flipped classroom as a blended, student-centered instructional model expanding active learning into class time
description: The article defines the flipped classroom as a model in which "students study instructional materials before class, typically online lectures, and apply what they learned in in-class activities". It is generally understood through blended learning, and its essential point is that "active learning activities are expanded", with in-class reciprocal actions distinguishing it from traditional teacher-centered lecture models. Instructors take on roles as curricular designers, instructors, and media developers.
requirements: Students must engage with pre-class video or audio instructional materials, and in-class time must feature interactive student-centered activities, per the article's inclusion criteria for studies of the approach.
constraints: Implementation barriers the article names include instructor hesitancy to adopt new approaches and students' diverse learning needs; effectiveness depends in large part on whether students actually use the available pre-class time effectively.
target_learning_goals: cognitive, affective, and interpersonal educational outcomes
examples: In the meta-analysis, included studies were required to define the flipped classroom as including the use of video or audio materials before class and featuring in-class activities.
key_sources: Hwan Young Jang and Hye Jeong Kim. (2020). A Meta-Analysis of the Cognitive, Affective, and Interpersonal Outcomes of Flipped Classrooms in Higher Education. Educ. Sci. 2020, 10, 115. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci10040115

article_title: The Factors Affecting Academic Achievement: A Systematic Review of Meta Analyses
citation: Koçak, Ö., Göksu, İ., & Göktaş, Y. (2021). The factors affecting academic achievement: a systematic review of meta analyses. International Online Journal of Education and Teaching, 8(1), 454-484. https://iojet.org
title: Nine-category taxonomy of variables influencing academic achievement
description: A taxonomy organizing the 254 variables found in meta-analyses of academic achievement into nine categories: "Psychological Characteristics", "Learning Theories and Teaching Strategies", "SES&SDC and Individual Characteristics", "Family", "Teacher", "Special Education", "School", "Educational Technology" and "Violence". Variables "with the effect sizes between -.799 and 3.170 were examined in nine categories", modeled on similar review studies (e.g., Hattie, 2015; Richardson et al., 2012). The review found the largest numbers of variables in the psychological, socio-economic/socio-demographic/individual, learning theories and teaching strategies, and family categories.
requirements: Variables were categorized by five experts separately, with multi-category variables re-examined against full texts and assigned by consensus
constraints: The review reports the relevant variables and ESs come from meta-analyses with different qualities and limitations and no limits were placed on education levels
target_learners: students across all levels of education, pre-school to higher education
target_learning_goals: understanding which factors influence academic achievement
examples: Inter-rater reliability of categorization was checked with Intraclass Correlation Coefficient analysis; the average measures ICC was .86, which according to Koo and Li (2016) indicates good reliability.
key_sources: Koçak, Ö., Göksu, İ., & Göktaş, Y. (2021). The factors affecting academic achievement: a systematic review of meta analyses. International Online Journal of Education and Teaching, 8(1), 454-484. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1286675

article_title: The Impact of Stratified Teaching on the Academic Performance of Chinese Middle School Students: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Shi, H., Cheung, E.S.T., & Cheung, A.C.K. (2020) The impact of stratified teaching on the academic performance of Chinese middle school students: A meta-analysis. Science Insights Education Frontiers, 7(1):735-760. https://doi.org/10.15354/sief.20.re012
title: Taxonomy of stratified teaching types: hierarchical grouped fix-class, hierarchical shift-class, and in-class hierarchical systems
description: The article defines stratified teaching as a strategy, model, and ideology in which teachers "divide students scientifically into groups of similar levels based on their current knowledge, abilities, and potential, and then teaches them accordingly". It organizes implementation into a taxonomy of three systems: the "hierarchical grouped fix-class teaching system", the "hierarchical shift-class teaching system", and the "in-class hierarchical teaching system". In-class stratification is further split into "dominant stratification", where students know their own and others' placement, and "recessive stratification", where only the teacher (or teacher and individual student/parent) knows. The meta-analysis uses this taxonomy to code and compare intervention modes.
requirements: Teachers assess students' current knowledge, abilities, and potential to assign levels, and at least two teachers teach the experimental and control groups separately per the article's inclusion criteria.
constraints: In the Chinese context, large-scale actual stratified teaching is not allowed, only small-scale experiments, according to the article.
target_learning_goals: academic performance in basic education subjects
examples: The 22 included studies were coded by intervention method into in-class dominant (PO), in-class recessive (NE), in-class general (GE), shift-class (TR), and combined (MI) modes.
key_sources: Shi, H., Cheung, E.S.T., & Cheung, A.C.K. (2020) The impact of stratified teaching on the academic performance of Chinese middle school students: A meta-analysis. Science Insights Education Frontiers, 7(1):735-760. https://doi.org/10.15354/sief.20.re012

article_title: The Impact of Stratified Teaching on the Academic Performance of Chinese Middle School Students: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Shi, H., Cheung, E.S.T., & Cheung, A.C.K. (2020) The impact of stratified teaching on the academic performance of Chinese middle school students: A meta-analysis. Science Insights Education Frontiers, 7(1):735-760. https://doi.org/10.15354/sief.20.re012
title: Base stratification on abilities, motivation, interests, and cognitive structure — not performance alone — or stratification becomes diversion
description: The article warns that stratified teaching works as differentiated instruction only when grouping reflects more than achievement scores. It states that "in most studies, stratified teaching stratification is based on student performance and does not take into account factors such as student abilities, motivation, interests, and cognitive structure", and that without considering these factors "the stratification will evolve into a diversion", no different from fast and slow class teaching. The principle directs implementers to group on a broader profile of learner characteristics.
requirements: Teachers must gather information on student abilities, motivation, interests, and cognitive structure before assigning strata.
constraints: The article notes stratified teaching follows the principle of teaching students according to their aptitude and advancing step by step, but in practice grouping often reduces to performance-based placement.
target_learning_goals: academic performance
personalized learning
examples: The article's problems section describes the risk that performance-based stratification becomes diversion comparable to fast and slow class teaching in some middle schools.
key_sources: Shi, H., Cheung, E.S.T., & Cheung, A.C.K. (2020) The impact of stratified teaching on the academic performance of Chinese middle school students: A meta-analysis. Science Insights Education Frontiers, 7(1):735-760. https://doi.org/10.15354/sief.20.re012

article_title: The Impact of Stratified Teaching on the Academic Performance of Chinese Middle School Students: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Shi, H., Cheung, E.S.T., & Cheung, A.C.K. (2020) The impact of stratified teaching on the academic performance of Chinese middle school students: A meta-analysis. Science Insights Education Frontiers, 7(1):735-760. https://doi.org/10.15354/sief.20.re012
title: Provide sustained psychological care and encouragement across all levels during stratified teaching to prevent labeling burden
description: The article reports that under any stratification mode, students "are often labeled with A, B, and C levels, which creates psychological problems for middle and low-level students with some kinds of hint". Teachers typically counsel students early in stratification, but later inattention can cause psychological imbalance, especially at the extremes. The principle requires care and encouragement throughout the whole implementation period, not only at the start.
requirements: Teachers must communicate and psychologically counsel students at different levels early in stratification and continue attention throughout implementation.
constraints: The article states the problem arises across recessive, dominant, and shift-class stratification alike.
target_learning_goals: academic performance
student well-being and motivation
examples: The article notes that lack of later-stage attention can easily cause students' psychological imbalance, especially those at the extremes.
key_sources: Shi, H., Cheung, E.S.T., & Cheung, A.C.K. (2020) The impact of stratified teaching on the academic performance of Chinese middle school students: A meta-analysis. Science Insights Education Frontiers, 7(1):735-760. https://doi.org/10.15354/sief.20.re012

article_title: Comprehensive Meta-Analysis of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder Psychosocial Treatments Investigated within between Group Studies
citation: Fabiano, G. A., Schatz, N. K., Aloe, A. M., Pelham, W. E., Jr., Smyth, A. C., Zhao, X., Merrill, B. M., Macphee, F., Ramos, M., Hong, N., Altszuler, A., Ward, L., Rodgers, D. B., Liu, Z., Ersen, R. K., & Coxe, S. (2021). Comprehensive Meta-Analysis of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder Psychosocial Treatments Investigated Within Between Group Studies. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543211025092
title: Organizing framework for ADHD psychosocial treatment evidence: treatment type × rater × proximal outcome domain
description: The article organizes its meta-analytic results within a three-parameter framework: treatment type, rater of the outcome, and domain of outcome assessed. Treatments are categorized as behavioral interventions (behavioral parent training, behavioral classroom management, behavioral peer intervention, behavioral family problem-solving, general behavioral), training interventions (cognitive, organizational skills, social skills, emotion regulation), and additional interventions (combination treatments, neurofeedback/biofeedback, academic accommodations, academic modifications, self-monitoring). The article states: "Results are therefore organized first by treatment type, then by source of the measure (i.e., parent, teacher, observation, child product), and finally by domain assessed." Raters are parent, teacher, observer, or child source; outcome domains include ADHD symptoms, impairment, comorbid externalizing behavior, and parenting behaviors/effectiveness-stress.
requirements: Primary studies must supply information permitting calculation of standardized mean differences between a treatment and a comparison condition, and measures must be codable by rater and proximal outcome domain.
constraints: The framework covers between-group treatment-outcome studies of participants under 18 with ADHD (or well-described characteristic behaviors) with IQ not below 70, excluding medication-only studies and laboratory investigations; the meta-analysis focused on proximal outcomes of treatment.
target_learners: children and adolescents under 18 diagnosed with ADHD
target_learning_goals: improve ADHD symptoms, impairment, and academic/social functioning through psychosocial and educational interventions
examples: The meta-analysis reports separate subgroup analyses (Tables 2–4) for each treatment type crossed with each rater and outcome domain, e.g., behavioral classroom management effects on teacher-rated ADHD symptoms.

article_title: A Meta-Analysis on the Effects of Synchronous Online Learning on Cognitive and Affective Educational Outcomes
citation: Florence Martin, Ting Sun, Murat Turk, and Albert D. Ritzhaupt. (2021). A Meta-Analysis on the Effects of Synchronous Online Learning on Cognitive and Affective Educational Outcomes. International Review of Research in Open and Distributed Learning, Volume 22, Number 3. https://www.irrodl.org/index.php/irrodl
title: Meta-analytic corpus of 19 primary studies with 27 independent effect sizes on synchronous online learning (2000–2019)
description: The corpus assembled by this meta-analysis comprises 19 scholarly publications (12 journal articles and 7 dissertations) published between 2000 and 2019, identified through seven search terms in six databases and screened with PRISMA procedures. As the article reports, "The final sample consisted of k = 27 independent effect sizes (across the four models) and N = 4,409 participants." Each study was coded on outcome features, methodological and pedagogical features, synchronous technology features, and demographics, with inter-rater agreement of 88.46% on initial coding.
requirements: Studies had to use experimental or quasi-experimental between-subjects designs comparing synchronous online with asynchronous or face-to-face conditions and provide adequate statistics for effect-size calculation
constraints: Only two studies reported behavioral outcomes, so that outcome type was excluded from the synthesis
Dependent effect sizes within studies were combined by weighted averaging, which the authors note "ignores any subject variability"
target_learning_goals: cognitive outcomes such as learning, achievement, and comprehension
affective outcomes such as satisfaction, emotions, attitudes, and motivation
examples: Primary studies spanned histology, computer science, business, education, medicine, math, and health disciplines, with 78.9% conducted in the United States
key_sources: Florence Martin, Ting Sun, Murat Turk, and Albert D. Ritzhaupt. (2021). A Meta-Analysis on the Effects of Synchronous Online Learning on Cognitive and Affective Educational Outcomes. International Review of Research in Open and Distributed Learning, Volume 22, Number 3. https://www.irrodl.org/index.php/irrodl

article_title: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Reading and Writing Interventions for Students with Disorders of Intellectual Development
citation: Bakken, R.K.; Næss, K.-A.B.; Lemons, C.J.; Hjetland, H.N. (2021). A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Reading and Writing Interventions for Students with Disorders of Intellectual Development. Educ. Sci. 2021, 11, 638. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci11100638
title: Effective reading interventions for students with disorders of ID combine phonics-based decoding (often with sight-word instruction), linguistic comprehension, and supplemental instruction adapted to adaptive and cognitive challenges
description: Across the nine included studies, reading programmes were phonics-based and frequently combined decoding with sight-word reading: "Five studies combined decoding with sight-word instructions". Targeted decoding skills included sound blending and segmentation, word recognition, text reading, fluency, and single word reading. Most interventions also included linguistic comprehension instruction, and almost all used supplemental strategies addressing adaptive and cognitive challenges such as explicit instruction, time delays, reinforcement, repeated practice, short sessions, and behaviour management.
requirements: Interventions must be adapted to participants' adaptive and cognitive skills, e.g., via explicit instruction, systematic prompting, and repeated practice opportunities
constraints: The review tested multifaceted interventions rather than individual content components, so the contribution of each component is unknown
target_learners: Students aged 4–19 with disorders of intellectual development (mild-to-moderate IQ range 41.5–58.4 in the included studies)
target_learning_goals: Word reading and decoding of taught and untrained words
Linguistic comprehension
examples: Browder et al. developed the Early Literacy Skills Builder adapted for AAC users; Burgoyne et al. combined phonics, text reading and sight-word instruction with games and graded books for students with Down syndrome

article_title: Measures Matter: A Meta-Analysis of the Effects of Educational Apps on Preschool to Grade 3 Children's Literacy and Math Skills
citation: James Kim, Joshua Gilbert, Qun Yu, Charles Gale. (2021). Measures Matter: A Meta-Analysis of the Effects of Educational Apps on Preschool to Grade 3 Children's Literacy and Math Skills. AERA Open. https://doi.org/10.1177/23328584211004183
title: Educational apps meta-analytic dataset and replication toolkit (36 studies, 285 effect sizes)
description: A meta-analytic dataset of 36 intervention studies of educational apps for preschool to Grade 3 literacy and math, yielding 285 effect sizes coded for methodological, participant, and intervention moderators including outcome type, control type, grade, dosage, app quality pillars, and constrained versus unconstrained skills. The authors state, "A replication toolkit including the data set and the Stata and R code is available from the authors upon request." Mean app quality was 2.4 with a low social interaction mean of 1.30.
requirements: Coded posttest means, standard deviations, or test statistics sufficient to compute Hedges's g for each study
constraints: Studies limited to English-language reports from January 2008 to June 2020 targeting literacy or math in preschool to Grade 3
target_learning_goals: literacy and mathematics skills
examples: Coded 36 studies with two raters; mean kappa was k = .94 across coded study characteristics
key_sources: James Kim, Joshua Gilbert, Qun Yu, Charles Gale. (2021). Measures Matter: A Meta-Analysis of the Effects of Educational Apps on Preschool to Grade 3 Children's Literacy and Math Skills. AERA Open. https://doi.org/10.1177/23328584211004183

article_title: Measures Matter: A Meta-Analysis of the Effects of Educational Apps on Preschool to Grade 3 Children's Literacy and Math Skills
citation: James Kim, Joshua Gilbert, Qun Yu, Charles Gale. (2021). Measures Matter: A Meta-Analysis of the Effects of Educational Apps on Preschool to Grade 3 Children's Literacy and Math Skills. AERA Open. https://doi.org/10.1177/23328584211004183
title: Science-of-learning account of why educational apps can improve early academic skills
description: The article proposes three mechanisms through which educational apps may improve young children's learning: the touchscreen medium itself, the one-to-one or small-group practice context, and gamified learning affordances. It states that "interactive educational applications can support active, engaging, targeted, and varied practice," that touchscreens spare young children fine-motor keyboard demands, and that apps may provide more time on task with supplemental supports similar to tutoring, plus personalization and gamified elements like scaffolding and rewards.
requirements: Apps must foster active, engaged, meaningful learning with high-quality social interactions and clear learning goals, plus deliberate practice with feedback and interleaved varied activities
constraints: The authors caution results may not generalize to apps neither based on principles from the science of learning nor subjected to rigorous experimental evaluations
target_learning_goals: literacy and mathematics skills
examples: Berkowitz et al.'s Bedtime Learning Together math app fostering parent-child co-engagement around daily math word problems, and Neuman's Learn With Homer with structured lessons and adult fidelity monitoring, cited as high-quality app examples
key_sources: James Kim, Joshua Gilbert, Qun Yu, Charles Gale. (2021). Measures Matter: A Meta-Analysis of the Effects of Educational Apps on Preschool to Grade 3 Children's Literacy and Math Skills. AERA Open. https://doi.org/10.1177/23328584211004183

article_title: A Systematic Review of the Effects of Physical Activity on Specific Academic Skills of School Students
citation: Loturco, I.; Montoya, N.P.; Ferraz, M.B.; Berbat, V.; Pereira, L.A. (2022). A Systematic Review of the Effects of Physical Activity on Specific Academic Skills of School Students. Educ. Sci. 2022, 12, 134. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci12020134
title: Physically active lessons integrating movement into academic subjects as a school learning design
description: This pattern integrates physical activity into regular academic lessons rather than adding separate exercise sessions. The review describes it as "the integration of physical activity into regular classes (especially mathematics)" and suggests it "could be an effective strategy to enhance learning in school-aged students." Interventions reviewed ranged from classroom-based activities within regular school practices to specific programs of active lessons embedded in math or English classes.
requirements: Interventions embedded movement within the regular instructional format of academic lessons rather than as separate sessions
constraints: Math improvements were described as more expected and consistent than language or reading improvements, especially in short- or mid-term (≤8 weeks) programs
target_learners: Kindergarten, elementary, middle, and high school students
target_learning_goals: Mathematics skills and general academic achievement
examples: Beck et al.'s inter-limb gross motor activities performed while solving mathematical questions; Mullender-Wijnsma et al.'s 2-year integration of physical activities into math and spelling lessons; Resaland et al.'s 90 min/week of physically active educational lessons
key_sources: Loturco, I.; Montoya, N.P.; Ferraz, M.B.; Berbat, V.; Pereira, L.A. (2022). A Systematic Review of the Effects of Physical Activity on Specific Academic Skills of School Students. Educ. Sci. 2022, 12, 134. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci12020134

article_title: A Systematic Review of the Effects of Physical Activity on Specific Academic Skills of School Students
citation: Loturco, I.; Montoya, N.P.; Ferraz, M.B.; Berbat, V.; Pereira, L.A. (2022). A Systematic Review of the Effects of Physical Activity on Specific Academic Skills of School Students. Educ. Sci. 2022, 12, 134. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci12020134
title: Corpus of 31 school-based physical activity intervention studies included in the meta-analysis
description: A set of 31 peer-reviewed studies identified through PubMed MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science searches following PRISMA guidelines, from which 24 used mathematics tests, 4 language tests, 10 reading assessments, and 9 composite scores. Intervention types comprised "increasing the volume of physical education classes, applying classroom-based activities in the regular school practices, promoting 'active' breaks between regular classes, and employing specific programs of 'active' lessons." Risk of bias was assessed with the Cochrane RoB 2.0 tool.
requirements: Included studies required quantitative pre- and post-intervention academic performance assessment and at least one physical activity intervention group with a comparison group
constraints: Studies assessing only acute effects, qualitative studies, and studies without full text or outcome data were excluded
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement in mathematics, language, reading, and composite measures
examples: Table 1 characterizes each study's country, participants, intervention, comparator, outcome measure, and overall risk of bias, with risks ranging from low risk to high risk
key_sources: Loturco, I.; Montoya, N.P.; Ferraz, M.B.; Berbat, V.; Pereira, L.A. (2022). A Systematic Review of the Effects of Physical Activity on Specific Academic Skills of School Students. Educ. Sci. 2022, 12, 134. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci12020134

article_title: Methodology to the Teaching of English as a Foreign Language: A Systematic Review
citation: Philominraj, A., Ranjan, R., Ubilla Rosales, L., Cocio, A., & Brauchy Castillo, J. G. (2023). Methodology to the Teaching of English as a Foreign Language: A Systematic Review. MEXTESOL Journal, 47(2). https://www.mextesol.net/journal/
title: PRISMA-screened corpus of 40 Chilean EFL methodology studies (2011–2021) from Web of Science, SCOPUS and SCIELO
description: The review's empirical corpus consists of 40 research studies retrieved from three databases and screened following PRISMA guidelines, with thematic analysis and snowball sampling. The authors state that "40 articles (Web of Science=05, SCOPUS = 16, SCIELO= 19)met the criteria for this systematic review" after screening 80 titles and checking 73 usable articles for duplicity against inclusion criteria (methodology, approach, strategies, EFL, Chile, teaching, English language) and exclusion criteria (students' perspective, teacher-centered, other subjects, other languages).
requirements: Inclusion criteria: studies on methodology, approach, strategies, EFL, Chile, and teaching, written in English, published 2011–2021 in the three named databases
constraints: The restriction to Web of Science, SCOPUS and SCIELO limited the search to published studies, excluding doctoral dissertations and master's theses
target_learners: Chilean primary, secondary and tertiary EFL learners and teacher-education populations covered by the reviewed studies
target_learning_goals: EFL communicative competence and teaching methodology in the Chilean context
examples: A PRISMA flow diagram (Figure 1) presents the search and inclusion/exclusion process from 80 initial titles to 40 final articles
key_sources: Philominraj, A., Ranjan, R., Ubilla Rosales, L., Cocio, A., & Brauchy Castillo, J. G. (2023). Methodology to the Teaching of English as a Foreign Language: A Systematic Review. MEXTESOL Journal, 47(2). https://www.mextesol.net/journal/

article_title: Methodology to the Teaching of English as a Foreign Language: A Systematic Review
citation: Philominraj, A., Ranjan, R., Ubilla Rosales, L., Cocio, A., & Brauchy Castillo, J. G. (2023). Methodology to the Teaching of English as a Foreign Language: A Systematic Review. MEXTESOL Journal, 47(2). https://www.mextesol.net/journal/
title: Chilean EFL research areas organized into four groups: social-science studies, ELT/curriculum studies, community-attitude studies, and linguistically driven policy studies
description: The review organizes the retrieved EFL research into an organizing taxonomy of four groups. It states that "EFLresearch from various disciplines and perspectives can be grouped under various areas of knowledge that gofrom social sciences(economics and sociology)to education (curriculum,didactics, and methodology) and humanities(linguistics and appliedlinguistics)". The four printed groups are: (a) social-science studies of socio-economic factors, motivation and self-regulation; (b) works addressing Chilean ELT and the English curriculum including initial teacher education; (c) studies on factors impacting communities' attitudes toward learning; and (d) research emphasizing linguistic rationale with concerns about national language policy.
requirements: The taxonomy presupposes the 40-study retrieved corpus and thematic analysis of the selected articles
constraints: The grouping applies to research on English in Chile published 2011–2021 in the three databases used
target_learners: EFL learners and teachers in Chilean primary, secondary and tertiary education
target_learning_goals: Understanding the landscape of EFL teaching methodology research in Chile
examples: Group (a) is instantiated by Kormos & Kiddle (2013) and Yilorm & Acosta (2016) on socio-economic factors, motivation and self-regulation in Chile
key_sources: Philominraj, A., Ranjan, R., Ubilla Rosales, L., Cocio, A., & Brauchy Castillo, J. G. (2023). Methodology to the Teaching of English as a Foreign Language: A Systematic Review. MEXTESOL Journal, 47(2). https://www.mextesol.net/journal/

article_title: Methodology to the Teaching of English as a Foreign Language: A Systematic Review
citation: Philominraj, A., Ranjan, R., Ubilla Rosales, L., Cocio, A., & Brauchy Castillo, J. G. (2023). Methodology to the Teaching of English as a Foreign Language: A Systematic Review. MEXTESOL Journal, 47(2). https://www.mextesol.net/journal/
title: Traditional and communicative EFL methodologies form a continuum rather than a dichotomy, aligned with Kumaravadivelu's post-method theory
description: The review argues that the traditional/communicative split in Latin American EFL programs is a false dichotomy. It states that "EFL programsin Latin Americaincluding Chilerefer to the communicative and traditional methodologies and the distinction between these seemsincreasingly to be a false dichotomy", and cites Beaumont and Chang (2011), who "consider communicative and traditional methodologies on a continuum wherein teachers pick up elementsfrom these methods to their teachingpractices". The review aligns this view with Kumaravadivelu's (1994, 2006) post-method theory, which it presents as superseding the traditional/communicative perspective.
requirements: Teachers select and combine elements from both traditional and communicative methods in their practices
constraints: The account concerns EFL programs in Latin America including Chile as described by the review
target_learners: EFL learners in Chilean and wider Latin American school and tertiary contexts
target_learning_goals: EFL communicative competence through context-sensitive methodological choices
examples: The review reports that training programs in its corpus involved approaches emphasizing collaboration among teachers of the local network to explore local methodologies
key_sources: Philominraj, A., Ranjan, R., Ubilla Rosales, L., Cocio, A., & Brauchy Castillo, J. G. (2023). Methodology to the Teaching of English as a Foreign Language: A Systematic Review. MEXTESOL Journal, 47(2). https://www.mextesol.net/journal/

article_title: Methodology to the Teaching of English as a Foreign Language: A Systematic Review
citation: Philominraj, A., Ranjan, R., Ubilla Rosales, L., Cocio, A., & Brauchy Castillo, J. G. (2023). Methodology to the Teaching of English as a Foreign Language: A Systematic Review. MEXTESOL Journal, 47(2). https://www.mextesol.net/journal/
title: Chilean national English curriculum combines the Communicative Approach with Natural Approach, Cooperative Learning, Content-Based Instruction and Task-Based Language Teaching
description: The review describes the Chilean National Curriculum's English programs as anchored in the Communicative Approach and supplemented by four further approaches promoting communication. It states: "Themain contributions come from: a) Natural Approach; b) CooperativeLearning; c) Content-Based Instruction and d) Task-Based Language teaching". The curriculum emphasizes development of critical and creative thinking, teaching of learning strategies, communicative tasks, connections, culture, the writing process, and ICT and multimodal texts (MINEDUC, 2015), with class activities involving pair work, role play, problem solving and collaborative group projects.
requirements: Class objectives address all language components (vocabulary, topics, grammar, strategies, functions) across the four skills of listening, reading, writing, and speaking
constraints: The pattern is prescribed by the Chilean Ministry of Education curriculum, mandatory from fifth grade (students 10 years old)
target_learners: Chilean students aged 10–18 in mandatory English schooling, plus tertiary learners
target_learning_goals: Communicative competence: using English to interact and communicate relevant messages in contextualized, meaningful ways
examples: Under the communicative approach, work activities are developed in pairs, roleplay, problem-solving, and collaborative group projects in which students negotiate meanings and exchange information

article_title: Does Context-Based Learning Increase Academic Achievement and Learning Retention?: A Review Based on Meta-Analysis
citation: Tutal, Ö (2023). Does Context-Based Learning Increase Academic Achievement and Learning Retention?: A Review based on Meta-Analysis. Journal of Practical Studies in Education, 4(5), 1-16. https://doi.org/10.46809/jpse.v4i5.71
title: Educators should consider incorporating context-based learning strategies into instructional practices to support achievement and retention
description: Based on its meta-analytic findings, the article recommends that educators adopt context-based learning, an approach that "establish[es] a meaningful connection between everyday experiences and educational content" and emphasizes "the use of context as a powerful tool for constructing and understanding concepts." The recommendation is grounded in the significant positive overall effects on achievement and retention relative to lecture-based instruction.
requirements: Content should be situated within the learner's horizon and connected to real-life experiences, social events, or scientifically valid situations
constraints: The recommendation rests on Turkish thesis studies with experimental or quasi-experimental designs; evidence on retention comes from only 10 studies
target_learners: Elementary, middle, high school and tertiary students
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement
Long-term retention of learned knowledge
examples: The meta-analysis synthesized 42 achievement studies and 10 retention studies, most conducted in science courses, comparing CBL to teacher-led instruction with pretest-posttest control group designs
key_sources: Tutal, Ö (2023). Does Context-Based Learning Increase Academic Achievement and Learning Retention?: A Review based on Meta-Analysis. Journal of Practical Studies in Education, 4(5), 1-16. https://doi.org/10.46809/jpse.v4i5.71

article_title: Does Context-Based Learning Increase Academic Achievement and Learning Retention?: A Review Based on Meta-Analysis
citation: Tutal, Ö (2023). Does Context-Based Learning Increase Academic Achievement and Learning Retention?: A Review based on Meta-Analysis. Journal of Practical Studies in Education, 4(5), 1-16. https://doi.org/10.46809/jpse.v4i5.71
title: Context-based learning as a constructivist instructional approach using real-world contexts to build and understand concepts
description: CBL is an instructional approach that recognizes the importance of both the social context within the learning environment and the practical, real-world context in knowledge acquisition. It promotes active student engagement, using "context as a powerful tool for constructing and understanding concepts," and aligns with a constructivist view of learning. Knowledge construction is stimulated through the recognition of the need-to-know within a given context, and contexts act as integrators bringing "coherence, connection, meaning, and relevance to the learning experience."
requirements: Contexts should be relevant and relatable to students' lives, drawing from real-life experiences, social events, or scientifically valid situations
constraints: The article notes CBL differs from traditional education in that content is situated within the learner's horizon from the outset rather than presented first and applied later
target_learners: Elementary, middle, high school and tertiary students
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding
Knowledge construction and application in real-life contexts
examples: The article describes a spiral curriculum approach where ideas introduced in one context are further developed and reinforced in other contexts

article_title: Learning How to Use Input-Based and Output-Based Form-Focused Instruction: A Meta-Analytic Comparison of Persian EFL Learners
citation: Schenck, A. (2024). Learning How to Use Input-Based and Output-Based Form-Focused Instruction: A Meta-Analytic Comparison of Persian EFL Learners. Journal of Second Language Acquisition and Teaching, 30.
title: Processability Theory's three-level morphosyntactic complexity taxonomy (intra-phrasal, inter-phrasal, clausal)
description: The article uses Processability Theory (Pienemann & Lenzing, 2015) to organize grammatical features into three complexity levels: intra-phrasal features modifying one phrase (e.g., past -ed, plural -s), inter-phrasal features requiring manipulation of multiple phrases (e.g., subject-auxiliary inversion, third person -s), and clausal features including subordinate clauses (e.g., conditionals, relative clauses). The theory holds that "specific target features are, in fact, teachable when grammatical complexity is just above a learner's English proficiency level", so timing of instruction matters. The article categorizes the 41 treatment groups by these levels.
requirements: Target features must be classifiable into intra-phrasal, inter-phrasal, or clausal categories
constraints: The article notes prior Processability Theory research examined only a limited number of grammatical features
target_learning_goals: Acquisition of English grammatical features of varying morphosyntactic complexity
examples: The meta-analysis categorized 41 treatment groups from 18 studies as 11 intra-phrasal, 21 inter-phrasal, and 9 clausal

article_title: A Meta-Analysis of the Experimental Evidence Linking Mathematics and Science Professional Development Interventions to Teacher Knowledge, Classroom Instruction, and Student Achievement
citation: Lynch, K., Gonzalez, K., Hill, H., & Merritt, R. (2025). A Meta-Analysis of the Experimental Evidence Linking Mathematics and Science Professional Development Interventions to Teacher Knowledge, Classroom Instruction, and Student Achievement. AERA Open. https://doi.org/10.1177/23328584251335302
title: Meta-analytic dataset of 46 experimental mathematics and science PD studies with 200 teacher-outcome and 126 student-achievement effect sizes
description: The dataset comprises randomized experimental studies of PK-12 mathematics and science PD published 2001 or later, each reporting both teacher and student outcomes. As the article states, "The final meta-analytic sample includes 46 studies contributing 200 effect sizes for teacher outcomes and 126 effect sizes for student achievement outcomes." Teacher outcomes were coded as knowledge or classroom instruction; moderators coded intervention features, PD foci, and contextual features.
requirements: Studies must employ a randomized experimental design comparing a treatment group to a business-as-usual control group and report sufficient data to calculate effect sizes for both teacher and student outcomes
constraints: Excludes non-randomized designs and interventions not involving in-service classroom teachers, such as researcher-delivered instruction
target_learning_goals: mathematics and science achievement
teacher knowledge
classroom instruction
examples: Screening located 12,086 records from database searches plus 1,402 from other sources, reduced to 840 studies passing preliminary relevance criteria

A Meta-Analysis of the Experimental Evidence Linking Mathematics and Science Professional Development Interventions to Teacher Knowledge, Classroom Instruction, and Student Achievement. citation: Lynch, K., Gonzalez, K., Hill, H., & Merritt, R. (2025). A Meta-Analysis of the Experimental Evidence Linking Mathematics and Science Professional Development Interventions to Teacher Knowledge, Classroom Instruction, and Student Achievement. AERA Open. https://doi.org/10.1177/23328584251335302
title: Logic model linking PD interventions to teacher knowledge, classroom instruction, and student outcomes
description: Adapted from Garrett et al. (2019), this model structures the meta-analysis: "teachers' participation in a PD may lead to changes in their knowledge (Path a) and/or changes in classroom instruction (Path b); changes in instruction may also operate through changes in knowledge (Path f)." Changes in teachers then affect student outcomes (Paths h and i), while interventions may also affect students directly through new materials and supports (Path c), with context and intervention characteristics as moderators (Paths d, e, and g). The present analyses test Paths a, b, d, e, h, and i.
requirements: Empirical tests require studies measuring both teacher-level outcomes (knowledge and/or instruction) and student achievement outcomes within the same randomized contrast
constraints: Prior meta-analyses primarily analyzed Paths b and i; Paths a and h were examined only via intervention-impact associations, not within-study correlations
target_learning_goals: mathematics and science achievement
teacher knowledge
classroom instruction
examples: The study examines Paths a and h — PD impacts on teacher knowledge and their link to student learning — which prior meta-analyses had not analyzed

title: A staged competency-based framework for geriatric dental education with 6 core competencies, 34 sub-competencies, and 72 enabling competencies
description: The review derives a three-level hierarchical competency framework mapping eight curricular themes onto six core competency domains. The article reports that "In total, 6 core competencies, 34 sub-competencies, and 72 enabling competencies, were identified." Core competencies guide program-level planning, sub-competencies inform course or module design, and enabling competencies support specific measurable learning outcomes and assessment criteria across undergraduate and postgraduate levels.

constraints: Specific learning outcomes "may require further contextual refinement according to educational level, institutional setting, and assessment purpose"

examples: The review mapped eight thematic categories to six competency domains, e.g., merging public health and aging-related changes into core competency 1

article_title: Medical students with specific learning disabilities: mixed-methods systematic review of the prevalence, academic performance, challenges, and perceived impact of support interventions.
citation: Pavletič Bernarda, Babuder Milena Košak, Homar Vesna. (2026). Medical students with specific learning disabilities: mixed-methods systematic review of the prevalence, academic performance, challenges, and perceived impact of support interventions. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09574-0
title: Performance outcomes versus learning processes: comparable scores do not indicate equitable learning conditions
description: The review's central integrative framework distinguishes "performance outcomes" (measurable indicators such as examination scores, progression, graduation) from "learning processes and experiences" (effort, strategies, cognitive load, emotional burden, institutional barriers). It uses this distinction to interpret the meta-analytic parity in accommodated MCQ assessments alongside qualitative reports of substantial compensatory effort, arguing that "comparable assessment outcomes may be achieved alongside substantial compensatory effort and should not be assumed to indicate equitable learning conditions." The framework reframes assessment design and support policy toward equity of learning conditions rather than parity of scores.
requirements: Requires mixed-methods synthesis combining performance data with students' reported experiences to operationalize the distinction
constraints: Developed from evidence geographically concentrated in UK medical education and focused mainly on dyslexia, limiting transferability; the authors note similar scores "may reflect successful compensation under accommodated conditions rather than the absence of educational disadvantage"
target_learners: undergraduate medical students with specific learning disabilities
target_learning_goals: equitable academic performance and progression
wellbeing and inclusion in medical education
examples: The review integrated meta-analytic MCQ parity findings (d = 0.045) with meta-aggregated qualitative accounts of extra preparation time and anxiety to argue equity requires looking beyond scores
