article_title: A scoping review of internet addiction and academic performance among health sciences students.
citation: Baghcheghi Nayereh; Koohestani Hamid Reza. (2026). A scoping review of internet addiction and academic performance among health sciences students. BMC Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-026-04883-x
title: Indirect-pathway model: internet addiction affects academic performance primarily through mediators rather than direct GPA effects
description: The review proposes that internet addiction's effect on academic performance is "complex, multifaceted, and predominantly indirect," exerted through intermediary factors rather than grade-based indicators. Key mediators named are mental health variables (depression and anxiety), academic burnout, sleep disruption, and surface learning approaches, which "may impair cognitive functioning and academic engagement." A proposed self-care pathway holds that late-night internet use reduces sleep, excessive online time erodes structured routines, and sedentary screen use displaces physical activity. A self-escape model explains the GPA paradox as deteriorating mental health and learning quality rather than direct effects.
requirements: Longitudinal mediation studies to test the directionality of the proposed pathways, as the article states the model requires such testing
constraints: Due to the predominance of cross-sectional designs, the variables should be interpreted as correlates and potential pathways rather than confirmed causal mechanisms
target_learners: Health sciences students in higher education (medicine, dentistry, nursing, pharmacy, allied health)
target_learning_goals: Academic performance (GPA, examination results) and quality of learning processes (learning approaches, engagement, burnout)
examples: The review interprets Colombian, Turkish, Egyptian, and Iranian null GPA findings alongside negative findings from Bangladesh, Pakistan, Egypt/Saudi, and Iran as support for mediated rather than direct effects

article_title: Systematic evaluation of the teaching effectiveness of flipped classroom mode in undergraduate preventive medicine courses in China.
citation: Zheng Hui, Ouyang Yun, Zeng Yifei, He Xinyu, Song Liping, Yu Xiangyuan. (2026). Systematic evaluation of the teaching effectiveness of flipped classroom mode in undergraduate preventive medicine courses in China. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2026.1896815
title: Flipped classroom as an inversion of knowledge delivery explained via zone of proximal development and cognitive-process staging
description: The article describes the flipped classroom as "a blended learning model that inverts the traditional teaching process" in which knowledge delivery shifts to before class and classroom time is used for interaction, case discussion, and problem-solving. It explains the observed advantages through the "zone of proximal development" theory: lower-order cognitive processes occur before class and higher-order processes (analyzing, synthesizing, evaluating, creating) occur in class, "thereby achieving knowledge internalization and transfer". This is the framework the authors use to interpret their pooled results.
requirements: Students independently acquire content before class via activities such as watching instructional videos and reading literature
constraints: The authors note it is difficult to fully account for variability arising from differences in teaching implementation even under a random-effects model
target_learners: undergraduate medical and preventive medicine students in China
target_learning_goals: theoretical knowledge in preventive medicine courses
self-directed learning
critical thinking
collaboration and problem-solving
examples: Included trials implemented FC variants such as FC + PBL, FC + MOOC, and FC + micro-lecture videos in epidemiology, health statistics, and environmental hygiene courses

article_title: AI for Clinical Competency Assessment: Scoping Review of Methods and Applications.
citation: Zhang Wenjia (Stella), Daniels Benjamin B, Mita Carol, Nguyen Hoang, Duong David B. (2026). AI for Clinical Competency Assessment: Scoping Review of Methods and Applications. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/92826
title: Three-category taxonomy of AI-SSP intended use: deliberate-practice educational tools, hybrid training-plus-assessment tools, and explicit assessment systems
description: The review organizes the 20 unique AI-SSP systems by their primary intended use into three categories: educational tools for deliberate practice, hybrid training-and-assessment tools, and systems focused explicitly on assessment. It reports that "The largest group, 9 (45%) of 20 systems, framed AI-SSPs primarily as deliberate practice or educational tools", that six (30%) were hybrid training and assessment tools combining SP interaction with structured feedback and scoring, and that the remaining five systems focused explicitly on assessment. The taxonomy shows that even systems with scoring components have most often been introduced as formative learning environments, with an increasing subset emphasizing automated scoring and performance analytics.
requirements: Systems must produce some form of quantitative score to be classified in this review, even when assessment is not the primary purpose
constraints: Classification reflects the studies' stated primary purposes as charted by the reviewers, not independent functional testing of the systems
target_learners: nursing, pharmacy, physiotherapy, and physician assistant trainees
target_learning_goals: history-taking
clinical reasoning and diagnosis
communication and empathy
counseling
examples: USC Standard Patient, CureFun, SOPHIE, AMTES, Turing Interactive Case Learning, 2-Sigma, VR-AI-ECS, and MedSimAI were among the named platforms mapped in Table 2

title: LLM-wrapped AI-SSP architectures using task-specific prompt layers and structural constraints to control simulated patient behavior
description: The review describes a dominant design approach in newer AI-SSP systems in which LLMs are embedded within controlled custom platforms or structured prompt pipelines rather than open-ended public chatbots. These systems combine a system prompt with case information, behavioral instructions, and constraints, and "Several other studies also separated the simulated patient prompt from the scoring or feedback prompt", using multiple task-specific prompt layers. Some systems added retrieval-augmented generation, structured case graphs, templates, or guardrails to constrain output, improve consistency, and reduce hallucinations, leading the review to conclude newer systems are mostly "LLM wrapped" rather than fully open-ended.
requirements: System prompts must combine case information, behavioral instructions, and constraints defining how the simulated patient should respond
constraints: The architectural constraints limit what information the model can use and how the patient responds, as described by the review
target_learners: health professions trainees including nursing, pharmacy, and physician assistant learners
target_learning_goals: history-taking
communication skills
clinical reasoning
examples: Holderried et al used a 2-part prompt with behavioral instructions and illness scripts; Hicke et al used instructor-provided templates for system prompts and separate evaluation prompts with JSON output; Li et al used a structured case graph for retrieval before generating responses

title: Deploy AI-SSPs to pursue scalable, more standardized clinical competency assessment, but treat validity and reliability across diverse learner groups as unproven
description: The review positions AI-SSPs as emerging infrastructures for clinical competency assessment rather than merely educational simulations, motivated by the resource intensity of OSCEs and documented evaluator-related bias, including halo and contrast effects, "with examiner stringency alone accounting for up to 29% of score variation in some OSCE settings". It concludes AI-SSPs could make assessment more scalable and potentially more standardized, while cautioning that more evidence is needed on validity and reliability across diverse learner or practitioner groups before large-scale deployment.

constraints: The review states more evidence is still needed to determine whether AI-SSPs achieve validity and reliability across diverse learner or practitioner groups; the evidence base is concentrated in high-income countries

history-taking

examples: The review's included studies spanned single-arm pilots, randomized controlled trials such as Brugge et al and Haut et al's SOPHIE trial, and a multisite quasi-experimental evaluation of MedSimAI with 410 unique learners across 3 US institutions

article_title: Effectiveness of the flipped classroom in medical education: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
citation: Wu Yaqiu, Cheng Meixiong. (2026). Effectiveness of the flipped classroom in medical education: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09526-8
title: Flipped-classroom mechanism: shifting initial content acquisition to pre-class activities frees class time for application-oriented practice with instructor facilitation
description: The review proposes that flipped classrooms work by reordering instructional flow: learners "review core concepts before class via videos or readings, whereas in-class time is used more often for problem solving, case discussion, and skills practice". Instructors act more as facilitators, giving real-time feedback and scaffolding based on learners' preparation and in-class performance. The review presents this as a mechanistic interpretation consistent with, but not directly tested by, the pooled effects.
requirements: Learners must access preparatory materials (e.g., videos or readings) before class
Class time must be used for discussion, practice, and application, with instructor facilitation and feedback
constraints: The mechanism is the authors' interpretation; the meta-analysis did not directly test mediating processes, and effects are context dependent given very high heterogeneity
target_learning_goals: Theoretical knowledge
Procedural/technical skills
Self-directed learning ability
Case analysis/problem-solving ability
Learner satisfaction
examples: Eighteen included studies used pre-class video teaching plus group learning, case discussion, or the Peyton four-step method in class, compared against traditional lecture-based teaching

title: Tailor flipped-classroom implementation to learner stage, course objectives, and available resources rather than assuming a uniform effect
description: Because pooled benefits in medical education come with very high heterogeneity and context-dependent effect sizes, the review recommends that "implementation should be tailored to learner stage, course objectives, and available resources rather than assuming a uniform effect across settings". Residents, particularly for procedural/technical skills and satisfaction, showed the largest benefits, so stage-specific deployment is advised. The review also suggests clear course structure and learning/technical support to reduce early adaptation burden.
requirements: Clear course structure and appropriate learning and technical support to reduce transition costs and improve adherence during adoption
constraints: Effects are context dependent; key outcomes (procedural/technical skills, self-directed learning) rest on k ≤ 4 studies; residents' larger effects partly rest on single studies and are exploratory
target_learning_goals: Procedural/technical skills
Self-directed learning ability
Learner satisfaction
examples: The review found larger resident effects for procedural/technical skills (between-subgroup p = 0.0131) and satisfaction (p = 0.0107), and recommends prioritizing under-studied domains in future studies

article_title: Instruments for Assessing Basic Life Support Knowledge in Secondary School Students: A Scoping Review and Expert Panel.
citation: Mecías‐Calvo M., Sobrido‐Prieto M., Navarro‐Patón R. (2026). Instruments for Assessing Basic Life Support Knowledge in Secondary School Students: A Scoping Review and Expert Panel. The Journal of School Health. https://doi.org/10.1111/josh.70223
title: Expert-panel framework of four key content domains for BLS knowledge assessment in secondary schools
description: A five-member interdisciplinary expert panel (evidence synthesis, Applied Didactics, school-based interventions, BLS and first aid education, and nursing education) convened in a structured 90-min virtual meeting defined the core domains for assessing secondary students' BLS knowledge. The panel agreed that "questionnaires should include at least four key domains: recognition of cardiac arrest, activation of emergency services, BLS sequence, and CPR maneuvers." Although these form a continuous chain of survival, the panel recommended assessing them separately "to better identify specific knowledge gaps." The panel also emphasized that unconsciousness alone is insufficient to identify cardiac arrest and that breathing assessment should be essential.
requirements: Assessment instruments should cover at least the four agreed key domains, assessed separately rather than as a single composite.
constraints: The panel recommends incorporating knowledge retention assessment only when study conditions allow, given logistical difficulties such as loss of follow-up in school settings.
target_learning_goals: basic life support knowledge including CPR and AED use
examples: The panel reviewed the scoping review findings and reached unanimous agreement through open discussion in a structured 90-min virtual meeting.

description: The expert panel proposed a reusable structure for designing comparable BLS knowledge questionnaires adaptable to different educational contexts. It classifies questionnaire content into three relevance levels: "mandatory (present in any questionnaire); recommended (depending on the scope of the training program or the time available); and optional (more specific or advanced aspects)." This classification supports instrument adaptation across varied program scopes and time constraints while preserving a common core of assessed content.
requirements: Questionnaire designers assign each content element to one of the three relevance levels to enable comparability across contexts.

examples: The panel proposed the classification to facilitate the design of comparable instruments adaptable to different educational contexts.

title: Schedule mandatory annual or semiannual BLS refresher sessions rather than one-off interventions, because knowledge deteriorates within months
description: A design recommendation for school health programming derived from the review's retention findings. Because most studies show BLS knowledge decays quickly, the review states that "school health programs should incorporate mandatory annual or semiannual refresher sessions into the curriculum rather than relying on one‐off interventions." Spaced, recurring instruction is positioned as the structural response to rapid knowledge loss documented across the reviewed studies.
requirements: Refresher sessions must be built into the school curriculum as mandatory rather than optional additions.
target_learning_goals: maintenance of basic life support knowledge over time
examples: The review found most studies confirm knowledge of BLS deteriorates rapidly within a matter of months, motivating the refresher recommendation.

title: Use standardized, psychometrically validated, and culturally/linguistically appropriate assessment tools to ensure uniform and equitable BLS training evaluation across schools
description: The review's central recommendation for school health policy and practice: BLS programs should employ standardized assessment tools incorporating all chain-of-survival elements, replacing brief ad hoc questionnaires. The authors state that "Education should focus on culturally and linguistically appropriate tools, with age‐appropriate response formats," which would improve reliability and fairness and "reduce inequalities between schools and countries." Standardized measurement is framed as the path to comparable assessments and equitable, inclusive BLS training.
requirements: Assessment instruments should include clearly defined domains such as BLS, CPR techniques, identification of cardiac arrest, calling emergency services, functional AED use, and scene safety.
constraints: Policies should promote implementation and evaluation in resource-limited settings to prevent increased disparities in emergency response capacity.

examples: The review identifies gaps in content regarding scene safety, initial recognition, and AED use that should be strengthened in future questionnaires.

description: The review adopts soft skills as an overarching category of non-technical, transferable competencies spanning intrapersonal capacities (self-awareness, emotional regulation, resilience) and interpersonal competencies (empathic communication, teamwork, leadership). Drawing on the World Economic Forum Education 4.0 Taxonomy, the K4D 21st Century Skills report, and the BESSI framework, it presents a synthesis in which frameworks "commonly identify three interrelated dimensions of soft skills" — how something is done, the values justifying it, and the discipline-specific knowledge behind it (Table 1).

title: keepin' it R.E.A.L. (kiR) resistance-skills curriculum
description: The keepin' it R.E.A.L. model teaches resistance strategies — Refusal, Explain, Avoid, Leave — "based on the premise that most children who initiate substance use at an early age do so not out of the desire to try it, but because they lack the requisite social skills to resist drug offers." It comprises 10 interactive classroom sessions, five videos scripted, acted and filmed by students, and booster activities after every session. Seven of the review's 43 studies examined its efficacy, including acculturation, entertainment-education and cross-national Mexican variants.
requirements: Delivery through interactive classroom sessions with accompanying videos and booster activities, as printed in Table 3.
constraints: Review-synthesised kiR outcomes varied across variants: original kiR showed no significant behavioural change in one trial, and the Acculturation Enhancement version increased substance use expectancies by 8th grade.
target_learners: Middle-school students (5th-8th grade in the reviewed kiR studies)
target_learning_goals: Drug-offer refusal, resistance skills, refusal self-efficacy, decision-making, and anti-drug expectancies
examples: The review describes 10 interactive classroom sessions, five student-scripted videos, and booster activities after every classroom session.

citation: Bajpai Tewari, D., Gautam, U., Jaiswal, V., Pooja, Mishra, A., & Das, P. (2026). Integrated Education Models for Addressing Substance Use Among Schoolchildren: A Scoping Review of School-Based Educational Interventions. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph23081073
title: Preventive, protective, and corrective classification of school-based substance use intervention models
description: The review organises school-based substance use intervention models along an approach axis with three branches: "preventive models are defined as those delivered to substance-naive populations before any use has occurred; protective models as those that build resilience or resistance skills in general or identified at-risk populations without requiring prior use; and corrective models as those explicitly designed to intervene with students who have already initiated substance use." This taxonomy frames the review's mapping, its synthesis via a socio-ecological framework, and its finding that the corrective branch is empty in the current evidence base.
requirements: Interventions must be evaluated in school settings with school administration involvement, per the review's eligibility criteria.
constraints: The review found all 43 examined models fell only into the preventive or protective branches; no corrective model was identified.
target_learners: School-going children and adolescents, including substance-naive, at-risk, and substance-using students
target_learning_goals: Preventing substance use initiation, building resilience and resistance skills, and intervening after initiation
examples: The review applies the classification across 33 distinct intervention models in Table 3, tagging each as preventive and protective or preventive.

article_title: Exploring the impact of immersive reality for enhancing clinical training in dental education: a systematic review.
citation: Ruslin Muhammad, Sjamsudin Endang, Hanafiah Olivia Avriyanti, Stevanie Carolina, Kurniawan Sri Hastuti, Anshar Muh, Boffano Paolo, Forouzanfar Tymour, Sukotjo Cortino. (2026). Exploring the impact of immersive reality for enhancing clinical training in dental education: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09739-x
title: Implement immersive reality as a complement to traditional dental education methods
description: The review recommends integrating immersive reality alongside, not instead of, conventional dental training: "The findings support implementing IR as a complement to traditional dental education methods." The conclusion frames IR as offering "a novel approach to dental education by combining immersive experiences with opportunities for skill development and student engagement". This positions IR simulators as supplementary practice environments that let students repeat procedures safely before clinical contact.
requirements: Institutional capacity for IR hardware and software, since the review states high costs pose barriers and technical maintenance expertise may be unavailable.
constraints: Assessment in the reviewed literature relies heavily on subjective self-reported surveys, which the authors note would be better complemented by quantitative measures like procedural time and error rates.
target_learning_goals: clinical procedural skills
motor skills
knowledge of dental procedures
examples: The included studies used IR for preclinical pulpotomy, cavity preparation, scaling, suturing and surgical planning training alongside conventional simulator practice.

article_title: Clinical teaching models for the instruction of healthcare trainees in the 21(st) century: a scoping review.
citation: Munguiko Clement, Masereka Enos Mirembe, Atukwatse Joseph, Smitha Joseph, Kateregga James, Nankinga Clare, Collete Alice Alum, Namujju Josephine, Akello Safina, Nalubega Sylivia. (2026). Clinical teaching models for the instruction of healthcare trainees in the 21st century: a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09710-w
title: Three pedagogical orientations organize contemporary clinical teaching models: learner-centred reasoning, procedural skills-based, and workplace-based reflective teaching
description: The review groups the eight mapped models into three dominant pedagogical orientations, stating they "can broadly be grouped according to their dominant pedagogical orientation, namely learner-centred reasoning models, procedural and skills-based models, and workplace-based reflective teaching models." Learner-centred reasoning models (OMP, SNAPPS, RIME, Aunt Minnie) emphasize clinical reasoning, diagnostic thinking, and metacognition; procedural models (STEPS, BOPPPS) emphasize deliberate practice and structured instructional sequencing; workplace-based models (MiPLAN, ED STAT) emphasize contextual learning, role modelling, and adaptive supervision in authentic settings.
requirements: The grouping assumes models can be assigned a dominant pedagogical orientation, which the review presents as a broad interpretive categorization rather than a mutually exclusive classification
constraints: The review presents this as a broad grouping of mapped models, not a validated typology
target_learners: healthcare trainees including medical, nursing, midwifery, and allied health students
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning
procedural skills acquisition
professionalism and workplace-based competence
examples: The review assigns OMP, SNAPPS, RIME, and Aunt Minnie to the reasoning orientation, STEPS and BOPPPS to procedural skills, and MiPLAN and ED STAT to workplace-based teaching

citation: Munguiko Clement, Masereka Enos Mirembe, Atukwatse Joseph, Smitha Joseph, Kateregga James, Nankinga Clare, Collete Alice Alum, Namujju Josephine, Akello Safina, Nalubega Sylivia. (2026). Clinical teaching models for the instruction of healthcare trainees in the 21st century: a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09710-w
title: Clinical teaching models share common design features: structured stepwise approaches, learner-centred instruction, active participation, feedback, and clinical reasoning promotion
description: Across the eight mapped models, the review identifies a recurring set of design features: "structured stepwise approaches, learner-centred instruction, active participation, feedback, and the promotion of clinical reasoning and competency development." The pattern operates as a design template for clinical teaching sessions: a defined step sequence guides the encounter, the learner is placed in an active role, and feedback and reasoning prompts are embedded within routine patient care. Most models additionally aim to improve teaching effectiveness, diagnostic accuracy, and learner engagement through experiential and reflective learning.
requirements: Implementation requires clinical educators who can deliver the structured steps and provide feedback within real clinical encounters
constraints: The review notes most models aim to improve teaching effectiveness, diagnostic accuracy, and learner engagement, but does not report outcome evidence for the pattern itself
target_learners: healthcare trainees in medicine, nursing, midwifery, and allied health disciplines
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning
competency development
learner engagement
examples: OMP operationalizes the pattern with five microteaching skills (get a commitment, probe for supporting evidence, teach general rules, reinforce what is done well, correct errors) within brief clinical encounters

article_title: Effectiveness of technology-enhanced learning in neuroanatomy education among health professionals - a systematic review.
citation: K Anniesmitha, Rao K G Mohandas, Aithal P Ashwini, Bandekar Nikita N., Mandal Tatiyana, George Bincy M. (2026). Effectiveness of technology-enhanced learning in neuroanatomy education among health professionals - a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09764-w
title: Integrate technology-enhanced learning with, rather than as a replacement for, traditional anatomy teaching
description: The review concludes that technology-enhanced learning works best as a complement to conventional neuroanatomy teaching rather than a substitute for it. It states that "technology-enhanced learning is most effective when integrated with, rather than used as a replacement for, traditional anatomy teaching approaches", grounding this in engagement gains alongside inconsistent objective knowledge outcomes.
requirements: Traditional neuroanatomy teaching environments (e.g., didactic lectures, cadaveric dissection) remain available as comparators or anchors alongside the technology-enhanced component.
constraints: The evidence base was restricted to randomised controlled trials and driven from undergraduate medical student populations, which the review states may limit generalisability.
Considerable heterogeneity in intervention types, pedagogical approaches and outcome measures limits the ability to draw generalised conclusions.
target_learning_goals: Neuroanatomical knowledge and spatial understanding of complex three-dimensional brain structures
examples: Across the nine included RCTs, control groups were generally exposed to traditional neuroanatomy educational environments while intervention groups used 3D visualisation, VR, stereoscopic lectures or AR tools.

article_title: Effect of classroom physical activity breaks on learning behaviors and academic achievements in university students: a systematic review.
citation: Deng Qianting; Wu Chongyun; Yang Luodan. (2026). Effect of classroom physical activity breaks on learning behaviors and academic achievements in university students: a systematic review. Int J Behav Nutr Phys Act. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12966-026-01936-7
title: Effort-recovery and physiological mechanisms account for effects of classroom activity breaks on learning
description: The review explains the benefits of activity breaks via the effort-recovery model, which 'emphasizes the dynamic and reversible nature of fatigue' alleviated by restorative activities, plus proposed physiological mechanisms: BDNF upregulation supporting synaptic plasticity and memory consolidation, acute increases in arousal and alertness, enhanced neurotransmitter dynamics (dopamine, norepinephrine, serotonin), reduced sympathetic activity with enhanced parasympathetic modulation, and improved executive function and brain network connectivity.
requirements: Proposed to operate when task demands are alleviated by restorative activities such as appropriate rest or physical exercise
constraints: The review presents these mechanisms as proposed explanations, not as directly tested within the included studies
target_learning_goals: sustained attention
classroom engagement
academic emotions
academic performance
examples: The review cites evidence that structured exercise breaks boosted vitality with effects sustained up to 20 min, while another study found emotional improvements diminishing within 30 min.

article_title: The Effectiveness of Simulation-Based Versus Patient-Based Clinical Education in Nursing: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
citation: Prothero, L., Abdulmohdi, N., Shaw, S., Edmonds, M., and Meads, C. (2026). The Effectiveness of Simulation‐Based Versus Patient‐Based Clinical Education in Nursing: A Systematic Review and Meta‐Analysis. Nursing Open 13, no. 9: e70689. https://doi.org/10.1002/nop2.70689
title: Future simulation-versus-patient-based evaluations should also measure clinical and patient-based outcomes
description: This principle states that comparisons of simulation-based education with patient-based clinical teaching should extend beyond student assessments to clinical and patient outcomes, because the review found "No studies assessed patient‐based clinical outcomes, patient acceptability of nursing care given or staff resource time for teaching of the students." Without such measures, equivalence in nursing competency cannot establish equivalence in care quality. The review also notes none of the studies described whether simulation teaching improved patient care.
requirements: Comparative designs with concurrent comparators and objectively assessed outcomes for both groups
constraints: Current evidence base contains no measured patient-based clinical outcomes, patient acceptability, or staff resource time
target_learning_goals: clinical skills and competencies in patient care
examples: The review's included studies used exams, OSCEs, knowledge tests, externally rated performance scores and clinical placement grades as outcome measures

article_title: Metacognitive regulation in physical therapists' clinical reasoning: a scoping review.
citation: Perdrix Yannick, Nael Jérémy, Dionne Eric, Pinsault Nicolas. (2026). Metacognitive regulation in physical therapists’ clinical reasoning: a scoping review. International Journal of Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13563282/
title: Integrative model of metacognitive regulation in physical therapists' clinical reasoning structured around five key characteristics
description: The review creates an integrative model synthesizing the relationships between the characteristics of metacognitive regulation (MR) during physical therapy clinical reasoning. The article states: "We therefore structured the results of the nature of metacognitive regulation around five key characteristics: the types, the timing, the tasks, the focals and the interactions." Type covers self-observation, self-judgment and self-reaction; timing covers concurrent or retrospective and pre-, during- or post-task; task covers cognitive, psychomotor, emotional, communicational or global management; focal is "the analysis grid with which metacognitive regulation is achieved"; and interaction covers the persons in interaction during MR. The model is presented as a comprehensive lens for educational and clinical settings.
requirements: Applies to task-dependent metacognitive regulation in clinical reasoning contexts; only task-dependent activities were considered in the review
constraints: Developed from a qualitative synthesis of 36 studies; the authors state further empirical research is needed to test its applicability in educational and clinical settings
target_learning_goals: Clinical reasoning
Metacognitive regulation
Reflective practice
examples: The article's Example 2: a PT student one week after placement, in a professional-practices workshop with two other students, recalls gestures performed and asks whether he attended to the patient's reactions in order to adjust the intensity of his gestures
key_sources: Perdrix Yannick, Nael Jérémy, Dionne Eric, Pinsault Nicolas. (2026). Metacognitive regulation in physical therapists’ clinical reasoning: a scoping review. International Journal of Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13563282/

article_title: Metacognitive regulation in physical therapists' clinical reasoning: a scoping review.
citation: Perdrix Yannick, Nael Jérémy, Dionne Eric, Pinsault Nicolas. (2026). Metacognitive regulation in physical therapists’ clinical reasoning: a scoping review. International Journal of Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13563282/
title: Four overarching purposes of metacognitive regulation in PT clinical reasoning: pedagogical, clinical, professional developmental and sociopolitical
description: Beyond the expected learning and quality-of-care purposes, inductive analysis organized the reported purposes of metacognitive regulation into four categories. The article states: "This review identifies four primary purposes of MR engagement: pedagogical (learning and consolidation), clinical (adaptation and safety), professional developmental (identity and responsibility), and sociopolitical (emancipation and transformation)." The pedagogical purpose positions MR as "a lever for learning" supporting clinical reasoning development; the clinical purpose concerns adjusting reasoning in real time to improve safety, quality and equity of care; the professional developmental purpose links MR to identity formation and epistemic vigilance; and the sociopolitical purpose is framed as a "critical emancipatory function of MR". The data suggest the four purposes are not mutually exclusive but often interwoven.
requirements: Derived from synthesis of reported purposes in the included literature on PT clinical reasoning
constraints: The first two purposes were expected from prior codes; the sociopolitical purpose emerged inductively and the review is descriptive, not prescriptive
target_learning_goals: Clinical reasoning development
Professional identity formation
Equity in care
examples: The article notes that metacognitive training may simultaneously reinforce professional identity and ethical sensitivity, and reflective peer interactions could contribute to all four purposes depending on context
key_sources: Perdrix Yannick, Nael Jérémy, Dionne Eric, Pinsault Nicolas. (2026). Metacognitive regulation in physical therapists’ clinical reasoning: a scoping review. International Journal of Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13563282/

article_title: Metacognitive regulation in physical therapists' clinical reasoning: a scoping review.
citation: Perdrix Yannick, Nael Jérémy, Dionne Eric, Pinsault Nicolas. (2026). Metacognitive regulation in physical therapists’ clinical reasoning: a scoping review. International Journal of Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13563282/
title: Existing assessment methods for MR in PT clinical reasoning: qualitative scored reflections and quantitative calibration/certainty measurement
description: The review identified only four studies assessing MR in PT clinical reasoning, organized into two categories. Qualitative-data-based assessments score student data from placement situations (peer blogging, a critical reflection assessment task marked out of 100, a guided personal reflective report worth 20% of the placement mark). One study quantifies MR by measuring calibration — "the correlation between performance judgment and actual performance" — and certainty, defined as "a subjective estimate of expected performance", via prediction and postdiction sections on assignments. The article concludes that "the proposals remain much more limited than for other professions" and none reported a qualitative or psychometric evaluation of their method.
requirements: Assessment must be task-dependent; five self-questionnaire-based articles were excluded on this ground
constraints: None of the four studies reported a qualitative or psychometric evaluation; communication was not specifically addressed by any method
target_learners: Physical therapy students on clinical placements
target_learning_goals: Self-assessment of clinical reasoning
Calibration of performance judgments
examples: The critical reflection assessment task based on placement situations, marked out of 100 with subjective markers

article_title: Efficacy of Hand Gestures and the Hand as Foot Teaching Method Compared to Traditional Methods in Medical and Dental Education: A Scoping Review.
citation: Vats Shivangi, Thomas Manuel S., Jathanna Vinod. (2026). Efficacy of Hand Gestures and the Hand as Foot Teaching Method Compared to Traditional Methods in Medical and Dental Education: A Scoping Review. Journal of Dental Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/jdd.70190
title: Shared pedagogical framework of gestural teaching methods: gestural simulation, analogical induction, and active engagement making the invisible visible
description: The review proposes that Air Anatomy, the Hand as Foot method, and non-verbal communication techniques rest on one pedagogical philosophy: "using the body as a dynamic, interactive tool to make the invisible visible." Its core principle is "turning abstract information into concrete, physical experiences." The framework identifies shared mechanisms — gestural simulation of anatomical structures, analogical induction by comparing familiar with complex systems, and enhanced engagement that transforms passive learning into an active, participatory process.
requirements: An educator who can shape and manipulate the hand to model the target anatomical structures or concepts during instruction
constraints: Hand as Foot is described as focusing on a specific analogy, upper limb for lower limb, while Air Anatomy is a broader application of gestural simulation
target_learners: medical and dental undergraduate and postgraduate students
target_learning_goals: spatial understanding of anatomy and complex physiological concepts
comprehension and retention of difficult knowledge points
examples: The review notes Hand as Foot might use "a clenched fist to represent the femoral head," while Air Anatomy might use cupped hands to "grip" the thalamus
key_sources: Vats Shivangi, Thomas Manuel S., Jathanna Vinod. (2026). Efficacy of Hand Gestures and the Hand as Foot Teaching Method Compared to Traditional Methods in Medical and Dental Education: A Scoping Review. Journal of Dental Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/jdd.70190

article_title: Efficacy of Hand Gestures and the Hand as Foot Teaching Method Compared to Traditional Methods in Medical and Dental Education: A Scoping Review.
citation: Vats Shivangi, Thomas Manuel S., Jathanna Vinod. (2026). Efficacy of Hand Gestures and the Hand as Foot Teaching Method Compared to Traditional Methods in Medical and Dental Education: A Scoping Review. Journal of Dental Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/jdd.70190
title: Use low-cost, equipment-free gestural teaching methods in educational settings with limited resources
description: The review presents Air Anatomy, the Hand as Foot method, and the pen and palm model as accessible, "no‐cost" or low-cost alternatives to expensive high-tech teaching aids like virtual reality or 3D models. Because "they can be implemented without special equipment," these techniques are "particularly valuable in educational settings with limited resources." In regions with limited medical education resources, an image-based teaching method can address the scarcity and simplicity of traditional teaching aids while also reducing teaching expenses.
requirements: An educator able to perform the gestural demonstrations; no special equipment
constraints: Evidence base is small: the review notes a scarcity of studies directly comparing the Hand as Foot method with conventional teaching, making relative effectiveness difficult to conclude
target_learners: medical and dental undergraduate and postgraduate students in resource-limited settings
target_learning_goals: understanding of anatomy and complex physiological concepts
examples: The review describes Hand as Foot in dentistry as a cost-effective, low-tech complement to extracted teeth, wax carving, and digital models

title: GRAVEN database of hand-gesture representations of neuroanatomy
description: GRAVEN is a database developed for teaching that applies gestures to represent the neurosurgical approach's blood vessels and nerves, containing pictures of hand gestures representing anatomy, nerves, and vessels. The review states that the "development of databases, such as GRAVEN, which include hand gesture representations of neuroanatomy, offers an accessible and cost‐effective way to supplement traditional teaching methods." These resources can be used for both in-class learning and self-study, providing flexibility and reinforcing learning outside the classroom.
requirements: Used in addition to traditional teaching techniques
constraints: Its studied use was limited to undergraduate students, excluding neurosurgery residents
target_learners: medical undergraduates studying neuroanatomy or neurosurgical approaches
target_learning_goals: recognition of neuroanatomical structures, nerves and vessels
examples: The review reports students using GRAVEN combined with traditional techniques showed significant improvement in academic performance

article_title: Effects of High-Fidelity Simulation Training on Learning Outcomes and Satisfaction for Practising Registered Nurses: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
citation: Zhou Jie, Zhang Guowen, Song Peige, Liaw Sok Ying, Luk Tzu Tsun. (2026). Effects of High‐Fidelity Simulation Training on Learning Outcomes and Satisfaction for Practising Registered Nurses: A Systematic Review and Meta‐Analysis. Journal of Clinical Nursing. https://doi.org/10.1111/jocn.70206
title: NLN Jeffries Simulation Theory outcome framework (knowledge, skills, self-confidence, satisfaction)
description: The review organises its outcome synthesis using the NLN Jeffries Simulation Theory framework, under which simulation learning outcomes are categorised into four types. As the review states, "Following the NLN Jeffries Simulation Theory framework, the outcomes were categorised as knowledge acquisition, professional skills, self‐confidence and learning satisfaction". Each category was separately meta-analysed, allowing effects, heterogeneity and study-design differences to be examined per outcome.
requirements: Outcome measures must be assignable to one of the four framework categories, with instruments identified per study.
constraints: The framework's four categories do not cover all potential learning outcomes; the review notes it could not examine outcomes such as clinical judgement and communication not reported in the reviewed studies.
target_learning_goals: Knowledge acquisition
Professional/clinical skills
Self-confidence
Learning satisfaction
examples: The review applied the framework to pool outcomes across eight studies, with data extracted including HFS design details (scenario, prebriefing, simulation and debriefing durations, manikin brand).

Effects of High‐Fidelity Simulation Training on Learning Outcomes and Satisfaction for Practising Registered Nurses: A Systematic Review and Meta‐Analysis. citation: Casimiro Urcos CN, Casimiro Urcos WH, Alberca Pintado NE, Ostos Miraval RM, Carrasco Muñoz MA, Piñas Rivera LC. (2026). Pedagogical Innovation in Digital Environments: A Systematic Review Focused on Higher Education. F1000Research 15:522. https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.176682.1
title: Three-category organizing framework: pedagogical innovations, digital environments, and higher-education experiences/results
description: The review organizes the literature into three analytic categories: pedagogical innovations (active methodologies such as PBL, flipped learning, collaborative learning), digital environments (evolving from LMS to instructional ecosystems with simulation, analytics, and collaboration layers), and higher-education experiences and results. Studies were coded to one of these categories, with the review aiming to "characterize how these categories have been investigated" through contributions, limitations, and results.
requirements: Studies must address at least one of the three analysis categories in a university context with explicit methodological design, defined sample, peer review, and accessible data
constraints: Excluded reviews, grey literature, articles without a specific sample or with unmitigated methodological bias
target_learning_goals: pedagogical innovation in digital environments
contributions and limitations of technology-mediated higher education
examples: The 39 included studies in Table 2 were classified as 1 = Pedagogical innovations; 2 = Digital environments; 3 = Higher education – experiences/outcomes

article_title: How do doctors build knowledge around obstetric emergencies? A scoping review.
citation: Stelling H, Burford B, Park S, McGurk L, Brown M E L, Vance G. (2026). How do doctors build knowledge around obstetric emergencies? A scoping review. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2026-119725
title: Three interconnected domains — training, context and experience — organise how O&G doctors build knowledge around obstetric emergencies
description: The review's organising framework maps knowledge-building for obstetric emergencies onto three domains: "training reflected structured and formal approaches to knowledge acquisition; context encompassed both local workplace realities and wider systemic influences; and experience captured knowledge developed through clinical encounters". Knowledge flows within and across domains through an interplay of knowledge "received" from published sources, colleagues, educators and patients and knowledge "embodied" through personal clinical experience and practice. The framework was generated inductively from 369 included sources and used to structure the synthesis and its recommendations.
requirements: Applicable to understanding how doctors (across all grades) acquire, develop and apply knowledge relevant to obstetric emergencies, spanning formal education, workplace conditions and clinical encounters
constraints: Developed for obstetric emergency knowledge-building among O&G doctors; the review notes barriers were considerably more frequently reported than enablers across these domains
target_learners: Obstetrics and gynaecology doctors across all grades
target_learning_goals: Building and applying knowledge for managing obstetric emergencies
examples: The synthesis of 369 papers was organised by thematic allocation across the training, context and experience domains (online supplemental file S5)

The Journal of Nursing Research. https://doi.org/10.1097/jnr.0000000000000772
title: Select gamification approaches by matching format to educational objectives, institutional technological capabilities, and implementation context
description: The review concludes that gamified learning's effectiveness depends critically on design characteristics, implementation quality, and alignment with objectives, so educators should "match formats to objectives, invest in faculty development, and pilot before scaling". Serious games are recommended where consistent knowledge gains are sought, gamified simulation for procedural skills, and scalable web/mobile formats in resource-constrained settings provided mastery goals, timely feedback, and assessment alignment are built in. The principle operationalizes the review's subgroup findings as implementation guidance for nursing curricula.

constraints: Formal statistical testing of between-subgroup differences was not conducted, so category-level guidance requires cautious interpretation

Clinical skill performance
Attitudes toward clinical skill learning

article_title: The impact of the learner role in healthcare simulation-based education on learning outcomes: a systematic review.
citation: Amechghal A, Naciri A, Takhdat K, Loubbairi S, Mellouki A, Lahlou L, Nassik H. (2026). The impact of the learner role in healthcare simulation-based education on learning outcomes: a systematic review. J Educ Eval Health Prof. https://doi.org/10.3352/jeehp.2026.23.24
title: Observational experiential learning framework integrating experiential, social, and social cognitive theories to support observer roles in simulation
description: The review describes Johnson's observational experiential learning framework, which "integrates experiential learning, social learning, and social cognitive theories to support the use of the observer role during SBE." It posits that learners "can initially acquire knowledge through either active participation or structured observation and subsequently transform this experience into clinical skills through reflection and conceptualization during debriefing." The framework is offered to bridge the gap left by the field's traditional reliance on Kolb's experiential learning theory and the underexplored Bandura social cognitive theory of vicarious learning.
requirements: Requires structured observation and reflective debriefing through which observed experience is transformed into learning
constraints: Bandura's social cognitive theory underpinning observational and vicarious learning "remains underexplored in the simulation literature" per the review
target_learners: Health professions students and practitioners in simulation-based education
target_learning_goals: Clinical knowledge and skill acquisition through observation and reflection
examples: Three included studies (Johnson 2019; Ham et al. 2024) explicitly cited Johnson's observational experiential learning framework alongside Kolb and Bandura

citation: Amechghal A, Naciri A, Takhdat K, Loubbairi S, Mellouki A, Lahlou L, Nassik H. (2026). The impact of the learner role in healthcare simulation-based education on learning outcomes: a systematic review. J Educ Eval Health Prof. https://doi.org/10.3352/jeehp.2026.23.24
title: Design observer roles as intentional pedagogy with defined learning objectives, validated observation tools, and active debriefing involvement
description: The review reframes the observer role "from a logistical compromise to an intentional teaching strategy," recommending that "observer roles should therefore be designed with defined learning objectives, validated observation tools, and active involvement in debriefing." It supports this with evidence that directed observation supported by checklists or role-specific forms may enhance active watching and listening, and that studies using structured observer tools reported outcomes as good as, or better than, those of active participants.
requirements: Faculty development and audiovisual infrastructure to support high-quality observer engagement
Defined learning objectives, validated observation tools, and active observer involvement in debriefing
constraints: Formal equivalence between roles has not been established; evidence concentrated in nursing programs in high-income countries
target_learners: Health professions students and trainees in simulation-based education
target_learning_goals: Knowledge, skills, and attitudinal outcomes comparable to active participation
examples: All 15 included studies involved observers in shared debriefing, and 7 studies used directed observation with checklists or role-specific forms

title: Preparedness for practice as a construct encompassing professional competence plus readiness to function independently across diverse work environments
description: The review frames preparedness for practice in the health professions as extending beyond clinical competence. It states that "The concept of 'preparedness for practice' in the health professions encompasses not only professional competence but also readiness to function independently across diverse work environments." Accordingly, being prepared "encompasses a wide range of cognitive and behavioural attributes to ensure a smooth transition" from university into the work environment, which the review operationalises through attributes such as clinical skills, communication, cultural competence, adaptability, and resilience.
requirements: Education must develop cognitive and behavioural attributes alongside clinical competence to support the transition into practice
constraints: The review's synthesis focuses on general clinical readiness; only two included studies addressed alternative settings or independent roles
target_learning_goals: Clinical competence
Independent functioning across diverse work environments
Professional behaviours

It reports that "assessment is mostly dominated by the use of instruments such as multiple choice questions and description questions and assessment methods in the form of tests or written or electronic-based tasks," with rubrics, inventories, concept maps, questionnaires, checklists, interviews, and peer/self-assessment also represented. article_title: Objective technical skills assessment in laparoscopic cholecystectomy: a systematic review of manual, kinematic, and AI-based tools.
citation: Mainwaring Elizabeth M. A., Guidozzi Nadia, James Jonnie P., Pantling Jai, Menon Nainika, Salem Riadh, Markar Sheraz R. (2026). Objective technical skills assessment in laparoscopic cholecystectomy: a systematic review of manual, kinematic, and AI-based tools. Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-026-13309-z
title: Messick's unified construct-validity framework as a six-domain framework for appraising surgical assessment tools
description: Messick's unified theory of validity, as applied in this review, appraises assessment quality across six domains: "content, response process, internal structure, generalisability, relations to other variables, and consequences". The review graded each domain as reported-limited, reported-partial, reported-strong, or not reported, and used the framework to compare manual, kinematic, and AI-based tools within a common structure. It was chosen to enable multidimensional evaluation beyond isolated performance metrics, which the authors argue is particularly important for AI systems where internal accuracy may be robust while educational and safety implications remain untested.
requirements: Application requires study-level reporting on each validity domain; the review supplemented it with MERSQI for methodological quality and COSMIN/QUADAS-2 for risk of bias.
constraints: The review states domain ratings aggregated at tool level may favour tools evaluated in single studies, whose performance has not been challenged across multiple cohorts or settings.
target_learning_goals: technical operative skill assessment
competency-based surgical training progression
examples: The review applied the framework to 46 manual study-tool evaluations, 6 kinematic systems, and 13 AI systems, summarising tool-level ratings in Tables 2, 4, and 6.

article_title: Evaluating the impact of simulation on patient outcomes in pediatric and neonatal critical care: a systematic review and critical appraisal of the evidence.
citation: Zanin A, Poletto E, Mencia S, Gawronski O, Jourdain G. (2026). Evaluating the impact of simulation on patient outcomes in pediatric and neonatal critical care: a systematic review and critical appraisal of the evidence. European Journal of Pediatrics 185(5):302. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00431-026-06925-3
title: Kirkpatrick four-level model with the Level 4a/4b distinction as a framework for evaluating simulation-based education
description: The review organizes its evidence synthesis around the Kirkpatrick model, "a widely used four-level framework for evaluating the effectiveness of educational interventions, including SBE". Level 1 assesses reaction, Level 2 learning, Level 3 behavior in clinical practice, and Level 4 results; the review adopts the subdivision of Level 4 into 4a (system-level process metrics such as response times and protocol adherence) and 4b (direct patient outcomes such as mortality and complications). This distinction structures its primary outcome coding and thematic synthesis.
requirements: Outcomes must be coded as 4a or 4b according to whether the primary metric is a process-based system measure or a direct patient health indicator
constraints: The review notes a fundamental challenge lies in capturing the complex transfer of learning from simulation environments to real-world clinical practice
target_learners: healthcare providers and trainees in pediatric and neonatal intensive care
target_learning_goals: clinical skills and teamwork in resuscitation and critical care procedures
examples: The review mapped each included study's outcomes to levels L1, L2, L3, 4a, and 4b in a structured table

citation: Zanin A, Poletto E, Mencia S, Gawronski O, Jourdain G. (2026). Evaluating the impact of simulation on patient outcomes in pediatric and neonatal critical care: a systematic review and critical appraisal of the evidence. European Journal of Pediatrics 185(5):302. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00431-026-06925-3
title: Five-element model of influences determining simulation's clinical impact (SBR model)
description: To explain why simulation outcomes diverge across contexts, the review introduces a model asserting that success depends on "the alignment of five interconnected elements": (1) individual competence (technical/nontechnical skills); (2) team dynamics (communication and leadership); (3) institutional culture (psychological safety and administrative support); (4) physical resources (equipment and staffing availability); and (5) system-level integration (adherence to national or local protocols). The model explains why single-center studies, which can more easily align the five layers, often show more significant results than multicenter trials.
requirements: Future simulation-based research designs must account for the synergy between these five elements to bridge the gap between training and patient-level results
constraints: The model is introduced by the authors to illustrate contextual divergence; it is an interpretive framework, not a tested result
target_learners: healthcare providers and trainees in pediatric and neonatal intensive care
target_learning_goals: translating simulation-acquired competence into real-world clinical practice
examples: The review maps the model onto its research recommendations, arguing future studies should move beyond Level 1 and 2 outcomes

article_title: Simulation-Based Education to Support Nurses' Critical Thinking in Delirium Recognition: A Scoping Review.
citation: EL Hussein Mohamed Toufic, Sheehan Dawson S., Hirst Sandra. (2026). Simulation‐Based Education to Support Nurses' Critical Thinking in Delirium Recognition: A Scoping Review. Journal of Advanced Nursing. https://doi.org/10.1111/jan.70640
title: Four interrelated domains of critical thinking developed through simulation for delirium recognition
description: The review organizes its synthesis around four interrelated domains through which simulation-based education develops critical thinking: cue recognition, clinical reasoning, metacognitive reflection, and communication and advocacy. The authors state that "simulation‐based education supports the development of critical thinking through four interrelated domains", each contributing uniquely to detecting, interpreting and acting on subtle, fluctuating delirium cues. The framework is anchored in Facione's critical-thinking definition, Tanner's Clinical Judgement Model stages of noticing, interpreting, responding and reflecting, and Kolb's experiential learning theory, positioning clinical reasoning as "not a linear sequence but an adaptive, context‐dependent skill".
requirements: Structured pre-briefings and debriefings, deliberate cue exposure and opportunities for reflection on diagnostic reasoning, emotional regulation and communication, per the review's implications section.
constraints: No included study directly measured critical thinking as an explicit outcome; the domains are extrapolated from consistent improvements in reasoning, reflection and decision accuracy.
target_learners: Practicing registered nurses in adult clinical settings
target_learning_goals: Delirium recognition
critical thinking
clinical judgement
interprofessional communication
examples: The review maps SP/OSCE simulations to cue recognition and screening accuracy, VR and theatre-based modalities to empathy and reflection, and multimodal programmes to documentation and communication behaviour change.

article_title: Mapping the evidence on public health competency assessment strategies in undergraduate medical education: a scoping review.
citation: Hernández Rincón Erwin Hernando, González Garcés Mariana, Montoya Jerónimo Cárdenas, Fernández Valeria Concha, Torres Mario Andrés Torres, Vargas Villafañe Nicolle Valeria, Chaves Natalia Castaño. (2026). Mapping the evidence on public health competency assessment strategies in undergraduate medical education: a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09976-0
title: Structural typology of public health competency assessment strategies organised into nine evaluative domains
description: The review proposes a structural typology (Table 3) that classifies assessment strategies into evaluative domains rather than by individual instruments. As the review states, "The analysis allowed identification of a structural typology of assessment strategies that transcends classification by individual instruments, organising itself into evaluative domains that reflect different levels of integration between competency, context and method (Table 3)." The domains span experiential evaluation in real-world contexts, evaluation in clinical settings, structured curricular evaluation, assessment of equity and social determinants competencies, structured simulation, technology-mediated assessment, longitudinal assessment, institutional/systems evaluation, and conceptual/normative development. Each domain pairs a central evaluative logic with representative strategies, competency level, context, instruments and educational contribution.
requirements: Applies to assessment of public health competencies in undergraduate medical education as mapped in the included studies
constraints: The typology is an inductive conceptual classification grounded in the 30 included studies, not a validated assessment framework
target_learning_goals: Public health competencies including epidemiology, health promotion, social determinants of health, community engagement and health advocacy
examples: The review maps community projects, service learning, fieldwork and patient-based learning into the experiential real-world domain, citing studies [10–13, 19, 26, 27, 33]

citation: Hernández Rincón Erwin Hernando, González Garcés Mariana, Montoya Jerónimo Cárdenas, Fernández Valeria Concha, Torres Mario Andrés Torres, Vargas Villafañe Nicolle Valeria, Chaves Natalia Castaño. (2026). Mapping the evidence on public health competency assessment strategies in undergraduate medical education: a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09976-0
title: Continuum of evaluative complexity spanning ten levels from cognitive assessment to normative/consensus assessment
description: The review establishes a continuum of evaluative complexity (Table 4) ranking assessment approaches from knowledge-centred measurement to assessment at educational-systems level. As printed: "Analysis of the identified strategies allowed establishment of a continuum of evaluative complexity, from approaches centred on knowledge to integrated models of assessment in real contexts (Table 4)." The ten levels run from cognitive assessment (low complexity), through skills, attitudinal, real performance-based, applied clinical, programmatic, population/institutional, and validated-instrument assessment, to longitudinal assessment and normative/consensus assessment. Levels were assigned by degree of contextual authenticity, integration of multiple competency domains, educational scope and proximity to real-world professional performance.
requirements: Intended to facilitate understanding of the progressive sophistication of assessment strategies in undergraduate medical education
constraints: Inductively derived from the included studies and explicitly "should not be interpreted as a validated assessment framework"; implementation of the highest-level consensus approaches remains limited
target_learning_goals: Public health competencies including knowledge, skills, attitudes and integrated applied competencies
examples: The review places examinations and questionnaires at Level 1, OSCEs and standardised patients at Level 2, and community projects, service learning and clinical rotations at Levels 4–5

article_title: Comparative effects of physical education teaching models on motor skill development in school-aged children and adolescents: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.
citation: Tian Qi, Liu Yaowen, Wang Ziyu, Qin Gang. (2026). Comparative effects of physical education teaching models on motor skill development in school-aged children and adolescents: a systematic review and network meta-analysis. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2026.1905122
title: Select and implement structured physical education teaching models according to student age, learning objectives, sport content, and teaching context
description: Because the network meta-analysis found no definitive hierarchy of teaching models — rankings shifted with outcome definition, age, and study inclusion — the authors recommend that model choice be made contextually rather than by universal ranking. They state: "In practice, physical education teachers should select and implement structured teaching models according to student age, learning objectives, sport content, and teaching context." The principle treats P-score orderings as conditional effect estimates rather than proof of universal superiority.
requirements: Structured teaching models must be implemented within school physical education contexts, with decisions matched to the available class time, student numbers, curriculum sequence, and evaluation processes the article describes
constraints: The article states the P-score ordering should be interpreted as conditional effect estimates, not proof that one teaching model is universally superior; significant inconsistency, sparse comparisons, and risk of bias preclude a definitive hierarchy
target_learners: School-aged children and adolescents in school physical education
target_learning_goals: Motor skill development, including motor competence, sport-specific technical execution, and game performance
examples: The 13-study under-18 primary network found only Hybrid TGfU-SE, Nonlinear, and Functional games had confidence intervals excluding zero versus Control, while Game-based, Sport Education, TGfU, Traditional, and Linear estimates were imprecise

Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2026.1905122
title: Nine-node harmonized taxonomy of physical education teaching models for network meta-analysis
description: The review harmonizes study-level intervention labels into a connected treatment network of nine nodes: "Control, Functional games, Game-based, Hybrid TGfU-SE, Linear, Nonlinear, Sport Education, TGfU, and Traditional." Labels were mapped "according to instructional logic rather than name alone" — e.g., classical, technical, and direct-instruction labels were assigned to Traditional or Linear by degree of explicit technical sequencing, and constraint-led approaches to Nonlinear. Control denotes minimal or regular PE; Traditional denotes structured teacher-centered instruction; Cooperative appears only in the broad sensitivity network. The harmonization was intended to preserve interpretability and network connectivity rather than erase pedagogical nuance.
requirements: Each study must provide an independent between-pedagogy contrast and sufficient quantitative information to derive a standardized mean difference within a connected treatment network
constraints: Studies with mixed cognitive-psychomotor, visual-motor integration, or cognitive-visual processing outcomes, university participants, or club settings were restricted to the broad sensitivity network; Cooperative was retained only in the broad network
target_learners: School-aged children and adolescents in school physical education
target_learning_goals: Motor skill development and motor-related performance outcomes
examples: Hybrid TGfU-SE and Functional games were kept as distinct nodes because their intervention structures were identifiable and connected

description: This principle holds that the educational value of technology-enhanced simulation resources depends on their pedagogical integration: "Simulation and immersive tools are more likely to support learning when they are embedded in structured curricula, facilitated by trained faculty, supported by deliberate practice and assessed through competency-based criteria." constraints: The review presents these as implementation hypotheses derived from indirect evidence and one direct study, not a finalized curriculum guideline
target_learners: Health sciences students in surgical training, including Surgical Instrumentation students
target_learning_goals: Psychomotor skill acquisition, procedural familiarity, learner confidence, safe transition to clinical practice
examples: The review recommends that programs define learning outcomes, ensure faculty training, combine low-cost and technology-enhanced resources when appropriate, use checklists or objective metrics, and evaluate both perception and performance.

title: Design pedagogy, not just technology: the benefit of combining laboratory modalities depends on complementary information
description: The review concludes that the advantage of virtual laboratories comes from the quality of the pedagogical design around them rather than from the technology itself. Modalities should be combined so that each contributes information the other cannot: real experiments supply the phenomenological referent while simulations supply representations physical apparatus cannot show, such as force vectors and dynamic graphs. The review states "the benefit depends on whether the combined components contribute complementary information, not simply more of it", so adding media without added information yields no gain.
requirements: The combined components must contribute complementary information rather than redundant content
Guidance must be matched to learners' prior knowledge to avoid adding cognitive load
constraints: One documented exception: virtual experiments plus video showed no advantage over virtual experiments alone
Skill outcomes resting on instrument handling, such as graph reading, are not fully replaceable by simulation
target_learners: Physics learners in secondary and higher education
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding
Inquiry skills
Motivation and self-efficacy
examples: Ben Ouahi et al. (2024) reported the largest electricity gains for a real-plus-virtual combination within a 5E cycle across 166 students, and Mihret et al. (2023) found a blended modality most effective for understanding the nature of science

citation: Esanu V, Marziali E, Gaspar O, Agoston S, Carciumaru T, Stoia A, Paun C, Colosi HA, Dindelegan G, Dirven C, Meling TR, Vasilic D, Volovici V. (2026). Microvascular errors of technique: a systematic review. Acta Neurochirurgica. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00701-026-06810-w
title: Validated error-assessment scoring tools for microsurgical training (ALI, MARS10, OSATS, GRS)
description: The review identifies validated scoring systems that quantify microsurgical errors and structure feedback: the Anastomosis Lapse Index (ALI), the Microsurgical Anastomosis Rating Scale (MARS10), the Global Rating Scale (GRS), and OSATS. It reports: "Several validated scoring tools (e.g., ALI, MARS10, OSATS) were identified as effective in quantifying errors and guiding feedback in training settings." OSATS comprises a task-specific checklist and a Global Rating Scale, evaluated with 20 surgeons on a chicken thigh model.
requirements: Errors must be clearly described and linked to outcomes such as anastomotic patency for a tool to qualify
constraints: The review notes the rat microvascular model may tolerate certain technical errors, raising concerns about ALI's sensitivity; OSATS is not itself a microsurgical error scale
target_learning_goals: objective evaluation of microsurgical skill acquisition and error recognition
examples: Nimmons et al.'s OSATS microvascular arterial anastomosis task lists 14 checked skills, from needle loading to tissue approximation

article_title: The Impact of Early Clinical Exposure on Competency Development in Dental Students: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
citation: Pang Xuefei, Wang Huilin, Li Jinggui, Gui Haijun, Cao Xia, Cai Ming. (2026). The Impact of Early Clinical Exposure on Competency Development in Dental Students: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. International Dental Journal. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.identj.2026.109483
title: Three-type taxonomy of early clinical exposure modalities
description: The article classifies ECE into three modalities defined by authenticity of interaction: real clinical interactions ("Students interact with real patients in authentic clinical settings"), simulated clinical interactions (simulated patients in "controllable, safe and repeatable" environments, e.g. standardised patients, OSCE, manikins), and virtual environment learning (digital interfaces "without direct interaction with a human"). The taxonomy structures the review's inclusion criteria and its subgroup analyses of differential effects by modality.
requirements: Studies must expose students to clinical environments and tasks before the traditional intensive clinical internship period to qualify as ECE
constraints: The classification rests on authenticity of interaction and task complexity as defined by the authors for dental education contexts
target_learners: dental students without prior clinical experience
target_learning_goals: clinical competency development across theoretical knowledge, clinical skills and self-efficacy
examples: Six included studies used virtual environments, 13 used simulated clinical interactions, and 8 used real clinical settings, as tabulated in the review's characteristics table

article_title: Profile of anatomy teachers of students in healthcare professions: a scoping review.
citation: Fevry Joanne, Fotsing Salomon, Merghem Meriem, Roberge Anne, Ramdani Rayan, Filion Isabelle, Domecq Marie-Cécile, Jalali Alireza. (2026). Profile of anatomy teachers of students in healthcare professions: a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08721-x
title: Anatomy teacher profile framework: academic background, professional training, disciplinary expertise and teaching responsibilities
description: This scoping review defines the profile of an anatomy teacher along four dimensions: the article states "the profile of an anatomy teacher is defined by their academic background, professional training, disciplinary expertise and teaching responsibilities." The framework structures the review's data extraction and synthesis, organizing findings on degrees, academic titles and contracts, teaching strategies, course content, and evaluation strategies across healthcare professions. It underpins the review's conclusion that no single profile exists.
requirements: Studies must describe or stratify the anatomy educator population in healthcare professions programs for the framework to apply
constraints: The review found no included study linking these profile dimensions to teaching or evaluation strategies
target_learners: anatomy educators in higher education health professions programs
target_learning_goals: effective teaching and assessment of human anatomy knowledge and skills
examples: The review charted degrees, academic titles, contracts, teaching strategies, content and evaluation strategies for 42 included studies using this framework
