article_title: Psychosocial factors associated with academic performance in medical students: a systematic review.
citation: Ríos Andrade Raúl, Peralta Ramírez Aziel Alejandro, Trujillo López Sergio. (2026). Psychosocial factors associated with academic performance in medical students: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08742-6
title: Biopsychosocial four-domain framework of psychosocial factors in medical student academic performance
description: The review organizes psychosocial factors using the biopsychosocial model originally proposed by Engel (1977), integrating psychological, social, and contextual dimensions relevant to medical education. It categorizes factors into four domains: affective symptoms (stress, anxiety, depression, distress, burnout); motivation and learning attitudes (intrinsic/extrinsic motivation, engagement, study habits); personality and trait-like characteristics (emotional intelligence, grit, resilience, coping styles); and social and environmental factors (perceived social support, socioeconomic disadvantage, learning environment, institutional climate). The framework frames academic achievement as resulting from "dynamic interactions between individual psychological functioning, social resources, and contextual demands."
requirements: Only studies evaluating one or more of these four domains in relation to academic performance were considered eligible.
constraints: The review states the predominance of cross-sectional designs and varied measurement tools precludes causal inference.
target_learning_goals: academic performance (GPA, examinations, licensing or OSCE scores)
key_sources: Ríos Andrade Raúl, Peralta Ramírez Aziel Alejandro, Trujillo López Sergio. (2026). Psychosocial factors associated with academic performance in medical students: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08742-6

article_title: Technology-based teaching to support health students' clinical skills in stroke recovery: a scoping review.
citation: Bower K, Scrivener K, Larkins S, Seaton C, Carlisle K. (2026). Technology-based teaching to support health students’ clinical skills in stroke recovery: a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08709-7
title: Blended learning as intentional integration of online and face-to-face learning opportunities
description: The review adopts Garrison and Kanuka's definition of blended learning as "the effective and intentional integration of online and face-to-face learning opportunities". It uses this framing to organise technology-based teaching for health students' stroke clinical skills, noting blended approaches in clinical placements have involved videoconferencing, blogging, chat rooms, social media and web-based resources. The review proposes a blended-learning approach could support student-resourced rural stroke recovery services.
requirements: Technology-based learning activities must be deliverable in less than 12 hours, synchronously or asynchronously, within a stroke-related clinical placement
Design should align with teaching and learning theories and defined student learning outcomes
constraints: Challenges are well-documented, predominantly the availability of information technology skills and infrastructure, particularly in under-resourced and rural locations
target_learners: Health students (medical, nursing, physiotherapy and allied health) on stroke-related clinical placements
target_learning_goals: Clinical skills for stroke recovery, including assessment, treatment planning, and communication with people with aphasia
examples: The review cites online education activities connecting rural placement students to external clinical educators, and wearable technology remotely connecting educators to nursing students for procedural task practice

article_title: Characterization of the learning environment for teaching pharmaceutical care: a scoping review.
citation: Ribeiro MAL, Hohenfeld DWA, Tavares TMA, Araújo-Neto FC, Mesquita AR, Brito GC, Lyra Jr DP. (2026). Characterization of the learning environment for teaching pharmaceutical care: a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08876-7
title: Five-component conceptualization of learning environments (personal, social, organizational, physical, virtual)
description: The review adopts a concept of learning environment, following Gruppen et al. (2018), that "Refers to experiences and personal perceptions, social interactions, culture, and organizational practice, and the physical and virtual settings in which learning occurs". It decomposes environments into five components: personal (student perceptions, growth, professional identity), social (relationships with faculty, administration and patients), organizational (policies, accreditation rules, curriculum resources, workload), physical (campuses, hospitals, clinics, community settings), and virtual (curriculum management tools, digital assistants, learning forums). The review uses this framework to classify the components identified in each included study (Table 4).
requirements: Studies must describe the environment in terms of the five components for classification under this framework
constraints: The review notes the absence of consensus on the definition of learning environment in the healthcare field limits multicenter research
target_learners: Pharmacy students in undergraduate and professional programs
target_learning_goals: Patient-centered pharmaceutical care competencies
examples: Table 4 classifies each included study's components; for example, Brown & Vosper (2013) was classified as spanning Personal, Social, Organizational, Physical, and Virtual components
key_sources: Ribeiro MAL, Hohenfeld DWA, Tavares TMA, Araújo-Neto FC, Mesquita AR, Brito GC, Lyra Jr DP. (2026). Characterization of the learning environment for teaching pharmaceutical care: a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08876-7

title: Student-centered active-methods pattern in pharmaceutical care teaching environments
description: The included studies' teaching environments reflect a transition from traditional teacher-centered models to student-centered pedagogical approaches using technological resources and active methods. The review reports that "Different methods were observed, and the most used were PBL (n = 2) and experience-based learning (n = 2)", alongside team-based learning, students as partners, competence-based learning, e-learning, and simulated activities. The pattern demands students be more active participants in the teaching and learning process.
requirements: Environments should explore the use of active methods
constraints: The review reports challenges in meeting the expectations of advanced students and the need for continuous innovation (e-learning study)
target_learning_goals: Pharmaceutical care competencies, clinical communication, dispensing skills, critical thinking
examples: Table 5 lists each study's strategy and main results, e.g., a PBL study where the "Prompts group overcame control group in all phases of problem solving"

article_title: Strategies for remediating clinical reasoning skill deficits in underperforming residents: a scoping review.
citation: Philip SJ, Cholifatul UF, Felicia CC, Nooreen A. (2026). Strategies for remediating clinical reasoning skill deficits in underperforming residents: a scoping review. J Educ Eval Health Prof. https://doi.org/10.3352/jeehp.2026.23.3
title: Daniel et al. clinical reasoning framework: seven domains grounded in illness script, dual-process, and cognitive load theory
description: The review adopts the clinical reasoning framework proposed by Daniel et al. as its conceptual foundation. The framework is grounded in illness script theory, dual-process theory, and cognitive load theory, and defines clinical reasoning as "a skill, process, or outcome wherein clinicians observe, collect, and interpret data to diagnose and treat patients." The construct is delineated into 7 domains: information gathering, hypothesis generation, problem representation, differential diagnosis, leading diagnosis, diagnostic justification, and management and treatment. The review uses these domains to align assessment and remediation with specific reasoning processes.
requirements: Educators must be able to identify precisely where within the reasoning process a learner's reasoning is breaking down for targeted intervention
constraints: The review notes that mapping specific remediation strategies to these domains remains challenging because several studies did not explicitly state the framework underpinning their interventions
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning for diagnosis and treatment
examples: The review aligns assessment methods with reasoning domains, noting think-aloud methods permit assessment across multiple clinical reasoning domains.
key_sources: Philip SJ, Cholifatul UF, Felicia CC, Nooreen A. (2026). Strategies for remediating clinical reasoning skill deficits in underperforming residents: a scoping review. J Educ Eval Health Prof. https://doi.org/10.3352/jeehp.2026.23.3

article_title: Strategies for remediating clinical reasoning skill deficits in underperforming residents: a scoping review.
citation: Philip SJ, Cholifatul UF, Felicia CC, Nooreen A. (2026). Strategies for remediating clinical reasoning skill deficits in underperforming residents: a scoping review. J Educ Eval Health Prof. https://doi.org/10.3352/jeehp.2026.23.3
title: Identification methods for clinical reasoning deficits span examination-based (oral, written, performance-based) and non-examination-based approaches
description: The review organizes the methods used to identify residents with clinical reasoning deficits into a taxonomy. It states these approaches "can be broadly categorized into examination-based and non–examination-based methods," with examination-based methods further divided into oral (case-based assessments, think-aloud exercises), written (script concordance tests, written simulated case evaluations), and performance-based assessments (OSCEs, direct observations, simulation exercises). Non-examination-based methods include interviews, chart reviews, ward-round performance evaluations, video reviews, intuitive recognition of poor performance cues, critical incident monitoring, and multisource feedback.
requirements: Stakeholders such as educators, supervisors, program directors, and remediation committees are involved in applying these identification methods
constraints: The review states no single assessment method is sufficient to comprehensively evaluate all domains of clinical reasoning
target_learners: medical residents with suspected clinical reasoning deficits
target_learning_goals: accurate identification of clinical reasoning skill deficits
examples: One study described combined use of OSCEs, script concordance testing, mini-CEX, and chart-stimulated recall for post-remediation assessment.
key_sources: Philip SJ, Cholifatul UF, Felicia CC, Nooreen A. (2026). Strategies for remediating clinical reasoning skill deficits in underperforming residents: a scoping review. J Educ Eval Health Prof. https://doi.org/10.3352/jeehp.2026.23.3

article_title: Strategies for remediating clinical reasoning skill deficits in underperforming residents: a scoping review.
citation: Philip SJ, Cholifatul UF, Felicia CC, Nooreen A. (2026). Strategies for remediating clinical reasoning skill deficits in underperforming residents: a scoping review. J Educ Eval Health Prof. https://doi.org/10.3352/jeehp.2026.23.3
title: Effective remediation requires early identification, comprehensive diagnostic assessment, and tailored, coaching-based interventions supported by institutional commitment
description: The review's central design recommendation is that remediation of clinical reasoning deficits should begin with precise diagnosis of where reasoning breaks down, followed by individualized, coaching-based intervention. It states that "Effective remediation requires early identification, comprehensive diagnostic assessment, and tailored, coaching-based interventions supported by institutional commitment." Addressing clinical reasoning as a discrete focus, when appropriate, enables targeted interventions on the underlying cognitive processes rather than diffusing effort across multiple domains.
requirements: Institutional commitment including structured remediation frameworks, dedicated remediation coordinators, and faculty development programs
constraints: The review cautions that approaches to identifying underperformance and implementing remediation may vary across sociocultural and institutional contexts
target_learning_goals: remediation of clinical reasoning skill deficits and return to safe practice
examples: The review recommends institutions adopt proactive mechanisms to identify and support struggling learners rather than relying solely on self-referral, since self-referral typically accounted for fewer than 10% of referrals.

article_title: Efficacy of mind maps and concept maps in enhancing academic performance among undergraduate medical students in the preclinical stage: a systematic review.
citation: Aljamal Husam, Alawneh Rama, Derbas Afnan, Edaibes Mohammad, Ahmed Aya, Amer Lama, Alzoubi Hiba, Serhan Hashem Abu Habuser. (2025). Efficacy of mind maps and concept maps in enhancing academic performance among undergraduate medical students in the preclinical stage: a systematic review. Advances in Health Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-025-10437-4
title: Two-feature taxonomy distinguishing concept maps from mind maps: hierarchy and explicit link naming
description: The review organizes the two visual mapping tools by two differentiating characteristics drawn from Santiago (2011). Concept maps are "hierarchical with the most important concept shown first", with subsidiary and tertiary concepts placed below, and they require "explicit naming of links" through verbs such as "includes" or "is part of", aiding accurate interpretation. Mind maps place the main idea at the center with ideas radiating outward with no obvious hierarchy, and their links are unnamed, leaving relationships implicit. The review includes both tools because they share the goal of enhancing knowledge organization and retention, and builds on the account that concept mapping rests on Ausubel's assimilation theory of learning.
requirements: Concept mapping requires links between concepts to be named explicitly through linking verbs
constraints: The two tools differ structurally despite a shared purpose of knowledge organization and retention
target_learning_goals: knowledge organization
knowledge retention
comprehension of complex medical information
examples: The review's included RCTs used concept mapping with clinical cases, mind mapping of neuroanatomy topics, and online testable pathogenesis maps

article_title: Analysis of research on gamification, critical thinking and academic performance: A systematic review in the context of higher education.
citation: Gamarra-Vargas NM, Cosio Borda RF, Quispe-Farfán PH, Bosmans Flores FG, Robladillo-Bravo LM. (2025). Analysis of research on gamification, critical thinking and academic performance: A systematic review in the context of higher education. F1000Research 14:913. https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.164232.1
title: Self-determination theory and gamified learning as the most relevant theoretical approaches for studying gamification
description: The review identifies the theoretical structures underpinning gamification research. Its analysis of the selected literature concludes that "the most relevant approaches for the study of gamification are self-determination and gamified learning". Self-determination theory positions motivation as the center of human behavior, so a subject motivated through gamified activities can develop critical thinking; Landers' gamified learning theory highlights benefits including favored academic performance. The review also lists other theoretical bases: relevance theory, the transtheoretical model of behavior change, cognitive load theory, constructivism, the technology acceptance model and social cognitive theory.
requirements: Studies of gamification adopt an explicit theoretical approach to understand its application and benefits, as the review's analysis of theoretical structures presupposes.
constraints: The theoretical-structure analysis rests on the review's qualitative reading of thematic networks, which its own reviewer noted lacks quantitative centrality metrics.
target_learning_goals: critical thinking
academic performance
motivation
examples: The review's WOS thematic network (Figure 12) links a motivation-centered cluster to games and critical thinking clusters, consistent with self-determination theory.

citation: Gilbert Valentin, Philip Pierre, Llorca Pierre-Michel, Samalin Ludovic. (2026). Use of artificial intelligence–enhanced virtual patients in educational approaches to medical interview training: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08804-9
title: Five-domain outcome taxonomy for AI-VP interview training research
description: The review organizes its synthesis of heterogeneous AI-VP studies around five inductively identified outcome domains. As the authors state, domains "included communication and interviewing performance, empathy and interpersonal skills, learner self-efficacy and engagement, feedback and evaluation mechanisms, and transfer to actual practice." This taxonomy structures the narrative synthesis, maps each included study's outcomes, and highlights where evidence is strongest (interview structure, questioning, feedback-supported empathy) and weakest (transfer to real practice). It serves as an organizing framework for future AI-VP evaluation studies.
requirements: Studies must report outcomes in terms that can be mapped to the five domains for cross-study comparison
constraints: Domains were identified inductively by two review authors from the eleven included studies; the quantitative synthesis was not performed due to marked heterogeneity between studies

empathy and interpersonal skills
learner self-efficacy and engagement
feedback and evaluation
transfer to actual practice
examples: The review's narrative synthesis sections are organized under these five outcome-domain headings

citation: Tappan Rachel S., Holland Elizabeth E., Roth Heidi R. (2026). Educational assessments in entry-level physical therapy education: a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08927-z
title: Miller's pyramid as an organizing framework for knowledge and skill assessment formats
description: Miller's pyramid is a four-level framework ordering assessment targets from factual knowledge to real-world performance: "Knows" (best assessed with written exams), "Knows How" (written or oral exams), "Shows How" (performance-based assessments with standardized simulations or oral exams with standardized scenarios), and "Does" (clinic-based performance assessments). The review uses it to map which assessment formats and construct types are prevalent in physical therapy education and to identify which levels are underrepresented.
requirements: Assessment format should match the pyramid level of the construct being assessed
constraints: The review applies it to faculty- and preceptor-rated assessments of knowledge and skills in entry-level physical therapy education only
target_learners: entry-level physical therapy (PT) and physical therapy assistant (PTA) students
target_learning_goals: clinical knowledge
procedural skills
communication skills
clinical performance
examples: The review mapped the 92 identified assessments onto the pyramid, finding performance-based assessments correspond to the Does and Shows How levels

title: Messick's five sources of validity evidence as the charting framework for assessment validity
description: The review categorizes validity evidence using the five sources from Messick's framework and the Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing: content, response process, internal structure, relations with other variables, and consequences. In contemporary frameworks, "validity is a characteristic of the proposed interpretation of scores" for a specific assessment use rather than a property of the assessment tool itself. Each study's evidence was rated on a four-point scale adapted from Ghaderi et al. and Beckman et al.
requirements: Specification of the assessment's intended interpretation and use before gathering validity evidence
constraints: The review notes a detailed discussion of contemporary validity theory is beyond the scope of the article

target_learning_goals: valid interpretation of assessment scores for progression and competency decisions
examples: Each included study's validity evidence was categorized into the five sources and rated 0-3 using the printed rating scale in Table 2

article_title: Competence and confidence of health care professionals in using clozapine: a qualitative systematic review and thematic synthesis.

description: The review's thematic synthesis of 34 studies organises the factors influencing health care professionals' competence and confidence in clozapine management into six analytical themes. As the review reports, "Six themes were identified: attitude toward and knowledge about clozapine, misconceptions (regarding side effects, monitoring and co-morbidities), guidelines, education, training and experience." The framework links these factors to clozapine underuse and variation in prescribing practice.

constraints: Based on 34 included studies, most using self-report surveys; only a few studies involved non-medical professionals

non-medical professionals such as nurses, pharmacists and allied health workers
target_learning_goals: competence in clozapine prescribing and management
confidence in adhering to guidelines and managing side effects

Each factor is elaborated into themes and subthemes derived by meta-ethnographic synthesis of qualitative studies, and the authors state the framework "provides a conceptual framework for nurses' competence in healthcare policy and for developing political or policy education or programs to strengthen this competence."

article_title: Refining competency benchmarks: a scoping review of Angoff standard-setting in dental education.
citation: Lin Galvin Sim Siang, Hisham Abdul Rauf Badrul, Majid Muhammad Nazmi Abdul, Foong Chan Choong, Ho Ting Khee, Friedlander Lara T. (2026). Refining competency benchmarks: a scoping review of Angoff standard-setting in dental education. BMC Oral Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12903-026-08195-9
title: Taxonomy of standard-setting methods: norm-referenced, criterion-referenced, and compromise approaches
description: The review organises standard-setting methods into three categories. Norm-referenced (relative) methods determine cut-off scores from assessment results by comparing candidates to peers, and are "not widely used for high-stakes examinations". Criterion-referenced (absolute) methods, such as the Angoff and Ebel methods, set the cut-off independently of assessment results relative to test content. Compromise methods, including Hofstee and Hofstee-Angoff, combine both approaches. The review uses this taxonomy to situate the Angoff method as a widely utilised criterion-referenced technique relying on expert judgment of the minimally competent candidate.
requirements: A panel of subject-matter experts to judge item difficulty and establish the cut-off score
constraints: Norm-referenced methods focus on relative comparison of performance and are not widely used for high-stakes examinations, per the review
target_learners: foreign-trained dentists taking licensure proficiency tests
target_learning_goals: establishing valid cut-off scores for summative competency assessment in dental education
examples: The review's ten included studies applied Angoff, Modified Angoff, Hofstee, Cohen, Modified Cohen, relative (Mean, SD), and Borderline Regression methods across MCQ, SAQ and OSCE assessments

title: Scoping review of Angoff standard-setting in dental education (ten primary studies, 2009–2023)
description: A scoping review following the Arksey and O'Malley five-stage framework and PRISMA-ScR reporting guidelines, prospectively registered on the Open Science Framework. The search of six databases and two major dental education journals up to May 2024 identified 1412 records, of which "ten articles were selected after screening", with substantial inter-rater agreement (Kappa 0.78). The included studies span eight countries, undergraduate and licensure contexts, and MCQ, SAQ and OSCE assessment formats, analysed through quantitative frequency and qualitative thematic analysis using NVivo 12.

constraints: Only English-language articles were included; article quality was not assessed; no included article involved postgraduate students, so findings are limited to undergraduate dental education

examples: Most included studies used retrospective designs, with only one prospective study (Schoonheim-Klein et al., Netherlands)

Competencies were categorized as either a peer support competency, as outlined by SAMHSA, or a clinical competency, defined as techniques or skills typically used by clinical providers. The final taxonomy was composed of 12 peer support competencies (e.g., collaboration and care, providing support, recovery planning, sharing lived experience of recovery) and 4 clinical competencies (mental health diagnosis and psychoeducation, basic counseling skills, case management, cognitive behavioral techniques), developed through thematic content analysis, two rounds of pilot coding by eight researchers, and expert panel review.

Peer supporters in mental health systems

Input modalities were text (11 of 15 studies), voice (5), or hybrid (1); output corresponded closely to input mechanisms; and avatar design distinguished 6 studies using 3D-embodied virtual patients from 9 using nonembodied interfaces. The review uses this taxonomy in Table 2 to characterize the field and support its design-implementation research question.

citation: Zerrouk Deyae, Kassab Kenza, El Asri Achraf, Zarrouq Btissame. (2026). BMC Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-026-04354-3
title: Valkenburg's three paradigms of media effects (selectivity, transactionality, conditionality)
description: The review invokes Patti M. Valkenburg's synthesis of media-effects models into three overarching paradigms to explain why social media use and its effects vary across university students. The selectivity paradigm holds that "users, including university students, can process only a limited portion of available content" shaped by their orientations and needs. The transactionality paradigm emphasizes that dispositions, developmental stages, and social contexts jointly shape both use patterns and effects, and the conditionality paradigm proposes effects are not uniform and may be strengthened or attenuated by personal traits, development, and context.
requirements: Frameworks are used to explain variability in social media effects among university students rather than to predict a uniform outcome
constraints: The review presents these as explanatory conceptual frameworks, not as tested within its own data
target_learners: university students in the MENA region
target_learning_goals: understanding variability in social media effects on academic performance
examples: The review uses the paradigms in its introduction to motivate examining PSMU and academic performance in a region of high prevalence

description: The review frames competence in palliative care as encompassing knowledge, skills, abilities, values, beliefs, attributes and behaviors, and links it to self-efficacy or confidence. It states that "Published research widely recognizes the role of confidence in both the development of competence and its demonstration in evaluative contexts", drawing on Bandura's account of self-efficacy shaped through social and environmental influences. In the synthesis, nurse managers' competence was demonstrated in performing diverse responsibilities and was closely tied to their confidence in leading complex care processes.

title: Four-category taxonomy of IPE learning activities: small-group, simulation, theoretical, and clinical
description: The review organizes IPE learning activities into a taxonomy of nine types under four categories. It states that "Nine types of learning activities were identified under four learning categories: (1) small-group; (2) simulation; (3) theoretical, and (4) clinical". Small-group covers case-based and problem-based discussion; simulation covers mannequin, virtual, standardized-patient, and role-play formats; theoretical covers modules and presentations; clinical covers supervised hands-on practice. The taxonomy was derived thematically from the 41 included studies and is intended to inform design of future IPE interventions.

title: Design IPE sessions around a clear topic, shared pre-reading, and explicit review of each profession's roles to reduce role ambiguity
description: The review's synthesis of teaching strategies supports preparing learners before collaborative activity. It reports that offering pre-reading materials establishes a shared foundation of knowledge and "may diminish perceptions of ambiguity in interprofessional training", while briefing sessions or printed materials on roles and responsibilities "established a foundation of mutual respect to enhance work efficiency and resolve interprofessional conflicts". Establishing a clear topic provides direction ensuring learners achieve desired outcomes and helps them recognize the importance of teamwork.

citation: Pinar Sedat Alp, Morrow Joseph J., Kong Chia Yew. (2025). A systematic review of the use of human body donor models for postgraduate laparoscopic surgical training. Anatomical Science International. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12565-025-00872-z
title: Four-type validity framework for evaluating surgical training models
description: The review organises its evaluation of body donor models around four validity types drawn from simulation literature: "face validity, construct validity, content validity, and predictive validity". Face validity concerns resemblance to a real-life procedure, construct validity the ability to distinguish experience levels, content validity the capacity to enhance knowledge and skills across settings, and predictive validity the translation of improved skills to real-life clinical settings. The review sorts its 55 included studies into groups by which validity type they assess, and uses this framework to diagnose where evidence is strongest (face validity) and weakest (predictive validity).

constraints: Only one included study assessed predictive validity, so the framework's highest-level evidence tier is nearly empty in this literature
target_learning_goals: laparoscopic surgical skills
anatomical knowledge
examples: The review categorised its 55 included studies into five discussion groups, including studies assessing content validity, construct validity, and comparative studies

title: ASReview Lab with the SAFE procedure for machine-learning-assisted systematic review screening
description: The review used ASReview Lab (version 2.1.1) to prioritize records for title-abstract screening via active learning, following the five-step SAFE stopping procedure: random training-set screening, model-prioritized review with the ELAS-u4 model, stopping after at least 50 consecutive irrelevant records, a second pass with ELAS-h3, and quality assurance of the 10 highest- and lowest-ranked unscreened records. The authors state that "ASReview was used to prioritize records for screening, and screening continued until the predefined stopping rules (SAFE…) were met." Of 2,822 deduplicated records, 477 were manually reviewed and 32 studies included.

constraints: Records ranked below the SAFE stopping point were not manually screened and were assumed irrelevant based on model predictions; the authors note potential model-related omissions as a technical challenge.
target_learners: researchers conducting systematic reviews in education and health professions education
target_learning_goals: efficient and transparent study screening in systematic reviews
examples: The review screened 2,822 records, manually reviewed 477 titles and abstracts, and included 32 studies; a second round with an independent training set identified no new relevant studies.

citation: McCarthy Roisin, Maher Liam, O'Dea Angela. (2026). Validation status of definitive airway management simulators: a systematic review. BJA: British Journal of Anaesthesia. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bja.2026.01.027
title: Five-domain validity framework for simulator evaluation (face, content, construct, concurrent, predictive)
description: The review organises simulator validation evidence using five validity domains defined from Van Nortwick and McDougall: face validity (realism to non-experts), content validity (expert-rated teaching effectiveness), construct validity (differentiating expertise levels), concurrent validity (correlation with a gold standard such as human anatomy), and predictive validity ("the extent to which performance on the simulator predicts future performance in real clinical settings"). Each domain carries specified assessment methods, e.g. I-CVI ≥0.80 for content and task time, errors, or OSATS scores for construct validity. The review uses this framework to categorise and rate all 29 simulators.
requirements: Studies must report empirical data on at least one validity domain to be included under this framework
constraints: Predictive validity for front-of-neck access procedures cannot be ethically or practically evaluated in real clinical settings, per the review
target_learning_goals: tracheal intubation
fibreoptic intubation
front-of-neck access procedures
examples: The review assigned each simulator a Level of Evidence (OCEBM-adapted, 1–4) and a Level of Recommendation (1 strongest to 4 weakest) based on validity evidence across these domains

title: Educators should exercise caution when interpreting simulator performance as evidence of clinical competence, and validation evidence should guide simulator selection
description: Because most airway simulators lack robust validation—particularly predictive validity linking simulator performance to clinical outcomes—the review recommends that educators and training institutions treat simulator performance cautiously and let validation evidence drive selection and endorsement of simulators for teaching and assessment. It further urges development of "a unified, transparent validation framework, supported by professional and academic consensus" to improve simulator design, comparability, and clinical relevance.
requirements: Validation evidence should be available and consulted when selecting or endorsing simulators for teaching and assessment
constraints: Current evidence base is limited: most studies were small, cross-sectional, underpowered, with short follow-up intervals restricting conclusions about durable skill transfer
target_learning_goals: tracheal intubation
fibreoptic intubation
front-of-neck access procedures
examples: The review found studies comparing airway devices on static manikin models drew clinical conclusions without verifying anatomical accuracy or transferability, motivating the caution recommendation

article_title: Simulation-Based Training for Nursing Students to Improve Patient Safety: Systematic Review.
citation: González-Sanz A, López-García JC, Sutil-Rodríguez E, Juárez-Vela R, Santos-Sánchez JÁ, Navas-Echazarreta N, Martínez-Sabater A, Sancho-Sanchez C. (2026). Simulation-Based Training for Nursing Students to Improve Patient Safety: Systematic Review. JMIR Nursing. https://doi.org/10.2196/87898
title: Taxonomy of simulation modalities and fidelity levels for patient safety education
description: The review organizes simulation-based education by modality and fidelity. Fidelity is "the degree to which the simulation reproduces the conditions of actual clinical practice," classified as low, medium, or high; modalities per the Healthcare Simulation Dictionary include role-playing, virtual or online simulations, task trainers, high-tech mannequins, and immersive simulations with standardized patients. Across the 20 included studies, high-fidelity simulators (n=9), standardized patients (n=8), virtual reality (n=4), role play (n=2), and board simulations (n=1) were used, with categories not mutually exclusive. The combination of modality and fidelity level allows simulation to be adapted to different educational contexts and clinical competencies.
requirements: Simulation design must not compromise the psychological and physical integrity of participants, per the review's framing of safe training processes
constraints: Modality categories are not mutually exclusive because several studies combined HFS with SP or VR
target_learning_goals: patient safety competencies including communication, teamwork, and medication safety
examples: High-fidelity simulation predominated, with 16 studies using this modality; low-fidelity role-playing was used for interprofessional communication, medication administration, and incident reporting

title: KAS-based AI application framework for nursing education with three primary dimensions and twelve sub-dimensions
description: The review proposes an AI application framework for nursing education grounded in the Knowledge-Attitude-Skill model, refining three primary dimensions into twelve secondary sub-dimensions (K1–K4, A1–A4, S1–S4). The article states that "By refining the three dimensions of knowledge, attitudes, and skills into 12 specific sub-dimensions, it offers educators clear guidance for systematically designing teaching objectives, organizing instructional content, and conducting teaching evaluations." It was built through a deductive-inductive hybrid coding of 23 included studies.

constraints: The framework requires ongoing updates because rapid AI advancement necessitates maintaining timeliness; it has not yet been empirically validated

citation: Wei W, Nielsen MS, Nielsen AB, Han Y, Russell L, Konge L, Cold KM. (2026). Hands-on Distance Simulation of Technical Skills: A Systematic Review. Simulation in Healthcare. https://doi.org/10.1097/SIH.0000000000000881
title: Three-format taxonomy of distance simulation delivery: home-based, facility-based, and mobile
description: The review classifies distance simulation delivery into three descriptive formats. "Home-based distance simulation" involves trainees using portable simulators at home or other remote locations; "facility-based distance simulation" has trainees physically at a training center receiving instruction remotely via telecommunication; and "mobile simulation" transports a simulator to the learners' location. The review used these categories to group studies and interpret implementation strategies, finding home-based formats in 64 studies, facility-based in 39, and mobile in 1.
requirements: Learners must have access to portable simulators or training facilities and to telecommunication channels connecting them with remote facilitators
constraints: The review notes home-based formats are only suitable for basic technical training because they typically lack advanced simulators and facilities
target_learning_goals: hands-on technical skills such as laparoscopic skills, suturing, and ultrasound
examples: Home-based microsurgical training used smartphone camera zoom as a microscope substitute, while 5 facility-based ophthalmic trainings required advanced microscopes at training centers

constraints: The review notes benefits of technologies like 3D printing and XR depend on local infrastructure and resource availability, and XR implementation is limited by high cost and reliance on stable high-speed Internet

The pilot comprised seven sessions totalling 10.5 h for 325 students; the implementation series of eleven lectures totalling 22 teaching hours reached over 1,500 students from 42 German-speaking medical schools. The review notes the lectures "can be transferred to all medical schools as they require no additional equipment, such as an onsite TK".

article_title: Augmented Reality in Surgical Training: Systematic Review of Its Impact on Technical Performance in Surgical Trainees.
citation: El Ashry M, El Ashry A, Khalique H, Abdalle Y, Yeung T. (2026). Augmented Reality in Surgical Training: Systematic Review of Its Impact on Technical Performance in Surgical Trainees. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/71572
title: Cognitive load and gaze-guidance account of AR's training benefit
description: The review frames AR's educational value through cognitive load theory: instruction should "minimize extraneous cognitive load while maximizing germane load, the mental effort directed toward schema formation". AR telestration and anatomical overlays bypass the cognitive translation step of converting verbal descriptions into spatial awareness by providing visual guidance colocated with the task. The expertise reversal effect predicts the same overlays that scaffold novices may act as extraneous load for experts with robust internal schemas. Eye-tracking evidence on reduced gaze latency is presented as the most direct experimental support for this mechanism.
requirements: AR overlays must be colocated with the task being performed to bypass the cognitive translation step
constraints: The review strictly defines AR as unidirectional overlay of digital data onto a physical field, excluding bidirectional spatially mapped mixed reality interactions
The same overlays may function as extraneous cognitive load for experts who have already developed robust internal schemas
target_learners: surgical trainees: medical students, residents, and fellows
target_learning_goals: technical surgical skill acquisition
spatial anatomical understanding
procedural accuracy
examples: Felinska et al's eye-tracking data showed AR reduced gaze latency from 2.04 to 0.21 seconds (P<.01, ηp²=0.95), which the review cites as confirming that AR telestration directs trainees' visual attention to operationally relevant structures more rapidly than verbal instruction

article_title: A Scoping Review of the Conceptualization, Operationalization, and Institutional Recognition of the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning in Health Professions Education: Using Institutional Logics to Understand Inconsistencies.
citation: Varpio L, Jones F, Lege-Matsuura J, Schultz K, Amiel J, Dunleavy K, Jensen GM, Jeffries PR, Ellaway R. (2026). A Scoping Review of the Conceptualization, Operationalization, and Institutional Recognition of the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning in Health Professions Education: Using Institutional Logics to Understand Inconsistencies. Perspectives on Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.5334/pme.2740
title: Institutional Logics and Besharov & Smith's compatibility–centrality model explain variable SoTL recognition across HPE organizations
description: Institutional logics are "socially constructed and historically informed patterns of practices, assumptions, values, and rules" through which individuals produce meaning and justify actions. Besharov and Smith's model positions logics on two continuous dimensions—compatibility (consistency of rules for action) and centrality (equal validity to organizational functioning)—yielding four ideal types: contested, aligned, estranged, and dominant. The review applies this to argue that SoTL recognition varies with alignment between the logics of research and teaching: revised P&T guidelines suggest aligned organizations, while reliance on research metrics suggests estranged or contested ones.
requirements: Both the logics of research and SoTL must be articulated with clear prescriptions for action so their compatibility can be assessed
constraints: The review notes organizations can fall between ideal types because centrality and compatibility exist in degrees; some articles listed both supportive and obstructing factors
target_learning_goals: institutional recognition of educational scholarship in promotion and tenure decisions
examples: The review interprets P&T guideline revisions as high centrality plus high compatibility (aligned organizations), and committees applying research metrics to SoTL as low centrality and low compatibility (estranged) or high centrality with low compatibility (contested)

title: A literature-based framework distinguishing scholarly teaching, SoTL, and educational research by definition, audience, evidence, advancement, and impact
description: Built from Medina et al.'s (2011) framework and augmented with Milner et al.'s (2023) three essential scholarship components—advancement of knowledge, dissemination, impact—this framework (Table 3) differentiates three activities. Scholarly teaching draws on others' work for a local audience; SoTL involves looking critically at student learning and sharing insights publicly so others can build on them, since "SoTL contributes to the expertise of others"; educational research uses quantitative, qualitative, or mixed designs for questions of broad relevance with national or international impact. The authors propose the distinctions reveal the logic of SoTL and support compatibility in P&T decisions.
requirements: Clear articulation of SoTL's prescriptions for action at the field level so P&T committees can create compatibility with the research logic
constraints: The authors note Boyer's expansive definition of scholarship, while historically supportive, has become problematic because an incredible scope of operationalizations has been identified as evidence of SoTL

target_learning_goals: distinguishing scholarly teaching from SoTL and educational research
documenting educational scholarship for promotion
examples: The framework's illustrative example traces one Team-Based Learning activity through all three categories: portfolio documentation (scholarly teaching), publication in MedEdPortal (SoTL), and a peer-reviewed study of the intervention's conceptual structure (educational research)

citation: Joly Louise, Nunes de Sousa Alexandra, Bardiau Marjorie, Dory Valérie, Bayot Marie, Lenoir Anne-Laure. (2026). Impact of emotional competence on clinical reasoning: a scoping review. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2025-113483
title: Mikolajczak's five-component emotional competence framework crossed with Young's clinical reasoning categorisation as the review's organising axis
description: The review organises its synthesis around two frameworks. EC is described in Mikolajczak's framework, which "includes five components: emotion identification, regulation, expression, use and understanding", each comprising three levels (knowledge, application ability, natural propensity), distinguishing EC from emotional intelligence. CR is categorised per Young et al into reasoning skills, performance, process, outcome, context and goals of reasoning. title: AI-augmented tutoring defined by two integration models: AI-substitutive and AI-augmentative
description: The review defines an AI tutoring (intelligent tutoring) system as "an educational platform driven by computer algorithms" that integrates performance assessment with personalized, goal-oriented feedback to guide surgical skill acquisition in a training context. title: Educational programs should adopt combined strategies targeting movement behaviors and dietary habits together rather than as independent domains
description: Because physical activity and nutrition likely interact through shared biological pathways, the review recommends integrated lifestyle approaches in educational and public health settings. It states that "Educational programs and public health initiatives would benefit from adopting combined strategies that simultaneously target movement behaviors and dietary habits, rather than treating them as independent domains." This follows its finding that only a small proportion of studies examined physical activity and nutrition within the same analytical framework.

constraints: The review cautions that findings from predominantly observational evidence should be translated into practice with appropriate caution and not interpreted as definitive proof of causal academic benefit

academic achievement
healthy lifestyle behaviors

citation: Hietaniemi, A.‐M., Ylimäki, S., Härkönen, H., Hannila, H.‐M., Tuomikoski, A.‐M., Oikarinen, A., Jansson, M., Pölkki, T., Kanste, O. & Kääriäinen, M. (2026). Nurses' Experiences and Perceptions of Evidence‐Based Healthcare Competence: A Qualitative Systematic Review. Journal of Advanced Nursing. https://doi.org/10.1111/jan.70399
title: JBI EBHC model: five sub‐dimensions of evidence‐based healthcare competence
description: The review organises nurses' EBHC competence using the JBI EBHC model framework (Jordan et al. 2019), which holds that evidence‐based practice "requires the integration of sub‐dimensions of EBHC (global health, evidence generation, evidence synthesis, evidence transfer and evidence implementation) into the healthcare system". The model defines EBHC competence for nurses as including knowledge, skills, values, attitudes, beliefs and experience. The review used the model's sub‐dimensions as the categorisation scheme for its meta‐aggregation of qualitative findings.
requirements: Nurses require competencies across all EBHC sub‐dimensions for the model to be realised in practice
constraints: In this review, no extracted findings were associated with the evidence synthesis sub‐dimension, so only four sub‐dimensions received synthesised findings
target_learning_goals: evidence‐based healthcare competence across global health, evidence generation, evidence synthesis, evidence transfer and evidence implementation
examples: The review categorised 89 extracted findings into 15 categories and four synthesised findings mapped onto the model's sub‐dimensions

description: The review's implication for the profession is that "Integration of EBHC into education, mentoring and adequate resources enhances nurses' competence, motivation and commitment to EBHC sub‐dimensions, while also strengthening their professional confidence and development". Synthesised findings support this: nurses described mentorship, supportive leadership, structured training programmes and practical workshops as enhancing evidence transfer and implementation. The principle directs nursing education and healthcare organisations to embed EBHC in curricula and provide mentoring and resources.

evidence implementation in clinical care
research engagement

article_title: Very short answer questions vs. multiple choice questions in health professions education: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
citation: Sher Ali, Arshad Muhammad Moin Ud Din, Abbas Mesum, Asghar Abdul Hannan, Khan Anees Hussain, Ali Junaid, Yaqoob Muhammad Ibrahim, Alam Rana Aftab, Akram Muhammad Bilal, Masood Muhammad Abdullah, Thakur Amit Kumar. (2026). Very short answer questions vs. multiple choice questions in health professions education: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09359-5
title: Cueing-effect account: MCQ recognition inflates scores while VSAQs require self-generated responses reflecting independent knowledge
description: The article's explanatory framework holds that MCQs are "susceptible to cueing effects, where recognition rather than recall may drive performance, potentially inflating student scores without truly reflecting independent knowledge". VSAQs mitigate this by requiring concise, self-generated responses of 1-4 words while retaining computer-markable logistics. The review uses this account to interpret lower VSAQ scores as more authentic assessment of independent knowledge and clinical reasoning rather than a learning deficiency.
requirements: VSAQs must be computer-markable with a limited word count (1-4 words) to retain logistical feasibility
constraints: Both formats require retrieval from memory; the principal distinction is that VSAQs reduce response cueing and place greater demands on answer generation
target_learners: undergraduate and postgraduate health professions education students
target_learning_goals: assessment of independent knowledge and clinical reasoning ability
examples: The review interprets the pooled score difference favoring MCQs as consistent with recognition-driven answering inflating MCQ scores, citing prior literature on MCQ overestimation of mastery.

article_title: Thinking and feeling matter: a second-order meta-analysis of student characteristics across developmental domains and their effect on academic outcomes.
citation: Erdem Cahit, Kaya Metin, Polat Mustafa, Eğmir Eray. (2026). Thinking and feeling matter: a second-order meta-analysis of student characteristics across developmental domains and their effect on academic outcomes. BMC Psychology, 14, 919. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-026-05035-x
title: Tripartite developmental-domains framework of student characteristics
description: The article organizes student characteristics into four themes across three developmental domains: positive emotions and positive personality traits (affective), cognitive abilities (cognitive), and psychomotor abilities (psychomotor). It states this "tripartite classification aligns with widely accepted educational taxonomies and developmental psychology frameworks". The framework deliberately focuses on positive attributes, in line with a positive psychology perspective, because the included first-order meta-analyses predominantly examined positive traits.
requirements: Meta-analyses must report adequate statistical data (correlations, Fisher's z, Cohen's d, odds ratios) to permit effect-size calculation
constraints: Negative emotional factors such as anxiety and neuroticism were considered beyond the scope of the synthesis
Psychomotor skills were limited to visual perception and motor functioning due to the limitation of studies in the dataset
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement across general and specific academic areas
examples: The 29 included first-order meta-analyses were coded into the four themes, with inter-rater reliability of Cohen's Kappa = 0.88

description: The ECOEnfSM scale (Assessment competences of Mental Health Nurses in Specialized Health Training Programs, Rivera, 2021) is a validated tool developed to assess the competences of mental health nurses during their residency training program in Spain. The review reports that Rivera Vicente (2021), a reliability and validity study with 40 MHNs, "Validated the scale ECOEnFSM. to assess mental health nursing competences in Spain", covering assessment, nursing diagnosis, intervention, evaluation, research, clinical management, teaching and interpersonal relationships. title: Three-domain thematic framework of individual, institutional, and educational factors shaping ALS competence maintenance
description: The review develops an inductive thematic structure organising reported influences on ALS competence maintenance into three overarching domains: individual (e.g., experience, self-confidence, stress and cognitive load, non-technical skills), institutional (e.g., assessment systems, institutional support, standardisation, training access), and educational (e.g., simulation-based training, feedback and debriefing, spaced repetition and LDHF models, gamification, blended learning). Sources contributing to multiple domains were coded across domains. The review states that "Three overarching domains (individual, institutional and educational) were developed through successive rounds of refinement."

article_title: The impact of experiential learning on healthcare students' attitudes towards dementia: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
citation: Wong Ion Hong, Gao Xiaoyu, Tan Zhengyi, Fang Yiping, Wang Qun, Lei Wai In, Van Iat Kio, Tan Meijing, Liu Ning, Wu Jianwei. (2026). The impact of experiential learning on healthcare students’ attitudes towards dementia: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Geriatrics. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12877-026-07573-w
title: Theoretical accounts of why experiential learning shifts dementia attitudes: Kolb's Experiential Learning Theory, Construal Level Theory, and the Affect Heuristic
description: The review interprets its pooled findings through three frameworks. Kolb's Experiential Learning Theory "posits that learning is most effective when learners actively engage with experiences, reflect, abstract conceptual knowledge, and apply it in practice", supporting hands-on interaction. Construal Level Theory holds that closer psychological distance promotes more concrete, personalized representations, so experiential learning "reduces this distance, replacing abstract stereotypes with tangible, empathetic impressions". The Affect Heuristic explains why brief, emotionally charged experiences such as simulations can rapidly shift attitudes by bypassing rational deliberation.
requirements: Interventions must involve active engagement with experiences and reflection, per Kolb's cycle as the review describes it
constraints: The review presents these as interpretive frameworks for its findings, not as mechanisms tested within the included studies
target_learners: healthcare undergraduate students (medical, nursing, gerontology, social work, physiotherapy, dentistry, occupational therapy, pharmacy)
target_learning_goals: positive attitudes towards individuals with dementia
empathy and person-centered care orientation
examples: The review uses the Affect Heuristic to explain why single-session formats such as dementia simulations or firsthand narratives yielded significant DAS improvements
key_sources: Wong Ion Hong, Gao Xiaoyu, Tan Zhengyi, Fang Yiping, Wang Qun, Lei Wai In, Van Iat Kio, Tan Meijing, Liu Ning, Wu Jianwei. (2026). title: Four-theme synthesized framework of nursing students' virtual simulation teaching experiences
description: A qualitative meta-synthesis framework organizing nursing students' experiences of VS teaching into four synthesized findings: "(1) emotional experiences; (2) advantages of VS teaching; (3) challenges of VS teaching; (4) students’ needs for VS teaching." It was built by integrating 65 themes and 156 sub-themes from 17 qualitative studies into nine categories through repeated comparison and thematic analysis following the JBI meta-aggregation approach. The framework serves as a theoretical foundation for optimizing VS teaching equipment and accommodating diverse cultural backgrounds and learning foundations in future educational design.

constraints: Only Chinese and English databases were searched, and included studies were predominantly from Asian and European countries, limiting adaptability of conclusions to multicultural contexts
target_learning_goals: clinical practice skills
clinical reasoning
professional identity and responsibility
examples: The synthesis drew on studies using semi-structured interviews and focus groups across computer-based and immersive VR platforms in eight countries

article_title: Rubric use in dental education: a systematic review of design, implementation, and educational impact.
citation: Gadbail Amol Ramchandra, Gondivkar Shailesh M., Yuwanati Monal B., Sonone Archana, Dhamande Mithilesh, Panchbhai Aarati, Hande Alka H., Patil Swati, Sarode Sachin C. (2026). Rubric use in dental education: a systematic review of design, implementation, and educational impact. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09218-3
title: Rubrics as criterion-referenced evaluation instruments with analytic and holistic types
description: A rubric is defined by the review as "an evaluation instrument that delineates explicit criteria alongside graduated levels of achievement", facilitating criterion-referenced feedback for formative and summative purposes. The review distinguishes rubrics from checklists, which simply mark task completion, and numeric rating scales, which give global scores without criterion-specific feedback. It organizes rubrics into two types: "analytic where individual criteria are assessed separately and holistic assessment where a student's overall performance is assessed via a single comprehensive rubric". This taxonomy frames the review's synthesis of rubric design and implementation in dental education.
requirements: Rubrics require explicit criteria paired with graduated performance levels and descriptive feedback for each level to deliver criterion-referenced feedback
constraints: The review notes limited cross-institutional validation restricts generalizability of rubric effectiveness claims across all dental education contexts
target_learning_goals: clinical competency assessment
psychomotor skills
clinical judgment
professional behaviors
self-assessment and reflective practice
examples: Most included studies (20/23) applied analytic rubrics providing criterion-specific scoring across dental specialties including restorative dentistry, periodontics, endodontics, prosthodontics, and oral surgery

article_title: Effectiveness of artificial intelligence-driven simulation in dental education: a systematic review and meta-analysis of learning outcomes.
citation: Gadbail Amol Ramchandra, Gondivkar Shailesh M., Yuwanati Monal B, Sonone Archana, Dhamande Mithilesh, Panchbhai Aarti, Hande Alka H, Patil Swati, Sarode Sachin C. (2026). Effectiveness of artificial intelligence-driven simulation in dental education: a systematic review and meta-analysis of learning outcomes. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09390-6
title: Unified ADS framework: AI-enabled decision-making, adaptive or automated feedback, and simulation environments approximating clinical tasks
description: The review groups technologically distinct modalities — immersive VR-haptic systems, intelligent tutoring systems, and generative AI platforms such as chatbots and virtual patients — under a unified ADS framework based on shared characteristics: "AI-enabled or algorithm-driven decision-making", "provision of adaptive or automated feedback", and "use of simulation-based environments that approximate clinical tasks". The framework enables synthesis across emerging technologies while acknowledging that differences in fidelity, interactivity, and targeted competencies may produce variability in effectiveness. Pedagogically, the modalities are grounded respectively in experiential and procedural learning, adaptive feedback and mastery learning, and constructivist and case-based reasoning approaches.
requirements: Interventions must incorporate AI-enabled or algorithm-driven decision-making, adaptive or automated feedback, and simulation-based environments replicating clinical or educational tasks to qualify as ADS under the review's operational definition.
constraints: The modalities differ substantially in technological architecture, level of immersion, interaction design, and intended learning outcomes, and should not be considered functionally equivalent interventions.
target_learning_goals: Psychomotor clinical skills
Clinical reasoning and cognitive skills
Affective outcomes such as confidence and motivation
examples: The review's twelve included studies spanned VR-haptic simulators with machine learning, ITS platforms, and GPT-based conversational virtual patients, all classified under the unified ADS framework.

article_title: Teaching clinical communication skills through virtual patient-based learning: an umbrella review of systematic reviews.
citation: Kalmring M, Chmelar S, Greimel P, Kaider M, Lang C, Roszipal B. (2026). Teaching clinical communication skills through virtual patient-based learning: an umbrella review of systematic reviews. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09374-6
title: Three-dimension framework differentiating immersive and virtual patient technologies: level of immersion, interaction design, and representational fidelity
description: The review proposes differentiating immersive and virtual patient technologies along three dimensions derived from the included reviews: "level of immersion", "interaction design", and "representational fidelity". Immersion ranges from screen-based platforms to VR/AR simulations; interaction design ranges from predefined menu-based responses to natural language interaction; representational fidelity ranges from static images and video-based responses to fully animated 3D environments. The review argues these differences likely influence learning outcomes, so interaction quality and feedback design, rather than technology alone, may be key mechanisms underlying communication skills training.
requirements: Reviews and primary studies must report enough detail on interaction quality, fidelity, and responsiveness for the dimensions to be distinguished
constraints: The review notes the included reviews rarely differentiated clearly between levels of technological sophistication and generally provided limited detail on interaction quality, fidelity, or responsiveness
target_learning_goals: clinical communication skills
examples: The review reports many virtual patient systems relied on predefined response options with limited interaction flexibility, while only a small number of studies incorporated typed or voice-based natural language input

article_title: Problem-based and related learning approaches in family medicine residency: a scoping review of four countries.
citation: Clemens Megan, Boparai Josheil Kaur, Dawe Russell, Avery Susan. (2026). Problem-based and related learning approaches in family medicine residency: a scoping review of four countries. Canadian Medical Education Journal. https://doi.org/10.36834/cmej.81284
title: Three categories of synchronous PBL delivery in family medicine residency curricula: standalone, adjunct, and blended
description: The review organizes how the 12 included studies integrated PBL into family medicine postgraduate curricula into three synchronous delivery categories. As the authors state, "We found three distinct categories of synchronous approaches to integrating PBL into family medicine PGME curricula: 1) standalone, 2) adjunct, and 3) blended." Standalone approaches use PBL as the primary instructional mode; adjunct approaches add PBL sessions to traditional lecture-based delivery; blended approaches integrate PBL within established curriculum methods such as rotations, conferences, and engaged-classroom sessions.
requirements: Synchronous delivery involving multiple learners, since real-time interaction and problem-solving are described as essential features of PBL
constraints: The taxonomy applies to synchronous formats only; asynchronous environments were excluded from the review
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning
self-directed learning
application of learning to clinical practice
examples: Klein et al. paired a large-group lecture academic half-day with a small-group PBL session on the same topic the following month, an adjunct approach

description: The review uses a medical-education adaptation of Kirkpatrick's four-level training-outcome model to categorize the heterogeneous outcomes reported across included studies. The adapted model, per the article, "encompasses the same four levels, with some modification: the learners' satisfaction with program content and delivery (Level 1), change in opinion about the topic (Level 2A), change in knowledge and/or skills (Level 2B), change in behavior (Level 3), and patient outcomes (Level 4)." constraints: The authors note the framework may have underrepresented process-based benefits such as enhanced teamwork and self-directed learning

description: The review uses the updated Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) to code and organize implementation determinants. Determinants were "mapped across CFIR’s five domains (Innovation, Outer setting, Inner setting, Individuals, and Implementation process)", coded one at a time to the domain, subdomain, and construct best reflecting the original description, with two researchers coding independently and discrepancies resolved by consensus. constraints: The review maps reported determinants rather than evaluating strength of evidence; no formal methodological quality appraisal was conducted

description: The review describes how the six included interventions, while sharing the goal of enhancing leadership competencies and fostering a supportive EBP environment, drew on different theoretical mechanisms: supportive leadership and team dynamics, organizational behavior, experiential learning and social networks, adult learning and leadership behavior, proactive behavior and organizational readiness, and self-efficacy and implementation science. description: Narrative medicine is defined in the article as "an approach to the use of narrative to collect and interpret information on the patient's experience of illness", encouraging physicians to focus on patients' real feelings rather than laboratory and imaging results. title: Allocate sufficient instructional hours so TBL interventions can mature before expecting full benefits
description: Based on their duration subgroup analysis, the authors recommend that curriculum designers give TBL enough time to reach its full effect, since studies lasting more than 4 weeks showed larger effect sizes than shorter ones. The recommendation is grounded in a subgroup contrast, not a manipulated optimum.

title: Kirkpatrick model mapping as the organising framework for evaluating technology-enhanced surgical training evidence
description: The review uses the Kirkpatrick model of training evaluation as its organising axis, mapping each included study's reported outcomes to a level: level 1 reaction, level 2 learning (simulator scores, kinematic metrics, R-OSATS), level 3 transfer to operative behaviour, and level 4 patient outcomes. It reports that "the available evidence is concentrated at level 2 (learning — simulator scores, kinematic metrics, R-OSATS)". This framework lets the review show that no study reached transfer or patient-level outcomes, bounding what the technology evidence can support.

constraints: No included study reported level 3 or level 4 outcomes, limiting extrapolation to clinical performance

title: Towle's six-level taxonomy of patient involvement in medical education
description: The review adopts Towle's taxonomy, which "delineates a continuum of patient involvement in medical education across six progressive levels." It runs from patients represented abstractly in case studies, through standardized or volunteer patients with scripted roles, patients sharing personal experiences, patient-teachers involved in instruction and evaluation, patients as equal partners in teaching, assessment, and curriculum development, up to sustained educator roles with participation in institutional governance and policy. The review uses it to distinguish genuine co-teaching from simulated-patient roles in its inclusion criteria.

target_learning_goals: attitudes toward people with disabilities
communication skills
inclusive healthcare practice
examples: The review excluded studies where individuals with Disorders of Intellectual Development participated only as simulated patients, applying the taxonomy's distinction between scripted roles and substantive instructional roles

title: Three-level iceberg organization of TB health educator competency: visible competencies, supporting competencies, and core drivers
description: The article organizes its seven-dimension competency system using the Iceberg Competency Model into three levels. Above the waterline are "Visible Competencies": professional knowledge base, communication and health education skills, and clinical practice and problem-solving skills, described as directly observable and measurable. Supporting competencies (learning and development, collaboration and resource integration) bridge to the deepest level, "Core Drivers": professionalism and self-management, and research and innovation competence, which the authors describe as hardest to cultivate but most enduring. The dimensions are presented as progressive and mutually reinforcing.
requirements: Requires the seven-dimension, 24-category, 63-element indicator system as the content being organized into the three iceberg levels
constraints: The three-level organization is the authors' interpretive mapping onto the Iceberg Competency Model, not an empirically tested structure

target_learning_goals: Professional competency development for TB health education practice
examples: Figure 3 depicts the seven dimensions stacked in trapezoids divided by a waterline into visible competencies, supporting competencies, and core drivers

title: Draft competency-profile for qualifying student P2P-teachers in human medicine

The draft "reflects the interplay of medical skills, on the one hand (yellow colors), and teaching skills (blue colors), on the other hand", treating them as two sides of the same coin without ranking them.

article_title: Innovative technologies in psychiatry education: a systematic review.
citation: Mokhtari Saba, Mokhtari Asieh, Shariat Seyed Vahid, Nazeri Astaneh Ali, Shalbafan Mohammadreza. (2026). Innovative technologies in psychiatry education: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09573-1
title: Kirkpatrick and Miller framework mapping of psychiatry education technology evidence
description: The review maps its included studies onto two established evaluation frameworks to locate the evidence's level. According to Kirkpatrick's model, most studies demonstrated effects at Level 2 (learning), with only a few reporting Level 1 (learner satisfaction) and none reaching Levels 3 or 4. On Miller's pyramid, most interventions addressed the 'knows' and 'knows how' levels, while HFSs and immersive VR achieved the 'shows how' level. The review uses this mapping to highlight "the critical gap in evidence for their long-term impact on professional practice and patient care."
requirements: Studies must report outcomes classifiable into Kirkpatrick levels or Miller pyramid levels for the mapping to apply
constraints: None of the included studies evaluated the 'does' level of actual clinical performance or patient outcomes (Kirkpatrick Levels 3–4)
target_learning_goals: psychiatric knowledge
clinical skills
attitudes such as empathy and stigma reduction
examples: The review classified the nine included trials' outcomes (knowledge tests, diagnostic reasoning tasks, OSATS skill demonstrations) within the two frameworks' levels

article_title: Structured approaches to improving outcomes of oral exam in medical and paramedical education: A systematic review and evidence-based framework.
citation: Torab-Miandoab A, Ghafourifard M, Habibi-Chenaran S, Ghaffarifar S. (2026). Structured approaches to improving outcomes of oral exam in medical and paramedical education: A systematic review and evidence-based framework. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0355461
title: Comprehensive evidence-based framework for optimized oral examination execution
description: The review distills its synthesis into a unified, multi-dimensional framework for implementing oral examinations in medical and paramedical education, organized across dimensions including type of exam, delivery mode, duration and timing, question types, content scope, and scoring methods. For each dimension it lists the full option space and names a "Best Evidence-Based Choice", recommending "Objective Structured Viva Examination (OSVE)/ Multi-station" as exam type, "Hybrid synchronous (face-to-face + online synchronous)" delivery, "8–12 minutes per station with buffer and timing signals", and case-based progressive disclosure with communication and ethical scenarios. The framework is presented in Table 6 and Fig 5 and is intended to optimize outcomes by enhancing effectiveness and reliability.
requirements: Adherence to the framework's evidence-based choices across dimensions (exam type, delivery, timing, question format, scoring) as the article states adherence is expected to optimize outcomes
constraints: Derived from a review whose included studies were predominantly limited by restricted generalizability (91.3%) and small samples (49.5%)
target_learners: Medical and paramedical students, residents, and trainees across undergraduate and postgraduate health professions education
target_learning_goals: Assessment of clinical reasoning, communication, professionalism, and professional competencies via oral examination
examples: The framework recommends multi-station OSVEs, hybrid delivery, combined rubrics, and AI-assisted scoring, per the review's conclusions

article_title: Cumulative Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs) and School Outcomes During Adolescence: A Scoping Review.
citation: Stoddard, S. A., Moore, C. R., Polick, C. S., & Moss, J. M. (2026). Cumulative Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs) and School Outcomes During Adolescence: A Scoping Review. The Journal of School Health. https://doi.org/10.1111/josh.70209
title: Biopsychosocial pathway framework linking cumulative ACE exposure to adolescent school outcomes
description: The review organizes mediational evidence through a biopsychosocial model in which cumulative ACE exposure may influence school outcomes through biopsychosocial, mental/behavioral health, and more proximal school processes. Repeated or chronic adversity may lead to toxic stress, disrupting executive functioning, emotion regulation, and other learning processes, which are then associated with behavioral health, engagement, attendance, achievement, and classroom functioning, ultimately relating to high school completion. The framework is illustrated in the review's Figure 2.
requirements: Longitudinal designs are recommended to test pathways from ACEs, distinct behavioral health symptoms, school engagement, disciplinary experiences, academic performance, and educational attainment
constraints: The review notes current mediational evidence is preliminary and that additional research on mediating pathways, protective factors, and at-risk subpopulations is a critical first step
target_learners: US adolescents aged 12-18 exposed to cumulative adverse childhood experiences
target_learning_goals: Improved school engagement, attendance, academic achievement, and high school completion
examples: The review's Figure 2 diagrams pathways linking cumulative ACE exposure to adolescent school outcomes through biopsychosocial, mental/behavioral health, and proximal school processes
