citation: Kaihlaniemi, J., Suonnansalo, P., Kääriäinen, M., Kaakinen, P., Litendahl, M., Paukkonen, L., Laukkonen, K., & Oikarinen, A. (2025). Patients' Experiences of Healthcare Professionals' Competence in Digital Counselling in Healthcare Settings—A Qualitative Systematic Review. Journal of Advanced Nursing. https://doi.org/10.1111/jan.16663
title: Digital counselling competence comprises three synthesised areas: efficient counselling, self-management support, and reciprocal relationship-building
description: The review's meta-aggregation of 41 findings from 16 qualitative studies yielded three synthesised findings describing the competence patients expect of healthcare professionals in digital counselling. As the review states, 'competence in digital counselling includes the competence to provide digital counselling that is efficient and enables counselling to be implemented in health care, supports patients to self-manage and establishes a reciprocal counselling relationship in a digital environment.' This framework organises patient expectations into actionable competence domains for professional development.
requirements: Digital counselling competence requires a range of mutually supportive knowledge, skills, attitudes and values, as competence is defined in the review's background.
constraints: The synthesis is based on qualitative studies of adult patients in healthcare settings where communication was reciprocal (text-based or video-mediated), excluding one-sided interactions such as chatbots or viewing digital material.

Understand patient expectations of digital counselling competence

citation: Frangi Duccio, Bardacci Yari, Magi Camilla Elena, El Aoufy Khadija, Longobucco Yari, Iovino Paolo, Amato Carla, Balestri Chiara, Forciniti Carolina, Rasero Laura, Iozzo Pasquale, Lucchini Alberto, Bambi Stefano. (2025). Exploring the use of low-cost simulation in nursing education: a scoping review. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2025-099968
title: Five-category taxonomy of low-cost simulation strategies in nursing education
description: The review organises low-cost simulation in nursing education into five inductively derived categories: task trainers, mannequin simulators, computer-based tools, hybrid forms and serious games. The categories were "inductively derived from the data during the data charting process". Hybrid forms, the largest group, "combine various tools, enhance training by integrating real-world materials with low-cost simulators". The taxonomy maps how each strategy addresses technical and non-technical competencies across clinical areas.
requirements: Studies must describe the simulation strategy and its educational application to be categorised
constraints: The literature lacks a standard cost benchmark, so no specific economic thresholds were applied; 'low-cost' status relied on authors' descriptions
target_learning_goals: Technical clinical skills
Non-technical skills including communication, teamwork and clinical reasoning
examples: Task trainers replicating individual body parts including 3D-printed tracheas
Serious games such as the board game GridlockED for multipatient environments

description: The review identifies inconsistent cost reporting as a central barrier to evaluating low-cost simulation: only 38% of included studies reported cost-related factors, and the authors state that "the lack of objective cost data limits the ability to validate this categorisation across contexts". The principle calls on researchers and educators to report cost items — materials, simulators, sessions, maintenance, instructor fees and consumables — when implementing or studying low-cost simulation.
requirements: Cost reporting should cover not only initial material and equipment expenses but also ongoing costs for maintenance, instructor fees, consumable materials and repeated sessions
constraints: The review notes the literature lacks a standard cost benchmark, complicating direct comparisons between studies
target_learning_goals: Cost-effective simulation-based clinical skills training
examples: The review found only 15 of 39 studies reported cost-related factors, with materials and simulator costs most frequently itemised

title: Extended reality simulators for robotic surgery training
description: Extended reality (XR) simulators, encompassing virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR), and mixed reality (MR), are tools for training robotic surgery novices outside the operating room. The article describes them as "safe, ethical, and repeatable alternatives that produce objective measures of performance and allow real-time feedback to trainees." The most popular simulator identified is the da Vinci Surgical Simulator (dVSS), with the Mimic dV-Trainer also commonly used across included studies.
requirements: Participants must be robotic novices who have never used a robotic surgical device, or have limited experience with robot-assisted surgeries.

title: Use extended reality simulators as a low-cost, low-risk environment for training robotic surgery novices
description: The article supports implementing extended reality simulators into surgical training programs as an alternative or complement to dry lab training. The authors conclude that "extended reality simulators allow for an increase in variability in situation tasks and repeatability that these other models do not offer." XR training significantly improved time to complete versus no training and produced comparable results to dry lab training on both outcome measures.
requirements: Simulators must produce objective measures of performance and allow real-time feedback to trainees.
constraints: The cost of a dVSS simulator is much less than a full da Vinci surgical robot, but still substantial (approximately $127,000).

citation: Serrano Carlos M., Atenas María J., Rodriguez Patricio J., Vervoorn Johanna M. (2025). From Virtual Reality to Reality: Fine‐Tuning the Taxonomy for Extended Reality Simulation in Dental Education. European Journal of Dental Education. https://doi.org/10.1111/eje.13064
title: XR-simulation taxonomy for dental education along the virtuality continuum
description: The article proposes a uniform taxonomy for extended reality (XR) simulation in dental education, categorising 141 reviewed articles into Virtual Reality (VR), Mixed Reality (MR), Augmented Reality (AR), Augmented Virtuality (AV) and Computer Simulation (CS). The taxonomy is built on recurring features identified across the literature: 'stereoscopic (3D) vision, users' immersion, interaction, modification possibilities and the presence of haptic feedback'. These features serve as 'building blocks' for general definitions of each category within the virtuality continuum, adapted from Milgram & Kishino.
requirements: Each study must include a theoretical description of XR and/or the investigated ITT to be categorised within the taxonomy.
constraints: The taxonomy was developed for dental/maxillofacial education and does not summarise learning outcomes or the effect of technology components on the learning process.
target_learning_goals: preclinical and clinical skills training using digital simulation

description: The review recommends that national authorities and regulators commission research exploring how well current prescribing assessments predict later workplace performance, "with particular regard to patient safety", and that institutions consider measuring predictive validity of their own assessments. description: The review recommends that trainers "utilize combined force- and motion-based assessment as objective measures of technical competency, to ensure patient safety and to improve surgical outcomes." article_title: The Implementation of Data-Driven Assessment into Laparoscopic Skills Training: A Systematic Review.
citation: Hardon Sem F., Horeman Tim, Reijers Sophie J. M., Schoonmade Linda J., Daams Freek, van der Peet Donald L. (2025). The Implementation of Data-Driven Assessment into Laparoscopic Skills Training: A Systematic Review. Surgical Innovation. https://doi.org/10.1177/15533506251336824
title: Data-driven assessment tools as automated sensor-based systems measuring continuous variables representing technical skills
description: The review defines data-driven assessment tools as "automated sensor-based systems or devices that measured and recorded continuous variables that represented technical skills." These technology-enhanced tools use single or combined metric assessment, distinguishing them from non-automated methods like stopwatches, counted errors, or assessment forms. The review categorizes assessed skills into instrument handling (path length, speed, smoothness), tissue manipulation (maximum forces, mean force, force penalties), suture integrity (breaking strength, knot loosening), and anastomotic integrity (air pressure leakage).

constraints: Studies reporting only time to complete a task measured by stopwatch, counted errors, or assessment forms were excluded as non-automated

Laparoscopic competency
examples: The most frequently used systems were LAP mentor, Forcesense, LAP sim, MIST VR, ProMIS, and Aurora

description: The review organizes the six included studies into three themes: "(1) preparation to care for people living with dementia, (2) impact of dementia care training and (3) experience of caring of people living with dementia." Preparation covers undergraduate curriculum needs; training impact covers knowledge, confidence and empathy outcomes; experience covers transition challenges, barriers and facilitators in acute care. title: ICAP framework for classifying cognitive engagement in wound care education
description: The review uses the ICAP framework by Chi and Wylie, which "distinguishes four modes of engagement: interactive, constructive, active and passive," to classify wound care teaching methods. It suggests "students' learning experience improves if students are actively engaging with the presented content," with interactive and constructive modes hypothesised as most effective. Most reviewed interventions used interactive or constructive modes such as hands-on clinical application and case-based discussions.

citation: Dorrestein L, Ritter C, De Mol Z, Wichtel M, Cary J, Vengrin C, Artemiou E, Adams CL, Ganshorn H, Coe JB, Barkema H, Hecker KG. (2025). Validity evidence for communication skills assessment in health professions education: a scoping review. BMJ Open 15(9):e096799. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2024-096799
title: Communication skills assessment studies should explicitly define the communication construct, clarify validity sources, and define the intended purpose and use of scores
description: The review recommends that gaps in validity evidence be addressed by studies that "explicitly defin[e] the communication skill construct(s) assessed, clarifying the validity source(s) reported and defining the intended purpose and use of the scores (ie, for learning and feedback, for decision making purposes)". This principle guides assessment design toward evidence-centred practice, linking construct definition, validation process and score interpretation. It stems directly from the review's finding that only 18% of studies defined the construct and only 10% used a validity framework.
requirements: A clear statement of the communication construct(s) to be measured before designing the assessment
Specification of the situation in which the assessment will be employed and the level of validity evidence needed
Employment of a validation process and continuous quality assurance of the assessment
constraints: Score interpretation is constrained by the heterogeneity of the definition of communication skills across the health professions and the reporting quality of the studies
target_learning_goals: Communication skills assessment for learning and feedback
Communication skills assessment for summative decision making
examples: The review's four-step evidence-centred design approach: stating the construct, listing validity evidence sought, specifying assessment methods, and interpreting the resulting data

This recommendation is grounded in the subgroup analyses showing larger and more consistent effects for longer, moderate-intensity interventions on mathematics and overall academic achievement. description: The review concludes that virtual dissection tables (VDTs) are best implemented as complementary components of anatomy education rather than replacements for cadaveric dissection. It distinguishes virtual laboratories (software-based simulation without real physical equipment) from remote laboratories (distance control of real equipment) and simulated laboratories (a broader category), preserving original terminology where studies used terms interchangeably.

title: Kolb's Experiential Learning Theory and Cognitive Load Theory as explanatory accounts of video-based virtual laboratory effectiveness
description: The review attributes the effectiveness of audiovisual virtual laboratories to two established learning theories. Kolb's Experiential Learning Theory "explains how virtual labs enable reflective observation and conceptual understanding without any hands-on experiences." Cognitive Load Theory suggests that "well-designed educational videos allow learners to have control on the pace and focus on key information, improving comprehension and retention, so unnecessary mental effort decreased." Together these theories clarify how video-based virtual labs work in online learning environments.
requirements: Well-designed educational videos that let learners control pace and focus on key information

citation: Rathleff Camilla Rams, Vergel John, Ryberg Thomas, Kristensen Jette Kolding, Telléus Patrik Kjaersdam. (2025). Medical students’ evaluation of digital problem-based learning: a mixed-methods systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07823-2
title: The ACAD framework categorizes DPBL design into social, epistemic, and set design
description: The Activity-Centered Analysis and Design (ACAD) model provides a metatheoretical framework for understanding complex learning situations by focusing on activities at the heart of student perceptions. In the context of DPBL, it categorizes instructional design options into three distinct categories: "social design" (how students engage with tasks individually, in groups, or as teams, including social roles), "epistemic design" (the tasks that students are asked to perform), and "set design" (the digital tools with which students interact). The review used this framework to categorize 453 student quotes and identify key design considerations for educators designing future DPBL interventions.
requirements: The framework requires categorization of student perceptions into social, epistemic, and set design modalities to identify design considerations.
target_learning_goals: Understanding how design choices in digital learning environments shape student experience

article_title: Learning curve for lateral lymph node dissection in rectal cancer - a systematic review of literature.
citation: Kehagias D., Baldari L., Cassinotti E., Boni L., Lampropoulos C., Kehagias I. (2025). Learning curve for lateral lymph node dissection in rectal cancer – a systematic review of literature. Techniques in Coloproctology. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10151-025-03214-3
title: Three-phase learning curve model: learning, competence, and proficiency
description: The review applies a standardized three-phase learning curve model consisting of learning, competence, and proficiency phases, supported by several studies in minimally invasive surgery. The learning curve follows a characteristic pattern: an initial phase of rapid learning and improvement, followed by a plateau phase indicating competence, and ultimately a phase of mastery or proficiency. Studies reporting only two phases were classified as learning and competence; studies with four phases were classified as two learning phases followed by competence and proficiency.

constraints: Several confounding factors can affect the shape and interpretation of a learning curve, including prior experience, individual background, and the availability of appropriate equipment

article_title: Diabetes knowledge of nurses in sub-Saharan Africa: a scoping review.

title: Scoping review framework mapping nurses' diabetes knowledge, care knowledge, and knowledge-acquisition factors in SSA hospitals
description: The review organises the literature around three review questions: nurses' knowledge of diabetes, nurses' knowledge of diabetes management or care, and factors hindering or promoting knowledge acquisition. It applied the Arksey and O'Malley scoping methodological framework, which "included the following steps: identifying the research question; searching for relevant studies; selecting studies; charting data; and collating, summarising and reporting the results." Primary outcomes covered knowledge of diabetes types, pathophysiology, diagnostics, medications and management; secondary outcomes covered personal, organisational and support-system barriers and facilitators.
requirements: Studies addressing nurses involved in care for adults with diabetes in hospital settings in SSA, published in English from 2000 to 2024.
constraints: The protocol was not pre-registered; studies were not formally assessed for quality; only English-language studies were included, possibly missing Francophone Africa.

examples: The review screened 2974 retrieved records and included 20 studies conducted across twelve SSA countries.

description: This scoping review proposes a two-category taxonomy for faculty development competencies in interprofessional health education. The first category covers interprofessional collaborative and facilitation competencies for IPE, drawing on the CIHC and IPEC frameworks. The second category covers pedagogical, theoretical, and methodological foundations including learning theories, teaching-learning strategies, and assessment processes. The review concludes that "the domains of competencies for faculty development in IPE can be divided into two groups: 1) Interprofessional collaborative and facilitation competencies for IPE and 2) Pedagogical, theoretical, and methodological foundations for faculty development in IPE."

article_title: Integrating Digital Technologies into the Teaching of Intercultural Competences: A Systematic Literature Mapping.
citation: Basantes-Andrade A, Bastidas-Amador G, Ruiz-Chagna C, Congo-Cervantes M, Quintana-Andrade G. (2025). Integration of digital technologies in the teaching of intercultural competences: systematic literature mapping. F1000Research 14:772. https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.167364.1
title: Systematic literature mapping as a methodological framework for analyzing digital intercultural competence research
description: The study applies systematic literature mapping (SLM) following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, defined as providing "a comprehensive overview of the available literature within a defined time frame, identifying trends, methodological approaches, and research gaps". SLM complements systematic literature review by offering "a preliminary exploratory analysis" before more restrictive SLR criteria. The method uses ten Kitchenham-based quality criteria on a Likert-type scale with a minimum inclusion threshold of 7 out of 10 points, applied by five independent reviewers with consensus-based discrepancy resolution.
requirements: Studies must be peer-reviewed, open-access articles in English or Spanish from Scopus, Web of Science, and SciELO, published between January 2005 and December 2024, directly addressing technology integration in intercultural competence teaching
constraints: No inferential statistical analyses, heterogeneity analyses, or sensitivity analyses were performed, as the mapping design did not include quantitative comparisons between groups
target_learning_goals: intercultural competence development through digital technologies
examples: Screening of 176 records through PRISMA 2020 identification, screening, and inclusion phases yielded 23 included studies assessed with a ten-criterion rubric

title: Six-theme framework for AI integration in orthopaedic education and training
description: The review organises its findings into six key themes: "(a) AI-driven simulation and Virtual Reality in Orthopaedic Training, (b) Adaptive Learning Platforms and Personalized Education Pathways, (c) Computer Vision and Objective Skill Assessment, (d) AI Applications in Orthopaedic Research, (e) Predictive Analytics for Surgical Education and Outcome Prediction, and (f) Challenges and Ethical Considerations in AI Integration." This framework maps the landscape of AI applications across orthopaedic education and research, distinguishing between mature technologies (VR/AR simulators) and nascent ones (generative AI), and highlighting cross-cutting concerns of bias, cost, validation gaps and ethical considerations.

constraints: Evidence is constrained by heterogeneity in study designs and outcome measures, precluding meta-analysis

citation: Dutt Deepaysh DCS, Hohnen Harry, Kulshrestha Subham, Razavi Hessom. (2025). Simulation models in direct ophthalmoscopy education: a systematic review. Canadian Medical Education Journal. https://doi.org/10.36834/cmej.79989
title: McGaghie's levels of simulation-based translational outcomes as applied to direct ophthalmoscopy simulation
description: The review applies McGaghie's proposed levels of simulation-based translational outcomes, adapted to direct ophthalmoscopy, as an effectiveness assessment framework. Levels range from "Internal acceptability" (trainee satisfaction with simulator, Level 1) through "Contained effects" (changes in performance using the simulator, Level 2), "Downstream effects" (changes in clinical behaviour, Level 3), "Target effects" (changes in patient outcomes, Level 4) and "Collateral effects" (hospital-wide or systems-level changes, Level 5). The review uses this scale alongside the Kirkpatrick Model and a Messick-based validity scale to rate each included study.
requirements: Each study's simulator design is rated against the five translational outcome levels, from internal acceptability to collateral effects
constraints: The framework as applied assesses simulation effectiveness at levels up to system-wide change, but most included studies reached only Level 1 or 2
target_learning_goals: Direct ophthalmoscopy technique
Fundus pathology identification
examples: The review rated each of the 37 included studies' effectiveness using this adapted scale, reported in Appendix A

description: The review organises community nurse training programs (CNTPs) by delivery method using Allen and Seaman's classification, distinguishing "online, hybrid and onsite training". title: Kirkpatrick's four levels of evidence for evaluating the attributable effect of teaching programs.
description: Kirkpatrick's framework outlines four ascending levels of attributable benefit of a teaching program: (1) how well trainees received a program, (2) measured learning, (3) change in behaviour attributable to the program, and (4) outcomes of training such as reduced cost or higher quality of outcomes. The review uses this framework to examine the quality of evidence available for RAS curricula assessment, noting that "The importance of an adequate before-and-after assessment approach with a control group and statistical considerations were highlighted as key to this evaluation."

title: The Modified Medical Education Research Study Quality Instrument (MMERSQI) for assessing study quality in medical education research.
description: The MMERSQI is a tool for assessing the quality of studies in medical education research, used in this review with a minimum score of 23.5 and a maximum score of 100. The review reports that "The modified MERSQI scoring does not differentiate between descriptive statistics or simple inferential statistics" and that "Points are doubled when modelling is used." The review used this tool to assess the methodological quality of the included studies, finding overall low quality.

ECE integrates early, often observational clinical experiences into pre-clinical years to contextualize theoretical knowledge. The authors recommend integration during early phases of medical training to enhance competency-based medical education.

citation: Yang Deng-Chi, Yu Yung-Chen, Lee Yi-Hsuan, Su Ruei-Ning, Lin Wei-Hung, Lai Pei-Chun. (2025). Geriatric core competencies for non-geriatricians and nurses: a scoping review. BMC Geriatrics. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12877-025-06806-8
title: Eighteen-domain integrated classification of geriatric core competencies
description: The review consolidates competencies from ten consensus studies into 18 distinct domains: basic, clinical, and social sciences of ageing, professionalism, communication, teamwork, disease and comorbidity, optimizing function, geriatric assessment, geriatric syndromes, pharmacologic/medication management, cognitive/dementia problems, falling and gait abnormalities, healthcare planning, palliative care, transitions of care, patient safety and quality care, and research. The authors state this "integrated domain-based classification" allowed them "to systematically organize and compare competencies across different sources." Pharmacologic/medication management and cognitive/dementia problems each appeared in seven of the ten studies.
requirements: Competencies must be derived from studies using structured consensus methods such as expert consensus or the Delphi method for comparability
constraints: The classification was applied to the ten included studies, mostly published before 2017 and mostly from American institutions

title: Bloom's revised taxonomy as a framework for classifying geriatric core competencies
description: The review applies Bloom's revised taxonomy (2001) to classify each competency verb into six cognitive process dimensions (Remembering, Understanding, Applying, Analyzing, Evaluating, Creating) and four knowledge dimensions (Factual, Conceptual, Procedural, Metacognitive Knowledge). The authors note "Bloom's taxonomy can serve as a useful framework for understanding and analysing the geriatric core competencies under review," and that applying this "taxonomical lens" highlighted the cognitive and knowledge-level distribution, not just frequency. Four researchers independently classified competencies, resolving discrepancies by consensus.
requirements: Classification requires examining each verb in the competencies and identifying the corresponding taxonomy category
constraints: The review notes Bloom's taxonomy had been applied to osteopathic competency analysis but not previously to geriatric core competencies
target_learning_goals: cognitive-level alignment of geriatric competency objectives

article_title: Angoff methods in standard setting in health professional education: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
citation: Kannan, S., & Gowri, S. (2025). Angoff methods in standard setting in health professional education: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education, 25, 1727. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08300-6
title: Angoff methods as a flexible family of standard-setting approaches
description: The article frames the Angoff method not as a single technique but as "a flexible family of approaches with distinct outcomes." The family includes Traditional Angoff, Modified Angoff, Angoff (Yes/No), Angoff Group (Yes/No), Three-level Angoff, and Mastery Angoff, each differing in how judges estimate borderline candidate performance. The choice of variant allows for the deliberate setting of more lenient or stringent standards, making variant selection a conscious decision aligned with assessment purpose and context.
requirements: Requires a panel of expert judges to estimate the probability that a minimally competent candidate would answer each test item correctly.
constraints: An uninformed choice of variant can lead to unintended pass rates.
target_learners: Undergraduate and postgraduate learners in medicine and other health professions
target_learning_goals: Establishing defensible cut scores for minimum competence in health professional assessments

title: Select the Angoff variant deliberately, aligned with assessment purpose and context
description: Because Angoff variants differ substantially in stringency and reliability, educators should select a specific variant as "a conscious decision aligned with the assessment's purpose and context." The Modified Angoff with a reality check is recommended as the preferred variant for psychometrically defensible and reliable processes, while the Angoff (Yes/No) method should be employed with caution and only alongside extensive judge training.

constraints: The choice of variant allows for deliberate setting of more lenient or stringent standards; an uninformed choice can lead to unintended pass rates.

title: Six-step TBL structure for ethics education
description: The review describes a recurring six-step TBL structure used across studies: pre-class preparation, individual readiness assurance test (iRAT), team readiness assurance test (tRAT), immediate feedback (tFAT), team application exercises (tAPP), and reflection. This structure was applied to ethics topics including medical ethics, bioethics, and research ethics, using frameworks such as the Four-Box Method for case analysis.

title: Human experts should routinely fact-check LLM-generated MCQ content and pilot questions before formal use
description: The article recommends that "Human experts within the field of study are required to routinely fact-check the question stem and answer key generated by AI to ensure that content is accurate, coherent, unbiased, and able to accurately discriminate between students". Educators should also consider piloting LLM-generated MCQs on a small subset of students prior to formal examination use, and constraining the LLM to specific reputable resources such as course textbooks.

description: The article identifies "seven pre-defined outcomes" for assessing MCQ quality: "question relevance, question clarity, distractor quality, question accuracy/correctness, item difficulty analysis, and item discrimination analysis (point biserial correlation and item discrimination index)". The item difficulty analysis assesses the proportion of examinees who respond correctly to a given item, whereas the item discrimination index reflects how well a given item distinguishes between high- and low-scoring students. This framework provides a structured approach for evaluating generated examination questions.

title: Triadic conceptualisation of empathy comprising cognitive, affective, and behavioural components
description: The review identifies a triadic model of empathy used in three included studies, encompassing cognitive, affective, and behavioural dimensions. Cognitive empathy refers to "understanding others’ emotions intellectually", affective empathy to "sharing and mirroring emotions", and behavioural empathy to "expressing empathy through verbal or nonverbal actions (e.g., supportive statements, gestures, or listening)". This framework underpins the review's analysis of how studies defined and assessed empathy.

description: The review organizes current LLM applications in dental education into a seven-domain taxonomy: dental examinations, educational information resources, perception of LLMs in dental education, assessment of students' assignments, preclinical support, generation of test questions, and virtual patients. The review states "This review identified seven major application scenarios of LLMs in dental education" and maps each domain to its occurrence frequency, with dental examinations dominating (n = 24). The taxonomy also extends to a developmental continuum, positioning LLM support across preclinical training, clinical practice, and specialty training stages.

article_title: Virtual reality simulation to teach communication for undergraduate nursing students: a scoping review.
citation: Deng Jing, Tan Yifei, Chen Jing, Guo Xiujing, Wang Ling, Xie Chuan. (2025). Virtual reality simulation to teach communication for undergraduate nursing students: a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08450-7
title: VR simulation as a pedagogical platform for communication skills training in undergraduate nursing education
description: The review organizes evidence on VR simulation for communication training around VR's core characteristics: "interaction, immersion, immediacy, participation, and presence". These enable high-fidelity, clinically relevant communication environments that provide a safe platform for practice with flexible scheduling and customizable learning experiences. The framework positions VR as enabling safe, private practice of high-risk scenarios and deliberate, repeated practice using standardized, on-demand scenarios, supporting simulation-based mastery learning and deliberate practice frameworks.

constraints: The review notes a demonstrable gap between technological capabilities and human performance, particularly in replicating complex therapeutic communication within clinical contexts

citation: Beyene Lise Saestad, Vikman Miriam Dubland, Fugleberg Bruaset Geir Tarje, Hem Marit Helene, Andersen Elisabeth, Hammervold Unn Elisabeth. (2025). What is known about the development of relational competence in the mental health education of healthcare professionals – a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08353-7
title: Kolb's experiential learning model as a framework for developing relational competence
description: The review uses Kolb's learning model as its explanatory framework for how relational competence develops. Learning is described as connecting new knowledge with existing understanding, either by "adding knowledge to existing understanding (assimilative learning) or by restructuring established understanding (accommodative learning)". Because relational competence involves personal change, the authors argue pedagogical methods must be linked to accommodative learning, with raising awareness, critical thinking, and reflection as central concepts. The learner moves between actor and observer roles through "concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualisation, and active experimentation".

target_learners: Students enrolled in health and social care education programs whose learning involves mental health-related topics

citation: Fikria Ainun; Setiawan Slamet; Munir Ahmad (2025). A Systematic Review of Technology-Enhanced Project-Based Language Learning: Theoretical Frameworks, Project Types, and Implications for Future Research and Practice. F1000Research. https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.165491.1
title: TEPBLL is grounded in five conceptual frameworks: social constructivism, sociocultural theory, incidental vocabulary learning, communicative language learning, and self-determination theory
description: This systematic review of 31 SSCI articles on technology-enhanced project-based language learning (TEPBLL) identifies the theoretical foundations of the field. The authors report that "the study involved five major categories of theoretical frameworks or concepts, as outlined in Table 3, encompassing social constructivism, sociocultural theory, incidental vocabulary learning, communicative language learning, and self-determination theory." Social constructivism was the most cited framework, with learners acting as "developers of knowledge" through interaction, while sociocultural theory foregrounds social and cultural activities and scaffolding. The review uses these categories to organize the TEPBLL literature and to suggest that future work could combine frameworks for novelty.
requirements: Articles must report the theoretical or conceptual framework underpinning the TEPBLL intervention for this taxonomy to apply
constraints: Derived from 31 SSCI-indexed empirical articles published 2015-2024; non-SSCI and non-empirical work excluded
target_learning_goals: language skills and knowledge through project-based learning with technology
examples: Coding of frameworks was done bottom-up: researchers read articles one at a time, noted frameworks, combined similar concepts, and prepared a list of main frameworks

title: Seven project types characterize TEPBLL: telecollaborative, digital storytelling, virtual reality, video making, mobile instant messaging-based, video conferencing, and audio-visual translation projects

The authors state that "The 31 coded articles had identified seven big umbrellas of project-based language learning type, details exposed in Table 4." Each type is illustrated with named systems: telecollaborative projects use tools such as Canvas, Wikipedia, and WeChat; digital storytelling uses SlideShare and iMovie; virtual reality projects use SVVR, iVR, and Google Tour Creator; video making uses Movie Maker and YouTube; mobile instant messaging projects use WhatsApp and WeChat; video conferencing uses Skype; and audio-visual translation uses SubESPSKills and Moodle.

citation: Mac Olivia, Marshall Sarah, McFadden Kathleen, Ayre Julie, McCaffery Kirsten J, Billah Sk Masum, Muscat Danielle M. (2026). title: Seven-domain framework of health literacy competencies for health professionals
description: The review developed a framework of seven domains of health professional health literacy competencies, iteratively and deductively refined from the data and informed by health literacy expertise. The domains cover knowledge of health literacy (performance-based and self-reported), self-efficacy to address health literacy, direct observation of ability to address health literacy, self-reported frequency of using health literacy techniques, and perceived effectiveness and behavioural intentions to address health literacy. The authors state these expert-informed, iteratively developed domains "provide a structured framework that others can use to target specific competencies and to adapt or develop new measurement tools".

Interpersonal: Communication, teamwork, relationship building, and the ability to influence others. citation: Wilkes S., Maggio L. A., Martin P. C., Melton J., Zheng B. (2026). Self-Directed Learning in Health Professions Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Perspectives on Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.5334/pme.2128
title: Knowles' andragogy as the foundational framework for self-directed learning in health professions education
description: The review frames self-directed learning primarily through Knowles' andragogy, defining SDL as "a process in which individuals take the initiative, with or without the help of others, in diagnosing their learning needs, formulating learning goals, identifying resources for learning, choosing and implementing appropriate learning strategies, and evaluating learning outcomes." The framework delineates three essential components: educators as facilitators rather than content sources, learner involvement in determining needs and resources, and learner direction of implementation and evaluation. The review uses these components as coding criteria and acknowledges that empirical evidence for andragogy itself is limited.
requirements: SDL interventions must involve learners in diagnosing learning needs, formulating goals, identifying resources, and evaluating outcomes to fully embody the framework
constraints: The authors note empirical evidence for andragogy itself is limited and its assumptions (e.g., that all adult learners inherently seek autonomy) have been critiqued

description: A design recommendation from the review's conclusions: educational outcome researchers should "collect and report on characteristics of participants in their research to ensure it is applicable for practice". The review argues comprehensive demographic reporting, including co-occurring conditions, gender identity beyond the binary, and personal and perceived racial and ethnic identity, is necessary for intersectional analysis and for including marginalised subgroups of autistic people. It further recommends combining large administrative datasets with primary data collection and collaborative, co-produced research design.

description: The review recommends that because first-year students often struggle with self-direction and teamwork, "PBL should begin with structured orientation sessions that introduce its goals and methods". title: Working definition of problem-based learning as a student-centred, facilitated small-group tutorial cycle organised by an authentic problem trigger
description: The review defines PBL as "a student-centred approach delivered through facilitated small-group tutorials in which an authentic problem scenario (the trigger) is presented first and serves as the main organiser of learning". Students analyse the trigger, identify learning needs, formulate objectives, complete self-directed study, and reconvene to integrate and apply new knowledge, with the tutor facilitating process rather than delivering content. What distinguishes PBL is that students generate the learning agenda from the problem and use a structured tutorial cycle; in case-based learning cases more often support consolidation of already-taught content, while inquiry-based learning may not use a problem trigger as the central organiser.
requirements: A tutor who facilitates process and discussion rather than delivers content
constraints: Distinguished from case-based learning and inquiry-based learning by the problem trigger as central curriculum organiser and the structured tutorial cycle

article_title: Effectiveness of E-Learning in Undergraduate ENT Education: A Mixed-Methods Systematic Review.
citation: Mughal Z, Gupta KK, di Traglia R, Fruhstorfer B. (2026). Effectiveness of E‐Learning in Undergraduate ENT Education: A Mixed‐Methods Systematic Review. The Laryngoscope. https://doi.org/10.1002/lary.70164
title: Four analytical themes explain the effectiveness of e‐learning in undergraduate ENT education
description: Thematic synthesis of qualitative and qualitized data from twenty studies generated 84 unique codes, consolidated into five descriptive themes and four overarching analytical themes. The review lists these as: "1. Educational impact of e‐learning is maximized with multimedia elements. 2. Autonomy and control over e‐learning media empowers students to take charge of their education and foster self‐directed learning skills. 3. Technical issues undermine the adaptability and flexibility of the e‐learning experience. 4. E‐learning is a complementary tool rather than a stand‐alone solution, and is most effective alongside traditional face‐to‐face teaching." These themes explain the quantitative findings, linking multimedia richness and learner autonomy to consistent knowledge and confidence gains, and technical barriers plus absent hands‐on practice to limited skill development.
requirements: Qualitative or qualitized learner perception data amenable to line‐by‐line coding, descriptive theme development, and analytical theme generation
constraints: Themes emerged from undergraduate ENT e‐learning contexts; the review notes the impersonal nature of e‐learning, lack of real‐time feedback, and technical barriers as detracting factors
target_learning_goals: ENT knowledge
clinical skills
learner confidence

description: The review concludes that e‐learning should be combined with traditional instructional methods rather than used alone. description: The review concludes that educational initiatives alone are unlikely to yield sustained improvements unless accompanied by enabling organisational conditions such as adequate staffing, access to pressure-relieving equipment, and embedding prevention protocols into routine workflows. title: Integrate synchronous feedback during remote teaching with self-directed virtual teaching to optimize psychomotor learning
description: The review recommends combining the flexibility of self-directed virtual teaching with real-time instructor feedback during remote teaching. It concludes that "Integrating the flexibility of SDVT with synchronous feedback during RT can optimize psychomotor learning while maintaining instructional oversight." This design recommendation follows from findings that synchronous feedback was a key advantage of RT over purely self-directed formats.

citation: Zhang YuKun, Wang YuWei, Jiang ManYu, Sun XiHui, Tang LiYoong. (2026). title: Kirkpatrick's four-level model as an organizing framework for evaluating NTS training outcomes in emergency care.
description: The review organises its synthesis of NTS training outcomes using Kirkpatrick's four-level model, covering reaction (Level 1), learning (Level 2), behavioural change (Level 3), and clinical results (Level 4). The authors state that "the outcomes of non-technical skills training were categorized according to Kirkpatrick's four-level model". Because no included study reported participants' reactions, the summary focused on Levels 2–4, "covering learning outcomes, behavioural performance, and clinical results". This mapping clarifies that the most consistent gains occur at the learning and behaviour levels, while evidence at the clinical outcome level remains sparse.
requirements: Outcomes must be classifiable into learning, behavioural, and clinical result levels for the framework to structure the synthesis.
constraints: No included study reported Level 1 reaction outcomes, so the framework's reaction level could not be populated.
target_learners: Healthcare professionals working in emergency departments
target_learning_goals: Non-technical skills including teamwork, communication, leadership, situational awareness, and decision-making

title: Mediational pathway in which NTS training shapes team cognition, coordination, and observable behaviours that are plausibly upstream of safety and timeliness outcomes.
description: The review proposes a conceptual mechanism account in which NTS training exerts its effects "primarily by shaping team cognition, coordination, and observable behaviours, rather than acting directly on distal clinical endpoints". Simulation followed by structured debriefing strengthens shared mental models and role clarity, reducing coordination losses; situation displays and checklists operate as "cognitive scaffolds that lower working-memory load, increase cue salience, and facilitate global monitoring and timely updates". Brief refreshers and micro-debriefs promote retrieval practice and error-based learning that consolidate habits.
requirements: Debriefing quality must be sufficient for simulation to strengthen shared mental models and role clarity.
constraints: The pathway is indirect: patient-level outcomes were infrequently evaluated, and the review notes the difficulty of attributing downstream clinical outcomes to educational interventions.
target_learners: Healthcare professionals working in emergency departments
target_learning_goals: Team cognition, coordination, and observable team behaviours in resuscitation and emergency care

title: An 11-cluster competency framework for academic global surgery education
description: The review developed a competency framework by organizing thematic clusters from identified academic global surgery programs. It consists of 11 clusters: Surgical Systems and Health Systems Science; Leadership and Management; Research and Scientific Inquiry; Clinical and Technical Excellence; Policy, Advocacy and Diplomacy; Health Equity and Social Determinants; Education and Mentorship; Ethics, Cultural Competency and Professionalism; Innovation and Implementation Science; Communication and Interdisciplinary Collaboration; and Emergency and Humanitarian Surgery. Each cluster includes related sub-competencies and representative examples drawn from program content, with relative emphasis ranging from "Very Common" to "Less Common".
requirements: Derived from a scoping review of peer-reviewed studies and grey literature describing academic global surgery programs between 2000 and 2024.
constraints: The framework reflects the programs captured in this review; the authors note no universally accepted core competency framework currently guides these programs.

title: Three-category taxonomy of AR/VR training technologies: haptic simulators, head-mounted devices, and software platforms
description: The review establishes a taxonomy classifying AR/VR educational interventions into three groups. As the authors state, different AR and VR tools were "categorized into three groups: haptic simulators, head-mounted devices, and software platforms". Haptic simulators are high-fidelity VR systems providing force-feedback; head-mounted displays offer immersive 3D visual environments often without tactile feedback; software-based platforms run on standard computers, tablets, or smartphones without specialized hardware. The taxonomy was applied to the 25 included randomized controlled trials and detailed in Tables 3, 4 and 5.

description: Moriña's (2021) framework on inclusive pedagogy draws heavily from previous research evidenced in a systematic review and is particularly relevant in higher education. It "encourages educators to reflect on their underlying (1) beliefs, (2) knowledge, (3) design and (4) actions of EDI approaches to T&L". The framework is rooted in the belief that students are valuable contributors to the T&L process and are seen as an asset to the T&L environment, shifting the focus from providing learning opportunities for most students to focusing on providing opportunities for all students.

title: Inclusive pedagogy is defined as an approach to teaching and learning that supports teachers to respond to individual differences between learners but avoids the marginalisation that can occur when some students are treated differently
description: The review adopts Florian and Spratt's (2013) definition of inclusive pedagogy as "an approach to teaching and learning that supports teachers to respond to individual differences between learners, but avoids the marginalisation that can occur when some students are treated differently". In adopting an inclusive pedagogical approach, educators not only encourage difference, they celebrate it, and see difference as a strength. This approach creates the optimal environment for the inclusion of all individuals through the intentional adoption of repeatable, flexible and individualized learning in an inclusive learning environment.
requirements: Educators need to have an in‐depth understanding of how and what students learn, and what students' individual needs are including disabilities.

Whilst they do not explicitly define inclusive pedagogy, they affirm the need for pedagogical approaches that are theoretically appropriate, equitable, inclusive, and responsive to diverse perspectives. The toolkit provides specific questions for educators wanting to adopt inclusive pedagogy, which promotes the inclusion of student views.

title: INACSL Standards of Best Practice for healthcare simulation
description: The International Nursing Association for Clinical Simulation and Learning (INACSL) Standards of Best Practice were the most widely adopted standards in the reviewed studies. Studies that embedded these standards evidenced a responsive approach to the inclusion of students through acknowledging the diversity among learners, and the adoption of psychological safety, needs assessments and flexible and repeatable learning. The INACSL Best Practice Standards indicate that "simulations should be designed with experts and learners" and evaluated by participants, peer clinicians, educators, stakeholders and all involved in the simulation.

citation: Aulakh Jasmine, Wahab Hana, Richards Christine, Bidaisee Satesh, Ramdass Prakash V. A. K. (2025). Self-directed learning versus traditional didactic learning in undergraduate medical education: a systemic review and meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06449-0
title: SDL should be incorporated into undergraduate medical curricula as an effective learning strategy
description: The authors recommend that self-directed learning be deliberately incorporated into undergraduate medical curricula, on the grounds that their meta-analysis found a significant pooled advantage in exam scores over traditional didactic learning. They state that "when used appropriately and strategically as a learning strategy, SDL can be beneficial to medical education and should be incorporated into the curriculum." Educators are encouraged to tailor curricular components and explore pedagogical approaches that support SDL.
requirements: Educators should provide technology-enhanced learning tools, mentorship or guidance, and a supportive learning environment that promotes autonomy and self-regulation, as stated by the authors.
constraints: The authors caution that SDL "may not be as beneficial as traditional in-classroom didactic lectures for selected cognitive competencies or knowledge acquisition for certain subject areas."
The practical SDL subgroup did not reach statistical significance, so the recommendation is best supported for theoretical SDL.
target_learning_goals: Cognitive performance and knowledge application in medical curricula
examples: The review's meta-analysis of 14 studies found SDL favoured over TDL in 11 studies, with a pooled mean difference of 2.399.

title: Self-Directed Learning as a theory of andragogy
description: The article frames Self-Directed Learning as "a theory of andragogy in which adult learners take their own initiative to identify and tailor their individual learning process and outcomes." It traces the theory to Garrison (1997), building on Malcolm Knowles' theory of andragogy, and specifies that SDL "requires the capacity to identify learning needs, select resources for learning, implement learning strategies and assess the outcomes achieved." In undergraduate medical education, SDL is operationalized through students formulating their own learning goals.

constraints: SDL was applied to a limited subset of topics within undergraduate medical curricula in the reviewed studies, which the authors note may skew perceptions of its effectiveness.

Critical thinking
examples: The review's included studies implemented SDL through formats such as case-based learning, problem-based learning, e-learning modules, and simulation-based training.

description: The review applies the Kirkpatrick model, "which is globally used to evaluate the results of training and learning programs", as its organizing framework for classifying learning effects beyond participant opinions. Level 2 captures changes in residents' knowledge and skills observed during video review, level 3 captures how residents change behaviour by optimising clinical care, and level 4 captures impact on patient and healthcare outcomes. The review explicitly excludes Kirkpatrick level 1 studies because that level "only measures their opinion on the method used".

article_title: Current level of rheumatology teaching amongst undergraduate medical students: a systematic literature review.
citation: Kouranloo K, Myall N, Christie J. (2025). Current level of rheumatology teaching amongst undergraduate medical students: a systematic literature review. Clinical Rheumatology. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10067-024-07297-5
title: Mandate a minimum required number of dedicated rheumatology teaching hours delivered by specialists
description: The review recommends that undergraduate programmes introduce a minimum dedicated number of rheumatology teaching hours delivered by specialists, because limited exposure has decreased student awareness of the specialty and is associated with poor career uptake. The authors state the need "to not only introduce a minimum hour of rheumatology-specific teaching delivered by the those in the specialty". This addresses the wide variation in hours (4–120 h) found across institutions.
requirements: Dedicated curriculum time allocated specifically to rheumatology
Delivery by rheumatology specialists rather than only adjacent specialties
constraints: Cross-sectional evidence base; the review notes results may not represent current teaching levels
target_learning_goals: rheumatology and musculoskeletal clinical knowledge
career awareness of rheumatology
examples: The review's included studies reported dedicated rheumatology hours ranging from 4 to 120 h per student
key_sources: Kouranloo K, Myall N, Christie J. (2025). Current level of rheumatology teaching amongst undergraduate medical students: a systematic literature review. Clinical Rheumatology. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10067-024-07297-5

article_title: Current level of rheumatology teaching amongst undergraduate medical students: a systematic literature review.
citation: Kouranloo K, Myall N, Christie J. (2025). Current level of rheumatology teaching amongst undergraduate medical students: a systematic literature review. Clinical Rheumatology. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10067-024-07297-5
title: Exposure pathway from undergraduate rheumatology teaching to specialty career choice
description: The review proposes an explanatory account in which undergraduate and Foundation Programme exposure to a specialty shapes students' awareness of what the specialty entails, which in turn influences career choice and ultimately workforce recruitment. The authors state that "the overall lack of exposure to rheumatology in undergraduate programmes has been associated with a lack of uptake of rheumatology as a career amongst medical students globally". Placement experience is described as "crucial in determining their future career choice".
requirements: Adequate exposure to the specialty throughout training
constraints: The pathway is an association drawn from cross-sectional surveys, not a tested causal model
target_learning_goals: informed specialty career choice
examples: The review cites only 154 of 4970 Foundation Programme jobs having dedicated rheumatology placement, mostly in London
key_sources: Kouranloo K, Myall N, Christie J. (2025). Current level of rheumatology teaching amongst undergraduate medical students: a systematic literature review. Clinical Rheumatology. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10067-024-07297-5

article_title: Learning by making - student-made models and creative projects for medical education: systematic review with qualitative synthesis.
citation: Yi Tan Yong, Shreyans Panwar, Vallabhajosyula Ranganath. (2025). Learning by making – student-made models and creative projects for medical education: systematic review with qualitative synthesis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06716-8
title: Explanatory schema relating learning processes activated by creative project-based lessons to effects on students and faculty
description: The review developed an explanatory framework from content analysis of 17 studies, organizing six themes — enhanced learning, collaborative learning, deep learning, student engagement, student disengagement, and faculty engagement — into "an explanatory schema relating learning processes activated by creative project-based lessons and the effects on students and faculty" (Fig. 2, Table 2). It links student-created models and projects to self-directed learning, cognitive load modulation, and metacognitive behaviours, mediated by mentorship and group learning.
requirements: Creative project-based lessons require student autonomy in design and production, team-based work, and consistent engagement from team members or mentors
constraints: Challenges include high task demands, cognitive and emotional intensiveness, and mismatch with students' professional identities
target_learning_goals: preclinical and clinical medicine topics
collaborative learning
deep learning
key_sources: Yi Tan Yong, Shreyans Panwar, Vallabhajosyula Ranganath. (2025). Learning by making – student-made models and creative projects for medical education: systematic review with qualitative synthesis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06716-8

article_title: Game-thinking; utilizing serious games and gamification in nursing education - a systematic review and meta-analysis.
citation: Nylén-Eriksen Mats, Stojiljkovic Marko, Lillekroken Daniela, Lindeflaten Katrin, Hessevaagbakke Elisabeth, Flølo Tone Nygaard, Hovland Olav Johannes, Solberg Ada Marie Svarstad Hansen Sylvia, Bjørnnes Ann Kristin, Tørris Christine. (2025). Game-thinking; utilizing serious games and gamification in nursing education – a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06531-7
title: Game-thinking as an umbrella term encompassing serious games and gamification
description: Game-thinking is presented as an umbrella term encompassing two game-based methods: serious games (SG) and gamification. The article defines SG as "full complete games that use all game design elements in various degrees for non-entertainment purposes" while "Gamification, however, applies one or a combination of game design elements in non-gaming contexts". Both share game design elements such as points, levels, avatars and leaderboards, and both represent the pedagogical design strategy of game-thinking in educational contexts.
requirements: Interventions must involve either serious games or gamification as defined by the article's eligibility criteria
constraints: The article notes a lack of consensus and uniformity in definitions, and that classifying studies into SG or gamification was challenging due to inconsistent or lacking definitions
target_learning_goals: academic achievement
student perceptions
key_sources: Nylén-Eriksen Mats, Stojiljkovic Marko, Lillekroken Daniela, Lindeflaten Katrin, Hessevaagbakke Elisabeth, Flølo Tone Nygaard, Hovland Olav Johannes, Solberg Ada Marie Svarstad Hansen Sylvia, Bjørnnes Ann Kristin, Tørris Christine. title: Nine attribute categories framework for game design elements
description: A proposed framework categorizes game design elements into nine attribute categories, aiming to consolidate research and facilitate comparisons between studies. The article notes that "A revised definition of gamification are suggested replacing game design elements with the attributes categories". The framework is recommended to improve health professions education and is used in this review to characterize interventions across included studies.
requirements: A classification system for game design elements to enable comparison across studies
constraints: The article notes that "the vast variety of these elements and the lack of standard classification system pose challenges across and within different research fields"
target_learning_goals: academic achievement

title: JBI critical appraisal checklists for RCT and quasi-experimental quality assessment
description: The Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) checklists were used to assess risk of bias and certainty of evidence. The article states that "The well-established JBI appraisal checklist for RCT´ (13 items), and the quasi-experimental checklist (9 items) assess internal validity". Studies were categorized as low quality when scoring < 50%, moderate quality with scores ≥ 50–70% and high when scoring > 70%.
requirements: Independent double-quality assessment by reviewers using the appropriate JBI checklist per study design
constraints: Quality categories are based on total scores: low < 50%, moderate 50–70%, high > 70%

article_title: Beyond traditional teaching: a systematic review of innovative pedagogical practices in higher education.
citation: Suyo-Vega JA, Fernández-Bedoya VH, Meneses-La-Riva ME. (2024). Beyond traditional teaching: a systematic review of innovative pedagogical practices in higher education. F1000Research. https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.143392.1
title: Three-category taxonomy of innovative pedagogical practices in higher education
description: The review organizes its findings into three distinct teaching strategies: "the first emphasizing student-centered approaches, the second showcasing the integration of educational technology, and the third highlighting evaluation and feedback methodologies." This taxonomy emerged from categorizing the 25 included articles and structures the review's analysis of strategies, pedagogical approaches, and their impact. It provides a framework for examining how innovative practices in university settings promote teaching and learning effectiveness.
requirements: Articles must address innovative pedagogical practices in university settings
constraints: Taxonomy derived from 25 articles published 2015-2023 in ERIC, Scopus, and ProQuest
target_learning_goals: improved teaching and learning effectiveness
key_sources: Suyo-Vega JA, Fernández-Bedoya VH, Meneses-La-Riva ME. (2024). Beyond traditional teaching: a systematic review of innovative pedagogical practices in higher education. F1000Research. https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.143392.1

article_title: Beyond traditional teaching: a systematic review of innovative pedagogical practices in higher education.
citation: Suyo-Vega JA, Fernández-Bedoya VH, Meneses-La-Riva ME. (2024). Beyond traditional teaching: a systematic review of innovative pedagogical practices in higher education. F1000Research. https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.143392.1
title: TPACK model as framework for effective technology-integrated teaching
description: The review draws on Mishra and Koehler's TPACK model, which "describes the intersection of pedagogical, technological, and content knowledge necessary for effective teaching." The model includes seven forms of knowledge intersection: pedagogical knowledge, content knowledge, technological knowledge, pedagogical content knowledge, technological pedagogical knowledge, technological content knowledge, and technological pedagogical content knowledge. The review uses this framework to analyze how faculty integrate technology with pedagogy and content in higher education teaching.
requirements: Faculty must develop technological skills and stay updated on technology-related topics
constraints: Framework applied to higher education context in this review
target_learning_goals: effective integration of technology, pedagogy, and content knowledge in teaching
key_sources: Suyo-Vega JA, Fernández-Bedoya VH, Meneses-La-Riva ME. (2024). Beyond traditional teaching: a systematic review of innovative pedagogical practices in higher education. F1000Research. https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.143392.1

article_title: Impact and perceptions of Active Learning Classrooms on reducing sedentary behaviour and improving physical and mental health and academic indicators in children and adolescents: A scoping review.
citation: Sánchez-López M, Violero-Mellado J, Martínez-Vizcaíno V, Laukkanen A, Sääkslahti A, Visier-Alfonso ME. (2025). Impact and perceptions of Active Learning Classrooms on reducing sedentary behaviour and improving physical and mental health and academic indicators in children and adolescents: A scoping review. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0317973
title: Active Learning Classrooms as flexible, student-centred learning environments
description: The review defines ALCs as "educational environments designed to facilitate not only physical movement within the classroom, but also active student-centred participation, even if unplanned". These spaces "typically include flexible, non-traditional furniture arrangements that support various collaborative and individualised working configurations". Interventions replace traditional furniture with versatile options such as standing desks, exercise balls and ottomans, often with polycentric layouts where the teacher does not occupy a central place.
requirements: flexible, non-traditional furniture arrangements supporting varied working configurations
constraints: interventions solely replacing desks with standing desks, fit balls or pedal desks were excluded as they do not modify classroom configuration or teaching-learning dynamics
target_learners: children and adolescents aged 3–18 in school classrooms
target_learning_goals: active student participation, collaboration and engagement in learning

article_title: Large Language Models in Dental Licensing Examinations: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
citation: Liu Mingxin, Okuhara Tsuyoshi, Huang Wenbo, Ogihara Atsushi, Nagao Hikari Sophia, Okada Hiroko, Kiuchi Takahiro. (2025). Large Language Models in Dental Licensing Examinations: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. International Dental Journal. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.identj.2024.10.014
title: Do not apply current LLMs to dental education or clinical diagnosis until their accuracy reaches the required threshold
description: The review concludes that applying LLMs to dental education and clinical diagnosis at this stage is high-risk and inappropriate. It reasons that "the integrate accuracy rates for GPT-3.5, GPT-4, and Bard were 54%, 72%, and 56%, respectively – falling significantly short of the 95% threshold" cited as required for medical education and clinical diagnostics. The principle therefore withholds deployment until accuracy improves.
requirements: LLM accuracy on dental knowledge must reach the 95% threshold the article cites before educational or clinical use
constraints: The article notes more advanced LLMs such as GPT-4o may show greater potential, but their performance in dental licensing examinations remains unknown
target_learning_goals: accurate dental knowledge acquisition
safe clinical diagnostic reasoning
examples: The review found integrated accuracies of 54% (GPT-3.5), 72% (GPT-4), and 56% (Bard), all below the cited 95% threshold
key_sources: Liu Mingxin, Okuhara Tsuyoshi, Huang Wenbo, Ogihara Atsushi, Nagao Hikari Sophia, Okada Hiroko, Kiuchi Takahiro. (2025). Large Language Models in Dental Licensing Examinations: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. International Dental Journal. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.identj.2024.10.014

article_title: Effectiveness of flipped classrooms in Chinese students of clinical medicine major undergoing clinical practice: a meta-analysis.
citation: Sun Xinrui, Yuan Xin, Zhang Linyu, Zhang Yi, Xiao Xue, Liu Hanmin, Ma Fang. (2025). Effectiveness of flipped classrooms in Chinese students of clinical medicine major undergoing clinical practice: a meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06737-3
title: Flipped classroom model: pre-class preparation, in-class interaction, post-class consolidation
description: The flipped classroom is a blended learning approach that "reverse[s] traditional teaching by requiring students to prepare key concepts at home and engage in collaborative activities during class time". In the included studies, this typically meant students watched teaching videos or micro-lectures before class (often via WeChat), followed by in-class interactive Q&A, case discussion, and teaching rounds, with post-class summary and review. Teachers act as "observers and guides of activities" rather than lecturers.
requirements: Requires students to prepare key concepts before class, typically via teaching videos or micro-lectures
constraints: Some students find pre-class preparation a burden and stressful; videos should be restricted to 20 minutes to be acceptable for most students
target_learners: Undergraduate clinical medicine students in clinical practice
target_learning_goals: Theoretical knowledge
Practical clinical skills
key_sources: Sun Xinrui, Yuan Xin, Zhang Linyu, Zhang Yi, Xiao Xue, Liu Hanmin, Ma Fang. (2025). Effectiveness of flipped classrooms in Chinese students of clinical medicine major undergoing clinical practice: a meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06737-3

article_title: AI in the Health Sector: Systematic Review of Key Skills for Future Health Professionals.
citation: Gazquez-Garcia J, Sánchez-Bocanegra CL, Sevillano JL. (2025). AI in the Health Sector: Systematic Review of Key Skills for Future Health Professionals. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/58161
title: Five-domain competency framework for AI use by health professionals
description: The review proposes a framework of five key competency areas deemed essential for integrating AI into clinical practice: "AI fundamentals, ethical and legal considerations, data analysis and management, communication and teamwork, and the evaluation of AI tools". Domains were derived by qualitative synthesis, with categories developed iteratively by grouping competencies that were conceptually aligned and ranked by frequency of appearance across the 7 included studies. Table S3 outlines competencies for each skill to guide educational programs and ongoing training.
requirements: Competencies should be considered only a first proposal, modifiable depending on the training program profile, technological developments, and evaluation of academic results
constraints: Derived from only 7 included studies with heterogeneous designs; no meta-analysis was performed due to heterogeneity
target_learning_goals: effective and safe use of AI technologies in clinical practice
key_sources: Gazquez-Garcia J, Sánchez-Bocanegra CL, Sevillano JL. (2025). AI in the Health Sector: Systematic Review of Key Skills for Future Health Professionals. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/58161

article_title: A scoping review of gamified applications in English language teaching: a comparative discussion with medical education.
citation: Zolfaghari Zahra, Karimian Zahra, Zarifsanaiey Nahid, Farahmandi Amir Yousef. (2025). A scoping review of gamified applications in English language teaching: a comparative discussion with medical education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06822-7
title: Taxonomy of gamification elements in TEFL applications
description: The review organizes the gamified TEFL literature around a taxonomy of game elements, counting the frequency with which each appears across the 33 included studies: "Feedback	23", challenge, points, leaderboard, leveling, time, badge, progress bar, story/narration, digital badges, avatar/character, and competition. This element inventory structures the review's comparative discussion with medical education, where feedback and competitive features are also central.
requirements: Studies must report the gamification elements used for the element-frequency mapping to apply
target_learners: English as a Foreign Language learners across primary, secondary, and higher education
target_learning_goals: language learning motivation and engagement
vocabulary, writing, speaking, reading, grammar, listening, and pronunciation skills

article_title: Virtual reality for assessment in undergraduate nursing and medical education - a systematic review.
citation: Neher Andrea N., Bühlmann Florian, Müller Martin, Berendonk Christoph, Sauter Thomas C., Birrenbach Tanja. (2025). Virtual reality for assessment in undergraduate nursing and medical education – a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06867-8
title: Align VR assessments with learning objectives and teaching methods through constructive alignment
description: The review concludes VR assessments should be integrated thoughtfully into a comprehensive pedagogical strategy rather than added as technology for its own sake. It states that "it is crucial to ensure that the technology is thoughtfully integrated into a comprehensive pedagogical strategy", guided by constructive alignment between learning objectives, teaching methods, and assessment. The review warns that complex VR scenarios ending in a single multiple-choice question waste the technology's potential.
requirements: Learning objectives, teaching methods, and VR assessments must be aligned; the review states "it is important to determine which learning objectives should be assessed in VR and train accordingly to achieve alignment between learning objectives, teaching, and assessment".
constraints: The review notes that simply integrating new technology into a training program does not inherently enhance its value.
target_learning_goals: Clinical competencies assessed in VR, e.g., Patient Care, communication skills, medical knowledge
examples: The review criticizes designing complex VR scenarios with detailed action sequences only to assess learners at the end with a single multiple-choice question answered by controller click.
key_sources: Neher Andrea N., Bühlmann Florian, Müller Martin, Berendonk Christoph, Sauter Thomas C., Birrenbach Tanja. (2025). Virtual reality for assessment in undergraduate nursing and medical education – a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06867-8

article_title: Nutritional Education in Medical Curricula and Clinical Practice: A Scoping Review on the Knowledge Deficit Amongst Medical Students and Doctors.
citation: Khiri Nasr and Kristy Howells. (2025). Nutritional Education in Medical Curricula and Clinical Practice: A Scoping Review on the Knowledge Deficit Amongst Medical Students and Doctors. Journal of Human Nutrition and Dietetics. https://doi.org/10.1111/jhn.70031
title: AfN undergraduate nutrition curriculum for medical doctors: 13 core competencies assessed through 11 graduation criteria
description: The Association for Nutrition, with the Academy of Medical Royal Colleges and the General Medical Council, launched an initiative to incorporate nutrition into UK undergraduate medical curricula, in which "13 core nutritional competencies have been developed, which are assessed through 11 graduation criteria". Competencies span Knowledge, Assessment and Skills in Intervention, covering healthy balanced diets, ethical and legal considerations, nutritional status evaluation (e.g., BMI), and initiating sensitive nutrition conversations and referrals.
requirements: National standardisation and adoption by medical schools with graduation benchmarks
target_learning_goals: nutrition science knowledge
nutritional assessment and intervention skills
