article_title: Simulation-Based Learning Supported by Technology to Enhance Critical Thinking in Nursing Students: Scoping Review.
citation: Stenseth Hege Vistven et al. (2025). Simulation-Based Learning Supported by Technology to Enhance Critical Thinking in Nursing Students: Scoping Review. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/58744
title: DeLone and McLean IS Success Model as an organizing framework for enablers and barriers of technology-supported SBL for critical thinking
description: The review used the DeLone and McLean model of information system success as a deductive lens to organize enablers and barriers identified inductively from included studies. The model "aims to evaluate the success of an IS and suggests that its dimensions are interrelated and influence each other." Dimensions include system quality, information quality, service quality, use and intention to use, satisfaction, and net benefits, each mapped to a theme such as affinity for technology, realism, accessibility, engagement and motivation, validation, return on investment, and enhanced critical thinking.
requirements: Themes were sorted into the model's predetermined categories through deductive analysis after inductive thematic analysis
constraints: The review notes its main findings on RQ 3 related primarily to the information quality and use and intention to use dimensions
target_learning_goals: critical thinking
clinical reasoning
clinical judgment
key_sources: Stenseth Hege Vistven et al. (2025). Simulation-Based Learning Supported by Technology to Enhance Critical Thinking in Nursing Students: Scoping Review. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/58744

article_title: Healthcare research and education: actively constructed research knowledge-a model for online systematic reviews and meta-analyses courses.
citation: El Ansari Walid, El-Ansari Kareem, Hany Mohamed. (2025). Healthcare research and education: actively constructed research knowledge–a model for online systematic reviews and meta-analyses courses. BMC Research Notes. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13104-025-07111-8
title: Model online SR/MA course design framework
description: The article proposes a model online SR/MA course that integrates self-paced and self-directed learning, high interactivity, expert-guided feedback, and PRISMA alignment. It is designed for busy medical and health students and clinicians, delivered via Moodle LMS, and structured so that learners progressively build skills across modules, culminating in a real learner-performed SR/MA project within virtual research teams. The framework emphasizes the 'human' factor through synchronous and asynchronous trainer-learner and learner-learner interactions.
requirements: Utilizes Moodle LMS for content delivery, assignment submission, and communication
Requires expert trainers with discipline-specific knowledge and SR/MA skills to provide individualized feedback
constraints: Designed for SR/MA training in health, medical, surgical and related fields
target_learning_goals: Conducting systematic reviews and meta-analyses
Applying PRISMA principles
Critical appraisal and quality assessment
key_sources: El Ansari Walid, El-Ansari Kareem, Hany Mohamed. (2025). Healthcare research and education: actively constructed research knowledge–a model for online systematic reviews and meta-analyses courses. BMC Research Notes. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13104-025-07111-8

article_title: Healthcare research and education: actively constructed research knowledge-a model for online systematic reviews and meta-analyses courses.
citation: El Ansari Walid, El-Ansari Kareem, Hany Mohamed. (2025). Healthcare research and education: actively constructed research knowledge–a model for online systematic reviews and meta-analyses courses. BMC Research Notes. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13104-025-07111-8
title: Seven-module progressive course structure with longitudinal manuscript preparation
description: The proposed course comprises seven modules, each with learning outcomes, interactive elements, and assessment methods. Preparation for the final module (Module 7, manuscript preparation) starts at the beginning of the course and continues as an ongoing thread across all modules in a 'building blocks' fashion. Successful completion of interactive elements in each module is a prerequisite for progression to the next module.
requirements: Successful completion of interactive elements in each module as prerequisite for progression
target_learning_goals: Systematic review methodology
Meta-analysis skills
Manuscript preparation
key_sources: El Ansari Walid, El-Ansari Kareem, Hany Mohamed. (2025). Healthcare research and education: actively constructed research knowledge–a model for online systematic reviews and meta-analyses courses. BMC Research Notes. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13104-025-07111-8

article_title: Healthcare research and education: actively constructed research knowledge-a model for online systematic reviews and meta-analyses courses.
citation: El Ansari Walid, El-Ansari Kareem, Hany Mohamed. (2025). Healthcare research and education: actively constructed research knowledge–a model for online systematic reviews and meta-analyses courses. BMC Research Notes. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13104-025-07111-8
title: Provide individualized expert feedback on assignments in online research training
description: The article recommends that online SR/MA courses provide individualized constructive feedback from expert trainers on assignments, as this enhances learning, improves teaching planning, and promotes trainees' autonomous learning abilities. The article states that evaluation and feedback are crucial from both teachers' and learners' perspectives, and that only the proposed course among those compared delivers this feature.
requirements: Expert trainers with both discipline-specific knowledge and SR/MA skills
Sufficient resources including planning and time
constraints: Providing individualized feedback necessitates expert trainers and further resources
target_learning_goals: Research synthesis skills
Autonomous learning
examples: The proposed course delivers one-on-one individualized feedback from expert trainers after each assignment.
key_sources: El Ansari Walid, El-Ansari Kareem, Hany Mohamed. (2025). Healthcare research and education: actively constructed research knowledge–a model for online systematic reviews and meta-analyses courses. BMC Research Notes. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13104-025-07111-8

article_title: Healthcare research and education: actively constructed research knowledge-a model for online systematic reviews and meta-analyses courses.
citation: El Ansari Walid, El-Ansari Kareem, Hany Mohamed. (2025). Healthcare research and education: actively constructed research knowledge–a model for online systematic reviews and meta-analyses courses. BMC Research Notes. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13104-025-07111-8
title: Embrace the human factor through synchronous and asynchronous communication in online courses
description: The article recommends that online courses deliberately incorporate the 'human' factor through broad trainer-learner and learner-learner networking via real-time messaging, online meetings, discussion forums, message boards, and emails. The article cites research showing that completely replacing classroom instruction with online instruction has negative consequences due to lack of the human factor, and that hybrid models yield more positive results.
requirements: Platforms supporting synchronous and asynchronous communication channels
constraints: Online courses might struggle to keep learners engaged and motivated and preserve sufficient social connections
target_learning_goals: Engagement and motivation
Social connection and community building
examples: The proposed course incorporates synchronous real-time messaging and online meetings alongside asynchronous discussion forums, message boards, and emails.

title: Moodle LMS platform for SR/MA course delivery
description: The proposed course utilizes the Moodle learning management system (LMS) platform for distributing training materials and assignments, enabling communication and feedback. The article states Moodle is recognized for its effectiveness in collaborative online learning and assessments, and enables a clear overview of course structure, supports synchronous and asynchronous communication, and provides a centralized hub for assignment submission and evaluation.

description: The review used Kirkpatrick's framework to categorize the levels of outcome evaluation performed in the included studies, sorting findings into "categories representing levels of outcome evaluation suggested in using Kirkpatrick's framework particularly reaction and learning outcome levels." This framework provided the structure for the review's content analysis, distinguishing reaction-level evaluations (perceptions and satisfaction) from learning-level evaluations (measured knowledge and skills). The review found that all included studies evaluated outcomes at only these two levels, with none reaching behavioral or organizational levels.

article_title: Digital Competence among Healthcare Leaders: A Mixed-Methods Systematic Review.
citation: Laakkonen Noora, Jarva Erika, Hammarén Mira, Kanste Outi, Kääriäinen Maria, Oikarinen Anne, Mikkonen Kristina. (2024). Digital Competence among Healthcare Leaders: A Mixed-Methods Systematic Review. Journal of Nursing Management. https://doi.org/10.1155/2024/8435248
title: Digital competence in healthcare as a multidimensional construct spanning technical, methodological, personal, and social skills
description: The review adopts a conception of digital competence as "the confident and critical use of Information Society Technology (IST) for work, leisure and communication" and reports, citing Mainz et al., that digital competence in healthcare can be divided into technical, methodological, personal, and social skills. Technical competencies encompass basic computer use, digital health skills, technology administration, and ethical and legal aspects; methodological include data processing and project management; personal include self-reflection and critical thinking; social include teamwork and communication. The review uses this framing to argue leaders' digital competence is broad and multifaceted.
requirements: Assessment of leaders' digital competence should address all four skill domains rather than only knowledge and skills
constraints: The review notes earlier leader-focused work focused on knowledge and skills, dismissing personal and social skills
target_learners: Healthcare leaders and managers in social and healthcare contexts
target_learning_goals: Digital competence development for leadership in digitalising healthcare
examples: The review's synthesis of leaders' experiences covers knowledge needs, implementation expertise, perceptions, and advocacy across these domains

citation: Rakesh, D., Lee, P. A., Gaikwad, A., & McLaughlin, K. A. (2025). Annual Research Review: Associations of socioeconomic status with cognitive function, language ability, and academic achievement in youth: a systematic review of mechanisms and protective factors. Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, 66(4), 417–439. https://doi.org/10.1111/jcpp.14082
title: Classification of mediators and moderators into stress, support, stimulation, child characteristics, and other contextual factors
description: The review classifies mediators and moderators of the SES-cognition/achievement association into five categories: stress, support, stimulation, child characteristics, and other contextual factors. Stressors reflect environmental experiences that are likely to require adaptation and overwhelm the coping resources of an average child. Support is defined as the provision of nurturing relationships, resources, and environments that offer emotional and practical assistance. Stimulation refers to the availability of enriching environmental inputs that facilitate learning opportunities for children. Other contextual factors include broader environmental elements such as neighborhood and school characteristics.
requirements: Factors not falling into the defined categories are classified as 'other'.

Academic achievement

title: Deprivation, rather than threat, is associated with cognitive outcomes like EF and language ability
description: The review discusses the distinction between deprivation and threat as forms of adversity, noting that the finding that cognitive stimulation mediates SES links with cognitive and language outcomes is consistent with the notion that deprivation, which is the absence of enriching cognitive and social inputs, rather than other types of adversities such as threat, is associated with cognitive outcomes like EF and language ability. This distinction is supported using network analyses.
requirements: This framework distinguishes deprivation (absence of enriching inputs) from threat as distinct forms of adversity with different cognitive outcomes.

title: ASReview: machine-learning-based tool for systematic review screening
description: The review used ASReview (Active learning for Systematic Reviews), a machine-learning-based tool to conduct systematic reviews. ASReview uses a combination of human input and machine learning to iteratively select and classify relevant research papers for inclusion. Starting from a randomly presented list of records, the researcher labels records as relevant or not relevant, and ASReview learns from this input and progressively reorders records from most to least relevant. Simulations indicate that screening a range of 8%–33% of records can identify at least 95% of the relevant records.
requirements: Selection criteria and stopping rule must be pre-established for ASReview to be effective.
constraints: ASReview is not entirely bias-free.
target_learning_goals: Systematic review methodology
examples: A total of 2062 papers (56% of the total) were screened using ASReview before reaching the stopping rule.

description: The Interprofessional Education Collaborative (IPEC) framework identifies "four core competencies of interprofessional collaboration": Values and Ethics, Roles and Responsibilities, Communication, and Teams and Teamwork. The review states these competencies "enhance patient care, promote population health and reduce healthcare costs". The review used this framework deductively, mapping inductively derived themes and sub-themes from 88 included studies onto the four IPEC competencies to determine which competencies IPE develops.

constraints: The review notes the extent to which IPE sessions foster acquisition of these competencies had not previously been investigated

target_learning_goals: interprofessional collaborative practice competencies: teamwork, communication, roles and responsibilities, values and ethics
examples: The review mapped 88 studies' competency outcomes onto the four IPEC competencies, finding Teams and Teamwork most frequently developed (65 instances)

The two themes are "personal professional growth and professional interactional skills/ competencies". citation: Mensour Emma A, Tran Carolyn, Li Toni, Mallawaarachchi Indika, Shaw Jennifer M, Blissett Sarah. (2025). title: PGME programs should consider incorporating PBL into curricula for its satisfaction and behavioural benefits at no detriment to knowledge acquisition
description: The review concludes that PBL strengthens attitudes and behaviours of residents "at no detriment to their acquisition of medical knowledge," and recommends that "PGME programs should consider incorporating PBL into curricula." The recommendation rests on the review's synthesis showing similar learning outcomes but improved satisfaction and self-reported behaviours with PBL.
requirements: PBL requires small-group facilitation, dedicated self-study time, and a reconvened discussion session with a facilitator
constraints: PBL instructional formats require more time and potentially more facilitators; scheduling within busy PGME contexts with variable attendance is a challenge

self-directed learning
teamwork and collaboration
examples: The review synthesized 21 studies in which PBL was embedded in existing programs (n=13) or delivered as additional sessions (n=8), mostly in person (n=19)

description: The review uses the Kirkpatrick Evaluation Model as its organizing framework, in which "reaction" assesses participant satisfaction, "learning" measures effect on knowledge and skill via scored examinations, "behaviour" describes observable shifts in thinking leading to practical changes, and "results" specifies impact on practice or patient care. title: Align ophthalmology curricula with ICO guidelines and extend training duration to raise trainee competency
description: The article recommends that "medical schools worldwide should work toward aligning their ophthalmology curricula with ICO guidelines" and that "Increasing the duration of exposure to ophthalmology, particularly in underserved areas, is essential". It further proposes standardized assessment tools such as OSCEs and international collaboration to build educational infrastructure in low- and middle-income countries. This follows from its regression findings that competency level and training duration are the strongest predictors of outcomes.

diagnostic skills in eye care

citation: Jia, M., Xin, T., Lina, Z., Baoling, Z., & Li, M. (2025). An analysis of the empirical research on SL/FL teaching and learning based on positive psychology: a systematic literature review. BMC Psychology, 13, 319. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-025-02576-5
title: Positive psychology frameworks (PERMA, EMPATHICS, Broaden-and-Build, Control-Value) structure SL/FL learning research
description: The review identifies several theoretical frameworks used to study positive psychology in SL/FL learning, including Seligman's PERMA model ("P: positive emotion. E: engagement. R: relationship. M: meaning. A: accomplishment"), Oxford's EMPATHICS model, the Broaden-and-Build Theory, and Control Value Theory. These frameworks are used both to design interventions (e.g. a 14-week PERMA-based listening and speaking intervention) and to organize the review's analysis of how positive emotions and traits influence language learning outcomes.
requirements: Studies applying these frameworks require structured intervention designs (e.g. the 14-week PERMA intervention) and measurement instruments such as the Foreign Language Enjoyment Scale and Grit Scale.
constraints: The review notes the reliance on self-report questionnaires may introduce bias, and most studies are cross-sectional, limiting causal inference.
target_learners: SL/FL learners at primary and secondary level
target_learning_goals: Language performance
Learning engagement
Well-being
examples: A 14-week intervention using Seligman's PERMA model on students' listening and speaking showed significant improvements compared to traditional teaching methods.

article_title: Comparing the seminar-case learning and lecture-based learning models in medical education: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
citation: Lou Jicheng, Guo Feng. (2025). Comparing the seminar-case learning and lecture-based learning models in medical education: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07041-w
title: The seminar-case learning (SCL) model as a combination of seminar learning and case-based learning
description: The SCL model is a teaching approach that "is a combination of seminar and case-based learning." It integrates "the efficient communication of seminar learning and the clinical thinking of case-based learning." In practice, a teacher selects a typical authentic case and distributes anonymized patient information to students before class. Students independently prepare responses, then during class the teacher gives a brief lecture, introduces the case, and facilitates group analysis and open seminar discussion.
requirements: Teachers require extensive medical knowledge, strong teaching skills, and experience to facilitate discussions and manage classroom interactions.
constraints: Double-blinding is not possible because teachers must implement different teaching methods across conditions.
target_learning_goals: Clinical thinking
Theoretical knowledge
Case analysis
Clinical skills
examples: Teachers send anonymized patient information to students via a chat software group prior to class, and students independently prepare responses to teacher-posed questions.

citation: Sekhavati P, Wild T, Martinez IDPC, Dion PM, Woo M, Ramlogan R, Boet S, Shorr R, Gu Y. (2025). Instructional design features in ultrasound‐guided regional anaesthesia simulation‐based training: a systematic review. Anaesthesia. https://doi.org/10.1111/anae.16527
title: Modified Kirkpatrick model for classifying simulation training outcomes
description: The review applies a modified Kirkpatrick model with four levels to classify outcomes of ultrasound‐guided regional anaesthesia simulation training. Level 1 assesses learners' perceptions including satisfaction and confidence; level 2 evaluates "knowledge acquisition, skills and attitudes"; level 3 examines behavioural changes in the professional setting such as transfer of skills to clinical practice; and level 4 measures outcomes of learners' actions such as patient outcomes and block success. The model structures the review's synthesis of which instructional design features accompany which outcome levels.

title: Network meta-analysis framework for ranking multiple teaching methods simultaneously
description: Network meta-analysis (NMA) is presented as "a new type of meta-analysis, which can compare the effectiveness of multiple interventions more intuitively and in detail, while traditional meta-analysis can only compare them in pairs". The article applies it with Stata 16.0's mvmeta package, using SMDs for continuous outcomes and ORs for binary outcomes, SUCRA curves to rank treatments probabilistically, node-splitting for inconsistency, and a league table for pairwise comparisons. It integrates direct and indirect evidence across 13 interventions.
requirements: Requires a connected network of comparative studies; interventions published in fewer than 3 literatures were excluded
constraints: Results are considered statistically insignificant if the 95% CI includes 1; heterogeneity was assessed via prediction intervals and node-splitting
target_learning_goals: comparative effectiveness evaluation of teaching methods
examples: The article ranked 13 teaching methods using SUCRA, with PBL + WeChat first for theoretical scores (88%) and PBL + CP first for medical record scores (99.9%)

title: Replace passive lecture-based learning with active, problem-oriented methods in resident standardized training
description: The article argues that LBL leaves students "only learning passively" and lacking independent thinking, and concludes that "the standardized training and education of resident physicians in China urgently need to change the teaching mode and awaken students' awareness of self-directed learning". It recommends actively altering teaching techniques to enhance mastery of clinical knowledge and skills, supported by NMA evidence that PBL-based methods outperform LBL across outcomes.
requirements: Requires teachers to take a guiding and supportive role, with students independently thinking through problems via group discussion or literature review
constraints: The article notes the shift is challenging for students facing heavy learning tasks and graduation pressure, accustomed to passive learning since youth
target_learners: internal medicine residents in standardized training in China
target_learning_goals: theoretical performance
clinical thinking
self-directed learning
examples: The NMA compared 13 interventions across 74 studies and found new methods significantly outperformed LBL on theoretical, practical, medical record, and satisfaction outcomes

article_title: Speech-Language Pathologists' Perceptions of Their Competence in Managing Stuttering: A Systematic Review with Narrative Synthesis.
citation: Alegre, E., Penman, A., Unicomb, R., & Scarinci, N. (2025). Speech–Language Pathologists' Perceptions of Their Competence in Managing Stuttering: A Systematic Review with Narrative Synthesis. International Journal of Language & Communication Disorders, 60(3), e70040. https://doi.org/10.1111/1460-6984.70040
title: Provide ongoing education, supportive work environments and opportunities for familiarity with people who stutter to enhance SLP competence in stuttering management
description: The review's clinical implications emphasise "the importance of ongoing education and support for SLPs to enhance their clinical competence in stuttering management". Specifically, targeted professional development, supportive work environments and familiarity with people who stutter can positively impact SLPs' confidence and proficiency. The review recommends SLPs whose caseloads include stuttering prioritise ongoing education, seek support to implement treatment where needed and pursue opportunities to gain experience with people who stutter.
requirements: SLPs whose caseloads include stuttering need access to targeted professional development and supportive work environments
constraints: The review notes it is unclear whether continuing professional education improves actual competence or only perceived competence
target_learning_goals: clinical competence in stuttering assessment and treatment

article_title: Team based learning pedagogy enhances the education quality: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
citation: Xie Zhi-Bo, Cheng Xin-Yu, Li Xiao-Yan, Zhang Yi-Fan. (2025). Team based learning pedagogy enhances the education quality: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07175-x
title: Team-Based Learning three-phase pedagogical framework
description: Team-Based Learning is a teacher-guided small-group learning method involving students in both individual and group activities, consisting of three phases: "preparation prior to class, readiness assurance progress, and application of course concepts". In the first phase, students complete out-of-class study through reading assignments determined by teachers. In the second stage, the Individual Readiness Assurance Test (IRAT) and Group Readiness Assurance Test (GRAT) evaluate students' readiness to apply knowledge from reading assignments. Finally, application exercises require students to apply acquired knowledge to solve problems.
requirements: Students complete out-of-class reading assignments determined by teachers before class
Individual and Group Readiness Assurance Tests are conducted in class
Application exercises require students to apply knowledge to solve problems
constraints: TBL demonstrates greater cost-effectiveness when implemented with a high student-to-faculty ratio
target_learning_goals: knowledge acquisition
critical thinking
knowledge retention
student engagement
examples: TBL has been adopted by many medical schools since its introduction in 1970
key_sources: Xie Zhi-Bo, Cheng Xin-Yu, Li Xiao-Yan, Zhang Yi-Fan. (2025). Team based learning pedagogy enhances the education quality: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07175-x

article_title: Team based learning pedagogy enhances the education quality: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
citation: Xie Zhi-Bo, Cheng Xin-Yu, Li Xiao-Yan, Zhang Yi-Fan. (2025). Team based learning pedagogy enhances the education quality: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07175-x
title: Generalize TBL pedagogy in medical education classrooms
description: Based on their meta-analytic findings of gratifying TBL effectiveness, the authors conclude that "TBL pedagogy is compatible with the present medical education and should be generalized in more classrooms". TBL not only enhances theoretical scores of medical students but also enables them to benefit from and enjoy the classes. The authors note TBL is suitable for medical students at any stage, particularly in group teaching involving a large number of students, and call for more global, high-quality studies and more standardized evaluation methods.
requirements: Teachers need to prepare in advance, including designing teaching units and preparing outlines for pre-study
constraints: Some included trials were non-randomized studies which could introduce bias
Some studies had small sample sizes
Only English-language literature was enrolled, potentially leading to publication bias
target_learning_goals: theoretical knowledge
student engagement
satisfaction
examples: The authors conclude TBL should be generalized in more classrooms based on pooled evidence of higher scores, retention, engagement and satisfaction

article_title: Motivation Theories and Constructs in Experimental Studies of Online Instruction: Systematic Review and Directed Content Analysis.
citation: Lesselroth Blake; Papadakis Stamatis; Lo Chung; Gavarkovs Adam PhD; Miller Erin PhD; Coleman Jaimie MPT; Gunasegaran Tharsiga HBSc; Kusurkar Rashmi A MD, PhD; Kulasegaram Kulamakan PhD; Anderson Melanie MLiS; Brydges Ryan PhD. (2025). Motivation Theories and Constructs in Experimental Studies of Online Instruction: Systematic Review and Directed Content Analysis. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/64179
title: Six-category taxonomy of motivational constructs targeted by instructional design strategies
description: The review organizes motivational constructs targeted by online design strategies into six a priori categories derived from prominent motivation theories and prior research. The authors state: "Our list included the following categories of motivational constructs: intrinsic value beliefs (eg, interest), extrinsic value beliefs (eg, instrumentality), competence and control beliefs (eg, self-efficacy), social connectedness (eg, relatedness), autonomy, and goals." Intrinsic value refers to value derived from completing an activity, whereas extrinsic value refers to value derived from outcomes external to the activity. This taxonomy served as the deductive coding scheme for the directed content analysis.
requirements: Coding requires a priori construct categories derived from established motivation theories and prior motivational research.
constraints: The categorization scheme was refined during coding from the published protocol, aggregating more constructs into fewer categories.
target_learning_goals: Learner motivation in online instruction
examples: The review used the taxonomy to code 46 experimental comparison studies of online motivational design strategies.

article_title: Motivation Theories and Constructs in Experimental Studies of Online Instruction: Systematic Review and Directed Content Analysis.
citation: Lesselroth Blake; Papadakis Stamatis; Lo Chung; Gavarkovs Adam PhD; Miller Erin PhD; Coleman Jaimie MPT; Gunasegaran Tharsiga HBSc; Kusurkar Rashmi A MD, PhD; Kulasegaram Kulamakan PhD; Anderson Melanie MLiS; Brydges Ryan PhD. (2025). Motivation Theories and Constructs in Experimental Studies of Online Instruction: Systematic Review and Directed Content Analysis. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/64179
title: Keller's ARCS model of motivational design
description: The review describes Keller's ARCS model as a model of motivational design stating that learners remain motivated when four conditions are met. As the review summarizes: "Keller's ARCS model states that, for learners to become and remain motivated to learn, their attention must be captured via feelings of curiosity, they must perceive instruction to be relevant to their current needs and long-term goals, they must feel confident that they can succeed, and they must feel satisfied with the intrinsic and extrinsic consequences of engaging with instruction." The ARCS model was among the most commonly used theories in the reviewed studies and was associated with studies most likely to target multiple motivational constructs.
requirements: Application requires attention, relevance, confidence, and satisfaction components to be addressed in instructional design.
target_learning_goals: Learner motivation in online instruction
examples: Studies informed by the ARCS model were most likely to report targeting multiple motivational constructs in the review.

article_title: Nurses' and Midwives' Experiences of Clinical Supervision in Practice: A Scoping Review.
citation: Gill‐Meeley, N., Hernon, O., Frawley, T., Cuddihy, C., & Smyth, S. (2025). Nurses' and Midwives' Experiences of Clinical Supervision in Practice: A Scoping Review. Journal of Clinical Nursing. https://doi.org/10.1111/jocn.17489
title: Clinical supervision is a formal process of professional support that aids nurses and midwives to develop professionally and learn from experience through structured reflection on their practice.
description: The review defines clinical supervision as "a formal process of professional support that aids nurses and midwives to develop professionally and learn from experience through structured reflection on their practice". Reflection on experiences from clinical practice is the foundation of clinical supervision, allowing professionals to review how they work. Beneficial outcomes include greater self-awareness, professional self-confidence and enhanced awareness of their own competence.
requirements: Structured reflection on practice
target_learning_goals: Professional development
Learning from experience

article_title: Simulation tools in neuro-oncological surgery: a scoping review of perioperative and training applications.
citation: Menna Grazia, Riva Dora, Marino Salvatore, Garber Jocelyn, Gerritsen Jasper Kees Wim, Mattogno Pier Paolo, Young Jacob Stewart, Olivi Alessandro, Doglietto Francesco, Berger Mitchel Stuart, Della Pepa Giuseppe Maria. (2025). Simulation tools in neuro-oncological surgery: a scoping review of perioperative and training applications. Journal of Neuro-Oncology. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11060-025-04972-8
title: Six-category taxonomy of simulation technologies in neuro-oncological surgery
description: The review organizes neuro-oncological simulation research into six categories: 3D models, AR, MR, and VR in presurgical planning and intraoperative navigation, plus AR and VR in surgical training. The review reports that "Augmented Reality (AR) in Presurgical Planning and Intraoperative Navigation: 25 articles" formed the largest group, while 3D models (5 articles) and VR for planning/navigation (4 articles) were least studied. The taxonomy maps distinct roles: 3D-printed models for presurgical planning, AR for intraoperative navigation overlay, and VR/MR for deeper real-time integration.
requirements: Studies must describe simulation-based interventions in neurosurgical oncology, including presurgical planning, intraoperative navigation, or skills acquisition in a training environment
constraints: Limited to studies published in English; heterogeneity of study designs prevented meta-analysis
target_learning_goals: surgical skill acquisition
tumor resection planning
intraoperative navigation

citation: Mohd Amiruddin Mohd Kassim, Sidi Muhammad Yusoff Azli Shah, Jane Tze Yn Lim, Tuti Iryani Mohd Daud. (2025). Online-Based and Technology-Assisted Psychiatric Education for Trainees: Scoping Review. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/64773
title: Five-method taxonomy of online-based and technology-assisted psychiatric education for trainees
description: The review organizes the literature on online-based and technology-assisted psychiatric education into five methods: videoconference, online modules/e-learning, virtual patients, software/applications, and social media. These methods were applied to objectives including "teaching theory knowledge, skills training, psychotherapy supervision, and information retrieval." The taxonomy is supported by a three-phase trend analysis (prior to 2015, 2015-2019, and 2020 onward) of 82 included articles.
requirements: Studies must include psychiatric trainees or residents and evaluate outcomes related to knowledge, skills, confidence, preference, or participant feedback
constraints: Based on English-language studies or those with English translations; review articles and purely descriptive accounts were excluded
target_learning_goals: psychiatric theory knowledge
clinical skills training
psychotherapy supervision
information retrieval

article_title: Self-directed learning in health professions: A mixed-methods systematic review of the literature.
citation: Berger-Estilita, Joana; Linda, Krista; Gogollari, Artemisa; Schmitz, Felix; Elfering, Achim; Guttormsen, Sissel (2025). Self-directed learning in health professions: A mixed-methods systematic review of the literature. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0320530
title: Person, Process, and Context framework as a structured lens for understanding SDL readiness among healthcare professionals
description: The review identifies "three factors—Person, Process, and Context— as a structured lens through which to understand how individual traits, learning methods, and environmental influences interact to facilitate SDL readiness among HCPs." Personal factors include intrinsic motivation, self-efficacy, and confidence in SDL abilities. Process factors include goal achievement strategies and support from digital tools. Contextual factors include social interactions, learning environment, learning programs, and organizational support with digital tools. The review uses this lens to organize both promoting factors and barriers to SDL in healthcare organizations.
requirements: The framework requires distinguishing individual traits, learning methods, and environmental influences when analyzing SDL readiness.
constraints: The review notes a clear separation between these factors is often lacking, causing terminological overlap, and that a distinct categorization between factors that promote or hinder SDL was first suggested in this publication.
target_learners: Healthcare professionals including nurses, pharmacists, and physicians in clinical settings
target_learning_goals: Self-directed learning readiness and continuous professional development
examples: The review's Table 2 categorizes promoting factors and barriers into Personal, Process, and Contextual factors, listing items such as intrinsic motivation, goal achievement strategies, and supportive organizational policies.
key_sources: Berger-Estilita, Joana; Linda, Krista; Gogollari, Artemisa; Schmitz, Felix; Elfering, Achim; Guttormsen, Sissel (2025). Self-directed learning in health professions: A mixed-methods systematic review of the literature. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0320530

article_title: Self-directed learning in health professions: A mixed-methods systematic review of the literature.
citation: Berger-Estilita, Joana; Linda, Krista; Gogollari, Artemisa; Schmitz, Felix; Elfering, Achim; Guttormsen, Sissel (2025). Self-directed learning in health professions: A mixed-methods systematic review of the literature. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0320530
title: Thirteen SDL models and frameworks applied in healthcare organizations, classified as personal, process, context, and combined models
description: The review identifies thirteen SDL models applied across twelve included studies, classified into "four combined models, five process models, three context models, and one personal model." Named models include Knowles' model on self-directed learning, Deci and Ryan's Self-Determination Theory, Zimmerman's Self-Directed Learning Theoretical Model, Karasek's Job Demands-Control model, Marsick and Watkins Models for Informal and Incidental Learning, and Tynjälä's 3P Model, among others. The review reports that only about one-third of included studies explicitly used or referenced such models, and that "a unified SDL model tailored to clinical settings remains absent."
requirements: Models must be adapted to the dynamic nature of roles and responsibilities among healthcare professionals, as the review finds a one-size-fits-all solution impractical.
constraints: The review states the challenges in creating a universal SDL model stem from the dynamic nature of roles among healthcare professionals, and that frameworks originating from sectors like business and technology require adaptation toward patient-centered outcomes, ethical practice, and clinical safety in healthcare.
target_learners: Healthcare professionals including nurses, pharmacists, and physicians
target_learning_goals: Understanding and applying SDL models in clinical and workplace learning contexts
examples: The review's Table 1 describes each model's type, description, and context of use, such as Cuyvers' Self-Regulation of Professional Learning model applied to nurses' self-regulated workplace learning in clinical wards.
key_sources: Berger-Estilita, Joana; Linda, Krista; Gogollari, Artemisa; Schmitz, Felix; Elfering, Achim; Guttormsen, Sissel (2025). Self-directed learning in health professions: A mixed-methods systematic review of the literature. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0320530

article_title: Changes in medical student attendance at in-person teaching sessions: a systematic review.
citation: Nagappan Palaniappan Ganesh, Tan Sapphire Rou Xi, Absar Shazia, Brown Samuel, Sayers Sarah, McManus Alex, Arora Anmol, Kuhn Isla, Khan Faris, Lau Edward, Tulinius Charlotte. (2025). Changes in medical student attendance at in-person teaching sessions: a systematic review. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2024-091768
title: Attendance as a marker of perceived relative utility of teaching sessions
description: The review proposes that attendance rates reflect the relative utility of teaching sessions compared with online material and other resources: "Attendance rates may, therefore, reflect the relative utility of teaching sessions compared with the utility of online material and other resources". Longitudinally measured attendance offers a gauge of session utility since students can compare information sources. This framework underpins the review's argument for voluntary attendance.
requirements: Attendance must be voluntary so rates reflect utility rather than compulsion
constraints: The review states this marker is unsuitable when attendance is compulsory
target_learning_goals: evaluating the usefulness of teaching sessions

title: Five-factor framework for improving the student learning experience in self-directed learning
description: The review identifies five key factors that improve the student learning experience in undergraduate clinical science programs that utilise self-directed learning: "curricular elements; educator influence; impact of peers, environment; and clinical placement experiences". This framework organises the findings of 19 included studies and provides a structure for educators to consider when designing curricula that incorporate self-directed learning.

lifelong learning

article_title: Effectiveness of non-technical skills training in intensive care units: a systematic review.
citation: Fernandes Pimenta Isac Davidson Santiago et al. (2025). Effectiveness of non-technical skills training in intensive care units: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07037-6
title: Kirkpatrick's four-level evaluation model applied to NTS training outcomes in ICUs
description: The review organizes outcomes using Kirkpatrick's evaluation model, encompassing reaction, learning, behaviors, and organizational results. Reaction covers "the participant's response to the training"; learning covers "acquisition of knowledge, skills and attitudes after training"; behavior covers "changes in participants' behavior in real or controlled care environments"; and results cover "measurable impacts of the training program at the organizational and health level." This framework structures the summary of findings table and GRADE certainty ratings.
requirements: Studies must report outcomes mappable to at least one of the four Kirkpatrick levels
constraints: Reaction outcomes have no comparison group and are only assessed after the intervention
target_learning_goals: Non-technical skills: teamwork, situational awareness, leadership, communication, decision-making

article_title: Effectiveness of non-technical skills training in intensive care units: a systematic review.
citation: Fernandes Pimenta Isac Davidson Santiago et al. (2025). Effectiveness of non-technical skills training in intensive care units: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07037-6
title: Use simulation-based training as the primary strategy for teaching non-technical skills in ICUs
description: The review identifies simulation training as the predominant teaching strategy across included studies, often combined with lectures, game play, online modules, interactive activities, and clinical case discussion. The authors cite the argument that "simulation-based training is the most effective for teaching NTS, promoting authentic use of communication, leadership, and teamwork techniques." Positive learning results in one study were attributed to simulation in the curriculum versus a classroom-based approach.
requirements: Facilitators with sufficient experience in learning, particularly for practical simulation contexts
constraints: Many programs combined simulation with traditional strategies; the relative contribution of each component was not isolated
target_learning_goals: Non-technical skills: teamwork, situational awareness, leadership, communication
examples: Included studies used simulation sessions with briefing and debriefing, often alongside lectures, game play, online modules and case discussions

citation: Cahyaningrum Yeny Dyah, Suhoyo Yoyo, Rahayu Gandes Retno. (2025). Facilitating clinical reasoning for medical students in clinical settings: a scoping review. Korean Journal of Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.3946/kjme.2025.333
title: Three-theme framework for clinical reasoning facilitation in clinical settings
description: This scoping review proposes an organizing framework comprising three themes for understanding how clinical reasoning is facilitated in clinical settings. The review states these themes "encompass the responsibilities of clinical teachers, strategies employed in the process of clinical reasoning, and factors that impact clinical reasoning learning in clinical settings." The framework maps facilitator roles (environment creation, process demonstration, assessment, technique implementation), specific facilitation techniques organized by thinking process, and internal/external influencing factors. It provides a structure for medical educators to optimize clinical reasoning instruction.

constraints: The review notes specific strategies that enhance clinical reasoning abilities need further investigation

Diagnostic reasoning
Clinical decision-making

article_title: Facilitating clinical reasoning for medical students in clinical settings: a scoping review.
citation: Cahyaningrum Yeny Dyah, Suhoyo Yoyo, Rahayu Gandes Retno. (2025). Facilitating clinical reasoning for medical students in clinical settings: a scoping review. Korean Journal of Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.3946/kjme.2025.333
title: Integrate clinical teachers' facilitation role with developing technology for clinical reasoning learning
description: The review recommends that lecturers' role in facilitating clinical reasoning be integrated with currently developing technology. It states that "lecturers' role in facilitating clinical reasoning also needs to be integrated with the currently developing technology." This principle directs clinical educators to leverage technological tools (such as virtual patient simulations) while maintaining attention to the source of information, ensuring students acquire clinical reasoning skills through both human facilitation and technological support.

constraints: The review notes the role of clinical teachers in facilitating virtual simulation learning may be vague
target_learning_goals: Clinical reasoning
examples: The review cites virtual patient case simulation as a technique where computer-based simulations provide realistic clinical scenarios for practicing clinical reasoning

citation: Hertz P , Rattenborg S , Haug TR , Houlind K , Konge L , Bjerrum F . (2024). Training and assessment for colorectal surgery and appendicectomy– a systematic review. Colorectal Dis. https://doi.org/10.1111/codi.16905
title: Messick's five-source validity framework for surgical assessment tools
description: The review applies a scoring tool based on the five sources of validity originally described by Messick: content, response process, internal structure, relation to other variables, and consequences. Assessment tools should ideally be supported by validity evidence from each of the five sources, though not necessarily within the same paper. The review used Ghaderi's toolbox, with scores from 0 to 15 points, to assess the validity evidence reported for each of the 31 identified assessment tools.
requirements: Validity evidence should be assessed against all five sources of validity
constraints: The review notes most studies reported validity using outdated terms, and only a very few described validity data using a current and recommended framework
target_learners: surgical trainees and residents in colorectal surgery

examples: The review's Table 1 maps each identified assessment tool against the five validity sources

article_title: Strategies to enhance clinical teaching and learning in undergraduate nursing education: A scoping review.
citation: Hobenu Kafui A., Adefuye Anthonio O., Naab Florence, Nyoni Champion N. (2025). Strategies to enhance clinical teaching and learning in undergraduate nursing education: A scoping review. PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0305789
title: Seven-theme taxonomy of strategies to enhance clinical teaching and learning in undergraduate nursing education
description: The review organises its findings into seven themes and 36 sub-themes: 'scaffolding the curriculum, transformative teaching and learning approaches, integrating simulation-based education, dedicated education units for clinical placement, applying technology in clinical education, developing interprofessional teamwork and collaboration, and integrating inter-country clinical experience'. The taxonomy was generated through inductive thematic analysis of 40 included articles, with initial coding by one author and co-coding with another, verified by two further authors. It maps the reported strategy space for nursing clinical education.
requirements: Peer-reviewed articles and dissertations published in English between January 2011 and September 2023 on strategies for undergraduate nursing clinical education
constraints: Included studies were undergraduate nursing populations; postgraduate and other health profession programmes were excluded

clinical teaching and learning

article_title: Determining the metrics of competence in robotic hysterectomy: a systematic review.
citation: Arcamo K, Murugappan S, Larkins K, Mohan H, Costello A, Pendlebury A, McNally O, McBain R. (2025). Determining the metrics of competence in robotic hysterectomy: a systematic review. Journal of Robotic Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11701-025-02471-6
title: Kern's six-step framework for curriculum development structures the review's approach to informing robotic hysterectomy curriculum design.
description: The review is situated within a structured curriculum development effort at the International Medical Robotics Academy (IMRA) using Kern's six-step approach. The authors state that the steps "Goals And Objectives and Evaluation And Feedback" serve to identify specific and measurable objectives and opportunities for formative feedback. This review addresses those sections of Kern's framework by evaluating existing performance metrics for robotic hysterectomy. The framework provides the organizing rationale for why valid metrics are a prerequisite for an effective training curriculum.
requirements: A structured curriculum development process, such as Kern's six-step approach, to identify measurable objectives and feedback opportunities.
target_learning_goals: acquiring technical competence in robotic hysterectomy

title: A metric- or competence-based educational pathway improves trainee performance and reduces intraoperative complications compared to a time- or case-based curriculum.
description: The review asserts that a metric- or competence-based educational pathway ensures learners reach the required knowledge, skills, and attitudes before progressing. It states that "Compared to a time- or case-based curriculum, a metric-based system has been shown to improve trainee performance and reduce intraoperative complications." The authors emphasize competency-based progression as an essential component of robotic hysterectomy training, straying from conventional volume-based training requirements.
requirements: Valid, procedure-specific performance metrics that reliably assess skill progression.
target_learning_goals: achieving competency-based progression in robotic surgical skills

title: Four-dimension framework of nurse managers' decision-making competency
description: The review proposes a conceptual framework organizing 15 core characteristics of nurse managers' decision-making competency into four higher-order dimensions: strategic and ethical decision-making, information synthesis and application, organizational and interpersonal decision-making, and professional growth and reflective decision-making. The article states that "These dimensions are not isolated; they are interconnected components supporting informed, ethical, and strategic decisions in complex healthcare environments." The framework integrates characteristics identified across the reviewed literature into a structured model.

constraints: Generalizability may be constrained in settings where structural or cultural conditions differ significantly from those described in the reviewed literature

title: Include practical, hands-on components in perineal tear education programmes rather than senior supervision alone.
description: The review concludes that effective education included practical components such as hands-on skills training in perineal anatomy, assessment and classification, rather than senior supervision alone. Workshops typically involved didactic education followed by a practical hands-on workshop or dissection lab. The practical element likely bolsters efficacy.
requirements: Training programmes should include hands-on skills practice in perineal anatomy, assessment and classification.
constraints: Findings should be interpreted and applied to different contexts with caution due to study heterogeneity and risk of bias.

Clinical assessment and classification of perineal tears

article_title: Whether case-based teaching combined with the flipped classroom is more valuable than traditional lecture-based teaching methods in clinical medical education: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
citation: Shi Xu-Ying, Lu Bing-Rui, Yin Qing, Wang Qiu-Wen, Fang Yong-Qi, Sun Zhi-Gang. (2025). Whether case-based teaching combined with the flipped classroom is more valuable than traditional lecture-based teaching methods in clinical medical education: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07465-4
title: Flipped Classroom Case Learning (FCCL) as an integrated pedagogical model
description: FCCL integrates the flipped classroom (FC) model — flexible, self-managed pre-class videos and in-class group activities — with case-based learning (CBL), a guided inquiry method linking theoretical knowledge to real-world clinical scenarios. The article describes this integration as a combined pedagogical model likely to yield synergistic benefits, producing a teaching effect where "1 + 1 > 2." Students engage in self-directed theoretical learning before class and case discussion and analysis during class, fostering long-term retention of knowledge and clinical analysis abilities, plus communication and collaboration skills.
requirements: Requires adequate pre-course preparation by students
Requires instructors to prepare learning materials such as instructional videos and case designs
constraints: Application in surgical education in Western countries requires careful consideration due to time conflicts from demanding schedules
target_learners: Undergraduate and graduate clinical medicine students and residents
target_learning_goals: Theoretical knowledge mastery
Clinical analysis skills
Communication and collaboration skills

article_title: The use of deliberate practice in simulation-based surgical training for laparoscopic surgery - a systematic review.
citation: Wickramasinghe D, Vincent J. (2025). The use of deliberate practice in simulation-based surgical training for laparoscopic surgery – a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07613-w
title: Deliberate Practice framework as an instructional design model for simulation-based surgical training
description: The review applies Ericsson's Deliberate Practice (DP) framework as an evaluative and design lens for simulation-based surgical training (SBST) in minimally invasive surgery. DP's "core components include clear goal definition, focused effort during learning, repeated practice until reaching desired proficiency, individual coaching, and immediate feedback". The review uses these components to assess adherence across ten studies, contrasting DP's aim of expert performance for all learners with discriminant, remedial-oriented models.
requirements: Requires clear goal definition, focused effort, repeated practice, individual coaching, and immediate feedback as stated core components
constraints: DP assumes minimal transfer of skills between apparently similar domains
Surgery lacks an explicit definition of expert performance, complicating DP application compared to sports and music
target_learning_goals: laparoscopic psychomotor skills
key_sources: Wickramasinghe D, Vincent J. (2025). The use of deliberate practice in simulation-based surgical training for laparoscopic surgery – a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07613-w

title: Structure simulation-based surgical training according to deliberate practice principles, including immediate feedback and stepwise task progression
description: The review concludes that DP is a useful instructional design tool for structuring SBST and that "Strict adherence to DP, however, is likely to produce superior training results than conventional training". Programs should incorporate immediate feedback, structured task progression, and repetition with attention to effort constraints between sessions.
requirements: Requires immediate feedback, stepwise task progression, and repeated practice sessions
constraints: Limited by resource requirements, particularly instructor commitment and equipment capable of real-time metrics

citation: de Azevedo Cardoso T, Aung H H, Yeh W-Y, Ozdamli F, Ignjatovic A, Spaic D, Bukumiric Z, Rajovic N, Markovic K, Savic M, Milin-Lazovic J, Grubor N, Milic N, Stanisavljevic D, Despotovic A, Bokonjic D, Vladicic Masic J, Janicijevic V, Masic S, Milic N. title: Implement the flipped classroom in medical curricula with preclass quizzes, active in-class activities, and alignment of activities with learning objectives.
description: The article recommends that flipped classroom implementation replace instructor-driven passive learning with student-centered active learning, supported by "preclass assessment (eg, quizzing) to maintain student engagement and enforce preparedness". It stresses that "clearly defined learning objectives and aligning classroom activities with those objectives are critical for effective implementation". The FC effect is reported highest when quizzes and problem-based learning exercises are used together.

Institutional efforts to ensure equitable access to digital resources

clinical reasoning and skills development

title: ECE delivery modalities taxonomy: clinical/hospital-based, simulation-based, community-based, and peer/professional shadowing
description: The review organizes early clinical exposure interventions into "four broad categories or modalities: clinical/hospital-based, simulation-based, community-based and peer/professional shadowing." Clinical ECE involves chairside observation and supervised patient contact; simulation builds procedural and communication skills in controlled environments before real patients; shadowing and community placements extend exposure through senior-peer observation and supervised immersion. The taxonomy maps how dental programs structure early patient contact.

constraints: The review notes interventions varied widely in duration, timing, and delivery mode, limiting direct comparison across modalities

description: The review finds that reliability and validity reporting varied across included studies, with about half providing clear validation evidence and others little or none. It concludes there is "necessity of employing standardized and validated outcome measures in ECE in dental education research for the sake of study comparability and enhancing confidence in results." Future studies should prioritize robust objective performance measures with multicentre designs and longitudinal follow-up.

Objective performance measures rather than sole reliance on self-report

It recommends that "findings support integrating multimodal, competency-based education into surgical training" and notes that "Standardized outcome measures and multicenter validation are needed to define optimal learning pathways." citation: Sterpu Irene, Herling Lotta, Nordquist Jonas, Rotgans Jerome, Acharya Ganesh. (2024). Team-based learning (TBL) in clinical disciplines for undergraduate medical students—a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04975-x
title: TBL as a three-phase structured active-learning method: preparation, readiness assurance (iRAT/tRAT), and application exercises
description: The review describes team-based learning as a structured pedagogical method that "unfolds across three distinct phases": individual pre-class study, an in-class readiness assurance phase in which students first take an individual quiz (iRAT, typically 15–25 multiple-choice questions) and then retake it in teams (tRAT) with discussion and immediate feedback, and a final application phase where teams tackle real-life exercises applying concepts to concrete medical contexts. The review uses this framework as the standard against which it judged whether the 49 included studies implemented full-concept or modified TBL.
requirements: Individual preparatory materials assigned before class
Small teams of roughly 5–7 students and immediate feedback after tRAT submission
constraints: The review found most clinical-discipline implementations omit one or more of these steps, most often peer review

teamwork

title: Kolb's experiential learning theory (KELT) and its four-mode experiential learning cycle
description: KELT describes the role experience plays in the learning process as a dynamic, holistic, multi-dimensional approach to human development, developed by Kolb from the works of Dewey, Lewin, and Piaget. Kolb defines learning as "the process whereby knowledge is created through the transformation of experience", resulting from grasping and transforming experience through a cyclical sequence of stages. The review uses KELT as the anchor framework for mapping EL in IPP education, noting its four-mode recursive cycle of concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualization, and active experimentation.
requirements: Learning is viewed as continuous and grounded in experience rather than as an outcome
Learners progress through the four modes of the experiential learning cycle
constraints: The review found only eight included articles used an EL-specific theory or model, two based specifically on KELT
target_learning_goals: interprofessional practice competencies
experiential learning
examples: The Leicester Model of Interprofessional Education incorporates elements of KELT with a 4-step education cycle for teaching interprofessional groups of students

title: TBL and PBL as distinct collaborative problem-solving designs differing in structure, group size, and teacher role
description: The article frames TBL and PBL as two learner-centered, collaborative problem-solving methods that differ in learning-activity sequence, group size and composition, problem nature and format, teacher role, and evaluation. PBL uses "small-group tutorials, typically comprising 8–10 students guided by a tutor", while TBL is designed for larger classes with teams of five to seven members, one teacher facilitating multiple self-managed teams, mandatory pre-reading assignments, tests of prior knowledge, and inter-team discussions with structured feedback. The meta-analysis compares outcomes arising from these two designs.
requirements: Both methods require professionally relevant problems and small-group learning as shared design features
constraints: The article notes specific implementation methods (course content, duration, frequency, group size, teacher role, learning resources) varied across included studies

practical clinical skills
learning interest
examples: The ten included trials spanned nine specialties including neurology, oncology, ophthalmology, general surgery, and stomatology, with TBL groups of 12–115 and PBL groups of 12–85 participants

article_title: Acute effect of physical activity on academic outcomes in school-aged youth: A systematic review and multivariate meta-analysis.
citation: Muntaner-Mas A, Morales JS, Martínez-de-Quel Ó, Lubans DR, García-Hermoso A. (2024). Acute effect of physical activity on academic outcomes in school-aged youth: A systematic review and multivariate meta-analysis. Scand J Med Sci Sports. https://doi.org/10.1111/sms.14479
title: Active breaks as the predominant form of acute physical activity in the reviewed interventions
description: Active breaks were the predominant form of physical activity in the included studies (10 out of 11). The article characterizes them as interventions that take into account "neither the embodiment (physical activity is not related to a learning task) nor the integration (there is no temporal overlap between movements and the learning task) concepts". Despite lacking these features, the review's findings suggest that human movement with minimal cognitive load may still improve academic performance, and the authors argue active breaks are an appealing strategy for educational contexts because timing and planning are key barriers to movement-based interventions.
requirements: A single bout of physical activity delivered during the school day, separate from the learning task
constraints: Active breaks lack embodiment and integration with academic content, which the authors note as a limitation relative to embodied learning techniques
target_learners: School-aged children and adolescents in classroom settings
target_learning_goals: Academic performance (mathematics, language) and classroom behavior
examples: Included interventions used active breaks of 4 to 30 minutes, with 20 minutes the most common bout duration, mostly applying acute aerobic exercise.

BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05306-4
title: Use the biopsychosocial model as the theoretical framework for PPS training programmes and holistic consultations
description: The review recommends educators utilise the biopsychosocial model, "endorsed by several of the included studies", as a theoretical framework for developing training that addresses the multifaceted presentation of PPS. It supports moving away from the biomedical model, breaking mind–body dualism, and structuring consultations around biological, psychological and social domains so patients take agency in their own care.
requirements: Training must be clearly intended to develop psychologically informed practice working holistically at the interface of somatic and psychological care
constraints: The review reports a gap in existing programmes around explanations of psychosocial and physiological interrelating factors, and that only one included study used a tool facilitating a structured consultation

patient self-management and agency

article_title: Development and applications of the Anaesthetists' Non-Technical Skills behavioural marker system: a systematic review.
citation: Kang Jiamin, Hu Jiale, Yan Chunji, Xing Xueyan, Tu Shumin, Zhou Fang. (2024). Development and applications of the Anaesthetists’ Non-Technical Skills behavioural marker system: a systematic review. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2023-075019
title: The ANTS behavioural marker system: four skill categories with 15 elements rated on 4-point Likert scales
description: The ANTS behavioural marker system is a framework developed and tested by Fletcher et al at the University of Aberdeen in 2002 for training and evaluating anaesthetists' performance. It "includes four skill categories necessary for good anaesthetic practice, including task management, teamwork, situation awareness and decision-making, with 15 elements and examples of good and bad behaviours for each element". It uses "a set of 4-point Likert scales to rate observed behaviours" with space for open comments, and supplies a common language for discussing non-technical skills and a framework for structuring teaching and debriefing.
requirements: Raters should conduct calibration and training in the system before using it for teaching and evaluation to ensure standardised judgement, as emphasised in the ANTS handbook
Assessment should be based only on behaviours observed directly, rated first at element level and then at the more general category level
constraints: The system cannot differentiate between NTS required for different scenarios and cannot capture and evaluate short scenarios
It does not distinguish between NTS required in a particular clinical setting and NTS in general
Over-reliance on assessment of the measure in the original study and failure to re-establish validity when modified or assessed in a new population or scenario
target_learning_goals: non-technical skills: task management, teamwork, situation awareness and decision-making
examples: Adapted NTS behavioural marker systems were developed for an organ procurement team, nurse anaesthetists and medical air ambulance teams using ANTS as the starting point

article_title: Large language models for generating medical examinations: systematic review.
citation: Artsi Yaara, Sorin Vera, Konen Eli, Glicksberg Benjamin S., Nadkarni Girish, Klang Eyal. (2024). Large language models for generating medical examinations: systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05239-y
title: Use LLMs as a supplementary tool for writing medical examinations until more conclusive evidence exists
description: The review concludes that LLMs can write MCQs for medical examinations but that their limitations, including hallucination and faulty items, cannot be ignored. It states that "LLMs may serve as a supplementary tool for writing medical examinations" until further study provides more conclusive evidence, and that AI should be viewed as a powerful tool best utilized by experienced professionals.
requirements: Cautious and critical evaluation of AI-generated questions, with awareness of AI limitations to avoid misuse and deterioration of medical education quality
constraints: Further research is needed on long-term effectiveness and impact; no reviewed study tested AI-generated MCQs in a real-world setting with medical students
target_learning_goals: generation of valid multiple-choice questions for medical examinations
examples: Five of eight reviewed studies demonstrated valid MCQs, yet all studies also presented faulty questions requiring modification

article_title: Findings Favor Haptics Feedback in Virtual Simulation Surgical Education: An Updated Systematic and Scoping Review.
citation: Sayed Azher, Aralia Mills, Jinzhi He, Taliah Hyjazie, Junko Tokuno, Andrea Quaiattini, and Jason M. Harley. (2024). Findings Favor Haptics Feedback in Virtual Simulation Surgical Education: An Updated Systematic and Scoping Review. Surgical Innovation. https://doi.org/10.1177/15533506241238263
title: Integrate haptic feedback in surgical virtual simulations as an adjunct to traditional teaching, with adequate simulator validation
description: The review concludes that haptic feedback generally enhances performance in surgical virtual simulations and should be integrated where possible, but positioned as a complement to — not a replacement for — traditional teaching methods. It states "Haptics generally enhances performance, complements traditional teaching methods, and offers personalized learning with adequate simulator validation". The review also stresses that simulator use for feedback requires adequate validation, since frequent feedback does not guarantee quality.
requirements: Adequate simulator validation before haptic VSs are used for feedback or training
constraints: Haptic feedback may not be universally effective for all task types; the review advises choosing the training method according to the specific task being trained
target_learning_goals: surgical procedural skills
instrument handling
clinical competencies
examples: The review notes that when exposure to animal models and cadavers is limited, such as for novices and medical students, virtual simulations with haptic feedback may be an invaluable alternative
key_sources: Sayed Azher, Aralia Mills, Jinzhi He, Taliah Hyjazie, Junko Tokuno, Andrea Quaiattini, and Jason M. Harley. (2024). article_title: Findings Favor Haptics Feedback in Virtual Simulation Surgical Education: An Updated Systematic and Scoping Review.
citation: Sayed Azher, Aralia Mills, Jinzhi He, Taliah Hyjazie, Junko Tokuno, Andrea Quaiattini, and Jason M. Harley. (2024). Findings Favor Haptics Feedback in Virtual Simulation Surgical Education: An Updated Systematic and Scoping Review. Surgical Innovation. https://doi.org/10.1177/15533506241238263
title: Taxonomy of replicated haptic interactions in surgical virtual simulations
description: The review organizes the haptic characteristics implemented across included studies into replicated interaction types: sense of collision or touch, drilling sensations, force changes from interacting with different tissue types, and haptic guidance along predefined paths. It reports that "sense of collision or touch (n = 12) ... drilling (n = 7) ... and force changes due to interactions with different tissue types (eg, skin, adipose tissue, vessels, n = 4) ... were the replicated haptic interactions", while 24 studies did not elaborate on the haptic characteristics provided. Delivery was most commonly via haptic arms (n = 23) or laparoscopic simulators (n = 10), often reinforced with visual and auditory cues for realism.
requirements: Haptic hardware such as haptic arms (eg, Phantom Omni) or laparoscopic simulator instrument handles/trocars to deliver force feedback
constraints: The review notes heterogeneity across surgical domains: dentistry and orthopedics emphasize drilling sensations with limited empirical support for their realism, while laparoscopic simulations lack replication of nuanced tactile properties of soft tissues and solid organs
target_learning_goals: surgical task performance
tissue handling
drilling skills
instrument manipulation
examples: The review describes the Phantom Omni arm, a mobile arm with six degrees of freedom that participants manipulate to feel haptic feedback generated via a control box

citation: Sten CW, Söderström K, Stensrud B, Nylund IB, Siqveland J. (2024). The effectiveness of virtual reality training on knowledge, skills and attitudes of health care professionals and students in assessing and treating mental health disorders: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05423-0
title: Classification of virtual patient training interventions into virtual standardized patient, interactive patient scenario, and virtual patient game designs
description: The review applies an updated classification of virtual patient interventions, based on Kononowicz et al. developed from Talbot et al.'s model, to categorize the VR training designs in the included studies. It distinguishes three designs: the virtual standardized patient, "a conversational agent that simulates clinical presentations for training purposes"; the interactive patient scenario, which "primarily uses text-based multimedia, enhanced with images and case histories"; and the virtual patient game using 3D avatars for clinical reasoning and team training. Four studies used VSPs, two IPS, and two VP games.
requirements: The classification requires expertise in VR systems and learning design; the review used advisers from VRINN, SIMInnlandet, and an experienced VP scholar to categorize interventions.
constraints: The VSP interventions classified in the review predate modern artificial intelligence but are considered conversational agents because they include an algorithm that answers questions.
target_learning_goals: mental health assessment and treatment skills
clinical interviewing
diagnostic reasoning
examples: In the review's Table 1, the eight included studies are each categorized as VSP, IPS, or VP game with their VR system, duration, comparison, and outcome measures.
