article_title: Surgical Sabermetrics: A Scoping Review of Technology-enhanced Assessment of Nontechnical Skills in the Operating Room.
citation: Howie Emma E., Ambler Olivia, Gunn Eilidh G.M., Dias Roger D., Wigmore Stephen J., Skipworth Richard J.E., Yule Steven J. (2024). Surgical Sabermetrics: A Scoping Review of Technology-enhanced Assessment of Nontechnical Skills in the Operating Room. Annals of Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1097/SLA.0000000000006211
title: Surgical sabermetrics: digital, sensor-based assessment of operative nontechnical skills organized by the NOTSS taxonomy with cognitive load as an added construct
description: Surgical sabermetrics is the practice of digital assessment for feedback and improvement in surgery, influenced by performance monitoring in elite sports. It integrates audio-visual capture of the operating room with sensor-based assessment of the surgeon and team, and clinical data. The review organizes the field by the NOTSS taxonomy (Situation Awareness, Decision-Making, Communication, Teamwork, Leadership) and introduces cognitive load as an additional nontechnical construct, defining nontechnical skills as "cognitive, social and personal resource skills that complement technical skills and contribute to safe and efficient task performance."
requirements: Studies must digitally measure at least one nontechnical skill per the NOTSS taxonomy, including CogL, in a surgical context
constraints: Objective metrics are proxy measures of performance variables of interest; interpretation of the surgical context is required to derive meaning, and ground truth is required to determine the validity
target_learning_goals: nontechnical skills assessment
cognitive load management
surgical performance improvement
examples: The review mapped 122 distinct objective digital metrics across 16 categories against NOTSS domains in Supplemental Table 2, with cardiovascular measures such as HRV the most frequently used (n=25 studies).

article_title: Differential attainment in assessment of postgraduate surgical trainees: a scoping review.
citation: Jones Rebecca L., Prusmetikul Suwimol, Whitehorn Sarah. (2024). Differential attainment in assessment of postgraduate surgical trainees: a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05580-2
title: Four-theme, three-level explanatory framework for causes of differential attainment in surgical training
description: The review organises proposed causes of differential attainment into four themes identified from the included literature: training culture, experience of assessment, social networks, and personal characteristics. It then maps these onto Regan de Bere et al.'s three levels — macro (high-level policy), meso (institutional or working environments) and micro (individual factors) — stating these levels "can be used to more deeply explore each of the four themes to enrich the discovery of causes of DA". The framework is the review's own thematic synthesis, not a tested model.
requirements: Causes must be explored through qualitative research, which the review says is more attuned to capturing the complexities of DA than the predominantly quantitative performance-metric literature
constraints: The review states there is a paucity of data explicitly addressing why DA occurs, so the framework rests on suggestive rather than causal evidence
target_learning_goals: equitable assessment and progression in surgical training
examples: The review cites Ellis et al. on variation in training experiences and access to supportive peers and role models, Woolf et al. on trainee perceptions that relationships with feedback-giving colleagues could affect ARCP results, and Roe et al.'s protective factors such as supportive supervisors and peer networks

title: Task-specific training framework of six key components for motor learning
description: The review organises its content assessment around six agreed key components of task-specific training for motor learning: practice structure, specificity, repetition, modification, progression, and feedback. The article defines TST as involving "goal directed practice, repetition, progressive challenge, and positive reinforcement to optimise motor learning". Each component was assessed in the included videos for whether demonstration and/or instruction was provided, forming the basis of the 0–12 suitability scoring system.

constraints: The scoring system was developed by the authors for this review, was subjective, and may have been affected by observer bias

It evaluates video content against the six key TST components, scoring "0 to 2 for each of the six TST components for a total possible score of 12": 2 if both demonstration and instruction were provided, 1 for either one, 0 for a missing component. Scores of 0–4 were considered unsuitable, 5–8 moderately suitable, and 9–12 very suitable.

title: Combine problem-based learning with case-based learning when designing clinical practical teaching for interventional procedures such as TACE
description: The article recommends the combined PBL+CBL teaching mode for TACE clinical education, concluding it "significantly improves the teaching effect and significantly improves the theoretical and surgical operations, meeting the requirements of clinical education." PBL supplies student-centered, question-guided group work while CBL anchors learning in real clinical cases that students investigate before teacher-led analysis. The authors suggest the combination allows more student-teacher interaction and helps forge a preliminary mind of clinical logic.

clinical thinking capacity

article_title: Problematic smartphone use and academic achievement: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
citation: Paterna, Adrian; Alcaraz-Ibáñez, Manuel; Aguilar-Parra, Jose M.; Salavera, Carlos; Demetrovics, Zsolt; Griffiths, Mark D. (2024). Problematic smartphone use and academic achievement: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of Behavioral Addictions. https://doi.org/10.1556/2006.2024.00014
title: Problematic smartphone use as a multidimensional behavioral pattern with psychological and physical symptoms
description: The article defines problematic smartphone use (PSU) as "a multidimensional behavioral pattern involving both psychological symptoms (e.g., salience and loss of control) and physical symptoms (e.g., tolerance and withdrawal), that may result in negative consequences in daily life". It treats PSU as a construct distinct from mere frequency or hours of use, which are "not necessarily problematic", and operationalizes it via psychometrically validated self-report instruments. The meta-analysis uses this construct as its predictor variable across studies.
requirements: PSU scores must derive from psychometrically-validated self-report instruments whose properties were formally tested in a peer-reviewed paper
constraints: The article notes there is no consensus on the definition and self-reported measurement of PSU, and aggregated scores prevented quantifying dimension-specific relationships
target_learners: elementary, middle school, high school, and tertiary students
target_learning_goals: academic achievement
reducing problematic smartphone use
examples: Included studies measured PSU with instruments such as the SAS-SV, PMPUQ, MPPUS and SABAS, scored continuously or categorically

article_title: Is there sufficient evidence for the association between executive dysfunction and academic performance in adolescents with major depressive disorder?: a systematic review.
citation: Urbańska-Grosz J, Walkiewicz M, Sitek EJ. (2023). European Child & Adolescent Psychiatry. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00787-023-02275-9
title: Executive functions as a multidimensional construct whose components relate differently to educational achievement across developmental stages
description: The review organises executive functions (EF) as a multi-dimensional construct encompassing prioritising, planning, initiating, maintaining and inhibiting goal-directed activity, monitoring performance, coordinating multiple activities and modifying strategy. It frames EF components as differentially important across education stages: inhibitory control matters at early school age, while planning multi-step activity gains importance once basic academic skills are mastered. The authors write that "EF as a multi-dimensional construct enable us to prioritise, plan, initiate, maintain and inhibit goal-directed activity, as well as monitor our performance, coordinate the performance of multiple activities, and modify our strategy".
requirements: Assessment must cover multiple EF components, as no single test captures all aspects; the review notes none of the included studies assessed all aspects of executive functions
constraints: Executive skills continue to evolve up to early adulthood, and the evolution of hot executive skills such as affective decision-making is unlikely to be linear, complicating study of EF in depressed adolescents

self-regulation strategies for classroom and individual study
examples: The review used this framework to classify the five included studies' measures into planning/decision-making, inhibitory control, working memory/attention, set-shifting and meta-tasking columns (Table 2), noting meta-tasking was never assessed

citation: Crean Daniel, Gordijn Bert, Kearns Alan J. (2024). Impact and Assessment of Research Integrity Teaching: A Systematic Literature Review. Science and Engineering Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11948-024-00493-1
title: Rest's four-stage ethical decision-making process as the organizing framework for evaluating RI teaching claims
description: The review organizes its analysis around Rest's (1986) distinction of four stages of the ethical decision-making process. As the article states, "Rest (1986) distinguishes four stages of the ethical decision-making process, i.e. awareness, reasoning, motivation, and action", and these stages "are often mentioned as aims / goals of RI teaching". The review built a rubric guided by these stages to classify whether each of 86 eligible sources claimed RI teaching improves or does not improve each stage, and whether claims carried primary or secondary evidence.
requirements: Sources must make claims about how RI teaching affects one or more of the four stages for the rubric to classify them
constraints: The review excluded the impact of mentors, role-models, advisors, or supervisors, focusing only on formal RI teaching
target_learners: researchers at undergraduate, postgraduate, and principal investigator levels
target_learning_goals: research integrity ethical awareness, reasoning, motivation, and action
examples: The rubric in Fig. 2 classified each eligible source's claims by stage, treating 'behaviour' as the term primarily used for action
key_sources: Crean Daniel, Gordijn Bert, Kearns Alan J. (2024). Impact and Assessment of Research Integrity Teaching: A Systematic Literature Review. Science and Engineering Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11948-024-00493-1

article_title: Objective assessment tools in laparoscopic or robotic-assisted gynecological surgery: A systematic review.
citation: Tesfai FM, Nagi J, Morrison I, Boal M, Olaitan A, Chandrasekaran D, Stoyanov D, Lanceley A, Francis N. (2024). Objective assessment tools in laparoscopic or robotic‐assisted gynecological surgery: A systematic review. Acta Obstet Gynecol Scand. https://doi.org/10.1111/aogs.14840
title: Contemporary five-aspect validity framework (adapted from Messick) for appraising surgical assessment tools
description: The review applies a contemporary framework of validity, adapted from Messick's validity framework, with five aspects: content, response process, internal structure, relationship to other variables, and consequences. Each aspect is scored 0–3, giving a maximum of 15, banded as limited (1–5), moderate (6–10) or substantial (11–15) validity. The scoring system was adapted from Beckman, Ghaderi, Haug and Grüter and modified for this review; separate scoring definitions are provided for manual tools and APMs, e.g. for APMs "Performance metrics were recorded by the simulator (i.e., eliminating rater bias)". The framework structures the review's per-tool validity tables.
requirements: Assessment of all five aspects requires data such as expert consensus or task analysis for content, rater training or blinding for response process, and reliability measures for internal structure
constraints: Scoring bands and definitions were modified by the authors for this review; the framework was applied only to technical-skills tools in laparoscopic or robotic-assisted gynecological surgery
target_learners: surgical trainees in minimally invasive gynecological surgery
target_learning_goals: objective assessment of technical surgical skills
proficiency-based progression in surgical training
examples: Each of the 37 tools was categorized along the five dimensions of the framework in Tables 3–7 and Table S2, producing the substantial/moderate/limited ranking in Table 8
key_sources: Tesfai FM, Nagi J, Morrison I, Boal M, Olaitan A, Chandrasekaran D, Stoyanov D, Lanceley A, Francis N. (2024). Objective assessment tools in laparoscopic or robotic‐assisted gynecological surgery: A systematic review. Acta Obstet Gynecol Scand. https://doi.org/10.1111/aogs.14840

article_title: Objective assessment tools in laparoscopic or robotic-assisted gynecological surgery: A systematic review.
citation: Tesfai FM, Nagi J, Morrison I, Boal M, Olaitan A, Chandrasekaran D, Stoyanov D, Lanceley A, Francis N. (2024). Objective assessment tools in laparoscopic or robotic‐assisted gynecological surgery: A systematic review. Acta Obstet Gynecol Scand. https://doi.org/10.1111/aogs.14840
title: Inventory of 37 objective assessment tools for minimally invasive gynecological surgery
description: The review assembles an inventory of 37 assessment tools for minimally invasive gynecological surgery, organized into manual global rating tools (e.g. OSATS, GOALS, GEARS, GRS, GERT), manual procedure-specific tools (e.g. OSA-LS, H-OSATS, OSA-TLH, RHAS, CAT-LSH, myTIPreport) and 11 automated performance metrics from VR simulators (e.g. da Vinci Surgical Simulation, LapSim, LapMentor, MIST, RobotiX Mentor, LapVR). The review states "There is a plethora of objective assessment tools in minimally invasive gynecological surgery" and provides validity evidence, MERSQI quality scores and level of evidence for each tool in Tables 3–8. It is offered as a resource for researchers, educators and practitioners.
requirements: Users should consult the per-tool validity evidence and MERSQI quality ratings before selecting a tool, since evidence strength varies widely
constraints: Excludes tools for open, intrauterine and vaginal surgery and nontechnical skills tools; only English-language studies were included
target_learners: surgical trainees in minimally invasive gynecological surgery
target_learning_goals: objective assessment of laparoscopic and robotic-assisted surgical technical skills
examples: The review reports that OSATS-family tools were used most frequently (n = 32 studies) and that the RobotiX Mentor simulator provided a pass/fail benchmark score of 75/110
key_sources: Tesfai FM, Nagi J, Morrison I, Boal M, Olaitan A, Chandrasekaran D, Stoyanov D, Lanceley A, Francis N. (2024). Objective assessment tools in laparoscopic or robotic‐assisted gynecological surgery: A systematic review. Acta Obstet Gynecol Scand. https://doi.org/10.1111/aogs.14840

article_title: What do we know about Objective Structured Clinical Examination in Sport and Exercise Medicine? A scoping review.
citation: El Sherif Reem, Shrier Ian, Paul-Tellier Pierre, Rodriguez Charo. (2024). What do we know about Objective Structured Clinical Examination in Sport and Exercise Medicine? A scoping review. Canadian Medical Education Journal. https://doi.org/10.36834/cmej.77841
title: Two-purpose framework for OSCE use in Sport and Exercise Medicine education
description: The review organises the included literature around two distinct uses of the OSCE in SEM and musculoskeletal education: summative competency assessment after training, and evaluation of educational interventions. It states OSCEs "were generally used for two different objectives in Sports Medicine and MSK education programs". Of the 22 included studies, 11 assessed knowledge/skills during or after a training program, 8 assessed an intervention, and 3 assessed and improved the OSCE tool itself. The framework maps study objectives, participants, and psychometric reporting across the field.
requirements: Studies must describe an OSCE or similar station-based, case-based assessment relevant to sport/exercise/MSK medicine training
constraints: The review excluded OSCEs used for assessment in general medical training or other specialties
target_learning_goals: musculoskeletal and sport medicine clinical skills, including history-taking, physical examination, and procedural skills
examples: The review coded each included study's objective in NVivo and reported the frequency of each objective category in Table 1.
key_sources: El Sherif Reem, Shrier Ian, Paul-Tellier Pierre, Rodriguez Charo. (2024). What do we know about Objective Structured Clinical Examination in Sport and Exercise Medicine? A scoping review. Canadian Medical Education Journal. https://doi.org/10.36834/cmej.77841

article_title: Impacts of blended learning with BOPPPS model on Chinese medical undergraduate students: a comprehensive systematic review and meta-analysis of 44 studies.
citation: Li Shuze, Wei Wei, Li Xiaofeng, Ma Li, Li Qiujuan, Sun Xiance, Chen Xin. (2024). Impacts of blended learning with BOPPPS model on Chinese medical undergraduate students: a comprehensive systematic review and meta-analysis of 44 studies. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05917-x
title: BOPPPS six-step teaching model
description: BOPPPS is a goal-oriented, student-centered teaching model divided into "six essential steps: bridge-in, objective, pre-assessment, participatory learning, and summary" (with post-assessment), originating from Canadian teacher skill training put forward by Douglas Kerrin in 1978. In the blended version, teachers use an online platform for pre-class introduction resources, online pre-tests of 10–20 exercises, in-class or online participatory discussions, group reporting and role-playing, post-testing, and in-class plus post-class summarization. The article treats the six stages as "a coherent, systematic, and actionable teaching design model" and evaluates its blended implementation against LBL.
requirements: An online teaching platform (e.g. Xuexi Tong, Rain Classes, MOOC) to deliver pre-class resources, tests, and discussions
Teachers able to evaluate and modify each of the six steps, which the article says makes it extremely convenient to implement
constraints: The article notes some students still reported poor classroom interaction in purely online courses, which the blended mode is said to compensate for
target_learners: Chinese medical undergraduate students in higher medical education
target_learning_goals: Medical theory knowledge
Practical skills
Autonomous learning ability
Classroom satisfaction and engagement
examples: In the pre-test phase teachers generate 10–20 exercises aligned with teaching objectives online; applied knowledge is taught through role-playing involving both students and teachers
key_sources: Li Shuze, Wei Wei, Li Xiaofeng, Ma Li, Li Qiujuan, Sun Xiance, Chen Xin. (2024). Impacts of blended learning with BOPPPS model on Chinese medical undergraduate students: a comprehensive systematic review and meta-analysis of 44 studies. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05917-x

article_title: Implementation of simulation training in the Intensive Care Units (ICU) during the COVID-19 pandemic: A scoping review.
citation: Nouira Hajer, Jaoued Oussama, Ouanes Islem, Jrad Maissa, Chtioui Soumaya, Gharbi Rim, Fekih Hassen Mohamed, Ben Sik Ali Habiba, Elatrous Souheil. (2024). Implementation of simulation training in the Intensive Care Units (ICU) during the COVID-19 pandemic: A scoping review. La Tunisie Médicale. https://doi.org/10.62438/tunismed.v102i8.4972
title: Kirkpatrick Model as the review's framework for stratifying training impact across four levels
description: The Kirkpatrick Model, first developed by Donald Kirkpatrick in 1959, is a tool for evaluating the effectiveness of a training program. The review uses it as its organizing evaluation axis: "The model stratifies the level of impact of training results according to four levels: performance and patient outcomes (level 4), behavioral change after training (level 3), individual learning (level 2), and participants' reactions to training (level 1)." Each included study's main results were sorted by the Kirkpatrick level investigated.
requirements: Training outcomes must be mapped to one of the four stratified levels for the model to structure evaluation as the review uses it
constraints: The review found the highest level, patient outcomes, was not assessed in any included study
target_learners: health care providers in critical care
target_learning_goals: evaluating the impact of simulation-based training programs
examples: The review sorted each included article's main results by the Kirkpatrick level investigated and synthesized findings across three thematic axes
key_sources: Nouira Hajer, Jaoued Oussama, Ouanes Islem, Jrad Maissa, Chtioui Soumaya, Gharbi Rim, Fekih Hassen Mohamed, Ben Sik Ali Habiba, Elatrous Souheil. (2024). Implementation of simulation training in the Intensive Care Units (ICU) during the COVID-19 pandemic: A scoping review. La Tunisie Médicale. https://doi.org/10.62438/tunismed.v102i8.4972

article_title: A systematic review of medical practitioners' retention and application of basic sciences to clinical practice.
citation: Albert Francis A., Seidu Abdul-Aziz, Mason Hannah M., Anderson Emma, Alele Faith O., Heggarty Paula, Hollins Aaron, Gupta Tarun Sen, Hays Richard B., McArthur Lawrie, Malau-Aduli Bunmi S. (2024). A systematic review of medical practitioners' retention and application of basic sciences to clinical practice. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05952-8
title: Encapsulated knowledge: basic science integrates into clinical concepts as expertise develops
description: Encapsulated knowledge is a form of transformed basic science knowledge that attaches relevant basic science knowledge to clinical scenarios and diagnoses. The review states that "integrated basic science knowledge aids in synthesising clinical presentations, reducing the need for detailed recall as clinical experience grows". It explains why detailed retention may diminish while the conceptual framework remains crucial for ongoing learning and clinical reasoning, and why specialist practice narrows working memory to encapsulated knowledge focused on the scope of practice.
requirements: Teaching basic sciences within a clinical context and introducing patient problems early in the curriculum, which the review states are essential for developing encapsulated knowledge
constraints: The review attributes the concept to Schmidt and Rikers and related literature rather than testing it directly in the included studies
target_learning_goals: integration of basic science with clinical reasoning
long-term retention of basic science knowledge
examples: The review cites the finding that students who learned causal explanations for symptoms retained diagnostic information better than those who learned epidemiological information
key_sources: Albert Francis A., Seidu Abdul-Aziz, Mason Hannah M., Anderson Emma, Alele Faith O., Heggarty Paula, Hollins Aaron, Gupta Tarun Sen, Hays Richard B., McArthur Lawrie, Malau-Aduli Bunmi S. (2024). A systematic review of medical practitioners' retention and application of basic sciences to clinical practice. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05952-8

article_title: Primary care physicians' knowledge and confidence in providing cancer survivorship care: a systematic review.
citation: Vos Julien A. M., Wollersheim Barbara M., Cooke Adelaide, Ee Carolyn, Chan Raymond J., Nekhlyudov Larissa. (2023). Primary care physicians’ knowledge and confidence in providing cancer survivorship care: a systematic review. Journal of Cancer Survivorship. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11764-023-01397-y
title: Nekhlyudov cancer survivorship care domains framework for characterizing PCP knowledge and confidence
description: The review organizes its outcomes using the five domains of quality cancer survivorship care proposed by Nekhlyudov et al.: prevention and surveillance for recurrences and new cancers; surveillance and management of physical effects; surveillance and management of psychosocial effects; surveillance and management of chronic medical conditions; and health promotion and disease prevention. The review states that quantitative outcomes "were analyzed using the framework method and mapped to the different domains of cancer survivorship care". Mapping outcomes to these domains reveals that confidence and knowledge vary across care domains, with gaps concentrated in physical effects and recurrence surveillance.
requirements: Outcomes must be classifiable into the five survivorship care domains to apply the mapping method
constraints: The review notes it did not address care coordination and communication, a sixth component of the quality framework
target_learners: Primary care physicians (PCPs, GPs, family physicians) providing cancer survivorship care
target_learning_goals: Knowledge and confidence in providing cancer survivorship care across its domains
examples: The review mapped quantitative outcomes from 33 papers to the domains and found most papers described physical effects (n = 19), psychosocial effects (n = 12), and recurrence surveillance (n = 14)
key_sources: Vos Julien A. M., Wollersheim Barbara M., Cooke Adelaide, Ee Carolyn, Chan Raymond J., Nekhlyudov Larissa. (2023). Primary care physicians’ knowledge and confidence in providing cancer survivorship care: a systematic review. Journal of Cancer Survivorship. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11764-023-01397-y

article_title: The efficacy of simulation-based learning versus non-simulation-based learning in endocrinology education: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
citation: Wu Zeyu, Huang Yiling, Lyu Ling, Huang Yu, Ping Fan. (2024). The efficacy of simulation-based learning versus non-simulation-based learning in endocrinology education: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06010-z
title: Three-type taxonomy of simulation techniques in endocrinology education: computer-based simulation, scenario-based simulation, and standardized patients
description: The article organizes the simulation interventions in the reviewed trials into three primary types. "Computer-based simulations employ software applications" offering adaptability and scalability for repetitive practice; "Scenario-based simulations utilize prearranged scenarios and settings," often with role-playing and tangible equipment; and "Standardized patients involve trained actors or volunteers who simulate real patient scenarios," supporting communication and clinical reasoning. The taxonomy structures both the included studies and the subgroup analysis by simulation technique.
requirements: Each technique requires interactive design, timely feedback, and a safe learning environment for developing medical skills, as the article states these are common features
constraints: The article notes notable disparities exist among the three methods, so their attributes are not interchangeable across learning goals
target_learning_goals: endocrine theoretical knowledge
clinical and communication skills
clinical decision-making
examples: In the included trials, 10 studies used standardized patients, 6 employed computer-based simulations, and 6 used scenario-based simulation methods

article_title: Essential core competencies for health policy graduates: a multi-method consensus type study.
citation: Doshmangir Leila, Alipouri Sakha Minoo, Mostafavi Hakimeh, Kabiri Neda, Ghaffarifar Saeideh, Takian Amirhossein. (2024). Essential core competencies for health policy graduates: a multi-method consensus type study. Health Research Policy and Systems. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12961-024-01221-8
title: A competency framework for health policy doctoral graduates organized into five competency categories with sub-categories and detailed skills
description: The article presents a finalized framework (Table 4) mapping five core competencies — health policy research, policy analysis, educational competencies, decision-making and multidisciplinary work — into sub-categories (e.g. leadership and management, evaluation, consultation, advocacy) and detailed skill lists. It was built by combining scoping-review domains with interview-derived competencies and refining them through expert consensus. Skills range from "Exploring databases and journals to retrieve relevant articles and documents" to cost-effectiveness analysis and advocacy for evidence use in decision-making.
requirements: Curricula must be aligned with the competencies, objectives and assessments, which the article calls essential to guarantee alignment
constraints: The competencies are presented in no particular order and were derived in the Iranian context with international input, so contextual tailoring is emphasized
target_learners: health policy doctoral students and post-doctoral graduates
target_learning_goals: health policy research
policy analysis
educational competencies
decision-making
multidisciplinary work
examples: The framework specifies research skills such as designing and implementing basic and advanced research, applying ethical principles to research, and translating and effectively presenting findings to stakeholders.
key_sources: Doshmangir Leila, Alipouri Sakha Minoo, Mostafavi Hakimeh, Kabiri Neda, Ghaffarifar Saeideh, Takian Amirhossein. (2024). Essential core competencies for health policy graduates: a multi-method consensus type study. Health Research Policy and Systems. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12961-024-01221-8

article_title: Essential core competencies for health policy graduates: a multi-method consensus type study.
citation: Doshmangir Leila, Alipouri Sakha Minoo, Mostafavi Hakimeh, Kabiri Neda, Ghaffarifar Saeideh, Takian Amirhossein. (2024). Essential core competencies for health policy graduates: a multi-method consensus type study. Health Research Policy and Systems. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12961-024-01221-8
title: Health policy curricula should be contextually tailored to foster multi-dimensional competencies complementing graduates' specific disciplines
description: The article concludes that curriculum appropriateness and contextual tailoring are crucial to foster multi-dimensional competencies that complement the specific disciplines of future health policy scholars, enabling them to serve their health systems towards health-system goals and sustainable development. This follows from the consensus finding that competencies span research, policy analysis, education, decision-making and multidisciplinary work, and from the observation that graduates often cannot secure positions matching their training.
requirements: Educational content should be continuously updated and identified by stakeholders from diverse disciplines
constraints: The article notes a paucity of attention to modifying higher education curricula in numerous countries, including Iran
target_learning_goals: preparation for academic and non-academic roles
serving health-system goals and sustainable development
examples: Iran's first health policy doctoral curriculum, developed over a decade ago, drew from nursing, medicine, midwifery, health education, social welfare, rehabilitation and management disciplines across four universities.

article_title: The status of interprofessional education for healthcare students in South Korea: a scoping review focusing on simulation-based education.
citation: Lee Sunmin, Kim Myung Chun, Kim Jongyoon. (2024). The status of interprofessional education for healthcare students in South Korea: a scoping review focusing on simulation-based education. Korean Journal of Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.3946/kjme.2024.304
title: Kirkpatrick's Expanded Outcomes Typology for categorizing educational effectiveness of IPE
description: The review applies Kirkpatrick's Expanded Outcomes Typology as its organizing framework for evaluating educational effectiveness, which "delineates four levels of educational effectiveness: reaction, attitude, behavior, and results". Simulation methods were classified by multidimensional aspects including human versus computer simulation and fidelity, as described by Elshama. The review uses these frameworks to categorize the ten included studies' outcome evaluations and to diagnose the field's concentration on lower levels.
requirements: Outcome measures must be mappable onto the four levels of reaction, attitude, behavior, and results
constraints: The review found most Korean simulation-based IPE studies only reached levels 1 and 2, with no study covering level 4
target_learning_goals: interprofessional collaboration competencies
teamwork and communication skills

article_title: The effectiveness of simulation-based learning (SBL) on students' knowledge and skills in nursing programs: a systematic review.
citation: Alharbi, A., Nurfianti, A., Mullen, R. F., McClure, J. D., & Miller, W. H. (2024). The effectiveness of simulation-based learning (SBL) on students’ knowledge and skills in nursing programs: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education, 24. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06080-z
title: Three-theme framework for synthesising SBL effects: acquisition, retention, and wider clinical performance
description: The review organises its narrative synthesis into three themes interpreting SBL's impact on nursing students. The first theme, "Impact of SBL on knowledge and skills acquisition", probes immediate effects on learner capabilities; the second, "Impact of SBL on retention of knowledge and skills", examines durability over time; the third, "Impact of SBL on wider clinical performance", concerns broader practice outcomes including self-confidence, satisfaction, clinical reasoning, self-efficacy and problem-solving. The framework structures how the review's 33 studies are compared across designs, interventions and outcome measures.
requirements: Studies must report knowledge, skills acquisition and/or retention outcomes in nursing student populations to be synthesised under the framework
constraints: The retention theme lacks universality due to limited long-term analyses and mixed results, as the review states
target_learning_goals: clinical knowledge acquisition
psychomotor clinical skills
retention of clinical competencies
clinical performance behaviours such as teamwork and self-efficacy
examples: The review categorises findings from 33 studies into the three themes, e.g., CPR skill gains under Theme 1, four-month BLS retention under Theme 2, and teamwork improvements under Theme 3
key_sources: Alharbi, A., Nurfianti, A., Mullen, R. F., McClure, J. D., & Miller, W. H. (2024). The effectiveness of simulation-based learning (SBL) on students’ knowledge and skills in nursing programs: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education, 24. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06080-z

article_title: The effectiveness of simulation-based learning (SBL) on students' knowledge and skills in nursing programs: a systematic review.
citation: Alharbi, A., Nurfianti, A., Mullen, R. F., McClure, J. D., & Miller, W. H. (2024). The effectiveness of simulation-based learning (SBL) on students’ knowledge and skills in nursing programs: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education, 24. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06080-z
title: Use simulation-based learning as a core teaching strategy in nursing education while continuing to evaluate and refine it
description: The review concludes that simulation-based learning is a potent teaching strategy within nursing education, supporting its use for building knowledge and clinical skills in safe, realistic environments. It pairs this endorsement with the requirement for "the ongoing evaluation and refinement of this approach", since acquisition evidence is stronger than retention evidence. Educators adopting SBL should therefore treat it as an evidence-supported but still-evolving method whose design, implementation and evaluation need continued study.
requirements: Ongoing evaluation and refinement of SBL interventions, as the review's conclusion states
constraints: Limited studies evaluated retention beyond five months, constraining generalisable claims regarding durability
Heterogeneity of study designs, risk of bias, and lack of long-term follow-up limit the evidence base
target_learning_goals: clinical knowledge and skills acquisition
life-support and emergency-response competencies
examples: The review's 33 included studies implemented SBL via high-, medium- and low-fidelity manikins, virtual simulation, serious games and virtual reality across CPR, critical care and decision-making topics
key_sources: Alharbi, A., Nurfianti, A., Mullen, R. F., McClure, J. D., & Miller, W. H. (2024). The effectiveness of simulation-based learning (SBL) on students’ knowledge and skills in nursing programs: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education, 24. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06080-z

article_title: Automated analysis of operative video in surgical training: scoping review.
citation: Dick L, Boyle CP, Skipworth RJE, Smink DS, Tallentire VR, Yule S. (2024). Automated analysis of operative video in surgical training: scoping review. BJS Open. https://doi.org/10.1093/bjsopen/zrae124
title: Three-domain taxonomy of automated operative video metrics: process, outcome and critical safety elements
description: The review organizes the metrics generated by automated video analysis into three domains: process metrics (for example movement of instruments), outcome metrics (for example intraoperative phase duration), and critical safety elements (for example critical view of safety in laparoscopic cholecystectomy). Process-based metrics "uniformly analysed motion" and were mostly generated by computer vision tracking, while outcome-based metrics were more diverse and largely generated from advanced AI-based analysis. The review uses this classification to describe the full range of metrics across the 13 included studies.
requirements: Automated analysis of real-world operative video footage with non-human assessment applied during or after the operation
constraints: No included study produced metrics for the assessment of non-technical skills
target_learning_goals: technical operative skill assessment and feedback
examples: Studies generated suturing scores for transanal total mesorectal excision, phase durations for laparoscopic cholecystectomy and cataract surgery, and heat maps showing areas of safe and unsafe dissection
key_sources: Dick L, Boyle CP, Skipworth RJE, Smink DS, Tallentire VR, Yule S. (2024). Automated analysis of operative video in surgical training: scoping review. BJS Open. https://doi.org/10.1093/bjsopen/zrae124

article_title: Automated analysis of operative video in surgical training: scoping review.
citation: Dick L, Boyle CP, Skipworth RJE, Smink DS, Tallentire VR, Yule S. (2024). Automated analysis of operative video in surgical training: scoping review. BJS Open. https://doi.org/10.1093/bjsopen/zrae124
title: Evidence corpus of 13 real-world operative video analytics studies
description: The review's evidence base comprises 13 studies applying automated video analysis to trainee-performed real-world operations, identified from 6736 screened articles. The median number of videos included for analysis was 69 (range 6–1107), with a total of 107 trainees and 152 attendings or experts reported across studies. Cataract surgery and cholecystectomy were the two most common operations assessed, and the mean adjusted MERSQI quality score was 12.73 out of 18. All studies were published within the last 10 years, with 8 within the last 5 years.
requirements: Studies must use real-world operations, trainee-performed video, automated analysis, and metrics with potential to facilitate feedback and training
constraints: Simulated or virtual reality settings were excluded, which the review notes may have under-represented minimally invasive surgery
target_learning_goals: automated assessment of operative technical performance
examples: Included study designs were predominantly prospective cohort studies (8), with 4 retrospective cohort studies and 1 qualitative study
key_sources: Dick L, Boyle CP, Skipworth RJE, Smink DS, Tallentire VR, Yule S. (2024). Automated analysis of operative video in surgical training: scoping review. BJS Open. https://doi.org/10.1093/bjsopen/zrae124

article_title: Teaching and learning clinical reasoning skill in undergraduate medical students: A scoping review.
citation: Delavari S, Barzkar F, Rikers MJP, Pourahmadi M, Soltani Arabshahi SK, Keshtkar A, Dargahi H, Yaghmaei M, Monajemi A. (2024). Teaching and learning clinical reasoning skill in undergraduate medical students: A scoping review. PLOS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0309606
title: Taxonomy of clinical reasoning educational interventions by focus (process- vs knowledge-oriented) and case presentation (serial cue vs whole cases)
description: The review organizes the 54 included studies' educational interventions along stated dimensions: strategies were presented "by serial cue or whole clinical cases that presented as process-oriented or knowledge-oriented". It also charts intervention duration, number of clinical cases, and whether the same cases were used for pretest, intervention and posttest, providing a dimensional map of the intervention space for clinical reasoning teaching in undergraduate medical education.
requirements: Studies must report the educational strategy, case presentation format, and purpose of the teaching approach for the dimensions to be charted
constraints: Based on 54 included studies published between January 1, 2010, and March 23, 2024, in four databases, excluding gray literature
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning skill
diagnostic accuracy
examples: Method of clinical case presentation in 28 and 13 studies were whole cases and serial cue, respectively; purpose of teaching approach of 34 and 13 studies were process- and knowledge-oriented, respectively
key_sources: Delavari S, Barzkar F, Rikers MJP, Pourahmadi M, Soltani Arabshahi SK, Keshtkar A, Dargahi H, Yaghmaei M, Monajemi A. (2024). Teaching and learning clinical reasoning skill in undergraduate medical students: A scoping review. PLOS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0309606

article_title: Designing a framework for curriculum building in systematic review competencies for librarians: a case report.
citation: Farris David P., Lebo Rachael A., Price Carrie. (2024). Designing a framework for curriculum building in systematic review competencies for librarians: a case report. Journal of the Medical Library Association : JMLA. https://doi.org/10.5195/jmla.2024.1930
title: Four-module curriculum structure mapping learning objectives to systematic review competencies and SRSS skills
description: The course is organized into four modules that together cover the systematic review searching workflow: consultation and pre-searching, searching, search strategy peer review, and search reporting. Each module is mapped in Table 1 to the learning objectives set by the MLA SR Workgroup and to corresponding SRSS skills (8–14). As the article states, "Four modules were established that would meet the course objectives: Module 1, consultation and pre-searching, Module 2, searching, Module 3, search strategy peer review, and Module 4, search reporting." The pattern is reusable for librarian evidence-synthesis training.
requirements: Objectives must be defined in advance by a competency framework (here the Townsend et al. six competencies and the SRSS skills) so modules can be mapped to them
constraints: The pilot in-person offering was four hours and online offerings two 2.5-hour sessions; the article notes building a full systematic review search is not feasible in the course context
target_learners: health science librarians, both new and experienced searchers earning the SRSS specialization
target_learning_goals: systematic review searching skills: reference interviewing, preliminary searching, database selection, comprehensive search strategy building, search peer review, and search reporting
examples: Online offerings divided into two 2.5-hour sessions with a breakout-group activity constructing a search string for one of three concepts, followed by instructors live-testing the full three-concept search strategy in PubMed
key_sources: Farris David P., Lebo Rachael A., Price Carrie. (2024). Designing a framework for curriculum building in systematic review competencies for librarians: a case report. Journal of the Medical Library Association : JMLA. https://doi.org/10.5195/jmla.2024.1930

article_title: Designing a framework for curriculum building in systematic review competencies for librarians: a case report.
citation: Farris David P., Lebo Rachael A., Price Carrie. (2024). Designing a framework for curriculum building in systematic review competencies for librarians: a case report. Journal of the Medical Library Association : JMLA. https://doi.org/10.5195/jmla.2024.1930
title: Townsend et al. six-competency framework for librarians involved in systematic reviews
description: A competency framework developed in 2017 by Townsend et al. for librarians involved in systematic reviews, adapted from Miller's Pyramid for Clinical Assessment, outlining six competency areas with smaller associated skills and indicators. The article's course objectives were intended to align with these competencies: "1) conducting a reference interview, 2) performing preliminary searches, 3) selecting appropriate resources to search, 4) building an extensive, comprehensive, and documented search strategy, 5) peer reviewing search strategies, and 6) reporting search methods." The MLA SRSS workgroup used the framework to define twenty-six fundamental skills on two Learning Pathways.
requirements: The framework is used to define course objectives and to derive the SRSS fundamental skills on Level I and Level II Learning Pathways
constraints: The article presents the framework as adapted from Miller's Pyramid for Clinical Assessment; it does not report validation data for the framework itself
target_learners: health science librarians supporting systematic reviews
target_learning_goals: systematic review competencies from reference interview through search reporting
examples: The instructors reviewed the Townsend et al. competencies and the Spencer and Eldredge librarian roles when initially planning and developing the curriculum
key_sources: Farris David P., Lebo Rachael A., Price Carrie. (2024). Designing a framework for curriculum building in systematic review competencies for librarians: a case report. Journal of the Medical Library Association : JMLA. https://doi.org/10.5195/jmla.2024.1930

article_title: Designing a framework for curriculum building in systematic review competencies for librarians: a case report.
citation: Farris David P., Lebo Rachael A., Price Carrie. (2024). Designing a framework for curriculum building in systematic review competencies for librarians: a case report. Journal of the Medical Library Association : JMLA. https://doi.org/10.5195/jmla.2024.1930
title: Essential Searching Skills for Librarians on Systematic Review Teams course
description: A required Level I core course in the Medical Library Association's Systematic Review Services Specialization, developed and taught by the authors across eleven cohorts from 2022 to 2024, with approximately thirty registered participants per class. Each class used a Slack channel for communication and an open course site on Open Science Framework with readings, handouts, slides, and activity instructions. PubMed is the primary platform because it is "fully accessible without restriction to anyone with internet access and incorporates the MeSH database of controlled vocabulary." The course includes a five-question pre-test, four modules, a breakout-group search-building activity, and an identical post-test.
requirements: Delivered within the SRSS, which requires eight required core courses and four electives; participants are added to a Slack channel and given access to the OSF course site
constraints: The abbreviated three-concept activity was chosen over a full systematic review search because building a full search can take several weeks and requires input from an actual research team
target_learners: librarians of all searching skill levels earning the Systematic Review Services Specialization
target_learning_goals: comprehensive search strategy development, controlled vocabulary use, search peer review via PRESS, and search reporting via PRISMA-S
examples: The pilot class was held in person at the MLA Annual Meeting in New Orleans in May 2022, with subsequent online offerings and a final in-person offering in Portland, Oregon in May 2024

article_title: Core Competencies for Serious Illness Conversations: An Integrative Systematic Review.
citation: Susanna Pusa, Rebecca Baxter, Sofia Andersson, Erik K. Fromme, Joanna Paladino, Anna Sandgren. (2024). Core Competencies for Serious Illness Conversations: An Integrative Systematic Review. Journal of Palliative Care. https://doi.org/10.1177/08258597241245022
title: Three-theme taxonomy of core competencies for serious illness conversations
description: The review proposes a taxonomy of clinician core competencies for serious illness conversations (SICs), defined as "a mixture of attributes comprising applied knowledge, skills, and attitudes". Thematic synthesis of 53 included articles produced three themes — conversation resources, intrapersonal capabilities, and interpersonal capabilities — with subthemes describing how each is applied, and a conceptual model (Figure 2) depicting circular interactions between the themes.
requirements: Competencies were sought only in articles pertaining to the Serious Illness Care Program and/or Serious Illness Conversation Guide
constraints: The review states that because it only examined SICP/SICG-related articles, the competencies likely reflect some of the program's or guide's content
target_learning_goals: conducting effective serious illness conversations with seriously ill patients
examples: The review screened 313 records at title/abstract, assessed 96 full texts, and included 53 articles appraised with Joanna Briggs Institute checklists and synthesized thematically
key_sources: Susanna Pusa, Rebecca Baxter, Sofia Andersson, Erik K. Fromme, Joanna Paladino, Anna Sandgren. (2024). Core Competencies for Serious Illness Conversations: An Integrative Systematic Review. Journal of Palliative Care. https://doi.org/10.1177/08258597241245022

article_title: Virtual reality simulation and real-life training programs for cataract surgery: a scoping review of the literature.
citation: Dormegny Lea, Lansingh Van Charles, Lejay Anne, Chakfe Nabil, Yaici Rémi, Sauer Arnaud, Gaucher David, Henderson Bonnie An, Thomsen Ann Sofia Skou, Bourcier Tristan. (2024). Virtual reality simulation and real-life training programs for cataract surgery: a scoping review of the literature. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06245-w
title: EyeSi and HelpMeSee virtual reality cataract surgery simulators
description: Two widely used virtual reality simulators for cataract surgery training. EyeSi is "a widespread, commercially-available cataract surgery simulator designed for phacoemulsification and vitreoretinal surgery self-guided training" mostly used in high-income countries. HelpMeSee "focuses on resource-limited areas in low- and middle-income countries", mainly training manual small incision cataract surgery with certified instructors and a reimbursement system. The review compared outcomes across 13 EyeSi studies and one HMS study.
requirements: Access to the simulator hardware, which the review notes is limited by acquisition and maintenance cost
constraints: EyeSi is mostly located in high-income countries while HMS is primarily found in low- and middle-income countries, illustrating unequal access to the technology
target_learners: Allied health personnel in resource-limited areas (HMS)
target_learning_goals: Cataract surgical skills (phacoemulsification, MSICS)
Patient safety in the operating room
examples: The HMS study in India used a 6-day, 35-hour training with 80% HMS simulator time plus a supervised surgery phase on actual patients
key_sources: Dormegny Lea, Lansingh Van Charles, Lejay Anne, Chakfe Nabil, Yaici Rémi, Sauer Arnaud, Gaucher David, Henderson Bonnie An, Thomsen Ann Sofia Skou, Bourcier Tristan. (2024). Virtual reality simulation and real-life training programs for cataract surgery: a scoping review of the literature. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06245-w

citation: Dormegny Lea, Lansingh Van Charles, Lejay Anne, Chakfe Nabil, Yaici Rémi, Sauer Arnaud, Gaucher David, Henderson Bonnie An, Thomsen Ann Sofia Skou, Bourcier Tristan. (2024). Virtual reality simulation and real-life training programs for cataract surgery: a scoping review of the literature. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06245-w
title: Use virtual reality simulation prior to performing real cataract surgery cases
description: The review concludes that virtual reality simulation appears to lead to safer outcomes than supervised surgical training on actual patients alone, "which encourages its use prior to performing real cases". Simulators enable repeated training on surgical steps without risking patient injury, and a VRS phase before surgery on actual patients, as in the HMS curriculum, may help reduce complication rates.
requirements: Access to a virtual reality simulator, which the review notes is limited by cost and unequal geographic distribution
constraints: Virtual reality simulators are sparsely distributed around the world with numerous access difficulties and lack of standardization between training programs
target_learners: Ophthalmology residents and trainees who have not yet completed specialty training
target_learning_goals: Safe cataract surgery performance in the operating room
Reduced intraoperative complications
examples: The review cites the HMS training curriculum and one EyeSi study that proposed a VRS phase prior to surgery on actual patients

article_title: Application of Emerging Teaching Models in Dental Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
citation: Pang Xuefei, Li Ling, Liu Xu, Wang Yan, Yang Bo. (2024). Application of Emerging Teaching Models in Dental Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. International Dental Journal. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.identj.2024.05.016
title: Taxonomy of four emerging student-centred teaching methods (PBL, CBL, TBL, FC) sharing student-centredness, group cooperation, and situational learning
description: The article organizes four emerging teaching methods — problem-based learning, case-based learning, team-based learning, and flipped classroom — by shared features and distinguishing characteristics (Table 1). All share that they "emphasize the central position of students", require students to "discuss and solve problems in small groups", and emphasize "placing learning in specific problems or case situations". They differ in orientation: PBL is problem-oriented, CBL is case-oriented using real clinical cases, TBL focuses on teamwork and communication skills, and FC is described as "a more student-centred teaching mode" requiring active participation. The review uses this taxonomy to structure its comparison against lecture-based learning.
requirements: Experimental groups must use only PBL, CBL, TBL, or FC without other educational tools, though auxiliary tools such as social media are allowed
constraints: No articles using TBL alone as the experimental teaching method were found meeting the inclusion criteria, so TBL is described but not meta-analytically evaluated
target_learners: dental undergraduates in every grade including interns
target_learning_goals: theoretical knowledge
clinical operational skills
critical thinking
self-directed learning
examples: The 29 included RCTs used PBL in 6 studies, CBL in 4 studies, FC in 16 studies, and combined methods in 3 studies
key_sources: Pang Xuefei, Li Ling, Liu Xu, Wang Yan, Yang Bo. (2024). Application of Emerging Teaching Models in Dental Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. International Dental Journal. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.identj.2024.05.016

article_title: Metaverse-based simulation: a scoping review of charting medical education over the last two decades in the lens of the 'marvelous medical education machine'.
citation: Popov Vitaliy, Mateju Natalie, Jeske Caris, Lewis Kadriye O. (2024). Metaverse-based simulation: a scoping review of charting medical education over the last two decades in the lens of the 'marvelous medical education machine'. Annals of Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1080/07853890.2024.2424450
title: Updated 'unstuck' model of medical education in which space converges with time and content, and assessment becomes multifaceted and multimodal
description: The review proposes an updated version of Friedman's 'marvelous medical education machine' framework in which the originally isolated space dimension 'is no longer isolated but converges with content and time'. In this model, learning occurs anywhere and anytime, content is customizable to individual learner needs, and assessment 'can occur at any point in the learning process', using varied methods and sources serving formative and summative purposes. The review uses this four-dimension framework (space, time, content, assessment) as its coding scheme to thematically analyze 173 publications.
requirements: Coding publications requires studies providing insights related to at least one of Friedman's dimensions: Time, Space, Content, or Assessment
constraints: The review notes significant heterogeneity in technologies, educational contexts, learner groups, and measured outcomes across the 173 included studies
target_learning_goals: clinical competencies including patient care, medical knowledge, procedural training, interprofessional teamwork, clinical reasoning, and critical thinking
examples: An innovative eXtended Reality International Grand Rounds study used XR to connect tens of trainees to the same content at the same time, allowing a learning event to occur at scale
key_sources: Popov Vitaliy, Mateju Natalie, Jeske Caris, Lewis Kadriye O. (2024). Metaverse-based simulation: a scoping review of charting medical education over the last two decades in the lens of the 'marvelous medical education machine'. article_title: Development and validation of a national clinical pharmacy competency framework for hospital pharmacists in Austria: a multi-method study.
citation: Stoll J. T., Böhmdorfer-McNair B., Jeske M., Weidmann A. E. (2024). Development and validation of a national clinical pharmacy competency framework for hospital pharmacists in Austria: a multi-method study. International Journal of Clinical Pharmacy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11096-024-01781-3
title: First national clinical pharmacy competency framework for hospital pharmacists in Austria
description: A bespoke national competency framework for Austrian hospital pharmacists, underpinned by the European Common Training Framework's Patient Care and Clinical Pharmacy Skills domain. It was built from 19 behaviour competencies reviewed for national appropriateness and amended by expert-panel comments, such as adding "within the legal authorizations in Austria" to the prescribing competency. The final version was translated into German and is being considered by the AAHP and the Austrian Chamber of Pharmacists.
requirements: Validation by representative national expert stakeholders
Consideration within the legal authorisations in Austria, as the article states the framework "should always be considered within the legal authorisations in Austria"
constraints: Developed for the Austrian hospital pharmacy context and legal setting
target_learners: undergraduate and postgraduate clinical pharmacy trainees
target_learning_goals: clinical pharmacy patient-care competencies
medication safety competencies
examples: The expert panel added notes distinguishing seamless care (focus on medicine management) from transfer of care (focus on communication) and agreed to include first aid as a competency because it is mandatory under Austrian law.

Development and validation of a national clinical pharmacy competency framework for hospital pharmacists in Austria: a multi-method study. article_title: Peer teachers as ultrasound instructors? - a systematic literature review of peer teaching concepts in undergraduate ultrasound education.
citation: Winter Lone, Neubauer Ricarda, Weimer Johannes, Dietrich Christoph F., Wittek Agnes, Schiestl Lina, Marinova Milka, Schäfer Valentin Sebastian, Strizek Brigitte, Recker Florian. (2024). Peer teachers as ultrasound instructors? – a systematic literature review of peer teaching concepts in undergraduate ultrasound education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06345-7
title: Develop comprehensive guidelines for peer tutor education to standardize training and ensure minimum standards
description: The review concludes that despite growing literature supporting peer teaching in ultrasound education, training concepts remain heterogeneous without a standardized system for training and qualifying peer teachers. It recommends that "Developing comprehensive guidelines for peer tutor education could increase acceptance and recognition of peer-assisted learning and ensure minimum training standards." This addresses the observed variability in formats, durations, assessments and certification across programs.
requirements: Training programs should include assessment of peer teachers' content-related, practical, and didactic competence, as the review's modified quality criteria emphasize
constraints: The review is limited to undergraduate medical ultrasound education in English or German literature up to November 21, 2023, excluding postgraduate settings
target_learners: medical students in undergraduate ultrasound education
medical students training as peer teachers
target_learning_goals: practical ultrasound scanning skills
theoretical ultrasound knowledge
peer teaching and didactic skills
examples: Included programs used course-based concepts (93.8%) and internships (50.0%) with a median training duration of about ten days, with objective assessments such as MCQ or OSCE in 56% of programs

BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06345-7

article_title: Simulate to stimulate? A systematic review of stress, learning, and performance in healthcare simulation.
citation: Vage A, Spence AD, McKeown G, Gormley GJ, Hamilton PK. (2024). Simulate to stimulate? A systematic review of stress, learning, and performance in healthcare simulation. The Ulster Medical Journal. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11591218/
title: Design simulation courses with structured briefing and debriefing and avoid relying on extensively stressful content as a learning tool
description: The review recommends that because simulation scenarios as sole learning tools are often ineffective and potentially detrimental, course designers should add adjunctive measures. It states that "adjunctive measures such as effective briefing and debriefing should be strongly considered in course design", and that extensively stressful content may not be as beneficial as previously thought.
requirements: Structured pre-scenario briefing and post-scenario debriefing processes, which the review associates with improved instructional and learning outcomes
constraints: The review notes substantial heterogeneity between studies and a paucity of evidence, so this recommendation rests on a sparse evidence base
target_learning_goals: clinical and procedural performance under stress
resuscitation and emergency skills
examples: The review found only two of eleven impaired-performance studies mentioned structured briefing and debriefing, while three performed neither brief nor debrief
key_sources: Vage A, Spence AD, McKeown G, Gormley GJ, Hamilton PK. (2024). Simulate to stimulate? A systematic review of stress, learning, and performance in healthcare simulation. The Ulster Medical Journal. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11591218/

article_title: The effect of problem-based learning on improving problem-solving, self-directed learning, and critical thinking ability for the pharmacy students: A randomized controlled trial and meta-analysis.
citation: Chen Tu, Zhao Yi-Jing, Huang Feng-Qing, Liu Qun, Li Ying, Alolga Raphael N., Zhang Lei, Ma Gaoxiang. (2024). title: Problem-based learning as a seven-step, student-centered, problem-driven instructional process
description: The article describes PBL as "a student-centered learning strategy that uses a problem as a starting point to facilitate learning", in which pharmacy students collaborate in small groups to improve cognitive capacities and clinical and critical thinking skills. It enumerates seven steps: identifying the problem, exploring prior knowledge, generating potential theories, identifying learning needs, individually gathering research, re-evaluating and applying new knowledge, and reflecting on the learning process. In this study PBL was implemented in the Authentication of Chinese Medicines course, an applied discipline on identifying and studying varieties and quality of Chinese medicines.
requirements: A problem used as the starting point for learning and small-group collaboration of students
constraints: The article's evidence base is pharmacy students in a Chinese pharmaceutical university course; the meta-analysis included only English and Chinese language articles
target_learning_goals: problem-solving ability
self-directed learning
critical thinking
communication skills
examples: The 17-week Authentication of Chinese Medicines course at China Pharmaceutical University was delivered in PBL format with about two hours a week, compared against lecture-based learning.

article_title: Simulation in podiatry teaching and learning: A scoping review.
citation: Anning Naomi, Tehan Peta. (2024). Simulation in podiatry teaching and learning: A scoping review. Journal of Foot and Ankle Research. https://doi.org/10.1002/jfa2.70020
title: Six-theme taxonomy of simulation purposes in podiatry education
description: The review organizes the podiatry simulation literature by the purpose of the simulation intervention, grouping studies into six themes: "skill improvement, communication and professionalism, clinical competencies and patient safety, educational enhancement, and anatomy and histology education". Content analysis of included studies was charted into tables by these purposes, alongside study design, participants, simulation modality, and main findings, to draw links between purpose, modality, and findings.
requirements: Content analysis of included studies charted by purpose of simulation intervention, study design, participants, modality, and main findings
constraints: Further quantitative synthesis was not possible due to the diverse scope of included data
target_learning_goals: clinical skills
communication and professionalism
clinical competencies
anatomy and histology knowledge
examples: Table 1 charts each included study under one of the six purpose categories, from anatomic wound models for diabetic foot ulcers to virtual microscopes for histology
key_sources: Anning Naomi, Tehan Peta. (2024). Simulation in podiatry teaching and learning: A scoping review. Journal of Foot and Ankle Research. https://doi.org/10.1002/jfa2.70020

article_title: Simulation in podiatry teaching and learning: A scoping review.
citation: Anning Naomi, Tehan Peta. (2024). Simulation in podiatry teaching and learning: A scoping review. Journal of Foot and Ankle Research. https://doi.org/10.1002/jfa2.70020
title: Learning outcomes in simulation depend more on scenario design, debriefing, and feedback than on simulator fidelity
description: Drawing on prior healthcare education research, the review argues that simulation effectiveness "relies less on fidelity and more on well‐designed clinical scenarios, appropriate debriefing, and effective feedback", which enhance learning outcomes regardless of the simulation's complexity. It treats low- and high-fidelity simulation as complementary, with fidelity matched to the learner's stage rather than treated as inherently superior.
requirements: well-designed clinical scenarios
appropriate debriefing
effective feedback
constraints: Prior research indicates mixed effectiveness between low- and high-fidelity simulations, with high-fidelity gains not always translating to clinical practice
target_learning_goals: clinical skills
decision-making
clinical competencies
examples: Included studies used low-fidelity models such as oranges, avocadoes, and a grapefruit ulcer model for initial practice, alongside high-fidelity mannequins and pulsatile flow simulators
key_sources: Anning Naomi, Tehan Peta. (2024). Simulation in podiatry teaching and learning: A scoping review. Journal of Foot and Ankle Research. https://doi.org/10.1002/jfa2.70020

article_title: Acceptance and use of extended reality in surgical training: an umbrella review.
citation: Esmaeel T, Elham T, Fereidooni Mahsa, Ayatollahi Haleh. (2024). Acceptance and use of extended reality in surgical training: an umbrella review. Systematic Reviews. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13643-024-02723-w
title: UTAUT as an organizing framework for factors influencing acceptance and use of XR in surgical training
description: The article uses the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) as its guiding framework for synthesizing findings across 44 included reviews. It states that the model "has four domains including performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, and facilitating conditions which offer valuable insights into the drivers and barriers faced by users." The review coded findings from the included systematic reviews into these four domains using qualitative software.
requirements: Findings from included reviews must be codable into the four UTAUT domains of performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, and facilitating conditions
constraints: The review reports significant heterogeneity across included studies, which precluded quantitative meta-analysis and required a qualitative framework synthesis
target_learning_goals: surgical skill acquisition
technology adoption in surgical training
examples: Two authors independently coded findings from the 44 included reviews using MAXQDA, categorizing them under the four UTAUT domains.
key_sources: Esmaeel T, Elham T, Fereidooni Mahsa, Ayatollahi Haleh. (2024). Acceptance and use of extended reality in surgical training: an umbrella review. Systematic Reviews. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13643-024-02723-w

article_title: Acceptance and use of extended reality in surgical training: an umbrella review.
citation: Esmaeel T, Elham T, Fereidooni Mahsa, Ayatollahi Haleh. (2024). Acceptance and use of extended reality in surgical training: an umbrella review. Systematic Reviews. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13643-024-02723-w
title: Successful integration of XR into surgical training requires careful curriculum design and resource allocation
description: The review concludes that adopting XR in surgical training is not just a matter of acquiring technology: "The successful integration of XR into surgical training necessitates careful curriculum design and resource allocation." It further states that adoption is facilitated by designing user-friendly interfaces and positive social influences, while financial and resource challenges must be overcome. The principle directs programs to plan curricula and allocate resources when introducing XR.
requirements: User-friendly interface design
resource availability
overcoming financial and technical limitations
constraints: The review notes financial and resource challenges must be overcome for XR to realize its potential in surgical training
target_learning_goals: surgical skill acquisition
procedural accuracy
examples: The review's conclusion recommends that future research focus on overcoming financial and resource barriers so XR can fully realize its potential in surgical training.

article_title: Acceptance and use of extended reality in surgical training: an umbrella review.
citation: Esmaeel T, Elham T, Fereidooni Mahsa, Ayatollahi Haleh. (2024). Acceptance and use of extended reality in surgical training: an umbrella review. Systematic Reviews. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13643-024-02723-w
title: Extended reality (VR, AR, MR) simulation systems for surgical training
description: Extended reality comprises virtual reality, augmented reality, and mixed reality technologies applied to surgical training. The article defines them: "VR tools immerse users in fully digital environments", "AR overlays digital content onto the real-world environment", and MR "blends both VR and AR, where digital and physical elements coexist and interact in real time." The review catalogs named simulators (e.g., LapSim, LAP Mentor, Eyesi, Microsoft HoloLens, da Vinci VR) used across specialties.
requirements: Resource availability and addressing technical and financial limitations for effective use
constraints: Included reviews note limitations such as lack of realistic haptic feedback in some VR simulators and lower realism of AR training compared to box trainers
target_learning_goals: surgical technical skills
procedural accuracy
nontechnical skills such as teamwork and decision-making
examples: Included reviews describe VR arthroscopy simulators (ARTHRO VR, ArthroS VR), laparoscopic simulators (LapSim, MIST-VR), ophthalmic simulators (Eyesi), and AR head-mounted displays (Microsoft HoloLens, Google Glass).
