article_title: Death of the paediatric manikin: a scoping review.
citation: Apara Teleireoluwa, Hogan Tom, Peterson Jennifer L H. (2024). Death of the paediatric manikin: a scoping review. BMJ Paediatrics Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjpo-2024-002941
title: Tripathy et al framework of three categories of simulated manikin death
description: The review cites a theoretical framework of simulated manikin death developed through a mixed-methods approach, outlining three categories by which manikin death may occur in a simulation session: 'expected death' (both facilitators and participants know death should be expected), 'unexpected death' (only participants are unaware), and 'death due to inaction/action' (death determined by participants' actions). The framework acknowledges these categories may have different impacts on participants, and the review uses it to frame why manikin death's educational effects vary across scenario designs.
requirements: The framework distinguishes categories by what facilitators and participants know prior to the scenario and by whether participant actions determine death
constraints: The review presents the framework as background from adult and general simulation literature, not as tested within the three included paediatric studies
target_learning_goals: preparing learners for death of patients in clinical practice
managing emotional responses during resuscitation scenarios
examples: The review introduces the framework when discussing how death of the manikin could feasibly occur in a variety of scenarios
key_sources: Apara Teleireoluwa, Hogan Tom, Peterson Jennifer L H. (2024). Death of the paediatric manikin: a scoping review. BMJ Paediatrics Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjpo-2024-002941

article_title: Death of the paediatric manikin: a scoping review.
citation: Apara Teleireoluwa, Hogan Tom, Peterson Jennifer L H. (2024). Death of the paediatric manikin: a scoping review. BMJ Paediatrics Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjpo-2024-002941
title: Debriefs after paediatric manikin death need skilled facilitation with designated time for emotional and communication discussion
description: The review concludes that the debrief has a crucial role in mitigating potentially negative impacts of paediatric manikin death. From the qualitative participant data, it would seem preferable for facilitators to use a debrief incorporating "designated time and space for discussion of the emotional and communication elements of the simulation scenario", while maintaining psychological safety through clear discouragement of blame. Facilitators should state at the debrief's start when death was a predetermined learning objective.
requirements: Experienced facilitators are needed to manage debriefs while maintaining psychological safety
Learning objectives for the scenario should be clearly articulated in the debrief
constraints: No specific debriefing model was evaluated in the included studies; the recommendation derives from qualitative participant data
target_learning_goals: processing emotional responses to patient death
reflecting on team resuscitation performance
examples: In the included studies, facilitator reassurance that death was a learning objective plus a facilitated debrief allowed participants to work through their discomfort
key_sources: Apara Teleireoluwa, Hogan Tom, Peterson Jennifer L H. (2024). Death of the paediatric manikin: a scoping review. BMJ Paediatrics Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjpo-2024-002941

article_title: Digital learning of clinical skills and its impact on medical students' academic performance: a systematic review.
citation: McGee RG, Wark S, Mwangi F, Drovandi A, Alele F, Malau-Aduli BS, The ACHIEVE Collaboration. (2024). Digital learning of clinical skills and its impact on medical students’ academic performance: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06471-2
title: Integrate traditional and digital teaching methods rather than replacing face-to-face training entirely
description: The review concludes that combining traditional and innovative digital methods yields the most comprehensive learning experience in clinical skills education. It states that "the integration of traditional and innovative digital teaching methods appeared to provide the most comprehensive learning experience", and that students in some studies still valued personal interaction and hands-on experience from face-to-face training. The principle is used to recommend a hybrid model leveraging digital flexibility while preserving practical skill development.
requirements: Digital tools must be carefully matched to the skills being taught, as the review states effectiveness varies by skill and context
constraints: Some students preferred digital tools as an addition to, not a replacement for, traditional teaching (Huang et al.)
target_learning_goals: clinical skills acquisition including history-taking, physical examination, communication skills, and clinical reasoning
examples: The review's included blended-learning studies (e.g. Viljoen 2020; Gong 2021) associated blended approaches with better immediate and delayed post-intervention test scores and higher theoretical and practical assessment scores
key_sources: McGee RG, Wark S, Mwangi F, Drovandi A, Alele F, Malau-Aduli BS, The ACHIEVE Collaboration. (2024). Digital learning of clinical skills and its impact on medical students’ academic performance: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06471-2

article_title: Training technical or non-technical skills: an arbitrary distinction? A scoping review.
citation: Gamborg ML, Salling LB, Rölfing JD, Jensen RD. (2024). Training technical or non-technical skills: an arbitrary distinction? A scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06419-6
title: TS and NTS as interrelated constructs whose separation in learning designs may be arbitrary
description: The review proposes that technical and non-technical skills are interrelated constructs rather than independent categories, based on the pattern that "the results strongly indicate a correlation between TS and NTS skills, suggesting that physicians who are proficient in their NTS, also perform well on their TS." It frames the conventional split in learning designs as possibly arbitrary, drawing on socio-cultural educational studies, motor learning accounts in which motor control results from continuous cognitive adaptation, Gibson's affordances, and self-regulated learning frameworks such as Zimmerman's circular model and Ziegler's actiotope model.
requirements: Future studies should simultaneously assess both skill sets to establish how improvement in TS is influenced by NTS and vice versa
constraints: The supporting socio-cultural studies were qualitative and cannot establish whether a clear relationship between TS and NTS exists
Quantitative studies in the review lacked theoretical presentation or discussion of how TS and NTS interact
target_learners: healthcare professionals and physicians in medical education
target_learning_goals: integration of technical and non-technical clinical skills
examples: The review cites Cleland et al. and Tsuda et al. as showing acquisition of TS happens in relation to other learners and teachers, and quotes Gibson (1979, p. 223): "we must perceive in order to move, but we must also move in order to perceive."
key_sources: Gamborg ML, Salling LB, Rölfing JD, Jensen RD. (2024). Training technical or non-technical skills: an arbitrary distinction? A scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06419-6

article_title: Training technical or non-technical skills: an arbitrary distinction? A scoping review.
citation: Gamborg ML, Salling LB, Rölfing JD, Jensen RD. (2024). Training technical or non-technical skills: an arbitrary distinction? A scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06419-6
title: Non-technical skills as a poorly defined construct in need of reconceptualization, with knowledge not qualifying as a skill
description: The review argues that NTS is poorly defined and therefore harder than TS to assess, noting that despite work on behavioural markers, consensus definitions and taxonomies, "there is still little consensus on how to assess NTS". During analysis the authors found several publications defining knowledge as an NTS; they argue knowledge "refers to the process of expanding a frame of mind, rather than an applicable skill" and is the foundation actions are based on rather than a skill itself, and they excluded studies defining knowledge as NTS without assessing other NTS aspects.
requirements: Research should validate the tools they use to assess NTS, using well established frameworks such as Kane's validity framework
constraints: Unclear definitions of NTS in the literature were an obstacle; the review applied a broad definition of NTS as all skills that are not body-kinetic skills, excluding knowledge-only studies
target_learners: healthcare professionals and physicians in medical education
target_learning_goals: accurate conceptualization and valid assessment of non-technical skills
examples: The review's broad working definition incorporated personal resources skills and cognitive skills in addition to traditionally defined NTS such as teamwork and communication.
key_sources: Gamborg ML, Salling LB, Rölfing JD, Jensen RD. (2024). Training technical or non-technical skills: an arbitrary distinction? A scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06419-6

article_title: Interventions to improve pharmacists' competency in chronic disease management: a systematic review of randomized controlled trials.
citation: Rendrayani Farida, Utami Auliasari M., Insani Widya N., Puspita Falerina, Alfian Sofa D., Nguyen Thang, Puspitasari Irma M. (2024). Interventions to improve pharmacists’ competency in chronic disease management: a systematic review of randomized controlled trials. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06393-z
title: EPOC taxonomy of intervention types for classifying health-professional competency interventions
description: The Cochrane Effective Practice and Organization of Care (EPOC) taxonomy classifies health-system interventions into four types. The review states: "Using the latest EPOC taxonomy [37], the interventions were further categorized into four types" — delivery arrangements, financial arrangements, governance arrangements, and implementation strategies — and uses it to organize its synthesis, arguing the taxonomy "ensures consistent classification and comparability" for decision-makers. In the included studies only implementation strategies and combined implementation strategies–delivery arrangements types appeared.
requirements: Interventions must be classifiable into one of the four EPOC types for consistent classification and comparability
constraints: No financial arrangements or governance arrangements interventions appeared among the 11 included RCTs
target_learners: pharmacists in community and hospital settings
target_learning_goals: knowledge, skills, and attitudes for chronic disease management
examples: The review classified all 11 included RCTs as implementation strategies (n = 8) or combined implementation strategies–delivery arrangements (n = 3)
key_sources: Rendrayani Farida, Utami Auliasari M., Insani Widya N., Puspita Falerina, Alfian Sofa D., Nguyen Thang, Puspitasari Irma M. (2024). Interventions to improve pharmacists’ competency in chronic disease management: a systematic review of randomized controlled trials. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06393-z

article_title: Effectiveness of Virtual Simulations Versus Mannequins and Real Persons in Medical and Nursing Education: Meta-Analysis and Trial Sequential Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
citation: Jiang N, Zhang Y, Liang S, Lyu X, Chen S, Huang X, Pan H. (2024). Effectiveness of Virtual Simulations Versus Mannequins and Real Persons in Medical and Nursing Education: Meta-Analysis and Trial Sequential Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/56195
title: Adopt virtual simulations as viable alternatives to face-to-face simulation where cost-utility and time-space flexibility matter
description: The article concludes that, given "favorable cost-utility plus high flexibility regarding time and space, VSs are viable alternatives to traditional face-to-face learning modalities." This rests on its meta-analytic finding of no significant effectiveness differences across four competencies, plus cited advantages: reduced instructor time, manpower, and space costs, repeatable training without patient harm, and automated documentation and evaluation of student performance.
requirements: Institutions must accept that comparative effectiveness evidence shows equivalence rather than superiority over mannequins and real persons
constraints: The article states the comparative effectiveness of VSs deserves follow-up as new technology emerges, and that undesirable usability may hinder the learning process
target_learners: pre- and postregistration medical and nursing students and staff
target_learning_goals: knowledge
procedural skills
clinical reasoning
communication skills
examples: The meta-analysis pooled 27 RCTs with 1480 participants comparing VSs to mannequins or real persons, finding no significant differences on any of the four outcomes
key_sources: Jiang N, Zhang Y, Liang S, Lyu X, Chen S, Huang X, Pan H. (2024). Effectiveness of Virtual Simulations Versus Mannequins and Real Persons in Medical and Nursing Education: Meta-Analysis and Trial Sequential Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/56195

article_title: Simulation-Based Education of Health Workers in Low- and Middle-Income Countries: A Systematic Review.
citation: Robinson SJA, Ritchie AMA, Pacilli M, Nestel D, McLeod E, Nataraja RM. (2024). Simulation-Based Education of Health Workers in Low- and Middle-Income Countries: A Systematic Review. Glob Health Sci Pract. https://doi.org/10.9745/GHSP-D-24-00187
title: Kirkpatrick four-level evaluation model applied to simulation-based education
description: The review uses the Kirkpatrick model as its evaluation framework, which "includes 4 levels: reaction, learning, behavior, and results," with Level 4 (results) denoting changes in final outcomes such as reduced patient length of stay. Studies were included only if they quantitatively evaluated at Level 4, clearly linked to patient outcomes rather than inferred from context. The review treats each level as requiring individual evaluation, since successful evaluation at Level 4 is not causally related to other levels.
requirements: Level 4 evaluations must be clearly linked to patient outcomes rather than being inferred from context
constraints: Evaluation at Level 4 is difficult to achieve; the model's focus on summative evaluation potentially neglects investigations of how changes occur
target_learners: health workers and health students in low- and middle-income countries
target_learning_goals: evaluating whether SBE programs change patient-level outcomes
examples: The review required Kirkpatrick Level 4 evaluation for inclusion, yielding 97 studies across 50 LMICs; only 9 studies evaluated all 4 levels
key_sources: Robinson SJA, Ritchie AMA, Pacilli M, Nestel D, McLeod E, Nataraja RM. (2024). Simulation-Based Education of Health Workers in Low- and Middle-Income Countries: A Systematic Review. Glob Health Sci Pract. https://doi.org/10.9745/GHSP-D-24-00187

article_title: Augmented reality for basic skills training in laparoscopic surgery: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
citation: Xiong Jian, Dai Xiaoqin, Zhang Yuyang, Liu Xingchao, Zhou Xiyuan. (2024). Augmented reality for basic skills training in laparoscopic surgery: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-024-11387-5
title: AR laparoscopic training systems reviewed: ProMIS, eoSim, ART, iSurgeon, and HoloPointer
description: The review catalogues the augmented reality systems used across the 12 included studies for basic laparoscopic skills training. As printed, "These studies utilized various AR systems-ProMIS, eoSim, ART, iSurgeon, and HoloPointer-across different laparoscopic scenarios, including simulated abdominal procedures, suturing tasks, and laparoscopic cholecystectomy". Three of the four meta-analyzed studies used the same system, iSurgeon, which the authors say supports reliability of the pooled assessments.
requirements: Studies must involve medical students, novice trainees, residents, or inexperienced surgeons learning basic laparoscopic skills
A defined comparison group or pre-post change in educational outcomes
constraints: Technological limitations such as limited realism, inadequate haptic feedback, and less intuitive user interfaces restricted AR's potential
Some studies lacked detailed reporting on AR functionalities, hindering interpretation
target_learning_goals: basic laparoscopic surgical skills
technical skills acquisition
reduced intraoperative errors
examples: Wild (2022) and Cizmic (2023) used iSurgeon for telestration during porcine laparoscopic cholecystectomy; Huettl (2023) used HoloPointer for LC with late residents/new fellows
key_sources: Xiong Jian, Dai Xiaoqin, Zhang Yuyang, Liu Xingchao, Zhou Xiyuan. (2024). Augmented reality for basic skills training in laparoscopic surgery: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-024-11387-5

article_title: Influences of school climate on emotional health and academic achievement of school-going adolescents in India: a systematic review.
citation: Podiya Jayalaxmi Kaniyagundi, Navaneetham Janardhana, Bhola Poornima. (2025). Influences of school climate on emotional health and academic achievement of school-going adolescents in India: a systematic review. BMC Public Health 25, 54. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-024-21268-0
title: School climate as a multidimensional collective experience shaping adolescent emotional health and academic achievement
description: The review adopts the National School Climate Center definition of school climate as "a collective experience of students, parents, teachers, and other staff, shaped by rules, goals, ethics, interaction patterns, methods of teaching and learning, and institutional structures" guaranteeing social, emotional, and physical safety. It organizes the eleven included studies around climate components—safety, relationships, peer support, teaching methodology, and institutional environment—and maps their interconnected influence on emotional health and academic outcomes (Fig. 2).
requirements: Understanding the perspectives of all stakeholders—teachers, students, parents, administrators, and staff—is essential, since climate aspects can be determined by the perceptions of school teachers and administrators
constraints: The review notes the concept includes cultural aspects, values, available resources, and social networks, and that few Indian studies have examined both outcome domains together
target_learners: school-going adolescents aged 13–16 in Indian secondary schools (grades 8–10)
target_learning_goals: emotional health and well-being
academic achievement
key_sources: Podiya Jayalaxmi Kaniyagundi, Navaneetham Janardhana, Bhola Poornima. (2025). Influences of school climate on emotional health and academic achievement of school-going adolescents in India: a systematic review. BMC Public Health 25, 54. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-024-21268-0

article_title: A Scoping Review of Interprofessional Simulation-Based Team Training Programs.
citation: Bochatay N, Ju M, O'Brien BC, van Schaik SM. (2025). A Scoping Review of Interprofessional Simulation-Based Team Training Programs. Simulation in Healthcare. https://doi.org/10.1097/SIH.0000000000000792
title: Power and intergroup relations theories as a lens for redesigning ISBTT
description: The review proposes that ISBTT programs implicitly rely on contact theory, whose prerequisite of equal status is rarely met in hierarchical healthcare teams. It argues that engaging with "theoretical concepts related to power and intergroup relations" — including French and Raven's social bases of power and Strauss's negotiated order perspective — can help programs explicitly address barriers to collaboration, inform debriefing content, and explain tensions such as inexperienced physician trainees leading experienced nurses.
requirements: Programs must engage with theoretical and conceptual frameworks developed to understand power and intergroup relations, as the review recommends
constraints: The review notes that while power dynamics are unlikely to change through education programs alone, programs can equip participants to navigate them
target_learners: Health professionals from at least 2 professions participating in simulation-based team training
target_learning_goals: Navigating power discrepancies and hierarchies in interprofessional teams
Managing conflict and building social capital in collaborative practice
examples: The review describes how the negotiated order perspective explains tensions when inexperienced physician trainees act as team leaders giving instructions to experienced nurses
key_sources: Bochatay N, Ju M, O'Brien BC, van Schaik SM. (2025). A Scoping Review of Interprofessional Simulation-Based Team Training Programs. Simulation in Healthcare. https://doi.org/10.1097/SIH.0000000000000792

article_title: Critical thinking and clinical skills by problem-based learning educational methods: an umbrella systematic review.
citation: Ge Wei-Li, Zhu Xia-Yin, Lin Jiang-Bo, Jiang Jian-Jun, Li Tao, Lu Yi-Fei, Mi Ya-Fei, Tung Tao-Hsin. (2025). Critical thinking and clinical skills by problem-based learning educational methods: an umbrella systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06951-z
title: Introduce organized learning early in the curriculum and gradually expand active, self-directed learning as students master foundational knowledge
description: The review recommends sequencing PBL against students' prior knowledge: because PBL "requires students to have a certain level of foundational knowledge and concepts", it may be limited in early teaching stages. The authors advise introducing organized learning early and expanding active, self-directed learning afterwards, and gradually increasing PBL teaching frequency as grade level rises.
requirements: Students must have mastered certain basic knowledge before PBL is expected to yield better critical thinking and skill outcomes
constraints: In fields requiring rigorous theoretical foundations, such as biostatistics, PBL may have limitations because it focuses on problem-solving rather than in-depth theoretical instruction
target_learners: undergraduate medical, nursing and dental students
target_learning_goals: critical thinking
clinical skills
problem-solving
examples: The review reports first-year medical students' critical thinking, problem-solving and self-direction showed no significant PBL advantage, supporting delayed rather than early PBL introduction
key_sources: Ge Wei-Li, Zhu Xia-Yin, Lin Jiang-Bo, Jiang Jian-Jun, Li Tao, Lu Yi-Fei, Mi Ya-Fei, Tung Tao-Hsin. (2025). Critical thinking and clinical skills by problem-based learning educational methods: an umbrella systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06951-z

article_title: Nurse Competency in Providing Spiritual Care and Associated Influencing Factors: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
citation: Kaiyue Wu, Xinsheng Wang, Linbo Sun, Jiayi Feng, Changping Song. (2025). Nurse Competency in Providing Spiritual Care and Associated Influencing Factors: A Systematic Review and Meta‐Analysis. Nursing Open. https://doi.org/10.1002/nop2.70192
title: Spiritual Care Competence Scale (SCCS) and its Chinese version
description: The SCCS, translated and revised by Van Leeuwen et al. (2009) from the Dutch version, evaluates the spiritual care competence of clinical nurses. The original has "six dimensions" — assessment and implementation, professional development and quality improvement, support, referral, spiritual attitude towards patients, and communication — with 27 items scored on a five-level Likert method (total 27–110). The Chinese version (Wei et al. 2017) has 22 items, total 22–110, Cronbach's α 0.974.
requirements: Included studies must explicitly use the SCCS scale, per the review's inclusion criteria
constraints: Cronbach's alpha of the original scale's dimensions ranged from 0.56 to 0.82, per the article
target_learning_goals: measuring spiritual care competence
key_sources: Kaiyue Wu, Xinsheng Wang, Linbo Sun, Jiayi Feng, Changping Song. (2025). Nurse Competency in Providing Spiritual Care and Associated Influencing Factors: A Systematic Review and Meta‐Analysis. Nursing Open. https://doi.org/10.1002/nop2.70192

article_title: Using Virtual Reality to Enhance Surgical Skills and Engagement in Orthopedic Education: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
citation: Li Ting, Yan Jingxin, Gao Xin, Liu Hangyu, Li Jin, Shang Yuanting, Tang Xiaoyu. (2025). Using Virtual Reality to Enhance Surgical Skills and Engagement in Orthopedic Education: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/70266
title: Adopt VR technology in orthopedic medical education to improve surgical competence, pending stronger validation
description: The article concludes that VR is an effective orthopedic education tool that improves knowledge, practical skills, engagement, and satisfaction, so adopting VR in medical education holds promise for improving orthopedic surgical competence. It recommends standardization of VR teaching technologies and validation through rigorous research methodologies such as multicenter RCTs to establish evidence-based practices and guidelines for integrating VR into medical education.
requirements: Standardization of VR teaching technologies and validation of educational outcomes through rigorous research methodologies, such as multicenter RCTs
constraints: The quality of this meta-analysis was limited by the notable heterogeneity in terms of VR platforms
the cost of VR headsets and associated hardware can be prohibitively high, with ongoing maintenance, updates, and software licensing renewals
target_learning_goals: orthopedic theoretical knowledge
surgical technical skills
clinical reasoning
learner engagement
examples: The meta-analysis pooled 23 RCTs (1091 participants) comparing VR teaching with traditional teaching across knowledge, operation, design, and engagement outcomes

article_title: AI-Powered Problem- and Case-based Learning in Medical and Dental Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
citation: Wei H, Dai Y, Yuan K, Li KY, Hung KF, Hu EM, Lee AHC, Chang JWW, Zhang C, Li X. (2025). AI-Powered Problem- and Case-based Learning in Medical and Dental Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. International Dental Journal. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.identj.2025.100858
title: Taxonomy of AI technologies applied to PBL/CBL in medical and dental education
description: The review organises AI-powered PBL/CBL implementations into intelligent tutoring systems (COMET, CC-Cruiser, LearnGuide, ChatGPT), intelligent information access systems, AI-generated decision-making systems such as Watson for Oncology, and generative and immersive technologies. It describes ITSs as "computer-based educational platforms which utilise AI and adaptive technologies to mimic human tutoring by providing real-time, customised and interactive feedback to learners". Generative models including LLMs, GANs, VAEs and diffusion models create synthetic multimodal cases, while VR, AR and haptic systems support virtual patients for practising communication, diagnosis, decision-making and treatment.
requirements: AI tools must be integrated into PBL/CBL with an appropriate comparison group for effectiveness evaluation
constraints: The review notes drawbacks such as slow annotation processes and presence of irrelevant information for information-access systems, and high hardware requirements for some platforms
target_learning_goals: knowledge acquisition
clinical reasoning capability
learner satisfaction
examples: COMET generated tutoring hints via Bayesian networks displayed in a discussion pane; METEOR reduced problem-scenario development time from 1 month to 4-5 hours per person using the UMLS Semantic Network
key_sources: Wei H, Dai Y, Yuan K, Li KY, Hung KF, Hu EM, Lee AHC, Chang JWW, Zhang C, Li X. (2025). AI-Powered Problem- and Case-based Learning in Medical and Dental Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. International Dental Journal. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.identj.2025.100858

article_title: AI-Powered Problem- and Case-based Learning in Medical and Dental Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
citation: Wei H, Dai Y, Yuan K, Li KY, Hung KF, Hu EM, Lee AHC, Chang JWW, Zhang C, Li X. (2025). AI-Powered Problem- and Case-based Learning in Medical and Dental Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. International Dental Journal. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.identj.2025.100858
title: Combine AI technology with skilled facilitators who verify AI-provided information and give personalised feedback
description: The review concludes that AI-powered PBL/CBL works best when human facilitators remain central: tutors educate students on using the AI system, verify the accuracy of AI-provided information, and provide personalised feedback. The authors state that "AI technology should be combined with skilled facilitators" to realise the full potential of the approach, positioning facilitators as accuracy checkers and feedback providers rather than replacements.
requirements: Facilitators must be trained to educate students on utilization of the AI-powered system/platform and verify the accuracy of the information provided by AI
constraints: The article frames this as a discussion-level recommendation, not a manipulated or tested condition
target_learning_goals: safe and accurate use of AI tools in PBL/CBL
clinical reasoning
examples: In the included RCTs, tutors/instructors verified AI-provided information and provided personalised feedback alongside ChatGPT-generated questions, simulated patients and interviews

article_title: Effectiveness of generative artificial intelligence-based teaching versus traditional teaching methods in medical education: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
citation: Li Juan, Yin Kaiyu, Wang Yida, Jiang Xiaoqin, Chen Dongxu. (2025). Effectiveness of generative artificial intelligence-based teaching versus traditional teaching methods in medical education: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07750-2
title: Meta-analytic evidence base of 11 RCTs comparing GAI-based and traditional teaching in medical students
description: A corpus of 11 randomized controlled trials comprising 786 medical students (395 GAI-based intervention, 391 traditional control), identified from 1200 initial records searched in PubMed, Cochrane Library, EMBASE, and Web of Science from January 2014 to January 2025. All studies were published 2024–2025, predominantly from Asian institutions (8 studies, 72.7%), with ChatGPT as the primary GAI tool in 9 studies (81.8%). The article states "ChatGPT was the primary GAI tool, utilized in 9 studies (81.8%)" and that 5 studies ran interventions exceeding one week.
requirements: Included studies enrolled medical students, used GAI-based teaching as the primary intervention, had a traditional teaching control, reported quantifiable knowledge or skill outcomes, and used an RCT design
constraints: Only one study included postgraduate participants; the population is primarily undergraduate medical students
target_learning_goals: medical knowledge acquisition
clinical practical skills
examples: Included trials spanned theory and practice courses, durations from 10 minutes to 4 weeks, and immediate or delayed assessment, as tabulated in Table 1

Effectiveness of generative artificial intelligence-based teaching versus traditional teaching methods in medical education: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. article_title: The effectiveness of case-based learning compared with lecture-based learning in pharmacy education: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
citation: Chen Min, Li Xinyao, Liu Qingming, Zhou Jing, Fan Xiaofang, Liu Yantao, Lin Yunzhu, Ni Jiaqi. (2025). The effectiveness of case-based learning compared with lecture-based learning in pharmacy education: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07927-9
title: Pharmacy courses suited to CBL over LBL require integrating theory with practice in complex, context-dependent scenarios
description: The review identifies course characteristics that make pharmacy courses suitable for CBL rather than LBL: courses that "require more than rote memorization, requiring students to integrate theoretical knowledge with practical application, navigate complex, context-dependent scenarios, and develop problem-solving and clinical reasoning skills." Examples the article names include Clinical Pharmacokinetics, Pharmacognosy, Clinical Pharmacology, and clinical pharmacy practicums, all emphasizing application of knowledge to real or simulated patient cases. The pattern links course type to CBL's strengths in contextualized, interactive learning.
requirements: Courses must emphasize application of knowledge to real or simulated patient cases and bridging theory and practice
constraints: The article states this characterization is based on the included studies' courses, spanning foundational drug mechanisms to direct patient care
target_learning_goals: problem-solving skills
clinical reasoning
communication and teamwork
theoretical mastery
examples: The included RCTs applied CBL in pharmacology, pharmacognosy, clinical pharmacy, clinical pharmacotherapeutics, human anatomy and physiology, clinical pharmacokinetics, and narcotic psychopharmacology courses
key_sources: Chen Min, Li Xinyao, Liu Qingming, Zhou Jing, Fan Xiaofang, Liu Yantao, Lin Yunzhu, Ni Jiaqi. (2025). The effectiveness of case-based learning compared with lecture-based learning in pharmacy education: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07927-9

article_title: Efficacy of problem-based learning combined with case-based learning versus lecture-based learning in orthopedic education: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
citation: Xiong Xianghua, Xu Jiongnan, Luo Mingyan, Niu Dongsheng, Bi Qing, Wang Zhaofu, Zhang Jun. (2025). Efficacy of problem-based learning combined with case-based learning versus lecture-based learning in orthopedic education: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07741-3
title: Select teaching methods flexibly: use LBL for foundational theory and PBL-CBL for clinical practice segments in orthopedic education
description: The article recommends matching teaching method to content type rather than replacing lecture teaching wholesale. It states that "teaching methods should be selected flexibly based on teaching content": during the foundational theoretical knowledge phase, LBL's advantages can be leveraged to build a solid knowledge framework, while in clinical practice segments PBL-CBL's strengths should be fully used to cultivate clinical reasoning and practical skills. The recommendation rests on the meta-analytic advantages of PBL-CBL and the authors' caution that PBL-CBL is less suitable for foundational knowledge.
requirements: Teachers need strong professional competence, clinical experience, and classroom management skills; extensive case repositories and facilities are needed, and students require strong self-directed learning abilities with extensive pre-class preparation.
constraints: The article states the PBL-CBL approach is less suitable for teaching foundational knowledge and may cause students to neglect systematic learning of foundational content; it is also time-consuming to prepare and implement, and generalizability beyond Chinese settings requires further verification.
target_learning_goals: Theoretical knowledge mastery
Clinical reasoning and practical skills
Teamwork and communication abilities
examples: The meta-analysis pooled 15 RCTs or Q-RCTs (980 participants) in which the intervention group received PBL combined with CBL and the control group received LBL, across clerks, interns, and residents.

title: Five teaching methods for empathy interventions: didactic, rehearsal, reflection, observation, and feedback

citation: Fahl Jan Torge, Duvivier Robbert, Reinke Laurens, Pierie Jean-Pierre E. N., Schönrock-Adema Johanna. (2023). title: Retrieval-and-reconsolidation account of the spacing effect in psychomotor skill learning
description: The review assembles mechanistic explanations for why spaced training works: each session begins with active retrieval of the skill memory, and "each retrieval results in more profound (re)consolidation into the memory", allowing new movements to be integrated into existing memory. It adds complementary accounts: adaptive consolidation signalling regular future use, rest and sleep providing muted sensory input that reduces retrograde interference, and reduced reactive inhibition. The review stresses these are theoretical explanations and the reality may involve multiple mechanisms at once.
requirements: Spacing must distribute practice of the same material over repeated encounters separated by interstudy intervals, so that active retrieval occurs at the start of each session
constraints: The review states these are just theoretical explanations and alleged mechanisms; the reality might be more complex and involve multiple mechanisms at the same time

examples: The review uses this account to interpret why spaced groups showed steeper learning curves and why sleep-containing intervals between sessions support consolidation

title: Expanded seven-step self-directed learning (SDL) framework for identifying SDL activities and assessment methods
description: The authors developed an SDL framework from a literature review of accreditation standards and guidelines across health professions education programs. It "comprises seven steps, each step of which involves various components or activities", and was used to develop research objectives, identify SDL components in included studies, and count the number of steps in reported SDL interventions. The authors state these steps "may serve as a framework for identifying SDL activities and/or SDL interventions discussed in research articles and assessment methods employed for studying outcomes of SDL interventions". It was built because there is no agreed-upon standard defining SDL, how it should be taught, or how it should be assessed.

citation: Taylor, T.A.H., Kemp, K., Mi, M., & Lerchenfeldt, S. (2023). Self-directed learning assessment practices in undergraduate health professions education: a systematic review. Medical Education Online, 28(1). https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2023.2189553
title: Assess self-directed learning with multiple assessments combining direct and indirect measures
description: The review recommends that evidence-based best practices for assessing SDL in undergraduate health professions education include multiple assessments with both direct and indirect measures, because each assessment type has distinct strengths and shortcomings. Direct measures such as objective exams provide "direct evidence of student learning", while indirect measures such as reflections, surveys, and focus groups provide information about students' perceptions and the learning process itself. The authors found less than half of reviewed studies (48.9%) used more than one assessment method, and multiple assessments were associated with higher study quality.
requirements: Use of more than one assessment method, blending direct measures (exams, presentations, papers) and indirect measures (reflections, surveys, focus groups)
constraints: The association between multiple assessments and quality is correlational; the review also notes internal knowledge exams were often administered shortly after the activity and did not test long-term retention
target_learning_goals: self-directed learning outcomes and lifelong learning skills
examples: The review found 69 studies used one assessment, 59 used two, and 13 used three; studies with one assessment had a mean MERSQI of 9.49 versus 11.25 and 11.27 for two and three assessments

article_title: Teaching heart valve surgery techniques using simulators: a systematic review.
citation: EL-Andari R, Bozso SJ, Kang JJH, Fialka NM, Adams C, Nagendran J. (2023). Teaching heart valve surgery techniques using simulators: a systematic review. Canadian Journal of Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1503/cjs.017921
title: Fidelity taxonomy of surgical simulators: low-, middle- and high-fidelity devices for valve surgery training
description: The review organizes heart valve surgery simulators along a fidelity axis: "Surgical simulators can generally be divided into low-and high-fidelity devices." Low-fidelity simulators use readily available, cost-effective materials (e.g., tubing, boxes, plastic cups) but lack realistic look and feel; high-fidelity simulators replicate actual anatomy using animal or human tissue and realistic procedures, at high cost. Middle-fidelity models (e.g., silicone-over-clay aortic roots) and patient-specific 3D-printed models sit between these poles. The review uses this taxonomy to describe aortic and mitral valve simulators and to frame cost-versus-realism trade-offs.
requirements: High-fidelity simulators require cost and accessibility resources; the review notes many are prohibitively expensive for widespread adoption into surgical programs.
constraints: Low-fidelity simulators "often do not provide a realistic look or feel"; even high-fidelity simulators cannot replicate individual patient variation, unexpected complications, and team communication skills.
target_learning_goals: heart valve repair and replacement surgical technique
minimally invasive and robotic valve procedures
examples: Examples include a sub-US$20 aortic simulator from household materials, a cadaver-based beating-heart model with intra-aortic balloon pump, and 3D-printed patient-specific mitral models from echocardiography data.

title: Cultural safety and related concepts form a contested conceptual landscape with distinct geopolitical origins, often used interchangeably and rarely critiqued
description: The review describes a family of overlapping concepts — cultural safety, cultural competence, cultural sensitivity, cultural responsiveness, cultural knowledge, cultural awareness, and cultural humility — that emerged from the included studies and were "often used interchangeably". It traces two concepts' origins: cultural safety emerged in New Zealand via a Māori nurse working within the health system, while cultural competence developed in the United States within the transcultural nursing movement. It highlights Baba's 2013 report distinguishing cultural safety, cultural competence, cultural awareness, and cultural sensitivity as a resource for consolidating terms. The review uses this landscape to argue the field needs conceptual clarity about which concepts are preferable in which contexts.
requirements: Concepts should be justified and clearly cited when chosen, and applied with attention to the socio-political and historical contexts in which they emerged
constraints: Only half of selected papers described or cited a cultural safety or similar concept, and less than a fifth provided a critique of one
target_learners: health, social work, and education professionals and students undertaking cultural safety training
target_learning_goals: understanding cultural safety and related concepts and their appropriate application in professional practice
examples: The review's Table 3 outlines definitions of cultural safety, cultural competence, cultural awareness, and cultural sensitivity drawn from Baba's 2013 report

description: The article develops a coding framework rating each intervention 0–2 on task characteristics (varied vs repetitive, group/team/opponent vs individual, divergent vs convergent, open-ended vs technical instruction) and environment characteristics (open vs fixed space, props vs no props), averaged into a combined creativity score from 0 to 14. title: Linear versus non-linear pedagogy as contrasting frameworks for teaching physical activity
description: The article contrasts two pedagogical models for physical education. Linear pedagogy involves acquiring technical skills through constant or block training with drills or fixed choreography reproduced until the motor skill is mastered, with variability limited. Non-linear pedagogy involves the teacher adjusting the task, the environment, or both: varying rules, participant numbers, using open-ended problem-solving instructions such as 'Show me any other way to...', changing space size or equipment. The article links non-linear practices to inhibiting routine movement patterns and flexibly switching between variable tasks, and notes they "can be more student-centred if applied appropriately".

constraints: The article states linear pedagogy may align with natural scaffolding of learning by executive function in the early phases until automaticity is achieved

self-regulation

title: Micro-, meso- and macro-level distinction of dementia care competencies
description: The review proposes that dementia care competencies operate at three system levels. Micro-level concepts are carried out by individual actors such as laypersons, caregivers and health professionals, including communication skills, facilitation skills, knowledge of signs and symptoms, partnering, and supporting responsive behaviours. examples: The discussion lists micro-level concepts such as communication skills and supporting individuals experiencing responsive behaviours, and meso/macro concepts such as infrastructure and workforce development

article_title: Asynchronous e-learning with technology-enabled and enhanced training for continuing education of nurses: a scoping review.
citation: Kimura Rika, Matsunaga Mayumi, Barroga Edward, Hayashi Naoko. (2023). Asynchronous e-learning with technology-enabled and enhanced training for continuing education of nurses: a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04477-w
title: TEET framework: classifying e-learning technologies into enabling and enhancing technological approaches
description: The technology-enabled and enhanced training (TEET) framework, adopted from Ngenzi et al. (2021), classifies the technological approaches of e-learning into two subcategories: enabling technologies (e.g., interactive online modules, videos, slides, online discussion forums, mobile devices, LMS) and enhancing technologies (e.g., computer simulation or virtual reality, resource access, scenario-based learning, gamification). The review states "The term technology-enabled and enhanced training (TEET) reflects the various contributions of technology to education" and uses it to map 60 studies of asynchronous e-learning for clinical nurses, alongside three delivery modes (face-to-face, blended, pure online).
requirements: Studies must describe whether the e-learning method is synchronous or asynchronous and which TEET option is used, per the review's inclusion criteria
constraints: TEET continues to evolve as it is closely aligned with technological advancements, per the article
target_learning_goals: continuing professional development knowledge and skills acquisition
examples: The review charted all 60 articles' modes of delivery and technological approaches using this classification in Tables 3 and 4

article_title: Effectiveness of SBAR-based simulation programs for nursing students: a systematic review.
citation: Yun Jungmi, Lee Yun Ji, Kang Kyoungrim, Park Jongmin. (2023). Effectiveness of SBAR-based simulation programs for nursing students: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04495-8
title: SBAR as a structured communication framework for clinical handover
description: SBAR (situation, background, assessment, recommendation) is a structured communication tool comprising "the communication of the patient's current situation, the background and causes of the situation, the assessment of the current condition, and the reporter's recommendations for further treatment." The review describes it as reliable, validated, easily implemented in hospital practice, and enabling clear communication in a short time. It is the intervention core of the simulation programs reviewed, embedded in scenarios, role-play, and reports.
requirements: Training programs must teach all four SBAR components so users perform SBAR as intended (fidelity)
constraints: The review notes programs in the included literature did not incorporate surveillance or monitoring of fidelity to SBAR
target_learning_goals: structured clinical communication
patient handover
patient safety competency
examples: Included programs embedded SBAR in orientation, lectures, role-play, scenario simulation, and debriefing, with durations between one and six hours
key_sources: Yun Jungmi, Lee Yun Ji, Kang Kyoungrim, Park Jongmin. (2023). Effectiveness of SBAR-based simulation programs for nursing students: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04495-8

article_title: Effectiveness of SBAR-based simulation programs for nursing students: a systematic review.
citation: Yun Jungmi, Lee Yun Ji, Kang Kyoungrim, Park Jongmin. (2023). Effectiveness of SBAR-based simulation programs for nursing students: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04495-8
title: SBAR simulation programs combine pre-briefing, role-play simulation, and debriefing/discussion over one to six hours
description: The reviewed interventions shared a recurring structure: "The interventions included in the analysis consisted of orientation, pre-briefing, role-play simulation, debriefing, or discussion." Program duration varied between one and six hours; in 8 studies pre-briefing lasted more than 60 minutes, and most Korean programs included at least 60 minutes of orientation, lecture, or education before scenario performance with role-play. Control conditions ranged from e-learning and self-learning to regular clinical practice and conventional lectures.
requirements: Sufficient pre-briefing time (more than 60 minutes in 8 of the included studies) before scenario performance
constraints: Programs differed in intervention period, components, and measurement methods, preventing integrated comparison of effects
target_learning_goals: communication clarity
clinical competence
critical thinking
examples: One study applied a four-phase clinical practicum with SBAR training (concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualization, active experimentation); another used a three-session program of 20-minute education, 15–20-minute role-play, and 10-minute group discussion
key_sources: Yun Jungmi, Lee Yun Ji, Kang Kyoungrim, Park Jongmin. (2023). Effectiveness of SBAR-based simulation programs for nursing students: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04495-8

article_title: Technology-enhanced simulation-based learning in orthodontic education: A scoping review.
citation: SIPIYARUK Kawin, KAEWSIRIRAT Prachworrakit, SANTIWONG Peerapong. (2023). Technology-enhanced simulation-based learning in orthodontic education: A scoping review. Dental Press Journal of Orthodontics. https://doi.org/10.1590/2177-6709.28.3.e2321354.oar
title: Taxonomy of technology-enhanced simulation formats and orthodontic topic areas in orthodontic education
description: The review organizes the 14 identified simulators along two axes: technology format and orthodontic topic area. Formats include 3D virtual, augmented reality, virtual reality, automaton, haptic, and scenario-based simulations; the review reports that "Five simulations were designed in a three-dimensional (3D) format", four adopted AR, two employed VR, and one each was scenario-based, automated facial landmark identification, and haptic. Topic areas span diagnosis and treatment planning, bracket positioning, clinical cases and procedures, facial landmark, removable appliance, and cephalometric tracing.
requirements: Simulations must be used for teaching or training orthodontic professionals or residents to fall within the taxonomy's scope
constraints: The taxonomy covers only the 16 articles and 14 simulators included under the review's 2000-2021 search criteria
target_learning_goals: orthodontic diagnosis and treatment planning
bracket positioning
psychomotor clinical skills
cephalometric tracing
examples: The review's Table 1 classifies each included simulator by learning topic, type and concept of simulation, research objectives, and reported educational outcomes
key_sources: SIPIYARUK Kawin, KAEWSIRIRAT Prachworrakit, SANTIWONG Peerapong. (2023). Technology-enhanced simulation-based learning in orthodontic education: A scoping review. Dental Press Journal of Orthodontics. https://doi.org/10.1590/2177-6709.28.3.e2321354.oar

article_title: Technology-enhanced simulation-based learning in orthodontic education: A scoping review.
citation: SIPIYARUK Kawin, KAEWSIRIRAT Prachworrakit, SANTIWONG Peerapong. (2023). Technology-enhanced simulation-based learning in orthodontic education: A scoping review. Dental Press Journal of Orthodontics. https://doi.org/10.1590/2177-6709.28.3.e2321354.oar
title: Use technology-enhanced simulations for repetitive practice with immediate feedback to support self-directed learning and patient safety
description: The review argues technology-enhanced simulations should be designed so learners can repeat tasks with immediate feedback: they "allow users to perform required tasks repetitively until the expected outcomes are achieved", and with immediate feedback they support self-directed learning, reducing the need for one-to-one instructor support. The authors explain task repetition through the 'role of failure', in which students rethink or reperform tasks based on feedback from failure, and note simulators let learners improve skills in a safe environment, reducing treatment risk and enhancing patient safety.
requirements: Immediate feedback within the simulation to support self-directed learning
Unlimited training sessions, which the review notes come despite high setup costs and trained staff requirements
constraints: The review presents this as an argument from cited literature rather than a tested result of this review
target_learners: dental undergraduates preparing for clinical practice
target_learning_goals: psychomotor clinical skills
orthodontic knowledge and skills
patient safety
examples: The review cites the haptic simulation allowing users to perform the required steps of orthodontic bracket placement on a virtual patient, and the scenario-based software providing questions with immediate feedback

article_title: Structured viva validity, reliability, and acceptability as an assessment tool in health professions education: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
citation: Abuzied Abdelhamid Ibrahim Hassan, Nabag Wisal Omer Mohamed. (2023). Structured viva validity, reliability, and acceptability as an assessment tool in health professions education: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04524-6
title: Five criteria of a good assessment tool in medical education: validity, reliability, acceptability, feasibility, and educational impact
description: The review adopts a framework in which the usefulness of an assessment method in medical education is judged against five elements. As the article states, "validity, reliability and acceptability are considered parts of the criteria used for determining the usefulness of a particular method of assessment, together with the feasibility and educational impact those five elements are the criteria of good assessment tool." The review applies this framework by evaluating structured viva on the first three criteria against agreed medical education standards.
requirements: Assessment tools should be evaluated against all five criteria to determine their usefulness in medical education
constraints: This review evaluates only validity, reliability, and acceptability; feasibility and educational impact are named but not systematically reviewed
target_learners: Health professions education learners and faculty
target_learning_goals: Judging the quality and usefulness of assessment methods
examples: The review structures its Results and Discussion sections around the validity, reliability, and acceptability of structured viva

article_title: Application of case-based learning in psychology teaching: a meta-analysis.
citation: Wu Fanghui, Wang Tao, Yin Danxu, Xu Xiaoxiao, Jin Cancan, Mu Nan, Tan Qingrong. (2023). Application of case-based learning in psychology teaching: a meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04525-5
title: Case-based learning as a student-centered pedagogy distinguished from problem-based learning by prior-knowledge use and teacher guidance
description: The article characterizes CBL as "a student-centered pedagogy that requires students’ active participation in analyzing and discussing cases provided by the teacher", aiming to prepare students for professional practice by applying theoretical knowledge to contextual situations. Cases must be relevant, realistic, engaging, challenging, and instructional, with group case discussion as the core process. The article distinguishes CBL from PBL: CBL requires prior knowledge and trained-teacher guidance, whereas PBL involves solving problems with little previous knowledge and less teacher control, producing more "unfocused tangents".
requirements: Authentic and effective teaching cases are described as the key content, with achievement largely depending on case construction and facilitation
Inquiry-based learning, most commonly group discussion, is regarded as the instruction process for CBL
constraints: The article notes no standardized definition of CBL has been acknowledged
Applying CBL brings challenges and higher expectations to both teachers and students
target_learners: undergraduate and vocational students in psychology-related courses
target_learning_goals: applying theoretical knowledge to contextual situations
problem-solving and critical thinking skills
knowledge transfer
examples: Included trials implemented CBL alone or combined with simulated teaching, team-based learning, PBL, or flipped classroom formats across medical, nursing, management, experimental, and introductory psychology courses
key_sources: Wu Fanghui, Wang Tao, Yin Danxu, Xu Xiaoxiao, Jin Cancan, Mu Nan, Tan Qingrong. (2023). Application of case-based learning in psychology teaching: a meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04525-5

article_title: Efficacy of high-fidelity simulation in advanced life support training: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
citation: Zeng Qin, Wang Kai, Liu Wei-xin, Zeng Jiu-zhi, Li Xing-lan, Zhang Qing-feng, Ren Shang-qing, Xu Wen-ming. (2023). Efficacy of high-fidelity simulation in advanced life support training: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04654-x
title: Achieve high efficacy of HF simulation-based ALS training through proper participants, well-designed courses, experienced instructors, and debriefing sessions
description: The article argues that HF simulation is "just a device that provides realistic feedback" and that high-efficacy ALS training additionally requires optimized course design, case scenarios, experienced instructors, and debriefing sessions. It links this to its moderator findings: benefits appeared for residents and senior students but not first-year students. Debriefing is described as providing feedback crucial to enhancing team performance.
requirements: High-efficacy ALS training needs optimized course design, case scenarios, experienced instructors, and debriefing sessions, per the article's discussion.
constraints: HF simulation is costly and time-consuming, requiring specialized personnel, equipment, and space; a cited cost-effectiveness analysis found HF programs had only a 6% probability of being cost-effective at a willingness to pay of $100 compared with LF programs.
target_learning_goals: advanced life support knowledge
ALS skill performance
teamwork behaviors
examples: The meta-analysis pooled 25 RCTs in which 998 trainees used HF manikins (SimMan 3G by Laerdal was the most widely used simulator) and 989 received LF simulation-based or traditional training.
key_sources: Zeng Qin, Wang Kai, Liu Wei-xin, Zeng Jiu-zhi, Li Xing-lan, Zhang Qing-feng, Ren Shang-qing, Xu Wen-ming. (2023). Efficacy of high-fidelity simulation in advanced life support training: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04654-x

article_title: Effectiveness of virtual reality in nursing education: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
citation: Liu Kai, Zhang Weiwei, Li Wei, Wang Ting, Zheng Yanxue. (2023). Effectiveness of virtual reality in nursing education: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04662-x
title: Sherman and Craig's four essential components of VR as the review's defining criterion for VR-based instruction
description: The review operationalizes VR instruction using the four essential components delineated by Sherman and Craig: "virtual world, immersion, sensory feedback, interactivity". Included studies' experimental groups had to employ VR technology implementing these components to establish varying degrees of immersion through diverse VR platforms. This definition distinguishes VR interventions from non-VR simulation controls such as high-fidelity/low-fidelity and mannequin simulation.
requirements: Experimental interventions must implement virtual world, immersion, sensory feedback, and interactivity to count as VR instruction
constraints: The criterion was applied only to randomized controlled trials in nursing student populations
target_learning_goals: theoretical knowledge
practical skills
satisfaction
critical thinking
examples: Included interventions ranged from immersive VR (Immer VR) to VR combined with online education and flipped-classroom VR animation micro-courses

article_title: Educational strategies and nursing theory to prepare leaners for NCLEX-RN.
citation: Almasloukh, K. B., Miner, M., Phillips, K., & Evans, M. (2023). Educational strategies and nursing theory to prepare leaners for NCLEX‐RN. Nursing Open, 10, 7144–7153. https://doi.org/10.1002/nop2.1998
title: Eight theories/models recur across NCLEX-RN preparation literature, with Tanner's clinical judgement model aligned stepwise to the NCSBN Clinical Judgement Measurement Model
description: The review identifies eight theories or models used in more than one reviewed article: Tanner's clinical judgement model, the NCJMM, Knowles' adult learning theory (andragogy), Bloom's three learning domains, Peplau's theory of interpersonal relations, Bandura's self-efficacy theory, self-determination theory of motivation, and Astin's input-environment-outcome model. The review maps Tanner's steps onto the NCJMM: "The first step in Tanner's clinical judgement model is noticing," paralleled by recognizing and analysing cues, through to reflection paralleled by refining hypotheses and evaluation. Theories were used in 19 of the reviewed studies.
requirements: Theories are used as frameworks guiding educational strategies for NCLEX-RN preparation, as charted across the 25 reviewed studies
constraints: The review found no favoured theory or framework that should guide NCLEX-RN preparation, and no clearly defined theory focusing on students' QOL
target_learners: pre-licensure nursing students preparing for the NCLEX-RN
target_learning_goals: clinical judgement
NCLEX-RN readiness
critical thinking
examples: The review's Table 3 lists the eight theories with their citing articles; the discussion details stepwise similarities between Tanner's model and the NCJMM

article_title: 3D printing as a pedagogical tool for teaching normal human anatomy: a systematic review.
citation: Brumpt Eléonore, Bertin Eugénie, Tatu Laurent, Louvrier Aurélien. (2023). 3D printing as a pedagogical tool for teaching normal human anatomy: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04744-w
title: 3D-printed anatomical models (3DPAMs) for teaching normal human anatomy
description: 3DPAMs are physical 3D-printed replicas of anatomically normal human structures used as pedagogical tools in anatomy teaching. They are typically designed from medical image data — "In 47 studies (69%), the 3DPAMs were designed from CT scans" — segmented and modelled in software such as Mimics or MeshMixer, and printed mostly by FDM in plastic, most often PLA. Reported advantages include visual and haptic qualities, reproducibility, customizability, manipulability, and integration of functional anatomy.
requirements: An image acquisition modality must be chosen; the review states choosing an appropriate image acquisition modality is key
Segmentation and modelling software plus a compatible printer are needed; professionals such as engineers, radiologists, graphic designers and anatomists were often required
constraints: The main disadvantages were design-related: consistency, lack of detail or transparency, overly bright colours, long printing time, and high cost
More realistic models require more expensive technologies and substantially longer design time
target_learning_goals: normal human anatomy knowledge
spatial understanding of complex anatomical regions
structure recognition
mental rotation ability
examples: Bone was printed in 51 of 68 articles; the cephalic region was the most studied (33 articles); plastic and its derivatives were used in 48 studies
key_sources: Brumpt Eléonore, Bertin Eugénie, Tatu Laurent, Louvrier Aurélien. (2023). 3D printing as a pedagogical tool for teaching normal human anatomy: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04744-w

article_title: Active learning in undergraduate classroom dental education- a scoping review.
citation: Perez Arnaldo, Green Jacqueline, Moharrami Mohammad, Gianoni-Capenakas Silvia, Kebbe Maryam, Ganatra Seema, Ball Geoff, Sharmin Nazlee. (2023). Active learning in undergraduate classroom dental education- a scoping review. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0293206
title: Kirkpatrick's four-level model used to classify outcome evaluations of active learning
description: The review used Kirkpatrick's Model (1998) to summarize evaluation data by level. The article states "This model suggests four levels of outcome evaluation, including reaction (satisfaction and perceived outcomes), learning (direct measures of outcomes such knowledge, skills, and attitudes), behavior (behavioral changes resulting from the intervention), and results (organizational changes resulting from the intervention)". Papers reporting more than one outcome level were classified separately to calculate evaluations per level. In this review, all outcome evaluations fell at the reaction and learning levels.
requirements: Evaluation data classified by level: reaction, learning, behavior, and results
constraints: All outcome evaluations in the reviewed classroom dental education literature were at reaction and learning levels only
target_learning_goals: evaluation of active learning interventions in classroom dental education
examples: The review classified 32 studies as reaction evaluations alone, 19 as learning evaluations alone, and 42 as combined reaction and learning evaluations
key_sources: Perez Arnaldo, Green Jacqueline, Moharrami Mohammad, Gianoni-Capenakas Silvia, Kebbe Maryam, Ganatra Seema, Ball Geoff, Sharmin Nazlee. (2023). Active learning in undergraduate classroom dental education- a scoping review. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0293206

article_title: Effectiveness of Flexible Bronchoscopy Simulation-Based Training: A Systematic Review.
citation: Gerretsen Eveline C.F. MSc, Chen Aoben MD, Annema Jouke T. MD, PhD, Groenier Marleen PhD, van der Heijden Erik H.F.M. MD, PhD, van Mook Walther N.K.A. MD, PhD, Smeenk Frank W.J.M. MD, PhD. (2023). Effectiveness of Flexible Bronchoscopy Simulation-Based Training: A Systematic Review. Chest. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chest.2023.05.012
title: Kirkpatrick four-level model for evaluating training impact
description: The review applies the Kirkpatrick model, described as "a four-level model to evaluate training impact: reaction (level 1), learning (level 2), behavior (level 3), and results (level 4)." In the FB SBT context, level 2 means improved skills in a simulation setting, level 3 improved bronchoscopy performance in a patient setting, and level 4 improved patient outcomes such as less discomfort or fewer complications. The review uses these levels to classify outcome measures and judge the relevance of included studies' results.
requirements: Outcome measures must be classifiable by whether they capture satisfaction, simulation-setting skill, patient-setting behavior, or patient outcomes
constraints: Level 1 (satisfaction) studies were excluded from this review as less relevant to its purpose
target_learners: novice pulmonology trainees learning flexible bronchoscopy
target_learning_goals: basic flexible bronchoscopy skills
examples: The review classified ten studies' outcomes as Kirkpatrick level 2 (simulation setting) and four studies' outcomes as level 3 (patient setting); no study reported level 4 outcomes
key_sources: Gerretsen Eveline C.F. MSc, Chen Aoben MD, Annema Jouke T. MD, PhD, Groenier Marleen PhD, van der Heijden Erik H.F.M. MD, PhD, van Mook Walther N.K.A. MD, PhD, Smeenk Frank W.J.M. article_title: Effectiveness of Flexible Bronchoscopy Simulation-Based Training: A Systematic Review.
citation: Gerretsen Eveline C.F. MSc, Chen Aoben MD, Annema Jouke T. MD, PhD, Groenier Marleen PhD, van der Heijden Erik H.F.M. MD, PhD, van Mook Walther N.K.A. MD, PhD, Smeenk Frank W.J.M. MD, PhD. (2023). Effectiveness of Flexible Bronchoscopy Simulation-Based Training: A Systematic Review. Chest. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chest.2023.05.012
title: Instructional design feature set for simulation training programs
description: The review assessed each training program against a set of instructional design features partially based on Issenberg et al: "Clinical variation, Curriculum integration, Instructor feedback, Group practice, Individualized learning, Mastery learning, Prestudy, Range in task difficulty," alongside general features such as duration and assessment method. Across the 14 studies, apart from clinical variation (present in nine studies) and prestudy (present in 10 studies), there was no dominant pattern of any other instructional feature. The set operationalizes how SBT programs can be described and compared.
requirements: Features not explicitly mentioned in a study were assumed not to be present, so coding depends on complete program descriptions
constraints: Three planned features (multiple learning strategies, number of learning modalities, repetition) were left out for definitional and redundancy reasons stated by the review

examples: Reviewers coded each of the 14 studies on the eight instructional features in Table 6, contacting authors when characteristics could not be extracted from publications

article_title: Determinants of academic achievement among higher education student found in low resource setting, A systematic review.
citation: Kassaw Chalachew, Demareva Valeriia. (2023). Determinants of academic achievement among higher education student found in low resource setting, A systematic review. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0294585
title: Four-category taxonomy of academic achievement determinants in low-resource higher education
description: The review organizes predictors of academic achievement into four operational categories: psychological factors ("mental pain, sleep quality, self-esteem, prosocial behavior, anxiety, depression, and suicidality"), biological factors (gender, age, and hormonal issues such as dysmenorrhea), facility-related factors (seating, lighting, technology, dormitories, and other physical conditions), and lifestyle factors (social media usage, premarital sex, sexual abstinence). Tables 1–4 map primary studies onto these categories, and Fig 2 summarizes the categorized factors associated with achievement in Ethiopian higher education.
requirements: Primary studies must report outcome variables and covariates with basic statistical analysis linking factors to academic performance
constraints: Limited to cross-sectional studies of Ethiopian higher education students published between 2013 and 2022
target_learners: higher education students in low-resource settings
target_learning_goals: academic achievement as measured by GPA and performance indicators
examples: Tables 1–4 assign each primary study's findings to the psychological, biological, facility, or lifestyle category; Fig 2 summarizes the categories.

article_title: Educational outcomes of recess in elementary school children: A mixed-methods systematic review.
citation: Howie Erin K., Perryman Kristi L., Moretta Joseph, Cameron Laura. (2023). Educational outcomes of recess in elementary school children: A mixed-methods systematic review. PLOS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0294340
title: Recess as a unique developmental opportunity beyond physical activity
description: The review frames recess as more than a physical activity bout: it combines physiological activity with being outdoors, social interaction, and creative free play, each with proposed developmental benefits. It notes recess "includes social interaction, where children have opportunities to develop social skills, practice conflict resolution, and problem-solving skills". This framework motivates examining recess effects on educational outcomes beyond what exercise alone explains.
requirements: Recess defined as a regular unstructured break in the school day, typically outdoors
constraints: The review excluded interventions where recess was manipulated into structured activity, so the framework applies to unstructured recess
target_learning_goals: social skills
problem solving
creativity
attention
examples: The review cites Piaget's classification of play stages and outdoor-walk studies as background for the framework

article_title: Educational outcomes of recess in elementary school children: A mixed-methods systematic review.
citation: Howie Erin K., Perryman Kristi L., Moretta Joseph, Cameron Laura. (2023). Educational outcomes of recess in elementary school children: A mixed-methods systematic review. PLOS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0294340
title: Daily recess duration may beneficially exceed the CDC-recommended 20 minutes when split into shorter periods
description: Based on the studies showing improved outcomes, the review suggests educational benefits may accrue from total daily recess longer than the CDC-recommended 20 minutes, and that the total can be divided into shorter periods. It states there "may be additional educational benefits of recess length longer than the CDC recommended 20 minutes per day, but that this can be broken up into shorter recess periods."
requirements: Evidence on optimal scheduling and meaningful outcomes to justify allocating additional school time
constraints: No dose-response was directly examined; the improved-outcome studies used 25 minutes or two 15-minute periods; evidence is described as limited
target_learning_goals: on-task behavior
academic achievement
classroom behavior
examples: Qualitative studies with specified durations used 40 minutes of daily recess or more, two split into shorter periods

article_title: Evaluation of video review tools for assessing non-technical skills in emergency department resuscitation teams: a systematic review.
citation: Alexander Emily G, Denny Fraser, Gordon Malcom WG, McKiernan Cieran, Lowe David J. (2023). Evaluation of video review tools for assessing non-technical skills in emergency department resuscitation teams: a systematic review. BMC Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12873-023-00895-7
title: Use T-NOTECHS as the tool of choice for assessing non-technical skills of ED resuscitation teams via video review
description: The review recommends T-NOTECHS for video-based assessment of NTS in ED resuscitation teams because it is validated, most studied, and balances usability, reliability and validity. It states that "when assessing NTS more holistically, T-NOTECHS demonstrates usability, reliability and validity". T-NOTECHS splits NTS into 5 categories on a 5-point Likert scale and provides score anchors to guide users.
requirements: Video recording of real-life resuscitations in the ED; reviewers can pause or rewind video for more accurate assessment
constraints: The conclusion that T-NOTECHS is the best tool is suggested but not proven fully due to small sample sizes; reliability varies across studies (ICC 0.48–0.94)
target_learning_goals: non-technical skills including leadership, communication, situational awareness, decision making and teamwork
examples: Six of the nine included studies used T-NOTECHS; the review recommends multi-centre studies with larger sample sizes to establish its utility, and suggests TTCA-24 where communication is identified as a weakness

Evaluation of video review tools for assessing non-technical skills in emergency department resuscitation teams: a systematic review.
