article_title: The effect of experiential learning interventions on physical activity outcomes in children: A systematic review.
citation: Varman Sumantla D., Jones Rachel A., Kelly Bridget, Hammersley Megan L., Parrish Anne-Maree, Stanley Rebecca, Cliff Dylan P. (2023). The effect of experiential learning interventions on physical activity outcomes in children: A systematic review. PLOS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0294987
title: Kolb's four-stage experiential learning model as the framework for physical activity interventions
description: The review frames experiential learning through David Kolb's four-stage model: "concrete experience", "reflective observation", "abstract conceptualization" and "active experimentation". Learners participate in hands-on activities, develop perspectives through reflection, identify the significance of the learning experience from which new behaviours emerge, and apply the new concept practically. Reflection is described as the key component enabling learners to relate knowledge and behaviour systematically. The review uses this model to characterise and categorise the interventions it synthesises.
requirements: Interventions must incorporate an experiential learning activity in which children play a central role, physically do something, and have some autonomy to be creative, problem-solve or be reflective
constraints: The review restricted included studies to randomised controlled trials, a post hoc protocol deviation deemed the most robust level of evidence
target_learning_goals: physical activity knowledge
physical activity attitudes
physical activity behaviour
key_sources: Varman Sumantla D., Jones Rachel A., Kelly Bridget, Hammersley Megan L., Parrish Anne-Maree, Stanley Rebecca, Cliff Dylan P. (2023). The effect of experiential learning interventions on physical activity outcomes in children: A systematic review. PLOS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0294987

article_title: The effect of experiential learning interventions on physical activity outcomes in children: A systematic review.
citation: Varman Sumantla D., Jones Rachel A., Kelly Bridget, Hammersley Megan L., Parrish Anne-Maree, Stanley Rebecca, Cliff Dylan P. (2023). The effect of experiential learning interventions on physical activity outcomes in children: A systematic review. PLOS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0294987
title: Experiential learning physical activity interventions structured as practical components plus theory components
description: The review categorises experiential learning physical activity interventions into practical components — outdoor and adventure activities, fitness activities and challenges, rhythmic and expressive movement activities, modified sports and games, and active play and tummy time — and theory components: "behaviour change and motivational strategies" and "information and education strategies". Most included studies (n = 8) used approaches from both theory categories, and the review considered both component types when interpreting intervention effects.
requirements: A practical component and a theory-based component, coordinated by a facilitator such as a teacher, educator or parent who provides structure such as basic instruction or questions invoking problem-solving or reflection
constraints: One study added environmental/organisational change strategies on top of both theory categories; the pattern as categorised covers only practical and theory components
target_learners: children aged birth to 12 years in schools, preschools, after-school and community settings
target_learning_goals: physical activity behaviour change
physical activity knowledge
physical activity attitudes and self-efficacy
examples: Eather et al. combined fitness activities and challenges with modified sports and games, plus behaviour change/motivational and information/education strategies, over 8 weeks in primary schools
key_sources: Varman Sumantla D., Jones Rachel A., Kelly Bridget, Hammersley Megan L., Parrish Anne-Maree, Stanley Rebecca, Cliff Dylan P. (2023). The effect of experiential learning interventions on physical activity outcomes in children: A systematic review. PLOS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0294987

article_title: Effect of e-learning program for improving nurse knowledge and practice towards managing pressure injuries: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
citation: Ding, Y., Qian, J., Zhou, Y., & Zhang, Y. (2024). Effect of e‐learning program for improving nurse knowledge and practice towards managing pressure injuries: A systematic review and meta‐analysis. Nursing Open, 11, e2039. https://doi.org/10.1002/nop2.2039
title: Evidence base of eight controlled trials of e-learning for pressure injury management (from 1054 screened citations)
description: The review's evidence corpus consists of eight interventional trials with independent comparison groups, identified from 1054 citations across EMBASE, SCOPUS, Cochrane Library, MEDLINE, Google Scholar, ScienceDirect and Clinicaltrials.gov searched to August 2022. The authors state they "included data from eight studies satisfying the inclusion criteria"; four studies reported knowledge outcomes and five reported classification skills. Studies were conducted mostly in Iran and European countries, with intervention-arm samples of 20 to 217.
requirements: Eligible studies had to be randomized or non-randomized controlled trials comparing e-learning against traditional lecture or no training
constraints: Unpublished grey literature and case reports/series were excluded
Publication bias assessment and meta-regression could not be performed due to the limited number of studies
target_learners: nurses in surgical, ICU, and general wards
target_learning_goals: pressure injury prevention and management knowledge
pressure ulcer classification skills
examples: Included trials spanned Beeckman et al. (2008) in Belgium (I = 217, C = 209, PUCLAS2 outcome) through van Gaal et al. (2010) in the Netherlands (I = 88, C = 136, EPUAP knowledge outcome).

article_title: Validity Evidence for Procedure-specific Competence Assessment Tools in Orthopaedic Surgery: A Scoping Review.
citation: Li Yibo, Chan Robert, Menon Matthew R.G., Ryan Joanna F., Mador Brett, Campbell Sandra M., Turner Simon R. (2024). Validity Evidence for Procedure-specific Competence Assessment Tools in Orthopaedic Surgery: A Scoping Review. JAAOS Global Research & Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5435/JAAOSGlobal-D-23-00065
title: Five-domain validity evidence framework for appraising surgical assessment tools
description: The review applies a five-domain validity framework, based on Messick's unitary view of validity and operationalized by Ghaderi et al, in which each assessment tool is scored on content, response process, internal structure, relation to other variables, and consequences, with a maximum score of 15. Two independent reviewers scored each of the 24 tools on these domains, with disagreements resolved by consensus. The framework is presented as having "good interrater reliability" when used in prior surgical specialties' reviews.
requirements: Two independent reviewers scoring each tool, with disagreements resolved by consensus decision
constraints: Scores are appraisals of published validity evidence, capped by the quality of the underlying studies
target_learning_goals: assessment of procedural technical competence in surgery
examples: Each of the 24 tools received domain scores in Table 2, e.g., the Shoulder Objective Practical Assessment Tool scored 3,1,2,2,1 for a total of 9 of 15

article_title: Use of problem-based learning in orthopaedics education: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
citation: Li Ting, Song Ruohong, Zhong Wenjie, Liao Wenao, Hu Jiang, Liu Xilin, Wang Fei. (2024). Use of problem-based learning in orthopaedics education: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05244-1
title: Adopt PBL in orthopaedics clinical teaching while planning for added study time demands and pressure
description: The review concludes that the PBL teaching model can significantly improve the quality of clinical teaching and is worth promoting and applying, because pooled results favour PBL on knowledge, skills, satisfaction and process abilities. At the same time it reports that students can feel higher levels of study pressure and experience less study time, so adoption should be paired with provision of learning space, time, and resources. The authors state the findings need to be further verified in multicentre, double-blind and large-sample RCTs.
requirements: PBL requires a high level of self-directed learning and collaboration skills from students
providing students with more learning space, time, and resources to support self-study and group discussions
constraints: all included studies were from China, and some pooled results were strongly subjective
only English and Chinese studies were included, which may have led to language bias and heterogeneity
half of the included studies did not provide detailed information on the frequency and duration of PBL interventions
risk of bias increased due to lack of information about randomization, allocation concealment, and blinding of outcome assessment in some studies
target_learning_goals: orthopaedics theoretical knowledge
procedural and clinical skills
problem-solving, independent learning, teamwork, communication and clinical reasoning abilities
examples: The review pooled 51 RCTs (4268 patients) comparing PBL with lecture-based learning across orthopaedics teaching topics such as basic theory, imageology, arthroscopy training and failure-case analysis.

article_title: Video Killed the Radio Star-A Meta-Analysis on Video-Based Coaching to Improve Surgical Skill.
citation: Anderson Steven Mark, Gillanders Sarahlouise, Hickey Anne, Offiah Gozie, Davis Niall. (2025). Video Killed the Radio Star—A Meta‐Analysis on Video‐Based Coaching to Improve Surgical Skill. World Journal of Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1002/wjs.12494
title: Video-based coaching as a mechanism for reproducing the trainee–trainer feedback relationship outside the operating room
description: Video-based coaching (VBC) is a training method in which "a coach provides individualized feedback on a trainee's performance after reviewing video footage of their performance together". The article positions VBC as reproducing the conventional trainee–trainer relationship of the apprenticeship model without the time constraints of the operating room and without the need for sophisticated simulation models. In the review, VBC sessions involved trainees watching video of their own performance with expert feedback, varying in session count, length and timing across the included RCTs.
requirements: Video footage of the trainee's performance and a coach able to review it with the trainee and deliver individualized feedback
constraints: All included studies scored a high risk of performance bias because it is not possible to blind participants or personnel to VBC or control
target_learning_goals: surgical technical skill acquisition
examples: In the included RCTs, coaching sessions ranged from a single session to 10, lasted 10 to 45 min, and occurred from immediately following the procedure to 2 weeks after it; 14 studies used one-to-one review of the video with a coach
key_sources: Anderson Steven Mark, Gillanders Sarahlouise, Hickey Anne, Offiah Gozie, Davis Niall. (2025). Video Killed the Radio Star—A Meta‐Analysis on Video‐Based Coaching to Improve Surgical Skill. World Journal of Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1002/wjs.12494

article_title: Video Killed the Radio Star-A Meta-Analysis on Video-Based Coaching to Improve Surgical Skill.
citation: Anderson Steven Mark, Gillanders Sarahlouise, Hickey Anne, Offiah Gozie, Davis Niall. (2025). Video Killed the Radio Star—A Meta‐Analysis on Video‐Based Coaching to Improve Surgical Skill. World Journal of Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1002/wjs.12494
title: Formally integrate video-based coaching into conventional surgical training programs
description: The article concludes that because VBC is an effective and versatile supplement to the apprenticeship model, "Training bodies around the world should now look at how best to formally integrate VBC into conventional surgical training". The recommendation rests on the meta-analytic evidence that VBC outperformed several routinely used forms of feedback, and on its demonstrated effectiveness across session counts, settings and coaching frameworks.
requirements: Access to video footage of trainee performance and capacity to deliver individualized coach feedback sessions
constraints: The article states further research is needed to establish how best VBC can be incorporated into surgical training curricula going forward
target_learning_goals: surgical technical skill acquisition
examples: The review demonstrated VBC to be effective in both simulated and live surgeries, whether delivered as a single session or over multiple sessions and across a wide range of coaching frameworks

article_title: Comparison of the Informed Health Choices Key Concepts Framework to other frameworks relevant to teaching and learning how to think critically about health claims and choices: a systematic review.
citation: Oxman Andrew D., García Laura Martínez. (2020). Comparison of the Informed Health Choices Key Concepts Framework to other frameworks relevant to teaching and learning how to think critically about health claims and choices: a systematic review. F1000Research 9:164. https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.21858.1
title: The IHC Key Concepts Framework: principles for evaluating the trustworthiness of treatment claims, organised as concepts, competences, and dispositions
description: The Informed Health Choices Key Concepts Framework is a structure of concepts, competences, and dispositions for evaluating the trustworthiness of claims about treatment effects and for making informed health choices. The article states that "The concepts are principles for evaluating the trustworthiness of treatment claims and the evidence used to support these, and for making informed choices." The current (2019) version includes 49 concepts in three groups (Claims, Comparisons, Choices), 20 competences in four groups, and 16 dispositions in four groups, and serves as a starting point for teachers, journalists, researchers and other intermediaries developing learning resources.
requirements: To be usable as a framework, sources must include a description of the purpose, a list of elements, and definitions of key terms, per the review's inclusion criteria
constraints: The framework targets treatment (intervention) claims about health, though people in other fields have found the concepts relevant for assessing claims about other types of interventions
target_learners: teachers, journalists, researchers and other intermediaries
target_learning_goals: assessing the trustworthiness of treatment claims
making informed health choices
examples: The 2019 framework's Table 1 organises concepts under Claims, Comparisons, and Choices; Table 2 lists competences such as recognising unfair treatment comparisons; Table 3 lists dispositions such as questioning the basis for treatment claims
key_sources: Oxman Andrew D., García Laura Martínez. (2020). citation: Oxman Andrew D., García Laura Martínez. (2020). title: Catalogue of 22 included frameworks relevant to teaching critical thinking about claims, comparisons, and choices
description: This element is the set of 22 frameworks the systematic review included, spanning critical thinking (e.g. Ennis's taxonomy, Paul's model, Halpern's list, Baron's model of the good thinker), logic and argumentation (logical fallacies, Allen's taxonomy, the evidence based reasoning framework), cognition (cognitive biases, metacognitive frameworks, epistemological models, the AIR model), scientific thinking (PISA scientific literacy, the K-12 science education framework, systems thinking, a model for scientific thinking), and evidence-based health care (health literacy, EBP core competencies, GRADE, Bradford-Hill criteria, critical appraisal, the Cochrane risk of bias tool, and the Catalogue of biases). evaluation of evidence supporting claims
informed choices

article_title: The impact of project ECHO on physician preparedness to treat opioid use disorder: a systematic review.
citation: Puckett, H. M., Bossaller, J. S., & Sheets, L. R. (2021). The impact of project ECHO on physician preparedness to treat opioid use disorder: a systematic review. Addiction Science & Clinical Practice, 16, 6. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13722-021-00215-z
title: Project ECHO as a case-based tele-mentoring model for extending specialist capacity to community providers
description: Project ECHO (Extension for Community Healthcare Outcomes) is described as "a collaborative tele-mentoring program in which specialists train health-care workers to treat medical conditions". It is explicitly distinguished from telemedicine: rather than a physician treating a patient remotely, it "connects learners with experienced specialists in order to improve services", so learners can implement new services after participation. Sessions are case-based, multi-disciplinary, and aimed at community and rural providers treating conditions such as OUD.
requirements: Requires specialists willing to facilitate case-based sessions and community providers (typically primary care) who attend and present cases
constraints: The review states the model is not traditional telemedicine and that a study by the Rand Corporation found building capacity to evaluate ECHO outcomes is a critical unmet need
target_learners: Primary care physicians and cross-disciplinary health care teams, especially in rural and underserved locations
target_learning_goals: Knowledge and self-efficacy for treating opioid use disorder, including buprenorphine prescribing
examples: The University of New Mexico OUD ECHO runs 2-hour case presentations facilitated by a physician specializing in OUD, a psychiatrist, a social worker, a psychiatric nurse, and a community health worker
key_sources: Puckett, H. M., Bossaller, J. S., & Sheets, L. R. (2021). The impact of project ECHO on physician preparedness to treat opioid use disorder: a systematic review. Addiction Science & Clinical Practice, 16, 6. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13722-021-00215-z

article_title: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of the Use of High-Fidelity Simulation in Obstetric Ultrasound.
citation: Dromey Brian P. MBChB, MRCOG; Peebles Donald M. MBBS, MD, MRCOG; Stoyanov Danail V. PhD. (2021). A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of the Use of High-Fidelity Simulation in Obstetric Ultrasound. Simulation in Healthcare. https://doi.org/10.1097/SIH.0000000000000485
title: Simulation as a waypoint to semiautonomous supervised clinical practice
description: The review frames high-fidelity ultrasound simulation not as a replacement for clinical training but as "a waypoint to allow the learner to transition to semiautonomous practice in a supervised, clinical setting." On this account, simulation is best used for acquisition of technical skills and image optimization, augments traditional learning, and, when integrated into curricula with self-directed learning, lets trainees contribute to clinical service while learning a complex skill. The framework draws an analogy to aviation, where simulators are integrated into training, assessment, and licensing.
requirements: Integration into training curricula rather than optional, unguided access
A strong focus on specific, objective, and measurable clinical outcomes with audit and curriculum revision based on learner feedback
constraints: Current simulators focus on technical skills proficiency while ignoring communication, distractions, and clinical management; none address the clinical context in which the trainee will eventually work
target_learners: novice ultrasound operators, including obstetrics and gynecology trainees, emergency medicine and radiology trainees, and allied health professionals
target_learning_goals: technical obstetric ultrasound skills
image optimization
transition to supervised clinical scanning
examples: The authors' own training curricula were challenged by simulation-based training and assessment, using simulation to augment traditional learning with objective outcomes and curriculum revision
key_sources: Dromey Brian P. MBChB, MRCOG; Peebles Donald M. MBBS, MD, MRCOG; Stoyanov Danail V. PhD. (2021). A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of the Use of High-Fidelity Simulation in Obstetric Ultrasound. Simulation in Healthcare. https://doi.org/10.1097/SIH.0000000000000485

article_title: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of the Use of High-Fidelity Simulation in Obstetric Ultrasound.
citation: Dromey Brian P. MBChB, MRCOG; Peebles Donald M. MBBS, MD, MRCOG; Stoyanov Danail V. PhD. (2021). A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of the Use of High-Fidelity Simulation in Obstetric Ultrasound. Simulation in Healthcare. https://doi.org/10.1097/SIH.0000000000000485
title: Integrate simulation training into the clinical curriculum with objective, measurable outcomes rather than case-count logbooks
description: The review recommends that "consideration ought to be given to integrate simulation training into the clinical curriculum," because trainees report clinical commitments as barriers to voluntary engagement and because curricula based on numbers of cases completed do not measure competence. It argues training programs should be "based on objective outcomes, rather than trainer reports and arbitrary numbers of cases recorded in a log book," with audit and revision based on learner feedback.
requirements: Formal guidance and scheduled access so trainees can engage despite clinical workload
Objective, measurable outcome measures for competence assessment
constraints: Even in research settings trainees reported clinical commitments as barriers to engaging with simulation training
target_learners: sonographers and midwives learning obstetric ultrasound
target_learning_goals: basic obstetric ultrasound competence
image optimization
readiness for supervised clinical scanning
examples: Monsky et al. mandated departmental-level simulator assessment before overnight call, then redesigned the residency program with 8 additional weeks of targeted transvaginal ultrasound training

article_title: The effectiveness of problem-based learning in gynecology and obstetrics education in China: A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
citation: Bi S, Liu R, Li J, Gu J. (2021). The effectiveness of problem-based learning in gynecology and obstetrics education in China: A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000024660
title: Pool of 38 randomized controlled trials comparing PBL with traditional teaching in Chinese gynecology and obstetrics education
description: The evidence base for this meta-analysis is a pool of randomized controlled trials published in Chinese between 2015 and 2020 comparing PBL with traditional teaching in obstetrics and gynecology courses. As the article states, "a total of 38 controlled studies with 1494 participants in the PBL group and 1511 participants in traditional teaching groups were included for this meta-analysis." Sample sizes ranged from 31 to 218 with a median of 71, mostly interns. Only studies with duration longer than 6 months were included in the meta-analysis.
requirements: Studies had to be randomized controlled trials comparing PBL with traditional teaching in Chinese obstetrics and gynecology education with usable outcome data
constraints: All included trials had unclear bias for blinding of participants, personnel, and outcome assessment; 16 studies were ambiguous about random sequence generation
target_learning_goals: theoretical knowledge
clinical practice skills
clinical operation skills
student satisfaction
examples: The search screened 519 records from Chinese and English databases and included 38 trials published 2015-2020, all in Chinese.

article_title: How Can Bullying Victimisation Lead to Lower Academic Achievement? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Mediating Role of Cognitive-Motivational Factors.
citation: Muthanna, S., Da Silva Nascimento, B., El-Asam, A., Hammuda, S., & Khattab, N. (2021). How Can Bullying Victimisation Lead to Lower Academic Achievement? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Mediating Role of Cognitive-Motivational Factors. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health, 18(5), 2209. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph18052209
title: Self-Determination Theory as the framework explaining how bullying victimisation undermines motivation and achievement
description: The article uses Self-Determination Theory as its explanatory framework for why victimisation lowers achievement. SDT "postulates that relatedness, autonomy, and competence are three important factors to maintain positive well-being", and the authors argue that negative school conditions such as peer rejection, social exclusion and bullying may undermine these needs, reducing motivation and aspirations, which in turn impairs academic achievement. Expectancy-value and achievement goal theories are cited as complementary accounts.
requirements: All three needs — relatedness, autonomy and competence — must be supported in students for them to feel motivated and achieve their highest academic potential, as the article states.
constraints: The article presents SDT as an interpretive framework supported by prior studies, not as a mechanism tested within the meta-analysis itself.
target_learners: children and adolescents in school settings (5–18 years)
target_learning_goals: academic motivation and aspirations
academic achievement
school engagement
examples: The authors interpret the meta-analytic mediation result through SDT: bullied students feel less connected to school, present lower academic motivation and reduced perceived academic competence, and lower educational aspirations than non-bullied peers.

article_title: Learning about stress from building, drilling and flying: a scoping review on team performance and stress in non-medical fields.

title: The 'team brain': an umbrella concept uniting shared mental model, transactive memory and situational awareness as team cognition supporting performance under stress
description: The review introduces the 'team brain' as an umbrella term under which three overlapping cognitive themes come together: shared mental model, transactive memory and situational awareness. All three "revolve around the development of a common view of the situation, for which communication is important". The authors propose that developing a team brain could increase team performance in stressful situations and improve patient outcomes, and that simulation training might help develop these cognitive structures.

constraints: The review states an integration of the three cognitive themes and team performance in stressful situations has not yet been specified; further research is needed before integrating the concept in training and education

team communication
shared situational understanding
examples: The review cites medical simulation studies in which surgery residents developed shared mental models after a stressful scenario and emergency department professionals showed increased transactive memory after trauma simulation.

article_title: Is project-based learning effective among kindergarten and elementary students? A systematic review.
citation: Ferrero Marta, Vadillo Miguel A., León Samuel P. (2021). Is project-based learning effective among kindergarten and elementary students? A systematic review. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0249627
title: PjBL as a student-centred inquiry approach defined by key elements: driving problem, final product, group work, student empowerment, teacher guidance, and adapted evaluation tools
description: The review characterizes PjBL (used to cover both project- and problem-based learning) as "active, student-centred methods of instruction that encourage students to work in collaborative groups on real-world questions or challenges" with teachers as facilitators. Its central elements are a problem driving the activities, a final artifact or product, group work, student empowerment, teacher-provided guidance and resources, and evaluation tools adapted to PjBL such as notebook entries or portfolios. The review built a 30-item scale from these principles to assess prerequisites and fidelity.
requirements: An intervention faithful to the PjBL approach should include all its essential components as defined in the literature
constraints: PjBL and PBL are often employed interchangeably among researchers and teachers due to difficulties in distinguishing or defining their key features
target_learning_goals: acquisition of content knowledge
higher-order thinking skills
examples: The review coded each included study against the key elements using a 30-item scale divided into prerequisites (Part A) and intervention fidelity (Part B)
key_sources: Ferrero Marta, Vadillo Miguel A., León Samuel P. (2021). Is project-based learning effective among kindergarten and elementary students? A systematic review. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0249627

article_title: Is project-based learning effective among kindergarten and elementary students? A systematic review.
citation: Ferrero Marta, Vadillo Miguel A., León Samuel P. (2021). Is project-based learning effective among kindergarten and elementary students? A systematic review. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0249627
title: Do not assume PjBL results from secondary and higher education transfer directly to kindergarten and primary students without monitoring
description: The review argues that because of considerable differences between senior and novice learners, what is effective in secondary or postsecondary settings may not transfer directly to younger students. It states that "it should not be assumed that novice learners possess the advanced self-regulation skills, prior knowledge, or group work skills" necessary for PjBL, so any attempt to translate this literature to kindergarten and primary students should be properly monitored.
requirements: Any attempt to translate the main results and conclusions of this literature to kindergarten and primary students should be properly monitored
constraints: The studies included in the review do not address how different learning profiles affect PjBL effectiveness, since all populations were students without special needs
target_learning_goals: content knowledge acquisition

citation: Schmidt MW, Köppinger KF, Fan C, Kowalewski K-F, Schmidt LP, Vey J, Proctor T, Probst P, Bintintan VV, Müller-Stich B-P, Nickel F. (2021). Virtual reality simulation in robot-assisted surgery: meta-analysis of skill transfer and predictability of skill. BJS Open. https://doi.org/10.1093/bjsopen/zraa066
title: Messick's unified construct validity framework for evaluating robotic VR simulators as assessment and selection tools
description: The article applies Messick's framework, which "conceptualizes all validity under one overarching framework of construct validity", to robotic VR simulators. Within it, concurrent validity asks how accurately simulator performances predict current intraoperative performance, informing credentialing, while predictive validity asks how accurately they predict future performance, informing selection of future robotic surgeons. The review uses this framework to organize its predictability studies and to argue that terminology around validity is often misunderstood and misused.
requirements: Evidence must distinguish concurrent from predictive validity questions when assessing simulator performance against operative performance
constraints: The review found that not a single study comprehensively evaluated the predictability of future operative performance
target_learners: surgical trainees and surgeons training in robot-assisted surgery
target_learning_goals: technical surgical skill assessment and credentialing in robot-assisted surgery
examples: The review grouped three cross-sectional studies as predictability (validity evidence) studies and pooled their correlation coefficients in a random-effects meta-analysis

title: Use robotic VR simulator training before operating on patients, as acquired skills transfer to the operating room
description: The review concludes that "Technical surgical skills acquired through robotic VR simulator training can be transferred to the operating room", so that "VR training can therefore be justified before operating on patients". The authors argue this supports including robotic VR simulators in dedicated training curricula and emphasizes simulation training before real operating room performance to ensure patient safety. Shortened operating times further justify simulators because operating room time is expensive.
requirements: Training curricula must be designed so that skills acquired on the simulator match the operative performance assessed; the article states exactly how best to implement simulators (duration of training, choice of tasks) requires further investigation
constraints: The evidence base is limited: only eight studies were eligible, transfer studies were too heterogeneous for quantitative synthesis, and the extent to which transfer applies remains unclear
target_learners: novice robotic surgeons, surgical residents, and credentialed surgeons naive to robot-assisted surgery
target_learning_goals: technical robotic surgical skill acquisition and transfer to operating room performance
examples: In the reviewed studies, intervention groups trained on dVSS or dV-Trainer tasks to proficiency before operating room assessment on human patients or live animal models

citation: Jørgensen Rasmus, Laursen Christian B., Konge Lars, Pietersen Pia Iben. (2021). Education in the placement of ultrasound-guided peripheral venous catheters: a systematic review. Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13049-021-00897-z
title: Kern's six-step model for curriculum development as an organizing framework for USG-PVC education
description: Kern's six-step model is a curriculum-development framework the review uses to structure its evaluation of existing USG-PVC education. The steps are "problem identification and general needs-assessment, targeted needs-assessment, setting goals and measurable objectives, educational strategies, implementation, and evaluation and feedback", with earlier steps revisited throughout. The review maps its findings onto these steps, finding needs assessments absent, curricula poorly described, and assessment tools rarely validity-tested.
requirements: Assessment tools preferably based on solid evidence of validity should be used to ensure the set goals and objectives
constraints: The review found no needs-assessment studies and a lack of defined curricula and competency-assurance tools in the included literature
target_learning_goals: competence in ultrasound-guided peripheral venous catheter placement
examples: The review used the model to evaluate existing knowledge: no needs-assessment studies were found, curricula generally included ultrasound physics, knobology, probe selection, vascular and nerve recognition, preparation, and complications, and only Primdahl's rating scale had explored validity evidence via Messick's framework

article_title: Characteristics of laparoscopic and open hernia repair simulation models: a systematic review.
citation: Pelly T., Vance-Daniel J., Linder C. (2021). Characteristics of laparoscopic and open hernia repair simulation models: a systematic review. Hernia. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8251686/
title: Three-domain validity framework for evaluating surgical simulation models
description: The review applies a three-domain validity framework to classify hernia repair simulation models. As the review defines it, "Face validity was defined as the physical realism of the simulator", construct validity as the ability to differentiate performance by experience level, and content validity as expert-judged suitability as a teaching modality. Each of the 27 included models is tabulated against these three domains plus educational impact and skill transfer.
requirements: Developers must assess models against the defined validity domains after design and implementation to establish educational value
constraints: The review notes the literature's validity definitions are nebulous and vary from those applied in this review, with a need for more consensus

target_learning_goals: technical competence in hernia repair procedures
examples: The review classified all 27 included models by face, construct and content validity, educational impact and transfer of skills to the operating theatre

title: GOALS-GH and GOALS-IH OSATS assessment tools for laparoscopic hernia repair
description: The GOALS-GH and GOALS-IH are Objective Structured Assessment of Technical Skills (OSATS) tools designed specifically for TEP and TAPP laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair and incisional hernia repair respectively. The review reports "Both were shown to have high inter-rater reliabilities (0.96, 95% CI 0.74–0.99) as well as construct validity", with good correlation between GOALS-IH scores and the number of laparoscopic procedures performed. The review recommends future model developers employ these tools for formal evaluation and comparison.
requirements: Developers of hernia repair models should employ these assessment tools or similar to allow formal evaluation of educational impact and comparison between models

target_learning_goals: assessment of operative performance in simulated and real laparoscopic hernia repair

article_title: The Influence of Academic Emotions on Learning Effects: A Systematic Review.
citation: Tan Jing, Mao Jie, Jiang Yizhang, Gao Ming. (2021). The Influence of Academic Emotions on Learning Effects: A Systematic Review. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph18189678
title: Two-dimensional (valence × arousal) classification of academic emotions into four groups
description: The review organizes academic emotions along two dimensions: valence (whether the stimulus is pleasant or unpleasant) and arousal (the emotional intensity a stimulus causes). Based on this classification it divides emotions into four groups: "positive arousal emotions (e.g., enjoyment, pride)", positive low-arousal emotions (e.g., relaxation), passive arousal emotions (e.g., anger, anxiety), and negative emotions (e.g., extreme depression, despair). This taxonomy underpins the review's comparisons of positive versus negative academic emotions on learning effects.
requirements: Academic emotions must be assessed with tools distinguishing valence and arousal, such as emotion scales or self-report instruments
constraints: The review notes arousal and potency produce different results in cognitive processes and on relevant neural matrices, so effects differ by emotion type
target_learning_goals: academic performance
learning strategies
motivation
cognitive load
examples: The review's included studies measured emotions with instruments such as PANAS, the Positive Emotion Self-Report Scale, and the Achievement Emotion Questionnaire

title: Barrows' core model of problem-based learning: six defining characteristics
description: The review adopts Barrows' 1996 overview as its defining model of problem-based learning and uses it as an inclusion criterion: articles not reporting these elements were excluded. The model specifies that "learning is student centred", "learning occurs in small student groups", tutors act as facilitators or guides, problems form the organizing focus and stimulus for learning, problems develop problem-solving skills, and new information is attained through self-directed learning. In this review it anchors the intervention category against traditional, tutor-led, teacher-centred instruction.

constraints: Applied in this review to undergraduate and postgraduate dental students learning oral medicine and radiology

problem-solving skills
self-directed learning
examples: Included PBL-type interventions ranged from syndicate learning and the one-minute preceptor to simulation, virtual, and blended learning, compared against tutor-led traditional methods

article_title: Analysis of Nurses' and Physicians' Attitudes, Knowledge, and Perceptions toward Fever in Children: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis.
citation: Vicens-Blanes, F., Miró-Bonet, R., & Molina-Mula, J. (2021). International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph182312444
title: Three-variable taxonomy (knowledge, attitudes, perceptions) for classifying outcomes of nurses' fever-management education
description: The review organizes the evaluation of educational programs for nurses around three outcome classes. Knowledge covers "understanding of fever physiology, fever management, and antipyretic drugs or measures"; attitudes cover changes in clinical practice with a febrile child, performance against febrile convulsions, and health education provided to parents; perceptions cover how parents, nursing colleagues, and physicians influence care of a febrile child and how much control professionals have over management. The meta-analysis pools studies separately within these three classes.
requirements: Studies must evaluate an educational program for nurses related to fever care for children and measure at least one of the three outcome classes.
For the quantitative synthesis, articles must report at least two statistical measures of the variables, shared through mean and standard deviation.
constraints: The review states the variables are "difficult to quantify", and some included programs used unvalidated questionnaires, which may restrict validity.
target_learners: nurses in hospital and community pediatric settings
target_learning_goals: knowledge of fever physiology and management
attitudes toward fever management practice
perceptions of control over febrile child management
examples: The review classified 41 articles by the variable they measured and pooled five program evaluations separately for knowledge, attitudes, and perceptions.

title: Do not use single non-cognitive factors in admissions decisions for rehabilitation science programs
description: The review concludes that no single non-cognitive factor was consistently related to clinical or academic performance across the 21 included studies, so evaluating a specific factor for admissions is not currently supported. It states there is "insufficient evidence currently to recommend the evaluation of a specific non-cognitive factor for admissions decisions." Educators should treat grit, self-efficacy, and stress as promising but unproven indicators.

constraints: All included studies were level 3 observational designs with low certainty, small samples, and few factors studied more than 4 times

article_title: Use of neuroimaging to measure neurocognitive engagement in health professions education: a scoping review.
citation: Toy, S., Huh, D. D., Materi, J., Nanavati, J., & Schwengel, D. A. (2022). Use of neuroimaging to measure neurocognitive engagement in health professions education: a scoping review. Medical Education Online, 27(1). https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2021.2016357
title: Information processing, neural efficiency, and dual processing theories frame interpretation of novice–expert brain activation differences
description: The review reports that included researchers adopted information processing, neural efficiency, and/or dual processing theory to inform their studies. These frameworks explain differences in brain activation between novices and experts: individuals are thought to better regulate working memory resources and "exhibit significantly less brain activation in the prefrontal cortex (PFC) while performing tasks within their area of expertise", and dual processing theory holds that with experience, slow analytical decision-making evolves into less-effortful intuitive judgements.
requirements: Studies must be designed to compare brain activation patterns across expertise levels or learning stages for the frameworks to be applied as the review describes
constraints: The review notes the current literature base does not provide clear markers for optimal PFC engagement levels, which may depend on context, task, and individual
target_learning_goals: neurocognitive engagement
clinical reasoning
psychomotor skill development
expertise development
examples: The review reports several clinical decision-making studies specifically examined whether dual processing theory could be verified by functional brain imaging

article_title: Evaluation of simulation models in neurosurgical training according to face, content, and construct validity: a systematic review.
citation: Chawla Shreya, Devi Sharmila, Calvachi Paola, Gormley William B., Rueda-Esteban Roberto. (2022). Evaluation of simulation models in neurosurgical training according to face, content, and construct validity: a systematic review. Acta Neurochirurgica. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00701-021-05003-x
title: Face, content, and construct validity framework for evaluating simulation models as educational tools
description: The review organises simulator evaluation around three validity types: "Face validity examines the realism of a simulator and difficulty level similarity in comparison to real training tasks, whilst content validity assesses the model's effectiveness during a specific skill training to improve participants' techniques". Construct validity is the objective method "that considers the ability of a simulator to differentiate levels of skill competence". The review applies this framework to cadaver, animal/placenta, synthetic, and VR models across four skull-base procedures, and names predictive validity as an ultimate, unassessed fourth type.
requirements: Subjective validity types (face and content) are evaluated by questionnaires; construct validity requires distinguishing participants at different levels of experience and expertise.
constraints: The review states there is no consensus on the gold standard to assess medical and surgical education outcomes, and predictive validity assessment is logistically impractical due to long-term follow-up requirements.
target_learning_goals: validating simulation-based training tools for surgical skill acquisition
examples: The review used this framework to synthesise 18 studies, finding all reported face validity, 11 content validity, and 6 construct validity.

title: Issenberg's features of high-fidelity medical simulations that lead to effective learning
description: The article invokes Issenberg and co-workers' account of the features needed for simulation to transform a principle into a lesson learned. The listed features include "provision of feedback, repetitive practice, curriculum integration, appropriate range of difficulty level, multiple learning strategies, simulation that captures clinical variation, a controlled environment, individualized learning, defined outcomes and simulator validity". The review uses this framework to interpret why simulation improved coronary anastomosis performance and to discuss curriculum design across the included trials.

time efficiency in task completion
examples: The review's included trials featured self-directed practice, instructional videos in three trials, and in-person education sessions in four trials

title: Case-based learning pedagogy as case-guided, teacher-prompted learning with a defined implementation sequence
description: CBL is a teaching model in which students analyse clinical cases and design treatment strategies while the teacher acts as "a prompter and guide to help students justify their analyses". The article describes an implementation sequence: "establishment of the case → case grouping and analysis → brainstorming → identifying instruction goals → new findings → exchanging results between groups → reaching learning consensus and integrating the consensus into clinical practice". It positions CBL as an element of competency-based education bridging theoretical and practical learning.
requirements: CBL curricula should be based on the sound fundamental knowledge background of the students
constraints: CBL had not been routine in Chinese dental education; the traditional teacher-centred model, variable school standards, scarce high-quality teaching teams and compressed course duration are stated inhibitory factors
target_learners: undergraduate and graduate dental students in China
target_learning_goals: clinical decision-making and comprehensive patient care
critical thinking
integration of preclinical knowledge into clinical application
examples: Included RCTs applied CBL across prosthodontics, endodontics, periodontology, orthodontics, oral medicine, general dentistry, oral anatomy and physiology, and oral histology and pathology

article_title: Research education and training for nurses and allied health professionals: a systematic scoping review.
citation: King, O., West, E., Lee, S., Glenister, K., Quilliam, C., Wong, S. A., & Beks, H. (2022). Research education and training for nurses and allied health professionals: a systematic scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03406-7
title: Modified Kirkpatrick educational outcomes typology as a multi-level framework for mapping research education outcomes
description: The review used Barr and colleagues' modified Kirkpatrick educational outcomes typology as its organising framework for classifying the outcomes that research education programs report. The typology "gives rise to the identification of outcome measures at multiple levels", reflecting that individuals, programs, organisational and other factors interact to produce various outcomes. The review mapped every included program's reported outcomes onto this typology, which exposed the concentration of evaluation at lower levels such as satisfaction and confidence.
requirements: Outcomes measured and reported in the papers must be mappable to the typology's levels or domains
constraints: The review notes complex interactions between individuals, programs, organisational and other factors make discernment between education interventions and other RCB strategy elements a fraught endeavour
target_learning_goals: research knowledge and skills
evidence-based practice capability
research capacity building
examples: Outcomes of the 68 included programs were mapped to the typology, revealing lower-level outcomes such as satisfaction, improved research knowledge and confidence dominated
