article_title: Research education and training for nurses and allied health professionals: a systematic scoping review.
citation: King, O., West, E., Lee, S., Glenister, K., Quilliam, C., Wong, S. A., & Beks, H. (2022). Research education and training for nurses and allied health professionals: a systematic scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03406-7
title: Evaluate research education programs rigorously and include longer-term, organisation-level outcomes, not only individual-level measures
description: The review concludes that evaluation of research education programs must be rigorous and, although programs target individuals, evaluation must extend to longer-term and broader organisation-level outcomes and impacts. The authors argue that "Examining this is critical to improving clinician-led health research and the translation of research into clinical practice". This principle responds directly to the review's finding that few programs measured organisational or practice outcomes and that evaluation methods were poorly described.
requirements: Evaluation must consider longer-term and broader organisation-level outcomes and impacts, not only individual satisfaction, knowledge and confidence
constraints: Discerning education interventions from other elements of multidimensional RCB strategies is a fraught endeavour, complicating attribution of organisation-level impacts
target_learners: program evaluators and health organisation leaders
target_learning_goals: research capacity building
clinician-led health research
translation of research into clinical practice
examples: The review mapped 68 programs' outcomes to the modified Kirkpatrick typology and found few evaluated with research milestones such as protocol completion, manuscript preparation, poster or conference presentation
key_sources: King, O., West, E., Lee, S., Glenister, K., Quilliam, C., Wong, S. A., & Beks, H. (2022). Research education and training for nurses and allied health professionals: a systematic scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03406-7

article_title: The frequency of assessment tools in arthroscopic training: a systematic review.
citation: Zhou Haixia, Xian Chengyao, Zhang Kai-Jun, Yang Zhouwen, Li Wei, Tian Jing. (2022). The frequency of assessment tools in arthroscopic training: a systematic review. Annals of Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1080/07853890.2022.2085317
title: Taxonomy of arthroscopic training assessment tools: objective metrics versus subjective scales
description: The review organizes arthroscopic skills assessment tools into two classes. Objective tools "depend on easy-to-measure metrics" such as completion time, instrument path length, hand movement, visual parameters and injuries, often generated by simulator built-in systems or external sensors. Subjective tools are scoring instruments with predetermined criteria — task-specific checklists and global rating scales (GRS) such as ASSET. The review uses this taxonomy to tabulate frequency and testing context across 28 studies and to argue for combined use.
requirements: Subjective scales require predetermined criteria to reduce subjectivity and make evaluation more reliable
GRS evaluation requires experts, with a specific training protocol for evaluators to improve inter-rater reliability
constraints: Motion-analysis parameters derived from simulators or external sensors are limited to simulated environments and not usable with real patients
GRS effectiveness in the clinical environment is not established; few studies evaluated validity and reliability of GRS in actual patients
target_learning_goals: arthroscopic technical skills such as diagnostic arthroscopy, triangulation and meniscectomy
examples: The review tabulated 28 studies by objective metric type and subjective tool type across simulator, cadaver, animal model and patient contexts (Tables 2–4).
key_sources: Zhou Haixia, Xian Chengyao, Zhang Kai-Jun, Yang Zhouwen, Li Wei, Tian Jing. (2022). The frequency of assessment tools in arthroscopic training: a systematic review. Annals of Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1080/07853890.2022.2085317

article_title: The frequency of assessment tools in arthroscopic training: a systematic review.
citation: Zhou Haixia, Xian Chengyao, Zhang Kai-Jun, Yang Zhouwen, Li Wei, Tian Jing. (2022). The frequency of assessment tools in arthroscopic training: a systematic review. Annals of Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1080/07853890.2022.2085317
title: Arthroscopic Surgical Skill Evaluation Tool (ASSET) global rating scale
description: ASSET is a global rating scale for arthroscopic surgical skills. The review describes that the "ASSET global rating scale consists of nine domains, including a weighted descriptor, 'additional complexity of procedure', as a control measure for special skills", with each domain discriminating novice, competent and expert levels on a 5-point Likert-type scale. It was the most frequently used GRS in the reviewed studies (10 studies) and, per the review, the only GRS demonstrating reliability in both simulated and clinical environments.
requirements: Experts are required for the evaluation process, and a specific training protocol is necessary for evaluators to improve inter-rater reliability
constraints: No validated criteria score exists for identifying minimum competency: ASSET did not have exactly the same criteria for identifying minimum competency in different studies
In operating-room use, rater agreement varied on individual ASSET domains, especially difficulty of procedure
target_learning_goals: arthroscopic surgical skill assessment across knee, shoulder, hip, ankle and wrist procedures
examples: Koehler et al. set a minimum score of 3 in each of eight domains for competence; Dwyer et al. instead used a criterion of an ASSET score of 24 or greater.
key_sources: Zhou Haixia, Xian Chengyao, Zhang Kai-Jun, Yang Zhouwen, Li Wei, Tian Jing. (2022). The frequency of assessment tools in arthroscopic training: a systematic review. Annals of Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1080/07853890.2022.2085317

article_title: The frequency of assessment tools in arthroscopic training: a systematic review.
citation: Zhou Haixia, Xian Chengyao, Zhang Kai-Jun, Yang Zhouwen, Li Wei, Tian Jing. (2022). The frequency of assessment tools in arthroscopic training: a systematic review. Annals of Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1080/07853890.2022.2085317
title: Combine subjective and objective assessment tools when evaluating arthroscopic skills training
description: The review recommends that assessment of arthroscopic skill training should not rely on a single tool class. Because objective metrics cannot identify weaknesses in specific skills and subjective scales have context limits, the authors conclude that "combined use of subjective and objective assessment tools can be applied to more situations and skills and can be the optimal way for assessment." Most reviewed studies (60.7%) already combined the two.
requirements: Both tool types must be available: objective metrics for measurable performance and GRS or checklists for rated performance
constraints: Heterogeneity in study designs, methodology and outcome measures precluded quantitative statistical analysis, and no included study directly compared objective with subjective measures
Evidence for other joints besides knee and shoulder was insufficient
target_learning_goals: arthroscopic technical skills, from basic diagnostic arthroscopy to advanced procedures such as meniscectomy
examples: Studies such as Waterman et al. used simulator completion time and probe distance alongside a 14-point diagnostic arthroscopy checklist and ASSET for patient performance.
key_sources: Zhou Haixia, Xian Chengyao, Zhang Kai-Jun, Yang Zhouwen, Li Wei, Tian Jing. (2022). The frequency of assessment tools in arthroscopic training: a systematic review. Annals of Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1080/07853890.2022.2085317

article_title: GENESISS 2-Generating Standards for In-Situ Simulation project: a systematic mapping review.
citation: Evans Kerry, Woodruff Jenny, Cowley Alison, Bramley Louise, Miles Giulia, Ross Alastair, Cooper Joanne, Baxendale Bryn. (2022). GENESISS 2—Generating Standards for In-Situ Simulation project: a systematic mapping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03401-y
title: Conceptual model of in-situ simulation in healthcare proposing four main ISS functions
description: The GENESISS project's phase-one conceptual model of ISS in healthcare proposes four main ISS functions, depicted in Figure 1 of this review. The model underpins the review's aim to develop evidence-based standards for healthcare professionals, educators and managers implementing ISS interventions in clinical practice. The review states that "A conceptual model of ISS was developed in phase one [33] which proposed four main ISS functions (Fig. 1)", and the mapping review's four evidence categories reflect these functions.
requirements: ISS terms and concepts require standardisation and integrated models of learning are required to provide a more comprehensive and cohesive strategic approach, as the review states
constraints: The model was developed in phase one of the GENESISS project and this article reports its use to frame a mapping review, not a direct empirical validation of the model
target_learning_goals: teamwork and non-technical skills
clinical skills and patient safety
system readiness and safety culture
examples: The review organised 69 included studies into categories reflecting the model's functions: assessment, system readiness and safety cultures, clinical skills and outcomes, and non-technical skills and confidence
key_sources: Evans Kerry, Woodruff Jenny, Cowley Alison, Bramley Louise, Miles Giulia, Ross Alastair, Cooper Joanne, Baxendale Bryn. (2022). GENESISS 2—Generating Standards for In-Situ Simulation project: a systematic mapping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03401-y

article_title: GENESISS 2-Generating Standards for In-Situ Simulation project: a systematic mapping review.
citation: Evans Kerry, Woodruff Jenny, Cowley Alison, Bramley Louise, Miles Giulia, Ross Alastair, Cooper Joanne, Baxendale Bryn. (2022). GENESISS 2—Generating Standards for In-Situ Simulation project: a systematic mapping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03401-y
title: In-situ simulation conducted in the actual clinical environment with real equipment and teams enables realism, equipment testing, safe transitions to new facilities and wider team participation
description: Across the included studies, the review summarises recurring benefits of conducting simulation in the real clinical setting rather than off-site. Teams perform with actual equipment and resources, equipment can be located and tested, transitions to new facilities are facilitated safely, and more team members can participate compared with off-site training. The review's Table 8 lists "Realism: Real setting enabling teams to perform with actual equipment and resources" among the benefits reported across all included studies.
requirements: ISS interventions are conducted in patient care settings rather than simulation laboratories or training suites, per the review's inclusion criteria
constraints: The review also reports limitations including high cancellation rate in high acuity areas, fidelity issues in key components of task completion, and possibility of training effect for pre-announced ISS
target_learning_goals: problem solving within real dynamic clinical settings
multidisciplinary team working
learning into practice
examples: Studies used ISS to test electronic health records in the ICU before go-live and to evaluate a new ED's capacity for emergent resuscitative processes while time remained for corrective actions
key_sources: Evans Kerry, Woodruff Jenny, Cowley Alison, Bramley Louise, Miles Giulia, Ross Alastair, Cooper Joanne, Baxendale Bryn. (2022). GENESISS 2—Generating Standards for In-Situ Simulation project: a systematic mapping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03401-y

article_title: The impact of virtual reality simulation training on operative performance in laparoscopic cholecystectomy: meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials.
citation: Humm Gemma; Mohan Helen Peter; Fleming Christina; Harries Rhiannon; Wood Christopher; Dawas Khaled; Stoyanov Danail; Lovat Laurence B. (2022). The impact of virtual reality simulation training on operative performance in laparoscopic cholecystectomy: meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials. BJS Open. https://doi.org/10.1093/bjsopen/zrac086
title: OSATS and GOALS global rating scales for assessing operative performance in laparoscopic cholecystectomy
description: The article uses two validated global rating scores as primary outcome measures: the Objective Structured Assessment of Technical Skill (OSATS) and the Global Operative Assessment of Laparoscopic Skills (GOALS). OSATS "was originally validated for direct observation in open surgery, and later validated in laparoscopic cholecystectomy", while GOALS "was developed and validated to assess the specific skilled required for laparoscopic surgery, including direct and delayed observation". GOALS domains include depth perception, bimanual dexterity, efficiency and tissue handling, with autonomy in direct observation. Both use continuous scales with minimum 1 and maximum 5 per category.
requirements: Blinded assessment; the article notes most studies used delayed video assessment of more than one assessor blinded to the intervention, giving low risk of detection bias
constraints: GOALS domain scores showed substantial heterogeneity across studies (I2 up to 83 per cent) in the pooled analyses
target_learners: Junior surgical trainees performing laparoscopic cholecystectomy
target_learning_goals: Objective assessment of technical surgical skill
examples: The meta-analyses pooled total OSATS, total GOALS, individual GOALS domains and time to completion of task as continuous outcomes
key_sources: Humm Gemma; Mohan Helen Peter; Fleming Christina; Harries Rhiannon; Wood Christopher; Dawas Khaled; Stoyanov Danail; Lovat Laurence B. (2022). The impact of virtual reality simulation training on operative performance in laparoscopic cholecystectomy: meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials. BJS Open. https://doi.org/10.1093/bjsopen/zrac086

article_title: Extended Reality in Neurosurgical Education: A Systematic Review.
citation: Iop A., El-Hajj V.G., Gharios M., de Giorgio A., Monetti F.M., Edström E., Elmi-Terander A., Romero M. (2022). Extended Reality in Neurosurgical Education: A Systematic Review. Sensors. https://doi.org/10.3390/s22166067
title: UP/UX metric framework for evaluating XR educational simulations
description: The review defines user performance (UP) as "a set of metrics that quantifies the efficiency and effectiveness of a surgical simulation carried out on an XR system", including accuracy, precision, surgical outcome, speed, and attempts per user. User experience (UX) accounts for how subjects perceive events, interactions, and feedback, organized into ten categories: usefulness, self-assessment, haptic interaction, ease of use, system feedback, comfort, time requirements, engagement, immersiveness, and realism. The framework is used to group indicators across the 31 included studies and to detect which metrics are shared versus study-specific.
requirements: Metrics must be classifiable as objective UP measures or subjective UX measures to allow grouping across studies
constraints: The review found UP metrics vary by procedure and UX questionnaires were mostly custom, hindering cross-study comparison
target_learning_goals: procedural knowledge and surgical skill acquisition in cranial neurosurgery
examples: Tumor resection studies grouped UP metrics into three tiers: percentage of tumor resected and healthy tissue volume (tier 1), time and instrument path length (tier 2), and kinematic force metrics (tier 3)
key_sources: Iop A., El-Hajj V.G., Gharios M., de Giorgio A., Monetti F.M., Edström E., Elmi-Terander A., Romero M. (2022). Extended Reality in Neurosurgical Education: A Systematic Review. Sensors. https://doi.org/10.3390/s22166067

article_title: Hot topics and frontier evolution in college flipped classrooms based on mapping knowledge domains.
citation: Sun Liyan, Yang Li, Wang Xue, Zhu Junqi, Zhang Xuesen. (2022). Hot topics and frontier evolution in college flipped classrooms based on mapping knowledge domains. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2022.950106
title: Three-phase flipped classroom teaching model: preparation before class, classroom activities, consolidation after class
description: The article synthesizes its keyword co-occurrence clusters into a three-topic structure and a flow chart of the flipped classroom teaching model (Figure 7): "this study identified three hot topics, namely, preparation before class, classroom activities and consolidation after class." Pre-class work centers on teacher-provided videos and materials via a learning management system; in-class work centers on active, student-centered collaborative activities; after-class work centers on tests, diversified assignments, and evaluation and redesign.
requirements: Teachers must provide pre-class learning materials through a learning management system and produce quality teaching videos
After-class evaluation and feedback collection to redesign teaching strategies
constraints: The topics are derived from keyword co-occurrence in a 2013–2021 Web of Science corpus of higher-education studies, not from a direct intervention test
target_learning_goals: autonomous learning
active learning
knowledge consolidation and transfer
examples: The article's Figure 7 summarizes the flipped classroom teaching mode process flow chart built from the three hot topics
key_sources: Sun Liyan, Yang Li, Wang Xue, Zhu Junqi, Zhang Xuesen. (2022). Hot topics and frontier evolution in college flipped classrooms based on mapping knowledge domains. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2022.950106

article_title: Hot topics and frontier evolution in college flipped classrooms based on mapping knowledge domains.
citation: Sun Liyan, Yang Li, Wang Xue, Zhu Junqi, Zhang Xuesen. (2022). Hot topics and frontier evolution in college flipped classrooms based on mapping knowledge domains. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2022.950106
title: Three-period frontier evolution of flipped-classroom research: exploration, adaptation, and growth periods
description: Using keyword time zone analysis (Figure 8), the article organizes the field's evolution into three phases: "the research frontier is divided into exploring period, adaptation period, and growth period." The exploration period (before 2015) covers the transition from traditional lectures, with teacher role change and high time investment; the adaptation period (2016–2018) centers on online learning, motivation, and critical thinking as technology costs fell; the growth period (2019–2021) centers on educational technology, control systems, and games, accelerated by COVID-19-driven online teaching.
requirements: Keyword starting-time data in CiteSpace to identify frontier periods
constraints: Period boundaries are the article's own classification of a Web of Science higher-education corpus from 2013 to 2021
target_learning_goals: understanding the research evolution of flipped-classroom pedagogy
examples: Keywords of the exploration period included student, classroom, lecture, software, engagement, and performance; the growth period added control system, learning system, and game
key_sources: Sun Liyan, Yang Li, Wang Xue, Zhu Junqi, Zhang Xuesen. (2022). Hot topics and frontier evolution in college flipped classrooms based on mapping knowledge domains. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2022.950106

article_title: A Systematic Review of Simulation-Based Training in Vascular Surgery.
citation: Haiser Alexander, Aydin Abdullatif, Kunduzi Basir, Ahmed Kamran, Dasgupta Prokar. (2022). A Systematic Review of Simulation-Based Training in Vascular Surgery. The Journal of Surgical Research. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jss.2022.05.009
title: Messick's modern validity framework with Beckman ratings and McGaghie-style translational outcomes (LoE 1-5) for evaluating surgical simulators
description: The review applies a two-part evaluation framework to vascular surgery simulators. Validity evidence is judged against Messick's five sources — content, response process, internal structure, relations to other variables, and consequences — each rated 0-2 with Beckman's scale, where 2 means "Data strongly supports the source of validity". Effectiveness is scored with an adapted McGaghie translational outcomes hierarchy from LoE 1 (trainee satisfaction) to LoE 5 (collateral effects such as "Cost saving; skill retention"). The authors argue modern unitary validity definitions are "vital in the in-depth assessment of simulators" and recommend the framework as standard practice.
requirements: Studies must report data for each validity source rather than discussion alone, since Beckman's rating 0 applies when there is discussion but no data presented.
Assessment of potential author bias and selective outcome reporting at study level.
constraints: The review found the framework underused: only 1.3% of studies featured all five validity criteria, and 25% used outdated conventional definitions such as face validity.
target_learning_goals: validity evidence for surgical skill assessment
translational effectiveness of simulation-based training
examples: The review rated the Inanimate OAR bench simulator 2/2 for content, response processes, internal structure, and consequences, and awarded LoE 2/5 for decreased simulated procedure time and supervisor interference.
key_sources: Haiser Alexander, Aydin Abdullatif, Kunduzi Basir, Ahmed Kamran, Dasgupta Prokar. (2022). A Systematic Review of Simulation-Based Training in Vascular Surgery. The Journal of Surgical Research. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jss.2022.05.009

article_title: Advances in e-learning in undergraduate clinical medicine: a systematic review.
citation: Delungahawatta T., Dunne S. S., Hyde S., Halpenny L., McGrath D., O'Regan A., Dunne C. P. (2022). Advances in e-learning in undergraduate clinical medicine: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03773-1
title: Connectivism as the learning-theoretic framing for e-learning in medical education
description: The review frames e-learning as "a pedagogical approach supported by the principles of connectivism learning theory", in which knowledge is "a fluid entity circulated through technology enabled networks". Learners filter information, develop perspectives, log into networks to share understanding, and repeat the cycle. The review uses this framework to analyse how individual e-learning elements collectively affect learning, and notes only 7 of 25 higher-impact studies described theoretical underpinnings.
requirements: Effective e-learning strategies should consider potential learning challenges encountered by the e-learner, and the roles of e-learner, e-teacher and host institution should be defined
constraints: Only 7 of 25 higher-impact reviewed studies (28%) described theoretical underpinnings; the review calls for future work to reference theoretical principles
target_learners: undergraduate medical students in clinical medicine
target_learning_goals: knowledge and skill acquisition in clinical medicine disciplines
examples: The review applied connectivism in its data extraction, examining how and when to use e-learning in undergraduate clinical medical education
key_sources: Delungahawatta T., Dunne S. S., Hyde S., Halpenny L., McGrath D., O'Regan A., Dunne C. P. (2022). Advances in e-learning in undergraduate clinical medicine: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03773-1

article_title: Advances in e-learning in undergraduate clinical medicine: a systematic review.
citation: Delungahawatta T., Dunne S. S., Hyde S., Halpenny L., McGrath D., O'Regan A., Dunne C. P. (2022). Advances in e-learning in undergraduate clinical medicine: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03773-1
title: Effective e-learning interventions combine interactivity, built-in assessment, asynchronous access and multimedia
description: The review identifies a recurring design pattern in effective undergraduate clinical medicine e-learning: interactive software, active-learning promotion such as built-in quizzes following cases, asynchronous use, multimedia platforms (slideshows, videos, images), ease of use and adaptability. Nineteen interventions had a built-in assessment, mostly multiple-choice questions, to evaluate whether learning improvement had taken place.
requirements: Quality assurance should be considered at the planning stage and built into e-learning interventions
constraints: Justification for the chosen assessment strategy was included in only two of the reviewed studies
target_learners: undergraduate medical students in clinical medicine
target_learning_goals: knowledge acquisition, skills development, and exam preparation in clinical disciplines
examples: Reviewed interventions enabled just-in-time learning through timely access to facts, revision aid use, and flipped-classroom designs where post-e-lecture sessions become interactive
key_sources: Delungahawatta T., Dunne S. S., Hyde S., Halpenny L., McGrath D., O'Regan A., Dunne C. P. (2022). Advances in e-learning in undergraduate clinical medicine: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03773-1

article_title: The effects of obstetric emergency team training on patient outcome: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
citation: Brogaard L, Glerup Lauridsen K, Løfgren B, et al. (2022). The effects of obstetric emergency team training on patient outcome: A systematic review and meta‐analysis. Acta Obstet Gynecol Scand. https://doi.org/10.1111/aogs.14263
title: Train entire labor and delivery units locally with in situ multiprofessional simulation-based team training
description: The review concludes that simulation-based team training works best when delivered locally in the actual care environment with all professional groups participating together. The authors state that "Studies with in situ multiprofessional simulation‐based training demonstrated the best effect" and that "local (in situ) multiprofessional training for all staff members is the most beneficial with regards to improving patient outcomes." Most included studies trained staff annually in one-day programs in the Labor and Delivery Unit.
requirements: Training should include all staff members of the Labor and Delivery Unit rather than a partial subset
constraints: None of the two RCTs demonstrated the same effect as cohort studies; only about 50% of studies used pre-defined guidelines or a previously described program; analysis of optimal training frequency was not possible because no studies used interventions more frequently than yearly
target_learners: Multiprofessional obstetric emergency teams in Labor and Delivery Units in high-resource settings
target_learning_goals: Managing obstetric emergencies such as shoulder dystocia, postpartum hemorrhage, umbilical cord prolapse, and emergency cesarean section
examples: The majority of included studies trained delivery ward staff in situ annually with one-day programs, e.g. PROMPT training in England and Australia; only a few trained in simulation centers
key_sources: Brogaard L, Glerup Lauridsen K, Løfgren B, et al. (2022). The effects of obstetric emergency team training on patient outcome: A systematic review and meta‐analysis. Acta Obstet Gynecol Scand. https://doi.org/10.1111/aogs.14263

article_title: Simulation-Based Education in Trauma Management: A Scoping Review.
citation: Larraga-García, B., Quintana-Díaz, M., & Gutiérrez, Á. (2022). Simulation-Based Education in Trauma Management: A Scoping Review. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health, 19(20). https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph192013546
title: Fidelity-based classification of clinical simulators (low, medium, high)
description: The review organizes clinical simulators by fidelity, defined as "the simulated model's relation to its closeness to reality being the main classification". Low-fidelity simulators are anatomical representations for simple tasks and basic motor skills; medium-fidelity simulators integrate low-complexity software to manipulate physiological variables for decision-making assessment; high-fidelity simulators are life-size mannequins with mechanical devices and computer technology for advanced techniques and critical situations. The review uses this taxonomy to characterize the simulation methods of the included trauma training studies.
requirements: Simulation methods should be matched to the skills to be trained, as the review states one method can be better than another depending on the skills targeted
constraints: The review reports that, per cited systematic reviews and a randomized trial, high-fidelity simulators show no important long-term advantage over low-fidelity ones for knowledge and skill improvement
target_learning_goals: trauma management technical skills
non-technical skills such as communication, leadership and decision making
examples: The review classified the 35 included studies' simulation methods using this fidelity framework, finding high-fidelity mannequins in 51.4% of courses
key_sources: Larraga-García, B., Quintana-Díaz, M., & Gutiérrez, Á. (2022). Simulation-Based Education in Trauma Management: A Scoping Review. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health, 19(20). https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph192013546

article_title: Comparison of ultrasonography learning between distance teaching and traditional methodology. An educational systematic review.
citation: Duarte ML, dos Santos LR, Iared W, Peccin MS. (2022). Comparison of ultrasonography learning between distance teaching and traditional methodology. An educational systematic review. São Paulo Medical Journal. https://doi.org/10.1590/1516-3180.2021.1047.R.19052022
title: Sixteen-study comparative evidence base on distance versus traditional ultrasonography teaching
description: The evidence base assembled by this systematic review: after screening 5,048 records and evaluating 61 in full, the reviewers included 16 studies of sufficient methodological quality comparing traditional and distance teaching of ultrasonography. Eleven studies evaluated doctors, residents or medical students, one evaluated nurses, and four evaluated physical therapy students in Spain. The review states that "from these, 16 presented sufficient methodological quality for their inclusion", and summarizes each study's design, learners, examination type, intervention and Kirkpatrick level in Table 2.
requirements: Studies had to compare teaching of ultrasonography for healthcare professionals between traditional methods and electronic means through distance-learning, e-learning, m-learning or web-based learning
constraints: One study (Socransky et al.) was excluded due to loss to follow-up of over 50% of initial participants; five studies involved no practical evaluation and relied only on questionnaires
target_learning_goals: improved ultrasound skills to achieve an accurate diagnosis
examples: Included studies taught FAST ultrasound, thoracic structures, pneumothorax, point-of-care ultrasound, musculoskeletal structures, and venous or arterial access procedures
key_sources: Duarte ML, dos Santos LR, Iared W, Peccin MS. (2022). Comparison of ultrasonography learning between distance teaching and traditional methodology. An educational systematic review. São Paulo Medical Journal. https://doi.org/10.1590/1516-3180.2021.1047.R.19052022

article_title: The effectiveness of problem based learning in improving critical thinking, problem-solving and self-directed learning in first-year medical students: A meta-analysis.
citation: Manuaba Ida Bagus Amertha Putra, No Yi, Wu Chien-Chih. (2022). The effectiveness of problem based learning in improving critical thinking, problem-solving and self-directed learning in first-year medical students: A meta-analysis. PLOS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0277339
title: PBL's three main learning objectives: deep content learning, problem analysis and solution development, and self-directed learning
description: The article frames problem-based learning as an approach in which students "learn actively using case-based peer-to-peer teaching" under a facilitator's guidance, aiming to integrate learned knowledge rather than implant it. It names "three main learning objectives": applying deep content learning, applying problem analysis skills to develop solutions, and applying self-directed learning to adapt learning styles. This framework organizes the three outcome domains the meta-analysis evaluates.
requirements: Implementation requires students to formulate their own learning goals from PBL scenarios, solve problems via literature and internet, and actively participate in group discussions under facilitator guidance
constraints: The article notes students familiar with teacher-centered methods tend to face difficulty applying the student-centered PBL method in higher education
target_learning_goals: critical thinking/knowledge
problem-solving
self-directed learning
examples: The meta-analysis evaluated each of the three objectives as a separate pooled outcome across the seven included studies
key_sources: Manuaba Ida Bagus Amertha Putra, No Yi, Wu Chien-Chih. (2022). The effectiveness of problem based learning in improving critical thinking, problem-solving and self-directed learning in first-year medical students: A meta-analysis. PLOS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0277339

article_title: Effectiveness of school-based CPR training among adolescents to enhance knowledge and skills in CPR: A systematic review.
citation: Zenani, N.E., Bello, B., Molekodi, M., & Useh, U., 2022, 'Effectiveness of school-based CPR training among adolescents to enhance knowledge and skills in CPR: A systematic review', Curationis 45(1), a2325. https://doi.org/10.4102/curationis.v45i1.2325
title: Chain of survival as the framework linking bystander CPR training to out-of-hospital cardiac arrest survival
description: The review frames school-based CPR training through the chain of survival: early recognition of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, activating the emergency response, early CPR with chest compressions, rapid defibrillation, and post-CPR care. Because these "critical linked interventions mostly rely on a layperson, who is often the first on the scene", training adolescents in school positions them to act promptly and to serve as CPR multipliers passing skills to family and friends.
requirements: Laypersons trained in the chain of survival links must be present at the scene of cardiac arrest
constraints: The framework is presented in the review's introduction as background rationale, not tested within the review itself
target_learning_goals: recognising cardiac arrest
activating emergency response
performing early CPR with chest compressions
examples: The review describes a pupil trained in CPR saving another pupil on the soccer field when a teacher is absent, acting according to the chain of survival links
key_sources: Zenani, N.E., Bello, B., Molekodi, M., & Useh, U., 2022, 'Effectiveness of school-based CPR training among adolescents to enhance knowledge and skills in CPR: A systematic review', Curationis 45(1), a2325. https://doi.org/10.4102/curationis.v45i1.2325

article_title: Performance effects of simulation training for medical students - a systematic review.
citation: McInerney Niall, Nally D., Khan M.F., Heneghan H., Cahill R.A. (2022). Performance effects of simulation training for medical students – a systematic review. GMS Journal for Medical Education. https://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2022-39/zma001572.shtml
title: Simulation-based medical education (SBME) as an adjunct to traditional undergraduate medical curricula
description: SBME uses a "device that presents a simulated patient (or part of a patient) that interacts appropriately with the actions taken by the simulation participant", allowing students to learn in a safe, controlled and standardised environment. Methods reviewed include artificial patient models such as SimMan (median 17.5 minutes per session) and standardized patients (median 82.5 minutes per session). The review validates SBME as an adjunct to the traditional didactic lecture-based curriculum for undergraduate medical students.

physical examination
clinical knowledge
management of emergency scenarios

article_title: Medical students’ satisfaction level with e-learning during the COVID-19 pandemic and its related factors: a systematic review.
citation: Tabatabaeichehr Mahbubeh, Babaei Samane, Dartomi Mahdieh, Alesheikh Peiman, Tabatabaee Amir, Mortazavi Hamed, Khoshgoftar Zohreh. (2022). Journal of Educational Evaluation for Health Professions. https://doi.org/10.3352/jeehp.2022.19.37
title: Corpus of 24 cross-sectional studies of medical students' e-learning satisfaction appraised with the AXIS tool
description: The review assembled a corpus of 24 cross-sectional studies enrolling 15,473 medical science students, mean age 20.84±2.06 years, 58.23% women, 73.45% studying clinical medicine, drawn from 14 countries. Quality was appraised with the AXIS tool, a 20-item instrument rating report quality, study design quality, and possible biases at three levels. The review reports that "21 studies ... were of high quality, 2 studies ... were of fair quality, and 1 study ... was of low quality."
requirements: Studies had to be cross-sectional designs focused on medical students' satisfaction with e-learning and related factors; letters, case reports, conference proceedings, experiments, qualitative designs, and reviews were excluded
constraints: Gray literature was not included; only English and Persian publications were searched
target_learners: medical science students, primarily undergraduate clinical medicine students
target_learning_goals: satisfaction with e-learning during the COVID-19 pandemic
examples: Searches of Scopus, PubMed, Web of Science, Iranmedex, and the Scientific Information Database yielded 3,554 studies, of which 24 remained after exclusions; satisfaction questionnaires were researcher-created in 23 studies and one used the reduced Students' Evaluation of Educational Quality.

article_title: Learning outcomes for communication skills across the health professions: a systematic literature review and qualitative synthesis.
citation: Denniston C, Molloy E, Nestel D, Woodward-Kron R, Keating JL. (2017). Learning outcomes for communication skills across the health professions: a systematic literature review and qualitative synthesis. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2016-014570
title: Four-domain taxonomy of communication skills learning outcomes: knowledge, content, process and perceptual skills
description: The review organises its final 205 learning outcomes into four themes, three of which derive from the seminal work of Kurtz, Silverman and Draper, with the research group adding a fourth theme, knowledge. Knowledge is defined as "An individual's understanding of information through which incoming data and/or experiences are processed and recorded"; content as what is communicated; process as how one communicates; and perceptual as awareness of self and others and how that impacts communication. The taxonomy structures the synthesised outcome list presented for educational design across the health professions.
requirements: Learning outcomes assigned to a theme must be judged against the theme definitions and the decision guide used in the qualitative synthesis
constraints: The authors present the list as a foundation for others to interpret rather than a prescriptive list, aligned with a social constructionist perspective
target_learners: health professionals across professions and levels of education, prequalification and postqualification
target_learning_goals: communication skills learning outcomes spanning knowledge, content, process and perceptual skills
examples: The final list presents content-domain outcomes in the chronological sequence of a healthcare interaction for ease of representation

article_title: Effect of classroom-based physical activity interventions on academic and physical activity outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
citation: Watson Amanda, Timperio Anna, Brown Helen, Best Keren, Hesketh Kylie D. (2017). Effect of classroom-based physical activity interventions on academic and physical activity outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis. The International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12966-017-0569-9
title: Taxonomy of classroom-based physical activity forms and academic-related outcome categories
description: The review organises classroom-based physical activity into three forms — active breaks, curriculum-focussed active breaks, and physically active lessons — defined as "physical activity carried out during regular class time", distinct from recess or lunch breaks. Academic-related outcomes are grouped into three categories: classroom behaviour (on-task and off-task behaviour), cognitive function (e.g. executive function), and academic achievement (standardised tests, progress monitoring tools, grades, perceived competence). This taxonomy structures the review's search, data extraction, meta-analysis grouping and conclusions.

constraints: The review notes there are no set definitions for classroom-based physical activity; the definitions were provided to maintain consistency and clarity

cognitive function
academic achievement

article_title: Longitudinal Associations Between Childhood Obesity and Academic Achievement: Systematic Review with Focus Group Data.
citation: Martin A, Booth JN, McGeown S, Niven A, Sproule J, Saunders DH, Reilly JJ. (2017). Longitudinal Associations Between Childhood Obesity and Academic Achievement: Systematic Review with Focus Group Data. Current Obesity Reports, 6(3), 297–313. https://doi.org/10.1007/s13679-017-0272-9
title: Physical Education should be a positive, supportive experience for children and adolescents with obesity
description: The review concludes that PE environments can be sites of weight-related teasing and perceived teacher bias for adolescents with obesity, and recommends that "Physical Education should be a positive experience for children and adolescents with obesity". This includes PE teachers understanding motivation processes and delivering educational experiences that teach the values and benefits of physical activity for sustained participation. The principle addresses the psychosocial barriers that may undermine both wellbeing and engagement in physical activity among learners with obesity.
requirements: PE teachers should understand the complexity of motivation processes to deliver positive PE experiences for adolescents with obesity
constraints: Evidence for teacher bias towards obese children is empirically inconsistent, per the review
target_learning_goals: physical literacy
psychosocial wellbeing in PE
examples: Focus group participants reported feeling ignored and excluded from activities by PE teachers, and classroom teachers were perceived as non-judgmental towards increased body weight

article_title: Longitudinal Associations Between Childhood Obesity and Academic Achievement: Systematic Review with Focus Group Data.
citation: Martin A, Booth JN, McGeown S, Niven A, Sproule J, Saunders DH, Reilly JJ. (2017). Longitudinal Associations Between Childhood Obesity and Academic Achievement: Systematic Review with Focus Group Data. Current Obesity Reports, 6(3), 297–313. https://doi.org/10.1007/s13679-017-0272-9
title: Executive function development as an explanation for age- and subject-specific obesity–achievement associations
description: The review proposes that obesity-related deficits in academic achievement may manifest only during adolescence because cognitive abilities related to academic achievement, social functioning and emotional control (executive functions such as reasoning, working memory, cognitive flexibility and inhibition) "develop steeply from the age of 6 years, develop throughout adolescence and reach adult levels at about age 20". Puberty-related neural reorganisation in the prefrontal cortex may explain why younger children show no association. The theory also proposes that non-verbal maths tasks invoke brain regions (prefrontal cortex, hippocampus) associated with obesity and energy-balance behaviours, potentially explaining why obesity is negatively associated with maths but not reading/language achievement.
requirements: Longitudinal data spanning the developmental period from childhood through adolescence
constraints: Proposed as a plausible explanation; the review calls for further research to understand these mechanisms
target_learning_goals: maths achievement
cognitive development
examples: The review cites evidence that working memory, reasoning, inhibition and cognitive flexibility are strongly associated with maths achievement and have been shown to be impaired in children and adolescents with obesity

article_title: The Effect of Problem-Based Learning on Improvement of the Medical Educational Environment: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
citation: Qin Yongjie, Wang Yungui, Floden Robert E. (2016). The Effect of Problem-Based Learning on Improvement of the Medical Educational Environment: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Medical Principles and Practice. https://doi.org/10.1159/000449036
title: Dundee Ready Education Environment Measure (DREEM)
description: DREEM is a standardized instrument for evaluating the medical educational environment, developed at Dundee University Medical School in 1997 by an international Delphi panel. It contains "50 items" scored 0–4 on a 5-point scale, with nine negative items reverse-scored, so higher scores indicate a more positive evaluation; the maximum score of 200 represents an ideal environment. It includes five subscales covering perceptions of learning, teachers, academic self-perceptions, atmosphere, and social self-perceptions, and has been translated into at least nine languages. This review used DREEM as the sole outcome measure.
requirements: Reports mean difference and standard deviation of DREEM scores for intervention and control groups
constraints: Used here only for medical/nursing educational environments
target_learning_goals: perceptions of the medical educational environment
examples: All six included RCTs measured the educational environment with DREEM after the PBL or LBL intervention

article_title: The Effect of Problem-Based Learning on Improvement of the Medical Educational Environment: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
citation: Qin Yongjie, Wang Yungui, Floden Robert E. (2016). The Effect of Problem-Based Learning on Improvement of the Medical Educational Environment: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Medical Principles and Practice. https://doi.org/10.1159/000449036
title: PBL small-group tutorial structure with facilitator tutor and five-step process
description: The article describes problem-based learning as "a nontraditional, active, inductive, student-centered approach to learning" that develops self-learning, collaboration, problem solving and critical thinking. Its distinguishing feature is small tutorial groups of 6–8 students with a tutor acting as facilitator or guide rather than expert or purveyor of knowledge. The PBL process follows five basic steps: problem analysis, establishment of learning objectives, collection of information, summarizing, and reflection. In the included trials, PBL was implemented in groups of 4–6 students with mentors or 15-student groups with scenarios.
requirements: Small tutorial groups with a tutor facilitating rather than lecturing
A problem or scenario as the trigger for learning
constraints: Contrasted throughout with traditional lecture-based learning characterized by large class sizes and instructor-driven delivery
target_learning_goals: self-learning
collaboration
problem solving
critical thinking
examples: In one included study, PBL groups of 4–6 students with one mentor followed a PBL process with one scenario every 2 weeks over 3 months

article_title: Descriptors for unprofessional behaviours of medical students: a systematic review and categorisation.
citation: Mak-van der Vossen M, van Mook W, van der Burgt S, Kors J, Ket JCF, Croiset G, Kusurkar R. (2017). Descriptors for unprofessional behaviours of medical students: a systematic review and categorisation. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-017-0997-x
title: Four-theme taxonomy of unprofessional behaviours of medical students
description: The review organises real-life unprofessional behaviours of undergraduate medical students into four behavioural themes. The included articles yielded "205 different descriptions of unprofessional behaviours, which were coded into 30 different descriptors, and subsequently classified into four behavioural themes: failure to engage, dishonest behaviour, disrespectful behaviour, and poor self-awareness." Each theme is defined in behavioural terms: failure to engage is "insufficiently handling one's tasks", dishonest behaviour covers "cheating, lying, plagiarism and not obeying rules and regulations", disrespectful behaviour "has a negative effect on other people", and poor self-awareness is "inappropriately handling one's own performance". The framework is offered as a shared vocabulary for educators documenting lapses.
requirements: Behaviours must be witnessed by stakeholders or admitted by students themselves, within the educational context, to fall under the framework
constraints: Behaviours are specific to students in undergraduate education and not all guideline domains for physicians were found
What is seen as unprofessional is dependent on time and cultural context
target_learners: preclinical and clinical undergraduate medical students
target_learning_goals: professionalism
recognition and documentation of unprofessional behaviour
examples: The review mapped its findings to the GMC's domains of concern for medical students, finding many similarities plus some new descriptors

citation: Mak-van der Vossen M, van Mook W, van der Burgt S, Kors J, Ket JCF, Croiset G, Kusurkar R. (2017). Descriptors for unprofessional behaviours of medical students: a systematic review and categorisation. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-017-0997-x
title: Give educators a common language of behaviour descriptors so unprofessional behaviour is acknowledged and reported
description: The review proposes its framework of 30 descriptors in four themes as a shared vocabulary for medical educators. It argues that a common understanding among educators about denominating unprofessional behaviours could lead to greater consistency in observing, describing and evaluating them, and that the list "might facilitate teachers to see and report unprofessional behaviours, and thus help to solve the problem of 'failure to fail'". Explicitly denominating behaviour serves two goals: creating a culture in which unprofessional behaviour is acknowledged, and targeting students who need extra guidance.
requirements: Educators conduct a conversation with the student about observed behaviours rather than only giving a fail
constraints: Only giving a fail is not enough; the behaviour list indicates which behaviours should prompt a discussion, aiming for contextual interpretation
target_learners: preclinical and clinical undergraduate medical students
target_learning_goals: professionalism
timely identification and remediation of unprofessional behaviour
examples: The review's Table 1 lists implications: a common language facilitates acknowledgment and discussion among teachers and students, and the behaviour list facilitates teachers to see and report unprofessional behaviours

title: Four-category coding framework for assessing the real-world authenticity of virtual patient collections
description: The article develops a coding framework with four main categories — patient data, patient representation, diagnoses, and setting — to analyze how well a virtual patient collection represents a relevant patient population and how patients are represented as persons. Codes cover sex, age, sexual orientation, BMI, disability, occupation, cultural/migration aspects, substance use, naming, social context, direct speech, emotions, multimedia, ICD-10 diagnoses, onset, setting, and scenario closure. The authors state: "We developed a coding framework to analyze the VP collection that is provided to medical students in the interdisciplinary year at LMU Munich and evaluate (1) its authenticity compared to the German population and (2) how the patient is represented as a person."

title: Choose between online and alternative training methods for licensed health professionals based on resources, expertise, and desired reach, since effectiveness for knowledge and clinical behaviour appears similar
description: The review's practical implication for educators: because online training may be as effective as alternative methods for providing knowledge and achieving desired clinical behaviour, the choice of method should be governed by contextual factors. The article states that "factors such as the availability of resources, expertise, and desired reach of an intervention may govern which training method is optimal in any given scenario." Online methods offer widespread access, personalised instruction, and regularly updated content, but face-to-face workshops remain the current gold standard.

citation: Moßhammer D, Graf J, Joos S, Hertkorn R. (2017). Physical examination in undergraduate medical education in the field of general practice – a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-017-1074-1
title: Five-category taxonomy of physical examination teaching and research in undergraduate medical education
description: The scoping review developed a content categorization of 117 articles using qualitative content analysis following Mayring. Articles were matched into five categories: "teaching methods" (CAT I), "teaching quality" (CAT II), "performance evaluation and assessment formats" (CAT III), "student views" (CAT IV) and "patient/ standardized patient perspective" (CAT V). Categories were derived inductively from the text material through an iterative six-step process, with inter-rater reliability of 0.88 (n = 103). The taxonomy represents the possible dimensions of assessment for physical examination education research.
requirements: Articles must concern undergraduate medical education with focus on general practice physical examination
constraints: Every article was assigned to only one category by main focus, though many articles could have been allocated to more than one category

title: Four-perspective framework for classifying the pedagogical foundations of educational games
description: The review adopts Wu's classification of educational games by pedagogical perspective: behaviourism (learning as operant conditioning prioritizing knowledge transmission), cognitivism (learners as information processors), humanism (person-centred experiential learning), and constructivism (knowledge construction through problem-solving and social interaction). The authors used these definitions to classify each of the 21 reviewed games and to judge game/pedagogy coherence, arguing that "a selection of a pedagogical perspective would not be indifferent in this case since it mirrors the intentions of game authors and determines the architecture of the games".

constraints: The review notes the connection between pedagogical perspectives and serious games is weak, with developers emphasizing practicality over theoretical foundations

skill development through repetition
problem-solving and knowledge construction
examples: Each of the 21 reviewed games was classified by reviewer pairs using Wu's definitions, with a third reviewer resolving disagreements; 76.2% of game designs were coherent with their pedagogical strategy

title: Corpus of 21 peer-reviewed studies of serious games in medical education (2011–2015)
description: A systematically assembled corpus of 21 peer-reviewed journal articles describing or assessing serious games or gamified apps in under- and postgraduate medical education, published 2011–2015 in English, Spanish, or Portuguese. From 494 initial records, 108 duplicates and 365 non-qualifying articles were excluded, leaving 21 studies. The corpus spans specialties including "phono audiology, laboratory, surgery, forensics, pathology, neurosurgery, and urology", with six games in physiology and anatomy, and was coded for study design, MERSQI quality, game attributes, pedagogical strategy, and pedagogical role.

constraints: The 5-year time frame was chosen due to high speed of innovation and obsolescence in games; no Spanish- or Portuguese-language games were found despite targeted searching

title: Flipped classroom as reversal of lecture and homework elements with pre-recorded videos before face-to-face active-learning sessions
description: The article adopts the educause conceptual framework of the flipped classroom as "a pedagogical strategy in which the typical lecture and homework elements of a course are reversed": students watch pre-recorded lectures before class and perform active learning activities such as exercises, projects, or discussions in class. The review restricts the definition to implementations with instructor-provided pre-class videos and a face-to-face meeting, excluding text-only pre-class reading and fully online courses.

A face-to-face class meeting must be included

description: Several descriptive articles reviewed define core lists of drugs and diseases that medical students should know for prescribing education. Orme et al. described "a list of 120 ‘core drugs’ that students should know in detail, and 47 drugs that students should be familiar with" plus core disease lists; Maxwell and Walley described 201 core drugs and 148 core diseases; Ross and Maxwell refined this into 98 drug classes and 125 therapeutic problems; Baker et al. developed a validated list of 100 commonly prescribed drugs based on prescribing data and a survey of 148 FY1 doctors.

title: The Kirkpatrick Model as a four-level framework for evaluating simulation-based training
description: The Kirkpatrick Model is an evaluation framework the review uses to classify the level of evaluation assessment completed for the training reported in each reviewed article. "The model consists of 4 levels: (1) participants responses—REACTION—to training (eg, satisfaction); (2) extent of knowledge, attitude, or skills gained—LEARNING; (3) extent to which desired behaviors are being used on the job—BEHAVIOR; and (4) extent to which desired behaviors are producing the desired outcomes in practice—RESULTS." citation: Albarqouni Loai, Hoffmann Tammy, Glasziou Paul. (2018). Evidence-based practice educational intervention studies: a systematic review of what is taught and how it is measured. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-018-1284-1
title: Six high-quality EBP assessment instruments (Fresno Test, Berlin Questionnaire, ACE tool, Taylor et al., Utrecht questionnaire, MacRae et al.)
description: The review identifies six instruments rated high quality because they achieved "≥3 types of established validity evidence". Four (Fresno Test, Berlin Questionnaire, Taylor et al., ACE tool) measure both EBP knowledge and skills; the Utrecht questionnaire measures knowledge and MacRae et al. measures skills. The Fresno Test, Berlin Questionnaire and ACE tool evaluate the ask, acquire, and appraise-and-interpret steps; none covers all five steps.
requirements: Instruments must be supported by established inter-rater reliability (if applicable), objective non-self-reported outcome measures, and multiple (≥3) types of established validity evidence, including discriminative validity
constraints: None of the six high-quality instruments was designed to evaluate all five EBP steps; the highest coverage is three steps
target_learners: Health professionals across undergraduate, postgraduate, and continuing education
target_learning_goals: Evidence-based practice knowledge, skills, and attitudes
examples: The Fresno Test consists of two clinical scenarios with 12 open-ended questions, needs about 40-60 min to complete and 10-15 min to mark using standardised grading rubrics

title: CREATE framework for classifying EBP assessment tools in education
description: The CREATE framework (Classification Rubric for EBP Assessment Tools in Education), developed in 2011, provides guidance for developing new EBP instruments by "purposively classifying the assessment domains (e.g. self-efficacy, knowledge, skills) and types (e.g. self-report, performance assessment) within the five EBP steps". The review uses its seven outcome-domain categories to organise the outcomes measured in included studies and cites it to help EBP educators identify the best available instruments.
requirements: New EBP instruments should be developed by classifying assessment domains and types within the five EBP steps

target_learning_goals: Evidence-based practice competence across the five EBP steps
examples: The review organised extracted outcome domains into the CREATE framework's seven categories, from reaction to the educational experience through benefit to patients

article_title: Evidence-based practice educational intervention studies: a systematic review of what is taught and how it is measured.
citation: Albarqouni Loai, Hoffmann Tammy, Glasziou Paul. (2018). Evidence-based practice educational intervention studies: a systematic review of what is taught and how it is measured. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-018-1284-1
title: EBP curricula should cover all five EBP steps, with greater emphasis on applying evidence with patients
description: Because most evaluated interventions teach only some EBP steps and neglect apply and reflect, the review argues "greater emphasis should be placed on teaching learners how to apply and the evidence in collaboration with individual patients such as through shared decision making". It notes the international consensus statement of 68 core EBP competencies may help harmonise intervention content. Educational packages addressing all EBP steps are needed to improve EBP teaching.
requirements: Educational packages and instruments which address all EBP steps are needed
constraints: The review notes that if interventions remain mostly focused on locating and appraising evidence, research evidence may be poorly translated into clinical practice

target_learning_goals: Applying research evidence in collaboration with patients, including shared decision making
examples: The review found only 10 of 85 controlled studies taught all five EBP steps, motivating the recommendation

description: The TDF is, in the article's words, "a comprehensive framework composed of 12 domains that synthesize 128 explanatory constructs drawing on 33 psychological theories associated with clinical behavior change." The review used it as the second step of a two-step analysis, directing coding of charted barriers and facilitators into the 12 domains for two units of analysis: physicians engaging in SDL and SDL developers implementing programs. The authors report this as the first TDF-guided directed coding in a scoping review on SDL in CPD.

Key domains were determined by frequency counts, which the authors say do not imply importance

article_title: Self-regulated learning in the clinical context: a systematic review.
citation: van Houten‐Schat Maaike A, Berkhout Joris J, van Dijk Nynke, Endedijk Maaike D, Jaarsma A Debbie, Diemers Agnes D. (2018). Self‐regulated learning in the clinical context: a systematic review. Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1111/medu.13615
title: Cyclical three-phase SRL models (Zimmerman, Knowles, Pintrich) frame SRL as goal setting, plan implementation and self-evaluation, but stem from classroom research
description: The review reports that included studies used the cyclical three-phase model of Zimmerman, the theoretical model of Knowles, or a framework based on Pintrich's principles. These theories "agree upon active engagement, goal setting, implementation of a plan and self‐evaluation of the process". The review also cites Sitzmann and Ely's categorisation of SRL processes into regulatory agent (goal setting), regulatory mechanism (planning, monitoring, strategies, motivation, emotion control) and regulatory appraisal (self-evaluation, attributions, self-efficacy). The authors caution these classroom-derived models cannot easily be applied to the complex clinical context.
requirements: A theoretical framework is needed to study SRL, though the review found one is often lacking in clinical-context studies
constraints: The review states these frameworks stemmed from classroom-setting research and, given the known influence of context on SRL, cannot be applied easily to the complex clinical context

article_title: A meta-analytic perspective on the valid use of subjective human judgement to make medical school admission decisions.
citation: Kreiter Clare, O'Shea Marie, Bruen Catherine, Murphy Paul, Pawlikowska Teresa. (2018). A meta-analytic perspective on the valid use of subjective human judgement to make medical school admission decisions. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2018.1522225
title: Format traditional interviews to yield a reliable score, e.g., by engaging each applicant in multiple independent interviews
description: The review concludes that the traditional interview's low reliability significantly limits its validity, but that its reliable variance is moderately predictive of relevant outcomes. It therefore recommends reformatting the interview so it produces a reliable score: 'if traditional subjective interviews can be formatted to yield a reliable score (e.g., by engaging an applicant in multiple independent interviews), it might significantly enhance its value as a subjective assessment'. This preserves the subjective component while addressing the measurement weakness the meta-analysis identified.
requirements: The interview must be reformatted so the score reflects comprehensive error sources, allowing an inference about maximum attainable validity
constraints: The recommendation is conditional ('might significantly enhance'), derived from reliability and validity coefficients rather than a direct test of the reformatted format
target_learning_goals: valid and reliable selection of applicants with potential to succeed as medical students and physicians
examples: The review's Table 1 aggregates G-study and repeat-interview alpha estimates showing reliabilities from r = .23 to r = .46 across medical education and employment studies

article_title: A meta-analytic perspective on the valid use of subjective human judgement to make medical school admission decisions.
citation: Kreiter Clare, O'Shea Marie, Bruen Catherine, Murphy Paul, Pawlikowska Teresa. (2018). A meta-analytic perspective on the valid use of subjective human judgement to make medical school admission decisions. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2018.1522225
title: Use constrained optimization rather than holistic review to incorporate subjective policy judgements transparently in admission decisions
description: The review argues that mechanical methods can incorporate subjective judgements in quantitative form, with weights reflecting explicitly stated values. It identifies constrained optimization (CO) as the most explicit and versatile such framework: 'CO methods are preferable to holistic review because they are transparent and treat all applicants equally while providing flexibility for programmes seeking to implement both subjective and objective policy decisions'. This follows from the meta-analytic finding that mechanical combination outperforms clinical judgement.
requirements: Subjective decisions about class composition and applicant attributes must be encoded as explicit weights or constraints within the optimization
constraints: Decisions about the relative importance of attributes such as communication skills, intellectual ability, and ethnicity/race remain inherently subjective because objective evidence of their relative importance does not exist
target_learning_goals: fair, transparent, and valid selection decisions incorporating subjective policy values
examples: The article cites the authors' prior work applying constrained optimization to admission decisions, including generating an alternate list when using constrained optimization to make admission decisions

article_title: Spatial cognition in minimally invasive surgery: a systematic review.
citation: Vajsbaher Tina, Schultheis Holger, Francis Nader K. (2018). Spatial cognition in minimally invasive surgery: a systematic review. BMC Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12893-018-0416-1
title: Visual working memory as a holistic framework for spatial cognition in MIS learning and performance
description: The review proposes shifting from studying isolated spatial abilities to a holistic account centered on working memory, the active 'mental workspace' that temporarily processes incoming stimuli, maintains focus, blocks unnecessary information and delegates cognitive processes. The component "responsible for processing and manipulating visuospatial stimuli is referred to as VWM". In MIS, novices' repeated gaze switches between monitor and instruments raise attentional demands, reduce effective WM capacity and produce cognitive overload; the framework aims to explain fragmentary findings on VSA, mental rotation and mental practice within one system.
requirements: Research and training must consider the functioning of the whole WM system rather than isolated spatial abilities
External and internal factors influencing the surgeon must be considered together
constraints: The framework is a theoretical narrative proposed by the authors; the review states its validity in practice still needs to be tested
target_learners: novice surgeons and surgical trainees learning minimally invasive surgery
target_learning_goals: MIS technical skill acquisition
intraoperative spatial orientation and attention allocation
reduction of cognitive load during surgery
examples: The review explains novice laparoscopic performance through simultaneous WM demands: retaining procedure steps, transforming the 2D image into a 3D representation, retrieving operative knowledge, and tracking instrument coordination

It "presents both transcribed and recorded conversations in real time", stopping the recording at chosen points so trainees can discuss whether the talk is helping or impeding preferred outcomes. The review presents CARM as a CA-based alternative to role play that overcomes some inauthenticity but removes real-time thinking, feedback on the simulation, and observing others approach the same task.

title: Debriefing with good judgment: a reflective-practice debriefing method using performance gaps to explore learner frames
description: Debriefing with good judgment is a well-established debriefing method in which the debriefer uses observations of performance gaps to explore learner frames and thought processes. It "uses a 3-phase (reaction, analysis, and summary) conversational approach based in reflective practice". In this curriculum it was used in one of each session's two scenarios to focus on mental models, teamwork, and thought processing to fill in performance gaps, and was chosen for its established track record and associated assessment tool.

title: Conceptual framework linking school green space to academic performance through five mechanisms
description: The review proposes a conceptual framework, adapted from Markevych and colleagues and incorporating pathways from another included study, mapping how green space near schools may influence academic outcomes. It states that green space "could influence different academic outcomes through one of five mechanisms: attention restoration, better mental health, more time outdoors, more physical activity, and better physical health", with confounding and moderating factors (parental, school/environmental, and individual characteristics) affecting these relationships. The framework is offered to synthesize mechanisms and guide future research variables.

constraints: The framework is a proposal for future research, not a tested model; the review found only weak evidence overall

title: Gallagher et al.'s six validation benchmarks for surgical simulation instruments
description: The review adopts an article by Gallagher et al. defining six types of validation benchmarks for surgical training instruments: face, content, construct, concurrent, discriminate and predictive validity. Construct validity is defined as "an evaluation of whether an instrument measures what it was designed to," usually tested as the ability to differentiate novices from experts. The review uses this taxonomy to categorize the validity evidence of each included study and to argue that future work should move to higher levels of validity.
requirements: Proving validity is described as a vital part of assessing simulator training
constraints: Face validity is described as highly subjective and difficult to use for broader conclusions
None of the included studies provided discriminate or predictive validity

target_learning_goals: valid assessment of surgical skills acquired through simulation
examples: The review categorizes four included studies as providing construct validity, one as providing face validity, and argues Jonas et al. could be argued to provide concurrent validity via enucleated pig eyes

description: The review organizes its field around COTS devices enabling touchless gesture-based human-computer interaction in surgical environments, where touching a mouse, keyboard or touchscreen breaks asepsis and antisepsis protocols. The article defines the category: "The term COTS refers to a device that can be taken from a shelf, that is, sold over the counter", noting they are low-cost, wireless, ergonomic, and allow manipulation with 6 degrees of freedom. The review uses this framework to classify 86 studies by device (Microsoft Kinect, Leap Motion Controller, Myo armband, cameras), clinical area, and type of use.

article_title: A systematic review and meta-analysis on the effects of physically active classrooms on educational and enjoyment outcomes in school age children.
citation: Bedard Chloe, St John Laura, Bremer Emily, Graham Jeffrey D., Cairney John. (2019). A systematic review and meta-analysis on the effects of physically active classrooms on educational and enjoyment outcomes in school age children. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0218633
title: Physically active lessons (movement integration) as an intervention category distinct from active breaks and active transitions
description: The review defines active classrooms as a teaching technique that "intentionally blends physical activities into core-content academic lessons to satisfy both the learning outcomes of the classroom without sacrificing time spent engaging in PA". Integrated activity may be related to the academic content (e.g., acting out a word's meaning) or unrelated (e.g., jumping to answer a math question). The review distinguishes this category from active breaks, which introduce PA without academic content, and active transitions, which use PA to move between tasks, and restricted inclusion to interventions that did not take away teaching time.

constraints: Excluded multi-component school-wide interventions where effects cannot be attributed to the active-lesson component alone; excluded activity-break comparators and post-secondary settings

target_learning_goals: academic performance across subjects such as mathematics, reading, spelling, language, geography, and science

It states the review "throws into sharp relief the urgent need to conduct more population-level research into the educational prospects of children in contact with CSC services, especially from the perspective of the child's journey through CSC services", which it found was the weakest point of the existing evidence base. Addressing this knowledge gap is framed as the first step to helping vulnerable children and young people.
requirements: Administrative data linked over time, since data on all children can be linked to fully examine their careers in the care system and through school

citation: Ramis Mary-Anne, Chang Anne, Conway Aaron, Lim David, Munday Judy, Nissen Lisa. (2019). Theory-based strategies for teaching evidence-based practice to undergraduate health students: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1698-4
title: Five theoretical frameworks underpin the theory-based undergraduate EBP interventions, but no single theory is aligned with EBP teaching and learning
description: The review identifies the theories used in the five included studies: Social Cognitive Theory (Bandura's self-efficacy construct), Rogers' Theory of Diffusion of Innovations, Cognitive Apprenticeship Theory, Cognitive Load Theory and Cognitive Flexibility Theory. CAT "posits social interactions between the learner and the expert form a base for further cognitive development", accomplished through "scaffolding, observation, modeling, mentoring, reflection and participation". The review concludes no single theory is yet aligned with EBP teaching and learning and that the most effective theory cannot be determined.

constraints: Due to heterogeneity in theories reported, populations and interventions it was not possible to confidently determine which theory was most effective

examples: Kim et al. grounded their intervention in SCT self-efficacy and Rogers' Diffusion of Innovations; Ashktorab et al. mapped each intervention stage to Rogers' five stages; Long et al. linked practice opportunities to CAT's reflection component
