citation: Coleman E., O'Connor E. (2019). The role of WhatsApp® in medical education; a scoping review and instructional design model. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1706-8
title: Three strategies for WhatsApp use in medical education: pre-defined curriculum, education without curriculum, and primarily non-educational use
description: The review organises the 23 included studies into three usage strategies distinguished by educational intent, curriculum presence, moderation, setting and scale. As printed, "Three strategies for WhatsApp use were apparent; primarily educational use with a pre-defined curriculum (n = 5), primarily educational use without a curriculum (n = 11), and primarily non-educational use (n = 7)." Curriculum groups were local, moderated and short-duration; non-educational groups were national or international and seldom moderated. The taxonomy anchors the authors' proposed design model.
requirements: Classification requires judging each study's primary purpose, curriculum presence, moderator presence and setting scale from the published report.
constraints: Derived from 23 studies published 2015–2018 in medical education; the review notes possible omission of relevant publications.
target_learning_goals: discipline-specific medical knowledge
clinical case discussion and information sharing
examples: The review tabulated all 23 studies against the strategies, finding moderated local groups for educational use and unmoderated national or international groups for primarily non-educational use.

citation: Coleman E., O'Connor E. (2019). The role of WhatsApp® in medical education; a scoping review and instructional design model. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1706-8
title: Proposed instant messenger learning design model combining the three WhatsApp strategies with the exploration-enactment-assessment framework
description: The authors propose an instructional design model for instant messenger application learning in medical education, intended to fill the theoretical vacuum they identified in the reviewed studies. It is "drawing from Dabbagh and Bannan-Ritland's exploration-enactment-evaluation learning design framework for online education [50], in turn informed by socio-cultural and constructivist theories (Fig. 2)". The model combines the three usage strategies and is offered as a resource for educators planning IMA use, standing distinct from generic technology-enhanced learning models.
requirements: Educators planning IMA use should apply the model to give learning activities a theory-driven instructional design foundation.
constraints: The review states further research is warranted to explore the utility of the design model; it had not itself been empirically evaluated.
target_learning_goals: theory-driven instructional design of instant messenger learning activities
examples: The model is presented in Fig. 2 as an adaptation of Dabbagh's framework mapped onto the three WhatsApp usage strategies identified in the review.

article_title: Team-based learning pedagogy enhances the quality of Chinese pharmacy education: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
citation: Lang Bingchen, Zhang Lingli, Lin Yunzhu, Han Lu, Zhang Chuan, Liu Yantao. (2019). Team-based learning pedagogy enhances the quality of Chinese pharmacy education: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1724-6
title: Generalize team-based learning in Chinese pharmacy classrooms where small-group effectiveness is needed with high student-faculty ratios
description: The article concludes that TBL pedagogy, an innovative and interactive small-group approach, is compatible with Chinese pharmacy education and recommends wider adoption. It argues TBL "provides the advantage that ensuring the effectiveness of small-group learning with high student faculty ratios", fitting understaffed pharmacy education, and states it "should be generalized in more Chinese classrooms" based on the meta-analytic evidence of higher test scores and improved student-reported abilities.
requirements: Teachers lay out discussion topics, raise questions or cases, organize pre-tests and post-tests and questionnaires, and evaluate effectiveness; student groups carry out preview, information searching, literature reading, group discussion, and summary report.
constraints: The evidence base shows substantial heterogeneity (I2 = 98%) and Egger's test indicated publication bias (p = 0.049); the authors call for more high-quality studies and more standardized evaluation methods.

target_learning_goals: Theoretical knowledge tested by objective tests
Learning enthusiasm, self-study ability, thinking ability, and communication skills

article_title: Efficacy of adaptive e-learning for health professionals and students: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
citation: Fontaine G, Cossette S, Maheu-Cadotte M-A, Mailhot T, Deschênes M-F, Mathieu-Dupuis G, Côté J, Gagnon M-P, Dubé V. (2019). Efficacy of adaptive e-learning for health professionals and students: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2018-025252
title: Five-subdomain taxonomy characterising the adaptivity process of adaptive e-learning environments
description: The review proposes that the adaptivity process of an AEE be characterised by five subdomains that "emerged from the review": "(1) Adaptivity method. (2) Adaptivity goals. (3) Adaptivity timing. (4) Adaptivity factors. (5) Adaptivity types". Method distinguishes designed (expert-based, 'if THIS, then THAT') from algorithmic adaptivity; goals cover effectiveness, efficiency, behaviour change and metacognitive processes; timing distinguishes beginning-only from throughout-training adaptation; factors are the learner data used (scores, actions, response time); types follow Knutov et al (content, navigation, multimedia, presentation, tools). The review applies this taxonomy to all 21 included AEEs.
requirements: Researchers should report adaptivity methods, goals, timing, factors and types clearly, and provide details on underlying algorithms or AEE architecture to ensure replicability
constraints: The taxonomy emerged from 21 studies in health professions education, mostly diagnostic-testing topics, and the review notes reporting on adaptivity was often unclear
target_learning_goals: knowledge acquisition
clinical skills development
clinical behaviour change
examples: In the reviewed studies, 11 AEEs employed designed adaptivity and 9 algorithmic adaptivity; content adaptivity was implemented in 20 of 21 AEEs and 17 of 21 integrated more than one adaptivity type

article_title: Efficacy of adaptive e-learning for health professionals and students: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
citation: Fontaine G, Cossette S, Maheu-Cadotte M-A, Mailhot T, Deschênes M-F, Mathieu-Dupuis G, Côté J, Gagnon M-P, Dubé V. (2019). Efficacy of adaptive e-learning for health professionals and students: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2018-025252
title: Three main adaptive e-learning platforms used in health professions education: SlideTutor, Smart Sparrow and PALM
description: The review identifies three main adaptive e-learning platforms across the 21 studies: "SlideTutor (n=4), Smart Sparrow (n=4) and the Perceptual Adaptive Learning Module (PALM, n=3)". SlideTutor is an AEE with algorithmic adaptivity providing dermopathology virtual-slide cases supervised by the system, using an expert knowledge base of evidence-diagnosis relationships to build a dynamic solution graph and determine the optimal instructional sequence. Smart Sparrow uses designed adaptivity, letting educators set adaptivity factors to specify how the system adapts the instructional sequence or provides feedback. PALM uses algorithmic adaptivity with adaptive response-time-based sequencing that dynamically spaces learning items based on each learner's accuracy and speed.
requirements: Educators or algorithms must specify adaptivity factors and the instructional sequence; PALM requires interactive learning trials generating accuracy and speed data
constraints: SlideTutor cases are specific to dermopathology virtual slides; Smart Sparrow custom learning paths "can be more or less personalised"
target_learning_goals: diagnostic accuracy
perceptual classification learning
clinical reasoning skills
examples: Studies using these platforms trained learners in dermopathology, diagnostic cytopathology, diagnostic imaging, electrocardiography and fetal heart rate interpretation

citation: Fontaine G, Cossette S, Maheu-Cadotte M-A, Mailhot T, Deschênes M-F, Mathieu-Dupuis G, Côté J, Gagnon M-P, Dubé V. (2019). Efficacy of adaptive e-learning for health professionals and students: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2018-025252
title: Eight practical considerations for designing and developing adaptive e-learning environments
description: Based on the review results, the authors present "eight practical considerations for the design and development of AEEs based on the results of this systematic review for educators and educational researchers" (Table 3): developing the educational content, selecting a theoretical framework, selecting the adaptivity method, selecting the adaptivity goal(s), selecting the adaptivity timing, selecting the adaptivity factor(s), selecting the adaptivity type(s), and determining technical resources and selecting the adaptive e-learning platform. The pattern operationalises the review's five-subdomain taxonomy as a design sequence, from content development through platform selection.
requirements: More pedagogical content must be developed than the planned session duration, since "it is necessary to develop more pedagogical content (eg, 60 min of learning) to reach the planned duration of each adaptive e-learning session (eg, 30 min of learning)"; a theoretical framework coherent with the adaptivity principles must be selected; technical resources and pre-existing software must be evaluated before development
constraints: The considerations are derived from a review of 21 studies in health professions education with generally high risk of bias and low-to-very-low quality of evidence
target_learning_goals: knowledge acquisition
skills development
clinical behaviour change
examples: The review's Table 3 lists the eight considerations with explanations, e.g. adaptivity goals may be to increase learning effectiveness, increase learning efficiency, modify behavioural predictors or improve cognitive/metacognitive processes

article_title: Blended learning models for introductory programming courses: A systematic review.
citation: Ali Alammary. (2019). Blended learning models for introductory programming courses: A systematic review. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0221765
title: Five blended learning models for introductory programming courses classified by where content delivery and practical activities take place
description: The review classifies forty blended learning approaches applied in introductory programming courses into five models: flipped, mixed, flex, supplemental, and online-practicing. The classification criterion is location of delivery: "This classification has been made according to where the content delivery and practical activities take place i.e., face-to-face or online." Each model is described with its own structure and example approaches from the included studies.
requirements: A course must have both face-to-face and online components to count as blended learning under the review's adopted definition
constraints: Classification derived from 38 studies in higher education introductory programming contexts
target_learning_goals: introductory programming concepts and problem-solving skills

citation: Ali Alammary. (2019). Blended learning models for introductory programming courses: A systematic review. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0221765
title: Five blended learning components classified by interaction type
description: The review draws on a prior classification of blended learning building blocks: "Alammary, Carbone [28] identified five different blended learning components. Two of them are face-to-face, while the other three are online components." The components are face-to-face instructor-led, face-to-face collaboration, online instructor-led, online collaboration, and online self-paced, each classified by the type of interaction it supports and each described with its pedagogical advantages.
requirements: Instructors mix components thoughtfully, using each method for what it does best
constraints: Component classification is grounded in constructivist learning theory as described in the review
target_learning_goals: flexible and interactive learning across delivery modes

article_title: Acute surgical wound-dressing procedure: Description of the steps involved in the development and validation of an observational metric.
citation: Hegarty Josephine, Howson Victoria, Wills Teresa, Creedon Sile A., Mc Cluskey Pat, Lane Aoife, Connolly Aine, Walshe Nuala, Noonan Brendan, Guidera Fiona, Gallagher Anthony G, Murphy Siobhan. (2019). Acute surgical wound‐dressing procedure: Description of the steps involved in the development and validation of an observational metric. International Wound Journal. https://doi.org/10.1111/iwj.13072
title: Proficiency-based progression training (PBPT): trainees practice until an unambiguously demonstrated quantitative performance benchmark is reached, with metric-based feedback
description: PBPT is a training approach for high-volume, high-risk technical and non-technical skills in which trainees receive precise feedback proximate to performance and "a quantitative performance benchmark to work towards" that "should be a valid representation of the procedure". It requires learners to practice until the benchmark is unambiguously demonstrated, relying on a comprehensive quantitative characterisation of the skill. In this study PBPT principles underpinned the six-stage development of the ANTT wound-dressing observational metric, whose metrics and operational definitions offer specific goals for a training curriculum.
requirements: A valid observational metric that quantitatively characterises the procedure, with operationally defined steps and errors, so feedback can delineate deviation from optimal performance
target_learners: trainee health care professionals learning acute surgical wound-dressing procedures
target_learning_goals: proficient performance of aseptic non-touch technique during acute surgical wound dressings
examples: The study's metric development process followed PBPT steps: literature scoping, video-based task analysis, stress testing for reliability, and Delphi validation of the resulting metric.

title: ANTT wound-dressing observational metric: a three-phase, 31-step tool defining the performance standard for acute surgical wound dressings
description: The ANTT wound-dressing observational metric is a scoring instrument deconstructed into three phases of explicitly defined, observable steps, each with a marked beginning point and endpoint, plus error and sentinel-error items. It "identifies the standard to be attained in the performance of acute surgical wound dressings" and can be scored for steps observed out of total steps and errors observed out of total potential errors. It functions as both an adjunct to an educational programme and a tool to assess practitioner performance in simulated and clinical practice contexts.
requirements: Training in the use of the metric to ensure consistency in its application
constraints: Developed and validated for acute surgical wounds healing by primary intention post-major surgeries in one region of Ireland; further clinical-context testing would enhance validity
target_learners: nurses performing acute surgical wound dressings
target_learning_goals: correct performance of aseptic non-touch technique in wound dressing
avoidance of errors and sentinel errors during the procedure
examples: Tables 2 and 3 enumerate the metric's phases and steps (e.g., disinfecting the trolley, donning sterile gloves using non-touch technique) and its errors and sentinel errors (e.g., failure to perform hand hygiene, violation of aseptic non-touch technique).

title: Six-stage iterative metric development pattern: scoping review, video capture, task analysis, reliability stress testing, and Delphi consensus
description: The article describes a reusable development sequence underpinned by PBPT principles: a team of clinicians, academics, and researchers developed the metric "using an iterative six‐stage process, culminating in a Delphi panel meeting". A scoping review supplied background perspective; forehead-mounted GoPro video recordings of real and simulated procedures were repeatedly and iteratively deconstructed into steps, errors, and sentinel errors; the metric was stress tested for clarity, scorability, and inter-rater reliability; and a Delphi panel verified face and content validity. The authors state this methodology provides a framework for developing validated metrics and performance standards.
requirements: A metric development group combining academic and clinical expertise (the study used 8 academic and 4 clinical experts)
video recordings capturing procedures from start to waste disposal and hand hygiene
constraints: The task analysis and initial stress testing took the team 2.5 days (20 hours); technical difficulties with the GoPro camera were encountered
target_learners: health care professionals being trained in procedural skills
target_learning_goals: objective characterisation and assessment of procedural skill performance
examples: Videos were recorded with a GoPro mounted on nurses' foreheads during routine wound dressings, with nurses self-selecting and not interrupted or guided during the procedure.

article_title: Effects of school-based physical activity on mathematics performance in children: a systematic review.
citation: Sneck S., Viholainen H., Syväoja H., Kankaapää A., Hakonen H., Poikkeus A.-M., Tammelin T. (2019). Effects of school-based physical activity on mathematics performance in children: a systematic review. The International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12966-019-0866-6
title: Mechanisms account proposing that PA affects mathematics performance via brain and cognition, executive functions, motor-cognitive development, and emotional engagement
description: The review organises candidate mediating mechanisms for PA effects on mathematics into several strands: brain structure and function effects, executive functions (inhibition, working memory, cognitive flexibility) that are associated with mathematics achievement, motor development and related cognitive skills such as visuospatial skills and rapid automatized naming, and emotional experiences linked to mathematical achievement including math anxiety. The review notes "the findings on links between PA interventions and cognitive performance in children are still relatively rare and inconsistent" and calls for merging neuroscientific, psychological and educational theorizing.
requirements: Further examination of cognitive skills, executive functions, behaviour and brain activation outcomes in future intervention studies to determine how or why PA might affect mathematics performance
constraints: The mechanisms remain hypothesised; the review reports that findings on links between PA interventions and cognitive performance are rare and inconsistent
target_learning_goals: Mathematics performance and underlying cognitive and emotional mediators
examples: The review cites a study in which children's motor skills explained almost 16% of the variation in mathematical measures, and one reporting increased prefrontal cortex activity after exercise

article_title: Is computer-assisted instruction more effective than other educational methods in achieving ECG competence amongst medical students and residents? A systematic review and meta-analysis.
citation: Viljoen Charle André, Scott Millar Rob, Engel Mark E, Shelton Mary, Burch Vanessa. (2019). Is computer-assisted instruction more effective than other educational methods in achieving ECG competence amongst medical students and residents? A systematic review and meta-analysis. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2018-028800
title: Modified Kirkpatrick framework for evaluating educational interventions in ECG training studies
description: The review applied a modified version of the Kirkpatrick framework to classify the outcomes of the included educational interventions. It appraises outcomes at levels measuring "participants' perceptions of (reactions to) the learning experience (level 1)", modification of attitudes and perceptions (level 2a), modification of knowledge and/or skills (level 2b), transfer to the workplace (level 3), change in organisational practice (level 4a) and benefits to patients (level 4b). All thirteen included studies reported level 2b outcomes; none reported level 3 or 4 outcomes.
requirements: Studies must measure an objective outcome such as acquisition or retention of ECG competence to be classified at level 2b
constraints: None of the included studies evaluated CAI at Kirkpatrick level 3, 4a or 4b, which the review calls a widely recognised ongoing shortcoming of health professions education research
target_learning_goals: ECG analysis and interpretation competence
examples: Eight studies reported participants' reactions to CAI (level 1) and three reported changes in attitudes and perceptions (level 2a), with variable and inconsistent preferences between CAI and lectures

article_title: Digital Learning to Improve Safe and Effective Prescribing: A Systematic Review.
citation: Bakkum, M.J., Tichelaar, J., Wellink, A., Richir, M.C. & van Agtmael, M.A. (2019). Digital Learning to Improve Safe and Effective Prescribing: A Systematic Review. Clinical Pharmacology and Therapeutics. https://doi.org/10.1002/cpt.1549
title: Taxonomy of digital learning resource types for prescribing education
description: The review classifies digital learning resources into defined types used to categorize interventions: e-learning, digital assessment, social component, podcasts, blended learning, virtual patient, virtual reality, augmented reality, and serious/educational games. E-learning is defined as a "Web‐based (online) or offline course offering a mixture of text, multimedia, and interactive elements," and blended learning as any DLR combined with face-to-face teaching. The taxonomy structures the review's analysis of which DLR types are used and how effective they are, with e-learning the most-used type (55 of 65 articles).
requirements: Articles must describe or evaluate at least one DLR for teaching safe and effective prescribing to graduate or undergraduate prescribers
constraints: Definitions were adapted from prior work (van den Berg et al. and Piovesan et al.) and applied with reviewer consensus decisions, limiting repeatability
target_learning_goals: safe and effective prescribing
rational pharmacotherapy
examples: The review categorized 55 articles as e-learning, 12 as blended learning, 6 as digital assessment, and 9 as unique interventions such as gamified e-learning, a text-based virtual patient, and informative podcasts

citation: Bakkum, M.J., Tichelaar, J., Wellink, A., Richir, M.C. & van Agtmael, M.A. (2019). Digital Learning to Improve Safe and Effective Prescribing: A Systematic Review. Clinical Pharmacology and Therapeutics. https://doi.org/10.1002/cpt.1549
title: Design prescribing DLRs with anytime-anywhere availability, manageable time demands, and directly applicable authentic content
description: From qualitative reports across included studies, the review compiles ten recommendations for future DLRs for safe and effective prescribing. The most appreciated element is availability: "By far the most appreciated feature of DLRs is the possibility to study anytime and anywhere," which promotes just-in-time learning and puts students in charge of their learning. Other recommendations include openness about required time investment with bite-size chunks, clear navigational structure for pace and revision, quizzes and game design principles, direct feedback, authentic content connected to clear learning goals, accessible and attractive design, multimedia presented in various ways, and relevant web links.
requirements: Content should have a clear connection with predefined and clearly communicated learning goals and be directly applicable
constraints: Digital communication channels such as web forums and email for peer and teacher contact remained largely unused by students
target_learning_goals: safe and effective prescribing
rational pharmacotherapy
examples: The review's Table 3 lists ten elements, with anytime-anywhere availability mentioned in 13 articles and authentic, applicable content in 12 articles

article_title: Professional Reasoning in Occupational Therapy: A Scoping Review.
citation: Márquez-Álvarez L.-J., Calvo-Arenillas J.-I., Talavera-Valverde M.-Á., Moruno-Millares P. (2019). Professional Reasoning in Occupational Therapy: A Scoping Review. Occupational Therapy International. https://doi.org/10.1155/2019/6238245
title: Three-phase historical development of professional reasoning research in occupational therapy: exploratory, transition, and consolidation
description: The review proposes that research on professional reasoning in occupational therapy evolved through three historical periods with distinct characteristics: "(a) exploratory phase (1982-1993), (b) transition phase (1994-2003), and (c) consolidation phase (2005-present)". The exploratory phase is characterised by nonempirical qualitative studies using ethnographic and phenomenological approaches; the transition phase shows considerable increase and diversification of studies with empirical work outweighing nonempirical; the consolidation phase shows a reversed trend with quantitative approaches predominating and more literature reviews. The phases are grounded in the statistically significant period-methodology associations the review reports.
requirements: The phase division rests on statistical comparison of articles grouped into 10-year periods, with articles published between 2015 and 2017 excluded from the statistical analyses
constraints: The phase characterisation derives from indexed-journal articles (original studies and reviews) published between 1982 and 2017 (n = 208)
A detailed analysis of the findings of the included papers was beyond the scope of the study, and scientific quality of the literature was not assessed
target_learning_goals: understanding the historical development of research on professional reasoning in occupational therapy
examples: The review classifies 1982–1993 as exploratory with similar numbers of nonempirical (n = 10) and empirical (n = 11) articles, mainly exploratory and descriptive; 1994–2003 as transition with qualitative phenomenological studies predominating among empirical work; and 2005 onward as consolidation with quantitative studies (n = 29) outweighing qualitative ones (n = 23) in 2004–2014.

article_title: Systematic review of the current status of cadaveric simulation for surgical training.

title: Adapted Kirkpatrick hierarchy for assessing educational impact of training interventions
description: The review structures its evidence synthesis around an adapted Kirkpatrick hierarchy (Fig. 1) with four levels: learner reaction/opinion (level 1), learner knowledge (level 2), learner behaviour (level 3), and change in patient outcome (level 4), described as "the highest level of impact assessment in educational research". Each included study was assigned to a level by its outcome measure type, enabling the review to show that higher-level evidence is scarcer and of variable quality.
requirements: Studies must attempt to measure educational impact to be assigned a level in the synthesis
constraints: Only one included study reached level 4 (patient outcome); most evidence sits at levels 1 and 3
target_learning_goals: surgical procedural skills acquired through cadaveric simulation
examples: The review classified its 51 included studies into level 1 (22 studies), level 2 (5), level 3 (23) and level 4 (1) syntheses

article_title: Active Commute in Relation to Cognition and Academic Achievement in Children and Adolescents: A Systematic Review and Future Recommendations.
citation: Phansikar, M.; Ashrafi, S.A.; Khan, N.A.; Massey, W.V.; Mullen, S.P. (2019). International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph16245103
title: Active commuting as a physically active context with distinctive cognitive-motor demands that may differ from leisure-time physical activity
description: The review frames active commuting to school as a form of leisure-time physical activity complementary to sport and chores, but argues it "may be unique in terms of some of its inherent cognitive-motor challenges": attentive navigation through outdoor life-space with distractions and dangers. In the discussion it contrasts ACS with leisure-time physical activity, suggesting the latter "calls for more neuromuscular complexity as compared to walking or bicycling", which may explain why leisure-time physical activity shows clearer academic benefits than ACS in the pooled mathematics analysis.
requirements: Understanding the ACS–cognition relationship requires accounting for dose (duration, frequency, intensity), mode, and whether commuting is done alone or in a group, as the review states these shape the activity received.
constraints: The review states ACS is not always discretionary for children, since they do not always choose their mode of transportation, and exposure to traffic and air pollution during commuting may counteract benefits.
target_learners: children and adolescents aged 4 to 18.5 years in primary and secondary schools
target_learning_goals: executive functioning
academic achievement including mathematics, language, and reading outcomes
examples: The review contrasts studies where ACS showed positive associations (visuospatial accuracy, d2 Test of Attention, working memory) with studies using the flanker task and verbal fluency that found none.

article_title: Revisiting the trajectory of medical students' empathy, and impact of gender, specialty preferences and nationality: a systematic review.
citation: Andersen Freja Allerelli, Johansen Ann-Sofie Bering, Søndergaard Jens, Andersen Christina Maar, Assing Hvidt Elisabeth. (2020). title: Two-component taxonomy of empathy: affective and cognitive empathy
description: The review organises empathy as a construct with distinct components, stating that "Empathy is usually categorised as either affective (emotional), cognitive or a combination of both". Affective empathy is described as compassion and the ability to enter into other peoples' feelings, while cognitive empathy is the ability to understand someone's situation without making it one's own. In the clinical setting, the review states it is predominantly the cognitive empathy type that is valued and strived for. The review applies this distinction when interpreting studies, for example one cross-sectional study that differentiated between emotional and cognitive empathy and found higher cognitive empathy in final-year students.
requirements: Measurement instruments must distinguish the component being measured, since scales such as the BEES and TEQ measure affective empathy while the RMET measures cognitive empathy
constraints: The review notes that many different definitions and understandings of empathy, and different ways of measuring it, have led to ambiguous results
target_learning_goals: clinical empathy in patient-physician relationships
examples: One included cross-sectional study differentiated between emotional and cognitive empathy and found a higher cognitive empathy level in final year students compared to first-year students

citation: Andersen Freja Allerelli, Johansen Ann-Sofie Bering, Søndergaard Jens, Andersen Christina Maar, Assing Hvidt Elisabeth. (2020). Revisiting the trajectory of medical students' empathy, and impact of gender, specialty preferences and nationality: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-1964-5
title: Jefferson Scale of Empathy – Student Version (JSPE-S)
description: The JSPE-S is the self-report instrument used by most included studies; the review describes it as measuring affective empathy and studying "the empathic relationship between the medical student and the patient". It consists of 20 items on a 7-point Likert scale, with a minimum of 20 and a maximum of 140 points, where a high score indicates a more empathic orientation. All cross-sectional studies except four, and all longitudinal studies except one, employed the JSPE-S. The review notes the scale focuses on thoughts and not actions, citing Sulzer.
requirements: Validated scales; the review notes all studies except one employed validated scales, and flags one study applying the English validated JSPE-S to students without English as their native language
constraints: Self-reporting questionnaires introduce reporting bias; self-reported empathy has only a vague association with the patient-physician relationship in the clinical setting, per the review's cited literature
target_learning_goals: measuring empathy levels across educational years, gender, specialty preference and nationality
examples: Cross-sectional sample sizes of included studies using the JSPE-S ranged from 129 to 5521 participants, and longitudinal samples from 72 to 1653

article_title: Content and outcomes of narrative medicine programmes: a systematic review of the literature through 2019.
citation: Remein Christy DiFrances C, Childs E, Pasco JC, Trinquart L, Flynn DB, Wingerter SL, Bhasin RM, Demers LB, Benjamin EJ. (2020). Content and outcomes of narrative medicine programmes: a systematic review of the literature through 2019. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2019-031568
title: Narrative medicine as a framework grounded in narrative competence for humane and effective medical practice
description: Narrative medicine (NM) is a framework for medicine and health sciences that values individuals' stories and experiences as integral to the lived experience of health and illness. The review attributes its foundational account to Rita Charon, who introduced the term in 2001 and asserted that "The effective practice of medicine requires narrative competence, that is, the ability to acknowledge, absorb, interpret, and act on the stories and plights of others." NM programmes operationalise this framework through close reading of published literature and creative/reflective writing, combined with group discussion and workshopping, aiming to cultivate narrative and clinical competencies.
requirements: Eligible NM training in the review had to include both essential components: textual analysis/close reading of published literature and creative/reflective writing embedded in the programmatic core.
constraints: The review notes the stated definition of NM was inconsistent even within publications meeting inclusion criteria, and its vocabulary reflects a particularly American viewpoint on academic health sciences education.
target_learners: medical, dental and health sciences students
target_learning_goals: narrative competence
empathy
reflection
relationship-building
professional identity formation
examples: Programmes in the review implemented the framework through reading published narratives and reflective writing (100% of programmes), group discussion (83.6%), sharing/workshopping writing (52.7%) and other narrative-based exercises such as patient interviews and portfolios.

article_title: The informal curriculum of family medicine - what does it entail and how is it taught to residents? A systematic review.
citation: Rothlind Erica, Fors Uno, Salminen Helena, Wändell Per, Ekblad Solvig. (2020). The informal curriculum of family medicine – what does it entail and how is it taught to residents? A systematic review. BMC Family Practice. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12875-020-01120-1
title: The informal curriculum in Family Medicine comprises three partly interrelated themes: cultural competence, medical professionalism, and dealing with uncertainty
description: A taxonomy developed by the review through narrative synthesis of nine studies addressing what Family Medicine residents learn outside the formal curriculum. The review states that 'Through the process of narrative synthesis three overall, and partly intersecting, elements constituting the informal curriculum of FM were developed: gaining cultural competence, achieving medical professionalism and dealing with uncertainty.' The themes are treated as partly intersecting rather than distinct, and the review treats informal and hidden curriculum terms as interchangeable for its purpose.
requirements: Articles discussing any aspect of the informal curriculum in relation to Family Medicine, identified through iterative literature searches
constraints: The element dealing with uncertainty was derived from only two included articles, which the review acknowledges limits depth
target_learners: postgraduate medical trainees in workplace-based training
target_learning_goals: cultural competence
medical professionalism
dealing with uncertainty
examples: The review included 9 studies for question 1 and 11 interventional studies for question 2, published between 2000 and 2019

title: Workplace informal learning comes in three types — implicit, reactive, and deliberate — differing in the learner's intention to learn
description: The review attributes this three-type framework to prior workplace-learning models (references 7 and 8). It states that 'In models focusing on workplace learning the concept of informal learning has been elaborated and different types have been outlined: implicit, reactive and deliberate', with the individual's intention to learn as the main difference between the three and of significance for how well knowledge is retained. Deliberate informal learning is described as goal-formulated learning with time set aside; reactive learning manages a work task with learning at best a byproduct.
requirements: A workplace-learning context in which goals can be formulated and time set aside for deliberate informal learning
constraints: The review attributes this framework to prior models rather than testing it; research on how informal learning takes place in the workplace is described as limited

retention of knowledge gained outside formal curricula

citation: Rothlind Erica, Fors Uno, Salminen Helena, Wändell Per, Ekblad Solvig. (2020). The informal curriculum of family medicine – what does it entail and how is it taught to residents? A systematic review. BMC Family Practice. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12875-020-01120-1
title: Formalize parts of the informal curriculum for Family Medicine residents to reduce dependency on individual supervisors and facilitate more retained learning
description: The review recommends complementing workplace-based experiential training with formalized training in aspects of the informal curriculum. It argues that 'formalizing parts of the informal curriculum would likely facilitate a shift from implicit or reactive informal learning to more deliberate forms, where a modification of skills and behaviors is also more probable to occur', and that this would reduce the dependency on the individual supervisor's interests or preferences by providing a more uniform base for all residents. The recommendation is grounded in the review's finding that formalized training currently appears lacking.
requirements: Awareness among supervisors of the areas in which they are likely to have great impact on their residents
Identification of gaps where formalized learning activities are needed
constraints: The review states the current literature is not sufficient to conclude how to best teach the informal curriculum
target_learning_goals: cultural competence
medical professionalism
dealing with uncertainty
examples: The review's 11 included interventions ranged from isolated workshops of 1–10 occasions to interventions integrated over at least 1 year, with small-group discussions the most common method

article_title: Active learning narrows achievement gaps for underrepresented students in undergraduate science, technology, engineering, and math.
citation: Theobald Elli J. et al. (2020). Active learning narrows achievement gaps for underrepresented students in undergraduate science, technology, engineering, and math. Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1916903117
title: Heads-and-hearts hypothesis: gap reduction requires combining deliberate practice with inclusive teaching
description: The article's proposed explanation for the extensive variation in active learning's effect on achievement gaps. It holds that "meaningful reductions in achievement gaps only occur when course designs combine deliberate practice with inclusive teaching". Deliberate practice supplies focused, scaffolded, feedback-rich effort; inclusive teaching supplies dignity, communicated confidence, and genuine interest in students' growth. The authors claim these elements act synergistically for underrepresented students facing stereotype threat, microaggressions, and underpreparation.
requirements: Course designs must combine deliberate practice with inclusive teaching; either element alone is hypothesized to be insufficient for meaningful gap reduction
constraints: Explicit and rigorous testing of the heads-and-hearts hypothesis has yet to be done, per the article
target_learners: undergraduate STEM students, especially students from minoritized groups in STEM
target_learning_goals: reduced achievement gaps in STEM examination scores and passing rates
retention of underrepresented students in STEM majors
examples: The article cites a general chemistry companion course combining psychological interventions addressing belonging and stereotype threat with study-skills training and intensive peer-led group problem-solving that narrowed gaps while controlling for self-selection bias
key_sources: Theobald Elli J. et al. (2020). Active learning narrows achievement gaps for underrepresented students in undergraduate science, technology, engineering, and math. Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1916903117

title: Deliberate-practice course design with four facets: focused effort, scaffolded exercises, immediate feedback, and repetition
description: The article enumerates the deliberate-practice elements it considers required for courses that reduce or eliminate achievement gaps: "1) extensive and highly focused efforts geared toward improving performance... 2) scaffolded exercises designed to address specific deficits in understanding or skills, 3) immediate feedback, and 4) repetition". It presents these as facets of evidence-based best practice in active learning, and pairs them with a culture of inclusion as the two key design elements.
requirements: Students work hard on relevant tasks; exercises are scaffolded to specific deficits; feedback is immediate; practice is repeated
constraints: The article presents this as a hypothesis component; rigorous testing of the combined design has yet to be done
target_learning_goals: improved performance on course assessments
narrowed achievement gaps
examples: High-intensity active-learning classrooms, where students spend a large reported proportion of class time on in-class activities, are consistent with the deliberate-practice element per the article

article_title: Academic Outcomes of School-Aged Children Born Preterm: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
citation: McBryde M, Fitzallen GC, Liley HG, Taylor HG, Bora S. (2020). Academic Outcomes of School-Aged Children Born Preterm: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. JAMA Network Open. https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2020.2027
title: Subskill taxonomy of reading and mathematics achievement used to profile preterm academic outcomes
description: The article demarcates reading and mathematics into higher- and lower-order subskills by investigating the content and structure of psychoeducational measures. Reading is categorized into "overall reading, decoding (lower-order skill), and reading comprehension (higher-order skill)", with decoding further split into word identification and pseudoword decoding. Mathematics is categorized into overall mathematics, mathematical knowledge, calculation, mathematical fluency, and applied problems, with applied problems defined as the highest-order skill requiring interpretation, approach selection, and accurate answers.
requirements: Academic outcomes assessed by validated, standardized tests reporting mean (SD) scores, normed to a mean (SD) of 100 (15) for comparability across measures
constraints: The demarcation of subskills came from the authors' own investigation of the psychoeducational measures' content and structure, not from an independently validated taxonomy
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension
decoding and word identification
mathematical knowledge, calculation, fluency, and applied problem solving
examples: All assessment measures were normed to a mean (SD) of 100 (15) and compared in this metric across the 33 included studies

citation: Engell, T., Kirkøen, B., Hammerstrøm, K. T., Kornør, H., Ludvigsen, K. H., & Hagen, K. A. (2020). Prevention Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11121-020-01091-w
title: Three-part taxonomy of intervention elements: practice, process, and implementation elements
description: The review distinguishes three discrete element types in interventions for children at risk. Practice elements are "specific activities or actions used to evoke or influence an outcome (e.g., positive reinforcement)"; process elements cover delivery forms and contexts such as home visitation; implementation elements are "discrete strategies to facilitate or enable the delivery of practice and process elements" such as ongoing training. The taxonomy organizes the review's coding matrices and frequency analyses of 147 identified elements.
requirements: Interventions must be described in enough detail (articles, manuals, or appendices) for coders to identify discrete elements
constraints: Frequency analyses do not merit conclusions about the effectiveness of elements; FVs are likely skewed by publication bias

target_learning_goals: academic achievement in reading, math, and grade point average
examples: Coders used consensus mapping with a priori listed elements plus discovery of 11 unanticipated elements, achieving 90.4% total coding agreement

citation: Liu CX, Ouyang WW, Wang XW, Chen D, Jiang ZL. (2020). title: Evidence base of 20 Chinese RCTs comparing PBL+LBL with LBL across specialized clinical courses
description: The meta-analysis's evidence base consists of 20 randomized controlled studies, all from China, identified from 126 records screened to 34 and finally included after full-text review. It involves "a total of 1817 students, including 910 students in PBL+LBL group and 907 group in LBL group". Courses span gynecology and obstetrics, hepatobiliary surgery, cardiothoracic surgery, dermatology, breast surgery, vascular surgery, general practice, internal medicine, general surgery, infectious diseases, and pediatrics. citation: Barba-Martín Raúl A., Bores-García Daniel, Hortigüela-Alcalá David, González-Calvo Gustavo. (2020). The Application of the Teaching Games for Understanding in Physical Education. Systematic Review of the Last Six Years. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph17093330
title: Teaching Games for Understanding (TGfU) model: game-centered sports teaching built on four pedagogical principles
description: TGfU emerged in the 1980s as an alternative to the technical method for teaching sports games, making understanding of sport the focus of learning and asking students to consider the "why" of doing something during the development of the game, rather than the "how". It develops tactics and skills in real or simulated game contexts to improve decision-making and problem-solving, with the teacher questioning students to build tactical awareness. The review describes it as resting on four pedagogical principles: transfer, modification-representation, modification-exaggeration and tactical complexity.
requirements: Implementation requires teachers to have thorough knowledge of the model itself and of each discipline to make appropriate modifications during development
constraints: The review notes misinterpretations of the model have occurred, leading the original creators to publish clarifications
target_learners: primary and secondary school Physical Education students
target_learning_goals: tactical awareness and decision-making in games

description: To establish common guidelines among sports, TGfU developed classifications grouping games mainly into four categories: target games, court or net/wall games, striking/fielding games, and territory or invasion games. The review explains that this lets "teachers help students to compare more easily the similarities of apparently different games", for example extrapolating between basketball and football as invasion games. This classification underpins the model's transfer principle.

citation: Wassenaar Thomas M., Williamson Wilby, Johansen-Berg Heidi, Dawes Helen, Roberts Nia, Foster Charlie, Sexton Claire E. (2020). title: AMSTAR-2 critical-domain framework for rating the confidence of systematic reviews
description: AMSTAR-2 is the quality-assessment framework the article uses to rate systematic reviews by overall confidence. Confidence is determined by evaluating seven critical domains — preregistration, literature search, justification for excluding studies, risk of bias assessment, appropriateness of meta-analytical methods, risk of bias in synthesis of results, and publication bias. A lack of addressing one or multiple critical domains yields a low or critically low rating; with no critical flaws, non-critical weaknesses determine a high or moderate rating. The article applied it with two independent reviewers to all 19 reviews.
requirements: Two independent reviewers scoring the reviews
Evaluation of both critical and non-critical domains to derive an overall confidence rating
constraints: The article notes it is not recommended to combine individual item ratings into an overall score; the total score was provided only to acknowledge a quality gradient and was not used in the synthesis
target_learning_goals: evaluating evidence quality on physical activity effects on cognition, academic achievement and the brain
examples: The article rated 17 of 19 included reviews as critically low confidence because they did not address multiple critical domains

title: Van Der Vleuten's utility index for evaluating assessment instruments
description: The utility index is a widely accepted framework, described by Van Der Vleuten, for appraising an evaluation instrument. The review uses it to appraise each technical skills-assessment tool, defining validity (with content, construct, and concurrent subtypes), reliability, feasibility/acceptability, educational impact, and cost-effectiveness. The authors state it is "a widely accepted framework for assessing an evaluation instrument" and summarize evidence for each tool against these criteria.
requirements: Assessment tools must be appraised across validity, reliability, feasibility/acceptability, and educational impact dimensions to establish utility evidence.
constraints: Cost-effectiveness was not evaluated in this review.

target_learning_goals: technical surgical skill and operative competence assessment

title: TBL readiness assurance sequence: preparation, IRAT, GRAT consensus discussion, appeals, and instructor feedback
description: The article describes TBL as an instructional activity sequence of three main stages — preparation, readiness assurance, and application of course concepts — in which the readiness assurance test determines "whether each participant is prepared for the next application step of TBL". Its sub-steps are the IRAT (individual MCQs), the GRAT (groups answer the same MCQs through "consensus-building discussion"), an appeals step to restore credit, and whole-class instructor feedback addressing misconceptions. The article uses this sequence as the structure across which it compares IRAT and GRAT performance.
requirements: Participants must come prepared to every session, with adequate reading materials assigned prior to class
Each student is held accountable for their contribution to team performance
The same scoring system is used for IRAT and GRAT when comparing them
target_learners: healthcare professions students (medical, nursing, dental, pharmacy)
target_learning_goals: preparation for application-stage problem solving
collaborative knowledge consolidation
examples: The 11 included studies all administered an IRAT followed by a GRAT on the same MCQ set, with six using percentage scoring and others using ranges such as 0–10, 0–14, and 0–20 points.

title: Mental practice as an umbrella concept spanning mental imagery, mental rehearsal and mental simulation, explained by neurophysiological, cognitive and motivational theories
description: The article construes mental practice as "the ‘symbolic’ mental rehearsal of a task in the absence of actual physical rehearsal", subsuming mental imagery, mental rehearsal and mental simulation, undertaken by surgeons prior to performing a task to improve knowledge, skills and behaviour. The six reviews explained MP through theories from functional neuroscience and the PETTLEP model to dual code theory, neuroplasticity, self-efficacy, cognitive load and goal-setting, with neurophysiological accounts proposing that imagining movements strengthens cortical representations or primes neuromuscular pathways. constraints: The article states there is still confusion about the boundaries of what constitutes simulation through mental practice and incomplete knowledge of the interplay between broader cognitive skills and psychomotor skills

citation: Snelgrove Huon; Gabbott Ben. (2020). Critical analysis of evidence about the impacts on surgical teams of ‘mental practice’ in systematic reviews: a systematic rapid evidence assessment (SREA). BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-02131-3
title: Adopt mental practice as an economical, sustainable addition to surgical training, including shared mental rehearsal within teams
description: The article concludes that in designing surgical training, team building and safety procedures, "MP has potential to improve performance and its application is highly economical, sustainable and feasible with current resources", offering an alternative to expensive technology-based simulation. It further proposes that teams can share their practical envisioning derived through MP to improve collective performance, positioning MP as an information-sharing practice proximal to the task and related to shared mental models, anticipatory thinking and situational awareness. Unlike reflective practice's retrospective review, MP privileges cultivating foresight.
requirements: Organisational support for MP resources, requiring organisational spaces, leadership and interpersonal expertise, for example instantiation in pre-surgical routines
constraints: The article states MP is still under theorised and little acknowledged, and that whether and how users apply MP post training remains largely unreported
target_learning_goals: surgical performance improvement
team coordination and safety
examples: The article cites recent research suggesting teams can share mental rehearsals to improve collective performance, and describes MP embedded in warm-up routines of attention management, stress control and goal-setting.

article_title: Improving Team Performance and Patient Safety on the Job Through Team Training and Performance Support Tools: A Systematic Review.
citation: Costar, D. M., & Hall, K. K. (2020). Improving Team Performance and Patient Safety on the Job Through Team Training and Performance Support Tools: A Systematic Review. Journal of Patient Safety. https://doi.org/10.1097/PTS.0000000000000746
title: Secure leadership involvement and project champions, and budget time to educate staff on a new teamwork tool's purpose and workflow fit, when implementing team training or performance support tools
description: Across the reviewed studies, the authors stress that leadership involvement and project champions are needed regardless of the specific teamwork practice used. Leadership support helps launch the practice, signals that tools are "critical to quality and safety of care rather than merely an additional administrative task", and reinforces sustained, correct use over time. Implementers should also educate staff on why a tool is being implemented, how it should be used, and how it fits established workflows.
requirements: Leadership endorsement and participation, plus time and due diligence to educate staff on the tool's purpose, use, and fit with established workflows, are needed for implementation and sustained compliance.
constraints: New protocols sometimes require greater time and team participation (e.g., longer handoffs, more team members completing checklist items), which the review notes may lead to some resistance and dissatisfaction.
target_learners: Frontline hospital staff in units such as operating rooms, intensive care units, emergency departments, and perinatal units
target_learning_goals: Sustained transfer of teamwork knowledge, skills, and attitudes to on-the-job performance; improved clinical processes and patient safety
examples: The review reports that leaders may endorse and promote training programs and participate in team training workshops, and that leadership can provide reinforcement when staff use support tools as intended.

article_title: The UK haemophilia specialist nurse: Competencies fit for practice in the 21st century.
citation: Pollard D, Harrison C, Dodgson S, Holland M, Khair K. (2020). The UK haemophilia specialist nurse: Competencies fit for practice in the 21st century. Haemophilia. https://doi.org/10.1111/hae.14002
title: HNA five-domain competency framework for haemophilia specialist nurses with four levels of practice
description: The UK Haemophilia Nurses Association competency framework organises haemophilia specialist nursing competence into five domains — clinical knowledge, clinical/direct care, communication and support, collaborative practice, and research — "supported by indicators for four levels of practice (beginner, competent, proficient and expert)". Each level's indicators provide a standard against which nurses can measure their personal practice, developed through three regional workshops with 66 nurses and consensus ranking of competence against time in practice. It updates the 2014 framework within Health Education England's multiprofessional advanced clinical practice structure.
requirements: Nurses and their managers use the framework to assess existing skills and knowledge and identify learning needs appropriate to personal development
constraints: The indicative timeframes for progressing between levels should be interpreted cautiously because the rate at which nurses gain experience depends on the level of clinical activity in their centre, prior roles and skill transferability
target_learners: UK haemophilia specialist nurses from beginner to expert level
target_learning_goals: Clinical knowledge of bleeding disorders
Clinical/direct care skills
Communication and support
Collaborative multidisciplinary practice
Research engagement
examples: Tables 1–5 print indicators for each domain at each of the four levels, e.g. level 1 clinical knowledge includes understanding the variety of bleeding disorders and their hereditary nature; level 4 includes prescribing replacement therapy in line with qualification.
key_sources: Pollard D, Harrison C, Dodgson S, Holland M, Khair K. (2020). The UK haemophilia specialist nurse: Competencies fit for practice in the 21st century. Haemophilia. https://doi.org/10.1111/hae.14002

article_title: The UK haemophilia specialist nurse: Competencies fit for practice in the 21st century.
citation: Pollard D, Harrison C, Dodgson S, Holland M, Khair K. (2020). The UK haemophilia specialist nurse: Competencies fit for practice in the 21st century. Haemophilia. https://doi.org/10.1111/hae.14002
title: Four-level progression structure with indicative practice timeframes for competency development
description: The framework structures competence progression as four levels, each with an indicative timeframe in haemophilia practice: "beginner, in practice for 0‐6 months (level 1)" through competent (over 6 months), proficient (18–24 months) and expert (a minimum of 3 years). The timeframes were derived by consensus at the HNA annual meeting where delegates ranked their own competence alongside time in practice. Each level's indicators let nurses gauge progression and identify areas for further education.
requirements: Indicators at each level provide a standard against which nurses can measure their personal practice
constraints: The article states the timeframes "should be interpreted cautiously" because experience gain depends on centre activity level and prior roles
target_learners: Haemophilia nurse specialists progressing from novice to advanced practice
target_learning_goals: Progressive development of specialist haemophilia nursing competence
examples: The HNA annual meeting in 2018 asked delegates to rank their own level of competence alongside time in haemophilia practice, producing a consensus based on average time in practice.

article_title: A systematic review of simulation-based training tools for technical and non-technical skills in ophthalmology.
citation: Lee Roxanne, Raison Nicholas, Lau Wai Yan, Aydin Abdullatif, Dasgupta Prokar, Ahmed Kamran, Haldar Shreya. (2020). A systematic review of simulation-based training tools for technical and non-technical skills in ophthalmology. Eye. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41433-020-0832-1
title: Dual-framework evaluation model: Messick's five-source validity framework combined with adapted McGaghie translational outcome levels
description: The review organises its appraisal of every simulator around two complementary frameworks. Validity is judged against Messick's modern validity framework, whose five sources are content, response processes, internal structure, relations to other variables and consequences, each rated 0–2 on a validated scale. Effectiveness is judged against "an adaptation of McGaghie's proposed levels of simulation-based translational outcomes", ranging from internal acceptability (level 1) through contained, downstream and target effects to collateral effects (level 5).
requirements: Studies must report outcome data addressable to at least one validity source or translational level; studies without original data were excluded.
constraints: The review carried out qualitative analysis due to the heterogeneity of study designs, so no pooled quantitative estimates are produced.
target_learners: medical students completing their ophthalmology attachment
target_learning_goals: technical surgical skills
non-technical skills in ophthalmic training
examples: Each row of the review's Tables 2–5 records per-study validity scores for the five Messick sources and a single effectiveness level for each simulator model.
key_sources: Lee Roxanne, Raison Nicholas, Lau Wai Yan, Aydin Abdullatif, Dasgupta Prokar, Ahmed Kamran, Haldar Shreya. (2020). A systematic review of simulation-based training tools for technical and non-technical skills in ophthalmology. Eye. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41433-020-0832-1

article_title: A systematic review of simulation-based training tools for technical and non-technical skills in ophthalmology.
citation: Lee Roxanne, Raison Nicholas, Lau Wai Yan, Aydin Abdullatif, Dasgupta Prokar, Ahmed Kamran, Haldar Shreya. (2020). A systematic review of simulation-based training tools for technical and non-technical skills in ophthalmology. Eye. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41433-020-0832-1
title: Eyesi Surgical virtual reality ophthalmic surgery simulator
description: The Eyesi Surgical (VRmagic, Mannheim, Germany) is "a high-fidelity virtual reality simulator designed for practising intraocular procedures". It combines a mannequin head housing a model eye, an operating microscope, instrument tracking sensors, and software modules for cataract and vitreoretinal surgery steps; the system records performance metrics, enabling scores and feedback to be generated. It is the most extensively assessed ophthalmic simulator in the review, with 33 validity studies.
requirements: Requires the hardware suite (mannequin head, model eye, operative microscope, instruments, foot pedals, touchscreen) and the VR software platform with its training modules.
constraints: Comprehensive validity evidence exists for the cataract modules; response-processes evidence remained limited even there.
target_learning_goals: cataract surgery skills
vitreoretinal surgery skills
examples: Studies in the review trained participants on forceps, anti-tremor, capsulorhexis and phacoemulsification tasks, with training times ranging from 20 minutes to mastery-learning formats.
key_sources: Lee Roxanne, Raison Nicholas, Lau Wai Yan, Aydin Abdullatif, Dasgupta Prokar, Ahmed Kamran, Haldar Shreya. (2020). A systematic review of simulation-based training tools for technical and non-technical skills in ophthalmology. Eye. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41433-020-0832-1

article_title: A systematic review of simulation-based training tools for technical and non-technical skills in ophthalmology.
citation: Lee Roxanne, Raison Nicholas, Lau Wai Yan, Aydin Abdullatif, Dasgupta Prokar, Ahmed Kamran, Haldar Shreya. (2020). A systematic review of simulation-based training tools for technical and non-technical skills in ophthalmology. Eye. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41433-020-0832-1
title: Use simulation to enable focussed, competency-based skills training before treating patients, and strengthen research before full curricular implementation
description: The review argues that the apprenticeship model, in which competence is assumed after a minimum number of procedures, is undermined by inconsistent clinical exposure and by quantity not equating to quality. "Simulation models offer a platform for trainees to improve their clinical and surgical skills, enabling focussed, competency-based training without putting patients at risk." Because most models lack robust evidence, the review recommends that "More robust research is needed to enable effective implementation of simulation tools into current training curriculums."
requirements: Objective assessment of proficiency prior to treating patients, using validated simulator metrics rather than procedure counts.
constraints: The review found poor quality of study design, predominance of descriptive reports, and few studies investigating effects on patient outcomes, so widespread curricular integration is not yet evidence-supported for most models.
target_learning_goals: clinical and surgical skills
competency-based progression
examples: The review's evidence base spans 131 studies across virtual reality, wet-lab, dry-lab and e-learning modalities, with the Eyesi family the only comprehensively investigated models.

article_title: Experiential Learning Interventions and Healthy Eating Outcomes in Children: A Systematic Literature Review.
citation: Varman Sumantla D., Cliff Dylan P., Jones Rachel A., Hammersley Megan L., Zhang Zhiguang, Charlton Karen, Kelly Bridget. (2021). Experiential Learning Interventions and Healthy Eating Outcomes in Children: A Systematic Literature Review. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph182010824
title: Design experiential learning interventions with multiple combined strategies, parent involvement, engaging hands-on activities, theory grounding, and targeted food behaviours
description: The review distils design implications for experiential learning interventions targeting children's healthy eating. It recommends that interventions "include multiple or a combination of experiential learning strategies", involve parents in activities such as cooking and gardening models, make strategies fun and engaging, ground them in behaviour change theory such as social cognitive theory, and target specific food behaviours such as "choose vegetables as snacks". These recommendations derive from patterns across the 25 included RCTs and CRCTs.
requirements: Interventions should include multiple or a combination of experiential learning strategies and be grounded on an effective behaviour change theory
constraints: The review notes the impact of individual experiential learning approaches could not be established because most studies used combinations
Evidence is limited by high risk of bias in most included studies
target_learners: children aged 0–12 years in preschool, primary school, and community settings
target_learning_goals: nutrition-related knowledge, attitudes, and dietary behaviours towards healthy eating
examples: The most effective primary school studies combined games, role-playing, food preparation/cooking, school gardens, and taste-testing; two high-effect studies involved parents directly in intervention activities
key_sources: Varman Sumantla D., Cliff Dylan P., Jones Rachel A., Hammersley Megan L., Zhang Zhiguang, Charlton Karen, Kelly Bridget. (2021). Experiential Learning Interventions and Healthy Eating Outcomes in Children: A Systematic Literature Review.
