article_title: The use of blogs in the education field: A qualitative systematic review
citation: Carlos R. del Blanco, Ivan García-Magariño. (2018). The use of blogs in the education field: A qualitative systematic review. https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.05421
title: Five-category taxonomy of blog effects in education derived through Grounded Theory synthesis
description: The review organizes its findings into five categories derived through Grounded Theory: "(1) eﬀects of blogging on reﬂective practice and learning, (2) eﬀects of blogging on learning engagement, (3) eﬀects of blogging on collaborative learning and students’ interaction, (4) eﬀects of blogging on social support, and (5) eﬀects of blogging on the development of s peciﬁc skills". One study can belong to more than one category since it can have addressed several topics. This taxonomy structures the review's synthesis of 47 empirical, peer-reviewed studies published between January 2011 and June 2013.
requirements: Studies must be empirical and peer-reviewed, published between January 2011 and June 2013, and focused on blogs in education without combining blogs with other web 2.0 tools
constraints: The taxonomy emerged from a qualitative evidence synthesis rather than a meta-analysis, because only 6 of 47 studies used an experimental design and most populations were too small to be statistically significant
target_learners: students across all education levels, from primary up to doctoral education
target_learning_goals: reflective practice
learning engagement
collaborative learning
social support
specific skills such as writing and ICT competencies
examples: Table 1 summarizes the 47 selected studies and their attributed categories across the five dimensions
key_sources: Carlos R. del Blanco, Ivan García-Magariño. (2018). The use of blogs in the education field: A qualitative systematic review. https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.05421

article_title: The use of blogs in the education field: A qualitative systematic review
citation: Carlos R. del Blanco, Ivan García-Magariño. (2018). The use of blogs in the education field: A qualitative systematic review. https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.05421
title: Blogs as educational Web 2.0 tools with four defining features
description: Blogs are Web 2.0 tools whose educational use the review examines. The article defines them by four features: "(1) reverse chronological order, (2) archival o f posts, (3) hypermedia content, and (4) ease of use". Ease of use is described as one of the keys for the popularity and fast spreading of blogs, since a blog can be created and managed without any specific knowledge in programming and databases. Other potential characteristics include a search engine, multi-user collaboration with different roles, and posting of comments for third-party users fostering dialog and feedback with the internet community.
requirements: A blog can be created and managed by a user without any speciﬁc knowledge in programming and databases
constraints: Studies that combined the use of blogs with other web 2.0 tools were discarded from the review to assess the actual efficiency of blogs and avoid uncontrolled relationships among several web technologies
target_learners: students across all education levels, from primary up to doctoral education
target_learning_goals: collaboration
communication
professional writing
information-gathering skills
examples: Herring et al. (2004) classified blogs by genre into filters, personal journals, and knowledge logs, with personal journals predominant
key_sources: Carlos R. del Blanco, Ivan García-Magariño. (2018). The use of blogs in the education field: A qualitative systematic review. https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.05421

article_title: Augmented Reality Technology in Teaching about Physics: A systematic review of opportunities and challenges
citation: Andrej Vidak, Iva Movre Šapić, Vanes Mešić, Vjeran Gomzi. (2023). Augmented Reality Technology in Teaching about Physics: A systematic review of opportunities and challenges. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci11110661
title: XReality framework classifying computer-enhanced realities by whether the real-world environment remains part of the experience
description: The XReality framework, attributed in the review to Rauschnabel et al., classifies computer-enhanced realities by whether the real-world environment remains part of the learning experience. If the real-world environment is at least visually part of the experience, the technology is augmented reality; otherwise it is virtual reality. The review quotes AR as "represents a combination of real and virtual content that is displayed in real time". Within the framework, assisted reality (text-based instructions overlaid on the physical environment) and mixed reality (seamless integration of more complex virtual and real objects) are subtypes of AR, and the term extended reality is suggested to be avoided.
requirements: The real-world environment must be at least visually part of the learning experience for a technology to count as augmented reality rather than virtual reality.
constraints: The framework suggests the umbrella term extended reality (XR) be completely avoided because VR does not extend the real-world environment but replaces its visual aspects.
target_learners: physics students at school and university level
target_learning_goals: distinguishing AR from VR and related reality technologies when selecting tools for physics instruction
examples: The review uses the framework operationally: reviewed papers were excluded when "the given educational technology does not constitute AR as defined in the XReality framework".
key_sources: Andrej Vidak, Iva Movre Šapić, Vanes Mešić, Vjeran Gomzi. (2023). Augmented Reality Technology in Teaching about Physics: A systematic review of opportunities and challenges. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci11110661

article_title: Augmented Reality Technology in Teaching about Physics: A systematic review of opportunities and challenges
citation: Andrej Vidak, Iva Movre Šapić, Vanes Mešić, Vjeran Gomzi. (2023). Augmented Reality Technology in Teaching about Physics: A systematic review of opportunities and challenges. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci11110661
title: Cognitive load theory applied to AR-based learning: germane load fostered, extraneous load minimized, intrinsic load adjusted
description: The review presents cognitive load theory as a relevant theory for AR-based physics learning: working memory is very limited in capacity and duration and may become overloaded, impeding learning. Learning environments induce three mutually additive load types — germane load from learning processes relevant to constructing target knowledge, extraneous load from information not relevant to learning, and intrinsic load from the inherent complexity of the task. For effective learning, "germane load should be fostered, extraneous load should be minimized and intrinsic load should be adjusted (e.g., by segmenting information)". The review links this to AR design via Mayer's multimedia principles, particularly spatial and temporal contiguity and segmenting.
requirements: AR learning environments must foster germane load, minimize extraneous load, and adjust intrinsic load, e.g., by segmenting information.
constraints: If learning with multiple representations is not introduced carefully, it may result in cognitive overload, per Ainsworth's account cited in the review.
target_learners: physics students at school and university level using AR applications
target_learning_goals: managing cognitive load when learning physics concepts with AR visualizations
examples: The review notes AR tools can place words and images near animated or physical objects, e.g., overlaying textual descriptions on real-world car engine parts, consistent with spatial contiguity.
key_sources: Andrej Vidak, Iva Movre Šapić, Vanes Mešić, Vjeran Gomzi. (2023). Augmented Reality Technology in Teaching about Physics: A systematic review of opportunities and challenges. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci11110661

article_title: Augmented Reality Technology in Teaching about Physics: A systematic review of opportunities and challenges
citation: Andrej Vidak, Iva Movre Šapić, Vanes Mešić, Vjeran Gomzi. (2023). Augmented Reality Technology in Teaching about Physics: A systematic review of opportunities and challenges. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci11110661
title: Ainsworth's three functions of multiple representations: complementary information, limiting interpretation, constructing deeper understanding
description: The review describes Ainsworth's theory of multiple representations as an account of how external representations such as AR visualizations support learning. Multiple representations can support learning in three ways: by allowing for complementary information or processes, by limiting the room for interpretation, and by providing the opportunity for constructing deeper understanding. The review illustrates the first function with light intensity distribution graphs paired with an image of a diffraction pattern, and the second with a video of motion alongside a corresponding real-time graph. It warns that "If not introduced carefully, learning with multiple representations may result in cognitive overload."
requirements: Multiple representations must be introduced carefully; otherwise learning with them may result in cognitive overload.
constraints: The theory is presented as relevant for reasoning about learning with visualizations generally, including AR-based learning.
target_learners: physics learners working with AR overlays combining graphs, images, videos and 3D objects
target_learning_goals: interpreting multiple coordinated representations of physical phenomena, e.g., motion videos with real-time graphs
examples: The review's example: a video of the motion potentially prevents the interpretation of a graph as the image of motion, illustrating the interpretation-limiting function.
key_sources: Andrej Vidak, Iva Movre Šapić, Vanes Mešić, Vjeran Gomzi. (2023). Augmented Reality Technology in Teaching about Physics: A systematic review of opportunities and challenges. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci11110661

article_title: Augmented Reality Technology in Teaching about Physics: A systematic review of opportunities and challenges
citation: Andrej Vidak, Iva Movre Šapić, Vanes Mešić, Vjeran Gomzi. (2023). Augmented Reality Technology in Teaching about Physics: A systematic review of opportunities and challenges. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci11110661
title: Embodied, grounded and distributed cognition accounts for AR-based physics learning
description: The review identifies embodied and grounded cognition, and distributed cognition, as theories relevant to AR-based learning. Embodied and grounded cognition holds that "cognitive activity is grounded in sensory–motor processes and situated in specific contexts and situations"; AR enables this by letting learners physically move AR markers to change the distance between simulated bodies or affect simulated meteor motion by moving through the classroom. Distributed cognition asserts that cognition is distributed across "internal human minds, external cognitive artifacts, and groups of people", so external representations such as AR visualizations facilitate learning by preventing cognitive overload in the coupled system of internal and external representations.
requirements: AR activities must couple learner bodily movement or external artifacts with the simulated content for the embodied/distributed accounts to apply.
constraints: These theories are offered as interpretive lenses for AR research rather than tested predictions within this review.
target_learners: physics students using body-tracking or marker-manipulation AR environments
target_learning_goals: learning physics through physically enacted and externally distributed representations
examples: Reviewed studies instantiate these accounts: Enyedy et al. tracked students' movements via ceiling cameras to display 3D objects, and Lindgren et al. had students impersonate meteors in a room-sized AR simulation.
key_sources: Andrej Vidak, Iva Movre Šapić, Vanes Mešić, Vjeran Gomzi. (2023). Augmented Reality Technology in Teaching about Physics: A systematic review of opportunities and challenges. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci11110661

article_title: Augmented Reality Technology in Teaching about Physics: A systematic review of opportunities and challenges
citation: Andrej Vidak, Iva Movre Šapić, Vanes Mešić, Vjeran Gomzi. (2023). Augmented Reality Technology in Teaching about Physics: A systematic review of opportunities and challenges. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci11110661
title: Corpus of 96 AR-in-physics-education articles (2012–2023) from Scopus and ERIC
description: The review's evidence base is a corpus of 96 peer-reviewed, English-language, original (non-review) articles on AR in teaching physics, published between January 1st, 2012 and January 1st, 2023, drawn from Scopus and ERIC. Both research and developmental (classroom physics) articles were included because both may be sources of ideas about AR-based physics learning. The corpus is organized in the review's Table 3 by authors, physics topics, research design and AR-based learning activity, covering topics from electrical circuits and magnetism to astronomy and states of matter.
requirements: Articles had to be peer-reviewed journal articles related to using AR in teaching physics, written in English, and published in the 2012–2023 window.
constraints: Review articles were excluded because they would not provide new, original information about teaching ideas in AR-based physics learning.
target_learners: physics education researchers and teachers seeking AR activity ideas
target_learning_goals: identifying AR-based learning activities and research designs for individual physics topics
examples: Included studies range from marker-based solar system overlays for elementary students to smartglasses-based magnetic field visualizations for university learners.

participation

article_title: Exploring gender differences in the Force Concept Inventory using a random effects meta-analysis of international studies
citation: Purwoko Haryadi Santoso, Bayu Setiaji, Wahyudi, Johan Syahbrudin, Syamsul Bahri, Fathurrahman, A. Suci Rizky Ananda, Yusuf Sodhiqin. (2024). Exploring gender differences in the Force Concept Inventory using a random effects meta-analysis of international studies. https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.16988
title: Interpret FCI scores with awareness of the magnitude and direction of gender performance gaps
description: The article recommends that researchers and educators interpret FCI scores while considering the gendered performance gaps the meta-analysis documented. It states that "When interpreting the FCI scores, they should consider the magnitude and direction of the discovered performance gaps", and that studying moderating variables such as students' background preparation can inform learning design to close the gaps. This principle applies the meta-analytic finding of a moderate male-favoring gap to assessment interpretation practice.
requirements: Educators and researchers must know the magnitude and direction of gender gaps documented for the assessment context they use
constraints: The meta-analysis analyzed only pre-instruction FCI data, so findings may be generalized with caution across testing conditions
target_learning_goals: accurate interpretation of Force Concept Inventory results for teaching and learning
examples: The meta-analysis of 38 studies found a moderate significant gap (g = 0.61) favoring male students, wider in NA-based studies
key_sources: Purwoko Haryadi Santoso, Bayu Setiaji, Wahyudi, Johan Syahbrudin, Syamsul Bahri, Fathurrahman, A. Suci Rizky Ananda, Yusuf Sodhiqin. (2024). Exploring gender differences in the Force Concept Inventory using a random effects meta-analysis of international studies. https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07190

article_title: Review Ecosystems to access Educational XR Experiences: a Scoping Review
citation: Shaun Bangay, Adam P.A. Cardilini, Sophie McKenzie, Maria Nicholas and Manjeet Singh. (2024). Review Ecosystems to access Educational XR Experiences: a Scoping Review. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.17243
title: A review ecosystem is the environment that hosts and maintains experiential reviews of interactive experiences
description: The article defines a review ecosystem as "the environment that hosts and maintains these reviews" of interactive applications such as games and eduXR experiences. It treats the ecosystem as a complex system extending beyond commercial interests to serve diverse stakeholders including educators, and analyzes existing game review ecosystems as the closest established equivalent for designing eduXR review environments.

constraints: Existing ecosystems for virtual reality experiences are either a sub-category of games or still in development stages, and eduXR experiences have little representation within these systems

article_title: Learning Outcomes, Assessment, and Evaluation in Educational Recommender Systems: A Systematic Review
citation: Nursultan Askarbekuly, Ivan Luković. (2024). Learning Outcomes, Assessment, and Evaluation in Educational Recommender Systems: A Systematic Review. https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.09500
title: Outcome-based approach: ERS evaluation should be rooted in the achievement of intended learning outcomes
description: The review adopts an outcome-based approach in which learning is defined through the achievement of intended learning outcomes, and argues that "the evaluation of educational recommender systems should be rooted in outcome-based assessment". Under this approach, target metrics should be learning-centered and derived from learning outcomes, and systems should verify that intended outcomes are achieved through assessment. The authors state that in their earlier works they demonstrated it is possible to align intended outcomes, learning activities, and learning assessment when building an educational product.
requirements: Intended learning outcomes must be defined for the learner, and assessment activities aligned with those outcomes, as in constructive alignment
constraints: The review acknowledges the outcome-oriented approach is not always applicable, for example in the affective learning domain where outcomes are open-ended rather than pre-defined
target_learners: learners in formal and informal e-learning settings
target_learning_goals: achievement of intended learning outcomes
competence, knowledge, and skill acquisition
examples: The review evaluates existing ERS research against this approach, checking what metrics systems optimize and how they verify outcome achievement

article_title: Learning Outcomes, Assessment, and Evaluation in Educational Recommender Systems: A Systematic Review
citation: Nursultan Askarbekuly, Ivan Luković. (2024). Learning Outcomes, Assessment, and Evaluation in Educational Recommender Systems: A Systematic Review. https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.09500
title: Three common approaches to implementing outcome-based assessment in ERS
description: The review outlines three approaches used within the reviewed ERS for outcome-based assessment: "outcomes and assessment were already in place as part of a formal course, or the assessment exercises automatically generated and graded, or their achievement was concluded from indirect observations". In the first, the system logs formal assessment results and optimizes recommendations accordingly, evaluating through experimental groups. In the second, a knowledge-based method models outcomes, assessment activities, and their relations within the system. In the third, traditional assessment is replaced with indirect measures indicative of learning, such as collaboration with other users.
requirements: The first approach requires course organizers to correctly define outcomes and align assessment activities; the second requires domain knowledge and significant manual effort composing outcomes, assessment, and their relations; the third requires the indirect measure to strongly correlate with learning
constraints: The first approach does not resolve the question of efficiency for informal settings; the second raises efficiency questions; the third necessitates identification of strong predictors of learning
target_learning_goals: measuring achievement of learning outcomes
assessing pedagogical effect of recommendations
examples: Three reviewed papers automated outcome-based assessment by linking parts of expected solutions to learning outcomes and updating the probability of achieving the outcome based on which parts of the program were written correctly

article_title: A Meta-analysis of College Students' Intention to Use Generative Artificial Intelligence
citation: Yifei Diao, Ziyi Li, Jiateng Zhou, Wei Gao and Xin Gong. (2024). A Meta-analysis of College Students' Intention to Use Generative Artificial Intelligence. Preprint submitted to Elsevier. https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.06712
title: Integrated theoretical framework combining TPB, TAM, UTAUT2 and EVT variables for GenAI intention
description: The article builds a comprehensive theoretical framework by integrating core variables from classic technology-acceptance theories: TPB (attitudes, subjective norms, perceived behavioural control), TAM (perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use), UTAUT2 (performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, facilitating conditions, hedonic motivation, price value, habit) and EVT (utility value, intrinsic value, costs). Variables with similar conceptions were merged — for example, "we utilised perceived cost that combines discussions on price value from UTAUT2 and costs from EVT" — and performance expectancy interiorises perceived usefulness and utility value. Nine antecedent variables were defined and meta-analysed against students' behavioural intention to use GenAI.
requirements: Variables with similar conceptions must be merged and those without sufficient empirical evidence eliminated to ensure accuracy and representativeness of meta-analytic results
constraints: Small sample sizes for some variables required merging; variables with effect sizes below 3 were deleted
target_learning_goals: understanding and predicting students' behavioural intention to use generative AI in learning
examples: The framework merged perceived cost (price value from UTAUT2 plus costs from EVT) and performance expectancy (interiorising perceived usefulness from TAM and utility value from EVT) into nine coded antecedent variables

article_title: A Systematic Review of Empirical Research on Graphing Numerical Data in K-12 STEM Education
citation: Verena Rufai, Dominik Thüsbj, Sarah Malonecj, Stefan Küchemanndi, Sebastian Becker-Genschowe, Markus Vogelf, Roland Brünkengj, Jochen Kuhnhi. (2024). A Systematic Review of Empirical Research on Graphing Numerical Data in K-12 STEM Education. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED
title: Graphing as a constructive generative activity within the ICAP framework
description: The review frames graphing as an active generative process located at the high end of Chi and Wylie's Interactive, Constructive, Active, and Passive (ICAP) framework. According to the framework, "the effectiveness of learning activities decreases from interactive to constructive and from active to passive activities as learner engagement declines." Generating a graphical representation solely based on numerical data is a constructive activity associated with considerable benefits. The review uses this framing, together with generative learning theory, to predict positive effects of graphing on learning.
requirements: The generated graphical representation is one learners have not seen during learning and is solely based on numerical data, which the review identifies as the condition for the activity to count as constructive.
constraints: The review notes that the way graphing is conducted, such as manually or via tools, might also influence the learning outcome.
target_learning_goals: Constructing convention-based graphical representations of numerical data
Interpreting and understanding graphical data representations

citation: Verena Rufai, Dominik Thüsbj, Sarah Malonecj, Stefan Küchemanndi, Sebastian Becker-Genschowe, Markus Vogelf, Roland Brünkengj, Jochen Kuhnhi. (2024). A Systematic Review of Empirical Research on Graphing Numerical Data in K-12 STEM Education. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED
title: Ainsworth's design, function, and task (DeFT) framework applied to self-generated graphs
description: The review describes Ainsworth's DeFT framework, which proposes that aspects of design, functions, and tasks should influence the creation of learning material with multiple representations. It considers five design parameters: "the number of representations, how the information is distributed across representations, the types of representations, the order of representations, and the amount of support needed to translate between representations." The review applies this framework to argue that self-generated graphs can serve all of Ainsworth's functions and that graphing includes the framework's cognitive tasks, since learners must choose and correctly generate a representation.
requirements: Learners need the ability to describe and use multiple representations appropriately, including choosing a representation based on context, task demands, personal ability, and goals.
constraints: The review restricts its scope to transformations within one register (treatments), such as creating a graph based on a table, and excludes transformations between registers (conversions).
target_learning_goals: Constructing and selecting appropriate graphical representations of numerical data
Translating between representations such as tables and graphs

title: Corpus of 50 peer-reviewed empirical studies on graphing in K-12 STEM education
description: The review assembles a corpus of 50 peer-reviewed empirical studies on graphing in K-12 STEM education identified in SCOPUS, ERIC, and PsychInfo using PRISMA-guided screening with ASReview and Rayyan. The studies were published between 1979 and 2024, with publication rates peaking around 2019 and 2020. Most studies were conducted in the USA, followed by Indonesia and Australia. Participant numbers ranged from three to 745, averaging 116 students (SD = 174), and most studies involved high school students (n=43).
requirements: Included studies examined self-generated or partially completed, convention-based graphical representations constructed from numerical data by K-12 students in STEM contexts.
constraints: Studies investigating graphing based on given verbal-textual or mathematical-symbolical information, function graphs not based on data, and pure graph interpretation of provided graphs were excluded.
target_learning_goals: Graph construction from numerical data

title: Typical implementation pattern of graphing activities in K-12 STEM studies
description: The review maps how graphing was typically implemented across the included studies. Most authors analyzed graphing in a problem-solving environment (n=36), with studies most often conducted in more than one lesson (n=22) or a single lesson (n=17). Participants mostly created graphs by hand (n=29), most frequently constructing line graphs (n=27), and mostly worked with bivariate data (n=34). Participants often did not receive any guidance about how to create graphs, although ten studies provided explicit instructions.
requirements: Graphing tasks require numerical data, either self-generated by students during experiments or provided to them.
constraints: Only one study was conducted in the researchers' lab; most studies took place in lessons or courses rather than controlled laboratory settings.
target_learners: K-12 students, most often high school students
target_learning_goals: Constructing graphs from numerical data in STEM problem-solving contexts

article_title: Towards Enhanced Learning through Presence: A Systematic Review of Presence in Virtual Reality Across Tasks and Disciplines
citation: Zheng Wei, Junxiang Liao, Lik-Hang Lee, Huamin Qu, and Xian Xu. (2025). Towards Enhanced Learning through Presence: A Systematic Review of Presence in Virtual Reality Across Tasks and Disciplines. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13845
title: Five-type presence taxonomy for VR learning environments: spatial, social, co-presence, self-presence, and cognitive presence
description: The review organizes VR presence research around five presence types identified across the included studies: spatial presence, social presence, co-presence, self-presence, and cognitive presence. The abstract states the review provides "a detailed classification and analysis of different types of presence in VR environments, including spatial presence, social presence, co-presence, self-presence, and cognitive presence." Each type is defined by its function: spatial presence concerns perceiving position and spatial relationships, cognitive presence concerns deep thinking and knowledge construction, social presence concerns interaction quality, co-presence concerns shared awareness, and self-presence concerns identity and embodiment. The taxonomy structures the review's data extraction (DE4), its mapping of presence types to task functions, and its design recommendations.
requirements: Studies must manipulate or measure at least one of the five presence types to be classifiable within this framework
constraints: Derived from 78 studies published 2020-2024 in VR education and collaboration contexts
target_learners: VR learners across education, engineering, and collaborative training contexts
target_learning_goals: Immersive learning engagement
Skill mastery
Collaborative competence
examples: The review's data extraction rubric (DE4) codes each of the 78 included studies by which of the five presence types it addresses

article_title: Scaling Success: A Systematic Review of Peer Grading Strategies for Accuracy, Efficiency, and Learning in Contemporary Education
citation: Paul, U., Mantravadi, A., Shah, J., Shah, S., Mylavarapu, S. V., Rashid, M. P., & Gehringer, E. (2025). Scaling Success: A Systematic Review of Peer Grading Strategies for Accuracy, Efficiency, and Learning in Contemporary Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.11677
title: Two-dimensional taxonomy of peer grading systems: evaluation approaches and reviewer weighting strategies
description: The review develops a taxonomy organizing peer-grading systems along two orthogonal dimensions: Evaluation Approaches (summative feedback via rating, ranking, and categorization, plus formative feedback) and Reviewer Weighting Strategies (calibration, back-evaluation, consensus, and reputation). It was built bottom-up: two authors independently analyzed all 122 included studies, identified features (11 and 10, with eight overlapping), and refined them through iterative discussion into the consolidated dimensions. The taxonomy serves as "a descriptive framework and a critical lens to assess the strengths and limitations of various peer-grading approaches across multiple factors such as accuracy, graders learning outcomes, engagement, and scalability."

understanding assessment criteria through grading others' work

article_title: Teaching with AI: A Systematic Review of Chatbots, Generative Tools, and Tutoring Systems in Programming Education
citation: Said Elnaffar, Farzad Rashidi, Abedallah Zaid Abualkishik. (2026). Teaching with AI: A Systematic Review of Chatbots, Generative Tools, and Tutoring Systems in Programming Education. International Journal of Learning, Teaching and Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.26803/ijlter.25.1.1
title: Framework for effective and responsible integration of AI tools in programming education
description: The review proposes a concise five-element framework for the effective and responsible integration of AI tools in programming education. It recommends utilizing AI to provide hints and guidance rather than full solutions, teaching learners to write clear prompts and evaluate AI output, adapting prompts to students' language and local practices, combining AI use with assessments and honor codes to prevent misuse, and maintaining instructor oversight to explain AI outputs and correct misunderstandings. The framework aims to elevate AI "from mere coding assistant to a tool that supports learning, thinking, and ethical use in programming courses".
requirements: Instructor active involvement to explain AI outputs, correct misunderstandings, and guide the learning process
Learners taught prompt skills including writing clear prompts, identifying errors in AI output, and evaluating results carefully
Assessments, simple detection tools, and honor codes combined with AI use to prevent misuse
constraints: The framework is proposed by the review based on its synthesis of 58 studies rather than empirically validated as a whole in this article
target_learning_goals: independent problem-solving and critical thinking
ethical and effective use of AI tools
programming skill development
examples: The review recommends step-by-step problem solving using AI for hints and guidance rather than full solutions, enabling students to think critically

citation: Majid Memari, Krista Ruggles. (2025). Artificial Intelligence in Elementary STEM Education: A Systematic Review of Current Applications and Future Challenges. https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.00105
title: Eight-category taxonomy of AI technologies in elementary STEM education
description: The review organizes the field into eight AI technology categories identified through preliminary scoping: intelligent tutoring systems and conversational AI, automated assessment and feedback, learning analytics and predictive modeling, computer vision for engagement monitoring, multimodal sensing and biometric analysis, adaptive content generation, educational robots and embodied AI, and extended reality with AI enhancement. Each category is defined by its primary functions, evidence level, and main limitations in Table 1, from "Personalized instruction, adaptive hints, dialogue-based scaffolding" for tutoring systems to "Immersive environments, spatial learning, adaptive simulations" for XR. The taxonomy structures the review's synthesis, distribution analysis, and gap identification.
requirements: Studies must address elementary-age populations (K-5/6, ages 5-12) and at least one of the eight AI technology categories applied to educational contexts
constraints: The taxonomy was built from publications 2020-2025 plus seminal earlier works, so it reflects the recent literature landscape rather than a stable classification
target_learning_goals: STEM learning outcomes across science, technology, engineering, and mathematics, individually or integrated
examples: The review used the eight categories to code all 258 included studies and report category shares (45% tutoring/conversational AI down to 4% XR)

article_title: Artificial Intelligence in Elementary STEM Education: A Systematic Review of Current Applications and Future Challenges
citation: Majid Memari, Krista Ruggles. (2025). Artificial Intelligence in Elementary STEM Education: A Systematic Review of Current Applications and Future Challenges. https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.00105
title: Learning-by-teaching paradigm with AI tutees grounded in cooperative learning mechanisms
description: The review articulates a theoretical framework in which elementary students learn by teaching artificial tutees rather than receiving instruction from AI tutors. This pedagogical inversion—positioning the child as expert and the AI as learner—is justified by analogy to cooperative learning: meta-analytic evidence shows peer explanation and collaborative problem-solving link social interaction to cognitive growth in elementary mathematics. Educational robots and teachable agents can be designed to systematically elicit these processes through programmed responses "signaling confusion, requesting clarification, or demonstrating partial understanding", creating structured opportunities for explanatory and metacognitive verbalization within STEM contexts.
requirements: Robot or agent responses must be programmed to elicit explanation, clarification requests, and monitoring of the tutee's understanding
Measurement should capture concept explanations, strategy statements, metacognitive verbalizations, and scaffolding behaviors in student-robot dialogue
constraints: Direct experimental evaluations of educational robots or teachable agents deployed in elementary STEM classrooms remain limited; the framework rests on theoretical parallels with cooperative peer learning rather than direct tests
target_learners: Elementary students ages 5-12 acting as tutors to AI tutees
target_learning_goals: Content knowledge, metacognitive skills, and explanatory elaboration in STEM domains
examples: The review describes children explaining mathematical concepts to a robot "student", which requires articulating understanding clearly and revealing their own misconceptions

article_title: Artificial Intelligence in Elementary STEM Education: A Systematic Review of Current Applications and Future Challenges
citation: Majid Memari, Krista Ruggles. (2025). Artificial Intelligence in Elementary STEM Education: A Systematic Review of Current Applications and Future Challenges. https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.00105
title: Spatial computing and learning analytics framework for XR-based elementary STEM learning
description: The review presents spatial computing as the paradigm underpinning educational XR designs: digital objects persist in users' physical environments with stable spatial registration, allowing learners to walk around, inspect from multiple angles, and manipulate three-dimensional STEM representations. Modern optical see-through head-mounted displays support multimodal interaction through eye-gaze tracking, voice commands, and hand gesture recognition, producing machine-readable behavioral traces including gaze vectors, hand trajectories, head pose, and environment point clouds. These telemetry streams enable multiple levels of learning analytics, from event-level logs to continuous kinematic features, supporting formative feedback, diagnostic learner profiles, and engagement measurement in elementary STEM.
requirements: Principled construct mapping linking observable behaviors to targeted STEM competencies, validated through empirical studies comparing automated behavioral indices to criterion measures
Secure data pipelines for capturing, storing, and preprocessing telemetry streams
constraints: Rigorous empirical evidence for XR effectiveness in elementary STEM contexts remains limited, with most validated implementations occurring in health professions training and higher education; publicly available multimodal behavioral datasets from children using XR systems for STEM learning do not exist
target_learners: Elementary students ages 5-12 using head-mounted displays or AR devices
target_learning_goals: Spatial reasoning, conceptual understanding, and procedural fluency in STEM through embodied manipulation of virtual objects
examples: The review describes AR systems combined with computer vision models detecting assembly errors in construction training, and proposes similar approaches for molecular assembly or circuit wiring tasks in elementary STEM
key_sources: Majid Memari, Krista Ruggles. (2025). Artificial Intelligence in Elementary STEM Education: A Systematic Review of Current Applications and Future Challenges. https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.00105

article_title: From Pilots to Practices: A Scoping Review of GenAI-Enabled Personalization in Computer Science Education
citation: Reihanian, I.; Hou, Y.; Sun, Q. (2026). From Pilots to Practices: A Scoping Review of GenAI-Enabled Personalization in Computer Science Education. AI. https://doi.org/10.3390/ai7010006
title: Exploration-first adoption framework for GenAI personalization in CS education
description: The review proposes an exploration-first deployment stance in which instructors and institutions "pilot small instrument interactions" and "scale in response to evidence, with learning-preserving defaults built into tools and policies." Concretely it specifies help-design defaults that preserve productive struggle (explanation-first hints, solution withholding, graduated hint ladders with reflection prompts), artifact grounding in student code, failing tests, and assignment specifications, human-in-the-loop audits of generated tests, items, and grades with logs retained for pedagogy and moderation, a pilot-measure-scale cycle, and enablement governance with vetted instances, data minimization, and allow-lists plus process evidence instead of AI detectors. The framework is the review's organizing proposal for moving from pilots to institutionalized practice.
requirements: Instructors and institutions pilot small instrumented interactions before scaling
Learning-preserving defaults built into tools and policies
Human-in-the-loop audits of generated tests, items, and grades with logs retained
Enablement governance: vetted or enterprise instances, data minimization, and prompt and version change logs
constraints: The review presents this as a proposal based on patterns in successful deployments, not a tested intervention; it states the aim is not to enforce hard thresholds but to encourage routine monitoring and structured decision-making
target_learners: Higher-education computer science learners and instructors
target_learning_goals: Preserving productive struggle while scaling personalized support
Durable learning and fairness in GenAI-enabled personalization
examples: The review's phased roadmap (Table 5) operationalizes the framework: foundation (working group, vendor vetting, policy template), pilot (1–2 sections with instrumented metrics), evaluation (process and outcome metrics, equity stratification), scale, and sustain phases with illustrative success indicators
key_sources: Reihanian, I.; Hou, Y.; Sun, Q. (2026). From Pilots to Practices: A Scoping Review of GenAI-Enabled Personalization in Computer Science Education. AI. https://doi.org/10.3390/ai7010006

article_title: From Pilots to Practices: A Scoping Review of GenAI-Enabled Personalization in Computer Science Education
citation: Reihanian, I.; Hou, Y.; Sun, Q. (2026). From Pilots to Practices: A Scoping Review of GenAI-Enabled Personalization in Computer Science Education. AI. https://doi.org/10.3390/ai7010006
title: Theoretical grounding: GenAI personalization as a mechanism for implementing evidence-based learning-science practices at scale
description: The review connects its design-pattern findings to four established learning-science constructs. Solution-withholding designs connect to desirable difficulties theory, where introducing challenges that require effort during learning can improve long-term retention and transfer; graduated hint ladders operationalize the distinction between productive and unproductive struggle. Course-aligned worked examples and Parsons problems reflect worked-example research and the key insight of fading, progressively reducing support as competence grows, with LLMs enabling dynamic, individualized fading at finer granularity than cohort-level progressions. Test-driven tutoring and rubric-guided feedback exemplify assessment for learning, making success criteria explicit and creating revision opportunities. Artifact-grounded assistance aligns with cognitive load theory, where context-aware hints reduce the load of translating generic advice to specific code. The review concludes that GenAI personalization is not pedagogically novel so much as a mechanism for implementing evidence-based practices at scale.
requirements: Designs must preserve theoretically grounded features (desirable difficulty, graduated scaffolding, and criterion transparency) rather than optimizing for superficial metrics
constraints: The review presents these as interpretive connections to explain why certain design patterns succeed, not as empirically tested mediations
target_learning_goals: Long-term retention and transfer
Schema construction and self-regulated improvement
examples: The review states that GenAI personalization appears most promising when it maintains challenge within the zone of proximal development while reducing unproductive struggle such as environment setup, obscure syntax errors, and tooling friction
key_sources: Reihanian, I.; Hou, Y.; Sun, Q. (2026). From Pilots to Practices: A Scoping Review of GenAI-Enabled Personalization in Computer Science Education. AI. https://doi.org/10.3390/ai7010006

article_title: Effects of Physics Teaching Materials on Student Critical Thinking and Creative Thinking Skills: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Serli Ahzari, Asrizal, Usmeldi. (2024). Effects of Physics Teaching Materials on Student' Critical Thinking and Creative Thinking Skills: A Meta-Analysis. Jurnal Penelitian Pembelajaran Fisika (JPPF). https://jppf.ppj.unp.ac.id/index.php/jppf/article/view/129627
title: Use modules and student worksheets as the physics teaching material formats most strongly associated with critical and creative thinking gains
description: The article recommends that physics educators and curriculum developers favor modules and student worksheets when designing materials for 21st-century thinking skills, because these formats showed the highest average effect sizes in its meta-analysis. It states "the use of modules and student worksheets in physics learning can make a significant contribution to improving students' critical skills and creative thinking skills." The recommendation rests on the stratified comparison of material types in Table 3.
requirements: Materials must be designed for high school physics learning contexts as in the sampled articles
constraints: Based on only 20 national-journal articles from 2019-2023, a scope the authors themselves flag as limited
target_learning_goals: critical thinking skills
creative thinking skills
examples: The meta-analysis coded 22 effect sizes across four material types and found modules (3.93) and student worksheets (3.97) in the high category while general teaching materials (0.23) were medium

article_title: Effects of Physics Teaching Materials on Student Critical Thinking and Creative Thinking Skills: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Serli Ahzari, Asrizal, Usmeldi. (2024). Effects of Physics Teaching Materials on Student' Critical Thinking and Creative Thinking Skills: A Meta-Analysis. Jurnal Penelitian Pembelajaran Fisika (JPPF). https://jppf.ppj.unp.ac.id/index.php/jppf/article/view/129627
title: Constructivist learning theory as the explanatory account for high effect sizes of modules and worksheets
description: The article interprets its meta-analytic findings through constructivist learning theory, which it describes as positing that "active engagement in knowledge construction is crucial for deep learning." It argues well-designed physics modules promote deeper cognitive processing through guided exploration and reflection, and that student worksheets scaffold higher-order thinking when they include explicit prompts for analysis and evaluation. This account is offered as the authors' interpretation of why modules and worksheets showed the largest effects.
requirements: Materials must actively engage learners in knowledge construction rather than passive reading
constraints: The article presents this as an interpretive alignment with literature, not as a mechanism tested within the meta-analysis
target_learning_goals: critical thinking skills
creative thinking skills
examples: The discussion links the module effect size (ES = 3.93) to constructivist principles citing Chen (2023), and worksheet scaffolding to Yulkifli et al. (2022)

article_title: Autoscoring Anticlimax: A Meta-analytic Understanding of AI's Short-answer Shortcomings and Wording Weaknesses
citation: Michael Hardy. (2026). Autoscoring Anticlimax: A Meta-analytic Understanding of AI's Short-answer Shortcomings and Wording Weaknesses. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.04820
title: Autoregressive training objective misalignment account of LLM autoscoring failure
description: The article proposes that LLM short-answer scoring failures follow from the autoregressive pretraining objective, which "rewards fluency, local coherence, and surface-form patterning" rather than the deep semantic comprehension, inferential reasoning, and rubric-grounded ordinal decision rules that scoring child-written text demands. Decoder-only architectures optimize unidirectional likelihood p(xt|x<t), while the signal that matters in grading is often bidirectional and non-local, better supported by encoder objectives that denoise and model p(xmasked|x context). This account explains the meta-analytic regularities: meaning dependence penalties, decoder underperformance, tokenizer/vocabulary effects, and prompt sensitivity.
requirements: Models trained autoregressively on internet text; scoring tasks requiring rubric-consistent ordinal judgments of child-written responses
constraints: The article states vocabulary size and tokenizer family are partially confounded with model families, so causal interpretations should be made cautiously; only the direction (and not the magnitude) of estimated coefficients should be considered
target_learners: K-12 students whose written short answers are scored
target_learning_goals: Trustworthy automated assessment of student learning from short constructed responses
examples: The meta-regression of 890 QWK results shows the read indicator negative across specifications and the gpt coefficient negative in the Bayesian fit, which the article links to autoregressive bias
key_sources: Michael Hardy. (2026). Autoscoring Anticlimax: A Meta-analytic Understanding of AI's Short-answer Shortcomings and Wording Weaknesses. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.04820

article_title: Autoscoring Anticlimax: A Meta-analytic Understanding of AI's Short-answer Shortcomings and Wording Weaknesses
citation: Michael Hardy. (2026). Autoscoring Anticlimax: A Meta-analytic Understanding of AI's Short-answer Shortcomings and Wording Weaknesses. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.04820
title: Design LLM scoring systems for robustness to child text by testing sensitivity to misspellings, invented words, and nonstandard morphology, and avoiding extremes of vocabulary size
description: The article states that "Tokenization and vocabulary design are not incidental implementation details; they are part of the reliability mechanism" for scoring child-written responses. Practitioners should "explicitly test sensitivity to misspellings, invented words, and nonstandard morphology, and avoid extremes of vocabulary size". This principle follows from the meta-analytic finding that extremely small vocabularies over-fragment idiosyncratic spellings while extremely large vocabularies include rare or under-trained tokens that behave unpredictably on out-of-distribution orthography, both reducing scoring reliability.
requirements: Explicit sensitivity testing during model selection or training for child-written responses; vocabulary design treated as part of the reliability mechanism
constraints: The article notes vocabulary size and tokenizer family are partially confounded with model families in the ecosystem
target_learners: K-12 students, especially younger children whose writing employs phonetic spelling and imperfect word approximations
target_learning_goals: Accurate and fair automated scoring of child-written short answers
examples: The article's observation that children learning to write often employ phonetic spelling and imperfect word approximations that are out-of-vocabulary for GPT models but easily decipherable for humans
key_sources: Michael Hardy. (2026). Autoscoring Anticlimax: A Meta-analytic Understanding of AI's Short-answer Shortcomings and Wording Weaknesses. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.04820

article_title: Autoscoring Anticlimax: A Meta-analytic Understanding of AI's Short-answer Shortcomings and Wording Weaknesses
citation: Michael Hardy. (2026). Autoscoring Anticlimax: A Meta-analytic Understanding of AI's Short-answer Shortcomings and Wording Weaknesses. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.04820
title: Treat meaning-dependent items as a separate evaluation regime rather than averaging them with surface-aligned items
description: The article recommends that "Meaning-dependent items should be evaluated and monitored separately" because if an assessment mixes surface-aligned and meaning-dependent items, "a single overall QWK obscures the most consequential failures". This principle operationalizes the meta-analytic finding that the read indicator is negative across specifications: items requiring semantic integration systematically lower LLM-human agreement. Monitoring these items separately makes the regime where rubric interpretation, negation, partial credit logic, and child-specific phrasing matter visible to practitioners.
requirements: Item-level classification of assessment items as meaning-dependent versus surface-aligned; separate monitoring pipelines for each regime
constraints: The article states this applies when an assessment mixes surface-aligned and meaning-dependent items
target_learners: K-12 students assessed with mixed item types
target_learning_goals: Detecting consequential LLM scoring failures on semantic-interpretation items
examples: The article's recommendation that practitioners avoid anthropomorphizing item difficulty and use human reliability metrics as quality control for labels rather than as a proxy for expected model behavior

article_title: Autoscoring Anticlimax: A Meta-analytic Understanding of AI's Short-answer Shortcomings and Wording Weaknesses
citation: Michael Hardy. (2026). Autoscoring Anticlimax: A Meta-analytic Understanding of AI's Short-answer Shortcomings and Wording Weaknesses. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.04820
title: ASAP-SAS corpus of short-answer scoring prompts and rubrics
description: The ASAP-SAS corpus "comprises diverse prompts and scoring rubrics for short answer scoring" and was the subject of a Kaggle competition from over a decade ago. It contains 10 rubric-scored items used across the meta-analyzed studies, with human-rater QWK benchmarks available for each item (Shermis, 2015). Despite sophisticated prompt engineering and fine-tuning, state-of-the-art models including frontier decoders fall short of human-level agreement on this corpus. The dataset is publicly available at https://www.kaggle.com/c/asap-sas.
requirements: Rubric-scored items with human rater agreement benchmarks for covariate control
constraints: The article notes state-of-the-art LLM autoscoring models on this publicly available dataset are not transferrable to other applications as they consist of computationally heavy ensembles fine-tuned to a single question
target_learners: K-12 students whose short answers populate the corpus
target_learning_goals: Benchmarking automated short-answer scoring against human agreement
examples: The meta-analysis aggregated 890 observed agreement coefficients from studies evaluating LLMs on this common set of J=10 rubric-scored items

article_title: Systematic reviews, systematic error and the acquisition of clinical knowledge.
citation: Mickenautsch Steffen. (2010). Systematic reviews, systematic error and the acquisition of clinical knowledge. BMC Medical Research Methodology. https://doi.org/10.1186/1471-2288-10-53
title: Analysis-synthesis unity model of clinical knowledge acquisition
description: The article proposes a model in which clinical knowledge acquisition depends on the interaction between analytic and synthetic processes rather than their opposition. Analytic knowledge from basic science and experience forms the basis for plausible hypothesis development, which is then tested through synthesis by trial, and systematic reviews unify isolated trial results. The article states that "The acquisition of clinical knowledge is based on the interaction between analysis and synthesis" and that systematic reviews inform the analytic knowledge of the clinician without replacing it.
requirements: A plausible hypothesis developed through analysis must precede hypothesis testing through synthesis
constraints: The article presents this as a philosophical proposition rather than an empirically tested model
target_learning_goals: understanding how clinical knowledge is acquired through the interaction of analysis and synthesis
examples: The article illustrates the model with the ART approach in dentistry: GV Black's extension for prevention concept as thesis, Mertz-Fairhurst's observation as antithesis, and Frencken's synthesis through selective caries removal
key_sources: Mickenautsch Steffen. (2010). Systematic reviews, systematic error and the acquisition of clinical knowledge. BMC Medical Research Methodology. https://doi.org/10.1186/1471-2288-10-53

article_title: Systematic reviews, systematic error and the acquisition of clinical knowledge.
citation: Mickenautsch Steffen. (2010). Systematic reviews, systematic error and the acquisition of clinical knowledge. BMC Medical Research Methodology. https://doi.org/10.1186/1471-2288-10-53
title: Include bias-controlling measures in clinical trial study designs
description: The article argues that empirical evidence on systematic error justifies including bias-controlling measures in clinical trial design. It states that "inclusion of bias-controlling measures; such as randomization, blinding and attrition control, into the study design of clinical trials is justified". These measures respectively address selection, performance/detection, and attrition bias, limiting over-estimation of treatment effects.
requirements: Randomization (random sequence allocation and allocation concealment), blinding, and intention-to-treat analysis must be applied to address each bias type
constraints: Trials investigating subjective outcome measures are especially at risk of over-estimation
target_learning_goals: designing clinical trials that limit systematic error and protect internal validity
examples: The article cites meta-epidemiological evidence that over-estimation from attrition bias can reach up to 25% and from inadequate randomization and blinding may reach above 50%
key_sources: Mickenautsch Steffen. (2010). Systematic reviews, systematic error and the acquisition of clinical knowledge. BMC Medical Research Methodology. https://doi.org/10.1186/1471-2288-10-53

citation: Walczak Jacek, Kaleta Anna, Gabryś Elżbieta, Kloc Krzysztof, Thangaratinam Shakila, Barnfield Gemma, Weinbrenner Susanne, Meyerrose Berit, Arvanitis Theodoros N, Horvath Andrea R, Zanrei Gianni, Kunz Regina, Suter Katja, Burnand Bernard, Arditi Chantal, Oude Rengerink Katrien, Harry Gee, Mol Ben WJ, Khan Khalid S. title: Develop educationally sound assessment tools for EBM teaching-the-teachers courses, designed as part of an ongoing evaluation cycle
description: The review concludes that because no well-developed assessment tools exist for EBM teacher courses, the effect of tutors' teaching skills is currently not measurable, and calls for developing educationally sound assessment tools to encourage clinically integrated EBM teaching. It states that "assessment tools need to be designed as a part of an ongoing evaluation cycle" to maintain course relevance and achieve intended objectives. Without such tools, it argues, it would be impossible to ascertain whether TTT courses have the desired effect.
requirements: Assessment tools should be educationally sound and designed as part of an ongoing evaluation cycle
constraints: The review notes existing assessment methods are very few and of poor quality, and identified tools were intended for traditionally conducted courses rather than clinically integrated courses
target_learners: Health care professionals with teaching responsibilities attending EBM teaching-the-teachers courses
target_learning_goals: Effective teaching of evidence-based medicine in clinical settings
examples: The review identified the components of Scherrer et al's twenty-three-question telephone-interview questionnaire as material that might be useful in initiating development of such an assessment tool

title: Kirkpatrick's four-level hierarchy for evaluating educational interventions

It states that "Evaluation of educational interventions must concern at least four dimensions embedded in Kirkpatrick's hierarchy, such as participant's satisfaction, learning (both knowledge and skills), behavioral change (understood as a transfer of knowledge and skills to workplace), and outcomes which are mainly considered as impact on patients". The review uses this hierarchy as a benchmark against which the included articles' assessment practices fall short.

title: Use RLOs as a supplement to, not a replacement for, other delivery approaches such as lectures

The feedback showed that "the RLOs supported learning but students still valued the lectures therefore we recommend that RLOs are used as a supplement but not to replace other delivery approaches". Some students reported needing lecturer support, while others wanted the RLO before the lecture as a basic introduction.

target_learning_goals: understanding meta-analysis concepts within evidence based practice
examples: Students received their usual lecture on meta-analysis and were then given time to work through the two RLOs in a computer lab
