title: RLO development process: storyboard, dual peer review, packaging and release
description: The article describes a quality-controlled development process for RLOs based on a well established methodology. Storyboards (written templates of proposed content) were developed through an iterative development cycle, sent to experts for peer review prior to development, and after a prototype was built the RLOs went through "a second internal peer review by experts and evaluation by students" before packaging and release.
requirements: Academic experts review storyboards for accuracy and appropriateness using a structured proforma
Second peer review assessing usability and appropriateness of media before release
target_learners: healthcare students who will use the resulting RLOs
target_learning_goals: accurate, usable e-learning resources for difficult statistical concepts
examples: Figure 1 shows the stages beginning with team meetings to scope content and ideas for analogies and media
key_sources: Bath-Hextall Fiona, Wharrad Heather, Leonardi-Bee Jo. (2011). Teaching tools in Evidence Based Practice: evaluation of reusable learning objects (RLOs) for learning about Meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3123313/

article_title: Assessing the patient safety competencies of healthcare professionals: a systematic review.
citation: Okuyama Ayako, Martowirono Kartinie, Bijnen Bart. (2011). Assessing the patient safety competencies of healthcare professionals: a systematic review. BMJ Quality & Safety. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3203526/
title: Match assessment methods to Miller's competency levels, using direct observation for higher levels
description: The review recommends that instructors understand the limitations of different assessment approaches and use a range of methods fitting the specific learning situations of Miller's four competency levels. It states that written examinations "tend to measure the potential to perform rather than actual work performance", so more advanced trainees should be assessed through direct observation in simulation scenarios or real practice for the higher competency levels.
requirements: Instructors must understand the limitations of different assessment approaches before selecting methods for each Miller level.
constraints: Written examinations tend to measure the potential to perform rather than actual work performance, limiting their use for higher competency levels.
target_learners: Physicians, residents, medical students, nurses, and nursing students in hospital settings
target_learning_goals: Patient safety competencies including knowledge, skills, and behaviour across Miller's four competency levels
examples: The review identified 20 tools for the 'shows how' and 'does' levels in the domains of managing safety risks, working in teams, and communicating effectively, including three suitable for emergency situations, two for surgery, and two for anaesthesiologists in training.
key_sources: Okuyama Ayako, Martowirono Kartinie, Bijnen Bart. (2011). Assessing the patient safety competencies of healthcare professionals: a systematic review. BMJ Quality & Safety. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3203526/

article_title: Assessing the patient safety competencies of healthcare professionals: a systematic review.
citation: Okuyama Ayako, Martowirono Kartinie, Bijnen Bart. (2011). Assessing the patient safety competencies of healthcare professionals: a systematic review. BMJ Quality & Safety. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3203526/
title: Combine or alternate assessment tools because no single tool covers all patient safety competency domains
description: The review states that each tool has its own strengths and limitations, so complementing methods must be sought to overcome these weaknesses. Because "no tool covered all the patient safety competency domains", the review recommends that tools should be combined or alternated, while noting that the various tools cover the domains unevenly.
requirements: Multiple assessment tools must be available covering complementary patient safety domains.
constraints: The various tools cover the domains unevenly, and more work is needed on 'contributing to safety culture', 'optimizing human and environmental factors', and 'recognizing, responding to, and disclosing adverse events'.
target_learners: Physicians, residents, medical students, nurses, and nursing students in hospital settings
target_learning_goals: Comprehensive assessment of patient safety competencies across all six Canadian Safety Competencies Framework domains
examples: The review found 25 tools assessing 'managing safety risks' but only four measuring 'optimising human and environmental factors', illustrating the uneven coverage that motivates combining tools.
key_sources: Okuyama Ayako, Martowirono Kartinie, Bijnen Bart. (2011). Assessing the patient safety competencies of healthcare professionals: a systematic review. BMJ Quality & Safety. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3203526/

article_title: Assessing the patient safety competencies of healthcare professionals: a systematic review.
citation: Okuyama Ayako, Martowirono Kartinie, Bijnen Bart. (2011). Assessing the patient safety competencies of healthcare professionals: a systematic review. BMJ Quality & Safety. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3203526/
title: Adapt context-specific assessment tools to each discipline rather than copying them across working environments
description: The review observes that the described tools were mainly applied in specific situations such as the operating theatre, anaesthesia, and crisis management, with few tools developed for daily practice in other workplaces. Because "The importance of context in measuring the higher competency levels means that such tools cannot simply be copied and used in other working environments", each discipline or speciality must adapt the tools to its own requirements.
requirements: Each discipline or speciality must adapt the tools to its own requirements before use in a new working environment.
constraints: Only a few tools have been developed for the assessment of competencies in daily practice in other workplaces.
target_learners: Physicians, residents, medical students, nurses, and nursing students in hospital settings
target_learning_goals: Assessment of higher-level patient safety competencies ('shows how' and 'does') in discipline-specific working environments
examples: The Anaesthetists' Non-Technical Skills System (ANTS) and the Non-Technical Skills System (NOTECHS) are available for assessing safety competencies in their respective clinical situations at the higher competency levels.
key_sources: Okuyama Ayako, Martowirono Kartinie, Bijnen Bart. (2011). Assessing the patient safety competencies of healthcare professionals: a systematic review. BMJ Quality & Safety. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3203526/

article_title: Assessing the patient safety competencies of healthcare professionals: a systematic review.
citation: Okuyama Ayako, Martowirono Kartinie, Bijnen Bart. (2011). Assessing the patient safety competencies of healthcare professionals: a systematic review. BMJ Quality & Safety. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3203526/
title: Provide sufficient rater-training for summative assessment with behavioural marker systems
description: The review identifies rater-training as a requirement for summative assessment, noting that the response process provides evidence that raters have been properly trained through faculty development. It reports that rater-training was described for nine tools (26%), "usually only once and briefly", and that in the majority of studies rater-training was either minimally described or not described at all.
requirements: Sufficient rater-training is a requirement for summative assessment.
constraints: In the majority of the studies rater-training was either minimally described or not described at all.
target_learners: Physicians, residents, medical students, nurses, and nursing students in hospital settings
target_learning_goals: Reliable summative assessment of patient safety competencies
examples: The review reports modest inter-rater reliability for some tools such as the ANTS and the Non-Technical Skills for Surgeons, linking limited rater-training to reliability concerns.
key_sources: Okuyama Ayako, Martowirono Kartinie, Bijnen Bart. (2011). Assessing the patient safety competencies of healthcare professionals: a systematic review. BMJ Quality & Safety. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3203526/

article_title: Assessing the patient safety competencies of healthcare professionals: a systematic review.
citation: Okuyama Ayako, Martowirono Kartinie, Bijnen Bart. (2011). Assessing the patient safety competencies of healthcare professionals: a systematic review. BMJ Quality & Safety. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3203526/
title: Miller's four competency levels as an organising framework for patient safety assessment
description: The review uses Miller's four competency levels — 'knows', 'knows how', 'shows how', and 'does' — as its central organising framework for categorising assessment tools. At each level "the trainee should be able to demonstrate the ability to imitate or replicate a protocol, apply principles in a familiar situation, adapt principles to new situations, and associate new knowledge with previously learned principles". The review maps all 34 identified tools onto these levels and argues that ideally a toolbox would assess each competency at the Miller level fitting the stage of training reached.
requirements: Assessment methods must fit the specific learning situations of Miller's four competency levels.
constraints: Competence is context dependent and can only be assessed in the work place.
target_learners: Physicians, residents, medical students, nurses, and nursing students in hospital settings
target_learning_goals: Patient safety competencies across knowledge, applied knowledge, simulated performance, and real practice
examples: The review categorised seven tools at the 'knows' level, three at 'knows how', nineteen at 'shows how' via simulation, and two at 'does' via direct observation of trainees with actual patients.
key_sources: Okuyama Ayako, Martowirono Kartinie, Bijnen Bart. (2011). Assessing the patient safety competencies of healthcare professionals: a systematic review. BMJ Quality & Safety. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3203526/

article_title: Assessing the patient safety competencies of healthcare professionals: a systematic review.
citation: Okuyama Ayako, Martowirono Kartinie, Bijnen Bart. (2011). Assessing the patient safety competencies of healthcare professionals: a systematic review. BMJ Quality & Safety. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3203526/
title: The Canadian Safety Competencies Framework's six domains as the content scope for patient safety assessment
description: The review adopts the Canadian Safety Competencies Framework, finalised by the Canadian Patient Safety Institute in 2008, as the content scope for selecting and analysing assessment tools. The framework "consists of six core competency domains: 1. Contributing to a culture of patient safety. 2. Working in teams for patient safety. 3. Communicating effectively for patient safety. 4. Managing safety risks. 5. Optimising human and environmental factors. 6. Recognising, responding to, and disclosing adverse events". Articles were included only if their assessment content covered these domains.
requirements: Assessment content must cover the domains of the Canadian Safety Competencies Framework.
constraints: The review excluded procedural or technical skills, medication safety skills, general clinical skills, diagnostic skills, and open disclosure skills.
target_learners: Physicians, residents, medical students, nurses, and nursing students in hospital settings
target_learning_goals: The six patient safety competency domains of the Canadian Safety Competencies Framework
examples: The review mapped each of the 34 tools to the six domains, finding 'managing safety risks' assessed by 25 tools and 'optimising human and environmental factors' by only four.
key_sources: Okuyama Ayako, Martowirono Kartinie, Bijnen Bart. (2011). Assessing the patient safety competencies of healthcare professionals: a systematic review. BMJ Quality & Safety. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3203526/

article_title: Persuasive features in web-based alcohol and smoking interventions: a systematic review of the literature.
citation: Lehto Tuomas MSc, Oinas-Kukkonen Harri PhD. (2011). Persuasive Features in Web-Based Alcohol and Smoking Interventions: A Systematic Review of the Literature. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3222186/
title: Persuasive Systems Design (PSD) model as a framework for analyzing Web-based health behavior change interventions
description: The PSD model is a framework for designing and evaluating persuasive systems, conceptualized by Oinas-Kukkonen and Harjumaa. It builds on multiple theoretical constructs, such as goal-setting theory, elaboration likelihood model, and theory of reasoned action/planned behavior. The model presents four categories of persuasive system principles: primary task support, dialogue support, system credibility, and social support. In this review, the PSD model was applied as the framework for identifying various persuasive techniques incorporated into Web-based substance use interventions, with the authors considering it "the most sophisticated persuasive design and evaluation method available" for this context.
requirements: The model requires analysis of the persuasion context, including recognizing the intent, the event, and the strategy for persuasion
constraints: The PSD model is described as yet relatively unknown in the literature
target_learners: Designers and evaluators of Web-based health behavior change interventions
target_learning_goals: Understanding and applying persuasive system design principles to support health behavior change
examples: The review applied the PSD model to categorize persuasive features across 23 RCTs of Web-based alcohol and smoking interventions
key_sources: Lehto Tuomas MSc, Oinas-Kukkonen Harri PhD. (2011). Persuasive Features in Web-Based Alcohol and Smoking Interventions: A Systematic Review of the Literature. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3222186/

article_title: A systematic review of the effects of residency training on patient outcomes.
citation: van der Leeuw Renée M, Lombarts Kiki MJMH, Arah Onyebuchi A, Heineman Maas Jan. (2012). A systematic review of the effects of residency training on patient outcomes. BMC Medicine. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3391170/
title: Provide adequate supervision, extra operation time and attention to individual resident competence to serve patient outcomes
description: The review concludes that residency programs can deliver safe, high-quality patient care while training residents if certain supports are in place. It states that "adequate supervision, room for extra operation time, and evaluation of and attention to the individual competence of residents throughout residency training could positively serve patient outcomes." Sixteen studies highlighted the need for supervision by showing similar outcomes for supervised residents or worse outcomes for unsupervised residents.
requirements: Faculty are primarily responsible for residents' learning and their support is essential, besides the additional time required
constraints: The balance between the investment in teaching (time and money) and delivering care is especially relevant for teaching hospitals; the review notes it would be interesting to determine how much dedicated supervision and additional time is needed
target_learning_goals: delivering safe, high-quality patient care during residency training
developing operative competence through supervised exposure
examples: Sixteen studies showed similar patient outcomes for supervised residents or worse outcomes for unsupervised residents; two large studies with samples over 5,000 patients found similar outcomes for faculty and supervised residents after case-mix adjustment
key_sources: van der Leeuw Renée M, Lombarts Kiki MJMH, Arah Onyebuchi A, Heineman Maas Jan. (2012). A systematic review of the effects of residency training on patient outcomes. BMC Medicine. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3391170/

article_title: Tools used to assess medical students competence in procedural skills at the end of a primary medical degree: a systematic review.
citation: Morris Marie C., Gallagher Tom K., Ridgway Paul F. (2012). Tools used to assess medical students competence in procedural skills at the end of a primary medical degree: a systematic review. Medical Education Online. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3427596/
title: Develop standardised assessment tools with proven reliability and validity for end-point procedural skills certification
description: The review's central recommendation is that medical education needs standardised tools with proven reliability and validity for assessing procedural skills competence at the end of medical training. It argues that "There is a need to develop standardised tools with proven reliability and validity for assessment of procedural skills competence at the end of medical training", so that graduates have comparable skill levels irrespective of country of training. Currently institution-specific checklists lead to inequity of assessment before qualification.
requirements: Tools must have established reliability and validity ensuring unambiguous identification of competence or incompetence in procedural skills
constraints: Procedural skills competence is a complex entity that is not easily objectively defined and is specific not generic
target_learners: medical students at the end of their primary medical degree
target_learning_goals: procedural skills competence prior to certification
examples: The review found no currently used tool in the pre-certification setting has established construct validity, motivating the call for new validated instruments
key_sources: Morris Marie C., Gallagher Tom K., Ridgway Paul F. (2012). Tools used to assess medical students competence in procedural skills at the end of a primary medical degree: a systematic review. Medical Education Online. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3427596/

article_title: Tools used to assess medical students competence in procedural skills at the end of a primary medical degree: a systematic review.
citation: Morris Marie C., Gallagher Tom K., Ridgway Paul F. (2012). Tools used to assess medical students competence in procedural skills at the end of a primary medical degree: a systematic review. Medical Education Online. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3427596/
title: Assess procedural competence with many methods by many people at regular intervals across the curriculum
description: The review concludes that single method, single testing of procedural skills is limited in ensuring clinical competence. It recommends that "Assessment needs to include many methods by many people at regular intervals across the primary training curriculum". This programmatic approach would allow students to receive feedback on their level of competence, be it novice, intermediate, advanced intermediate or expert, and whether they are meeting expected levels for their training stage.
requirements: Provided construct validity of a global assessment tool is assured in the undergraduate setting
constraints: The review notes the assertion of competence in a simulated setting does not guarantee transferability of the skill to the workplace
target_learners: medical students from first to final year of training
target_learning_goals: procedural skills competence development and feedback across the curriculum
examples: The review suggests a global assessment tool could be used incrementally on a yearly basis from first to final year, allowing feedback on competence level relative to peers
key_sources: Morris Marie C., Gallagher Tom K., Ridgway Paul F. (2012). Tools used to assess medical students competence in procedural skills at the end of a primary medical degree: a systematic review. Medical Education Online. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3427596/

article_title: Tools used to assess medical students competence in procedural skills at the end of a primary medical degree: a systematic review.
citation: Morris Marie C., Gallagher Tom K., Ridgway Paul F. (2012). Tools used to assess medical students competence in procedural skills at the end of a primary medical degree: a systematic review. Medical Education Online. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3427596/
title: Establish an international expert consensus on minimum procedural competence required for certification
description: The review calls for an international consensus statement by expert academic clinicians defining the minimum level of competence required in procedural skills at the end point of medical training. It states "Fundamentally an international consensus statement by expert academic clinicians is required depicting the minimum level of competence required in procedural skills at the end point of medical training". Achieving below this expert-agreed level would be a barrier to certification in the interest of public safety.
requirements: Expert academic clinicians must agree the minimum competence level
constraints: The degree of competence could be further honed and improved during residency
target_learners: graduating medical students entering the clinical workforce
target_learning_goals: minimum safe procedural skills competence at certification
examples: The review argues this would ensure the mobile workforce has transferable skill sets irrespective of country of training, making graduates truly fit for practice
key_sources: Morris Marie C., Gallagher Tom K., Ridgway Paul F. (2012). Tools used to assess medical students competence in procedural skills at the end of a primary medical degree: a systematic review. Medical Education Online. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3427596/

article_title: Tools used to assess medical students competence in procedural skills at the end of a primary medical degree: a systematic review.
citation: Morris Marie C., Gallagher Tom K., Ridgway Paul F. (2012). Tools used to assess medical students competence in procedural skills at the end of a primary medical degree: a systematic review. Medical Education Online. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3427596/
title: Item-specific procedural skills checklists as an assessment method
description: Item-specific checklists are one of the two methods of procedural skills assessment the review found in current pre-registration practice, with six of the tools taking this form. They examine all components of a skill and can be used by inexperienced examiners with little instruction, but are time consuming to devise, have issues with reliability and validity, are often site specific and not standardised, and are used mostly in low stakes exams for formative assessment or in the early clinical years.
requirements: High volumes of content specific tools must be devised, which is time consuming
constraints: Often site specific not standardised; used mostly in low stakes exams for formative assessment or in the early clinical years
target_learners: medical students being assessed on procedural skills
target_learning_goals: summative and formative assessment of discrete procedural skills
examples: O'Connor's 21-item weighted suturing/intubation checklist reporting κ of 0.65 suture and 0.71 intubation; Kovacs' 24-item weighted airway checklist reporting κ of 0.93
key_sources: Morris Marie C., Gallagher Tom K., Ridgway Paul F. (2012). Tools used to assess medical students competence in procedural skills at the end of a primary medical degree: a systematic review. Medical Education Online. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3427596/

article_title: Tools used to assess medical students competence in procedural skills at the end of a primary medical degree: a systematic review.
citation: Morris Marie C., Gallagher Tom K., Ridgway Paul F. (2012). Tools used to assess medical students competence in procedural skills at the end of a primary medical degree: a systematic review. Medical Education Online. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3427596/
title: Global rating scales for procedural skills assessment
description: Global rating scales are the second method of procedural skills assessment found in current pre-registration practice, with two of the identified tools taking this form. They assess broader examiner abilities with regard to safety and professionalism, report IRR of 0.85 and construct validity with surgical skills abilities, and can be used with certainty in high stakes certification exams, but require expert examiners to assess candidates.
requirements: Need expert examiners to assess candidates
constraints: Cost – need expert examiners to assess candidates
target_learners: medical students assessed by expert practitioners
target_learning_goals: assessment of procedural competence including professionalism and safety
examples: McKinley's generic procedural skills global tool with 4 themes and 42 items, 12 of them procedural, reporting a κ of 0.79 and predicted reliability of 0.79
key_sources: Morris Marie C., Gallagher Tom K., Ridgway Paul F. (2012). Tools used to assess medical students competence in procedural skills at the end of a primary medical degree: a systematic review. Medical Education Online. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3427596/

article_title: Tools used to assess medical students competence in procedural skills at the end of a primary medical degree: a systematic review.
citation: Morris Marie C., Gallagher Tom K., Ridgway Paul F. (2012). Tools used to assess medical students competence in procedural skills at the end of a primary medical degree: a systematic review. Medical Education Online. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3427596/
title: Competence-performance gap in simulated procedural skills assessment
description: The review raises the concern that certifying competence in a simulated setting does not guarantee the skill transfers to the workplace, framing the challenge of teaching for transfer. It states that "The assertion of competence in a simulated setting does not, however, guarantee the transferability of the skill to the workplace", and that medical educators must facilitate students to be consistent in competent performance irrespective of whether the setting is simulated or an emotionally charged clinical area. Engum's tool, in which students performed real rather than simulated cannulation, is presented as addressing this potential gap.
requirements: Assessment approaches must consider whether simulated competence reflects actual clinical performance
constraints: The transfer claim is supported by unpublished data cited by the authors (MM, PFR, 2012)
target_learners: medical students assessed in simulated settings before practice
target_learning_goals: transfer of procedural skills from simulation to clinical practice
examples: Engum's IV cannulation tool assessed students performing real rather than simulated procedures, which the review says addresses the potential competence-performance gap

article_title: The role of feedback in improving the effectiveness of workplace based assessments: a systematic review.
citation: Saedon H, Salleh S, Balakrishnan A, Imray CHE, Saedon M. (2012). The role of feedback in improving the effectiveness of workplace based assessments: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education, 12, 25. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3432628/
title: Kirkpatrick's four levels of educational outcomes as a synthesis framework for WBA feedback evidence
description: The review uses Kirkpatrick's four levels of educational outcomes to organise and grade the evidence from included WBA feedback studies. The framework ranges from learners' reactions (Level 1) through learning of skills and knowledge (Level 2) and changes in learner behaviour (Level 3) to wider changes in the delivery of care (Level 4). Findings were grouped by type of intervention and described according to levels of outcome, with the review concluding that "The highest Kirkpatrick level reached by any of the studies was level 3 which indicates a change in behaviour".
requirements: Studies must report outcomes that can be mapped to one of the four Kirkpatrick levels for the framework to grade the evidence
constraints: The review found no included study reached Level 4, so the framework could not certify wider changes in delivery of care for WBA feedback
target_learning_goals: formative assessment feedback effectiveness
changes in clinical practice behaviour
examples: The review grouped the 15 included studies by type of intervention and described findings according to Kirkpatrick levels of outcome, finding most evidence at Levels 2 and 3
key_sources: Saedon H, Salleh S, Balakrishnan A, Imray CHE, Saedon M. (2012). The role of feedback in improving the effectiveness of workplace based assessments: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education, 12, 25. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3432628/

article_title: The role of feedback in improving the effectiveness of workplace based assessments: a systematic review.
citation: Saedon H, Salleh S, Balakrishnan A, Imray CHE, Saedon M. (2012). The role of feedback in improving the effectiveness of workplace based assessments: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education, 12, 25. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3432628/
title: WBA feedback should be specific and action-based to be effective for improving practice
description: The review concludes that for MSF to be a useful tool, the way it is used must be improved: "Comments should be provided and these should be specific and action-based." This principle holds that written feedback accompanying workplace based assessments should contain specific, actionable comments rather than global judgements or numerical scores alone, because global judgements do not indicate how trainees should behave to improve their practice.
requirements: Assessors must provide written comments rather than only numerical scores
Comments must be specific and action-based to inform a change in practice
constraints: Time constraints of a busy clinical workload, regarding WBA as cumbersome, lack of training on how to provide feedback, and lack of trust in the formative nature of assessment currently limit implementation
target_learning_goals: improving clinical performance through formative feedback
examples: The review reports that the greater space for free text in the TAB tool allows valuable information to be transmitted back to the trainee which they can use to inform a change in practice, rather than simply a numerical score
key_sources: Saedon H, Salleh S, Balakrishnan A, Imray CHE, Saedon M. (2012). The role of feedback in improving the effectiveness of workplace based assessments: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education, 12, 25. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3432628/

article_title: The role of feedback in improving the effectiveness of workplace based assessments: a systematic review.
citation: Saedon H, Salleh S, Balakrishnan A, Imray CHE, Saedon M. (2012). The role of feedback in improving the effectiveness of workplace based assessments: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education, 12, 25. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3432628/
title: Multisource feedback (MSF) as a workplace based assessment method
description: Multisource feedback (MSF) is a workplace based assessment method in which feedback and scoring are provided by multiple assessors and compiled and fed back to educational supervisors. Tools include the Sheffield Peer Review Assessment Tool (SPRAT) and team assessment of behaviour (TAB). MSF "has the sole purpose of providing feedback of doctors' practice and behaviours", and the review found most evidence supporting feedback from WBAs comes from MSF studies, with 7 of 15 included studies focusing on MSF.
requirements: Multiple assessors including patients, co-workers and medical colleagues
Free-text comment capacity to transmit actionable information
constraints: Unregulated self-selection of assessors introduces leniency bias, as reported in the review
target_learners: postgraduate doctors in training across specialties including general practice, general medicine, general surgery, dermatology, paediatrics and anaesthetics
target_learning_goals: formative assessment of professional behaviour and clinical skills
examples: Archer et al's analysis of SPRAT data from 4770 paediatric trainees in the UK, and Violato et al's 5-year longitudinal study of 250 general practice doctors in Canada
key_sources: Saedon H, Salleh S, Balakrishnan A, Imray CHE, Saedon M. (2012). The role of feedback in improving the effectiveness of workplace based assessments: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education, 12, 25. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3432628/

article_title: The role of feedback in improving the effectiveness of workplace based assessments: a systematic review.
citation: Saedon H, Salleh S, Balakrishnan A, Imray CHE, Saedon M. (2012). The role of feedback in improving the effectiveness of workplace based assessments: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education, 12, 25. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3432628/
title: Mini-clinical evaluation exercise (mini-CEX) as a workplace based assessment method
description: The mini-clinical evaluation exercise (mini-CEX) is a workplace based assessment method in which an assessor observes a trainee's clinical encounter and provides feedback and scoring. The review found 3 included studies based on mini-CEX, in anaesthetics training in New Zealand and in primary care and internal medicine in the United States. Studies showed "a positive effect of feedback and a perceived very positive educational impact", with the mini-CEX facilitating feedback even where a strong feedback culture was absent.
requirements: Written feedback fields on the form for strengths, areas for improvement and agreed actions
Sufficient time allowed for feedback during the encounter
constraints: The review reports feedback is offered less frequently than is desirable, and other WBAs such as mini-CEX and DOPS did not show clear evidence of leading to a change in behaviour
target_learners: postgraduate doctors in training, including anaesthetics trainees and primary care and internal medicine residents
target_learning_goals: formative assessment of clinical skills including medical interviewing, physical examination and counselling
examples: Weller et al's analysis of 331 mini-CEX forms in anaesthetics, and Holmboe et al's videotaping of 107 feedback sessions showing recommendations focused on medical interviewing, physical examination and counselling
key_sources: Saedon H, Salleh S, Balakrishnan A, Imray CHE, Saedon M. (2012). The role of feedback in improving the effectiveness of workplace based assessments: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education, 12, 25. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3432628/

article_title: Teaching meta-analysis using MetaLight.
citation: Thomas James, Graziosi Sergio, Higgins Steve, Coe Robert, Torgerson Carole, Newman Mark. (2012). Teaching meta-analysis using MetaLight. BMC Research Notes. https://doi.org/10.1186/1756-0500-5-571
title: MetaLight: free software application for teaching and learning meta-analysis
description: MetaLight is a freely available software application that runs simple meta-analyses and contains specific functionality to facilitate the teaching and learning of meta-analysis. It is a lightweight application that aims to support the teaching of meta-analysis, designed primarily as a teaching aid for use in the classroom and for conducting student assignments. Its interface has been designed to develop understanding of the relationship between effect sizes and their appearance on the forest plot, the impact of selecting a fixed or random effects model, and how funnel plots are constructed.
requirements: Requires the Microsoft Silverlight browser plugin and internet access to run in a web browser, or can run 'out of browser' if needed
constraints: Intended primarily as a tool for teaching and learning rather than for advanced analyses such as meta-regression and Bayesian meta-analysis
target_learners: students learning meta-analysis in higher education
target_learning_goals: understanding meta-analysis methods
interpreting forest plots and funnel plots
understanding fixed and random effects models
examples: Developed to support a series of ESRC-funded workshops to develop capacity in meta-analysis in education in the UK, running from April 2008 to March 2009
key_sources: Thomas James, Graziosi Sergio, Higgins Steve, Coe Robert, Torgerson Carole, Newman Mark. (2012). Teaching meta-analysis using MetaLight. BMC Research Notes. https://doi.org/10.1186/1756-0500-5-571

article_title: Construct-level predictive validity of educational attainment and intellectual aptitude tests in medical student selection: meta-regression of six UK longitudinal studies.
citation: McManus IC, Dewberry Chris, Nicholson Sandra, Dowell Jonathan S, Woolf Katherine, Potts Henry WW. (2013). Construct-level predictive validity of educational attainment and intellectual aptitude tests in medical student selection: meta-regression of six UK longitudinal studies. BMC Medicine. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3827328/
title: Construct-level predictive validity (CLPV) framework for interpreting selection-measure validity
description: The article develops and applies the construct-level predictive validity framework following Hunter, Schmidt and Le (2006): the estimate of the "true predictor-outcome correlation" between the underlying construct measured by a selection test and the underlying knowledge measured in later examinations, correcting for restriction of range, measurement unreliability and right-censorship. It argues that raw correlations within selected entrants are of "little real interest" because selectors need to know how all applicants would have performed. The framework is operationalized via an MCMC-adapted HSL method that yields standard errors and confidence intervals, and is applied in a meta-regression of 57 coefficients from six UK cohorts.
requirements: Requires predictor distributions in both entrants and applicants, plus reliability estimates for predictor (in applicants) and outcome (in entrants)
Requires the Hunter-Schmidt-Le method adapted for right-censored predictors and ordinal/binary outcomes via MCMC
constraints: The Hunter et al. method can produce erroneous results if the predictor measure is heavily right-censored, as with A-levels where many candidates hold maximum grades
CLPV standard errors must be estimated from MCMC chain variability; equivalent N is about a quarter of actual N
target_learners: medical school applicants and entrants in UK selection contexts
target_learning_goals: predicting subsequent undergraduate and postgraduate medical training performance from selection measures
examples: Applied to six UK cohorts (Westminster, 1980, 1985, 1990, UCLMS, UKCAT-12) covering entry years 1972–2009, yielding 57 CLPV coefficients meta-regressed by predictor, outcome stage and year of entry
key_sources: McManus IC, Dewberry Chris, Nicholson Sandra, Dowell Jonathan S, Woolf Katherine, Potts Henry WW. (2013). Construct-level predictive validity of educational attainment and intellectual aptitude tests in medical student selection: meta-regression of six UK longitudinal studies. BMC Medicine. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3827328/

article_title: Construct-level predictive validity of educational attainment and intellectual aptitude tests in medical student selection: meta-regression of six UK longitudinal studies.
citation: McManus IC, Dewberry Chris, Nicholson Sandra, Dowell Jonathan S, Woolf Katherine, Potts Henry WW. (2013). Construct-level predictive validity of educational attainment and intellectual aptitude tests in medical student selection: meta-regression of six UK longitudinal studies. BMC Medicine. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3827328/
title: The 'dark variance' account of unexplained performance variance in medical selection
description: The article proposes that even after educational attainment's strong CLPVs (accounting for perhaps 65% of true variance in first-year performance), the remaining ~35% of variance — after measurement error, range restriction and right-censorship are taken into account — constitutes a 'dark variance' whose nature is not yet properly characterized, analogous to dark matter in astrophysics. The authors suggest some of it probably relates to factors unpredictable at selection such as illness or life events, and some to personality, motivation or study skills. This account sets a theoretical limit on any single selection predictor and motivates searching for additional predictor constructs.
requirements: A predictor (educational attainment) with CLPV substantially below one, so that remaining outcome variance must be explained by other, statistically independent constructs
constraints: The nature of the dark variance is not yet properly characterized; the article offers only probable candidate factors (illness, life events, personality, motivation, study skills) without measuring them
target_learners: medical students and medical school applicants
target_learning_goals: explaining variance in undergraduate and postgraduate medical examination performance beyond prior educational attainment
examples: The conclusion states educational attainment accounts for perhaps 65% of true variance in first-year performance, raising the question of the remaining 35%
key_sources: McManus IC, Dewberry Chris, Nicholson Sandra, Dowell Jonathan S, Woolf Katherine, Potts Henry WW. (2013). Construct-level predictive validity of educational attainment and intellectual aptitude tests in medical student selection: meta-regression of six UK longitudinal studies. BMC Medicine. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3827328/

article_title: Construct-level predictive validity of educational attainment and intellectual aptitude tests in medical student selection: meta-regression of six UK longitudinal studies.
citation: McManus IC, Dewberry Chris, Nicholson Sandra, Dowell Jonathan S, Woolf Katherine, Potts Henry WW. (2013). Construct-level predictive validity of educational attainment and intellectual aptitude tests in medical student selection: meta-regression of six UK longitudinal studies. BMC Medicine. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3827328/
title: Judge selection measures by construct-level predictive validity, not by correlations within the selected group
description: The article argues that a key error in selection research is assessing validity via correlations among those already admitted, which are inevitably depressed by restriction of range and can lead to wrongly concluding that measures like A-level grades are of little value. Instead, selectors should estimate the construct-level predictive validity — the true predictor-outcome correlation applicable to the whole applicant pool — using corrections for range restriction, unreliability and right-censorship. The article demonstrates this with six UK cohorts, showing CLPVs (.450 mean) far exceed raw entrant correlations (.171 mean).
requirements: Data on predictor score distributions in both applicants and entrants, plus reliability estimates for predictors and outcomes
Statistical correction methods (e.g., the MCMC-adapted Hunter-Schmidt-Le approach) to infer the true correlation from entrant data
constraints: Estimates depend on assumptions about underlying distributions; the method can be erroneous for heavily right-censored predictors unless specifically adapted
CLPVs are estimated less reliably than conventional correlations (equivalent N about a quarter of actual N)
target_learners: medical school applicants and admissions selectors in UK and comparable selection contexts
target_learning_goals: accurate evaluation of how well selection measures predict future training performance
examples: The article cites Sir George Smart's 1973 claim that A-level grades had low correlation with medical school performance, and Burt's 1943 'time-honoured fallacy' of judging selection efficiency by order-of-merit prediction within the selected group, as instances of the error the principle corrects

Construct-level predictive validity of educational attainment and intellectual aptitude tests in medical student selection: meta-regression of six UK longitudinal studies. BMC Medicine. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3827328/

title: Six UK longitudinal cohort studies of medical student selection and performance (1972–2009 entry)
description: A set of six prospective cohort studies providing the data for the meta-regression: the Westminster Study (entry 1972–1980, with full AH5), the 1980, 1985 and 1990 St. Mary's cohort studies (with applicant as well as entrant data; the 1990 cohort also has an abbreviated AH5), the UCLMS Cohorts (entry 2001–2004, detailed follow-up including MRCP(UK)), and the UKCAT-12 Study (entry 2007–2009, 12 medical schools, largest study, UKCAT and first-year outcomes). Four are proper selection studies with applicant data enabling range-restriction correction; outcomes span basic medical science, finals, MRCP(UK) and Specialist Register entry.
requirements: Applicant as well as entrant predictor distributions for range-restriction correction (available in four of the six studies)
Longitudinal linkage of selection data to undergraduate and postgraduate outcomes via GMC numbers and examination records
constraints: The Westminster and UCLMS cohorts have entrant data only, so selection ratios for them were modeled rather than observed
UKCAT-12 outcomes analyzed here are limited to first-year performance
target_learners: UK medical school applicants and entrants, 1972–2009 entry years
target_learning_goals: predicting undergraduate medical examination performance and postgraduate outcomes (MRCP(UK), Specialist Register) from secondary-school attainment and aptitude tests
examples: The UKCAT-12 study alone contributed 1,666, 1,768 and 1,442 entrants in 2007, 2008 and 2009 respectively, with applicant distributions for A-levels, GCSEs and UKCAT shown in Figures 3 and 4

article_title: The effect of virtual endoscopy simulator training on novices: a systematic review.
citation: Qiao Weiguang, Bai Yang, Lv Ruxi, Zhang Wendi, Chen Yuqing, Lei Shan, Zhi Fachao. (2014). The Effect of Virtual Endoscopy Simulator Training on Novices: A Systematic Review. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0089224
title: Use virtual endoscopy simulator training as an alternative to conventional teaching for novice gastroscopy learners
description: The review concludes that virtual endoscopy simulator training, in which novices follow a structured training schedule on a virtual endoscopy simulator, can substitute for bedside teaching for gastroscopy novices. It states that "virtual simulator training method could be considered as an alternative to conventional teaching for novices", based on pooled RCT evidence showing superior independent completion and less required assistance for gastroscopy. The recommendation is limited to gastroscopy; the review explicitly finds no supporting data for colonoscopy.
requirements: Novices receive a structured training schedule based on the virtual endoscopy simulator, as defined in the review's inclusion criteria
constraints: The review concludes no data is available to support simulator training effectiveness for colonoscopy
GRADE rated the gastroscopy completion evidence low due to imprecision and lack of instructor blinding
target_learning_goals: Independent completion of gastroscopy procedures
Reduced assistance requirements during endoscopy
examples: The review pooled 15 RCTs (n=354), 9 for colonoscopy and 6 for gastroscopy training, comparing simulator training with bedside teaching or other interventions
key_sources: Qiao Weiguang, Bai Yang, Lv Ruxi, Zhang Wendi, Chen Yuqing, Lei Shan, Zhi Fachao. (2014). The Effect of Virtual Endoscopy Simulator Training on Novices: A Systematic Review. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0089224

article_title: The effect of virtual endoscopy simulator training on novices: a systematic review.
citation: Qiao Weiguang, Bai Yang, Lv Ruxi, Zhang Wendi, Chen Yuqing, Lei Shan, Zhi Fachao. (2014). The Effect of Virtual Endoscopy Simulator Training on Novices: A Systematic Review. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0089224
title: Virtual endoscopy simulators (Accu-Touch, GI Mentor, EASIE, ScopeGuide 3-D imager, virtual reality sigmoidoscopy simulator)
description: Virtual endoscopy simulators are computer-based training systems that let novices practice gastrointestinal endoscopy without procedure-related errors to patients. The review identifies the specific systems used across included trials: "the Accu-Touch colonoscopy simulator", "the GI Mentor virtual endoscopy simulator", "the Erlangen Active Simulator for Interventional Endoscopy (EASIE)", "the simulated ScopeGuide 3-D imager view" and "virtual reality sigmoidoscopy simulator". These systems offer interactive video technology and computer graphics simulation responding in real time to the user's endoscopic movements.
requirements: Interactive video technology or computer graphics simulation that displays endoscopic images in real time in response to the user's endoscopic movements
constraints: No procedure-related errors to patients, per the review's stated advantage over bedside teaching
target_learning_goals: Gastroscopy and colonoscopy procedural skills
Endoscopic manual skills acquisition
examples: Simulator systems were used across 15 RCTs conducted mostly in the USA (8 studies), with 4 in Germany, 2 in Italy, 2 in Austria, and 1 each in Sweden, UK, Denmark, France, Canada and Netherlands

article_title: Problem-based learning in pharmaceutical education: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
citation: Galvao Tais F., Silva Marcus T., Neiva Celiane S., Ribeiro Laura M., Pereira Mauricio G. (2014). Problem-Based Learning in Pharmaceutical Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. The Scientific World Journal. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3950357/
title: Problem-based learning as an educational method for pharmacy education
description: Problem-based learning (PBL) is an educational method focused on self-directed learning, small group discussion with facilitators, and working through problems to acquire knowledge. In a PBL course, the instructor helps students develop problem solving skills, self-directed learning, collaboration skills and intrinsic motivation, leading students to identify what they know, what they need to know, and how and where to access new information. The review applies this method to pharmacy education, where students learn by working with real-life cases.
requirements: Small group discussion of cases led by a facilitator
Working through problems to acquire knowledge
constraints: The review notes the main barriers for implementing PBL are teacher and staff training and a necessary reduction in class size
target_learning_goals: problem solving skills
self-directed learning
collaboration skills
intrinsic motivation
examples: Included studies used small group discussion of cases led by a facilitator, with or without problem solving, across externship, clerkship, and continuing education contexts

article_title: Digital asthma self-management interventions: a systematic review.
citation: Morrison D, Wyke S, Agur K, Cameron EJ, Docking RI, MacKenzie AM, McConnachie A, Raghuvir V, Thomson NC, Mair FS. (2014). Digital Asthma Self-Management Interventions: A Systematic Review. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3958674/
title: Metareview method: systematic review of systematic reviews with AMSTAR quality filtering to map effectiveness evidence and identify research gaps
description: The article uses a review-of-reviews design: comprehensive multi-database searching identified 29 systematic reviews of digital asthma self-management interventions, which were then quality-appraised with AMSTAR so that only reviews meeting predetermined standards (at least 50% of quality indicators plus documented quality assessment of included studies) advanced to data extraction. This yielded 10 reviews describing 19 RCTs whose outcomes were synthesized narratively by outcome domain. The authors frame this as an approach that has "proven helpful in synthesizing a broad base of literature in order to identify research gaps and inform future intervention programs".
requirements: Included reviews must meet AMSTAR quality thresholds including documented quality assessment of their included studies
constraints: Meta-analysis was not possible due to heterogeneity and inadequate information provision within reviews
Data are an extra step away from original research, increasing possibility of reporting errors
target_learning_goals: asthma self-management knowledge and skills
self-care behaviors such as medication use and action plan use
examples: Searches of 14 databases identified 3810 unique citations; 29 reviews met inclusion criteria and 10 passed AMSTAR appraisal

article_title: Transfer of learning and patient outcome in simulated crisis resource management: a systematic review.
citation: Boet Sylvain, Bould M. Dylan, Fung Lillia, Qosa Haytham, Perrier Laure, Tavares Walter, Reeves Scott, Tricco Andrea C. (2014). Transfer of learning and patient outcome in simulated crisis resource management: a systematic review. Canadian Journal of Anaesthesia. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4028539/
title: Kirkpatrick's four-level hierarchy as a classification tool for communicating learning outcome levels in healthcare education evaluation
description: Kirkpatrick's hierarchy classifies learning outcomes resulting from educational interventions in healthcare into four levels: Level 1 (Reaction) measures how learners perceive the educational intervention; Level 2 (Learning) measures acquisition of skills/knowledge/attitudes in a non-clinical setting; Level 3 (Behaviour) measures "learners' behavioural changes in the professional setting, i.e., transfer of learning to the clinical setting"; and Level 4 (Results) measures the effect of learners' actions, i.e., improved patient outcomes. This review used a modified Kirkpatrick model to set eligibility, deliberately focusing on Levels 3 and 4 and excluding studies measuring only Levels 1 and 2. Multiple levels are possible within a single study.
requirements: Outcomes must be measured at the level being claimed — behavioural change in the workplace for Level 3 or patient outcome for Level 4, rather than learner reactions or learning measured in a simulated environment
constraints: The review states Kirkpatrick does not adequately capture studies where the main outcome measure was survival of the simulated patient, and the classification may not accurately capture all higher-level learning outcomes in simulation education because the model was not originally developed for simulation education
target_learners: Healthcare providers including physicians, nurses, respiratory therapists, physician assistants, perfusionists, and paramedics at all levels of practice
target_learning_goals: Non-technical crisis resource management skills such as communication, leadership, task management, teamwork, situation awareness, and decision-making
examples: The review included studies measuring identifiable CRM skills at Levels 3 and 4 and excluded papers measuring Kirkpatrick Levels 1 and 2 outcomes because they focus simply on learner reactions and learning measured in a simulated environment
key_sources: Boet Sylvain, Bould M. Dylan, Fung Lillia, Qosa Haytham, Perrier Laure, Tavares Walter, Reeves Scott, Tricco Andrea C. (2014). Transfer of learning and patient outcome in simulated crisis resource management: a systematic review. Canadian Journal of Anaesthesia. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4028539/

article_title: Transfer of learning and patient outcome in simulated crisis resource management: a systematic review.
citation: Boet Sylvain, Bould M. Dylan, Fung Lillia, Qosa Haytham, Perrier Laure, Tavares Walter, Reeves Scott, Tricco Andrea C. (2014). Transfer of learning and patient outcome in simulated crisis resource management: a systematic review. Canadian Journal of Anaesthesia. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4028539/
title: Continue simulation programs over time rather than treating them as one-time interventions, since teamwork gains decay without ongoing training
description: The review's evidence indicates that simulation-based CRM training effects on workplace behaviour are not automatically durable: in the interrupted time series study, "All CTS measures returned to baseline during the decay phase" once the in situ simulation program stopped, and in another study transfer of CRM skills in the workplace was not retained after a month. This principle holds that simulation-based CRM training should be designed as a continuing program rather than a single time-limited intervention, because observed behavioural gains in the clinical setting erode when training is discontinued.
requirements: Ongoing delivery of the simulation program — the benefits of in situ simulation were observed while the program ran and were lost when it was not continued
constraints: All of the studies included in this review involved one time-limited intervention on a small number of subjects; the authors note it is possible that modification of patient outcome requires a whole series of interventions on many subjects
target_learners: Multidisciplinary trauma and emergency teams, including physicians, residents, nurses, technicians, pharmacists, and respiratory therapists
target_learning_goals: Sustained transfer of teamwork and communication behaviours to real clinical settings
examples: The interrupted time series study compared teamwork behaviours over four periods — pre-test baseline, didactic-based phase, simulation phase, and decay phase — and found all CTS measures returned to baseline during the decay phase

citation: Boet Sylvain, Bould M. Dylan, Fung Lillia, Qosa Haytham, Perrier Laure, Tavares Walter, Reeves Scott, Tricco Andrea C. (2014). title: Simulation-based crisis resource management (CRM) training programs for healthcare teams
description: Simulation-based CRM training programs teach non-technical skills — task management, teamwork, situation awareness, and decision-making — that can be safely practiced in a simulated crisis, with the ultimate goal of increasing patient safety and producing better patient outcomes. Eight of the nine included studies used "a combination of didactic and simulation training approaches in teaching CRM principles", and one study used only simulated mock codes. Interventions included high-fidelity simulation, in situ simulation delivered in the clinical setting, and mock code programs, compared against no intervention or didactic teaching alone.
requirements: The intervention must include simulation-based CRM teaching; interventions not explicitly mentioning CRM terms but teaching relevant non-technical skills during a medical crisis also qualified
constraints: The review excluded papers where teaching and/or assessment of technical skills could not be separated from non-technical skills in an acute care context, and excluded studies measuring only simulated outcomes
target_learners: Healthcare providers including physicians, nurses, respiratory therapists, physician assistants, perfusionists, and paramedics, from trainees to staff
target_learning_goals: Non-technical CRM skills — leadership, communication, task management, decision-making, situation awareness, and teamwork — applied to emergency and high-stakes clinical situations
examples: One study randomized trauma teams to simulation-enhanced CRM teaching or no extra teaching and compared outcomes during real trauma activations; another randomized subjects to scenario-based didactic sessions or scenario-based, simulator-enhanced teaching

article_title: Educational technologies in problem-based learning in health sciences education: a systematic review.
citation: Jun J, Bridges SM. (2014). Educational Technologies in Problem-Based Learning in Health Sciences Education: A Systematic Review. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/jmir.3240
title: Eight roles for technology in learning as an organizing framework for educational technology in PBL
description: The review adopts a framework of 8 roles for technology in learning drawn from the educational literature, used to identify studies for inclusion and to organize analysis of how technologies support PBL. The roles span access to and structuring of information, curriculum platform, communications media, thinking tools, rich contexts for learning, collaboration spaces, a perspective toolkit, and "Scaffolding". The framework frames the review's focus on whether technological affordances support or detract from the scaffolding of student learning in face-to-face tutorials and self-directed learning.
requirements: Technologies must be analyzed against the specific role they play in the PBL cycle rather than as generic additions
constraints: The framework is applied to postsecondary health sciences education in medicine, dentistry, and speech and hearing sciences where PBL is the key pedagogy
target_learners: postsecondary health sciences students in medicine, dentistry, and speech and hearing sciences
target_learning_goals: flexible knowledge
effective problem-solving skills
self-directed learning skills
collaborative teamwork skills
intrinsic motivation
examples: The review used the 8 roles to classify interventions into learning software and digital learning objects, IWBs and plasma screens, and LMSs
key_sources: Jun J, Bridges SM. (2014). Educational Technologies in Problem-Based Learning in Health Sciences Education: A Systematic Review. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/jmir.3240

article_title: Educational technologies in problem-based learning in health sciences education: a systematic review.
citation: Jun J, Bridges SM. (2014). Educational Technologies in Problem-Based Learning in Health Sciences Education: A Systematic Review. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/jmir.3240
title: Educational technologies in PBL should support scaffolding to reduce cognitive load
description: The review argues that educational technologies in PBL are most effective when they support scaffolding of student learning. It states this is particularly the case where such technologies support scaffolding thereby reducing cognitive load and allowing students to learn in complex domains. Technologies including software, 3D models, LMSs, and IWBs can assist students in problem-solving processes by making disciplinary thinking explicit, structuring tasks, and embedding expert guidance.
requirements: Thoughtful instructional design approaches when adapting traditional systems or designing new programs for inquiry-based learning
constraints: Additional cognitive burden due to higher levels of complexity was seen as a possible limitation to effective implementation
target_learners: postsecondary health sciences students in PBL curricula
target_learning_goals: problem-solving in complex domains
reduced perceived cognitive load
examples: The review reports that dedicated software can help learners to construct explanations, structure tasks, and make them more manageable
key_sources: Jun J, Bridges SM. (2014). Educational Technologies in Problem-Based Learning in Health Sciences Education: A Systematic Review. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/jmir.3240

article_title: Educational technologies in problem-based learning in health sciences education: a systematic review.
citation: Jun J, Bridges SM. (2014). Educational Technologies in Problem-Based Learning in Health Sciences Education: A Systematic Review. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/jmir.3240
title: Learning software and digital learning objects as PBL interventions
description: Learning software and digital learning objects were the most frequently examined technology type in the review, with 20 of 28 studies. Software included interactive distance learning programs, concept mapping, 3D visualization, CD-ROMs, Web-based learning portfolios, online virtual/simulated patients, video cases, online cases, and surgical decision-making simulations. The review reports these were used as an aid/supplement or a replacement for traditional formats such as lectures, dissection, and clinical practice, and for bridging the gap between theoretical knowledge and clinical practice.
requirements: Integration of a computer-based learning tool into the curriculum is as important as the optimization of the software itself
constraints: One study found the PBL video scenario to be cumbersome and not imitating real life, therefore of little educational value
target_learners: undergraduate and postgraduate health sciences students
target_learning_goals: knowledge construction
clinical decision-making
collaboration outside the classroom
examples: The review reports that 91% of respondents rated the ErgoROM CD-ROM as either excellent or very good
key_sources: Jun J, Bridges SM. (2014). Educational Technologies in Problem-Based Learning in Health Sciences Education: A Systematic Review. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/jmir.3240

article_title: Educational technologies in problem-based learning in health sciences education: a systematic review.
citation: Jun J, Bridges SM. (2014). Educational Technologies in Problem-Based Learning in Health Sciences Education: A Systematic Review. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/jmir.3240
title: Interactive whiteboards and plasma screens as PBL interventions
description: Interactive whiteboards (IWBs) and plasma screens were examined in 5 of the 28 reviewed studies, all arising in the 7 years before the review plus one 2005 plasma screen study. IWBs were used to support whole-group engagement in PBL tutorials, enable data sharing and construction of shared understandings about patients, and expand the scaffolding choices available to instructors. The review reports that the integration of face-to-face and virtual modalities through a single PBL group's use of an IWB was seamless and supported whole-group engagement.
requirements: IT support must be provided for all students and facilitators when IWBs are installed in PBL tutorial rooms
constraints: There are limited studies to show the relative advantages or disadvantages of using IWBs in health sciences education
target_learners: undergraduate medical and dental students in PBL tutorials
target_learning_goals: collaborative problem solving
shared visualization and argumentation
whole-group engagement
examples: The review reports that IWBs were installed in all PBL tutorial rooms in a 5-year undergraduate dental PBL curriculum

citation: Jun J, Bridges SM. (2014). Educational Technologies in Problem-Based Learning in Health Sciences Education: A Systematic Review. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/jmir.3240
title: Learning management systems as PBL interventions
description: Learning management systems (LMSs) were examined in 3 of the 28 reviewed studies, including WebCT, VMS Portal, and iSUS. LMSs combine course or subject management and pedagogical tools to offer a means of designing, building, and delivering online learning environments. The review reports positive effects including practical guidance about what to learn and how to learn, feedback on accumulated real patient learning, peer comparison, and self-management support, with students perceiving LMSs as the most useful means of communication and resource delivery for PBL.
requirements: Monitoring, support, and development are important for efficient and positive implementation of an LMS in PBL curricula
constraints: Insufficient support, resources, and training might result in less successful implementation of educational technologies
target_learners: medical students in PBL curricula including placement students
target_learning_goals: self-directed learning
communication and resource delivery
managing the learning environment
examples: The review reports that a Web-based LMS included 66 placement students in a PBL medical curriculum with questionnaire responses from 100% of students
