article_title: Educating medical trainees on medication reconciliation: a systematic review.
citation: Ramjaun Aliya, Sudarshan Monisha, Patakfalvi Laura, Tamblyn Robyn, Meguerditchian Ari N. (2015). Educating medical trainees on medication reconciliation: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4373246/
title: Combine didactic sessions, role-play and experiential learning to educate medical students in medication reconciliation
description: The review concludes that a combination of didactic sessions, role-play exercises and experiential learning at the undergraduate level may be effective in educating medical students in how to conduct medication reconciliation. None of the studies concerning the education of medical students relied solely on didactic methods, and 5 out of 7 included an experiential component.
requirements: Interventions should combine didactic teaching with active practice components rather than relying solely on didactic methods
constraints: None of the included student studies assessed more objective outcomes such as increase in skill or accuracy in performing medication reconciliation
target_learners: Undergraduate medical students (clerkship and pre-clinical years)
target_learning_goals: Conducting accurate medication reconciliation
Safe patient transitions of care
examples: Bray-Hall et al. combined introductory didactic sessions, faculty role-play demonstration, self-study, direct patient care and small-group reflection
Lindquist et al. used pharmacist instruction, a standardized patient demonstration, small-group medication history-taking and class reflection
key_sources: Ramjaun Aliya, Sudarshan Monisha, Patakfalvi Laura, Tamblyn Robyn, Meguerditchian Ari N. (2015). Educating medical trainees on medication reconciliation: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4373246/

article_title: The effectiveness of the problem-based learning teaching model for use in introductory Chinese undergraduate medical courses: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
citation: Zhang Yanqi, Zhou Liang, Liu Xiaoyu, Liu Ling, Wu Yazhou, Zhao Zengwei, Yi Dali, Yi Dong. (2015). The Effectiveness of the Problem-Based Learning Teaching Model for Use in Introductory Chinese Undergraduate Medical Courses: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0120884
title: Apply PBL preferentially in laboratory course settings where small-group work aligns with hands-on assessment
description: The article's subgroup analysis and discussion support applying the PBL teaching model preferentially in laboratory course settings, where the authors state that "laboratory courses are typically conducted in small groups, which is more suitable for PBL teaching model adoption" and that laboratory exams "focus more on execution and analytical skills." The meta-analytic evidence shows the examination score advantage of PBL over LBL is roughly three times larger in laboratory courses (SMD = 2.01) than in theory courses (SMD = 0.72).
requirements: Laboratory courses conducted in small groups, as the article states these are more suitable for PBL teaching model adoption
constraints: In theory courses with limited teaching conditions, students may be divided into groups but remain in one classroom that can exceed 100 students, limiting PBL suitability
target_learners: Undergraduate medical students in introductory courses (freshman to junior-year)
target_learning_goals: Execution and analytical skills assessed in laboratory course examinations
examples: The meta-analysis found the laboratory course subgroup examination score SMD was 2.01 versus 0.72 for theory courses, a statistically significant difference (P<0.001).
key_sources: Zhang Yanqi, Zhou Liang, Liu Xiaoyu, Liu Ling, Wu Yazhou, Zhao Zengwei, Yi Dali, Yi Dong. (2015). The Effectiveness of the Problem-Based Learning Teaching Model for Use in Introductory Chinese Undergraduate Medical Courses: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0120884

article_title: The effectiveness of the problem-based learning teaching model for use in introductory Chinese undergraduate medical courses: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
citation: Zhang Yanqi, Zhou Liang, Liu Xiaoyu, Liu Ling, Wu Yazhou, Zhao Zengwei, Yi Dali, Yi Dong. (2015). The Effectiveness of the Problem-Based Learning Teaching Model for Use in Introductory Chinese Undergraduate Medical Courses: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0120884
title: PBL teaching model as defined by Kinkade: small-group, case-based learning with hypotheses and out-of-class objectives
description: The article adopts Kinkade's definition of the PBL teaching model as "a curriculum of carefully selected activities that test the learner's critical knowledge acquisition, problem-solving, self-directed learning, and team-participation capacities." Students work in small groups, generate hypotheses about a given case and learning objectives, work outside of class hours to fulfill learning objectives, and then reconvene and solve the problem. In the reviewed studies, PBL was applied for one semester in experimental groups, either alone or combined with LBL, with teachers facilitating student learning through experimentation, clinical cases, and seminars.
requirements: Small-group student work with case materials and learning objectives
Out-of-class work to fulfill learning objectives before reconvening to solve the problem
constraints: In the reviewed Chinese studies, PBL was applied for only one semester, and in combination courses less than half of lessons used PBL methods due to teaching condition limitations
target_learners: Undergraduate medical students in introductory courses
target_learning_goals: Critical knowledge acquisition, problem-solving, self-directed learning, and team-participation capacities
examples: The 31 included studies applied PBL in disciplines including clinical medicine, integrative Chinese and western medicine, and pharmaceutical science, across 15 courses including anatomy, biochemistry, and physiology.
key_sources: Zhang Yanqi, Zhou Liang, Liu Xiaoyu, Liu Ling, Wu Yazhou, Zhao Zengwei, Yi Dali, Yi Dong. (2015). The Effectiveness of the Problem-Based Learning Teaching Model for Use in Introductory Chinese Undergraduate Medical Courses: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0120884

article_title: Medical wikis dedicated to clinical practice: a systematic review.
citation: Brulet A, Llorca G, Letrilliart L. (2015). Medical Wikis Dedicated to Clinical Practice: A Systematic Review. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4392552/
title: Professional medical wikis may be improved by using clinical cases, developing more detailed transparency and editorial policies, and involving postgraduate and continuing medical education learners
description: The review concludes that professional medical wikis can be improved along three lines: using clinical cases, developing more detailed transparency and editorial policies, and involving postgraduate and continuing medical education learners. The authors state: "Professional medical wikis may be improved by using clinical cases, developing more detailed transparency and editorial policies, and involving postgraduate and continuing medical education learners." Clinical case reports support the emergence of concrete questions of practice and are likely to meet strong clinical interest.
requirements: Editorial policies and user disclosures require both technical and policy supports, since almost only purpose-built platforms are able to manage detailed user data
constraints: The effectiveness of collaborative writing applications in medical education requires further research
target_learners: practicing physicians in continuing medical education
target_learning_goals: building clinical knowledge relevant to practice
archiving, sharing, discussing, and gradually improving clinical case materials
examples: Clinical cases were reported on nine of the 25 wikis; the review notes frequent clinical case reports support the emergence of concrete questions of practice

Among eight medical wikis including learners' contributions, five include spontaneous undergraduate or postgraduate contributions and three have a formal educational goal targeting postgraduate students or practicing physicians in CME
key_sources: Brulet A, Llorca G, Letrilliart L. (2015). Medical Wikis Dedicated to Clinical Practice: A Systematic Review. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4392552/

article_title: Medical wikis dedicated to clinical practice: a systematic review.
citation: Brulet A, Llorca G, Letrilliart L. (2015). Medical Wikis Dedicated to Clinical Practice: A Systematic Review. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4392552/
title: Four information properties framework for assessing medical wiki relevancy for clinicians: accuracy, readability, reliability, and currency
description: The review proposes assessing the relevancy of medical wikis for clinicians according to four information properties: accuracy, readability, reliability, and currency. The authors state: "the relevancy for clinicians of the medical wikis can be discussed according to four information properties: accuracy, readability, reliability, and currency." Accuracy may be impaired in wikis not displaying a review policy; readability was assessed with the Flesch reading ease test; reliability through the 16-criterion information framework; and currency through editorial activity rates.
requirements: Assessment requires site disclosures, sampled articles, and activity data from the wikis themselves
constraints: No validated quality-assessment tool is currently fitted either to wikis or to a professional audience, per the review
target_learning_goals: evaluating the trustworthiness and usability of collaborative clinical knowledge resources
examples: The review applied the framework to conclude that no medical wiki meets all four information properties needed by clinicians
key_sources: Brulet A, Llorca G, Letrilliart L. (2015). Medical Wikis Dedicated to Clinical Practice: A Systematic Review. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4392552/

article_title: Medical wikis dedicated to clinical practice: a systematic review.
citation: Brulet A, Llorca G, Letrilliart L. (2015). Medical Wikis Dedicated to Clinical Practice: A Systematic Review. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4392552/
title: Wiki medium as an asynchronous communication tool embodying learning principles based on constructivism and cooperation
description: The review frames the wiki medium, as an asynchronous communication tool, as embodying learning principles based on constructivism and cooperation. The authors state: "From a theoretical point of view, the wiki medium, as an asynchronous communication tool, embodies learning principles based on constructivism and cooperation [94]." This framing underpins the recommendation to involve learners in medical wikis, since learners' contributions can be part of their curricula as an alternative to mere volunteering.
requirements: Learners' contributions require a formal educational goal or curricular integration to represent an alternative to volunteering
constraints: The effectiveness of collaborative writing applications in medical education requires further research
target_learners: practicing physicians in continuing medical education
target_learning_goals: collaborative knowledge building
archiving, sharing, discussing, and gradually improving clinical case materials
examples: Three wikis had a formal educational goal targeting postgraduate students or practicing physicians in continuous medical education, including Orthochina and UCLA Radiology Residents Pediatric Imaging
key_sources: Brulet A, Llorca G, Letrilliart L. (2015). Medical Wikis Dedicated to Clinical Practice: A Systematic Review. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4392552/

article_title: A scoping review of medical education research in family medicine.
citation: Webster F, Krueger P, MacDonald H, Archibald D, Telner D, Bytautas J, Whitehead C. (2015). A scoping review of medical education research in family medicine. BMC Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4407512/
title: Ten-topic-area taxonomy of family medicine education research
description: The review organizes family medicine education research into a set of topic areas identified through scoping review of 624 articles. The authors state: "The following research topic areas were identified: continuing education, curriculum development, undergraduate education, teaching methods, assessment techniques, selection of entrants, non-clinical skills, professional and faculty development, clinical decision-making and resident well-being." This taxonomy maps the field's substantive foci and serves as a benchmark for assessing future changes in educational scholarship.
requirements: Articles must focus exclusively on family medicine trainees and practitioners and/or primary care with an explicit focus on medical education
constraints: Derived from literature published 2002 to 2012 in English only; commentaries and purely descriptive curriculum papers excluded
target_learning_goals: mapping the substantive topic areas of family medicine education research
key_sources: Webster F, Krueger P, MacDonald H, Archibald D, Telner D, Bytautas J, Whitehead C. (2015). A scoping review of medical education research in family medicine. BMC Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4407512/

article_title: A scoping review of medical education research in family medicine.
citation: Webster F, Krueger P, MacDonald H, Archibald D, Telner D, Bytautas J, Whitehead C. (2015). A scoping review of medical education research in family medicine. BMC Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4407512/
title: Engage methodologists throughout the research process to strengthen education research
description: The review proposes that weak methodological reporting and narrow methodological range in family medicine education research can be addressed by involving methodologists across all stages of research. The authors state the problem "could be ameliorated by better engagement of methodologists throughout the research process." This principle treats methodological expertise as a collaborative, integrated resource rather than a post-hoc consultancy, aiming to improve rigour and diversity of research designs in education scholarship.
requirements: Research teams must include or consult methodologists from the design stage onward
constraints: Stated in the context of family medicine education research where 75% of studies were quantitative and most lacked explicit methodology
target_learning_goals: improving methodological rigour and diversity in education research
examples: The review found 65% of quantitative and 86% of qualitative studies did not explicitly identify methodology, motivating this recommendation
key_sources: Webster F, Krueger P, MacDonald H, Archibald D, Telner D, Bytautas J, Whitehead C. (2015). A scoping review of medical education research in family medicine. BMC Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4407512/

article_title: A scoping review of medical education research in family medicine.
citation: Webster F, Krueger P, MacDonald H, Archibald D, Telner D, Bytautas J, Whitehead C. (2015). A scoping review of medical education research in family medicine. BMC Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4407512/
title: Explicitly ground education research in theoretical frameworks
description: The review recommends that family medicine education research be explicitly theoretically informed, arguing that articulation of underlying assumptions is needed for researchers to critically engage with study findings. The authors state: "research should be explicitly theoretically informed; this can be achieved by engaging scholars with diverse areas of theoretical expertise." The principle addresses the observed lack of stated research paradigms and epistemological assumptions in the field.
requirements: Research must articulate its underlying theoretical framework and epistemological assumptions
constraints: Recommended for a field where most studies did not identify methodology; authors note broader medical education research shares this limitation
target_learning_goals: strengthening theoretical grounding and critical engagement in education research
examples: The authors cite Bunniss and Kelly's argument that articulation of underlying assumptions is needed to critically engage with findings
key_sources: Webster F, Krueger P, MacDonald H, Archibald D, Telner D, Bytautas J, Whitehead C. (2015). A scoping review of medical education research in family medicine. BMC Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4407512/

article_title: A scoping review of medical education research in family medicine.
citation: Webster F, Krueger P, MacDonald H, Archibald D, Telner D, Bytautas J, Whitehead C. (2015). A scoping review of medical education research in family medicine. BMC Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4407512/
title: Scoping review methodology (Arksey and O'Malley framework, advanced by Levac et al.)
description: The review employed a scoping review approach designed to 'map' literature in a particular area, illuminating key concepts and main sources and types of evidence. The authors used "the methodologically rigorous scoping review approach proposed by Arksey and O'Malley and advanced by Levac, Colquhoun, and O'Brien", involving five stages: identifying research questions, identifying relevant studies, study selection, charting the data, and collating, summarizing and reporting results. Unlike systematic reviews, it does not explicitly aim to assess study quality but can identify research gaps.
requirements: Five-stage process: research questions, relevant studies, study selection, data charting, and collating/summarizing/reporting
constraints: Does not explicitly aim to assess the quality of studies; suited to complex topics not extensively reviewed with many study designs
target_learning_goals: mapping the state of a research field and identifying gaps
examples: Applied here to 817 full-text articles screened from 2002 to 2012, yielding 624 included articles from 40 countries
key_sources: Webster F, Krueger P, MacDonald H, Archibald D, Telner D, Bytautas J, Whitehead C. (2015). A scoping review of medical education research in family medicine. BMC Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4407512/

article_title: The impact of feedback of intraoperative technical performance in surgery: a systematic review.
citation: Trehan Abhishek, Barnett-Vanes Ashton, Carty Matthew J, McCulloch Peter, Maruthappu Mahiben. (2015). The impact of feedback of intraoperative technical performance in surgery: a systematic review. BMJ Open. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4480038/
title: Intraoperative performance feedback as a means to improve efficiency of surgical training
description: The review defines feedback as "the provision of information pertaining to the operator's surgical performance with the aim of improving subsequent performance". It frames feedback on intraoperative technical performance as a response to declining operating-theatre time for trainees, positioning it as a key component of future surgical training programmes. Across the three included RCTs, feedback was delivered orally after each procedure, with contents covering outcomes, and in one study benchmarking relative to peers.
requirements: Feedback must pertain to the operator's surgical performance with the aim of improving subsequent performance
Delivery after each procedure as in all included studies
constraints: Optimum means and circumstances of feedback delivery are not yet established
May not be effective in some circumstances or when delivered inappropriately
target_learning_goals: intraoperative technical skill acquisition
reduction of procedural errors
improved operative efficiency
examples: All three included studies delivered oral feedback after each procedure; one used video footage review with a 60 min structured feedback session
key_sources: Trehan Abhishek, Barnett-Vanes Ashton, Carty Matthew J, McCulloch Peter, Maruthappu Mahiben. (2015). The impact of feedback of intraoperative technical performance in surgery: a systematic review. BMJ Open. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4480038/

article_title: The impact of feedback of intraoperative technical performance in surgery: a systematic review.
citation: Trehan Abhishek, Barnett-Vanes Ashton, Carty Matthew J, McCulloch Peter, Maruthappu Mahiben. (2015). The impact of feedback of intraoperative technical performance in surgery: a systematic review. BMJ Open. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4480038/
title: Future intraoperative feedback research should systematically vary source, facilitator, frequency, duration and content
description: The review states that future studies should consider the effect of study variables including source (oral/written), facilitator (expert/non-expert), frequency (every procedure/once daily/weekly/monthly) and duration of feedback (months/years), plus surgeon involvement, standardised assessment means, content, timing relative to the procedure, and opportunities for discussion, correction and learning. This agenda responds to the finding that the optimum means and circumstances of feedback dissemination remain unknown. It also names benchmarking and feedback based on intraoperative recordings reviewed later as variables to test.
requirements: Standardised means of assessing surgical performance, which may be both generic and procedure-specific
constraints: Current evidence base is limited to three RCTs, most with simulated procedures and short follow-up
target_learning_goals: establishing optimum feedback delivery for surgical skill acquisition
examples: The review enumerates variables: source, facilitator, frequency, duration, surgeon involvement, assessment standardisation, content, timing, discussion opportunities, benchmarking, and other interventions such as guidelines and instructional videos
key_sources: Trehan Abhishek, Barnett-Vanes Ashton, Carty Matthew J, McCulloch Peter, Maruthappu Mahiben. (2015). The impact of feedback of intraoperative technical performance in surgery: a systematic review. BMJ Open. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4480038/

article_title: How well do health professionals interpret diagnostic information? A systematic review.
citation: Whiting Penny F, Davenport Clare, Jameson Catherine, Burke Margaret, Sterne Jonathan A C, Hyde Chris, Ben-Shlomo Yoav. (2015). How well do health professionals interpret diagnostic information? A systematic review. BMJ Open. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4521525/
title: Report diagnostic test accuracy using natural frequencies rather than probabilities to support health professionals' probabilistic reasoning
description: The review concludes that presenting test accuracy information as natural frequencies — joint frequencies of two events, such as the number of women who test positive and have breast cancer — rather than as conditional probabilities improves health professionals' post-test probability estimation and speed of calculations. The authors state that presenting probabilities as frequencies may improve understanding of test accuracy information and note this approach has been embraced by the Cochrane Collaboration and GRADE.
requirements: The diagnostic scenario must provide prevalence, sensitivity and specificity information that can be converted into natural frequency counts
constraints: Evidence for improved estimation comes from five studies including three RCTs; the review notes further research is needed on how presentation format influences disease management decisions
target_learners: health professionals including doctors, nurses, midwives and physiotherapists
target_learning_goals: interpreting diagnostic test accuracy information
estimating post-test probability of disease
examples: Five studies including three RCTs found more accurate post-test probability estimation with natural frequencies than probabilities
Two studies found professionals spent an average of 25% more time assessing probability-format scenarios
key_sources: Whiting Penny F, Davenport Clare, Jameson Catherine, Burke Margaret, Sterne Jonathan A C, Hyde Chris, Ben-Shlomo Yoav. (2015). How well do health professionals interpret diagnostic information? A systematic review. BMJ Open. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4521525/

article_title: How well do health professionals interpret diagnostic information? A systematic review.
citation: Whiting Penny F, Davenport Clare, Jameson Catherine, Burke Margaret, Sterne Jonathan A C, Hyde Chris, Ben-Shlomo Yoav. (2015). How well do health professionals interpret diagnostic information? A systematic review. BMJ Open. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4521525/
title: Use visual aids alongside frequency or probability formats to further improve post-test probability estimation
description: The review reports that visual aids to present information, applied to both probabilities and natural frequencies, further improved health professionals' post-test probability estimation beyond format effects alone. One RCT found natural frequencies with graphical aids produced the highest proportion of correct estimates at 73%, compared with 68% for probabilities with graphical aids, 48% for natural frequencies alone and 23% for probabilities alone. The authors recommend visual presentation as a means of facilitating improved understanding of diagnostic information.
requirements: Graphical displays must be designed to correspond with the accuracy information being presented, such as probability modifying plots or circle graphics
constraints: The review states this finding was based on a single study, limiting generalisability
target_learners: health professionals including doctors and other clinicians
target_learning_goals: estimating post-test probability of disease
interpreting diagnostic test results
examples: One RCT compared natural frequencies and probabilities each with and without graphical aids, finding the combined format produced the highest proportion of correct estimates
key_sources: Whiting Penny F, Davenport Clare, Jameson Catherine, Burke Margaret, Sterne Jonathan A C, Hyde Chris, Ben-Shlomo Yoav. (2015). How well do health professionals interpret diagnostic information? A systematic review. BMJ Open. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4521525/

article_title: Online technology use in physiotherapy teaching and learning: a systematic review of effectiveness and users' perceptions.
citation: Mącznik Aleksandra K., Ribeiro Daniel Cury, Baxter G. David. (2015). Online technology use in physiotherapy teaching and learning: a systematic review of effectiveness and users’ perceptions. BMC Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4587774/
title: Technology effectiveness varies by type: websites for practical skills, discussion boards for knowledge and reflective thinking
description: The review organizes its findings around a mapping between technology type and learning outcome. Websites containing web-based tutorials, videos and patient-therapist simulations support practical skills performance, while discussion boards support knowledge acquisition, critical thinking and reflective thinking. As the review states, "The effectiveness of interventions varied according to the technology used." This framework suggests educators should match technology choice to intended learning outcome rather than treating online technology as a uniform category.
requirements: Educators must identify the intended learning outcome before selecting a technology type
constraints: Based on heterogeneous study designs and outcome measures that precluded meta-analysis
target_learning_goals: practical skills performance
knowledge acquisition
critical and reflective thinking
examples: Websites with web-based tutorials and video repositories improved practical skills; discussion forums improved knowledge acquisition measured by final marks
key_sources: Mącznik Aleksandra K., Ribeiro Daniel Cury, Baxter G. David. (2015). Online technology use in physiotherapy teaching and learning: a systematic review of effectiveness and users’ perceptions. BMC Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4587774/

article_title: Which intervention design factors influence performance of community health workers in low- and middle-income countries? A systematic review.
citation: Kok Maryse C, Dieleman Marjolein, Taegtmeyer Miriam, Broerse Jacqueline EW, Kane Sumit S, Ormel Hermen, Tijm Mandy M, de Koning Korrie AM. (2014). Which intervention design factors influence performance of community health workers in low- and middle-income countries? A systematic review. Health Policy and Planning. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4597042/
title: Preliminary conceptual framework of factors influencing CHW performance with three outcome levels
description: The review developed a preliminary conceptual framework (Figure 1) dividing factors influencing CHW performance into three main categories: broad contextual factors, health system factors and intervention design factors. It differentiates "CHW performance outcome measures at three levels (Figure 1): CHW level, mediating processes and end-user level", with CHW-level outcomes including self-esteem, motivation, attitudes, competencies, adherence to standards and procedures, job satisfaction and capacity to facilitate community agency. The framework guided data extraction and categorization of findings, and new subcategories deriving from the literature were added where needed.
requirements: The framework was developed from reading selected international literature and used as the basis for data extraction and categorization of findings
constraints: This review limits itself to presenting intervention design factors; broad contextual and health system factors are presented in a separate article
target_learners: community health workers in low- and middle-income countries
target_learning_goals: CHW motivation, competencies, job satisfaction and adherence to standards and procedures
examples: The framework was used to structure the data extraction form and thematic coding of all 140 included studies
key_sources: Kok Maryse C, Dieleman Marjolein, Taegtmeyer Miriam, Broerse Jacqueline EW, Kane Sumit S, Ormel Hermen, Tijm Mandy M, de Koning Korrie AM. (2014). Which intervention design factors influence performance of community health workers in low- and middle-income countries? A systematic review. Health Policy and Planning. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4597042/

article_title: Effectiveness of problem-based learning in Chinese pharmacy education: a meta-analysis.
citation: Zhou Jiyin, Zhou Shiwen, Huang Chunji, Xu Rufu, Zhang Zuo, Zeng Shengya, Qian Guisheng. (2016). Effectiveness of problem-based learning in Chinese pharmacy education: a meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-016-0546-z
title: Adopt PBL as an optional, supplementary teaching method in Chinese pharmacy education, tailored to local institutional needs
description: The article concludes that PBL pedagogy, shown to outperform lecture-based teaching in pooled Chinese pharmacy trials, should be adopted incrementally rather than as wholesale replacement. It states "PBL methods could be an optional, supplementary method of pharmaceutical teaching in China", and that institutions "should revise PBL curricula according to their own needs, which would maximize the effectiveness of PBL". This positions PBL as a context-sensitive addition to existing pharmacy curricula, not a one-size-fits-all mandate.
requirements: Institutional capacity for smaller tutorial groups and teacher training, since the article notes main obstacles include training of teachers and staff and necessary decreases in class size
constraints: Chinese pharmacy education has special teaching conditions (limited equipment, varied institutional standards, traditional teacher-oriented methods) making direct imitation of foreign PBL models difficult
target_learners: Undergraduate pharmacy students in Chinese colleges and universities
target_learning_goals: Theoretical pharmacy knowledge
Professional reasoning and self-directed learning skills
examples: The 16 included trials implemented PBL across disciplines such as pharmaceutical analysis, natural medicine chemistry, and biopharmaceutics, each with tutorial groups of roughly 4–22 students over one or two semesters
key_sources: Zhou Jiyin, Zhou Shiwen, Huang Chunji, Xu Rufu, Zhang Zuo, Zeng Shengya, Qian Guisheng. (2016). Effectiveness of problem-based learning in Chinese pharmacy education: a meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-016-0546-z

article_title: Effectiveness of problem-based learning in Chinese pharmacy education: a meta-analysis.
citation: Zhou Jiyin, Zhou Shiwen, Huang Chunji, Xu Rufu, Zhang Zuo, Zeng Shengya, Qian Guisheng. (2016). Effectiveness of problem-based learning in Chinese pharmacy education: a meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-016-0546-z
title: PBL as an active-learning pedagogy that engages students more deeply than teacher-oriented lecture formats
description: The article frames PBL's advantage through an active-engagement mechanism: "Learning is most effective when students are actively involved in PBL". In PBL, "teachers and other faculty personnel in a PBL program engage more with students", and the model "can inspire students to engage in proactive learning and thinking initiatives, facilitating a stronger grasp of experimental processes and logic". The authors also note PBL "encourages students to think about and resolve practical problems" and may help students apply knowledge to work situations, improve professional reasoning, and encourage self-directed learning during professional careers.
requirements: Teacher and faculty engagement with students in tutorial settings
Problem-centered curriculum design rather than factual-knowledge dissemination
constraints: The article presents this as the authors' interpretation of why PBL outperformed lectures, not as a directly tested mechanism in the included trials
target_learners: Undergraduate pharmacy students in Chinese higher education
target_learning_goals: Proactive learning and thinking initiatives
Application of knowledge to practical work situations
Self-directed learning during professional careers
key_sources: Zhou Jiyin, Zhou Shiwen, Huang Chunji, Xu Rufu, Zhang Zuo, Zeng Shengya, Qian Guisheng. (2016). Effectiveness of problem-based learning in Chinese pharmacy education: a meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-016-0546-z

article_title: Effectiveness of problem-based learning in Chinese pharmacy education: a meta-analysis.
citation: Zhou Jiyin, Zhou Shiwen, Huang Chunji, Xu Rufu, Zhang Zuo, Zeng Shengya, Qian Guisheng. (2016). Effectiveness of problem-based learning in Chinese pharmacy education: a meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-016-0546-z
title: Corpus of 16 Chinese-language randomized controlled trials of PBL in pharmacy education (2006–2014, pooled n = 1826)
description: The meta-analysis assembles a corpus of 16 articles (representing 17 studies) published in Chinese between 2006 and 2014, previously inaccessible to non-Chinese-speaking researchers. "The sample sizes ranged from 28 to 112 participants and the pooled sample size was 1826 (PBL group = 929, control group = 897)". Studies spanned pharmacy disciplines including pharmaceutical analysis, natural medicine chemistry, biopharmaceutics and pharmacokinetics, pharmaceutical formulation design, and others, with intervention lengths of one to two semesters.
requirements: Chinese-language database access (CNKI, VIP, Wanfang, CBM) for retrieval
constraints: All studies were conducted in mainland China; none assessed long-term professional achievements of pharmacists
target_learners: Undergraduate pharmacy students in Chinese colleges and universities
target_learning_goals: Theoretical examination performance in pharmacy coursework

article_title: A qualitative analysis of virtual patient descriptions in healthcare education based on a systematic literature review.
citation: Hege Inga, Kononowicz Andrzej A., Tolks Daniel, Edelbring Samuel, Kuehlmeyer Katja. (2016). A qualitative analysis of virtual patient descriptions in healthcare education based on a systematic literature review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-016-0655-8
title: Five-category concept map of virtual patient descriptions in healthcare education
description: The article develops a concept map synthesizing how virtual patients are described in the healthcare education literature. Five main categories were developed inductively-deductively, "stemming from a Simulation-based model developed by Issenberg" and the authors' shared understanding of VPs; the categories represent the life-cycle and environment of a VP with three main actors: the patient, the teacher who creates a VP, and the learner who engages with a VP, plus the VP itself as learning activity and the curriculum as environment. The map visualizes concepts and relations using CMap software and is offered as a dynamic resource for educators and researchers.
requirements: A coding frame with categories, subcategories, indicators, examples from the data, and decision rules
constraints: Based on researchers' and educators' views in the literature; the authors state it is unclear to what extent this represents other perspectives, such as the learners'
Related search terms such as case-based learning were deliberately excluded, so additional concepts might be revealed when expanding to such terms
target_learning_goals: Understanding the concept space of virtual patients in healthcare education
examples: The authors extracted 185 VP descriptions from 375 educational articles published 1991 through 2014 and coded them with a frame whose subcategories were developed by subsumption, reaching saturation after coding 10% of the descriptions

title: Involve patients more deeply in virtual patient development beyond providing multimedia material
description: The article recommends moving patients beyond their current role as donors of authentic material in VP development. Patients could act as reviewers or feedback-givers to ensure their perspective is adequately represented and valued, especially for VPs presenting a patient's perspective, where "a deeper inclusion of patients into the VP development seems indispensable". Future VP development and research should focus on including patients beyond multimedia elements and investigate effects on perceived authenticity and learner engagement.
requirements: Willingness of VP developers to involve patients as reviewers or feedback-givers rather than only as material sources
constraints: The article states this recommendation rests on the observation that patients are currently under-valued; effects on perceived authenticity and learner engagement are proposed research questions, not demonstrated findings
target_learning_goals: Authentic representation of the patient perspective in virtual patient scenarios
examples: The article suggests patients could act as reviewers or feedback-givers to ensure their perspective is adequately represented and valued in VP development

title: Develop and share virtual patients collaboratively to lower creation effort and costs
description: The article describes collaborative development and exchangeability as approaches to lower the effort and production costs of virtual patients. Medical schools have undertaken efforts to collaboratively develop and use VPs, and approaches have focused on "the exchangeability of virtual patients"; the eViP project focused on exchangeability among different institutions and across VP systems. Educators would benefit from a sophisticated study investigating the multifaceted costs of VP creation, use, and maintenance depending on the underlying VP technology.
requirements: Institutional collaboration or sharing infrastructure for VP development and exchange
constraints: The article notes branching cases are more difficult to construct and more expensive compared with linear cases, a cost factor that sharing initiatives must address
target_learning_goals: Cost-effective creation and maintenance of virtual patient cases
examples: The group of Berman et al. implemented a model to collaboratively develop VPs and share infrastructure costs among institutions; the eViP project focused on exchangeability of virtual patients among institutions and across VP systems

article_title: Use of theory in computer-based interventions to reduce alcohol use among adolescents and young adults: a systematic review.
citation: Tebb Kathleen P., Erenrich Rebecca K., Jasik Carolyn Bradner, Berna Mark S., Lester James C., Ozer Elizabeth M. (2016). Use of theory in computer-based interventions to reduce alcohol use among adolescents and young adults: a systematic review. BMC Public Health 16, 517. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-016-3183-x
title: Modified Painter classification system for theory use in interventions (mentioned, applied, measured)
description: The review applies a modified version of Painter et al.'s classification system to categorize how each CBI uses theory. A CBI is classified as "mentioned" if an established broad theory is named, "applied" if any associated article describes how the theory informed the intervention, and "measured" if any article includes at least one measure of a construct within the theoretical framework. The authors state the classification system "offers a guiding framework for reporting how theory based principles can be applied to computer based interventions".
requirements: Requires review of all articles associated with a given CBI to classify mention, application, and measurement of theory
constraints: The 'measured' category departs from Painter's 'tested' category, which required over half of a theory's constructs to be measured; the fourth Painter category, building or creating theory, was not used because it was not applicable
target_learning_goals: preventing or reducing alcohol use through computer-based interventions
examples: Applied to 42 unique CBIs, with Tables 1 and 2 listing each intervention's theories, application descriptions, and measured constructs
key_sources: Tebb Kathleen P., Erenrich Rebecca K., Jasik Carolyn Bradner, Berna Mark S., Lester James C., Ozer Elizabeth M. (2016). title: Corpus of 42 unique computer-based alcohol interventions for youth (100 articles, 1999–2014)
description: The review assembles a corpus of 42 unique computer-based interventions targeting alcohol use among adolescents and young adults, drawn from 100 retained articles published between 1999 and 2014. The search "yielded a total of 600 unique articles", of which 500 were excluded. Thirty of the 42 interventions were studied exclusively in the United States; 33 were delivered in school settings and the remainder in home or clinic settings, with study sample sizes ranging from 59 to 20,150 participants.
requirements: Included interventions delivered their main component via computer, tablet or smartphone and targeted alcohol use among ages 12-21
constraints: Interventions intended to treat a substance use disorder, non-English articles, protocols, and studies without outcomes were excluded
target_learning_goals: alcohol use prevention and reduction
examples: Nearly all interventions had at least one study measuring alcohol use as a primary outcome (n = 37); other common outcomes included binge drinking (n = 17) and perceived alcohol norms (n = 14)

article_title: What Are We Looking for in Computer-Based Learning Interventions in Medical Education? A Systematic Review.
citation: Taveira-Gomes T, Ferreira P, Taveira-Gomes I, Severo M, Ferreira MA. (2016). What Are We Looking for in Computer-Based Learning Interventions in Medical Education? A Systematic Review. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/jmir.5461
title: Four latent classes characterize educational software in medical CBL research: multimedia, text, Web conference, and instructional
description: The review used latent class analysis on educational software variables from 251 articles, selecting four classes by best interpretability and lowest BIC. It reports: "We uncovered 4 latent classes for educational software, characteristically making use of multimedia (115/251, 45.8%), text (64/251, 25.5%), Web conferencing (54/251, 21.5%), and instructional design principles (18/251, 7.2%)." The multimedia class uses interactive websites with text, images, audio, and video plus quizzes and clinical cases; the instructional class is a small group of highly interactive multimedia apps built on multiple instructional design principles.
requirements: Class assignment requires software feature variables reported in at least 2% of studies; variables reported in <2% were excluded from the model
constraints: Classes describe the 2003–2013 medical education literature only; the instructional class contains just 18 studies (7.2%)
target_learning_goals: characterizing CBL software features in medical education research
key_sources: Taveira-Gomes T, Ferreira P, Taveira-Gomes I, Severo M, Ferreira MA. (2016). What Are We Looking for in Computer-Based Learning Interventions in Medical Education? A Systematic Review. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/jmir.5461

title: Three latent classes characterize intervention end points in medical CBL research: knowledge and attitudes, knowledge-attitudes-skills, and online activity
description: A second latent class model grouped the 212 intervention studies by measured end points. The review reports: "We found 3 classes for intervention outcomes: knowledge and attitudes (175/212, 82.6%), knowledge, attitudes, and skills (11.8%), and online activity (12/212, 5.7%)." The dominant class assesses knowledge and attitudes only; a small class adds skills assessment; the smallest measures online activity such as number of posts and reads, with knowledge and skill assessment nearly absent.
requirements: Class models were fitted on end point variables reported in at least 2% of studies, with class number chosen by lowest BIC and interpretability
constraints: Derived from the 212 of 251 articles reporting interventions on the end points of interest
target_learning_goals: characterizing outcome measurement in CBL intervention research

title: CBL research should continue shifting toward student-centered models, measuring online activity, and reporting instructional design
description: The review's forward-looking principle: "The shift to student-centered models needs to continue," supported by empowering students to study at their own pace, richer interactions with materials, and facilitated communication. It further recommends real-time collection of student activity with objective performance assessment for predictive value, and reporting instructional design considerations so intervention effects can be attributed.
requirements: Studies should report instructional design considerations and comparable comparison arms so intervention effects can be assessed
constraints: Only a few current reports put students at the center of the education process, focusing usually on teaching-related aspects

engagement
predicting learning outcomes
examples: The review highlights social media, reward-based systems, collaborative user-generated content, and 3D virtual worlds as approaches to promote student-centered CBL

article_title: Educational strategies for teaching evidence-based practice to undergraduate health students: systematic review.
citation: Kyriakoulis Konstantinos, Patelarou Athina, Laliotis Aggelos, Wan Andrew C, Matalliotakis Michail, Tsiou Chrysoula, Patelarou Evridiki. (2016). Educational strategies for teaching evidence-based practice to undergraduate health students: systematic review. Journal of Educational Evaluation for Health Professions. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5066070/
title: Use a multifaceted approach when teaching EBP to undergraduate health students
description: The review concludes that a multifaceted approach may be best suited when teaching EBM to health students. Multifaceted interventions combine methods such as lectures, computer sessions, small group discussions, journal clubs, and assignments, and were "more likely to improve knowledge, skills, and attitude compared to SI or no interventions". The principle directs curriculum designers to combine multiple instructional formats rather than relying on a single delivery method.
requirements: Combination of multiple teaching strategies (e.g., lectures, computer sessions, small group discussions, journal clubs, and assignments) rather than a single format
constraints: The review notes this is based on existing evidence that MI were "more likely to improve" outcomes, not a meta-analytic pooled estimate; heterogeneity prevented meta-analysis
target_learners: Undergraduate health students (medical, nursing, pharmacy, physiotherapy, dentistry)
target_learning_goals: EBP competence including knowledge, skills, and attitudes
examples: Included multifaceted interventions combined lectures, practicals, group discussions, teamwork, and students' presentations (Spain nursing study); lectures, seminars, online search, and answering worksheets (Jordan medical study); and didactic, small-group sessions and EBP assignments (US medical study)

title: Single versus multifaceted intervention categorization scheme for EBP teaching studies
description: The review categorizes the educational interventions in its 20 included studies into two types: single interventions (SI) covering a workshop, conference, lecture, journal club, or e-learning, and multifaceted interventions (MI) where a combination of strategies had been assessed. This categorization organizes the review's synthesis and underpins its conclusion that multifaceted approaches may be best suited for teaching EBM to health students.
requirements: Educational interventions that can be classified as either a single format or a combination of formats
constraints: The categorization was applied to studies of EBP teaching for undergraduate health students published 2005–2015

examples: The review lists 13 studies as single interventions and 6 as multifaceted interventions in its synthesis of results

title: Validated EBP assessment instruments (Fresno test, Berlin questionnaire, EBP competence questionnaire, and related tools)
description: The review identifies a set of validated instruments used to assess EBP learning outcomes across its included studies: the Fresno test, the Berlin questionnaire, the Taylor questionnaire, the Scale of efficacy toward EBP, the EBP competence questionnaire, and a validated instrument for assessment of EBP related knowledge. These tools measure EBP knowledge, skills, and attitudes and anchor the review's finding that "validated tools to assess knowledge and skill acquisition exist and have been widely used".

Administration pre- and post-intervention to measure change
constraints: The review notes similar validated tools to determine the extent to which attitudes change after an educational intervention are lacking

title: Web-based evidence-based research (EBR) tool usable from computer, smartphone, or iPad
description: One included study tested a web-based, evidence-based research tool that is usable from a computer, smartphone, or iPad, designed to improve learners' overall online research and critical appraisal skills in EBP. The review reports this tool produced "a significant improvement in overall research skills among the nursing and nutrition student group" across three studies (quasi-experimental and two RCTs). It exemplifies the technology-based delivery the review identifies as rising.

Learners engaged in EBP tasks requiring online research and critical appraisal
constraints: Evidence comes from three studies by one research team (nursing n=158, nutrition n=80, pharmacy n=79) as summarized in the review

examples: The tool was evaluated in a quasi-experimental study with nursing students and two randomized controlled trials with nutrition and pharmacy students, with pre-post mean differences favoring intervention groups

title: EBP as a learnable skill framework for undergraduate health education
description: The review frames EBP as "a learnable skill", stating that "the question is not whether EBP can or should be taught, but how to best teach". This framework positions EBP competence—knowledge, skills, and attitudes—as an teachable outcome that educational interventions can improve, and organizes the review's synthesis around identifying which teaching strategies best build that competence. It treats EBP as comprising domains of research question formulation, sources of evidence, evidence appraisal, and implementation into practice.
requirements: Curriculum time and instructional strategies dedicated to EBP teaching
Assessment instruments capable of measuring EBP competence change
constraints: The review notes increase in EBP competency is dependent on a variety of factors including prior training, exposure to epidemiology, research design, biostatistics, and organizational culture and support toward EBP, none of which were adjusted for in included studies
target_learners: Undergraduate health students across medical, nursing, pharmacy, physiotherapy, and dentistry disciplines
target_learning_goals: EBP competence: knowledge, skills, and attitudes for clinical decision-making incorporating research evidence
examples: The review's 20 included studies all evaluated educational interventions designed to increase EBP competence, supporting the premise that EBP is teachable

article_title: Assessing the effectiveness of problem-based learning in physical diagnostics education in China: a meta-analysis.
citation: Wang, J., Xu, Y., Liu, X., Xiong, W., Xie, J., & Zhao, J. (2016). Assessing the effectiveness of problem-based learning in physical diagnostics education in China: a meta-analysis. Scientific Reports. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5093758/
title: Problem-based learning as a student-centered approach using real problems in tutor-led small groups
description: The article characterizes problem-based learning (PBL) as "an educational approach usually characterized by the use of real problems as a context for students to acquire knowledge and develop skills". Unlike the traditional teaching model, "PBL approach is student-centered": students learn a subject "through the experience of problem solving in a tutor-led small group". In this meta-analysis PBL is the experimental intervention, compared against traditional teaching in Chinese physical diagnostics courses, with knowledge and skill scores as outcomes.
requirements: Real problems used as the context for acquiring knowledge and developing skills
A tutor-led small group in which students learn through problem solving
constraints: The article notes evidence that the PBL teaching model is not superior to the traditional approach with respect to the acquisition of factual knowledge, and that effects may differ across subjects
target_learners: Medical students in Chinese medical schools studying physical diagnostics (clinical diagnostics)
target_learning_goals: Acquiring basic clinical knowledge and theoretical knowledge of physical diagnostics
Developing clinical skills: history taking, physical examination, and diagnostic reasoning
examples: Thirteen controlled studies in Chinese physical diagnostics courses implemented PBL in the experimental group and traditional teaching in the control group, generally over one semester

article_title: Does a PBL-based medical curriculum predispose training in specific career paths? A systematic review of the literature.
citation: Tsigarides Jordan, Wingfield Laura R., Kulendran Myutan. (2017). Does a PBL-based medical curriculum predispose training in specific career paths? A systematic review of the literature. BMC Research Notes. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5219658/
title: Personality-based selection hypothesis for PBL-career associations
description: The review proposes that any association between PBL curricula and career choice may arise because problem-based learning appeals to students with particular personality characteristics due to its open and group-based nature. The review cites Holen et al. finding that "students that were outgoing, curious, sociable and conscientious appreciated a PBL curriculum" and Bexelius et al. finding that graduates choosing surgical careers scored higher in conscientiousness. It also notes the hypothesis that problem-based curricula may be more likely to produce graduates who select primary care careers.
requirements: The hypothesis requires that personality traits influence both preference for PBL curricula and subsequent career path selection
constraints: The review presents this as argument and cited hypothesis rather than as a tested result of the included studies
target_learning_goals: career choice formation in medical education
examples: The review cites Holen et al. on students who appreciated PBL curricula and Bexelius et al. on conscientiousness among surgical career choosers as supporting background

article_title: The Effectiveness of Teamwork Training on Teamwork Behaviors and Team Performance: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Controlled Interventions.
citation: McEwan D., Ruissen G.R., Eys M.A., Zumbo B.D., Beauchamp M.R. (2017). The Effectiveness of Teamwork Training on Teamwork Behaviors and Team Performance: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Controlled Interventions. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0169604
title: Four-dimension framework of teamwork: preparation, execution, reflection, and interpersonal dynamics
description: The article organizes teamwork into behaviors that regulate team performance and behaviors that keep the team together, following Lewin's locomotion and maintenance processes. Regulation spans behaviors "before/in preparation for team task performance," during execution (communication, coordination, cooperation), and after task completion (reflection, monitoring, adjustment), while a fourth dimension covers interpersonal dynamics such as conflict management and social support. The meta-analysis used these four dimensions to code targeted and measured dimensions of interventions.
requirements: Interventions and measures must be codable into the preparation, execution, reflection, and/or interpersonal-dynamics dimensions
constraints: The article notes 29 teamwork frameworks exist with differing numbers and labelling of dimensions; this framework reflects the generally agreed multi-behavior structure
target_learners: team members in health care, aviation, military, academic, industry, and laboratory settings
target_learning_goals: teamwork behaviors including goal setting, communication, coordination, reflection, conflict management, and social support
examples: Each included intervention was coded for which of the four dimensions it targeted and which were measured as outcomes

article_title: Airway management education: simulation based training versus non-simulation based training-A systematic review and meta-analyses.
citation: Sun Yanxia, Pan Chuxiong, Li Tianzuo, Gan Tong J. (2017). Airway management education: simulation based training versus non-simulation based training-A systematic review and meta-analyses. BMC Anesthesiology. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12871-017-0313-7
title: Seventeen-study comparative evidence base on simulation versus non-simulation airway management training
description: The review assembled a corpus of 17 published comparative trials evaluating SBT against NSBT for airway management training, identified from six databases from inception to May 2016. Studies covered techniques including direct laryngoscopy, flexible laryngoscopy or bronchoscopy, bag-mask-ventilation, cricoid pressure and surgical airway, with a "Median sample size of included studies was 60 (range 6–245)" and median MERSQI score 13.5 (range 9.5–16).
requirements: Comparative trials featuring SBT as the educational intervention and NSBT as the comparison group, with assessment of learner and/or patient outcomes
constraints: Data from letters, case reports, reviews or abstracts were excluded
Some studies could not be included in pooled analyses because of missing data
target_learners: Residents and physicians with limited airway management experience
target_learning_goals: Airway management techniques including laryngoscopy, intubation, bag-mask-ventilation, cricoid pressure and surgical airway
examples: Thirteen of the 17 studies were randomized controlled trials; four were non-randomized two-group designs

article_title: A real-world approach to Evidence-Based Medicine in general practice: a competency framework derived from a systematic review and Delphi process.
citation: Galbraith Kevin, Ward Alison, Heneghan Carl. (2017). A real-world approach to Evidence-Based Medicine in general practice: a competency framework derived from a systematic review and Delphi process. BMC Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5415750/
title: Real-world EBM competency framework for general practice: mindfulness, pragmatism, and knowledge of the patient
description: The article proposes a three-competency framework for Evidence-Based Medicine in general practice, derived from a systematic review and Delphi consensus. It states: "A simple competency framework was constructed, that acknowledges the constraints of real-world general practice: (1) mindfulness - in one's approach towards EBM itself, and to the influences on decision-making; (2) pragmatism - in one's approach to finding and evaluating evidence; and (3) knowledge of the patient - as the most useful resource in effective communication of evidence." Mindfulness means open awareness of biases and influences on decisions; pragmatism means using trusted pre-appraised evidence sources rather than systematic searching; knowledge of the patient means using the therapeutic relationship to judge when and how to communicate evidence. The framework is intended for GP training, continuing professional development, and routine care.
requirements: Further validation of the framework as an educational resource and as a strategy for actual practice, as the authors state
constraints: Deliberately excludes search and critical-appraisal skills as core competencies, based on the review's finding that these lacked credibility for routine general practice work
target_learning_goals: Applying evidence-based medicine in routine general practice
Communicating evidence to patients
Reflecting on decision-making influences
examples: A clinical scenario in which a GP considers prescribing a sleeping tablet, pauses to check her reasoning (mindfulness), consults the TRIP database for a pre-appraised synopsis (pragmatism), and tailors the recommendation to the patient's preferences (knowledge of the patient)
key_sources: Galbraith Kevin, Ward Alison, Heneghan Carl. (2017). A real-world approach to Evidence-Based Medicine in general practice: a competency framework derived from a systematic review and Delphi process. BMC Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5415750/

article_title: Systematic review of the effect of training interventions on the skills of health professionals in promoting health behaviour, with meta-analysis of subsequent effects on patient health behaviours.
citation: Hatfield Thomas G., Withers Thomas M., Greaves Colin J. (2020). Systematic review of the effect of training interventions on the skills of health professionals in promoting health behaviour, with meta-analysis of subsequent effects on patient health behaviours. BMC Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-020-05420-1
title: Healthcare professional training for behaviour change interventions should combine educational and practical elements rather than education alone
description: The review concludes that effective training of healthcare professionals who deliver health behaviour change interventions should include both educational components (e.g. presentations, workshops) and practical components (e.g. opportunities to practise techniques learnt, case study evaluation). In the narrative synthesis, "Training using both educational and practical elements seemed to be more effective, significantly improving 52% of outcomes, whereas education only training significantly improved only 23% of outcomes." The review advises policymakers that education-only components are unlikely to suffice.
requirements: Training must be delivered to healthcare professionals whose role involves contact with patients and delivery of care or treatment
Practical elements must provide opportunities to practise techniques learnt, such as case study evaluation or practising taught elements
constraints: Evidence base is 12 RCTs all judged high risk of bias for delivery-quality outcomes
The advantage of combined training is a descriptive percentage comparison, not a tested difference
target_learners: Physiotherapists and other healthcare professionals delivering health behaviour change interventions
target_learning_goals: Communication skills for behaviour change counselling
Delivery of intended intervention content
examples: Nine of the 12 included studies added practical elements such as providing opportunities to practice techniques learnt on top of educational elements like presentations and workshops
key_sources: Hatfield Thomas G., Withers Thomas M., Greaves Colin J. (2020). Systematic review of the effect of training interventions on the skills of health professionals in promoting health behaviour, with meta-analysis of subsequent effects on patient health behaviours. BMC Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-020-05420-1
